_meta.purpose: Gold-standard, source-verified disease knowledge base for the AI Symptom->Disease->Treatment engine. Every entry is researched disease-by-disease against real MBBS/MD-level clinical guidelines (WHO, NICE, British Society of Gastroenterology/Haematology, ICMR, India MoHFW). Nothing here is hallucinated. Any number that could not be independently verified is marked confidence:'moderate' with a note. doctor_approval_required is ALWAYS true. IMPORTANT SCOPE RULE: the AI's own output (ai_suggests) is test(s) + candidate medicine(s) + real efficacy %, stated directly with no disclaimer clutter — the mandatory doctor-approval gate is the safety mechanism, not hedging text. Dose/duration/route/monitoring are doctor_reference_only, for the Registered Medical Practitioner alone to decide. CONSULTATION FLOW (mirrors a real doctor visit): Step 1 — patient states their complaint in their own words. Step 2 — AI asks consultation_questions (real, gold-standard history-taking, one at a time, like a doctor would). Step 3 — AI outputs ai_suggests (test + medicine + efficacy %) plus symptom_mechanisms (plain-language reason the medicine should resolve the specific symptom reported) for the doctor to review and finally decide.

iron_deficiency_anaemia.name: Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA)

core.name: Fatigue / generalized weakness
core.note: Most common presenting complaint

core.name: Shortness of breath on exertion
core.note: Dyspnoea; worsens as Hb falls

specific_signs.name: Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)
specific_signs.note: Textbook-classic but actually uncommon in practice — do not over-weight

specific_signs.name: Restless legs (associated)
specific_signs.note: Commonly cited association, not independently re-verified this session

symptoms.severity_gradient: Mild anaemia is often near-asymptomatic or mild fatigue only. As Hb falls, dyspnoea/tachycardia/palpitations become prominent. Severe cases show tachycardia and signs of cardiac strain (ankle oedema, dyspnoea at rest).

staged_severity_model.source: Merck Manual Professional — Anemias Caused by Deficient Erythropoiesis

stages.name: Iron-store depletion
stages.criteria: Ferritin <30 ng/mL, Hb/serum iron still normal

stages.name: Iron-restricted erythropoiesis
stages.criteria: Transferrin saturation <15%, mild anaemia begins, RBC morphology still normal
stages.symptoms: Early mild symptoms: pallor, fatigue, weakness, mild dyspnoea

stages.name: True IDA
stages.criteria: Microcytic/hypochromic RBCs, progressively worsening anaemia
stages.symptoms: Late/severe-only symptoms: pica, glossitis, cheilosis, koilonychia

additional_real_findings.finding: Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome — painless progressive dysphagia (solids-only) + esophageal web + IDA triad. Rare but real; recognized risk factor for upper-GI squamous cell carcinoma.
additional_real_findings.confidence: high (well-documented, though the syndrome itself is rare)

additional_real_findings.finding: Cognitive impairment independent of anaemia severity — iron deficiency alone (even without anaemia) lowers cognitive scores in children and geriatric patients. In children: developmental delay, reduced school performance, behavioural disorders.

Presents non-classically — falls, frailty progression, reduced mobility, delirium, dementia-like decline, depression — often misattributed to normal ageing rather than recognized as IDA. Increased fall risk via impaired postural stability/bioenergetic capacity.
additional_real_findings.source: PMC4077071; Medical News Today clinical review

additional_real_findings.finding: Maternal: preterm labour, higher C-section rate, postpartum haemorrhage, maternal death (severe cases). Fetal: low birth weight, small-for-gestational-age.
Postpartum depression association — mixed evidence, at least one study found no significant association, weak link to antenatal anxiety only.
additional_real_findings.confidence: low/mixed — flag as unconfirmed, do not present as established

additional_real_findings.finding: Diminished cell-mediated immunity, impaired phagocytic activity/oxidative burst, dendritic cell dysfunction -> real increased susceptibility to infection.
additional_real_findings.confidence: high for mechanism; moderate for clinical-impact size

additional_real_findings.finding: High-output cardiac failure and pulmonary hypertension in severe/chronic untreated IDA, via hyperdynamic circulation + hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Late-stage finding, not common.
additional_real_findings.confidence: high for mechanism, but severe/late-stage only

symptoms.not_included_no_real_evidence: Athlete/sports-anaemia-specific presentation and thyroid-metabolism/temperature-dysregulation-beyond-cold-intolerance were searched for but no additional real, distinct clinical findings were found — not fabricated as filler.
red_flags: Tachycardia or signs of new/worsening heart failure (ankle oedema, dyspnoea at rest)
Hb < 8 g/dL — India Anaemia Mukt Bharat threshold for urgent referral to a Medical Officer / District Hospital
Any sign of active GI bleeding (melaena / haematochezia) — urgent real-doctor GI referral, never primary-care iron therapy alone
Pregnancy with anaemia — always requires real obstetric review, never AI-only management

consultation_questions.note: Step 2 of the flow — asked one at a time after the patient's initial complaint, mirroring real gold-standard clinical history-taking (OSCE-style / Geeky Medics + Medscape-cross-validated). Confidence: high on content, moderate on exact wording since primary pages were paywalled/blocked this session.

ordered.q: Since when have you been feeling this tiredness/weakness, and has it been getting worse, better, or staying the same?
ordered.why: Chronic, gradually-worsening course favours a nutritional cause like IDA over a sudden acute process

ordered.q: Do you get breathless, feel your heart racing, or feel dizzy when you exert yourself (climbing stairs, walking fast)?
ordered.why: Gauges severity and cardiac compensation for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity

ordered.q: What does your diet usually look like — do you eat meat/eggs/fish regularly, or are you vegetarian/vegan?
ordered.why: Vegetarians/vegans have a real, elevated risk of dietary iron deficiency

ordered.q: Have you had any unusual cravings — for ice, clay, chalk, or starch?
ordered.why: Pica/pagophagia is a fairly specific sign of IDA that patients rarely mention unless asked directly

ordered.q: (If applicable) How heavy are your periods — are you soaking through pads/tampons quickly, or passing clots?
ordered.why: Menorrhagia is a leading, systematically under-reported cause of IDA in women

ordered.q: Have you noticed black or tarry stools, or any blood in your stool? Any known stomach ulcers or heartburn?
ordered.why: Screens for occult GI bleeding — the other leading cause of IDA, and a red-flag if positive

ordered.q: Do you regularly take painkillers like ibuprofen/aspirin, or any blood thinners?
ordered.why: NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants are a real, verified cause of occult GI blood loss

ordered.q: Have you lost weight recently without trying to?
ordered.why: Red-flag question — screens for malabsorption or an underlying wasting disease

ordered.q: Have you ever had stomach/intestinal surgery, such as a gastric bypass?
ordered.why: Real, verified cause of iron malabsorption

ordered.q: Are you currently pregnant, or have you been pregnant recently?
ordered.why: Changes both the risk profile and the entire management pathway

ordered.q: Does anyone in your family have anaemia or a history of stomach/bowel cancer?
ordered.why: Relevant to the differential diagnosis and how urgently to refer

ordered.q: Is there anything in particular you're worried it might be?
ordered.why: Standard closing consultation question — not diagnostic, but part of a real gold-standard consultation structure

symptom_mechanisms.note: Step 3 add-on — plain-language reason the AI's suggested medicine should resolve the SPECIFIC symptom the patient reported. Every mechanism below is real, verified physiology, not invented.

items.reason: Iron is needed both to make haemoglobin (which carries oxygen to your tissues) AND as a direct fuel-cell component inside your cells' mitochondria (iron-sulfur centres in the respiratory chain). Low iron weakens both systems, so you feel tired even before anaemia is severe. Once iron is replenished, both oxygen delivery and cellular energy production recover.

Lower haemoglobin means your blood carries less oxygen, so your heart beats faster and your breathing quickens to compensate, especially on exertion. Restoring iron restores haemoglobin and oxygen-carrying capacity, which is why these symptoms ease as your levels normalise.
Pallor is a direct visible sign of lower haemoglobin concentration in your blood. As haemoglobin rises with treatment, normal colour returns.

items.symptom: Sore/smooth tongue, cracked mouth corners, brittle nails, hair thinning
items.reason: The cells lining your tongue/mouth and the cells that grow your nails and hair divide and renew very fast, and that renewal depends on an iron-dependent enzyme (ribonucleotide reductase) needed to build new DNA. These tissues run out of iron first, which is why they show visible signs early. Iron repletion lets these high-turnover tissues resume normal renewal.

This is a real, well-recognised association with iron deficiency and typically resolves once iron is replenished, though the exact brain mechanism behind the craving itself is not firmly established in the literature.
items.confidence: association is high; underlying mechanism is not verified

hb_cutoffs_anaemia_who_2024.source: WHO 2024 Guideline on haemoglobin cutoffs to define anaemia (first major revision since 1968)

other_markers.ferritin_caveat: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant — falsely normal or raised in inflammation/infection. Must be interpreted alongside CRP/clinical context.

ai_suggests.note: This is the ONLY part the AI itself outputs to the doctor's approval queue: test(s) to order + candidate medicine(s), each with a real efficacy number where the literature actually supports one. Dose, duration, route, monitoring are doctor_reference_only below, for the doctor's own decision. Final decision is always the doctor's.

recommended_tests.test: CBC (Hemoglobin, MCV, RBC count, platelets, WBC)

recommended_tests.role: Ordered together with CBC — single best confirmatory test for IDA specifically
Confirmatory add-on when ferritin is equivocal (e.g. concurrent inflammation)
Reviewed alongside CBC to confirm microcytic/hypochromic morphology

ai_suggests.tests_source: ARUP Consult; Hematology.org; BC Government Clinical Guidelines; Medscape — consistent across all sources (confidence: high)

candidate_medicines.name: Ferrous Sulfate (oral iron)
candidate_medicines.efficacy: 72.8% of adult patients are Hb responders (≥1.0 g/dL rise) by day 14; of those, 92.9% reach a ≥2.0 g/dL rise by day 42–56

candidate_medicines.name: Ferrous Fumarate (oral iron, alternative)
candidate_medicines.efficacy: No real efficacy difference vs Ferrous Sulfate found in the literature — oral iron salts differ in GI tolerability, not cure rate
candidate_medicines.efficacy_basis: Consistent absence-of-difference finding across comparative studies

candidate_medicines.name: Ferrous Gluconate (oral iron, alternative)
candidate_medicines.efficacy: Same as Ferrous Fumarate — efficacy equivalent to Ferrous Sulfate, differs on tolerability only
candidate_medicines.efficacy_basis: Consistent absence-of-difference finding across comparative studies

candidate_medicines.name: Ferric Carboxymaltose (IV iron, if oral not suitable)
candidate_medicines.efficacy: Mean Hb rise 0.45 g/dL greater than IV iron sucrose (95% CI 0.08–0.83); ferritin +37.32 ng/mL higher (95% CI 18.98–55.65). Comparable end-point efficacy to oral Ferrous Sulfate but reached in 2 weeks vs 12 weeks. 'Achieved normal Hb' rate NOT statistically significant vs iron sucrose (RR 1.77, 95% CI 0.98–3.20)
candidate_medicines.confidence: high for Hb/ferritin mean-difference figures; moderate for the normal-Hb-achievement RR (not statistically significant)

ai_suggests.efficacy_honesty_note: Clinical trials do not report a single 'cure %'. The real, honestly-reportable proxy metrics are Hb response rate and Hb/ferritin normalization rate, each tied to a defined threshold and time point — that is what is shown above, not an invented unqualified cure percentage.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine used for IDA (not just the AI's lean candidate list above) — each with real effectiveness data, a real pharmacological reason why, source, and honesty confidence flag. Reference/research backing, not the AI's direct patient-facing output.

medicines.name: Ferrous Sulfate
medicines.effectiveness: 72.8% Hb-responder rate (>=1.0 g/dL rise) by day 14 (pooled 5-RCT); pediatric case 95% Hb-normalization at 3 months (n=19, small)
medicines.reason_why: Non-heme iron absorption is hepcidin-gated - each dose triggers a ~24h hepcidin spike via the ferroportin-degradation pathway, capping fractional absorption (~16.3% on consecutive-day dosing) regardless of dose size; GI intolerance further limits achievable dose/adherence. This is why efficacy plateaus well below 100% and response is gradual.
medicines.source: Haematologica/PMC4697898; PMC7496601
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Ferrous Fumarate / Gluconate / Ascorbate
medicines.effectiveness: No significant efficacy difference vs ferrous sulfate in comparative trials; ferrous ascorbate specifically has no clean modern responder-% located despite being the most common form used in India
medicines.reason_why: All are simple Fe2+ salts absorbed via the same DMT1 duodenal transporter and subject to the identical hepcidin ceiling - the counter-ion changes solubility/GI irritation, not the rate-limiting absorption mechanism.
medicines.source: Comparative RCT literature
medicines.confidence: high for equivalence; ferrous ascorbate % not independently verified

medicines.name: Ferrous Bisglycinate (chelated)
medicines.effectiveness: >2x higher bioavailability vs ferrous sulfate/fumarate; RCT in pregnancy showed superior Hb+ferritin rise and significantly fewer GI effects vs ferrous glycine sulfate. No single unified % across trials, but consistently directionally superior
medicines.reason_why: The glycine-chelated structure is taken up partly via the PepT1 amino-acid transporter, partially bypassing the DMT1/hepcidin bottleneck, and resists gastric-pH dissociation - delivering iron to the enterocyte more efficiently while reacting less with luminal contents (hence less GI irritation).
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Iron Hydroxide Polymaltose Complex (IPC)
medicines.effectiveness: Mixed real evidence: one meta-analysis found equivalence to ferrous sulfate; a larger, more recent systematic review found it LESS effective (MD -0.81 g/dL, 95% CI -1.08 to -0.53, 6 studies/368 patients) but far better tolerated (14.9% vs 34.1% adverse-reaction rate, p<0.001)
medicines.reason_why: Its non-ionic, high-MW structure requires active carrier-mediated uptake instead of passive Fe2+/DMT1 diffusion - slower and less efficient, but avoids free ionic iron catalyzing luminal oxidative irritation.
medicines.source: PMC3206382; BMC Pediatrics meta-analysis 10.1186/s12887-026-07561-4
medicines.confidence: high, but genuinely mixed across studies - report both findings, don't pick a winner

medicines.name: Heme Iron Polypeptide (Proferrin)
medicines.effectiveness: Comparable Hb outcome to IV iron sucrose (117 vs 113 g/L at 6mo, CKD trial, p=0.37); no responder-% reported
medicines.reason_why: Heme iron is absorbed via a separate heme-transporter pathway (HCP1) rather than DMT1, giving it a real absorption advantage independent of the non-heme hepcidin ceiling - though this trial's endpoint is mean Hb, not a responder percentage.
medicines.source: Ovid/Acta Medica; PMC3606612
medicines.confidence: moderate - real trials, but only mean-Hb endpoints, no %

medicines.name: Ferric Maltol (Accrufer) - oral, FDA-approved
medicines.effectiveness: 67% responder rate (Hb >=2g/dL) at week 12, AEGIS-H2H ITT, vs 84% for ferric carboxymaltose (non-inferiority NOT met)
medicines.reason_why: A stable, non-ionic Fe3+-maltol complex releases iron more gradually across the gut than ionic salts, improving tolerability, but its ceiling effectiveness genuinely falls short of IV therapy per the head-to-head trial.
medicines.confidence: high - real, named RCT, real %

medicines.name: Alternate-day oral dosing (strategy, not a drug)
medicines.effectiveness: 21.8% cumulative fractional absorption alternate-day vs 16.3% consecutive-day (p=0.001), ~34% relative gain
medicines.reason_why: Lets hepcidin (elevated ~24h post-dose) decay back to baseline between doses, unmasking higher fractional absorption on each subsequent dose.
medicines.source: Real RCT (hepcidin-based dosing study)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Iron Sucrose
medicines.effectiveness: 2.49 g/dL mean Hb rise by week 8 (FERWON-IDA, n=1512); separately 98.3% achieved Hb>=2g/dL by 8wk in one China RCT vs FCM
medicines.reason_why: IV as a class bypasses gut absorption and hepcidin regulation entirely - iron is delivered directly, bound to transferrin in circulation. Iron sucrose specifically is capped at ~200mg/session by labile-iron toxicity risk, requiring 5+ sessions for full repletion.
medicines.source: FERWON-IDA/PMC6772897; Springer/MedScience 2023
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Ferric Carboxymaltose (FCM)
medicines.effectiveness: +0.45 g/dL greater mean Hb rise vs iron sucrose (95% CI 0.08-0.83, 14 trials/4,757 patients); GI-bleed-specific meta-analysis RR 1.24 (95% CI 1.14-1.34) favoring FCM; pregnancy meta-analysis SMD +0.89 g/dL favoring FCM. 'Achieved normal Hb' vs iron sucrose was NOT statistically significant in the broadest analysis (RR 1.77, CI 0.98-3.20) - effect size is population/endpoint-dependent
medicines.reason_why: Its carbohydrate-shell nanoparticle allows up to 1000mg in a single infusion, taken up by reticuloendothelial macrophages that slowly release iron to transferrin - enabling full repletion in 1-2 sessions vs iron sucrose's 5+ sessions, explaining the faster time-to-response.
medicines.source: PMC12099480; pregnancy meta-analysis
medicines.confidence: high, with an honestly-flagged non-significant sub-endpoint

medicines.name: Ferric Derisomaltose / Iron Isomaltoside
medicines.effectiveness: FERWON-IDA: non-inferior to iron sucrose at week 8 (~2.49 g/dL both arms) but significantly faster response in first 2 weeks; comparable/slightly better safety (0.3% vs 0.4% serious hypersensitivity). Note: a separate analysis found 79.0% responder rate vs 70.0% for FCM, while another indirect comparison found RR 1.18 (95% CI 0.96-1.45, NS) favoring FCM - two real analyses disagree on direction
medicines.reason_why: Same stable-carbohydrate-complex mechanism as FCM (large single doses, controlled slow release), avoiding labile-iron toxicity - faster time-to-target without more adverse events.
medicines.source: FERWON-IDA/PMC6772897; ASH/Blood 2022; PMC10862635
medicines.confidence: high figures, but genuinely conflicting between studies - report both, don't pick one as definitive

medicines.name: Ferumoxytol
medicines.effectiveness: 81.1% achieved Hb>=2.0 g/dL at week 5 vs 5.5% placebo (pivotal RCT AMAG-FER-IDA-301); non-inferior to FCM (1.4 vs 1.6 g/dL mean rise)
medicines.reason_why: A superparamagnetic iron-oxide nanoparticle coated for controlled reticuloendothelial uptake, similar release kinetics to FCM, permitting large single-dose repletion.
medicines.source: Wiley/AJH 10.1002/ajh.23582
medicines.confidence: high - real, large placebo-controlled RCT

medicines.name: Low-MW Iron Dextran, Ferric Gluconate
medicines.effectiveness: No distinct modern responder-% located (older agents, largely superseded)
medicines.reason_why: Same class mechanism as other IV irons (transferrin-mediated delivery bypassing gut) but largely displaced by newer agents (FCM, derisomaltose, ferumoxytol) with better single-dose capacity and safety data.
medicines.source: Not independently verified this session
medicines.confidence: not verified - do not fabricate a number

medicines.name: Vitamin C (adjunct, not standalone)
medicines.effectiveness: Hb +0.14 g/dL (95% CI 0.08-0.20), ferritin +3.23 ug/L - statistically significant but explicitly 'clinically unimportant' per the review authors; a separate meta-analysis found the effect not statistically significant at all
medicines.reason_why: Ascorbic acid reduces dietary Fe3+ to the more absorbable Fe2+ form and forms a soluble chelate resisting luminal inhibitors - a real mechanism, but downstream absorption is still hepcidin-capped, so the net clinical effect is small.
medicines.source: ScienceDirect 2024 meta-analysis (11 RCTs, 1930 patients)
medicines.confidence: high confidence the real effect is small/negligible - not a cure booster

medicines.name: Probiotic adjunct (L. plantarum 299v)
medicines.effectiveness: Not a standalone Hb-response % - real trial shows ~3x reduction in GI intolerance, ~5x reduction in treatment discontinuation when added to oral iron
medicines.reason_why: Modulates gut microbiota/mucosal environment to reduce iron-induced GI irritation, improving adherence rather than absorption itself.
medicines.confidence: moderate - real RCT-derived, but metric is adherence/tolerability, not cure rate

medicines.name: Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (EPO)
medicines.effectiveness: No real evidence supports EPO for PURE IDA - indicated only for anaemia of CKD/chronic disease with functional iron deficiency
medicines.reason_why: EPO stimulates marrow erythropoiesis but does not address the underlying substrate (iron) deficit - giving EPO without correcting iron deficiency can worsen functional iron deficiency. Established hematology consensus, not merely absent data.
medicines.source: General hematology consensus
medicines.confidence: high confidence this is NOT indicated - must be actively excluded from the AI's candidate list for pure IDA

exhaustive_medicine_survey.no_new_drug_class_note: No qualitatively new IDA drug class was found in 2023-2026 searches beyond derisomaltose (already established ~2020) and the alternate-day oral dosing optimization - stated honestly rather than inventing a 'breakthrough'.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real responder percentages come from DIFFERENT trials using DIFFERENT Hb-rise thresholds and timepoints (e.g. >=1.0 g/dL at day 14 vs >=2.0 g/dL at week 12) - ranking them together is directionally useful (IV generally outperforms oral) but is NOT a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Medicines with no single comparable responder-% (bisglycinate, ferrous fumarate/gluconate/ascorbate, heme iron polypeptide, IPC, low-MW dextran, ferric gluconate, vitamin C, probiotics) are excluded from this ranked list for that reason, not because they are ineffective.

doctor_reference_only._note: Reference detail for the Registered Medical Practitioner. The AI does not decide or output any of this — dose, duration, route and monitoring are entirely the doctor's call.

first_line_oral.drug: Ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily (≈65 mg elemental iron/day)
first_line_oral.dosing_note: NICE 2021 moved to once-daily dosing (away from twice/thrice-daily). Emerging real evidence supports alternate-day dosing for higher fractional absorption and fewer GI side effects — not yet universal first-line.
first_line_oral.how_to_take: Empty stomach preferred for absorption; take with food if GI intolerance; avoid tea/coffee/dairy/calcium/antacids within 2 hours; a vitamin-C source aids absorption
first_line_oral.duration: Continue 3 months AFTER Hb normalizes, to replenish iron stores — this is longer than the time needed to correct the anaemia itself

india_specific_protocol_anaemia_mukt_bha.women_reproductive_age: 100 mg elemental iron + 0.5 mg folic acid, daily
india_specific_protocol_anaemia_mukt_bha.pregnant_women: 60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid, daily, from 2nd trimester (14th week) through pregnancy
india_specific_protocol_anaemia_mukt_bha.severe_hb_below_8: Urgent referral; IM iron is a formal treatment option under AMB for severe cases
india_specific_protocol_anaemia_mukt_bha.source: Government of India, MoHFW — Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme (2018–)

if_oral_fails_iv_iron.dosing_formula: Ganzoni formula: Total iron deficit (mg) = body weight (kg) x (target Hb - actual Hb, g/dL) x 2.4 + iron stores (500 mg if body weight >=35 kg; 15 mg/kg if <35 kg)

blood_transfusion.note: Reserved for severe, symptomatic cases needing rapid Hb rise. Common clinical convention is symptomatic + Hb < 7 g/dL, but no single universal numeric threshold was independently verified this session.

monitoring.expected_response: ~2 g/dL (20 g/L) rise over 3-4 weeks if adherent and diagnosis correct
monitoring.after_normalization: Continue iron 3 more months for store repletion, then periodic checks at 3/6/12/24 months

mandatory_specialist_referral: Men and postmenopausal women with new, unexplained IDA — upper AND lower GI investigation (gastroscopy + colonoscopy) should be considered FIRST-LINE per BSG 2021, to rule out GI malignancy. This is a hard rule the AI must always surface, never skip.
No response to adequate therapy -> Haematology

stages.name: Sufficient
stages.criteria: 25-OH-Vitamin D >30 ng/mL

stages.criteria: 25-OH-Vitamin D 20-30 ng/mL (some sources: 10-30)

stages.name: Deficient - clinical disease
stages.criteria: 25-OH-Vitamin D <20 ng/mL; clinical rickets/osteomalacia/myopathy manifest below ~10 ng/mL (25 nmol/L); frank rickets typically <5 ng/mL

additional_real_findings.finding: Maternal vitamin D deficiency -> congenital rickets, neonatal hypocalcaemic seizures/convulsions, craniotabes/wide sutures/rachitic rosary/tetany in newborns, secondary hyperparathyroidism. Real mortality signal in case series (5/25 stillborn, 3/25 neonatal death in one series); lower birth weight/head circumference, small-for-gestational-age.

Real coexistence of osteomalacia within 'osteoporotic' hip fractures in >50 age group. KEY DIFFERENTIATOR for the AI: osteoporosis is classically asymptomatic until fracture, while osteomalacia causes bone pain/tenderness/proximal weakness BEFORE fracture.

Distinct entity (CKD-MBD) — bone pain, deformity, fracture risk plus PTH/FGF23 derangement; radiographically distinguished from nutritional osteomalacia by subperiosteal resorption, 'salt-and-pepper' skull, 'rugger-jersey' spine (vs Looser zones in nutritional osteomalacia).
Long-term anticonvulsant therapy is a real, named cause of osteomalacia (induces vitamin D catabolism).
Dark skin + low sun exposure, malabsorption syndromes, obesity, older age.

symptoms.severity_gradient: Subclinical vitamin D insufficiency is asymptomatic. As 25-OH-D falls below ~20 ng/mL, mild bone pain/fatigue/proximal weakness appear. Below ~10 ng/mL (osteomalacia) or with prolonged severe deficiency in children (rickets), classic skeletal deformities, Looser zones, and hypocalcaemic complications develop.
red_flags: Hypocalcaemic tetany/seizures/convulsions (paediatric and neonatal) — real emergency
Cardiomyopathy and death risk in severe untreated hypocalcaemia
Neurological complications: hydrocephalus, benign intracranial hypertension, craniosynostosis (rickets)
Pathological fractures, severe skeletal deformity
Suspected CKD-related renal osteodystrophy — needs real nephrology workup, not simple vitamin D replacement

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine used for Rickets/Osteomalacia, each with real effectiveness data, a real pharmacological reason why, source, and honesty confidence flag.

medicines.name: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3)
medicines.effectiveness: Standard first-line; single high-dose (90,000 or 300,000 IU 'stoss' therapy) achieves 90.7% complete radiographic healing (Thacher score = 0) at 12 weeks in nutritional rickets (both doses equal efficacy, n=43/group)
medicines.reason_why: D3 is the natural human form, synthesized in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol; binds vitamin D-binding protein and undergoes hepatic 25-hydroxylation then renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation to the active hormone.
medicines.source: PMC6330863 (real RCT, n=86 completers)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2)
medicines.effectiveness: Inferior to D3: meta-analysis (22 studies, n=1,277) found D3 raises total 25(OH)D by 15.69 nmol/L more than D2 (95% CI 9.46-21.93); D2 also reduces PTH less. No independent responder-% for D2 alone.
medicines.reason_why: D2 (plant/fungal-derived) has lower vitamin-D-binding-protein affinity and faster hepatic clearance than D3; the effect gap narrows at low/food-fortification doses but is clear at supplemental/therapeutic doses.
medicines.source: PMC8538717 (large meta-analysis)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Calcifediol (25-OH-vitamin D3)
medicines.effectiveness: Achieves >50% higher circulating 25-OH-D3 than equivalent cholecalciferol dosing; faster onset (raises levels within days vs weeks). Figure is from one comparative study, not a meta-analysis.
medicines.reason_why: Bypasses the rate-limiting hepatic 25-hydroxylation step entirely (it IS the 25-hydroxylated product already) and has higher relative affinity for vitamin D-binding protein - relevant for liver-impaired or malabsorptive patients.
medicines.confidence: high for mechanism/direction; the >50% figure is single-study, not consensus

medicines.name: Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2-D3, active hormone)
medicines.effectiveness: 'Complete correction of the abnormal phenotype' in Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets Type 1 (VDD1) - a real, qualitative but definitive clinical outcome, not a trial percentage
medicines.reason_why: VDD1 is caused by genetic 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency - the kidney cannot activate vitamin D at all, so calcitriol is direct hormone replacement, not substrate supplementation; this is why it is curative here specifically, unlike in nutritional deficiency.
medicines.source: StatPearls NBK526025
medicines.confidence: high mechanism; no responder-% exists because the real outcome reported is binary/qualitative

medicines.name: Alfacalcidol (1-alpha-OH-D3, prodrug of calcitriol)
medicines.effectiveness: In renal osteodystrophy/haemodialysis: 82% of patients achieved >=30% PTH reduction (vs 93% for paricalcitol in the same 86-patient comparative study) - note this is a renal-osteodystrophy population, not nutritional rickets
medicines.reason_why: Requires only one hepatic hydroxylation step (not renal) to become active calcitriol - usable even when kidneys can't perform the second (renal) activation step, unlike plain vitamin D3.
medicines.source: Endokrynologia Polska comparative trial
medicines.confidence: high - real comparative trial; paricalcitol numerically outperformed it

medicines.name: Calcium (alone or + vitamin D) - for calcium-deficiency rickets
medicines.effectiveness: Real NEJM RCT (Nigerian children): calcium alone and calcium+vitamin D both produced better healing than vitamin D alone. Exact healing % not accessible (source paywalled) - real directional finding only, no fabricated percentage
medicines.reason_why: In populations with adequate vitamin D but genuinely low dietary calcium intake, the rate-limiting substrate is calcium itself, not activated vitamin D - so supplementing the actually-deficient substrate resolves the mineralization defect that vitamin D alone cannot fix.
medicines.confidence: high confidence in the real directional finding; no exact percentage independently verified

medicines.name: Phosphate + Calcitriol (conventional XLH therapy)
medicines.effectiveness: Real phase 3 trial control arm: rickets severity score improved by only 0.7 (of a 0-10 scale, baseline ~3.2) over 40 weeks; 6-Minute-Walk-Test percent-predicted distance unchanged (76% to 75%)
medicines.reason_why: Treats the biochemical consequence (low phosphate) but does not address the causal excess FGF23 hormone that drives renal phosphate wasting in XLH - so healing is partial and slow.
medicines.source: PMC7179969 (NEJM phase 3 trial control arm)
medicines.confidence: high - real phase 3 RCT control-arm data

medicines.name: Burosumab (anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody) - for XLH specifically
medicines.effectiveness: Real phase 3 RCT (n=61 children): rickets severity score improved by 2.0 vs 0.7 for conventional therapy (baseline ~3.2/10) over 40 weeks; 6MWT percent-predicted distance rose 62% to 72% (vs unchanged with conventional therapy) - described as 'significantly greater clinical improvement'
medicines.reason_why: Directly neutralizes the causal excess FGF23 hormone (the actual genetic defect in XLH), restoring renal phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D activation at the source - a fundamentally different, disease-modifying mechanism vs simply supplementing phosphate/calcitriol downstream.
medicines.confidence: high for the real trial numbers reported; categorical responder-% (RGI-C) exists in the paper but not independently confirmed this session

exhaustive_medicine_survey.no_new_drug_class_note: Burosumab (FDA-approved 2018, still the newest real disease-modifying option for XLH) is the most significant real treatment-class innovation found; no qualitatively newer agent located in 2023-2026 searches for nutritional rickets/osteomalacia beyond established vitamin D/calcium/phosphate management.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Very few medicines in this disease have a clean, single, comparable responder-percentage in the real literature (unlike IDA) - most real outcomes here are reported as mean score changes, qualitative correction, or relative comparisons. Only two entries below have a genuine standalone %; the rest are real but not percentage-rankable, and are NOT excluded for being less effective - only because no clean % exists.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) - stoss therapy
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete radiographic healing (Thacher score=0) at 12 weeks, nutritional rickets

ranked_high_to_low.name: Alfacalcidol
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Patients achieving >=30% PTH reduction, renal osteodystrophy/haemodialysis population (not nutritional rickets)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Endokrynologia Polska

ischaemic_heart_disease.name: Ischaemic Heart Disease (IHD) / Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)
ischaemic_heart_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Unlike every disease researched before this one, IHD/CAD has a true minute-to-minute emergency window. Any presentation matching STEMI/NSTEMI-pattern chest pain (crushing, prolonged, unrelieved by rest/nitroglycerin), cardiogenic shock signs (hypotension, cold clammy skin, altered mental status, oliguria), malignant arrhythmias, or cardiac arrest MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now) - this is a hard, non-negotiable rule, not a suggestion to route through AI/doctor review.
ischaemic_heart_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Ischaemic Heart Disease / Coronary Artery Disease is NOT curable in the sense of removing the underlying atherosclerotic disease process - the plaque burden, once formed, does not disappear and the disease is managed, not eliminated, for life. Three real, trial-proven exceptions to a purely one-way disease course are documented in this entry: (1) 'Aborted' myocardial infarction - when a completely occluded artery is reopened ultra-early, the acute event itself can be genuinely prevented rather than merely treated: 13.3% of a large tenecteplase-trial cohort (n=5,470) met strict aborted-MI criteria (>=50% ST resolution, enzyme rise <=2x ULN CK/CKMB or <=5x ULN troponin), rising to 17.1% with faster (86-minute) prehospital thrombolysis versus 4.5% with slower (123-minute) in-hospital thrombolysis, and up to about 25% of patients treated within the first hour of symptom onset per a dedicated review synthesis - genuine, complete prevention of infarct/scar formation for that one event, but real only for the single acute STEMI episode in patients who reach a reperfusion-capable pathway within roughly one to two hours, and it does nothing to the underlying atherosclerotic disease, which persists and can cause a future event without full secondary prevention (see curative_option below for the full real trial data); (2) plaque regression: intensive LDL-lowering demonstrably shrinks, not just halts, existing coronary plaque on intravascular ultrasound - GLAGOV (evolocumab + statin, mean LDL-C 36.6 mg/dL) produced -0.95% percent-atheroma-volume change versus +0.05% with statin alone, and ASTEROID (high-intensity rosuvastatin alone) produced regression in the majority of treated arteries - but this is roughly 1% shrinkage of plaque volume, not disease elimination, and no trial has shown intensive lipid-lowering alone reduces recurrent-event risk to zero; (3) combination secondary-prevention pharmacotherapy (antiplatelet/DAPT + high-intensity statin +/- ezetimibe/PCSK9i/bempedoic acid + beta-blocker/ACE-inhibitor/MRA where indicated + colchicine +/- low-dose anticoagulation) each independently lowers recurrent MACE or mortality risk by roughly 13-38% relative to not using that specific agent (see effectiveness_ranked_table below for every real, sourced number) - substantial and worth stacking, but even maximal guideline-directed therapy leaves a real residual event rate; no single medicine or combination in the real literature reduces IHD/CAD recurrent-event risk to zero, or to the near-100% crystal-free, flare-free state real in gout's treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy. Real 2024 evidence (REDUCE-AMI) also honestly narrows one long-assumed benefit: routine long-term beta-blockers after MI showed NO mortality/reinfarction benefit in a modern, promptly-reperfused, preserved-ejection-fraction population (HR 0.96, ns) - the classic 23-42% beta-blocker mortality reductions cited in this entry come from older, largely non-reperfused, higher-risk trial populations and should not be uncritically assumed to apply at the same magnitude to every modern patient (they do still clearly apply to reduced-ejection-fraction/heart-failure patients post-MI). The honest bottom line: treat the acute event as fast as humanly possible - call emergency services immediately for chest pain, since minutes of delay measurably change whether the heart muscle dies - then commit to full, continuous, guideline-directed secondary prevention for life; there is no cure, but the real trial evidence shows the disease's future event rate can be substantially cut with unbroken adherence to it.

curative_option.name: Ultra-Early Reperfusion Achieving 'Aborted' Myocardial Infarction (STEMI Only) - Real Prevention of the Acute Infarct When Treatment Starts Within Roughly 1-2 Hours of Symptom Onset; NOT a Cure of the Underlying Coronary Atherosclerosis
curative_option.note: IHD/CAD as a chronic arterial disease is never cured - the atherosclerotic plaque burden persists for life regardless of treatment (see the plaque-regression evidence in this entry, which shows real but modest shrinkage, not elimination). But the single most curative-feeling real event in the whole disease is a genuine, trial-documented phenomenon: when a completely occluded coronary artery in an evolving ST-elevation MI is reopened fast enough, the heart muscle downstream of the blockage can be salvaged before it dies, so no infarct - and no permanent scar - ever forms, an outcome termed 'aborted myocardial infarction' (>=50% ST-segment resolution plus only a trivial biomarker rise: CK/CK-MB <=2x or troponin <=5x the upper limit of normal). This is the real closest thing to preventing the event outright rather than merely treating it after the fact, but it applies only to that one acute STEMI episode, only to patients who reach effective reperfusion within about one to two hours of symptom onset, and it does nothing to the coronary atherosclerosis itself, which remains and requires the full, lifelong secondary-prevention medicine regimen documented throughout this entry to avoid a future event.

real_trial_data.assent3_substudy_incidence: 13.3% (727 of 5,470 STEMI patients receiving tenecteplase-based reperfusion) met strict aborted-MI criteria - Taher T et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2004;44:38-47 (PMID 15234403)
real_trial_data.time_to_treatment_is_the_key_driver: In a dedicated comparison, aborted MI occurred in 17.1% of 468 patients given prehospital thrombolysis (mean time-to-needle 86 minutes) versus 4.5% of 264 patients given in-hospital thrombolysis (mean time-to-needle 123 minutes, p=0.05 for the time difference) - the earlier the artery was opened, the more likely the infarct was prevented rather than merely limited (PMID 19234016)
real_trial_data.review_synthesis: Verheugt FW et al. (Eur Heart J 2006;27:901-904, PMID 16543251) synthesise the wider reperfusion literature: over 10% of all successfully reperfused patients overall, and up to approximately 25% of those specifically treated within the first hour of symptom onset, achieve aborted infarction; the review explicitly proposes aborted MI as the ideal target of reperfusion therapy rather than merely 'a good outcome'
real_trial_data.pharmacoinvasive_vs_primary_pci_comparis: STREAM trial substudy: aborted MI in 11.1% of the pharmacoinvasive (immediate prehospital/early fibrinolysis) arm versus 6.9% of the primary-PCI (necessarily delayed by transfer) arm - consistent with earlier drug-based reperfusion outrunning the time needed to mobilise a catheterisation lab in some real-world settings (Sinnaeve PR et al., Circulation 2014;130:1139-1145, PMID 24916050)

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect: for the single acute STEMI episode being treated, sufficiently fast reperfusion can genuinely prevent that infarct from ever forming - there is no scar, no permanent muscle loss, and no reduction in ejection fraction from that event, which is as close to 'the heart attack never happened' as real cardiology gets. Not curative: the coronary atherosclerotic disease that caused the occlusion is completely unaffected by how fast it was treated - the plaque, the other diseased segments, and the underlying risk factors are all still there, unchanged, immediately afterward - so aborting one MI does not lower the future risk of another one; that risk reduction only comes from the medicines documented throughout this entry (antiplatelets, statins +/- ezetimibe/PCSK9i/bempedoic acid, beta-blockers/ACE-inhibitors where indicated, colchicine), taken indefinitely.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients who do not recognise symptoms and call for emergency care immediately (median real-world total ischaemic time in most health systems is several hours, far beyond the roughly one-to-two-hour window in which aborted MI becomes common); patients with NSTEMI/non-occlusive disease (aborted MI as defined here is a STEMI/complete-occlusion concept); and patients whose infarct is already established by the time they reach any form of reperfusion, for whom the goal shifts from 'abort' to 'minimise infarct size' (still real and worthwhile, but a different, smaller benefit).
curative_option.important_caveat: None of the aborted-MI figures above come from a randomised trial of 'abort vs not' - they are observational/subgroup findings within reperfusion trials showing that patients who happened to be treated faster were more likely to abort their infarct, so some of the association could reflect that faster-presenting patients also had smaller, more proximal, more treatable occlusions to begin with, not time-to-treatment alone; the qualitative conclusion (faster reperfusion tracks with better myocardial salvage) is nonetheless extremely well established across decades of reperfusion research (it is literally why 'door-to-balloon time' and 'time is muscle' are core emergency-cardiology doctrine), even though the exact percentages above should be read as real but imperfectly controlled estimates.
curative_option.source: Taher T, Fu Y, Wagner GS, et al., 'Aborted myocardial infarction in patients with ST-segment elevation: Insights from the ASSENT-3 trial electrocardiographic substudy', J Am Coll Cardiol 2004;44:38-47 (PMID 15234403); 'Does prehospital thrombolysis increase the proportion of patients who have an aborted myocardial infarction?' (PMID 19234016); Verheugt FW, Gersh BJ, Armstrong PW, 'Aborted myocardial infarction: a new target for reperfusion therapy', Eur Heart J 2006;27:901-904 (PMID 16543251); Sinnaeve PR et al., 'Aborted myocardial infarction in ST-elevation myocardial infarction: insights from STREAM', Circulation 2014;130:1139-1145 (PMID 24916050)
curative_option.confidence: high for the time-to-treatment/aborted-MI association and the underlying-disease-unchanged boundary; moderate for the precise percentages, which come from observational/subgroup analyses rather than a dedicated randomised trial of the abort phenomenon itself

core_by_acs_type.name: Stable angina
core_by_acs_type.note: Exertional chest tightness/pressure, radiates to left arm/jaw/neck/back; brought on by exertion, relieved by rest/nitroglycerin within minutes

core_by_acs_type.name: Unstable angina
core_by_acs_type.note: New-onset, occurs at rest, worsening pattern (more frequent/severe/prolonged), or does NOT respond to rest/nitroglycerin - ischaemia WITHOUT biomarker release

core_by_acs_type.name: Acute MI (STEMI/NSTEMI)
core_by_acs_type.note: Severe chest pain/pressure, diaphoresis, nausea/vomiting, dyspnoea, sense of impending doom, dizziness, cold sweats, palpitations, occasional loss of consciousness

core_by_acs_type.name: Silent ischaemia
core_by_acs_type.note: No symptoms despite real myocardial oxygen deprivation - well-documented, especially in diabetics (autonomic neuropathy blunts pain perception)

core_by_acs_type.name: Atypical presentation (women/diabetics)
core_by_acs_type.note: Fatigue, dyspnoea, epigastric discomfort, indigestion, palpitations, sweating rather than classic chest pain - real, clinically important, historically underdiagnosed pattern

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: ECG: ST depression
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Stable/unstable angina, NSTEMI

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: ECG: ST elevation
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: STEMI - defining criterion

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Troponin kinetics
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Rises within 2-3h of injury, peaks ~9-12h (high-sensitivity assays); cTnI elevated 7-10 days, cTnT up to 14 days; STEMI typically monophasic peak - more peaks/re-elevation associates with worse complications, lower ejection fraction, higher mortality

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: S4 gallop, signs of heart failure
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Raised JVP, pulmonary crackles, peripheral oedema - if ischaemia has caused ventricular dysfunction

staged_severity_model.source: Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) 1976 original guideline; MDCalc; MSD Manual
staged_severity_model.confidence: high - standard, verified, widely-used clinical grading

stages.name: CCS Class I
stages.criteria: Ordinary activity does not cause angina

stages.name: CCS Class II
stages.criteria: Slight limitation
stages.symptoms: Angina walking/stairs rapidly, uphill, after meals, cold/wind, emotional stress, shortly after waking, or walking >2 blocks/climbing >1 flight at normal pace

stages.name: CCS Class III
stages.criteria: Marked limitation
stages.symptoms: Angina walking 1-2 blocks or climbing 1 flight at normal pace/conditions

stages.name: CCS Class IV

stages.symptoms: Angina at rest or with any activity

symptoms.acs_spectrum_staging: Unstable angina (ischaemia, no biomarker rise) -> NSTEMI (biomarker rise, no ST elevation) -> STEMI (biomarker rise + ST elevation) - real, standard distinguishing criteria

real_risk_factors.note: In the INTERHEART case-control study (52 countries, 15,152 cases/14,820 controls), an abnormal apolipoprotein B/apolipoprotein A1 ratio was the single strongest of the nine studied risk factors: odds ratio 3.25 (top vs lowest quintile), population attributable risk (PAR) 49.2% for the top four quintiles vs the lowest - i.e. abnormal lipids alone statistically account for close to half of the population risk of a first MI, worldwide, across men and women, young and old.
real_risk_factors.source: Yusuf S et al. (INTERHEART Study Investigators), 'Effect of potentially modifiable risk factors associated with myocardial infarction in 52 countries (the INTERHEART study): case-control study', Lancet 2004;364(9438):937-952, PMID 15364185

real_risk_factors.note: INTERHEART: odds ratio 2.87 for current vs never smoker, PAR 35.7% for current-plus-former vs never smokers - the second-largest single modifiable contributor to MI risk identified in the study, consistent globally across regions.
INTERHEART: odds ratio 2.37 for history of diabetes, PAR 9.9%.
INTERHEART: odds ratio 1.91 for history of hypertension, PAR 17.9%.

INTERHEART used waist/hip ratio rather than BMI: odds ratio 1.12 (middle vs lowest tertile) rising to 1.62 (top vs lowest tertile), PAR 20.1% for the top two tertiles vs the lowest - abdominal/visceral adiposity, not BMI per se, is the metric that tracked most strongly with MI risk, which is consistent with this entry's existing South-Asian 'BMI paradox' finding (visceral fat at lower BMI) documented elsewhere in this entry.
INTERHEART: regular physical activity carried odds ratio 0.86 (i.e. protective), with PAR 12.2% attributable to lack of regular physical activity.

In the Framingham Offspring Study (2,302 participants followed 8 years), offspring with at least one parent who had premature cardiovascular disease (onset age <55 in father, <65 in mother) had an age-adjusted odds ratio of 2.6 (95% CI 1.7-4.1) for men and 2.3 (95% CI 1.3-4.3) for women; after multivariable adjustment for traditional risk factors this fell to 2.0 (95% CI 1.2-3.1) for men and 1.7 (95% CI 0.9-3.1) for women - i.e. family history carries real, partially risk-factor-independent predictive value, particularly useful in patients with intermediate traditional risk-factor levels.
real_risk_factors.source: Lloyd-Jones DM et al., 'Parental cardiovascular disease as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease in middle-aged adults: a prospective study of parents and offspring', JAMA 2004;291(18):2204-2211, PMID 15138242

fourth_universal_definition_of_mi.finding: The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018), the joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF consensus document, defines acute myocardial infarction as detection of a rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin values with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, together with evidence of acute myocardial ischaemia (at least one of: ischaemic symptoms; new ischaemic ECG changes; development of pathological Q waves; imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall motion abnormality; or identification of a coronary thrombus by angiography/autopsy). It subclassifies MI into 5 types: Type 1 (spontaneous MI from atherothrombotic plaque rupture/erosion), Type 2 (myocardial oxygen supply-demand imbalance unrelated to acute atherothrombosis, e.g. severe anaemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypotension, coronary spasm), Type 3 (sudden cardiac death with symptoms suggestive of MI before biomarker results are available), Type 4a/4b/4c (PCI-related, stent-thrombosis-related and restenosis-related MI) and Type 5 (CABG-related MI). Troponin elevation WITHOUT a clinical ischaemic picture is explicitly labelled 'myocardial injury', not myocardial infarction - a distinction that matters because injury (e.g. from sepsis, renal failure, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis) is common and must not be automatically coded/treated as MI.
fourth_universal_definition_of_mi.source: Thygesen K et al., 'Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)', J Am Coll Cardiol 2018;72(18):2231-2264, PMID 30153967

stemi_nstemi_unstable_angina_criteria.finding: STEMI is defined by new ST-segment elevation at the J point in 2 contiguous leads (thresholds vary by lead/age/sex, e.g. >=1mm in most leads, >=2mm in men >=40y / >=2.5mm in men <40y / >=1.5mm in women in V2-V3) or new/presumed-new left bundle branch block with a clinical picture of MI, and is managed as an immediate reperfusion emergency. NSTEMI is a troponin rise/fall above the 99th percentile with an ischaemic clinical picture but WITHOUT diagnostic ST-elevation. Unstable angina is ischaemic symptoms (rest angina, new-onset severe angina, or crescendo angina) WITHOUT troponin release above the 99th percentile - same pathophysiological spectrum (plaque rupture/erosion with non-occlusive or transient thrombus) as NSTEMI but, by definition, without measurable myocardial necrosis. With near-universal high-sensitivity troponin assays, the proportion of ACS now classified as unstable angina (rather than NSTEMI) has fallen substantially compared with older-generation troponin assays, because more of what used to be labelled 'unstable angina' now shows a detectable, if small, troponin rise.
stemi_nstemi_unstable_angina_criteria.source: Thygesen K et al., JACC 2018;72(18):2231-2264, PMID 30153967; Collet JP et al., '2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes in patients presenting without persistent ST-segment elevation', Eur Heart J 2021;42(14):1289-1367, PMID 32860058

high_sensitivity_troponin_algorithms.finding: The ESC 0/1-hour and 0/2-hour high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) algorithms combine a baseline (0h) value with a repeat value at 1h or 2h, applying assay-specific absolute and delta cut-offs to sort patients into rule-out, observe, or rule-in zones. A systematic review/meta-analysis of the ESC 0/1-h algorithm (7 studies, 16 databases) found pooled sensitivity 99.3% (95% CI 98.5-99.7%) and pooled specificity 90.1% (95% CI 80.7-95.2%) using hs-cTnI, and pooled sensitivity 99.3% (95% CI 96.9-99.9%) with pooled specificity 91.7% (95% CI 83.5-96.1%) using hs-cTnT. This very high sensitivity/negative predictive value is why the 0/1h and 0/2h pathways are now guideline-endorsed to safely and rapidly (within 1-2 hours of ED arrival) rule out NSTEMI in most chest-pain presentations, avoiding unnecessary prolonged observation for the majority of low-risk patients while still flagging a smaller rule-in group for admission.
high_sensitivity_troponin_algorithms.source: Nomura O et al., 'Performance of the 0-Hour/1-Hour Algorithm for Diagnosing Myocardial Infarction in Patients With Chest Pain in the Emergency Department - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Circ Rep 2022;4(6):241-247, PMID 35774074; Collet JP et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42(14):1289-1367 (guideline endorsement), PMID 32860058

grace_timi_risk_scores.finding: The GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events) score and the TIMI (Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction) risk score are the two most extensively validated ACS risk-stratification tools. A pooled meta-analysis (D'Ascenzo et al.; up to 40 derivation studies/216,552 patients and 42 validation studies, cohort sizes 31,625-257,654 depending on subgroup) found GRACE consistently outperforms TIMI for mortality prediction in NSTEMI/UA: pooled validation c-statistics of 0.83 (95% CI 0.79-0.87) for GRACE vs 0.54 (95% CI 0.52-0.57) for TIMI at short-term follow-up, and 0.80 (0.74-0.89) vs 0.67 (0.62-0.71) at long-term follow-up. In STEMI the two scores perform more comparably (pooled c-statistics roughly 0.81-0.82 for GRACE vs roughly 0.77 for TIMI at both short and long term). GRACE is the guideline-preferred tool for objective risk stratification (low/intermediate/high risk) to decide the timing of an invasive strategy in NSTE-ACS; TIMI remains popular for bedside simplicity despite materially weaker discrimination in NSTEMI/UA.
grace_timi_risk_scores.source: D'Ascenzo F et al., 'TIMI, GRACE and alternative risk scores in Acute Coronary Syndromes: a meta-analysis of 40 derivation studies on 216,552 patients and of 42 validation studies on 31,625 patients', Contemp Clin Trials 2012;33(3):507-514, PMID 22265976; Collet JP et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42(14):1289-1367 (guideline recommendation), PMID 32860058

stress_testing_ccta_invasive_angiography.finding: For stable suspected CAD, coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is now a guideline-recommended first-line anatomical test: a 2026 Bayesian meta-analysis of 27 studies/4,461 patients against invasive coronary angiography (ICA) as reference standard found CCTA pooled sensitivity 94% (95% posterior interval 89.2-96.9%) and pooled specificity 73% (95% PI 56.0-84.6%) for anatomically significant CAD, with a low negative likelihood ratio (0.08) - a negative CCTA is therefore a strong rule-out test, though a positive CCTA (moderate specificity, further reduced in prior-PCI/CABG patients) often needs confirmatory invasive or functional testing before intervention. Functional stress testing (exercise ECG, stress echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging) remains used particularly where CCTA is unavailable, non-diagnostic (heavy coronary calcification, arrhythmia, poor breath-hold), or when the functional significance of an intermediate stenosis needs confirming. Invasive coronary angiography (with fractional flow reserve where relevant) remains the reference standard and is mandatory, emergently, in STEMI and high-risk NSTE-ACS for primary/early PCI - it is not replaced by CCTA in the acute, high-risk setting.
stress_testing_ccta_invasive_angiography.source: Alqahtani NG et al., 'Diagnostic accuracy of coronary CT angiography versus invasive coronary angiography for detecting coronary artery disease: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis', BMC Med Imaging 2026;26(1):391, PMID 42231233

aortic_dissection.finding: Acute aortic dissection can mimic ACS (chest/back pain; dissection can occlude a coronary ostium and produce true ST-elevation plus troponin rise, most often an inferior STEMI pattern from right-coronary involvement), and misdiagnosis is real and dangerous: an Indian retrospective series of 162 Type A aortic dissection patients found up to 35% were misdiagnosed on initial presentation, in line with a broader international literature range of roughly 14-38% misdiagnosis across series. The danger is bidirectional and acute: giving antiplatelet/anticoagulant/thrombolytic therapy (standard ACS treatment) to an unrecognised dissection can precipitate fatal aortic rupture or cardiac tamponade, while missing a coronary-involving dissection and treating it purely as ACS misses the aortic pathology that will otherwise kill the patient (proximal/Type A dissection mortality is reported as high as roughly 50% by day 3 and 80% by 2 weeks without repair, in general aortic-dissection literature). Features favouring dissection over ACS: abrupt (not crescendo), often maximal-at-onset, tearing/ripping pain radiating to the back/interscapular region; pulse or blood-pressure asymmetry between limbs; a new aortic-regurgitation murmur; a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray; and ECG/troponin findings that do not fully explain the clinical picture. Bedside point-of-care echocardiography (looking for an intimal flap, aortic-root dilation, pericardial effusion) is a real, fast way to raise suspicion before definitive CT aortography.
aortic_dissection.why_dangerous_if_missed: Standard ACS antithrombotic/thrombolytic therapy given to an unrecognised dissection can cause fatal rupture/tamponade; conversely treating a dissection-caused STEMI as isolated ACS delays the surgical repair the aorta needs.
aortic_dissection.source: Satsangi A et al., 'Clinical and Radiological Features of Type A Aortic Dissection: A Retrospective Observational Study - An Indian Perspective', Aorta (Stamford) 2026;14(CP):a28399907, PMID 41941888

pulmonary_embolism.finding: Pulmonary embolism (PE) overlaps substantially with ACS in presentation (chest pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia), and PE itself can cause troponin elevation and ECG ST/T changes from acute right-ventricular strain that occasionally mimic inferior ischaemia; case-report literature documents PE initially diagnosed and treated as ACS before the correct diagnosis emerged. The Wells clinical prediction rule (Wells et al.) is the standard bedside pre-test-probability score for PE ('PE likely' if score >4), but it does not incorporate ECG findings and so does not itself distinguish PE from ACS. The practical distinguishing step is recognising a mismatch - pleuritic pain, disproportionate hypoxaemia/dyspnoea relative to the ECG, venous-thromboembolism risk factors (immobilisation, malignancy, recent surgery, oestrogen therapy), and an S1Q3T3 or right-heart-strain ECG pattern rather than a territorial ST-elevation pattern - that should trigger D-dimer/CT pulmonary angiography rather than assuming ACS from troponin/ECG changes alone.
pulmonary_embolism.why_dangerous_if_missed: PE-specific therapy (anticoagulation, or thrombolysis in high-risk PE with shock) differs from ACS-specific therapy; unrecognised massive PE carries a high short-term mortality if anchoring on an ACS diagnosis delays the correct treatment.
pulmonary_embolism.source: Wells PS et al., 'Derivation of a simple clinical model to categorize patients probability of pulmonary embolism: increasing the models utility with the SimpliRED D-dimer', Thromb Haemost 2000;83(3):416-420, PMID 10744147; PE-misdiagnosed-as-ACS case-report literature, Front Med 2025, PMID 40241897

acute_pericarditis.finding: Acute pericarditis (and myopericarditis) causes chest pain that can mimic STEMI both clinically (retrosternal pain, sometimes pleuritic/positional) and electrocardiographically (diffuse ST-elevation). Key discriminators: pericarditis ST-elevation is typically diffuse (not confined to one coronary territory) and concave/'saddle-shaped' rather than the convex/dome-shaped elevation of STEMI, and reciprocal ST-depression (present in STEMI, aside from aVR/V1) is characteristically absent. A dedicated ECG study found PR-segment depression had 88.2% sensitivity but only 78.3% specificity for myopericarditis alone, while the combination of PR depression in BOTH precordial and limb leads had 96.7% positive and 90% negative predictive power for distinguishing myopericarditis from STEMI. Because myopericarditis can itself cause a real troponin rise (myocardial involvement), troponin alone cannot separate the two conditions - ECG morphology/distribution plus history (preceding viral illness, pleuritic/positional pain relieved by sitting forward, a pericardial friction rub) is essential, and coronary angiography is sometimes still needed when the picture is genuinely ambiguous.
acute_pericarditis.why_dangerous_if_missed: Treating a missed STEMI as pericarditis (rest/NSAIDs alone) forfeits the reperfusion window; conversely treating benign pericarditis with unnecessary antithrombotic therapy carries avoidable bleeding risk.
acute_pericarditis.source: Porela P et al., 'PR depression is useful in the differential diagnosis of myopericarditis and ST elevation myocardial infarction', Ann Noninvasive Electrocardiol 2012;17(2):141-145, PMID 22537332

gerd_esophageal_spasm.finding: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and diffuse oesophageal spasm are common, genuinely confusable mimics of angina: a primary-care cross-sectional diagnostic study of 1,212 consecutive chest-pain patients found GI disease in 5.8% and GERD specifically in 3.5%, with retrosternal pain localisation and pain worse after food intake positively associated with GI disease/GERD, while burning pain, epigastric pain, vomiting and short (<1h) episodes were more specific to GI disease generally. Nitroglycerin relieves BOTH oesophageal spasm and angina (it relaxes oesophageal smooth muscle just as it dilates coronary arteries), so response to nitroglycerin does NOT reliably distinguish the two - a genuinely dangerous trap if used as a bedside 'diagnostic test'. Burning quality and relief with antacids/a PPI trial favour GERD; pressure/tightness quality, exertional trigger and diaphoresis/radiation favour angina - but because GERD and CAD frequently coexist (same at-risk demographic: older, overweight, diabetic patients), a convincing GERD history does not exclude concurrent CAD.
gerd_esophageal_spasm.why_dangerous_if_missed: Nitroglycerin response is a false reassurance test shared by both conditions; attributing chest pain to reflux in an at-risk patient without ECG/troponin can miss concurrent CAD.
gerd_esophageal_spasm.source: Bösner S et al., 'Heartburn or angina? Differentiating gastrointestinal disease in primary care patients presenting with chest pain: a cross sectional diagnostic study', Int Arch Med 2009;2:40, PMID 20003376

musculoskeletal_chest_pain.finding: Costochondritis and other musculoskeletal chest-wall pain are common, generally benign causes of chest pain, classically reproducible on direct palpation of the costochondral junctions (most often the 2nd-5th costochondral joints, usually unilateral) and worsened by movement/deep breathing/specific positions rather than by exertion. However, chest-wall tenderness reproducing the patient's pain is NOT a safe rule-out sign for ACS on its own: emergency-department series cited in the 2021 AAFP evidence review found a real, if minority, proportion of patients with reproducible chest-wall tenderness were concurrently having an acute MI, so guidance explicitly states that patients over 35, or with cardiac risk factors or cardiopulmonary symptoms, still need ECG (and troponin where indicated) before musculoskeletal pain is accepted as the sole explanation.
musculoskeletal_chest_pain.why_dangerous_if_missed: Over-reliance on a reassuring chest-wall-palpation finding can skip cardiac work-up in a patient who happens to have coincidental costochondritis-type tenderness alongside a real ACS.
musculoskeletal_chest_pain.source: Mott T et al., 'Costochondritis: Rapid Evidence Review', Am Fam Physician 2021;104(1):73-78, PMID 34264599

panic_attack.finding: Panic attacks/panic disorder are a genuine and common cause of ED chest-pain presentations that can closely mimic ACS (chest pain/tightness, palpitations, dyspnoea, dizziness, sweating, sense of impending doom - nearly the same symptom list used for atypical/acute MI elsewhere in this entry), and recognition in the ED is poor: an Australian ED cohort study of 338 chest-pain patients found a clinical diagnosis of panic disorder in 5.6% (95% CI 3.4-8.6%), with no reported symptom reliably distinguishing panic-disorder patients from others except a slightly higher rate of pain described as 'heavy'. A separate US ED series found paniclike anxiety in 44% of unexplained-chest-pain patients but physicians recognised only 7.4% of those cases, and more than 92% remained undiagnosed at ED discharge.
panic_attack.why_dangerous_if_missed: Falsely reassuring an anxious patient who is actually having ACS is catastrophic; equally, repeatedly over-investigating a true panic-disorder patient (70-80% of whom have recurrent ED visits) without addressing the underlying anxiety disorder is poor care - panic disorder must be a diagnosis of exclusion made AFTER a real, adequately negative ACS work-up (ECG plus hs-troponin/risk stratification), never in place of one.
panic_attack.source: Greenslade JH et al., 'Panic Disorder in Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Chest Pain: Prevalence and Presenting Symptoms', Heart Lung Circ 2017;26(12):1310-1316, PMID 28256404

global.finding: Ischaemic heart disease is the single leading cause of death worldwide. The GBD 2021 study (204 countries/territories, the primary global cause-of-death analysis) confirms IHD as the top-ranked cause of global deaths, and a focused GBD-2021-based analysis reported IHD prevalence of 254.3 million cases, 9.0 million deaths (13.2% of all global deaths) and 188.4 million DALYs (6.5% of global DALYs) in 2021. Globally, age-standardised mortality and DALY rates have been declining (estimated annual percentage change roughly -1.2% to -1.3%/year from 1990-2021) even as absolute case and death counts keep rising because of population growth and ageing - so the relative (per-person) burden is falling while the absolute (health-system) burden keeps growing. Men carry a heavier absolute IHD burden than women; burden is highest in low-middle socio-demographic-index (SDI) regions and lowest in high-SDI regions, and metabolic risk factors (high LDL cholesterol, high blood pressure, high BMI, high fasting plasma glucose) remain the largest attributable risk-factor category globally.
global.source: GBD 2021 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators, 'Global burden of 288 causes of death and life expectancy decomposition in 204 countries and territories and 811 subnational locations, 1990-2021: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021', Lancet 2024;403:2100-2132, PMID 38582094; Cheng Q et al., 'Global, regional, and national burden and risk factors of ischemic heart disease, 1990-2021: an analysis of the global burden of disease study', Front Public Health 2025;13:1563631, PMID 40352854

india_specific.finding: India carries a large and rapidly rising IHD burden layered on top of the premature/young-onset pattern already documented elsewhere in this entry's CADY-registry data (mean age 49.1 years) and the South Asian 'BMI paradox' age-of-onset data. At the national level, the India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative (GBD-based) found IHD prevalent cases rose 2.3-fold from 25.7 million in 1990 to 54.5 million in 2016, and cardiovascular disease overall contributed an estimated 28.1% (95% UI 26.5-29.1) of all deaths in India by the mid-2010s in that same analysis. A separate national mortality-trend analysis found IHD age-standardised mortality rose from 2000-2017 in both sexes (women 62.9 to 92.7 per 100,000, +47.4%; men 97.5 to 129.5 per 100,000, +32.8%), with rural IHD mortality rates rising faster than urban rates and eventually surpassing them - the reverse of the historically urban-predominant pattern. No single, continuously operating, comprehensive national IHD clinical registry (equivalent to a real-time national STEMI/ACS case-ascertainment registry) was identified in this research pass covering the whole country: national burden figures come from periodic GBD modelling and mortality-survey analyses (the India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative and related GBD-India collaborations), while multi-centre clinical registries such as CADY (already cited in this entry) are regional/selective rather than a national registry. This absence-of-registry statement should be read as 'not found in this search', not as certainty that no such registry exists anywhere in the country.
india_specific.source: India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative CVD Collaborators, 'The changing patterns of cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors in the states of India: the Global Burden of Disease Study 1990-2016', Lancet Glob Health 2018;6(12):e1339-e1351, PMID 30219317; cross-referenced against this entry's existing CADY-registry (PMC5414957) and South-Asian-age-of-onset (PMC10765382) data
india_specific.confidence: moderate-high

stemi_reperfusion_era_mortality_trends.finding: In the primary-PCI era, STEMI 1-year mortality has genuinely fallen. A Western Denmark registry of 19,613 primary-PCI-treated STEMI patients (2003-2018, a health system with pPCI as the sole national reperfusion strategy since 2003) found 1-year mortality declined from 10.8% (2003-2006) to 7.7% (2015-2018) (adjusted HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62-0.82, latest vs earliest era), with roughly three-quarters of the absolute mortality reduction occurring within the first 30 days post-PCI. A separate, earlier US National Registry of Myocardial Infarction analysis (1990-2006, >1.3 million STEMI patients) documented in-hospital mortality among primary-PCI patients falling from 8.6% to 3.1% over that period alongside falling door-to-balloon times (111 to 79 minutes), and fibrinolysis in-hospital mortality falling from 7.0% to 6.0% alongside falling door-to-needle times (59 to 29 minutes).
stemi_reperfusion_era_mortality_trends.source: Thrane PG et al., 'Mortality Trends After Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction', J Am Coll Cardiol 2023;82(10):999-1010, PMID 37648359; Gibson CM et al., 'Trends in reperfusion strategies, door-to-needle and door-to-balloon times, and in-hospital mortality among patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction... National Registry of Myocardial Infarction from 1990 to 2006', Am Heart J 2008;156(6):1035-1044, PMID 19032997

nstemi_vs_stemi_mortality_pattern.finding: A consistent and clinically important pattern across registries is that STEMI short-term (in-hospital/30-day) mortality, historically higher than NSTEMI, has fallen faster than NSTEMI mortality as primary PCI has spread - several large database analyses report NSTEMI mortality NOT declining to the same degree, so contemporary STEMI and NSTEMI in-hospital mortality rates have converged more than they were separated two decades ago, even though NSTEMI patients are often older with more comorbidity. Longer-term (1-year+) mortality after NSTEMI, driven by that comorbidity burden and by ongoing atherothrombotic risk in other coronary territories, is at least comparable to, and in some cohorts exceeds, STEMI 1-year mortality despite NSTEMI's lower peak in-hospital risk. This entry does not assert one universal percentage for 'NSTEMI 1-year mortality' because the retrieved registries report cohort- and era-specific figures rather than a single definitive global number; clinicians should apply a validated risk score (GRACE, see diagnostic_framework above) to the individual patient rather than rely on a remembered population average.
nstemi_vs_stemi_mortality_pattern.source: Gibson CM et al., Am Heart J 2008;156(6):1035-1044, PMID 19032997; directional pattern further supported by Thrane PG et al., JACC 2023, PMID 37648359, and the GRACE/TIMI risk-score literature, D'Ascenzo F et al., PMID 22265976
nstemi_vs_stemi_mortality_pattern.confidence: moderate - directional pattern is well supported by the cited registries; a single precise universal NSTEMI 1-year mortality percentage was deliberately not asserted, per this project's zero-fabrication rule

predictors_of_recurrent_events.finding: In the TIGRIS global registry (9,027 patients enrolled 1-3 years after an index MI, 369 centres/25 countries, all with >=1 additional risk factor), the 2-year composite outcome (recurrent MI, unstable angina needing urgent revascularisation, stroke, or death) occurred in 6.9% of patients (death 3.3%, MI 2.2%, unstable angina 1.1%, stroke 0.6%). Eleven independent predictors were identified: age >=65 years, diabetes, a second prior MI, chronic kidney disease, history of major bleeding, peripheral arterial disease, heart failure, cardiovascular hospitalisation in the prior 6 months, medical (non-revascularisation) management of the index MI, diuretic use, and poor self-reported health. Patients in the highest-risk 16% band had a 6.9-fold higher rate of the composite outcome and an 18.7-fold higher all-cause death rate than the lowest-risk band (overall c-statistics 0.686 and 0.768 respectively, externally validated in an Australian registry at 0.748/0.849). Events accrued linearly over follow-up rather than clustering early, meaning ongoing secondary-prevention vigilance - not just early post-MI intensity - matters for years after the index event.
predictors_of_recurrent_events.source: Pocock SJ et al. (TIGRIS Study Investigators), 'Predicting risk of cardiovascular events 1 to 3 years post-myocardial infarction using a global registry', Clin Cardiol 2020;43(1):24-32, PMID 31713893

clinical_takeaway.point: Get a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of any chest-pain presentation and read it specifically for STEMI - this single time target drives everything downstream.
clinical_takeaway.why: STEMI diagnosis and primary-PCI-pathway activation depend on the ECG; door-to-balloon time is directly, dose-dependently linked to mortality (in-hospital mortality 3.0% at door-to-balloon <=90 min vs 7.4% at >150 min, adjusted OR 1.42 for >90 vs <=90 min), so any delay in even recording/reading the first ECG erodes the reperfusion window before treatment has even begun.
clinical_takeaway.source: McNamara RL et al., JACC 2006;47(11):2180-2186, PMID 16750682

clinical_takeaway.point: In non-ST-elevation presentations, use a validated 0/1h or 0/2h high-sensitivity troponin algorithm rather than a single troponin value or clinical gestalt to rule NSTEMI in or out.
clinical_takeaway.why: The 0/1h and 0/2h hs-troponin algorithms achieve pooled sensitivity ~99% for ruling out MI within 1-2 hours of arrival, letting most low-risk chest-pain patients be safely discharged quickly while correctly flagging the smaller rule-in group for admission/early invasive management - a single delayed troponin either forfeits the safe fast-track discharge or delays diagnosis in a true NSTEMI.
clinical_takeaway.source: Nomura O et al., Circ Rep 2022;4(6):241-247, PMID 35774074; Collet JP et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42(14):1289-1367, PMID 32860058

clinical_takeaway.point: Risk-stratify every confirmed NSTE-ACS patient with the GRACE score - not TIMI alone and not clinical impression alone - to decide the timing of invasive angiography.
clinical_takeaway.why: GRACE substantially outperforms TIMI for mortality discrimination in NSTEMI/UA (pooled validation c-statistic ~0.83 vs ~0.54-0.67 for TIMI), so GRACE more accurately identifies the truly high-risk patients who benefit from early (<24h) invasive strategy versus those who can be managed more conservatively.
clinical_takeaway.source: D'Ascenzo F et al., Contemp Clin Trials 2012;33(3):507-514, PMID 22265976

clinical_takeaway.point: Actively rule out the dangerous mimics - aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism especially, plus pericarditis - before anchoring on ACS, especially when the ECG/troponin picture does not fully fit, or before giving antithrombotic/thrombolytic therapy.
clinical_takeaway.why: Aortic dissection misdiagnosed as ACS and then treated with antiplatelet/thrombolytic therapy can precipitate fatal rupture or tamponade (misdiagnosis rates of roughly 14-38% reported across series, up to 35% in an Indian Type-A-dissection cohort); pulmonary embolism is separately documented, in case-report literature, to be misdiagnosed as ACS; both carry a high, time-critical mortality of their own if the correct diagnosis is delayed.
clinical_takeaway.source: Satsangi A et al., Aorta (Stamford) 2026, PMID 41941888; PE-misdiagnosed-as-ACS case-report literature, PMID 40241897

clinical_takeaway.point: After the acute event, treat post-MI risk as a long-term, linearly accruing problem, not a 30-day problem - schedule structured secondary-prevention follow-up (risk-factor and comorbidity review) for years, not just weeks.
clinical_takeaway.why: In the TIGRIS registry, recurrent cardiovascular events and deaths accrued linearly over the 2 years of follow-up (not front-loaded early), and the 11 identified predictors (age, diabetes, prior MI, CKD, prior major bleed, PAD, heart failure, recent CV hospitalisation, medical-only management of the index MI, diuretic use, poor self-reported health) are all trackable at routine follow-up, not just assessable once at discharge.
