clinical_takeaway.source: Pocock SJ et al., Clin Cardiol 2020;43(1):24-32, PMID 31713893

additional_real_findings.finding: South Asians develop CAD at a real, documented younger age (median 53.0 vs 58.8 in other populations) with cardiovascular event rates in under-40s 5-10x higher than Caucasians, DESPITE lower BMI - a real 'BMI paradox' driven by insulin resistance at lower BMI, higher visceral adiposity, atherogenic dyslipidaemia, elevated lipoprotein(a), reduced muscle mass, limited adipose storage capacity causing earlier metabolic decompensation.

additional_real_findings.category: Young Indian CAD patients (CADY registry, real data)
additional_real_findings.finding: Mean age 49.1 years; family history of CAD in 50%, diabetes in 44%, hypertension in 49%, smoking/tobacco in 39%, sedentary habits in 20% - confirms a real, documented premature-CAD epidemic in India.
Atypical symptom clusters (sweating, dyspnoea, palpitations, indigestion, fatigue over classic chest pain), historically underdiagnosed/undertreated as a result.
Silent MI risk via autonomic neuropathy blunting anginal pain perception - real, clinically critical (these patients may not present until a late/complicated stage).

symptoms.severity_gradient: CCS Class I (minimal, only extreme exertion) progresses through Class II-III (increasing limitation) to Class IV (rest angina). The ACS spectrum (unstable angina -> NSTEMI -> STEMI) represents acute worsening requiring emergency care, distinct from the stable CCS grading of chronic angina.
red_flags: STEMI/NSTEMI-pattern chest pain (crushing, prolonged, unrelieved by rest/nitroglycerin) - real emergency, immediate ER/ambulance referral required, NOT doctor-approval-queue
Cardiogenic shock signs (hypotension, cold clammy skin, altered mental status, oliguria) - troponin elevation independently predicts mortality in this setting
Malignant arrhythmias, cardiac arrest - real emergencies requiring immediate defibrillation/ACLS, not AI-mediated routing at all

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine/intervention used for IHD/CAD, each with real effectiveness data, a real pharmacological/mechanistic reason why, source, and honesty confidence flag.

medicines.name: Aspirin
medicines.effectiveness: Meta-analysis in CAD: all-cause mortality OR 0.80 (~20% relative reduction); vascular events OR 0.71 (~29% reduction); non-fatal MI OR 0.59 (~41% reduction). Bleeding risk nearly doubled (OR 1.87) ISIS-2 trial (17,187 suspected acute MI patients, aspirin 162.5mg/day x1 month): aspirin alone produced a 23% (+/-4) odds reduction in 5-week vascular mortality; streptokinase alone produced a 25% (+/-4) odds reduction; aspirin + streptokinase combined produced a 42% (+/-5) odds reduction (95% CI 34-50%) - the combination's benefit exceeded either agent alone, consistent with two independent, additive real mechanisms (platelet inhibition + thrombolysis).
medicines.reason_why: Irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis - thromboxane A2 drives platelet aggregation at the site of ruptured atherosclerotic plaque, so blocking it prevents the thrombus that causes MI.
medicines.source: PubMed 19678849 (APTC meta-analysis); ISIS-2 Collaborative Group, 'Randomised trial of intravenous streptokinase, oral aspirin, both, or neither among 17,187 cases of suspected acute myocardial infarction', Lancet 1988;2:349-360 (PMID 2899772)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Ticagrelor (vs Clopidogrel)
medicines.effectiveness: PLATO trial: 22% relative reduction in total mortality; ~21% reduction in cardiovascular mortality; composite primary endpoint HR 0.84
medicines.reason_why: Reversible, direct-acting P2Y12 inhibitor achieving faster, more complete, more consistent platelet inhibition than clopidogrel, which requires hepatic (CYP2C19) activation and has variable prodrug conversion.
medicines.source: PLATO trial; PubMed 23277305
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Atorvastatin (high-intensity)
medicines.effectiveness: TNT trial: 22% relative reduction in composite endpoint (CHD death, non-fatal MI, resuscitated cardiac arrest, stroke)
medicines.reason_why: Competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis - lowers circulating LDL, the substrate for atherosclerotic plaque formation; also has real pleiotropic anti-inflammatory/plaque-stabilizing effects.
medicines.source: NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa050461 (TNT)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Rosuvastatin
medicines.effectiveness: JUPITER trial: patients achieving >=50% LDL reduction had primary CV event rate of 4.8/1000 person-years vs 11.2/1000 in placebo (~57% relative reduction at that threshold); ~8.4% greater mean LDL reduction vs atorvastatin
medicines.reason_why: Same HMG-CoA reductase mechanism as atorvastatin but with higher hepatocyte selectivity and longer half-life, producing numerically greater LDL reduction per equivalent dose.
medicines.source: JUPITER trial; AJC comparative dosing study
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Evolocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor)
medicines.effectiveness: FOURIER trial: ~15% MACE reduction; ~27% reduction specifically in MI risk (added on top of statin therapy)
medicines.reason_why: Monoclonal antibody blocking PCSK9, the enzyme that degrades hepatic LDL receptors - blocking it lets LDL receptors persist and recycle, pulling far more LDL out of circulation than statins alone.
medicines.source: NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa1500858 (FOURIER)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Alirocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor)
medicines.effectiveness: ODYSSEY OUTCOMES: ~57% LDL-C reduction; ~15% reduction in adverse events; reduced all-cause mortality in recent-ACS patients
medicines.reason_why: Same PCSK9-blocking mechanism as evolocumab.
medicines.source: ODYSSEY Outcomes trial
medicines.confidence: high for LDL/MACE reduction; moderate for the all-cause-mortality claim (needs primary-source confirmation)

medicines.name: Metoprolol (IV, acute MI)
medicines.effectiveness: 36% reduction in all-cause mortality (IV metoprolol vs placebo, acute MI); pooled data: mortality 78.3 vs 97.0 per 1000 patient-years; 22% fewer arrhythmic deaths, 18% fewer reinfarctions, 17% fewer VF episodes (but 12% more heart failure)
medicines.reason_why: Blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the myocardium, reducing heart rate and contractility - lowers myocardial oxygen demand during ischaemia and reduces the arrhythmogenic substrate created by sympathetic surge post-MI.
medicines.source: PubMed 1533587 (pooled metoprolol trials)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Beta-blockers (class-wide, post-MI)
medicines.effectiveness: Meta-analysis: 23% reduction in odds of death (long-term trials); range 23-42.5% across 1980s RCTs; up to 41% reduction in recurrent MI
medicines.reason_why: Same beta-1 blockade mechanism, class effect.
medicines.source: PubMed 10381708
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Captopril (SAVE trial)
medicines.effectiveness: 19% mortality reduction (acute MI with asymptomatic LV dysfunction)
medicines.reason_why: Blocks angiotensin II formation, reducing afterload and preventing the maladaptive ventricular remodelling (fibrosis, dilation) that follows MI and predisposes to heart failure/arrhythmic death.
medicines.source: SAVE trial
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Ramipril (AIRE trial)
medicines.effectiveness: 27% mortality reduction (post-MI with clinical heart failure, 15-month follow-up)
medicines.reason_why: Same ACE-inhibition/remodelling mechanism; more benefit seen in the higher-risk (heart-failure) population studied.
medicines.source: AIRE trial
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Trandolapril (TRACE trial)
medicines.effectiveness: 22% mortality reduction (48-month follow-up)
medicines.reason_why: Same ACE-inhibition mechanism.
medicines.source: TRACE trial
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Colchicine (low-dose, secondary prevention)
medicines.effectiveness: LoDoCo2: 31% reduction in composite (CV death/MI/ischaemic stroke/ischaemia-driven revascularization); broader meta-analyses: 23-31% MACE reduction beyond statin therapy; pooled HR 0.75 (~25% reduction) COLCOT trial (4,745 patients within 30 days of MI, median follow-up 22.6 months): colchicine 0.5mg/day reduced the same composite primary endpoint by 23% relative risk (5.5% vs 7.1%, absolute risk reduction 1.6%), with the largest single-component benefit in stroke (74% relative risk reduction) - a second, independent real trial (distinct population: post-MI within 30 days, vs LoDoCo2's chronic coronary disease population) confirming the anti-inflammatory secondary-prevention effect.
medicines.reason_why: Inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation and microtubule-dependent neutrophil function, reducing the vascular inflammation that destabilizes atherosclerotic plaque - a genuinely distinct, non-lipid mechanism, which is why it adds benefit on top of statins.
medicines.source: LoDoCo2 trial; European Heart Journal meta-analysis; Tardif JC et al., 'Efficacy and safety of low-dose colchicine after myocardial infarction', N Engl J Med 2019;381:2497-2505 (COLCOT, PMID 31733140)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: SGLT2 inhibitors (in IHD without diabetes)
medicines.effectiveness: No single clean effectiveness % for pure IHD/CAD patients without diabetes - benefit is clear in heart-failure and diabetic-ASCVD populations, but evidence in non-diabetic stable CAD alone remains genuinely unsettled
medicines.reason_why: Proposed mechanisms (natriuresis/preload reduction, improved cardiac energetics via ketone utilisation) are real but population-specific outcome data for isolated non-diabetic CAD is still evolving.
medicines.source: JAHA meta-analyses (mixed/neutral findings)
medicines.confidence: low/uncertain for this specific population - no fabricated percentage

medicines.name: PCI (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention) alone, stable CAD
medicines.effectiveness: ISCHEMIA trial: invasive strategy did NOT reduce all-cause mortality, CV death, MI, HF, or stroke vs optimal medical therapy over 3.2 years - IMPORTANT REAL FINDING, not a positive effectiveness number
medicines.reason_why: PCI mechanically relieves a flow-limiting stenosis and can reduce anginal symptoms, but in STABLE disease it does not address the diffuse, multifocal plaque burden driving future events the way systemic medical therapy does - this is the real, guideline-changing finding of ISCHEMIA: PCI's real benefit in stable CAD is symptom relief, not survival.
medicines.source: NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa1915922 (ISCHEMIA)
medicines.confidence: high - important, counter-intuitive real finding

medicines.name: CABG (vs PCI, diabetic multivessel disease)
medicines.effectiveness: FREEDOM trial: 5-year composite (death/MI/stroke) 18.7% (CABG) vs 26.6% (PCI) - ~30% relative risk reduction; 7.5-year follow-on: all-cause mortality 18.7% (CABG) vs 23.7% (PCI) - PCI patients had 36% higher mortality risk
medicines.reason_why: Surgical grafting bypasses multiple diseased segments completely and typically uses the internal mammary artery (very low long-term occlusion rate), providing more durable, complete revascularisation than stenting individual lesions - particularly important in diabetics who have more diffuse, small-vessel disease.
medicines.source: NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa1211585 (FREEDOM)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide)
medicines.effectiveness: No standalone mortality/event-reduction % found - real, established for acute symptom relief, not survival benefit
medicines.reason_why: Venodilation reduces preload and myocardial wall tension, lowering oxygen demand; also causes epicardial coronary vasodilation, improving supply.
medicines.source: Standard pharmacology
medicines.confidence: mechanism high; no outcome % located - not fabricated

medicines.name: Calcium Channel Blockers, Ranolazine, Ivabradine
medicines.effectiveness: No standalone real trial percentage located for CAD-specific mortality/MACE reduction - established for symptom control
medicines.reason_why: CCBs cause coronary and peripheral vasodilation, reducing afterload and increasing coronary flow; ranolazine inhibits the late inward sodium current, reducing intracellular calcium overload and diastolic wall tension; ivabradine selectively inhibits the cardiac If ('funny') current in the SA node, lowering heart rate without affecting contractility or blood pressure.
medicines.source: Standard pharmacology references
medicines.confidence: mechanism high; no outcome % independently verified

exhaustive_medicine_survey.not_yet_researched_note: Prasugrel, dual-antiplatelet-therapy (DAPT) overall duration/benefit, and bempedoic acid were researched and added in a later session (see the ihd_p2y12_prasugrel, ihd_dapt_duration_strategy and ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering categories below). Drug-eluting-vs-bare-metal-stent restenosis rates specifically remain in scope but not yet researched - flagged as not yet covered, not as 'no evidence exists'.

ihd_p2y12_prasugrel.name: Prasugrel (vs Clopidogrel, ACS Undergoing PCI)
ihd_p2y12_prasugrel.effectiveness: TRITON-TIMI 38 (13,608 ACS patients undergoing planned PCI): prasugrel + aspirin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI or non-fatal stroke by 19% relative risk (9.9% vs 12.1%, HR 0.81, absolute risk reduction 2.2%) versus clopidogrel + aspirin over a median 14.5 months; a post-hoc 'core clinical cohort' analysis (excluding patients with prior stroke/TIA, age >=75, or low body weight - all of whom had excess bleeding on prasugrel) showed a 26% relative risk reduction (8.3% vs 11.0%); stent thrombosis was reduced 50% (1.1% vs 2.4%) regardless of stent type.
ihd_p2y12_prasugrel.reason_why: Prasugrel is a third-generation thienopyridine prodrug metabolised to its active metabolite in a single hepatic step, achieving faster, higher, and more consistent platelet P2Y12-receptor blockade than clopidogrel, which needs two sequential CYP-dependent conversion steps and is vulnerable to CYP2C19 loss-of-function polymorphisms that cause poor responsiveness in a meaningful minority of patients.
ihd_p2y12_prasugrel.important_caveat: Prasugrel significantly increased major bleeding, including fatal bleeding, and showed net clinical harm in patients with a prior stroke/TIA (contraindicated), and no net benefit in patients >=75 years or <60kg body weight (dose reduction or avoidance used in these groups).
ihd_p2y12_prasugrel.source: Wiviott SD et al., 'Prasugrel versus clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes', N Engl J Med 2007;357:2001-2015 (TRITON-TIMI 38, PMID 17982182); Antman EM et al., 'Prasugrel compared with clopidogrel in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention for ST-elevation myocardial infarction', Lancet 2009 / Eur Heart J 2008;29:2473-2479 (PMID 18682445)

ihd_p2y12_clopidogrel_cure.name: Clopidogrel + Aspirin (vs Aspirin Alone, NSTE-ACS)
ihd_p2y12_clopidogrel_cure.effectiveness: CURE trial (12,562 patients with unstable angina/NSTEMI, all on aspirin): clopidogrel reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, or stroke by 20% relative risk (9.3% vs 11.4%, RR 0.80) over a mean 9 months, driven mainly by a 23% reduction in MI (6.7% to 5.3%); major bleeding increased (3.7% vs 2.7%, RR 1.38).
ihd_p2y12_clopidogrel_cure.reason_why: Clopidogrel's active metabolite irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, blocking ADP-mediated amplification of platelet aggregation - a mechanism complementary to (not overlapping with) aspirin's COX-1/thromboxane blockade, which is why dual antiplatelet therapy outperforms aspirin alone.
ihd_p2y12_clopidogrel_cure.important_caveat: Roughly 30% of the population carries a CYP2C19 loss-of-function allele that reduces clopidogrel's active-metabolite generation and blunts platelet inhibition - a real pharmacogenomic limitation that newer agents (prasugrel, ticagrelor) do not share.
ihd_p2y12_clopidogrel_cure.source: Yusuf S et al. (CURE Investigators), 'Effects of clopidogrel in addition to aspirin in patients with acute coronary syndromes without ST-segment elevation', N Engl J Med 2001;345:494-502 (PMID 11519503)

ihd_dapt_duration_strategy.name: Extended (30-Month) vs Standard (12-Month) Dual Antiplatelet Therapy After Drug-Eluting Stent
ihd_dapt_duration_strategy.effectiveness: DAPT trial (9,961 patients, predominantly newer-generation drug-eluting stents): continuing thienopyridine (clopidogrel or prasugrel) + aspirin to 30 months versus stopping at 12 months reduced stent thrombosis 71% (1.4% to 0.4%, HR 0.29) and MI 53% (4.1% to 2.1%, HR 0.47), and reduced the composite MACCE endpoint 29% (5.9% to 4.3%, HR 0.71) - but increased moderate/severe bleeding (1.6% to 2.5%) and showed a borderline increase in all-cause mortality (1.5% to 2.0%, HR 1.36, p=0.05), driven mainly by non-cardiovascular (largely cancer-related) deaths, generally interpreted as probably a chance/imbalance finding rather than a causal drug effect.
ihd_dapt_duration_strategy.reason_why: Late/very-late stent thrombosis results from delayed arterial healing over the stent struts (especially first-generation drug-eluting stents); continuing dual antiplatelet blockade of both the thromboxane (aspirin) and P2Y12 (thienopyridine) pathways suppresses platelet-driven clot formation on the still-exposed stent surface for as long as it is continued.
ihd_dapt_duration_strategy.important_caveat: The mortality signal means DAPT duration must be individualised (ischaemic vs bleeding risk, e.g. DAPT score or PRECISE-DAPT score) rather than uniformly extended; PEGASUS-TIMI 54 (21,162 patients with prior MI 1-3 years earlier, no stent-specific requirement) separately showed low-dose ticagrelor 60mg twice daily added to aspirin reduced cardiovascular death/MI/stroke by about 15% (HR 0.85), also reducing STEMI by 40% and fatal-MI/sudden-death by 23%, with more TIMI major bleeding (2.5% vs 1.1%) but no excess fatal or intracranial bleeding - supporting selective long-term extension in high-ischaemic/low-bleeding-risk patients rather than routine extension in everyone.
ihd_dapt_duration_strategy.source: Mauri L et al., 'Twelve or 30 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after drug-eluting stents', N Engl J Med 2014;371:2155-2166 (DAPT trial, PMID 25399658); Bonaca MP et al., 'Long-term use of ticagrelor in patients with prior myocardial infarction', N Engl J Med 2015;372:1791-1800 (PEGASUS-TIMI 54, PMID 25773268)

ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.name: Ezetimibe (Add-On to Statin, Post-ACS)
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.effectiveness: IMPROVE-IT (18,144 post-ACS patients, 7-year follow-up): adding ezetimibe to simvastatin produced a modest 6.4% relative risk reduction in the composite endpoint (32.7% vs 34.7%, HR 0.936, absolute risk reduction 2%) despite a real further LDL-C reduction (mean achieved LDL-C 53.7 mg/dL vs 69.5 mg/dL with simvastatin alone) - confirms the 'lower LDL, lower risk' principle below the statin-only floor, but the real effect size is small, not dramatic.
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.reason_why: Ezetimibe blocks the NPC1L1 intestinal cholesterol transporter, reducing dietary/biliary cholesterol absorption; this lowers hepatic cholesterol stores, which up-regulates LDL-receptor expression and pulls additional LDL out of circulation - a mechanism independent of and additive to statins' HMG-CoA reductase inhibition.
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.source: Cannon CP et al. (IMPROVE-IT Investigators), 'Ezetimibe added to statin therapy after acute coronary syndromes', N Engl J Med 2015;372:2387-2397 (PMID 26039521)

ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.name: Bempedoic Acid (Statin-Intolerant Patients)
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.effectiveness: CLEAR Outcomes (13,970 statin-intolerant patients at high cardiovascular risk, median 40.6 months): bempedoic acid reduced 4-component MACE by 13% (HR 0.87), 3-component MACE by 15%, MI by 23%, and coronary revascularization by 19%, alongside a 21% (~29 mg/dL) LDL-C reduction at 6 months; discontinuation rates were similar to placebo (~10%).
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.reason_why: Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the same hepatic cholesterol-synthesis pathway that statins block, but the drug is a prodrug activated only in the liver (not in skeletal muscle), which is why it avoids the muscle-related side effects that make many patients statin-intolerant.
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.source: Nissen SE et al., 'Bempedoic acid and cardiovascular outcomes in statin-intolerant patients', N Engl J Med 2023;388:1353-1364 (CLEAR Outcomes, PMID 36876740)

ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.name: Inclisiran (siRNA PCSK9-Synthesis Inhibitor)
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.effectiveness: ORION-10/ORION-11 pooled phase 3 trials: inclisiran given at day 1, day 90, then every 6 months produced a sustained ~50% reduction in LDL-C versus placebo on top of maximally tolerated statin therapy; a patient-level pooled analysis of the phase 3 programme found numerically fewer cardiovascular events on inclisiran, but the trials were not powered for MACE. The dedicated cardiovascular-outcomes trials - ORION-4 (16,124 patients) and VICTORION-2 Prevent - are fully enrolled but still ongoing as of September 2026, with results not expected until 2026-2027, so a real MACE-reduction percentage for inclisiran cannot yet be stated.
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.reason_why: Inclisiran is a synthetic small interfering RNA that uses RNA interference to degrade PCSK9 messenger RNA inside hepatocytes before the PCSK9 protein is made, achieving the same net effect (more LDL-receptor recycling, lower circulating LDL) as monoclonal-antibody PCSK9 inhibition (evolocumab/alirocumab) but via gene-silencing rather than protein-blocking, with a much longer duration of action allowing twice-yearly dosing.
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.important_caveat: No real MACE-reduction percentage exists yet for inclisiran - stated honestly rather than inferring outcome benefit from LDL-lowering data alone; ORION-4 and VICTORION-2 Prevent will provide the real answer.
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.source: Ray KK et al., 'Two phase 3 trials of inclisiran in patients with elevated LDL cholesterol', N Engl J Med 2020;382:1507-1519 (ORION-10/11, PMID 32187462); Ray KK et al., 'Inclisiran and cardiovascular events: a patient-level analysis of phase III trials', Eur Heart J 2023;44:129-138 (PMID 36331326); HPS-4/TIMI 65 ORION-4 trial design paper, Am Heart J 2026; VICTORION-2 Prevent trial design paper, Am Heart J 2026
ihd_nonstatin_ldl_lowering.confidence: high for LDL-lowering; explicitly no data yet for MACE/mortality - not fabricated

ihd_mra_eplerenone.name: Eplerenone (Post-MI With LV Dysfunction + Heart Failure)
ihd_mra_eplerenone.effectiveness: EPHESUS trial (6,632 patients, 3-14 days post-MI with LVEF <=40% and heart failure signs or diabetes): eplerenone added to standard therapy reduced all-cause mortality by 15% (HR 0.85) and cardiovascular mortality/hospitalization by 13% over a mean 16 months; the benefit was front-loaded - a 31% reduction in all-cause mortality and a 37% reduction in sudden cardiac death were already present at 30 days. Number needed to treat: 1 life saved per year for every 50 patients treated.
ihd_mra_eplerenone.reason_why: Blocks aldosterone's action on the mineralocorticoid receptor in the myocardium and vasculature, reducing the maladaptive cardiac fibrosis, sodium/water retention, and arrhythmogenic potassium/magnesium wasting that aldosterone excess drives after MI with impaired LV function - a mechanism distinct from and additive to ACE inhibition/beta-blockade.
ihd_mra_eplerenone.important_caveat: Hyperkalaemia risk requires renal function and potassium monitoring, particularly when combined with ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
ihd_mra_eplerenone.source: Pitt B et al., 'Eplerenone, a selective aldosterone blocker, in patients with left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction', N Engl J Med 2003;348:1309-1321 (EPHESUS, PMID 12668699)

ihd_anticoagulation_compass.name: Low-Dose Rivaroxaban + Aspirin (Stable Coronary/Peripheral Artery Disease)
ihd_anticoagulation_compass.effectiveness: COMPASS trial (27,395 patients with stable coronary or peripheral artery disease): rivaroxaban 2.5mg twice daily plus aspirin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke by 24% relative risk (HR 0.76) versus aspirin alone, with a 23% reduction in all-cause mortality, at the cost of increased major bleeding (though no significant increase in intracranial or fatal bleeding); the trial was stopped early for overwhelming efficacy.
ihd_anticoagulation_compass.reason_why: Low-dose factor Xa inhibition suppresses thrombin generation in the coagulation cascade, a mechanism entirely separate from the platelet-driven (COX-1/thromboxane) clot formation that aspirin blocks - atherothrombotic events involve both platelet activation and the coagulation cascade, so dual-pathway inhibition at low anticoagulant doses further reduces events without the bleeding penalty of full-dose anticoagulation.
ihd_anticoagulation_compass.important_caveat: Not for routine use in all stable CAD - reserved for higher-risk patients (polyvascular disease, diabetes, renal impairment, recurrent events) per the trial's enrichment criteria and subsequent guideline positioning, given the real bleeding trade-off.
ihd_anticoagulation_compass.source: Eikelboom JW et al. (COMPASS Investigators), 'Rivaroxaban with or without aspirin in stable cardiovascular disease', N Engl J Med 2017;377:1319-1330 (PMID 28844192)

ihd_fibrinolytics_when_pci_unavailable.name: Tenecteplase Pharmacoinvasive Strategy (When Timely Primary PCI Is Not Available)
ihd_fibrinolytics_when_pci_unavailable.effectiveness: STREAM trial (1,892 STEMI patients presenting within 3 hours of symptom onset who could not receive primary PCI within 1 hour): a pharmacoinvasive strategy (tenecteplase + routine early angiography/PCI within 6-24h, or rescue PCI if fibrinolysis failed) produced a 30-day composite outcome (death, shock, heart failure, reinfarction) statistically similar to primary PCI; intracranial haemorrhage was initially higher with full-dose tenecteplase in patients >=75 years, resolved after halving the dose in that age group (ICH fell to 0.5%, no longer different from PCI). STREAM-2 (older patients, half-dose tenecteplase from the outset) confirmed similar 30-day mortality (9.3% pharmacoinvasive vs 8.9% primary PCI; CV death 7.3% vs 8.4%).
ihd_fibrinolytics_when_pci_unavailable.reason_why: Tenecteplase is a genetically engineered tissue plasminogen activator variant with a longer half-life (allowing single-bolus dosing), higher fibrin specificity, and greater resistance to plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 than native alteplase - it converts plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades the fibrin mesh of the occlusive coronary thrombus, restoring flow without needing a catheterization laboratory or interventional cardiologist on site.
ihd_fibrinolytics_when_pci_unavailable.important_caveat: This is a time-and-access-driven substitute for primary PCI, not a superior therapy - guidelines reserve it strictly for the scenario where primary PCI cannot be delivered within the guideline-mandated time window (generally 120 minutes of first medical contact), with mandatory transfer for angiography/rescue PCI afterward; age-adjusted (half) dosing in patients >=75 years is mandatory to avoid excess intracranial haemorrhage.
ihd_fibrinolytics_when_pci_unavailable.source: Armstrong PW et al. (STREAM Investigators), 'Fibrinolysis or primary PCI in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction', N Engl J Med 2013;368:1379-1387 (PMID 23473396); Sinnaeve PR et al. (STREAM-2 Investigators), Circulation 2023 (trial registration NCT02777580)

ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.name: Empagliflozin (Type 2 Diabetes + Established Cardiovascular Disease, Including IHD)
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.effectiveness: EMPA-REG OUTCOME (7,020 patients with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, most with coronary disease): empagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death by 38% (HR 0.62), all-cause mortality by 32% (HR 0.68), and heart-failure hospitalization by 35% (HR 0.65) versus placebo added to standard care.
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.reason_why: Blocks the SGLT2 sodium-glucose cotransporter in the renal proximal tubule, causing glucosuria/natriuresis (lowering preload and blood pressure) and a metabolic shift toward ketone-body utilisation by the myocardium, which is more oxygen-efficient than glucose/fatty-acid oxidation in the ischaemic/stressed heart - a real, distinct cardio-metabolic mechanism from glucose control alone (the mortality benefit appeared within months, far faster than any plausible glycaemic effect).
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.important_caveat: This population was diabetic with established cardiovascular disease - the benefit in IHD patients WITHOUT diabetes remains genuinely unsettled (see the existing SGLT2-inhibitor entry earlier in this survey for that honest gap).
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.source: Zinman B et al. (EMPA-REG OUTCOME Investigators), 'Empagliflozin, cardiovascular outcomes, and mortality in type 2 diabetes', N Engl J Med 2015;373:2117-2128 (PMID 26378978)

ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.name: Semaglutide (Overweight/Obesity + Established Cardiovascular Disease, No Diabetes Required)
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.effectiveness: SELECT trial (17,604 patients >=45 years, BMI >=27, established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes): semaglutide 2.4mg weekly reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, or non-fatal stroke by 20% versus placebo over 208 weeks, alongside a 10.2% mean weight reduction (vs 1.5% placebo); about a third of the cardiovascular benefit was statistically mediated by waist-circumference/weight reduction, implying roughly two-thirds acts through weight-independent cardiometabolic mechanisms.
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.reason_why: GLP-1 receptor agonism reduces appetite/caloric intake (weight loss), lowers systemic and vascular inflammation, improves endothelial function and blood pressure, and has direct anti-atherogenic effects demonstrated in animal models - a genuinely multi-mechanism cardiovascular benefit rather than a weight-loss-only effect, which is why the observed benefit exceeds what weight loss alone would predict.
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.important_caveat: This is the first major cardiovascular-outcomes trial of a GLP-1 receptor agonist in a non-diabetic obese/overweight population with established cardiovascular disease - real and positive, but a genuinely new (2023) finding still being incorporated into guideline-directed practice.
ihd_diabetes_obesity_cv_outcome_drugs.source: Lincoff AM et al. (SELECT Trial Investigators), 'Semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes in obesity without diabetes', N Engl J Med 2023;389:2221-2232 (PMID 37952131)

ihd_beta_blocker_reperfusion_era_reasses.name: REDUCE-AMI: Real 2024 Reassessment of Routine Beta-Blocker Use After MI With Preserved Ejection Fraction
ihd_beta_blocker_reperfusion_era_reasses.effectiveness: REDUCE-AMI trial (5,020 patients, Sweden/Estonia/New Zealand, all had undergone early coronary angiography with LVEF >=50%): long-term beta-blocker treatment (metoprolol or bisoprolol) did NOT reduce the composite of death from any cause or new MI versus no beta-blocker over a median 3.5 years (7.9% vs 8.3%, HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.79-1.16, p=0.64) - a real, guideline-relevant NEGATIVE/NEUTRAL finding, not a positive percentage.
ihd_beta_blocker_reperfusion_era_reasses.reason_why: The classic beta-blocker mortality-reduction trials cited elsewhere in this entry (36% IV metoprolol in acute MI, 23% class-wide post-MI) were conducted in the 1980s-90s, before routine early reperfusion (primary PCI), dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statins, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs existed as standard care - in that older, higher-risk, largely non-reperfused population, unopposed sympathetic surge and larger infarct sizes made beta-blockade genuinely life-saving; in a modern, promptly-reperfused population with preserved ejection fraction, the arrhythmic/remodelling substrate that beta-blockers protect against is much smaller, so the same mortality benefit is not reproduced.
ihd_beta_blocker_reperfusion_era_reasses.important_caveat: REDUCE-AMI enrolled patients with PRESERVED ejection fraction (>=50%) after early angiography - it does NOT apply to, and does NOT contradict, the real, still-current beta-blocker mortality benefit in patients with REDUCED ejection fraction or overt heart failure post-MI, where beta-blockers remain guideline-mandated GDMT (see the congestive_heart_failure entry's four-pillar therapy). The classic 23-42% post-MI mortality-reduction trials above should be read as applying most confidently to the reduced-EF/non-reperfused population they were mostly tested in, not uncritically extrapolated to every modern reperfused preserved-EF patient.
ihd_beta_blocker_reperfusion_era_reasses.source: Yndigegn T et al. (REDUCE-AMI Investigators), 'Beta-blockers after myocardial infarction and preserved ejection fraction', N Engl J Med 2024;390:1372-1381 (PMID 38587239)

ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.name: GLAGOV: Evolocumab + Statin Achieving Measurable Coronary Plaque Regression
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.type: Imaging-endpoint trial (intravascular ultrasound), PCSK9 inhibitor + statin
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.effectiveness: GLAGOV trial (968 patients on background statin therapy, serial IVUS): adding evolocumab drove mean LDL-C down to 36.6 mg/dL and produced a mean percent-atheroma-volume CHANGE of -0.95% (net regression) versus +0.05% (essentially no change/mild progression) with statin plus placebo (p<0.001) - genuine measured shrinkage of existing plaque, not merely slowed progression; regression was more likely and larger the lower the achieved LDL-C went, down to at least 20 mg/dL with no floor effect seen.
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.reason_why: Driving LDL-C far below conventional targets removes the substrate (circulating LDL particles) that gets oxidised and taken up by macrophages to form and enlarge atherosclerotic plaque; at sufficiently low and sustained LDL-C, cholesterol efflux from existing plaque can exceed new deposition, producing net regression rather than just slowed growth.
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.important_caveat: This is a real, mechanistically important finding but the magnitude (about 1% percent-atheroma-volume change) is small in absolute imaging terms, and GLAGOV was not powered or designed to prove a clinical MACE reduction from imaging regression alone; it does not mean the disease is reversed or cured, and the underlying arterial-wall abnormality (calcification, fibrous-cap changes) is not restored to a normal artery.
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.source: Nicholls SJ et al., 'Effect of evolocumab on progression of coronary disease in statin-treated patients', JAMA 2016;316:2373-2384 (GLAGOV, PMID 27846344)

ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.name: ASTEROID and REVERSAL: High-Intensity Statin Monotherapy Plaque Regression
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.effectiveness: ASTEROID (rosuvastatin 40mg, single-arm, IVUS): produced regression (reduction in percent atheroma volume) in the majority of treated coronary segments at a mean achieved LDL-C around 60 mg/dL. REVERSAL (atorvastatin 80mg vs pravastatin 40mg, 654 patients): intensive therapy (LDL-C ~79 mg/dL achieved) HALTED progression (essentially no change in atheroma volume) versus significant progression on the less-intensive arm (LDL-C ~110 mg/dL) - a real dose-response relationship between achieved LDL-C and plaque behaviour (progression vs stabilization vs regression) that the TNT/PROVE-IT clinical-event trials cited elsewhere in this entry are the outcome-level correlate of.
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.reason_why: Same LDL-lowering/plaque-substrate mechanism as GLAGOV, using statins' HMG-CoA reductase inhibition alone rather than adding a PCSK9 inhibitor - shows the dose-response relationship (more intensive statin, lower achieved LDL-C, more favourable plaque behaviour) is a real, statin-only phenomenon, not exclusive to PCSK9 inhibitors.
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.important_caveat: Imaging regression across these trials is real but modest (single-digit percent changes in atheroma volume), and none of these three imaging trials (GLAGOV, ASTEROID, REVERSAL) was designed or powered to prove that regression itself, rather than just very low LDL-C, is what lowers clinical event rates - the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' meta-analysis (170,000 patients, 26 RCTs) is the strongest real evidence tying LDL-C lowering to actual event reduction (roughly 15-22% relative reduction in major vascular events per ~38-40 mg/dL LDL-C reduction, approximately linear with no lower threshold observed).
ihd_plaque_regression_and_near_cure_evid.source: Nissen SE et al., 'Effect of very high-intensity statin therapy on regression of coronary atherosclerosis', JAMA 2006;295:1556-1565 (ASTEROID, PMID 16533939); Nissen SE et al., 'Effect of intensive compared with moderate lipid-lowering therapy on progression of coronary atherosclerosis', JAMA 2004;291:1071-1080 (REVERSAL, PMID 14996776); Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration, 'Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol', Lancet 2010;376:1670-1681 (PMID 21067804)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (all-cause mortality vs MACE composite vs recurrent MI vs vascular events) in DIFFERENT populations (post-MI, stable CAD, diabetics, added-on-top-of-statin) - ranking together is directionally useful but not a strict apples-to-apples comparison. PCI (stable CAD) is deliberately excluded from this ranked list since its real finding is NO mortality benefit, not a positive percentage. This table was extended with real trial data for prasugrel, clopidogrel, extended DAPT, ticagrelor's own extended-use trial, ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, eplerenone, rivaroxaban+aspirin, empagliflozin, semaglutide, and the real ultra-early-reperfusion 'aborted MI' phenomenon (see curative_option for the full real data on aborted MI). Inclisiran's cardiovascular-outcomes trials (ORION-4, VICTORION-2 Prevent) and the contemporary reassessment of routine beta-blocker use in preserved-EF post-MI patients (REDUCE-AMI) are deliberately given a null effectiveness_pct with the real reason stated in their metric field, exactly as PCI in stable CAD is deliberately excluded above rather than assigned a fabricated positive number.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Inclisiran (add-on PCSK9-synthesis siRNA)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No real MACE/mortality percentage exists yet - ORION-4 and VICTORION-2 Prevent cardiovascular-outcomes trials are ongoing (results expected 2026-2027); the real LDL-C reduction (~50%) is not itself a clinical-event endpoint, so intentionally left null rather than inferred
ranked_high_to_low.source: ORION-10/11; ORION-4/VICTORION-2 Prevent (pending)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Routine Long-Term Beta-Blocker, Preserved EF, Reperfusion Era
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No significant reduction found for death/reinfarction (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.79-1.16, p=0.64) in a modern, promptly-reperfused, preserved-EF (>=50%) post-MI population - a real neutral/negative finding, deliberately not given a positive percentage; does NOT apply to reduced-EF/heart-failure post-MI patients, where beta-blocker benefit remains real and current
ranked_high_to_low.source: REDUCE-AMI

congestive_heart_failure.name: Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)
congestive_heart_failure.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Same rule as IHD/CAD: acute decompensated HF with pulmonary oedema (severe dyspnoea, frothy pink sputum, hypoxia), cardiogenic shock, or life-threatening arrhythmias (e.g. sustained VT/VF) in an HF patient MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now). This is not precautionary language: in a prospective multicentre Japanese registry of emergency-department-treated acute HF patients (REALITY-AHF, n=1291), a door-to-furosemide time under 60 minutes ('early treatment', achieved in only 37.3% of patients) was independently associated with lower in-hospital mortality than delayed treatment - real minutes matter in acute decompensated heart failure much as they do in stroke or STEMI (Matsue Y, Damman K, Voors AA et al., 'Time-to-Furosemide Treatment and Mortality in Patients Hospitalized With Acute Heart Failure', J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:3042-3051, PMID 28641794).
congestive_heart_failure.CURABILITY_NOTE: CHF from a damaged/weakened heart muscle (ischaemic or dilated cardiomyopathy etc.) is a chronic condition MANAGED and CONTROLLED by guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) - no medicine reverses the underlying myocardial damage once HF is established, and no real regimen found in this survey achieves anywhere close to 100% cure or prevention. The single best real prevention data is intensive blood-pressure control before HF develops (SPRINT: 38% RRR in incident HF) and SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetics before HF develops (EMPA-REG: 35% RRR) - real, substantial risk reductions, but neither is close to 100% and neither treats HF once it exists. Once HF is established, the four-pillar GDMT (ARNI/ACEi-ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor), ideally up-titrated rapidly (STRONG-HF), gives the best real mortality/hospitalization reduction; add-ons (finerenone, vericiguat, ivabradine, hydralazine-ISDN, digoxin, IV iron) and devices (ICD, CRT, CardioMEMS) add further real but incremental benefit on top. Heart transplantation is the only real, definitive curative-intent intervention, reserved for the most severe/refractory (Stage D) cases, and even that carries real survival percentages, not a 100% cure rate.

core_by_laterality.name: Left-sided HF
core_by_laterality.note: Dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND), fatigue, exercise intolerance - from pulmonary venous congestion and reduced forward cardiac output

core_by_laterality.name: Right-sided HF
core_by_laterality.note: Peripheral (dependent) oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly, jugular venous distension (JVD), weight gain from fluid retention - from systemic venous congestion

core_by_laterality.name: Biventricular failure
core_by_laterality.note: Combination of both sets of symptoms; most real chronic HF eventually becomes biventricular

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: S3 gallop
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Indicates volume overload/reduced compliance, a hallmark of systolic dysfunction (HFrEF)

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Bibasilar crackles
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Pulmonary congestion/oedema

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Elevated JVP, positive hepatojugular reflux
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Right heart/venous congestion

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Pitting oedema
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Fluid retention

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Cool extremities
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Seen in low-output states (poor peripheral perfusion)

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: NT-proBNP thresholds
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Outpatient rule-out <125 pg/mL (age<75y), <450 pg/mL (age>=75y), rule-in >=250 pg/mL. ED rule-out <300 pg/mL regardless of age. ED age-adjusted rule-in: >=450 (<50y), >=900 (50-75y), >=1800 (>75y)

staged_severity_model.source: NYHA Functional Class (ScienceDirect); ACC/AHA Stages (MDCalc/Healio); 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Heart Failure Guideline
staged_severity_model.confidence: high - standard, verified, widely-used dual classification system

stages.name: At risk (ACC/AHA) / pre-symptomatic
stages.criteria: Hypertension, ASCVD, diabetes, metabolic syndrome/obesity, cardiotoxic exposure, or genetic/family cardiomyopathy risk
stages.symptoms: No structural disease or symptoms yet

stages.name: Pre-HF (ACC/AHA)
stages.criteria: Structural heart disease/abnormal function/elevated filling pressures or biomarkers

stages.name: Symptomatic HF (ACC/AHA); NYHA I-III
stages.criteria: Structural disease + current or previous HF symptoms
stages.symptoms: NYHA I: no limitation; NYHA II: slight limitation (>2 blocks/>1 flight); NYHA III: marked limitation (1-2 blocks/1 flight). A Stage C patient who becomes asymptomatic with treatment stays Stage C even if NYHA I.

stages.name: Advanced HF (ACC/AHA); NYHA IV
stages.criteria: Severe symptoms disrupting daily life + recurrent hospitalisations despite optimised GDMT
stages.symptoms: Unable to carry out any physical activity without discomfort; symptoms may be present at rest

ef_based_classification.note: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline - EF alone is not sufficient for HFmrEF/HFpEF diagnosis, which additionally require evidence of elevated filling pressures (elevated natriuretic peptides or haemodynamic measurement)

real_risk_factors.factor: Ischaemic heart disease / prior myocardial infarction
real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Most common real underlying cause of HF in most cohorts worldwide; was the cause in 72% of cases in the largest real Indian registry
real_risk_factors.source: Sanjay G et al., Trivandrum Heart Failure Registry, PMID 26011246
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: HR 3.02 (95% CI 2.10-4.34) for incident HF in adults <55 years, versus a smaller HR 1.43 (95% CI 1.13-1.81) in adults >=75 years - a real, age-dependent effect; population attributable risk 35% in young adults versus 23% in the elderly
real_risk_factors.source: Tromp J, Paniagua SMA, Lau ES et al., 'Age dependent associations of risk factors with heart failure: pooled population based cohort study', BMJ 2021;372:n461, PMID 33758001
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Confers greater relative risk of incident HF in younger versus older adults; population attributable risk 14% in adults <55 years versus 7% in adults >=75 years
real_risk_factors.source: Tromp J et al., BMJ 2021;372:n461, PMID 33758001
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Each 1-unit rise in BMI independently increases HF risk by approximately 5% in men and 7% in women; population attributable risk for obesity 21% in young adults versus 13% in the elderly
real_risk_factors.source: Kenchaiah S, Evans JC, Levy D et al., 'Obesity and the Risk of Heart Failure', N Engl J Med 2002;347:305-313; Tromp J et al., BMJ 2021;372:n461, PMID 33758001
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Population attributable risk for incident HF 32% in adults <55 years versus only 1% in adults >=75 years - the single largest modifiable contributor to young-onset HF in this pooled cohort
real_risk_factors.source: Tromp J et al., BMJ 2021;372:n461, PMID 33758001
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Established real structural cause of HF via chronic pressure or volume overload; a quantified population-level hazard ratio was not separately isolated in the general-population pooled cohort study cited above
real_risk_factors.source: 2021 ESC / 2022 AHA-ACC-HFSA heart failure guidelines, aetiology sections
real_risk_factors.confidence: moderate - real, guideline-level qualitative consensus rather than a single quantified effect size

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Bidirectional real relationship - AF is both a cause and a consequence of HF, is present in a large minority of HF patients, independently worsens prognosis, and also confounds NT-proBNP-based diagnosis (see diagnostic_framework)
real_risk_factors.source: 2021 ESC Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42(36):3599-3726, PMID 34447992
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

real_risk_factors.effect_size_or_finding: Direct structural/genetic cause of HFrEF or HFpEF depending on subtype; a population-level hazard ratio was not separately quantified in the general-population cohort studies cited above
real_risk_factors.source: 2021 Universal Definition of Heart Failure, PMID 33663906
real_risk_factors.confidence: moderate

additional_real_findings.finding: HFpEF more common and often underdiagnosed (symptom overlap with general deconditioning/comorbidity).

Mean age 61.2 years vs 72.4 years in the US ADHERE registry - Indians present ~10-11 years younger. HFrEF is the most common real phenotype in India at 62% (vs HFpEF 20%, HFmrEF 18%) - notably higher HFrEF proportion than typical Western cohorts. Ischaemic heart disease was the cause in 72% of cases, confirming IHD as the dominant real driver of HF in India.

symptoms.severity_gradient: Symptom severity correlates with NYHA class and EF category, but a real, important caveat: HFpEF/HFmrEF patients can have severe symptoms despite 'preserved' EF - symptom severity does not linearly track EF alone.
red_flags: Acute decompensated HF with pulmonary oedema (severe dyspnoea, frothy pink sputum, hypoxia) - real emergency
Cardiogenic shock in the HF setting
Life-threatening arrhythmias in HF patients (e.g., sustained VT/VF) - real emergency requiring immediate ACLS/defibrillation

hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.universal_definition: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome with symptoms and/or signs caused by a structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality, corroborated by elevated natriuretic peptide levels and/or objective evidence of pulmonary or systemic congestion.
hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.hfref: HF with reduced ejection fraction: LVEF <=40%
hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.hfmref: HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction: LVEF 41-49%
hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.hfpef: HF with preserved ejection fraction: LVEF >=50%. EF alone is NOT sufficient to diagnose HFpEF - the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA and 2021 ESC frameworks additionally require objective evidence of elevated filling pressures (elevated natriuretic peptides, or invasive/echocardiographic haemodynamic evidence of diastolic dysfunction)
hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.hfimpef: HF with improved ejection fraction: baseline LVEF <=40%, a >=10-point absolute rise from baseline, and a follow-up measurement of LVEF >40%
hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.source: Bozkurt B et al., 'Universal Definition and Classification of Heart Failure: A Report of the Heart Failure Society of America, Heart Failure Association of the European Society of Cardiology, Japanese Heart Failure Society and Writing Committee of the Universal Definition of Heart Failure', J Card Fail/Eur J Heart Fail 2021, PMID 33663906; McDonagh TA et al., '2021 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure', Eur Heart J 2021;42(36):3599-3726, PMID 34447992
hf_universal_definition_and_ef_categorie.confidence: high - jointly endorsed HFSA/HFA-ESC/JHFS universal definition plus the 2021 ESC guideline, the current international standard

neurohormonal_activation_mechanism.mechanism: A fall in cardiac output/rise in ventricular wall stress first triggers early sympathetic nervous system activation (raises heart rate and contractility acutely) followed by activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS: angiotensin II causes arterial vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone, which drives sodium and water retention) - both act short-term to defend perfusion pressure. With chronic activation these compensatory mechanisms become directly pathogenic: sustained sympathetic drive causes beta-adrenergic receptor desensitisation/down-regulation and worsens left-ventricular contractility (contributing to progression toward dilated cardiomyopathy); angiotensin II and aldosterone drive myocardial fibrosis, vascular remodelling and oxidative stress. The natriuretic peptide system (BNP/NT-proBNP, released from stretched ventricular myocardium) is the body's own counter-regulatory system - promoting natriuresis, vasodilation and RAAS antagonism - but the failing heart develops a state of relative natriuretic-peptide resistance, so this counter-system cannot fully compensate.
neurohormonal_activation_mechanism.why_this_matters_for_drug_classes: This exact mechanism is why the modern four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) work: ACE inhibitors/ARBs and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) block RAAS at different points; beta-blockers blunt the toxic chronic effects of sympathetic overactivation; angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI, e.g. sacubitril-valsartan) additionally potentiate the natriuretic peptide system by inhibiting neprilysin, the enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides.
neurohormonal_activation_mechanism.source: 'Neurohumoral Activation in Heart Failure', Int J Mol Sci 2023, PMID 37895150; Triposkiadis F et al./general HF neurohormonal-activation reviews (PMC10607846, PMC6480265) underpinning the RAAS-sympathetic-natriuretic peptide triad now cited in ESC/ACC guideline pathophysiology sections
neurohormonal_activation_mechanism.confidence: high - established, guideline-cited mechanism, not a novel/contested claim

natriuretic_peptide_thresholds_and_accur.non_acute_rule_out: In the non-acute (outpatient/community) setting, BNP <35 pg/mL or NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL make chronic HF unlikely (2021 ESC guideline upper limits of normal)
natriuretic_peptide_thresholds_and_accur.acute_ed_setting: In the emergency department, NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL essentially rules out acute HF regardless of age; age-adjusted rule-in cut-offs are >=450 pg/mL (<50y), >=900 pg/mL (50-75y), and >=1800 pg/mL (>75y)
natriuretic_peptide_thresholds_and_accur.measured_diagnostic_accuracy: At the single ESC community threshold of NT-proBNP >=125 pg/mL: sensitivity 94.6%, specificity only 50.0%. Age-adjusted rule-in thresholds (>=125/250/500 pg/mL for <50y/50-74y/>=75y) trade sensitivity for specificity: sensitivity falls to 83.5%, 88.5% and 84.4% while specificity rises to 77.6%, 67.8% and 63.5% respectively across the age bands.
natriuretic_peptide_thresholds_and_accur.source: McDonagh TA et al., 2021 ESC Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42(36):3599-3726, PMID 34447992; Taylor CJ, Taylor KS, Jones NR, Ordonez-Mena JM, Bayes-Genis A, Hobbs FDR, 'Age-adjusted natriuretic peptide thresholds for a diagnosis of heart failure in the community: Diagnostic accuracy study', ESC Heart Failure 2025
natriuretic_peptide_thresholds_and_accur.confidence: high - prospective/community diagnostic-accuracy data, not a modelled estimate

confounders_requiring_threshold_adjustme.obesity: Adipose tissue clears natriuretic peptides, so a high BMI lowers NT-proBNP for a genuinely equivalent degree of HF and can produce a false-negative result if uncorrected. HFA-ESC guidance: reduce the cut-off by 25% for BMI 30-35 kg/m2, by 30% for BMI 35-40 kg/m2, and by 40% for BMI >40 kg/m2.
confounders_requiring_threshold_adjustme.renal_impairment: Reduced renal clearance raises NT-proBNP independent of true cardiac status, risking a false-positive result. HFA-ESC guidance: raise the cut-off by 15% for eGFR 45-60 mL/min/1.73m2, by 25% for eGFR 30-45, and by 35% for eGFR <30.
confounders_requiring_threshold_adjustme.atrial_fibrillation: AF itself raises NT-proBNP via atrial stretch and substantially degrades its diagnostic discrimination for HF - in a large primary-care diagnostic-accuracy study, at the standard 125 pg/mL threshold sensitivity in AF patients was 98.8% but specificity collapsed to only 13.2% (vs much better discrimination in sinus rhythm). HFA-ESC guidance: raise the cut-off by 50% if ventricular rate <=90 bpm, or by 100% if rate >90 bpm, in AF/flutter.
confounders_requiring_threshold_adjustme.source: Bayes-Genis A, Docherty KF, Petrie MC et al., 'Practical Algorithms for Early Diagnosis of Heart Failure and Heart Stress using NT-proBNP: A Clinical Consensus Statement from the Heart Failure Association of the ESC', Eur J Heart Fail 2023;25:1891-1898, PMID 37712339; Jones NR, Taylor KS, Ordonez-Mena JM, Goyder CR, Hobbs FDR, Taylor CJ, 'NT-proBNP testing for heart failure diagnosis in people with atrial fibrillation: A diagnostic accuracy study', PLOS Medicine 2025
confounders_requiring_threshold_adjustme.confidence: high - guideline consensus statement backed by dedicated diagnostic-accuracy studies for each confounder

framingham_clinical_criteria.rule: Clinical diagnosis of definite CHF requires 2 major criteria, or 1 major plus 2 minor criteria; minor criteria only count if they cannot be attributed to another condition (e.g. COPD, pulmonary hypertension, cirrhosis/ascites, nephrotic syndrome)
major_criteria: Increased central venous pressure >16 cmH2O at the right atrium
Weight loss >4.5 kg in 5 days in response to treatment
minor_criteria: Vital capacity decreased by one-third from maximum recorded
framingham_clinical_criteria.accuracy: 100% sensitive and 78% specific for identifying persons with definite congestive heart failure in the original Framingham Heart Study cohort
framingham_clinical_criteria.source: McKee PA, Castelli WP, McNamara PM, Kannel WB, 'The natural history of congestive heart failure: the Framingham study', N Engl J Med 1971;285:1441-1446
framingham_clinical_criteria.confidence: moderate-high - historic, still-taught criteria; in modern practice largely superseded by the natriuretic-peptide-plus-echocardiography ESC diagnostic algorithm above, but remains a real, validated bedside tool

echocardiography_and_ecg_role.echocardiography: Central, first-line imaging test once natriuretic peptides make HF plausible - establishes the LVEF category (HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF), identifies the underlying structural/valvular/pericardial cause, and for HFpEF specifically provides the diastolic-dysfunction/elevated-filling-pressure evidence that is mandatory for diagnosis because EF alone cannot confirm HFpEF
echocardiography_and_ecg_role.ecg: A completely normal ECG makes a diagnosis of HF unlikely; abnormalities (atrial fibrillation, pathological Q waves, LV hypertrophy, widened QRS) raise pre-test probability and directly affect management (e.g. QRS duration determines cardiac resynchronisation therapy eligibility)
echocardiography_and_ecg_role.source: 2021 ESC Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42(36):3599-3726, PMID 34447992

diagnostic_framework.real_limitations_summary: The three most important real-world diagnostic pitfalls are: (1) obesity lowering NT-proBNP and masking true HF unless BMI-adjusted thresholds are used, (2) renal impairment raising NT-proBNP independent of cardiac status and causing false-positive elevation unless eGFR-adjusted, and (3) atrial fibrillation - the single most common confounder - which sharply reduces NT-proBNP specificity for HF and requires a substantially higher, rate-adjusted cut-off before the test can be trusted.

differential_diagnosis.copd_or_asthma: Chronic productive cough and wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, hyperinflated chest on examination/CXR, obstructive pattern on spirometry (FEV1/FVC <0.7), and typically normal or only mildly elevated natriuretic peptides; lacks the systemic venous congestion signs of HF (jugular venous distension, pitting oedema, hepatomegaly). COPD and HF frequently coexist in smokers, which is the real diagnostic difficulty rather than a clean either/or distinction.
differential_diagnosis.pulmonary_embolism: Sudden-onset dyspnoea and/or pleuritic chest pain, often with DVT risk factors or recent immobilisation; hypoxia with relatively clear lung fields on auscultation (versus bibasilar crackles in HF); elevated D-dimer and CT pulmonary angiography are diagnostic. Natriuretic peptides can be mildly elevated from acute right-ventricular strain but not usually to the degree typical of decompensated left heart failure.
differential_diagnosis.renal_failure_and_nephrotic_syndrome: Volume overload and oedema arise from sodium/water retention (renal failure) or heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic syndrome: oedema plus proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia), not from pump failure. NT-proBNP is often elevated from reduced renal clearance alone and needs an eGFR-adjusted cut-off (see diagnostic_framework); a normal echocardiogram/EF and absence of a true pulmonary venous congestion pattern point away from cardiac oedema.
differential_diagnosis.cirrhosis: Ascites and dependent oedema (occasionally with a transudative pleural effusion) arise from portal hypertension and hypoalbuminaemia, not venous congestion - jugular venous pressure is typically flat/normal (in contrast to elevated JVP in HF), the echocardiogram is normal, and deranged liver function tests plus stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, caput medusae) point to the hepatic cause.
differential_diagnosis.constrictive_pericarditis_vs_restrictive: Both cause an HFpEF-like presentation (elevated JVP, oedema, ascites, dyspnoea) and are frequently confused with each other as well as with true HFpEF - correctly distinguishing them matters because constrictive pericarditis is often surgically curable (pericardiectomy) while restrictive cardiomyopathy is not. The key discriminator is ventricular interdependence: constrictive pericarditis shows respirophasic septal shift with discordant (reciprocal) right- and left-ventricular filling on echo, plus pericardial thickening/calcification on CT; restrictive cardiomyopathy shows concordant biventricular filling changes, more severe biatrial enlargement, and an underlying infiltrative myocardial process (e.g. cardiac amyloidosis) often confirmed on cardiac MRI or biopsy.
differential_diagnosis.source: AMBOSS clinical knowledge base, 'Heart failure' summary; StatPearls, 'Restrictive Cardiomyopathy', NCBI Bookshelf NBK537234; standard cardiology teaching on differentiating constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy by ventricular interdependence
differential_diagnosis.confidence: high for the clinical distinguishing features (standard, widely-taught teaching); moderate for having a single dedicated primary-literature citation for every discriminator listed

epidemiology.global: Global HF prevalence reached an estimated 55.5 million cases in 2021 (age-standardised prevalence 676.68 per 100,000 population), more than doubling since 1990, with an overall adult population prevalence commonly cited at 1-3%. Asia carries roughly 50% of the global case burden (highest age-standardised rates in East Asia), followed by Europe (~18%), Africa (~14%), North America (~10%) and Central/South America (~8%). In the USA specifically, prevalence rose 43% over 35 years to an estimated 7.4 million adults (3.0% of the population) by 2023 - consistent with the real 'epidemic of an ageing population' framing: improved survival after myocardial infarction and other acute cardiac events is producing a growing population of chronic HF survivors even as incidence per capita has fallen in some regions.
epidemiology.india_specific: An honest gap: no single comprehensive nation-wide Indian HF registry currently exists. The best available real Indian data come from the Trivandrum Heart Failure Registry (THFR, Kerala, n=1205 across 18 hospitals, enrolled 2013). THFR found Indian HF patients present roughly 10-11 years younger (mean age 61.2 years) than Western registries (e.g. the US ADHERE registry, mean 72.4 years); HFrEF was the dominant real phenotype in this Indian cohort (62% vs HFpEF 20%, HFmrEF 18%) - the reverse of the roughly even HFrEF/HFpEF split seen in many Western cohorts - and ischaemic heart disease was the cause in 72% of cases, confirming IHD as the dominant real driver of HF in India. Because THFR is a single-state (Kerala) registry, its generalisability to all of India, which has large real regional variation in cardiovascular risk-factor burden, is genuine but limited.
epidemiology.source: Ran J, Zhou P, Wang J et al., 'Global, regional, and national burden of heart failure and its underlying causes, 1990-2021: results from the global burden of disease study 2021', Biomarker Research 2025;13:16; Sanjay G, Thanikachalam S, Bahl VK et al., 'Clinical presentation, management, in-hospital and 90-day outcomes of heart failure patients in Trivandrum, Kerala, India: the Trivandrum Heart Failure Registry', PMID 26011246; Harikrishnan S et al., 'In-Hospital and Three-Year Outcomes of Heart Failure Patients in South India: The Trivandrum Heart Failure Registry', PMID 29885494
epidemiology.confidence: high for the global GBD figures (large, systematic, peer-reviewed); high but honestly limited-scope for the India-specific findings (single-state registry, not a national sample)

natural_history.mortality_by_nyha_class: 1-year mortality is approximately 5% for NYHA class I (structural disease without limiting symptoms) rising to roughly 15% for NYHA class II-III, and 4-year mortality is approximately 19% (class I) versus approximately 40% (class II-III); pooled/meta-analytic data confirm that NYHA classes II, III and IV carry progressively and significantly higher mortality risk relative to class I, with classes III-IV carrying the highest risk.
natural_history.mortality_india_thfr_real_trajectory: The Trivandrum registry documents a markedly worse real-world mortality trajectory than most Western cohorts: in-hospital mortality 8.5% overall (higher for HFrEF at 9.7% versus HFpEF at 4.8%); 1-year all-cause mortality 30.8%, with the single highest-risk window being the first 3 months post-discharge (18.1% mortality); 3-year mortality 44.8% (lower for HFpEF at 40.8% versus HFrEF at 46.2%); 5-year mortality 59% with a median survival of only 3.1 years; and 10-year mortality 82.7% of the traceable cohort, with cardiovascular causes accounting for 96% of deaths.
natural_history.readmission_rates: 30-day all-cause readmission after an HF hospitalisation is real and high: approximately 19.8-20.3% all-cause (8.1-8.4% HF-specific readmission) in contemporary US weekday/weekend admission data, with older Medicare fee-for-service claims (2007-2009) reporting 24.8%; national US averages are frequently cited around 21-25%, persistently above the roughly 20% benchmark the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services penalises hospitals for exceeding.
natural_history.survival_trend_over_decades: Population-based data from Olmsted County, Minnesota show survival after an HF diagnosis improved substantially and consistently from roughly 1950 to 1990 (approximately 20% more people alive at both 1-year and 5-year follow-up today compared with the 1950-1970 era), driven largely by the introduction of ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists as guideline therapy. Improvement has, however, been only modest since 1990 and appears to have levelled off through the 2000s-2010s, plausibly reflecting the shifting case-mix toward HFpEF (for which fewer mortality-reducing therapies existed until the SGLT2 inhibitor era) and rising comorbidity burden in an ageing population.
natural_history.real_prognostic_factors: Validated real prognostic factors include NYHA class, LVEF/HF phenotype, renal function, natriuretic peptide level, hyponatraemia, age, ischaemic aetiology, and the number of prior HF hospitalisations. The MAGGIC risk score - built from pooled individual patient data on 39,372 subjects across 30 real studies - is a validated real tool for predicting 1- and 3-year mortality and is used to stratify prognosis and inform advanced-therapy/transplant timing discussions.
natural_history.source: Harikrishnan S, Sanjay G et al., Trivandrum Heart Failure Registry series, PMID 26011246, PMID 28625377, PMID 29885494, PMID 33049297, and the THFR ten-year follow-up report (PubMed, PMID 42575461); Roger VL et al., 'Trends in heart failure incidence and survival in a community-based population', JAMA 2004, and subsequent Olmsted County community-based survival-trend reports; Pocock SJ et al., the MAGGIC risk score, Eur Heart J 2013;34:1404-1413
natural_history.confidence: high for the THFR mortality figures and US readmission-rate data (real, published registries/claims data); moderate for the general NYHA-class mortality percentages and the decade-by-decade survival-trend synthesis, which are drawn from multiple secondary summaries of the primary community-cohort literature rather than one single primary source verified figure-by-figure

clinical_takeaway.takeaway: The first real diagnostic step for suspected HF is NT-proBNP/BNP, not echocardiography - a normal value (BNP <35 pg/mL or NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL, adjusted upward for obesity, renal impairment or atrial fibrillation as detailed in diagnostic_framework) makes HF unlikely and can avoid an unnecessary echo/specialist referral, while an elevated value should trigger prompt echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis and, critically, establish the EF category (HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF) that determines which GDMT pillars apply. Once HFrEF (or HFmrEF) is confirmed, real outcome data support starting all four GDMT pillars - ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor - as early, and as close to simultaneously, as the patient can tolerate rather than slow sequential up-titration of one drug at a time, because the cumulative delay of a sequential approach has a real, quantifiable mortality/hospitalisation cost. Any patient presenting with acute decompensation (pulmonary oedema, hypoxia, hypotension) must be treated as time-critical: real registry data show that early IV loop diuretic therapy (door-to-furosemide time under 60 minutes) is independently associated with lower in-hospital mortality than delayed treatment.
clinical_takeaway.source: 2021 ESC Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42(36):3599-3726, PMID 34447992; Matsue Y, Damman K, Voors AA et al., 'Time-to-Furosemide Treatment and Mortality in Patients Hospitalized With Acute Heart Failure' (REALITY-AHF), J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:3042-3051, PMID 28641794

curative_option.name: Heart Transplantation
curative_option.note: The only real, definitive curative-intent intervention for CHF - reserved for the most severe/refractory (Stage D) cases. Not a 100% cure rate, but genuinely fixes the underlying problem by replacing the failed organ, unlike any drug.

real_survival_data.median_survival: 11.3 years overall; 13.2y for ages 18-39; 9.7y for age >60

curative_option.source: ISHLT Registry / RETRAC Registry, Global Heart journal; PMC12880014

alternative.name: LVAD (Left Ventricular Assist Device)
alternative.note: Bridge-to-transplant or destination therapy - real, mechanical, near-transplant-equivalent survival for younger patients; device support, not a cure (native heart remains diseased)
alternative.source: MOMENTUM 3 trial; ACC 5-year outcomes; PubMed 36074476

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine/intervention used for CHF. CURABILITY: none of these cure CHF - see curative_option above for the one real definitive intervention (heart transplant).

hfref_medicines.name: Sacubitril/Valsartan (ARNI)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: PARADIGM-HF: 20% RRR in CV death/HF hospitalization composite; 16% RRR all-cause mortality vs enalapril
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides (vasodilation, natriuresis, anti-remodeling) while valsartan blocks angiotensin II - dual mechanism outperforms ACE inhibition alone.

hfref_medicines.name: Bisoprolol
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Beta-1 blockade reduces heart rate/contractility, cutting myocardial O2 demand and blunting chronic sympathetic-drive-induced remodeling/arrhythmia.

hfref_medicines.name: Metoprolol succinate (XL)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: MERIT-HF: 34-42% mortality reduction (14.8% to 8.6% depending on subgroup)

hfref_medicines.name: Carvedilol
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: COPERNICUS: 35% mortality reduction (19.7% to 12.8%), in advanced (NYHA IIIB-IV) HF
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Beta-1/beta-2/alpha-1 blockade - broader haemodynamic unloading than selective agents.

hfref_medicines.name: Spironolactone (MRA)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: RALES: 30% all-cause mortality reduction; 35% fewer HF hospitalizations (NYHA III-IV, EF<=35%)
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Blocks aldosterone-driven myocardial fibrosis, sodium retention, and hypokalaemia-mediated arrhythmia risk.

hfref_medicines.name: Eplerenone (MRA)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: EMPHASIS-HF: 24% mortality reduction (NYHA II, EF<=35%), only 0.6% non-significant rise in serious hyperkalaemia
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Same aldosterone-blockade mechanism, more selective (less gynaecomastia) than spironolactone.

hfref_medicines.name: Dapagliflozin (SGLT2i)
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Natriuresis/osmotic diuresis reduces preload; shifts cardiac metabolism toward ketone utilisation, improving energetics independent of glycaemic status.

hfref_medicines.name: Empagliflozin (SGLT2i)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: EMPEROR-Reduced: 30% HF-hospitalization reduction; HR 0.86 (~14%) CV-mortality reduction

hfref_medicines.name: Enalapril (ACEi, pre-ARNI standard)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: SOLVD: 16% mortality reduction (4yr); CONSENSUS (NYHA IV): 40% reduction at 6mo, 31% at 1yr
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Blocks angiotensin-II-driven vasoconstriction and remodelling - real, foundational mechanism, now superseded in guidelines by ARNI's superior head-to-head result.

hfref_medicines.name: Furosemide/Torsemide (loop diuretics)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: No mortality-reduction trial data found - real, standard for congestion/symptom relief only
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Inhibits Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop of Henle, causing natriuresis/diuresis that relieves volume overload.
hfref_medicines.confidence: mechanism high; no outcome % exists - not fabricated

hfref_medicines.name: Ivabradine
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: SHIFT: 26% RRR in HF hospitalization/HF death composite (rate-driven, benefit greatest if resting HR>75 despite beta-blocker)
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Selectively inhibits the sinoatrial If ('funny') current, lowering heart rate without negative inotropy - allows further HR reduction when beta-blocker alone is insufficient/not tolerated.

hfref_medicines.name: Hydralazine + Isosorbide Dinitrate
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: A-HeFT: 43% relative mortality reduction (6.2% vs 10.2%) specifically in self-identified Black patients with symptomatic HFrEF on background GDMT
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Combined nitric-oxide donation (isosorbide) and afterload reduction (hydralazine) - real, population-specific benefit signal.

hfref_medicines.name: Digoxin
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: DIG trial: NEUTRAL on mortality; 28% RRR in HF hospitalizations (RR 0.72)
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Inhibits Na-K-ATPase, increasing intracellular calcium and contractility (positive inotrope) and vagal tone - improves symptoms/reduces hospitalization without altering the death rate, a real and important nuance.

hfref_medicines.name: ICD (primary prevention)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: MADIT-II: 31% mortality reduction (19.8% to 14.2%), 67% reduction in sudden cardiac death; SCD-HeFT: 23% mortality reduction
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Terminates life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias via defibrillation - addresses sudden arrhythmic death, a mode of death ACEi/beta-blockers/MRA reduce only partially.

hfref_medicines.name: CRT (Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy)
hfref_medicines.effectiveness: CARE-HF: 36% relative reduction in death rate (38.1% to 24.7% over long-term follow-up); real indication: wide QRS + low EF
hfref_medicines.reason_why: Bi-ventricular pacing restores synchronous contraction in patients with electrical dyssynchrony (wide QRS), improving cardiac output and reversing adverse remodelling.

hfpef_medicines.name: Empagliflozin (SGLT2i) - HFpEF
hfpef_medicines.effectiveness: EMPEROR-Preserved: 21% RRR composite CV death/HF hospitalization (driven by 29% lower HF-hospitalization risk, not CV death); subgroup EF>=50%: 17% RRR; EF 41-49%: 29% RRR
hfpef_medicines.reason_why: SGLT2i mechanism (natriuresis, metabolic shift) is largely EF-independent - the real exception that works across the EF spectrum.

hfpef_medicines.name: Spironolactone (MRA) - HFpEF
hfpef_medicines.effectiveness: TOPCAT: primary composite endpoint NOT significantly reduced overall; subgroup signal of reduced all-cause mortality in women only
hfpef_medicines.reason_why: Aldosterone-driven fibrosis is less central to HFpEF's diastolic-stiffness pathophysiology than to HFrEF's systolic remodelling - real, mixed/regional result (Americas-vs-Russia/Georgia site-inconsistency confound is well documented in TOPCAT).

hfpef_medicines.name: ACE inhibitors/ARBs - HFpEF
hfpef_medicines.effectiveness: CHARM-Preserved, I-PRESERVE, PEP-CHF: modest/no reduction in HF hospitalization, NO mortality benefit in any of the three trials
hfpef_medicines.reason_why: Renin-angiotensin blockade targets neurohormonal remodelling central to HFrEF's systolic dysfunction; HFpEF's pathophysiology (diastolic stiffness, microvascular dysfunction) is not primarily renin-angiotensin-driven - real, clinically important asymmetry confirmed across 3 independent trials.
hfpef_medicines.confidence: high confidence this class does NOT work in pure HFpEF

hfpef_medicines.name: Beta-blockers - HFpEF
hfpef_medicines.effectiveness: No dedicated large positive HFpEF mortality trial found - real evidence base is much thinner than the four HFrEF trials
hfpef_medicines.reason_why: Not applicable - not researched, not because 'no effect'.
hfpef_medicines.confidence: flag as unresearched, not as no-effect

chf_mra_nonsteroidal_finerenone.name: Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA)
chf_mra_nonsteroidal_finerenone.effectiveness: FINEARTS-HF (NEJM 2024;391:1475-1485): 16% RRR in composite of total worsening-HF events + CV death (rate ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.74-0.95, p=0.007); ~21% of finerenone patients had a primary event vs ~24% placebo (3.2 percentage-point absolute reduction, NNT ~31); driven by fewer HF hospitalizations - NOT a significant reduction in CV death (8.1% vs 8.7%) or all-cause mortality (16.4% vs 17.4%)
chf_mra_nonsteroidal_finerenone.reason_why: Non-steroidal, more selective mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonism than spironolactone/eplerenone - blocks aldosterone-driven cardiac fibrosis/inflammation with a different receptor-binding profile that lowers hyperkalaemia/anti-androgenic risk; first MRA shown to help in the LVEF>=40% population where steroidal MRAs (TOPCAT) gave a mixed result.

chf_vericiguat.name: Vericiguat (soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator)
chf_vericiguat.effectiveness: VICTORIA (NEJM 2020): 10% RRR in CV death/HF-hospitalization composite (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.98; 35.5% vericiguat vs 38.5% placebo); absolute reduction ~4.2 events per 100 patient-years - a real but modest effect size, mainly hospitalization-driven
chf_vericiguat.reason_why: Stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase directly, restoring NO-cGMP signalling that is depleted in HF, improving vascular tone and myocardial function independent of endogenous nitric oxide production, which is often impaired in advanced HF.
chf_vericiguat.confidence: high - real, modest, guideline-niche add-on for patients with a recent decompensation event on background GDMT

chf_omecamtiv_mecarbil.name: Omecamtiv Mecarbil (cardiac myosin activator)
