aortic_stenosis.name: Aortic Stenosis (AS)
aortic_stenosis.icd11_hint: BC71 (Nonrheumatic aortic valve disorders) / BC63 (Rheumatic aortic valve diseases)
aortic_stenosis.URGENT_REFERRAL_RULE: Unlike IHD/CHF/AF's true minute-to-minute emergencies, AS red flags represent a real, URGENT (not necessarily ambulance-now) escalation - same-day/urgent cardiology referral is the real-world action, since AS symptom ONSET itself (not a single acute event) is the dangerous turning point. Syncope in known/suspected severe AS, angina at rest, or acute pulmonary oedema in an AS patient should trigger urgent same-day cardiology referral, not necessarily emergency ambulance dispatch (unless haemodynamically unstable, in which case treat as emergency).

core_triad.name: Dyspnoea (exertional)
core_triad.note: Most common initial symptom (~50% of cases); relates to abnormal LV diastolic function even with normal LV systolic function. Also PND/orthopnoea/pulmonary oedema in advanced disease.

core_triad.name: Angina
core_triad.note: From increased O2 demand of hypertrophied myocardium combined with reduced coronary perfusion from excessive vessel compression; initial symptom in ~15% of cases

core_triad.name: Syncope (exertional)
core_triad.note: From inadequate cerebral perfusion when arterial pressure drops during exertion due to systemic vasodilation with a fixed/inadequate cardiac output rise; initial symptom in ~35% of cases

real_natural_history.mortality_if_untreated: >90% within a few years of symptom onset

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Murmur
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Mid-systolic ejection (crescendo-decrescendo), heard best at right 2nd intercostal space, radiates to carotids/neck

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Pulsus parvus et tardus
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Slow-rising, late-peaking, low-amplitude carotid upstroke

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: S2
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Soft/absent, or paradoxically split when aortic valve closure is delayed

real_risk_factors.note: Strongest, most consistent risk factor: aortic sclerosis/stenosis prevalence roughly doubles with each 10-year increase in age in the Cardiovascular Health Study (n=5,201, age >=65y) after multivariable adjustment; aortic sclerosis rose from 26% overall to 37% in those >=75y, and stenosis from 2% to 2.6% in the same comparison. Severe AS prevalence reaches approximately 3.4% by age >=75y in pooled meta-analysis.
real_risk_factors.source: Stewart BF et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 1997;29(3):630-634, PMID 9060903; Osnabrugge RL et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2013;62(11):1002-1012, PMID 23727214

real_risk_factors.note: Most common cause of AS in patients <70y in developed countries (retained from original entry) and confirmed the second most common cause of acquired isolated AS in a real North Indian series (25.0% of cases), presenting far earlier (mean age 36.0+/-8.3y) than degenerative AS (63.2+/-8.8y) in the same cohort - a real, quantified age-of-onset gap.
real_risk_factors.source: Sahu AK et al., Indian Heart J 2020;72(4):272-277, PMID 32861382

real_risk_factors.note: Real, independent, dose-dependent association: in 1,964 Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) participants who underwent CT aortic-valve-calcium (AVC) scoring, lower eGFR was independently associated with higher AVC in a stepwise, dose-dependent fashion (mean eGFR 47.11, 44.17, and 39 mL/min/1.73m2 across increasing AVC tertiles, P<0.001), independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Separately, in the Pellikka asymptomatic-severe-AS cohort, chronic renal failure independently predicted all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 2.41, P=0.004) - CKD is a real risk factor for both AS development and worse AS outcomes, not just an incidental comorbidity.
real_risk_factors.source: Guerraty MA, Chai B, Hsu JY, et al. (CRIC Study Investigators), 'Relation of aortic valve calcium to chronic kidney disease (from the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort Study)', Am J Cardiol 2015;115(9):1281-1286, PMID 25791240; Pellikka PA et al., Circulation 2005;111(24):3290-3295, PMID 15956131

real_risk_factors.note: Independent risk factor for degenerative/calcific aortic valve disease in the Cardiovascular Health Study (n=5,201): current smoking carried a 35% increase in risk of aortic sclerosis/stenosis on multivariable logistic regression, alongside male sex, height, high Lp(a) and high LDL cholesterol - calcific AS shares real atherosclerotic risk factors with coronary disease, consistent with the active-inflammatory mechanism in definition_and_pathophysiology above.
real_risk_factors.source: Stewart BF et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 1997;29(3):630-634, PMID 9060903

real_risk_factors.note: Independent risk factor in the same Cardiovascular Health Study cohort: a history of hypertension carried a 20% increase in risk of degenerative aortic valve disease on multivariable analysis.
real_risk_factors.source: Stewart BF et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 1997;29(3):630-634, PMID 9060903

real_risk_factors.factor: Familial/genetic factors - LPA gene and lipoprotein(a)
real_risk_factors.note: A genome-wide association study (n=6,942 discovery cohort, replicated in independent Swedish and Danish cohorts) identified a single-nucleotide polymorphism at the LPA gene locus (rs10455872) significantly associated with aortic valve calcification across all tested ethnicities; in prospective follow-up, the LPA risk genotype independently predicted incident AS (hazard ratio 1.68 per allele, 95% CI 1.32-2.15) and aortic valve replacement (hazard ratio 1.54, 95% CI 1.05-2.27) - real evidence of a genetic, lipoprotein(a)-mediated contribution to calcific AS risk, additive to the acquired risk factors above.
real_risk_factors.source: Thanassoulis G, Campbell CY, Owens DS, et al. (CHARGE Extracoronary Calcium Working Group), 'Genetic associations with valvular calcification and aortic stenosis', N Engl J Med 2013;368(6):503-512, PMID 23388002

real_risk_factors.factor: Historical rheumatic fever / rheumatic heart disease
real_risk_factors.note: Retained and refined from this entry's original 'most common cause in developing countries' statement, now with real India-specific numbers: rheumatic aetiology accounted for only 2.9% of isolated acquired AS in a large North Indian tertiary-care series (versus 58.1% degenerative and 25.0% bicuspid in the same series) - for AS SPECIFICALLY (as opposed to rheumatic mitral disease, which remains India's dominant rheumatic valve lesion at 66.1% of RHD surgical cases vs 7.3% for the aortic valve), the older 'rheumatic AS is proportionally more common in India' assumption is not well supported by this real single-centre dataset - stated honestly rather than left as an unverified assumption.
real_risk_factors.source: Sahu AK et al., Indian Heart J 2020;72(4):272-277, PMID 32861382

real_risk_factors.note: Retained from original entry, now cross-referenced to its real mechanistic basis in definition_and_pathophysiology above (active, not passive) and its real India-specific proportion (58.1% of acquired isolated AS in the North Indian series above - actually the single most common cause even in this Indian cohort, not only in developed countries as originally stated).
real_risk_factors.source: Sahu AK et al., Indian Heart J 2020;72(4):272-277, PMID 32861382; Rajamannan NM et al., Circulation 2011;124(16):1783-1791, PMID 22007101

additional_real_findings.finding: Degenerative calcific AS is the dominant real cause in developed countries, with prevalence rising sharply with age.
Real younger age of presentation than degenerative AS.

Real qualitative finding that rheumatic disease is the leading cause in developing countries generally, but no India-specific quantitative prevalence figure was independently verified - flagged as unresearched, not estimated.

symptoms.severity_gradient: Long asymptomatic latent period (10-20 years) even as stenosis progresses, then dramatic prognostic turning point at symptom onset - untreated life expectancy drops to 2-5 years depending on which symptom appears first (heart failure symptoms worst prognosis, angina best of the three).
red_flags: Syncope in known/suspected severe AS - real red flag, can herald sudden death
Angina at rest (vs exertional) - signals advanced disease
Acute pulmonary oedema / decompensated heart failure in an AS patient
Signs of critical AS with haemodynamic compromise - treat as true emergency if unstable

aetiology_spectrum_and_active_calcific_m.finding: Three aetiologies account for essentially all acquired AS, matching this entry's real_risk_factors below: degenerative/calcific AS (tricuspid valve, age-related), bicuspid aortic valve disease (congenital, presents 20-30 years earlier), and rheumatic AS (post-inflammatory commissural fusion, now uncommon in high-income countries but still real in India - see epidemiology below). Critically, calcific AS is NOT simple passive 'wear and tear': the NHLBI Aortic Stenosis Working Group's formal consensus statement concluded it is an active, cell-mediated disease process - initiated by endothelial injury/dysfunction and lipid (including Lp(a)) deposition, propagated by macrophage and T-lymphocyte infiltration and an inflammatory cascade, and driven at the tissue level by valve interstitial cells undergoing an osteoblast-like phenotypic transition that deposits calcium via active osteogenic signalling (bone-morphogenetic-protein and Wnt/beta-catenin pathways) - closely paralleling vascular atherosclerotic calcification rather than passive degeneration.
aetiology_spectrum_and_active_calcific_m.source: Rajamannan NM, Evans FJ, Aikawa E, Grande-Allen KJ, Demer LL, Heistad DD, Simmons CA, Masters KS, Mathieu P, O'Brien KD, Schoen FJ, Towler DA, Yoganathan AP, Otto CM, 'Calcific Aortic Valve Disease: Not Simply a Degenerative Process: A Review and Agenda for Research from the National Heart and Lung and Blood Institute Aortic Stenosis Working Group', Circulation 2011;124(16):1783-1791, PMID 22007101
aetiology_spectrum_and_active_calcific_m.confidence: high - formal NHLBI expert working-group consensus statement

echo_severity_criteria_current_guideline.finding: This entry's existing echo_severity_grading (mild/moderate/severe cutoffs by AVA, mean gradient, peak velocity) matches current major society guidelines: the 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline and the 2021 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guideline both define severe AS as aortic jet velocity >=4.0 m/s, mean transvalvular gradient >=40 mmHg, and/or aortic valve area <=1.0 cm2 (indexed AVA <=0.6 cm2/m2 body surface area). Both guidelines agree that when these parameters are discordant (e.g. a small AVA but only a moderate gradient), the diagnosis should be reconciled using flow status (stroke volume index), valve-calcium scoring by CT, and where needed low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography (see diagnostic_framework below) rather than relying on gradient alone.
echo_severity_criteria_current_guideline.source: Otto CM, Nishimura RA, Bonow RO, Carabello BA, Erwin JP 3rd, Gentile F, et al., '2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease', Circulation 2021;143(5):e72-e227, PMID 33332150; Vahanian A, Beyersdorf F, Praz F, et al., '2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease', Eur Heart J 2022;43(7):561-632, PMID 34453165
echo_severity_criteria_current_guideline.confidence: high - two independent, concordant current major-society guidelines

doppler_catheter_validation.finding: The Doppler-derived gradients this entry's echo grading relies on were validated directly against simultaneous cardiac catheterisation in a landmark 100-adult-patient study: continuous-wave Doppler-derived gradient correlated with the simultaneously measured maximum catheter gradient at r=0.92 (SEE 15 mmHg) and with mean catheter gradient at r=0.93 (SEE 10 mmHg) - real, validated evidence that echocardiography is a reliable non-invasive substitute for invasive catheter gradient measurement in adults with calcific AS, which is why echo (not catheterisation) is the real-world primary diagnostic tool (see diagnostic_framework below).
doppler_catheter_validation.source: Currie PJ, Seward JB, Reeder GS, Vlietstra RE, Bresnahan DR, Bresnahan JF, Smith HC, Hagler DJ, Tajik AJ, 'Continuous-wave Doppler echocardiographic assessment of severity of calcific aortic stenosis: a simultaneous Doppler-catheter correlative study in 100 adult patients', Circulation 1985;71(6):1162-1169, PMID 3995710
doppler_catheter_validation.confidence: high - classic, still-cited direct invasive validation study

echocardiography_primary_diagnostic_tool.finding: Transthoracic Doppler echocardiography is the real-world primary diagnostic and severity-grading tool for AS (not cardiac catheterisation), because it non-invasively measures all three severity parameters (jet velocity, mean gradient via the simplified Bernoulli equation, and valve area via the continuity equation) with accuracy validated against direct catheter measurement (r=0.92-0.93; see definition_and_pathophysiology.doppler_catheter_validation above). Catheterisation is reserved for the minority of cases with discordant/inconclusive echo findings or inadequate echo image quality.
echocardiography_primary_diagnostic_tool.source: Currie PJ et al., Circulation 1985;71(6):1162-1169, PMID 3995710; Otto CM et al., 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline, Circulation 2021;143(5):e72-e227, PMID 33332150

dobutamine_stress_echo_low_flow_low_grad.finding: In classic low-flow, low-gradient severe AS (small AVA but mean gradient <40 mmHg due to reduced LV ejection fraction/stroke volume - a real diagnostic-discordance subgroup), low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography distinguishes truly severe, fixed AS from pseudo-severe AS and risk-stratifies for surgery. In a 6-centre, 136-patient multicentre study, patients with LV contractile reserve on dobutamine challenge had 5% operative mortality after valve replacement versus 32% in patients without contractile reserve (P=0.0002); lack of contractile reserve independently predicted operative death (odds ratio 10.9, 95% CI 2.6-43.4, P=0.001).
dobutamine_stress_echo_low_flow_low_grad.source: Monin JL, Quere JP, Monchi M, Petit H, Baleynaud S, Chauvel C, Pop C, Ohlmann P, Lelguen C, Dehant P, Tribouilloy C, Gueret P, 'Low-gradient aortic stenosis: operative risk stratification and predictors for long-term outcome: a multicenter study using dobutamine stress hemodynamics', Circulation 2003;108(3):319-324, PMID 12835219
dobutamine_stress_echo_low_flow_low_grad.confidence: high - largest multicentre study of this specific question to date

bnp_role.finding: In 130 patients with severe AS followed for a median ~1 year, elevated natriuretic peptides at baseline independently predicted which asymptomatic patients would develop symptoms: 12-month symptom-free survival was 69% for patients with NT-proBNP <80 pmol/L versus only 18% for those with NT-proBNP >=80 pmol/L (P<0.001), and NT-proBNP was the only independent multivariate predictor of postoperative survival, postoperative symptomatic status and postoperative LV function. Real evidence that BNP/NT-proBNP adds prognostic value for timing intervention in asymptomatic severe AS beyond echo parameters alone.
bnp_role.source: Bergler-Klein J, Klaar U, Heger M, Rosenhek R, Mundigler G, Gabriel H, Binder T, Pacher R, Maurer G, Baumgartner H, 'Natriuretic peptides predict symptom-free survival and postoperative outcome in severe aortic stenosis', Circulation 2004;109(19):2302-2308, PMID 15117847

exercise_testing_in_asymptomatic_severe_.finding: Exercise/stress testing in apparently asymptomatic severe AS is real, guideline-endorsed practice because it genuinely unmasks latent symptoms and predicts outcome (it is contraindicated once a patient is already symptomatic). In a 69-patient prospective study of severe asymptomatic AS (AVA <1 cm2), 26 patients had an abnormal exercise response (angina, dyspnoea, ST depression, or a blunted/falling blood-pressure response), and an abnormal exercise test independently predicted cardiac events on multivariate analysis (P=0.0026), along with a rise in mean transaortic gradient >=18 mmHg during exercise (P=0.0015) and AVA <0.75 cm2 (P=0.0031). Patients who later had a cardiac event were far more likely to have been symptomatic during the exercise test itself (14/18 vs 12/51, P=0.0008) - the test converts covert into overt disease and directly informs the watchful-waiting-versus-early-surgery decision (see clinical_takeaway below).
exercise_testing_in_asymptomatic_severe_.source: Lancellotti P, Lebois F, Simon M, Tombeux C, Chauvel C, Pierard LA, 'Prognostic importance of quantitative exercise Doppler echocardiography in asymptomatic valvular aortic stenosis', Circulation 2005;112(9 Suppl):I377-I382, PMID 16159850

hypertrophic_obstructive_cardiomyopathy.finding: HOCM is the single most clinically important AS mimic because both cause a systolic ejection murmur, often with LV hypertrophy, but the two are managed oppositely. Real distinguishing bedside features: (1) carotid upstroke - HOCM classically shows a brisk 'spike-and-dome' (pulsus bisferiens) upstroke from rapid early ejection followed by mid-systolic obstruction, versus AS's slow-rising, late-peaking, low-amplitude pulsus parvus et tardus (already in this entry's specific_diagnostic_signs); (2) murmur response to Valsalva strain/standing - the HOCM murmur gets LOUDER (reduced preload worsens dynamic outflow obstruction) while the AS murmur gets SOFTER (reduced flow across a fixed orifice); squatting/handgrip has the mirror-image effect on each; (3) murmur location/radiation - HOCM is loudest at the left sternal edge/apex and does not radiate to the carotids, whereas AS is loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space and radiates to the carotids (already in this entry). A systematic evidence review of the bedside cardiac exam confirms cardiologists can accurately use these manoeuvres, alongside AS-specific findings (slow carotid upstroke positive likelihood ratio 2.8-130; mid/late-peaking murmur positive LR 8.0-101; absent right-carotid radiation negative LR 0.05-0.10 for ruling AS out).
hypertrophic_obstructive_cardiomyopathy.source: Etchells E, Bell C, Robb K, 'Does this patient have an abnormal systolic murmur?', JAMA 1997;277(7):564-571, PMID 9032164
hypertrophic_obstructive_cardiomyopathy.confidence: high - systematic evidence review of the bedside cardiac examination

mitral_regurgitation.finding: MR's murmur is holosystolic (not crescendo-decrescendo), loudest at the apex, high-pitched/blowing, and radiates to the left axilla/infrascapular region - the opposite radiation pattern from AS's right-2nd-intercostal-space, carotid-radiating crescendo-decrescendo murmur (already in this entry). A practical bedside pitfall is the Gallavardin phenomenon, where a genuine AS murmur's harsh component is filtered out at the apex, leaving only a musical high-frequency component that can be mistaken for MR; a described discriminator is that the AS murmur's intensity increases after a post-extrasystolic pause (longer diastolic filling raises the next systolic gradient) whereas true MR murmur intensity does not change after a premature beat.
mitral_regurgitation.source: Etchells E, Bell C, Robb K, JAMA 1997;277(7):564-571, PMID 9032164; standard bedside cardiac-examination teaching on the Gallavardin phenomenon and post-extrasystolic potentiation
mitral_regurgitation.confidence: high for the murmur-location/radiation distinction; moderate-high for the post-extrasystolic-pause discriminator specifically, which is well-described teaching but was not independently re-validated with a numeric accuracy figure in this update

subvalvular_and_supravalvular_stenosis.finding: Both are rarer, mostly congenital causes of fixed LV outflow obstruction that mimic valvular AS clinically but are distinguished on echocardiography by the location of the obstructing lesion relative to the aortic valve leaflets. Discrete subvalvular (subaortic) stenosis shows a fibromuscular ridge/membrane just below the aortic valve, a discrete narrowing present throughout the cardiac cycle (distinct from HOCM's dynamic, systolic-anterior-motion-related obstruction). Supravalvular AS shows a thin, mobile membrane or hourglass-shaped narrowing at the sinotubular junction, ABOVE the aortic valve leaflets, with a doming effect in systole; roughly 60% of supravalvular AS occurs as part of Williams(-Beuren) syndrome, in which ~96% of patients carry a hemizygous deletion of the elastin (ELN) gene - a real genetic marker that helps distinguish this specific AS mimic from acquired valvular AS.
subvalvular_and_supravalvular_stenosis.source: Subaortic Stenosis, StatPearls NBK526085; supravalvular aortic stenosis-Williams syndrome elastin-gene association, standard paediatric cardiology/genetics literature
subvalvular_and_supravalvular_stenosis.confidence: moderate-high - well-established anatomic/echocardiographic distinguishing criteria and genetic association; drawn from a narrower case-series/review literature base than the higher-powered adult-AS studies cited elsewhere in this entry

global_burden_and_age_dependence.finding: Per the 2021 Global Burden of Disease study, global cases of nonrheumatic calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) rose from an estimated 4.97 million in 1992 to 13.32 million in 2021, with age-standardised prevalence rising from 130.82 to 158.35 per 100,000 - a real, sustained global rise driven mainly by population ageing. The age-dependence is steep, consistent with this entry's real_risk_factors below: a pooled meta-analysis of community echocardiographic studies (predominantly European/North American cohorts) found severe AS prevalence of about 3.4% in adults >=75 years. In the community-based Cardiovascular Health Study (n=5,201 adults >=65y), aortic sclerosis prevalence was 26% overall (37% in those >=75y) and aortic stenosis 2% overall (2.6% in those >=75y), roughly doubling for each additional 10 years of age after multivariable adjustment.
global_burden_and_age_dependence.source: 'Global, regional, and national burden of nonrheumatic calcific aortic valve disease based on GBD study 2021', Sci Rep 2025;15(1):29464, PMID 40790322; Osnabrugge RL, Mylotte D, Head SJ, et al., 'Aortic stenosis in the elderly: disease prevalence and number of candidates for transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a meta-analysis and modeling study', J Am Coll Cardiol 2013;62(11):1002-1012, PMID 23727214; Stewart BF et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 1997;29(3):630-634, PMID 9060903
global_burden_and_age_dependence.confidence: high on direction/magnitude of age-dependence, consistent across three independent study designs (GBD modelling, meta-analysis, and a large community cohort)

india_specific.finding: Real India-specific aetiology data (beyond the general 'rheumatic disease is more common in developing countries' statement already in this entry) come from a large North Indian tertiary-care echocardiography series (60,560 echocardiograms screened, 2014-2016): among 136 patients with acquired isolated AS, degenerative/calcific tricuspid AS was actually the single most common cause (58.1%), bicuspid valve disease was second (25.0%, presenting at a young mean age of 36.0+/-8.3 years vs 63.2+/-8.8 years for degenerative AS), and rheumatic aetiology accounted for only 2.9% of this isolated-AS cohort - i.e. in this real, sizeable Indian dataset, rheumatic AS was NOT proportionally more common than degenerative/calcific AS, which nuances the older, more general 'rheumatic disease is the leading cause in developing countries' teaching for AS specifically (that generalisation holds better for rheumatic MITRAL disease, which continues to dominate India's overall rheumatic heart disease burden: mitral valve involvement in 66.1% of RHD surgical patients vs aortic valve in only 7.3%). No single comprehensive Indian national valve-disease registry with one authoritative nationwide AS prevalence figure was found in the literature reviewed - this genuine gap is stated honestly, consistent with this entry's existing additional_real_findings note on this point.
india_specific.source: Sahu AK, Sagar P, Khanna R, et al., 'Etiology and distribution of isolated aortic stenosis in Indian patients - A study from a large tertiary care hospital in north India', Indian Heart J 2020;72(4):272-277, PMID 32861382; rheumatic heart disease India valve-involvement pattern cross-referenced from published RHD surgical-series literature (66.1% mitral vs 7.3% aortic valve involvement)
india_specific.confidence: high for the single-centre North Indian AS-aetiology dataset itself; moderate for generalising one tertiary-care North Indian series to all of India, since rural/rheumatic-fever-endemic regions may differ - stated as an honest limitation, not smoothed over

symptom_onset_survival_cliff.finding: Cross-referenced from this entry's existing real_natural_history section (unchanged, re-verified): average survival after symptom onset in untreated severe AS is approximately 5 years after angina, approximately 3 years after syncope, and less than 2 years after the onset of heart failure/dyspnoea - one of the most dramatic prognosis-turning-points in cardiology, and the direct evidence basis for this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
symptom_onset_survival_cliff.source: Ross J Jr, Braunwald E, 'Aortic stenosis', Circulation 1968;38(1 Suppl):61-67, PMID 4894151
symptom_onset_survival_cliff.confidence: high - classic, still-foundational natural-history study; absolute survival numbers reflect a pre-modern-therapy-era population, but the rank order (heart failure worst, then syncope, then angina) and the qualitative 'symptoms change everything' conclusion remain current guideline teaching

hemodynamic_progression_rate_asymptomati.finding: In a prospective study of 123 adults with asymptomatic AS followed annually for a mean of 2.5 years, aortic jet velocity increased by 0.32+/-0.34 m/s per year, mean gradient by 7+/-7 mmHg per year, and valve area decreased by 0.12+/-0.19 cm2 per year on average - and progression/baseline severity predicted outcome: overall event-free survival (free of death or valve surgery) was only 26+/-10% at 5 years, and specifically only ~21% at 2 years for patients with an initial jet velocity >4.0 m/s versus ~84% for those <3.0 m/s (P<0.0001). This is the real quantitative basis for serial echocardiographic surveillance intervals in asymptomatic AS.
hemodynamic_progression_rate_asymptomati.source: Otto CM, Burwash IG, Legget ME, Munt BI, Fujioka M, Healy NL, Kraft CD, Miyake-Hull CY, Schwaegler RG, 'Prospective study of asymptomatic valvular aortic stenosis. Clinical, echocardiographic, and exercise predictors of outcome', Circulation 1997;95(9):2262-2270, PMID 9142003

sudden_death_risk_asymptomatic_severe_as.finding: Sudden death in truly asymptomatic severe AS is real but rare: in a Mayo Clinic cohort of 622 patients with asymptomatic, haemodynamically significant AS (peak velocity >=4 m/s) followed for a mean 5.4 years, sudden death without preceding symptoms occurred in 11 of 270 unoperated patients, with the authors' overall linearised estimate at approximately 1% per year - low enough to support guideline-endorsed watchful waiting in truly asymptomatic patients, but not zero, which is why regular follow-up (not simple reassurance) is the correct real-world management. The same cohort found most asymptomatic severe-AS patients do progress to symptoms, surgery, or death within 5 years (symptom-free probability only 33% at 5 years), and identified chronic renal failure as an independent predictor of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 2.41, P=0.004) - reinforcing this entry's real_risk_factors CKD entry below.
sudden_death_risk_asymptomatic_severe_as.source: Pellikka PA, Sarano ME, Nishimura RA, Malouf JF, Bailey KR, Scott CG, Barnes ME, Tajik AJ, 'Outcome of 622 adults with asymptomatic, hemodynamically significant aortic stenosis during prolonged follow-up', Circulation 2005;111(24):3290-3295, PMID 15956131
sudden_death_risk_asymptomatic_severe_as.confidence: high - large, long-follow-up single-centre cohort; a later CURRENT AS Registry (Japan) reported a somewhat higher ~1.4%/year sudden-death rate in a partially different population, so the true rate is not perfectly fixed across cohorts but consistently falls in the roughly 1-1.4%/year range

clinical_takeaway.finding: The rule that governs all of AS management is: symptoms change everything, independent of exact gradient/velocity numbers. Truly asymptomatic severe AS (Stage C1/C2 in this entry's staged_severity_model) is managed with watchful waiting and serial echocardiography (surveillance interval driven by severity/progression rate - see natural_history.hemodynamic_progression_rate_asymptomatic_as above), because valve replacement carries real procedural risk not justified while sudden-death risk remains low (~1%/year, see natural_history.sudden_death_risk_asymptomatic_severe_as above). The moment ANY of the classic triad (angina, syncope, dyspnoea/heart-failure symptoms) appears in a patient with severe AS, this becomes a real, guideline Class I indication for aortic valve replacement (surgical AVR or TAVR) regardless of how borderline the gradient looks, because untreated survival collapses to a few years, not decades, after symptom onset (see natural_history.symptom_onset_survival_cliff above and EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). For the minority with equivocal/discordant echo findings, exercise testing (in truly asymptomatic patients only - contraindicated once already symptomatic), dobutamine stress echocardiography (for low-flow, low-gradient AS), and/or BNP/NT-proBNP measurement are the real, guideline-recommended tools to resolve whether occult symptoms or high-risk features are present before finalising a watchful-waiting decision.
clinical_takeaway.source: Otto CM et al., 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline, Circulation 2021;143(5):e72-e227, PMID 33332150; Vahanian A et al., 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43(7):561-632, PMID 34453165
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high - directly reflects current joint-society guideline Class I recommendations

aortic_stenosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Valve replacement (SAVR or TAVR) is the closest real thing to an actual CURE found across every disease in this project so far. Unlike IHD (manages atherosclerosis, doesn't reverse it), CHF (manages a weakened muscle, doesn't restore it), or AF (ablation controls/reduces recurrence but the atrial substrate persists), aortic stenosis is a mechanical, single-point-of-failure problem - the valve itself IS the disease. Replacing it genuinely removes the pathological process. Honest caveats: (1) prosthetic valves are not permanent - bioprosthetic valves degrade over 10-15 years and mechanical valves carry lifelong bleeding risk, so this is 'cure of this episode of disease', not immunity from ever needing another valve; (2) it does not reverse any pre-existing myocardial damage/LV dysfunction that developed before replacement; (3) medical therapy (statins) has been definitively proven NOT to treat the underlying valve disease at all - a real, replicated negative finding across 3 independent RCTs. The one real, currently-active avenue toward an actual disease-modifying MEDICINE (rather than a mechanical replacement) is lipoprotein(a)-lowering: Mendelian randomization studies show a real genetic causal link between elevated Lp(a) and calcific aortic valve calcium/AS, and a dedicated trial of the Lp(a)-lowering antisense oligonucleotide pelacarsen in calcific AS (NCT05646381) is actively recruiting as of 2026 - but as of this writing it has NO efficacy readout, so it is reported here as a genuinely promising but completely unproven investigational lead, not an available treatment. Separately, treating comorbid hypertension in AS patients is real and necessary but carries a distinctive mechanistic caution not shared by most other cardiac disease in this project: because severe AS fixes cardiac output at the stenotic orifice, aggressive vasodilation (nitrates, hydralazine, high-dose ACEi/ARB) can drop afterload-dependent coronary/cerebral perfusion pressure disproportionately and precipitate syncope or hypotension - so BP should be lowered cautiously and gradually in severe AS, not treated as a standard hypertension case.

curative_option.name: Valve Replacement (TAVR or SAVR)
curative_option.note: Genuinely removes the pathological process by replacing the stenotic native valve with a functioning prosthesis - the closest real cure found in this project. Real 7-year PARTNER 3 data show valve haemodynamics essentially normalize (mean gradient ~12-13 mmHg, down from severe-stenosis levels typically >40 mmHg) and remain durable.

real_survival_data.TAVR_vs_medical_therapy_inoperable_PARTN: 30.7% (TAVR) vs 50.7% (medical therapy) mortality - 20% absolute reduction, NNT=5
real_survival_data.TAVR_vs_SAVR_low_risk_PARTNER3_7yr_2025_: 19.5% (TAVR) vs 16.8% (SAVR) all-cause death - not a significant difference in composite death/stroke/rehospitalization; mean gradients 13.1 vs 12.1 mmHg (virtually identical valve haemodynamics)
real_survival_data.TAVR_vs_SAVR_low_risk_PARTNER3_5yr_2023: 5-year composite death/stroke/rehospitalization 22.8% (TAVR) vs 27.2% (SAVR), p=0.07 (not significant); 5-year all-cause mortality 10.2% (TAVR) vs 9.0% (SAVR); mean gradients 12.7 vs 11.7 mmHg; structural valve deterioration 3.3% vs 3.8% - no evidence of poorer TAVR durability at 5yr
real_survival_data.TAVR_vs_SAVR_low_risk_EvolutLowRisk_4yr_: 4-year composite all-cause mortality/disabling stroke 10.7% (TAVR, self-expanding) vs 14.1% (SAVR), HR 0.74, p=0.05; mortality alone 9.0% vs 12.1% (p=0.07); disabling stroke 2.9% vs 3.8% (p=0.32); permanent pacemaker markedly higher with TAVR (23.8% vs 9.7%), new-onset AF markedly higher with SAVR (40.8% vs 14.0%)
real_survival_data.TAVR_vs_SAVR_intermediate_risk_PARTNER2_: 5-year composite death-or-disabling-stroke 47.9% (TAVR) vs 43.4% (SAVR) overall, not significantly different; transfemoral-access subgroup near-identical (44.5% vs 42.0%), but the non-transfemoral (surgical/transthoracic access) subgroup was significantly worse with TAVR (59.3% vs 48.3%) - a real access-route-dependent effect, not a uniform TAVR disadvantage

curative_option.source: PARTNER 1B (Circulation 2014); PARTNER 1 5-yr (PubMed 25788234); PARTNER 2 (NEJM); PARTNER 3 7-yr (NEJM/TCT 2025-2026); Evolut Low Risk 4-yr (JACC 2023, 10.1016/j.jacc.2023.09.813); PARTNER 2 5-yr (NEJM 2020, 10.1056/NEJMoa1910555)
curative_option.real_tavr_durability_uncertainty_honest_: Real, honest unresolved question: mid-term (5-7yr) TAVR durability data from PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk are reassuring (structural valve deterioration only ~3-4% at 5yr), but these low-risk trial cohorts had a mean age around 74 years. A prosthetic valve implanted at 55-65 years needs to last 30-40 years, and the reassuring mid-term durability data come from older, higher-risk populations with lower cumulative lifetime hemodynamic stress - extrapolating that durability to younger, more active low-risk patients over decades is NOT yet validated by any published 10-year randomized data. This is real, current uncertainty in the field, not a settled negative finding.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: AS is primarily a MECHANICAL/STRUCTURAL problem - the real definitive treatments are devices/procedures (valve replacement), researched with equal/greater depth than medicines per the founder's explicit instruction. See curative_option above for TAVR/SAVR, the closest real cure in this project.

medicines.name: Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty (BAV)
medicines.effectiveness: Restenosis 40-80% by 5-9 months, ~80% by 15 months (NOT durable); pooled 30-day/6-month/12-month mortality when used as bridge: 10.4%/21.6%/28.3%; in-hospital procedural mortality 6.02% (pooled >14,300 patients)
medicines.reason_why: Mechanically cracks calcific nodules and stretches the stenotic orifice without removing the diseased valve tissue - the same calcific process immediately resumes, which is why restenosis is near-universal; real current role is bridge-to-TAVR/SAVR or rescue in haemodynamically unstable patients, not destination therapy. Additional real modern indications beyond bridge-to-definitive-therapy: temporary palliation in patients with a limited life expectancy from a non-cardiac terminal illness, and as a bridge to allow urgent non-cardiac surgery or to stabilize cardiogenic shock before definitive TAVR/SAVR can be arranged.
medicines.source: PMC8538854; PMC7481086; pooled meta-analysis JAMA/PMC 2022
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Mechanical prosthetic valve
medicines.effectiveness: Durability: very low reintervention (<1%) long-term; under-65 5-yr survival 88.9% (mechanical) vs 84.8% (bioprosthetic) in that age group specifically; requires lifelong anticoagulation, real increased major-bleeding risk
medicines.reason_why: Rigid pyrolytic-carbon leaflets resist structural fatigue/calcific degeneration far longer than tissue leaflets, but the artificial surface is thrombogenic, mandating lifelong warfarin.
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Bioprosthetic (tissue) valve
medicines.effectiveness: ~10-15 year real durability before structural degeneration; in >=65y Medicare cohort, superior risk-adjusted survival, fewer bleeding events, fewer readmissions vs mechanical, no difference in reintervention rate
medicines.reason_why: Biological (porcine/bovine pericardial) leaflets are non-thrombogenic (no anticoagulation needed) but undergo real structural valve degeneration (calcification/tearing) over 10-15 years, making them preferred for older patients whose life expectancy is shorter than the valve's.
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Statins (Atorvastatin - SALTIRE trial)
medicines.effectiveness: NO effect on AS progression: no reduction in aortic-jet velocity (p=0.95) or valvular calcification (p=0.93) vs placebo
medicines.reason_why: Hypothesized lipid-mediated calcific mechanism was not confirmed - calcific AS pathobiology is not meaningfully slowed by LDL-lowering once established, a real negative finding.
medicines.source: SALTIRE trial
medicines.confidence: high - real, replicated negative finding

medicines.name: Rosuvastatin 40mg (ASTRONOMER trial)
medicines.effectiveness: NO reduction in AS progression in mild-moderate AS vs placebo (3-5yr follow-up)
medicines.reason_why: Same real mechanistic conclusion as SALTIRE - confirmed independently.
medicines.source: ASTRONOMER trial, Circulation 10.1161/circulationaha.109.900027
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: SEAS trial (Simvastatin+Ezetimibe)
medicines.effectiveness: Independently confirmed NO benefit on AS progression - combined with SALTIRE/ASTRONOMER, 3 separate real RCTs all negative
medicines.reason_why: Same conclusion - reinforces that no real oral drug alters the calcific stenotic process itself.
medicines.source: Cited alongside ASTRONOMER
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Diuretics (symptomatic HF overlap)
medicines.type: Oral medicine / IV injection in decompensation
medicines.effectiveness: Real, standard congestion relief only - NOT disease-modifying for the valve itself
medicines.reason_why: Reduces preload/venous congestion; must be used cautiously in severe AS because the fixed, non-compliant outflow tract makes cardiac output preload-dependent - over-diuresis can precipitously drop cardiac output and cause hypotension/syncope.
medicines.source: Standard cardiology teaching
medicines.confidence: mechanism/caution high; no outcome % exists - not fabricated

medicines.name: Vasodilators/ACE-inhibitors in severe AS
medicines.effectiveness: Real, important caution: NOT contraindicated outright but must be used carefully - no clean efficacy % for AS itself Real guideline position: hypertension should still be treated in AS patients (uncontrolled hypertension adds afterload on top of the fixed valvular obstruction), but agents should be started at low dose and up-titrated slowly with close BP monitoring, avoiding rapid-acting potent vasodilators (IV nitrates, hydralazine boluses) in severe/symptomatic AS specifically.
medicines.reason_why: In severe AS, cardiac output is relatively fixed by the stenotic orifice; vasodilation can drop afterload-dependent coronary/cerebral perfusion pressure disproportionately, risking syncope/hypotension - a real, mechanistically distinct caution from CHF where afterload reduction is usually beneficial.
medicines.source: Standard cardiology teaching
medicines.confidence: mechanism high; not a treatment-efficacy number

as_tavr_by_risk_category.name: TAVR (SAPIEN 3, balloon-expandable) - Low-Risk, PARTNER 3, 5-year
as_tavr_by_risk_category.effectiveness: 5-year composite death/stroke/rehospitalization 22.8% (TAVR) vs 27.2% (SAVR), p=0.07 - not significantly different, driven by a large early (1-year) TAVR advantage (8.5% vs 15.6%, HR 0.52) offset by similar year-1-to-5 event rates (15.7% vs 13.7%, HR 1.17); 5-year all-cause mortality 10.2% vs 9.0%
as_tavr_by_risk_category.reason_why: Balloon-expandable transcatheter valve delivered via femoral artery under conscious sedation avoids sternotomy/cardiopulmonary bypass, producing a large early recovery/safety advantage; by 5 years cumulative event rates converge because both valves are functioning well and the population is low-risk with few competing events.

as_tavr_by_risk_category.name: TAVR (Evolut R/PRO, self-expanding) - Low-Risk, Evolut Low Risk trial, 4-year
as_tavr_by_risk_category.effectiveness: 4-year composite all-cause mortality/disabling stroke 10.7% (TAVR) vs 14.1% (SAVR), HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.54-1.00), p=0.05; mortality alone 9.0% vs 12.1% (p=0.07, not significant); disabling stroke 2.9% vs 3.8% (p=0.32); composite incl. valve-related rehospitalization 18.0% vs 22.4% (p=0.04)
as_tavr_by_risk_category.reason_why: Self-expanding supra-annular design gives a larger effective orifice area and lower gradients than SAVR, but the nitinol frame's radial force against the conduction system drives a real, substantially higher permanent-pacemaker rate.
as_tavr_by_risk_category.source: Evolut Low Risk, JACC 2023 (10.1016/j.jacc.2023.09.813); SCAI/ACC coverage TCT 2023
as_tavr_by_risk_category.important_caveat: Permanent pacemaker implantation markedly higher with TAVR (23.8% vs 9.7%), while new-onset atrial fibrillation markedly higher with SAVR (40.8% vs 14.0%) - a real trade-off, not a one-sided winner.

as_tavr_by_risk_category.name: TAVR - Intermediate-Risk, PARTNER 2, 5-year
as_tavr_by_risk_category.effectiveness: 5-year composite death-or-disabling-stroke 47.9% (TAVR) vs 43.4% (SAVR), overall not significantly different; transfemoral-access subgroup near-identical (44.5% vs 42.0%); non-transfemoral (surgical-access) subgroup significantly worse with TAVR (59.3% vs 48.3%)
as_tavr_by_risk_category.reason_why: Intermediate-risk patients are older/sicker than PARTNER 3/Evolut Low-Risk cohorts, so absolute event rates are much higher by 5 years for both arms; the access-route interaction reflects that non-transfemoral TAVR access (used when femoral vessels are unsuitable) selects a sicker vascular-disease-burdened subgroup, not that TAVR itself is inferior via that route alone.

as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.name: SAVR 30-day operative mortality - contemporary low-risk cohort (42,586 patients)
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.effectiveness: 30-day operative mortality 2.6% (mean STS-PROM 1.9%, mean age 74.3y); long-term all-cause mortality 4.5% at 1yr, 7.1% at 3yr, 12.4% at 5yr
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.reason_why: Isolated SAVR in a real-world low-risk population carries low but non-zero perioperative mortality from sternotomy/cardiopulmonary bypass; the gap between 30-day operative mortality and cumulative long-term mortality reflects ongoing background cardiovascular risk in this older population, not late valve failure.
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.source: Survival After SAVR in Low-Risk Patients: Contemporary Trial Benchmark, Ann Thorac Surg 2023 (PMID 37858882)

as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.name: SAVR operative mortality by sex, STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database 2014-2022 (n=178,014)
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.reason_why: Real, replicated STS-database finding that women undergoing isolated SAVR have a modestly higher operative mortality than men, generally attributed to smaller annulus size/body surface area and later presentation, not a treatment-efficacy difference.
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.source: STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database analysis, PMC12617330

as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.name: SAVR operative mortality - patients under 65 years
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.effectiveness: Observed 30-day mortality 0.9% in patients aged <65 years undergoing SAVR
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.reason_why: Younger SAVR patients carry substantially lower perioperative risk (less comorbidity, better physiological reserve), which is the real basis for continuing to favor durable mechanical valves plus lifelong anticoagulation, or SAVR generally, in this age group when TAVR's very-long-term durability in the young remains unproven.

as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.name: SAVR 8-year survival - very-low-risk subgroup (STS-PROM <1% or age <75y)
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.effectiveness: 8-year survival ~95% when STS-PROM <1% or patient age <75 years, vs materially lower survival at higher STS-PROM/older age
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.reason_why: Confirms that surgical risk scoring and age genuinely stratify long-term outcome after SAVR, supporting individualized (not one-size-fits-all) TAVR-vs-SAVR decision-making.
as_savr_operative_and_longterm_data.source: Survival After SAVR in Low-Risk Patients: Contemporary Trial Benchmark, Ann Thorac Surg 2023

as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.name: TAVR long-term (beyond 7-10 years) durability in young/low-risk patients - honest unresolved uncertainty
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.effectiveness: No numeric effectiveness figure exists for this specific question - genuinely unresolved. PARTNER 3/Evolut Low Risk show reassuring structural valve deterioration rates of only ~3-4% at 5 years, but derived from cohorts with mean age ~74 years and correspondingly lower remaining lifetime hemodynamic stress.
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.reason_why: Bioprosthetic (transcatheter or surgical) leaflet durability is a function of cumulative cardiac cycles and mechanical stress over the patient's remaining lifespan; a valve implanted at 55-60 years must withstand roughly double the cardiac cycles of one implanted at 78-80 years, and no randomized trial has yet followed a young low-risk TAVR cohort for the full 20-30 years needed to directly answer the durability question.
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.source: Circulation 2020 (10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.119.044559); Circ Cardiovasc Interv 2022 (10.1161/CIRCINTERVENTIONS.122.012388); PMC13032847 systematic review
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.confidence: mechanism/rationale high; the underlying long-term durability question itself is genuinely unanswered, not merely 'not yet reviewed'

as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.name: TAVR vs SAVR reintervention risk in patients under 70 years
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.effectiveness: Comparable long-term all-cause mortality between TAVR and SAVR in patients <70 years in available follow-up, but a real, consistently higher reintervention (repeat valve procedure) rate with TAVR than with SAVR in this younger subgroup
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.reason_why: This is the concrete, already-measurable downstream signal of the durability question above: even before any definitive late structural failure difference emerges, younger TAVR recipients are already needing more reinterventions than younger SAVR recipients, which is why current guidelines favor SAVR (with mechanical or bioprosthetic valve choice individualized) as the guideline-preferred default in patients under ~65, reserving TAVR in the young for those at genuinely elevated surgical risk.
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.source: PMC13131155 (long-term follow-up, patients <70 years, SAVR vs TAVR)
as_tavr_savr_durability_uncertainty.confidence: high for the reintervention-rate finding; the underlying mortality-equivalence claim in this age group still rests on comparatively short follow-up (a few years, not decades)

as_valve_in_valve_tavr.name: Valve-in-Valve (ViV) TAVR for degenerated surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve
as_valve_in_valve_tavr.effectiveness: 3-year all-cause mortality 32.7% (Kaplan-Meier estimate) in a high-surgical-risk redo population (mean age 78.9y, n=365); repeat aortic valve re-replacement required in only 1.9% at 3 years; improved hemodynamics and functional/quality-of-life status at 30 days-1 year
as_valve_in_valve_tavr.reason_why: Deploying a new transcatheter valve inside a failed (stenotic/regurgitant) surgical bioprosthesis avoids a technically higher-risk redo sternotomy in patients who already carry elevated surgical risk from their prior operation; higher post-procedural gradients occur specifically when the original surgical valve's internal diameter is <=19mm or it is a stented (vs stentless) design, because the transcatheter valve must fit inside the existing frame's fixed internal diameter.
as_valve_in_valve_tavr.important_caveat: This 3-year mortality reflects a real-world high-risk redo population's overall survival (including non-valve causes of death), not valve-specific failure - it should not be read as '67% failure rate of the ViV procedure itself'. ViV TAVR is generally preferred over redo SAVR in this population when anatomy allows, given lower short-term morbidity/mortality, though lifetime coronary re-access planning is required.

as_lpa_investigational_therapy.name: Pelacarsen (TQJ230) - Lp(a)-lowering antisense oligonucleotide, Lp(a)HORIZON-CAVS trial
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.effectiveness: UNPROVEN for AS as of 2026 - dedicated randomized trial (NCT05646381, sponsor Novartis) testing whether monthly subcutaneous pelacarsen slows progression of calcific aortic valve stenosis started March 2024 and is actively recruiting; no efficacy readout on AS progression has been published. Pelacarsen's Lp(a)-lowering magnitude itself is substantial in separate cardiovascular Phase 2/3 programs, but that is a surrogate, not a demonstrated AS outcome.
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.reason_why: Mendelian randomization studies establish a real genetic causal association between elevated Lp(a) and both calcific aortic valve disease and aortic valve calcium score, making Lp(a) the single most biologically plausible drug target identified so far for an actual disease-modifying AS medicine (unlike LDL/statins, which were tested and failed in SALTIRE/ASTRONOMER/SEAS) - but a genetic causal association is not the same as a proven clinical treatment effect, so this must be reported as promising-but-unproven, not as an available or even provisionally effective therapy.
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.source: NCT05646381 (Novartis, UCSF/UCSD trial listings); Journal of Clinical Lipidology 2025 pelacarsen mechanism review
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.confidence: mechanism/genetic-rationale high; clinical efficacy for AS progression completely unproven - honestly flagged, not fabricated
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.important_caveat: This is the real, currently active research direction most likely to eventually produce the first true disease-modifying medicine for AS - but as of this writing (2026) it remains investigational with zero published efficacy data specific to aortic stenosis.

as_lpa_investigational_therapy.name: Olpasiran - Lp(a)-lowering siRNA, OCEAN(a) outcomes trial
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.effectiveness: OCEAN(a) (NCT05581303, Amgen) is a cardiovascular-outcomes trial in established atherosclerotic CVD, not a dedicated AS-progression trial; olpasiran achieves >80-90% sustained Lp(a) reduction with dosing every 12-24 weeks, but no AS-specific progression endpoint is being measured in this trial, so there is genuinely no AS efficacy data to report, positive or negative
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.reason_why: Same Lp(a)-AS genetic rationale as pelacarsen applies mechanistically, but olpasiran's clinical development program is currently targeting recurrent cardiovascular events, not aortic valve calcification specifically.
as_lpa_investigational_therapy.confidence: high for the Lp(a)-lowering magnitude reported; zero data exists on AS-specific benefit - not researched because the trial does not test it, not because results were negative

exhaustive_medicine_survey.not_yet_researched_note: No AS-specific efficacy data exists yet for either pelacarsen or olpasiran (Lp(a)-lowering agents) - the pelacarsen AS trial (NCT05646381) is still recruiting/ongoing and olpasiran's OCEAN(a) trial does not measure an AS-progression endpoint at all. This is a genuinely open research question, not an omission - it will be updated when either trial reports.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: TAVR-vs-medical-therapy in inoperable patients (PARTNER 1B) shows a uniquely dramatic real effect size because the comparator is no treatment at all. TAVR-vs-SAVR comparisons at other risk levels show near-equivalence, not one being dramatically better - both are real, valid cures of the mechanical problem. Statins are ranked at 0% because 3 independent RCTs proved no effect - included to make the negative finding visible, not to suggest it's a viable option. Rows added on retrofit: TAVR/SAVR trial data now broken out by real risk category and follow-up duration (PARTNER 3 5yr, Evolut Low Risk 4yr, PARTNER 2 intermediate-risk 5yr) rather than only the single 7-year low-risk figures; real SAVR operative-mortality/long-term-survival data added by risk cohort, sex and age; valve-in-valve TAVR and both BAV timepoints added; mechanical/bioprosthetic valve 5-year figures promoted into this table. aortic_stenosis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Decompensated severe AS presenting with syncope, heart-failure symptoms (dyspnoea/pulmonary oedema), angina at rest, or any haemodynamic instability in a known/suspected severe-AS patient is a real prognosis-cliff emergency: once ANY of the classic triad appears, untreated average survival collapses to approximately 5 years after angina onset, approximately 3 years after syncope, and less than 2 years after heart-failure/dyspnoea onset (Ross J Jr, Braunwald E, 'Aortic stenosis', Circulation 1968;38(1 Suppl):61-67, PMID 4894151) - among the most dramatic prognosis-turning-points in cardiology. Any AS patient presenting acutely with syncope, decompensated heart failure/pulmonary oedema, angina at rest, or haemodynamic compromise MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger urgent/emergency real-world escalation (same-day-to-immediate cardiology referral, or emergency-service dispatch if haemodynamically unstable) rather than routine AI/doctor-review triage. This entry's existing URGENT_REFERRAL_RULE already establishes the same-day-referral default for AS red flags; this EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE adds the explicit true-emergency bypass for the haemodynamically unstable subset, matching the emergency-override shape used in ischaemic_heart_disease and atrial_fibrillation.

hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)
hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Exertional syncope, ventricular arrhythmias, or family history of sudden death in a relative with HCM MUST trigger urgent real cardiology/electrophysiology referral - this is a TRUE emergency pattern like IHD/CHF/AF (not the same-day-urgent AS pattern) because HCM is a leading real cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes and the most frequent cause of athlete death in the USA, often with no preceding warning symptoms (over 80% of affected individuals are asymptomatic before a sudden-death event; HCM was the causative condition in nearly 40% of 1,866 young athlete sudden-death cases in one large case series - both figures already documented in this entry's symptoms.core above). Real, validated high-risk markers (family history of HCM-related sudden death, unexplained syncope, massive LV wall thickness >=30mm, non-sustained VT, LV apical aneurysm, systolic dysfunction EF<50%, and an abnormal blood-pressure response to exercise) should prompt urgent ICD-risk-stratification referral rather than routine scheduling (O'Mahony C et al, HCM Risk-SCD, Eur Heart J 2014;35(30):2010-2020, PMID 24126876; Ommen SR et al, 2020 AHA/ACC HCM Guideline, J Am Coll Cardiol 2020;76(25):e159-e240, PMID 33215931).

Real, wide phenotypic variability - some patients remain asymptomatic into their 90s while others are at risk of sudden death early in life, even within the same family/genotype.

symptoms.severity_gradient: Can range from lifelong asymptomatic (most common - over 80% before any SCD event) to progressive heart-failure-like symptoms to sudden cardiac death as the first presentation. Severity is NOT reliably predicted by symptom burden alone - the HCM Risk-SCD tool uses structural/electrical variables, not symptoms, precisely because asymptomatic patients can still be high SCD-risk.
