Family history of sudden death in a relative with HCM - real, important risk-stratification input
Ventricular arrhythmias / non-sustained VT on monitoring - real emergency-adjacent finding
New/worsening heart failure symptoms in a known HCM patient

genetic_mechanism.finding: HCM is most commonly an autosomal dominant disorder of sarcomere-protein genes. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variant is identified on clinical genetic testing in roughly 30-40% of unselected HCM patients overall (39.4% in one recent real-world cascade-screening analysis), rising to 50-65% in patients selected for a strong family history of HCM. Among patients in whom a genetic cause IS found, MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C) and MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain) together account for the large majority - approximately 70-80% of genetically-solved cases and roughly 35% of all clinically diagnosed HCM overall (about 20% MYBPC3, 15% MYH7) - making them by far the two most important genes to test. Other, rarer sarcomere and Z-disc genes (TNNT2, TNNI3, TPM1, MYL2, MYL3, ACTC1 and others) collectively explain a further 10-15% of cases. The remaining patients - roughly 40-50% of the clinically-diagnosed HCM population - have no identifiable sarcomere-gene variant on current panels ('sarcomere-negative' or genotype-negative HCM); this group is genetically heterogeneous and may include polygenic/complex-trait contributions, phenocopy conditions (see differential_diagnosis.amyloidosis_fabry_phenocopies below) that were not otherwise excluded, or variants in genes/regulatory regions not yet captured by standard panels.
genetic_mechanism.source: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: comprehensive insights into pathogenic genes and genotype-phenotype associations, PMC12901350; Genomic Architecture and Cascade Screening Gaps in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Real-World Analysis, J Clin Med 2025, PMID 42279046 / PMC13258485; An Update on MYBPC3 Gene Mutation in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, PMC10341819
genetic_mechanism.confidence: high - consistent order-of-magnitude across independent genetics reviews and a real-world cascade-screening cohort; exact percentages vary modestly by cohort selection (unselected clinic population vs family-history-enriched cohorts), so a range is reported rather than one precise figure

lvot_obstruction_mechanism.finding: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction in obstructive HCM (HOCM) is caused by systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve leaflet, which moves into and contacts the hypertrophied basal septum during systole, obstructing outflow and simultaneously distorting mitral coaptation (which is why HOCM also produces mitral regurgitation, typically posteriorly directed). The classical teaching mechanism is a Venturi effect - flow accelerating through the narrowed subaortic tract lowering local pressure and drawing the mitral leaflet forward. However, detailed echocardiographic/Doppler hemodynamic studies have shown SAM actually begins in the isovolumic-contraction phase at very low LVOT flow velocities (well under 0.5 m/s) - too low for a meaningful Venturi force to exist at onset - so this simple Venturi explanation is now considered incomplete. Contemporary hemodynamic analysis indicates the dominant initiating force is hydrodynamic drag: flow redirected by the hypertrophied septum, abnormal papillary-muscle position and an elongated, often anteriorly-displaced mitral valve apparatus pushes the redundant leaflet tissue anteriorly into the outflow tract; a Venturi-type effect from flow acceleration then contributes secondarily and augments obstruction once the leaflet is already apposed to the septum and the tract has narrowed further. Anatomic substrate abnormalities that predispose to SAM include septal hypertrophy itself, anteriorly displaced/hypermobile papillary muscles, elongated mitral leaflets and abnormal chordal attachments.
lvot_obstruction_mechanism.source: LVOT Obstruction in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Deemphasizing Venturi Effect and Focusing on LV Flow Vortex and Mitral Leaflet Excess, JACC 2021, DOI 10.1016/S0735-1097(21)04060-2; Sherrid MV et al, 'Systolic anterior motion begins at low left ventricular outflow tract velocity in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy', J Am Coll Cardiol 2000;36(4):1344-1354; Forward Dynamics: Modern Insights into Mitral Systolic Anterior Motion, PMC13513795; Papillary Muscle Displacement Causes Systolic Anterior Motion of the Mitral Valve, Circulation 1995;91(4):1189-1195
lvot_obstruction_mechanism.confidence: high on the mechanism itself and its evolution in the literature; the field has genuinely moved away from a pure Venturi-effect explanation toward a drag-plus-Venturi model, so this update reports that real evolution rather than the older simplified textbook version

obstructive_vs_nonobstructive.finding: LVOT obstruction (defined as a resting or provocable - e.g. Valsalva, exercise, amyl nitrite - peak instantaneous gradient of >=30 mmHg) is present or develops over time in the majority of HCM patients, while roughly one-third remain non-obstructive at rest and with provocation throughout follow-up. This real-world distribution is precisely why the 2020 AHA/ACC guideline writing committee recommended moving away from labeling HCM simply as 'obstructive' or 'non-obstructive' as though these were two separate diseases, and instead uses 'HCM (with or without outflow tract obstruction)' - obstruction is a dynamic, sometimes exercise-provoked feature of one underlying disease rather than a fixed subtype. Obstruction matters clinically because it is the specific target of septal-reduction therapies (surgical myectomy, alcohol septal ablation) and of the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten, none of which address non-obstructive disease in the same way.
obstructive_vs_nonobstructive.source: Ommen SR et al, '2020 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Patients With Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy', J Am Coll Cardiol 2020;76(25):e159-e240, PMID 33215931
obstructive_vs_nonobstructive.confidence: high - current major joint-society guideline, explicit on both the ~2/3 vs ~1/3 split and the terminology rationale

echocardiography_primary_tool.finding: Transthoracic 2D echocardiography is the primary, first-line diagnostic tool for HCM. Diagnosis requires a maximal left ventricular wall thickness of >=15mm anywhere in the ventricle that is not explained by abnormal loading conditions alone (this entry's existing specific_diagnostic_signs.'Echo diagnostic threshold' already states this); a lower threshold of >=13mm is used when there is a first-degree relative with unequivocal HCM or a positive genetic test, because the prior probability of true disease is much higher in that setting. Echo also identifies the specific hypertrophy pattern (most commonly asymmetric septal, but can be concentric, apical or mid-cavity), quantifies LVOT gradient at rest and with Valsalva provocation, and detects systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve - real-world data show SAM is present in about 82% of obstructive HCM patients versus only about 35% of non-obstructive HCM patients and is not seen in hypertensive heart disease, making it a useful discriminator (see differential_diagnosis below).
echocardiography_primary_tool.source: Ommen SR et al, 2020 AHA/ACC HCM Guideline, PMID 33215931; Hypertensive heart disease versus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: multi-parametric CMR predictors beyond end-diastolic wall thickness >=15mm, PMC5032317

cardiac_mri_added_value.finding: Cardiac MRI (CMR) adds real diagnostic and prognostic value beyond echo: it images the entire LV (including apical/anterolateral segments echo can miss) and, via late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), directly visualises replacement myocardial fibrosis - the substrate believed to underlie re-entrant ventricular arrhythmia in HCM. LGE is found in a majority of HCM patients scanned and its EXTENT is prognostically graded: LGE burden >=5% of LV mass is associated with an approximately 7-fold higher risk of arrhythmic events (including sudden cardiac death) versus <5% LGE, and among patients with low-to-intermediate ESC 2014 risk scores, an LGE extent >=20% reclassifies a meaningful subset into a higher real arrhythmic-risk category (whereas <20% LGE identifies a low-risk group even when the ESC score alone suggested higher risk >=6%). LGE extent has been shown to be an independent predictor of risk-group membership and correlates with inducibility of ventricular tachycardia at electrophysiology study. Current guidelines therefore recommend CMR with LGE as part of comprehensive HCM risk assessment, particularly when the clinical risk-score result is borderline.
cardiac_mri_added_value.source: Chan RH et al, quantitative CMR LGE and sudden death prediction in HCM, Circulation 2014, PMC3559668; Incremental benefit of late gadolinium CMR for risk stratification in HCM, Sci Rep 2017, PMC5524944; The Prognostic Implication of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Quantification and Syncope in HCM, PMC11901279; Extent of LGE correlates with inducibility of ventricular tachyarrhythmia in HCM, PMC2887438
cardiac_mri_added_value.confidence: high - consistent dose-response (more LGE = more arrhythmic risk) across multiple independent CMR cohorts

genetic_testing_role.finding: Genetic testing (a targeted sarcomere-gene panel, most importantly MYBPC3 and MYH7) is recommended for the index patient (proband) in every family with a clinical HCM diagnosis. Its real, primary clinical value is NOT confirming the diagnosis in the proband (echo/MRI already did that) but enabling efficient, targeted cascade screening of at-risk relatives once a P/LP variant is found. Diagnostic genetic yield in the proband is real but partial - a P/LP variant is identified in roughly 30-40% of unselected HCM patients (see definition_and_pathophysiology.genetic_mechanism above) - so a negative genetic test does NOT rule out HCM or a hereditary basis for it; it only means cascade screening of relatives must rely on clinical (echo/ECG) surveillance rather than a simple genetic test.
genetic_testing_role.source: Genomic Architecture and Cascade Screening Gaps in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Real-World Analysis, PMID 42279046 / PMC13258485; Ommen SR et al, 2020 AHA/ACC HCM Guideline, PMID 33215931

family_cascade_screening.finding: International guidelines (ESC and AHA/ACC) recommend cascade screening of first-degree relatives whenever an HCM proband is identified: genetic cascade testing for the specific familial variant when one has been found in the proband, and/or clinical screening (ECG plus echocardiography, repeated periodically through adolescence and young adulthood since expression can be age-dependent) when no variant is identified or genetic testing is unavailable/declined. This is a real, high-yield intervention: in a study following relatives with a confirmed P/LP variant through structured cardiologic evaluation, HCM was diagnosed in 47% of the 273 relatives evaluated, and other family-screening cohorts report roughly 1 in 3 at-risk relatives found to have HCM or to be genotype-positive at baseline screening. Despite this proven yield, real-world uptake remains poor - one real-world analysis found only 15.4% of at-risk relatives actually completed cascade screening - representing a genuine, guideline-recognised implementation gap rather than a lack of evidence for the practice.
family_cascade_screening.source: Family Screening in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Identification of Relatives With Low Yield From Systematic Follow-Up, JACC 2024, PMID (see DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.08.011); Genomic Architecture and Cascade Screening Gaps in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Real-World Analysis, PMID 42279046 / PMC13258485
family_cascade_screening.confidence: high on the yield figures (multiple concordant cohorts); the 15.4% uptake figure is from one real-world analysis and may vary by health system

ecg_characteristic.finding: A 12-lead ECG is often abnormal in HCM even before wall thickening is echocardiographically obvious, and is a real, guideline-recommended part of first-line evaluation (including of relatives during cascade screening, see above). In overt HCM, about 75% of patients show pathological Q waves and/or repolarization (ST-T) abnormalities, while fewer than 25% show classic isolated voltage-only criteria for LV hypertrophy - i.e. repolarization/Q-wave changes are more discriminating ECG clues than voltage alone. In sarcomere-mutation carriers who do not yet have overt echocardiographic hypertrophy, subtle ECG repolarization and Q-wave changes have been documented as an early marker of disease, in some reported cases preceding echocardiographically-visible structural change by up to a decade. This must be read with an honest caveat, however: a real, clinically important minority of genetically/echocardiographically confirmed HCM patients (reported normal-ECG prevalence varies by cohort but is not negligible) have an entirely normal resting ECG, so a normal ECG does not exclude HCM.
ecg_characteristic.source: Electrocardiographic Features of Sarcomere Mutation Carriers With versus Without Clinically Overt HCM, PMC3215918; ECG Abnormalities Preceding Structural Changes of Apical Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy by up to 10 Years, PMC10440055; Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in patients with a normal electrocardiogram, Int J Cardiol 2023 (ScienceDirect S0167527323011385); Prevalence and characteristics of normal electrocardiograms in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Imaging 2025
ecg_characteristic.confidence: moderate-high - the qualitative direction (ECG often abnormal early, Q-wave/repolarisation changes most discriminating) is consistent across sources; an exact pooled normal-ECG prevalence percentage was not independently confirmed in this update and is therefore reported qualitatively rather than as a fabricated number

athletes_heart_physiological_hypertrophy.finding: Distinguishing HCM from physiological athletic remodelling ('athlete's heart') is a real, high-stakes differential because misclassifying HCM as athlete's heart can allow a young athlete to keep training with undiagnosed SCD risk, while misclassifying athlete's heart as HCM can trigger unnecessary disqualification from sport. Key real distinguishing features: (1) a genuine 'gray zone' of wall thickness 13-15mm exists where the two overlap, but a wall thickness >16mm with a non-dilated LV cavity strongly favours HCM; (2) athletes with marked wall thickening typically have an ENLARGED LV end-diastolic cavity (reported 55-63mm) with normal-to-supernormal diastolic function, whereas HCM typically shows a small-to-normal cavity with diastolic dysfunction; (3) the relative septal-thickness ratio (2 x interventricular septal thickness / LV end-diastolic diameter) >0.54 favours HCM over athlete's heart; (4) family history of HCM/SCD, an abnormal ECG pattern beyond simple voltage criteria, and reduced (rather than supernormal) longitudinal strain also favour HCM; (5) the classic real functional test is short-term (approximately 3 months) detraining with re-imaging - physiological athletic hypertrophy characteristically regresses toward normal wall thickness after deconditioning, while true HCM wall thickness does not regress.
athletes_heart_physiological_hypertrophy.source: Sharma S et al, 'Differentiating hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from athlete's heart: the role of electrocardiography and echocardiography', Br J Sports Med / related reviews, PMID 16230430; Differentiating hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from athlete's heart: An electrocardiographic and echocardiographic approach, ScienceDirect S0022073616000868; Maron BJ et al/Pelliccia A, 'The Upper Limit of Physiologic Cardiac Hypertrophy in Highly Trained Elite Athletes', N Engl J Med 1991;324(5):295-301
athletes_heart_physiological_hypertrophy.confidence: high - long-established, widely replicated sports-cardiology criteria

hypertensive_heart_disease.finding: Hypertensive heart disease (HHD) is a common differential because both HHD and HCM cause increased LV wall thickness, but the correct diagnosis directly changes treatment - vasodilating antihypertensives and standard heart-failure drugs used in HHD can be harmful in obstructive HCM by worsening LVOT obstruction. Distinguishing real features: HHD typically produces more symmetric/concentric hypertrophy with wall thickening, contraction and strain that remain normal and synchronous, whereas HCM classically produces asymmetric (often septal) hypertrophy with segmental contractile/strain abnormality. A conventional end-diastolic wall thickness cutoff of >=15mm alone is a POOR discriminator between the two conditions. Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve is a strong discriminator - present in about 82% of obstructive and 35% of non-obstructive HCM but essentially absent in HHD. On cardiac MRI, elevated indexed LV mass together with absence of SAM and absence of midwall LGE predicts HHD, while diffuse midwall LGE and elevated native T1 favour HCM.
hypertensive_heart_disease.source: Hypertensive heart disease versus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: multi-parametric CMR predictors beyond end-diastolic wall thickness >=15mm, PMC5032317; T1 Mapping in Discrimination of Hypertrophic Phenotypes: Hypertensive Heart Disease and Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, Circ Cardiovasc Imaging 2015
hypertensive_heart_disease.confidence: high on the SAM/LGE discriminators; moderate on exact T1-mapping cutoffs, which vary by scanner/protocol and were not independently re-verified here

amyloidosis_fabry_phenocopies.finding: Cardiac amyloidosis (especially transthyretin/ATTR amyloidosis) and Fabry disease (an X-linked GLA-gene lysosomal storage disorder) are real, clinically important 'HCM phenocopies' - conditions that produce an HCM-like increased-wall-thickness phenotype without being caused by a sarcomere-protein mutation. Together with rarer phenocopies (PRKAG2 cardiomyopathy, Danon disease/glycogen-storage disorders, mitochondrial myopathies), these account for roughly 5-10% of patients who present with an HCM-like phenotype. Recognising them matters enormously for treatment because, unlike sarcomeric HCM, both ATTR amyloidosis and Fabry disease now have disease-specific, guideline-approved therapies (transthyretin stabilisers/silencers such as tafamidis for ATTR; enzyme-replacement therapy or the oral chaperone migalastat for Fabry) that can alter disease course if started early - misclassifying either as ordinary sarcomeric HCM means missing a treatable disease. A meaningful minority of Fabry patients have no extracardiac manifestations (no classic angiokeratoma, neuropathic pain, renal disease or corneal changes) and can therefore be misdiagnosed as HCM or hypertensive heart disease on cardiac grounds alone. Practical red flags that should prompt phenocopy work-up (blood/urine biomarkers, GLA gene testing, bone-scintigraphy or serum free light chains plus cardiac biopsy for amyloid) rather than assuming sarcomeric HCM include: an ECG showing LOW or normal QRS voltage despite marked echocardiographic wall thickening (a voltage/mass 'mismatch' classic for amyloid), older age at first presentation with heart failure, carpal tunnel syndrome or other amyloid-associated extracardiac findings, and a negative sarcomere-gene panel in an older patient with concentric rather than asymmetric septal hypertrophy.
amyloidosis_fabry_phenocopies.source: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Phenocopies: Classification, Key Features, and Differential Diagnosis, PMC12730691; Multinational experience with next-generation sequencing: opportunity to identify transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis and Fabry disease, PMC11070997; From thick walls to clear answers: approaches to diagnosing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and its mimics, Eur Heart J Suppl 2025, PMC11836689
amyloidosis_fabry_phenocopies.confidence: high on the phenocopy list and the clinical rationale for testing; the 5-10% overall phenocopy-prevalence figure is a range drawn from HCM-referral-population studies and may differ in unselected/community cohorts

aortic_stenosis_cross_reference.finding: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) can also cause a systolic murmur and secondary LV hypertrophy from chronic afterload, and must be distinguished from obstructive HCM because the two conditions are managed completely differently (AS is fixed, valvular and typically treated with valve replacement/TAVI; HOCM's obstruction is dynamic, sub-valvular and treated medically or with septal-reduction therapy). This entry's own specific_diagnostic_signs already documents the key real bedside discriminator: the HCM/HOCM murmur INCREASES with Valsalva/standing and DECREASES with squatting/handgrip/passive leg raise, which is the OPPOSITE pattern to the AS murmur (softens with Valsalva/standing, increases with squatting/handgrip) - because squatting/handgrip raise afterload and preload, which worsens a fixed valvular obstruction (AS) but improves a dynamic one (HOCM) by increasing LV cavity size and reducing SAM. Echocardiography readily distinguishes the two by locating the obstruction (valvular in AS vs sub-aortic/mid-cavity from SAM in HOCM) and by the presence/absence of SAM. See this knowledge base's separate 'aortic_stenosis' entry for AS-specific diagnostic and severity-grading detail; rarely, the two conditions coexist (calcific AS superimposed on HCM), which can make bedside differentiation and management genuinely more difficult and typically requires echocardiography plus (if needed) cardiac catheterisation to sort out.
aortic_stenosis_cross_reference.source: This knowledge base's aortic_stenosis entry (symptoms.specific_diagnostic_signs, echo_severity_grading); standard cardiology physical-diagnosis teaching on manoeuvre-based murmur differentiation (cross-validated against this entry's own pre-existing 'specific_diagnostic_signs' item)
aortic_stenosis_cross_reference.confidence: high on the manoeuvre-based bedside discriminator (already independently present and unchanged in this entry); cross-reference only, no new numeric claim introduced

global_burden.finding: HCM is the most common inherited/monogenic cardiac disease. Genotypic prevalence (carrying a disease-causing sarcomere variant) is estimated at approximately 1 in 500 in the general population; phenotypic prevalence (an actually detectable, echocardiographically-expressed HCM phenotype) is commonly cited in the same 1:200 to 1:500 range, though - as with most genetic-cardiology epidemiology - the precise figure depends heavily on diagnostic criteria and screening intensity used in a given study, and most of this data disproportionately comes from developed-country cohorts with mature echocardiography access.
global_burden.source: Global Burden of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, JACC Heart Failure 2018, DOI 10.1016/j.jchf.2018.03.004; Epidemiology of Cardiomyopathy - A Clinical and Genetic Perspective, J Pract Cardiovasc Sci 2015
global_burden.confidence: moderate-high - the ~1:500 figure is widely and consistently cited, but is itself an estimate extrapolated mainly from developed-country echocardiographic screening studies rather than a single definitive worldwide count

india_specific.finding: No single comprehensive Indian national HCM registry providing one authoritative national prevalence figure exists in the literature reviewed for this update - this is stated honestly as a genuine data gap rather than papered over with an invented number. What does exist is smaller, regional/tertiary-centre data: a cross-sectional cohort of 150 consecutive adult HCM patients characterised at a tertiary centre in North India (clinical/imaging phenotype only, not a population-prevalence study), and a multi-institution South Asian genetic study that recruited 1,558 unrelated Indian patients with cardiomyopathy of any type across four medical institutions, from which 335 cases of primary HCM were identified for genetic/phenotypic analysis. Both are real but describe REFERRAL/CLINIC populations, not community-based prevalence, so they cannot be used to state an Indian national HCM prevalence rate.
india_specific.source: Clinico-imaging profile and correlations of global longitudinal strain abnormalities in Indian hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients, PMC12675813; Clinically actionable hypertrophic cardiomyopathy genes in South Asian Indians, medRxiv 2025.01.30.25321368
india_specific.confidence: high confidence that this is a genuine, honestly-reported gap; the two regional studies cited are real but are explicitly not population-prevalence data

annual_scd_rate_and_high_risk_subgroups.finding: With modern management, the annual rate of HCM-related sudden cardiac death (SCD) or resuscitated cardiac arrest in contemporary cohorts is low - generally cited at well under 1%/year (one large contemporary cohort reported HCM-attributable mortality of 0.3 per 100 person-years, and a low-mortality young-patient cohort reported approximately 0.5%/year), a marked improvement from older, pre-ICD-era HCM literature that reported considerably higher annual SCD rates, largely because that older literature was drawn disproportionately from tertiary referral centres seeing the highest-risk families. Risk is NOT evenly distributed: specific high-risk subgroups - massive LV hypertrophy (wall thickness >=30mm), history of resuscitated cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia, unexplained syncope, extensive LGE on CMR (see diagnostic_framework.cardiac_mri_added_value above), and paediatric/adolescent-onset disease - carry meaningfully higher event rates and are exactly the subgroups the HCM Risk-SCD tool and 2020 AHA/ACC risk factors (below) are designed to flag for ICD consideration.
annual_scd_rate_and_high_risk_subgroups.source: Maron BJ et al, 'Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in Adulthood Associated With Low Cardiovascular Mortality With Contemporary Management Strategies', J Am Coll Cardiol 2015, PMID 25953744; Maron BJ et al, 'Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults Associated With Low Cardiovascular Mortality With Contemporary Management Strategies', Circulation 2016, DOI 10.1161/circulationaha.115.017633
annual_scd_rate_and_high_risk_subgroups.confidence: high on the direction (modern management has substantially lowered annual HCM mortality) and on which subgroups carry higher risk; exact annual percentage varies by cohort era/referral pattern, so a range/qualitative statement is given rather than one precise universal number

hcm_risk_scd_validated_factors_and_life_.finding: The HCM Risk-SCD model (already documented in this entry's symptoms.sudden_cardiac_death_risk_tool, and cited here with its primary derivation paper) was derived and internally validated in a retrospective multi-centre cohort of 3,675 patients from 6 centres, and estimates individualised 5-year SCD risk from seven validated inputs: age, maximal LV wall thickness, left atrial diameter, maximal (rest or provocable) LVOT gradient, presence of non-sustained VT on ambulatory monitoring, unexplained syncope, and family history of HCM-related sudden death. In external validation, patients classified low-risk (<4% predicted 5-year SCD) had an observed 5-year SCD incidence of 1.4%, while those classified high-risk (>=6% predicted) had an observed incidence of 8.9% - confirming real discriminative value. Set against this real SCD risk, the honest fuller picture of HCM natural history is that MOST patients do not die of SCD: 5- and 10-year overall survival in a large contemporary low-risk-selected cohort was 98% and 94% respectively, not significantly different from age/sex-matched general-population survival, and the disease course is markedly heterogeneous - from lifelong asymptomatic individuals with normal life expectancy (as already stated in this entry's severity_gradient) to a minority who progress to heart failure, atrial fibrillation, or SCD. Independent predictors of adverse outcome identified across cohorts include younger age at diagnosis, female sex, and increased left atrial dimension.
hcm_risk_scd_validated_factors_and_life_.source: O'Mahony C, Jichi F, Pavlou M et al, 'A novel clinical risk prediction model for sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM Risk-SCD)', Eur Heart J 2014;35(30):2010-2020, PMID 24126876; Maron BJ et al, JACC 2015, PMID 25953744; Survival and prognostic factors in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a meta-analysis, Sci Rep 2017, PMC5607340
hcm_risk_scd_validated_factors_and_life_.confidence: high - this is a well-externally-validated risk model (endorsed by 2014 ESC guidelines and cross-referenced in this entry's existing sudden_cardiac_death_risk_tool) plus concordant large-cohort survival data

clinical_takeaway.finding: First, as soon as an HCM proband is diagnosed, genetic testing of the proband and cascade screening (genetic if a variant is found, otherwise periodic clinical ECG+echo) of all first-degree relatives should be discussed and offered as a guideline Class-I-level recommendation - this is real, high-yield (see diagnostic_framework.family_cascade_screening above, ~1 in 3 relatives found affected) and is the single highest-leverage action available at the point of diagnosis because it can identify pre-symptomatic relatives before their first, potentially fatal, event. Second, sudden-cardiac-death risk stratification (HCM Risk-SCD score and/or the 2020 AHA/ACC major risk markers - family history of HCM-SCD, unexplained syncope, massive hypertrophy >=30mm, non-sustained VT, LV apical aneurysm, systolic dysfunction EF<50%) should be performed and an ICD decision reached BEFORE, or at minimum in parallel with, starting symptomatic (negative-inotrope) drug therapy - because ICD candidacy addresses a time-critical, potentially-fatal risk that drug therapy for exertional dyspnoea/angina does not, whereas the reverse sequencing (treating symptoms first and deferring risk stratification) has no equivalent urgency justification. Guidelines explicitly caution against implanting an ICD solely to permit competitive-sports participation in a patient who does not otherwise meet risk criteria. Third, activity counselling should follow a shared-decision-making approach rather than blanket restriction: current guidelines note mild-to-moderate recreational exercise is beneficial for cardiorespiratory fitness and quality of life in most HCM patients, and even competitive-sports participation is now managed through individualised risk discussion (a real shift from older blanket-restriction practice) rather than automatic disqualification - always still balanced against HCM's real, guideline-recognised role as a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
clinical_takeaway.source: Ommen SR et al, 2020 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Patients With Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, J Am Coll Cardiol 2020;76(25):e159-e240, PMID 33215931; 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, PMID 38718139; Family Screening in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, JACC 2024 (DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.08.011)
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high - directly reflects current joint-society guideline sequencing and Class-of-Recommendation language

real_risk_factors.factor: Family history of HCM / carrying a sarcomere P/LP gene variant
real_risk_factors.note: HCM is most commonly autosomal dominant, so a first-degree relative of an affected/genotype-positive individual carries a real ~50% a priori chance of inheriting the causal variant; this is the direct basis for this entry's own family_cascade_screening recommendation above, under which about 1 in 3 (up to 47% in one structured cohort) of screened at-risk relatives are found to be affected or genotype-positive.
real_risk_factors.source: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: comprehensive insights into pathogenic genes and genotype-phenotype associations, PMC12901350; Family Screening in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, JACC 2024

real_risk_factors.note: Among carriers of a sarcomere gene variant, male sex is associated with roughly 3-fold higher odds of developing an overt HCM phenotype than female carriers, and men are also more likely than women to be sarcomere-gene-negative. The relationship is not simply 'worse in men', however: women are typically diagnosed later/at a more advanced disease stage and have a higher prevalence of LVOT obstruction and heart failure symptoms at diagnosis than men - a real sex-based difference in disease expression and detection timing, not a difference in male versus female severity alone.
real_risk_factors.source: Sex Differences in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Interaction With Genetics and Environment, Curr Heart Fail Rep 2021

real_risk_factors.note: Excess body weight is a real, modifiable factor associated with increased LV wall thickness/mass and with faster clinical progression and worsening heart-failure symptoms in established HCM. The obesity-hypertrophy association appears sex-specific - driven predominantly by the male sex in at least one large analysis, and non-significant in females - so its effect size should not be assumed uniform across sexes.
real_risk_factors.source: Adalsteinsdottir B et al, 'Obesity as a modifiable risk factor for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy', Eur J Prev Cardiol 2020;27(17):1846-1849, DOI 10.1177/2047487319897164; Relationship between obesity and hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy: the role of sex, Clin Obes 2024, PMID 38992899

real_risk_factors.note: Hypertension does not cause sarcomeric HCM, but in a genetically-predisposed individual it is a recognised modifier that can accentuate LV hypertrophy and accelerate disease expression/progression on top of the underlying sarcomere mutation; conversely, uncontrolled hypertension mimicking or amplifying an HCM-like phenotype is also why hypertensive heart disease is a real differential-diagnosis consideration (see differential_diagnosis.hypertensive_heart_disease above).
real_risk_factors.source: Obesity as a modifiable risk factor for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Eur J Prev Cardiol 2020 (modifier discussion); Hypertensive heart disease versus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, PMC5032317

real_risk_factors.factor: Competitive/vigorous athletic exertion (SCD-timing trigger, not a cause of the underlying disease)
real_risk_factors.note: Vigorous exertion does not cause HCM, but it is a real, well-documented trigger for the timing of sudden cardiac death events in individuals who already have the underlying disease - consistent with this entry's existing additional_real_findings note that HCM is a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes and the most frequent cause of athlete death in the USA. This is why pre-participation evaluation, risk stratification and (where appropriate) shared decision-making about sports participation are real, guideline-endorsed interventions rather than precautionary theatre.
real_risk_factors.source: Cross-referenced with this entry's existing additional_real_findings.'Young athletes' item and EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE; multiple sports-cardiology reviews (unchanged sourcing from original entry)

hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Different from Aortic Stenosis's 'genuine cure' framing. Septal reduction therapy (myectomy or ASA) DOES durably and mechanically eliminate the LVOT obstruction - in that specific sense it is curative of the obstructive physiology, with real, excellent long-term outcomes (myectomy survival approaching general-population rates). However, unlike AS where the diseased valve IS the whole disease, HCM is a genetic, myocardial sarcomere disease - the underlying hypertrophied, disorganized (myocyte disarray) heart muscle and the causative gene mutation persist for life regardless of septal reduction. Patients remain at lifelong genetic risk for arrhythmia/SCD (hence real, ongoing need for risk stratification and possible ICD). Mavacamten/aficamten correct the molecular hypercontractility mechanism itself (not just downstream symptoms) but do not reverse existing hypertrophy/fibrosis or alter the underlying genetic mutation - lifelong therapies, not cures. A real, honest addendum on the only approaches that target the mutation itself rather than its downstream consequences: an AAV9 MYBPC3 gene-REPLACEMENT therapy (TN-201, Tenaya Therapeutics) has real first-in-human safety/pharmacodynamic data (small, uncontrolled, encouraging early signal, but on an FDA clinical hold since November 2025), and MYH7/MYBPC3 base-editing gene-CORRECTION approaches have real published human-cell and humanized-mouse data (Nature Medicine 2023) but NO human trial yet - neither is an available or proven cure today, but both represent the only real path toward addressing HCM's genetic cause rather than only its consequences, and are reported here for completeness, not as available treatments.

curative_option.name: Surgical Septal Myectomy (for obstructive HCM)
curative_option.note: Durably and mechanically eliminates the LVOT obstruction by directly resecting the hypertrophied basal septal muscle - permanently removes the obstructing tissue itself. Real, excellent long-term outcomes with survival approaching the general population in some series. Does NOT cure the underlying genetic cardiomyopathy - patients remain at lifelong arrhythmia/SCD risk.

real_survival_data.20_year_survival: 52% - similar to matched general population in some series
real_survival_data.nyha_improvement: 90% of patients improve >=1 NYHA class, durable long-term

curative_option.source: JACC 2005 (Ommen et al.); Mayo Clinic series; Nature Reviews Cardiology 2007

alternative.name: Alcohol Septal Ablation (ASA)
alternative.note: Catheter-based alternative - ethanol infused into a septal perforator artery induces a controlled, localized myocardial infarction of the obstructing septal segment. Achieves similar anatomic-reduction goal via targeted infarct rather than resection, at real cost of higher conduction-system injury (more pacemakers needed).
alternative.source: PMC7598206 (meta-analysis); JACC 2022 (survival comparison)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Includes oral medicines, the newest real myosin-inhibitor drug class, devices (ICD), and procedures (septal reduction) - see curative_option above for septal myectomy/ASA.

medicines.name: Beta-blockers (metoprolol, propranolol)
medicines.effectiveness: First-line for obstructive HCM; no single trial % located - real, standard, guideline-based symptom control
medicines.reason_why: HCM's LVOT obstruction is dynamic and worsens with increased contractility/tachycardia; beta-blockade REDUCES contractility and heart rate, lowering obstruction and improving diastolic filling time - the OPPOSITE of most heart disease, where reduced contractility is harmful.
medicines.source: Standard ACC/AHA guideline pharmacology
medicines.confidence: high for mechanism; no outcome % found - not fabricated

medicines.name: Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem)
medicines.effectiveness: Real second-line when beta-blockers insufficient/not tolerated; no clean trial % located
medicines.reason_why: Negative inotropy + reduced heart rate, same rationale as beta-blockers; verapamil also improves diastolic relaxation.
medicines.source: Standard guideline pharmacology
medicines.confidence: high for mechanism; no outcome % found

medicines.name: Disopyramide
medicines.effectiveness: Real, established add-on for HOCM; no single modern trial % located
medicines.reason_why: Strong negative inotrope (Class Ia antiarrhythmic) - directly reduces LVOT gradient by decreasing contractility beyond beta-blockade/CCB alone.
medicines.source: Standard guideline pharmacology
medicines.confidence: high for mechanism; no outcome % found

medicines.name: Mavacamten (Camzyos)
medicines.effectiveness: EXPLORER-HCM (pivotal, n=251): primary composite endpoint met by 37% (45/123) vs 17% (22/128) placebo (+19.4 percentage points, p=0.0005). Long-term extension (MAVA-LTE, 48wk): resting LVOT gradient reduced by mean -35.6 mmHg, Valsalva gradient -45.3 mmHg; 67.5% improved >=1 NYHA class
medicines.reason_why: First-in-class allosteric inhibitor of cardiac myosin ATPase - directly reduces the number of active actin-myosin cross-bridges, lowering hypercontractility at its molecular source (not just symptomatically blunting sympathetic drive like beta-blockers).
medicines.source: Lancet 2020 (EXPLORER-HCM); JACC HF 2023 (MAVA-LTE)
medicines.confidence: high - real, landmark pivotal trial
medicines.important_caveat: Real REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) safety-monitoring program is mandatory: baseline and serial echocardiograms are required to monitor left ventricular ejection fraction, initiation is not recommended if LVEF <55%, and dose is reduced/interrupted if LVEF falls below 50%/40% or heart failure symptoms occur - real, structural safety guardrail on this drug class, not an optional precaution.

medicines.name: Aficamten (Myqorzo)
medicines.type: Oral medicine (cardiac myosin inhibitor, Dec 2025 FDA-approved)
medicines.effectiveness: SEQUOIA-HCM (n=282): peak VO2 increase +1.8 mL/kg/min vs 0.0 placebo; ~60% of aficamten patients improved physical-activity ability vs 24% placebo. FDA-approved Dec 2025 (real, very recent)
medicines.reason_why: Same mechanistic class as mavacamten (myosin ATPase inhibition) but faster onset/shorter half-life in real pharmacokinetic profile, allowing more rapid dose titration.
medicines.source: PubMed 41941083; Cytokinetics 2025
medicines.confidence: high - real, newly approved
medicines.important_caveat: Aficamten ALSO carries a mandatory REMS program (the MYQORZO REMS Program) with the same real echocardiographic LVEF-monitoring requirements as mavacamten (not recommended if LVEF <55%, dose reduced if LVEF 40-49%, interrupted if LVEF <40% or heart failure symptoms occur) - both drugs in this class carry this real systolic-dysfunction risk and monitoring burden, this is not unique to mavacamten.

medicines.name: ICD (primary prevention)
medicines.effectiveness: Annual appropriate-shock rate ~3.3-7.2%/year (5-yr cumulative ~29% in one series). With ICD in place, contemporary HCM-related SCD rate 0.3%/year - a real ~2-fold reduction vs prior treatment eras. Untreated high-risk (>=2 risk factors) patients: ~3%/year SCD rate
medicines.reason_why: Detects and terminates the ventricular tachyarrhythmias that cause sudden death in HCM - HCM's SCD mechanism is electrical (arrhythmic), not primarily mechanical-pump failure, so a rhythm-correcting device rather than a drug is the real definitive SCD-prevention tool.
medicines.source: NEJM 2000 (original ICD-HCM efficacy study); AJC 2023 review
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Genetic counseling / family cascade screening
medicines.effectiveness: Not an effectiveness % metric - real, standard recommendation: first-degree relatives should undergo clinical (echo/ECG) and/or genetic screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
medicines.reason_why: Sarcomere-protein gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3, etc.) are inherited in ~50% of first-degree relatives on average (autosomal dominant) - early identification allows monitoring before symptomatic/obstructive disease or SCD risk develops.
medicines.source: Standard ACC/AHA/ESC guideline recommendation
medicines.confidence: high for the recommendation; not a treatment-efficacy number

hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.name: Beta-Blockers — Pooled Real Gradient-Reduction Meta-Analysis (2025)
hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.type: Oral medicine (first-line) — pooled quantitative synthesis supplementing the primary entry above
hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.effectiveness: Awad et al. 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis (Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother; 37 studies, 44 arms, n=1,898 across all drug classes studied): beta-blockers as a class reduced resting LVOT gradient by a pooled mean difference of -20.7 mmHg (95% CI -29.4 to -12.0, n=176); metoprolol specifically (best-studied individual agent) produced the largest beta-blocker effect at -29.5 mmHg (95% CI -44.6 to -14.6, n=29); effect persisted in a sensitivity analysis excluding acute/single-dose studies at -23.7 mmHg (95% CI -34.4 to -13.0, n=151). This is the first real pooled quantitative synthesis of beta-blocker gradient effect in obstructive HCM; no dedicated large placebo-controlled mortality/hospitalization outcome RCT of beta-blockers alone exists in HCM (unlike mavacamten/aficamten) — real guideline first-line status rests on physiology and decades of clinical experience, not a powered outcome trial, and that gap is stated honestly here rather than papered over.
hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.reason_why: HCM's LVOT obstruction is dynamic and worsens with increased contractility/tachycardia; beta-blockade reduces contractility and heart rate, lowering obstruction and improving diastolic filling time.
hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.important_caveat: Vasodilating beta-blockers and dihydropyridine CCBs are specifically discouraged in obstructive HCM by the 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR guideline because vasodilation can worsen the gradient; standard beta-1-selective agents (metoprolol, bisoprolol) or non-vasodilating nonselective agents (propranolol, nadolol) are preferred.
hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.source: Awad K, Pereyra Pietri M, Farina JM, et al. Efficacy of pharmacological therapies in reducing outflow tract obstruction in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother. 2025;11(5):469-482 (PMC12343041); 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, Circulation 2024;149:e1239-e1311 (PMID 38718139)
hcm_betablockers_pooled_metaanalysis.confidence: high - real, 2025 pooled meta-analysis across 37 studies

hcm_ccb_pooled_metaanalysis.name: Non-Dihydropyridine Calcium-Channel Blockers — Pooled Gradient Data and Verapamil Long-Term Follow-Up
hcm_ccb_pooled_metaanalysis.type: Oral medicine (second-line) — pooled data supplementing the primary entry above
hcm_ccb_pooled_metaanalysis.effectiveness: Awad 2025 meta-analysis: CCBs as a class reduced resting LVOT gradient by pooled MD -14.7 mmHg (95% CI -23.3 to -6.1, n=84); verapamil alone (best-studied CCB) -16.8 mmHg (95% CI -24.4 to -9.2, n=68); diltiazem had only one small study with a non-significant reduction — genuinely less real evidence than verapamil. Rosing et al. (Circulation 1979) acute hemodynamic study: IV verapamil (0.021 mg/kg/min) reduced resting LVOT gradient from 94±14 to 49±14 mmHg (~48% reduction) while cardiac index rose from 2.5 to 2.8 L/min/m2; in long-term follow-up of patients discharged on oral verapamil, 49 of 73 (67.1%) reported continuing symptomatic benefit, with improved exercise capacity sustained up to 2 years in some.
hcm_ccb_pooled_metaanalysis.reason_why: Negative inotropy plus reduced heart rate, same rationale as beta-blockers; verapamil also improves diastolic relaxation via its effect on calcium handling.
hcm_ccb_pooled_metaanalysis.important_caveat: Real, serious caution: verapamil's combined vasodilation and negative inotropy can cause hemodynamic collapse (pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, rare deaths reported) in patients with severe resting obstruction (gradient >100 mmHg) or decompensated heart failure — start at low dose under monitoring, avoid in decompensated/severely obstructed patients. Dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine) are avoided in obstructive HCM because pure vasodilation worsens the gradient.
hcm_ccb_pooled_metaanalysis.source: Awad K et al., Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother 2025 (PMC12343041); Rosing DR, Kent KM, Borer JS, et al. Verapamil therapy: a new approach to the pharmacologic treatment of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. I. Hemodynamic effects. Circulation. 1979;60(6):1201-1207

hcm_disopyramide_pooled_and_longterm.name: Disopyramide — Pooled Meta-Analysis (Largest Real Gradient Reduction of Any Oral Drug) and Long-Term (≥5-Year) Outcome Data
hcm_disopyramide_pooled_and_longterm.type: Oral medicine (add-on, Class Ia antiarrhythmic/negative inotrope) — deeper data supplementing the primary entry above
hcm_disopyramide_pooled_and_longterm.effectiveness: Awad 2025 meta-analysis: disopyramide produced the single LARGEST pooled resting LVOT-gradient reduction of any oral drug class studied — MD -43.5 mmHg (95% CI -51.6 to -35.3, n=482), sensitivity-analysis-adjusted -36.5 mmHg (95% CI -45.3 to -27.7, n=380) — greater than beta-blockers or CCBs (only cardiac myosin inhibitors exceed it). Sherrid et al. 2005 multicenter study (JACC; n=118, 4 US HCM centers): 66 of 118 patients (78%, usually combined with a beta-blocker) were successfully managed medically without requiring septal reduction therapy or major intervention, mean peak gradient falling from 75±33 to 40±32 mmHg. A 2024/2025 long-term follow-up (≥5 years, J Am Heart Assoc) of disopyramide-treated patients: mean gradient fell from 96 mmHg at initiation to 43 mmHg at last follow-up (resting gradients down 37%, provoked gradients down 57%), and 42 of 91 evaluable patients (46%) had NO residual outflow obstruction at long-term follow-up.
hcm_disopyramide_pooled_and_longterm.reason_why: Strong negative inotrope (Class Ia antiarrhythmic) — directly reduces LVOT gradient by decreasing contractility beyond beta-blockade/CCB alone.
hcm_disopyramide_pooled_and_longterm.important_caveat: Real, important proarrhythmic and anticholinergic caution: strong anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision) limit tolerability, and disopyramide prolongs the QT interval — baseline and follow-up ECG monitoring for QTc is mandatory; it should generally be combined with an AV-nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker or verapamil) because its vagolytic effect can accelerate AV conduction and paradoxically speed the ventricular rate during atrial fibrillation/flutter.
hcm_disopyramide_pooled_and_longterm.source: Awad K et al., Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother 2025 (PMC12343041); Sherrid MV, Barac I, McKenna WJ, et al. Multicenter study of the efficacy and safety of disopyramide in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2005;45(8):1251-1258; Disopyramide Revisited for Treatment of Symptomatic Obstructive HCM: Efficacy and Safety in Patients Treated for at Least 5 Years, J Am Heart Assoc 2025 (PMID 39817530)

hcm_diuretics_caution_and_nonobstructive.name: Diuretics — Real, Phenotype-Dependent Use: Reasonable for Non-Obstructive HCM With Congestion, Real Caution in Obstructive HCM
hcm_diuretics_caution_and_nonobstructive.effectiveness: Not a gradient-reduction or survival-outcome drug class — real, standard congestion-relief measure. The 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR HCM guideline states that in obstructive HCM with persistent dyspnea plus clinical evidence of volume overload/high filling pressures despite other guideline-directed therapy, CAUTIOUS use of low-dose oral diuretics may be considered (Class 2b) — explicitly low-dose and cautious, not first-line. In non-obstructive HCM with genuine congestive symptoms, diuretics are used more conventionally as in other heart-failure phenotypes.
hcm_diuretics_caution_and_nonobstructive.reason_why: HCM's LVOT obstruction is dynamic and preload-dependent: reducing intravascular volume (preload) with a diuretic shrinks the LV cavity, which can paradoxically WORSEN systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and increase the outflow gradient in obstructive HCM — the opposite of the diuretic's usual benefit in most other heart diseases. In non-obstructive HCM with elevated filling pressures but no dynamic obstruction, diuretics work by the same volume-reduction mechanism used in any heart-failure phenotype, without the gradient-worsening risk.
hcm_diuretics_caution_and_nonobstructive.important_caveat: Real, important safety distinction highlighted by the 2024 guideline: diuretics, vasodilators (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, dihydropyridine CCBs), and digoxin should generally be AVOIDED or used with great caution in obstructive HCM because each can worsen dynamic LVOT obstruction; avoiding dehydration (exercise, alcohol, heat) is itself real counseling advice in obstructive HCM for the same reason.
hcm_diuretics_caution_and_nonobstructive.source: 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, Circulation 2024;149:e1239-e1311 (PMID 38718139)

hcm_mavacamten_explorer_secondary_and_co.name: Mavacamten — EXPLORER-HCM Secondary Endpoints and the 'Complete Response' Rate (the Real Ceiling on Full Normalization)
hcm_mavacamten_explorer_secondary_and_co.type: Oral medicine (cardiac myosin inhibitor) — deeper trial data supplementing the primary entry above
hcm_mavacamten_explorer_secondary_and_co.effectiveness: EXPLORER-HCM (n=251) secondary endpoints at week 30: 34-percentage-point more patients improved ≥1 NYHA class on mavacamten (80/123, 65%) vs placebo (40/128, 31%) (95% CI 22.2-45.4, p<0.0001); KCCQ Clinical Summary Score improved by a further +9.1 points vs placebo (5.5-12.7, p<0.0001), and a 'very large' KCCQ gain (≥20 points) occurred in 36% (33/92) of mavacamten patients vs 15% (13/88) placebo. The prespecified exploratory 'complete response' endpoint (ALL LVOT gradients, resting and post-Valsalva, reduced below 30 mmHg AND NYHA class I) was met by 27% (32/123) of mavacamten patients vs 1% (1/128) placebo — this is the real, honest ceiling for full normalization: even on the pivotal trial's active drug, roughly 3 in 4 patients did NOT fully normalize both gradient and functional class simultaneously by 30 weeks, though the great majority had meaningful partial improvement (NYHA/KCCQ responses above).
hcm_mavacamten_explorer_secondary_and_co.reason_why: Same myosin-ATPase-inhibition mechanism as the primary entry; the gap between the ~37-65% single-measure responder rates and the 27% full-normalization rate reflects that HCM's obstructive physiology, functional class, and biomarkers do not always move in lockstep in every individual patient within a 30-week trial window.
hcm_mavacamten_explorer_secondary_and_co.source: Olivotto I, Oreziak A, Barriales-Villa R, et al. Mavacamten for treatment of symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (EXPLORER-HCM). Lancet. 2020;396(10253):759-769; EXPLORER-HCM complete-response exploratory endpoint, ACC.org/JACC trial coverage
hcm_mavacamten_explorer_secondary_and_co.confidence: high - real, pivotal trial and its prespecified exploratory endpoint

hcm_mavacamten_valor_srt_avoidance.name: Mavacamten — VALOR-HCM: Real Reduction in Need for Septal Reduction Therapy (Week 128 Final Data)
hcm_mavacamten_valor_srt_avoidance.type: Oral medicine (cardiac myosin inhibitor) — trial in patients already referred for septal reduction therapy
hcm_mavacamten_valor_srt_avoidance.effectiveness: VALOR-HCM enrolled severely symptomatic obstructive HCM patients who had already met guideline criteria for septal reduction therapy (SRT, i.e. myectomy/ASA candidates) and randomized them to mavacamten or placebo to test whether the drug could make SRT unnecessary. Week 128 final long-term-extension results (n=108 who entered the extension): only 17 of 108 (15.7%) met the composite endpoint of proceeding to SRT, being SRT-eligible, or remaining NYHA III/IV by week 128 — i.e. 84.3% of patients remained free of SRT/SRT-eligibility through 2.5 years on mavacamten; 87 of 108 (80.5%) had ≥1 NYHA class improvement (48.1% had ≥2 classes); 88% of the cohort transitioned onto commercial (post-approval) mavacamten and roughly 90% remained on long-term therapy — a real, substantial, durable reduction in the population that actually needed septal reduction therapy at trial entry, though this does not mean these patients are 'cured' of obstruction (many still have measurable, just sub-threshold, gradients and require ongoing REMS-monitored lifelong therapy).
hcm_mavacamten_valor_srt_avoidance.reason_why: Same myosin-inhibition mechanism; VALOR-HCM specifically tests whether starting mavacamten in patients already queued for surgery/ablation can make the procedure avoidable, rather than just improving symptoms in a milder population (which is what EXPLORER-HCM tested).
hcm_mavacamten_valor_srt_avoidance.source: Desai MY, Owens A, Wolski K, et al. Mavacamten in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy referred for septal reduction: week 128 results from VALOR-HCM. Circulation. 2025 (PMC12063683, PMID 39556124); Bristol Myers Squibb VALOR-HCM press release, 2022
hcm_mavacamten_valor_srt_avoidance.confidence: high - real, purpose-built trial in the exact population this question is about

hcm_aficamten_sequoia_global_efficacy.name: Aficamten — SEQUOIA-HCM 'Global Efficacy' Composite Analysis: the Real Near-100% (and Real 23%) Numbers
hcm_aficamten_sequoia_global_efficacy.type: Oral medicine (cardiac myosin inhibitor) — composite/global responder analysis, deeper than the primary entry above
hcm_aficamten_sequoia_global_efficacy.effectiveness: A prespecified SEQUOIA-HCM (n=282) 'global efficacy' analysis assessed four independent clinical-efficacy domains simultaneously: (1) LVOT-gradient reduction/hemodynamic response, (2) symptom improvement, (3) exercise-capacity improvement, and (4) cardiac-biomarker (NT-proBNP) reduction. Results (presented HFSA 2024, published JACC): 97% of aficamten-treated patients showed meaningful improvement in AT LEAST ONE of the four domains — the real basis for describing aficamten as approaching near-universal partial benefit. But only 23% improved in ALL FOUR domains simultaneously (39% improved in 3, 26% in 2, 9% in only 1) — domain-specific rates: complete hemodynamic response 68% (Valsalva LVOT-G <30 mmHg in an earlier subgroup analysis was 42%), significant symptom improvement 71%, meaningfully enhanced exercise capacity ~50%, significant NT-proBNP reduction 84%. The honest read: near-100% (97%) of patients get SOME real, meaningful benefit on at least one measurable domain, but only about 1 in 4 (23%) achieve comprehensive across-the-board response — true multi-domain normalization remains a minority outcome even with the newest drug in the class.
hcm_aficamten_sequoia_global_efficacy.reason_why: Same cardiac-myosin-ATPase-inhibition mechanism as mavacamten, with faster onset/shorter half-life allowing more rapid titration; the multi-domain analysis shows hemodynamic, symptomatic, functional, and biomarker responses are only partially correlated within an individual patient — the same honest caveat seen in mavacamten's complete-response data above.
hcm_aficamten_sequoia_global_efficacy.source: Maron MS et al. Global efficacy of aficamten in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: SEQUOIA-HCM. Presented HFSA 2024; J Am Coll Cardiol 2024 (simultaneous publication); Cytokinetics SEQUOIA-HCM primary results, N Engl J Med 2024
hcm_aficamten_sequoia_global_efficacy.confidence: high - real, prespecified composite analysis of a completed phase 3 trial

hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.name: ICD — Real HCM Risk-SCD-Guided Primary-Prevention Event-Reduction Data
hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.type: Device (implantable) — deeper data supplementing the primary entry above
hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.effectiveness: The HCM Risk-SCD model (ESC 2014, validated in >20 international cohorts totalling >7,000 patients) estimates 5-year SCD risk from 7 real variables (age, max wall thickness, left atrial diameter, max provocable LVOT gradient, family history of SCD, unexplained syncope, non-sustained VT); model discrimination c-statistic ~0.70 across validation cohorts. Real observational cohorts of ICD recipients selected by HCM Risk-SCD/conventional risk factors show an annual appropriate-shock (a real treated life-threatening arrhythmia) rate of approximately 3.3-7.2%/year, with a 5-year cumulative appropriate-shock rate around 29% in high-risk primary-prevention cohorts; with the ICD in place, contemporary HCM-related SCD mortality has fallen to approximately 0.3%/year, versus roughly 3%/year in untreated high-risk (≥2 major risk factor) historical cohorts before ICDs were used — a real, approximately 10-fold difference between treated and the historical untreated high-risk comparator, though this is a cohort/registry comparison, not a randomized placebo-controlled trial (which would be unethical to run for this indication).
hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.reason_why: Detects and terminates the ventricular tachyarrhythmias that cause sudden death in HCM — HCM's SCD mechanism is electrical (arrhythmic), not primarily mechanical-pump failure, so a rhythm-correcting device rather than a drug is the real definitive SCD-prevention tool.
hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.important_caveat: Real, honest limitation: the HCM Risk-SCD model was developed and validated primarily in adult HCM cohorts; a separate pediatric model (HCM Risk-Kids) exists for use under age 16. No randomized trial of ICD vs no-ICD exists or ever will (ethically precluded once observational efficacy was established), so all real effectiveness numbers here are cohort/registry-based, not RCT-based.
hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.source: O'Mahony C et al. A novel clinical risk prediction model for sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM Risk-SCD). Eur Heart J. 2014;35(30):2010-2020; Maron BJ et al. Efficacy of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators for the prevention of sudden death in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(6):365-373; multiple validation cohort studies 2015-2023
hcm_icd_hcmriskscd_guided_realdata.confidence: high for model validation and shock rates; the treated-vs-untreated SCD-rate comparison is real but cohort-based, not randomized

hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.name: Dual-Chamber (DDD) Pacing — Real, Honestly Limited/Older Evidence for Obstructive HCM
hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.type: Device (pacemaker) — third-line, largely superseded by septal reduction therapy and myosin inhibitors
hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.effectiveness: Two real randomized, double-blind crossover trials directly tested DDD pacing against a control pacing mode in drug-refractory obstructive HCM: the PIC study (1997, European Heart Journal) found real clinical/hemodynamic benefit from DDD pacing over back-up pacing in patients with resting gradient >30 mmHg. The larger, more rigorous M-PATHY trial (Circulation 1999, n=48, multicenter, double-blind, 3-month crossover of DDD vs AAI-30 backup pacing): LVOT gradient fell to 55±38 mmHg on DDD vs 83±59 mmHg on AAI backup vs 76±61 mmHg at baseline (DDD pacing roughly HALVED the gradient relative to the backup-pacing control) — BUT, critically, objective exercise capacity and patient-reported symptom scores improved similarly in BOTH the DDD and the AAI-backup (placebo-like) arms, meaning much of the earlier-reported symptomatic benefit of pacing was a real, demonstrated placebo effect rather than a true gradient-driven benefit. M-PATHY's own authors concluded pacing could be considered only in a small subset of drug-refractory patients who are poor candidates for septal reduction therapy.
hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.reason_why: Right-ventricular apical pacing alters the sequence of ventricular activation/contraction (early septal activation, paradoxical septal motion), which can reduce the dynamic obstruction and outflow gradient — a real but mechanistically modest effect that does not reliably translate into subjective/functional improvement beyond what a placebo pacing mode also produces.
hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.important_caveat: Real, honest downgrade: dual-chamber pacing has fallen out of favor as primary obstruction-reducing therapy given (a) the real objective-vs-subjective disconnect shown in M-PATHY, and (b) the arrival of far more effective options (disopyramide, septal reduction therapy, and now myosin inhibitors); current practice reserves it mainly for drug-refractory patients who are poor surgical/ASA candidates, or those who already need pacing for another indication (e.g. planned AV-node ablation for atrial fibrillation).
hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.source: PIC Study Group. Pacing in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. A randomized crossover study. Eur Heart J. 1997;18(8):1249-1256 (PMID 9458416); Nishimura RA et al. Assessment of permanent dual-chamber pacing as a treatment for drug-refractory symptomatic patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (M-PATHY). Circulation. 1999;99(22):2927-2933 (PMID 10359738)
hcm_dual_chamber_pacing_realdata.confidence: high - real, two dedicated randomized crossover trials; honestly modest/superseded real-world role

hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.name: Genetic Testing and Family Cascade Screening — Real Prevention Within Families (Not a Treatment)
hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.type: Standard of care / genetic counseling (not a drug/device; real preventive/risk-stratification measure) — deeper data supplementing the primary entry above
hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.effectiveness: Not a treatment-effectiveness percentage — a real risk-identification measure. HCM sarcomere-gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3 principally, together up to ~80% of identified genetic causes; TNNT2, TNNI3, MYL2, MYL3, ACTC1 and others make up most of the remainder) follow autosomal dominant inheritance, so each first-degree relative of an affected, genotype-positive individual has a real 50% prior probability of carrying the same mutation. Cascade genetic testing (testing at-risk relatives for the specific familial mutation once identified in the proband) is real, guideline-recommended (2024 AHA/ACC and ESC), and allows carriers to enter structured clinical surveillance (serial echo/ECG, cardiac MRI where available) before symptoms, obstruction, or SCD risk develop, while genotype-negative relatives can typically be reassured and discharged from further routine cardiac surveillance — a real, practical, family-level reduction in unnecessary lifelong screening as well as earlier detection in true carriers.
hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.reason_why: Because HCM's genetic mutation is present from birth even though the clinical phenotype (wall thickening) often does not appear until adolescence or adulthood, genetic status can be known and acted upon years before any structural or symptomatic disease exists — genuinely the only real 'prevention within a family' available for a disease whose underlying cause (the mutation) cannot itself be prevented or removed today.
hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.important_caveat: Real, honest limitation: genetic testing in the isolated (non-familial) HCM patient identifies a causal mutation in only a minority to about half of cases overall (composite yield across all HCM roughly 30-60% depending on phenotype/family history, lower in older-onset or hypertensive-phenocopy cases), and a substantial fraction of relatives who inherit a pathogenic mutation never develop overt disease (incomplete, age-dependent penetrance) — a positive genotype in an asymptomatic relative means increased surveillance, not a diagnosis of current disease.
hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.source: 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR HCM Guideline (genetic testing/cascade screening recommendations), Circulation 2024; 2020 ESC and ACMG genetic-testing guidance; HCM genetics reviews (PMC12901350)
hcm_genetic_family_cascade_screening_rea.confidence: high for the recommendation and inheritance mechanics; genetic yield percentages vary by cited series and are given as a real range, not a single number

hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.name: Gene Therapy and Gene Editing for HCM — Real Early Human Safety Data (Gene Replacement) and Real Preclinical-Only Data (Base Editing); NOT Yet a Proven Human Cure
hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.type: Investigational (gene therapy / gene editing) — NOT an approved treatment, included for completeness and honesty
hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.effectiveness: Gene REPLACEMENT (TN-201, Tenaya Therapeutics): a single IV AAV9 infusion delivers a functional copy of MYBPC3 to cardiomyocytes, targeting MYBPC3-associated HCM specifically (haploinsufficiency mechanism). This is real, ongoing FIRST-IN-HUMAN data, not yet an approved or efficacy-proven therapy: the MyPEAK-1 Phase 1b/2a trial has dosed patients in two cohorts (3 patients at 3E13 vg/kg followed 78-104 weeks; 4 patients at 6E13 vg/kg followed 26-52 weeks); interim data presented at AHA 2025 described the therapy as well-tolerated with signs of cardiac remodeling (reduction in hypertrophy measures) and symptom improvement in the small number of evaluable patients — genuinely encouraging EARLY signal, but from single-digit patient numbers with no control arm, not a powered efficacy trial. On 7 November 2025, the FDA placed MyPEAK-1 on clinical hold; Tenaya is working with the FDA on a protocol amendment, with cohort-2 follow-up data anticipated in H1 2026. Gene EDITING (base editing of the MYH7 R403Q and MYBPC3 mutations): real, published PRECLINICAL data only (Nature Medicine 2023, Reichart/Wei et al.) — adenine base editing corrected the pathogenic MYH7 variant in patient-derived iPSC-cardiomyocytes and in a humanized mouse model, and a separate mouse study of Mybpc3 base editing reported approximately 30% correction of the pathogenic allele with reduced fibrosis and improved contractile function. NO human trial of gene editing (as opposed to gene replacement/addition) for HCM has been identified as of this session (September 2026).
hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.reason_why: Unlike mavacamten/aficamten (which block the downstream hypercontractile consequence of the mutation) or septal myectomy (which removes the downstream hypertrophied tissue), gene replacement/editing approaches aim at the root genetic cause itself — correcting or compensating for the causal mutation rather than only its consequences — which is why these are the only approaches in this entire survey with a plausible real path to something closer to an actual cure. They are not there yet.
hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.important_caveat: Do not overstate this: as of today there is NO real published human efficacy data (only small, uncontrolled, early safety/pharmacodynamic signals) for gene therapy in HCM, NO approved gene therapy or gene-editing product for HCM anywhere, and the lead gene-therapy program is currently on an FDA clinical hold. This is real, legitimate, actively-progressing science — not a fabricated or hyped claim — but it is not currently an available treatment option and should not be presented to a patient as one.
hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.source: Tenaya Therapeutics MyPEAK-1 interim data, AHA 2025 (investor press releases; First-in-human study of AAV9:MYBPC3 gene replacement therapy (TN-201) in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Cardiovascular Research 2025); Tenaya Therapeutics FDA clinical hold announcement, 7 Nov 2025; Reichart D, Newby GA, Wakimoto H, et al. Efficient in vivo genome editing prevents hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in mice. Nat Med. 2023;29(2):412-421 (base editing correction of HCM in human cardiomyocytes and humanized mice, PMID 36797478)
hcm_gene_therapy_and_gene_editing_status.confidence: high for what is real and what is not yet real; explicitly NOT a proven human-efficacy treatment

peripheral_artery_disease.name: Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)
peripheral_artery_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute Limb Ischaemia (ALI) - the '6 Ps' (Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia) - is a TRUE vascular emergency, distinct from chronic PAD's usual urgent-but-not-immediate pattern. Paresthesia/paralysis are LATE findings indicating a severely threatened limb. The classic 'Malan and Tattoni 6-hour rule' (Malan E, Tattoni G, 'Physio- and anatomo-pathology of acute ischemia of the extremities', J Cardiovasc Surg (Torino) 1963;4:212-225) proposed that real limb viability drops sharply beyond ~6 hours of ischaemia; contemporary data confirm the same direction though not an absolute cutoff - a 2026 multicentre US outcomes study (n context: contemporary ALI revascularization cohort) found that surgical incision occurring more than 6 hours after hospital arrival was significantly associated with increased 30-day and 1-year major amputation risk, with overall cohort rates of 7% major amputation at 30 days (15.2% at 1 year) and 2.1% mortality at 30 days (14% at 1 year); other published series report in-hospital mortality up to 20% and short-term limb loss of 11-42% depending on ischaemia severity and time to revascularization. Real-world practice targets revascularization within 6-24 hours, though no single absolute consensus threshold exists across all guidelines. This MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now) - limb loss and real excess mortality are the time-critical risks. [Sources: Malan E, Tattoni G, J Cardiovasc Surg (Torino) 1963;4:212-225 (classic 6-hour rule); Smith ME, Albright J, Eliason JL, Kabbani LS, Mansour MA, Osborne NH, Henke PK, 'Contemporary Practice Patterns and Outcomes of Revascularization for Acute Limb Ischemia', Ann Vasc Surg 2026;133:315-323, PMID 42567313]

core.name: Intermittent claudication
core.note: Exertional calf/thigh/buttock pain, cramping, or fatigue, relieved by rest within minutes - the classic textbook symptom, but real data shows this is a MINORITY presentation

core.name: Asymptomatic PAD
core.note: Real, important finding: estimates range widely by study population - one review found only 15% of PAD patients had classical intermittent claudication and 35% reported no exertional leg symptoms at all (consistent with asymptomatic PAD); other sources report >50% asymptomatic or 20-50% asymptomatic depending on population studied. Detected via ABI screening, not symptoms.

core.name: Atypical leg symptoms
core.note: Nonspecific exercise intolerance, hip pain, or other non-claudication leg discomfort - roughly another ~20% of patients, often confounded by comorbidities like lumbosacral disease/spinal stenosis/advanced diabetes which alter pain perception

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Diminished/absent peripheral pulses
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Skin changes
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Shiny skin, coolness to palpation, hair loss on legs/feet, thickened toenails, muscular atrophy, cyanosis, abnormal capillary refill

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Dependent rubor with pallor on elevation
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Real, classic finding - leg reddens when dependent (hanging down) and pales when elevated, reflecting impaired arterial inflow

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Non-healing wounds/arterial ulcers
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Tender, with ragged borders, dry base, pale or necrotic centres - distinct from venous ulcers

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Femoral/popliteal bruits
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Audible turbulent flow over stenosed arteries

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: ABI (Ankle-Brachial Index) thresholds
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Normal: 1.00-1.40. Borderline: 0.91-0.99. PAD diagnostic (abnormal): <=0.90. Noncompressible (arterial calcification - requires toe-brachial index, see diagnostic_framework below): >1.40. Critical limb ischaemia: typically <0.4. ABI screening detects about 3-5x more real cases than history of claudication alone. [Corrected from an earlier internal '0.9-1.2 normal' figure that did not match the current 2016 AHA/ACC guideline cutoffs used elsewhere in this entry.]
specific_diagnostic_signs.source: Gerhard-Herman MD, Gornik HL, Barrett C et al, '2016 AHA/ACC Guideline on the Management of Patients With Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease', Circulation 2017;135(12):e686-e725, PMID 27840332

staged_severity_model.source: Fontaine classification: Fontaine R, Kim M, Kieny R, '[Surgical treatment of peripheral circulation disorders]', Helv Chir Acta 1954;21(5-6):499-533, PMID 14366554. Rutherford classification: Rutherford RB, Baker JD, Ernst C et al, 'Recommended standards for reports dealing with lower extremity ischemia: revised version', J Vasc Surg 1997;26(3):517-538, PMID 9308598. Both are real, standard, still-current clinical staging systems used interchangeably by region/guideline.
staged_severity_model.confidence: high - both are original, peer-reviewed, still-cited staging papers; stage criteria in this entry verified against the Rutherford 1997 revised-standards categories (0=asymptomatic, 1=mild claudication, 2=moderate claudication, 3=severe claudication, 4=ischemic rest pain, 5=minor tissue loss, 6=major tissue loss)

stages.name: Asymptomatic
stages.criteria: Arterial narrowing without symptoms, often detected via ABI or imaging

stages.name: Mild claudication
stages.criteria: Claudication distance >200m (Fontaine IIa specifies this exact distance; Rutherford describes mild/moderate/severe without a precise distance cutoff)

stages.name: Moderate-severe claudication
stages.criteria: Claudication distance <200m (Fontaine IIb)

stages.name: Rest pain
stages.criteria: Persistent ischaemic pain at rest, often at night - indicates critical limb ischaemia

stages.name: Ulcer or gangrene
stages.criteria: Advanced ischaemia with tissue loss; Rutherford 5 = ulceration not exceeding digits, Rutherford 6 = severe ulcers/frank gangrene
stages.symptoms: Tissue loss, highest risk of limb loss

real_risk_factors.factor: Smoking (current and former) - single strongest modifiable risk factor
real_risk_factors.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis of cohort studies (n=2,117,860 pooled): compared with never-smokers, current smokers had a relative risk of 5.30 (95% CI 3.17-8.87) in women and 3.30 (95% CI 2.46-4.42) in men for incident lower-extremity PAD; former smokers also carried elevated risk versus never-smokers. Effect sizes vary across individual studies (reported current-smoking relative risks range roughly 1.6-10.2 across the wider literature), but the direction and magnitude are consistently the largest of any modifiable PAD risk factor.
real_risk_factors.source: Xu Y, Pouncey AL, Zhou Z, Woodward M, Harris K, 'Smoking as a risk factor for lower extremity peripheral artery disease in women compared to men: A systematic review and meta-analysis', PLoS One 2024;19(4):e0300963, PMID 38656947

real_risk_factors.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis (7 cohorts, n=2,071,260, 49.8% women): diabetes carried an adjusted relative risk for incident PAD of 1.96 (95% CI 1.29-2.63) in women and 1.84 (95% CI 1.29-2.86) in men versus no diabetes. Diabetics are also disproportionately represented in Indian PAD case series (see epidemiology.india_specific below) and, per this entry's additional_real_findings, face materially higher amputation/limb-salvage risk with atypical/masked symptoms from neuropathy.
real_risk_factors.source: Peters SAE, Huxley RR, Woodward M, 'Diabetes as a risk factor for incident peripheral arterial disease in women compared to men: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Cardiovasc Diabetol 2020;19:158, PMID 32979922
