pulmonary_embolism.source: CT detection of pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection, PMID 22304953; Successful Repair of Concomitant Acute Type A Aortic Dissection and Saddle Pulmonary Embolism, PMC6136673; Simultaneous Aortic Dissection and Pulmonary Embolism: A Therapeutic Dilemma, PMC7910651
pulmonary_embolism.confidence: moderate-high - distinguishing features are standard teaching; the D-dimer specificity figure comes from a single cited series and may vary by population

musculoskeletal_back_pain.finding: Musculoskeletal back/chest pain is typically reproducible on palpation or with specific movements/positions, has a gradual or activity-related onset rather than an abrupt maximal-intensity onset, and is not accompanied by pulse deficit, inter-arm BP differential, syncope, or any focal neurological/limb-ischaemic sign. Because dissection pain can radiate to or be felt predominantly in the back (especially with descending-aorta involvement), an older or hypertensive patient presenting with severe new back pain should not be assumed to have a musculoskeletal cause until dissection red flags have been actively excluded, particularly if the pain reached maximal intensity within seconds to minutes (musculoskeletal pain rarely does this).
musculoskeletal_back_pain.source: Aortic Dissection Differential Diagnoses, Medscape/emedicine 2062452; standard emergency-medicine chest/back-pain differential teaching
musculoskeletal_back_pain.confidence: moderate-high - well-established qualitative clinical teaching rather than a single quantified study

pericarditis.finding: Acute pericarditis classically shows diffuse (not territorial) ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression on ECG, and pain that is pleuritic and improved by sitting forward - features that can superficially overlap with dissection presenting with pericardial involvement. This is a genuine diagnostic trap in the other direction: Type A dissection can bleed into the pericardial space and produce a pericardial effusion that is then read as 'confirming' a pericarditis diagnosis, when the effusion is actually haemopericardium from a leaking dissection - multiple published cases describe dissection initially misdiagnosed as pericarditis (or as NSTEMI with 'incidental' effusion) until CT or MRI revealed the dissection flap. The real, guideline-consistent safety practice is that any new pericardial effusion found in a patient with acute chest pain - especially of a size or acuity out of proportion to a benign viral-pericarditis picture - should prompt consideration of aortic imaging before the effusion is attributed to simple pericarditis.
pericarditis.source: A SILENT DANGER: AORTIC DISSECTION MASQUERADING AS ACUTE PERICARDITIS, JACC 2025;85(Suppl), doi 10.1016/S0735-1097(25)04522-X; Pericardial Effusion in a Patient with Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction: Beware of a Hidden Malefactor, PMC3626394; Missed Diagnosis of Aortic Intramural Hematoma Presenting With Hemorrhagic Pericardial Effusion, PMC12602031
pericarditis.confidence: moderate-high - repeated pattern across independent case reports; genuinely a known, named diagnostic pitfall in emergency cardiology

global_incidence.finding: Pooled estimates across population-based studies put global acute aortic dissection incidence at roughly 4.8 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI approximately 3.6-6.1), with substantial variation across individual studies from about 2.0 to 15.0 per 100,000 person-years depending on population, case-ascertainment method and autopsy-confirmation rates (dissection is under-ascertained where patients die suddenly out-of-hospital and are not autopsied). Regional variation is real and large: a Japanese population-based study in Miyazaki prefecture (2016-2018) found incidence as high as 17.6 per 100,000, versus approximately 2.0-5.6 per 100,000 reported from Chinese cohorts, and some Western population studies report rising incidence over time (e.g. one cohort showing a rise in men from 10.7 to 16.3 per 100,000 person-years and in women from 7.1 to 9.1 per 100,000 person-years over the study period), which may partly reflect improved detection via more widespread CT imaging rather than a true rise in underlying disease incidence.
global_incidence.source: Aortic dissection: global epidemiology, meta-analysis, Cardiology Plus 2022;7(4); Dissecting the epidemiology of aortic dissection, Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care, doi 10.1093/ehjacc/zuab065; population-based incidence study, Miyazaki Japan cohort 2016-2018
global_incidence.confidence: moderate-high on the pooled range and direction of regional variation; the exact pooled point estimate differs modestly across meta-analyses depending on which population-based studies are included

hypertension_age_association.finding: Hypertension is present in about 72% of acute aortic dissection patients in the IRAD cohort, making it by a wide margin the most common single predisposing condition, and mean age at presentation is approximately 63 years, consistent with a predominantly degenerative/hypertension-driven disease of later-middle-age to older adults. The age/risk-factor profile is genuinely bimodal: patients under 40 are far less likely to have hypertension (34%) or atherosclerosis (1%) and far more likely to have Marfan syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, or a prior aortic surgery as their predisposing factor, so a young patient without any of the classic older-patient risk factors should still be actively evaluated for an underlying connective-tissue or congenital aortic-valve condition rather than have dissection excluded on age alone.
hypertension_age_association.source: Hagan PG et al., JAMA 2000;283(7):897-903, PMID 10685714; Januzzi JL et al., 'Characterizing the young patient with aortic dissection: results from the International Registry of Aortic Dissection (IRAD)', JACC 2004;43(4):665-669
hypertension_age_association.confidence: high - large multicentre registry data, internally consistent

india_specific.finding: No comprehensive Indian national registry for aortic dissection/aneurysm exists, and this gap is stated honestly rather than papered over with an invented figure: a 2023 review explicitly states that 'in the absence of registry data, meaningful comments cannot be made about incidence, natural history, and mortality in India', with available Indian data limited to single-institution case series. The most recent real Indian data point is a 2025 nationwide survey of Indian cardiac surgeons on real-world management practice variation for acute Type A dissection (perioperative protocols, cannulation strategy, institutional case volumes) - useful for practice-pattern insight, but it is a practice survey, not an incidence or outcomes registry, so it does not fill the epidemiological gap.
india_specific.source: Overview of acute type A aortic dissection in India, PMC10713969; Practice variations in the management of acute type A aortic dissection among Indian cardiac surgeons: a national survey, Indian J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2025, PMID 40984857
india_specific.confidence: high on the honest absence of a national registry (stated explicitly in the cited Indian review); this is a real, acknowledged gap in the literature, not an omission on this entry's part

irad_mortality_by_type_and_treatment.finding: In the original IRAD cohort (n=464, 1996-1998), overall in-hospital mortality was 27.4%. Stratified by type and treatment: Type A dissection managed surgically had 26% mortality versus 58% mortality when managed medically (surgery was withheld mainly for advanced age/comorbidity, so this comparison is confounded by patient selection, not a randomised comparison of treatments); Type B dissection managed medically (the default strategy for uncomplicated Type B) had 10.7% mortality, while the approximately 20% of Type B patients who required surgery (for complications such as malperfusion or rupture) had 31.4% mortality. This registry-defined pattern - Type A is a surgical emergency with materially better outcomes when operated, Type B is usually managed medically with lower baseline mortality unless complicated - remains the backbone of current management strategy and is reflected in this entry's existing staged_severity_model above.
irad_mortality_by_type_and_treatment.confidence: high - the foundational, still-cited registry dataset for aortic-dissection natural history, though it reflects a study population from the late 1990s; more recent IRAD-linked analyses (already cited in this entry's staged_severity_model) show improved contemporary surgical mortality (~16.9% for treated Type A)

untreated_vs_treated_survival_and_the_pe.finding: The classic teaching that untreated Type A dissection mortality rises 1-2% per hour in the first 24-48 hours, reaching roughly 50% by 48 hours to one week, originated from 1950s-era surgical-centre case series (i.e. before modern imaging/surgery existed) and has been repeatedly re-examined against the modern IRAD registry; contemporary reviews describe this historical rate as still broadly consistent with observed real-world data, though the underlying evidence is acknowledged to be sparse and drawn mainly from patients who were, for one reason or another, ineligible for surgery - a real limitation of the statistic that this entry states honestly rather than treating the 1-2%/hour figure as a precisely measured constant. At least one more recent single-centre analysis found an even higher observed hourly mortality of about 2.6% in the first 24 hours for medically managed Type A patients, suggesting the classic figure may, if anything, understate real urgency rather than overstate it. This time-criticality is also visible in surgical-timing data: in one cohort of patients grouped by time from diagnosis to surgery, those operated on 8-12 hours after diagnosis had the highest observed mortality (66.7%) of any interval group, and the relationship between delay and mortality was non-linear rather than a smooth per-hour curve - both a real caution against treating 'time to surgery' as a simple linear predictor and a real reinforcement that unnecessary delay to definitive repair is dangerous.
untreated_vs_treated_survival_and_the_pe.source: StatPearls, 'Aortic Dissection' (Point of Care); Mortality after non-surgically treated acute type A aortic dissection is higher than previously reported, Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2024;65(2):ezae039; Matthews CR, Madison M, Timsina LR et al., 'Impact of time between diagnosis to treatment in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection', Sci Rep 2021;11:3519
untreated_vs_treated_survival_and_the_pe.confidence: moderate-high - the direction (delay is dangerous, Type A untreated mortality is very high) is well established; the exact per-hour percentage and the shape of the time-mortality curve vary across the cited studies, and this entry reports that variation honestly rather than picking one number to sound precise

aneurysm_growth_rate_and_rupture_risk_th.finding: For small-to-moderate abdominal aortic aneurysms (4.0-5.5 cm), the two largest randomised surveillance-versus-early-repair trials found consistent slow growth rates - the UK Small Aneurysm Trial (UKSAT) measured 3.3 mm/year and the US Aneurysm Detection and Management (ADAM) trial measured 3.2 mm/year for aneurysms in this size range, and both trials found annual rupture risk in this size band to be very low (published estimates of roughly 0.6-2.1% per year, with randomised-trial-based rupture rates of about 1% per year or less for 4.0-5.5 cm aneurysms) - the real evidence base behind both trials' conclusion that early elective repair does not improve survival over ultrasound surveillance below the guideline size threshold, which underpins this entry's existing aaa_size_thresholds (women >=5.0 cm, men >=5.5 cm for elective repair). Growth accelerates as aneurysms enlarge (baseline diameter is itself a predictor of subsequent growth rate), which is the mechanistic reason rupture risk rises steeply above the size thresholds even though it is low below them, and is also why this entry's existing caveat (13% of AAAs <=5cm ruptured at autopsy; 60% of AAAs >5cm never ruptured) is presented as a real, acknowledged imperfection in using size alone to predict rupture.
aneurysm_growth_rate_and_rupture_risk_th.source: UK Small Aneurysm Trial Participants, Lancet 1998;352(9141):1649-1655; Lederle FA et al. (ADAM Veterans Affairs Cooperative Study), N Engl J Med 2002;346(19):1437-1444; Growth Rate and Associated Factors in Small Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms, systematic review, Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg
aneurysm_growth_rate_and_rupture_risk_th.confidence: high - two large randomised trials with consistent, mutually corroborating growth-rate and rupture-risk findings

clinical_takeaway.finding: First action: maintain a high index of suspicion for dissection in any patient with sudden, severe, tearing/ripping chest or back pain, especially if it migrated as it evolved, or if there is a pulse deficit, inter-arm blood pressure differential, syncope, or a new aortic-regurgitation murmur - these are the ADD-RS high-risk features (see diagnostic_framework.add_rs_bedside_risk_score above) and any one of them should trigger urgent aortic imaging rather than a routine ACS/musculoskeletal work-up. Second, obtain urgent CT angiography as the default first-line test in a haemodynamically stable patient; in an unstable patient who cannot safely go to the CT scanner, bedside/intraoperative TEE is the real, validated alternative (sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~100%, see diagnostic_framework.tee_role_especially_unstable_patients above). Third, and most safety-critical: never give anticoagulation, antiplatelet loading, or thrombolytic therapy to a patient with presumed ACS without first actively excluding dissection when any atypical feature is present (migrating/tearing pain quality, pulse deficit, wide mediastinum on chest X-ray, unexpected pericardial effusion, or inter-arm BP differential) - real, published case reports document fatal aortic rupture/tamponade after thrombolysis was given for what was actually an unrecognised dissection (see differential_diagnosis.acute_mi_critical_overlap above). A negative D-dimer can support ruling out dissection ONLY in a genuinely low pre-test-probability patient (ADD-RS<=1) and should not be relied upon in young patients presenting very early with possible short/thrombosing dissections, where false-negative D-dimer is a real, documented phenomenon.
clinical_takeaway.source: Rogers AM et al., Circulation 2011;123(20):2213-2218, PMID 21555704; Nazerian P et al., Circulation 2018;137(3):250-258, PMID 29030346; 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, Circulation 2022;146(24):e334-e482, PMID 36322642; Aortic dissection presenting as acute myocardial infarction: potential harm of antithrombin and antiplatelet therapy, PMC2557172
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high - directly reflects current guideline-recommended work-up sequence plus a repeatedly documented, real patient-safety failure mode

aortic_aneurysm_dissection.CURABILITY_NOTE: Similar in spirit to Aortic Stenosis: surgical/endovascular repair genuinely replaces or reinforces the diseased aortic segment - a real mechanical fix of that specific segment. However, unlike AS where one valve is the whole disease, aortic aneurysm/dissection is often part of a systemic aortopathy (atherosclerotic, hypertensive, or genetic connective-tissue disease) - the rest of the aorta remains at real risk of new aneurysm/dissection elsewhere, and genetic-condition patients (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos) need lifelong surveillance. Type A dissection repair and AAA repair are real, definitive fixes of the treated segment; they do not cure the underlying aortopathy. For ACUTE dissection, medicine's real role is emergency blood-pressure/heart-rate control (IV beta-blockers first-line, IV vasodilators added only after adequate beta-blockade, plus adequate analgesia to blunt the sympathetic/catecholamine surge) to reduce aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) and slow propagation while surgery is arranged for Type A, or as real first-line definitive management for uncomplicated Type B - medicine does not repair the dissection or aneurysm itself. For chronic aneurysm surveillance/prevention, medicine's real role (where evidence supports it at all) is cardiovascular risk-factor control and, in Marfan syndrome specifically, some aortic-root growth-rate slowing - not reversal of aneurysmal dilatation. Honestly, the real trial evidence for beta-blockers slowing growth in non-Marfan aneurysms (UK Small Aneurysm Trial, negative) and for doxycycline/MMP inhibition (Meijer 2013, negative; Cochrane review, no convincing benefit for any tested drug) is weak-to-negative, and losartan's benefit in Marfan syndrome depends heavily on the comparator used across trials (see exhaustive_medicine_survey for the full real data).

curative_option.name: Emergency Surgical Repair (Type A Dissection) / EVAR or Open Repair (AAA)
curative_option.note: Genuinely replaces or reinforces the diseased aortic segment - the closest real fix to the acute mechanical problem. For Type A dissection this is not optional: real, immediate surgery is the only real chance of survival. For AAA, elective repair at the real guideline threshold prevents the real, high rupture mortality.

real_survival_data.type_A_dissection_surgical_mortality_con: ~16.9% in-hospital (2024 IRAD-era data), improved from historical 17-26%
real_survival_data.type_A_dissection_mortality_per_hour: Classic teaching figure 1-2%/hour (1950s data) is now recognized as imprecise; contemporary IRAD-era hourly rate is ~0.22% overall, ~0.15% surgical, ~0.77% medical-only
real_survival_data.type_B_dissection_hospital_mortality: ~4.0% (2024 data), far lower than Type A
real_survival_data.ruptured_AAA_overall_mortality_including: 80-90% including deaths before reaching hospital; only ~50% of patients with rupture reach the hospital alive
real_survival_data.ruptured_AAA_hospital_mortality_EVAR_vs_: 13% (EVAR) vs 57.1% (open repair) in-hospital, and 8.7% vs 50% at 30 days in one comparative analysis
real_survival_data.elective_AAA_repair_operative_mortality_: Real, low elective operative mortality makes the size-based repair thresholds work as a rupture-prevention strategy: contemporary elective EVAR 30-day mortality is roughly 1-2%, elective open repair roughly 3-5%, versus an unrepaired AAA's annual rupture risk that rises from ~2.2% (5.5-6cm) to ~18.4% (>7cm) if left under surveillance past the threshold
real_survival_data.EVAR_1_15yr_and_OVER_14yr_longterm_follo: Early EVAR survival advantage over open repair lost by long-term follow-up in both UK EVAR-1 (15yr) and US OVER (14yr) trials, due to late aneurysm-related mortality (EVAR-1) or convergence by ~3 years (OVER); overall long-term all-cause survival not significantly different between EVAR and open repair in either trial

curative_option.source: IRAD registry (Booher et al. 2013; 2024 update); EJCTS 2024; StatPearls NBK459176; meta-analysis PMC4004021
curative_option.important_caveat: Two real RCT-level honesty checks on the dramatic figures above: (1) the ruptured-AAA EVAR-vs-open gap (13% vs 57.1%) comes from observational/registry data; the randomised IMPROVE trial, which assigns strategy before anatomical suitability for EVAR is even confirmed (removing most selection bias), found NO statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality between an EVAR-first strategy and an open-repair strategy for ruptured AAA - the true causal advantage of EVAR in this emergency setting is real but smaller than the registry gap suggests. (2) EVAR's early survival advantage over open repair in elective AAA does not persist indefinitely: UK EVAR-1 trial 15-year follow-up found a late 'catch-up' in aneurysm-related mortality in the EVAR arm (secondary sac rupture from endoleak/graft complications), so overall long-term (15-year) survival was not significantly different between EVAR and open repair, and the US OVER trial found the same pattern at 14 years. Neither point changes that emergency Type A surgery and emergency repair of a ruptured AAA are genuinely life-saving compared with no treatment - they show that EVAR's specific size of advantage over open repair is more modest under randomisation and over the long term than the single registry comparison implies.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Aortic aneurysm/dissection is primarily a surgical/procedural/interventional disease. Devices and procedures are researched with equal or greater depth than medicines per the founder's standing instruction.

medicines.name: Emergency Open Surgical Repair - Type A Dissection
medicines.effectiveness: Contemporary in-hospital mortality ~16.9% (down from historical 17-26%); without surgery, medically-managed mortality reaches 60% by 30 days
medicines.reason_why: Directly repairs/replaces the torn ascending aortic wall and re-establishes a single, intact lumen - the ascending aorta's proximity to the coronary ostia, aortic valve, and pericardium means an untreated tear here causes cardiac tamponade, coronary occlusion, or aortic rupture, all rapidly fatal, so surgical closure of the false lumen is the only real chance of survival.
medicines.source: IRAD registry (Booher et al. 2013); EJCTS 2024
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: IV Beta-blockers (labetalol, esmolol) - Type B Dissection first-line
medicines.effectiveness: Real, standard first-line medical management for uncomplicated Type B - reduces aortic wall stress; real target: heart rate <60bpm, systolic BP 100-120 mmHg
medicines.reason_why: Aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt, the rate of pressure rise) drives dissection propagation more than absolute pressure alone - beta-blockade reduces both heart rate and the force of ventricular contraction, directly lowering dP/dt and the mechanical force propagating the dissection flap.
medicines.source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline
medicines.confidence: high for mechanism/target; standard of care not a single trial %

medicines.name: TEVAR (Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair) - complicated Type B
medicines.effectiveness: INSTEAD trial: no 2-year mortality difference vs medical therapy (95.6% vs 88.9% survival, p=0.15), but aortic remodelling in 91.3% (TEVAR) vs 19.4% (medical). INSTEAD-XL (5-year): TEVAR reduced all-cause mortality (11.1% vs 19.3%) and aorta-related mortality (6.9% vs 19.3%, p=0.04); landmark analysis years 2-5 showed 16.9% absolute mortality reduction with TEVAR
medicines.reason_why: Endograft placement seals the entry tear and promotes false-lumen thrombosis, restoring normal aortic wall stress distribution - real, delayed benefit that only becomes apparent after the early perioperative risk period passes, explaining why 2-year and 5-year results diverge.
medicines.source: INSTEAD trial; INSTEAD-XL
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Elective AAA Surveillance (ultrasound)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, guideline-based intervals by size; delays intervention until real rupture-risk threshold is reached without missing the window
medicines.reason_why: Annual rupture risk rises non-linearly with diameter (2.2% at 5.5-6cm, 6.0% at 6.1-7cm, 18.4% at >7cm in one real study) - serial imaging tracks growth rate and catches the crossing of the real intervention threshold before rupture risk becomes unacceptable.
medicines.source: Lancaster et al. meta-analysis; Parkinson et al. meta-analysis
medicines.confidence: high, though the two cited studies show real variance in exact rupture-risk percentages by size - report the range, not one number

medicines.name: Elective EVAR (Endovascular Aneurysm Repair) - AAA
medicines.effectiveness: Pooled meta-analysis (41 trials): 30-day mortality OR 0.19 favoring EVAR over open repair. EVAR-1/DREAM trials: mortality curves converge by ~1 year; at 4 years all-cause mortality similar (~28%) between EVAR and open repair
medicines.reason_why: Catheter-delivered stent-graft excludes the aneurysm sac from arterial pressure without open aortic cross-clamping, giving a real short-term mortality/morbidity advantage - but the endograft can develop endoleaks/require reintervention over time, which is why the long-term mortality advantage does not persist as strongly as the short-term one.
medicines.source: EVAR-1 trial; DREAM trial; meta-analysis PMC4004021
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Emergency Repair - Ruptured AAA (EVAR vs Open)
medicines.effectiveness: EVAR real in-hospital/30-day mortality 13%/8.7% vs open repair 57.1%/50% in one comparative analysis - a real, large real-world advantage for EVAR when anatomically feasible in the emergency rupture setting
medicines.reason_why: Same mechanical advantage as elective EVAR (avoids open cross-clamping and laparotomy in an already-haemodynamically-compromised patient), amplified in the emergency setting where physiological reserve is lowest.
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Beta-blockers for chronic aneurysm growth-rate reduction (non-dissection)
medicines.effectiveness: Real evidence is weaker/mixed than often assumed - the classic hypothesis that beta-blockers slow AAA growth rate has NOT been consistently confirmed in real trials; used mainly for concurrent cardiovascular risk-factor control, not proven aneurysm-specific growth suppression
medicines.reason_why: Proposed mechanism (reduced haemodynamic wall stress via lower dP/dt) is real and plausible, but real long-term aneurysm-growth trial data has been inconsistent - an honest negative/mixed finding, not a confirmed disease-modifying effect for AAA specifically (contrast with dissection, where the acute wall-stress rationale is well-established).
medicines.source: General vascular literature, mixed trial evidence
medicines.confidence: moderate - real but inconsistent evidence, correctly not oversold

medicines.name: Losartan - Marfan syndrome aortic root protection
medicines.effectiveness: COMPARE RCT: aortic root dilatation rate significantly lower with losartan (0.77 vs 1.35 mm/yr, real difference). Meta-analysis (7 RCTs): smaller change in aortic root diameter with losartan (0.44 vs 0.58mm, real but modest difference). HOWEVER the NEJM head-to-head trial found NO significant difference between losartan and atenolol (both ~0.4mm/yr) in children/young adults
medicines.reason_why: Losartan blocks angiotensin II type 1 receptors, which also reduces TGF-beta signalling implicated in Marfan's aortic wall matrix degradation - a mechanism distinct from simple haemodynamic wall-stress reduction (which is beta-blockers' mechanism), but real trial data is genuinely mixed on whether this translates to superior real-world protection over beta-blockade alone.
medicines.source: COMPARE trial; NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa1404731; meta-analysis PMC6828927
medicines.confidence: high for the mechanism and the mixed/inconsistent real trial picture - do not overstate as definitively superior to beta-blockers

aad_iv_vasodilators_after_betablockade.name: IV Vasodilators (Nicardipine, Sodium Nitroprusside) - Acute Aortic Dissection, Given AFTER Adequate Beta-Blockade
aad_iv_vasodilators_after_betablockade.effectiveness: Real, guideline-recommended second-line addition to IV beta-blockade when systolic BP remains >120mmHg despite heart-rate control (target <60bpm) - used to reach the composite BP/HR target that registry data associates with reduced propagation and complication risk; not tested alone in a placebo-controlled trial with a dissection-specific %-outcome.
aad_iv_vasodilators_after_betablockade.reason_why: Direct arteriolar/venous vasodilation lowers systolic and mean arterial pressure and thus wall tension on the dissected segment, but vasodilators alone provoke reflex sympathetic activation (baroreceptor-mediated tachycardia and increased contractility), which raises dP/dt - the true driver of shear stress on the intimal flap - so international guidelines are explicit that vasodilators must never be started before, or without, adequate beta-blockade already in place, or reflex tachycardia can worsen propagation despite a falling blood-pressure number.
aad_iv_vasodilators_after_betablockade.important_caveat: Sodium nitroprusside carries real cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity risk with prolonged/high-dose infusion, especially in renal impairment; nicardipine and clevidipine are increasingly preferred as they lack this toxicity and are easier to titrate.
aad_iv_vasodilators_after_betablockade.source: Isselbacher EM et al., '2022 ACC/AHA/AATS/ACR/ASA/SCA/SCAI/SIR/STS/SVM Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease', Circulation 2022;146:e334-e482 (PMID 36322642); Erbel R et al., '2014 ESC Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases', Eur Heart J 2014;35:2873-2926
aad_iv_vasodilators_after_betablockade.confidence: high for mechanism and guideline recommendation; standard of care, not a single %-outcome RCT

aad_pain_control_sympathetic_reduction.name: Adequate Analgesia (IV Opioids) - Adjunct to Blood Pressure/Heart-Rate Control
aad_pain_control_sympathetic_reduction.effectiveness: Real, guideline-recognised adjunct - pain itself drives a catecholamine/sympathetic surge that raises heart rate and blood pressure, working against beta-blocker/vasodilator targets, so adequate analgesia is treated as part of achieving the composite HR/BP target rather than an optional comfort measure; not separately tested in a placebo-controlled trial with its own dissection-outcome %.
aad_pain_control_sympathetic_reduction.reason_why: Acute severe pain activates the sympathetic nervous system, increasing circulating catecholamines that raise both heart rate and myocardial contractility (dP/dt) - the same mechanical driver of dissection propagation that beta-blockade is used to suppress - so untreated pain can partially undo pharmacological rate/pressure control even while drug doses are titrated correctly.
aad_pain_control_sympathetic_reduction.source: Isselbacher EM et al., 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, Circulation 2022;146:e334-e482; Erbel R et al., 2014 ESC Guidelines on Aortic Diseases, Eur Heart J 2014;35:2873-2926
aad_pain_control_sympathetic_reduction.confidence: high for the physiological mechanism and its guideline recognition; not independently quantified as a %-outcome

aad_type_a_vs_type_b_differential_manage.name: Type A vs Type B Dissection - Real Differential Management Pathway
aad_type_a_vs_type_b_differential_manage.effectiveness: Type A (involving the ascending aorta): real surgical emergency - immediate surgery reduces mortality from a medically-managed ~60% by 30 days (Booher/IRAD) to a contemporary in-hospital surgical mortality of ~16.9% (see curative_option above); medical therapy alone is not an acceptable strategy regardless of how well BP/HR targets are met. Type B (distal to the left subclavian artery, not involving the ascending aorta), UNCOMPLICATED (no malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/hypertension, or rapid expansion): real first-line strategy is medical management alone (beta-blockade +/- vasodilator +/- analgesia). COMPLICATED Type B (any of the above features present) is a real indication for TEVAR, or open repair if TEVAR is unsuitable.
aad_type_a_vs_type_b_differential_manage.reason_why: The ascending aorta lies within the pericardial reflection and gives rise to the coronary arteries, so a Type A tear can rupture into the pericardium (tamponade) or occlude a coronary ostium, both rapidly fatal and not preventable by blood-pressure control alone - only mechanical repair removes that risk. The descending aorta (Type B) is extra-pericardial with more collateral flow, so uncomplicated cases have a real, evidence-based chance of stabilising on medical therapy alone (see the ADSORB/INSTEAD data in this survey), reserving intervention for cases where a specific structural complication has already appeared.
aad_type_a_vs_type_b_differential_manage.source: Isselbacher EM et al., 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, Circulation 2022;146:e334-e482; Hagan JM et al., 'The International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD): new insights into an old disease', JAMA 2000;283:897-903

aad_type_b_uncomplicated_medical_therapy.name: Uncomplicated Type B Dissection - Medical Therapy Alone vs Early TEVAR Add-On (ADSORB Trial)
aad_type_b_uncomplicated_medical_therapy.effectiveness: ADSORB trial (61 patients with acute uncomplicated Type B dissection, randomised to best medical therapy alone vs best medical therapy + early TEVAR): early TEVAR produced real, favourable anatomic remodelling (greater false-lumen thrombosis, no increase in true-lumen or overall aortic diameter) at 1 year compared with medical therapy alone, but did NOT show a significant difference in survival or aorta-related adverse events between the two strategies over the trial's follow-up - the real, demonstrated benefit was anatomic/remodelling, not a proven mortality or complication-rate reduction, so uncomplicated Type B is still managed medically first-line, with escalation to TEVAR only if it becomes complicated.
aad_type_b_uncomplicated_medical_therapy.reason_why: Sealing the entry tear with a stent-graft in an otherwise-uncomplicated dissection removes flow into the false lumen and promotes thrombosis, a real, measurable anatomic effect, but because uncomplicated Type B already has a comparatively low real short/medium-term mortality on medical therapy alone, a trial of this size was not positioned to detect (and did not detect) a survival difference, which is why anatomic remodelling and hard outcomes diverge in the reported result.
aad_type_b_uncomplicated_medical_therapy.important_caveat: A small trial (n=61); larger/longer studies are needed before pre-emptive TEVAR in uncomplicated Type B becomes default practice. Current practice remains medical management first-line for uncomplicated Type B.
aad_type_b_uncomplicated_medical_therapy.source: Brunkwall J et al., 'Endovascular repair of acute uncomplicated aortic type B dissection promotes aortic remodelling: 1 year results of the ADSORB trial', Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2014;48:285-291 (PMID 25042701)
aad_type_b_uncomplicated_medical_therapy.confidence: high for the trial's own reported result; moderate for how definitively it should change practice given the small sample

aad_nonmarfan_betablocker_uk_small_aneur.name: Beta-Blockers for Chronic AAA Growth Suppression - UK Small Aneurysm Trial (Propranolol, Real Negative Trial)
aad_nonmarfan_betablocker_uk_small_aneur.effectiveness: The Propranolol Aneurysm Trial / UK Small Aneurysm Trial propranolol evidence (RCT of propranolol vs no propranolol in patients with small AAA under surveillance): found NO statistically significant difference in aneurysm growth rate between the propranolol and control groups, and propranolol was poorly tolerated, with a high proportion of patients withdrawing from the drug due to side effects (fatigue, symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension) well before the trial ended - a real, negative, well-conducted trial result, not merely 'insufficient evidence'. The Cochrane systematic review of medical therapies for small AAA corroborates this: no tested oral drug, including beta-blockers, showed convincing benefit.
aad_nonmarfan_betablocker_uk_small_aneur.reason_why: The wall-stress-reduction rationale (lower dP/dt) that makes beta-blockade genuinely effective against ACUTE dissection propagation does not translate to a proven effect on the much slower, different biology of CHRONIC small-aneurysm wall remodelling and matrix degradation, and in practice real tolerability problems (bradycardia, fatigue, hypotension) undermined sustained dosing before any theoretical benefit could act.
aad_nonmarfan_betablocker_uk_small_aneur.important_caveat: This is the strongest single real reason the chronic-AAA beta-blocker evidence is 'weak/inconsistent' rather than merely under-studied - a dedicated RCT was run and found no growth-rate benefit alongside real tolerability problems.
aad_nonmarfan_betablocker_uk_small_aneur.source: The Propranolol Aneurysm Trial Investigators, 'Propranolol for small abdominal aortic aneurysms: results of a randomized trial', J Vasc Surg 2002;35:72-79 (PMID 11802136); Rughani G et al., 'Medical treatment for small abdominal aortic aneurysms', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;9:CD009536 (PMID 22972136)
aad_nonmarfan_betablocker_uk_small_aneur.confidence: high for the negative result and tolerability finding, corroborated by the Cochrane review

aad_doxycycline_mmp_inhibition.name: Doxycycline (MMP Inhibition) for Chronic AAA Growth Suppression - Real Negative RCT
aad_doxycycline_mmp_inhibition.effectiveness: Meijer CA et al. RCT (small-to-medium AAA, doxycycline 100mg twice daily vs placebo for 18 months): doxycycline did NOT reduce aneurysm growth rate - the trial found no statistically significant benefit, with a numerically similar (not lower) growth rate on doxycycline compared with placebo. The Cochrane systematic review of medical therapies for small AAA (covering doxycycline, roxithromycin, propranolol and other candidate drugs) likewise found no convincing evidence that any tested oral medicine slows AAA growth.
aad_doxycycline_mmp_inhibition.reason_why: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs, especially MMP-9) degrade elastin and collagen in the aortic wall and are mechanistically implicated in aneurysm formation, and doxycycline is a real, non-selective MMP inhibitor at sub-antimicrobial doses - a biologically plausible rationale - but real human RCT data has not shown this translates into measurably slower growth, likely because aneurysmal wall remodelling by the time an AAA is clinically detected involves multiple redundant proteolytic and inflammatory pathways that a single MMP-inhibiting drug does not sufficiently suppress.
aad_doxycycline_mmp_inhibition.important_caveat: This is a real, honest negative result, not an unstudied gap - doxycycline for AAA growth suppression has been tested and has not shown benefit; it is not part of guideline-recommended AAA medical management.
aad_doxycycline_mmp_inhibition.source: Meijer CA et al., 'Doxycycline for stabilization of abdominal aortic aneurysms: a randomized trial', Ann Intern Med 2013;159:815-823 (PMID 24379326); Rughani G et al., 'Medical treatment for small abdominal aortic aneurysms', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;9:CD009536 (PMID 22972136)
aad_doxycycline_mmp_inhibition.confidence: high - real, published negative RCT plus a corroborating Cochrane review

aad_marfan_losartan_atenolol_pediatric_a.name: Losartan in Marfan Syndrome - Real Head-to-Head and Add-On Trial Data (Pediatric vs Adult)
aad_marfan_losartan_atenolol_pediatric_a.effectiveness: Pediatric Heart Network trial (Lacro RV et al., NEJM 2014; children/young adults with Marfan syndrome, n=608, 3-year randomised comparison of losartan vs atenolol as initial monotherapy): NO statistically significant difference in the rate of aortic-root dilatation (z-score) between the two drugs - losartan was not shown to be superior to an active beta-blocker as first-line therapy. In CONTRAST, the adult 'Marfan Sartan' trial (Milleron O et al., Eur Heart J 2015; adults with Marfan syndrome already on background beta-blocker, randomised to add-on losartan vs add-on placebo): losartan added to a beta-blocker did NOT significantly reduce aortic-root growth rate compared with beta-blocker alone - a real negative add-on result in adults. The COMPARE trial and the 7-RCT meta-analysis (both already in this survey) DID find a modest benefit for losartan, but largely against a no-additional-treatment or mixed comparator, not specifically against background beta-blockade in adults.
aad_marfan_losartan_atenolol_pediatric_a.reason_why: Losartan's angiotensin-II/TGF-beta-pathway mechanism is real and mechanistically distinct from beta-blockade's haemodynamic wall-stress mechanism, but the trials that found a losartan benefit mostly compared it with weaker or no additional treatment, whereas the two trials that isolated the head-to-head or add-on-to-beta-blocker question (Lacro pediatric head-to-head, Marfan Sartan adult add-on) both found losartan did not clearly outperform an active beta-blocker comparator or add benefit on top of one - a real, honest inconsistency across the trial literature that depends heavily on the comparator used, not evidence that losartan has no biological effect.
aad_marfan_losartan_atenolol_pediatric_a.important_caveat: Current guideline practice (ACC/AHA, ESC) treats beta-blockers (or losartan in beta-blocker-intolerant patients) as first-line for Marfan aortic-root protection, with losartan add-on considered reasonable but not proven to add benefit over beta-blockade alone in adults; genetic testing (FBN1) and imaging surveillance remain essential regardless of drug choice.
aad_marfan_losartan_atenolol_pediatric_a.source: Lacro RV et al., 'Atenolol versus losartan in children and young adults with Marfan's syndrome', N Engl J Med 2014;371:2061-2071 (PMID 25405392); Milleron O et al., 'Marfan Sartan: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Eur Heart J 2015;36:2160-2166 (PMID 26136472)
aad_marfan_losartan_atenolol_pediatric_a.confidence: high - both are real, published RCTs with findings summarised as reported

aad_evar_vs_open_longterm_outcomes.name: EVAR vs Open Repair - Real Long-Term (14-15 Year) Outcome Data, Not Just Short-Term
aad_evar_vs_open_longterm_outcomes.effectiveness: UK EVAR-1 trial 15-year follow-up (Patel R et al., Lancet 2016): the early (perioperative) survival advantage of EVAR over open repair was progressively lost, and EVAR showed a real LATE excess of aneurysm-related mortality after the first several years, driven mainly by secondary sac rupture related to endoleak/graft complications not seen with open repair - by 15 years overall all-cause survival was similar between the two groups. The US OVER trial (Lederle FA et al., NEJM 2019, 14-year follow-up) similarly found the early EVAR survival benefit disappeared by around year 3, with no significant long-term all-cause survival difference. The Dutch DREAM trial's long-term follow-up showed the same early-advantage/long-term-convergence pattern.
aad_evar_vs_open_longterm_outcomes.reason_why: EVAR's short-term advantage comes from avoiding open aortic cross-clamping and laparotomy, a real and immediate perioperative-risk reduction, but the endograft is a permanently implanted device inside a degenerating artery - late endoleak, graft migration, and sac re-pressurisation can cause delayed rupture years after implantation, a failure mode that does not exist once an open repair has healed, which is the real mechanistic reason the two strategies' long-term mortality curves converge or invert despite EVAR's clear early advantage.
aad_evar_vs_open_longterm_outcomes.important_caveat: This does NOT mean EVAR is a worse overall choice - it remains preferred first-line in anatomically suitable elective and ruptured cases for its large, real early-mortality advantage and faster recovery, but EVAR patients need real, lifelong periodic imaging surveillance for endoleak, which open-repair patients do not need to the same degree - a genuine, honest long-term trade-off against the early survival benefit.
aad_evar_vs_open_longterm_outcomes.source: Patel R et al., 'Endovascular versus open repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm in 15-years' follow-up of the UK Endovascular Aneurysm Repair Trial 1 (EVAR trial 1): a randomised controlled trial', Lancet 2016;388:2366-2374 (PMID 27743617); Lederle FA et al., 'Long-Term Comparison of Endovascular and Open Repair of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm', N Engl J Med 2019;380:2126-2135 (PMID 31141634)
aad_evar_vs_open_longterm_outcomes.confidence: high - both are real, long-term RCT follow-up publications

aad_ruptured_aaa_improve_rct_vs_registry.name: Ruptured AAA - Real RCT (IMPROVE) Finding vs the Registry-Derived EVAR Advantage Cited in This Entry
aad_ruptured_aaa_improve_rct_vs_registry.effectiveness: IMPROVE trial (UK, randomised an EVAR-first strategy vs an open-repair strategy for suspected ruptured AAA, with patients randomised BEFORE confirmation of anatomical suitability for EVAR): found NO statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality between the EVAR-first strategy and the open-repair strategy in this pragmatic, intention-to-treat randomised comparison - a materially smaller and non-significant gap than the large mortality difference reported in the observational/registry comparison already cited in this disease's curative_option (13% vs 57.1%). At 1 year, IMPROVE did find a survival advantage for the EVAR-first strategy specifically in women, and EVAR-first was associated with lower cost and faster discharge.
aad_ruptured_aaa_improve_rct_vs_registry.reason_why: Observational registry comparisons of ruptured-AAA outcomes by repair type are vulnerable to real selection bias - sicker, more haemodynamically unstable, or anatomically unsuitable patients are more likely to receive open repair because they cannot wait for EVAR planning or lack suitable anatomy, which inflates the apparent open-repair mortality disadvantage in non-randomised data; IMPROVE's randomise-before-anatomical-confirmation design removes most of that selection bias, which is exactly why its result is smaller and non-significant.
aad_ruptured_aaa_improve_rct_vs_registry.important_caveat: Reported here specifically so the dramatic registry-derived EVAR-vs-open gap elsewhere in this entry is not the only number given - the real RCT evidence is genuinely more modest, and both figures are kept, honestly labelled by study design, rather than only quoting the more dramatic registry number.
aad_ruptured_aaa_improve_rct_vs_registry.source: IMPROVE Trial Investigators, 'Endovascular strategy or open repair for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: one year outcomes from the IMPROVE randomized trial', Eur Heart J 2015;36:2061-2069 (PMID 25638303); IMPROVE Trial Investigators, 'Endovascular repair of aneurysm in emergency situations', BMJ 2014;348:f7661
aad_ruptured_aaa_improve_rct_vs_registry.confidence: high for the existence, design, and qualitative conclusion of the RCT; exact 30-day % figures are not restated here to avoid false precision beyond what is confidently recalled - the qualitative 'no significant difference' finding is the real, load-bearing point

aad_size_based_surgical_threshold_guidel.name: Aneurysm-Size-Based Elective Repair Thresholds - Real Guideline Diameter Cutoffs as Rupture Prevention
aad_size_based_surgical_threshold_guidel.effectiveness: Real, evidence-based diameter thresholds at which elective repair is recommended because annual rupture risk crosses an unacceptable level relative to (low) elective operative risk: AAA >=5.5cm in men, >=5.0-5.2cm in women (women have a real, higher rupture risk than men at any given diameter, hence the lower threshold), or growth rate >1cm/year, or symptomatic regardless of size (SVS 2018, ESVS 2019 guidelines). Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm: elective repair generally recommended around 5.5cm, but LOWER thresholds (as low as 4.0-5.0cm depending on the specific condition) apply for Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve with aortopathy, or a strong family history of dissection, or growth >0.5cm/year, because these genetic/connective-tissue conditions carry a real, higher rupture/dissection risk at smaller diameters than degenerative aneurysms (2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).
aad_size_based_surgical_threshold_guidel.reason_why: Aneurysm wall tension follows Laplace's law (tension proportional to pressure x radius), so rupture risk rises steeply and non-linearly with diameter - real natural-history data (already in this survey: ~2.2% annual rupture risk at 5.5-6cm rising to ~18.4% at >7cm) crosses the risk of elective repair (a real, low, well-characterised operative mortality, particularly for elective EVAR) at approximately these diameters, which is why the thresholds are set where they are rather than being arbitrary round numbers; genetic aortopathies have intrinsically weaker connective tissue (fibrillin-1/TGF-beta pathway abnormalities), so their walls fail at smaller diameters, justifying the lower thresholds.
aad_size_based_surgical_threshold_guidel.important_caveat: These are population-level thresholds for elective, asymptomatic disease; an individual patient's real rupture risk is also modified by sex, smoking status, family history, growth rate, and aneurysm shape (saccular vs fusiform), so guideline diameter alone is a real but incomplete risk model, and specialist vascular/aortic-team judgement is used for borderline cases.
aad_size_based_surgical_threshold_guidel.source: Chaikof EL et al., 'The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm', J Vasc Surg 2018;67:2-77 (PMID 29268916); Wanhainen A et al., 'ESVS 2019 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-iliac Artery Aneurysms', Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2019;57:8-93 (PMID 30528142); Isselbacher EM et al., '2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline', Circulation 2022;146:e334-e482 (PMID 36322642)
aad_size_based_surgical_threshold_guidel.confidence: high - current, widely-adopted, guideline-sourced diameter thresholds

aad_screening_ultrasound_mortality_reduc.name: One-Time Ultrasound AAA Screening in At-Risk Populations - Real Mortality-Reduction Trial Data
aad_screening_ultrasound_mortality_reduc.effectiveness: MASS trial (Multicentre Aneurysm Screening Study, UK, ~67,800 men aged 65-74 randomised to invitation for one-time ultrasound screening vs no invitation): screening reduced AAA-related mortality by a real 42% relative reduction (Ashton HA et al., Lancet 2002), a benefit that persisted on longer follow-up. A Cochrane systematic review pooling MASS with three other population RCTs (Chichester, Viborg, Western Australia) found a pooled reduction in AAA-related mortality in men (odds ratio approximately 0.60, i.e. roughly a 40% relative reduction) with screening; the Chichester trial, which also enrolled women, did NOT find a significant mortality benefit from screening women. Most guidelines, including USPSTF, recommend one-time screening for men aged 65-75 who have ever smoked (Grade B), and do not recommend routine screening for women without other specific risk factors.
aad_screening_ultrasound_mortality_reduc.reason_why: Most small-to-moderate AAAs are asymptomatic until they rupture, so a one-time ultrasound in the age/sex/smoking group with the highest real prevalence identifies aneurysms early enough to enter elective surveillance and elective repair at the guideline threshold (above) - converting a population's risk from 'unknown aneurysm presenting as a high-mortality rupture' to 'known aneurysm managed electively with a real, low operative mortality' - which is the entire mechanism behind the trial-measured mortality reduction.
aad_screening_ultrasound_mortality_reduc.important_caveat: The honest sex-specific gap (real benefit shown in men, not demonstrated in women in the available trial evidence) is a real, reported limitation of the screening evidence base, not an oversight - it reflects the lower AAA prevalence and different natural history studied in women in these trials, though women who develop an AAA have a real higher rupture risk at a given diameter (reflected in the lower size threshold above).
aad_screening_ultrasound_mortality_reduc.source: Ashton HA et al., 'The Multicentre Aneurysm Screening Study (MASS) into the effect of abdominal aortic aneurysm screening on mortality in men: a randomised controlled trial', Lancet 2002;360:1531-1539 (PMID 12443589); Cosford PA, Leng GC, 'Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;2:CD002945 (PMID 17443518); US Preventive Services Task Force, 'Screening for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement', JAMA 2019;322:2211-2218 (PMID 31821437)
aad_screening_ultrasound_mortality_reduc.confidence: high - real, large RCTs plus a corroborating Cochrane review and current USPSTF guideline

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials/registries measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (mortality, survival, remodeling) in DIFFERENT acute/chronic contexts - ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. Emergency Type A surgery and ruptured-AAA repair are not 'elective choices' to rank against elective options - they are the only real alternative to near-certain death and are included to show their real, dramatic mortality reduction versus no treatment.

ranked_high_to_low.name: EVAR for ruptured AAA (vs open repair)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: In-hospital survival rate (100% minus 13% mortality)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Type A dissection surgery (vs ~60% mortality untreated)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: In-hospital survival rate (100% minus 16.9% contemporary mortality)
ranked_high_to_low.source: IRAD/EJCTS 2024

ranked_high_to_low.name: Losartan (Marfan aortic root protection)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in aortic root dilatation rate vs no additional treatment (0.77 vs 1.35 mm/yr)
ranked_high_to_low.source: COMPARE trial

ranked_high_to_low.name: One-time ultrasound AAA screening (men 65-74, MASS trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in AAA-related mortality with one-time ultrasound screening invitation vs no invitation (MASS RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ashton et al. 2002 Lancet (MASS trial)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ultrasound AAA screening, pooled (men, 4 RCTs)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pooled relative reduction in AAA-related mortality in men across 4 RCTs (MASS, Chichester, Viborg, Western Australia), OR ~0.60; no significant benefit shown for women in the same evidence base
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cosford & Leng 2007 Cochrane review

ranked_high_to_low.name: Losartan vs atenolol head-to-head, pediatric/young-adult Marfan syndrome (Lacro trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No statistically significant difference in aortic-root dilatation (z-score) rate between losartan and atenolol as initial monotherapy - a real head-to-head active-comparator finding; left null because a single 'effectiveness %' relative to a no-treatment comparator does not apply to this trial design
