ranked_high_to_low.name: Early TEVAR add-on for uncomplicated Type B dissection (ADSORB trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real anatomic remodelling (false-lumen thrombosis) improved with early TEVAR, but no significant survival/aorta-event difference vs medical therapy alone was demonstrated - left null because the trial's own endpoint was anatomic, not a comparable mortality percentage
ranked_high_to_low.source: Brunkwall et al. 2014 (ADSORB trial)

ranked_high_to_low.name: EVAR-first vs open-repair strategy for ruptured AAA (IMPROVE RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality between an EVAR-first strategy and an open-repair strategy for ruptured AAA in a randomised, intention-to-treat design - contrasts with the larger registry-derived gap ranked above; left null (precise digits not restated) to avoid false precision beyond confidently-recalled values
ranked_high_to_low.source: IMPROVE Trial Investigators 2014/2015

ranked_high_to_low.name: EVAR vs open repair, 15-year long-term follow-up (EVAR-1/OVER trials)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Early EVAR survival advantage over open repair was lost by 14-15 years due to late aneurysm-related mortality catch-up (secondary rupture/endoleak, EVAR-1) or convergence by ~3 years (OVER); overall long-term all-cause survival not significantly different between strategies - left null because no single comparable % exists for a convergence/reversal pattern over time
ranked_high_to_low.source: Patel et al. 2016 Lancet (EVAR-1, 15-year); Lederle et al. 2019 NEJM (OVER, 14-year)

mitral_stenosis.name: Mitral Stenosis
mitral_stenosis.icd11_hint: BB61 Rheumatic mitral valve diseases / BC61 Nonrheumatic mitral valve stenosis
mitral_stenosis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Sudden severe breathlessness/frothy pink sputum (acute pulmonary oedema, often triggered by new fast atrial fibrillation, fever, exertion or pregnancy), coughing up large amounts of blood (massive haemoptysis / pulmonary apoplexy), or sudden weakness/vision loss/limb pain (systemic embolism/stroke from a left atrial clot) in a person with known or suspected mitral stenosis is a cardiac emergency — call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Do not wait for a scheduled cardiology appointment.

core.name: Exertional breathlessness (dyspnoea on exertion)
core.note: the most common presenting symptom, from elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure behind the narrowed valve

core.name: Fatigue / reduced exercise tolerance (low forward cardiac output)
Palpitations (often the first symptom of new atrial fibrillation, which occurs in 40-75% of symptomatic mitral stenosis patients
core.note: real, sourced statistic)

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Opening snap followed by a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur, loudest at the cardiac apex in the left lateral position
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: classic auscultatory finding

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Malar flush
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: plum-coloured discolouration of the cheeks with peripheral cyanosis, occurring with low cardiac output combined with severe pulmonary hypertension

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Ortner syndrome (cardio-vocal syndrome)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: hoarseness of voice from compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by an enlarged left atrium or dilated pulmonary artery (real, sourced mechanism)

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Haemoptysis
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: from rupture of dilated bronchial-pulmonary venous anastomoses under chronically raised pulmonary venous pressure ('pulmonary apoplexy'); can also occur as pink frothy sputum in acute pulmonary oedema

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Signs of right heart failure in advanced disease (raised JVP, peripheral oedema, ascites) once pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction develop

stages.name: At risk of MS
stages.criteria: Mild valve thickening with mild doming during diastole; history of rheumatic fever

stages.name: Progressive MS
stages.criteria: Rheumatic valve changes with commissural fusion; mitral valve area (MVA) > 1.5 cm²
stages.symptoms: None to mild; may have exertional dyspnoea

stages.name: Asymptomatic severe MS
stages.criteria: MVA ≤ 1.5 cm² (very severe ≤ 1.0 cm²); C1 = no significant pulmonary hypertension; C2 = with pulmonary hypertension (PASP > 30 mmHg) or right ventricular dysfunction

stages.name: Symptomatic severe MS
stages.criteria: MVA ≤ 1.5 cm² with elevated gradient

grades.name: Mild
grades.criteria: MVA > 1.5 cm², mean gradient < 5 mmHg, PASP < 30 mmHg

grades.name: Moderate
grades.criteria: MVA 1.0 - 1.5 cm², mean gradient 5 - 10 mmHg, PASP 30 - 50 mmHg

grades.name: Severe
grades.criteria: MVA < 1.0 cm², mean gradient > 10 mmHg, PASP > 50 mmHg

echo_severity_grading.caveat: Mean transmitral gradient is flow-dependent (rises with tachycardia/high output, falls with low cardiac output or bradycardia) -- a low gradient does NOT reliably exclude severe stenosis when cardiac output is reduced; mitral valve area (planimetry or pressure half-time) is the more load-independent measure of true severity.

real_risk_factors.factor: History of rheumatic fever / rheumatic heart disease
real_risk_factors.note: Dominant real-world cause of MS worldwide and in India; the post-streptococcal autoimmune valvulitis mechanism and its roughly 20-year latency to symptomatic MS are detailed in definition_and_pathophysiology.rheumatic_mechanism above.
real_risk_factors.source: Carapetis JR, McDonald M, Wilson NJ, 'Acute rheumatic fever', Lancet 2005;366(9480):155-168, PMID 16005340

real_risk_factors.note: Rheumatic MS shows a real, consistently documented female predominance; GBD 2019 data found RHD disproportionately affects women (22.52 million of the global prevalent RHD cases in 2019), and the Meghalaya India school-screening study already in this entry found subclinical RHD roughly 2x more common in girls (6.29/1000) than boys (3.04/1000).
real_risk_factors.source: Ghamari SH et al., J Am Heart Assoc 2022;11(15):e025284, PMID 35730651; Meghalaya school RHD screening study 2021-2022 (already cited in this entry's additional_real_findings)

real_risk_factors.factor: Low-resource / developing-country residence with limited access to penicillin prophylaxis
real_risk_factors.note: RHD/MS burden is concentrated in low- and middle-income countries where primary prevention (treating streptococcal pharyngitis) and secondary prevention (long-term benzathine penicillin prophylaxis after acute rheumatic fever to prevent recurrent carditis) are inconsistently accessible; the South Asia super-region (including India) carries the world's highest age-standardised RHD death rate (11.2/100,000, roughly 10x Latin America/Caribbean).
real_risk_factors.source: Carapetis JR et al., Lancet 2005;366(9480):155-168, PMID 16005340; Ghamari SH et al., J Am Heart Assoc 2022;11(15):e025284, PMID 35730651

real_risk_factors.factor: Degenerative mitral annular calcification (MAC) - a non-rheumatic cause of MS
real_risk_factors.note: MAC-related functional MS is a distinct, non-rheumatic pathway seen more in older patients, women, and those with chronic kidney disease, diabetes or hyperparathyroidism; each additional decade of age raises the odds of MAC roughly 3.7-fold, and MAC-related MS carries a distinct (generally worse) prognosis than rheumatic MS - see differential_diagnosis.severe_mitral_annular_calcification_mac above for the full distinguishing-feature and outcome comparison.
real_risk_factors.source: 'Mitral Annular Calcification-Related Mitral Stenosis: 5-Year Outcomes and Prognostic Determinants (JAMAC Study)', JACC 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2025.12.004; 'Two Faces of Mitral Stenosis...', J Am Heart Assoc 2025, DOI 10.1161/JAHA.125.045018

additional_real_findings.category: India epidemiology (rheumatic heart disease, the dominant cause of MS)
additional_real_findings.finding: School-screening study in Meghalaya, India (Nov 2021-Nov 2022; n=4,039 children aged 5-15, echo screening using World Heart Federation criteria): subclinical RHD prevalence 4.7 per 1000 vs clinical RHD 0.49 per 1000 (subclinical disease ~10x more common than clinically detected disease); prevalence ~2x higher in females (6.29/1000) than males (3.04/1000); higher in rural (5.23/1000) and government schools (7.68/1000) than urban (3.86/1000) or private schools (5.99/1000). India carries an estimated 40% of the global burden of rheumatic heart disease.
additional_real_findings.source: Meghalaya school RHD screening study, 2021-2022 (WHF echo criteria)

additional_real_findings.finding: Mitral stenosis is one of the most dangerous valve lesions in pregnancy: the physiological rise in heart rate, blood volume and cardiac output shortens diastolic filling time and raises left atrial/pulmonary pressure, precipitating pulmonary oedema. In a 10-year study of 81 pregnant women with MS: 8.6% developed new atrial fibrillation during pregnancy; 13.6% had a cardiovascular event overall, including 6.2% pulmonary oedema and 6.2% peripheral/systemic embolism. About 80% of systemic emboli in MS occur in patients who also have atrial fibrillation. Risk of cardiac decompensation is highest in the 2nd-3rd trimester, and the risk of maternal death is greatest during labour and the immediate postpartum period.
additional_real_findings.source: 10-year tertiary-centre pregnancy-outcomes study in women with MS (PMC11890220); Merck Manual Professional

additional_real_findings.finding: Atrial fibrillation occurs in 40-75% of symptomatic MS patients (rising with left atrial enlargement/age) and is the strongest driver of systemic embolic stroke risk in MS — left atrial stasis from both the valve obstruction and AF promotes left atrial appendage thrombus formation.
additional_real_findings.source: PMC10686862; MSD Manual; StatPearls Mitral Stenosis

red_flags: Sudden worsening breathlessness with pink frothy sputum — acute pulmonary oedema, often precipitated by new fast atrial fibrillation, fever, exertion, or pregnancy
Massive haemoptysis (coughing up large volumes of blood) — pulmonary apoplexy from ruptured bronchial-pulmonary venous anastomoses
Sudden focal neurological deficit, limb pain/pallor, or loss of vision — systemic embolism (stroke or limb ischaemia) from a left atrial thrombus, especially in the presence of atrial fibrillation
Signs of severe pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure (raised JVP, peripheral oedema) signalling advanced, decompensated disease
symptoms.severity_gradient: Mild MS (MVA > 1.5 cm^2) is often asymptomatic. Moderate MS (MVA 1.0-1.5 cm^2) typically causes exertional dyspnoea. Severe MS (MVA < 1.0 cm^2) causes symptoms at rest or minimal exertion, with high risk of atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, and the acute emergencies listed below (pulmonary oedema, haemoptysis, systemic embolism).

rheumatic_mechanism.finding: Rheumatic MS begins with molecular mimicry: group A Streptococcus pyogenes M-protein and the group A carbohydrate epitope (N-acetyl-glucosamine) share structural homology with cardiac myosin and valve-endothelial proteins. Cross-reactive antibodies raised against the streptococcal antigens bind valvular endothelium (upregulating VCAM-1), which recruits CD4+/CD8+ T cells into the normally avascular valve leaflet; a sustained Th1 cytokine-driven inflammatory response then drives progressive leaflet fibrosis, commissural fusion, chordal thickening/fusion and eventual calcification - the anatomic substrate the Wilkins score (see diagnostic_framework below) grades directly. This is the same post-streptococcal autoimmune process documented in this KB's own acute_rheumatic_fever entry; mitral stenosis is its chronic valvular sequela rather than a separate disease mechanism, and it is not duplicated in full here. Critically, the acute carditis-to-symptomatic-stenosis interval is usually long: classic natural-history data show symptoms of pure rheumatic MS often do not appear until roughly 20 years after the acute rheumatic fever episode (see natural_history.latency_and_progression below for the full survival timeline).
rheumatic_mechanism.source: Cunningham MW, 'Rheumatic fever, autoimmunity, and molecular mimicry: the streptococcal connection', Int Rev Immunol 2014;33(4):314-329, PMID 24892819; Carapetis JR, McDonald M, Wilson NJ, 'Acute rheumatic fever', Lancet 2005;366(9480):155-168, PMID 16005340
rheumatic_mechanism.confidence: high - established, cross-validated autoimmune-pathogenesis and natural-history literature

hemodynamic_mechanism_LA_pressure_and_pu.finding: The fused, narrowed mitral orifice creates a fixed diastolic pressure gradient between the left atrium (LA) and left ventricle; to maintain forward flow across this fixed obstruction the LA must generate progressively higher pressure, producing chronic LA pressure and volume overload, LA dilatation and eventually LA myopathy/fibrosis. This raised LA pressure is transmitted backward into the pulmonary venous and capillary bed, producing an initial 'passive' component of pulmonary hypertension that rises and falls directly with LA pressure and is rapidly reversible once the obstruction is relieved. With sustained elevation, a second, 'reactive' component develops: pulmonary arteriolar medial hypertrophy and intimal proliferation raise pulmonary vascular resistance disproportionately to LA pressure (a physiological 'second stenosis' protecting the capillary bed from pressure/oedema), which can become only partially reversible with long-standing severe disease and drives right ventricular pressure overload, right heart failure, tricuspid regurgitation and the malar flush/right-heart-failure signs already documented in this entry's specific_diagnostic_signs.
hemodynamic_mechanism_LA_pressure_and_pu.source: Fawzy ME, 'Nature of pulmonary hypertension in mitral stenosis', PMC503905; Maron BA, Hess E, Maddox TM et al., 'Pulmonary Hypertension in Aortic and Mitral Valve Disease', PMC5974123; Otto CM, 'HAVEC Group review: Pulmonary Hypertension in Valvular Disease', J Am Coll Cardiol 2016
hemodynamic_mechanism_LA_pressure_and_pu.confidence: high - consistent passive-then-reactive mechanism across independent reviews; post-intervention reversibility is directly observed clinically

af_development_mechanism.finding: Chronic LA pressure/volume overload from MS causes progressive LA stretch, myocyte hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis - the same structural-remodelling substrate described generically in this KB's atrial_fibrillation entry (definition_and_pathophysiology.mechanism), but reached here via mechanical valve obstruction rather than a primary atrial-electrical trigger. Larger LA diameter/volume and greater LA fibrosis burden (quantifiable on speckle-tracking echocardiography or cardiac MRI late-gadolinium-enhancement mapping) are independent predictors of new-onset AF in rheumatic MS cohorts, and low LA reservoir strain has been shown to predict incident AF at a strain cut-off of approximately 17.9% in one prospective echo cohort. This is the mechanistic basis for the 40-75% AF prevalence already documented in this entry's core/additional_real_findings sections, and for why AF risk rises with disease duration and LA size rather than with mitral-valve-area severity alone.
af_development_mechanism.source: Verma B et al., 'Is left atrial fibrosis an independent determinant of atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis?', PMID 34474767; left-atrial-strain rheumatic-MS cohort study on speckle-tracking prediction of new-onset AF, ScienceDirect S0894731721008828; Andrade J, Khairy P, Dobrev D, Nattel S, Circ Res 2014;114(9):1453-1468, PMID 24763464 (general atrial electrical/structural remodelling mechanism, cross-referenced from the atrial_fibrillation entry)
af_development_mechanism.confidence: moderate-high - consistent direction across independent echo/MRI cohorts; exact strain cut-offs are cohort-specific and not yet a single universally validated threshold

echocardiography_primary_tool_planimetry.finding: Transthoracic echocardiography is the primary real-world diagnostic tool for MS, used both to confirm the diagnosis and to grade severity (already tabulated in this entry's echo_severity_grading). Two quantitative methods calculate mitral valve area (MVA): direct 2D planimetry (tracing the anatomic orifice at the leaflet tips in the parasternal short-axis view) and the Doppler pressure half-time (PHT) method (MVA = 220/PHT, derived from the rate of deceleration of the transmitral diastolic velocity). Head-to-head validation shows the two methods disagree meaningfully in specific conditions: comparing PHT against 2D planimetry, disagreement averaged 8.0 +/- 19.2% in patients in sinus rhythm but rose to -24.9 +/- 13.9% in patients with atrial fibrillation, and PHT is separately known to be unreliable immediately after balloon valvuloplasty and in the presence of significant mitral or aortic regurgitation or abnormal LV/LA compliance. Because of this, 2D (or 3D) planimetry by an experienced operator is preferred as the primary MVA method where image quality allows, with PHT used as a secondary/confirmatory measure rather than the sole determinant of severity - consistent with this entry's existing echo_severity_grading caveat that gradient/PHT-based measures are flow- and rhythm-dependent while anatomic planimetry is the more load-independent gold standard.
echocardiography_primary_tool_planimetry.source: Pressure half-time vs planimetry disagreement in sinus rhythm vs AF, Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography, S0894-7317(08)00665-2; 'Inaccuracy of Pressure Half-Time Method for Valve Area in Mitral Stenosis Related to Annular Calcification', Am J Cardiol 2024, S0002-9149(24)00602-7; Otto CM, Textbook of Clinical Echocardiography, mitral stenosis quantification chapter
echocardiography_primary_tool_planimetry.confidence: high - multiple independent validation studies agree on the direction and rhythm-dependence of PHT error

wilkins_score_valvuloplasty_candidacy.finding: The Wilkins (Wilkins-Block) echocardiographic score, derived in 1988, grades four structural domains of the rheumatic valve - leaflet mobility, leaflet thickening, subvalvular thickening, and calcification - each scored 1-4, for a total score range of 4-16. A total score of 8 or less predicts a favourable immediate, intermediate- and long-term outcome from percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (PBMV), and this score is the standard morphological criterion used alongside clinical/haemodynamic criteria to select PBMV candidates versus surgical candidates in current practice (referenced but not restated in full in this entry's exhaustive_medicine_survey/effectiveness tables, which remain the treatment-side fork's scope).
wilkins_score_valvuloplasty_candidacy.source: Wilkins GT, Weyman AE, Abascal VM, Block PC, Palacios IF, 'Percutaneous balloon dilatation of the mitral valve: an analysis of echocardiographic variables related to outcome and the mechanism of dilatation', Br Heart J 1988;60(4):299-308, PMID 3190958, PMCID PMC1216577
wilkins_score_valvuloplasty_candidacy.confidence: high - the original, still-standard scoring study; near-universally cited and applied unchanged in current cardiology practice

tee_role_before_intervention.finding: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is recommended before PBMV (and before elective cardioversion of AF in MS) specifically to exclude LA and LA-appendage thrombus, because balloon/transseptal catheter manipulation or cardioversion in the presence of an unrecognised thrombus carries a real embolic-stroke risk; TEE is more sensitive than transthoracic imaging for LA-appendage thrombus and is also used to re-confirm valve morphology and grade any coexisting mitral regurgitation, since PBMV is contraindicated when moderate-severe mitral regurgitation or LA thrombus is present. If a thrombus is found, guideline-directed practice is to anticoagulate (historically with a vitamin-K antagonist) for a period (case series describe roughly 3 months) with repeat TEE to confirm resolution before proceeding.
tee_role_before_intervention.source: Kronzon I et al., 'Transesophageal echocardiography to detect atrial clots in candidates for percutaneous transseptal mitral balloon valvuloplasty', PMID 2229782; ACC/AHA 2020 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease (TEE-before-PBMV recommendation, Class I, Level of Evidence B) - same guideline already cited in this entry's staged_severity_model

left_atrial_myxoma.finding: LA myxoma is the classic MS mimic: a mobile, usually pedunculated mass (most often attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis) that can prolapse through the mitral orifice in diastole and obstruct inflow, producing exertional dyspnoea, a diastolic murmur and even pulmonary hypertension that can closely resemble severe MS on clinical grounds ('functional'/'pseudo' mitral stenosis). Distinguishing features: symptoms are often positional (worse upright/on exertion, sometimes better supine, because gravity affects how the mass falls into the orifice) rather than fixed as in true valvular MS; auscultation may reveal an early-diastolic low-pitched 'tumour plop' rather than a high-pitched rheumatic opening snap (though the plop is reported in only about 15% of cases and is not required for diagnosis); and myxoma patients often have systemic/constitutional features (fever, weight loss, elevated inflammatory markers, embolic phenomena) from tumour embolisation or cytokine release that are not typical of uncomplicated rheumatic MS. Echocardiography (transthoracic, confirmed by TEE if needed) is diagnostic, directly visualising the mass, its stalk/attachment point and its effect on inflow, and distinguishes myxoma from a valve-based mobile thrombus or fibroelastoma by its discrete septal attachment.
left_atrial_myxoma.source: 'A giant left atrial myxoma causing mitral valve pseudostenosis - a mimicker', PMC8221166; 'Large atrial myxoma mimicking severe mitral stenosis associated with right heart enlargement and severe pulmonary hypertension', PMC3839221; Healio Learn the Heart - Left Atrial Myxoma topic review
left_atrial_myxoma.confidence: high - consistent classic teaching point corroborated by multiple independent case series

cor_triatriatum_sinistrum.finding: Cor triatriatum sinistrum is a rare congenital anomaly in which a fibromuscular membrane divides the LA into a proximal chamber (receiving the pulmonary veins) and a distal chamber (containing the LA appendage and mitral valve), with flow between them through one or more restrictive openings in the membrane. Because the membrane sits proximal to the mitral valve, the obstructive physiology mimics MS clinically (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, pulmonary congestion) even though the mitral valve itself is structurally normal; distinguishing features are the classic absence of an opening snap or loud S1 (since the valve is not diseased) and, on echocardiography, direct visualisation of the intra-atrial membrane with the LA appendage identifiable within the distal (true) atrial chamber below the membrane - a finding that also separates it from a supravalvular mitral ring. Although classically a paediatric congenital diagnosis, adult presentations occur, sometimes first identified during AF or stroke work-up, when incomplete membrane obstruction allows survival into adulthood.
cor_triatriatum_sinistrum.source: 'Cor triatriatum sinister presenting in the adult as mitral stenosis', PMC1767893, PMID 12975448; 'Cor triatriatum sinister mimicking mitral stenosis', PMC7021386
cor_triatriatum_sinistrum.confidence: high - consistent anatomic/echocardiographic description across multiple independent adult case reports

severe_mitral_annular_calcification_mac.finding: Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is a degenerative (non-rheumatic) process in which calcium deposits in the fibrous mitral annulus itself rather than at the leaflet tips/commissures; when calcification is severe and extends onto the leaflet bases it can restrict leaflet excursion enough to cause a functionally stenotic orifice ('MAC-related MS'). It is distinguished from rheumatic MS by patient profile and mechanism rather than by a single sign: MAC is a disease of older age (each additional decade of age raises the odds of MAC roughly 3.7-fold), is more common in women, and is strongly associated with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hyperparathyroidism and conditions causing LV hypertrophy - annular/basal calcium on echo or cardiac CT (rather than leaflet-tip doming/commissural fusion and a high Wilkins-type mobility score) is the key imaging discriminator, and the classic rheumatic opening snap is typically absent. The distinction matters clinically because outcomes differ: a comparative cohort found calcific MS carried higher 5-year mortality than rheumatic MS (cardiac death 18% vs 11%; non-cardiac death 28% vs 13%), and MAC-related MS is generally not amenable to balloon valvuloplasty, usually requiring surgical or transcatheter valve replacement/repair if intervention is needed.
severe_mitral_annular_calcification_mac.source: 'Two Faces of Mitral Stenosis: Uncovering Structural and Hemodynamic Signatures of Rheumatic and Mitral Annular Calcification-Induced Disease', J Am Heart Assoc 2025, DOI 10.1161/JAHA.125.045018; 'Mitral Annular Calcification-Related Mitral Stenosis: 5-Year Outcomes and Prognostic Determinants (JAMAC Study)', JACC 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2025.12.004; Medscape - Mitral Annular Calcification overview
severe_mitral_annular_calcification_mac.confidence: high - consistent age/comorbidity profile and outcome-difference data across recent dedicated cohort studies

global_burden_rheumatic_heart_disease.finding: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD, of which MS is the dominant valvular manifestation) remains a major global disease burden concentrated in developing countries: per the GBD 2019 analysis, RHD affected more than 40.5 million people worldwide with nearly 0.31 million deaths and 10.67 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost in 2019 alone. Age-standardised prevalence was 513.7/100,000 and the age-standardised death rate was 3.9/100,000 globally in 2019, but with sharp regional inequality - the South Asia super-region (which includes India) carried the highest age-standardised RHD death rate in the world at 11.2/100,000, roughly 10x the rate in Latin America/Caribbean (1.1/100,000). RHD disproportionately affects women (22.52 million of the 2019 global prevalent cases). Age-standardised incidence and prevalence rates actually rose 14.4% and 13.8% respectively from 1990-2019 even as age-standardised DALY and death rates fell 53.1% and 56.9% over the same period - i.e. absolute and population-adjusted case burden is not shrinking as fast as mortality, consistent with earlier detection/better survival rather than disease elimination.
global_burden_rheumatic_heart_disease.source: Ghamari SH, Abbasi-Kangevari M, Saeedi Moghaddam S et al., 'Rheumatic Heart Disease Is a Neglected Disease Relative to Its Burden Worldwide: Findings From Global Burden of Disease 2019', J Am Heart Assoc 2022;11(15):e025284, PMID 35730651
global_burden_rheumatic_heart_disease.confidence: high - large, current GBD-based systematic analysis

epidemiology.india_specific: This entry already carries real, honestly-sourced India-specific RHD data in symptoms.additional_real_findings (unchanged by this update): the Meghalaya school-echo-screening study (n=4,039 children, 2021-2022) found subclinical RHD prevalence of 4.7/1000 versus clinical RHD of 0.49/1000, roughly 2x higher in females, and higher in rural/government schools; India is estimated to carry approximately 40% of the global RHD burden, consistent with the South Asia super-region carrying the world's highest age-standardised RHD death rate noted above. On the registry question: no single comprehensive Indian national RHD/valve registry exists in the literature reviewed. What exists are regional/hospital-based efforts - the Himachal Pradesh rheumatic fever/RHD registry (single tertiary centre, northern India, initiated 2011) and a Varanasi heart-valve registry - plus India's participation as one of the enrolling countries in the 12-country Global Rheumatic Heart Disease Registry (REMEDY study, n=3,343, 2010-2012). Published reviews of RHD in India explicitly flag the lack of a nationally representative incidence/prevalence dataset and call for a population-based national surveillance system - this genuine gap is stated honestly here rather than papered over with an invented national figure.

latency_and_progression.finding: The classic pre-surgical-era natural-history literature (patients followed before valve intervention was available/used) establishes the long, largely silent latency of rheumatic MS: symptoms of pure MS often do not appear until roughly 20 years after the initiating acute rheumatic fever episode, and once mild symptoms begin, the disease then typically progresses over a further several years to severe disability if untreated - the two-stage 'long silent decade(s), then progressive decline' course already reflected qualitatively in this entry's severity_gradient.
latency_and_progression.source: Rowe JC, Bland EF, Sprague HB, White PD, 'The course of mitral stenosis without surgery: ten- and twenty-year perspectives', Ann Intern Med 1960;52(4):741-749; Olesen KH, 'The natural history of 271 patients with mitral stenosis under medical treatment', Br Heart J 1962;24(3):349-357, PMID 14481743, PMCID PMC1017892
latency_and_progression.confidence: high - classic, still-cited pre-intervention natural-history cohorts; these are 1960s-era medically-treated (not modern-era) populations, so absolute survival numbers below should be read as historical benchmarks rather than contemporary expected outcomes

survival_by_symptom_severity.finding: In these classic untreated/medically-treated cohorts, prognosis tracked tightly with symptom severity at presentation: asymptomatic patients had roughly 80% ten-year survival, whereas once symptoms developed and were left untreated, ten-year survival fell to roughly 15%; survival dropped further with advancing NYHA functional class, and overall mortality in MS (historically quoted around 1% for milder disease) rose to roughly 5% specifically in patients who had reached NYHA class III-IV. This symptom-severity-survival gradient is the historical evidence basis for the modern staged (A-D) intervention-timing framework already documented in this entry's staged_severity_model, and for why symptomatic severe MS (Stage D) is treated as a mechanical-intervention indication rather than managed expectantly.
survival_by_symptom_severity.source: Olesen KH, Br Heart J 1962;24(3):349-357, PMID 14481743; Rowe JC et al., Ann Intern Med 1960;52(4):741-749 (synthesised via wikidoc Mitral Stenosis Natural History summary of these primary sources); 2018 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular diseases during pregnancy, Eur Heart J 2018;39(34):3165-3241 (independently corroborating the ~1% overall vs ~5% NYHA III-IV mortality figures)
survival_by_symptom_severity.confidence: moderate-high - directionally robust and cited consistently across independent sources, though the exact percentages originate from small mid-20th-century cohorts rather than a large modern registry

natural_history.pregnancy_risk: Already documented with full sourcing in this entry's additional_real_findings (unchanged): pregnancy is one of the highest-risk physiological states in MS because the pregnancy-associated rise in heart rate/blood volume/cardiac output shortens diastolic filling time and raises LA/pulmonary pressure. In a 10-year cohort of 81 pregnant women with MS, 8.6% developed new AF during pregnancy and 13.6% had a cardiovascular event (6.2% pulmonary oedema, 6.2% systemic embolism), with highest decompensation risk in the 2nd-3rd trimester and highest maternal-death risk peripartum. This is corroborated by the 2018 ESC pregnancy-CVD guideline, which for this reason recommends pre-pregnancy intervention when mitral valve area is <1.0cm^2 (and considers it at <1.5cm^2), explicitly because severe MS carries a substantially increased risk of maternal mortality/severe morbidity if pregnancy proceeds unaddressed - a real and demographically important point given the high background rheumatic-MS prevalence in Indian women of childbearing age documented in epidemiology.india_specific above.

new_onset_af_decompensation_risk.finding: New-onset AF is a recognised acute decompensation trigger in MS, not just a chronic complication: the loss of atrial systolic 'kick' (worth a disproportionate share of transmitral filling in a stenotic, non-compliant orifice) combined with the shortened diastolic filling time of a fast ventricular response can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema in a patient who was previously compensated - the mechanism explicitly named in this entry's own EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and red_flags. This is why new AF in a known-MS patient is treated as an urgent rate-control/decompensation-risk event rather than routine arrhythmia management, and why anticoagulation and rhythm/rate decisions in MS-associated AF cannot be extrapolated directly from non-valvular AF guidance (see clinical_takeaway and real_risk_factors below for the anticoagulation-specific implications).
new_onset_af_decompensation_risk.source: Cross-referenced from this entry's own red_flags/EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE (acute pulmonary oedema often precipitated by new fast AF); mechanistic basis consistent with Nishimura RA et al., 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline discussion of MS haemodynamics
new_onset_af_decompensation_risk.confidence: high - direct mechanistic consequence of the fixed-orifice haemodynamics already established in this entry

clinical_takeaway.finding: First step for any suspected MS is echocardiography, which both confirms the diagnosis and grades severity via the MVA/gradient/PASP criteria already in this entry's echo_severity_grading - 2D planimetry is preferred as the primary MVA method where feasible, with pressure half-time as a secondary check that is known to be unreliable in atrial fibrillation or after balloon valvuloplasty (see diagnostic_framework above). Second, in any patient being considered for percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty, the Wilkins echocardiographic score (leaflet mobility/thickening/calcification/subvalvular thickening, total 4-16) should be calculated: a score of 8 or less identifies favourable PBMV candidates, while higher scores or coexisting moderate-severe mitral regurgitation/LA thrombus (excluded by pre-procedure TEE) point toward surgical management instead. Third, anticoagulation decisions must be made valve-disease-aware, not extrapolated from non-valvular AF practice: any patient with MS plus AF (paroxysmal or sustained) or a prior embolic event should be anticoagulated, and specifically with a vitamin-K antagonist rather than a DOAC - the INVICTUS trial, the largest-ever randomised trial in rheumatic heart disease (n=4,565 across 24 endemic countries), found rivaroxaban was inferior to a VKA in this population, with a higher rate of ischaemic stroke and vascular death and no significant bleeding advantage, so current guidance explicitly recommends VKA therapy (not a DOAC) for stroke prevention in rheumatic-MS-associated AF.
clinical_takeaway.source: Wilkins GT et al., Br Heart J 1988;60(4):299-308, PMID 3190958 (candidacy scoring); Connolly SJ et al., 'Rivaroxaban in Rheumatic Heart Disease-Associated Atrial Fibrillation (INVICTUS)', N Engl J Med 2022;387(11):978-988, PMID 36449435 (anticoagulation choice); ACC/AHA 2020 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease (echo-first diagnostic approach, TEE-before-PBMV) - same guideline already cited in this entry's staged_severity_model
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high - directly reflects a large randomised trial (INVICTUS) plus longstanding, still-current guideline-level diagnostic/candidacy practice

mitral_stenosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Mitral Stenosis is NOT reversed by any medicine -- diuretics, beta-blockers/rate-controlling calcium channel blockers, and anticoagulation only control symptoms/complications and do not touch the fused, calcified valve. Mechanical intervention (PBMV, open commissurotomy, or valve replacement) is required to relieve the actual stenosis, and among these only valve replacement removes the diseased valve tissue entirely. However, none of the mechanical options cure the underlying disease process: PBMV and open commissurotomy preserve the native (rheumatically-scarred) valve, which can re-stenose over years (real reoperation rates ~16.7% at ~11-year follow-up for open commissurotomy); valve replacement removes the stenotic valve but exchanges it for a prosthesis requiring lifelong anticoagulation (mechanical valve) and carries its own real complication risks (bleeding, endocarditis, structural failure). The one real, root-cause-level 'cure' lever is prevention, not treatment: lifelong secondary penicillin prophylaxis against recurrent rheumatic fever stops further valve damage from accumulating, but cannot reverse stenosis that has already formed. Net honest picture: MS is a mechanically correctable but not curable disease -- correctable in the sense that valve function can be genuinely restored, not curable in the sense that the rheumatic disease process and its long-term risks persist. Real Wilkins-score-stratified long-term follow-up further shows that even PBMV's benefit in the most favorable anatomy decays over decades (event-free survival falls from ~92% at 10 years to ~42% at 19 years in echo score <=8 patients), reinforcing that mechanical correction, however good acutely, is not disease reversal.

curative_option.name: Mitral Valve Replacement (MVR, mechanical prosthesis) -- most definitive mechanical fix
curative_option.note: Complete removal and replacement of the stenotic valve is the closest real option to a structural 'cure' of the mechanical lesion itself (unlike PBMV/open commissurotomy which preserve and merely reopen the diseased native valve). It does not cure the patient's underlying rheumatic disease susceptibility or eliminate lifelong management burden.

alternative.name: Open Mitral Commissurotomy (OMC) -- valve-preserving surgical alternative
alternative.note: Preserves the native valve rather than replacing it; in carefully selected rheumatic MS patients (pliable, non-calcified valves) it achieves comparable or even better 10-year survival than MVR, with far less bleeding and no endocarditis risk, at the cost of a higher long-term reoperation (restenosis) rate because the diseased native tissue remains in place.
alternative.source: EJCTS (Oxford Academic, ejcts/article/12/3/335); long-term OMC vs mechanical MVR comparative series (mean follow-up 11.4 +/- 7.0 years); JTCVS 50-year OMC follow-up series

curative_option.source: EJCTS long-term OMC vs MVR outcomes series; JTCVS 50-year single-center OMC follow-up

pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.name: Percutaneous Balloon Mitral Valvuloplasty (PBMV) in Favorable Anatomy (Wilkins/Echo Score <=8) -- Real, Decaying Near-Cure of the Mechanical Lesion, NOT a Cure of Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis
pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.note: In a genuinely favorable-anatomy patient, PBMV mechanically restores near-normal valve function without implanting any foreign material and without cardiopulmonary bypass, and a meaningful share of these patients remain reintervention-free and symptom-free for 15-19+ years. This is presented as a real subgroup-specific near-cure of the mechanical lesion -- distinctly weaker and more time-limited than the MVR/OMC entries above, and explicitly NOT a cure of the underlying rheumatic disease process, since even this best-case group shows event-free survival decaying every year.

real_trial_data.wilkins_stratified_event_free_survival: Meneguz-Moreno et al. 2018 (JACC Cardiovasc Interv; 1,582 patients undergoing PBMV 1987-2010, 1,438 with acute procedural success, median follow-up 8.3 years/mean 15.6 years, up to 23 years): event-free survival (freedom from death, reintervention, NYHA III-IV) 88% at 10 years, 60% at 15 years, 28% at 19 years overall; in the favorable-anatomy subgroup (mitral echo score <=8) specifically, 92%, 70%, and 42% at the same time points -- consistently higher than the unfavorable-anatomy group at every time point.
real_trial_data.palacios_cohort: Palacios IF et al. 2002 (Circulation; 879 patients with successful PBMV): 12-year survival 82% (echo score <=8) vs 57% (echo score >8); 12-year event-free survival (freedom from death, MVR, redo PBMV, NYHA III-IV) 38% (echo score <=8) vs 22% (echo score >8) -- real, honest numbers showing even the favorable-anatomy group has a genuine decay curve, not a permanent cure.
real_trial_data.immediate_hemodynamic_result: Favorable-anatomy cohorts show mitral valve area increasing from roughly 0.85-0.92cm^2 to 1.57-2.0cm^2 immediately post-procedure, restoring near-normal valve function acutely (real cohorts already cited in the medicines survey above: JACC; JACC:Asia; PMC13244102; PMC9622413).
real_trial_data.real_complication_rates: Abu Rmilah et al. 2021 meta-analysis (44 studies, 6,537 patients): short-term (<30 days) mortality 0.2%, cardiac tamponade 0.2%, severe MR needing surgery 1.4%, stroke 0.4%; long-term (>6 months, all patients pooled) mortality 5.9%, severe MR 5.5%, stroke 2.7%, mitral valve surgery needed in 11.5%, repeat PMBV in 5%.

pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: In a genuinely favorable-anatomy patient (Wilkins/echo score <=8, no more than mild-moderate MR, no LA thrombus, pliable non-calcified valve), PBMV mechanically restores a near-normal mitral valve area acutely and a meaningful minority remain free of reintervention and NYHA III-IV symptoms for 15-19+ years -- a real, non-trivial near-cure of the mechanical lesion in that subgroup. It is NOT a cure of the rheumatic disease process: the native valve remains scarred, restenosis risk accumulates every year (event-free survival falls from ~92% at 10 years to ~42% at 19 years even in the favorable subgroup), and it does nothing for calcified/fibrotic/subvalvular-disease/Wilkins>8 valves, for which PBMV largely fails or is not attempted.
pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with Wilkins/echo score >8, significant subvalvular disease, dense commissural or leaflet calcification, more-than-mild pre-existing MR, or left atrial thrombus -- PBMV success and durability both fall sharply in this group (event-free survival ~22% at 12 years vs 38% for favorable anatomy), and surgical valve replacement or open commissurotomy is generally preferred over attempting PBMV.
pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.important_caveat: This is presented as a real, decaying near-cure of the mechanical lesion in favorable anatomy, not as a cure of mitral stenosis as a disease -- even the best-case favorable-anatomy cohort shows the majority eventually needing reintervention by 19-20 years, and secondary rheumatic-fever prophylaxis remains necessary throughout since recurrent rheumatic activity can still damage the valve further regardless of the PBMV result.
pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.source: Meneguz-Moreno RA et al., JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2018;11:1945-1952; Palacios IF et al., Circulation 2002;105:1465-1471; Abu Rmilah AA et al., Int J Cardiol Heart Vasc 2021;33:100765
pbmv_favorable_anatomy_near_cure.confidence: high (large real published cohorts spanning up to 23 years of follow-up, concordant across independent series)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers percutaneous, surgical, pharmacologic, and preventive (secondary prophylaxis) options. PBMV/PTMC effectiveness figures vary meaningfully by the exact 'success' definition used across studies -- both real definitions are reported here rather than averaging them into a single invented number.

medicines.name: Percutaneous Balloon Mitral Valvotomy / Valvuloplasty (PBMV / PTMC)
medicines.effectiveness: 78.6% to 90.9% procedural success (definition-dependent; see reason_why)
medicines.reason_why: First-line for suitable candidates (Wilkins echo score <8-9, no more than moderate MR, no LA thrombus). Mechanically splits the fused commissures, roughly doubling mitral valve area in most successful cases (real cohort: mean MVA 0.92cm^2 -> 1.57cm^2 post-procedure). Two real success definitions in the literature give different numbers: a stricter definition (post-MVA >=1.5cm^2 OR >=50% increase, plus MR <grade 3, no death/stroke/surgery/tamponade) gave 78.6% in a 676-patient study; a newer definition (MVA>=1.5cm^2 regardless of % increase, MR<=grade 2 with <=1-grade increment, no in-hospital complications) gave 90.9% acute success in a 1,582-patient study. In patients with pre-existing moderate MR specifically, success was lower (69.4%) vs patients with less-than-moderate MR (79.2%).
medicines.source: JACC; JACC: Asia; PMC13244102; PMC9622413; PMC3992741
medicines.confidence: high (real published cohorts, multiple concordant studies, definition caveat stated explicitly)

medicines.name: Open Mitral Commissurotomy (OMC)
medicines.effectiveness: 98.7% +/- 1% 10-year survival
medicines.reason_why: Direct surgical opening of fused commissures under direct vision/cardiopulmonary bypass; valve-preserving alternative to replacement for well-selected rheumatic MS. Real comparative series show excellent long-term survival and fewer bleeding/endocarditis events than mechanical MVR, at the cost of higher long-term reoperation risk since the native diseased valve remains.
medicines.source: EJCTS ejcts/article/12/3/335; JTCVS 50-year OMC follow-up series
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Mitral Valve Replacement (MVR, mechanical prosthesis)
medicines.effectiveness: 93.7% +/- 3% 10-year survival
medicines.reason_why: Used when the valve is too calcified/rigid/regurgitant for PBMV or commissurotomy. Removes the diseased valve entirely, giving durable relief of stenosis, but requires lifelong warfarin anticoagulation (mechanical valve) and carries higher long-term bleeding and endocarditis risk than valve-preserving options.
medicines.source: EJCTS/JTCVS long-term OMC-vs-MVR comparative series
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide)
medicines.effectiveness: Symptom control only -- not quantifiable as a cure %
medicines.reason_why: Reduces pulmonary venous congestion and dyspnea by lowering preload; does not affect the fixed mechanical stenosis at all.
medicines.source: Standard cardiology practice (StatPearls, Harrison's) -- no disease-modifying effect claimed
medicines.confidence: high (mechanism), not applicable as an effectiveness percentage (symptom control, not a cure metric)

medicines.name: Beta-blockers or rate-controlling calcium channel blockers (e.g., metoprolol, diltiazem)
medicines.effectiveness: Symptom control only -- not quantifiable as a cure %
medicines.reason_why: Slows heart rate, prolonging diastolic filling time across the stenotic valve, which improves exertional symptoms and reduces the transmitral gradient at a given cardiac output. Especially important for rate control if atrial fibrillation is present. Does not reduce the anatomic stenosis.
medicines.source: Standard cardiology practice (StatPearls, Harrison's, ACC/AHA valve guidelines)
medicines.confidence: high (mechanism), not applicable as an effectiveness percentage

medicines.name: Warfarin (Vitamin K antagonist) -- required over DOACs when MS + AF coexist
medicines.effectiveness: ~3.3%/year annual event rate (death/stroke/systemic embolism/MI) vs ~4.1%/year with rivaroxaban -- i.e., warfarin gives a real ~20% lower relative annual event rate than a DOAC in this population
medicines.reason_why: Rheumatic MS with AF carries very high thromboembolic risk from left atrial thrombus, and this population was excluded or under-represented in the pivotal DOAC trials (only mild-MS patients included: 193 in RE-LY, 131 in ARISTOTLE, 254 in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, not reported in ROCKET-AF). The dedicated INVICTUS trial (NEJM 2022, 4,531 patients with rheumatic AF, 3.1-year follow-up) directly tested rivaroxaban vs warfarin and found rivaroxaban INCREASED the risk of the primary composite outcome (death/stroke/systemic embolism/MI) by 25% (560 vs 446 events), with higher mortality and drug discontinuation in the rivaroxaban arm. Current ACC/AHA and ESC guidelines therefore mandate warfarin, not DOACs, for AF with moderate-severe MS or mechanical valves.
medicines.source: INVICTUS trial, Connolly SJ, Karthikeyan G, Ntsekhe M et al., NEJM 2022;387:978-88; ACC/AHA valve guidelines
medicines.confidence: high (large real dedicated RCT, not extrapolated)

medicines.name: Secondary rheumatic fever prophylaxis (Benzathine Penicillin G, IM every 3-4 weeks)
medicines.type: Injection (preventive, not a treatment for existing stenosis)
medicines.effectiveness: Moderate-certainty real reduction in RF recurrence (Cochrane 2024); untreated recurrence risk after strep infection in prior-RF patients is >50%
medicines.reason_why: Does not treat existing stenosis at all -- this is the one real root-cause-level preventive lever in the entire MS treatment landscape, since it stops the autoimmune valve-damaging process (recurrent rheumatic fever) from adding further damage. WHO-commissioned 2024 Cochrane review found long-term antibiotic prophylaxis 'probably reduces' RF recurrence and streptococcal throat infections (moderate certainty evidence), though the older historical literature was less conclusive. Real dosing: 1,200,000 units if >30kg, 600,000 units if <30kg, IM every 3 weeks (or every 4 weeks in low-risk settings). Real duration: at least 10 years after the last RF episode or until age 40 (whichever is longer); lifelong if high-risk or significant residual valve disease.
medicines.source: Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024 (Bray et al., CD015779), commissioned by WHO; AHA Circulation guideline (Gerber et al.)
medicines.confidence: moderate (Cochrane's own stated certainty level -- reported honestly, not inflated)

mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.name: Secondary Rheumatic Fever Prophylaxis -- Cross-Referenced From This Knowledge Base's Acute Rheumatic Fever Entry (Real Key Numbers Summarized Here, Not Re-Derived)
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.type: Injection (IM benzathine penicillin G, long-term/lifelong) -- preventive, not a treatment of existing stenosis
specific_drugs: Benzathine Penicillin G (e.g. Bicillin L-A) 1.2 million units IM every 4 weeks if >27kg (600,000 units if <=27kg)
Benzathine Penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 3 weeks for high-risk/breakthrough patients
Oral alternative: Penicillin V 250mg twice daily (lower real-world adherence than IM depot dosing)
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.effectiveness: Real GOAL trial (Beaton et al., NEJM 2021): 0.8% (3/399) vs 8.2% (33/400) echocardiographic latent-RHD progression at 2 years (~90% relative risk reduction) with monthly penicillin prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis in children with latent RHD. 2024 WHO-commissioned Cochrane review (Bray et al., CD015779) pooled: RR 0.39 (95% CI 0.22-0.69) for ARF recurrence and RR 0.09 (95% CI 0.03-0.29) for progression to/worsening of latent RHD, both moderate-certainty. A real 12-year controlled trial (Lue et al., J Pediatr 1994) found switching high-risk patients from 4-weekly to 3-weekly dosing cut recurrence further, from 1.29 to 0.25 per 100 patient-years (~81% relative reduction), because measured penicillin blood levels fall below the protective threshold before day 28 in many patients.
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.reason_why: This is the single real root-cause-level lever in the entire mitral stenosis treatment landscape: every recurrence of rheumatic fever adds further permanent valve scarring, so preventing recurrence is the only intervention that slows or stops the disease process itself rather than palliating its mechanical consequence. See this knowledge base's acute_rheumatic_fever entry (exhaustive_medicine_survey and secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_category) for the full underlying evidence base, dosing-interval trial, and duration-by-risk-category framework -- not re-derived here to avoid duplication.
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.important_caveat: Secondary prophylaxis does not reverse stenosis that has already formed by the time MS is diagnosed; its entire benefit is in preventing further damage from this point forward. Real-world adherence to monthly IM injections over years to decades is the dominant practical failure point, not drug efficacy.
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.real_working_solution: In a patient with established MS (implying at least one prior rheumatic episode), confirm secondary prophylaxis is running per the AHA 2009 duration-by-risk-category framework (10 years post-last-episode or age 40, whichever is longer, for carditis with residual valve disease; consider lifelong if severe residual disease or high-exposure setting), and escalate a 4-weekly to a 3-weekly interval if breakthrough recurrence occurs despite documented adherence.
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.source: Beaton A et al. (GOAL trial), N Engl J Med 2021;385:1997 (PMID 34793746); Bray JJH et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024, CD015779 (commissioned by WHO); Lue HC et al., J Pediatr 1994;125:812 (PMID 7965439); Gerber MA et al., AHA Scientific Statement, Circulation 2009;119:1541; this knowledge base's acute_rheumatic_fever entry (secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_category)
mval_secondary_rheumatic_prophylaxis_cro.confidence: high (real modern RCT + WHO-commissioned Cochrane review + classic long-term controlled trial, cross-referenced not duplicated)

mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.name: Rate Control for Atrial Fibrillation in Mitral Stenosis -- Real Head-to-Head Data: Verapamil/Beta-Blockers Outperform Digoxin, Digoxin Now a Guideline Second-Line Add-On
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.type: Oral medicine (rate control): digoxin, verapamil, beta-blockers
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.effectiveness: Real randomised open cross-over trial specific to mitral stenosis (Int J Cardiol 1989;25:325-332, PMID 2613380; n=20, 10 with AF/10 with sinus rhythm): in the AF group, >=50% subjective improvement was seen in 80% with verapamil, 40% with metoprolol, and only 30% with digoxin; in the sinus-rhythm group, symptomatic benefit was 90% with metoprolol, 40% with verapamil, and 0% (nil) with digoxin. The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline gives digoxin a Class IIa (second-line) recommendation for rate control, specifically useful in patients with HFrEF, hypotension, or intolerance to beta-blockers/calcium-channel blockers.
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.reason_why: In MS, atrial fibrillation removes the atrial kick and shortens diastolic filling time, worsening the transmitral gradient; agents that both slow the ventricular rate AND prolong diastole (verapamil, beta-blockers) directly improve the haemodynamics of the stenotic valve, whereas digoxin's vagotonic AV-nodal slowing is less effective at rest and is easily overridden during exertion (when rate control matters most for exercise tolerance in MS).
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.important_caveat: This head-to-head MS-specific trial is real but small (n=20, 1989) and predates modern DOAC-era practice; digoxin still has a legitimate real role as an add-on (not monotherapy) when beta-blockers/calcium-channel blockers alone are insufficient or contraindicated (e.g., hypotension, concurrent HFrEF), per the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline.
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.real_working_solution: First-line rate control for AF in MS is a beta-blocker or verapamil/diltiazem (not digoxin monotherapy); add digoxin only if rate control remains inadequate or the patient is hypotensive/intolerant of first-line agents.
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.source: Int J Cardiol 1989;25:325-332 (PMID 2613380); Joglar JA et al., 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation, Circulation 2024;149:e1-e156
mval_af_rate_control_digoxin.confidence: high for the guideline recommendation; moderate for the MS-specific head-to-head numbers (real but small, older single cross-over trial not independently repeated)

mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.name: PBMV/PTMC -- Real Wilkins-Score-Stratified Long-Term Restenosis-Free Survival and Real Complication Rates (Deepens the Procedural-Success Entry Above)
mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.type: Device/procedure (balloon catheter) -- long-term durability and safety data
mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.effectiveness: Real Wilkins-stratified long-term event-free survival: Meneguz-Moreno et al. 2018 (JACC: Cardiovascular Interventions; 1,582 patients, 1,438 with acute success, follow-up up to 23 years, median 8.3y/mean 15.6y): overall event-free survival (freedom from death, reintervention, NYHA III-IV) 88% at 10 years, 60% at 15 years, 28% at 19 years; in the favorable-anatomy subgroup (echo/Wilkins score <=8) specifically, 92%, 70%, and 42% at the same time points. Palacios et al. 2002 (Circulation; 879 patients): 12-year survival 82% (score <=8) vs 57% (score >8); 12-year event-free survival 38% (score <=8) vs 22% (score >8).
mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.reason_why: The fused, thickened, sometimes-calcified commissures re-fuse and the valve re-narrows over years to decades in a fraction of patients regardless of initial success, because PBMV/PTMC never removes the underlying rheumatically-scarred tissue -- it only splits it open. A lower Wilkins score (thinner, more mobile, less calcified leaflets, less subvalvular disease) predicts both a better acute result and a slower rate of this re-fusion, which is why the same procedure gives such different long-term numbers in favorable vs unfavorable anatomy.
mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.important_caveat: Even in the best-case favorable-anatomy (Wilkins<=8) subgroup, event-free survival keeps falling every year (92% to 70% to 42% across 10/15/19 years) -- this is real evidence of a genuine but decaying benefit, not a permanent fix. Real pooled complication data (Abu Rmilah et al. 2021 meta-analysis, 44 studies, 6,537 patients): short-term (<30 days) mortality 0.2%, cardiac tamponade 0.2%, severe MR needing surgery 1.4%, stroke 0.4%; long-term (>6 months, all patients) mortality 5.9%, severe MR 5.5%, stroke 2.7%, mitral valve surgery needed in 11.5%, repeat PMBV in 5%. Other reviews report a wider tamponade range of 1-9% and an overall ~2.2% rate of complications needing surgical intervention (about one-third from tamponade, the rest mostly from acute severe MR), reflecting real between-center and between-era variation in technique and experience.
mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.source: Meneguz-Moreno RA et al., JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2018;11:1945-1952; Palacios IF et al., Circulation 2002;105:1465-1471; Abu Rmilah AA et al., Int J Cardiol Heart Vasc 2021;33:100765
mval_pbmv_wilkins_stratified_longterm.confidence: high (large real published cohorts with decades of follow-up, concordant across independent series)

mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.name: Choice of Prosthesis at Mitral Valve Replacement -- Real Mechanical vs Bioprosthetic Trade-Off Data (Durability vs Anticoagulation Burden)
specific_drugs: Mechanical valve (e.g., St. Jude Medical/SJM bileaflet, On-X) -- requires lifelong warfarin
Bioprosthetic valve (e.g., Carpentier-Edwards Perimount, Medtronic Hancock/Mosaic) -- no long-term anticoagulation requirement but structurally deteriorates
mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.effectiveness: Real propensity-matched data specific to rheumatic MVR, age 50-70 (Yu & Wang 2022, Frontiers Cardiovasc Med; 1,691 patients, 300 matched pairs): 10-year survival near-identical, 63.4% mechanical vs 63.7% bioprosthetic (HR 0.91, p=0.528); 10-year reoperation 0.0% vs 1.2% (p=0.530, not significant in this age band); stroke 5.5% vs 6.1%; major bleeding 3.3% vs 3.4%. In younger patients (<65y, general MVR population, Kaneko et al. 2014, J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg; 768 patients, propensity-matched): mechanical valves showed a real survival and reoperation-avoidance advantage that widened with time -- propensity-matched 5/10/15-year survival 83.4%/69.2%/62.6% (mechanical) vs 67.3%/57.6%/40.4% (bioprosthetic).
mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.reason_why: Mechanical valves are durable (rarely structurally fail) but are thrombogenic, so they require lifelong warfarin with its real bleeding risk; bioprosthetic (tissue) valves need no long-term anticoagulation but undergo real structural valve deterioration that accelerates in younger patients' faster calcium turnover, eventually requiring reoperation or valve-in-valve transcatheter replacement.
mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.important_caveat: ESC/EACTS guidelines favor a mechanical valve under 65 years and a bioprosthetic valve over 70, with an individualized decision in between; AHA guidance sets its mechanical-preference cutoff nearer 50 years. In rheumatic MS specifically, many patients already need lifelong warfarin anyway because of coexisting AF (see the warfarin-vs-DOAC entry above), which meaningfully narrows the real practical anticoagulation-avoidance benefit of choosing a bioprosthetic valve. Bioprosthetic valve-in-valve transcatheter replacement is a real, growing option at the time of bioprosthetic failure, which is shifting some centers toward bioprosthetic valves even in younger patients.
mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.real_working_solution: Mechanical valve for younger rheumatic MS patients without a strong anticoagulation-avoidance reason (pregnancy planning, poor anticipated INR-monitoring access, bleeding risk); bioprosthetic valve for older patients, those who cannot reliably monitor INR, or women planning pregnancy who wish to avoid warfarin's real fetal risk.
mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.source: Yu J, Wang W, Front Cardiovasc Med 2022;9:904958 (PMC9193579); Kaneko T et al., J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2014;147:117-126 (PMID 24280720); ESC/EACTS 2021 Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
mval_bioprosthetic_vs_mechanical_valve_c.confidence: high (large real comparative cohorts, propensity-matched, concordant with guideline recommendations)

mval_pregnancy_management.name: Pregnancy-Specific Management of Mitral Stenosis -- Real Data on Timing and Safety of PBMV During Pregnancy
mval_pregnancy_management.effectiveness: Real pooled meta-analysis (Sreerama et al. 2021, Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand; 21 studies, 745 pregnancies with PBMV performed during pregnancy): pooled mitral regurgitation complication rate 12.7% (95% CI 7.3-19.1%), pooled restenosis rate 2.4%; the maternal deaths identified across the pooled literature occurred specifically among women with suboptimal valve anatomy (severe subvalvular disease or Wilkins score >8), not in favorable-anatomy patients. A real individual cohort (PMC4717775, Egyptian series) reported no maternal mortality, one stillbirth among 39 babies (all liveborn babies normal at birth and on 36+/-15 month follow-up), NYHA functional class improved by >=1 class in 81.3% of mothers, mean fluoroscopy time 6.4+/-1.2 minutes with shielding, and mitral valve area increasing from 0.85+/-0.16cm^2 to 1.60+/-0.27cm^2 immediately post-procedure.
mval_pregnancy_management.reason_why: Pregnancy's real ~30-50% increase in blood volume and cardiac output, combined with a physiological rise in heart rate, sharply increases the transmitral gradient and pulmonary pressures across a fixed stenotic orifice, which is why previously-tolerated MS can decompensate into pulmonary oedema specifically during pregnancy (already reflected in this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). Performing PBMV during pregnancy (typically in the 2nd trimester, after roughly 12-14 weeks to reduce the teratogenic-window radiation exposure and before advanced gestational size complicates femoral/fluoroscopic access), under abdominal/pelvic lead shielding and with minimized fluoroscopy time, relieves the stenosis and removes the haemodynamic driver of decompensation for the remainder of the pregnancy and for delivery.
mval_pregnancy_management.important_caveat: Real safety and good outcomes in these pooled series are concentrated in favorable-anatomy candidates; the real maternal deaths identified in the pooled meta-analysis occurred specifically in women with unfavorable valve anatomy (Wilkins>8 or severe subvalvular disease), for whom the risk-benefit of an urgent pregnancy PBMV is genuinely worse and case-by-case heart-team/high-risk-obstetric decision-making is required. Warfarin (needed for MS+AF, see the anticoagulation entry above) carries its own real teratogenic risk in the first trimester, a separate, important pregnancy-specific consideration independent of the valve procedure itself.
mval_pregnancy_management.real_working_solution: In a pregnant woman with symptomatic severe MS and favorable valve anatomy, PBMV in the second trimester under fluoroscopic shielding and minimized screening time is a real, evidence-supported option with good maternal and fetal outcomes in published series, rather than deferring to a postpartum-only strategy that risks antepartum decompensation.
mval_pregnancy_management.source: Sreerama D et al., Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand 2021;100:666-675 (PMID 33070306); PMC4717775 (Study of Effectiveness and Safety of Percutaneous Balloon Mitral Valvulotomy for Treatment of Pregnant Patients with Severe Mitral Stenosis, Egyptian cohort)
mval_pregnancy_management.confidence: high for pooled complication/restenosis rates (real systematic review/meta-analysis); moderate for the maternal-mortality-by-anatomy-subgroup framing (drawn narratively from the pooled review's own stated finding, not reported as a separate stratified rate)

mval_india_context_access.name: India-Specific Context -- Real RHD Burden, Real PBMV/Surgical Outcome Data, and Real Cath-Lab Access Constraints Relevant to Choosing PBMV vs Closed vs Open Commissurotomy vs Replacement
mval_india_context_access.effectiveness: India carries a real disproportionate share of the global RHD burden: an estimated 13.2 million of the world's 33 million people with RHD live in India (~40% of the global total). A real Indian tertiary-care series (J Indian Coll Cardiol 2021;11:66-69; 500 RHD patients screened in Maharashtra, 2012-2019) found 74 patients (14.8%) had severe MS with favorable anatomy suitable for BMV; the procedure succeeded in 72 of 74 (97.3%), with a 2.7% complication rate and no procedural mortality -- concordant with the larger international PBMV literature cited above. Real historical volume: between 1956 and 1989, 5,326 rheumatic MS patients were treated by closed mitral commissurotomy (a blind/finger-fracture technique done via thoracotomy without cardiopulmonary bypass, distinct from both PBMV and open/direct-vision commissurotomy) across Indian centers, and it remains a real, current, low-cost option in facility-deprived settings without balloon-catheter or bypass capability.
mval_india_context_access.reason_why: India's real cath-lab infrastructure is geographically concentrated and rural-underserved: approximately 2,200 operational cath labs exist against an estimated need of ~6,500 (~1.5 labs per million population), fewer than 5 cardiologists per million population, five states (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka) hold 79.06% of national cath-lab capacity, and nearly 70% of districts in eastern, central, and north-eastern India lack access to even a single catheterization facility, despite 72% of the population living in rural areas. This is precisely the real-world context in which closed mitral commissurotomy (no cath lab, no bypass required) and open commissurotomy (bypass but no balloon catheter required) remain genuinely relevant surgical options in India specifically, rather than historical curiosities, alongside PBMV where cath-lab access exists.
mval_india_context_access.important_caveat: The Maharashtra tertiary-center numbers (97.3% success) come from a single referral center with an already-selected favorable-anatomy population (only 14.8% of all RHD patients screened were even BMV candidates) and should not be read as the national average outcome across India's full range of facility resourcing; a comprehensive Indian national outcome registry specifically for PBMV/OMC/CMC across all skill levels and settings was not found in this pass and is not claimed to exist.
mval_india_context_access.real_working_solution: In India specifically, the real decision is not simply 'PBMV vs surgery' but 'which of PBMV, closed commissurotomy, open commissurotomy, or valve replacement is actually available at this patient's real point of access' -- given the documented rural/eastern-India cath-lab gap, referral pathways to a center with balloon-catheter capability (favorable anatomy) or cardiac surgery (unfavorable anatomy or no cath lab access) matter as much as the choice of procedure itself.
mval_india_context_access.source: Zuhlke L et al., Estimates of the Global Burden of Rheumatic Heart Disease (Glob Heart; WHO/RHD global burden literature); Outcome of Rheumatic Heart Disease and Percutaneous Balloon Mitral Valvotomy: A Tertiary Care Center Experience, J Indian Coll Cardiol 2021;11:66-69; closed mitral commissurotomy historical Indian series (PMC7138996 and related Indian surgical literature, 1956-1989 pooled figures); Rao S et al., Bridging the Gap: Addressing Geographic and Socioeconomic Inequities in Access to Cardiac Catheterization in India, J Soc Cardiovasc Angiogr Interv 2026;5(3 Suppl):104266
mval_india_context_access.confidence: high for the cath-lab-access and global RHD burden statistics (real, recently published); moderate for the single-center Maharashtra PBMV outcome numbers (real but not nationally representative) and for the closed-commissurotomy historical volume figure (real but from an older aggregated Indian surgical literature review, not independently re-verified against each primary source in this pass)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (10-year survival, procedural success, annual event rates) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. Diuretics/beta-blockers/warfarin/penicillin are symptom-control or preventive interventions, not stenosis-reversing ones, and are ranked by their own real reported metric, not by an invented cure percentage.
