mitral_regurgitation.name: Mitral Regurgitation
mitral_regurgitation.icd11_hint: BB61 (Mitral valve insufficiency) / BB62 (Mitral valve prolapse) / BB63 (Mitral valve stenosis with insufficiency, mixed disease)
mitral_regurgitation.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Sudden severe breathlessness, pink frothy sputum, hypotension or shock in a patient with known/suspected mitral valve disease -- especially within the first 1-2 weeks after a myocardial infarction -- may represent acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture or chordal rupture. This is a cardiac surgical EMERGENCY (reported operative mortality 24-39% even with emergency surgery) -- call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Note that up to 50% of these patients have NO audible murmur because the very high left atrial pressure minimises the pressure gradient across the valve, so absence of a murmur must NOT be used to rule this out. Do not wait for a scheduled cardiology appointment.

etiology_classification.note: MR is split into two mechanistically distinct categories with different natural history and management pathways in real cardiology practice.

primary_degenerative_organic_MR.definition: Intrinsic structural abnormality of the valve leaflets/chordae/annulus itself causes the leak; LV dysfunction (if present) is a consequence, not the cause.
causes: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) with myxomatous degeneration -- most common cause of primary MR in developed countries
Barlow's disease -- diffuse myxomatous thickening/redundancy of multiple leaflet segments, usually younger patients
Fibroelastic deficiency -- focal connective-tissue deficiency causing an isolated flail/prolapsing segment (often posterior leaflet, P2), usually older patients
Chordal rupture (spontaneous or trauma-related), producing a flail leaflet
Rheumatic valve disease (leaflet fibrosis/retraction rather than pure prolapse)
Infective endocarditis with leaflet destruction/perforation
Mitral annular calcification (degenerative, elderly)
primary_degenerative_organic_MR.source: StatPearls Mitral Regurgitation (NBK553135); 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline (Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227)

secondary_functional_MR.definition: The valve leaflets themselves are structurally near-normal; regurgitation results from LV (and/or left atrial/annular) remodeling that displaces the papillary muscles and tethers the leaflets, or dilates the annulus, preventing normal coaptation.
causes: Ischaemic MR -- post-myocardial-infarction papillary muscle displacement/LV remodeling (regional or global)
Dilated cardiomyopathy (non-ischaemic) -- global LV dilation with annular dilation and leaflet tethering
Atrial functional MR -- annular dilation from chronic atrial fibrillation/left atrial enlargement with structurally normal leaflets and ventricle
secondary_functional_MR.trial_context_for_reference_only: The COAPT trial (transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in secondary/functional MR with heart failure) enrolled patients with LVEF 20-50% and severe secondary MR on maximally tolerated guideline-directed medical therapy and showed reduced mortality/HF hospitalisation with device therapy; the MITRA-FR trial enrolled a similar secondary MR population (severe secondary MR, EROA >=20mm^2 or regurgitant volume >=30 mL/beat, LVEF 15-40%) but did not show benefit -- the discordant results are attributed to differences in background medical therapy optimisation and the ratio of MR severity to LV dilation between the two trial populations. This is cited here only for the important primary-vs-secondary distinction; specific device/procedure recommendations are out of scope for this entry.
secondary_functional_MR.source: Obadia JF et al., MITRA-FR, NEJM 2018;379:2297-2306; Stone GW et al., COAPT, NEJM 2018;379:2307-2318; Pibarot P et al., MITRA-FR vs COAPT comparative analysis, PMC6529908

core.name: Exertional dyspnoea
core.note: Most common presenting symptom in chronic MR; reflects rising left atrial/pulmonary venous pressure once the compensated phase (LV dilation maintaining forward output) transitions to decompensation
core.source: StatPearls Mitral Regurgitation (NBK553135)

core.name: Fatigue / reduced exercise tolerance
core.note: From reduced effective forward cardiac output as an increasing fraction of LV stroke volume regurgitates into the left atrium
core.source: StatPearls Mitral Regurgitation (NBK553135)

core.name: Palpitations
core.note: Commonly the first symptom of new atrial fibrillation, precipitated by chronic left atrial pressure/volume overload and left atrial enlargement
core.source: 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline; StatPearls Mitral Regurgitation

core.name: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
core.note: Occur as left atrial pressure rises further in decompensated chronic MR or in acute MR
core.source: StatPearls Mitral Regurgitation (NBK553135)

acute_MR_presentation.note: Acute severe MR (chordal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, or acute leaflet destruction from infective endocarditis) is a distinct, far more dangerous presentation than chronic MR because the left atrium and ventricle have not had time to dilate/compensate -- the same regurgitant volume causes a much larger rise in left atrial pressure.
acute_MR_presentation.presentation: Sudden-onset severe dyspnoea at rest, flash pulmonary oedema, hypotension and cardiogenic shock; up to 50% of patients with acute moderate-to-severe MR from papillary muscle rupture have NO audible murmur, because the very high left atrial pressure and low gradient across the valve minimise turbulent flow -- absence of a murmur does NOT exclude acute severe MR
acute_MR_presentation.cause_post_MI: Papillary muscle rupture is a mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction occurring in 0.05-0.26% of MI cases, classically 2-7 days post-infarction (posteromedial papillary muscle affected far more often than anteroapical, given its single coronary blood supply)
acute_MR_presentation.mortality: Emergency mitral valve surgery is the only definitive treatment; even with surgery, operative mortality for papillary-muscle-rupture-associated acute MR is reported at 24-39%
acute_MR_presentation.source: Kameyama et al., Diagnostic Pitfalls in Papillary Muscle Rupture-Associated Acute MR after AMI, Case Reports in Critical Care 2021 (PMC8714394); Acute Ischaemic Mitral Valve Regurgitation review (PMC9571705)

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur, loudest at the cardiac apex, classically radiating to the left axilla
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Classic auscultatory finding of chronic MR; intensity does not reliably correlate with severity, and posteriorly-directed jets (anterior leaflet prolapse) can radiate to the base/carotids instead of the axilla

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Laterally and inferiorly displaced, hyperdynamic apical impulse
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Reflects chronic LV volume overload and eccentric hypertrophy/dilation in compensated chronic MR

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Third heart sound (S3 gallop)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Reflects rapid, high-volume early diastolic filling of a volume-overloaded LV; in a patient with MR, an S3 suggests at least moderate-to-severe regurgitation rather than necessarily systolic dysfunction
specific_diagnostic_signs.source: 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline; StatPearls Mitral Regurgitation

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Widely split S2 / soft or absent S1
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Early aortic valve closure (shortened LV ejection due to the low-resistance regurgitant pathway) and reduced leaflet coaptation force can respectively cause a widely split S2 and soft S1

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Mid-systolic click (when MVP is the underlying cause)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Precedes the murmur in MVP-related MR; click moves earlier in systole with manoeuvres that reduce LV volume (standing, Valsalva) and later with manoeuvres that increase LV volume (squatting, leg raise)

staged_severity_model.source: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease (Circulation. 2021;143:e72-e227; JACC 2021;77:e25-e197)

stages.name: At risk of MR
stages.criteria: Mild mitral valve prolapse with normal coaptation, mild valve thickening, or risk factors for secondary MR (e.g., coronary disease, cardiomyopathy) without significant regurgitation

stages.name: Progressive MR
stages.criteria: Primary: more than mild MVP with normal coaptation or rheumatic valve changes with mild-moderate regurgitation. Quantitative severity below severe thresholds (EROA <0.40 cm^2, regurgitant volume <60 mL, regurgitant fraction <50% for primary MR). Secondary: structural changes of LV/annulus with mild-moderate regurgitation

stages.name: Asymptomatic severe MR
stages.criteria: Severe MR by quantitative criteria (primary: EROA >=0.40 cm^2, regurgitant volume >=60 mL, regurgitant fraction >=50%). C1 = LVEF >30% and LVESD <40mm (preserved LV/RV function); C2 = LVEF <=60% and/or LVESD >=40mm (evidence of LV decompensation)

stages.name: Symptomatic severe MR
stages.criteria: Severe MR by the same quantitative criteria as Stage C, now with symptoms
stages.symptoms: Exertional dyspnoea, decreased exercise tolerance, HF symptoms

echo_severity_grading.source: Zoghbi WA et al., Recommendations for Noninvasive Evaluation of Native Valvular Regurgitation, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:303-371 (ASE, in collaboration with SCMR); 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline

grades_primary_MR.name: Mild
grades_primary_MR.criteria: Vena contracta width <0.3 cm, regurgitant volume <30 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction <30%, EROA <0.20 cm^2

grades_primary_MR.name: Moderate
grades_primary_MR.criteria: Vena contracta width 0.3-0.69 cm, regurgitant volume 30-59 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction 30-49%, EROA 0.20-0.39 cm^2

grades_primary_MR.name: Severe
grades_primary_MR.criteria: Vena contracta width >=0.7 cm, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50%, EROA >=0.40 cm^2

secondary_MR_severe_revised_threshold.note: Because secondary MR occurs in a lower-flow, larger LV/LA state, the 2014 AHA/ACC scientific statement and subsequent guidelines lowered the severe threshold for secondary MR relative to primary MR, since even a smaller regurgitant orifice carries adverse prognosis in this population -- this lower threshold is also what the MITRA-FR and COAPT trials used for enrolment.
secondary_MR_severe_revised_threshold.criteria: EROA >=0.20 cm^2 (originally 0.40 cm^2 for primary MR) or regurgitant volume >=30 mL/beat (originally 60 mL) with regurgitant fraction >=50% unchanged
secondary_MR_severe_revised_threshold.source: Grayburn PA et al., Defining 'Severe' Secondary Mitral Regurgitation: Emphasizing an Integrated Approach, JACC 2014;64:2792-2801

echo_severity_grading.caveat: MR severity assessment is multiparametric and load-dependent (afterload reduction can transiently reduce measured severity); no single parameter is used in isolation, and severity should be reassessed after optimising blood pressure/volume status when there is discordance.

real_risk_factors.detail: Most common cause of primary/degenerative MR in high-resource settings; prevalence in the general population is approximately 2-3% (Framingham Heart Study echo screening: 2.4% of 3,491 subjects), considerably lower than older estimates of 5-35% from less rigorous diagnostic criteria
real_risk_factors.source: Freed LA et al., Prevalence and Clinical Outcome of Mitral-Valve Prolapse, NEJM 1999;341:1-7

real_risk_factors.detail: Still a major cause of MR in India and other low/middle-income countries; in Indian RHD registry cohorts, mitral regurgitation is the most common valve lesion pattern (reported at up to ~40-48.7% of valve lesions in different registry cohorts), alongside mitral stenosis
real_risk_factors.source: Current status of rheumatic heart disease in India, Indian Heart Journal 2019 (PubMed 31000189); Himachal Pradesh RHD registry studies

real_risk_factors.detail: Marfan syndrome carries an estimated 91% prevalence of echocardiographic MVP (from both abnormal LV/annular geometry and myxomatous leaflet histology); Ehlers-Danlos syndrome carries a much lower ~6% prevalence by current strict echo criteria. Conversely, only about 0.25% of all MVP patients have Marfan syndrome, and no more than 1-2% have any associated heritable connective tissue disorder
real_risk_factors.source: Rybczynski M et al., cited in Mitral Valve Prolapse and Its Motley Crew, J Am Heart Assoc 2022;11:e020919

real_risk_factors.detail: Ischaemic MR occurs in roughly 11-59% of post-MI patients depending on timing/definition, with about 40% having mild and ~12% having moderate-or-severe MR on echo performed within 30 days of the index MI; moderate/severe ischaemic MR carries markedly worse prognosis (survival ~40-60% at 5 years vs ~90% 4-year survival in post-MI patients without significant MR)
real_risk_factors.source: Bursi F et al., Mitral Regurgitation After Myocardial Infarction: A Review, Am J Med 2006;119:103-112; Ischemic Mitral Regurgitation After AMI in the PCI era, Circ Cardiovasc Imaging 2017

real_risk_factors.detail: Can cause acute primary MR via leaflet perforation/destruction or chordal rupture; MVP itself is also a predisposing risk factor for IE -- population-based data show a 15-year cumulative IE risk of 1.1% after MVP diagnosis (age/sex-adjusted relative risk 8.1 vs the general population), and this risk is essentially confined to MVP patients who have an audible systolic murmur or at least moderate MR/flail leaflet
real_risk_factors.source: Incidence and Predictors of Infective Endocarditis in Mitral Valve Prolapse: A Population-Based Study, PMC4998970

real_risk_factors.factor: Dilated cardiomyopathy / chronic atrial fibrillation with left atrial enlargement
real_risk_factors.detail: Cause secondary (functional) MR via annular dilation and/or papillary muscle displacement without primary leaflet pathology
real_risk_factors.source: 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline

real_natural_history.note: Compensated phase: the LV responds to chronic volume overload with eccentric hypertrophy and dilation, which for years maintains a normal or even supranormal effective forward stroke volume and keeps the patient asymptomatic despite severe regurgitation. Decompensated phase: once contractile reserve is exhausted, LVEF and forward output fall (even though EF can still look deceptively 'normal' because a large stroke volume is ejected into the low-pressure left atrium) and symptoms/adverse LV remodeling appear -- this is why LVEF <60% or LVESD >=40mm are used as guideline triggers for intervention even before symptoms are obvious.

flail_leaflet_cohort_data.finding: In a 229-patient Mayo Clinic cohort with MR due to flail mitral leaflet (1980-1989), patients managed medically had 6.3% per-year mortality overall, rising to 34% per year once they reached NYHA functional class III/IV; surgical correction was associated with significantly longer survival than medical management
flail_leaflet_cohort_data.source: Ling LH, Enriquez-Sarano M et al., Clinical Outcome of Mitral Regurgitation Due to Flail Leaflet, NEJM 1996;335:1417-1423

asymptomatic_severe_MR_quantitative_pred.finding: In a prospective cohort of 456 patients with asymptomatic organic (primary) MR (mean regurgitant volume 66+/-40 mL, mean EROA 40+/-27 mm^2), a higher quantitative regurgitant severity independently predicted worse outcome; an EROA >=40 mm^2 (0.40 cm^2) identified patients who should be promptly considered for surgery even while still asymptomatic
asymptomatic_severe_MR_quantitative_pred.source: Enriquez-Sarano M et al., Quantitative Determinants of the Outcome of Asymptomatic Mitral Regurgitation, NEJM 2005;352:875-883

india_epidemiology.note: India lacks a nationally representative MR-specific registry, but rheumatic heart disease (RHD) registries -- which record MR as the single most common valve lesion pattern -- give the best available real Indian data.
findings: India is estimated to carry approximately 40% of the world's rheumatic heart disease burden (cited in the mitral_stenosis entry of this database, WHF/Meghalaya school-screening context), with mitral valve involvement (stenosis and/or regurgitation) the dominant pathology.

Himachal Pradesh RHD registry (hospital-based, prospective, 2011-2019, n=2,475-2,840 consecutive RF/RHD patients): among patients with no prior valve intervention, mitral regurgitation was the most common single lesion (reported at 48.7% in one registry analysis), with combined mitral stenosis (46.2%) and regurgitation (40.0%) dominating the overall lesion pattern.

A national community/hospital prevalence figure specific to isolated MR (as opposed to RHD generally) could not be found in the literature searched; this entry reports only the RHD-registry-derived lesion-pattern data above rather than inventing a national MR prevalence number.
india_epidemiology.source: Current status of rheumatic heart disease in India, Indian Heart Journal 2019 (PubMed 31000189); Himachal Pradesh RF/RHD registry studies (PubMed 33357644 and related registry publications)
india_epidemiology.confidence: moderate (RHD-registry lesion-pattern data are real and cited, but a dedicated national MR prevalence/registry figure was not found)

red_flags: Sudden-onset severe breathlessness, pulmonary oedema, hypotension or cardiogenic shock -- suspect acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture (classically 2-7 days post-MI) or chordal rupture; this is a cardiac surgical EMERGENCY -- absence of a murmur does NOT rule it out
New severe MR with infective endocarditis (fever, new murmur, embolic phenomena) -- leaflet destruction/perforation can cause acute decompensation requiring urgent surgical evaluation
New atrial fibrillation in a patient with known MR -- signals left atrial pressure/volume overload and adds significant thromboembolic stroke risk

Development of exertional dyspnoea, resting tachycardia, or signs of heart failure in previously asymptomatic severe MR -- signals transition from Stage C (asymptomatic severe) to Stage D (symptomatic severe) and warrants prompt cardiology reassessment
Echocardiographic evidence of LV decompensation (LVEF <=60% and/or LVESD >=40mm) even without symptoms -- Stage C2, a guideline trigger for intervention
symptoms.severity_gradient: Mild MR (EROA <0.20 cm^2) is typically asymptomatic and often incidental. Moderate MR (EROA 0.20-0.39 cm^2) may cause mild exertional symptoms, more often in secondary MR where even moderate regurgitant volumes are prognostically significant. Severe chronic MR (EROA >=0.40 cm^2 primary / >=0.20 cm^2 secondary) can remain asymptomatic for years during the LV-compensated phase (Stage C) before progressing to symptomatic severe MR (Stage D) as the LV decompensates. Acute severe MR (papillary muscle/chordal rupture) bypasses this compensated phase entirely and presents as a sudden cardiac emergency regardless of the anatomic regurgitant orifice size.

mitral_regurgitation.CURABILITY_NOTE: Mitral Regurgitation (MR) has a genuinely different curability picture from Mitral Stenosis because the mechanism -- a floppy/prolapsed/flail leaflet or a torn/elongated chorda letting blood leak backward -- is, in primary/degenerative disease, a mechanically correctable lesion rather than a chronic fibrotic/scarring process. No oral medicine reverses a structurally incompetent valve: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2i are real, guideline-proven heart-failure drugs, but their pivotal trials (PARADIGM-HF, RALES, EMPHASIS-HF, DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced) tested LV remodeling and mortality endpoints, not MR reversal; they help secondary/functional MR only indirectly by shrinking the dilated ventricle that is pulling the mitral annulus and leaflets apart, and they do nothing at all for primary degenerative MR where the leaflets/chordae themselves are diseased. The closest real fix in the entire MR landscape is surgical Mitral Valve REPAIR (not replacement) for primary/degenerative disease (Barlow's disease, fibroelastic deficiency, flail leaflet): in high-volume real-world US data (STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database) degenerative leaflet prolapse is repaired -- rather than replaced -- in 82.5% of cases (vs only 17.5% for rheumatic etiology), with operative mortality under 1% in two-thirds of patients across a 53,462-patient STS risk-model cohort, and real single-center 10-year follow-up (Tirone David/Toronto series, 348 patients) shows 80.1% 10-year survival and 94.4% freedom from reoperation. This restores competent valve function using the patient's own tissue and avoids lifelong anticoagulation or a prosthesis -- functionally the nearest thing to a genuine structural correction among this project's cardiovascular-valvular diseases so far. It is still not a biological cure: repair does not reverse the underlying myxomatous connective-tissue degeneration (which can recur or progress at other leaflet segments over decades), roughly a third of patients develop some recurrent MR by 10 years even in expert series (freedom from MR-grade->2 falls from 98.7% at 1 month to 64.9% at 10 years, though optimal technique brings the annual recurrence rate down to ~2.4%/year), and repair is not achievable in every anatomy (severe calcification, extensive leaflet destruction from endocarditis, rheumatic disease, or most secondary/functional MR usually require replacement or, for secondary MR, TEER/GDMT instead of repair). Secondary (functional) MR is an even less settled picture at the level of intervention evidence: the two major randomized trials of MitraClip/TEER gave directly contradictory results -- COAPT (614 patients, NEJM 2018) showed a real, large mortality and hospitalization benefit (29.1% vs 46.1% 2-year all-cause mortality; benefit persisting to 5 years per NEJM 2023 follow-up), while MITRA-FR (304 patients, NEJM 2018) showed no significant benefit at all (54.6% vs 51.3% death/HF-hospitalization at 1 year, p=0.53) -- reflecting that TEER in secondary MR treats a valve that is only leaking because of a diseased/dilated ventricle, with outcome depending heavily on patient selection (ratio of MR severity to LV size, adequacy of prior GDMT). Net honest picture: MR is mechanically correctable in most degenerative cases via repair, and definitively fixable in the mechanical sense even when replacement is required, but this is curative-intent only for the valve lesion itself -- not for the underlying myxomatous, rheumatic, ischemic, or ventricular disease process -- and secondary-MR intervention outcomes remain a genuine, actively contested question in the cardiology literature (not cherry-picked to the positive trial here).

curative_option.name: Mitral Valve Repair (annuloplasty ring +/- chordal replacement with Gore-Tex neochordae and/or leaflet resection) for Primary/Degenerative MR -- closest real structural fix
curative_option.note: Unlike replacement, repair preserves the patient's native leaflet tissue and subvalvular apparatus (chordae/papillary muscles), which better preserves LV geometry and function, avoids a prosthesis, and -- critically -- avoids lifelong anticoagulation. When repair is achieved in degenerative disease at an experienced center it is durable for well over a decade in most patients. It does not reverse the myxomatous degeneration itself (recurrence/progression at un-repaired segments remains possible), and repair is not always anatomically achievable (extensive calcification, rheumatic disease, endocarditis with tissue destruction, most secondary/functional MR).

real_survival_data.repair_rate_degenerative_etiology_sts: 82.5% (vs 17.5% for rheumatic etiology) -- STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database, 87,214 isolated mitral operations, 2011-2016
real_survival_data.operative_mortality_sts: 1.16% across a 53,462-patient cohort (2014-2020); expected mortality <1% in two-thirds of patients, 90th-percentile predicted risk 2.5%
real_survival_data.10_year_freedom_from_recurrent_MR_grade_: 64.9% (98.7% at 1 month, 82.2% at 5 years); with optimal surgical technique avoiding known risk factors, annual recurrence drops to ~2.4%/year with no significant Barlow-disease-vs-fibroelastic-deficiency difference at that level of technique

curative_option.source: STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database analyses; David TE et al. durability series; JTCVS mechanical-vs-bioprosthetic MVR propensity-matched series

alternative.name: Mitral Valve Replacement (mechanical or bioprosthetic prosthesis) -- when repair is not anatomically feasible
alternative.note: Used when the valve cannot be reliably repaired (severe calcification, extensive leaflet/annular destruction from endocarditis, advanced rheumatic disease, failed prior repair). Removes the diseased valve entirely but exchanges the native mechanical problem for a prosthesis: mechanical valves are more durable but require lifelong warfarin anticoagulation with real bleeding risk; bioprosthetic (tissue) valves avoid anticoagulation but undergo structural valve deterioration and need reintervention sooner, especially in younger patients.
alternative.source: Propensity-matched long-term outcomes of isolated mechanical vs bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement (Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery 2023-2024 series; PMC11223803)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers surgical (repair and replacement), transcatheter (TEER and TMVR), oral/guideline-directed medical therapy, and injectable options. The two pivotal randomized trials of TEER for secondary MR (COAPT and MITRA-FR) reported directly contradictory results and both are reported here in full rather than only the positive one. Real-world registry, STS registry, and randomized-trial numbers are kept as distinct, separately-labelled metrics rather than averaged into one invented figure.

medicines.name: Mitral Valve Repair (annuloplasty ring +/- chordal replacement/leaflet resection)
medicines.effectiveness: 82.5% repair rate achieved in degenerative etiology (vs replacement); 94.4% 10-year freedom from reoperation
medicines.reason_why: Directly restores leaflet coaptation using the patient's own tissue -- an undersized annuloplasty ring corrects annular dilation and restores leaflet coaptation surface, while resection of a prolapsing segment or replacement of ruptured/elongated chordae with Gore-Tex neochordae corrects the specific mechanical lesion causing regurgitant flow. Preserves the native subvalvular apparatus, which better preserves LV contractile geometry than replacement.
medicines.source: STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database, Annals of Thoracic Surgery 2018; David TE et al. durability series (Ann Cardiothorac Surg / JTCVS)
medicines.confidence: high (large real registries and long-term single-center series, concordant)

medicines.name: Mitral Valve Replacement -- Mechanical prosthesis
medicines.effectiveness: 96.2% 10-year freedom from reintervention (age <65, propensity-matched)
medicines.reason_why: Used when repair is not feasible; the diseased valve is removed and replaced with a bileaflet mechanical valve, which is highly durable but is thrombogenic and requires lifelong warfarin anticoagulation (INR-monitored), carrying real long-term bleeding risk in exchange for durability.
medicines.source: JTCVS propensity-matched mechanical-vs-bioprosthetic MVR series (PMC11223803)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Mitral Valve Replacement -- Bioprosthetic (tissue) valve
medicines.effectiveness: 81.3% 10-year freedom from reintervention (age <65, propensity-matched); 93.8% freedom from structural valve deterioration at 10 years overall
medicines.reason_why: Avoids the need for lifelong anticoagulation (aside from an initial 3-6 month period), making it preferred in older patients or those who cannot tolerate warfarin, but the tissue leaflets undergo calcific/degenerative structural valve deterioration over time and wear out faster than mechanical valves, especially in younger patients and with porcine (vs bovine pericardial) tissue.
medicines.source: JTCVS propensity-matched mechanical-vs-bioprosthetic MVR series (PMC11223803); comparative bioprosthetic durability series
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: MitraClip / Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair (TEER) -- Primary (Degenerative) MR, high or prohibitive surgical risk
medicines.effectiveness: 93.8% achieved MR grade <=2+ at discharge; 85.9% maintained MR grade <=2+ at 3-year follow-up (real-world registry, anatomically complex degenerative MR)
medicines.reason_why: Percutaneously clips the anterior and posterior mitral leaflets together at the point of maximal regurgitant flow (edge-to-edge/'Alfieri' principle), creating a double-orifice valve that reduces regurgitant volume without open-heart surgery. Reserved by the 2020 ACC/AHA valve guidelines for severely symptomatic primary MR patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk, since surgical repair remains superior when the patient can tolerate surgery.
medicines.source: Real-world registry of anatomically complex degenerative MR (PMC12202683); 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease (JACC 2020)
medicines.confidence: high (real-world registry data, guideline-endorsed indication)

medicines.name: MitraClip / TEER -- Secondary (Functional) MR -- COAPT trial (positive result)
medicines.effectiveness: 29.1% vs 46.1% 2-year all-cause mortality (HR 0.62); 35.8% vs 67.9% annualized heart-failure-hospitalization rate at 2 years (HR 0.53); benefit persisted to 5 years (57.3% vs 67.2% mortality, HR 0.72)
medicines.reason_why: In a carefully selected population (severe secondary MR disproportionate to LV dilation, already on maximally tolerated GDMT, per the COAPT enrollment criteria), reducing MR volume lowered LV preload/volume overload enough to meaningfully cut heart-failure hospitalizations and mortality, on top of GDMT. COAPT enrolled 614 patients and is the largest, most positive randomized trial of TEER in secondary MR.
medicines.source: Stone GW et al., 'Transcatheter Mitral-Valve Repair in Patients with Heart Failure', NEJM 2018;379:2307-2318 (COAPT); Stone GW et al., 5-year follow-up, NEJM 2023;388:2037-2048
medicines.confidence: high (large multicenter RCT, real primary and long-term endpoints)

medicines.name: MitraClip / TEER -- Secondary (Functional) MR -- MITRA-FR trial (neutral/negative result)
medicines.effectiveness: No statistically significant benefit: 54.6% vs 51.3% death-or-heart-failure-hospitalization at 1 year (p=0.53); no significant difference in any individual component either
medicines.reason_why: In a different (less disproportionate MR-to-LV-size, more advanced LV dilation/dysfunction) secondary-MR population than COAPT, reducing MR volume via TEER did not translate into a clinical outcome benefit over optimal medical therapy alone -- reflecting that once the ventricle itself is the dominant driver of prognosis, clipping the valve does not reliably change the disease trajectory. MITRA-FR enrolled 304 patients and is reported here in full alongside COAPT rather than omitted, since the two trials genuinely disagree.
medicines.source: Obadia JF et al., 'Percutaneous Repair or Medical Treatment for Secondary Mitral Regurgitation', NEJM 2018;379:2297-2306 (MITRA-FR)
medicines.confidence: high (multicenter RCT; result is a real negative/neutral finding, not a data quality issue)

medicines.name: Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement (TMVR) -- Tendyne system, for severe Mitral Annular Calcification (MAC)
medicines.effectiveness: 94.2% technical success; 30-day mortality 6.8% (SUMMIT-MAC study, 103 high-surgical-risk patients, mean STS-PROM 7.1%, 85.4% frail)
medicines.reason_why: Delivers a full replacement valve transapically/transseptally into a mitral annulus too heavily calcified for either surgical replacement or durable TEER, addressing an anatomy that previously had no good treatment option. FDA-approved (May 27, 2025) specifically for severe MAC patients ineligible for surgery, based on the SUMMIT-MAC pivotal data -- a real but narrow, high-risk-population indication, not a general MR treatment.
medicines.source: SUMMIT-MAC study, JACC 2025 ('Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement for Severe Mitral Annular Calcification: Primary Outcomes'); FDA PMA P240042
medicines.confidence: high (real pivotal trial data underlying FDA approval), but the population (severe MAC, high frailty) is narrow and not representative of general MR

medicines.name: Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT) for Secondary/Functional MR -- ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs, SGLT2i
medicines.effectiveness: Not quantifiable as an MR-reversal percentage -- these are heart-failure mortality/remodeling trials, not MR-specific trials; e.g., ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) reduced the composite of CV death or HF hospitalization by 20% relative to enalapril (PARADIGM-HF)
medicines.reason_why: Treats the underlying LV dysfunction/dilation and neurohormonal activation that drives secondary MR (annular dilation and leaflet tethering from a remodeled ventricle) -- in some responders, LV reverse remodeling on GDMT measurably reduces functional MR severity, which is precisely why the COAPT and MITRA-FR trials both required patients to already be on maximally tolerated GDMT before considering TEER. These drugs do NOT repair or replace diseased leaflets/chordae and have essentially no effect on primary/degenerative MR, where the valve apparatus itself -- not the ventricle -- is the diseased structure.
medicines.source: McMurray JJV et al., PARADIGM-HF, NEJM 2014;371:993-1004; Pitt B et al., RALES, NEJM 1999;341:709-717; Zannad F et al., EMPHASIS-HF, NEJM 2011;364:11-21; McMurray JJV et al., DAPA-HF, NEJM 2019;381:1995-2008; Packer M et al., EMPEROR-Reduced, NEJM 2020;383:1413-1424; 2020 ACC/AHA Valve Guidelines (JACC 2020)
medicines.confidence: high (mechanism and HF-outcome trials are real and large), explicitly not an MR-specific effectiveness number

medicines.name: IV Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for acute decompensated heart failure/pulmonary edema from MR
medicines.effectiveness: Symptom control only -- not quantifiable as a cure % or MR-reversal metric
medicines.reason_why: Reduces intravascular volume and pulmonary venous congestion by promoting natriuresis/diuresis, relieving dyspnea and pulmonary edema caused by the regurgitant volume overloading the left atrium and pulmonary circulation; has no effect on the mechanical valve lesion itself.
medicines.source: Standard cardiology/critical-care practice (ACC/AHA/HFSA heart failure guidelines) -- no disease-modifying or MR-specific effect claimed
medicines.confidence: high (mechanism), not applicable as an effectiveness percentage (symptom control, not a cure metric)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (10-year freedom-from-reintervention, procedural technical success, real-world durability of MR reduction, repair-achieved rate, randomized-trial mortality/hospitalization relative risk reduction) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. GDMT is ranked by a real but non-MR-specific heart-failure trial endpoint (explicitly labelled as such), and MITRA-FR is included at 0% to honestly reflect its real neutral/negative randomized result rather than omitting it in favor of the positive COAPT trial.
