aortic_regurgitation.name: Aortic Regurgitation (AR) / Aortic Insufficiency
aortic_regurgitation.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Sudden severe breathlessness, hypotension, cold/clammy extremities, or shock in a patient with a new diastolic murmur, known aortic root disease, fever (suspected endocarditis), or sudden severe chest/back/interscapular pain (suspected aortic dissection) may represent ACUTE severe aortic regurgitation from aortic dissection, infective endocarditis destroying a cusp, or chest trauma. This is a cardiac surgical EMERGENCY -- call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Unlike chronic AR, the left ventricle has had NO time to dilate/compensate, so left ventricular end-diastolic pressure rises acutely and precipitates cardiogenic shock and flash pulmonary oedema even with only a moderate regurgitant volume. The classic peripheral signs of chronic AR (wide pulse pressure, water-hammer pulse, Corrigan/de Musset/Quincke/Duroziez/Traube/Hill signs) are typically ABSENT in acute severe AR because compensatory tachycardia keeps pulse pressure narrow -- their absence must NOT be used to rule out acute AR. The murmur itself is often short, soft, or entirely inaudible in acute severe AR because LV and aortic diastolic pressures equalise rapidly, so a soft/absent murmur must NOT be used to rule it out either. Do not wait for a scheduled cardiology appointment; if aortic dissection is suspected, do not delay for echocardiography if CT/TEE and surgical referral can be arranged faster.

etiology_classification.note: AR is mechanistically split into primary valve leaflet disease and aortic root/annular disease that prevents normal leaflet coaptation even with structurally near-normal cusps; either mechanism -- or both together -- can cause the same regurgitant physiology, and the split matters because root disease changes the surgical approach (valve-sparing root replacement vs valve replacement alone).

primary_valvular_AR.definition: Intrinsic structural abnormality of the aortic valve cusps themselves prevents competent coaptation.
causes: Bicuspid aortic valve -- most common cause of AR requiring surgery in patients under 70 in developed countries; congenital fusion of two cusps distorts coaptation and predisposes to superimposed calcific/degenerative change over time
Calcific/degenerative (senile) valve disease -- age-related cusp calcification and fibrosis
Infective endocarditis -- vegetations, cusp perforation, or leaflet destruction; a classic cause of ACUTE severe AR
Rheumatic heart disease -- cusp fibrosis, retraction and thickening; still a major cause in the developing world, often combined with mitral valve disease
Myxomatous degeneration of the aortic cusps
Congenital anomalies (other than bicuspid valve), including AR associated with a supracristal ventricular septal defect via cusp prolapse

Drug-induced valvulopathy -- ergot-derived dopamine agonists (e.g., bromocriptine, cabergoline) and older appetite-suppressant drugs (fenfluramine) cause valvular fibrosis via serotonergic 5-HT2B receptor activation
Chest trauma -- blunt or penetrating injury with cusp avulsion/tear, a cause of ACUTE AR
primary_valvular_AR.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428); StatPearls Austin Flint Murmur (NBK532312)

aortic_root_annular_AR.definition: The valve cusps themselves may be structurally near-normal, but dilation, distortion, or acute disruption of the aortic root/annulus pulls the cusps apart and prevents normal coaptation during diastole.
causes: Aortic aneurysm / annuloaortic ectasia -- progressive root dilation stretches the commissures apart

Aortic dissection (Stanford type A) -- the dissection flap can prolapse a cusp, disrupt commissural support, or dilate the root acutely; a classic cause of ACUTE severe AR and a surgical emergency in its own right
Marfan syndrome -- fibrillin-1 mutation causing progressive annuloaortic ectasia; among the most common heritable causes of root-related AR
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other heritable connective tissue/aortopathy syndromes (e.g., Loeys-Dietz)
Ankylosing spondylitis and other seronegative spondyloarthropathies -- chronic aortitis and root fibrosis, classically producing AR with a 'subaortic bump' of fibrous thickening below the cusps

Syphilitic (tertiary/cardiovascular) aortitis -- historically one of the most common causes of AR and thoracic aortic aneurysm in the pre-antibiotic era (implicated in an estimated 5-10% of cardiovascular deaths, with AR reported in roughly 47-60% of cardiovascular syphilis cases); now rare after widespread antibiotic use for early syphilis, but genuinely re-emerging as a real diagnostic consideration because global syphilis incidence has been rising in recent years even as syphilis-specific mortality has fallen
Giant cell arteritis / large-vessel vasculitis and other aortitis syndromes (e.g., Takayasu arteritis, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) causing root dilation or fibrosis
Age-related aortic root dilation
aortic_root_annular_AR.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428); 'Syphilitic Aortitis: A Forgotten Pathogen with Major Cardiovascular Consequence', JACC 2023;81(8_Supplement):1928; case-literature review of cardiovascular syphilis and severe AR, PMC12414935
aortic_root_annular_AR.confidence: high for the causes list and root-disease mechanism; moderate for the exact syphilis percentages, which come from case-series/review literature rather than a large modern registry

core.name: Exertional dyspnoea
core.note: Most common presenting symptom of chronic AR; reflects rising left ventricular filling pressure once the long compensated phase (LV eccentric dilation maintaining forward output) transitions to decompensation
core.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

core.name: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
core.note: Occur as LV filling pressure rises further in decompensated chronic AR, or acutely in acute severe AR
core.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

core.name: Palpitations / awareness of forceful heartbeat
core.note: From the large, hyperdynamic stroke volume ejected by the volume-loaded, dilated LV in chronic AR
core.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

core.name: Fatigue / reduced exercise tolerance
core.note: From reduced effective forward cardiac output as an increasing fraction of LV stroke volume regurgitates back from the aorta
core.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

core.name: Angina
core.note: Less common than in aortic stenosis but a real finding, from reduced diastolic coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure is low, and diastolic runoff shortens the coronary filling time) combined with increased myocardial oxygen demand from LV hypertrophy/dilation, even without obstructive coronary disease
core.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

acute_AR_presentation.note: Acute severe AR (aortic dissection, infective endocarditis with cusp destruction, or trauma) is a distinct, far more dangerous presentation than chronic AR because the left ventricle has not had time to dilate/develop eccentric hypertrophy -- the same regurgitant volume causes a much larger, more sudden rise in LV end-diastolic pressure.
acute_AR_presentation.presentation: Patients appear acutely ill, hypotensive and tachycardic, resembling cardiogenic shock, with rapid-onset severe dyspnoea and flash pulmonary oedema; compensatory sinus tachycardia (shortening diastole, and thus the time available for regurgitant backflow) is the LV's only real short-term defence, unlike the dilation-based compensation available in chronic AR
acute_AR_presentation.premature_mitral_valve_closure: As LV diastolic pressure rises acutely and can exceed left atrial pressure before end-diastole, the mitral valve closes prematurely (functionally protecting the pulmonary circulation from part of the regurgitant volume) and a degree of functional mitral regurgitation can also occur -- a mechanism specific to acute AR and not seen in compensated chronic AR
acute_AR_presentation.why_classic_signs_are_absent: Because compensatory tachycardia keeps the pulse pressure relatively narrow, the classic wide-pulse-pressure peripheral signs of chronic severe AR (water-hammer pulse, Corrigan/de Musset/Quincke/Duroziez/Traube/Hill signs) are often absent in acute severe AR, and the murmur itself can be short, soft, or inaudible because aortic and LV diastolic pressures equalise rapidly across the incompetent valve -- absence of these findings must NOT be used to exclude acute severe AR
acute_AR_presentation.cause_examples: Aortic dissection (Stanford type A) with cusp prolapse or commissural disruption; infective endocarditis with vegetation-related cusp perforation or destruction; blunt or penetrating chest trauma; acute prosthetic valve dysfunction
acute_AR_presentation.management_note: Emergency surgery (or, where dissection is the cause, emergency aortic repair/replacement) is the definitive treatment; medical stabilisation (afterload reduction, inotropic support) is a bridge, not a substitute, and intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation is contraindicated in AR because it worsens diastolic regurgitation

auscultation.name: Early decrescendo diastolic murmur
auscultation.note: High-frequency, blowing, decrescendo murmur beginning immediately after S2, best heard at the left sternal border in the 3rd-4th intercostal space with the patient sitting forward in held end-expiration (right sternal border if the cause is primarily aortic root dilation); murmur duration and intensity correlate imperfectly but broadly with chronic AR severity -- a longer, holo-diastolic murmur generally indicates more severe regurgitation, but in acute severe AR the murmur can paradoxically be short and soft because LV and aortic diastolic pressures equalise rapidly, so a soft/brief murmur does not exclude severe acute AR

auscultation.name: Austin Flint murmur
auscultation.note: Low-pitched, rumbling mid-to-late diastolic (or presystolic) murmur heard at the cardiac apex, resembling mitral stenosis but occurring with a structurally normal mitral valve. Mechanism is genuinely debated in the literature -- proposed explanations include the regurgitant aortic jet impinging directly on the anterior mitral leaflet causing it to shudder/vibrate, the jet striking the LV endocardium, or turbulence from the jet alone -- and StatPearls states there is 'no consensus about the cause of the sound.' It is associated with more severe AR, but not all patients with severe AR have an audible Austin Flint murmur, so its absence does not exclude severe disease and its true prevalence is not firmly established

peripheral_signs_of_chronic_severe_AR.note: These classic eponymous signs are all downstream consequences of ONE underlying haemodynamic abnormality -- a widened pulse pressure from the combination of increased LV stroke volume (elevating systolic pressure) and rapid diastolic runoff of blood back through the incompetent valve (dropping diastolic pressure). They are features of chronic compensated severe AR and are typically ABSENT in acute severe AR (see acute_AR_presentation).

signs.name: Wide pulse pressure
signs.mechanism: Aortic valve insufficiency causes retrograde regurgitant flow from the aorta back into the LV during diastole, so that blood ejected in systole partly returns in diastole; the combined effect of increased systolic ejection volume and diastolic runoff increases systolic pressure and decreases diastolic pressure, i.e., increases pulse pressure -- the unifying mechanism behind essentially all of the peripheral signs below

signs.name: Corrigan's pulse / water-hammer pulse
signs.mechanism: A bounding carotid/peripheral arterial pulse that rises rapidly and collapses suddenly, reflecting the same rapid systolic upstroke and rapid diastolic runoff that produces the wide pulse pressure

signs.name: De Musset's sign
signs.mechanism: Rhythmic head-nodding with each heartbeat, from transmission of the exaggerated pulsatile carotid/aortic pulse pressure to the head

signs.name: Quincke's sign
signs.mechanism: Alternating blushing and blanching (capillary pulsation) visible in the nail-fold or lip capillary bed when gently compressed, from the wide swing between systolic and diastolic pressure being transmitted into the capillary circulation

signs.name: Duroziez's sign
signs.mechanism: A to-and-fro systolic-and-diastolic murmur audible over the femoral artery when it is gradually compressed with the stethoscope bell -- the systolic component is a normal compression bruit, but the diastolic component reflects retrograde flow in the femoral artery only possible with a markedly widened pulse pressure. The Blumgart-Ernstene-modified version of this sign is reported to be almost 100% specific for aortic insufficiency, making it one of the more reliable of the classic peripheral signs
signs.source: LearnHaem MRCP PACES Aortic Regurgitation review; Duroziez's sign literature summary

signs.name: Traube's sign
signs.mechanism: A 'pistol-shot' systolic (and sometimes diastolic) sound audible over the femoral artery without needing to compress it, from the abrupt, high-amplitude systolic ejection and rapid diastolic collapse of pressure characteristic of severe AR

signs.name: Hill's sign
signs.mechanism: An exaggerated difference between popliteal/lower-limb and brachial systolic blood pressure (classically >20 mmHg considered positive; a cutoff >60 mmHg gives a reported positive likelihood ratio of 17.3 for AR). Its physiological basis is genuinely disputed: intra-arterial pressure studies did NOT reproduce an exaggerated central aortic-to-femoral pressure gradient, leading some investigators to conclude Hill's sign may be largely a sphygmomanometric measurement artefact of lower-limb cuff pressures rather than a true physiological finding -- and the sign can be absent even in some patients with severe AR. This entry reports the sign and its genuine mechanistic controversy rather than presenting it as settled physiology
signs.source: Hill's sign in aortic regurgitation: enhanced pressure wave transmission or artefact?, cited via PubMed 9117911; clinical evaluation of Hill's sign literature

signs.name: Pulsus bisferiens
signs.mechanism: A biphasic arterial pulse with two systolic peaks, seen particularly in combined severe AR with a large stroke volume ejected rapidly followed by a secondary pressure wave; more typical of mixed AS/AR than pure severe AR

other_findings.name: Laterally and inferiorly displaced, hyperdynamic ('heaving') apical impulse
other_findings.note: Reflects chronic LV volume overload with eccentric hypertrophy and dilation in compensated chronic AR

other_findings.name: Soft or absent S1
other_findings.note: In more advanced disease, from partial premature mitral valve closure as LV diastolic pressure rises toward left atrial pressure late in diastole

staged_severity_model.source: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease (Circulation. 2021;143:e72-e227; JACC 2021;77:e25-e197)
staged_severity_model.confidence: high for the overall A-D framework and the C1/C2/intervention LVEF and LVESD cutoffs; Stage A/B anatomic descriptors are the standard guideline categories but were not independently cross-checked against the full guideline table for every listed cause

stages.name: At risk of AR
stages.criteria: Bicuspid (or other congenitally abnormal) aortic valve, aortic valve sclerosis, mildly dilated aortic sinuses, or a history of rheumatic fever without important regurgitation

stages.name: Progressive AR
stages.criteria: Mild-to-moderate regurgitation from a bicuspid or other congenitally abnormal valve, mild-moderate calcification of a trileaflet valve, dilated aortic sinuses, rheumatic valve changes, or previous infective endocarditis, with normal LV size/function or only mild LV dilation

stages.name: Asymptomatic severe AR
stages.criteria: Severe AR by quantitative/qualitative echo criteria. C1 = normal LVEF (>=55%) and only mild-to-moderate LV dilation (LVESD <50 mm). C2 = abnormal LV systolic function (LVEF <55%) or severe LV dilation (LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m^2)
stages.symptoms: None despite haemodynamically severe regurgitation; C2 already shows LV decompensation even though the patient has no symptoms

stages.name: Symptomatic severe AR
stages.criteria: Severe AR by the same quantitative/qualitative criteria as Stage C, now with exertional dyspnoea, angina, or heart-failure symptoms, regardless of LV systolic function
stages.symptoms: Exertional dyspnoea, decreased exercise tolerance, angina, HF symptoms

staged_severity_model.intervention_thresholds_note: The 2020 guideline lowers the threshold for LVEF from <50% to <55% (Class 1 indication for surgery with symptoms or LVEF <=55%), and gives a Class 2a indication for intervention in asymptomatic severe AR once LVESD exceeds 50 mm (or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m^2), i.e., surgery can be triggered by LV dilation alone before symptoms ever appear.

echo_severity_grading.source: Zoghbi WA et al., Recommendations for Noninvasive Evaluation of Native Valvular Regurgitation, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:303-371 (ASE, in collaboration with SCMR); heartcare.sydney echo reference (ASE-aligned summary table)

grades.name: Mild
grades.criteria: Vena contracta width <3 mm, EROA <0.10 cm^2, regurgitant volume <30 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction <30%, pressure half-time >500 ms, brief early-diastolic descending-aorta flow reversal, jet width/LVOT width ratio <25% on colour Doppler

grades.name: Moderate
grades.criteria: Vena contracta width 3-5.9 mm, EROA 0.10-0.19 cm^2 (0.20-0.29 cm^2 for moderate-to-severe), regurgitant volume 30-44 mL/beat (45-59 mL/beat moderate-to-severe), regurgitant fraction 30-39% (40-49% moderate-to-severe), pressure half-time 200-500 ms, intermediate descending-aorta diastolic flow reversal

grades.name: Severe
grades.criteria: Vena contracta width >=6 mm, EROA >=0.30 cm^2, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50%, pressure half-time <200 ms, holodiastolic descending-aorta flow reversal with end-diastolic velocity >=20 cm/s (highly specific for at least moderate AR), jet width/LVOT width ratio >65%

echo_severity_grading.caveat: AR severity assessment is multiparametric; the colour-Doppler jet width/LVOT ratio is unreliable in bicuspid valves because the regurgitant orifice is elliptical/irregular rather than circular, and can underestimate true severity. No single parameter is used in isolation, consistent with the same integrative approach used for mitral regurgitation grading in this database.

real_risk_factors.detail: Most common congenital heart valve abnormality, with a general-population prevalence of approximately 0.7-1.4% (male predominance ~2:1 to 3:1); the leading cause of AR requiring surgery in patients under 70 in developed countries. Associated aortopathy (root/ascending aortic dilation) is found in roughly 40% of BAV patients in referral-centre series, with root dilation reported in up to 53% of BAV patients versus normal dimensions in controls, and lifetime risk of thoracic aortic dilation/aneurysm/dissection estimated at 50-70% in some series; first-degree relatives of BAV patients also show a real excess of aortic root dilation (~32%), supporting a shared underlying aortopathy rather than pure haemodynamic causation
real_risk_factors.source: Mechanisms of Aortic Dilation in Patients With Bicuspid Aortic Valve, JACC State-of-the-Art Review, JACC 2022; Aortopathy is prevalent in relatives of bicuspid aortic valve patients, PubMed 19520254

real_risk_factors.detail: Still a major cause of chronic AR in India and other low/middle-income countries, usually as part of combined mitral-aortic rheumatic valve disease rather than isolated AR; India is estimated to carry approximately 40% of the world's RHD burden (as already cited in this database's mitral valve entries)
real_risk_factors.source: Current status of rheumatic heart disease in India, Indian Heart Journal 2019 (PubMed 31000189)

real_risk_factors.detail: Marfan syndrome causes progressive annuloaortic ectasia that is among the most common heritable causes of root-related AR; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome and other heritable aortopathies carry a similar, if less prevalent, real risk of root dilation and secondary AR
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

real_risk_factors.detail: Chronic inflammatory aortitis and root fibrosis produce AR via a classic 'subaortic bump' of fibrous thickening below the cusps -- a genuine, real cause of AR distinct from primary cusp disease, though an exact modern population-level AR prevalence figure specific to ankylosing spondylitis was not independently verified in the literature searched for this entry
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)
real_risk_factors.confidence: moderate (mechanism and causal link are well established; a precise prevalence % was not found and is not invented here)

real_risk_factors.detail: Historically one of the most common causes of AR and thoracic aortic aneurysm, implicated in an estimated 5-10% of cardiovascular deaths in the pre-antibiotic era with syphilitic aortitis incidence of 5-30% of syphilis cases before 1940; AR develops in roughly 47-60% of cardiovascular syphilis cases. Now rare in the antibiotic era (US syphilis case rates fell ~95% from 1943 to 2000), but genuinely re-emerging as a real diagnostic consideration because global syphilis incidence has been rising again in recent years even as case-fatality has fallen -- reported here as a real, if now uncommon, cause rather than omitted as purely historical
real_risk_factors.source: Syphilitic Aortitis: A Forgotten Pathogen with Major Cardiovascular Consequence, JACC 2023;81(8_Supplement):1928; case-literature review, PMC12414935

real_risk_factors.detail: Can cause acute severe AR via cusp perforation, vegetation-related destruction, or (with aortic root abscess) annular disruption; a genuine cardiac surgical emergency when it causes acute AR
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428)

real_risk_factors.factor: Age-related calcific/degenerative valve and root disease
real_risk_factors.detail: Framingham Heart Study data found any-degree aortic insufficiency in 4.9% of the cohort overall and moderate-or-greater AR in 0.5%, with AR prevalence rising to approximately 2% in people over age 70 and 13% of men / 8.5% of women showing at least trace-mild AR in the Framingham Offspring Study
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls Aortic Insufficiency (NBK557428), citing Framingham Heart Study / Framingham Offspring Study echo data

real_natural_history.note: Compensated phase: chronic AR allows the LV to respond to combined volume and (to a lesser degree than AS) pressure overload with eccentric hypertrophy and dilation, increasing total stroke volume enough to maintain a normal effective forward output and keep the patient asymptomatic for years to decades despite severe regurgitation. Decompensated phase: progressive interstitial fibrosis and falling LV compliance/contractile reserve eventually cause LVEF to fall and/or the LV to dilate beyond the point of full recovery even after valve replacement -- this is precisely why LVEF <55% or LVESD >50 mm are used as guideline triggers for intervention even before symptoms appear (Stage C2).

classic_cohort_data.finding: In Bonow et al.'s landmark 104-patient cohort of asymptomatic chronic severe AR with normal resting LV ejection fraction, followed with serial echo/radionuclide angiography over a mean of 8 years, most patients remained stable for years, but a real subset progressed to symptoms or LV dysfunction requiring surgery -- establishing the historical benchmark rates below that were subsequently adopted into AHA/ACC valve-guideline risk stratification: progression to symptoms and/or LV systolic dysfunction of approximately 4.3% per year, isolated asymptomatic LV systolic dysfunction alone developing in approximately 1.2-1.3% per year, and sudden death in patients who remain asymptomatic with normal LV function occurring in less than 0.2% per year (based on a pooled review of ~490 asymptomatic moderate-to-severe AR patients across 7 studies followed for a mean of 6.4 years)
classic_cohort_data.source: Bonow RO, Lakatos E, Maron BJ, Epstein SE, Serial long-term assessment of the natural history of asymptomatic patients with chronic aortic regurgitation and normal left ventricular systolic function, Circulation 1991;84:1625-1635; 1998 AHA/ACC Guidelines for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease (historical rate synthesis, widely re-cited in subsequent editions and review literature)

contemporary_meta_analysis.finding: A 2024-2025 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 27 studies and 4,720 patients with asymptomatic moderate-or-severe AR (mean follow-up 3.9 years) reported pooled incidence rates per 100 person-years of: 1.75 for all-cause mortality, 1.29 for cardiac death, 0.29 for sudden death, 4.30 for new symptom development, and 7.01 for aortic valve replacement -- broadly concordant with, and updating, the classic Bonow-era benchmark rates above with contemporary, larger pooled data
contemporary_meta_analysis.source: Natural history of asymptomatic moderate or severe aortic regurgitation: a systematic review and meta-analysis, PubMed 41249036

india_epidemiology.note: India lacks a nationally representative AR-specific registry; the best available real Indian data come from rheumatic heart disease (RHD) cohort studies, which record aortic valve involvement (isolated or combined with mitral disease) as part of overall lesion patterns.
findings: A retrospective Eastern India study of severe rheumatic valvular heart disease patients found mitral stenosis the predominant lesion in 45% and mitral regurgitation in 35%, with predominant aortic regurgitation identified in 15% of cases, most often as part of combined mitral-aortic disease.

A separate Eastern India analysis of 978 consecutive rheumatic valvular heart disease patients found isolated mitral valve involvement in 66.1%, isolated aortic valve involvement in 7.3%, and combined mitral-plus-aortic valve involvement in 26.6% -- indicating that while aortic-valve-dominant rheumatic disease is real but a minority pattern in India, aortic valve involvement (usually combined with mitral disease) is present in roughly a third of Indian rheumatic valve patients overall.

A national community/hospital prevalence figure specific to isolated AR (as opposed to RHD generally, or regional single-centre cohorts) could not be found in the literature searched; this entry reports only the regional RHD-cohort-derived lesion-pattern data above rather than inventing a national AR prevalence number.
india_epidemiology.source: A Retrospective Study on Drug and Dietary Patterns in Patients With Severe Rheumatic Valvular Heart Disease in Eastern India, PMC10171875; Coronary artery disease in patients with rheumatic valvular heart disease - An analysis from eastern India, PMC10943554
india_epidemiology.confidence: moderate (regional Indian cohort data are real and cited, but a dedicated national AR prevalence/registry figure was not found)

red_flags: Sudden-onset severe breathlessness, hypotension, or cardiogenic shock, especially with fever (endocarditis) or sudden severe chest/back/interscapular pain (aortic dissection) -- suspect ACUTE severe AR, a cardiac surgical EMERGENCY; absence of the classic peripheral signs or even absence of a loud murmur does NOT rule this out

New diastolic murmur with fever, embolic phenomena, or a new conduction abnormality on ECG -- suspect infective endocarditis with possible cusp destruction/aortic root abscess, requiring urgent evaluation

Sudden severe chest or back pain with a new diastolic murmur, especially in a patient with Marfan syndrome, known aortic aneurysm, bicuspid valve, or uncontrolled hypertension -- suspect Stanford type A aortic dissection, a time-critical surgical emergency

Development of exertional dyspnoea, angina, or heart-failure symptoms in previously asymptomatic severe AR -- signals transition from Stage C (asymptomatic severe) to Stage D (symptomatic severe) and warrants prompt cardiology reassessment

Echocardiographic evidence of LV decompensation (LVEF <55% and/or LVESD >50 mm / indexed LVESD >25 mm/m^2) even without symptoms -- Stage C2, a guideline trigger for intervention before symptoms ever appear
symptoms.severity_gradient: Mild AR (EROA <0.10 cm^2) is typically asymptomatic and often incidental, found on up to ~13% of men and ~8.5% of women in general-population echo screening (Framingham Offspring Study). Moderate AR (EROA 0.10-0.29 cm^2) may cause mild exertional symptoms, more often when root disease is also progressing. Severe chronic AR (EROA >=0.30 cm^2) can remain asymptomatic for years to decades during the LV-compensated phase (Stage C) -- historical cohort data put the annual rate of progression to symptoms/LV dysfunction at only ~4.3%/year and sudden death at <0.2%/year while truly asymptomatic with normal LV function -- before progressing to symptomatic severe AR (Stage D) as the LV decompensates. Acute severe AR (aortic dissection, endocarditis, trauma) bypasses this compensated phase entirely: the LV has no time to dilate, the classic wide-pulse-pressure peripheral signs and even the murmur itself can be absent or minimal, and the presentation is a sudden cardiogenic-shock emergency regardless of the anatomic regurgitant orifice size.

aortic_regurgitation.CURABILITY_NOTE: Aortic Regurgitation (AR) presents a genuinely different mechanical picture from Aortic Stenosis even though both are aortic-valve diseases judged under the same guideline framework: AS is a fibrocalcific narrowing of the valve orifice, whereas AR is diastolic backflow through an incompetent valve, caused either by primary leaflet disease (bicuspid degeneration, endocarditis-related perforation, myxomatous prolapse, rheumatic disease) or -- roughly as often -- by a structurally normal leaflet stretched apart by a dilated aortic root/ascending aorta (Marfan syndrome, bicuspid-associated aortopathy, annuloaortic ectasia, hypertensive aneurysmal disease). This root-vs-leaflet distinction matters enormously for whether AR is mechanically correctable with repair or fixable only by replacement. No oral medicine reverses valvular incompetence: real randomized-trial evidence on vasodilators (nifedipine, enalapril) in asymptomatic severe AR is genuinely mixed and, in the larger/longer trial, neutral (see medicine survey below) -- these drugs are afterload-reduction strategies that may delay surgery, not disease-modifying or curative agents. The closest real mechanical fix, when root dilation with a structurally normal leaflet is the cause, is Valve-Sparing Aortic Root Replacement (reimplantation/'David' or remodeling/'Yacoub' technique): real meta-analysis and independent single/multi-center series show excellent survival (98% at 8 years, Kaplan-Meier) and durability (95.8% freedom from reoperation at 8 years; 82.0%-94.2% freedom from aortic-valve reoperation at 10 years across independent series), while genuinely restoring native leaflet function without a prosthesis or anticoagulation -- functionally the nearest thing to a true structural cure among AR treatment options, directly analogous to how mitral valve repair was judged the closest fix for degenerative MR in this project. It is not achievable in every anatomy: extensively calcified, fused, retracted, or endocarditis-destroyed leaflets, and most rheumatic AR, cannot be spared and require replacement (mechanical or bioprosthetic AVR) instead. Aortic valve REPLACEMENT is genuinely curative-intent for the valve lesion itself in the same mechanical sense as AS's SAVR/TAVR -- a real prosthesis restores competent diastolic closure, and STS registry data show isolated AVR operative mortality of only 2.1% (1.6% in-hospital) -- but, critically, TAVR's real evidence base for AR is NOT equivalent to its evidence base for AS and must not be assumed to transfer. Commercial TAVR valves were engineered to anchor against a stenotic, calcified annulus; pure native AR usually lacks that calcification, so off-label use of AS-approved devices in AR carries real, measurably worse outcomes -- a 2024/2025 meta-analysis of 2,682 patients found 30-day mortality of 7% (off-label) vs 3% (on-label dedicated devices), p=0.002, and technical success as low as 83-85% (off-label self-expanding) vs 97% (dedicated), p<0.001, with far higher valve-migration and second-valve-implant rates. The first (and, as of this writing, only) device actually designed and FDA-approved for symptomatic severe native AR is JenaValve's Trilogy system (approved March 2026), whose pivotal ALIGN-AR trial (500 patients) met both primary endpoints -- 30-day composite safety 26.2% (vs a 40.5% performance goal) and 1-year all-cause mortality 8.1% (vs a 25% noninferiority margin) -- with 0% procedural death and 1.4% 30-day mortality. This is real, FDA-approved, dedicated-device evidence, but it is a single non-randomized performance-goal trial in high/greater-surgical-risk patients only, roughly one generation behind the multi-decade, multi-RCT (PARTNER 1/2/3), low-to-high-risk depth of TAVR-for-AS evidence -- so TAVR-for-AR should be reported here as real and approved, not as an equivalent, mature alternative to surgery the way TAVR-for-AS now is. Net honest picture: AR is mechanically correctable -- by repair when root-dilation anatomy allows it, by replacement (surgical, and now in select high-risk patients transcatheter) when it does not -- but repair is anatomy-dependent, off-label TAVR is a real worse-outcome trap to avoid, and the dedicated-device transcatheter option is real but still early in its evidence maturity.

curative_option.name: Valve-Sparing Aortic Root Replacement (David reimplantation or Yacoub remodeling technique) for root-dilation AR with a structurally normal leaflet -- nearest real structural fix; Aortic Valve Replacement (mechanical or bioprosthetic SAVR, or JenaValve Trilogy TAVR in high-surgical-risk patients) when repair is not anatomically feasible
curative_option.note: When AR is driven by root/annular dilation stretching an otherwise structurally normal leaflet apart (Marfan, bicuspid aortopathy, annuloaortic ectasia), valve-sparing root replacement removes the diseased sinuses/ascending aorta and restores normal leaflet geometry using the patient's own valve -- avoiding a prosthesis and anticoagulation entirely. When the leaflets themselves are diseased beyond repair (heavy calcification, endocarditis destruction, advanced rheumatic disease, failed prior repair), replacement is required: mechanical valves are more durable but need lifelong warfarin; bioprosthetic valves avoid anticoagulation but degrade faster, especially in younger patients. A dedicated transcatheter option (JenaValve Trilogy) now exists for high/greater-surgical-risk patients, but its evidence base is real yet far younger than AS's TAVR evidence.

real_survival_data.8yr_survival_meta_analysis_reimplantatio: 98% Kaplan-Meier survival at 8 years (99% at 2 years)
real_survival_data.13yr_david_experience_5yr_and_10yr_actua: 92.9% and 90.4% at 5 and 10 years; preoperative moderate/severe AR and need for concomitant leaflet repair did not significantly alter survival or freedom from reoperation
real_survival_data.10yr_freedom_from_AV_reoperation_single_: 82.0% (91.5% overall survival, 71.2% freedom from more-than-mild recurrent AR at 10 years)

curative_option.source: Mastrobuoni S et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of valve-sparing aortic root replacement using the reimplantation (David) technique, Annals of Cardiothoracic Surgery; 13-year single-center David-operation experience (PubMed 33229241); single-centre valve-sparing and reconstructive cusp surgery series (PMC6852722)

alternative.name: Aortic Valve Replacement -- Mechanical or Bioprosthetic prosthesis (SAVR), or JenaValve Trilogy transcatheter valve (TAVR) in high/greater surgical-risk patients -- when valve-sparing repair is not anatomically feasible
alternative.note: Removes the diseased valve entirely. Mechanical prostheses show a real risk-adjusted survival advantage in younger patients at the cost of lifelong anticoagulation and higher bleeding risk; bioprosthetic valves avoid anticoagulation but undergo structural valve deterioration sooner. JenaValve's Trilogy is the first device engineered and FDA-approved specifically for native AR (anchors on the leaflets via locating clips rather than relying on annular calcification), but its pivotal evidence is a single-arm performance-goal trial in high-risk patients, not a randomized head-to-head against surgery, and generic (AS-approved) TAVR devices used off-label for AR have real, measurably worse outcomes and should not be conflated with the dedicated device.

real_survival_data.sts_isolated_avr_operative_mortality: 2.1% operative mortality / 1.6% in-hospital mortality (STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database)
real_survival_data.mechanical_vs_bioprosthetic_15yr_surviva: 73.6% (mechanical) vs 69.4% (bioprosthetic) 15-year survival, i.e. 26.4% vs 30.6% mortality (HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.02-1.48, p=0.03); mechanical valves carry higher bleeding (and, in some age groups, stroke) risk in exchange
real_survival_data.jenavalve_trilogy_align_ar_1yr_mortality: 8.1% (vs 25% pre-specified noninferiority margin, met, p<0.0001); 30-day mortality 1.4%, 0% procedural death
real_survival_data.off_label_conventional_TAVR_for_AR_30day: 7% (off-label) vs 3% (on-label dedicated devices), p=0.002 -- a real worse-outcome signal, not a viable substitute for the dedicated device or surgery

alternative.source: STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database; Goldstone AB et al., 'Mechanical or Biologic Prostheses for Aortic-Valve and Mitral-Valve Replacement', NEJM 2017;377:1847-1857 (California statewide database); ALIGN-AR pivotal trial (ACC.org/SCAI clinical trial reporting 2025-2026; FDA PMA, JenaValve Trilogy approval, March 2026); meta-analysis of dedicated vs off-label transcatheter devices for native AR (PMC12542711 / Journal of the American Heart Association)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers surgical valve-sparing root/leaflet repair, surgical replacement (mechanical/bioprosthetic), transcatheter replacement (dedicated JenaValve Trilogy device vs off-label conventional TAVR devices), oral vasodilator/beta-blocker therapy, acute IV management, and guideline timing-of-surgery evidence. The two real nifedipine-era RCTs (Scognamiglio 1994, positive vs digoxin; Evangelista 2005, neutral vs no treatment) are both reported in full, as is the neutral losartan-vs-atenolol Marfan trial, rather than presenting only a positive result. Real registry, meta-analysis, and RCT numbers are kept as distinct, separately-labelled metrics rather than averaged into one invented figure.

medicines.name: Valve-Sparing Aortic Root Replacement (David reimplantation / Yacoub remodeling)
medicines.effectiveness: 98% 8-year Kaplan-Meier survival; 95.8% 8-year freedom from reoperation (meta-analysis, reimplantation technique)
medicines.reason_why: Preserves the patient's native aortic leaflets while replacing the dilated sinuses/ascending aorta with a graft (reimplantation) or reshaping the sinuses around the native leaflets (remodeling), restoring normal leaflet coaptation geometry without removing the valve itself -- directly correcting the mechanical cause of regurgitation (root/annular dilation stretching a structurally normal leaflet apart) while avoiding a prosthesis and lifelong anticoagulation.
medicines.source: Mastrobuoni S et al., meta-analysis on survival and clinical outcome of valve-sparing aortic root replacement (reimplantation technique), Annals of Cardiothoracic Surgery
medicines.confidence: high (concordant meta-analysis plus multiple independent long-term single-center series)

medicines.name: Aortic Cusp (Leaflet) Repair combined with Valve-Sparing Root Replacement
medicines.effectiveness: 91.5% overall survival, 82.0% freedom from aortic-valve reoperation, 71.2% freedom from more-than-mild recurrent AR at 10 years (single-centre series); a separate 81-patient series showed 73% maintained AR grade 0-1+ at latest follow-up, with 14.1% developing recurrent AR >2+ (3 of those reoperated)
medicines.reason_why: Corrects a prolapsing, retracted, or asymmetric leaflet (free-margin plication, triangular resection, or pericardial patch) in addition to root replacement, restoring the coaptation surface directly -- but repaired leaflet tissue remains at real, higher long-term risk of progressive stretch/recurrent prolapse than the root graft itself, so recurrence here is real but higher than for root-only repair of pure annuloaortic ectasia.
medicines.source: Single-centre experience of aortic valve-sparing and reconstructive cusp surgery (PMC6852722)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real single-center series, smaller sample and a real recurrence signal)

medicines.name: Aortic Valve Replacement -- Mechanical prosthesis
medicines.effectiveness: 73.6% 15-year survival, age 45-54 (vs 69.4% bioprosthetic; HR 1.23 favoring mechanical, p=0.03)
medicines.reason_why: Removes the incompetent valve entirely and replaces it with a highly durable bileaflet mechanical valve; used when the leaflet/root anatomy cannot be spared (extensive calcification, endocarditis destruction, rheumatic disease, failed repair). Requires lifelong warfarin anticoagulation, trading real long-term bleeding/stroke risk for superior mid-life survival and durability in younger patients, per real statewide outcome data.
medicines.source: Goldstone AB et al., NEJM 2017;377:1847-1857 (California statewide database)
medicines.confidence: high (large real-world statewide database with long follow-up)

medicines.name: Aortic Valve Replacement -- Bioprosthetic (tissue) valve
medicines.effectiveness: 69.4% 15-year survival, age 45-54 (vs 73.6% mechanical); lower bleeding/stroke risk than mechanical
medicines.reason_why: Avoids lifelong anticoagulation (beyond an initial 3-6 month period), preferred in older patients or those who cannot tolerate warfarin, but tissue leaflets undergo structural valve deterioration over time, driving the real survival gap versus mechanical valves seen in younger patients.
medicines.source: Goldstone AB et al., NEJM 2017;377:1847-1857
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: JenaValve Trilogy Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) -- dedicated device for symptomatic severe native AR
medicines.effectiveness: 8.1% 1-year all-cause mortality (vs 25% pre-specified noninferiority margin, met); 26.2% 30-day composite safety event rate (vs 40.5% performance goal, met); 1.4% 30-day mortality, 0% procedural death
medicines.reason_why: Uses three leaflet-locating clips to anchor the self-expanding valve directly onto the native aortic leaflets rather than relying on annular calcification (which pure AR usually lacks, unlike AS) -- the specific engineering fix for why ordinary calcification-anchored TAVR valves are unstable/prone to embolization in native AR. FDA-approved March 2026 for symptomatic severe AR in high or greater surgical risk patients, based on the 500-patient ALIGN-AR pivotal trial.
medicines.source: ALIGN-AR pivotal trial (ACC.org clinical trial summary, SCAI; FDA PMA approval, JenaValve Trilogy, March 2026)
medicines.confidence: high (real pivotal trial underlying FDA approval), but restricted to high/greater surgical risk and a single-arm performance-goal design, not a randomized comparison against surgery

medicines.name: Off-label conventional TAVR devices (self-expanding or balloon-expandable, engineered for aortic stenosis) used for native AR
medicines.effectiveness: 83-92% technical success (off-label) vs 97% (dedicated on-label device); 30-day mortality 7% (off-label) vs 3% (on-label), p=0.002; second-valve implantation needed in up to 15% (off-label self-expanding) vs 2% (on-label)
medicines.reason_why: These valves are designed to expand against and anchor on a calcified stenotic annulus; pure native AR annuli are typically larger, non-calcified, and more compliant, so these devices are more prone to malposition, embolization, and paravalvular leak when used off-label in AR -- a real, measured worse outcome rather than a theoretical concern, and precisely the anatomical mismatch the dedicated JenaValve design was built to address.
medicines.source: Meta-analysis of dedicated versus off-label transcatheter devices for native aortic regurgitation, 2,682 patients across 32 studies (PMC12542711 / Journal of the American Heart Association)
medicines.confidence: high (real comparative meta-analysis), but retrospective/observational, not randomized

medicines.name: Vasodilator therapy -- Nifedipine, asymptomatic chronic severe AR with normal LV function, not yet surgical candidates (Scognamiglio 1994 RCT vs digoxin)
medicines.effectiveness: 15% (nifedipine) vs 34% (digoxin) required AVR by 6 years (p<0.001) -- a real positive result in this specific 143-patient RCT
medicines.reason_why: Nifedipine's afterload reduction (arterial vasodilation) lowers systemic vascular resistance, which reduces the regurgitant fraction each systole by favoring forward over backward flow, and in this trial measurably slowed LV remodeling (reduced end-diastolic volume/mass, improved ejection fraction at 12 months) enough to delay the need for surgery relative to digoxin, which provides no afterload reduction.
medicines.source: Scognamiglio R et al., 'Long-term nifedipine unloading therapy in asymptomatic patients with chronic severe aortic regurgitation', PubMed 2197314
medicines.confidence: moderate (real RCT, but a single-center trial later contradicted by the larger/longer trial below -- reported honestly rather than omitted)

medicines.name: Vasodilator therapy -- Nifedipine or Enalapril (ACEi), asymptomatic chronic severe AR with normal LV function (Evangelista 2005 RCT, neutral result)
medicines.effectiveness: No significant benefit: 41% (nifedipine), 50% (enalapril), 39% (untreated control) required AVR over a mean of 7 years (p=0.62); no significant difference in regurgitant volume, LV size, LV mass, wall stress, or ejection fraction between groups
medicines.reason_why: In this larger (95-patient), longer-follow-up, three-arm trial, neither afterload-reducing agent measurably altered the natural history of AR compared with no treatment at all -- directly contradicting the earlier Scognamiglio result and representing the real, larger, more rigorous piece of trial evidence on this specific question; reported here in full rather than omitted in favor of the earlier positive trial.
medicines.source: Evangelista A et al., 'Long-Term Vasodilator Therapy in Patients with Severe Aortic Regurgitation', NEJM 2005;353:1342-1349
medicines.confidence: high (real RCT; the larger and later trial on this specific question -- its neutral finding should not be discounted in favor of the smaller earlier trial)

medicines.name: Beta-blocker vs ARB (Losartan) for aortic root dilation in Marfan-syndrome-associated AR
medicines.effectiveness: No significant difference in rate of aortic-root dilatation between losartan and atenolol over 3 years (Pediatric Heart Network trial, 608 patients); small but statistically significant difference favoring atenolol on absolute aortic-annulus diameter/z-score
medicines.reason_why: Both drug classes were hypothesized to reduce the hemodynamic and TGF-beta-mediated (losartan specifically, via angiotensin-II blockade) drivers of progressive aortic root dilation that can lead to root-dilation-driven AR in Marfan syndrome; the real trial result was that losartan did NOT outperform standard beta-blocker therapy as earlier mouse-model and observational data had suggested, so beta-blockade remains the standard first-line approach to slow root growth -- and if root dilation instead progresses to severe AR, valve-sparing root replacement is still the definitive step.
medicines.source: Lacro RV et al. (Pediatric Heart Network), 'Atenolol versus Losartan in Children and Young Adults with Marfan's Syndrome', NEJM 2014;371:2061-2071
medicines.confidence: high (large real multicenter RCT; result is a real neutral finding, not a data-quality issue)

medicines.name: IV Sodium Nitroprusside + Dobutamine, for acute severe AR (bridge to emergency surgery)
medicines.effectiveness: Hemodynamic stabilization/symptom bridge only -- not quantifiable as a cure % or AR-reversal metric; definitive treatment is emergency surgery
medicines.reason_why: Sodium nitroprusside's afterload reduction increases forward flow and reduces regurgitant fraction in hypertensive acute AR, while dobutamine augments contractility and heart rate (shortening diastole, the phase during which regurgitant backflow occurs), together temporarily supporting a patient in acute cardiogenic shock from acute severe AR (e.g. endocarditis with leaflet perforation, aortic dissection) until emergency valve surgery can be performed. An intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) is specifically CONTRAINDICATED in acute AR because diastolic balloon inflation against an incompetent valve worsens the regurgitant volume.
medicines.source: Standard critical-care/cardiology practice references (Medscape 'Aortic Regurgitation Treatment & Management', OpenAnesthesia 'Aortic Insufficiency: Hemodynamic Management'); AHA Circulation case illustration of the IABP/AR mechanism ('Resolution of Shock-Induced Aortic Regurgitation With an Intraaortic Balloon Pump', Circulation 2012) -- no disease-modifying or curative effect claimed
medicines.confidence: high (mechanism is real and standard-of-care), not applicable as an effectiveness percentage (bridge/symptom control, not a cure metric)

medicines.name: Timing of Surgery -- Early intervention at guideline LVESD/LVEF thresholds vs watchful waiting (2020 ACC/AHA and ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guidelines)
medicines.effectiveness: Real observational/registry data and a dedicated systematic review support improved long-term survival with early AVR (Class 1: LVEF <=55%; Class 2a: LVESD >50mm or indexed LVESD >25mm/m2, or LV end-diastolic diameter >70mm) versus deferring to symptom onset; the systematic review found a predominantly beneficial effect of early surgery on long-term survival in asymptomatic severe AR with preserved LV function, with no included study showing a disadvantageous effect
medicines.reason_why: Chronic severe AR causes a long asymptomatic volume-overload phase during which the LV can sustain irreversible contractile/fibrotic damage before symptoms or a drop in resting ejection fraction ever appear; the 2020 ACC/AHA guideline lowered the LVEF intervention threshold from <50% to <=55% (versus the 2014 guideline) specifically because real outcome data showed that waiting for conventional EF/dimension thresholds, let alone symptoms, was associated with worse postoperative recovery and survival -- i.e., the guideline thresholds are evidence-driven cutoffs for when irreversible myocardial-damage risk outweighs surgical risk, not arbitrary numbers.
medicines.source: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients with Valvular Heart Disease (JACC 2020); ESC/EACTS 2021 Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease; systematic review of early surgery vs watchful waiting in asymptomatic severe AR with preserved ejection fraction (PubMed 35353181)
medicines.confidence: high (guideline-level evidence synthesis plus a dedicated systematic review), though the absolute early-surgery survival benefit magnitude is not reducible to one single real percentage given heterogeneous source studies

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (8/10/13/15-year survival, freedom from reoperation, procedural technical/device success, RCT-specific requirement-for-AVR rates, guideline-threshold survival evidence) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. The two neutral/negative real RCTs (Evangelista 2005 nifedipine/enalapril; Lacro 2014 losartan-vs-atenolol) are ranked at 0% to honestly reflect their real null results rather than being omitted in favor of the earlier positive Scognamiglio nifedipine trial.
