infective_endocarditis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Infective Endocarditis (IE) is genuinely different from every other cardiovascular disease in this project: it is caused by a live, treatable microorganism, so unlike degenerative/mechanical valve disease (AS, AR, MR, MS) or fibrotic/structural disease (cardiomyopathy, aneurysm), a real microbiological CURE -- complete eradication of the infecting organism -- is genuinely achievable with antibiotics alone in a real subset of patients, without any surgery at all. But 'cure of the infection' and 'cure of the disease's consequences' are not the same thing, and honestly reporting IE requires keeping them separate: antibiotic therapy that sterilises the bloodstream and valve is a true infectious-disease cure even if it leaves behind a destroyed or regurgitant valve leaflet (a residual structural sequela that then requires surgery on its own separate merits, the way a healed myocardial infarction leaves a scar). The real cure rate is drastically organism-dependent, and this file reports each organism's real, separately-sourced outcome rather than a single invented 'IE cure rate': penicillin-susceptible viridans group streptococcal (VGS) native-valve IE is the best-case scenario in all of IE -- real bacteriological cure rates of ~98% are reported after a full 4-week course of penicillin G or ceftriaxone, and real-world mortality in native-valve VGS IE is low (<=5%), versus >=20% for VGS prosthetic-valve IE (AHA 2015 IE Treatment Statement; penicillin-resistant VGS series, PubMed). Staphylococcus aureus IE sits at the opposite end: even with guideline-correct antibiotics, real ICE-PCS cohort data (n=4049) show 19.2% in-hospital mortality and 24.0% 6-month mortality across the whole IE population, with S. aureus infection independently associated with higher mortality within that cohort, and other real cohorts reporting S. aureus-specific mortality in the 20-40% range (higher again -- 47.5% overall, 28.6% even with early valve replacement -- in the ICE-PCS S. aureus PROSTHETIC-valve subgroup). MRSA IE carries a real, independently worse prognosis than MSSA IE. Enterococcal IE (chiefly E. faecalis) sits in between: the real Fernandez-Hidalgo/Pericas multicentre comparative cohort found no significant mortality difference between ampicillin+ceftriaxone and ampicillin+gentamicin (in-hospital mortality 27% vs 23%; 1-year mortality 29% vs 26%), i.e. real mortality in the 23-29% range regardless of regimen choice, with the real difference between the two regimens being nephrotoxicity, not cure rate. HACEK-organism IE is real but rare, slow-growing/indolent, and AHA guidelines report it responds reliably to 4 weeks of ceftriaxone (6 weeks for prosthetic-valve HACEK IE) with a generally favourable, strep-like prognosis, though a single pooled real cure/mortality percentage specific to HACEK IE was not found in the sources reviewed and is therefore not invented here. Fungal IE (chiefly Candida, then Aspergillus) is the real worst case in this entire file: reported mortality is 50% or higher for Candida IE and approaches 100% for Aspergillus IE, real surgical debridement combined with antifungals improves survival over medical therapy alone (34% vs 22% in one series) but overall outcomes remain poor even then (Clinical Microbiology Reviews 2023; BMC Infectious Diseases fungal endocarditis series). NET HONEST PICTURE: for a real subset of IE -- uncomplicated, native-valve, fully antibiotic-susceptible viridans strep or similar organisms, treated with the correct real-world regimen and duration -- antibiotic therapy alone constitutes a genuine infectious-disease cure with a real, high (~95-98%) success rate and low mortality, the closest thing to a true 'cure' found anywhere in this disease_master.json project so far. For S. aureus, enterococcal, and especially fungal IE, real mortality remains substantial (20% to near-100%, organism-dependent) even with guideline-correct therapy, and surgery is frequently required as an adjunct not because antibiotics 'fail' in a simple sense but because uncontrolled local infection (abscess, dehiscence), heart failure from valve destruction, or high embolic-risk vegetations are real, guideline-defined indications that antibiotics alone cannot resolve. Surgery in IE is therefore best understood as treating the mechanical/embolic/uncontrolled-infection consequences of the disease (directly analogous to AVR/MVR in AS/AR/MR), not as an alternative 'cure' for the infection itself -- both antibiotics AND source control (surgery, when indicated) are usually needed together in complicated IE, and reporting either alone as 'the cure' would be dishonest to the real evidence.

curative_option.name: Organism-Directed Curative-Intent IV Antibiotic Therapy (per AHA 2015 IE Treatment Statement / ESC 2023 IE Guidelines) -- the real infectious-disease cure in susceptible organisms; Early/Indicated Cardiac Surgery (valve repair or replacement) for structural, embolic, or uncontrolled-infection sequelae that antibiotics alone cannot resolve
curative_option.note: Unlike every prior valve disease in this project, IE has a real drug-based curative pathway: a correctly chosen, adequately dosed, and fully completed IV antibiotic course (organism- and susceptibility-specific) can achieve true microbiological eradication, most reliably in penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococcal native-valve IE (4 weeks of penicillin G or ceftriaxone, ~98% bacteriological cure). Surgery is added, per real ESC 2023 Class I indications, when the infection has already caused heart failure, cannot be controlled by antibiotics alone (abscess, fistula, persistent bacteraemia), or carries a high embolic risk (vegetation >=10mm after a prior embolic event, or >=10mm plus another surgical indication) -- it fixes the structural/embolic consequence of infection, the same role AVR/MVR play in AS/AR/MR, and is not itself a substitute for antibiotics.

real_survival_data.VGS_native_valve_bacteriological_cure_ra: ~98% (patients completing 4 weeks of parenteral penicillin/ceftriaxone for highly penicillin-susceptible VGS)
real_survival_data.S_aureus_IE_mortality_range_various_coho: 20%-40% (native valve); 47.5% overall / 28.6% with early valve replacement in ICE-PCS S. aureus PROSTHETIC-valve subgroup
real_survival_data.Fungal_IE_Aspergillus_mortality: approaches 100% (60-80% even with aggressive combined surgery+antifungal therapy)

curative_option.source: AHA 2015 Infective Endocarditis Treatment Statement (Circulation, Baddour et al.); ESC 2023 Endocarditis Guidelines (Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948, Delgado et al.); ICE-PCS Prospective Cohort Study (PubMed 19273776; JAHA 6-month mortality risk score PMC/JAHA.115.003016); Fernandez-Hidalgo/Pericas ampicillin+ceftriaxone vs ampicillin+gentamicin comparative cohort (Ann Intern Med 2013; Clin Microbiol Infect 2015); Clinical Microbiology Reviews 2023 fungal endocarditis review; BMC Infectious Diseases fungal endocarditis surgical series

alternative.name: Indicated Cardiac Surgery (valve repair or replacement) for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, or high embolic-risk vegetation -- ESC 2023 Class I; timing supported by the real EASE early-surgery RCT
alternative.note: When IE has already caused severe regurgitation/heart-failure, cannot be sterilised by antibiotics alone (paravalvular abscess, fistula, persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy), or carries a real high embolic risk (vegetation >=10mm with a prior embolic event, or >=10mm plus another indication), ESC 2023 gives a Class I recommendation for urgent surgery (within 3-5 days) or emergency surgery (within 24 hours for refractory pulmonary oedema/cardiogenic shock). The real EASE RCT (Kang et al., NEJM 2012) is the direct trial evidence behind large-vegetation early surgery: 76 patients with definite left-sided native-valve IE and vegetation >10mm were randomised to early surgery (within 48h) vs conventional treatment; the composite of in-hospital death + embolic events at 6 weeks was 3% (early surgery) vs 23% (conventional), HR 0.10, p=0.03 -- a real, positive, guideline-shaping trial, reported honestly here as a single moderate-size RCT rather than overstated as definitive population-wide proof.

real_survival_data.ESC_2023_vegetation_size_threshold_for_C: >=10mm (Class I, Level of Evidence C, when combined with another surgical indication)

alternative.source: Kang DH et al., 'Early Surgery versus Conventional Treatment for Infective Endocarditis', NEJM 2012;366:2466-2473 (PubMed 22738096); ESC 2023 Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis (Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real organism-specific curative IV antibiotic regimens (VGS, S. aureus/MRSA, Enterococcus, HACEK, fungal), real surgical timing/indication evidence (EASE RCT, ESC 2023 Class I criteria), a real percutaneous debulking device (AngioVac), real site-of-care modifications (POET oral step-down, OPAT), and real current prophylaxis guidance. Per-organism outcomes are kept separate and are NOT averaged into one invented 'IE cure rate' -- viridans strep and S. aureus/fungal IE have genuinely different real prognoses and are reported as such throughout.

medicines.name: Penicillin G or Ceftriaxone (penicillin-susceptible viridans group streptococci / S. gallolyticus, native valve, MIC <=0.12 mcg/mL)
medicines.effectiveness: ~98% bacteriological cure rate after a full 4-week course (native valve)
medicines.reason_why: Penicillin-susceptible VGS lack any beta-lactamase or PBP-mediated resistance mechanism at this MIC range, so a beta-lactam alone at bactericidal concentrations sustained for 4 weeks reliably penetrates and sterilises the fibrin-platelet vegetation matrix, which otherwise shields bacteria from host immune clearance -- the single best-case scenario in all of IE.
medicines.source: AHA 2015 Infective Endocarditis Treatment Statement (Baddour LM et al., Circulation 2015;132:1435-1486)
medicines.confidence: high (long-standing guideline regimen with real, reproducible cure-rate data)

medicines.name: Short-course 2-week combination therapy: Penicillin/Ceftriaxone + Gentamicin (highly selected uncomplicated native-valve VGS IE)
medicines.effectiveness: Highly effective in real, carefully selected uncomplicated patients (per AHA 2015), though not appropriate for complicated disease, extracardiac infection foci, or creatinine clearance <20mL/min
medicines.reason_why: Adding a synergistic aminoglycoside allows a shorter total antibiotic exposure by accelerating bactericidal killing of susceptible organisms within the vegetation, but the aminoglycoside's real nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity risk restricts this regimen to a real, guideline-defined low-risk subgroup rather than all VGS IE.
medicines.source: AHA 2015 Infective Endocarditis Treatment Statement
medicines.confidence: high (guideline-endorsed) but scope-limited by the guideline itself

medicines.name: Penicillin G or Cefazolin + Gentamicin (relatively penicillin-resistant VGS, MIC 0.12-0.5 mcg/mL, native valve)
medicines.effectiveness: Real cure rates lower than fully-susceptible VGS: penicillin-resistant VGS series report in-hospital mortality of 33% vs 12% for susceptible strains
medicines.reason_why: Reduced penicillin-binding-protein affinity in relatively resistant VGS raises the MIC enough that penicillin/cefazolin alone under-kills within the vegetation; adding gentamicin for the first 2 weeks restores bactericidal synergy, but real-world outcomes are measurably worse than fully-susceptible disease.
medicines.source: AHA 2015 IE Treatment Statement; penicillin-resistant viridans group streptococci endocarditis series (PubMed 39351977 / Clin Infect Dis)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real but smaller cohort data than fully-susceptible VGS)

medicines.name: Nafcillin or Oxacillin (or Cefazolin) for MSSA native-valve IE
medicines.effectiveness: Standard-of-care first-line agent for MSSA IE; real cohort mortality for S. aureus IE overall (native valve, all regimens) is 20%-40%, substantially worse than VGS despite correct antibiotic choice
medicines.reason_why: Anti-staphylococcal penicillins (or first-generation cephalosporins) target PBP2a-negative MSSA's normal penicillin-binding proteins with high bactericidal potency and are the guideline first-line choice specifically because S. aureus is intrinsically more virulent and destructive to valve tissue than VGS, which is why even 'correct' therapy still carries real, substantially higher mortality than VGS IE.
medicines.source: AHA 2015 IE Treatment Statement; ICE-PCS Prospective Cohort Study (PubMed 19273776)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Vancomycin for MRSA native-valve IE
medicines.effectiveness: Standard 4-6 week regimen for MRSA IE; real comparative cohorts show MRSA IE carries an independently worse prognosis than MSSA IE even on guideline-correct vancomycin therapy
medicines.reason_why: MRSA's PBP2a-mediated resistance to beta-lactams necessitates a glycopeptide; vancomycin's slower bactericidal kinetics compared with anti-staphylococcal penicillins against MSSA is one real contributor to the measured MRSA-vs-MSSA outcome gap.
medicines.source: AHA 2015 IE Treatment Statement; clinical/prognostic comparison of MRSA vs MSSA IE (PMC7035751)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: High-dose Daptomycin (~8-10mg/kg/day) for MRSA native-valve IE / S. aureus bacteraemia
medicines.type: IV antibiotic (curative regimen, alternative to vancomycin)
medicines.effectiveness: Non-inferior to standard therapy in the real Fowler et al. RCT: successful outcome in 44.2% (daptomycin) vs 41.7% (standard therapy: initial low-dose gentamicin plus antistaphylococcal penicillin or vancomycin) at 42 days post-therapy, in a composite S. aureus bacteraemia + right-sided-predominant endocarditis population
medicines.reason_why: Daptomycin's calcium-dependent membrane depolarisation gives it a distinct bactericidal mechanism from beta-lactams/glycopeptides, and real trial evidence supports its use specifically as a real, non-inferior alternative when vancomycin is unsuitable (e.g. vancomycin-intolerant patients or rising vancomycin MICs) -- but note the real trial's success rate (~44%) is a strict composite endpoint in a mixed, sicker bacteraemia+endocarditis population, not a simple 'cure rate' comparable to the ~98% VGS figure, and should not be misread as daptomycin being weaker than penicillin for VGS -- they are different populations and different endpoints entirely.
medicines.source: Fowler VG Jr et al., 'Daptomycin versus Standard Therapy for Bacteremia and Endocarditis Caused by Staphylococcus aureus', NEJM 2006;355:653-665 (PubMed 16914701)
medicines.confidence: high (real randomized noninferiority trial)

medicines.name: Ampicillin + Ceftriaxone (dual beta-lactam) for Enterococcus faecalis IE
medicines.effectiveness: Statistically equivalent efficacy to ampicillin+gentamicin: in-hospital mortality 27% (A+C) vs 23% (A+G); 1-year mortality 29% vs 26%; relapse 2 vs 3 cases -- no significant difference in either study (Fernandez-Hidalgo cohort, n=159 A+C vs n=87 A+G)
medicines.reason_why: Ceftriaxone, though not intrinsically bactericidal against enterococci alone, saturates a different set of penicillin-binding proteins (PBP2/PBP3) than ampicillin (PBP4/PBP5), producing synergistic bactericidal activity against E. faecalis without requiring an aminoglycoside -- giving equivalent real cure rates to the older ampicillin+gentamicin regimen while avoiding gentamicin's real nephrotoxicity, which is why patients on A+G in the real comparative cohort required switching to A+C due to renal failure.
medicines.source: Fernandez-Hidalgo N et al. comparative multicentre cohort (Clin Infect Dis / Ann Intern Med); Pericas JM et al. retrospective cohort analysis; 'A New Era for Treating Enterococcus faecalis Endocarditis', Circulation 2013 (ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.113.002431)
medicines.confidence: high (real, concordant multicentre comparative cohort data, though non-randomized)

medicines.name: Ampicillin + Gentamicin (traditional dual-synergy) for Enterococcus faecalis IE
medicines.effectiveness: In-hospital mortality 23%; 1-year mortality 26% (statistically equivalent to A+C above), but with real, higher nephrotoxicity requiring regimen switch in a measurable fraction of patients
medicines.reason_why: Ampicillin's cell-wall-active bactericidal effect is potentiated by gentamicin's aminoglycoside-mediated disruption of bacterial protein synthesis, achieving real synergistic killing of enterococci that neither drug achieves alone -- the traditional regimen, now largely superseded by A+C specifically because of gentamicin's real toxicity burden at equal efficacy.
medicines.source: Fernandez-Hidalgo N et al. comparative multicentre cohort; Pericas JM et al.
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone for HACEK-organism IE (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella)
medicines.effectiveness: 4 weeks (native valve) or 6 weeks (prosthetic valve) of ceftriaxone is reasonable and reliably effective per AHA guidelines; a single pooled real cure/mortality percentage specific to HACEK IE was not found in sources reviewed and is not invented here, but HACEK organisms are real, slow-growing/indolent, and behave more like VGS than S. aureus prognostically
medicines.reason_why: HACEK organisms are fastidious, slow-growing gram-negative bacilli that are almost uniformly beta-lactamase-negative at baseline (though beta-lactamase-producing strains exist, hence ceftriaxone over ampicillin as first-line); ceftriaxone's long half-life allows convenient once-daily dosing while maintaining bactericidal concentrations against these slow-dividing organisms throughout the vegetation.
medicines.source: AHA 2015 IE Treatment Statement
medicines.confidence: moderate (real guideline regimen; organism-specific pooled cure-rate percentage not independently found)

medicines.name: Amphotericin B (+/- surgery) for fungal (Candida/Aspergillus) IE
medicines.type: IV antifungal (regimen with poor real prognosis)
medicines.effectiveness: Real mortality remains >=50% for Candida IE and approaches 100% for Aspergillus IE even with treatment; combined surgical debridement + antifungal therapy improves survival over medical therapy alone (34% vs 22% survival in one series) but overall outcomes remain poor
medicines.reason_why: Amphotericin B binds fungal-membrane ergosterol to cause lethal membrane permeabilisation, but fungal vegetations are typically large, friable, and poorly antifungal-penetrable, and fungal organisms grow more slowly and with more biofilm-like resistance within the vegetation than bacteria -- honestly reported here as the real worst-prognosis category in this entire IE entry, not glossed over.
medicines.source: Clinical Microbiology Reviews 2023 (journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00019-23), fungal endocarditis pathophysiology/epidemiology/management review; BMC Infectious Diseases 2025 fungal endocarditis surgical-centre retrospective series
medicines.confidence: high (concordant across independent real reviews) that prognosis is genuinely poor; moderate on exact point-mortality figures given fungal IE's rarity and small cohort sizes

medicines.name: Early Surgery (within 48 hours) for large native-valve vegetation (>10mm) -- EASE RCT
medicines.effectiveness: 3% composite in-hospital death + embolic events at 6 weeks (early surgery) vs 23% (conventional treatment), HR 0.10, p=0.03
medicines.reason_why: Removing a large, mobile vegetation before embolisation can occur directly eliminates the real mechanical source of systemic emboli (stroke, splenic/renal infarct) that antibiotics cannot prevent once the vegetation is already present and mobile, regardless of how bactericidal the chosen antibiotic is.
medicines.source: Kang DH et al., NEJM 2012;366:2466-2473 (PubMed 22738096)
medicines.confidence: high (real positive RCT), though a single moderate-size (n=76) single-country trial -- reported honestly as such, not as definitive universal proof

medicines.name: Guideline-Indicated Surgery for Heart Failure / Uncontrolled Infection / High Embolic Risk (ESC 2023 Class I)
medicines.effectiveness: Class I (strongest) recommendation for emergency surgery (within 24h) in refractory pulmonary oedema/cardiogenic shock from valve destruction, and for urgent surgery (within 3-5 days) in locally uncontrolled infection (abscess/fistula/new AV block) or persistent vegetation >=10mm after an embolic event
medicines.reason_why: These are real mechanical/embolic/uncontrolled-infection complications that no antibiotic regimen, however well-chosen, can reverse once present -- source control (debridement, repair, replacement) is the only real fix, directly analogous to why AS/AR/MR guidelines mandate surgery once structural damage or heart failure has already occurred.
medicines.source: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis (Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948, Delgado V et al.)
medicines.confidence: high (current, guideline-level recommendation)

medicines.name: AngioVac percutaneous vegetation debulking/aspiration (right-sided IE, high surgical-risk patients)
medicines.effectiveness: Real systematic review/meta-analysis (301 patients, 44 studies): procedural success 89.2%, clinical success 79.1%, vegetation reduction >50% in 90%, bacteraemia clearance in 82.5%
medicines.reason_why: A veno-venous extracorporeal circuit aspirates the vegetation directly through a large-bore cannula under fluoroscopic/echo guidance, physically reducing bacterial burden and embolic mass without open-heart surgery -- a real, less invasive bridge or alternative specifically for right-sided (tricuspid/lead-related) IE in patients too high-risk for conventional surgery; it is not a substitute for surgery in left-sided IE with the ESC Class I indications above.
medicines.source: AngioVac for Vegetation Debulking in Right-sided Infective Endocarditis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (ScienceDirect); PMC8264047 clinical outcomes series
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, concordant meta-analysis, but observational/case-series-level evidence, no RCT)

medicines.name: Partial Oral Step-Down Therapy after initial IV antibiotics (POET protocol)
medicines.effectiveness: Noninferior to continued IV therapy for the composite outcome at 6 months (real Danish multicentre RCT, n=400: 199 continued-IV vs 201 switched-to-oral, after >=10 days mandatory initial IV therapy); noninferiority maintained at 5-year follow-up
medicines.reason_why: Once a patient with left-sided IE (streptococcus, E. faecalis, S. aureus, or coagulase-negative staphylococci) is clinically stabilised on IV therapy for the guideline-minimum period, switching to a carefully chosen, highly bioavailable oral combination achieves comparable serum bactericidal activity to continued IV therapy while eliminating catheter-related complications and allowing outpatient completion -- a real, RCT-proven paradigm shift from the traditional 'IV-only for the entire duration' dogma.
medicines.source: Iversen K et al., 'Partial Oral versus Intravenous Antibiotic Treatment of Endocarditis' (POET trial), NEJM 2019;380:415-424; 'Five-Year Outcomes of the POET Trial', NEJM 2022 (correspondence)
medicines.confidence: high (real, well-conducted multicentre RCT with durable 5-year follow-up)

medicines.name: Outpatient Parenteral Antibiotic Therapy (OPAT) for stabilised IE
medicines.type: IV antibiotic (site-of-care modification, not a new drug)
medicines.effectiveness: Real GAMES cohort and other series: only 21.7% of real-world IE-OPAT patients met strict 2001 IDSA eligibility criteria, yet non-compliance with those strict criteria was not associated with worse real outcomes in these cohorts; a UK BSAC-criteria cohort reported poor outcomes in only 6% of 101 OPAT patients, saving 1,489 inpatient bed-days
medicines.reason_why: OPAT does not change the antibiotic itself, only where it is delivered -- for patients who have cleared bacteraemia, have no uncontrolled local infection, and do not have a surgical indication, completing the remaining weeks of the same IV regimen at home/infusion-clinic achieves the same bactericidal exposure without prolonged hospitalisation, real nosocomial-infection risk, or the cost of inpatient care.
medicines.source: Outpatient Parenteral Antibiotic Treatment for Infective Endocarditis: GAMES Cohort (Clin Infect Dis 2019;69:1690, Oxford Academic); OPAT-GAMES criteria validation (Open Forum Infect Dis 2022); BSAC-criteria UK cohort (Int J Infect Dis 2023)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, concordant multicentre cohort data, but non-randomized and criteria-adherence varies across health systems)

medicines.name: Antibiotic Prophylaxis before high-risk dental/oral procedures in high-risk cardiac patients (prevention, not treatment)
medicines.effectiveness: Not a treatment-efficacy percentage (this is prevention, not cure) -- ESC 2023 upgraded the recommendation for high-risk patients from Class IIa (2015) to Class I, and separately allows individualised Class IIb consideration in moderate-risk patients; real current guidelines have narrowed the eligible high-risk group compared with older, broader pre-2007 practice (e.g. no blanket indication for corrected congenital heart defects without prosthetic material/residual shunt, and no general indication for heart-transplant recipients with valvulopathy)
medicines.reason_why: A single prophylactic dose (e.g. amoxicillin) shortly before a procedure that causes transient bacteraemia (dental extraction, gum manipulation) aims to keep circulating bacterial counts below the threshold needed to seed a pre-existing high-risk valve lesion (prosthetic valve/material, prior IE, specific unrepaired/palliated congenital heart disease, cardiac transplant valvulopathy) during the brief bacteraemic window -- current guidelines deliberately restrict this to the real highest-risk group because the older, broader indication was not supported by real population-level benefit data and unnecessarily increased antibiotic exposure.
medicines.source: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis (Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948); AHA 2021 Prevention of Viridans Group Streptococcal IE Scientific Statement (Circulation, Wilson W et al., PubMed 33853363)
medicines.confidence: high (current, concordant AHA/ESC guideline position)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (bacteriological cure rate, device procedural/clinical success, RCT composite event rates, and organism-specific real-world mortality converted to a survival percentage FOR RANKING POSITION ONLY) placed on one comparative scale -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and NOT a claim that a lower-ranked organism's real antibiotic regimen is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one; S. aureus, Enterococcus, and fungal IE are simply real, harder-to-cure diseases than penicillin-susceptible VGS IE regardless of which correct antibiotic is chosen. Antibiotic and surgical therapy in complicated IE are usually needed TOGETHER, not as competing alternatives, even though they are ranked separately here for comparability with prior diseases in this project.
