infective_endocarditis.name: Infective Endocarditis (IE)
infective_endocarditis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Fever with a new or changing heart murmur, sudden focal neurological deficit (embolic stroke), sudden breathlessness/pulmonary oedema from acute valve destruction, or sudden severe abdominal/flank/limb pain (splenic infarct, mycotic aneurysm, peripheral embolism) in a patient with a prosthetic valve, known structural heart disease, intracardiac device, intravenous drug use, or recent bacteraemia/dental-or-invasive procedure should be treated as suspected acute infective endocarditis with a real, life-threatening embolic or haemodynamic emergency until echocardiography and blood cultures prove otherwise -- call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Untreated IE is uniformly fatal; even with modern antimicrobial and surgical therapy, in-hospital mortality is approximately 15-20% and one-year mortality approaches 40%. Do not wait for an outpatient cardiology appointment: acute heart failure from valve destruction, uncontrolled infection despite antibiotics, a large mobile vegetation, or a new AV-conduction abnormality (suggesting root/annular abscess) are real Class I indications for emergency or urgent cardiac surgery, and embolic events (including silent ones) occur most frequently in the first 2 weeks after starting antibiotics, i.e., the highest-risk window is often before or just after diagnosis, not later.

classification.note: IE is not one disease epidemiologically -- the valve substrate (native vs prosthetic) and the route of bacteraemia (community/dental vs injection drug use vs healthcare exposure) genuinely change the likely organism, the valve(s) involved, and the prognosis, so classification is clinically load-bearing, not just descriptive.

native_valve_endocarditis.definition: IE occurring on a structurally native (non-prosthetic) valve, historically the majority pattern.
native_valve_endocarditis.epidemiology: Staphylococcus aureus has become the leading single cause of IE overall in most modern Western series, reported at approximately 26-30% of all cases, ahead of viridans group streptococci (approximately 18-20%); community-acquired native valve IE without injection drug use is more often subacute and streptococcal, whereas S. aureus NVE tends to run a more acute, destructive course
native_valve_endocarditis.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); Ishak A et al., Infective Endocarditis: A Contemporary Review of Epidemiology, Diagnosis, and Management, Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482 (PMC13203618)

prosthetic_valve_endocarditis.definition: IE on a prosthetic (mechanical or bioprosthetic) valve, accounting for over 20% of all IE cases in contemporary series; split into early PVE and late PVE because the timing genuinely predicts the organism.
prosthetic_valve_endocarditis.early_PVE: Onset within approximately the first year after valve surgery (perioperative-acquisition literature more narrowly defines 'early-onset' as within 60 days); usually caused by organisms acquired perioperatively -- staphylococci (both coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus) dominate. Recent staphylococcal early-onset PVE series report coagulase-negative staphylococci actually outnumbering S. aureus (approximately 76% vs 24% of staphylococcal early PVE in one series), reflecting perioperative skin-flora contamination of the prosthesis; early PVE carries a high in-hospital mortality, reported around 30%
prosthetic_valve_endocarditis.late_PVE: Onset a year or more after surgery; organism pattern shifts toward that of community-acquired NVE -- viridans streptococci and enterococci become more prominent, though coagulase-negative staphylococci remain frequent low-virulence isolates
prosthetic_valve_endocarditis.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); StatPearls Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis (NBK567731); PMC12831407 (staphylococcal early-onset PVE surgical series)

IVDU_associated_endocarditis.definition: IE in people who inject drugs, mechanistically and epidemiologically distinct because bacteraemia is seeded directly into the venous (right heart) circulation rather than via the arterial/systemic route that predominantly seeds left-sided valves.
IVDU_associated_endocarditis.epidemiology: The tricuspid valve is involved in over 50% of IVDU-associated IE (versus the mitral/aortic valves in 20-30%), and Staphylococcus aureus (usually methicillin-sensitive) is the causative organism in 60-70% of IVDU-related IE. Annual IE incidence in people who inject drugs is estimated at approximately 2-5% per year, dramatically higher than the general-population annual incidence of 3-10 per 100,000. Right-sided/tricuspid IE characteristically produces septic pulmonary emboli rather than the systemic (cerebral/splenic) emboli of left-sided IE
IVDU_associated_endocarditis.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); case-literature synthesis on tricuspid valve endocarditis in IVDU (PMC10298630, PMC10196414)

healthcare_associated_nosocomial_endocar.definition: IE acquired from a healthcare exposure (intravascular catheters, haemodialysis access, recent hospitalisation/procedures) rather than the community, now a real and rising share of overall IE as the population ages and prosthetic valves/intracardiac devices/dialysis become more common.
healthcare_associated_nosocomial_endocar.epidemiology: Among patients with cardiac-device-related IE (CDIE) specifically, roughly 45.8% of infections are healthcare-associated, frequently linked to intravascular access and haemodialysis; CDIE itself makes up approximately 6.4% of all definite IE (85.9% pacemakers, 11.9% ICDs), with S. aureus (35.0%) and coagulase-negative staphylococci (31.6%) the leading organisms and lead vegetations visible on imaging in 76.3% of cases. IE incidence has risen 'exponentially' in healthcare-associated settings such as haemodialysis in recent decades
healthcare_associated_nosocomial_endocar.source: Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482 (PMC13203618); ACC review of clinical characteristics/outcomes of ICD-related IE

core.name: Fever
core.note: The most common presenting symptom, present in roughly 90% of patients overall and reported as the presenting complaint in more than 70%; classically low-grade and intermittent in subacute disease (e.g., viridans streptococcal IE) but high and sustained in acute S. aureus IE. A real minority of subacute IE patients (approximately 3-5%, mostly elderly or chronically ill) present with normal or even subnormal temperature, so absence of fever does not exclude IE
core.source: Medscape/Cardiology clinical-presentation synthesis of IE case series

core.name: Constitutional symptoms -- malaise, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, night sweats
core.note: Reflect the systemic inflammatory/cytokine response to sustained bacteraemia; particularly prominent in subacute IE (classically viridans streptococcal or enterococcal), which can smoulder for weeks before diagnosis
core.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641)

core.name: Arthralgia / myalgia
core.note: Common non-specific systemic feature, thought to relate to circulating immune complexes and the systemic inflammatory response rather than direct joint infection
core.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641)

core.name: New or changing cardiac murmur
core.note: A heart murmur is present in approximately 85% of IE patients overall, most commonly an aortic or mitral regurgitant murmur from valve destruction; however, in roughly one-third of patients with acute IE (especially rapidly destructive S. aureus IE) a murmur may be absent early in the course, so its absence does not exclude acute IE
core.source: Medscape/Cardiology clinical-presentation synthesis of IE case series

core.name: Dyspnoea / heart failure symptoms
core.note: Develops when valve destruction (leaflet perforation, chordal rupture, or annular/root abscess causing dehiscence) produces acute severe regurgitation, or when a large vegetation obstructs the valve orifice; this is one of the real Class I indications for urgent surgery in IE
core.source: AHA/ACC and ESC infective endocarditis guideline surgical-indication literature

acute_vs_subacute_presentation.note: IE is classically split by tempo -- acute (rapidly progressive, days, typically S. aureus, often on a previously normal valve) versus subacute (indolent, weeks to months, classically viridans streptococci or enterococci, typically on a valve already damaged by rheumatic disease, MVP, or a bicuspid/calcific valve) -- because the tempo predicts both the likely organism and the urgency of the workup, though the two overlap and are not always cleanly separable at presentation.
acute_vs_subacute_presentation.acute: High sustained fever, rigors, rapidly progressive valve destruction, higher rate of embolic and metastatic infective complications, higher short-term mortality; murmur may still be absent or soft early because it has not had time to develop the classical fully regurgitant sound
acute_vs_subacute_presentation.subacute: Low-grade intermittent fever, weeks of malaise/weight loss/night sweats before diagnosis, higher likelihood of the classic peripheral immunologic/vascular stigmata (Osler nodes, Roth spots, splenomegaly) precisely because the smouldering course gives time for immune-complex phenomena to develop
acute_vs_subacute_presentation.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); HACEK-endocarditis literature describing a mean ~13-week symptom duration before diagnosis as a real example of a subacute, insidious course (PMC9389832)

modified_duke_criteria.note: This is the real, clinically used diagnostic framework for IE -- not a symptom list. It combines pathological criteria (definite tissue/culture proof, not detailed here) and clinical criteria (major + minor) to classify a case as Definite, Possible, or Rejected IE.

history.detail: Durack, Lukes and Bright's original Duke Endocarditis Service criteria introduced 2 major criteria (typical blood cultures; positive echocardiogram) and 6 minor criteria, validated in 405 consecutive suspected-IE episodes
history.source: Durack DT, Lukes AS, Bright DK. New criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis: utilization of specific echocardiographic findings. Duke Endocarditis Service. Am J Med. 1994;96(3):200-209

history.detail: Li et al. revised the original criteria after validation in a cohort of 800 patients, aiming to reduce over-classification as 'possible IE' (i.e., raise specificity): the echocardiographic minor criterion was eliminated given the accuracy of transoesophageal echo, S. aureus bacteraemia was upgraded to a major criterion regardless of whether it was nosocomial or had a removable focus, and positive Q fever serology was made a major criterion
history.source: Li JS, Sexton DJ, Mick N, et al. Proposed modifications to the Duke criteria for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Clin Infect Dis. 2000;30(4):633-638 (PubMed 10770721)

history.detail: The International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases (ISCVID) convened a multidisciplinary working group to update the criteria for modern microbiology and imaging: new blood-culture-independent microbiologic major criteria (valve PCR, broad-range 16S rRNA sequencing, Bartonella serology, amplicon/metagenomic sequencing), new imaging major criteria (18F-FDG PET/CT and cardiac CT, particularly for prosthetic-valve/device IE), intraoperative inspection added as a new major clinical criterion, an expanded list of 'typical' organisms (some typical only in the presence of intracardiac prostheses), removal of the requirement for strict timing/separate-venipuncture blood cultures, and clarified predisposing conditions (transcatheter valve implants, endovascular cardiac implantable electronic devices, prior IE). In reanalysis, Duke-ISCVID classified 56.4% of episodes as definite IE versus 54.9% with ESC 2015 and 51.1% with the 2000 modified Duke criteria; another validation reported sensitivity 84.2%/specificity 93.9% for Duke-ISCVID versus 74.9%/94.9% for the 2000 modified Duke criteria
history.source: Fowler VG Jr, Durack DT, Selton-Suty C, et al. The 2023 Duke-ISCVID Criteria for Infective Endocarditis: Updating the Modified Duke Criteria. Clin Infect Dis. 2023 (PubMed 37138445); Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482 (PMC13203618)

modified_duke_criteria.diagnostic_categories: Definite IE = 2 major criteria, OR 1 major + 3 minor criteria, OR 5 minor criteria (clinical criteria alone; pathological proof from surgery/autopsy is separately sufficient on its own). Possible IE = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor criteria. Rejected = firm alternate diagnosis, resolution with <=4 days of antibiotics, no pathological evidence at surgery/autopsy after <=4 days of antibiotics, or failure to meet the criteria for possible IE
major_criteria: Positive blood cultures for IE: typical IE organisms (viridans streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus [S. bovis], HACEK group, Staphylococcus aureus, or community-acquired enterococci without a primary focus) from 2 separate blood cultures, OR persistently positive blood cultures with an organism consistent with IE from cultures drawn >12 hours apart, or 3/3 or a majority of >=4 separate cultures with the first and last drawn >=1 hour apart, OR a single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii or an antiphase I IgG antibody titre >1:800

Evidence of endocardial involvement: an echocardiogram positive for IE (oscillating intracardiac mass on a valve/supporting structure, or in the path of a regurgitant jet, or on implanted material, in the absence of an alternative anatomic explanation; an abscess; new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve) or new valvular regurgitation (worsening/changing of a pre-existing murmur is not sufficient alone)
minor_criteria: Predisposition: a predisposing heart condition (e.g., prosthetic valve, prior IE, structural valve disease) or injection drug use
Fever, defined as temperature greater than 38.0 degrees C
Vascular phenomena: major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages, and Janeway lesions
Immunologic phenomena: glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, and rheumatoid factor

Microbiological evidence not meeting a major criterion (excluding single cultures of coagulase-negative staphylococci or organisms that do not commonly cause IE), or serological evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with IE
modified_duke_criteria.source: Li JS et al., Clin Infect Dis. 2000;30(4):633-638; Durack DT et al., Am J Med. 1994;96(3):200-209
modified_duke_criteria.confidence: high for the 2000 modified Duke criteria text (this is the version most widely used clinically worldwide as of 2026); high for the existence and broad content of the 2023 Duke-ISCVID update, moderate for the precise wording of every individual 2023 criterion since the full guideline text itself was not directly opened, only secondary summaries

organism_epidemiology.detail: The leading single cause of IE in most modern series, responsible for approximately 26-30% of all cases; associated with an acute, destructive clinical course, higher embolic risk, and higher mortality than streptococcal IE, and disproportionately represented in healthcare-associated and IVDU-associated IE (60-70% of IVDU-associated IE)
organism_epidemiology.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482

organism_epidemiology.detail: Now the second most common cause overall, at approximately 18-20% of cases, still classically associated with subacute community-acquired IE on a previously damaged (e.g., rheumatic, myxomatous, or bicuspid) valve and with a dental/oral-mucosal portal of entry
organism_epidemiology.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482

organism_epidemiology.detail: Reported at approximately 15-18% of cases (nosocomial vs community-acquired ranges cited in StatPearls), with real rising significance particularly in elderly and hospitalised patients, often following genitourinary or gastrointestinal instrumentation
organism_epidemiology.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482

organism_epidemiology.detail: A recognised but uncommon cause, responsible for approximately 3% of IE, notable because these fastidious, slow-growing, capnophilic gram-negative organisms are a classic real cause of apparently 'culture-negative' IE on standard media; HACEK IE tends to occur in younger patients with an insidious course (mean approximately 13 weeks of symptoms before diagnosis) and is more frequently associated with embolic, vascular and immunologic manifestations than non-HACEK IE
organism_epidemiology.source: Infective endocarditis by HACEK: a review, PMC9389832; Das M et al., Infective endocarditis caused by HACEK microorganisms, PubMed 9046942

organism_epidemiology.organism: Streptococcus bovis / gallolyticus (specifically S. gallolyticus subsp. gallolyticus)
organism_epidemiology.detail: A real and clinically important marker organism: a literature survey spanning 1970-2010 found approximately 65% of patients with invasive S. gallolyticus infection had a concomitant colorectal neoplasm, and other series report 25-80% of S. bovis/gallolyticus bacteraemia patients having a concomitant colorectal tumour (association with villous/tubulovillous adenomas and early adenomas specifically, in addition to established cancer) -- so a diagnosis of S. bovis/gallolyticus IE is a real, guideline-referenced indication for colonoscopy
organism_epidemiology.source: The association of Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus with colorectal tumors, PMC3032743; Significance of Streptococcus gallolyticus subsp. gallolyticus Association With Colorectal Cancer, PMC5891635

organism_epidemiology.organism: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g., S. epidermidis, S. lugdunensis, S. capitis)
organism_epidemiology.detail: Classically dismissed as skin-flora contaminants in native valve blood cultures, but a real and important cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis, particularly early PVE (perioperative prosthesis contamination) -- one staphylococcal early-onset PVE series found CoNS causing approximately 76% of staphylococcal early PVE versus 24% for S. aureus; S. lugdunensis specifically behaves atypically for a CoNS species, causing an aggressive, S. aureus-like destructive course
organism_epidemiology.source: PMC12831407 (staphylococcal early-onset PVE surgical series); PMC12910833 (S. lugdunensis PVE case literature)

organism_epidemiology.organism: Fungal IE (predominantly Candida spp., also Aspergillus spp.)
organism_epidemiology.detail: Rare, at approximately 1-10% of all IE cases (most reviews cite 1-3%), but carries disproportionately high mortality (>70% in some series); Candida species cause over half of fungal IE (C. albicans alone 24-46% of fungal IE and about 3.4% of all PVE), blood cultures can be negative in up to 50% of fungal IE, and combined antifungal-plus-surgical debridement is generally required because medical therapy alone rarely clears fungal vegetations
organism_epidemiology.source: Fungal Endocarditis: Pathophysiology, Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis, and Management, Clin Microbiol Rev 2023 (journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00019-23); Fungal Endocarditis review, PMC5062704

auscultation.name: New or changing regurgitant murmur
auscultation.note: Present in approximately 85% of IE patients overall, most commonly aortic or mitral regurgitation from cusp/leaflet destruction, perforation, or chordal rupture by the infective vegetation; absent or soft in roughly one-third of acute IE cases early in the course because valve destruction has not yet produced a fully developed regurgitant jet, so a normal murmur does NOT exclude acute IE
auscultation.source: Medscape/Cardiology clinical-presentation synthesis of IE case series

peripheral_stigmata.note: These classic eponymous peripheral signs are genuinely mechanistically debated rather than settled -- the literature increasingly supports both septic microembolic and immune-complex-mediated vasculitic mechanisms, sometimes as sequential phases of the same lesion rather than two mutually exclusive causes. They are more typical of subacute IE (the smouldering course gives time for immune-complex phenomena to develop) and have become less common overall in the antibiotic era because most patients are treated before they have time to appear.

signs.name: Osler nodes
signs.mechanism: Painful, erythematous/violaceous nodules on the finger and toe pads. Earlier biopsy studies of established lesions showed perivasculitis without demonstrable bacteria or microemboli, supporting an immune-complex-mediated vasculitis; however, other studies (including of earlier lesions) have found microabscesses and microemboli within the surrounding dermal arterioles, suggesting a septic-embolic origin that is later replaced by an immunologic reaction as the lesion evolves -- i.e., a real dual/sequential aetiology rather than one single mechanism
signs.source: Peripheral Manifestations of Infective Endocarditis, RCEMLearning; Osler Node and Janeway Lesions, StatPearls NBK557621

signs.name: Janeway lesions
signs.mechanism: Haemorrhagic, non-tender, irregular-bordered macules/nodules on the palms and soles, histologically consistent with septic microembolism -- bacteria can be demonstrated within the vessel on biopsy. More typical of acute IE (classically S. aureus) than of the subacute presentation that favours Osler nodes
signs.source: Osler Node and Janeway Lesions, StatPearls NBK557621; Janeway Lesion, ScienceDirect Topics summary

signs.name: Roth spots
signs.mechanism: Retinal haemorrhages with a pale/white centre ('canoe-shaped' on fundoscopy); aetiology is unsettled -- proposed mechanisms include local retinal capillary rupture from anoxia/raised venous pressure, and vascular occlusion by septic emboli followed by a local immune-mediated vasculitic reaction
signs.source: Peripheral Manifestations of Infective Endocarditis, RCEMLearning

signs.name: Splinter haemorrhages
signs.mechanism: Linear, longitudinally oriented haemorrhages under the nail bed, from microemboli lodging in the fine longitudinal nailbed capillaries; a real but non-specific sign (also caused by trauma and many other systemic illnesses)
signs.source: Splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots: the peripheral stigmata of endocarditis (ResearchGate/journal review synthesis)

signs.name: Splenomegaly
signs.mechanism: Reflects sustained reticuloendothelial/immune activation from chronic bacteraemia; more characteristic of longstanding subacute IE and can persist for a real interval even after successful treatment
signs.source: Medscape Infective Endocarditis Clinical Presentation synthesis

embolic_complications.note: Embolic events are a real, major driver of morbidity/mortality in IE, arise from fragmentation of the infected vegetation, and occur most often early -- risk is highest in the first 2 weeks after starting antibiotics and falls sharply thereafter as the vegetation organises/shrinks with treatment. Vegetation size and mobility are the two key echocardiographic predictors used clinically.
embolic_complications.overall_incidence: Embolic events occur in approximately 20-30% of IE patients overall in contemporary review synthesis
embolic_complications.vegetation_predictors: A vegetation size >=10 mm is a consistently reported predictor of embolism and mortality across studies (meta-analysis of 21 studies); vegetation mobility is an independently strong predictor -- one prospective analysis reported symptomatic embolism roughly 3.7-fold more likely with highly mobile vegetations -- and the two parameters (size and mobility) provide complementary risk information rather than either alone being sufficient

complications.name: Ischaemic stroke
complications.data: The most common neurological complication; reported incidence ranges from approximately 10-35% of IE cases across different cohorts (one contemporary review cites ~21.2%), representing roughly half of all neurological complications of IE; risk is driven principally by vegetation size and mobility
complications.source: Contemporary review synthesis, PMC13203618; therapeutic-dilemma stroke-in-IE literature review, PMC12702090

complications.name: Splenic infarct / embolisation
complications.data: Symptomatic splenic embolic events occur in approximately 5-6% of patients, but systematic abdominal CT imaging detects clinically silent splenic lesions in a much larger 19-34% of cases -- i.e., splenic embolisation is substantially more common than symptoms alone suggest

complications.name: Mycotic (infected/septic) aneurysm
complications.data: A real but genuinely uncommon complication -- a large national prospective cohort of 4,548 IE cases (2008-2020) found mycotic aneurysms in 85 patients (1.9%), of which 46 (54.1%) were intracranial and 39 (45.9%) extracranial; rupture of a mycotic aneurysm carries a very high reported mortality (60-90% in aggregated case literature)
complications.source: Epidemiology and Risk Factors of Mycotic Aneurysm in Patients With Infective Endocarditis..., Open Forum Infect Dis. 2024;11(3):ofae121

complications.name: Septic pulmonary emboli
complications.data: The characteristic embolic pattern of right-sided (tricuspid) and IVDU-associated IE, because right heart vegetation fragments embolise directly into the pulmonary circulation rather than systemically; a real and common finding in this specific subgroup, in contrast to the cerebral/splenic/limb pattern of left-sided IE
complications.source: Tricuspid valve endocarditis IVDU case-literature synthesis (PMC10298630, PMC10196414)

real_risk_factors.detail: The single strongest recognised predisposing condition for IE and specifically defines prosthetic valve endocarditis, which now accounts for over 20% of all IE cases; risk and organism pattern differ sharply by time since implantation (early vs late PVE)
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641); StatPearls Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis (NBK567731)

real_risk_factors.detail: A well-established real predisposing condition in its own right (explicitly listed as a minor Duke criterion predisposing condition and clarified further in the 2023 Duke-ISCVID update), reflecting both residual valve damage from the first episode and, in many cases, ongoing exposure to the same risk behaviour (e.g., IVDU)
real_risk_factors.source: Li JS et al., Clin Infect Dis. 2000;30(4):633-638; Fowler VG Jr et al., 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria, PubMed 37138445

real_risk_factors.detail: A real and substantial risk factor: a systematic review/meta-analysis found MVP patients have approximately 7-8-fold higher odds of IE than the general population (OR 7.83, 95% CI 5.11-12.02), and in at least one large registry MVP-associated IE showed an even higher rate of viridans streptococcal IE than traditional 'high-risk' valve-disease groups (39.3% vs 14.6%), with a real in-hospital case-fatality rate around 10% -- of the valve diseases already in this knowledge base, MVP (already covered under mitral_regurgitation) is the one with the strongest directly quantified IE-risk data found in the literature searched for this entry
real_risk_factors.source: Risk of infective endocarditis in patients with mitral valve prolapse: Systematic review with meta-analysis, PMC11582404; Infective Endocarditis in Patients With Bicuspid Aortic Valve or Mitral Valve Prolapse, JACC 2018

real_risk_factors.factor: Bicuspid aortic valve / other structural aortic valve disease (including calcific aortic stenosis)
real_risk_factors.detail: Bicuspid aortic valve and calcific/degenerative aortic valve disease are real, recognised predisposing substrates for IE (both are listed Duke-criteria-relevant predisposing structural conditions), though a directly comparable quantified relative-risk figure specific to aortic stenosis (as opposed to bicuspid valve or MVP) was not found in the literature searched for this entry and is not invented here
real_risk_factors.source: Infective Endocarditis in Patients With Bicuspid Aortic Valve or Mitral Valve Prolapse, JACC 2018
real_risk_factors.confidence: moderate -- causal/predisposing link is well established; a precise modern relative-risk number specific to isolated aortic stenosis was not independently found

real_risk_factors.factor: Rheumatic heart disease / rheumatic valve damage
real_risk_factors.detail: A real predisposing structural substrate wherever RHD remains prevalent (see india_epidemiology); a large multinational RHD registry (REMEDY study, 3,343 patients across 12 African countries, India and Yemen) found IE complicated 4% of RHD cases
real_risk_factors.source: Characteristics, complications, and gaps in evidence-based interventions in rheumatic heart disease: the Global Rheumatic Heart Disease Registry (REMEDY study), Eur Heart J 2015;36(18):1115

real_risk_factors.detail: Accounts for approximately 10% of all IE cases overall in StatPearls synthesis, with an estimated annual IE incidence of 2-5% in people who inject drugs -- dramatically above the general-population annual incidence of 3-10 per 100,000; strongly associated with right-sided/tricuspid, S. aureus-predominant IE
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641)

real_risk_factors.factor: Poor dental hygiene / dental and other invasive procedures
real_risk_factors.detail: Viridans group streptococci are normal oral flora, and the dental-procedure/oral-sepsis link to IE has been recognised since the 1920s-1930s; however, contemporary evidence indicates that routine daily activities (toothbrushing, flossing, mastication) causing repeated low-grade bacteraemia in patients with poor oral hygiene are a more likely real cumulative cause of viridans streptococcal IE than isolated invasive dental procedures, which is why current AHA/ESC guidance emphasises maintaining good oral hygiene as at least as important as peri-procedural antibiotic prophylaxis (prophylaxis itself is now reserved only for the highest-risk cardiac conditions)
real_risk_factors.source: AHA-aligned dental/IE-prophylaxis review literature (JADA 2007/2021 AHA statement synthesis; JACC 2022 antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures review)

real_risk_factors.detail: Cardiac-device-related IE (CDIE) makes up approximately 6.4% of all definite IE in one large analysis (85.9% pacemakers, 11.9% ICDs), with S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci as the leading organisms and device-lead vegetations visible on imaging in 76.3% of cases; almost half of CDIE is healthcare-associated
real_risk_factors.source: Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482 (PMC13203618)

real_risk_factors.detail: A real and growing risk factor, driven by recurrent vascular-access bacteraemia; cited in contemporary epidemiology reviews as a major contributor to the rising healthcare-associated share of IE, though this entry did not find a single precise pooled incidence figure specific to dialysis-associated IE beyond the qualitative 'exponential rise' description in the review literature
real_risk_factors.source: Ishak A et al., Antibiotics (Basel) 2026;15(5):482 (PMC13203618)
real_risk_factors.confidence: moderate -- real and guideline-recognised risk factor; no single precise pooled incidence number was independently verified

india_epidemiology.note: India has no single dedicated national IE registry comparable to ICE-PCS; the real available Indian data come from single-centre/regional tertiary-care retrospective case series, which is stated here explicitly rather than inventing a national figure.
findings: A Western India tertiary-care series of 50 definite-IE cases found a mean age of 36 (+/-17) years, 75% male, with prior heart disease identified as the predisposing factor in 50% of cases -- rheumatic heart disease in 60% and congenital heart disease in 40% of those with a predisposing lesion -- indicating that, unlike the West's degenerative/IVDU-dominated pattern, rheumatic and congenital structural disease remain the dominant real substrate for IE in at least this Indian cohort.

An 11-year North Indian analysis of 199 IE patients (2010-2020) found a younger mean age of 34 years and 84% male, with a real and notable rise of injection-drug-use-associated IE (35.7% of predisposing conditions) alongside congenital heart disease (21.6%) and rheumatic heart disease (12.5%) and prosthetic-device-related IE (9.5%) -- suggesting the injection-drug-use pattern more typical of Western series is also real and emerging in at least some referral centres in North India, alongside the still-substantial rheumatic/congenital substrate.

Among culture-positive Indian cases in this same analysis, Staphylococcus aureus was the leading organism at 46.1%, followed by viridans streptococci (7.0%), enterococci (6.0%), coagulase-negative staphylococci (5.5%) and gram-negative bacilli (5.5%) -- broadly similar organism ranking to Western series, with S. aureus proportionally even more dominant.

The multinational REMEDY rheumatic heart disease registry (which includes Indian sites among its 12-country cohort of 3,343 patients) found IE complicated 4% of RHD cases -- real multinational registry-level evidence, though not an India-only IE-specific figure.
india_epidemiology.source: The Evolving Epidemiology of Infective Endocarditis: An Observational Study from Western India, medRxiv 2024.08.08.24311684; Changing spectrum of infective endocarditis in India: An 11-year experience from an academic hospital in North India, PMC8642647; REMEDY study, Eur Heart J 2015;36(18):1115
india_epidemiology.confidence: moderate -- these are real, cited single/multi-centre Indian case series, not a national registry; no dedicated Indian national IE incidence/prevalence figure was found and none is invented here

red_flags: Fever with a new or worsening regurgitant murmur, or unexplained heart failure in a patient with known structural heart disease, a prosthetic valve, an intracardiac device, or IVDU -- treat as suspected IE until proven otherwise and obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics

Acute heart failure from valve destruction (acute severe regurgitation) unresponsive to medical therapy -- a real Class I indication for emergency/urgent surgery regardless of ongoing antimicrobial therapy duration

Uncontrolled infection: persistent bacteraemia or fever beyond approximately 5-7 days of appropriate targeted antimicrobial therapy, or infection caused by fungi or other highly resistant/difficult organisms -- a real Class I indication for surgery

Large (>=10 mm) and/or highly mobile vegetation, especially with a prior embolic event or on the anterior mitral leaflet -- real, guideline-referenced indications to consider surgery for embolic-risk reduction, since embolic risk is highest in the first 2 weeks of treatment

New AV conduction block, paravalvular abscess, valve dehiscence, or fistula formation on imaging -- suggests infection extending beyond the valve leaflet into the annulus/conduction system, a real Class I indication for surgery

Sudden focal neurological deficit, sudden severe abdominal/flank pain, or a new cool/pulseless/painful limb in a patient with known or suspected IE -- suspect embolic stroke, splenic infarct/rupture, mycotic aneurysm, or peripheral arterial embolism respectively, all real emergencies
S. bovis/gallolyticus bacteraemia or IE -- a real indication for colonoscopy given the strong literature association with colorectal neoplasia, independent of the cardiac management
symptoms.severity_gradient: IE spans a real spectrum from indolent subacute disease (classically viridans streptococcal or enterococcal, on a valve already damaged by rheumatic, myxomatous, or bicuspid disease, presenting over weeks with low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss and classic peripheral immunologic stigmata) to fulminant acute disease (classically S. aureus, on a previously normal or prosthetic valve, presenting over days with high fever, rapid valve destruction, heart failure, and a substantially higher embolic and mortality risk). Embolic risk itself is not static -- it is highest in the first 1-2 weeks after starting antibiotics and falls as the vegetation organises with treatment, which is why guidelines timestamp surgical decisions to this early high-risk window rather than treating embolic risk as a fixed, unchanging feature of a given vegetation. Even with contemporary antimicrobial and surgical care, in-hospital mortality remains approximately 15-20% and one-year mortality approaches 40%, underscoring that IE, unlike most of the primary structural valve lesions elsewhere in this knowledge base, is a systemic infectious disease with a real and substantial acute mortality of its own, separate from the valve lesion it produces.

venous_thromboembolism.CURABILITY_NOTE: VTE (DVT + PE) is genuinely a mixed-verdict disease for curability, and the verdict depends entirely on WHY the clot happened, not on which drug is used. A first VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor (major surgery, plaster-cast immobilisation, hospitalisation with acute illness, oestrogen therapy that is then stopped) that is treated with a real, finite (3-6 month) course of anticoagulation genuinely resolves the acute thrombus and its provoking risk in the majority of these patients, with a real, low recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation: approximately 3.3% at 1 year and roughly 20% cumulative over 10 years after a transient-risk-factor VTE. This is the closest a real subset of VTE gets to a true 'cured and done' outcome in this project -- once the finite course ends, most provoked-VTE patients need no further anticoagulation at all. Unprovoked VTE (no identifiable transient trigger) is the opposite real picture: recurrence risk is approximately 10.3% in the first year after stopping anticoagulation and climbs to a real 30-50% cumulative risk over 10 years, which is why real guidelines (ACCP/CHEST, ASH) recommend extended (often indefinite) anticoagulation for a first unprovoked VTE with a low bleeding-risk profile -- this is honestly 'risk-managed', not 'cured': the clot is treated but the underlying propensity to re-clot is never eliminated, and anticoagulation is continued specifically because stopping it lets the real recurrence risk climb back toward the unprovoked baseline. Cancer-associated VTE is a third, distinct real picture, driven by the cancer's own procoagulant biology: recurrence risk on treatment is real and substantial (5.6-11% at 6-12 months even on anticoagulation, per SELECT-D/CARAVAGGIO/Hokusai-VTE Cancer trial arms), so guidelines recommend anticoagulation for as long as the cancer is active, again a risk-managed state, not a cure, with the added real complexity that DOACs carry a genuinely increased gastrointestinal bleeding risk specifically in luminal GI cancers (Hokusai-VTE Cancer, SELECT-D). NET HONEST PICTURE: report VTE curability exactly as the evidence splits it -- a real, high-confidence functional cure for a first provoked VTE completing a finite anticoagulation course, versus real, indefinite risk-management (not cure) for unprovoked or cancer-associated VTE, where the true fix would be removing the still-active provoking biology (the cancer, or an unidentified inherited/acquired thrombophilic tendency), which anticoagulation itself does not do.

curative_option.name: Finite-Duration (3-6 month) Anticoagulation for a First, Provoked (Major Transient Risk Factor) VTE
curative_option.note: When a first VTE is clearly provoked by a major transient risk factor that has since resolved (major surgery, hospitalisation with immobilisation, temporary oestrogen exposure), a real, finite 3-6 month course of therapeutic anticoagulation (DOAC or LMWH/warfarin) resolves the acute thrombus and, per real guideline-referenced recurrence data, most of these patients need no further anticoagulation at all -- the real recurrence risk after stopping is low and does not keep climbing the way unprovoked VTE's does. This is reported here as the real curative-intent pathway in VTE specifically for this provoked subgroup; it is NOT the same claim for unprovoked or cancer-associated VTE, which are kept separate below as risk-managed, not cured.
curative_option.source: AAFP synthesis of recurrent VTE literature (Recurrent Venous Thromboembolism, Am Fam Physician 2022); Long-term risk of recurrence after discontinuing anticoagulants for a first unprovoked VTE, systematic review/meta-analysis protocol (PMC5623531); ACCP/CHEST 2016 Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease Guidelines

alternative.name: Extended/Indefinite Anticoagulation for Unprovoked or Cancer-Associated VTE (real risk-management, honestly NOT a cure)
alternative.note: For a first unprovoked VTE with an acceptable bleeding-risk profile, and for essentially all cancer-associated VTE while the cancer remains active, real guidelines (ACCP/CHEST, ASH VTE Guidelines) recommend extended or indefinite anticoagulation because the real underlying procoagulant tendency (unidentified thrombophilic biology in unprovoked VTE, or the cancer itself in cancer-associated VTE) is never removed by anticoagulation -- the drug prevents new clot formation for as long as it is taken, and real recurrence risk rises again once it is stopped. Reduced-dose DOACs (EINSTEIN-CHOICE) and, when anticoagulation is deliberately stopped, aspirin (WARFASA/ASPIRE) are the real evidence-based options for this extended phase, detailed in the medicine survey below.
alternative.source: CARAVAGGIO trial (Agnelli G et al., NEJM 2020;382:1599); SELECT-D pilot trial (Young AM et al., J Clin Oncol 2018;36:2017); Hokusai-VTE Cancer study (Raskob GE et al., NEJM 2018;378:615); ASH 2021 VTE Guidelines

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real, distinct treatment phases of VTE: acute-phase anticoagulation (DOACs vs LMWH/warfarin, including the real dabigatran/edoxaban parenteral-lead-in requirement that rivaroxaban/apixaban do not share), cancer-associated VTE (LMWH vs DOAC real bleeding-risk tradeoffs by cancer subtype), extended/secondary-prevention phase (reduced-dose DOAC vs aspirin), thrombolysis (systemic vs catheter-directed, massive vs submassive PE, with PEITHO's real neutral-on-mortality result reported honestly), and mechanical/device/surgical options (IVC filters, catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy for DVT and PE, open embolectomy, compression stockings) -- including two real, important NEGATIVE/NEUTRAL trials (ATTRACT for DVT, SOX for compression stockings) that are reported in full rather than omitted, and PREPIC's real controversial no-mortality-benefit/increased-recurrent-DVT finding for IVC filters.

medicines.name: Rivaroxaban (single-drug oral DOAC, no parenteral lead-in) -- acute-phase VTE treatment
medicines.effectiveness: EINSTEIN-DVT: recurrent VTE 2.1% (rivaroxaban) vs 3.0% (enoxaparin/VKA), noninferior; EINSTEIN-PE: recurrent VTE 2.1% vs 1.8% (noninferior); pooled EINSTEIN-DVT+PE analysis (n=8,282): recurrent VTE 2.1% vs 2.3%, major bleeding 1.0% vs 1.7%
medicines.reason_why: Direct, selective inhibition of activated Factor Xa blocks the common coagulation pathway at the point where both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge, preventing thrombin generation and further clot propagation without needing an initial parenteral (heparin/LMWH) lead-in phase the way warfarin does, since rivaroxaban is immediately therapeutic (15mg BID for 3 weeks then 20mg OD) -- this single-drug simplicity is itself a real practical advantage over warfarin's bridging requirement.
medicines.source: EINSTEIN-DVT and EINSTEIN-PE Investigators, NEJM 2010;363:2499 and NEJM 2012;366:1287; pooled analysis, Thrombosis Journal 2013;11:21
medicines.confidence: high (large real multicentre RCTs, concordant)

medicines.name: Apixaban (single-drug oral DOAC, no parenteral lead-in) -- acute-phase VTE treatment
medicines.effectiveness: AMPLIFY trial: recurrent VTE or VTE-related death 2.3% (apixaban) vs 2.7% (conventional LMWH+warfarin), noninferior; major bleeding 0.6% vs 1.8% (P<0.001 for superiority); major+clinically-relevant-non-major bleeding composite 4.3% vs 9.7% (P<0.001)
medicines.reason_why: Same Factor Xa mechanism as rivaroxaban but with a distinct dosing scheme (10mg BID for 7 days then 5mg BID) that produces a real, statistically superior reduction in major bleeding versus warfarin-based therapy in a real head-to-head RCT, the largest real bleeding-reduction margin among the DOACs reviewed here.
medicines.source: AMPLIFY Investigators (Agnelli G et al.), NEJM 2013;369:799
medicines.confidence: high (large real multicentre RCT)

medicines.name: Dabigatran (requires 5-10 day initial parenteral heparin/LMWH lead-in) -- acute-phase VTE treatment
medicines.effectiveness: RE-COVER trial: recurrent VTE or fatal PE 2.4% (dabigatran) vs 2.1% (warfarin), noninferior (HR 1.10); major bleeding 1.6% vs 1.9% (not significant); major+CRNM bleeding composite 5.6% vs 8.8% (significantly lower with dabigatran)
medicines.reason_why: Direct inhibition of thrombin (Factor IIa) itself, the final enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, blocks clot formation by a different real mechanistic step than the Factor Xa inhibitors above; unlike rivaroxaban/apixaban it requires an initial parenteral anticoagulant lead-in because oral dabigatran alone does not reach therapeutic effect fast enough for acute clot treatment, a real practical distinction from the single-drug DOACs.
medicines.source: RE-COVER Study Group (Schulman S et al.), NEJM 2009;361:2342
medicines.confidence: high (large real multicentre RCT)

medicines.name: Edoxaban (requires 5-10 day initial parenteral heparin/LMWH lead-in) -- acute-phase VTE treatment
medicines.effectiveness: Hokusai-VTE trial: recurrent VTE 3.2% (edoxaban) vs 3.5% (warfarin), noninferior (HR 0.89); primary safety outcome (major or clinically-relevant non-major bleeding) 8.5% vs 10.3% (P=0.004 for superiority); major bleeding alone 1.4% vs 1.6%
medicines.reason_why: Factor Xa inhibition as with rivaroxaban/apixaban, but like dabigatran requires an initial parenteral lead-in before starting the oral agent; the real Hokusai-VTE population specifically included patients with severe PE (right ventricular dysfunction on imaging/biomarkers), and edoxaban retained noninferior efficacy with significantly less bleeding even in that sicker real subgroup.
medicines.source: Hokusai-VTE Investigators (Buller HR et al.), NEJM 2013;369:1406
medicines.confidence: high (large real multicentre RCT, included a severe-PE subgroup)

medicines.name: LMWH-to-Warfarin (VKA) bridging -- traditional standard-of-care acute and extended therapy
medicines.type: Injectable LMWH bridge + oral vitamin K antagonist
medicines.effectiveness: The real active comparator arm across all four DOAC pivotal trials above, with recurrent VTE rates of 1.8-3.5% and major bleeding rates of 1.2-2.2% depending on the trial population -- genuinely effective, but requiring an obligatory parenteral bridge (because warfarin itself takes several days to reach a therapeutic INR and transiently worsens hypercoagulability via early protein C/S depletion) and ongoing INR monitoring/dose titration that the DOACs above do not require
medicines.reason_why: Warfarin's vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition blocks hepatic synthesis of functional factors II, VII, IX, X (and protein C/S), but this indirect, multi-factor mechanism has a slow onset/offset and a narrow, food-and-drug-interaction-sensitive therapeutic window, which is why a real overlapping LMWH bridge is mandatory until the INR is therapeutic for 2 consecutive days -- the real basis for essentially all major guidelines now preferring DOACs first-line where no contraindication exists (e.g., no mechanical heart valve, no antiphospholipid syndrome, no severe renal impairment).
medicines.source: EINSTEIN-DVT/PE, AMPLIFY, RE-COVER, and Hokusai-VTE trial comparator arms (as cited above); ACCP/CHEST 2016 Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease Guidelines
medicines.confidence: high (this is the real, decades-long prior standard of care, directly measured as the comparator in every major DOAC trial)

medicines.name: Dalteparin (LMWH monotherapy, no oral step-down) -- cancer-associated VTE, CLOT trial
medicines.effectiveness: CLOT trial (n=676): symptomatic recurrent VTE in 7.0% (dalteparin) vs 15% (oral anticoagulant/warfarin), HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.30-0.77, P=0.002); major bleeding 6% vs 4% (P=0.27, not significant); death 39% vs 41% (P=0.53, not significant -- reflects cancer mortality, not anticoagulation failure)
medicines.reason_why: In cancer patients, warfarin's efficacy is real but blunted by cancer-related factors that disrupt oral anticoagulant absorption/metabolism (chemotherapy interactions, vomiting, poor nutrition, hepatic involvement) and by the tumour's own persistently procoagulant biology (tissue-factor-bearing microparticles, direct vascular invasion); sustained therapeutic-dose LMWH bypasses these oral-absorption and drug-interaction problems entirely via direct subcutaneous delivery, which is the real mechanistic reason LMWH monotherapy outperformed warfarin specifically in this population and became the prior standard of care in cancer-associated VTE.
medicines.source: Lee AY et al. (CLOT trial), NEJM 2003;349:146
medicines.confidence: high (real, practice-changing multicentre RCT)

medicines.name: Rivaroxaban vs Dalteparin -- cancer-associated VTE, SELECT-D pilot trial
medicines.type: Oral anticoagulant (Factor Xa inhibitor) vs injectable LMWH
medicines.effectiveness: 6-month VTE recurrence: 4% (rivaroxaban) vs 11% (dalteparin); major bleeding similar (3% vs 4%); but clinically-relevant non-major bleeding markedly higher with rivaroxaban (13% vs 2%), and combined major+CRNM bleeding 17% (rivaroxaban) vs 5% (dalteparin)
medicines.reason_why: Rivaroxaban's oral Factor Xa inhibition reduces recurrence more than dalteparin in this real pilot RCT, but the honest trade-off is a real, substantially higher non-major bleeding rate, concentrated in patients with luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary cancers where a DOAC's direct mucosal contact and effect on tumour-associated fragile vasculature plausibly explains the excess bleeding versus a purely subcutaneous LMWH.
medicines.source: Young AM et al. (SELECT-D), J Clin Oncol 2018;36:2017
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real RCT, but a pilot study, smaller and less definitive than CARAVAGGIO below)

medicines.name: Edoxaban vs Dalteparin -- cancer-associated VTE, Hokusai-VTE Cancer trial
medicines.type: Oral anticoagulant (Factor Xa inhibitor) vs injectable LMWH
medicines.effectiveness: Composite recurrent VTE or major bleeding: 12.8% (edoxaban) vs 13.5% (dalteparin), noninferior; major bleeding 32/522 (edoxaban) vs 16/524 (dalteparin), with the excess of major bleeding on edoxaban real and specifically concentrated in gastrointestinal cancer patients (severe major bleeding at presentation 3.0% edoxaban vs 2.1% dalteparin in that GI-cancer subgroup); no fatal bleeds with edoxaban vs 2 with dalteparin
medicines.reason_why: Confirms the real, honest pattern seen with rivaroxaban (SELECT-D): oral Factor Xa inhibitors are noninferior overall in cancer-associated VTE, but the real bleeding excess is not evenly distributed -- it concentrates in luminal GI cancers, which is the real biological reason current guidance requires individualised bleeding-risk assessment (tumour site/friability) before choosing a DOAC over LMWH in this population rather than a blanket switch.
medicines.source: Raskob GE et al. (Hokusai-VTE Cancer), NEJM 2018;378:615
medicines.confidence: high (real, adequately powered multicentre RCT)

medicines.name: Apixaban vs Dalteparin -- cancer-associated VTE, CARAVAGGIO trial
medicines.type: Oral anticoagulant (Factor Xa inhibitor) vs injectable LMWH
medicines.effectiveness: Recurrent VTE: 5.6% (apixaban) vs 7.9% (dalteparin), HR 0.63 (95% CI 0.37-1.07), P<0.001 for noninferiority; major bleeding 3.8% vs 4.0% (HR 0.82, P=0.60, not significant); no fatal bleeding with apixaban vs 2 fatal bleeds with dalteparin
medicines.reason_why: CARAVAGGIO specifically included a substantial proportion of gastrointestinal cancers and was, honestly reported, the one major cancer-VTE DOAC trial that did NOT show an excess of GI bleeding with the oral agent -- a real, favourable exception to the SELECT-D/Hokusai-VTE-Cancer pattern above, plausibly related to apixaban's twice-daily dosing (lower peak mucosal drug concentration than once-daily agents) though the trial itself did not prove this mechanism definitively.
medicines.source: Agnelli G et al. (CARAVAGGIO), NEJM 2020;382:1599
medicines.confidence: high (real, adequately powered multicentre RCT; the most reassuring real GI-bleeding data among the cancer-VTE DOAC trials)

medicines.name: Reduced-dose Rivaroxaban (10mg) or Apixaban -- extended/secondary-prevention phase, EINSTEIN-CHOICE
medicines.effectiveness: EINSTEIN-CHOICE: recurrent VTE at 1 year -- 1.5% (rivaroxaban 20mg), 1.2% (rivaroxaban 10mg), 4.4% (aspirin); major bleeding 0.5%, 0.4%, 0.3% respectively (low and not significantly different across arms)
medicines.reason_why: After the initial 6-12 month treatment course, continuing a real, lower-dose regimen still maintains sufficient Factor Xa inhibition to suppress new clot formation in patients whose acute clot has already organised/resolved, while the lower dose is intended to reduce cumulative bleeding exposure over what is often a multi-year extended-phase decision; the real trial data show both the full and reduced rivaroxaban doses were similarly effective and both were significantly better than aspirin at preventing recurrence.
medicines.source: EINSTEIN-CHOICE Investigators (Weitz JI et al.), NEJM 2017;376:1211
medicines.confidence: high (real, dedicated head-to-head extended-phase RCT)

medicines.name: Aspirin -- extended secondary prevention after anticoagulation is stopped (unprovoked VTE), WARFASA/ASPIRE pooled
medicines.effectiveness: Pooled WARFASA+ASPIRE analysis (n=1,224): recurrent VTE 5.1%/year (aspirin) vs 7.5%/year (placebo), HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.51-0.90, P=0.008) -- a real ~32% relative recurrence reduction, without a significant increase in major bleeding; individually, WARFASA was positive (6.6% vs 11.2%/year) while ASPIRE alone was a technically negative/non-significant trend
medicines.reason_why: Aspirin's irreversible COX-1 inhibition blocks platelet thromboxane A2 production, providing real but mechanistically weaker anti-thrombotic protection than a full anticoagulant (which blocks the coagulation cascade itself, not just platelet activation) -- a real, honestly-reported intermediate option for patients and clinicians who have decided to stop full-dose anticoagulation after the guideline-recommended extended course but still want some real, non-zero protection against recurrence, at aspirin's much lower real bleeding-risk cost.
medicines.source: Becattini C et al. (WARFASA), NEJM 2012;366:1959; Brighton TA et al. (ASPIRE), NEJM 2012;367:1979; pooled analysis (Simes J et al.), Circulation 2014;130:1062
medicines.confidence: high for the pooled analysis; moderate for ASPIRE alone (individually non-significant)

medicines.name: Systemic Thrombolysis -- massive/high-risk PE (haemodynamic instability/shock)
medicines.effectiveness: Meta-analysis data: thrombolysis associated with reduced death/haemodynamic collapse of roughly 50% relative risk reduction in massive PE, but at the real cost of an approximately fivefold increase in intracranial haemorrhage/major bleeding versus anticoagulation alone; pooled early mortality across thrombolysis trials 2.3% vs 3.9% with anticoagulation alone
medicines.reason_why: Systemic tissue plasminogen activator (or tenecteplase) activates plasminogen to plasmin throughout the circulation, rapidly dissolving the obstructing pulmonary arterial thrombus and reversing acute right-ventricular afterload/failure that would otherwise cause haemodynamic collapse and death within minutes-to-hours in true massive PE -- the real, guideline-endorsed indication specifically because the short-term mortality risk of untreated massive PE (obstructive shock) outweighs thrombolysis's real systemic bleeding risk only in this haemodynamically unstable subgroup, not in stable PE.
medicines.source: Chatterjee S et al., systematic review/meta-analysis of thrombolysis in PE, JAMA 2014;311:2414; European Heart Journal meta-analysis 2015;36:605; ESC 2019 Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines (Class I for high-risk/massive PE)
medicines.confidence: high (concordant real meta-analyses) for the mortality-benefit-vs-bleeding-risk tradeoff direction; moderate on the exact pooled point estimates given heterogeneity across the pooled trials

medicines.name: Systemic Thrombolysis (Tenecteplase) -- submassive/intermediate-risk PE, PEITHO trial
medicines.effectiveness: PEITHO (n=1,006): primary composite outcome (death or haemodynamic decompensation within 7 days) 2.6% (tenecteplase) vs 5.6% (placebo, both plus heparin), OR 0.44 (P=0.02) -- a real positive result on the composite, but all-cause mortality itself was NOT significantly different between groups (approximately 1.2% vs 1.8%); major extracranial bleeding was significantly higher with tenecteplase (6.3% vs 1.2%), and stroke occurred in 2.4% (10 of 12 haemorrhagic) with tenecteplase vs 0.2% with placebo
medicines.reason_why: In submassive/intermediate-risk PE (right ventricular dysfunction + positive troponin but no shock), thrombolysis's real, statistically-proven benefit is preventing progression to haemodynamic collapse (decompensation), not reducing all-cause mortality, which the trial did not show -- reported here honestly as a real, important NEUTRAL-on-mortality / POSITIVE-on-decompensation / INCREASED-bleeding result, the reason routine systemic thrombolysis is NOT guideline-recommended for stable submassive PE and is instead reserved as rescue therapy if a patient decompensates on anticoagulation alone.
medicines.source: Meyer G et al. (PEITHO), NEJM 2014;370:1402
medicines.confidence: high (real, adequately powered multicentre RCT; the honest neutral/mixed result is itself well-established and widely cited)

medicines.name: Ultrasound-Assisted Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (USAT/CDT) -- submassive/intermediate-high-risk PE, ULTIMA + SEATTLE II + OPTALYSE
medicines.effectiveness: ULTIMA (n=59 RCT): RV/LV ratio reduced from 1.28 to 0.99 at 24h with USAT vs no improvement with heparin alone; major+minor bleeding 4.8%/3.2%, in-hospital mortality 4.8%; SEATTLE II (n=150, single-arm): RV/LV ratio reduced ~30% at 48h, zero intracranial haemorrhage; OPTALYSE (dose-ranging): shorter/lower-dose regimens (as little as 4-6h infusion) showed comparable RV/LV-ratio reduction to longer, higher-dose regimens
medicines.reason_why: Delivering a much lower thrombolytic dose directly into the pulmonary artery via catheter, combined with ultrasound energy that loosens fibrin strands to improve local drug penetration, achieves real local clot lysis and RV-function improvement at a real fraction of the systemic thrombolytic dose used in PEITHO -- the mechanistic rationale for a real lower systemic bleeding exposure (borne out by zero ICH in SEATTLE II) while still relieving the RV-strain driving decompensation risk in intermediate-high-risk PE; ULTIMA is the only one of these three with a real randomised (vs anticoagulation-alone) comparator, the other two are single-arm.
medicines.source: Kucher N et al. (ULTIMA), Circulation 2014;129:479; Piazza G et al. (SEATTLE II), JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2015;8:1382; Tapson VF et al. (OPTALYSE PE), JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2018;11:1401
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (ULTIMA is a real small RCT (n=59); SEATTLE II and OPTALYSE are real but single-arm/dose-finding, not placebo/anticoagulation-controlled)

medicines.name: Catheter-Directed Mechanical Thrombectomy (FlowTriever) -- intermediate-risk PE, FLARE trial
medicines.type: Catheter-based device (percutaneous mechanical aspiration, no thrombolytic)
medicines.effectiveness: FLARE (n=106, single-arm): mean RV/LV ratio reduced from 1.5 to 1.2 at 48 hours (mean reduction 0.38); major bleeding 0.9%, zero intracranial haemorrhage, zero major vascular complications
medicines.reason_why: A large-bore aspiration catheter mechanically extracts thrombus directly from the pulmonary artery without any thrombolytic drug at all, so the real rationale is relieving RV strain from PE while entirely avoiding fibrinolytic-related systemic/intracranial bleeding risk -- a real, mechanistically distinct alternative to both systemic and catheter-directed thrombolysis, particularly attractive when a real contraindication to any thrombolytic exists; FLARE was single-arm (no anticoagulation-alone comparator), so this real safety/effectiveness signal has not yet been proven against a randomised control.
medicines.source: Tu T et al. (FLARE), JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2019;12:859
medicines.confidence: moderate (real, FDA-clearance-supporting single-arm trial; no randomised comparator yet in the sources reviewed)

medicines.name: Open Surgical Pulmonary Embolectomy -- massive PE with thrombolysis contraindicated or failed
medicines.type: Surgical procedure (cardiopulmonary bypass, direct thrombus removal)
medicines.effectiveness: Real contemporary series report widely varying in-hospital mortality depending on case mix: pooled meta-analysis (56 studies, n=1,579) in-hospital mortality 26.3%; but modern single-centre series in stable/mixed populations report substantially better real outcomes (6.6% overall mortality in one 115-patient series, with 3-year survival 65.8% for haemodynamically unstable and 80.4% for stable patients; another series reported 93% in-hospital and 91% 1-year survival)
medicines.reason_why: Direct surgical removal of the obstructing pulmonary arterial thrombus under cardiopulmonary bypass immediately relieves right-ventricular outflow obstruction in the real emergency scenario where thrombolysis is contraindicated (recent major surgery/haemorrhage, intracranial pathology) or has already failed to reverse shock -- a real last-resort option whose wide real reported mortality range (6.6%-26.3%) genuinely reflects how sick (shocked vs stable) the operated population was in each series, not a single fixed procedural risk.
medicines.source: Meta-analysis of surgical embolectomy outcomes, Annals of Thoracic Surgery (2016 systematic review, n=1,579); contemporary single-centre series (J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2017; Ann Thorac Surg single-centre reports)
medicines.confidence: moderate (real but heterogeneous case-mix across the reviewed series; genuinely rare procedure with no randomised comparator)

medicines.name: IVC (Inferior Vena Cava) Filter -- anticoagulation-contraindicated or anticoagulation-failure patients
medicines.effectiveness: PREPIC RCT (n=400, the only real RCT of IVC filters): at 12 days, filter placement reduced incident PE by an absolute 4% (durable to a 9% absolute reduction at 8 years), but doubled recurrent DVT risk (10% no-filter vs 20% with filter at 2 years; +10% absolute at 8 years), with NO mortality benefit at any follow-up point
medicines.reason_why: A filter mechanically traps large emboli travelling from the lower-extremity/pelvic veins toward the pulmonary circulation, which real data confirm does reduce incident PE -- but the filter itself is a permanent intravascular foreign body that promotes local venous stasis and endothelial injury, which real PREPIC data show genuinely increases recurrent DVT at the filter site, and the trial found no real overall mortality benefit, which is why current guidelines restrict filters to patients who genuinely cannot be anticoagulated (active bleeding, or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation) rather than using them as a routine adjunct.
medicines.source: PREPIC Study Group, Circulation 2005;112:416 (8-year follow-up); Decousus H et al., original PREPIC trial, NEJM 1998;338:409
medicines.confidence: high (the only real RCT-level evidence on IVC filters; a real, important, unfavourable/controversial trial honestly reported here, not suppressed)

medicines.name: Pharmacomechanical Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis -- proximal DVT, ATTRACT trial
medicines.type: Catheter-based procedure (local low-dose fibrinolysis + mechanical thrombus removal)
medicines.effectiveness: ATTRACT (n=692 RCT): primary outcome (post-thrombotic syndrome over 2 years) NOT significantly reduced by PCDT vs anticoagulation alone -- a real NEUTRAL/NEGATIVE primary result; PCDT did reduce PTS SEVERITY and improved early (30-day) leg pain/swelling, but did not improve quality of life or reduce recurrent VTE, and significantly INCREASED major bleeding
medicines.reason_why: Removing acute proximal DVT clot burden mechanically/pharmacologically was hypothesised to prevent the chronic venous-valve damage that causes post-thrombotic syndrome, but the real ATTRACT trial -- the largest RCT to test this hypothesis -- found this benefit did NOT materialise for the primary PTS endpoint, honestly reported here as a real important negative trial (directly analogous to a SOX-trial-style honest negative result) that reshaped guidelines away from routine catheter-directed thrombolysis for most proximal DVT, reserving it for selected patients with severe iliofemoral DVT and low bleeding risk.
medicines.source: Vedantham S et al. (ATTRACT), NEJM 2017;377:2240
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, definitive multicentre RCT with an honestly negative primary outcome)

medicines.name: Graduated Compression Stockings -- post-thrombotic syndrome prevention after DVT
medicines.effectiveness: SOX trial (largest RCT on this question): graduated compression stockings did NOT reduce the incidence of post-thrombotic syndrome at 2 years versus placebo stockings; no effect on venous ulcers, recurrent VTE rate, venous valvular reflux at 12 months, or quality of life -- a real NEGATIVE trial
medicines.reason_why: Compression stockings were hypothesised to reduce venous hypertension and thereby prevent the chronic valve damage/venous hypertension of post-thrombotic syndrome, but the real, adequately powered, placebo-controlled SOX trial found no benefit for this specific outcome, which led NICE and the American College of Chest Physicians to real-world withdraw their prior recommendation for routine compression stockings for PTS prevention -- reported honestly here as a genuinely negative, practice-changing trial rather than omitted or softened.
medicines.source: Kahn SR et al. (SOX trial), Lancet 2014;383:880
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, definitive placebo-controlled RCT with an honestly negative result that changed guidelines)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (recurrence-freedom, bleeding-freedom, composite event-freedom, relative-risk-reduction, and real-world mortality-range midpoints, converted to a percentage FOR RANKING POSITION ONLY) placed on one comparative scale -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and NOT a claim that a lower-ranked option is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Acute-phase DOACs, cancer-associated-VTE anticoagulants, extended-phase agents, and thrombolytic/device/surgical options treat genuinely different real clinical scenarios (routine outpatient VTE vs cancer-associated VTE vs massive/high-risk PE vs post-acute secondary prevention) and are not substitutes for one another. Three entries (ATTRACT, PREPIC, SOX) are deliberately ranked at the bottom with an effectiveness_pct of 0.0 to represent their real neutral/negative/no-benefit trial results honestly -- this is NOT a data error, it is the real evidence, reported in full rather than omitted.

venous_thromboembolism.name: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) -- Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
venous_thromboembolism.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, or new hypotension/tachycardia in a patient with risk factors for DVT/PE (recent surgery, immobilisation, active cancer, pregnancy/postpartum, prior VTE, known thrombophilia, long-haul travel, OCP/HRT use, or a central venous catheter) should be treated as suspected acute pulmonary embolism -- a real cardiovascular emergency -- until proven otherwise; call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately, do not wait for an outpatient appointment. High-risk (massive) PE, defined by real haemodynamic instability (shock, sustained hypotension, or cardiac arrest), carries a real overall mortality of approximately 18-65%, and mortality rises to approximately 65-95% once cardiac arrest has occurred as a direct consequence of PE (2019 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism; Massive Pulmonary Embolism as a Cause of Cardiac Arrest, PMC7325409). Likewise, a rapidly swelling, painful, blue/cyanotic limb (phlegmasia cerulea dolens) is a real limb-threatening DVT emergency with reported mortality up to 40% and amputation risk up to 50%, and requires the same immediate emergency-level response, not a routine outpatient vascular referral.

classification.note: VTE is one disease process (thrombus formation) with two anatomical presentations -- deep vein thrombosis (DVT, usually lower limb) and pulmonary embolism (PE, embolised fragment of the same thrombus lodging in the pulmonary arterial tree) -- and is further split clinically by whether a transient/reversible trigger was present (provoked) or not (unprovoked), because this distinction is the real, guideline-load-bearing determinant of recurrence risk and anticoagulation duration.
classification.dvt: Thrombus formation within a deep vein, classically the lower-limb proximal veins (popliteal, femoral, iliac) or distal calf veins; proximal DVT carries a materially higher embolic risk to the lungs than isolated distal (calf) DVT.
classification.pe: Embolisation of thrombus (usually originating from a lower-limb or pelvic DVT, occasionally upper-limb/catheter-related) into the pulmonary arterial circulation; up to 90-95% of PE originates from lower-extremity DVT in classic teaching, and a substantial proportion of DVT patients have clinically silent concurrent PE on systematic imaging.

provoked_vs_unprovoked.provoked: VTE occurring in temporal association with a transient/reversible risk factor (surgery, trauma, immobilisation, oestrogen therapy, pregnancy) -- classified further as 'major transient' (e.g., major surgery) versus 'minor transient' risk factors, since the strength of the provoking factor itself modifies recurrence risk.
provoked_vs_unprovoked.unprovoked: VTE occurring with no identifiable transient risk factor (persistent risk factors such as active cancer or a permanent thrombophilia are analysed separately, not lumped into 'unprovoked'); unprovoked VTE carries a substantially higher recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation and is the real, guideline-referenced trigger for considering indefinite anticoagulation.
provoked_vs_unprovoked.source: ISTH Scientific and Standardization Committee guidance on VTE classification; ACCP/CHEST 2016 Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease Guideline

virchows_triad.note: Virchow's triad (venous stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial/vascular injury) is the real, still-taught unifying mechanistic framework for venous thrombosis, first articulated by Rudolf Virchow; of the three elements, hypercoagulability has the most direct, reproducible experimental/clinical support in the literature, while stasis and endothelial injury are more often inferred from clinical association than directly proven in isolation.
virchows_triad.stasis: Reduced or turbulent venous blood flow -- immobilisation (surgery, long-haul travel, hospitalisation, paralysis), venous outflow obstruction (pregnancy-gravid uterus, pelvic mass), or valvular incompetence -- allows activated clotting factors and platelets to accumulate locally near the valve pockets of deep veins rather than being washed out and diluted by flowing blood, and promotes local hypoxia of the venous endothelium that itself upregulates prothrombotic surface molecules.
virchows_triad.hypercoagulability: A shift in the blood's own protein/cellular balance toward clot formation -- inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden causing activated protein C resistance, prothrombin G20210A gene mutation causing elevated prothrombin levels, antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency), acquired states (malignancy releasing tissue factor and procoagulant microparticles, pregnancy's physiological rise in clotting factors VII/VIII/X/fibrinogen with falling protein S, oestrogen therapy's hepatic-synthesis-driven rise in clotting factors and fall in natural anticoagulants, antiphospholipid antibodies interfering with phospholipid-dependent anticoagulant reactions) -- tips the normal pro-/anti-coagulant equilibrium toward net thrombin generation.
virchows_triad.endothelial_injury: Direct damage or activation of the venous endothelial lining -- central venous catheterisation, surgical/trauma-related vessel wall injury, prior DVT-related valve scarring, or inflammatory/cytokine-mediated endothelial activation (e.g., sepsis, vasculitis, smoking-derived chemical injury) -- exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor, and converts the endothelium's normal antithrombotic surface (thrombomodulin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, heparan sulfate) into a prothrombotic one, triggering local platelet adhesion and the coagulation cascade.
virchows_triad.clinical_honesty_note: The literature itself flags that, of the three components, hypercoagulability is the most directly and repeatedly demonstrated in venous thrombosis, whereas isolated experimental proof of stasis or endothelial injury alone causing venous thrombosis is comparatively less robust -- most real clinical VTE arises from a combination of two or more elements acting together (e.g., surgery = stasis from immobilisation + endothelial injury from the operation + a transient hypercoagulable acute-phase response), not from a single isolated mechanism.
virchows_triad.source: Virchow Triad, StatPearls (NBK539697); Virchow's triad in 'silent' deep vein thrombosis, J Vasc Surg Venous Lymphat Disord 2019 (ScienceDirect S2213-333X(19)30170-2)

core.name: DVT -- unilateral leg swelling
core.note: The most characteristic DVT sign; calf circumference >3cm larger than the asymptomatic leg is one of the 9 items in the Wells DVT clinical prediction rule, reflecting venous outflow obstruction distal to the thrombus
core.source: Wells PS et al., Value of assessment of pretest probability of deep-vein thrombosis in clinical management, Lancet 1997;350:1795-1798

core.name: DVT -- unilateral leg pain / calf tenderness
core.note: Localised tenderness along the deep venous system is a core Wells DVT criterion; pain is typically dull/aching and worsens with dependency or walking
core.source: Wells PS et al., Lancet 1997;350:1795-1798

core.name: DVT -- warmth and erythema of the affected limb
core.note: Reflects local venous congestion and the inflammatory response to thrombus within the vessel wall; often accompanies swelling and can mimic cellulitis, which is itself a common alternative diagnosis captured by the '-2 points' item in the Wells DVT score
core.source: StatPearls Deep Venous Thrombosis (clinical presentation synthesis)

core.name: DVT -- dilated collateral (nonvaricose) superficial veins
core.note: A recognised Wells DVT criterion; reflects blood being diverted through the superficial system around an obstructed deep venous segment
core.source: Wells PS et al., Lancet 1997;350:1795-1798

core.name: PE -- dyspnoea
core.note: The single most frequent PE symptom: new dyspnoea (exertional or at rest) was present in 79% of confirmed-PE patients in PIOPED II, with onset within seconds to minutes in 87% of these patients
core.source: Pineda LA et al./Stein PD et al., Clinical Characteristics of Patients with Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Data from PIOPED II, Am J Med 2007;120:871-879

core.name: PE -- pleuritic chest pain
core.note: Reported in approximately 47-66% of confirmed PE cases across PIOPED I and PIOPED II (65% had the pleuritic-pain-or-haemoptysis syndrome in PIOPED I versus 41% in PIOPED II), typically reflecting peripheral pulmonary infarction with pleural irritation
core.source: PIOPED I and PIOPED II data synthesis (Am J Med 2007;120:871-879)

core.name: PE -- tachycardia
core.note: Heart rate >100/min occurred in only 24-30% of PE patients without prior cardiopulmonary disease in PIOPED data, i.e. a real minority -- so a normal heart rate does NOT exclude PE, though tachycardia is a component of the Wells score, Geneva score, and PESI
core.source: PIOPED data synthesis (Am J Med 2007;120:871-879)

core.name: PE -- hemoptysis
core.note: A less common but classic PE symptom, part of the 'pleuritic pain or hemoptysis' syndrome tracked in PIOPED (65% in PIOPED I, 41% in PIOPED II for the combined syndrome); reflects pulmonary infarction with alveolar haemorrhage
core.source: PIOPED I/II data synthesis

core.name: PE -- syncope
core.note: A real marker of haemodynamically significant PE (transient obstructive shock from acute right ventricular pressure overload); syncope at presentation is one of the clinical features that should prompt urgent risk stratification for high-risk/massive PE
core.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543-603 (Konstantinides SV et al.)

core.name: PE -- tachypnoea
core.note: Respiratory rate >=20/min occurred in 54-70% of PE patients without prior cardiopulmonary disease in PIOPED data; combining dyspnoea, tachypnoea, or pleuritic chest pain captured 92% of confirmed PE patients
core.source: PIOPED data synthesis (Am J Med 2007;120:871-879)

homans_sign.definition: Calf pain on passive dorsiflexion of the foot with the knee extended, historically taught as a DVT sign.
homans_sign.real_diagnostic_accuracy: Genuinely poor and clinically unreliable: published series report sensitivity of only 10-54% and specificity of 39-89%, a range wide enough that a positive test neither confirms nor a negative test excludes DVT; Homan's sign is present in only about one-third of confirmed DVT cases and is falsely positive in a real minority of patients without DVT. Both ACCP/CHEST and NICE guidelines omit Homan's sign from their DVT diagnostic pathways, and compression ultrasound (sensitivity and specificity both exceeding 94% for proximal DVT) is the real diagnostic standard instead.
homans_sign.source: Clinical examination diagnostic-accuracy literature synthesis on Homan's sign (sensitivity 10-54%, specificity 39-89%); ACCP/CHEST and NICE DVT diagnostic guideline structure
homans_sign.confidence: moderate -- the sensitivity/specificity range is concordant across multiple secondary clinical-examination sources, though a single primary index study reporting this exact range was not independently opened for this entry
