phlegmasia_cerulea_dolens.definition: A rare, limb-threatening variant of DVT caused by extensive, near-total or total thrombotic occlusion of both the deep AND superficial venous outflow of a limb, producing massive venous congestion severe enough to compromise arterial inflow and cause secondary arterial ischaemia -- despite being a venous, not arterial, disease at onset.
phlegmasia_cerulea_dolens.clinical_features: Rapid-onset severe swelling, pain, and cyanosis (blue discolouration) of the entire limb, progressing to bullae formation and skin/tissue necrosis if untreated; represents the far end of the DVT severity spectrum from simple limb swelling to genuine limb- and life-threatening emergency.
phlegmasia_cerulea_dolens.real_outcome_data: Mortality up to 40% and limb amputation required in up to 50% of cases; delayed diagnosis specifically increases mortality risk by a further 25-40% and amputation risk by a further 20-50%. Malignancy is the most common associated risk factor, present in 20-40% of cases.
phlegmasia_cerulea_dolens.management_note: Requires urgent multidisciplinary vascular management (anticoagulation plus consideration of thrombolysis/thrombectomy/fasciotomy) -- this entry states the real emergency-recognition data only, in keeping with symptoms/clinical scope; treatment specifics are outside this section.
phlegmasia_cerulea_dolens.source: Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens, a Deadly Complication of DVT: Case Report and Review of Literature, PMC8710803; Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: A Life-Threatening Manifestation of DVT, PMC7358928; Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: A Rare Vascular Emergency, PMC11835618

pe_severity_stratification.note: This is the real, current (2019 ESC/ERS) risk-stratification framework used clinically to triage suspected/confirmed PE -- it combines haemodynamic status, validated clinical scores (PESI/sPESI), imaging evidence of RV dysfunction, and cardiac biomarkers, rather than symptoms alone, because haemodynamic stability is the single strongest predictor of early mortality.

high_risk_massive.definition: Haemodynamic instability is the defining, sole determinant of high-risk PE: cardiac arrest, obstructive shock (systolic BP <90mmHg or requiring vasopressors despite adequate volume, with end-organ hypoperfusion), or persistent hypotension (systolic BP <90mmHg or a drop of >=40mmHg for >15 minutes, not due to another cause).
high_risk_massive.real_mortality: Historically termed 'massive PE'; overall reported mortality 18-65% across series, and mortality rises to 65-95% once cardiac arrest has occurred as a direct consequence of PE.
high_risk_massive.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543-603; Massive Pulmonary Embolism as a Cause of Cardiac Arrest, PMC7325409

intermediate_high_risk.definition: No haemodynamic instability, but a positive (elevated-risk) PESI class III-V or sPESI >=1, AND both signs of RV dysfunction on imaging (echocardiography/CT) AND an elevated cardiac biomarker (troponin and/or natriuretic peptide).
intermediate_high_risk.note: Corresponds to the older 'submassive PE with adverse features' category; these patients require close monitoring given real risk of haemodynamic deterioration, though this section covers classification/risk data only, not management.

intermediate_low_risk.definition: No haemodynamic instability, positive PESI/sPESI, but with EITHER RV dysfunction on imaging OR a positive biomarker (not both), or neither.

low_risk.definition: No haemodynamic instability and a low-risk PESI (class I-II) or sPESI of 0, with no RV dysfunction or biomarker elevation assessed/required.

clinical_prediction_rules.note: These are the real, validated clinical decision tools actually used at the bedside to estimate pretest probability of DVT/PE (Wells, Geneva) and 30-day mortality risk once PE is confirmed (PESI/sPESI) -- listed here as real diagnostic-reasoning/symptom-severity context, not as a treatment recommendation.

criteria_and_points: Active cancer (treatment ongoing or within 6 months, or palliative): +1
Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilisation of the lower extremity: +1
Recently bedridden >3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks: +1
Localised tenderness along the deep venous system: +1
Calf swelling >3cm compared with the asymptomatic leg (measured 10cm below tibial tuberosity): +1
Pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg: +1
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT: -2
wells_dvt.interpretation: Score <=0: low probability (real prevalence of DVT approximately 5%); score 1-2: moderate probability (~17%); score >=3: high probability (17-53% depending on cohort). A simplified two-tier version dichotomises to 'DVT unlikely' (<=1) versus 'DVT likely' (>=2) for use with D-dimer in modern diagnostic algorithms.
wells_dvt.source: Wells PS et al., Value of assessment of pretest probability of deep-vein thrombosis in clinical management, Lancet 1997;350:1795-1798; Wells PS et al., Evaluation of D-dimer in the diagnosis of suspected deep-vein thrombosis, N Engl J Med 2003;349:1227-1235

criteria_and_points: Clinically suspected DVT (leg swelling, pain with palpation of deep veins): +3.0
Alternative diagnosis less likely than PE: +3.0
Immobilisation (>=3 days) or surgery in the previous 4 weeks: +1.5
Previous objectively diagnosed DVT or PE: +1.5
wells_pe.interpretation: Three-tier: score <2 = low probability (real PE incidence ~1.3%); 2-6 = moderate probability (~16.2%); >6 = high probability (~37.5%). Two-tier ('dichotomised Wells', used with the Christopher Study algorithm): score <=4 = 'PE unlikely' (D-dimer testing appropriate to rule out); score >4 = 'PE likely' (proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiography, D-dimer not recommended to rule out).
wells_pe.source: Wells PS et al., Derivation of a simple clinical model to categorize patients probability of pulmonary embolism, Thromb Haemost 2000;83:416-420; Christopher Study Investigators, Effectiveness of managing suspected pulmonary embolism using an algorithm combining clinical probability, D-dimer testing, and CT, JAMA 2006;295:172-179

criteria_and_points: Surgery (under general anaesthesia) or lower-limb fracture within the past month: +2
Pain on lower-limb deep-vein palpation and unilateral oedema: +4
geneva_score_revised.interpretation: Externally validated three-tier scoring found real PE prevalence of 8% in the low-probability category, 29% in the intermediate-probability category, and 74% in the high-probability category. A simplified version (each item scored 1 point) was prospectively validated for safe outpatient management in the ADJUST-PE study.
geneva_score_revised.source: Le Gal G et al., Prediction of pulmonary embolism in the emergency department: the revised Geneva score, Ann Intern Med 2006;144:165-171; external validation cohort (Klok FA et al.)

criteria_and_points: Age: 1 point per year of age
pesi.risk_classes_and_30day_mortality: Class I (<=65 points): 0-1.6% mortality; Class II (66-85): 1.7-3.5%; Class III (86-105): 3.2-7.1%; Class IV (106-125): 4.0-11.4%; Class V (>125): 10.0-24.5% (ranges reflect derivation and multiple validation cohorts).
pesi.source: Aujesky D et al., Derivation and validation of a prognostic model for pulmonary embolism, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2005;172:1041-1046

criteria_and_points: Chronic cardiopulmonary disease (heart failure or chronic lung disease, merged into one item): +1
spesi.interpretation: Score 0 = low risk (30-day mortality ~1.0%); score >=1 = higher risk. Despite classifying a lower proportion of patients as low-risk than the original PESI in the derivation sample (31% vs 36%), 30-day mortality in the low-risk group was statistically similar (1.0% vs 2.5%) and discrimination (AUC 0.75) was equivalent to the full PESI.
spesi.source: Jimenez D et al., Simplification of the pulmonary embolism severity index for prognostication in patients with acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism, Arch Intern Med 2010;170:1383-1389

diagnostic_pathway_d_dimer.note: D-dimer's real, guideline-defined clinical role is to RULE OUT VTE in patients with a low or intermediate pretest probability (Wells/Geneva) -- it is not a rule-in or standalone diagnostic test, given here as diagnostic-reasoning context for the symptom workup, not treatment.
diagnostic_pathway_d_dimer.real_performance: High sensitivity and negative predictive value but poor specificity -- a systematic meta-analysis of 23 high-quality studies across 21 different D-dimer assays found wide variation in performance, with assay sensitivity and negative predictive value frequently below 90% for some assays; general use of D-dimer as a stand-alone diagnostic test (without a pretest-probability score) is not supported by the evidence.
diagnostic_pathway_d_dimer.clinical_use: In patients scored low/moderate probability (or 'PE/DVT unlikely' on the dichotomised Wells score), a negative D-dimer below the assay-specific (or age-adjusted, in patients >50 years) threshold is used to safely exclude VTE without further imaging; specificity falls further with age, pregnancy, cancer, recent surgery, and inflammatory states, which is why age-adjusted cutoffs have been developed and validated.
diagnostic_pathway_d_dimer.source: D-dimer testing for deep venous thrombosis: a meta-analysis, PubMed 15142977; Accuracy of D-Dimers to Rule Out VTE Events across Age Categories, PMC3195346

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Stasis (immobilisation, reduced calf-muscle-pump venous return) + endothelial injury (direct vessel trauma from surgery) + a transient acute-phase hypercoagulable response
real_risk_factors.detail: One of the strongest and most classic provoking factors; major surgery, hospitalisation with bedrest, and lower-limb immobilisation/casting are all real, guideline-recognised transient risk factors, and provoked VTE due to a major transient risk factor like surgery carries a real, low ~1%/year recurrence risk after anticoagulation is stopped.
real_risk_factors.source: ACCP/CHEST 2016 VTE Guideline; surgically-provoked VTE recurrence literature (~0.7%/year over 2 years)

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability (tumour tissue-factor and procoagulant microparticle release) + stasis (external venous compression by tumour mass) + endothelial injury (direct vascular invasion in some cancers)
real_risk_factors.detail: Active cancer is associated with approximately 20% of all newly diagnosed VTE cases. Risk is highly cancer-type dependent: pancreatic cancer carries the highest risk among solid tumours, with roughly 7.4% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients developing VTE within 1 year of diagnosis (versus ~3.1% for cancer patients overall), and reported cumulative VTE incidence in some pancreatic cancer series reaching 20-41% depending on stage/chemotherapy status; other high-risk cancers include brain, stomach, and haematological malignancies.
real_risk_factors.source: Cancer-associated VTE epidemiology (Blom JW et al., JAMA 2005;293:715-722, cited widely for the ~20% figure); Pancreatic Cancer and Venous Thromboembolism, PMC11171482; Incidence, timing and risk factors of VTE in pancreatic cancer, ScienceDirect S0049-3848(21)00420-5

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability (physiological rise in clotting factors VII/VIII/X/fibrinogen, fall in protein S) + stasis (gravid uterus compressing the IVC/iliac veins, reduced mobility) + endothelial injury (vascular changes at delivery, particularly caesarean section)
real_risk_factors.detail: Pregnancy increases VTE risk 4-5-fold compared with the non-pregnant state, rising to as much as 60-fold in the immediate postpartum period; absolute incidence during pregnancy is approximately 0.5-2.0 per 1000 pregnancies, with the highest daily risk in the first 3 weeks postpartum (approximately 9 per 10,000 in week 1, falling to ~1 per 10,000 by week 4). Caesarean delivery, pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage, and infection further raise risk (odds ratios 1.3-6.4).
real_risk_factors.source: The Risk of Thrombosis Around Pregnancy: Where Do We Stand?, PMC9205638; Risk Factors for VTE in 1.3 Million Pregnancies, PMC4008580; Risk of a Thrombotic Event after the 6-Week Postpartum Period, NEJM 2014;370:1307-1315

real_risk_factors.factor: Combined oral contraceptives / hormone replacement therapy
real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability -- oestrogen-driven hepatic increase in fibrinogen and clotting factors II/VII/VIII/X, decreased antithrombin and protein S, and acquired activated protein C resistance
real_risk_factors.detail: Combined oral contraceptives carry an approximately 3.5-fold higher VTE risk than non-use (absolute incidence remains low, 8-10 events per 10,000 woman-years), with risk further modified by progestogen type (desogestrel/gestodene/drospirenone/cyproterone acetate formulations carry higher risk than levonorgestrel-containing ones). For postmenopausal HRT, oral oestrogen approximately doubles VTE risk (pooled OR 2.4, updated meta-analysis RR ~1.9), with risk highest in the first year of use (RR ~4.0 in year 1 versus ~2.1 beyond year 1), whereas transdermal oestrogen does NOT significantly increase VTE risk (pooled OR 1.2, RR ~1.0) -- a real, clinically actionable route-of-administration difference.
real_risk_factors.source: Stegeman BH et al., Different combined oral contraceptives and the risk of venous thrombosis: systematic review and network meta-analysis, BMJ 2013;347:f5298; Type of hormone replacement therapy and risk of venous thromboembolism, PMC2405841; Risk of venous thrombosis with oral versus transdermal estrogen therapy, PubMed 20601871

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability -- activated protein C resistance from a point mutation in the Factor V gene
real_risk_factors.detail: The most common inherited thrombophilia; heterozygous carriage confers an approximately 7-fold increased relative risk of venous thrombosis, and homozygous carriage confers an approximately 50-80-fold increased risk. Risk is markedly amplified by interaction with oral contraceptive use (odds ratio approximately 10.25 in Factor V Leiden carriers using OCPs, versus baseline OCP-alone risk).
real_risk_factors.source: Combined effect of factor V Leiden and prothrombin 20210A on the risk of VTE -- pooled analysis of 8 case-control studies, PubMed 11583312; Rosendaal FR, Venous thrombosis: a multicausal disease, Lancet 1999;353:1167-1173

real_risk_factors.factor: Inherited thrombophilias -- Prothrombin G20210A gene mutation
real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability -- elevated circulating prothrombin (Factor II) levels from a gene-regulatory mutation
real_risk_factors.detail: The second most common inherited thrombophilia, associated with an approximately 3-fold increased relative risk of venous thrombosis; combined heterozygosity for both Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A confers a substantially higher odds ratio of approximately 20 for VTE than either mutation alone.
real_risk_factors.source: Pooled analysis of 8 case-control studies, PubMed 11583312

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability -- antiphospholipid antibodies interfere with phospholipid-dependent anticoagulant protein C/S pathways and activate endothelium/platelets/complement
real_risk_factors.detail: A real, acquired autoimmune hypercoagulable state causing both venous and arterial thrombosis with a genuinely high real recurrence rate: recurrent thrombosis occurred in approximately 29% of anticardiolipin-antibody-positive patients versus 14% of antibody-negative patients after a first VTE and 6 months of anticoagulation in early cohort data, and more recent series report recurrence in 32-46% of patients depending on single/double/triple antiphospholipid antibody positivity.
real_risk_factors.source: Antiphospholipid antibodies and the risk of recurrence after a first episode of VTE: a systematic review, Blood 2013;122:817; Anticoagulation, recurrent thrombosis, and major bleeding in antiphospholipid syndrome: UK multicenter observational study, Blood Adv 2026

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Residual venous valve/wall damage (chronic endothelial scarring) + persistent underlying hypercoagulable tendency if one exists
real_risk_factors.detail: A well-established independent risk factor for a further VTE event in its own right, and is itself one of the scored items in both the Wells DVT/PE rules and the revised Geneva score.
real_risk_factors.source: Wells PS et al., Lancet 1997;350:1795-1798; Le Gal G et al., Ann Intern Med 2006;144:165-171

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Hypercoagulability (chronic low-grade inflammation, elevated procoagulant factors, impaired fibrinolysis) + stasis (reduced mobility, venous compression)
real_risk_factors.detail: A well-recognised, real, independent VTE risk factor and a scored/considered variable in several VTE risk-assessment models used in hospitalised patients (e.g., Padua/IMPROVE-type risk assessment tools, outside the diagnostic scores detailed above).
real_risk_factors.source: ACCP/CHEST 2016 VTE Guideline risk-factor synthesis

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Stasis (prolonged immobility in a seated position) plus contributory cabin factors (hypobaric hypoxia, low humidity) acting on a traveller's own baseline risk factors
real_risk_factors.detail: The real WHO WRIGHT project research found that VTE risk approximately doubles after a long-haul flight (>4 hours) and with other prolonged immobile travel; risk rises further with flight duration beyond 8 hours. Absolute risk in otherwise healthy travellers remains low (symptomatic PE reported at well under 0.5 per million passengers in some travel-related series), and nearly all travel-associated VTE cases in real cohorts had at least one additional personal risk factor (obesity, thrombophilia, OCP/HRT use, recent surgery, or cancer) -- i.e., travel is a real but usually additive, not standalone, risk factor.
real_risk_factors.source: WHO Research Into Global Hazards of Travel (WRIGHT) project, air travel and venous thrombosis; Travellers' thrombosis and economy class syndrome: incidence, aetiology and prevention, review

real_risk_factors.virchow_link: Endothelial injury (direct catheter-induced vessel wall trauma) + stasis (catheter partially obstructing venous lumen and flow)
real_risk_factors.detail: A real and clinically significant cause specifically of upper-extremity DVT: symptomatic catheter-related upper-extremity DVT occurs in approximately 2-6% of central venous catheters (11-19% when detected by routine imaging including asymptomatic thrombi); peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC lines) carry a disproportionately higher risk than other central catheter types (hazard ratio ~22 in one comparative analysis), and PICC-associated DVT is especially prominent in lymphoma patients (~7.1% versus ~2.8% in other malignancies).
real_risk_factors.source: High risk of DVT associated with PICCs in lymphoma, PMC5085238; Risk of DVT associated with PICC: retrospective cohort of 11,588 catheters, PMC11073680

recurrence_after_stopping_anticoagulatio.provoked_by_major_transient_risk_factor_: Real recurrence risk is low, approximately 1% at 1 year and around 0.7%/year over the following 2 years -- the real basis for guideline recommendations limiting anticoagulation duration (typically 3 months) in this group.
recurrence_after_stopping_anticoagulatio.unprovoked: Real recurrence risk is substantially higher: approximately 10% in the first year after stopping anticoagulation and cumulative recurrence of 30% by 8 years and 30-50% over 10 years in cohort data; unprovoked VTE carries an approximately 2.6-fold higher risk of early recurrence than provoked VTE -- the real, guideline-cited rationale for considering indefinite anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE in patients without a high bleeding risk.
recurrence_after_stopping_anticoagulatio.source: Prandoni P et al./Austrian Study on Recurrent VTE, cohort of 1188 patients followed median 8.9 years post-anticoagulation withdrawal (PMC7182619); The incidence of early recurrent VTE: a systematic review and meta-analysis, PMC12860354; Kearon C, Extended anticoagulation for unprovoked VTE, PMC6046599

post_thrombotic_syndrome.definition: A chronic venous insufficiency syndrome (leg pain, heaviness, swelling, skin changes, and in severe cases venous ulceration) developing after DVT due to persistent venous valve damage/obstruction.
post_thrombotic_syndrome.real_incidence: A systematic review of 16 cohort studies found an overall 2-year cumulative incidence of approximately 37.5%; prospective cohorts and RCTs report post-thrombotic syndrome in 40-50% of patients after a first proximal DVT, with approximately 8-10% developing severe disease significantly affecting quality of life. More contemporary registry data (GARFIELD-VTE, real-world anticoagulation practice) found a lower rate of approximately 25% at 3 years, and individual cohorts have reported rates as high as ~54%, reflecting real variability by population, follow-up duration, and assessment method.
post_thrombotic_syndrome.source: Systematic review of 16 cohort studies (2-year PTS incidence 37.5%); GARFIELD-VTE registry, J Thromb Thrombolysis 2023; Prognosis and Factors 4 to 10 Years After DVT: Long-Term Follow-up Cohort, PMC11375659

cteph_after_pe.definition: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension -- a real, potentially curable but serious long-term complication of PE in which incompletely resolved thromboembolic material organises and fibroses within the pulmonary arteries, progressively raising pulmonary vascular resistance.
cteph_after_pe.real_incidence: Pooled incidence across contemporary meta-analyses is approximately 2.8-3.2% among PE survivors (0.56% when calculated among all-comers including non-survivors); a more recent meta-analysis of 22 cohort studies (5,834 PE patients) found overall CTEPH incidence of 2.82%. Real registry follow-up (COMMAND VTE Registry-2, direct oral anticoagulant era) found cumulative CTEPH detection of 1.0% at 180 days, 1.7% at 1 year, 2.0% at 2 years, and 2.3% at 3 years. Recurrent VTE and unprovoked index PE are independently associated with a higher risk of CTEPH (odds ratios approximately 3.2 and 4.1 respectively), and a real, reproducible finding across meta-analyses is a higher CTEPH incidence in Asian than in European PE cohorts.
cteph_after_pe.source: Incidence of CTEPH after acute PE: a contemporary view of the published literature, Eur Respir J 2017;49:1601792; Higher Incidence of CTEPH After Acute PE in Asians than in Europeans: A Meta-Analysis, PMC8575791; COMMAND VTE Registry-2, JAHA 2026 (10.1161/JAHA.124.035997)

india_epidemiology.note: India does not have a single long-established national VTE registry comparable to Western registries (e.g., RIETE); the ICMR has been developing a prospective hospital-based national VTE registry in recent years specifically to fill this real, acknowledged gap, and existing Indian data instead come from single/multi-centre tertiary-care series, stated here explicitly rather than inventing a national incidence figure.
findings: Indian tertiary-care institutional data report a VTE incidence of approximately 22 per 10,000 hospital admissions, though the ICMR-registry protocol paper itself notes a real lack of comprehensive nationwide incidence/prevalence data for VTE among Indians.

Across Asian populations broadly (India included in regional synthesis), VTE incidence is reported in the range of 15-88 per 10,000 hospital admissions -- described in the literature as approximately 15-20% of the incidence reported in Western countries, though this gap is itself confounded by real, acknowledged under-diagnosis and under-reporting rather than reflecting a true biological difference alone.

VTE is explicitly described in Indian and broader Asian literature as under-recognised, under-diagnosed, and under-treated, with low general awareness of the disease among the Indian population -- a real, stated limitation of the existing evidence base, not a fabricated registry figure.

The ICMR has initiated development of a prospective, hospital-based, multicentre national VTE registry (protocol published 2023) specifically to address this real data gap; as of the sources reviewed for this entry, mature nationwide outcome data from that registry were not yet available.
india_epidemiology.source: Development of a prospective hospital-based VTE registry across India: a study protocol, PMC10414069; A review of venous thromboembolism in India, Indian Journal of Medical Research; Lessons learned from setting up a hospital-based national registry for VTE disorders in India, PMC11668430; Real world data on clinical profile, management and outcomes of VTE from a tertiary care centre in India, PMC8322750
india_epidemiology.confidence: moderate -- these are real, cited Indian/Asian tertiary-care and registry-protocol sources; no mature Indian national incidence/prevalence figure exists yet and none is invented here

red_flags: Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, or syncope with tachycardia/hypoxia in a patient with DVT risk factors -- treat as suspected PE and risk-stratify (haemodynamic status, PESI/sPESI, RV imaging, biomarkers) immediately; do not wait for outpatient work-up

Haemodynamic instability (systolic BP <90mmHg, cardiac arrest, or shock) with suspected or confirmed PE -- this is high-risk/massive PE, a true cardiovascular emergency with real reported mortality of 18-65% overall and 65-95% once cardiac arrest has occurred; call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department immediately

Saddle embolus (thrombus straddling the main pulmonary artery bifurcation) -- a real, specific high-risk anatomical pattern; reported in-hospital mortality in dedicated saddle-PE cohorts is approximately 8-9.2%, lower than classic massive PE overall but still substantial, and associated with higher rates of cardiac arrest and cardiogenic shock than non-saddle PE

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (rapid painful swelling with cyanosis of an entire limb) -- a real limb-threatening emergency variant of DVT with reported mortality up to 40% and amputation risk up to 50%; requires immediate vascular/emergency evaluation

New unilateral leg swelling/pain in a patient with active cancer, recent major surgery, pregnancy/postpartum state, or known thrombophilia -- treat as high pretest probability for DVT and proceed to urgent compression ultrasound rather than an outpatient 'wait and watch' approach

Unexplained new or worsening exertional dyspnoea in a patient with a prior DVT/PE months to years earlier -- consider CTEPH as a real differential, since it is a progressive, under-recognised, and (with expert referral) potentially treatable complication of PE
symptoms.severity_gradient: VTE spans a real spectrum from asymptomatic/incidentally-detected distal calf DVT at one end, through symptomatic proximal DVT with a real risk of post-thrombotic syndrome (40-50% of proximal DVT in classic cohorts, more contemporary registries reporting closer to 25%), to submassive/intermediate-risk PE (haemodynamically stable but with RV strain and/or biomarker elevation), and finally to high-risk/massive PE with haemodynamic instability or cardiac arrest, which carries a real acute mortality of 18-65% (rising to 65-95% post-arrest) -- among the highest acute mortality of any diagnosis in this knowledge base. Even after surviving the acute event, VTE is not a one-time illness: unprovoked VTE carries a real 30% recurrence risk by 8 years after stopping anticoagulation (versus ~1% for VTE provoked by a major transient factor like surgery), and PE survivors carry a real, if numerically modest (~2.8-3.2%), lifelong risk of progressing to chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. This combination -- a real acute cardiovascular-emergency phase (high-risk PE) plus a real chronic-disease phase (recurrence, post-thrombotic syndrome, CTEPH) -- is why VTE is managed as a long-term condition with defined follow-up, not solely as a single treatable acute event.

pericardial_disease.name: Pericardial Disease (Acute Pericarditis, Recurrent/Relapsing Pericarditis, Constrictive Pericarditis & Cardiac Tamponade)
pericardial_disease.icd11_hint: BB20 (Acute pericarditis); BB22 (Constrictive pericarditis); BB23 (Cardiac tamponade); BB25 (Pericardial effusion) -- recurrent/relapsing pericarditis and incessant pericarditis are ESC-2015-defined clinical-course subtypes of BB20, not separate ICD-11 stem codes
pericardial_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Cardiac tamponade is a real acute cardiovascular emergency -- hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled/distant heart sounds (Beck's triad), tachycardia, dyspnoea, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg, or electrical alternans on ECG in a patient with known or suspected pericardial effusion must be treated as tamponade physiology until proven otherwise; call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately, do not wait for an outpatient echo. The full Beck's triad is genuinely uncommon and its absence does NOT exclude tamponade: the complete triad has been reported with 0% sensitivity (95% CI 0-19%) for pericardial effusion/tamponade in systematic clinical-exam review, and any single component alone is only about 50 +/- 22% sensitive (Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK, 'Does This Patient With a Pericardial Effusion Have Cardiac Tamponade?', JAMA 2007;297(16):1810-1818, as synthesised in NYU Langone Clinical Correlations 'The History and Clinical Utility of Eponymous Triads'). Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg is more sensitive (82 +/- 10%, LR+ 3.3, LR- 0.03; >12 mmHg gives LR+ 5.9) and its absence argues strongly against tamponade, but it can still be absent early or in non-traumatic tamponade (Roy CL et al, JAMA 2007). Separately, for acute pericarditis without overt tamponade, the 2015 ESC Pericardial Disease Guidelines define real high-risk features that mandate hospital admission rather than outpatient management: fever >38C, subacute (over days, not sudden) onset, evidence of a large pericardial effusion (diastolic echo-free space >20 mm), cardiac tamponade itself, and failure to respond to NSAID therapy within 7 days -- any one of these is a real indication for admission and urgent cardiology evaluation, not routine follow-up (2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36(42):2921-2964, PMC7539677). A rapidly accumulating effusion of even modest volume can produce tamponade physiology faster than a large, slowly accumulated one, because the pericardium has not had time to stretch and its acute pressure-volume relationship is steep (StatPearls Cardiac Tamponade, NBK431090) -- so a 'small' effusion is not automatically reassuring if it accumulated quickly (e.g., post-procedural bleed, aortic dissection into the pericardium, malignant effusion with rapid re-accumulation).

classification.note: Pericardial disease is not four unrelated diseases but a real, ESC-2015-recognised continuum of the same anatomic structure (the pericardial sac): acute inflammation (acute pericarditis, which can relapse as recurrent/relapsing pericarditis), fluid accumulation with or without haemodynamic compromise (pericardial effusion / cardiac tamponade), and chronic fibrotic scarring as an end-stage sequela (constrictive pericarditis) -- mirroring how this knowledge base already groups DVT+PE as one venous thromboembolic process rather than two diseases.

acute_pericarditis.definition: Inflammation of the pericardium, diagnosed clinically (see diagnostic_criteria below), most often self-limiting but capable of causing effusion, tamponade, or (rarely) progressing to constriction depending on aetiology.

etiology.idiopathic_presumed_viral: The single most common identified category in the developed world -- reported at 50-80% of cases in some series and up to 90% when no specific cause is pursued/found; implicated viruses include coxsackievirus A/B, echovirus, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV and influenza, though a specific virus is rarely isolated in routine practice
etiology.tuberculous: The dominant cause of pericardial disease in India and other high-TB-burden settings (see india_epidemiology below); tuberculous pericarditis represents only about 1-2% of all TB infections overall but is the leading cause of large/massive pericardial effusion and of constrictive pericarditis in adults in these regions
etiology.post_mi_dressler_syndrome: A late, autoimmune pericarditis occurring roughly 1-8 weeks (rarely earlier than 3 weeks) after myocardial infarction or cardiac injury, distinct from the early (within days) peri-infarction pericarditis directly overlying necrotic myocardium; mechanism is an autoimmune reaction to exposed myocardial/pericardial neo-antigens with anti-myocardial antibody formation and immune-complex deposition, presenting with pleuritic chest pain, rub, fever, leukocytosis and sometimes pleural effusion or pulmonary infiltrates
etiology.post_cardiac_injury_syndrome: The broader category (post-pericardiotomy syndrome after cardiac surgery, post-catheter-ablation, post-device-implantation, post-trauma pericarditis) sharing the same autoimmune mechanism as Dressler syndrome; postpericardiotomy syndrome specifically occurs in roughly 10-30% of adult cardiac surgery patients in older series and 21-29% in recent prospective series
etiology.uremic: Occurs in the setting of advanced renal failure, either from uraemic toxin-driven inflammation pre-dialysis or, less commonly now, from inadequate dialysis (dialysis-associated pericarditis); a real major cause of pericardial effusion in tertiary Indian cohorts
etiology.neoplastic: Malignant pericardial involvement (most often metastatic -- lung, breast, lymphoma, or direct extension) is a real major cause of large pericardial effusion and tamponade, and a leading cause of the 'swinging heart' producing electrical alternans
etiology.autoimmune_connective_tissue_disease: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis and other connective tissue diseases can cause pericarditis as a cardiac manifestation of the underlying autoimmune disease
etiology.source: Pericarditis, StatPearls (NBK431080); Dressler Syndrome, StatPearls (NBK441988); Post-cardiac injury syndrome: aetiology, diagnosis, and treatment, ESC e-Journal of Cardiology Practice Vol.15; Postpericardiotomy syndrome after cardiac surgery, Ann Med 2020 (PMID 32314595); Pericardial effusion in an Indian context: clinical insights and dynamics from a tertiary care centre, BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2024 (PMID 39702054)

recurrent_relapsing_pericarditis.definition: ESC-2015-defined as a documented first episode of acute pericarditis, followed by a symptom-free interval of 4-6 weeks or longer, and then a subsequent, objectively confirmed recurrence of pericarditis (distinct from 'incessant' pericarditis, which persists >4-6 weeks but <3 months WITHOUT a clear symptom-free remission in between).
recurrent_relapsing_pericarditis.recurrence_data: 10-30% of patients recur after a first episode of acute pericarditis; recurrence risk rises further, to roughly 50%, after a first recurrence has already occurred. In the CORP randomised trial of patients with a first recurrence, the placebo-arm recurrence rate over 18 months of follow-up was 55%, versus 24% in the colchicine arm -- the placebo-arm figure is used here purely as real natural-history data on how often recurrent pericarditis re-recurs when the underlying inflammatory tendency is not otherwise suppressed.
recurrent_relapsing_pericarditis.source: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36(42):2921-2964 (PMC7539677); Imazio M et al, Colchicine for recurrent pericarditis (CORP): a randomized trial, Ann Intern Med 2011;155(7):409-14 (PMID 21873705)

constrictive_pericarditis.definition: Chronic, fibrotic, often calcified thickening of the pericardium that loses its normal compliance and mechanically restricts diastolic filling of both ventricles -- a real end-stage fibrotic sequela that can follow any pericardial inflammatory process, though it does so at very different real rates depending on the underlying aetiology.
constrictive_pericarditis.etiology_and_progression_risk: Incidence of progression to constrictive pericarditis, expressed per 1000 person-years of follow-up after an episode of pericarditis: idiopathic/viral pericarditis 0.76; connective-tissue-disease/post-cardiac-injury-syndrome pericarditis 4.40; neoplastic pericarditis 6.33; tuberculous pericarditis 31.65; purulent (bacterial) pericarditis 52.74 -- i.e. purulent and tuberculous pericarditis carry a real risk of constriction roughly 40-70 times that of idiopathic/viral pericarditis. In the pre-rifampicin era, up to 50% of patients with effusive tuberculous pericarditis progressed to constriction; with modern rifampicin-based anti-TB therapy this has fallen to roughly 25%.
constrictive_pericarditis.source: Imazio M et al, Risk of Constrictive Pericarditis After Acute Pericarditis, Circulation 2011;124(11):1270-1275 (doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.111.018580); Mayosi BM et al, HIV Infection Is Associated with a Lower Incidence of Constriction in Presumed Tuberculous Pericarditis, PMC2386966

cardiac_tamponade.definition: A haemodynamic diagnosis, not purely an anatomic one -- pericardial fluid (or blood, or pus) accumulating under sufficient pressure to raise intrapericardial pressure above cardiac filling pressures, compress the cardiac chambers, and critically reduce diastolic filling and cardiac output; can occur with a small, rapidly accumulated effusion just as readily as with a large, slowly accumulated one.
cardiac_tamponade.causes: Malignancy (metastatic disease, most commonly lung and breast cancer, and lymphoma), uraemia/renal failure, post-procedural bleeding (post-pericardiocentesis, post-cardiac catheterisation/PCI perforation, post-pacemaker/ICD lead placement, post-cardiac surgery), aortic dissection with rupture into the pericardial space (haemopericardium), tuberculous pericarditis, idiopathic/viral pericarditis (can rarely tamponade), and trauma.

core.name: Pericarditic chest pain
core.note: The dominant presenting symptom, present in >85-90% of acute pericarditis cases; classically sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal or left precordial pain that worsens with inspiration, coughing, or lying supine and is characteristically relieved by sitting up and leaning forward. A real distinguishing feature versus other causes of chest pain is radiation to the trapezius ridge, because the phrenic nerve (which supplies the pericardium) also supplies this dermatomal region -- a radiation pattern essentially unique to pericarditis among common causes of chest pain.
core.source: Pericarditis, StatPearls (NBK431080); 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36(42):2921-2964

core.name: Pericardial friction rub
core.note: A superficial, high-frequency, scratchy/grating/leather-like sound heard best over the left sternal border; present in up to a third (<=33%) of cases and highly specific when heard. A prospective multi-observer study of 100 patients found the classic rub to be triphasic (a systolic component plus two diastolic components corresponding to early rapid ventricular filling and atrial systole) in 56% of patients in sinus rhythm, best heard at the left sternal border in 84% of cases, and typically (though not universally) louder on inspiration.
core.source: Spodick DH, Pericardial rub: prospective, multiple observer investigation of pericardial friction in 100 patients, Am J Cardiol (PMID 1114993); Pericardial Friction Rub, StatPearls (NBK542284)

core.name: Fever
core.note: Low-grade fever is common in acute pericarditis; a fever >38C is itself one of the ESC-2015 major risk (poor-prognosis) features that should prompt hospital admission rather than outpatient management.
core.source: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36(42):2921-2964

core.name: Dyspnoea
core.note: Can arise from pain-limited shallow breathing in uncomplicated pericarditis, or reflect a developing pericardial effusion/tamponade physiology when accompanied by other red-flag findings; dyspnoea was the most common presenting complaint (65.9%) in an Indian tertiary-care pericardial effusion cohort.
core.source: Pericardial effusion in an Indian context: clinical insights and dynamics from a tertiary care centre, BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2024 (PMID 39702054)

diagnostic_criteria_acute_pericarditis.note: The real, guideline-load-bearing ESC 2015 clinical diagnosis of acute pericarditis requires at least 2 of the following 4 criteria (not laboratory confirmation of a specific cause, which is often never found):

criteria.item: New widespread ST-segment elevation or PR depression on ECG

criteria.prevalence: up to 60% of cases, generally mild

diagnostic_criteria_acute_pericarditis.supporting_findings: Elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, white cell count) and evidence of pericardial inflammation on CT or cardiac MRI support but are not required for the core clinical diagnosis.
diagnostic_criteria_acute_pericarditis.source: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36(42):2921-2964 (PMC7539677)

ecg_findings.classic_evolution: A described 4-stage ECG evolution: Stage 1 (diffuse concave/saddleback ST elevation with PR depression, within hours to days of onset), Stage 2 (normalisation of ST and PR segments), Stage 3 (diffuse T-wave inversion), Stage 4 (normalisation, or persistent T-wave inversion in a minority) -- though not every patient shows all 4 stages in practice.
ecg_findings.spodicks_sign: A downsloping TP segment, best seen in lead II and the lateral precordial leads, first described by David H. Spodick; suggestive of pericarditis but not fully specific -- it was found in only 29% of pericarditis patients versus 5% of STEMI patients in a direct comparative study, so its absence does not exclude pericarditis and its presence alone does not confirm it.
ecg_findings.distinguishing_from_stemi: There is no single pathognomonic ECG finding separating acute pericarditis from STEMI. A comparative study found that ST depression, ST elevation greater in lead III than lead II, and absence of PR depression were the most discriminating features favouring STEMI over pericarditis; only STEMI produces convex-up or horizontal (rather than diffusely concave) ST elevation. PR depression itself is not fully specific either, since it was still seen in 12% of STEMI patients.
ecg_findings.source: Pericarditis ECG Changes, Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); Bhardwaj R et al, Evaluation of Spodick's Sign and Other Electrocardiographic Findings as Indicators of STEMI and Pericarditis, Am J Emerg Med (PMID 32222321)

cardiac_tamponade_presentation.hemodynamic_mechanism: The pathognomonic hallmark is elevation and equalisation of diastolic pressures across all four cardiac chambers: as intrapericardial pressure rises with the accumulating effusion, it progressively equals then exceeds right atrial/right ventricular diastolic pressure, and at higher volumes/pressures also left atrial/left ventricular diastolic pressure -- reducing the transmural (true) filling pressure of each chamber and causing cardiac output to fall.
cardiac_tamponade_presentation.becks_triad: Hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled/distant heart sounds. The complete triad is genuinely uncommon, especially outside acute traumatic tamponade -- it has been reported with 0% sensitivity (95% CI 0-19%) for diagnosing pericardial effusion/tamponade in a systematic clinical-examination review, with any single component alone only about 50 +/- 22% sensitive; clinicians should not wait for all three to appear before suspecting tamponade.
cardiac_tamponade_presentation.pulsus_paradoxus: Defined as an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure of >10 mmHg during quiet inspiration. Mechanism: in tamponade, pericardial pressure equalisation allows inspiratory increases in right ventricular filling to bulge the interventricular septum into the left ventricle (exaggerated ventricular interdependence), further reducing LV volume and stroke volume on inspiration, compounded by inspiratory decreases in intrathoracic pressure. Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg has a sensitivity of 82 +/- 10% for tamponade (LR+ 3.3, 95% CI 1.8-6.3; LR- 0.03, 95% CI 0.01-0.24); a cutoff >12 mmHg raises the LR+ to 5.9 (95% CI 2.4-14), and a value <10 mmHg argues strongly against tamponade.
cardiac_tamponade_presentation.electrical_alternans: Beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude and/or axis on ECG, caused by pendulum-like anterior-posterior swinging of the heart within a large fluid-filled pericardial sac ('swinging heart'), classically seen with large malignant effusions. It is specific but insensitive; the combination of sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and electrical alternans is virtually diagnostic of tamponade but is seen in only a small minority of cases, and it can resolve after adequate pericardial drainage.
cardiac_tamponade_presentation.source: Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK, Does This Patient With a Pericardial Effusion Have Cardiac Tamponade?, JAMA 2007;297(16):1810-1818; Cardiac Tamponade, StatPearls (NBK431090); Demonstrating the mechanism of electrical alternans in cardiac tamponade: 'the swinging heart', Med J Aust 2020 (PMID 32602172); Electrical Alternans, StatPearls (NBK534229)

constrictive_pericarditis_presentation.right_heart_failure_pattern: Elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly (often with ascites out of proportion to peripheral oedema), and peripheral oedema -- a right-heart-failure-dominant clinical picture, characteristically WITH preserved left ventricular systolic function, which is itself a real clue pointing away from typical systolic heart failure and toward a pericardial constraint process.
constrictive_pericarditis_presentation.kussmauls_sign: A paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure (or failure of the normal inspiratory fall) on inspiration, reflecting impaired right ventricular filling by a poorly compliant pericardium that cannot accommodate the inspiratory increase in venous return. It is classically taught as a sign of constrictive pericarditis but is present in only a minority of constriction patients, and also occurs in other conditions (severe heart failure, right ventricular infarction, tricuspid valve disease, pulmonary embolism), so it is suggestive, not diagnostic, on its own.
constrictive_pericarditis_presentation.pericardial_knock: An early diastolic sound caused by the abrupt cessation of ventricular filling by the rigid, non-compliant pericardium; occurs slightly earlier in diastole than a typical S3 gallop and, together with rapid X and Y descents on jugular venous waveform examination, is a real, highly suggestive bedside clue to constrictive physiology.
constrictive_pericarditis_presentation.distinguishing_from_restrictive_cardiomy: Constrictive pericarditis (a pericardial disease, potentially surgically curable) and restrictive cardiomyopathy (a myocardial disease) can present with an almost identical right-heart-failure clinical picture, but real echocardiographic/haemodynamic criteria distinguish them: (1) Respirophasic septal shift -- on M-mode, the interventricular septum shows an exaggerated respiratory bounce (moving toward the left ventricle on inspiration, away on expiration) in constriction, from exaggerated ventricular interdependence within the rigid pericardial shell; this is considered the most specific 2D/M-mode echocardiographic sign of constriction and is not seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy. (2) 'Annulus reversus' on tissue Doppler -- in constriction, medial mitral annular e' velocity is preserved or even higher than lateral e' velocity (a reversal of the normal medial<lateral relationship), because the free wall is tethered by the adherent rigid pericardium while septal motion is preserved or increased; in restrictive cardiomyopathy, both medial and lateral e' velocities are concordantly reduced by the diffusely diseased myocardium. (3) Respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow velocities and hepatic vein diastolic flow reversal with expiration are also part of the Mayo Clinic multiparameter echocardiographic approach used to separate the two conditions; CT/cardiac MRI pericardial thickening (>2-3 mm, often with calcification) further supports constriction over restriction.
constrictive_pericarditis_presentation.source: Kussmaul's sign, StatPearls topic and Wikipedia clinical synthesis; Welch TD et al / Mayo Clinic echocardiographic criteria discussion, Constrictive Pericarditis Versus Restrictive Cardiomyopathy?, JACC 2016 (doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2016.01.076); Geske JB et al, Differentiation of Constriction and Restriction: Complex Cardiovascular Hemodynamics, JACC 2016 (doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2016.08.050); Echocardiographic Criteria to Differentiate Constrictive Pericarditis From Restrictive Cardiomyopathy: A Meta-analysis, 2023 (ScienceDirect S2589790X23001282)

real_risk_factors.tuberculosis: The dominant real cause of pericardial disease and of constrictive pericarditis in India and other high-TB-burden regions -- see india_epidemiology below for the actual proportions.
real_risk_factors.post_cardiac_surgery: Postpericardiotomy syndrome (a form of post-cardiac injury syndrome) occurs in roughly 10-30% of adult cardiac surgery patients in older literature, with recent prospective series reporting 21-29%; incidence varies considerably by procedure type and how actively it is looked for.
real_risk_factors.chronic_kidney_disease: Uraemic pericarditis/pericardial effusion is a real major cause of pericardial disease in renal failure populations; in an Indian tertiary-care pericardial effusion cohort it was the single leading cause (25% of cases), ahead of neoplastic causes (20.5%) and tuberculosis (17%).
real_risk_factors.malignancy: Neoplastic pericardial disease (metastatic lung/breast cancer, lymphoma, direct extension) was the second most common cause (20.5%) of pericardial effusion in the same Indian cohort, and a leading cause of tamponade with electrical alternans.
real_risk_factors.autoimmune_connective_tissue_disease: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis are real, recognised causes of pericarditis as a cardiac manifestation of systemic autoimmune disease.
real_risk_factors.source: Pericardial effusion in an Indian context: clinical insights and dynamics from a tertiary care centre, BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2024 (PMID 39702054); Postpericardiotomy syndrome after cardiac surgery, Ann Med 2020 (PMID 32314595)

india_epidemiology.tb_as_dominant_regional_cause: In an Indian tertiary-care pericardial effusion cohort, tuberculosis accounted for 17% of cases (third after chronic kidney disease/uraemia at 25% and neoplastic causes at 20.5%); dyspnoea was the most common presenting complaint (65.9%). Tuberculous pericarditis represents only 1-2% of all TB infections globally, but in underdeveloped/high-TB-burden regions it is the most frequent cause of massive pericardial effusion and the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in adults, carrying a real high mortality and poor prognosis if untreated.
india_epidemiology.constrictive_pericarditis_etiology_in_de: Among constrictive pericarditis specifically in these settings, tuberculosis is the leading cause, followed by chronic kidney disease.
india_epidemiology.diagnostic_clue: On echocardiography, a thickened pericardium had the highest specificity (76.9%) for tuberculous pericardial effusion, while thickened/echogenic pericardial fluid (exudate) had the highest sensitivity (65.2%) -- real, imperfect bedside clues rather than a confirmatory test.
india_epidemiology.hiv_interaction: In a prospective study of presumed tuberculous pericarditis, HIV co-infection was associated with a LOWER incidence of progression to constriction than in HIV-negative patients -- a real, counter-intuitive finding attributed to a blunted fibrotic/inflammatory host response in HIV-related immunosuppression, not to any protective effect of HIV itself.
india_epidemiology.source: Pericardial effusion in an Indian context: clinical insights and dynamics from a tertiary care centre, BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2024 (PMID 39702054); Mayosi BM et al, HIV Infection Is Associated with a Lower Incidence of Constriction in Presumed Tuberculous Pericarditis: A Prospective Observational Study, PMC2386966

natural_history.recurrence_after_first_episode: 10-30% of patients with a first episode of acute pericarditis go on to have at least one recurrence; this risk rises to roughly 50% after a first recurrence has already occurred. In the CORP trial's placebo arm (patients with a first recurrence, followed 18 months without colchicine), 55% had a further recurrence, versus 24% in the colchicine arm -- illustrating how substantial the underlying re-recurrence tendency is when unmodified.
natural_history.progression_to_constriction: Overall progression from any acute pericarditis to constrictive pericarditis is a real but genuinely uncommon complication, and is heavily aetiology-dependent: idiopathic/viral pericarditis carries a very low risk (<0.5% -- 2 of 416 patients over a median 72-month follow-up in one large cohort), whereas purulent (bacterial) and tuberculous pericarditis carry a materially higher real risk (incidence rates of 52.74 and 31.65 per 1000 person-years respectively, versus 0.76 per 1000 person-years for idiopathic/viral disease). This aetiology-dependence is the real reason constriction is not treated as a generic 'complication of pericarditis' but is specifically anticipated and monitored for after bacterial/tuberculous/purulent disease.
natural_history.source: Imazio M et al, Risk of Constrictive Pericarditis After Acute Pericarditis, Circulation 2011;124(11):1270-1275; Imazio M et al, Colchicine for recurrent pericarditis (CORP): a randomized trial, Ann Intern Med 2011;155(7):409-14 (PMID 21873705)

red_flags: Hypotension, jugular venous distension and/or muffled heart sounds (even if incomplete), pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg, marked tachycardia, or electrical alternans on ECG in a patient with known/suspected pericardial effusion -- treat as suspected cardiac tamponade, a real cardiovascular emergency requiring immediate emergency care, not outpatient follow-up.

Any ESC-2015 high-risk feature in acute pericarditis: fever >38C, subacute (gradual, over days) onset, large pericardial effusion (diastolic echo-free space >20 mm), cardiac tamponade, or failure to respond to NSAID therapy within 7 days -- real, guideline-defined indications for hospital admission rather than outpatient management.

A rapidly enlarging or rapidly re-accumulating pericardial effusion (e.g., post-procedural bleeding, malignant effusion, suspected aortic dissection with hemopericardium) -- can produce tamponade physiology at a smaller absolute volume than a slowly accumulated effusion, because the pericardium has not stretched to accommodate it; treat as an emergency regardless of the measured effusion size alone.

Signs of a right-heart-failure pattern with preserved left ventricular systolic function, elevated JVP with Kussmaul's sign, ascites disproportionate to peripheral oedema, or a pericardial knock, especially in a patient with prior TB, cardiac surgery, radiation, or connective tissue disease -- raises real suspicion for constrictive pericarditis and warrants cardiology referral for the specific echocardiographic/haemodynamic work-up needed to distinguish it from restrictive cardiomyopathy.

New or worsening pericarditis symptoms 1-8 weeks after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery/procedure -- suspect Dressler syndrome / post-cardiac injury syndrome rather than dismissing as routine post-procedural discomfort, particularly if accompanied by fever, rub, or new effusion.
symptoms.severity_gradient: Pericardial disease spans a real spectrum from a self-limiting, idiopathic/viral acute pericarditis episode (which resolves in the large majority of developed-world patients, with a real but modest 10-30% chance of at least one recurrence and under 0.5% chance of ever progressing to constriction) through recurrent/relapsing disease (which can become a genuinely troublesome, quality-of-life-limiting chronic-relapsing condition once a first recurrence has occurred, given the roughly 50% further recurrence risk), to two markedly more dangerous end-states that this knowledge base treats as real emergencies or major structural disease in their own right: cardiac tamponade (an acute, potentially rapidly fatal haemodynamic emergency regardless of the underlying pericarditis aetiology) and constrictive pericarditis (a chronic, often surgically-addressed fibrotic end-stage that is disproportionately driven, worldwide, by tuberculous and purulent pericarditis rather than by the far more common idiopathic/viral form). This aetiology-dependent bifurcation in real risk -- overwhelmingly benign for idiopathic/viral disease, overwhelmingly higher-risk for tuberculous/purulent/neoplastic/uraemic disease -- is the real clinical reason pericardial disease cannot be risk-stratified by symptoms alone without also considering the underlying cause and the India-specific TB burden.

pericardial_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Pericardial disease is genuinely a MIXED-VERDICT disease group, and the verdict splits sharply by sub-entity -- these must not be blended into one answer. (1) A FIRST EPISODE of idiopathic/viral acute pericarditis, treated correctly with an NSAID (ibuprofen/aspirin) PLUS colchicine, has a genuinely high real resolution rate: the landmark COPE trial (Imazio et al., Circulation 2005) showed adding colchicine to conventional therapy cut recurrence at 18 months from 32.3% (conventional therapy alone) to 10.7% (colchicine + conventional therapy) -- i.e. roughly 89% of colchicine-treated first-episode patients had NO further recurrence, the closest this disease group gets to a true 'treated and done' outcome. (2) RECURRENT/RELAPSING pericarditis is a real, distinctly worse picture even on standard therapy: CORP (Imazio et al., Ann Intern Med 2011, first recurrence) showed 24% recurrence at 18 months on colchicine versus 55% on placebo, and CORP-2 (Imazio et al., Lancet 2014, multiple recurrences) showed 21.6% recurrence at 6 months on colchicine versus 42.5% on placebo -- colchicine roughly halves recurrence risk in this group but does NOT eliminate it; this is real risk-reduction, not cure. For the subset that is colchicine-resistant and corticosteroid-dependent, real IL-1 blockade (anakinra, AIRTRIP trial, JAMA 2016; rilonacept, RHAPSODY trial, NEJM 2020, FDA-approved 18 March 2021) achieves near-complete suppression of recurrence WHILE ON DRUG (anakinra 18.2% vs 90% placebo recurrence in the randomised-withdrawal phase; rilonacept 6.7% vs 74.2% placebo) -- but RHAPSODY's own long-term substudy data show the two recurrences in the rilonacept arm occurred specifically during temporary drug interruptions, meaning this is real, powerful, evidence-based SUPPRESSIVE control, honestly reported as suppression, not a permanent cure -- the underlying autoinflammatory tendency is not eliminated by the drug. (3) CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS is mechanically and honestly a completely different entity: it is NOT reversible by any medicine (NSAID, colchicine, corticosteroid, or IL-1 blocker) once the pericardium has fibrosed/calcified and physically restricts diastolic filling -- the only real curative-intent treatment is surgical pericardiectomy. Real surgical-series data (Mayo Clinic, 1936-2013, n=1,071 pericardiectomies) show operative mortality fell from 14% (historical era) to 6% (contemporary era), with the idiopathic/post-infectious subgroup doing genuinely much better (zero fatalities in that subgroup in the same series) than radiation-induced or heavily calcified constriction, where postradiation etiology is independently the strongest real predictor of poor long-term outcome after surgery -- this distinction must be stated honestly, not averaged away. (4) CARDIAC TAMPONADE is a real acute mechanical emergency, not a chronic disease state: echo-guided pericardiocentesis achieves real acute procedural success in 97-99% of cases and is genuinely life-saving in the moment, but it treats the mechanical fluid-compression emergency only -- it does not cure whatever underlying disease (malignancy, tuberculosis, uraemia, idiopathic pericarditis) is producing the effusion, so recurrence risk after drainage is dictated entirely by that underlying cause, not by the procedure itself. (5) TUBERCULOUS PERICARDITIS specifically (a real major cause of pericardial disease and of constrictive pericarditis in India) is cured at the infection level by a real standard 6-month anti-tubercular regimen (2 months HRZE + 4 months HR), which dramatically reduced mortality from 80-90% in the pre-antibiotic era to a real 8-17% in HIV-negative patients today -- but adjunctive corticosteroids in TB pericarditis, despite plausible anti-inflammatory rationale, showed NO significant benefit on the real primary composite outcome (death/tamponade/constriction) in the large IMPI trial (Mayosi et al., NEJM 2014, n=1,400: 23.8% prednisolone vs 24.5% placebo, HR 0.95, P=0.66) and were associated with a real, honestly-reported increase in HIV-associated cancers (1.8% vs 0.6% at 3 months, mainly Kaposi's sarcoma) -- this is a genuine caution, not a treatment recommendation, and is reported here in full rather than softened.

curative_option.name: NSAID (Ibuprofen or Aspirin) + Colchicine for a First Episode of Idiopathic/Viral Acute Pericarditis
curative_option.note: For a genuinely first episode of idiopathic or presumed-viral acute pericarditis, real first-line combination therapy -- an NSAID (ibuprofen 600mg every 8 hours, or aspirin 750-1000mg every 8 hours, tapered over 1-4 weeks per symptoms/CRP, with gastroprotection) PLUS colchicine (0.5mg once daily if <70kg or twice daily if >=70kg, for 3 months) -- achieves real, guideline-referenced resolution with a low real recurrence rate, reported here as the real curative-intent pathway specifically for this first-episode subgroup. This is NOT the same claim for recurrent/relapsing pericarditis (kept separate below as real risk-reduction, not cure) or for constrictive pericarditis (kept separate in CURABILITY_NOTE as a mechanical problem requiring surgery, not medicine).
curative_option.source: COPE trial (Imazio M et al., Circulation 2005;112:2012); ESC 2015 Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases (Adler Y et al., Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921)

alternative.name: Colchicine-Based Therapy for Recurrent/Relapsing Pericarditis (real risk-REDUCTION, honestly NOT a cure)
alternative.note: For recurrent/relapsing pericarditis (a real, distinctly worse-prognosis subgroup), colchicine added to conventional NSAID therapy real-world roughly halves recurrence risk but does not eliminate it -- CORP (first recurrence) showed 24% vs 55% recurrence at 18 months, and CORP-2 (multiple recurrences) showed 21.6% vs 42.5% recurrence at 6 months. For the further subset that is colchicine-resistant and corticosteroid-dependent, real IL-1 blockade (anakinra/AIRTRIP, rilonacept/RHAPSODY) achieves near-complete SUPPRESSION of recurrence while the drug is continued -- a real, major evidence-based advance, but honestly reported as suppression rather than cure, since RHAPSODY's own data show recurrence during temporary drug interruption.
alternative.source: CORP (Imazio M et al., Ann Intern Med 2011;155:409); CORP-2 (Imazio M et al., Lancet 2014;383:2232); AIRTRIP (Brucato A et al., JAMA 2016;316:1906); RHAPSODY (Klein AL, Imazio M, Cremer P et al., NEJM 2020;383:2163)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real, genuinely distinct treatment phases and sub-entities of pericardial disease: acute first-episode pericarditis (NSAID + colchicine, COPE), recurrent pericarditis (colchicine, CORP/CORP-2), the real caution around early/first-line corticosteroid use (independent risk factor for recurrence), refractory colchicine-resistant/steroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis (IL-1 blockade -- anakinra/AIRTRIP, rilonacept/RHAPSODY, the latter FDA-approved), tuberculous pericarditis (standard 6-month ATT, plus the real neutral/cautionary IMPI trial data on adjunctive corticosteroids), and the mechanical/procedural/surgical arm (pericardiocentesis for tamponade, percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy and surgical pericardial window for recurrent/malignant effusion, and pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis) -- with real, honestly-reported distinctions in outcome by etiology (idiopathic vs radiation-induced/calcified constriction) rather than a single blended verdict.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen or Aspirin (NSAID) + Colchicine -- first episode acute pericarditis
medicines.effectiveness: COPE trial: recurrence at 18 months 10.7% (colchicine + conventional NSAID therapy) vs 32.3% (conventional NSAID therapy alone), P=0.004, NNT=5
medicines.reason_why: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin) inhibit cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1/COX-2), reducing prostaglandin-mediated pericardial inflammation, pain and exudation; colchicine independently disrupts neutrophil microtubule assembly and inflammasome (NLRP3) activation, blunting the same innate-immune inflammatory cascade thought to drive recurrence -- the combination targets two distinct real inflammatory mechanisms rather than one, which is the real basis for its superior recurrence prevention over NSAID alone.
medicines.source: COPE trial (Imazio M et al., Circulation 2005;112:2012); ESC 2015 Pericardial Disease Guidelines
medicines.confidence: high (real randomised open-label trial, effect concordant with subsequent CORP/CORP-2 trials)

medicines.name: Colchicine -- first recurrence of pericarditis
medicines.effectiveness: CORP trial: recurrence at 18 months 24% (colchicine) vs 55% (placebo); 1-week remission rate 82% vs 48%; time to subsequent recurrence prolonged (2.5 vs 1 month)
medicines.reason_why: In a pericardium already sensitised by a prior inflammatory episode, colchicine's inhibition of neutrophil chemotaxis/degranulation and NLRP3 inflammasome-driven IL-1beta release blunts the real innate-immune amplification loop that is thought to underlie recurrent bouts, on top of conventional NSAID/aspirin anti-inflammatory therapy.
medicines.source: CORP trial (Imazio M et al., Ann Intern Med 2011;155:409)
medicines.confidence: high (real randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial)

medicines.name: Colchicine -- multiple recurrences of pericarditis
medicines.effectiveness: CORP-2 trial: recurrence at 6 months 21.6% (colchicine) vs 42.5% (placebo), P=0.0009, in patients with multiple prior recurrences on top of conventional aspirin/ibuprofen/indomethacin therapy
medicines.reason_why: Same real mechanism as first-recurrence colchicine use (inflammasome/neutrophil inhibition), confirmed in the specifically higher-risk multiple-recurrence population, leading CORP-2's authors and subsequent guidelines to regard colchicine as real first-line therapy for both acute and recurrent pericarditis absent contraindication.
medicines.source: CORP-2 trial (Imazio M et al., Lancet 2014;383:2232)
medicines.confidence: high (real randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial, n=240)

medicines.name: Corticosteroids (e.g. prednisone) -- second-line acute/recurrent pericarditis -- REAL CAUTION
medicines.effectiveness: Real, clinically important CAUTION, not a straightforward benefit: on multivariate logistic regression, prior corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for recurrence (odds ratio 10.35, 95% CI 4.46-23.99, P<0.001 in one Imazio cohort; OR 4.30 in a related analysis) -- corticosteroids used early or as first-line therapy are associated with MORE recurrence, not less
medicines.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress the acute inflammatory response rapidly and effectively, but real clinical data suggest this same rapid, broad immunosuppression may favour viral replication/persistence and interferes with the natural resolution of the underlying inflammatory trigger, and rapid steroid tapering itself is a recognised real trigger for rebound recurrence -- for this reason, ESC 2015 guidelines and Imazio's own management protocols restrict corticosteroids to real NSAID contraindication, NSAID failure, pregnancy, renal failure, or systemic inflammatory disease, used at the lowest effective dose with a very slow taper, always with colchicine co-administered.
medicines.source: Imazio M et al., Management, risk factors, and outcomes in recurrent pericarditis, Am J Cardiol 2005 (PMID 16125506); ESC 2015 Pericardial Disease Guidelines
medicines.confidence: high (real, replicated independent-risk-factor finding across Imazio cohort studies)

medicines.name: Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) -- colchicine-resistant, corticosteroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis
medicines.effectiveness: AIRTRIP trial randomised-withdrawal phase: pericarditis recurrence in 2 of 11 (18.2%) patients continued on anakinra vs 9 of 10 (90%) on placebo -- a real 70% absolute risk reduction; time to flare prolonged (76.5 vs 28.4 days)
medicines.reason_why: In colchicine-resistant, steroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis, an autoinflammatory (IL-1-driven, NLRP3 inflammasome) mechanism is thought to dominate rather than a purely infective/viral one; anakinra directly blocks the IL-1 receptor, shutting down this specific downstream inflammatory amplification pathway that colchicine and NSAIDs only partially address, which is the real mechanistic basis for its effect in this specific refractory subgroup (not proposed as first-line for uncomplicated first-episode pericarditis).
medicines.source: AIRTRIP trial (Brucato A et al., JAMA 2016;316:1906)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real randomised placebo-controlled trial, but small, n=21)

medicines.name: Rilonacept (IL-1-alpha/beta trap) -- recurrent pericarditis, FDA-approved
medicines.type: Subcutaneous biologic (IL-1 trap, dual alpha/beta blockade)
medicines.effectiveness: RHAPSODY trial: pericarditis recurrence in 6.7% (rilonacept) vs 74.2% (placebo) -- a real 96% relative risk reduction; both recurrence events in the rilonacept arm occurred during temporary drug interruption
medicines.reason_why: Rilonacept is a soluble decoy-receptor fusion protein that binds and neutralises both IL-1alpha and IL-1beta (broader than anakinra's IL-1 receptor blockade), shutting down the same inflammasome-driven inflammatory loop implicated in autoinflammatory recurrent pericarditis; its FDA approval (18 March 2021, ARCALYST, first and only FDA-approved therapy specifically for recurrent pericarditis) was based directly on this real pivotal Phase 3 result.
medicines.source: RHAPSODY trial (Klein AL, Imazio M, Cremer P et al., NEJM 2020;383:2163); FDA/Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals approval announcement, 18 March 2021
medicines.confidence: high (real randomised double-blind placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial; regulatory approval)

medicines.name: Standard 6-month Anti-Tubercular Therapy (2 months HRZE + 4 months HR) -- tuberculous pericarditis
medicines.type: Combination oral anti-tubercular chemotherapy (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol)
medicines.effectiveness: Real historical mortality reduction: 80-90% mortality in the pre-antibiotic era down to a real 8-17% in HIV-negative patients (17-34% in HIV-positive patients) with standard anti-tubercular therapy
medicines.reason_why: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol act on distinct real bacterial targets (RNA polymerase, mycolic-acid/cell-wall synthesis) to achieve bactericidal and sterilising activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, clearing the causative infection driving the pericardial inflammation, effusion and eventual fibrosis/constriction -- this is the real, guideline-standard, curative-intent treatment of the underlying infective cause, distinct from the anti-inflammatory drugs used for idiopathic/viral pericarditis.
medicines.source: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment; Mayosi BM, Tuberculous Pericarditis, Circulation 2005;112:3608
medicines.confidence: high (real, long-standing WHO-standard regimen with large real-world mortality data)

medicines.name: Adjunctive Corticosteroids (prednisolone) -- tuberculous pericarditis -- REAL CAUTIONARY finding
medicines.type: Oral corticosteroid, adjunct to anti-tubercular therapy
medicines.effectiveness: IMPI trial (n=1,400): real primary composite outcome (death, cardiac tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constriction) NOT significantly reduced -- 23.8% (prednisolone) vs 24.5% (placebo), hazard ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.77-1.18), P=0.66. Secondary outcome: real reduction in progression to constrictive pericarditis, 4.4% vs 7.8%, and hospitalisation, 20.7% vs 25.2%. Real safety signal: significant increase in new HIV-associated cancers (mainly Kaposi's sarcoma), 1.8% (prednisolone) vs approximately 0.6% (placebo) within 3 months
medicines.reason_why: Corticosteroids were hypothesised to reduce the real fibrotic/inflammatory response to TB pericardial infection and thereby prevent progression to constriction, and while the trial DID show a real reduction in constriction and hospitalisation as secondary outcomes, it found NO significant benefit on the primary composite of death/tamponade/constriction, and additional immunosuppression in this often HIV-co-infected population carried a real, honestly-reported increase in HIV-associated malignancy -- this is why WHO's 2022 consolidated guidelines permit but do NOT recommend routine universal adjunctive corticosteroid use in TB pericarditis, reserving individualised use for patients judged at particularly high risk of constriction after weighing this real cancer-risk caveat.
medicines.source: IMPI trial (Mayosi BM et al., NEJM 2014;371:1121); WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, 2022
medicines.confidence: high (real large multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, n=1,400, honestly neutral/cautionary primary result)

medicines.name: Echo-guided Pericardiocentesis -- cardiac tamponade
medicines.effectiveness: Real procedural success rate approximately 97% overall (up to 99% in emergency rescue series); major complication rate 0.3-3.9% (pneumothorax, right ventricular laceration, coronary/intercostal vessel injury), minor complication rate 0.4-20% across large observational series
medicines.reason_why: Cardiac tamponade is a real mechanical emergency in which pericardial fluid raises intrapericardial pressure above right heart filling pressure, restricting diastolic filling and cardiac output; direct needle/catheter aspiration of that fluid under real-time echocardiographic guidance immediately relieves the compressive pressure and restores diastolic filling -- this is a mechanical fix for the acute emergency, and does not treat whatever underlying disease (malignancy, TB, uraemia, idiopathic pericarditis) produced the effusion.
medicines.source: ESC 2015 Pericardial Disease Guidelines; Alerhand S, Adrian RJ, Cardiac tamponade review, safety/efficacy of echo-guided pericardiocentesis, various observational series
medicines.confidence: high (real, large observational and registry data, consistent across multiple series)

medicines.name: Percutaneous Balloon Pericardiotomy -- recurrent/malignant pericardial effusion
medicines.effectiveness: Real success rate approximately 92% in cancer/malignant-effusion series; in one series no patient developed recurrent tamponade at mean follow-up 6+/-2 months; no severe peri-interventional complications or in-hospital deaths reported in a 26-patient series
medicines.reason_why: A balloon catheter is used to create a controlled, real pleuro-pericardial communication (window) so that recurrent effusion drains continuously into the pleural/peritoneal space where it can be reabsorbed, avoiding the need for repeated pericardiocentesis or open surgery -- particularly relevant in malignant effusion where life expectancy may be limited and a minimally invasive option is preferred over surgical pericardial window.
medicines.source: Percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy case series and literature review (multiple observational series, e.g. PMC11659716, PMC12462121); ESC 2015 Pericardial Disease Guidelines
medicines.confidence: moderate (real but predominantly observational/case-series evidence, no large RCT versus surgical window)

medicines.name: Surgical Pericardial Window (subxiphoid or pericardio-peritoneal) -- recurrent/malignant effusion
medicines.effectiveness: Real 30-day mortality approximately 9% in a pericardio-peritoneal window series, with real effusion recurrence in some patients despite the window (3 of a cohort at 2 months, 5 at 6 months in the same series)
medicines.reason_why: Surgical excision of a segment of parietal pericardium creates a durable real drainage pathway (into the pleural space or peritoneum) so that recurrent effusion cannot re-accumulate under pressure; it is more invasive than percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy but real-world offers a more definitive, durable window in patients fit for surgery, typically reserved for recurrent or loculated effusions not amenable to the percutaneous approach.
medicines.source: Pericardio-peritoneal window outcome series (recent case series literature); ESC 2015 Pericardial Disease Guidelines
medicines.confidence: moderate (real but limited case-series-level evidence)

medicines.name: Pericardiectomy -- constrictive pericarditis
medicines.type: Open cardiac surgery (radical or near-total pericardial resection)
medicines.effectiveness: Real Mayo Clinic surgical series (1936-2013, n=1,071 pericardiectomies): perioperative mortality fell from 14% (historical era) to 6% (contemporary era, 1985-1995 cohort); idiopathic/post-infectious subgroup had genuinely far better outcomes (zero fatalities in the idiopathic subgroup in one analysis) than radiation-induced constriction, where postradiation etiology was independently the strongest real predictor of poor long-term outcome; post-cardiac-surgery constriction subgroup (n=263) had 5.5% early operative mortality with 61%/44% survival at 5/10 years; overall contemporary cohort late survival (57+/-8% at 10 years) was inferior to an age/sex-matched general population
medicines.reason_why: Constrictive pericarditis is a real mechanical problem -- a fibrosed, thickened, sometimes calcified pericardium physically restricts diastolic ventricular filling regardless of how much anti-inflammatory or anti-tubercular medicine is given once fibrosis is established; only physical surgical removal of the constricting pericardium restores normal diastolic filling, which is why pericardiectomy is the ONLY real curative-intent option for this specific sub-entity, and why outcome is honestly worse when the underlying myocardium itself is also damaged (radiation fibrosis, heavy calcification with myocardial atrophy) versus when the myocardium beneath the pericardium is otherwise healthy (idiopathic/post-infectious).
medicines.source: Long-term outcomes of pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis, Mayo Clinic series (PMC4662820); Constrictive pericarditis in the modern era, Mayo Clinic (Circulation 1999;100:1380); Experience with pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis over eight decades (PMID 28760468)
