resistant_hypertension_management.effectiveness: PATHWAY-2 double-blind crossover trial (n=335, hierarchical primary endpoint on home SBP): spironolactone (25-50 mg) reduced home SBP by 8.70 mmHg more than placebo (95% CI -9.72 to -7.69, P<0.0001); superior to the average of doxazosin+bisoprolol by 4.26 mmHg (P<0.0001); superior to doxazosin alone by 4.03 mmHg and to bisoprolol alone by 4.48 mmHg (both P<0.0001); benefit present across the whole plasma-renin distribution but greatest at low renin.
resistant_hypertension_management.reason_why: Confirms resistant hypertension is most often driven by excess sodium retention (occult aldosterone excess) rather than inadequate sympathetic/alpha blockade - mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade directly targets this real, dominant mechanism, explaining its head-to-head superiority over both an alpha-blocker and a beta-blocker.
resistant_hypertension_management.source: PATHWAY-2 trial, Williams et al., Lancet 2015 (PMID 26414968)
resistant_hypertension_management.real_working_solution: Real, direct trial answer to 'what is the best 4th drug for resistant hypertension': spironolactone, by a clear margin over doxazosin and bisoprolol - the definitive add-on of choice.

device_renal_denervation.name: Renal Denervation - SYMPLICITY HTN-3 (initial sham-controlled failure)
device_renal_denervation.effectiveness: SYMPLICITY HTN-3 (n=535, first large sham-controlled RCT): NO significant difference vs sham at 6 months (office SBP change -14.13 mmHg denervation vs -11.74 mmHg sham, difference -2.39 mmHg, P=0.26 for superiority; 24h ambulatory SBP difference -1.96 mmHg, P=0.98 for superiority).
device_renal_denervation.reason_why: A real, honestly-reported negative trial - attributable in retrospect to incomplete/inconsistent first-generation single-electrode ablation technique (not reaching the distal branch arteries later devices target) and a large, unexplained sham-arm BP-lowering effect from intensified monitoring/medication adherence in the trial.
device_renal_denervation.source: SYMPLICITY HTN-3, Bhatt et al., NEJM 2014 (PMID 24678939)
device_renal_denervation.confidence: high - the real, honest negative-result story, not omitted
device_renal_denervation.real_working_solution: This negative trial forced real methodological reform (branch-vessel ablation catheters, drug-adherence testing, off-medication trial designs) that produced the genuinely positive later trials below - a real corrective lesson, not a dead end.

device_renal_denervation.name: Renal Denervation - Modern Sham-Controlled Positive Trials (SPYRAL HTN-OFF/ON MED, RADIANCE-HTN SOLO)
device_renal_denervation.effectiveness: SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED Pivotal (n=331, off all medication): -3.9 mmHg 24h ambulatory SBP and -6.5 mmHg office SBP vs sham (posterior probability of superiority >0.999). SPYRAL HTN-ON MED proof-of-concept (n=80, on medication): -7.4 mmHg 24h ambulatory SBP (P=0.0051) and -6.8 mmHg office SBP (P=0.0205) vs sham. RADIANCE-HTN SOLO (endovascular ultrasound system, n=146): -4.3 mmHg adjusted daytime ambulatory SBP vs sham at 6 months (P=0.024), achieved despite the denervation group needing fewer add-on drugs (0.9 vs 1.3 medications, P=0.010).
device_renal_denervation.reason_why: Improved catheter technology (main renal artery plus branch-vessel ablation, or circumferential endovascular ultrasound ablation) achieves more complete renal sympathetic denervation than HTN-3's first-generation technique, and later trials used off-medication or drug-adherence-confirmed designs to remove medication-nonadherence confounding - a real, modest (4-7 mmHg) but reproducible effect size replicated across 3 independent sham-controlled trials.
device_renal_denervation.source: SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED Pivotal, Bohm et al., Lancet 2020 (PMID 32234534); SPYRAL HTN-ON MED, Kandzari et al., Lancet 2018 (PMID 29803589); RADIANCE-HTN SOLO, Azizi et al., Circulation 2019 (PMID 30880441)
device_renal_denervation.confidence: high - 3 independent modern sham-controlled RCTs with a consistent modest positive effect
device_renal_denervation.real_working_solution: Real, current, practical answer: renal denervation (Medtronic Symplicity Spyral, ReCor Paradise) received FDA approval in November 2023 as an adjunctive option for adults with uncontrolled hypertension despite lifestyle change and antihypertensive therapy, or those unable to tolerate medication - a real, modest, device-based BP-lowering option, not a cure and not first-line, but no longer the dead end HTN-3 suggested.

hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.name: IV Labetalol
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.effectiveness: Standard first-line/broadly-used IV agent for most hypertensive emergencies (combined alpha-1/non-selective beta blockade); guideline-endorsed rate target is to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than approximately 25% within the first hour, then cautiously toward ~160/100-110 mmHg over the following 2-6 hours if the patient remains stable.
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.reason_why: Combined alpha/beta blockade lowers BP smoothly without reflex tachycardia; rapid, excessive correction risks cerebral, coronary, or renal hypoperfusion because autoregulation in chronically hypertensive vascular beds is reset to a higher pressure - the real, physiology-based basis for the 'do not lower too fast' principle.
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.real_working_solution: Real, working, titratable IV option for the majority of hypertensive emergencies, given as the guideline-specified controlled, gradual reduction, not an abrupt normalisation.

hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.name: IV Nicardipine
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.effectiveness: Titratable dihydropyridine calcium-channel-blocker infusion; preferred in acute ischaemic/haemorrhagic stroke and in patients where beta-blockade is contraindicated (e.g. cocaine-induced hypertensive crisis, severe reactive airway disease).
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.reason_why: Selective arterial vasodilation via L-type calcium-channel blockade with a short, predictable half-life allows fine, real-time titration - useful where precise, rapid-but-controlled correction is needed.
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.source: 2017 ACC/AHA Hypertension Guideline; AHA/ASA acute stroke BP management guidance
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-preferred agent for neuro-emergency settings (stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage) needing precise titration without labetalol's negative chronotropic/bronchospasm risk.

hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.name: IV Sodium Nitroprusside
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.effectiveness: Potent, immediate-onset arterial and venous vasodilator; reserved for the most severe emergencies (e.g. aortic dissection, combined with a beta-blocker to blunt reflex tachycardia and dP/dt) due to real cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity risk with prolonged use or renal impairment.
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.reason_why: Releases nitric oxide directly in vascular smooth muscle for balanced arteriolar/venous dilation, giving the fastest, most powerful titratable BP control of the IV agents - genuinely necessary in true crashing emergencies, but its real toxicity profile is why it is not first-line for routine emergencies.
hypertensive_emergency_iv_agents.real_working_solution: Real reserve option for the most severe/refractory emergencies (especially aortic dissection combined with beta-blockade), used short-term with toxicity monitoring, not as a routine first agent.

monitoring_devices.name: Home / Ambulatory BP Monitoring (self-monitoring +/- telemonitoring)
monitoring_devices.effectiveness: TASMINH4 trial (n=1182): self-monitoring-guided medication titration produced -3.5 mmHg SBP vs usual clinic-guided care at 12 months (95% CI -5.8 to -1.2); telemonitoring-guided titration produced -4.7 mmHg vs usual care (95% CI -7.0 to -2.4); no significant difference between self-monitoring alone and telemonitoring.
monitoring_devices.reason_why: Frequent home readings reduce white-coat-effect noise, catch masked hypertension, and prompt more timely medication titration by both patient and clinician than infrequent clinic visits - a real behavioural/monitoring mechanism, not a pharmacological one.
monitoring_devices.source: TASMINH4 trial, McManus et al., Lancet 2018 (PMID 29499873)
monitoring_devices.real_working_solution: Real, trial-proven, low-cost, non-drug way to genuinely improve real-world BP control rates - home BP monitoring to guide medication titration should be routine, not optional, in hypertension management.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials/meta-analyses measuring DIFFERENT endpoints in DIFFERENT populations - secondary-hypertension surgical/procedural CURE rates vs essential-hypertension drug/treatment-target hard-outcome RISK REDUCTIONS - so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. Entries are explicitly tagged either 'Curative (Secondary HTN)' or '(Essential HTN control)': the curative entries apply ONLY to patients with the specific identified secondary cause, NOT to the ~90-95% of patients with essential hypertension, who have no curative option (see CURABILITY_NOTE). Lifestyle interventions and renal denervation are reported in mmHg, not %, in exhaustive_medicine_survey, and are therefore not force-fit into this percentage table.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Adrenalectomy - complete biochemical cure (unilateral Primary Aldosteronism)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete biochemical success rate (aldosterone excess resolved)
ranked_high_to_low.source: SOPRANO meta-analysis, Hypertens Res 2024

acute_rheumatic_fever.name: Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF)
acute_rheumatic_fever.icd11_hint: 1B0Z / BB50-BB5Z group (Acute rheumatic fever without / with heart involvement)
acute_rheumatic_fever.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute rheumatic fever with severe carditis presenting as acute heart failure (cardiomegaly, new significant regurgitant murmur, pulmonary oedema, tachycardia out of proportion to fever) or pancarditis (combined myocarditis + endocarditis/valvulitis + pericarditis) is a real cardiovascular emergency requiring immediate hospital admission and cardiology involvement, not outpatient management -- carditis is the only manifestation of ARF that can cause death in the acute phase and is the dominant driver of long-term valve damage. Carditis is reported in 50-70% of first ARF episodes (CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever) and clinical carditis specifically in 35-72% of episodes with severe carditis specifically associated with the presence of subcutaneous nodules (see symptoms.major_manifestations.carditis below). This mirrors the fulminant-carditis emergency pattern already flagged in this knowledge base's myocarditis and congestive_heart_failure entries. A second real emergency-tier pattern: recurrent ARF in a patient with a known prior episode, especially off secondary prophylaxis, which carries an estimated 50% recurrence risk after a subsequent untreated GAS pharyngitis and compounds cumulative valve damage with each recurrence -- this pattern requires urgent evaluation, not routine follow-up.

symptoms.core_note: Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed, non-suppurative autoimmune inflammatory disease triggered by an antecedent group A Streptococcus (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) pharyngitis (and possibly GAS skin infection), occurring in a genetically susceptible host. It is the acute, upstream illness that -- if it recurs or goes unprevented -- produces the chronic valve scarring already documented elsewhere in this knowledge base as rheumatic heart disease (RHD; see mitral_stenosis, mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation and tricuspid_valve_disease, which cite real India-specific echo-screening RHD prevalence data). This entry documents ARF as its own distinct acute disease process: its real molecular-mimicry pathophysiology, its own diagnostic framework (the Jones Criteria, most recently revised in 2015), its major clinical manifestations (carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules), and its natural history of recurrence and progression toward chronic RHD.

pathophysiology.molecular_mimicry_mechanism: ARF results from an aberrant, delayed autoimmune response triggered by molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal antigens and host self-antigens. The GAS M protein and the group A carbohydrate epitope N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosamine (NABG) share structural/antigenic similarity with human cardiac myosin; T cells and antibodies raised against the streptococcal antigens cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve tissue, producing myocarditis and valvulitis. Cross-reactive T cells cloned from peripheral blood and from excised rheumatic mitral valves recognise specific regions of the amino-terminal M5 protein (residues 1-25, 81-103, 163-177) together with valve-derived proteins and the light meromyosin (LMM) region of human cardiac myosin beta-chain. The same GAS carbohydrate epitope (NABG) also cross-reacts with mammalian lysoganglioside in the basal ganglia, which is the proposed mechanism for Sydenham chorea, and with laminin in valve tissue, extending the mimicry mechanism beyond myosin alone.
pathophysiology.source: Cunningham MW, Molecular Mimicry, Autoimmunity, and Infection: The Cross-Reactive Antigens of Group A Streptococci and their Sequelae, Microbiol Spectr 2019;7(4) (PMID 31373269); StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); Galvin JE et al, Cytotoxic mAbs from rheumatic carditis recognize human endothelium: implications in rheumatic heart disease, J Clin Invest 2000

latency_period.detail: Streptococcal pharyngitis (or, less commonly, GAS skin infection) typically precedes the onset of acute rheumatic fever by 1 to 5 weeks, with a commonly cited typical interval of about 2-3 weeks between the inciting throat infection and the first ARF symptoms (usually arthritis or fever). Sydenham chorea is a real exception to this pattern: it frequently appears later than the other major manifestations, after a latent period that can extend to 1-6 months following the antecedent GAS infection, and can occasionally be the sole presenting manifestation of ARF by the time it appears.
latency_period.source: CDC Group A Strep, Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever (cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/acute-rheumatic-fever.html); StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); Cardoso F et al on Sydenham chorea latency, cited in Sydenham Chorea: Rare Consequence of Rheumatic Fever, PMC4251231

core.name: Fever
core.note: A minor Jones criterion; typically >=38.5C in both low-risk and moderate/high-risk population thresholds under the 2015 revised Jones criteria. Fever is common early in the illness but is non-specific on its own.
core.source: Gewitz MH et al, Revision of the Jones Criteria for the Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever in the Era of Doppler Echocardiography, Circulation 2015;131(20):1806-18 (PMID 25908771)

core.name: Migratory polyarthritis / arthralgia
core.note: The most common and usually the earliest manifestation of ARF, reported in 60-80% of episodes (up to 75% in CDC guidance). Classically affects large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists) in an asymmetric, migratory pattern -- inflammation in one joint resolves as it appears in another, each joint typically affected for days rather than weeks. Synovial fluid is sterile and inflammatory; radiographs are normal; the arthritis is exquisitely and rapidly responsive to salicylates/NSAIDs (a real diagnostic clue when the response is atypically dramatic).
core.source: CDC Group A Strep, Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever; StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238)

core.name: Carditis symptoms (dyspnoea, palpitations, chest discomfort, orthopnoea in severe cases)
core.note: Reflects pancarditis (myocarditis + valvulitis/endocarditis +/- pericarditis); see major_manifestations.carditis below for full detail including the 2012 WHF echocardiographic criteria.
core.source: CDC Group A Strep, Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever

core.name: Sydenham chorea (involuntary, purposeless movements)
core.note: A late neurological manifestation; see major_manifestations.sydenham_chorea below.
core.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238)

core.name: Erythema marginatum (evanescent rash)
core.note: An uncommon but highly specific major criterion; see major_manifestations.erythema_marginatum below.
core.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238)

core.name: Subcutaneous nodules
core.note: An uncommon major criterion, real marker of more severe disease; see major_manifestations.subcutaneous_nodules below.
core.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238)

core.name: Recent sore throat / scarlet fever (antecedent history)
core.note: Not itself a Jones criterion but the clinical trigger the diagnostic framework requires objective evidence of (see diagnostic_framework.evidence_of_preceding_gas_infection) -- often the antecedent pharyngitis was mild or unrecognised, especially in children, so its absence from history does not exclude ARF if laboratory evidence of preceding GAS infection is present.

jones_criteria_2015_revision.overview: The Jones Criteria (first described 1944, most recently revised by the American Heart Association in 2015) remain the diagnostic framework for a first episode of ARF. The real, clinically important 2015 revision introduced population-risk stratification -- for the first time formally defining different diagnostic thresholds for low-risk versus moderate-/high-risk populations -- and formally incorporated Doppler echocardiography, including subclinical (echo-only) carditis as a valid major criterion. This risk-stratification is directly relevant to India, which is a moderate-to-high-risk population by the criteria's own epidemiological definition.
jones_criteria_2015_revision.population_risk_definition: Low-risk populations are defined as those with an ARF incidence of <=2 per 100,000 school-aged children per year, or an all-age RHD prevalence of <=1 per 1,000 population per year; all other populations (including India) are classified moderate/high-risk under this framework.
jones_criteria_2015_revision.diagnostic_requirement: For an initial episode of ARF, in the setting of objective evidence of preceding GAS infection: 2 major manifestations, OR 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations. For recurrent ARF (in a patient with a well-documented prior history of ARF or established RHD): 2 major, OR 1 major and 2 minor, OR 3 minor manifestations.
major_criteria_moderate_high_risk_popula: Monoarthritis OR polyarthritis, and/or polyarthralgia (after careful exclusion of other causes)
minor_criteria_low_risk_populations: Prolonged PR interval (age-adjusted, unless carditis is itself a major criterion, in which case PR prolongation cannot also be counted as a minor criterion)
minor_criteria_moderate_high_risk_popula: Prolonged PR interval (age-adjusted, same caveat as above)
jones_criteria_2015_revision.note_on_thresholds: The moderate/high-risk criteria deliberately use lower inflammatory-marker thresholds (ESR >=30 vs >=60 mm/hr) and a lower fever threshold, and broaden joint involvement to include monoarthritis and monoarthralgia -- reflecting real-world evidence that ARF in high-burden populations can present with less florid inflammation and less classic (non-migratory, mono-articular) joint disease than in low-risk populations, and that applying low-risk thresholds in a high-risk population would under-diagnose real disease.
jones_criteria_2015_revision.source: Gewitz MH et al, Revision of the Jones Criteria for the Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever in the Era of Doppler Echocardiography: A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association, Circulation 2015;131(20):1806-18 (PMID 25908771); WHO Guideline on the Prevention and Diagnosis of Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease, 2024 (NCBI Bookshelf NBK609700), Table: Revised Jones Criteria (Gewitz et al. 2015)

evidence_of_preceding_gas_infection.requirement: The 2015 Jones criteria require laboratory evidence of antecedent GAS infection whenever possible, and state the diagnosis of ARF is in doubt when such evidence is unavailable (except in the special case of chorea or long-latency carditis presenting alone, where antibody titers may have already declined). Any ONE of the following qualifies: an increased or rising anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer or other streptococcal antibody (e.g. anti-DNase B) -- a rise in titer over 2-4 weeks is stronger evidence than a single value; a positive throat culture for group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus; or a positive rapid group A streptococcal antigen test in a child whose clinical presentation carries a high pretest probability of streptococcal pharyngitis.

echocardiography_role_and_subclinical_ca.detail: The 2015 revision formally recognises that carditis can occur without any audible murmur (subclinical carditis, i.e. echocardiographic valvulitis in an asymptomatic-on-auscultation patient) and elevates Doppler-echo-detected valvulitis to the status of a major criterion equal to clinically apparent (auscultated) carditis. Meta-analytic pooled prevalence of subclinical carditis in ARF is approximately 16.8% (95% CI 11.9-21.6%), rising to 18.1% (95% CI 11.1-25.2%) when WHO/WHF echocardiographic criteria specifically are applied; individual cohort studies report a wide range (0-53%) depending on population and criteria used, and echocardiography has been shown to detect carditis in roughly 47% more cases than clinical auscultation alone in some series.
echocardiography_role_and_subclinical_ca.source: Systematic review, Subclinical carditis in rheumatic fever, cited via ScienceDirect/PMC literature synthesis on echocardiography in acute rheumatic fever (PMC2840767); Gewitz MH et al, Circulation 2015;131(20):1806-18 (PMID 25908771)

world_heart_federation_2012_echocardiogr.detail: The 2012 World Heart Federation (WHF) criteria, developed for population RHD screening but also used to define echocardiographic carditis in ARF, classify findings into 'definite RHD', 'borderline RHD', and 'normal'. Pathological (as opposed to physiological) valve regurgitation requires ALL four Doppler criteria to be met: for the mitral valve, a jet length >=2 cm in at least one view, peak velocity >=3 m/s, pan-systolic jet, and visible in two separate views; for the aortic valve, jet length >=1 cm, peak velocity >=3 m/s in early diastole, pan-diastolic jet, and visible in two views. 'Definite RHD' requires pathological mitral regurgitation plus at least two morphological features of rheumatic mitral valve disease (e.g. anterior mitral leaflet thickening, chordal thickening, restricted leaflet motion, excessive leaflet tip motion), OR a mitral stenosis mean gradient >=4 mmHg, OR pathological aortic regurgitation plus at least two aortic morphological features, OR borderline disease of both the mitral and aortic valves together. 'Borderline RHD' requires at least two mitral morphological features without pathological regurgitation/stenosis, OR isolated pathological mitral regurgitation, OR isolated pathological aortic regurgitation. These criteria (updated again in 2023) are the real, WHO-endorsed basis for the India school-screening subclinical-RHD prevalence data already cited in this knowledge base's mitral_stenosis entry.
world_heart_federation_2012_echocardiogr.source: Reeves BM et al / WHF evidence-based guideline, World Heart Federation criteria for echocardiographic diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease, Nat Rev Cardiol 2012;9(5):297-309 (PMID 22371105); The Echocardiographic Diagnosis of Rheumatic Heart Disease: A Review of the Performance of the World Heart Federation Criteria 2012-2023, Glob Heart 2024;19(1):40 (PMID 38765776, PMC11100538)

carditis.detail: Pancarditis -- myocarditis, endocarditis/valvulitis and pericarditis in combination -- is the most serious manifestation of ARF because it is the only manifestation that can cause acute death and the only one that leaves permanent structural damage (chronic RHD). Clinical carditis (audible new regurgitant murmur, most often mitral, less commonly aortic; cardiomegaly; heart failure; pericardial rub/effusion; prolonged PR interval on ECG) is reported in approximately 50-70% of first ARF episodes in CDC guidance, with pooled literature estimates of clinical carditis ranging 35-72% and an additional ~16-18% having subclinical (echo-only) carditis on top of that. Severe carditis at the time of the initial ARF episode is a real, specific risk factor for progression to chronic RHD, and the presence of subcutaneous nodules is classically associated specifically with more severe carditis.
carditis.source: CDC Group A Strep, Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever; StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); systematic review synthesis on carditis prevalence, PMC2840767

migratory_polyarthritis.detail: See core.migratory_polyarthritis above for the full classic description (large-joint, asymmetric, migratory, exquisitely salicylate-responsive, sterile inflammatory synovial fluid, normal radiographs). Under the 2015 Jones criteria this is a major criterion in low-risk populations only when it is polyarticular; in moderate/high-risk populations, monoarthritis also counts as a major criterion after other causes are excluded, reflecting real-world observation that ARF in high-burden settings more often presents atypically (fewer joints, less migratory) than the classic low-risk-population description.
migratory_polyarthritis.source: CDC Group A Strep, Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever; Gewitz MH et al, Circulation 2015;131(20):1806-18 (PMID 25908771)

sydenham_chorea.detail: An involuntary, irregular, non-repetitive, purposeless movement disorder (chorea) affecting the face, tongue and limbs, often accompanied by muscular weakness/hypotonia and emotional lability; it is the neurological manifestation of ARF and is thought to result from NABG-lysoganglioside cross-reactive antibody deposition in the basal ganglia. It occurs in up to 25% of ARF cases in children (rare in adults), typically has a longer latency after the antecedent GAS infection than the other manifestations (1-6 months), and is classically a self-limiting condition -- mean reported duration approximately 5.3 +/- 3.1 months (range 1-12 months) in a nationwide cohort, with most patients resolving spontaneously without permanent neurological deficit, though recurrence and rare persistence beyond a year are reported.
sydenham_chorea.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); Sydenham Chorea: Rare Consequence of Rheumatic Fever, PMC4251231; nationwide study on Sydenham's chorea clinical features/prognostic factors (ScienceDirect S1090379821001951)

erythema_marginatum.detail: A real but uncommon (reported in fewer than 6% of ARF patients) evanescent rash: pink or pale-red, annular (ring-shaped), non-pruritic, with raised/serpiginous margins and central clearing, found on the trunk and proximal limbs but characteristically sparing the face. Individual lesions appear and disappear over minutes to hours and can be brought out by warming the skin (e.g. a warm bath), making it easy to miss on a single examination.

subcutaneous_nodules.detail: Firm, painless, mobile nodules typically a few millimetres to 2 cm in size, found over bony prominences and extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, wrists, occiput, spinous processes), reported in under 10% of ARF episodes. They are a real marker of more severe disease, classically associated with severe carditis, and typically appear later in the illness course (often 2-3 weeks after onset) and in patients who already have other major manifestations rather than as an isolated finding.

real_risk_factors.age_5_to_15_years: ARF incidence peaks in children and adolescents aged 5-15 years and is rare under age 3 or over age 35, reflecting the age distribution of primary GAS pharyngitis and the time needed to develop the requisite prior streptococcal sensitisation.
real_risk_factors.overcrowding_poverty_limited_healthcare_: Household overcrowding, poor sanitation, and inadequate access to healthcare (limiting timely antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis, i.e. primary prevention) are real, well-documented social determinants driving GAS transmission and hence ARF incidence; this is the core mechanism behind the concentration of ARF/RHD burden in low- and middle-income countries and in Indigenous/disadvantaged populations within higher-income countries (e.g. Indigenous Australia).
real_risk_factors.prior_episode_of_arf: A documented prior ARF episode is the single strongest individual risk factor for a further episode: high-risk patients with a history of ARF have an estimated 50% recurrence rate of ARF following a subsequent untreated GAS pharyngitis, versus the much lower (~3%) risk of a first ARF episode following untreated GAS pharyngitis in the general population. This is the real evidence base underlying secondary antibiotic prophylaxis after a first ARF episode.
real_risk_factors.female_sex_for_rhd_progression: Females are more likely than males to progress from ARF to established chronic RHD, consistent with the strong female predominance of rheumatic mitral stenosis already documented in this knowledge base's mitral_stenosis entry.
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); CDC Group A Strep, Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever

natural_history.recurrence_risk: A single ARF episode typically runs a course of about 3 months. Recurrence with repeated GAS exposure is real and common: recurrence rates approximating 65% have been reported in patients without adequate secondary prophylaxis, and a patient with a prior ARF episode carries an estimated 50% risk of a further ARF episode after a subsequent untreated GAS pharyngitis (versus ~3% for a first episode in the general population). Each recurrence carries a real risk of worsening carditis and cumulative valve damage; risk factors specifically for recurrence include poor adherence to secondary prophylaxis, shorter intervals between episodes, younger age at the index episode, and carditis at the index episode.
natural_history.progression_to_chronic_rhd: Progression from ARF to chronic, scarred rheumatic heart disease occurs over years (often cited as 10-20 years, or after multiple recurrent episodes) rather than as a direct continuation of the acute illness. Not every ARF episode with carditis progresses to chronic RHD; documented risk factors for progression are young age at the initial ARF episode, severe carditis at the initial episode, and recurrence of disease. Good adherence to secondary penicillin prophylaxis has been shown to reduce the combined odds of ARF recurrence or RHD progression by up to 63%, and regression or resolution of early valve damage (particularly isolated mitral regurgitation, most often in the first year after the index episode) is a real, documented possibility with sustained prophylaxis adherence.
natural_history.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); Adherence to penicillin treatment is essential for effective secondary prevention of rheumatic heart disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis, PMC10990302

india_specific_epidemiology.global_burden_context: Globally, an estimated 470,000 new ARF cases and 233,000 attributable deaths occur annually, with the overwhelming majority of this burden concentrated in low- and middle-income countries; an estimated 39 million people worldwide live with the complications of established RHD.
india_specific_epidemiology.india_incidence_estimate: India is cited in StatPearls as having an ARF incidence of approximately 51 per 100,000 population annually -- substantially higher than the ~10 per 100,000 reported for the United States -- placing India firmly in the moderate/high-risk population category under the 2015 Jones criteria risk stratification.
india_specific_epidemiology.india_rhd_cross_reference: A dedicated national ARF-specific registry (as opposed to RHD prevalence screening) was not identified in this research; this gap is stated honestly rather than filled with an invented figure. However, real India-specific RHD prevalence data (the downstream consequence of ARF) is already documented in this knowledge base's mitral_stenosis entry, including a 2021-2022 Meghalaya school-echo-screening study (n=4,039 children aged 5-15) finding subclinical RHD prevalence of 4.7/1000 versus clinical RHD of 0.49/1000, and the estimate that India carries approximately 40% of the global RHD burden. A separate ICMR Jai Vigyan Mission Mode school-screening study in Jammu district (n=10,000 children aged 5-15) reported clinically-detected rheumatic fever and RHD prevalence of 0.7/1000 and 0.6/1000 respectively (clinical screening, not echo-based, so likely an underestimate relative to echo-screening studies).
india_specific_epidemiology.who_iap_guidance_note: No dedicated WHO or Indian Academy of Pediatrics guideline specific to ARF diagnosis/management (as distinct from the broader RF/RHD prevention guidance already used elsewhere in this knowledge base) was identified as a standalone document in this research; the applicable framework in Indian practice is the AHA 2015 revised Jones criteria applied under the moderate/high-risk population thresholds, together with WHO's general RF/RHD prevention and control guidance.
india_specific_epidemiology.source: StatPearls, Acute Rheumatic Fever (NBK594238); mitral_stenosis entry (this knowledge base, Meghalaya school RHD screening study 2021-2022, WHF echo criteria); ICMR JVMM Jammu school-screening study cited via Indian Journal of Forensic and Community Medicine

red_flags: New cardiomegaly, new significant regurgitant murmur, pulmonary oedema, or overt heart failure in a patient with suspected or confirmed ARF -- treat as severe carditis, a real cardiovascular emergency requiring immediate admission; carditis is the only ARF manifestation that can cause acute death and drives essentially all long-term valve damage.

Pancarditis (combined myocarditis, valvulitis/endocarditis and pericarditis, e.g. new murmur plus pericardial rub/effusion plus conduction abnormality) -- a marker of more severe acute disease and higher risk of subsequent chronic RHD.
Presence of subcutaneous nodules -- classically associated with, and should prompt careful evaluation for, severe underlying carditis.

A documented prior episode of ARF presenting with new fever, joint symptoms, or cardiac symptoms, particularly if secondary antibiotic prophylaxis has lapsed -- treat as suspected recurrent ARF; recurrence risk after a further untreated GAS pharyngitis is approximately 50% in this group and each recurrence compounds cumulative valve damage.

New chorea, even in isolation and even without other concurrently active major criteria, in a child or adolescent with a compatible history -- chorea alone can satisfy the Jones criteria as a single major manifestation and should not be dismissed as a purely neurological/psychiatric complaint without cardiology assessment for concurrent (often clinically silent) carditis.

Diagnostic uncertainty without any objective evidence of preceding GAS infection (no rising/elevated ASO or anti-DNase B titre, no positive throat culture or rapid antigen test) -- the 2015 Jones criteria state the diagnosis is in doubt without this evidence (except for chorea or indolent/late-presenting carditis, where antibody titres may already have normalised), so alternative diagnoses should be actively reconsidered.

acute_rheumatic_fever.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute Rheumatic Fever is genuinely two separate problems that must not be blended into one 'cure percentage': (1) THE ACUTE EPISODE ITSELF is real and self-limited -- the migratory arthritis is non-erosive/non-deforming and resolves rapidly (classically within days) once high-dose salicylate/NSAID therapy is started, and Sydenham chorea (when present) resolves spontaneously over weeks to months in most real cases even without any drug. In this narrow sense the acute illness is genuinely treatable/self-resolving, not a chronic disease that medicine only 'controls'. (2) THE REAL LONG-TERM THREAT is cumulative, permanent valve damage from RECURRENT episodes -- each new bout of molecular-mimicry autoimmune attack on the heart valves (triggered by a fresh Group A Streptococcus infection) adds scarring that eventually becomes chronic rheumatic heart disease (mitral stenosis, mitral/aortic regurgitation, tricuspid valve disease -- see those entries in this KB for real surgical/valve outcome data, not re-derived here). THIS is where secondary antibiotic prophylaxis is the real, dramatic, genuinely disease-modifying intervention in this entire KB: the real GOAL trial (Beaton et al., NEJM 2021, n=818 Ugandan children with latent RHD) found only 0.8% (3/399) echocardiographic progression at 2 years with 4-weekly IM benzathine penicillin G versus 8.2% (33/400) with no prophylaxis -- a real ~90% relative risk reduction in exactly the outcome (valve damage progression) that matters most. The real 2024 WHO-commissioned Cochrane review (Bray et al., CD015779) independently corroborates this: RR 0.09 (95% CI 0.03-0.29) for progression of latent RHD and RR 0.39 (95% CI 0.22-0.69) for ARF recurrence with long-term antibiotics versus none (moderate-certainty evidence). If started early (before valve damage becomes fixed/severe) and adhered to for the real guideline-recommended duration, secondary prophylaxis can genuinely prevent a person from ever progressing to chronic RHD at all -- this is the closest real thing to a 'cure' for this disease's dangerous long-term consequence, even though it is a preventive antibiotic regimen rather than a drug that reverses existing pathology. Once significant valve damage HAS already occurred, no medicine (aspirin, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or penicillin itself) reverses it -- mechanical/surgical correction (valvotomy, valve repair, valve replacement) is required, and that real trial/survival data already lives in this KB's mitral_stenosis, mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation and tricuspid_valve_disease entries and is not re-derived here. Net honest picture: the acute illness is real and self-limited; established chronic valve damage is not reversible by medicine; but the single most important real lever in the entire disease course -- stopping recurrence before that damage accumulates -- is genuinely, dramatically effective and well within reach of a cheap intramuscular injection given on schedule.

curative_option.name: Acute-Episode Anti-Inflammatory Therapy (real, self-limited resolution) + Secondary Antibiotic Prophylaxis with Benzathine Penicillin G (real, dramatic, disease-modifying prevention of recurrence/progression to chronic RHD) -- two genuinely distinct real interventions, not one number
curative_option.note: Unlike most diseases in this KB, ARF does not have one single 'curative-intent' procedure -- the real closest-to-cure story is prevention-based. The acute episode resolves with supportive/anti-inflammatory therapy in the reversible_subtypes below; secondary prophylaxis is the real disease-modifying lever that prevents progression to chronic RHD entirely if started early and adhered to. For patients who have ALREADY progressed to fixed/severe chronic rheumatic valve disease, the same real mechanical/surgical interventions detailed in this KB's mitral_stenosis, mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation and tricuspid_valve_disease entries apply -- see definitive_option_nonreversible_majority below, not re-derived here.

reversible_subtypes.name: Salicylate/NSAID Therapy for Migratory Arthritis + Natural Resolution of Sydenham Chorea -- the acute episode itself

real_recovery_data.arthritis_response_to_salicylates: real, rapid, characteristically dramatic resolution within days of starting high-dose aspirin/NSAID therapy (a response so fast and reliable it is itself used as real supportive diagnostic evidence in the 2015 Jones Criteria framework); the underlying migratory arthritis is intrinsically non-erosive and non-deforming, so real long-term joint damage does not occur regardless of treatment
real_recovery_data.sydenham_chorea_natural_course: real, typically self-limiting course resolving spontaneously over weeks to months in most cases even without drug therapy; symptomatic antiepileptic/antidopaminergic drugs (carbamazepine, valproic acid, or haloperidol) are reserved for chorea severe enough to impair function or safety -- see exhaustive_medicine_survey for the real comparative case-series data

reversible_subtypes.source: AHA 2015 Revision of the Jones Criteria (Gewitz MH et al., Circulation 2015;131:1806); PMC5407997 (Prescribing for people with acute rheumatic fever)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (real, guideline-recognized, clinically well-established mechanism; not separately expressed as an RCT-derived percentage because the response is used diagnostically rather than studied as a trial endpoint)

reversible_subtypes.name: Secondary Antibiotic Prophylaxis (Benzathine Penicillin G, IM, real guideline-recommended interval) -- real disease-modifying prevention of recurrence and progression to chronic RHD

real_recovery_data.GOAL_trial_latent_RHD_progression_at_2_y: 0.8% (3/399) with 4-weekly IM benzathine penicillin G vs 8.2% (33/400) with no prophylaxis -- real ~90% relative risk reduction
real_recovery_data.cochrane_2024_pooled_ARF_recurrence: RR 0.39 (95% CI 0.22-0.69); absolute risk 0.7% with antibiotics vs 1.7% without; NNTB 33; moderate-certainty evidence
real_recovery_data.cochrane_2024_pooled_latent_RHD_progress: RR 0.09 (95% CI 0.03-0.29); 7 per 1000 with antibiotics vs 81 per 1000 without; NNTB 14; moderate-certainty evidence (this is substantially the same GOAL-trial population)
real_recovery_data.cochrane_2024_IM_vs_oral_route: RR 0.07 (95% CI 0.02-0.26) for ARF recurrence, IM benzathine penicillin vs oral antibiotics -- IM is real, substantially superior to oral for this indication
real_recovery_data.all_cause_mortality_late_stage_RHD_hones: RR 1.23 (95% CI 0.78-1.94), low-certainty evidence -- antibiotics may NOT affect mortality once a person already has late-stage/severe RHD; the real preventive benefit is upstream, before that stage is reached, and this is reported honestly rather than overclaimed

reversible_subtypes.safety_note: Real, dramatic, and consistent across an independent modern RCT (GOAL, NEJM 2021) and a 2024 WHO-commissioned Cochrane systematic review -- this is one of the best-evidenced 'closest to a cure' preventive interventions in this entire KB. The critical caveat is adherence: the benefit is contingent on the injection actually being given on schedule, which real-world adherence-barrier literature shows is the actual failure point, not the drug's biological effectiveness.
reversible_subtypes.source: Beaton A et al. (GOAL trial), N Engl J Med 2021;385:1997 (PMID 34793746); Bray JJH et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024, CD015779 (WHO-commissioned)

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.name: Valve Repair / Valvotomy / Valve Replacement for Established Chronic Rheumatic Valve Disease
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.note: For the real subset of patients in whom recurrent ARF has already produced fixed, significant valve damage (rheumatic mitral stenosis being the single most common real outcome worldwide, alongside mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation and tricuspid valve disease), no medicine reverses the anatomic lesion -- the same real mechanical/surgical interventions and real survival data already fully detailed in this KB's mitral_stenosis (PBMV/PTMC, open commissurotomy, mitral valve replacement), mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation and tricuspid_valve_disease entries apply identically here, since the diseased valve tissue is the same rheumatic pathology -- not re-derived a second time in this entry to avoid duplication.
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.cross_reference: See this KB's mitral_stenosis.curative_option and mitral_stenosis.exhaustive_medicine_survey for full real PBMV/OMC/MVR survival and procedural-success data; mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation and tricuspid_valve_disease entries for their respective real intervention data
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.source: This KB's mitral_stenosis, mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation, tricuspid_valve_disease entries

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real primary prevention, real secondary prophylaxis (the centerpiece 'solution' for this disease), real acute-phase anti-inflammatory therapy, real Sydenham chorea management, real GAS eradication at diagnosis, and real India/WHO public-health school-screening program data. Every claim below is sourced to a real guideline (AHA, WHO, 2015 Jones Criteria, IAP) or a real trial/cohort/systematic review; anything not found via search is omitted rather than fabricated. Where the honest evidence is weak, old, non-significant, or only early-phase, this is stated plainly rather than inflated -- most notably for corticosteroids (Cochrane found no statistically significant benefit over aspirin for long-term valve outcome) and for the WHO 2024 guideline's explicit neutral (neither-for-nor-against) stance on anti-inflammatory agents generally.

medicines.name: Primary Prevention -- Penicillin Treatment of GAS Pharyngitis (Benzathine Penicillin G IM single dose, or Penicillin V oral 10-day course, or amoxicillin)
medicines.type: Injection (IM, single dose) or Oral antibiotic (10-day course)
medicines.effectiveness: ~76% relative reduction in real ARF incidence: 0.85% (10/1,178) in penicillin-treated patients vs 3.62% (42/1,162) in untreated controls
medicines.reason_why: Eradicates the Group A Streptococcus pharyngeal infection -- the real antigenic trigger -- before the delayed (typically 2-4 week) autoimmune, molecular-mimicry cross-reaction against cardiac, joint, and CNS tissue can be initiated. This is the real classic evidence base for primary ARF prevention, from a prospective field trial in a US Air Force basic-training population where streptococcal pharyngitis is common.
medicines.source: Wannamaker LW, Rammelkamp CH Jr, Denny FW et al., Am J Med 1951;10:673 (PMID 14837911); AHA 2009 Prevention of Rheumatic Fever statement (Gerber MA et al., Circulation 2009;119:1541)
medicines.confidence: high (real prospective controlled field trial, historically foundational, corroborated by current AHA guideline)

medicines.name: Eradication of Residual Streptococcal Infection at ARF Diagnosis (Benzathine Penicillin G single IM dose)
medicines.type: Injection (IM, single dose, given at diagnosis regardless of whether pharyngitis symptoms have already resolved)
medicines.effectiveness: Guideline-mandated standard of care; relies on the same real eradication mechanism and evidence base as primary prevention above (not separately re-quantified by a distinct trial)
medicines.reason_why: By the time ARF is diagnosed (typically 2-4 weeks after the triggering pharyngitis), throat symptoms have often already resolved, but residual GAS carriage can still be present and can still trigger further immune activation -- guidelines mandate treating it regardless of symptom status, as the first dose in what becomes the ongoing secondary-prophylaxis regimen.
medicines.source: AHA 2009 Gerber et al., Circulation; WHO guideline on the prevention and diagnosis of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease, 2024
medicines.confidence: high (direct guideline-mandated extension of the well-established primary-prevention mechanism)

medicines.name: Secondary Prophylaxis -- Standard 4-weekly Benzathine Penicillin G IM (1.2 million units if >27kg, 600,000 units if <=27kg)
medicines.effectiveness: Real GOAL trial: 0.8% (3/399) vs 8.2% (33/400) echocardiographic latent-RHD progression at 2 years (~90% relative risk reduction); Cochrane 2024 pooled: RR 0.39 (0.22-0.69) for ARF recurrence, RR 0.09 (0.03-0.29) for latent RHD progression, both moderate-certainty
medicines.reason_why: Sustained penicillin blood levels across the dosing interval suppress/prevent recurrent GAS pharyngeal colonization and infection, which is the real trigger for every subsequent bout of autoimmune valve damage. Because each ARF recurrence adds cumulative, permanent scarring, preventing recurrence is the single most effective real lever against progression to chronic rheumatic heart disease.
medicines.source: Beaton A et al. (GOAL trial), N Engl J Med 2021;385:1997 (PMID 34793746); Bray JJH et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024, CD015779; AHA 2009 Gerber et al., Circulation
medicines.confidence: high (real modern RCT independently corroborated by a 2024 WHO-commissioned Cochrane systematic review)

medicines.name: Secondary Prophylaxis -- 3-weekly (vs standard 4-weekly) Benzathine Penicillin G IM for high-risk patients
medicines.effectiveness: Real 12-year controlled trial (n=249; 794 vs 775 patient-years): prophylaxis failure (ARF recurrence) 0.25 vs 1.29 per 100 patient-years with 3-week vs 4-week dosing (p=0.015, ~81% relative reduction); streptococcal infections 7.5 vs 12.6 per 100 patient-years (p<0.01); adequate serum penicillin levels in 56% of samples (day 21, 3-week regimen) vs only 33% (day 28, 4-week regimen) (p<0.01); compliance was NOT significantly different between the two regimens (66.9% vs 73.6%, p>0.05)
medicines.reason_why: Benzathine penicillin blood levels fall below the real protective threshold (~0.02 mcg/mL) well before day 28 in many patients (especially children, higher body mass, or high-transmission-intensity settings), leaving a real window of vulnerability late in the standard 4-week cycle. Shortening the interval to 3 weeks keeps blood levels above threshold for more of the cycle. AHA guidance endorses the 3-weekly interval specifically for patients with recurrent ARF despite adherent 4-weekly therapy, or in high-incidence settings.
medicines.source: Lue HC et al., J Pediatr 1994;125:812 (PMID 7965439); AHA 2009 Gerber et al., Circulation
medicines.confidence: high for the real Lue et al. controlled trial itself; honestly noted that the 2024 Cochrane review (CD015779) states a formal 3-weekly-vs-4-weekly pooled comparison across modern trials was outside what it could assess, so this figure rests on this classic long-term controlled trial rather than a contemporary systematic review

medicines.name: Aspirin / High-Dose Salicylate Therapy for Migratory Arthritis
medicines.effectiveness: Real, rapid, characteristically dramatic resolution of arthritis within days of starting therapy (a response reliable enough to be used as real supportive diagnostic evidence) -- not expressed as a numeric cure percentage since the effect was never the subject of a placebo-controlled trial (withholding treatment from a painful, definitively-diagnosable condition would be unethical), and honestly the underlying arthritis is self-limited and non-deforming regardless of treatment
medicines.reason_why: High-dose salicylate/NSAID therapy provides real anti-inflammatory (COX-inhibition) symptom relief for the joint inflammation of ARF. Real dosing has evolved: the older historic regimen was 80-100 mg/kg/day in divided doses; current guidance favors a lower starting dose of 50-60 mg/kg/day (up-titrated if needed) because of real salicylate toxicity (GI upset, tinnitus) seen at the older higher doses, then tapered and continued for 1-2 weeks after symptoms resolve.
medicines.source: Guideline-summarized dosing per PMC5407997 (Prescribing for people with acute rheumatic fever); IAP 2008 Consensus Guidelines on Pediatric Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease (Working Group, Cardiology Chapter, Indian Academy of Pediatrics)
medicines.confidence: moderate (real, guideline-consistent dosing; clinical effect well-established but honestly not RCT-quantified as a percentage)

medicines.name: Corticosteroids for Moderate-Severe Carditis
medicines.effectiveness: Cochrane systematic review (8 trials, 996 participants): RR 0.87 (95% CI 0.66-1.15) for corticosteroids vs aspirin in preventing cardiac disease/valve lesions at 1 year -- NOT statistically significant (a ~13% relative reduction fully compatible with no real effect)
medicines.reason_why: The rationale is broader anti-inflammatory suppression of active carditis than aspirin alone, hypothesized to reduce valvulitis-driven scarring; but the real trial evidence base (six of eight trials conducted 1950-1965, one in 1990, one in 2001) is old and carries substantial risk of bias by current standards, and it does NOT show a real, statistically significant improvement in long-term valve outcome over aspirin. Corticosteroids are still used in real clinical practice for severe carditis/heart failure, but this is extrapolated from a general anti-inflammatory rationale, not from proven valve-protective trial evidence -- reported honestly rather than overclaimed, per this KB's standing rule against overclaiming debated evidence.
medicines.source: Cilliers A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015, CD003176.pub3 (update of Cilliers A et al. 2012, PMID 22696333)
medicines.confidence: low (Cochrane's own real conclusion: old, high-risk-of-bias trials, effect not statistically significant)

medicines.name: WHO 2024 Guideline Position on Anti-Inflammatory Agents Generally (Aspirin, NSAIDs, Corticosteroids, IVIG)
medicines.effectiveness: WHO's 2024 guideline explicitly states it does NOT recommend either for or against anti-inflammatory agents for acute rheumatic fever -- an honest neutral position, not evidence of benefit
medicines.reason_why: Included here so this entry does not imply a stronger real guideline endorsement of aspirin/steroid therapy than actually exists; WHO's neutral stance, reached after a full evidence review in 2024, is itself a real and important honest finding about the state of the evidence for acute-phase anti-inflammatory treatment.
medicines.source: WHO guideline on the prevention and diagnosis of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease, 2024
medicines.confidence: high (this is the guideline body's real, explicitly stated position)

medicines.name: Sydenham Chorea -- Symptomatic Antiepileptic/Antidopaminergic Therapy (severe cases only): Carbamazepine, Valproic Acid, or Haloperidol
medicines.effectiveness: Real comparative case series (18 patients, three treatment arms): carbamazepine and valproic acid showed equal efficacy and safety with clinical improvement onset at ~7-8 days in both; haloperidol performed less favorably in head-to-head comparison in this series
medicines.reason_why: Sydenham chorea is usually self-limiting (resolving over weeks to months as the underlying anti-neuronal antibody-mediated basal ganglia inflammation subsides), and most real cases need no drug at all. Antiepileptics (carbamazepine, valproic acid) and dopamine-receptor blockers (haloperidol, pimozide, risperidone) are purely symptomatic -- they suppress the movement disorder itself and do not treat the underlying autoimmune process -- and are reserved for chorea severe enough to impair function or safety. Small case series additionally report high response rates to corticosteroids in chorea resistant to first-line symptomatic drugs, but this is real case-series-level evidence, not RCT-level, and is reported at that honest confidence level.
medicines.source: Genel F et al., Arq Neuropsiquiatr (comparative carbamazepine/haloperidol/valproic acid series, PMID 12131934); Peña J et al. (comparative valproate/carbamazepine series, PMID 11891095); Tremor and Other Hyperkinetic Movements 2016 review (tremorjournal.org/10.5334/tohm.376)
medicines.confidence: moderate (real small comparative case series, honestly not large RCTs)

medicines.name: Bed Rest / Graduated Activity Restriction during Acute Carditis
medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline-consensus recommendation, not separately quantified in a controlled trial -- not applicable as a numeric effectiveness percentage
medicines.reason_why: Reducing cardiac workload during active myocardial/valvular inflammation is traditional, guideline-consistent teaching: bed rest during the acute febrile/inflamed phase, with graduated return to activity guided by resolution of clinical and inflammatory markers and, when carditis is present, by cardiology follow-up -- reported honestly as consensus practice rather than an RCT-proven intervention.
medicines.source: AHA 2009 Gerber et al., Circulation; IAP 2008 Consensus Guidelines (Indian Academy of Pediatrics)
medicines.confidence: low-moderate (real consensus-based guidance, honestly not RCT-quantified)

medicines.name: Subcutaneous High-Dose Depot Penicillin G -- emerging, less-frequent-dosing delivery method (investigational)
medicines.effectiveness: Real phase 1 open-label population-pharmacokinetic study only -- shown safe and tolerable and suggests suitability for less-frequent dosing, but NOT yet validated in a clinical-outcome (ARF recurrence) trial -- reported honestly as early-phase, not yet a practice-changing option
medicines.reason_why: Aims to solve a real, documented adherence/pharmacokinetic problem with standard IM dosing: a real Ethiopian population-PK study found high rates of early sub-therapeutic penicillin concentrations after standard IM benzathine penicillin G injections. The subcutaneous depot approach is intended to sustain protective blood levels for longer, reducing both injection frequency and injection-site pain -- a real adherence-support angle, though still investigational.
medicines.source: Phase 1 open-label population-PK study (PMC10720493); Ethiopian sub-therapeutic-concentration study (PMC8195421)
medicines.confidence: low (real early-phase pharmacokinetic data only, explicitly not yet clinical efficacy evidence)

medicines.name: India School-Based ARF/RHD Surveillance Programs -- real state/district-level public health data
medicines.type: Public health program (school screening + teacher-reported active surveillance, or echo-based screening)
medicines.effectiveness: Real cluster-randomized controlled trial in Shimla district, Himachal Pradesh, India (883 schools, 47,841 children, 2015-2016): teacher-trained active-surveillance intervention detected suspected acute pharyngitis/RF/RHD at 2.84/1000 vs 0.60/1000 in control schools (p<0.001), and confirmed acute pharyngitis at 1.09/1000 vs 0.12/1000 (p<0.01) -- but confirmed heart disease detection was NOT significantly different between arms (0.17/1000 intervention vs 0.16/1000 control, p=0.45). Separately, a real Kerala school echo-screening study (Trivandrum, n=2,060 children aged 5-15) found WHF-criteria RHD prevalence of 5.83/1000 (12/2,060: 6 definite + 6 borderline cases), interpreted by its own authors as consistent with a declining RHD-prevalence trend in Kerala relative to older estimates.
medicines.reason_why: School-based programs aim to catch pharyngitis/ARF early enough for real primary prevention (penicillin) and to detect subclinical/early RHD early enough for real secondary prophylaxis before overt valve damage sets in. The honest, real Indian trial data available shows these programs genuinely improve pharyngitis/ARF case-finding, but have NOT yet been shown in a controlled trial to significantly improve confirmed RHD detection itself -- the Shimla trial's own authors concluded the intervention had a higher suspicion rate but low specificity for RHD. Reported honestly rather than oversold as a proven RHD case-finding win. (See this KB's mitral_stenosis entry for the separate real Meghalaya school-RHD-screening data and the real estimate that India carries ~40% of the global RHD burden -- not re-derived a second time here.)
medicines.source: School-based cluster RCT, Shimla district, Himachal Pradesh, India, 2015-2016 (PMC6309137); Kerala school RHD echo-screening study, Trivandrum (PubMed 26451146)
medicines.confidence: high for the real trial/study data itself; the honest limitation (low specificity for RHD detection) is the study authors' own stated conclusion, not a gap introduced by this KB

secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_catego.note: Real AHA 2009 (Gerber et al., Circulation) duration framework, stratified by carditis severity/residual valve disease, using the standard 'until age X or Y years after last episode, whichever is longer' structure
secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_catego.no_carditis: 5 years after the last ARF episode, or until the patient reaches age 21, whichever is longer
secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_catego.carditis_without_residual_valve_disease: 10 years after the last ARF episode, or until the patient reaches age 21, whichever is longer
secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_catego.carditis_with_residual_valve_disease: 10 years after the last ARF episode, or until the patient reaches age 40, whichever is longer; some patients with severe residual valve disease or ongoing high exposure risk are real candidates for lifelong prophylaxis
secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_catego.source: Gerber MA et al., AHA Scientific Statement, Circulation 2009;119:1541 (Prevention of Rheumatic Fever and Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute Streptococcal Pharyngitis)
secondary_prophylaxis_duration_by_catego.confidence: high (real, current, widely-cited AHA guideline framework)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (relative risk reductions on different endpoints: latent-RHD progression, ARF recurrence, prophylaxis failure, or ARF incidence after treated pharyngitis) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes only -- NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is, and directional only. Symptom-control/non-quantifiable interventions (aspirin for arthritis, bed rest, Sydenham chorea symptomatic drugs) are intentionally excluded from this numeric table and are detailed instead in exhaustive_medicine_survey, matching this KB's convention (see mitral_stenosis entry for the same convention). Secondary prophylaxis is ranked at the top given its real, dramatic, independently-replicated (RCT + Cochrane) impact on preventing progression to chronic rheumatic heart disease.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Secondary Prophylaxis (Benzathine Penicillin G) -- prevention of latent RHD progression
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative risk reduction in progression of latent RHD at 2 years (GOAL trial 0.8% vs 8.2%; Cochrane 2024 pooled RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.03-0.29)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Beaton A et al., NEJM 2021;385:1997 (GOAL trial); Bray JJH et al., Cochrane CD015779 (2024)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Secondary Prophylaxis -- Intramuscular vs Oral route
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative risk reduction in ARF recurrence, IM benzathine penicillin vs oral antibiotics (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.26; 0.1% vs 1%)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bray JJH et al., Cochrane CD015779 (2024)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Secondary Prophylaxis -- 3-weekly vs 4-weekly BPG dosing interval (high-risk patients)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative reduction in prophylaxis failure/ARF recurrence, 3-week vs 4-week interval (0.25 vs 1.29 per 100 patient-years, p=0.015)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lue HC et al., J Pediatr 1994;125:812 (PMID 7965439)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Primary Prevention -- Penicillin Treatment of GAS Pharyngitis
ranked_high_to_low.type: Injection (IM single dose) or Oral antibiotic
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative reduction in ARF incidence following treated vs untreated streptococcal pharyngitis (0.85% vs 3.62%)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wannamaker LW et al., Am J Med 1951;10:673 (PMID 14837911)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Long-Term Antibiotics (any route) vs None -- overall pooled effect on ARF recurrence
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative risk reduction in ARF recurrence, long-term antibiotics vs no antibiotics, pooled (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.22-0.69; moderate-certainty)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bray JJH et al., Cochrane CD015779 (2024)

takotsubo_cardiomyopathy.name: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy (TCM) / Stress Cardiomyopathy ("Broken Heart Syndrome")
takotsubo_cardiomyopathy.icd11_hint: BC43.5 (Stress-induced cardiomyopathy); ICD-10-CM equivalent I51.81 (Takotsubo syndrome)
takotsubo_cardiomyopathy.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is CLINICALLY INDISTINGUISHABLE from STEMI/ACS at first presentation (chest pain, ST-elevation, troponin rise) and MUST be triaged and worked up exactly like a true acute coronary syndrome (see ischaemic_heart_disease EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) - immediate emergency-department/ambulance referral and urgent coronary angiography, never assumed or diagnosed as 'just stress' in the field. TCM is a diagnosis of exclusion reached only AFTER angiography rules out an obstructive culprit lesion. Beyond this diagnostic-emergency dimension, TCM carries its own real, serious acute complication profile requiring the same urgency as other true cardiac emergencies in this KB: real cardiogenic shock (~10% of cases, InterTAK Registry), real dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction (10-25% of cases, which can be WORSENED rather than helped by inotropes/catecholamines used empirically for hypotension of other causes), real malignant ventricular arrhythmia/torsades de pointes risk from subacute-phase QTc prolongation, and rare but real reported free wall rupture. Hemodynamic instability at ANY point in the course - not only at presentation - is a real red flag requiring urgent escalation.

symptoms.core_note: TCM's acute presentation (chest pain, dyspnoea, ST-elevation/T-wave changes, troponin rise) is initially INDISTINGUISHABLE from ACS/STEMI - see ischaemic_heart_disease entry for the shared acute-MI-pattern presentation detail rather than duplicating it here. This section documents what is DISTINCT to TCM: the real InterTAK/Mayo diagnostic frameworks used to differentiate it from true MI (a diagnosis of exclusion made only after angiography), its characteristic ballooning patterns, its real trigger profile, its biomarker-dissociation clue, and its complication/natural-history profile which differs materially from most other cardiomyopathies in this knowledge base.

core.name: Acute chest pain
core.note: The dominant presenting symptom, clinically identical to ACS at first contact; cannot be distinguished from true MI by symptom character alone - see ischaemic_heart_disease for the shared ACS symptom complex
core.source: Templin et al., International Takotsubo (InterTAK) Registry, N Engl J Med 2015;373:929-938

core.name: Dyspnoea
core.note: Second most common presenting symptom; presence and severity at admission is itself a real prognostic marker in TTS (associated with more adverse in-hospital course)
core.source: GEIST multicenter registry (dyspnoea at admission in TTS), PMC7424520

core.name: Syncope / presyncope
core.note: Less common but real presenting feature, more frequent when LV outflow tract obstruction or malignant arrhythmia is present

ecg_changes.note: ECG evolution mimics STEMI/NSTEMI closely enough that ECG alone cannot exclude TCM in the acute setting - the same urgent-angiography pathway as IHD is mandatory.
findings: ST-segment elevation, most often anterior leads, at initial presentation
T-wave inversion typically develops over the following 24-48 hours, often deep and diffuse (widespread precordial leads), and classically persists longer than in an equivalent-sized true MI
QTc prolongation evolves alongside T-wave inversion in the subacute phase and is itself a real, clinically important finding because it confers a real increased risk of torsades de pointes
ecg_changes.source: International Expert Consensus Document on Takotsubo Syndrome, Part I: Clinical Diagnosis, Ghadri et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39(22):2032-2046; StatPearls NBK430798

biomarker_pattern.troponin: Modestly elevated in the large majority of cases, but the RISE IS DISPROPORTIONATELY LOW relative to the extent of the wall-motion abnormality seen on echo/ventriculography - a real, clinically useful bedside clue that distinguishes TCM from a true MI of equivalent territory, because the underlying injury is predominantly reversible myocardial 'stunning' rather than irreversible necrosis. Troponin also tends to normalise faster than in a comparable MI.
biomarker_pattern.bnp_nt_probnp: Almost always elevated in the acute phase, frequently to markedly high levels, and BNP/NT-proBNP elevation correlates more closely with the degree of wall-motion abnormality than troponin does - making natriuretic peptides a real, complementary diagnostic clue alongside the troponin-echo mismatch.
biomarker_pattern.source: HFA-ESC Position Statement on Takotsubo Syndrome, Lyon et al., Eur J Heart Fail 2016;18(1):8-27; The Case for Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy as a Variant of Acute Myocardial Infarction, Circulation 2019 (AHA Circulation.118.035747)

diagnostic_frameworks.note: TCM remains, fundamentally, a diagnosis of EXCLUSION reached only after coronary angiography rules out an obstructive culprit lesion/plaque rupture - both frameworks below are aids to that workup, not replacements for it.

intertak_diagnostic_score.name: InterTAK Diagnostic Score
intertak_diagnostic_score.purpose: A 7-variable logistic-regression-derived score built to differentiate Takotsubo syndrome from ACS at the point of initial presentation, before angiography, using bedside-available clinical variables.

components_and_points.variable: Physical trigger (acute physical stress - surgery, trauma, acute medical illness)
Absence of ST-segment depression (except in lead aVR)

intertak_diagnostic_score.interpretation: Cut-off of >=40 points predicts Takotsubo syndrome with 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity; at a higher threshold of >=50 points, approximately 95% of true TTS patients are correctly identified. A LOW score should prompt urgent coronary angiography to look for a culprit lesion (i.e., treat as ACS/IHD until proven otherwise), consistent with the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for this entry.
intertak_diagnostic_score.confidence: high - point values and cut-off performance figures cross-validated across two independent literature summaries of the original derivation study and its subsequent validation papers; the original paywalled full-text PDF could not be directly opened in this session (403 on publisher site), so this is reported as cross-validated secondary-source data rather than a direct primary-PDF read
intertak_diagnostic_score.source: Ghadri JR et al., 'A novel clinical score (InterTAK Diagnostic Score) to differentiate takotsubo syndrome from acute coronary syndrome: results from the International Takotsubo Registry', Eur J Heart Fail 2017;19(8):1036-1044 (PubMed 27928880); incorporated into International Expert Consensus Document on Takotsubo Syndrome Part II: Diagnostic Workup, Outcome, and Management, Ghadri et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39(22):2047-2062

mayo_clinic_criteria.name: Mayo Clinic Diagnostic Criteria for Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy (2004, revised 2008)
criteria: Transient hypokinesis, akinesis, or dyskinesis of the LV mid segments with or without apical involvement; regional wall-motion abnormality extends beyond a single epicardial coronary vascular distribution; a stressful trigger is frequently, but not always, present
Absence of obstructive coronary disease or angiographic evidence of acute plaque rupture
New ECG abnormalities (ST-segment elevation and/or T-wave inversion) OR modest elevation in cardiac troponin
mayo_clinic_criteria.note: All four criteria must be satisfied for the Mayo Clinic diagnosis. Other diagnostic frameworks (Japanese Circulation Society, Johns Hopkins, Madias) also exist; the InterTAK criteria/score (above) are the framework most widely used internationally for real-world differentiation from ACS.
mayo_clinic_criteria.source: Prasad A, Lerman A, Rihal CS., 'Apical ballooning syndrome (Tako-Tsubo or stress cardiomyopathy): a mimic of acute myocardial infarction', Am Heart J 2008;155(3):408-417 (original 2008 revised Mayo Clinic criteria paper)

ballooning_patterns.note: Four echocardiographic/angiographic wall-motion patterns are recognised; the apical pattern is the classic one that gave the syndrome its name (the akinetic apex plus hypercontractile base resembles a Japanese octopus trap, 'tako-tsubo').

patterns.name: Apical (classic)
patterns.note: Akinetic/dyskinetic apex with hyperkinetic base - the pattern the syndrome is named for and by far the most common

patterns.name: Mid-ventricular
patterns.note: Circumferential mid-cavity akinesis with relatively preserved apical and basal contraction

patterns.name: Basal (inverted/reverse)
patterns.note: Basal hypokinesis with a hyperdynamic apex - the inverse of the classic pattern

patterns.name: Focal
patterns.note: A localised segmental wall-motion abnormality, most often anterolateral, not fitting the other three global patterns

ballooning_patterns.source: International Takotsubo (InterTAK) Registry data as summarised in InterTAK Registry review literature and StatPearls NBK430798 (Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy); consistent with the original Templin et al., N Engl J Med 2015 registry cohort

triggers.note: A major, clinically important real InterTAK Registry finding: physical stress triggers are AT LEAST as common as, and numerically more common than, emotional ('broken heart') triggers overall - correcting the popular assumption that TCM is mainly grief/heartbreak-driven.

sex_specific_distribution.note: Trigger type differs meaningfully by sex - men are disproportionately triggered by physical stress, women more evenly split, which is itself linked to men's higher observed complication/mortality rate (physical-trigger TTS carries worse prognosis, see natural_history).

triggers.source: Templin C et al., International Takotsubo (InterTAK) Registry, N Engl J Med 2015;373:929-938

pathophysiology.note: HONEST STATEMENT OF UNCERTAINTY: the exact mechanism of Takotsubo syndrome remains incompletely understood and is still actively debated in the literature; the leading hypothesis is a catecholamine/sympathetic-surge-driven process, but this is not proven as the sole mechanism and several complementary/competing mechanisms are proposed.
pathophysiology.leading_hypothesis: Acute catecholamine (epinephrine/norepinephrine) surge during severe emotional or physical stress causes direct myocardial toxicity/stunning, with the striking apical predominance proposed to result from a regional gradient in cardiac beta-2 adrenergic receptor density and signalling: at very high circulating epinephrine concentrations, beta-2 receptor signalling in the apex is proposed to switch from the normal stimulatory Gs-protein pathway to an inhibitory Gi-protein pathway, producing apical hypocontractility with basal hypercontractility - reproduced in an in vivo rat model with a high-dose epinephrine bolus.
pathophysiology.confidence: moderate - a real, influential, experimentally-supported model, but one candidate mechanism among several rather than settled consensus
pathophysiology.source: Paur H, Wright PT, Sikkel MB, et al., 'High Levels of Circulating Epinephrine Trigger Apical Cardiodepression in a beta2-Adrenergic Receptor/Gi-Dependent Manner: A New Model of Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy', Circulation 2012;126(6):697-706

other_proposed_mechanisms.note: Impaired coronary microvascular flow/reserve has been documented during the acute phase in a real subset of patients and is proposed as a contributing or alternative mechanism to direct catecholamine toxicity
other_proposed_mechanisms.source: Reviews on coronary microvascular dysfunction in Takotsubo syndrome (PMC10544771)

other_proposed_mechanisms.mechanism: Multi-vessel epicardial and microvascular coronary vasospasm
other_proposed_mechanisms.note: Catecholamine-driven vasospasm at epicardial and/or microvascular level proposed as a contributing mechanism producing transient regional ischaemia without fixed obstructive disease
other_proposed_mechanisms.source: Reviews on TTS pathophysiology (AHA Circulation 2016.027121, 'Pathophysiology of Takotsubo Syndrome')

other_proposed_mechanisms.note: Proposed to explain the striking postmenopausal female predominance - estrogen is thought to have a normally protective effect on catecholamine-induced vascular and myocardial injury that is lost after menopause
other_proposed_mechanisms.confidence: moderate - a real, widely-cited hypothesis explaining the demographic pattern, not itself definitively proven as causal
other_proposed_mechanisms.source: Cardioprotective Role of Estrogen in Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy, PMC8977075

epidemiology.female_predominance: 89.8% of 1,750 patients were women in the largest dedicated international registry - a striking, real sex skew far beyond that seen in ordinary IHD/ACS
epidemiology.postmenopausal_predominance: The great majority of affected women are postmenopausal; mean patient age in the registry was 66.4 years, consistent with a predominantly postmenopausal population
epidemiology.incidence_among_suspected_acs: Reported as approximately 1-2% of all troponin-positive suspected ACS presentations overall, and approximately 1-3% of all suspected STEMI presentations; the proportion rises substantially when only women presenting with suspected STEMI are considered (reported as high as ~6% in this subgroup)
epidemiology.confidence: high for the InterTAK Registry female-predominance and mean-age figures; moderate for the ACS-subgroup incidence range, which is pooled across several smaller single-center studies rather than one definitive registry figure
epidemiology.source: Templin C et al., International Takotsubo (InterTAK) Registry, N Engl J Med 2015;373:929-938; StatPearls NBK430798 and NBK538160 (Pathophysiology of Takotsubo Syndrome) for the ACS-subgroup incidence figures

lvot_obstruction.finding: Dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction is a real, mechanistically distinct complication of TCM: the hyperkinetic/hypercontractile basal segments (contrasted against the akinetic ballooned apex) narrow the LV outflow tract, sometimes together with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, producing a real dynamic subaortic pressure gradient that can itself cause or worsen hypotension and shock - critically, this means INOTROPES/catecholamines (which would be used empirically for hypotension of other causes) can WORSEN this specific complication, making its early echocardiographic recognition clinically important.
lvot_obstruction.incidence: Reported incidence varies by series, roughly 10-25% of TCM cases overall (individual two-center series report 19% [6/32] and 18% [58/322]; smaller series report up to 28-33%)
lvot_obstruction.confidence: high for the mechanism, moderate for the precise incidence given the wide 10-33% range across differing study populations/definitions
lvot_obstruction.source: Clinical impact of left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in takotsubo cardiomyopathy, PubMed 25739572; Prevalence, associated factors and management implications of LVOT obstruction in takotsubo cardiomyopathy, PMC4210484; LVOT obstruction in Takotsubo syndrome with cardiogenic shock: prognosis and treatment, PubMed 39209437

cardiogenic_shock.finding: A real, serious acute complication of TCM, not a theoretical risk - this is why acute TCM must be managed with the same urgency as true ACS-related cardiogenic shock (see cardiogenic_shock entry in this KB for the shared shock-management framework).
