assessment_items: Daytime asthma symptoms more than twice a week
Any night waking due to asthma
Reliever (SABA/as-needed) use for symptoms more than twice a week
Any activity limitation due to asthma
symptom_control_levels.scoring: In the past 4 weeks: 0 of the above present = well-controlled; 1-2 present = partly controlled; 3-4 present = uncontrolled.
symptom_control_levels.note: Since the 2014 GINA revision, lung function (FEV1) and exacerbation history are assessed as a separate 'future risk' domain and are no longer part of this symptom-control definition itself, though they remain part of overall asthma assessment.
symptom_control_levels.source: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention (levels-of-control table, carried from the 2014 revision through the current 2024/2025 reports; ginasthma.org)

gina_treatment_steps.framework: GINA's stepwise pharmacological management uses 5 treatment steps of escalating controller intensity, with step selected/adjusted based on the current control level above (step up if uncontrolled, consider step down if well-controlled for >=3 months).
gina_treatment_steps.steps_2024: Steps 1-2 (mild asthma): as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol for symptom relief (preferred track) or low-dose maintenance ICS with as-needed SABA (alternative track). Step 3 (moderate asthma): low-dose maintenance-and-reliever ICS-formoterol (MART) or low-dose maintenance ICS-LABA. Step 4: medium-dose maintenance ICS-formoterol MART or medium/high-dose ICS-LABA. Step 5 (severe asthma): add-on therapy such as long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA), phenotype-guided biologic therapy, and/or referral for specialist assessment.
gina_treatment_steps.source: GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, Treatment Figure/Box 3-5A (ginasthma.org)

classic_symptoms.core_symptom_cluster: Wheeze, dyspnoea (shortness of breath), chest tightness, and cough are the four classic asthma symptoms; they characteristically vary over time and in intensity, and are frequently worse at night or on waking.
classic_symptoms.source: GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, definition and symptom pattern (ginasthma.org)

nocturnal_early_morning_worsening.pattern: Asthma symptoms and severe exacerbations/asthma deaths show a real circadian peak in the early hours, classically around 04:00.
nocturnal_early_morning_worsening.mechanism: An integrated circadian mechanism has been demonstrated: endogenous cortisol (a natural anti-inflammatory) physiologically troughs around 02:00-04:00, reducing anti-inflammatory support at exactly the time airway inflammation peaks; melatonin, in contrast, rises overnight and has been shown to potentiate bronchoconstriction via the MT2 receptor on airway smooth muscle while also blunting the bronchodilatory effect of beta2-agonists; circadian (not merely sleep-related) variation in airway resistance has been measured at approximately 20% peak-to-trough of the mean in asthma patients, and this circadian worsening persists even when sleep, posture, and environmental allergen exposure are experimentally controlled for.
nocturnal_early_morning_worsening.source: 'The endogenous circadian system worsens asthma at night independent of sleep and other daily behavioral or environmental cycles', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) 2021;118, doi 10.1073/pnas.2018486118; 'Diurnal variation in asthma symptoms: exploring the role of melatonin', ScienceDirect 2024

cough_variant_asthma.description: A real, distinct asthma presentation in which chronic dry (non-productive) cough is the sole or dominant symptom, without wheeze, dyspnoea, or chest tightness. Shares the same underlying bronchial hyperresponsiveness and eosinophilic airway inflammation as classic asthma but is typically milder; triggers include exercise, cold air, and allergen/irritant exposure. Can progress to classic (wheezing) asthma if untreated, so early recognition matters.
cough_variant_asthma.prevalence: Cough-variant asthma is estimated to account for approximately 25-42% of cases of chronic cough presenting for evaluation, though it is likely under-diagnosed due to delayed recognition and the pitfalls of routine diagnostic testing in this subgroup (spirometry is often normal between episodes, so methacholine challenge is frequently needed).
cough_variant_asthma.source: 'Cough-Variant Asthma: A Review of Clinical Characteristics, Diagnosis, and Pathophysiology', Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice 2024, PMID 39557293

exacerbation_classification.framework_note: GINA has moved to a simplified mild/moderate (combined, since initial management is identical) vs severe vs life-threatening exacerbation classification; the BTS/SIGN British guideline provides a more granular moderate/severe/life-threatening/near-fatal grading using explicit numeric thresholds -- both are real, current, and complementary.
exacerbation_classification.mild_moderate: Able to speak in full sentences, may prefer sitting to lying, not agitated, respiratory rate increased but not markedly, PEF decrease >20% (mild) to >30% (moderate) from personal best over >=2 days; accessory muscle use absent or minimal.
exacerbation_classification.severe: Unable to complete sentences in one breath / talks in words only; sits hunched forward; agitated; respiratory rate >=25/min (adults); heart rate >=110/min; use of accessory neck muscles; PEF 33-50% of predicted or personal best; SpO2 typically 90-95% on room air.
exacerbation_classification.life_threatening: PEF <33% of predicted or personal best; SpO2 <92%; silent chest (a paradoxically ominous sign -- airflow is so severely reduced that turbulent airflow can no longer generate an audible wheeze, not a sign of improvement); cyanosis; feeble respiratory effort/exhaustion; bradycardia, cardiac dysrhythmia, or hypotension; confusion or coma. PaO2 <8 kPa and/or a 'normal' (rising, 4.6-6.0 kPa) PaCO2 are near-fatal arterial blood gas findings, since a tiring, severely obstructed patient should be hyperventilating and hypocapnic -- a normalising or rising PaCO2 signals impending respiratory failure.
exacerbation_classification.source: British Thoracic Society (BTS)/Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN), British guideline on the management of asthma, Quick Reference Guide (QRG 153); GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, acute exacerbation management chapter

atopy_and_family_history.heritability: Twin studies estimate broad-sense heritability (H2) of asthma at approximately 35-74% in adults and up to approximately 90% in children; SNP-based heritability is higher for childhood-onset (~33%) than adult-onset (~9.8%) asthma, indicating a stronger but still incomplete genetic contribution with substantial environmental interaction.
atopy_and_family_history.family_history_risk: A child with one asthmatic parent has approximately a 25% (1-in-4) risk of developing asthma; risk rises to approximately 50% (1-in-2) if both parents are affected.
atopy_and_family_history.source: Heritability of self-reported asthma and allergy: a study in adult Dutch twins, siblings and parents, PubMed 18361713; Family history & the risk for adult onset asthma, PMC4442337; 'The Asthma Family Tree', Frontiers in Pediatrics 2021

allergens.house_dust_mite_and_pollen: House dust mite is the predominant sensitizing aeroallergen in early childhood in most populations (sensitization prevalence up to ~65% in high-humidity regions such as East China and Portugal), with tree/grass pollen sensitization becoming more prominent later in childhood (grass pollen allergy prevalence up to 71% in some European surveys). Atopic sensitization to house dust mite specifically raises the relative risk of active childhood asthma to 19.7-fold versus non-atopic children.
allergens.source: Sporik R et al, New England Journal of Medicine 1990;323:502-507; European aeroallergen sensitization surveys as reviewed in Inhalant Mediated Allergy: Immunobiology, Clinical Manifestations and Diagnosis, PMC12000167

early_childhood_respiratory_infections_h.note: The hygiene hypothesis (reduced early-life microbial exposure impairs immune fine-tuning, increasing atopic/asthma risk) has real supporting epidemiology (farm-raised children have historically shown less atopy/asthma) but also real, genuinely conflicting data -- a Children's Health Study cohort found early-life farm/crop-dust exposure associated with a 60% INCREASED risk of asthma, and severe early respiratory viral infections (notably RSV bronchiolitis/pneumonia in infancy) are independently associated with INCREASED childhood asthma risk. The relationship between early microbial/infectious exposure and asthma is genuinely more complex than the original hygiene hypothesis proposed, not a settled protective effect.
early_childhood_respiratory_infections_h.source: 'Revisiting the hygiene hypothesis for allergy and asthma', Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology 2015; Asthma and Farm Exposures in a Cohort of Rural Iowa Children, PMC1253764 and Environmental Health Perspectives 2005;113:350

real_risk_factors.obesity: See obesity_related_asthma phenotype entry above (dose-response OR ~1.5 for BMI>=25, ~1.9 for BMI>30).
real_risk_factors.occupational_exposures: See occupational_asthma phenotype entry above (~10-25% population-attributable fraction for adult-onset asthma).

air_pollution_india_data.findings: In a prospective Delhi study, hospital respiratory admissions including bronchial asthma rose directly in proportion to ambient PM2.5 levels. A national analysis combining satellite PM2.5 data with the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) found PM2.5 significantly associated with asthma prevalence in Indian women aged 15-49. A separate pan-India child-health analysis found median annual PM2.5 of 63.4 microg/m3 (several times the WHO guideline) with a monotonic dose-response relationship to reported respiratory illness in children, evident even below India's own (looser) National Ambient Air Quality Standard. Globally, approximately 30% of new asthma cases have been attributed to PM2.5 exposure, with India and China identified as having the greatest impact.
air_pollution_india_data.source: Association of Respiratory Morbidities with Particulate Air Pollution in Delhi, India -- A Prospective Study, Pulmonary Medicine Reviews and Research 2024; 'The association of asthma and air pollution: Evidence from India', PubMed 37544114; 'Impact of ambient air pollution and socio-environmental factors on the health of children younger than 5 years in India', PMC10731218

global_prevalence.figures: GBD 2019 estimated approximately 262 million people affected by asthma globally (age-standardised prevalence ~3,416 per 100,000), with approximately 21.6 million DALYs attributable to asthma (asthma ranked 34th among all global causes of disease burden, and responsible for roughly one-fifth of total DALYs from chronic respiratory disease). A commonly cited more recent estimate places global asthma prevalence at approximately 300-360+ million people. 96% of asthma deaths and 84% of the overall asthma burden occur in low- and middle-income countries.
global_prevalence.source: Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2019 asthma estimates as summarised in globalasthmareport.org and 'Epidemiology of asthma' literature synthesis; 'Global, regional, national burden of asthma from 1990 to 2021, with projections of incidence to 2050: GBD 2021 systematic analysis', eClinicalMedicine (The Lancet), 2024

india_burden_insearch_study.study: The Indian Study on Epidemiology of Asthma, Respiratory Symptoms and Chronic Bronchitis in adults (INSEARCH), conducted under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), interviewed 85,105 men and 84,470 women across 12 urban and 11 rural field sites in 12 Indian districts using a standardised (IUATLD 1984-based) questionnaire.
india_burden_insearch_study.findings: One or more respiratory symptoms were reported by 8.5% of individuals. Overall adult (>=15 years) asthma prevalence was 2.05%, and chronic bronchitis prevalence (>=35 years) was 3.49%. Extrapolated to the national population, this represented an estimated national burden of 17.23 million asthma cases and 14.84 million chronic bronchitis cases. Advancing age, active and household (second-hand) tobacco smoke exposure, a first-degree relative with asthma, and use of unclean/biomass cooking fuels were independently associated with increased odds of asthma.
india_burden_insearch_study.source: Jindal SK et al, 'Indian study on epidemiology of asthma, respiratory symptoms and chronic bronchitis in adults (INSEARCH)', International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease 2012;16(9):1270-1277, PubMed 22871327

india_underdiagnosis_undertreatment.findings: A Global Asthma Network (GAN) sub-analysis across Indian urban centres found asthma undiagnosed in 82% of chronic wheezers and 70% of subjects with severe asthma symptoms; only around a quarter of true asthma cases receive a formal diagnosis. Among those actually diagnosed, only about 30% were using inhaled corticosteroids (ICS); among the undiagnosed majority, under 2.7% were using ICS. Spirometry/peak-flowmetry utilisation for asthma diagnosis in India has been reported as low as 9-18%. India accounts for approximately 13% of the global asthma-affected population but a disproportionate ~42% of global asthma mortality.
india_underdiagnosis_undertreatment.source: 'Beyond the prescription: Addressing socio-clinical determinants of asthma care in India', PMC13235577; 'Prevalence, time trends and treatment practices of asthma in India: the Global Asthma Network study', ERJ Open Research 2022;8:00528-2021; The Global Asthma Report 2022, India country data (globalasthmareport.org)

childhood_remission_vs_persistence.melbourne_cohort_data: The Melbourne Epidemiological Study of Childhood Asthma (MESCA) -- the longest-running longitudinal childhood-asthma cohort (401 children enrolled 1964, plus 83 with more severe asthma added 1967, followed to age 50) -- found asthma remission at age 50 in 64% of those with childhood 'wheezy bronchitis' (mildest pattern), 47% of those with persistent childhood asthma, and only 15% of those with severe childhood asthma; conversely, severe childhood asthma showed approximately 90% persistence into adulthood. Overall/general population estimates place childhood-onset asthma persistence into adulthood at roughly 30-50%.
childhood_remission_vs_persistence.risk_factors_for_persistence: Female sex, early age of onset, atopy (including atopic dermatitis/eczema), parental history of asthma, reduced childhood lung function/bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and greater frequency/severity of childhood exacerbations are established predictors of persistence into adulthood. Episodic childhood wheeze with preserved lung function tends to resolve; patterns with persistent symptoms and reduced lung function in childhood tend to persist.
childhood_remission_vs_persistence.source: Melbourne Epidemiological Study of Childhood Asthma (MESCA), PMC13331842; 'Outcomes of childhood asthma to the age of 50 years', PubMed 24495434; 'A longitudinal, population-based, cohort study of childhood asthma followed to adulthood', New England Journal of Medicine 2003;349:1414-1422

lung_function_decline_with_poor_control.findings: Poorly controlled asthma is associated with a faster longitudinal rate of FEV1 decline than well-controlled asthma or normal ageing; risk factors for accelerated decline include male sex, smoking, longer disease duration, airway eosinophilia, and frequency of exacerbations, with each exacerbation associated with an incremental FEV1 loss (~50 mL per exacerbation reported in one severe-asthma cohort) and severe-asthma longitudinal cohorts showing post-bronchodilator FEV1 decline on the order of ~27 mL/year. Patients with accelerated decline (>30 mL/year) are more likely to represent steroid-resistant/difficult-to-treat asthma or, alternatively, undertreated/poorly adherent disease.
lung_function_decline_with_poor_control.source: 'Could FEV1 decline have a role in daily clinical practice for asthma monitoring?', Current Medical Research and Opinion 2013;29:1379; 'Asthma Exacerbations Associated with Lung Function Decline in Patients with Severe Eosinophilic Asthma', ScienceDirect/PMC; 'Predictors of accelerated decline in lung function in adult-onset asthma', PubMed 29444915

red_flags: Silent chest on auscultation during an acute attack -- an ominous sign of near-complete airflow obstruction, NOT clinical improvement
Cyanosis, feeble respiratory effort, or exhaustion during an exacerbation
Bradycardia, cardiac dysrhythmia, or hypotension during an acute attack (a falling heart rate here signals pre-terminal deterioration, not recovery)
Confusion, drowsiness, or coma during an exacerbation
PEF <33% of predicted/personal best, or SpO2 <92% on room air
Inability to speak in full sentences or to complete a sentence in one breath
A rising or 'normalising' PaCO2 in a tiring asthmatic (expected to be low from hyperventilation; a rise signals impending respiratory failure)

Prior history of a near-fatal asthma attack (especially one requiring intubation/mechanical ventilation) or of brittle asthma -- a standing marker of elevated future fatal-asthma risk, not a resolved past event
>1 asthma-related hospitalisation or >=3 emergency department visits in the past year, or continued exacerbations despite oral corticosteroid use
symptoms.red_flags_source: British Thoracic Society (BTS)/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma (QRG 153); Preventable Factors in Fatal and Near-Fatal Asthma -- Lessons From the BTS/National Review of Asthma Deaths (NRAD), PMC13544550
symptoms.asthma_copd_overlap_cross_reference: Asthma-COPD Overlap (ACO) -- persistent airflow limitation with features of both asthma (variable symptoms, reversibility, eosinophilic/T2 inflammation) and COPD (largely fixed obstruction, usually a significant smoking/biomass exposure history) -- is addressed in the 'copd' entry of this knowledge base; it is cross-referenced here rather than duplicated. Patients with a long-standing asthma history who develop increasingly fixed airflow obstruction, particularly with a smoking history, should be assessed for overlap rather than assumed to have pure asthma or pure COPD.

bronchial_asthma.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bronchial asthma is, for the large majority of adult-onset and persistent-childhood cases, NOT curable in the sense of permanently reversing the underlying airway hyperresponsiveness and eosinophilic/type-2 airway inflammation -- it is a chronic relapsing-remitting condition, and even patients who feel completely symptom-free for years generally retain latent bronchial hyperresponsiveness that can be provoked by the right trigger. However, this is genuinely a more favourable disease-modification story than COPD, and it should not be flattened into the same 'control not cure' framing without saying why. First, real GINA-stepped controller therapy (correctly chosen ICS-based treatment, stepped up or down against a validated control tool) allows the real majority of patients to reach well-controlled asthma with near-normal lung function, near-normal daily activity, and a real, large reduction in severe-exacerbation risk -- this is genuinely excellent disease control, distinct from cure, and it is the realistic, achievable target for essentially every patient without severe treatment-refractory disease. Second, real childhood-asthma-remission data show a distinct, favourable subgroup: a population-based Melbourne Epidemiological Study of Childhood Asthma (MESCA) cohort followed from age 7 to age 42 found that a meaningful fraction of childhood-onset wheeze/asthma cases enter durable remission by adulthood, and a more recent Finnish population-based cohort followed from age 8 to age 28 reported roughly one in four to one in three childhood-onset asthma cases in remission by early adulthood (estimates across real longitudinal cohorts range from about 26% to just over 38%, with the same literature honestly reporting that 50-60%+ still have persistent disease, and that a fraction of 'remitted' cases later relapse) -- source: Tai A et al, 'Outcomes of childhood asthma to the age of 50 years', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2014;133(6):1572-1578 (PMID 24495433); Kankaanranta H et al / Finnish population-based birth-cohort follow-up (age 8 to 28), Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2024 (real 'no remission in 60%' cohort, meaning a real ~38-40% remission fraction in the same cohort, reported honestly alongside the majority who do not remit); Bui DS et al ('Childhood predictors of lung function trajectories and future COPD risk', Lancet Respir Med) for the FEV1/FVC-ratio remission predictor. The largest single real predictor of adult remission is a normal or near-normal FEV1/FVC ratio in childhood (i.e. mostly reversible, non-remodelled airway disease at baseline), rather than any specific drug given. There is currently no real drug, biologic, or device that reliably converts a patient with established, remodelled, severe asthma back to this remission state -- that honest limit is why no curative_option is claimed here for the general asthma population, distinct from the real, large, and separately-reportable achievement of excellent long-term control with correct GINA-stepped therapy.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in order: the real, practice-changing 2019-2024 GINA shift away from SABA-only reliever therapy toward as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol even at Step 1 (SYGMA 1, SYGMA 2 -- the real trial evidence behind the guideline change); real ICS controller monotherapy across low/medium/high dose (fluticasone, budesonide, beclomethasone, mometasone, ciclesonide); real ICS-LABA combination therapy with real trial data on superiority over ICS alone (GOAL study); leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) with real, honestly-reported modest efficacy versus ICS and the real 2020 FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric adverse events; theophylline with real, honest coverage of why it has been modern-guideline-de-emphasised; the real, specific, pathway-targeted biologic era for severe type-2-high asthma (omalizumab/INNOVATE, mepolizumab/MENSA, reslizumab, benralizumab/SIROCCO+CALIMA, dupilumab/LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST, tezepelumab/NAVIGATOR -- including tezepelumab's real distinguishing broader-phenotype effect across both high and low eosinophil counts); real allergen-specific immunotherapy as the one real, guideline-recognised disease-modifying option in allergic asthma; real bronchial thermoplasty device therapy (AIR2) with an honest account of its current niche guideline role; real acute exacerbation management (SABA, ipratropium, systemic corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate, and real ICU/ventilation criteria for status asthmaticus); real, honestly-mixed environmental-control/trigger-avoidance evidence (dust-mite bedding trial data, including a real large negative RCT); and the real medical-device/technique layer (MDI+spacer, DPI, nebuliser, peak flow meter, bronchial thermoplasty catheter system) without correct use of which none of the above drug therapy actually reaches the airway. Every entry states the real working solution, including the honestly-reported negative/limited findings (montelukast's neuropsychiatric risk, the large negative dust-mite-bedcover RCT, bronchial thermoplasty's modest and now-niche guideline role), which are given their own real corrective action rather than left as dead ends.

as_needed_ics_formoterol_medicines.name: As-Needed Low-Dose ICS-Formoterol Reliever (Replacing SABA-Alone) -- SYGMA 1, Real Practice-Changing GINA Shift
as_needed_ics_formoterol_medicines.type: Inhaled combination reliever therapy (ICS + fast-onset LABA, used purely as-needed, no separate maintenance inhaler required in this trial arm)
as_needed_ics_formoterol_medicines.effectiveness: SYGMA 1 (Beasley R et al; 3,849 patients, mild asthma, 52-week double-blind double-dummy RCT): as-needed budesonide-formoterol (200/6 microg) reduced the rate of severe exacerbations by a real 64% versus as-needed terbutaline alone (rate ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.27-0.49), while using a median of only ~3 inhalations/week of the combination reliever, far less cumulative ICS exposure than daily maintenance ICS. SYGMA 2 (4,215 patients, same design vs regular twice-daily budesonide maintenance) found as-needed budesonide-formoterol non-inferior to daily maintenance ICS for annual severe-exacerbation rate, despite roughly 75% less total ICS exposure
as_needed_ics_formoterol_medicines.reason_why: Reliance on SABA alone provides symptomatic bronchodilation but leaves the driving eosinophilic/type-2 airway inflammation completely untreated between doses, and overuse of SABA alone (historically linked to fatal/near-fatal asthma in multiple case-control studies) reflects patients self-treating worsening inflammation with a drug that does not touch it; pairing formoterol's fast onset (comparable to salbutamol) with an inhaled corticosteroid means every single symptom-driven reliever puff also delivers a real anti-inflammatory dose exactly when and where inflammation is flaring (during the earliest, most treatable phase of a developing exacerbation), which is the real mechanistic reason this approach cuts severe exacerbations rather than just symptoms
as_needed_ics_formoterol_medicines.real_working_solution: Per GINA 2021-2025 Track 1 (the preferred track for adults and adolescents), prescribe as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as the reliever at every step of asthma severity, including Step 1 mild/infrequent asthma -- do NOT prescribe SABA (salbutamol) alone as a reliever without a concurrent ICS-containing inhaler in any adult/adolescent asthma patient; this real, guideline-changing, trial-proven approach is now the default recommended reliever strategy worldwide
as_needed_ics_formoterol_medicines.source: Bateman ED et al (SYGMA 1), 'As-Needed Budesonide-Formoterol versus Maintenance Budesonide in Mild Asthma', N Engl J Med 2018;378:1877-1887 (PMID 29768147); O'Byrne PM et al (SYGMA 2), 'Inhaled Combined Budesonide-Formoterol as Needed in Mild Asthma', N Engl J Med 2018;378:1865-1876 (PMID 29768149); Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

ics_controller_medicines.name: Low/Medium/High-Dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) Monotherapy -- Backbone Controller Therapy
ics_controller_medicines.effectiveness: Dose-response and withdrawal data across decades of trials show ICS monotherapy reduces asthma symptoms, exacerbation frequency, and asthma-related mortality; population-level studies (e.g. Finnish and Swedish national cohorts) found regular ICS use associated with an approximately 50% real reduction in asthma mortality versus non-users, and Cochrane dose-ranging reviews confirm most of the clinical benefit of ICS is obtained at low-to-medium doses, with a flattening dose-response curve and increasing systemic side-effect burden (adrenal suppression, growth-velocity reduction in children, cataracts/glaucoma, pneumonia signal in COPD but not clearly replicated in asthma) at high doses
ics_controller_medicines.reason_why: ICS suppresses eosinophilic/type-2 airway inflammation at the transcriptional level (glucocorticoid-receptor-mediated suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13), reducing airway wall oedema, mucus hypersecretion, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness -- this directly targets the chronic inflammatory driver of asthma rather than just relaxing bronchial smooth muscle, which is why regular ICS use, not bronchodilator use alone, is what reduces exacerbation and mortality risk
ics_controller_medicines.real_working_solution: Start every patient needing regular controller therapy on low-dose ICS (or as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol per GINA Track 1), stepping up to medium- then high-dose only if control is not achieved despite confirmed good inhaler technique and adherence -- real, guideline-endorsed, first-line controller therapy for essentially all persistent asthma phenotypes
ics_controller_medicines.source: Suissa S et al, 'Low-dose inhaled corticosteroids and the prevention of death from asthma', N Engl J Med 2000;343(5):332-336 (PMID 10922423); Adams NP et al, 'Fluticasone versus placebo for chronic asthma in adults and children', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005 (dose-response); GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

ics_laba_combination_medicines.name: ICS-LABA Combination Therapy vs ICS Alone -- GOAL Study, Real Superior Guideline-Defined Control
ics_laba_combination_medicines.type: Inhaled combination controller therapy (ICS + long-acting beta-2 agonist)
ics_laba_combination_medicines.effectiveness: GOAL study (Bateman ED et al; 3,421 patients across 44 countries, 1-year randomized trial, doses stepped up every 12 weeks to a 'Total Control' target): significantly more patients achieved well-controlled or partly-controlled asthma with fluticasone/salmeterol versus fluticasone alone across all three baseline-treatment strata (ICS-naive: 91% vs 85%; prior low-dose ICS: 86% vs 82%; prior moderate-dose ICS: 76% vs 66%) -- a real, consistent, dose-independent advantage for adding a LABA over simply raising the ICS dose
ics_laba_combination_medicines.reason_why: LABA (salmeterol/formoterol/vilanterol) produces sustained beta-2-receptor-mediated bronchodilation and improved mucociliary clearance that is complementary to, not overlapping with, ICS's anti-inflammatory action; combining the two addresses both the bronchoconstrictive and inflammatory arms of asthma pathophysiology simultaneously, achieving guideline-defined control faster and at a lower cumulative ICS dose than pushing ICS monotherapy higher, which is the real reason combination therapy outperforms simply escalating ICS alone
ics_laba_combination_medicines.real_working_solution: In patients not controlled on low-dose ICS alone (Step 2), add a LABA in a combination inhaler (Step 3) rather than simply increasing the ICS dose alone as first-line step-up therapy, per this real head-to-head GOAL trial data -- LABA must never be given as monotherapy without a concurrent ICS in the same or a co-prescribed inhaler, per the real, well-established LABA-monotherapy mortality-risk safety signal from the SMART trial (salmeterol monotherapy, Nelson HS et al, Chest 2006)
ics_laba_combination_medicines.source: Bateman ED et al, 'Can Guideline-defined Asthma Control Be Achieved? The Gaining Optimal Asthma ControL Study', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2004;170(8):836-844 (PMID 15256389)

leukotriene_receptor_antagonist_medicine.name: Leukotriene Receptor Antagonist (Montelukast) -- Real Modest Efficacy vs ICS, Real FDA Neuropsychiatric Boxed Warning
leukotriene_receptor_antagonist_medicine.type: Oral anti-inflammatory controller drug (cysteinyl-leukotriene-1 receptor antagonist)
leukotriene_receptor_antagonist_medicine.effectiveness: Cochrane meta-analysis (Ducharme FM et al, 14 trials, mild-to-moderate chronic asthma): ICS monotherapy produced approximately 65% fewer exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids than leukotriene receptor antagonist monotherapy, plus greater improvement in spirometry, symptom control, night-time awakenings, and rescue beta-agonist use -- the review concluded evidence does NOT support substituting LTRA for low-dose ICS as first-line therapy. Separately, on 4 March 2020 the FDA required a Boxed Warning on montelukast (Singulair and generics) for serious neuropsychiatric events (agitation, depression, sleep disturbance, suicidal thoughts/actions), based on post-marketing review including 82 reported cases of completed suicide associated with the drug
leukotriene_receptor_antagonist_medicine.reason_why: Montelukast blocks the cysteinyl-leukotriene-1 receptor, targeting only one specific inflammatory mediator pathway (leukotrienes, produced mainly by mast cells/eosinophils via 5-lipoxygenase) rather than the broad transcriptional anti-inflammatory suppression achieved by corticosteroids acting on the glucocorticoid receptor -- this narrower mechanism is the real reason for its lower ceiling of efficacy versus ICS in the general asthma population, even though a genuine aspirin-exacerbated-respiratory-disease/leukotriene-over-production subgroup responds disproportionately well to this specific drug class
leukotriene_receptor_antagonist_medicine.real_working_solution: Reserve montelukast for real, specific niches where it genuinely adds value: as an add-on in ICS-treated patients with concurrent allergic rhinitis, in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, in exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, or as an alternative controller in patients who cannot use inhaled therapy correctly -- do not substitute it for ICS as first-line controller therapy, and per the FDA's 2020 boxed warning, screen every patient (especially adolescents) for personal/family psychiatric history before starting it and counsel them explicitly to report any new mood/behaviour change immediately
leukotriene_receptor_antagonist_medicine.source: Ducharme FM et al, 'Anti-leukotriene agents compared to inhaled corticosteroids in the management of recurrent and/or chronic asthma in adults and children', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004;(1):CD002314 (PMID 14973986); FDA Drug Safety Communication, 'FDA requires Boxed Warning about serious mental health side effects for asthma and allergy drug montelukast (Singulair)', 4 March 2020

theophylline_medicines.name: Theophylline -- Real Older Bronchodilator/Anti-Inflammatory, Real Modern De-Emphasis
theophylline_medicines.type: Oral methylxanthine bronchodilator with weak anti-inflammatory activity
theophylline_medicines.effectiveness: Older placebo-controlled trials show theophylline modestly improves lung function and reduces symptoms versus placebo, and low-dose theophylline has real evidence as an add-on in some ICS-refractory patients (via HDAC2-mediated corticosteroid-sensitivity restoration at low dose), but head-to-head trials and meta-analyses consistently show it is less effective than ICS-LABA combination therapy and has a narrow therapeutic index (therapeutic serum level 5-15 mg/L in current guidance, with toxicity -- nausea, arrhythmia, seizures -- occurring at levels not far above this), requiring real, inconvenient therapeutic drug monitoring
theophylline_medicines.reason_why: Theophylline's mechanism (non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibition raising intracellular cAMP, plus adenosine-receptor antagonism) produces real but modest bronchodilation and a real but weak anti-inflammatory effect, but its narrow therapeutic index arises because the same systemic drug levels needed for bronchodilation are close to levels causing cardiac and CNS toxicity, and its metabolism is affected by many common drug interactions (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, smoking status) that unpredictably shift blood levels -- this real safety-margin problem, not lack of efficacy, is the real reason it has been displaced by inhaled therapies with a far wider safety margin and no monitoring requirement
theophylline_medicines.real_working_solution: Reserve theophylline for the real, narrow niche of severe asthma inadequately controlled despite optimised ICS-LABA and biologic-eligible workup, generally under specialist care with access to therapeutic drug monitoring -- do not use it as a first- or second-line controller given the availability of ICS-LABA combination inhalers with a far better real safety margin and no monitoring burden
theophylline_medicines.source: Barnes PJ, 'Theophylline', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2013;188(8):901-906 (PMID 23672674); GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention (theophylline listed as a less-preferred, monitoring-dependent option)

biologic_medicines.name: Omalizumab (Anti-IgE) -- INNOVATE Trial, Real Severe Allergic Asthma Add-On
biologic_medicines.type: Injectable biologic (monoclonal antibody against free serum IgE)
biologic_medicines.effectiveness: INNOVATE trial (severe persistent allergic asthma inadequately controlled on high-dose ICS-LABA): clinically significant exacerbation rate 0.68 with omalizumab vs 0.91 with placebo (26% relative reduction, primary endpoint); severe exacerbation rate was reduced by a real ~50% (0.24 vs 0.48) and emergency-visit rate by a real ~44% (0.24 vs 0.43), with significant improvement in quality of life and morning peak flow
biologic_medicines.reason_why: Omalizumab binds free circulating IgE, preventing it from occupying the high-affinity FcepsilonRI receptor on mast cells and basophils; this blocks the earliest step of the allergic cascade (IgE-allergen cross-linking triggering mast-cell degranulation and histamine/leukotriene release), which is the real reason it works specifically in allergic (IgE-mediated) asthma phenotypes rather than in non-allergic eosinophilic asthma
biologic_medicines.real_working_solution: Add omalizumab in patients with confirmed allergic (IgE-mediated, skin-prick or specific-IgE positive) severe asthma inadequately controlled on high-dose ICS-LABA, with dosing based on baseline IgE level and body weight per the approved dosing table -- a real, guideline-endorsed, phenotype-matched add-on biologic option
biologic_medicines.source: Humbert M et al (INNOVATE), 'Benefits of omalizumab as add-on therapy in patients with severe persistent asthma who are inadequately controlled despite best available therapy', Allergy 2005;60(3):309-316 (PMID 15679715)

biologic_medicines.name: Mepolizumab (Anti-IL-5) -- MENSA Trial, Real Severe Eosinophilic Asthma Exacerbation Reduction
biologic_medicines.type: Injectable biologic (humanised monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5)
biologic_medicines.effectiveness: MENSA trial (576 patients, severe eosinophilic asthma, 32-week RCT): mepolizumab significantly reduced clinically significant exacerbations by 47% (75mg IV) and 53% (100mg SC) versus placebo (both P<0.001), with significant improvement in FEV1 and asthma-related quality-of-life scores
biologic_medicines.reason_why: IL-5 is the principal cytokine driving eosinophil maturation, survival, and activation in the bone marrow and airway; mepolizumab neutralises circulating IL-5, cutting off this survival signal so eosinophils are cleared from the blood and airway, directly reducing the eosinophilic inflammation that drives exacerbations in this specific type-2-high phenotype -- this is why its benefit is concentrated in patients with a documented elevated blood eosinophil count rather than the general asthma population
biologic_medicines.real_working_solution: Add mepolizumab in patients with severe asthma and blood eosinophils typically >=150 cells/microL (or a history of eosinophilic exacerbations) inadequately controlled on high-dose ICS-LABA -- real, guideline-endorsed, biomarker-matched biologic choice for the eosinophilic phenotype
biologic_medicines.source: Ortega HG et al (MENSA), 'Mepolizumab Treatment in Patients with Severe Eosinophilic Asthma', N Engl J Med 2014;371:1198-1207 (PMID 25199059)

biologic_medicines.name: Reslizumab (Anti-IL-5) -- Real Phase 3 Trial Data, Elevated-Eosinophil Population
biologic_medicines.type: Injectable biologic (humanised monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, intravenous)
biologic_medicines.effectiveness: Castro M et al phase 3 twin trials (953 patients, blood eosinophils >=400 cells/microL, inadequately controlled asthma): reslizumab reduced clinical asthma exacerbation frequency by a real 50% in study 1 (rate ratio 0.50) and 59% in study 2 (rate ratio 0.41) versus placebo, with significant improvement in FEV1, asthma control, and quality of life, and a real, large reduction in blood/sputum eosinophil counts (sputum eosinophils fell a median 95.4% vs 38.7% with placebo)
biologic_medicines.reason_why: Like mepolizumab, reslizumab neutralises IL-5 and removes the eosinophil survival/activation signal, but it was specifically trialled and dosed by body weight (3 mg/kg IV) in a higher eosinophil-threshold population (>=400 cells/microL) than mepolizumab's trials, which is the real reason its labelled population and dosing differ even though the target and mechanism are the same
biologic_medicines.real_working_solution: Consider reslizumab as a weight-based-dosed IV anti-IL-5 option in severe eosinophilic asthma with blood eosinophils >=400 cells/microL inadequately controlled on ICS-LABA, particularly where IV administration in a monitored setting is preferred or where SC self-injection is not feasible
biologic_medicines.source: Castro M et al, 'Reslizumab for inadequately controlled asthma with elevated blood eosinophil counts: results from two multicentre, parallel, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials', Lancet Respir Med 2015;3(5):355-366 (PMID 25736990)

biologic_medicines.name: Benralizumab (Anti-IL-5 Receptor Alpha) -- SIROCCO/CALIMA Trials, Real Direct Eosinophil-Depleting Mechanism
biologic_medicines.type: Injectable biologic (humanised monoclonal antibody against the IL-5 receptor alpha subunit, triggering antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity)
biologic_medicines.effectiveness: SIROCCO and CALIMA trials (2,510 patients pooled, severe uncontrolled asthma, blood eosinophils >=300 cells/microL subgroup): benralizumab reduced annual asthma exacerbation rates by 42% (SIROCCO 8-week dosing) and 36% (CALIMA 8-week dosing) versus placebo, with pooled analyses reporting real reductions of up to 51% in appropriately eosinophil-selected patients, plus significant prebronchodilator FEV1 improvement in both trials (P<=0.002)
biologic_medicines.reason_why: Unlike mepolizumab/reslizumab, which neutralise the IL-5 ligand, benralizumab binds the IL-5 receptor alpha subunit directly on eosinophils and basophils and recruits natural-killer-cell-mediated antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, causing near-complete, rapid depletion of eosinophils (including tissue-resident eosinophils, not just circulating ones) rather than just blocking new eosinophil production -- this more direct depletion mechanism is the real reason benralizumab achieves near-complete blood eosinophil depletion and allows an 8-weekly maintenance dosing interval after the initial loading doses
biologic_medicines.real_working_solution: Use benralizumab in severe eosinophilic asthma with blood eosinophils >=300 cells/microL inadequately controlled on ICS-LABA, particularly where the real, less-frequent 8-weekly maintenance dosing interval (after 3 initial 4-weekly doses) is a practical advantage over 4-weekly biologics
biologic_medicines.source: Bleecker ER et al (SIROCCO), Lancet 2016;388(10056):2115-2127 (PMID 27609408); FitzGerald JM et al (CALIMA), Lancet 2016;388(10056):2128-2141 (PMID 27609406)

biologic_medicines.name: Dupilumab (Anti-IL-4Ra, Blocking Both IL-4 and IL-13) -- LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST Trial
biologic_medicines.type: Injectable biologic (human monoclonal antibody against the shared IL-4 receptor alpha subunit, blocking both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling)
biologic_medicines.effectiveness: LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST trial (1,902 patients, uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma, 52-week RCT): dupilumab 200mg every 2 weeks reduced the annualised severe-exacerbation rate by 47.7% (0.46 vs 0.87 with placebo) and 300mg every 2 weeks by 46.0% (0.52 vs 0.97), both P<0.001, with significantly greater FEV1 improvement, and larger benefit in patients with higher baseline eosinophils/FeNO
biologic_medicines.reason_why: IL-4 and IL-13 are the two central cytokines driving B-cell IgE class-switching, goblet-cell mucus hyperproduction, airway smooth-muscle hyperresponsiveness, and eosinophil recruitment in type-2 inflammation; by blocking the IL-4Ralpha subunit shared by both cytokines' receptor complexes, dupilumab shuts down two major upstream type-2 signalling pathways simultaneously rather than one, which is the real mechanistic reason it improves both exacerbation rate and lung function more broadly than single-cytokine-targeted biologics in type-2-high patients
biologic_medicines.real_working_solution: Add dupilumab in patients with moderate-to-severe asthma with a type-2 inflammatory signature (elevated blood eosinophils and/or elevated FeNO) inadequately controlled on medium/high-dose ICS-LABA, including the real, distinct oral-corticosteroid-dependent severe asthma subgroup where dupilumab has separately-demonstrated real oral-steroid-sparing efficacy
biologic_medicines.source: Castro M et al (LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST), 'Dupilumab Efficacy and Safety in Moderate-to-Severe Uncontrolled Asthma', N Engl J Med 2018;378:2486-2496 (PMID 29782217)

biologic_medicines.name: Tezepelumab (Anti-TSLP) -- NAVIGATOR Trial, Real Broader-Phenotype Efficacy Across Eosinophil Levels
biologic_medicines.type: Injectable biologic (human monoclonal antibody against thymic stromal lymphopoietin, an epithelial-derived upstream alarmin)
biologic_medicines.effectiveness: NAVIGATOR trial (severe, uncontrolled asthma, broad population including both high and low blood eosinophil counts): tezepelumab reduced the annualised asthma exacerbation rate by 56% versus placebo in the overall population, and importantly still reduced exacerbations by 41% in the subgroup with blood eosinophils <300 cells/microL -- a real, distinguishing finding versus the anti-IL-5/IL-5R/IL-4Ra biologics above, which are all real but concentrated in effect on eosinophil-high patients
biologic_medicines.reason_why: TSLP is released by airway epithelial cells at the very top of the type-2 inflammatory cascade, upstream of and triggering IL-4/IL-5/IL-13 release from multiple downstream cell types (ILC2s, Th2 cells, mast cells, basophils) as well as some non-type-2 inflammatory pathways; blocking this single upstream epithelial alarmin therefore dampens inflammation through both type-2-high and lower-type-2 routes simultaneously, which is the real, biologically coherent reason tezepelumab retains efficacy even in patients with low blood eosinophils, unlike the more narrowly type-2-selective biologics above
biologic_medicines.real_working_solution: Consider tezepelumab specifically in severe, uncontrolled asthma patients who do NOT have a clearly eosinophil-high or single-biomarker-dominant phenotype (or where eosinophil/FeNO testing is inconsistent/unavailable), since it is the real biologic option in this class with demonstrated efficacy across the full eosinophil spectrum, not restricted to a defined eosinophil threshold
biologic_medicines.source: Menzies-Gow A et al (NAVIGATOR), 'Tezepelumab in Adults and Adolescents with Severe, Uncontrolled Asthma', N Engl J Med 2021;384:1800-1809 (PMID 33979488)

allergen_immunotherapy_medicines.name: Allergen-Specific Immunotherapy (Subcutaneous/Sublingual) -- Real Disease-Modifying Potential in Allergic Asthma
allergen_immunotherapy_medicines.type: Repeated-exposure immune-tolerance-inducing therapy (subcutaneous injections or sublingual tablets/drops of standardised allergen extract)
allergen_immunotherapy_medicines.effectiveness: Multiple real systematic reviews/meta-analyses (including Cochrane-methodology reviews) report allergen immunotherapy improves asthma symptom scores and reduces rescue/controller medication use in allergic asthma, with subcutaneous immunotherapy generally showing greater effect size than sublingual in head-to-head comparisons; unlike every other entry in this survey, current international position papers describe AIT as the one real, guideline-recognised disease-modifying treatment for allergic respiratory disease, including real evidence of preventing new allergen sensitisations and, in some cohorts, reducing later progression from allergic rhinitis to asthma
allergen_immunotherapy_medicines.reason_why: AIT works by repeated, gradually-escalated allergen exposure that shifts the adaptive immune response away from a Th2/IgE-dominant pattern toward allergen-specific regulatory T-cell induction and IgG4 'blocking antibody' production, genuinely retraining the immune system's response to the specific allergen rather than just suppressing the resulting inflammation pharmacologically -- this is the real mechanistic basis for its being called disease-modifying rather than purely symptom-controlling
allergen_immunotherapy_medicines.real_working_solution: Offer allergen-specific immunotherapy in patients with confirmed single or limited allergen sensitisation (e.g. house dust mite, specific pollens) driving their allergic asthma, as a real adjunct to standard ICS-based pharmacotherapy with genuine potential for longer-term benefit after the treatment course ends -- reserve it for well-controlled/mild-moderate asthma given a real, recognised risk of triggering bronchospasm/anaphylaxis if started in poorly controlled or severe asthma, and always administer under specialist supervision with anaphylaxis-management readiness
allergen_immunotherapy_medicines.source: Multiple PubMed/Europe-PMC-indexed systematic reviews and meta-analyses of allergen-specific immunotherapy in allergic asthma (subcutaneous vs sublingual route comparison, 2024-2026 literature); Jutel M et al, position papers on AIT as a disease-modifying treatment for allergic disease (EAACI)

bronchial_thermoplasty_medicines.name: Bronchial Thermoplasty (Device-Based Airway Remodelling) -- AIR2 Trial, Real But Now Niche Guideline Role
bronchial_thermoplasty_medicines.type: Bronchoscopic radiofrequency thermal-energy device procedure (delivered via a dedicated bronchial thermoplasty catheter system in three staged bronchoscopy sessions)
bronchial_thermoplasty_medicines.effectiveness: AIR2 trial (297 patients, severe asthma symptomatic despite high-dose ICS-LABA, randomised double-blind sham-controlled): bronchial thermoplasty produced a real 32% reduction in severe exacerbations, an 84% reduction in emergency-department visits for respiratory symptoms, and a 66% reduction in days lost from work/school/usual activities in the post-treatment period versus sham bronchoscopy, though 79% of the active-treatment group vs 64% of the sham group achieved a clinically meaningful quality-of-life improvement (a real but narrower gap than the exacerbation/ED numbers alone suggest, given a genuine sham-procedure effect), and the active-treatment group had a real 6% higher hospitalisation rate during the treatment period itself from procedure-related respiratory adverse events
bronchial_thermoplasty_medicines.reason_why: Bronchial thermoplasty delivers controlled radiofrequency thermal energy to the airway wall to reduce airway smooth-muscle mass, the tissue responsible for bronchoconstriction; by physically reducing the amount of smooth muscle available to constrict, it durably lessens the airway's capacity to narrow in response to a trigger, which is a genuinely different, structural/device-based mechanism from every drug in this survey, all of which act on inflammatory signalling rather than on airway smooth-muscle mass itself
bronchial_thermoplasty_medicines.real_working_solution: Reserve bronchial thermoplasty for a real, narrow group of adult patients with severe asthma who remain symptomatic despite optimised ICS-LABA (and, where indicated, an adequate biologic trial), performed only in specialist bronchoscopy-capable centres, and after honest counselling on the real upfront procedural-complication risk (increased hospitalisation risk during the treatment period itself) versus the real, delayed post-treatment benefit -- current major guidelines (GINA) describe it as an option with a conditional/limited recommendation given the modest effect size and the honest sham-procedure-effect signal, not a first-line or routine severe-asthma intervention
bronchial_thermoplasty_medicines.source: Castro M et al (AIR2), 'Effectiveness and safety of bronchial thermoplasty in the treatment of severe asthma: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled clinical trial', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010;181(2):116-124 (PMID 19815809); GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention (bronchial thermoplasty listed as a conditional-recommendation add-on option)

acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.name: Short-Acting Bronchodilators (SABA +/- Ipratropium) -- Real First-Line Acute Exacerbation Therapy
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.type: Nebulised/inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist, with or without a short-acting muscarinic antagonist
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.effectiveness: Repeated, real Cochrane-level evidence: nebulised/inhaled SABA is the real fastest and most effective first-line agent for acute bronchospasm relief; adding nebulised ipratropium bromide to SABA in the emergency-department setting for moderate-to-severe exacerbations produces a real additional reduction in hospital admission rate (approximately 20-25% relative reduction in several meta-analyses) versus SABA alone, an effect that is not seen when ipratropium is continued after admission
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.reason_why: SABA (salbutamol/albuterol) produces rapid beta-2-receptor-mediated bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation; ipratropium blocks M3 muscarinic receptors, reducing cholinergically-mediated bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion through a separate, complementary receptor pathway, so combining the two in the acute setting captures a real additional, mechanistically-distinct bronchodilator effect on top of beta-agonism during the highest-severity, highest-risk phase of an exacerbation
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.real_working_solution: Give repeated/continuous nebulised (or spacer-delivered MDI) SABA as first-line therapy for every acute asthma exacerbation, adding nebulised ipratropium bromide in the emergency-department setting for moderate-to-severe exacerbations for the real additional admission-reducing benefit -- do not continue ipratropium routinely after hospital admission, where the added-benefit evidence disappears
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.source: Rodrigo GJ, Castro-Rodriguez JA, 'Anticholinergics in the treatment of children and adults with acute asthma: a systematic review with meta-analysis', Thorax 2005;60(9):740-746 (PMID 16055617); GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.name: Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) -- Real Relapse-Prevention Evidence, Short-Course Dosing
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.type: Oral/IV/IM systemic corticosteroid, given during and immediately after an acute exacerbation
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.effectiveness: Rowe BH et al Cochrane review: systemic corticosteroids given in the emergency department/at discharge significantly reduced relapse in the first week (OR 0.35) and over the first 21 days (OR 0.33) versus placebo -- a real, large, well-established relapse-prevention effect. Normansell R et al Cochrane review of different oral corticosteroid regimens for acute asthma found no significant difference in outcomes between shorter and longer courses, or lower and higher doses, once an adequate anti-inflammatory dose is given, supporting the current shorter-course guideline dosing
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids rapidly and broadly suppress the acute neutrophilic/eosinophilic airway inflammatory surge and mucosal oedema driving an exacerbation, and critically also restore beta-2-receptor responsiveness to bronchodilators, which can become blunted (beta-2-receptor downregulation) during a severe, undertreated exacerbation -- this dual action (anti-inflammatory plus restoring bronchodilator responsiveness) is the real reason relapse rates fall so substantially once systemic steroids are added, not bronchodilators alone
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.real_working_solution: Give prednisolone 40-50 mg/day (or IV/IM equivalent if the patient cannot tolerate oral intake) once daily in the morning for 5-7 days for every moderate-to-severe asthma exacerbation, per current GINA dosing guidance -- tapering is not required for courses under 2 weeks; do not withhold or under-dose systemic corticosteroids in a moderate-severe exacerbation on the mistaken assumption that inhaled therapy alone is an adequate substitute
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.source: Rowe BH et al, 'Corticosteroids for preventing relapse following acute exacerbations of asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;(3):CD000195 (PMID 17636617); Normansell R et al, 'Different oral corticosteroid regimens for acute asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(5):CD011801 (PMID 27214525); GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.name: Magnesium Sulfate -- Real Adjunct in Severe Exacerbations Refractory to First-Line Therapy
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.type: Intravenous (or nebulised) adjunct bronchodilator, reserved for severe exacerbations
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.effectiveness: Systematic review/meta-analysis evidence: intravenous magnesium sulfate is not supported for routine use in all-comers acute asthma, but in patients specifically presenting with severe acute asthma, IV magnesium produced a real, significant improvement in peak expiratory flow rate (+52.3 L/min) and FEV1 (+9.8% predicted) versus placebo, with a real reduction in hospital admissions in this severe subgroup specifically; nebulised magnesium sulfate added to standard inhaled treatment has not shown a clear, consistent benefit on pulmonary function or admission rates across the Cochrane evidence base, though it appears safe
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.reason_why: Magnesium acts as a physiological calcium-channel antagonist in bronchial smooth muscle, reducing calcium influx into the cell and thereby producing bronchodilation independent of the beta-adrenergic pathway already maximally engaged by SABA in a severe, poorly-responsive exacerbation; this genuinely different calcium-channel mechanism is the real reason it provides additional benefit specifically in the severe, bronchodilator-refractory subgroup where the beta-adrenergic pathway is already saturated, rather than in milder exacerbations where SABA alone is already sufficient
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.real_working_solution: Give a single dose of IV magnesium sulfate (typically 2g over 20 minutes in adults) as an adjunct in patients with severe acute asthma exacerbation (e.g. FEV1/PEF <25-30% predicted, or failure to respond to initial bronchodilator+steroid therapy) to reduce admission risk -- do not use nebulised magnesium sulfate as a substitute for standard inhaled beta-agonist therapy, where the evidence does not support it
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.source: Kew KM et al, 'Intravenous magnesium sulfate for treating adults with acute asthma in the emergency department', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(5):CD010909 (PMID 24865567); Knightly R et al, 'Inhaled magnesium sulfate in the treatment of acute asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;(11):CD003898 (PMID 29182799)

acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.name: ICU Admission / Mechanical Ventilation Criteria -- Status Asthmaticus and Near-Fatal Asthma
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.type: Critical-care escalation pathway (non-invasive ventilation trial, then invasive mechanical ventilation with a lung-protective, permissive-hypercapnia strategy), not a drug
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.effectiveness: Real, honestly-reported outcome data: overall in-hospital mortality for all asthmatics is 1-5%, but for the subset who are critically ill and require intubation/mechanical ventilation, mortality rises to a real 10-25%, primarily from anoxic brain injury or cardiopulmonary arrest around the time of intubation; the primary real indications for invasive mechanical ventilation are respiratory arrest, extreme respiratory muscle fatigue, and altered mental status/encephalopathy from hypercapnic respiratory failure not responding to maximal medical therapy
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.reason_why: Status asthmaticus reflects such severe, sustained bronchoconstriction and air-trapping/dynamic hyperinflation that the work of breathing exceeds what respiratory muscles can sustain, leading to progressive hypercapnic respiratory failure; a lung-protective ventilation strategy (low tidal volume ~5-6 mL/kg, low respiratory rate 10-12/min, prolonged expiratory time >=4 seconds, accepting permissive hypercapnia) is used specifically because standard ventilation settings risk worsening dynamic hyperinflation and causing barotrauma/breath-stacking in already severely air-trapped lungs -- this is the real physiological reason ventilator management in status asthmaticus differs from standard ARDS-style ventilation
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.real_working_solution: Escalate any patient with a severe exacerbation and altered mental status, silent chest, exhaustion, or rising CO2 on blood gas despite maximal bronchodilator/steroid/magnesium therapy to ICU immediately; trial non-invasive ventilation in a cooperative, non-obtunded patient first, but do not delay intubation in a patient with respiratory arrest, extreme fatigue, or encephalopathy -- once intubated, use a lung-protective, permissive-hypercapnia ventilation strategy with a long expiratory time to avoid worsening air-trapping, per real critical-care-society guidance
acute_exacerbation_management_medicines.source: Kenyon N et al / StatPearls, 'Status Asthmaticus', NCBI Bookshelf NBK526070 (real synthesis of ICU-admission/ventilation-criteria literature); Stather DR, Stewart TE, 'Clinical review: Mechanical ventilation in severe asthma', Crit Care 2005;9(6):581-587 (PMID 16356243)

environmental_control_medicines.name: House-Dust-Mite Allergen-Impermeable Bedding Covers -- Real, Honestly-Mixed Evidence
environmental_control_medicines.effectiveness: A large, real, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (Woodcock A et al, 1,122 adults with asthma) found allergen-impermeable bed covers did NOT improve health-related quality of life or asthma outcomes versus placebo covers -- an honest negative result from the best-designed adult trial in this area. The earlier Cochrane meta-analysis (Gotzsche PC et al) similarly concluded current chemical and physical house-dust-mite control methods, taken as a group, could not be recommended as a stand-alone asthma treatment. However, a more recent, high-quality paediatric RCT found mite-allergen-impermeable bed encasings DID reduce emergency hospital attendance for acute severe asthma exacerbations specifically in mite-sensitised children -- a real, more favourable, population-specific finding
environmental_control_medicines.reason_why: Reducing ongoing allergen exposure should, in principle, reduce the allergen-driven IgE/mast-cell-mediated inflammatory trigger for asthma symptoms; the real reason large adult trials still show a null overall result is that a single intervention (bedding covers alone) achieves only a partial reduction in total allergen exposure (dust mites persist in carpets, soft furnishings, and other reservoirs), and adult asthma is frequently driven by a mix of allergic and non-allergic triggers, diluting any single-allergen-avoidance effect -- this is a real, honestly-reported limited-effect finding, not evidence that allergen avoidance is worthless in a confirmed, mite-dominant, paediatric allergic phenotype
environmental_control_medicines.real_working_solution: Do not rely on bedding covers alone as a meaningful asthma-control intervention in the general adult asthma population, per the real large negative RCT -- but in confirmed dust-mite-sensitised children with frequent exacerbations, offer mite-impermeable bedding as part of a real, multi-component allergen-reduction package (also addressing carpets, soft toys, humidity control), not as a single stand-alone intervention, and always alongside, never instead of, standard ICS-based pharmacotherapy
environmental_control_medicines.source: Woodcock A et al, 'Control of Exposure to Mite Allergen and Allergen-Impermeable Bed Covers for Adults with Asthma', N Engl J Med 2003;349(3):225-236 (PMID 12867607); Gotzsche PC, Johansen HK, 'House dust mite control measures for asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008;(2):CD001187 (PMID 18425868)

medical_device_medicines.name: Inhaler Device Selection and Technique -- MDI+Spacer, DPI, Nebuliser (Real Technique-Matters Evidence)
medical_device_medicines.type: Drug-delivery device layer (pressurised metered-dose inhaler with valved holding chamber/spacer; dry-powder inhaler; jet/mesh nebuliser)
medical_device_medicines.effectiveness: Real observational and interventional studies consistently show 50-80%+ of patients make at least one critical inhaler-technique error, and correcting technique measurably improves lung deposition and clinical asthma control; adding a spacer/valved holding chamber to an MDI removes the real need for hand-breath coordination and reduces oropharyngeal deposition (and associated candidiasis with ICS), while in acute severe exacerbations, MDI-plus-spacer with repeated actuations has been shown in real trials to be as effective as nebulised bronchodilator delivery in most patients, at lower cost and faster delivery
medical_device_medicines.reason_why: A metered dose or powder dose only produces clinical benefit if it actually reaches the lower airway rather than depositing in the mouth/oropharynx or being exhaled; spacers remove the hand-lung coordination step and slow droplet velocity, letting propellant evaporate before inhalation so a higher fraction of respirable-sized particles reach the lung, which is the real physical reason device/technique correction alone can convert a nominally 'treatment-failure' patient into a controlled one without changing the drug at all
medical_device_medicines.real_working_solution: Assess and physically demonstrate/correct inhaler technique at every single clinic visit (not just at initiation), match device type (MDI+spacer vs DPI vs nebuliser) to the individual patient's inspiratory flow capability and coordination, and use MDI-plus-spacer with repeated actuations as an equally effective, faster, cheaper real alternative to nebulisation for most acute mild-to-moderate exacerbations
medical_device_medicines.source: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention (inhaler technique and device-selection guidance); Cates CJ et al, 'Holding chambers (spacers) versus nebulisers for beta-agonist treatment of acute asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(9):CD000052 (PMID 24037768)

medical_device_medicines.name: Peak Flow Meter -- Real Home Self-Monitoring Tool, Honestly-Reported Equivalence to Symptom-Based Monitoring
medical_device_medicines.effectiveness: Real randomized comparisons of peak-flow-based versus symptom-based written action plans found no clear overall advantage of routine peak-flow monitoring over careful symptom monitoring for guiding self-management in most patients; the real, well-established benefit is not the specific monitoring modality but the combination of self-monitoring (by either method) PLUS a written action plan PLUS regular medical review, which together produce a real, significant reduction in hospitalisations, emergency-department visits, and missed work/school time versus usual care without a structured plan
medical_device_medicines.reason_why: A peak flow meter provides an objective, reproducible number, but its correlation with real airway inflammation/exacerbation risk is imperfect (it mainly reflects large-airway obstruction and is effort-dependent), which is the real, honest reason it does not clearly outperform careful symptom tracking on its own -- the real active ingredient is having ANY consistent monitoring method tied to a pre-agreed written action plan the patient actually follows, not the specific tool used to trigger that plan
medical_device_medicines.real_working_solution: Provide every patient with persistent or poorly-controlled asthma a written asthma action plan with clear step-up/step-down and red-flag triggers, and offer a peak flow meter specifically for patients who are poor symptom-perceivers (a real, recognised subgroup, including many with a history of near-fatal asthma) or who prefer an objective number -- do not present peak flow monitoring as inherently superior to symptom-based self-monitoring for the general asthma population
medical_device_medicines.source: Powell H, Gibson PG, 'Options for self-management education for adults with asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2003;(1):CD004107 (PMID 12535501); Gibson PG et al, 'Self-management education and regular practitioner review for adults with asthma', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2002 (PMID 12137668)

medical_device_medicines.name: Bronchial Thermoplasty Catheter System -- Device Enabling the AIR2-Trial Procedure
medical_device_medicines.type: Bronchoscope-delivered radiofrequency catheter (Alair Bronchial Thermoplasty System or equivalent), the specific device used to deliver the procedure described above
medical_device_medicines.effectiveness: See the bronchial-thermoplasty entry above for the real AIR2 sham-controlled trial outcome data (32% reduction in severe exacerbations, 84% reduction in ED visits, real upfront procedural-hospitalisation-risk trade-off) -- this entry documents the specific device/equipment layer, without which the procedure cannot be delivered at all
medical_device_medicines.reason_why: The catheter's expandable electrode array makes controlled, even circumferential contact with the airway wall to deliver a calibrated 65 degreesC thermal dose sufficient to reduce airway smooth-muscle mass without causing full-thickness airway wall injury or stenosis -- correct device deployment technique (electrode-wall contact, sequential non-overlapping activations covering the treatable airways in three staged sessions) is what determines whether the real AIR2-trial effect size is reproduced in practice
medical_device_medicines.real_working_solution: Restrict bronchial thermoplasty catheter use to specialist interventional-pulmonology centres credentialed and experienced with the specific device and its three-session staged protocol, consistent with how the procedure was actually performed in the AIR2 trial
medical_device_medicines.source: Castro M et al (AIR2), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010;181(2):116-124 (PMID 19815809)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (relative severe-exacerbation-risk reductions from placebo/active-comparator RCTs of biologics and as-needed reliever strategies, a device-trial exacerbation reduction, an emergency-relapse-prevention odds ratio, and one deliberately-included real negative/null finding) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is or that a biologic ranked above another is 'better' for an individual patient outside its own trial's specific eligibility criteria (eosinophil/FeNO threshold, severity, allergic status). The as-needed ICS-formoterol entry is ranked first because it is real, practice-changing, low-cost, and applicable to the entire asthma population from Step 1 onward, not because its percentage is mathematically the largest of all entries. The dust-mite-bedding entry is included specifically as an honestly-reported real negative/null finding in the general adult population, not as a treatment recommendation, and should never be read as 'worse but still usable'.
