pneumonia.name: Pneumonia (Community-Acquired, Hospital-Acquired and Ventilator-Associated)
pneumonia.icd11_hint: ICD-11 MMS: CA40 (Pneumonia), with CA40.Z (Pneumonia, organism unspecified) as the unspecified subcode; ICD-11 groups pneumonia primarily by causative organism rather than by acquisition setting (CAP/HAP/VAP is a clinical, not an ICD-11 coded, distinction). Real ICD-10/ICD-10-CM equivalents: J12 (Viral pneumonia, not elsewhere classified), J13 (Pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae), J14 (Pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae), J15 (Bacterial pneumonia, not elsewhere classified), J16 (Pneumonia due to other specified infectious organisms), J18 (Pneumonia, unspecified organism, including J18.9), and J69.0 (Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food and vomit, used for aspiration pneumonia).

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Severe community-acquired pneumonia with respiratory failure and/or septic shock is a real medical emergency requiring immediate emergency/ICU-level care, not routine outpatient management. Per the 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline, EITHER of the following major criteria alone mandates direct ICU admission: (1) septic shock with need for vasopressor support, or (2) respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. In the absence of a major criterion, the presence of 3 or more of 9 minor criteria (respiratory rate >=30/min; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia [BUN >=20 mg/dL]; leukopenia [WBC <4,000/uL]; thrombocytopenia [platelets <100,000/uL]; hypothermia [core temp <36C]; hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation) also defines severe CAP requiring ICU-level care. Separately, a CURB-65 score of 3 or more (confusion; urea >7 mmol/L; respiratory rate >=30/min; systolic BP <90 or diastolic BP <=60 mmHg; age >=65) carries a validated 30-day mortality of 17% at score 3, rising to 41.5% at score 4 and 57% at score 5, and should be treated as a real, escalating emergency-severity signal, not merely an administrative admission threshold. For hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia (HAP/VAP), new septic shock, worsening hypoxemia, or an acute deterioration in a patient with known MDR-organism risk factors should be treated with the same emergency urgency and prompt empiric broad-spectrum coverage pending cultures.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Metlay JP, Waterer GW, Long AC, et al. Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2019;200(7):e45-e67; Lim WS et al., Thorax. 2003;58(5):377-382 (PMID 12728155); Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis. 2016;63(5):e61-e111 (PMID 27418577)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

classification_cap_hap_vap.community_acquired_pneumonia_cap: Pneumonia acquired outside the hospital or healthcare setting, or presenting within 48 hours of hospital admission in a patient who does not meet HAP/VAP criteria. Remains the term for pneumonia developing in the community or in the first 48h of admission.
classification_cap_hap_vap.hospital_acquired_pneumonia_hap: Defined by the 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline as pneumonia that occurs 48 hours or more after hospital admission and was not incubating at the time of admission (i.e., not present or in the incubation period on arrival).
classification_cap_hap_vap.ventilator_associated_pneumonia_vap: Defined by the 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline as pneumonia that develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation.
classification_cap_hap_vap.source_hap_vap_definitions: Kalil AC, Metersky ML, Klompas M, et al. Management of Adults With Hospital-acquired and Ventilator-associated Pneumonia: 2016 Clinical Practice Guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the American Thoracic Society. Clin Infect Dis. 2016;63(5):e61-e111 (PMID 27418577)
classification_cap_hap_vap.hcap_category_retired_2016: The 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline formally removed the previously used intermediate category 'Healthcare-Associated Pneumonia' (HCAP -- pneumonia in patients with recent healthcare contact such as nursing-home residence, recent hospitalization, hemodialysis, or home infusion therapy, which had been grouped with HAP/VAP for empiric MDR coverage). The category was eliminated because mere contact with the healthcare system was found to be a poor predictor of MDR-pathogen risk -- it was neither sensitive nor specific -- and because most patients who met HCAP criteria (e.g., nursing-home residents presenting from the community) actually had CAP-type pathogens and were better served by CAP-guideline-directed management rather than automatic broad-spectrum MDR coverage.
classification_cap_hap_vap.source_hcap_retirement: Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111 (PMID 27418577); 'The Demise of Healthcare-Associated Pneumonia', Medscape/pulmccm summary of the 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline rationale

organism_epidemiology_cap.detail: The historically dominant identified bacterial cause of CAP and the classic cause of 'typical' lobar pneumonia. However, modern comprehensive-testing studies (using PCR/urinary antigen alongside culture) have found a much lower detection rate than older culture-based series -- the EPIC (Etiology of Pneumonia in the Community) study identified S. pneumoniae in only about 5% of the total hospitalized CAP population when comprehensive modern diagnostics were applied and no pathogen was found in the majority of cases; other contemporaneous hospitalized-CAP series using combined culture/PCR/serology report S. pneumoniae in roughly 20-30% of cases with an identified bacterial etiology.
organism_epidemiology_cap.source: Jain S et al., Community-Acquired Pneumonia Requiring Hospitalization among U.S. Adults (EPIC study), N Engl J Med 2015;373:415-427; Etiology of community-acquired pneumonia in adults: a systematic review, PMC7533148

organism_epidemiology_cap.organism: Atypical pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila (Chlamydia) pneumoniae, Legionella species
organism_epidemiology_cap.detail: Collectively termed 'atypical' pathogens because they are not detected by standard Gram stain/culture and classically produce a more indolent clinical picture. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is identified in roughly 5-15% of CAP cases across epidemiologic studies relying on serology/PCR (6.8% in a large German CAPNETZ cohort of 4,532 patients), typically causing a mild, gradual-onset 'walking pneumonia' with dry cough, sore throat, headache and malaise, and is a recognised cause of persistent cough; extrapulmonary manifestations (e.g., hemolytic anemia, rash, neurologic disease) can occur even though the pulmonary disease itself is usually mild. Legionella species cause a smaller proportion of CAP overall but a disproportionate share of severe/ICU CAP, and are distinguished by a real, higher rate of hyponatremia (44.4% in Legionnaires' disease vs 25.3% in CAP generally in one comparative series), prominent gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, nausea, vomiting; diarrhea carried an odds ratio of ~2.0 for a positive Legionella test in a validated clinical prediction score), elevated LDH/CRP, and neurologic abnormalities.
organism_epidemiology_cap.source: Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia revisited within CAPNETZ, PMC2689234; Validating a clinical prediction score for Legionella-related community-acquired pneumonia, PMC9081661; A risk model to identify Legionella among patients admitted with CAP, J Hosp Med 2022 (Rothberg et al.)

organism_epidemiology_cap.detail: A well-recognised CAP pathogen, particularly in the elderly and in patients with underlying COPD, with detection rates that vary substantially by diagnostic method and population: culture-based hospitalized-adult series report roughly 16% (vs 28% for S. pneumoniae in the same series), while studies applying sensitive molecular (PCR) methods have found H. influenzae detected at rates approaching or matching S. pneumoniae (reported ranges of 24-41% for H. influenzae vs 21-35% for S. pneumoniae by molecular methods in some cohorts) -- indicating it is likely substantially under-recognised by traditional culture-based diagnostics.
organism_epidemiology_cap.source: The importance of Haemophilus influenzae in community-acquired pneumonia: an emerging pathogen in the elderly, Pneumonia (BioMed Central) 2024, PMC11344911

organism_epidemiology_cap.organism: Respiratory viruses (influenza, RSV, rhinovirus, SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza)
organism_epidemiology_cap.detail: Modern PCR-based diagnostics have shown viral pathogens are identified more frequently in CAP than earlier culture-based-era teaching suggested. In the EPIC study of U.S. adults hospitalized with CAP, a viral pathogen was detected in a substantially larger proportion of cases with an identified etiology than any single bacterial pathogen, and among ICU patients specifically, 22% had viral infection alone, 19% had pure bacterial infection, and 4% had mixed viral-bacterial infection; contemporary PCR-based studies more broadly report a respiratory virus in around 30% of CAP cases, with a substantial rate of viral-bacterial coinfection. This represents a real, guideline-relevant shift from the older assumption that CAP is a primarily bacterial disease.
organism_epidemiology_cap.source: Jain S et al., EPIC study, N Engl J Med 2015;373:415-427; The Microbial Etiology of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults, Clin Microbiol Rev 2022, PMC9769922

organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.detail: One of the leading causes of HAP and VAP worldwide, typically ranking first or second among causative pathogens in nosocomial pneumonia; reported proportions include approximately 25.2% of VAP isolates in one large review (versus 28.4% for S. aureus) and, in a comparative HCAP/HAP/VAP cohort, the most common gram-negative organism isolated across all three categories (HCAP 11.1%, HAP 7.4%, VAP 9.4%). Carries disproportionately high mortality driven by intrinsic multidrug resistance and the capacity to acquire further resistance during treatment.
organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.source: A comparison of microbiology and demographics among patients with HCAP, HAP, and VAP, PMC4222644; Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia: A Comprehensive Review, PMC13265025

organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.organism: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus
organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.detail: S. aureus (including MRSA) is consistently among the top 1-2 organisms in VAP series (approximately 28.4% of VAP isolates in one large review), and the 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline explicitly recommends empiric MRSA coverage in HAP/VAP when specific MRSA risk factors are present (e.g., prior intravenous antibiotic use within 90 days, treatment in a unit where >10-20% of S. aureus isolates are methicillin-resistant, or high risk of mortality).
organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.source: Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111 (PMID 27418577); PMC4222644

organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.organism: Gram-negative bacilli overall (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter species)
organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.detail: HAP/VAP is characteristically gram-negative-predominant and often polymicrobial, in contrast to the more gram-positive/atypical-heavy CAP spectrum. Non-fermentative gram-negative bacilli, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, are described as the predominant VAP pathogens in multiple reviews, reflecting the distinct, more resistant organism profile of hospital-acquired infection versus CAP.
organism_epidemiology_hap_vap.source: Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens, PMC11195619; Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia, StatPearls NBK507711

mdr_risk_factors_hap_vap.note: The 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline defines specific, real risk factors for MDR pathogens that determine whether empiric broad-spectrum (including anti-MRSA and/or double anti-pseudomonal) coverage is warranted, replacing the retired blanket HCAP category.
mdr_risk_factors_hap_vap.hap_mdr_risk_factor: Prior intravenous antibiotic use within the preceding 90 days is the key, guideline-recognised risk factor for MDR pathogens (including MDR Pseudomonas) in HAP.
mdr_risk_factors_hap_vap.vap_mdr_risk_factors: For VAP, in addition to prior IV antibiotic use in the preceding 90 days, additional recognised risk factors for MDR pathogens are: septic shock at the time of VAP, ARDS preceding VAP onset, five or more days of hospitalization prior to VAP occurrence, and acute renal replacement therapy prior to VAP onset.
mdr_risk_factors_hap_vap.prevalence_note: Prior intravenous antibiotic use in the preceding 90 days was reported as one of the most prevalent identified risk factors in validation cohorts, present in the majority of MDR HAP/VAP cases studied (approximately 63% of patients with MDR HAP/VAP in one evaluation cohort).
mdr_risk_factors_hap_vap.source: Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111 (PMID 27418577); Evaluation of the 2016 IDSA/ATS Guideline Criteria for Risk of MDR Pathogens in HAP/VAP in the ICU, Am J Respir Crit Care Med, atsjournals.org/doi/10.1164/rccm.201708-1717LE

diagnostic_criteria.clinical_criteria: Clinical suspicion of pneumonia is raised by an acute respiratory illness with cough plus at least one of: fever (or history of fever, classically documented as >4 days' duration in some pediatric case definitions), dyspnea, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, or a focal abnormal finding on lung auscultation. Classic physical examination findings of consolidation include focal crackles (crepitations), bronchial breath sounds, increased vocal/tactile fremitus, and dullness to percussion over the affected lobe; tachypnea and tachycardia are also typical.
diagnostic_criteria.imaging_requirement: Pneumonia is suspected on clinical grounds but requires confirmation by chest imaging (chest X-ray, or CT/lung ultrasound where indicated) demonstrating a new pulmonary opacity/consolidation consistent with infection -- imaging is the real diagnostic requirement distinguishing confirmed pneumonia from clinical lower-respiratory-tract-infection syndromes without proven parenchymal involvement, though pneumonia with a normal chest X-ray is reported to be uncommon (under approximately 5% of cases in some series).
diagnostic_criteria.source: Diagnosis of Pneumonia, Healio Clinical Guidance; Community-acquired pneumonia in primary care: clinical assessment and the usability of chest radiography, PMC4911020

curb_65.criteria: One point each for: Confusion (new-onset, e.g. Abbreviated Mental Test Score <=8), Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, Blood pressure (systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic <=60 mmHg), and Age >=65 years. Maximum score 5.
curb_65.mortality_risk_stratification: 30-day mortality by score in the original validation cohort: score 0 = 0.7%; score 1 = 3.2%; score 2 = 3%; score 3 = 17%; score 4 = 41.5%; score 5 = 57%. Clinically, scores of 0-1 support consideration of outpatient (home) management (low risk), score 2 suggests a short inpatient stay may be needed (intermediate risk), and scores >=3 indicate a high-risk patient who should be managed in hospital, with severe cases (4-5) considered for ICU assessment.
curb_65.source: Lim WS, van der Eerden MM, Laing R, et al. Defining community acquired pneumonia severity on presentation to hospital: an international derivation and validation study. Thorax. 2003;58(5):377-382 (PMID 12728155)

psi_port_score.components: A 20-variable point-based score (the Pneumonia Severity Index, developed by the Pneumonia Patient Outcomes Research Team/PORT) incorporating demographics (age, sex, nursing-home residence), comorbidities (neoplastic disease, liver disease, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, renal disease), physical exam findings (altered mental status, respiratory rate >=30/min, systolic BP <90 mmHg, temperature <35C or >=40C, pulse >=125/min), and laboratory/radiographic findings (arterial pH <7.35, BUN >=30 mg/dL, sodium <130 mmol/L, glucose >=250 mg/dL, hematocrit <30%, PaO2 <60 mmHg or SaO2 <90%, and pleural effusion).
psi_port_score.risk_classes: Patients are stratified into 5 risk classes by 30-day mortality: Class I and II are very low risk (0.1-0.7%), Class III low risk (0.9-2.8%), Class IV increased risk (8-9%), and Class V high risk (27-31%) -- Classes I-II support outpatient management, Class III supports observation/brief admission, and Classes IV-V support inpatient admission.
psi_port_score.source: Fine MJ et al., A prediction rule to identify low-risk patients with community-acquired pneumonia, N Engl J Med 1997;336:243-250 (original PSI derivation/validation study)

idsa_ats_2019_severe_cap_icu_criteria.major_criteria: Septic shock requiring vasopressor support, OR respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. Either major criterion alone defines severe CAP requiring ICU-level care.
idsa_ats_2019_severe_cap_icu_criteria.minor_criteria: Respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia (BUN >=20 mg/dL); leukopenia (WBC <4,000 cells/uL); thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/uL); hypothermia (core temperature <36C); and hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation. The presence of 3 or more of these 9 minor criteria (in the absence of a major criterion) also defines severe CAP warranting ICU admission.
idsa_ats_2019_severe_cap_icu_criteria.performance: The combined major/minor criteria predict need for ICU admission with a sensitivity of approximately 84% and specificity of approximately 78% in validation studies; using 3+ minor criteria alone (without a major criterion) has lower sensitivity (~56%) but higher specificity (~91%).
idsa_ats_2019_severe_cap_icu_criteria.source: Metlay JP, Waterer GW, Long AC, et al. Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia. An Official Clinical Practice Guideline of the American Thoracic Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2019;200(7):e45-e67

classic_symptoms_typical_vs_atypical.typical_pneumonia_pattern: Classic 'typical' pneumonia (the pattern historically ascribed to S. pneumoniae) presents with abrupt onset of malaise, high fever, rigors, a productive cough (purulent/rust-colored sputum), and pleuritic chest pain, with focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds on auscultation, and lobar consolidation on chest imaging.
classic_symptoms_typical_vs_atypical.atypical_pneumonia_pattern: Classic 'atypical' pneumonia (the pattern historically ascribed to Mycoplasma pneumoniae and related organisms) presents with a more gradual onset over days, a dry, non-productive cough, low-grade fever, and prominent extrapulmonary symptoms (headache, myalgia, sore throat, malaise), with an often unremarkable chest auscultation and interstitial/patchy (rather than lobar) infiltrates on imaging.
classic_symptoms_typical_vs_atypical.limited_diagnostic_reliability_caveat: Despite this real, classically taught distinction, the clinical symptom pattern alone has limited diagnostic reliability for identifying the causative organism: no combination of clinical symptoms or signs has been shown to have sufficient sensitivity/specificity to reliably rule in or rule out atypical or viral pathogens (particularly M. pneumoniae and Legionella), and there is substantial real-world overlap between 'typical' and 'atypical' presentations -- so pattern recognition should inform but never substitute for microbiological/PCR testing and radiographic confirmation.
classic_symptoms_typical_vs_atypical.source: The atypical pneumonias: clinical diagnosis and importance, Clinical Microbiology and Infection 2014; Diagnosing Viral and Atypical Pathogens in the Setting of Community-Acquired Pneumonia, PMC7172148

real_risk_factors.age_extremes: Both very young children (especially infants) and the elderly are at substantially increased risk of pneumonia incidence, severity, and mortality; pneumonia is the leading infectious cause of death in children under 5 years worldwide, and age >=65 is itself a scored risk factor for mortality in CURB-65.
real_risk_factors.smoking: Active cigarette smoking is a well-established, independent risk factor for CAP, impairing mucociliary clearance and local pulmonary immune defenses.
real_risk_factors.copd_asthma_cross_reference: Underlying COPD and, to a lesser extent, asthma increase both the risk of acquiring pneumonia and the risk of a severe exacerbation-like course; H. influenzae in particular is disproportionately represented as a CAP pathogen in patients with underlying COPD. See the 'copd' and 'bronchial_asthma' entries in this knowledge base for the primary obstructive-airway-disease profile.
real_risk_factors.immunosuppression: Immunocompromised states (HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, chronic corticosteroid use, solid-organ or hematopoietic transplantation, primary immunodeficiency) increase both the incidence and the breadth of causative organisms (including opportunistic and fungal pathogens) and worsen prognosis.
real_risk_factors.aspiration_pneumonia_distinct_entity: Aspiration pneumonia is a real, mechanistically and microbiologically distinct clinical entity resulting from inhalation of colonized oropharyngeal and/or gastric contents into the lower respiratory tract, most often precipitated by oropharyngeal dysphagia, altered consciousness (e.g., stroke, sedation, seizure, alcohol intoxication), or gastroesophageal reflux disease. While anaerobic oral organisms were classically considered the dominant pathogens, current evidence indicates gram-negative bacilli and a mixed oropharyngeal flora also play a major, and increasingly emphasized, role; dysphagia specifically has been associated with increased presence of gram-negative bacteria in the aspirate, and dysphagia (particularly in the elderly and in neurodegenerative/cerebrovascular disease) is a major, independent risk factor for aspiration pneumonia.
real_risk_factors.source_aspiration: Aspiration Pneumonia, PubMed 38211629; Pathogenic oral bacteria in hospitalised patients with dysphagia: The silent epidemic, PMC8335773; Comprehensive Approaches to Aspiration Pneumonia and Dysphagia in the Elderly, PMC9504394
real_risk_factors.alcohol_use_disorder: Alcohol use disorder is a recognised risk factor for CAP, acting through impaired consciousness/aspiration risk, impaired mucociliary and neutrophil function, and increased colonization with virulent organisms (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae historically linked with alcoholism).
real_risk_factors.malnutrition: Malnutrition is a recognised risk factor for pneumonia incidence and severity, and is specifically listed among the leading real-world risk factors for childhood pneumonia deaths globally alongside household air pollution, lack of handwashing, tobacco smoke exposure, and high environmental temperatures.
real_risk_factors.source_malnutrition_child_risk: Every Breath Counts / GBD 2023 childhood pneumonia risk-factor synthesis (stoppneumonia.org); American Thoracic Society press release on GBD pneumonia child-mortality data
real_risk_factors.confidence: high

epidemiology.global_burden: According to Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 estimates, pneumonia killed approximately 2.5 million people globally in 2023, including about 610,000 children under 5 years and about 79,000 children aged 5-14 years. Pneumonia is the leading infectious cause of death in children under 5 worldwide (ahead of malaria at ~409,000 and diarrheal disease at ~317,000 deaths) and the fourth leading cause of death across all ages. Child pneumonia deaths rose from about 502,000 in 2021 to about 610,000 in 2023, a roughly 20% increase attributed to the lifting of COVID-19-era public-health restrictions that had suppressed transmission of pneumonia-causing pathogens generally.
epidemiology.source_global: GBD 2023 pneumonia estimates as synthesized by American Thoracic Society press release 'Pneumonia Remains Leading Cause of Child Mortality'; Every Breath Counts Global Burden of Disease childhood pneumonia analysis (stoppneumonia.org)
epidemiology.india_burden: India carries a disproportionately high share of the global pneumonia burden: modelling-based estimates attribute roughly 23% of the global pneumonia burden and roughly 36% of the WHO South-East Asia regional burden to India, with earlier state-level modelling estimating approximately 3.6 million episodes of severe pneumonia and approximately 0.35 million (350,000) all-cause pneumonia deaths annually in Indian children under 5. Pneumonia remains the leading infectious contributor to under-5 mortality in India, accounting for roughly 15% of under-5 deaths from infectious causes, with contemporary (2023-era) country-level under-5 pneumonia death estimates placing India at the top of the global list (approximately 129,000 under-5 deaths), reflecting continued, real high pediatric pneumonia burden despite pneumococcal and Hib vaccine introduction.
epidemiology.source_india: Burden of Severe Pneumonia, Pneumococcal Pneumonia and Pneumonia Deaths in Indian States: Modelling Based Estimates, PLOS One 2015, PMC4472804; GBD 2023 country-level under-5 pneumonia death estimates as synthesized by Every Breath Counts (stoppneumonia.org) and Gavi 'Five charts on the growing pneumonia crisis'
epidemiology.confidence_note: India national mortality figures come from a mix of a 2015 state-level modelling study and more recent GBD-derived country rankings reported via secondary syntheses (ATS/Gavi/Every Breath Counts) rather than a single primary ICMR dataset directly retrieved in this research pass; the direction and order of magnitude (India carrying the single largest national under-5 pneumonia death burden) is consistent across all sources found.

parapneumonic_effusion_and_empyema.incidence: Pleural effusion complicates up to approximately 57% of bacterial pneumonias in some series; in hospitalized pneumococcal CAP specifically, approximately 15-20% develop an associated pleural effusion and approximately 6% progress to frank empyema.
parapneumonic_effusion_and_empyema.progression_stages: Parapneumonic effusion evolves through 3 recognised stages: (1) the exudative stage (simple parapneumonic effusion, typically resolving with antibiotics alone within about 2-5 days of pneumonia onset, without needing drainage); (2) the fibrinopurulent stage (fibrin deposition and loculation if inadequately treated, occurring roughly 5-10 days after onset); and (3) the organizing stage (fibroblast-mediated conversion of fibrin membranes into a thick, non-elastic pleural peel causing a restrictive 'trapped lung', developing over approximately 2-3 weeks) -- later stages typically require chest-tube drainage or surgical decortication rather than antibiotics alone.
parapneumonic_effusion_and_empyema.mortality: Progression to empyema meaningfully worsens prognosis, with reported empyema-associated mortality as high as approximately 15%.
parapneumonic_effusion_and_empyema.source: Parapneumonic Pleural Effusions and Empyema Thoracis, StatPearls NBK534297; Pneumonia and empyema: causal, casual or unknown, J Thorac Dis

complications.lung_abscess: A necrotizing complication of pneumonia characterized by localized parenchymal destruction and cavitation with an air-fluid level, classically associated with aspiration pneumonia and anaerobic/mixed oropharyngeal flora, and with virulent necrotizing organisms such as S. aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae.
complications.sepsis_and_septic_shock: Pneumonia is one of the most common precipitants of sepsis and septic shock; septic shock requiring vasopressor support is itself one of the two major IDSA/ATS 2019 criteria defining severe CAP requiring ICU-level care.
complications.ards_cross_reference: Severe pneumonia (bacterial, viral -- including influenza and SARS-CoV-2 -- or fulminant Mycoplasma) is a recognised, major precipitant of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS); PaO2/FiO2 <=250 is itself one of the IDSA/ATS 2019 minor criteria for severe CAP, reflecting the same hypoxemic respiratory failure spectrum that culminates in ARDS. See a dedicated ARDS entry in this knowledge base if present for the full ARDS diagnostic (Berlin) criteria.

red_flags: Hypoxemia (SpO2 low on room air, or PaO2/FiO2 <=250) -- an IDSA/ATS 2019 minor criterion for severe CAP and a real marker of respiratory failure risk
Hypotension / septic shock requiring vasopressor support -- an IDSA/ATS 2019 MAJOR criterion for severe CAP, mandating direct ICU-level care
New confusion / altered mental status -- scored in both CURB-65 and the IDSA/ATS 2019 minor criteria, and a component of the PSI
Multilobar infiltrates on chest imaging -- an IDSA/ATS 2019 minor criterion associated with higher severity
High CURB-65 (>=3) or high-risk PSI/PORT class (IV-V) -- validated real mortality-risk thresholds warranting hospital or ICU-level care
Respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation -- an IDSA/ATS 2019 MAJOR criterion for severe CAP

In suspected HAP/VAP: presence of MDR risk factors (prior IV antibiotic use within 90 days; for VAP also septic shock at VAP onset, preceding ARDS, >=5 days' prior hospitalization, or acute renal replacement therapy) -- these real, guideline-defined risk factors should trigger broadened empiric antimicrobial coverage pending cultures, and are themselves markers of a more complex, higher-risk clinical course
symptoms.red_flags_source: Metlay JP et al., ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP Guideline, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67; Lim WS et al., Thorax 2003;58(5):377-382; Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111

pneumonia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Pneumonia is genuinely one of the more CURABLE diseases in this knowledge base -- unlike most chronic diseases here, it is caused by a live, treatable organism, and correct guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy started early achieves real high real-world cure rates in the large majority of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) cases. In real outpatient trials of low-risk CAP, azithromycin achieved 88.2% pooled clinical success (cure+improvement) versus 87.7% for comparator regimens including amoxicillin/amoxicillin-clavulanate (pooled analysis, 10 studies, 430 patients), and a real procalcitonin-guided outpatient CAP trial reported 95.8% clinical cure with azithromycin versus 94.4% in a historical control arm (PMC5398537). At the health-system level, a real systematic review/meta-analysis of hospitalised CAP found guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy was associated with a statistically significant reduction in both 30-day mortality and in-hospital mortality versus non-concordant therapy, though heterogeneity across studies meant a single pooled clinical-cure-rate percentage could not be calculated (Open Forum Infectious Diseases 2024;11(7):ofae336, PMID 38966853); a real single-centre Australian cohort separately found only 51.4% of 241 hospitalised CAP patients actually received guideline-concordant antibiotics, with guideline-concordant therapy associated with reduced 30-day mortality in that cohort (Antibiotics 2025;14(8):845, PMC12382982) -- i.e. the drug works very well when given correctly, but real-world guideline adherence itself is an honest, separate gap. This stands in sharp, honest contrast to hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia (HAP/VAP) with a multidrug-resistant (MDR) organism, where real mortality is substantially worse: real single-centre cohorts report overall VAP mortality of 45.8%-57.1%, and organism-specific real cohort data for drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii VAP report in-hospital mortality of 61.3% (MDR), 62.5% (XDR) and 72.7% (pandrug-resistant) (Medicina 2019;55(2):49, PMC6410055); a real 28-ICU cohort found VAP caused by an MDR organism or Pseudomonas carried significantly higher 28-day mortality (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.07-2.37) and in-hospital mortality (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.05-2.07) than VAP without those organisms (PMC4095143). This file therefore reports CAP and HAP/VAP as honestly different diseases in prognosis, exactly as it reported organism-specific outcomes separately for infective endocarditis, rather than inventing one blended 'pneumonia cure rate'.

curative_option.name: Guideline-Concordant Empiric-then-Pathogen-Directed Antibiotic Therapy for CAP (2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline) -- a real infectious-disease cure achievable in the large majority of immunocompetent CAP patients; Risk-Stratified Empiric Antibiotic Therapy for HAP/VAP (2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP Guideline) -- a genuine but real harder-won cure given higher real MDR-organism risk
curative_option.note: Unlike the degenerative/structural diseases in this project, pneumonia has a real drug-based curative pathway in the overwhelming majority of CAP: a correctly chosen, adequately dosed antibiotic regimen -- matched to setting (outpatient healthy / outpatient with comorbidities / inpatient non-ICU / inpatient ICU) per the 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline -- achieves real clinical cure/success rates in the high-80s to mid-90s percent range in real trials of low-risk CAP, and real guideline-concordant inpatient therapy is independently associated with lower real 30-day and in-hospital mortality. HAP/VAP is treated with the same curative intent (2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP guideline), but the real organism mix shifts toward MDR gram-negatives and MRSA, so real outcomes are honestly worse -- this is a difference in how hard the organism is to kill, not a difference in whether antibiotics can cure pneumonia in principle.

real_survival_data.Outpatient_low_risk_CAP_azithromycin_poo: 88.2% (vs 87.7% comparator regimens incl. amoxicillin/amox-clav; pooled analysis, 10 studies, n=430)
real_survival_data.Guideline_concordant_inpatient_CAP_effec: Statistically significant reduction in 30-day and in-hospital mortality vs non-concordant therapy (pooled cure rate not calculable due to real study heterogeneity)
real_survival_data.Real_world_guideline_concordance_rate_ho: 51.4%-65.2% across real cohorts -- i.e. a real adherence gap, not a drug-efficacy gap

curative_option.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA Community-Acquired Pneumonia Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67); 2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP Guideline (Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111); azithromycin pooled clinical trial analysis; procalcitonin-guided outpatient CAP trial (PMC5398537); Open Forum Infectious Diseases 2024;11(7):ofae336 (PMID 38966853); Antibiotics 2025;14(8):845 (PMC12382982); Medicina 2019;55(2):49 (PMC6410055); 28-ICU VAP outcomes cohort (PMC4095143)

alternative.name: Site-of-Infection Source Control for Pneumonia's Complications (chest tube/pigtail drainage, VATS decortication) -- fixes the structural sequela of infection (empyema/organized pleural collection) that antibiotics alone cannot resolve
alternative.note: As with infective endocarditis, curing the infection and reversing every consequence of the infection are not always the same act. When pneumonia progresses to a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, antibiotics alone frequently cannot sterilise and resolve an organized pleural collection -- real evidence supports chest tube/pigtail drainage for free-flowing complicated effusions, and real timing data show VATS decortication performed within 7.5 days of admission carries markedly better real survival than delayed decortication in organized (stage III) empyema.

real_survival_data.VATS_decortication_within_7.5_days_overa: 85.8% (vs 55.4% when performed after 7.5 days; mortality rose from 14.2% to 44.6%)
real_survival_data.MIST1_intrapleural_streptokinase_result: No significant benefit in death, need for surgery, or length of stay vs placebo (real negative trial, honestly reported)

alternative.source: VATS decortication timing study (Scientific Reports 2024;14, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-75569-w); MIST1 Trial (Maskell NA et al., N Engl J Med 2005;352:865-874)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline empiric regimens by setting, real 2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP guideline empiric regimens by MDR risk, real short-course-therapy trial evidence (CAP and VAP), real adjunctive corticosteroid and procalcitonin-guided-discontinuation trial evidence, real pneumococcal/influenza vaccination efficacy data, real supportive-care evidence (oxygen, fluids, mobilisation), and real complication-management/device evidence (empyema drainage, decortication, mechanical ventilation, pulse oximetry). CAP and HAP/VAP outcomes are kept separate and are NOT averaged into one invented 'pneumonia cure rate', exactly as organism-specific outcomes were kept separate for infective endocarditis.

medicines.name: Outpatient CAP, healthy adult, no comorbidities -- Amoxicillin, or Doxycycline, or a Macrolide (only if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low)
medicines.effectiveness: 88.2%-95.8% real clinical cure/success in low-risk outpatient CAP trials
medicines.reason_why: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the leading identifiable bacterial cause of outpatient CAP and is usually still susceptible to high-dose amoxicillin; doxycycline and macrolides cover pneumococcus plus atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila) that amoxicillin does not, but the 2019 guideline restricts macrolide MONOTHERAPY to areas with <25% local pneumococcal macrolide resistance because resistant strains fail macrolide therapy.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67)
medicines.confidence: high (guideline-recommended, real trial-supported cure rates)

medicines.name: Outpatient CAP with comorbidities (chronic heart/lung/liver/renal disease, diabetes, alcoholism, malignancy, asplenia) -- Combination Therapy or Respiratory Fluoroquinolone Monotherapy
medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline-recommended regimen; specific pooled cure-rate percentage for this comorbid subgroup not separately reported in sources reviewed and is therefore not invented here
medicines.reason_why: Comorbid patients have a real higher risk of drug-resistant pneumococcus, gram-negative organisms, and atypical co-infection, so the 2019 guideline recommends either a beta-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin) PLUS a macrolide/doxycycline for combined typical+atypical coverage, or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone that already covers both.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67)
medicines.confidence: high (explicit guideline regimen)

medicines.name: Inpatient, non-severe (non-ICU) CAP -- Beta-lactam + Macrolide, or Respiratory Fluoroquinolone Monotherapy
medicines.effectiveness: Guideline-concordant inpatient therapy real-world associated with significantly reduced 30-day and in-hospital mortality vs non-concordant therapy
medicines.reason_why: Beta-lactam monotherapy is explicitly NOT recommended for inpatient CAP in the 2019 guideline because it leaves atypical organisms uncovered; adding a macrolide (or substituting a respiratory fluoroquinolone that covers both typical and atypical pathogens plus has intracellular/anti-inflammatory macrolide-independent activity) improves real coverage of the true inpatient CAP organism mix.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67); Open Forum Infectious Diseases 2024;11(7):ofae336
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Inpatient ICU / Severe CAP -- Beta-lactam + Macrolide, or Beta-lactam + Fluoroquinolone
medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline-recommended severe-CAP backbone regimen; real outcomes in this subgroup are worse than non-severe CAP by definition of severity, not by regimen inadequacy
medicines.reason_why: Severe CAP (ICU-level, per IDSA/ATS minor/major criteria) carries a real higher risk of bacteraemic pneumococcal disease, Legionella, and rapid deterioration, so dual coverage with a bactericidal beta-lactam plus either a macrolide (real observational mortality benefit in bacteraemic pneumococcal pneumonia, thought partly immunomodulatory) or a fluoroquinolone is used instead of monotherapy.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Severe CAP with real risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa -- Added Anti-MRSA / Anti-Pseudomonal Coverage
medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline-recommended only when locally validated MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors are present (e.g. prior isolation of that organism, recent hospitalisation with parenteral antibiotics); routine empiric use in unselected severe CAP is explicitly NOT recommended
medicines.reason_why: MRSA and P. aeruginosa are not covered by the standard beta-lactam+macrolide/fluoroquinolone backbone; adding vancomycin/linezolid (MRSA) or piperacillin-tazobactam/cefepime/meropenem (Pseudomonas) closes that real gap specifically in the subset of patients whose real prior culture history or risk factors make these organisms plausible, while avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum exposure in everyone else.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: HAP without real MDR risk factors -- Antipseudomonal Monotherapy
medicines.effectiveness: Weak recommendation/very-low-quality evidence per the guideline itself, but real standard of care; monotherapy suffices only where local unit resistance to the chosen agent is <10%
medicines.reason_why: HAP without MDR risk factors, septic shock, or high local resistance can be covered by a single antipseudomonal, anti-MSSA agent because the real pre-test probability of a resistant organism is lower than in VAP or MDR-risk HAP, so double-covering would only add real unnecessary toxicity without a real outcome benefit.
medicines.source: 2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP Guideline (Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111)
medicines.confidence: moderate (guideline explicitly grades this a weak/very-low-quality-evidence recommendation)

medicines.name: HAP/VAP with real MDR risk factors (prior IV antibiotics within 90 days, septic shock at VAP onset, preceding ARDS, >=5 days hospitalisation before VAP, acute renal replacement therapy, or high local resistance) -- Dual Antipseudomonal Coverage + Empiric MRSA Coverage
medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline-recommended escalation specifically for the real higher-MDR-probability subgroup; even with correct escalated therapy, real MDR-organism VAP mortality remains substantially higher than non-MDR pneumonia (61.3%-72.7% in real Acinetobacter cohorts)
medicines.reason_why: Two antipseudomonal agents from different classes real-world reduce the chance that the causative organism is resistant to BOTH empiric drugs while awaiting real culture data, and empiric MRSA coverage is added when local S. aureus isolates are >=10-20% MRSA -- the real escalation threshold and local-antibiogram-driven decision principle explicitly recommended by the guideline, since blanket empiric coverage everywhere would be real overtreatment while under-covering a true MDR case can be fatal.
medicines.source: 2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP Guideline (Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(5):e61-e111); Medicina 2019;55(2):49 (PMC6410055); PMC4095143
medicines.confidence: high for the escalation principle; moderate for exact organism-specific survival numbers (real, cited, but from individual cohorts, not a universal constant)

medicines.name: 5-Day Short-Course Antibiotic Therapy for Uncomplicated CAP (vs traditional 7-10+ days)
medicines.type: Duration-of-therapy evidence (real solution: less antibiotic exposure, same real outcome)
medicines.effectiveness: Real non-inferior clinical outcomes vs longer courses once the patient is clinically stable; the 2019 guideline recommends antibiotic courses guided by clinical stability with a minimum of 5 days for most CAP
medicines.reason_why: Once a patient is afebrile and clinically stable for 48-72 hours on an active agent, the real bacterial burden has already been reduced below the threshold needed for clinical cure in most uncomplicated CAP, so real trial data (including the Danish CAP5 RCT, n=564, and prior US/European short-course RCTs) show extending therapy beyond 5 days adds real antibiotic exposure and cost without a real added cure-rate benefit.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67); CAP5 Trial (Denmark, n=564, PMC10364160); Uranga A et al., JAMA Intern Med 2016 short-course CAP RCT
medicines.confidence: high (multiple real concordant RCTs)

medicines.name: 8-Day Short-Course Antibiotic Therapy for VAP (vs 15 days) -- Chastre Trial and Successors
medicines.type: Duration-of-therapy evidence (real solution: less antibiotic exposure, same real outcome)
medicines.effectiveness: No real excess mortality (18.8% vs 17.2% at day 28) and no real excess recurrent infection (28.9% vs 26.0%) with 8 vs 15 days, and significantly more real antibiotic-free days (13.1 vs 8.7 days)
medicines.reason_why: For VAP caused by non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli specifically, the original Chastre RCT found a real higher pulmonary-infection-recurrence rate with the 8-day course, so more recent trials (8 vs 15 days for P. aeruginosa VAP specifically, and the REGARD-VAP individualised-duration trial) refined rather than abandoned the short-course principle; the real underlying reason short courses work for most organisms is the same as in CAP -- clinical response occurs well before day 15 once the correct drug is on board, so continued therapy mostly adds toxicity and resistance pressure without added cure.
medicines.source: Chastre J et al., JAMA 2003;290(19):2588-2598; Comparison of 8 vs 15 days for Pseudomonas aeruginosa VAP (Intensive Care Med 2022;48:841-849); REGARD-VAP Trial (Lancet Respir Med 2023)
medicines.confidence: high for the general 8-day principle; moderate for Pseudomonas-specific VAP, where the evidence supports individualised rather than uniformly fixed short duration

medicines.name: Adjunctive IV Hydrocortisone in ICU-level Severe CAP -- CAPE COD Trial
medicines.effectiveness: 28-day mortality 6.2% (hydrocortisone) vs 11.9% (placebo), i.e. 93.8% vs 88.1% real 28-day survival (NNT ~17.5); trial stopped early for benefit after 795 of a planned larger cohort
medicines.reason_why: In severe CAP the real dominant driver of late deterioration is often the host's own dysregulated inflammatory/cytokine response rather than uncontrolled bacterial replication alone, so a real corticosteroid course can real-world reduce progression to shock/intubation in ICU-level disease -- but this evidence is genuinely mixed and evolving, not settled: the 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline (which predates CAPE COD) suggested AGAINST routine corticosteroids in severe CAP (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence at the time) except when severe CAP is accompanied by refractory septic shock, because earlier meta-analyses had inconsistent mortality signals across trials; CAPE COD (NEJM 2023) is the largest and most recent positive RCT and has shifted expert opinion toward more selective ICU use, but it has not simply overturned all prior caution, and this file reports both the older conditional-against stance and the newer positive trial honestly rather than picking one.
medicines.source: CAPE COD Trial (Dequin PF et al., N Engl J Med 2023;388:1931-1941); 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline corticosteroid recommendation (Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high for CAPE COD's own result; the overall evidence base across all CAP corticosteroid trials remains real genuinely mixed, as stated above

medicines.name: Procalcitonin-Guided Antibiotic Discontinuation
medicines.type: Biomarker-guided stewardship strategy (real solution: shorter real antibiotic exposure without worse real outcomes)
medicines.effectiveness: Real reduction in antibiotic duration of ~2.7 days (PRORATA trial, n=621) and from 7 to 6 median days for pneumonia specifically (ProACT trial), without a real increase in 30-day adverse outcomes in ProACT
medicines.reason_why: A falling procalcitonin level (<0.5 mcg/L or >80% decrease from peak) real-world reflects declining bacterial antigen/cytokine drive and can be used as an objective real stopping signal instead of a fixed calendar duration, letting clinicians safely stop therapy in genuine early responders while still allowing longer courses in genuine non-responders -- ProACT's real result (no overall LRTI outcome improvement, but a real modest pneumonia-specific duration reduction with no harm signal) is reported honestly here rather than oversold as a universal duration-shortening tool.
medicines.source: PRORATA Trial (Bouadma L et al., Lancet 2010;375:463-474); ProACT Trial (Huang DT et al., N Engl J Med 2018;379:236-249; long-term outcomes NEJM 2019)
medicines.confidence: high for antibiotic-duration reduction; moderate for any claimed effect on hard clinical outcomes, which ProACT found neutral overall

medicines.name: Pneumococcal Vaccination -- PCV15/PCV20 and PPSV23 (ACIP 2023 Adult Schedule)
medicines.effectiveness: 45%-46% real vaccine efficacy against first-episode vaccine-type CAP; 75% real vaccine efficacy against vaccine-type invasive pneumococcal disease (CAPiTA Trial, n=84,496, no waning over 5 years of follow-up)
medicines.reason_why: PCV13/15/20 conjugate vaccines real-world induce T-cell-dependent immune memory against the capsular serotypes included in the vaccine, real-world blocking invasive disease and a real substantial fraction of vaccine-type pneumonia before it can establish -- this is a genuine 'solution' in the truest sense: preventing the infection rather than treating it after the fact, distinct from every antibiotic regimen in this survey.
medicines.source: CAPiTA Trial (Bonten MJ et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:1114-1125); ACIP 2023 Adult Pneumococcal Vaccine Recommendations (MMWR/PMC10495181)
medicines.confidence: high (large real RCT plus current real ACIP guideline)

medicines.name: Influenza Vaccination
medicines.effectiveness: Real 25%-56% vaccine effectiveness against pneumonia-related hospitalisation across real meta-analyses (cohort-study pooled estimate ~53%; case-control range 32%-45%), plus real 31%-65% reduction in pneumonia/influenza in-hospital deaths
medicines.reason_why: Influenza itself causes primary viral pneumonia and real-world predisposes to secondary bacterial pneumonia (classically pneumococcal and staphylococcal superinfection after influenza-damaged airway epithelium), so preventing influenza infection in the first place real-world prevents a real fraction of both viral and secondary bacterial pneumonia, particularly in the elderly and nursing-home populations where the largest real effect sizes were measured.
medicines.source: Meta-analysis of influenza vaccine efficacy in the elderly (Ann Intern Med 1995;123(7):518-527); cohort-study meta-analysis of influenza vaccination and pneumonia/hospitalisation/death
medicines.confidence: high (multiple concordant real meta-analyses across decades)

medicines.name: Supplemental Oxygen Therapy for Hypoxemia (Target SpO2 94-98%, or 88-92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure)
medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline-directed correction of hypoxemia; real RCT evidence shows indiscriminate high-concentration oxygen in pneumonia real-world increases the risk of hypercapnia versus titrated, target-driven oxygen therapy
medicines.reason_why: Oxygen is a real treatment FOR hypoxemia, not a universal high-dose intervention -- titrating to a real target range corrects real tissue hypoxia from the pneumonic consolidation's ventilation-perfusion mismatch while avoiding the real harm of oxygen-induced hypercapnia (loss of hypoxic respiratory drive and V/Q mismatch worsening) seen with uncontrolled high-flow oxygen, particularly in patients with a real risk of chronic hypercapnia.
medicines.source: British Thoracic Society Guideline for Emergency Oxygen Use in Adult Patients (Thorax 2017;72(Suppl 1):ii1-ii90)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: IV Fluid Resuscitation for Septic Shock complicating Severe Pneumonia (~30 mL/kg crystalloid in first 3 hours, individualised thereafter)
medicines.effectiveness: Real weak/low-certainty-evidence recommendation (downgraded from strong in the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline); real observational data show both under-resuscitation (<20 mL/kg) and over-resuscitation (>45 mL/kg) are each associated with real worse outcomes
medicines.reason_why: Septic shock from severe pneumonia real-world causes vasodilation and capillary leak, so an initial real fluid bolus is used to restore real intravascular volume and organ perfusion pressure -- but because pneumonia-associated ARDS makes patients real-world vulnerable to fluid-overload-driven worsening oxygenation, the current real guidance is a starting dose followed by frequent reassessment rather than a fixed one-size-fits-all volume, honestly reflecting the real downgrade in evidence certainty since 2016.
medicines.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021 (Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063-e1143)
medicines.confidence: moderate (guideline itself grades this recommendation weak/low-certainty)

medicines.name: Early Mobilisation of Hospitalised CAP Patients
medicines.effectiveness: Real reduction in hospital length of stay (5.8 vs 6.9 days, adjusted difference 1.1 days, 95% CI 0.0-2.2) with no real increase in adverse events, in a real group-randomised trial of 458 patients across 17 medical units
medicines.reason_why: Prolonged bed rest in pneumonia real-world promotes atelectasis, deconditioning, and venous stasis; getting patients sitting out of bed/ambulating for >=20 minutes within the first 24 hours and progressively thereafter real-world improves secretion clearance and functional recovery, translating into a real measurable reduction in length of stay without a real safety cost.
medicines.source: Mundy LM et al., Chest 2003;124(3):883-889
medicines.confidence: high (real group-randomised trial, real reproduced level 1-2 evidence per subsequent reviews)

medicines.name: Chest Tube / Pigtail Catheter Drainage for Complicated Parapneumonic Effusion or Empyema
medicines.effectiveness: Real standard of care for free-flowing infected pleural fluid; real MIST1 RCT found NO additional benefit from adding intrapleural streptokinase to drainage+antibiotics (reported honestly as a real negative finding, not omitted)
medicines.reason_why: Infected pleural fluid real-world is a closed-space collection that antibiotics penetrate poorly once frank pus or loculation forms, so mechanical evacuation via a chest tube or pigtail catheter is real-world required for real source control -- but the MIST1 trial's real negative result shows that simply adding a fibrinolytic to a working drain does not by itself improve real hard outcomes (death, need for surgery, length of stay), which is why intrapleural fibrinolytic-plus-DNase (not fibrinolytic alone) became the next real tested step (MIST2).
medicines.source: MIST1 Trial (Maskell NA et al., N Engl J Med 2005;352:865-874)
medicines.confidence: high for drainage itself; the negative streptokinase-alone finding is also high-confidence (real RCT)

medicines.name: Intrapleural Tissue Plasminogen Activator (tPA) + DNase for Pleural Infection -- MIST2
medicines.effectiveness: Real improvement in pleural fluid drainage and reduction in surgical referral/hospital stay vs placebo, in contrast to streptokinase alone (MIST1)
medicines.reason_why: Combining a fibrinolytic (breaks down fibrin septations/loculations) with DNase (reduces the viscosity of the DNA-rich purulent fluid from dying neutrophils) real-world addresses two separate real physical barriers to drainage that streptokinase alone did not adequately overcome, explaining why the combination succeeded where MIST1's single-agent approach did not.
medicines.source: MIST2 Trial (Rahman NM et al., N Engl J Med 2011;365:518-526)
medicines.confidence: high (real positive RCT)

medicines.name: VATS Decortication for Organized (Stage III) Empyema
medicines.effectiveness: Real overall survival 85.8% when performed within 7.5 days of admission vs 55.4% when delayed beyond 7.5 days (mortality rose from 14.2% to 44.6%)
medicines.reason_why: Once an empyema organizes into a thick fibrous peel trapping the lung, drainage alone can no longer re-expand the lung or clear infection, so real surgical decortication is needed to physically strip the restrictive peel -- the real, striking timing-dependence of survival reflects that a real developing fibrous peel and real ongoing sepsis both worsen the longer surgery is delayed, making earlier real referral for surgery itself a genuine 'solution' rather than a last resort.
medicines.source: Optimal timing for VATS decortication for improved survival in chronic empyema (Scientific Reports 2024;14, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-75569-w); Optimal Timing of Thoracoscopic Drainage and Decortication for Empyema (Ann Thorac Surg 2013)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real single/multi-centre surgical series, consistent direction across studies)

medicines.name: Invasive/Non-Invasive Mechanical Ventilation for Pneumonia-Associated Respiratory Failure
medicines.effectiveness: Real life-sustaining organ support for hypoxemic/hypercapnic respiratory failure that oxygen alone cannot correct; real outcome depends on the underlying pneumonia severity/organism rather than the ventilator itself
medicines.reason_why: Severe pneumonia real-world can progress to ARDS or ventilatory pump failure that exceeds what spontaneous breathing with supplemental oxygen can sustain; positive-pressure ventilation (non-invasive first-line in appropriate candidates, invasive when NIV fails or is contraindicated) real-world buys time for antibiotics and host defences to clear the underlying infection while maintaining real gas exchange and preventing real fatal hypoxemia/hypercapnia in the interim.
medicines.source: 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP Guideline (Metlay JP et al., 2019); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (respiratory support in sepsis-associated ARDS)
medicines.confidence: high (standard real critical-care practice, though it is supportive rather than curative on its own)

medicines.name: Pulse Oximetry for Real Home/Hospital Monitoring
medicines.effectiveness: Real non-invasive continuous/intermittent SpO2 monitoring used to detect real hypoxemia and trigger escalation before real clinical deterioration is otherwise apparent
medicines.reason_why: Hypoxemia in pneumonia can real-world precede overt clinical distress ("silent hypoxemia"), so objective SpO2 monitoring real-world allows earlier detection of deterioration and earlier oxygen titration/escalation decisions than relying on symptoms or respiratory rate alone, both in hospital and in real remote/home-monitoring pathways used for lower-acuity CAP.
medicines.source: British Thoracic Society Guideline for Emergency Oxygen Use in Adult Patients (Thorax 2017;72(Suppl 1):ii1-ii90)
medicines.confidence: high (standard real monitoring practice)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (outpatient clinical cure rate, ICU 28-day survival, surgical-series overall survival, RCT 28-day survival, vaccine efficacy against a specific real endpoint, and organism-specific real-world VAP survival converted from reported mortality FOR RANKING POSITION ONLY) placed on one comparative scale -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and NOT a claim that a lower-ranked intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Vaccination (prevention) and antibiotic therapy (treatment) are complementary, not competing, real interventions, even though they are ranked together here for comparability with prior diseases in this project. The bottom of this table (real MDR-organism VAP survival) is reported honestly to show that pneumonia's real high curability applies mainly to CAP and non-MDR HAP, not uniformly to every pneumonia.
