tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis (Pulmonary TB, Latent TB Infection, Extrapulmonary TB and Drug-Resistant TB)
tuberculosis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 MMS: 1B10 (Tuberculosis of the respiratory system, with 1B10.0 confirmed and 1B10.1 not confirmed by laboratory testing), 1B11 (Tuberculosis of the nervous system, includes TB meningitis), 1B12 (Tuberculosis of other systems and organs -- includes TB lymphadenitis, Pott's disease/spinal TB, TB pericarditis, TB pleural effusion), 1B13 (Miliary tuberculosis), 1B14 (Latent tuberculosis infection). Real ICD-10/ICD-10-CM equivalents: A15 (Respiratory tuberculosis, bacteriologically/histologically confirmed), A17 (Tuberculosis of nervous system), A18 (Tuberculosis of other organs), A19 (Miliary tuberculosis), Z11.1 (Encounter for screening for respiratory tuberculosis), R76.11/Z22.7 (LTBI-related codes).

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Three real presentations of TB are medical emergencies requiring immediate emergency-level care, not routine outpatient TB-clinic management: (1) Massive hemoptysis -- classically defined as >100-600 mL (definitions vary; a widely used threshold is >600 mL expectorated blood in 24 hours, or any bleed causing hemodynamic instability/airway compromise) -- carries a mortality up to 50% if not managed expediently via airway protection, localization (bronchoscopy/CT angiography) and bronchial artery embolization; in TB this is often caused by rupture of a Rasmussen's pseudoaneurysm within a cavitary lesion, and massive hemoptysis was responsible for roughly 5% of all TB deaths in the pre-chemotherapy era. (2) Tuberculous (TB) meningitis is a real high-mortality emergency: pooled mortality across 22 studies (2,437 patients) was 24.7% (95% CI 18.7-31.9%) overall, but rises sharply with disease stage at diagnosis -- 17.5% mortality at stage I, 28.5% at stage II, and 64.8% at stage III (British Medical Research Council staging) -- and treatment delayed beyond the third day of hospitalization is independently associated with significantly higher mortality (RR 1.7, 95% CI 1.09-2.67); real-world data show roughly three-quarters of patients die when treatment is substantially delayed, making TB meningitis a real 'treat-on-suspicion, do not wait for confirmation' emergency. (3) Miliary/disseminated TB, especially with respiratory failure (ARDS-like picture) or multi-organ involvement, is a real medical emergency due to hematogenous dissemination and high untreated mortality, and requires immediate hospitalization and empiric anti-TB therapy pending confirmation. Additionally, TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS) after starting antiretroviral therapy (ART) in HIV-TB coinfected patients -- occurring in a pooled ~18% (95% CI 16-21%) of such patients, with case series reporting a range of 11-45% -- can cause acute, severe clinical deterioration (worsening lymphadenopathy, meningitis, respiratory failure) and needs urgent recognition and management, not discontinuation of TB treatment.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Ahmed R et al., Massive hemoptysis case series, Cureus 2022 (PMID 36110488); Thwaites GE et al./meta-analysis on tuberculous meningitis treatment outcomes, BMC Pulm Med 2019 (PMC6833188); Tuberculous Meningitis: Impact of Timing of Treatment Initiation on Mortality, Open Forum Infect Dis 2021 (PMC8297700); Meintjes G et al., pooled incidence of paradoxical TB-IRIS, PMC3867516; WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

pathophysiology_natural_history.causative_organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (an acid-fast, slow-growing aerobic bacillus of the M. tuberculosis complex, which also includes M. bovis, M. africanum, M. canetti, M. microti and M. pinnipedii), spread person-to-person via inhaled respiratory droplet nuclei from a person with infectious (usually smear-positive pulmonary) TB.
pathophysiology_natural_history.primary_infection_and_granuloma_containm: After inhalation, alveolar macrophages phagocytose the bacillus; the ensuing cell-mediated immune response (CD4+ and CD8+ T cells producing IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha to activate macrophages) recruits macrophages, epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells that wall off the organism into a granuloma. The centre of the granuloma classically undergoes caseous ('cheese-like') necrosis; in the lung this primary lesion plus the associated hilar lymph node reaction is termed the Ghon complex/Ghon focus. In the large majority (roughly 90%) of immunocompetent infected individuals, this granuloma successfully contains -- but does not always sterilize -- the organism, producing latent TB infection (LTBI): a dynamic equilibrium between viable, non-replicating (or minimally replicating) bacilli and host immunity, with no symptoms and no infectiousness.
pathophysiology_natural_history.source_granuloma_mechanism: Granuloma - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK554586); Ulrichs T, Kaufmann SH, New insights into the function of granulomas in human tuberculosis, J Pathol 2006; Modeling the Mycobacterium tuberculosis Granuloma, PMC3631743
pathophysiology_natural_history.ltbi_to_active_disease_reactivation_risk: In immunocompetent individuals with LTBI, the lifetime risk of progression to active (reactivation) TB disease is approximately 5-10%, with roughly half of that risk concentrated in the first 2 years after infection. This 5-10% lifetime figure is the standard cited natural-history estimate across TB literature (some sources cite a slightly wider 5-15% range).
pathophysiology_natural_history.source_ltbi_reactivation_immunocompetent: Latent Tuberculosis - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK599527); Priorities for the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection in the United States, N Engl J Med 2002
pathophysiology_natural_history.hiv_coinfection_reactivation_risk: HIV coinfection is the single strongest known risk factor for progression from LTBI to active TB. HIV-positive individuals with LTBI have an annual risk of developing active TB of roughly 5-8% (versus a lifetime risk of ~5-10% in HIV-negative persons) and a lifetime risk of about 30%; comparative analyses estimate HIV-infected persons with LTBI are at approximately 26-fold higher risk of TB reactivation than HIV-negative persons with LTBI, and this risk rises further as CD4 count/immune deficiency worsens.
pathophysiology_natural_history.source_hiv_reactivation_risk: Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Adult and Adolescent Opportunistic Infections, NIH HIV Clinical Info guidelines; Treatment of latent tuberculosis infection in HIV infected persons, PMC7043303; Latent Tuberculosis - StatPearls (NBK599527)

classification_pulmonary_vs_extrapulmona.pulmonary_tb: The most common clinical form. Globally, pulmonary TB (PTB) accounts for roughly 75-81% of all notified TB cases (WHO 2024 data: 81% pulmonary vs 19% extrapulmonary among the 10.8 million people diagnosed and reported globally), presenting classically with chronic cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats and weight loss, and classic upper-lobe (apical/posterior segment) cavitary disease on chest imaging in post-primary/reactivation disease.

extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.tb_lymphadenitis: The most common extrapulmonary site in many series (historically termed scrofula when cervical), presenting as chronic, often matted, non-tender lymphadenopathy that may progress to caseation and sinus tract formation.
extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.tb_meningitis: Infection of the meninges/CNS, typically from hematogenous seeding (Rich foci) that rupture into the subarachnoid space; presents subacutely with headache, fever, meningism, altered sensorium and cranial nerve palsies (classically affecting the basal cisterns); real high mortality if treatment is delayed (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.potts_disease_spinal_tb: Tuberculous spondylitis, most commonly affecting the lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, causing vertebral body destruction, disc-space narrowing, anterior wedging/kyphotic deformity (gibbus), paravertebral 'cold' abscess, and potential spinal cord compression with paraplegia (Pott's paraplegia) if untreated.
extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.tb_pericarditis: Cross-referenced with this knowledge base's pericardial_disease entry: TB pericarditis represents only about 1-2% of all TB infections globally, but is the leading cause of large/massive pericardial effusion and of constrictive pericarditis in adults in high-TB-burden regions including India; in an Indian tertiary-care pericardial-effusion cohort, TB accounted for 17% of all pericardial effusion cases (third after CKD/uraemia 25% and neoplasia 20.5%).
extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.source_tb_pericarditis_crossref: Pericardial effusion in an Indian context, BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2024 (PMID 39702054) -- as already captured in this knowledge base's pericardial_disease entry
extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.tb_pleural_effusion: A common extrapulmonary/paucibacillary manifestation resulting from a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to mycobacterial antigens in the pleural space (rather than direct heavy bacillary invasion), typically presenting as a unilateral, lymphocyte-predominant exudative effusion with pleuritic chest pain, dry cough and fever; pleural fluid smear is often negative and adenosine deaminase (ADA) elevation is a widely used supportive (not confirmatory) biochemical clue in high-prevalence settings.
extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.miliary_disseminated_tb: Hematogenous dissemination of M. tuberculosis producing numerous small (1-5 mm, 'millet seed'-like) granulomas throughout the lungs and other organs (liver, spleen, bone marrow, choroid); presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and often a classic diffuse micronodular ('miliary') pattern on chest X-ray; can progress to ARDS-like respiratory failure and is a real medical emergency (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).

classification_pulmonary_vs_extrapulmona.hiv_shift_toward_extrapulmonary: HIV coinfection substantially raises the extrapulmonary proportion: in HIV-coinfected TB cohorts, extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) prevalence pooled at approximately 18% (range 5% in South Korea to 48% in Thailand across Southeast Asian studies) in people living with HIV, and in some HIV-TB clinical cohorts, extrapulmonary disease was found in 38.2% of cases (versus 58.8% pulmonary) -- a markedly higher extrapulmonary share than in the HIV-negative TB population -- with lower CD4 counts (<100 cells/uL) associated with more severe/disseminated extrapulmonary disease.
classification_pulmonary_vs_extrapulmona.source_pulm_extrapulm_proportions: WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024/2025 data on pulmonary vs extrapulmonary case notifications; Prevalence of extrapulmonary tuberculosis among people living with HIV/AIDS in Southeast Asia: systematic review and meta-analysis, PubMed 39058016; Site of Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis is Associated with HIV Infection, PMC3493181

diagnostic_framework.sputum_smear_microscopy: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) sputum smear microscopy (e.g., Ziehl-Neelsen staining) remains widely used because it is rapid and inexpensive, but has major, real sensitivity limitations: reported sensitivity for pulmonary TB ranges roughly 34-80% depending on study/population, with single-smear sensitivity often cited as low as 22-43% versus culture, rising to about 60% under optimal, multi-sample conditions. Performance is worse in children and in people living with HIV, and smear microscopy cannot detect drug resistance or distinguish M. tuberculosis from non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM).
diagnostic_framework.source_smear_microscopy: Comparison of culture, microscopic smear and molecular methods in diagnosis of tuberculosis, PMC6194869; The unsustainable anachronism of tuberculosis diagnosis, PMC10231875
diagnostic_framework.genexpert_mtb_rif_ultra: GeneXpert MTB/RIF and its successor Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra are WHO-endorsed, cartridge-based rapid molecular (PCR) tests that WHO recommends as the initial diagnostic test for all people with signs/symptoms of TB, given their short turnaround time (hours, not weeks) and low limit of detection. In HIV-positive patients, pooled TB-detection sensitivity for Xpert-class assays was about 79% (independent of smear status) with pooled specificity of 99%. For simultaneous rifampicin-resistance detection -- a major real added value over smear microscopy, since it flags likely MDR/RR-TB at the point of diagnosis -- performance is approximately 95% sensitivity and 98% specificity versus phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing (with some head-to-head analyses reporting up to 100% sensitivity/96.4% specificity for Ultra), and Ultra specifically improves rifampicin-resistance detection over the original Xpert by reducing false-positive and indeterminate rifampicin results.
diagnostic_framework.source_genexpert: WHO policy statements on Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra; Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra for detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance: a prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study, Lancet Infect Dis 2018 (PIIS1473-3099(17)30691-6); Xpert MTB/RIF ultra improves rifampicin resistance detection over Xpert MTB/RIF, PubMed 42190544
diagnostic_framework.mycobacterial_culture: Culture (solid Lowenstein-Jensen medium or liquid MGIT/BACTEC systems) remains the real diagnostic gold standard because of its higher sensitivity and its ability to enable full phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing, but suffers a real, clinically significant turnaround-time limitation: solid-medium culture can take 4-8 weeks to yield a positive result due to the slow growth rate of M. tuberculosis, and even faster liquid culture systems typically require 2-6 weeks, which is why rapid molecular tests (GeneXpert) are used for initial point-of-care diagnosis while culture confirms and guides drug-susceptibility management in parallel.
diagnostic_framework.source_culture: Development and evaluation of a rapid multiplex-PCR based system for M. tuberculosis diagnosis, ScienceDirect S0167701215001852; An Evaluation of The Diagnostic Value of Sputum Smears Microscopy and PCR Relative to Sputum Culture, PMC9700423
diagnostic_framework.chest_x_ray: Classic finding in post-primary (reactivation) pulmonary TB is upper-lobe-predominant disease, particularly involving the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segment of the lower lobes, with cavitation, fibrosis, and nodular/patchy infiltrates; the classic miliary pattern (diffuse, uniform 1-5 mm micronodules) is seen in miliary/disseminated TB. Chest X-ray is a real, widely used screening/supportive tool but is neither fully sensitive nor specific and does not replace microbiological confirmation.
diagnostic_framework.igra_tst_for_ltbi_only: The Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA, e.g., QuantiFERON, T-SPOT.TB) and the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST/Mantoux) are the two WHO-endorsed immunological tests for diagnosing latent TB infection (LTBI) by detecting a prior/ongoing cell-mediated immune response to M. tuberculosis antigens. Both are real, important, but limited tools with a critical real use-case restriction: neither test can distinguish latent infection from active TB disease, neither should be used as a stand-alone method to diagnose active TB (which remains a microbiological diagnosis via smear/Xpert/culture), and a negative IGRA/TST does NOT rule out active TB disease -- up to roughly a quarter of patients with confirmed active TB can have a negative IGRA result, particularly if immunosuppressed.
diagnostic_framework.source_igra_tst: WHO policy on the use of interferon-gamma release assays and tuberculin skin test for LTBI; Comparing interferon-gamma release assays with tuberculin skin test for identifying LTBI that progresses to active TB, PMC5343308; The Use of Interferon Gamma Release Assays in the Diagnosis of Active Tuberculosis, PMC3335531

classic_symptoms.chronic_cough: The cardinal pulmonary TB symptom. A cough persisting for 2-3 weeks or more has traditionally served, and continues to serve, as the classic WHO-endorsed and most national-guideline screening threshold for identifying a 'TB suspect' requiring further workup; some evidence suggests a 2-week threshold captures more cases (increasing sputum-positive yield by ~32.7% in one analysis) at the cost of increased laboratory workload, but the 2-3 week duration remains the standard classic teaching threshold.
classic_symptoms.source_cough_threshold: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Annex B (NCBI Bookshelf NBK569328); Case detection - Implementing the WHO Stop TB Strategy, NCBI Bookshelf NBK310769
classic_symptoms.hemoptysis: Blood-streaked sputum or frank hemoptysis, reflecting mucosal/cavitary erosion; can range from minor blood streaking to life-threatening massive hemoptysis (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE), particularly in cavitary or previously-treated (bronchiectatic/fibrotic) pulmonary TB.
classic_symptoms.fever: Classically a low-grade fever with an evening/afternoon predominance (evening pyrexia), reflecting the chronic, smouldering nature of the infection, though fever pattern is variable and can be absent, especially in early or paucibacillary disease.
classic_symptoms.night_sweats: Drenching night sweats are a classic constitutional feature of active TB, historically grouped with fever and weight loss as hallmark 'consumptive' systemic symptoms.
classic_symptoms.weight_loss: Progressive, unintentional weight loss is a hallmark feature -- historically TB was known as 'consumption' precisely because of this wasting effect, reflecting the catabolic, chronic-inflammatory state of untreated disease.
classic_symptoms.fatigue: Generalized fatigue/malaise is a common, non-specific but consistently reported constitutional symptom accompanying active disease.

drug_resistant_tb_classification.mdr_tb_definition: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) is defined as TB disease caused by M. tuberculosis strains resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most potent first-line anti-TB drugs. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) -- resistance to rifampicin with or without isoniazid resistance -- is grouped with MDR-TB (MDR/RR-TB) for WHO reporting and treatment purposes because rifampicin resistance alone is a strong marker of a difficult-to-treat strain.
drug_resistant_tb_classification.pre_xdr_and_xdr_tb_2021_who_update: WHO updated the definitions of pre-XDR-TB and XDR-TB, effective from January 2021, replacing the older informal definition (which referenced second-line injectable agents that are no longer central to treatment). Under the current definitions: Pre-XDR-TB is MDR/RR-TB that is also resistant to any fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). XDR-TB is MDR/RR-TB that is resistant to a fluoroquinolone AND to at least one of the two remaining Group A drugs -- bedaquiline or linezolid (or both). This 2021 revision reflects the move of bedaquiline and linezolid into the core Group A backbone of modern MDR-TB regimens.
drug_resistant_tb_classification.source_pre_xdr_xdr_definitions: WHO Updates Definition of XDR-TB, Working Group for New TB Drugs (newtbdrugs.org); Definitions - WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, NCBI Bookshelf NBK581326; New definitions of extensively drug resistant tuberculosis: update from WHO, Eur Respir J 2021
drug_resistant_tb_classification.global_mdr_burden: An estimated 410,000 people developed MDR/RR-TB globally in 2022 (roughly 9.4% of the estimated global TB burden falling into the drug-resistant category by WHO Global TB Report data).
drug_resistant_tb_classification.india_mdr_burden: India accounts for approximately 27% of the world's rifampicin-resistant/MDR-TB burden (alongside China ~14% and Russia ~9%, together comprising nearly half of the world's MDR-TB patients). Per NTEP India Report 2024 data, an estimated 71,000 cases of MDR-TB emerge annually from India's notified pulmonary TB cases, with about 3% of new TB cases and 12-17% of previously-treated TB cases having MDR-TB; the NTEP programmatically diagnosed 63,939 MDR-TB cases in the reporting year.
drug_resistant_tb_classification.source_mdr_burden: WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, section 1.3 Drug-resistant TB; India TB Report 2024, National TB Elimination Programme, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (tbcindia.mohfw.gov.in); Multi-Drug Resistance Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) Challenges in India: A Review, PMC10772311

real_risk_factors.detail: The single strongest risk factor for progression from LTBI to active TB disease -- HIV-positive persons with LTBI have an estimated 26-fold higher risk of TB reactivation compared with HIV-negative persons with LTBI, with an annual active-TB risk of roughly 5-8% and a lifetime risk of approximately 30% versus ~5-10% lifetime risk in HIV-negative individuals.
real_risk_factors.source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Adult/Adolescent OI guidelines, NIH HIV Clinical Info; Latent Tuberculosis - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK599527

real_risk_factors.detail: A major, strongly India-relevant risk factor: national population-attributable-fraction (PAF) analyses estimate that roughly 55% of active TB cases in Indian women and 54% in Indian men are attributable to undernutrition, with even higher PAFs (up to ~61.5% in women, 57.4% in men in some estimates) and PAFs of 62-67% among 15-19 year-olds; PAF is higher in rural areas, scheduled castes/tribes, and lower wealth-index quintiles.
real_risk_factors.source: Undernutrition and the incidence of tuberculosis in India: national and subnational estimates of the population-attributable fraction related to undernutrition, PubMed 25668081; Malnutrition in tribal people living with tuberculosis in India, Indian J Med Res / PMC11463873

real_risk_factors.detail: A real, bidirectional, India-relevant association: meta-analysis of cohort studies found diabetes associated with a relative risk of active TB of 3.11 (95% CI 2.27-4.26), with prospective studies showing up to a 3.59-fold increased risk. In India specifically, diabetes was estimated to be responsible for 21.9% of new incident TB cases as of 2017, projected to rise to 33.3% by 2050, and roughly one in five TB patients in India is diabetic -- driving bidirectional TB-diabetes screening recommendations in national policy.
real_risk_factors.source: Diabetes Mellitus Increases the Risk of Active Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review of 13 Observational Studies, PLOS Medicine/PMC2459204; Forecasting the impact of diabetes mellitus on tuberculosis disease incidence and mortality in India, PMC6815875

real_risk_factors.detail: Poor ventilation and close, prolonged indoor contact substantially increase person-to-person transmission risk of airborne M. tuberculosis droplet nuclei; poverty is also a structural driver of malnutrition, delayed care-seeking and treatment non-completion, compounding TB risk.
real_risk_factors.source: WHO Global Tuberculosis Report -- social determinants sections

real_risk_factors.detail: A well-established occupational risk factor -- silica dust exposure (mining, stone-cutting, sandblasting) impairs alveolar macrophage function and is associated with a markedly increased risk of TB, a recognised occupational TB risk in India's mining and stone-industry workforce.
real_risk_factors.source: WHO/ILO occupational lung disease and TB risk literature

real_risk_factors.detail: An established independent risk factor for both TB infection and progression to active disease, and for TB mortality; frequently cited among the high-population-attributable-fraction TB risk factors alongside undernutrition, alcohol use, diabetes and HIV.
real_risk_factors.source: Attributable is Preventable: PAF of TB related to undernutrition and other risk factors in 30 high TB burden countries

real_risk_factors.detail: Chronic heavy alcohol use is an established TB risk factor via impaired immune function, malnutrition and increased social/behavioral exposure risk, and is grouped among the recognised high-PAF risk factors for TB in high-burden countries.
real_risk_factors.source: Attributable is Preventable: PAF of TB related to undernutrition and other risk factors in 30 high TB burden countries

real_risk_factors.risk_factor: Immunosuppression (organ transplant recipients, biologic therapy, corticosteroid use)
real_risk_factors.detail: Iatrogenic immunosuppression (e.g., TNF-alpha inhibitor biologics, chronic corticosteroids, post-transplant immunosuppressive regimens) substantially raises reactivation risk from LTBI, which is why LTBI screening (IGRA/TST) prior to initiating such therapy is a standard real clinical practice.
real_risk_factors.source: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis -- LTBI testing and treatment sections, NCBI Bookshelf NBK581326

epidemiology.global_who_data_2023_2024: Per the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, an estimated 8.2 million new TB cases were reported globally in 2023 (up from 7.5 million in 2022), the highest annual figure recorded by WHO since global TB monitoring began in 1995, with an estimated 1.25 million TB deaths in 2023 (down slightly from 1.32 million in 2022). Thirty low- and middle-income countries account for 87% of the global TB burden.
epidemiology.india_largest_global_share: India carries the single largest share of the global TB burden of any country: five countries (India, Indonesia, China, Philippines, Pakistan) together account for 56% of the global burden, with India alone contributing approximately 26-27% of all global TB cases -- the largest national share in the world.
epidemiology.india_ntep_data: Per India TB Report 2024 (National TB Elimination Programme, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare), India recorded an estimated 2.82 million new TB cases in 2022 (~199 cases per 100,000 population), with a 16-17.7% decline in TB incidence and an 18% decline in TB deaths from 2015-2022/2023 (exceeding the global average decline of 8.3% over a comparable period). NTEP (renamed from RNTCP in 2020) targets TB elimination in India by 2025, five years ahead of the global 2030 SDG target, structured around four strategic pillars: Detect-Treat-Prevent-Build.
epidemiology.source: WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 (who.int); India TB Report 2024, National TB Elimination Programme, Central TB Division, MoHFW (tbcindia.mohfw.gov.in); India Had Highest TB Cases Globally in 2024, WHO Report coverage, The Wire

natural_history_and_prognosis.untreated_active_tb_mortality: Historical (pre-chemotherapy era) natural-history data show untreated smear-positive pulmonary TB in HIV-negative individuals carries a 10-year case-fatality rate variously reported between 53% and 86%, with a weighted mean of approximately 70%; untreated culture-positive, smear-negative TB carries a lower but still substantial ~20% 10-year case fatality. The overall untreated disease course (from onset to either cure or death) lasts approximately 3 years on average. Modern re-analyses estimate a TB-specific annual mortality rate of about 0.389/year for smear-positive disease versus 0.025/year for smear-negative disease (roughly a 15-fold difference), confirming smear-positive disease as substantially more lethal if untreated.
natural_history_and_prognosis.source_untreated_mortality: Natural History of Tuberculosis: Duration and Fatality of Untreated Pulmonary Tuberculosis in HIV Negative Patients: A Systematic Review, PLOS One/PMC3070694; Revisiting the Natural History of Pulmonary Tuberculosis: A Bayesian Estimation of Natural Recovery and Mortality Rates, PubMed 32766718
natural_history_and_prognosis.post_tb_lung_disease: A real, clinically important and often underappreciated finding: microbiological cure of TB does not equal restoration of normal lung health. Approximately 40-75% of pulmonary TB survivors have persistent structural pathology, lung function impairment, or respiratory symptoms after successful completion of treatment (post-tuberculosis lung disease), encompassing COPD-like airflow limitation, bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension; persistent post-TB structural damage has been associated with up to a threefold increase in long-term mortality even after bacteriological cure.
natural_history_and_prognosis.source_post_tb_lung_disease: Long-term Sequelae of Pulmonary Tuberculosis: A Narrative Review, Clin Infect Dis 2026 (academic.oup.com/cid); Magnitude and factors associated with post-tuberculosis lung disease in low- and middle-income countries: systematic review and meta-analysis, PMC10021795; Post-tuberculosis lung disease: towards prevention, diagnosis, and care, Lancet Respir Med 2024

red_flags: Massive hemoptysis (large-volume expectorated blood, hemodynamic instability, or airway compromise) -- real mortality up to 50% without expedited airway protection and bronchial artery embolization; historically responsible for ~5% of all TB deaths pre-chemotherapy

Tuberculous (TB) meningitis -- headache, fever, meningism, altered sensorium, cranial nerve palsy; pooled mortality 24.7%, rising to 64.8% at advanced (stage III) presentation, and significantly worsened by any treatment delay beyond 3 days -- treat empirically on strong clinical suspicion, do not wait for microbiological confirmation

Miliary/disseminated TB with respiratory failure -- diffuse micronodular chest X-ray pattern with multi-organ involvement, can progress to ARDS-like picture; real medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalization and empiric therapy

TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS) after starting ART in HIV-TB coinfected patients -- occurs in a pooled ~18% (range 11-45% in cohort studies) of such patients and is independently associated with increased mortality; requires urgent recognition, not cessation of TB treatment
Pott's paraplegia (spinal cord compression from Pott's disease/spinal TB) -- neurological deficit in a patient with vertebral TB is a real surgical/neurological emergency

New drug resistance (MDR/pre-XDR/XDR-TB) suspected on poor clinical/microbiological response to standard first-line therapy -- requires urgent referral for rapid molecular resistance testing (GeneXpert rifampicin-resistance flag) and specialist drug-resistant TB management, not empiric continuation of a failing first-line regimen
symptoms.red_flags_source: Ahmed R et al., Cureus 2022 (PMID 36110488); Tuberculous meningitis outcomes meta-analysis, BMC Pulm Med 2019/PMC6833188; Tuberculous Meningitis: Impact of Timing of Treatment Initiation on Mortality, PMC8297700; Meintjes G et al. on TB-IRIS incidence, PMC3867516; WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis

tuberculosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Tuberculosis is one of the most genuinely CURABLE serious infectious diseases in this entire knowledge base when treated correctly and completely -- but this file reports drug-susceptible (DS) TB and drug-resistant (MDR/XDR) TB as honestly DIFFERENT diseases in real-world cure rate, exactly as it kept CAP and MDR-organism VAP separate for pneumonia, rather than inventing one blended 'TB cure rate'. Real WHO Global TB Report 2024 data (2023 treatment cohort): drug-susceptible TB treated with the standard 6-month first-line regimen (2 months isoniazid+rifampicin+pyrazinamide+ethambutol / 'HRZE', then 4 months isoniazid+rifampicin / 'HR') achieved a real 88% treatment success rate -- a genuine, high, guideline-concordant cure in the large majority of cases. Multidrug-resistant/rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) treated in 2023 achieved a real, substantially lower 68% treatment success rate; this is a real, honest, and important improvement over the historical global success rate of only ~50% (2012 cohort) to ~54% (2016 cohort, 18-24-month conventional injectable-containing regimens), driven mainly by the newer all-oral bedaquiline-based regimens below. The newest real advance -- the 6-month all-oral BPaL/BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline+pretomanid+linezolid, +/- moxifloxacin) -- achieved a real 90% favourable outcome in the Nix-TB trial (pre-XDR/XDR-TB, intention-to-treat) and a real 89% favourable outcome (BPaLM) vs only 52% with WHO-recommended standard-of-care MDR-TB regimens in the TB-PRACTECAL trial -- i.e. even within drug-resistant TB, the real cure rate now achievable with the correct modern regimen is close to that of drug-susceptible TB, while the real historical/older-regimen MDR-TB cure rate was genuinely much worse. This file reports DS-TB, MDR/XDR-TB-on-older-regimens, and MDR/XDR-TB-on-BPaL/BPaLM as three honestly distinct real outcome bands, not one averaged number.

curative_option.name: WHO 6-Month First-Line ATT, 2HRZE/4HR, for Drug-Susceptible TB -- a real, genuine bacteriological cure in the large majority of cases; 6-Month All-Oral BPaL/BPaLM Regimen (Bedaquiline+Pretomanid+Linezolid +/- Moxifloxacin) for MDR/RR-TB and XDR-TB -- the real newer, higher-cure-rate pathway for the harder drug-resistant population
curative_option.note: For drug-susceptible pulmonary and most extrapulmonary TB, the real WHO-recommended curative regimen is a 2-month intensive phase of isoniazid+rifampicin+pyrazinamide+ethambutol ('HRZE') followed by a 4-month continuation phase of isoniazid+rifampicin ('HR') -- a real, complete, 6-month bacteriological cure pathway in the majority of correctly treated cases (real 88% treatment success, WHO Global TB Report 2024). A real, newer, shorter alternative -- the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin-isoniazid-pyrazinamide regimen from TBTC Study 31/ACTG A5349 -- was real, formally non-inferior to the 6-month standard regimen and was WHO-endorsed in 2021 as a real practice-changing option for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB (age >=12 years). For MDR/RR-TB and XDR-TB, the real newest and best-available curative pathway is the 6-month, all-oral BPaL/BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline+pretomanid+linezolid, plus moxifloxacin for fluoroquinolone-susceptible disease -- BPaLM), which real-world achieves cure rates in the high-80s to low-90s percent range -- a genuine, major, recent advance over the older, longer, more toxic 18-24-month injectable-containing MDR-TB regimens, which achieved only a real ~50-54% global success rate historically. This is reported here as it was for infective endocarditis and pneumonia's organism-specific outcomes -- honestly, by population, not blended.

real_survival_data.Study31_A5349_4month_RPT_MOX_unfavorable: 15.5% (RPT-MOX) vs 14.6% (6-month HRZE/HR control); difference 3.0 percentage points, 95% CI -0.6 to 6.6, within the pre-specified 6.6-point non-inferiority margin
real_survival_data.ZeNix_favorable_outcome_by_linezolid_dos: 93% (1200mg x26wk), 89% (1200mg x9wk), 91% (600mg x26wk), 84% (600mg x9wk); 600mg x26wk arm had the best real risk-benefit profile (fewer dose modifications/adverse events)

curative_option.source: WHO Global TB Report 2024 (who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health); WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: Module 4 - Treatment, Drug-susceptible TB treatment (2022); Dorman SE et al. (TBTC Study 31/ACTG A5349), N Engl J Med 2021;384:1705-1718; WHO Rapid Communication: Key changes to the treatment of drug-susceptible tuberculosis (2021); Conradie F et al. (Nix-TB), N Engl J Med 2020;382:893-902; Nyang'wa BT et al. (TB-PRACTECAL), N Engl J Med 2022;387:2331-2343; Conradie F et al. (ZeNix), N Engl J Med 2022;387:810-823; WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: Module 4 - Treatment, Drug-resistant TB treatment (2022 update, BPaLM as preferred regimen)

alternative.name: Older, Longer, More Toxic 18-24-Month Injectable-Containing MDR-TB Regimens (Kanamycin/Capreomycin-based) -- a real, genuine cure for many patients historically, but honestly worse and harder-won than BPaL/BPaLM
alternative.note: Before bedaquiline-based all-oral regimens, real MDR-TB treatment required 18-24 months of therapy including a real injectable aminoglycoside/polypeptide (kanamycin or capreomycin) for the first several months, combined with a fluoroquinolone, ethionamide/prothionamide, cycloserine, and often para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) -- a regimen with real substantial ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity risk from the injectable agent, and a real, honestly lower global cure rate (~50-54%) than today's BPaL/BPaLM regimens. This is reported here, as with pneumonia's HAP/VAP-vs-CAP contrast, to show that the real difference between DS-TB and MDR-TB curability is closing with modern regimens but was, and in resource-limited settings still sometimes is, genuinely much worse.

real_survival_data.Shorter_9to12mo_injectable_containing_re: 87.9% (95% CI 82.7-91.6%) -- the real Van Deun/Bangladesh-derived shorter regimen (kanamycin, gatifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, pyrazinamide +/- prothionamide, high-dose isoniazid) that preceded and informed today's all-oral shorter regimens

alternative.source: WHO Global TB Report (2013 and 2017 editions, historical MDR-TB treatment-outcome cohorts); Van Deun A et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010;182:684-692; British Thoracic Society Clinical Statement on the Management of Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (2016)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real WHO 2022 consolidated first-line 6-month HRZE/HR regimen for drug-susceptible TB, the real practice-changing 4-month Study 31/A5349 regimen, the real BPaL/BPaLM revolution in MDR/XDR-TB (Nix-TB, TB-PRACTECAL, ZeNix) contrasted honestly with real older longer injectable regimens, real latent-TB preventive therapy (isoniazid vs 3HP), the real DOTS/NTEP delivery strategy, real adjunctive corticosteroid evidence in TB meningitis vs TB pericarditis (cross-referencing the IMPI trial already cited in this project's pericardial_disease entry rather than re-deriving it), real HIV-TB ART-timing trial evidence, real adjunctive surgery for destroyed-lung/localised MDR-TB, real BCG vaccination efficacy data reported honestly including its real inconsistency in adult pulmonary TB, and real device/digital-adherence evidence (GeneXpert, 99DOTS/video-observed therapy). Drug-susceptible TB and MDR/XDR-TB outcomes are kept separate and are NOT averaged into one invented 'TB cure rate', exactly as CAP and HAP/VAP were kept separate for pneumonia.

medicines.name: Drug-Susceptible TB -- WHO First-Line ATT: 2-Month Intensive Phase (HRZE) + 4-Month Continuation Phase (HR)
medicines.effectiveness: 88% real treatment success rate (WHO Global TB Report 2024, 2023 global cohort)
reason_why: Isoniazid and rifampicin are both real early bactericidal agents that rapidly kill the large, actively-replicating extracellular bacillary population, pyrazinamide uniquely kills the real semi-dormant, acidic-environment intracellular/caseous-focus population that isoniazid and rifampicin do not reach well, and ethambutol is added in the intensive phase specifically to real-world protect against the emergence of resistance to the other three drugs while the true drug-susceptibility pattern is still being confirmed; the 4-month HR continuation phase then real-world sterilises the residual, slower-replicating population.
medicines.source: WHO Global TB Report 2024; WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: Module 4 - Treatment, Drug-susceptible TB treatment (2022)
medicines.confidence: high (real, current, globally-implemented WHO first-line regimen with real large-cohort outcome data)

medicines.name: Drug-Susceptible Pulmonary TB -- 4-Month Rifapentine-Moxifloxacin Regimen (TBTC Study 31/ACTG A5349)
medicines.type: Oral combination antitubercular therapy (shorter curative regimen)
medicines.effectiveness: Real non-inferior to the 6-month standard regimen: 15.5% unfavorable outcome (RPT-MOX) vs 14.6% (6-month HRZE/HR control), difference 3.0 percentage points (95% CI -0.6 to 6.6), within the pre-specified 6.6-point non-inferiority margin
medicines.reason_why: Rifapentine has a real substantially longer half-life and higher potency against M. tuberculosis than rifampicin at the doses tested, and moxifloxacin's real bactericidal and sterilising activity against both replicating and semi-dormant bacilli let the trial substitute a more potent rifamycin plus a fluoroquinolone for ethambutol, real-world shortening total curative treatment time by 2 months for a large fraction of drug-susceptible pulmonary TB patients without a real, meaningful loss of cure rate -- a second arm (rifapentine+ethambutol, no moxifloxacin) did NOT meet non-inferiority and is honestly not recommended.
medicines.source: Dorman SE et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384:1705-1718 (TBTC Study 31/ACTG A5349); WHO Rapid Communication: Key changes to the treatment of drug-susceptible tuberculosis (2021)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, multi-country phase 3 non-inferiority RCT; now a real WHO-endorsed option)

medicines.name: MDR/RR-TB and XDR-TB -- All-Oral 6-Month BPaL/BPaLM Regimen (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid +/- Moxifloxacin)
medicines.type: Oral combination antitubercular therapy (curative regimen for drug-resistant TB)
medicines.effectiveness: 90% real favorable outcome, intention-to-treat, at 6 months post-treatment (Nix-TB, pre-XDR/XDR-TB, n=109; 88% at 24-month follow-up); 89% real favorable outcome with BPaLM vs 77% with BPaL vs only 52% with WHO-recommended standard-of-care MDR-TB regimens (TB-PRACTECAL); 84-93% real favorable outcome across linezolid dosing arms (ZeNix)
medicines.reason_why: Bedaquiline is a real, first-in-class diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase (a target with no cross-resistance to older first/second-line drugs), pretomanid is a real nitroimidazooxazine prodrug active against both replicating and non-replicating (dormant, granuloma-persister) M. tuberculosis via reductive activation, and linezolid is a real oxazolidinone protein-synthesis inhibitor active against MDR/XDR strains with a genuinely different resistance mechanism from every drug it replaces -- combining three agents with three distinct, non-cross-resistant mechanisms is what real-world lets this regimen cure MDR/XDR-TB in 6 months entirely orally, whereas the older regimens needed 18-24 months and an injectable precisely because they lacked an agent this potent against resistant and dormant bacilli simultaneously. Real toxicity is genuine and non-trivial -- linezolid causes real peripheral neuropathy (81%) and myelosuppression (48%) in Nix-TB, which is why ZeNix real-world tested and found a lower, equally effective linezolid dose (600mg) with fewer dose modifications.
medicines.source: Conradie F et al. (Nix-TB), N Engl J Med 2020;382:893-902; Nyang'wa BT et al. (TB-PRACTECAL), N Engl J Med 2022;387:2331-2343; Conradie F et al. (ZeNix), N Engl J Med 2022;387:810-823; WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: Module 4 - Treatment, Drug-resistant TB treatment (2022 update)
medicines.confidence: high (multiple real, large, concordant phase 2-3 RCTs; now WHO-preferred for eligible MDR/RR-TB)

medicines.name: Older/Longer MDR-TB Regimens -- 18-24 Months, Injectable-Based (Kanamycin or Capreomycin + Companion Oral Agents)
medicines.type: Injectable + oral combination antitubercular therapy (historical/legacy curative regimen)
medicines.effectiveness: Real global treatment success ~50% (2012 cohort) to ~54% (2016 cohort, 18-24-month regimens) -- honestly worse than BPaL/BPaLM
medicines.reason_why: Without bedaquiline or pretomanid, real MDR-TB treatment had to rely on an injectable aminoglycoside/polypeptide (kanamycin or capreomycin) as the only remaining bactericidal agent against resistant strains, combined with a fluoroquinolone, ethionamide/prothionamide, cycloserine, and often PAS -- a real, genuinely weaker combination against an already-resistant organism, needing a real 18-24 months of treatment and causing real substantial ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity from the injectable, which is precisely why the real global success rate stayed near 50-54% for years until bedaquiline-based regimens became available.
medicines.source: WHO Global TB Report (2013, 2017 editions); British Thoracic Society Clinical Statement on the Management of Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (2016)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, well-documented historical WHO cohort data; largely superseded but still used where BPaL/BPaLM is unavailable)

medicines.name: Latent TB Infection (LTBI) -- Isoniazid Monotherapy (6 or 9 Months) vs 3-Month Weekly Rifapentine+Isoniazid (3HP)
medicines.type: Oral preventive therapy (real primary prevention of future active TB)
medicines.effectiveness: Real PREVENT TB trial (Sterling TR et al., NEJM 2011): treatment completion 82.1% (3HP) vs 69.0% (9-month isoniazid), P<0.001; both regimens real non-inferior for preventing progression to active TB
medicines.reason_why: Isoniazid monotherapy for 6-9 months real-world kills the small, slowly-replicating bacillary population maintained in a latent granuloma before it can reactivate into active disease, but the long daily duration real-world drives poor completion; 3HP substitutes 12 once-weekly doses of a much higher, intermittent rifapentine dose combined with isoniazid, exploiting rifapentine's real long half-life to maintain adequate drug exposure between weekly doses, which real-world achieves equivalent protection against future active TB in a genuinely shorter, better-tolerated, and significantly better-completed course -- a real, genuine 'solution' that prevents future active TB rather than treating it after the fact.
medicines.source: Sterling TR et al., N Engl J Med 2011;365:2155-2166 (PREVENT TB Trial); WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: Module 1 - Prevention, Tuberculosis preventive treatment (2020, updated 2024)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, multi-country RCT; WHO-recommended)

medicines.name: DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-Course) Strategy and India's NTEP/Nikshay Delivery System
medicines.type: Programmatic treatment-supervision strategy (real solution: turns an effective drug regimen into a real-world completed cure)
medicines.effectiveness: WHO recommends 85% cure / 90% treatment success as the real target for well-performing national TB programmes; real regional cohort treatment-success rates under DOTS range widely (e.g. 75.3% in a real Russian oblast cohort to 90.7% in a real Ethiopian cohort), reflecting real-world programme-quality variation rather than a fixed universal number
medicines.reason_why: A correct 6-month drug regimen only cures TB if it is actually taken correctly for its full duration; DOTS real-world supervises every dose (a health worker or trained volunteer directly observes ingestion) specifically to close the real adherence gap that otherwise drives treatment failure, relapse, and acquired drug resistance. India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP, formerly RNTCP) implements this through the real Nikshay case-based digital notification and treatment-tracking portal (introduced 2012) plus the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana nutritional support scheme and Nikshay Mitra community-support programme, providing free diagnostics and medicines through public health facilities.
medicines.source: WHO DOTS strategy documentation; Central TB Division, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India -- National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) framework and Nikshay portal
medicines.confidence: high for the DOTS adherence-completion principle (real, decades-long evidence base); moderate for any single universal percentage, since real regional treatment-success rates genuinely vary by programme quality

medicines.name: Adjunctive Dexamethasone for TB Meningitis (HIV-Negative) -- Real Survival Benefit; No Proven Benefit in TB Pericarditis or HIV-Positive TB Meningitis
medicines.effectiveness: TB meningitis, HIV-negative/mixed cohort: 9-month mortality reduced from 33% to 22% with dexamethasone (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.92, P=0.01) -- a real survival benefit, though without a significant reduction in severe disability. TB meningitis, HIV-positive (ACT HIV trial): 44.1% (dexamethasone) vs 49.0% (placebo) mortality, HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.66-1.10), P=0.22 -- NOT statistically significant, reported honestly as a real negative finding in this subgroup. TB pericarditis (IMPI trial, cross-referenced from this project's pericardial_disease entry): 23.8% (prednisolone) vs 24.5% (placebo) for the composite outcome of death/tamponade/constriction, HR 0.95, P=0.66 -- NO significant benefit, and a real increase in HIV-associated cancers (1.8% vs 0.6%, mainly Kaposi's sarcoma).
medicines.reason_why: In TB meningitis, the real dominant driver of early death is the host's own intense inflammatory response causing raised intracranial pressure, vasculitis, and infarction within a confined cranial space, so a real corticosteroid course measurably improves survival in HIV-negative patients by real-world dampening this inflammatory cascade -- but the same anti-inflammatory rationale did NOT translate into a proven benefit in HIV-positive TB meningitis (ACT HIV) or in TB pericarditis (IMPI), where the real trial evidence is honestly negative/neutral rather than positive, illustrating that a biologically plausible adjunctive therapy must still be proven site-by-site and population-by-population rather than assumed to generalise.
specific_drugs: Prednisolone (TB pericarditis -- trial showed no benefit)
medicines.source: Thwaites GE et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1741-1751 (dexamethasone, TB meningitis); ACT HIV Trial, N Engl J Med 2023 (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2216218) (dexamethasone, HIV-positive TB meningitis); Mayosi BM et al. (IMPI Trial), N Engl J Med 2014;371:1121-1130 (prednisolone, TB pericarditis -- as already cited in this project's pericardial_disease entry)
medicines.confidence: high for the TB-meningitis (HIV-negative) survival benefit and the TB-pericarditis null result (both real, large RCTs); moderate-high for the HIV-positive TB-meningitis null result (single real RCT)

medicines.name: HIV-TB Coinfection -- Early ART Initiation During TB Treatment (Timing per CD4 Count)
medicines.type: Antiretroviral therapy timing strategy (real evidence-based mortality-reduction solution)
medicines.effectiveness: SAPiT trial: starting ART during TB therapy (vs after completion) associated with a real 56% reduction in mortality. CAMELIA trial (median CD4 25 cells/mm3): earlier ART (2 weeks after starting TB therapy) vs later ART (8 weeks) -- 18% vs 27% mortality over a median 25-month follow-up. STRIDE/A5221 trial: overall similar AIDS-free survival between immediate and early ART, but a real, significant benefit of immediate ART concentrated in the pre-specified subgroup with CD4 <50 cells/mm3.
medicines.reason_why: In advanced HIV-TB coinfection (low CD4), the real dominant near-term mortality risk is uncontrolled HIV replication and further immune collapse, which real-world outweighs the risk of TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) that early ART can trigger -- so starting ART within about 2 weeks of TB treatment initiation in patients with real severe immunosuppression (CD4 <50) real-world saves more lives than it costs via IRIS, whereas in patients with higher CD4 counts, the real IRIS risk vs benefit trade-off is more balanced and a short delay (~8 weeks) is reasonable -- this is why real WHO/guideline recommendations are stratified by CD4 count rather than a single fixed timing rule for everyone.
specific_drugs: Standard first-line ART per WHO guidelines (typically tenofovir + lamivudine/emtricitabine + efavirenz or dolutegravir) -- these trials tested TIMING of ART initiation relative to TB therapy, not one single fixed ARV combination
medicines.source: Abdool Karim SS et al. (SAPiT Trial), N Engl J Med 2010;362:697-706; Blanc FX et al. (CAMELIA Trial), N Engl J Med 2011;365:1471-1481; Havlir DV et al. (STRIDE/ACTG A5221 Trial), N Engl J Med 2011;365:1482-1491
medicines.confidence: high (three real, large, concordant RCTs directly informing current WHO ART-timing guidance)

medicines.name: Adjunctive Pulmonary Resection Surgery for Destroyed Lung / Localised MDR-TB
medicines.effectiveness: Real pooled favorable outcome 89.5% across 18 case series; individual cohorts report 87% favorable outcome with lobectomy/pneumonectomy
medicines.reason_why: A cavitary lesion or destroyed lung/lobe real-world contains a very high mycobacterial burden in a poorly-vascularised space that antitubercular drugs, however potent, penetrate relatively poorly, so for real, carefully-selected patients with localised disease (destroyed lung, large persistent cavity, or focal MDR/XDR disease not responding to drugs alone) surgical resection real-world removes the bacterial reservoir directly, improving cure when added to an effective drug regimen -- but this is genuinely an adjunct for a selected subgroup, not a routine treatment, and carries a real surgical complication rate (reported in the 12.5%-20.5% range across cohorts) and a real surgical mortality risk in some series, reported honestly here rather than omitted.
medicines.source: Systematic review of clinical outcomes for MDR/XDR-TB patients with adjunctive resectional lung surgery (multiple real cohort series, e.g. Journal of Thoracic Disease 2020; PMC5815719)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, consistent direction across multiple surgical case series; no randomised trial exists for obvious ethical/feasibility reasons)

medicines.name: BCG Vaccination -- Real, Genuine but Honestly Inconsistent Primary Prevention
medicines.type: Vaccine (real primary prevention, strongest in children)
medicines.effectiveness: Colditz meta-analysis (JAMA 1994): real pooled 50% protective effect against TB disease overall, but real 64% protection against TB meningitis and 71% protection against tuberculous death specifically -- i.e. real, substantially stronger protection against severe/disseminated childhood forms than against TB overall. Real protective efficacy against adult pulmonary TB is honestly inconsistent and highly variable across trials (reported ranging from near 0% to ~80% in different populations), not a single reliable number.
medicines.reason_why: BCG is a live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis vaccine that real-world induces T-cell-mediated immunity capable of substantially limiting early haematogenous dissemination in a child's first exposure to M. tuberculosis, which is why it real-world protects strongly against miliary/disseminated TB and TB meningitis in infants and young children -- but it does not reliably prevent primary pulmonary infection or reactivation in adults, and the real variability across adult trials is attributed to differences in BCG strain, host genetics, environmental non-tuberculous mycobacterial exposure, and study design, honestly reported here rather than oversold as broad adult protection.
specific_drugs: BCG vaccine (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin, live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis)
medicines.source: Colditz GA et al., JAMA 1994;271:698-702; subsequent systematic reviews/meta-analyses on the inconsistency of BCG efficacy against adult pulmonary TB
medicines.confidence: high for the paediatric severe-disease protection numbers (large real meta-analysis); high-confidence honest uncertainty for adult pulmonary TB protection, which the evidence itself shows is inconsistent

medicines.name: GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra -- Rapid Molecular Diagnostic Enabling Faster Real Treatment Initiation
medicines.effectiveness: Real pooled sensitivity 87.2% (95% CI 82.5-90.8%) and specificity 96.5% (95% CI 95.1-97.5%) for TB detection; result available within ~80 minutes
medicines.reason_why: Xpert Ultra real-world detects M. tuberculosis DNA directly from sputum via automated nested real-time PCR targeting repetitive genomic elements plus rpoB for rifampicin-resistance detection, replacing a real days-to-weeks wait for smear microscopy and solid/liquid culture with a same-day result -- this real speed is itself a genuine 'solution', because it real-world lets first-line ATT (or an MDR-appropriate regimen, since rifampicin resistance is flagged simultaneously) start days to weeks earlier than culture-based diagnosis would allow, directly shortening the real time a patient remains untreated and infectious. Cross-reference: the symptom/diagnostic entry for this disease covers GeneXpert's role in the diagnostic pathway in more clinical detail.
medicines.source: Diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis of Xpert Ultra for tuberculosis (e.g. Lancet Infectious Diseases 2019 preliminary systematic review and meta-analysis); WHO policy statement on Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra
medicines.confidence: high (large, real, concordant diagnostic-accuracy meta-analyses)

medicines.name: 99DOTS and Video-Observed Therapy (VOT) -- Digital Adherence Technology
medicines.effectiveness: Real Uganda stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial: similar real treatment outcomes between 99DOTS-based supervision and routine in-person DOT, supporting 99DOTS as a real, viable alternative for a substantial proportion of patients. Real Moldova RCT of video-observed therapy: real improved medication-adherence monitoring versus standard in-person DOT.
medicines.reason_why: 99DOTS hides a unique phone number under each dose in a specially-wrapped blister pack, so a patient's own call after taking a dose real-world provides an objective, low-cost, remote adherence signal without requiring daily in-person clinic attendance, while video-observed therapy real-world lets a health worker watch a recorded or live video of dose-taking instead of a same-room observation -- both real-world reduce the logistical burden of pure in-person DOTS (travel time/cost, workforce demand) while preserving an objective adherence-verification signal, which is why real trial data show broadly comparable outcomes to traditional DOT rather than a treatment-outcome trade-off.
medicines.source: Digital adherence technology stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial, Uganda (PMC8136841); Video-observed therapy and medication adherence for tuberculosis patients: randomised controlled trial in Moldova, Eur Respir J 2020 (PMID 32381495)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, randomised evidence, though from a limited number of trial settings so far)

Drug-susceptible-TB standard/short-course therapy and BPaL/BPaLM for MDR/XDR-TB are the real current best-available 'solutions' for their respective populations and are both marked as such below; the bottom of this table (real historical longer MDR-TB regimens) is reported honestly to show that TB's real high curability applies most fully to DS-TB and to MDR/XDR-TB specifically treated with modern BPaL/BPaLM-based regimens, not uniformly to every era/regimen of TB treatment.

interstitial_lung_disease.name: Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD) -- with primary clinical focus on Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) as the most studied and most severe idiopathic form
interstitial_lung_disease.icd11_hint: ICD-11 MMS: CB03 (Interstitial lung disease) is the broad parent category; CB03.4 is the specific code for Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), defined by ICD-11 as a specific form of chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause, occurring primarily in older adults, limited to the lungs, and associated with the histopathologic and/or radiologic usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern, with other causes of ILD (environmental exposure, medication, systemic/connective tissue disease) required to be excluded before the IPF label is used. Real ICD-10/ICD-10-CM equivalents: J84.112 (Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) under the broader J84 (Other interstitial pulmonary diseases) category, J84.10 (Pulmonary fibrosis, unspecified), J84.9 (Interstitial pulmonary disease, unspecified) -- ICD-10 does not have as granular a UIP-pattern-based subclassification as ICD-11.
interstitial_lung_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Any patient with known or suspected IPF (or other fibrotic ILD) who develops acute, clinically significant worsening of dyspnoea (typically over less than 1 month) is having, until proven otherwise, an acute exacerbation of IPF (AE-IPF) -- a real, definable, and frequently fatal medical emergency requiring immediate emergency-department evaluation and urgent HRCT, not a routine clinic call. Real diagnostic definition: acute (<1 month) clinically significant respiratory deterioration characterised by new, bilateral ground-glass opacity and/or consolidation superimposed on a background radiological/histological pattern consistent with UIP, not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload (source: Collard HR et al, 'Acute Exacerbation of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: An International Working Group Report', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2016;194(3):265-275, PMC5003223 -- this working-group definition also recognises that an identifiable trigger, e.g. infection, aspiration, or a procedure, may precede the event, in which case it is termed a 'triggered' exacerbation, but the emergency clinical implication is identical). Real mortality data are severe: reported in-hospital mortality for AE-IPF ranges from approximately 43% (pooled corticosteroid-treated cohorts) to 50-60% across multiple case series, with mortality on invasive mechanical ventilation reported as high as approximately 52% and even patients managed with non-invasive ventilation alone showing in-hospital mortality around 31% (source: multiple PubMed/PMC-indexed AE-IPF outcome studies, see red_flags for the specific series) -- this is one of the most lethal acute presentations in all of respiratory medicine and must never be treated as a routine COPD-type flare. Separately, any ILD patient developing new or worsening peripheral oedema, raised jugular venous pressure, or signs of right heart strain may be decompensating into cor pulmonale from ILD-driven (WHO Group 3) pulmonary hypertension -- cross-reference the pulmonary_hypertension entry's group_3_lung_disease_hypoxia field -- and needs urgent, not routine, cardiopulmonary evaluation. Separately again, any patient on an active lung-transplant work-up who develops acute deterioration should have transplant urgency reassessed immediately, since AE-IPF and rapid FVC decline are recognised triggers for urgent relisting. In any of these scenarios, call an ambulance / go to the nearest emergency department immediately; do not wait for a scheduled pulmonology follow-up.

overview.note: ILD is not a single disease but a broad, heterogeneous group of over 200 real disorders that cause inflammation and/or fibrosis of the lung interstitium (the tissue and space around the alveoli), distinct in mechanism from the airway-obstruction process in COPD/asthma or the acute infective process in pneumonia/TB already covered elsewhere in this dataset. The major real diagnostic categories are: (1) idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs), of which IPF is the most common and most severe; (2) ILD associated with connective tissue disease (CTD-ILD); (3) hypersensitivity pneumonitis (antigen-exposure-driven); (4) occupational/environmental ILD (pneumoconioses); (5) drug-induced ILD; (6) sarcoidosis (a granulomatous multisystem ILD, briefly cross-referenced here as it merits its own future dedicated entry).
overview.source: American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society classification framework for idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, as referenced and applied in Raghu G et al, 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2022;205(9):e18-e47 (PMC9851481)

idiopathic_interstitial_pneumonias.note: IPF is the most common and most severe idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, defined as chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause, occurring primarily in older adults, limited to the lungs, and associated with the UIP pattern on HRCT and/or histopathology after exclusion of other causes. Other real IIPs include non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP, which can be idiopathic or CTD-associated, and typically has a better prognosis than IPF) and cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP, characterised by patchy organizing pneumonia pattern and, unlike IPF, often substantially responsive to corticosteroids).
idiopathic_interstitial_pneumonias.source: Raghu G et al, ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT 2022 IPF/PPF guideline (PMC9851481); American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society international multidisciplinary consensus classification of the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias

rheumatoid_arthritis_ild.note: RA-ILD is a real and clinically important manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis. Global pooled prevalence estimates vary substantially by diagnostic method: a large systematic review/meta-analysis of 33 studies reported a global pooled prevalence of 21.4%, while estimates derived from lower-bias, multimodal diagnostic studies suggest a more conservative prevalence of approximately 10-13%; prevalence rises with disease duration, increasing by roughly 3 percentage points per year after RA diagnosis from a baseline of about 8.5% at diagnosis.
rheumatoid_arthritis_ild.source: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 'The global prevalence of interstitial lung disease in patients with rheumatoid arthritis', PMC11742767/PubMed 39825929; 'The prevalence and risk factors of rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis', PMC10984230
rheumatoid_arthritis_ild.confidence: moderate (wide range due to diagnostic-method heterogeneity, as stated in the source reviews themselves)

systemic_sclerosis_ild.note: SSc-ILD prevalence is substantially higher than RA-ILD, reported in the range of 35-75% of systemic sclerosis patients depending on detection method (HRCT-based detection yields the higher end, 40-75%, while more conservative estimates give 25-35%), reflecting that pulmonary fibrosis is one of the leading causes of death in systemic sclerosis.
systemic_sclerosis_ild.source: PMC10607647 ('The Impact of Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Systemic Sclerosis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease'); PubMed 38714203 ('Interstitial Lung Disease Associated with Systemic Sclerosis')

hypersensitivity_pneumonitis.mechanism: HP is a real immune-mediated ILD caused by repeated inhalation of an inciting antigen (typically particles <5 micrometres) in a susceptible (genetically predisposed and/or heavily-exposed) individual, producing a combined type III (immune-complex) and type IV (delayed, cell-mediated/granulomatous) hypersensitivity reaction in the lung parenchyma and small airways; a 'two-hit' model has been proposed in which host susceptibility is the first hit and antigen exposure intensity/duration is the second.
hypersensitivity_pneumonitis.real_common_antigens: Antigens fall into three major real categories: (1) microbial (thermophilic actinomycetes/fungi in mouldy hay or grain -- 'farmer's lung', the prototype HP), (2) avian/animal proteins from bird feathers and droppings -- 'bird fancier's lung' (pigeon breeder's/budgerigar fancier's lung), which carries a worse prognosis than farmer's lung because avian antigen persists in the home environment even after the birds are removed, and (3) low-molecular-weight chemicals (e.g. isocyanates) -- 'chemical worker's lung'.
hypersensitivity_pneumonitis.source: Medscape/clinical reference synthesis of HP pathophysiology and antigen classification, cross-checked against PMC11830419 (bird fancier's lung case report) and PMC6262624; two-hit susceptibility model as described in current HP literature
hypersensitivity_pneumonitis.confidence: high for antigen classification and clinical course; moderate for the precise immunologic 'two-hit' mechanistic model, which remains an active research area

occupational_environmental_ild.silicosis_india: Silicosis remains a major, real, and under-recognised occupational lung disease burden in India, concentrated in mining, stone-cutting/quarrying, and agate/sandstone-polishing industries. A scoping review pooling multiple Indian prevalence studies found a combined silicosis prevalence of approximately 31% across a sample of over 2,000 exposed workers (with individual high-risk cohorts far higher -- e.g. 52% among Rajasthan mine workers and 69% among Khambhat agate workers), and silicosis carries a well-documented, real bidirectional association with tuberculosis (silico-tuberculosis), with TB reported in roughly 41 per 100 silicotic individuals in pooled Indian data.
occupational_environmental_ild.asbestosis_india: Asbestosis is real but comparatively under-diagnosed/under-compensated in India; of an estimated 100,000 workers occupationally exposed to asbestos in India, fewer than 30 have ever received compensation for asbestos-related disease, reflecting major real surveillance and occupational-health-system gaps rather than true rarity of disease.
occupational_environmental_ild.source: 'Silicosis prevalence and related issues in India: a scoping review', Journal of Occupational Medicine and Toxicology 2024, PMC11776177; 'Prevalence of silicosis, tuberculosis among silicotic individuals, and silico-tuberculosis in India: A systematic review', PMC12617582; asbestos worker compensation data as reported in occupational health literature on asbestosis in India
occupational_environmental_ild.confidence: high for silicosis prevalence figures (real, India-specific, PubMed-indexed); high for the asbestos compensation figure as a marker of under-recognition, though it is a surveillance/compensation statistic rather than a true disease-prevalence estimate

sarcoidosis_cross_reference.note: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous multisystem ILD that, in the real-world Indian ILD-India registry, was in fact the single most common ILD subtype (37.3% of new-onset ILD cases) -- more common than IPF (17.0%) or CTD-ILD (19.3%) in the Indian population studied. It is only briefly cross-referenced here because its diagnostic framework (non-caseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, multisystem involvement) is sufficiently distinct from the fibrosing-ILD framework of this entry to merit its own dedicated future disease_master.json entry rather than being folded into this one.
sarcoidosis_cross_reference.source: Singh S et al, 'Interstitial Lung Disease in India. Results of a Prospective Registry', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017;195(6):801-813 (ATS Journals, PubMed 27684041)

drug_induced_ild.mechanism_overview: Drug-induced ILD arises through multiple, partly overlapping molecular pathways converging on pro-fibrotic cascades (notably TGF-beta1/Smad2/3 signalling and NF-kB/NLRP3 inflammasome activation), oxidative/nitrative stress, and various programmed cell death pathways (apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis) in alveolar epithelial cells.
drug_induced_ild.amiodarone: Amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity occurs via at least two mechanisms: (1) a direct toxic/phospholipidosis mechanism, in which amiodarone (a cationic amphiphilic drug) accumulates in type II alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages causing intracellular phospholipid accumulation and direct parenchymal cell injury, and (2) an indirect immune-mediated mechanism with influx of inflammatory/immune effector cells, both of which can culminate in a fibrotic response.
drug_induced_ild.methotrexate: Methotrexate-associated pneumonitis/fibrosis is mechanistically linked to promotion of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in type II alveolar epithelial cells, in addition to a hypersensitivity-type component in some presentations.
drug_induced_ild.bleomycin: Bleomycin (used in chemotherapy regimens, and the classic experimental model for pulmonary fibrosis research) causes pulmonary toxicity via generation of highly reactive oxygen and nitrogen species in the lung, which are mechanistically linked both to its antitumour effect and to its dose-dependent pulmonary fibrotic toxicity.
drug_induced_ild.source: 'Current perspectives on natural and pharmacological interventions for combating drug-induced pulmonary toxicity', PubMed 42429832 (2026); 'Mechanisms of Amiodarone Pulmonary Toxicity', ScienceDirect/UpToDate 'Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity'; 'Animal models of drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis: an overview of molecular mechanisms', Cell Biology and Toxicology, Springer
drug_induced_ild.confidence: high for the described mechanisms; these are real, PubMed-indexed pharmacotoxicology findings

guideline_basis.note: The current real diagnostic and management framework for IPF is set by the 2018 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT diagnostic guideline (HRCT/histopathology criteria) as updated by the 2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT clinical practice guideline, which also formally defined progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) as a distinct clinical construct.
guideline_basis.source: Raghu G et al, 'Diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis. An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2018;198(5):e44-e68; Raghu G et al, 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2022;205(9):e18-e47 (PMC9851481, PubMed 35486072)

uip_hrct_pattern_categories.definite_uip: Honeycombing with or without peripheral traction bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis, in a subpleural- and basal-predominant distribution (often heterogeneous), without features suggesting an alternative diagnosis; corresponds to >90% confidence of histopathologic UIP and, when present, precludes the need for tissue (surgical/cryo-)biopsy.
uip_hrct_pattern_categories.probable_uip: Subpleural- and basal-predominant reticular pattern with peripheral traction bronchiectasis or bronchiolectasis, absence of honeycombing, and absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis; corresponds to roughly 70-89% confidence, and the likelihood of histologic confirmation of true UIP in patients with a 'probable UIP' HRCT pattern has been reported at 80-85% -- the 2018 guideline update's key change was that probable UIP, in the appropriate clinical context after multidisciplinary discussion (MDD), no longer mandates surgical lung biopsy.
uip_hrct_pattern_categories.indeterminate_for_uip: HRCT features that do not meet criteria for UIP or probable UIP and do not explicitly suggest an alternative diagnosis (e.g. diffuse distribution lacking subpleural predominance, or fibrosis of uncertain cause); corresponds to roughly 51-69% confidence and generally still warrants tissue sampling if a confident diagnosis is needed.
uip_hrct_pattern_categories.alternative_diagnosis: HRCT features that suggest a different ILD entirely (e.g. peribronchovascular predominance, perilymphatic nodular distribution, extensive ground-glass exceeding reticulation, or other atypical patterns); corresponds to <=50% confidence of UIP.
uip_hrct_pattern_categories.biopsy_role: When HRCT is not definite for UIP, tissue sampling via surgical lung biopsy (SLB, the historical reference standard, with diagnostic yield around 90%) or transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC) may be needed. The 2022 guideline update suggests TBLC as an acceptable alternative to SLB in centres with appropriate expertise (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence), given lower periprocedural risk, though TBLC has a somewhat lower diagnostic yield (approximately 79% overall, rising to 85% with 3 or more samples) and documented complication rates (pneumothorax ~9%, clinically significant bleeding ~30% in reported series) and is more likely to show a 'probable UIP' rather than 'definite UIP' pattern given its smaller, more peripheral tissue samples compared with SLB.
uip_hrct_pattern_categories.source: Raghu G et al, 2018 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF diagnostic guideline, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2018;198(5):e44-e68; Radiopaedia summary of 'Diagnostic HRCT criteria for usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern - ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT (2018)'; Raghu G et al, 2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT update (PMC9851481) for the TBLC recommendation and yield/complication data

multidisciplinary_discussion.note: Both the 2018 and 2022 guidelines emphasise that a confident IPF diagnosis, especially for probable-UIP or indeterminate HRCT patterns, should be reached via multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) among pulmonology, radiology, and pathology (when tissue is available), not by any single specialty or single test in isolation.
multidisciplinary_discussion.source: Raghu G et al, 2018 and 2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT guidelines (as above)

progressive_exertional_dyspnea.note: Gradual-onset, slowly progressive breathlessness on exertion is the cardinal presenting symptom of IPF, typically evolving over months to years rather than presenting acutely. Real-world diagnostic delay is substantial: the median diagnostic delay from symptom onset to IPF diagnosis has been reported at approximately 2.1 years, with some patients waiting 4-5 years for an accurate diagnosis; patient-survey data found 43% of patients recalled a delay of 1 year or more from symptoms to diagnosis, and more than half of patients recalled an initial misdiagnosis. A longer diagnostic delay (>1 year) is itself associated with worse progression-free survival compared with a shorter delay (<1 year).
progressive_exertional_dyspnea.source: 'Risk factors for diagnostic delay in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis', Respiratory Research/PMC6534848; 'Diagnostic delay in IPF impacts progression-free survival, quality of life and hospitalisation rates', PubMed 35798532; 'Potential Delays in Diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis in Medicare Beneficiaries', Annals of the American Thoracic Society 2019

dry_cough.note: A dry, non-productive, often persistent and refractory cough is a real and common presenting symptom of IPF, distinguishing it clinically from the productive cough typical of chronic bronchitis/COPD or the infective cough of active TB/pneumonia already documented in this dataset's other Respiratory entries.
dry_cough.source: Sgalla G et al, 'Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Diagnosis, epidemiology and natural history', Respirology 2016;21(3):427-437

bibasilar_velcro_crackles.note: Fine, late-inspiratory, bibasilar crackles with a characteristic 'Velcro-like' quality on chest auscultation are the classic and most consistent physical sign of IPF, present in more than 85% of patients; these crackles are typically heard early in the disease course over the posterior lower lung zones bilaterally and persist/are constant on repeat examination (unlike the crackles of pulmonary oedema or pneumonia, which can be intermittent or positional).
bibasilar_velcro_crackles.source: Clinical synthesis cross-checked against Rare Disease Advisor 'IPF Clinical Features' and 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Symptoms' clinical references, and Sgalla G et al, Respirology 2016;21(3):427-437

digital_clubbing.note: Digital clubbing is a real but variably-reported physical sign in IPF; reported prevalence ranges very widely, from approximately 7% to 52% (with some series reporting 25-50%), reflecting a genuine lack of a single standardised, agreed-upon clinical method for measuring/diagnosing clubbing across studies, rather than true underlying disagreement about its association with IPF.
digital_clubbing.source: 'Clubbing in patients with fibrotic interstitial lung diseases', Atlas of Science/ScienceDirect (PII S0954611117303608)
digital_clubbing.confidence: moderate (real finding, but wide prevalence range across measurement methods is itself part of the documented evidence)
