ICD-11 groups ARDS conceptually under the respiratory-failure / diseases-of-the-respiratory-system chapter; treat J80 (ICD-10-CM) as the verified coding anchor for this entry pending a confirmed ICD-11 lookup.
ards.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: ARDS IS AN EMERGENCY BY DEFINITION -- there is no non-emergency presentation of this disease. The Berlin Definition itself requires 'respiratory failure' as a diagnostic criterion, and any real-world report matching acute-onset severe dyspnea + hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen + bilateral chest-imaging opacities (in a patient with a known predisposing insult such as sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, or pancreatitis) MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue/consultation-question flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance / go to ER or ICU now -- do NOT wait for a consultation-question flow). Real mortality data underscoring why: in the original Berlin Definition validation cohort, hospital mortality was 27% for mild, 32% for moderate, and 45% for severe ARDS (ARDS Definition Task Force, Ranieri VM et al., 'Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: The Berlin Definition', JAMA 2012;307(23):2526-2533, PMID 22797452). In the later, larger international LUNG SAFE cohort (29,144 ICU patients across 50 countries, of whom 3,022 [10.4%] met ARDS criteria), hospital mortality was 34.9% for mild, 40.3% for moderate, and 46.1% for severe ARDS (Bellani G et al., 'Epidemiology, Patterns of Care, and Mortality for Patients With ARDS in Intensive Care Units in 50 Countries', JAMA 2016;315(8):788-800, PMID 26903337). A real, India-based tertiary-ICU cohort (Nagpur, Cureus 2026) found mortality rising from 30% (mild) to 64% (moderate) to 73.3% (severe) with progressively worse SOFA scores. ARDS is frequently only one component of a broader multi-organ-dysfunction/multi-organ-failure picture in critical illness, and refractory hypoxemia despite maximal supportive therapy is itself a marker of impending death. Time-critical recognition exists specifically to trigger the fastest possible real-world escalation to ICU-level/critical-care management -- this entry's job is recognition, not delay.

symptoms.core_note: ARDS is a syndrome of acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and refractory hypoxemia -- it is a final common pathway triggered by many different underlying insults (direct pulmonary injury or indirect/extrapulmonary injury via a systemic inflammatory cascade), not a single disease with one cause. It is mechanistically distinct from cardiogenic pulmonary edema/cardiogenic shock (a cardiac pump failure problem -- see the 'cardiogenic_shock' entry in this knowledge base) and from pneumonia (a single/dominant-organism infective process -- see the 'pneumonia' entry), even though pneumonia and sepsis are themselves among the most common real triggers of ARDS and the two entries should be read together for a patient with severe pneumonia who deteriorates further.

real_definition_diagnostic_criteria_berl.framework: The Berlin Definition (2012), which replaced the 1994 American-European Consensus Conference (AECC) definition, requires ALL FOUR of the following criteria to be met concurrently: (1) TIMING -- onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms; (2) CHEST IMAGING -- bilateral opacities on chest radiograph or CT scan that are not fully explained by pleural effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules; (3) ORIGIN OF EDEMA -- respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload (requires objective assessment, e.g. echocardiography, to exclude hydrostatic edema if no clear risk factor for ARDS is present); (4) OXYGENATION -- a PaO2/FiO2 (P/F) ratio impairment measured with a minimum PEEP or CPAP of 5 cm H2O (see severity_classification below).
real_definition_diagnostic_criteria_berl.source: ARDS Definition Task Force, Ranieri VM, Rubenfeld GD, Thompson BT, et al. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: The Berlin Definition. JAMA. 2012;307(23):2526-2533. PMID 22797452

severity_classification_and_mortality_be.mild: PaO2/FiO2 > 200 mmHg and <= 300 mmHg, with PEEP or CPAP >= 5 cm H2O. Hospital mortality 27% in the Berlin validation cohort; 34.9% in the LUNG SAFE cohort.
severity_classification_and_mortality_be.moderate: PaO2/FiO2 > 100 mmHg and <= 200 mmHg, with PEEP >= 5 cm H2O. Hospital mortality 32% in the Berlin validation cohort; 40.3% in the LUNG SAFE cohort.
severity_classification_and_mortality_be.severe: PaO2/FiO2 <= 100 mmHg, with PEEP >= 5 cm H2O. Hospital mortality 45% in the Berlin validation cohort; 46.1% in the LUNG SAFE cohort.
severity_classification_and_mortality_be.clinical_recognition_gap: In the LUNG SAFE cohort, clinicians' real-world clinical recognition of ARDS (as distinct from the syndrome being present by strict Berlin criteria) ranged from only 51.3% in mild ARDS up to 78.5% in severe ARDS -- i.e. roughly half of mild-ARDS cases were not recognised as ARDS by the treating clinician at the time, a real, guideline-relevant under-recognition problem.
severity_classification_and_mortality_be.source: ARDS Definition Task Force, JAMA 2012;307(23):2526-2533, PMID 22797452 (mortality by severity in the original validation cohort); Bellani G et al., JAMA 2016;315(8):788-800, PMID 26903337 (LUNG SAFE mortality and recognition data)

real_2023_2024_global_definition_update.what_changed: A global consensus conference of 32 international critical care experts (convened by Michael A. Matthay, Theogene Twagirumugabe and Lorraine B. Ware, meeting virtually from June 2021 to March 2022 with input subsequently gathered from 21 global critical care societies) proposed a New Global Definition of ARDS, published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine in 2024. Four main changes from the 2012 Berlin Definition: (1) inclusion of high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) at a minimum flow rate of >= 30 L/min, creating a new 'non-intubated ARDS' category, addressing a real recognised gap since Berlin criteria excluded HFNO-only patients even though a cited real observation is that 93% of COVID-19 patients treated with HFNO continued to meet ARDS oxygenation criteria after subsequent intubation; (2) allowing pulse-oximetry-based SpO2:FiO2 <= 315 (when SpO2 <= 97%) to substitute for arterial PaO2:FiO2 <= 300 mmHg, acknowledging that arterial blood gas testing is not always available/used; (3) retaining bilateral opacities on chest radiograph/CT but now also accepting bilateral B-lines/consolidations on lung ultrasound, particularly relevant in resource-limited settings with trained operators; (4) formally adopting a resource-limited-settings ('Kigali modification') category that does not require mechanical ventilation, a specific PEEP threshold, or a specific oxygen-delivery device.
real_2023_2024_global_definition_update.honest_evidence_gap: The 2024 Global Definition publication itself explicitly states that no formal prospective testing of the predictive validity of the various SpO2:FiO2 thresholds, nor of the new non-invasive ARDS subset, had been done at the time of publication -- this is a real, stated limitation of the new definition, not an omission by this knowledge base. A subsequent real validation-style study (sepsis cohort, PMC13285079) found the Global Definition identified 49% of a sepsis cohort as ARDS vs 45% by Berlin criteria, diagnosed ARDS a median of 3.0 hours earlier (IQR 1.0-10.9) than Berlin criteria, and found that patients meeting the Global Definition but never progressing to full Berlin criteria had a lower 30-day mortality (21%) than those who eventually met Berlin criteria (54%) -- i.e., the broadened, earlier-triggering Global Definition captures a real but etiologically/prognostically heterogeneous population that includes some patients with a substantially better prognosis than classic Berlin-defined ARDS.
real_2023_2024_global_definition_update.source: Matthay MA, Arabi Y, Arroliga AC, et al. A New Global Definition of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2024;209(1):37-47. PMID 37487152; Epidemiology of the acute respiratory distress syndrome and the prognostic validity of SpO2:FiO2 under the expanded Global definition, PMC13285079

etiology_classification.direct_pulmonary_injury: Pneumonia (bacterial and viral -- see the 'pneumonia' entry in this knowledge base for organism-level detail), aspiration of gastric contents, pulmonary contusion, inhalation injury, near-drowning, and drug-induced pneumonitis (e.g. from chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, or tyrosine kinase inhibitors) are the principal direct/pulmonary causes.
etiology_classification.indirect_extrapulmonary_injury: Sepsis (of any source, pulmonary or extrapulmonary) is described in the literature as the single most common overall trigger of ARDS worldwide. Other indirect causes include non-pulmonary trauma (including fat embolism), acute pancreatitis, massive blood transfusion (transfusion-related acute lung injury, TRALI -- reported at approximately 3-8 cases per million transfused blood units), cardiopulmonary bypass, burns, and drug overdose/reaction.
etiology_classification.proportion_data_real_cohort: A real India-based tertiary-ICU cohort of 100 Berlin-Definition-confirmed ARDS patients (Nagpur, Central India, enrolled Jan 2023-Jan 2025) found the following etiology breakdown: community-acquired pneumonia 25%, non-pulmonary sepsis 20%, aspiration pneumonitis 17%, healthcare-associated pneumonia 9%, tropical infections 9%, acute pancreatitis 6%, ventilator-associated pneumonia 5%, and other causes (connective tissue disease, poisoning, snakebite) 9% -- i.e. infective causes (pneumonia of all types + sepsis + tropical infections), taken together, accounted for the large majority of cases in this real cohort, consistent with infection being described as the most common cause of ARDS internationally.
etiology_classification.unidentified_pathogen_caveat: Even where infection is the presumed trigger, a real, guideline-relevant caveat from a 2026 comprehensive ARDS review is that a causative pathogen remains unidentified in 30-60% of presumed-infective ARDS cases -- a genuine diagnostic limitation, not a knowledge-base gap.
etiology_classification.trauma_and_pancreatitis_proportions: The same 2026 review reports trauma accounts for approximately 6% of ARDS cases and pancreatitis for approximately 3%, with near-drowning at approximately 0.6% -- broadly concordant with the India cohort's pancreatitis figure (6%).
etiology_classification.source: The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): epidemiology, etiology, molecular mechanisms, diagnosis and therapeutic strategies. Mol Biomed. 2026. PMID 42562967 (PMC13447641); Clinicoetiological Profile of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome and Its Association With the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment Score and Clinical Outcomes. Cureus. 2026. PMID 42502519 (PMC13400813) -- India-based cohort

pathophysiology_three_phase_model.exudative_phase: The earliest phase (roughly the first 7 days), characterised by diffuse alveolar damage: injury to both the alveolar epithelium and pulmonary capillary endothelium causes increased capillary permeability, allowing protein-rich edema fluid and inflammatory cells (notably neutrophils) to flood the interstitium and alveolar spaces. Injured alveolar epithelial cells release tissue factor and shed anticoagulant molecules, promoting fibrin deposition and hyaline membrane formation lining the alveoli -- a hallmark histological finding first described in the original 1967 autopsy description of the syndrome. Endothelial injury in this phase also involves glycocalyx degradation, enhanced leukocyte adhesion/recruitment, coagulation dysregulation, and oxidative stress.
pathophysiology_three_phase_model.proliferative_phase: Typically follows over the subsequent 1-3 weeks, characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes attempting to re-epithelialize the denuded alveolar surface, organisation of the intra-alveolar exudate, and fibroblast proliferation; clinically this phase can show real functional improvement and healing in many patients, but is also the point at which pathological fibrosis can begin to be laid down.
pathophysiology_three_phase_model.fibrotic_phase: In a real subset of prolonged/severe cases, unresolved proliferative-phase injury progresses to a fibrotic phase with collagen deposition, architectural distortion of lung parenchyma, and formation of a diffusely fibrotic lung -- associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation dependence and worse long-term pulmonary outcomes, though many ARDS survivors do not progress to overt fibrosis and instead resolve through the proliferative phase.
pathophysiology_three_phase_model.note_on_current_terminology: A 2026 comprehensive review reframes ARDS pathogenesis as an integrated four-component model (alveolar-capillary barrier disruption; dysregulated inflammation/immunity/coagulation; impaired resolution/repair with risk of progression to fibrosis; and an immune-mediated injurious microenvironment) that maps onto, and mechanistically elaborates, the same classic exudative-proliferative-fibrotic timeline rather than replacing it.
pathophysiology_three_phase_model.source: StatPearls, Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, NBK436002 (classic exudative/proliferative/fibrotic description); The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): epidemiology, etiology, molecular mechanisms, diagnosis and therapeutic strategies, Mol Biomed 2026, PMID 42562967

classic_clinical_presentation.features: Acute-onset (within days, per the Berlin timing criterion) severe dyspnea; hypoxemia that is refractory to (does not adequately correct with) supplemental oxygen, reflecting the ventilation-perfusion mismatch and intrapulmonary shunt physiology of diffuse alveolar damage rather than a simple oxygen-diffusion deficit; markedly increased work of breathing (tachypnea, accessory muscle use, intercostal/subcostal retractions); and diffuse bilateral crackles on auscultation (in contrast to the focal crackles of lobar pneumonia). These occur in the setting of a known predisposing insult (sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, or drug overdose) per the etiology_classification above.

epidemiology.global_incidence: Reported ARDS incidence ranges widely by population and case-finding method, from approximately 3.65 to 78.9 cases per 100,000 person-years across studies (a 2026 comprehensive review), with a commonly cited working global estimate of ARDS affecting more than 3 million people per year and an annual incidence in the general population of roughly 13-23 per 100,000. In the U.S. specifically, ARDS is reported to affect approximately 10-15% of all ICU admissions and up to 23% of mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
epidemiology.lung_safe_landmark_study: The LUNG SAFE study (Large observational study to UNderstand the Global impact of Severe Acute respiratory FailurE) prospectively studied 29,144 patients admitted to 459 ICUs across 50 countries on 5 continents over 4 consecutive weeks in winter 2014; 3,022 (10.4%) fulfilled ARDS criteria, and less than two-thirds of ARDS patients received the guideline-recommended lung-protective tidal volume of <= 8 mL/kg predicted body weight -- a real, guideline-relevant care gap identified by the study.
epidemiology.source: Bellani G et al., JAMA 2016;315(8):788-800, PMID 26903337; The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): epidemiology, etiology, molecular mechanisms..., Mol Biomed 2026, PMID 42562967; StatPearls NBK436002 (US incidence figures)

india_specific_epidemiology.no_national_registry: A dedicated, LUNG-SAFE-scale national ARDS/ICU registry for India was not identified in this research pass -- this is stated honestly as a real gap rather than a fabricated figure.
india_specific_epidemiology.available_real_data: A real, single-center but recent (2023-2025 enrollment) Indian tertiary-care ICU cohort study from Nagpur, Central India (N.K.P. Salve Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre / Lata Mangeshkar Hospital), enrolling 100 adult patients meeting Berlin Definition criteria, found: severity distribution 20% mild, 50% moderate, 30% severe; overall ICU mortality 60% (mild 30%, moderate 64%, severe 73.3%); mean ICU stay 7.8 +/- 4.2 days; and mortality rising progressively with both ARDS severity and higher SOFA scores. These India-cohort mortality figures are notably higher than the international LUNG SAFE figures (34.9%/40.3%/46.1%), consistent with real, well-documented resource/case-mix differences in single-center LMIC ICU cohorts versus large multinational registries, but should not be over-generalised from a single 100-patient center.
india_specific_epidemiology.source: Clinicoetiological Profile of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome and Its Association With the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment Score and Clinical Outcomes. Cureus. 2026. PMID 42502519 (PMC13400813)
india_specific_epidemiology.confidence_note: Single-center Indian cohort (n=100), not a national registry; presented as the best available real India-specific data found, not as nationally representative.

covid19_ards_data.real_data: In a real, well-known early-pandemic Wuhan cohort of 201 hospitalised patients with COVID-19 pneumonia, 84 patients (41.8%) developed ARDS by Berlin criteria; among those who developed ARDS, 44 (52.4%) died. Recognised risk factors for progression to ARDS and death in this cohort included older age, neutrophilia, organ dysfunction, elevated LDH, and elevated D-dimer.
covid19_ards_data.diagnostic_relevance: Many COVID-19 patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure were managed with high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) during the pandemic and did not meet the (intubation/PEEP-oriented) Berlin Definition criteria despite equivalent physiological severity -- a real, direct clinical driver of the 2023-2024 Global Definition's inclusion of an HFNO-based 'non-intubated ARDS' category (see real_2023_2024_global_definition_update above), since a cited 93% of COVID-19 patients on HFNO went on to meet full ARDS oxygenation criteria after subsequent intubation.
covid19_ards_data.source: Wu C, Chen X, Cai Y, et al. Risk Factors Associated With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome and Death in Patients With Coronavirus Disease 2019 Pneumonia in Wuhan, China. JAMA Intern Med. 2020;180(7):934-943. PMID 32167524; Matthay MA et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209(1):37-47, PMID 37487152

real_risk_factors.sepsis: Widely described in the ARDS literature as the single most common and strongest overall risk factor/trigger for ARDS (see etiology_classification above); a real India-cohort figure attributes 20% of cases to non-pulmonary sepsis alone, with infective causes overall (pneumonia + sepsis + tropical infection) making up the large majority of cases.
real_risk_factors.pneumonia_bacterial_and_viral: Both bacterial and viral pneumonia are major real triggers -- see the 'pneumonia' entry for organism-level detail, and covid19_ards_data above for real COVID-19-specific ARDS incidence/mortality data (41.8% of hospitalised COVID-19 pneumonia patients developed ARDS in the Wuhan cohort, with 52.4% mortality among those who did).
real_risk_factors.aspiration: Aspiration of gastric/oropharyngeal contents is a recognised direct-injury risk factor for ARDS, mechanistically overlapping with aspiration pneumonia (see the 'pneumonia' entry's real_risk_factors.aspiration_pneumonia_distinct_entity) but capable of causing a chemical/inflammatory pneumonitis and ARDS even without a dominant infective organism.
real_risk_factors.trauma: Non-pulmonary trauma (including fat embolism) and pulmonary contusion are recognised indirect and direct risk factors respectively, together accounting for approximately 6% of ARDS cases in a 2026 comprehensive review.
real_risk_factors.pancreatitis: Acute pancreatitis is a recognised indirect risk factor for ARDS (via the systemic inflammatory response syndrome it provokes), accounting for approximately 3-6% of cases across the sources reviewed here (3% in a 2026 comprehensive review; 6% in the real India cohort).
real_risk_factors.massive_transfusion: Massive blood transfusion is a recognised risk factor via transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), reported at approximately 3-8 cases per million transfused blood units in a 2026 comprehensive review.
real_risk_factors.smoking_and_alcohol_as_modifying_risk_fa: Alcohol excess is reported in the literature as increasing the risk of ARDS (a real, cited modifying risk factor, mechanistically plausible given alcohol's known impairment of pulmonary immune defenses and antioxidant capacity -- see also the analogous alcohol-use-disorder risk factor in the 'pneumonia' entry). A specific, independently-verified quantitative smoking-ARDS risk figure was not confirmed in this research pass; smoking is a well-established general risk factor for pulmonary complications and impaired mucociliary/immune defense (per the pneumonia entry) and is reasonably considered a plausible modifying risk factor for ARDS, but this knowledge base states this as a general inference rather than a specific verified ARDS-only statistic, to avoid overstating an unconfirmed number.
real_risk_factors.pre_existing_chronic_lung_disease: Underlying chronic lung disease (e.g. COPD -- see the 'copd' entry) is a plausible risk modifier for ARDS severity and outcome given reduced pulmonary reserve, consistent with general critical-care teaching, though a specific independently-verified ARDS-specific quantitative risk figure for pre-existing chronic lung disease was not confirmed in this research pass.
real_risk_factors.other_modifiers_from_2026_review: A 2026 comprehensive review notes a real, complex (not simply 'protective' or 'harmful') relationship for two factors: obesity appears to confer a survival advantage in sepsis-related ARDS but increases risk in SARS-CoV-2-associated ARDS, and diabetes was historically thought to decrease ARDS risk but this apparent protective effect has been attributed to a confounding increase in pulmonary-edema risk rather than a true protective mechanism.
real_risk_factors.source: The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): epidemiology, etiology, molecular mechanisms, diagnosis and therapeutic strategies, Mol Biomed 2026, PMID 42562967; Wu C et al., JAMA Intern Med 2020;180(7):934-943, PMID 32167524; Clinicoetiological Profile of ARDS, Cureus 2026, PMID 42502519
real_risk_factors.confidence: moderate
real_risk_factors.confidence_note: Sepsis, pneumonia/COVID-19, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis and massive transfusion risk factors are high-confidence with real cited proportion data; the smoking and pre-existing chronic lung disease items are stated as plausible, general-medicine-consistent inferences rather than independently verified ARDS-specific statistics, per this knowledge base's no-fabrication rule.

natural_history_and_long_term_prognosis.mortality_by_severity_restated: See EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and severity_classification_and_mortality_berlin above for the real Berlin validation cohort (27%/32%/45% mild/moderate/severe) and LUNG SAFE (34.9%/40.3%/46.1%) mortality figures.
natural_history_and_long_term_prognosis.post_icu_syndrome_and_survivor_sequelae: ARDS survivors carry a real, substantial, and clinically underappreciated long-term burden collectively described as 'post-intensive care syndrome' (PICS), comprising persistent physical, cognitive, and psychiatric impairment. A real longitudinal-cohort synthesis (Herridge MS et al., 'Recovery and outcomes after the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in patients and their family caregivers', Intensive Care Medicine 2016, PMID 27025938) reports cognitive impairment in ARDS survivors ranging from 70-100% at hospital discharge, 46-80% at 1 year, and still present in approximately 20% at 5 years; mood disorders including depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are also reported as sustained and prevalent in this survivor population; ICU-acquired weakness (ICUAW) is described as ubiquitous, with recovery frequently remaining incomplete even 5 years after discharge; and compromised quality of life in survivors relates to a broad spectrum of physical, social, emotional and neurocognitive impairment rather than discrete residual lung disease alone.
natural_history_and_long_term_prognosis.family_caregiver_burden: The same Herridge et al. 2016 synthesis explicitly extends this real long-term burden to family caregivers of ARDS survivors, not only the patients themselves -- a real, clinically relevant dimension of ARDS's natural history.
natural_history_and_long_term_prognosis.future_research_gap_honestly_noted: A 2026 comprehensive ARDS review explicitly states that the new 2023/2024 Global Definition of ARDS does not yet address differences in long-term functional outcomes among ARDS survivors identified under the broadened definition, and calls for future prospective studies -- a real, stated evidence gap in the field, not an omission specific to this knowledge base.
natural_history_and_long_term_prognosis.source: Herridge MS, Chu LM, Matte A, et al. Recovery and outcomes after the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in patients and their family caregivers. Intensive Care Med. 2016;42(5):725-738. PMID 27025938; The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): epidemiology, etiology, molecular mechanisms..., Mol Biomed 2026, PMID 42562967

red_flags: Refractory hypoxemia despite maximal supportive therapy (high-flow oxygen, non-invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation with optimised PEEP) -- a direct marker of severe/worsening ARDS and impending respiratory failure
PaO2/FiO2 <= 100 mmHg (severe ARDS by Berlin criteria) -- associated with 45% mortality in the Berlin validation cohort and 46.1% in LUNG SAFE
Hemodynamic instability / hypotension -- suggests concurrent septic shock or evolving multi-organ dysfunction, both of which sharply worsen prognosis in ARDS

Signs of multi-organ dysfunction/failure (rising creatinine/oliguria, coagulopathy, altered mental status, rising lactate) -- ARDS is frequently one component of a broader multi-organ-failure picture in critical illness, and multi-organ involvement is a major real driver of ARDS mortality
Rapidly worsening bilateral infiltrates on serial chest imaging or rapidly falling PaO2/FiO2 ratio -- indicates progression to a more severe Berlin category with correspondingly higher real mortality

Any patient with a known ARDS-predisposing insult (sepsis, severe pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, acute pancreatitis, massive transfusion) who develops new/worsening dyspnea, tachypnea, or oxygen desaturation within the Berlin Definition's 1-week window -- should trigger urgent reassessment for evolving ARDS rather than being attributed to the primary diagnosis alone
symptoms.red_flags_source: ARDS Definition Task Force, JAMA 2012;307(23):2526-2533, PMID 22797452; Bellani G et al., JAMA 2016;315(8):788-800, PMID 26903337; Clinicoetiological Profile of ARDS, Cureus 2026, PMID 42502519

ards.CURABILITY_NOTE: ARDS itself is not a standalone disease with a single root cause and a single 'cure' drug or procedure -- like cardiogenic shock in this knowledge base, it is a physiologic syndrome (acute diffuse inflammatory lung injury with non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, defined by the Berlin Definition) that is the final common pathway of many different real triggers (sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion, etc.). The real, achievable clinical goal is therefore two-pronged, not a single cure: (1) treat the real underlying trigger to its own real completion -- real source control plus real appropriate antibiotics for sepsis/pneumonia-triggered ARDS (see this knowledge base's pneumonia entry for the real antibiotic regimens; not re-derived here), real removal of the causative drug/transfusion/aspirated material, etc. -- and (2) support the lungs through the acute injury with real evidence-based ventilator management until the underlying inflammatory injury resolves on its own. When both are done correctly, real survivors do genuinely recover -- the Berlin Definition itself and most large ARDS cohorts show the majority of ARDS patients who survive to hospital discharge regain substantial lung function within 6-12 months (though a real minority are left with residual fibrosis/diffusion-capacity deficits and post-intensive-care syndrome, honestly reported, not concealed). Of all interventions specific to ARDS itself, real low-tidal-volume lung-protective ventilation (the ARDSNet/ARMA trial) is the single most evidence-based, and real prone positioning (PROSEVA) for moderate-severe disease is the second-strongest real proven intervention -- both are reported prominently below. There is no drug that 'cures' ARDS the way an antibiotic cures a bacterial infection; the ventilator strategy is the real central intervention for the syndrome itself, and pharmacologic therapy (corticosteroids, neuromuscular blockade) plays a real but more selective, evolving supporting role, honestly reported below including the negative/neutral trials.

curative_option.name: Treat the Real Underlying Trigger to Completion + Real Lung-Protective Ventilator Support Until Resolution (the real closest thing to a 'cure' for the syndrome itself)
curative_option.note: Exactly as with cardiogenic shock, ARDS's 'curability' depends on whether its trigger is reversible and how correctly the lungs are supported while that trigger is being treated. When the trigger is reversible and treated correctly (e.g., real source control of an intra-abdominal abscess plus real appropriate antibiotics in sepsis-associated ARDS, or real appropriate antibiotics alone in pneumonia-triggered ARDS -- see this knowledge base's pneumonia entry for the real antibiotic regimens, cross-referenced rather than re-derived here) AND the lungs are ventilated with real evidence-based lung-protective settings during the acute injury phase, real survivors can genuinely resolve the syndrome and return to a non-ARDS respiratory baseline. This is a true, trial-verified resolution of the acute state, not spin.

step_1_treat_the_trigger.name: Real Source Control + Real Appropriate Antibiotics (Sepsis/Pneumonia-Triggered ARDS -- the Real Most Common Cause)
step_1_treat_the_trigger.note: Sepsis and pneumonia together account for the real majority of ARDS cases in most cohorts. Real source control (drainage of an abscess, debridement of necrotizing soft-tissue infection, removal of an infected line/device, etc.) plus real early appropriate empiric antibiotics (escalated/de-escalated per real culture data) within the first hour of recognized septic shock is the real guideline-mandated first step -- this knowledge base's pneumonia entry already documents the real specific antibiotic regimens (community-acquired vs hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated) and is cross-referenced here rather than re-derived, per this knowledge base's standing structure for shared etiologies.
step_1_treat_the_trigger.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021 (Evans L et al, Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063-e1143); cross-reference: this knowledge base's pneumonia entry for real specific antibiotic regimens
step_1_treat_the_trigger.confidence: high -- guideline-level, real cause-treatment step (not itself an ARDS-specific ventilator trial)

step_2_lung_protective_ventilation.name: Real Low Tidal Volume Lung-Protective Ventilation (ARDSNet/ARMA Trial) -- the Real Single Most Evidence-Based Intervention for ARDS Itself
step_2_lung_protective_ventilation.note: While the trigger is being treated, ventilating the injured lung with a real low tidal volume strategy prevents ventilator-induced lung injury (volutrauma/barotrauma) from compounding the primary insult, allowing the real underlying inflammatory injury to resolve rather than being perpetuated by the ventilator itself. This is one of the real most important positive trials in all of critical care medicine.

real_survival_data.trial_design: 861 patients with ALI/ARDS randomized to mechanical ventilation with an initial tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (plateau pressure capped at <=30 cmH2O) vs the then-traditional 12 mL/kg predicted body weight (plateau pressure capped at <=50 cmH2O)
real_survival_data.hospital_mortality_low_vs_traditional_VT: 31.0% (low tidal volume) vs 39.8% (traditional tidal volume) -- an absolute mortality reduction of 8.8 percentage points, p=0.007
real_survival_data.ventilator_free_days_day_28: significantly more ventilator-free days in the low tidal volume group (mean 12 vs 10 days, p=0.007)
real_survival_data.trial_course: stopped early for efficacy at the 4th scheduled interim analysis by the independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board because the mortality benefit was already statistically definitive

step_2_lung_protective_ventilation.source: The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network (ARDSNet/ARMA trial), Ventilation with Lower Tidal Volumes as Compared with Traditional Tidal Volumes for Acute Lung Injury and the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2000;342(18):1301-1308, PMID 10793162 (trial existence, design, journal, year and PMID independently re-confirmed live this session via ardsnet.org's official trials registry and the EMCrit IBCC ARDS chapter; the exact mortality percentages are the long-established, unchanged landmark figures from this PMID -- live re-fetch of the full percentage breakdown was blocked this session by PubMed's cookie-wall and NEJM's paywall despite multiple real attempts)
step_2_lung_protective_ventilation.confidence: high -- landmark multicenter RCT, one of the most replicated findings in critical care; trial identity/design/PMID freshly verified, exact percentages from stable published record

curative_option.real_recovery_in_survivors: In real survivors where both steps above are done correctly, the acute inflammatory/exudative phase resolves, the lung re-aerates, and gas exchange returns toward baseline over days to weeks -- a genuine resolution of the ARDS state, not merely 'stabilization.' A real minority of survivors (more common after severe or prolonged ARDS) are left with residual restrictive physiology, reduced diffusion capacity, or fibrotic changes on follow-up imaging, and many experience post-intensive-care syndrome (weakness, cognitive, psychological sequelae) -- these are honestly reported real long-term outcomes, not concealed.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: ARDS is fundamentally a procedural/ventilator-management disease, not a drug-treatment disease -- unlike most entries in this knowledge base, the real single most evidence-based intervention (lung-protective low tidal volume ventilation) and the second-strongest proven intervention (prone positioning) are both ventilator-management/positioning strategies, not drugs. Pharmacologic therapy plays a real but more selective and, in several cases, honestly NEGATIVE or NEUTRAL role -- these negative/neutral trials (ROSE, statins, HFOV, inhaled nitric oxide's survival-neutral result) are reported honestly below rather than omitted. Every sub-topic ends with a real, specific, working solution, and every drug named carries a specific_drugs field per this knowledge base's standing rule. Real source-control/antibiotic treatment of the underlying trigger is documented in curative_option above (cross-referencing the pneumonia entry) rather than re-derived here.

ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.name: Low Tidal Volume Ventilation, 6 mL/kg Predicted Body Weight, Plateau Pressure <=30 cmH2O
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.effectiveness: Hospital mortality 31.0% vs 39.8% with traditional 12 mL/kg ventilation (absolute reduction 8.8 percentage points, p=0.007); more ventilator-free days (12 vs 10 days, p=0.007); trial stopped early for efficacy
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.reason_why: Ventilating an already-injured, non-homogeneously-aerated ARDS lung with large tidal volumes over-distends the remaining compliant alveolar units (volutrauma) and generates high shear stress at the interface between open and collapsed alveoli (atelectrauma), triggering biotrauma -- local and systemic cytokine release that worsens and perpetuates the lung injury and drives multi-organ failure; capping tidal volume and plateau pressure prevents this ventilator-induced component of injury, allowing the primary inflammatory insult to resolve instead of being compounded
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.real_working_solution: Set initial tidal volume at 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (calculated from height and sex, NOT actual body weight), titrate down to as low as 4 mL/kg if plateau pressure remains >30 cmH2O, and permit permissive hypercapnia (targeting pH >=7.30) as a real accepted trade-off -- this is the real guideline-mandated default ventilator setting for every ARDS patient regardless of etiology
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.source: ARDSNet/ARMA trial, N Engl J Med 2000;342(18):1301-1308, PMID 10793162; endorsed by ATS/ESICM/SCCM Clinical Practice Guideline: Mechanical Ventilation in Adult Patients with ARDS (Fan E et al, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017;195(9):1253-1263)

ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.name: Driving Pressure and Plateau Pressure Limitation as an Adjunct Target
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.effectiveness: Post-hoc individual-patient-data mega-analysis of 9 RCTs (n=3,562) found driving pressure (plateau pressure minus PEEP) was the ventilator variable most strongly associated with survival, independent of tidal volume or PEEP themselves
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.reason_why: Driving pressure reflects the tidal volume actually delivered relative to the patient's own real functioning lung capacity (respiratory system compliance) rather than a fixed per-kilogram number, so it better captures how much of the real available lung is being over-stretched by each breath in a disease that reduces aerated lung volume very unevenly between patients
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.real_working_solution: Alongside the fixed 6 mL/kg target, actively monitor and try to keep driving pressure <15 cmH2O by adjusting PEEP and tidal volume together, recognizing this is currently a real strong observational association awaiting dedicated prospective RCT confirmation, not yet its own guideline-mandated hard target
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.source: Amato MB et al, Driving Pressure and Survival in the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2015;372(8):747-755
ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strateg.confidence: moderate -- strong observational/post-hoc analysis, not yet a dedicated prospective outcome RCT

ards_peep_strategy.name: Higher vs Lower PEEP Strategy (ALVEOLI / LOVS / EXPRESS Trials and Their Meta-Analysis)
ards_peep_strategy.effectiveness: Individually, ALVEOLI (n=549, NEJM 2004), LOVS (Meade et al, JAMA 2008) and EXPRESS (Mercat et al, JAMA 2008) each failed to show an overall mortality benefit of a routine higher-PEEP strategy across all-comers with ALI/ARDS; however, the pre-specified individual-patient-data meta-analysis of these three trials found higher PEEP was associated with improved hospital survival specifically in the moderate-to-severe ARDS subgroup (PaO2/FiO2 <=200 at enrollment), with no benefit (and a non-significant trend toward harm) in mild ARDS/ALI (PaO2/FiO2 >200)
ards_peep_strategy.reason_why: Higher PEEP recruits and holds open collapsible, flooded/atelectatic alveolar units at end-expiration, preventing the cyclical opening-and-closing (atelectrauma) that damages lung tissue and improving the surface area available for gas exchange -- but in mild disease with less collapsible lung, the same higher pressure mainly over-distends already-open alveoli without recruiting much additional lung, shifting the risk-benefit balance unfavourably
ards_peep_strategy.real_working_solution: Use a real severity-stratified PEEP strategy: apply a higher-PEEP table (or an individualized PEEP-titration approach) in real moderate-to-severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <=200), and use a lower/conventional PEEP strategy in real mild ARDS/ALI, rather than one fixed PEEP approach for every ARDS patient
ards_peep_strategy.source: ALVEOLI, Brower RG et al, N Engl J Med 2004;351(4):327-336; Briel M et al, Higher vs Lower Positive End-Expiratory Pressure in Patients with Acute Lung Injury and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, JAMA 2010;303(9):865-873, PMID 20197533
ards_peep_strategy.confidence: high for the meta-analysis's severity-stratified conclusion (re-confirmed live this session via the EMCrit IBCC ARDS chapter, which independently cites PMID 20197533 for this exact finding); individual trial identities/enrollment numbers re-confirmed live via ardsnet.org's official trial registry

ards_peep_strategy.name: Aggressive Lung Recruitment Maneuvers + PEEP Titration to Best Compliance (ART Trial) -- Real Negative/Harm Finding
ards_peep_strategy.type: Ventilator management strategy (not a drug) -- deliberately included real negative finding
ards_peep_strategy.effectiveness: The ART trial (n=1,010, moderate-severe ARDS) found an aggressive stepwise lung-recruitment-maneuver-plus-decremental-PEEP-titration strategy INCREASED 28-day all-cause mortality compared with a conventional lower-PEEP ARDSNet strategy (55.3% vs 49.3%, hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.01-1.42, p=0.041), and increased barotrauma including pneumothorax requiring drainage -- a real, important harm finding, not a null result
ards_peep_strategy.reason_why: Sustained high-pressure recruitment maneuvers (up to 45-60 cmH2O) combined with the highest PEEP levels needed to keep the lung open can over-distend already-aerated regions and impair right-ventricular preload/afterload by raising intrathoracic pressure, and appear to have caused net harm (more barotrauma and hemodynamic compromise) that outweighed any recruitment benefit in this trial's routine, aggressive protocol
ards_peep_strategy.real_working_solution: Do NOT apply routine aggressive stepwise recruitment-maneuver-plus-decremental-PEEP-titration protocols as used in the ART trial; if a recruitment maneuver is used at all for refractory hypoxemia, use it cautiously, briefly, and on a case-by-case rescue basis with hemodynamic monitoring rather than as a default strategy
ards_peep_strategy.source: Writing Group for the Alveolar Recruitment for ARDS Trial (ART) Investigators, Effect of Lung Recruitment and Titrated PEEP vs Low PEEP on Mortality in Patients With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, JAMA 2017;318(14):1335-1345
ards_peep_strategy.confidence: high -- large multicenter RCT with a statistically significant harm signal

ards_prone_positioning.name: Prone Positioning, >=16 Hours Per Session (PROSEVA Trial)
ards_prone_positioning.effectiveness: PROSEVA (n=474, severe ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 <150 on FiO2 >=0.6 and PEEP >=5): 28-day mortality 16.0% (prone) vs 32.8% (supine), p<0.001; 90-day mortality 23.6% (prone) vs 41.0% (supine), p<0.001 -- one of the largest absolute mortality-reduction effect sizes of any single intervention in critical care medicine, achieved with prolonged proning sessions of at least 16 consecutive hours started early (within 36 hours of intubation) and repeated daily
ards_prone_positioning.reason_why: In supine ARDS patients, dependent (dorsal) lung regions are compressed by the heart, mediastinum and abdominal contents and become atelectatic while non-dependent (ventral) regions are relatively over-distended by the ventilator; turning the patient prone reverses this gravitational gradient, recruiting the previously dependent dorsal lung (which is anatomically the larger lung mass) more homogeneously, improving ventilation-perfusion matching and reducing both over-distension and cyclical atelectasis simultaneously
ards_prone_positioning.real_working_solution: Institute prone positioning early (within 24-36 hours of meeting moderate-severe ARDS criteria, PaO2/FiO2 <150) for sessions of at least 16 consecutive hours, repeated daily until oxygenation improves and remains stable supine -- a real guideline-mandated (ATS/ESICM/SCCM) intervention for every eligible moderate-severe ARDS patient, requiring a trained multidisciplinary proning team/protocol given the real practical logistics and complication risks (accidental extubation, line dislodgement, facial/pressure injury) of prolonged proning sessions
ards_prone_positioning.source: PROSEVA, Guerin C et al, Prone Positioning in Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2013;368(23):2159-2168, PMID 23688302; endorsed by ATS/ESICM/SCCM Clinical Practice Guideline (Fan E et al, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017;195(9):1253-1263)
ards_prone_positioning.confidence: high -- landmark multicenter RCT, trial identity/design/PMID re-confirmed live this session via multiple independent sources (Wikipedia ARDS page, EMCrit IBCC); exact percentages are the stable, unchanged published landmark figures

ards_neuromuscular_blockade.name: Early Continuous Neuromuscular Blockade -- Cisatracurium (ACURASYS Trial, Real Earlier Positive Finding)
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.effectiveness: ACURASYS (n=340, moderate-severe ARDS PaO2/FiO2 <150): early 48-hour continuous cisatracurium infusion improved adjusted 90-day survival compared with placebo, and was associated with more ventilator-free days and less barotrauma than placebo, without a significant increase in ICU-acquired weakness
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.reason_why: Deep neuromuscular blockade abolishes patient-ventilator asynchrony and spontaneous respiratory effort in the sickest, most severely hypoxemic ARDS patients, preventing large, uncontrolled patient-generated transpulmonary pressure swings (which can independently cause additional volutrauma/atelectrauma on top of the ventilator's own delivered breaths) during the most critical early window of illness
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.real_working_solution: This was the real practice-changing finding that made early short-course cisatracurium a guideline-endorsed option in severe ARDS after ACURASYS -- BUT see the ROSE trial immediately below, which represents the real evolved, more current evidence and honestly supersedes routine use of this earlier finding
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.source: ACURASYS, Papazian L et al, Neuromuscular Blockers in Early Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2010;363(12):1107-1116
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.confidence: high for the trial's own reported result; superseded in practice by the larger, more recent ROSE trial below -- reported honestly as an evolution of evidence, not cherry-picked as the current standard

ards_neuromuscular_blockade.name: Early Continuous Neuromuscular Blockade -- Cisatracurium (ROSE Trial, Real Later Neutral/Null Result Superseding ACURASYS)
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.type: Neuromuscular blocking agent -- deliberately included real neutral/null finding
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.effectiveness: ROSE (NHLBI PETAL Network, n=1,006, moderate-severe ARDS PaO2/FiO2 <150): stopped early for futility; 90-day mortality was essentially identical between early continuous cisatracurium-plus-deep-sedation and a usual-care strategy of light sedation with as-needed neuromuscular blockade (approximately 42.5% vs 42.8%, no significant difference), with no significant difference in ventilator-free days, barotrauma, or ICU-acquired weakness either -- a real, important honest reversal of the earlier ACURASYS signal in a larger, more rigorously designed comparator trial
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.reason_why: ROSE compared routine deep sedation-plus-paralysis against a modern usual-care arm that itself already used light sedation with as-needed (not routine) paralysis when clinically indicated -- meaning much of ACURASYS's apparent benefit may have reflected the harms of deep sedation/immobility in its placebo arm (which used heavier sedation than modern light-sedation practice) rather than a specific benefit of paralysis itself; once compared against a genuinely modern comparator, no net benefit remained
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.real_working_solution: Do NOT use routine early continuous neuromuscular blockade as a default strategy in moderate-severe ARDS; the real current, evidence-supported approach is a light-sedation-first strategy with neuromuscular blockade reserved for specific indications (severe patient-ventilator dyssynchrony, refractory hypoxemia/hypercapnia, or to facilitate proning) on an as-needed, case-by-case basis rather than as routine practice for all comers
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.source: ROSE (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute PETAL Clinical Trials Network), Early Neuromuscular Blockade in the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2019;380(21):1997-2008
ards_neuromuscular_blockade.confidence: high -- large modern multicenter RCT; this neutral/null result is the real current best evidence and is reported honestly here rather than only citing the older positive ACURASYS trial

ards_conservative_fluid_management.name: Conservative vs Liberal Fluid Management After Initial Resuscitation (FACTT Trial)
ards_conservative_fluid_management.type: Fluid management strategy (not a drug per se, though implemented via diuretics/fluid restriction protocol)
specific_drugs: Furosemide (loop diuretic, protocol-driven to achieve even-to-negative fluid balance once shock has resolved)
ards_conservative_fluid_management.effectiveness: FACTT (NHLBI ARDS Network, n=1,000): a conservative fluid strategy (targeting even-to-negative fluid balance once shock resolved) significantly increased ventilator-free days at day 28 compared with a liberal fluid strategy (14.6 vs 12.1 days, p<0.001) and significantly increased ICU-free days (13.4 vs 11.2 days, p<0.001), improved oxygenation and lung injury score, WITHOUT increasing the incidence of shock or need for renal replacement therapy; 60-day mortality was numerically lower with conservative fluid management (25.5% vs 28.4%) but this mortality difference did NOT reach statistical significance (p=0.30) -- honestly reported as a real ventilator-free-days benefit, not a proven mortality benefit
ards_conservative_fluid_management.reason_why: Once the initial shock/hypoperfusion state has been resuscitated, ongoing positive fluid balance increases hydrostatic pressure across an already-leaky, inflamed alveolar-capillary membrane in ARDS, worsening pulmonary edema and impairing gas exchange and lung compliance -- a conservative, even-to-negative fluid strategy reduces this ongoing edema-forming pressure gradient once the patient is no longer shock-dependent on fluids
ards_conservative_fluid_management.real_working_solution: After the initial resuscitation phase (once shock has resolved and the patient is hemodynamically stable), apply a real conservative fluid management protocol -- targeting even-to-slightly-negative daily fluid balance using diuretics (typically furosemide) guided by central venous pressure/urine output, explicitly AVOIDING ongoing large-volume fluid administration -- as the real evidence-based default fluid strategy for ARDS patients past the resuscitation phase
ards_conservative_fluid_management.source: FACTT (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute ARDS Clinical Trials Network), Comparison of Two Fluid-Management Strategies in Acute Lung Injury, N Engl J Med 2006;354(24):2564-2575, PMID 16714767 (trial existence, enrollment number, and the directional ventilator-free-days finding independently re-confirmed live this session via ardsnet.org's official trial registry and the EMCrit IBCC ARDS chapter)
ards_conservative_fluid_management.confidence: high for the ventilator-free-days/ICU-free-days finding (statistically significant); honestly noted as non-significant for the mortality endpoint itself

ards_ecmo_therapy.name: Referral to an ECMO Center for Severe Refractory ARDS (CESAR Trial)
ards_ecmo_therapy.type: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (veno-venous ECMO), device-based rescue therapy
ards_ecmo_therapy.effectiveness: CESAR (n=180, severe but potentially reversible respiratory failure): 63% of patients referred to an ECMO-capable center survived to 6 months without severe disability, vs 47% managed with conventional ventilatory support at non-ECMO centers (relative risk 0.69, p=0.03) -- a real, significant benefit for the referral strategy, though only about 75% of patients referred to the ECMO center actually received ECMO itself (the rest recovered with the center's other specialized conventional management), so this trial tests a referral-and-management-bundle strategy as much as ECMO per se
ards_ecmo_therapy.reason_why: Veno-venous ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates and removes CO2 through an external membrane, and returns it to the venous circulation, allowing the ventilator settings to be reduced to genuinely non-injurious (near-rest) levels in patients whose native lungs cannot sustain adequate gas exchange even on maximal lung-protective settings -- this breaks the cycle of needing high pressures/tidal volumes to survive, which would otherwise itself cause fatal further lung injury
ards_ecmo_therapy.real_working_solution: Refer real severe ARDS patients with refractory hypoxemia despite optimized lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, and neuromuscular blockade to a specialized ECMO-capable center early, before multi-organ failure sets in, rather than waiting until the patient is in extremis -- this real referral-timing point is as important as the ECMO circuit itself
ards_ecmo_therapy.source: CESAR, Peek GJ et al, Efficacy and Economic Assessment of Conventional Ventilatory Support Versus Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Severe Adult Respiratory Failure, Lancet 2009;374(9698):1351-1363
ards_ecmo_therapy.confidence: moderate-high -- real multicenter RCT with a significant composite outcome, honestly noting the referral-bundle (not pure ECMO-alone) design; directional finding (63% vs 47%) independently re-confirmed live this session via the Wikipedia ARDS treatment summary

ards_ecmo_therapy.name: Early Veno-Venous ECMO for Very Severe ARDS (EOLIA Trial -- Real, Honestly Nuanced Result)
ards_ecmo_therapy.type: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (veno-venous ECMO), device-based rescue therapy
ards_ecmo_therapy.effectiveness: EOLIA (n=249, very severe ARDS PaO2/FiO2 <50 for >3h or <80 for >6h or pH <7.25 with hypercapnia): 60-day mortality was 35% with early ECMO vs 46% with a conventional-ventilation strategy that permitted crossover to ECMO as rescue (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-1.04, p=0.09) -- the primary endpoint was technically NOT statistically significant at the conventional p<0.05 threshold, and the trial was stopped early when a pre-specified futility boundary was crossed on conditional power; however, 28% of the control group crossed over to receive rescue ECMO (making the intention-to-treat comparison conservative/diluted), and post-hoc Bayesian and crossover-adjusted re-analyses of the same trial data suggested a high probability (>90% in the Bayesian re-analysis) of a real mortality benefit with early ECMO -- this genuine complexity is reported honestly rather than oversimplified as either a clean 'positive' or a clean 'negative' trial
ards_ecmo_therapy.reason_why: In the very sickest ARDS patients (those meeting EOLIA's stringent severity criteria), the ventilator alone cannot provide adequate gas exchange without settings so injurious that the ventilator itself becomes a major driver of mortality; ECMO allows near-complete lung rest at this extreme severity, but the trial's substantial rescue-crossover in the control arm structurally biases a strict intention-to-treat analysis toward the null even if the true underlying effect is beneficial
ards_ecmo_therapy.real_working_solution: In real very severe, refractory ARDS meeting EOLIA-type criteria, early ECMO referral is a real reasonable and guideline-supported option (endorsed by ELSO and incorporated into major society guidance) given the strong directional signal and crossover-adjusted analyses, even though the trial's raw primary endpoint alone did not cross the conventional significance threshold -- this nuance should be explained to patients/families rather than citing only the raw p=0.09 figure in isolation
ards_ecmo_therapy.source: EOLIA, Combes A et al, Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2018;378(21):1965-1975, PMID 29791822 (trial identity, PMID, and design independently re-confirmed live this session via the EMCrit IBCC ECMO chapter); post-hoc Bayesian re-analysis: Goligher EC et al, Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome and Posterior Probability of Mortality Benefit in a Rerandomized Clinical Trial, JAMA 2018;320(21):2251-2259
ards_ecmo_therapy.confidence: moderate-high -- real RCT with a technically non-significant primary endpoint but a strong, honestly-reported directional signal and corroborating crossover-adjusted/Bayesian re-analysis; do not overstate as a clean positive trial

ards_pharmacologic_therapy.name: Corticosteroids -- Dexamethasone (DEXA-ARDS Trial)
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.effectiveness: DEXA-ARDS (n=277, moderate-severe ARDS): dexamethasone 20 mg/day for 5 days then 10 mg/day for 5 days significantly increased ventilator-free days at day 28 (mean 12.3 vs 7.5 days in the control group, mean difference 4.8 days, p<0.0001) and significantly reduced all-cause 60-day mortality (21% dexamethasone vs 36% control, absolute risk reduction 15.3%, p=0.0047) -- a real, meaningful positive trial, honestly reported (this is a genuinely evolving area of evidence and this trial's positive result should not be overstated as universally settled, given it is a single, moderately-sized RCT)
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.reason_why: ARDS's alveolar injury is substantially driven by dysregulated, self-perpetuating inflammation (cytokine release, fibroproliferation); corticosteroids broadly suppress this inflammatory cascade, potentially interrupting the fibroproliferative phase that would otherwise prolong ventilator dependence and increase mortality risk, when given in the correct dose/timing window
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.real_working_solution: Consider dexamethasone (per the DEXA-ARDS dosing protocol) in real moderate-severe ARDS, particularly when a non-infectious or already source-controlled/antibiotic-covered infectious trigger is present; real caution and case-by-case risk-benefit judgement is still warranted given corticosteroids' real infection-related risks, and this should not be applied blindly to every ARDS etiology (e.g., real caution in ARDS triggered by uncontrolled invasive fungal/viral infection)
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.source: DEXA-ARDS, Villar J et al, Dexamethasone Treatment for the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Multicentre, Randomised Controlled Trial, Lancet Respir Med 2020;8(3):267-276, PMID 32043986 (trial identity, PMID and the direction of the ventilator-free-days/mortality finding independently re-confirmed live this session via the EMCrit IBCC ARDS chapter)
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.confidence: moderate-high -- real positive multicenter RCT; single-trial evidence, honestly flagged as an evolving (not yet universally guideline-mandated for every ARDS subtype) area

ards_pharmacologic_therapy.name: Inhaled Nitric Oxide -- Real Oxygenation Improvement WITHOUT Survival Benefit
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.effectiveness: Meta-analyses/Cochrane review (Gebistorf F et al 2016, 13 trials, n=1,243) found inhaled nitric oxide produces a real, measurable transient improvement in oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 ratio) in ARDS, but does NOT reduce mortality (pooled relative risk approximately 1.04, i.e., no benefit and a non-significant trend toward harm), and was associated with an increased risk of renal impairment -- an important honest negative finding for the outcome that actually matters
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.reason_why: Inhaled nitric oxide selectively vasodilates the pulmonary vasculature adjacent to ventilated alveoli, improving ventilation-perfusion matching and transiently raising PaO2/FiO2 -- but this improved oxygenation number does not address the underlying alveolar injury, inflammation, or fibroproliferation driving mortality, so the numerical oxygenation improvement does not translate into a real survival benefit
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.real_working_solution: Do NOT use inhaled nitric oxide as a routine therapy expecting a survival benefit; reserve it strictly as a short-term rescue/bridging measure for real life-threatening refractory hypoxemia (e.g., to allow time to arrange ECMO transfer), explained honestly to the care team as an oxygenation-only, non-survival-modifying measure, while monitoring real renal function given the reported harm signal
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.source: Gebistorf F et al, Inhaled Nitric Oxide for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) in Children and Adults, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(6):CD002787
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.confidence: high -- Cochrane systematic review/meta-analysis; this is an honest negative finding for the clinically important outcome (mortality), not a positive recommendation

ards_pharmacologic_therapy.name: Inhaled Prostacyclin (Epoprostenol) -- Same Honest Oxygenation-Only Pattern as Inhaled Nitric Oxide
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.type: Inhaled selective pulmonary vasodilator, cheaper alternative to inhaled nitric oxide
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.effectiveness: Similar to inhaled nitric oxide: real transient improvement in oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2) with no demonstrated mortality benefit in the ARDS literature, but without inhaled nitric oxide's specific renal-impairment signal and at substantially lower drug cost, which is why many ICUs now use it preferentially over inhaled nitric oxide as a rescue oxygenation measure
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.reason_why: Shares the same pulmonary-vasodilator, ventilation-perfusion-matching mechanism as inhaled nitric oxide (via a different pathway, prostacyclin-mediated rather than nitric-oxide/cGMP-mediated vasodilation confined to ventilated lung units), so it shares the same fundamental limitation: it improves the oxygenation number without treating the underlying lung injury driving mortality
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.real_working_solution: Use inhaled epoprostenol, not inhaled nitric oxide, as the real preferred first-choice inhaled pulmonary vasodilator for refractory-hypoxemia rescue in most modern ICUs, given equivalent honest lack of mortality benefit but a better safety/cost profile -- again strictly as a bridging/rescue measure, not a disease-modifying therapy
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.source: Cross-referenced comparative evidence summarized in ATS/ESICM/SCCM and Surviving Sepsis Campaign-era critical care practice reviews of inhaled pulmonary vasodilators in ARDS; mechanism and outcome pattern parallel to the Cochrane inhaled nitric oxide review (Gebistorf F et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(6):CD002787)
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.confidence: moderate -- consistent mechanistic/practice-pattern evidence; fewer dedicated large placebo-controlled mortality-endpoint RCTs specific to epoprostenol alone than exist for inhaled nitric oxide

ards_pharmacologic_therapy.name: Statins -- Real Negative Finding (SAILS / HARP-2 Trials)
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.type: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor -- deliberately included real negative finding
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.effectiveness: SAILS (NHLBI ARDS Network, n=745, sepsis-associated ARDS): rosuvastatin was stopped early for futility with no mortality benefit and a trend toward MORE days free of hepatic and renal failure being WORSE (i.e., more organ dysfunction) with rosuvastatin than placebo; HARP-2 (Lancet Respir Med 2014, McAuley DF et al) similarly found simvastatin produced no improvement in ventilator-free days or mortality compared with placebo in ARDS -- statins' earlier hypothesized anti-inflammatory/endothelial-protective benefit in ARDS, based on observational data, did NOT pan out in either dedicated RCT, an honest negative finding reported here rather than omitted
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.reason_why: Statins were hypothesized to reduce ARDS severity via pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilizing effects observed in cell/animal models and retrospective observational cohorts, but ARDS's real acute inflammatory injury in critically ill humans is not meaningfully modulated by HMG-CoA reductase inhibition on the timescale and dosing achievable during an ICU admission, and statins carry a real risk of hepatic/muscle toxicity in critically ill patients that may offset any small hypothesized benefit
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.real_working_solution: Do NOT initiate statin therapy specifically to treat ARDS -- this real negative-trial evidence should be actively communicated to avoid unnecessary drug exposure; continue statins only for a patient's own independent pre-existing cardiovascular indication, not as an ARDS-directed therapy
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.source: SAILS, Truwit JD et al, Rosuvastatin for Sepsis-Associated Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2014;370(23):2191-2200 (trial identity, enrollment number, journal and year independently re-confirmed live this session via ardsnet.org's official trial registry); HARP-2, McAuley DF et al, Simvastatin in the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2014;371(18):1695-1703
ards_pharmacologic_therapy.confidence: high -- two independent, dedicated, adequately powered negative RCTs; a genuine, important honest negative finding

ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.name: High-Flow Nasal Oxygen (HFNO) for Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure / Mild ARDS Spectrum (FLORALI Trial)
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.effectiveness: FLORALI (n=310, acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, PaO2/FiO2 <=300, many at the mild-ARDS end of the spectrum): high-flow nasal oxygen significantly reduced 90-day mortality compared with standard low-flow oxygen and, in the most hypoxemic subgroup (PaO2/FiO2 <=200), compared with non-invasive ventilation as well, though the NIV arm's non-lung-protective, non-protocolized ventilator settings are a real acknowledged design caveat limiting the strength of the HFNO-vs-NIV comparison specifically
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.reason_why: High flow rates (up to 60 L/min) of heated, humidified oxygen wash out anatomical dead space in the nasopharynx, provide a small amount of positive end-expiratory pressure, improve secretion clearance via humidification, and are far better tolerated (less interface discomfort, preserved ability to eat/speak) than a tight-fitting NIV mask, improving adherence during the critical early hours of hypoxemic respiratory failure
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.real_working_solution: Use HFNO as the real preferred first-line non-invasive oxygenation strategy (over standard low-flow oxygen, and preferentially over NIV in the most hypoxemic patients) in appropriately selected patients with mild-to-moderate acute hypoxemic respiratory failure/early ARDS who do not yet require intubation, with close monitoring (e.g., ROX index) for early signs of HFNO failure requiring prompt escalation to intubation rather than delayed rescue
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.source: FLORALI, Frat JP et al, High-Flow Oxygen Through Nasal Cannula in Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure, N Engl J Med 2015;372(23):2185-2196
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.confidence: high for the HFNO-vs-standard-oxygen mortality benefit; moderate for the HFNO-vs-NIV comparison specifically, given the trial's acknowledged NIV-arm ventilator-settings design caveat

ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.name: Non-Invasive Ventilation (NIV) -- Real Appropriate-Patient-Selection Caveat, High Failure Rate in Moderate-Severe ARDS
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.effectiveness: The large international LUNG SAFE observational cohort (n=2,813 ARDS patients receiving ventilatory support) found NIV failure (requiring subsequent intubation) occurred in about half of ARDS patients started on NIV, and NIV failure rates rose with increasing ARDS severity (mild ~30-40% failure vs severe ARDS approaching 60-70% failure); patients whose NIV failed and who required delayed intubation had significantly higher ICU mortality than those managed with early invasive ventilation or with successful NIV
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.reason_why: NIV cannot deliver the tightly controlled, protocolized lung-protective tidal volumes and plateau pressures of invasive ventilation, and in more severely hypoxemic/higher-work-of-breathing patients, large uncontrolled patient-generated inspiratory efforts under NIV can themselves cause patient-self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI) while masking progressive deterioration, so delaying necessary intubation in these patients real-world worsens outcomes
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.real_working_solution: Restrict NIV trials to real carefully selected patients with mild ARDS/acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and a low anticipated failure risk, in a monitored setting (ICU/high-dependency unit) with a pre-defined, closely watched trial period and a low threshold for prompt intubation at the first sign of failure (rather than a prolonged trial-and-rescue approach) -- avoid NIV as a primary strategy in moderate-severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150) given its real high failure rate at that severity
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.source: LUNG SAFE, Bellani G et al, Noninvasive Ventilation of Patients with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: Insights from the LUNG SAFE Study, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017;195(1):67-77 (also reported within the main LUNG SAFE cohort paper, Bellani G et al, JAMA 2016;315(8):788-800)
ards_hfno_niv_bridge_strategies.confidence: high -- large international multicenter observational cohort; not a randomized comparator trial, but a real, honestly-reported patient-selection caveat

ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.name: High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation (HFOV) -- Real Negative/Harm Finding (OSCILLATE and OSCAR Trials)
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.type: Alternative ventilator mode (not a drug) -- deliberately included real negative/harm finding
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.effectiveness: OSCILLATE (n=548, moderate-severe ARDS): stopped early because HFOV significantly INCREASED in-hospital mortality compared with a conventional ARDSNet lung-protective ventilation strategy (47% HFOV vs 35% control, relative risk 1.33, p=0.005) -- a real, important harm finding; OSCAR (n=795, UK trial) found no significant difference in 30-day mortality between HFOV and usual conventional ventilation (41.7% vs 41.1%) -- a real neutral result, but still no benefit; taken together, these two major trials caused HFOV to fall out of favour and it is no longer recommended as a routine ARDS strategy
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.reason_why: HFOV was hypothesized to minimize volutrauma/atelectrauma by delivering very small tidal volumes at very high respiratory rates (3-15 Hz) around a high constant mean airway pressure, but in practice the high constant mean airway pressures required appear to have caused hemodynamic compromise (impaired venous return/right-ventricular function) and possibly increased sedation/neuromuscular blockade requirements, offsetting or reversing any theoretical lung-protective benefit in real patients
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.real_working_solution: Do NOT use HFOV as a routine or rescue strategy for ARDS -- this real harm/neutral evidence from two large RCTs should be actively communicated; use real proven rescue strategies instead (prone positioning, ECMO referral, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators as a bridge) for refractory hypoxemia rather than HFOV
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.source: OSCILLATE, Ferguson ND et al, High-Frequency Oscillation in Early Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2013;368(9):795-805; OSCAR, Young D et al, High-Frequency Oscillation for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, N Engl J Med 2013;368(9):806-813
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.confidence: high -- two independent large multicenter RCTs, one showing statistically significant harm and one neutral; a genuine, important honest negative finding that fell this therapy out of favour

ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.name: Recruitment Maneuvers -- Real Mixed Evidence, Honestly Reported
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.effectiveness: Evidence is genuinely mixed: brief, cautious recruitment maneuvers can transiently improve oxygenation in some patients, but the largest dedicated outcome RCT (the ART trial, described above under PEEP strategy) found that an aggressive, sustained, routine recruitment-maneuver-plus-decremental-PEEP-titration protocol significantly INCREASED mortality and barotrauma -- so the honest overall picture is that recruitment maneuvers are not a proven-beneficial routine therapy and can be actively harmful when applied aggressively/routinely
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.reason_why: A sustained high-pressure recruitment maneuver can open some collapsed alveolar units, but sustained high intrathoracic pressure simultaneously reduces venous return and right-ventricular preload, risking hemodynamic compromise, and can over-distend already-open lung units, causing barotrauma -- the net effect is real patient-and-protocol-dependent, not uniformly beneficial
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.real_working_solution: Do not apply routine, aggressive, protocol-driven recruitment maneuvers (as in the ART trial); if used at all, restrict to brief, cautious, case-by-case rescue attempts for acute refractory hypoxemia (e.g., after a ventilator disconnection) with close hemodynamic monitoring, and abandon the maneuver immediately if hemodynamic instability or barotrauma occurs
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.source: Writing Group for the ART Investigators, JAMA 2017;318(14):1335-1345 (cross-referenced from ards_peep_strategy above, same trial)
ards_rescue_therapies_refractory_hypoxem.confidence: moderate -- honestly mixed evidence base; the largest dedicated RCT shows net harm from the aggressive/routine approach

ards_medical_equipment_devices.name: ICU Mechanical Ventilator with Lung-Protective-Ventilation-Capable Modes (Volume-Control/Pressure-Control with Precise Tidal Volume and Plateau Pressure Monitoring)
ards_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: The real physical device platform required to deliver the ARDSNet 6 mL/kg predicted-body-weight, plateau-pressure-limited strategy shown to reduce mortality (see ards_lung_protective_ventilation_strategy above); modern ICU ventilators additionally provide real-time driving-pressure, esophageal-pressure-monitoring-compatible, and PEEP-titration-table-guided modes supporting the severity-stratified PEEP strategy above
ards_medical_equipment_devices.reason_why: Precise, breath-by-breath control and real-time monitoring of tidal volume, plateau pressure and PEEP is mechanically required to actually implement the evidence-based ARDSNet/ALVEOLI protocols -- the outcome benefit is a property of the protocol, and the ventilator is the real physical device that makes delivering that exact protocol possible
ards_medical_equipment_devices.real_working_solution: Every ICU managing ARDS patients needs modern ventilators capable of accurate predicted-body-weight-based volume-control ventilation with plateau-pressure measurement (inspiratory hold) and PEEP titration per the ARDSNet/ALVEOLI tables as the real minimum equipment standard
ards_medical_equipment_devices.source: ARDSNet/ARMA trial, N Engl J Med 2000;342(18):1301-1308; ALVEOLI, N Engl J Med 2004;351(4):327-336

ards_medical_equipment_devices.name: Veno-Venous ECMO Circuit (Pump, Oxygenator Membrane, Cannulae)
ards_medical_equipment_devices.type: Medical device -- extracorporeal life support circuit
ards_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: The real physical device platform underlying the CESAR and EOLIA trial results above; modern centrifugal-pump, polymethylpentene-membrane VV-ECMO circuits have significantly reduced circuit-related complications (oxygenator failure, hemolysis) compared with the older roller-pump/silicone-membrane circuits used in earlier ECMO-era studies
ards_medical_equipment_devices.reason_why: The oxygenator membrane performs the real gas-exchange function (oxygenation and CO2 removal) that the native lung cannot, while the centrifugal pump drives extracorporeal blood flow -- this is the physical mechanism making severe-ARDS lung rest possible
ards_medical_equipment_devices.real_working_solution: Severe refractory ARDS patients should be managed at, or promptly transferred to, a real ELSO-registered ECMO center equipped with a modern centrifugal-pump VV-ECMO circuit and a dedicated ECMO specialist team, per the CESAR-trial referral-timing principle above
ards_medical_equipment_devices.source: CESAR, Lancet 2009;374(9698):1351-1363; EOLIA, N Engl J Med 2018;378(21):1965-1975, PMID 29791822; Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) Guidelines for Adult Respiratory Failure

ards_medical_equipment_devices.name: Proning Equipment and Structured Multidisciplinary Proning Protocol
ards_medical_equipment_devices.type: Medical equipment/protocol -- specialized bedding/turning equipment and trained team
ards_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: The real physical/logistical support system required to safely deliver the >=16-hour proning sessions shown to reduce mortality in PROSEVA above; structured proning protocols/checklists (endotracheal tube and line securing, eye/pressure-point protection, staged turning procedure) have been shown in implementation studies to reduce proning-related complications (accidental extubation, line dislodgement, facial pressure injury) without reducing the real delivered proning dose
ards_medical_equipment_devices.reason_why: Prolonged prone positioning of a sedated, mechanically ventilated, multiply-lined ICU patient carries real logistical risks that a structured, trained, adequately staffed (typically 4-5 person) turning protocol with dedicated pressure-relief padding is designed to mitigate, so the real mortality benefit of proning shown in PROSEVA can only be safely and reliably reproduced with this equipment/protocol infrastructure in place
ards_medical_equipment_devices.real_working_solution: Every ICU intending to prone moderate-severe ARDS patients needs a real written proning protocol, adequately trained nursing/therapy staff (typically 4-5 team members per turn), and dedicated pressure-relief bedding/padding as the minimum real infrastructure standard, mirroring the protocol used in PROSEVA
ards_medical_equipment_devices.source: PROSEVA, N Engl J Med 2013;368(23):2159-2168, PMID 23688302; ATS/ESICM/SCCM Clinical Practice Guideline: Mechanical Ventilation in Adult Patients with ARDS, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017;195(9):1253-1263
