type_1_diabetes.source: CDC 'A U.S. Report Card' diabetes statistics; PubMed 30181166 (Prevalence of diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among US adults in 2016 and 2017); NCBI PMC8563635 (Type 1 diabetes in 2017: global estimates of incident and prevalent cases)
type_1_diabetes.confidence: high - consistent across US CDC data and global epidemiology literature; the exact global percentage varies by source region so a range is given rather than one false-precise number

type_2_diabetes.mechanism: Real combination of insulin resistance (impaired tissue response to insulin, principally in muscle, liver, and adipose tissue) plus a real RELATIVE (not absolute) insulin deficiency as beta-cell compensatory capacity fails over time.
type_2_diabetes.proportion: The overwhelming majority of diabetes cases - approximately 90-95% of all diagnosed cases in the US (91.2% in one large adult cohort), and an even larger global majority.

gestational_diabetes_mellitus.definition: A real, distinct pregnancy-specific entity - glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy, driven by placental-hormone-induced insulin resistance. Real, well-documented future-risk marker for T2DM (see real_risk_factors below).
gestational_diabetes_mellitus.note: Cross-reference: not a standalone entry in this KB; its acute maternal/fetal obstetric management sits outside this disease's non-pregnant adult scope, but its role as a T2DM risk factor is covered here.

mody.mechanism: Real distinct MONOGENIC form of diabetes - autosomal dominant heterozygous pathogenic variants in any of 11+ known genes (e.g. HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK), typically causing a primary beta-cell defect rather than insulin resistance or autoimmunity. Classically presents before age 25-30 with a strong multi-generational family history, often without obesity or autoantibodies.
mody.proportion: Real but genuinely uncommon - estimated at approximately 1-5% of all diabetes cases, with prevalence-in-later-onset-diabetes cohort estimates as low as 0.16-0.52% among those diagnosed after age 40 (UK Biobank / US Geisinger MyCode data), versus a higher ~4% figure quoted specifically among younger-onset diabetes patients. MODY is real, clinically significant despite its rarity because correct genetic diagnosis changes treatment (e.g. sulfonylurea response in HNF1A-MODY) - though that treatment implication itself is outside this entry's symptoms-only scope.
mody.source: AAFP 'Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young: Rapid Evidence Review' (2022); medRxiv/PMC preprint 'MODY is prevalent in later-onset diabetes...' 2025 (UK Biobank and Geisinger MyCode cohort analysis); PMC9697644
mody.confidence: moderate-high - the 1-5% headline range is widely cited, but exact prevalence is cohort-dependent and MODY is substantially under-diagnosed in real-world practice per the same sources

lada.mechanism: A real, distinct SLOW-ONSET autoimmune form of diabetes - immunologically similar to T1DM (autoantibody-positive, chiefly GAD65, present in ~90% of LADA cases) but with a slower rate of beta-cell destruction, so patients initially retain enough endogenous insulin to be managed like T2DM before progressing to insulin dependence.
lada.diagnostic_clues: Real, described clinical suspicion triggers: adult onset (classically >30 years), NOT obese/overweight, coexisting personal or family autoimmune disease (e.g. autoimmune thyroiditis), and deteriorating glycemic control despite escalating oral hypoglycemic/incretin-based therapy that would normally be expected to work in true T2DM. Confirmed by autoantibody testing (GAD-65, IA-2, ZnT8, ICA - a 4-antibody panel gives ~98% detection per Labcorp/clinical lab sources).
lada.misclassification_burden: Real and clinically important - up to an estimated 12% of patients clinically labelled 'Type 2 diabetes' may actually have LADA, and misclassification is associated with delayed insulin initiation, worse glycemic control, and increased complication risk.
lada.source: Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine, 'Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults: Not type 1, not type 2, a little of both' (2025); PMC12522475 'Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges'; Labcorp LADA diagnostic testing article
lada.confidence: high for the conceptual/diagnostic-clue framing; moderate for the exact 12% misclassification figure since it derives from a subset of studied T2DM cohorts, not a universal rate

diabetes_thresholds.note: fasting defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours
must be performed in a lab using an NGSP-certified/DCCT-standardized assay
classic symptoms = polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss, or hyperglycemic crisis

diagnostic_criteria_ada.confirmation_rule: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia with acute metabolic decompensation, diagnosis requires two abnormal test results from the same sample or two separate test samples (can be the same test repeated, or two different tests).
diagnostic_criteria_ada.source: American Diabetes Association, '2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025', Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl.1):S27, PMID 39651986
diagnostic_criteria_ada.confidence: high - directly sourced from the current (2025) ADA Standards of Care, the real actual current guideline

classic_symptoms.name: Polyuria
classic_symptoms.note: Real mechanism: once plasma glucose exceeds the renal tubular reabsorptive threshold (~180 mg/dL), glucose spills into the urine and acts as an osmotically active solute, dragging water with it (osmotic diuresis) - the real physiological basis of polyuria in uncontrolled hyperglycemia.

classic_symptoms.name: Polydipsia
classic_symptoms.note: Real, directly downstream of osmotic-diuresis-driven fluid loss and resulting intracellular/extracellular dehydration triggering thirst.

classic_symptoms.name: Polyphagia
classic_symptoms.note: Real - relative/absolute insulin deficiency impairs cellular glucose uptake and utilisation, so tissues signal a starvation-like state despite hyperglycemia, driving increased hunger.

classic_symptoms.name: Unexplained weight loss
classic_symptoms.note: Real, and classically MORE PROMINENT in T1DM - reflects a real catabolic state: absolute insulin deficiency forces the body to break down fat and muscle for energy despite calorie intake, unlike the often-preserved or increased weight typical at T2DM onset.

classic_symptoms.name: Fatigue
classic_symptoms.note: Real, from impaired cellular glucose utilisation plus dehydration from osmotic diuresis.

classic_symptoms.name: Blurred vision
classic_symptoms.note: Real, acute-hyperglycemia-driven osmotic change in lens/vitreous water content altering refractive index - typically reversible with glycemic correction, DISTINCT from chronic diabetic retinopathy (see chronic microvascular complications).

classic_symptoms.name: Slow-healing wounds
classic_symptoms.note: Real - chronic hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function, microvascular perfusion, and collagen synthesis.

classic_symptoms.name: Recurrent infections
classic_symptoms.note: Real - classically genital candidiasis, urinary tract infections, and skin infections; chronic hyperglycemia impairs innate immune (neutrophil) function.

core_presentation.source: ADA Standards of Care 2025 clinical presentation section; StatPearls 'Diabetes Mellitus' overview physiology
core_presentation.confidence: high - standard, well-replicated MBBS/MD-level clinical teaching

dka.more_common_in: T1DM (classic presenting feature in ~25-40% of new-onset T1DM in some cohorts), but real and increasingly documented in T2DM too, especially under metabolic stress (infection, MI) or with SGLT2-inhibitor use (euglycemic DKA).
dka.diagnostic_criteria: Plasma glucose >250 mg/dL (except euglycemic DKA), arterial pH <7.3, serum bicarbonate <18 mEq/L, positive ketonemia/ketonuria, elevated anion gap (>10-12).
dka.mortality: Real case-fatality rate approximately 1-5% in general/high-income-country populations, depending on age and comorbidity; mortality is substantially higher when DKA is complicated by concurrent bacterial infection.
dka.source: Kitabchi AE et al., 'Hyperglycemic Crises in Adult Patients With Diabetes', Diabetes Care 2009;32(7):1335 (original ADA severity classification, still cited/reaffirmed); ADA/EASD 'Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report', Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257; StatPearls 'Adult Diabetic Ketoacidosis' NBK560723

hhs.more_common_in: T2DM, typically in older patients, often precipitated by infection, stroke, or non-adherence.
hhs.diagnostic_criteria: Plasma glucose >600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L); effective serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg (or total osmolality >320 mOsm/kg); near-absence of significant ketoacidosis - pH >=7.3, bicarbonate >=15 mEq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L.
hhs.mortality_contrast: Real, important, somewhat counterintuitive finding: despite LESS severe acid-base derangement than DKA, HHS carries HIGHER mortality - commonly cited ranges of 5-20% for HHS versus ~1-5% (some sources: 0.2-1% in high-income countries) for DKA, attributed to the older age and greater comorbidity burden of typical HHS patients rather than to the metabolic disturbance itself.
hhs.source: AAFP 'Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State' (2017); Endotext 'Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar Syndrome' NBK620700; Diabetes Care 2014;37(11):3124 'Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State: A Historic Review'
hhs.confidence: high for the criteria and the directional mortality contrast; the exact mortality percentage range varies modestly across cited sources so a range rather than one number is given

severe_hypoglycemia.definition: Hypoglycemia severe enough to require assistance from another person for recovery (ADA definitional framework), reflecting neuroglycopenia impairing the patient's own capacity to self-treat.
severe_hypoglycemia.glucose_thresholds: General hypoglycemia commonly defined at plasma glucose <70 mg/dL; adrenergic symptoms typically appear <54-55 mg/dL; neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness) typically appear <48-50 mg/dL. Note: patients with chronically poor glycemic control can experience symptomatic hypoglycemia at higher absolute glucose values due to an altered symptomatic 'set point'.
severe_hypoglycemia.diagnostic_framework: Whipple's triad - (1) a low plasma glucose measurement, (2) symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia, (3) resolution of those symptoms when glucose is corrected.
severe_hypoglycemia.source: StatPearls 'Hypoglycemia' NBK534841; Wikipedia 'Whipple's triad' (summarising the original 1938 diagnostic framework)

diabetic_retinopathy.staging: Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR, early stage - microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, macular oedema risk) progressing to Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR, advanced stage - pathological retinal neovascularisation, risk of vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment).
diabetic_retinopathy.burden: Real - diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of blindness in working-age adults; roughly one-third of people with diabetes show signs of retinopathy and about 10% develop vision-threatening retinopathy/vision loss.
diabetic_retinopathy.source: PMC9971534 'Diabetic retinopathy as the leading cause of blindness and early predictor of cascading complications'; CDC 'Vision Loss and Diabetes'

diabetic_nephropathy.staging: Staged by KDIGO framework combining albuminuria category (normal <30 mg/g; microalbuminuria/moderately increased 30-300 mg/g; macroalbuminuria/severely increased >300 mg/g) and eGFR category (CKD defined as eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m^2 and/or presence of albuminuria, staged G1-G5).
diabetic_nephropathy.burden: Real - diabetic nephropathy/diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and of patients starting renal replacement therapy (dialysis) in the United States and many other countries worldwide.
diabetic_nephropathy.source: KDIGO CKD guideline framework as summarised in PMC2761852 'Diabetic nephropathy' and StatPearls 'Chronic Kidney Disease' NBK535404

diabetic_neuropathy.subtypes: Peripheral (predominantly sensory, distal symmetric, 'stocking-glove' pattern, with motor features in advanced disease) and Autonomic (cardiac autonomic neuropathy most studied subtype; also gastrointestinal, genitourinary, sudomotor autonomic dysfunction).
diabetic_neuropathy.prevalence: Real, very high burden - diabetic peripheral neuropathy affects more than half of people with long-standing diabetes in pooled estimates; individual studies report prevalence in the ~44-51% range by questionnaire/foot-examination methods respectively. Cardiac autonomic neuropathy prevalence as high as 31% (possible) to 66% (definite) in high-foot-ulcer-risk cohorts in one study.
diabetic_neuropathy.foot_ulcer_amputation_risk: Peripheral neuropathy is the key initiating factor for diabetic foot ulceration (implicated in >60% of ulcers) and the leading cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation in most high-income countries. People with diabetes have a real ~15% lifetime risk of developing a diabetic foot ulcer, and WHO data indicate lower-limb amputations are roughly 10 times more common in people with diabetes than without. Cross-reference: peripheral_artery_disease entry in this KB covers the co-existing macrovascular ischaemic contribution to diabetic foot disease.
diabetic_neuropathy.source: StatPearls 'Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy' NBK442009; PMC5367231 (cardiac autonomic neuropathy in high-foot-ulcer-risk T2DM); WHO diabetic foot/amputation data as cited in the reviewed neuropathy literature

chronic_macrovascular_complications.note: Diabetes real-world macrovascular disease is covered in depth in this KB's own dedicated entries - cross-reference ischaemic_heart_disease (diabetic autonomic neuropathy is a real, documented cause of blunted anginal pain perception and 'silent ischaemia', and diabetics/women show a real atypical-presentation pattern of fatigue/dyspnoea/epigastric discomfort rather than classic chest pain) and peripheral_artery_disease (diabetes is a major real accelerant of lower-limb atherosclerosis, compounding the neuropathic diabetic-foot risk above).

chd_risk_equivalent_concept.concept: Real, historically influential risk-stratification concept - the NCEP Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) guidelines (2001) classified diabetes as a 'coronary heart disease risk equivalent', meaning a person with diabetes but no prior MI should be risk-stratified and treated for cardiovascular prevention as aggressively as a person who has already survived a myocardial infarction (defined operationally as a >20% 10-year CHD risk).
chd_risk_equivalent_concept.origin: This concept originated from Haffner SM et al., 'Mortality from coronary heart disease in subjects with type 2 diabetes and in nondiabetic subjects with and without prior myocardial infarction', New England Journal of Medicine 1998, a landmark Finnish population study finding that 7-year MI incidence in diabetics without prior MI was statistically indistinguishable from non-diabetics WITH prior MI.
chd_risk_equivalent_concept.current_status: Real, ongoing clinical debate - subsequent systematic reviews/meta-analyses (from ~2009 onward) found the 'risk equivalence' does not hold uniformly across all diabetic subgroups (varies with diabetes duration, concomitant risk factors, and population studied), so it is now understood as a historically important but imperfect heuristic rather than an absolute rule.
chd_risk_equivalent_concept.source: NCEP ATP III Guidelines (NIH/NHLBI, 2001); Haffner SM et al., NEJM 1998;339:229-234; American College of Cardiology, 'Is Diabetes Really a CHD Risk Equivalent?' (2016) summarising the subsequent controversy
chd_risk_equivalent_concept.confidence: high for the concept's real origin and content; the 'current status' controversy point is explicitly flagged as real, ongoing debate rather than settled fact

hba1c.role: Real gold-standard marker of average glycemic control over the preceding ~2-3 months (reflecting glucose bound to circulating haemoglobin over the red-cell lifespan).
hba1c.targets: General ADA target for many nonpregnant adults: A1C <7% (53 mmol/mol) as a common general goal, with the 2025 Standards of Care explicitly framing goals as individualized (the 'four Ms' approach) - less stringent targets (e.g. <7.5-8%) are appropriate for patients with limited life expectancy, extensive comorbidity, or high hypoglycemia risk, while more stringent targets may suit selected patients if achievable without significant hypoglycemia.
hba1c.source: ADA, '6. Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025', Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl.1):S128

cgm.role: Real, increasingly used monitoring tool - continuous glucose monitoring provides real-time interstitial glucose trends and a 'time-in-range' metric (ADA-referenced general target ~70% time-in-range for many adults), supplementing or in some regimens replacing fingerstick self-monitoring. Per the 2025 ADA Standards, current evidence is NOT yet sufficient to support CGM specifically for the initial SCREENING or DIAGNOSIS of prediabetes/diabetes - its established real-world role is ongoing management monitoring, not diagnosis.
cgm.source: ADA Standards of Care 2025 (Diagnosis and Classification section noting insufficient evidence for CGM in diagnosis; Glycemic Goals section for time-in-range framing)

real_risk_factors.note: Real, single strongest modifiable risk factor for T2DM. Meta-analysis-derived relative risk rises steeply with BMI category: overweight RR ~1.5-2.92, Class I obesity RR ~2.5, Class II RR ~3.6, Class III RR ~5.1, with some high-BMI subgroup estimates reported as high as RR ~7.3-38.8 depending on population and BMI cutoff used.
real_risk_factors.source: StatPearls 'Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes' NBK592412; meta-analysis data summarised across multiple prospective cohort studies (ScienceDirect 2010 pooled meta-analysis)
real_risk_factors.confidence: high for the directional/strength finding; the exact RR number varies materially by study and BMI cutoff so a range is given

real_risk_factors.note: Real, well-established polygenic contribution to T2DM risk; MODY represents the rare monogenic extreme (see classification above).
Real, established independent modifiable risk factor, synergistic with obesity.

Real, strong future-T2DM risk marker - lifetime risk of T2DM after a GDM pregnancy is estimated at approximately 50-60%, with cumulative incidence of 20-60% within 10 years of the index pregnancy in various cohorts, and hazard ratio remaining elevated for over 35 years post-pregnancy in some registry data.
real_risk_factors.source: Mayo Clinic Press summary of GDM follow-up literature; Diabetes Care 2022;45(4):864 'Persistence of Risk for Type 2 Diabetes After Gestational Diabetes Mellitus'; Sri Lankan community cohort study PMC5482451
real_risk_factors.confidence: high for the directional/magnitude finding; the exact percentage varies by cohort and follow-up duration so a range is given

real_risk_factors.factor: South Asian / Indian ethnicity ('Asian Indian phenotype')
real_risk_factors.note: Real, well-documented, clinically important ethnicity-specific risk finding highly relevant to this India-focused KB. South Asians/Asian Indians develop T2DM at real LOWER BMI thresholds than Western (Caucasian) populations - one cited comparison found the BMI in South Asians conferring equivalent diabetes risk to a BMI >30 kg/m^2 in White populations was only ~22 kg/m^2. The underlying mechanism is the real, described 'thin-fat Indian' phenotype: normal or low overall BMI/lean mass but disproportionately increased truncal/visceral adiposity, associated with insulin resistance from adolescence onward.
real_risk_factors.source: American Diabetes Association journal 'Diabetes in South Asians: Is the Phenotype Different?', Diabetes 2014;63(1):53; PubMed 11701707 'Body fat distribution and insulin resistance in healthy Asian Indians and Caucasians'; PMC8191592 'Diabetes and Cardiometabolic Risk in South Asian Youth'
real_risk_factors.confidence: high - consistent, well-replicated finding across multiple independently fetched sources

global.finding: An estimated 589 million adults worldwide were living with diabetes in 2024, projected to reach 853 million by 2050.
global.source: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition (2025)

india.finding: India has an estimated 89.8 million adults (aged 20-79) living with diabetes as of 2024 - ranking second globally only to China, and accounting for roughly 1 in every 7 adults with diabetes worldwide. India also has the second-highest number of undiagnosed diabetes cases globally. Projected to rise 75% to approximately 156.7 million by 2050.
india.source: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition (2025); PMC13289985 'A Global Wake-up Call: The 2025 IDF Diabetes Atlas and what it Means for India'

india.finding: The ICMR-INDIAB-17 national metabolic disease survey (113,043 individuals, 31 states/UTs, 2008-2020) estimated 10.1 crore (~101 million) Indians have diabetes and a further 13.6 crore (~136 million) have prediabetes - giving India its widely-used popular description as the 'diabetes capital of the world'. The same study found overall weighted prevalence of prediabetes 15.3%, hypertension 35.5%, and generalised obesity 28.6%, indicating major co-occurring metabolic disease burden.
india.source: ICMR-INDIAB-17, Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2023 ('Metabolic non-communicable disease health report of India'); Journal of the Indian Institute of Science summary (Springer 2023)
india.confidence: high - real, recent, large national research-programme figures with directly fetched citations
india.note: The ICMR-INDIAB (~101 million) and IDF Atlas (~89.8 million) figures differ because of different survey years, methodologies, and age-bands sampled - both are real, current, guideline/registry-sourced numbers and are presented here without forcing false reconciliation.

prediabetes_to_t2dm_progression.annual_conversion_rate: Real, well-documented progression - approximately 5-10% of people with prediabetes convert to overt T2DM annually in general-population cohorts, though this varies enormously by baseline risk: pooled cohort analyses show 1-year conversion ranging from under 1% to >40% depending on baseline HbA1c/risk stratum, and up to 70% of people with prediabetes are estimated to develop diabetes over their lifetime, especially if overweight/obese.
prediabetes_to_t2dm_progression.source: Multiple cohort studies as summarised via PMC7284825, PMC4390315 (Japanese HbA1c-stratified cohort), and Lancet Global Health individual-patient pooled analysis (Obesity, Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease Collaboration, 19 prospective cohorts)
prediabetes_to_t2dm_progression.confidence: high for the directional 5-10%/year general estimate; the wide stratified range is itself a real, important finding rather than noise

ukpds_dcct_legacy_effect.finding: Real, landmark, and somewhat counterintuitive finding from two of the most important trials in diabetes history: early, tight glycemic control confers LONG-TERM benefit that persists for decades even after glycemic control in the previously-intensive group later converges with or worsens relative to the previously-standard-therapy group - termed the 'legacy effect' (UKPDS, type 2 diabetes) or 'metabolic memory' (DCCT/EDIC, type 1 diabetes).
ukpds_dcct_legacy_effect.dcct_edic_data: In EDIC follow-up, participants who had averaged HbA1c ~7.2% during the original DCCT intensive-therapy period showed, ~20 years later, a 63% reduced risk of retinopathy, 54% reduced risk of kidney disease, 60% reduced risk of neuropathy, and 30% reduced risk of cardiovascular events compared with the conventional-therapy group - despite HbA1c differences between groups having narrowed after the trial ended.
ukpds_dcct_legacy_effect.ukpds_data: UKPDS follow-up (>80,000 person-years) similarly found that benefits of early tight glycemic control in newly-diagnosed T2DM persisted for decades despite the early loss of the within-trial HbA1c difference between intensive and conventional groups.
ukpds_dcct_legacy_effect.clinical_implication: Real, important argument for early, aggressive glycemic control at diagnosis rather than a 'treat to target later' approach, since early hyperglycemic exposure appears to leave a durable biological imprint (proposed mechanisms include oxidative stress, advanced glycation end-products, and epigenetic changes).
ukpds_dcct_legacy_effect.source: DCCT/EDIC Research Group, 'Understanding Metabolic Memory...', Diabetes Care 2021;44(10):2216; UKPDS long-term follow-up as summarised in Diabetes on the Net 'UKPDS at 44 years' and Springer 'Legacy Effects from DCCT and UKPDS' (Curr Atheroscler Rep 2010)
ukpds_dcct_legacy_effect.confidence: high - both DCCT/EDIC and UKPDS are landmark, extensively replicated/cited trials and the legacy-effect/metabolic-memory finding is one of the most robust conclusions in diabetes clinical science

red_flags: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) - real emergency, see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) - real emergency, HIGHER mortality than DKA, see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE
Severe hypoglycemia requiring third-party assistance - real emergency, see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE
Sudden vision loss or new floaters/flashes - real red flag for vitreous haemorrhage/tractional retinal detachment from proliferative diabetic retinopathy, needs urgent ophthalmology review

New foot ulcer, especially with surrounding cellulitis, malodour, or exposed bone/tendon - real red flag for limb-threatening diabetic foot infection/osteomyelitis, cross-reference peripheral_artery_disease for co-existing ischaemic contribution
Rapidly rising creatinine/falling eGFR or new heavy proteinuria - real red flag for accelerating diabetic nephropathy toward end-stage renal disease
Chest pain, dyspnoea, or unexplained fatigue/epigastric discomfort in a diabetic patient - real red flag for atypical/silent myocardial ischaemia, cross-reference ischaemic_heart_disease entry

diabetes_mellitus.CURABILITY_NOTE: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic, progressive metabolic disease that is NOT cured by standard pharmacotherapy alone - lifelong drug therapy for the majority of patients aims at durable glycaemic CONTROL to reduce microvascular/macrovascular complication risk, not reversal of the underlying beta-cell dysfunction/insulin-resistance pathophysiology. However, T2DM is one of the real few chronic metabolic diseases in this knowledge base with a genuine near-cure pathway: metabolic/bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy) can induce real, durable diabetes REMISSION in a substantial proportion of appropriate patients (STAMPEDE trial - 29% Roux-en-Y and 23% sleeve-gastrectomy patients met the primary HbA1c <=6.0% endpoint at 5 years vs only 5% with intensive medical therapy alone), and real intensive lifestyle intervention with a structured, primary-care-delivered very-low-calorie diet can likewise induce real T2DM remission in a real, specific, practice-relevant population (DiRECT trial - 46% remission at 12 months and 36% still in remission at 2 years in the intervention arm vs 4% and a much lower rate respectively in controls, with remission strongly tied to the amount of weight lost). Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) has NO cure with current standard therapy - it is an autoimmune beta-cell-destructive disease requiring lifelong exogenous insulin - though islet-cell or whole-pancreas transplantation exists as a real, narrow option for select severe/brittle cases with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia unawareness, reported honestly below including its real graft-survival limits and mandatory lifelong immunosuppression trade-off.

curative_option.name: T2DM Remission Pathways (Bariatric/Metabolic Surgery & Intensive Lifestyle Intervention) and T1DM Islet-Cell/Pancreas Transplantation (Narrow, Selected Cases)
curative_option.note: These are the real closest-to-a-cure pathways in diabetes care. For T2DM, surgical and intensive-lifestyle remission is real and reproducible in trials but is NOT universal or guaranteed durable in every patient - relapse to hyperglycaemia occurs in a meaningful fraction over time, especially with weight regain. For T1DM, islet/pancreas transplantation is a real option but is reserved for a narrow subset (recurrent severe hypoglycaemia with unawareness, or already undergoing kidney transplantation) because of the real, permanent immunosuppression burden and finite graft survival - it is not offered as first-line therapy to the general T1DM population, for whom insulin remains the only option (see definitive_option_nonreversible_majority below and exhaustive_medicine_survey for standard care).

reversible_subtypes.name: Metabolic/Bariatric Surgery-Induced T2DM Remission (Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass / Sleeve Gastrectomy)
reversible_subtypes.note: Real, randomized head-to-head evidence against intensive medical therapy in obese T2DM patients (BMI 27-43). Both procedures produced far higher rates of the primary glycaemic endpoint than medical therapy alone at 5 years, with gastric bypass numerically superior to sleeve gastrectomy and requiring fewer diabetes medications at follow-up. Honest caveat: the trial's primary endpoint (HbA1c <=6.0% with or without medication) is a stringent glycaemic-control endpoint, not a strict off-all-medication remission definition, and mean HbA1c in the surgery arms (7.3-7.4% at 5 years, down from 9.3-9.5% at baseline) shows genuine but incomplete normalisation in many patients.

real_recovery_data.primary_endpoint_gastric_bypass_5yr: 29% (HbA1c <=6.0%) vs 5% with intensive medical therapy alone
real_recovery_data.primary_endpoint_sleeve_gastrectomy_5yr: 23% (HbA1c <=6.0%) vs 5% with intensive medical therapy alone
real_recovery_data.cohort: STAMPEDE trial, 150 randomized, 134 completing 5-year follow-up, BMI 27-43

reversible_subtypes.source: STAMPEDE trial, Schauer et al., NEJM 2017 (5-year outcomes, PMID 28199805); original 3-year outcomes Schauer et al., NEJM 2014 (PMID 24679060)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - the only randomized surgery-vs-medical-therapy trial in T2DM with 5-year follow-up
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, randomized-trial-proven: bariatric/metabolic surgery is the single most effective real intervention for durable glycaemic remission/near-remission in obese T2DM patients, and should be actively discussed as a genuine disease-modifying option, not reserved as a last resort for weight loss alone.

reversible_subtypes.name: Intensive Lifestyle Intervention / Very-Low-Calorie-Diet-Induced T2DM Remission (DiRECT Trial)
reversible_subtypes.note: A real, practice-changing UK primary-care-based cluster-randomised trial: an 825-853 kcal/day total diet replacement for 3-5 months, followed by structured food reintroduction and long-term weight-loss maintenance support, delivered by ordinary GP practice staff (not a specialist obesity clinic) - demonstrating remission is achievable in routine primary care, not only in trial-specialist settings. Remission was strongly weight-loss-dependent: over 80% of those who lost more than 15 kg were still in remission at both 12 and 24 months.

real_recovery_data.remission_rate_if_lost_over_15kg: >80% still in remission at 12 and 24 months
real_recovery_data.remission_definition: HbA1c <6.5% (<48 mmol/mol) after >=2 months off all antidiabetic medication
real_recovery_data.cohort: DiRECT trial, 306 patients, UK primary care, T2DM duration <6 years, not on insulin

reversible_subtypes.source: DiRECT trial, Lean et al., Lancet 2018 (PMID 29465180); 2-year durability Lean et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019 (PMID 30852132)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - large, real cluster-randomised primary-care trial, a genuinely important and often-underappreciated finding
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, GP-delivered, drug-free route to genuine T2DM remission: structured very-low-calorie total diet replacement plus long-term weight-maintenance support achieves remission in roughly half of appropriately selected early-duration T2DM patients (<6 years, not yet on insulin) - this should be offered as a real first-line option, not only pharmacotherapy.

reversible_subtypes.name: Islet Cell Transplantation for Select Severe/Brittle Type 1 Diabetes (Recurrent Severe Hypoglycaemia)
reversible_subtypes.note: Real, but narrow-indication option - reserved for T1DM patients with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness despite optimized insulin therapy, or those already requiring immunosuppression for a kidney transplant (islet-after-kidney). Honest caveat: full, sustained insulin independence is not universal or permanent - many recipients revert to needing some exogenous insulin over years, though C-peptide production and protection from severe hypoglycaemia often persist even after partial graft function loss. Lifelong immunosuppression carries real infection/malignancy risk, which is why this is not offered to the general T1DM population.

real_recovery_data.registry_comparison_vs_standard_care: CITR islet-transplant recipients achieved HbA1c <7.0% AND freedom from severe hypoglycaemic events in 71-80% over 5 years vs 21-33% with standard insulin therapy (T1D Exchange registry controls)
real_recovery_data.cohort: Clinical Islet Transplantation Consortium CIT-08 study (islet-alone n=48, islet-after-kidney n=24), up to 8 years follow-up; CITR vs T1D Exchange registry comparison (n=71 vs n=213)

reversible_subtypes.source: CIT-08 study, Diabetes Care 2022 (PMID 36260350); CITR vs T1D Exchange registry comparison, Diabetes Care 2025
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - prospective multicentre consortium study plus real-world registry comparison
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, evidence-backed option for the narrow subgroup of T1DM patients with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia unawareness refractory to optimized insulin/CGM therapy: islet transplantation achieves insulin independence in the majority initially and durably protects against severe hypoglycaemia in >90%, even when full insulin independence later wanes - a genuine rescue option, not a population-wide cure.

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.name: Standard Lifelong Pharmacotherapy (T2DM Majority Not Achieving/Maintaining Remission) and Lifelong Insulin Therapy (T1DM - No Cure Exists With Standard Care)
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.note: For the majority of T2DM patients who are not candidates for or do not achieve/maintain surgical or lifestyle-induced remission, and for essentially all T1DM patients outside the narrow transplant-eligible subgroup above, no medicine or device currently cures the underlying disease. The real, achievable goal is durable glycaemic control via the pharmacotherapy, insulin regimens, and monitoring strategies detailed in exhaustive_medicine_survey below, which real, large trials (UKPDS, DCCT/EDIC, EMPA-REG OUTCOME, LEADER and others) show meaningfully reduces microvascular and macrovascular complications and mortality - but this is genuinely lifelong management, not cure.
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes - 2024/2025/2026; UKPDS; DCCT/EDIC

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real drug class, insulin regimen, device, and acute/chronic complication management option used in diabetes mellitus, each ending in a stated real working solution per the standing rule. CURABILITY: none of these cure T1DM or the majority of T2DM - see curative_option above for the real remission/transplant pathways that exist for a subset of patients. Every drug CLASS below carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific medicines.

diabetes_t2dm_first_line_pharmacotherapy.name: Metformin
diabetes_t2dm_first_line_pharmacotherapy.effectiveness: UKPDS 34 (n=1704 overweight T2DM patients, median 10.7 years): metformin reduced any diabetes-related endpoint by 32% (95% CI 2-52, P=0.002), diabetes-related death by 42% (P=0.017), and all-cause mortality by 36% (P=0.011) vs conventional diet-alone therapy; combined UKPDS 33+34 analysis showed a 19% risk reduction (2-33%, P=0.033) for diabetes-related endpoints vs other intensive therapies.
diabetes_t2dm_first_line_pharmacotherapy.reason_why: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity via AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway activation, lowering blood glucose without stimulating insulin secretion - the only first-line agent shown in a randomized trial to reduce diabetes-related death and all-cause mortality, not just glycaemia.
diabetes_t2dm_first_line_pharmacotherapy.confidence: high - landmark 20-year UK Prospective Diabetes Study
diabetes_t2dm_first_line_pharmacotherapy.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-universal first-line drug for essentially all newly diagnosed T2DM patients (absent contraindication) - the only oral agent with randomized-trial-proven mortality benefit, cheap, weight-neutral-to-modestly-weight-reducing, and low hypoglycaemia risk.

diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.name: SGLT2 Inhibitors (Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors)
diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.type: T2DM pharmacotherapy - real cardiovascular and renal outcome-trial-proven class
diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.effectiveness: EMPA-REG OUTCOME (empagliflozin, n=7020, established CVD): 38% RRR cardiovascular death (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.77, P<0.0001), 32% RRR all-cause mortality (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57-0.82). DECLARE-TIMI 58 (dapagliflozin, n=17,160, broad CV-risk population): reduced composite CV death/hospitalization-for-heart-failure (4.9% vs 5.8%, P=0.005), driven by HHF reduction (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61-0.88); did not significantly reduce MACE. CREDENCE (canagliflozin, n=4401, diabetic nephropathy with albuminuria): 30% RRR in the primary renal composite of ESKD/doubling-creatinine/renal-or-CV-death (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.59-0.82, P=0.00001); 32% RRR ESKD alone (HR 0.68); 39% RRR hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.61). DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin, n=4304, CKD with/without diabetes): 39% RRR in the primary kidney-composite outcome (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51-0.72); 31% RRR all-cause mortality (HR 0.69).
diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.reason_why: Blocks glucose reabsorption at the SGLT2 transporter in the renal proximal tubule, causing glucosuria (lowering blood glucose independent of insulin) plus natriuresis, reduced intraglomerular pressure, and favourable cardiac/renal haemodynamic effects - explaining why the cardiovascular and renal benefits appear far larger and faster than glycaemic control alone could produce.
diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.source: EMPA-REG OUTCOME, Zinman et al., NEJM 2015 (PMID 26378978); DECLARE-TIMI 58, Wiviott et al., NEJM 2019 (PMID 30415602); CREDENCE, Perkovic et al., NEJM 2019 (PMID 30990260); DAPA-CKD, Heerspink et al., NEJM 2020 (PMID 32970396)
diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.confidence: high - four large independent randomized outcome trials with concordant cardiorenal benefit; see this KB's congestive_heart_failure entry for the parallel HFrEF/HFpEF-specific SGLT2i outcome data
diabetes_t2dm_sglt2_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-elevated (ADA/EASD) second pillar of T2DM care, independent of HbA1c target achieved: SGLT2 inhibitors should be added early in any T2DM patient with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease/albuminuria, given hard mortality/renal-failure-prevention benefit, not merely glycaemic effect.

diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.name: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (including Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonism)
diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.type: T2DM pharmacotherapy - real transformative weight-loss AND cardiovascular-outcome-proven class
diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.effectiveness: LEADER (liraglutide, n=9340, high CV risk): 13% RRR primary MACE (13.0% vs 14.9%, HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.97); 15% RRR all-cause mortality (HR 0.85, P=0.02). SUSTAIN-6 (semaglutide, n=3297, high CV risk): 26% RRR primary MACE (6.6% vs 8.9%, HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.95, P=0.02 for superiority) - one of the largest CVOT effect sizes among the class. SURPASS trials (tirzepatide, n>5000 across SURPASS 1-6): HbA1c reduction of 1.9-2.6 percentage points and body-weight reduction of 6.2-12.9 kg over 40-52 weeks, exceeding both insulin glargine and other GLP-1 receptor agonists head-to-head (highest dose: -2.58% HbA1c and -11.7 kg vs glargine, which caused +1.9 kg weight gain, at 52 weeks).
diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.reason_why: Activates GLP-1 receptors to enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and act centrally to reduce appetite; tirzepatide additionally co-agonises the GIP receptor, producing synergistic incretin effects - together explaining both the marked weight loss and the real cardiovascular-event reduction seen independent of glycaemic control alone.
diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.source: LEADER, Marso et al., NEJM 2016 (PMID 27295427); SUSTAIN-6, Marso et al., NEJM 2016 (PMID 27633186); SURPASS program summary, multiple NEJM/Lancet publications 2021-2022
diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.confidence: high - multiple large randomized CVOTs plus a large head-to-head phase 3 program
diabetes_t2dm_glp1_receptor_agonists.real_working_solution: Real, genuinely transformative modern drug class: GLP-1 receptor agonists (and dual-agonist tirzepatide) are now guideline-preferred injectable add-ons for T2DM patients with obesity and/or established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, delivering simultaneous real HbA1c reduction, substantial weight loss, and hard cardiovascular-event risk reduction in a single drug class.

diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.name: DPP-4 Inhibitors (Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 Inhibitors)
diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.type: T2DM pharmacotherapy - modest efficacy, cardiovascular-neutral class
diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.effectiveness: TECOS (sitagliptin, n=14,671): noninferior to placebo for primary MACE composite (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.88-1.09) and no increase in heart-failure hospitalization (HR 1.00); complete cardiovascular neutrality. CARMELINA (linagliptin, high CV/renal-risk T2DM): non-inferior for MACE and no increase in heart-failure hospitalization, confirming CV safety in a fragile, high-renal-risk population.
diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.reason_why: Inhibits the DPP-4 enzyme that normally degrades endogenous incretins (GLP-1, GIP), modestly prolonging their glucose-lowering action - a gentler, oral, weight-neutral mechanism than injectable GLP-1 receptor agonists, but with correspondingly smaller HbA1c and no cardiovascular-outcome benefit.
diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.source: TECOS, Green et al., NEJM 2015 (PMID 26052984); CARMELINA, Rosenstock et al., JAMA 2019
diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.confidence: high - two large dedicated cardiovascular outcome trials, both confirming neutrality (neither benefit nor harm)
diabetes_t2dm_dpp4_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Real, well-tolerated, weight-neutral, low-hypoglycaemia-risk oral add-on for T2DM patients who need modest additional glycaemic lowering without the injection, GI side-effects, or cost of a GLP-1 receptor agonist - honestly positioned as cardiovascular-neutral, not cardioprotective.

diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.name: Sulfonylureas
diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.type: T2DM pharmacotherapy - real-world widely used, real hypoglycaemia-risk caveat
diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.effectiveness: ADVANCE trial (gliclazide MR-based intensive control, n=11,140, target HbA1c <=6.5%): 10% RRR in the composite primary macro/microvascular outcome, driven mainly by a 21% RRR in new/worsening diabetic nephropathy; no significant increase in mortality with intensive gliclazide-based control.
diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.reason_why: Stimulates pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels, independent of ambient glucose level - effective and inexpensive, but this glucose-independent insulin release is exactly why hypoglycaemia risk is real and clinically significant, unlike metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, or DPP-4 inhibitors.
diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.source: ADVANCE trial, Patel et al., NEJM 2008 (PMID 18539916)
diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.confidence: high - large randomized outcome trial specifically using gliclazide
diabetes_t2dm_sulfonylureas.real_working_solution: Real, effective, low-cost glucose-lowering option, particularly valuable where cost limits access to newer classes (as in much real-world Indian/global practice) - ADVANCE shows a genuine renal-protective benefit with gliclazide specifically, but the real, honest trade-off is a materially higher hypoglycaemia risk than metformin/SGLT2i/DPP-4i, requiring patient education and cautious dosing, especially in the elderly.

diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.name: Pioglitazone (Thiazolidinedione)
diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.type: T2DM pharmacotherapy - real macrovascular signal, real side-effect caveats
diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.effectiveness: PROactive trial (n=5238, established macrovascular disease): non-significant 10% RRR in the primary composite endpoint, but a significant 16% RRR in the main secondary endpoint of all-cause death/MI/stroke (mean follow-up 34.5 months); real safety signals included an imbalance in fracture risk (especially in women) and an initial imbalance in bladder-cancer cases (14 vs 5) that did not persist in longer-term follow-up.
diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.reason_why: Activates PPAR-gamma nuclear receptors, improving peripheral insulin sensitivity in adipose tissue and muscle - a genuinely insulin-sensitizing mechanism distinct from insulin secretagogues, but PPAR-gamma activation also drives fluid retention/oedema, weight gain, and bone-remodelling changes that explain its real heart-failure and fracture-risk caveats.
diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.source: PROactive trial, Dormandy et al., Lancet 2005 (PMID 16214598); 6-year observational follow-up 2013 (PMID 23859428)
diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.confidence: high - large dedicated macrovascular outcome trial, honestly including its negative/mixed signals
diabetes_t2dm_thiazolidinediones.real_working_solution: Real, still-used insulin-sensitizing option, particularly useful in patients with significant insulin resistance/NAFLD, but the real, guideline-documented caveats (contraindicated in heart failure, increased fracture risk in women, monitor for bladder-cancer history) mean it is a second/third-line choice with active risk-benefit discussion, not a default first agent.

diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.name: Basal-Bolus Insulin Therapy - Rapid-Acting Analog Insulins (Prandial/Bolus Component)
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.type: T1DM disease-modifying therapy - the only option; rapid-acting bolus component
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.effectiveness: DCCT (n=1441, T1DM): intensive insulin therapy (multiple daily injections targeting near-normal glycaemia) reduced retinopathy onset/progression by 76% and 54% respectively, nephropathy by 34-56%, and neuropathy by 60% vs conventional therapy, establishing that near-physiologic prandial insulin replacement genuinely prevents microvascular complications.
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.reason_why: Rapid-acting insulin analogs (modified amino-acid sequence vs human insulin) dissociate from hexamers faster after subcutaneous injection, producing an onset/peak/duration profile that mimics physiologic post-meal insulin release far more closely than regular human insulin, reducing both post-prandial hyperglycaemia and delayed post-meal hypoglycaemia.
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.source: DCCT, DCCT Research Group, NEJM 1993 (PMID 8366922); DCCT/EDIC 30-year follow-up, Diabetes Care 2016 (PMID 26681715)
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.confidence: high - the foundational, practice-defining T1DM intensive-therapy trial
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.real_working_solution: Real, only disease-modifying option for T1DM: rapid-acting insulin analogs dosed at meals (carbohydrate-counted, correction-factor-adjusted) as the bolus component of basal-bolus therapy remain the real, guideline-standard prandial insulin-replacement strategy.

diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.name: Basal-Bolus Insulin Therapy - Long-Acting Analog Insulins (Basal Component)
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.type: T1DM disease-modifying therapy - the only option; long-acting basal component
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.effectiveness: The DCCT/EDIC legacy-effect finding directly supports basal-bolus intensive regimens: 6.5 years of intensive glycaemic control early in T1DM produced a real 30% reduction in cardiovascular events and death, persisting more than 20 years after the intensive-control period ended ("metabolic memory"), specifically attributable to the HbA1c difference achieved during DCCT via intensive basal-bolus therapy.
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.reason_why: Long-acting analogs form stable subcutaneous depots (via isoelectric-point precipitation for glargine, or albumin-binding for detemir/degludec) giving a flat, prolonged, near-peakless basal insulin profile that suppresses hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight, substantially reducing the nocturnal-hypoglycaemia risk seen with older NPH insulin.
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.source: DCCT/EDIC 20-year cardiovascular follow-up, Nathan et al., NEJM 2005/Diabetes Care 2016 update (PMID 26681715)
diabetes_t1dm_insulin_basal_bolus_therap.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-standard basal component of lifelong T1DM insulin therapy: once/twice-daily long-acting analog insulin, combined with rapid-acting bolus insulin, is the real working answer for T1DM glycaemic management, with the DCCT/EDIC legacy effect providing the real, hard-outcome justification for pursuing intensive control from diagnosis.

diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.name: Hybrid Closed-Loop / Automated Insulin Delivery ("Artificial Pancreas") Systems
diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.type: T1DM device therapy - real CGM-integrated automated insulin dosing
specific_drugs: Tandem t:slim X2 with Control-IQ technology
diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.effectiveness: iDCL/DCLP3 trial (Control-IQ, n=168, 6 months): time-in-range (glucose 70-180 mg/dL) increased from 61% at baseline to 71% with closed-loop control, while remaining unchanged at 59% in the sensor-augmented-pump control group; overnight time-in-range reached 76% vs 59% in controls, with less hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia and better HbA1c in the closed-loop group.
diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.reason_why: An algorithm on the pump reads real-time continuous glucose monitor data and automatically adjusts basal insulin delivery (and, in newer systems, auto-correction boluses) every few minutes, replacing fixed basal rates with a continuously glucose-responsive delivery pattern that better approximates physiologic beta-cell function than any fixed-dose regimen.
diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.source: Control-IQ pivotal trial (iDCL/DCLP3), Brown et al., NEJM 2019 (PMID 31618560)
diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.confidence: high - large randomized multicentre trial with a dedicated non-closed-loop control arm
diabetes_t1dm_automated_insulin_delivery.real_working_solution: Real, trial-proven, guideline-endorsed technology upgrade over standard pump/injection therapy: hybrid closed-loop automated insulin delivery genuinely increases time-in-range and reduces both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia, and should be offered to T1DM patients as the real current standard-of-care device option where accessible.

diabetes_glycemic_targets_monitoring.name: ADA-Recommended Individualized HbA1c Targets and Treatment-Intensification Strategy
diabetes_glycemic_targets_monitoring.type: Glycaemic-target strategy - real guideline-driven, real trial-justified
diabetes_glycemic_targets_monitoring.effectiveness: ADA Standards of Care: general target HbA1c <7% (53 mmol/mol) for most non-pregnant adults; a stricter <6.5% target is considered for younger, comorbidity-free patients if achievable without significant hypoglycaemia; a relaxed 7.5-8% target is recommended for patients with multiple comorbidities, limited life expectancy, or hypoglycaemia history. The DCCT/EDIC 'legacy effect'/metabolic-memory finding shows that early intensive control (achieving lower HbA1c for the first 6.5 years after T1DM diagnosis) produces a real 30% cardiovascular-event/death reduction persisting >20 years later, even after the glycaemic difference between groups disappeared - meaning delayed intensification does NOT recapture the same benefit.
diabetes_glycemic_targets_monitoring.reason_why: Chronic hyperglycaemia drives glycation-mediated vascular and neural injury (advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress) that appears to leave a persistent molecular 'memory' in tissues even after glucose is later normalized - explaining why early, sustained glycaemic control produces a legacy cardiovascular benefit that late-onset control cannot fully replicate.
diabetes_glycemic_targets_monitoring.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes - 2024/2025/2026; DCCT/EDIC 30-year follow-up, Diabetes Care 2016 (PMID 26681715)
diabetes_glycemic_targets_monitoring.real_working_solution: Real, actionable clinical implication: treatment should be intensified promptly at diagnosis in fit patients (not deferred), individualizing the numeric HbA1c target by age/comorbidity/hypoglycaemia-risk per ADA criteria - the real, hard-outcome-trial-justified principle that early control produces a durable legacy benefit that later intensification cannot fully recover.

diabetes_dka_management.name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) - IV Insulin, Fluid, and Electrolyte Replacement Protocol
diabetes_dka_management.type: Acute complication management - real, guideline-standardized emergency protocol
diabetes_dka_management.effectiveness: 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report on hyperglycaemic crises: diagnosis now requires (1) hyperglycaemia (glucose >=200 mg/dL or known diabetes), (2) ketosis (beta-hydroxybutyrate >=3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones 2+), and (3) metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L), replacing the older anion-gap-based criterion for greater accuracy; management is protocolized as isotonic fluid resuscitation, continuous IV (or, in mild-moderate uncomplicated cases, subcutaneous) insulin, and proactive potassium replacement before/alongside insulin to prevent insulin-induced hypokalaemia-related arrhythmia.
diabetes_dka_management.reason_why: Insulin deficiency drives unchecked lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis (producing the acidosis) plus severe osmotic diuresis (producing volume/electrolyte depletion) - correcting all three simultaneously (fluids first to restore perfusion, insulin to switch off ketogenesis, potassium replacement because insulin drives extracellular potassium back into cells) is why the protocol targets all three, not glucose-lowering alone.
diabetes_dka_management.source: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report, ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS, Diabetes Care 2024 (PMID 38907703)
diabetes_dka_management.real_working_solution: Real, standardized, life-saving protocol: isotonic-fluid-first resuscitation, continuous IV insulin infusion (or protocolized subcutaneous insulin for mild-moderate uncomplicated DKA outside intensive care), and scheduled potassium monitoring/replacement is the real working answer to DKA, now further refined by beta-hydroxybutyrate-based diagnosis and resolution criteria.

diabetes_hhs_management.name: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) - Fluid-Predominant Management Protocol
diabetes_hhs_management.type: Acute complication management - real, guideline-standardized, distinct from DKA
diabetes_hhs_management.effectiveness: Per the same 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report, HHS (severe hyperglycaemia, usually >600 mg/dL, with marked hyperosmolality and altered mental status, but WITHOUT significant ketoacidosis, distinguishing it from DKA) is managed with a fluid-predominant strategy - larger and more gradual isotonic fluid replacement than DKA (given the typically greater free-water deficit and older, more comorbid patient population), with insulin infusion added once volume resuscitation has begun and typically at lower relative doses, since profound hyperglycaemia alone (without significant acidosis) responds well to rehydration.
diabetes_hhs_management.reason_why: HHS occurs in patients with enough residual endogenous insulin to suppress ketogenesis but not enough to prevent severe hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis - so the dominant physiological problem is profound dehydration/hyperosmolality rather than acidosis, which is why fluid resuscitation (not insulin) is the primary and most urgent intervention, given more cautiously than in DKA because HHS patients are typically older with more cardiac/renal comorbidity.
diabetes_hhs_management.source: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report, ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS, Diabetes Care 2024 (PMID 38907703)
diabetes_hhs_management.real_working_solution: Real, distinct-from-DKA working protocol: gradual, carefully monitored isotonic fluid resuscitation as the primary intervention (given the typically older, comorbid HHS population), with insulin added cautiously after volume status is addressed, correctly recognizing HHS as a fluid/osmolality emergency rather than primarily an insulin-deficiency/acidosis emergency.

diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.name: Glucagon for Severe Hypoglycaemia (Including Newer Non-Injectable Formulations)
diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.type: Acute complication management - real rescue therapy for severe hypoglycaemia
diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.effectiveness: Two randomized crossover trials comparing 3 mg nasal glucagon (Baqsimi) to 1 mg injectable glucagon for insulin-induced hypoglycaemia found nasal glucagon non-inferior: treatment success (glucose rise to >=70 mg/dL or >=20 mg/dL from nadir within 30 minutes) was achieved in 100% (nasal) vs 100% (injectable) in Study 1, and 98.8% vs 100% in Study 2, with mean time to success of 11.6 vs 9.9 minutes respectively - a clinically trivial difference given nasal glucagon requires no reconstitution or injection technique from a rescuer.
diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.reason_why: Glucagon mobilizes hepatic glycogen stores to rapidly raise blood glucose regardless of route; the real practical breakthrough of the nasal formulation is that it removes the reconstitution/injection-technique failure points of the traditional emergency kit (which historically caused real-world administration failures by untrained bystanders/family members during a genuine emergency), improving real-world rescue success even though the pharmacologic mechanism is unchanged.
diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.source: FDA approval trials for Baqsimi, described in Clinical Review Report NCBI Bookshelf 2020 (based on two randomized crossover trials)
diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.confidence: high - randomized noninferiority trials underpinning FDA approval
diabetes_severe_hypoglycemia_glucagon.real_working_solution: Real, practical, guideline-endorsed rescue option: nasal glucagon (Baqsimi) or the ready-to-use dasiglucagon auto-injector should be prescribed alongside insulin therapy for any patient at risk of severe hypoglycaemia, given their real-world ease-of-use advantage over the older reconstitution-required injectable kit, translating into faster, more reliable bystander-administered rescue.

diabetes_nephropathy_management.name: ACE Inhibitors / ARBs for Diabetic Nephropathy
diabetes_nephropathy_management.type: Chronic complication management - real renoprotective drug class, real trial-proven in both T1DM and T2DM
diabetes_nephropathy_management.effectiveness: Captopril Collaborative Study Group trial (captopril, n=409, T1DM with nephropathy): slower doubling of serum creatinine (12.1% vs 21.3%, P=0.007, NNT 11), an effect independent of blood-pressure lowering alone. RENAAL (losartan, n=1513, T2DM with nephropathy): 28% risk reduction in end-stage renal disease (19.6% vs 25.5%, P=0.002). IDNT (irbesartan, n=1715, T2DM with nephropathy): 20% RRR vs placebo (P=0.02) and 23% RRR vs amlodipine (P=0.006) in the composite renal endpoint.
diabetes_nephropathy_management.reason_why: ACE inhibitors/ARBs preferentially dilate the glomerular efferent arteriole (by blocking angiotensin II), reducing intraglomerular hyperfiltration pressure that drives progressive nephron loss in diabetic kidney disease - a real, blood-pressure-independent renoprotective mechanism, which is why these trials showed benefit beyond what BP control alone (e.g. amlodipine, in IDNT) achieved.
diabetes_nephropathy_management.source: Captopril Collaborative Study Group, Lewis et al., NEJM 1993 (PMID 8413456); RENAAL, Brenner et al., NEJM 2001 (PMID 11565517); IDNT, Lewis et al., NEJM 2001
diabetes_nephropathy_management.confidence: high - three separate landmark randomized trials spanning both T1DM (captopril) and T2DM (losartan, irbesartan); cross-reference this KB's hypertension entry for the same drug class's blood-pressure-outcome data
diabetes_nephropathy_management.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-standard, disease-modifying therapy: ACEi (T1DM evidence base) or ARB (T2DM evidence base) should be started in any diabetic patient with albuminuria/nephropathy regardless of blood pressure level, given the real, BP-independent renoprotective effect demonstrated across three separate landmark trials.

diabetes_retinopathy_management.name: Panretinal Photocoagulation and Anti-VEGF Injections for Diabetic Retinopathy
diabetes_retinopathy_management.type: Chronic complication management - real, trial-compared procedural and pharmacologic options
diabetes_retinopathy_management.effectiveness: DRCR.net Protocol S (n=305 eyes with proliferative diabetic retinopathy): intravitreal ranibizumab was non-inferior, and over 2 years actually superior, to panretinal (laser) photocoagulation for visual-acuity outcomes, and produced significantly lower rates of vision-impairing diabetic macular oedema; ranibizumab-treated eyes also had less peripheral visual-field loss than laser-treated eyes.
diabetes_retinopathy_management.reason_why: Panretinal laser photocoagulation destroys peripheral ischaemic retina to reduce the angiogenic (VEGF) drive for pathologic neovascularisation, at the cost of some peripheral visual field; anti-VEGF agents directly neutralize vascular endothelial growth factor, treating the underlying angiogenic stimulus without destroying retinal tissue, explaining their real visual-acuity and visual-field advantage - at the cost of requiring repeated intravitreal injections rather than a largely one-time procedure.
diabetes_retinopathy_management.source: DRCR.net Protocol S, Writing Committee, JAMA 2015 (PMID 25693010); 5-year outcomes, Gross et al., JAMA Ophthalmol 2018
diabetes_retinopathy_management.confidence: high - large randomized DRCR.net multicentre trial
diabetes_retinopathy_management.real_working_solution: Real, trial-proven current standard: anti-VEGF injection (ranibizumab or equivalent) is now a real, evidence-preferred first option over immediate panretinal photocoagulation for proliferative diabetic retinopathy where sustained follow-up for repeated injections is feasible, given its superior visual-acuity and visual-field preservation; laser photocoagulation remains a real, effective, durable option where injection follow-up adherence is a concern.

diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.name: Neuropathic Pain Agents for Painful Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy
diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.type: Chronic complication management - real, trial-proven symptomatic pain control
diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.effectiveness: Randomized comparative trials (e.g. the BLOSSOM phase IV trial and multiple head-to-head RCTs) show pregabalin and duloxetine produce clinically significant pain improvement in a large majority of patients (88.3% pregabalin vs 86.9% duloxetine achieving significant improvement at 12 weeks in BLOSSOM); meta-analyses show pregabalin/duloxetine reduce pain severity by 30-50% versus placebo, with duloxetine 60 mg/day showing efficacious relief of neuropathic pain in the original Goldstein et al. placebo-controlled trial.
diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.reason_why: Gabapentin/pregabalin bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in dorsal-horn neurons, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release and dampening central pain sensitization; duloxetine is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that enhances descending inhibitory pain pathways - two distinct, real, complementary mechanisms for peripheral-nerve-injury-driven neuropathic pain, which is why either class (or combination) is used depending on side-effect profile (sedation/oedema with pregabalin vs GI/orthostatic effects with duloxetine).
diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.source: Goldstein et al., duloxetine RCT, Pain 2005 (PMID 15733628); BLOSSOM phase IV trial 2023; meta-analysis of duloxetine vs pregabalin/gabapentin, PMC 2009
diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.confidence: high - multiple placebo-controlled RCTs and head-to-head comparative trials with consistent effect sizes
diabetes_neuropathy_pain_management.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-first-line symptomatic options for painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy: gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine each produce real, clinically meaningful pain reduction in the majority of patients and are interchangeable first choices, with selection individualized by comorbidity (duloxetine favoured with comorbid depression; pregabalin/gabapentin favoured when sedation at night is desirable).

diabetes_prevention_program.name: Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) - Lifestyle Intervention and Metformin for T2DM Primary Prevention
diabetes_prevention_program.type: Primary prevention - real, major trial in prediabetic populations
specific_drugs: Metformin (850 mg twice daily, prevention-dose regimen)
diabetes_prevention_program.effectiveness: DPP trial (n=3234 adults with prediabetes, mean 2.8 years): intensive lifestyle intervention (goal >=7% weight loss plus >=150 min/week physical activity) reduced T2DM incidence by 58% vs placebo; metformin reduced incidence by 31% vs placebo (incidence rates: 11.0, 7.8, and 4.8 cases per 100 person-years in placebo, metformin, and lifestyle groups respectively). The DPP Outcomes Study (21-year follow-up) showed the median time without developing diabetes was extended by 3.5 years (lifestyle) and 2.5 years (metformin) vs placebo, i.e. a durable, not merely transient, effect.
diabetes_prevention_program.reason_why: Both interventions target the same root pathophysiology (insulin resistance driven by excess adiposity) before beta-cell failure becomes irreversible - structured weight loss/exercise directly reduces adiposity-driven insulin resistance, while metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and modestly improves insulin sensitivity, explaining why lifestyle intervention (which addresses the root cause more completely) outperformed metformin by nearly 2-fold.
diabetes_prevention_program.source: Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group, NEJM 2002 (PMID 11832527); 21-year outcomes, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025
diabetes_prevention_program.confidence: high - one of the largest, most influential primary-prevention trials in all of internal medicine, still cited in every major diabetes guideline
diabetes_prevention_program.real_working_solution: Real, major, guideline-foundational primary-prevention answer: for adults with prediabetes, structured intensive lifestyle intervention should be offered as first-line prevention (58% RRR, durable over 21 years), with metformin as a real, effective alternative/adjunct (31% RRR) particularly for those unable to sustain lifestyle change or at higher risk (younger, more obese, history of gestational diabetes).

diabetes_medical_devices_equipment.name: Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGM), Glucometers, and Insulin Delivery Devices
diabetes_medical_devices_equipment.type: Medical equipment/devices - real, trial-proven glycaemic monitoring and delivery technology
diabetes_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: DIAMOND trial (n=158 T1DM patients on multiple daily injections, baseline HbA1c 7.5-9.9%, 24 weeks): CGM (Dexcom G4 Platinum) produced significantly better glycaemic control than self-monitored blood glucose 4x/day, reducing both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia exposure - the first trial to show CGM benefit specifically in patients using injections rather than a pump, expanding the real evidence base for CGM beyond pump users.
diabetes_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: CGM measures interstitial glucose continuously (every few minutes) via a subcutaneous sensor, revealing real-time trends and rate-of-change information that intermittent capillary fingerstick testing cannot show, allowing patients and automated systems (see automated insulin delivery above) to react to and prevent excursions rather than only detect them after the fact.
diabetes_medical_devices_equipment.source: DIAMOND trial, Beck et al., JAMA 2017 (PMID 28118453)
diabetes_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Real, trial-proven technology: CGM improves glycaemic control even in patients on standard multiple-daily-injection therapy (not only pump users), and is now guideline-recommended for essentially all T1DM patients and insulin-treated T2DM patients where accessible, alongside standard glucometers for backup/calibration and insulin pens for reliable, accurate, more comfortable insulin delivery than vial-and-syringe.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials/meta-analyses measuring DIFFERENT endpoints in DIFFERENT populations - T2DM remission/prevention rates vs pharmacotherapy hard-outcome relative risk reductions vs transplant insulin-independence rates - so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. T2DM remission pathways (bariatric surgery, DiRECT) and the Diabetes Prevention Program's incidence-reduction data are ranked prominently given their genuine disease-modifying/preventive impact, distinct from lifelong add-on pharmacotherapy for established disease.

ranked_high_to_low.name: DiRECT - T2DM remission at 12 months (intensive lifestyle/very-low-calorie diet)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Diabetes remission rate (HbA1c <6.5% off all medication) at 12 months
ranked_high_to_low.source: DiRECT trial, Lancet 2018

ranked_high_to_low.name: Islet cell transplantation - insulin independence (select severe T1DM)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Insulin independence achieved (islet-alone/islet-after-kidney recipients)
ranked_high_to_low.source: CIT-08 study, Diabetes Care 2022

ranked_high_to_low.name: Diabetes Prevention Program - intensive lifestyle intervention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: T2DM incidence relative risk reduction vs placebo
ranked_high_to_low.source: Diabetes Prevention Program, NEJM 2002

thyroid_disorders.name: Thyroid Disorders (Hypothyroidism including Hashimoto's Thyroiditis - primary and secondary/central forms; Hyperthyroidism including Graves' Disease, Toxic Multinodular Goiter, Toxic Adenoma, Subacute/Silent/Postpartum Thyroiditis as linked entities)
thyroid_disorders.icd11_hint: 5A00 Hypothyroidism; 5A02 Thyrotoxicosis (covers Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma - ICD-11 does not appear to carry a dedicated Graves'-specific subcode distinct from 5A02 Thyrotoxicosis in the sources checked); 5A03 Thyroiditis (covers subacute/de Quervain, silent, and postpartum thyroiditis); 5A01 Nontoxic goitre
thyroid_disorders.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct endocrine EMERGENCIES must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now): (1) Myxedema Coma - the decompensated end-stage of severe untreated/undertreated hypothyroidism. Real precipitating factors identified in 77.6% of cases, most commonly infection, followed by cold exposure, and also including sedative/narcotic drugs, trauma, burns, stroke, and non-adherence to thyroid replacement. Real mortality is high and inconsistently reported across studies - a systematic review covering 2004-2024 (698 patients) found an overall mortality of 38.8%, a Japanese national inpatient database found 29.5%, and older/smaller series report ranges from 20-25% up to 50-60% without prompt treatment; cardiac complications, low Glasgow Coma Scale, and advanced age are independent mortality predictors. (2) Thyroid Storm - the decompensated end-stage of severe untreated/undertreated hyperthyroidism, real diagnostic framework is the Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS, 1993): points are summed across thermoregulatory dysfunction (temperature, 0 to +30), CNS effects (absent 0, mild/agitation +10, moderate delirium-psychosis-extreme lethargy +20, severe seizures-coma +30), GI-hepatic dysfunction (absent 0, moderate diarrhoea/nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain +10, severe unexplained jaundice +20), heart rate (0 to +25 as rate rises), congestive heart failure (absent 0, mild pedal oedema +5, moderate bibasilar rales +10, severe pulmonary oedema +15), atrial fibrillation (absent 0, present +10), and precipitating event (absent 0, present +10); a total score >=45 is highly suggestive of thyroid storm requiring ICU admission, 25-44 indicates impending storm warranting close monitoring, and <25 makes storm unlikely. Real precipitating factors include infection, thyroidal/nonthyroidal surgery, certain medications (anaesthetics, pseudoephedrine, amiodarone), iodinated contrast exposure, diabetic ketoacidosis, exogenous thyroid hormone overdose, stroke, myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism. Real mortality is estimated at 8-25% despite modern ICU-level treatment. Both conditions are real acute killers and must never be queued through routine doctor-approval workflow.

hashimotos_thyroiditis.mechanism: Real chronic autoimmune thyroiditis - lymphocytic infiltration plus T-cell-driven cytotoxicity and autoantibodies directed against thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) causing progressive glandular inflammation, fibrosis, and loss of functioning thyroid tissue. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg positivity, together with elevated TSH and low free T4, delineates Hashimoto's as the cause.
hashimotos_thyroiditis.proportion: Real, leading cause of hypothyroidism specifically in iodine-sufficient regions (e.g. USA, most of Europe, and post-iodization India), where iodine deficiency has been largely corrected.
hashimotos_thyroiditis.source: StatPearls 'Hashimoto Thyroiditis' NBK459262; PMC12907336 'Hashimoto's thyroiditis: from pathogenesis to clinical management'; Endocrine Society 'Hashimoto Disease' patient library
hashimotos_thyroiditis.confidence: high - consistently and independently stated across StatPearls, PubMed-indexed reviews, and the Endocrine Society

iodine_deficiency.mechanism: Insufficient dietary iodine impairs thyroid hormone synthesis (iodine is an obligate substrate for T4/T3 production), leading to compensatory TSH rise, goiter formation, and eventually overt hypothyroidism if deficiency is severe/prolonged.
iodine_deficiency.proportion: Real, LEADING cause of hypothyroidism GLOBALLY (as distinct from iodine-sufficient regions, where autoimmune disease predominates). Iodine-deficiency-related hypothyroidism is estimated to affect approximately 2.2 billion people worldwide who live in iodine-deficient areas, with iodine deficiency disorders overall affecting over 200 million people and being the most common preventable cause of brain damage/mental retardation worldwide; 1.5 billion people are estimated to be at risk.
iodine_deficiency.india_context: Real, historically severe relevance to India - India ran the National Goitre Control Programme from 1962 (renamed the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme, NIDDCP, in 1992). Pre-programme goiter prevalence surveys found a range as wide as 1.5-44.5% across different districts; of 414 districts surveyed across all 29 states and 7 union territories, 337 were found endemic (IDD prevalence >5%), and an ICMR national survey found no Indian state entirely free of iodine deficiency risk. The programme is considered a genuine public-health success, with an estimated 92% of the population now consuming iodised salt, though full universal coverage has not yet been reached.
iodine_deficiency.source: WHO 'Iodine deficiency' NLiS data brief; Archives of Medical Science 'The burden of iodine deficiency'; Indian Journal of Medical Research (PMC6366256) 'National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme: Current status & future strategy'; PMC3818611 'Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD) control in India'
iodine_deficiency.confidence: high for the global leading-cause statement and the India programme history; moderate for the precise 92%-coverage figure since it is a programme self-reported adequacy estimate rather than an independent audit

secondary_central_hypothyroidism.mechanism: Real, distinct entity where the thyroid gland itself is structurally normal but hypothyroidism results from inadequate TSH drive due to pituitary (secondary) or hypothalamic TRH (tertiary) dysfunction - most commonly pituitary macroadenoma (mass effect or post-surgical/post-radiation hypopituitarism), but also Sheehan's syndrome, traumatic brain injury, or infiltrative/granulomatous pituitary disease. Usually occurs as part of combined (multihormonal) hypopituitarism rather than isolated TSH deficiency.
secondary_central_hypothyroidism.proportion: Real, genuinely rare compared to primary hypothyroidism - estimated prevalence in the general population ranges from about 1 in 16,000 to 1 in 100,000 (some estimates 1 in 20,000-80,000), and it accounts for roughly 1 in 1000 (about 0.1%) of all hypothyroidism cases. Approximately 50% of acquired central hypothyroidism cases are attributable specifically to pituitary macroadenomas.
secondary_central_hypothyroidism.diagnostic_distinction: Real, key diagnostic distinguishing feature from primary hypothyroidism: TSH is LOW or INAPPROPRIATELY NORMAL (not elevated) despite a low free T4, because the defect lies upstream of the thyroid gland itself - see diagnostic_framework below.
secondary_central_hypothyroidism.source: StatPearls 'Hypothyroidism' NBK519536; ScienceDirect 'Central Hypothyroidism: Advances in Etiology, Diagnostic Challenges, Therapeutic Targets, and Associated Risks'; Endocrine Connections 2019 'The diagnosis and management of central hypothyroidism in 2018'
secondary_central_hypothyroidism.confidence: high for the mechanism and diagnostic-distinction points; moderate for the exact prevalence figures since central hypothyroidism is rare enough that estimates vary across the cited sources
