who_standard_global.cutoffs: Underweight <18.5 kg/m^2; Normal range 18.5-24.9 kg/m^2; Overweight (pre-obese) 25.0-29.9 kg/m^2; Obese Class I 30.0-34.9 kg/m^2; Obese Class II 35.0-39.9 kg/m^2; Obese Class III (severe/morbid obesity) >=40.0 kg/m^2.
who_standard_global.source: WHO Obesity and overweight fact sheet; WHO BMI classification (standard adult cutoffs used worldwide for non-Asian-specific populations)

who_asia_pacific_cutoffs.cutoffs: Real, distinct, LOWER Asia-Pacific BMI classification adopted by WHO Western Pacific Regional Office / International Obesity Task Force (2000) for Asian populations: Underweight <18.5 kg/m^2; Normal 18.5-22.9 kg/m^2; Overweight (at risk) 23.0-24.9 kg/m^2; Obese Class I 25.0-29.9 kg/m^2; Obese Class II >=30.0 kg/m^2.
who_asia_pacific_cutoffs.rationale: Real, well-documented finding that at any given BMI, people of Asian descent carry a higher percentage body fat and visceral adiposity than Caucasians, and develop type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk at a substantially lower BMI than the standard WHO cutoffs - this directly parallels the 'thin-fat Indian phenotype' already documented in this KB's diabetes_mellitus entry.
who_asia_pacific_cutoffs.source: WHO Western Pacific Region / IASO/IOTF, 'The Asia-Pacific Perspective: Redefining Obesity and its Treatment' (2000); Lancet 2004;363(9403):157 'Appropriate body-mass index for Asian populations and its implications for policy and intervention strategies' (WHO Expert Consultation)

classification_bmi.clinical_note: Cross-reference: this real, lower Asian BMI cutoff is the same underlying ethnicity-specific principle already established in this KB's diabetes_mellitus entry ('Asian Indian phenotype' / 'thin-fat Indian' - normal or low overall BMI/lean mass but disproportionate truncal/visceral adiposity and insulin resistance). A person may be classified as metabolically obese despite a BMI that would read as 'normal' or merely 'overweight' on the standard WHO scale.

western_ncep_atp_iii.cutoffs: Men >102 cm (40 inches); Women >88 cm (35 inches).

india_asian_specific.cutoffs: Real, India-specific lower thresholds per the Misra et al. Consensus Statement for Asian Indians: abdominal obesity (Action Level 2, used as the metabolic-syndrome waist criterion) at waist circumference >=90 cm in men and >=80 cm in women; a lower Action Level 1 (>=78 cm men, >=72 cm women) is defined as an early warning threshold for moderate risk warranting lifestyle counselling. These are also the IDF's designated South Asian ethnic-specific waist cutoffs (90 cm men / 80 cm women), lower than the IDF's Europid cutoffs (94 cm men / 80 cm women).
india_asian_specific.source: Misra A, Chowbey P, Makkar BM, et al. 'Consensus Statement for Diagnosis of Obesity, Abdominal Obesity and the Metabolic Syndrome for Asian Indians...' J Assoc Physicians India 2009;57:163 (PMID 19582986); IDF Worldwide Definition of the Metabolic Syndrome (2006 consensus, Alberti et al., Diabetic Medicine 2006;23(5):469)
india_asian_specific.note: Some individual Indian regional studies have proposed slightly different optimal cutoffs (e.g. one study derived 90 cm men / 85 cm female as most sensitive/specific in its cohort), but the Misra consensus 90/80 figure is the one in standing national and IDF ethnic-specific use for diagnostic criteria purposes.

ncep_atp_iii_revised.rule: Diagnosis requires any 3 of the following 5 criteria.
components: Waist circumference: Men >102 cm (40 in), Women >88 cm (35 in) [Western cutoffs; see india_asian_specific above for the modified Asian/Indian threshold commonly substituted in South Asian populations]
Triglycerides >=150 mg/dL (or on drug treatment for elevated triglycerides)
HDL cholesterol: Men <40 mg/dL, Women <50 mg/dL (or on drug treatment for reduced HDL)
Blood pressure >=130/85 mmHg (or on antihypertensive drug treatment with a history of hypertension)

Fasting glucose >=100 mg/dL (or on drug treatment for elevated glucose) - this glucose threshold was lowered from the original ATP III (2001) figure of >=110 mg/dL by the 2004 AHA/NHLBI scientific statement update, to align with the ADA's revised impaired-fasting-glucose cutoff.
ncep_atp_iii_revised.source: NCEP ATP III (2001), Circulation 2002;106:3143; Grundy SM et al. 'Diagnosis and Management of the Metabolic Syndrome: AHA/NHLBI Scientific Statement' Circulation 2005;112(17):2735

idf_2005_consensus.rule: Central obesity (mandatory, by ethnicity-specific waist circumference) PLUS any 2 of the remaining 4 components.
idf_2005_consensus.mandatory_component: Central obesity by ethnicity/region-specific waist circumference cutoff (e.g. South Asian: Men >=90 cm, Women >=80 cm; Europid: Men >=94 cm, Women >=80 cm).
additional_components_any_2_of_4: Triglycerides >=150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) or specific treatment
HDL cholesterol <40 mg/dL (1.03 mmol/L) in men, <50 mg/dL (1.29 mmol/L) in women, or specific treatment
Blood pressure: systolic >=130 or diastolic >=85 mmHg, or treatment of previously diagnosed hypertension
Fasting plasma glucose >=100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes
idf_2005_consensus.source: Alberti KGMM, Zimmet P, Shaw J. 'Metabolic syndrome - a new world-wide definition. A Consensus Statement from the International Diabetes Federation' Diabetic Medicine 2006;23(5):469 (PMID 16681555)

metabolic_syndrome_diagnostic_criteria.key_practical_difference: NCEP ATP III treats all 5 components as equally weighted (any 3 of 5, waist circumference optional). IDF makes central/abdominal obesity an obligatory gatekeeper criterion (reflecting visceral adiposity as the pathophysiologic core, see pathophysiology below) plus any 2 of the remaining 4. Applying Asian/Indian ethnic-specific waist cutoffs (90/80 cm) instead of Western cutoffs (102/88 cm) within either framework substantially raises the number of Indians who meet the abdominal-obesity/metabolic-syndrome threshold at a lower absolute waist size - a real, clinically important source of under-diagnosis if Western cutoffs are mistakenly applied in Indian patients.

visceral_central_adiposity.mechanism: Real, well-established distinction: visceral/intra-abdominal (central) fat is metabolically far more dangerous than subcutaneous (peripheral/gluteofemoral) fat. Visceral adipocytes are more lipolytically active, drain directly via the portal circulation delivering free fatty acids straight to the liver, and are the principal source of the pro-inflammatory adipokine secretion described below - explaining why waist circumference (a proxy for visceral fat) is a stronger predictor of cardiometabolic risk than BMI alone at a population level.
visceral_central_adiposity.source: PMC11416200 'A Comprehensive Review of Metabolic Syndrome and Its Role in Cardiovascular Disease and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Mechanisms, Risk Factors, and Management'

adipokine_dysregulation.leptin_resistance: Real phenomenon in obesity: despite markedly elevated circulating leptin levels (leptin is secreted in proportion to fat mass), the hypothalamic satiety response to leptin becomes blunted (central leptin resistance), so appetite suppression fails despite high leptin - a key driver of the positive energy balance that sustains obesity. This is mechanistically distinct from the rare monogenic congenital leptin DEFICIENCY described under etiology below.
adipokine_dysregulation.adiponectin_reduction: Real, paradoxical inverse relationship: adiponectin (an insulin-sensitising, anti-inflammatory, anti-atherogenic adipokine) is REDUCED in obesity as adipose tissue expands, unlike most other adipokines. Lower adiponectin correlates with worse insulin resistance and higher cardiovascular risk.

chronic_low_grade_inflammation.mechanism: Real mechanism: hypertrophied, hypoxic visceral adipocytes and infiltrating macrophages within adipose tissue secrete increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6, CRP), producing a state of chronic low-grade systemic inflammation. This inflammatory milieu directly interferes with insulin-receptor signalling (via serine phosphorylation of IRS-1, among other pathways), linking obesity-associated inflammation mechanistically to insulin resistance and atherogenesis.
chronic_low_grade_inflammation.source: PMC11416200; Hotamisligil GS, 'Inflammation and metabolic disorders' Nature 2006;444:860 (foundational review, cited across current literature)

insulin_resistance_central_link.mechanism: Real, central unifying mechanistic link of the metabolic syndrome: excess free fatty acid flux from visceral fat, adipokine dysregulation, and chronic inflammation together impair insulin signalling in skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue. The resulting compensatory hyperinsulinemia (before beta-cell decompensation to overt T2DM) itself worsens hypertension (via renal sodium retention and sympathetic activation), dyslipidemia (via increased hepatic VLDL/triglyceride synthesis and reduced HDL), and directly promotes further visceral fat deposition - a self-reinforcing cycle. This is why insulin resistance, rather than any single one of the 5 diagnostic components, is considered the pathophysiologic core of metabolic syndrome.

etiological_classification.primary_lifestyle_driven: The overwhelming majority of obesity cases - a real, chronic positive energy balance from the interaction of dietary intake, physical inactivity, and an underlying polygenic genetic susceptibility (no single monogenic cause).

congenital_leptin_deficiency.mechanism: Real, rare autosomal recessive LEP gene mutation causing congenital leptin deficiency - severe early-onset hyperphagia, intense food-seeking behaviour, and extreme obesity from infancy, predominantly reported in consanguineous families. Distinct from the leptin RESISTANCE seen in common obesity (see pathophysiology above).
congenital_leptin_deficiency.source: Springer 'Monogenic forms of childhood obesity due to mutations in the leptin gene' Mol Cell Pediatr 2014 (PMC4644131)

mc4r_mutations.mechanism: Real, the single COMMONEST identified monogenic cause of severe obesity - loss-of-function mutations in the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) gene, which is expressed in the hypothalamus and is a key downstream mediator of leptin/POMC-pathway satiety signalling. Pathogenic MC4R variants are found in up to 5.8% of individuals with severe childhood-onset obesity, though population-level prevalence of pathogenic variants is much lower (~0.3% in one UK birth cohort).
mc4r_mutations.source: NEJM 2003;348:1085 'Clinical Spectrum of Obesity and Mutations in the Melanocortin 4 Receptor Gene'

secondary_obesity.hypothyroidism: Cross-reference: covered in this KB's thyroid_disorders entry - hypothyroidism causes a real but generally modest weight gain (mostly fluid/myxedematous, with only a minor true fat-mass component), and is a real, clinically important cause to screen for and exclude in any new unexplained weight gain.
secondary_obesity.cushing_syndrome: Real secondary cause - endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoid excess produces a characteristic real central/truncal obesity pattern with relative sparing (or wasting) of the limbs, plus other classic Cushingoid stigmata (moon facies, buffalo hump, violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising) that should be distinguished from simple central adiposity.
secondary_obesity.medication_induced: Real, common and under-recognised cause - agents including certain antipsychotics (e.g. olanzapine, clozapine), some antidepressants, sulfonylureas and insulin, corticosteroids, and some antiepileptics/anticonvulsants are well-documented to cause clinically significant weight gain.
secondary_obesity.source: StatPearls NBK459333 'Obesity'; StatPearls Cushing Syndrome NBK470218

acanthosis_nigricans.finding: Real, highly prevalent and clinically useful marker of underlying insulin resistance - velvety, hyperpigmented, thickened plaques classically at the neck (nape), axillae, and groin/other skin flexures. In middle-aged adults it has been shown to be a highly prevalent AND specific clinical sign of insulin resistance across the full spectrum of glucose tolerance, and is a well-documented early marker for metabolic syndrome in pediatric/adolescent patients, often co-occurring with skin tags (acrochordons).
acanthosis_nigricans.source: PubMed 31769902 'Acanthosis nigricans in middle-age adults: A highly prevalent and specific clinical sign of insulin resistance'; StatPearls NBK431057 'Acanthosis Nigricans'

core_presentation.functional_limitations: Real, well-documented physical morbidity independent of specific comorbid diagnoses - reduced exercise tolerance and dyspnoea on exertion, joint pain and reduced mobility from mechanical loading (see osteoarthritis cross-reference below), gastroesophageal reflux, urinary incontinence (increased intra-abdominal pressure), and skin-fold intertrigo/fungal infections in skin creases.
core_presentation.psychosocial_impact: Real, well-documented and clinically significant - weight-based stigma and discrimination (including within healthcare settings), depression and anxiety at higher prevalence than the general population, reduced health-related quality of life, and body-image disturbance. This is a real contributor to both under-presentation for care and to the sedentary/dietary behaviour patterns that perpetuate obesity, not merely a downstream consequence of it.
core_presentation.confidence: moderate-high - directional findings well-replicated in the literature; exact prevalence figures for psychosocial comorbidity vary widely by population studied

associated_comorbidities_cross_reference: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - covered in full in this KB's diabetes_mellitus entry; insulin resistance from central adiposity is the shared core mechanism (see pathophysiology above).

Hypertension - covered in full in this KB's hypertension entry; obesity-related hypertension mechanistically involves insulin-resistance-driven renal sodium retention and sympathetic activation (see pathophysiology above).

Dyslipidemia - the characteristic obesity/metabolic-syndrome lipid pattern (raised triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL particles) is captured directly within the metabolic_syndrome_diagnostic_criteria above.
Obstructive Sleep Apnea - covered in full in this KB's obstructive_sleep_apnea entry; obesity (particularly central/neck adiposity) is its dominant risk factor.

Ischaemic Heart Disease / Coronary Artery Disease - covered in full in this KB's ischaemic_heart_disease entry; metabolic syndrome confers a real, meta-analytically confirmed increased risk of incident cardiovascular disease (RR ~1.53, 95% CI 1.26-1.87) and coronary heart disease specifically (RR ~1.52, 95% CI 1.37-1.69).

NAFLD/MASLD (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease, now re-termed Metabolic dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease) - real, extremely common hepatic manifestation of insulin resistance and central obesity; not a separate standalone entry in this KB at present, flagged here as a real, expected comorbidity to screen for (e.g. via liver enzymes/ultrasound) in any obese or metabolic-syndrome patient.

Certain cancers - real, epidemiologically established association between obesity and increased risk of several cancers (including endometrial, breast [postmenopausal], colorectal, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, renal, and pancreatic cancer), attributed to chronic hyperinsulinemia, elevated bioavailable sex steroids, and chronic inflammation.

Osteoarthritis - real, well-documented association via both direct mechanical joint-loading (particularly knee OA) and a systemic pro-inflammatory/metabolic contribution (adipokine-mediated cartilage effects), not purely a mechanical-load phenomenon.

real_risk_factors.note: Real, well-established modifiable risk factor for both weight gain and, independently, for metabolic syndrome development at any given weight.

Real, established risk factor - diets high in refined carbohydrates, added sugars (including sugar-sweetened beverages), and energy-dense/ultra-processed foods, with low fibre/whole-food content, are consistently associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome development.

Real, substantial polygenic heritability of BMI and fat distribution (twin and family studies estimate heritability in the range of ~40-70%), distinct from the rare monogenic syndromes listed under etiology above.

Real, well-documented association, though its direction varies by setting - in India's 'double burden' context (see epidemiology below), obesity is increasingly prevalent across both higher and lower socioeconomic strata and across urban and rural areas, unlike the classical high-income-country pattern of obesity concentrated in lower socioeconomic groups.

Real, independently documented risk factor - short sleep duration is associated with dysregulation of appetite-regulating hormones (increased ghrelin, decreased leptin signalling effect) and higher obesity/metabolic syndrome risk; conversely adequate sleep (6-8 hours) has been shown to be protective against weight regain after weight loss.

global.finding: Global obesity prevalence in adults rose from 6.4% in 1990 to 16.06% in 2022 (overweight rose from 17.5% to 28.0% over the same period), based on a pooled analysis of 3,663 population-representative studies covering 222 million children, adolescents and adults. Worldwide obesity prevalence has more than tripled since 1980, and by 2022 more than 1 billion people globally were living with obesity, with close to 3 billion living with either overweight or obesity.
global.source: NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), Lancet 2024 'Worldwide trends in underweight and obesity from 1990 to 2022: a pooled analysis of 3663 population-representative studies' (PMID 38432237); WHO Obesity and overweight fact sheet

india.finding: The ICMR-INDIAB national study (a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of 113,043 adults aged >=20 years across 31 Indian states/union territories, 2008-2020) found an overall weighted prevalence of generalised obesity of 28.6% and abdominal obesity of 39.5%. A more recent ICMR-INDIAB-23 analysis further reported a high prevalence of 'metabolic obesity' phenotypes, including a substantial proportion of 'Metabolically Obese Non-Obese' individuals (i.e. metabolically unhealthy despite a normal/non-obese BMI) - directly illustrating the Asian/Indian lower-BMI-threshold-for-risk principle described above.
india.double_burden_note: Real, well-documented and India-specific epidemiological phenomenon: India simultaneously carries a persistent burden of undernutrition/underweight in parts of its population alongside a rapidly rising obesity and metabolic syndrome burden - the so-called 'double burden of malnutrition' - making obesity screening relevant even in populations traditionally not considered at classical Western-style obesity risk.
india.source: Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2023, ICMR-INDIAB national cross-sectional study; PubMed 40844097 'High prevalence of metabolic obesity in India: The ICMR-INDIAB national study (ICMR-INDIAB-23)', Indian Journal of Medical Research

natural_history.metabolic_syndrome_progression: Real, meta-analytically confirmed progression risk: individuals with metabolic syndrome have an increased risk of all-cause mortality (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.17-1.56), incident cardiovascular disease (RR 1.53, 95% CI 1.26-1.87), coronary heart disease (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.37-1.69), and stroke (RR 1.76, 95% CI 1.37-2.25), in addition to a well-established substantially increased risk of progression to overt type 2 diabetes mellitus (insulin resistance being the shared core mechanism - see pathophysiology above).
natural_history.source_progression: Mottillo S et al. 'The Metabolic Syndrome and Cardiovascular Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' J Am Coll Cardiol 2010;56(14):1113 (PMID 20863953)
natural_history.weight_regain_natural_history: Real, well-documented and clinically important natural history finding: weight regain after unsustained/time-limited lifestyle intervention is the norm rather than the exception. In one real-world cohort, 52% of patients who lost weight on a structured diet intervention had regained weight by a mean follow-up of ~37 months; more broadly, five years after completing a structured lifestyle weight-loss programme, average maintained weight loss falls to only around 3.2% of initial body weight in typical cohorts, with most weight regain occurring within the first 36-48 weeks after the intervention ends. This underscores that obesity behaves as a chronic, relapsing condition requiring sustained (not time-limited) management rather than a one-time correctable event.
natural_history.source: European Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2026, 'Long-term weight maintenance after a low-carbohydrate diet: a real-world retrospective cohort study'; Cambridge Core, Proceedings of the Nutrition Society, 'Long-term weight status in regainers after weight loss by lifestyle intervention'
natural_history.confidence: high for the directional finding (regain is the norm); exact percentages vary materially by intervention type and cohort, so ranges are given rather than one false-precision figure

red_flags: Severe/morbid obesity (BMI >=40, or >=35 with comorbidity) with signs of respiratory compromise - daytime hypersomnolence, morning headache, and hypercapnia raise concern for Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS, historically 'Pickwickian syndrome') - a real, distinct entity from simple OSA, defined by daytime alveolar hypoventilation (awake PaCO2 >45 mmHg) in an obese patient without an alternative respiratory/neuromuscular/metabolic cause, though it very frequently coexists with OSA (cross-reference this KB's obstructive_sleep_apnea entry).

Rapid, unexplained weight gain over a short period - real red flag for an underlying secondary cause (Cushing syndrome, hypothyroidism, medication effect - see etiological_classification above) rather than simple lifestyle-driven obesity, and warrants targeted endocrine workup.

Signs of established end-organ complications at presentation - e.g. new acanthosis nigricans plus polyuria/polydipsia suggesting undiagnosed T2DM, resistant hypertension, or exertional dyspnoea/leg oedema suggesting evolving cardiovascular or right-heart complications - real triggers for urgent comprehensive metabolic and cardiovascular evaluation rather than routine lifestyle counselling alone.
Source: StatPearls NBK542216 'Obesity-Hypoventilation Syndrome'; StatPearls NBK470218 'Cushing Syndrome'; clinical synthesis consistent with the mechanisms and thresholds cited above.

obesity_metabolic_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Obesity/metabolic syndrome is a chronic, relapsing disease that is NOT durably reversed by lifestyle intervention alone in the majority of patients (weight regain is the norm once intensive lifestyle support is withdrawn - see Look AHEAD and DiRECT durability data below). However, it is one of the real few chronic metabolic diseases in this knowledge base with a genuine, reproducible near-cure pathway: bariatric/metabolic surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy) produces real, durable substantial weight loss (16-18% total body weight still maintained at 15-20 years, SOS study) and real substantial reductions in overall mortality (adjusted HR 0.71-0.76) and diabetes incidence (adjusted HR 0.17) in the real large majority of appropriate patients, and is the single most effective durable intervention available today. Separately, real newer GLP-1/dual-GIP-GLP-1-agonist pharmacotherapy (tirzepatide, semaglutide) has recently achieved real substantial mean weight loss (16-22.5% of body weight in pivotal trials) that for the first time approaches surgical results in some patients - a real genuinely transformative advance in obesity pharmacotherapy compared with older agents (5-10% typical). Honest caveat on pharmacotherapy: unlike surgery, its effect is NOT a cure but requires continued/lifelong dosing - the STEP 1 extension trial showed patients regained two-thirds of lost weight within one year of stopping semaglutide, so pharmacotherapy is a real, powerful, but ongoing chronic-disease-management tool, not a one-time fix like surgery can be.

curative_option.name: Bariatric/Metabolic Surgery (Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass & Sleeve Gastrectomy) - the Real Closest Thing to a Cure - and GLP-1/Dual-Agonist Pharmacotherapy for the Non-Surgical Majority
curative_option.note: Real, reproducible, randomized and prospective-controlled evidence shows bariatric/metabolic surgery is genuinely disease-modifying, not just symptom control: it produces durable substantial weight loss and real reductions in mortality, diabetes incidence, and cardiovascular events that persist for 15-20+ years in the large majority of appropriate patients. For the far larger population who are not candidates for or decline surgery, real newer GLP-1/dual-agonist pharmacotherapy is now the most effective non-surgical option, with efficacy approaching (though on average still below) surgical results, but requiring continued treatment to sustain effect (see exhaustive_medicine_survey and CURABILITY_NOTE).

reversible_subtypes.name: Bariatric/Metabolic Surgery-Induced Durable Weight Loss & Mortality Reduction (SOS Study)
reversible_subtypes.note: The Swedish Obese Subjects (SOS) study is the largest and longest prospective, matched-controlled (non-randomized, for ethical reasons) trial of bariatric surgery vs usual care, with up to 24 years of mortality follow-up. Surgery types in the cohort were gastric bypass (13%), banding (19%), and vertical banded gastroplasty (68%) - reflecting 1987-2001 practice; modern practice favours Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, which produce numerically greater weight loss than banding/VBG in later comparative studies.

real_recovery_data.weight_change_surgery_10yr: -17% total body weight (control group +1% at 10 years)
real_recovery_data.overall_mortality_adjusted_hr: 0.71 (about 29-30% relative risk reduction) vs usual care over median 24-year follow-up
real_recovery_data.diabetes_incidence_adjusted_hr: 0.17 (about 83% relative risk reduction) vs usual care
real_recovery_data.cohort: SOS study, n=4047 (2010 surgery, 2037 matched usual-care controls), inclusion BMI >=34 kg/m2 (men) or >=38 kg/m2 (women), age 37-60 years

reversible_subtypes.source: Sjostrom et al., NEJM 2007 (mortality, PMID 17715408); Sjostrom et al., NEJM 2012 (Life Expectancy after Bariatric Surgery in SOS, PMID 25007858); Sjostrom, J Intern Med 2013 review (PMID 23163728)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - largest, longest-follow-up controlled bariatric surgery outcomes study in existence
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, prospectively-controlled, two-decade-plus proof that bariatric/metabolic surgery produces durable substantial weight loss and real reductions in all-cause mortality, diabetes incidence, and myocardial infarction in the real large majority of appropriate obese patients - the single most disease-modifying intervention available for obesity today.

reversible_subtypes.name: Comparative Procedure Choice - Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass vs Sleeve Gastrectomy (Modern Practice)
reversible_subtypes.note: Modern bariatric practice has shifted toward Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG), which produce greater weight loss than the older banding/VBG procedures dominant in the original SOS cohort. Randomized trials (SM-BOSS, SLEEVEPASS) and pooled 5-year meta-analyses show RYGB yields modestly greater weight loss and better metabolic (T2DM/dyslipidaemia) resolution than LSG, at the cost of a technically more complex operation with more anatomical rearrangement.

real_recovery_data.metabolic_resolution: T2DM and dyslipidaemia resolution rates higher after RYGB than LSG in pooled comparative cohorts

reversible_subtypes.source: 5-year systematic review and meta-analysis, BMC Surgery 2024; SM-BOSS/SLEEVEPASS randomized trials
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - randomized trials plus large pooled meta-analysis
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, comparative-trial-based guidance: both RYGB and LSG are real effective options; RYGB is modestly more effective for weight loss and metabolic resolution, LSG is technically simpler with a different complication profile - procedure choice should be individualised, not a barrier to offering surgery.

reversible_subtypes.name: Real, Current Candidacy Criteria for Bariatric/Metabolic Surgery (ASMBS/IFSO 2022, incl. Asian-Population Threshold)
reversible_subtypes.note: The 2022 ASMBS/IFSO joint guideline (updating the 1991 NIH consensus criteria of BMI>=40, or >=35 with comorbidity) lowered and broadened eligibility, and explicitly adjusts thresholds downward for Asian populations because of their disproportionate cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI.

real_recovery_data.standard_bmi_ge_35: MBS recommended regardless of presence/absence/severity of comorbidities
real_recovery_data.standard_bmi_30_to_34_9_with_comorbidity: MBS should be considered with comorbid metabolic disease (T2DM, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, OSA, MASLD, CKD, PCOS, GERD)
real_recovery_data.asian_population_threshold: clinical obesity suggested at BMI >25 kg/m2; MBS should be offered at BMI >27.5 kg/m2 in Asian populations (evidence base drawn predominantly from Asian patients with concomitant T2DM)

reversible_subtypes.source: 2022 ASMBS/IFSO Indications for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery guideline, Surg Obes Relat Dis 2022 (PMID 36336720)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - current joint society guideline
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, current, guideline-based candidacy screen: use BMI>=35 (any comorbidity status) or BMI 30-34.9 with a qualifying metabolic comorbidity as the standard threshold, and apply the lower Asian-population threshold (BMI>=27.5, generally with a comorbidity) rather than under-referring lower-BMI Asian patients who carry equivalent cardiometabolic risk.

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.name: GLP-1/Dual-GIP-GLP-1-Agonist Pharmacotherapy (Tirzepatide, Semaglutide) for Patients Not Undergoing Surgery
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.note: For the much larger population who are ineligible, decline, or are awaiting bariatric surgery, real newer incretin-based pharmacotherapy is now the most effective chronic medical option, with tirzepatide showing the largest mean weight loss of any approved drug and, in a minority of patients, weight loss overlapping the lower range of surgical outcomes - see exhaustive_medicine_survey below for full trial data. This is real, durable disease CONTROL with continued treatment, not a cure: efficacy is contingent on ongoing dosing (STEP 1 extension trial - two-thirds of lost weight regained within 1 year of stopping semaglutide).
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.source: SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022, PMID 35658024); STEP 1 (NEJM 2021, PMID 33567185); STEP 1 extension (Diabetes Obes Metab 2022, PMID 35441470)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real surgical, endoscopic, pharmacological, lifestyle, behavioural, and device-based option used in obesity/metabolic syndrome, each ending in a stated real working solution per the standing rule. CURABILITY: bariatric/metabolic surgery is the real closest thing to a cure (see curative_option above); GLP-1/dual-agonist pharmacotherapy is real, powerful, but ongoing chronic management, not a cure. Every drug CLASS below carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific medicines. Metabolic syndrome component management (hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hyperglycaemia) is cross-referenced to the hypertension, ischaemic_heart_disease, and diabetes_mellitus entries rather than re-derived, per standing instruction.

obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.name: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
specific_drugs: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (surgical procedure, not a drug)
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.effectiveness: SOS study: -23% total body weight at 2 years, -16 to -18% sustained at 15-20 years (mixed cohort); modern comparative data: 26.0% total body weight loss and 67.1% excess BMI loss at 5 years, superior T2DM/dyslipidaemia resolution vs sleeve gastrectomy.
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.reason_why: Creates a small gastric pouch bypassing most of the stomach and proximal small bowel, combining marked restriction of intake with altered gut-hormone signalling (increased GLP-1/PYY, reduced ghrelin) that suppresses appetite and improves insulin sensitivity independent of weight loss alone.
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.source: SOS study, NEJM 2007/2012; 5-year RYGB vs LSG meta-analysis, BMC Surgery 2024
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.real_working_solution: Real, most metabolically effective standard bariatric procedure - produces the greatest durable weight loss and metabolic-comorbidity resolution of the two mainstream operations; the closest thing to a cure for obesity and its metabolic complications in appropriate candidates.

obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.name: Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy (LSG)
specific_drugs: Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy (surgical procedure, not a drug)
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.effectiveness: 22.5% total body weight loss and 58.8% excess BMI loss at 5 years (modestly less than RYGB); real, durable, guideline-endorsed as a standalone definitive procedure, not only a staging step.
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.reason_why: Removes approximately 80% of the stomach along the greater curvature, producing a tubular gastric remnant that markedly restricts intake volume and substantially reduces ghrelin-producing fundal tissue, reducing hunger.
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.source: 5-year RYGB vs LSG systematic review and meta-analysis, BMC Surgery 2024; SM-BOSS/SLEEVEPASS randomized trials
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.real_working_solution: Real, technically simpler, single-organ, non-rerouted alternative to RYGB with slightly lower but still substantial and durable weight loss and metabolic benefit - appropriate first-choice procedure for many patients, particularly where RYGB's malabsorptive complication profile (dumping syndrome, marginal ulcer, internal hernia) is a greater concern.

obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.name: Current Candidacy Criteria (ASMBS/IFSO 2022) Including Asian-Population BMI Threshold
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.type: Guideline-based patient-selection criterion, not a drug/procedure itself
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.effectiveness: Broadened 1991 NIH BMI>=40 (or >=35 with comorbidity) criteria to BMI>=35 regardless of comorbidity, BMI 30-34.9 with qualifying metabolic comorbidity, and a lower Asian-population threshold of BMI>=27.5 (obesity flagged from BMI>25) reflecting real elevated cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI in Asian patients.
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.reason_why: Visceral-adiposity-driven cardiometabolic risk (T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidaemia) occurs at lower absolute BMI in Asian populations than in Western populations for a given amount of visceral fat, so a uniform Western BMI cutoff systematically under-refers appropriate Asian candidates.
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.source: 2022 ASMBS/IFSO Indications for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery guideline, Surg Obes Relat Dis 2022 (PMID 36336720)
obesity_bariatric_metabolic_surgery.real_working_solution: Real, current, actionable eligibility screen for referring patients (including lower-BMI Asian patients who are frequently under-referred) to a bariatric surgical evaluation.

obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.name: Semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.effectiveness: STEP 1 trial: mean weight loss 14.9% (semaglutide) vs 2.4% (placebo) at 68 weeks; 86.4% of patients achieved >=5% weight loss vs 31.5% with placebo.
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.reason_why: GLP-1 receptor agonism slows gastric emptying and acts on hypothalamic appetite centres to reduce hunger and caloric intake, while also improving insulin secretion and peripheral insulin sensitivity.
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.source: STEP 1 trial, Wilding et al., NEJM 2021 (PMID 33567185)
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed, highly effective non-surgical option achieving weight loss roughly 3x that of older anti-obesity drugs - honest caveat: requires continued dosing, as two-thirds of lost weight is regained within a year of stopping (STEP 1 extension trial).

obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.name: Tirzepatide (Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonist)
specific_drugs: Tirzepatide (Zepbound, obesity-indicated formulation; Mounjaro, diabetes formulation)
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.effectiveness: SURMOUNT-1 trial: mean weight loss 16.0% (5 mg), 21.4% (10 mg), 22.5% (15 mg) vs 2.4% placebo at 72 weeks; 89-96% of patients achieved >=5% weight loss vs 28% placebo. Head-to-head SURMOUNT-5: tirzepatide produced 20.2% vs semaglutide's 13.7% weight loss at 72 weeks (superior on 5 key secondary endpoints).
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.reason_why: Combines GIP receptor agonism with GLP-1 receptor agonism, producing synergistic appetite suppression and improved insulin sensitivity beyond GLP-1 agonism alone, which explains its numerically superior weight loss over semaglutide in direct comparison.
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.source: SURMOUNT-1, Jastreboff et al., NEJM 2022 (PMID 35658024); SURMOUNT-5 head-to-head trial, NEJM 2025
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.confidence: high - large randomized placebo-controlled trial plus head-to-head RCT
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.real_working_solution: Real, genuinely transformative recent pharmacological advance - the highest mean weight loss of any approved anti-obesity drug, at the top dose (22.5%) approaching the lower range of surgical weight-loss outcomes for a meaningful subset of patients, while remaining a non-surgical, reversible option; requires continued treatment to sustain effect.

obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.name: Older/First-Generation GLP-1 Receptor Agonist (Liraglutide) - Comparative Context
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.effectiveness: Modest compared with semaglutide/tirzepatide - typically 5-8% weight loss in pivotal trials (SCALE program), superseded in efficacy by once-weekly semaglutide and tirzepatide but still a real, approved option where those agents are unavailable or not tolerated.
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.reason_why: Same GLP-1 receptor mechanism as semaglutide but shorter half-life (daily dosing) and lower receptor potency/dose, producing consistently smaller weight loss in head-to-head-adjacent trial programs.
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.source: SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial program
obesity_glp1_dual_agonist_pharmacotherap.real_working_solution: Real, earlier-generation but still guideline-approved option; superseded in average efficacy by semaglutide/tirzepatide but a real fallback where those are contraindicated, unavailable, or not tolerated.

obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.name: Orlistat
specific_drugs: Orlistat (Xenical, prescription 120 mg; Alli, OTC 60 mg)
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.effectiveness: Comparatively modest: about 44% of patients achieved >=5% weight loss at 1 year in comparative-efficacy analyses - the lowest of the standard older anti-obesity agents.
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.reason_why: Inhibits pancreatic and gastric lipases, blocking absorption of about 30% of ingested dietary fat, which is excreted unabsorbed - a mechanical, non-appetite-suppressing mechanism, which explains its comparatively modest efficacy and characteristic GI (steatorrhoea) side effects.
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.source: Kumar & Aronne, comparative efficacy review, Obesity 2015
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.real_working_solution: Real, oral, non-systemic, over-the-counter-available option with a distinct (non-appetite) mechanism - honestly modest efficacy compared with incretin-based therapy, best reserved for patients wanting a non-injectable option or as adjunct therapy, with GI tolerability being the main real-world limiting factor.

obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.name: Phentermine-Topiramate Extended-Release
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.effectiveness: Highest efficacy among the older oral agents: about 9.8% mean weight loss at the top dose in pivotal trials (EQUIP/CONQUER), with about 75% of patients achieving >=5% weight loss at 1 year.
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.reason_why: Phentermine (a sympathomimetic appetite suppressant acting via hypothalamic norepinephrine release) is combined with topiramate (an anticonvulsant with independent appetite-suppressing and satiety-enhancing central effects), giving additive efficacy beyond either agent alone.
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.source: EQUIP and CONQUER pivotal trials; Kumar & Aronne comparative efficacy review, Obesity 2015
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.real_working_solution: Real, most effective oral (non-injectable) anti-obesity drug combination prior to the GLP-1/dual-agonist era - a real working solution for patients wanting an oral option, with a teratogenicity contraindication (topiramate) requiring contraception counselling in women of childbearing potential.

obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.name: Naltrexone-Bupropion Sustained-Release
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.type: Opioid antagonist + dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor combination (oral)
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.effectiveness: Comparatively modest to moderate: about 6.1-6.5% mean weight loss vs about 1.2-1.9% placebo in the COR trial program at 28 and 56 weeks; about 55% of patients achieved >=5% weight loss at 1 year.
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.reason_why: Bupropion stimulates hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons to reduce appetite, while naltrexone blocks opioid-receptor-mediated auto-inhibition of those same POMC neurons, prolonging and potentiating the appetite-suppressing signal.
obesity_older_antiobesity_pharmacotherap.real_working_solution: Real, oral, non-teratogenic option with an additional real, independently useful effect on food-craving/reward behaviour, useful particularly in patients with a strong hedonic/craving-driven eating pattern - honestly more modest average weight loss than phentermine-topiramate or incretin-based agents.

obesity_lifestyle_intervention.name: Intensive Lifestyle Intervention / Structured Very-Low-Calorie-Diet Programs (DiRECT Trial Cross-Reference)
specific_drugs: Not applicable - structured diet/behavioural program (e.g., Counterweight-Plus total-diet-replacement protocol used in DiRECT)
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.effectiveness: DiRECT trial (see diabetes_mellitus entry for full data): 46% T2DM remission at 12 months and continued remission in 36% at 2 years, strongly tied to amount of weight lost (>=15 kg associated with the highest remission rates) - real evidence that structured, primary-care-delivered intensive lifestyle intervention is a genuine, practice-relevant remission pathway in early-duration T2DM/obesity, though weight regain over time is a real honest limitation.
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.reason_why: A structured, clinically-supervised very-low-calorie total-diet-replacement phase followed by staged food reintroduction and long-term weight-maintenance support produces large enough sustained caloric deficit and weight loss to reverse hepatic and pancreatic fat accumulation, the mechanistic driver of the Twin Cycle Hypothesis of T2DM.
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.source: DiRECT trial, Lean et al., Lancet 2018 (cross-referenced in full in the diabetes_mellitus entry)
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.real_working_solution: Real, foundational, guideline-recommended first step for all patients with obesity/metabolic syndrome regardless of whether surgery or pharmacotherapy is later added - structured, supervised programs (not unstructured advice) are what produced DiRECT's real remission results, and lifestyle intervention remains a required foundation underneath pharmacotherapy and surgery alike, not a stand-alone substitute for them once significant obesity/comorbidity is present.

obesity_lifestyle_intervention.name: Look AHEAD Trial - Long-Term Intensive Lifestyle Intervention (Honest Cardiovascular-Neutral Finding)
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.type: Long-term intensive lifestyle intervention, large randomized outcome trial
specific_drugs: Not applicable - structured diet + physical activity behavioural intervention
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.effectiveness: Real, honest, sobering finding: despite significant, sustained weight loss and improved cardiovascular risk factors (glycaemic control, lipids, blood pressure) over a median ~10 years in 5,145 overweight/obese T2DM patients, intensive lifestyle intervention did NOT reduce the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, hospitalization for angina): hazard ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.83-1.09, P=0.51) - the trial was stopped early for futility on this endpoint.
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.reason_why: The intervention achieved real weight loss and metabolic improvement, but the trial's null cardiovascular result illustrates that surrogate risk-factor improvement does not automatically guarantee a hard cardiovascular outcome benefit at the population level - possibly reflecting good background cardiovascular care in both arms diluting a detectable difference, and/or that lifestyle-intervention-scale weight loss (a few kg net difference over time given real-world regain) was insufficient to modify hard events the way bariatric surgery's larger, more durable weight loss does.
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.confidence: high - large multicentre randomized controlled trial, stopped for futility on pre-specified analysis
obesity_lifestyle_intervention.real_working_solution: Real, honestly-reported non-cardiovascular benefits remain genuine and clinically meaningful (less sleep apnea, less depression, improved mobility, fewer diabetes medications needed, improved quality of life, lower long-term costs) - lifestyle intervention should be recommended for those real benefits and as the necessary foundation for other therapies, but clinicians and patients should not be told to expect it alone to reduce hard cardiovascular events the way bariatric surgery (SOS) or intensive risk-factor pharmacotherapy does.

obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.name: Hypertension Component - Cross-Referenced to hypertension Entry
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.type: Metabolic syndrome component management - blood pressure
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.effectiveness: See hypertension entry's first_line_drug_classes for full real outcome-trial data on these specific agents - not re-derived here per standing cross-reference instruction. SOS data above additionally shows bariatric surgery itself lowers blood pressure and increases diuresis as a direct mechanical/metabolic effect of weight loss.
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.reason_why: Weight loss (surgical, pharmacological, or lifestyle) reduces sympathetic nervous system activation and RAAS activity that obesity itself drives, so blood pressure improvement is a real, partially weight-loss-mediated effect layered on top of first-line antihypertensive drug therapy.
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.source: hypertension entry (cross-referenced); SOS study blood-pressure sub-analysis (PMC3510228)
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.real_working_solution: Real working solution: treat hypertension per the hypertension entry's guideline-based first-line agents, while recognising that real, meaningful weight loss from any of the interventions above provides additional, partially independent blood-pressure benefit.

obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.name: Dyslipidaemia Component - Cross-Referenced to ischaemic_heart_disease Entry (Statins)
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.effectiveness: See ischaemic_heart_disease entry's statin medicines for full real outcome-trial data (TNT, JUPITER) - not re-derived here per standing cross-reference instruction.
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.reason_why: Obesity-associated dyslipidaemia (elevated triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL particles) is addressed primarily by high-intensity statin therapy per standard cardiovascular risk guidelines, independent of the weight-loss intervention chosen.
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.real_working_solution: Real working solution: apply the same high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin or rosuvastatin) used in the ischaemic_heart_disease entry to metabolic-syndrome-associated dyslipidaemia, per standard cardiovascular risk-based statin-initiation guidelines.

obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.name: Hyperglycaemia Component - Cross-Referenced to diabetes_mellitus Entry (Metformin's Particular Relevance)
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.effectiveness: See diabetes_mellitus entry's diabetes_t2dm_first_line_pharmacotherapy for full real UKPDS 34 mortality-benefit data - not re-derived here. Metformin carries particular relevance in metabolic syndrome because it is weight-neutral-to-modestly-weight-reducing (unlike sulfonylureas/insulin, which tend to cause weight gain), making it a rational glycaemic first-line choice specifically in patients whose glycaemic abnormality arises from obesity-driven insulin resistance.
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.reason_why: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity via AMPK activation, directly targeting the insulin-resistance pathophysiology that links obesity to hyperglycaemia in metabolic syndrome, without the weight-gain side effect of insulin secretagogues.
obesity_metabolic_syndrome_component_man.real_working_solution: Real working solution: use metformin as in the diabetes_mellitus entry for the glycaemic component of metabolic syndrome, favouring it specifically over weight-gain-prone glucose-lowering agents in this obesity-driven population; GLP-1/dual-agonist therapy above provides simultaneous weight loss AND glycaemic benefit where indicated.

obesity_behavioral_psychological_support.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for Obesity - Adjunctive Role
specific_drugs: Not applicable - structured psychotherapy (individual or group CBT-OB protocol)
obesity_behavioral_psychological_support.effectiveness: Meta-analyses of randomized trials show a medium, statistically significant effect size for CBT on weight loss and weight-loss maintenance versus usual/minimal care; network meta-analysis found CBT was the most effective psychological/behavioural approach, ahead of standard behavioural therapy (BT), usual care, and minimal care, though the CBT-vs-BT difference itself was not large.
obesity_behavioral_psychological_support.reason_why: CBT-OB techniques (self-monitoring, goal-setting, stimulus control, behavioural substitution, cognitive restructuring of body-image and eating-related thoughts) address the cognitive and behavioural drivers of overeating and treatment non-adherence that purely biological therapies do not target, improving adherence to and durability of whichever primary weight-loss intervention (lifestyle, drug, or surgery) is chosen.
obesity_behavioral_psychological_support.source: CBT for lifestyle changes in obesity/T2DM systematic review and meta-analysis, Sci Rep 2023; CBT vs BT network meta-analysis, J Clin Psychol Med Settings 2024
obesity_behavioral_psychological_support.confidence: moderate-high - multiple meta-analyses of randomized trials
obesity_behavioral_psychological_support.real_working_solution: Real, evidence-based ADJUNCTIVE therapy (not a primary/stand-alone weight-loss treatment) - should be offered alongside lifestyle, pharmacological, or surgical therapy, particularly for patients with disordered-eating patterns, poor treatment adherence, or difficulty sustaining weight loss, and is a real component of comprehensive pre- and post-bariatric-surgery psychological care.

obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.name: Endoscopic Sleeve Gastroplasty (ESG)
specific_drugs: Endoscopic Sleeve Gastroplasty using an endoscopic suturing device (e.g., Apollo OverStitch)
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.effectiveness: MERIT trial (randomized, class 1-2 obesity): ESG plus lifestyle modification produced significantly greater weight loss than lifestyle modification alone; comparative cohort data show mean total body weight loss around 26.5-28.7 kg (roughly 15-18% TBWL) at 6-12 months, generally more durable than intragastric balloon.
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.reason_why: Endoscopic full-thickness sutures placed transorally reduce gastric volume and compliance in a manner mechanically analogous to (but less extensive than) surgical sleeve gastrectomy, without any incision, abdominal access, or organ removal.
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.source: MERIT trial, Lancet 2022; IGB vs ESG systematic review and meta-analysis, PMID 32399847
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.confidence: high - randomized controlled trial (MERIT) plus multiple comparative meta-analyses
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.real_working_solution: Real, incision-free, day-procedure option for class 1-2 obesity (BMI 30-40) not wanting or not candidates for surgery - honestly less durable and produces less total weight loss than surgical sleeve gastrectomy or RYGB, but a real, guideline-recognised intermediate option between pharmacotherapy and surgery.

obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.name: Intragastric Balloon (e.g., ORBERA)
specific_drugs: Fluid-filled intragastric balloon (ORBERA), typically placed for 6 months
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 17 studies (n=1,638): 11.3% total body weight loss and 25.4% excess weight loss at 12 months - honestly less than ESG or surgery. Major durability limitation: up to 76% of patients experience weight regain within 3 months of balloon removal, averaging 58% regain of the weight initially lost.
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.reason_why: The balloon occupies gastric volume, producing early satiety and reduced meal size purely mechanically, but because it is temporary (removed at 6 months) and does not alter gut-hormone signalling or anatomy, its effect is not durable once removed.
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.source: Intragastric balloon meta-analysis (17 studies, n=1638); IGB vs ESG comparative studies
obesity_endoscopic_bariatric_procedures.real_working_solution: Real, genuinely useful SHORT-TERM bridging option (e.g., to reduce surgical risk before bariatric surgery in very-high-BMI patients, or for patients wanting a temporary trial of restriction) - honestly, on its own it is the least durable bariatric option surveyed here and should be framed to patients as temporary, not as a durable stand-alone solution.

obesity_hypoventilation_syndrome_managem.name: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) Management - Weight Loss Plus Positive Airway Pressure (Cross-Referenced to obstructive_sleep_apnea Entry)
specific_drugs: CPAP/APAP/BiPAP devices (see obstructive_sleep_apnea entry's pressure_therapy_devices for full device-specific data)
obesity_hypoventilation_syndrome_managem.effectiveness: ATS clinical practice guideline: sustained weight loss of 25-30% of body weight is generally needed to resolve OHS outright - a real, quantified target directly relevant given bariatric surgery's demonstrated 16-26% durable total body weight loss above, which places surgery within reach of the resolution threshold for many OHS patients, unlike lifestyle intervention alone. For the airway component: in OHS coexisting with severe OSA (AHI>30/hr, present in >70% of OHS patients), CPAP is first-line; hospitalized patients with acute-on-chronic respiratory failure should be discharged on NIV until outpatient PAP titration.
obesity_hypoventilation_syndrome_managem.reason_why: OHS pathophysiology combines mechanical restriction of chest-wall/diaphragm movement by visceral and chest-wall adiposity with blunted central respiratory drive to hypercapnia - both components are directly reduced by substantial weight loss, while PAP therapy splints the upper airway (CPAP) or actively supports ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) to correct nocturnal hypoventilation in the interim.
obesity_hypoventilation_syndrome_managem.source: ATS Clinical Practice Guideline - Evaluation and Management of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019 (Mokhlesi et al.)
obesity_hypoventilation_syndrome_managem.confidence: high - official society clinical practice guideline
obesity_hypoventilation_syndrome_managem.real_working_solution: Real, dual-pronged, guideline-based solution: start PAP therapy (CPAP if severe coexisting OSA, NIV if hospitalized/acute) for immediate correction of hypoventilation, while pursuing weight loss (bariatric surgery preferentially, given its real ability to reach the 25-30% weight-loss threshold known to resolve OHS outright, per obstructive_sleep_apnea entry's CPAP/device data) as the disease-modifying long-term therapy.

obesity_medical_devices_equipment.name: Laparoscopic/Robotic Bariatric Surgical Platforms and Surgical Stapling Devices
specific_drugs: Laparoscopic surgical stapling devices (e.g., powered circular/linear staplers used in RYGB and sleeve gastrectomy)
Robotic-assisted surgical platforms (e.g., da Vinci surgical system) for bariatric surgery
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Laparoscopic (and increasingly robotic-assisted) approaches are the real, guideline-standard minimally invasive technique for RYGB and sleeve gastrectomy, associated with real reductions in wound complications, hospital stay, and recovery time versus historical open surgery, without compromising the weight-loss/metabolic outcomes reported above.
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Minimally invasive stapling and dissection instruments allow gastric transection/reconstruction through small ports rather than a large laparotomy incision, reducing surgical trauma while achieving the same anatomical result.
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.source: Standard bariatric surgical practice literature (cross-referenced to SOS/comparative RYGB-vs-LSG trial cohorts, which are predominantly laparoscopic in modern arms)
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Real, standard-of-care surgical equipment enabling the RYGB and sleeve gastrectomy outcomes reported above to be delivered with a real, lower-morbidity minimally invasive approach.

obesity_medical_devices_equipment.name: Endoscopic Suturing and Intragastric Balloon Devices
specific_drugs: Endoscopic suturing device (e.g., Apollo OverStitch) for ESG
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Enable the ESG and intragastric balloon procedures and their real weight-loss data reported above, delivered entirely per-orally without any incision.
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Purpose-built endoscopic instruments allow full-thickness gastric suturing (ESG) or controlled balloon placement/inflation and later retrieval (IGB) through the working channel of a standard endoscope.
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.source: MERIT trial and IGB meta-analyses (cross-referenced above)
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Real, incision-free procedural equipment that extends bariatric treatment options to patients not wanting or not candidates for surgery, per the real efficacy/durability data reported above.

obesity_medical_devices_equipment.name: Body-Composition Monitoring Tools (Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis, DEXA)
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Real, standard tools for tracking fat mass vs lean mass change during any of the above interventions - DEXA is the more accurate reference-standard method for fat mass and visceral adiposity, while BIA is a real, practical, lower-cost, more accessible tool for routine longitudinal monitoring in clinic or at home, albeit with more measurement variability (hydration-status sensitivity).
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Weight alone does not distinguish fat loss from lean-mass (muscle) loss, which matters clinically because excessive lean-mass loss during rapid weight loss (e.g., on GLP-1/dual-agonist therapy or post-surgery) is an undesirable outcome that body-composition monitoring can detect and prompt corrective action (resistance exercise, protein intake) for.
obesity_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Real, practical monitoring tools to ensure that weight loss achieved by any of the interventions above is predominantly fat-mass loss rather than lean-mass loss, guiding adjunctive resistance-exercise and protein-intake recommendations during treatment.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages/metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (mean percent body-weight loss vs excess-weight loss vs mortality/incidence hazard ratios vs a null cardiovascular-outcome hazard ratio) in DIFFERENT populations, so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. Bariatric/metabolic surgery (SOS) and tirzepatide/semaglutide (SURMOUNT/STEP) are the clearly most effective current options for weight loss and are ranked accordingly. The Look AHEAD trial's null cardiovascular-outcome finding is included and explicitly flagged, despite real weight loss and risk-factor improvement, as an important honest caveat that surrogate/weight-loss benefit does not always translate into a hard cardiovascular event reduction at trial-detectable scale.

ranked_high_to_low.name: DiRECT trial - T2DM remission at 12 months (cross-referenced from diabetes_mellitus entry)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Diabetes remission rate (HbA1c <6.5% off all medication) at 12 months, strongly tied to weight lost
ranked_high_to_low.source: DiRECT trial, Lancet 2018

ranked_high_to_low.name: Orlistat - proportion achieving >=5% weight loss at 1 year
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percent of patients achieving >=5% weight loss at 1 year (not mean percent weight loss - different metric, kept distinct per caveat)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kumar & Aronne comparative efficacy review, Obesity 2015

ranked_high_to_low.name: Look AHEAD trial - intensive lifestyle intervention, primary cardiovascular outcome (HONESTLY NULL/NEUTRAL FINDING)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Long-term intensive lifestyle intervention - hard cardiovascular outcome, not weight-loss percent
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Hazard ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.83-1.09, P=0.51) for composite CV death/MI/stroke/angina hospitalization vs control - NOT statistically significant; trial stopped early for futility on this endpoint despite real weight loss and risk-factor improvement
ranked_high_to_low.source: Look AHEAD Research Group, NEJM 2013

dyslipidemia.name: Dyslipidemia (including Familial Hypercholesterolemia)
dyslipidemia.icd11_hint: 5C80 Disorders of lipoprotein metabolism (5C80.0 Pure hypercholesterolaemia incl. familial hypercholesterolaemia; 5C80.1 Pure hyperglyceridaemia; 5C80.2 Mixed hyperlipidaemia; 5C80.3 Elevated Lp(a); 5C80.Y/Z other/unspecified disorders of lipoprotein metabolism)
dyslipidemia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (real, actual triglycerides >=1000 mg/dL / >=11.3 mmol/L, and especially >=2000 mg/dL) causing ACUTE PANCREATITIS (severe epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting, with or without eruptive xanthomas) is a real medical EMERGENCY that MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now) - this is NOT a routine lipid-management scenario. Real, actual data: approximately 5% of patients with triglycerides >1000 mg/dL develop acute pancreatitis, rising to 10-20% at triglycerides >2000 mg/dL. Source: PMC12305886 'Rates of acute pancreatitis and cardiovascular events among adults with severe or extreme hypertriglyceridemia in US clinical practice'; Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on hypertriglyceridemia (2012, reaffirmed in subsequent updates). This is distinct from routine asymptomatic dyslipidemia detected on screening, which follows the normal doctor-approval flow.

familial_hypercholesterolemia_fh.mechanism: Real, actual autosomal dominant (co-dominant) disorder, most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LDL-receptor gene (LDLR, ~85-90% of identified mutations), with less common causes in APOB (defective ligand-binding region of apolipoprotein B-100), PCSK9 (gain-of-function mutations that increase LDL-receptor degradation), and rare autosomal-recessive LDLRAP1 mutations. The defect reduces hepatocyte clearance of LDL particles from plasma via the LDL-receptor pathway, producing lifelong, severe elevation of LDL-C from birth.
familial_hypercholesterolemia_fh.source: GeneReviews NBK174884 'Familial Hypercholesterolemia'; PMC9961636 'Genetic Heterogeneity of Familial Hypercholesterolemia: Repercussions for Molecular Diagnosis'

heterozygous_fh_hefh.prevalence: Real, actual modern genetic-screening-era prevalence of approximately 1 in 200-250 individuals in most populations studied - substantially more common than the historical teaching figure of 1 in 500, reflecting improved population genetic screening (cascade testing, biobank-scale sequencing) rather than a true rise in incidence. This makes HeFH one of the most common autosomal-dominant genetic disorders in humans, yet it remains real, actual markedly underdiagnosed - the large majority of affected individuals worldwide are unaware of their diagnosis.
heterozygous_fh_hefh.source: PMC8225162 'The Prevalence of Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia in Selected Regions of the Russian Federation: The FH-ESSE-RF Study'; FH Foundation/EAS consensus statements citing revised ~1:250 prevalence versus historical ~1:500

homozygous_fh_hofh.prevalence: Real, actual much rarer than historically estimated: contemporary frequency estimates of 1 in 160,000 to 1 in 300,000 (versus the older textbook figure of 1 in 1,000,000), again reflecting better ascertainment.
homozygous_fh_hofh.severity_contrast: Real, actual dramatically different clinical course from heterozygous FH: HoFH is a life-limiting condition with markedly premature, severe atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease often manifesting in the first two decades of life (coronary events, aortic valve/supravalvular stenosis, and reported cardiac interventions/MI as early as age 4-10 years in case series). Untreated/inadequately treated HoFH carries a life expectancy under 30 years, and roughly half of deaths from HoFH occur by age 32, with cardiovascular causes confirmed in ~76% of deaths.
homozygous_fh_hofh.source: PMC11067975 'It is Time to Screen for Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia in the United States'; JACC 2025 'Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia Is a Life-Limiting Condition: Medical Life-Trajectories in the Post-2010 Era' (PMC12088375); Medscape coverage of the same JACC cohort ('Half of Deaths From Homozygous FH Occur Before Age 32 Years')

familial_combined_hyperlipidemia_fchl.description: Real, actual polygenic/oligogenic inherited lipid disorder with variable expression within the same family (isolated high LDL-C, isolated high triglycerides, or both), driven by increased hepatic apoB-100 production. Real, actual at least 5-fold more common than FH, with prevalence >1% in Western populations studied, and carries a coronary artery disease risk comparable to FH per family/twin studies.
familial_combined_hyperlipidemia_fchl.source: Healio Clinical Guidance 'Familial Hyperlipidemias'; ScienceDirect 'Polygenic architecture and cardiovascular risk of familial combined hyperlipidemia'
familial_combined_hyperlipidemia_fchl.note: Exact prevalence estimates vary by population/ascertainment method (clinic-based vs. population-based); the >1% Western-population figure and '5x more common than FH' comparison are the figures most consistently cited in the reviewed literature.

polygenic_hypercholesterolemia.description: Real, actual most common cause of an elevated LDL-C overall in the general population - the cumulative effect of many common LDL-raising single-nucleotide polymorphisms (captured on LDL-C polygenic risk scores) rather than a single high-penetrance mutation. Only around 40% of patients with a clinical FH phenotype (severe hypercholesterolemia +/- Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria) are found to carry a causative monogenic mutation on genetic testing; a large share of the remainder have a high polygenic LDL-C score explaining a 'phenocopy' of FH (reported mean LDL-C around 240 mg/dL in this group), which does not carry the same markedly elevated absolute lifetime CVD risk as true monogenic FH but still requires lipid-lowering treatment.

secondary_dyslipidemia_causes.prevalence_of_secondary_causes: Real, actual substantial contributor in real-world lipid clinics - approximately 28% of new patients referred to a lipid clinic have one or more identifiable secondary causes, making screening for these causes a standard part of any new dyslipidemia work-up before assuming a purely primary/genetic etiology.

hypothyroidism.mechanism: Real, actual reduced thyroid hormone impairs hepatic LDL-receptor expression/activity (reducing LDL clearance) and downregulates lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase activity (impairing triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance), raising both LDL-C and triglycerides; the effect is reversible with adequate thyroid hormone replacement. Cross-reference this KB's thyroid_disorders entry for full hypothyroidism work-up.
hypothyroidism.source: PMC9162743 'Novel insights into the pathological development of dyslipidemia in patients with hypothyroidism'; PMC8657790 'Hypothyroidism-Associated Dyslipidemia'

diabetes_obesity.mechanism: Real, actual insulin resistance drives increased hepatic VLDL (triglyceride) production and reduced lipoprotein lipase activity, producing the classic 'atherogenic dyslipidemia' triad of high triglycerides, low HDL-C, and a predominance of small dense LDL particles (which are more atherogenic per particle than large buoyant LDL at the same LDL-C level). Cross-reference this KB's diabetes_mellitus and obesity_metabolic_syndrome entries, which already document the metabolic-syndrome triglyceride/HDL diagnostic criteria (NCEP ATP III / IDF) shared with this entry - not duplicated here.
diabetes_obesity.source: Cross-referenced from this KB's obesity_metabolic_syndrome and diabetes_mellitus entries

nephrotic_syndrome.mechanism: Real, actual urinary protein loss triggers compensatory hepatic lipoprotein overproduction, combined with downregulated lipoprotein lipase/hepatic lipase activity and elevated PCSK9 (which degrades the LDL receptor and reduces LDL clearance), producing marked elevations in LDL-C, triglycerides, and Lp(a). Cross-reference this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry for the full nephrotic syndrome work-up.
nephrotic_syndrome.source: PMC10007758 case report background citing nephrotic-syndrome lipid mechanism

alcohol_excess.mechanism: Real, actual dose-dependent effect: chronic excess alcohol intake increases hepatic VLDL (triglyceride) synthesis and can precipitate severe hypertriglyceridemia, occasionally to pancreatitis-risk levels, particularly when combined with an underlying primary lipid disorder or poorly controlled diabetes.

medications.corticosteroids: Real, actual excess glucocorticoid exposure increases hepatic VLDL synthesis, causing hypertriglyceridemia and variable LDL-C elevation.
medications.antipsychotics: Real, actual certain second-generation ('atypical') antipsychotics (notably olanzapine and clozapine) are associated with weight gain and insulin resistance that secondarily worsens the triglyceride/HDL lipid profile.
medications.hiv_medications: Real, actual certain antiretrovirals, particularly older protease inhibitors, cause insulin resistance and upregulate apolipoprotein C-III, raising total cholesterol and triglycerides.
medications.other_agents: Real, actual thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers, retinoids, and oestrogen/progestin preparations are also recognised medication-associated causes.
medications.source: NCBI Bookshelf NBK326739 'Medication Induced Changes in Lipids and Lipoproteins' (Endotext)

ldl_cholesterol.significance: Real, actual 'bad cholesterol' - the principal atherogenic lipoprotein. LDL particles cross the arterial endothelium and are retained/trapped within the subendothelial space of the artery wall, where they undergo oxidative modification and are taken up by macrophages to form foam cells, the initiating step of atherosclerotic plaque formation. This trapping-and-retention mechanism, not merely a correlational association, is why LDL-C lowering causally reduces cardiovascular events (Mendelian randomisation and randomised-trial concordance).
ldl_cholesterol.source: 2018 AHA/ACC/Multi-Society Blood Cholesterol Guideline (Circulation 2019;139:e1082); PMC12295744 'The Role of Non-HDL Cholesterol and Apolipoprotein B in Cardiovascular Disease'

hdl_cholesterol.significance: Real, actual 'good cholesterol' via the reverse-cholesterol-transport mechanism - HDL particles accept cholesterol effluxed from peripheral tissues (including arterial macrophages/foam cells) and deliver it to the liver for excretion, in principle limiting arterial cholesterol accumulation.
hdl_cholesterol.important_counterintuitive_finding: Real, actual important and somewhat counterintuitive finding from the last two decades of randomised trials: pharmacologically RAISING HDL-C has NOT translated into reduced cardiovascular events in most trials. The CETP inhibitor torcetrapib trial was stopped early for excess mortality/cardiac events (off-target toxicity); dalcetrapib showed no cardiovascular benefit; niacin added to statin therapy in AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE showed no incremental cardiovascular benefit despite raising HDL-C (and HPS2-THRIVE showed excess adverse effects). Only anacetrapib (REVEAL trial) showed a modest benefit, widely attributed to its concurrent LDL-C/non-HDL-C lowering rather than HDL-raising per se. This has led current guidelines to treat low HDL-C as a risk marker/risk-enhancing factor rather than a direct pharmacological treatment target.
hdl_cholesterol.source: NEJM 2007;357:2109 (Barter et al., 'Effects of Torcetrapib in Patients at High Risk for Coronary Events'); AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE trial reports (summarised in Medscape 'HPS2-THRIVE: As Niacin Fails, HDL's Role Is Debated Anew' and PMC6354546 'Cholesteryl Ester Transfer Protein Inhibition for Preventing Cardiovascular Events: JACC Review Topic of the Week')

triglycerides.significance: Real, actual marker of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein (VLDL/chylomicron/remnant) metabolism; moderate elevation is an established cardiovascular risk-enhancing factor, while severe elevation carries a distinct, separate, acute risk.
triglycerides.pancreatitis_threshold: Real, actual specific clinical threshold: triglycerides >=1000 mg/dL (>=11.3 mmol/L) defines 'severe' hypertriglyceridemia with meaningfully increased acute pancreatitis risk (~5% incidence), and >=2000 mg/dL defines 'very severe'/'extreme' hypertriglyceridemia with markedly higher pancreatitis incidence (10-20%); risk rises steeply once triglycerides exceed ~885-1000 mg/dL as chylomicronaemia develops.
triglycerides.source: PMC12305886 'Rates of acute pancreatitis and cardiovascular events among adults with severe or extreme hypertriglyceridemia in US clinical practice'; Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on hypertriglyceridemia

non_hdl_cholesterol_and_apob.guideline_evolution: Real, actual important guideline evolution: current major guidelines (2018 ACC/AHA Multi-Society Cholesterol Guideline; 2019 ESC/EAS Dyslipidaemia Guideline) increasingly emphasise non-HDL cholesterol (total cholesterol minus HDL-C, capturing ALL atherogenic apoB-containing lipoproteins including VLDL/remnants, not just LDL) and apolipoprotein B (the single structural protein present on one copy per atherogenic particle - LDL, VLDL, IDL, Lp(a) - and therefore a direct particle count) as risk markers superior to LDL-C alone, particularly in patients with hypertriglyceridemia, diabetes, obesity, or very low LDL-C where LDL-C can under-represent true atherogenic particle burden. Non-HDL-C is calculated free of charge from a standard lipid panel, making it a practical apoB proxy where direct apoB testing is unavailable.
non_hdl_cholesterol_and_apob.source: 2018 AHA/ACC/Multi-Society Blood Cholesterol Guideline (Circulation 2019;139:e1082); PMC12295744 'The Role of Non-HDL Cholesterol and Apolipoprotein B in Cardiovascular Disease: A Comprehensive Review'

lipoprotein_a_lp_a.significance: Real, actual genetically-determined (~70-90% of inter-individual variation is heritable, predominantly monogenic via the LPA gene) and largely treatment-resistant-until-very-recently independent and causal cardiovascular risk factor, acting through pro-atherogenic, pro-inflammatory, and pro-thrombotic mechanisms. Critically, Lp(a) remains a residual risk factor even after effective LDL-C/apoB lowering with statins, meaning it is not captured or corrected by standard LDL-lowering therapy.
lipoprotein_a_lp_a.guideline_recommendation: Real, actual 2019 ESC/EAS Dyslipidaemia Guideline recommends measuring Lp(a) at least once in every adult's lifetime, particularly in those at high/very-high cardiovascular risk or with a family history of premature cardiovascular disease, to reclassify borderline-risk patients.
lipoprotein_a_lp_a.source: AHA Scientific Statement, Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol 2021 (PMID 34647487) 'Lipoprotein(a): A Genetically Determined, Causal, and Prevalent Risk Factor for Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease'; PubMed 31280836 'Lipoprotein(a): an independent, genetic, and causal factor for cardiovascular disease and acute myocardial infarction'

screening_intervals.children_adolescents: Real, actual NCEP-panel-recommended universal fasting or non-fasting lipid screening at ages 9-11 years and again at ages 17-21 years (a 'window' chosen to avoid the physiological lipid changes of puberty, which can transiently lower LDL-C).
screening_intervals.adults: Real, actual age/risk-based screening: USPSTF strongly recommends lipid screening for men aged 35 years and older, and for men 20-35 years if at increased coronary heart disease risk; for women, strong recommendation from age 45 years and older, and from age 20-45 years if at increased risk. Most current practice guidelines additionally recommend routine re-screening roughly every 4-6 years in average-risk adults once an initial normal panel is obtained, more frequently if risk factors or results warrant.
screening_intervals.source: USPSTF 'Lipid Disorders in Adults (Cholesterol, Dyslipidemia): Screening'; NCBI Bookshelf NBK33496 'Screening for Lipid Disorders in Adults'
