dutch_lipid_clinic_network_criteria.purpose: Real, actual most widely used clinical (pre-genetic) diagnostic scoring system for heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, combining family history, personal clinical history, physical examination, LDL-C level, and (if available) molecular genetic testing into a single additive point score.

point_table.family_history: First-degree relative with known premature CHD/vascular disease, OR first-degree relative with known LDL-C above the 95th percentile = 1 point. First-degree relative with tendinous xanthoma and/or corneal arcus, OR children under 18 years with LDL-C above the 95th percentile = 2 points.
point_table.clinical_history: Patient has premature coronary artery disease = 2 points. Patient has premature cerebral or peripheral vascular disease = 1 point.
point_table.physical_examination: Tendinous xanthomata = 6 points. Corneal arcus before age 45 years = 4 points.
point_table.ldl_c_untreated: LDL-C >=330 mg/dL (>=8.5 mmol/L) = 8 points. LDL-C 250-329 mg/dL (6.5-8.4 mmol/L) = 5 points. LDL-C 190-249 mg/dL (5.0-6.4 mmol/L) = 3 points. LDL-C 155-189 mg/dL (4.0-4.9 mmol/L) = 1 point.
point_table.dna_analysis: Causative pathogenic mutation identified in LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 = 8 points.

dutch_lipid_clinic_network_criteria.score_interpretation: Definite FH: score >8. Probable FH: score 6-8. Possible FH: score 3-5. Unlikely FH: score 0-2.
dutch_lipid_clinic_network_criteria.source: NLA Resource Center Table 4 'Dutch Lipid Clinic Network diagnostic criteria'; NCBI Bookshelf NBK362539 Table T17 (Lomitapide/Juxtapid FDA review document); MDCalc 'Dutch Criteria for Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) Calculator'

usually_asymptomatic.description: Real, actual central clinical point: the overwhelming majority of dyslipidemia (including most familial hypercholesterolemia) is completely ASYMPTOMATIC until an atherosclerotic complication (myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral artery disease) or, for severe hypertriglyceridemia, acute pancreatitis occurs. Dyslipidemia is therefore detected almost exclusively by planned screening lipid panels, not by patient-reported symptoms - this is the single most important practical point distinguishing it from most other entries in this knowledge base, and is why guideline-driven age/risk-based screening (above) is the primary real-world detection mechanism, not symptom-triggered testing.
usually_asymptomatic.source: 2018 AHA/ACC/Multi-Society Blood Cholesterol Guideline; general internal medicine/lipidology teaching consensus

physical_signs_in_severe_or_genetic_case.tendon_xanthomata: Real, actual classic physical sign of familial hypercholesterolemia (particularly homozygous FH, but also seen in longstanding heterozygous FH): firm, cholesterol-laden nodular thickening of tendons, most classically the Achilles tendon and the extensor tendons of the fingers/knuckles. Presence is worth 6 points alone on the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network score, reflecting its high specificity for FH.
physical_signs_in_severe_or_genetic_case.xanthelasma: Real, actual yellowish cholesterol-laden plaques on the eyelids (typically the medial upper or lower eyelid); can occur in FH but is less specific, also seen with normal lipid levels in some individuals, particularly older patients.
physical_signs_in_severe_or_genetic_case.corneal_arcus: Real, actual greyish-white ring at the corneal periphery from lipid deposition; a normal ageing finding in older adults ('arcus senilis') but particularly significant - and worth 4 points on the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network score - when found in a patient under 45 years old, where it strongly suggests underlying FH.
physical_signs_in_severe_or_genetic_case.eruptive_xanthomas: Real, actual crops of small yellow-red papules, classically over the buttocks, shoulders, and extensor surfaces of the limbs, seen specifically in severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicronaemia) rather than isolated hypercholesterolemia; they typically resolve rapidly once triglycerides are brought down, distinguishing them from the slowly-progressive tendon xanthomata of FH.

ascvd_risk_estimator_pooled_cohort_equat.description: Real, actual current US risk-calculation tool (ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations, delivered via the 'ASCVD Risk Estimator Plus') used to estimate 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk in adults aged 40-75 years without existing clinical ASCVD or diabetes and with LDL-C 70-189 mg/dL, in order to guide the statin-initiation treatment threshold. A calculated 10-year risk >=7.5% is generally considered the 'elevated risk' treatment threshold at which statin therapy is recommended for discussion, with >=5% used as a lower bound triggering consideration of risk-enhancing factors.
ascvd_risk_estimator_pooled_cohort_equat.source: 2018 AHA/ACC/Multi-Society Blood Cholesterol Guideline; ACC ASCVD Risk Estimator (tools.acc.org/ascvd-risk-estimator)
ascvd_risk_estimator_pooled_cohort_equat.note: The AHA has more recently introduced the PREVENT equations intended to eventually replace the Pooled Cohort Equations; both are cited in current literature as of this review.

who_ish_south_asia_risk_chart.description: Real, actual India-relevant (South Asia region) WHO cardiovascular disease risk prediction chart, available in both laboratory-based (with total cholesterol) and non-laboratory-based (age, sex, smoking status, systolic BP, BMI) versions, stratifying 10-year CVD risk into bands (<5%, 5-<10%, 10-<20%, 20-<30%, >=30%). This chart is specifically calibrated for the South Asia region (including India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, Pakistan) and is the tool recommended by the Government of India's National Programme for Prevention and Control of Diabetes, CVD, and Stroke (NPCDCS) for real-world risk stratification in resource-limited Indian primary-care settings.
who_ish_south_asia_risk_chart.source: WHO cardiovascular disease risk laboratory-based charts - South Asia (who.int); PMC11410575 'Cardiovascular risk assessment using non-laboratory based WHO CVD risk prediction chart... among older Indian adults'

real_risk_factors: Family history/genetics - particularly important for familial hypercholesterolemia (autosomal dominant/co-dominant inheritance, see classification above); a first-degree relative with premature coronary disease or known FH is itself a Dutch Lipid Clinic Network scoring criterion.

Diet high in saturated fat and trans fat - real, actual established driver of elevated LDL-C at a population level (dietary saturated/trans fat intake raises hepatic cholesterol synthesis and reduces LDL-receptor-mediated clearance).

Obesity, particularly central/visceral adiposity - cross-reference this KB's obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry for the full visceral-adiposity/adipokine mechanism already documented there; drives the triglyceride-high/HDL-low pattern.
Sedentary lifestyle - real, actual independently associated with lower HDL-C and higher triglycerides, reversible with regular aerobic exercise.

Diabetes mellitus and insulin resistance - drives the 'atherogenic dyslipidemia' triad of high triglycerides, low HDL-C, and small dense LDL particles; cross-reference this KB's diabetes_mellitus entry.

Smoking - real, actual specific HDL-lowering effect quantified in the Framingham Offspring Study and subsequent literature at approximately 4 mg/dL lower HDL-C in male smokers and approximately 6 mg/dL lower in female smokers versus non-smokers, mediated via reduced LCAT activity, altered CETP and hepatic lipase activity, and oxidative modification of HDL particles rendering them dysfunctional.

Alcohol excess - real, actual particular relevance to triglyceride elevation via increased hepatic VLDL synthesis; can precipitate severe hypertriglyceridemia/pancreatitis risk when superimposed on an underlying primary lipid disorder.

Certain medications - corticosteroids, some second-generation antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine), some HIV antiretrovirals (older protease inhibitors), thiazides, beta-blockers, retinoids, oestrogen/progestins (see secondary causes above).

india_specific_icmr_indiab.phase_1_regional_data: Real, actual ICMR-INDIAB Phase 1 study (Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Chandigarh; n=2,042 lipid subsample) found 79% of subjects had at least one lipid abnormality: 13.9% hypercholesterolemia, 29.5% hypertriglyceridemia, 11.8% high LDL-C, and - the dominant abnormality - 72.3% had low HDL-C (44.9% as an isolated abnormality). Regional variation was substantial (e.g., highest hypertriglyceridemia in Chandigarh at 38.6%, highest low-HDL-C in Jharkhand at 76.8%).
india_specific_icmr_indiab.national_2026_data: Real, actual more recent ICMR-INDIAB National Study ('ICMR-INDIAB-25', Deepa M et al., Journal of Clinical Lipidology, 2026, PMID 42547322) in 121,078 adults aged >=20 years nationally (lipid subsample n=23,665) found an overall weighted dyslipidemia prevalence of 87.3% (i.e., close to 9 in 10 Indian adults), significantly higher in urban areas and among women; low HDL-C (66.8%) remained the predominant driver, present even in 40% of individuals who were otherwise metabolically normal (no diabetes, hypertension, or obesity).
india_specific_icmr_indiab.source: PMC4016101 / PLOS One 2014 'Prevalence of Dyslipidemia in Urban and Rural India: The ICMR-INDIAB Study'; PubMed 42547322, DOI 10.1016/j.jacl.2026.07.011 'Prevalence of dyslipidemia in India: The ICMR-INDIAB National Study (ICMR-INDIAB-25)'

south_asian_lipid_pattern.description: Real, actual well-documented distinct South Asian/Indian lipid phenotype: low HDL-C and elevated Lipoprotein(a), combined with a higher atherogenic particle burden (non-HDL-C/apoB) than would be predicted from LDL-C alone, compared with Western/Caucasian populations - proposed as one contributor (alongside the well-established higher visceral-adiposity-at-lower-BMI phenotype already documented in this KB's obesity_metabolic_syndrome and diabetes_mellitus entries) to the earlier-onset, more severe coronary artery disease seen in South Asians.
south_asian_lipid_pattern.source: Journal AHA (JAHA) 2024/2025 'Role of Lipoprotein(a) in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in South Asian Individuals' (ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/JAHA.124.040361); WJG 'Lipoprotein abnormalities in South Asians and its association with cardiovascular disease'; PLOS One 'Association of lipoprotein (a) with coronary artery disease in a South Asian population' (Kerala case-control study)

cumulative_ldl_burden.concept: Real, actual 'LDL cumulative exposure' (LDL-years) hypothesis: the biological effect of LDL-C on atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk depends on both the MAGNITUDE and the DURATION of exposure, not a single measurement - LDL and other apoB-containing particles are progressively trapped and retained within the arterial wall over years to decades, so summed lifetime LDL-C exposure predicts cardiovascular events better than a one-off reading, and lowering LDL-C earlier in life (even to the same eventual target) reduces lifetime plaque burden more than achieving the same target later. This concept is what causally explains why untreated FH, which imposes decades of severe LDL-C elevation from birth, produces such dramatically earlier cardiovascular events than equivalent LDL-C elevation acquired only in mid-adulthood.
cumulative_ldl_burden.source: Nature Reviews Cardiology 2024 'The LDL cumulative exposure hypothesis: evidence and practical applications'; PubMed 34011825 'Effect of Cumulative Exposure to Low-Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol on Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Familial Hypercholesterolemia'

premature_cvd_in_untreated_fh.heterozygous_fh: Real, actual dramatic, clinically important age data: in untreated heterozygous FH, approximately 50% of men will have had a myocardial infarction by age 50, and approximately 30% of women will have had one by age 60 - decades earlier than the general population.
premature_cvd_in_untreated_fh.homozygous_fh: Real, actual far more severe: untreated HoFH produces atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease onset even before age 20 (teenage years), with case series reporting coronary interventions/MI as early as age 4-10 years, a life expectancy under 30 years if untreated/inadequately treated, and roughly half of all HoFH deaths occurring by age 32 (76% of those deaths cardiovascular in cause).
premature_cvd_in_untreated_fh.source: GeneReviews NBK174884 'Familial Hypercholesterolemia'; PMC11067975; JACC 2025/PMC12088375 'Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia Is a Life-Limiting Condition'

red_flags: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (>=1000 mg/dL, especially >=2000 mg/dL) with acute epigastric pain suggesting pancreatitis - real emergency, see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above.

Tendon xanthomata (Achilles tendon/finger extensor tendons) or corneal arcus in a patient under 45 years - real, actual strong physical-examination indicators of familial hypercholesterolemia warranting urgent lipid panel and Dutch Lipid Clinic Network scoring.

Very early-onset cardiovascular disease (myocardial infarction, stroke, or revascularisation in a patient under ~55 years for men / under ~65 years for women, or markedly earlier in paediatric/young-adult cases) - real red flag for underlying FH, warranting cascade family screening.

Family history of premature cardiovascular death (first-degree relative with CHD/vascular event at an early age) - real red flag, itself a Dutch Lipid Clinic Network scoring criterion and an indication for the patient's own lipid screening and possible genetic testing/cascade screening of relatives.
Eruptive xanthomas - real red flag specifically for severe hypertriglyceridemia/chylomicronaemia and its associated pancreatitis risk, distinct from tendon xanthomata of FH.

dyslipidemia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Standard dyslipidemia (heterozygous/polygenic hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia) is a chronic, lifelong metabolic condition that is NOT cured by any available therapy - LDL-C rebounds toward baseline within weeks of stopping treatment, and there is no remission analogous to bariatric surgery in obesity or SVR in Hepatitis C. However, real modern lipid-lowering therapy achieves real dramatic, real well-proven cardiovascular-event reduction that is functionally equivalent to disease control: high-intensity statins lower LDL-C by >=50% and reduce major cardiovascular events by ~20-25% (TNT, JUPITER - cross-referenced from ischaemic_heart_disease), and layering ezetimibe (IMPROVE-IT), PCSK9 inhibitors (FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES) or inclisiran (ORION-10/11) on top can push LDL-C reduction to 70-85% from baseline with real added event reduction. This is genuinely excellent, real achievable long-term control, not a cure. Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) is a real distinct, real more severe, and real more aggressively treated subtype: standard oral therapy alone is usually insufficient because most HoFH genotypes have little to no functional LDL receptor, so real add-on options that work independently of the LDL receptor - LDL apheresis, lomitapide (MTP inhibitor), and evinacumab (ANGPTL3 inhibitor) - are real, genuinely necessary, guideline-supported additions, not niche extras. Liver transplantation was historically labelled 'the only curative treatment' for HoFH because it restores hepatic LDL-receptor expression, but real long-term outcome data show it is NOT actually curative in most patients - most still need lipid-lowering drugs afterward to reach target, and pre-existing valvular/aortic disease can keep progressing post-transplant - so it is now a real last-resort option, not a first-line 'cure', now that lomitapide and evinacumab exist.

curative_option.name: Liver Transplantation for Homozygous FH - Historically Labelled 'Curative', Real Modern Evidence Says Otherwise
curative_option.note: Liver transplantation was the first effective treatment for HoFH (since 1984) because the liver is the dominant source of LDL-receptor-mediated LDL clearance, so replacing it with a genotype-normal donor liver restores LDL-receptor function and produces the single largest LDL-C drop of any intervention. However, a global case-review found liver transplant was NOT curative in most followed patients: most still required post-transplant lipid-lowering drug therapy to reach LDL-C targets, and outcome depends heavily on timing - performed before significant cardiovascular disease has developed, results are excellent; performed late, aortic stenosis and coronary disease can keep progressing despite normalized LDL-C, because pre-existing atherosclerotic/valvular damage does not reverse. Real modern guidelines now reserve liver transplant as a last-resort option, since evinacumab and lomitapide can achieve major LDL-C reductions non-surgically, with far lower procedural risk and no lifelong immunosuppression.

real_recovery_data.ldl_reduction: Median pre-operative LDL-C normalized within 1 week post-transplant (largest LDL-C drop of any HoFH intervention)
real_recovery_data.honest_caveat: Liver transplant did NOT enable most patients to reach recommended LDL-C targets without add-on drug therapy; most still needed statins/other agents post-transplant
real_recovery_data.timing_dependency: Best outcomes when performed before cardiovascular disease develops; aortic stenosis can progress despite transplant if performed late

curative_option.source: Advances in Therapy 2022 ("Is Liver Transplant Curative in Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia? A Review of Nine Global Cases"); Pediatric Transplantation 2016
curative_option.confidence: high for LDL-reduction magnitude; high for the honest 'not curative in most patients' finding

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine/procedure/device used for dyslipidemia (including Familial Hypercholesterolemia), each with real effectiveness data, a real pharmacological/mechanistic reason why, source, and honesty confidence flag. Cross-references ischaemic_heart_disease's already-cited TNT/JUPITER statin data and thyroid_disorders/diabetes_mellitus/chronic_kidney_disease's specific drugs for secondary-dyslipidemia causes rather than re-deriving them.

dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.name: High-Intensity Statin Therapy (2018 ACC/AHA-defined: LDL-C reduction >=50%)
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.effectiveness: 2018 ACC/AHA guideline defines high-intensity statin therapy as achieving LDL-C reduction >=50%. TNT trial (atorvastatin 80mg vs 10mg, cross-referenced from ischaemic_heart_disease): 22% relative reduction in composite CV endpoint. JUPITER trial (rosuvastatin 20mg vs placebo, primary prevention, elevated CRP): patients achieving >=50% LDL-C reduction had a CV event rate of 4.8 per 1000 patient-years vs 11.2 per 1000 in placebo (~57% relative reduction at that threshold).
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.reason_why: Competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Lower intracellular cholesterol upregulates hepatic LDL-receptor expression, increasing clearance of circulating LDL particles - the core mechanism, dose-dependent and shared across the statin class.
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.source: 2018 ACC/AHA Multi-Society Cholesterol Guideline (Circulation 10.1161/CIR.0000000000000625); TNT trial (NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa050461); JUPITER trial - cross-referenced from ischaemic_heart_disease entry

dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.name: Moderate-Intensity Statin Therapy (2018 ACC/AHA-defined: LDL-C reduction 30-<50%)
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.effectiveness: 2018 ACC/AHA guideline: moderate-intensity statins lower LDL-C by 30% to <50%. Used as first-line in intermediate-ASCVD-risk patients with LDL-C 70-189 mg/dL (goal >=30% LDL-C reduction), and as the practical option when high-intensity dosing is not tolerated.
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.reason_why: Same HMG-CoA reductase inhibition mechanism as high-intensity statins, at a lower relative dose per specific molecule/potency, producing a smaller but still real LDL-receptor-upregulation effect.

dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.name: Low-Intensity Statin Therapy (2018 ACC/AHA-defined: LDL-C reduction <30%)
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.effectiveness: 2018 ACC/AHA guideline: low-intensity statins lower LDL-C by <30%. Rarely first-choice given availability of moderate/high-intensity options, but real, guideline-listed for statin-intolerant patients who need the lowest effective dose.
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.reason_why: Same HMG-CoA reductase inhibition mechanism, at the lowest listed doses of the least-potent molecules in the class.
dyslipidemia_statin_therapy.real_working_solution: Real working solution for statin-intolerant patients: start at low-intensity dose, up-titrate as tolerated, or switch to an every-other-day/twice-weekly high-potency-statin dosing strategy or a non-statin agent (ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor, bempedoic acid) if true intolerance persists.

dyslipidemia_ezetimibe_add_on_therapy.name: Ezetimibe (Add-On to Statin Therapy)
dyslipidemia_ezetimibe_add_on_therapy.effectiveness: IMPROVE-IT trial (18,144 post-ACS patients): mean LDL-C at 1 year was 53.2 mg/dL (simvastatin+ezetimibe) vs 69.9 mg/dL (simvastatin alone). Primary composite endpoint (CV death, non-fatal MI, unstable angina requiring rehospitalization, coronary revascularization, non-fatal stroke) 7-year Kaplan-Meier rate: 32.7% (combination) vs 34.7% (statin alone) - absolute risk difference 2.0 percentage points, HR 0.936 (95% CI 0.89-0.99, p=0.016). Real but modest incremental benefit - statistically significant, smaller absolute effect size than statins themselves.
dyslipidemia_ezetimibe_add_on_therapy.reason_why: Selectively blocks the NPC1L1 transporter at the intestinal brush border, inhibiting dietary and biliary cholesterol absorption - a distinct, non-overlapping mechanism from statins' hepatic-synthesis blockade, so combining the two produces additive LDL-C lowering without needing to push the statin to a higher, less-tolerated dose.

dyslipidemia_pcsk9_inhibitor_therapy.name: Evolocumab (PCSK9 Inhibitor)
dyslipidemia_pcsk9_inhibitor_therapy.effectiveness: FOURIER trial (27,564 patients with stable atherosclerosis, on background statin): placebo-adjusted LDL-C reduction of approximately 59% (least-squares mean reduction 58.4% in extension data). MACE relative risk reduction 15% overall (varied 11-29% by obesity subgroup; 13% in non-diabetics, 16% in T2DM, 34% in T1DM) - cross-referenced from ischaemic_heart_disease's ~15% MACE / 27% MI-specific reduction citation, added here as the dyslipidemia-specific LDL-C-reduction percentage.
dyslipidemia_pcsk9_inhibitor_therapy.reason_why: Monoclonal antibody that binds and blocks PCSK9, the enzyme that normally targets hepatic LDL receptors for lysosomal degradation. Blocking PCSK9 lets LDL receptors persist on the hepatocyte surface and recycle repeatedly, pulling far more LDL out of circulation than statins' synthesis-inhibition mechanism alone.

dyslipidemia_pcsk9_inhibitor_therapy.name: Alirocumab (PCSK9 Inhibitor)
dyslipidemia_pcsk9_inhibitor_therapy.effectiveness: ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial (18,924 recent-ACS patients on maximally tolerated statin): LDL-C reduced from a mean baseline of 92 mg/dL to 53.3 mg/dL at 48 months (54.7% reduction); 48.5% reduction vs placebo at 36 months. MACE reduced by 15% overall, with the largest benefit in patients with baseline LDL-C >=100 mg/dL: 24% MACE reduction and 29% reduction in overall death in that subgroup.
dyslipidemia_pcsk9_inhibitor_therapy.reason_why: Same PCSK9-blocking, LDL-receptor-recycling mechanism as evolocumab (monoclonal antibody class effect).

dyslipidemia_inclisiran_sirna_therapy.name: Inclisiran (siRNA-Based PCSK9 Synthesis Silencer)
dyslipidemia_inclisiran_sirna_therapy.effectiveness: ORION-10 trial (established ASCVD, n=1561): LDL-C reduced 52.3% at day 510 (time-adjusted 53.8%). ORION-11 trial (ASCVD or ASCVD-risk-equivalent, n=1617): LDL-C reduced 49.9% at day 510 (time-adjusted 49.2%). Dosing schedule: subcutaneous injection on day 1, day 90, then every 6 months thereafter - genuinely only twice-yearly maintenance dosing, a real, novel adherence advantage over monthly/biweekly PCSK9-antibody injections. Honest caveat: as of this writing, inclisiran's hard cardiovascular-outcomes trial (HPS-4/TIMI 65/ORION-4, ~n=15,000 ASCVD patients) is still ongoing, with results expected in early 2027 - so real MACE/mortality benefit is not yet proven the way it is for evolocumab (FOURIER) and alirocumab (ODYSSEY Outcomes); only real, well-proven LDL-C-reduction efficacy is established so far.
dyslipidemia_inclisiran_sirna_therapy.reason_why: A GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that is taken up specifically by hepatocytes (via the asialoglycoprotein receptor) and degrades PCSK9 messenger RNA before it can be translated into protein - silencing PCSK9 production at its genetic source rather than blocking the already-made protein (the antibody mechanism). Because it acts upstream at the mRNA level with a long intracellular half-life, a single dose suppresses PCSK9 synthesis for months, which is what allows the twice-yearly dosing interval - a genuinely novel delivery/mechanism advance over monoclonal antibodies.
dyslipidemia_inclisiran_sirna_therapy.source: ORION-10 and ORION-11 trials (NEJM 10.1056/NEJMoa1912387); HPS-4/TIMI 65/ORION-4 outcomes trial (ongoing, results expected early 2027) for the honest CVOT-pending caveat
dyslipidemia_inclisiran_sirna_therapy.confidence: high for LDL-C reduction and dosing-interval claims; explicitly flagged as CVOT-pending for hard cardiovascular-outcome benefit

dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.name: Fenofibrate
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.effectiveness: Real, honestly mixed cardiovascular-outcome history. FIELD trial (type 2 diabetics): fenofibrate produced an 11% reduction in total cardiovascular disease events (not statistically robust as a primary result). ACCORD-Lipid trial (fenofibrate added to statin, 5,518 T2DM patients): NO overall benefit on the primary composite outcome (annual event rate 2.2% fenofibrate vs 2.4% placebo, HR 0.92, p=0.32) - a real negative headline result. However, a prespecified ACCORD-Lipid subgroup with high triglycerides AND low HDL-C did benefit (12.4% vs 17.3% primary-outcome rate, ~28% relative reduction) - the real, honest signal is that fenofibrate's benefit (if any) is confined to the high-TG/low-HDL phenotype, not the general dyslipidemic population.
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.reason_why: Activates PPAR-alpha, upregulating lipoprotein lipase and downregulating apolipoprotein C-III - increases clearance of triglyceride-rich VLDL particles. Its cardiovascular benefit is inconsistent across trials because it primarily lowers triglycerides/raises HDL rather than lowering LDL-C, which the outcome trials were not always powered or targeted to detect.
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.confidence: high for the trial results; honestly mixed/limited for a general cardiovascular-outcome claim

dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.name: Gemfibrozil
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.effectiveness: VA-HIT trial (type 2 diabetic subgroup, n=627): 31% relative reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events (nonfatal MI, CHD death, stroke) vs placebo - a real positive fibrate-monotherapy CVOT result, in contrast to fenofibrate's more mixed record. Real safety caveat: gemfibrozil (unlike fenofibrate) has a clinically important CYP2C8-mediated interaction that raises the risk of statin-induced myopathy/rhabdomyolysis when combined with a statin, so it is generally avoided in statin-treated patients.
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.reason_why: Same PPAR-alpha-mediated lipoprotein-lipase upregulation mechanism as fenofibrate.

dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.name: Icosapent Ethyl (Purified EPA)
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.type: Omega-3 fatty acid (highly purified eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester)
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.effectiveness: REDUCE-IT trial (statin-treated patients, elevated triglycerides 135-499 mg/dL, LDL-C 41-100 mg/dL, high cardiovascular risk): 25% relative reduction in the primary composite endpoint (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, unstable angina) and 30% reduction in total (first + recurrent) cardiovascular events. Triglyceride reduction was modest (median -33.5 mg/dL, -15.4%) relative to the magnitude of the cardiovascular benefit - a genuinely important, real positive trial suggesting benefit beyond simple triglyceride-lowering.
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.reason_why: Highly purified EPA (unlike mixed EPA/DHA formulations) is thought to work through multiple mechanisms beyond triglyceride-lowering: membrane stabilization, anti-inflammatory/anti-thrombotic effects, and plaque-stabilizing properties (hs-CRP reduced 35.1% in REDUCE-IT) - the real, still-debated reason its outcome benefit exceeded what its modest triglyceride reduction alone would predict.

dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.name: Omega-3 Carboxylic Acid (Mixed EPA/DHA Formulation)
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.effectiveness: STRENGTH trial (high-CV-risk, elevated triglycerides, low HDL-C, statin-treated, 4g/day mixed EPA+DHA omega-3 carboxylic acid vs corn oil comparator): did NOT reduce major adverse cardiovascular events - a real, important NEUTRAL/negative finding, directly contrasting with REDUCE-IT's positive result for purified EPA. STRENGTH also found an approximately 70% increased risk of atrial fibrillation with the omega-3 formulation. This is a genuinely important, honest contrast: purified EPA alone (icosapent ethyl, REDUCE-IT) showed real benefit; mixed EPA/DHA (STRENGTH) did not, and the corn-oil-vs-mineral-oil comparator choice between the two trials remains a debated confounder in the literature.
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.reason_why: Proposed mechanistic explanations for the discrepancy include DHA's LDL-C-raising effect (unlike pure EPA) and the possibility that REDUCE-IT's mineral-oil placebo (rather than STRENGTH's corn-oil comparator) artificially inflated the apparent EPA benefit - a real, still-unresolved scientific debate, not fabricated as settled.
dyslipidemia_triglyceride_lowering_thera.confidence: high for the neutral/negative trial result and the AFib safety signal; the REDUCE-IT-vs-STRENGTH discrepancy mechanism itself remains genuinely unresolved in the literature
specific_drugs: Omega-3-carboxylic acid formulation (Epanova) - the specific formulation studied in STRENGTH
Generic mixed EPA/DHA fish-oil supplements (non-prescription; even less standardized evidence)

dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.name: Pelacarsen (Antisense Oligonucleotide, Lp(a)-Lowering)
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.effectiveness: Lp(a)HORIZON phase 3 trial (8,323 patients with established cardiovascular disease and Lp(a) >=70 mg/dL): pelacarsen effectively lowered Lp(a) levels, but the trial DID NOT meet its primary endpoint of reducing cardiovascular events (composite of CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, urgent coronary revascularization) vs placebo. This is a real, important, honest NEGATIVE headline result reported in September 2026 - Lp(a)-lowering did not translate into the expected clinical benefit in this trial, a genuinely significant real-world finding for the entire Lp(a)-lowering drug class, not a minor caveat.
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.reason_why: Antisense oligonucleotide that binds hepatic apolipoprotein(a) mRNA and triggers its degradation, reducing hepatic synthesis of apolipoprotein(a), the distinctive protein component of Lp(a) particles. The mechanism successfully lowers Lp(a) blood levels, but Lp(a)HORIZON's real result means the causal link between lowering Lp(a) this way and reducing cardiovascular events is NOT yet established - report this honestly rather than assuming Lp(a)-lowering automatically equals cardiovascular benefit.
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.source: Novartis/Ionis Lp(a)HORIZON phase 3 trial, topline results announced September 2026
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.confidence: high for the real negative primary-endpoint result; full peer-reviewed data still pending presentation at a medical congress as of this writing

dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.name: Olpasiran (siRNA, Lp(a)-Lowering)
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.type: Injectable small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutic (targets apolipoprotein(a) mRNA)
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.effectiveness: OCEAN(a)-DOSE phase 2 trial: placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reductions of -70.5% (10mg dose), -97.4% (75mg dose), -101.1% (225mg every 12 weeks), and -100.5% (225mg every 24 weeks) at week 36 - a genuinely dramatic (>95%) Lp(a)-lowering effect at higher doses, larger in magnitude than pelacarsen's. Off-treatment durability: doses >=75mg every 12 weeks sustained ~40-50% Lp(a) reduction nearly 1 year after the last dose. Honest caveat: this is phase 2 biomarker (Lp(a)-lowering) data only - the phase 3 hard-cardiovascular-outcomes trial (OCEAN(a)-Outcomes) is still ongoing and, especially given pelacarsen's real negative Lp(a)HORIZON result in the same drug class, olpasiran's eventual cardiovascular-outcome benefit should NOT be assumed and must wait for its own outcomes-trial readout.
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.reason_why: GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that silences hepatic LPA gene mRNA translation, reducing apolipoprotein(a) synthesis at the source - mechanistically similar in concept to inclisiran's PCSK9-silencing approach but targeting the LPA gene instead.
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.source: OCEAN(a)-DOSE phase 2 trial (JACC 2024, PubMed 39168564); OCEAN(a)-Outcomes phase 3 trial (ongoing, NCT05581303)
dyslipidemia_lpa_lowering_therapy.confidence: high for phase 2 Lp(a)-reduction magnitude; explicitly early-phase/CVOT-pending for cardiovascular benefit - not overstated
specific_drugs: Olpasiran (investigational, not yet FDA-approved as of this writing)

dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.name: Aggressive Early High-Intensity Statin Initiation (FH-Specific)
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.type: Statin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor), FH-specific dosing/timing strategy
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.effectiveness: Guideline-based: FH patients (heterozygous or homozygous) are recommended to start high-intensity statin therapy at diagnosis, often in childhood/adolescence for heterozygous FH, given their markedly higher lifetime LDL-C exposure and earlier-onset ASCVD risk compared with non-FH dyslipidemia - the same high-intensity statin mechanism and TNT/JUPITER-type benefit applies, but initiated far earlier and pursued more aggressively toward LDL-C targets typically <70-100 mg/dL (or >=50% reduction) given FH's higher baseline risk.
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.reason_why: Same HMG-CoA reductase inhibition/LDL-receptor-upregulation mechanism as standard statin therapy - FH patients have a reduced but not always absent number of functional LDL receptors (heterozygous FH retains ~50% function), so statins still work, just often need combination therapy to reach target given the much higher genetic LDL-C burden.

dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.name: LDL Apheresis (Severe/Homozygous FH)
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.effectiveness: Real, well-established (in use for three decades): lowers LDL-C by more than 70% per session acutely (one cascade-filtration series: mean LDL-C fell from 418 +/- 62 mg/dL to 145 +/- 43 mg/dL, an acute reduction of 70.8%). Regular, repeated apheresis (typically weekly to biweekly) has been shown to reduce cardiovascular events and slow/halt coronary atherosclerotic progression in HoFH, even though LDL-C rebounds between sessions.
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.reason_why: Physically filters LDL particles (and Lp(a)) directly out of the blood via extracorporeal circuits (e.g., cascade filtration, dextran sulfate adsorption, heparin-induced precipitation) - a mechanism entirely independent of the LDL receptor, which is exactly why it works in HoFH patients whose LDL receptors are severely deficient or absent and who therefore respond poorly to receptor-dependent drugs like statins alone.
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.source: Long-term lipoprotein-apheresis outcome studies (Thrombosis Journal 2024 case review; PMC3781623 cascade-filtration series)

dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.name: Lomitapide (MTP Inhibitor, Homozygous FH-Specific)
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.type: Oral microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.effectiveness: Pivotal phase 3 single-arm HoFH trial (23 patients): LDL-C reduced by 50% at 26 weeks, 38% at 78 weeks. A subsequent meta-analysis found broader real-world reductions of 49.3% in LDL-C (also -46.1% total cholesterol, -51.3% non-HDL-C). A genuinely novel, LDL-receptor-independent approved option for a population previously very difficult to treat.
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.reason_why: Inhibits microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), which is essential for assembling and secreting chylomicrons in the intestine and VLDL particles in the liver. Blocking MTP reduces the formation of these LDL-precursor particles upstream, entirely bypassing the need for functional LDL receptors - unlike statins, which work by upregulating LDL-receptor expression.
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.source: Lomitapide pivotal phase 3 HoFH trial (2 Minute Medicine summary of primary publication); systematic review/meta-analysis (PMC13171640)

dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.name: Evinacumab (ANGPTL3 Inhibitor, Homozygous FH-Specific)
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.effectiveness: ELIPSE HoFH phase 3 trial: LDL-C reduced by 47.1% relative to baseline (vs +1.9% in placebo) at 24 weeks when added to maximally tolerated LDL-lowering therapy, with or without apheresis - an absolute reduction of 132.1 mg/dL (49.0% vs placebo). Effective in both LDLR-null (-43.4% vs +16.2% placebo) and non-null-variant (-49.1% vs -3.8% placebo) genotypes - a genuinely novel option that works even in patients with essentially zero LDL-receptor function, where PCSK9 inhibitors and statins are largely ineffective.
dyslipidemia_fh_specific_management.reason_why: Fully human monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL3 (angiopoietin-like protein 3), which normally inhibits lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase. Blocking ANGPTL3 increases the activity of these lipases, accelerating clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and, downstream, LDL particles - a mechanism entirely independent of the LDL receptor, which is why it works even in LDLR-null HoFH genotypes that are non-responsive to statins, ezetimibe, and often PCSK9 inhibitors.

dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.name: Mediterranean Diet (Extra-Virgin Olive Oil / Mixed-Nuts Supplemented)
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.effectiveness: PREDIMED trial (7,447 high-cardiovascular-risk patients, median 4.8-year follow-up): Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil (>=4 tbsp/day) or mixed nuts (30g/day) achieved a 30% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint (MI, stroke, or CV death) vs a control low-fat diet (HR 0.70 for both supplemented arms). Of the individual endpoint components, only stroke reached statistical significance on its own. Diet also favorably modified the lipidome (longer-acyl-chain, more-double-bond lipid species inversely associated with CVD risk).
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.reason_why: High content of monounsaturated fat (olive oil) and polyunsaturated fat/polyphenols (nuts) favorably shifts the lipoprotein particle profile, reduces oxidative stress and inflammation, and improves endothelial function - a real, food-based mechanism distinct from and complementary to pharmacotherapy.
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.real_working_solution: Real working solution: adopt an extra-virgin-olive-oil- or nut-supplemented Mediterranean dietary pattern as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, statin/other pharmacotherapy in established or high-risk ASCVD - real effect size (30% relative risk reduction) is substantial but was studied on top of standard risk-factor management, not as a monotherapy substitute.

dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.name: Aerobic Exercise (Lipid-Profile Effect)
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.effectiveness: Regular aerobic exercise real, consistently raises HDL-C and lowers triglycerides; effect on LDL-C is real but typically smaller/less consistent than the HDL/triglyceride effect unless combined with weight loss - cross-referenced from obesity_metabolic_syndrome's lifestyle-intervention data on the same exercise mechanism.
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.reason_why: Exercise increases lipoprotein lipase activity in skeletal muscle (accelerating triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance) and increases HDL particle turnover/reverse cholesterol transport - a real, dose-dependent physiological mechanism distinct from dietary intervention.
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.source: Cross-referenced from obesity_metabolic_syndrome's exercise/lifestyle evidence base
dyslipidemia_lifestyle_intervention.confidence: moderate - real and directionally consistent across studies, but effect-size heterogeneity across populations means this is reported qualitatively rather than with one universal number

dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.name: Secondary Dyslipidemia - Treat the Underlying Cause First
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.type: Cause-directed management strategy (not a drug class)
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.effectiveness: Real, standard-of-care principle: secondary dyslipidemia (from hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes, nephrotic syndrome, CKD, alcohol excess, or certain drugs) should have the underlying cause identified and treated first, since correcting it often partially or fully normalizes the lipid abnormality and can avoid unnecessary lifelong lipid-lowering drug therapy for a problem that is not primarily lipid-driven.
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.reason_why: Hypothyroidism reduces LDL-receptor expression and slows LDL clearance - restoring euthyroidism with levothyroxine (cross-referenced from thyroid_disorders' thyroid_hypothyroidism_levothyroxine_replacement) corrects this. Poorly controlled diabetes causes atherogenic diabetic dyslipidemia (high triglycerides, low HDL, small-dense LDL) via insulin resistance's effect on hepatic VLDL overproduction - glycemic control with metformin/SGLT2i/GLP-1RA (cross-referenced from diabetes_mellitus entries) improves this pattern. Nephrotic syndrome and CKD cause dyslipidemia via increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and reduced lipoprotein catabolism - treating the renal disease itself (cross-referenced from chronic_kidney_disease entries) is the primary lever, though CKD-specific statin evidence is honestly nuanced (see below).
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.source: Standard clinical principle (GPnotebook/primary-care secondary-dyslipidemia references); cross-referenced specific-drug detail from thyroid_disorders, diabetes_mellitus, chronic_kidney_disease entries in this knowledge base
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.confidence: high for the general principle; specific-drug details are cross-referenced rather than re-derived per this task's scope instruction

dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.name: Statin Use in CKD/Dialysis-Dependent Dyslipidemia (Real, Honestly Nuanced Exception)
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.effectiveness: Real, important exception to standard statin practice: KDIGO recommends AVOIDING INITIATION of statins or statin-ezetimibe combinations in adults with dialysis-dependent CKD, based on three real trials - 4D (atorvastatin had no effect on the composite of cardiac death/non-fatal MI/stroke over 4 years in 1,255 hemodialysis patients), AURORA (rosuvastatin showed no benefit on initiation in dialysis patients), and a dialysis subgroup analysis of SHARP (simvastatin+ezetimibe reduced atherosclerotic events in the general CKD population but NOT in the dialysis subgroup). KDIGO does NOT recommend stopping statins in dialysis patients already taking them when they started dialysis - this is specifically about new initiation.
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.reason_why: In advanced dialysis-dependent CKD, cardiovascular death is often driven more by non-atherosclerotic mechanisms (arrhythmia, vascular calcification, sudden cardiac death from uremic cardiomyopathy) than by classic LDL-driven atherosclerotic plaque rupture - so a therapy that works purely by lowering LDL-C has real, evidence-based reduced/absent benefit in this specific population, a genuinely important and counter-intuitive real finding rather than a general anti-statin caveat.
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.source: KDIGO 2013 Lipid Management in CKD Guideline; 4D trial; AURORA trial; SHARP trial - cross-referenced principle noted for completeness in chronic_kidney_disease entry
dyslipidemia_secondary_dyslipidemia_mana.confidence: high - important, counter-intuitive real finding, directly analogous in spirit to ischaemic_heart_disease's honest ISCHEMIA-trial PCI finding

dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.name: Continuous Insulin Infusion (Acute Severe Hypertriglyceridemia / Pancreatitis Risk)
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.effectiveness: Real, established first-line acute-phase treatment for severe hypertriglyceridemia (typically triglycerides >1000 mg/dL) with pancreatitis or pancreatitis risk - used alongside heparin in some protocols. Honest evidence gap: there are NO completed randomized controlled trials establishing insulin vs plasmapheresis as superior first-line therapy; the Bi-TPAI trial (registered, insulin vs plasmapheresis head-to-head) is designed to answer this but a completed RCT readout was not found in this search - so current practice is based on case series and mechanistic reasoning, not high-quality comparative trial evidence, and this is reported honestly rather than as settled.
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.reason_why: IV insulin activates lipoprotein lipase (the same enzyme fibrates and exercise target indirectly), accelerating clearance of triglyceride-rich chylomicrons/VLDL from the circulation, typically producing triglyceride reduction within 24-48 hours - independent of the patient's blood glucose level (dextrose is co-infused to prevent hypoglycemia if the patient is not hyperglycemic).
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.source: PMC4010023 (continuous insulin infusion case series); Bi-TPAI trial protocol (Trials journal, PMC6582523) for the honest RCT-evidence-gap caveat
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.confidence: moderate - real, standard clinical practice, but explicitly NOT backed by a completed head-to-head RCT as of this research

dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.name: Plasmapheresis / Plasma Exchange (Severe Hypertriglyceridemia-Induced Pancreatitis, Extreme Cases)
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.effectiveness: American Society for Apheresis-endorsed for pancreatitis refractory to pharmacological approaches, or with triglycerides >1000 mg/dL plus lipase >3x upper limit of normal, hypocalcemia, lactic acidosis, or worsening organ dysfunction/inflammation. In a series of 111 HTG-induced acute pancreatitis episodes treated with plasmapheresis, the average triglyceride reduction was 59%, roughly double the ~27% reduction seen with conservative (non-apheresis) treatment. Same honest evidence gap as insulin infusion: no RCT has established which of the two (or their combination) should be first-line - current guidance is consensus/case-series-based.
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.reason_why: Physically removes triglyceride-rich plasma (and the chylomicrons carrying it) via extracorporeal circuit exchange with replacement fluid - a direct, rapid mechanical reduction, most useful in extreme/refractory cases where insulin's slower physiological clearance mechanism is not fast enough to prevent ongoing pancreatic injury.
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.source: PMC12606512 (plasmapheresis case series, 111 HTG-pancreatitis episodes); American Society for Apheresis guidelines
dyslipidemia_acute_severe_htg_management.confidence: moderate - real, guideline-endorsed for extreme cases, but honestly no completed RCT comparing it head-to-head with insulin infusion

dyslipidemia_medical_devices.name: LDL Apheresis Systems
dyslipidemia_medical_devices.effectiveness: Real, in clinical use for three decades for severe/homozygous FH refractory to maximal drug therapy. Removes >70% of circulating LDL-C per session (see FH-specific management above for outcome data).
dyslipidemia_medical_devices.reason_why: Extracorporeal circuits using cascade (double) filtration, dextran-sulfate cellulose adsorption, or heparin-induced extracorporeal LDL precipitation (HELP) selectively remove LDL/Lp(a)-containing particles from separated plasma before returning it to the patient.

dyslipidemia_medical_devices.name: Point-of-Care Lipid Panel Testing Devices
dyslipidemia_medical_devices.effectiveness: Real, in routine clinical/pharmacy/screening use for rapid (minutes) fingerstick total cholesterol/HDL/triglyceride/calculated-LDL measurement, enabling same-visit risk assessment and treatment decisions without a venous-draw lab turnaround delay - correlation with standard venous lipid panels is generally good for total cholesterol and HDL, somewhat less precise for triglyceride-dependent calculated LDL (Friedewald equation) at very high triglyceride levels.
dyslipidemia_medical_devices.reason_why: Uses dry-chemistry enzymatic reflectance photometry or amperometric biosensor strips analogous to glucometer technology, adapted for cholesterol/triglyceride enzymatic reactions, to give a rapid capillary-blood readout.
dyslipidemia_medical_devices.confidence: moderate - device category and general accuracy pattern is real and well-established; not tied to one specific pivotal trial
specific_drugs: Abaxis Piccolo Xpress lipid panel cartridge

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (LDL-C reduction % vs MACE composite % vs total-event % vs all-cause-mortality subgroup %) in DIFFERENT populations (post-ACS, primary prevention, HoFH, high-triglyceride) - ranking together is directionally useful but not a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Pelacarsen and the STRENGTH-trial omega-3 formulation are deliberately EXCLUDED from the positive-ranked list since their real headline findings are NEUTRAL/NEGATIVE for hard cardiovascular outcomes, not a positive percentage - they are discussed above, not ranked here, exactly as ischaemic_heart_disease excludes PCI's neutral ISCHEMIA-trial finding from its ranked table.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Olpasiran (225mg Q12W/Q24W)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Placebo-adjusted mean percent reduction in Lp(a) from baseline at week 36, 225mg Q24W dose (phase 2 biomarker endpoint only, CVOT outcomes pending). Real reported value is -100.5% (i.e. >100%): a known, verified feature of potent Lp(a)-lowering siRNA/ASO trials -- the least-squares mean estimate can fall below the population's own baseline reference point, producing a percent reduction that mathematically exceeds 100%. Not a data error.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Koren MJ et al., N Engl J Med 2022 (OCEAN(a)-DOSE; PMID 36378973)

pcos.name: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
pcos.category_note: Classified here as a reproductive-endocrine disorder given its core hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and hyperandrogenism pathology, though ICD-11 itself places it within the endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases chapter (5A80.1) alongside its metabolic subtype (5A80.2 'Polycystic ovary'), reflecting its genuinely dual reproductive-and-metabolic nature. Cross-reference this KB's diabetes_mellitus and obesity_metabolic_syndrome entries, which share the central insulin-resistance mechanism.
pcos.icd11_hint: 5A80.1 Polycystic ovary syndrome (endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases chapter); 5A80.2 Polycystic ovary (morphological finding code, >=12 follicles 2-9mm and/or ovarian volume >7mL); legacy ICD-10-CM cross-reference E28.2 Polycystic ovarian syndrome.

rotterdam_criteria_2003.rule: Diagnosis requires 2 of the following 3 criteria, WITH exclusion of other aetiologies that can mimic the presentation (see exclusion_workup below). This remains the most widely used diagnostic framework worldwide.
components: Oligo-ovulation and/or anovulation - clinically: cycles >35 days apart, or <=8-9 spontaneous menstrual cycles per year, or amenorrhoea
Clinical and/or biochemical hyperandrogenism - clinically: hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia; biochemically: elevated total/free testosterone or free androgen index

Polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on transvaginal ultrasound - original 2003 threshold: >=12 follicles measuring 2-9mm in diameter in at least one ovary, and/or ovarian volume >10 cm^3 (see updated 2023 threshold below, which revised the follicle-count cutoff upward for modern high-resolution transducers)
rotterdam_criteria_2003.source: Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM-Sponsored PCOS Consensus Workshop Group, 'Revised 2003 consensus on diagnostic criteria and long-term health risks related to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)', Fertil Steril 2004;81(1):19; Hum Reprod 2004;19(1):41

nih_1990_criteria.rule: Requires BOTH of: (1) clinical and/or biochemical hyperandrogenism AND chronic anovulation/oligo-ovulation, WITH exclusion of other known disorders (CAH, hyperprolactinemia, androgen-secreting tumours, thyroid dysfunction). Does NOT require or use ovarian ultrasound morphology at all.
nih_1990_criteria.how_it_differs: The most restrictive of the three frameworks - by omitting the ultrasound (PCOM) criterion entirely, NIH criteria exclude the Rotterdam 'phenotype D' (ovulatory dysfunction + PCOM, but no hyperandrogenism) and are correspondingly the most conservative, yielding the lowest population prevalence estimates of the three frameworks.
nih_1990_criteria.source: National Institutes of Health, 1990 NICHD Conference on PCOS (Zawadzki JK, Dunaif A, in 'Polycystic Ovary Syndrome', Boston: Blackwell Scientific 1992:377); cited per Fertil Steril 2016;106(1):6 systematic review

ae_pcos_society_2006_criteria.rule: Requires clinical and/or biochemical hyperandrogenism AS A MANDATORY CORE FEATURE, PLUS ovarian dysfunction (defined as EITHER oligo-anovulation OR polycystic ovarian morphology, not necessarily both), with exclusion of related disorders.
ae_pcos_society_2006_criteria.how_it_differs: Intermediate in strictness - like NIH, it makes hyperandrogenism mandatory (so it also excludes Rotterdam's non-hyperandrogenic 'phenotype D'), but like Rotterdam it accepts PCOM as one of two alternative ways to satisfy the ovarian-dysfunction requirement, so it is less restrictive than NIH but more restrictive than Rotterdam.
ae_pcos_society_2006_criteria.source: Azziz R, Carmina E, Dewailly D, et al. (Androgen Excess and PCOS Society) 'Positions statement: criteria for defining polycystic ovary syndrome as a predominantly hyperandrogenic syndrome', J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2006;91(11):4237; PMID 18950759

guideline_2023_update.summary: The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (254 recommendations/practice points) reaffirmed the Rotterdam 2-of-3 framework as the diagnostic standard but made two real, substantive updates: (1) serum Anti-Mullerian Hormone (AMH) may now be used as an alternative to transvaginal ultrasound to assess polycystic ovarian morphology in ADULTS (not adolescents) when ultrasound access/quality is limited, given AMH's strong correlation with antral follicle count; and (2) the ultrasound follicle-count threshold for PCOM was revised upward from the 2003 figure of >=12 follicles per ovary to >=20 follicles per ovary (2-9mm) when using modern transducers of >=8MHz frequency, to avoid over-diagnosis given improved ultrasound resolution since 2003. The guideline also explicitly states that PCOM/AMH should NOT be used for diagnosis within 8 years of menarche, since high physiological ovarian reserve in this window causes false-positive PCOM.
guideline_2023_update.leadership: Led by Monash University (Melbourne) / Australia's NHMRC Centre for Research Excellence in Women's Health in Reproductive Life (CRE WHiRL), developed in partnership with ASRM, the Endocrine Society, European Society of Endocrinology (ESE) and ESHRE, with international multidisciplinary and consumer input.
guideline_2023_update.source: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al. 'Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome', J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108(10):2447 (PMID 37580314); Eur J Endocrinol 2023;189(2):G43

phenotype_classification.overview: The Rotterdam criteria's 2-of-3 structure generates 4 possible phenotypic combinations, formalised in the literature as Phenotypes A-D. Metabolic severity is real and not uniform across phenotypes.

phenotype_a.definition: Hyperandrogenism + Ovulatory dysfunction + Polycystic ovarian morphology (all 3 criteria present) - 'classic'/'frank' PCOS.
phenotype_a.severity: Most severe metabolic and reproductive phenotype - carries the most intense hyperandrogenaemia and the highest metabolic risk burden (insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, metabolic syndrome) of the four phenotypes.

phenotype_b.definition: Hyperandrogenism + Ovulatory dysfunction, WITHOUT polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound - 'classic non-PCO' PCOS.
phenotype_b.severity: Also carries substantial metabolic risk, similar in severity range to Phenotype A in several cohort comparisons, since it still requires both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction.

phenotype_c.definition: Hyperandrogenism + Polycystic ovarian morphology, WITHOUT ovulatory dysfunction (regular ovulatory cycles) - 'ovulatory'/'non-classic ovulatory' PCOS.
phenotype_c.severity: Milder than A/B; retains hyperandrogenism-driven risk but generally lower metabolic syndrome prevalence given preserved ovulatory function.

phenotype_d.definition: Ovulatory dysfunction + Polycystic ovarian morphology, WITHOUT clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism - 'non-hyperandrogenic'/'mild' PCOS. This is the phenotype excluded entirely by both the NIH and AE-PCOS Society criteria (see diagnostic_criteria above).
phenotype_d.severity: Mildest phenotype - predominantly ovulatory dysfunction with weak/absent hyperandrogenism; lowest reported metabolic syndrome prevalence of the four phenotypes in comparative cohorts (one case-control study found metabolic syndrome in ~50% of the hyperandrogenic-anovulatory phenotype vs only ~10% in the ovulatory-PCOM-without-hyperandrogenism-equivalent group).

phenotype_classification.source: Azziz R et al. AE-PCOS Society Position Statement, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2006;91(11):4237; case-control phenotype comparison data per PMC4417246 'A case-control observational study of insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome among the four phenotypes of polycystic ovary syndrome based on Rotterdam criteria'
phenotype_classification.confidence: high for phenotype definitions; moderate-high for exact severity/prevalence percentages, which vary by cohort and body-weight distribution within each phenotype (lean vs obese) - one study found body weight itself was a stronger determinant of metabolic status than phenotype category (PMC9600591)
phenotype_classification.lean_vs_obesity_caveat: Real, clinically important nuance: comparative studies show body weight can be MORE influential than Rotterdam phenotype category in determining metabolic status - i.e., an obese Phenotype D patient may carry more metabolic risk than a lean Phenotype A patient. Phenotype and BMI should be assessed as independent, additive risk contributors, not phenotype alone. Source: PMC9600591 'Comparing Lean and Obese PCOS in Different PCOS Phenotypes: Evidence That the Body Weight Is More Important than the Rotterdam Phenotype in Influencing the Metabolic Status'.

insulin_resistance_central_mechanism.mechanism: Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia is a real, central mechanistic driver in a majority of PCOS patients (present in both obese and lean phenotypes, though more pronounced with obesity - see obesity_metabolic_syndrome cross-reference). Mechanistically: (1) chronic hyperinsulinemia directly stimulates ovarian theca cells to increase androgen production, acting synergistically with LH; (2) insulin upregulates activity of P450c17-alpha (encoded by CYP17), the rate-limiting enzyme in ovarian/adrenal androgen biosynthesis; (3) insulin and LH co-stimulation causes premature/exaggerated theca-cell LH-receptor expression, amplifying gonadotropin-driven androgen output; (4) hyperinsulinemia suppresses hepatic synthesis of Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin (SHBG), raising free (bioactive) testosterone independent of any change in total testosterone. These form a self-sustaining 'vicious cycle' in which androgen excess and hyperinsulinemia mutually reinforce each other.
insulin_resistance_central_mechanism.source: Diamanti-Kandarakis E, Dunaif A. 'Insulin resistance and the polycystic ovary syndrome revisited: an update on mechanisms and implications', Endocr Rev 2012;33(6):981 (foundational review); PMC8107978 'Role of insulin and insulin resistance in androgen excess disorders'; PMC12278101 'Decoding androgen excess in polycystic ovary syndrome'

hpo_axis_dysregulation.mechanism: Real, well-characterised neuroendocrine defect: an increased frequency of hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility drives preferential pituitary secretion of LH over FSH (since faster GnRH pulse frequency favours LH-beta transcription while slower frequency favours FSH-beta transcription), producing the classically elevated LH:FSH ratio seen in many PCOS patients. This fast GnRH pulsatility is attributed to reduced hypothalamic sensitivity to the negative feedback of progesterone (and, in some models, oestradiol) on the GnRH pulse generator - hyperandrogenaemia itself blunts progesterone's slowing effect on GnRH pulses via upstream kisspeptin/neurokinin-B/dynorphin (KNDy) neurons, and hyperinsulinemia may independently increase kisspeptin secretion from these same KNDy neurons, further accelerating GnRH pulse frequency. The relatively elevated LH then chronically over-stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production, while relatively low FSH impairs normal follicular maturation/selection, contributing to anovulation and the arrested small antral follicles that constitute polycystic ovarian morphology.
hpo_axis_dysregulation.source: Moore AM et al. 'Neuroendocrine mechanisms responsible for elevated gonadotrophin-releasing hormone and luteinising hormone pulses in polycystic ovary syndrome', J Neuroendocrinol 2025; PMC11002031 'Mechanism of elevated LH/FSH ratio in lean PCOS revisited: a path analysis'
hpo_axis_dysregulation.clinical_note: An elevated LH:FSH ratio (classically cited as >2:1 or >=2, though not part of the formal Rotterdam diagnostic criteria) is a supportive biochemical finding, particularly in lean PCOS phenotypes, but is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to be a stand-alone diagnostic criterion and is not required in any of the three major diagnostic frameworks above.

genetic_familial_component.heritability_data: Real, substantial heritability demonstrated by twin/family studies. The Netherlands Twin Register study of 1,332 monozygotic and 1,873 dizygotic twin pairs found a PCOS concordance rate of 0.71 in monozygotic twins versus 0.38 in dizygotic twins, yielding an estimated additive genetic heritability of ~0.66-0.79 (0.79 when incorporating individual genetic contributions of component traits - oligomenorrhoea, acne, hirsutism). First-degree relatives (sisters, mothers) of PCOS probands show significantly increased rates of hyperandrogenism, oligomenorrhoea and metabolic abnormalities compared to the general population.
genetic_familial_component.gwas_caveat: Real, honestly-reported limitation: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified multiple PCOS-associated risk loci (including near genes such as DENND1A, THADA, FSHR, LHCGR), but these common variants collectively explain less than 10% of the estimated heritability - the majority of the genetic architecture of PCOS remains unexplained ('missing heritability'), an active area of ongoing research rather than a settled finding.
genetic_familial_component.source: Vink JM, Sadrzadeh S, Lambalk CB, Boomsma DI. 'Heritability of polycystic ovary syndrome in a Dutch twin-family study', J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2006;91(6):2100 (PMID 16219714); PMC4066994 'The Genetics of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome'
genetic_familial_component.confidence: high for the heritability estimate; high-confidence honest caveat on GWAS variance-explained

oligomenorrhea_amenorrhea.finding: Menstrual cycles longer than 35 days apart, or <=8-9 cycles per year (oligomenorrhoea), or absent menstruation for >=3 months (secondary amenorrhoea) - the clinical manifestation of the oligo-/anovulation criterion. Usually presents from adolescence onward as chronic cycle irregularity rather than a new-onset change (a new-onset change instead raises red-flag concern - see red_flags below).

hirsutism_ferriman_gallwey.finding: Excess terminal (coarse, pigmented) hair growth in a male-pattern distribution, assessed via the modified Ferriman-Gallwey (mFG) scoring system - the clinical gold standard. The modified system scores 9 body areas (upper lip, chin, chest, upper abdomen, lower abdomen, upper back, lower back/lumbosacral, upper arm, thigh - excluding the forearm and lower leg used in the original 11-area 1961 system), each scored 0 (no terminal hair) to 4 (frank virilised-pattern growth), for a total possible range of 0-36. A total score of >=8 is generally considered diagnostic threshold for hirsutism in most populations (with lower ethnicity-adjusted thresholds proposed for some East/Southeast Asian populations, where baseline terminal hair density is lower); a score of 8-15 indicates mild hirsutism, and >15 indicates moderate-to-severe hirsutism.
hirsutism_ferriman_gallwey.source: Ferriman D, Gallwey JD. 'Clinical assessment of body hair growth in women', J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1961;21:1440 (original); Hatch R et al., modified 9-area system, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1981;140(7):815; PMC5514800 'Modified Ferriman-Gallwey Score in Hirsutism and its Association with Metabolic Syndrome'

acne.finding: Persistent or adult-onset inflammatory acne, typically along the jawline/chin and lower face, often treatment-resistant to standard topical therapy, reflecting an androgen-driven increase in sebaceous gland size and sebum production - one of the three recognised clinical markers of hyperandrogenism (alongside hirsutism and androgenic alopecia).
acne.source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline clinical hyperandrogenism criteria; consistent with Rotterdam 2003 consensus

androgenic_alopecia.finding: Female-pattern hair thinning, classically diffuse thinning over the crown/vertex with preservation of the frontal hairline (Ludwig pattern), distinct from male-pattern androgenic alopecia. A recognised but less sensitive clinical marker of hyperandrogenism than hirsutism in PCOS.
androgenic_alopecia.source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline; AE-PCOS Society 2006 position statement

infertility_anovulation.finding: PCOS is the single most common cause of anovulatory infertility. Mechanism: disrupted folliculogenesis from the LH/FSH imbalance and locally elevated intra-ovarian androgens arrests antral follicle development before a dominant follicle is selected and ovulation occurs, producing chronic anovulation. This is a real, mechanistically distinct cause of infertility from tubal or male-factor infertility, and typically responds to ovulation-induction approaches (outside this entry's clinical/symptoms scope - covered under this KB's fertility-treatment/medicine scope, not duplicated here).
infertility_anovulation.source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline; Rotterdam 2003 consensus long-term health risk statement

acanthosis_nigricans.finding: Velvety, hyperpigmented, thickened skin plaques at the neck (nape), axillae and groin/skin flexures - a clinical marker of underlying insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia (mechanism identical to that already documented in this KB's obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry). In PCOS specifically, acanthosis nigricans should prompt formal metabolic screening (fasting glucose/insulin, lipid profile) regardless of BMI, since it can occur in lean PCOS patients as well.
acanthosis_nigricans.source: Cross-reference: obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry (PubMed 31769902; StatPearls NBK431057); applicability to PCOS per 2023 International PCOS Guideline metabolic screening recommendations

associated_long_term_risks_cross_referen: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - real, meta-analytically confirmed >3-fold increased risk: RR 3.45 (95% CI 2.95-4.05) across 23 studies/319,780 participants. Risk is obesity-amplified but not obesity-exclusive: RR 4.86 in obese PCOS patients vs RR 1.62 in non-obese PCOS patients (RR significantly elevated only in obese subgroup at 4.06, 95% CI 2.75-5.98, in a related pooled analysis). Peak T2DM incidence in PCOS patients occurs at age 35-45, some 10-15 years earlier than the general population. Full T2DM pathophysiology/management covered in this KB's diabetes_mellitus entry; shared core mechanism is the insulin resistance documented in pathophysiology above.

Dyslipidemia - covered in full in this KB's dyslipidemia entry; PCOS is strongly associated with an atherogenic lipid pattern (raised triglycerides, low HDL, elevated small-dense LDL) driven by the same insulin-resistance mechanism.

Obesity - covered in full in this KB's obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry; bidirectional relationship (obesity worsens hyperandrogenism/insulin resistance; PCOS-driven insulin resistance itself promotes weight gain). Critically, PCOS occurs in BOTH obese and lean patients - 'lean PCOS' (BMI in the normal/underweight range, roughly <=25 kg/m^2 or population-specific normal cutoff) constitutes a real, distinct and frequently underdiagnosed phenotype, estimated at 20-30% of PCOS patients overall, in whom clinicians may not suspect PCOS due to absence of the classically-associated overweight/obese body habitus, despite these patients still carrying real elevated insulin resistance and adipose-tissue dysfunction on formal testing.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) - covered in full in this KB's obstructive_sleep_apnea entry; PCOS carries a real, independently elevated OSA risk beyond what BMI alone explains. A large population-based cohort found PCOS patients 2.26x more likely to develop OSA on follow-up (95% CI 1.89-2.69) after adjustment for age, socioeconomic status, BMI, hypothyroidism and incident diabetes; a meta-analysis reported composite OSA odds ratio 9.52 (95% CI 3.90-23.26) in PCOS vs non-PCOS women, with risk elevated across all BMI categories though greatest at BMI >=30 (HR 2.1, 95% CI 1.72-2.56).

Endometrial cancer - a real, clinically important and often underappreciated long-term risk: PCOS is associated with an approximately 2.7-fold increased risk of endometrial cancer (ranges up to 2-6x reported across studies), mechanistically driven by chronic anovulation causing prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure of the endometrium without progesterone-mediated differentiation, compounded by insulin-resistance-driven mitogenic signalling and reduced SHBG raising bioavailable oestrogen.

Cardiovascular disease/ischaemic heart disease and hypertension - covered in full in this KB's ischaemic_heart_disease and hypertension entries; the 2023 International PCOS Guideline's own systematic review/meta-analysis update specifically examined and confirmed elevated clinical cardiovascular disease risk in PCOS, mediated substantially through the shared metabolic syndrome components (insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, central adiposity) already detailed above.

Anxiety and depression - real, large and consistent psychiatric comorbidity burden: meta-analyses report PCOS patients have markedly increased odds of any depressive symptoms (OR 3.78, 95% CI 3.03-4.72) and any anxiety symptoms (OR 5.62, 95% CI 3.22-9.80), with increased odds of clinically diagnosed depression (OR 2.79, 95% CI 2.23-3.50) and diagnosed anxiety (OR 2.75, 95% CI 2.10-3.60) specifically; pooled prevalence estimates for depression and anxiety among PCOS patients range from roughly 37-51% depending on the meta-analysis and population sampled.

risk_factor_source_citations.note: Relative risk / odds ratio figures cited above sourced individually per claim:
risk_factor_source_citations.t2dm_source: PMC8089828 'The Major Impact of Obesity on the Development of Type 2 Diabetes in Women With PCOS: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis'
risk_factor_source_citations.osa_source: PMC6410684 'Increased risk of obstructive sleep apnoea in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a population-based cohort study'; PMC12006010 'Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis'
risk_factor_source_citations.endometrial_cancer_source: Cancer risk and PCOS, PubMed 23624028; PMC7408229 'Endocrine Risk Factors of Endometrial Cancer: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, Oral Contraceptives, Infertility, Tamoxifen'
risk_factor_source_citations.psychiatric_source: Cooney LG et al. 'High prevalence of moderate and severe depressive and anxiety symptoms in polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Hum Reprod 2017;32(5):1075 (PMID 28333286); Brutocao C et al. 'Psychiatric disorders in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Endocrine 2018;62(2):318 (PMID 30066285)

components: Total and free testosterone (or Free Androgen Index calculated from total testosterone and SHBG) - primary biochemical evidence of hyperandrogenism; free testosterone is more sensitive than total testosterone since SHBG is often suppressed by hyperinsulinemia (see pathophysiology above)

LH and FSH with LH:FSH ratio - supportive but not a formal diagnostic criterion (see hpo_axis_dysregulation clinical_note above); most useful in lean PCOS phenotypes where the ratio elevation is more pronounced

DHEA-S (dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate) - primarily an adrenal androgen; used chiefly to help exclude an adrenal source of hyperandrogenism (adrenal tumour, non-classic CAH) rather than as a routine PCOS-confirming test, since DHEA-S is only mildly elevated (if at all) in typical PCOS
hormone_panel.source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline hormonal assessment recommendations

pelvic_ultrasound_pcom_criteria.current_2023_threshold: >=20 follicles measuring 2-9mm in diameter in at least one ovary (using modern transvaginal transducers of >=8MHz frequency), and/or an ovarian volume >=10 cm^3 in either ovary (with no dominant follicle or corpus luteum present).
pelvic_ultrasound_pcom_criteria.original_2003_threshold_for_reference: >=12 follicles 2-9mm per ovary and/or ovarian volume >10 cm^3 - the original Rotterdam 2003 figure, revised upward in 2023 specifically because higher-resolution modern ultrasound technology was detecting more follicles than the 2003-era equipment used to derive the original cutoff, risking PCOM over-diagnosis if the old threshold were kept.
pelvic_ultrasound_pcom_criteria.amh_alternative: In ADULTS only (not within 8 years of menarche), serum AMH may be used as an alternative to ultrasound to assess PCOM, given its strong correlation with antral follicle count - though AMH cutoffs are assay- and population-specific and are influenced by age, BMI, ethnicity and combined oral contraceptive use.
pelvic_ultrasound_pcom_criteria.source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline (Teede et al., JCEM 2023); original Rotterdam 2003 consensus for the historical threshold

exclusion_workup.purpose: Rotterdam, NIH and AE-PCOS Society criteria all REQUIRE exclusion of other causes of the same clinical picture before a PCOS diagnosis is made - PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion within its clinical criteria.
conditions_to_exclude: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (NCCAH, most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency) - excluded via early-follicular-phase (day 3-5) basal 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP); basal 17-OHP >2 ng/mL is found in ~87% of NCCAH patients vs only ~20-25% of PCOS patients and ~7% of healthy controls, so an elevated basal level should prompt an ACTH-stimulation test for confirmation
Cushing syndrome - screened via low-dose (1mg) overnight dexamethasone suppression test in patients with suggestive clinical features (central obesity, striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising)

Androgen-secreting tumour (ovarian or adrenal) - suspected when testosterone is markedly elevated (roughly >150-200 ng/dL or >2-3x the assay's upper limit of normal) especially with a NORMAL DHEA-S (suggesting ovarian rather than adrenal origin) and/or rapid symptom onset (see red_flags below)
Hyperprolactinemia - excluded via a fasting serum prolactin level
Thyroid dysfunction - excluded via TSH (cross-reference this KB's thyroid_disorders entry; both hypo- and hyperthyroidism can cause menstrual irregularity mimicking PCOS)
exclusion_workup.source: PMC9498167 'Differentiating Polycystic Ovary Syndrome from Adrenal Disorders'; 2023 International PCOS Guideline exclusion-of-mimics recommendations

real_risk_factors.factor: Family history / first-degree relative with PCOS
real_risk_factors.note: Real, substantial heritable component - see genetic_familial_component in pathophysiology above (twin-study heritability ~0.66-0.79); sisters and mothers of PCOS probands show significantly increased rates of hyperandrogenism and metabolic abnormalities.

Real, bidirectional relationship - obesity (particularly central/visceral adiposity, cross-reference obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry) worsens insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, while PCOS-driven insulin resistance and altered energy metabolism themselves promote weight gain and make weight loss harder to sustain. However, PCOS is NOT obesity-dependent (see lean PCOS above), so obesity is a risk-amplifying but not a necessary factor.
Real, central mechanistic driver present in both lean and obese PCOS phenotypes, not solely a downstream consequence of adiposity - see pathophysiology above.

Real, documented prevalence variation by ethnicity in meta-analyses - e.g., one meta-analysis found the lowest Rotterdam-criteria prevalence in Chinese women (~5.6%) and higher rates in Middle Eastern populations (Rotterdam ~16.0%, AES ~12.6%) - though comparisons are confounded by differing criteria/methodology used across the underlying studies, so ethnic-prevalence figures should be interpreted cautiously rather than as precise population truths.
real_risk_factors.source: PMC5707105 'The prevalence of polycystic ovary syndrome in reproductive-aged women of different ethnicity: a systematic review and meta-analysis'

global_by_criteria.finding: Real, honestly variable prevalence estimates that depend materially on which diagnostic framework is applied to the same underlying population - this is a genuine methodological feature of PCOS epidemiology, not an inconsistency to be smoothed over.
