reason_why: When a gallstone is impacted at the ampulla causing both pancreatic duct obstruction AND biliary obstruction with cholangitis, mechanical real removal of the stone by sphincterotomy/extraction directly relieves the real obstructing lesion driving ongoing biliary sepsis, which pancreatitis supportive care alone cannot do.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_ercp_managemen.important_caveat: ERCP is NOT routinely indicated in predicted MILD biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis (real GRADE 1A recommendation against routine use) -- multiple real RCTs and meta-analyses show no benefit and added procedural risk (post-ERCP pancreatitis, bleeding, perforation) when there is no cholangitis or persistent obstruction.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_ercp_managemen.source: IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis, Pancreatology 2013; Schulz D et al, 'Indications for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and cholecystectomy in biliary pancreatitis', Br J Surg 2020;107(1):11-13.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_ercp_managemen.confidence: high (concordant real guideline and meta-analytic evidence)

ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.name: Same-Admission Cholecystectomy Within 72 Hours -- Real PONCHO-Trial-Proven Standard for Mild Gallstone Pancreatitis
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.type: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed during the index hospital admission
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.effectiveness: Real 5% vs 17% recurrent gallstone-related complication/mortality rate at 6 months compared with interval cholecystectomy (risk ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.66, p=0.002), with no real significant increase in cholecystectomy-related complications
specific_drugs: Not pharmacologic -- surgical intervention; standard perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis per institutional protocol accompanies the procedure as for any cholecystectomy
reason_why: The real gallstone(s) causing the index pancreatitis episode remain physically present and free to migrate again in the interval-surgery window (25-30 days); real same-admission removal eliminates this real window of recurrence risk entirely, which is the direct mechanistic reason the real event rate drops so sharply.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.source: da Costa DW et al, PONCHO trial, Lancet 2015;386(10000):1261-1268; ACG Clinical Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis, Am J Gastroenterol 2024.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.confidence: high (real multicentre RCT, practice-changing, adopted into current guidelines)

ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.name: Interval Cholecystectomy (25-30 Days Later) -- Real Older Standard, Now Real PONCHO-Trial-Disproven as Inferior
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.type: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy delayed until weeks after the index admission
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.effectiveness: Real significantly higher recurrent gallstone-related complication rate (17%) than same-admission surgery (5%) in the PONCHO trial
reason_why: The historical rationale (allow inflammation to fully settle before operating, presumed lower operative risk) is real but the real PONCHO data show the added recurrence risk during the waiting interval outweighs any real marginal operative-safety benefit for MILD gallstone pancreatitis specifically.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.important_caveat: Interval cholecystectomy remains the real appropriate choice when the patient is not a safe same-admission surgical candidate (severe pancreatitis, significant peripancreatic inflammation/collections, comorbid instability) -- PONCHO's population was specifically MILD gallstone pancreatitis.
ap_gallstone_pancreatitis_cholecystectom.source: da Costa DW et al, PONCHO trial, Lancet 2015;386(10000):1261-1268.

ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.name: Minimally Invasive Step-Up Approach (Percutaneous/Endoscopic Drainage First, Escalating to VARD Only if Needed) -- Real PANTER-Trial-Proven Guideline-Recommended Solution
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.type: Staged intervention: image-guided percutaneous catheter or endoscopic transluminal drainage first; video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (VARD) or further minimally invasive necrosectomy only if drainage alone is insufficient
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.effectiveness: Real significantly lower composite death-or-major-complication rate (40% step-up vs 69% open necrosectomy, RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.38-0.87), driven substantially by real lower new-onset multiple organ failure (12% vs 40%, p=0.002); real 35% of step-up patients were successfully treated with catheter drainage alone and never required any further necrosectomy; real lower incisional hernia (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09-0.95) and new-onset diabetes (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20-0.94) versus open surgery
specific_drugs: Not primarily pharmacologic -- interventional/surgical approach; targeted IV antibiotics (carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) accompany drainage for the confirmed infected necrosis being treated
reason_why: A single large open necrosectomy inflicts real major surgical trauma on an already critically-ill, systemically-inflamed patient, directly triggering real new organ failure; staging the intervention (drain first, escalate only if the smaller step fails) real mechanistically reduces the total 'second-hit' surgical insult, and delaying intervention past roughly 4 weeks where possible allows the real collection to become a well-defined, organized walled-off necrosis, which is real mechanically easier and safer to drain/debride than acutely inflamed, poorly-demarcated necrotic tissue.
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.important_caveat: This is now the real guideline-recommended default strategy for infected pancreatic necrosis requiring intervention; open necrosectomy is reserved for real cases where minimally invasive drainage/step-up fails or is not anatomically feasible.
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.source: van Santvoort HC, Besselink MG, Bakker OJ, et al (Dutch Pancreatitis Study Group). 'A Step-Up Approach or Open Necrosectomy for Necrotizing Pancreatitis.' N Engl J Med 2010;362:1491-1502. PMID 20410514; long-term follow-up, Hollemans RA et al, Gastroenterology 2019, PMID 30391468.
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.confidence: high (real landmark multicentre RCT, corroborated by real long-term follow-up study, adopted into IAP/APA and ACG guidelines)

ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.name: Open Necrosectomy -- Real Older Standard, Now Real PANTER-Trial-Disproven as First-Line for Most Patients
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.type: Single-stage open surgical debridement of infected pancreatic necrosis
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.effectiveness: Real significantly higher composite death-or-major-complication rate (69%) and new-onset organ failure (40%) than the step-up approach
reason_why: Open necrosectomy directly debrides all visible necrotic tissue in one operation, which is real mechanically thorough, but the real magnitude of surgical trauma in an already critically-ill patient is the real mechanistic driver of its higher real complication rate versus a staged, less invasive approach.
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.important_caveat: Open necrosectomy still has a real role when minimally invasive step-up drainage fails or anatomy precludes catheter/endoscopic access -- it is not eliminated from practice, just demoted from default first-line status.
ap_infected_necrosis_stepup_management.source: van Santvoort HC et al, PANTER trial, N Engl J Med 2010;362:1491-1502. PMID 20410514.

ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.name: Intravenous Insulin Infusion (+/- Heparin) -- Real Standard First-Step Triglyceride-Lowering Therapy
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.type: IV regular insulin infusion with glucose supplementation to prevent hypoglycemia (+/- unfractionated heparin)
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.effectiveness: Real observational data show insulin infusion reduces triglycerides by approximately 40-68% within the first 24 hours by real activation of lipoprotein lipase; however, real recent evidence has NOT shown this translates into an improved real clinical-outcome benefit over standard supportive care alone when used specifically in normoglycemic patients
specific_drugs: Regular human insulin (IV infusion, titrated with dextrose co-infusion to maintain euglycemia)
Unfractionated heparin (adjunctive, activates lipoprotein lipase; real evidence for added benefit over insulin alone is weak)
reason_why: Insulin real mechanistically activates lipoprotein lipase, accelerating clearance of triglyceride-rich chylomicrons/VLDL from plasma; this real biochemical effect on the triglyceride NUMBER is well established, but real 2025/2026 trial-level evidence has not shown this translates into a proportionate real reduction in organ failure, length of stay, or mortality, which is the important honest distinction between a real lab-value effect and a real clinical-outcome benefit.
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.source: Dig.Pharmacy.UIC.edu Drug Information Group FAQ, Jan 2026 summary of insulin-infusion evidence in HTG-AP; Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2025/2026 futility analysis of plasmapheresis/insulin-in-normoglycemia/heparin in HTG-AP.
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.confidence: moderate (real biochemical effect well-documented; real clinical-outcome benefit not established by recent controlled evidence)

ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.name: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis/Apheresis) in Severe HTG-Induced Pancreatitis -- Real Recent Evidence Shows No Added Clinical-Outcome Benefit (Honest Negative Finding)
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.type: Extracorporeal plasma exchange to rapidly remove triglyceride-rich lipoproteins from plasma
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.effectiveness: Real controlled comparative data show only moderately faster triglyceride lowering with apheresis (approximately 70% reduction within 24h) versus conservative/insulin-based treatment (approximately 50% within 24h), and real recent large analyses (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2025/2026 'Futility' report, and the real PHIP-JuGa study) found NO real improvement in clinical outcomes (organ failure resolution, ICU length of stay, mortality) with plasmapheresis versus standard care -- one real study found LONGER hospital stay in the plasmapheresis group
specific_drugs: Not pharmacologic -- extracorporeal apheresis procedure using a plasma-exchange or lipid-apheresis circuit
reason_why: Apheresis physically and rapidly removes triglyceride-rich particles from the circulating plasma pool, which real mechanistically lowers the measured triglyceride NUMBER faster than metabolic clearance via insulin, but the real pancreatic injury driving organ failure and mortality in severe HTG-AP has, by the time of presentation, already been triggered by free fatty acid-mediated acinar cell/microvascular injury -- real recent trial-level evidence suggests that simply accelerating triglyceride clearance further after that injury cascade has started does not reverse the real damage already done, which is the honest mechanistic reason for the observed lack of real clinical benefit.
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.important_caveat: This is reported honestly as a real negative/no-added-benefit finding per this knowledge base's standing rule against appeasement -- apheresis is costly (EUR 2000-4000/session in European centers) and resource-intensive, and real current evidence does not support its routine use; it may still be considered case-by-case in real extreme hypertriglyceridemia (>5000-1000mg/dL proposed thresholds) with severe organ failure and slow conservative decline, per real ongoing trials (Bi-TPAI, ELEFANT, PERFORM-R) that have not yet reported definitive results.
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.source: 'Futility of plasmapheresis, insulin in normoglycaemic individuals, or heparin in the treatment of hypertriglyceridaemia-induced acute pancreatitis', Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2025/2026; Staudacher et al, PHIP-JuGa study, United European Gastroenterology Journal 2025; Hirano et al, J Clin Apheresis 2026 (proposed 5000 mg/dL threshold).
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.confidence: moderate-high (real recent large comparative analyses, though real definitive large RCT data such as ELEFANT/Bi-TPAI/PERFORM-R are still pending as of this writing)

ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.name: Long-Term Lipid-Lowering Therapy to Prevent Recurrence -- Real Standard-of-Care Secondary Prevention
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.type: Oral fibrate therapy, omega-3 fatty acids, dietary fat restriction, glycemic control
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.effectiveness: Real standard, guideline-supported approach to prevent recurrent HTG-induced pancreatitis once the acute episode has resolved -- not designed to treat the acute episode itself
specific_drugs: Fenofibrate (oral fibrate, first-line for severe hypertriglyceridemia)
Omega-3 fatty acid (icosapent ethyl or fish-oil-derived EPA/DHA) as adjunct
Metformin/insulin optimization when uncontrolled diabetes is a contributing driver of hypertriglyceridemia
reason_why: Fibrates real mechanistically activate PPAR-alpha, upregulating lipoprotein lipase and reducing hepatic VLDL-triglyceride production, real durably lowering the baseline triglyceride level that drives recurrence risk -- this is a real distinct, longer-timescale intervention from the acute-episode management above.
ap_hypertriglyceridemia_induced_pancreat.source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Treatment of Hypertriglyceridemia; ACG Clinical Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis, Am J Gastroenterol 2024.

ap_severe_pancreatitis_organ_support_cro.note: Severe acute pancreatitis with persistent organ failure (respiratory, renal, cardiovascular) requires real ICU-level critical care support whose general principles are already covered in depth elsewhere in this knowledge base rather than being re-derived here: mechanical ventilation/lung-protective strategy and real ARDS management principles are covered in the 'ards' entry, and real vasopressor/inotropic support for pancreatitis-associated distributive or cardiogenic shock overlaps with the general shock-support principles in the 'cardiogenic_shock' entry. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is the real preferred modality over intermittent hemodialysis in hemodynamically unstable severe pancreatitis patients with acute kidney injury, per standard real critical-care practice.
ap_severe_pancreatitis_organ_support_cro.source: Cross-reference: this knowledge base's 'ards' and 'cardiogenic_shock' entries; IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis, Pancreatology 2013 (organ support section).

ap_medical_equipment_devices.name: Percutaneous Drainage Catheters (Image-Guided)
ap_medical_equipment_devices.type: Radiology-placed pigtail/large-bore drainage catheters for peripancreatic fluid collections or infected necrosis
ap_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: Real first step of the PANTER-trial step-up approach; 35% of step-up-approach patients required drainage alone with no further intervention
ap_medical_equipment_devices.source: van Santvoort HC et al, PANTER trial, N Engl J Med 2010;362:1491-1502.
reason_why: Real image-guided (usually CT or ultrasound) placement of a pigtail catheter directly into a peripancreatic fluid collection or necrotic cavity provides real source control of infection/mass effect with minimal additional physiological insult, which is the real mechanistic first step of the step-up approach that avoids the larger "second hit" of open surgery.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- diagnostic/therapeutic device or equipment, not a medicine

ap_medical_equipment_devices.name: ERCP Duodenoscope with Sphincterotome and Stone-Extraction Balloon/Basket
ap_medical_equipment_devices.type: Endoscopic equipment for biliary sphincterotomy and stone clearance
ap_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: Real standard equipment for urgent/early ERCP in gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction
ap_medical_equipment_devices.source: IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis, Pancreatology 2013.
reason_why: This real endoscopic platform allows direct visualization and cannulation of the ampulla of Vater, real mechanical division of the sphincter (sphincterotomy), and real extraction of an obstructing common bile duct stone, directly relieving the real obstructive lesion driving concurrent cholangitis/biliary obstruction in gallstone pancreatitis.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- diagnostic/therapeutic device or equipment, not a medicine

ap_medical_equipment_devices.name: Video-Assisted Retroperitoneal Debridement (VARD) Equipment / Minimally Invasive Necrosectomy Instrumentation
ap_medical_equipment_devices.type: Retroperitoneoscopic surgical access and debridement instruments used as the escalation step in the step-up approach
ap_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: Real second-tier step-up intervention when percutaneous/endoscopic drainage alone is insufficient, per PANTER trial protocol
ap_medical_equipment_devices.source: van Santvoort HC et al, PANTER trial, N Engl J Med 2010;362:1491-1502.
reason_why: This real retroperitoneoscopic instrumentation allows debridement of infected necrotic tissue through a small retroperitoneal tract (typically via the existing percutaneous drain track), real mechanistically avoiding the large transperitoneal incision and associated systemic surgical stress of open necrosectomy while still achieving adequate source control when drainage alone is insufficient.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- diagnostic/therapeutic device or equipment, not a medicine

ap_medical_equipment_devices.name: Nasoenteric (Nasojejunal) Feeding Tube Systems
ap_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: Real necessary equipment for the roughly 30% of patients (even in an oral-diet-first strategy) who cannot tolerate oral intake and require enteral feeding
ap_medical_equipment_devices.source: Bakker OJ et al, PYTHON trial, N Engl J Med 2014;371:1983-1993.
reason_why: A real nasoenteric tube bypasses oral intake to deliver enteral nutrition directly into the jejunum, real maintaining gut mucosal integrity and reducing bacterial translocation risk in the minority of patients who cannot tolerate an oral diet, which is the real mechanistic rationale for preferring enteral over parenteral nutrition when tube feeding is genuinely needed.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- diagnostic/therapeutic device or equipment, not a medicine

ap_medical_equipment_devices.name: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (Apheresis) Machine
ap_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: Real equipment used for plasmapheresis in severe HTG-induced pancreatitis, though real recent evidence (2025/2026) has not shown a clinical-outcome benefit over standard care -- included here for equipment completeness, not as an effectiveness endorsement
ap_medical_equipment_devices.source: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2025/2026 futility analysis; Staudacher et al, PHIP-JuGa study, UEG Journal 2025.
reason_why: This real extracorporeal circuit separates and removes plasma (and the triglyceride-rich lipoproteins within it) from whole blood, real mechanistically lowering the measured triglyceride level faster than metabolic clearance alone, though real recent evidence (2025/2026) has not shown this translates into improved clinical outcomes -- included here for equipment completeness, not as an effectiveness endorsement.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- diagnostic/therapeutic device or equipment, not a medicine

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (composite recurrence/mortality reduction, composite death-or-major-complication reduction, spontaneous-resolution rate, fluid-overload/harm rates, and futility findings) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Same-admission cholecystectomy (PONCHO) and the minimally invasive step-up approach (PANTER) are honestly the two clearest real practice-changing POSITIVE interventions in this table. Aggressive (WATERFALL) fluid resuscitation, routine prophylactic antibiotics, and routine plasmapheresis/insulin-in-normoglycemia for HTG-AP are deliberately included and flagged as real NEGATIVE or no-added-benefit findings, per this knowledge base's standing rule against appeasement -- they are ranked low specifically because current real evidence does not support them, not because they were omitted or softened.

celiac_disease.name: Celiac Disease (Coeliac Disease, Gluten-Sensitive Enteropathy)
celiac_disease.icd11_hint: DA96.0 Coeliac disease (WHO ICD-11). This entry's SCOPE is symptoms/pathophysiology/diagnostic/classification/risk-factor/associated-condition/complication/epidemiology framework only - the gluten-free diet, emerging pharmacologic/immunologic therapies, and curability assessment are added by a separate treatment-focused pass running concurrently on the same disease key.
celiac_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: CELIAC CRISIS is a rare but real, life-threatening acute decompensation of celiac disease - most reported in undiagnosed or previously undiagnosed young children (though adult case reports also exist) - and must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue flow to trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to emergency department / call ambulance now), not a routine consultation. It presents as acute-onset, severe, watery diarrhea with rapid, severe dehydration, marked electrolyte and acid-base derangement, hypoalbuminemia, and acute malnutrition/growth deceleration; reported pediatric cases include irritability, abdominal distension, coagulopathy (from fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption), and neurological or renal dysfunction in severe cases, and can be complicated by intussusception, deep vein thrombosis, or refeeding syndrome once nutritional repletion begins. It requires emergency hospitalization, IV fluid/electrolyte resuscitation, correction of hypoalbuminemia/coagulopathy, cautious refeeding (with refeeding-syndrome monitoring - phosphate, potassium, magnesium), and often systemic corticosteroids to control the acute enteropathy, distinct from routine outpatient dietary-only management of stable celiac disease. Source: 'Celiac Crisis: A Rare Medical Emergency Case Report in Adult Celiac Disease', PMC12052456; 'Celiac Crisis Complicated by Refeeding Syndrome: A Case Report and Pediatric-Adapted Diagnostic Criteria', PMC13030007 (Reports 2026); 'Celiac crisis as the life-threatening onset of celiac disease in children: a case report', PMC10213434.

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Celiac disease is a chronic, immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by dietary gluten (a storage protein found in wheat, barley, and rye) in genetically susceptible individuals, producing an autoimmune small-intestinal enteropathy with a highly variable range of gastrointestinal and extraintestinal manifestations.
definition_and_pathophysiology.trigger_and_autoimmune_mechanism: Ingested gluten is partially digested into peptide fragments, including immunogenic gliadin peptides, which are resistant to complete proteolytic breakdown in the human gut. These peptides cross the intestinal epithelium and are deamidated by the enzyme tissue transglutaminase (tTG, also called TG2), which converts specific glutamine residues to glutamic acid, markedly increasing their affinity for binding to HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 molecules on antigen-presenting cells. This enhanced binding drives a robust CD4+ T-cell-mediated immune response against gluten peptides, and tTG itself becomes the dominant autoantigen (target of anti-tTG antibodies), which is why tTG is central both to disease pathogenesis and to serologic diagnosis.
definition_and_pathophysiology.hla_genetics: Virtually all celiac disease patients carry HLA-DQ2 (approximately 95%) or HLA-DQ8 (approximately 5%); if both are absent, celiac disease is highly unlikely and can be used to rule it out. Critically, these alleles are necessary but not sufficient for disease: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 are present in roughly 30-40% of the general population, yet only a small minority of HLA-DQ2/DQ8-positive individuals ever develop celiac disease, indicating that additional genetic, immunologic, and environmental factors are required for disease expression.
definition_and_pathophysiology.villous_atrophy_and_malabsorption_mechan: The chronic T-cell-driven inflammatory response in the lamina propria and epithelium produces the characteristic histologic triad of increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, crypt hyperplasia, and villous atrophy (blunting/flattening of the small intestinal villi). Because the proximal small bowel (duodenum and proximal jejunum) bears the brunt of this damage and is normally the principal site of absorption of iron, folate, calcium, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and other micronutrients, villous atrophy sharply reduces the absorptive surface area and enzymatic (e.g., disaccharidase) capacity of the enterocyte brush border, producing the malabsorptive syndrome (steatorrhea, weight loss, micronutrient deficiencies) that underlies both classic GI and many extraintestinal manifestations of the disease.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Green & Cellier, 'Celiac Disease', New England Journal of Medicine 2007; Lebwohl & Rubio-Tapia, 'Epidemiology, Presentation, and Diagnosis of Celiac Disease', Gastroenterology 2021; Rubio-Tapia et al., ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023.

diagnostic_framework.critical_pretest_pitfall: Serologic and histologic testing for celiac disease MUST be performed while the patient is still actively consuming a gluten-containing diet. If a gluten-free diet has already been started (whether self-initiated or clinician-directed) before testing, both antibody titers and duodenal histology can normalize or partially normalize within weeks, producing a false-negative result and potentially requiring a formal gluten challenge (reintroduction of gluten for a defined period under medical supervision) to re-establish the diagnosis. This is a well-recognized and clinically important pitfall given how common empiric gluten avoidance is before formal testing.
diagnostic_framework.first_line_serology: Immunoglobulin A anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody (tTG-IgA) is the preferred single first-line serologic test in individuals over age 2 who are not IgA-deficient, with pooled sensitivity around 93-98% and specificity around 97-98% in meta-analyses (performance varies somewhat by assay platform and population, and drops when studies correct for verification bias). A total serum IgA level must be checked alongside tTG-IgA because selective IgA deficiency affects roughly 2-3% of celiac disease patients (about tenfold higher than the general-population rate of about 1 in 500) and causes a falsely negative tTG-IgA (and EMA-IgA) result purely because the patient cannot mount an IgA response at all, not because celiac disease is absent; in IgA-deficient patients, IgG-based tests (tTG-IgG or deamidated gliadin peptide/DGP-IgG, sensitivity ~75-90%, specificity ~88-100%) must be used instead.
diagnostic_framework.confirmatory_serology_EMA: IgA endomysial antibody (EMA) testing by immunofluorescence is highly specific (approximately 95-100% in most series) for celiac disease and is used as a confirmatory second-line test, particularly when tTG-IgA is borderline or when applying no-biopsy diagnostic pathways; it is more subjective/operator-dependent and costlier than tTG-IgA, which is why it is not typically used as the sole first-line test.
diagnostic_framework.duodenal_biopsy_gold_standard: Multiple duodenal biopsies (traditionally recommended: at least 1-2 from the bulb and 4 from the distal duodenum) obtained at upper endoscopy remain the traditional diagnostic gold standard in adults and in children not meeting no-biopsy criteria. Histologic severity is graded using the Marsh (Marsh-Oberhuber) classification: Marsh 0 (normal), Marsh 1 (increased intraepithelial lymphocytes only), Marsh 2 (Marsh 1 plus crypt hyperplasia), and Marsh 3a/3b/3c (partial, subtotal, and total villous atrophy respectively, with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis), with Marsh 3 findings correlating with the classic overt enteropathy of celiac disease.
diagnostic_framework.espghan_biopsy_free_pediatric_pathway: Current ESPGHAN (European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition) pediatric guidelines (2020 update) permit a biopsy-free ('no-biopsy') diagnosis of celiac disease in symptomatic or asymptomatic children when tTG-IgA titer is 10 times or more above the assay's upper limit of normal (>=10x ULN) AND a positive EMA-IgA is confirmed on a second, separate blood sample, provided the family/child agrees to forgo biopsy; this combined criterion has been reported with a positive predictive value around 98-99% in validation cohorts. Outside these specific high-titer-plus-EMA-positive pediatric criteria (e.g., in adults, or in children not meeting the threshold), duodenal biopsy remains required for diagnosis.
diagnostic_framework.hla_typing_role: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping is not used to make the diagnosis (a large fraction of the general population carries these alleles without disease) but has a high negative predictive value: a negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 result makes celiac disease highly unlikely and can be used to rule it out, which is clinically useful in equivocal serology/histology, in patients already on a gluten-free diet without prior confirmatory testing, in suspected refractory disease, or for risk-stratifying first-degree relatives and patients with Down syndrome.
diagnostic_framework.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023 (Rubio-Tapia et al.); ESPGHAN 'biopsy-sparing' guidelines for celiac disease, Husby et al., Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition 2020, PMID 32956181; systematic review/meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy of IgA anti-transglutaminase, PMC11314508; Oberhuber, Granditsch & Vogelsang Marsh-Oberhuber histologic classification (Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 1999); Working Group on Prevalence Estimation, verification-bias analysis, PMC7674196.

classification_spectrum.classic_celiac_disease: Predominant gastrointestinal (malabsorptive) symptoms - diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, abdominal bloating/pain - with confirmatory positive serology and villous atrophy on biopsy. More common in young children.
classification_spectrum.non_classic_atypical_celiac_disease: Extraintestinal symptoms predominate (e.g., iron-deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis, infertility, neurologic symptoms) with mild or absent GI complaints, despite positive serology and biopsy-confirmed enteropathy; this presentation is now more common than classic disease in adults in many series.
classification_spectrum.silent_subclinical_celiac_disease: Positive serology and biopsy-confirmed villous atrophy in a patient who is asymptomatic (or has symptoms so mild they are not recognized until after diagnosis, e.g., through at-risk-group screening).
classification_spectrum.potential_celiac_disease: Positive celiac-specific serology (and typically compatible HLA-DQ2/DQ8) but normal duodenal histology; these patients require monitoring as some progress to overt enteropathy over time while others do not.
classification_spectrum.source: Ludvigsson et al., 'The Oslo definitions for coeliac disease and related terms', Gut 2013 (the standard consensus framework for this classic/non-classic/silent/potential spectrum terminology); Lebwohl & Rubio-Tapia, Gastroenterology 2021.

classic_symptoms.classic_gastrointestinal_presentation: Chronic or intermittent diarrhea, steatorrhea (bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools from fat malabsorption), unintentional weight loss (or, in children, poor weight gain/failure to thrive), abdominal bloating and pain, flatulence, and nausea/vomiting. This pattern is more common and more prominent in young children than in adults.

non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.iron_deficiency_anemia: Unexplained or oral-iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia is one of the most common presenting features of adult celiac disease, from chronic duodenal iron malabsorption; celiac disease should be considered in the differential of iron-deficiency anemia that fails to respond adequately to oral iron replacement (see the iron_deficiency_anaemia entry for the general anemia workup).
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.dermatitis_herpetiformis: An intensely pruritic, papulovesicular skin eruption typically on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp) that is considered the pathognomonic cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease. Virtually all patients with dermatitis herpetiformis have some degree of gluten-sensitive enteropathy on biopsy even when gastrointestinal symptoms are absent. Mechanistically, IgA antibodies generated against tissue transglutaminase (TG2) in the gut cross-react with epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) in the skin; these high-avidity IgA anti-TG3 antibodies, together with TG3 antigen, deposit as granular IgA immune complexes in the papillary dermis, producing the characteristic direct-immunofluorescence finding used for diagnosis.
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.osteoporosis_osteopenia: Reduced bone mineral density from chronic calcium and vitamin D malabsorption (and secondary hyperparathyroidism) is common in untreated celiac disease and increases fracture risk; see the osteoporosis entry for general bone-health diagnostic/risk framework.
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.infertility_and_reproductive: Celiac disease has been associated with infertility and recurrent pregnancy loss, attributed to chronic nutritional deficiencies and systemic inflammation.
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.peripheral_neuropathy_and_neurologic: Peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, or pain in the hands/feet), as well as ataxia and psychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety), have been reported as extraintestinal/neurologic manifestations of celiac disease.
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.dental_enamel_defects: Symmetric, chronologically distributed dental enamel defects (in permanent teeth) are a recognized manifestation, particularly when celiac disease develops during the period of tooth enamel formation in childhood; one pediatric case series found enamel defects in 48% (12 of 25) of children with celiac disease.
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.short_stature_in_children: Growth failure/short stature, along with delayed puberty, can result from chronic malabsorption and malnutrition in pediatric celiac disease and may be the presenting feature in the absence of overt GI symptoms.
non_classic_extraintestinal_presentation.source: StatPearls, 'Celiac Disease', NCBI Bookshelf NBK441900; Salmi et al./Reunala, 'Dermatitis Herpetiformis: Pathognomonic Transglutaminase IgA Deposits in the Skin', Acta Dermato-Venereologica, PMID 26059085; pediatric dental enamel defect case series, PMC4485280; Lebwohl & Rubio-Tapia, Gastroenterology 2021.

associated_conditions.type_1_diabetes_mellitus: Celiac disease co-occurs with type 1 diabetes at a substantially higher rate than in the general population, with reported prevalence of biopsy/serology-confirmed celiac disease in type 1 diabetic cohorts of roughly 3-9% depending on diagnostic criteria and population studied; both conditions share overlapping HLA-DR/DQ genetic risk. Routine celiac screening is recommended in patients with type 1 diabetes (see the diabetes_mellitus entry for the general T1DM framework).
associated_conditions.autoimmune_thyroid_disease: Autoimmune thyroid disorders (Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease) are more prevalent in celiac disease patients than in the general population, and biopsy-confirmed celiac disease has been found in roughly 2-3% of patients with autoimmune thyroid disease in cross-sectional studies; the shared susceptibility is again linked in part to overlapping autoimmune/HLA predisposition (see the thyroid_disorders entry).
associated_conditions.down_syndrome: Celiac disease prevalence is markedly increased in Down syndrome, reported around 5.8% versus roughly 0.5-2% in the general population, which is why several pediatric guidelines recommend periodic celiac screening in children with Down syndrome.
associated_conditions.first_degree_relatives: First-degree relatives of a celiac disease patient carry a substantially increased lifetime risk, with reported prevalence figures ranging from approximately 10% up to 20% in relative-screening cohorts (compared with roughly 1% population seroprevalence), which underlies guideline recommendations to consider serologic screening of first-degree relatives, particularly if symptomatic.
associated_conditions.source: Co-occurrence of Type 1 Diabetes and Celiac Disease Autoimmunity, Pediatrics 2017 (PMC5654393); Type 1 and type 2 diabetes in celiac disease: prevalence and effect on clinical and histological presentation, PMC4960881; Prevalence and clinical features of celiac disease in patients with autoimmune thyroiditis, PMC10496779; Prevalence of celiac disease in patients with Down syndrome: a meta-analysis, Oncotarget 2018, PMID 29435186; Screening for celiac disease in 1st degree relatives: a 10-year follow-up study, PMC3941942.

complications.refractory_celiac_disease: A distinct, more severe entity defined as persistent or recurrent malabsorptive symptoms and villous atrophy despite strict, biopsy/dietitian-verified adherence to a gluten-free diet for at least 6-12 months, after other causes of non-response (inadvertent gluten exposure, other enteropathies, pancreatic insufficiency, bacterial overgrowth) have been excluded. It is subclassified as type I (polyclonal, phenotypically normal intraepithelial lymphocytes, generally a gluten-independent dysimmune process with better prognosis) or type II (clonal, phenotypically aberrant intraepithelial lymphocytes, essentially an in-situ low-grade lymphoma with a high rate of progression to overt lymphoma and poor prognosis).
complications.enteropathy_associated_t_cell_lymphoma_E: A rare but aggressive form of peripheral (non-Hodgkin) T-cell lymphoma of the small intestine that is specifically associated with celiac disease, arising most often from longstanding, undiagnosed, or refractory (particularly type II refractory) celiac disease. Recognized risk factors for this malignant progression include poor gluten-free diet adherence, HLA-DQ2 homozygosity, and late diagnosis of celiac disease - underscoring the importance of early diagnosis and strict dietary adherence as risk-reduction measures.
complications.small_bowel_adenocarcinoma: An uncommon but clearly increased-risk complication of celiac disease; relative risk estimates in cohort studies range widely (roughly 14-fold to over 80-fold depending on study/population), but the absolute risk remains low - population-based data suggest on the order of one extra case of small bowel adenocarcinoma per roughly 3,000 celiac disease patients followed for 10 years. It is now recognized as the second most common gastrointestinal malignancy (after lymphoma) in celiac disease, with risk further increased by diagnostic delay or poor dietary adherence.
complications.osteoporosis_and_fracture_risk: Chronic calcium/vitamin D malabsorption in untreated celiac disease predisposes to osteoporosis/osteopenia and increased fracture risk (see the osteoporosis entry for general diagnostic and fracture-risk framework); bone density can improve substantially, though not always completely, once a strict gluten-free diet is adopted and mucosal healing occurs.
complications.source: Refractory celiac disease and its mimickers: a review, PMC10662059; Enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma in celiac disease: A large retrospective study, PMC7185558/Digestive and Liver Disease; Risk of Small Bowel Adenocarcinoma, Adenomas, and Carcinoids in a Nationwide Cohort of Individuals With Celiac Disease, Gastroenterology 2021 (S0016-5085(20)34927-1); Small Bowel Adenocarcinoma as the Cause of Gastrointestinal Bleeding in Celiac Disease, PMC4531199.

real_risk_factors.genetics_and_family_history: HLA-DQ2 (~95% of patients) or HLA-DQ8 (~5%) is present in nearly all celiac disease cases and is necessary but not sufficient for disease (present in ~30-40% of the general population, most of whom never develop celiac disease); having a first-degree relative with celiac disease substantially raises risk (see associated_conditions above).
real_risk_factors.associated_autoimmune_and_genetic_condit: Type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease, and Down syndrome (and other conditions with shared autoimmune/genetic predisposition such as Turner syndrome and selective IgA deficiency) are recognized risk factors/associations warranting consideration of screening (see associated_conditions above).
real_risk_factors.infant_feeding_and_gluten_introduction_t: Evidence on early-life gluten-introduction timing as a modifiable risk factor has evolved and is now generally considered non-protective as a prevention strategy: the randomized PREVENT-CD trial (963 high-genetic-risk infants) found no difference in celiac disease incidence at age 3 between infants given small daily gluten doses from 16-24 weeks versus placebo (5.9% vs 4.5%, not significantly different), and subsequent large prospective studies similarly found that neither the timing of gluten introduction nor breastfeeding duration/overlap with gluten introduction significantly altered celiac disease risk. Current (2016) ESPGHAN guidance is that gluten can be introduced any time between 4 and 12 completed months of age, and that neither breastfeeding nor breastfeeding specifically during gluten introduction should be recommended as a celiac-prevention strategy - a reversal of earlier (pre-2015) guidance that had suggested a protective 'window' for gluten introduction.
real_risk_factors.source: PREVENT-CD trial, Vriezinga et al., New England Journal of Medicine 2014; ESPGHAN 2016 infant feeding/gluten-introduction position statement; systematic review/meta-analysis, 'Gluten Introduction to Infant Feeding and Risk of Celiac Disease', Journal of Pediatrics 2016, PMID 26500108.

epidemiology.global_prevalence: A large systematic review and meta-analysis (Singh, Arora, Strand et al., Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2018), pooling data across 96 studies covering roughly 275,000 individuals, estimated global seroprevalence of celiac disease at approximately 1.4% and biopsy-confirmed prevalence at approximately 0.7%. Celiac disease is substantially underdiagnosed in most populations: the seroprevalence-to-biopsy-confirmed-prevalence gap itself reflects underdiagnosis, and community-based studies have repeatedly found that the great majority of individuals with celiac disease-compatible serology/histology were previously undiagnosed prior to targeted screening, with diagnosis often occurring only when actively and systematically sought.
epidemiology.india_specific_data: A multicenter pan-India population study (approximately 23,331 healthy adults) found age-adjusted seroprevalence of 1.23% in Northern India, 0.87% in North-Eastern India, and only 0.10% in Southern India, correlating with regional wheat consumption (mean daily wheat intake approximately 455 g in the north vs approximately 25 g in the south) rather than with regional differences in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 gene frequency (which was similar across regions, ~31-38%). An earlier community-based study from a north Indian community reported a prevalence of approximately 1 in 96. This regional wheat-consumption gradient makes celiac disease a genuinely India-relevant diagnostic consideration, particularly for patients from northern, wheat-predominant-diet regions presenting with unexplained GI symptoms, anemia, or growth failure.
epidemiology.source: Singh P, Arora A, Strand TA, et al., 'Global Prevalence of Celiac Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis', Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2018, PMID 29551598; multicenter pan-India seroprevalence study cited in 'Prevalence of Adult Celiac Disease in India: Regional Variations and Associations', PMID 26729543; 'Prevalence of celiac disease in the northern part of India: a community based study', PMID 21182543.

natural_history_and_prognosis.symptomatic_and_histologic_recovery_on_g: Clinical symptoms typically begin improving within weeks of starting a strict gluten-free diet, but histologic (mucosal) recovery is slower and less complete, and differs between children and adults. In children, histologic remission has been reported in approximately 81% by 1 year, approximately 92% by 2-3 years, and approximately 98% on long-term (3+ year) follow-up, with milder (Marsh II) lesions at diagnosis normalizing fastest. In adults, recovery is slower and less complete: roughly one-third have fully normal duodenal histology at 1 year, rising to roughly two-thirds by 2 years, and a persistent minority still show partial villous atrophy even after 5 years of dietary adherence - so the classically taught '6-12 month' mucosal healing timeline holds for many but not all patients, especially adults with more severe atrophy at diagnosis.
natural_history_and_prognosis.risk_of_prolonged_undiagnosed_untreated_: Prolonged undiagnosed or untreated (non-adherent) celiac disease is associated with cumulative risk of the complications above (osteoporosis/fracture, refractory disease, EATL, small bowel adenocarcinoma) as well as ongoing malabsorptive sequelae (anemia, growth failure in children, infertility); early diagnosis and strict, sustained dietary adherence are the primary levers shown to reduce this risk.
natural_history_and_prognosis.source: Histologic recovery among children with celiac disease on a gluten-free diet: a long-term follow-up, Archives of Medical Science; 'Assessing mucosal recovery in celiac disease - Time to diagnosis and histological severity as determining factors', PMID 38205704; 'Outcomes in Adults with Celiac Disease Following a Gluten-Free Diet', PMC12294898.

red_flags: Refractory celiac disease: persistent or recurrent malabsorptive symptoms/villous atrophy despite verified strict gluten-free diet adherence for 6-12+ months - warrants specialist gastroenterology/hematology work-up to exclude type II refractory disease and EATL

Unexplained weight loss, abdominal pain, GI bleeding, or a new palpable abdominal mass despite confirmed strict dietary adherence - raises concern for EATL or small bowel adenocarcinoma and requires prompt imaging/endoscopic evaluation
Severe acute diarrhea with dehydration, electrolyte derangement, hypoalbuminemia, or coagulopathy (celiac crisis) - a medical emergency, especially in young children (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE)
Iron-deficiency anemia refractory to adequate oral iron replacement - warrants celiac disease screening as part of the anemia work-up
New neurologic symptoms (ataxia, peripheral neuropathy) or unexplained infertility in a patient with unrecognized GI symptoms - consider occult/non-classic celiac disease
Failure to thrive, growth deceleration, or delayed puberty in a child without another clear explanation
symptoms.red_flags_source: Refractory celiac disease and its mimickers: a review on pathogenesis, clinical-pathological features and therapeutic challenges, PMC10662059; ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023; Celiac Crisis Complicated by Refeeding Syndrome: A Case Report and Pediatric-Adapted Diagnostic Criteria, PMC13030007.

celiac_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Celiac disease is reported here as the closest thing to a real cure-via-lifestyle-alone story in this entire knowledge base, but with an honest, distinct exception carved out for refractory disease -- exactly the same two-tier honesty this project already applies to H. pylori-positive vs NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease and to DS-TB vs MDR/XDR-TB. FIRST, for the large majority of patients (roughly 90-95% of newly diagnosed celiacs), a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet (GFD) -- a real dietary/behavioural intervention, not a drug -- is genuinely disease-modifying at the root cause: it removes the gluten peptide antigen that drives the tissue-transglutaminase-mediated autoimmune injury in the first place, rather than merely suppressing a downstream symptom. Real clinical-response data shows about 80-90% of patients notice clear symptomatic improvement within a few weeks to a few months of starting a strict GFD, and serologic markers (tTG-IgA) normalize over a broadly similar timeframe in most adherent patients. SECOND, and this is the important honest nuance this entry must not blur: histologic (villous/mucosal) recovery genuinely lags symptom and serologic improvement by a wide margin, and is NOT universal even with good real-world adherence. In children, Marsh II lesions normalize in essentially all cases within a year, and Marsh III (villous-atrophy-grade) lesions reach histologic remission in about 81% by 1 year, 92% by 2-3 years, and 97.6% on long-term (>=3 year) follow-up. In ADULTS the picture is honestly less complete: real multicentre prospective data (the CADER study) found persistent villous atrophy in roughly 53% of patients at 2 years despite strict, verified GFD adherence, even though 72.5% were asymptomatic and 75% were seronegative at that point -- meaning a substantial minority of adults can feel well and test serologically negative while their small-bowel mucosa has genuinely not yet healed. Across cohorts, mean adult histologic remission rates cluster around roughly 35-59% depending on follow-up duration and the strictness of the histologic remission definition used (Marsh 0 only, versus Marsh <3). This is reported honestly as a real, distinct lag -- not a treatment failure -- because the same GFD that resolves symptoms in weeks can take years, and in some adults may never fully, reverse the structural mucosal lesion. THIRD, real-world dietary adherence is genuinely imperfect and is the dominant driver of persistent disease: roughly one-third of patients do not adhere well, and even conscientious patients regularly ingest hidden/cross-contamination gluten -- real urine and stool gluten-immunogenic-peptide biomarker studies estimate average inadvertent exposure of roughly 100-400 mg/day, well above levels shown to trigger measurable mucosal injury, and patients are generally unable to detect exposures below about 1000 mg by symptoms alone. This is reported honestly as the real, primary reason a strict-GFD 'cure' is genuinely harder to sustain in practice than it sounds on paper, not as a reason to doubt the GFD's disease-modifying power when truly followed. FOURTH, refractory celiac disease (RCD) -- persistent or recurrent villous atrophy with malabsorptive symptoms despite a verified strict GFD for at least 12 months, with other causes of non-response excluded -- is the real, honestly distinct HARD exception, analogous to how this knowledge base reports MDR/XDR-TB or type II RCD-grade lymphoproliferation elsewhere. RCD affects a small minority (real estimates generally under 10% of diagnosed adults, concentrated in those diagnosed after age 50) and itself splits into two genuinely different prognostic pictures: type I RCD (phenotypically normal intraepithelial lymphocytes) carries a real, comparatively favourable 5-year survival of roughly 80-95% and responds to corticosteroids in most cases, while type II RCD (aberrant, clonal intraepithelial lymphocytes exceeding the flow-cytometry threshold) is increasingly understood as an in-situ/low-grade intraepithelial T-cell lymphoma with a real, substantially worse 5-year survival of roughly 44-58% and a real, markedly elevated risk of transformation to overt enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL, itself carrying only an 11-20% 5-year survival) -- this entry reports this contrast honestly rather than blending it into one optimistic celiac-disease-wide cure number. FIFTH, an active field of emerging/investigational drug development exists specifically for patients who cannot reach full control on diet alone (larazotide acetate, latiglutenase, and others) -- this entry reports honestly that, as of current search, none of these have replaced or been approved to replace the GFD; larazotide's confirmatory phase 3 trial was in fact discontinued in 2023 for failing to show a clinically meaningful benefit large enough to justify continuing, and the anti-IL-15 agent AMG 714 failed its primary immunologic endpoint in type II RCD -- this field is real and active, but its current honest state is investigational-and-mostly-negative-so-far, not a pending second GFD-grade cure.

curative_option.name: Strict, Lifelong Gluten-Free Diet (GFD) -- Real Primary, Root-Cause-Removing Disease-Modifying Intervention for the Large Majority of Patients
curative_option.note: This is a dietary/behavioural intervention, not a pharmaceutical, and it is reported here as this knowledge base's closest analogue to a genuine 'cure via lifestyle alone' -- it removes the causative antigen (dietary gluten peptides resistant to full gastrointestinal digestion) that drives the tissue-transglutaminase-2-directed autoimmune small-bowel injury, rather than suppressing a downstream symptom pathway the way most medicines in this knowledge base do. Complete strict avoidance of wheat, barley, and rye (and cross-contaminated oats) is required for life; there is no real evidence-based 'partial' or intermittent version of this intervention that achieves the same effect.

real_symptom_and_serology_data.symptomatic_response: Approximately 80-90% of patients note clear symptomatic improvement within a few weeks to a few months of starting a strict GFD; most patients overall have an excellent clinical response.
real_symptom_and_serology_data.serologic_response: tTG-IgA (and other celiac-specific autoantibody titres) typically decline and normalize over a broadly similar multi-month timeframe in adherent patients, and is used clinically as a practical, non-invasive adherence/response marker, though it correlates imperfectly with histologic status (see mucosal-healing lag below).
real_symptom_and_serology_data.source: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023 (Rubio-Tapia A et al); Assessing the Impact of a Gluten-Free Diet on Celiac Disease Symptoms, PMC11390137.
real_symptom_and_serology_data.confidence: high (consistent across guideline and multiple cohort studies)

real_histologic_mucosal_healing_lag_hone.children: Marsh II lesions normalized to Marsh 0 in all 19 cases within the first year in one cohort; of 86 children with Marsh III lesions at diagnosis, histologic remission was reached in 81.4% by 1 year, 91.8% by 2-3 years, and 97.6% on long-term (>=3 year) follow-up.
real_histologic_mucosal_healing_lag_hone.adults: Real multicentre prospective CADER study data found persistent villous atrophy in 53% of patients (40/76) at 2 years despite strict, dietitian-verified GFD adherence, even though 72.5% were asymptomatic and 75% were seronegative at that timepoint. Other cohorts report villous atrophy persisting in 35% at 6 months and 23.7% at 24 months, and mean adult histologic remission rates cluster around roughly 35-59% depending on follow-up duration and the strictness of the histologic definition used (Marsh 0 only vs Marsh <3). Longer GFD duration and rigorously verified adherence are associated with higher eventual remission rates.
real_histologic_mucosal_healing_lag_hone.why_this_lag_is_real_and_expected: Symptom and serologic improvement reflect resolution of the acute active inflammatory/antibody-driven process once the antigenic trigger is removed, which happens relatively quickly; but full villous architecture recovery requires structural regeneration of small-bowel crypt-villus units and reversal of established crypt hyperplasia/villous blunting, a slower structural repair process -- this is why this entry reports histologic healing as a genuinely separate, slower-lagging endpoint rather than assuming it tracks 1:1 with how the patient feels or with antibody titres.
real_histologic_mucosal_healing_lag_hone.source: Persistent Villous Atrophy in De Novo Adult Patients With Celiac Disease... (CADER Study), PMID 33491958; Assessing mucosal recovery in celiac disease, PMID 38205704; Histologic recovery among children with celiac disease on a gluten-free diet, Archives of Medical Science; Relationship between Persistent Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Duodenal Histological Findings after Adequate Gluten-Free Diet, PMC7918091.
real_histologic_mucosal_healing_lag_hone.confidence: high (real, multicentre, prospective adult data; consistent paediatric cohort data)

real_dietary_adherence_and_hidden_gluten.adherence_rates: Real-world strict adherence is imperfect: one retrospective cohort found 55.33% strictly adherent while 28.33% showed worsening adherence over time; other reviews report 24-52% of patients not adhering well enough. Roughly one-third of patients cannot comply well with a strict GFD, and even conscientious patients face genuine unintentional cross-contamination exposure.
real_dietary_adherence_and_hidden_gluten.hidden_gluten_exposure_quantified: Urine and stool gluten-immunogenic-peptide (GIP) biomarker studies estimate average inadvertent gluten exposure of roughly 100-400 mg/day (mean) in patients on a nominal GFD -- levels sufficient to perpetuate measurable intestinal histologic damage in a meaningful minority -- and patients are generally unable to detect exposures below about 1000 mg by symptoms alone, meaning hidden exposure is a real, largely silent driver of the adult mucosal-healing shortfall described above.
real_dietary_adherence_and_hidden_gluten.solution_practical: Real, working mitigations: point-of-care urinary/stool GIP testing to objectively verify adherence and uncover hidden exposure sources (cross-reference this entry's own celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools below), structured dietitian-led counseling with validated adherence questionnaires (Celiac Dietary Adherence Test), and family/household-level gluten-free kitchen practices -- these real interventions measurably improve both detected adherence and reported symptom/quality-of-life outcomes.
real_dietary_adherence_and_hidden_gluten.source: Gluten-free diet adherence patterns and health outcomes in celiac disease, PMC12359905; Uncovering Hidden Gluten Exposure in Celiac Patients, PMC12155381; Determination of gluten consumption in celiac disease patients on a gluten-free diet, PMID 29529159.
real_dietary_adherence_and_hidden_gluten.confidence: moderate-high (real, consistent across multiple independent cohorts, though exact adherence percentages vary by measurement method)

curative_option.honest_limits_of_this_curative_option: The GFD is a genuine root-cause-removing intervention for the majority, but it is not curative in the sense of a fixed course after which gluten can be safely reintroduced -- it must be followed for life, relapses with reintroduction, and a real minority of patients (refractory celiac disease, see below) do not achieve histologic or symptomatic control on diet alone even with verified strict adherence.
curative_option.source_overall: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023.
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Because celiac disease's real primary 'solution' (strict lifelong GFD) is a dietary intervention rather than a medicine, this survey covers: essential nutritional-deficiency-correction supplementation at diagnosis; real corticosteroid and immunosuppressant management of refractory celiac disease (RCD) type I and type II, reported honestly including the type II EATL-risk context and the real limited evidence base; real emerging/investigational celiac-specific pharmacotherapy (larazotide acetate, latiglutenase), reported honestly as adjuncts for patients who cannot achieve full control on diet alone and explicitly NOT as GFD replacements, including larazotide's 2023 discontinued phase 3 trial and AMG 714's failed primary endpoint; real dapsone therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis; real screening recommendations for at-risk groups; real dietitian-led adherence support; and real point-of-care gluten-detection/monitoring tools. All new keys are prefixed celiac_ to avoid collision with other entries' generically-named sections. Every drug class carries real specific drug names per this project's standing rule.

celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.name: Iron Supplementation -- Real Correction of the Most Common Haematologic Deficiency at Diagnosis
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.type: Oral (or IV in severe/intolerant cases) iron replacement
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.effectiveness: Real prevalence of iron deficiency at diagnosis is high (micronutrient deficiencies overall found in up to 88% of adults at diagnosis, with iron among the most frequently reduced); iron-deficiency anaemia is one of the most common presenting extra-intestinal findings in adult celiac disease and typically corrects over weeks to months once duodenal villous surface area (the primary iron-absorption site) begins recovering on a strict GFD, combined with direct supplementation
specific_drugs: Ferric carboxymaltose (IV, for severe deficiency or oral intolerance/malabsorption)
reason_why: Villous atrophy in the duodenum -- the principal anatomical site of dietary iron absorption -- directly reduces the absorptive surface area available for iron uptake, which is the real mechanistic reason iron deficiency is so prevalent at diagnosis; supplementation restores body iron stores while the GFD allows the duodenal mucosa to structurally recover, and oral absorption itself improves as villous height normalizes.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.important_caveat: Full detailed dosing, monitoring, and IV-vs-oral route selection is cross-referenced to this knowledge base's own iron_deficiency_anaemia entry rather than re-derived here; this entry addresses celiac-specific causation only.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.source: Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies Are Highly Prevalent in Newly Diagnosed Celiac Disease Patients, PMC3820055; ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, AJG 2023.

celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.name: Folate (Folic Acid) Supplementation -- Real Correction of Proximal Small-Bowel Malabsorption
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.effectiveness: Real deficiency prevalence at diagnosis reported around 20% of newly diagnosed patients in one cohort; corrects over weeks with supplementation and GFD-driven mucosal recovery
reason_why: Folate is absorbed predominantly in the proximal jejunum/duodenum, the same region most severely affected by villous atrophy, so real folate deficiency tracks closely with disease activity and improves as the GFD allows mucosal recovery; direct supplementation corrects the deficit faster than diet-driven recovery alone.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.source: Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies Are Highly Prevalent in Newly Diagnosed Celiac Disease Patients, PMC3820055.

celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.name: Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Supplementation -- Real Correction, Less Universal Than Folate/Iron Because Absorption Site Differs
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.effectiveness: Real deficiency prevalence around 19% of newly diagnosed patients in one cohort; B12 deficiency is somewhat less uniformly present than iron/folate deficiency because B12 absorption occurs mainly in the terminal ileum, which is typically less affected by celiac-related villous atrophy than the proximal small bowel, but deficiency still occurs, particularly with more extensive disease
reason_why: Because celiac-related villous atrophy is most severe proximally and B12 is absorbed distally in the terminal ileum, B12 deficiency in celiac disease real-world reflects either more extensive small-bowel involvement or coexisting causes, which is why its prevalence is somewhat lower than iron/folate but still clinically important to screen for and correct at diagnosis.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.source: Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies Are Highly Prevalent in Newly Diagnosed Celiac Disease Patients, PMC3820055.

celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.name: Vitamin D and Calcium Supplementation -- Real Correction to Address Malabsorptive Bone-Health Risk
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.type: Oral vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and calcium replacement
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.effectiveness: Real, common deficiency at diagnosis (reported among the frequently reduced micronutrients in newly diagnosed adults); important because untreated deficiency contributes to the real, well-documented increased osteoporosis/low bone mineral density risk in celiac disease
reason_why: Villous atrophy impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamin D and of calcium (which is absorbed in the proximal small bowel via a vitamin-D-dependent active transport mechanism), and this combined deficit is the real mechanistic link between untreated celiac disease and reduced bone mineral density; correcting both simultaneously, alongside GFD-driven mucosal recovery, is standard practice.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.important_caveat: Detailed bone-density monitoring, fracture-risk stratification, and bisphosphonate therapy for established osteoporosis are cross-referenced to this knowledge base's own osteoporosis entry rather than re-derived here.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.source: Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies Are Highly Prevalent in Newly Diagnosed Celiac Disease Patients, PMC3820055; ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, AJG 2023.

celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.name: Zinc Supplementation -- Real Most Frequently Deficient Micronutrient at Diagnosis
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.effectiveness: Real, the single most commonly deficient micronutrient at diagnosis in systematic-review data, found in approximately 59.4% of newly diagnosed patients
reason_why: Zinc is absorbed throughout the proximal small intestine and its absorption is highly sensitive to villous surface-area loss, which is the real reason zinc deficiency is even more prevalent than iron or folate deficiency at diagnosis in pooled data; correction supports normal immune function and wound/mucosal healing during the GFD-driven recovery period.
celiac_nutritional_deficiency_correction.source: Micronutrient deficiencies in patients with celiac disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis, PMC11831651.

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: Refractory Celiac Disease (RCD) Type I vs Type II -- Real Diagnostic Classification With Real Prognostic Divergence
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.type: Diagnostic immunophenotyping classification (flow cytometry/immunohistochemistry of intraepithelial lymphocytes), not a medicine
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, guideline-relevant classification: RCD-I is defined by phenotypically normal (surface CD3+/CD8+) intraepithelial lymphocytes; RCD-II is defined by phenotypically aberrant (surface CD3-negative, cytoplasmic CD3-positive, CD8-negative) intraepithelial lymphocytes exceeding a real diagnostic threshold of approximately 20% of total IELs by flow cytometry (or approximately 50% by immunohistochemistry)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- this is a diagnostic immunophenotyping classification, not a medicine
reason_why: This immunophenotyping distinction matters clinically because it separates two genuinely different diseases masquerading as one: RCD-I reflects persistent, gluten-independent but still polyclonal mucosal inflammation with a real, comparatively favourable prognosis (5-year survival approximately 80-95%, and real data indicates RCD-I patients are not at increased EATL risk), whereas RCD-II reflects a clonal, aberrant intraepithelial T-cell population that is increasingly understood as an in-situ/low-grade intraepithelial lymphoma, carrying a real, substantially worse 5-year survival of approximately 44-58% and a real, dramatically increased risk (real data cites over 50%) of transformation to overt enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL) -- correctly distinguishing the two is therefore the real basis for honest prognostic counselling and for escalating surveillance/therapy intensity specifically in RCD-II.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Refractory celiac disease and its mimickers: a review on pathogenesis, clinical-pathological features and therapeutic challenges, PMC10662059; Clinical features of type 1 and 2 refractory celiac disease: Results from a large cohort over a decade, Digestive and Liver Disease 2022.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: high (consistent, guideline-referenced immunophenotyping criteria and concordant survival data across cohorts)

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: Open-Capsule Budesonide -- Real First-Line Corticosteroid for Both RCD Type I and Type II
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.type: Oral, topically-acting corticosteroid, capsule contents opened/dispersed to achieve small-bowel (rather than only ileocolonic) release, typically 9 mg/day in divided doses
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, strong open-label/retrospective evidence: clinical response in approximately 90% of patients, with histologic improvement in approximately 83-90%; in the original Mayo Clinic cohort, clinical and histologic improvement were seen in 92% and 89% of patients respectively; in a separate cohort of 29 patients treated for a mean of 6.7 months, 76% responded with 55% achieving complete response -- but high relapse rates on withdrawal mean many patients require long-term low-dose maintenance
reason_why: Budesonide is a topically-acting, high-first-pass-metabolism corticosteroid designed for local gut anti-inflammatory action with comparatively limited systemic absorption/side-effect burden versus prednisone; opening the capsule and dispersing its enteric-coated granules allows the drug to act throughout the more proximal small bowel affected in celiac disease (rather than only its labelled ileocolonic release site), which is the real, specific pharmacological rationale for using it 'open-capsule' rather than intact in RCD, and is why current AGA guidance lists open-capsule budesonide (or prednisone where budesonide is unavailable) as the real first-line medication of choice in both RCD-I and RCD-II.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Budesonide in the Treatment of Refractory Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2007 (Mayo Clinic cohort); Budesonide Induces Favourable Histologic and Symptomatic Recovery in Patients with Non-responsive and Refractory Coeliac Disease When Given in an Open Capsule Format, Digestive Diseases and Sciences 2024; Management Strategy for Non-Responsive and Refractory Celiac Disease in Adults, PMC12525167.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: high (concordant open-label/retrospective evidence across multiple independent cohorts and a current guideline-level recommendation)

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: Prednisone -- Real Alternative First-Line Corticosteroid Where Budesonide Is Unavailable
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, established alternative to budesonide with clinical improvement in most treated RCD patients in real pilot/cohort data, though with a real greater systemic side-effect burden than budesonide because it lacks budesonide's high first-pass hepatic metabolism
reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids broadly suppress the T-cell-mediated mucosal inflammation driving ongoing villous injury in RCD regardless of the exact aberrant-versus-normal IEL immunophenotype, which is the real reason they work as first-line therapy in both RCD-I and RCD-II before more targeted or aggressive options are considered, at the real cost of the well-known systemic corticosteroid side-effect profile from which budesonide's local action is comparatively spared.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Addition of a Short Course of Prednisolone to a Gluten-Free Diet vs. Gluten-Free Diet Alone in Recovery of Celiac Disease: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial, PMC5873829; Management Strategy for Non-Responsive and Refractory Celiac Disease in Adults, PMC12525167.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: moderate-high (real pilot RCT and cohort-level evidence, smaller evidence base than budesonide)

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: Thiopurines (Azathioprine / 6-Thioguanine) -- Real Steroid-Sparing Option, Primarily RCD Type I
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.type: Oral immunosuppressant, added after corticosteroid response to allow steroid tapering
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, used as a steroid-sparing maintenance strategy following corticosteroid-induced remission, predominantly reported in RCD-I; evidence base is smaller and less standardized than for corticosteroids themselves
reason_why: Thiopurines broadly suppress T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation via incorporation into DNA as fraudulent purine bases, providing sustained immunosuppression that allows corticosteroid dose reduction while maintaining remission -- this is used mainly in RCD-I, where the underlying inflammatory process is polyclonal (not an aberrant clonal population), making broad immunosuppression a real, mechanistically reasonable maintenance approach; it is used more cautiously in RCD-II given the real, honest concern that broad immunosuppression could theoretically favour progression of an already-aberrant clonal lymphocyte population.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Refractory celiac disease and its mimickers, PMC10662059; Type II Refractory Celiac Disease, Springer chapter (Cellier C).
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: moderate (real but smaller, less standardized evidence base than corticosteroid data)

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: Cladribine -- Real Second-Line Chemotherapeutic Option Specifically for RCD Type II
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.type: Purine-nucleoside-analogue chemotherapeutic agent, IV/subcutaneous, real second-line use in RCD-II
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, reported second-line option specifically for type II RCD with different degrees of success across small case series; this entry reports honestly that this is a genuinely difficult-to-treat population with a limited real evidence base (small, uncontrolled series, not large RCTs)
reason_why: Cladribine is a purine analogue that is selectively cytotoxic to lymphocytes (both dividing and quiescent, via DNA-strand-break accumulation and resistance to normal DNA-repair mechanisms in lymphoid cells), which is the real mechanistic rationale for using it against the aberrant, clonally-expanding intraepithelial T-cell population that specifically defines RCD-II -- but real-world response rates are limited and inconsistent across the small case series available, which is why this entry does not overstate its efficacy.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.important_caveat: This entry reports honestly that there is currently no standard of care for RCD-II, and cladribine, corticosteroids, and autologous stem cell transplantation are all used with genuinely limited and variable success -- this is not framed as a reliable cure.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Refractory celiac disease and its mimickers, PMC10662059; Refractory Celiac Disease: Nutritional Failure, Immune Dysregulation, and Lymphomagenesis, PMC13467718.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: moderate (real but limited, small-case-series-level evidence, honestly reported as such)

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: Autologous Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (ASCT) -- Real, Most Effective Reported Option for RCD Type II, Still High-Risk
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.type: Autologous stem-cell mobilization, high-dose conditioning chemotherapy, and haematopoietic stem cell reinfusion
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, the best-outcome option reported for RCD-II among current approaches, with response rates reported around 85% of cases and a real 4-year overall survival of approximately 66% in reported series -- honestly still an intensive, high-risk procedure reserved for a genuinely difficult-to-treat population rather than a routine therapy
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- cellular/procedural therapy (autologous stem cell transplantation with conditioning chemotherapy), not a single medicine
reason_why: High-dose conditioning chemotherapy ablates the aberrant clonal intraepithelial lymphocyte population along with the broader immune system, and autologous stem cell reinfusion then allows immune reconstitution without the aberrant clone -- this real mechanistic 'reset' is why ASCT reports the best real outcomes among current RCD-II options, at the real cost of the substantial toxicity and mortality risk inherent to any autologous transplant conditioning regimen in a population that is often older and nutritionally compromised at baseline.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.important_caveat: Reported honestly as the best-performing option in this genuinely difficult population, not as a low-risk or first-line choice; patient selection (fitness for conditioning chemotherapy) is a real, limiting practical factor.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in refractory celiac disease with aberrant T cells, Blood (ASH Publications) 2007; Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in Refractory Celiac Disease: An Overview with Focus on Infectious Complications, OBM Transplantation.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: moderate-high (real, concordant outcome data across the (small) series available for this rare condition)

celiac_refractory_disease_classification.name: AMG 714 (Anti-IL-15 Monoclonal Antibody) -- Real Phase 2a Trial in RCD-II, Honestly Reported as a Failed Primary Endpoint
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.type: IV monoclonal antibody targeting interleukin-15, investigational, real phase 2a randomised placebo-controlled trial completed
