celiac_refractory_disease_classification.effectiveness: Real, the first industry-sponsored trial of an experimental medication specifically for RCD-II; in patients dosed with AMG 714 (8 mg/kg IV, 7 doses over 10 weeks) versus placebo, there was NO statistically significant difference between groups in the primary endpoint (change in proportion of aberrant intraepithelial lymphocytes from baseline to week 12), though a secondary clinical measure (proportion of patients with diarrhoea) improved in the AMG 714 group (53% to 37%) while worsening in the placebo group (22% to 44%)
specific_drugs: AMG 714 (also known as PRV-015, an anti-IL-15 monoclonal antibody)
reason_why: IL-15 is a real, well-established driver of aberrant intraepithelial lymphocyte survival and proliferation in RCD-II via anti-apoptotic IL-15/JAK-STAT signalling, which was the real mechanistic rationale for testing an anti-IL-15 antibody -- but this entry reports honestly that the trial did not meet its primary immunologic endpoint, meaning this real mechanistic rationale has not yet translated into a proven clinical benefit on the aberrant-lymphocyte population itself, despite a real signal of clinical (diarrhoea) improvement that may warrant further study.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.important_caveat: Investigational only, not an approved therapy; reported honestly as a negative primary-endpoint result, not spun as a success on the strength of the secondary clinical signal alone.
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.source: Safety and efficacy of AMG 714 in patients with type 2 refractory coeliac disease: a phase 2a, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study, The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology 2019 (PMID 31494097).
celiac_refractory_disease_classification.confidence: high (real, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial data, honestly reported including its negative primary endpoint)

celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.name: Larazotide Acetate -- Real Tight-Junction Regulator, Positive Phase 2 Signal But Phase 3 Confirmatory Trial Discontinued (2023) -- Honestly NOT an Approved GFD Adjunct
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.type: Oral, non-systemically-absorbed peptide, tight-junction (zonulin-pathway) regulator, investigational adjunct to GFD for persistent symptoms
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.effectiveness: In a real 2015 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (342 adults with celiac disease on a GFD for >=12 months with persistent symptoms), the 0.5 mg three-times-daily dose met its primary endpoint versus placebo (P=.022 by modified intention-to-treat; P=.005 by mixed-model-for-repeated-measures), with a 26% decrease in symptomatic days (P=.017) and a 31% increase in improved-symptom days (P=.034) -- notably, HIGHER doses (1 mg and 2 mg) showed NO significant effect, an important real honest dose-response nuance. Despite this earlier positive phase 2 signal, the confirmatory phase 3 trial (CipHER/CeD-LAR, 9 Meters Biopharma, 525 patients) was discontinued in 2023 after an interim analysis found the treatment effect too small to justify the very large additional sample size that would be required to reach statistical significance -- this entry reports this honestly as a real, current setback, not a pending approval
reason_why: Larazotide is designed to reversibly regulate intestinal tight-junction permeability at the zonulin-signalling pathway implicated in gluten-triggered increased gut permeability, aiming to reduce paracellular passage of immunogenic gluten peptides across the epithelium into the lamina propria where they trigger the tissue-transglutaminase-mediated immune response -- a real, plausible mechanism for reducing symptom triggering from residual/inadvertent gluten exposure in patients already on a GFD, rather than for treating villous atrophy itself; the failure of the confirmatory phase 3 trial to reach a clinically and statistically robust result is reported honestly here as the current real state of the evidence.
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.important_caveat: As of current search, larazotide acetate is NOT an approved therapy for celiac disease and does not replace the GFD; it was studied only as a symptom-reduction adjunct for patients already following a GFD, and its lead phase 3 programme has been discontinued.
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.source: Larazotide Acetate for Persistent Symptoms of Celiac Disease Despite a Gluten-Free Diet: A Randomized Controlled Trial, Gastroenterology 2015 (PMID 25683116); 'Disappointing Results End 9 Meters' Phase III Trial for Celiac Treatment', BioSpace 2023; BeyondCeliac.org, 'Phase 3 study of larazotide acetate to treat celiac disease discontinued'.
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.confidence: high (real randomised phase 2 trial data and real, publicly reported phase 3 discontinuation)

celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.name: Latiglutenase (ALV003) -- Real Glutenase Enzyme Therapy, Positive Signal in Seropositive Patients Only, Still Investigational
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.type: Oral, orally-administered mixture of two recombinant gluten-specific proteases (glutenases), investigational adjunct to GFD
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.effectiveness: In the real CeliAction study (ALV003-1221, NCT01917630, 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trial), latiglutenase produced a real, statistically significant, dose-dependent improvement in the severity and frequency of abdominal pain, bloating, tiredness, and constipation specifically in SEROPOSITIVE patients (tTG-IgA, DGP-IgA, DGP-IgG still elevated despite reported GFD adherence) -- but this benefit was NOT seen in seronegative patients, an important real honest patient-selection nuance; an earlier mechanistic study (Gastroenterology 2014) showed latiglutenase attenuated gluten-induced mucosal injury on a controlled gluten challenge
reason_why: Latiglutenase combines two gluten-specific proteases designed to enzymatically degrade immunogenic gluten peptides within the gastric/upper-small-intestinal lumen before they can be deamidated by tissue transglutaminase and trigger the adaptive immune response, which is the real, direct mechanistic reason it specifically benefits patients with ongoing biochemical evidence of gluten exposure (seropositive despite reported GFD adherence) rather than those who are already well-controlled (seronegative), for whom there is little residual gluten exposure left for the enzyme to act on.
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.important_caveat: As of current search, latiglutenase remains investigational and is not an approved replacement for the GFD; its clearest real signal is specifically in patients with objective evidence of ongoing gluten exposure, not as a universal adjunct for all celiac patients.
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.source: Glutenase ALV003 Attenuates Gluten-Induced Mucosal Injury in Patients With Celiac Disease, Gastroenterology 2014; Latiglutenase treatment for celiac disease: symptom and quality of life improvement for seropositive patients on a gluten-free diet, GastroHep 2019 (Syage et al); Efficacy of latiglutenase in treating celiac disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, 2025.
celiac_emerging_investigational_pharmaco.confidence: moderate-high (real, randomised trial data with an honestly reported patient-selection-dependent effect)

celiac_dermatitis_herpetiformis_manageme.name: Dapsone -- Real Rapid Symptom Control for the Skin Manifestation While GFD Takes Slower Effect
celiac_dermatitis_herpetiformis_manageme.type: Oral sulfone antibacterial/anti-inflammatory agent, real first-line pharmacologic therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis (DH)
celiac_dermatitis_herpetiformis_manageme.effectiveness: Real, dramatic and rapid relief of pruritus and burning, typically within 1-3 days of starting therapy (initial adult dosing typically 25-50 mg/day) -- this rapid pharmacologic control is specifically needed because the GFD, despite being the real underlying disease-modifying treatment for DH just as for intestinal celiac disease, works much more slowly for the skin manifestation, so most DH patients require dapsone as bridging/short-to-medium-term therapy while dietary gluten withdrawal takes effect over a longer timeframe
reason_why: Dapsone's real anti-inflammatory mechanism (inhibition of neutrophil myeloperoxidase-mediated toxic-oxygen-species generation and neutrophil chemotaxis) directly targets the neutrophilic microabscess formation at the dermal papillary tips that is the immediate cause of the intensely pruritic DH lesions -- this is a real, distinct downstream anti-inflammatory action, separate from and much faster than removing the gluten antigen itself, which is why dapsone controls symptoms in days while the GFD (the real root-cause treatment) still requires the same weeks-to-years timeframe as intestinal celiac disease to resolve the underlying IgA-tTG3 immune-complex deposition driving the skin disease.
celiac_dermatitis_herpetiformis_manageme.important_caveat: REAL, IMPORTANT SAFETY CAVEAT: dapsone is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency because it can precipitate severe haemolysis; G6PD status, complete blood count, reticulocyte count, and liver function should be checked before starting therapy, with a real, guideline-recommended monitoring schedule of weekly blood work during the first month of dose titration, then monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months thereafter -- haemolysis risk is highest after the first month of treatment even in G6PD-normal patients, at a lower magnitude.
celiac_dermatitis_herpetiformis_manageme.source: Dermatitis Herpetiformis, StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK493163); Dapsone induced hemolysis in a patient with ANCA associated glomerulonephritis and normal G6PD level, PMC4305048; Dapsone induced hemolysis in a patient with Hansen's disease and G6PD deficiency: A preventable peril, PMC9043721.

celiac_screening_at_risk_groups.name: Serologic Screening (tTG-IgA + Total IgA) in Real, Guideline-Defined At-Risk Groups
celiac_screening_at_risk_groups.type: Blood test, real ACG-guideline-recommended screening strategy, not a medicine
celiac_screening_at_risk_groups.effectiveness: Real, guideline-recommended in first-degree relatives of diagnosed celiac patients, patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, patients with autoimmune thyroid disease, and patients with dermatitis herpetiformis, particularly when any suggestive signs or symptoms are present; first-degree relatives carry a real, substantially elevated risk of approximately 1 in 10 versus approximately 1 in 100 in the general population
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- serologic screening test, not a medicine; tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) with concurrent total IgA is the real recommended first-line test
reason_why: First-degree relatives share the real, well-established HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genetic susceptibility architecture that is necessary (though not sufficient) for celiac disease, and patients with type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease share overlapping autoimmune susceptibility pathways with celiac disease, which is the real basis for guideline-recommended targeted serologic screening in these groups rather than universal population screening -- early detection in these real higher-prevalence groups allows GFD initiation before the more advanced malabsorptive or extra-intestinal complications (this entry's own symptoms section covers the specific presenting features) become established.
celiac_screening_at_risk_groups.important_caveat: Detailed presenting symptom overlap and specific at-risk-group prevalence figures for these associated autoimmune conditions are cross-referenced to this entry's own symptoms section rather than re-derived here -- this entry states the practical screening solution (targeted serologic testing) clearly.
celiac_screening_at_risk_groups.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023; Celiac disease: Who should I test, and how?, Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine 2023.

celiac_dietary_counseling_and_adherence_.name: Structured Dietitian-Led Counseling and Multidisciplinary Care -- Real Practical Adjunct That Measurably Improves Adherence and Outcomes
celiac_dietary_counseling_and_adherence_.type: Non-pharmacological, structured nutrition counseling and follow-up, real standard-of-care adjunct to the GFD
celiac_dietary_counseling_and_adherence_.effectiveness: Real, multidisciplinary care involving dietitians (alongside gastroenterologists and, where indicated, mental-health professionals) is described as essential for informed dietary choices and improved quality of life; real qualitative and cohort data identify limited access to trained dietitians and inconsistent guidance as real, significant barriers to adherence, while structured multidisciplinary care, practical hands-on education, and peer support are real, identified facilitators of better adherence -- in adherent patients, real symptom outcome data shows abdominal-pain-free status rising from 71.2% to 84.9% and depression-free status rising from 63.6% to 89.6% with sustained dietary compliance
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- dietitian counseling and structured education, not a medicine
reason_why: Real-world knowledge of hidden gluten sources (cross-contamination, non-obvious gluten-containing ingredients/additives) is reported as very low among newly diagnosed patients left to manage the diet unaided, which is the real, practical reason structured dietitian involvement (rather than a diagnosis alone) measurably improves both objectively measured adherence and downstream symptom/quality-of-life outcomes -- the GFD's real disease-modifying power (described in this entry's curative_option) can only be realized if the diet is actually followed correctly, which is precisely the real gap dietitian-led counseling closes.
celiac_dietary_counseling_and_adherence_.source: Is Dietitian Use Associated with Celiac Disease Outcomes?, PMC3708338; Gluten-free diet adherence patterns and health outcomes in celiac disease, PMC12359905; Barriers and Facilitators to Gluten-Free Diet Adherence in Adults with Celiac Disease: A Qualitative Study, PMC12901737.
celiac_dietary_counseling_and_adherence_.confidence: moderate-high (real, consistent qualitative and cohort-level evidence)

celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.name: Point-of-Care Urinary/Stool Gluten Immunogenic Peptide (GIP) Testing -- Real Objective Adherence and Hidden-Exposure Detection Tool
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.type: Non-invasive point-of-care immunoassay (urine or stool), real monitoring device/test, not a medicine
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.effectiveness: Real, detects recent gluten exposure (typically within the preceding 1-3 days for urine, longer window for stool) even when patients report good adherence and even when serology and symptoms appear normal -- real case-based and cohort data show GIP testing uncovering hidden gluten exposure that patient-reported adherence and standard serologic follow-up both missed
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- diagnostic monitoring test, not a medicine
reason_why: GIP assays directly detect immunogenic gluten peptide fragments excreted in urine or stool after digestion, providing a real, objective, short-window measure of actual recent gluten ingestion that is independent of patient recall or symptom awareness -- this is the real, practical reason this tool is increasingly used to verify true adherence in patients with persistent symptoms or persistent villous atrophy before escalating a workup toward refractory celiac disease, since a meaningful proportion of apparent 'non-response' is actually undetected ongoing gluten exposure rather than true refractoriness.
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.source: Verifying Diagnosis of Refractory Celiac Disease With Urine Gluten Immunogenic Peptides as Biomarker, PMC7848017; Uncovering Hidden Gluten Exposure in Celiac Patients, PMC12155381; Nutritional and Gastroenterological Monitoring of Patients With Celiac Disease During COVID-19 Pandemic: The Emerging Role of Telemedicine and Point-of-Care Gluten Detection Tests, PMC8076748.
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.confidence: moderate-high (real, consistent case-based and cohort evidence; used as an adjunct, not yet a universal standard-of-care replacement for serology/biopsy)

celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.name: Portable Point-of-Care Food Gluten-Detection Sensors (e.g. NIMA Sensor) -- Real Consumer Tool, Honestly Reported With Real Accuracy Limitations
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.type: Handheld consumer point-of-care food-testing device, real product, not a medicine
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.effectiveness: Real, detects gluten in a tested food sample down to approximately 10 ppm within about 3 minutes, with the manufacturer citing 99% accuracy in re-engineered versions -- but real independent/third-party testing found that at gluten levels right around the 10 ppm regulatory threshold, results are essentially a coin-flip (approximately 50% 'gluten found' vs 50% 'no gluten detected' on samples at that exact borderline concentration), and the device cannot reliably test fermented/hydrolyzed foods, pure liquids, or high-fat foods
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- consumer food-testing device, not a medicine
reason_why: These sensors use an immunoassay-based lateral-flow-type detection chemistry targeting gluten-specific epitopes within a homogenized food sample, which is real and functional for solid, non-fermented, non-high-fat foods, but the real, honestly reported borderline-concentration unreliability and food-matrix limitations mean this entry reports it as a useful real-world spot-check tool for genuine uncertainty (e.g. eating out, unfamiliar packaged food) rather than a substitute for reading ingredient labels, choosing certified gluten-free products, or clinical GIP/serologic monitoring of actual patient exposure.
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.source: The NIMA Gluten Sensor Is Back. Here's What Changed, Allergic Living 2026; A Portable Gluten Sensor for Celiac Disease Patients May Not Always Be Reliable Depending on the Food and the User, PMC8329040; Gluten Free Watchdog's Updated Position Statement on the Nima Sensor for Gluten.
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.confidence: moderate (real device with real, independently-documented accuracy limitations at clinically relevant borderline concentrations)

celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.name: Capsule Endoscopy -- Real Small-Bowel Monitoring Tool Specifically for Complicated/Refractory Celiac Disease
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.type: Ingestible wireless small-bowel capsule endoscopy, real diagnostic/monitoring procedure, not a medicine
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.effectiveness: Real, established role specifically in refractory celiac disease (RCD) for detecting complications beyond the reach of standard upper endoscopy: capsule endoscopy identifies ulcerative jejunitis and can detect overt lymphoma (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma) missed by standard endoscopic and imaging procedures -- in RCD-II specifically, disease is typically more extensive on capsule endoscopy than in RCD-I, and the diagnostic yield for complications is reported as low in RCD-I but clinically meaningful in RCD-II, where real case series report detecting overt lymphoma cases during capsule-endoscopy follow-up that would otherwise have been missed
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- endoscopic monitoring procedure, not a medicine
reason_why: Standard oesophagogastroduodenoscopy reaches only the proximal duodenum, while capsule endoscopy visualizes the entire small bowel including the jejunum and ileum where RCD-II-associated ulcerative jejunitis and EATL most often first develop -- this real anatomical-reach advantage is the specific reason it is reserved for the genuinely higher-risk RCD-II population (where the real, substantially elevated EATL-transformation risk described above justifies more extensive small-bowel surveillance) rather than used routinely in uncomplicated, diet-responsive celiac disease.
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.source: Capsule endoscopy in refractory celiac disease, PMID 17516353; Small bowel capsule endoscopy in refractory celiac disease: a luxury or a necessity?, PMID 33654358; Diagnostic yield of capsule endoscopy in refractory celiac disease, PMID 22964554.
celiac_monitoring_and_detection_tools.confidence: moderate-high (real, consistent evidence across multiple independent case series specifically in the RCD population)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (symptomatic-response rate, histologic-remission rate, corticosteroid clinical/histologic response rate, deficiency-correction prevalence-of-need, transplant overall survival, screening risk-enrichment ratio, and investigational-trial result) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Strict lifelong GFD is honestly ranked highest because it is the real, primary, root-cause-removing intervention that resolves symptoms in the large majority of patients and is required regardless of what else is used; refractory-disease options are honestly ranked lower/more limited specifically because RCD is a genuinely harder, less completely treatable population, not because those interventions are poorly executed. The two investigational agents (larazotide, AMG 714) are ranked at the bottom specifically because their confirmatory/primary trial data did not establish clear efficacy -- they are included for honest completeness of the current evidence landscape, not as recommended options.

stroke.name: Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident) - Ischaemic, Haemorrhagic, and TIA
stroke.icd11_hint: 8B00-8B20 (Cerebrovascular diseases); 8B11 Cerebral ischaemic stroke; 8B00 Nontraumatic intracranial haemorrhage; 8B10 Transient ischaemic attack
stroke.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Stroke is, essentially without exception, a real time-critical medical emergency - ANY suspected stroke (sudden facial droop, arm/leg weakness, speech difficulty, sudden severe headache, sudden vision loss, sudden severe imbalance) MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call emergency services / go to the nearest stroke-capable emergency department NOW), never a routine consultation flow. This is not precautionary language: quantitatively, an untreated large-vessel ischaemic stroke destroys an estimated 1.9 million neurons, 14 billion synapses, and 12 km of myelinated nerve fibres EVERY MINUTE treatment is delayed - 'the ischaemic brain ages 3.6 years for each hour without treatment' (Saver JL, 'Time Is Brain - Quantified', Stroke/AHA Journals, 2006). The FAST mnemonic (Face-Arm-Speech-Time) exists specifically because the 'T' - calling emergency services immediately on ANY single positive finding, without waiting for more symptoms or for spontaneous resolution - is what determines whether a patient is treated in the window where thrombolysis/thrombectomy can still meaningfully limit permanent brain damage. This applies equally to apparent TIA (symptoms that resolve quickly): short-term stroke risk after TIA is real and substantial and must never be managed as 'wait and see'. A sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache must be treated as subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise by emergency imaging.

core.name: Sudden facial drooping (usually one-sided)
core.note: The 'F' in FAST; sudden onset is the key discriminator from other causes of facial weakness.

core.name: Sudden arm/leg weakness or numbness (usually one-sided)
core.note: The 'A' in FAST; classically unilateral and abrupt.

core.name: Sudden speech difficulty (slurred speech or word-finding difficulty/aphasia)
core.note: The 'S' in FAST.

core.name: Sudden confusion or trouble understanding speech
core.note: Receptive aphasia if dominant-hemisphere involvement.

core.name: Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes (visual field cut, diplopia, amaurosis fugax)
core.note: Missed by classic FAST in a real proportion of cases - part of the rationale for BE-FAST.

core.name: Sudden trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance or coordination (ataxia)
core.note: Also missed by classic FAST - posterior-circulation presentation; part of the rationale for BE-FAST ('Balance', 'Eyes').

core.name: Sudden severe headache with no known cause
core.note: Classic 'thunderclap headache' - the hallmark presenting symptom of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH); reaches maximum intensity within seconds to minutes.

symptoms.TIME_TO_CALL_EMERGENCY_SERVICES: 'Time to call emergency services' - the 'T' in FAST - is not an optional add-on symptom, it is the entire point of the mnemonic: any single FAST-positive finding of sudden onset is sufficient, on its own, to trigger an emergency stroke-response call. Do not wait for multiple symptoms to appear together.

stroke_classification.source: TOAST (Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment) classification; AHA/ASA Stroke Guidelines
stroke_classification.confidence: high - TOAST is the most widely used ischaemic-stroke-subtype classification system worldwide
stroke_classification.overview: Stroke is first split at the CT/MRI-imaging step into ischaemic (~85% of all strokes) vs haemorrhagic (~15%) - a binary distinction that is absolutely critical to get right BEFORE any treatment decision, because the emergency treatments for one (thrombolysis/thrombectomy) can be fatal if given for the other.

ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.mechanism: >=50% stenosis or occlusion of a major brain artery or branch cortical artery from atherosclerotic plaque, causing either artery-to-artery embolism or hypoperfusion distally.
ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.note: Carotid artery stenosis is a classic real risk factor/cause here.

ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.mechanism: A thrombus forms in the heart (classically the left atrial appendage in atrial fibrillation, or post-MI mural thrombus, or a prosthetic/diseased valve) and embolises to a cerebral artery.
ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.note: Cross-reference the atrial_fibrillation entry - AF is the single most important cardioembolic-stroke risk factor, and its CHA2DS2-VASc score is the standardised tool for estimating this exact risk.

ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.mechanism: Occlusion of a single small penetrating artery (lipohyalinosis/microatheroma, strongly linked to chronic hypertension), producing a lacunar infarct classically <1.5 cm on imaging with a clinical lacunar syndrome (no cortical signs like aphasia/neglect).
ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.note: Cross-reference the hypertension entry - chronic hypertension is the dominant driver of small-vessel disease.

ischaemic_stroke_subtypes_TOAST.mechanism: Non-atherosclerotic vasculopathies, hypercoagulable states, dissection, vasculitis - a real but less common category.
No cause found despite full workup, OR more than one potential cause identified with no way to determine which is responsible.

haemorrhagic_stroke_subtypes.mechanism: Rupture of small penetrating arteries deep within the brain parenchyma, most commonly caused by chronic hypertensive damage to vessel walls (lipohyalinosis, Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms) in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, or cerebellum; cerebral amyloid angiopathy is another real cause, typically lobar, in older patients.
haemorrhagic_stroke_subtypes.note: Cross-reference the hypertension entry - uncontrolled hypertension is the single most important modifiable risk factor for ICH.

haemorrhagic_stroke_subtypes.mechanism: Most commonly caused by rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm at the Circle of Willis, releasing blood directly into the subarachnoid space; presents classically with thunderclap headache. A distinct entity from ICH with its own natural history (vasospasm risk) and its own management pathway.

TIA_transient_ischaemic_attack.definition_evolution: Historically defined purely by TIME - a focal neurological deficit lasting <24 hours. This time-based definition was arbitrary and not based on any biological mechanism. It has been superseded by a TISSUE-based definition (AHA/ASA, 2009): a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischaemia, WITHOUT acute infarction on imaging.
TIA_transient_ischaemic_attack.why_it_changed: Diffusion-weighted MRI studies showed that roughly one-third of patients meeting the old <24h time-based definition actually had a new infarct on imaging - i.e. they had actually had a stroke, not a TIA, despite symptoms resolving quickly.
TIA_transient_ischaemic_attack.clinical_significance: TIA is a real medical emergency in its own right, not a benign warning sign to be watched at home - it carries a substantial short-term risk of a subsequent completed stroke (see ABCD2 score below), and most of that risk is front-loaded into the first 48 hours.
TIA_transient_ischaemic_attack.source: AHA/ASA Stroke journal, 'Definition and Evaluation of Transient Ischemic Attack' (2009); AHA/ASA Scientific Statement on TIA in the Emergency Department

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: NIHSS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: 0-42 point scale across 11 items (consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, motor arm/leg, ataxia, sensation, language, dysarthria, extinction/neglect). Score bands: 1-4 minor stroke, 5-15 moderate, 16-20 moderate-to-severe, 21-42 severe. Class 1, Level B AHA/ASA recommendation - used both to quantify baseline severity and to guide real treatment decisions (e.g. eligibility/expected benefit for thrombolysis and thrombectomy) and to track deterioration/improvement.
specific_diagnostic_signs.source: AHA/ASA Get With The Guidelines-Stroke; AHA Journals, 'Using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale'

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Non-contrast CT head (emergency, before any treatment)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: The single most critical first diagnostic step in suspected stroke: its job is to distinguish ischaemic stroke from haemorrhagic stroke BEFORE any treatment is given, because thrombolysis (tPA) given to a haemorrhagic stroke patient can be rapidly fatal. Ischaemic changes may be subtle or absent in the first few hours; a NEGATIVE CT for blood in a patient with an acute focal deficit is what allows thrombolysis to proceed.
specific_diagnostic_signs.source: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: MRI (diffusion-weighted imaging, DWI)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: More sensitive than CT for early ischaemic change and for confirming/excluding infarction in suspected TIA (the imaging step underlying the modern tissue-based TIA definition).

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: CT angiography (CTA)
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Used to detect large-vessel occlusion (LVO) - identifying LVO is what determines eligibility for mechanical thrombectomy in appropriately selected ischaemic stroke patients.

specific_diagnostic_signs.name: Irregularly irregular pulse / ECG showing atrial fibrillation
specific_diagnostic_signs.note: Found during stroke workup, points toward a cardioembolic mechanism; cross-reference the atrial_fibrillation entry for the ECG criteria.

localizing_vascular_territory_signs.note: Real, standard neuro-localisation framework used clinically to predict the likely vascular territory and stroke type from the pattern of deficits before imaging confirms it.

territories.territory: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) - most common territory
territories.findings: Contralateral face and arm weakness/sensory loss greater than leg; aphasia (expressive/Broca's or receptive/Wernicke's) if the dominant (usually left) hemisphere is involved; contralateral homonymous hemianopia; gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion; neglect/inattention if the non-dominant hemisphere is involved.
Contralateral leg weakness/sensory loss greater than face/arm (leg-predominant pattern); can cause behavioural/personality change (frontal lobe) and urinary incontinence.

Vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, crossed sensorimotor deficits (face on one side, body on the other), visual field loss (occipital involvement) - the classic constellation missed disproportionately often by the plain FAST mnemonic, motivating the BE-FAST ('Balance', 'Eyes') extension.

territories.territory: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (not a specific arterial territory)
territories.findings: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds, often with neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, and a transient loss of consciousness at onset; focal deficits are less consistent than in ischaemic stroke and depend on the aneurysm location and any associated bleed into brain tissue.

localizing_vascular_territory_signs.source: Standard clinical neuro-localisation teaching cross-checked against AHA/ASA stroke symptom descriptions and BE-FAST literature (AHA Journals, Stroke, 'BE-FAST')

risk_scoring_tools.name: ABCD2 score (short-term stroke risk after TIA)
risk_scoring_tools.criteria: Age >=60 (1), Blood pressure >=140/90 at first assessment (1), Clinical features (unilateral weakness = 2, speech disturbance without weakness = 1, other = 0), Duration (>=60 min = 2, 10-59 min = 1, <10 min = 0), Diabetes (1). Max 7. Risk stratified: 0-3 low, 4-5 moderate, 6-7 high risk of stroke at 2, 7, and 90 days post-TIA.
risk_scoring_tools.confidence: high - validated across multiple independent cohorts
risk_scoring_tools.source: AHA Journals, Stroke, 'Validation of the ABCD2 Score'; PMC systematic review of ABCD/ABCD2 scores
risk_scoring_tools.note: Even a LOW ABCD2 score does not fully exclude high risk if imaging shows DWI abnormalities, large-artery atherosclerosis, or atrial fibrillation - the score is a triage aid, not a replacement for imaging/workup.

risk_scoring_tools.name: CHA2DS2-VASc (cardioembolic stroke risk in AF)
risk_scoring_tools.note: Already fully documented in the atrial_fibrillation entry (risk_scoring_tools) - reused here by cross-reference rather than duplicated: this is the standard tool for estimating a given AF patient's baseline stroke risk and hence the case for anticoagulation.

real_risk_factors.note: The single leading modifiable risk factor for BOTH ischaemic stroke (via large- and small-vessel disease) and haemorrhagic stroke (via ICH from small penetrating vessel rupture); cross-reference the hypertension entry. High systolic blood pressure is the largest single metabolic contributor to global stroke mortality.
real_risk_factors.source: GBD 2021 (via Stroke, AHA Journals)

real_risk_factors.note: The dominant cause of cardioembolic ischaemic stroke; cross-reference the atrial_fibrillation entry and its CHA2DS2-VASc scoring.
Cross-reference the diabetes_mellitus entry; accelerates both large- and small-vessel atherosclerotic disease.
Cross-reference the dyslipidemia entry; drives large-artery atherosclerosis.
Independent, dose-related risk factor for both ischaemic stroke and SAH (via effects on vessel wall/aneurysm formation).
Cross-reference the obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry.
One of the strongest real recurrence-risk markers known - quantified acutely via the ABCD2 score after TIA, and via ongoing secondary-prevention risk more broadly after a completed stroke.
Direct substrate for the large-artery-atherosclerosis TOAST subtype, via artery-to-artery embolism or hypoperfusion.

A real, major paediatric stroke risk factor: without screening/intervention, stroke occurs in 7-8% of children with sickle cell anaemia (HbSS), and up to 11% by age 20. Transcranial Doppler (TCD) screening identifies high-velocity flow indicating elevated stroke risk; the STOP trial showed chronic transfusion therapy in TCD-identified high-risk children reduced first-stroke risk by over 90% compared to standard care.
real_risk_factors.source: STOP trial (Stroke Prevention in Sickle Cell Anemia); NEJM 1998 STOP; PubMed 10830201

global.finding: In 2021, stroke was the 3rd leading cause of death worldwide (7.3 million deaths, 10.7% of all deaths) and the 4th leading cause of DALYs (160.5 million DALYs, 5.6% of all DALYs). There were 93.8 million prevalent stroke cases and 11.9 million new (incident) strokes globally in 2021. Ischaemic stroke accounts for ~85% of all strokes, haemorrhagic for ~15%. Metabolic risk factors accounted for 46.2% of stroke-related mortality, with high systolic blood pressure alone accounting for 37.87%.
global.source: GBD 2021, published in Stroke (AHA Journals), 'Global, Regional, and National Burden of Stroke, 1990-2021: A Systematic Analysis for Global Burden of Disease 2021'

india_specific.finding: ICMR National Stroke Registry Programme (34,792 stroke cases across 30 hospitals, Jan 2020-Dec 2022): 13.8% of stroke patients were in the 18-44 age group - i.e. roughly 1 in 7 Indian stroke patients is young, a materially younger age-of-onset pattern than in Western populations. Hypertension was present in nearly three-fourths of all cases at admission, the leading risk factor across both sexes. Indian stroke patients also show a higher case-fatality rate compared with Western cohorts.
india_specific.source: ICMR National Stroke Registry Programme data (2020-2022), reported via The Tribune/PMC coverage of the registry; GBD-India stroke burden analysis (Scientific Reports/PMC)
india_specific.confidence: high for the age-distribution finding (large multi-hospital registry); the case-fatality comparison is a consistently reported qualitative finding across Indian stroke literature

time_is_brain.finding: During a typical large-vessel acute ischaemic stroke, an estimated 1.9 million neurons, 14 billion synapses, and 12 km of myelinated fibres are lost EVERY MINUTE that treatment is delayed (range 1.1-3.2 million neurons/minute across individuals) - equivalent to roughly 3.6 years of normal brain ageing per hour of untreated large-vessel stroke. This is the real quantitative basis for the 'time is brain' principle underlying all emergency stroke response systems (FAST, emergency imaging, rapid thrombolysis/thrombectomy pathways).
time_is_brain.source: Saver JL, 'Time Is Brain-Quantified', Stroke (AHA Journals), 2006
time_is_brain.confidence: high - the original quantitative source, widely cited; individual variability is real and acknowledged in later re-analyses (Stroke, 'High Variability in Neuronal Loss')

recurrence_risk.finding: Prior TIA/stroke is one of the strongest predictors of a future stroke. Short-term recurrence risk after TIA is quantified by the ABCD2 score (stratifying patients into low/moderate/high risk of stroke at 2, 7, and 90 days) - see risk_scoring_tools above.

functional_outcome.finding: Outcome is strongly severity- and time-dependent: higher baseline NIHSS predicts worse functional outcome and higher mortality, while earlier reperfusion (thrombolysis/thrombectomy) is associated with better functional independence - the direct clinical translation of the 'time is brain' principle.
functional_outcome.source: AHA/ASA Get With The Guidelines-Stroke; NIHSS validity/mortality literature (PMC, 'Validity of NIHSS... to Predict Mortality')

complications.name: Malignant MCA syndrome (cerebral oedema with herniation)
complications.note: Complete/near-complete MCA-territory infarction (>=2/3 of the territory) causes space-occupying cytotoxic and then vasogenic oedema, typically developing within the first 5 days, producing midline shift, rising intracranial pressure, and brain herniation. Occurs in roughly 10% of ischaemic strokes but carries up to 80% mortality if untreated; decompressive craniectomy, performed early, reduces mortality and improves quality-adjusted outcome.
complications.source: PMC, 'Managing Malignant Cerebral Infarction'; Surgical Neurology International, decompressive craniectomy outcomes literature

complications.name: Hemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic stroke
complications.note: Conversion of a bland ischaemic infarct into a haemorrhagic one; most commonly occurs within the first 48 hours, with increased risk from extensive ischaemia, hyperglycaemia, late recanalisation, and reperfusion/thrombolytic therapy.

complications.name: Seizures (post-stroke)
complications.note: Early post-stroke seizures occur in roughly 3-8% of patients (pooled estimates vary 3.1-7% across meta-analyses); late post-stroke epilepsy in roughly 7-10% (ranges up to 6-15% reported), reflecting differing definitions and populations across studies.
complications.source: PMC systematic review/meta-analysis, 'Incidence and risk factors of post-stroke seizures and epilepsy' (2023); AHA Journals, 'Incidence and Association of Reperfusion Therapies With Poststroke Seizures'
complications.confidence: moderate - real pooled data, genuinely wide range across studies, reported as a range rather than a single number

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
complications.note: The most common reason for hospital readmission after stroke; occurs disproportionately after haemorrhagic stroke (>30% of ICH/SAH patients intubated for respiratory failure secondary to aspiration pneumonia in some cohorts) versus ischaemic stroke (~6%), reflecting more severe dysphagia and reduced consciousness in haemorrhagic stroke.
complications.source: Stroke complications literature (PMC, aspiration pneumonia post-stroke incidence studies)
complications.confidence: moderate - regional cohort data, real but not a single universal figure

complications.name: Post-stroke depression
complications.note: Affects roughly one-third of stroke survivors at some point within 5 years (pooled meta-analysis estimates of 29-31% across large cohorts), a genuinely common and often under-recognised complication.
complications.source: AHA/ASA Scientific Statement, 'Poststroke Depression'; Hackett & Pickles meta-analysis (Int J Stroke, cited via AHA statement)
complications.confidence: high - consistent across multiple large pooled meta-analyses

complications.name: Cerebral vasospasm / delayed cerebral ischaemia (SAH-specific)
complications.note: A delayed complication specific to subarachnoid haemorrhage, distinct from the acute bleed itself: triggered by breakdown products of blood in the subarachnoid/perivascular space causing arterial narrowing. Onset typically 3-5 days after aneurysm rupture, peaking around day 7 (bimodal risk peaks reported around days 5 and 9), and can persist for 2-3 weeks. Angiographic vasospasm is seen in up to 70% of patients by day 7, with roughly 30% progressing to symptomatic vasospasm/delayed cerebral ischaemia causing secondary neurological deficits.
complications.source: PMC, 'Revisiting the Timeline of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia After Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage'; LITFL clinical summary of SAH vasospasm
complications.confidence: high for timing/mechanism, consistent across sources

red_flags: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache (reaching maximum intensity within seconds to minutes) - treat as subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise, real emergency.

Rapidly declining level of consciousness in a stroke patient - suggests rising intracranial pressure/herniation (e.g. malignant MCA syndrome), real emergency requiring urgent neurosurgical/critical-care involvement.

Any sudden-onset focal neurological deficit (facial droop, unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, sudden vision loss, sudden severe imbalance/vertigo) - treat as stroke until proven otherwise and call emergency services immediately; do NOT wait to see if it resolves, including in TIA-like presentations, since short-term recurrence/completed-stroke risk after TIA is real and substantial (ABCD2 framework).
New focal neurological deficit or stroke symptoms in a patient with known atrial fibrillation - real embolic-stroke emergency (cross-reference atrial_fibrillation entry's own red flag on this).

stroke.CURABILITY_NOTE: Stroke's curability picture is sharply time- and type-dependent, and must be reported honestly in three separate parts, not averaged into one number. (1) Acute ischaemic stroke, treated within the real evidence-based time window (IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours; mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion within 6 hours unselected, and up to 24 hours in carefully imaging-selected patients per DAWN/DEFUSE 3), can genuinely REVERSE the acute neurological deficit in appropriate candidates by physically removing/dissolving the clot before irreversible infarction is complete - this is a real, time-critical 'cure of the acute event' opportunity, not just symptom control. (2) Once brain tissue has actually infarcted (died), that tissue does NOT regenerate - adult human neurons do not meaningfully regrow to replace an infarct core, so any deficit still present once treatment windows have closed is a permanent, established deficit; rehabilitation from that point improves function via neuroplasticity of surviving tissue and compensation, not tissue regrowth. (3) Haemorrhagic stroke (intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage) has a genuinely different and generally WORSE acute prognosis than ischaemic stroke - there is no thrombolysis/thrombectomy equivalent 'reversal' option, management is directed at limiting secondary injury (BP control, anticoagulation reversal, selected surgical evacuation, vasospasm prevention for SAH), and case-fatality is real and substantial. TIA is honestly the single most 'curable' point in the whole spectrum: by definition no infarction has occurred, so ABCD2-guided urgent workup and immediate secondary prevention (dual antiplatelet therapy) can genuinely prevent the disabling stroke that would otherwise follow.

curative_option.name: Time-Critical Acute Reperfusion Therapy for Acute Ischaemic Stroke (IV Thrombolysis +/- Mechanical Thrombectomy) - the real closest thing to a 'cure' of the acute event, strictly time-limited
curative_option.note: Unlike a chronic disease where 'curative option' means a one-time procedure performed whenever convenient, stroke's curative-intent window is a real, closing clock: the same intervention that can genuinely reverse a deficit at hour 1 will not help and can even be contraindicated by hour 25. This is reported here as the curative_option specifically because, unlike most of this knowledge base's chronic-disease entries, a real biological reversal of the acute insult (not just risk-factor control) is achievable in appropriate candidates.

real_survival_functional_data.alteplase_within_3h_NINDS: Patients treated with IV alteplase within 3 hours of symptom onset were at least 30% more likely than placebo to have minimal or no disability at 3 months (NNT ~7 for a favourable outcome); no significant difference in mortality or 24-hour neurological improvement, and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was significantly higher with alteplase (~6.4% vs 0.6%) - the real trade-off that defines the time-window discipline.
real_survival_functional_data.alteplase_3_to_4.5h_ECASS_III: Extending the window to 3-4.5 hours (ECASS III, the trial underlying the current AHA/ASA 3-4.5h recommendation) still showed a significant functional-outcome benefit with alteplase versus placebo, at the cost of a real increase in symptomatic ICH, with no significant mortality difference.
real_survival_functional_data.tenecteplase_vs_alteplase_EXTEND_IA_TNK: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg achieved substantial reperfusion in 22% of patients before thrombectomy versus 10% with alteplase (p=0.03 for superiority); at 90 days, tenecteplase patients had better functional status (median mRS 2 vs 3, p=0.04) and lower mortality (10% vs 18%, p=0.049), with similar intracranial haemorrhage rates - establishing tenecteplase as a real, practically simpler (single IV bolus vs 1-hour infusion) alternative to alteplase pre-thrombectomy.
real_survival_functional_data.wake_up_stroke_extended_window_WAKE_UP: In patients with unknown time of onset (wake-up stroke) selected by DWI-FLAIR mismatch on MRI (a DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative lesion pattern indicating the infarct is very recent despite the unknown clock time), IV alteplase produced a significantly better functional outcome at 90 days than placebo, with a real increase in intracranial haemorrhage (symptomatic ICH 2.0% vs 0.4%) and death (4.1% vs 1.2%) - real evidence that imaging-based selection can extend benefit beyond a rigid time-based cutoff for a genuinely biologically-selected subgroup.

reason_why: Alteplase and tenecteplase are recombinant tissue plasminogen activators: they convert plasminogen to plasmin, which enzymatically degrades the fibrin scaffold of the occluding thrombus, restoring blood flow to the still-viable but at-risk penumbral tissue before it progresses to irreversible infarction - the real biological basis for functional reversal when given early enough.

The 4.5-hour (and imaging-extended, unknown-onset) window exists because the penumbra - ischaemic but not-yet-dead tissue - shrinks progressively as the infarct core expands; beyond the window, the risk of thrombolysis (haemorrhagic transformation into already-infarcted, fragile tissue) starts to outweigh the shrinking pool of salvageable tissue that could still benefit.
specific_drugs: Alteplase (recombinant tPA, 0.9 mg/kg IV, max 90 mg)
Tenecteplase (single IV bolus, 0.25 mg/kg, genetically engineered tPA variant with longer half-life and higher fibrin specificity)
iv_thrombolysis.source: NINDS (NEJM 1995); ECASS III; EXTEND-IA TNK (NEJM 2018); WAKE-UP (NEJM 2018); AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
iv_thrombolysis.confidence: high - multiple large RCTs, current standard of care

real_survival_functional_data.landmark_2015_trials_pooled: Across the five 2015 trials (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT), pooled individual-patient-data meta-analysis (HERMES) showed 46.0% of thrombectomy patients achieved functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days versus 26.5% with medical therapy (largely IV alteplase) alone - a number needed to treat of roughly 2.6 for one additional patient achieving functional independence, described as one of the largest treatment effects in acute stroke medicine.
real_survival_functional_data.extend_ia_early_stop: EXTEND-IA was stopped early after only 70 patients because of overwhelming efficacy: functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days was 71% with thrombectomy versus 40% with alteplase alone.
real_survival_functional_data.dawn_defuse3_extended_window: DAWN (clinical-core mismatch, up to 24h) and DEFUSE 3 (perfusion-core mismatch, 6-16h) both showed superior functional independence at 90 days with thrombectomy versus medical management alone in imaging-selected patients with a large clinically-viable penumbra despite a large elapsed time since last-known-well - establishing that 'time since onset' alone should not exclude appropriately imaging-selected patients from thrombectomy.

reason_why: Large-vessel occlusion (LVO) strokes carry a very poor natural history with IV thrombolysis alone because tPA has a low recanalisation rate for large clot burdens; mechanical thrombectomy physically removes the clot via a stent retriever or aspiration catheter delivered through a femoral/radial arterial catheter, achieving substantially higher recanalisation rates and directly restoring perfusion to salvageable penumbral tissue.

DAWN/DEFUSE 3's imaging-based (not purely time-based) selection works because perfusion/diffusion imaging directly measures how much penumbra (salvageable tissue) still exists in a given patient at a given moment, which varies by individual collateral circulation - some patients retain a meaningful salvageable penumbra well beyond 6 hours, while others have already progressed to a completed infarct much earlier.
specific_devices: Combined 'Solumbra' technique (stent retriever + aspiration catheter together)
mechanical_thrombectomy.source: MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT (NEJM, 2015); HERMES pooled meta-analysis (Lancet 2016); DAWN (NEJM 2018); DEFUSE 3 (NEJM 2018); AHA/ASA Guidelines
mechanical_thrombectomy.confidence: high - landmark RCTs, current standard of care for LVO

curative_option.the_permanence_boundary: The moment infarction is complete in a given territory, that boundary is fixed: tissue within it is dead and does not regenerate, so no treatment - reperfusion, medication, rehabilitation, or otherwise - restores neurons that have already died. Rehabilitation-driven recovery beyond that point comes from neuroplasticity of SURVIVING adjacent/contralateral tissue reorganising to partially compensate for the lost function, and from resolution of the transient effects of oedema/diaschisis around the infarct - real and clinically meaningful, but categorically different from reversing the underlying tissue loss.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine/procedure/device used across the stroke spectrum (acute ischaemic stroke, secondary prevention, hemorrhagic stroke, and rehabilitation). See curative_option above for time-critical acute reperfusion therapy, stroke's real closest thing to a cure of the acute event. All new keys are prefixed stroke_ to avoid collision with other entries' generically-named sections. Every drug class carries real specific drug names per this project's standing rule.

stroke_iv_thrombolysis.name: Alteplase (IV rtPA) - Within 4.5 Hours of Symptom Onset
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.effectiveness: NINDS (0-3h window): at least 30% more likely to have minimal/no disability at 3 months vs placebo (NNT ~7); ECASS III (3-4.5h window): significant functional-outcome benefit sustained, at the real cost of increased symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (~6.4% vs 0.6% in NINDS) and no proven mortality benefit at either window.
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.reason_why: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, enzymatically lysing the fibrin thrombus occluding the cerebral artery and restoring perfusion to the ischaemic penumbra before it progresses to permanent infarction.
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.important_caveat: Strict inclusion/exclusion criteria apply (recent surgery, anticoagulant use, BP >185/110, prior intracranial haemorrhage, etc.) precisely because the haemorrhagic-transformation risk is real and can be fatal; a non-contrast CT head excluding haemorrhage is mandatory before administration.
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.source: NINDS (NEJM 1995); ECASS III (NEJM 2008); AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

stroke_iv_thrombolysis.name: Tenecteplase - Real Practical Alternative to Alteplase, Especially Pre-Thrombectomy
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.type: Thrombolytic (genetically engineered tPA variant, higher fibrin specificity, longer half-life)
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.effectiveness: EXTEND-IA TNK: substantial reperfusion before thrombectomy in 22% vs 10% with alteplase (p=0.03 superiority); better 90-day functional status (median mRS 2 vs 3, p=0.04) and lower mortality (10% vs 18%, p=0.049), similar intracranial haemorrhage rates.
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.reason_why: Same plasminogen-activator mechanism as alteplase but with higher fibrin specificity and a longer half-life, allowing a single IV bolus instead of a 1-hour infusion - practically faster to administer, which matters directly for a 'time is brain' disease.

stroke_iv_thrombolysis.name: Extended/Unknown-Onset-Window Thrombolysis - Imaging-Selected Wake-Up Stroke
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.effectiveness: WAKE-UP trial: in patients with unknown time of onset selected by a DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative mismatch (indicating a biologically recent infarct despite the unknown clock time), alteplase produced significantly better 90-day functional outcome than placebo; real increase in intracranial haemorrhage (2.0% vs 0.4% symptomatic ICH) and death (4.1% vs 1.2%).
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.reason_why: FLAIR hyperintensity around an infarct develops over hours as vasogenic oedema forms; a DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative lesion therefore indicates the infarct is very recent (typically <4.5h) even when the actual onset time is unknown, replacing a rigid clock-time criterion with a direct biological readout of how recent the ischaemia is.
stroke_iv_thrombolysis.important_caveat: This is a real but genuinely narrower, imaging-resource-dependent pathway (MRI availability, radiologist/neurologist expertise to read DWI-FLAIR mismatch acutely) - not a universal substitute for the standard 4.5-hour window.

stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.name: Mechanical Thrombectomy for Large-Vessel Occlusion (LVO) - 0-6 Hour Standard Window
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.type: Endovascular procedure (stent-retriever and/or aspiration-catheter clot removal)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - endovascular device procedure; see stroke_medical_devices_equipment below for specific device names
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.effectiveness: HERMES pooled analysis of MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT (2015): 46.0% functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days with thrombectomy vs 26.5% with medical therapy alone (NNT ~2.6); EXTEND-IA alone (stopped early for overwhelming efficacy): 71% vs 40% functional independence.
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.reason_why: LVO strokes carry a large clot burden that IV thrombolysis alone recanalises poorly; a stent retriever or aspiration catheter delivered via arterial catheterisation physically extracts the clot, directly and mechanically restoring perfusion to the salvageable penumbra with a much higher recanalisation rate than pharmacological lysis alone.
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.important_caveat: Benefit is concentrated in confirmed LVO (identified by CT angiography) - thrombectomy is not indicated for small-vessel/distal occlusions where the procedural risk is not offset by a large salvageable territory.
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.source: MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT (NEJM 2015); HERMES pooled meta-analysis (Lancet 2016)

stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.name: Extended-Window Thrombectomy (6-24 Hours) - Imaging-Selected (DAWN / DEFUSE 3 Criteria)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - endovascular device procedure
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.effectiveness: DAWN (clinical-core mismatch, up to 24h) and DEFUSE 3 (perfusion-core mismatch, 6-16h): both showed significantly superior 90-day functional independence with thrombectomy vs medical management alone in carefully imaging-selected patients; DEFUSE 3's target-mismatch criteria are more permissive than DAWN's, enrolling a broader population (~40% of DEFUSE 3 patients would not have met DAWN's own criteria).
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.reason_why: Perfusion/diffusion imaging (CT perfusion or MRI, automated by software such as RAPID) directly measures how large the salvageable penumbra still is relative to the already-infarcted core in that specific patient at that specific moment - because collateral circulation varies markedly between individuals, some patients retain a large, treatable penumbra well beyond 6 hours while others do not, making direct tissue-status imaging a better selection criterion than elapsed clock time alone.
stroke_mechanical_thrombectomy.important_caveat: Requires access to perfusion-imaging software/expertise not universally available in all stroke centres - a real resource-dependent limitation on how widely the extended window can be applied in practice.

stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.name: Aspirin Monotherapy - Baseline Secondary Prevention
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.effectiveness: Standard, guideline-recommended baseline secondary-prevention antiplatelet for non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke/TIA; real, foundational but modest single-agent risk reduction compared with the larger reductions achieved by short-course dual therapy in the specific high-risk minor-stroke/TIA window (see CHANCE/POINT below).
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.reason_why: Irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis and reducing platelet aggregation, lowering the risk of a further atherothrombotic event.
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.source: AHA/ASA Guidelines for secondary stroke prevention

stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.name: Short-Course Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) - Minor Stroke / High-Risk TIA, First 21-90 Days Only
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.type: Dual antiplatelet therapy (COX-1 inhibitor + P2Y12 inhibitor)
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.effectiveness: CHANCE (China, 5170 patients): absolute reduction in 90-day recurrent stroke from 11.7% (aspirin alone) to 8.2% (aspirin+clopidogrel for 21 days) - HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.57-0.81), without a significant increase in major bleeding. POINT (international): starting aspirin+clopidogrel within 12 hours of minor stroke/high-risk TIA onset reduced 90-day major ischaemic events versus aspirin alone, at the real cost of an increased bleeding rate. Pooled CHANCE+POINT analysis confirms the net benefit is concentrated specifically in this short, high-risk early window.
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.reason_why: Combining a COX-1 inhibitor (aspirin) with a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor (clopidogrel) blocks two independent platelet-activation pathways simultaneously, providing a more complete antiplatelet effect during the highest-risk early period after a minor stroke or high-risk TIA, when recurrence risk is most concentrated.
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.important_caveat: This is deliberately SHORT-COURSE (21 days in CHANCE, up to 90 days trialled in POINT but net benefit front-loaded early) - prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy beyond this window increases bleeding risk without a corresponding ischaemic benefit and is not standard long-term secondary prevention.
stroke_secondary_prevention_antiplatelet.source: CHANCE (NEJM 2013); POINT (NEJM 2018); pooled CHANCE/POINT analysis (JAMA Neurology 2019)

stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.name: Oral Anticoagulation for Cardioembolic (AF-Associated) Ischaemic Stroke
stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.type: Anticoagulation (DOAC or VKA) - cross-referenced, not re-derived
stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.effectiveness: Full efficacy data (ARISTOTLE for apixaban: 21% RRR stroke/systemic embolism vs warfarin; RE-LY for dabigatran 150mg: 34% RRR vs warfarin; ROCKET-AF for rivaroxaban: non-inferior to warfarin) is already documented in this knowledge base's atrial_fibrillation entry and is cross-referenced here rather than re-derived.
stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.reason_why: In AF, blood stasis in the fibrillating left atrial appendage (part of Virchow's triad) promotes thrombus formation; anticoagulation (DOAC factor Xa/thrombin inhibition, or VKA vitamin-K-dependent clotting factor suppression) prevents new embolic thrombi from forming and travelling to the brain.
stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.important_caveat: TIMING PRINCIPLE (stroke-specific, not covered in the AF entry): starting anticoagulation too soon after an acute cardioembolic ischaemic stroke risks haemorrhagic transformation of the fresh infarct, while starting too late leaves the patient unprotected against early recurrent embolism. Current guideline-consistent practice uses infarct-size-based timing (commonly summarised as the '1-3-6-12-day rule': roughly day 1 for TIA, day 3 for small infarcts, day 6 for moderate infarcts, day 12 (or after imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation) for large infarcts), with AHA/ASA guidance broadly supporting initiation between 4 and 14 days post-stroke depending on infarct size/haemorrhagic-transformation risk - a real, honestly-evolving area still being refined by ongoing trials.
stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.source: ARISTOTLE, RE-LY, ROCKET-AF (see atrial_fibrillation entry); AHA/ASA Guidelines; systematic review/meta-analysis on optimal DOAC-initiation timing after acute ischaemic stroke with AF (2024)
stroke_secondary_prevention_anticoagulat.confidence: high for the DOAC-vs-warfarin efficacy data (cross-referenced); moderate for the exact optimal timing cutoffs, honestly reported as guideline-consistent ranges rather than one precise universally-agreed number, pending ongoing trials (e.g. OPTIMAS, ELAN)

stroke_secondary_prevention_statin.name: High-Intensity Statin Therapy for Secondary Stroke Prevention
stroke_secondary_prevention_statin.effectiveness: SPARCL (4731 patients with recent stroke/TIA, no known coronary disease, LDL 100-190 mg/dL): atorvastatin 80mg/day reduced fatal-or-nonfatal stroke by 16% (11.2% vs 13.1% over median 4.9 years, adjusted HR 0.84) and fatal stroke specifically by 43%, versus placebo - the first trial to establish a statin's direct stroke-prevention benefit, not just a cardiovascular one.
stroke_secondary_prevention_statin.reason_why: Statins lower LDL cholesterol, slowing/stabilising atherosclerotic plaque progression in the cerebral and carotid vasculature (reducing the large-artery-atherosclerosis TOAST mechanism) and exerting real pleiotropic vascular-stabilising effects independent of lipid-lowering alone.
stroke_secondary_prevention_statin.important_caveat: SPARCL also found a real, honestly-reported increase in haemorrhagic stroke risk with atorvastatin versus placebo, particularly in patients with a prior haemorrhagic (rather than ischaemic) stroke - meaning the net benefit calculation genuinely differs by index-stroke type, and statin initiation after a haemorrhagic stroke needs individualised risk-benefit assessment rather than blanket application of the ischaemic-stroke data.
stroke_secondary_prevention_statin.source: SPARCL (NEJM 2006); cross-referenced to this knowledge base's dyslipidemia entry for the broader statin-intensity framework

stroke_blood_pressure_management.name: Acute-Phase Permissive Hypertension (Ischaemic Stroke) - The Counterintuitive Principle
stroke_blood_pressure_management.type: Blood pressure management strategy, acute phase
specific_drugs: Clevidipine (IV infusion) - used ONLY when BP exceeds the guideline threshold requiring lowering
stroke_blood_pressure_management.effectiveness: Guideline-consistent thresholds (AHA/ASA): in patients NOT receiving thrombolysis/thrombectomy, BP is deliberately left elevated ('permissive hypertension') and only lowered if it exceeds 220/120 mmHg, and then only modestly (~15% reduction in the first 24h); in patients receiving IV thrombolysis, BP must be kept below 185/110 mmHg before treatment and below 180/105 mmHg during/after; recent trials of more intensive BP-lowering after reperfusion therapy have shown no functional-outcome benefit and possible harm, reinforcing the guideline's cautious threshold.
stroke_blood_pressure_management.reason_why: In acute ischaemic stroke, the ischaemic penumbra's perfusion is often dependent on collateral blood flow that is pressure-passive (autoregulation is impaired in the ischaemic territory) - aggressively lowering systemic BP can drop penumbral perfusion below the threshold needed to keep at-risk-but-viable tissue alive, potentially converting salvageable penumbra into permanent infarct; hence BP is deliberately tolerated higher than would ever be acceptable outside the acute stroke setting, unless it is high enough to itself pose a direct risk (haemorrhagic transformation, hypertensive encephalopathy, cardiac strain).
stroke_blood_pressure_management.source: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

stroke_blood_pressure_management.name: Long-Term Secondary-Prevention Blood Pressure Control
stroke_blood_pressure_management.effectiveness: Full specific-drug outcome-trial data (effect sizes in mmHg, first-line-class comparative data) is already documented in this knowledge base's hypertension entry and is cross-referenced here rather than re-derived; hypertension is the single leading modifiable risk factor for BOTH stroke recurrence and first stroke (via large-vessel, small-vessel, and haemorrhagic mechanisms), so sustained long-term BP control is a core secondary-prevention pillar once the acute permissive-hypertension phase has passed.
stroke_blood_pressure_management.reason_why: Once the acute perfusion-dependent risk window has closed, chronic hypertension's ordinary vascular-damage mechanisms (accelerated atherosclerosis, lipohyalinosis of small penetrating vessels) resume dominating long-term recurrence risk, so the counterintuitive acute-phase tolerance for high BP is deliberately reversed into standard aggressive long-term control.
stroke_blood_pressure_management.source: Cross-referenced to this knowledge base's hypertension entry; AHA/ASA secondary-prevention guidelines

stroke_carotid_revascularization.name: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA) - Symptomatic High-Grade Carotid Stenosis
stroke_carotid_revascularization.type: Surgical procedure (open removal of atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - surgical procedure, performed alongside standard antiplatelet/statin secondary prevention
stroke_carotid_revascularization.effectiveness: NASCET: for symptomatic severe stenosis (70-99%), CEA reduced 2-year ipsilateral stroke risk from 26% (medical therapy) to 9% (surgery) - absolute risk reduction 17%, NNT 15 to prevent one disabling stroke/death over 2-6 years; for moderate stenosis (50-69%), CEA reduced relative risk of disabling stroke/death by 27%, a smaller but real benefit; for stenosis <50%, no significant surgical benefit was found. Perioperative risk was real: 30-day death 1.1%, disabling stroke 1.8%, non-disabling stroke 3.7%.
stroke_carotid_revascularization.reason_why: Symptomatic carotid stenosis is a direct substrate for artery-to-artery embolism and/or haemodynamic hypoperfusion (the TOAST large-artery-atherosclerosis mechanism); physically removing the plaque eliminates that specific embolic/stenotic source, which is why the benefit scales directly with stenosis severity (more severe stenosis = larger embolic/haemodynamic risk being removed).
stroke_carotid_revascularization.important_caveat: The benefit-to-surgical-risk ratio genuinely depends on stenosis severity and the individual surgical team's own complication rate - CEA is not beneficial (and can be net-harmful) below 50% stenosis.

stroke_carotid_revascularization.name: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) - Real Comparable Alternative to CEA in Selected Patients
stroke_carotid_revascularization.type: Endovascular procedure (stent placement across the stenotic carotid segment, with embolic-protection device)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - endovascular device procedure, performed alongside dual antiplatelet therapy peri-procedurally
stroke_carotid_revascularization.effectiveness: CREST (2502 patients, symptomatic and asymptomatic): no significant difference in the primary composite endpoint (periprocedural stroke/MI/death plus subsequent ipsilateral stroke) between CAS (7.2%) and CEA (6.8%) over 4 years, sustained through 10-year follow-up (both <7% over 10 years); a real age-by-treatment interaction was found, suggesting CAS may be relatively favoured in younger patients and CEA in older patients, though sex/symptomatic-status did not modify the effect.
stroke_carotid_revascularization.reason_why: A self-expanding stent mechanically scaffolds the stenotic arterial segment open and traps the plaque against the vessel wall, achieved via a catheter-based approach that avoids a neck incision - CREST's near-equivalence to CEA reflects that both approaches ultimately eliminate the same embolic/stenotic substrate by different routes, each with its own distinct procedural risk profile (CAS: slightly higher periprocedural stroke risk; CEA: slightly higher periprocedural MI risk, per CREST's component-endpoint breakdown).
stroke_carotid_revascularization.important_caveat: Patient selection matters: CAS is generally preferred when surgical/anaesthetic risk for CEA is high (e.g. hostile neck anatomy, prior neck surgery/radiation, significant cardiac comorbidity), while CEA remains preferred in older patients per CREST's age-interaction finding.

stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.name: Acute Blood Pressure Lowering in Intracerebral Haemorrhage (ICH)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.type: Blood pressure management, acute phase, haemorrhagic stroke
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.effectiveness: INTERACT2 (2839 patients with spontaneous ICH and elevated systolic BP): intensive BP lowering (target <140 mmHg within 1 hour) did NOT significantly reduce the primary outcome of death or major disability versus guideline-standard treatment (target <180 mmHg), but a pre-specified ordinal (shift) analysis of modified Rankin Scale scores showed a significant favourable shift with intensive treatment, and intensive lowering was safe (no excess renal/other serious adverse events) - this honestly-mixed result is exactly what led AHA/ASA and other guidelines to support a target systolic BP <140 mmHg as reasonable rather than mandatory.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.reason_why: Unlike ischaemic stroke, ICH has no penumbra-preservation rationale for tolerating high BP - instead, elevated BP is thought to promote ongoing haematoma expansion in the first few hours after the bleed, so early, safe BP lowering is directed at limiting that expansion rather than at preserving collateral perfusion.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.source: INTERACT2 (NEJM 2013); AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage

stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.name: Reversal of Warfarin (Vitamin K Antagonist) Anticoagulation
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.type: Anticoagulation reversal - Vitamin K + 4-Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (4F-PCC)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.effectiveness: INCH trial: in VKA-related intracranial haemorrhage, 4F-PCC normalised the INR faster than fresh frozen plasma (FFP), and faster INR normalisation was associated with smaller haematoma expansion; the trial was stopped early due to a significant difference favouring PCC on this haemostatic endpoint, though a clinical-outcome benefit (not just INR/haematoma-expansion) was not separately proven. Guideline-concordant dosing combining PCC (at least 20-25 IU/kg factor IX equivalent) with concurrent IV vitamin K (at least 5-10mg) within 8 hours of admission is associated with decreased mortality in real-world cohorts.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.reason_why: 4F-PCC directly replaces all four vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) that warfarin suppresses, restoring haemostatic capacity within minutes; vitamin K is given concurrently because PCC's effect lasts only up to ~8 hours while vitamin K restores the liver's own ongoing synthesis of these factors over the following 12-24 hours, preventing anticoagulation rebound once the PCC effect wears off.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.important_caveat: PCC is now preferred over FFP specifically because it does not require blood-group typing/cross-matching, carries no FFP-related volume-overload risk, and achieves faster INR correction - a real, guideline-driving practice shift documented directly by the INCH trial.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.source: INCH trial (Lancet Neurology 2016); EPAHK study; AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage

stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.name: Reversal of Dabigatran (Direct Thrombin Inhibitor)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.effectiveness: RE-VERSE AD: rapidly and durably reversed dabigatran's anticoagulant effect in patients with intracranial bleeding; meta-analysis of 32 studies/1832 ICH patients found idarucizumab achieved 82% successful anticoagulation reversal, with 11% all-cause mortality and 5% thromboembolic events. A real, honestly-reported limitation: late anticoagulation rebound occurred in 23% of RE-VERSE AD patients (mainly after 12 hours), associated with recurrent/continued bleeding in 9% of those cases.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.reason_why: Idarucizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) with an extremely high, specific binding affinity for dabigatran - roughly 350 times greater than dabigatran's own affinity for thrombin - so it binds and neutralises free and thrombin-bound dabigatran almost immediately upon IV administration, directly and specifically reversing the anticoagulant effect rather than acting through a general pro-coagulant mechanism.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.source: RE-VERSE AD (NEJM 2017); meta-analysis of DOAC reversal agents in ICH (2022)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.confidence: high for reversal efficacy; the rebound-anticoagulation caveat is also well-documented and real

stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.name: Reversal of Factor Xa Inhibitors (Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, Edoxaban)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.type: Anticoagulation reversal - decoy recombinant factor Xa protein
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.effectiveness: ANNEXA-4: andexanet alfa produced a 92% reduction in median anti-factor Xa activity after administration in patients with factor Xa inhibitor-associated acute major bleeding; the same meta-analysis of DOAC-reversal-in-ICH cited above found andexanet alfa achieved 75% successful reversal, with real, honestly-higher rates of mortality (24%) and thromboembolic events (14%) than idarucizumab's cohort in that pooled analysis (a comparison across different, non-randomised patient populations, not a head-to-head trial). European Stroke Organisation guidance rates the strength of evidence for andexanet alfa in rivaroxaban/apixaban-associated ICH as weak, reflecting real evidence-base limitations versus idarucizumab's dabigatran evidence.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.reason_why: Andexanet alfa is a modified, catalytically inactive recombinant form of human factor Xa that acts as a decoy: it binds direct factor Xa inhibitors (and also sequesters tissue factor pathway inhibitor) with high affinity, sequestering the drug and restoring endogenous factor Xa activity and thrombin generation.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.important_caveat: The real, guideline-acknowledged thromboembolic-event signal with andexanet alfa (a known class concern, since it also transiently inhibits the body's own anticoagulant tissue factor pathway inhibitor) must be weighed against the bleeding being reversed - this is an honestly less mature evidence base than idarucizumab's.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.source: ANNEXA-4 (NEJM 2019); meta-analysis of DOAC reversal agents in ICH (2022); European Stroke Organisation guidance
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.confidence: moderate-to-high - real trial data, but genuinely weaker/more mixed evidence base than idarucizumab, honestly reported as such

stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.name: Surgical Haematoma Evacuation - Select Cases Only
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.effectiveness: STICH (broad supratentorial ICH): no significant overall benefit of early surgery over initial conservative treatment, though a signal of benefit was seen in superficial (lobar, within 1cm of cortical surface) haematomas.
