STICH II (specifically superficial lobar ICH, 10-100mL, no intraventricular extension): unfavourable outcome at 6 months in 59% (early surgery) vs 62% (initial conservative treatment) - a 3.7-percentage-point difference that did NOT reach statistical significance (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.62-1.20, p=0.367), with 21% crossover from conservative to delayed surgery complicating interpretation. Honest bottom line: routine early surgical evacuation is NOT proven to improve outcomes for most spontaneous supratentorial ICH, and is reserved for specific scenarios (large haematoma causing mass effect/herniation, cerebellar haemorrhage with brainstem compression/hydrocephalus, or clinical deterioration) rather than applied routinely.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.reason_why: The STICH/STICH-II neutral results reflect a real biological tension: evacuating the haematoma reduces mass effect and secondary injury, but the surgical access itself causes additional injury to surrounding brain tissue, and for many supratentorial locations these two effects roughly cancel out at a population level - unlike cerebellar haemorrhage, where the posterior fossa's rigid, space-limited compartment makes mass effect and brainstem compression/hydrocephalus a much more clearly surgery-responsive emergency.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.important_caveat: Cerebellar haemorrhage >3cm with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus is the one ICH-location scenario with a genuinely stronger, more consistent case for urgent surgical evacuation, distinct from the neutral supratentorial STICH/STICH-II data.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.source: STICH (Lancet 2005); STICH II (Lancet 2013); AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.confidence: high for the neutral supratentorial finding (large RCTs); the cerebellar-haemorrhage exception is standard neurosurgical teaching cross-checked against the same AHA/ASA guideline

stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.name: Decompressive Hemicraniectomy - Malignant MCA Infarction (Ischaemic Stroke Complication, Cross-Referenced)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.type: Neurosurgical procedure (bone-flap removal to allow room for swelling)
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.effectiveness: Pooled analysis of DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET (patients aged 18-60 with malignant MCA infarction, treated within 48h): decompressive surgery increased survival from 29% to 78% (absolute risk reduction 50%, NNT 2 for survival); more patients achieved mRS<=4 (75% vs 24%) and mRS<=3 (43% vs 21%) - a genuinely large, consistent effect across all three trials, but with the real honest caveat that many survivors remain moderately-to-severely disabled (the trials increased survival more dramatically than they increased good functional outcome).
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.reason_why: Malignant MCA infarction causes space-occupying cerebral oedema within a rigid skull; removing a section of skull (the bone flap) gives the swelling brain somewhere to expand into rather than compressing against the skull and herniating, directly preventing the fatal secondary injury of brain herniation even though it does not reduce the primary infarct itself.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.important_caveat: This is the real evidence base cross-referenced from this entry's own 'malignant MCA syndrome' complication (see symptoms/complications) - the honest trade-off is markedly increased SURVIVAL with a real, substantial proportion of survivors remaining significantly disabled, a trade-off patients/families must be counselled on explicitly.
stroke_hemorrhagic_ich_management.source: Pooled analysis of DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET (Lancet Neurology 2007)

stroke_sah_management.name: Aneurysm Securing - Endovascular Coiling vs Neurosurgical Clipping
stroke_sah_management.type: Definitive aneurysm treatment (endovascular or open surgical)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - endovascular (coiling) or neurosurgical (clipping) procedure
stroke_sah_management.effectiveness: ISAT (2143 patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms suitable for either technique): endovascular coiling gave a 23% relative risk reduction and 7% absolute risk reduction in death/significant disability at 1 year compared with surgical clipping (22.7% dependent/dead with coiling vs 30.6% with clipping); the survival/independence benefit of coiling persisted through at least 7 years of follow-up (18-year UK cohort follow-up confirmed continued durability). The real trade-off: late aneurysm rebleeding and need for re-treatment is more common after coiling than after clipping.
stroke_sah_management.reason_why: Coiling occludes the aneurysm from within its lumen via a catheter (avoiding a craniotomy and brain retraction), while clipping mechanically occludes the aneurysm neck from outside via open surgery; ISAT's outcome difference reflects that, for aneurysms anatomically suitable for both techniques, the less invasive endovascular approach causes less peri-procedural brain injury, while its real durability trade-off (higher re-treatment/rebleeding rate) reflects a real difference in the completeness/permanence of aneurysm occlusion achieved by packing coils versus a mechanical clip.
stroke_sah_management.important_caveat: ISAT specifically enrolled aneurysms judged suitable for EITHER technique by the treating team - it does not mean every aneurysm is coilable; anatomy (wide neck, location, associated haematoma requiring simultaneous evacuation) still determines which technique is feasible for a given patient.

stroke_sah_management.name: Nimodipine - Real, Well-Established Vasospasm/Outcome-Improving Intervention Specific to SAH
specific_drugs: Nimodipine (oral, 60mg every 4 hours for 21 days, standard regimen)
stroke_sah_management.effectiveness: British Aneurysm Nimodipine Trial (1989) and subsequent meta-analyses: poor outcome (death or severe disability) was reduced by roughly 40% in nimodipine-treated aneurysmal SAH patients versus placebo, with a real reduction in cerebral infarction attributable to vasospasm and a probable trend toward improved mortality - one of the most well-established, guideline-mandated pharmacological interventions specific to any single stroke subtype in this entire disease.
stroke_sah_management.reason_why: Nimodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with relatively selective cerebrovascular activity; it blocks calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, real evidence points to it improving outcome more through a direct neuroprotective effect on ischaemic neurons than through simply dilating spastic vessels (angiographic vasospasm reduction has not always tracked as closely with the clinical benefit as the neuroprotection hypothesis would predict), but either mechanism converges on the same real, reproducible outcome benefit.
stroke_sah_management.important_caveat: Unlike most interventions in this survey, nimodipine's benefit is SAH-specific - it is not used for ischaemic stroke or ICH, and is given orally on a fixed 21-day course routinely (not titrated to angiographic vasospasm severity).
stroke_sah_management.source: British Aneurysm Nimodipine Trial (BMJ 1989); Cochrane/other meta-analyses of calcium antagonists for aneurysmal SAH

stroke_rehabilitation.name: Early, Structured, Multidisciplinary Post-Stroke Rehabilitation
stroke_rehabilitation.type: Rehabilitation - physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language therapy, multidisciplinary stroke-unit care
specific_drugs: Not a drug - structured multidisciplinary rehabilitation programme
stroke_rehabilitation.effectiveness: Organised stroke-unit, multidisciplinary rehabilitative care is real, guideline-endorsed standard of care associated with improved functional outcome and reduced mortality/dependency compared with less organised general-ward care (long-established Cochrane Stroke Unit Trialists' Collaboration evidence). AVERT (2104 patients): very-early (within 24h), high-dose, high-frequency mobilisation resulted in a LOWER proportion of patients with a favourable 3-month outcome (mRS 0-2) than usual care, an honest, counter-intuitive negative finding for that specific high-dose protocol; a pre-specified dose-response analysis within AVERT suggested that shorter, more frequent (rather than fewer, longer) very-early sessions may still be beneficial - the real, nuanced conclusion is 'get moving early, but not in large single high-dose sessions in the first 24 hours.'
stroke_rehabilitation.reason_why: Structured rehabilitation drives neuroplasticity-based recovery: repetitive, task-specific practice promotes reorganisation of surviving peri-infarct and contralateral cortex to partially assume functions of the infarcted territory, and coordinated multidisciplinary input (physio/OT/speech/nursing/medical) reduces complications (aspiration pneumonia, DVT, contractures, depression) that otherwise independently worsen functional outcome. AVERT's specific negative finding for high-dose very-early mobilisation is thought to reflect a real, mechanistically-plausible risk: excessively early, prolonged, high-intensity activity in the first 24 hours may transiently compromise penumbral perfusion or provoke early neurological worsening in a subset of patients before the tissue has stabilised.
stroke_rehabilitation.important_caveat: Do NOT interpret AVERT as 'mobilisation is bad' - it specifically found the trialled HIGH-DOSE, first-24-hour protocol underperformed usual care; standard, guideline-based rehabilitation (beginning within the first few days, once medically stable, progressively increased) remains real and beneficial and is not the same intervention AVERT tested negatively.
stroke_rehabilitation.source: Cochrane Stroke Unit Trialists' Collaboration; AVERT (Lancet 2015)

stroke_tia_urgent_workup.name: ABCD2-Score-Guided Urgent TIA Workup and Immediate Secondary Prevention
stroke_tia_urgent_workup.type: Risk-stratified urgent diagnostic pathway + immediate pharmacotherapy
specific_drugs: Aspirin + Clopidogrel (short-course, per CHANCE/POINT above, for high-ABCD2-risk patients)
Anticoagulation if AF-driven cardioembolic mechanism is found on workup
stroke_tia_urgent_workup.effectiveness: The ABCD2 score (Age, Blood pressure, Clinical features, Duration, Diabetes; max 7) stratifies patients into low (0-3), moderate (4-5), and high (6-7) risk of a completed stroke at 2, 7, and 90 days after a TIA - real, validated across multiple independent cohorts - and directly determines urgency: high-risk patients are triaged for same-day/urgent brain and vascular imaging plus immediate initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy (per CHANCE/POINT) and statin therapy, converting the TIA-to-stroke risk window into a genuinely actionable, treatable emergency rather than a 'watch and wait' presentation.
stroke_tia_urgent_workup.reason_why: TIA represents transient ischaemia that has NOT yet progressed to infarction - by definition it is the single most reversible/preventable point in the entire stroke spectrum, because the underlying cause (large-artery stenosis, cardioembolic source, small-vessel disease) is still present and about to cause a real disabling stroke unless identified and treated within the highest-risk early days.
stroke_tia_urgent_workup.important_caveat: Even a LOW ABCD2 score does not fully exclude high risk if imaging shows a DWI abnormality (meaning a small infarct already occurred, i.e. it was technically a minor stroke, not a TIA), large-artery atherosclerosis, or atrial fibrillation - the score is a triage aid to prioritise urgency, not a replacement for full imaging/cardiac workup in every patient.
stroke_tia_urgent_workup.source: AHA Journals, Stroke, 'Validation of the ABCD2 Score'; CHANCE; POINT; SPARCL

stroke_medical_devices_equipment.name: Stent Retrievers - Solitaire FR, Trevo XP
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: The stent-retriever devices used in the pivotal 2015 thrombectomy trials (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT); deployed across the thrombus for 5-10 minutes to ensnare the clot within the stent's mesh before withdrawal restores flow and removes the clot; comparative studies suggest Trevo XP achieves shorter procedure times and fewer stent passages than Solitaire FR in some series, though both are real guideline-endorsed devices with strong outcome evidence behind the class as a whole.
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: A self-expanding stent-mesh structure is deployed past the occlusion, expands to interdigitate with and capture the thrombus, and is then withdrawn along with the captured clot back through the catheter, mechanically extracting the obstruction rather than relying on pharmacological dissolution.
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.source: Cross-referenced to MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT (NEJM 2015)

stroke_medical_devices_equipment.name: Aspiration/Direct-Aspiration Catheters - Penumbra System (ADAPT Technique)
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.type: Endovascular mechanical thrombectomy device (large-bore aspiration catheter)
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: The ADAPT ('a direct aspiration first pass technique') FAST study reported >97% revascularisation rates with groin-puncture-to-revascularisation times of 37 minutes or less using Penumbra aspiration devices; frequently combined with a stent retriever in the 'Solumbra' technique (localised aspiration at the thrombus site while the stent retriever captures it, reducing thrombus fragmentation/distal embolisation).
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: A large-bore catheter is advanced to directly contact the thrombus face, and continuous vacuum aspiration draws the clot into and through the catheter, physically removing it without needing to first cross and traverse the full length of the thrombus with a stent-retriever wire.
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.source: ADAPT FAST study; cross-referenced to Penumbra System device literature

stroke_medical_devices_equipment.name: Carotid Stents
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.type: Endovascular device (self-expanding stent with embolic-protection filter)
specific_drugs: Self-expanding carotid stent systems used in CREST
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: See stroke_carotid_revascularization above - CREST established near-equivalence to CEA in the appropriately selected population.
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Mechanically scaffolds the stenotic carotid segment open; an accompanying embolic-protection device (a distal filter) is used during deployment to catch any plaque debris dislodged during the procedure before it can embolise to the brain.

stroke_medical_devices_equipment.name: External Ventricular Drain (EVD) - Hydrocephalus Complicating SAH/ICH
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.type: Neurosurgical device (catheter draining CSF from the lateral ventricle to an external collection system)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - neurosurgical CSF-diversion device
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Real, standard-of-care emergency intervention for acute obstructive hydrocephalus complicating SAH (from blood obstructing CSF outflow/reabsorption) or large ICH with intraventricular extension - a genuinely life-saving bridge that relieves acutely raised intracranial pressure while the underlying cause (aneurysm, haematoma) is definitively treated; also allows real-time intracranial pressure monitoring.
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Blood products in the subarachnoid space or ventricular system impair CSF reabsorption via the arachnoid granulations (or directly obstruct the ventricular system), causing CSF to accumulate faster than it drains; an EVD catheter placed into the lateral ventricle provides a direct, controllable external outflow path, immediately lowering intracranial pressure until the obstruction resolves or is treated.
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.source: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage; AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
stroke_medical_devices_equipment.confidence: high - standard, long-established neurosurgical practice cross-checked against current AHA/ASA guidelines

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages/metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (functional independence at 90 days, relative/absolute stroke-risk reduction, survival, reperfusion rate, INR-normalisation surrogate) in DIFFERENT populations (acute ischaemic stroke, secondary prevention, hemorrhagic stroke) - ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. Time-critical acute reperfusion (thrombolysis/thrombectomy) is honestly ranked at the top not merely by its own percentage but because it is the one real point in the entire ischaemic-stroke spectrum capable of reversing an acute deficit before permanent infarction, per curative_option above; hemorrhagic-stroke interventions are honestly ranked reflecting their genuinely worse real-world outcomes and more limited evidence bases (STICH/STICH-II neutral, andexanet alfa's weaker evidence than idarucizumab's) rather than any errors in how they were executed.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Decompressive hemicraniectomy (malignant MCA infarction, DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET pooled)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Absolute survival increase (78% vs 29%), NNT 2 for survival
ranked_high_to_low.source: DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET pooled analysis, Lancet Neurology 2007

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mechanical thrombectomy for LVO (HERMES pooled, 2015 trials)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Absolute functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days
ranked_high_to_low.source: HERMES pooled meta-analysis, Lancet 2016

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mechanical thrombectomy (EXTEND-IA, stopped early for efficacy)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Absolute functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days, single trial
ranked_high_to_low.source: EXTEND-IA, NEJM 2015

ranked_high_to_low.name: Carotid endarterectomy, severe stenosis 70-99% (NASCET)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk reduction in disabling stroke/death vs medical therapy
ranked_high_to_low.source: NASCET, NEJM 1991

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nimodipine (aneurysmal SAH)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in poor outcome (death/severe disability)
ranked_high_to_low.source: British Aneurysm Nimodipine Trial, BMJ 1989

ranked_high_to_low.name: Idarucizumab (dabigatran reversal, ICH meta-analysis)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Successful anticoagulation reversal rate
ranked_high_to_low.source: Meta-analysis of DOAC reversal agents in ICH, 2022

ranked_high_to_low.name: Andexanet alfa (factor Xa inhibitor reversal, ANNEXA-4)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Reduction in median anti-factor Xa activity (surrogate, not clinical-outcome endpoint)
ranked_high_to_low.source: ANNEXA-4, NEJM 2019

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.icd11_hint: 8A60-8A6Z (Epilepsy or seizures); 8A61 Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; 8A65 Status epilepticus
epilepsy.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Status epilepticus is a real, life-threatening neurological emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely, triggering immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW), never a routine consultation flow. By the current ILAE 2015 operational definition (Trinka E et al., Epilepsia 2015), a convulsive seizure lasting >=5 minutes (t1), or recurrent seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them, IS status epilepticus and requires emergency treatment to be started immediately - waiting for the seizure to 'run its course' beyond 5 minutes is not appropriate. Beyond 30 minutes (t2), risk of long-term neuronal injury and mortality rises sharply: overall status epilepticus mortality is 9-37% depending on aetiology and duration, and outcomes are significantly worse once t2 is reached versus resolution within the t1-t2 window (BMC Neurology 2022, 'Timing matters'). This applies to ANY suspected prolonged seizure activity, first-ever seizure with failure to regain consciousness, or cluster seizures without recovery between them - these must never be managed as 'wait and see' at home.

definition_ILAE_2014.criteria: ILAE 2014 practical clinical definition (Fisher et al.): Epilepsy is a disease of the brain defined by ANY of: (1) at least two unprovoked (or reflex) seizures occurring >24 hours apart; (2) one unprovoked (or reflex) seizure and a probability of further seizures similar to the general recurrence risk (at least ~60%) after two unprovoked seizures, occurring over the next 10 years; (3) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.
definition_ILAE_2014.recurrence_risk_basis: The 60% figure is derived from natural-history data showing the risk of a third seizure after two unprovoked seizures is approximately 3 in 4 (95% CI ~60-90%); the Task Force reasoned that a single unprovoked seizure carrying a similarly high recurrence risk should logically also be classified as epilepsy. The >60% figure is an approximate guideline, not a sharp cutoff.
definition_ILAE_2014.resolution: Epilepsy is considered 'resolved' for individuals who had an age-dependent epilepsy syndrome but are now past the applicable age, or who have remained seizure-free for the last 10 years, with no seizure medicines for the last 5 years.
definition_ILAE_2014.critical_distinction: A single PROVOKED (acute symptomatic) seizure - e.g. due to fever, acute alcohol withdrawal, acute hypoglycaemia, acute head trauma, or acute stroke at the time of the insult - does NOT by itself constitute epilepsy, because the seizure is attributable to a transient systemic or acute CNS insult rather than an enduring predisposition to unprovoked seizures.
definition_ILAE_2014.source: Fisher RS et al., 'ILAE Official Report: A practical clinical definition of epilepsy', Epilepsia 2014;55(4):475-482 (ILAE Guideline PDF, ilae.org/files/ilaeGuideline/Definition2014.pdf)
definition_ILAE_2014.confidence: high - the current official ILAE definition in clinical use worldwide

classification_ILAE_2017_seizure_types.framework: The ILAE 2017 operational classification of seizure types is based on where the seizure begins in the brain (onset), using semiology (signs/symptoms) as the basis for categorisation.

three_top_level_categories.description: Originates within networks limited to one cerebral hemisphere; may be discretely localised or more widely distributed. Further subdivided by AWARENESS (focal aware vs focal impaired awareness - awareness is used as a classifier specifically for focal seizures) and by the first prominent sign/symptom into MOTOR onset (e.g. automatisms, atonic, clonic, epileptic spasms, hyperkinetic, myoclonic, tonic) or NON-MOTOR onset (autonomic, behaviour arrest, cognitive, emotional, sensory).

Originates at some point within, and rapidly engages, bilaterally distributed networks. Subdivided into motor (tonic-clonic, clonic, tonic, myoclonic, myoclonic-tonic-clonic, myoclonic-atonic, atonic, epileptic spasms) and non-motor/absence (typical, atypical, myoclonic, eyelid myoclonia).

Used when the onset is not witnessed or data are insufficient to classify as focal or generalized; may still show defining motor (tonic-clonic, epileptic spasms) or non-motor features, and may later be reclassified as focal or generalized onset with more information.

classification_ILAE_2017_seizure_types.focal_to_bilateral_tonic_clonic: A focal seizure that spreads to involve bilaterally distributed networks is termed 'focal to bilateral tonic-clonic' - this term formally REPLACES the older term 'secondarily generalized seizure' under the 2017 framework.
classification_ILAE_2017_seizure_types.terminology_retired: The 2017 revision retired the terms 'partial' (replaced by 'focal'), 'simple partial', 'complex partial', 'dyscognitive', 'psychic', and 'secondarily generalized'.
classification_ILAE_2017_seizure_types.source: Fisher RS et al., 'Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: Position Paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology', Epilepsia 2017;58(4):522-530; Fisher RS et al., 'Instruction manual for the ILAE 2017 operational classification of seizure types', Epilepsia 2017;58(4):531-542
classification_ILAE_2017_seizure_types.confidence: high - current official ILAE seizure classification

classification_epilepsy_syndromes.framework_note: Epilepsy syndrome diagnosis is the third and most specific level of ILAE epilepsy diagnosis (after seizure type and epilepsy type), combining seizure types, EEG, and imaging features, typically age-dependent - accurate syndromic diagnosis guides antiseizure medicine choice and prognosis.

named_syndromes.features: A genetic generalized epilepsy syndrome with onset typically in adolescence; classic triad of early-morning myoclonic jerks (especially after waking or sleep deprivation), generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and (in a subset) absence seizures. EEG shows generalized 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges, often photosensitive.
named_syndromes.source: ILAE Epilepsy Diagnosis manual (epilepsydiagnosis.org), 'Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy'; ILAE Classification and Definition of Epilepsy Syndromes

named_syndromes.features: Usually presents between 3-5 years of age; characterised by multiple seizure types (predominantly tonic, atonic, and atypical absence seizures), an EEG pattern of slow (<=2.5 Hz) generalized spike-and-wave discharges with abnormal background activity while awake, and fast (10-20 Hz) generalized paroxysmal fast activity/polyspikes during sleep. Associated with intellectual disability and is typically drug-resistant.

named_syndromes.syndrome: Dravet Syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy)
named_syndromes.features: Onset in the first year of life, classically with prolonged febrile and afebrile hemiclonic or generalized seizures, later evolving into multiple treatment-resistant seizure types (myoclonic, atypical absence, focal) with developmental regression/intellectual disability. Approximately 70-80% of cases are associated with SCN1A gene variants (loss-of-function, sodium channel), >90% of which arise de novo.
named_syndromes.source: epilepsydiagnosis.org, 'Dravet Syndrome (DS)' diagnostic criteria; OMIM #607208 Dravet Syndrome; PMC8739186, 'SCN1A Mutation-Beyond Dravet Syndrome: A Systematic Review'

named_syndromes.syndrome: Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy with Hippocampal Sclerosis (MTLE-HS)
named_syndromes.features: The most common surgically remediable focal epilepsy syndrome in adults; seizures typically arise from the hippocampus/mesial temporal structures, often preceded by an epigastric rising sensation or other aura, with impaired awareness and oroalimentary automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing). MRI shows hippocampal atrophy on T1 with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the affected hippocampus - the defining structural correlate.
named_syndromes.source: MedLink Neurology, 'Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis'; epilepsydiagnosis.org 'Familial Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy'

named_syndromes.features: Onset typically age 4-10 years; brief (typically 4-20 second) staring spells with abrupt onset/offset and immediate return to baseline (no postictal confusion), often provoked by hyperventilation; EEG shows classic generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
named_syndromes.source: ILAE Epilepsy Diagnosis manual, epilepsy syndrome classification

classification_epilepsy_syndromes.source: ILAE Classification and Definition of Epilepsy Syndromes (ilae.org); epilepsydiagnosis.org syndrome pages
classification_epilepsy_syndromes.confidence: high for syndrome-defining clinical/EEG features - these are long-established, consistently described diagnostic criteria

etiology.framework: ILAE recognises six (non-hierarchical, non-mutually-exclusive) etiologic categories: structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune, and unknown - a given patient's epilepsy may fall into more than one category simultaneously.

structural.note: Includes stroke (cross-reference the stroke entry - post-stroke seizures occur in ~3-8% early and epilepsy in ~7-10% late per pooled meta-analyses), traumatic brain injury, brain tumour, and cortical malformations (e.g. focal cortical dysplasia). In a paediatric hospital cohort, an identifiable structural aetiology was found in 18.8% of patients.
structural.source: Epilepsy & Behavior 2024, paediatric hospital-based ILAE 2017/2022 classification study; cross-reference this knowledge base's stroke entry (complications: post-stroke seizures/epilepsy)

structural_TBI_specific.note: Post-traumatic epilepsy risk rises steeply with injury severity: cumulative incidence over ~30 years is approximately 2% after mild TBI, 4% after moderate TBI, and >15% after severe TBI; risk exceeds 50% in severe injuries with dural penetration and cortical injury. A contemporary Norwegian cohort found 11.8% cumulative incidence at 2 years and 13.2% at 5 years after severe TBI, and epilepsy risk overall was 7.4-fold higher after severe brain injury versus the general population.
structural_TBI_specific.source: Annegers JF et al. cohort data (NCBI Bookshelf, 'Epilepsy after Traumatic Brain Injury'); Frontiers in Neurology 2024, 'Risk of epilepsy after traumatic brain injury: a nationwide Norwegian matched cohort study'

genetic.note: A presumed genetic aetiology was assigned in 35.7% of a paediatric epilepsy cohort - the single largest identified category. Specific gene-epilepsy associations include SCN1A (sodium channel) variants in ~70-80% of Dravet syndrome (>90% de novo) and in the milder Genetic Epilepsy with Febrile Seizures Plus (GEFS+) spectrum.
genetic.source: Epilepsy & Behavior 2024 paediatric cohort study; PMC8739186 SCN1A systematic review; Rare Disease Advisor, 'Dravet Syndrome Genetics'

infectious_neurocysticercosis_india.note: Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium larval CNS infection) is a major, India/developing-world-relevant cause of epilepsy. Real Indian proportion data: 40% of epilepsy patients in a rural Northwest India cohort had CT/MRI evidence of past or recent neurocysticercosis; 24.8% of active epilepsy cases in a Uttarakhand community study; 61.2% of active epilepsy patients in a hospital-based Assam study met definitive/probable neurocysticercosis criteria; 42.2% in an Assam tea-garden community study; and 13.7% of 451 people with epilepsy in a rural South Indian community had epilepsy specifically attributable to calcified-stage neurocysticercosis. Regional variation in Indian epilepsy prevalence is partly explained by regional variation in neurocysticercosis prevalence.
infectious_neurocysticercosis_india.source: PMC3420514, 'Active Epilepsy as Indicator of Neurocysticercosis in Rural Northwest India'; PMC9341139, 'High prevalence of neurocysticercosis among patients with epilepsy...Assam'; PubMed 21339656, 'Neurocysticercosis and its impact on crude prevalence rate of epilepsy in an Indian community'; PMC8016991, 'Neurocysticercosis in patients with active epilepsy...tea garden community of Assam'; PubMed 31376678, 'Prevalence, clinical characteristics, and seizure outcomes of epilepsy due to calcific...neurocysticercosis...south India'
infectious_neurocysticercosis_india.confidence: high - multiple independent Indian community/hospital studies converge on neurocysticercosis as a major real contributor, though the exact proportion varies substantially (13.7%-61.2%) by region and diagnostic criteria used

metabolic.note: Metabolic aetiology (e.g. inborn errors of metabolism, GLUT1 deficiency) was identified in 1.7% of a paediatric epilepsy cohort - a real but comparatively small proportion of the total.

immune.note: Immune aetiology (e.g. autoimmune/antibody-mediated encephalitis presenting with seizures) was identified in 0.8% of the same paediatric cohort - the smallest identified category, but an important one to consider because it is potentially treatable with immunotherapy.

unknown_idiopathic.note: An unknown aetiology (following negative/normal laboratory, genetic/metabolic, and imaging workup) was assigned in 30.3% of the same paediatric cohort - a substantial real proportion even with modern diagnostic workup.

etiology.cross_reference: Stroke, traumatic brain injury, and structural cortical lesions are structural causes shared with this knowledge base's stroke entry; neurocysticercosis is highlighted separately here as an India-specific infectious cause not covered elsewhere in this knowledge base.

EEG.role_and_limitation: EEG supports diagnosis and helps localise/classify seizure type and syndrome, but a NORMAL interictal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy - this is an important diagnostic caveat. Overall EEG sensitivity for epilepsy is under 50%: approximately 30-55% of routine EEGs in patients with confirmed epilepsy, and even 9-10% of prolonged video-EEG studies, show no interictal epileptiform discharges. Sensitivity of a single first EEG is only ~50-55%, rising to as high as 92% with repeated studies, sleep recordings, and activation techniques (hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep deprivation).
EEG.source: PMC/onlinelibrary Wiley, Benbadis S, 'The role of EEG in patients with suspected epilepsy', Epileptic Disorders 2020; PubMed 16197858, EEG interictal sensitivity/specificity
EEG.confidence: high - consistently reported diagnostic limitation across the epileptology literature

video_EEG_and_PNES.role: Prolonged video-EEG monitoring, correlating clinical semiology on video with simultaneous EEG during a typical habitual event, is the gold-standard method for distinguishing true epileptic seizures from Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizures (PNES) - achieving a definitive diagnosis in up to ~90% of monitored patients.
video_EEG_and_PNES.why_it_matters: PNES is a genuinely important, often-missed differential: up to 75% of people ultimately diagnosed with PNES were initially misdiagnosed with epilepsy, 20-30% of patients initially labelled as having drug-resistant epilepsy actually have PNES, and PNES accounts for more than 90% of misdiagnoses seen at specialist epilepsy centres, with an average diagnostic delay of 7-10 years before correct diagnosis.
video_EEG_and_PNES.source: StatPearls, 'Psychogenic Nonepileptic Seizures'; Psychiatric Times, 'The Diagnosis of Psychogenic Nonepileptic Seizures'; ScienceDirect, 'Proposal for best practice in the use of video-EEG when psychogenic non-epileptic seizures are a possible diagnosis'
video_EEG_and_PNES.confidence: high - consistent figures across multiple epileptology sources, though exact percentages vary modestly by study population

MRI_brain.role: MRI brain is the key structural-imaging investigation, most important for identifying an epileptogenic structural lesion - classically hippocampal sclerosis in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, seen as hippocampal atrophy on T1-weighted imaging plus T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the affected hippocampus, and also cortical malformations, tumours, and post-traumatic/post-stroke gliotic scarring. A real limitation: hippocampal sclerosis escapes detection on routine visual inspection in roughly 10% of focal epilepsy cases, improved by dedicated quantitative hippocampal volumetry/T2 signal analysis.
MRI_brain.source: MedLink Neurology, 'Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis'; AJNR 2014, '3T MRI Quantification of Hippocampal Volume and Signal...Improves Detection of Hippocampal Sclerosis'; Radiology Assistant, 'Epilepsy - Role of MRI'

core.name: Focal aware seizures
core.note: Awareness is preserved throughout. Symptoms depend on the cortical location of onset: motor (jerking/stiffening of one limb/side), sensory (tingling, visual flashes, unusual smell/taste), autonomic (epigastric rising sensation, flushing, piloerection), or psychic (deja vu, fear, altered perception). Formerly termed 'simple partial seizures' (term retired under ILAE 2017).
core.source: ILAE 2017 operational seizure classification (Fisher et al., Epilepsia 2017)

core.name: Focal impaired-awareness seizures
core.note: Awareness is impaired for at least part of the seizure; classically accompanied by automatisms - lip-smacking, chewing, fumbling with clothing/objects, or wandering - and a period of post-ictal confusion. Formerly termed 'complex partial seizures' (term retired under ILAE 2017).
core.source: ILAE 2017 operational seizure classification

core.name: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS)
core.note: Classic two-phase seizure: a tonic phase (sudden loss of consciousness, sustained muscle stiffening, often with a cry as air is forced past a closed glottis, and falling if standing), followed by a clonic phase (rhythmic jerking of the limbs). Frequently followed by a period of post-ictal confusion and, when there is unilateral post-ictal weakness, this is termed Todd's paralysis (typically resolving within 48 hours).
core.source: ILAE 2017 operational seizure classification

core.name: Absence seizures
core.note: Brief (typically 4-20 seconds), abrupt-onset and abrupt-offset staring spells with impaired awareness but no falling and no post-ictal confusion; may be accompanied by subtle eyelid fluttering or automatisms. Classic in childhood absence epilepsy, where hyperventilation reliably provokes an episode and EEG shows generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
core.source: ILAE Epilepsy Diagnosis manual, childhood absence epilepsy

core.name: Myoclonic seizures
core.note: Sudden, brief, shock-like jerks of a muscle or muscle group, without loss of consciousness; classically occur shortly after waking in Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy, often provoked by sleep deprivation.
core.source: ILAE Epilepsy Diagnosis manual, Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy

status_epilepticus.operational_definition: ILAE 2015 conceptual/operational definition uses two time points: t1 (the time point beyond which a seizure should be regarded as an 'abnormally prolonged seizure' and emergency treatment should be started) and t2 (the time point beyond which there is risk of long-term consequences, including neuronal injury). For convulsive (tonic-clonic) status epilepticus, t1 = 5 minutes and t2 = 30 minutes. Equivalently, status epilepticus is operationally defined as continuous seizure activity lasting >=5 minutes, OR recurrent seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them.
status_epilepticus.mortality: Overall mortality of status epilepticus ranges from 9% to 37%, strongly dependent on aetiology and duration of status; seizures lasting more than 30 minutes carry significantly higher mortality than those lasting 10-29 minutes, and patients reaching t2 (30 minutes) have markedly increased mortality and unfavourable functional outcomes compared with those who resolve within the t1-t2 window.
status_epilepticus.source: Trinka E et al., 'A definition and classification of status epilepticus - Report of the ILAE Task Force on Classification of Status Epilepticus', Epilepsia 2015 (PubMed 26336950); BMC Neurology 2022, 'Timing matters: there are significant differences in short-term outcomes between two time points of status epilepticus'
status_epilepticus.confidence: high - current official ILAE operational definition and its mortality correlation are well replicated

real_risk_factors.note: A presumed genetic aetiology accounts for a substantial proportion (~36% in one paediatric cohort) of epilepsy overall; specific channelopathy genes such as SCN1A are directly causal in defined syndromes (Dravet syndrome, GEFS+).
real_risk_factors.source: Epilepsy & Behavior 2024 paediatric cohort study; PMC8739186

real_risk_factors.note: Simple febrile seizures carry only a modestly elevated subsequent epilepsy risk of about 2%. Complex/prolonged febrile seizures (focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hours) carry a substantially higher risk of 5-10% (some series report 6-8%); risk rises further with earlier age of onset, abnormal neurodevelopment, abnormal EEG, or family history of epilepsy.
real_risk_factors.source: AAFP, 'Febrile Seizures: Risks, Evaluation, and Prognosis'; Neurology 2012, 'Long-term risk of developing epilepsy after febrile seizures'; MedLink Neurology, 'Febrile seizures'

real_risk_factors.note: See etiology.infectious_neurocysticercosis_india above - a major, India-relevant cause with real proportion data across multiple regional Indian studies (13.7%-61.2% of epilepsy cohorts depending on region/criteria).
real_risk_factors.source: See etiology section citations above

real_risk_factors.note: Risk of post-traumatic epilepsy rises steeply with severity: ~2% after mild TBI, ~4% after moderate TBI, >15% (up to >50% with dural penetration/cortical injury) after severe TBI.
real_risk_factors.source: NCBI Bookshelf, 'Epilepsy after Traumatic Brain Injury'; Frontiers in Neurology 2024 Norwegian cohort study

real_risk_factors.note: Cross-reference the stroke entry: early post-stroke seizures occur in ~3-8% of patients and late post-stroke epilepsy in ~7-10% (ranges up to 6-15% across meta-analyses).
real_risk_factors.source: Cross-reference: this knowledge base's stroke entry, complications.Seizures (post-stroke)

real_risk_factors.note: Perinatal brain injury and cortical malformations are recognised structural causes of paediatric-onset epilepsy, contributing to the structural-aetiology category alongside acquired lesions.

global.finding: Around 50 million people worldwide have epilepsy, one of the most common neurological diseases globally. Nearly 80% of people with epilepsy live in low- and middle-income countries. The estimated proportion of the general population with active epilepsy at any given time is 4-10 per 1000 people. An estimated 5 million people are newly diagnosed with epilepsy each year; annual incidence is ~49 per 100,000 in high-income countries versus up to 139 per 100,000 in low- and middle-income countries.
global.source: WHO, 'Epilepsy' fact sheet, updated 7 February 2024 (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/epilepsy)

india_specific.finding: Indian epilepsy prevalence studies (1964 onward) range from 2.5 to 11.9 per 1000 population; a meta-analysis of 20 studies (598,910 people) found a pooled crude prevalence of 5.35 per 1000 (adjusted 5.33 per 1000, 95% CI 4.25-6.41), broadly comparable between rural (5.47/1000) and urban (5.11/1000) areas, with higher rates among males, rural populations, and lower socioeconomic groups.
india_specific.source: PMC3548390, 'Epidemiology and treatment gap of epilepsy in India'; Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology, 'Epilepsy in India I: Epidemiology and public health' (PubMed 26425001)
india_specific.confidence: high - consistent across multiple large Indian epidemiological reviews/meta-analyses

india_treatment_gap.finding: The epilepsy treatment gap (proportion of people with epilepsy not receiving adequate/regular antiseizure treatment) in India ranges from 22% to 50% in suburban/urban areas up to 40-90% in rural areas. Globally, the treatment gap is estimated at 75% in low-income countries and 50% in middle-income countries. At least 12-15 million Indians have epilepsy, implying well over 10 million untreated or inadequately treated patients in India alone; unaffordable treatment cost, drug unavailability, and social stigma/superstition are cited as major drivers.
india_treatment_gap.source: PMC7887495, 'Epilepsy Treatment Gap in India: Is It Too High a Peak to Scale?'; PMC7657297, 'Bridging The Gap in Epilepsy Treatment in A Resource-Limited Setting'; PMC3021924, 'Epilepsy Care in Developing Countries'
india_treatment_gap.confidence: high - concept and wide range are consistently reported across Indian and global epilepsy-care literature; the exact percentage varies by region as noted

seizure_freedom_with_treatment.finding: In the landmark Kwan & Brodie cohort of 470 previously untreated patients started on monotherapy, 47% became seizure-free with their first antiseizure drug, and a further 14% became seizure-free with a second or third drug. However, failure of the first drug carries only a ~10% chance of seizure freedom with subsequent drug trials, and only ~4% of the entire cohort achieved seizure freedom after two prior drug failures - the empirical basis for defining drug-resistant epilepsy after two adequately-trialled, tolerated antiseizure medicines have failed. WHO separately estimates that up to 70% of people with epilepsy could live seizure-free if properly diagnosed and treated - the gap between this figure and real-world outcomes reflects diagnostic delay, treatment gap, and access barriers rather than a ceiling on drug efficacy itself.
seizure_freedom_with_treatment.source: Kwan P, Brodie MJ, 'Effectiveness of first antiepileptic drug', Epilepsia 2001 (PubMed 11737159); WHO Epilepsy fact sheet 2024
seizure_freedom_with_treatment.confidence: high - Kwan & Brodie is the foundational, widely-replicated dataset defining drug-resistant epilepsy

SUDEP.finding: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) is the leading cause of epilepsy-related death in adults, with an incidence of approximately 1.2 per 1000 person-years in the general epilepsy population, rising to 2.46-5.94 per 1000 person-years (accounting for 14.7-17.4% of deaths) in drug-resistant epilepsy; incidence in children is lower, at 0.22 per 1000 patient-years. The single leading risk factor is the occurrence and frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (risk rises with >=3 GTCS per year); other major risk factors include lack of antiseizure drug treatment, polytherapy (>=3 drugs, reflecting more severe/refractory disease), nocturnal seizures, longer epilepsy duration, and intellectual disability. Proposed mechanism: a seizure-induced, centrally-mediated disruption of cardiorespiratory function leading to terminal apnoea and/or cardiac arrest.
SUDEP.source: Neurology 2017, AAN/AES Practice Guideline Summary, 'Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy incidence rates and risk factors'; PMC5613169, 'Ranking the Leading Risk Factors for Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy'
SUDEP.confidence: high - AAN/AES practice guideline based on systematic review, genuinely important and often under-recognised mortality risk

red_flags: Status epilepticus (continuous seizure activity >=5 minutes, or recurrent seizures without full recovery between them) - a real life-threatening neurological emergency requiring immediate emergency treatment; mortality 9-37% and rises sharply beyond 30 minutes of ongoing seizure activity.

New focal neurological deficit during or after a seizure (persisting well beyond the expected post-ictal Todd's paralysis window, or with atypical features) - raises concern for an underlying structural lesion (tumour, stroke, abscess) that needs urgent brain imaging.

Signs of raised intracranial pressure accompanying new-onset seizures (severe headache, vomiting, papilloedema, declining consciousness) - suggests a structural intracranial cause requiring emergency neuroimaging and neurosurgical input.

First-ever seizure in an adult, or any seizure with fever/meningism/altered sensorium - must be urgently evaluated for an acute provoked cause (CNS infection, metabolic derangement) before being labelled epilepsy.

epilepsy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Epilepsy's curability picture must be reported in two honestly separate parts, not averaged into one number. (1) For the real majority of patients, epilepsy is genuinely, meaningfully controllable with appropriately chosen antiseizure drug (AED) therapy: in the landmark Kwan & Brodie prospective cohort (525 previously untreated patients, Glasgow, 1984-1997), 333 patients (63%) became completely seizure-free during treatment or after it was stopped, with seizure-free rates similar for a single established drug (67%) and a single newer drug (69%) (Kwan P, Brodie MJ, 'Early Identification of Refractory Epilepsy', NEJM 2000;342:314-319, PMID 10660394). A commonly cited round figure of 'roughly 70% seizure-free, roughly 30% drug-resistant' is used across ILAE/WHO literature and later cohorts as a directional summary of this same finding, and is reported here alongside the precise original 63% figure for honesty rather than rounding it up silently. The remaining ~30-37% who fail two adequately chosen, tolerated AED trials meet the ILAE 2010 consensus definition of drug-resistant epilepsy (Kwan P et al, Epilepsia 2010, 'Definition of drug resistant epilepsy'). (2) For a real, substantial fraction of this drug-resistant ~30% - specifically those with well-localized drug-resistant focal epilepsy such as mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis - epilepsy surgery is a genuinely distinct, curative-intent option, not just another rung of medical management: the only randomized controlled trial of epilepsy surgery (Wiebe S et al, NEJM 2001) found 58% of surgical patients versus 8% of medically-managed patients were free of seizures impairing awareness at 1 year (P<0.001) - see curative_option below. This real cure option is honestly and extensively documented as being under-referred in real-world practice (see epilepsy_surgery below), which is itself a genuine, well-documented care gap distinct from any biological limit on the surgery's own efficacy.

curative_option.name: Resective Epilepsy Surgery for Well-Localized Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy (e.g. Anterior Temporal Lobectomy for Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy with Hippocampal Sclerosis) - Real Genuine Seizure-Freedom Cure Option, Distinct from Lifelong Medical Management
curative_option.note: Unlike AED therapy, which suppresses seizures for as long as the drug is taken, resective surgery physically removes the epileptogenic zone - in appropriately selected, well-localized cases this is a real biological cure of the seizure disorder, not lifelong symptom suppression, and a substantial proportion of surgical patients are able to eventually taper off AEDs entirely under specialist supervision.

real_survival_functional_data.wiebe_2001_RCT: Wiebe S et al, 'A Randomized, Controlled Trial of Surgery for Temporal-Lobe Epilepsy', NEJM 2001;345:311-318 (the only RCT of epilepsy surgery ever conducted, stopped early for efficacy): 80 adults with temporal-lobe epilepsy randomized to anteromesial temporal resection plus AEDs versus AEDs alone for 1 year. At 1 year, the cumulative proportion free of seizures impairing awareness was 58% in the surgical group versus 8% in the medical group (P<0.001); the surgical group also had significantly better quality of life (P<0.001). Four surgical patients (10%) had adverse effects of surgery.
real_survival_functional_data.real_world_center_data: A contemporary real-world referral-center series of 29 temporal lobectomies found 27 patients (93%) completely seizure-free and 2 (7%) with >90% improvement - even higher than the RCT figure, though from a smaller, single-center, non-randomized cohort with its own selection effects.

reason_why: In well-localized mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis, the seizure-generating tissue (the sclerotic hippocampus and adjacent mesial temporal structures) is a discrete, surgically accessible focus rather than a diffusely distributed abnormality - resecting it removes the actual anatomical substrate generating the seizures, rather than pharmacologically raising the seizure threshold everywhere in the brain as AEDs do.

This is why surgery can achieve genuine, drug-independent seizure freedom in a way no AED can: AEDs work only as long as they are present at adequate brain concentration, whereas removing the epileptogenic tissue eliminates the source itself.
curative_option.the_underutilization_care_gap: Epilepsy surgery is real and well-documented to be dramatically under-referred and delayed in practice: real-world data show fewer than 1% of potentially eligible drug-resistant patients are ever referred for surgical evaluation, and among those who are referred, the average time from seizure onset to surgery is approximately 20 years in the United States, with real single-center data showing patients waited an average of 18 years before being seen at a specialist epilepsy center and 39% self-referred without their neurologist having discussed surgery with them at all. This is a genuine, well-documented care gap - not a reflection of the surgery's own efficacy, which the Wiebe RCT already established - and clinicians should refer patients meeting the ILAE drug-resistant definition (two failed adequately-trialled AEDs) for surgical video-EEG/imaging evaluation far earlier than current real-world practice typically does.
curative_option.important_caveat: This curative-intent pathway applies specifically to well-localized, surgically accessible epileptogenic foci (classically mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis on MRI, and other single well-defined lesional foci); it is not a universal option for multifocal, poorly-localized, or eloquent-cortex-overlapping epilepsy, for whom neurostimulation (below) is the real alternative once resective surgery is not feasible.
curative_option.source: Wiebe S et al, NEJM 2001;345:311-318 (PMID 11484687); real-world epilepsy-surgery-utilization literature (Englot DJ, Epilepsia 2025 'Perils and progress in epilepsy surgery utilization'; barriers-to-referral literature, PMC11705306/PMC5912964)
curative_option.confidence: high - the RCT is small (80 patients) but is the only randomized surgical-epilepsy trial ever done and its effect size is large and highly statistically significant; the underutilization data is consistent across multiple independent real-world cohorts

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine/procedure/device used across the epilepsy spectrum (first-line AED selection by seizure type, newer adjunctive AEDs, status epilepticus emergency management, epilepsy surgery, neurostimulation, ketogenic diet, neurocysticercosis-specific treatment, and SUDEP prevention). See curative_option above for resective epilepsy surgery, epilepsy's real closest thing to a genuine cure for well-localized drug-resistant focal disease. All new keys are prefixed epilepsy_ to avoid collision with other entries' generically-named sections. Every drug class carries real specific drug names per this project's standing rule.

epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.name: Lamotrigine - First-Line, SANAD II-Confirmed Standard for Newly Diagnosed Focal Epilepsy
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.effectiveness: SANAD II (Lancet 2021, 990 patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, open-label non-inferiority RCT): lamotrigine achieved superior 12-month remission compared with both levetiracetam (hazard ratio 1.32 favouring lamotrigine) and zonisamide (hazard ratio 1.37 favouring lamotrigine) on per-protocol analysis. The trial concluded lamotrigine should remain first-line for focal epilepsy and that levetiracetam/zonisamide are not supported as first-line alternatives.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.reason_why: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in a use-dependent manner, preferentially in rapidly-firing epileptic neurons, stabilising neuronal membranes and reducing the sustained repetitive firing that underlies focal seizure propagation, while its favourable side-effect/tolerability profile allows patients to remain on an effective dose for longer, which SANAD II found translated into materially better real-world remission rates than levetiracetam or zonisamide.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.source: Marson A et al, 'The SANAD II study of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of levetiracetam, zonisamide, or lamotrigine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy', Lancet 2021;397:1363-1374 (PMID 33838757)
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.confidence: high - large pragmatic multicentre UK RCT, the current best head-to-head comparative-effectiveness evidence for focal-epilepsy first-line choice

epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.name: Levetiracetam - Widely-Used Alternative, Real Comparative Data Now Shows It Is Not First-Line
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.effectiveness: SANAD II found levetiracetam inferior to lamotrigine for 12-month remission in focal epilepsy (HR 1.32 favouring lamotrigine); levetiracetam remains real and effective in absolute terms (many patients do achieve remission on it) and is favoured in specific real clinical situations - rapid IV loading capability, minimal drug-drug interactions, and no need for slow titration - but the head-to-head trial data does not support it as the default first choice when lamotrigine is tolerable.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.reason_why: Binds synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), modulating neurotransmitter vesicle release and dampening hypersynchronous neuronal firing - a mechanism distinct from sodium-channel blockade, useful when carbamazepine/lamotrigine are contraindicated or when rapid IV loading is needed (e.g. peri-operatively), but SANAD II's real comparative data shows this mechanism does not translate into superior remission versus lamotrigine for routine first-line focal-epilepsy use.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.important_caveat: Real, well-documented behavioural/psychiatric side effects (irritability, mood change) occur in a meaningful minority and are an important part of the real-world tolerability picture SANAD II's remission data reflects.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.source: Marson A et al, SANAD II (Lancet 2021;397:1363-1374, PMID 33838757)

epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.name: Carbamazepine - Older Real Comparator, Still a Real Effective First-Line Option
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.effectiveness: Predates SANAD II and was the SANAD I (2007) comparator; remains a real, effective, guideline-listed first-line option for focal epilepsy in many settings including India (low cost, long real-world track record), though lamotrigine's SANAD II data and generally better tolerability profile has shifted UK/Western first-line preference.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.reason_why: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in a use-dependent fashion (mechanistically similar in principle to lamotrigine, but a distinct chemical class with a different side-effect/interaction profile), reducing sustained high-frequency neuronal firing underlying focal seizures.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.important_caveat: Real, serious HLA-B*1502-associated Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis risk in patients of Han Chinese/Southeast Asian/South Asian ancestry - genotyping before starting is a real, guideline-recommended safety step in populations with meaningful HLA-B*1502 prevalence.
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.source: SANAD I (Marson A et al, Lancet 2007, the original 2007 trial comparing carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and other AEDs for focal epilepsy); ILAE first-line AED guidance
epilepsy_first_line_focal_aeds.confidence: moderate-high - SANAD I is an older but real RCT; carbamazepine's real-world first-line role, especially in India, is well-documented though not re-tested head-to-head against lamotrigine in SANAD II

epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.name: Valproate - SANAD II-Confirmed Most Effective First-Line AED for Generalized/Unclassifiable Epilepsy, But With a Critical Teratogenicity Warning
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.type: Antiseizure drug (multiple mechanisms: sodium-channel blockade, GABA-transaminase inhibition, T-type calcium-channel effects)
specific_drugs: Sodium valproate / Valproic acid (Depakote, Epival, Encorate)
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.effectiveness: SANAD II (Lancet 2021, 520 patients with newly diagnosed generalized or unclassifiable epilepsy): levetiracetam was found INFERIOR to valproate for both 12-month and 24-month remission, and was neither clinically effective nor cost-effective compared with valproate - establishing valproate as the real more-effective first-line drug for this seizure category specifically.
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.reason_why: Valproate acts through multiple complementary mechanisms - use-dependent sodium-channel blockade, inhibition of GABA transaminase (raising inhibitory GABA levels), and T-type calcium-channel modulation relevant to absence seizures - giving it genuinely broader-spectrum efficacy across generalized seizure types (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic) than levetiracetam, which SANAD II's remission data reflects.
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.important_caveat: CRITICAL, WELL-DOCUMENTED SAFETY WARNING: valproate is a real, potent human teratogen. First-trimester exposure causes fetal valproate syndrome - a dose-related (reported in the 500-1000 mg/day range and higher) pattern of neural tube defects, congenital heart defects, limb defects, genitourinary defects, and characteristic facial dysmorphism, plus a substantially increased risk of neurodevelopmental impairment/lower IQ in exposed children. Because of this real, well-established risk, current guidance (MHRA/EMA Pregnancy Prevention Programme, ACOG, ILAE) is that valproate should generally be AVOIDED in women/girls of childbearing potential whenever an effective alternative exists, and used only with informed consent, effective contraception, and specialist oversight when no alternative controls seizures - SANAD II's own authors explicitly frame their generalized-epilepsy data as informing exactly this benefit-versus-harm discussion for girls and women of childbearing potential, for whom lamotrigine or levetiracetam (both real, less teratogenic alternatives with somewhat lower but still real efficacy in generalized epilepsy) should generally be preferred first.
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.source: Marson A et al, 'The SANAD II study of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of valproate versus levetiracetam for newly diagnosed generalised and unclassifiable epilepsy', Lancet 2021;397:1375-1386 (PMID 33838758)
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.confidence: high - large pragmatic multicentre UK RCT

epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.name: Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam - Real Preferred Alternatives to Valproate in Women/Girls of Childbearing Potential
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.type: Antiseizure drugs (sodium-channel blocker; SV2A modulator, respectively)
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.effectiveness: Both are real, effective alternatives for generalized/unclassifiable epilepsy when valproate's teratogenicity risk is unacceptable; SANAD II's own generalized-epilepsy trial found valproate more effective than levetiracetam specifically, so this is an honest efficacy-versus-safety trade-off, not a claim that these agents match valproate's efficacy - they are recommended specifically because avoiding fetal valproate syndrome is judged to outweigh the real, quantified reduction in seizure-control efficacy for this specific patient population.
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.reason_why: Neither drug carries valproate's teratogenicity profile at anything like the same magnitude of documented risk, making them the real preferred substitution when the patient is, or may become, pregnant - the clinical decision is a real, guideline-endorsed benefit-risk trade-off (accepting somewhat lower population-level seizure-control efficacy in exchange for avoiding a well-documented, severe, irreversible fetal harm).
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.source: Marson A et al, SANAD II generalized-epilepsy trial (Lancet 2021;397:1375-1386); MHRA/EMA valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme guidance
epilepsy_first_line_generalized_aeds.confidence: high for the safety rationale; moderate for exact comparative efficacy versus valproate in this substitution scenario (not a head-to-head RCT of this specific clinical decision)

epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.name: Lacosamide - Adjunctive Focal Seizures, Selective Slow Sodium-Channel Inactivation
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.type: Antiseizure drug (selective enhancer of sodium-channel slow inactivation)
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.effectiveness: Pooled analysis of Phase II/III adjunctive trials in adults with uncontrolled partial-onset (focal) seizures: 50% responder rate was significantly higher than placebo at all tested doses, e.g. one pivotal trial reported 40.5% responders on lacosamide 400 mg/day versus 25.8% on placebo (p=0.01); another reported 33%/41%/38% responders at 200/400/600 mg/day versus 22% on placebo (p<0.01 for 400 and 600 mg/day).
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.reason_why: Unlike traditional sodium-channel blockers (phenytoin, carbamazepine) which act on the channel's fast-inactivation gating, lacosamide selectively enhances the SLOW inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels - a mechanistically distinct action that reduces long-term channel availability specifically during the sustained, repetitive high-frequency firing characteristic of an epileptic focus, without disrupting normal physiological neuronal firing, making it a genuinely complementary add-on mechanism in patients already on a fast-inactivation-acting AED.
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.source: Ben-Menachem E et al and Chung S et al, pivotal Phase III adjunctive lacosamide trials (summarised in Halasz P et al, pooled Phase II/III analysis, Epilepsia 2009-2010); PeerJ 2013 meta-analysis of lacosamide adjunctive therapy
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.confidence: high - multiple independent placebo-controlled Phase III RCTs with a consistent dose-response signal

epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.name: Perampanel - Adjunctive Focal (+/- Secondary Generalized) Seizures, First-in-Class AMPA-Receptor Antagonist
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.effectiveness: Three pivotal Phase III trials (studies 304, 305, 306; 1480 patients total) in drug-resistant partial-onset seizures: Study 306's 50% responder rates were 17.9% (placebo), 20.6% (2mg), 28.5% (4mg, p=0.0132 vs placebo), and 34.9% (8mg, p=0.0003 vs placebo); Study 304's 8mg arm achieved a 37.6% responder rate. Long-term extension study 307 showed responder rates rising over time with continued treatment (41.4% at weeks 14-26 to 62.7% at weeks 92-104).
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.reason_why: Perampanel is the first clinically available drug in the class of selective, non-competitive AMPA-receptor antagonists: it blocks AMPA-receptor-mediated fast excitatory glutamatergic synaptic transmission (rather than acting on sodium/calcium channels or GABA like most other AEDs), directly reducing the excessive excitatory neurotransmission that drives seizure propagation - a genuinely distinct mechanism of action that makes it a rational add-on in patients whose seizures persist despite drugs acting through other mechanisms.
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.source: French JA et al and Krauss GL et al, perampanel Phase III trials 304/305/306 (Neurology/Epilepsia, 2012); French JA et al, extension study 307 (Epilepsia 2013, PMID 22905878)
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.confidence: high - three independent placebo-controlled Phase III RCTs plus long-term extension data

epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.name: Brivaracetam - Adjunctive Focal Seizures, High-Affinity SV2A Ligand
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.effectiveness: Phase III adjunctive trials in uncontrolled focal-onset seizures: an Asian Phase III RCT found 50% responder rates of 19.0% (placebo), 41.1% (brivaracetam 50mg/day), and 49.3% (brivaracetam 200mg/day), both doses p<0.0001 versus placebo; a separate Chinese Phase III RCT found 48.89% responders on brivaracetam 200mg/day versus 23.86% on placebo (OR 3.12, 95% CI 1.63-5.99, p=0.0006); an earlier mixed focal/generalized trial found a 30.3% responder rate versus 16.7% placebo (p=0.006).
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.reason_why: Brivaracetam binds synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) with roughly 15-30-fold higher affinity and greater selectivity than levetiracetam, modulating vesicular neurotransmitter release more potently at the same receptor site - a rational option specifically for patients who partially respond to or poorly tolerate levetiracetam, since it acts through the same validated target with a refined pharmacological profile.
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.source: Inoue Y et al, Asian Phase III brivaracetam trial (Epilepsia Open 2024); Chinese Phase III brivaracetam trial (2025); earlier brivaracetam adjunctive trials (Epilepsia 2014, PMID 24256083/24116853)
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.confidence: high - multiple independent placebo-controlled Phase III RCTs across different populations with a consistent effect

epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.name: Cenobamate - Real Remarkably High Seizure-Freedom Rate for Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy, Dual Mechanism
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.type: Antiseizure drug (dual mechanism: sodium-channel inactivation enhancer + positive allosteric GABA-A modulator)
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.effectiveness: Pivotal Phase II/III dose-response RCT (Krauss GL et al, Lancet Neurology 2020; 437 patients with focal seizures refractory to >=1 prior AED randomized to placebo or cenobamate 100/200/400mg/day): 21% of patients on cenobamate 400mg/day achieved complete seizure freedom during the 12-week maintenance period - described in the trial literature as approximately 3-10 times higher than the seizure-freedom rates achieved by any other new AED tested in similarly designed drug-resistant-focal-epilepsy trials since the 1990s. Real-world multicentre cohort data (12-month follow-up) found seizure freedom in 62.5% of cenobamate-treated patients versus 43.7% with perampanel and 16.6% with brivaracetam in the same comparison, with 83.0% 12-month treatment retention.
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.reason_why: Cenobamate acts through a dual, complementary mechanism - it preferentially inhibits the persistent (late) component of the voltage-gated sodium current far more potently than the transient component (enhancing slow inactivation even more strongly than lacosamide), while simultaneously acting as a positive allosteric modulator at a non-benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor - combining a sodium-channel-based and a GABAergic mechanism in a single molecule, which is the mechanistic rationale proposed for why its seizure-freedom rate in drug-resistant focal epilepsy trials has been substantially higher than single-mechanism newer AEDs.
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.important_caveat: Requires a real, mandatory slow up-titration schedule (over 12+ weeks) specifically because rapid titration was associated with a serious hypersensitivity reaction (including DRESS syndrome) in early trials - real, guideline-documented safety requirement, not optional.
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.source: Krauss GL et al, 'Safety and efficacy of adjunctive cenobamate (YKP3089) in patients with uncontrolled focal seizures', Lancet Neurology 2020;19:38-48 (PMID 31871104); real-world multicentre cenobamate effectiveness study (Epilepsia Open, 2024-2025)
epilepsy_newer_adjunctive_aeds.confidence: high for the pivotal RCT's seizure-freedom finding (genuinely unusual magnitude for a drug-resistant population); moderate-high for the real-world comparative figures (non-randomized, retrospective real-world cohort, not a head-to-head RCT against perampanel/brivaracetam)

epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.name: First-Line: Benzodiazepines - IV Lorazepam or IM/Buccal Midazolam
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.type: Antiseizure drug (GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator), emergency first-line
specific_drugs: Diazepam (IV or rectal, alternative first-line agent per AES 2016 guideline)
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.effectiveness: RAMPART trial (Silbergleit R et al, NEJM 2012; 893 evaluable prehospital status epilepticus patients treated by paramedics): at ED arrival, seizures were absent without need for rescue therapy in 329/448 (73.4%) of patients given intramuscular midazolam versus 282/445 (63.4%) given intravenous lorazepam - an absolute difference of 10 percentage points (95% CI 4.0-16.1), meeting pre-specified criteria for BOTH noninferiority AND superiority of IM midazolam (p<0.001), because IM midazolam can be given immediately without needing IV access, which is often difficult/delayed in a convulsing prehospital patient.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.reason_why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators at the GABA-A receptor, potentiating the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter (GABA) to rapidly terminate the hypersynchronous, self-sustaining seizure activity of status epilepticus; the RAMPART finding that IM midazolam outperformed IV lorazepam in the real prehospital setting reflects a route-of-administration/time-to-treatment effect (immediate IM injection versus the real delay of establishing IV access in a convulsing patient) rather than a difference in the underlying GABAergic mechanism itself.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.important_caveat: GABA-A receptor efficiency of benzodiazepines is time-dependent and falls with prolonged seizure duration (receptor internalization) - this is the real pharmacological rationale for treating status epilepticus as fast as possible and for escalating promptly to second-line therapy if benzodiazepines fail, rather than repeating benzodiazepine doses indefinitely.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.source: Silbergleit R et al, 'Intramuscular versus Intravenous Therapy for Prehospital Status Epilepticus' (RAMPART), NEJM 2012;366:591-600 (PMID 22335736)
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.confidence: high - large multicentre double-blind RCT, directly changed US EMS/AES 2016 practice guidelines

epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.name: Second-Line: Fosphenytoin, Valproate, or Levetiracetam (Benzodiazepine-Refractory Status Epilepticus)
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.type: Antiseizure drugs (sodium-channel blocker; multi-mechanism; SV2A modulator, respectively) - IV infusion
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.effectiveness: ESETT trial (Kapur J et al, NEJM 2019; double-blind, response-adaptive randomized comparative-effectiveness trial in benzodiazepine-refractory established status epilepticus): all three agents showed approximately equal, roughly 50% efficacy for seizure cessation plus improved alertness by 60 minutes without additional anticonvulsant - levetiracetam 52% (95% CI 41-62%), fosphenytoin 49% (95% CI 38-61%), valproate 52% (95% CI 41-63%) - with similar rates of adverse events across all three, establishing genuine real equipoise between the three agents for this indication.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.reason_why: These three agents act through genuinely different mechanisms (sodium-channel blockade for fosphenytoin, multi-mechanism GABAergic/sodium-channel/calcium-channel action for valproate, SV2A modulation for levetiracetam) yet ESETT found essentially equivalent real-world efficacy (~50% each) for terminating benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus - meaning agent choice in practice can reasonably be guided by patient-specific factors (comorbidities, drug interactions, hepatic/renal function) rather than by an efficacy hierarchy, since none of the three real trial arms outperformed the others.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.important_caveat: Only fosphenytoin carries formal FDA indication for status epilepticus among the three ESETT agents in adults; levetiracetam and valproate are real, guideline-supported, evidence-based off-label uses per ESETT and the AES 2016 guideline.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.source: Kapur J et al, 'Randomized Trial of Three Anticonvulsant Medications for Status Epilepticus' (ESETT), NEJM 2019;381:2103-2113 (PMID 31774955)
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.confidence: high - large NIH-funded multicentre double-blind adaptive RCT, directly informs current second-line agent selection

epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.name: Third-Line: Continuous Anesthetic Infusion for Refractory Status Epilepticus
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.type: Anesthetic agents (GABA-A potentiators / NMDA antagonist) - continuous IV infusion under EEG monitoring
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.effectiveness: AES 2016 evidence-based guideline (Glauser T et al, Epilepsy Currents 2016): if second-line therapy fails to terminate status epilepticus (refractory status epilepticus), treatment options at this stage are anesthetic doses of thiopental, midazolam, pentobarbital, or propofol, all administered with continuous EEG monitoring to titrate to burst-suppression or seizure cessation - this stage carries real, substantially higher morbidity/mortality reflecting both the severity of truly refractory status epilepticus itself and the risks of deep anesthesia (hypotension, need for mechanical ventilation, infection).
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.reason_why: At this refractory stage, seizure activity has typically become self-sustaining through GABA-A receptor internalization (reducing benzodiazepine efficacy) and NMDA-receptor upregulation - continuous anesthetic-dose infusions achieve much deeper, more sustained GABA-A potentiation (or, for agents with NMDA-antagonist activity, block the upregulated excitatory pathway directly) than intermittent bolus dosing can, which is why titration to EEG burst-suppression, not just clinical seizure cessation, is the real guideline-recommended endpoint at this stage.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.important_caveat: Requires ICU-level care with continuous EEG monitoring and usually mechanical ventilation - this is real, resource-intensive critical care, appropriately reserved for genuinely benzodiazepine- and second-line-drug-refractory cases.
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.source: Glauser T et al, 'Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults: Report of the Guideline Committee of the American Epilepsy Society', Epilepsy Currents 2016;16:48-61
epilepsy_status_epilepticus_management.confidence: high - current standing AES practice guideline synthesizing the available evidence for this treatment stage

epilepsy_surgery.name: Resective Epilepsy Surgery (Anterior Temporal Lobectomy) for Drug-Resistant Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy
epilepsy_surgery.type: Neurosurgical procedure (resection of the epileptogenic zone)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - neurosurgical resection procedure, performed alongside continued AED therapy which is often tapered post-operatively under specialist supervision
epilepsy_surgery.effectiveness: See curative_option above for full real trial data (Wiebe et al NEJM 2001: 58% surgical vs 8% medical seizure-freedom at 1 year, P<0.001) - reproduced here as the exhaustive-survey entry for completeness.
epilepsy_surgery.reason_why: Physically removes the discrete, surgically accessible epileptogenic focus (classically the sclerotic hippocampus and mesial temporal structures) rather than pharmacologically suppressing seizure activity brain-wide, giving it genuine curative potential distinct from any AED - see curative_option and epilepsy_surgery's underutilization note above for the real, well-documented referral gap that limits how many eligible patients actually receive this option.
epilepsy_surgery.real_working_solution: For patients meeting the ILAE drug-resistant-epilepsy definition (two failed adequately-trialled, tolerated AEDs) with a well-localized single focus on video-EEG/MRI workup, timely referral to a comprehensive epilepsy surgery center for evaluation is the real, evidence-based working solution - not indefinite trial-and-error cycling through additional AEDs, which the real-world referral-delay data shows is exactly what happens far too often in practice.
