epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.name: Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) - Drug-Resistant Epilepsy Not Amenable to Resection
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.type: Implantable neurostimulation device (intermittent cervical vagus nerve stimulation)
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.effectiveness: Real long-term single-center/cohort outcome data show seizure reduction increasing progressively with duration of therapy: mean seizure-frequency reduction of 35.7% at 6 months rising to 66.8% at 84 months (7 years) in one long-term series; responder rates (>=50% seizure reduction) of 38.4%/51.4%/63.6%/77.8% at years 1/2/10/17 in another long-term series, with 10.8-20.5% of patients (higher in pediatric cohorts) eventually achieving seizure freedom for >=1 year.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.reason_why: An implanted pulse generator delivers intermittent electrical stimulation to the left cervical vagus nerve, which projects via the nucleus tractus solitarius to widespread brainstem and forebrain structures (locus coeruleus, thalamus, limbic structures) involved in seizure network modulation - the real, honestly-described mechanism is desynchronization of pathological cortical network activity rather than resection of a specific focus, which is why VNS's real benefit accrues progressively over years rather than immediately, and is offered specifically to patients whose epilepsy is not amenable to resective surgery (multifocal, poorly localized, or eloquent-cortex-overlapping foci).
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.important_caveat: VNS very rarely produces complete seizure freedom (responder-rate data above is predominantly a partial seizure-reduction benefit) - it is a real, valuable option to reduce seizure burden, not a cure, and should not substitute for a genuine resective-surgery evaluation when the patient is in fact a resection candidate.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.source: Multiple long-term VNS outcome cohort studies (Acta Epileptologica 2022, 'Long-term outcomes and prognosis factors of vagus nerve stimulation'; long-term single-center follow-up studies, 2018-2025)
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.confidence: moderate-high - consistent real-world long-term cohort data across multiple independent centers, though VNS lacks a large modern placebo-controlled RCT of this design (device implantation is not practically sham-controllable for years of follow-up)

epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.name: Responsive Neurostimulation (RNS System) - Focal Drug-Resistant Epilepsy, 1-2 Seizure Foci
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.type: Implantable closed-loop neurostimulation device (cortical/subcortical electrodes detect epileptiform activity and deliver responsive stimulation)
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.effectiveness: RNS System pivotal trial (Morrell MJ et al, Neurology 2011/2014; 191 randomized subjects): active stimulation produced -37.9% change in seizures versus -17.3% with sham stimulation during the blinded period. Long-term open-label follow-up showed progressive improvement: median seizure reduction of 44% at 1 year, 53% at 2 years, and 75% at 9 years, with 73% of patients achieving >=50% seizure reduction at 9 years; the long-term SUDEP rate with the RNS System (2.8 per 1000 patient-stimulation-years) was significantly lower than comparable drug-resistant-epilepsy populations without the device.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.reason_why: Unlike VNS's open-loop, scheduled stimulation, the RNS System continuously monitors intracranial EEG from electrodes placed directly at the identified seizure focus/foci and delivers stimulation only in direct response to detected early ictal/epileptiform activity - a real closed-loop, focus-targeted mechanism designed specifically for patients with 1-2 well-identified but non-resectable (eloquent cortex, bilateral, or otherwise surgically inaccessible) seizure foci, which is why its long-term seizure-reduction trajectory (progressively improving over 9 years) differs from a one-time resective cure but still achieves genuinely substantial, real, guideline-recognized benefit.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.source: Morrell MJ et al, RNS System Pivotal Trial (Neurology 2011, 2014, PMID 24621228); Nair DR et al, nine-year prospective RNS outcome study (Neurology 2020, PMID published under 10.1212/WNL.0000000000010154)
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.confidence: high - randomized double-blind sham-controlled pivotal trial plus prospective long-term (9-year) open-label follow-up with a consistent progressive-improvement signal

epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.name: Deep Brain Stimulation of the Anterior Nucleus of the Thalamus (ANT-DBS) - SANTE Trial
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.type: Implantable neurostimulation device (bilateral anterior thalamic nucleus stimulation)
specific_drugs: Medtronic DBS System (anterior thalamic nucleus target)
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.effectiveness: SANTE trial (Fisher R et al; 110 adults with refractory partial-onset seizures randomized to bilateral ANT-DBS): median seizure-frequency reduction from baseline was 41% at 1 year, 69% at 5 years, and 75% at 7 years, with responder rates of 43% at 1 year and 68% at 5 years; at 5 years, 16% of subjects were seizure-free for at least 6 months continuously. FDA-approved for focal epilepsy in 2018 based on this trial.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.reason_why: The anterior thalamic nucleus is a real, well-connected relay hub within the Papez circuit/limbic network implicated in seizure propagation from multiple cortical regions; bilateral stimulation here modulates a shared downstream network rather than a single cortical focus, making ANT-DBS a rational option specifically for multifocal or non-localizable drug-resistant epilepsy where neither resection nor a single-focus RNS placement is feasible - the trial's progressively improving seizure-reduction trajectory over years mirrors RNS's pattern and is attributed to gradual, stimulation-induced network-level neuromodulatory changes rather than an acute lesional effect.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.important_caveat: SANTE's long-term follow-up (10-year Salanova 2021 analysis) explicitly reported on SUDEP incidence in this population as a real safety endpoint given DBS-treated patients remain a drug-resistant, SUDEP-at-risk population by definition; the reported SUDEP rate with DBS was comparable to other neuromodulation therapies for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, not a new added risk beyond the population's own baseline risk.
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.source: Fisher R et al, SANTE pivotal trial (Epilepsia 2010); Salanova V et al, 'The SANTE study at 10 years of follow-up' (Epilepsia 2021, PMID 34042175)
epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices.confidence: high - randomized double-blind sham-controlled pivotal trial with long-term (7-10 year) prospective follow-up showing a consistent progressive-improvement signal similar to RNS

epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.name: Classic Ketogenic Diet - Real Evidence-Based Non-Pharmacologic Option, Particularly for Pediatric Drug-Resistant Epilepsy
epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.type: Non-pharmacologic metabolic therapy (high-fat, low-carbohydrate, adequate-protein diet inducing sustained ketosis)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - classic 4:1 (fat:carbohydrate+protein by weight) ketogenic diet, medically supervised; modified Atkins diet and low-glycemic-index treatment are real, better-tolerated variant regimens used particularly in adolescents/adults
epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.effectiveness: Neal EG et al, Lancet Neurology 2008 (the landmark RCT: 145 children aged 2-16 with drug-resistant epilepsy, >=2 failed AEDs, randomized to immediate ketogenic diet versus delayed-start control): at 3 months, mean seizures were 62.0% of baseline in the diet group versus 136.9% in controls (a real 75% relative reduction, 95% CI 42.4-107.4%, p<0.0001); 28/73 children (38%) on the diet achieved >50% seizure reduction versus 4/72 (6%) of controls (p<0.0001), and 5/73 (7%) achieved >90% seizure reduction versus none of the controls.
epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.reason_why: Sustained ketosis shifts the brain's primary fuel source from glucose to ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate); proposed real mechanisms include ketone-body-mediated enhancement of GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission, reduced glutamatergic excitatory neurotransmission, altered adenosine signalling, and improved mitochondrial energy stability - collectively raising the seizure threshold through a genuinely different (metabolic, not synaptic-receptor) route than any AED, which is the real physiological reason it retains efficacy even in patients who have already failed multiple different AED mechanisms.
epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.important_caveat: Requires real, structured dietetic supervision (constipation, vomiting, lack of energy, and hunger were the most frequent side effects in the Neal 2008 trial; long-term risks include growth restriction, kidney stones, and dyslipidemia) - it is a real, resource-intensive therapy requiring a trained ketogenic-diet team, not a simple home dietary change.
epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.source: Neal EG et al, 'The ketogenic diet for the treatment of childhood epilepsy: a randomised controlled trial', Lancet Neurology 2008;7:500-506 (PMID 18456557)
epilepsy_ketogenic_diet.confidence: high - the landmark randomized controlled trial establishing ketogenic diet efficacy in pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy, widely replicated in subsequent cohorts

epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.name: Albendazole + Corticosteroids (Dexamethasone) - Active/Viable Neurocysticercosis Cysts
epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.effectiveness: Garcia HH et al, NEJM 2004 (Cysticercosis Working Group in Peru, double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, 120 patients with living cysticerci and seizures): albendazole 800mg/day plus dexamethasone 6mg/day for 10 days significantly reduced seizure recurrence versus placebo, with the seizure benefit specifically demonstrated for generalized tonic-clonic seizures; combined albendazole+corticosteroid therapy was found in subsequent real Indian pediatric cohort studies (Chandigarh, North India) to be the most efficacious regimen for both preventing seizure recurrence and promoting radiological lesion resolution over ~1 year of follow-up, superior to either agent alone.
epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.reason_why: Albendazole is a benzimidazole antiparasitic that binds parasite beta-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerization and killing the viable larval cyst; because dying cysts provoke an acute host inflammatory response around the lesion (which is itself a real trigger for seizures and can transiently worsen perilesional oedema), co-administered corticosteroids suppress this inflammatory reaction, reducing the real risk of a treatment-induced seizure flare while the antiparasitic clears the underlying living organism that is the actual cause of the epilepsy in these patients - directly treating the underlying infectious cause rather than only suppressing the resulting seizures with an AED.
epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.important_caveat: This regimen is specific to VIABLE/ACTIVE cysts (seen as a cystic lesion with a visible scolex, or an enhancing lesion, on CT/MRI) - it is not indicated for purely calcified (dead, burnt-out) neurocysticercosis lesions, which are managed with AEDs alone since there is no longer a living organism to treat; cross-reference this knowledge base's epilepsy symptoms/etiology infectious_neurocysticercosis_india content for the real, substantial India-specific prevalence data (up to 40-61% of epilepsy cohorts in some Indian regional studies) that makes this a genuinely India-relevant, not merely academic, treatment pathway.
epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.real_working_solution: For a patient with new-onset seizures and a solitary cysticercal lesion confirmed on neuroimaging, combined albendazole+corticosteroid therapy directly treats the underlying infectious cause and is the real working solution - alongside, not instead of, standard AED seizure control during the active-cyst treatment period.
epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.source: Garcia HH et al, 'A Trial of Antiparasitic Treatment to Reduce the Rate of Seizures Due to Cerebral Cysticercosis', NEJM 2004;350:249-258 (PMID 14724304); Indian (Chandigarh) randomized trial of corticosteroids vs albendazole vs combination in children with solitary cysticercus granuloma (PMID 15224704)
epilepsy_neurocysticercosis_specific_man.confidence: high - real double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (Garcia 2004) plus a separately-conducted real India-specific pediatric RCT relevant to this knowledge base's India context

epilepsy_sudep_prevention.name: Optimal Seizure Control - The Real Primary SUDEP-Risk-Reduction Strategy
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.type: Preventive strategy (achieved through the full AED/surgery/neurostimulation/ketogenic-diet armamentarium documented in this survey, not a separate intervention)
specific_drugs: Not a specific drug - achieved via the seizure-control modalities documented throughout this exhaustive_medicine_survey (first-line AEDs, newer adjunctive AEDs, epilepsy surgery, neurostimulation, ketogenic diet)
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.effectiveness: AAN/AES practice guideline systematic review (Neurology 2017) identifies the occurrence and frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) as the single leading, most robustly established SUDEP risk factor, with risk rising specifically with >=3 GTCS per year; other major risk factors (lack of AED treatment, polytherapy reflecting more refractory disease, nocturnal seizures, longer epilepsy duration) are themselves markers of poorer seizure control. Because GTCS frequency is the dominant, modifiable risk driver identified across the evidence base, achieving genuine seizure control - by whichever real modality in this survey actually controls the patient's seizures (first-line AEDs for the ~63-70% who respond, or surgery/neurostimulation/ketogenic diet for drug-resistant patients) - is the real, evidence-supported primary SUDEP-prevention strategy, rather than any single dedicated 'anti-SUDEP' drug or device.
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.reason_why: The leading proposed SUDEP mechanism is a seizure-induced, centrally-mediated disruption of cardiorespiratory function (terminal apnoea and/or cardiac arrest) that is triggered specifically by generalized tonic-clonic seizures - since GTCS is the trigger, preventing GTCS from occurring (via effective, appropriately-escalated seizure treatment) removes the proximate cause, which is why seizure control itself, achieved through whichever real treatment modality actually works for a given patient, is the primary risk-reduction lever rather than a separate pharmacological or device-based 'SUDEP prevention' intervention distinct from epilepsy treatment itself.
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.source: Harden C et al / AAN-AES, 'Practice guideline summary: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy incidence rates and risk factors', Neurology 2017;88:1674-1680; Sveinsson O et al ranking-of-risk-factors analysis (PMC5613169)
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.confidence: high - AAN/AES systematic-review-based practice guideline, consistent with the broader SUDEP epidemiological literature

epilepsy_sudep_prevention.name: Nocturnal Supervision - Real, Adjunctive, Lower-Certainty Evidence
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.type: Supervision/monitoring strategy (adjunctive to seizure control, not a substitute for it)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - supervision/monitoring intervention (co-sleeping/room-sharing, seizure-detection devices, listening devices), adjunctive to the primary seizure-control strategies above
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.effectiveness: Cochrane systematic review (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, summarized in NICE evidence review) found limited, very-low-certainty evidence that nocturnal supervision - defined as another person present in the same room at night, or regular checks/listening-device monitoring - reduces SUDEP incidence, reflecting genuine benefit signal but a real, honestly-reported evidence-quality limitation (few, small, non-randomized studies) rather than a lack of real-world clinical adoption.
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.reason_why: If SUDEP is mechanistically driven by an unwitnessed postictal cardiorespiratory event during or after a nocturnal seizure, a supervising person present to reposition the patient (supine-to-prone or recovery position) and provide tactile/verbal stimulation could interrupt the proposed apnoea/asystole cascade before it becomes fatal - a real, biologically plausible adjunctive mechanism, reported here honestly alongside its genuinely limited quality of supporting evidence rather than being overstated as proven.
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.source: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 'Treatments for the prevention of Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP)' (PMID 32239759); NICE evidence review, 'Reducing the risk of seizure-related mortality, including SUDEP'
epilepsy_sudep_prevention.confidence: low-moderate - honestly reported as very-low-certainty evidence by the Cochrane review itself, despite being a widely recommended real clinical practice

epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.name: EEG / Video-EEG Monitoring - Diagnostic and Presurgical Localization
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.type: Diagnostic medical equipment (scalp electroencephalography, inpatient video-EEG telemetry, intracranial/stereo-EEG for presurgical mapping)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - scalp EEG, inpatient video-EEG telemetry units, intracranial/stereo-EEG (SEEG) electrode arrays for presurgical localization
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Standard, guideline-mandated diagnostic tool for epilepsy classification (ILAE 2017 seizure-type framework - cross-reference this knowledge base's epilepsy symptoms/diagnostic_framework content) and, specifically for surgical candidacy, video-EEG telemetry with concordant MRI is the real prerequisite step that identifies whether a patient has the well-localized single focus that makes them a genuine candidate for the resective-surgery cure pathway documented under epilepsy_surgery/curative_option above - without this step, surgical candidacy cannot be honestly assessed at all.
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Correctly classifying seizure type/epilepsy syndrome (cross-reference the concurrently-authored symptoms/diagnostic_framework content in this same entry) is the real prerequisite for every treatment decision documented in this survey - choosing lamotrigine/valproate-class first-line therapy by seizure type, judging drug-resistance, and identifying resective-surgery candidacy via video-EEG/MRI concordance are all directly downstream of accurate EEG-based localization and classification.
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.source: ILAE 2017 classification framework; standard comprehensive-epilepsy-center presurgical evaluation protocols (cross-referenced to this entry's own diagnostic_framework content, not re-derived)
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.confidence: high - established, universally guideline-mandated diagnostic standard

epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.name: Implantable Neurostimulation Devices - VNS, RNS, and ANT-DBS Systems
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.type: Medical devices (implantable neurostimulators, see epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices above for the full real trial data on each)
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: See epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices above (VNS Therapy System, RNS System, Medtronic ANT-DBS System) for the full real trial evidence base for each device's seizure-reduction effectiveness.
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Listed here as the equipment/devices catalogue entry for completeness; the underlying mechanisms and trial evidence for each are fully documented under epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices above rather than re-derived here.
epilepsy_medical_devices_equipment.source: Cross-referenced to epilepsy_neurostimulation_devices above (Morrell MJ et al Neurology 2011/2014/2020; Fisher R et al/Salanova V et al Epilepsia 2010/2021; VNS long-term cohort literature)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages/metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (seizure freedom at 1 year, complete seizure freedom during a 12-week maintenance period, 50% responder rate, absence of seizures at ED arrival, relative seizure-frequency reduction) in DIFFERENT populations (newly diagnosed epilepsy, benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus, drug-resistant focal epilepsy already failing multiple AEDs, pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy) - ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. Resective epilepsy surgery for well-localized drug-resistant focal epilepsy is honestly ranked at the top not merely by its own percentage but because, per curative_option above, it is the one real point in the drug-resistant-epilepsy spectrum capable of genuine, drug-independent seizure freedom rather than lifelong pharmacological suppression; first-line AED therapy is ranked immediately after because it is the real primary solution that already resolves epilepsy for the majority (63-70%) of all newly diagnosed patients, before drug-resistance ever becomes relevant.

parkinsons_disease.name: Parkinson's Disease
parkinsons_disease.icd11_hint: 8A00.0 Parkinson disease (8A00.00 sporadic, 8A00.01 familial); 8A00.1 Atypical parkinsonism (e.g. 8A00.10 progressive supranuclear palsy); 8A00.2 Secondary parkinsonism; ICD-10 G20
parkinsons_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute akinetic crisis / parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome (PHS) is a real, rare, potentially fatal emergency in a person with Parkinson's disease and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow, triggering immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (go to the nearest emergency department NOW). Trigger pattern: a known Parkinson's patient with sudden severe worsening (marked rigidity/near-total immobility) together with fever, reduced consciousness, sweating/tachycardia/labile blood pressure (autonomic instability), especially after missed, reduced or stopped anti-parkinsonian medicines (including inability to swallow tablets, vomiting/gastro-intestinal illness, or a hospital stay/surgery where doses were delayed) or after a new dopamine-blocking medicine such as an antipsychotic or metoclopramide. Newman et al. describe PHS as resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with rigidity, pyrexia and reduced conscious level, possible autonomic instability and raised creatine kinase, complicated by acute renal failure, aspiration pneumonia, DVT/PE and DIC; mortality of up to 4% is reported, with a further one-third of survivors left with permanent sequelae, and prognosis improves with early recognition (Newman EJ et al., Neurocrit Care 2009;10:136-140). The patient or carer must be told never to stop or skip anti-parkinsonian medicines abruptly and not to wait at home if this picture appears.

definition.finding: Parkinson disease (PD) is the second-most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 2-3% of the population aged >=65 years. Neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, which causes striatal dopamine deficiency, and intracellular inclusions containing aggregates of alpha-synuclein are the neuropathological hallmarks. Multiple other cell types throughout the central and peripheral autonomic nervous system are also involved, probably from early disease onwards, which is why PD carries many non-motor symptoms alongside the cardinal motor features. ICD-11 (8A00.0) describes PD as a gradual-onset progressive degenerative disease whose cardinal manifestations include bradykinesia plus one of tremor, rigidity or postural instability.
definition.source: Poewe W et al., 'Parkinson disease', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17013; WHO ICD-11 MMS 8A00.0 Parkinson disease (icd.who.int)
definition.confidence: high - review-level statement of the accepted definition and pathological hallmarks

core_pathology_alpha_synuclein_lewy_bodi.finding: The characteristic pathological hallmark is progressive loss of dopaminergic (neuromelanin-containing) neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta with intraneuronal Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, which contain alpha-synuclein (alpha-synuclein was identified as a component of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites in 1997). Familial evidence supports a causal role for alpha-synuclein: a missense mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene (SNCA, A53T) was identified in an Italian kindred and three unrelated Greek families with autosomal-dominant PD, a specific molecular alteration linked to the disorder.
core_pathology_alpha_synuclein_lewy_bodi.source: Spillantini MG et al., 'Alpha-synuclein in Lewy bodies', Nature 1997;388:839-840; Polymeropoulos MH et al., 'Mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene identified in families with Parkinson's disease', Science 1997;276:2045-2047; Poewe W et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17013

nigral_neuron_loss_at_symptom_onset.finding: Motor symptoms appear only after a substantial part of the nigrostriatal system is already lost, but the exact percentage depends on WHAT is measured (nigral cell bodies vs striatal terminals/dopamine). Verified primary data: (1) Fearnley & Lees (post-mortem, 20 PD cases): pigmented nigral neuron loss in PD is exponential with about 45% lost in the first decade, greatest in the lateral ventral tier (average 91%); the presymptomatic phase was estimated at about 5 years, and at the onset of symptoms there was an estimated 68% cell loss in the lateral ventral tier and 48% in the caudal nigra as a whole (control ageing loss is only 4.7% per decade). (2) Kordower et al. (28 PD brains, 1-27 years post-diagnosis): 50-90% loss of tyrosine-hydroxylase-positive nigral neurons from the earliest time points studied with only marginal additional loss thereafter, while dopaminergic fibre markers in the dorsal putamen were virtually completely lost by 4 years after diagnosis. (3) Kish et al. (8 PD brains): dopamine in the putamen was nearly completely depleted, with under 1% remaining in its caudal portions, and motor deficits were attributed mainly to putaminal dopamine loss.
nigral_neuron_loss_at_symptom_onset.note_on_commonly_quoted_60_80_percent: The often-quoted 'about 60-80% of dopaminergic neurons lost before symptoms' is NOT attributed to a single primary source here because none was verified; the primary measurements above give the honest ranges (about 48-68% nigral neuron loss by region at onset; 50-90% TH-positive neuron loss at early diagnosis; near-complete putaminal dopamine/terminal loss). Cheng et al. propose (as a hypothesis) that ongoing degeneration of axons, rather than cell bodies, is the main determinant of clinically apparent progression.
nigral_neuron_loss_at_symptom_onset.source: Fearnley JM & Lees AJ, Brain 1991;114:2283-2301 (PMID 1933245); Kordower JH et al., 'Disease duration and the integrity of the nigrostriatal system in Parkinson's disease', Brain 2013;136:2419-2431 (PMID 23884810); Kish SJ, Shannak K, Hornykiewicz O, N Engl J Med 1988;318:876-880 (PMID 3352672); Cheng HC, Ulane CM, Burke RE, Ann Neurol 2010 (PMID 20517933)
nigral_neuron_loss_at_symptom_onset.confidence: high for the individual post-mortem measurements; moderate for any single 'percent at onset' number because it varies by region, method and case series

basal_ganglia_circuit_mechanism.finding: In the Albin-Young-Penney functional-anatomy model, hypokinetic disorders such as PD result from a complex series of changes in the activity of striatal projection-neuron subpopulations that increase basal ganglia output, which is the circuit-level explanation for slowness and reduced movement amplitude when striatal dopamine is lost.
basal_ganglia_circuit_mechanism.source: Albin RL, Young AB, Penney JB, 'The functional anatomy of basal ganglia disorders', Trends Neurosci 1989;12:366-375 (PMID 2479133)
basal_ganglia_circuit_mechanism.confidence: high for the classic model; it is a simplification and does not explain every symptom

braak_proposed_staging.finding: Braak et al. proposed, from incidental and symptomatic autopsy cases, that alpha-synuclein pathology begins in the dorsal motor nucleus of the glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves and the anterior olfactory nucleus, then ascends through the brainstem (reaching the substantia nigra), then the anteromedial temporal mesocortex and finally the neocortex. This is a proposed topographical staging procedure. It is often invoked to explain why olfactory loss, constipation and sleep disturbance can precede the motor syndrome and why cognitive impairment appears later, but that symptom-to-stage mapping is an interpretation.
braak_proposed_staging.source: Braak H et al., 'Staging of brain pathology related to sporadic Parkinson's disease', Neurobiol Aging 2003;24:197-211 (PMID 12498954)
braak_proposed_staging.confidence: high that this is what the staging model proposes; the clinical mapping of specific symptoms to specific Braak stages is an interpretation

non_dopaminergic_and_late_disease_featur.finding: In the 20-year Sydney cohort the main problems of late disease relate to non-levodopa-responsive features, and the authors conclude that the diverse features of advanced PD 'go far beyond a lack of dopamine'. Smell loss in PD correlates with reduced neuron numbers in the locus coeruleus, raphe nuclei and nucleus basalis of Meynert, implicating cholinergic, noradrenergic and serotonergic deficits.
non_dopaminergic_and_late_disease_featur.source: Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844 (PMID 18307261); Doty RL, 'Olfactory dysfunction in Parkinson disease', Nat Rev Neurol 2012;8:329-339 (PMID 22584158)

diagnosis_is_clinical_no_definitive_biom.finding: PD is diagnosed clinically. WHO states that PD is a clinical diagnosis that can be made by neurologists and by trained non-specialist health workers, and the MDS criteria state that PD diagnoses are generally made clinically, with ancillary tests permitted only as a single supportive item. There is no established confirmatory laboratory or imaging test that proves idiopathic PD in life; definite diagnosis rests on neuropathology (nigral neuron loss with alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy pathology). The limitation is real: in a meta-analysis of 20 studies (11 with pathology as gold standard) pooled accuracy of clinical diagnosis was 80.6% (95% CrI 75.2-85.3%), 73.8% when made mainly by non-experts, and 79.6% (initial) rising to 83.9% (after follow-up) when made by movement-disorder experts; using UK Brain Bank criteria the pooled accuracy was 82.7%. The original clinico-pathological series found nigral Lewy bodies in only 76 of 100 cases diagnosed prospectively as idiopathic PD (24 had other pathology: progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, Alzheimer-type pathology, basal ganglia vascular disease), improving to 82% accuracy on retrospective application of the criteria. Under-diagnosis also occurs: in the EUROPARKINSON community surveys 24% of people found to have PD were newly detected by the survey.
diagnosis_is_clinical_no_definitive_biom.source: WHO fact sheet 'Parkinson disease' (updated 9 August 2023, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/parkinson-disease); Postuma RB et al., 'MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease', Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Rizzo G et al., 'Accuracy of clinical diagnosis of Parkinson disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Neurology 2016;86:566-576 (PMID 26764028); Hughes AJ et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55:181-184 (PMID 1564476); de Rijk MC et al., EUROPARKINSON study, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1997;62:10-15 (PMID 9010393)
diagnosis_is_clinical_no_definitive_biom.confidence: high - accuracy figures are from a Bayesian meta-analysis and a landmark clinico-pathological series

MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.framework: Step 1 is to establish PARKINSONISM: bradykinesia (slowness of movement AND decrement in amplitude or speed, or progressive hesitations/halts, as movement continues) in combination with rest tremor, rigidity, or both. Limb bradykinesia must be documented. Postural instability is NOT part of the MDS definition of parkinsonism due to PD (it 'often occurs in later stages of PD, but its presence early in disease suggests an alternative diagnosis'). Step 2 is to decide whether PD is the cause using three feature classes: absolute exclusion criteria, red flags, and supportive criteria.

definition_of_features_in_criteria.bradykinesia: Slowness plus decrement in amplitude/speed; assessed with finger tapping, hand movements, pronation-supination, toe and foot tapping (MDS-UPDRS 3.4-3.8). The decrement is a feature sometimes not seen in parkinsonism from alternate conditions.
definition_of_features_in_criteria.rigidity: Judged on slow passive movement of major joints with the patient relaxed; 'lead-pipe' velocity-independent resistance not solely reflecting failure to relax (distinct from spasticity or paratonia). Cogwheeling is often present but may reflect tremor incidentally felt; isolated cogwheeling without lead-pipe rigidity does NOT meet the minimum requirement for rigidity.
definition_of_features_in_criteria.rest_tremor: 4-6 Hz tremor in the fully resting limb that is suppressed during movement initiation; re-emergent tremor with prolonged posture can occur but tremor must also be seen at rest; isolated postural or kinetic tremor does NOT qualify.

MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.clinically_established_PD: Requires (1) absence of absolute exclusion criteria, (2) at least two supportive criteria, and (3) no red flags. Designed to maximise specificity (at least ~90% will have PD).
MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.clinically_probable_PD: Requires absence of absolute exclusion criteria AND red flags counterbalanced by supportive criteria: 1 red flag needs at least 1 supportive criterion; 2 red flags need at least 2 supportive criteria; more than 2 red flags excludes probable PD. Designed to balance sensitivity and specificity (at least ~80% of probable-PD patients truly have PD).
supportive_criteria: 1. Clear and dramatic beneficial response to dopaminergic therapy (returned to normal or near-normal function initially; or, if not documented, marked improvement with dose increases/marked worsening with decreases (>30% change in UPDRS-III or a reliable history), or unequivocal on/off fluctuations that at some point included predictable end-of-dose wearing off).
3. Rest tremor of a limb documented on examination (past or current).
4. Olfactory loss (anosmia or clear hyposmia) or cardiac sympathetic denervation on MIBG scintigraphy.
absolute_exclusion_criteria: Unequivocal cerebellar abnormalities (cerebellar gait, limb ataxia, cerebellar oculomotor abnormalities).
Downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, or selective slowing of downward vertical saccades.
Probable behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia or primary progressive aphasia within the first 5 years of disease.
Parkinsonian features restricted to the lower limbs for more than 3 years.
Treatment with a dopamine receptor blocker or dopamine-depleting agent in a dose and time-course consistent with drug-induced parkinsonism.
Absence of observable response to high-dose levodopa despite at least moderate disease severity.
Unequivocal cortical sensory loss, clear limb ideomotor apraxia, or progressive aphasia.
Normal functional neuroimaging of the presynaptic dopaminergic system.
Documentation of an alternative condition known to produce parkinsonism and plausibly connected to the symptoms, or the expert's judgement that an alternative syndrome is more likely than PD.
red_flags: Rapid progression of gait impairment requiring regular wheelchair use within 5 years of onset.
Complete absence of motor progression over 5 or more years (unless explained by treatment).
Early bulbar dysfunction within 5 years (severe dysphonia/dysarthria - speech unintelligible most of the time - or severe dysphagia requiring soft food, NG tube or gastrostomy).
Inspiratory respiratory dysfunction (diurnal or nocturnal inspiratory stridor or frequent inspiratory sighs).

Severe autonomic failure in the first 5 years (orthostatic BP fall >=30 mmHg systolic or >=15 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing without other cause, or severe urinary retention/incontinence - in men with erectile dysfunction and not due to prostate disease).
Recurrent (more than once a year) falls from impaired balance within 3 years of onset.
Disproportionate anterocollis (dystonic) or hand/foot contractures within the first 10 years.
Absence of ANY common non-motor feature (sleep dysfunction, autonomic dysfunction such as constipation/urgency/orthostasis, hyposmia, psychiatric dysfunction) despite 5 years of disease.
Otherwise unexplained pyramidal tract signs (pyramidal weakness or clear pathological hyperreflexia).
Bilateral symmetric parkinsonism with no side predominance by history or examination.
MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.other_key_points: Dementia is NOT an exclusion criterion for PD regardless of when it occurs relative to parkinsonism onset. Time matters: diagnostic accuracy rises with follow-up because progression, treatment response and hallmarks of other diseases may not have emerged early. Mild non-specific parkinsonian signs occur in up to 25% of elderly people without PD, so the criteria aim to separate PD from these.
MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.validation: Postuma 2018 (626 parkinsonism patients, 8 centres, expert diagnosis as gold standard): 94.5% of PD patients met MDS probable-PD criteria (5.5% false-negative); 88.5% of non-PD patients were correctly identified (11.5% false-positive); overall accuracy for probable PD 92.6%; 59.3% of PD and 1.6% of non-PD patients met clinically established PD. UK Brain Bank criteria performed worse (sensitivity 89.2%, specificity 79.2%, accuracy 86.4%). Caveat: the gold standard was expert clinical diagnosis, not autopsy. A 2025 scoping review of 28 autopsy-based articles found that supranuclear gaze palsy, rapid progression to wheelchair need, and bilateral symptoms were reported in more than 5% of pathologically confirmed PD, so individual exclusions/red flags are not absolute in practice; excellent levodopa response and rest tremor were the most useful supportive features.
MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.source: Postuma RB, Berg D et al., 'MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease', Mov Disord 2015;30(12):1591-1601 (DOI 10.1002/mds.26424); Postuma RB et al., 'Validation of the MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease', Mov Disord 2018 (PMID 30145797); Fox SH et al., 'Revisiting the 2015 MDS diagnostic criteria for Parkinson disease: insights from autopsy-confirmed cases', npj Parkinson's Disease 2025 (PMID 41390531)
MDS_2015_clinical_diagnostic_criteria.confidence: high - criteria text taken from the published MDS criteria table (Table 1 executive summary)

UK_PDS_Brain_Bank_criteria.framework: Three steps. Step 1 (parkinsonian syndrome): bradykinesia AND at least one of muscular rigidity, 4-6 Hz rest tremor, or postural instability not caused by primary visual, vestibular, cerebellar or proprioceptive dysfunction. Step 2 (exclusion criteria) includes repeated strokes with stepwise progression, repeated head injury, definite encephalitis, oculogyric crises, neuroleptic treatment at symptom onset, more than one affected relative, sustained remission, strictly unilateral features after 3 years, supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, early severe autonomic involvement, early severe dementia with memory/language/praxis disturbance, and Babinski sign. Step 3 (supportive criteria): three or more required for 'definite' PD - unilateral onset, rest tremor, progressive disorder, persistent asymmetry affecting the onset side most, excellent (70-100%) levodopa response, severe levodopa-induced chorea, levodopa response for 5 years or more, and clinical course of 10 years or more.
UK_PDS_Brain_Bank_criteria.difference_from_MDS: The Brain Bank criteria count postural instability as a Step-1 feature; the MDS criteria do not, and MDS adds red-flag/supportive weighing and olfactory/MIBG markers.
UK_PDS_Brain_Bank_criteria.source: Hughes AJ, Daniel SE, Kilford L, Lees AJ, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55:181-184 (PMID 1564476); criteria table reproduced in NCBI Bookshelf NBK379754 'UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank Diagnostic Criteria'

dopamine_transporter_imaging_DaTscan.role: 123I-ioflupane (FP-CIT/DaTscan) SPECT images presynaptic dopamine transporter binding. An abnormal scan shows nigrostriatal degeneration (supports PD, atypical parkinsonism or dementia with Lewy bodies); a NORMAL scan supports a non-degenerative cause such as essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism. In 248 patients with unclassified parkinsonism, FP-CIT SPECT distinguished PD from essential tremor (odds ratio 82), from vascular parkinsonism (OR 61) and from drug-induced parkinsonism (OR 36) but NOT from atypical parkinsonian syndromes (OR 1). The MDS criteria use normal presynaptic dopaminergic imaging as an absolute exclusion criterion for PD, but state explicitly that dopaminergic imaging does not qualify for separating PD from atypical parkinsonian syndromes. NICE NG71 advises considering 123I-FP-CIT SPECT for people with tremor when essential tremor cannot be clinically differentiated from parkinsonism, and advises against acute levodopa or apomorphine challenge tests in differential diagnosis.
dopamine_transporter_imaging_DaTscan.limitation: DaTscan supports the presence of nigrostriatal degeneration; it does not diagnose PD specifically and does not replace clinical assessment.
dopamine_transporter_imaging_DaTscan.source: Vlaar AM et al., Eur Neurol 2008;59:258-266 (PMID 18264015); Cummings JL et al., Brain 2011;134:3146-3166 (PMID 21810889); Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; NICE guideline NG71 'Parkinson's disease in adults' (nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71), recommendation wording verified through search-result excerpts of the NICE page (page itself returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch)
dopamine_transporter_imaging_DaTscan.confidence: high for Vlaar/Cummings/MDS statements; moderate-high for NICE wording (verified via search excerpt, not full-page read)

response_to_levodopa_as_supportive_featu.finding: A clear, dramatic response to dopaminergic therapy is supportive criterion 1 in the MDS criteria, and, conversely, absence of observable response to high-dose levodopa despite at least moderate severity is an absolute exclusion criterion. In the UK Brain Bank criteria an excellent (70-100%) levodopa response is a supportive feature. Levodopa response is therefore supportive, not proof: MSA patients can occasionally respond, and response may not be evaluable early.
response_to_levodopa_as_supportive_featu.source: Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Hughes AJ et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55:181-184; Tamura M et al., Front Neurol 2023;14:1293732 (levodopa-responsive MSA-P case)

alpha_synuclein_seed_amplification_assay.finding: An emerging (not yet routine) biomarker: in the PPMI cohort (1123 participants, cerebrospinal fluid) the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay had 87.7% sensitivity for PD (95% CI 84.9-90.5) and 96.3% specificity versus healthy controls (93.4-99.2). Sensitivity was 98.6% in sporadic PD with the typical olfactory deficit but lower in LRRK2 PD (67.5%) and in sporadic PD without olfactory deficit (78.3%); 44 of 51 (86%) prodromal participants with RBD or hyposmia were positive, as were 8% of non-manifesting LRRK2/GBA carriers. It is a research-stage tool; the 2015 MDS clinical criteria do not include it, and it does not replace clinical diagnosis.
alpha_synuclein_seed_amplification_assay.source: Siderowf A et al., 'Assessment of heterogeneity among participants in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative cohort using alpha-synuclein seed amplification: a cross-sectional study', Lancet Neurol 2023;22:407-417 (PMID 37059509)
alpha_synuclein_seed_amplification_assay.confidence: high for the reported PPMI numbers; clinical-use status stated cautiously

core.name: Bradykinesia (slowness with decrement) - the core defining motor feature
core.note: Current MDS criteria make bradykinesia the mandatory feature: slowness of movement plus decrement in amplitude or speed (or progressive hesitations/halts) as a movement is repeated, documented in the limbs on finger/hand/foot tapping and pronation-supination. The MDS note combines the older terms bradykinesia (slowness) and akinesia/hypokinesia (reduced amplitude): both are generally present, though not always together. Mechanistically it follows from striatal dopamine loss increasing basal ganglia output (Albin model).
core.source: Postuma RB et al., MDS clinical diagnostic criteria, Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Albin RL et al., Trends Neurosci 1989;12:366-375

core.name: Rest tremor (classically 'pill-rolling' hand tremor)
core.note: Defined in the MDS criteria as a 4-6 Hz tremor in the fully resting limb that is SUPPRESSED during movement initiation - this rest-predominant behaviour is the distinguishing feature from essential tremor, which the MDS Tremor Task Force defines as an isolated bilateral upper-limb ACTION tremor of at least 3 years' duration without other neurological signs. Postural or kinetic tremor alone does not meet MDS criteria for parkinsonism, although a re-emergent tremor on holding a posture can occur in PD. 'Pill-rolling' is the classical descriptive term for the thumb-finger rest tremor; it is not itself defined in the MDS criteria. Rest tremor is not universal: in one series of 253 untreated patients 67% of women and 48% of men presented with tremor, and tremor-onset patients were older at onset with slower motor deterioration. Rest tremor of a limb is a supportive criterion because it is less common in alternative conditions.
core.source: Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Bhatia KP et al., 'Consensus statement on the classification of tremors', Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87 (PMID 29193359; ET definition verified via search excerpt); Haaxma CA et al., 'Gender differences in Parkinson's disease', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007;78:819-824 (PMID 17098842)

core.name: Rigidity (lead-pipe, often with 'cogwheel' quality)
core.note: Increased resistance to slow passive movement of major joints in a relaxed patient. MDS criteria define it as lead-pipe, velocity-independent resistance; cogwheeling is often present and may partly reflect tremor superimposed on raised tone ('may reflect tremor incidentally felt'), and isolated cogwheeling without lead-pipe rigidity does not qualify. Mechanism: in a robot-assisted study of 20 PD patients and 25 controls, rigidity was accompanied by increased long-latency stretch reflexes (not short-latency reflexes) that rose with stretch velocity only in PD, and the authors state that the pathophysiological underpinning of parkinsonian rigidity remains incompletely understood.
core.source: Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Asci F et al., 'Rigidity in Parkinson's disease: evidence from biomechanical and neurophysiological measures', Brain 2023;146:3705-3718 (PMID 37018058)

core.name: Postural instability (typically a later feature)
core.note: Postural instability is a feature of parkinsonism but is not part of the MDS definition of PD-parkinsonism because it 'often occurs in later stages of PD, but its presence early in disease suggests an alternative diagnosis'. Recurrent falls within 3 years of onset is an MDS red flag. It defines Hoehn and Yahr stage 3 (impaired postural reflexes). In the 20-year Sydney cohort, falls had occurred in 87% of survivors.
core.source: Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Hoehn MM & Yahr MD, Neurology 1967;17:427-442; Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844

core.name: Asymmetric onset and persistent asymmetry
core.note: Unilateral onset and persistent asymmetry are UK Brain Bank supportive features; bilateral symmetric parkinsonism with no side predominance is an MDS red flag. Lower-limb-only parkinsonism for more than 3 years is an MDS absolute exclusion.
core.source: Hughes AJ et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55:181-184; Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601

core.name: Gait freezing, speech and swallowing problems (mainly later disease)
core.note: In 20-year survivors of the Sydney cohort: freezing 81%, moderate dysarthria 81%, choking 48%. Early severe bulbar dysfunction (within 5 years) is instead an MDS red flag pointing away from idiopathic PD.
core.source: Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844 (PMID 18307261); Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601

non_motor_symptoms_and_prodromal_phase.framing: Non-motor symptoms are clinically important and often under-recognised. The MDS criteria treat absence of ANY common non-motor feature after 5 years of disease as a red flag, and treat olfactory loss as a supportive criterion.

features.name: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) - key prodromal marker
features.note: Idiopathic RBD (iRBD) is a powerful early sign of a synucleinopathy: PD, dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) or multiple system atrophy (MSA) - not PD alone. Multicentre cohort of 1280 polysomnography-confirmed iRBD patients from 24 centres (mean follow-up 4.6 years): conversion to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome 6.3% per year, 73.5% converting by 12 years. Predictors of conversion included abnormal quantitative motor testing (HR 3.16), objective motor signs (HR 3.03), olfactory deficit (HR 2.62), mild cognitive impairment, erectile dysfunction (HR 2.13), abnormal DAT scan (HR 1.98) and constipation (HR 1.67). Earlier cohorts: Iranzo et al. - 36 of 44 (82%) developed a defined neurodegenerative syndrome (16 PD, 14 DLB, 1 MSA, 5 MCI), with disease-free survival 65.2% at 5, 26.6% at 10 and 7.5% at 14 years; Postuma 2009 (Montreal) - 12-year risk 52.4%. RBD is also common once PD is established: pooled RBD prevalence in PD 46% (meta-analysis), or 23.6% for RBD symptoms in newly diagnosed PD versus 3.4% in controls.
features.source: Postuma RB et al., Brain 2019;142:744-759 (PMID 30789229); Iranzo A et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:443-453 (PMID 23562390); Postuma RB et al., Neurology 2009;72:1296-1300 (PMID 19109537); Maggi G et al., Sleep Med Rev 2023;68:101759 (PMID 36708642); Zhang J et al., BMC Neurol 2017;17:23 (PMID 28160778)

features.name: Hyposmia / anosmia - prodromal and supportive feature
features.note: Olfactory dysfunction is present in approximately 90% of early-stage PD and can precede motor symptoms by years. In the Honolulu-Asia Aging Study (2,267 men aged 71-95 without PD or dementia) impaired olfaction predated clinical PD by at least 4 years: age-adjusted PD incidence fell from 54.5 per 10,000 person-years in the lowest odour-identification quartile to 8.4 in the highest. Smell loss is less marked or absent in MSA, corticobasal degeneration and PSP, so olfactory testing can help differential diagnosis; MDS criteria accept olfactory loss as a supportive criterion.
features.source: Doty RL, Nat Rev Neurol 2012;8:329-339 (PMID 22584158); Ross GW et al., Ann Neurol 2008;63:167-173 (PMID 18067173); Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601

features.name: Constipation
features.note: Premorbid constipation is associated with later PD: pooled OR 2.27 (95% CI 2.09-2.46) across 9 studies with 741,593 participants; OR 2.13 (1.78-2.56) when constipation was assessed more than 10 years before diagnosis, i.e. it can predate PD by over a decade. It is a risk marker and a common non-motor feature, not diagnostic on its own.
features.source: Adams-Carr KL et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2016;87:710-716 (PMID 26345189)

features.name: Depression
features.note: Systematic review (36 independent articles): weighted prevalence of major depressive disorder 17% of PD patients, minor depression 22%, dysthymia 13%, clinically significant depressive symptoms 35% - substantial but lower than generally assumed; population studies report lower rates than clinic-based studies.
features.source: Reijnders JS et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:183-189 (PMID 17987654)

features.name: Anxiety
features.note: Meta-analysis (45 quality-assessed articles): average point prevalence of anxiety disorders in PD 31%; clinically significant anxiety symptoms 25.7% by rating-scale cut-offs.
features.source: Broen MP et al., Mov Disord 2016;31:1125-1133 (PMID 27125963)

features.name: Cognitive impairment and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD)
features.note: PDD is dementia arising in the context of established PD. Systematic review: 24.5% (95% CI 17.4-31.5) of PD patients have dementia (31.1% in the four best-quality studies), and PDD accounts for 3-4% of all dementia; the MDS Task Force reports dementia incidence in PD increased up to six-fold with point prevalence close to 30%, older age and akinetic-rigid form raising risk. Timing: dementia is an early-onset problem only in DLB - by the DLB Consortium 1-year rule, dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism is labelled DLB, whereas parkinsonism preceding dementia by more than 1 year is labelled PDD. Cumulative risk is high with long survival: in the Sydney cohort dementia was present in 83% of 20-year survivors. PDD is characterised by impaired attention, memory, executive and visuospatial function with hallucinations, apathy and affective change; there is no specific ancillary test.
features.source: Aarsland D et al., Mov Disord 2005;20:1255-1263 (PMID 16041803); Emre M et al., Mov Disord 2007;22:1689-1707 (PMID 17542011); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453; 1-year rule wording verified via search excerpt); Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844 (PMID 18307261)

features.name: Orthostatic hypotension (autonomic dysfunction)
features.note: Pooled point prevalence of orthostatic hypotension in PD 30.1% (95% CI 22.9-38.4) from 25 studies, with large heterogeneity so interpret with caution. Symptomatic postural hypotension 48% in 20-year Sydney survivors. Severe autonomic failure within the first 5 years is an MDS red flag for MSA-type atypical parkinsonism rather than early PD.
features.source: Velseboer DC et al., Parkinsonism Relat Disord 2011;17:724-729 (PMID 21571570); Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844; Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601

features.name: Sialorrhoea (drooling)
features.note: Systematic review of 8 studies: pooled prevalence of drooling 56% (95% CI 44-67) in PD versus 14% (3-25) in healthy controls, relative risk 5.5 (2.1-14.4); rates ranged 32-74% depending on definition (highest when nocturnal drooling was included).
features.source: Kalf JG et al., J Neurol 2009;256:1391-1396 (PMID 19288042)

features.name: Other sleep disturbance, urinary symptoms and psychosis (later disease)
features.note: Meta-analysis: excessive daytime sleepiness 35% and insomnia 44% of PD patients. Sydney 20-year survivors: excessive daytime sleepiness 70%, urinary incontinence 71%, hallucinations 74%, fractures 35%.
features.source: Maggi G et al., Sleep Med Rev 2023;68:101759 (PMID 36708642); Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844 (PMID 18307261)

prodromal_PD_framework.finding: The MDS research criteria for prodromal PD define the stage where early signs of PD neurodegeneration are present but classic motor diagnosis is not yet possible, using a Bayesian likelihood-ratio approach (probable prodromal PD = at least 80% certainty). They are for research only because no proven disease-modifying therapy exists. The 2019 update increased the positive likelihood ratio of olfactory loss and added diabetes, global cognitive deficit, physical inactivity and low plasma urate in men as markers.
prodromal_PD_framework.source: Berg D et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1600-1611 (PMID 26474317); Heinzel S et al., Mov Disord 2019;34:1464-1470 (PMID 31412427)

staging_hoehn_and_yahr.description: The Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) scale (original 1967 description, 5 stages) grades global severity and is heavily weighted toward postural instability.

stages.description: Unilateral involvement only, usually with minimal or no functional disability.
Bilateral or midline involvement without impairment of balance.
Bilateral disease with mild to moderate disability and impaired postural reflexes; physically independent.
Severely disabling disease; still able to walk or stand unassisted.
Confinement to bed or wheelchair unless aided.

staging_hoehn_and_yahr.modified_scale_and_limitations: A 'modified H&Y' adds stages 1.5 and 2.5 and is widely used. The MDS Task Force found strengths (wide use; higher stages correlate with dopaminergic imaging loss and with other motor/disability scales) and weaknesses (mixes impairment with disability, is non-linear, weighted toward postural instability, ignores non-motor problems), and recommends using the original form for describing groups and treating it as most valid in the mid-range (stages 2-4).
staging_hoehn_and_yahr.source: Hoehn MM & Yahr MD, 'Parkinsonism: onset, progression and mortality', Neurology 1967;17:427-442 (PMID 6067254); Goetz CG et al., 'Movement Disorder Society Task Force report on the Hoehn and Yahr staging scale: status and recommendations', Mov Disord 2004;19:1020-1028 (PMID 15372591); stage wording reproduced in NCBI Bookshelf NBK379751 (PD REHAB trial monograph, 'Hoehn and Yahr stages')
staging_hoehn_and_yahr.confidence: high - classic scale; stage wording cross-checked against a published monograph

classification_of_parkinsonism.framework: 'Parkinsonism' is the syndrome (bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity). Idiopathic PD is one cause. ICD-11 separates primary (Parkinson disease, 8A00.0), atypical (8A00.1) and secondary (8A00.2) parkinsonism. Distinguishing them matters because prognosis, levodopa response and reversibility differ.
classification_of_parkinsonism.idiopathic_PD: The commonest cause of degenerative parkinsonism: nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss with alpha-synuclein Lewy pathology, asymmetric onset, good levodopa response, prodromal non-motor phase (see other sections).

drug_induced.finding: Drug-induced parkinsonism (DIP) is caused by dopamine-receptor blockade or dopamine depletion. Culprits: antipsychotics (phenothiazines, butyrophenones, thioxanthenes, sulpiride), 'hidden neuroleptics' prescribed as anti-nausea/anti-vomiting drugs (metoclopramide and other benzamides), dopamine depleters (reserpine, tetrabenazine), alpha-methyldopa, and calcium-channel blockers such as flunarizine and cinnarizine. Clinically it is often bilateral, associated with tardive dyskinesia and may lack resting tremor. French pharmacovigilance series (155 cases): 69% arose within 3 months of starting the drug, a second peak at 12 months was mainly calcium-channel blockers, central dopamine antagonists accounted for 49% of suspect drugs, and 88.7% had a favourable course after partial or complete withdrawal - so it is often reversible, but a drug-induced cause can also unmask underlying PD. FP-CIT SPECT is typically normal in DIP (OR 36 for PD vs DIP). Flunarizine-induced parkinsonism with depression was described in 12 patients (partial or complete improvement on withdrawal in most) - relevant in India where flunarizine/cinnarizine are widely prescribed for vertigo and migraine.
drug_induced.source: Montastruc JL et al., 'Drug-induced parkinsonism: a review', Fundam Clin Pharmacol 1994;8:293-306 (PMID 7851836); Bondon-Guitton E et al., Mov Disord 2011;26:2226-2231 (PMID 21674626); Chouza C et al., Lancet 1986;1:1303-1304 (PMID 2872433); Vlaar AM et al., Eur Neurol 2008;59:258-266; MDS criteria absolute exclusion #5

vascular_parkinsonism.finding: Vascular parkinsonism is a contested syndrome. A critical appraisal found that no structural imaging pattern is specific, white-matter MRI hyperintensities correlate poorly with parkinsonism, 'definite' vascular parkinsonism results from infarcts or haemorrhages involving the substantia nigra/nigrostriatal pathway, and many reported cases are pseudovascular (true PD or another degenerative parkinsonism with non-specific MRI change) or higher-level gait disorders such as normal-pressure hydrocephalus. FP-CIT SPECT distinguishes PD from vascular parkinsonism (OR 61).
vascular_parkinsonism.source: Vizcarra JA et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:886-894 (PMID 25997420); Vlaar AM et al., Eur Neurol 2008;59:258-266

normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.finding: Idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) presents in the elderly with gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence (the gait-cognitive-urinary triad) and can mimic parkinsonism with a magnetic, short-stepped gait (higher-level gait disorder). The 2005 evidence-based guidelines (Relkin et al.) classify iNPH as probable, possible or unlikely, address shunt surgery as its treatment and note that Class I evidence is scarce. It matters because it is a potentially treatable mimic that needs neuroimaging (ventriculomegaly) rather than a dopaminergic drug; the wording 'potentially reversible' reflects treatability by CSF diversion in selected patients, not a guaranteed outcome.
normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.source: Relkin N et al., 'Diagnosing idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus', Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S4-16 (PMID 16160425); Vizcarra JA et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:886-894
normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.confidence: moderate-high - triad and guideline classification verified via guideline title/search summaries; detailed imaging thresholds not extracted

atypical_parkinsonian_syndromes_parkinso.overview: Atypical parkinsonian syndromes are DLB, multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD). Prevalence: DLB about 0.4% of the elderly; MSA and PSP each 5-10 per 100,000; CBD about 1 per 100,000. They are synucleinopathies (DLB, MSA) and tauopathies (PSP, CBD).

syndromes.name: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)
syndromes.key_features: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early postural instability with falls (Richardson-type presentation); less commonly parkinsonism-predominant (PSP-P) or frontotemporal dementia (PSP-FTD) presentations. MDS-PSP criteria use four predictor domains: ocular motor dysfunction, postural instability, akinesia and cognitive dysfunction. Downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is an MDS absolute exclusion for PD.
syndromes.source: Levin J et al., Dtsch Arztebl Int 2016;113:61-69 (PMID 26900156); Hoglinger GU et al., Mov Disord 2017;32:853-864 (PMID 28467028); Williams DR & Lees AJ, Lancet Neurol 2009;8:270-279 (PMID 19233037)

syndromes.name: Multiple system atrophy (MSA)
syndromes.key_features: Alpha-synuclein deposition in oligodendrocytes (glial cytoplasmic inclusions); autonomic failure combined with parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C). Second consensus: probable MSA needs sporadic progressive adult-onset disease with rigorously defined autonomic failure and POORLY levodopa-responsive parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia. New MDS MSA criteria (2022) add 'clinically established' and 'clinically probable' categories and require MRI markers for clinically established MSA.
syndromes.source: Gilman S et al., Neurology 2008;71:670-676 (PMID 18725592); Wenning GK et al., Mov Disord 2022;37:1131-1148 (PMID 35445419); Levin J et al., 2016

syndromes.name: Corticobasal degeneration (CBD) / corticobasal syndrome
syndromes.key_features: Markedly asymmetrical parkinsonism with apraxia or cortical sensory disturbance; four phenotypes (corticobasal syndrome, frontal behavioural-spatial syndrome, non-fluent/agrammatic primary progressive aphasia, PSP syndrome). Cortical sensory loss or limb ideomotor apraxia is an MDS absolute exclusion for PD.
syndromes.source: Armstrong MJ et al., Neurology 2013;80:496-503 (PMID 23359374); Levin J et al., 2016; Postuma RB et al., 2015

syndromes.name: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
syndromes.key_features: Dementia with later parkinsonism; consensus criteria give increased diagnostic weight to REM sleep behaviour disorder and MIBG scintigraphy; dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism suggests DLB rather than PDD.
syndromes.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453); Levin J et al., 2016

why_poor_levodopa_response.finding: In PD the lesion is predominantly PRESYNAPTIC (nigral neurons), while striatal neurons bearing dopamine receptors are relatively preserved, so replacing dopamine works. In MSA (and PSP) degeneration also involves postsynaptic striatal/putaminal neurons (dopamine-receptor-bearing) from an early stage, so extra dopamine has little to act on. Supporting data: in a levodopa-responsive MSA-P autopsy case the putaminal neuron number and dopamine-receptor immunoreactivity were preserved, whereas levodopa-unresponsive MSA-P controls had significant putaminal neuronal loss and reduced receptor immunoreactivity, with severe nigral loss in all. PSP has even more severe presynaptic dopaminergic loss than PD (caudate DAT function 34.1% lower). Because presynaptic imaging is abnormal in both PD and atypical syndromes, DaTscan cannot separate them (OR 1). Levodopa response in atypical parkinsonism is poor, or wanes early, but not always absent (levodopa-responsive MSA-P exists).
why_poor_levodopa_response.source: Tamura M et al., Front Neurol 2023;14:1293732 (PMID 38033780); Kaasinen V et al., J Nucl Med 2019;60:1757-1763 (PMID 30979821); Vlaar AM et al., Eur Neurol 2008;59:258-266; Gilman S et al., Neurology 2008;71:670-676
why_poor_levodopa_response.confidence: moderate-high - mechanism supported by autopsy/imaging literature; the single-case autopsy is illustrative, not proof for all patients

classification_of_parkinsonism.practical_differential_note: Most useful clinical clues to atypical parkinsonism in the MDS criteria are red flags and exclusions: early falls, rapid progression to wheelchair, early bulbar dysfunction, early severe autonomic failure, inspiratory stridor, supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, pyramidal signs, symmetric onset and poor levodopa response. Even so, clinico-pathological data show that in the original series 24 of 100 clinically diagnosed idiopathic PD had another pathology (PSP, MSA, Alzheimer-type, vascular).
classification_of_parkinsonism.source: Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601; Hughes AJ et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55:181-184

real_risk_factors.note: Prevalence rises steeply with age: pooled worldwide rates per 100,000 were 41 (age 40-49), 107 (50-59), 428 (60-69), 1,087 (70-79) and 1,903 (80 and over; bands 55-64 and 65-74 also reported as 173 and 425 in the same meta-analysis). PD affects 2-3% of people aged >=65.
real_risk_factors.source: Pringsheim T et al., Mov Disord 2014;29:1583-1590 (PMID 24976103); Poewe W et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17013

real_risk_factors.factor: Family history / genetics (LRRK2, GBA, SNCA, PRKN)
real_risk_factors.note: WHO states family history increases risk. LRRK2 G2019S: 1% of sporadic and 4% of hereditary PD (higher in the Middle East and southern Europe); age-related penetrance 28% at 59, 51% at 69, 74% at 79 years; LRRK2 PD is clinically more benign than idiopathic PD. GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations: odds ratio 5.43 for PD across 16 centres (5,691 patients); found in about 15% of Ashkenazi Jewish patients and 3% of non-Ashkenazi patients (7% on full sequencing), with earlier onset and more affected relatives. SNCA A53T causes autosomal-dominant PD (Polymeropoulos 1997). PRKN (parkin) mutations cause autosomal-recessive juvenile parkinsonism (Kitada 1998).
real_risk_factors.source: Healy DG et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7:583-590 (PMID 18539534); Sidransky E et al., N Engl J Med 2009;361:1651-1661 (PMID 19846850); Polymeropoulos MH et al., Science 1997;276:2045-2047; Kitada T et al., Nature 1998;392:605-608 (PMID 9560156); WHO PD fact sheet 2023

real_risk_factors.note: Meta-analysis of 7 population-based incidence studies: relative risk of PD about 1.5 in men versus women. GBD 2016: male-to-female ratio of age-standardised prevalence 1.40 (95% UI 1.36-1.43) in 2016 and 1.37 in 1990. Women have a later age at onset (about 2.1 years) and 16% higher striatal FP-CIT binding at symptom onset, and more often present with tremor (67% vs 48%); the authors hypothesise an oestrogen-related protective effect - a hypothesis, not proven.
real_risk_factors.source: Wooten GF et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2004;75:637-639 (PMID 15026515); GBD 2016 Parkinson's Disease Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:939-953 (PMID 30287051); Haaxma CA et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007;78:819-824 (PMID 17098842)

real_risk_factors.note: Agricultural Health Study nested case-control (110 PD cases, 358 controls): PD associated with complex-I-inhibiting pesticides (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.0-2.8), including rotenone (OR 2.5, 1.3-4.7), and with oxidative-stress pesticides (OR 2.0), including paraquat (OR 2.5, 1.4-4.7). Meta-analysis of 104 studies: exposure to pesticides or solvents is a risk factor; paraquat and maneb/mancozeb about 2-fold; rural living also associated. WHO: exposure to air pollution, pesticides and solvents 'may increase risk'. Association evidence; not every exposed person develops PD.
real_risk_factors.source: Tanner CM et al., Environ Health Perspect 2011;119:866-872 (PMID 21269927); Pezzoli G & Cereda E, Neurology 2013;80:2035-2041 (PMID 23713084); WHO PD fact sheet 2023

real_risk_factors.factor: Inverse association with cigarette smoking and coffee/caffeine (real epidemiological finding - NOT a recommendation)
real_risk_factors.note: Meta-analysis (44 case-control + 4 cohort studies for smoking; 8 + 5 for coffee): relative risk of PD 0.59 (0.54-0.63) for ever-smokers, 0.39 (0.32-0.47) for current smokers, and 0.69 (0.59-0.80) for coffee drinkers versus non-drinkers, with dose-response. Caution on interpretation: the prodromal phase of PD raises the possibility of reverse causation. Mendelian-randomisation studies are mixed: one found an inverse association with genetically predicted smoking initiation (OR 0.74, 0.60-0.93) with no significant association for alcohol or coffee, and genetic liability to PD was not associated with smoking; another found smoking continuation (OR 0.64) and alcohol intake (OR 0.79) associated with lower PD risk and not explained by survival bias alone. So the smoking association may be real, the coffee association is less consistent, and the biology is not established. This does NOT mean smoking is protective or advisable: smoking causes lung cancer, COPD and cardiovascular disease and no clinical guideline recommends smoking or caffeine to prevent PD.
real_risk_factors.source: Hernan MA et al., Ann Neurol 2002;52:276-284 (PMID 12205639); Domenighetti C et al., J Parkinsons Dis 2022;12:267-282 (PMID 34633332); Dominguez-Baleon C et al., Sci Rep 2021;11:13980 (PMID 34234189)

real_risk_factors.factor: Constipation and other prodromal states (risk markers, not causes)
real_risk_factors.note: Constipation (OR 2.27), hyposmia and iRBD are associated with later PD but are early manifestations of the disease process rather than independent causal risk factors.
real_risk_factors.source: Adams-Carr KL et al., 2016 (PMID 26345189); Berg D et al., MDS prodromal criteria, Mov Disord 2015 (PMID 26474317)

global.finding: GBD 2016: 6.1 million people (95% UI 5.0-7.3) had PD in 2016 versus 2.5 million (2.0-3.0) in 1990; crude prevalence rose 74.3% and age-standardised prevalence 21.7%, so the rise is not only from ageing. PD caused 3.2 million DALYs and 211,296 deaths in 2016. WHO (2023, GBD 2019-based): over 8.5 million people with PD in 2019; prevalence doubled in 25 years; 329,000 deaths (over 100% increase since 2000); 5.8 million DALYs (81% increase since 2000). Dorsey et al. describe PD as the fastest-growing neurological disorder in the world, with numbers projected to double again to over 12 million by 2040 (over 17 million if longevity, declining smoking and industrialisation are also factored in). Earlier projection: 4.1-4.6 million over age 50 in the 15 most populous nations in 2005, doubling to 8.7-9.3 million by 2030.
global.source: GBD 2016 Parkinson's Disease Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:939-953 (PMID 30287051); WHO fact sheet 'Parkinson disease' (9 August 2023); Dorsey ER et al., 'The Emerging Evidence of the Parkinson Pandemic', J Parkinsons Dis 2018;8:S3-S8 (PMID 30584159); Dorsey ER et al., Neurology 2007;68:384-386 (PMID 17082464)
global.confidence: high for the published figures; GBD 2016 (6.1 M) and WHO/GBD 2019 (8.5 M) are different estimation rounds and should not be mixed as one series

regional_and_ethnic_variation.finding: Age-specific prevalence at 70-79 years was 1,601 per 100,000 in North America/Europe/Australia versus 646 in Asia. A review of Eastern versus Western studies found PD prevalence and incidence slightly lower in the East, with male predominance more obvious in Western studies. European community surveys of people aged 65+ found age-adjusted PD prevalence of 1.6%.
regional_and_ethnic_variation.source: Pringsheim T et al., Mov Disord 2014;29:1583-1590; Abbas MM et al., Mov Disord Clin Pract 2018;5:14-28 (PMID 30363342); de Rijk MC et al., 1997 (PMID 9010393)

india_specific.finding: Indian PD data are sparse. A 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis (1980-2019) identified only 3 community-based PD prevalence studies (121 cases) and pooled a prevalence of 0.8 per 1,000 population (95% CI 0.4-1.3), with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 95%). A 1988 door-to-door survey of the Parsi community of Bombay (14,010 people; 46 with PD, 25 men, 21 women) found a much higher prevalence (about 328 per 100,000 by simple arithmetic; the abstract prints the figure as '328.3 per 1000', apparently a unit error), rising consistently with age and slightly higher in men - this is a single, unusual endogamous community and should not be generalised to India. India-specific GBD PD estimates were not retrieved in this pass.
india_specific.source: Dhiman V et al., Neurol India 2021;69:294-301 (PMID 33904437); Bharucha NE et al., Arch Neurol 1988;45:1321-1323 (PMID 3264148)
india_specific.confidence: moderate - real but sparse and heterogeneous Indian data; stated as such rather than extrapolated

progressive_course.finding: PD is progressive. In the Sydney multicentre cohort (newly diagnosed, followed 20 years) 100 of 136 (74%) had died; mortality fell in the first 3 years of treatment, then rose relative to the general population, with a standardised mortality ratio of 3.1 at 15-20 years. Among 20-year survivors: dementia 83%, falls 87%, freezing 81%, fractures 35%, hallucinations 74%, excessive daytime sleepiness 70%, urinary incontinence 71%, symptomatic postural hypotension 48%, choking 48%; only one lived independently and 48% were in nursing homes. Late disability is dominated by non-levodopa-responsive features.
progressive_course.source: Hely MA et al., 'The Sydney multicenter study of Parkinson's disease: the inevitability of dementia at 20 years', Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844 (PMID 18307261)
progressive_course.confidence: high - single long-term cohort; survivors are a selected group

motor_fluctuations_and_dyskinesia_with_l.finding: Meta-analysis of the levodopa literature (74 publications): in the modern era motor fluctuations (wearing-off) were nil in year 1 of levodopa but affected about 40% of patients by 4-6 years, and dyskinesias affected just under 40% by 4-6 years; the authors note these are incidence data and the prevalence of clinically important morbidity may be substantially less. 'Wearing-off' means predictable end-of-dose return of symptoms; 'on-off' means abrupt, less predictable swings between good and poor motor states; levodopa-induced dyskinesia is involuntary choreiform/dystonic movement, mostly at peak dose. Presence of dyskinesia and end-of-dose wearing-off are MDS supportive criteria for PD.
motor_fluctuations_and_dyskinesia_with_l.source: Ahlskog JE & Muenter MD, Mov Disord 2001;16:448-458 (PMID 11391738); Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601

dopaminergic_terminal_loss_trajectory.finding: Post-mortem study: dopaminergic markers in the dorsal putamen showed a modest loss at 1 year after diagnosis, variable moderate-to-marked loss at 3 years, and virtually complete loss by 4 years and thereafter; nigral TH-positive neuron loss was already 50-90% at the earliest time points with little further loss.
dopaminergic_terminal_loss_trajectory.confidence: high for the data; small sample per time point

phenotype_variation.finding: Tremor-onset patients had a 38% slower UPDRS-III deterioration in one cohort; LRRK2 PD is more benign (fewer falls, less dyskinesia, better cognition and olfaction) than idiopathic PD; GBA-mutation carriers present earlier with more affected relatives.
phenotype_variation.source: Haaxma CA et al., 2007 (PMID 17098842); Healy DG et al., 2008 (PMID 18539534); Sidransky E et al., 2009 (PMID 19846850)

acute_akinetic_crisis_parkinsonism_hyper.definition_and_mechanism: Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome is a rare but potentially fatal complication most commonly following reduction or cessation of anti-parkinsonian medicines. It resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rigidity, pyrexia and reduced conscious level, with possible autonomic instability and raised creatine kinase. NMS is probably caused by reduced dopaminergic activity in the hypothalamus and striatum and occurs with dopamine antagonists or withdrawal of dopamine agonists in patients with parkinsonism.
acute_akinetic_crisis_parkinsonism_hyper.complications: Acute renal failure, aspiration pneumonia, deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism, disseminated intravascular coagulation.
acute_akinetic_crisis_parkinsonism_hyper.outcome: Mortality of up to 4% has been reported, and a further one-third of patients have permanent sequelae; prognosis improves with early recognition and management. Patients and physicians should be warned against sudden reduction in anti-parkinsonian medicines.
acute_akinetic_crisis_parkinsonism_hyper.broader_acute_akinesia: In a 675-patient cohort followed 12 years, 26 developed acute akinesia (sudden motor deterioration persisting 48 hours or more despite treatment); in 17 the akinesia began with an infection or after surgery and appeared unrelated to treatment changes, in 9 it coincided with gastrointestinal disease or drug manipulation and showed NMS features; UPDRS motor score rose by 31.4 points within 2-3 days, lasted about 11 days, recovery was incomplete in 10, and 4 of 26 (15%) died. Triggers to ask about: missed/late/reduced doses, vomiting or gut illness, infection, surgery (including deep brain stimulation surgery where medicine is withheld), and new dopamine-blocking drugs.
acute_akinetic_crisis_parkinsonism_hyper.source: Newman EJ, Grosset DG, Kennedy PG, 'The parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome', Neurocrit Care 2009;10:136-140 (PMID 18712508); Onofrj M & Thomas A, 'Acute akinesia in Parkinson disease', Neurology 2005;64:1162-1169 (PMID 15824341); Granner MA & Wooten GF, Semin Neurol 1991;11:228-235 (PMID 1947485); Kim JH et al., Neurosurgery 2010;66:E1029 (PHS after DBS, PMID 20404676)
acute_akinetic_crisis_parkinsonism_hyper.confidence: high for definition, features and figures as quoted; incidence figures come from a single-centre cohort
