red_flags: Acute akinetic crisis / parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome: sudden severe rigidity/immobility with fever, drowsiness or confusion and autonomic instability, especially after missed or stopped anti-parkinsonian medicines or a new dopamine-blocking drug - a life-threatening emergency (mortality up to 4%, plus about one-third with permanent sequelae).

Signs pointing to an atypical parkinsonian syndrome rather than idiopathic PD (MDS red flags/exclusions): recurrent falls within 3 years of onset; rapid progression needing a wheelchair within 5 years; early severe bulbar dysfunction (unintelligible speech, severe dysphagia) within 5 years; severe early autonomic failure (orthostatic BP fall >=30/15 mmHg, urinary retention/incontinence with erectile dysfunction) within 5 years; inspiratory stridor; disproportionate anterocollis or contractures; pyramidal signs; bilateral symmetric onset.
Downward vertical gaze palsy/slow downward saccades (PSP) or cerebellar signs (MSA-C) - MDS absolute exclusion criteria for PD.
Absent or poor response to adequate levodopa despite at least moderate severity - MDS absolute exclusion criterion; suggests atypical parkinsonism or a non-PD cause and needs specialist review.

Early dementia or hallucinations: dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism suggests DLB rather than PDD; early behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia or aphasia (within 5 years) excludes PD; cortical sensory loss or limb apraxia suggests CBD.
Gait-cognitive-urinary triad with a magnetic, short-stepped gait in an older adult: consider normal-pressure hydrocephalus (needs neuroimaging; potentially treatable, not a levodopa problem).

Parkinsonism beginning within weeks to months of starting an antipsychotic, metoclopramide-type anti-emetic, flunarizine/cinnarizine, calcium-channel blockers or other dopamine-antagonist drugs: drug-induced parkinsonism (MDS absolute exclusion when the dose/time-course fits); review the medicine list urgently as this is often reversible on withdrawal.
Stepwise deterioration with vascular risk factors and lower-body-predominant signs: consider vascular parkinsonism/stroke (cross-reference the stroke entry in this knowledge base).
Normal presynaptic dopaminergic imaging (DaTscan) in a patient labelled PD - MDS absolute exclusion; think essential tremor, drug-induced or functional parkinsonism.
Bulbar dysfunction, choking or aspiration episodes in an established patient (choking in 48% of 20-year survivors): aspiration pneumonia risk requires prompt swallowing assessment.
Lower-limb-only parkinsonism for more than 3 years, or complete absence of progression over 5 years without treatment explanation: red flag/exclusion - reconsider the diagnosis.

parkinsons_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Parkinson's disease is NOT curable, and this must be stated plainly rather than hedged. The underlying neurodegeneration (progressive loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons plus wider non-dopaminergic involvement) continues regardless of any treatment used today. Every therapy in this entry - levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B/COMT inhibitors, amantadine, apomorphine, continuous levodopa infusions and deep brain stimulation (DBS) - controls SYMPTOMS; none of them stops or reverses the disease. That is the honest and important difference from stroke or epilepsy in this knowledge base, which each carry a real curative-intent option; Parkinson's disease has none, so no curative_option key is provided (same convention as COPD, asthma and osteoporosis). What the evidence DOES show: (1) Symptomatic control is real and often dramatic, especially early. In ELLDOPA (361 early-PD patients, 40 weeks + 2-week washout) total UPDRS worsened by 7.8 units on placebo but changed by -1.4 units on carbidopa-levodopa 600 mg/day (p<0.001) (Fahn et al, NEJM 2004, PMID 15590952). (2) That benefit is not permanent: in the modern-era literature motor fluctuations were nil in the first year of levodopa but appeared in about 40% of patients by 4-6 years, with dyskinesias just under 40% by 4-6 years (Ahlskog & Muenter, Mov Disord 2001, PMID 11391738); after 20 years of follow-up in the Sydney cohort 74% had died, dementia was present in 83% of survivors, and the dominant problems were non-levodopa-responsive features (falls 87%, freezing 81%, dysarthria 81%, hallucinations 74%) (Hely et al, Mov Disord 2008, PMID 18307261). (3) No disease-modifying treatment is proven: the MDS Evidence-Based Medicine review states there are no clinically useful interventions to prevent or delay disease progression (Fox et al, Mov Disord 2018, PMID 29570866); levodopa itself showed no disease-modifying effect in the LEAP delayed-start trial (UPDRS difference 1.0 point, 95% CI -1.5 to 3.5, p=0.44; Verschuur et al, NEJM 2019, PMID 30673543); rasagiline 1 mg met the ADAGIO delayed-start end points but 2 mg did not, so the authors advised caution (Olanow et al, NEJM 2009, PMID 19776408); once-weekly exenatide showed no effect in a 194-patient phase 3 trial (MDS-UPDRS III off-medication +5.7 vs +4.5 points, p=0.47; Vijiaratnam et al, Lancet 2025, PMID 39919773), and the Lancet later attached an Expression of Concern to that paper (Lancet 2026;407:2588, PMID 42330995) after a regulatory inspection at one trial site; lixisenatide showed a small 12-month phase 2 signal (MDS-UPDRS III -0.04 vs +3.04 points, p=0.007, with nausea in 46%) that still needs larger trials (Meissner et al, NEJM 2024, PMID 38598572). (4) DBS gives substantial, durable improvement in motor fluctuations, dyskinesia and tremor for well-selected advanced patients, but in the 10-year VA/NINDS CSP 468F follow-up bradykinesia, axial-symptom and quality-of-life gains faded, cognitive impairment worsened, and the authors report that non-motor symptoms progressed (Ostrem et al, Front Neurol 2025, PMID 41626017) - i.e. DBS is not disease-modifying either. (5) Two mimics ARE genuinely reversible and must not be missed: drug-induced parkinsonism (favourable evolution in 88.7% after withdrawal of the suspect drug) and normal-pressure hydrocephalus (shunt surgery); both are covered in pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has Parkinson's disease: a stepwise symptom-control ladder - levodopa-based therapy at the lowest dose that gives satisfactory control, add-on drugs for wearing-off and dyskinesia, device-aided therapy (DBS, intestinal levodopa gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa or apomorphine infusion) when oral therapy fails, active treatment of non-motor symptoms, structured exercise and allied-health therapy, and an emergency plan that never allows abrupt stopping of dopaminergic drugs.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine, procedure and device used for Parkinson's disease, in the order: (1) levodopa-carbidopa (most effective symptomatic therapy; honest 'honeymoon' and motor-complication timeline); (2) dopamine agonists with the impulse-control-disorder safety signal; (3) MAO-B inhibitors with the honest disease-modification evidence; (4) COMT inhibitors; (5) amantadine for dyskinesia; (6) apomorphine, inhaled levodopa and istradefylline for OFF episodes; (7) continuous infusion therapies (intestinal levodopa gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa, apomorphine infusion); (8) deep brain stimulation (landmark trials, long-term outcome, candidate selection, adaptive DBS); (9) acute akinetic crisis / parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome; (10) non-motor symptoms (constipation, orthostatic hypotension, REM sleep behaviour disorder, psychosis and dementia); (11) exercise, physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy; (12) secondary/drug-induced parkinsonism and normal-pressure hydrocephalus; (13) the honest disease-modification trial record; (14) medical equipment and devices. Parkinson's disease has NO curative option, so no curative_option key exists (see CURABILITY_NOTE). All new keys are prefixed pd_ to avoid collision with other entries. Every drug class carries real specific drug names per this project's standing rule, and every entry names its actual trial, guideline or FDA label; where a number could not be retrieved from the primary source it is not stated.

pd_levodopa_carbidopa.name: Carbidopa-Levodopa (Immediate-Release) - The Most Effective Symptomatic Therapy for Parkinson's Motor Symptoms
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.type: Dopamine precursor combined with a peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (dopa-decarboxylase) inhibitor
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.effectiveness: ELLDOPA (361 patients with early PD; 40 weeks of treatment then 2-week washout): total UPDRS changed by +7.8 units on placebo, +1.9 on carbidopa-levodopa 150 mg/day, +1.9 on 300 mg/day and -1.4 on 600 mg/day (p<0.001) - a clear dose-dependent improvement. PD MED (1,620 newly diagnosed patients randomised to levodopa, dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor, median 3-year follow-up, up to 7 years): PDQ-39 mobility scores averaged 1.8 points better with levodopa than with levodopa-sparing therapy (95% CI 0.5-3.0, p=0.005), EQ-5D utility 0.03 better (p=0.0002), and only 2% (11/528) discontinued levodopa for side effects versus 28% on dopamine agonists and 23% on MAO-B inhibitors. The PD MED authors describe the advantage as 'very small but persistent' (the minimally important difference on that scale is 6 points), i.e. levodopa is best but the gap to alternatives is modest in early disease.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.reason_why: Parkinson's disease is a state of striatal dopamine deficiency caused by loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons. Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine by the surviving neurons; carbidopa does not cross the barrier and blocks peripheral decarboxylation, so more levodopa reaches the brain and peripheral nausea and hypotension are reduced. Levodopa is repeatedly described in the primary trial literature as the most effective therapy for Parkinson's disease (Olanow et al, Lancet Neurol 2014).
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.important_caveat: Levodopa does NOT slow the disease. In LEAP (445 early-PD patients, 80 weeks), the change in UPDRS was -1.0 (early start) versus -2.0 (delayed start), difference 1.0 point (95% CI -1.5 to 3.5, p=0.44), which the authors interpret as no disease-modifying effect; rates of dyskinesia and fluctuations did not differ significantly between groups. In ELLDOPA the dopamine-transporter imaging decline was larger on levodopa (-6%, -4%, -7.2% vs -1.4% on placebo), which the authors say is uncertain to interpret (either faster loss of terminals or a pharmacological effect on the transporter). The FDA label carries warnings for sudden sleep onset during daily activities and impulse-control behaviours.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.real_working_solution: Start levodopa when symptoms impair quality of life and use the LOWEST dose that gives satisfactory control (dyskinesia and wearing-off risk is dose-dependent - see next entry); LEAP gives no evidence that starting early harms the disease course, so fear of 'levodopa toxicity' is not a reason to withhold it from a symptomatic patient.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.source: Fahn S et al (ELLDOPA), N Engl J Med 2004 (PMID 15590952); PD Med Collaborative Group, Lancet 2014;384:1196-1205 (PMID 24928805); Verschuur CVM et al (LEAP), N Engl J Med 2019;380:315-324 (PMID 30673543); MDS Evidence-Based Medicine review, Fox SH et al, Mov Disord 2018;33:1248-1266 (PMID 29570866); FDA Sinemet label (DailyMed)

pd_levodopa_carbidopa.name: Long-Term Levodopa Motor Complications - 'Honeymoon' Period, Wearing-Off and Dyskinesia (Honest Incidence and Timeline)
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.type: Natural history / adverse-effect profile of chronic levodopa therapy (not a separate drug)
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.effectiveness: Ahlskog & Muenter pooled 74 publications (112 treatment intervals): in modern-era series motor fluctuations (wearing-off) were nil during the first year of levodopa but affected approximately 40% of patients by 4-6 years, and dyskinesias were slightly under 40% by 4-6 years; patients whose PD began before the levodopa era had dyskinesias much earlier (median 50% by 5-6 months), probably because of longer pre-existing disease. The authors stress these are incidence figures and that clinically important prevalence 'may be substantially less'. In the Sydney 20-year cohort, drug-induced dyskinesia and end-of-dose failure were experienced by most patients. In the STRIDE-PD data (745 patients), risk of both dyskinesia and wearing-off rose with levodopa dose (p<0.001 for both); predictors of dyskinesia in rank order were young age at onset, higher levodopa dose, low body weight, North American region, entacapone-containing regimen, female gender and higher UPDRS Part II.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.reason_why: Levodopa has a short plasma half-life, and as nigrostriatal terminals are lost the brain's ability to buffer dopamine falls, so each dose produces a shorter 'on' period (wearing-off) and pulsatile receptor stimulation that promotes dyskinesia. Experimental work cited by the LCIG trial authors links motor complications to non-physiological, intermittent drug delivery that can be reduced by continuous delivery.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.important_caveat: Because the numbers are incidence data from a mixture of eras and populations they should not be read as the fate of every patient; in the trials cited the dyskinesias were often mild, but an early-onset (young) patient on a high dose is at the highest risk.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.real_working_solution: Prevent: lowest effective levodopa dose (STRIDE-PD authors: 'use the lowest dose of l-dopa that provides satisfactory clinical control to minimize the risk of both dyskinesia and wearing-off'). Treat wearing-off: COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor, dopamine agonist, extended-release levodopa. Treat dyskinesia: amantadine. If these fail: DBS or continuous infusion (entries below).
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.source: Ahlskog JE, Muenter MD, Mov Disord 2001;16:448-458 (PMID 11391738); Warren Olanow C et al (STRIDE-PD analysis), Mov Disord 2013;28:1064-1071 (PMID 23630119); Hely MA et al, Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844 (PMID 18307261)

pd_levodopa_carbidopa.name: Extended-Release Carbidopa-Levodopa - Fewer Daily Doses and Less OFF Time in Fluctuating Disease
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.type: Oral extended-release levodopa formulation (with decarboxylase inhibitor)
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.effectiveness: ADVANCE-PD phase 3 (393 patients with at least 2.5 h/day of OFF time randomised double-blind after open-label titration): OFF time as a percentage of waking hours ended at 23.82% on extended-release versus 29.79% on immediate-release (mean difference -5.97 percentage points, 95% CI -9.05 to -2.89), while using fewer doses (3.6 vs 5.0 per day). The MDS Evidence-Based Medicine review lists levodopa extended-release as clinically useful for treating motor fluctuations.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.reason_why: A longer-acting release profile keeps plasma levodopa above the therapeutic threshold for longer, so each dose covers more of the day and fewer troughs occur.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.important_caveat: The gain is modest (about 6 percentage points of the waking day) and was shown in patients with at least 2.5 h/day of OFF time.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.real_working_solution: Use in patients whose wearing-off is predictable and who would benefit from fewer daily doses before escalating to device-aided therapy.
pd_levodopa_carbidopa.source: ADVANCE-PD phase 3 trial, Lancet Neurol 2013;12:346-356 (PMID 23485610); MDS EBM review, Mov Disord 2018 (PMID 29570866); FDA Rytary label (DailyMed)

pd_dopamine_agonists.name: Non-Ergot Dopamine Agonists (Pramipexole, Ropinirole) - Levodopa-Sparing Initial Therapy With Fewer Motor Complications
pd_dopamine_agonists.effectiveness: CALM-PD (301 early-PD patients): initial pramipexole gave significantly less wearing-off, dyskinesia or on-off fluctuation (28%) than levodopa (51%) (hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.30-0.66, p<0.001), but UPDRS improved more on levodopa (9.2 vs 4.5 points, p<0.001) and somnolence was more frequent on pramipexole (32.4% vs 17.3%, p=0.003). At 6 years complications were 50.0% with initial pramipexole vs 68.4% with initial levodopa (p=0.002), disabling dyskinesias were uncommon in both, and daily-living scores did not differ (79.9 vs 82.5, p=0.19). Ropinirole study (268 early-PD patients, 5 years): cumulative dyskinesia 20% with ropinirole vs 45% with levodopa (hazard ratio for remaining dyskinesia-free 2.82, 95% CI 1.78-4.44, p<0.001), 34% of completers on ropinirole never needed levodopa; the 10-year extension (42 vs 27 patients) kept a lower dyskinesia incidence (adjusted OR 0.3, p=0.046) with no difference in daily-living or PDQ-39 scores. Against this, PD MED found levodopa gave better patient-rated mobility and only 2% stopped for side effects versus 28% of the dopamine-agonist group. The MDS EBM review rates non-ergot dopamine agonists clinically useful as early monotherapy and as adjunct.
pd_dopamine_agonists.reason_why: Agonists directly stimulate striatal dopamine receptors, bypass the failing presynaptic dopamine synthesis, and have longer half-lives than levodopa, giving less pulsatile stimulation - the proposed reason for fewer motor complications.
pd_dopamine_agonists.important_caveat: Fewer dyskinesias comes at a price: weaker motor benefit, more somnolence, oedema, hallucinations and the impulse-control-disorder risk detailed in the next entry. The delayed-levodopa strategy is therefore a rational choice mainly for younger patients (young age at onset is the top-ranked predictor of dyskinesia in STRIDE-PD - this link to agonist choice is clinical inference, not a randomised finding) who are carefully screened for impulsivity; PD MED shows MAO-B inhibitors were at least as effective as agonists as a levodopa-sparing option. The FDA labels for both drugs warn of sudden sleep onset during daily activities (including driving) and of impulse-control behaviours.
pd_dopamine_agonists.real_working_solution: Use an agonist as levodopa-sparing therapy only in selected younger patients after discussing impulse-control and sleepiness risks (and driving), titrate slowly, and add levodopa when disability requires it - the trials show this strategy is safe and delays dyskinesia.
pd_dopamine_agonists.source: Parkinson Study Group (CALM-PD), JAMA 2000;284:1931-1938 (PMID 11035889); CALM-PD extended follow-up, Arch Neurol 2009;66:563-570 (PMID 19433655); ropinirole vs levodopa 5-year study, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1484-1491 (PMID 10816186) and 10-year follow-up, Mov Disord 2007;22:2409-2417 (PMID 17894339); PD Med Collaborative Group, Lancet 2014 (PMID 24928805); FDA Mirapex and Requip XL labels (DailyMed)

pd_dopamine_agonists.name: Rotigotine Transdermal Patch - Continuous Dopaminergic Stimulation for Fluctuating and Early Disease
pd_dopamine_agonists.type: Non-ergot dopamine agonist delivered as a 24-hour transdermal patch
pd_dopamine_agonists.effectiveness: CLEOPATRA-PD (204 rotigotine, 201 pramipexole, 101 placebo; levodopa-treated patients with wearing-off, 6 months): mean change in OFF time -2.5 h with rotigotine, -2.8 h with pramipexole and -0.9 h with placebo; rotigotine versus placebo -1.58 h (95% CI -2.27 to -0.90); rotigotine was non-inferior to pramipexole. The FDA label lists Parkinson's disease (and restless legs syndrome) as indications.
pd_dopamine_agonists.reason_why: The patch delivers the agonist at a steady rate through the skin, avoiding gastrointestinal absorption problems and giving continuous rather than pulsatile receptor stimulation.
pd_dopamine_agonists.important_caveat: Same class-effect risks as other agonists (impulse-control disorders, somnolence). The transdermal route also matters clinically because patients who cannot swallow are a real problem in the acute akinetic crisis (see that entry, where rotigotine patches are described only in case reports).
pd_dopamine_agonists.real_working_solution: Patch rotigotine is a practical option for patients who need an agonist but have swallowing difficulty or erratic oral absorption.
pd_dopamine_agonists.source: Poewe W et al (CLEOPATRA-PD), Lancet Neurol 2007;6:513-520 (PMID 17509486); FDA Neupro label (DailyMed)

pd_dopamine_agonists.name: Dopamine-Agonist Safety Signals - Impulse-Control Disorders, Withdrawal Syndrome and Ergot Valvulopathy (With Real Fixes)
pd_dopamine_agonists.type: Class adverse-effect profile of dopamine agonists (and other dopaminergic drugs)
specific_drugs: Ergot-derived agonists with valvulopathy risk: pergolide, cabergoline (avoid; use non-ergot agonists)
pd_dopamine_agonists.effectiveness: Impulse-control disorders (ICDs): in a cross-sectional study of 3,090 treated PD patients at 46 North American centres, an ICD was present in 13.6% (pathological gambling 5.0%, compulsive sexual behaviour 3.5%, compulsive buying 5.7%, binge eating 4.3%) and 3.9% had two or more. ICDs were more common with a dopamine agonist than without (17.1% vs 6.9%; OR 2.72, 95% CI 2.08-3.54, p<0.001) and frequency was similar for pramipexole and ropinirole (17.7% vs 15.5%; OR 1.22, p=0.14), i.e. a class effect. Other independent associations: levodopa use, younger age, unmarried status, current smoking and a family history of gambling problems. Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (DAWS): 5 of 26 patients (19%) who tapered an agonist developed a severe stereotyped withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, panic, depression, dysphoria, pain, orthostatic hypotension, drug craving) refractory to levodopa; all five had baseline ICDs and higher agonist exposure. Ergot agonists: in a UK primary-care cohort of 11,417 antiparkinsonian-drug users, current pergolide use (incidence-rate ratio 7.1, 95% CI 2.3-22.3) and cabergoline use (4.9, 95% CI 1.5-15.6) raised the rate of cardiac-valve regurgitation, but other agonists did not.
pd_dopamine_agonists.reason_why: The widely accepted hypothesis is that agonists (especially D3-preferring ones) over-stimulate the relatively spared mesolimbic reward circuitry, producing compulsive reward-seeking; abrupt agonist reduction after high cumulative exposure produces a dopaminergic withdrawal state; ergot derivatives activate 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves (the accepted mechanism for the valvulopathy). These mechanisms are hypotheses and were not tested in the trials cited.
pd_dopamine_agonists.important_caveat: The prevalence figures are from a cross-sectional study (association, not incidence) and DAWS numbers come from a small single-centre retrospective cohort; both are precise real signals but not exact population rates.
pd_dopamine_agonists.real_working_solution: Screen for gambling, sexual, buying and eating behaviours at every visit and warn patient and family before starting any agonist. The FDA pramipexole label states that these behaviours are 'generally reversible upon dose reduction or treatment discontinuation'; therefore if an ICD appears, reduce or stop the agonist (slowly, monitoring closely for DAWS, especially in those with ICDs and high agonist doses). Use non-ergot agonists only.
pd_dopamine_agonists.source: Weintraub D et al, Arch Neurol 2010;67:589-595 (PMID 20457959); Rabinak CA, Nirenberg MJ, Arch Neurol 2010;67:58-63 (PMID 20065130); Schade R et al, N Engl J Med 2007;356:29-38 (PMID 17202453); FDA Mirapex label (DailyMed)

pd_mao_b_inhibitors.name: Selegiline and Rasagiline - Mild Symptomatic Monotherapy in Early PD; Disease-Modification Claim Honestly Unproven
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.effectiveness: DATATOP (800 untreated early-PD patients): deprenyl reduced the risk of reaching disability requiring levodopa (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.41-0.62, p<0.001; median time to end point delayed by about 9 months), but motor ratings improved in the first 3 months and worsened after withdrawal, i.e. a symptomatic effect is entangled with any protective effect; the authors state the mechanism 'remains unclear'. TEMPO (404 patients, 26 weeks): total UPDRS was 4.20 units better than placebo with rasagiline 1 mg (95% CI -5.66 to -2.73, p<0.001) and 3.56 units better with 2 mg (p<0.001). ADAGIO delayed-start (1,176 patients, 72 weeks): rasagiline 1 mg met all three hierarchical end points (UPDRS worsening 2.82 vs 4.52 points for early vs delayed start, p=0.02) but 2 mg did not (3.47 vs 3.11, p=0.60); the authors' conclusion is that 1 mg was 'consistent with a possible disease-modifying effect' but 'the study results must be interpreted with caution' because the two doses disagreed. In PD MED, initial MAO-B inhibitor therapy scored 1.4 PDQ-39 mobility points better than a dopamine agonist (95% CI 0.0-2.9, p=0.05) with 23% discontinuing for side effects. MDS EBM review: selegiline and rasagiline are clinically useful monotherapy in early PD, and there is no clinically useful intervention to prevent or delay progression.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.reason_why: MAO-B breaks down dopamine in the striatum; inhibiting it raises synaptic dopamine and prolongs the effect of levodopa, giving a mild symptomatic benefit with a once-daily oral tablet.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.important_caveat: Disease modification is NOT established: DATATOP is confounded by symptomatic effect, and ADAGIO's dose inconsistency prevents a conclusion. Effects are mild compared with levodopa. The Azilect label states tyramine restriction is not required at recommended doses but very high-tyramine foods (over 150 mg) could still cause severe hypertension; the label also warns about sleep attacks and impulse-control behaviours.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Reasonable first choice for a patient with mild disability who wants a well-tolerated, once-daily, low-burden levodopa-sparing option (PD MED: at least as effective as an agonist with fewer ICD/somnolence concerns), or as an add-on to reduce OFF time - but do not prescribe it for the claim of slowing the disease.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.source: Parkinson Study Group (DATATOP), N Engl J Med 1989;321:1364-1371 (PMID 2509910) and 1993;328:176-183 (PMID 8417384); Parkinson Study Group (TEMPO), Arch Neurol 2002;59:1937-1943 (PMID 12470183); Olanow CW et al (ADAGIO), N Engl J Med 2009;361:1268-1278 (PMID 19776408); PD Med Collaborative Group, Lancet 2014 (PMID 24928805); MDS EBM review, Mov Disord 2018 (PMID 29570866); FDA Azilect label (DailyMed)

pd_mao_b_inhibitors.name: Safinamide - Add-On MAO-B Inhibitor With Glutamate Modulation for Wearing-Off
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.type: Reversible MAO-B inhibitor with non-dopaminergic (glutamate-release-modulating) action
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.effectiveness: Randomised 24-week trial (549 levodopa-treated patients with more than 1.5 h/day OFF time): daily ON time without troublesome dyskinesia rose +1.42 h with safinamide vs +0.57 h with placebo (least-squares mean difference 0.96 h, 95% CI 0.56-1.37 h); premature discontinuation for adverse events was 4.4% vs 3.6%. The FDA label indicates safinamide as adjunctive treatment to levodopa/carbidopa in patients experiencing OFF episodes, and the MDS EBM review lists it as clinically useful for motor fluctuations.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.reason_why: It raises striatal dopamine by MAO-B inhibition and adds an effect on glutamatergic transmission that is described in the trial as 'dopaminergic and nondopaminergic actions'.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.important_caveat: The gain is under 1 hour of extra good ON time per day; it is an incremental add-on, not a substitute for optimising levodopa.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Add to levodopa when wearing-off persists after dose optimisation and a once-daily tablet is preferred.
pd_mao_b_inhibitors.source: Schapira AHV et al, JAMA Neurol 2017;74:216-224 (PMID 27942720); FDA Xadago label (DailyMed); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866)

pd_comt_inhibitors.name: Entacapone and Opicapone - COMT Inhibitors to Extend Each Levodopa Dose in Wearing-Off
pd_comt_inhibitors.type: Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitors, given as adjuncts to levodopa
pd_comt_inhibitors.effectiveness: Entacapone, placebo-controlled trial (205 patients with motor fluctuations, 24 weeks): 'on' time (about 10 h per day at baseline) rose by 5.0 percentage points, more in patients with a small baseline 'on' fraction (<55%). Opicapone (BIPARK I, 600 randomised: opicapone 5, 25, 50 mg once daily vs placebo vs entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose, 14-15 weeks): change in OFF time -116.8 min with opicapone 50 mg vs -56.0 min with placebo (difference -60.8 min, 95% CI -97.2 to -24.4, p=0.0015) and non-inferior to entacapone (-96.3 min; difference -26.2 min, p=0.0051); opicapone 5 mg and 25 mg were not significantly different from placebo (p=0.056 and 0.080). Commonest adverse event was dyskinesia (18 patients on 50 mg vs 5 on placebo), followed by insomnia and constipation. In the PD MED adjunct trial (500 patients uncontrolled on levodopa) MAO-B inhibitors gave PDQ-39 mobility scores 4.2 points better than COMT inhibitors (p=0.03). The FDA label indicates opicapone 50 mg as adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa for OFF episodes, and the MDS review lists entacapone and opicapone as clinically useful for motor fluctuations.
pd_comt_inhibitors.reason_why: COMT converts levodopa to 3-O-methyldopa in the periphery; blocking it slows levodopa elimination, lengthens its half-life, and keeps brain dopamine higher between doses, shortening OFF time.
pd_comt_inhibitors.important_caveat: Do NOT start a COMT inhibitor together with levodopa in early, non-fluctuating PD: in STRIDE-PD (747 patients, 134 weeks) starting with levodopa-carbidopa-entacapone produced a shorter time to dyskinesia (hazard ratio 1.29, p=0.04) and more dyskinesia (42% vs 32%, p=0.02) than levodopa-carbidopa, with no significant difference in time to wearing-off; the higher levodopa-equivalent dose in the entacapone arm may explain this. Tolcapone carries an FDA warning of potentially fatal acute fulminant liver failure and is only for patients who cannot use other adjuncts.
pd_comt_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Add a COMT inhibitor when predictable end-of-dose wearing-off appears; opicapone once-daily 50 mg is the convenient option, entacapone the long-standing one, and dose-reduce levodopa if dyskinesia emerges.
pd_comt_inhibitors.source: Parkinson Study Group, Ann Neurol 1997;42:747-755 (PMID 9392574); Ferreira JJ et al (BIPARK I), Lancet Neurol 2016;15:154-165 (PMID 26725544); Stocchi F et al (STRIDE-PD), Ann Neurol 2010;68:18-27 (PMID 20582993); PD MED adjunct trial, JAMA Neurol 2022;79:131-140 (PMID 34962574); FDA Ongentys and Tasmar labels (DailyMed); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866)

pd_amantadine_dyskinesia.name: Amantadine (Immediate- and Extended-Release) - The Real Drug for Levodopa-Induced Dyskinesia
pd_amantadine_dyskinesia.effectiveness: Immediate-release, double-blind crossover trial (18 patients, 14 completers): amantadine reduced dyskinesia severity by 60% (p=0.001) during an intravenous levodopa infusion without reducing the antiparkinsonian effect of levodopa, and improved diary-recorded motor fluctuations. Extended-release, EASE LID 3 (randomised, 13 weeks): Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale changed by -20.7 vs -6.3 with placebo (treatment difference -14.4, 95% CI -20.4 to -8.3, p<0.0001) and OFF time by -0.5 h vs +0.6 h (difference -1.1 h, p=0.0199); adverse events led to discontinuation in 19% vs 8% (dry mouth 13.5%, nausea 13.5%, insomnia 10.8%, orthostatic hypotension 10.8%, visual hallucinations 8.1%). EASE LID 2 (2-year open-label, 223 patients, mean PD duration 11.7 years): 57.8% completed, median treatment 1.9 years, MDS-UPDRS Part IV remained low through week 100 (about 6.9-7.3 points); adverse events were falls 32.7%, hallucinations 24.2%, peripheral oedema 16.1%, constipation 13.5%. The MDS EBM review lists amantadine as clinically useful for dyskinesia; the FDA Gocovri label lists dyskinesia and adjunctive treatment of OFF episodes.
pd_amantadine_dyskinesia.reason_why: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia involves hyperfunction of glutamate NMDA receptors on striatal neurons (the mechanistic view stated in the crossover trial); amantadine blocks that receptor, reducing involuntary movements without removing the dopaminergic benefit.
pd_amantadine_dyskinesia.important_caveat: Hallucinations and falls were among the commonest adverse events, which limits use in the elderly or cognitively impaired; abrupt discontinuation has been reported as a trigger of akinetic crisis (see that entry) so it must be tapered, not stopped suddenly.
pd_amantadine_dyskinesia.real_working_solution: First-line drug for troublesome peak-dose dyskinesia; if hallucinations or cognitive decline limit it, or dyskinesia stays disabling, move to DBS or continuous infusion.
pd_amantadine_dyskinesia.source: Verhagen Metman L et al, Neurology 1998;50:1323-1326 (PMID 9595981); Oertel W et al (EASE LID 3), Mov Disord 2017;32:1701-1709 (PMID 28833562); EASE LID 2, J Parkinsons Dis 2020;10:543-558 (PMID 31929122); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866); FDA Gocovri label (DailyMed)

pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.name: Apomorphine (Injection and Sublingual Film) - On-Demand Rescue From OFF Episodes
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.effectiveness: Sublingual film phase 3 (109 patients with at least 2 h/day OFF time; 12-week maintenance): the 30-minute post-dose change in MDS-UPDRS Part III at week 12 was -11.1 with apomorphine vs -3.5 with placebo (difference -7.6, 95% CI -11.5 to -3.7, p=0.0002); oropharyngeal side effects occurred in 31% vs 7% and led to discontinuation in 17% vs 2%; transient nausea in 28%, somnolence 13%. The FDA Apokyn label indicates acute, intermittent treatment of hypomobility 'off' episodes (end-of-dose wearing-off and unpredictable on-off) in advanced PD.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.reason_why: Apomorphine is a fast-acting dopamine agonist that bypasses gut absorption, so it can turn a patient ON within minutes when oral levodopa has failed or is delayed.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.important_caveat: Nausea is common on initiation (28% in the sublingual trial) and antiemetic pre-treatment is recommended when starting apomorphine formulations (post-hoc analysis of the phase 3 study); in the sublingual trial only 63% completed the study and one patient with known cardiac risk factors had a fatal cardiac arrest. The akinetic-crisis literature pairs apomorphine with domperidone.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.real_working_solution: Use for predictable morning OFF or sudden unpredictable OFF; escalate to continuous infusion if OFF episodes are frequent.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.source: Olanow CW et al, Lancet Neurol 2020;19:135-144 (PMID 31818699); FDA Apokyn label (DailyMed); Pötter-Nerger M et al, J Neural Transm 2024 (PMID 39153024) for the domperidone pairing

pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.name: Inhaled Levodopa and Istradefylline - Additional Add-Ons for OFF Episodes
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.type: Inhaled levodopa powder; selective adenosine A2A receptor antagonist
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.effectiveness: Inhaled levodopa (CVT-301 84 mg, 36-patient crossover for early-morning OFF): 66.7% were ON at 30 minutes vs 44.5% with placebo (p=0.040); cough was the commonest adverse event (11.1% vs 2.8%). Istradefylline (12-week trial, 395 levodopa-treated patients): OFF time fell 4.35% of waking day (20 mg, p=0.026) and 4.49% (60 mg, p=0.024) relative to placebo, which equals -0.64 h (p not significant for the 20 mg dose) and -0.77 h (95% CI -1.44 to -0.11) in absolute hours; common adverse events were dyskinesia, nausea, dizziness and hallucinations. FDA labels: Inbrija for intermittent treatment of OFF episodes; Nourianz 20 mg as adjunct for OFF episodes.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.reason_why: Inhalation delivers levodopa through the lung directly into the bloodstream, skipping the delayed gastric emptying common in PD; adenosine A2A antagonism removes an inhibitory brake on the indirect striatal pathway independent of dopamine.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.important_caveat: Effect sizes are modest (istradefylline under 1 hour/day; inhaled levodopa data here are from a small crossover study, not a large efficacy trial).
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.real_working_solution: Options for patients whose OFF episodes persist despite an optimised oral regimen and who are not yet candidates for device-aided therapy.
pd_off_episode_rescue_and_other_adjuncts.source: CVT-301 morning-OFF study, Parkinsonism Relat Disord 2019;62:175-180 (PMID 30992235); istradefylline 6002-US-006 study, Neurology 2008;70:2233-2240 (PMID 18519872); FDA Inbrija and Nourianz labels (DailyMed)

pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.name: Levodopa-Carbidopa Intestinal Gel (LCIG, Duodopa/Duopa) - Continuous Jejunal Infusion for Advanced Fluctuating PD
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.type: Continuous enteral levodopa-carbidopa gel delivered by portable pump through a percutaneous gastrojejunostomy tube
specific_drugs: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel / enteral suspension (Duodopa; US brand Duopa)
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.effectiveness: First double-blind controlled demonstration of continuous delivery (12-week, double-dummy, 71 patients): mean OFF time fell by 4.04 h with LCIG vs 2.14 h with immediate-release oral levodopa-carbidopa (difference -1.91 h, 95% CI -3.05 to -0.76, p=0.0015); ON time without troublesome dyskinesia rose 4.11 h vs 2.24 h (difference 1.86 h, p=0.0059). Adverse events occurred in 35 of 37 (95%) LCIG patients (5 [14%] serious) vs 34 of 34 (100%) oral patients (7 [21%] serious), mainly related to the gastrojejunostomy tube. FDA approved Duopa on 12 January 2015 (16-hour infusion via PEG-J). The MDS EBM review lists levodopa intestinal infusion as clinically useful for motor fluctuations.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.reason_why: The trial authors' rationale: motor complications reflect non-physiological intermittent drug delivery, and a continuous infusion into the small intestine removes the gastric-emptying variability and plasma level swings of oral tablets.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.important_caveat: Needs a surgically/endoscopically placed tube and pump; adverse events are frequent and tube-related. The label requires evaluating vitamin B6 levels before treatment.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.real_working_solution: Best for advanced fluctuating patients who want a non-brain-surgery option or are not DBS candidates because of age, cognition or comorbidity.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.source: Olanow CW et al, Lancet Neurol 2014;13:141-149 (PMID 24361112); FDA Duopa label and approval (12 Jan 2015, DailyMed / AbbVie); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866)

pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.name: Continuous Subcutaneous Foslevodopa-Foscarbidopa (Vyalev) - Newer Non-Surgical 24-Hour Infusion
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.type: Soluble levodopa/carbidopa prodrugs delivered as 24-hour/day subcutaneous infusion through a single infusion site
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.effectiveness: Phase 3 double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled 12-week trial (141 randomised: 74 foslevodopa-foscarbidopa vs 67 oral immediate-release levodopa-carbidopa; at least 2.5 h/day OFF time): ON time without troublesome dyskinesia increased 2.72 h vs 0.97 h (difference 1.75 h, 95% CI 0.46-3.05, p=0.0083) and OFF time fell 2.75 h vs 0.96 h (difference -1.79 h, 95% CI -3.03 to -0.54, p=0.0054). Adverse events 85% vs 63% (serious 8% vs 6%); infusion-site events were erythema 27%, pain 26%, cellulitis 19%, oedema 12%; premature discontinuation for adverse events was 22% vs 1%. The 52-week open-label study (244 enrolled; 137 completed, 107 discontinued) showed at week 52 ON time without troublesome dyskinesia +3.8 h and OFF time -3.5 h, morning akinesia falling from 77.7% to 27.8%, with serious adverse events in 25.8%. FDA approved Vyalev on 16 October 2024 for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced PD.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.reason_why: A soluble prodrug formulation allows continuous 24-hour levodopa delivery without a gastrojejunostomy or brain surgery.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.important_caveat: Infusion-site reactions are the price: nearly one in five had cellulitis and 22% stopped for adverse events in the randomised trial; in the open-label year 107 of 244 discontinued. The effect is about 1.75 h/day more good ON time than oral immediate-release levodopa-carbidopa; head-to-head comparisons with LCIG or DBS were not found, so cross-trial comparison is not valid. The label advises evaluating vitamin B6 levels.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.real_working_solution: A genuinely newer option for advanced fluctuating patients who prefer a non-surgical, non-tube route; rotate the infusion site and treat site infections promptly.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.source: Soileau MJ et al, Lancet Neurol 2022;21:1099-1109 (PMID 36402160); 52-week open-label study, Neurol Ther 2023;12:1937-1958 (PMID 37632656); FDA Vyalev label and approval (16-17 Oct 2024, DailyMed / AbbVie)

pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.name: Subcutaneous Apomorphine Infusion - Continuous Dopamine-Agonist Therapy for Persistent Fluctuations
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.type: Continuous subcutaneous dopamine-agonist infusion by pump
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.effectiveness: TOLEDO double-blind placebo-controlled 12-week trial (107 randomised, patients with motor fluctuations despite optimised oral therapy; 3-8 mg/h during 16 waking hours, mean final dose 4.68 mg/h): OFF time fell 2.47 h/day vs 0.58 h/day with placebo (difference -1.89 h/day, 95% CI -3.16 to -0.62, p=0.0025). The FDA Onapgo label indicates treatment of motor fluctuations in adults with advanced PD.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.reason_why: Continuous subcutaneous infusion gives steady dopaminergic stimulation without needing gut absorption.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.important_caveat: The TOLEDO abstract reports apomorphine was well tolerated without unexpected safety findings (its adverse-event list was truncated in the retrieved abstract); class risks (nausea, impulse-control disorders) apply, and in the acute akinetic-crisis literature a transient lack of apomorphine response was described.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.real_working_solution: Option for advanced fluctuating patients who are not candidates for DBS or intestinal gel; open-label studies cited in the TOLEDO abstract report reduced dyskinesia and lower levodopa dose with apomorphine infusion.
pd_continuous_infusion_therapies.source: Katzenschlager R et al (TOLEDO), Lancet Neurol 2018;17:749-759 (PMID 30055903); FDA Onapgo label (DailyMed)

pd_deep_brain_stimulation.name: Deep Brain Stimulation (STN or GPi) vs Best Medical Therapy for Advanced PD - Landmark Comparative Trials
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.type: Neurosurgical implanted neurostimulation (bilateral subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna DBS)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - implanted pulse generator with bilateral STN or GPi leads, used together with continued carbidopa-levodopa and other antiparkinsonian drugs
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.effectiveness: VA CSP 468 (Weaver et al, JAMA 2009): 255 patients with advanced PD (Hoehn and Yahr 2 or more off medication; 25% aged 70 or older) - STN DBS n=60, GPi DBS n=61, best medical therapy n=134, 6-month outcomes. DBS patients gained a mean 4.6 h/day of ON time without troubling dyskinesia versus 0 h/day for medical therapy (between-group difference 4.5 h/day, 95% CI 3.7-5.4, p<0.001); clinically meaningful motor improvement (5 points or more) in 71% vs 32%; significant improvement in the PD quality-of-life summary measure and in 7 of 8 domain scores (p<0.001); small decrements in some information-processing tests; at least one serious adverse event in 49 DBS patients vs 15 medical (p<0.001), including 39 surgery-related events and 1 death from cerebral haemorrhage. Deuschl et al, NEJM 2006 (randomised-pairs trial): 156 patients under 75 years, 6 months - PDQ-39 improved by 9.5 points and UPDRS-III by 19.6 points more with STN stimulation than with medication alone (p=0.02 and p<0.001); serious adverse events 13% vs 4%, including a fatal intracerebral haemorrhage. UK PD SURG (Williams et al, Lancet Neurol 2010; 366 patients, open-label, 1 year): PDQ-39 summary index improved 5.0 points with surgery vs 0.3 with medical therapy (difference -4.7, 95% CI -7.6 to -1.8, p=0.001); mobility domain -8.9 and activities-of-daily-living domain -12.4 points; the authors judged the differences clinically meaningful but 'surgery is not without risk'. EARLYSTIM (Schuepbach et al, NEJM 2013): 251 patients with early motor complications (mean age 52, mean duration 7.5 years) - PDQ-39 improved 7.8 points with STN stimulation vs 0.2-point worsening with medical therapy (difference 8.0, p=0.002), with superior motor disability, daily living, motor complications and good-mobility time; serious adverse events 54.8% vs 44.1%, with 17.7% related to implantation or the device. The MDS EBM review rates bilateral STN and GPi DBS clinically useful for motor fluctuations and dyskinesia.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.reason_why: High-frequency stimulation of the STN or GPi is thought to normalise the abnormal basal-ganglia network firing patterns of the dopamine-depleted state, reducing the severity of OFF-state motor symptoms and allowing lower levodopa doses (which lowers dyskinesia).
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.important_caveat: DBS improves symptoms but does NOT slow or cure the disease (see the long-term entry). It carries real surgical risk (intracranial haemorrhage deaths occurred in two of the randomised trials) and STN stimulation can worsen depression, apathy, impulsivity, verbal fluency and executive function in a subset of patients (expert-consensus statement).
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.real_working_solution: For an appropriately selected advanced or early-fluctuating patient, DBS is the largest-effect option for motor fluctuations, dyskinesia and tremor; EARLYSTIM (mean disease duration 7.5 years) supports considering referral as soon as troublesome motor complications emerge.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.source: Weaver FM et al (CSP 468), JAMA 2009;301:63-73 (PMID 19126811); Deuschl G et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355:896-908 (PMID 16943402); Williams A et al (PD SURG), Lancet Neurol 2010;9:581-591 (PMID 20434403); Schuepbach WMM et al (EARLYSTIM), N Engl J Med 2013;368:610-622 (PMID 23406026); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866); Bronstein JM et al, Arch Neurol 2011;68:165 (PMID 20937936)

pd_deep_brain_stimulation.name: STN vs GPi Target Choice and Real 10-Year Outcome (VA/NINDS CSP 468 and CSP 468F)
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.type: Neurosurgical implanted neurostimulation - target selection and long-term follow-up
specific_drugs: Not a drug - STN DBS or GPi DBS lead placement (bilateral)
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.effectiveness: 24-month comparison (299 patients, 152 GPi vs 147 STN): change in blinded off-medication/on-stimulation UPDRS-III did not differ (p=0.50) and self-reported function was similar; STN patients needed lower dopaminergic drug doses (p=0.02); a visuomotor processing-speed measure declined more after STN (p=0.03); depression worsened after STN but improved after GPi (p=0.02); serious adverse events 51% GPi vs 56% STN. 10-year follow-up (CSP 468F, 156 patients enrolled; data for 68 GPi/49 STN at 7 years and 49 GPi/28 STN at 10 years): off-medication UPDRS-III improvement from baseline in the GPi cohort was 39.9% at 2 years, 16.4% at 7 years and 22.3% at 10 years (p=0.10 at 10 years) and in the STN cohort 34.9%, 16.9% and 32.8% (p<0.001 at every time point); tremor and rigidity showed the greatest and most durable gains, UPDRS-IV motor complications and diaries improved long-term with medication reductions in both targets; bradykinesia, axial symptoms and quality of life (PDQ-39 no longer improved at 7 and 10 years) faded and more severe cognitive impairment developed.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.reason_why: Both targets are nodes of the basal-ganglia motor circuit; STN stimulation acts more directly on levodopa requirement, whereas GPi stimulation has less impact on mood and processing speed in these data.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.important_caveat: The 10-year cohort is a subset of the original randomised patients (attrition) and non-motor symptoms progressed regardless of target - DBS treats the motor complications of PD, not the disease.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.real_working_solution: Choose the target individually: GPi where mood, cognition or dyskinesia-with-drug-reduction issues weigh most; STN where reducing medication is the goal (both effective per CSP 468).
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.source: Follett KA et al (CSP 468), N Engl J Med 2010;362:2077-2091 (PMID 20519680); Ostrem JL et al (CSP 468F), Front Neurol 2025;16:1728999 (PMID 41626017)

pd_deep_brain_stimulation.name: DBS Candidate Selection - Levodopa Responsiveness as the Key Predictor of Success
specific_drugs: Not a drug - preoperative levodopa challenge and multidisciplinary DBS-team assessment
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.effectiveness: International expert consensus (Bronstein et al, Arch Neurol 2011): PD patients without significant active cognitive or psychiatric problems who have medically intractable motor fluctuations, intractable tremor or intolerance of medication adverse effects are good candidates; surgery is best done by an experienced stereotactic neurosurgeon within a multidisciplinary team; programming takes 3 to 6 months; DBS improves levodopa-responsive symptoms, dyskinesia and tremor. In 54 STN-DBS patients, younger age and levodopa responsiveness predicted a favourable response, and individual symptoms that improve with a suprathreshold levodopa dose are likely to improve with stimulation (Charles et al, Neurology 2002). In a meta-analysis of 37 STN-DBS cohorts, motor (UPDRS-III) improvement averaged 27.55 points (52%), activities of daily living (UPDRS-II) 13.35 points (50%), levodopa-equivalent dose fell 55.9%, dyskinesia fell 69.1%, daily OFF periods fell 68.2% and PDQ-39 improved 34.5%; larger improvements were independently associated with higher baseline levodopa responsiveness, higher baseline motor score and longer disease duration (Kleiner-Fisman et al, Mov Disord 2006).
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.reason_why: Symptoms that respond to dopamine replacement are the ones mediated by circuits DBS can modulate; symptoms that do not respond to levodopa (many axial symptoms, freezing, cognitive decline) generally do not respond to DBS either.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.important_caveat: Contraindicating features in the consensus statement are significant active cognitive or psychiatric problems; STN DBS can worsen mood and executive function in a subset. The referral threshold is 'good levodopa response but disabling motor complications despite optimised drugs', not 'drugs have failed'.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.real_working_solution: Do a formal levodopa challenge (off vs on UPDRS-III), cognitive and psychiatric screening, and refer to a DBS-experienced team; CSP 468 included patients aged 70 or older (25% of the trial), and the German trial was restricted to those under 75, so age alone is not an absolute bar.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.source: Bronstein JM et al, Arch Neurol 2011;68:165 (PMID 20937936); Charles PD et al, Neurology 2002;59:932-934 (PMID 12297584); Kleiner-Fisman G et al, Mov Disord 2006;21 Suppl 14:S290-S304 (PMID 16892449); Weaver FM et al, JAMA 2009 (PMID 19126811)

pd_deep_brain_stimulation.name: Adaptive (Closed-Loop) DBS - Newest Real Advance, Still Early Evidence
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.type: Implanted neurostimulation that adjusts stimulation automatically to sensed brain activity
specific_drugs: Not a drug - Medtronic BrainSense Adaptive DBS on Percept implantable neurostimulators
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.effectiveness: FDA approved Medtronic's BrainSense Adaptive DBS system for Parkinson's disease on 24 February 2025, with the approval reported as based on the ADAPT-PD trial; I could not retrieve the peer-reviewed ADAPT-PD numbers, so none are stated here. The one peer-reviewed study retrieved is a blinded randomised crossover feasibility pilot of only four patients in which adaptive DBS improved motor symptoms and quality of life relative to clinically optimised continuous DBS (Oehrn et al, Nat Med 2024).
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.reason_why: The device senses the patient's own neural signals (for example STN oscillations that mark high versus low dopaminergic states) and raises or lowers stimulation automatically, instead of delivering a constant amount.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.important_caveat: Evidence base is small and early: four-patient pilot plus a regulatory approval whose trial data were not retrieved here. Same non-disease-modifying limits as conventional DBS.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.real_working_solution: Ask the DBS centre whether the implanted or planned device supports adaptive mode; use conventional optimised DBS where it does not.
pd_deep_brain_stimulation.source: Medtronic FDA approval announcement, 24 Feb 2025 (news.medtronic.com); Oehrn CR et al, Nat Med 2024;30:3345-3356 (PMID 39160351)

pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.name: Acute Akinetic Crisis / Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia Syndrome - Emergency Restoration of Dopaminergic Therapy plus Supportive Care
pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.type: Neurological emergency (multi-pillar management: trigger treatment, supportive care, dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic drugs)
specific_drugs: Carbidopa-levodopa via nasogastric or PEG tube
Amantadine sulphate intravenous (described in the German guideline literature)
Diazepam (muscle-tone reduction); dantrolene and bromocriptine (used in case reports)
pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.effectiveness: Definition (German Society of Neurology guideline group): an acute, potentially life-threatening, levodopa-resistant severe worsening of rigidity and akinesia with high fever, disturbed consciousness, dysphagia and autonomic symptoms, often after interruption of dopaminergic medication or an infection; about 0.3% of PD patients per year. Outcome: mortality of 4% to 23% in published cohorts; in a Japanese cohort 68.7% achieved complete remission but 31.3% had a permanent residual deterioration, mortality 4%; complications include aspiration pneumonia 19.2%, disseminated intravascular coagulation 8.1% and acute renal failure 5.1%; recovery took 4 to 26 days. Management (four pillars, consensus/case-report based): (1) treat the trigger - antibiotics for infection, correct electrolytes and glucose, stop neuroleptics and antiemetics; (2) supportive - monitor vital signs, cooling and antipyretics, IV fluids, thrombosis prophylaxis; (3) prevent and treat rhabdomyolysis, renal failure and DIC, with intensive care if needed; (4) dopaminergic therapy - restart and adjust levodopa early, giving it by nasogastric or PEG tube if dysphagia; apomorphine s.c. (0.7-8 mg/h, with domperidone) or rotigotine patch as alternatives; non-dopaminergic - IV amantadine sulphate or diazepam. In the DBS-failure case series retrieved, most patients recovered after the battery or pulse generator was replaced or stimulation reactivated, whereas deaths were reported when re-implantation was late or not done.
pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.reason_why: Abrupt loss of dopaminergic stimulation (missed levodopa, gut absorption failure, DBS battery depletion or infection, dopamine-blocking drugs) produces a hypodopaminergic hypermetabolic state resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with rigidity generating heat and rhabdomyolysis; the review also proposes cytokine-driven transient levodopa resistance.
pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.important_caveat: Evidence is case reports, case series and expert guideline consensus - no randomised trials were found. Apomorphine response may be delayed: in 16 patients no motor improvement appeared for 2 to 10 days at 150-200 mg/day and 4 died. Tube feeding reduces levodopa absorption (see solution). Antipyretics, lithium and abrupt amantadine withdrawal are also reported triggers.
pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.real_working_solution: NEVER stop dopaminergic drugs abruptly (including in the perioperative period and in hospitalised, nil-by-mouth patients); if oral intake fails, use nasogastric levodopa, rotigotine patch or apomorphine; give tube feeds at night with dopaminergic drugs by day, stop feeds 1 hour before and after levodopa, or use tube feed with protein 0.8 g/kg/day; check the DBS system (battery, infection) in any DBS patient with this picture; treat as an ICU-level emergency.
pd_acute_akinetic_crisis_phs.source: Pötter-Nerger M et al, J Neural Transm 2024;131:1199-1207 (PMID 39153024); Pötter-Nerger M, Löhle M, Höglinger G, J Neurol 2024;271:6485-6493 (PMID 39192030); Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome case series and literature review, Cureus 2022;14:e29646 (PMID 36320988)

pd_non_motor_constipation.name: Constipation in PD - Macrogol (Polyethylene Glycol), Lubiprostone and Probiotic-Prebiotic Fibre
pd_non_motor_constipation.type: Osmotic laxative; chloride-channel activator; dietary/probiotic intervention
specific_drugs: Macrogol (polyethylene glycol) electrolyte solution (Movicol-type osmotic laxatives)
Fermented milk with multiple probiotic strains and prebiotic fibre
pd_non_motor_constipation.effectiveness: Macrogol: double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 57 PD patients for 8 weeks - responder rates were significantly higher at 4 weeks (p<0.0003) and 8 weeks (p<0.0012), bowel-movement frequency (p<0.002) and stool consistency (p<0.006) improved, only 2 patients (12.5%) on placebo needed rescue rectal laxatives vs none on macrogol, and UPDRS-III and PDQ-39 did not change (macrogol did not affect the course of PD). Lubiprostone (54 patients, up to 48 mcg/day, 4 weeks): marked or very marked global improvement in 64.0% (16/25) vs 18.5% (5/27) on placebo (p=0.001). Probiotic-prebiotic fermented milk (120 patients with Rome III constipation, 4 weeks): complete bowel movements per week rose 1.2 vs 0.1 (difference 1.1, 95% CI 0.4-1.8, p=0.002); 3 or more weekly complete bowel movements in 58.8% vs 37.5% (p=0.030) and an increase of one or more in 53.8% vs 25.0% (p=0.004) - Class I evidence per the authors.
pd_non_motor_constipation.reason_why: PD slows colonic transit through autonomic and enteric-nervous-system involvement; osmotic laxatives retain water in the stool, lubiprostone activates chloride channels to increase intestinal fluid, and prebiotic fibre plus probiotics increase stool bulk and change gut flora.
pd_non_motor_constipation.important_caveat: Studies are short (4 to 8 weeks) and small; lubiprostone was tested for 4 weeks only. Fluids and fibre alone were not tested in isolation in these trials.
pd_non_motor_constipation.real_working_solution: Use dietary fibre/probiotic-prebiotic fermented milk and macrogol (tested, well tolerated, no worsening of motor scores); lubiprostone is an additional randomised-tested option.
pd_non_motor_constipation.source: Zangaglia R et al, Mov Disord 2007;22:1239-1244 (PMID 17566120); Ondo WG et al, Neurology 2012;78:1650-1654 (PMID 22573627); Barichella M et al, Neurology 2016;87:1274-1280 (PMID 27543643); MDS non-motor EBM review, Seppi K et al, Mov Disord 2019;34:180-198 (PMID 30653247)

pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.name: Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension in PD - Droxidopa and Midodrine (With Non-Drug Measures)
pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.type: Norepinephrine pro-drug; peripheral alpha-1 agonist; non-pharmacological measures
specific_drugs: Non-drug: support stockings, fluid expansion, head-of-bed elevation (label-cited measures)
pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.effectiveness: Droxidopa, PD-specific study nOH306B (171 patients): at week 1 improvement on the dizziness/lightheadedness item was 2.3 vs 1.3 with placebo (p=0.018) and standing systolic BP rose 6.4 vs 0.7 mmHg (nominal p=0.032), but differences at weeks 2, 4 and 8 were not statistically significant and 12.4% vs 6.1% withdrew for adverse events; the earlier nOH306A interim cohort (51 patients) failed its futility analysis (OHQ composite change -2.2 vs -2.1, p=0.98). Mixed-cause nOH phase 3 (162 responders including PD, MSA, pure autonomic failure): OHQ composite improved 0.90 units over placebo (p=0.003) and standing systolic BP rose 11.2 vs 3.9 mmHg, at 7 days. Midodrine 10 mg three times daily (171 neurogenic OH patients, not PD-specific, 6-week study): standing systolic BP improved at all time points (p<0.001), symptoms by week 2 (p=0.001) and global relief ratings (p=0.03 patient, p<0.001 investigator), with pilomotor reactions, urinary retention and supine hypertension as main adverse effects. FDA labels: midodrine carries a boxed warning for marked supine hypertension (systolic BP above 200 mmHg), is reserved for patients 'considerably impaired despite standard clinical care' including support stockings, fluid expansion and lifestyle changes, and notes that clinical benefit in daily activities has not been verified; droxidopa carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension (elevate the head of the bed, monitor supine BP) and its label states effectiveness beyond 2 weeks has not been established.
pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.reason_why: In PD, sympathetic noradrenergic denervation stops norepinephrine release on standing (droxidopa is converted to norepinephrine by dopa-decarboxylase); midodrine constricts arterioles and veins directly to raise standing BP.
pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.important_caveat: Both drugs raise supine BP, which is a real danger in bed-bound elderly PD patients; evidence for droxidopa in PD specifically is weaker than in mixed-cause trials (one PD cohort failed its primary end point at week 8 and the later cohort's benefit was only significant at week 1). Amantadine ER caused orthostatic hypotension in 10.8% vs 0% in EASE LID 3, so a medication review is part of the work-up.
pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.real_working_solution: Non-drug first (compression stockings, adequate fluids, head-of-bed elevation, avoidance of triggering drugs), then midodrine or droxidopa with supine BP monitoring for symptomatic patients; review medications that can lower BP (for example amantadine ER, per EASE LID 3).
pd_non_motor_orthostatic_hypotension.source: Kaufmann H et al, Neurology 2014;83:328-335 (PMID 24944260); Hauser RA et al (nOH306B), Mov Disord 2015;30:646-654 (PMID 25487613); nOH306A, Parkinsonism Relat Disord 2014;20:57-65 (PMID 24326693); Midodrine Study Group, JAMA 1997;277:1046-1051 (PMID 9091692); FDA Northera and midodrine labels (DailyMed)

pd_non_motor_rbd.name: REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder in PD - Clonazepam, Melatonin and Transdermal Rivastigmine (Honest Evidence)
pd_non_motor_rbd.type: Benzodiazepine; pineal hormone; cholinesterase inhibitor; safe-sleeping-environment measures
pd_non_motor_rbd.effectiveness: AASM 2023 clinical practice guideline: 'good practice statement' that a safe sleeping environment (removing objects that could injure, padding furniture, floor mat, sleeping separately if severe) is essential; conditional suggestions for clonazepam and immediate-release melatonin in secondary RBD due to a medical condition, and for transdermal rivastigmine in RBD due to Parkinson disease; conditional suggestion AGAINST deep brain stimulation for RBD; drug discontinuation for drug-induced RBD. Real PD trial: prolonged-release melatonin 4 mg for 8 weeks in 30 PD patients did NOT reduce RBD (3.4 events/week vs 3.6 on placebo, difference 0.2, 95% CI -3.2 to 3.6, p=0.92). The MDS non-motor EBM review found no randomised trial meeting its criteria for RBD in PD.
pd_non_motor_rbd.reason_why: In RBD the muscle atonia that normally accompanies REM sleep is lost, so dream enactment occurs; clonazepam and melatonin are thought to reduce this, and cholinergic deficiency is a proposed contributor in PD, which is the rationale for rivastigmine.
pd_non_motor_rbd.important_caveat: Guideline strength is conditional (low-certainty evidence); the only PD-specific randomised melatonin trial was negative and small (15 per group); the AASM abstract gives no PD-specific clonazepam trial numbers and its remarks on clonazepam adverse effects were not retrievable, so check them in the full guideline before prescribing.
pd_non_motor_rbd.real_working_solution: Make the bedroom safe first (this is the one strongly-worded good-practice item); then try immediate-release melatonin or clonazepam per AASM; use transdermal rivastigmine if PD dementia or cognitive impairment coexists.
pd_non_motor_rbd.source: Howell M et al (AASM guideline), J Clin Sleep Med 2023;19:759-768 (PMID 36515157); Gilat M et al, Mov Disord 2020;35:344-349 (PMID 31674060); Seppi K et al (MDS non-motor EBM review), Mov Disord 2019;34:180-198 (PMID 30653247)

pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.name: Parkinson's Disease Psychosis - Pimavanserin or Low-Dose Clozapine; Avoid Dopamine-Blocking Antipsychotics
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.type: Selective serotonin 5-HT2A inverse agonist; atypical antipsychotic with low D2 affinity
specific_drugs: Clozapine (low dose 6.25-50 mg/day; Clozaril and generics)
AVOID: haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, and other dopamine-blocking antipsychotics
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.effectiveness: Pimavanserin phase 3 (199 patients, 6 weeks, 40 mg/day): SAPS-PD fell 5.79 points vs 2.73 with placebo (difference -3.06, 95% CI -4.91 to -1.20, p=0.001; Cohen's d 0.50) with no worsening of motor function; 10 discontinued for adverse events vs 2 on placebo. FDA label: indicated for hallucinations and delusions associated with PD psychosis, 34 mg once daily, with the class boxed warning of increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (the drug is approved for dementia-related psychosis only when it is PD-related). Observational data in a 2024 review (two Medicare studies of about 21,700 patients each) found pimavanserin mortality comparable to or lower than other atypical antipsychotics. Clozapine (randomised double-blind, 60 patients, mean 24.7 mg/day, 4 weeks): Clinical Global Impression improved 1.6 vs 0.5 points and all three psychosis measures improved significantly 'without worsening parkinsonism'; weekly blood counts were required. Olanzapine failed: in two randomised studies it produced no significant psychosis benefit over placebo and was significantly WORSE than placebo on UPDRS total, motor and daily-living scores.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.reason_why: PD psychosis is driven by dopaminergic drugs plus serotonergic/cholinergic changes; pimavanserin acts on 5-HT2A receptors and has no dopamine-blocking activity, and clozapine has very low D2 occupancy at these doses, so parkinsonism is not worsened.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.important_caveat: Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics worsen parkinsonism: the trial above showed olanzapine worsened UPDRS scores; central dopaminergic antagonists caused 49% of drug-induced parkinsonism reports in a pharmacovigilance series and 28 of its reports were worsening of pre-existing idiopathic PD; risperidone and amisulpride are named triggers of akinetic crisis. Clozapine requires blood-count monitoring (agranulocytosis). Any antipsychotic in dementia carries mortality risk.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.real_working_solution: Use pimavanserin or low-dose clozapine (with blood counts); never use haloperidol or other dopamine-blocking antipsychotics in PD.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.source: Cummings J et al, Lancet 2014;383:533-540 (PMID 24183563); Parkinson Study Group, N Engl J Med 1999;340:757-763 (PMID 10072410); Breier A et al, Biol Psychiatry 2002;52:438-445 (PMID 12242060); Bondon-Guitton E et al, Mov Disord 2011;26:2226-2231 (PMID 21674626); Pötter-Nerger M et al, J Neural Transm 2024 (PMID 39153024); FDA Nuplazid label (DailyMed)

pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.name: Parkinson's Disease Dementia - Rivastigmine (Evidence-Based Cholinesterase Inhibitor)
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.effectiveness: EXPRESS trial (541 patients with mild-to-moderate dementia at least 2 years after PD diagnosis, 24 weeks, 3-12 mg/day): ADAS-cog improved 2.1 points from 23.8 on rivastigmine vs 0.7-point worsening on placebo (p<0.001); clinically meaningful ADCS-CGIC improvement 19.8% vs 14.5% and worsening 13.0% vs 23.1% (p=0.007); all secondary outcomes were better; adverse events were nausea 29.0% vs 11.2%, vomiting 16.6% vs 1.7%, tremor 10.2% vs 3.9%. The MDS EBM review lists rivastigmine as possibly useful as adjunct for motor symptoms including gait.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.reason_why: PD dementia has a prominent cholinergic deficit; inhibiting cholinesterases raises acetylcholine in cortex.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.important_caveat: Benefit is 'moderate and similar to those reported in trials of rivastigmine for Alzheimer's disease'; tremor increase and gastrointestinal effects are real.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.real_working_solution: Use rivastigmine for PD dementia, titrating slowly; treat psychosis separately as above.
pd_non_motor_psychosis_dementia.source: Emre M et al (EXPRESS), N Engl J Med 2004;351:2509-2518 (PMID 15590953); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866)

pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.name: Exercise and Physiotherapy - Real Functional Benefit; Disease-Slowing Evidence Only Preliminary
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.type: Structured physical exercise (aerobic/treadmill, tai chi, physiotherapy)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - physiotherapy-guided exercise programmes; high-intensity treadmill training; tai chi
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.effectiveness: Cochrane review of physiotherapy vs no intervention (39 trials, 1,827 participants): short-term (under 3 months) improvements in gait speed (0.04 m/s), 2- or 6-minute walk (13.37 m), freezing of gait questionnaire (-1.41), Timed Up & Go (-0.63 s), Functional Reach (2.16 cm), Berg Balance (3.71 points) and clinician-rated UPDRS - differences small, at or near minimal clinically important change for some, and trial quality only mixed. SPARX phase 2 (128 de novo PD patients not on medication, 6 months): UPDRS motor change with high-intensity treadmill exercise (80-85% max heart rate, 4 days/week) was 0.3 points vs 3.2 with usual care (p=0.03) - only the high-intensity arm passed the non-futility threshold; adherence was 2.8 days/week. Tai chi (195 patients, 24 weeks): better maximum excursion than resistance training (+5.55 percentage points, 95% CI 1.12-9.97) and stretching (+11.98), fewer falls than stretching, no serious adverse events. ParkinsonNet networks in a cluster-randomised trial (699 patients) did not change health outcomes (primary score 47.7 vs 48.3) but cost less (euro727 saved over 24 weeks). The MDS EBM review rates physiotherapy clinically useful adjunct and exercise-based movement strategy training and formalised patterned exercises possibly useful.
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.reason_why: Exercise trains the motor system to compensate for dopamine loss (cueing, amplitude and balance training) and may have neuroplastic effects; the SPARX signal on disease severity is preliminary.
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.important_caveat: Honest limit: exercise improves function and possibly slows functional decline, but a proven disease-modifying effect is not established - SPARX was a phase 2 feasibility-plus-futility trial and I did not locate published results of the phase 3 confirmatory trial SPARX3 (NCT04284436, primary end point MDS-UPDRS III at 12 months).
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.real_working_solution: Prescribe regular exercise for every patient (aerobic or tai chi, physiotherapy for gait/balance/falls) from diagnosis; it was feasible and safely prescribed in the trials, helps function now, and has a preliminary progression signal in a randomised phase 2 trial.
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.source: Tomlinson CL et al (Cochrane), CD002817 2013 (PMID 24018704); Schenkman M et al (SPARX), JAMA Neurol 2018;75:219-226 (PMID 29228079); Li F et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:511-519 (PMID 22316445); Munneke M et al (ParkinsonNet), Lancet Neurol 2010;9:46-54 (PMID 19959398); MDS EBM review (PMID 29570866)

pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.name: Speech Therapy (LSVT LOUD) and Occupational Therapy - Daily-Function Gains
specific_drugs: Not a drug - Lee Silverman Voice Treatment (LSVT LOUD) speech therapy; home-based occupational therapy
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.effectiveness: LSVT (33 patients randomised to LSVT vs respiratory therapy): significantly greater gains in voice loudness (SPL) and pitch variability immediately after treatment, maintained at 24 months. Occupational therapy (191 patients, multicentre assessor-masked trial, 10 weeks home-based): self-perceived performance in daily activities (COPM) at 3 months was 1.2 points higher than usual care (95% CI 0.8-1.6).
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.reason_why: Speech treatment retrains high-effort loud phonation that counters hypophonia; occupational therapy teaches compensatory strategies and environmental change for daily tasks.
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.important_caveat: LSVT trial was small (33 patients); OT effect is on patient-perceived performance, not on motor scores.
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.real_working_solution: Refer for LSVT-type voice therapy at the first sign of soft speech and for occupational therapy when daily tasks become difficult.
pd_exercise_and_allied_therapy.source: Ramig LO et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2001;71:493-498 (PMID 11561033); Sturkenboom IH et al, Lancet Neurol 2014;13:557-566 (PMID 24726066)

pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.name: Drug-Induced Parkinsonism - Stop or Substitute the Offending Drug (Genuinely Reversible Mimic)
specific_drugs: Central dopamine-blocking drugs (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, risperidone, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
Other reported causes: antidepressants, calcium-channel blockers, H1 antihistamines, lithium, valproic acid, amiodarone, anticholinesterases, trimetazidine
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.effectiveness: French pharmacovigilance review (155 cases of drug-induced or -worsened parkinsonism among 20,855 adverse reactions, 1993-2009): 69% appeared within 3 months of starting the suspect drug and 20% around 12 months (mainly calcium-channel blockers); suspect drugs were central dopaminergic antagonists 49%, antidepressants 8%, calcium-channel blockers 5%, peripheral dopaminergic antagonists 5%, H1 antihistamines 5%; the three cardinal symptoms were found in only 37.4%; evolution was favourable in 88.7% after partial or complete withdrawal; 28 cases were worsening of pre-existing idiopathic PD; about 50% involved drugs other than antipsychotics; 43.9% were classified serious.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.reason_why: These drugs block striatal D2 receptors (or otherwise reduce dopaminergic transmission), producing the same rigidity and bradykinesia as dopamine loss; removing the drug restores function.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.important_caveat: This is a description of pharmacovigilance reports (not a controlled trial); cases in which parkinsonism persists after withdrawal may reflect underlying PD unmasked by the drug, and drug-induced parkinsonism can coexist with PD.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.real_working_solution: Review every medication in any new parkinsonism, stop or substitute the culprit (never treat the drug-induced syndrome by adding more drugs), and re-assess after withdrawal; for necessary antipsychotic therapy in PD, use the agents in the psychosis entry.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.source: Bondon-Guitton E et al, Mov Disord 2011;26:2226-2231 (PMID 21674626)

pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.name: Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus - Shunt Surgery as a Genuinely Reversible Mimic of Parkinsonism (Not a PD Treatment)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - lumboperitoneal shunt (tested in SINPHONI-2)
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.effectiveness: SINPHONI-2 (open-label randomised trial in 93 patients aged 60-85 with idiopathic NPH, lumboperitoneal shunt within 1 month vs postponed 3 months): improvement of 1 or more points on the modified Rankin scale at 3 months in 65% (32/49) immediate vs 5% (2/44) postponed (difference 61%, 95% CI 42-68, p<0.0001); at 12 months after surgery 67% vs 58% (p=0.496); serious adverse events in 22% (19/87) over 12 months, commonest cerebral infarction (7%). Systematic review of shunt surgery in iNPH (64 studies, 3,063 patients): improvement in an average of 71% with an average 1% mortality; in the last 5 years' studies improvement 82%, mortality 0.2% and combined common complications 8.2%.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.reason_why: NPH is enlarged ventricles with normal CSF pressure causing gait disturbance, cognitive decline and urinary symptoms that can mimic parkinsonism; diverting CSF relieves the pressure on periventricular pathways.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.important_caveat: SINPHONI-2 was open-label (not masked) and used lumboperitoneal shunts; I did not retrieve a placebo-controlled shunt trial. Shunt does NOT treat idiopathic Parkinson's disease and only applies when the diagnosis is truly NPH.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.real_working_solution: In any patient whose parkinsonism-like picture includes gait disturbance, cognitive decline, urinary symptoms and ventriculomegaly on imaging (see the symptoms section for the NPH description), refer for NPH assessment - shunting is a real, reversible fix for that mimic.
pd_secondary_parkinsonism_and_mimics.source: Kazui H et al (SINPHONI-2), Lancet Neurol 2015;14:585-594 (PMID 25934242); Toma AK et al, Acta Neurochir 2013;155:1977-1980 (PMID 23975646)

pd_disease_modification_evidence.name: Disease-Modification Trial Record - Levodopa, MAO-B Inhibitors, GLP-1 Agonists and Exercise (Honest: Nothing Proven)
pd_disease_modification_evidence.type: Summary of every attempt to slow progression
pd_disease_modification_evidence.effectiveness: MDS Evidence-Based Medicine review (through 2016): 'There are no clinically useful interventions to prevent/delay disease progression.' LEAP (445 patients, 80 weeks): no disease-modifying effect of levodopa (difference 1.0 UPDRS point, p=0.44). ADAGIO: rasagiline 1 mg 'consistent with a possible disease-modifying effect' but 2 mg not; interpret with caution. Exenatide-PD3 (194 patients, 96 weeks, off-medication MDS-UPDRS III): +5.7 vs +4.5 points, adjusted difference 0.92 (95% CI -1.56 to 3.39), p=0.47 - no evidence of benefit; the Lancet subsequently published an Expression of Concern (2026) after a regulatory inspection at one site. Lixisenatide (LIXIPARK, 156 patients, 12 months): MDS-UPDRS III -0.04 vs +3.04 (difference 3.08, 95% CI 0.86-5.30, p=0.007), off-medication score at 14 months 17.7 vs 20.6, but nausea 46% and vomiting 13% and the authors call for longer, larger trials. Exercise: SPARX phase 2 signal (see exercise entry).
pd_disease_modification_evidence.reason_why: The goal of a disease-modifying drug is to slow the loss of dopaminergic neurons; none has yet shown that effect in a definitive trial.
pd_disease_modification_evidence.important_caveat: Because symptomatic drugs mask the disease during delayed-start designs, apparent early gains can be symptomatic; only delayed-start or long washout designs can separate the two.
pd_disease_modification_evidence.real_working_solution: Working solution: because no proven disease-modifying therapy exists, treat symptoms optimally, encourage exercise, and consider enrolment in a confirmatory disease-modification trial (GLP-1 agonist studies are the current focus).
