pd_disease_modification_evidence.source: Fox SH et al, Mov Disord 2018;33:1248-1266 (PMID 29570866); Verschuur CVM et al, N Engl J Med 2019 (PMID 30673543); Olanow CW et al, N Engl J Med 2009 (PMID 19776408); Vijiaratnam N et al, Lancet 2025;405:627-636 (PMID 39919773); Lancet Expression of Concern 2026;407:2588 (PMID 42330995); Meissner WG et al, N Engl J Med 2024;390:1176-1185 (PMID 38598572)

pd_medical_devices_equipment.name: DBS Implantable System - Pulse Generator, Leads, Programmer and Adaptive-Sensing Hardware
specific_drugs: Not a drug - implanted pulse generator (IPG) with STN/GPi leads (for example Medtronic Percept with BrainSense sensing and adaptive mode)
pd_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Device behind the DBS trials above: bilateral leads connected by extension cables to a chest-wall IPG that is programmed for 3 to 6 months (consensus statement) to reach optimal results; an FDA-approved adaptive DBS version (24 February 2025) senses brain activity in daily life. In the DBS-failure literature, IPG battery depletion or infection has caused parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome that recovered after battery replacement or reactivation in the case reports retrieved.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: The IPG delivers programmed high-frequency pulses to the target nucleus; loss of stimulation abruptly removes the therapeutic effect (DBS withdrawal syndrome).
pd_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Infection is the most commonly reported complication; the system needs lifelong follow-up and battery replacement.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Schedule IPG battery checks and replace before depletion; treat any DBS patient with sudden severe rigidity/fever as a possible device failure.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.source: Bronstein JM et al, Arch Neurol 2011 (PMID 20937936); Medtronic FDA approval, 24 Feb 2025; Cureus 2022 case series (PMID 36320988)

pd_medical_devices_equipment.name: Infusion Pump Systems - LCIG PEG-J Pump, Subcutaneous Foslevodopa Pump and Apomorphine Pump
pd_medical_devices_equipment.type: External programmable infusion pumps with dedicated delivery tubing/cannulae
specific_drugs: Not a drug - portable pump delivering levodopa-carbidopa gel via PEG-J (Duopa/Duodopa), foslevodopa-foscarbidopa via a single subcutaneous site (Vyalev), or apomorphine via subcutaneous cannula (Onapgo)
pd_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Duopa is delivered through a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy with jejunal extension (PEG-J) by a small portable pump over 16 continuous hours; Vyalev is the first 24-hour subcutaneous levodopa-based infusion approved (16-17 October 2024); apomorphine infusion in TOLEDO ran 16 waking hours. All three are backed by the randomised trials above.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Pumps make continuous, individually titrated dosing possible instead of intermittent tablets.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Tube-related complications (LCIG) and infusion-site reactions (SC) are the main real burdens; the label for levodopa infusions advises evaluating vitamin B6 levels.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Choose the delivery system together with a movement-disorder team by patient preference and ability to manage the equipment (carer support helps).
pd_medical_devices_equipment.source: Olanow CW et al, Lancet Neurol 2014 (PMID 24361112); Soileau MJ et al, Lancet Neurol 2022 (PMID 36402160); Katzenschlager R et al, Lancet Neurol 2018 (PMID 30055903); FDA Duopa/Vyalev/Onapgo labels (DailyMed)

pd_medical_devices_equipment.name: Wearable Motion Monitoring (Parkinson's KinetiGraph) and Patient Motor Diaries
pd_medical_devices_equipment.type: Wrist-worn movement sensor and patient-completed diary
specific_drugs: Not a drug - Personal KinetiGraph (PKG) wrist-worn system; Hauser-style ON/OFF/dyskinesia home diary
pd_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: The PKG is an FDA-cleared wearable (K140086, 22 August 2014; second-generation K161717, 20 September 2016; continuous home use cleared 11 March 2022) that quantifies bradykinesia, tremor, motor fluctuations and dyskinesia with correlation to medication timing. Patient diaries record ON, OFF and dyskinesia time and are the primary outcome in all of the fluctuation trials cited above. I retrieved qualitative clinic evaluations of PKG use but no randomised trial showing improved outcomes, so no efficacy percentage is stated.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Continuous accelerometry captures fluctuations that are missed in a 15-minute clinic visit and gives an objective record for adjusting doses or judging DBS/infusion candidacy.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Clearance shows analytic validity, not proven outcome benefit; PKG is a support tool, not a treatment.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Use PKG or diaries before escalating to device-aided therapy and after each programming change.
pd_medical_devices_equipment.source: PKG Health clearance summary (K140086, K161717, 2022 clearance); trial diaries per Olanow CW et al, Lancet Neurol 2014 (PMID 24361112) and Soileau MJ et al (PMID 36402160)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT end points (UPDRS points, hours of OFF/ON time, percent responders, PDQ-39 points, bowel movements, mmHg, psychosis scale points) in different populations (early PD, advanced fluctuating PD, PD with dementia or psychosis, and two non-PD mimics), so the ordering is directional judgement (size of benefit on each option's own metric combined with evidence quality), NOT a common-scale percentage ranking; effectiveness_pct appears only where a genuine percent exists and is otherwise 'N/A (see metric)'. IMPORTANT: NONE of these treatments is disease-modifying or curative - they are all SYMPTOMATIC. Parkinson's disease is not curable and the neurodegeneration continues under every option listed, which distinguishes it honestly from stroke, epilepsy and other entries in this knowledge base that do carry a real cure pathway (see CURABILITY_NOTE). The two reversible mimics (rank 6 shunt for normal-pressure hydrocephalus, rank 15 drug withdrawal for drug-induced parkinsonism) are ranked by their own trial or pharmacovigilance metric but apply only when that mimic is the correct diagnosis, not to idiopathic PD. The last two rows (0.0) record documented negative results, not zero-quality drugs: melatonin failed its only PD-specific RBD trial, and no proven disease-modifying agent exists. Percentages of 0.0 for those rows mean 'no proven benefit'.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Carbidopa-levodopa (Sinemet; levodopa-benserazide; extended-release Rytary)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Total UPDRS change at 42 weeks -1.4 units (600 mg/day) vs +7.8 units on placebo (ELLDOPA, dose-dependent, p<0.001); better patient-rated mobility than dopamine agonists/MAO-B inhibitors in PD MED (PDQ-39 mobility 1.8 points, p=0.005; small margin). Good-or-excellent motor response to levodopa in pathologically confirmed idiopathic PD (graded-response subset): 37.5% excellent + 45.7% good = 83.2% (280 cases across 12 studies, 1971-2018); levodopa response is a core diagnostic feature of PD, not a universal-scale efficacy number.
ranked_high_to_low.source: ELLDOPA, NEJM 2004 (PMID 15590952); PD MED, Lancet 2014 (PMID 24928805); Pitz et al, Mov Disord Clin Pract 2020 systematic review (PMID 32071945)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Bilateral STN or GPi deep brain stimulation (advanced PD, selected candidates)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Patients with clinically meaningful motor improvement (5 points or more) at 6 months: 71% DBS vs 32% best medical therapy; +4.5 h/day ON time without troubling dyskinesia vs medical therapy (p<0.001); serious adverse events 49 vs 15 patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Weaver et al (CSP 468), JAMA 2009 (PMID 19126811)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (Duodopa/Duopa)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: OFF time -1.91 h/day vs oral immediate-release levodopa (95% CI -3.05 to -0.76); -4.04 h/day from baseline; double-blind, 12 weeks (Olanow 2014 RCT, n=71). Responder rate (>=1 h/day improvement in OFF time from baseline) in a separate 54-week open-label PEG-J study: 84.0% (272/324 patients).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Olanow et al, Lancet Neurol 2014 (PMID 24361112); responder rate from Fernandez et al phase 3 open-label study (NCT00335153), as tabulated in systematic evaluation of LCIG responder characteristics (PMC5784118)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa (Vyalev)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: ON time without troublesome dyskinesia +1.75 h/day and OFF time -1.79 h/day vs oral levodopa-carbidopa (12-week double-blind); 22% discontinued for adverse events vs 1%. Responder rate (>=1 h/day OFF-time reduction) in a pooled responder analysis of two phase 3 trials: 82.6% foslevodopa-foscarbidopa vs 50.0% oral levodopa-carbidopa (p<0.001).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Soileau et al, Lancet Neurol 2022 (PMID 36402160); responder analysis presented at MDS International Congress 2022 ("Impact of foslevodopa/foscarbidopa on key clinical and patient-reported outcomes", MDS Abstracts)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (Onapgo)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: OFF time -1.89 h/day vs placebo (95% CI -3.16 to -0.62), 12-week double-blind (TOLEDO trial). Patient Global Impression of Change rated as improved: 79.1% apomorphine vs 23.5% placebo at week 12 (secondary endpoint of the same trial, per FDA ONAPGO prescribing information Clinical Studies section and Sunovion/Supernus FDA-approval summaries).
ranked_high_to_low.source: TOLEDO, Lancet Neurol 2018 (PMID 30055903); PGIC data per ONAPGO (apomorphine) FDA prescribing information, DailyMed, Clinical Studies (Study 1/NCT02006121)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lumboperitoneal/ventriculoperitoneal shunt for normal-pressure hydrocephalus (reversible MIMIC, not a Parkinson's treatment)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Improvement of 1 or more mRS points at 3 months: 65% immediate shunt vs 5% postponed (open-label, p<0.0001); 71% average improvement in a 64-study review
ranked_high_to_low.source: SINPHONI-2, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 25934242); Toma et al, Acta Neurochir 2013 (PMID 23975646)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Amantadine extended-release (Gocovri) / amantadine for levodopa-induced dyskinesia
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale -14.4 points vs placebo (95% CI -20.4 to -8.3, p<0.0001); OFF time -1.1 h vs placebo; 19% vs 8% discontinued for adverse events (EASE LID 3 trial alone). Responder rate (>=50% reduction in ON time with dyskinesia) in the pooled EASE LID + EASE LID 3 analysis: 53% amantadine ER vs 26% placebo (n=100 vs 96).
ranked_high_to_low.source: EASE LID 3, Mov Disord 2017 (PMID 28833562); pooled responder analysis, Frontiers in Neurology 2021 (10.3389/fneur.2021.645706)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rotigotine patch / pramipexole as adjunct in wearing-off
ranked_high_to_low.metric: OFF time -1.58 h/day vs placebo for rotigotine (95% CI -2.27 to -0.90); pramipexole -2.8 h vs placebo -0.9 h; rotigotine non-inferior to pramipexole. Responder rate (>=30% reduction in daily off-time): rotigotine 59.7% (120/201) vs placebo 35% (35/100); pramipexole 67% (134/200).
ranked_high_to_low.source: CLEOPATRA-PD, Lancet Neurol 2007 (PMID 17509486)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rasagiline / selegiline (early monotherapy or adjunct)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Total UPDRS -4.20 units vs placebo with rasagiline 1 mg at 26 weeks (TEMPO); selegiline delayed need for levodopa (hazard ratio 0.50, DATATOP, confounded by symptomatic effect). Pre-specified TEMPO responder analysis (responder = <3-unit total UPDRS worsening at 26 weeks): rasagiline 1 mg 66% (p=0.004 vs placebo), rasagiline 2 mg 67% (p=0.001), placebo 49%.
ranked_high_to_low.source: TEMPO, Arch Neurol 2002 (PMID 12470183); DATATOP, NEJM 1993 (PMID 8417384)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Opicapone 50 mg once daily / entacapone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: OFF time -60.8 min vs placebo for opicapone 50 mg (95% CI -97.2 to -24.4, p=0.0015), non-inferior to entacapone. BIPARK-I responder analysis (>=1 h/day OFF-time reduction, overall population): opicapone 50 mg 70%, entacapone 58%, placebo 48%.

alzheimers_disease.name: Alzheimer's Disease
alzheimers_disease.icd11_hint: 8A20 Dementia due to Alzheimer disease (8A20.0 with early onset, 8A20.1 with late onset, 8A20.2 atypical, 8A20.3 mixed, 8A20.Z unspecified); ICD-10 G30 / F00

definition.finding: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the commonest cause of dementia, a clinical syndrome of acquired, progressive cognitive and functional decline. The neuropathological hallmarks are extracellular amyloid-beta (Abeta) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau, together with neuronal and synaptic loss and reactive gliosis/neuroinflammation. Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent form of dementia, accounting for approximately 60-70% of dementia cases worldwide.
definition.source: WHO/Alzheimer's Disease International dementia statistics summary (alzint.org/about/dementia-facts-figures/dementia-statistics); WHO Global Health Estimates 2019 / GBD 2019

amyloid_beta_plaques.finding: Amyloid-beta peptides (mainly Abeta40 and the more aggregation-prone Abeta42) are cleaved from amyloid precursor protein (APP, on chromosome 21) by beta- and gamma-secretase and accumulate as extracellular neuritic plaques. Autosomal-dominant mutations in APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 (the catalytic component of gamma-secretase) alter Abeta processing and cause early-onset familial AD with essentially complete penetrance, which is the strongest genetic evidence that Abeta accumulation is causally upstream in at least this form of the disease.
amyloid_beta_plaques.source: The landscape of autosomal-dominant Alzheimer's disease: global distribution and age of onset, Brain 2025;148:2429 (PMID 39903689); DIAN study data on APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 variant pathogenicity
amyloid_beta_plaques.confidence: high for the genetics of autosomal-dominant AD; the inference that this proves the mechanism in the far more common sporadic late-onset disease is a central and still-debated extrapolation (see amyloid_cascade_hypothesis_debate below)

tau_neurofibrillary_tangles.finding: Hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates intracellularly as neurofibrillary tangles, spreading in a stereotyped, hierarchical anatomical sequence described by Braak and Braak: transentorhinal cortex (stage I-II), hippocampus/limbic structures (stage III-IV), then association and finally primary neocortex (stage V-VI). Tangle burden and its topographical spread correlate more closely with regional neuronal loss and with the clinical/cognitive stage than plaque burden does.
tau_neurofibrillary_tangles.source: Braak H, Braak E, staging framework as applied to AD tau pathology; entorhinal/hippocampal tau and episodic memory decline literature, e.g. Maass A et al., J Neurosci 2018;38:530 (PMID 29192126) on entorhinal tau and memory decline in aging
tau_neurofibrillary_tangles.confidence: high for the anatomical staging description; correlation strength estimates vary by cohort

cholinergic_deficit.finding: There is marked loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert (the principal source of cortical acetylcholine), first reported by Whitehouse et al in 1981/1982. This cholinergic deficit correlates with cognitive decline and is the pharmacological basis for cholinesterase-inhibitor therapy, but the 'cholinergic hypothesis' as a complete explanation of AD has been challenged because cholinergic loss is neither the earliest nor the only major deficit.
cholinergic_deficit.source: Whitehouse PJ et al., 'Alzheimer disease: evidence for selective loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis', Ann Neurol 1981;10:122-126; review of the cholinergic hypothesis and its challenges, Hampel H et al., Brain 2018;141:1917 (cholinergic system in pathophysiology and treatment of AD)

synaptic_loss_best_correlate.finding: In a direct comparison of neuropathological measures against antemortem cognitive test scores, Terry and colleagues found that synapse loss (measured in the frontal and temporal neocortex) was a stronger correlate of cognitive impairment than either plaque count or neurofibrillary tangle count, establishing synaptic loss (rather than plaques or tangles per se) as the pathological change that tracks most closely with clinical severity.
synaptic_loss_best_correlate.source: Terry RD et al., 'Physical basis of cognitive alterations in Alzheimer's disease: synapse loss is the major correlate of cognitive impairment', Ann Neurol 1991;30:572-580

neuroinflammation_and_trem2.finding: Microglia surround and respond to amyloid plaques; genome-wide association studies identified rare variants in TREM2 (triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2) as a risk factor for late-onset AD with an effect size similar to a single APOE-e4 allele. TREM2 controls microglial phagocytosis, survival and the transition to a 'disease-associated microglia' (DAM) state, linking innate immune/neuroinflammatory signalling mechanistically to amyloid and tau pathology. Neuroinflammation is now regarded as a third, interacting pillar of AD pathophysiology alongside amyloid and tau, not merely a bystander reaction.
neuroinflammation_and_trem2.source: TREM2 and microglial immunity in Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms, genetics, and therapeutic opportunities, PMC12956735 (2025 review); TREM2-dependent effects on microglia in Alzheimer's disease, Front Aging Neurosci 2018 (disease-associated microglia/DAM concept)
neuroinflammation_and_trem2.confidence: high for the genetic association and microglial biology; the precise causal weight of neuroinflammation relative to amyloid/tau in driving symptoms is still an active research question

amyloid_cascade_hypothesis_debate.finding_history_of_failure: The amyloid cascade hypothesis (that Abeta accumulation is the initiating, upstream event that triggers tau pathology, synaptic/neuronal loss and dementia) drove two decades of anti-amyloid drug development that largely failed clinically despite reducing amyloid. Two phase 3 trials of bapineuzumab (an anti-amyloid antibody) in mild-to-moderate AD showed no benefit on clinical outcomes despite biomarker evidence of reduced Abeta accumulation and downstream phospho-tau change. Solanezumab failed three phase 3 programmes: EXPEDITION 1 and 2 (1012 and 1040 patients with mild-to-moderate AD) did not improve cognition or function; EXPEDITION 3 (2129 patients with mild AD) was stopped for futility; and the A4 trial in preclinical (amyloid-positive, cognitively normal) AD also failed its primary endpoint. These repeated failures fuelled real scientific debate about whether amyloid-beta itself is the right therapeutic target, or whether treatment in these trials came too late in the disease course.
amyloid_cascade_hypothesis_debate.source: Salloway S et al. (bapineuzumab), N Engl J Med 2014;370:322-333; Doody RS et al. (EXPEDITION 1/2 solanezumab), N Engl J Med 2014;370:311-321 (PMID 24450890); Honig LS et al. (EXPEDITION 3), N Engl J Med 2018;378:321-330; Sperling RA et al. (A4 study), reported via NeurologyLive coverage of the trial's primary-endpoint failure

definition_and_pathophysiology.finding_recent_positive_trials: More recently, anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies given at an early disease stage have shown statistically significant, if modest, slowing of clinical decline alongside near-complete amyloid clearance on PET: the phase 3 CLARITY-AD trial of lecanemab and the phase 3 TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial of donanemab both showed a roughly 25-35% relative slowing of decline on the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) compared with placebo over 18 months, with donanemab-treated participants at the very earliest (low tau) stage showing about 60% slowing and 47% having no measurable clinical progression at one year. These are the first large randomised trials to show a clinical benefit that tracks with amyloid removal, which is read by many in the field as support for a causal (if not sole) role for amyloid, while critics note the clinical effect sizes are small, are accompanied by real safety signals (ARIA-E in 12.6% with lecanemab and 24% with donanemab; ARIA-H in 17.3% and 31.4% respectively), and do not by themselves resolve whether amyloid removal alone is sufficient therapy.

research_integrity_concern_verified.finding: A well-documented, verified research-integrity concern exists in this field, separate from and not proof against the broader amyloid hypothesis: a highly influential 2006 Nature paper by Sylvain Lesne (University of Minnesota) that first described a specific amyloid-beta oligomer, 'Abeta*56', and linked it to memory impairment in rats, was found after a Science magazine investigation (2022) to contain images with signs of manipulation (duplicated/altered western blot bands); the paper had been cited by roughly 2,300 subsequent articles and coincided with a large rise in NIH funding for amyloid-oligomer research. The paper was formally retracted in 2024 following the investigation. This is a real, confirmed case of alleged data manipulation in one specific, highly-cited paper about one specific amyloid oligomer species - it is not evidence that amyloid plaques/tau pathology themselves are fabricated, and it long postdates and is separate from the original plaque/tangle pathology described by Alois Alzheimer and from the genetic evidence in autosomal-dominant AD.
research_integrity_concern_verified.source: Piller C, 'Blots on a field?', Science, 21 July 2022 (investigation into Lesne image manipulation allegations); Alzforum news coverage 'Sylvain Lesne, Who Found Abeta*56, Accused of Image Manipulation'; 2024 retraction of Lesne SD et al., Nature 2006;440:352-357
research_integrity_concern_verified.confidence: high that the investigation, allegations and 2024 retraction occurred as described; the broader implication for the amyloid hypothesis is a subject of genuine, ongoing scientific debate rather than a settled fact

definition_and_pathophysiology.honest_synthesis: The honest state of the debate: amyloid and tau pathology, synaptic loss, cholinergic deficit and neuroinflammation are all real, well-documented features of AD; genetic evidence from autosomal-dominant AD and Down syndrome (extra APP copy) supports a causal role for Abeta in at least those forms; the 2006 Lesne Abeta*56 paper describing one specific oligomer is confirmed to have been built on manipulated images and was retracted; two decades of most anti-amyloid trials failed clinically despite biomarker success; and the most recent lecanemab/donanemab trials show a real, modest, statistically significant clinical benefit tracking with amyloid removal. No single one of these facts alone settles whether amyloid is the primary upstream driver of sporadic late-onset AD in the way the strongest form of the amyloid cascade hypothesis proposed.

NIA_AA_2011_criteria.finding: The 2011 National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) workgroups revised the 1984 criteria into three companion papers covering three stages of increasing severity: (1) core clinical criteria for dementia due to AD (probable/possible AD dementia, with a research-only category incorporating biomarkers); (2) mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD; and (3) preclinical AD (biomarker-positive, cognitively unimpaired, for research use only). Core clinical criteria for all-cause dementia require cognitive/behavioural symptoms that interfere with usual function, represent a decline from a previous level, are not explained by delirium or major psychiatric disease, and involve impairment in at least two of: memory, reasoning/complex-task handling, visuospatial ability, language, or personality/behaviour.
NIA_AA_2011_criteria.source: McKhann GM et al., 'The diagnosis of dementia due to Alzheimer's disease: recommendations from the NIA-AA workgroups', Alzheimers Dement 2011;7:263-269 (PMID 21514250); Albert MS et al., 'The diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease: recommendations from the NIA-AA workgroups', Alzheimers Dement 2011;7:270-279 (PMID 21514249); Sperling RA et al., 'Toward defining the preclinical stages of Alzheimer's disease: recommendations from the NIA-AA workgroups', Alzheimers Dement 2011;7:280-292 (PMID 21514248)

AA_2024_biological_definition_vs_IWG_cli.finding: In 2024 two competing revised frameworks were published. The Alzheimer's Association (AA) Workgroup (chaired by Clifford Jack) proposed a purely biological definition: AD is defined by the presence of amyloid and tau (and other) biomarkers regardless of clinical symptoms, so that detecting AD neuropathologic change by biomarkers is itself equivalent to diagnosing the disease, even in a cognitively normal person (staged 'Core 1' plasma/CSF/PET biomarkers such as p-tau217 are proposed as sufficient for biological diagnosis). The International Working Group (IWG) published a competing 2024 update explicitly rejecting a purely biological label, arguing that amyloid-positive but cognitively normal individuals (and more generally biomarker-positive people without qualifying cognitive symptoms) should NOT be told they have 'Alzheimer's disease', out of concern for how a biological-only label would be understood by patients and society, and for premature use of blood tests to justify treatment. The clinical-biological construct instead requires biomarker-confirmed AD pathology PLUS a specific amnestic (or other AD-typical) clinical syndrome. This is a genuine, unresolved disagreement between two major expert bodies, not merely a terminology footnote.
AA_2024_biological_definition_vs_IWG_cli.source: Jack CR Jr et al. (Alzheimer's Association Workgroup), 'Revised criteria for diagnosis and staging of Alzheimer's disease', Alzheimers Dement 2024 (DOI 10.1002/alz.13859); International Working Group 2024 update (as summarised in 'New Alzheimer's disease diagnostic criteria 2024: Biological vs Clinical-biological criteria' and 'What is biological Alzheimer's disease?', PMC11165693)
AA_2024_biological_definition_vs_IWG_cli.confidence: high that this disagreement is real and public; both frameworks are described here without endorsing either as settled

DSM5_major_and_mild_neurocognitive_disor.finding: DSM-5 replaced the term 'dementia' with major neurocognitive disorder (and introduced mild neurocognitive disorder for a lesser degree of impairment not yet compromising independence). Major neurocognitive disorder due to AD requires insidious onset and gradual progression in at least two cognitive domains (memory/learning plus at least one other), steady decline without extended plateaus, no evidence of mixed aetiology, and (for the 'probable' label) either a causative genetic mutation or this specific clinical/progression pattern; mild neurocognitive disorder requires similar features but decline not severe enough to compromise independence in everyday activities.
DSM5_major_and_mild_neurocognitive_disor.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5/DSM-5-TR neurocognitive disorders criteria, as summarised in Major Neurocognitive Disorder (Dementia), StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf NBK557444

biomarkers_csf.finding: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers - lowered Abeta42 (or a lowered Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, which corrects for individual variation in total amyloid production) plus raised total tau and phosphorylated tau (p-tau181) - reflect amyloid deposition and neurodegeneration/tangle pathology respectively. Against amyloid-PET status, CSF Abeta42/40 achieved sensitivity/specificity of about 0.94/0.82, and p-tau181/Abeta42 about 0.96/0.69 in one comparative analysis; against neuropathology at autopsy, CSF Abeta42/total-tau achieved about 97% sensitivity and 83% specificity for identifying early AD in one series, and INNOTEST CSF Abeta42 alone predicted neuritic plaque presence at autopsy with AUC 0.87 (80% sensitivity, 82% specificity) in another. Exact numbers vary by assay platform and cohort, but the general pattern (better performance for ratios than for single analytes) is consistent.
biomarkers_csf.source: Multiple comparative CSF-biomarker-vs-amyloid-PET/autopsy studies summarised in 'Diagnostic Biomarkers of Amyloid and Tau Pathology in Alzheimer's Disease', J Prev Alzheimers Dis 2024; 'Detailed comparison of amyloid PET and CSF biomarkers for identifying early Alzheimer disease', Neurology (PMID range referenced in that review); Tapiola T et al., Arch Neurol 2009 (INNOTEST CSF Abeta42 autopsy correlation, PMID 19273758)
biomarkers_csf.confidence: moderate-high - figures are drawn from several distinct cohorts/platforms rather than one single definitive number, and this is stated explicitly rather than presenting one number as universal

biomarkers_pet.finding: Amyloid PET (using tracers such as florbetapir, flutemetamol or florbetaben) visually classifies a scan as amyloid-positive or -negative; visual reads achieve sensitivities of about 88-98% and specificities of about 88-100% for discriminating absent/sparse versus moderate/frequent neuritic plaque density at autopsy. Tau PET (e.g. flortaucipir) images neurofibrillary tangle burden and its topography broadly follows the Braak staging sequence, and tau-PET Braak-stage assignment correlates with the degree of episodic memory impairment.
biomarkers_pet.source: Amyloid PET visual-read accuracy figures as summarised in comparative CSF/PET biomarker reviews (J Prev Alzheimers Dis 2024); tau-PET Braak-stage clinical correlation, 'Clinical Correlates of the PET-based Braak Staging Framework in Alzheimer's Disease', 2024
biomarkers_pet.confidence: high for the general accuracy range; exact figures depend on tracer and reference standard

plasma_p_tau217_and_fda_cleared_blood_te.finding: Plasma phosphorylated tau at position 217 (p-tau217) is the most accurate blood-based biomarker developed so far, with areas under the ROC curve of about 0.93-0.96 for detecting AD pathology against PET/CSF reference standards. In May 2025 the FDA cleared the Fujirebio Lumipulse G pTau217/beta-amyloid1-42 plasma ratio test as the first blood test for aiding diagnosis of AD, intended for adults aged 55+ with signs/symptoms of cognitive impairment; in a large multicentre study (1767 participants) the plasma ratio showed high diagnostic accuracy and reduced the proportion of clinically ambiguous ('intermediate') results to under 10%. In one head-to-head validation in secondary care, plasma p-tau217-based testing gave 89-91% accuracy, 89-95% positive predictive value and 77-90% negative predictive value versus amyloid-PET/CSF status. The 2024 Alzheimer's Association biological-definition framework treats accurate plasma assays such as p-tau217 as 'Core 1' biomarkers sufficient, on their own, for a biological diagnosis - which is precisely the point of clinical disagreement with the IWG framework above.
plasma_p_tau217_and_fda_cleared_blood_te.source: FDA news release on Lumipulse G pTau217/beta-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio clearance (2025), as reported in 'FDA Approves First Alzheimer's Diagnostic Blood Test', MedCentral, and 'FDA approval of the Lumipulse G PTau217/beta-amyloid 1-42 plasma ratio test: a new era in accessible Alzheimer's diagnosis', PMC12889242; head-to-head Lumipulse/SIMOA comparison, medRxiv 2024.05.02.24306780 / PMC11788209
plasma_p_tau217_and_fda_cleared_blood_te.confidence: high for FDA clearance and the reported accuracy figures; note plasma p-tau217 aids diagnosis alongside clinical assessment and is not a stand-alone population screening test

MRI_medial_temporal_atrophy.finding: Structural MRI showing disproportionate medial temporal lobe (hippocampal/entorhinal) atrophy supports a diagnosis of AD and helps exclude other structural causes of cognitive decline (tumour, subdural haematoma, hydrocephalus, significant cerebrovascular disease); it is a supportive, non-specific biomarker of neurodegeneration in the NIA-AA 'N' (neurodegeneration) category rather than a marker specific to AD pathology, since medial temporal atrophy also occurs in normal ageing and in other dementias.
MRI_medial_temporal_atrophy.source: NIA-AA 2011/2018 A/T/N biomarker framework as described in Sperling RA et al. 2011 (PMID 21514248) and subsequent NIA-AA research framework publications

MMSE_MoCA_cutoffs_and_limitations.finding: The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) are widely used bedside screening tools, not diagnostic tests. In comparative studies the MoCA generally outperforms the MMSE for detecting mild cognitive impairment (MoCA identifies roughly 90% of MCI cases versus roughly 18-45% for the MMSE in some comparisons), with one direct comparison reporting MoCA sensitivity/specificity of about 90.2%/87.2% for dementia versus 78.4%/76.9% for the MMSE. A commonly used MoCA cutoff for detecting dementia is a score below 20-21 (sensitivity about 0.79, specificity about 0.80 in one analysis), while cutoffs of 23-25 are used for MCI depending on the method; a one-point correction is conventionally added to the raw MoCA score for people with 12 or fewer years of education. Both tools are education- and language-biased: older or less-educated people are at higher risk of false-positive (over-called impairment) results, and neither tool substitutes for a full clinical/biomarker work-up.
MMSE_MoCA_cutoffs_and_limitations.source: Comparative MMSE/MoCA sensitivity-specificity studies summarised in 'Comparative methods for determining MoCA, MMSE, and CDR cut-offs in Alzheimer's disease: insights from the ADNI study', PMC12961348; 'Accuracy of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment tool for detecting mild cognitive impairment: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Alzheimers Dement 2023 (Islam et al.)
MMSE_MoCA_cutoffs_and_limitations.confidence: moderate-high - cutoffs vary meaningfully by population/study and this variability is stated rather than presenting one universal number

autopsy_historical_gold_standard.finding: Definitive diagnosis of AD has historically rested on post-mortem neuropathological examination demonstrating a sufficient density and distribution of neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (e.g. CERAD neuritic-plaque scoring combined with Braak neurofibrillary staging), because no biomarker or clinical test in life has been perfectly concordant with pathology. This remains true even as biomarker-based 'biological diagnosis' has been proposed for research and, increasingly, clinical use (see AA 2024 criteria above); autopsy series continue to be used to validate the accuracy of clinical criteria and biomarkers (e.g. the 82.7% pooled accuracy of clinical AD-type dementia diagnosis against pathology reported in comparative dementia-diagnosis accuracy literature).
autopsy_historical_gold_standard.source: CERAD/Braak neuropathological diagnostic criteria as the historical reference standard used throughout the biomarker-validation literature cited above (e.g. Tapiola T et al., Arch Neurol 2009, PMID 19273758, using autopsy neuritic-plaque score as the gold standard)

preclinical_AD.finding: Preclinical AD (NIA-AA Stage 1: amyloidosis alone; Stage 2: amyloidosis plus neurodegeneration; Stage 3: the above plus subtle cognitive changes not yet meeting MCI criteria) describes biomarker-positive, clinically normal individuals, and is a research construct, not (under the 2011/IWG framework) a clinical diagnosis to be given to patients. A systematic review/meta-analysis estimated overall prevalence of preclinical AD (any stage) at about 22% (95% CI 18-26%) in cognitively normal populations, rising steeply with age from about 16.5% at 53 years to about 53% at 86 years; risk of progression to symptomatic disease rises across the stages, estimated at about 20% (Stage 1), 38% (Stage 2) and 73% (Stage 3).
preclinical_AD.source: Sperling RA et al., Alzheimers Dement 2011;7:280-292 (PMID 21514248); prevalence/progression meta-analysis, 'Prevalence and risk of progression of preclinical Alzheimer's disease stages: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Alzheimers Res Ther 2018

MCI_due_to_AD_and_conversion_rates.finding: MCI due to AD (Albert 2011 criteria) requires a cognitive complaint/decline (typically memory) with objective impairment on testing, essentially preserved independence in daily activities, and no dementia, together with supportive AD biomarkers. Reported annual conversion rates from MCI to dementia (all-cause or AD) are commonly cited as roughly 10-15% per year, though pooled estimates vary substantially by setting and follow-up duration: a large recent meta-analysis of 89 studies (mean follow-up 5.2 years) found conversion risk of 41.5% (38.3-44.7%) in clinic-based cohorts versus 27.0% (22.0-32.0%) in population-based cohorts, and conversion rates in individual studies have ranged as widely as 14.5% to 87%, reflecting real heterogeneity in how MCI is defined and ascertained rather than a single fixed number.
MCI_due_to_AD_and_conversion_rates.source: Albert MS et al., Alzheimers Dement 2011;7:270-279 (PMID 21514249); pooled conversion-rate meta-analysis as reported across MCI-to-dementia systematic reviews (e.g. Salemme et al., Alzheimers Dement Diagn Assess Dis Monit 2025; McGrattan et al., Alzheimers Dement Transl Res Clin Interv 2022, PMID for LMIC review)
MCI_due_to_AD_and_conversion_rates.confidence: moderate-high - the honest range (roughly 10% to over 40% depending on population) is given rather than a single number to avoid overstating precision

CDR_scale.finding: The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) combines cognitive and functional assessment across six domains (memory, orientation, judgment/problem-solving, community affairs, home/hobbies, personal care) into a 5-point global stage: CDR 0 (normal), 0.5 (very mild/questionable, includes MCI), 1 (mild), 2 (moderate), 3 (severe). The CDR-Sum-of-Boxes (CDR-SB), which sums the six domain scores rather than collapsing them to one global stage, is the primary efficacy outcome used in modern anti-amyloid antibody trials (e.g. lecanemab CLARITY-AD, donanemab TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2) because it is more sensitive to change than the global CDR score alone.
CDR_scale.source: Clinical Dementia Rating scale as used and described in dementia-staging comparative literature (PMC12047750) and in the lecanemab/donanemab phase 3 trial primary-outcome reporting cited above

GDS_and_FAST_stages.finding: Reisberg's Global Deterioration Scale (GDS) defines 7 stages of cognitive decline (from no impairment to very severe), and the companion Functional Assessment Staging Test (FAST), also 7 stages, stages the same progression by functional/activities-of-daily-living criteria (the last two GDS stages are subdivided into more FAST sub-stages), which is particularly useful for staging advanced dementia in long-term-care and hospice settings where cognitive testing is no longer feasible. A person's GDS (cognitive) stage and FAST (functional) stage can differ at a given point in the illness.
GDS_and_FAST_stages.source: Reisberg B, Global Deterioration Scale and Functional Assessment Staging (FAST), as described in comparative dementia-staging-scale reviews ('The GDS/FAST Staging System', and dementia stages overview literature)
GDS_and_FAST_stages.confidence: high for the scale structure; exact stage-duration figures are setting-dependent and not stated here to avoid overprecision

mild_moderate_severe_clinical_dementia_s.finding: Clinically, AD dementia is commonly divided into mild (early difficulty with instrumental activities such as finances/driving, word-finding difficulty, mild disorientation, still largely independent), moderate (needs assistance with basic activities of daily living, more marked language/behavioural problems, increasing disorientation, may develop wandering or agitation) and severe (loses ability to communicate coherently, generally requires full assistance with all ADLs, eventual loss of ambulation, swallowing difficulty). These labels map approximately onto CDR 1 / CDR 2 / CDR 3 and GDS/FAST mid-to-late stages respectively.
mild_moderate_severe_clinical_dementia_s.source: Cross-referenced against CDR and GDS/FAST stage descriptions above; consistent with standard clinical staging terminology used across the dementia-staging literature cited
mild_moderate_severe_clinical_dementia_s.confidence: moderate-high - this is a widely used clinical convention rather than a single formally numbered criterion set

core.name: Episodic memory loss - typically the first and defining symptom
core.note: New-learning/recent-memory impairment (repeating questions, forgetting recent conversations/events, misplacing items) is usually the earliest and most prominent symptom because the earliest tau pathology (Braak stage I-II) affects the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, the principal input/output relay of the hippocampus via the perforant pathway; hippocampal/entorhinal dysfunction impairs the formation of new episodic memories while older, well-consolidated memories are relatively preserved early on. This is the amnestic-onset pattern required by the NIA-AA and DSM-5 'typical' AD criteria, though non-amnestic (atypical) presentations exist (see atypical_variants below).
core.source: Maass A et al., 'Entorhinal Tau Pathology, Episodic Memory Decline, and Neurodegeneration in Aging', J Neurosci 2018;38:530 (PMID 29192126); Braak/Braak staging framework

core.name: Language impairment (anomia, word-finding difficulty, progressing to impaired comprehension)
core.note: As disease spreads to temporo-parietal association cortex, word-finding difficulty and reduced verbal fluency appear, progressing over years to impaired comprehension and eventually reduced verbal output; this differs from the primary progressive aphasia variants (see atypical variants) where language impairment is the presenting and dominant feature rather than a later addition to amnestic decline.
core.source: DSM-5 major neurocognitive disorder domain criteria (language); NIA-AA 2011 core clinical criteria (McKhann et al., PMID 21514250)

core.name: Visuospatial dysfunction
core.note: Difficulty with spatial orientation, getting lost in familiar places, and impaired visuoconstructional tasks emerge as parietal and occipito-parietal regions become involved; when visuospatial impairment is the presenting, dominant feature (rather than a mid-stage addition), this defines the posterior cortical atrophy variant.
core.source: DSM-5 major neurocognitive disorder domain criteria (visuospatial); Crutch SJ et al., consensus classification of posterior cortical atrophy, Alzheimers Dement 2017

core.name: Executive dysfunction
core.note: Impaired planning, organisation, multitasking and reasoning about complex tasks (e.g. managing finances, medications) is part of the NIA-AA core clinical criteria for dementia and typically becomes more prominent as frontal-executive networks are affected in mid-stage disease, contributing heavily to loss of instrumental activities of daily living.
core.source: McKhann GM et al., Alzheimers Dement 2011;7:263-269 (PMID 21514250)

core.name: Apraxia (impaired learned motor skills despite intact motor/sensory function)
core.note: Difficulty performing previously learned motor sequences (dressing, using utensils/tools) develops as the disease progresses and parietal cortex is affected; it contributes substantially to loss of independence in moderate-to-severe disease and is distinct from the primary motor/sensory deficits seen in stroke or Parkinsonism.
core.source: DSM-5/NIA-AA cognitive-domain criteria; standard clinical dementia literature on functional decline

atypical_variants.name: Posterior cortical atrophy (PCA) - the 'visual variant' of AD
atypical_variants.note: PCA presents with progressive, prominent visuospatial and visuoperceptual deficits (difficulty judging distances/reading/recognising objects or faces, Balint's or Gerstmann's syndrome features) with relatively preserved memory and insight early on, reflecting atrophy/hypometabolism concentrated in parietal and occipital cortex rather than the medial temporal lobe. Onset is typically earlier than typical AD (commonly mid-fifties to early sixties) and affects women more than men (about 60% vs 40% in cohort data). PCA affects an estimated 5% (range up to about 15%, given under-recognition) of AD presentations, and is caused by AD pathology at autopsy in the majority of cases; the 2017 international consensus (Crutch et al.) established a three-level classification (syndrome, then intermediate, then likely-cause level) to standardise diagnosis. Notably, PCA and logopenic-variant PPA are reported to be MORE specific for underlying AD neuropathology at autopsy than a diagnosis of 'probable AD dementia' made using the typical amnestic criteria.
atypical_variants.source: Crutch SJ et al., 'Consensus classification of posterior cortical atrophy', Alzheimers Dement 2017;13:870-884; PCA epidemiology/demographics as summarised in Lancet Neurol 2023 international cohort/IPD meta-analysis and Alzforum coverage 'Posterior Cortical Atrophy Is a Form of Young-Onset Alzheimer's'; specificity-for-AD-pathology finding, 'Posterior cortical atrophy and logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia are more specific for Alzheimer's disease pathology than probable Alzheimer's disease', Brain Commun 2024/PMC13457939

atypical_variants.name: Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia (lvPPA) - the 'language variant' of AD
atypical_variants.note: lvPPA presents with impaired single-word retrieval and impaired sentence/phrase repetition, with relatively preserved articulation, grammar and single-word comprehension (distinguishing it from the semantic and nonfluent/agrammatic PPA variants, which are usually associated with frontotemporal lobar degeneration rather than AD). Imaging shows asymmetric (left greater than right) atrophy of the posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal lobes, posterior cingulate and medial temporal lobes. Autopsy, amyloid-PET positivity and elevated CSF tau/Abeta ratio confirm that lvPPA is, in the majority of cases, a language-led presentation of underlying AD pathology, and (as above) may be even more specific for AD pathology than the standard amnestic presentation.
atypical_variants.source: Gorno-Tempini ML et al., PPA classification criteria (nonfluent/agrammatic, semantic, logopenic variants); lvPPA-AD pathological association and imaging pattern as summarised in 'Patterns of longitudinal brain atrophy in the logopenic variant of primary progressive aphasia', PMC3880853; Brain Commun 2024/PMC13457939 (specificity finding as above)

behavioral_and_psychological_symptoms_of.framing: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are extremely common, cause much of the caregiver burden, and often prompt medical attention as much as the cognitive symptoms themselves. The Cache County population-based study followed 408 incident dementia cases with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory over 5+ years and found that at least one neuropsychiatric symptom was present in 56% of participants at baseline, rising to 76-87% at later visits.

features.name: Apathy
features.note: Rose from 20% at baseline to 51% by 5.3 years of follow-up in the Cache County cohort - the single symptom with the steepest rise, and one of the symptoms (with depression and anxiety) that participants were most likely to newly develop.
features.source: Cache County Study, point and 5-year period prevalence of neuropsychiatric symptoms in dementia, as summarised via Johns Hopkins/PubMed record (PMID 17607801)

features.name: Depression
features.note: 29% at baseline, rising to 41-47% at later visits in the Cache County cohort.

features.name: Anxiety
features.note: 14% at baseline, rising to 24-32% at later visits.

features.name: Agitation/aggression
features.note: Fluctuated between 13% and 24% across follow-up visits.

features.name: Delusions
features.note: 18% at baseline, rising to 34-38% at later visits.

features.name: Hallucinations (mainly visual)
features.note: 10% at baseline, rising to 19-24% at later visits; when hallucinations are a very early, prominent feature (occurring before or with only mild dementia), dementia with Lewy bodies should be strongly considered instead of/alongside AD (see differential_dementias below).

features.name: Sleep disturbance
features.note: Common across the disease course and contributes heavily to caregiver burden; disrupted sleep-wake cycles and 'sundowning' (worsening confusion/agitation in the evening) are frequently reported clinical phenomena in AD, though this entry does not assign a single verified population prevalence figure to 'sundowning' specifically because none was retrieved in this research pass.
features.source: General BPSD literature; Cache County Study for related neuropsychiatric symptom prevalence (PMID 17607801)

adl_loss.finding: Progression follows a broadly predictable functional trajectory: loss of instrumental activities of daily living (finances, driving, medication management) in mild disease, then loss of basic activities of daily living (dressing, bathing, toileting, continence) in moderate-to-severe disease, culminating in complete dependence for all care, loss of ambulation, and eventual mutism in end-stage disease. This functional decline is formally captured by the FAST scale (see staging above).
adl_loss.source: GDS/FAST staging literature; DSM-5/NIA-AA functional-decline criteria for progression from mild to major neurocognitive disorder

dysphagia_and_aspiration_pneumonia.finding: Swallowing difficulty (dysphagia) is common in advanced AD and is a major driver of late-stage mortality via aspiration pneumonia. In a 22-year US retrospective analysis, aspiration pneumonia was implicated in 115,284 deaths among older adults (over 65) with AD, and elderly dementia patients carry roughly double the risk of pneumonia-related mortality compared with those without dementia; about 25% of an AD cohort was hospitalised for incident pneumonia during follow-up in a matched cohort study. Aspiration pneumonia specifically carries a much worse prognosis than non-aspiration pneumonia in older patients (median survival about 62 days versus 274 days in one comparative series).
dysphagia_and_aspiration_pneumonia.source: 'Aspiration Pneumonia Related Mortality in Older Adults with Alzheimer's Disease: A 22-Year Retrospective Analysis', Neurology 2025 (conference abstract P3-11.010); 'Risk factors of pneumonia in persons with and without Alzheimer's disease: a matched cohort study', PMC10084638; aspiration-versus-non-aspiration pneumonia survival comparison as reported in the aspiration-pneumonia-in-dementia mortality literature
dysphagia_and_aspiration_pneumonia.confidence: moderate-high - figures come from specific retrospective cohorts and conference-abstract-level reporting rather than a single definitive registry

immobility_and_terminal_decline.finding: Loss of ambulation, contractures, pressure injuries and profound immobility characterise the terminal phase of AD, and together with dysphagia/aspiration and general frailty account for the fact that AD/dementia is a leading underlying or contributing cause of death in older adults, even though it is frequently under-recorded as the immediate cause of death on death certificates (pneumonia or another acute event is often listed instead).
immobility_and_terminal_decline.source: General natural-history literature on advanced dementia terminal-stage care and cause-of-death under-recording, consistent with the aspiration-pneumonia mortality data cited above

red_flags: Rapidly progressive dementia (severe decline over weeks to a few months rather than years): raises suspicion for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) or another rapidly progressive dementia cause (autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis, CNS infection, metabolic derangement) rather than typical AD; in CJD, dementia is typically the presenting feature, followed by pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs (about 88%), visuospatial/cerebellar signs (about 74%), myoclonus (about 62%, usually appearing later) and akinetic mutism (about 46%, an end-stage feature); EEG periodic sharp-wave complexes, characteristic MRI DWI/FLAIR cortical ribboning or basal ganglia signal change, and CSF 14-3-3 protein or real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) testing support the diagnosis. This needs urgent neurology referral, not routine dementia work-up.

New focal neurological deficits (hemiparesis, visual field loss, aphasia of sudden onset, etc.): suggests a stroke, mass lesion or other structural cause rather than typical AD and needs urgent imaging (cross-reference this knowledge base's stroke entry).

Acute or subacute confusion, fluctuating attention, or altered consciousness superimposed on baseline dementia: suggests delirium (infection, drug toxicity/interaction, metabolic derangement, dehydration, urinary retention/constipation) rather than progression of AD itself, and is a medical emergency requiring identification and treatment of the precipitant - delirium is not diagnostic of AD progression and its cause must be found.

Prominent, very early visual hallucinations, marked fluctuation in cognition/alertness, or spontaneous parkinsonism at or before dementia onset: suggests dementia with Lewy bodies rather than AD; this distinction matters clinically because DLB patients have severe, sometimes fatal, sensitivity to antipsychotic drugs.

Early, prominent personality/behavioural change (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive/ritualistic behaviour) or early language breakdown with relatively preserved memory, especially with onset before age 65: suggests behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia or a non-logopenic PPA variant rather than typical AD.
Sudden stepwise deterioration, or dementia with a clear temporal relationship to a stroke, with vascular risk factors and focal deficits: suggests vascular or mixed vascular-AD dementia.

Cognitive impairment with a gait disturbance (magnetic, short-stepped gait) and urinary incontinence in an older adult: raises normal-pressure hydrocephalus, a potentially treatable mimic - needs neuroimaging before being labelled as AD.

New cognitive decline with systemic clues (weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, recent travel/exposure history, known HIV risk, heavy alcohol use, or medication changes especially anticholinergics/benzodiazepines/opioids): mandates exclusion of a reversible/treatable cause before accepting a diagnosis of AD (see differential_dementias below).

Any dementia presentation before age 65 (early-onset), especially with a strong family history across generations: raises the possibility of autosomal-dominant AD (APP/PSEN1/PSEN2) and warrants genetic counselling and consideration of testing (see real_risk_factors below).

vascular_dementia.finding: Vascular dementia (cross-referenced in full in this knowledge base's stroke entry) is characterised by a temporal relationship to cerebrovascular events, a stepwise (rather than smoothly progressive) decline, prominent executive dysfunction and gait disturbance relative to memory loss, focal neurological signs, and MRI evidence of infarcts, lacunes or extensive white-matter disease. Mixed vascular-AD pathology is extremely common (see mixed_dementia below), so the distinction is often one of relative contribution rather than a clean either/or.
vascular_dementia.source: Cross-reference to this KB's stroke entry; standard vascular-cognitive-impairment diagnostic literature

dementia_with_lewy_bodies.finding: DLB (also briefly covered in this KB's parkinsons_disease entry) core clinical features are fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention/alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behaviour disorder (upgraded to a core clinical feature in the 2017 consensus criteria). One core feature supports possible DLB; two or more support probable DLB. By the DLB Consortium's 1-year rule, dementia arising before or within 1 year of parkinsonism onset is labelled DLB, whereas parkinsonism preceding dementia by more than 1 year is labelled Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) - the same underlying alpha-synuclein pathology, staged differently by symptom sequence.
dementia_with_lewy_bodies.source: McKeith IG et al., 'Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium', Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

frontotemporal_dementia.finding: Behavioural-variant FTD (bvFTD) presents with early, prominent personality and behavioural change (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, ritualistic/compulsive behaviour, dietary change) with relative sparing of episodic memory and visuospatial function early on, reflecting predominantly frontal (and sometimes anterior temporal) rather than posterior/medial-temporal involvement; onset is often before age 65. FTD is a clinical and pathological family distinct from AD (tauopathies or TDP-43 proteinopathies rather than amyloid/tau-AD pathology in most cases), though clinical overlap with AD is common enough that neuroimaging/behavioural-history distinction matters practically.
frontotemporal_dementia.source: FTD-versus-AD differentiating features as summarised in comparative dementia-syndrome literature (Cherrier MM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 1997, on FTD-vs-vascular mental-status differences, and general bvFTD consensus criteria literature)

mixed_dementia.finding: Pure single-pathology dementia is the exception rather than the rule in older brains at autopsy. In the Religious Orders Study/Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) cohort, pure AD pathology (with no other significant co-pathology) was found in only about 10% of participants despite AD being the most common single clinical diagnosis, and harmonised analysis across six community-based autopsy cohorts (including UK MRC CFAS and ROSMAP) found that more than 80% of older individuals harboured mixed degenerative-plus-vascular (or other) pathology; over 230 distinct combinations of co-existing pathologies have been catalogued. The practical takeaway is that most real-world dementia in older adults reflects combined pathology (commonly AD plus cerebrovascular disease, or AD plus Lewy body pathology), so a clean single-disease label is often an oversimplification even when one pathology clinically predominates.
mixed_dementia.source: 'The prevalence, correlation, and co-occurrence of neuropathology in old age: harmonisation of 12 measures across six community-based autopsy studies of dementia', PMC9977689; Rush Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project cognition-neuropathology literature, PMC3157574

reversible_treatable_mimics_and_standard.finding: A minority but clinically critical fraction of apparent dementia is due to a reversible or partially reversible cause. Estimates of the proportion of dementia presentations attributable to potentially reversible conditions have ranged widely across eras and settings (older literature cited figures approaching 20%; a more recent geriatric-clinic study found the reported frequency of reversible/partly-reversible dementia ranging 0-23% depending on the population studied, with individual condition prevalence in one geriatric clinic series of hypothyroidism 2.6%, B12 deficiency 1.7%, and normal-pressure hydrocephalus 0.9% among dementia patients) - i.e. these causes are real but not the majority explanation, and 'reversibility' in practice is often partial rather than complete cure. Depression (pseudodementia), alcohol-related cognitive impairment, normal-pressure hydrocephalus and B12 deficiency together account for more than half of identified reversible-dementia cases in reviewed series. The conditions that MUST be actively excluded before accepting a diagnosis of AD/irreversible dementia are: hypothyroidism (TSH), vitamin B12 deficiency (serum B12 +/- methylmalonic acid/homocysteine), normal-pressure hydrocephalus (gait-cognition-urinary triad plus neuroimaging showing ventriculomegaly), depression/pseudodementia (mood history and screening), drug effects (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids and other sedating/cognition-impairing medicines - medication reconciliation is essential), neurosyphilis (VDRL/RPR and treponemal testing where risk factors are present), chronic subdural haematoma (history of falls/anticoagulation plus CT/MRI), HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HIV testing where risk factors present), and chronic heavy alcohol use (history, thiamine status). The standard basic dementia work-up therefore includes: full blood count, renal and liver function, TSH, vitamin B12 (+/- folate), calcium, glucose/HbA1c, and structural neuroimaging (CT or MRI) in essentially every new dementia presentation, with syphilis/HIV serology, EEG or CSF studies added when specific risk factors or atypical features (rapid progression, young age, focal signs) are present.
reversible_treatable_mimics_and_standard.source: Prevalence-of-reversible-dementia literature as summarised via 'Prevalence of potentially reversible conditions in dementia and mild cognitive impairment in a geriatric clinic', PMID 21794050, and 'How Reversible are Reversible Dementias?', touchNEUROLOGY; standard reversible-dementia workup as described in AAFP 'Diagnostic Approach to the Confused Elderly Patient'
reversible_treatable_mimics_and_standard.confidence: moderate-high - the honest, wide range of reported reversible-dementia prevalence across different eras/settings is stated explicitly rather than picking one figure to imply false precision

real_risk_factors.note: Incidence and prevalence of AD/dementia rise steeply and roughly exponentially with age from the mid-60s onward; age is consistently identified as the dominant non-modifiable risk factor across essentially all epidemiological studies of AD.
real_risk_factors.source: WHO/ADI dementia statistics (alzint.org); GBD 2019-based WHO estimates

real_risk_factors.note: The APOE-e4 allele is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset (sporadic) AD. The landmark Farrer et al. 1997 JAMA meta-analysis (40 research teams, 5,930 AD cases and 8,607 controls) reported that, relative to the common e3/e3 genotype, one copy of e4 (e3/e4 heterozygotes) confers an odds ratio of roughly 3-4-fold increased AD risk, and two copies (e4/e4 homozygotes) confer roughly 9-15-fold increased risk (an odds ratio of about 14.9 has been specifically reported for e4/e4 in Caucasian cohorts in this meta-analysis), with the association's strength varying by age, sex and ethnic group. APOE-e4 is a risk-modifying gene, not a deterministic one: many e4 carriers never develop AD, and some non-carriers do.
real_risk_factors.source: Farrer LA et al., 'Effects of age, sex, and ethnicity on the association between apolipoprotein E genotype and Alzheimer disease: a meta-analysis', JAMA 1997;278:1349-1356 (PMID 9343467)

real_risk_factors.factor: Autosomal-dominant genetic mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) - rare but fully penetrant early-onset disease
real_risk_factors.note: Mutations in APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2 cause autosomal-dominant Alzheimer's disease (ADAD), typically with early onset (before age 65, often much earlier) and essentially complete penetrance (PSEN2 mutations are rarer and more variably penetrant than APP/PSEN1). Age at symptom onset is relatively consistent within families carrying the same PSEN1 mutation, more variable for PSEN2/APP; PSEN1 mutations are generally associated with earlier onset than PSEN2 or APP mutations. The Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN) has catalogued 550 variants across these three genes, of which 279 are classified pathogenic/likely pathogenic. ADAD accounts for a small minority of all AD cases but is central to research (including the anti-amyloid antibody trials) because carriers can be identified and studied before symptom onset.
real_risk_factors.source: 'The landscape of autosomal-dominant Alzheimer's disease: global distribution and age of onset', Brain 2025;148:2429 (PMID 39903689); Bateman RJ et al. (DIAN), 'Clinical and biomarker changes in dominantly inherited Alzheimer's disease', N Engl J Med 2012;367:795-804

real_risk_factors.note: Down syndrome, which occurs in roughly 1 in 1,000 births, is the most common genetic cause of early-onset AD because the APP gene resides on chromosome 21, so trisomy 21 causes lifelong APP over-expression. Essentially all individuals with Down syndrome develop the neuropathological hallmarks (plaques and tangles) of AD by around age 40, and by age 65 roughly two-thirds of people with Down syndrome have a clinical dementia diagnosis - i.e. an extra APP copy alone accelerates the disease by decades, though triplication of other chromosome-21 genes may also contribute.
real_risk_factors.source: 'A genetic cause of Alzheimer disease: mechanistic insights from Down syndrome', PMC4678594; Down syndrome-AD epidemiology as summarised in ALZFORUM 'Trisomy 21' mutation database entry

real_risk_factors.note: Women make up roughly two-thirds of AD cases and have a higher estimated lifetime risk of developing AD than men (about 1 in 5 for women versus about 1 in 10 for men in commonly cited US figures), a difference only partly explained by women's longer life expectancy; hormonal (menopause-related oestrogen decline), genetic (X-chromosome-linked factors) and sex-specific risk-factor-burden differences (e.g. depression, hypertension, diabetes associations found to be stronger in women in some cohorts) are proposed contributing mechanisms, though the field states plainly that the full explanation for the sex difference is not yet settled.
real_risk_factors.source: Sex differences in Alzheimer's disease risk literature, PMC11313277 ('Sex and Gender Differences in Alzheimer's Disease: Genetic, Hormonal, and Inflammation Impacts') and related sex-differences reviews (ScienceDirect, PMC11715427)

real_risk_factors.factor: The 14 Lancet Commission modifiable risk factors (2024 update) - potentially preventable fraction of dementia cases
real_risk_factors.note: The 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention and care update estimates that modifying 14 risk factors across the life course could prevent or delay approximately 45% of dementia cases worldwide (up from 12 factors and about 40% in the 2020 report). The 14 factors are: less education (early life); hearing loss, high LDL cholesterol, depression, traumatic brain injury, physical inactivity, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, obesity, and excessive alcohol consumption (midlife); and social isolation, air pollution, and untreated vision loss (later life) - the 2024 update specifically added high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss to the 2020 list of 12 factors. This is a population-attributable-fraction estimate (i.e. the theoretical maximum benefit if a risk factor were eliminated entirely across the population), not a guarantee for any individual, and it applies to all-cause dementia, not AD pathology specifically.
real_risk_factors.source: Livingston G et al., 'Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2024 report of the Lancet standing Commission', Lancet 2024 (thelancet.com/article/S0140-6736(24)01296-0); Alzheimer Europe summary of the 2024 Lancet Commission's 14 modifiable risk factors

global.finding: WHO estimated 55 million people living with dementia worldwide in 2023 (using WHO Global Health Estimates 2019/GBD 2019-based methodology), projected to rise to 139 million by 2050; already about 60% of people with dementia live in low- and middle-income countries, projected to rise to about 71% by 2050. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, accounting for an estimated 60-70% of all dementia cases.
global.source: WHO Global Health Estimates 2019/GBD 2019-based dementia figures, as summarised by Alzheimer's Disease International (alzint.org/about/dementia-facts-figures/dementia-statistics)

india_specific.finding: The Longitudinal Aging Study in India - Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia (LASI-DAD), the first nationally representative study of dementia in India (an ancillary study of LASI, itself covering 72,262 people, with a dedicated LASI-DAD sub-sample of 4,096 participants using neuropsychological testing plus informant reports and DSM-5 criteria), estimated dementia prevalence among adults aged 60+ at 7.4% in Wave 1, implying over 8.8 million Indians aged 60+ living with dementia; a nationwide study additionally found dementia more prevalent among women than men and in rural versus urban areas, with substantial state-to-state variation. Separately, the Dementia India Report (Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India, ARDSI) estimated 3.7 million people with dementia in India in 2010, projected to reach 5.29 million by 2020. No dedicated national dementia registry for India was identified in this research pass - the LASI-DAD survey and periodic ARDSI reports are the main sources of national-level Indian dementia data rather than a continuously operating registry, and this absence-of-registry statement should be treated as 'not found in this search', not as a certainty that no such registry exists anywhere in the country.
india_specific.source: LASI-DAD study design and Wave 1 prevalence, PMC7742243 and related LASI-DAD publications; 'Prevalence of dementia in India: National and state estimates from a nationwide study', Alzheimers Dement 2023 (Lee J et al., PMID 36637034); Dementia India Report 2010/2020, ARDSI, as summarised via STRiDE India situation report (stride-dementia.org/india-situation-report) and rural India library summary
india_specific.confidence: moderate-high for the LASI-DAD prevalence figure (a real, nationally representative, peer-reviewed estimate); the registry statement is explicitly hedged as a search-based non-finding rather than a confirmed absence

survival.finding: AD/dementia shortens survival, though reported median survival varies considerably by age at diagnosis, dementia severity at diagnosis and study methodology; one matched cohort study reported a median follow-up of 4.5 years in the AD cohort versus 5.2 years in the matched non-AD cohort (a relative, not absolute, survival comparison). This entry does not state a single 'years of survival after diagnosis' figure as a universal fact because retrieved sources gave cohort-specific relative comparisons rather than one definitive absolute median-survival number applicable to all patients; clinicians should counsel using locally validated prognostic tools/cohort data rather than a single global number.
survival.source: Matched-cohort AD survival comparison as reported in pneumonia-risk-in-AD cohort literature (PMC10084638)
survival.confidence: moderate - stated as a relative comparison from one cohort rather than a definitive universal figure, per this project's zero-fabrication rule

causes_of_death.finding: Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in advanced AD (115,284 deaths attributed to aspiration pneumonia among over-65s with AD in a 22-year US retrospective analysis), reflecting the dysphagia and immobility of late-stage disease; dementia is frequently under-recorded as the true underlying cause of death on death certificates, with pneumonia or another acute terminal event listed instead.
causes_of_death.source: 'Aspiration Pneumonia Related Mortality in Older Adults with Alzheimer's Disease: A 22-Year Retrospective Analysis of Mortality Trends', Neurology 2025 conference abstract

caregiver_burden.finding: Caregiver burden in AD/dementia is large and well quantified in the US context: an estimated 11.46 million unpaid Alzheimer's/dementia caregivers in the US in 2023 provided about 18.4 billion hours of unpaid care (valued at roughly $347 billion); the total lifetime cost of care for a person with dementia was estimated at $405,262 (2024 dollars), about 70% of which falls on family caregivers as unpaid care and out-of-pocket costs; 70% of dementia caregivers report that coordinating care is itself stressful. These are US-specific figures and are presented as such rather than extrapolated globally.
caregiver_burden.source: '2024 Alzheimer's disease facts and figures', Alzheimers Dement 2024 (PMID 38689398); Alzheimer's Association 2024 caregiver-burden report coverage (alz.org/news/2024/new-alzheimers-association-report-reveals-top-stressors-caregivers)
caregiver_burden.confidence: high for the US figures cited; explicitly not generalised to other countries including India, where separate (and less complete) data exist

FINGER_trial.finding: The Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER, 1,260 at-risk older adults aged 60-77, 2-year multidomain intervention of diet, exercise, cognitive training and vascular-risk monitoring versus general health advice) was the first large long-term RCT to show a significant multidomain-lifestyle benefit on cognition in an at-risk population: the intervention group's composite cognitive score improved more than the control group's (a small but statistically significant between-group difference, Cohen's d approximately 0.13). This established proof-of-concept that a structured multidomain lifestyle programme can measurably affect cognitive trajectory in at-risk older adults, launching the World-Wide FINGERS network of replication trials.
FINGER_trial.source: Ngandu T et al., 'A 2 year multidomain intervention of diet, exercise, cognitive training, and vascular risk monitoring versus control to prevent cognitive decline in at-risk elderly people (FINGER): a randomised controlled trial', Lancet 2015;385:2255-2263

US_POINTER_trial.finding: US POINTER (2,111 older adults at risk of cognitive decline across 5 US sites, 2-year trial comparing a structured, higher-support multidomain lifestyle intervention against a self-guided lower-support version) reported in 2025 (JAMA, presented at AAIC 2025) that the structured intervention produced greater cognitive improvement than the self-guided version, with benefit estimated as equivalent to protecting cognition from 1-2 years of normal age-related decline; benefits were reported consistently across age, sex, ethnicity, cardiovascular-health status and APOE-e4 genotype. This is the largest US-based replication of the FINGER approach and the first to show benefit is achievable at scale in a diverse population.
US_POINTER_trial.source: U.S. POINTER Study Results, Alzheimer's Association (alz.org/us-pointer/study-results); AAIC 2025 news release (aaic.alz.org/releases-2025/us-pointer-study-results-announced.asp); published JAMA 28 July 2025

SPRINT_MIND_trial.finding: SPRINT MIND (a pre-specified cognitive sub-study of SPRINT, 9,361 hypertensive adults at elevated cardiovascular risk randomised to intensive systolic BP control, target <120 mmHg, versus standard control, target <140 mmHg) found that intensive blood-pressure control significantly reduced the risk of MCI by about 19% and reduced the combined risk of MCI or probable dementia by about 15%, although the trial was stopped early (for cardiovascular benefit) before it had statistical power to show a significant reduction in probable dementia alone as a standalone endpoint. A subsequent long-term follow-up (median 6.9 years) continued to show a lower probable-dementia incidence rate in the intensive-treatment group (8.5 per 1,000 person-years) versus standard treatment (10.2 per 1,000 person-years), i.e. the benefit persisted well after the original intensive-treatment protocol ended. This is real evidence that a specific, aggressively treated modifiable vascular risk factor (hypertension) measurably reduces cognitive-impairment risk, complementing (not replacing) the multidomain-lifestyle evidence above.
SPRINT_MIND_trial.source: SPRINT MIND Investigators, JAMA 2019;321:553-561 (primary results); long-term follow-up, 'Long-Term Effect of Intensive vs Standard Blood Pressure Control on Mild Cognitive Impairment and Probable Dementia in SPRINT', Neurology 2025

prevention_and_lifestyle_clinical_course.practical_synthesis: None of FINGER, US POINTER or SPRINT MIND is a cure or a guarantee of prevention for any individual; each demonstrates a real, statistically significant but modest reduction in cognitive-decline/MCI risk from a specific, well-defined intervention (multidomain lifestyle programme, or intensive BP control) in an at-risk population over a defined trial period. They support the Lancet Commission's modifiable-risk-factor framework (above) with genuine randomised evidence rather than only observational association, and they belong to the prevention/risk-reduction side of the picture, not to disease-modifying drug treatment (which belongs to the treatment-focused pass of this knowledge base).

clinical_takeaway.point: Exclude reversible/treatable mimics FIRST, in every new dementia presentation, before accepting a diagnosis of AD.
clinical_takeaway.why: Hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, depression/pseudodementia, medication effects (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids), neurosyphilis, chronic subdural haematoma, HIV and alcohol-related cognitive impairment are all real, identifiable and at least partially treatable causes that can mimic AD; the standard basic work-up (blood count, renal/liver function, TSH, B12, calcium, glucose, structural neuroimaging, plus targeted syphilis/HIV serology or CSF/EEG when red flags are present) should precede a settled diagnosis.
clinical_takeaway.source: Reversible-dementia and standard confused-elderly-patient work-up literature cited in differential_dementias_and_reversible_causes above

clinical_takeaway.point: Use clinical criteria (NIA-AA 2011 / DSM-5) plus, where available, biomarkers to support - not replace - clinical judgement; be aware the field itself is split on whether a biomarker-positive, symptom-free person should be told they have 'Alzheimer's disease'.
clinical_takeaway.why: The 2024 Alzheimer's Association biological-definition framework and the 2024 IWG clinical-biological framework disagree on this point; over-interpreting a positive amyloid-PET, CSF or plasma p-tau217 result in a cognitively normal person as a diagnosis of 'disease' can cause real harm (anxiety, insurance/employment implications, premature treatment decisions) that the clinical-biological camp is specifically trying to avoid.
clinical_takeaway.source: Jack CR Jr et al., Alzheimers Dement 2024 (AA framework); IWG 2024 update as summarised above

clinical_takeaway.point: Stage the patient (CDR/GDS-FAST/clinical mild-moderate-severe) - staging drives realistic prognosis discussion, safety planning (driving, finances, home safety) and caregiver support planning, and should happen at diagnosis, not be deferred.
clinical_takeaway.why: Functional trajectory (ADL loss, then dysphagia/immobility) is broadly predictable once staged, and caregiver burden (18.4 billion unpaid hours/year in the US alone) is enormous and rises with disease stage, so early, honest staging allows caregivers to plan rather than being caught unprepared.
clinical_takeaway.source: GDS/FAST and CDR staging literature; 2024 Alzheimer's disease facts and figures (PMID 38689398) cited above
