clinical_takeaway.point: Screen for and actively manage BPSD (especially depression, apathy, anxiety and, later, agitation/psychosis) at every visit - these symptoms are near-universal by mid-disease and drive most of the caregiver distress and institutionalisation risk, independent of the cognitive score.
clinical_takeaway.why: By 5 years post-diagnosis 76-87% of patients in the Cache County cohort had at least one neuropsychiatric symptom, and apathy alone rose from 20% to 51%; these are modifiable targets for non-pharmacological and (where indicated) pharmacological management even though they do not change the underlying neurodegeneration.
clinical_takeaway.source: Cache County Study (PMID 17607801)

clinical_takeaway.point: Actively discuss modifiable-risk-factor reduction (per the Lancet Commission's 14 factors) and refer to a structured multidomain lifestyle programme where available (FINGER/World-Wide FINGERS/US POINTER model) or optimise blood pressure aggressively (per SPRINT MIND) in at-risk or early-stage patients - this is real, trial-proven risk reduction, not folk advice.
clinical_takeaway.why: Up to an estimated 45% of dementia cases are attributable to 14 modifiable factors across the life course, and randomised trial evidence (not just observational association) now exists for both multidomain lifestyle intervention and intensive BP control reducing MCI/cognitive-decline risk.
clinical_takeaway.source: Livingston G et al., Lancet 2024 (Lancet Commission); Ngandu T et al., Lancet 2015 (FINGER); SPRINT MIND Investigators, JAMA 2019 and Neurology 2025 follow-up

clinical_takeaway.point: Keep a high index of suspicion for a non-typical presentation (early-onset before 65, prominent visual/language/behavioural-first symptoms, or rapid progression) and refer promptly - these patterns point to atypical AD variants, a different dementia entirely, autosomal-dominant AD, or a rapidly progressive dementia needing urgent work-up, and are frequently missed if the clinician anchors only on the classic amnestic-onset picture.
clinical_takeaway.why: PCA and lvPPA are, if anything, more specific for underlying AD pathology than the 'typical' amnestic presentation, yet are commonly misdiagnosed for years because they don't fit the classic memory-loss picture; rapidly progressive dementia needs urgent CJD/autoimmune work-up, not routine AD management.
clinical_takeaway.source: Crutch SJ et al., 2017; Brain Commun 2024/PMC13457939 (PCA/lvPPA AD-specificity); CJD red-flag literature cited above

alzheimers_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Alzheimer's disease is NOT curable, and this must be stated plainly. No drug or device in this entry stops or reverses the underlying neurodegeneration (amyloid-beta plaque and tau neurofibrillary tangle accumulation, synaptic loss, neuroinflammation, neuronal death) described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry; every treatment below is either symptomatic (cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, BPSD management, sleep/dysphagia/falls/delirium management) or, for the anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies, modestly DISEASE-MODIFYING (it slows, but does not stop or reverse, the rate of clinical decline). The honest state of disease-modifying therapy: in CLARITY-AD (1795 participants with early AD, 18 months), lecanemab (Leqembi) reduced decline on the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) by 27% versus placebo (treatment difference -0.45, P=0.00005) (van Dyck CH et al., N Engl J Med 2023;388:9-21). In TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (1736 participants with early symptomatic AD, 18 months), donanemab (Kisunla) slowed decline on CDR-SB by 29% and on iADRS by 22% in the combined population, with participants at the earliest (low/medium tau) stage showing larger, roughly 60% slowing and some showing no measurable progression at one year (Sims JR et al., JAMA 2023;330:512-527, PMID 37459141). These are real, statistically significant, regulator-reviewed results - but a 27-29% SLOWING of decline over 18 months is not a cure, not a stop, and not a reversal: cognition and function still decline in the treated group, just somewhat more slowly than on placebo. Both drugs carry a real, sometimes serious safety signal - amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), swelling (ARIA-E) or microhaemorrhage (ARIA-H) on MRI - that occurs more often, and more severely, in APOE-e4 homozygotes, which is why APOE genotyping and scheduled monitoring MRIs are part of appropriate use. A third anti-amyloid antibody, aducanumab (Aduhelm), received controversial FDA accelerated approval in 2021 on a biomarker surrogate without convincing clinical-benefit data, was never meaningfully adopted clinically after CMS restricted coverage to trial participants, and was discontinued by Biogen in 2024 for commercial (not primarily safety) reasons; it is included here only as history, not as a current treatment option. As of this research (September 2026) no CDSCO approval, import licence or listing for lecanemab or donanemab was located, so their availability in India could not be verified and should not be assumed. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has Alzheimer's disease: (1) start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild-to-moderate disease, or memantine for moderate-to-severe disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated - modest, real, guideline-endorsed symptomatic benefit; (2) where the person has confirmed amyloid pathology and MCI/mild dementia, is APOE-genotyped, and can access the required MRI-monitored infusion/injection programme, lecanemab or donanemab for real (if modest) disease-modifying slowing, with honest discussion of ARIA risk; (3) treat BPSD with non-drug measures first (the DICE approach), reserving SSRIs, brexpiprazole or (short-term, lowest-dose) other antipsychotics for standardised, risk-benefit-justified use, and actively avoiding benzodiazepines and anticholinergics; (4) proactively manage the real drivers of morbidity and mortality - dysphagia/aspiration risk, falls, delirium, sleep disturbance, caregiver burnout - and start advance-care-planning/palliative-care conversations early, because tube feeding has not been shown to prolong survival or improve outcomes in advanced dementia (Finucane TE et al., JAMA 1999;282:1365-1370) and comfort-focused, hand-feeding-based care is the evidence-based approach in that stage. This stepwise, honest package - not any single pill - is the real standard of care.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for Alzheimer's disease: symptomatic cognitive-enhancer drugs, disease-modifying anti-amyloid antibodies, behavioural/psychological symptom (BPSD) management, and management of the complications that actually drive morbidity, hospitalisation and death in dementia (dysphagia, falls, delirium, sleep disturbance, caregiver burden, and end-of-life care). Diagnostic biomarkers (CSF, PET, plasma p-tau217) are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms/diagnostic_framework entry and are not duplicated here.

ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.name: Donepezil - First-Line Cholinesterase Inhibitor for Mild-to-Moderate Alzheimer's Disease
specific_drugs: Donepezil (Aricept and generics, 5-10 mg once daily; 23 mg extended-release for moderate-severe disease)
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.effectiveness: Cochrane review (Birks JS, Harvey RJ, 2018 update, 30 trials): after 24-26 weeks, donepezil improved cognition on the ADAS-Cog (0-70 scale) by a mean of -2.67 points versus placebo (95% CI -3.31 to -2.02, 1130 participants, 5 studies) and produced small benefits in function and global clinical impression; the review rates this moderate-quality evidence of a real but small benefit across mild, moderate and severe AD. NICE technology appraisal TA217 recommends donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine as monotherapy options for managing mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.reason_why: AD involves substantial loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert (the main source of cortical acetylcholine), first described by Whitehouse et al in 1981-82, and this cholinergic deficit correlates with cognitive decline. Donepezil reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down synaptic acetylcholine, increasing cholinergic neurotransmission at surviving synapses and partially compensating for this deficit.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.important_caveat: The benefit is symptomatic and modest (a few points on a 70-point cognitive scale); donepezil does not alter the underlying amyloid/tau pathology or slow neurodegeneration. Common adverse effects are cholinergic (nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, muscle cramps, bradycardia/syncope in susceptible patients); caution is needed with concurrent bradycardia-causing drugs.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Start at the lowest dose (5 mg/day) and titrate to 10 mg/day after 4-6 weeks as tolerated; continue as long as the patient/family perceive net benefit and tolerability is acceptable, and do not withhold or stop it because 'it will only be a small effect' - the Cochrane-quantified small effect is real and NICE-endorsed.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.source: Birks JS, Harvey RJ, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;6:CD001190 (Cochrane Library, doi 10.1002/14651858.CD001190.pub3); NICE TA217 (nice.org.uk/guidance/ta217)

ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.name: Rivastigmine (Oral Capsule and Transdermal Patch) - Comparable Efficacy, Patch Reduces GI Side Effects
specific_drugs: Rivastigmine transdermal patch 4.6/9.5/13.3 mg/24h (Exelon Patch and generics)
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.effectiveness: Cochrane review (Birks JS et al 2015, 13 trials, 12-52 week duration): rivastigmine at higher oral doses (6-12 mg/day) produced clinically meaningful benefits on cognition and activities of daily living versus placebo, though at the cost of more cholinergic gastrointestinal adverse effects at those doses; the review found no difference between rivastigmine and placebo on behavioural change or carer burden as a group-level outcome. The IDEAL trial (1195 patients aged 50-85 with mild-to-moderate AD, 24 weeks, industry-sponsored) supported FDA approval of the transdermal patch, which delivers comparable plasma exposure and efficacy to the oral capsule with a better gastrointestinal tolerability profile, particularly at the 9.5 mg/24h patch dose.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.reason_why: Rivastigmine is a 'pseudo-irreversible' carbamate inhibitor of both acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (the second cholinesterase enzyme, which becomes relatively more important as AD progresses), giving broader cholinergic enhancement than a pure acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Continuous transdermal delivery avoids the peak plasma concentrations that drive oral-dose gastrointestinal side effects.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.important_caveat: Nausea and vomiting are dose-limiting with oral capsules, especially during up-titration; the patch reduces but does not eliminate this. Skin application-site reactions occur with the patch and rotation of application site is required.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Prefer the transdermal patch over oral capsules when gastrointestinal tolerability is a concern or when adherence with multiple daily oral doses is difficult (a common practical problem in dementia caregiving), titrating from the 4.6 mg/24h to 9.5 mg/24h patch after 4 weeks.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.source: Birks JS, Grimley Evans J, Iakovidou V et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;4:CD001191 (doi 10.1002/14651858.CD001191.pub4); IDEAL trial as summarised in FDA Exelon Patch approval record and rivastigmine transdermal systematic review, Expert Rev Neurother 2025 (doi 10.1080/14737175.2025.2527211)

ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.name: Galantamine - Consistent Cognitive Benefit, No Additional Benefit Above 16 mg/day
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.type: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with additional nicotinic-receptor-modulating activity
specific_drugs: Galantamine (Razadyne/Reminyl and generics; extended-release once-daily formulation available)
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.effectiveness: Cochrane review found galantamine produces consistent positive effects on cognition, function and behaviour over trials lasting 3-6 months, with no additional cognitive benefit from doses above 16 mg/day, and a rate of gastrointestinal adverse events similar to the other cholinesterase inhibitors. NICE TA217 recommends galantamine, alongside donepezil and rivastigmine, as a monotherapy option for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.reason_why: Galantamine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and additionally acts as an allosteric potentiating ligand at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, a proposed (though not conclusively proven to be clinically superior) second mechanism for enhancing cholinergic transmission.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.important_caveat: As with all cholinesterase inhibitors, the benefit is symptomatic, not disease-modifying, and gastrointestinal side effects limit up-titration in some patients.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Use as an alternative first-line cholinesterase inhibitor to donepezil/rivastigmine, titrating to but not beyond 16 mg/day (extended-release) since higher doses add side effects without added cognitive benefit.
ad_cholinesterase_inhibitors.source: Cochrane review of galantamine for Alzheimer's disease/mild cognitive impairment as summarised in NICE TA217 and the AAN/Cochrane cholinesterase-inhibitor evidence base

ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.name: Memantine Monotherapy - Moderate-to-Severe Alzheimer's Disease
specific_drugs: Memantine (Namenda and generics; 5 mg titrated weekly to 20 mg/day; extended-release once-daily formulation available)
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.effectiveness: NICE TA217 recommends memantine monotherapy for people with moderate Alzheimer's disease who are intolerant of or have a contraindication to cholinesterase inhibitors, and for people with severe Alzheimer's disease generally. Randomised trials in moderate-to-severe AD (e.g. the pivotal MEM-MD-02 trial in patients already stable on donepezil) show memantine produces significant benefits over placebo in cognition, function, behaviour and global clinical status.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.reason_why: In AD, chronic low-level glutamate excess causes sustained, pathological NMDA-receptor activation that is proposed to contribute to excitotoxic neuronal injury and to impair normal synaptic signal-to-noise discrimination. Memantine blocks the NMDA receptor in a voltage-dependent, low-affinity manner that preferentially blocks this pathological tonic activation while allowing normal, high-amplitude synaptic (learning-related) NMDA signalling to proceed - a mechanistically distinct approach from cholinesterase inhibition.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.important_caveat: Generally well tolerated; dizziness, headache and constipation are the most common adverse effects. It is not indicated as monotherapy for mild AD, where cholinesterase inhibitors are preferred.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.real_working_solution: Use memantine as the primary symptomatic agent once AD reaches the moderate-severe stage, either alone (if a cholinesterase inhibitor is not tolerated) or added to an existing cholinesterase inhibitor.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.source: NICE TA217 (nice.org.uk/guidance/ta217); MEM-MD-02 trial as summarised in Tariot PN et al., JAMA 2004;291:317-324 and subsequent combination-therapy analyses

ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.name: Memantine + Donepezil Combination Therapy - Real Trial Evidence, but No Proven Added Benefit Over Donepezil Alone
specific_drugs: Memantine + Donepezil (fixed-dose combination: Namzaric; or the two drugs prescribed separately)
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.effectiveness: The DOMINO-AD trial (a 2x2 factorial RCT in patients already on donepezil with moderate-severe AD) and pooled meta-analyses of acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor-plus-memantine combinations found that continuing donepezil (with or without adding memantine) was more cost-effective than stopping donepezil, but found NO significant additional cognitive/functional benefit of adding memantine to donepezil over donepezil alone at the group level - i.e. combination therapy is not proven superior to donepezil monotherapy, even though earlier single trials (e.g. MEM-MD-02, which specifically added memantine to donepezil-stable patients) had shown a positive combination effect versus donepezil-plus-placebo.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.reason_why: Cholinergic enhancement (donepezil) and NMDA-receptor modulation (memantine) are mechanistically complementary in principle, which is why the combination was tested, but the group-level trial evidence has not consistently shown the combination beats donepezil alone.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.important_caveat: This is a genuinely mixed evidence picture (positive in some trials, null in DOMINO-AD and pooled analyses); the honest summary is 'reasonable to consider in an individual patient, not proven superior as a routine strategy'.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.real_working_solution: Reasonable to add memantine to an existing cholinesterase inhibitor in moderate-severe disease on a trial basis with individual reassessment, but do not present the combination to families as guaranteed to outperform a single agent - the trial evidence does not support that claim as a population-level fact.
ad_nmda_antagonist_memantine.source: DOMINO-AD trial cost-effectiveness/efficacy analyses, PMC5724694/PMC5316146 lineage; meta-analysis of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors combined with memantine for moderate-to-severe AD, Swiss Med Wkly (smw.ch); Howard R et al. (DOMINO-AD), N Engl J Med 2012;366:893-903

ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.name: Lecanemab (Leqembi) - Anti-Amyloid Monoclonal Antibody, Real Modest Disease-Modifying Slowing in Early AD
ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.type: Humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody against amyloid-beta protofibrils
specific_drugs: Lecanemab-irmb (Leqembi) IV infusion 10 mg/kg every 2 weeks; Leqembi IQLIK subcutaneous autoinjector 360 mg once weekly for maintenance dosing after 18 months of IV therapy
ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.effectiveness: CLARITY-AD (phase 3, 1795 participants with MCI due to AD or mild AD dementia, confirmed amyloid pathology, 18 months, randomised stratified by APOE4 status): lecanemab reduced decline on the CDR-Sum-of-Boxes by 27% versus placebo (treatment difference -0.45, P=0.00005); it slowed ADCOMS decline by 24% and slowed loss of activities of daily living (ADCS MCI-ADL) by 37%, all at 18 months. The FDA converted its accelerated approval to traditional approval in July 2023 on the strength of this confirmatory trial. On 29 August 2025 the FDA approved the LEQEMBI IQLIK subcutaneous autoinjector (360 mg/1.8 mL, administered in about 15 seconds) for once-weekly maintenance dosing after the initial 18 months of biweekly IV infusion, giving patients an at-home dosing option; it launched in the US on 6 October 2025.
ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.reason_why: Lecanemab binds soluble amyloid-beta protofibrils (a proposed neurotoxic aggregation intermediate) with high selectivity and clears cerebral amyloid on PET; because CLARITY-AD showed a real slowing of clinical decline that tracked with amyloid removal, it is read by many in the field as evidence supporting a causal (though not necessarily sole) role for amyloid-beta in driving progression, addressing part of the honest amyloid-cascade-hypothesis debate covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry.
ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.important_caveat: ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) occurred in a substantial minority: ARIA-E (oedema/effusion) in 12.6% and ARIA-H (microhaemorrhage/haemosiderosis) in 17.3% of the lecanemab group; both ARIA-E and ARIA-H were more frequent, and clinically more severe, in APOE-e4 carriers, with the highest risk in e4/e4 homozygotes versus heterozygotes versus non-carriers - which is why APOE genotyping before starting therapy and a scheduled MRI monitoring programme (baseline plus periodic surveillance scans during the highest-risk early dosing period) are required parts of appropriate use, not optional add-ons. Eligibility is restricted to confirmed amyloid-positive MCI or mild AD dementia - it is not indicated for moderate/severe AD or for amyloid-negative patients. As of this research (September 2026) no CDSCO approval or import licence for lecanemab was located; its availability in India could not be verified.
ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.real_working_solution: Offer lecanemab to appropriately selected patients (confirmed amyloid pathology, MCI or mild AD dementia, informed of ARIA risk and able to attend the required infusion/injection and MRI monitoring schedule), with APOE4 genotyping used to counsel on individualised ARIA risk rather than as an automatic exclusion.
ad_anti_amyloid_lecanemab.source: van Dyck CH et al. (CLARITY-AD), N Engl J Med 2023;388:9-21; FDA traditional approval announcement 2023; Eisai FDA approval release for LEQEMBI IQLIK subcutaneous autoinjector, 29 August 2025 (eisai.com/news/2025/news202559.html); Medscape/Pharmacy Times/AJMC coverage of the 2025 subcutaneous approval

ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.name: Donanemab (Kisunla) - Anti-Amyloid Monoclonal Antibody, Larger Slowing in the Earliest (Low-Tau) Stage
ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.type: Humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody against pyroglutamate-modified, plaque-specific amyloid-beta
specific_drugs: Donanemab-azbx (Kisunla) IV infusion 700 mg for first 3 doses then 1400 mg every 4 weeks
ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.effectiveness: TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (phase 3, 1736 participants with early symptomatic AD - MCI or mild dementia - confirmed amyloid AND tau pathology, 18 months): in the combined population donanemab slowed decline on CDR-SB by 29% and on the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) by 22% versus placebo. In the pre-specified low/medium-tau subgroup (the earliest-stage participants), the slowing was substantially larger - roughly 60% on some measures - and a meaningful proportion of these earliest-stage participants showed no measurable clinical progression at one year, the strongest single signal in the anti-amyloid antibody trials that treating earlier in the disease course produces a larger effect. The FDA approved donanemab in July 2024 based on these results.
ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.reason_why: Donanemab selectively targets a pyroglutamate-modified form of amyloid-beta found specifically in already-formed insoluble plaques (rather than soluble protofibrils, lecanemab's target), which produces very rapid and near-complete plaque clearance on amyloid PET in responders; TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 used a novel tau-PET-based, response-driven dosing strategy (stopping antibody infusions once plaque clearance was achieved) rather than fixed-duration dosing.
ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.important_caveat: ARIA rates were numerically higher than with lecanemab: ARIA-E occurred in 24% and ARIA-H in 31.4% of the donanemab group (versus 13.6% ARIA-H on placebo); most cases were mild-to-moderate and asymptomatic, but 1.6% of participants had serious ARIA, and ARIA-attributed deaths were reported in the trial, underscoring that this is a real, not theoretical, safety signal requiring the same APOE genotyping and MRI-monitoring discipline as lecanemab. As of this research (September 2026) no CDSCO approval or import licence for donanemab was located; its availability in India could not be verified.
ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.real_working_solution: Offer donanemab to appropriately selected, amyloid-and-tau-confirmed early AD patients under the same APOE-genotyping-plus-scheduled-MRI-monitoring framework as lecanemab, counselling that starting treatment as early in the biomarker-confirmed disease course as possible produced the largest observed benefit in the pivotal trial.
ad_anti_amyloid_donanemab.source: Sims JR et al. (TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2), JAMA 2023;330:512-527 (PMID 37459141); Eli Lilly investor release on TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 topline results; TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 long-term extension results, 2025-2026 (PMID 41330788)

ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.name: Aducanumab (Aduhelm) - Historical Entry Only: Controversial Accelerated Approval, Discontinued 2024
ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.type: Humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody against aggregated amyloid-beta (historical, no longer marketed)
ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.effectiveness: Aducanumab received FDA accelerated approval in June 2021 based on its ability to reduce amyloid plaque (a surrogate biomarker), despite its two pivotal phase 3 trials (ENGAGE and EMERGE) giving conflicting clinical results - one trial was stopped for futility and the other showed a modest positive signal - which made the clinical-benefit evidence far weaker and more contested than for lecanemab or donanemab. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) restricted reimbursement in April 2022 to patients enrolled in qualifying clinical trials, which effectively prevented meaningful real-world uptake.
ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.reason_why: Same anti-amyloid mechanism class as lecanemab/donanemab (binds aggregated amyloid-beta), but approved on a biomarker surrogate without the same strength of confirmed clinical-benefit data.
ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.important_caveat: On 31 January 2024 Biogen announced it was discontinuing aducanumab, with production ending in November 2024; the company stated explicitly that this was to reprioritise resources toward Leqembi (lecanemab) and other pipeline candidates, NOT because of a new safety or efficacy finding. It should not be prescribed or recommended today - it is documented here only for historical completeness and honesty about the field's trial record.
ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.real_working_solution: Not applicable as a current treatment option; patients previously on aducanumab were transitioned off it by May-November 2024 depending on trial-vs-prescription status, per Biogen's discontinuation timeline.
ad_anti_amyloid_aducanumab_historical.source: Biogen discontinuation announcement, 31 January 2024 (alz.org/news/2024/alzheimers-drug-aducanumab-aduhelm-discontinued; CNN, 31 Jan 2024); CMS national coverage determination, April 2022

ad_bpsd_nonpharmacologic_first_line.name: The DICE Approach (Describe-Investigate-Create-Evaluate) - Real, Guideline-Endorsed Non-Drug First-Line Framework for BPSD
specific_drugs: Not applicable (non-drug; structured caregiver/clinician behavioural-assessment protocol)
ad_bpsd_nonpharmacologic_first_line.effectiveness: The DICE approach (developed by Kales, Gitlin and Lyketsos) structures behavioural symptom management into four steps - Describe the specific behaviour and its context, Investigate medical/environmental/caregiver contributors, Create an individualised non-drug treatment plan, Evaluate whether it is working - and is endorsed by AAN/AGS/APA consensus guidance as the recommended first-line approach: clinicians should prescribe psychotropic drugs only after meaningful non-drug efforts have been tried, except when severe depression, psychosis or aggression pose an immediate safety risk.
ad_bpsd_nonpharmacologic_first_line.reason_why: Most BPSD (agitation, wandering, resistance to care) is triggered or worsened by an identifiable, modifiable proximate cause - pain, an unmet need, overstimulation/understimulation, a caregiving approach that provokes distress, or an underlying medical problem such as infection or constipation - so systematically finding and correcting that cause treats the behaviour at its source rather than only sedating the symptom.
ad_bpsd_nonpharmacologic_first_line.important_caveat: Requires trained, consistent caregiver/clinician engagement and time; it is not a quick fix and does not replace urgent pharmacological intervention when there is immediate danger to the patient or others.
ad_bpsd_nonpharmacologic_first_line.real_working_solution: Use DICE as the default first response to any new or worsening BPSD, reserving the pharmacological options below for behaviours that remain severe, dangerous or highly distressing after a genuine non-drug attempt.
ad_bpsd_nonpharmacologic_first_line.source: Kales HC, Gitlin LN, Lyketsos CG, 'Management of neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia in clinical settings: recommendations from a multidisciplinary expert panel', J Am Geriatr Soc 2014;62:762-769; Psychiatric News/Psychopharmacology Institute summaries of the DICE approach (diceapproach.com)

ad_bpsd_ssri_management.name: Citalopram for Agitation (CitAD Trial) - Real Efficacy, Real QTc-Prolongation Risk
specific_drugs: Citalopram (used off-label for AD agitation, at doses studied up to 30 mg/day)
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.effectiveness: CitAD (186 AD patients with moderate-severe agitation, US/Canada, JAMA 2014): 40% of citalopram-treated participants had moderate-or-marked improvement in agitation versus 26% on placebo (odds ratio 2.13, 95% CI 1.23-3.69, P=0.007) - a real, statistically significant benefit.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.reason_why: Serotonergic dysregulation is implicated in agitation and irritability in dementia; SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin availability, which is proposed to reduce agitation independent of any antidepressant effect.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.important_caveat: The same CitAD trial found a clinically important QTc-prolongation signal: citalopram increased QTc by 18.1 ms more than placebo by week 3 (95% CI 6.1-30.1, P=0.004), with more participants having a rise of 30 ms or more (7 vs 1). This is exactly why the FDA had already capped citalopram at 20 mg/day in patients over 60 for QT reasons, and it means baseline/follow-up ECG and avoidance of other QT-prolonging drugs are required before and during use for agitation, at a dose (30 mg/day) above the FDA's usual elderly cap.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.real_working_solution: Reserve for agitation not controlled by non-drug measures, checking baseline ECG/electrolytes and avoiding co-prescription of other QT-prolonging drugs; citalopram is a real, effective, but cardiac-risk-bearing option, not a risk-free 'just an antidepressant' choice.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.source: Porsteinsson AP et al. (CitAD), JAMA 2014;311:682-691; Porsteinsson AP et al., 'Changes in QTc Interval in the CitAD Randomized Trial', PLoS ONE 2014;9:e98426 (PMC4051660)

ad_bpsd_ssri_management.name: Sertraline for Depression in Alzheimer's Disease (DIADS-2) - Real Negative Trial, Honestly Reported
specific_drugs: Sertraline (commonly used off-label for depression/anxiety in AD despite this negative trial)
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.effectiveness: DIADS-2 (131 patients meeting criteria for depression of Alzheimer's disease, 24-week randomised multicentre trial, target dose 100 mg/day) found NO significant treatment effect of sertraline on depression outcomes at 12 or 24 weeks, and no benefit even in the subgroup meeting major- versus minor-depression criteria.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.reason_why: Depression in AD may have a distinct pathophysiology (neurodegeneration-driven rather than purely monoaminergic) from depression in cognitively normal people, which may explain why a drug class effective in primary depression did not separate from placebo here.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.important_caveat: This is a genuine negative trial for a commonly prescribed off-label use; it does not mean SSRIs are never appropriate in AD (citalopram has real trial-proven benefit for agitation, above), but it means clinicians should not assume sertraline will treat comorbid depression in AD on this evidence.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.real_working_solution: Do not rely on sertraline monotherapy as a proven fix for depression in AD; treat depression symptoms with a broader approach (non-drug measures, treating pain/isolation/unmet needs per DICE, and individualised trial with close monitoring) rather than presenting an SSRI as guideline-proven for this specific indication.
ad_bpsd_ssri_management.source: Rosenberg PB et al. (DIADS-2), Am J Psychiatry 2010;167:136-145 (PubMed 20087081); DIADS-2 study coordinating centre (jhuccs1.us/diads2)

ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.name: Brexpiprazole (Rexulti) - First and Only FDA-Approved Drug Specifically for Agitation in Alzheimer's Dementia
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.effectiveness: FDA approved brexpiprazole on 10 May 2023 specifically for agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer's disease - the first and only drug with this specific approved indication in the US. Two phase 3, 12-week, randomised, placebo-controlled fixed-dose trials showed brexpiprazole reduced agitation symptoms by 31% compared with placebo, with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement confirmed in the full published Study 213 results in JAMA Neurology.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.reason_why: Brexpiprazole's partial agonist activity at serotonin 5-HT1A and dopamine D2 receptors and antagonist activity at 5-HT2A and noradrenergic alpha-1B/2C receptors is proposed to dampen the dopaminergic/serotonergic circuit hyperactivity underlying agitation while producing less sedation/extrapyramidal burden than older antipsychotics.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.important_caveat: It carries the same class-wide boxed warning as every antipsychotic used in elderly dementia patients (see ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid below): increased risk of death, mainly from cardiovascular or infectious causes, versus placebo in this population. It is FDA-approved for this specific indication (unlike risperidone, which is not), but the mortality-risk boxed warning still applies and use should be time-limited and at the lowest effective dose with regular reassessment for taper.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.real_working_solution: Use brexpiprazole (rather than an off-label antipsychotic) when agitation is severe/dangerous and has not responded to DICE-based non-drug measures, at the lowest effective dose, with a planned reassessment/taper, and with the mortality risk explicitly discussed with the family.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.source: Otsuka/Lundbeck FDA approval announcement, 10 May 2023; Alzheimer's Association statement on FDA approval of brexpiprazole (alz.org/news/2023); JAMA Neurology publication of full Study 213 results

ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.name: Risperidone (Off-Label) for Severe Agitation/Psychosis - Real Modest Efficacy, Not FDA-Approved for This Use
specific_drugs: Risperidone (used off-label for severe agitation/psychosis in AD)
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.effectiveness: Risperidone has real, modest trial-supported efficacy for severe agitation and psychosis in dementia and is the most extensively studied antipsychotic in this population, but it is explicitly NOT FDA-approved for dementia-related psychosis/agitation; its own US label states this directly.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.reason_why: Dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptor antagonism reduces psychotic symptoms and agitation, the same general mechanism shared by other atypical antipsychotics used off-label in this population.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.important_caveat: In April 2005 the FDA issued a black-box warning, based on a meta-analysis of 17 placebo-controlled trials in 5,377 elderly dementia patients, that atypical antipsychotics as a class carry a 1.6-1.7-fold increased risk of death (approximately 4.5% vs 2.6% mortality), mostly from cardiovascular events (heart failure, sudden death) or infection (pneumonia); this warning was extended to first-generation (typical) antipsychotics such as haloperidol three years later. 'RISPERDAL is not approved for use in patients with dementia-related psychosis' is stated in its own FDA label.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.real_working_solution: Reserve for severe, dangerous psychosis/agitation unresponsive to non-drug measures and to FDA-approved brexpiprazole, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration, with the boxed mortality warning explicitly disclosed and documented as part of informed consent.
ad_bpsd_antipsychotics.source: FDA black-box warning for atypical antipsychotics in dementia, April 2005, as summarised in Psychiatric News (psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/pn.43.14.0001); risperidone (Risperdal) FDA label (accessdata.fda.gov)

ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.name: Pimavanserin (Nuplazid) for Dementia-Related/Alzheimer's Psychosis - Real, Honest Regulatory Failure
ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.type: 5-HT2A inverse agonist/antagonist (approved ONLY for a different, narrower indication)
specific_drugs: Pimavanserin (Nuplazid) - FDA-approved only for hallucinations/delusions in Parkinson's disease psychosis, NOT for Alzheimer's/dementia-related psychosis
ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.effectiveness: The HARMONY trial supported a 2020 supplemental application for the broader indication of 'dementia-related psychosis', but on 5 April 2021 the FDA declined to approve it, stating the positive HARMONY result appeared to be driven mainly by the Parkinson's-disease-dementia subgroup rather than by Alzheimer's disease or other dementia subtypes, and that the trial was not large enough across subgroups to support approval. Acadia resubmitted for the narrower Alzheimer's-disease-psychosis indication in February 2022; an FDA advisory committee voted 9-3 on 17 June 2022 that the evidence did not show effectiveness for this specific indication, and the FDA formally declined approval on 5 August 2022, recommending an additional dedicated trial.
ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.reason_why: 5-HT2A inverse agonism is a genuinely distinct, non-dopamine-blocking mechanism (which is why it remains a real option in Parkinson's disease psychosis, where dopamine-blocking antipsychotics are dangerous), but the AD/dementia-related-psychosis clinical evidence specifically has not met the FDA's effectiveness bar twice.
ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.important_caveat: This is a genuine, twice-repeated regulatory rejection for Alzheimer's/dementia-related psychosis specifically - it should not be presented to patients/families as an approved or evidence-proven option for AD psychosis.
ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.real_working_solution: Do not use pimavanserin for Alzheimer's-disease psychosis outside a clinical trial; it remains an approved, real option specifically for Parkinson's disease psychosis (cross-reference this knowledge base's parkinsons_disease entry), where its non-dopamine-blocking mechanism is a genuine advantage.
ad_bpsd_pimavanserin_status.source: Acadia Pharmaceuticals Complete Response Letter announcements, 5 April 2021 and 5 August 2022 (acadia.com/en-us/media/news-releases); Medscape 'FDA Panel Rejects Pimavanserin for Alzheimer's Psychosis'; Alzheimer Europe news coverage of both rejections

ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.name: Medications to Actively AVOID in Alzheimer's Disease - Benzodiazepines, Anticholinergics, and the Beers Criteria
ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.type: Negative/avoidance guidance (not a treatment, a real safety framework)
specific_drugs: Benzodiazepines (e.g. lorazepam, alprazolam, diazepam) - avoid routine use
Anticholinergic bladder antimuscarinics (e.g. oxybutynin) - avoid where alternatives exist
Antipsychotics generally - see boxed-warning entry above; use only when clearly justified
ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.effectiveness: The American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria explicitly lists benzodiazepines and strongly anticholinergic drugs as potentially inappropriate in older adults with dementia/cognitive impairment because they worsen cognition, increase fall and fracture risk, and can precipitate delirium; this is a consensus safety framework rather than a single randomised trial, but it is the standard, guideline-level basis for deprescribing decisions in dementia care.
ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.reason_why: Benzodiazepines cause sedation, worsen memory encoding and increase fall/hip-fracture and paradoxical-agitation risk in a brain already vulnerable from neurodegeneration; anticholinergic drugs directly antagonise the cholinergic system that cholinesterase inhibitors are trying to support, so they work pharmacologically against the disease's own symptomatic treatment.
ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.important_caveat: Short-term, carefully monitored benzodiazepine use may still be justified for acute severe distress or specific procedures, but routine/chronic use for agitation or insomnia should be actively avoided and existing prescriptions reviewed for deprescribing.
ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.real_working_solution: Perform medication reconciliation at every visit specifically looking for benzodiazepines, anticholinergics and unnecessary antipsychotics, and deprescribe them using a structured taper, replacing them with the DICE non-drug approach and, where truly needed, the FDA-approved or trial-supported options above.
ad_bpsd_medications_to_avoid.source: American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (updated editions); standard reversible-dementia/confused-elderly-patient medication-review literature cited in this knowledge base's differential_dementias_and_reversible_causes symptoms entry

ad_sleep_disturbance_management.name: Suvorexant - Only Drug With a Dedicated Phase 3 Trial for Insomnia Specifically in Alzheimer's Disease
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.effectiveness: In a dedicated phase 3 polysomnography trial (285 participants aged 50-90 with mild-moderate AD dementia and insomnia), suvorexant met its primary and secondary efficacy endpoints: total sleep time improved by 28.2 minutes versus placebo and wake-after-sleep-onset improved by about 16 minutes, over 4 weeks. The FDA approved an expanded indication for suvorexant for insomnia specifically in people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease dementia on this basis.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.reason_why: Orexin (hypocretin) neurons promote wakefulness; suvorexant blocks both orexin receptor subtypes, reducing wake-drive to allow sleep onset and maintenance, a mechanism distinct from GABA-ergic sedative-hypnotics.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.important_caveat: Falls were numerically more common with suvorexant than placebo (2% vs 0%) in the trial, alongside somnolence (4% vs 1%) and dry mouth; fall risk must be weighed given how much falls already matter in dementia.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.real_working_solution: Prefer suvorexant over benzodiazepine or non-benzodiazepine 'Z-drug' sedative-hypnotics for AD-associated insomnia, since it has dedicated positive AD-specific trial evidence and avoids the benzodiazepine-class cognitive/fall risks flagged above, while still monitoring for its own fall-risk signal.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.source: Merck FDA approval release, suvorexant phase 3 AD-dementia insomnia trial (merck.com news release); Practical Neurology/AASM/NeurologyLive coverage of the FDA expanded indication

ad_sleep_disturbance_management.name: Trazodone for Agitation/Sleep - Real, Honestly Insufficient Evidence Base
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.type: Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI), sedating antidepressant, used off-label
specific_drugs: Trazodone (widely used off-label for sleep/agitation in dementia, typically 25-150 mg at night)
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.effectiveness: A Cochrane review (Martinon-Torres G et al) concluded there is insufficient evidence to recommend trazodone for BPSD, based on only two small trials of differing design (16 and 6 weeks); some smaller individual trials found trazodone improved agitation versus placebo in institutionalised AD patients, and a head-to-head trial found trazodone had efficacy for agitation similar to haloperidol but was better tolerated.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.reason_why: Trazodone's antihistaminic and serotonergic-antagonist sedative properties promote sleep and may reduce agitation through sedation and mood effects, without the dopamine-receptor-blocking mortality signal of antipsychotics.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.important_caveat: The evidence base is genuinely thin and mixed - this is honestly reported as 'commonly used, plausibly helpful in individual patients, but not proven at the level of a Cochrane-endorsed treatment'; orthostatic hypotension and falls are real risks in this population.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.real_working_solution: A reasonable low-risk trial option for sleep/mild agitation once non-drug measures and suvorexant (for insomnia specifically) have been considered, precisely because its mortality/safety profile is more favourable than antipsychotics even though its efficacy evidence is weaker.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.source: Martinon-Torres G, Fioravanti M, Grimley Evans J, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004:CD004990; comparative trazodone-vs-haloperidol trial, Int J Geriatr Psychiatry (PubMed 9169246)

ad_sleep_disturbance_management.name: Melatonin for Sleep-Wake Disturbance - Real, Honestly Weak/Inconsistent Evidence
specific_drugs: Melatonin (over-the-counter in most markets; prolonged-release formulations studied in related neurodegenerative sleep disorders)
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.effectiveness: Evidence specifically for melatonin improving sleep-wake disturbance in Alzheimer's disease is weak and inconsistent across small trials; by contrast, a dedicated randomised trial of prolonged-release melatonin 4 mg for REM sleep behaviour disorder in Parkinson's disease (a related neurodegenerative population, cross-referenced in this knowledge base's parkinsons_disease entry) found NO benefit (3.4 vs 3.6 RBD events/week, P=0.92).
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.reason_why: Melatonin normally signals circadian phase to the suprachiasmatic nucleus; endogenous melatonin secretion is disrupted in AD, which is the physiological rationale for supplementation, but restoring the signal exogenously has not reliably translated into a proven clinical sleep benefit in this specific population.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.important_caveat: Very low risk profile is its main practical advantage, but families should be told honestly that the evidence for meaningful benefit in AD-specific sleep disturbance is weak, not that it is a proven fix.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.real_working_solution: Reasonable to trial given its very low risk before escalating to suvorexant or trazodone, but do not oversell expected benefit; the negative PD-RBD trial in a closely related neurodegenerative population is the clearest randomised signal available and it was negative.
ad_sleep_disturbance_management.source: Gilat M et al. (PD melatonin/RBD negative trial), Mov Disord 2020;35:344-349 (PMID 31674060); general AD-sleep-disturbance melatonin evidence summarised in dementia sleep-management reviews

ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.name: Oral Assisted Feeding and Careful Hand-Feeding - The Real Evidence-Based Alternative to Tube Feeding in Advanced Dementia
specific_drugs: Not applicable (feeding technique/care protocol, not a drug)
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.effectiveness: The foundational Finucane TE et al systematic review (JAMA 1999) found NO published randomised trial evidence that percutaneous feeding tubes prevent aspiration pneumonia, prolong survival, reduce pressure sores/infection risk, improve function, or provide palliation in advanced dementia; of seven observational controlled studies examined, none showed a survival benefit for tube feeding. This finding has been repeatedly reaffirmed and underlies the American Academy of Family Physicians' Choosing Wisely recommendation: 'Don't insert percutaneous feeding tubes in individuals with advanced dementia. Instead, offer oral assisted feeding.'
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.reason_why: Dysphagia and aspiration risk in advanced dementia stem from generalised cortical/brainstem-coordinated swallowing dysfunction and progressive frailty, problems a feeding tube bypasses mechanically but does not treat; tube feeding does not prevent reflux/aspiration of gastric or oral secretions and carries its own complication burden (tube-site infection, need for physical/chemical restraint, no reduction in aspiration risk).
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.important_caveat: This is a genuinely difficult, emotionally loaded decision for families; the evidence supports NOT defaulting to a feeding tube, but this requires careful, compassionate advance discussion (see ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_care below), not a purely clinical directive delivered without support.
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.real_working_solution: In advanced dementia with dysphagia, use careful hand-feeding with texture-modified diets and a trained caregiver/speech-language-therapy-guided feeding technique as the evidence-based default, reserving feeding-tube discussion for reversible, non-advanced-dementia causes of dysphagia.
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.source: Finucane TE, Christmas C, Travis K, 'Tube feeding in patients with advanced dementia: a review of the evidence', JAMA 1999;282:1365-1370 (PMID 10527184); AAFP Choosing Wisely recommendation on percutaneous feeding tubes (aafp.org/pubs/afp/collections/choosing-wisely/94.html)

ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.name: Aspiration Pneumonia Prevention - Oral Care, Positioning and Swallowing Assessment
specific_drugs: Not applicable (oral hygiene protocols, upright positioning during/after meals, texture-modified diets, speech-language-therapy swallowing assessment)
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.effectiveness: Aspiration pneumonia was implicated in 115,284 deaths among over-65s with AD in a 22-year US retrospective analysis (cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms/late_stage_and_functional_decline entry); this makes systematic prevention (rather than only treating pneumonia once it occurs) a high-value, if less dramatic, treatment-side intervention.
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.reason_why: Oral bacterial colonisation plus impaired airway-protective reflexes (cough, swallow coordination) is the mechanistic pathway from dysphagia to aspiration pneumonia; reducing oral bacterial load and keeping the patient upright during and after oral intake reduces both the inoculum and the mechanical risk of aspiration.
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.important_caveat: No single randomised trial in this specific knowledge-base research pass quantified a precise percentage reduction from a combined oral-care-plus-positioning bundle in AD specifically; this entry is graded moderate confidence and stated as a logical, widely-recommended bundle rather than as a single verified numeric effect size.
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.real_working_solution: Build routine oral hygiene, upright positioning for all oral intake, and a low threshold for formal swallowing (speech-language pathology) assessment into every advanced-AD care plan, rather than waiting for a first aspiration pneumonia episode to trigger these measures.
ad_dysphagia_nutrition_aspiration_preven.source: Aspiration pneumonia mortality data cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms entry (Neurology 2025 conference abstract, P3-11.010); general aspiration-prevention nursing-care literature

ad_falls_prevention.name: Exercise-Based Fall-Prevention Interventions in Cognitive Impairment/Dementia - Real, Honestly Modest and Fragile Evidence
ad_falls_prevention.effectiveness: A systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise-based fall-prevention interventions in community-dwelling older adults with cognitive impairment (9 RCTs, 1411 participants, mean age 78) found a statistically significant approximately 30% reduction in the RATE of falls (incidence rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.52-0.95), but honestly notes this was driven by only 4 of 12 comparisons and became non-significant when the most-effective studies were removed (low certainty evidence); exercise had NO significant effect on the number of PEOPLE who fell at least once (risk ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.90-1.14).
ad_falls_prevention.reason_why: Structured balance/strength/gait exercise improves postural control and lower-limb strength, which are proposed mechanisms for reducing fall frequency even when it cannot be expected to prevent every individual fall, given that dementia itself impairs gait/attention/executive control over balance.
ad_falls_prevention.important_caveat: This is a genuinely fragile, low-certainty evidence base - report it honestly as 'a real but modest and statistically fragile reduction in fall RATE, not a proven reduction in the proportion of people who fall', not as a strong guaranteed benefit.
ad_falls_prevention.real_working_solution: Offer structured, supervised balance/strength exercise as part of a falls-prevention plan in early-to-moderate dementia (where participation is feasible), combined with home-safety assessment and medication review (removing sedatives/anticholinergics, above) as the practical fall-reduction package, rather than relying on exercise alone.
ad_falls_prevention.source: 'Efficacy of exercise-based interventions in preventing falls among community-dwelling older persons with cognitive impairment: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis', Age and Ageing 2021;50:1557-1565 (academic.oup.com/ageing)

ad_delirium_prevention.name: Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) - Real, Trial-Proven Multicomponent Delirium Prevention
specific_drugs: Not applicable (structured protocol addressing cognitive impairment, sleep deprivation, immobility, visual/hearing impairment and dehydration)
ad_delirium_prevention.effectiveness: The original controlled clinical trial of HELP (Inouye SK et al, 852 hospitalised patients aged 70+) reduced the incidence of delirium by 40% by systematically identifying and intervening on six modifiable delirium risk factors using a trained interdisciplinary team and volunteers; HELP has since been implemented in more than 200 hospitals worldwide and is a standard recommended intervention for hospitalised dementia patients, who are at particularly high delirium risk.
ad_delirium_prevention.reason_why: Delirium in a hospitalised dementia patient is a superimposed, usually multifactorial acute confusional state (infection, drug toxicity, dehydration, sensory deprivation, sleep disruption, immobility); systematically correcting each of these modifiable contributors reduces the cumulative risk of tipping a vulnerable, already cognitively impaired brain into delirium.
ad_delirium_prevention.important_caveat: This is a hospital-system-level intervention requiring trained staff/volunteers, not a bedside drug order; its benefit is for PREVENTING delirium in hospitalised dementia patients, and this knowledge base's red_flags/symptoms entry already covers recognising delirium once it has occurred as a mimic of AD progression.
ad_delirium_prevention.real_working_solution: Any hospital admitting a person with Alzheimer's disease should apply a HELP-type protocol (or equivalent local delirium-prevention pathway) proactively, rather than only reacting once delirium has developed.
ad_delirium_prevention.source: Inouye SK et al., 'A Multicomponent Intervention to Prevent Delirium in Hospitalized Older Patients', N Engl J Med 1999;340:669-676; Commonwealth Fund summary of the Hospital Elder Life Program

ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.name: REACH II Structured Caregiver Intervention - Real Trial-Proven Reduction in Caregiver Burden
specific_drugs: Not applicable (in-home/telephone caregiver-support sessions addressing safety, self-care, social support, problem behaviours, and mood)
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.effectiveness: REACH II (Resources for Enhancing Alzheimer's Caregiver Health II), a randomised multisite trial of 495 dementia caregiver-care-recipient dyads across 5 US cities and 3 ethnic groups (Hispanic, white, African American), delivered 9 in-home plus 3 telephone sessions over 6 months versus brief check-in calls; intervention caregivers reported significantly better self-rated health, sleep quality, physical health and emotional health, with less burden, at 6 months, and this benefit was consistent across the three ethnic groups studied.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.reason_why: Caregiver burden and burnout in AD directly affect the quality and safety of care the patient receives and are a leading driver of premature nursing-home placement; a structured programme addressing the caregiver's own health, safety knowledge and coping skills is therefore itself a real treatment-side intervention for the patient's overall care trajectory, not only a caregiver-welfare measure.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.important_caveat: Requires trained interventionists and a structured multi-session delivery model; unstructured, informal 'caregiver advice' has not been shown to reproduce this benefit.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.real_working_solution: Refer every identified primary caregiver to a structured REACH-II-model programme (or local equivalent, e.g. Alzheimer's Association / ARDSI-affiliated caregiver-support services in India) as a standard part of the treatment plan, not an optional afterthought.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.source: Belle SH et al. (REACH II), Ann Intern Med 2006;145:727-738; 'Enhancing Caregiver Health: Findings from the REACH II Intervention', J Am Geriatr Soc 2009/PMC2819276

ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.name: Caregiver Burden - Real Scale of the Problem (Why This Matters as Much as Any Drug)
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.type: Epidemiological/health-economic context (not a treatment itself, but the case for treating the caregiver)
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.effectiveness: An estimated 11.46 million unpaid Alzheimer's/dementia caregivers in the US in 2023 provided about 18.4 billion hours of unpaid care (valued at roughly $347 billion); the total lifetime cost of care for a person with dementia was estimated at $405,262 (2024 dollars), about 70% of which falls on family caregivers as unpaid care and out-of-pocket costs; 70% of dementia caregivers report that coordinating care is itself stressful (US-specific figures, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms/natural_history entry).
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.reason_why: This scale of burden is the real-world reason caregiver-support interventions (REACH II above) and non-drug BPSD management (DICE above) are treatment-side priorities, not optional extras, in Alzheimer's disease management.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.important_caveat: These are US-specific figures and are not extrapolated to India, where separate (and less complete) caregiver-burden data exist.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.real_working_solution: Explicitly budget clinical time and referral pathways for caregiver support at every visit, treating caregiver wellbeing as a measurable component of the patient's own care quality.
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.source: '2024 Alzheimer's disease facts and figures', Alzheimers Dement 2024 (PMID 38689398); Alzheimer's Association 2024 caregiver-burden report
ad_caregiver_support_and_safety_planning.confidence: high for the US figures cited

ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.name: Early Advance Care Planning and Palliative-Care Integration in Alzheimer's Disease
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.type: Structured advance-care-planning and palliative-care process (not a drug)
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.effectiveness: Mitchell SL et al. (323 nursing-home residents with advanced dementia followed 18 months, N Engl J Med 2009) found that 54.8% died within 18 months, with pneumonia (probability 41.1%), febrile episodes (52.6%) and eating problems (85.8%) as common complications; 6-month mortality after pneumonia was 46.7%. Distressing symptoms (dyspnoea 46.0%, pain 39.1%) were common, and 40.7% of residents underwent at least one burdensome intervention (hospitalisation, ER visit, parenteral therapy, or tube feeding) in the last 3 months of life - the paper's central finding was that health-care proxies who understood the poor prognosis and expected clinical course were significantly less likely to have their relative undergo these burdensome interventions, establishing that PROACTIVE PROGNOSTIC COMMUNICATION ITSELF changes the pattern of end-of-life care received.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.reason_why: Advanced dementia is a terminal illness with a predictable complication trajectory (eating problems, febrile episodes/pneumonia, described above); when families and clinicians discuss this trajectory and the evidence against feeding tubes (Finucane, above) BEFORE a crisis, care decisions in the crisis itself are more likely to match the patient's/family's actual goals rather than defaulting to aggressive, low-yield interventions.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.important_caveat: This is a genuinely difficult conversation that requires skill and compassion, and 'palliative' does not mean 'no treatment' - symptom control (pain, dyspnoea), infection treatment decisions, and comfort-focused feeding remain active, real treatment choices within a palliative-care framework.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.real_working_solution: Initiate advance-care-planning discussions (healthcare proxy/power of attorney, goals of care, explicit discussion of feeding-tube evidence, hospitalisation preferences) at or soon after diagnosis while the patient can still participate, and revisit them at each major stage transition (CDR/GDS-FAST staging, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms entry) rather than waiting for a medical crisis to force the decision.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.source: Mitchell SL, Teno JM, Kiely DK et al., 'The Clinical Course of Advanced Dementia', N Engl J Med 2009;361:1529-1538 (PMID 19828530)

ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.name: Driving Safety and Legal/Financial Capacity Assessment
specific_drugs: Not applicable (on-road driving assessment; formal capacity evaluation for financial/legal decision-making)
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.effectiveness: Loss of instrumental activities of daily living - specifically finances and driving - is one of the earliest and most consistently described functional changes in mild AD (cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms/late_stage_and_functional_decline entry), making proactive assessment of these two specific domains a concrete, actionable early treatment-side task rather than a vague 'monitor function' instruction.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.reason_why: Executive dysfunction and impaired complex-task handling (core NIA-AA clinical criteria, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms entry) directly impair the judgement and multitasking that safe driving and financial decision-making require, often before memory loss alone would prompt concern.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.important_caveat: Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate; a global 'incompetent' label is both clinically inaccurate and legally inappropriate - formal capacity assessment should be tied to the specific decision in question (e.g. a will, a specific financial transaction, driving) rather than applied globally.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.real_working_solution: Discuss driving safety and financial/legal capacity (power of attorney, advance directives) explicitly at diagnosis or MCI stage, before impairment progresses to the point where the patient cannot meaningfully participate in the decision, using formal on-road assessment or occupational-therapy driving evaluation and formal capacity assessment where there is doubt, rather than relying on family impression alone.
ad_advance_care_planning_and_palliative_.source: NIA-AA 2011 core clinical criteria for functional decline (McKhann GM et al., PMID 21514250); standard dementia-care safety-planning literature cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms/clinical_takeaway entry

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Ginkgo Biloba - Real, Definitive Negative Trial for Dementia Prevention
specific_drugs: Ginkgo biloba extract (120 mg twice daily studied; widely sold over-the-counter)
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: The GEM trial (Ginkgo Evaluation of Memory, 3069 community volunteers aged 75+, median 6.1-year follow-up, JAMA 2008) found ginkgo biloba did NOT reduce the incidence of all-cause dementia or Alzheimer's disease (277 dementia cases on ginkgo vs 246 on placebo) - a real, adequately powered, definitive negative result, not an inconclusive one.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: Proposed antioxidant/vasodilatory mechanisms did not translate into a measurable reduction in dementia incidence in this large, long-duration randomised trial.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: Not applicable beyond the negative result itself; the GuidAge trial (long-term ginkgo in France) similarly failed to show benefit for AD prevention.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not recommend ginkgo biloba for dementia prevention or treatment; direct patients/families instead to the real, trial-proven modifiable-risk-factor and multidomain-lifestyle evidence (FINGER/US POINTER/SPRINT MIND, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms entry).
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: DeKosky ST et al. (GEM trial), JAMA 2008;300:2253-2262 (PMID 19017911); Vellas B et al. (GuidAge), Lancet Neurol 2012

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: NSAIDs (Naproxen, Celecoxib) for Prevention - Real Negative Trial, Real Harm Signal
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (historical/negative for this indication)
specific_drugs: Naproxen sodium, Celecoxib (studied for AD prevention; NOT recommended for this purpose)
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: ADAPT (2528 elderly participants with family history of dementia, randomised to naproxen, celecoxib or placebo) found neither drug delayed incident dementia or cognitive decline; naproxen was associated with a hazard ratio of 1.63 (95% CI 1.04-2.55) for cardiovascular/cerebrovascular events versus placebo and appeared to slightly HASTEN cognitive decline, leading to early trial termination in December 2004 after a related trial (APC) showed increased cardiovascular risk with celecoxib.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: The neuroinflammation-targeting rationale (reduce microglial/inflammatory contribution to AD pathology, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms/definition_and_pathophysiology entry) did not translate into clinical benefit and NSAIDs carried real cardiovascular harm in this elderly population.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: This is specifically about NSAIDs for AD PREVENTION/TREATMENT - it is not a statement about NSAID use for other indications (e.g. short-term analgesia), which carries its own separate risk-benefit calculation.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not prescribe or recommend naproxen or celecoxib for Alzheimer's disease prevention or treatment; the anti-inflammatory hypothesis in AD remains a research question (see neuroinflammation_and_trem2 in this knowledge base's symptoms entry), not a treatment-ready target.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: ADAPT Research Group, 'Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Events in the Randomized, Controlled Alzheimer's Disease Anti-Inflammatory Prevention Trial (ADAPT)', PLoS Clin Trials 2006/PMC1851724; ADAPT cognitive-outcome results, Arch Neurol 2008 (PMID 18474729)

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Postmenopausal Hormone Therapy (Estrogen +/- Progestin) - Real Trial Showing INCREASED Dementia Risk
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: Hormone replacement therapy (historical/negative and harmful for this indication)
specific_drugs: Conjugated equine estrogen (CEE), CEE + medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) - NOT recommended for dementia prevention
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: WHIMS (Women's Health Initiative Memory Study) found combined estrogen-plus-progestin INCREASED the risk of probable dementia (hazard ratio 2.05, 95% CI 1.21-3.48, 45 vs 22 cases per 10,000 person-years, P=0.01) in women aged 65+, equivalent to 23 additional dementia cases per 10,000 women per year - the opposite of the hypothesised protective effect, leading to early termination of this arm of the WHI study in July 2002.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: The hypothesis that estrogen's neuroprotective effects in younger/perimenopausal biology would extend to reducing dementia risk when started in women already aged 65+ was not supported; started late (well after menopause), hormone therapy instead appeared to increase cerebrovascular/cognitive risk in this specific age group.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: This finding is specific to hormone therapy STARTED in women 65 or older for dementia prevention; it does not by itself resolve the separate, ongoing 'critical window' hypothesis debate about hormone therapy started near the menopausal transition for other indications, which is outside this AD-treatment entry's scope.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not use postmenopausal hormone therapy as a dementia-prevention or Alzheimer's-treatment strategy in older women; this is a real, guideline-changing negative-and-harmful trial result, not a null/inconclusive one.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Shumaker SA et al. (WHIMS estrogen+progestin), JAMA 2003;289:2651-2662 (PMID 12771112); WHI study termination announcement, July 2002

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Statins for Alzheimer's Treatment - Real Negative Trials (LEADe, CLASP) Despite Epidemiological Interest
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (negative for AD treatment; remains indicated for cardiovascular risk reduction on its own separate merits)
specific_drugs: Atorvastatin (LEADe trial, 80 mg/day), Simvastatin (CLASP trial) - NOT proven to treat or slow Alzheimer's disease
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: The LEADe trial (atorvastatin 80 mg/day vs placebo, 72 weeks, in mild-moderate AD already on donepezil) found no significant clinical benefit despite a 50.2% reduction in LDL cholesterol by month 3; pooled analyses across statin trials found no beneficial effect on the ADAS-cog cognitive scale. A systematic review concluded there is insufficient evidence to recommend statins for the treatment of dementia.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: Epidemiological/observational association between high cholesterol and AD risk did not translate into a treatment effect when tested prospectively in randomised trials of people who already had AD, illustrating that association is not causation for treatment purposes.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: This is specifically about using statins to TREAT already-diagnosed AD; it says nothing against statin use for its proven, separate indication of cardiovascular/stroke risk reduction (cross-reference this knowledge base's dyslipidemia and stroke entries), which remains appropriate on its own merits when clinically indicated.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not prescribe or continue statins specifically as an Alzheimer's disease treatment; treat cardiovascular risk factors on their own separate, real evidence base (e.g. SPRINT MIND for blood pressure, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's symptoms entry, is a real modifiable-risk intervention, unlike statins for AD treatment).
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Feldman HH et al. (LEADe trial), Neurology 2010;74:956-964; CLASP trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00053599); statins-for-dementia systematic review, Cochrane/PubMed (PMID 20687089)

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Solanezumab - Three Repeated Phase 3 Failures Across the Disease Spectrum (EXPEDITION 1/2/3, A4)
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody targeting soluble, monomeric amyloid-beta (failed programme)
specific_drugs: Solanezumab - development discontinued for these indications
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: EXPEDITION 1 and 2 (1012 and 1040 patients with mild-moderate AD) did not improve cognition or function; EXPEDITION 3 (2129 patients with mild AD, amyloid-confirmed, 80 weeks) was formally published in NEJM in 2018 showing NO significant slowing of cognitive decline on ADAS-Cog; the A4 trial (preclinical, amyloid-positive but cognitively normal participants) also failed its primary endpoint. This is the third consecutive phase 3 miss for solanezumab.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: Solanezumab targets soluble monomeric amyloid-beta rather than the aggregated protofibril (lecanemab) or plaque-specific pyroglutamate-amyloid (donanemab) forms targeted by the drugs that later succeeded, which in hindsight is proposed as part of why it did not clear plaque or produce clinical benefit as effectively.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: Solanezumab's repeated, well-powered failures across mild AD, prodromal AD (EXPEDITION programme) and preclinical AD (A4) are part of the honest amyloid-cascade-hypothesis debate documented in this knowledge base's symptoms entry, and are real evidence that not every anti-amyloid mechanism works, even though lecanemab/donanemab (different target epitopes) later succeeded.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Solanezumab is not an available or recommended treatment; the amyloid-antibody class options with real proven benefit are lecanemab and donanemab specifically, above - the class as a whole is not interchangeable.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Doody RS et al. (EXPEDITION 1/2), N Engl J Med 2014;370:311-321 (PMID 24450890); Honig LS et al. (EXPEDITION 3), N Engl J Med 2018;378:321-330; Sperling RA et al. (A4), reported via NeurologyLive coverage

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Gantenerumab - Real Phase 3 Failure (GRADUATE 1/2, 2022) Despite a Successful Drug Class
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody targeting aggregated amyloid-beta (failed programme)
specific_drugs: Gantenerumab - development discontinued after these results
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: GRADUATE I and II (2000 participants combined, 27 months, subcutaneous dosing) found gantenerumab slowed CDR-SB decline by only -0.31 points (P=0.0954) and -0.19 points (P=0.2998) respectively versus placebo - neither statistically significant - with lower-than-expected amyloid removal on PET, prompting Roche to discontinue the gantenerumab development programme (including open-label extension and the Skyline secondary-prevention trial) in November 2022.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: Despite targeting aggregated amyloid-beta (the same general target class as lecanemab/donanemab), gantenerumab achieved less potent plaque clearance than expected at the doses used, illustrating that within-class differences in binding epitope, affinity and achieved target engagement - not just 'being an anti-amyloid antibody' - determine clinical success.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: This failure sits alongside lecanemab/donanemab's real successes in the SAME broad drug class, which is why this entry does NOT conclude 'anti-amyloid antibodies don't work' - it concludes 'this specific molecule, at the doses tested, did not achieve sufficient target engagement to produce a clinical effect'.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Gantenerumab is not an available or recommended treatment; use lecanemab or donanemab specifically, where the plaque-clearance and clinical-benefit evidence is real and statistically significant.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Roche/Genentech GRADUATE 1/2 topline results, November 2022, as reported by CNN, ALZFORUM ('Gantenerumab Falls Short in Phase 3') and Alzheimer Europe

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Verubecestat - Real BACE-Inhibitor Phase 3 Failure With Net Harm (EPOCH), a Cautionary Mechanistic Lesson
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: BACE1 (beta-secretase) inhibitor - blocks amyloid-beta production upstream (failed programme)
specific_drugs: Verubecestat - development discontinued after these results
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: EPOCH (78-week phase 3 trial in mild-moderate AD, verubecestat 12 mg and 40 mg vs placebo) was terminated early for futility; verubecestat reduced CSF amyloid-beta as intended but produced NO clinical benefit, and adverse events (rash, falls and injuries, sleep disturbance, suicidal ideation, weight loss, hair-colour change) were more common than with placebo. A companion trial in prodromal AD (APECS) was also terminated early.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: BACE1 cleaves many substrates beyond amyloid precursor protein, so blocking it upstream (rather than clearing already-formed amyloid, as the successful antibodies do) produced broader off-target biological effects and real harm without compensating benefit - a genuinely informative mechanistic lesson about WHERE in the amyloid pathway to intervene.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: This is one of the clearer examples in AD drug development of a treatment that both failed to help AND caused real, documented harm, not merely a neutral null result.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: BACE inhibitors as a class have not produced a successful AD treatment; do not use verubecestat or other BACE inhibitors outside a research setting.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Egan MF et al. (EPOCH), N Engl J Med 2018;378:1691-1703; further verubecestat EPOCH safety analysis, Alzheimers Res Ther 2019 (PMC6685277)

ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Semaglutide (Oral GLP-1) - Real 2025 Phase 3 Failure Despite Biomarker Improvement (EVOKE/EVOKE+)
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.type: GLP-1 receptor agonist (failed for this indication despite proven benefit in type 2 diabetes/obesity)
specific_drugs: Oral semaglutide 14 mg - NOT proven effective for Alzheimer's disease
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: EVOKE and EVOKE+ (3808 participants aged 55-85 with amyloid-confirmed MCI or mild AD dementia, combined) reported topline results on 24 November 2025: semaglutide reduced several CSF Alzheimer's biomarkers by up to 10% (p-tau181, p-tau217, non-phosphorylated tau181/205, and neuroinflammation/neurodegeneration/synaptic-function markers YKL-40, total tau, neurogranin) but did NOT confirm superiority over placebo on the primary clinical endpoint, change in CDR-SB - i.e. real biomarker movement without a matching real clinical benefit, leading Novo Nordisk to discontinue the planned 1-year extension period.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: GLP-1 receptor agonism has plausible neuroprotective/anti-inflammatory mechanisms under active investigation, and the biomarker changes suggest SOME biological effect on AD-relevant pathways, but this again illustrates (as with the amyloid-cascade debate in this knowledge base's symptoms entry) that a biomarker change does not guarantee a clinical benefit.
