ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: This is a genuinely recent (late 2025), well-powered negative clinical trial that should be reported honestly rather than as 'GLP-1 drugs are promising for Alzheimer's' based on the biomarker data alone.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not use semaglutide or other GLP-1 agonists as an Alzheimer's disease treatment on current evidence; semaglutide/tirzepatide remain real, separately-proven treatments for type 2 diabetes and obesity (cross-referenced in this knowledge base's diabetes_mellitus and obesity_metabolic_syndrome entries) on their own merits.
ad_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Novo Nordisk topline EVOKE/EVOKE+ results announcement, 24 November 2025 (Alzheimer Europe, NeurologyLive); EVOKE/EVOKE+ trial design, PubMed 39780249; Lancet 2026 full publication

ad_medical_devices_equipment.name: Medical Equipment/Devices - MRI Surveillance for ARIA, Infusion/Injection Systems for Anti-Amyloid Antibodies, Subcutaneous Autoinjector
ad_medical_devices_equipment.type: Medical devices/equipment required for safe delivery and monitoring of disease-modifying therapy
specific_drugs: Not applicable (devices, not drugs): brain MRI (for baseline and scheduled ARIA-surveillance scans), IV infusion equipment (lecanemab, donanemab), Leqembi IQLIK subcutaneous autoinjector, APOE genotyping laboratory test
ad_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Scheduled MRI surveillance during the highest-risk early dosing period is how ARIA (occurring in 12.6-31.4% of patients across the lecanemab/donanemab trials, above) is detected before it becomes clinically dangerous, and APOE genotyping (a laboratory test, not an imaging device) is used to individualise risk counselling and monitoring intensity; these are not optional accessories to anti-amyloid antibody therapy but integral, required components of its safe use per the trials' own protocols and subsequent appropriate-use guidance.
ad_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: ARIA is usually asymptomatic when first detectable on MRI but can progress to symptomatic oedema or haemorrhage; catching it on a scheduled scan allows dose interruption before serious harm occurs, which is the entire rationale for the monitoring requirement.
ad_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: This monitoring infrastructure (access to MRI, infusion centres, and follow-up capacity) is a real practical barrier to anti-amyloid antibody access in resource-limited settings, including much of India where CDSCO approval/availability for these drugs was not verified in this research pass (see CURABILITY_NOTE and the lecanemab/donanemab entries above).
ad_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Do not initiate lecanemab or donanemab without the infrastructure to deliver the full APOE-genotyping-plus-scheduled-MRI-monitoring protocol used in the pivotal trials; the subcutaneous autoinjector (Leqembi IQLIK) reduces but does not eliminate the infusion-centre/monitoring burden since it is for maintenance dosing only, after the initial 18 months of monitored IV therapy.
ad_medical_devices_equipment.source: CLARITY-AD and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial protocols and ARIA-monitoring requirements as reported above; Eisai LEQEMBI IQLIK approval release, 29 August 2025

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-drug DICE-based BPSD management (first-line for agitation/behavioural symptoms)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: AAN/AGS/APA consensus: recommended first-line for all BPSD except immediate safety risk; no single 'percent effective' figure exists because it is individualised, but it is the top-ranked real intervention because it has no mortality/ARIA/QTc risk and is guideline-mandated before any drug
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kales HC et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2014;62:762-769

ranked_high_to_low.name: Memantine - moderate-severe AD
ranked_high_to_low.metric: CIBIC-plus responder rate (no worsening of global impression at 24 weeks) 55% (109/198) with memantine+donepezil vs 45% (89/197) with placebo+donepezil (MEM-MD-02, N=404); NICE TA217-recommended; significant benefit vs placebo on cognition/function/behaviour/global status
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tariot PN et al., JAMA 2004;291:317-324 (PMID 14734594)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Citalopram - agitation (CitAD)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 40% moderate/marked improvement vs 26% placebo (OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.23-3.69, P=0.007); QTc +18.1 ms vs placebo at week 3 (P=0.004)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Porsteinsson AP et al. (CitAD), JAMA 2014;311:682-691

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) - delirium prevention in hospitalised dementia patients
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Delirium incidence reduced 40% vs usual care in the original controlled trial (852 patients aged 70+)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Inouye SK et al., N Engl J Med 1999;340:669-676

ranked_high_to_low.name: REACH II structured caregiver intervention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinically significant depression (CES-D>=15) at 6 months fell 44.5% relative to control (12.6% intervention vs 22.7% control; computed as (22.7-12.6)/22.7), 495 dyads, 3 ethnic groups; also significantly better self-rated health, sleep, physical and emotional health vs brief check-in calls
ranked_high_to_low.source: Belle SH et al., Ann Intern Med 2006;145:727-738

ranked_high_to_low.name: Risperidone (off-label) - severe agitation/psychosis
ranked_high_to_low.type: Atypical antipsychotic (not FDA-approved for this indication)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: BEHAVE-AD responder rate ('very much'/'much' improved) 59% with risperidone (~1 mg/day) vs 26% with placebo at endpoint (p<0.001); however class-wide 1.6-1.7x mortality risk (approx. 4.5% vs 2.6%) per FDA 2005 black-box warning meta-analysis of 17 trials/5377 patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Katz IR et al, J Clin Psychiatry 1999;60:107-115 (efficacy); FDA black-box warning, April 2005 (mortality risk); risperidone FDA label

ranked_high_to_low.name: Suvorexant - insomnia in mild-moderate AD dementia
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Responder rate (>=50-minute improvement in total sleep time at end of trial) 62% with suvorexant (83/134) vs 45% with placebo (62/137) over 4 weeks, 285 participants; total sleep time +28.2 min vs placebo overall; falls 2% vs 0%
ranked_high_to_low.source: Herring WJ et al (dedicated phase 3 AD-insomnia polysomnography trial); Merck FDA approval release

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral assisted hand-feeding vs percutaneous feeding tube - advanced dementia dysphagia
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No RCT or observational evidence that tube feeding prolongs survival, reduces aspiration, improves function or provides palliation vs careful hand-feeding; AAFP Choosing Wisely recommends against tubes
ranked_high_to_low.source: Finucane TE et al., JAMA 1999;282:1365-1370

ranked_high_to_low.name: Trazodone - agitation/sleep (off-label)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Insufficient evidence per Cochrane (2 small trials); individual trials show benefit vs placebo and efficacy similar to haloperidol with better tolerability
ranked_high_to_low.source: Martinon-Torres G et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004:CD004990

ranked_high_to_low.name: Melatonin - sleep-wake disturbance in AD
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Weak/inconsistent evidence in AD specifically; negative in the one dedicated RCT in a related neurodegenerative population (PD-RBD: 3.4 vs 3.6 events/week, P=0.92)
ranked_high_to_low.source: General AD sleep literature; Gilat M et al. (PD-RBD), Mov Disord 2020 (PMID 31674060)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Memantine + donepezil combination vs donepezil alone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No significant added group-level benefit over donepezil alone in DOMINO-AD/pooled meta-analyses, despite an earlier positive single trial (MEM-MD-02)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Howard R et al. (DOMINO-AD), N Engl J Med 2012;366:893-903

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT end points (ADAS-Cog points, CDR-Sum-of-Boxes percent slowing, percent agitation responders, incidence rate ratios, hours/minutes of sleep, delirium incidence, or a directional judgement for non-pharmacological/framework interventions that have no single percent), so the ordering is directional judgement (size and quality of benefit on each option's own metric, weighted by safety) NOT a common-scale percentage ranking; effectiveness_pct appears only where a genuine, directly comparable percent exists. IMPORTANT: only rows 4 and 5 (lecanemab, donanemab) are disease-modifying in the sense of measurably slowing the rate of decline; every other 'working' row (1-3, 6-16) is purely symptomatic and does not alter the underlying neurodegeneration - see CURABILITY_NOTE. Rows with effectiveness_pct of 0.0 (17-27) are documented REAL NEGATIVE or REJECTED results, not zero-quality drugs incorrectly tested - each is reported here specifically so it is not mistakenly recommended; several (pimavanserin, aducanumab) are approved/available for a DIFFERENT indication or were withdrawn for non-safety reasons, which the individual entries above explain. Lecanemab and donanemab availability in India could not be verified via CDSCO in this research pass and should not be assumed.

multiple_sclerosis.name: Multiple Sclerosis
multiple_sclerosis.icd11_hint: 8A40 Multiple sclerosis (8A40.0 relapsing-remitting, 8A40.1 primary progressive, 8A40.2 secondary progressive, 8A40.Z unspecified); ICD-10 G35

definition.finding: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (brain, spinal cord, optic nerves) characterised by multifocal areas of demyelination, variable axonal/neuronal loss, and astrogliosis, disseminated in space (multiple CNS sites) and time (multiple episodes). It is the leading non-traumatic cause of neurological disability in young adults.
definition.source: Thompson AJ et al., 'Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria', Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173 (PMID 29275977); Reich DS et al., 'Multiple Sclerosis', N Engl J Med 2018;378:169-180 (PMID 29320652)

autoimmune_mechanism_relapse.finding: MS relapses are driven by autoreactive, myelin-directed CD4+ (Th1/Th17) and CD8+ T-cells that cross the blood-brain barrier, together with B-cells and antibody-mediated mechanisms, triggering focal perivascular inflammatory demyelinating lesions in white and grey matter. Acute lesions show macrophage/microglia-mediated stripping of myelin from axons, relative sparing of axons acutely, oligodendrocyte injury/death, and reactive astrogliosis; this focal inflammatory activity, visible as new/enlarging T2 or gadolinium-enhancing lesions on MRI, underlies clinical relapses. B-cells contribute independently of antibody production via antigen presentation and cytokine secretion, which is the rationale for B-cell-depleting therapies.
autoimmune_mechanism_relapse.source: Reich DS et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:169-180 (PMID 29320652); Dendrou CA et al., 'Immunopathology of multiple sclerosis', Nat Rev Immunol 2015;15:545-558 (PMID 26250739)

mechanism_of_progression.finding: Progressive MS (both primary and secondary progressive) is driven less by acute focal relapsing inflammation and more by chronic, compartmentalised CNS inflammation (meningeal tertiary lymphoid-like follicles, smouldering/'slowly expanding' or paramagnetic-rim lesions with iron-laden activated microglia at the lesion edge), diffuse microglial activation in normal-appearing white matter, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive axonal degeneration/neurodegeneration that becomes progressively less responsive to conventional anti-inflammatory disease-modifying therapy. This mechanistic split (acute focal relapse-driven inflammation vs chronic compartmentalised/neurodegenerative progression) explains why relapse-targeted immunotherapies control relapse rate well but have much smaller effects on progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA - progression independent of relapse activity).
mechanism_of_progression.source: Absinta M et al., 'Association of Chronic Active Multiple Sclerosis Lesions With Disability In Vivo', JAMA Neurol 2019;76:1474-1483 (PMID 31403674); Kuhlmann T et al., 'Multiple sclerosis progression: time for a new mechanism-driven framework', Lancet Neurol 2023;22:78-88 (PMID 36410373)

ebv_as_likely_necessary_cause.finding: A landmark longitudinal study of >10 million US military personnel (1993-2013) found the risk of MS increased 32-fold after Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (801 MS cases identified; only 1 of 801 was EBV-seronegative at MS onset) but was not increased after infection with other viruses including cytomegalovirus, which controls for general changes in immune surveillance. Serum neurofilament light chain (a marker of neuroaxonal damage) rose only after EBV seroconversion, not before, supporting a causal, temporally-ordered role. The authors conclude EBV infection is a likely necessary (though not sufficient) cause of MS, since virtually no MS occurs without prior EBV infection.
ebv_as_likely_necessary_cause.source: Bjornevik K et al., 'Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis', Science 2022;375:296-301 (PMID 35025605, DOI 10.1126/science.abj8222)
ebv_as_likely_necessary_cause.confidence: high - large longitudinal cohort with pre-disease serial serum sampling, a rare and strong design for causal inference in MS epidemiology

genetic_risk_hla.finding: The HLA class II allele HLA-DRB1*15:01 (in linkage with HLA-DQB1*06:02, forming the DR15 haplotype) is the single strongest common genetic risk variant for MS in populations of European ancestry, with case-control odds ratios generally in the range of ~3 (reported as OR 2.84-3.53 in recent independent case-control cohorts); it is markedly more common in MS cases than controls. Genetics alone account for only a minority of overall MS risk (twin/family studies), and genetic risk interacts with EBV and other environmental factors (e.g., HLA-DRB1*15:01 carriers who are EBV-infected have substantially higher MS risk than either factor alone) - i.e. gene-environment interaction, not genetics in isolation.
genetic_risk_hla.source: International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium, Nat Genet 2013 (DRB1*15:01 as primary MS risk locus); Albanian case-control study, medRxiv 2025 (OR 3.53, 95% CI 2.01-6.19); Russian population study (OR 2.84, 95% CI 2.17-3.72)
genetic_risk_hla.confidence: moderate-high - the DRB1*15:01 association itself is very well replicated; the specific ORs cited vary by population studied and should be read as illustrative, not a single universal number

mcdonald_2017_criteria.finding: MS is diagnosed using the 2017 McDonald criteria, which require demonstrating dissemination in space (DIS - lesions in >=2 of 4 characteristic CNS locations: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and dissemination in time (DIT - simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, OR a new T2/enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI, OR CSF-specific oligoclonal bands as a substitute for DIT) in a patient with a typical clinically isolated syndrome, after excluding better explanations. The 2017 revision (versus 2010) additionally allowed CSF oligoclonal bands to substitute for DIT, allowed symptomatic lesions to count towards DIS/DIT, and allowed cortical lesions to count towards DIS - changes that permit earlier diagnosis. A validation study reported the 2017 DIS criteria had 87% sensitivity (95% CI 76-94), 73% specificity (50-89) and 83% overall accuracy (74-91) for identifying MS.
mcdonald_2017_criteria.source: Thompson AJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173 (PMID 29275977); DIS diagnostic-accuracy validation study, PMC11514922

mcdonald_2024_revision.finding: A 2024/2025 international consensus revision of the McDonald criteria (published Lancet Neurology, 2025) further refines diagnosis to improve specificity while preserving sensitivity: it recognises the optic nerve as a fifth topography that can count towards dissemination in space; it allows newer, more specific MRI biomarkers - the central vein sign (a thin vein running through the centre of a lesion, characteristic of true MS demyelinating lesions) and paramagnetic rim lesions (chronic active/'smouldering' lesions with an iron-laden microglial rim) - to be used as supportive/confirmatory evidence in specific situations; it allows CSF kappa free light chains as an alternative biomarker to oligoclonal bands; and it permits radiologically isolated syndrome to be classified as MS under defined conditions. It also recommends stricter diagnostic thresholds in patients over 50 or with vascular risk factors, to reduce misdiagnosis in populations more prone to non-specific white-matter lesions.
mcdonald_2024_revision.source: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria, Lancet Neurol 2025 (PMID 40975101); AJR 2026 radiologist guide to the 2024 update (PMID 41439773)
mcdonald_2024_revision.confidence: moderate - this is a very recent (2025-published) revision; real-world adoption/validation data are still accumulating, unlike the well-established 2017 criteria

mri_findings.finding: Characteristic MRI findings include ovoid periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles along the axis of medullary veins ('Dawson's fingers', reflecting perivenular demyelination), juxtacortical/cortical lesions, infratentorial (brainstem/cerebellar) lesions, and spinal cord lesions (typically <2 vertebral segments long, in contrast to the longitudinally extensive lesions of NMOSD). Gadolinium-contrast-enhancing lesions indicate active, acute inflammation with blood-brain-barrier breakdown and typically enhance for a few weeks before resolving, providing MRI evidence of dissemination in time when both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions co-exist on a single scan.
mri_findings.source: Thompson AJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173 (PMID 29275977); Filippi M et al., 'MRI criteria for the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis', Lancet Neurol 2016;15:292-303 (PMID 26822746)

csf_oligoclonal_bands.finding: CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (IgG bands present in CSF but not in a paired serum sample, detected by isoelectric focusing) are found in up to ~95% of confirmed MS patients and support the diagnosis; a large tertiary-centre cohort reported CSF-specific OCB sensitivity of 92.8% and specificity of 90.4% for MS, while the Mayo Clinic reference laboratory reports ~74% sensitivity and ~89% specificity using a >=2-unique-band cutoff (numbers vary by cohort and cutoff). OCB positivity is not MS-specific (also seen in CNS infections, neurosarcoidosis, some autoimmune/paraneoplastic disorders) and in the 2017 McDonald criteria functions specifically as a substitute for dissemination in time, not dissemination in space.
csf_oligoclonal_bands.source: Austrian tertiary-centre OCB study, PubMed 41405159; Mayo Clinic Laboratories OLIG test overview; Thompson AJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173 (PMID 29275977)
csf_oligoclonal_bands.confidence: moderate-high - sensitivity/specificity figures vary meaningfully between reported cohorts/methods and should not be quoted as one fixed number

optic_nerve_vep.finding: Visual evoked potentials (VEP), which measure conduction delay along the optic nerve/visual pathway, can detect subclinical optic nerve demyelination (delayed but preserved-amplitude P100 latency) even without a history of clinically apparent optic neuritis, and historically served as a paraclinical criterion for dissemination in space; under the 2024 McDonald revision the optic nerve itself (via VEP, optical coherence tomography, or MRI orbital imaging showing optic nerve lesion/enhancement) can now count as one of the five topographies for dissemination in space.
optic_nerve_vep.source: AJR 2026 radiologist guide to the 2024 McDonald update (PMID 41439773); MedLink Neurology 2024 McDonald revision summary

differential_diagnosis_nmosd.finding: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is a distinct, must-exclude autoimmune astrocytopathy (not a variant of MS) caused by pathogenic IgG antibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4), the main CNS water channel expressed on astrocyte foot processes; it classically causes severe, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 vertebral segments) and severe/bilateral optic neuritis, is diagnosed using the 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis (IPND) criteria (>=1 of 6 core clinical characteristics plus AQP4-IgG seropositivity, with stricter combined clinical+MRI requirements if AQP4-IgG is negative/unknown), and - critically for management - most MS disease-modifying therapies (especially interferon-beta and natalizumab) can worsen NMOSD, so correctly distinguishing the two conditions before starting treatment is a real patient-safety issue, not an academic distinction.
differential_diagnosis_nmosd.source: Wingerchuk DM et al., 'International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders', Neurology 2015;85:177-189 (PMID 26092914)

differential_diagnosis_mogad.finding: MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is a second, distinct must-exclude demyelinating disease, caused by IgG antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, presenting with optic neuritis (often bilateral, disc-swelling-predominant), myelitis, or ADEM-like encephalopathy; it is diagnosed per the 2023 international MOGAD diagnostic criteria (one of six core clinical phenotypes plus a positive cell-based-assay MOG-IgG result, with additional supporting clinical/MRI features required when the antibody titre is low or unavailable, specifically to prevent misclassification of MS or false-positive low-titre results as MOGAD). The 2023 criteria performed with 97% sensitivity and 100% specificity (no false positives) in a validation cohort. MOGAD has a different treatment approach (early, often prolonged, immunosuppression with a lower threshold for maintenance therapy after relapses) and a generally more monophasic/relapsing-but-different course than MS, so AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG antibody testing should be routine in any new suspected demyelinating CNS syndrome, not reserved for atypical cases.
differential_diagnosis_mogad.source: Banwell B et al., '2023 international consensus criteria for MOGAD', Lancet Neurol 2023 (as summarised in PMC11136770); validation cohort data (PMC11244737)

disease_course_classification_lublin_201.note: A first clinical episode suggestive of CNS demyelination lasting >=24 hours, without yet meeting full dissemination-in-time criteria for MS. Conversion to clinically definite MS after a first attack ranges widely by criteria/follow-up used - reported figures include ~63% converting to a second clinical attack over 20 years, and 30-82% converting under 2010 McDonald criteria depending on baseline MRI lesion burden (patients with an abnormal baseline brain MRI convert far more often and faster than those with a normal scan).
disease_course_classification_lublin_201.source: Lublin FD et al., 'Defining the clinical course of multiple sclerosis: the 2013 revisions', Neurology 2014;83:278-286 (PMID 24871874); CIS long-term conversion studies as summarised in PMC3503301 and related literature

disease_course_classification_lublin_201.note: Incidental MRI findings meeting MS-like lesion criteria in a person with no clinical symptoms attributable to demyelination. RIS converts to a first clinical event (i.e., becomes clinically apparent MS) in roughly a quarter to a third of cases over 5 years (one cohort reported a 34% 5-year conversion rate to first clinical event); under the 2024 McDonald revision, RIS meeting specific criteria can now be formally classified as MS even before a clinical event occurs.
disease_course_classification_lublin_201.source: Okuda DT et al., 'Radiologically isolated syndrome' natural-history literature (PubMed 25538833); Lancet Neurol 2025 2024 McDonald revision (PMID 40975101)

disease_course_classification_lublin_201.note: The most common presenting phenotype, accounting for approximately 85-90% of MS patients at initial diagnosis; characterised by clearly defined relapses (acute/subacute new or worsening neurological symptoms lasting >=24 hours) with full or partial recovery and no disease progression between relapses.
disease_course_classification_lublin_201.source: Lublin FD et al., Neurology 2014;83:278-286 (PMID 24871874); Klineova S, Lublin FD, 'Clinical Course of Multiple Sclerosis', Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med 2018;8:a028928 (PMC6120692)

disease_course_classification_lublin_201.note: A phase of steadily accumulating disability, with or without occasional relapses, that develops after an initial relapsing-remitting course. Historically, in the pre-disease-modifying-therapy era, roughly 50% of untreated RRMS patients transitioned to SPMS within about 10-15 years and up to a majority by 25-30 years of disease; more recent cohorts (reflecting widespread DMT use) report the 25-40% range progressing to SPMS by 6-10 years, with median time-to-transition estimates now ranging from about 10 to 23 years depending on the cohort and treatment era, indicating that disease-modifying therapy meaningfully delays (without eliminating) the relapsing-to-progressive transition.
disease_course_classification_lublin_201.source: AJMC review, 'Understanding the Transition From RRMS to SPMS'; PMC11968352 (SPMS diagnosis/activity-detection review); Lublin FD et al., Neurology 2014;83:278-286 (PMID 24871874)

disease_course_classification_lublin_201.note: Steadily worsening neurological function from onset, without early relapses, accounting for approximately 10-15% of all MS. Onset is typically later than RRMS (average symptom onset around the late 30s to 40s) and affects men and women in roughly equal numbers, unlike RRMS which is markedly female-predominant.
disease_course_classification_lublin_201.source: Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers, PPMS overview; Lublin FD et al., Neurology 2014;83:278-286 (PMID 24871874)

core.name: Optic neuritis
core.note: Often the first presenting symptom of MS, typically causing subacute, usually unilateral, painful (pain on eye movement) vision loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Population/clinic-based estimates suggest optic neuritis is the initial manifestation in roughly 20% of MS patients. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) long-term follow-up found the cumulative risk of a subsequent MS diagnosis after a first isolated optic neuritis episode was 40% at 10 years and 50% at 15 years overall, rising to about 25% at 10 years and 25% at 15 years in patients with a normal baseline brain MRI, versus a much higher risk (>70% at 15 years) in those with >=1 baseline brain MRI lesion - i.e. baseline MRI lesion burden is the single strongest predictor of conversion.
core.source: Optic Neuritis Study Group, 'Longitudinal study of visual outcome in optic neuritis: ONTT', and 15-year follow-up data (as summarised in PMC4214814 and related ONTT literature)

core.name: Sensory disturbances (numbness, tingling, paraesthesia)
core.note: Among the most common presenting and lifetime symptoms in MS, reflecting demyelinating lesions anywhere along central sensory pathways (spinal cord, brainstem, thalamus, sensory cortex); can be patchy, asymmetric, and does not follow a single peripheral nerve or dermatomal distribution, which helps distinguish it from peripheral neuropathy.
core.source: Reich DS et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:169-180 (PMID 29320652)

core.name: Lhermitte's sign
core.note: A transient, electric-shock-like sensation radiating down the spine and often into the limbs, triggered by neck flexion (occasionally extension/rotation), reflecting a demyelinating lesion in the cervical spinal cord's dorsal columns. Reported in roughly 36% of MS patients in one clinical series; it is not specific to MS (also seen in cervical spondylotic myelopathy, B12 deficiency, radiation myelopathy) but is a useful bedside localising sign to cervical cord pathology.
core.source: Lhermitte's sign prevalence study (PMC3968359, PubMed 24800049); StatPearls, 'Lhermitte Sign' (NBK493237)

core.name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
core.note: A brainstem sign caused by a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, producing impaired adduction of the affected eye on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye; reported in roughly 15-52% of MS patients across studies, and bilateral INO in a young adult is considered highly suggestive of MS.
core.source: Population-based INO-in-MS prevalence study, ScienceDirect S2211034822003364; classic INO-in-MS clinical spectrum study, PubMed 4026628

core.name: Motor weakness and spasticity
core.note: Corticospinal tract involvement produces limb weakness (often asymmetric) and upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses/Babinski sign, clonus); spasticity is a major contributor to gait impairment, pain, and disability over the disease course and is a common target of symptomatic (not disease-modifying) treatment.
core.source: Reich DS et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:169-180 (PMID 29320652)

core.name: Cerebellar ataxia and tremor
core.note: Cerebellar/cerebellar-pathway involvement produces limb and gait ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysarthria (scanning speech); the combination of nystagmus, intention tremor and scanning/staccato speech is classically referred to as 'Charcot's triad', though this eponymous grouping is now considered historical rather than diagnostically central.
core.source: Reich DS et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:169-180 (PMID 29320652)

core.name: Bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction
core.note: Very common and frequently under-reported: bladder dysfunction (urgency, frequency, incomplete emptying, retention) has been reported in up to 80-96% of MS patients in some series, bowel dysfunction (constipation and/or faecal incontinence) in roughly 29-54% (a large Italian multicentre study found 44.7% with a bowel/bladder deficit overall - 17.3% bowel, 40% bladder), and sexual dysfunction (diminished desire, arousal/erectile dysfunction, anorgasmia) in over half of patients in several cohorts. These three domains are interrelated and also correlate with cognitive dysfunction, and are frequently missed unless specifically asked about.
core.source: Nortvedt MW et al., Mult Scler 2007 (PubMed/journals.sagepub.com abstract 1352458506071210); Italian multicentre bowel-dysfunction study, PMC8857096; sexual-dysfunction-in-MS cohort literature (PubMed 8908666)

core.name: Fatigue
core.note: One of the most common and most disabling MS symptoms, reported by roughly 55-90% of patients depending on the measurement tool and threshold used (a 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis reported ~59% with clinically significant fatigue; other series report up to ~80-92%). Nearly 40% of patients describe fatigue as their single most disabling symptom, and it is a leading cause of early workforce departure; MS-related fatigue is distinct from depression or sleep disorders though it commonly co-exists with both and should be actively screened for.
core.source: Global prevalence of fatigue in MS systematic review/meta-analysis, Front Neurol 2024 (PMC11479926); MS Care Center (Pittsburgh) fatigue overview

core.name: Cognitive impairment
core.note: Affects roughly 40-70% of MS patients at some point in the disease course, most commonly involving processing speed, episodic memory, and executive function (with relative preservation of general intelligence and long-established semantic knowledge until later stages); cognitive impairment correlates with, but is not fully explained by, physical disability (EDSS), and independently impacts employment and quality of life, so routine cognitive screening (e.g., SDMT) is recommended rather than relying on physical disability as a proxy.
core.source: Bladder/bowel/cognitive interplay review, einj.org 2040346.173; cognitive impairment prevalence figures consistent with MS clinical-course literature (Klineova/Lublin, PMC6120692)

core.name: Uhthoff's phenomenon (heat sensitivity)
core.note: A transient (typically resolving within 24 hours), stereotyped worsening of existing neurological deficits (classically transient visual blurring after exercise in a patient with prior optic neuritis, but any previously affected pathway can be involved) triggered by a rise in core body temperature - from hot weather, exercise, fever, hot baths/saunas. The mechanism is temperature-dependent slowing/conduction block of action potentials along previously demyelinated axons (demyelinated axons are exquisitely temperature-sensitive), not new inflammatory demyelination; reported in roughly 60-80% of MS patients at some point in their disease. Because it is fully reversible with cooling and does not reflect new tissue damage, it is explicitly excluded from the clinical definition of a 'true relapse'.
core.source: StatPearls, 'Uhthoff Phenomenon' (NBK470244); MS Trust patient-information summary on Uhthoff's phenomenon

core.name: Depression
core.note: Markedly more common in MS than the general population: lifetime risk of major depression has been estimated as high as 50% in MS versus 10-15% in the general population, and a meta-analysis found 37% prevalence of major depressive disorder in early-phase MS with an overall any-depression prevalence around 25%. Depression in MS is under-recognised and under-treated relative to its prevalence, and is the single most consistent risk factor for suicidal ideation in this population, making routine depression screening (not just physical symptom review) a core part of MS follow-up.
core.source: Meta-analysis of depression prevalence in MS as summarised in suicide/depression review literature; Wiley Health Science Reports 2026 suicidal-ideation meta-analysis (10.1002/hsr2.72331)

core.name: Suicidality
core.note: A real, elevated, and often under-addressed risk: pooled estimates report suicidal ideation in roughly 20-23% of MS patients, suicide attempts in ~3.4%, and a standardised mortality ratio for suicide about twice that of the general population (suicide accounts for ~2.1% of total deaths in MS cohorts). Depression and anxiety are the most consistently reported risk factors, alongside social isolation and loss of independence/function - all of which are modifiable targets for proactive screening and intervention, not inevitable consequences of the disease.
core.source: Suicide/suicidal-ideation-in-MS meta-analyses (Wiley 10.1155/2023/1067257; Wiley Health Science Reports 2026, 10.1002/hsr2.72331; PMC12417961)

true_relapse_definition.finding: A true clinical relapse is defined as a monophasic episode of patient-reported symptoms and objective neurological findings typical of MS, reflecting an acute or subacute focal/multifocal CNS inflammatory demyelinating event, lasting at least 24 hours, occurring in the absence of fever or infection, and separated from a preceding relapse by at least 30 days.
true_relapse_definition.source: Standard MS relapse definition as used in regulatory trials and clinical practice, summarised in Neurology Clinical Practice, 'Infection, Relapses, and Pseudo-Relapses in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis' (10.1212/CPJ.0000000000200493)

pseudorelapse.finding: A pseudorelapse is a temporary recrudescence (re-emergence) of prior, already-existing neurological deficits in the setting of a systemic stressor - most often infection, fever, heat exposure/exercise (Uhthoff's phenomenon), or significant psychosocial stress - without new inflammatory demyelinating activity. Because true relapse and pseudorelapse can look clinically identical at the bedside, infection (especially urinary tract infection) must be actively screened for and treated before a new symptom flare is labelled and treated as a true relapse; one cohort study found nearly a 3-fold higher relapse rate in the 2 weeks before through 5 weeks after an infection compared with infection-free periods, underscoring how tightly the two are linked in practice.
pseudorelapse.source: Neurology Clinical Practice, 'Infection, Relapses, and Pseudo-Relapses in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis' (10.1212/CPJ.0000000000200493); Cleveland Clinic Mellen Center relapse-management approach

red_flags: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion (a large, >2 cm, mass-like MRI lesion with oedema, mass effect, and often ring/open-ring enhancement): mimics a brain tumour or abscess both clinically and radiologically, frequently causes cortical signs (altered mental status, visual field deficits) atypical for a routine MS plaque, and requires extensive work-up (often including CSF analysis and sometimes biopsy) to exclude neoplasm, infection or another inflammatory process before treating as MS.

Rapidly progressive course inconsistent with typical MS (severe deficits accumulating over days without a clear relapsing-remitting or slowly progressive pattern): should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and urgent exclusion of NMOSD, MOGAD, CNS infection, CNS lymphoma, or an autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis rather than assuming an unusually aggressive MS course.

Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (spinal cord lesion spanning >=3 vertebral segments) or severe bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis: atypical for MS (whose spinal lesions are usually short-segment) and should trigger urgent AQP4-IgG (NMOSD) and MOG-IgG (MOGAD) antibody testing, since both conditions require different treatment and can be worsened by some MS therapies.

Onset after age 50 or significant vascular risk factors with non-specific white-matter lesions: raises the risk of MS misdiagnosis, since small-vessel ischaemic white-matter disease can mimic MS lesions on MRI; the 2024 McDonald criteria explicitly recommend a stricter diagnostic threshold in this group.

real_risk_factors.factor: Sex (female predominance, and a rising female:male ratio)
real_risk_factors.note: MS relapsing-onset disease shows a strong and, in several Western cohorts, increasing female predominance - Canadian national data show the female:male ratio rising from under 2:1 in patients born in the 1930s to over 3:1 in those born 1976-1980 (about a 0.85% per-year increase in the ratio), and Danish data show women's MS risk more than doubling over 25 years while remaining essentially unchanged in men. The trend is too rapid to be explained by genetics alone and is thought to reflect changing environmental/lifestyle exposures (e.g., smoking patterns, obesity, reproductive patterns) rather than a shift in underlying biology; PPMS, notably, does not show this female predominance and affects the sexes roughly equally.
real_risk_factors.source: Disanto G, Ramagopalan SV, 'On the sex ratio of multiple sclerosis', Mult Scler 2013 (10.1177/1352458512447594); Canadian sex-ratio cohort data as summarised in Ajdacic-Gross V et al., Mult Scler 2019 (10.1177/1352458519838780)

real_risk_factors.note: See pathophysiology above: EBV infection increases MS risk 32-fold and is considered a likely necessary cause of MS (Bjornevik et al., Science 2022).
real_risk_factors.source: Bjornevik K et al., Science 2022;375:296-301 (PMID 35025605)

real_risk_factors.note: See pathophysiology above: the strongest common genetic risk allele, with reported case-control odds ratios of roughly 3 in recent cohorts, acting in combination with (not instead of) environmental risk factors.
real_risk_factors.source: International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium, Nat Genet 2013; population-specific case-control studies as cited above

real_risk_factors.note: MS prevalence and incidence show a well-documented latitude gradient - lowest near the equator, increasing towards higher latitudes with lower ambient UVB exposure - and this gradient correlates with population vitamin D status. Lower childhood/adolescent sun exposure and lower vitamin D levels are independently associated with higher MS risk in multiple studies, though as an observational/ecological association it cannot alone prove causation as strongly as the EBV cohort data; a 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis found the large majority (~73%) of MS patients had deficient vitamin D at the time of study.
real_risk_factors.source: Frontiers in Neurology 2022 vitamin D/MS review; 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis on vitamin D deficiency and MS, Mult Scler Relat Disord (S2211034824003810)

real_risk_factors.note: A large meta-analysis (14,573 cases, 579,812 controls) found an odds ratio for MS in ever-smokers of 1.54 (95% CI 1.46-1.63); the association appears stronger in men than women and in current smokers versus past smokers, and smoking is also linked to faster disease progression to SPMS in established MS, not just to onset risk.
real_risk_factors.source: Smoking and multiple sclerosis meta-analysis literature (PMC3020969, PMC4806598)

real_risk_factors.note: A systematic review/meta-analysis found significantly increased MS risk with obesity in childhood (effect size 1.37, 95% CI 1.09-1.74), adolescence (1.56, 95% CI 1.20-2.03), or either period (1.56, 95% CI 1.07-2.28); overweight (not just obesity) in adolescence was also associated with increased risk (1.41, 95% CI 1.26-1.59). Normal BMI in childhood/adolescence was protective by comparison.
real_risk_factors.source: Childhood and Adolescent Environmental Risk Factors for Multiple Sclerosis: systematic review with meta-analysis, PMC12560250

global.finding: According to the MS International Federation's Atlas of MS (2023 update, data collected 2022, covering 125 countries representing 91% of the world's population), an estimated 2.9 million people worldwide are living with MS, with a pooled incidence of 2.1 new cases per 100,000 people per year across the 81 countries reporting incidence data - equivalent to someone in the world being diagnosed with MS roughly every 5 minutes. 30 of 31 countries providing an updated prevalence figure reported an increase compared with the previous Atlas edition; at least 30,000 children and teenagers under 18 are estimated to be living with MS, likely an underestimate given limited paediatric-MS data in many countries.
global.source: MS International Federation, 'New prevalence and incidence data now available in the Atlas of MS', 21 August 2023 (msif.org)
global.confidence: high - large multi-country collaborative surveillance effort, though country-level data quality/completeness varies considerably

india_specific.finding: India has traditionally been considered a low-prevalence zone for MS, but published estimates have risen over time and remain limited by the absence of a nationwide registry and formally conducted large-scale epidemiological studies. Hospital-based data from the 1970s suggested a prevalence of only about 0.17-1.33 per 100,000; more recent estimates put current prevalence at roughly 7-10 per 100,000 nationally (with the 2013 Atlas of MS citing a broader 5-20 per 100,000 range, itself considered likely an underestimate given limited MRI/neurologist access historically), and some sources report figures as high as 20-40 per 100,000 in better-surveyed urban populations. A notably higher prevalence (~21 per 100,000) has been reported in the small, well-characterised Parsi community of Mumbai. Indian authors describe the true burden as likely under-ascertained ('iceberg') due to limited rural healthcare access and diagnostic capacity, rather than genuinely reflecting very low disease occurrence.
india_specific.source: 'Multiple sclerosis in India: an overview', Ann Indian Acad Neurol; 'Multiple sclerosis in India: Iceberg or volcano', ScienceDirect S0165572817300589; 'Epidemiology and genetic aspects of multiple sclerosis in India', Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2015
india_specific.confidence: low-moderate - explicitly limited by the absence of a nationwide registry; figures across sources range severalfold and should be read as the best available approximations, not a precise national rate

edss_and_disability.finding: Disability in MS is most widely tracked using the Kurtzke Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), a 0-10 scale in half-point increments driven substantially by ambulation: scores 1.0-4.5 indicate a patient who can still walk unaided; EDSS 6.0 indicates the need for intermittent or unilateral constant walking assistance (cane, single crutch, or brace) to walk about 100 metres, with or without resting; EDSS 6.5 indicates bilateral walking-aid dependence; scores 7.0 and above indicate wheelchair dependence. EDSS 6.0 is a commonly used clinically meaningful disability milestone in natural-history and trial literature because it marks the transition from independent to aided ambulation.
edss_and_disability.source: Kurtzke JF, 'Rating neurologic impairment in multiple sclerosis: an expanded disability status scale (EDSS)', Neurology 1983;33:1444-1452 (the original EDSS reference, as reflected in current EDSS scale documentation, e.g. Australian National Blood Authority criteria and MS Trust/Physiopedia summaries)

pregnancy_prims_study.finding: The Pregnancy in Multiple Sclerosis (PRIMS) study, the seminal prospective cohort on this question, found the annualised relapse rate fell progressively through pregnancy, reaching its lowest point in the third trimester (0.2 relapses/year versus 0.7 in the year before pregnancy - roughly a 70% reduction), followed by a rebound increase in the first 3 months postpartum (1.2 relapses/year, i.e. higher than the pre-pregnancy baseline), with about one-third of women experiencing at least one postpartum relapse; from the second trimester after delivery onward the relapse rate returned to pre-pregnancy levels. Women with greater disease activity in the year before and during pregnancy had the highest risk of early postpartum relapse. This means pregnancy itself is relapse-protective in the short term but requires proactive postpartum relapse-risk counselling and monitoring, not reassurance that the reduced-relapse state will persist.
pregnancy_prims_study.source: Confavreux C et al., 'Rate of pregnancy-related relapse in multiple sclerosis', N Engl J Med 1998;339:285-291 (PMID 9682040) - the original PRIMS study; Vukusic S et al., 'Pregnancy and multiple sclerosis (the PRIMS study): clinical predictors of post-partum relapse', Brain 2004;127:1353-1360 (PMID 15130950)

life_expectancy.finding: MS shortens life expectancy: pooled cohort/registry data indicate a reduction of roughly 6-14 years depending on the cohort, with a large meta-analysis (15 studies, ~160,000 patients, 1949-2013) finding an all-cause standardised mortality ratio of 2.61 (95% CI 2.58-2.65) - i.e., people with MS have roughly 2.6-fold higher mortality than the age/sex-matched general population. A 60-year Norwegian cohort found median life expectancy of 74.7 years in MS patients versus 81.8 years in the general population (72.2 years for men with MS, 77.2 years for women with MS); Finnish cohort data reported life expectancy shortened by about 7-9 years, with survival diverging from matched controls most clearly within the first decade after diagnosis. Modern disease-modifying therapy is expected to improve on these historical figures, but most published mortality cohorts predate widespread high-efficacy DMT use, so current life-expectancy gaps for newly diagnosed patients are likely somewhat narrower than these historical numbers suggest.
life_expectancy.source: Meta-analysis of all-cause SMR in MS (15 studies, 1949-2013) as summarised in mscare.org and related MS-mortality literature; Norwegian 60-year MS cohort study (mscare.org summary); Finnish nationwide MS mortality/life-expectancy cohort studies (PMC12048406; Eur J Neurol 2024, onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ene.16480)
life_expectancy.confidence: moderate - the direction and rough magnitude (several years' reduction, ~2-3x mortality ratio) are well replicated, but the exact number of years lost varies meaningfully by cohort, era, and country, and most large cohorts substantially predate current high-efficacy DMT use

clinical_takeaway.point: On any first CNS demyelinating-type episode (optic neuritis, myelitis, brainstem/cerebellar syndrome), get an early contrast-enhanced brain and spinal cord MRI plus CSF analysis (cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands/kappa free light chains) as first-line investigations - do not wait for a second clinical attack before starting the diagnostic work-up.
clinical_takeaway.why: The 2017/2024 McDonald criteria allow MRI dissemination in space and time (and CSF-specific oligoclonal bands as a substitute for dissemination in time) to establish an MS diagnosis after a single clinical episode, and MRI lesion burden at presentation is the strongest available predictor of conversion to clinically definite MS - waiting for a second attack delays a diagnosis that is often already achievable.
clinical_takeaway.source: Thompson AJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173 (PMID 29275977); ONTT baseline-MRI conversion-risk data

clinical_takeaway.point: Always test for AQP4-IgG (NMOSD) and MOG-IgG (MOGAD) antibodies before committing to an MS diagnosis or starting an MS disease-modifying therapy, especially if the presentation includes severe/bilateral optic neuritis or a long spinal cord lesion (>=3 vertebral segments).
clinical_takeaway.why: NMOSD and MOGAD are distinct diseases with different treatment approaches, and several standard MS disease-modifying therapies (e.g., interferon-beta, natalizumab) can worsen NMOSD - misclassifying either condition as MS is a real, avoidable harm, not a labelling technicality.
clinical_takeaway.source: Wingerchuk DM et al., Neurology 2015;85:177-189 (PMID 26092914); Banwell B et al., 2023 international MOGAD consensus criteria

clinical_takeaway.point: Refer promptly to neurology once MS is diagnosed or strongly suspected, since early initiation of disease-modifying therapy (started at the CIS/early-RRMS stage) meaningfully changes the disease trajectory compared with delayed treatment.
clinical_takeaway.why: MS pathology (focal inflammatory demyelination and, over time, progressive neurodegeneration) begins accumulating from the earliest clinical stages, and this knowledge base's scope for this entry is diagnosis/clinical features only - treatment-specific efficacy data will be added in the companion treatment-focused entry - but the clinical principle that earlier treatment initiation is associated with better long-term disability outcomes is well established in the MS literature.
clinical_takeaway.source: Reich DS et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:169-180 (PMID 29320652)

clinical_takeaway.point: Before labelling any new or worsening symptom a 'relapse', actively screen for and treat infection (especially urinary tract infection) and check for heat/fever exposure (Uhthoff's phenomenon), since both commonly cause pseudorelapses that mimic true relapses but do not need relapse-specific (e.g., high-dose steroid) treatment.
clinical_takeaway.why: A true relapse requires >=24 hours duration in the absence of fever/infection, and infection roughly triples relapse-like symptom rates in the surrounding weeks - treating a pseudorelapse as a true relapse exposes the patient to unnecessary steroid treatment while the real driver (the infection) goes unaddressed.
clinical_takeaway.source: Neurology Clinical Practice, 'Infection, Relapses, and Pseudo-Relapses in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis' (10.1212/CPJ.0000000000200493)

clinical_takeaway.point: Screen every MS patient for depression and suicidal ideation at routine visits, not only when they volunteer mood symptoms.
clinical_takeaway.why: Lifetime major depression risk in MS runs as high as 50% (versus 10-15% in the general population), suicidal ideation is reported in roughly one-fifth of MS patients, and suicide mortality is about double the general-population rate - depression is both under-recognised and the single strongest modifiable risk factor for suicidality in this population.
clinical_takeaway.source: MS depression/suicidality meta-analyses cited under 'core' symptoms above (Wiley 10.1155/2023/1067257; Wiley Health Science Reports 2026, 10.1002/hsr2.72331)

multiple_sclerosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Multiple sclerosis is NOT curable, and this must be stated plainly: no drug in this entry stops, reverses or repairs the underlying chronic immune-mediated demyelination and progressive neurodegeneration described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry. What IS real is a genuine, trial-proven tier of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) that measurably reduce relapse frequency and, for several agents, slow disability accumulation - these are real disease-course-modifying treatments, not symptomatic band-aids, but they slow the disease, they do not cure it or reverse existing damage. The honest efficacy landscape by tier: platform injectables (interferon beta-1a/1b, glatiramer acetate) reduce relapse rate by roughly 27-34% versus placebo (PRISMS, IFNB MS Study Group, Johnson 1995); oral moderate-efficacy agents (teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) reduce it by roughly 31-53% versus placebo (TEMSO/TOWER, DEFINE/CONFIRM); and high-efficacy agents (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine) reduce it by roughly 46-72% versus placebo or active comparator in their respective pivotal trials, with alemtuzumab (72% versus interferon at 5 years, CARE-MS extension) and natalizumab (68% versus placebo, AFFIRM) showing the largest effect sizes, each balanced against a real, specific safety signal (alemtuzumab: ~28% secondary autoimmunity; natalizumab: ~4.2/1000 PML risk, JCV-status-dependent). PRIMARY PROGRESSIVE MS (PPMS) has genuinely very limited DMT options compared with relapsing MS: ocrelizumab (ORATORIO) is the main evidence-based option, and even there the benefit is real but modest (12-week confirmed progression in 32.9% of ocrelizumab-treated patients versus 39.3% on placebo) - it slows PPMS progression, it does not stop or reverse it, and this gap should be stated honestly rather than implied away. For an ACUTE RELAPSE specifically (a separate question from long-term disease-course modification), high-dose IV or equivalent-dose oral methylprednisolone speeds recovery from that relapse (ONTT, COPOUSEP), and plasma exchange is a real, trial-proven salvage option when steroids fail (Weinshenker RCT) - but relapse treatment does not substitute for an ongoing DMT. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has MS: (1) treat any acute relapse promptly with high-dose methylprednisolone (IV or equivalent oral dose), escalating to plasma exchange if steroid-refractory; (2) start a disease-modifying therapy as early as possible after diagnosis - matched to disease activity level, patient preference for dosing route/frequency, and (in India specifically) real cost/access constraints, using off-label rituximab as a substantially more affordable practical alternative to ocrelizumab/natalizumab where cost is the barrier; (3) treat the specific symptoms that are actually present (spasticity, fatigue, bladder dysfunction, trigeminal neuralgia/neuropathic pain, walking impairment, depression, sexual dysfunction) with the real, evidence-graded options in this survey, honestly setting expectations where the evidence is modest (dalfampridine helps about one-third of patients) or genuinely limited (MS-specific antidepressant and PDE5-inhibitor trial evidence); (4) refer for structured physiotherapy, occupational therapy and exercise programmes throughout the disease course, since these have real, Cochrane-level evidence independent of DMT choice; and (5) plan pregnancy and DMT continuation/washout individually with the neurology team rather than reflexively stopping all treatment. This stepwise, honestly-tiered package - not any single drug - is the real standard of care, and 'no cure' does not mean 'nothing meaningfully works'.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for multiple sclerosis: acute relapse treatment, disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) across efficacy tiers with real pivotal-trial relapse-rate data, symptomatic management of the specific symptoms documented in this knowledge base's symptoms entry (spasticity, fatigue, bladder dysfunction, neuropathic pain/trigeminal neuralgia, walking impairment, depression, sexual dysfunction), rehabilitation, pregnancy/DMT safety, vitamin D, and honestly-reported failed/unproven treatments. Diagnostic criteria and disease-course classification are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms/diagnostic_framework and disease_course_classification_lublin_2013 entries and are not duplicated here.

ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.name: High-Dose Intravenous Methylprednisolone - First-Line Acute Relapse Treatment (ONTT)
specific_drugs: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate IV (Solu-Medrol and generics), typically 1 g/day for 3-5 days
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.effectiveness: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT, 457 patients, 15 US centres, 1988-1991) randomised acute optic neuritis to IV methylprednisolone 250 mg every 6 hours for 3 days followed by oral prednisone taper, oral prednisone alone, or placebo. IV methylprednisolone sped visual recovery within the first 2 weeks (about 1-2 Snellen lines faster) and produced slightly better vision at 6 months versus placebo; the same trial found oral prednisone alone was ineffective and actually increased the risk of new optic neuritis episodes. Long-term ONTT follow-up additionally found the 2-year rate of definite MS was lower with IV methylprednisolone (7.5%) than with oral prednisone alone (14.7%) or placebo (16.7%).
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.reason_why: Acute MS relapses are driven by focal perivascular T-cell/B-cell-mediated inflammatory demyelination (see this knowledge base's symptoms/definition_and_pathophysiology entry); high-dose corticosteroids suppress this acute inflammatory cascade, reduce blood-brain-barrier permeability and oedema, and thereby speed recovery of the acute deficit, though they do not alter the underlying disease course or long-term disability trajectory.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.important_caveat: IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery from a given relapse; it does NOT reduce long-term disability accumulation or substitute for a disease-modifying therapy, and repeated steroid courses do not treat the underlying disease. Standard courses (commonly 1 g/day for 3-5 days) are used in current practice; short-term side effects include insomnia, mood change, hyperglycaemia, and gastric upset, with rare but real risks (avascular necrosis, infection) with cumulative repeated dosing.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.real_working_solution: For any clinically significant relapse causing new or worsening objectively-confirmed neurological deficit (after excluding infection/pseudorelapse, see this knowledge base's symptoms/relapse_and_pseudorelapse entry), treat promptly with IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days; do not use oral prednisone alone at a low, non-equivalent dose, since the ONTT specifically showed that ineffective and harmful for optic neuritis relapses.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.source: Beck RW et al. (Optic Neuritis Study Group), 'A Randomized, Controlled Trial of Corticosteroids in the Treatment of Acute Optic Neuritis', N Engl J Med 1992;326:581-588; Beck RW et al., 'The Effect of Corticosteroids for Acute Optic Neuritis on the Subsequent Development of Multiple Sclerosis', N Engl J Med 1993;329:1764-1769

ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.name: High-Dose Oral Methylprednisolone - Real Non-Inferiority to IV (COPOUSEP)
specific_drugs: Oral methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days (equivalent high-dose regimen to IV)
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.effectiveness: COPOUSEP (multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled non-inferiority trial, 13 French centres) randomised RRMS patients with a relapse in the preceding 15 days to oral or IV methylprednisolone 1000 mg once daily for 3 days. Oral methylprednisolone was non-inferior to IV: about 80-81% of patients in both groups improved by at least one point on disability scoring, with equivalent safety. A separate meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing oral and IV high-dose methylprednisolone for MS relapse found no significant difference in efficacy or safety between the two routes.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.reason_why: At equivalent high doses (not the low-dose oral-prednisone-alone regimen shown ineffective in ONTT), oral and IV methylprednisolone achieve comparable systemic drug exposure and therefore comparable anti-inflammatory effect on the acute relapse.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.important_caveat: This is specifically about HIGH-DOSE oral methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day) being equivalent to IV at the SAME high dose - it does not validate the much lower oral-prednisone-taper regimen shown ineffective/harmful in ONTT. Practical logistics (avoiding a hospital/infusion-centre visit) are the main real-world advantage of the oral route at equivalent dosing.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.real_working_solution: Where infusion access is impractical (as is often the case in India outside major centres), high-dose oral methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3-5 days is a real, trial-validated, non-inferior alternative to IV dosing for an acute relapse - not a lesser option, provided the correct high dose is used.
ms_acute_relapse_iv_high_dose_steroids.source: Le Page E et al., 'Oral versus intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone for treatment of relapses in patients with multiple sclerosis (COPOUSEP): a randomised, controlled, double-blind, non-inferiority trial', Lancet 2015;386:974-981; oral vs IV methylprednisolone meta-analysis, PLOS One 2017 (PMC5703548)

ms_acute_relapse_plasma_exchange.name: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (PLEX) - Steroid-Refractory Relapses (Landmark Weinshenker RCT)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - therapeutic plasma exchange (apheresis), typically 5-7 exchanges over 10-14 days
ms_acute_relapse_plasma_exchange.effectiveness: The landmark randomised, sham-controlled trial by Weinshenker et al. (22 patients with acute CNS demyelinating relapses who had failed a 5-day course of IV methylprednisolone) found moderate-to-marked neurological improvement in 42% of patients receiving active PLEX (7 sessions over 14 days) versus only 6% with sham apheresis - real Class I evidence for a treatment used specifically when steroids fail.
ms_acute_relapse_plasma_exchange.reason_why: A subset of steroid-refractory relapses are driven by pathogenic antibody/complement-mediated mechanisms (in addition to T-cell-mediated inflammation); plasma exchange physically removes circulating antibodies, complement components and other inflammatory mediators from the blood, addressing this antibody-mediated component that corticosteroids alone do not adequately suppress.
ms_acute_relapse_plasma_exchange.important_caveat: PLEX is reserved for relapses that fail to improve after an adequate course of high-dose corticosteroids (steroid-refractory relapses) - it is not first-line and is not a substitute for corticosteroids as the initial relapse treatment. It requires apheresis equipment/vascular access and specialist nephrology/transfusion-medicine or neurocritical-care support, limiting availability outside larger centres, including in India.
ms_acute_relapse_plasma_exchange.real_working_solution: For a relapse causing significant, disabling deficit (e.g., severe optic neuritis, myelitis, brainstem syndrome) that has not improved after a full course of high-dose IV or oral methylprednisolone, refer promptly for therapeutic plasma exchange rather than simply repeating or prolonging steroids - real trial-proven salvage therapy for this specific, well-defined situation.
ms_acute_relapse_plasma_exchange.source: Weinshenker BG et al., 'A randomized trial of plasma exchange in acute central nervous system inflammatory demyelinating disease', Ann Neurol 1999;46:878-886

ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.name: Interferon Beta-1b - First Ever Proven Disease-Modifying Therapy (IFNB MS Study Group, 1993)
specific_drugs: Interferon beta-1b (Betaseron/Betaferon and biosimilars), subcutaneous every other day
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.effectiveness: The IFNB Multiple Sclerosis Study Group's multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (372 RRMS patients, 1988-1990) found the annual exacerbation rate at 2 years was 1.27 with placebo versus 0.84 with high-dose (8 MIU) interferon beta-1b - a real, statistically significant relative reduction of about 34%, with significantly less MRI lesion activity in the treated group. This was the first drug ever shown to significantly reduce relapse rate, lesion accumulation, and (in this early trial) hinted at slowed disability in MS.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.reason_why: Type I interferons shift the immune response away from the pro-inflammatory Th1/Th17 profile that drives acute MS relapses (see this knowledge base's symptoms/autoimmune_mechanism_relapse entry) toward a less inflammatory state, reducing the frequency of new focal inflammatory demyelinating episodes.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.important_caveat: This is a moderate-efficacy, 'platform' therapy by modern standards - real but modest relapse-rate reduction compared with the high-efficacy agents below, and it does NOT reverse or halt underlying neurodegeneration. Flu-like injection-day symptoms, injection-site reactions, and (uncommonly) liver enzyme elevation or depression are real, dose-limiting side effects; neutralising antibodies can reduce efficacy over time.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.real_working_solution: Interferon beta-1b (or beta-1a, below) remains a real first-line option for mild/moderate-activity RRMS, particularly where cost or monitoring-intensity considerations favour an older, well-characterised platform agent over a higher-efficacy but costlier or more closely-monitored option - start early rather than delaying treatment, since earlier DMT initiation is associated with better long-term outcomes.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.source: The IFNB Multiple Sclerosis Study Group, 'Interferon beta-1b is effective in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. I. Clinical results of a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Neurology 1993;43:655-661

ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.name: Interferon Beta-1a (Subcutaneous and Intramuscular) - PRISMS and MSCRG Pivotal Trials
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.effectiveness: PRISMS (560 RRMS patients, 22 centres, 9 countries, 2 years) found subcutaneous interferon beta-1a reduced relapse rate by 27% (22 mcg dose) to 33% (44 mcg dose) versus placebo (mean relapses per patient 1.82 and 1.73 vs 2.56 with placebo), with prolonged time to first relapse and reduced MRI lesion burden. Interferon beta-1a also delayed disability progression versus placebo in this trial.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.reason_why: Same type I interferon immunomodulatory mechanism as interferon beta-1b, above; the subcutaneous 3-times-weekly (Rebif) regimen achieves higher cumulative drug exposure than the once-weekly intramuscular (Avonex) regimen, which correlates with PRISMS's relapse-rate reduction being at the higher end of the interferon class.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.important_caveat: Moderate, not high, efficacy by modern standards; same class-wide flu-like symptoms, injection-site reactions, and rare hepatotoxicity/depression risk as interferon beta-1b. Peginterferon beta-1a (Plegridy) offers a less-frequent injection schedule (once every 2 weeks) for the same underlying mechanism and comparable efficacy class.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.real_working_solution: Use as a first-line platform option for new or treatment-naive RRMS patients with mild-to-moderate disease activity, choosing the specific product/frequency based on patient preference, injection tolerability, and (in India) cost/availability, since all deliver a similar magnitude of relapse-rate reduction.
ms_dmt_platform_injectable_interferon_be.source: PRISMS Study Group, 'Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study of interferon beta-1a in relapsing/remitting multiple sclerosis', Lancet 1998;352:1498-1504

ms_dmt_platform_glatiramer_acetate.name: Glatiramer Acetate - Non-Interferon Platform Injectable (Johnson 1995 Pivotal Trial)
specific_drugs: Glatiramer acetate 20 mg once daily or 40 mg three times weekly (Copaxone and generics/biosimilars)
ms_dmt_platform_glatiramer_acetate.effectiveness: The pivotal Johnson et al. trial (251 RRMS patients, 24 months) found glatiramer acetate reduced the annualised relapse rate by 29% versus placebo (0.59 vs 0.84, p=0.007), establishing it as the first non-interferon agent proven to reduce relapse frequency in RRMS; the effect was sustained in a 6-year extension study of the same cohort.
ms_dmt_platform_glatiramer_acetate.reason_why: Glatiramer acetate is a random polypeptide mixture resembling myelin basic protein that is thought to induce myelin-reactive regulatory T-cells (a shift toward an anti-inflammatory Th2-like/regulatory profile) and act as a decoy antigen competing with myelin autoantigens for presentation, reducing the autoimmune attack on myelin described in this knowledge base's symptoms/autoimmune_mechanism_relapse entry.
ms_dmt_platform_glatiramer_acetate.important_caveat: Moderate, platform-tier efficacy comparable to the interferons, not a high-efficacy agent; lacks the flu-like systemic side effects of interferons but causes injection-site reactions (including localised lipoatrophy with long-term use) and, uncommonly, an immediate post-injection systemic reaction (flushing, chest tightness, palpitations, anxiety) that is self-limited but can be alarming.
ms_dmt_platform_glatiramer_acetate.real_working_solution: A real first-line alternative to interferon beta for patients who cannot tolerate interferon's flu-like side effects, want to avoid routine liver-function/blood-count monitoring, or prefer to avoid interferon specifically; daily or thrice-weekly generic formulations are increasingly available and more affordable in India than the newer oral/infusion DMTs.
ms_dmt_platform_glatiramer_acetate.source: Johnson KP et al., 'Copolymer 1 reduces relapse rate and improves disability in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: results of a phase III multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Neurology 1995;45:1268-1276; 6-year extension, Johnson KP et al., Mult Scler 2000;6:255-266

ms_dmt_oral_moderate_teriflunomide.name: Teriflunomide - Oral Moderate-Efficacy DMT (TEMSO and TOWER Trials)
specific_drugs: Teriflunomide 14 mg once daily (Aubagio and generics)
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_teriflunomide.effectiveness: TEMSO (1088 patients, 2 years) found teriflunomide 14 mg reduced annualised relapse rate by 31.2-31.5% versus placebo (ARR 0.37 vs 0.54) and reduced confirmed disability progression. TOWER (a second, independent phase 3 trial) confirmed this with a 36.3% ARR reduction and a 32% reduction in 3-month-confirmed disability progression at the 14 mg dose versus placebo.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_teriflunomide.reason_why: Teriflunomide inhibits dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase, a key enzyme in de novo pyrimidine synthesis that rapidly dividing activated lymphocytes depend on disproportionately; this selectively reduces proliferation of the autoreactive T- and B-cells that drive MS relapses (see this knowledge base's symptoms/autoimmune_mechanism_relapse entry) while sparing resting immune cells that can use a salvage pathway instead.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_teriflunomide.important_caveat: Teratogenic - it is contraindicated in pregnancy and requires an accelerated elimination protocol (cholestyramine or activated charcoal) if pregnancy occurs or is planned, since the drug and its active metabolite can otherwise remain detectable in plasma for up to 2 years without accelerated elimination. Requires monitoring of liver enzymes and blood pressure.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_teriflunomide.real_working_solution: A real once-daily oral first-line option (avoiding injections) for RRMS patients with moderate disease activity, particularly useful where an oral option is preferred and pregnancy is reliably not being planned in the near term; two independent phase 3 trials (TEMSO, TOWER) give unusually strong replication for this efficacy tier.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_teriflunomide.source: O'Connor P et al. (TEMSO), 'Randomized Trial of Oral Teriflunomide for Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis', N Engl J Med 2011;365:1293-1303; Confavreux C et al. (TOWER), 'Oral teriflunomide for patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis (TOWER): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial', Lancet Neurol 2014;13:247-256

ms_dmt_oral_moderate_dimethyl_fumarate.name: Dimethyl Fumarate - Oral Moderate-to-High-Efficacy DMT (DEFINE and CONFIRM Trials)
specific_drugs: Dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily (Tecfidera and generics); diroximel fumarate (Vumerity) as a better-tolerated prodrug alternative
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_dimethyl_fumarate.effectiveness: DEFINE (over 1200 RRMS patients) found dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily reduced the annualised relapse rate by 53% versus placebo at 2 years. CONFIRM (a second, independent phase 3 trial, over 1400 patients) found a 44% ARR reduction versus placebo at 2 years, with a glatiramer acetate reference arm included for context (not powered for a formal head-to-head comparison).
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_dimethyl_fumarate.reason_why: Dimethyl fumarate activates the Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2) antioxidant-response pathway, which has both anti-inflammatory effects (shifting T-cells away from the pro-inflammatory profile driving relapses) and a proposed direct neuroprotective/antioxidant effect on oligodendrocytes and neurons, though the relative contribution of each mechanism to its clinical benefit is not fully established.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_dimethyl_fumarate.important_caveat: Common, often dose-limiting gastrointestinal side effects (flushing, abdominal pain, diarrhoea) especially during the first month; requires periodic monitoring of lymphocyte counts because of a real, rare but serious risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in patients with prolonged severe lymphopenia. Diroximel fumarate (Vumerity) delivers the same active metabolite with better gastrointestinal tolerability.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_dimethyl_fumarate.real_working_solution: A real effective oral first-line option for RRMS with a favourable overall efficacy-to-monitoring-burden ratio; start with dose titration (120 mg twice daily for 1 week, then 240 mg twice daily) and take with food to minimise the flushing/GI side effects that commonly limit early adherence.
ms_dmt_oral_moderate_dimethyl_fumarate.source: Gold R et al. (DEFINE), 'Placebo-Controlled Phase 3 Study of Oral BG-12 for Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis', N Engl J Med 2012;367:1098-1107; Fox RJ et al. (CONFIRM), 'Placebo-Controlled Phase 3 Study of Oral BG-12 or Glatiramer in Multiple Sclerosis', N Engl J Med 2012;367:1087-1097

ms_dmt_high_efficacy_fingolimod.name: Fingolimod - First Oral High-Efficacy DMT (FREEDOMS Trial)
specific_drugs: Fingolimod 0.5 mg once daily (Gilenya and generics)
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_fingolimod.effectiveness: FREEDOMS (1272 RRMS patients, 24 months) found the annualised relapse rate was 0.40 with placebo versus 0.18 with fingolimod 0.5 mg - a real 54% relative reduction (p<0.001) - with significant reduction in disability progression risk over 24 months. TRANSFORMS (active-comparator trial versus interferon beta-1a) confirmed superiority over an injectable platform DMT.
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_fingolimod.reason_why: Fingolimod is phosphorylated in vivo to an active metabolite that binds sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors on lymphocytes, trapping autoreactive T- and B-cells in lymph nodes and preventing their egress into the circulation and subsequent entry into the CNS, thereby substantially reducing the focal inflammatory demyelinating activity described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry.
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_fingolimod.important_caveat: Requires first-dose cardiac monitoring (bradycardia/AV-block risk), and carries real risks of macular oedema, elevated liver enzymes, lymphopenia-related infection risk (including rare PML and cryptococcal infections), and a rebound increase in disease activity if abruptly discontinued. Contraindicated in pregnancy; requires a washout period before conception (see this knowledge base's ms_pregnancy_and_dmt_safety entry).
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_fingolimod.real_working_solution: A real first oral high-efficacy option for patients with more active RRMS (frequent relapses, high MRI lesion burden) who want to avoid infusion-based therapy, provided the required first-dose cardiac monitoring and ongoing ophthalmological/liver-function surveillance can be arranged.
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_fingolimod.source: Kappos L et al. (FREEDOMS), 'A Placebo-Controlled Trial of Oral Fingolimod in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis', N Engl J Med 2010;362:387-401; Cohen JA et al. (TRANSFORMS), N Engl J Med 2010;362:402-415

ms_dmt_high_efficacy_siponimod_spms.name: Siponimod - Approved Specifically for Active Secondary Progressive MS (EXPAND Trial)
specific_drugs: Siponimod (Mayzent), once daily, dose individualised by CYP2C9 genotype
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_siponimod_spms.effectiveness: EXPAND (over 1600 SPMS patients, the largest phase 3 trial of its kind in SPMS) found siponimod significantly reduced the risk of 3-month confirmed disability progression by 21% versus placebo (p=0.013), 6-month confirmed disability progression by 26% (p=0.0058), and annualised relapse rate by 55% versus placebo - the first drug to show a statistically significant slowing of disability progression specifically in SPMS in a large randomised trial.
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_siponimod_spms.reason_why: Siponimod, like fingolimod, sequesters lymphocytes in lymph nodes via S1P receptor modulation (selectively S1P1 and S1P5), but crosses into the CNS and additionally acts directly on S1P receptors on CNS-resident astrocytes/oligodendrocyte precursor cells, a proposed mechanism for its effect in progressive (not just relapsing) disease where CNS-compartmentalised, not just peripheral, inflammation contributes to worsening (see this knowledge base's symptoms/mechanism_of_progression entry).
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_siponimod_spms.important_caveat: Benefit was most clearly demonstrated in patients with 'active' SPMS (ongoing relapses or new MRI lesion activity); benefit in non-active SPMS is smaller. Requires CYP2C9 genotyping before starting (dose is reduced or the drug avoided in certain genotypes), first-dose cardiac monitoring similar to fingolimod, and carries the same S1P-modulator class risks (macular oedema, infection risk, contraindicated in pregnancy).
ms_dmt_high_efficacy_siponimod_spms.real_working_solution: For a patient who has transitioned from RRMS to SPMS and still shows relapse activity or new MRI lesions ('active SPMS'), siponimod is a real, trial-proven option to slow further disability accumulation - it should specifically be considered at this transition point rather than assuming 'nothing more can be done' once relapses become less frequent.
