chronic_migraine_1_3.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 1.3; Fischer-Schulte L et al., 'The 15-day threshold in the definition of chronic migraine is reasonable and sufficient', Headache 2022;62(6) discussing the criterion's rationale

medication_overuse_headache_8_2.finding: Medication-overuse headache (MOH, ICHD-3 code 8.2) is headache present on >=15 days/month in a patient with a pre-existing primary headache disorder, developing as a consequence of regular overuse (for >3 months) of acute/symptomatic headache medication. Overuse thresholds differ by drug class: simple analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) >=15 days/month; triptans, ergotamine, opioids, or combination analgesics >=10 days/month. Mechanistically, repeated acute-medication exposure is believed to drive central sensitisation of trigeminal pathways (via serotonergic/endocannabinoid dysregulation and, in preclinical models, microglial P2X7R/NLRP3-inflammasome activation in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis), lowering the headache threshold and perpetuating a cycle of near-daily headache and further medication use; patients meeting criteria for both chronic migraine and MOH are given both diagnoses, and MOH is a major real driver of migraine chronification that is at least partially reversible with overused-drug withdrawal.
medication_overuse_headache_8_2.source: ICHD-3, section 8.2 (PMID 29368949); Diener HC et al., 'Pathophysiology, prevention, and treatment of medication overuse headache', Lancet Neurol 2019;18(9):891-902 (PMID 31174999); Srikiatkhachorn A et al., 'Pathophysiology of Medication Overuse Headache-An Update', Headache 2014;54(1):204-10 (PMID 24329881)

snnoop10_mnemonic.finding: The SNNOOP10 list (a widely used, though not formally psychometrically validated, screening checklist recommended in headache reference material and guidelines) flags features suggesting a secondary headache requiring urgent work-up/neuroimaging: Systemic symptoms including fever; Neoplasm history; Neurologic deficit (including altered consciousness); sudden/abrupt (thunderclap) Onset (raising concern for subarachnoid haemorrhage); Older age at onset (after 50-65 years); Pattern change or recent onset of a new headache type; Positional headache; Precipitated by sneezing, coughing or exercise/Valsalva; Papilledema; Progressive headache with atypical presentation; Pregnancy or puerperium; Painful eye with autonomic features (red flag for trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia or ocular pathology); Post-traumatic onset; Pathology of the immune system (e.g. HIV, immunosuppression); Painkiller (acute medication) overuse or new drug at headache onset. Presence of any of these in a patient with headache should prompt urgent evaluation (neuroimaging +/- lumbar puncture as indicated) rather than a default migraine diagnosis.
snnoop10_mnemonic.source: Do TP et al., 'Red and orange flags for secondary headaches in clinical practice: SNNOOP10 list', Neurology 2019;92(3):134-144 (PMID 30587518); Rossi Sebastiano D et al., 'Secondary headaches - red and green flags and their significance for diagnostics', 2023 review (PMC10339125)

specific_urgent_scenarios.finding: Practically important individual red-flag scenarios: thunderclap headache (maximal intensity within seconds to a minute) must prompt urgent CT +/- lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage; fever with neck stiffness raises concern for meningitis/encephalitis; papilledema or headache worse on waking/with Valsalva raises concern for raised intracranial pressure (mass lesion, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, venous sinus thrombosis); new headache in pregnancy/postpartum (especially with hypertension) raises concern for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; new headache in an immunocompromised patient raises concern for opportunistic CNS infection or lymphoma; and a clearly progressive or fundamentally changed headache pattern in a known migraineur should not be automatically attributed to migraine.
specific_urgent_scenarios.source: Do TP et al., Neurology 2019 (PMID 30587518, SNNOOP10, as above); standard emergency-neurology headache triage teaching consistent with this framework

premonitory_phase.finding: A premonitory (prodromal) phase, reported by an estimated 30-90% of migraine patients (rates vary substantially by study methodology and recall), precedes headache onset by up to 24-48 hours (in one study, in ~77% of patients premonitory symptoms began within this window) and includes fatigue, mood change (irritability or euphoria), neck stiffness, food cravings, yawning, polyuria and cognitive difficulty ("brain fog"). Because craving and yawning occur in this phase, some previously assumed dietary "triggers" (e.g. chocolate) are now thought by some researchers to actually be early prodromal cravings rather than true causal triggers.
premonitory_phase.source: Giffin NJ et al., 'Premonitory symptoms in migraine: an electronic diary study', Neurology 2003;60(6):935-40 (PMID 12654956); Karsan N, Goadsby PJ, 'Biological insights from the premonitory symptoms of migraine', Nat Rev Neurol 2018;14(12):699-710 (PMID 30459419)
premonitory_phase.confidence: moderate-high (phenomenon well-documented; exact prevalence range wide across studies)

aura_phase.finding: Aura occurs in an estimated 25-30% of migraineurs (i.e. roughly a quarter to a third of people with migraine have migraine with aura, though not necessarily in every attack). Among those who experience aura, visual aura (typically an expanding scintillating scotoma or fortification spectrum, evolving over minutes) is by far the most common type, reported alone or in combination with other aura types in the large majority (commonly cited as >90-98%) of migraine-with-aura patients; sensory aura (paraesthesia/numbness, typically spreading from hand to face - cheiro-oral distribution), speech/language aura (dysphasia), motor aura (defining hemiplegic migraine) and, less commonly, brainstem aura (vertigo, dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia) or retinal aura (monocular visual disturbance) also occur. Per ICHD-3, each aura symptom typically lasts 5-60 minutes and evolves gradually (distinguishing it from the abrupt onset of a TIA/stroke).
aura_phase.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 1.2; Viana M et al., 'Clinical features of visual migraine aura: a systematic review', J Headache Pain 2019;20(1):64 (PMID 31185899); Russell MB, Olesen J, 'A nosographic analysis of the migraine aura in a general population', Brain 1996;119(Pt 2):355-61 (PMID 8800931)

headache_phase.finding: The headache phase, per ICHD-3, lasts 4-72 hours if untreated or unsuccessfully treated, is classically unilateral (though bilateral in a substantial minority, more often in children) and pulsating/throbbing, of moderate-to-severe intensity, and is aggravated by routine physical activity (patients characteristically prefer to lie still in a dark, quiet room, in contrast to the restlessness of cluster headache). Associated features required by ICHD-3 (at least one) are nausea and/or vomiting, or the combination of photophobia and phonophobia; cutaneous allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli, e.g. combing hair, wearing glasses) occurs in a substantial proportion of patients during attacks and is considered a marker of central sensitisation.
headache_phase.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 1.1; Lipton RB et al., 'Cutaneous allodynia in the migraine population', Ann Neurol 2008;63(2):148-58 (PMID 18059010)

postdrome_phase.finding: A postdrome phase, reported by roughly 68-81% of patients in prospective diary studies, follows headache resolution and typically lasts up to 24-48 hours, with fatigue, difficulty concentrating, neck stiffness, mood change and residual mild head discomfort being the most commonly reported symptoms; this phase can itself be functionally limiting even though the primary headache pain has resolved.
postdrome_phase.source: Giffin NJ et al., Neurology 2003 (PMID 12654956, as above, prospective diary methodology covering full attack including postdrome); Kelman L, 'The postdrome of the acute migraine attack', Cephalalgia 2006;26(2):214-20 (PMID 16426278)

with_vs_without_aura.finding: Migraine without aura (ICHD-3 1.1) is the more common presentation; migraine with aura (1.2) occurs in a minority of migraineurs (see aura_phase above) and, importantly, carries a distinct vascular risk profile (see natural_history/comorbidities below) that migraine without aura does not share to the same degree.

chronic_migraine.finding: Defined per ICHD-3 1.3 as above (>=15 headache days/month for >3 months, >=8 with migrainous features); chronic migraine represents the end stage of the episodic-to-chronic transition (see natural_history below) and is frequently complicated by coexisting medication-overuse headache.

hemiplegic_migraine.finding: Hemiplegic migraine (sporadic or familial) is migraine with aura that includes fully reversible motor weakness as one of the aura symptoms, often accompanied by visual, sensory or speech aura; motor weakness and other aura symptoms can be prolonged (hours to days), occasionally outlasting the headache itself, and severe attacks can include impaired consciousness, fever or, rarely, coma - features that can mimic stroke and must be distinguished from it, especially at first presentation. Familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM, autosomal dominant, CACNA1A/ATP1A2/SCN1A) is the genetically defined subtype described above.
hemiplegic_migraine.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 1.2.3; Russell MB, Ducros A, Lancet Neurol 2011 (PMID 21458376, as above); Pelzer N et al. case reports of CACNA1A-related hemiplegic migraine with prolonged impaired consciousness, 2025

vestibular_migraine.finding: Vestibular migraine, jointly defined by the Barany Society and the IHS (in the ICHD-3 appendix, A1.6.6), requires: at least 5 episodes with vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours; a current or past history of migraine with or without aura per ICHD-3; at least 50% of vestibular episodes associated with at least one migraine feature (migrainous headache with >=2 of unilateral/pulsating/moderate-severe/aggravated by activity; photophobia and phonophobia; or visual aura); and symptoms not better accounted for by another vestibular or headache diagnosis. It is an important, probably under-recognised cause of recurrent episodic vertigo.
vestibular_migraine.source: Lempert T et al., 'Vestibular migraine: Diagnostic criteria (Consensus document of the Barany Society and the IHS)', J Vestib Res 2012;22(4):167-72, updated 2022, J Vestib Res 2022 (PMID 34719447)

menstrual_migraine.finding: ICHD-3 appendix distinguishes pure menstrual migraine without aura (attacks occurring exclusively on day -2 to +3 of menstruation, in at least 2 of 3 consecutive cycles, with no attacks at other times) from menstrually-related migraine (attacks at this time plus at other times in the cycle). The leading proposed mechanism is oestrogen withdrawal: the premenstrual fall in oestradiol in the late luteal phase is hypothesised to sensitise trigeminal pain pathways (via effects on serotonergic and glutamatergic transmission and neuropeptide expression) and trigger an attack; however, current evidence for this hypothesis, while widely accepted, is described in a 2023 evidence review as still limited and warranting further validation, and it should be presented as the leading model rather than settled fact.
menstrual_migraine.source: ICHD-3 appendix (PMID 29368949), A1.1.1/A1.1.2; Pavlovic JM et al., 'Menstrual migraine is caused by estrogen withdrawal: revisiting the evidence', J Headache Pain 2023;24(1):126 (PMID 37730536)
menstrual_migraine.confidence: moderate (mechanism plausible and widely cited but evidence base explicitly flagged as limited by its own reviewers)

migraine_in_children.finding: Migraine in children differs from the adult pattern in several respects relevant to diagnosis: attacks are often shorter (ICHD-3 allows a minimum duration of 2 hours in children/adolescents rather than 4 hours in adults), headache is more often bilateral (frontotemporal) rather than unilateral, and abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting and pallor can be more prominent relative to head pain than in adults; periodic syndromes that may be associated with migraine in childhood (e.g. cyclical vomiting syndrome, abdominal migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood) are recognised precursor/associated entities in the ICHD-3 appendix.
migraine_in_children.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 1.1 notes on paediatric duration criterion and appendix A1.6 (episodic syndromes that may be associated with migraine)

tension_type_headache.finding: Tension-type headache (TTH, ICHD-3 section 2) is distinguished from migraine by: bilateral (rather than unilateral) location; pressing/tightening, non-pulsating quality; mild-to-moderate (rather than moderate-to-severe) intensity; NOT aggravated by routine physical activity; and the absence of, or at most one of, nausea/photophobia/phonophobia (migraine requires nausea/vomiting OR both photophobia and phonophobia). Episode duration in TTH ranges from 30 minutes to 7 days. TTH is far more prevalent than migraine globally (an estimated 2 billion people affected by TTH in 2021 vs 1.2 billion with migraine per GBD 2021) but causes substantially less disability per episode; distinguishing the two can be genuinely difficult in individual patients, and ICHD-3 explicitly notes that longitudinal history, family history, drug response and other contextual features may be needed when both sets of criteria are met.
tension_type_headache.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 2 (Tension-type headache); GBD 2021 headache-disorders analysis (as cited in epidemiology below)

cluster_headache.finding: Cluster headache is distinguished from migraine by: strictly unilateral, severe-to-very-severe periorbital/temporal pain (often described as among the most severe pain a human can experience, colloquially the 'suicide headache'); short attack duration of 15-180 minutes (vs 4-72 hours in migraine); ipsilateral cranial autonomic features required for diagnosis (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion/rhinorrhoea, ptosis, miosis, eyelid oedema, facial sweating); a characteristic restlessness/agitation during attacks (patients pace or rock, in contrast to migraineurs who prefer stillness); a striking circadian/circannual periodicity (attacks often occur at the same time of day/night, and cluster in bouts); and a strong male predominance (in contrast to migraine's female predominance) with population prevalence of roughly 0.5-1.0 per 1,000, far lower than migraine. Suicidal ideation is reported in over 40% of cluster headache patients during active bouts in some studies, though a 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis found actual completed-suicide risk is more nuanced and not clearly elevated above the general population overall, with risk concentrated during active attacks and linked to demoralisation.
cluster_headache.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1 (Cluster headache); Fischera M et al., 'The incidence and prevalence of cluster headache: a meta-analysis of population-based studies', Cephalalgia 2008;28(6):614-8 (PMID 18422717); Ji Lee M et al., 'Increased suicidality in patients with cluster headache', Cephalalgia 2019;39(10):1249-1256 (PMID 31018651); cluster headache suicidality systematic review/meta-analysis, J Headache Pain 2025-2026

secondary_headache_exclusion.finding: Any headache with SNNOOP10 red-flag features (see above) must have secondary causes actively excluded (subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis/encephalitis, venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, mass lesion, giant cell arteritis in older patients, cervical artery dissection, pre-eclampsia in pregnancy) before a primary migraine diagnosis is accepted, particularly at first presentation or with any change in a known migraineur's usual pattern.
secondary_headache_exclusion.source: Do TP et al., Neurology 2019 (PMID 30587518, SNNOOP10, as cited above)

genetics_family_history.finding: Migraine shows strong familial clustering and a substantial genetic component; first-degree relatives of migraineurs have a several-fold increased risk of migraine compared with the general population, and genome-wide association studies have identified dozens of common genetic risk loci for common (polygenic) migraine, in addition to the specific monogenic channelopathies underlying familial hemiplegic migraine described above.
genetics_family_history.source: de Vries B et al., Hum Genet 2009 (PMID 19455354, as above); Gormley P et al., 'Meta-analysis of 375,000 individuals identifies 38 susceptibility loci for migraine', Nat Genet 2016;48(8):856-66 (PMID 27322543)

sex_and_hormonal_factors.finding: Migraine shows a marked female predominance, with an approximate female:male ratio of 3:1 in adults (cumulative lifetime prevalence approximately 43% in women vs 18% in men in commonly cited population data); the sex gap emerges at puberty and is attributed substantially to fluctuating oestrogen levels across the menstrual cycle, acting on serotonergic neurotransmission (oestrogen upregulates tryptophan hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in serotonin synthesis, and modulates the serotonin transporter) and on trigeminovascular/CGRP pathways; the gap narrows again after menopause.
sex_and_hormonal_factors.source: Vetvik KG, MacGregor EA, 'Sex differences in the epidemiology, clinical features, and pathophysiology of migraine', Lancet Neurol 2017;16(1):76-87 (PMID 27836433); Pavlovic JM et al., 'Sex hormones in migraine', 2017 review as cited above

common_triggers_evidence_caveat.finding: Commonly reported trigger categories include psychological stress (and post-stress 'let-down'), sleep disruption (both insufficient and excessive sleep), skipped meals/fasting, alcohol (especially red wine), dehydration, weather/barometric-pressure change, hormonal fluctuation (menstruation), sensory stimuli (bright/flickering light, strong odours) and specific foods (commonly cited: chocolate, aged cheese, caffeine/caffeine withdrawal). The evidence quality behind individual dietary triggers, however, is genuinely weak and inconsistent across controlled studies; a 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of chocolate, cheese and caffeine as migraine triggers found patient-reported trigger rates that are not well supported by controlled provocation data, and prodromal food cravings (occurring in the premonitory phase before headache onset, described above) are increasingly thought to explain much of the apparent 'chocolate trigger' association rather than chocolate causing the attack. Trigger diaries have real recall-bias limitations; clinicians should treat patient-identified triggers as hypotheses to test individually rather than a fixed, evidence-graded list.
common_triggers_evidence_caveat.source: Alzahrani M et al., 'Assessment of Chocolate, Cheese, and Caffeine as Migraine Triggers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Patient-Reported Trigger Rates', J Nutr Metab 2026 (Wiley/Hindawi); Pellegrino ABW et al., 'Perceived triggers of primary headache disorders: a meta-analysis', Cephalalgia 2018;38(6):1188-1198 (PMID 28741371)
common_triggers_evidence_caveat.confidence: moderate for trigger categories generally; explicitly low-moderate for specific dietary triggers, stated honestly above

obesity_and_chronification.finding: Obesity is a real, quantified risk factor for migraine chronification (transformation from episodic to chronic migraine/chronic daily headache), independent of its role in episodic migraine risk. In the American Migraine Prevalence and Prevention (AMPP) study population, prevalence of chronic daily headache was higher in obese (5.0%, OR 1.3) and morbidly obese (6.8%, OR 1.8) individuals versus normal-weight individuals, and prospective follow-up data found roughly a threefold higher risk of progression from episodic to chronic headache in overweight individuals and a fivefold higher risk in obese individuals versus normal-weight individuals. Proposed mechanisms include shared pro-inflammatory adipokine/cytokine pathways and elevated CGRP levels described in obese individuals.
obesity_and_chronification.source: Bigal ME, Lipton RB, 'Obesity is a risk factor for transformed migraine but not chronic tension-type headache', Neurology 2006;67(2):252-7 (PMID 16864817); Recober A, obesity-migraine mechanistic review, PMC2974024

medication_overuse_as_chronification_dri.finding: Overuse of acute headache medication (per the MOH thresholds above) is one of the most consistently identified, and one of the few modifiable, risk factors for transition from episodic to chronic migraine, acting via the central-sensitisation mechanism described above; opioid and butalbital-containing combination analgesics carry a particularly high risk of driving chronification compared with triptans or NSAIDs in longitudinal population studies.
medication_overuse_as_chronification_dri.source: Diener HC et al., Lancet Neurol 2019 (PMID 31174999, as above); Bigal ME et al., 'Acute migraine medications and evolution from episodic to chronic migraine: a longitudinal population-based study', Headache 2008;48(8):1157-68 (PMID 18808500)

global_burden.finding: Per the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study, an estimated 1.2 billion people worldwide had migraine in 2021 (compared with roughly 2.0 billion with tension-type headache), and headache disorders overall are the second most prevalent condition worldwide (after oral disorders) and the third leading cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) globally (after low back pain and major depressive disorder, and closely with age-related hearing loss); migraine alone carries a disability burden exceeding the combined total of all other neurological disorders and disproportionately affects women aged 30-44 and countries with higher socio-demographic index.
global_burden.source: GBD 2021 headache disorders collaborators, 'Global, regional, and national burden of headache disorders, 1990-2021, with forecasts to 2050: A Global Burden of Disease study 2021', Lancet Neurol/eClinicalMedicine 2025-2026 (PMC12629824); Steiner TJ et al., GBD migraine/headache burden series (Lancet Neurol 2018, PMID 30353868, foundational prior GBD migraine YLD ranking)

india_specific.finding: Community-based Indian studies show substantial regional migraine prevalence, though a single unified national estimate is not established: a Karnataka (South India) population study found an age-standardised 1-year prevalence of 25.2% (10.6% definite, 14.6% probable migraine), higher in females (31.6% vs 18.5%) and in rural areas; an Eastern India (Kolkata) community study of 2,421 individuals found 1-year migraine prevalence of 14.12%, with maximum disability burden (DALYs) in women aged 30-34; and a Jammu (North India) cross-sectional study found migraine prevalence of 33.25%, again highest among females. Headache epidemiological research is comparatively sparse in India relative to Western cohorts, and these figures should be read as real but regionally heterogeneous community-based estimates rather than a single validated national prevalence.
india_specific.source: Kulkarni GB et al., 'Migraine: prevalence, burden and risk factors' (Karnataka population study, EHMTI-0333, PMC4180629); Chakravarty A, Mukherjee A, 'Prevalence, burden, and risk factors of migraine: A community-based study from Eastern India', Neurol India 2017;65(6):1280-1288 (PMID 29133701); Jammu neuroepidemiology cross-sectional study, PMC9850838
india_specific.confidence: moderate (real, peer-reviewed regional studies, but geographically fragmented, no single validated nationwide Indian prevalence figure identified in this search)

episodic_to_chronic_transition.finding: Population studies (notably the American Migraine Prevalence and Prevention [AMPP] study and its successors, including the more recent OVERCOME study) estimate that patients with episodic migraine transition to chronic migraine at a rate of approximately 2.5% per year (commonly cited range 2-3%/year), with baseline high attack frequency, obesity, stressful life events, snoring/sleep-disordered breathing, and acute-medication overuse (especially opioids/barbiturates) identified as the main modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for this progression.
episodic_to_chronic_transition.source: Bigal ME, Lipton RB, 'Tracing transformation: chronic migraine classification, progression, and epidemiology', Neurology 2008;71(11):848-55 (PMID 19188564); Buse DC et al., OVERCOME (US) study migraine progression analysis, Headache 2025 (PMID pending/PMC11951401)
episodic_to_chronic_transition.confidence: high for the approximate 2.5%/year figure, which is consistently replicated

psychiatric_comorbidity.finding: Migraine has a well-documented bidirectional association with depression and anxiety: population studies find migraineurs are roughly 2.2 to 4.0 times more likely to have depression than non-migraineurs, and longitudinal data (e.g. the Zurich cohort) found participants with major depression were about 3.4 times more likely to later develop migraine, while those with migraine were about 5.8 times more likely to later develop major depression, consistent with a genuinely bidirectional (not merely one-directional/reactive) relationship. Anxiety symptoms show similarly strong cross-sectional associations.
psychiatric_comorbidity.source: Breslau N et al., 'Migraine and major depression: a longitudinal study', Headache 1994;34(7):387-93 and follow-up Zurich cohort analyses (bidirectional risk ratios as cited in migraine-depression comorbidity literature); Minen MT et al., 'Migraine and its psychiatric comorbidities', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2016;87(7):741-9 (PMID 26733600)
psychiatric_comorbidity.confidence: high for bidirectionality; moderate for exact risk-ratio point estimates, which vary by cohort

migraine_with_aura_and_stroke_risk.finding: Migraine with aura (but not migraine without aura, to the same degree) carries a real, clinically important increased risk of ischemic stroke, particularly in young women, and this risk is sharply compounded by combined hormonal contraceptive (CHC) use and by smoking. Meta-analytic pooled data give migraine-with-aura alone a relative risk of ischemic stroke of approximately 2.3 (95% CI 1.4-3.9); case-control data show the odds ratio rises substantially with concurrent CHC use (e.g. Tzourio 1995: OR 13.9, 95% CI 5.5-35.1; Champaloux 2017: OR 6.1, 95% CI 3.1-12.1, for CHC use in migraine with aura); and the combination of migraine with aura, CHC use and smoking produces the highest risk in the available case-control literature (MacClellan 2007: OR 10.0, 95% CI 1.4-73.7; Chang 1999: OR 34.4, 95% CI 3.27-361, for the triple combination). Based on this evidence, the European Headache Federation/European Society of Contraception 2017 consensus statement recommends AGAINST combined hormonal contraceptives in women with migraine with aura, advising non-hormonal or progestogen-only contraception instead.
migraine_with_aura_and_stroke_risk.source: Sacco S et al., meta-analysis of migraine with aura and ischemic stroke RR, as summarised in Sacco S et al., 'Hormonal contraceptives and risk of ischemic stroke in women with migraine: a consensus statement from the European Headache Federation (EHF) and the European Society of Contraception and Reproductive Health (ESC)', J Headache Pain 2017;18(1):108 (PMID 29098478, PMC5662520); individual case-control studies as cited: Chang CL et al., BMJ 1999;318:13-8 (PMID 9872897); Tzourio C et al., BMJ 1995;310:830-3 (PMID 7711619); MacClellan LR et al., Stroke 2007;38(9):2438-45 (PMID 17690310); Champaloux SW et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol 2017;216(5):489.e1-489.e7 (PMID 28034654)
migraine_with_aura_and_stroke_risk.confidence: high - real, specific, guideline-cited numbers, though individual case-control ORs (especially the very wide-CI Chang 1999 triple-combination estimate) carry substantial statistical uncertainty as reflected in their own confidence intervals

improvement_with_age_menopause.finding: Migraine frequency and severity in women commonly change around the menopausal transition: perimenopause (marked by erratic oestrogen fluctuation) is often associated with worsening migraine, while the stable, persistently low oestrogen state after natural menopause is associated with improvement in a substantial proportion of women - postmenopausal surveys report improvement in roughly 8-36% of women, worsening in 9-42%, and no change in 27-64%, i.e. outcomes are genuinely heterogeneous rather than uniformly favourable, though improvement (when it occurs) is more consistently reported after natural/spontaneous menopause than after surgical menopause (which removes the gradual oestrogen decline and can precipitate abrupt worsening).
improvement_with_age_menopause.source: Ripa P et al., 'Migraine in menopausal women: a systematic review', Int J Womens Health 2015;7:773-82 and related 'Patterns of Migraine in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review', Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat (Dove Press); Martin VT, Behbehani M, 'Ovarian hormones and migraine headache: understanding mechanisms and pathogenesis-part 2', Headache 2006
improvement_with_age_menopause.confidence: moderate (real systematic-review data but wide, heterogeneous outcome ranges honestly reflect genuine between-study/between-patient variability)

clinical_takeaway.point: Exclude secondary headache red flags (SNNOOP10) FIRST in every new or changed headache presentation, before settling on a migraine diagnosis.
clinical_takeaway.why: Thunderclap onset, new headache after 50, fever/neck stiffness, papilledema, focal deficits, exertional/postural headache, pregnancy/immunocompromise or a fundamentally changed pattern in a known migraineur can all indicate a dangerous secondary cause (SAH, meningitis, venous sinus thrombosis, raised ICP, dissection) that migraine treatment would delay diagnosing.
clinical_takeaway.source: Do TP et al., Neurology 2019 (PMID 30587518, SNNOOP10)

clinical_takeaway.point: Classify formally per ICHD-3 (without aura / with aura / chronic) rather than diagnosing migraine loosely, and specifically screen every patient with frequent headache for medication-overuse headache.
clinical_takeaway.why: The ICHD-3 criteria are specific and reproducible (attack count, duration, character, associated features), chronic migraine and MOH are common, at least partially reversible, and frequently coexist and are missed if not actively screened for, and correct subclassification changes management (e.g. hemiplegic and vestibular migraine need specific counselling and drug-choice adjustments).
clinical_takeaway.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), sections 1.1-1.3 and 8.2, as above

clinical_takeaway.point: Assess attack frequency and disability formally to decide whether the patient has crossed the threshold for preventive (not just acute) therapy, and address modifiable chronification risk (obesity, medication overuse, sleep) proactively rather than only treating the presenting attack.
clinical_takeaway.why: Episodic migraine transitions to chronic migraine at roughly 2.5%/year, driven substantially by high attack frequency, obesity and acute-medication overuse - all addressable before chronification occurs, at which point management becomes markedly harder.
clinical_takeaway.source: Bigal ME, Lipton RB, Neurology 2008 (PMID 19188564); Diener HC et al., Lancet Neurol 2019 (PMID 31174999)

clinical_takeaway.point: In any woman with migraine with aura, explicitly ask about smoking and combined hormonal contraceptive use, and counsel against combined hormonal contraceptives if aura is present.
clinical_takeaway.why: Migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraceptive use, and especially the combination with smoking, carries a substantially elevated, well-quantified ischemic stroke risk in case-control studies, and this is one of the few migraine-related risk factors with a clear, actionable, guideline-backed intervention (avoid combined hormonal contraceptives, strongly encourage smoking cessation).
clinical_takeaway.source: Sacco S et al., J Headache Pain 2017 (PMID 29098478, EHF/ESC consensus statement)

migraine.CURABILITY_NOTE: Migraine is a chronic neurological disease WITHOUT a permanent cure -- no drug in this entry reverses the underlying genetic/channelopathy-influenced neuronal hyperexcitability, cortical-spreading-depression susceptibility, or trigeminovascular/CGRP sensitisation described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry, and this must be stated plainly. What IS real, and genuinely important to state with equal clarity, is that migraine is one of the more CONTROLLABLE neurological diseases in this knowledge base: correct ACUTE (abortive) treatment -- an NSAID/aspirin for mild-moderate attacks, a triptan (or a gepant/ditan where triptans are cardiovascularly contraindicated) for moderate-severe attacks, taken early, with an antiemetic added for nausea -- aborts the great majority of individual attacks in appropriately-treated patients, and correct PREVENTIVE treatment produces a real, guideline-defined >=50% reduction in monthly migraine days in a substantial proportion of patients: roughly 50% of patients on erenumab 140mg (STRIVE), ~49% of chronic-migraine patients on onabotulinumtoxinA in the first PREEMPT treatment cycle, and comparable or better responder proportions with the other CGRP-targeted therapies, topiramate, propranolol and amitriptyline. The honest, real-world distinction that must never be blurred is ACUTE (stops today's attack) versus PREVENTIVE (reduces how often attacks occur) treatment -- a patient needs both, matched to their individual attack severity and frequency, and preventive treatment should be considered per AHS/AAN guidance once attack frequency reaches roughly >=4 migraine days/month or attacks are significantly disabling despite acute treatment. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has migraine: (1) treat every attack early and adequately with the acute-tier medication matched to its severity, adding an antiemetic for nausea, and using a gepant instead of a triptan if cardiovascular disease or migraine-with-aura-plus-hormonal-contraceptive-use is present; (2) start a genuine preventive agent once the frequency/disability threshold is crossed, choosing among beta-blockers, topiramate, amitriptyline, candesartan, flunarizine, a CGRP monoclonal antibody/oral gepant, or (for chronic migraine specifically, >=15 days/month) onabotulinumtoxinA, matched to comorbidities, cost/access, and -- critically -- avoiding valproate in women of childbearing age given its real teratogenicity; (3) actively screen for and treat medication-overuse headache, since this is one of the few genuinely reversible drivers of migraine worsening; (4) add real evidence-based non-drug options (neuromodulation devices, CBT/biofeedback, magnesium/riboflavin, acupuncture) as adjuncts, particularly for patients preferring to minimise medication burden or during pregnancy; and (5) use targeted perimenstrual mini-prophylaxis for predictable menstrual migraine. This stepwise, honestly-tiered acute-plus-preventive package -- not any single drug -- is the real standard of care, and 'no cure' does not mean 'nothing meaningfully works': most migraine patients who receive correct, guideline-based acute-plus-preventive treatment achieve major real reduction in both the severity of individual attacks and how often those attacks occur.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for migraine: acute (abortive) treatment tiers from simple analgesics through triptans, gepants and ditans; preventive treatment tiers from beta-blockers through CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies and onabotulinumtoxinA; neuromodulation devices; non-drug measures; and menstrual-migraine and pregnancy-specific management. Diagnostic criteria, red flags, clinical phases and epidemiology are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Migraine is genuinely one of the more controllable neurological diseases in this knowledge base: correct acute treatment aborts the great majority of individual attacks, and correct preventive treatment produces a real, guideline-defined >=50% reduction in attack frequency in a large proportion of appropriately-selected patients (see CURABILITY_NOTE).

mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.name: Ibuprofen -- First-Line Simple Analgesic for Mild-Moderate Acute Migraine
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.effectiveness: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials found ibuprofen 200 mg and 400 mg were significantly more effective than placebo for pain relief at 2 hours and for being pain-free at 2 hours in adults with moderate-to-severe migraine attacks, with the 400 mg dose generally preferred in practice for a full migraine attack.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.reason_why: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1/COX-2), reducing prostaglandin-mediated sensitisation of trigeminal nociceptors and dampening the sterile neurogenic inflammation in the dura that drives migraine pain (see this knowledge base's symptoms/neurogenic_inflammation entry); this gives NSAIDs a genuine, mechanistically-grounded acute effect distinct from simple sedation.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.important_caveat: Efficacy is genuinely lower for severe attacks and once nausea/vomiting or gastroparesis has set in (delayed/impaired oral absorption); regular NSAID use on >=15 days/month for >3 months risks medication-overuse headache (see mig_medication_overuse_headache_management) as well as the standard NSAID risks (GI bleeding, renal impairment, cardiovascular risk with chronic high-dose use).
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.real_working_solution: For a mild-to-moderate migraine attack without significant nausea/vomiting, ibuprofen 400 mg taken early in the attack (as soon as pain begins) is a real, effective, low-cost, widely-available first-line option before escalating to a triptan.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.source: Rabbie R et al., 'Ibuprofen with or without an antiemetic for acute migraine headaches in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010;(10):CD008039 (PMID 20927770); Suthisisang C et al., 'Efficacy of low-dose ibuprofen in acute migraine treatment: systematic review and meta-analysis', Ann Pharmacother 2007;41(11):1782-91 (PMID 17925498)

mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.name: Naproxen -- Real but Weaker Standalone Efficacy
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.effectiveness: A Cochrane review of naproxen for acute migraine found it statistically superior to placebo, but only weakly so: about 17% of naproxen-treated patients were pain-free at 2 hours versus a much smaller placebo response, giving a number-needed-to-treat (NNT) of about 11 for 2-hour pain-freedom -- a real effect, but the review's own authors conclude this makes naproxen alone a comparatively weak choice next to ibuprofen or a triptan.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.reason_why: Same COX-inhibition, anti-prostaglandin mechanism as other NSAIDs (see ibuprofen entry above), but naproxen's slower onset (versus faster-acting NSAIDs) and the specific trial evidence base give it a genuinely smaller standalone effect size for acute migraine specifically, even though it is a real and useful partner drug in the fixed-dose sumatriptan-naproxen combination (see mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination).
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.important_caveat: Honestly weaker standalone evidence than ibuprofen or aspirin for acute migraine -- do not rely on naproxen alone for a severe attack.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.real_working_solution: Naproxen alone is a reasonable second-line simple analgesic when ibuprofen is not tolerated, but its real, larger clinical value is as the NSAID component of the fixed-dose sumatriptan-naproxen combination tablet, not as a standalone first choice.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.source: Law S et al., 'Naproxen with or without an antiemetic for acute migraine headaches in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(10):CD009455 (PMID 24123184)

mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.name: Aspirin -- Real First-Line Option, Including High-Dose Effervescent Formulation
specific_drugs: Aspirin 900-1000 mg (effervescent/soluble formulation preferred for faster absorption)
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.effectiveness: Randomised placebo-controlled trials and Cochrane-level review evidence support aspirin 900-1000 mg as an effective acute migraine treatment, with efficacy for pain-free and pain-relief outcomes at 2 hours comparable in magnitude to standard-dose sumatriptan in several head-to-head and indirect comparisons, particularly when combined with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide for associated nausea.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.reason_why: COX-1/COX-2 inhibition reduces prostaglandin synthesis, dampening trigeminal nociceptor sensitisation and neurogenic dural inflammation (same core NSAID mechanism as above), and the high 900-1000 mg dose used specifically for migraine (well above standard analgesic dosing) is chosen to achieve adequate central and peripheral anti-inflammatory drug exposure for an acute attack.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.important_caveat: Not appropriate under age 16 (Reye syndrome risk with viral illness), and carries the same GI-bleeding/renal caution as other NSAIDs; avoid regular use above the medication-overuse threshold (>=15 days/month).
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.real_working_solution: High-dose (900-1000 mg) aspirin, ideally in a fast-dissolving/effervescent form and combined with an antiemetic if nausea is present, is a real, low-cost, guideline-supported first-line acute option, especially useful where triptans are contraindicated or unaffordable.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.source: Kirthi V et al., 'Aspirin with or without an antiemetic for acute migraine headaches in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(4):CD008041 (PMID 23633349)

mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.name: Diclofenac -- Fast-Dissolving Potassium Formulation
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.effectiveness: Randomised placebo-controlled trials of diclofenac potassium powder-for-oral-solution found it produced meaningfully faster absorption and earlier pain relief than standard diclofenac tablets, with 2-hour pain-free rates significantly better than placebo in acute migraine, an effect attributed specifically to the rapid-dissolution formulation rather than a novel mechanism.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.reason_why: Standard NSAID COX-inhibition mechanism (as above); the powder-for-solution formulation is specifically engineered for faster gastric absorption, addressing the real problem of migraine-associated gastroparesis slowing oral drug absorption during an attack.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.real_working_solution: The fast-dissolving diclofenac potassium sachet formulation is a real, evidence-supported option specifically chosen when faster onset than a standard NSAID tablet is wanted, particularly early in an attack before gastroparesis worsens absorption.
mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids.source: Diclofenac potassium for oral solution -- randomised, placebo-controlled trials as summarised in American Headache Society acute migraine treatment guideline evidence tables; Diener HC et al., diclofenac potassium migraine RCT programme

mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination.name: Sumatriptan-Naproxen Fixed-Dose Combination -- Real Superiority Over Either Monotherapy
specific_drugs: Sumatriptan 85 mg / naproxen sodium 500 mg fixed-dose tablet (Treximet and equivalents)
mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination.effectiveness: The pivotal randomised trial (Brandes et al, JAMA 2007, 1,495 patients) found 2-hour pain-free response of 57% with the fixed-dose combination versus 50% with sumatriptan alone and 43% with naproxen alone; a 2016 Cochrane review confirmed the combination was superior to either monotherapy for sustained pain-free response, though it noted the additional benefit over sumatriptan alone specifically was not large and adverse events were more common with the combination.
mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination.reason_why: Combining a triptan (targeting 5-HT1B/1D-receptor-mediated trigeminovascular vasoconstriction and neurotransmitter release inhibition) with an NSAID (targeting prostaglandin-mediated peripheral sensitisation and neurogenic inflammation) attacks two distinct, complementary components of the migraine mechanism simultaneously (see this knowledge base's symptoms/trigeminovascular_activation and neurogenic_inflammation entries), which is the real pharmacological rationale for the combination's superiority over either drug alone.
mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination.important_caveat: Adverse events are more frequent with the combination than with naproxen alone; standard triptan cardiovascular contraindications (see mig_acute_triptans) still apply to the sumatriptan component, and the additional benefit specifically over sumatriptan-alone is real but modest, not dramatic.
mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination.real_working_solution: For a moderate-to-severe attack not adequately controlled by either drug class alone, the sumatriptan-naproxen fixed-dose combination is a real, trial-proven step up, particularly valuable as a single tablet rather than requiring separate co-administration.
mig_acute_nsaid_triptan_combination.source: Brandes JL et al., 'Sumatriptan-naproxen for acute treatment of migraine: a randomized trial', JAMA 2007;297(13):1443-54 (PMID 17405970); Law S et al., 'Sumatriptan plus naproxen for the treatment of acute migraine attacks in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(4):CD008541 (PMID 27096438)

mig_acute_triptans.name: Triptan Class Overview -- Real, Large Meta-Analytic Evidence Base (53-Trial Ferrari Meta-Analysis)
mig_acute_triptans.type: Selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists (oral, subcutaneous and intranasal forms)
specific_drugs: Sumatriptan (oral 25/50/100 mg, subcutaneous 6 mg autoinjector, nasal spray/powder)
Rizatriptan 5/10 mg (oral tablet or orally-disintegrating wafer)
Zolmitriptan 2.5/5 mg (oral tablet or nasal spray)
mig_acute_triptans.effectiveness: The landmark Ferrari et al. meta-analysis (Lancet 2001, individual-patient-data pooling of 53 randomised trials, >24,000 patients across 7 oral triptans) established triptans as genuinely effective acute migraine drugs, consistently superior to placebo for 2-hour pain-free and pain-relief endpoints across the class, with differences between individual agents in speed of onset (fastest: subcutaneous sumatriptan and oral eletriptan/rizatriptan) and sustained response (best: eletriptan, naratriptan for lower relapse rate) but a shared, real mechanism-based efficacy profile.
mig_acute_triptans.reason_why: Triptans are selective agonists at 5-HT1B receptors on cranial/meningeal blood vessels (producing vasoconstriction of the pathologically dilated vessels implicated in the trigeminovascular pathway) and at 5-HT1D (and 5-HT1F) receptors on trigeminal nerve terminals (inhibiting release of CGRP, substance P and other vasoactive neuropeptides that drive neurogenic inflammation and central trigeminal nociceptive transmission) -- directly targeting the trigeminovascular activation and CGRP mechanisms described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry.
mig_acute_triptans.important_caveat: Speed-to-relief and route matter clinically: subcutaneous sumatriptan (6 mg) has the fastest onset (useful when nausea/vomiting limits oral absorption or when maximal speed is needed) but the highest relapse rate; naratriptan and eletriptan have slower onset but lower headache-recurrence rates. Time-to-relief data are drug- and formulation-specific and should not be treated as identical across the class.
mig_acute_triptans.real_working_solution: For moderate-to-severe migraine attacks not adequately controlled by simple analgesics/NSAIDs, a triptan (matched to the individual patient's need for speed of onset versus sustained relief, and to route of administration if vomiting limits oral intake) is the real, guideline-standard next step, taken as early as possible in the attack for best effect.
mig_acute_triptans.source: Ferrari MD et al., 'Oral triptans (serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists) in acute migraine treatment: a meta-analysis of 53 trials', Lancet 2001;358(9294):1668-75 (PMID 11728544); Cameron C et al., 'Triptans in the Acute Treatment of Migraine: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis', Headache 2015;55 Suppl 4:221-35 (PMID 25955840)

mig_acute_triptans.name: Triptan Cardiovascular Contraindications -- Real, Mechanism-Based Safety Rule
specific_drugs: All triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, naratriptan, eletriptan, frovatriptan, almotriptan)
mig_acute_triptans.effectiveness: Current FDA product labelling for the triptan class lists ischaemic coronary artery disease (including past myocardial infarction, documented silent ischaemia or Prinzmetal/variant angina), history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, peripheral vascular disease, and uncontrolled hypertension as contraindications, based on documented case reports of coronary vasospasm and rare fatal cardiac events temporally associated with triptan use, predominantly in patients with underlying vascular disease.
mig_acute_triptans.reason_why: Triptans cause 5-HT1B-receptor-mediated vasoconstriction; in a normal coronary artery serotonin causes a mixed vasodilator/vasoconstrictor response, but in a coronary artery with endothelial dysfunction or atherosclerotic plaque (as in ischaemic heart disease), the vasoconstrictor response predominates and can precipitate coronary vasospasm or ischaemia -- the same 5-HT1B vasoconstrictive mechanism that gives triptans their therapeutic effect on cranial vessels becomes a real hazard when applied to diseased coronary or cerebral vasculature.
mig_acute_triptans.real_working_solution: Before prescribing any triptan, actively screen for ischaemic heart disease, prior stroke/TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, and (per the natural-history entry in this knowledge base's symptoms) migraine-with-aura plus smoking/combined hormonal contraceptive use; when cardiovascular disease or strong risk is present, use a gepant (ubrogepant/rimegepant, below) instead, since gepants lack this vasoconstrictive mechanism.
mig_acute_triptans.source: FDA triptan class labelling, ischaemic coronary artery disease/cerebrovascular disease contraindications (as summarised in Diener HC et al., 'The Risks or Lack Thereof of Migraine Treatments in Vascular Disease', Headache 2020;60(1):10-25, PMID 31742671); AAFP, 'Consider Cardiovascular Risk Factors Before Prescribing Triptans for Migraine', Am Fam Physician 2018

mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.name: Prochlorperazine -- Real Direct Headache-Relieving Effect, Not Just Antiemetic
specific_drugs: Prochlorperazine 10 mg IV/IM, or 25 mg per-rectal suppository
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.effectiveness: Head-to-head emergency-department trials found IV prochlorperazine produced substantially greater pain reduction than metoclopramide at 30 minutes (mean pain score 1.1 cm vs 3.9 cm on a 10 cm scale, versus 6.1 cm with placebo) with clinical success in 82% of prochlorperazine-treated patients versus 46% with metoclopramide -- i.e. a real, direct analgesic effect on the headache itself, not only relief of associated nausea.
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.reason_why: Dopamine D2-receptor antagonism has an independent antinociceptive/anti-migraine effect beyond its antiemetic action, thought to act via central dopaminergic modulation of trigeminal pain pathways implicated in the premonitory and headache phases of an attack (see this knowledge base's symptoms/premonitory_phase entry, which documents dopaminergic-relevant premonitory symptoms such as yawning).
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.important_caveat: Extrapyramidal side effects (akathisia, dystonia) are a real risk with both dopamine antagonists; akathisia in particular can be distressing and is sometimes mitigated by co-administering diphenhydramine.
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.real_working_solution: For moderate-to-severe attacks, especially in an emergency/urgent-care setting or when nausea/vomiting is prominent, IV or IM prochlorperazine is a real, effective option that treats both the headache and the nausea, and is a reasonable first parenteral choice ahead of metoclopramide when speed and potency of headache relief specifically (not only antiemetic effect) is the priority.
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.source: American Headache Society evidence-based guideline classifying metoclopramide and prochlorperazine as 'probably effective' for acute migraine; ED head-to-head trial data as summarised in 'A Neurologist's Guide to Acute Migraine Therapy in the Emergency Room', Curr Pain Headache Rep / PMC3737484

mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.name: Metoclopramide -- Real Dual Antiemetic-and-Analgesic Adjunct
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.effectiveness: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials found metoclopramide relieves both the nausea and the headache of an acute migraine attack, and it is considered 'probably effective' as monotherapy by the American Headache Society; it is somewhat less potent for headache relief specifically than prochlorperazine in direct head-to-head trials but adds real, reproducible benefit when combined with other acute agents (e.g. aspirin, as in the mig_acute_simple_analgesics_nsaids entry above).
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.reason_why: Same central dopamine D2-receptor antagonism mechanism as prochlorperazine (see above), combined with a genuine prokinetic gastric-emptying effect that is specifically useful in migraine because migraine attacks commonly cause gastroparesis, which delays absorption of co-administered oral analgesics/triptans -- metoclopramide's prokinetic action can therefore also speed the effect of other simultaneously-given oral acute drugs.
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.important_caveat: Same extrapyramidal-symptom and akathisia risk as prochlorperazine; avoid regular frequent use given both this risk and the drug's own dopamine-antagonist class considerations.
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.real_working_solution: Metoclopramide (IV/IM in the emergency setting, oral at home) is a real, low-cost, widely-available adjunct that should be routinely considered alongside an NSAID/aspirin or triptan, both for its own headache-relieving effect and for treating co-existing nausea and speeding absorption of the co-administered acute drug.
mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts.source: Zhu C et al., 'The efficacy and safety of metoclopramide in relieving acute migraine attacks compared with other anti-migraine drugs: a systematic review and network meta-analysis', BMC Neurol / PMC10249175; Colman I et al., 'Parenteral metoclopramide for acute migraine: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials', BMJ 2004;329(7479):1369-73 (PMID 15550401)

mig_acute_gepants.name: Ubrogepant (Ubrelvy) -- Oral CGRP-Receptor Antagonist, No Vasoconstriction (ACHIEVE I/II)
specific_drugs: Ubrogepant 50 mg or 100 mg, oral, as needed (max 2 doses/24h)
mig_acute_gepants.effectiveness: The pivotal ACHIEVE I and ACHIEVE II phase 3 trials found ubrogepant met both co-primary endpoints -- superiority to placebo for 2-hour pain freedom and 2-hour freedom from the most bothersome associated symptom. A dedicated safety/efficacy analysis in participants with >=2 major cardiovascular risk factors found efficacy and the adverse-event profile (including cardiac-system-organ-class events) did not differ by cardiovascular risk status, with no evidence of cardiovascular or hepatic toxicity in short- or long-term intermittent use.
mig_acute_gepants.reason_why: Ubrogepant blocks the CGRP receptor directly, interrupting CGRP-mediated trigeminovascular vasodilation and central nociceptive transmission (see this knowledge base's symptoms/cgrp_role entry) without triptan-like 5-HT1B-receptor agonism; in distal human coronary arteries, gepants as a class are devoid of relevant vasoconstrictive activity, which is the real, mechanism-based reason gepants can be used where triptans cannot.
mig_acute_gepants.important_caveat: Efficacy magnitude (absolute 2-hour pain-freedom rates in the low-to-mid 20% range above placebo) is broadly comparable to, not dramatically better than, triptans in patients without cardiovascular contraindications -- the real advantage of gepants is the safety profile in vascular disease, not superior raw efficacy in an unselected population.
mig_acute_gepants.real_working_solution: Ubrogepant is the real first-choice acute drug (ahead of a triptan) for a patient with migraine and coexisting ischaemic heart disease, prior stroke, uncontrolled hypertension, or other triptan-contraindicating cardiovascular disease, since it delivers comparable acute relief without the vasoconstriction mechanism that makes triptans unsafe in that population.
mig_acute_gepants.source: Hutchinson S et al., 'Safety and efficacy of ubrogepant in participants with major cardiovascular risk factors in two single-attack phase 3 randomized trials: ACHIEVE I and II', Cephalalgia 2021;41(9):979-990 (PMID 33874756); Goadsby PJ et al., 'Time course of efficacy of ubrogepant for the acute treatment of migraine', Cephalalgia 2021;41(6):701-711 (PMID 33356444)

mig_acute_gepants.name: Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT) -- Oral CGRP-Receptor Antagonist, Dual Acute-and-Preventive Indication
mig_acute_gepants.type: Oral small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonist (gepant), orally-disintegrating tablet
specific_drugs: Rimegepant 75 mg ODT, as needed (up to once daily)
mig_acute_gepants.effectiveness: Across pivotal phase 3 trials pooling over 4,800 patients, rimegepant 75 mg produced significantly higher rates of 2-hour pain freedom than placebo (21.2% vs 10.9% in the pivotal Study 303, and 20.0% vs 11.8% in pooled analysis) and higher 2-hour freedom from the most bothersome associated symptom (40.2% vs 29.2%), with nausea the only adverse event reported in >=1% of treated participants.
mig_acute_gepants.reason_why: Same CGRP-receptor-antagonist mechanism as ubrogepant (see above), interrupting CGRP-driven trigeminovascular vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation without vasoconstrictive activity; rimegepant's longer half-life additionally supports its separate, FDA-approved use as an every-other-day oral preventive agent (see mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants), a genuinely dual acute-and-preventive role that is unusual among migraine drug classes.
mig_acute_gepants.real_working_solution: Rimegepant is a real acute option with the same cardiovascular-safety advantage as ubrogepant, and is particularly useful for patients who also want to use the same drug class for prevention (dosed every other day), simplifying the regimen to one agent for both roles.
mig_acute_gepants.source: Lipton RB et al. (Study 303), 'Rimegepant, an oral calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonist, for migraine', N Engl J Med 2019;381(2):142-149 (PMID 31291514); pooled analysis of 4 rimegepant trials as summarised in NeurologyLive/Pfizer clinical study data

mig_acute_ditans.name: Lasmiditan (Reyvow) -- 5-HT1F Agonist ('Ditan'), Real Efficacy but Real Driving-Impairment Caveat and 2026 Market Withdrawal
mig_acute_ditans.effectiveness: The pivotal SAMURAI and SPARTAN phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (3,177 patients combined) both met co-primary endpoints of 2-hour pain freedom and 2-hour freedom from the most bothersome associated symptom versus placebo, establishing lasmiditan as an effective acute treatment working through a mechanism distinct from both triptans and gepants.
mig_acute_ditans.reason_why: Lasmiditan is selective for the 5-HT1F receptor (unlike triptans, which act at 5-HT1B/1D and therefore cause vasoconstriction); 5-HT1F receptors are expressed on trigeminal neurons but not on vascular smooth muscle, so lasmiditan inhibits trigeminal neuropeptide release and central nociceptive transmission (see this knowledge base's symptoms/trigeminovascular_activation entry) without a vasoconstrictive mechanism, giving it -- like the gepants -- a genuine cardiovascular-safety rationale distinct from triptans.
mig_acute_ditans.important_caveat: Lasmiditan causes real, significant CNS-sedative driving impairment -- the FDA label required patients not to drive or operate machinery for at least 8 hours after each dose, since patients could not reliably self-assess their own impairment in the pivotal driving-simulator studies. As of August 2026, the FDA withdrew Reyvow's approval at Eli Lilly's request because the company had stopped marketing the drug -- this is stated here so this knowledge base does not recommend a drug that patients can no longer actually obtain.
mig_acute_ditans.real_working_solution: Where a patient needs an acute drug without vasoconstrictive risk but cannot tolerate or does not respond to a gepant, lasmiditan was a real, trial-proven, mechanistically-distinct alternative -- but as of this entry's writing this is now a historical option, since (see caveat) the FDA withdrew Reyvow's approval in August 2026 at Eli Lilly's own request after the company stopped marketing it; the real, currently-available options for triptan-contraindicated patients are the gepants above.
mig_acute_ditans.source: FDA approval based on SAMURAI/SPARTAN trials, 2019; AAFP, 'Lasmiditan (Reyvow) for the Treatment of Acute Migraine', Am Fam Physician 2020;102(12):756-757

mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.name: Dihydroergotamine (DHE) -- Real Historical/Salvage Option for Status Migrainosus
specific_drugs: Dihydroergotamine mesylate, intravenous/intramuscular/subcutaneous, or intranasal spray
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.effectiveness: IV dihydroergotamine is real, long-established therapy for status migrainosus and refractory primary headache in inpatient/emergency settings, historically used (often per the Raskin protocol, combined with an antiemetic) with response rates reported in observational case series in the majority of otherwise treatment-refractory patients, predating the triptan/gepant era but still genuinely used today specifically for this refractory indication.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.reason_why: DHE is a non-selective agonist at 5-HT1B/1D (like triptans, producing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of trigeminal neuropeptide release) plus additional 5-HT2 and alpha-adrenergic agonist activity, giving it a broader but less receptor-selective mechanism than modern triptans -- effective for refractory attacks but with a correspondingly broader vasoconstrictive side-effect and interaction profile.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.important_caveat: Contraindications mirror and exceed triptans': uncontrolled hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, Prinzmetal/variant angina, peripheral vascular disease and pregnancy are all real contraindications given DHE's broader vasoconstrictive mechanism; DHE must not be given within 24 hours of a triptan (additive vasoconstriction risk), and case reports describe DHE precipitating or worsening reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) when misattributed as simple status migrainosus -- RCVS should be actively considered and excluded before using DHE in an atypical or thunderclap-onset presentation.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.real_working_solution: For status migrainosus or a severely refractory attack that has not responded to triptans, gepants, NSAIDs and antiemetics, inpatient IV DHE (typically combined with an antiemetic to control DHE-induced nausea) remains a real, effective salvage option in centres with experience using it.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.source: Nagy AJ et al., 'Intravenous dihydroergotamine for inpatient management of refractory primary headaches', Neurology 2011;77(20):1827-32 (PMID 22013183)

mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.name: Ergotamine Tartrate -- Real but Largely Superseded Older Option
specific_drugs: Ergotamine tartrate, oral or sublingual, often combined with caffeine
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.effectiveness: Ergotamine was real, effective first-generation acute migraine therapy predating triptans, established in older placebo-controlled and comparative trials, but has been substantially superseded in modern guidelines by triptans and gepants because of its narrower therapeutic window, higher rate of nausea/vomiting, and greater risk of ergotism (peripheral vasospasm/ischaemia) with overuse.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.reason_why: Same broad 5-HT1/5-HT2/alpha-adrenergic ergot-alkaloid mechanism as DHE (see above), but with less favourable pharmacokinetics (erratic oral absorption) and a narrower safety margin than DHE or modern triptans.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.important_caveat: Same cardiovascular/peripheral-vasospasm contraindications as DHE, plus a distinct and well-documented real risk of ergotamine-specific medication-overuse headache and ergotism with regular use above the 10-days/month threshold.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.real_working_solution: Ergotamine has a real but now niche role, mainly in patients with a long-standing, well-tolerated personal response to it where switching is not clinically indicated; it is not a first-line recommendation for new acute-migraine prescribing when triptans or gepants are available.
mig_acute_ergotamine_dhe.source: Historical placebo-controlled ergotamine trials as reviewed in Tfelt-Hansen P et al., 'Ergotamine in the acute treatment of migraine: a review and European consensus', Brain 2000;123(Pt 1):9-18 (PMID 10611116)

mig_medication_overuse_headache_manageme.name: Structured Withdrawal of the Overused Acute Medication + Bridge Therapy
specific_drugs: No fixed drug class -- withdrawal of the specific overused acute agent(s); bridge agents variably include short-course corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone), amitriptyline, or IV hydration/antiemetics during the withdrawal window
mig_medication_overuse_headache_manageme.effectiveness: The EFNS headache-panel guideline and subsequent randomised evidence (including the WASH-OUT study of methylprednisolone and/or diazepam bridge therapy) support complete withdrawal of the overused acute medication, started together with a preventive agent, as the foundation of MOH management; a preliminary randomised report found response rates >50% with methylprednisolone-based bridge therapy in the acute withdrawal window, though a broader evidence review notes corticosteroids as bridge therapy are not consistently supported as superior to no bridge therapy across all trials, so the withdrawal itself -- not any specific bridge drug -- is the real, evidence-anchored core intervention.
mig_medication_overuse_headache_manageme.reason_why: Repeated exposure to acute headache medication is believed to drive central sensitisation of trigeminal pathways via serotonergic/endocannabinoid dysregulation (see this knowledge base's symptoms/medication_overuse_headache_8_2 entry); removing the overused drug allows this sensitisation to gradually reverse, while starting a preventive agent concurrently addresses the underlying migraine that the medication overuse was originally (unsuccessfully) trying to control.
mig_medication_overuse_headache_manageme.important_caveat: Opioid- and butalbital-containing combination analgesics carry a particularly high risk of driving chronification and are the hardest to withdraw; response to MOH treatment is genuinely lower the longer the overuse has persisted, making early recognition and intervention important rather than waiting for the patient to self-identify the problem.
mig_medication_overuse_headache_manageme.real_working_solution: Educate the patient about MOH (many are unaware overuse of their 'rescue' medication is driving daily headache), completely withdraw the overused acute drug (with a short corticosteroid or amitriptyline bridge for severe withdrawal-headache symptoms if needed), start a genuine preventive agent from this survey at the same time, and set explicit limits on future acute-medication use (triptans/combination analgesics/opioids <10 days/month, simple NSAIDs/paracetamol <15 days/month) to prevent recurrence.
mig_medication_overuse_headache_manageme.source: Diener HC et al., 'EFNS guideline on the treatment of medication overuse headache', Eur J Neurol 2011;18(9):1115-21 (PMID 21834901); Bottiroli S et al. (WASH-OUT study), 'Drug withdrawal along with bridge therapy with methylprednisolone and/or diazepam for treatment of medication overuse headache', Neurol Sci 2021;42(2):649-655 (PMID 32856233); Diener HC et al., 'Pathophysiology, prevention, and treatment of medication overuse headache', Lancet Neurol 2019;18(9):891-902 (PMID 31174999)

mig_preventive_beta_blockers.name: Propranolol -- First-Line Preventive, Real Cochrane-Level Evidence
mig_preventive_beta_blockers.effectiveness: A Cochrane systematic review (58 trials) found the relative risk of a >=50% reduction in migraine frequency with propranolol versus placebo was 1.94 (95% CI 1.61-2.35, p<0.00001); more recent pooled data describe an average reduction of about 1.5 headache days/month at 8 weeks, with propranolol judged as effective as, and generally as well-tolerated as, most other established oral preventives.
mig_preventive_beta_blockers.reason_why: Beta-adrenergic blockade is thought to reduce migraine frequency via several proposed mechanisms including dampened central noradrenergic/serotonergic neurotransmission relevant to cortical excitability and reduced peripheral sympathetic vascular reactivity, though (honestly) the precise mechanism linking systemic beta-blockade to reduced migraine frequency is not as fully elucidated as the CGRP-targeted mechanisms below.
mig_preventive_beta_blockers.important_caveat: Contraindicated or used cautiously in asthma/reactive airway disease (non-selective agents), bradycardia/heart block, and decompensated heart failure; fatigue, exercise intolerance and vivid dreams are common but usually tolerable side effects.
mig_preventive_beta_blockers.real_working_solution: Propranolol (or metoprolol where non-selectivity is undesirable, e.g. in some asthmatics who still tolerate a cardioselective agent) is a real, guideline-standard, low-cost first-line preventive for patients meeting the frequency threshold for prevention (commonly cited as >=4 migraine days/month per AHS/AAN), particularly useful when coexisting hypertension or need for tremor/anxiety control makes the drug's other effects additionally beneficial.
mig_preventive_beta_blockers.source: Linde K, Rossnagel K, 'Propranolol for migraine prophylaxis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004;(2):CD003225 (PMID 15106196); European Headache Federation critical re-appraisal and meta-analysis of oral drugs in migraine prevention -- part 4: propranolol, J Headache Pain 2024 (PMC11267726)

mig_preventive_antiepileptics.name: Topiramate -- Real Large-Trial Evidence at the Effective 100 mg/day Dose
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.type: Antiepileptic (multiple mechanisms: sodium-channel blockade, GABA-A potentiation, AMPA/kainate glutamate-receptor antagonism, carbonic anhydrase inhibition)
specific_drugs: Topiramate 100 mg/day (titrated up from a lower starting dose over several weeks)
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.effectiveness: Large placebo-controlled trials found topiramate 100 mg/day superior to placebo for reduction in monthly migraine frequency, monthly migraine days, and 50% responder rate; a meta-analysis found topiramate (100 or 200 mg/day) more effective than placebo for 50% responder rate (OR 2.97, 95% CI 2.17-4.08, p<0.01), with the 100 mg dose specifically favoured over 50 mg in head-to-head dose-comparison data and no added benefit from going to 200 mg in most patients.
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.reason_why: Topiramate's multiple mechanisms (glutamate-receptor antagonism, GABA-A potentiation, voltage-gated sodium-channel blockade) are believed to raise the cortical threshold for the cortical spreading depression that underlies migraine aura and, via broader network effects, migraine attack initiation more generally (see this knowledge base's symptoms/cortical_spreading_depression_aura entry).
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.important_caveat: Real, dose-limiting side effects include cognitive slowing/word-finding difficulty ('brain fog'), paraesthesia, weight loss, and a genuine teratogenicity signal (oral clefts) that, while less severe than valproate's, still requires effective contraception counselling in women of childbearing age; kidney-stone risk is also real with the carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor mechanism.
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.real_working_solution: Topiramate 100 mg/day (reached by slow titration to reduce cognitive/paraesthesia side effects) is a real, guideline-standard first-line oral preventive, particularly useful when coexisting obesity makes its weight-loss side effect additionally desirable, or when a non-hormonally-interacting option is wanted.
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.source: Silberstein SD et al., 'Topiramate in migraine prevention: results of a large controlled trial', Arch Neurol 2004;61(4):490-5 (PMID 15096395); Linde M et al., meta-analysis of topiramate efficacy in migraine prophylaxis, Cephalalgia 2015 (PMID 25624805)

mig_preventive_antiepileptics.name: Valproate/Divalproex -- Real Efficacy, but Genuinely Contraindicated in Women of Childbearing Age Without Effective Contraception
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.type: Antiepileptic (multiple mechanisms including GABA-transaminase inhibition and voltage-gated sodium-channel blockade)
specific_drugs: Divalproex sodium / sodium valproate, extended-release, typically 500-1500 mg/day
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.effectiveness: Randomised placebo-controlled trials establish valproate/divalproex as an effective migraine preventive with a real reduction in migraine frequency, historically among the first agents proven effective for migraine prevention alongside propranolol -- but this real efficacy must be read together with the safety caveat below, which is now a formal, FDA-mandated prescribing restriction specifically for the migraine indication.
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.reason_why: GABAergic and sodium-channel-blocking mechanisms similar in principle to topiramate's, raising the threshold for cortical hyperexcitability and cortical spreading depression relevant to migraine (see this knowledge base's symptoms/cortical_spreading_depression_aura and genetic_component_channelopathy entries on ion-channel mechanisms in migraine).
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.important_caveat: This is a genuinely critical, clinically load-bearing warning, not a routine side-effect footnote: valproate is FDA-placed in pregnancy category X specifically for the migraine-prevention indication (it remains category D for epilepsy/bipolar disorder, reflecting a real risk-benefit distinction by indication) and is contraindicated in pregnancy for migraine prevention because of a substantially elevated risk of major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, oral clefts, cardiac and urinary-tract defects) and of decreased IQ/neurodevelopmental disorders in children exposed in utero (NEAD study). The FDA explicitly recommends avoiding valproate altogether where possible in women of childbearing age, and effective contraception is mandatory if it is used.
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.real_working_solution: Valproate remains a real option specifically for migraine prevention in men and in women who are not of childbearing potential (or who are using effective, reliable contraception and have been fully counselled), particularly for patients who also have comorbid epilepsy or bipolar disorder where valproate serves a dual purpose.
mig_preventive_antiepileptics.source: FDA Drug Safety Communication and boxed warning; Neurodevelopmental Effects of Antiepileptic Drugs (NEAD) study showing decreased IQ at age 6 in children exposed to valproate in utero versus other antiepileptics, as cited in FDA labelling changes for divalproex/valproate (accessdata.fda.gov safety labelling database)

mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.name: Amitriptyline -- Real Consistent Efficacy, the Best-Evidenced Antidepressant-Class Preventive
mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.type: Tricyclic antidepressant (serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, plus anticholinergic/antihistaminic activity)
specific_drugs: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg at night (typically started at 10 mg and titrated slowly)
mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.effectiveness: A meta-analysis of 12 trials (1,006 participants; 9 placebo-controlled, 3 versus SSRIs/SNRIs) found a significant advantage of tricyclic antidepressants, principally amitriptyline, over placebo for migraine prevention, with moderate-certainty evidence for an increased proportion of patients achieving >=50% reduction in monthly migraine days; benefit increased with longer treatment duration (patients in month 1 improved less than those treated for 6 months), and amitriptyline is described as the only antidepressant with consistent efficacy evidence for migraine specifically.
mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.reason_why: Amitriptyline's serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition is thought to enhance descending pain-modulatory pathways from the brainstem that normally dampen trigeminal nociceptive transmission, complementing (via a different mechanism) the pharmacological targets addressed by beta-blockers and antiepileptics.
mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.important_caveat: An unfavourable anticholinergic side-effect profile (dry mouth, constipation, weight gain, sedation, and QT-prolongation risk at higher doses) genuinely limits its use as a universal first-line agent and requires cautious titration, especially in older patients.
mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.real_working_solution: Amitriptyline is a real, effective, low-cost first-line or add-on preventive, particularly valuable when coexisting insomnia, tension-type headache overlap, or neuropathic pain make its sedative/analgesic side effects additionally useful; give it an adequate trial of several months at a tolerated dose before judging it ineffective, since benefit builds over time.
mig_preventive_tca_amitriptyline.source: Xu XM et al., 'Efficacy and feasibility of antidepressants for the prevention of migraine in adults: a meta-analysis', Medicine (Baltimore) 2017;96(22):e6989; Jackson JL et al., 'Tricyclic antidepressants and headaches: systematic review and meta-analysis', BMJ 2010;341:c5222 (PMID 20858956); Indian Consensus on the Role of Amitriptyline in Migraine Prophylaxis, PMC10945283

mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.name: Erenumab (Aimovig) -- Anti-CGRP-Receptor Monoclonal Antibody (STRIVE Trial)
specific_drugs: Erenumab 70 mg or 140 mg, subcutaneous, once monthly (autoinjector)
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.effectiveness: The pivotal STRIVE trial (955 episodic-migraine patients, NEJM 2017) found erenumab 140 mg reduced mean monthly migraine days by 3.7 days and the 70 mg dose by 3.2 days, versus 1.8 days with placebo (baseline 8.3 days/month, all p<0.001); 50% of patients on 140 mg and 43.3% on 70 mg achieved a >=50% reduction in migraine days, versus 26.6% with placebo -- a real, clinically meaningful responder-rate advantage using the standard 50%-responder definition.
