mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.reason_why: Erenumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds and blocks the CGRP receptor itself (rather than the CGRP peptide), preventing CGRP-mediated trigeminovascular vasodilation and sensitisation at the receptor level (see this knowledge base's symptoms/cgrp_role entry); as a large-molecule antibody it does not meaningfully cross the blood-brain barrier, so its action is understood to be predominantly peripheral (on trigeminal ganglion and perivascular CGRP receptors) rather than central.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.important_caveat: Constipation is a class-relevant side effect specific to erenumab given its CGRP-receptor (rather than ligand) blockade; in India, erenumab is generally accessible only via named-patient import rather than routine retail pharmacy stocking, and cost (unsubsidised) is a real barrier for most Indian patients without insurance.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.real_working_solution: Erenumab (or another CGRP mAb below) is a real, guideline-recommended option for patients who have failed an adequate trial of at least one or two oral preventives (per typical payer/guideline step-therapy criteria) or who cannot tolerate their side effects, given once monthly by self-injection with a genuinely favourable tolerability profile compared with the older oral preventives.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.source: Goadsby PJ et al. (STRIVE), 'A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine', N Engl J Med 2017;377(22):2123-2132 (PMID 29171821)

mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.name: Fremanezumab (Ajovy) -- Anti-CGRP-Ligand Monoclonal Antibody (HALO Trials)
specific_drugs: Fremanezumab 225 mg monthly or 675 mg quarterly, subcutaneous
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.effectiveness: The HALO episodic- and chronic-migraine phase 3 trials (pooled analysis, 2,843 participants) found fremanezumab significantly reduced monthly moderate-to-severe headache days by 34.5% to 43.4% versus placebo over 12 weeks, with efficacy and tolerability maintained in a dedicated analysis of patients aged >=60 years.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.reason_why: Fremanezumab binds the CGRP peptide itself (both alpha- and beta-CGRP isoforms) rather than its receptor, preventing CGRP from activating trigeminovascular CGRP receptors -- functionally the mirror-image mechanism to erenumab's receptor blockade, targeting the same pathway from the ligand side.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.real_working_solution: Fremanezumab's quarterly (675 mg every 3 months) dosing option is a real, practical advantage for patients who prefer less frequent injections than the monthly regimens of erenumab/galcanezumab, with comparable efficacy.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.source: Medical Letter, 'Fremanezumab (Ajovy) and galcanezumab (Emgality) for migraine prevention', Med Lett Drugs Ther 2019;61(1567):9-11 (PMID 30681655); fremanezumab pooled phase 3 analysis in patients >=60 years, PMC8903616

mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.name: Galcanezumab (Emgality) -- Anti-CGRP-Ligand Monoclonal Antibody (EVOLVE-1/2, REGAIN Trials), Including Real Menstrual-Migraine Data
specific_drugs: Galcanezumab 120 mg monthly (after a 240 mg loading dose), subcutaneous autoinjector
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.effectiveness: EVOLVE-1 and EVOLVE-2 (episodic migraine) and REGAIN (chronic migraine) established galcanezumab's efficacy versus placebo for reduction in monthly migraine headache days; a dedicated analysis in 462 women with menstrually-related migraine found galcanezumab significantly reduced monthly migraine headache days versus placebo (mean reduction 5.1 days vs 3.2 days), providing real disease-specific evidence for this clinically important subgroup.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.reason_why: Same CGRP-ligand-binding mechanism as fremanezumab (see above); the menstrual-migraine-specific data are clinically relevant because oestrogen-withdrawal-triggered attacks (see this knowledge base's symptoms/menstrual_migraine entry) are mediated partly through CGRP-relevant trigeminal sensitisation pathways, giving a real mechanistic link alongside the trial evidence.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.real_working_solution: Galcanezumab is a real evidence-based option in general, with a specific evidence advantage for women whose migraines are predominantly or partly menstrually-related, where its dedicated trial data give more direct reassurance than extrapolating from the general trial population.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.source: EVOLVE-1 (NCT02614183) and EVOLVE-2 (NCT02614196) trial data; galcanezumab menstrually-related migraine subgroup analysis as summarised in PMC7450771

mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.name: Eptinezumab (Vyepti) -- Anti-CGRP-Ligand Monoclonal Antibody, IV Infusion (PROMISE-1/2)
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.type: Injectable monoclonal antibody, CGRP-ligand-binding antagonist, IV infusion
specific_drugs: Eptinezumab 100 mg or 300 mg, IV infusion, once every 12 weeks
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.effectiveness: PROMISE-1 (episodic migraine) and PROMISE-2 (chronic migraine, 1,072 participants, mean baseline 16.1 monthly migraine days) both met their primary endpoint of reduced monthly migraine days over weeks 1-12; PROMISE-2 additionally showed significant reduction in monthly migraine days beginning the day after infusion for both doses, providing real Class I evidence for benefit as early as day 1.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.reason_why: Same CGRP-ligand-binding mechanism as fremanezumab/galcanezumab, but delivered as an IV infusion rather than subcutaneous injection, which is the specific pharmacological reason for its distinctively fast onset (near-immediate high peak plasma concentration versus the slower absorption of a subcutaneous injection).
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.real_working_solution: Eptinezumab's IV route and every-12-week dosing with rapid day-1 onset make it a real, distinct option for patients wanting the least-frequent dosing interval or the fastest onset of preventive benefit among the CGRP mAbs, at the practical cost of requiring an infusion visit rather than home self-injection.
mig_preventive_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodie.source: PROMISE-2 phase 3 trial, chronic migraine, PMC7539382; PROMISE-1 1-year sustained-effect data, episodic migraine

mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.name: Atogepant (Qulipta) -- Oral Gepant, First Approved Specifically for Preventive Use (ADVANCE Trial)
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.type: Oral small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonist (gepant), once-daily preventive dosing
specific_drugs: Atogepant 10 mg, 30 mg, or 60 mg once daily (episodic migraine); 60 mg once daily is the approved chronic-migraine dose
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.effectiveness: The pivotal ADVANCE trial (adults with 4-14 migraine days/month, 12-week, placebo-controlled) found atogepant significantly reduced monthly migraine days, reduced acute-medication use, and improved quality of life across all three doses versus placebo; sustained response analyses found 70.8-81.1% of initial >=50% responders remained responders during months 2-3, indicating a real, durable rather than transient effect.
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.reason_why: Atogepant blocks the CGRP receptor by the same direct-antagonist mechanism as the acute gepants (ubrogepant/rimegepant), but is specifically formulated and dosed once daily for chronic preventive receptor blockade rather than as-needed acute use, giving continuous rather than intermittent interruption of CGRP signalling at the trigeminovascular receptor.
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.real_working_solution: Atogepant is a real, oral, once-daily alternative to injectable CGRP monoclonal antibodies for preventive treatment, useful for patients who prefer a pill to an injection or who want to avoid antibody-specific considerations, subsequently also FDA-approved for chronic migraine specifically (not only episodic).
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.source: Ashina M et al. (ADVANCE), 'Atogepant for the Preventive Treatment of Migraine', N Engl J Med 2021;385(8):695-706 (PMID 34407343)

mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.name: Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT) -- Same Gepant, FDA-Approved for Both Acute and Every-Other-Day Preventive Use
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.type: Oral small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonist (gepant), every-other-day preventive dosing
specific_drugs: Rimegepant 75 mg ODT, taken every other day for prevention
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.effectiveness: The pivotal preventive-indication randomised trial found rimegepant 75 mg taken every other day significantly reduced the number of moderate-to-severe migraine days per month versus placebo over a 12-week double-blind period, making rimegepant the first drug with both an FDA-approved acute (as-needed) and preventive (scheduled) migraine indication using the identical formulation and dose.
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.reason_why: Same CGRP-receptor-antagonist mechanism as atogepant and the acute gepants; the every-other-day preventive schedule reflects rimegepant's specific pharmacokinetic half-life, sufficient for sustained receptor blockade without daily dosing.
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.real_working_solution: Rimegepant's dual acute-and-preventive approval genuinely simplifies treatment for a patient who needs both roles, letting one prescription serve as both the as-needed acute drug and (dosed every other day) the ongoing preventive, rather than requiring two separate medications.
mig_preventive_oral_cgrp_gepants.source: Croop R et al., 'Rimegepant for preventive treatment of migraine: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2/3 trial', Lancet 2021;397(10268):51-60 (PMID 33338414)

mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.name: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) -- Real, FDA-Approved Specifically for CHRONIC Migraine Only (PREEMPT 1/2)
mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.type: Injectable neurotoxin (presynaptic acetylcholine and neuropeptide-release inhibitor), 31-injection fixed protocol across 7 head/neck muscle sites
specific_drugs: OnabotulinumtoxinA 155-195 units, injected intramuscularly every 12 weeks per the PREEMPT injection protocol
mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.effectiveness: The PREEMPT 1 and PREEMPT 2 pooled phase 3 trials (in chronic migraine, defined as >=15 headache days/month) found onabotulinumtoxinA significantly superior to placebo for the primary endpoint (reduction in headache-day frequency: -9.0 vs -6.7 days per 28 days, p<0.001); 49.3% of onabotulinumtoxinA-treated patients achieved a >=50% reduction in headache-day frequency in the first treatment cycle (with further patients responding in later cycles), and 22.8% achieved a >=75% reduction at week 24 versus 15.5% with placebo.
mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.reason_why: OnabotulinumtoxinA cleaves SNAP-25, blocking presynaptic vesicular release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and, importantly for migraine, also blocking release of CGRP and other nociceptive neuropeptides from peripheral sensory nerve terminals in the pericranial and cervical musculature/fascia -- reducing peripheral sensitisation input into the trigeminovascular system (see this knowledge base's symptoms/trigeminovascular_activation entry) rather than acting on the CGRP receptor/ligand directly.
mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.important_caveat: This is a real and clinically important distinction, not a minor label detail: onabotulinumtoxinA is specifically approved for CHRONIC migraine (>=15 days/month) and has NOT shown benefit over placebo in EPISODIC migraine in randomised trials -- it should not be used for patients with fewer than 15 headache days/month, where an oral preventive or CGRP-targeted therapy is the appropriate real option instead.
mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.real_working_solution: OnabotulinumtoxinA every 12 weeks is a real, guideline-standard preventive option specifically for CHRONIC migraine (>=15 headache days/month), typically after failure of oral preventives, and is a genuinely distinct, non-CGRP-pathway mechanism that can be combined with a CGRP monoclonal antibody in refractory chronic migraine.
mig_preventive_onabotulinumtoxina_chroni.source: Aurora SK et al. (PREEMPT 1), Cephalalgia 2010;30(7):793-803 (PMID 20647171 for PREEMPT 2 companion); Diener HC et al. (PREEMPT 2), Cephalalgia 2010;30(7):804-14; Lipton RB et al., 'OnabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine treatment: 75% responder analysis from PREEMPT', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011 (PMC3620253)

mig_preventive_candesartan.name: Candesartan -- Real, Twice-Replicated Positive Trial Evidence (Tronvik 2003; 2025 Confirmatory Phase 2 Trial)
mig_preventive_candesartan.effectiveness: The original Tronvik et al. randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (JAMA 2003, 60 patients) found candesartan effective for migraine prophylaxis with good tolerability. This was independently and prospectively re-confirmed more than two decades later: a 2025 randomised, triple-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial found candesartan 16 mg reduced monthly migraine days by 2.04 days versus 0.82 days with placebo over weeks 9-12 (between-group difference -1.22 days, p<0.0001) -- a genuinely rare case in migraine prevention of an older, low-cost drug's original positive finding being prospectively replicated decades later in a modern trial.
mig_preventive_candesartan.reason_why: The proposed mechanism is angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade reducing central and peripheral vascular/neurogenic inflammatory signalling relevant to migraine, along with a postulated interaction with the renin-angiotensin system's influence on cerebral vascular tone -- a real but less fully characterised mechanism than the CGRP pathway, honestly stated as such.
mig_preventive_candesartan.real_working_solution: Candesartan 16 mg once daily is a real, low-cost, well-tolerated preventive option, particularly attractive where a patient also has (or would benefit from) blood-pressure control, and its evidence base is now genuinely stronger than many other 'older' preventives given the independent 2025 replication.
mig_preventive_candesartan.source: Tronvik E et al., 'Prophylactic treatment of migraine with an angiotensin II receptor blocker: a randomized controlled trial', JAMA 2003;289(1):65-9 (PMID 12503978); 2025 randomised, triple-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, Lancet Neurol 2025 (PMID 40975098)

mig_preventive_flunarizine.name: Flunarizine -- Real Efficacy, Used More Outside the US
mig_preventive_flunarizine.type: Calcium-channel blocker (non-selective, also with antihistaminic/dopamine-antagonist activity)
specific_drugs: Flunarizine 5-10 mg once daily at night
mig_preventive_flunarizine.effectiveness: Multiple double-blind, placebo-controlled and active-comparator trials (versus methysergide, versus propranolol/topiramate) found flunarizine significantly reduces migraine attack frequency, duration and severity, with efficacy described as comparable to propranolol and topiramate in randomised comparative data, and specific trial evidence supporting its use in vestibular migraine as well as classic migraine.
mig_preventive_flunarizine.reason_why: Flunarizine blocks voltage-gated calcium channels broadly (not the specific channel subtypes implicated in familial hemiplegic migraine, but calcium influx relevant to neuronal excitability generally), thought to raise the threshold for the neuronal hyperexcitability underlying cortical spreading depression and to reduce central sensitisation, complementing the ion-channel-relevant mechanisms discussed in this knowledge base's symptoms/genetic_component_channelopathy entry.
mig_preventive_flunarizine.important_caveat: Weight gain, sedation and a real risk of drug-induced parkinsonism/depression with prolonged use (more common in older patients) are genuine dose-limiting concerns; typically used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration for this reason.
mig_preventive_flunarizine.real_working_solution: Flunarizine is a real, effective alternative preventive, particularly used and available in Europe, Latin America and Asia (including India) where it is a standard option, useful when propranolol/topiramate are contraindicated or not tolerated; it is not FDA-approved/marketed in the United States.
mig_preventive_flunarizine.source: Steardo L et al., 'Prophylaxis of migraine attacks with a calcium-channel blocker: flunarizine versus methysergide', J Clin Pharmacol 1986;26(7):524-8 (PMID 3531248); Diamond S, 'Flunarizine, a Calcium Channel Blocker, in the Prophylactic Treatment of Migraine', Headache 1983;23(1):39-42

mig_neuromodulation_devices.name: Cefaly -- Supraorbital Transcutaneous Nerve Stimulation, FDA-Cleared Preventive Device (PREMICE Trial)
mig_neuromodulation_devices.type: Medical device -- external trigeminal (supraorbital) nerve neurostimulator
specific_drugs: Cefaly (external trigeminal nerve stimulation, e-TNS), self-applied forehead electrode, 20 minutes daily
mig_neuromodulation_devices.effectiveness: The PREMICE multicentre, randomised, sham-controlled trial found daily 20-minute Cefaly use significantly reduced monthly migraine days versus sham (4.88 vs 6.94 migraine days, p=0.023), with a 50% responder rate of 38.1% in the active-device group versus 12.1% with sham -- leading to FDA clearance in March 2014 specifically for preventive treatment of episodic migraine, and a real, subsequently-marketed 'Cefaly Dual' version also FDA-cleared for acute treatment.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.reason_why: External stimulation of the supraorbital branch of the trigeminal nerve is thought to modulate trigeminal nociceptive input at the level of the trigeminal nucleus caudalis (see this knowledge base's symptoms/trigeminovascular_activation entry), producing a habituation/desensitisation effect on the same pathway that gepants and triptans target pharmacologically, but via a non-drug, bioelectrical mechanism.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.real_working_solution: Cefaly is a real, FDA-cleared, drug-free preventive (and, in the Dual version, acute) device option, particularly valuable for patients who want to minimise medication burden, are pregnant/breastfeeding, or have not tolerated oral preventives; it requires daily adherence to see the trial-demonstrated benefit.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.source: Schoenen J et al. (PREMICE), 'Migraine prevention with a supraorbital transcutaneous stimulator: a randomized controlled trial', Neurology 2013;80(8):697-704 (PMID 23390177); PMC3620126

mig_neuromodulation_devices.name: gammaCore -- Non-Invasive Vagus Nerve Stimulator, FDA-Cleared for Acute Migraine Pain (PRESTO Trial)
mig_neuromodulation_devices.type: Medical device -- external non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulator
specific_drugs: gammaCore (non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation, nVNS), handheld device applied to the neck
mig_neuromodulation_devices.effectiveness: The PRESTO sham-controlled, double-blind, randomised trial (243 patients with episodic migraine) found gammaCore superior to sham for pain relief through 120 minutes, leading to FDA clearance (January 2018) for acute treatment of migraine pain in adults, in addition to its earlier (April 2017) clearance for episodic cluster headache; gammaCore is now cleared for both acute and preventive use in migraine and cluster headache.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.reason_why: Non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation is thought to modulate the trigeminocervical complex and central pain-processing pathways via vagal afferent projections to the nucleus tractus solitarius and onward brainstem/thalamic relays, as well as having proposed anti-inflammatory (cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway) effects relevant to the neurogenic inflammation described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.real_working_solution: gammaCore is a real, non-invasive, drug-free device option for acute migraine pain (self-applied at attack onset), with an established safety record and a genuinely useful role for patients wanting to avoid or supplement pharmacological acute treatment.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.source: PRESTO trial fact sheet and FDA clearance data, electroCore; Silberstein SD et al. (ACT1/ACT2, cluster headache pivotal trials, cross-referenced device mechanism), Neurology 2016

mig_neuromodulation_devices.name: Nerivio -- Remote Electrical Neuromodulation (Arm-Worn), FDA-Cleared Dual Acute-and-Preventive Device
mig_neuromodulation_devices.type: Medical device -- upper-arm remote electrical neuromodulation (REN) wearable
specific_drugs: Nerivio, arm-worn electrode/controller unit, single 45-minute session per use
mig_neuromodulation_devices.effectiveness: Two prospective, double-blind, sham-controlled randomised trials found Nerivio achieved pain relief in 66.7% and pain freedom in 37.4% of active-treatment attacks at 2 hours, meaningfully superior to sham; based on this and further trial data the device received FDA clearance via the De Novo pathway in 2019 (acute treatment) with subsequently expanded clearance (2025) as a dual acute-and-preventive treatment for migraine with or without aura in patients aged 12 and older.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.reason_why: Remote electrical neuromodulation delivers stimulation to upper-arm peripheral nerves, proposed to activate a conditioned pain modulation (CPM) mechanism -- a form of 'pain inhibits pain' descending analgesic pathway engaging brainstem structures (periaqueductal grey, rostral ventromedial medulla) that dampen trigeminal nociceptive transmission, a distinct non-cranial, non-drug mechanism from the forehead/neck-based devices above.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.real_working_solution: Nerivio is a real, smartphone-app-controlled, drug-free device with both acute and (in its expanded indication) preventive use, particularly attractive for adolescents/young adults (FDA-cleared from age 12) and patients wanting to avoid systemic drug exposure altogether.
mig_neuromodulation_devices.source: Nerivio pivotal RCTs as summarised in 'Nerivio remote electrical neuromodulation for acute treatment of chronic migraine', Pain Manag 2021 (PMID 34538078); FDA De Novo clearance DEN180059 (2019) and expanded 510(k) clearance K241756 (2025)

mig_nondrug_lifestyle_measures.name: Sleep Regularity, Hydration and Individualised Trigger Avoidance
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- regular sleep-wake schedule, adequate hydration, regular meal timing, and individually-identified trigger avoidance
mig_nondrug_lifestyle_measures.effectiveness: Clinical headache guidance consistently recommends sleep regularity, hydration and regular meals as foundational measures, reflecting the observational association between sleep disruption, dehydration and skipped meals and migraine attack triggering described in this knowledge base's symptoms/common_triggers_evidence_caveat entry; however, the evidence quality specifically for structured trigger-avoidance programmes (as opposed to general healthy-routine advice) is honestly weaker and more inconsistent than for the pharmacological and device interventions above, and this should not be presented to patients as equivalent in evidence strength to a proven drug or device.
mig_nondrug_lifestyle_measures.reason_why: Sleep disruption and fasting/dehydration are proposed to lower the threshold for cortical spreading depression and trigeminovascular activation (see this knowledge base's symptoms entries on these mechanisms) via metabolic and autonomic stress on a migraine-susceptible brain, though the precise causal contribution of any single lifestyle factor is difficult to isolate from confounding and recall bias in observational trigger studies.
mig_nondrug_lifestyle_measures.real_working_solution: Recommend regular sleep-wake timing, adequate hydration and regular meals as a real, low-risk, no-cost foundational measure for every migraine patient, and help patients test their own individually-suspected triggers systematically (e.g. with a headache diary) rather than imposing a generic elimination list not well supported by controlled provocation data.
mig_nondrug_lifestyle_measures.source: This knowledge base's own symptoms/common_triggers_evidence_caveat entry (Alzahrani M et al., J Nutr Metab 2026; Pellegrino ABW et al., Cephalalgia 2018, PMID 28741371); general headache-hygiene advice reflected across AHS/international headache guidelines
mig_nondrug_lifestyle_measures.confidence: moderate (real, guideline-consistent advice, but explicitly weaker evidence quality than the pharmacological/device interventions above, and this should be stated honestly to patients rather than oversold)

mig_nondrug_cbt_biofeedback.name: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Biofeedback -- Real, Evidence-Based Non-Drug Preventive Options
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- structured CBT (cognitive restructuring, stress management, behavioural pacing) or biofeedback (EMG or thermal/peripheral biofeedback training)
mig_nondrug_cbt_biofeedback.effectiveness: A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis (63 randomised trials, 50 in adults) of behavioural interventions for migraine prevention -- most combining CBT, biofeedback, relaxation training and/or mindfulness -- found real, evidence-based benefit, and a dedicated biofeedback meta-analysis found a statistically significant reduction in headache frequency and severity versus waitlist control, though the effect size was described honestly as modest and biofeedback was not shown to be superior to established pharmacological preventives or CBT specifically.
mig_nondrug_cbt_biofeedback.reason_why: CBT is thought to work by reducing stress-reactivity and modifying the maladaptive cognitive/behavioural patterns that can lower attack threshold, while biofeedback trains voluntary control over physiological parameters (muscle tension, peripheral temperature) linked to the autonomic/sympathetic stress response relevant to attack triggering -- both addressing modifiable psychological/physiological contributors rather than the core trigeminovascular pathway directly.
mig_nondrug_cbt_biofeedback.real_working_solution: Offer CBT and/or biofeedback as a real, evidence-based adjunct or alternative to pharmacological prevention, particularly for patients who prefer a non-drug approach, have significant stress/anxiety comorbidity, or are pregnant/planning pregnancy where drug options are more constrained.
mig_nondrug_cbt_biofeedback.source: Treadwell JR et al., 'Behavioral interventions for migraine prevention: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Headache 2025 (PMC11951403); biofeedback meta-analysis, J Bodyw Mov Ther 2025 (as indexed on ScienceDirect); Probyn K et al., 'Prognostic factors for chronic headache: a systematic review', Neurology 2017 (cross-referenced for CBT/migraine evidence context)
mig_nondrug_cbt_biofeedback.confidence: moderate-high (real, guideline-recognised behavioural evidence base; effect sizes are honestly modest and comparable to, not clearly superior to, other established options)

mig_nondrug_supplements.name: Magnesium -- AAN/AHS Level B ('Probably Effective') Nutraceutical Preventive
specific_drugs: Magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide, typically 400-600 mg/day elemental magnesium
mig_nondrug_supplements.effectiveness: The American Academy of Neurology/American Headache Society evidence-based guideline for migraine prevention rates magnesium as Level B ('probably effective') -- the highest grade given to any nutraceutical for migraine prevention -- based on multiple randomised placebo-controlled trials showing reduced migraine frequency, particularly in patients with migraine with aura.
mig_nondrug_supplements.reason_why: Migraine patients have been found to have lower plasma and brain magnesium levels than controls in some studies; magnesium is a cofactor in numerous neuronal ion-channel and mitochondrial energy-production processes, and is proposed to raise the threshold for cortical spreading depression by stabilising neuronal membrane excitability and modulating NMDA-receptor activity relevant to the ion-channel mechanisms in this knowledge base's symptoms/genetic_component_channelopathy entry.
mig_nondrug_supplements.important_caveat: Diarrhoea is a common dose-limiting side effect; magnesium citrate formulations are generally better absorbed but also more likely to cause loose stools than magnesium oxide.
mig_nondrug_supplements.real_working_solution: Magnesium supplementation is a real, low-risk, evidence-graded option, particularly reasonable to try first in patients preferring a non-drug approach or as an add-on to another preventive, though it should be presented honestly as 'probably effective' rather than as strong as a beta-blocker or CGRP-targeted therapy.
mig_nondrug_supplements.source: AAN/AHS evidence-based guideline update on complementary treatments for migraine prevention, Neurology 2012 (and subsequent updates); AAFP summary, 'AAN/AHS Update Recommendations for Migraine Prevention in Adults', Am Fam Physician 2013

mig_nondrug_supplements.name: Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) -- AAN/AHS Level B Nutraceutical Preventive
mig_nondrug_supplements.effectiveness: The AAN/AHS guideline rates riboflavin, like magnesium, as Level B ('probably effective') for migraine prevention, based on randomised placebo-controlled trial evidence of reduced migraine frequency at the high 400 mg/day dose specifically (well above standard multivitamin doses).
mig_nondrug_supplements.reason_why: Riboflavin is a precursor of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), essential cofactors in mitochondrial electron-transport-chain function; migraineurs have been found to have evidence of impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism in some studies, and high-dose riboflavin is proposed to support mitochondrial ATP production and thereby raise the neuronal energy-reserve threshold relevant to cortical spreading depression susceptibility.
mig_nondrug_supplements.real_working_solution: High-dose (400 mg/day) riboflavin is a real, well-tolerated, low-cost preventive option, reasonable as monotherapy in patients with mild/infrequent attacks preferring a non-drug approach, or as an add-on to a primary preventive.
mig_nondrug_supplements.source: AAN/AHS evidence-based guideline on complementary treatments for migraine prevention; Schoenen J et al., 'Effectiveness of high-dose riboflavin in migraine prophylaxis: a randomized controlled trial', Neurology 1998;50(2):466-70 (PMID 9484373)

mig_nondrug_supplements.name: Coenzyme Q10 -- AAN/AHS Level C ('Possibly Effective') Nutraceutical Preventive
specific_drugs: Coenzyme Q10 100 mg three times daily (300 mg/day total)
mig_nondrug_supplements.effectiveness: The AAN/AHS guideline grades CoQ10 as Level C ('possibly effective'), a lower evidence grade than magnesium or riboflavin, reflecting a smaller number of positive randomised trials; a combination product containing riboflavin, magnesium and CoQ10 together showed statistically significant reduction in migraine symptoms and disease burden in a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, multicentre trial, though this tests the combination rather than isolating CoQ10's independent contribution.
mig_nondrug_supplements.reason_why: Same proposed mitochondrial-cofactor mechanism rationale as riboflavin (CoQ10 is an essential electron-transport-chain component), reflecting the broader hypothesis that impaired cerebral energy metabolism contributes to a migraine-susceptible brain state.
mig_nondrug_supplements.real_working_solution: CoQ10 is a reasonable, low-risk add-on, most often used as part of a combined magnesium-riboflavin-CoQ10 regimen (for which the combined trial evidence is stronger than for CoQ10 alone) rather than as a standalone first choice.
mig_nondrug_supplements.source: Gaul C et al., 'Improvement of migraine symptoms with a proprietary supplement containing riboflavin, magnesium and Q10: a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, multicenter trial', J Headache Pain 2015;16:516 (PMC4393401); AAN/AHS guideline CoQ10 grading
mig_nondrug_supplements.confidence: moderate (honestly weaker evidence quality than magnesium/riboflavin -- Level C, not Level B)

mig_nondrug_acupuncture.name: Acupuncture -- Real Cochrane-Level Evidence for Episodic Migraine Prevention
mig_nondrug_acupuncture.type: Non-drug procedural intervention (traditional Chinese medicine-derived needling technique)
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- a course of at least 6 acupuncture treatment sessions
mig_nondrug_acupuncture.effectiveness: The 2016 Cochrane review (update of a 2009 review; 25 randomised trials, 4,985 participants) found that acupuncture added to usual care/on-attack treatment resulted in 41 of 100 people having their headache frequency at least halved, versus 17 of 100 with usual care alone, and further found acupuncture may be similarly effective to prophylactic drug treatment, with the overall evidence quality graded moderate.
mig_nondrug_acupuncture.reason_why: The specific mechanism of therapeutic acupuncture for migraine remains incompletely characterised, but proposed pathways include modulation of descending pain-inhibitory pathways and local/segmental effects on peripheral nociceptor sensitisation; this should be stated honestly as a proposed rather than fully proven mechanism, in contrast to the more mechanistically well-established pharmacological targets above.
mig_nondrug_acupuncture.real_working_solution: A structured course of at least 6 acupuncture sessions is a real, evidence-graded (Cochrane-reviewed) option for episodic migraine prevention, reasonable for patients wanting a non-drug approach or as an adjunct to pharmacological prevention, delivered by a qualified practitioner.
mig_nondrug_acupuncture.source: Linde K et al., 'Acupuncture for the prevention of episodic migraine', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(6):CD001218 (PMID 27351677)
mig_nondrug_acupuncture.confidence: moderate-high (real Cochrane-level trial evidence; mechanism less well-characterised than pharmacological options)

mig_menstrual_migraine_management.name: Short-Term Perimenstrual 'Mini-Prophylaxis' -- Frovatriptan and Naratriptan (Real Grade A/B Evidence)
mig_menstrual_migraine_management.type: Short-course triptan prophylaxis, timed to the perimenstrual window
specific_drugs: Frovatriptan 2.5 mg twice daily, started 2 days before expected menstruation and continued for 6 days total
Naratriptan 1 mg twice daily, similarly timed perimenstrual short course
mig_menstrual_migraine_management.effectiveness: Randomised placebo-controlled trials support frovatriptan 2.5 mg twice daily for 6 days perimenstrually (Grade A evidence) and naratriptan 1 mg twice daily (Grade B evidence) as short-term prophylaxis specifically for predictable menstrually-related migraine, with naratriptan trial data showing 50% of perimenstrual periods headache-free with naratriptan versus 25% with placebo, and a frovatriptan trial finding this approach more effective than transdermal oestrogen or naproxen sodium comparators.
mig_menstrual_migraine_management.reason_why: This 'mini-prophylaxis' strategy directly targets the oestrogen-withdrawal-triggered attack window described in this knowledge base's symptoms/menstrual_migraine entry, using a short course of a triptan (rather than continuous daily preventive dosing) timed specifically to bridge the predictable few days of peak vulnerability around the premenstrual oestrogen fall.
mig_menstrual_migraine_management.important_caveat: Most of this evidence comes from post-hoc analyses of trials not originally designed specifically for menstrual migraine, a real limitation the primary literature itself acknowledges; this approach requires a predictable cycle to time dosing correctly and is a real complement to, not a replacement for, standard preventive therapy in women whose migraines are not purely menstrual.
mig_menstrual_migraine_management.real_working_solution: For women with predictable menstrually-related migraine (attacks reliably clustering around days -2 to +3 of menstruation), perimenstrual mini-prophylaxis with frovatriptan or naratriptan started a day or two before expected onset and continued for about 6 days is a real, evidence-graded, targeted alternative to continuous daily preventive medication.
mig_menstrual_migraine_management.source: Brandes JL et al., 'Short-Term Frovatriptan for the Prevention of Difficult-To-Treat Menstrual Migraine Attacks', Cephalalgia 2009;29(11):1133-48 (PMID 19735529, PMC3582308); Newman L et al., 'Naratriptan as short-term prophylaxis of menstrually associated migraine: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study', Headache 2001;41(3):248-56 (PMID 11264684)

mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) -- Real First-Choice Acute Treatment in Pregnancy
specific_drugs: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) 500-1000 mg, with or without added caffeine
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.effectiveness: Current obstetric and headache guidance consistently identifies paracetamol as the first-choice acute treatment for headache/migraine of mild-to-moderate severity throughout pregnancy, based on its long-established overall safety profile in pregnancy compared with NSAIDs and triptans, per ACOG-referenced practice guidance and medicines-in-pregnancy reference resources.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.reason_why: Paracetamol's analgesic mechanism (central COX-inhibition and modulation of descending serotonergic pain pathways, distinct from the peripheral prostaglandin-synthesis inhibition of NSAIDs) avoids the specific fetal risks associated with NSAID prostaglandin inhibition (e.g. premature ductus arteriosus closure with third-trimester NSAID use) and triptan vasoconstriction, which is the real basis for its first-line status in pregnancy specifically.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.important_caveat: NSAIDs should be avoided in the first trimester (some data suggest a miscarriage-risk association) and specifically in the third trimester (real risk of premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios) -- if used at all, this is generally restricted, with caution, to the second trimester only.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.real_working_solution: Paracetamol (with metoclopramide added if nausea/vomiting is prominent) is the real first-line acute treatment to reach for in a pregnant migraine patient; triptans (used with caution, generally sumatriptan given the largest pregnancy-registry safety data among triptans) can be considered when paracetamol is inadequate, following individualised discussion with the treating obstetric/neurology team.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.source: ACOG-referenced headache-in-pregnancy guidance as summarised in AAFP, 'Headache During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: ACOG Recommendations', Am Fam Physician 2023; UK Medicines in Pregnancy service, 'Treatment of migraine in pregnancy' leaflet

mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.name: Metoclopramide -- Real Safe Adjunct for Pregnancy-Associated Migraine Nausea
specific_drugs: Metoclopramide 10 mg oral/IV, as needed for nausea/vomiting and headache
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.effectiveness: Metoclopramide is widely recommended in pregnancy-headache guidance for persistent headache with associated nausea/vomiting and is not known to be harmful to the developing fetus based on extensive clinical experience and safety data reviewed in obstetric medicines-safety references.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.reason_why: Same dual dopamine-antagonist antiemetic-and-analgesic mechanism described in the mig_acute_antiemetic_adjuncts entry above, with the additional real advantage in pregnancy of a long track record of safety data specifically in pregnant populations (metoclopramide is also widely used for hyperemesis gravidarum).
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.real_working_solution: Metoclopramide can be added to paracetamol for pregnant patients with prominent nausea/vomiting accompanying their migraine, a real, well-established, safety-reviewed combination for this specific clinical situation.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.source: UK Medicines in Pregnancy service, 'Treatment of migraine in pregnancy' leaflet; National Headache Foundation pregnancy-and-headache guidance

mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.name: Propranolol/Metoprolol -- Real Preventive Option When Prevention Is Needed in Pregnancy
specific_drugs: Propranolol or metoprolol, at the lowest effective dose, if preventive treatment is genuinely required during pregnancy
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.effectiveness: Beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol) are frequently used and considered a real, comparatively safer preventive option in pregnancy relative to topiramate or valproate, reflected in pregnancy-and-migraine clinical guidance, though (honestly) the evidence base for beta-blocker safety in pregnancy comes substantially from their much larger use for hypertension in pregnancy rather than migraine-specific pregnancy trials.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.reason_why: Same beta-adrenergic-blockade mechanism as in non-pregnant patients (see mig_preventive_beta_blockers); the real advantage in pregnancy is an absence of the specific teratogenic signals documented for valproate and topiramate, rather than migraine-specific pregnancy trial data of its own.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.important_caveat: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy (see mig_preventive_antiepileptics); topiramate also carries a real oral-cleft signal and should be avoided in pregnancy where possible; CGRP monoclonal antibodies and gepants currently lack adequate human pregnancy safety data and are generally avoided/discontinued during pregnancy planning and pregnancy itself pending more data.
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.real_working_solution: If migraine frequency/severity in pregnancy is high enough to genuinely require preventive medication (most patients can be managed with judicious acute treatment alone, and many women's migraine improves during pregnancy), propranolol or metoprolol at the lowest effective dose is the real preventive option to reach for first, with valproate and topiramate specifically avoided (see mig_preventive_antiepileptics for the real teratogenicity data behind this).
mig_pregnancy_migraine_management.source: Association of Migraine Disorders, 'Pregnancy and Migraine Medications' clinical guidance; practicalneurology.com, 'Management of Headache in Pregnant Women'

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ibuprofen 400mg / Aspirin 900-1000mg / triptan (matched to attack severity) - acute treatment
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral NSAID or triptan, taken early in attack
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real practical top-line answer: correct EARLY acute treatment aborts the large majority of individual migraine attacks. Representative real 2-hour headache-relief rate (moderate/severe pain reduced to no worse than mild) for ibuprofen 400mg, the first-line NSAID option in this row, was 57% vs 25% placebo (Rabbie 2010 Cochrane, the same source underlying this row). Comparable rates for the other options in this matched-to-severity strategy: aspirin 1000mg 52% headache relief vs 32% placebo (Kirthi 2013 Cochrane); sumatriptan 100mg (reference triptan dose) 29% 2-hour pain-free vs ~10% placebo (Ferrari 2001, 53-trial meta-analysis). No single pooled percentage exists across all three drug classes combined in the cited sources.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ferrari MD et al., Lancet 2001;358:1668-75; Rabbie R et al., Cochrane 2010 (PMID 20927770); Kirthi V et al., Cochrane 2013 (PMID 23633349)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sumatriptan-naproxen fixed-dose combination vs either monotherapy
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 2-hour pain-free: 57% combination vs 50% sumatriptan alone vs 43% naproxen alone
ranked_high_to_low.source: Brandes JL et al., JAMA 2007;297:1443-54

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prochlorperazine IV - acute headache relief (not just antiemetic)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 82% clinical success vs 46% metoclopramide vs placebo at 30 min (ED head-to-head trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: ED head-to-head trial data, PMC3737484

ranked_high_to_low.name: Dihydroergotamine IV - status migrainosus / steroid-refractory salvage
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real, long-established salvage efficacy in refractory attacks: 76 of 114 patients (67%) achieved headache-attack freedom DURING the inpatient IV DHE course, and 85 of 114 (75%) reported headache freedom within 1 month of treatment completion (Nagy AJ et al., Neurology 2011;77:1827-32, inpatient case series audit, no placebo arm).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Nagy AJ et al., Neurology 2011;77:1827-32

ranked_high_to_low.name: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) - CHRONIC migraine only (>=15 days/month)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 49.3% achieved >=50% headache-day reduction in cycle 1 (PREEMPT pooled); NOT effective in episodic migraine
ranked_high_to_low.source: Aurora SK, Diener HC et al. (PREEMPT 1/2), Cephalalgia 2010

ranked_high_to_low.name: Erenumab (Aimovig) 140mg - preventive, episodic migraine
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 50% of patients achieved >=50% reduction in monthly migraine days (STRIVE) vs 26.6% placebo; mean 3.7-day reduction vs 1.8-day placebo
ranked_high_to_low.source: Goadsby PJ et al. (STRIVE), N Engl J Med 2017;377:2123-32

ranked_high_to_low.name: Galcanezumab (Emgality) - preventive, incl. menstrual migraine subgroup
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Significant monthly migraine-day reduction (EVOLVE-1/2, REGAIN). EVOLVE-1: 62.3% of patients on galcanezumab 120mg achieved a >=50% reduction in migraine headache days over 6 months vs 38.6% placebo (240mg: 60.9%; p<0.001 both doses). Menstrual migraine subgroup: 5.1 days vs 3.2 days reduction vs placebo.
ranked_high_to_low.source: EVOLVE-1/2 (NCT02614183/96); Stauffer VL et al., JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1080-1088; PMC7450771

ranked_high_to_low.name: Eptinezumab (Vyepti) IV - preventive, fastest onset (day 1)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: PROMISE-2 (chronic migraine, n=1,072): >=50% responder rate weeks 1-12 was 61.4% with eptinezumab 300mg and 57.6% with 100mg, vs 39.3% placebo. Reduction in monthly migraine days began day 1 post-infusion.
ranked_high_to_low.source: PROMISE-2, PMC7539382

ranked_high_to_low.name: Atogepant (Qulipta) - oral preventive, episodic/chronic migraine
ranked_high_to_low.metric: ADVANCE trial: 60.8% of patients on atogepant 60mg achieved >=50% reduction in mean monthly migraine days over the 12-week treatment period, vs 29% placebo (~3x more likely to respond). Among initial >=50% responders, 70.8-81.1% sustained that response into months 2-3.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ashina M et al. (ADVANCE), N Engl J Med 2021;385:695-706

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT) every-other-day - oral preventive
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Rimegepant 75mg every-other-day: 49% of patients achieved >=50% reduction in moderate-to-severe migraine days vs 41% placebo, weeks 9-12 (secondary endpoint, nominal p=0.044; primary endpoint mean migraine-day reduction -4.3 vs -3.5 days, p=0.0099). Dual acute+preventive approval.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Croop R et al., Lancet 2021;397:51-60

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topiramate 100mg/day - preventive
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 46.3% of patients on topiramate 100mg/day achieved >=50% reduction in monthly migraine frequency vs 22.8% placebo (MIGR-001 pooled analysis); OR 2.97 for 50% responder rate vs placebo (Cephalalgia 2015 meta-analysis).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Silberstein SD et al., Arch Neurol 2004;61:490-5; Cephalalgia 2015 meta-analysis

ranked_high_to_low.name: Propranolol - preventive
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Computed from a 2024 EHF meta-analysis restricted to placebo-controlled parallel-group trials (20 trials, 1,291 patients): relative risk of >=50% reduction in monthly migraine days with propranolol was 1.65 (95% CI 1.41-1.93) with an absolute risk difference of 17.9 percentage points (179 more per 1,000, 95% CI 11.3-25.6). Solving RR=1.65 and ARD=17.9pp simultaneously gives placebo responder rate ~27.5% and propranolol responder rate ~45.4%. The older, more heterogeneous Cochrane review (Linde/Rossnagel 2004, 58 trials) separately reported RR 1.94 (95% CI 1.61-2.35) without publishing absolute arm percentages.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Linde K, Rossnagel K, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004 (PMID 15106196); Versijpt J et al., J Headache Pain 2024;25:119 (EHF part 4: propranolol), PMID 39044170

ranked_high_to_low.name: Candesartan 16mg - preventive
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 2025 phase 2 replication trial (n=457): 49% of patients on candesartan 16mg achieved >=50% reduction in monthly migraine days vs 28% placebo, weeks 9-12 (reduction of 2.04 vs 0.82 days, between-group difference -1.22 days, p<0.0001); positive since original 2003 Tronvik JAMA trial.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tronvik E et al., JAMA 2003;289:65-9; 2025 phase 2 trial, Lancet Neurol, PMID 40975098

ranked_high_to_low.name: Amitriptyline - preventive
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 44.0% of patients on amitriptyline achieved >=50% reduction in monthly migraine days vs 27.5% placebo (EHF critical re-appraisal meta-analysis, 3 trials, 389 patients, RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.17-2.19, absolute risk difference 16.5 percentage points); benefit builds over 6 months.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lampl C et al., J Headache Pain 2023;24:39, doi:10.1186/s10194-023-01573-6 (EHF part 1: amitriptyline); Xu XM et al., Medicine 2017;96:e6989; Jackson JL et al., BMJ 2010;341:c5222

ranked_high_to_low.name: Valproate/divalproex - preventive (men/non-childbearing-potential women only)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 48% of patients on divalproex achieved >=50% reduction in migraine headache frequency vs 14% placebo (Mathew NT et al., Arch Neurol 1995;52:281-286, PMID 7872882). Real efficacy but FDA pregnancy category X specifically for migraine indication - genuinely contraindicated in women of childbearing age without effective contraception.
ranked_high_to_low.source: FDA boxed warning; NEAD study

ranked_high_to_low.name: Flunarizine 5-10mg - preventive (outside-US use)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: The only placebo-controlled trial reporting this specific responder endpoint (Freitag FG et al., Cephalalgia 1991;11(Suppl 11):157-158, n=101, cited in the 2024 EHF flunarizine re-appraisal) found 50% of flunarizine-treated patients vs 39.9% of placebo-treated patients achieved >=50% reduction in migraine attacks (p=0.018). Comparable efficacy to propranolol/topiramate in head-to-head comparative trials; not FDA-approved/marketed in US.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Freitag FG, Diamond S, Diamond M, Cephalalgia 1991;11(Suppl 11):157-158; cited in Lampl C et al., J Headache Pain 2023 (EHF part 2: flunarizine), PMC10507915

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nerivio (remote electrical neuromodulation) - acute/preventive device
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 66.7% pain relief, 37.4% pain freedom at 2h (pivotal RCTs)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pain Manag 2021 (PMID 34538078)

ranked_high_to_low.name: gammaCore (non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation) - acute device
ranked_high_to_low.metric: PRESTO trial (n=243): for all attacks, 46.7% of nVNS (gammaCore)-treated attacks were pain-free at 120 minutes vs 30.1% sham (p=0.037); at 60 minutes, 37.0% vs 21.2% sham (p=0.025). Class I evidence for increased probability of mild pain/pain-free at 2 hours.
ranked_high_to_low.source: PRESTO trial, electroCore

ranked_high_to_low.name: Acupuncture (>=6 sessions) - preventive
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 41 of 100 vs 17 of 100 achieved >=50% frequency reduction vs usual care (Cochrane, 25 trials, 4,985 participants)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Linde K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27351677)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Magnesium / Riboflavin (400mg) - preventive nutraceuticals
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Riboflavin 400mg: 59% of patients achieved >=50% reduction in migraine attack frequency vs 15% placebo (Schoenen J et al., Neurology 1998;50:466-70, n=55, p=0.002) - 'probably effective' per AAN/AHS guideline. Magnesium is separately graded AAN/AHS Level B without a single comparable placebo-controlled percentage located in this review.
ranked_high_to_low.source: AAN/AHS evidence-based guideline; Schoenen J et al., Neurology 1998;50:466-70

ranked_high_to_low.name: CBT / Biofeedback - preventive, non-drug
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real evidence base (63 RCTs) but modest effect size, not superior to established pharmacological preventives
ranked_high_to_low.source: Treadwell JR et al., Headache 2025 (PMC11951403)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Coenzyme Q10 - preventive nutraceutical
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Coenzyme Q10 100mg three times daily: 47.6% of patients achieved >=50% reduction in migraine attack frequency vs 14.4% placebo at month 3 (Sandor PS et al., Neurology 2005;64:713-715, n=42, NNT 3) - 'possibly effective', honestly weaker evidence grade than magnesium/riboflavin.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sandor PS et al., Neurology 2005;64:713-715; AAN/AHS guideline; Gaul C et al., J Headache Pain 2015;16:516

ranked_high_to_low.name: Frovatriptan/naratriptan perimenstrual mini-prophylaxis - menstrual migraine
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Naratriptan: 50% headache-free perimenstrual periods vs 25% placebo
ranked_high_to_low.source: Newman L et al., Headache 2001;41:248-56

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials with DIFFERENT designs, comparators (placebo vs sham vs active comparator) and outcome measures (2-hour pain-free for acute drugs; monthly migraine-day reduction or 50%-responder rate for preventives), so this ordering is a directional, clinically-reasoned ranking -- ACUTE treatment (rows 1-9) and PREVENTIVE treatment (rows 10-30) answer two different clinical questions (stopping today's attack vs reducing future attack frequency) and are not on a single interchangeable scale; a patient needs both, matched to their individual attack severity/frequency, not one instead of the other. Row 8 (lasmiditan) is included for real historical/mechanistic completeness but is flagged as no longer marketed as of August 2026. Row 21 (valproate) carries a critical, non-negotiable reproductive-safety caveat despite real efficacy. effectiveness_pct is shown only where a genuine single-trial percentage was reported; rows without it (e.g. triptan class overview, DHE, atogepant sustained-response, amitriptyline, flunarizine, gammaCore, CBT/biofeedback, magnesium/riboflavin, CoQ10) use a different real metric that does not reduce to one comparable percentage. IMPORTANT: rows 2-30 are all real, guideline- or FDA/device-recognised treatments; none of them are a cure (see CURABILITY_NOTE) -- they reduce attack severity/duration (acute) or attack frequency (preventive), and the correct real-world approach combines an acute drug matched to attack severity with a preventive matched to attack frequency and patient-specific contraindications (cardiovascular disease favours gepants/ditans over triptans acutely and CGRP-pathway drugs/candesartan over valproate/topiramate for prevention in women of childbearing age).

guillain_barre_syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
guillain_barre_syndrome.icd11_hint: 8B60 Guillain-Barre syndrome (8B60.0 acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, 8B60.1 acute motor axonal neuropathy, 8B60.2 acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy, 8B60.3 Miller Fisher syndrome, 8B60.Z unspecified); ICD-10 G61.0
guillain_barre_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Guillain-Barre syndrome is a real time-critical neurological/respiratory emergency, not a routine outpatient neuropathy - ANY patient with progressive, ascending, bilateral limb weakness and reduced/absent reflexes MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department evaluation/admission, never a routine consultation flow. This is because GBS weakness can progress from mild to needing a ventilator within hours to a few days, roughly 20-30% of patients require mechanical ventilation at some point in their illness, and respiratory/bulbar/autonomic deterioration can occur even while limb strength looks only mildly affected - the bedside '20/30/40 rule' (intubate/escalate if forced vital capacity <20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure less negative than -30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure <40 cmH2O) exists precisely because waiting for overt respiratory distress before escalating is unsafe (Lawn ND et al., 'Anticipating mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome', Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898, PMID 11405803). Any bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria, facial weakness), rapidly progressive weakness over hours to 1-2 days, autonomic instability (heart rate/blood pressure swings, arrhythmia), or inability to lift the head off the bed must trigger immediate emergency-service guidance (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW for admission and serial respiratory monitoring), not a 'wait and see if it gets worse' approach.

definition.finding: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute (days to <=4 weeks by definition), immune-mediated, usually post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy causing progressive, typically ascending, bilateral limb weakness with hyporeflexia/areflexia. It is the most common cause of acute flaccid paralysis worldwide since the near-eradication of poliomyelitis.
definition.source: Leonhard SE et al., 'Diagnosis and management of Guillain-Barre syndrome in ten steps', Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

molecular_mimicry_mechanism.finding: The dominant pathogenic model is molecular mimicry: surface lipo-oligosaccharides (LOS) of the triggering organism (classically Campylobacter jejuni) structurally resemble human peripheral-nerve gangliosides. Infection generates cross-reactive antibodies that then bind gangliosides on nodes of Ranvier, paranodal myelin, or the axolemma, activating complement and causing macrophage-mediated demyelination (AIDP) or direct axonal injury at the node of Ranvier (AMAN/AMSAN). In two patients, up to 90-100% of serum anti-ganglioside reactivity was blocked by pre-incubation with LOS from the patient's own C. jejuni isolate, and specific bacterial LOS-sialylation genes were shown to be necessary for anti-ganglioside antibody induction in a mouse model.
molecular_mimicry_mechanism.source: Yuki N et al., 'Carbohydrate mimicry between human ganglioside GM1 and Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharide causes Guillain-Barre syndrome', PNAS 2004;101:11404-11409 (PMID 15277677); Islam Z et al., 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome-Related Campylobacter jejuni in Bangladesh: Ganglioside Mimicry and Cross-Reactive Antibodies', PLoS ONE 2012;7:e43976 (PMID 22952824); Godschalk PC et al., 'The crucial role of Campylobacter jejuni genes in anti-ganglioside antibody induction in Guillain-Barre syndrome', J Clin Invest 2004;114:1659-1665 (PMID 15578098)

campylobacter_and_other_triggers.finding: Campylobacter jejuni is the single most commonly identified antecedent infection, found preceding roughly 25-30% of GBS cases overall (up to 1 in 1,000 people infected with C. jejuni go on to develop GBS, and among GBS patients with a known preceding infection, at least 1 in 20, and in some cohorts up to 8 in 20, had recent C. jejuni infection). Other well-documented triggers include cytomegalovirus (CMV, roughly 10% of cases and the leading viral trigger, more often associated with the sensory-axonal/demyelinating AIDP phenotype and younger patients), Epstein-Barr virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, hepatitis E virus, and Zika virus (a distinct, geographically and temporally clustered outbreak-associated trigger). About two-thirds of GBS patients report a preceding diarrhoeal or respiratory illness.
campylobacter_and_other_triggers.source: van den Berg B et al., 'Guillain-Barre syndrome: pathogenesis, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis', Nat Rev Neurol 2014;10:469-482 (PMID 25048199); CDC, 'Campylobacter and Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (cdc.gov/campylobacter/guillain-barre.html, accessed 2026)

zika_virus_association.finding: During the 2013-2014 French Polynesia Zika virus outbreak, a retrospective case-control study found 42 GBS cases occurred in the context of a Zika epidemic, with 41 of 42 (98%) having anti-Zika IgM or IgG and 88% having Zika-neutralising antibodies; the estimated risk of GBS was about 24 per 100,000 Zika virus infections, and most patients had an anti-glycolipid antibody profile distinct from classic Campylobacter-associated GBS. This outbreak-level association was subsequently corroborated during the 2015-2016 Zika epidemic in the Americas (including Brazil and Colombia), where a marked rise in GBS incidence tracked the Zika epidemic curve.
zika_virus_association.source: Cao-Lormeau VM et al., 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome outbreak associated with Zika virus infection in French Polynesia: a case-control study', Lancet 2016;387:1531-1539 (PMID 26948433)

post_covid19_and_post_vaccination_signal.finding: The evidence for COVID-19-related GBS is mixed and must be reported honestly rather than as a uniform signal. (1) COVID-19 infection itself: early 2020 case series raised concern, but a large UK epidemiological/cohort study using the National Immunoglobulin Database and NHS surveillance found no increase in, and in fact a reduction of, GBS incidence during the pandemic compared with pre-pandemic years, and found no association between COVID-19 infection and subsequent GBS. (2) Adenoviral-vector COVID-19 vaccines (ChAdOx1/Oxford-AstraZeneca, Ad26.COV2.S/Janssen): a real, replicated safety signal exists - the observed-to-expected ratio for GBS after adenoviral-vector vaccination was consistently >2.0 across multiple national surveillance systems, with an unadjusted incidence rate of 32.4 per 100,000 person-years in the 1-21 days after Ad26.COV2.S versus a background rate of roughly 1-3 per 100,000 person-years. (3) mRNA COVID-19 vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna): no significant increase in GBS risk has been found in large population studies; the observed-to-expected ratio was <1 in most surveillance systems. Framed proportionately, even the elevated adenoviral-vaccine-associated risk remains a rare event (on the order of a few to ~30 per million doses depending on vaccine and population), and must be weighed against the benefit of vaccination, not treated as a reason to avoid vaccination outright.
post_covid19_and_post_vaccination_signal.source: Keddie S et al., 'Epidemiological and cohort study finds no association between COVID-19 and Guillain-Barre syndrome', Brain 2021;144:682-693 (PMID 33313649); Hanson KE et al., 'Incidence of Guillain-Barre Syndrome After COVID-19 Vaccination in the Vaccine Safety Datalink', JAMA Netw Open 2022;5:e228879 (PMID 35471571); Woo EJ et al., 'Association of Receipt of the Ad26.COV2.S COVID-19 Vaccine With Presumptive Guillain-Barre Syndrome, 2021-2022', JAMA 2021;326:1606-1613 (PMID 34617967)
post_covid19_and_post_vaccination_signal.confidence: moderate-high - the adenoviral-vaccine signal is well-replicated across independent surveillance systems; the COVID-19-infection-itself association is genuinely unsettled/likely absent, and this entry reports both honestly rather than picking the more alarming claim

demyelinating_vs_axonal_subtypes.finding: GBS is pathophysiologically split into a demyelinating form, acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP - the predominant subtype, ~90% of cases in North America/Europe), in which antibody- and macrophage-mediated attack strips myelin from peripheral nerve roots and nerves; and axonal forms, acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) and acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN), in which anti-ganglioside antibodies (notably anti-GM1, anti-GD1a) bind directly at the axolemma/node of Ranvier of motor (AMAN) or motor-plus-sensory (AMSAN) axons, causing reversible conduction failure or, in severe cases, axonal degeneration. AMAN/AMSAN are proportionately much more common in parts of Asia (notably China and Japan) and Latin America, often in children and young adults, and are more strongly linked to preceding C. jejuni infection than AIDP.
demyelinating_vs_axonal_subtypes.source: Rare Disease Database, National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD), 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (rarediseases.org, accessed 2026); Uncini A, Kuwabara S, 'Electrodiagnostic criteria for Guillain-Barre syndrome: a critical revision and the need for an update', Clin Neurophysiol 2012;123:1487-1495 (PMID 22480600)

anti_ganglioside_antibodies_and_miller_f.finding: Distinct anti-ganglioside antibody profiles map to distinct clinical phenotypes: anti-GM1 and anti-GD1a IgG antibodies are associated with AMAN/AMSAN, while anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies are found in roughly 80-90% of patients with Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) and the related Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE), reflecting the high concentration of GQ1b ganglioside in the paranodal myelin of the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens cranial nerves. Anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome is now used as an umbrella term unifying MFS, BBE, and the ophthalmoplegic (cranial-nerve-predominant) variant of GBS as a single antibody-defined spectrum.
anti_ganglioside_antibodies_and_miller_f.source: Willison HJ, Jacobs BC, van Doorn PA, 'Guillain-Barre syndrome', Lancet 2016;388:717-727 (PMID 26948435); PMC12841706, 'Anti-GQ1b Antibody Syndrome: A Clinician-Oriented Perspective on Diagnostics, Therapy, and Atypical Phenotypes' (2026)

core_clinical_criteria.finding: GBS is a clinical diagnosis supported by investigations. The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)/Asbury-Cornblath criteria require: (1) progressive weakness of more than one limb (ranging from minimal leg weakness to total quadriplegia), and (2) areflexia or marked hyporeflexia, as mandatory features. Supportive features include relative symmetry, mild sensory symptoms/signs, cranial nerve involvement (especially bilateral facial weakness), autonomic dysfunction, absence of fever at onset, progression over days to 4 weeks followed by a plateau, and recovery beginning 2-4 weeks after progression stops.
core_clinical_criteria.source: Asbury AK, Cornblath DR, 'Assessment of current diagnostic criteria for Guillain-Barre syndrome', Ann Neurol 1990;27 Suppl:S21-24 (PMID 2194422); Fokke C et al., 'Diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome and validation of Brighton criteria', Brain 2014;137:33-43 (PMID 24163275)

brighton_collaboration_criteria.finding: The Brighton Collaboration criteria (2011), validated by Fokke et al. in a cohort of 493 patients, grade diagnostic certainty into 4 levels based on how much supporting data is available: Level 1 (highest certainty) requires bilateral flaccid limb weakness plus decreased/absent deep tendon reflexes in weak limbs, a monophasic illness pattern with nadir between 12 hours and 28 days, plus CSF albuminocytologic dissociation AND supportive nerve conduction study findings; Level 2 drops the CSF requirement; Level 3 drops the nerve conduction study requirement; Level 4 requires only the clinical pattern plus exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Applying these criteria, roughly 62% of clinically diagnosed GBS patients met Brighton Level 1, and a further 27% met Level 2, showing most real-world GBS is confirmable to a high level of diagnostic certainty using clinical features plus readily available CSF/electrodiagnostic testing.
brighton_collaboration_criteria.source: Fokke C et al., 'Diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome and validation of Brighton criteria', Brain 2014;137:33-43 (PMID 24163275); Sejvar JJ et al., 'Guillain-Barre syndrome and Fisher syndrome: case definitions and guidelines for collection, analysis, and presentation of immunization safety data', Vaccine 2011;29:599-612 (PMID 20600491)

csf_albuminocytologic_dissociation.finding: The classic CSF finding is albuminocytologic dissociation - elevated protein with a normal white cell count (typically <50 cells/microL, usually <10) - reflecting inflammation of nerve roots without meningeal cellular infiltration. This finding is time-dependent and often absent early: in one cohort, albuminocytologic dissociation was present in only about 57% of patients when lumbar puncture was performed within 4 days of weakness onset, rising to about 84% when performed after 4 days, and to roughly 90% by the second week of illness. A normal CSF protein in the first few days does NOT exclude GBS.
csf_albuminocytologic_dissociation.source: Wong AH et al., 'Cerebrospinal fluid protein in Guillain-Barre syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis' and CSF-timing data reviewed in 'Guillain-Barre syndrome and albuminocytological dissociation: a narrative review', Ann Med Surg 2025 (PMC12689043); Fokke C et al., Brain 2014;137:33-43 (PMID 24163275)

nerve_conduction_studies.finding: Electrodiagnostic (nerve conduction) studies help confirm the diagnosis and subclassify AIDP versus AMAN/AMSAN, but can be normal or non-specific in the first 1-2 weeks, so a normal early study does not exclude GBS. AIDP electrodiagnostic criteria (Uncini/Hadden-type criteria) require features of demyelination: prolonged distal motor latencies, reduced conduction velocities, prolonged or absent F-waves, and conduction block/abnormal temporal dispersion; AIDP is also associated with higher CSF protein and 'sural sparing' (abnormal upper-limb sensory responses with a relatively preserved sural sensory response). AMAN/AMSAN instead show reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes with relatively preserved conduction velocities and distal latencies, reflecting axonal loss/nodal conduction failure rather than demyelination; AMSAN additionally shows reduced/absent sensory nerve action potentials.
nerve_conduction_studies.source: Uncini A, Kuwabara S, 'Electrodiagnostic criteria for Guillain-Barre syndrome: a critical revision and the need for an update', Clin Neurophysiol 2012;123:1487-1495 (PMID 22480600); comparative NCS data reviewed in PMC4240930, 'Comparison of electrophysiological findings in axonal and demyelinating Guillain-Barre syndrome'

mri_findings.finding: Spinal MRI with contrast can show smooth enhancement of the cauda equina/lumbosacral nerve roots (and sometimes the intrathecal cranial nerves in Miller Fisher/Bickerstaff variants), reflecting blood-nerve-barrier breakdown at inflamed roots; this is a supportive but non-specific finding and MRI is used mainly to exclude mimics such as spinal cord compression or transverse myelitis rather than to positively confirm GBS.
mri_findings.source: van den Berg B et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2014;10:469-482 (PMID 25048199)
mri_findings.confidence: moderate - MRI nerve-root enhancement is a well-recognised but non-specific supportive sign, primarily used to exclude structural/cord mimics

aidp.finding: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) is the classic and most common subtype in North America and Europe (roughly 90% of GBS cases in these regions), presenting with symmetric ascending weakness, areflexia, and variable sensory symptoms, driven by macrophage/complement-mediated demyelination of nerve roots and peripheral nerves.

aman_amsan.finding: Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) causes pure motor weakness with axonal conduction failure/degeneration at the node of Ranvier and relative sparing of sensory function; acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN) additionally involves sensory axons and tends to be more severe with slower, less complete recovery. Both are proportionately much more frequent in China, Japan, and parts of Latin America than in Europe/North America, and are more tightly linked to preceding C. jejuni infection and anti-GM1/anti-GD1a antibodies.
aman_amsan.source: Uncini A, Kuwabara S, Clin Neurophysiol 2012;123:1487-1495 (PMID 22480600); NORD, 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (rarediseases.org, accessed 2026)

miller_fisher_syndrome.finding: Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) presents with the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia (external, sometimes with pupillary involvement), ataxia (predominantly a sensory/cerebellar-type gait and limb ataxia), and areflexia, usually WITHOUT significant limb weakness. Anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies are detectable in roughly 80-90% of cases. MFS accounts for a minority of the overall GBS spectrum but is the most common of the regional/localized variants; it is generally more benign than classic GBS, with most patients recovering spontaneously over weeks to a few months, though IVIG is often given to hasten recovery.
miller_fisher_syndrome.source: PMC12841706, 'Anti-GQ1b Antibody Syndrome: A Clinician-Oriented Perspective on Diagnostics, Therapy, and Atypical Phenotypes' (2026); Willison HJ et al., Lancet 2016;388:717-727 (PMID 26948435)

bickerstaff_brainstem_encephalitis.finding: Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE) is a more severe, brainstem-involving relative of MFS, defined by the triad of progressive ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, AND altered consciousness (or hyperreflexia, distinguishing it from the areflexia of MFS/GBS), reflecting direct brainstem involvement rather than a purely peripheral nerve process. BBE, MFS and the ophthalmoplegic variant of GBS are now understood to lie on a single anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome spectrum, and can evolve from one phenotype into another over days without a change in antibody serostatus.
bickerstaff_brainstem_encephalitis.source: Odaka M et al. foundational BBE case series, discussed in PMC12841706, 'Anti-GQ1b Antibody Syndrome' (2026); PMC12351415, 'Acute Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis in a Middle-Aged Male' (2025)

pharyngeal_cervical_brachial_variant.finding: The pharyngeal-cervical-brachial (PCB) variant presents with rapidly progressive oropharyngeal (dysphagia, dysarthria), neck, and shoulder/arm weakness with upper-limb areflexia, sparing leg strength - it can be mistaken for a brainstem stroke or myasthenic crisis because of the bulbar-predominant, non-ascending pattern. It is associated with anti-GT1a IgG antibodies (which cross-react with anti-GQ1b assays in some cases).
pharyngeal_cervical_brachial_variant.source: Mizoguchi K et al., 'Two species of antiganglioside antibodies in a patient with a pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1994;57:1121-1123 (PMID 8089683); Koga M et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1999

ascending_weakness_and_progression_timel.finding: The hallmark presentation is symmetric, usually ascending, weakness - typically beginning distally in the legs and progressing proximally and to the arms over hours to days, accompanied by paraesthesias in the hands and feet (often preceding objective weakness). By definition, progression occurs over no more than 4 weeks (most patients reach their nadir within 2 weeks, and around 50% within the first week); progression beyond 4 weeks should prompt reconsideration toward acute-onset CIDP rather than GBS. Deep tendon reflexes are reduced or absent, often early and even in limbs that are not yet clinically weak.
ascending_weakness_and_progression_timel.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214); Asbury AK, Cornblath DR, Ann Neurol 1990;27 Suppl:S21-24 (PMID 2194422)

cranial_nerve_and_facial_involvement.finding: Cranial nerve involvement is common: facial weakness (often bilateral, i.e. facial diplegia) occurs in roughly half of patients, making it one of the most frequent atypical/localizing findings; bulbar weakness (dysphagia, dysarthria) affecting cranial nerves IX/X occurs in a substantial minority and raises aspiration risk; extraocular (III, IV, VI) involvement occurs particularly in Miller Fisher/Bickerstaff variants. In a small proportion of cases (roughly 5%) cranial nerve involvement is the presenting feature and only later descends to involve the limbs.
cranial_nerve_and_facial_involvement.source: Emedicine/Medscape clinical review of GBS presentation, cross-referenced with rural-practice cranial neuropathy cohort study, J Neurosci Rural Pract (ruralneuropractice.com); Willison HJ et al., Lancet 2016;388:717-727 (PMID 26948435)

autonomic_dysfunction.finding: Autonomic dysfunction is common and clinically important, reported in roughly 50-66% of GBS patients in different series (one Mexican cohort found dysautonomia in 44.3% of patients, most commonly tachycardia, followed by constipation, bradycardia, excessive sweating, and hypertension/labile blood pressure). Autonomic instability can cause potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias (including severe bradycardia and asystole, particularly during suctioning/vagal stimulation in ventilated patients), wide blood pressure swings, paralytic ileus, and urinary retention, and is an independent reason for continuous cardiac monitoring in moderate-to-severe GBS, separate from the respiratory indication.
autonomic_dysfunction.source: Autonomic dysfunction cohort data reviewed in PMC13467141, 'Autonomic Dysfunction After Guillain-Barre Syndrome: Evidence from Comprehensive Autonomic Testing' (2026); Zaeem Z et al. and related Mexican-cohort dysautonomia data cited in GBS clinical reviews

pain.finding: Pain is common but historically under-recognised in GBS - it is not just a sensory neuropathy of numbness but frequently a significant pain syndrome. Roughly 70% of patients report subjective sensory complaints, with limb pain reported in about one-third (36%) of patients in one series, and back pain reported across a wide range (13-62%) depending on the cohort and how pain was ascertained; pain can precede weakness and, if unrecognised, delays diagnosis (e.g. GBS presenting as acute back pain).
pain.source: Clinical pain-prevalence data reviewed in PMC8478257, 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome Presenting as an Acute Back Pain'; emedicine/Medscape GBS clinical presentation review

respiratory_muscle_weakness.finding: Respiratory (diaphragmatic and intercostal) muscle weakness is the single most feared complication: approximately 20-30% of GBS patients require mechanical ventilation at some point in their illness, most often triggered within the first 1-2 weeks. Deterioration can be rapid, which is why serial (not one-off) bedside respiratory monitoring is mandatory once a patient is admitted, rather than waiting for clinical dyspnoea, which is often a late sign in a weak patient who cannot generate the effort to appear breathless.
respiratory_muscle_weakness.source: Busl KM et al., 'Guidelines for Neuroprognostication in Adults with Guillain-Barre Syndrome', Neurocrit Care 2023 (PMID pending indexing; Neurocritical Care Society guideline); Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898 (PMID 11405803)

EMERGENCY_red_flags: Rapidly progressive weakness (reaching inability to walk within hours to 1-2 days, or weakness that is clearly worsening from one assessment to the next) - a marker of aggressive disease trajectory that should prompt ICU-level monitoring even before overt respiratory failure develops (Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683, PMID 31541214).

Bulbar dysfunction (dysphagia, dysarthria, weak cough, pooling of secretions) with aspiration risk - an indication for urgent airway assessment and often prophylactic intubation, independent of the vital-capacity numbers (Busl KM et al., Neurocrit Care 2023 Neurocritical Care Society GBS neuroprognostication guideline).
