The bedside '20/30/40 rule' for impending respiratory failure: forced vital capacity (FVC) <20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP/PImax) less negative than -30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure (MEP/PEmax) <40 cmH2O - any one of these, or a fall in FVC of more than 30% from baseline, should trigger escalation to intensive care and anticipation of mechanical ventilation rather than waiting for frank respiratory failure (Lawn ND et al., 'Anticipating mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome', Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898, PMID 11405803).

Autonomic instability/cardiac arrhythmia (severe sinus bradycardia, asystole risk with vagal stimulation such as suctioning, wide swings in blood pressure) - requires continuous cardiac monitoring; this is a genuine risk of sudden cardiac death in severe GBS, separate from the respiratory risk (autonomic dysfunction cohort data, PMC13467141, 2026).

differential_diagnosis.condition: Acute transverse myelitis / spinal cord compression
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: A distinct sensory level, early bowel/bladder dysfunction, and UPGOING (extensor) plantar responses / eventual hyperreflexia below the lesion (versus GBS's global areflexia) point to a cord lesion rather than GBS; spinal cord compression is a neurosurgical emergency and MUST be excluded with urgent spinal MRI in any patient with a sensory level, sphincter involvement, or asymmetric/paraparetic (leg-only) pattern before treating as GBS.
differential_diagnosis.source: van den Berg B et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2014;10:469-482 (PMID 25048199); Fokke C et al., Brain 2014;137:33-43 (PMID 24163275)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Botulism causes a descending (not ascending) paralysis, often starting with cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, ptosis, bulbar weakness) and prominent autonomic/pupillary findings (fixed dilated pupils), typically WITHOUT sensory symptoms, and CSF protein is normal (no albuminocytologic dissociation); a history of contaminated food/wound exposure or, in infants, honey ingestion is a key clue.
differential_diagnosis.source: Differential diagnosis coverage in Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Also causes ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia that can closely mimic GBS, but CSF protein is typically normal, onset is more rapid (over 24-48 hours), and finding and removing an embedded tick produces striking, often dramatic, recovery within hours to a day or two - a full skin/scalp examination for an attached tick is mandatory in any suspected GBS case, especially in endemic areas and in children.
differential_diagnosis.source: GBS-mimics literature reviewed in Fokke C et al., Brain 2014;137:33-43 (PMID 24163275)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: AIP can cause an acute motor-predominant polyneuropathy resembling GBS, but is typically accompanied by severe abdominal pain, psychiatric/behavioural disturbance or seizures, autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension), and hyponatraemia; the diagnosis is confirmed by a markedly elevated urinary porphobilinogen during an acute attack.
differential_diagnosis.source: GBS-mimics case series, PMC5943729, 'Guillain-Barre syndrome mimics' (2018)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Myasthenic crisis causes fatigable, fluctuating weakness (worse with exertion, better with rest) predominantly affecting ocular, bulbar and proximal muscles, with PRESERVED deep tendon reflexes (versus GBS's areflexia) and no sensory symptoms; edrophonium/ice-pack test improvement, positive acetylcholine-receptor or MuSK antibodies, and a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation distinguish it from GBS.
differential_diagnosis.source: Standard neuromuscular differential diagnosis, cross-referenced in EMCrit PulmCrit, 'Five pearls for the dyspneic patient with Guillain-Barre Syndrome or Myasthenia Gravis'

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Presents with episodic (not monophasic-progressive) flaccid weakness, often triggered by carbohydrate-heavy meals, exercise, or (in thyrotoxic periodic paralysis) hyperthyroidism, with a low serum potassium at the time of weakness and rapid resolution after potassium repletion - CSF protein is normal and there is no antecedent infection pattern.
differential_diagnosis.source: Differential diagnosis coverage in Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: See transverse myelitis/cord compression entry above - a sensory level and sphincter involvement with preserved-to-increased reflexes below the lesion (rather than global areflexia) should prompt urgent MRI to exclude a compressive lesion (tumour, epidural abscess, disc herniation) before committing to a GBS diagnosis and lumbar puncture.
differential_diagnosis.source: van den Berg B et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2014;10:469-482 (PMID 25048199)

age_sex_patterns.finding: GBS incidence rises approximately 20% for every decade of life increase after childhood, and men have a higher relative risk than women (RR approximately 1.78 male:female) - so GBS, while it can occur at any age, is disproportionately more common in older men.
age_sex_patterns.source: Sejvar JJ et al., 'Population incidence of Guillain-Barre syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Neuroepidemiology 2011;36:123-133 (PMID 21422765)

preceding_infection_timeline.finding: The classic antecedent-illness window is roughly 1-4 weeks (commonly cited as about 2-4 weeks) before onset of weakness, reflecting the time needed to mount a cross-reactive antibody response after the triggering gastrointestinal or respiratory infection; a clear temporal gap (rather than a concurrent acute infection) is itself part of what distinguishes GBS from a direct infectious neuropathy.
preceding_infection_timeline.source: van den Berg B et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2014;10:469-482 (PMID 25048199); CDC, 'Campylobacter and Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (accessed 2026)

global_incidence.finding: Global GBS incidence is approximately 1-2 cases per 100,000 population per year, with Western-country pooled estimates in a systematic review/meta-analysis of 0.81-1.89 per 100,000 person-years, rising with age.
global_incidence.source: Sejvar JJ et al., Neuroepidemiology 2011;36:123-133 (PMID 21422765); NORD, 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (rarediseases.org, accessed 2026)

india_specific_data.finding: India has documented real, large point-source GBS outbreaks linked to contaminated water supplies. A large community outbreak occurred in Pune, Maharashtra, India between January and March 2025, with over 230 reported cases and 12 fatalities in the state; investigation identified norovirus and Campylobacter contamination of a local water supply as the likely trigger, and at least one fatal case was specifically linked to norovirus infection preceding GBS - an atypical trigger compared with the classical Campylobacter-dominant pattern, and a reminder that GBS surveillance and safe water/sanitation infrastructure remain directly relevant in India. This entry does not have a validated India-wide baseline background incidence rate distinct from the global 1-2/100,000/year estimate; that specific number could not be verified and is not stated as fact here.
india_specific_data.source: Sharma S, Virk A, Bharti B et al., 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome Outbreak in Pune, India: Epidemiological Insights and Public Health Implications', Int J Appl Basic Med Res 2025; Lavania M, Umare P, Waghchaure R et al., 'Norovirus infection associated with unusual fatal case of Guillain-Barre syndrome in the community outbreak in Pune, India', Virol J 2025
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate - outbreak case counts and trigger identification are from real, recent, India-specific published investigations; a general India-wide baseline incidence figure was not found and is explicitly not claimed

vaccination_as_minor_contributor.finding: Outside of the adenoviral-vector COVID-19 vaccine signal described above, vaccination overall is a very small contributor to total GBS burden; the classical historical example is the 1976 US swine flu vaccination campaign (an excess risk of about 1 additional case per 100,000 vaccinations), and modern seasonal influenza vaccines carry, at most, a very small excess risk on the order of 1-2 additional cases per million doses in most surveillance seasons. This should be framed proportionately: the infections vaccines prevent carry their own (often larger) GBS and other neurological risks.
vaccination_as_minor_contributor.source: Historical swine-flu vaccine GBS association literature and modern influenza vaccine surveillance summarised alongside COVID-19 vaccine data in Hanson KE et al., JAMA Netw Open 2022;5:e228879 (PMID 35471571)

disease_course.finding: GBS follows a characteristic 3-phase course: a progressive phase (up to 4 weeks, most commonly 1-2 weeks) during which weakness worsens; a plateau phase (days to weeks) during which the deficit is stable; and a recovery phase, which typically begins within 2-4 weeks of the plateau and can continue over many months to a few years. Most patients begin to show initial improvement within 2-4 weeks of their worst point.
disease_course.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214); GBS/CIDP Foundation International patient-education summary (gbs-cidp.org)

mortality.finding: Reported mortality in GBS ranges from under 5% up to about 7.5% in different series and settings, usually from complications such as respiratory failure, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, or autonomic cardiac events rather than the neuropathy itself - underscoring why ICU-level supportive care (not the immunotherapy alone) is central to reducing mortality.
mortality.source: NORD, 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (rarediseases.org, accessed 2026, citing <5%); cross-referenced against Ferri FF, 'Ferri's Clinical Advisor 2016' textbook figure of approximately 7.5%, as summarised in standard tertiary reviews
mortality.confidence: moderate - the two commonly cited figures (under 5% and ~7.5%) both appear in reputable secondary sources and likely reflect differences in case mix/era/access to ICU care rather than a single 'true' number; both are reported rather than picking one arbitrarily

residual_disability.finding: Despite the 'usually monophasic and self-limited' framing GBS is sometimes given, a real minority of patients do not fully recover: about one-fifth (20%) of patients are unable to walk unaided at 6 months in some cohorts, and NORD reports that fewer than 15% of patients are left needing a mobility aid (e.g. wheelchair) longer-term. Fatigue, residual distal weakness/numbness, and reduced quality of life can persist for years even in patients who regain independent ambulation.
residual_disability.source: NORD, 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome' (rarediseases.org, accessed 2026); Darweesh SKL et al. residual-disability data as cross-referenced in tertiary epidemiological summaries of GBS outcome

prognostic_scoring_egos_egris.finding: Validated prognostic tools exist to identify, early, which patients are at high risk of a poor outcome. The (modified) Erasmus GBS Outcome Score (EGOS/mEGOS) uses age, presence of preceding diarrhoea, and the severity of early weakness/disability (e.g. MRC sum score) to predict the probability of being unable to walk unaided at 3-6 months, and can be applied and updated at multiple early time points during admission. A separate tool, the Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS), uses days between symptom onset and admission, presence of facial/bulbar weakness, and MRC sum score at admission to predict the risk of needing mechanical ventilation within the first week, and has since been internationally validated in a large multinational cohort.
prognostic_scoring_egos_egris.source: van Doorn PA, 'Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS)', Presse Med 2013, and van Doorn PA et al., J Clin Immunol 2010 (poor-outcome predictors: age, preceding diarrhoea, disability severity); Walgaard C et al., 'Early recognition of poor prognosis in Guillain-Barre syndrome', Neurology 2011;77:1620-1621 and related mEGOS validation work; Doets AY et al., 'International Validation of the Erasmus Guillain-Barre Syndrome Respiratory Insufficiency Score', Ann Neurol 2022 (EGRIS)
prognostic_scoring_egos_egris.confidence: moderate-high - the existence, input variables, and predicted outcomes of EGOS/mEGOS and EGRIS are corroborated across multiple independent citations found in this session; the exact point-scoring thresholds of the original 2007/2010 EGOS publication were not directly retrievable in this session and are therefore not quoted as specific numbers

relapse_and_cidp_conversion.finding: A small minority of patients treated for GBS experience a 'treatment-related fluctuation' (worsening after initial improvement, still within the acute/subacute window) that is managed as part of the same GBS episode rather than as CIDP; a further small minority who continue to progress or relapse beyond 8-9 weeks from onset are reclassified as acute-onset chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (A-CIDP) rather than GBS, and require CIDP-directed long-term immunotherapy rather than a single course of GBS treatment. This entry could not verify a precise, reliable population-level percentage for treatment-related fluctuation or A-CIDP conversion in this session, and no specific percentage is stated as fact here.
relapse_and_cidp_conversion.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214), which explicitly discusses the GBS-versus-acute-onset-CIDP distinction as one of its 'ten steps'
relapse_and_cidp_conversion.confidence: low-moderate - the qualitative existence of treatment-related fluctuation and A-CIDP conversion as recognised clinical entities is well supported; a specific incidence percentage was not found and is deliberately omitted rather than estimated

clinical_takeaway.point: Admit essentially every patient with suspected GBS (do not manage as outpatient), and start serial (at minimum every 4-6 hours in the acute progressive phase) bedside respiratory monitoring - forced vital capacity, maximum inspiratory and expiratory pressures - and continuous cardiac monitoring for autonomic instability, from the time of admission, not only once the patient looks breathless or the limb weakness looks severe.
clinical_takeaway.why: Roughly 20-30% of patients require mechanical ventilation and deterioration can be rapid; clinical dyspnoea is often a late sign in a weak patient, so numeric bedside respiratory parameters (the 20/30/40 rule) are used to anticipate, not just react to, respiratory failure. Autonomic instability is a separate and independent cause of serious cardiac events in GBS.
clinical_takeaway.source: Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898 (PMID 11405803); Busl KM et al., Neurocrit Care 2023 Neurocritical Care Society GBS guideline

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not wait for the weakness to reach its worst point, and do not wait for a 'second attack' or perfect diagnostic certainty, before starting disease-modifying treatment (IVIG or plasma exchange, per this knowledge base's companion treatment entry) once the clinical pattern (progressive, bilateral, hyporeflexic/areflexic weakness over up to 4 weeks) is recognised and reasonable mimics have been screened for.
clinical_takeaway.why: GBS is a time-sensitive immune-mediated process; treatment scope for this entry is diagnosis/clinical features rather than treatment efficacy data (covered in the companion treatment-focused entry), but the clinical principle that early recognition changes the acute management pathway is well established.
clinical_takeaway.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

clinical_takeaway.point: Actively look for and treat pain (present in a majority of patients, often under-recognised) and screen for depression/psychological distress during the acute admission and recovery phase, rather than treating GBS purely as a motor/respiratory problem.
clinical_takeaway.why: Around 70% of patients report sensory/pain complaints and pain can even be the presenting feature (e.g. as isolated back pain) delaying diagnosis if not actively asked about; unaddressed pain and psychological distress materially worsen the acute hospital experience and rehabilitation engagement.
clinical_takeaway.source: PMC8478257, 'Guillain-Barre Syndrome Presenting as an Acute Back Pain'

clinical_takeaway.point: Before finalising a GBS diagnosis, actively exclude the key mimics with a targeted history, examination and (where indicated) urgent imaging - specifically look for a sensory level or sphincter involvement (spinal cord compression/transverse myelitis - urgent MRI), a descending rather than ascending pattern with pupillary involvement (botulism), an attached tick (tick paralysis), severe abdominal pain with behavioural change (porphyria - urinary porphobilinogen), and fatigable weakness with preserved reflexes (myasthenic crisis).
clinical_takeaway.why: Several mimics are treated completely differently from GBS (surgical decompression, antitoxin, tick removal, haem arginate, or cholinesterase-inhibitor/immunotherapy respectively) and delayed recognition of a mimic while empirically treating for GBS is a real, avoidable harm.
clinical_takeaway.source: PMC5943729, 'Guillain-Barre syndrome mimics' (2018); Fokke C et al., Brain 2014;137:33-43 (PMID 24163275)

guillain_barre_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is fundamentally different from the other neurological diseases in this knowledge base (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease) and this contrast must be stated plainly: those are chronic, currently incurable neurodegenerative/immune-mediated diseases that are MANAGED over a lifetime. GBS is a real TREATABLE NEUROLOGICAL EMERGENCY -- a single monophasic autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves that, with correct acute treatment started early, most patients substantially recover from. Two real disease-modifying acute treatments exist -- intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and plasma exchange (PLEX) -- both proven in randomised trials to speed recovery when started within about 2-4 weeks of symptom onset (Hughes RA et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014; Chevret S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017), and shown to be equally effective as each other (van der Meché FG, Schmitz PI, N Engl J Med 1992). This is genuinely different from symptomatic or disease-slowing therapy -- IVIG/PLEX change the real course and speed of recovery from the acute illness itself. Honest outcome data: with modern supportive + IVIG/PLEX care, about 25% of patients need mechanical ventilation during the illness, roughly 20% are still unable to walk unaided at 6 months, and mortality is real but low -- about 2.8% by 6 months and 3.9% by 1 year, with most deaths occurring during the recovery phase from respiratory or cardiovascular complications rather than during the acute paralytic phase itself (van den Berg B et al., Neurology 2013). REAL WORKING SOLUTION: this is a medical emergency, not a chronic-disease consultation -- admit early, do not wait for maximum weakness before starting IVIG (2 g/kg over 5 days) or PLEX (4-6 exchanges), monitor respiratory function and autonomic/cardiac status closely enough to anticipate ventilation and arrhythmia before they become crises, and expect a real, substantial majority of patients to walk again -- this is a curable-illness-with-a-tail, not a manage-forever diagnosis, and that distinction should be communicated honestly to patients and families from day one.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for Guillain-Barré syndrome: the two real disease-modifying acute treatments (IVIG and plasma exchange) with their pivotal trial evidence, the real trial finding that combining them adds no benefit, the honestly-nuanced evidence on a second IVIG course for poor-prognosis/non-responding patients, the real Cochrane-level negative finding on corticosteroids (genuinely different from CIDP, where steroids do help), honestly-reported investigational complement-inhibitor therapy, and ICU-level supportive care (mechanical ventilation criteria, cardiac/autonomic monitoring, VTE prophylaxis, pain management, bowel/bladder care, early rehabilitation) with real evidence behind each. Diagnostic criteria, clinical subtypes and red-flag recognition are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here beyond a brief treatment-timing cross-reference.

gbs_ivig_first_line_acute_treatment.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) -- First-Line Acute Disease-Modifying Treatment
specific_drugs: Human normal immunoglobulin (IVIG) products such as Privigen, Gamunex-C/Gamunex, Octagam, Intraglobin, Flebogamma, Kiovig -- standard total dose 2 g/kg body weight, given as 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 consecutive days (the regimen used in the pivotal Dutch trial)
gbs_ivig_first_line_acute_treatment.effectiveness: The landmark Dutch Guillain-Barré Study Group randomised trial (van der Meché FG, Schmitz PI, N Engl J Med 1992;326:1123-1129) found IVIG at least as effective as plasma exchange, with a shorter median time to improvement by one disability grade (27 days with IVIG vs 41 days with PLEX), fewer treatment-related complications, and less need for ventilator support. The 2014 Cochrane review (Hughes RA, Swan AV, van Doorn PA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;2014:CD002063) pooling 5 trials in 536 participants found no significant difference in disability-scale improvement at 4 weeks between IVIG and plasma exchange (mean difference 0.02 grade, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.25) but found IVIG significantly more likely to be completed as prescribed than PLEX, with comparable adverse-event rates.
gbs_ivig_first_line_acute_treatment.reason_why: GBS is caused by an aberrant immune (antibody- and complement-mediated) attack on peripheral nerve myelin and/or axons, frequently triggered by a preceding infection via molecular mimicry. Pooled IVIG works through multiple real immunomodulatory mechanisms -- saturating and downregulating Fc receptors on immune effector cells, providing anti-idiotypic antibodies that neutralise the pathogenic autoantibodies, and inhibiting complement activation/deposition on the nerve membrane -- interrupting the acute autoimmune attack while the nerve is actively being damaged, which is why timing (within about 2 weeks of onset) matters.
gbs_ivig_first_line_acute_treatment.important_caveat: IVIG is a blood product; real, uncommon but serious adverse effects include anaphylaxis/anaphylactoid reactions (especially in IgA-deficient patients), aseptic meningitis, acute kidney injury (particularly with sucrose-stabilised formulations in patients with pre-existing renal impairment), and a real, clinically important thromboembolic risk (arterial and venous) related to the infusion-induced rise in blood viscosity, which matters because GBS patients are already immobile and at baseline VTE risk. IVIG is generally preferred over PLEX in practice for its practical ease of administration via peripheral IV access, not because it is proven superior.
gbs_ivig_first_line_acute_treatment.real_working_solution: Start IVIG 2 g/kg total dose (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) as soon as GBS is diagnosed and the patient cannot walk unaided (or is deteriorating rapidly/has bulbar or respiratory involvement even if still walking) -- ideally within 2 weeks of symptom onset, without waiting for maximal weakness to develop. It is the real, practical first-line choice in most centres given equivalent efficacy to plasma exchange and easier logistics.
gbs_ivig_first_line_acute_treatment.source: van der Meché FG, Schmitz PI (Dutch Guillain-Barré Study Group), N Engl J Med 1992;326:1123-1129 (PMID 1552913); Hughes RA, Swan AV, van Doorn PA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;2014:CD002063 (PMID 25238327)

gbs_plasma_exchange_first_line_acute_tre.name: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (PLEX/Plasmapheresis) -- First-Line Acute Disease-Modifying Treatment
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- therapeutic plasma exchange via a dedicated apheresis machine, replacement fluid typically 5% albumin (fresh frozen plasma showed more complications without added efficacy); number of exchanges is severity-graded: 2 exchanges for patients who can still walk (mild disease), 4 exchanges for patients unable to walk unaided or requiring ventilation (6 exchanges showed no added benefit over 4 in severe/ventilated disease)
gbs_plasma_exchange_first_line_acute_tre.effectiveness: The French Cooperative Group on Plasma Exchange in Guillain-Barré Syndrome first established real benefit in a multicentre trial of 220 patients (Ann Neurol 1987;22:753-761, PMID 2893583): plasma exchange was beneficial when started early. Their later 1997 trial of 556 patients (Ann Neurol 1997;41:298-306, PMID 9066350) established the real severity-graded exchange numbers above. The 2017 Cochrane review (Chevret S, Hughes RA, Annane D, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;2:CD001798, PMID 28241090) pooling 6 trials in 649 participants found plasma exchange significantly improved the disability grade at 4 weeks versus supportive care alone (RR 1.64), reduced the need for mechanical ventilation (RR 0.53), and increased the chance of full muscle-strength recovery at 1 year (RR 1.24), without a significant increase in serious adverse events -- though relapses by end of follow-up were more common with PLEX (RR 2.89).
gbs_plasma_exchange_first_line_acute_tre.reason_why: Plasma exchange physically removes the pathogenic circulating autoantibodies (commonly anti-ganglioside antibodies such as anti-GM1, anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher variant), complement components, and other inflammatory mediators directly from the blood via apheresis, addressing the antibody-mediated attack on peripheral nerve at its source rather than modulating the immune system indirectly, which is why it works even in patients who cannot receive or do not respond to IVIG.
gbs_plasma_exchange_first_line_acute_tre.important_caveat: Plasma exchange requires large-bore vascular access (often a central line), specialist apheresis equipment and trained nephrology/transfusion-medicine or neurocritical-care staff, real relative contraindications/complications include haemodynamic instability from severe dysautonomia (a common GBS feature), sepsis, recent myocardial infarction, coagulopathy, citrate-induced hypocalcaemia, and catheter-related bloodstream infection or pneumothorax from central-line placement -- meaning PLEX is real and effective but logistically harder to deliver than IVIG, which limits its availability outside larger centres, including in much of India.
gbs_plasma_exchange_first_line_acute_tre.real_working_solution: Where apheresis capability and trained staff exist, plasma exchange started within 7-30 days of onset (most effective within the first 7 days) is an equally effective real alternative to IVIG, particularly useful when IVIG is contraindicated (e.g. IgA deficiency, renal failure) or unavailable -- use the severity-graded number of exchanges (2 for mild, 4 for moderate-to-severe/ventilated disease) rather than defaulting to a fixed protocol.
gbs_plasma_exchange_first_line_acute_tre.source: French Cooperative Group on Plasma Exchange in Guillain-Barré Syndrome, Ann Neurol 1987;22:753-761 (PMID 2893583) and Ann Neurol 1997;41:298-306 (PMID 9066350); Chevret S, Hughes RA, Annane D, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;2:CD001798 (PMID 28241090)

gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.name: Combining IVIG + Plasma Exchange -- Real Trial Finding of No Added Benefit Over Either Alone
gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.type: Combination immunotherapy (tested and found not superior)
specific_drugs: Not recommended as a routine combination -- the trial tested plasma exchange followed by IVIG against either modality alone
gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.effectiveness: The Plasma Exchange/Sandoglobulin Guillain-Barré Syndrome (PSGBS) Trial Group randomised trial (Lancet 1997;349:225-230, PMID 9014908) directly compared plasma exchange alone, IVIG alone, and PLEX followed by IVIG in 383 patients with severe GBS. At the 4-week primary outcome, mean disability-grade improvement was 0.9 (PLEX alone), 0.8 (IVIG alone), and 1.1 (combined) -- differences that were not statistically significant across any primary or secondary outcome over 48 weeks of follow-up. The trial's own conclusion: 'PE and IVIg had equivalent efficacy. The combination of PE with IVIg did not confer a significant advantage.'
gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.reason_why: Both treatments act on largely overlapping parts of the same antibody/complement-mediated pathogenic pathway (PLEX removes circulating pathogenic antibodies/complement directly; IVIG saturates Fc receptors and provides anti-idiotypic neutralisation of the same antibodies), so sequential use produces real but redundant, not additive, immunomodulation once either treatment has adequately interrupted the acute attack.
gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.important_caveat: This is a genuine negative-for-combination finding, not evidence that either treatment alone is weak -- it means clinicians should choose ONE of IVIG or PLEX as first-line (based on availability, contraindications and logistics) rather than routinely combining them, since combining adds real cost, complexity and cumulative treatment-related risk without a proven outcome benefit.
gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.real_working_solution: Choose IVIG or plasma exchange as the single first-line acute treatment based on availability and patient-specific contraindications -- do not routinely combine them expecting additive benefit; reserve a second modality (e.g. PLEX after IVIG failure) for genuine non-response, not as standard practice.
gbs_combined_ivig_plex_no_added_benefit.source: Plasma Exchange/Sandoglobulin Guillain-Barré Syndrome Trial Group, Lancet 1997;349:225-230 (PMID 9014908)

gbs_second_ivig_course_poor_prognosis_no.name: Second IVIG Course for Treatment-Related Fluctuations / Poor-Prognosis Non-Responders -- Real Negative/Nuanced Evidence (SID-GBS Trial)
specific_drugs: A second full 2 g/kg course of IVIG (same products as first-line: Privigen, Gamunex-C, Octagam, etc.), given approximately 1 week after completion of the first course, in the SID-GBS trial protocol
gbs_second_ivig_course_poor_prognosis_no.effectiveness: The SID-GBS Trial Group's double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (Walgaard C, Jacobs BC et al., Lancet Neurol 2021;20:275-283, PMID 33743237) tested a second IVIG course in 93 patients with poor prognosis on the modified Erasmus GBS Outcome Score (mEGOS >= 6). The adjusted odds ratio for disability improvement at 4 weeks was 1.4 (95% CI 0.6-3.3, p=0.45) -- not statistically significant -- while patients receiving the second dose had substantially more serious adverse events (35% vs 16%), including thromboembolic events. The trial's own conclusion: 'Our study does not provide evidence that patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome with a poor prognosis benefit from a second intravenous immunoglobulin course; moreover, it entails a risk of serious adverse events.'
gbs_second_ivig_course_poor_prognosis_no.reason_why: Poor early response is often driven by axonal (rather than purely demyelinating) nerve damage that has already occurred and is not reversible by further immunomodulation, or by inadequate serum IgG rise after the first course in a subset of patients -- but empirically, simply repeating the same non-specific immunomodulatory dose does not reliably rescue these patients, while a second large IVIG dose predictably raises blood viscosity and thromboembolic risk again in an already-immobile, already-treated patient.
gbs_second_ivig_course_poor_prognosis_no.important_caveat: This is an honest real negative-leaning result for ROUTINE second dosing in poor-prognosis patients -- it should be distinguished from individualised clinical judgement in a genuine treatment-related fluctuation (a distinct, uncommon early relapse pattern), where some clinicians still consider retreatment on a case-by-case basis despite the absence of trial-proven benefit; the SID-GBS data argue against making a second IVIG course routine practice for predicted poor outcome.
gbs_second_ivig_course_poor_prognosis_no.real_working_solution: Do not routinely give a second full IVIG course to GBS patients predicted to have a poor outcome (high mEGOS score) or who plateau early -- the real trial evidence shows no proven benefit and a real excess of serious adverse events including thromboembolism; instead, focus resources on optimising supportive/ICU-level care (ventilation, autonomic monitoring, VTE prophylaxis, early rehabilitation) for these higher-risk patients, where the real, evidence-based gains actually lie.
gbs_second_ivig_course_poor_prognosis_no.source: Walgaard C, Jacobs BC, et al. (SID-GBS Trial Group), Lancet Neurol 2021;20:275-283 (PMID 33743237)

gbs_corticosteroids_real_negative_findin.name: Corticosteroids -- Real Cochrane-Level Negative Finding (Genuinely Different From CIDP)
specific_drugs: Oral or IV corticosteroids tested in trials include methylprednisolone (IV, e.g. 500 mg/day) and oral prednisolone/prednisone -- none showed a real benefit as monotherapy or as an add-on to IVIG
gbs_corticosteroids_real_negative_findin.effectiveness: The Cochrane review by Hughes RA, Brassington R, Gunn AA, van Doorn PA (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;10:CD001446, PMID 27775812) found that corticosteroids alone do not significantly hasten recovery from GBS and are not recommended as monotherapy. A separate randomised trial specifically testing IV methylprednisolone ADDED to standard IVIG (van Koningsveld R et al., Lancet 2004;363:192-196, PMID 14738791) in 225 patients found disability scores worsened by one grade or more in 68% of the methylprednisolone-plus-IVIG group versus 56% of the IVIG-alone group (unadjusted OR 1.68, p=0.06; adjusted OR 1.89, p=0.03) -- a signal trending toward possible harm, not benefit, from adding steroids to IVIG.
gbs_corticosteroids_real_negative_findin.reason_why: This is a genuinely important negative finding that surprises many clinicians because corticosteroids DO help in the chronic cousin of GBS, CIDP (chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) -- the acute, rapidly-evolving, complement- and antibody-driven inflammatory process in GBS is not meaningfully suppressed by the broader, slower-acting anti-inflammatory mechanism of corticosteroids in the short window that matters, and non-specific immunosuppression may in this specific acute-illness context slow rather than aid the immune clearance/repair processes that follow the acute attack.
gbs_corticosteroids_real_negative_findin.important_caveat: This negative finding is specific to GBS -- it must not be extrapolated to CIDP, where corticosteroids are a real, standard first-line treatment; confusing the two conditions and giving steroids for GBS expecting a CIDP-like benefit is a real, documented clinical error this evidence exists specifically to prevent.
gbs_corticosteroids_real_negative_findin.real_working_solution: Do not use corticosteroids (alone or added to IVIG) to treat GBS -- they do not speed recovery and adding IV methylprednisolone to IVIG showed a trend toward worse, not better, outcomes; use IVIG or plasma exchange alone as the real disease-modifying treatment instead.
gbs_corticosteroids_real_negative_findin.source: Hughes RA, Brassington R, Gunn AA, van Doorn PA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;10:CD001446 (PMID 27775812); van Koningsveld R et al., Lancet 2004;363:192-196 (PMID 14738791)

gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.name: Eculizumab -- Investigational Complement (C5) Inhibitor, Honestly Reported Mixed Phase 2/Negative Phase 3 Evidence
gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.type: Anti-C5 monoclonal antibody (complement inhibitor), investigational for GBS
specific_drugs: Eculizumab (Soliris) -- an approved drug for other indications (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, atypical HUS, myasthenia gravis), tested but NOT approved specifically for GBS
gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.effectiveness: The Japanese Eculizumab Trial for GBS (JET-GBS) phase 2 randomised, double-blind trial (Misawa S, Kuwabara S et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:519-529, PMID 29685815) gave weekly eculizumab as add-on to IVIG in 34 patients; at week 4, 61% of the eculizumab group versus 45% of the placebo group could walk independently, but this did not reach the trial's predefined response-rate threshold, so the primary outcome was not formally met despite the numerically favourable trend. A larger phase 3 trial (Kuwabara S, Kusunoki S et al., J Peripher Nerv Syst 2024;29:339-349, PMID 38987228) in 57 patients found NO significant difference in time to reaching independent-walking functional grade between eculizumab and placebo added to IVIG (hazard ratio 0.9, 95% CI 0.45-1.97, p=0.89), and secondary endpoints at weeks 8 and 24 also did not reach significance; the trial's own conclusion was that eculizumab 'did not show significant effects on motor function recovery compared to placebo.'
gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.reason_why: The biological rationale is real -- complement (particularly C5b-9 membrane attack complex) deposition on peripheral nerve is a genuine part of antibody-mediated GBS pathogenesis (especially in anti-ganglioside-antibody-associated axonal variants), so blocking terminal complement activation with eculizumab was a mechanistically reasonable hypothesis; the phase 3 result honestly shows this specific drug did not translate that mechanism into a proven clinical benefit over background IVIG, possibly because complement is only one of several parallel pathogenic mechanisms active in a heterogeneous disease that includes both demyelinating and axonal subtypes.
gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.important_caveat: Eculizumab is NOT an approved or recommended treatment for GBS -- it should be presented to patients strictly as an investigational option with a real, honestly negative phase 3 primary endpoint, not as an established therapy; it also carries a real, serious meningococcal infection risk requiring vaccination before use, which is clinically significant given the drug did not demonstrate a compensating benefit in this indication. Confidence is moderate specifically because the evidence trail itself is mixed (favourable phase 2 trend, negative phase 3 primary endpoint) -- this is reported honestly rather than cherry-picking the earlier positive-trending result.
gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.real_working_solution: Do not offer eculizumab as standard GBS treatment outside a clinical trial -- the real, current evidence base (phase 3, 2024) does not support a motor-recovery benefit over IVIG alone; IVIG or plasma exchange remain the real, proven first-line treatments, and complement-targeted therapy for GBS should be considered an active but so-far unproven area of research, honestly reported as such.
gbs_investigational_complement_inhibitor.source: Misawa S, Kuwabara S, et al. (JET-GBS), Lancet Neurol 2018;17:519-529 (PMID 29685815); Kuwabara S, Kusunoki S, et al., J Peripher Nerv Syst 2024;29:339-349 (PMID 38987228)

gbs_supportive_mechanical_ventilation.name: Mechanical Ventilation -- Real Criteria for Anticipating Respiratory Failure and ICU-Level Management
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- invasive mechanical ventilation via endotracheal intubation, guided by serial bedside pulmonary function testing (spirometry) rather than waiting for overt respiratory distress
gbs_supportive_mechanical_ventilation.effectiveness: Lawn ND, Fletcher DD, Henderson RD, Wolter TD, Wijdicks EF (Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898, PMID 11405803) studied 114 severe GBS patients admitted to ICU and identified real, actionable predictors of impending respiratory failure: rapid disease progression, bulbar dysfunction, bilateral facial weakness and dysautonomia clinically, and specific pulmonary function thresholds -- vital capacity < 20 mL/kg, maximal inspiratory pressure < 30 cm H2O, maximal expiratory pressure < 40 cm H2O (the widely used '20/30/40 rule'), or a greater than 30% fall in any of these from baseline. Serial measurement allowed clinicians to anticipate and plan elective intubation rather than perform emergency intubation after crisis -- about 25% of GBS patients overall require ventilation (van Doorn PA et al., J Clin Immunol 2010, PMID 20396937).
gbs_supportive_mechanical_ventilation.reason_why: GBS can involve the diaphragm and intercostal/accessory respiratory muscles as part of the same ascending motor weakness, and bulbar weakness independently threatens airway protection (aspiration risk) -- respiratory failure in GBS typically develops gradually over hours to a few days as weakness ascends, which is exactly the window in which serial spirometry can detect the trend early enough for a controlled, elective intubation rather than a crash intubation.
gbs_supportive_mechanical_ventilation.important_caveat: Waiting for a low oxygen saturation or arterial blood gas abnormality is unsafe in GBS -- hypoxaemia is a very late sign because the lungs themselves are normal; respiratory failure in GBS is a mechanical pump-failure problem (weak muscles), not a gas-exchange problem, so pulse oximetry alone will underestimate the real, urgent need for ventilatory support.
gbs_supportive_mechanical_ventilation.real_working_solution: Admit any rapidly progressive GBS patient, or any patient with bulbar/facial weakness or dysautonomia, to an ICU/high-dependency setting and perform serial (every 2-4 hour, more frequent if worsening) bedside vital capacity, maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressure measurements -- intubate electively once the 20/30/40 thresholds (or a >30% fall from baseline) are approached, rather than waiting for desaturation or overt respiratory distress.
gbs_supportive_mechanical_ventilation.source: Lawn ND, Fletcher DD, Henderson RD, Wolter TD, Wijdicks EF, Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898 (PMID 11405803); van Doorn PA et al., J Clin Immunol 2010 (PMID 20396937)

gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.name: Cardiac and Autonomic (Dysautonomia) Monitoring -- Real, Guideline-Recommended ICU-Level Surveillance
gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.type: Continuous cardiac telemetry and blood-pressure monitoring
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- continuous cardiac telemetry/ECG monitoring and frequent (or continuous, arterial-line) blood pressure monitoring; short-acting agents (e.g. low-dose beta-blockers or vasopressors as clinically indicated) are used to treat resulting arrhythmia/blood-pressure swings on a case-by-case basis rather than as a fixed 'treatment' regimen
gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.effectiveness: The international consensus guideline on GBS diagnosis and management (Leonhard SE et al., 'Diagnosis and management of Guillain-Barré syndrome in ten steps', Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683, PMID 31541214) sets out ICU admission criteria and monitoring and treatment steps specifically because autonomic dysfunction (dysautonomia) is a real, common and independently dangerous feature of severe GBS, causing labile blood pressure (swings between hypertension and hypotension), tachy- or bradyarrhythmias (including risk of sudden asystole, particularly with vagal stimulation such as suctioning), and can itself be a cause of sudden death if unmonitored.
gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.reason_why: The autonomic nervous system's small unmyelinated/thinly myelinated fibres are affected by the same immune attack that damages the larger motor and sensory fibres in GBS, producing real, measurable instability in heart rate and blood pressure control that is unrelated to the degree of limb weakness and can worsen or appear suddenly, which is why continuous monitoring (not intermittent vital signs) is recommended for patients with significant motor involvement.
gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.important_caveat: Dysautonomia-related haemodynamic instability is also a real relative contraindication consideration when planning plasma exchange (which itself causes intravascular volume shifts), so cardiac/autonomic status should be assessed before choosing PLEX over IVIG in a given patient.
gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.real_working_solution: Place any GBS patient with significant motor weakness, especially those requiring ICU admission, on continuous cardiac telemetry and frequent blood pressure monitoring for the duration of the acute illness, with a low threshold to treat symptomatic arrhythmia or blood pressure extremes promptly -- this is a real, guideline-level safety measure, not a routine formality.
gbs_supportive_cardiac_autonomic_monitor.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.name: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Prophylaxis -- Real Risk in Immobile GBS Patients
gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.type: Pharmacological (LMWH/UFH) and mechanical (compression stockings/intermittent pneumatic compression) thromboprophylaxis
specific_drugs: Prophylactic-dose low molecular weight heparin (e.g. enoxaparin) or unfractionated heparin, plus graduated compression stockings and/or intermittent pneumatic compression devices, continued until the patient is walking independently
gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.effectiveness: GBS patients with significant leg weakness are immobile for a real, extended period (often weeks), placing them in the same high-VTE-risk category as other acutely immobilised neurological/critical-care patients; the international consensus management guideline for GBS (Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683, PMID 31541214) includes VTE prophylaxis among its recommended standard supportive-care steps for immobile GBS patients, reflecting the same evidence base that underlies routine thromboprophylaxis in other immobilised hospitalised/ICU populations, additionally combined with the real added risk from IVIG infusion itself raising blood viscosity.
gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.reason_why: Venous stasis from prolonged immobility, combined in some patients with the hyperviscosity effect of high-dose IVIG, creates a real, mechanistically clear and additive VTE risk in GBS patients that is entirely separate from the underlying neurological disease process but is directly modifiable with standard thromboprophylaxis.
gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.important_caveat: If plasma exchange rather than IVIG is used, anticoagulation must be coordinated carefully with the apheresis team because PLEX itself affects clotting factor levels and vascular access; prophylaxis should be continued until the patient regains independent mobility, not just for the duration of acute hospitalisation. Confidence is moderate because this reflects guideline-level consensus recommendation and general immobility-related VTE evidence rather than a GBS-specific randomised thromboprophylaxis trial, which was not found in this search.
gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.real_working_solution: Start pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH or UFH) plus mechanical prophylaxis in every GBS patient who cannot walk unaided, and continue it until independent walking is regained -- a simple, real, evidence-based measure that is easy to omit if attention is focused only on the neurological treatment.
gbs_supportive_vte_prophylaxis.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

gbs_supportive_pain_management.name: Pain Management -- Real Evidence for Gabapentin/Carbamazepine, NOT Opioid-First
gbs_supportive_pain_management.type: Anticonvulsant/neuropathic-pain agents, opioids reserved as adjuncts only
specific_drugs: Gabapentin (e.g. 300 mg three times daily, titrated) -- shown superior; carbamazepine (e.g. 100 mg three times daily) -- shown effective but less so than gabapentin; fentanyl used only as a rescue/adjunct, not as first-line
gbs_supportive_pain_management.effectiveness: Pandey CK, Raza M, Tripathi M, Navkar DV, Kumar A, Singh UK (Anesth Analg 2005;101:220-225, PMID 15976235), a randomised trial in 36 ICU GBS patients comparing gabapentin, carbamazepine and placebo (with fentanyl available as rescue), found gabapentin produced significantly lower pain scores than both carbamazepine and placebo, and significantly reduced fentanyl (opioid) consumption compared with placebo, with gabapentin showing the more pronounced and sustained reduction in opioid requirement across the study period; the authors concluded gabapentin is more effective than carbamazepine for GBS-associated pain.
gbs_supportive_pain_management.reason_why: Pain in GBS is predominantly neuropathic (dysaesthetic limb pain, radicular back pain from nerve-root inflammation) rather than nociceptive, so agents that dampen aberrant peripheral-nerve/dorsal-horn neuronal excitability (gabapentin, carbamazepine) target the real underlying mechanism directly, whereas opioids treat pain non-specifically and add real risks (respiratory depression, constipation worsening the bowel dysmotility already common in GBS, sedation masking neurological deterioration) without addressing the neuropathic mechanism.
gbs_supportive_pain_management.important_caveat: Respiratory depression from opioids is a particularly important real risk in GBS specifically because these patients already have a real, evolving risk of respiratory muscle weakness -- opioid sedation can mask or precipitate respiratory failure, reinforcing why gabapentin/carbamazepine, not opioids, should be first-line.
gbs_supportive_pain_management.real_working_solution: Treat GBS-associated neuropathic pain first-line with gabapentin (preferred based on the trial data) or carbamazepine as an alternative, reserving opioids strictly as a short-term rescue adjunct rather than a first-line strategy, particularly in patients with any degree of respiratory compromise.
gbs_supportive_pain_management.source: Pandey CK, Raza M, Tripathi M, Navkar DV, Kumar A, Singh UK, Anesth Analg 2005;101:220-225 (PMID 15976235)

gbs_supportive_bowel_bladder_care.name: Bowel and Bladder Care -- Real Supportive Management of Autonomic/Immobility-Related Dysfunction
specific_drugs: Not a specific drug class -- scheduled bladder catheterisation (intermittent or indwelling, per severity) for autonomic urinary retention, and a bowel regimen (stool softeners, laxatives, scheduled toileting) for autonomic/immobility-related constipation and ileus risk
gbs_supportive_bowel_bladder_care.effectiveness: The international consensus GBS management guideline (Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683, PMID 31541214) includes bladder and bowel management among the standard supportive-care steps for GBS patients with significant motor/autonomic involvement, reflecting real clinical need: urinary retention from autonomic involvement and severe constipation/ileus from a combination of autonomic dysfunction, immobility and opioid avoidance (or, if used, opioid-related slowing) are both common and require active, scheduled management rather than reactive treatment.
gbs_supportive_bowel_bladder_care.reason_why: Autonomic nerve fibres controlling bladder detrusor tone and gut motility are affected by the same immune attack causing limb weakness, and immobility independently slows gut transit -- both problems are mechanistically predictable and preventable with proactive, scheduled care rather than being left to develop into urinary retention/UTI or ileus/faecal impaction.
gbs_supportive_bowel_bladder_care.important_caveat: Untreated urinary retention risks recurrent urinary tract infection and renal injury, while untreated severe constipation/ileus risks bowel perforation in rare cases -- both are real, preventable complications rather than minor inconveniences, and both should be actively screened for rather than assumed absent. Confidence is moderate because this reflects guideline-level consensus supportive-care recommendation rather than a dedicated GBS-specific randomised bowel/bladder-management trial.
gbs_supportive_bowel_bladder_care.real_working_solution: Institute scheduled bladder assessment (with catheterisation as needed) and a proactive bowel regimen from admission in any GBS patient with significant motor or autonomic involvement, rather than waiting for retention or severe constipation to become symptomatic.
gbs_supportive_bowel_bladder_care.source: Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.name: Early Rehabilitation and Physiotherapy -- Real Evidence for Improved Recovery
gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.type: Structured physiotherapy/occupational therapy and exercise programme
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- structured, individually-graded physiotherapy (passive-then-active range-of-motion exercise, progressive strengthening, gait/mobility training) and occupational therapy, started as early as safely possible and continued through the recovery phase
gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.effectiveness: A systematic review of exercise interventions in GBS patients (Simatos Arsenault N, Vincent PO, Yu BH, Bastien R, Sweeney A, Physiother Can 2016;68:367-376, PMID 27904236) found that structured exercise/physiotherapy programmes were associated with real improvements in muscle strength, functional mobility and quality of life during GBS recovery, without evidence of harm from appropriately-graded activity.
gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.reason_why: GBS recovery depends on real peripheral nerve remyelination and axonal regeneration over weeks to months, a biological process that physiotherapy does not accelerate directly, but structured, progressively-graded rehabilitation helps prevent real secondary complications of prolonged immobility (contractures, disuse muscle atrophy beyond the neurological deficit itself, pressure injuries, deconditioning) and helps translate regained nerve function into regained functional mobility as efficiently as possible.
gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.important_caveat: Rehabilitation intensity must be carefully graded to the patient's fatigue and current strength -- overly aggressive exercise in the very early, still-progressing phase of GBS (before the disease has plateaued) is generally avoided in favour of gentle passive range-of-motion and positioning, with active strengthening escalated once the patient is in the stable/recovery phase.
gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.real_working_solution: Involve physiotherapy and occupational therapy early in the GBS admission -- starting with passive range-of-motion/positioning to prevent contractures during the acute/plateau phase, then progressing to active, graded strengthening and mobility/gait training as recovery begins -- as a real, evidence-supported part of the treatment plan rather than an afterthought started only after hospital discharge.
gbs_rehabilitation_early_physiotherapy.source: Simatos Arsenault N, Vincent PO, Yu BH, Bastien R, Sweeney A, Physiother Can 2016;68:367-376 (PMID 27904236)

gbs_medical_devices_equipment.name: Medical Equipment/Devices -- Apheresis Machines, IVIG Infusion Pumps, Ventilators, Cardiac Telemetry, Spirometers
gbs_medical_devices_equipment.type: Diagnostic/monitoring and treatment-delivery devices supporting acute GBS management
specific_drugs: IV infusion pump (for controlled-rate IVIG infusion)
Invasive mechanical ventilator (ICU-grade, for respiratory failure)
Continuous cardiac telemetry/ECG monitor and arterial-line blood pressure monitoring (for dysautonomia surveillance)
Bedside spirometer (for serial vital capacity/maximal inspiratory-expiratory pressure measurement to anticipate ventilation need)
Intermittent pneumatic compression device (for VTE prophylaxis in immobile patients)
gbs_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Each device is directly load-bearing for a proven intervention described above: the apheresis machine delivers the Cochrane-proven plasma exchange treatment; the infusion pump delivers the controlled-rate IVIG regimen used in the pivotal Dutch trial; the ventilator provides real life-saving support for the ~25% of patients who develop respiratory failure; cardiac telemetry detects the real, guideline-flagged dysautonomia-related arrhythmia risk; serial spirometry is the specific real tool behind the Lawn et al. '20/30/40' ventilation-anticipation criteria; and pneumatic compression devices deliver mechanical VTE prophylaxis for immobile patients.
gbs_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: GBS management is genuinely device-and-monitoring-intensive because the disease threatens multiple organ systems simultaneously (respiratory muscles, cardiac autonomic control, mobility) through a single underlying immune process, so real outcome depends as much on the monitoring/support infrastructure around the two core disease-modifying treatments (IVIG/PLEX) as on the treatments themselves.
gbs_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Apheresis machines and ICU-level ventilator/monitoring capacity are not universally available outside larger tertiary centres, which is a real, practical determinant of whether PLEX (versus IVIG, which needs only a standard infusion pump) is a feasible choice in a given hospital, including in much of India.
gbs_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Manage acute GBS in a centre with ICU-level ventilator, cardiac monitoring and serial pulmonary-function-testing capability at minimum; reserve plasma exchange for centres with functioning apheresis equipment and trained staff, defaulting to IVIG via standard infusion pump where apheresis is not available.
gbs_medical_devices_equipment.source: Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898 (PMID 11405803); Chevret S, Hughes RA, Annane D, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;2:CD001798 (PMID 28241090); Leonhard SE et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683 (PMID 31541214)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG (2 g/kg over 5 days) OR Plasma Exchange, started early -- Real Top-Line Answer
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Interim analysis of the pivotal head-to-head trial (n=150): strength improved by >=1 disability grade at 4 weeks in 53% of IVIG-treated patients vs 34% of plasma-exchange-treated patients; IVIG also showed faster median time to 1-grade improvement (27 vs 41 days) and fewer complications. The Cochrane pooled analysis across all trials found no significant overall difference between the two treatments (MD 0.02 grade, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.25), so IVIG and PLEX are considered equally effective real disease-modifying treatments when started within about 2-4 weeks of onset.
ranked_high_to_low.source: van der Meché FG, Schmitz PI, N Engl J Med 1992;326:1123-1129 (PMID 1552913); Hughes RA, Swan AV, van Doorn PA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;2014:CD002063 (PMID 25238327)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Plasma Exchange vs Supportive Care Alone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Significantly greater 4-week disability-grade improvement (RR 1.64), reduced need for mechanical ventilation (RR 0.53), and greater full-strength recovery at 1 year (RR 1.24) vs supportive care alone
ranked_high_to_low.source: Chevret S, Hughes RA, Annane D, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;2:CD001798 (PMID 28241090)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Serial Spirometry-Guided Elective Intubation ("20/30/40 rule")
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Identifies impending respiratory failure (vital capacity <20 mL/kg, MIP <30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O, or >30% fall from baseline) early enough for planned elective intubation rather than emergency intubation, in a disease where ~25% of patients ultimately need ventilation
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898 (PMID 11405803); van Doorn PA et al., J Clin Immunol 2010 (PMID 20396937)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Gabapentin for GBS-Associated Neuropathic Pain (vs Carbamazepine/Placebo)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Computed from reported raw values: gabapentin 300mg TID reduced Day-1 rescue opioid (fentanyl) consumption to 340.1 +/- 34.3 microg vs 590.4 +/- 35.0 microg with placebo in ICU GBS patients, a 42.4% reduction ((590.4-340.1)/590.4), alongside significantly lower numeric pain-rating-scale scores throughout the 7-day trial, in a randomised trial of 36 ICU GBS patients vs both carbamazepine and placebo.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pandey CK et al., Anesth Analg 2005;101:220-225 (PMID 15976235)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early Physiotherapy/Rehabilitation
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Associated with real improvements in strength, functional mobility and quality of life during recovery in a systematic review, without evidence of harm from appropriately-graded activity
ranked_high_to_low.source: Simatos Arsenault N et al., Physiother Can 2016;68:367-376 (PMID 27904236)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combined IVIG + Plasma Exchange -- Real Negative-for-Combination Finding
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No statistically significant advantage over either modality alone at 4 weeks or over 48 weeks of follow-up (mean improvement 1.1 combined vs 0.9 PLEX vs 0.8 IVIG, not significant)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Plasma Exchange/Sandoglobulin GBS Trial Group, Lancet 1997;349:225-230 (PMID 9014908)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Eculizumab (Complement C5 Inhibitor) -- Real Negative Phase 3 Primary Endpoint
ranked_high_to_low.type: Investigational anti-C5 monoclonal antibody, add-on to IVIG
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Phase 2 JET-GBS trial: at week 4, 61% of eculizumab-treated patients (14 of 23, 90% CI 42-78) were walking independently vs 45% with placebo (5 of 11, 90% CI 20-73) - a favourable numerical trend, but the primary efficacy threshold was not met since the lower CI bound (42%) did not clear the predefined 50% response bar. The subsequent phase 3 trial was negative (HR 0.9, 95% CI 0.45-1.97, p=0.89 for time to independent walking).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Misawa S, Kuwabara S, et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:519-529 (PMID 29685815); Kuwabara S, Kusunoki S, et al., J Peripher Nerv Syst 2024;29:339-349 (PMID 38987228)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Corticosteroids (Alone or Added to IVIG) -- Real Negative Finding, Unlike CIDP
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real negative finding: GBS disability score WORSENED by >=1 grade at 4 weeks in 68% of patients (76 of 112) given methylprednisolone added to IVIG, vs 56% (63 of 113) given IVIG alone (adjusted OR 1.89, p=0.03 after adjusting for age/baseline disability) - i.e. a trend toward WORSE, not better, outcomes with added steroid. No significant benefit was seen for corticosteroid monotherapy either (Cochrane).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hughes RA, Brassington R, Gunn AA, van Doorn PA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;10:CD001446 (PMID 27775812); van Koningsveld R et al., Lancet 2004;363:192-196 (PMID 14738791)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials with DIFFERENT comparators (some versus supportive care/placebo, some head-to-head against an active comparator such as PLEX or IVIG) and different outcome scales, so this ordering is a directional judgement, NOT a single directly-comparable percentage scale -- effectiveness_pct is shown only where a genuine relative-risk figure was reported and could be converted to an approximate percent (row 2); other rows use their own real, differently-shaped metric that does not reduce to a single number. Rows 1-5 are REAL WORKING, evidence-positive interventions (rank 1, IVIG or PLEX started early, is the practical top-line answer for the disease-modifying treatment decision); rows 6-9 are documented REAL NEGATIVE or non-superior findings, reported here specifically so they are not mistakenly used instead of the real working alternatives above them -- do not combine IVIG+PLEX routinely, do not add corticosteroids, do not routinely repeat IVIG in poor-prognosis patients, and do not present eculizumab as an approved GBS treatment. IMPORTANT: unlike a chronic-disease ranked table, every row here concerns a single, largely monophasic acute illness -- see CURABILITY_NOTE for why GBS should be framed as a treatable emergency, not a lifelong management condition.

myasthenia_gravis.name: Myasthenia Gravis
myasthenia_gravis.icd11_hint: 8C61 Myasthenia gravis (WHO ICD-11 foundation, disorder of the neuromuscular junction); legacy ICD-10 G70.0 Myasthenia gravis
myasthenia_gravis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Myasthenic crisis - respiratory failure from MG-related weakness of the diaphragm, accessory respiratory and/or bulbar muscles, requiring ventilatory support - is a real, life-threatening neurological emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely, triggering immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW), never a routine consultation flow. In a real Indian tertiary-care cohort of 64 MG patients, 21.9% developed at least one myasthenic crisis (median 8.5 months from onset), 57.1% of those needed prolonged ventilation, and half had recurrent crises - so a known MG patient with new or rapidly worsening breathlessness, difficulty swallowing/handling secretions, or slurred/nasal speech must never be managed as 'wait and see' at home, because myasthenic patients can decompensate to ventilatory failure without the obvious tachypnoea/accessory-muscle distress seen in other causes of respiratory failure (Kalita J, Kohat AK, Misra UK, 'Predictors of outcome of myasthenic crisis', Neurol Sci 2014;35(7):1109-1114, PMID 24497206; Wendell LC, Levine JM, 'Myasthenic crisis', Neurohospitalist 2011;1(1):16-22, PMID 23983833). The most frequent identifiable triggers are infection, recent surgery, and tapering/withdrawal of medication (Kalita J et al., 2014, PMID 24497206) - so any of these in a known MG patient, combined with new bulbar or respiratory symptoms, should be treated as a probable impending crisis rather than routine illness. Certain medications (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, intravenous magnesium, beta-blockers, D-penicillamine, and some anaesthetic/neuromuscular-blocking agents) can precipitate or worsen crisis and should never be newly started in an MG patient without checking this risk first (Barrons RW, Pharmacotherapy 1997;17(6):1220-1232, PMID 9399604; Petrucelli N, Barra ME, Koehl JL, Neurohospitalist 2024;14(1):52-57, PMID 38235027; Marriott M, Schwery A, VandenBerg A, Am J Health Syst Pharm 2023;80(5):249-257, PMID 36373673).

definition.finding: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) in which autoantibodies attack postsynaptic membrane components at the motor endplate, most commonly the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR), producing the cardinal clinical feature of fluctuating, fatigable skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with sustained or repeated activity and improves with rest.
definition.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, 'Myasthenia gravis: subgroup classification and therapeutic strategies for a heterogeneous disease', Lancet Neurol 2015;14(10):1023-1036 (PMID 26376969)

achr_antibody_mechanism.finding: Anti-AChR antibodies are present in roughly 80-85% of patients with generalized MG and a lower proportion (approximately 50%) of patients with purely ocular MG. These IgG1/IgG3 antibodies cause weakness through three complementary mechanisms at the postsynaptic membrane: complement-mediated membrane attack complex formation that destroys the folded postsynaptic membrane (reducing AChR density and simplifying the junctional folds), antigenic modulation (cross-linking and accelerated internalisation/degradation of AChRs), and direct functional blockade of the acetylcholine-binding site - the net effect being a reduced safety margin for neuromuscular transmission.
achr_antibody_mechanism.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969); Vincent A, 'Unravelling the pathogenesis of myasthenia gravis', Nat Rev Immunol 2002;2(10):797-804

musk_antibody_subtype.finding: Anti-muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) antibodies define a distinct MG subgroup found in a minority of AChR-antibody-negative patients. In a characterised MuSK-positive cohort (n=17), the phenotype was markedly different from typical AChR-MG: 82.4% had predominant facial and bulbar muscle involvement (rather than limb/ocular predominance), the group was 88% female, and 70.6% had onset before age 40. MuSK antibodies are predominantly IgG4, act mainly by disrupting agrin/LRP4/MuSK postsynaptic clustering signalling (a largely non-complement-fixing mechanism, unlike AChR-antibody disease), and this subgroup responds poorly to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and is essentially never associated with thymoma.
musk_antibody_subtype.source: Lavrnic D, Losen M, Vujic A, et al., 'The features of myasthenia gravis with autoantibodies to MuSK', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005;76(8):1099-1102 (PMID 16024887); Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

lrp4_and_seronegative.finding: Anti-LRP4 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4) antibodies are found in a small subset of patients who are AChR- and MuSK-antibody negative; LRP4 is the agrin receptor required for MuSK activation and AChR clustering, so anti-LRP4 antibodies impair the same clustering pathway disrupted in MuSK-MG. Even after AChR, MuSK and LRP4 testing, a residual group remains 'seronegative' on standard assays (clinical MG with no detectable antibody by routine clinical testing); some of these patients have low-affinity AChR antibodies detectable only on cell-based assays, so 'seronegative' status is partly an assay-sensitivity issue rather than proof of a distinct autoimmune mechanism.
lrp4_and_seronegative.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969); Budhram A, Ismail OZ, Sangam K, et al., 'Improving sensitivity of autoantibody testing for myasthenia gravis using cell-based assays', Front Neurol 2026 (PMID 42491105)

thymus_role.finding: The thymus is central to MG pathogenesis in the AChR-antibody-positive subgroup: thymic follicular hyperplasia (ectopic germinal centres producing anti-AChR-secreting B cells) is characteristic of early-onset AChR-MG, while a thymic epithelial tumour (thymoma) is found in a meaningful minority of MG patients overall, particularly in later-onset AChR-positive disease. In an Indian tertiary-referral cohort of 81 MG patients, 19 underwent thymectomy, of whom 16 had thymoma and 3 had thymic hyperplasia on histology. Thymoma is essentially never seen in MuSK-MG. This thymic link is the pathophysiological rationale for thymectomy in AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG (a treatment-side decision, not covered in this entry).
thymus_role.source: Misra UK et al., 'A study of comorbidities in myasthenia gravis', Acta Neurol Belg 2020;120(1):59-64 (PMID 30972663); Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

bedside_clinical_tests.finding: Fatigable weakness is demonstrated at the bedside by sustained upgaze (worsening ptosis after 30-60 seconds), repeated blinking or limb exercise producing increasing weakness, and improvement of ptosis after rest or ice application. The ice-pack test (cooling the affected eyelid, which improves neuromuscular transmission) is a simple bedside test for ptosis: in an Asian cohort, the conventional ice-pack test had 43.3% sensitivity and 100% specificity for ocular MG overall (only 27.8% sensitive for mild ptosis specifically), while adding sustained upgaze to the ice-pack test raised sensitivity to 73.3% (72.2% for mild ptosis) with specificity of 96.7% - i.e. the test is highly specific when positive but not sensitive enough alone to exclude MG when negative.
bedside_clinical_tests.source: Kee HJ, Yang HK, Hwang JM, Park KS, 'Evaluation and validation of sustained upgaze combined with the ice-pack test for ocular myasthenia gravis in Asians', Neuromuscul Disord 2019;29(4):296-301 (PMID 30704861)

serologic_antibody_testing.finding: Serum AChR-binding antibody testing is the first-line serologic test, positive in approximately 80-85% of generalized MG and roughly 50% of ocular MG; if AChR-antibody-negative, anti-MuSK antibody testing should follow (positive in a further small subset, historically reported higher in some series but generally a minority of AChR-negative patients); anti-LRP4 antibody testing can be considered in patients negative for both. Cell-based assays improve detection of low-affinity AChR antibodies missed by standard radioimmunoassay/ELISA in some 'seronegative' patients.
serologic_antibody_testing.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969); Budhram A et al., Front Neurol 2026 (PMID 42491105)

repetitive_nerve_stimulation.finding: Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at low frequency (2-3 Hz) is the standard electrodiagnostic screening test: a decrement of 10% or more in compound muscle action potential amplitude (or area) between the first and a later response (typically the 4th or 5th) is considered abnormal. Diagnostic sensitivity is test- and population-dependent - a 2025 study found amplitude-decrement-alone sensitivity of only 29.6%, area-decrement-alone 38%, and a combined amplitude-plus-area approach 43.7% in a mixed outpatient cohort, whereas a 2023 inpatient study of more severely affected, hospitalised MG patients found RNS sensitivity of 83.3% - illustrating that RNS is considerably more sensitive in clinically more severe/generalized disease than in mild or purely ocular disease.
repetitive_nerve_stimulation.source: Fonseca A, Almeida M, Duque C, et al., 'Enhancing diagnostic sensitivity in Myasthenia Gravis: the combined role of CMAP area and amplitude decrements', Clin Neurophysiol 2025;174:169-172 (PMID 40279946); Clifford KM, Wu CK, Post D, et al., 'Utility of Repetitive Nerve Stimulation in the Diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis in the Inpatient Setting', Neurohospitalist 2023;13(4):364-370 (PMID 37701254)

single_fiber_emg.finding: Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG), which measures jitter (variability in neuromuscular transmission time between paired muscle fibres of the same motor unit), is regarded as the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test for a defect of neuromuscular transmission - a 2026 study in a low-prevalence ocular MG cohort found SFEMG abnormal in 100% of patients who truly had a neuromuscular transmission disorder. Its high sensitivity comes at the cost of low specificity (jitter can be abnormal in other neuromuscular/motor neuron disorders), so it is used mainly when RNS and antibody testing are negative but clinical suspicion remains high.
single_fiber_emg.source: Gomez Y, Puwanant A, Caress JB, 'Predictive Value of Single-Fiber Electromyography for Ocular Myasthenia Gravis in a Low Prevalence Cohort', J Clin Neurophysiol 2026 (PMID 42138399); Morena JM, 'Electrodiagnostic Approach to Defects of Neuromuscular Transmission', Muscle Nerve 2026;74(1):10-21 (PMID 41630490)

edrophonium_tensilon_test.finding: The edrophonium (Tensilon) test - a rapid-onset, short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor given intravenously to look for transient improvement in a weak muscle (classically ptosis) - was historically the classic bedside pharmacologic test for MG. It is now formally archived/largely obsolete in current practice: edrophonium is not reliably available in many countries, the test carries a real risk of cholinergic side effects including bradyarrhythmia (requiring atropine and cardiac monitoring on standby), and it has been superseded by the combination of antibody testing, electrodiagnostics and the safer ice-pack test for ptosis.
edrophonium_tensilon_test.source: Naji A, Owens ML, 'Edrophonium (Archived)', StatPearls, StatPearls Publishing, 2023 (PMID 32119453)

thymoma_imaging_screening.finding: Because thymoma is present in a clinically important minority of newly diagnosed MG patients (disproportionately in AChR-antibody-positive disease) and can itself require surgical management, cross-sectional chest imaging (CT, or MRI where CT is contraindicated) of the anterior mediastinum is a standard part of the diagnostic work-up in every newly diagnosed MG patient to look for thymoma, independent of age or antibody status.
thymoma_imaging_screening.source: Misra UK et al., Acta Neurol Belg 2020 (PMID 30972663); Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

mgfa_clinical_classes.finding: The Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical classification grades a patient's worst-ever status into five classes: Class I - any ocular muscle weakness only (may include eye-closure weakness), with normal strength elsewhere; Class II - mild weakness affecting muscles other than ocular muscles (may also have ocular weakness of any severity), subdivided IIa (predominantly limb/axial) and IIb (predominantly oropharyngeal/respiratory); Class III - moderate weakness of non-ocular muscles (IIIa limb/axial-predominant, IIIb oropharyngeal/respiratory-predominant); Class IV - severe weakness of non-ocular muscles (IVa limb/axial-predominant, IVb oropharyngeal/respiratory-predominant, including use of a feeding tube without intubation); Class V - defined by the need for intubation, with or without mechanical ventilation, to maintain the airway (except when used during routine postoperative management). This classification standardises severity description for research and clinical communication but is a point-in-time/worst-ever descriptor, not a stand-alone diagnostic tool.
mgfa_clinical_classes.source: Jaretzki A 3rd, Barohn RJ, Ernstoff RM, et al., 'Myasthenia gravis: recommendations for clinical research standards', Neurology 2000;55(1):16-23 (PMID 10891897)

ocular_vs_generalized.finding: MG can remain purely ocular (weakness confined to the levator palpebrae and extraocular muscles) or progress to generalized disease. In a Spanish single-centre series, 62 of 91 MG patients (68%) had ocular onset, and binocular diplopia was the most frequent initial symptom (51.7% of ocular-onset cases); 50% of the ocular-onset group progressed to generalized MG at a median of 6 months. In a separate US academic cohort followed for a mean of 3 years, 12 of 59 (about 20%) of ocular MG patients treated with pyridostigmine alone progressed to generalized ('transformed') MG, versus none of those treated with prednisone - consistent with most generalization occurring within the first 2-3 years of disease and being influenced by early treatment choice (a treatment-side point, noted here only for its bearing on natural history/counselling).
ocular_vs_generalized.source: Diaz-Maroto I, Garcia-Garcia J, Sanchez-Ayaso PA, et al., 'Ocular myasthenia gravis and risk factors for developing a secondary generalisation: description of a Spanish series', Neurologia (Engl Ed) 2023;38(4):229-235 (PMID 35637136); Mittal MK, Barohn RJ, Pasnoor M, et al., 'Ocular myasthenia gravis in an academic neuro-ophthalmology clinic: clinical features and therapeutic response', J Clin Neuromuscul Dis 2011;13(1):46-52 (PMID 22361625)
