musk_vs_achr_pattern.finding: MuSK-MG and AChR-MG are clinically distinguishable subgroups rather than a single phenotype: MuSK-MG (see pathophysiology section) is markedly bulbar/facial-predominant with frequent tongue and facial muscle atrophy, disproportionate neck-extensor and respiratory involvement, a female preponderance, younger age of onset, poor response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (which can sometimes worsen MuSK-MG), and essentially no thymoma association - in contrast to classical generalized AChR-MG's proximal-limb, ocular and bulbar pattern with a recognised thymoma/thymic-hyperplasia association.
musk_vs_achr_pattern.source: Lavrnic D et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005 (PMID 16024887); Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

core_feature.finding: The defining clinical feature is fluctuating, fatigable weakness of voluntary (striated) muscle that characteristically worsens with sustained or repeated use and over the course of the day, and improves with rest - distinguishing it from most other causes of weakness, which are typically constant or improve with activity (as in some myopathies) rather than fatigue with it.
core_feature.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

ocular_symptoms.finding: Ptosis (often asymmetric or alternating) and binocular diplopia are the most common presenting features of MG, reflecting the ocular and periocular muscles' particular vulnerability to fatigable weakness; in the Spanish ocular-onset series, diplopia was the single most frequent initial symptom (51.7%), and ocular onset accounted for 68% of the overall MG cohort. Pupillary responses are always spared in MG (a useful bedside discriminator from third-nerve palsy or other causes of ptosis/diplopia with pupil involvement).
ocular_symptoms.source: Diaz-Maroto I et al., Neurologia (Engl Ed) 2023 (PMID 35637136)

bulbar_symptoms.finding: Bulbar muscle involvement produces dysarthria (a nasal or 'mushy' quality that worsens with prolonged speaking), dysphagia (particularly for solids or fatiguing towards the end of a meal, with risk of aspiration), and facial/masticatory weakness (a 'myasthenic snarl' on smiling, jaw fatigue with chewing). Bulbar-predominant presentation is especially characteristic of MuSK-MG.
bulbar_symptoms.source: Lavrnic D et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005 (PMID 16024887); Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

limb_and_axial_symptoms.finding: Limb weakness in generalized MG is typically proximal greater than distal (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or raising the arms overhead, worsening with repetition), often with neck-extensor weakness causing 'dropped head' by the end of the day; deep tendon reflexes and sensation remain normal, which helps distinguish MG from most peripheral neuropathies and myelopathies.
limb_and_axial_symptoms.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

respiratory_involvement.finding: Diaphragmatic and intercostal (respiratory) muscle weakness is the most dangerous manifestation of MG because it can progress to ventilatory failure (myasthenic crisis, covered separately below); it may develop gradually with disease progression or, more dangerously, acutely with an intercurrent precipitant, and can be present without dramatic limb weakness, so respiratory function must be actively assessed rather than inferred from limb strength alone.
respiratory_involvement.source: Wendell LC, Levine JM, 'Myasthenic crisis', Neurohospitalist 2011;1(1):16-22 (PMID 23983833)

definition_and_frequency.finding: Myasthenic crisis is defined as respiratory failure due to MG-related weakness of the diaphragm and/or accessory respiratory and bulbar muscles severe enough to require ventilatory support (invasive or non-invasive). In an Indian tertiary-care cohort of 64 MG patients followed a median of 48 months, 14 patients (21.9%) developed at least one myasthenic crisis, at a median of 8.5 months from disease onset; of those, 8/14 (57.1%) required prolonged ventilation, and half of the crisis patients had 2-4 recurrent crisis episodes over follow-up - underscoring that crisis is a recurring risk, not a one-off event, once it has occurred.
definition_and_frequency.source: Kalita J, Kohat AK, Misra UK, 'Predictors of outcome of myasthenic crisis', Neurol Sci 2014;35(7):1109-1114 (PMID 24497206); Wendell LC, Levine JM, Neurohospitalist 2011 (PMID 23983833)

precipitating_factors.finding: In the same Indian cohort, the identifiable precipitants of myasthenic crisis were infection (6 of 14 crisis episodes with a documented trigger), surgery (5), tapering or withdrawal of medication (2), and a contrast-media reaction (1) - i.e. intercurrent infection and perioperative medication changes are the dominant real-world triggers, well before dramatic 'idiopathic' worsening.
precipitating_factors.source: Kalita J, Kohat AK, Misra UK, Neurol Sci 2014 (PMID 24497206)

medications_that_worsen_mg.finding: A defined list of drug classes can precipitate or worsen MG weakness and must be used with caution or avoided, especially in a patient with any respiratory or bulbar compromise: aminoglycoside antibiotics (historically the class most frequently implicated in drug-induced neuromuscular blockade), fluoroquinolone and macrolide antibiotics, intravenous magnesium, beta-blockers (including labetalol, documented as one of the agents most often associated with acute exacerbation in a recent inpatient medication-exposure study), D-penicillamine (can itself induce a myasthenic syndrome), and neuromuscular-blocking/certain anaesthetic agents used during surgery (which require anaesthetic teams to be explicitly informed of the MG diagnosis). Clinicians should check any new medication against this list before prescribing in a known MG patient.
medications_that_worsen_mg.source: Barrons RW, 'Drug-induced neuromuscular blockade and myasthenia gravis', Pharmacotherapy 1997;17(6):1220-1232 (PMID 9399604); Petrucelli N, Barra ME, Koehl JL, 'Evaluation of Medication Exposure on Exacerbation of Disease in Patients With Myasthenia Gravis', Neurohospitalist 2024;14(1):52-57 (PMID 38235027); Marriott M, Schwery A, VandenBerg A, 'Myasthenia gravis: what does a pharmacist need to know?', Am J Health Syst Pharm 2023;80(5):249-257 (PMID 36373673)

bedside_respiratory_monitoring.finding: Patients with worsening bulbar or respiratory symptoms require serial bedside monitoring of forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF), because a falling trend on serial measurements can signal impending ventilatory failure before overt distress or hypoxia appear (myasthenic patients can look deceptively comfortable until they decompensate suddenly, since they may lack the accessory-muscle recruitment/tachypnoea typical of other causes of respiratory failure); a single normal measurement does not exclude clinically worsening respiratory compromise, so the trend and clinical bulbar/respiratory exam matter as much as any single number. This entry does not state specific numeric FVC/NIF cut-offs, since a verified sourced number for those exact thresholds could not be confirmed.

lambert_eaton_myasthenic_syndrome.finding: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is the key autoimmune mimic of MG but is mechanistically and clinically distinct: it is caused by antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC), present in roughly 90% of LEMS patients, which impair presynaptic acetylcholine release. Clinically, LEMS causes proximal limb weakness that classically improves (rather than worsens) with brief sustained exercise, is frequently accompanied by autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic symptoms) and depressed/absent deep tendon reflexes that can transiently normalise after exercise - findings not seen in MG. Electrodiagnostically, LEMS is distinguished from MG by an incremental (rather than decremental) response of compound muscle action potential amplitude on high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation or after brief maximal voluntary contraction. LEMS is strongly paraneoplastic: approximately half of LEMS patients have or go on to be found to have small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), and a validated clinical prediction score (the Dutch-English DELTA-P score) can stratify SCLC risk from readily available clinical variables (age, smoking, weight loss, performance status, bulbar involvement, erectile dysfunction, VGCC antibody level) with derivation/validation-cohort AUCs of 94.4-94.6%.
lambert_eaton_myasthenic_syndrome.source: Wijdicks EFM (author series), 'Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic syndrome: early diagnosis is key', Degener Neurol Neuromuscul Dis 2019;9:27-37 (PMID 31191084); Titulaer MJ, Maddison P, Sont JK, et al., 'Clinical Dutch-English Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome tumor association prediction score accurately predicts small-cell lung cancer in the LEMS', J Clin Oncol 2011;29(7):902-908 (PMID 21245427)

botulism.finding: Botulism, caused by botulinum toxin blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release, can mimic MG or LEMS with descending, fatigable-appearing weakness, ptosis, diplopia and bulbar symptoms, but is distinguished by an acute/subacute onset (over hours to days, from a food, wound, or infant-gut toxin source), early and prominent autonomic features (fixed/dilated pupils, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention - pupillary involvement is a key discriminator since MG spares pupils), and a descending pattern beginning with cranial nerves; RNS in botulism can show an incremental response similar to LEMS because the underlying defect is also presynaptic.
botulism.source: Clinical differential-diagnosis reasoning consistent with the presynaptic-versus-postsynaptic NMJ disease framework in Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969) and the LEMS review (PMID 31191084)

gbs_and_miller_fisher.finding: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) and its Miller Fisher variant can be confused with MG when presenting with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and bulbar weakness, but GBS/Miller Fisher is a peripheral-nerve/root disorder, so it characteristically produces areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes, preserved or brisk in MG), sensory/ataxic features in Miller Fisher (ataxia, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia triad, often with anti-GQ1b antibodies), an ascending or acute monophasic course rather than fluctuating fatigability, and albuminocytologic dissociation on CSF analysis - features not expected in MG.
gbs_and_miller_fisher.source: Clinical differential-diagnosis reasoning consistent with Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

thyroid_eye_disease_and_other_ptosis_dip.finding: Thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy) can cause diplopia and eyelid signs but typically shows lid retraction/lid lag (rather than ptosis), proptosis, restrictive extraocular myopathy on orbital imaging, and periorbital oedema/conjunctival injection, without fatigability; other structural mimics of ptosis/diplopia to exclude include third-nerve palsy (with pupil involvement, unlike MG), Horner syndrome (ptosis with miosis, not fatigable), and mitochondrial disease (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, which is typically fixed/non-fatigable and symmetric).
thyroid_eye_disease_and_other_ptosis_dip.source: Clinical differential-diagnosis reasoning consistent with Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969)

age_sex_bimodal_pattern.finding: MG has a well-described bimodal age-of-onset/sex distribution: early-onset disease (roughly before age 40-50) predominates in women and is more strongly associated with thymic hyperplasia and AChR antibodies, while late-onset disease (after age 50-60) has a male predominance and is more often associated with thymoma or a normal/atrophic thymus. MuSK-MG in particular skews strongly female and younger (88% female, 70.6% onset before 40 in the characterised cohort discussed above).
age_sex_bimodal_pattern.source: Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969); Lavrnic D et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005 (PMID 16024887)

autoimmune_and_thymic_comorbidity.finding: MG is associated with other autoimmune disease at a rate well above the general population, and with thymic pathology specifically. In the Indian tertiary-referral cohort, 71 of 81 MG patients (88%) had at least one comorbidity, 8 (10%) had a co-existing autoimmune comorbidity, and thymic pathology (thymoma or hyperplasia) was found in all 19 patients who underwent thymectomy (16 thymoma, 3 hyperplasia) - consistent with the broader literature's recognition of autoimmune thyroid disease as the most frequently reported co-existing autoimmune condition in MG cohorts internationally.
autoimmune_and_thymic_comorbidity.source: Misra UK et al., Acta Neurol Belg 2020 (PMID 30972663)

global_burden.finding: A pooled systematic review of 55 population-based epidemiological studies spanning 1950-2007 (1.7 billion person-years of observation) found an overall MG incidence of 5.3 per million person-years (95% CI 4.4-6.1; range 1.7-21.3 across studies), an AChR-MG-specific incidence of 7.3 per million person-years, a MuSK-MG incidence of only 0.1-0.32 per million person-years, and an overall MG prevalence of 77.7 per million persons (95% CI 64.0-94.3; range 15-179 across studies) - i.e. roughly 1 in 12,900 people, though with wide variation by region and case-ascertainment method. MG-attributable mortality across included studies ranged from 0.1 to 0.9 per million person-years.
global_burden.source: Carr AS, Cardwell CR, McCarron PO, McConville J, 'A systematic review of population based epidemiological studies in Myasthenia Gravis', BMC Neurol 2010;10:46 (PMID 20565885)

india_specific_data.finding: Dedicated India-specific population-level incidence/prevalence studies for MG are sparse; the available real Indian data are hospital/tertiary-referral cohort studies rather than nationwide registries. A Sanjay Gandhi Post Graduate Institute (Lucknow) cohort of 64 MG patients (median age 45, range 6-84) found that 21.9% developed myasthenic crisis over a median 48-month follow-up, and a related 81-patient cohort from the same centre found comorbidities in 88% of patients. A 2026 review from NIMHANS, Bengaluru specifically addresses sex-specific and reproductive-health aspects of MG in Indian practice, though without population-level Indian incidence/prevalence figures. This entry does not state a specific India-wide MG prevalence/incidence number, since no such verified population-based Indian study could be found.
india_specific_data.source: Kalita J, Kohat AK, Misra UK, Neurol Sci 2014 (PMID 24497206); Misra UK et al., Acta Neurol Belg 2020 (PMID 30972663); Menon D, Vengalil S, Nashi S, Nalini A, 'Women and Myasthenia Gravis', Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2026;29(3):327-335 (PMID 42262806)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate

disease_course.finding: In the largest published lifetime-course cohort (1,976 MG patients followed 1940-2000), the most severe weakness and the highest mortality risk occurred during the first 1-2 years after symptom onset, with the clinical course thereafter significantly influenced by age and sex; many patients who survive and are treated through this early high-risk window subsequently stabilise or improve, consistent with the general clinical teaching that MG is a fluctuating disease which, with modern immunotherapy, can achieve pharmacologic remission or minimal-manifestation status in a substantial proportion of patients (a treatment-outcome point, only referenced here for its bearing on natural-history counselling).
disease_course.source: Grob D, Brunner N, Namba T, Pagala M, 'Lifetime course of myasthenia gravis', Muscle Nerve 2008;37(2):141-149 (PMID 18059039)

modern_mortality.finding: With modern immunotherapy and ICU-level respiratory support, in-hospital mortality for MG (including admissions for myasthenic crisis) is now low: a nationwide Spanish population-based study of hospitalisations for MG (2016-2022) found in-hospital mortality remained low and stable at a mean of 2.6% across the study period, a marked improvement from the pre-mechanical-ventilation era when uncontrolled respiratory failure carried a much higher case-fatality rate; this entry does not state a specific historical (pre-1960s) mortality percentage, since no verified sourced figure for that specific historical comparison could be found in this session.
modern_mortality.source: 'Trends in hospitalisation, myasthenic crisis and intensive care use in myasthenia gravis: a nationwide population-based study in Spain (2016-2022)', Neurol Res Pract 2026 (PMID 42015252)

pregnancy_and_mg.finding: Pregnancy in a woman with MG requires close multidisciplinary (neurology-obstetric) monitoring because the disease course is unpredictable during pregnancy and the postpartum period carries a recognised risk of exacerbation; a 2026 review focused on reproductive-health aspects of MG explicitly identifies pregnancy planning, contraception, teratogenic risk of certain MG medications, postpartum exacerbation risk, and neonatal complications as core clinical considerations, though it does not itself provide a quantified percentage risk of exacerbation, which this entry therefore does not state.
pregnancy_and_mg.source: Menon D, Vengalil S, Nashi S, Nalini A, 'Women and Myasthenia Gravis', Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2026;29(3):327-335 (PMID 42262806)

transient_neonatal_myasthenia.finding: Transient neonatal myasthenia is a self-limited neuromuscular transmission disorder in infants born to mothers with MG, caused by transplacental transfer of maternal anti-AChR (or anti-MuSK) IgG antibodies; affected infants can show hypotonia, poor suck/feeding, weak cry, and respiratory difficulty in the first days of life, which resolves as maternal antibody is cleared from the neonatal circulation. A verified sourced numeric incidence percentage and precise median duration for transient neonatal myasthenia could not be confirmed from the sources reviewed in this session and are therefore not stated here; clinically, the key action point is that any infant of a myasthenic mother should be observed for these features after delivery.
transient_neonatal_myasthenia.source: General mechanism consistent with Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969); numeric incidence/duration not independently verified this session
transient_neonatal_myasthenia.confidence: low-moderate (mechanism well established; specific incidence/duration numbers not verified)

clinical_takeaway.finding: First, confirm the diagnosis objectively rather than on clinical impression alone: AChR-antibody testing (and MuSK/LRP4 if AChR-negative), supported by electrodiagnostics (RNS, or SFEMG if RNS/antibodies are negative but suspicion remains), and a simple bedside ice-pack test for ptosis when available. Second, image the chest (CT/MRI) in every newly diagnosed MG patient to screen for thymoma, regardless of age or antibody status. Third, actively screen for and educate the patient about myasthenic crisis red flags - new or worsening dysarthria, dysphagia, or breathlessness, especially in the setting of infection, recent surgery, or a tapered/missed medication dose - since these are the dominant real-world precipitants, and bedside respiratory assessment (not reassurance from normal limb strength) should guide urgency. Fourth, before prescribing any new medication to a known MG patient, check it against the list of drugs that can worsen MG (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, intravenous magnesium, beta-blockers, D-penicillamine, and anaesthetic/neuromuscular-blocking agents), and ensure any anaesthetic team is explicitly informed of the MG diagnosis before surgery.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesised from Gilhus NE, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26376969); Kalita J, Kohat AK, Misra UK, Neurol Sci 2014 (PMID 24497206); Barrons RW, Pharmacotherapy 1997 (PMID 9399604); Petrucelli N et al., Neurohospitalist 2024 (PMID 38235027); Marriott M et al., Am J Health Syst Pharm 2023 (PMID 36373673)

myasthenia_gravis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Myasthenia gravis (MG) does not have a single drug that reverses the underlying autoimmune attack on the neuromuscular junction in every patient, and that must be stated plainly. But MG is genuinely one of the more treatable neurological autoimmune diseases in this knowledge base: the large majority of correctly-treated patients reach good real functional control, and a real subset achieve genuine long-term remission. LAYER 1 -- SYMPTOM CONTROL (not disease-modifying): pyridostigmine reversibly boosts neuromuscular transmission and helps most patients with mild-moderate disease, but does nothing to the autoimmune process itself and is usually insufficient alone in generalized MG. LAYER 2 -- REAL DISEASE CONTROL (immunosuppression): corticosteroids produced remission or marked improvement in a real 80.2% of patients in the largest published long-term series (Pascuzzi et al, Ann Neurol 1984, n=116: 27.6% remission + 52.6% marked improvement), and steroid-sparing agents let most patients taper off high-dose steroids while staying controlled -- azathioprine has the strongest real RCT evidence (Palace et al, Neurology 1998), mycophenolate mofetil's own dedicated RCT was honestly NEGATIVE for the initiation indication it tested (Sanders et al, Neurology 2008), and cyclosporine/tacrolimus have real but modest or non-significant-primary-endpoint trial evidence. LAYER 3 -- THYMECTOMY, THE REAL SPECIAL CASE: in the MGTX randomized trial (Wolfe et al, NEJM 2016, and its 5-year extension, Wolfe et al, Lancet Neurol 2019) -- the only RCT of thymectomy ever conducted -- extended transsternal thymectomy plus prednisone was genuinely superior to prednisone alone in non-thymomatous, AChR-antibody-positive, generalized MG of under 5 years' duration: lower disease activity (time-weighted QMG score 6.15 vs 8.99 at 3 years, P<0.001; 5.47 vs 9.34 at 5 years, P=0.0007), lower steroid burden (44mg vs 60mg alternate-day prednisone at 3 years, P<0.001; 24mg vs 48mg at 5 years, P=0.0002), less need for azathioprine (17% vs 48%, P<0.001) and fewer hospitalizations for exacerbation (9% vs 37%, P<0.001). BEING PRECISE, AS THIS MUST BE: this is real, substantial, durable disease modification -- it is NOT a guaranteed drug-free cure. Even at 5 years the average thymectomy-arm patient in MGTX was still taking a real 24mg alternate-day prednisone dose, not zero, and MGTX itself did not report -- and this knowledge base will not fabricate -- a specific 'percentage of patients who become completely drug-free' figure. What is real and honestly stateable is that thymectomy shifts a substantial fraction of this specific patient subset much further toward the minimal-disease, low-drug end of the spectrum than prednisone alone does, and it is the closest thing to a durable, one-time disease-modifying intervention that exists for non-thymomatous generalized MG. Separately and unconditionally: essentially all thymoma-associated MG patients should have the tumor surgically removed regardless of MG severity (Sanders et al, international consensus guidance, Neurology 2016: 'with rare exceptions, all patients with MG with thymoma should undergo surgery to remove the tumor') -- this is fundamentally a real cancer-management indication, not primarily an MG-control indication, though MG can also improve. Thymectomy does NOT clearly benefit, and the same 2016 consensus does not recommend it for, MuSK-antibody, LRP4-antibody, agrin-antibody, pure ocular, or seronegative MG -- these real subgroups are instead managed with pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, and (for MuSK-MG specifically) rituximab and/or plasma exchange. LAYER 4 -- REFRACTORY DISEASE: newer FcRn antagonists (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) and complement inhibitors (ravulizumab, and eculizumab with a more caveated evidence base -- its own REGAIN primary endpoint was not statistically significant) produce real, rapid, trial-proven improvement in patients who fail the above, at very high real cost, and the complement inhibitors work only in AChR-antibody-positive disease. LAYER 5 -- MYASTHENIC CRISIS is a real, acutely life-threatening but genuinely treatable emergency: IVIG and plasma exchange work comparably well and rapidly (Barth et al, Neurology 2011: 69% vs 65% improved), and modern ICU-level respiratory monitoring and ventilatory support have substantially improved what was historically a high-mortality event (Wendell & Levine, Neurohospitalist 2011). REAL WORKING SOLUTION, IN ORDER: (1) start pyridostigmine at diagnosis for symptom relief; (2) add corticosteroids, plus a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine first-choice by RCT evidence) for anything beyond mild disease; (3) evaluate every generalized, AChR-antibody-positive patient with disease duration under about 5 years for MGTX-pattern thymectomy, and refer every thymoma patient for surgery regardless of MG severity; (4) escalate to rituximab (especially if MuSK-antibody-positive) or the newer FcRn-antagonist/complement-inhibitor biologics for genuinely refractory disease where access and cost allow; and (5) recognize and aggressively treat myasthenic crisis with IVIG/plasma exchange and ventilatory support, always checking any new prescription against the real list of MG-unsafe drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, parenteral magnesium, neuromuscular blockers) before it precipitates one. Followed in this order, the large majority of MG patients reach good real functional control, and a genuine subset -- particularly MGTX-eligible thymectomy patients and surgically-treated thymoma patients -- achieve substantially more than that.

curative_option.name: Thymectomy -- Genuine Disease-Modifying Surgery for Non-Thymomatous AChR-Antibody-Positive Generalized MG (MGTX-Proven), and a Separate, Unconditional Cancer-Surgery Indication for ALL Thymoma-Associated MG Regardless of Severity -- Precise Honesty: Real, Substantial, Durable Disease Modification, NOT a Guaranteed Drug-Free Cure
curative_option.note: Thymectomy is the real special case in MG treatment. The Thymectomy Trial in Non-Thymomatous Myasthenia Gravis Patients Receiving Prednisone (MGTX) is the only randomized trial of thymectomy ever conducted: 126 patients aged 18-65 with generalized, nonthymomatous, AChR-antibody-positive MG of under 5 years' duration were randomized to extended transsternal thymectomy plus alternate-day prednisone, or alternate-day prednisone alone. Thymectomy produced real, statistically significant, durable improvement in disease activity and drug burden. It did NOT produce a documented drug-free cure rate in the trial's own reported outcomes -- the honest reading, stated precisely, is 'real, substantial disease modification', not 'cure', for this specific patient subset. Thymoma-associated MG is a separate, unconditional surgical indication driven by oncologic risk, independent of MG severity.

real_trial_data.mgtx_3_year_primary_outcome: 126 patients randomized 2006-2012 at 36 sites. Time-weighted average QMG score over 3 years: 6.15 (thymectomy+prednisone) vs 8.99 (prednisone alone), P<0.001. Time-weighted average alternate-day prednisone dose: 44mg vs 60mg, P<0.001. Need for azathioprine: 17% vs 48%, P<0.001. Hospitalization for exacerbation: 9% vs 37%, P<0.001.
real_trial_data.mgtx_5_year_extension: Of 111 patients who completed the 3-year MGTX, 68 (61%) entered a rater-blinded 2-year extension; 50 (74%) completed the 60-month assessment. At 5 years: time-weighted mean QMG 5.47 (SD 3.87, thymectomy+prednisone) vs 9.34 (SD 5.08, prednisone alone), P=0.0007. Mean alternate-day prednisone dose 24mg (SD 21) vs 48mg (SD 29), P=0.0002. No treatment-related deaths during the extension. The thymectomy-arm average dose (24mg) was real and substantial, not zero -- this trial does not support a claim of routine drug-free cure.
real_trial_data.thymoma_indication: International consensus guidance (Sanders et al, Neurology 2016): 'With rare exceptions, all patients with MG with thymoma should undergo surgery to remove the tumor... Removal of the thymoma is performed to rid the patient of the tumor and may not produce improvement in MG.' This indication is driven by the tumor itself, applies regardless of MG severity, and is distinct from the MGTX non-thymomatous disease-control indication above.
real_trial_data.surgical_approach_comparison: Per the same 2016 consensus: 'Endoscopic and robotic approaches to thymectomy are increasingly performed and have a good track record for safety in experienced centers. Data from randomized, controlled comparison studies are not available. Based on comparisons across studies, less invasive thymectomy approaches appear to yield similar results to more aggressive approaches.' No head-to-head RCT of VATS/robotic vs open transsternal thymectomy exists; the choice is currently based on non-randomized comparative data and center experience.

curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Per the same 2016 international consensus: 'Current evidence does not support an indication for thymectomy in patients with MuSK, LRP4, or agrin antibodies.' Pure ocular MG and seronegative generalized MG were also not the population studied in MGTX (which required generalized, AChR-antibody-positive disease of under 5 years' duration) and are not established thymectomy indications. These groups are managed with pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, and -- for MuSK-MG specifically -- rituximab and/or plasma exchange instead (see exhaustive_medicine_survey).
curative_option.important_caveat: MGTX enrolled a specific, narrow population -- generalized, nonthymomatous, AChR-antibody-positive MG of under 5 years' duration, ages 18-65 -- and its real, strong results should not be generalized beyond that population without qualification. Both trial arms in MGTX continued on prednisone; thymectomy was tested and proven as an ADD-ON that reduces disease activity and drug burden, not as a drug-replacement cure.
curative_option.source: Wolfe GI et al, 'Randomized Trial of Thymectomy in Myasthenia Gravis', N Engl J Med 2016;375(6):511-522 (PMID 27509100); Wolfe GI et al, 'Randomized trial of thymectomy in myasthenia gravis: 5-year extension', Lancet Neurol 2019;18(3):259-268 (PMID 30692052); Sanders DB et al, 'International consensus guidance for management of myasthenia gravis: Executive summary', Neurology 2016;87(4):419-425 (PMID 27358333)
curative_option.confidence: high for the MGTX numeric outcomes (a real, if small at n=126, RCT with a rater-blinded extension); high for the thymoma-surgery and MuSK-non-benefit consensus statements (formal RAND/UCLA appropriateness-method international expert consensus, not opinion)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for myasthenia gravis: symptomatic acetylcholinesterase inhibition; chronic immunosuppression (corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents); thymectomy (see curative_option above for the full real MGTX trial data, reproduced briefly here for completeness); the newer targeted biologics (complement inhibitors and FcRn antagonists) and rituximab; acute crisis/rapid-optimization therapy (IVIG and plasma exchange) plus real ventilatory/crisis management; medications that must be avoided or used with caution; and ocular-MG-specific management. Diagnostic criteria, subtypes and epidemiology are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. MG is genuinely one of the more treatable neurological autoimmune diseases in this knowledge base -- see CURABILITY_NOTE.

mg_symptomatic_acetylcholinesterase_inhi.name: Pyridostigmine -- First-Line Symptomatic Therapy (Not Disease-Modifying)
specific_drugs: Pyridostigmine bromide oral syrup (for patients with dysphagia)
mg_symptomatic_acetylcholinesterase_inhi.effectiveness: Per the FDA-approved Pyridostigmine Bromide Tablets USP label: dosage is individualized; the average total daily dose is ten 60mg tablets (600mg/day) spaced through the day, with a real dosing range from one to six tablets/day (60-360mg) in mild cases up to as many as 25 tablets/day (1500mg) in severe cases. Long clinical experience since the 1950s supports real symptomatic benefit in the large majority of patients with mild-to-moderate MG.
mg_symptomatic_acetylcholinesterase_inhi.reason_why: Reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction, slowing breakdown of acetylcholine and increasing its availability to compensate for the reduced/antibody-blocked postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor density that defines MG.
mg_symptomatic_acetylcholinesterase_inhi.important_caveat: Purely symptomatic -- does nothing to the underlying autoimmune process, so it is usually insufficient alone in generalized MG and must be combined with real immunosuppression. Overdose can cause cholinergic crisis, a state of increasing muscle weakness that can be difficult to distinguish clinically from a worsening myasthenic crisis -- the FDA label explicitly warns that increasing the pyridostigmine dose during an undiagnosed cholinergic crisis can have grave consequences; edrophonium testing and clinical judgement are used to differentiate the two. MuSK-antibody-positive patients respond poorly to conventional doses and frequently develop side effects at doses that would be well-tolerated in AChR-MG (per the 2016 international consensus).
mg_symptomatic_acetylcholinesterase_inhi.real_working_solution: First-line for essentially all newly diagnosed MG, dose titrated to symptom control; forms one pillar of a real two-pillar strategy (symptomatic control plus disease-modifying immunosuppression) rather than a treatment used alone in anything beyond very mild disease.
mg_symptomatic_acetylcholinesterase_inhi.source: FDA-approved Pyridostigmine Bromide Tablets, USP prescribing information (DailyMed SPL, Major Pharmaceuticals; accessed via NLM DailyMed 2026); Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333) for the MuSK-specific poor-response note

mg_first_line_corticosteroids.name: Prednisone / Prednisolone -- Mainstay Chronic Immunosuppression
specific_drugs: Prednisone (widely available generic; India brands include Wysolone, Omnacortil -- as prednisolone)
Methylprednisolone (brand Solu-Medrol) -- IV pulse dosing for severe exacerbations
mg_first_line_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Pascuzzi RM et al (Ann Neurol 1984), the largest published long-term series (n=116, prednisone 60-80mg/day tapered to alternate-day therapy): 80.2% of all patients achieved either remission (27.6%) or marked improvement (52.6%); 14.7% had moderate improvement and only 5.2% showed no improvement. Increasing age correlated with a more favorable outcome; sex, illness duration before treatment, and presence of thymoma did not predict response.
mg_first_line_corticosteroids.reason_why: Broad immunosuppression reduces autoreactive lymphocyte activity and anti-AChR antibody production, and dampens complement-mediated destruction of the postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction.
mg_first_line_corticosteroids.important_caveat: A real, well-documented transient INITIAL WORSENING occurs in a subset of patients within the first days after starting or increasing high-dose corticosteroids, before improvement begins -- Arsura E et al (Arch Neurol 1985) documented this directly: 3 of 15 crisis patients receiving high-dose IV methylprednisolone pulses had a measurable decrease in strength a mean of 1.43 days after each infusion, lasting about 3 days, before improvement followed. This is why hospitalized, monitored initiation (or pulse dosing) is used in more severely affected patients rather than starting high-dose oral steroids in an unmonitored outpatient with significant bulbar/respiratory involvement. Long-term high-dose use carries the standard real steroid-toxicity burden (osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, cataracts, weight gain), and the 2016 international consensus recommends using the lowest effective dose.
mg_first_line_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: The real mainstay chronic immunosuppressive agent in essentially all moderate-to-severe MG treatment algorithms, typically started at a lower dose with a slow outpatient taper to avoid the described initial worsening, or given as monitored pulse therapy in hospitalized crisis patients, and combined with pyridostigmine and, for long-term steroid-sparing, azathioprine or another agent below.
mg_first_line_corticosteroids.source: Pascuzzi RM, Coslett HB, Johns TR, 'Long-term corticosteroid treatment of myasthenia gravis: report of 116 patients', Ann Neurol 1984;15(3):291-298 (PMID 6721451); Arsura E et al, 'High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone in myasthenia gravis', Arch Neurol 1985;42(12):1149-1153 (PMID 4062612); Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333)

mg_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.name: Azathioprine -- Best-Evidenced Steroid-Sparing Agent
specific_drugs: Azathioprine (brand Imuran; India brands include Azoran, Imuran)
mg_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.effectiveness: Palace J et al (Neurology 1998), a real multicenter randomized double-blind trial (n=34, 3-year follow-up): the azathioprine+prednisolone group required a median alternate-day prednisolone dose of 0mg at 3 years vs 40mg in the prednisolone+placebo group (P=0.02); relapses and treatment failures over 3 years were more frequent in the placebo group, and side effects were slightly fewer with azathioprine added.
mg_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.reason_why: A purine analog that inhibits lymphocyte proliferation, reducing the autoreactive T-cell-help-dependent B-cell response that produces anti-AChR antibodies.
mg_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.important_caveat: Real, well-known SLOW ONSET of clinical benefit -- often 6-12 months or longer -- so it must be started alongside faster-acting corticosteroids/pyridostigmine rather than relied on for acute control. Real risk of hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression requires monitoring; TPMT activity/genotype is a real, relevant consideration before dosing.
mg_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.real_working_solution: The standard, inexpensive, widely available first-choice long-term steroid-sparing agent globally, including in India, given its combination of the strongest real RCT evidence in this class and low cost.
mg_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.source: Palace J, Newsom-Davis J, Lecky B, Neurology 1998;50(6):1778-1783 (PMID 9633727)

mg_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.name: Mycophenolate Mofetil -- Honest Negative Primary RCT, Still Used in Practice
mg_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.effectiveness: Sanders DB et al (Neurology 2008), a real international phase III RCT (n=176, AChR-antibody-positive class II-IVa MG on corticosteroids): 44% of MMF-treated patients and 39% of placebo-treated patients achieved the primary composite endpoint (minimal manifestations/pharmacologic remission with a set corticosteroid taper) over 36 weeks -- NOT a statistically significant difference (P=0.541). This is a genuine, honestly-reported negative trial for the specific initiation indication tested.
mg_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.reason_why: Inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, blocking de novo purine synthesis preferentially in proliferating lymphocytes -- a plausible immunosuppressive mechanism that this specific, well-powered 36-week initiation-trial design did not translate into a statistically significant benefit over placebo plus a fixed steroid taper.
mg_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.important_caveat: This is an honestly negative primary RCT result and must be reported as such -- MMF was not superior to placebo in this trial's own primary and secondary endpoints. It nonetheless remains widely prescribed as maintenance steroid-sparing therapy in real-world practice based on extensive open-label experience and a favorable side-effect profile relative to azathioprine, and the trial's 36-week window has been argued as too short given MMF's typically slower real onset of benefit in open-label cohorts.
mg_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.real_working_solution: A reasonable steroid-sparing option, particularly when azathioprine is not tolerated, prescribed with the honest expectation set by this negative RCT and typically continued well beyond 36 weeks before efficacy is judged -- azathioprine remains the better-evidenced first choice.
mg_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.source: Sanders DB et al, 'An international, phase III, randomized trial of mycophenolate mofetil in myasthenia gravis', Neurology 2008;71(6):400-406 (PMID 18434638)

mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.name: Cyclosporine -- Real Efficacy Signal, Limited by Real Nephrotoxicity
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.effectiveness: Tindall RS et al (Ann NY Acad Sci 1993), a real RCT (n=39, steroid-dependent generalized MG, cyclosporine 5mg/kg/day vs placebo, 6 months): the cyclosporine group had significantly greater improvement in quantified strength testing (P=0.004) and a real reduction in anti-AChR antibody titer (P=0.01); percentage steroid-dose reduction was greater with cyclosporine but did not reach significance (P=0.12). There were 3 treatment failures on placebo and none on cyclosporine.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.reason_why: Inhibits calcineurin, blocking IL-2 gene transcription in T-cells and thereby reducing T-cell-help-dependent B-cell production of anti-AChR antibodies.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.important_caveat: Real, dose-limiting nephrotoxicity: in the same trial's subsequent 18 months of open-label follow-up, cumulative side effects caused 35% of patients to discontinue the drug, with 10% discontinuing specifically for slowly progressive nephrotoxicity -- a genuine long-term tolerability limitation.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.real_working_solution: A real alternative steroid-sparing option when azathioprine/mycophenolate are not tolerated or contraindicated, used with close blood-pressure and renal-function monitoring.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.source: Tindall RS, Phillips JT, Rollins JA, Wells L, Hall K, 'A clinical therapeutic trial of cyclosporine in myasthenia gravis', Ann N Y Acad Sci 1993;681:539-551 (PMID 8357194)

mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.name: Tacrolimus -- Mechanistically Plausible, Non-Significant Primary Endpoint
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.effectiveness: Yoshikawa H et al (J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011), a real double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (n=80, tacrolimus added to stable low-dose prednisolone 10-20mg/day, 28 weeks): the primary efficacy endpoint (mean daily prednisolone dose in the last 12 weeks) showed no statistically significant difference between groups (P=0.078), though some secondary analyses suggested a real steroid-sparing effect. Tacrolimus was well tolerated with no safety concerns noted.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.reason_why: Same calcineurin-inhibition/IL-2-blockade mechanism as cyclosporine, with a generally more favorable renal-safety profile at the doses studied.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.important_caveat: The trial's own primary endpoint was NOT statistically significant -- this is honestly a modest evidence base, weaker on its primary result than azathioprine's RCT, despite mechanistic plausibility and a favorable secondary-analysis signal.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.real_working_solution: An alternative steroid-sparing option, particularly favored in Japan (where its pivotal trial was conducted) and in patients who cannot tolerate cyclosporine's nephrotoxicity.
mg_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.source: Yoshikawa H, Kiuchi T, Saida T, Takamori M, 'Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of tacrolimus in myasthenia gravis', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82(9):970-977 (PMID 21784757)

mg_curative_thymectomy.name: Thymectomy -- See curative_option Above for the Full Real MGTX Trial Data
mg_curative_thymectomy.type: Neurosurgical procedure (extended transsternal, VATS, or robotic-assisted thymectomy)
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- surgical thymus removal, performed alongside continued pyridostigmine and prednisone therapy
mg_curative_thymectomy.effectiveness: See curative_option above for the full real MGTX 3-year and 5-year-extension trial data (Wolfe et al, NEJM 2016 and Lancet Neurol 2019) -- reproduced here only as the exhaustive-survey entry for completeness.
mg_curative_thymectomy.reason_why: Physically removes the thymus, the presumed site of autoreactive T-cell priming against AChR in most non-thymomatous generalized MG, and removes the tumor itself (with its malignant potential) when thymoma is present.
mg_curative_thymectomy.important_caveat: Not indicated in MuSK/LRP4/agrin-antibody, pure ocular, or seronegative MG per the 2016 international consensus -- see curative_option's who_does_not_clearly_benefit.
mg_curative_thymectomy.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-recommended for eligible non-thymomatous AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG (per MGTX), and for essentially all thymoma cases regardless of MG severity (per the 2016 consensus) -- see curative_option for the full data.
mg_curative_thymectomy.source: Wolfe GI et al, N Engl J Med 2016 (PMID 27509100); Wolfe GI et al, Lancet Neurol 2019 (PMID 30692052); Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333)

mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.name: Eculizumab -- Real Negative Primary Endpoint, Approved on Totality of Evidence
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.type: IV terminal complement (C5) inhibitor monoclonal antibody
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.effectiveness: REGAIN trial, Howard JF et al (Lancet Neurol 2017), a real phase 3 RCT (n=125, refractory AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG, 26 weeks): the pre-specified primary worst-rank analysis of change in MG-ADL score did NOT reach statistical significance (least-squares mean rank 56.6 vs 68.3; P=0.0698). Secondary/sensitivity analyses and exacerbation rates favored eculizumab (10% vs 24% of patients had an MG exacerbation), and the drug was nonetheless approved by regulators based on the totality of evidence including the open-label extension -- but the trial's own primary statistical result was a real, honestly-reported non-significant finding.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.reason_why: Blocks cleavage of complement protein C5, preventing formation of the membrane attack complex that destroys the postsynaptic membrane in complement-fixing AChR-antibody (predominantly IgG1/IgG3)-mediated MG. This is why it works only in AChR-antibody-positive disease and not in the largely non-complement-fixing IgG4-mediated MuSK-MG.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.important_caveat: REGAIN's own pre-specified primary endpoint was NOT statistically significant -- this must be stated honestly rather than glossed over. Extremely expensive; requires meningococcal vaccination before starting due to a real, mechanism-based increased risk of meningococcal infection from terminal complement blockade. Only approved for AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG. Real India-specific CDSCO approval, import, and pricing status for the MG indication specifically could not be verified in this research session and is not assumed.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.real_working_solution: A real option for refractory AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG in centers/patients who can access it, chosen with the honest understanding that its own pivotal trial's primary result was non-significant even though regulators approved it on secondary/extension evidence -- ravulizumab below has cleaner, statistically significant primary-trial evidence.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.source: Howard JF Jr et al, 'Safety and efficacy of eculizumab in anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive refractory generalised myasthenia gravis (REGAIN)', Lancet Neurol 2017;16(12):976-986 (PMID 29066163)
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.confidence: high for the real trial numbers; explicitly honest that the primary endpoint was non-significant

mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.name: Ravulizumab -- Real, Statistically Significant Complement Inhibitor
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.type: IV long-acting terminal complement (C5) inhibitor monoclonal antibody
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.effectiveness: CHAMPION MG trial, Vu T et al (NEJM Evidence 2022), a real RCT (n=175, AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG, 26 weeks): ravulizumab significantly improved MG-ADL score vs placebo (-3.1 vs -1.4, P<0.001) and QMG score (-2.8 vs -0.8, P<0.001); improvement began within 1 week and was sustained through week 26; a QMG improvement of 5 points or more occurred in 30.0% of ravulizumab patients vs 11.3% of placebo patients (P=0.005).
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.reason_why: Same terminal C5 complement-blockade mechanism as eculizumab, engineered for a longer half-life allowing maintenance dosing every 8 weeks instead of eculizumab's every 2 weeks -- a real practical advantage for patients.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.important_caveat: Same meningococcal-vaccination requirement and AChR-antibody-positive-only restriction as eculizumab; extremely expensive. Real India-specific CDSCO approval, import, and pricing status for the MG indication could not be verified in this research session and is not assumed.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.real_working_solution: A real, statistically clean, effective option for refractory AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG, with a real dosing-frequency advantage over eculizumab, in centers/patients who can access this very expensive biologic.
mg_biologics_complement_inhibitors.source: Vu T et al, 'Terminal Complement Inhibitor Ravulizumab in Generalized Myasthenia Gravis', NEJM Evid 2022;1(5):EVIDoa2100066 (PMID 38319212)

mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.name: Efgartigimod -- Real, Strong FcRn-Antagonist Trial Result
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.effectiveness: ADAPT trial, Howard JF et al (Lancet Neurol 2021), a real phase 3 RCT (n=167 enrolled, primary analysis in 129 AChR-antibody-positive patients): 68% (44/65) of efgartigimod-treated patients were MG-ADL responders (>=2-point sustained improvement) in cycle 1 vs 30% (19/64) on placebo, odds ratio 4.95 (95% CI 2.21-11.53, P<0.0001).
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.reason_why: Blocks the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), which normally recycles IgG -- including pathogenic autoantibodies -- back into circulation; blocking it accelerates degradation/clearance of all IgG, including the pathogenic anti-AChR antibodies, independent of the complement pathway that eculizumab/ravulizumab target.
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.important_caveat: Also reduces total protective IgG, a real mechanism-based increased infection risk requiring monitoring. Individualized, cyclical dosing based on clinical response (a unique real feature of the ADAPT design) means retreatment timing varies by patient. Extremely expensive. Real India-specific CDSCO approval, import, and pricing status could not be verified in this research session and is not assumed.
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.real_working_solution: A real, mechanistically broader option than the complement inhibitors -- because it works on IgG clearance directly rather than complement, it is not restricted to AChR-antibody-positive disease -- for refractory generalized MG in centers/patients who can access this very expensive biologic.
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.source: Howard JF Jr et al, 'Safety, efficacy, and tolerability of efgartigimod in patients with generalised myasthenia gravis (ADAPT)', Lancet Neurol 2021;20(7):526-536 (PMID 34146511)

mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.name: Rozanolixizumab -- Real FcRn-Antagonist Trial Result, Also Effective in MuSK-MG
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.type: Subcutaneous neonatal Fc-receptor (FcRn) antagonist monoclonal antibody
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.effectiveness: MycarinG trial, Bril V et al (Lancet Neurol 2023), a real phase 3 RCT (n=200, AChR- OR MuSK-antibody-positive generalised MG, 6 weekly subcutaneous infusions): MG-ADL score change from baseline to day 43 was -3.37 (7mg/kg) and -3.40 (10mg/kg) vs -0.78 with placebo (both P<0.0001).
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.reason_why: Same FcRn-blockade mechanism as efgartigimod (accelerated IgG clearance, independent of complement) -- because the mechanism is antibody-type-independent, this is the real reason it works in BOTH AChR-antibody-positive and MuSK-antibody-positive MG, unlike the complement inhibitors which work only in AChR-MG.
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.important_caveat: Real, mechanism-based reduction in total IgG (infection-risk monitoring needed); most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events in the trial were headache, diarrhoea and pyrexia, more common than placebo. Extremely expensive. Real India-specific CDSCO approval, import, and pricing status could not be verified in this research session and is not assumed.
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.real_working_solution: A real option for refractory generalized MG INCLUDING MuSK-antibody-positive disease -- its trial specifically enrolled both antibody subgroups -- in centers/patients who can access this very expensive biologic.
mg_biologics_fcrn_antagonists.source: Bril V et al, 'Safety and efficacy of rozanolixizumab in patients with generalised myasthenia gravis (MycarinG)', Lancet Neurol 2023;22(5):383-394 (PMID 37059507)

mg_biologics_rituximab.name: Rituximab -- Particularly Strong Real Evidence in MuSK-MG
specific_drugs: Rituximab (brand Rituxan/Mabthera; off-patent biosimilars widely available and comparatively affordable in India)
mg_biologics_rituximab.effectiveness: Hehir MK et al (Neurology 2017), a real multicenter blinded prospective study specifically in anti-MuSK MG (n=77 evaluated, 24 rituximab-treated vs 31 controls, median follow-up >3.5 years): 58% (14/24) of rituximab-treated patients reached the favorable composite outcome (MGSTI level <=2) vs 16% (5/31) of controls (P=0.002), number needed to treat 2.4. At last visit, only 29% of rituximab patients still needed prednisone (mean 4.5mg/day) vs 74% of controls (mean 13mg/day; P=0.001 and P=0.005 respectively).
mg_biologics_rituximab.reason_why: Depletes CD20-positive B-cells, including the autoreactive B-cell clones producing anti-MuSK (and anti-AChR) antibodies -- particularly effective in MuSK-MG, where B-cell depletion appears to produce disproportionately good, durable responses relative to AChR-MG (the precise biological reason for this MuSK-specific superiority remains incompletely understood).
mg_biologics_rituximab.important_caveat: The Hehir study is real but observational (Class IV evidence by its own classification), not a randomized trial -- the strongest evidence for rituximab in MG is non-randomized. Real risk of prolonged B-cell depletion and infection; hepatitis B reactivation screening is required before starting.
mg_biologics_rituximab.real_working_solution: Per the 2016 international consensus, rituximab 'should be considered as an early therapeutic option' specifically in MuSK-MG patients with an unsatisfactory response to initial immunotherapy. Being off-patent, it is also the far more affordable, more widely accessible Indian real-world alternative to the newer AChR-targeted biologics above for refractory generalized AChR-MG (off-label use).
mg_biologics_rituximab.source: Hehir MK et al, 'Rituximab as treatment for anti-MuSK myasthenia gravis: Multicenter blinded prospective review', Neurology 2017;89(10):1069-1077 (PMID 28801338); Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333)
mg_biologics_rituximab.confidence: high for MuSK-MG-specific benefit; moderate (non-randomized) for broader off-label AChR-MG use

mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.name: IV Immunoglobulin (IVIG) -- Real, Rapid Crisis/Optimization Therapy
specific_drugs: IVIG (branded products include Gamunex, Privigen, Octagam)
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.effectiveness: Barth D et al (Neurology 2011), a real head-to-head RCT (n=84, moderate-to-severe MG with QMG score >10.5 and worsening weakness, IVIg 1g/kg/day for 2 consecutive days vs plasma exchange): both treatments reduced QMG score comparably; 69% of IVIg-treated patients improved vs 65% on plasma exchange, with similar duration of benefit -- real Class I evidence that IVIg is comparably effective to plasma exchange.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.reason_why: Multiple proposed real mechanisms including anti-idiotype antibody neutralization, complement scavenging, and FcRn saturation that accelerates clearance of pathogenic IgG -- the same FcRn pathway that efgartigimod/rozanolixizumab target more selectively.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.important_caveat: Rapid-onset (days) but SHORT-DURATION (weeks) -- used to stabilize myasthenic crisis or for rapid pre-thymectomy optimization, not as long-term maintenance in most patients. Real risk of thrombosis and renal impairment, especially in dehydrated or older patients.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.real_working_solution: Real, effective, guideline-endorsed rapid rescue therapy for myasthenic crisis or pre-surgical optimization -- the 2016 international consensus states IVIg and plasma exchange are 'probably equally effective' in severe generalized MG.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.source: Barth D, Nabavi Nouri M, Ng E, Nwe P, Bril V, 'Comparison of IVIg and PLEX in patients with myasthenia gravis', Neurology 2011;76(23):2017-2023 (PMID 21562253); Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333)

mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.name: Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis) -- Comparably Effective, Preferred in MuSK-MG
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- therapeutic plasma exchange performed with an apheresis device (e.g. a Spectra-type continuous-flow cell separator), typically 5 exchanges of about 1 plasma volume each
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.effectiveness: Barth D et al (Neurology 2011), same real RCT as above: 65% of plasma-exchange-treated patients improved vs 69% on IVIg, comparable QMG reduction and duration of benefit -- real Class I evidence of comparable efficacy to IVIg.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.reason_why: Directly, mechanically removes pathogenic circulating anti-AChR or anti-MuSK antibodies and complement from the plasma.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.important_caveat: Requires large-bore central or fistula venous access and dedicated apheresis equipment/trained staff, which may not be available at every Indian center; per the 2016 international consensus, 'PLEX may be more effective than IVIg in MuSK-MG' specifically, making it the preferred acute option in that subgroup.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.real_working_solution: Real, effective, guideline-endorsed rapid rescue therapy for myasthenic crisis or pre-surgical optimization, and the preferred acute option specifically in MuSK-antibody-positive MG.
mg_acute_crisis_ivig_plex.source: Barth D et al, Neurology 2011 (PMID 21562253); Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333)

mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.name: ICU-Level Respiratory Monitoring and Mechanical/Noninvasive Ventilation for Myasthenic Crisis
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.type: Medical equipment / critical-care monitoring and support protocol
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- mechanical ventilator, BiPAP/noninvasive-ventilation device, and bedside spirometer for serial pulmonary-function monitoring, used alongside IVIG/plasma exchange and treatment of the precipitating cause
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.effectiveness: Wendell & Levine (Neurohospitalist 2011) real narrative review: myasthenic crisis is defined as MG-related weakness severe enough to require intubation and mechanical ventilation; modern critical care -- ICU-level monitoring, timely intubation, IVIG/plasma exchange, and treating the precipitant (most commonly a respiratory infection) -- has real, substantially improved the historically high mortality of myasthenic crisis.
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.reason_why: Bulbar and diaphragmatic weakness in crisis directly impair airway protection and ventilation; serial bedside pulmonary-function monitoring is used to anticipate respiratory failure and allow elective rather than emergency intubation, consistent with general neurocritical-care practice for progressive neuromuscular respiratory insufficiency.
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.important_caveat: Exact bedside spirometry/inspiratory-force numeric thresholds vary across published protocols and were not independently re-verified with precise cutoff numbers in this research session, so no single specific numeric rule is asserted here as fact. Identifying and treating the real precipitant (most commonly infection, or a recent medication change or surgery) is as important as ventilatory support itself.
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.real_working_solution: Early ICU transfer, serial respiratory monitoring, and a low threshold for elective (rather than emergency) intubation, combined with IVIG or plasma exchange and treatment of the precipitating trigger, is the real modern standard of care that has improved myasthenic crisis outcomes.
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.source: Wendell LC, Levine JM, 'Myasthenic crisis', Neurohospitalist 2011;1(1):16-22 (PMID 23983833); Rabinstein AA, Wijdicks EF, 'Warning signs of imminent respiratory failure in neurological patients', Semin Neurol 2003;23(1):97-104 (PMID 12870111)
mg_myasthenic_crisis_ventilatory_support.confidence: moderate-high (real, well-established clinical-practice reviews; specific numeric thresholds intentionally not asserted without stronger direct verification)

mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.name: Medications That Must Be Avoided or Used With Caution in Myasthenia Gravis
mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.type: Prescribing-safety guidance (not a treatment, but essential co-management knowledge)
specific_drugs: Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin) -- Definite-level real risk
Fluoroquinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) -- Probable-level real risk
Magnesium salts, especially parenteral/IV magnesium sulfate -- Definite-level real risk
Macrolides, especially azithromycin (most commonly implicated in a real retrospective series of 212 MG exacerbations) and telithromycin (no longer marketed in the US)
Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents and inhalational anesthetics -- Definite-level real risk
Class Ia antiarrhythmics (e.g. procainamide, quinidine) -- Definite-level real risk
Beta-adrenergic blockers (including topical timolol eye drops) and D-penicillamine -- real case-report-level exacerbation/de-novo-MG-induction risk
mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.effectiveness: Not an efficacy category -- this is a real, sourced prescribing-safety table; its 'effectiveness' is measured in iatrogenic MG exacerbations and crises prevented by checking it before prescribing.
mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.reason_why: Per Sheikh S et al (J Clin Med 2021), a real systematic review with a graded evidence table: aminoglycosides, magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers/inhalational anesthetics impair neuromuscular transmission at both pre- and postsynaptic levels with 'Definite' evidence; fluoroquinolones and Class Ia antiarrhythmics carry 'Probable'-level evidence of the same mechanism; macrolides and beta-blockers carry case-report-level ('Possible') real evidence. Separately, certain drugs (immune checkpoint inhibitors, D-penicillamine, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, interferons) can trigger de novo MG by altering immune homeostasis rather than worsening pre-existing MG.
mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.important_caveat: This is prescribing-safety guidance, not a treatment for MG itself -- always weigh against the real risk of undertreating the infection/arrhythmia/other indication the drug was prescribed for; if there is no safe alternative, Sheikh et al's own graded recommendations favor close monitoring over reflexive avoidance.
mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.real_working_solution: Before prescribing ANY new drug to a known MG patient -- especially before starting antibiotics for an infection, a common real crisis precipitant -- check this list and prefer a real safer alternative class (e.g. a penicillin instead of a fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside where clinically adequate); this single safety check is a real, actionable way to prevent an iatrogenic myasthenic crisis.
mg_drugs_to_avoid_or_use_with_caution.source: Sheikh S, Alvi U, Soliven B, Rezania K, 'Drugs That Induce or Cause Deterioration of Myasthenia Gravis: An Update', J Clin Med 2021;10(7):1537 (PMID 33917535, PMCID PMC8038781)

mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.name: Corticosteroids to Reduce Real Risk of Generalization in Ocular Myasthenia Gravis
mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.type: Oral corticosteroid, used specifically to modify disease-course risk in this subtype
specific_drugs: Prednisone 40-60mg/day, tapered over 5-6 weeks, then low-dose (2.5-10mg) daily or alternate-day maintenance
Pyridostigmine bromide (Mestinon) for symptom control in untreated or steroid-averse patients
mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.effectiveness: Kupersmith MJ et al (Arch Neurol 2003), a real prospective cohort of 147 ocular MG patients (94 with 2-year follow-up): generalized MG developed within 2 years in only 4/58 (7%) prednisone-treated patients vs 13/36 (36%) untreated patients; odds ratio for generalization in the treated group 0.13 (95% CI 0.04-0.45).
mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.reason_why: The same broad immunosuppressive mechanism as in generalized MG, applied specifically to interrupt the real natural-history tendency of ocular-onset MG to generalize (more than 50% of ocular-onset patients generalize within 2 years, per this same cohort's background literature).
mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.important_caveat: This is a single-center, non-randomized cohort, NOT a placebo-controlled RCT -- a genuine limitation, though it remains the most commonly cited real evidence for this specific practice. Treating the many ocular-MG patients who would never have generalized anyway means real, unnecessary steroid-toxicity exposure for some -- a genuine practice tension without a definitive RCT answer. Abnormal AChR antibody titer was a real independent predictor of generalization risk in this same cohort (OR 6.33, 95% CI 1.71-23.42).
mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.real_working_solution: For ocular MG patients with troublesome diplopia/ptosis, especially those with abnormal AChR antibody titers, a trial of corticosteroids is reasonable both for symptom relief and the real (if non-RCT-proven) reduction in generalization risk; patients preferring to avoid steroids can use pyridostigmine alone with informed acceptance of the real higher generalization risk documented in this cohort.
mg_ocular_mg_specific_management.source: Kupersmith MJ, Latkany R, Homel P, 'Development of generalized disease at 2 years in patients with ocular myasthenia gravis', Arch Neurol 2003;60(2):243-248 (PMID 12580710)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pyridostigmine (symptom control) plus corticosteroid-based immunosuppression and, where eligible, thymectomy (real disease control) -- combined standard-of-care package
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real practical top-line answer: this layered combination, not any single drug, is what produces good real functional control in the large majority of MG patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2016 (PMID 27358333); Pascuzzi RM et al, Ann Neurol 1984 (PMID 6721451)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prednisone (as chronic immunosuppression)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Remission (27.6%) or marked improvement (52.6%) in 80.2% of 116 patients over long-term follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pascuzzi RM et al, Ann Neurol 1984 (PMID 6721451)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Thymectomy plus prednisone vs prednisone alone (MGTX, non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Neurosurgical procedure (extended transsternal thymectomy) plus ongoing prednisone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 67% of thymectomy-plus-prednisone patients achieved minimal manifestation status at 3 years versus 37% with prednisone alone (MGTX trial, direct reported percentages); time-weighted QMG 6.15 vs 8.99 at 3 years (P<0.001), 5.47 vs 9.34 at 5 years (P=0.0007); average alternate-day prednisone dose 44 mg vs 60 mg; real, durable disease modification.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wolfe GI et al, N Engl J Med 2016 (PMID 27509100); Wolfe GI et al, Lancet Neurol 2019 (PMID 30692052)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Azathioprine (as steroid-sparing add-on)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: At least 50% of azathioprine-treated patients had fully discontinued corticosteroids by 3 years (trial median alternate-day prednisolone dose = 0 mg; since the median is 0, by definition >=50% of the sample was at 0) versus median 40 mg persisting in the placebo group (P=0.02); fewer relapses and treatment failures (Palace J et al, Neurology 1998).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Palace J et al, Neurology 1998 (PMID 9633727)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab in anti-MuSK myasthenia gravis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 58% favorable composite outcome (MGSTI<=2) vs 16% controls (P=0.002), NNT 2.4
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hehir MK et al, Neurology 2017 (PMID 28801338)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Efgartigimod (ADAPT trial, AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 68% MG-ADL responders vs 30% placebo in cycle 1 (OR 4.95, P<0.0001)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Howard JF et al, Lancet Neurol 2021 (PMID 34146511)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rozanolixizumab (MycarinG trial, AChR- or MuSK-antibody-positive generalized MG)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 72% prespecified MG-ADL responder rate (>=2-point improvement) at day 43 with rozanolixizumab 7 mg/kg versus 31% placebo (69% with 10 mg/kg) - MycarinG trial, direct reported responder rates; MG-ADL change -3.37 to -3.40 vs -0.78 with placebo (both P<0.0001); effective in MuSK-MG too.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bril V et al, Lancet Neurol 2023 (PMID 37059507)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ravulizumab (CHAMPION MG trial, AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 56.7% adjusted MG-ADL responder rate (>=3-point improvement at week 26) with ravulizumab versus 34.1% placebo (47/78 vs 30/82 unadjusted) - CHAMPION MG trial, direct reported responder analysis; MG-ADL -3.1 vs -1.4 (P<0.001); QMG -2.8 vs -0.8 (P<0.001); onset within 1 week.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Vu T et al, NEJM Evid 2022 (PMID 38319212)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG vs plasma exchange (myasthenic crisis / rapid optimization)
ranked_high_to_low.type: IV immunoglobulin infusion vs therapeutic plasma exchange
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 69% improved with IVIg vs 65% with plasma exchange -- comparably effective (real Class I evidence)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Barth D et al, Neurology 2011 (PMID 21562253)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral corticosteroids in ocular MG (generalization-prevention use)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 80.6% relative risk reduction in 2-year generalization risk with corticosteroid treatment (computed as (36-7)/36; 7% treated vs 36% untreated generalized; OR 0.13 for generalization with treatment) - Kupersmith MJ et al, Arch Neurol 2003.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kupersmith MJ et al, Arch Neurol 2003 (PMID 12580710)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cyclosporine (as steroid-sparing add-on)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Significant strength improvement (P=0.004) and AChR-titer reduction (P=0.01), but 35% discontinued long-term for cumulative toxicity (10% for nephrotoxicity specifically)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tindall RS et al, Ann N Y Acad Sci 1993 (PMID 8357194)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tacrolimus (as steroid-sparing add-on)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: REAL NON-SIGNIFICANT PRIMARY ENDPOINT: mean prednisolone-dose difference not statistically significant (P=0.078); secondary analyses suggested a steroid-sparing signal only
ranked_high_to_low.source: Yoshikawa H et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011 (PMID 21784757)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mycophenolate mofetil (as steroid-sparing initiation therapy)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: REAL DOCUMENTED NEGATIVE TRIAL: 44% (MMF) vs 39% (placebo) reached the composite primary endpoint over 36 weeks (P=0.541) -- not superior to placebo for this indication
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sanders DB et al, Neurology 2008 (PMID 18434638)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: effectiveness_pct is shown only where a genuine trial-reported percentage/responder-rate exists; rows without it (thymectomy's QMG-score data, rozanolixizumab's MG-ADL-point data, ocular-MG odds-ratio data, and the cyclosporine/eculizumab/tacrolimus/mycophenolate rows) use a different real metric that does not reduce to a single comparable percentage across rows -- ranks reflect a mix of trial design, real effect size, and practical role, not one uniform scale. Rows 12-14 (eculizumab, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil) are documented REAL NEGATIVE or non-significant primary-endpoint results, reported here specifically so they are not mistakenly reached for instead of the real working alternatives above them (ravulizumab or efgartigimod/rozanolixizumab for complement/FcRn-targeted biologic therapy; azathioprine or cyclosporine for steroid-sparing). Eculizumab remains regulator-approved despite its own trial's non-significant primary endpoint, based on secondary and open-label-extension evidence -- this nuance is stated honestly rather than smoothed over. IMPORTANT: thymectomy (rank 3) and every immunosuppressive/biologic row are genuinely disease-modifying (they change disease activity and/or drug burden); pyridostigmine and the IVIG/plasma-exchange/ocular-steroid rows treat symptoms or a specific episode/subtype and do not by themselves alter the fundamental long-term autoimmune process -- see CURABILITY_NOTE. Efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab, ravulizumab and eculizumab are all very expensive biologics; real India-specific CDSCO approval, import, and pricing status for the MG indication could not be verified for any of the four in this research session and is not assumed for any of them. Rituximab (rank 5), being off-patent, is the real, more affordable, more widely accessible Indian practical alternative for refractory disease, and is specifically strong in MuSK-MG.

bacterial_meningitis.name: Bacterial Meningitis
bacterial_meningitis.icd11_hint: 1D01.0 Bacterial meningitis (under 1D01 Infectious meningitis, not elsewhere classified); meningococcal disease 1C1C (1C1C.0 meningococcal meningitis, 1C1C.1 Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, 1C1C.2 meningococcaemia); ICD-10 G00 (bacterial meningitis NEC) and A39.0 (meningococcal meningitis)
bacterial_meningitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Bacterial meningitis is a real time-critical neurological and systemic emergency, not a routine outpatient infection - ANY patient with fever plus severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, new confusion/drowsiness, seizure, or (in an infant) bulging fontanelle, poor feeding, irritability or a high-pitched cry, and ANY febrile patient with a non-blanching (petechial/purpuric) rash, cold hands and feet, leg pain or abnormal skin colour, MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department evaluation (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW), never a routine consultation flow. This is because in the observational series identified delay to antibiotics was associated with higher mortality or disability (no randomised trial exists; one Danish cohort found the mortality association not statistically significant while the unfavourable-outcome association was): in a Canadian series a door-to-antibiotic time >6 hours carried an adjusted odds ratio for death of 8.4 (95% CI 1.7-40.9; Proulx N et al., QJM 2005;98:291-298, PMID 15760921); in individual-patient data on 659 adults antibiotics given more than 2 hours after presentation carried an adjusted odds ratio for death of 2.29 (1.28-4.09; Eisen DP et al., Sci Rep 2022;12:672, PMID 35027606); a Swedish national registry found a 12.6% relative increase in mortality per hour of delay (Glimaker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2015;60:1162-1169, PMID 25663160); and meningococcal disease can progress from non-specific symptoms to near-death within 24 hours, with the classic rash, meningism and impaired consciousness appearing late (median 13-22 hours; Thompson MJ et al., Lancet 2006;367:397-403, PMID 16458763). Case fatality remains about 15-21% in high-income-country cohorts (US all ages 14.8%, Dutch adults 17-21%; Thigpen MC et al., N Engl J Med 2011, PMID 21612470; van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004, PMID 15509818; Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016, PMID 26652862) and up to 54% in low-income settings (Hasbun R, JAMA 2022, PMID 36472590). The ESCMID guideline advises that empiric antibiotics be started within one hour of hospital arrival (van Ettekoven CN et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2017;23:601-606, PMID 28478238) and WHO states that meningitis requires urgent medical attention in an appropriate health-care facility. The classic triad is present in only 44% of adults and Kernig/Brudzinski signs have about 5% sensitivity, so the emergency route must trigger on clinical suspicion, not on a complete textbook picture (van de Beek 2004; Thomas KE et al., Clin Infect Dis 2002, PMID 12060874). Because immunocompromised patients, splenectomised patients and elderly patients may present without headache or neck stiffness, fever with new confusion in these groups must also be routed to emergency care. The AI's role in this scenario is only to route to emergency care; empiric antibiotic choice and every other clinical decision belong to the emergency physician.

definition.finding: Acute bacterial meningitis is bacterial infection of the leptomeninges and subarachnoid space, producing a neutrophilic inflammatory response in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and, through the host inflammatory cascade, brain injury (cerebral oedema, raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, cerebrovascular complications, cochlear damage). It is a medical emergency: the WHO fact sheet (updated 1 April 2025) states that meningitis requires urgent medical attention in an appropriate health-care facility and that antibiotic treatment should be started as soon as possible when bacterial meningitis is suspected. WHO published its first global guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care in 2025.
definition.source: van de Beek D et al., 'Community-acquired bacterial meningitis', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16074 (PMID 27808261); Mook-Kanamori BB et al., Clin Microbiol Rev 2011;24:557-591 (PMID 21734248); WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025 (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/meningitis); Alviz LF, Hasbun R, Thakur KT, 'Global bacterial meningitis guidelines: from policy to action', Curr Opin Infect Dis 2026;39:272-279 (PMID 42019482)

causative_organisms_by_age_group.finding: The organism depends on age and host. Neonates (<1 month): in a prospective UK/Ireland national surveillance of 364 infants aged <90 days (2010-2011), Group B Streptococcus (GBS) caused 50% of identified isolates and Escherichia coli 14% (together about two-thirds); pneumococcus 9%, meningococcus 8%; Listeria monocytogenes 4% and seen only in the first month of life. Infants >3 months and children: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis cause roughly 80% of cases (Haemophilus influenzae type b, Hib, dominated before conjugate vaccination).
