Adults: S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis cause 75-90% of cases; in a Dutch nationwide adult cohort (1,412 episodes, 2006-2014) S. pneumoniae caused 72%; a US population surveillance of 2003-2007 (all ages) found S. pneumoniae 58.0%, GBS 18.1%, N. meningitidis 13.9%, H. influenzae 6.7%, L. monocytogenes 3.4%. Older adults and immunocompromised patients: atypical organisms rise - in Dutch patients aged >=80 years, L. monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli together caused 33% of episodes versus 18% in younger adults; in adults on immunosuppressive medication L. monocytogenes caused 40% and S. pneumoniae 41% of episodes; Listeria meningitis in the Netherlands (1985-2014) peaked in neonates and in older adults (peak at age 87 years). A global meta-analysis (56 studies) confirms S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis predominate in all regions but the mix varies widely by age and region (E. coli and S. pneumoniae most common in African neonates).
causative_organisms_by_age_group.source: Okike IO et al., Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e150-e157 (PMID 24997051); Schuchat A et al., N Engl J Med 1997;337:970-976 (PMID 9395430); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819; read via PMC2901656); Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347 (PMID 26652862); Thigpen MC et al., N Engl J Med 2011;364:2016-2025 (PMID 21612470); van Soest TM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2022;70:2060-2069 (PMID 35352336); van Veen KEB et al., J Neuroimmune Pharmacol 2017;12:213-218 (PMID 27613024); Koopmans MM et al., J Infect 2017;75:12-19 (PMID 28419853); Oordt-Speets AM et al., PLoS One 2018;13:e0198772 (PMID 29889859)

post_vaccination_epidemiologic_shift.finding: Conjugate vaccines changed the organism mix and the age profile. US active surveillance (22 counties) found that between 1986 and 1995, five years after Hib conjugate vaccines were licensed for infants, estimated bacterial meningitis cases fell 55% (12,920 to 5,755), H. influenzae meningitis cases fell 94%, and the median age of patients rose from 15 months to 25 years, so bacterial meningitis became predominantly a disease of adults. In 1995 the rates per 100,000 were S. pneumoniae 1.1, N. meningitidis 0.6, GBS 0.3, L. monocytogenes 0.2, H. influenzae 0.2. From 1998-1999 to 2006-2007 (after pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and GBS screening in pregnancy) US incidence fell a further 31% (2.00 to 1.38 per 100,000) and median age rose from 30.3 to 41.9 years, but case fatality did not change significantly (15.7% to 14.3%). A Lancet review concluded H. influenzae meningitis has been near-eliminated where Hib vaccine is used, all-age pneumococcal meningitis fell only about 25% despite >90% reductions in vaccine-serotype disease, and serogroup C meningococcal meningitis was near-eliminated in several high-income countries. Globally, GBD 2016 found Hib went from the most common cause of incident meningitis in 1990 (780,070 cases) to the least common in 2016 (397,297 cases; -49.1%), and GBD 2019 found deaths in children <5 years fell 76.5% for H. influenzae and 72.3% for N. meningitidis between 1990 and 2019.
post_vaccination_epidemiologic_shift.source: Schuchat A et al., N Engl J Med 1997;337:970-976 (PMID 9395430); Thigpen MC et al., N Engl J Med 2011;364:2016-2025 (PMID 21612470); McIntyre PB et al., Lancet 2012;380:1703-1711 (PMID 23141619); GBD 2016 Meningitis Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:1061-1082 (PMID 30507391); GBD 2019 Meningitis Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2023;22:685-711 (PMID 37479374)

route_of_cns_invasion.finding: Most community-acquired cases follow mucosal colonisation of the nasopharynx (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae) then invasion of the bloodstream, survival in the bloodstream, and crossing of the blood-brain barrier or blood-CSF barrier into the subarachnoid space, where the bacteria multiply freely. For pneumococcus the adhesin CbpA binds the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor to translocate across the nasopharyngeal epithelium and later binds the laminin receptor at the cerebral endothelium; N. meningitidis and H. influenzae use a CbpA-homologue to bind the same receptor. Meningococcal type IV pili recruit the Par3/Par6/PKCzeta polarity complex in brain endothelial cells, which opens intercellular junctions and lets bacteria cross. Pathogens can cross the barrier transcellularly, paracellularly, or inside infected phagocytes ('Trojan horse'). GBS and E. coli K1 in neonates arise by vertical/hematogenous spread from the mother or gut colonisation. Non-haematogenous routes are contiguous spread from otitis/sinusitis/mastoiditis and direct entry via CSF leak, basilar skull fracture or a cochlear implant (see risk_factors_and_epidemiology).
route_of_cns_invasion.source: Doran KS et al., 'Host-pathogen interactions in bacterial meningitis', Acta Neuropathol 2016;131:185-209 (PMID 26744349; full text via PMC4713723); Coureuil M et al., Science 2009;325:83-87 (PMID 19520910); Kim KS, Nat Rev Microbiol 2008;6:625-634 (PMID 18604221); Mook-Kanamori BB et al., Clin Microbiol Rev 2011;24:557-591 (PMID 21734248)

inflammatory_cascade_and_raised_icp.finding: Once bacteria are in the subarachnoid space, bacterial products (e.g. pneumococcal cell wall, toxins) activate host innate immune receptors and resident microglia, releasing cytokines, chemokines, proteolytic enzymes and oxidants; this raises blood-brain barrier permeability, recruits neutrophils (CSF pleocytosis) and produces the tissue damage that is a main driver of death and sequelae, in addition to direct bacterial toxicity. The consequences are cerebral oedema, cerebral ischaemia, hydrocephalus, cerebrovascular involvement and seizures. A 2024 systematic review states that intracranial pressure (ICP) is elevated in up to 93% of patients with acute bacterial meningitis, multifactorially: cerebral oedema of vasogenic, cytotoxic or interstitial type, loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation with vasodilation, venous thrombophlebitis with venous congestion, and hydrocephalus from impaired CSF circulation/reabsorption; brain herniation is the most feared consequence and raised ICP and its consequences are among the primary causes of death.
inflammatory_cascade_and_raised_icp.source: Koedel U, Scheld WM, Pfister HW, Lancet Infect Dis 2002;2:721-736 (PMID 12467688); Scheld WM et al., J Infect Dis 2002;186 Suppl 2:S225-S233 (PMID 12424702); Doran KS et al., Acta Neuropathol 2016;131:185-209 (PMID 26744349); El-Hajj VG et al., 'Detection and management of elevated intracranial pressure in the treatment of acute community-acquired bacterial meningitis: a systematic review', Neurocrit Care 2024;41:228-243 (PMID 38356077)
inflammatory_cascade_and_raised_icp.confidence: high - the 'up to 93%' figure is an upper bound cited in that review from small ICP-monitoring series in severely ill patients, not a prevalence in all patients with meningitis

classic_triad_sensitivity.finding: The classic triad (fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status) is often incomplete. In the Dutch nationwide cohort of 696 culture-proven adult episodes, the full triad was present in only 44%, but 95% had at least two of the four symptoms headache, fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status; on admission 14% were comatose and 33% had focal neurological abnormalities. In a later Dutch cohort of patients aged >=80 years the triad was present in 43% (60/139). A systematic review of adult examination findings found that absence of all three of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status effectively rules out meningitis in the populations studied (sensitivity 99-100% for the presence of at least one of the three), but individual history items are poor (pooled sensitivity for headache 50%, for nausea/vomiting 30%). Practical consequence: absence of the triad does not exclude bacterial meningitis; in a Canadian series, absence of the triad was an independent predictor of >6 h delay to antibiotics (OR 4.9).
classic_triad_sensitivity.source: van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818); van Soest TM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2022;70:2060-2069 (PMID 35352336); Attia J et al., JAMA 1999;282:175-181 (PMID 10411200); Proulx N et al., QJM 2005;98:291-298 (PMID 15760921)

kernig_brudzinski_nuchal_rigidity.finding: Classic meningeal signs are insensitive. In 297 prospectively evaluated adults with suspected meningitis (Thomas et al., 2002), Kernig's sign had sensitivity 5% (LR+ 0.97), Brudzinski's sign sensitivity 5% (LR+ 0.97) and nuchal rigidity sensitivity 30% (LR+ 0.94), none discriminating meningitis (>=6 CSF WBC/microL) from no meningitis; nuchal rigidity had sensitivity/NPV 100% only in the 4 patients with >=1000 CSF WBC/microL. In a US emergency-department cohort of 230 neurologically intact adults undergoing LP, sensitivity for CSF pleocytosis was 2% for Kernig, 2% for Brudzinski, 13% for nuchal rigidity and 21% for jolt accentuation of headache (specificity 97%, 98%, 80% and 82%). A rural teaching-hospital study in India (Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences, Sevagram, Maharashtra; 190 patients aged >=12 years with acute encephalitis syndrome, meningitis in 52% by CSF WBC >5/microL) found no physical sign discriminated meningitis: nuchal rigidity LR+ 1.33 / LR- 0.86, jolt accentuation LR+ 5.52 (95% CI 0.67-44.9), Kernig LR+ 1.84, Brudzinski LR+ 1.69 (none of the LR+ 95% confidence intervals excluded 1: nuchal rigidity 0.89-1.98, jolt accentuation 0.67-44.9, Kernig 0.77-4.35, Brudzinski 0.65-4.37). An older review reported jolt accentuation (in patients with fever and headache) sensitivity 100% and specificity 54%, but that small-study estimate was not reproduced in the two later cohorts. In children, meningeal signs on examination raise likelihood (LR+ 4.5; neck stiffness 4.0; Kernig 3.5; Brudzinski 2.5) and their absence lowers it modestly (LR- 0.41), but no single feature is diagnostic. Practical takeaway: neither presence nor absence of meningeal signs should decide whether to do an LP or give antibiotics.
kernig_brudzinski_nuchal_rigidity.source: Thomas KE et al., Clin Infect Dis 2002;35:46-52 (PMID 12060874); Nakao JH et al., Am J Emerg Med 2014;32:24-28 (PMID 24139448); Waghdhare S et al., Clin Neurol Neurosurg 2010;112:752-757 (PMID 20615607); Attia J et al., JAMA 1999;282:175-181 (PMID 10411200); Curtis S et al., Pediatrics 2010;126:952-960 (PMID 20974781)

csf_pattern_bacterial.finding: CSF analysis is the principal diagnostic test. Typical bacterial pattern (IDSA 2004): WBC usually 1000-5000 cells/mm3 with neutrophil predominance (typically 80-95%), glucose <40 mg/dL in about 50-60% of patients, CSF-to-serum glucose ratio <=0.4 (80% sensitive, 98% specific) and elevated protein in virtually all patients. In a derivation study of 422 patients with acute bacterial or viral meningitis, each of CSF glucose <1.9 mmol/L (34 mg/dL), CSF:blood glucose ratio <0.23, CSF protein >2.2 g/L, CSF leukocytes >2000/mm3 or CSF polymorphonuclear leukocytes >1180/mm3 predicted bacterial (versus viral) meningitis with >=99% certainty, but none could rule bacterial meningitis out. A systematic review of adult data found CSF:blood glucose ratio <=0.4 (LR 18, 95% CI 12-27), CSF WBC >=500/microL (LR 15, 10-22) and CSF lactate >=3.5 mmol/L (31.5 mg/dL; LR 21, 14-32) accurately diagnosed bacterial meningitis. Important exceptions: a low CSF WBC (<1000/mm3) occurs in a substantial minority (46% of patients on immunosuppressive medication) and is itself a marker of poor prognosis in adults; partial antibiotic pre-treatment lowers culture and lactate yield (see microbiology entry).
csf_pattern_bacterial.source: Tunkel AR et al., 'Practice guidelines for the management of bacterial meningitis', Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903; values read from full text on academic.oup.com); Spanos A, Harrell FE, Durack DT, JAMA 1989;262:2700-2707 (PMID 2810603); Straus SE, Thorpe KE, Holroyd-Leduc J, JAMA 2006;296:2012-2022 (PMID 17062865); Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590); van Veen KEB et al., J Neuroimmune Pharmacol 2017;12:213-218 (PMID 27613024); van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818)
csf_pattern_bacterial.confidence: high for Spanos/Straus/Hasbun values (checked in PubMed abstracts); moderate for the IDSA numeric ranges (read from the guideline full text via a retrieval summariser, not re-checked against the PDF)

csf_pattern_viral_aseptic.finding: Viral (aseptic) meningitis: mononuclear (lymphocytic) pleocytosis, typically about 50-1000 cells x10^6/L (may be neutrophilic early in the course), protein about 0.4-0.8 g/L, and CSF:serum glucose ratio >=0.5 (normal), versus polymorphonuclear predominance and CSF:serum glucose <0.5 in the bacterial column of the same BMJ review table. Enteroviruses are by far the most common identified cause at all ages; in adults with confirmed aetiology enterovirus accounted for 46%, HSV-2 31%, varicella zoster virus 11% and HSV-1 4%. Most cases are self-limiting with a good prognosis, but the review states bacterial and viral meningitis cannot reliably be differentiated clinically, so all suspected cases need hospital assessment; PCR is 3- to 1000-fold more sensitive than viral culture. HSV-2 meningitis can recur. In children with CSF pleocytosis, the validated Bacterial Meningitis Score (below) is used to identify those at very low risk of bacterial meningitis.
csf_pattern_viral_aseptic.source: Logan SA, MacMahon E, 'Viral meningitis', BMJ 2008;336:36-40 (PMID 18174598; read via PMC2174764)
csf_pattern_viral_aseptic.confidence: moderate - numeric ranges taken from the BMJ review table as retrieved through a summariser, not from the primary studies

csf_pattern_tuberculous.finding: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is subacute rather than hyperacute; length of history was one of five independent predictors (with age, blood WBC, CSF WBC and CSF neutrophil proportion) in a Vietnamese study of 251 adults (143 TBM, 108 bacterial meningitis). The characteristic CSF is lymphocytic pleocytosis of about 10-500 cells/microL with >50% lymphocytes, protein >1 g/L (frequently 1-3 g/L) and glucose <2.2 mmol/L or CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.5 (40-50% in the review table); these ranges are commonly used in TBM research definitions; the profile is non-specific, overlaps with viral and fungal meningitis, and can be neutrophil-predominant early or mild in people living with HIV. Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF had sensitivity 70% (16/23) against the uniform case definition in HIV-infected Ugandan adults (Xpert 43%, culture 43%), so a negative test does not exclude TBM. TBM outcomes: >100,000 new cases/year and mortality approaching 50% with HIV (Nat Rev Neurol review); pooled adult risk of death 24.7% and neurological sequelae in 50.9% of survivors, with death in 64.8% of stage III and 53.4% of HIV-positive patients. See the separate 'tuberculosis' entry (symptoms.classification_pulmonary_vs_extrapulmonary.extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.tb_meningitis) for the TB-specific work-up and treatment.
csf_pattern_tuberculous.source: Thwaites GE et al., Lancet 2002;360:1287-1292 (PMID 12414204); Marais S et al., 'Tuberculous meningitis: a uniform case definition for use in clinical research', Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:803-812 (PMID 20822958); Leiva-Ordonez JE, Quintero B, Diagnostics (Basel) 2026;16 (PMID 41750700; PMC12939813); Bahr NC et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18:68-75 (PMID 28919338); Wilkinson RJ et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2017;13:581-598 (PMID 28884751); Wang MG et al., BMC Pulm Med 2019;19:200 (PMID 31694599; PMC6833188)
csf_pattern_tuberculous.confidence: high for Thwaites/Bahr/Wilkinson/Wang (checked in abstracts); moderate for the CSF numeric cut-offs (taken from a 2026 review table summarising the Marais case definition; the Marais paper itself was not accessible in full text)

csf_lactate.finding: CSF lactate helps separate bacterial from aseptic meningitis. A meta-analysis of 33 studies found pooled sensitivity 0.93 (95% CI 0.89-0.96), specificity 0.96 (0.93-0.98), LR+ 22.9 and LR- 0.07, with an optimal cut-off around 35 mg/dL; however, prior antibiotic treatment lowered sensitivity to 0.49 (0.23-0.75). Takeaway: a low CSF lactate argues against bacterial meningitis only if the patient has not already received antibiotics.
csf_lactate.source: Sakushima K et al., J Infect 2011;62:255-262 (PMID 21382412)

csf_and_blood_culture_gram_stain.finding: Gram stain sensitivity ranges from about 50% to 90% (69-93% in pneumococcal and 50-65% in Hib meningitis in children); CSF culture was positive in about 85% in the absence of prior antibiotic treatment, and yield falls after antibiotics. In a paediatric series, after >=50 mg/kg of a third-generation cephalosporin, meningococcal CSF cultures were sterile in all patients by 2 hours (3 of 9 within 1 hour, the earliest at 15 minutes), the first sterile pneumococcal CSF culture occurred at 4.3 hours (5 of 7 negative at 4-10 hours), and GBS cultures remained positive through the first 8 hours; blood cultures were positive in 74% without pre-treatment and in 57-68% of cases whose CSF cultures were negative. IDSA 2004 states that blood samples must be obtained for culture before or concurrent with LP.
csf_and_blood_culture_gram_stain.source: Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819; PMC2901656); Kanegaye JT, Soliemanzadeh P, Bradley JS, Pediatrics 2001;108:1169-1174 (PMID 11694698); Tunkel AR et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903)
csf_and_blood_culture_gram_stain.confidence: high for Hasbun and Kanegaye (abstracts); moderate for percentages read from the Brouwer review full text via summariser

pcr_multiplex_and_latex_agglutination.finding: Multiplex PCR (BioFire FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel, 14 targets, about 1 hour): in a multicentre evaluation of 1,560 prospectively collected CSF specimens sensitivity/positive percentage agreement was 100% for 9 of 14 analytes (enterovirus 95.7%, HHV-6 85.7%; L. monocytogenes and N. meningitidis were not observed in that study, GBS had 1 false positive and 1 false negative). A meta-analysis of 13 studies (3,764 patients; 8 pooled) found summary sensitivity 90% (95% CI 86-93%) and specificity 97% (94-99%); false-positive detections were 11.4% before and 4% after adjudication, highest for S. pneumoniae then S. agalactiae, and false negatives were mostly HSV-1/2, enterovirus and Cryptococcus. Takeaway: a positive S. pneumoniae PCR should be interpreted alongside CSF cell counts/culture, and a negative panel does not exclude HSV or bacterial meningitis. Latex agglutination has variable sensitivity (reported ranges 78-100% for Hib, 59-100% pneumococcal, 22-93% meningococcal) and cannot rule out disease; PCR sensitivities of 88% (H. influenzae), 92% (S. pneumoniae) and 94% (N. meningitidis) were reported in one study.
pcr_multiplex_and_latex_agglutination.source: Leber AL et al., J Clin Microbiol 2016;54:2251-2261 (PMID 27335149); Tansarli GS, Chapin KC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2020;26:281-290 (PMID 31760115); Brouwer MC et al., Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819; latex/PCR ranges read via PMC2901656)
pcr_multiplex_and_latex_agglutination.confidence: high for multiplex-panel figures (abstracts); moderate for latex/PCR ranges (summariser reading of the Brouwer review)

ct_before_lp_indications.finding: Neuroimaging before LP is intended to detect a mass lesion or brain shift that could precipitate herniation. In a prospective study of 301 adults with suspected meningitis (235 had CT before LP), CT was abnormal in 24% and showed mass effect in 5%; features associated with abnormal CT were age >=60 years, immunocompromise, history of CNS disease, seizure within the preceding week, and abnormal level of consciousness, inability to answer two consecutive questions or follow two consecutive commands, gaze palsy, abnormal visual fields, facial palsy, arm drift, leg drift and abnormal language. None of these were present in 96 patients (41%), of whom 93 had a normal CT (negative predictive value 97%) and the 3 misclassified patients had no herniation after LP. IDSA 2004 adopted these features as the criteria for CT first; a 2022 JAMA review adds papilledema. A Houston cohort of 202 adults found IDSA-based criteria missed 0% of major intracranial findings, versus 20.8% (UK), 41.7% (ESCMID) and 70.8% (Swedish) - but 4 patients (1.9%) had herniation and all 4 met every guideline's criteria. Conversely, Swedish registry data associate imaging-first pathways with delay and worse outcome: immediate LP without prior CT was associated with antibiotics 1.6 hours earlier and a favourable outcome (2015 study), and in 815 adults prompt LP versus imaging-preceded LP had adjusted OR 0.38 (95% CI 0.18-0.77) for death and 2.11 (1.47-3.00) for favourable outcome, with benefit irrespective of mental status or immunosuppression; adherence to the IDSA imaging recommendation gave aOR 1.09 (0.61-1.95) for mortality and 0.59 (0.42-0.82) for favourable outcome. These are observational registry findings (confounding by indication is possible), and international guidelines disagree.
ct_before_lp_indications.source: Hasbun R et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1727-1733 (PMID 11742046); Tunkel AR et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903); Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590); Park N, Nigo M, Hasbun R, Clin Neuroradiol 2022;32:857-862 (PMID 35181803); Glimaker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2015;60:1162-1169 (PMID 25663160); Glimaker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2018;66:321-328 (PMID 29020334)

lp_contraindications.finding: Contraindications to immediate LP are: a space-occupying intracranial lesion or brain shift (herniation risk), coagulation disorder, local skin infection at the puncture site, and the need for haemodynamic stabilisation before further procedures. Historical paediatric evidence supports caution: in 445 children with bacterial meningitis, cerebral herniation occurred in 4.3% (19 children), 12 of 19 episodes occurred in the first 12 hours after LP (OR 32.6, 95% CI 8.5-117.3 for the temporal association) and CT was normal in 5 of 14 episodes scanned around the time of herniation, so a normal CT does not guarantee LP is safe. If LP must be deferred, antibiotics should not be deferred with it (see clinical_takeaway).
lp_contraindications.source: van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22 Suppl 3:S37-S62 (PMID 27062097; contraindication list read from a search-result excerpt of the guideline text because the full text was not retrievable); Rennick G, Shann F, de Campo J, BMJ 1993;306:953-955 (PMID 8490469)
lp_contraindications.confidence: high for Rennick (abstract); moderate for the ESCMID contraindication list (excerpt only)

clinical_prediction_rules.finding: Bacterial Meningitis Score (BMS, children 29 days to 19 years with CSF pleocytosis >=10 WBC/microL and no antibiotics before LP): classifies a child as very low risk if ALL of the following are absent - positive CSF Gram stain, CSF absolute neutrophil count >=1000/microL, CSF protein >=80 mg/dL, peripheral blood absolute neutrophil count >=10,000/microL, and seizure before or at presentation. In the validation cohort of 3,295 children with pleocytosis (121 with bacterial meningitis, 3.7%), sensitivity was 98.3% (95% CI 94.2-99.8%) and negative predictive value 99.9% (99.6-100%); the only 2 missed cases were both <2 months old. It was validated retrospectively and only in children aged 29 days to 19 years without antibiotics before LP, so it does not cover neonates, pre-treated children or adults, and it cannot replace clinical judgement when the child is unwell. Adult prognostic (not diagnostic) staging: Aronin et al. found hypotension, altered mental status and seizures independently predicted adverse outcome (low/intermediate/high risk stages with 9%, 33%, 56% adverse outcome) and that progression to high-risk stage before antibiotics was associated with adverse outcome. TBM versus bacterial meningitis in adults: the Thwaites rule (age, length of history, blood WBC, CSF WBC, CSF neutrophil proportion) was 86% sensitive and 79% specific when tested prospectively (Vietnam; 251-adult derivation set).
clinical_prediction_rules.source: Nigrovic LE et al., JAMA 2007;297:52-60 (PMID 17200475); Aronin SI, Peduzzi P, Quagliarello VJ, Ann Intern Med 1998;129:862-869 (PMID 9867727); Thwaites GE et al., Lancet 2002;360:1287-1292 (PMID 12414204)

door_to_antibiotic_time_and_outcome.finding: Observational evidence consistently links delayed antibiotics to worse outcome in bacterial meningitis, although no randomised trial exists and sicker patients may be treated sooner, so the estimates are associations. (1) Canadian retrospective series of 123 adult episodes (Proulx 2005): case fatality 13%; adjusted OR for death 8.4 (95% CI 1.7-40.9) for door-to-antibiotic time >6 hours; delays were associated with transfer without antibiotics (OR 21.8), a head CT then LP then antibiotics sequence (OR 5.6) and absence of the classic triad (OR 4.9). (2) Eisen 2022, individual patient data of 659 adults (Australia, Denmark, UK; propensity-matched): adjusted OR for death 2.29 (1.28-4.09) when antibiotics were given >2 hours after presentation, and OR 1.79 (1.03-3.14) for neurological impairment when >3 hours. (3) Swedish national registry (Glimaker 2015): each hour of treatment delay was associated with a 12.6% relative increase in mortality; after guideline revision favouring prompt LP, mortality fell from 11.7% to 6.9% and sequelae from 49% to 38%. (4) Danish East cohort (Koster-Rasmussen 2008): each hour of delay raised the odds of unfavourable outcome by 9% (OR 1.09/h, 1.01-1.19), by 30% per hour among adults treated within 12 h. (5) French PNEUMOREA ICU study of 156 pneumococcal meningitis adults (Auburtin 2006): an interval >3 hours from admission to antibiotics was independently associated with 3-month mortality (OR 14.12, 3.93-50.9). (6) North Denmark cohort (Bodilsen 2016; 173 adults): delay >6 h versus <=2 h gave adjusted RR 1.6 (0.8-3.2) for in-hospital mortality (not statistically significant) and RR 1.5 (1.0-2.2) for unfavourable outcome at discharge; 31% of patients were diagnosed only after admission and had 30% versus 14% mortality. (7) Adult prognostic staging: Aronin 1998 (269 adults) found adverse outcome more common when the patient's prognostic stage advanced to high risk before antibiotics were given. Weakest/most conflicting result: the Danish cohort's mortality estimate did not reach significance. Practical consequence: the ESCMID guideline advises starting empiric antibiotics within one hour of hospital arrival in all suspected cases.
door_to_antibiotic_time_and_outcome.source: Proulx N et al., QJM 2005;98:291-298 (PMID 15760921); Eisen DP et al., Sci Rep 2022;12:672 (PMID 35027606); Glimaker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2015;60:1162-1169 (PMID 25663160); Koster-Rasmussen R, Korshin A, Meyer CN, J Infect 2008;57:449-454 (PMID 19000639); Auburtin M et al., Crit Care Med 2006;34:2758-2765 (PMID 16915106); Bodilsen J et al., BMC Infect Dis 2016;16:392 (PMID 27507415); Aronin SI et al., Ann Intern Med 1998;129:862-869 (PMID 9867727); van Ettekoven CN, van de Beek D, Brouwer MC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2017;23:601-606 (PMID 28478238; summary of ESCMID 2016 guideline, PMID 27062097)
door_to_antibiotic_time_and_outcome.confidence: high that delay is associated with worse outcome; moderate for any single effect size because all are observational and estimates differ widely (OR 1.09 per hour to OR 14.12 for >3 hours)

meningococcal_disease_speed_of_progressi.finding: In 448 UK children with meningococcal disease (103 fatal), most had only non-specific symptoms in the first 4-6 hours but were close to death by 24 hours; the classic features (haemorrhagic rash, meningism, impaired consciousness) developed late (median onset 13-22 hours), whereas early symptoms of sepsis (leg pains, cold hands and feet, abnormal skin colour) occurred in 72% at a median of 8 hours - well before the median admission time of 19 hours; only 51% were sent to hospital after the first consultation. A case-control study of 143 fatal and 355 surviving UK children found suboptimal in-hospital care independently associated with death: not being looked after by a paediatrician, insufficient supervision of junior staff, and failure to give adequate inotropes; OR for death 8.7 (95% CI 2.3-33) with two failures. Plasma endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) at admission tracked severity in 45 patients: fatality was 0%, 14%, 27% and 86% for levels <25, 25-700, 700-10,000 and >10,000 ng/L.
meningococcal_disease_speed_of_progressi.source: Thompson MJ et al., Lancet 2006;367:397-403 (PMID 16458763); Ninis N et al., BMJ 2005;330:1475 (PMID 15976421); Brandtzaeg P et al., J Infect Dis 1989;159:195-204 (PMID 2492587)

adult_symptom_frequencies.finding: In adult bacterial meningitis the most common symptoms are headache (84%), fever (74%), stiff neck (74%), nausea (62%) and altered mental status (median Glasgow Coma Scale 11, IQR 9-14). The CDC describes meningitis as sudden onset of fever, headache, stiff neck, nausea, vomiting, photophobia and altered mental status. A verified numeric frequency for photophobia in bacterial meningitis was not found and is not stated. Individually these symptoms are weak discriminators (pooled sensitivity of headache 50% and of nausea/vomiting 30% in a systematic review of adult examination findings), which is why the diagnosis rests on CSF examination rather than symptom count.
adult_symptom_frequencies.source: Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590); CDC Pink Book, Chapter 14 Meningococcal Disease (cdc.gov/pinkbook/hcp/table-of-contents/chapter-14-meningococcal-disease.html); Attia J et al., JAMA 1999;282:175-181 (PMID 10411200)
adult_symptom_frequencies.confidence: high for percentages; photophobia frequency deliberately omitted

altered_consciousness_and_seizures.finding: Depressed consciousness is common and prognostic: 14% of Dutch adults were comatose on admission and a low Glasgow Coma Scale score, tachycardia, positive blood culture, elevated ESR and thrombocytopenia predicted unfavourable outcome. Seizures occurred in 17% (121/696) of adults; patients with seizures had 41% mortality versus 16% without, seizures were more likely with pneumococcal infection, low GCS and focal cerebral abnormalities, and the authors advise a low threshold for anticonvulsant therapy when seizures are suspected.
altered_consciousness_and_seizures.source: van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818); Zoons E et al., Neurology 2008;70:2109-2115 (PMID 18305232)

infant_and_child_specific_presentation.finding: In infants and children the picture is non-specific and neck stiffness may be absent. A systematic review of 10 prospective studies found the following raised the likelihood of bacterial meningitis in children: history of bulging fontanelle (LR+ 8.0), neck stiffness (LR+ 7.7), seizures outside the febrile-convulsion age range (LR+ 4.4), reduced feeding (LR+ 2.0); on examination jaundice (LR+ 5.9), toxic or moribund appearance (LR+ 5.8), meningeal signs (LR+ 4.5), neck stiffness (LR+ 4.0), bulging fontanelle (LR+ 3.5), Kernig (LR+ 3.5), raised tone (LR+ 3.2), temperature >40 C (LR+ 2.9), Brudzinski (LR+ 2.5); the absence of meningeal signs (LR- 0.41) and an abnormal cry (LR- 0.30) lowered the likelihood, and absence of fever did not exclude meningitis (LR- 0.70). For neonates, clinical signs are often subtle, infants can have negative blood cultures and normal CSF parameters, lumbar punctures are frequently deferred and CSF cultures can be compromised by prior antibiotics; prompt antibiotics are essential. CDC lists refusal to feed, irritability (not wanting to be held or touched), bulging fontanelle (up to about 6 months), high-pitched cry or moaning, leg pain, cold extremities and abnormal skin colour as features that should prompt suspicion in a baby or young child.
infant_and_child_specific_presentation.source: Curtis S et al., Pediatrics 2010;126:952-960 (PMID 20974781); Ku LC, Boggess KA, Cohen-Wolkowiez M, Clin Perinatol 2015;42:29-45 (PMID 25677995); Thompson MJ et al., Lancet 2006;367:397-403 (PMID 16458763)
infant_and_child_specific_presentation.confidence: high; CDC infant symptom list read from a search-result excerpt of CDC meningitis guidance (moderate)

meningococcal_petechial_purpuric_rash.finding: Meningococcaemia classically causes a petechial or purpuric (non-blanching) rash often accompanied by hypotension, shock, acute adrenal haemorrhage and multiorgan failure; abrupt onset of fever, chills, cold hands and feet, severe aches, vomiting, diarrhoea and rash is typical (CDC). The rash is a late sign (median onset 13-22 hours in children) and is not required for the diagnosis; absence of rash was a risk factor for unfavourable outcome in the Dutch adult cohort. Among 233 UK children presenting with any non-blanching rash, 11% had proven meningococcal infection; those with meningococcal disease were more likely to be ill, febrile (>38.5 C), have purpura and capillary refill >2 s; no child with a rash confined to the distribution of the superior vena cava had meningococcal infection, no child with CRP <6 mg/L had it, and 5 meningococcal children had axillary temperature <37.5 C, so lack of fever does not exclude it. The authors of the UK study conclude that children with fever, purpura and delayed capillary refill should be admitted and treated without delay.
meningococcal_petechial_purpuric_rash.source: CDC Pink Book, Chapter 14 Meningococcal Disease (cdc.gov/pinkbook); Thompson MJ et al., Lancet 2006;367:397-403 (PMID 16458763); Wells LC et al., Arch Dis Child 2001;85:218-222 (PMID 11517104); van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818)

atypical_presentations_elderly_and_immun.finding: Patients on immunosuppressive medication (6% of 1,447 Dutch episodes) were less likely to present with headache or neck stiffness and in 46% had CSF leukocytes <1000/mm3; 25% died and 45% had unfavourable outcome. In patients aged >=80 years case fatality was 50% (75/149), the triad was present in only 43%, and only 30% had a favourable outcome. Practical consequence: fever with confusion in an elderly or immunosuppressed patient should trigger LP/antibiotic consideration even without headache or meningism, and Listeria has to be considered in empiric coverage in these groups (treatment details are in the companion treatment entry).
atypical_presentations_elderly_and_immun.source: van Veen KEB et al., J Neuroimmune Pharmacol 2017;12:213-218 (PMID 27613024); van Soest TM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2022;70:2060-2069 (PMID 35352336); Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590)

EMERGENCY_red_flags: Fever with any non-blanching (petechial/purpuric) rash, cold hands and feet, leg pain, abnormal skin colour, prolonged capillary refill or hypotension - suspected meningococcal septicaemia; early sepsis features precede the rash and the illness can progress from non-specific symptoms to near-death within 24 hours (Thompson MJ et al., Lancet 2006, PMID 16458763; Wells LC et al., Arch Dis Child 2001, PMID 11517104; CDC Pink Book Chapter 14).

Depressed consciousness, falling Glasgow Coma Scale, hypotension or seizures at presentation - the three baseline features that independently predicted adverse outcome (56% adverse outcome in the high-risk stage); 14% of adults are comatose on admission, a low Glasgow Coma Scale score predicts unfavourable outcome, and seizures carried 41% versus 16% mortality (Aronin SI et al., Ann Intern Med 1998, PMID 9867727; van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004, PMID 15509818; Zoons E et al., Neurology 2008, PMID 18305232).

Signs of raised intracranial pressure or impending herniation - acute neurological deterioration, new focal deficit, gaze palsy, facial palsy, limb drift, abnormal language, deteriorating level of consciousness, papilledema; raised ICP is reported in up to 93% of patients in the reviewed series and herniation occurred in 4.3% of children in a series of 445, mostly within 12 hours of an LP (Hasbun R et al., N Engl J Med 2001, PMID 11742046; Hasbun R, JAMA 2022, PMID 36472590; El-Hajj VG et al., Neurocrit Care 2024, PMID 38356077; Rennick G et al., BMJ 1993, PMID 8490469).

Fever in a neonate or young infant with poor feeding, irritability, high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, jaundice, seizures or a toxic/moribund appearance - clinical signs in neonates are often subtle and blood cultures/CSF can be normal, so prompt antibiotics are essential (Curtis S et al., Pediatrics 2010, PMID 20974781; Ku LC et al., Clin Perinatol 2015, PMID 25677995).

Absence of fever, neck stiffness or the classic triad does NOT exclude bacterial meningitis - afebrile presentation was associated with an adjusted OR of 39.4 for death (95% CI 4.3-358.1, very wide) in a Canadian series, absence of the triad predicted >6-hour antibiotic delay (OR 4.9), and 5 meningococcal children had a temperature <37.5 C (Proulx N et al., QJM 2005, PMID 15760921; Wells LC et al., Arch Dis Child 2001, PMID 11517104; Thomas KE et al., Clin Infect Dis 2002, PMID 12060874).

Fever with new confusion or drowsiness in patients aged >=60-80 years or on immunosuppressive medication, splenectomy/asplenia, complement deficiency or eculizumab/ravulizumab - typical features can be absent, septic shock is common in splenectomised patients (63% in one cohort) and eculizumab recipients have a 1,000- to 2,000-fold increased meningococcal incidence even after vaccination (van Veen KEB et al., PMID 27613024; Adriani KS et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2013, PMID 23628588; McNamara LA et al., MMWR 2017, PMID 28704351).

Any patient with suspected bacterial meningitis in whom antibiotic delay is looming because of transfer, CT or LP sequencing - delay of >2 hours was associated with an adjusted OR of 2.29 for death in an individual-patient-data analysis and transfer without antibiotics with an OR of 21.8 for >6-hour delay (Eisen DP et al., Sci Rep 2022, PMID 35027606; Proulx N et al., QJM 2005, PMID 15760921).

overall_sequelae_burden.finding: A meta-analysis of 132 papers found a median risk of at least one major or minor sequela after hospital discharge of 19.9% (IQR 12.3-35.3%); at least one major sequela 12.8% (7.2-21.1%); by organism, major sequelae occurred in 24.7% after pneumococcal, 9.5% after Hib and 7.2% after meningococcal meningitis. Hearing loss was the most common major sequela (33.9%) and 19.7% had multiple impairments. The risk of a major sequela was about twice as high in African (25.1%) and South-East Asian WHO-region (21.6%) studies as in European studies (9.4%). WHO states 1 in 5 survivors may have long-lasting after-effects; a 2022 JAMA review reports up to 24% of survivors with chronic neurological sequelae and mortality up to 54% in low-income countries. The authors conclude most reported sequelae could have been averted by Hib, pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination.
overall_sequelae_burden.source: Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414); WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025; Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590)

hearing_loss.finding: Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common sequela and is caused by cochlear damage from the meningeal inflammation (labyrinthitis). Danish nationwide data on 343 survivors of pneumococcal meningitis: of 240 who had audiometry, 129 (54%) had a hearing deficit, 16 (7%) profound unilateral and 16 (7%) profound bilateral loss, and 39% of those with hearing loss (50/129) had not been suspected of hearing loss at discharge; risk factors were advanced age, female sex, comorbidity, disease severity, low CSF glucose, high CSF protein and pneumococcal serotype (12F worse than 6B). Dutch adult survivors of pneumococcal meningitis assessed at a median of 2 years: hearing loss in 27% (21/79). In a cohort study in Niger (meningitis belt), hearing loss significantly disabled 31.3% of the exposed subjects and 10.4% had serious deafness. Figures differ with population, definition and audiometric testing, but the practical point is constant: audiometry should be performed for all survivors, and the ESCMID guideline recommends follow-up for hearing loss in survivors.
hearing_loss.source: Worsoe L et al., Clin Infect Dis 2010;51:917-924 (PMID 20815735); Kloek AT et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2020;26:1361-1367 (PMID 32006689); Jusot JF et al., BMC Infect Dis 2013;13:228 (PMID 23687976); Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414); van Ettekoven CN et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2017;23:601-606 (PMID 28478238)

hydrocephalus.finding: In the Dutch nationwide cohort (2006-2009; 577 episodes) hydrocephalus complicated 5% (26 episodes), was communicating in all but one, was already present on admission in 69%, was most often due to S. pneumoniae (54%) and L. monocytogenes (15%), and was an independent predictor of death (OR 7.81, 95% CI 2.91-20.8): 50% died and 69% had unfavourable outcome; only 6 patients had a CSF diversion procedure and all who were shunted died or had poor outcome.

seizures_and_epilepsy.finding: Acute seizures occur in 17% of adults (121/696), carry 41% versus 16% mortality, and are associated with pneumococcal disease, severe inflammation, low GCS and focal cerebral lesions (focal abnormalities 41% versus 14%). Seizures are one of the six standard 'major sequelae' categories in the global sequelae meta-analysis, but a separately verified figure for the long-term incidence of post-meningitic epilepsy was not obtained and is not stated here.
seizures_and_epilepsy.source: Zoons E et al., Neurology 2008;70:2109-2115 (PMID 18305232); Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414)
seizures_and_epilepsy.confidence: high for acute seizures; long-term epilepsy incidence intentionally not stated

cognitive_impairment.finding: Pooled analysis of 155 adult survivors (79 pneumococcal, 76 meningococcal) versus 72 healthy controls found cognitive impairment in 32%, mainly cognitive slowness, stable over time and similar between pneumococcal and meningococcal survivors (pneumococcal survivors worse on memory tasks). In Dutch pneumococcal survivors 1-5 years after illness (n=80), 34% had persistent neurological sequelae, 14% (11/79) had cognitive impairment on formal testing, and 71% (53/75) reported cognitive slowness, with lower quality-of-life scores than controls.
cognitive_impairment.source: Hoogman M et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007;78:1092-1096 (PMID 17353256); Kloek AT et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2020;26:1361-1367 (PMID 32006689)

cerebral_infarction_and_cerebrovascular.finding: Cerebral infarction occurred in 25% (174/696) of Dutch adults with bacterial meningitis: 36% in pneumococcal, 9% in meningococcal and 28% in meningitis caused by other bacteria; it was associated with older age, otitis/sinusitis, immunocompromise, lower GCS, lower CSF WBC and higher ESR, and with unfavourable outcome (OR 3.37, 95% CI 2.19-5.21).
cerebral_infarction_and_cerebrovascular.source: Schut ES et al., Neurocrit Care 2012;16:421-427 (PMID 21989842)

raised_icp_and_herniation.finding: Raised ICP is a common intermediate complication (up to 93% in severe cases in the reviewed series) and a leading cause of death; brain herniation is its most feared consequence. In children, herniation occurred in 4.3% of 445 cases and in 45% of the children who died (14 of 31).
raised_icp_and_herniation.source: El-Hajj VG et al., Neurocrit Care 2024;41:228-243 (PMID 38356077); Rennick G et al., BMJ 1993;306:953-955 (PMID 8490469)

mortality_by_organism_and_setting.finding: Global meta-analysis of 371 studies (157,656 episodes, 108 countries, 1935-2019): overall case fatality 18%, falling from 32% before 1961 to 15% after 2010; by pathogen Listeria monocytogenes 27%, S. pneumoniae 24%, H. influenzae 11%, N. meningitidis 9%. Dutch adult cohorts: 21% overall in 1998-2002 (pneumococcal 30% vs meningococcal 7%) and 17% in 2006-2014. US surveillance 1998-2007: 14.8%. UK/Ireland infants <90 days: overall 8%, pneumococcal 19%, GBS 5%, preterm 17% versus term 4%. Adults >=80 years: 50%. CDC gives 10-15% overall case-fatality for meningococcal disease even with appropriate antibiotics and up to 20% of survivors with permanent sequelae. Mortality is up to 54% in low-income countries.
mortality_by_organism_and_setting.source: van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802 (PMID 39093565); van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818); Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347 (PMID 26652862); Thigpen MC et al., N Engl J Med 2011;364:2016-2025 (PMID 21612470); Okike IO et al., Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e150-e157 (PMID 24997051); van Soest TM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2022;70:2060-2069 (PMID 35352336); CDC Pink Book Chapter 14; Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590)

waterhouse_friderichsen_syndrome.finding: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage classically caused by meningococcal sepsis, presenting with shock, petechial rash, abdominal pain and non-specific headache, fatigue and vomiting; prognosis is poor despite treatment. In a pathology series of 65 patients who died of bacterial infections, adrenal haemorrhage was present in 39 (60%); bacteria or bacterial antigens were found in the adrenal glands in 31 (79%) of those with haemorrhage, including 14 with N. meningitidis, and the authors suggest bacteria may play a pathogenic role - N. meningitidis was the most frequent organism but a broad range of bacteria (pneumococcus, group A streptococcus, Rickettsia rickettsii, S. aureus etc.) can cause adrenal lesions, so it is not specific to meningococcus. Meningococcal endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) levels correlate with the severity of shock, organ failure and death: plasma levels >700 ng/L correlated with severe septic shock, adult respiratory distress syndrome, renal impairment and death in 45 patients. The precise sequence linking endotoxaemia to adrenal bleeding was not established by the sources cited here and is not stated as fact.
waterhouse_friderichsen_syndrome.source: Rijal R et al., Vitam Horm 2024;124:449-461 (PMID 38408808); Guarner J et al., Mod Pathol 2008;21:1113-1120 (PMID 18500257); Brandtzaeg P et al., J Infect Dis 1989;159:195-204 (PMID 2492587); CDC Pink Book Chapter 14
waterhouse_friderichsen_syndrome.confidence: high for the associations; the mechanism beyond adrenal haemorrhage is deliberately limited

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Usually less toxic, lymphocytic (mononuclear) CSF pleocytosis of about 50-1000 cells x10^6/L (neutrophilic early), protein about 0.4-0.8 g/L and normal CSF:serum glucose ratio (>=0.5); enteroviruses cause most identified cases, HSV-2 and VZV are next in adults. Bacterial and viral meningitis cannot reliably be separated clinically, and early viral CSF can be neutrophilic, so antibiotics are given until bacterial meningitis is excluded; in children with pleocytosis the Bacterial Meningitis Score (sensitivity 98.3%, NPV 99.9%) can identify very-low-risk cases. Values on the bacterial side of the cut-offs (CSF lactate around 35 mg/dL or higher, CSF:blood glucose ratio <=0.4) favour bacterial disease, with the antibiotic-pretreatment caveat for lactate.
differential_diagnosis.source: Logan SA, MacMahon E, BMJ 2008;336:36-40 (PMID 18174598); Nigrovic LE et al., JAMA 2007;297:52-60 (PMID 17200475); Sakushima K et al., J Infect 2011;62:255-262 (PMID 21382412); Straus SE et al., JAMA 2006;296:2012-2022 (PMID 17062865)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Subacute (days to weeks) course rather than hours; length of history is a predictor separating TBM from bacterial meningitis; CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis 10-500 cells/microL with >50% lymphocytes, protein >1 g/L (often 1-3 g/L), low glucose (<2.2 mmol/L or ratio <0.5), and (per the tuberculosis entry) cranial nerve palsies classically affecting the basal cisterns; but neutrophil predominance can occur early and CSF alone is non-specific. Diagnostic rule (Thwaites 2002) was 86% sensitive/79% specific prospectively; Xpert Ultra sensitivity was 70% against the uniform case definition. TBM mortality pooled 24.7% (64.8% stage III; 53.4% HIV-positive) so it must be considered in any subacute meningitis with low CSF glucose (Thwaites suggests applying the rule to adults with meningitis and low CSF glucose), especially where TB is prevalent or HIV is present. Cross-reference: tuberculosis entry (extrapulmonary_tb_major_sites.tb_meningitis and red_flags).
differential_diagnosis.source: Thwaites GE et al., Lancet 2002;360:1287-1292 (PMID 12414204); Marais S et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:803-812 (PMID 20822958); Bahr NC et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18:68-75 (PMID 28919338); Wang MG et al., BMC Pulm Med 2019;19:200 (PMID 31694599); Wilkinson RJ et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2017;13:581-598 (PMID 28884751)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Herpes simplex (HSV) encephalitis and other viral encephalitis
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma with clinical evidence of neurological dysfunction: behavioural change, acute cognitive dysfunction, speech disturbance, focal deficits and seizures (in 113 virologically proven HSV encephalitis cases, behavioural change, fever, confusion and speech disturbance were characteristic). Altered mental status is early in encephalitis but does not reliably separate encephalitis from bacterial meningitis; CSF typically shows mild mononuclear pleocytosis with mildly to moderately raised protein, and CSF/imaging can be normal early in proven HSV disease. HSV CSF PCR has reported sensitivity 96-98% and specificity 95-99% in adults; MRI may show temporal lobe oedema/haemorrhage and bilateral temporal involvement is nearly pathognomonic. IDSA advises starting acyclovir in all patients with suspected encephalitis as soon as possible, pending results of diagnostic studies. The multiplex CSF panel misses some HSV cases (false negatives most often HSV-1/2, enterovirus, Cryptococcus).
differential_diagnosis.source: Tunkel AR et al., 'The management of encephalitis: clinical practice guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America', Clin Infect Dis 2008;47:303-327 (PMID 18582201; statements read from academic.oup.com full text); Whitley RJ et al., JAMA 1982;247:317-320 (PMID 6275134); Tansarli GS, Chapin KC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2020;26:281-290 (PMID 31760115)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: SAH classically presents with a thunderclap (instantly peaking) headache reaching maximal intensity within 1 hour, and neck pain/stiffness or limited neck flexion are themselves part of the validated Ottawa SAH Rule, so meningism cannot separate SAH from meningitis on its own. In neurologically intact patients with headache peaking within 1 hour, the Ottawa SAH Rule had 100% sensitivity (95% CI 97.2-100%) but only 15.3% specificity; non-contrast third-generation CT read by a radiologist was 100% sensitive (97.0-100%) when done within 6 hours of headache onset and 92.9% overall (89.0-95.5%), (SAH in these studies was defined by blood on CT, xanthochromia, or red cells in the final CSF tube with positive angiography, so a negative CT is not an absolute exclusion outside that early window). These derivations apply only to the stated headache population and not to patients with fever and altered consciousness, where bacterial meningitis is the parallel emergency and antibiotics must not wait.
differential_diagnosis.source: Perry JJ et al., JAMA 2013;310:1248-1255 (PMID 24065011); Perry JJ et al., BMJ 2011;343:d4277 (PMID 21768192)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Partially treated bacterial meningitis / culture-negative meningitis after antibiotics
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Prior oral or parenteral antibiotics lower CSF culture yield (meningococcus can be sterile within 2 hours and pneumococcus from about 4 hours of parenteral third-generation cephalosporin) and lower the sensitivity of CSF lactate (0.93 overall to 0.49 with pre-treatment), so a partly treated bacterial meningitis can look like aseptic meningitis; PCR panels and blood cultures (positive in 57-68% of cases with negative CSF culture in one paediatric series) can still give the answer.
differential_diagnosis.source: Kanegaye JT et al., Pediatrics 2001;108:1169-1174 (PMID 11694698); Sakushima K et al., J Infect 2011;62:255-262 (PMID 21382412); Tansarli GS, Chapin KC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2020;26:281-290 (PMID 31760115)

age_extremes.finding: Incidence is highest in neonates/young infants and older adults. UK/Ireland surveillance found an annual incidence of 0.38 per 1,000 live births for confirmed bacterial meningitis in infants <90 days, unchanged since the 1980s; Dutch Listeria meningitis peaked in neonates (0.61 per 100,000 live births) and at age 87 years (0.53 per 100,000 of that age). After conjugate vaccination the median age of US patients rose from 15 months in 1986 to 25 years in 1995, and in a later US surveillance from 30.3 years (1998-1999) to 41.9 years (2006-2007). Adults >=80 years had 50% case fatality. Advanced age is also a major risk factor for unfavourable outcome.
age_extremes.source: Okike IO et al., Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e150-e157 (PMID 24997051); Koopmans MM et al., J Infect 2017;75:12-19 (PMID 28419853); Schuchat A et al., N Engl J Med 1997;337:970-976 (PMID 9395430); Thigpen MC et al., N Engl J Med 2011;364:2016-2025 (PMID 21612470); van Soest TM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2022;70:2060-2069 (PMID 35352336)

immunocompromise_splenectomy_complement_.finding: Splenectomy or functional hyposplenia accounted for 2.5% (24/965) of adult bacterial meningitis episodes in a Dutch cohort; all were pneumococcal, septic shock was more frequent (63% versus 24%), mortality was 25% and only 32% of patients (6/19 with known status) had been adequately vaccinated against pneumococcus. Complement deficiency is most important for Neisseria: terminal complement (C5-C9) or properdin deficiencies are associated with recurrent or invasive neisserial infection, whereas early-component deficiency (C1-C3), asplenia and agammaglobulinaemia predispose to pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus; complement deficiency was identified in 3% of 176 Dutch meningococcal patients tested (from 7,732 patients over 1959-1992) but in 33% of those infected with uncommon or non-groupable serogroups, which is why screening is advised for recurrent disease or unusual serogroups in people aged >=5 years. Patients receiving the terminal complement inhibitor eculizumab have a 1,000- to 2,000-fold higher meningococcal incidence, with 16 US cases in 2008-2016, 14 of whom had received at least one meningococcal vaccine dose. 6% of Dutch adult episodes occurred in patients using immunosuppressive medication, in whom Listeria caused 40%.
immunocompromise_splenectomy_complement_.source: Adriani KS et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2013;88:571-578 (PMID 23628588); Figueroa JE, Densen P, Clin Microbiol Rev 1991;4:359-395 (PMID 1889047); Overturf GD, Clin Infect Dis 2003;36:189-194 (PMID 12522751); Fijen CA et al., Clin Infect Dis 1999;28:98-105 (PMID 10028078); McNamara LA et al., MMWR 2017;66:734-737 (PMID 28704351); van Veen KEB et al., J Neuroimmune Pharmacol 2017;12:213-218 (PMID 27613024)

crowding_and_outbreak_data.finding: In a meta-analysis of paediatric/adolescent case-control studies, household overcrowding (OR 2.52, 95% CI 1.75-3.63), smoke exposure (OR 2.10, 1.00-4.39), kissing (OR 2.00), and recent respiratory tract infection (OR 3.13, 2.02-4.86) increased invasive meningococcal disease risk. In a US college surveillance, freshmen living in dormitories had the highest incidence (5.1 per 100,000) and an independently elevated risk versus other students (matched OR 3.6, 95% CI 1.6-8.5). CDC estimates about 10% of adolescents and adults are asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriers of N. meningitidis at any given time. In India, a 2026 expert consensus lists outbreaks from 1966 (Delhi: 616 cases, case-fatality 20.9%) to 2022-2023 (Kolkata), with serogroup A predominant and emerging C, W and Y; a systematic-review prevalence of 12.1% (case fatality 12.8%) in epidemics versus 0.76% (case fatality 3.0%) in endemic settings is quoted there. WHO describes the African meningitis belt as extending from Senegal to Ethiopia; group A meningococcal conjugate vaccination has reduced epidemic disease there (see unvaccinated_status_and_vaccine_impact).
crowding_and_outbreak_data.source: Spyromitrou-Xioufi P, Tsirigotaki M, Ladomenou F, Eur J Pediatr 2020;179:1017-1027 (PMID 32405695); Bruce MG et al., JAMA 2001;286:688-693 (PMID 11495618); CDC Pink Book Chapter 14; Dutta AK et al., Hum Vaccin Immunother 2026;22:2676385 (PMID 42446494); WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025; GBD 2016 Meningitis Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:1061-1082 (PMID 30507391)
crowding_and_outbreak_data.confidence: high for case-control and college data; moderate for Indian outbreak figures which come from an expert-consensus abstract summarising the literature

unvaccinated_status_and_vaccine_impact.finding: Vaccination is the most effective prevention. Most reported sequelae could have been averted by Hib, pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines (Edmond 2010). In the African meningitis belt, MenAfriVac (serogroup A conjugate) reduced incidence of suspected meningitis by 57% (95% CI 55-59) in vaccinated versus unvaccinated populations across nine countries and reduced confirmed group A disease by more than 99% in fully vaccinated populations, though non-A serogroup incidence rate ratio was higher after campaigns (IRR 2.76, 1.21-6.30). In the Netherlands, adult bacterial meningitis incidence fell from 1.72 to 0.94 per 100,000 between 2007-08 and 2013-14 with herd protection from paediatric conjugate vaccines and no evidence of serotype/serogroup replacement. Only 32% of splenectomised meningitis patients had adequate pneumococcal vaccination.
unvaccinated_status_and_vaccine_impact.source: Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414); Trotter CL et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:867-872 (PMID 28545721); Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347 (PMID 26652862); Adriani KS et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2013;88:571-578 (PMID 23628588)

csf_leak_skull_fracture_otitis_sinusitis.finding: Basilar skull fractures predispose to meningitis through direct communication with the paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx or middle ear, and CSF leakage carries a greater risk; a Cochrane review of 5 randomised trials (208 participants) found no significant reduction in meningitis with prophylactic antibiotics compared with control. Cochlear implants: in 4,264 US children implanted before age 6 years (1997-2002), the incidence of pneumococcal meningitis was 138.2 cases per 100,000 person-years, more than 30 times the age-matched general population; risk was associated with an implant with a positioner (adjusted OR 4.5, 95% CI 1.3-17.9) and with the joint presence of inner-ear malformation and CSF leak (adjusted OR 9.3, 1.2-94.5). Contiguous otitis/sinusitis is a recognised predisposing condition (22% and 16% of patients >=80 years had otitis/sinusitis and pneumonia respectively) and is associated with cerebral infarction risk.
csf_leak_skull_fracture_otitis_sinusitis.source: Ratilal BO et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;CD004884 (PMID 25918919); Reefhuis J et al., N Engl J Med 2003;349:435-445 (PMID 12890842); van Soest TM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2022;70:2060-2069 (PMID 35352336); Schut ES et al., Neurocrit Care 2012;16:421-427 (PMID 21989842)

global_burden.finding: GBD 2016: global meningitis deaths fell 21.0% between 1990 and 2016 (403,012 to 318,400) while incident cases rose (2.50 million to 2.82 million); the highest incidence and mortality were in the peri-Sahelian African meningitis belt, and pneumococcus caused the largest number of years lived with disability (634,458). GBD 2019: 236,000 deaths (95% UI 204,000-277,000) and 2.51 million incident cases in 2019; 112,000 deaths and 1.28 million cases in children <5 years; age-standardised mortality fell from 7.5 to 3.3 per 100,000 between 1990 and 2019; S. pneumoniae caused 18.1% of all-age meningitis deaths, N. meningitidis 13.6% and Klebsiella pneumoniae 12.2%. Bacterial meningitis incidence ranges from about 0.9 per 100,000 per year in high-income to 80 per 100,000 in low-income countries. WHO: around 1 in 6 people who get bacterial meningitis die and 1 in 5 have severe complications. WHO set goals (Defeating meningitis by 2030 roadmap) to eliminate bacterial meningitis epidemics, reduce vaccine-preventable cases by 50% and deaths by 70%.
global_burden.source: GBD 2016 Meningitis Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:1061-1082 (PMID 30507391); GBD 2019 Meningitis Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2023;22:685-711 (PMID 37479374); Hasbun R, JAMA 2022;328:2147-2154 (PMID 36472590); WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025
global_burden.confidence: high for GBD/Hasbun numbers (abstracts); moderate for the WHO 2030 roadmap targets (from a search-result summary of the WHO roadmap, not from the primary document)

india_specific_data.finding: India has no verified single national, mandatory, all-age bacterial meningitis notification system in the sources I could access; what exists is hospital-based sentinel surveillance in children plus modelled estimates. Pre-Hib-vaccine sentinel surveillance in Chennai, Lucknow, New Delhi and Vellore (children 1-23 months, 2008-2010): among 708 children with abnormal CSF, 89 had a confirmed bacterial pathogen, of which Hib caused 70%, S. pneumoniae 13% and GBS 8%; the proportions of abnormal CSF and of probable bacterial meningitis caused by Hib were 74% and 58% lower at Vellore (41% Hib-conjugate vaccine coverage among suspected cases) than at the sites with 1-8% coverage, and a referral hospital saw annual Hib meningitis admissions fall from 10.7 to 3.8 after private-sector Hib vaccine use. A later 11-hospital sentinel network (children 1-59 months, 2012-2016; 12,941 suspected cases, 586 lab-confirmed [4.5%]) found S. pneumoniae 74.2%, H. influenzae 22.2% and N. meningitidis 3.6%, Hib case fatality 12.3%, PCV13 serotypes causing 72% of pneumococcal cases, penicillin non-susceptibility 57% and multidrug resistance in 43.7% of tested isolates (different population and testing methods from the earlier network, so it is not a like-for-like trend). Post-PCV sentinel data (32 hospitals, 19 states, 2019-2022; 12,971 children; 303 with pneumococcal meningitis): the proportion of children with pneumococcal meningitis fell from 3.5% (pre-PCV) to 1.8% (early and post-PCV), the share of PCV10-SII serotypes among serotyped cases fell from 41.4% to 25.9%, and in-hospital case fatality was 6.9%; India introduced PCV13 in select high-burden sites in 2017 and moved to nationwide PCV10-SII in 2021. Modelled estimates suggest deaths in Indian children aged 1-59 months from pneumococcal disease fell from 166,000 (2000) to 68,700 (2015) (-58%) and from Hib from 82,600 to 15,600 (-81%) - these are deaths from all pneumococcal/Hib disease (pneumonia and meningitis), not meningitis alone. A South Asia meta-analysis estimated incidence of childhood (1-59 months) bacterial meningitis at 105 per 100,000 per year but flagged it as an underestimate. For meningococcal disease, a 2026 expert consensus calls surveillance weak, recommends mandatory reporting and sentinel surveillance, and states the true burden is under-estimated. I could not verify an India-wide adult bacterial meningitis incidence figure or a dated schedule for national pentavalent (Hib) roll-out; neither is stated.
india_specific_data.source: Ramachandran P et al., Indian J Med Res 2013;137:712-720 (PMID 23703338); Verghese VP et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2009;28:738-740 (PMID 19633518); Jayaraman Y et al., Vaccine 2021;39:3737-3744 (PMID 34074545); Chethrapilly Purushothaman GK et al., Lancet Reg Health Southeast Asia 2026;50:100790 (PMID 42291471); Wahl B et al., Lancet Glob Health 2019;7:e735-e747 (PMID 31097277); Ali M et al., Vaccine 2018;36:5846-5857 (PMID 30145101); Dutta AK et al., Hum Vaccin Immunother 2026;22:2676385 (PMID 42446494)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate to high - each number is from a real abstract; the statement about the absence of a national system is an absence-of-evidence statement from the sources accessed and should not be read as proof that none exists

clinical_takeaway.point: Suspected bacterial meningitis is an emergency: give empiric intravenous antibiotics as soon as possible - ESCMID advises within one hour of hospital arrival - and do not delay them for imaging, transfer or LP in an unstable patient. Antibiotic choice, dexamethasone and doses are in the companion treatment entry and are for the treating doctor.
clinical_takeaway.why: Every large observational series links delay to worse outcome (aOR for death 2.29 when >2 hours; 12.6% relative mortality increase per hour in a national registry; OR 8.4 for >6 hours), and IDSA 2004 explicitly allows antimicrobial therapy before LP or before CT. No randomised trial exists, so effect sizes are approximate.
clinical_takeaway.source: van Ettekoven CN et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2017 (PMID 28478238; ESCMID 2016 guideline PMID 27062097); Tunkel AR et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004 (PMID 15494903); Eisen DP et al., Sci Rep 2022 (PMID 35027606); Glimaker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2015 (PMID 25663160); Proulx N et al., QJM 2005 (PMID 15760921)

clinical_takeaway.point: Draw blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose only if this does not delay treatment, and perform the LP as early as it is safe; if LP has to be delayed, start antibiotics first (with adjunctive treatment as set out in the treatment entry) and do the LP afterwards.
clinical_takeaway.why: Blood cultures were positive in 57-68% of pre-treated patients whose CSF cultures were sterile, and meningococcal CSF can be sterile within 2 hours of parenteral cephalosporin while pneumococcal CSF stays positive about 4 hours; blood cultures and PCR therefore preserve the aetiological diagnosis when CSF cannot be obtained in time. IDSA states blood must be cultured before or concurrent with LP.
clinical_takeaway.source: Kanegaye JT et al., Pediatrics 2001 (PMID 11694698); Tunkel AR et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004 (PMID 15494903); Tansarli GS, Chapin KC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2020 (PMID 31760115)

clinical_takeaway.point: Decide on CT before LP by clinical criteria, not routinely: image first only if age >=60 years, immunocompromise, prior CNS disease, seizure in the past week, or abnormal level of consciousness, gaze palsy, visual field defect, facial palsy, limb drift, abnormal language (papilledema also counts). Absence of all of these had a 97% negative predictive value for CT mass effect. Note that guidelines disagree (Swedish registry data favour prompt LP without CT even with impaired mental status) and imaging must never delay antibiotics.
clinical_takeaway.why: Hasbun 2001 found abnormal CT in 24% and mass effect in 5%; the IDSA-criteria missed no major intracranial finding in a 202-patient Houston cohort while ESCMID and Swedish criteria missed 41.7% and 70.8%, yet Swedish national data (815 adults) associated prompt LP with lower mortality (aOR 0.38) than imaging-first pathways. The evidence is observational.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hasbun R et al., N Engl J Med 2001 (PMID 11742046); Park N et al., Clin Neuroradiol 2022 (PMID 35181803); Glimaker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2018 (PMID 29020334)

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not rule bacterial meningitis out on the absence of fever, neck stiffness, Kernig/Brudzinski signs or the classic triad; proceed to LP/antibiotics on clinical suspicion, and in fever plus non-blanching rash or early sepsis signs in a child treat as meningococcal disease immediately without waiting for the rash to spread or for CSF.
clinical_takeaway.why: Triad present in only 44% (95% had >=2 of 4 features); Kernig and Brudzinski sensitivity 5% and nuchal rigidity 30% in adults; meningococcal rash appears at a median 13-22 hours whereas sepsis symptoms appear at about 8 hours; afebrile presentation carried an adjusted OR of 39.4 for death (very wide CI 4.3-358.1).
clinical_takeaway.source: van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004 (PMID 15509818); Thomas KE et al., Clin Infect Dis 2002 (PMID 12060874); Thompson MJ et al., Lancet 2006 (PMID 16458763); Proulx N et al., QJM 2005 (PMID 15760921)

clinical_takeaway.point: Keep the differential open while treating: send CSF for cell count, glucose/protein with paired blood glucose (ratio), lactate, Gram stain and culture, and PCR (multiplex panel, HSV, TB if subacute or low glucose); start acyclovir if encephalitis is suspected; consider TBM (see 'tuberculosis' entry) in subacute meningitis with lymphocytic CSF and low glucose; in children with pleocytosis and no antibiotics before LP, the Bacterial Meningitis Score identifies very-low-risk cases (not neonates or adults).
clinical_takeaway.why: Bacterial and viral meningitis cannot be distinguished clinically; CSF glucose ratio <=0.4 (LR 18), WBC >=500 (LR 15) and lactate >=3.5 mmol/L (LR 21) are strong rule-in tests but none rules out; HSV encephalitis and TBM are treatable and time-sensitive mimics.
clinical_takeaway.source: Straus SE et al., JAMA 2006 (PMID 17062865); Logan SA, MacMahon E, BMJ 2008 (PMID 18174598); Tunkel AR et al., Clin Infect Dis 2008 (PMID 18582201); Nigrovic LE et al., JAMA 2007 (PMID 17200475); Thwaites GE et al., Lancet 2002 (PMID 12414204)

clinical_takeaway.point: After survival, arrange audiometry for every survivor, screen for cognitive, motor and seizure sequelae, and check vaccination/immune status (asplenia, complement deficiency, eculizumab, CSF leak or cochlear implant) especially after pneumococcal or recurrent/unusual-serogroup meningococcal meningitis.
clinical_takeaway.why: 54% of Danish pneumococcal survivors who had audiometry had a hearing deficit and 39% of them were not suspected of hearing loss at discharge; 32% of adult survivors had cognitive impairment; complement deficiency is found in about a third of patients with meningococcal disease due to uncommon serogroups.
clinical_takeaway.source: Worsoe L et al., Clin Infect Dis 2010 (PMID 20815735); Hoogman M et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007 (PMID 17353256); Fijen CA et al., Clin Infect Dis 1999 (PMID 10028078); van Ettekoven CN et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2017 (PMID 28478238)

bacterial_meningitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bacterial meningitis is genuinely CURABLE, and this must be stated plainly because it is the opposite of the chronic neurological diseases in this knowledge base (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, myasthenia gravis, migraine), which are managed but not eliminated. It is an acute bacterial infection of the meninges: correct antibiotics, started promptly, actually kill the organism and end the infection, and most patients who receive prompt correct treatment survive (pooled global case fatality was 15% after 2010, i.e. about 85% survive; van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802, PMID 39093565). The honest counterweight is equally real and is stated with equal clarity. (1) It is a time-critical emergency: WHO states that bacterial meningitis can become fatal within 24 hours; in a 123-case adult series the adjusted odds of death were 8.4 times higher (95% CI 1.7-40.9) when door-to-antibiotic time exceeded 6 hours (Proulx N et al., QJM 2005;98:291-298, PMID 15760921), and in an east-Danish cohort each hour of antibiotic delay raised the odds of an unfavourable outcome by about 9% (OR 1.09/h), and by 30% per hour (OR 1.30/h) among adults who still received adequate antibiotics within 12 hours (Koster-Rasmussen R et al., J Infect 2008;57:449-454, PMID 19000639). (2) Mortality is real even with treatment: pooled case fatality was 18% overall, falling from 32% before 1961 to 15% after 2010, and is highest for Listeria (27%) and pneumococcus (24%) and lowest for meningococcus (9%) and Haemophilus influenzae type b (11%) (van Ettekoven 2024); WHO summarises this as roughly 1 in 6 people with bacterial meningitis dying (WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025). (3) Cure of the infection does not mean an undamaged nervous system: about 1 in 5 survivors has lasting sequelae (median risk of at least one major or minor sequela 19.9%, of a major sequela 12.8%, and of a major sequela after pneumococcal meningitis 24.7%; hearing loss is the commonest major sequela; Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328, PMID 20417414), 54% of audiometry-tested Danish pneumococcal-meningitis survivors had a hearing deficit and 39% of those had not been suspected of hearing loss at discharge (Worsoe L et al., Clin Infect Dis 2010;51:917-924, PMID 20815735), and cognitive impairment (mainly slowness) was found in 32% of adult survivors (Hoogman M et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007;78:1092-1096, PMID 17353256). This is why hearing and neurological follow-up are part of the treatment, not an afterthought. REAL WORKING SOLUTION: (a) suspect it early and give IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (plus vancomycin where pneumococcal resistance is a concern, plus ampicillin if age over 50-60 years, pregnancy or immunocompromise) within the first hour of arrival -- never delay antibiotics for CT or lumbar puncture in an unstable patient; (b) give dexamethasone with, or just before, the first antibiotic dose in suspected bacterial meningitis (WHO 2025 strong recommendation, low certainty): the landmark adult trial cut the relative risk of death to 0.48 and of an unfavourable outcome to 0.59 (de Gans J, van de Beek D, N Engl J Med 2002;347:1549-1556, PMID 12432041), although trials in high-HIV, low-income settings did not reproduce a benefit; (c) narrow therapy once organism and sensitivities are known and finish the organism-specific course; (d) give chemoprophylaxis to close contacts of meningococcal (and, where indicated, Hib) disease; (e) treat raised intracranial pressure, seizures and hydrocephalus in a monitored setting; (f) test hearing before discharge; and (g) vaccinate -- Hib, pneumococcal conjugate and meningococcal vaccines are the real primary prevention. This is a curable emergency with a real residual-damage tail: not a manage-forever diagnosis, and not a minor infection either.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for bacterial meningitis: empiric antibiotic regimens by age group and risk factor (neonates; infants, children and adults; over-50/immunocompromised with Listeria cover; post-neurosurgical, head-trauma and CSF-shunt patients; low-resource fallbacks) with real doses; organism-directed de-escalation and durations (Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria, group B streptococcus, Gram-negative bacilli and staphylococci); the timing rule that antibiotics must not be delayed for lumbar puncture or imaging; adjunctive dexamethasone with the landmark trials and their real neutral and negative counterparts; adjuncts that do not work (glycerol, hypothermia, activated protein C, fluid restriction); chemoprophylaxis and infection control for meningococcal and Hib contacts; vaccination as primary prevention (Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, meningococcal ACWY/B/A); management of raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, seizures and vascular/ENT complications; hearing screening and rehabilitation; and the medical equipment and devices involved. Diagnostic criteria, clinical signs and red-flag recognition are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here beyond treatment-timing cross-references. Guideline status, verified in this research: the 2004 IDSA bacterial meningitis guideline (Tunkel AR et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284) is listed as ARCHIVED on idsociety.org and no newer IDSA community-acquired bacterial meningitis guideline was found; more recent guidance exists and is used alongside it: the ESCMID 2016 guideline, the IDSA 2017 healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis guideline, the German 2023 guideline, and the WHO 2025 guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care (the first global WHO meningitis guideline; excludes neonates and healthcare-associated meningitis). NICE guideline NG240 (published 19 March 2024) also exists; its content could not be retrieved in this research and it is not cited for specific claims. Bacterial meningitis is genuinely curable with prompt correct antibiotic therapy but carries real mortality if treatment is delayed and real residual-sequelae risk even after cure (see CURABILITY_NOTE).

bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.name: Empiric Antibiotics for Neonatal Bacterial Meningitis -- Ampicillin plus Gentamicin or Cefotaxime
bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.type: Empiric intravenous combination antibiotic therapy, neonates (birth to about 6 weeks)
specific_drugs: Early-onset (first week of life): ampicillin 150 mg/kg/day divided every 8 h PLUS either gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day divided every 12 h OR cefotaxime 100-150 mg/kg/day divided every 8-12 h

Late-onset (about 1 to 6 weeks of life): ampicillin 200 mg/kg/day divided every 6-8 h PLUS either an aminoglycoside (gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg/day every 8 h, tobramycin 7.5 mg/kg/day every 8 h, or amikacin 30 mg/kg/day every 8 h) OR cefotaxime 150-200 mg/kg/day divided every 6-8 h
Ceftriaxone is NOT a neonatal substitute for cefotaxime (see caveat)
bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.effectiveness: IDSA 2004 empiric regimen for age 0-4 weeks: ampicillin plus either cefotaxime or an aminoglycoside (doses above as tabulated in Brouwer 2010, Table 2, adapted from IDSA 2004 with permission). The regimen is chosen for the organisms that cause neonatal disease -- Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus), Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes in the first week, with staphylococci and other Gram-negative bacilli added in late-onset disease. Honest evidence status: a systematic review (Pediatrics 2024 supplement) found only 2 randomised trials of antibiotic regimens for meningitis in infants aged 0-59 days (168 infants, 1976-2015), neither compared a current WHO-recommended regimen, intrathecal gentamicin added nothing to systemic ampicillin/gentamicin, and 10 versus 14 days showed no mortality difference (very low certainty; Mathias S et al., Pediatrics 2024;154, PMID 39087804) -- the regimens above rest on guideline consensus and microbiology, not on head-to-head neonatal trials. The WHO 2025 meningitis guideline excludes neonates aged 0-28 days from its scope and refers to the WHO pocket book of hospital care for children.
bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.reason_why: Ampicillin is essential because expanded-spectrum cephalosporins have no useful activity against Listeria monocytogenes (Brouwer 2010), which is a real cause of early neonatal meningitis; cefotaxime or an aminoglycoside covers E. coli and other Gram-negative bacilli. Gentamicin is added largely for in-vitro synergy -- CSF gentamicin concentrations are only minimally above the MIC, so its role is debated (Brouwer 2010).
