bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.important_caveat: Ceftriaxone label (FDA, Hospira, revision 2026-01-19): contraindicated in premature neonates up to a post-menstrual age of 41 weeks, in hyperbilirubinaemic neonates (displaces bilirubin from albumin, risk of bilirubin encephalopathy), and in neonates 28 days or younger who need or are expected to need calcium-containing IV solutions including parenteral nutrition (fatal ceftriaxone-calcium precipitation in lungs and kidneys reported). Adjunctive dexamethasone in neonatal meningitis is unproven -- the only small alternate-allocation trial (52 neonates) showed no effect and there are insufficient data to recommend it (Brouwer 2010; IDSA 2004).
bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.real_working_solution: Start ampicillin plus cefotaxime (or ampicillin plus gentamicin) immediately in any neonate with suspected meningitis or sepsis -- do not wait for lumbar puncture results -- obtain CSF and blood cultures, and continue until cultures guide narrowing. Organism-directed duration: group B streptococcus 14-21 days, aerobic Gram-negative bacilli 21 days (or 2 weeks after the first sterile CSF culture, documented by repeat lumbar puncture), Listeria 21 days (IDSA 2004). Use cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone, as the neonatal third-generation cephalosporin.
bm_empiric_therapy_neonates.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Mathias S et al., Pediatrics 2024;154 (PMID 39087804); WHO 2025 (scope exclusion of neonates)

bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.name: Third-Generation Cephalosporin Backbone -- Ceftriaxone or Cefotaxime (Infants Over 1 Month, Children, Adults Under 50 Years)
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.type: Empiric intravenous third-generation cephalosporin, first-line for community-acquired bacterial meningitis
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone, adults: 2 g IV every 12 h (4 g/day); children: 80-100 mg/kg/day every 12-24 h (FDA label: initial 100 mg/kg, maximum 4 g, then 100 mg/kg/day once daily or divided every 12 h, maximum 4 g/day)
Cefotaxime, adults: 8-12 g/day divided every 4-6 h; children: 225-300 mg/kg/day divided every 6-8 h
Penicillin G 24 million units/day every 4 h may be considered as monotherapy only where penicillin resistance is under 1%
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.effectiveness: IDSA 2004: third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) are recommended for childhood bacterial meningitis (A-I) and for pneumococcal and meningococcal meningitis due to penicillin-resistant strains (A-III), are the empiric drugs of choice for Haemophilus influenzae type b because of chloramphenicol resistance, and showed greater efficacy than chloramphenicol and cefuroxime. WHO 2025: strong recommendation (very low certainty evidence) that IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime be given as empiric treatment for suspected or probable acute bacterial meningitis in children and adults; ceftriaxone is preferred over cefotaxime during meningococcal and pneumococcal epidemics. ESCMID 2016 advises starting empiric treatment within one hour of arrival with the choice differentiated by age, risk factors and local pneumococcal resistance, and the German guideline (2023) recommends ceftriaxone 2 x 2 g/day. Route: in a Malawian trial in adults (465 patients, 90% HIV-positive) IM ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily was not inferior to IV (deaths 128/229 IM vs 121/230 IV; OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.61-1.27), which supports IM dosing when IV access is not immediately possible (Scarborough M et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2441-2450, PMID 18077809; WHO 2025 remark: give IM if IV cannot be secured).
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.reason_why: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis cause 75-90% of adult and about 80% of paediatric (over 3 months) community-acquired cases (Brouwer 2010), and a third-generation cephalosporin has excellent CSF penetration under inflammatory conditions and broad activity against both (Brouwer 2010).
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.important_caveat: Do not reconstitute or dilute ceftriaxone with calcium-containing diluents such as Ringer's or Hartmann's solution, and do not infuse it simultaneously through the same line as calcium-containing IV fluids; outside the neonatal period it may be given sequentially if the line is flushed between infusions (FDA label). Beta-lactam allergy: WHO advises investigating the allergy, notes cephalosporins can be used safely in most non-severe penicillin allergy, and says all beta-lactams should be avoided after a previous life-threatening reaction; IDSA 2004 lists meropenem (A-I) as an alternative to cefotaxime/ceftriaxone and fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin) for patients who cannot receive standard therapy.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.real_working_solution: Give IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) as the first antibiotic on clinical suspicion, within the first hour, after blood cultures if that causes no delay. Add vancomycin (next entry) where pneumococcal cephalosporin resistance is a concern, and ampicillin (entry after that) for Listeria risk. Use IM ceftriaxone when IV access cannot be obtained at once.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); Scarborough M et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2441-2450 (PMID 18077809); ceftriaxone FDA label via openFDA (Hospira, 2026-01-19)

bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.name: Vancomycin (or Rifampin) Added to the Cephalosporin -- Penicillin/Cephalosporin-Resistant Pneumococcus
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.type: Empiric glycopeptide add-on for resistant pneumococcal meningitis
specific_drugs: Vancomycin, children: 60 mg/kg/day divided every 6 h; adults: 30-60 mg/kg/day divided every 8-12 h (German guideline: 2 x 1 g/day as a guide value with serum levels), target trough 15-20 micrograms/mL
Rifampin 600 mg once daily (German guideline) as an alternative add-on to the cephalosporin -- never as monotherapy
Alternative for cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus: meropenem 6 g/day divided every 8 h (adults), or moxifloxacin with an expanded-spectrum cephalosporin
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.effectiveness: IDSA 2004: vancomycin is not recommended for non-resistant strains and must never be used alone; it is added to a third-generation cephalosporin for penicillin- or cephalosporin-resistant pneumococci (A-III), and rifampin is added only if clinical or bacteriological response is delayed (A-III). WHO 2025: conditional recommendation (very low certainty) to add IV vancomycin in areas with high prevalence of penicillin or third-generation-cephalosporin resistance in S. pneumoniae; rifampin can substitute for vancomycin in low-tuberculosis-burden settings, and only when vancomycin is unavailable or contraindicated in high-TB-burden settings. India-specific: in a hospital sentinel network across India (3,104 suspected paediatric cases, 257 confirmed) S. pneumoniae caused 82.9% of confirmed meningitis in children under 5 and showed considerable resistance to penicillin and cefotaxime (Jayaraman Y et al., PLoS One 2018;13:e0197198, PMID 29768458).
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.reason_why: Some pneumococci have altered penicillin-binding proteins that lower the potency of penicillin and cephalosporins; vancomycin acts on a different target (cell-wall precursors) and restores coverage, while rifampin adds a different mechanism (RNA-polymerase inhibition) but induces rapid resistance when used alone.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.important_caveat: Dexamethasone may reduce vancomycin penetration into CSF (German guideline, citing experimental resistant-pneumococcal meningitis data, Paris MM et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1994;38:1320-1324). IDSA 2004 still recommends dexamethasone for adults with suspected/proven pneumococcal meningitis even if the isolate proves resistant, with close follow-up, and notes rifampin may benefit patients receiving vancomycin plus a cephalosporin plus dexamethasone. Rifampin is not a routine add-on and, in high-TB-burden settings, WHO restricts it to when vancomycin is unavailable.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.real_working_solution: In regions with documented pneumococcal cephalosporin resistance (the Indian sentinel data above show considerable resistance) start ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, monitor vancomycin troughs, and drop vancomycin as soon as the isolate is shown cephalosporin-susceptible.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819) (Table 2); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); Jayaraman Y et al., PLoS One 2018;13:e0197198 (PMID 29768458)

bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.name: Ampicillin (or Amoxicillin) Added for Listeria -- Age Over 50-60 Years, Pregnancy, Immunocompromise
specific_drugs: Ampicillin 12 g/day divided every 4 h (adults; German guideline 6 x 2 g/day) added to ceftriaxone (plus vancomycin where needed)
Impaired cellular immunity (IDSA 2004): vancomycin PLUS ampicillin PLUS either cefepime or meropenem
Penicillin-allergic alternative for proven Listeria: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.effectiveness: IDSA 2004 empiric regimen for age over 50 years: vancomycin plus ampicillin plus ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (add ampicillin whenever Listeria is a suspected pathogen). WHO 2025 (strong recommendation, very low certainty) adds IV ampicillin or amoxicillin when any Listeria risk factor is present: age over 60 years, pregnancy, immunosuppressive therapy, organ transplantation, malignancy, advanced HIV disease, diabetes mellitus, end-stage kidney disease, liver cirrhosis or alcohol use disorder. Listeria is not a trivial add-on: pooled case fatality for Listeria meningitis is 27% (van Ettekoven 2024) and in a Dutch nationwide cohort Listeria caused 162 of 2,664 adult bacterial meningitis episodes (6%) with 31% case fatality (Brouwer MC, van de Beek D, EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922, PMID 37007737).
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.reason_why: Listeria monocytogenes has intrinsic resistance to cephalosporins; ampicillin and penicillin are highly active (Brouwer 2010), so a cephalosporin-only regimen leaves the elderly and immunocompromised uncovered for this organism.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.important_caveat: IDSA 2004 sets the age threshold at over 50 years while WHO 2025 uses over 60 years plus a broader risk-factor list; the practical difference is the 50-60-year band without other risk factors, where local judgement applies.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.real_working_solution: For anyone over 50 (IDSA) or over 60 (WHO), pregnant, or with any listed Listeria risk factor, give ampicillin or amoxicillin together with the cephalosporin from the first dose, and stop it only when culture excludes Listeria.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Brouwer MC, van de Beek D, EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922 (PMID 37007737); van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802 (PMID 39093565)

bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.name: Low-Resource Fallback -- Chloramphenicol plus Ampicillin/Amoxicillin/Benzylpenicillin, and Single-Dose IM Ceftriaxone in Epidemics
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.type: Alternative empiric regimens when third-generation cephalosporins are unavailable
specific_drugs: Chloramphenicol IV (dose per national formulary; not standardised in the sources read) PLUS benzylpenicillin, ampicillin or amoxicillin -- only when ceftriaxone or cefotaxime are not immediately available
Where Hib vaccine coverage is low, prefer ampicillin or amoxicillin over benzylpenicillin as the partner drug
Epidemic meningococcal meningitis: ceftriaxone (single dose was non-inferior to oily chloramphenicol in the Niger trial; WHO 2025 advises 5 days of parenteral ceftriaxone in meningococcal epidemics)
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.effectiveness: WHO 2025 conditional recommendation (very low certainty): chloramphenicol with benzylpenicillin/ampicillin/amoxicillin should be considered for empiric treatment only when ceftriaxone or cefotaxime are not immediately available; in meningococcal epidemics WHO strongly recommends 5 days of parenteral ceftriaxone (very low certainty). In a randomised non-inferiority trial in Niger (510 suspected cases over 2 months of age) single-dose ceftriaxone and single-dose oily chloramphenicol had identical 72-hour treatment-failure rates of 9% (risk difference 0.3%, 90% CI -3.8 to 4.5) and similar case fatality (6% vs 5%) (Nathan N et al., Lancet 2005;366:308-313, PMID 16039333). The Cochrane review of pre-admission antibiotics found this to be the only qualifying trial and rated the evidence moderate quality (Sudarsanam TD et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;6:CD005437, PMID 28613408).
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.reason_why: IDSA 2004 notes that resistance to chloramphenicol developed among Haemophilus influenzae type b, one reason third-generation cephalosporins replaced it as the empiric drugs of choice; it remains a stop-gap where they are unavailable.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.real_working_solution: Use ceftriaxone whenever it can be obtained; if it truly cannot, chloramphenicol plus an aminopenicillin is the WHO-endorsed stop-gap, and in confirmed meningococcal epidemics short-course parenteral ceftriaxone is the evidence-backed simplification.
bm_empiric_therapy_infants_children_adul.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Nathan N et al., Lancet 2005;366:308-313 (PMID 16039333); Sudarsanam TD et al., Cochrane 2017;6:CD005437 (PMID 28613408); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.name: Vancomycin plus an Anti-Pseudomonal Beta-Lactam (Cefepime, Ceftazidime or Meropenem) -- Post-Neurosurgery, Head Trauma, CSF Shunt/Drain, Nosocomial Meningitis
bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.type: Empiric IV therapy for healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis
specific_drugs: Vancomycin 30-45 mg/kg/day divided every 8-12 h (target trough 15-20 micrograms/mL in seriously ill adults on intermittent dosing)
PLUS ONE of: ceftazidime 6 g/day divided every 8 h; cefepime 6 g/day divided every 8 h; meropenem 6 g/day divided every 8 h (adults)
Basilar skull fracture or recurrent community-acquired meningitis: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone or cefotaxime instead (pneumococcus predominates)

Beta-lactam anaphylaxis where meropenem is contraindicated: aztreonam or ciprofloxacin for Gram-negative cover; MSSA: nafcillin or oxacillin; MRSA: vancomycin; Acinetobacter: meropenem (carbapenem-resistant: colistimethate sodium or polymyxin B given IV and intraventricularly); rifampin added in combination when intracranial/spinal hardware is present
bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.effectiveness: IDSA 2004 (as tabulated in Brouwer 2010 and Medscape's reproduction) recommends vancomycin plus ceftazidime, cefepime or meropenem for head trauma, neurosurgery or CSF shunt; IDSA 2017 healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis guideline recommends vancomycin plus an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, ceftazidime or meropenem) chosen from local susceptibility, and the German guideline (2023) recommends vancomycin plus meropenem or ceftazidime (or cefepime), adding metronidazole after surgery involving mucous membranes. Durations per IDSA 2017: S. aureus or Gram-negative bacilli 10-14 days (some experts 21 days for Gram-negatives); coagulase-negative staphylococci or Propionibacterium acnes 10 days if minimal CSF inflammation and few symptoms, 10-14 days if significant; 10-14 days after the last positive CSF culture when cultures stay positive. Intraventricular therapy: clamp the drain 15-60 minutes and titrate to CSF concentrations 10-20 times the MIC.
bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.reason_why: After neurosurgery, trauma or shunting the pathogens shift from pneumococcus/meningococcus to staphylococci and aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter), which need anti-pseudomonal and MRSA-active cover. Acinetobacter ceftazidime resistance rose from 30% to 68% and cefepime resistance from 20% to 62% between 1999 and 2008 in US surveillance, so the local antibiogram matters, and meropenem is described as the carbapenem of choice (Brouwer 2010).
bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.important_caveat: Cefepime: a 2026 Bayesian meta-analysis of 110 randomised trials (22,608 patients, all indications, not meningitis-specific) found a 94.4% posterior probability that all-cause mortality was higher with cefepime than other beta-lactams (OR 1.10, 95% credible interval 0.98-1.24; OR 1.17 in published peer-reviewed trials) (Sohani ZN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2026;9:e2633017, PMID 42720951); this supports choosing meropenem or ceftazidime where local susceptibility allows, but it does not override an individual culture-guided decision. Meropenem's US label lists bacterial meningitis only for paediatric patients 3 months and older (40 mg/kg every 8 h, up to 2 g every 8 h); its adult meningitis use rests on IDSA (A-I) guideline recommendation, and the cefepime label text retrieved lists no meningitis indication.
bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.real_working_solution: Start vancomycin plus meropenem (or ceftazidime, or cefepime according to the local antibiogram) after any neurosurgical procedure, head trauma with CSF contact, or shunt/drain, take CSF (and shunt/drain) cultures before the first dose if possible, and de-escalate to the narrowest active agent when the organism is known; imipenem is avoided because of seizure risk (IDSA 2004, D-II).
bm_empiric_therapy_post_neurosurgical_sh.source: Tunkel AR et al. (IDSA), Clin Infect Dis 2017;64:e34-e65 (PMID 28203777) (recommendations read via Medscape's Meningitis Guidelines page, emedicine.medscape.com/article/232915); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.name: Meningococcal Meningitis -- Penicillin G/Ampicillin if Susceptible, Ceftriaxone/Cefotaxime if Not; 5-7 Days
bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.type: Organism-directed IV therapy after culture and susceptibility (Neisseria meningitidis)
specific_drugs: Penicillin MIC under 0.1 micrograms/mL: penicillin G 24 million units/day divided every 4 h, or ampicillin 12 g/day divided every 4 h
Penicillin MIC 0.1 micrograms/mL or above: ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 h or cefotaxime (IDSA alternatives: cefepime, chloramphenicol, a fluoroquinolone, meropenem)
Ceftriaxone-resistant meningococcus (German guideline, MIC over 0.125 mg/L): meropenem
bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.effectiveness: Duration: IDSA 2004 7 days; WHO 2025 Table 3.2 5-7 days; German guideline 7-10 days; during meningococcal epidemics WHO strongly recommends 5 days of parenteral ceftriaxone (very low certainty). Outcome data: pooled case fatality of meningococcal meningitis is 9% (van Ettekoven 2024); in 696 Dutch adults mortality was 7% for meningococcal versus 30% for pneumococcal meningitis (van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859, PMID 15509818); the median risk of a major sequela is 7.2% (Edmond 2010), the lowest of the three main pathogens. Penicillin resistance is rising: in Germany meningococcal penicillin resistance was 5.9% (2019), 3.9% (2020) and 8.5% (2021), so the German guideline advises against penicillin until susceptibility is known, while noting that switching a working cephalosporin to penicillin gives questionable benefit.
bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.reason_why: Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus that is usually highly susceptible to beta-lactams; in the Cochrane prophylaxis review rifampin was less effective than ceftriaxone at eradicating carriage at 1-2 weeks (RR 5.93 for failure; see chemoprophylaxis entry).
bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.important_caveat: Dexamethasone gave no mortality benefit in meningococcal meningitis in the Cochrane subgroup analysis (Brouwer 2015), and WHO 2025 gives a strong recommendation AGAINST routine corticosteroids during meningococcal epidemics; the German guideline says corticosteroids may be considered in meningococcal meningitis when hearing impairment is present.
bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.real_working_solution: Treat with ceftriaxone until susceptibility is known, narrow to penicillin G or ampicillin only when the MIC confirms susceptibility and local policy permits, complete 5-7 days, and start chemoprophylaxis for close contacts at once.
bm_directed_therapy_neisseria_meningitid.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read) (Table 3.2); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818); van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802 (PMID 39093565); Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414)

bm_directed_therapy_streptococcus_pneumo.name: Pneumococcal Meningitis -- Susceptibility-Tiered Therapy (Penicillin, Ceftriaxone, Vancomycin plus Ceftriaxone); 10-14 Days
bm_directed_therapy_streptococcus_pneumo.type: Organism-directed IV therapy after culture and susceptibility (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
specific_drugs: Penicillin MIC 0.06 micrograms/mL or below: penicillin G or ampicillin (alternatives: cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, chloramphenicol)
Penicillin-nonsusceptible (MIC 0.12 micrograms/mL or above) but cephalosporin-susceptible: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (alternatives: cefepime, meropenem)

Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone MIC 1.0 micrograms/mL or above: vancomycin PLUS ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (alternative: vancomycin plus moxifloxacin; WHO also lists rifampicin plus ceftriaxone/cefotaxime, or vancomycin plus rifampicin)
Dosing as for empiric therapy: ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 h (adults), vancomycin trough 15-20 micrograms/mL
bm_directed_therapy_streptococcus_pneumo.effectiveness: Duration 10-14 days (IDSA 2004; WHO 2025 Table 3.2; German guideline 10-14 days); during pneumococcal epidemics WHO conditionally recommends 10 days of parenteral ceftriaxone. IDSA 2004 advises repeat CSF analysis in patients who have not responded after 48 hours of appropriate therapy, particularly resistant strains and those given dexamethasone (A-III), but not routinely. Pneumococcus is the most lethal and most damaging of the common causes: pooled case fatality 24% (van Ettekoven 2024), 30% in Dutch adults (van de Beek 2004), and the median risk of a major sequela is 24.7% (Edmond 2010). Pneumococcal meningitis is also where the best adjunctive-dexamethasone evidence lies (see the dexamethasone entries).
bm_directed_therapy_streptococcus_pneumo.reason_why: Susceptibility varies by isolate, so the tiering keeps the narrowest effective drug while ensuring cephalosporin-resistant strains receive a second, mechanistically different agent (vancomycin or rifampin).
bm_directed_therapy_streptococcus_pneumo.real_working_solution: Send CSF and blood cultures with susceptibility testing before or immediately after the first dose, continue ceftriaxone (plus vancomycin if the MIC is 1.0 or above or is not yet known in a high-resistance setting), give dexamethasone if not already started, repeat the lumbar puncture at 48 hours only if the patient is not improving, and complete 10-14 days.
bm_directed_therapy_streptococcus_pneumo.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read) (Table 3.2); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802 (PMID 39093565); van de Beek D et al., N Engl J Med 2004;351:1849-1859 (PMID 15509818); Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414)

bm_directed_therapy_haemophilus_influenz.name: Haemophilus influenzae Meningitis -- Ampicillin if Beta-Lactamase-Negative, Ceftriaxone/Cefotaxime if Positive; 7-10 Days
bm_directed_therapy_haemophilus_influenz.type: Organism-directed IV therapy after culture and susceptibility (Haemophilus influenzae, mainly type b in the unvaccinated)
specific_drugs: Beta-lactamase-negative: ampicillin (alternatives: cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, cefepime, chloramphenicol, aztreonam, a fluoroquinolone)
Beta-lactamase-positive: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (alternatives: cefepime, chloramphenicol, aztreonam, a fluoroquinolone)
Beta-lactamase-negative but ampicillin-resistant: meropenem (alternatives: cefepime, chloramphenicol, aztreonam, a fluoroquinolone)
bm_directed_therapy_haemophilus_influenz.effectiveness: Duration: IDSA 2004 7 days; WHO 2025 Table 3.2 7-10 days; German guideline 7-10 days. Pooled case fatality 11% (van Ettekoven 2024); paediatric meta-analysis mortality 4%, adult mortality 6-14%, and hearing loss in up to 16% of children and 10-25% of adults (Brouwer 2010). Dexamethasone is best supported for Hib meningitis in children (severe hearing loss RR 0.34 in the 2015 Cochrane review; see dexamethasone entries). Vaccination has changed the picture: WHO notes a drastic decline in invasive Hib disease with conjugate vaccine but a growing number of cases caused by non-b serotypes and non-typeable strains.
bm_directed_therapy_haemophilus_influenz.reason_why: Ampicillin fails against beta-lactamase-producing strains and against the ampicillin-resistant beta-lactamase-negative subgroup, so a beta-lactamase result or MIC is needed before narrowing; expanded-spectrum cephalosporins became the standard therapy once chloramphenicol-resistant and beta-lactamase-producing strains emerged (Brouwer 2010).
bm_directed_therapy_haemophilus_influenz.real_working_solution: Treat empirically with ceftriaxone, narrow to ampicillin only when the isolate is beta-lactamase negative and ampicillin-susceptible, give dexamethasone with the first dose in children with suspected or proven Hib, and complete 7-10 days; give household rifampin chemoprophylaxis per the Hib entry.
bm_directed_therapy_haemophilus_influenz.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read) (Table 3.2, section 1.6.3); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802 (PMID 39093565)

bm_directed_therapy_listeria_monocytogen.name: Listeria Meningitis -- Ampicillin (or Penicillin G) with Consideration of an Aminoglycoside; Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole if Penicillin-Allergic; 21 Days
specific_drugs: Ampicillin 12 g/day divided every 4 h (or penicillin G 24 million units/day) -- backbone

Gentamicin as an optional synergistic partner (IDSA 2004 table footnote: 'addition of an aminoglycoside should be considered'; German guideline dose 3-6 mg/kg/day once daily with serum-level monitoring)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for penicillin-allergic patients (German guideline also lists meropenem)
bm_directed_therapy_listeria_monocytogen.effectiveness: Duration 21 days (WHO 2025 Table 3.2; IDSA 2004 'Listeria monocytogenes, 21 days or longer'). Pooled case fatality 27% (van Ettekoven 2024) and 31% (51 of 162 episodes) in a Dutch nationwide cohort, with an unfavourable outcome in 56% (Brouwer MC, van de Beek D, EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922, PMID 37007737). Honest evidence on the aminoglycoside: it has enhanced killing in vitro, but retrospective clinical data showed no benefit, and in a cohort of 118 listeriosis patients renal failure was more common in the aminoglycoside group with a possible mortality signal after adjustment (Mitja O et al., J Antimicrob Chemother 2009;64:416-423, as cited in Brouwer 2010; the study is retrospective and confounded by indication). Ampicillin or penicillin is therefore the evidence-backed core, and gentamicin is an optional add-on whose benefit is unproven.
bm_directed_therapy_listeria_monocytogen.reason_why: Listeria is intracellular and intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; ampicillin and penicillin are highly active, and combining an aminoglycoside is based on in-vitro synergy rather than clinical trial proof.
bm_directed_therapy_listeria_monocytogen.important_caveat: Dexamethasone in Listeria meningitis is genuinely contested: the French MONALISA cohort found higher mortality with adjunctive dexamethasone in neurolisteriosis (OR 4.58, 95% CI 1.50-13.98), whereas the later Dutch nationwide cohort found adjunctive dexamethasone associated with a lower rate of unfavourable outcome (adjusted OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.81); both are observational. See the dedicated dexamethasone entry.
bm_directed_therapy_listeria_monocytogen.real_working_solution: When Gram-positive bacilli or Listeria grow, switch (or add) ampicillin at full dose for 21 days; use gentamicin only with monitoring of renal function and levels if the treating team elects the combination; use trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if the patient is truly penicillin-allergic.
bm_directed_therapy_listeria_monocytogen.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read) (Table 3.2); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); Brouwer MC, van de Beek D, EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922 (PMID 37007737)

bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.name: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) Meningitis -- Penicillin G or Ampicillin; 14-21 Days
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.type: Organism-directed IV therapy (neonates, and older adults with comorbidity)
specific_drugs: Penicillin G or ampicillin (in neonates commonly combined with an aminoglycoside)
Alternatives: cefotaxime, ceftriaxone (outside the neonatal restrictions above), vancomycin
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.effectiveness: Duration 14-21 days (IDSA 2004; WHO 2025 Table 3.2). Neonatal mortality 7-27% (a large study of 276 cases: 14%), adult mortality 25-30%, and one-third of surviving neonates had sequelae including spastic quadriplegia, severe intellectual disability, hemiparesis, deafness or blindness (Brouwer 2010). The penicillin-plus-aminoglycoside neonatal combination has been standard although group B streptococci are frequently aminoglycoside-resistant; the choice rests on animal experiments showing better outcomes than penicillin alone (Brouwer 2010).
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.reason_why: Group B streptococcus remains susceptible to penicillin, ampicillin and cephalosporins; macrolide and aminoglycoside resistance is common.
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.real_working_solution: Treat with high-dose penicillin G or ampicillin for 14-21 days guided by clinical and CSF response; prevention in the newborn relies on intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis of colonised mothers (meta-analysis estimate of a 30-fold reduction in early-onset disease, with heterogeneous trials; Brouwer 2010).
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read) (Table 3.2); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.name: Aerobic Gram-Negative Bacillary Meningitis (Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas) and Staphylococcal Meningitis -- Culture-Directed; About 21 Days for Gram-Negatives
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.type: Organism-directed IV therapy for uncommon community-acquired and healthcare-associated pathogens
specific_drugs: Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus): ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (alternatives: aztreonam, a fluoroquinolone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, meropenem, ampicillin; German guideline: also cefepime) -- 21 days
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: ceftazidime or cefepime (alternatives: aztreonam, meropenem, ciprofloxacin) -- 21 days

Methicillin-susceptible S. aureus: nafcillin or oxacillin (German guideline: cefazolin, flucloxacillin); methicillin-resistant: vancomycin (alternatives linezolid, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, daptomycin); S. epidermidis: vancomycin, consider rifampin
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.effectiveness: IDSA 2004 (tabulated in Medscape's reproduction and Brouwer 2010) gives 21 days for Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas; in neonates the duration of Gram-negative therapy should be set partly by repeated lumbar punctures documenting CSF sterilisation (IDSA A-III). For healthcare-associated infections IDSA 2017 gives 10-14 days for S. aureus or Gram-negative bacilli (some experts 21 days for Gram-negatives). After the introduction of expanded-spectrum cephalosporins the prognosis of Gram-negative bacillary meningitis improved substantially, but multidrug resistance (Acinetobacter, ESBL/carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales) is a growing threat in post-neurosurgical patients (Brouwer 2010).
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.reason_why: These organisms appear after neurosurgery, head trauma, in neonates, or with bacteraemia from a distant focus, and their susceptibility varies widely, so treatment must follow the CSF culture and MIC rather than a fixed regimen.
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.real_working_solution: Identify the organism and MIC, choose the narrowest agent that reaches CSF, treat about 21 days for Gram-negative bacilli (10-14 days for S. aureus in healthcare-associated disease per IDSA 2017), and manage any hardware or parameningeal focus (see the complications entries).
bm_directed_therapy_group_b_streptococcu.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Tunkel AR et al. (IDSA), Clin Infect Dis 2017;64:e34-e65 (PMID 28203777); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.name: Do Not Delay Antibiotics for Lumbar Puncture or Imaging -- Real Timing Evidence (First-Hour Rule)
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.type: Treatment-timing rule for suspected bacterial meningitis
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) IV plus dexamethasone, started immediately after blood cultures, before CT or lumbar puncture whenever either is expected to cause delay
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.effectiveness: Delay costs lives. Proulx et al. (123 cases of adult bacterial meningitis, case fatality 13%): adjusted odds of death 8.4 (95% CI 1.7-40.9) for door-to-antibiotic time over 6 hours; the sequence head CT, then lumbar puncture, then antibiotics was associated with a door-to-antibiotic time over 6 hours (OR 5.6) (QJM 2005;98:291-298, PMID 15760921). Koster-Rasmussen et al. (187 culture-positive cases in east Denmark): antibiotic delay independently predicted an unfavourable outcome (OR 1.09 per hour; OR 1.30 per hour among adults treated within 12 hours), and the median time to adequate antibiotics was 1 h 39 min (J Infect 2008;57:449-454, PMID 19000639). Guidelines: WHO 2025 (strong recommendation, very low certainty) says treatment should not be delayed for cranial imaging or when lumbar puncture is deferred, regards the first hour as the golden window, and states that any delay in diagnostic investigations should not delay therapy; ESCMID 2016 advises starting empiric treatment within one hour of arrival; the German guideline advises within 1 hour and strictly avoiding a delay over 3 hours; IDSA 2004 says empiric antibiotics should not be delayed pending Gram stain or other diagnostic tests.
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.reason_why: Bacteria multiply and release inflammatory products in the subarachnoid space without host defences, so every hour of untreated infection adds to brain injury; treatment-first sacrifices some culture yield but saves neurons and lives.
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.important_caveat: Both delay studies are observational (retrospective), so confounding by illness severity is possible; the direction of association is consistent across studies and guidelines, but neither is a randomised trial. Prior antibiotics reduce culture yield (CSF culture positivity fell from 88% to 70% and from 66% to 62% in two large series; Brouwer 2010), but Gram stain often still identifies the organism: in an Indian series of 535 suspected cases Gram stain identified the organism in 36 of 55 pretreated patients (65%) versus culture in 5 (9%) (Brouwer 2010).
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.real_working_solution: Sequence for an unstable or slow-to-image patient: blood cultures, then IV antibiotics plus dexamethasone at once, then imaging if indicated, then lumbar puncture when safe. In a stable patient with no imaging indication, take blood cultures, do the lumbar puncture promptly, and give antibiotics immediately after (WHO good-practice statement: lumbar puncture as soon as possible, preferably before antimicrobials, unless contraindicated or deferred).
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Proulx N et al., QJM 2005;98:291-298 (PMID 15760921); Koster-Rasmussen R et al., J Infect 2008;57:449-454 (PMID 19000639); van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22 Suppl 3:S37-S62 (PMID 27062097), as summarised in van Ettekoven CN, van de Beek D, Brouwer MC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2017;23:601-606 (PMID 28478238); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.name: Cranial Imaging Before Lumbar Puncture -- Who Really Needs It
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.type: Selective pre-lumbar-puncture CT/MRI to avoid herniation
specific_drugs: CT head (or MRI) only for defined risk features; antibiotics and dexamethasone are given BEFORE the scan if imaging is delayed
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.effectiveness: WHO 2025: cranial imaging should NOT be performed routinely (strong recommendation against, very low certainty). Where imaging is readily accessible, perform it before lumbar puncture if any of: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new-onset seizures (adults), or a severe immunocompromised state (strong recommendation, very low certainty). Where imaging is not accessible, defer lumbar puncture while these features persist but do not delay treatment. IDSA 2004 lists immunocompromise, seizure within the previous week (adults), papilloedema, abnormal level of consciousness and focal neurological deficit as reasons for CT first (B-II). The evidence base: in 301 adults with suspected meningitis, 235 had CT before lumbar puncture, 24% were abnormal and 5% showed mass effect; when none of the baseline features (age 60 or over, immunocompromise, CNS disease history, seizure within a week, abnormal consciousness, inability to follow commands, gaze palsy, abnormal visual fields, facial palsy, arm or leg drift, abnormal language) was present, CT was normal in 93 of 96 (negative predictive value 97%) (Hasbun R et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1727-1733, PMID 11742046).
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.reason_why: Lumbar puncture in the presence of a mass lesion or marked brain swelling risks herniation, but most patients with meningitis have no such lesion, and the clinical features above identify those who do.
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.real_working_solution: Apply the WHO/IDSA feature list rather than scanning everyone; if a feature is present, give antibiotics and dexamethasone first, scan, and do the lumbar puncture only if no mass effect; monitor closely after the puncture because a few patients deteriorate despite a clear scan (German guideline recommendation 16).
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); Hasbun R et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1727-1733 (PMID 11742046); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.name: Antibiotics Before Hospital Admission -- Real (Limited) Evidence
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.type: Pre-admission parenteral antibiotic when transfer is likely to be delayed
specific_drugs: Parenteral antibiotic (IV; IM if no IV line can be secured) -- WHO does not specify a single agent; the only randomised comparison used IM ceftriaxone versus IM oily chloramphenicol
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.effectiveness: WHO 2025 (conditional recommendation, very low certainty): consider empiric parenteral antimicrobial treatment before admission or transfer when acute bacterial meningitis is strongly suspected and a clinically significant delay in transfer is likely. The Cochrane review of pre-admission antibiotics found NO randomised trial comparing pre-admission antibiotics with none; the one included open-label non-inferiority trial (510 participants, Niger epidemic) showed single-dose IM ceftriaxone non-inferior to oily chloramphenicol for mortality (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.57-2.56) (Sudarsanam TD et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;6:CD005437, PMID 28613408).
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.reason_why: The rationale is time: pre-admission dosing shortens time to first effective antibiotic when transport delay is expected.
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.important_caveat: There is no randomised evidence that pre-admission antibiotics reduce mortality versus no antibiotics; the recommendation is a conditional, expert-consensus one.
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.real_working_solution: In a remote setting with strong suspicion and expected delay, give one parenteral dose of ceftriaxone (IV if a line is in place, otherwise IM) before transfer and communicate this to the receiving team so lumbar puncture is done as soon as possible on arrival.
bm_timing_of_antibiotics_lumbar_puncture.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Sudarsanam TD et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;6:CD005437 (PMID 28613408); Nathan N et al., Lancet 2005;366:308-313 (PMID 16039333)

bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.name: Short-Course Ceftriaxone Evidence -- 5 versus 10 Days in Children; 5-Day Meningococcal Epidemic Regimen
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.type: Evidence for shortened antibiotic duration in uncomplicated cases
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone IV for 5 days (children over 2 months who are clinically stable at day 5 with pneumococcal, Hib or meningococcal meningitis) instead of 10 days
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.effectiveness: Molyneux et al.: double-blind placebo-controlled equivalence trial in 1,004 children aged 2 months to 12 years in ten hospitals (Bangladesh, Egypt, Malawi, Pakistan, Vietnam) given 5 versus 10 days of ceftriaxone: 2 relapses in the 5-day arm (one HIV-infected child), none in the 10-day arm, no bacteriological failures (Lancet 2011;377:1837-1845, PMID 21620467). Karageorgopoulos et al. meta-analysis of 5 paediatric RCTs (383 patients): short (4-7 days) versus long (7-14 days) ceftriaxone showed no difference in clinical success (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.73-2.11), neurological complications (OR 0.60, 0.29-1.27) or hearing impairment (OR 0.59, 0.28-1.23), with shorter hospital stay (-2.17 days) (Arch Dis Child 2009;94:607-614, PMID 19628879). WHO 2025: 5 days of parenteral ceftriaxone in meningococcal epidemics (strong, very low certainty) and 10 days in pneumococcal epidemics (conditional).
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.reason_why: Bacteria in CSF are cleared early with effective bactericidal therapy; late failures are rare when the patient is clinically stable, so the marginal benefit of longer courses is small.
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.important_caveat: The evidence is paediatric, non-neonatal and excludes cases unstable at day 5; the Karageorgopoulos meta-analysis could not analyse by organism and its authors call the data limited. Neonates, immunocompromised patients and complicated cases need longer, individualised courses.
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.real_working_solution: For a stable child who has completed 5 days of ceftriaxone for pneumococcal, Hib or meningococcal meningitis, stopping is evidence-supported; for adults, follow organism-specific durations (7-14 days) because comparable adult randomised data were not found in the Karageorgopoulos meta-analysis.
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.source: Molyneux E et al., Lancet 2011;377:1837-1845 (PMID 21620467); Karageorgopoulos DE et al., Arch Dis Child 2009;94:607-614 (PMID 19628879); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.name: Empiric Course When No Pathogen Is Found; Re-Puncture and Response Monitoring
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.type: Duration and monitoring rules for culture-negative or slow-responding meningitis
specific_drugs: Same empiric antibiotics (for example ceftriaxone with or without vancomycin/ampicillin) continued or extended as below; no new drug class
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.effectiveness: WHO 2025 (conditional, very low certainty): in non-epidemic settings with suspected or probable acute bacterial meningitis and no pathogen identified, empiric therapy may be stopped after 7 days if the person has clinically recovered, defined as all of the following for at least 48 hours: resolution of fever, resolution of vital-sign abnormalities, resolution of altered consciousness, and normal mental status. If there is no clinical recovery within one week, extend antibiotics and repeat the diagnostic work-up including a repeat lumbar puncture if no contraindication. IDSA 2004: repeat CSF analysis for patients not responding after 48 hours of appropriate therapy (A-III), particularly resistant strains or those who received dexamethasone, but not routinely.
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.reason_why: Non-response at 48 hours or one week signals a wrong drug, resistant organism, undrained focus or complication rather than the need for more of the same drug.
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.real_working_solution: Reassess daily; if clinically recovered for 48 hours with no pathogen and 7 days done, stop; if not recovering, repeat the lumbar puncture, review resistance, search for a parameningeal focus or intracranial complication, and extend treatment.
bm_duration_and_response_monitoring.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.name: Dexamethasone in Adults -- de Gans 2002 Landmark Trial, Cochrane 2015 and Nationwide Implementation Data
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.type: Adjunctive corticosteroid (anti-inflammatory) given with the first antibiotic dose
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days, first dose 15-20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic dose (de Gans trial regimen)
Alternatives when dexamethasone cannot be given (WHO 2025): IV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone at equivalent dosage
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.effectiveness: de Gans J, van de Beek D (N Engl J Med 2002;347:1549-1556, PMID 12432041): randomised double-blind multicentre trial, 301 adults (157 dexamethasone, 144 placebo). Unfavourable outcome at 8 weeks: relative risk 0.59 (95% CI 0.37-0.94, P=0.03); death: relative risk 0.48 (95% CI 0.24-0.96, P=0.04); in pneumococcal meningitis unfavourable outcome was 26% versus 52% (RR 0.50, 0.30-0.83); gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 2 dexamethasone versus 5 placebo patients. Cochrane 2015 (Brouwer MC et al., CD004405, PMID 26362566; 25 studies, 4,121 participants): overall mortality reduction was non-significant (17.8% vs 19.9%, RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.80-1.01) and in adults RR 0.74 (0.53-1.05), but corticosteroids reduced severe hearing loss (RR 0.67, 0.51-0.88), any hearing loss (RR 0.74, 0.63-0.87) and neurological sequelae (RR 0.83, 0.69-1.00), and reduced mortality in pneumococcal meningitis (RR 0.84, 0.72-0.98). Real-world implementation in the Netherlands (Brouwer MC et al., Neurology 2010;75:1533-1539, PMID 20881273): dexamethasone given with or before the first antibiotic dose in 84% of pneumococcal episodes in 2006-09 versus 3% in 1998-2002; mortality 20% versus 30% (P=0.001), hearing loss 12% versus 22%, unfavourable outcome 39% versus 50% (OR 0.63, 0.46-0.86) -- a historical-control comparison (Class III evidence). In 1,412 Dutch adult episodes 2006-14, adjunctive dexamethasone (given in 89%) was associated with an adjusted OR of 0.54 (0.39-0.73) for unfavourable outcome (Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347, PMID 26652862). WHO 2025: strong recommendation (low certainty) to start IV corticosteroids with the first antibiotic dose in children and adults with suspected bacterial meningitis in non-epidemic settings where lumbar puncture can be performed.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.reason_why: Dexamethasone dampens the subarachnoid inflammatory response (cytokine release triggered when antibiotics lyse bacteria), which drives cerebral oedema, vasculitis and hearing-nerve injury; the benefit is time-dependent (WHO 2025: beneficial effects likely decrease as the delay in administration increases), which is why it is given before or with the first antibiotic dose.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.important_caveat: Honest neutral/negative findings that qualify the picture: an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 5 trials (2,029 patients) found no significant reduction in death (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.79-1.19) or in death/severe neurological sequelae, only a reduction of hearing loss among survivors (24.1% vs 29.5%, OR 0.77, 0.60-0.99), and concluded the benefit for any subgroup remains unproven (van de Beek D et al., Lancet Neurol 2010;9:254-263, PMID 20138011); the Cochrane 2015 review found no effect on severe hearing loss when only high-quality studies were analysed and an increase in recurrent fever (RR 1.27, 1.09-1.47).
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.real_working_solution: Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours with (or 10-20 minutes before) the first antibiotic dose to every adult with suspected bacterial meningitis where lumbar puncture is available, and continue for 4 days only if pneumococcal (or Hib) disease is confirmed or remains likely.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.source: de Gans J, van de Beek D, N Engl J Med 2002;347:1549-1556 (PMID 12432041); Brouwer MC et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;CD004405 (PMID 26362566); Brouwer MC et al., Neurology 2010;75:1533-1539 (PMID 20881273); Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347 (PMID 26652862); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.name: Dexamethasone in Children -- Hib and Hearing-Loss Evidence, Weaker and Mixed Elsewhere
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.type: Adjunctive corticosteroid in paediatric bacterial meningitis
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 2-4 days (IDSA 2004, A-I), first dose 10-20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic
Equivalent regimen quoted in the Cochrane review and Brouwer 2010: 0.6 mg/kg/day for 4 days, first dose before or with the first antibiotic
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.effectiveness: Strongest signal is in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis and for hearing loss: Odio CM et al. (N Engl J Med 1991;324:1525-1531, PMID 2027357; 101 infants and children, dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 days, first dose 15-20 minutes before cefotaxime): neurological or audiological sequelae 14% (7/51) versus 38% (18/48), P=0.007. McIntyre PB et al. meta-analysis (JAMA 1997;278:925-931, PMID 9302246): Hib severe hearing loss combined OR 0.31 (0.14-0.69); in pneumococcal meningitis only studies giving dexamethasone early (with or before antibiotics) suggested protection (severe hearing loss OR 0.09, 0.0-0.71); gastrointestinal bleeding rose with duration (0.5% in controls, 0.8% with 2 days, 3.0% with 4 days), so the authors suggested limiting to 2 days may be optimal. Cochrane 2015: severe hearing loss in children with Hib meningitis RR 0.34 (0.20-0.59) but no reduction in non-Haemophilus meningitis; in high-income countries severe hearing loss RR 0.51 (0.35-0.73). IDSA 2004 states use in children with pneumococcal meningitis is controversial and that data are insufficient for neonates. WHO 2025 (strong, low certainty) covers children as well as adults, with a maximum of 4 days.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.reason_why: Same mechanism as in adults: dampening of the antibiotic-induced inflammatory surge that damages the cochlea and brain; the hearing endpoint is where the effect is most consistent.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.important_caveat: Weaker and mixed evidence in children outside Hib: the Malawian trial (598 children) found no effect (relative risk of death 1.00, 95% CI 0.80-1.25; sequelae 28% vs 28%) (Molyneux EM et al., Lancet 2002;360:211-218, PMID 12133656), and a US retrospective cohort of 2,780 children found no association of adjuvant corticosteroids with mortality at any age (Mongelluzzo J et al., JAMA 2008;299:2048-2055, PMID 18460665). Cochrane 2015 found no benefit in low-income countries.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.real_working_solution: In children in high-income-country settings (where the positive trials were done) with suspected bacterial meningitis, give 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours with the first antibiotic dose, continue up to 4 days if Hib or pneumococcus is confirmed or likely, and stop if the CSF is not consistent with bacterial meningitis or a non-pneumococcal/non-Hib organism is found.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.source: Odio CM et al., N Engl J Med 1991;324:1525-1531 (PMID 2027357); McIntyre PB et al., JAMA 1997;278:925-931 (PMID 9302246); Brouwer MC et al., Cochrane 2015;CD004405 (PMID 26362566); IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.name: Dexamethasone Timing, Continuation and Stop Rules
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.type: Practical administration rules for adjunctive dexamethasone
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone adults 10 mg IV every 6 hours; children 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours; maximum 4 days
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.effectiveness: Timing: IDSA 2004 recommends the first dose 10-20 minutes before (or at least with) the first antimicrobial dose (A-I), and says patients who have already received antimicrobials should not be given dexamethasone because it is unlikely to improve outcome (A-I). WHO 2025 says the beneficial effects are likely to decrease as the delay increases, so give it with the first antibiotic dose or as soon as possible after; the German guideline (2023) suggests it may be considered up to a few hours after starting antibiotics if it was not given at the start. Continuation: IDSA 2004 continues dexamethasone only if Gram-positive diplococci are seen on CSF Gram stain or S. pneumoniae is cultured; WHO 2025 continues up to a maximum of 4 days if CSF is consistent with bacterial meningitis (including when S. pneumoniae or Hib is detected) and discontinues it if the CSF is not consistent with bacterial meningitis or a pathogen other than S. pneumoniae/Hib is detected; the German guideline gives 4 days if pneumococci are found or pneumococcal meningitis is probable. Populations: WHO states the recommendations also apply to people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy with undetectable viral load (under 50 copies/microlitre), but corticosteroids have not proven beneficial in advanced HIV disease; corticosteroids should not be given for cerebral malaria.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.reason_why: WHO 2025 states that the beneficial effects of corticosteroids are likely to decrease as the delay in administration increases.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.real_working_solution: Give the first dexamethasone dose with the first antibiotic dose (before lumbar puncture results), then use CSF Gram stain/culture to decide: continue up to 4 days for pneumococcus or Hib (or when pneumococcal disease remains probable), stop for other organisms or non-bacterial CSF.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.source: IDSA 2004: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, Kaufman BA, Roos KL, Scheld WM, Whitley RJ, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267-1284 (PMID 15494903) -- archived on idsociety.org; recommendations read via the AAFP summary (Smith L, Am Fam Physician 2005;71:2003-2008) and the IDSA tables reproduced in Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.name: Dexamethasone in High-HIV / Low-Income Settings -- Real Neutral Trial Results
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.type: Real negative and qualified adjunctive-corticosteroid trial evidence
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone 16 mg twice daily for 4 days (Malawi adult trial regimen)
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.effectiveness: Scarborough M et al. (N Engl J Med 2007;357:2441-2450, PMID 18077809): 465 adults in Blantyre, Malawi, 90% HIV-positive, dexamethasone 16 mg twice daily for 4 days versus placebo: death at 40 days 129/231 versus 120/228, OR 1.14 (0.79-1.64), no benefit for proven pneumococcal disease, disability, hearing or adverse events. Nguyen TH et al. (N Engl J Med 2007;357:2431-2440, PMID 18077808): 435 Vietnamese adolescents and adults: intention-to-treat no significant reduction in death at 1 month (RR 0.79, 0.45-1.39) or death/disability at 6 months (OR 0.74, 0.47-1.17), but in microbiologically confirmed bacterial meningitis (300 patients) death at 1 month RR 0.43 (0.20-0.94) and death/disability at 6 months OR 0.56 (0.32-0.98); no benefit in 'probable' cases, where tuberculous meningitis may explain an excess of deaths with dexamethasone. Cochrane 2015: no beneficial effect of corticosteroids in low-income countries. WHO 2025: corticosteroids have not proven beneficial in advanced HIV disease.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.reason_why: The reasons for the difference are not established; the trial populations differ from the European adult trial (advanced HIV in the Malawi trial, and in the Vietnam trial 'probable' cases in which tuberculous meningitis may explain an excess of deaths with dexamethasone).
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.real_working_solution: Use dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose where microbiologically confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial (especially pneumococcal) meningitis is likely and the patient is not in advanced HIV disease; recognise that in high-HIV settings the benefit is unproven and do not delay antibiotics for it.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.source: Scarborough M et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2441-2450 (PMID 18077809); Nguyen TH et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2431-2440 (PMID 18077808); Brouwer MC et al., Cochrane 2015 (PMID 26362566); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.name: Dexamethasone in Listeria Meningitis -- Contested Observational Evidence
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours (Dutch standard regimen) -- do not stop solely because Listeria is suspected on current Dutch evidence; French evidence argues the opposite
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.effectiveness: Charlier C et al., MONALISA nationwide French cohort (818 listeriosis cases, 252 neurolisteriosis; Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:510-519, PMID 28139432): neurolisteriosis mortality was higher in patients who received adjunctive dexamethasone (OR 4.58, 95% CI 1.50-13.98, P=0.008). Brouwer MC, van de Beek D (EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922, PMID 37007737): Dutch nationwide prospective cohort of 162 Listeria monocytogenes meningitis episodes (2006-2022): dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose in 58%; adjusted OR for unfavourable outcome 0.40 (0.19-0.81); the authors concluded dexamethasone should not be withheld if Listeria is suspected or detected and note that guidelines based on the French cohort advise stopping dexamethasone when the pathogen is detected.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.reason_why: Whether dexamethasone-induced immunosuppression worsens an intracellular infection (Listeria) or whether the observed harm reflects confounding is unresolved; both cohorts are observational.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.important_caveat: Conflicting observational data; no randomised trial of dexamethasone in Listeria meningitis exists in the sources reviewed.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.real_working_solution: Because the two large observational cohorts disagree, the decision to continue dexamethasone once Listeria is identified should be made by the treating infectious-disease team on the individual case; ampicillin at full dose is the non-negotiable component either way.
bm_adjunctive_dexamethasone.source: Charlier C et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:510-519 (PMID 28139432); Brouwer MC, van de Beek D, EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922 (PMID 37007737)

bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.name: Glycerol -- Real Negative Adult Trial and Cochrane Osmotic-Therapy Review
specific_drugs: Glycerol 75 mL orally four times daily for 4 days (highest tolerated dose in the Malawi trial; not recommended)
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.effectiveness: Ajdukiewicz KM et al. (Lancet Infect Dis 2011;11:293-300, PMID 21334262): double-blind trial in 265 Malawian adults with bacterial meningitis and high HIV prevalence, stopped early: death by day 40 was 63% with glycerol versus 49% with placebo (adjusted OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.3-4.2, P=0.003), no benefit for death and disability. Cochrane 2018 (Wall EC et al., CD008806, PMID 29405037; 5 trials, 1,451 participants): glycerol probably has little or no effect on death (RR 1.08, 0.90-1.30, moderate certainty), may reduce neurological disability (RR 0.73, 0.53-1.00, low certainty) and deafness (RR 0.64, 0.44-0.93). WHO 2025 (conditional recommendation against, low certainty): glycerol should not be used routinely in children and adults with suspected, probable or confirmed bacterial meningitis, and the GDG judged this applicable to all settings because glycerol was independently associated with mortality in the resource-limited HIV-prevalent trials. The German guideline also recommends against routine glycerol.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.reason_why: Osmotic therapies were proposed to draw extravascular fluid out of the brain and reduce cerebral oedema (Cochrane 2018 rationale); glycerol did not reduce death and in the adult African trial was associated with higher mortality.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.real_working_solution: Do not add glycerol; use the proven combination (prompt antibiotics plus dexamethasone) and, for impending herniation, the ICP measures in the raised-ICP entries.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.source: Ajdukiewicz KM et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2011;11:293-300 (PMID 21334262); Wall EC et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;CD008806 (PMID 29405037); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.name: Induced Hypothermia -- Real Negative Trial (Trial Stopped Early for Excess Mortality)
specific_drugs: Cold-saline 4 C loading then cooling to 32-34 C for 48 hours (trial regimen; not recommended)
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.effectiveness: Mourvillier B et al. (JAMA 2013;310:2174-2183, PMID 24105303): open-label randomised trial in 49 French ICUs, 98 comatose adults (GCS 8 or below) with community-acquired bacterial meningitis, stopped early on the request of the data and safety monitoring board: mortality 51% (25/49) with hypothermia versus 31% (15/49) with standard care (RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.05-3.77, P=0.04); unfavourable outcome at 3 months 86% versus 74% (RR 2.17, 0.78-6.01, not significant); 77% had pneumococcal meningitis. The German guideline recommends against routine hypothermia.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.reason_why: Cooling was tried because induced hypothermia helps in other conditions with global cerebral hypoxia; in severe bacterial meningitis it did not improve outcome and the data monitoring board stopped the trial for excess mortality; the mechanism of harm is not established.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.real_working_solution: Do not use induced hypothermia in bacterial meningitis; treat fever with standard antipyresis and manage raised ICP with the measures below.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.source: Mourvillier B et al., JAMA 2013;310:2174-2183 (PMID 24105303); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.name: Activated Protein C -- Real Negative Finding for Bacterial Meningitis
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.type: Sepsis adjunct (tested retrospectively, not recommended in meningitis)
specific_drugs: Activated protein C (drotrecogin alfa) -- not recommended for bacterial meningitis
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.effectiveness: Brouwer 2010: activated protein C reduced mortality in severe sepsis but cannot be advised for patients at low risk of death because of bleeding; a retrospective analysis of 4,096 patients in activated-protein-C trials found intracranial haemorrhage in 6% of the 128 adults with meningitis, so it cannot be recommended for bacterial meningitis.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.reason_why: The problem is bleeding: activated protein C carried a 6% intracranial haemorrhage rate in adults with meningitis in the retrospective analysis.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.real_working_solution: Do not use activated protein C for meningitis; meningococcal or pneumococcal sepsis is managed with standard sepsis care and antibiotics.
bm_adjunctive_therapies_not_supported.source: Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_fluid_management.name: Maintenance Fluids -- Do Not Routinely Restrict Fluids
bm_fluid_management.type: Isotonic fluid management, not fluid restriction
specific_drugs: Maintenance fluids preferably orally or by enteric (nasogastric) tube; if IV is needed, isotonic solutions such as Ringer's lactate or normal saline
Moderate fluid restriction only if syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is clinically suggested and there is no shock or hypovolaemia
bm_fluid_management.effectiveness: WHO 2025 (conditional recommendation against, very low certainty): fluid intake should not be routinely restricted in children and adults with suspected, probable or confirmed acute bacterial meningitis. Cochrane 2016 (Maconochie IK, Bhaumik S, CD004786, PMID 27813057; 3 trials, 420 children, no adult trials): no significant difference in death between maintenance and restricted fluid (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.53-1.27) or acute severe neurological sequelae (RR 0.67, 0.41-1.08), but a significant advantage for maintenance fluid for spasticity (RR 0.50, 0.27-0.93) and seizures at 72 hours (RR 0.59, 0.42-0.83); evidence low to very low quality. A 2026 systematic review of the two randomised trials (407 children) found restriction did not significantly change mortality (RR 1.19, 0.77-1.85) or neurological sequelae (RR 1.31, 0.74-2.30) (Netravathi M et al., BMC Med 2026, PMID 42472812).
bm_fluid_management.reason_why: Earlier practice restricted fluids because of hyponatraemia attributed to raised antidiuretic hormone (Netravathi 2026); the Cochrane review notes that both over- and under-hydration are associated with adverse outcomes, and the randomised data (children only) show no benefit from restriction, with some secondary outcomes favouring maintenance fluids.
bm_fluid_management.important_caveat: If Ringer's lactate is used for maintenance or resuscitation, do not mix it with ceftriaxone in the same line or diluent (calcium precipitation risk per the ceftriaxone FDA label; contraindicated with calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates 28 days or younger).
bm_fluid_management.real_working_solution: Give normal maintenance fluids (oral or nasogastric where possible, isotonic IV otherwise), correct shock with fluid resuscitation, monitor sodium, and restrict moderately only for suspected SIADH without shock.
bm_fluid_management.source: Maconochie IK, Bhaumik S, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;CD004786 (PMID 27813057); Netravathi M et al., BMC Med 2026 (PMID 42472812); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.name: Meningococcal Chemoprophylaxis for Close Contacts -- Ceftriaxone, Ciprofloxacin, Rifampin (Azithromycin Not Routine)
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.type: Post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis of close contacts (carriage eradication)
specific_drugs: Rifampin orally for 2 days: infants under 1 month 5 mg/kg every 12 h; 1 month and older 10 mg/kg every 12 h (maximum 600 mg per dose); adults and adolescents over 60 kg 600 mg every 12 h (German/RKI table)
Ceftriaxone single IM dose: 125 mg for under 15 years; 250 mg for 15 years and older
Ciprofloxacin single oral dose 20 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg), age 1 month and older (adults 500 mg)
Azithromycin single oral dose 10 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) -- not recommended routinely; equivalent to rifampin for nasopharyngeal eradication in one study
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.effectiveness: WHO 2025 (strong recommendation, very low certainty): in sporadic disease, single-dose parenteral ceftriaxone or oral ciprofloxacin should be given to close contacts of laboratory-confirmed meningococcal disease (during large epidemics, to close contacts of clinically suspected cases), according to known susceptibility patterns; rifampicin should be considered (conditional) when ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin cannot be given. WHO defines close contacts, in the 7 days before symptom onset until 24 hours after the index case starts appropriate antibiotics, as people with prolonged exposure within 1 metre (for example household contacts) and people directly exposed to the index case's oral secretions (kissing, mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, endotracheal intubation). Prophylaxis should start as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of identifying the index case; later than 14 days after case identification it likely has limited or no benefit (WHO 2025; NJDOH 2025).
