Evidence (Cochrane 2013, Zalmanovici Trestioreanu A et al., CD004785, PMID 24163051; 24 studies, 2,531 randomised participants plus 4,354 cluster-randomised): no cases of meningococcal disease occurred in the trials, so effectiveness against disease could not be measured directly; against placebo at one week, ciprofloxacin (RR of carriage 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.12), rifampin (RR 0.17, 0.13-0.24), minocycline (RR 0.28) and penicillin (RR 0.47, 0.24-0.94) eradicated N. meningitidis carriage; no trial compared ceftriaxone with placebo, but rifampin was less effective than ceftriaxone after 1-2 weeks (RR 5.93, 1.22-28.68); resistant isolates appeared after rifampin.
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.reason_why: The risk of secondary meningococcal disease is 400- to 800-fold higher in close contacts than in the general population (WHO 2025), and prophylaxis works by clearing the organism from the contact's nasopharynx before it invades.
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.important_caveat: Ciprofloxacin resistance is rising: CDC advises health departments to preferentially use rifampin, ceftriaxone or azithromycin instead of ciprofloxacin when both (1) two or more invasive meningococcal cases caused by ciprofloxacin-resistant strains and (2) at least 20% of reported invasive cases being ciprofloxacin-resistant occur in a local catchment area in a rolling 12 months (Berry I et al., MMWR 2024;73:99-103, PMID 38329923); WHO also says the antibiotic should follow local susceptibility. Rifampin is not recommended in pregnant women, can interfere with oral contraceptive efficacy and some seizure and anticoagulant medications, stains body fluids red and can stain soft contact lenses; prophylaxis is generally not recommended for asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriers because efficacy beyond a few weeks is unproven (NJDOH 2025). Vaccination status does not remove the need for prophylaxis (NJDOH: prophylaxis regardless of vaccination status); for household and household-like contacts of a case with a vaccine-preventable serogroup (A, C, W, Y, B) the German guideline also recommends post-exposure vaccination in addition to chemoprophylaxis.
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.real_working_solution: Identify close contacts at once, give one of the regimens above within 24 hours, choose the agent by the local ciprofloxacin-resistance pattern (see caveat), tell contacts to seek care immediately for fever, and if the index patient was treated with penicillin G give an eradication course (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) before discharge (German guideline).
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); New Jersey Department of Health Communicable Disease Service Manual, Invasive Meningococcal Disease chapter, January 2025 (reproducing AAP Red Book 2024 and CDC regimens; full text read); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122) (Table 6, RKI rifampin/ciprofloxacin regimens); Zalmanovici Trestioreanu A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;CD004785 (PMID 24163051); Berry I et al., MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2024;73:99-103 (PMID 38329923)

bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.name: Droplet Precautions and Contact Surveillance After a Meningococcal or Hib Case
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- droplet precautions (single room or cohorting, surgical mask) for the patient
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.effectiveness: NJDOH 2025 (invasive meningococcal disease) and the AAP Red Book 2024 (invasive Hib disease) both recommend droplet precautions in addition to standard precautions through 24 hours after initiation of effective antimicrobial therapy; the NJDOH chapter recommends personal surveillance of close contacts for at least 10 days from last exposure and, for childcare centres, prophylaxis for all attendees in the index child's class (not for classmates from kindergarten upward, where close contacts are more defined). For air travel, prophylaxis is recommended for anyone seated directly next to the index case on a flight over 8 hours, or within one seat in any direction on a flight of any duration if the index case was coughing or vomiting (NJDOH 2025).
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.reason_why: Meningococcus and Hib spread by respiratory droplets and oropharyngeal secretions, and precautions are recommended until 24 hours after effective therapy begins (NJDOH; Red Book; the German guideline states contagiousness is no longer expected after 24 hours).
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.real_working_solution: Isolate for 24 hours after the first effective dose, notify public health (invasive meningococcal disease is immediately reportable in New Jersey per NJDOH), identify close contacts, give prophylaxis, and counsel contacts on early symptoms.
bm_chemoprophylaxis_meningococcal_contac.source: New Jersey Department of Health Communicable Disease Service Manual, Invasive Meningococcal Disease chapter, January 2025 (reproducing AAP Red Book 2024 and CDC regimens; full text read); AAP Red Book 2024-2027, Haemophilus influenzae infections chapter, pp. 403-404 (full text of the chapter read)

bm_chemoprophylaxis_haemophilus_influenz.name: Rifampin Chemoprophylaxis for Household Contacts of Invasive Hib Disease
bm_chemoprophylaxis_haemophilus_influenz.type: Post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis (Haemophilus influenzae type b)
specific_drugs: Rifampin orally once daily for 4 days: 20 mg/kg (maximum 600 mg); adults 600 mg per dose; infants under 1 month dose not established (some experts use 10 mg/kg)
If rifampin is contraindicated, a single dose of ceftriaxone can be considered (durability of eradication not well established)
bm_chemoprophylaxis_haemophilus_influenz.effectiveness: Red Book 2024 (Table 3.10): chemoprophylaxis is recommended for ALL household contacts (people residing with the index patient, or non-residents who spent 4 or more hours with them on at least 5 of the 7 days before admission) when the household includes at least 1 child under 4 years who is unimmunised or incompletely immunised, a child under 12 months who has not completed the primary Hib series, or an immunocompromised child of any age or immunisation status; also for preschool/childcare contacts when 2 or more cases occur within 60 days and unimmunised/incompletely immunised children attend; and for the index patient if under 2 years (or in a household with a susceptible contact) and treated with a regimen other than cefotaxime or ceftriaxone. It is NOT recommended for households with no children under 4 years, when all contacts are immunocompetent and appropriately immunised, for contacts of a single childcare case, for index patients over 2 years or treated with a full cefotaxime/ceftriaxone course, or for pregnant people. Rifampin eradicates Hib from the pharynx in about 95% of carriers and decreases the risk of secondary invasive illness; most secondary household cases occur in the first week, so start as soon as possible, although starting 7 or more days after hospitalisation of the index case may still help (Red Book 2024, referencing CDC ACIP 2014, MMWR Recomm Rep 2014;63(RR-1):1-14).
bm_chemoprophylaxis_haemophilus_influenz.reason_why: Unimmunised young children in a household with an invasive Hib case are at increased risk of secondary disease; rifampin removes the carried organism.
bm_chemoprophylaxis_haemophilus_influenz.real_working_solution: Give rifampin for 4 days to all household contacts (including adults) when the criteria above are met, and complete or update the Hib vaccination of any under-immunised child.
bm_chemoprophylaxis_haemophilus_influenz.source: AAP Red Book 2024-2027, Haemophilus influenzae infections chapter, pp. 403-404 (full text of the chapter read)

bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.name: Haemophilus influenzae Type b (Hib) Conjugate Vaccine -- Real Primary Prevention
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.type: Conjugate vaccine (monovalent or in pentavalent DPT-HepB-Hib combination)
specific_drugs: Hib conjugate vaccine (monovalent), or the pentavalent DPT-HepB-Hib vaccine used in India's programme
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.effectiveness: Burden before/around vaccine scale-up: Hib caused about 8.13 million serious illnesses and 371,000 deaths in children under 5 in 2000, judged 'almost entirely vaccine preventable' (Watt JP et al., Lancet 2009;374:903-911, PMID 19748399). Impact: estimated Hib deaths in children aged 1-59 months fell by 90% (uncertainty range 78-96%) between 2000 and 2015 as vaccine use expanded (Wahl B et al., Lancet Glob Health 2018;6:e744-e757, PMID 29903376). WHO states Hib vaccine is used in most national childhood immunisation programmes worldwide. India: the introduction of Hib as the pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib) vaccine in two states is described in Gupta SK et al., Indian Pediatr 2012;49:707-709 (PMID 23024078), and India still had the largest number of estimated Hib deaths (15,600) in 2015 (Wahl 2018). WHO 2025 (section 1.6.3) notes reports of a growing number of non-b serotype and non-typeable H. influenzae cases, which the Hib vaccine does not cover.
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.reason_why: Conjugating the Hib capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein makes the vaccine T-cell dependent so infants respond and nasopharyngeal carriage falls, reducing both direct and herd disease.
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.real_working_solution: Ensure every infant completes the Hib-containing primary series and booster per the national schedule; treat any under-immunised child in a household with a Hib case per the chemoprophylaxis entry.
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.source: Watt JP et al., Lancet 2009;374:903-911 (PMID 19748399); Wahl B et al., Lancet Glob Health 2018;6:e744-e757 (PMID 29903376); Gupta SK et al., Indian Pediatr 2012;49:707-709 (PMID 23024078); WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025; WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.name: Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV7/PCV13/PCV10) -- Real Primary Prevention of Invasive Pneumococcal Disease Including Meningitis
specific_drugs: PCV7 (Prevnar), PCV13 (Prevnar 13), 10-valent PCV including PNEUMOSIL (used in India's universal immunisation programme)
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.effectiveness: Cochrane 2009 (Lucero MG et al., CD004977, PMID 19821336; 6 RCTs, 57,015 vaccinated children): pooled vaccine efficacy against vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease 80% (95% CI 58-90%), all-serotype invasive disease 58% (29-75%). US population data after PCV7 licensure: invasive pneumococcal disease in children under 2 years fell 69% (188.0 to 59.0 per 100,000), vaccine-serotype disease fell 78%, disease from penicillin-nonsusceptible strains fell 35%, and adults also benefited through herd protection (Whitney CG et al., N Engl J Med 2003;348:1737-1746, PMID 12724479). Netherlands adults 2006-14: incidence of adult bacterial meningitis fell from 1.72 to 0.94 per 100,000 per year, most sharply for pneumococcal serotypes in the paediatric vaccine, with no evidence of serotype replacement (Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347, PMID 26652862). India: pneumococcus caused 82.9% of confirmed meningitis in Indian children under 5 in the sentinel network and over 90% of identified serotypes were covered by PCV13 (Jayaraman Y et al., PLoS One 2018;13:e0197198, PMID 29768458); PCV was introduced phase-wise and rolled out nationwide by 2021 (Kumar P et al., Vaccines 2025;13, PMID 40333310).
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.reason_why: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines induce serotype-specific antibody and reduce carriage, protecting vaccinated infants and, by reduced transmission, unvaccinated adults.
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.important_caveat: Vaccine efficacy against all-serotype disease (58%) is lower than against vaccine serotypes (80%) because non-vaccine serotypes remain; in the Cochrane review the 11% reduction in all-cause mortality did not reach statistical significance (95% CI -1 to 21%).
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.real_working_solution: Complete the PCV schedule in infancy; after recovery from pneumococcal meningitis, ESCMID advises pneumococcal vaccination to prevent recurrence, and patients with recurrent meningitis, complement deficiency or splenectomy should be vaccinated (Brouwer 2010).
bm_prevention_vaccination_hib_and_pneumo.source: Lucero MG et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;CD004977 (PMID 19821336); Whitney CG et al., N Engl J Med 2003;348:1737-1746 (PMID 12724479); Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347 (PMID 26652862); Jayaraman Y et al., PLoS One 2018;13:e0197198 (PMID 29768458); Kumar P et al., Vaccines 2025;13 (PMID 40333310); van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22 Suppl 3:S37-S62 (PMID 27062097), as summarised in van Ettekoven CN, van de Beek D, Brouwer MC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2017;23:601-606 (PMID 28478238); Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

bm_prevention_vaccination_meningococcal.name: Meningococcal Vaccines -- MenACWY, MenB (4CMenB/Bexsero, Trumenba), MenABCWY (Penbraya), MenAfriVac and Men5CV
specific_drugs: MenACWY conjugate: Menveo (MenACWY-CRM), MenQuadfi; MenB: Bexsero (4CMenB), Trumenba (MenB-fHbp); pentavalent MenABCWY: Penbraya (vaccines listed as available in the US as of January 2025)
MenAfriVac (PsA-TT, serogroup A conjugate) for the African meningitis belt; Men5CV (serogroups A, C, W, Y, X), the first pentavalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine, prequalified by WHO in 2023
bm_prevention_vaccination_meningococcal.effectiveness: MenACWY adolescent programme, England: after vaccination of 13-18 year olds began in 2015, MenW cases in 14-18 year olds fell (incidence rate ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.17-0.76) and MenY cases fell (0.21, 0.07-0.59); overall vaccine effectiveness against MenCWY combined was 94% (80-99) (Campbell H et al., Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2022;6:96-105, PMID 34883094). MenB, England infants (4CMenB, two-dose priming plus 12-month booster): group B disease incidence 75% lower in fully eligible cohorts (63 observed vs 253 expected cases; incidence rate ratio 0.25, 0.19-0.36), an estimated 277 cases prevented over 3 years; adjusted vaccine effectiveness point estimates 52.7% (two-dose) and 59.1% (two-dose plus booster) but with very wide confidence intervals (-33.5 to 83.2 and -31.1 to 87.2) (Ladhani SN et al., N Engl J Med 2020;382:309-317, PMID 31971676). MenAfriVac, Chad: 1.8 million people aged 1-29 vaccinated; 2012 meningitis incidence 2.48 per 100,000 in vaccinated regions versus 43.8 per 100,000 elsewhere (incidence rate ratio 0.096, 0.046-0.198), and serogroup A carriage fell (adjusted OR 0.019) (Daugla DM et al., Lancet 2014;383:40-47, PMID 24035220); across nine African countries 2010-15, suspected meningitis incidence fell 57% in vaccinated versus unvaccinated populations and confirmed group A disease fell by more than 99% in fully vaccinated populations, but the incidence rate ratio for non-A serogroups was higher after campaigns (2.76, 1.21-6.30), meaning other serogroups need surveillance (Trotter CL et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:867-872, PMID 28545721). WHO 2025 calls vaccination the primary control intervention against meningococcal disease.
bm_prevention_vaccination_meningococcal.reason_why: Conjugate vaccines induce immune memory and reduce nasopharyngeal carriage, which is why the adolescent (high-carriage) programme produced herd protection; protein-based MenB vaccines target subcapsular antigens because the group B capsule is poorly immunogenic.
bm_prevention_vaccination_meningococcal.important_caveat: Vaccine effectiveness estimates for 4CMenB against group B disease have very wide confidence intervals crossing zero in the infant analysis, so the population-level incidence drop (75%) is the more informative number; MenAfriVac data are observational surveillance analyses.
bm_prevention_vaccination_meningococcal.real_working_solution: Follow the national schedule for MenACWY (the UK programme targets adolescents) and MenB (the UK programme targets infants); vaccinate patients with recurrent meningococcal meningitis due to complement deficiency or splenectomy (Brouwer 2010); in the meningitis belt use MenAfriVac/Men5CV campaigns; for household contacts of a vaccine-preventable-serogroup case add post-exposure vaccination to (not instead of) chemoprophylaxis (German guideline).
bm_prevention_vaccination_meningococcal.source: Campbell H et al., Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2022;6:96-105 (PMID 34883094); Ladhani SN et al., N Engl J Med 2020;382:309-317 (PMID 31971676); Daugla DM et al., Lancet 2014;383:40-47 (PMID 24035220); Trotter CL et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:867-872 (PMID 28545721); New Jersey Department of Health Communicable Disease Service Manual, Invasive Meningococcal Disease chapter, January 2025 (reproducing AAP Red Book 2024 and CDC regimens; full text read); WHO Meningitis fact sheet, 1 April 2025; WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.name: Osmotic Agents for Impending Brain Herniation -- Mannitol, Sorbitol, Hypertonic Saline (Temporary Measure; No Meningitis-Specific Randomised Trial)
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.type: Hyperosmolar therapy for acute intracranial hypertension
specific_drugs: Mannitol 20% IV (German guideline: temporary osmotherapy with 20% mannitol may be considered); hypertonic saline or sorbitol as alternatives per WHO (doses per institutional neurocritical protocol -- not standardised in the meningitis sources reviewed)
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.effectiveness: WHO 2025 remark: osmotic agents other than glycerol, such as mannitol, sorbitol and hypertonic saline, can be used as a temporary measure for increased intracranial pressure in children and adults with bacterial meningitis and signs of impending brain herniation (rapid change in level of consciousness, hypertension, bradycardia, loss of pupillary reaction); interventions with a more durable effect (ventilatory support, decompressive craniectomy) may be needed; mannitol is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines; the GDG lists the effect of osmotic agents other than glycerol in bacterial meningitis as a research gap. German guideline (2023, recommendation 25): for raised ICP, elevate the upper body to 30 degrees, deep sedation, external ventricular drainage; in ventilated patients short-term hyperventilation to pCO2 32-35 mm Hg may be considered; temporary osmotherapy with 20% mannitol may be considered. Neurocritical Care Society cerebral-oedema guideline (Cook AM et al., Neurocrit Care 2020;32:647-666, PMID 32227294): hyperosmolar therapy may help reduce ICP in other neurological insults, but neurological outcomes do not appear to be affected, and corticosteroids appear helpful in reducing cerebral oedema in bacterial meningitis. Preclinical only: hypertonic saline attenuated brain oedema more than mannitol in a rabbit bacterial-meningitis model (Liu S et al., Crit Care Med 2011;39:1467-1473, PMID 21336112).
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.reason_why: Hyperosmolar agents draw water out of oedematous brain tissue across the blood-brain barrier gradient, lowering ICP briefly, which buys time for definitive measures.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.important_caveat: No randomised trial of mannitol or hypertonic saline specifically in bacterial meningitis was identified (the Cochrane osmotic-therapy review found only glycerol trials); the recommendation is expert-consensus, and hyperosmolar therapy has not been shown to improve neurological outcome in other brain injuries.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.real_working_solution: For a deteriorating patient with signs of impending herniation give mannitol or hypertonic saline as a bridge, secure the airway and ventilate, elevate the head 30 degrees, and move rapidly to CSF drainage/ICP-targeted care or neurosurgical decompression; do not use osmotic agents prophylactically as a substitute for antibiotics and dexamethasone.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); Cook AM et al., Neurocrit Care 2020;32:647-666 (PMID 32227294); Liu S et al., Crit Care Med 2011;39:1467-1473 (PMID 21336112)

bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.name: ICP Monitoring and ICP-Targeted Neurointensive Care (CSF Drainage via External Ventricular Drain)
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.type: Neurocritical-care strategy for severe meningitis with impaired consciousness
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- continuous ICP monitor and external ventricular drain (EVD) with targets ICP under 20 mm Hg and cerebral perfusion pressure over 50 mm Hg, plus mechanical ventilation and sedation
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.effectiveness: Glimaker M et al. (PLoS One 2014;9:e91976, PMID 24667767): prospectively designed intervention-control study of 105 adults aged 16-75 with community-acquired bacterial meningitis and severely impaired consciousness; 52 received ICP-targeted treatment in a neurointensive unit (external ventricular catheter CSF drainage in 48, osmotherapy in 21, hyperventilation in 13, external cooling in 9, gram-dose methylprednisolone in 3, deep barbiturate sedation in 2) and 53 received conventional intensive care; all received ventilation, sedation, antibiotics and corticosteroids per guidelines. Mortality at 2 months was 10% (5/52) versus 30% (16/53) (relative risk reduction 68%, p under 0.05), and full recovery was 54% (28) versus 32% (17). Lindvall P et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2004;38:384-390, PMID 14727209): 18 patients with severe bacterial meningitis had neurointensive care, 15 had continuous ICP measurement; 14 of 15 developed ICP of at least 15 mm Hg, 10 of 15 (67%) survived, mean ICP was significantly higher and cerebral perfusion pressure markedly lower in non-survivors, and ICP fell gradually in survivors. German guideline recommendation 24: EVD if clinically relevant hydrocephalus is present, and EVD may be suggested even without hydrocephalus on CT when consciousness is reduced and otherwise unexplained.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.reason_why: In severe bacterial meningitis ICP rises and cerebral perfusion pressure falls (Lindvall: mean ICP significantly higher and CPP markedly lower in non-survivors); controlling ICP to protect perfusion pressure is the mechanism proposed for the survival difference.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.important_caveat: The Glimaker comparison is a prospectively designed intervention-control study, not a randomised trial; the Lindvall report is a small uncontrolled series. WHO 2025 notes that people with raised ICP require intensive-care monitoring and adequate infrastructure and workforce.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.real_working_solution: For adults with severely impaired consciousness (for example coma) admit to a neurointensive setting with ICP monitoring/EVD where available, target ICP under 20 mm Hg and CPP over 50 mm Hg, and combine with standard antibiotics and dexamethasone.
bm_raised_intracranial_pressure_manageme.source: Glimaker M et al., PLoS One 2014;9:e91976 (PMID 24667767); Lindvall P et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004;38:384-390 (PMID 14727209); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_hydrocephalus_management.name: Hydrocephalus -- External Ventricular Drainage and Shunting
bm_hydrocephalus_management.type: Neurosurgical CSF diversion for meningitis-associated hydrocephalus
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- external ventricular drain (EVD), serial lumbar punctures in selected communicating cases, and ventriculoperitoneal shunt for persistent hydrocephalus
bm_hydrocephalus_management.effectiveness: Kasanmoentalib ES et al. (Neurology 2010;75:918-923, PMID 20820003): in a Dutch nationwide adult cohort hydrocephalus complicated 26 of 577 episodes (5%), was communicating in all but 1, was already present on admission in 69%, and was an independent predictor of death (OR 7.81, 95% CI 2.91-20.8); 13 of 26 (50%) died and 69% had an unfavourable outcome. Six patients had an intervention (2 serial lumbar punctures, 4 EVD; median 12 hours from diagnosis to CSF diversion); all who were shunted died or had a poor outcome. German guideline recommendation 24: in clinically relevant internal hydrocephalus place an EVD; consider EVD even without CT hydrocephalus in otherwise unexplained reduced consciousness.
bm_hydrocephalus_management.reason_why: Hydrocephalus raises ICP; CSF diversion lowers the pressure while antibiotics and dexamethasone treat the infection.
bm_hydrocephalus_management.important_caveat: The 'uniformly poor outcome after neurosurgical intervention' reflects a very small series of patients who were already the most severely ill, and cannot be read as evidence that drainage is harmful.
bm_hydrocephalus_management.real_working_solution: Image promptly if consciousness falls or hydrocephalus is suspected and place an EVD for clinically relevant hydrocephalus; decisions on permanent shunting rest with neurosurgery, as the sources reviewed give no evidence-based threshold.
bm_hydrocephalus_management.source: Kasanmoentalib ES et al., Neurology 2010;75:918-923 (PMID 20820003); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_seizure_management.name: Seizures in Bacterial Meningitis -- Benzodiazepine First-Line, Then Fosphenytoin/Phenytoin; Stop Within 3 Months if No Recurrence
bm_seizure_management.type: Acute anti-seizure treatment and short-term prophylaxis
specific_drugs: Status epilepticus (American Epilepsy Society 2016, Level A): IM midazolam, IV lorazepam, IV diazepam, or IV phenobarbital as initial therapy in adults; in children IV lorazepam or IV diazepam (Level A); fosphenytoin preferred over phenytoin when both are available, phenytoin acceptable (Level A)
Weight-based doses per the AES algorithm and national formulary (not reproduced in the abstract read)
bm_seizure_management.effectiveness: Zoons E et al. (Neurology 2008;70:2109-2115, PMID 18305232): seizures occurred in 121 of 696 Dutch adult episodes (17%); death occurred in 41% of patients with seizures versus 16% without (p under 0.001); seizures were linked to severe CNS and systemic inflammation, structural lesions, pneumococcal meningitis and predisposing conditions; antiepileptic drugs were given in 82% of patients with seizures; the authors advise a low threshold for starting anticonvulsants when seizure is clinically suspected. Glauser T et al., Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults, Epilepsy Curr 2016;16:48-61 (PMID 26900382): 38 randomised trials, only 4 class I; respiratory depression is lower with benzodiazepine than placebo in convulsive status epilepticus, showing untreated status itself causes respiratory compromise. WHO 2025 (conditional recommendation, very low certainty): in children and adults with acute symptomatic seizures from meningitis, anti-seizure medicines should be continued for no longer than three months in the absence of recurring seizures; choice depends on semiology, comorbidity, availability, cost and side effects, with specific considerations for older adults, HIV, and women and girls of childbearing potential (refer to WHO mhGAP).
bm_seizure_management.reason_why: Seizures in meningitis are associated with severe CNS and systemic inflammation and structural CNS lesions (Zoons 2008) and with a much higher case fatality, hence the low threshold to treat.
bm_seizure_management.important_caveat: Meningitis-specific randomised evidence for one anti-seizure drug over another was not identified; the drug tiers come from general status-epilepticus evidence, and IDSA 2004 advises avoiding imipenem because of seizure risk (D-II).
bm_seizure_management.real_working_solution: Treat seizures as status epilepticus per AES steps (benzodiazepine first), start maintenance anticonvulsants with a low threshold, search for structural lesions or venous thrombosis if seizures persist, and plan withdrawal within 3 months if seizure-free.
bm_seizure_management.source: Zoons E et al., Neurology 2008;70:2109-2115 (PMID 18305232); Glauser T et al., Epilepsy Curr 2016;16:48-61 (PMID 26900382); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read)

bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.name: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis, Vasculopathy and Parameningeal Focus -- Heparin, Nimodipine/Corticosteroids, Source Control
bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.type: Management of specific intracranial and ENT complications
specific_drugs: Sinus venous thrombosis: therapeutic-range intravenous heparin
Vasculopathy: nimodipine and/or corticosteroids may be considered (intra-arterial blood-pressure monitoring if IV nimodipine is used)
Parameningeal focus (sinusitis, mastoiditis, otitis media): rapid surgery to clear the focus
bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.effectiveness: German guideline (Klein M et al., Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44, PMID 37649122): recommendation 19 (strong consensus) rapid surgery to clear a parameningeal infectious focus detected clinically or on CT; recommendation 26 (strong consensus) nimodipine and/or corticosteroids may be considered for vasculopathy; recommendation 27 (strong consensus) intravenous heparin in the therapeutic range is suggested for sinus vein thrombosis; recommendation 18 adds aciclovir while herpes simplex encephalitis remains possible.
bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.reason_why: Vasculopathy and sinus vein thrombosis are recognised complications, and a contiguous ENT focus (sinusitis, mastoiditis) is a source of the meningeal infection (German guideline).
bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.important_caveat: These are consensus recommendations from one national guideline; controlled trial evidence for anticoagulation or nimodipine in meningitis-associated vascular complications was not identified in the sources reviewed.
bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.real_working_solution: When a patient deteriorates or has focal deficits after starting therapy, image for infarction, venous thrombosis, abscess or subdural collection, and treat the specific complication and any ENT focus in parallel with antibiotics.
bm_cerebrovascular_complications_and_foc.source: Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.name: Formal Audiological Screening Before Discharge (Twice) and Early Hearing Rehabilitation / Cochlear-Implant Evaluation
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.type: Post-recovery screening, rehabilitation and implantation pathway
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- formal audiological screening (before discharge, or within 4 weeks if not possible; repeat if normal), then hearing aids, cochlear or middle-ear implants, and speech-language therapy as indicated
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.effectiveness: WHO 2025 (strong recommendation, very low certainty): in children and adults with acute meningitis from any cause, formal audiological screening should be done before discharge, or within four weeks of discharge if not possible; those screened before discharge and found normal should have a second formal screening because a small number develop hearing loss later; when hearing loss is detected, urgent referral for hearing rehabilitation or evaluation for cochlear implantation is crucial to prevent rapid speech impairment from loss of auditory feedback and to avoid cochlear ossification in eligible people; hearing rehabilitation should be provided as soon as possible (strong, very low certainty). ESCMID 2016 also advises evaluating survivors for hearing loss. Why it matters: 54% of 240 audiometry-tested Danish pneumococcal-meningitis survivors had a hearing deficit, 7% had bilateral profound loss, and 39% of those with a deficit were not suspected of hearing loss at discharge (Worsoe L et al., Clin Infect Dis 2010;51:917-924, PMID 20815735); hearing loss is the commonest major sequela of bacterial meningitis (Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328, PMID 20417414). Old caveat: in a 1993 study evoked otoacoustic emissions gave traces for only 54.7% of ears in children with meningitis and was judged not practical as a pre-discharge check with the technology then available (Fortnum H et al., Br J Audiol 1993;27:227-231, PMID 8312845); WHO 2025 nonetheless recommends formal screening.
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.reason_why: Loss of auditory feedback impairs speech rapidly, and cochlear ossification can close the window for implantation, so timing of detection and referral matters (WHO 2025).
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.real_working_solution: Book audiometry before discharge (or within 4 weeks) for every survivor, repeat it, refer straight away for hearing aids or cochlear-implant assessment if abnormal, and offer speech-language therapy.
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Worsoe L et al., Clin Infect Dis 2010;51:917-924 (PMID 20815735); Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414); van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22 Suppl 3:S37-S62 (PMID 27062097), as summarised in van Ettekoven CN, van de Beek D, Brouwer MC, Clin Microbiol Infect 2017;23:601-606 (PMID 28478238); Fortnum H et al., Br J Audiol 1993;27:227-231 (PMID 8312845)

bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.name: Neurological and Cognitive Follow-Up, Rehabilitation and Psychological Support
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- structured clinical assessment for sequelae, rehabilitation services (physiotherapy, occupational, speech-language, educational), and psychological support
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.effectiveness: WHO 2025: children and adults with acute meningitis from any cause should be reviewed for sequelae before discharge and at follow-up, with at least one clinical assessment within four weeks of discharge and referral to appropriate services when sequelae are found (strong recommendation, very low certainty); rehabilitation should be provided as soon as possible (strong, very low certainty); psychological support should be offered to patients and caregivers where available. Burden: median risk of at least one major or minor sequela after bacterial meningitis is 19.9% and of a major sequela 12.8% (Edmond 2010), about 1 in 5 survivors is left with long-term complications (WHO 2025), and cognitive impairment was found in 32% of adult survivors, mainly cognitive slowness, that was stable over time (Hoogman M et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007;78:1092-1096, PMID 17353256).
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.reason_why: Sequelae include hearing loss, seizures, limb weakness and difficulties with vision, speech, language, memory and communication (WHO Meningitis fact sheet); WHO recommends rehabilitation as soon as possible once sequelae are found.
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.real_working_solution: Schedule a follow-up visit within 4 weeks of discharge, screen hearing, vision, cognition, behaviour, motor function and seizures, and refer early to rehabilitation and psychology.
bm_hearing_screening_and_sequelae_rehabi.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Edmond K et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10:317-328 (PMID 20417414); Hoogman M et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007;78:1092-1096 (PMID 17353256)

bm_medical_devices_equipment.name: Medical Equipment/Devices -- CT/MRI, Lumbar Puncture Set, ICP Monitor and External Ventricular Drain, Mechanical Ventilator, Infusion Pumps, Audiometry Equipment
bm_medical_devices_equipment.type: Diagnostic, monitoring and treatment-delivery devices supporting bacterial meningitis management
specific_drugs: CT scanner (and MRI) for selective pre-lumbar-puncture imaging and complication detection
Lumbar puncture needle and manometer (CSF opening pressure, Gram stain, culture, PCR)
Intracranial pressure monitor and external ventricular drain (EVD) with CSF collection system
Mechanical ventilator (for airway protection, sedation and controlled ventilation in comatose or herniating patients)
IV infusion pumps and IV/IM administration sets for timed antibiotics and dexamethasone
Audiometry / formal audiological screening equipment, hearing aids and cochlear implants
bm_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Each device supports a proven or guideline-recommended step above: selective CT before lumbar puncture per WHO 2025/IDSA 2004 (Hasbun 2001 negative predictive value 97% when no risk features); CSF sampling for Gram stain, culture, PCR and cell counts that direct therapy; ICP monitor and EVD underlying the ICP-targeted mortality reduction (10% vs 30%, Glimaker 2014); ventilation and sedation delivered to all patients in that study; and audiological screening plus implantation per WHO 2025 to prevent cochlear ossification.
bm_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Bacterial meningitis is device-supported because the organism is treated with drugs but complications (herniation, hydrocephalus, seizures, hearing loss) are prevented or treated with equipment.
bm_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Neurointensive-care capacity (ICP monitoring, EVD, ventilation), CT and audiology/cochlear-implant services are not available at every hospital, which is a real determinant of outcome; WHO 2025 notes that people with raised ICP require intensive-care monitoring and adequate infrastructure and workforce, and that the guideline is intended for first- and second-level facilities including in LMICs.
bm_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Ensure a hospital pathway that gives antibiotics without waiting for imaging, has CT and neurosurgical/neurointensive backup for deteriorating patients, and links to audiology before discharge.
bm_medical_devices_equipment.source: Hasbun R et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1727-1733 (PMID 11742046); Glimaker M et al., PLoS One 2014;9:e91976 (PMID 24667767); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, Geneva: World Health Organization; 2025 (ISBN 978-92-4-010804-2; full text read); Klein M et al., German guidelines on community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis in adults, Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Immediate empiric IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (plus vancomycin and/or ampicillin as indicated) within the first hour, given BEFORE any CT/lumbar-puncture delay -- Real Top-Line Answer
ranked_high_to_low.metric: In-hospital mortality reduced 71.5% relative to delayed treatment when antibiotics were given within 6 hours of admission vs after 6 hours (7.5% [6/80] vs 26.3% [10/38] mortality; computed as (26.3-7.5)/26.3), 123 adult cases, adjusted OR for death 8.4 (95% CI 1.7-40.9) for delay >6h; each hour of delay raised odds of unfavourable outcome by 9-30%; WHO 2025 and ESCMID 2016 recommend starting within 1 hour
ranked_high_to_low.source: Proulx N et al., QJM 2005;98:291-298 (PMID 15760921); Koster-Rasmussen R et al., J Infect 2008;57:449-454 (PMID 19000639); van Ettekoven CN et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2424802 (PMID 39093565); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, 2025

ranked_high_to_low.name: Adjunctive dexamethasone in adults, given with (or 10-20 minutes before) the first antibiotic dose -- de Gans 2002
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Randomised, 301 adults: relative risk of death 0.48 (95% CI 0.24-0.96), of unfavourable outcome 0.59 (0.37-0.94); pneumococcal meningitis unfavourable outcome 26% vs 52%. The percentage shown is the relative reduction in mortality. Later trials in high-HIV, low-income settings did not reproduce a mortality benefit (see rows 15-16)
ranked_high_to_low.source: de Gans J, van de Beek D, N Engl J Med 2002;347:1549-1556 (PMID 12432041)

ranked_high_to_low.name: ICP-targeted neurointensive care (EVD CSF drainage, ICP under 20 mm Hg, CPP over 50 mm Hg) for adults with severely impaired consciousness
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Mortality at 2 months 10% (5/52) vs 30% (16/53) with conventional intensive care (relative risk reduction 68%, p under 0.05); full recovery 54% vs 32%. Non-randomised intervention-control study; the percentage shown is the authors' relative mortality reduction
ranked_high_to_low.source: Glimaker M et al., PLoS One 2014;9:e91976 (PMID 24667767); Lindvall P et al., Clin Infect Dis 2004;38:384-390 (PMID 14727209)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine -- primary prevention of invasive pneumococcal disease (including meningitis)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pooled efficacy against vaccine-serotype invasive disease 80% (95% CI 58-90%), all-serotype invasive disease 58% (29-75%); US invasive disease under 2 years fell 69% after PCV7; Dutch adult bacterial meningitis incidence fell from 1.72 to 0.94 per 100,000/year with no serotype replacement
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lucero MG et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;CD004977 (PMID 19821336); Whitney CG et al., N Engl J Med 2003;348:1737-1746 (PMID 12724479); Bijlsma MW et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16:339-347 (PMID 26652862)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hib conjugate vaccine -- primary prevention of Hib meningitis and disease
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Estimated Hib deaths in children 1-59 months fell 90% (uncertainty range 78-96%) from 2000 to 2015 as vaccine use expanded; Hib disease judged almost entirely vaccine preventable (population-level estimate, not a trial efficacy figure)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wahl B et al., Lancet Glob Health 2018;6:e744-e757 (PMID 29903376); Watt JP et al., Lancet 2009;374:903-911 (PMID 19748399)

ranked_high_to_low.name: MenAfriVac (serogroup A conjugate) -- African meningitis belt
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Confirmed group A meningitis incidence reduced by more than 99% in fully vaccinated populations across nine countries; suspected meningitis incidence 57% lower; Chad 2012 incidence 2.48 vs 43.8 per 100,000 (IRR 0.096); non-A serogroups rose after campaigns (IRR 2.76, 1.21-6.30), so surveillance and multivalent vaccine (Men5CV) matter
ranked_high_to_low.source: Trotter CL et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:867-872 (PMID 28545721); Daugla DM et al., Lancet 2014;383:40-47 (PMID 24035220)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Meningococcal ACWY conjugate vaccine -- UK adolescent programme
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Overall vaccine effectiveness against MenCWY 94% (95% CI 80-99); MenW incidence in 14-18 year olds IRR 0.35 (0.17-0.76), MenY IRR 0.21 (0.07-0.59)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Campbell H et al., Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2022;6:96-105 (PMID 34883094)

ranked_high_to_low.name: 4CMenB (Bexsero) infant programme -- group B meningococcal disease, England
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Group B disease incidence 75% lower in fully eligible cohorts (63 observed vs 253 expected cases; IRR 0.25, 0.19-0.36); adjusted vaccine effectiveness point estimates 52.7% (two-dose) and 59.1% (with booster) but with very wide confidence intervals crossing zero; the percentage shown is the incidence reduction
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ladhani SN et al., N Engl J Med 2020;382:309-317 (PMID 31971676)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Meningococcal chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (ciprofloxacin, rifampin, ceftriaxone; azithromycin not routine)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Carriage eradication at one week vs placebo: ciprofloxacin RR 0.04 (0.01-0.12), rifampin RR 0.17 (0.13-0.24), penicillin RR 0.47; rifampin less effective than ceftriaxone at 1-2 weeks (RR 5.93). No disease cases occurred in the trials, so this is a carriage surrogate, not a disease-reduction figure. Percentage shown is ciprofloxacin's relative reduction in carriage
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zalmanovici Trestioreanu A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;CD004785 (PMID 24163051); WHO guidelines on meningitis, 2025; Berry I et al., MMWR 2024;73:99-103 (PMID 38329923)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rifampin chemoprophylaxis for household contacts of invasive Hib disease
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Eradicates Hib from the pharynx in about 95% of carriers and decreases the risk of secondary invasive illness in exposed household contacts (20 mg/kg once daily, maximum 600 mg, for 4 days)
ranked_high_to_low.source: AAP Red Book 2024-2027, Haemophilus influenzae infections chapter, pp. 403-404

ranked_high_to_low.name: Short-course ceftriaxone (5 days) in stable children; single-dose IM ceftriaxone in meningococcal epidemics; IM ceftriaxone when IV access is not possible
ranked_high_to_low.type: Treatment simplification with real RCT support
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relapse-free/bacteriological cure rate 99.6% with 5-day ceftriaxone (494/496 children, 2 relapses) vs 100% with 10-day standard course (508/508, 0 relapses) in 1,004 children, demonstrating equivalence; single-dose ceftriaxone vs oily chloramphenicol in epidemic meningococcal meningitis: 9% treatment failure in both arms; IM vs IV ceftriaxone in Malawian adults: deaths 128/229 vs 121/230 (OR 0.88, 0.61-1.27)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Molyneux E et al., Lancet 2011;377:1837-1845 (PMID 21620467); Nathan N et al., Lancet 2005;366:308-313 (PMID 16039333); Scarborough M et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2441-2450 (PMID 18077809)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mannitol / hypertonic saline as a temporary bridge for impending herniation -- Real Evidence Gap
ranked_high_to_low.type: Hyperosmolar therapy (expert consensus, no meningitis-specific RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: WHO 2025 and the German guideline allow it as a temporary measure for signs of impending herniation; no randomised trial in bacterial meningitis was identified, and hyperosmolar therapy has not been shown to improve neurological outcome in other brain injuries
ranked_high_to_low.source: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care, 2025; Klein M et al., Neurol Res Pract 2023;5:44 (PMID 37649122); Cook AM et al., Neurocrit Care 2020;32:647-666 (PMID 32227294)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Dexamethasone in high-HIV / low-income settings -- Real Neutral Trial Results
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Malawi (465 adults, 90% HIV-positive): death at 40 days OR 1.14 (0.79-1.64); Vietnam (435): intention-to-treat RR death 0.79 (0.45-1.39), benefit confined to microbiologically confirmed cases (RR 0.43, 0.20-0.94); Cochrane 2015: no benefit in low-income countries; WHO: not proven beneficial in advanced HIV
ranked_high_to_low.source: Scarborough M et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2441-2450 (PMID 18077809); Nguyen TH et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2431-2440 (PMID 18077808); Molyneux EM et al., Lancet 2002;360:211-218 (PMID 12133656)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Dexamethasone in Listeria meningitis -- Contested Observational Evidence
ranked_high_to_low.metric: French MONALISA cohort: higher neurolisteriosis mortality with dexamethasone (OR 4.58, 1.50-13.98); Dutch nationwide cohort: adjusted OR for unfavourable outcome 0.40 (0.19-0.81); no randomised trial
ranked_high_to_low.source: Charlier C et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17:510-519 (PMID 28139432); Brouwer MC, van de Beek D, EClinicalMedicine 2023;58:101922 (PMID 37007737)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Glycerol adjuvant therapy -- Real Negative Finding (Do Not Use)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Malawian adults: death by day 40 63% with glycerol vs 49% with placebo (adjusted OR 2.4, 1.3-4.2); Cochrane 2018: no effect on death (RR 1.08, 0.90-1.30); WHO 2025: conditional recommendation against routine use
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ajdukiewicz KM et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2011;11:293-300 (PMID 21334262); Wall EC et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;CD008806 (PMID 29405037)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Induced hypothermia in comatose adults -- Real Negative Finding (Trial Stopped Early for Excess Mortality)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Mortality 51% (25/49) with cooling to 32-34 C vs 31% (15/49) with standard care (RR 1.99, 1.05-3.77); unfavourable outcome at 3 months 86% vs 74% (not significant)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Mourvillier B et al., JAMA 2013;310:2174-2183 (PMID 24105303)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Routine fluid restriction -- No Benefit (Do Not Restrict Routinely)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Three trials, 420 children: no significant difference in death (RR 0.82, 0.53-1.27) or acute severe neurological sequelae (RR 0.67, 0.41-1.08); maintenance fluid better for spasticity and seizures; low-quality evidence; WHO 2025 conditional recommendation against routine restriction
ranked_high_to_low.source: Maconochie IK, Bhaumik S, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;CD004786 (PMID 27813057); Netravathi M et al., BMC Med 2026 (PMID 42472812)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Activated protein C -- Not Recommended in Bacterial Meningitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Intracranial haemorrhage in 6% of 128 adults with meningitis among 4,096 patients in activated-protein-C trials
ranked_high_to_low.source: Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D, Clin Microbiol Rev 2010;23:467-492 (PMID 20610819)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials, cohorts and surveillance analyses with different comparators and outcome scales, so this ordering is a directional, practical judgement, NOT a single directly comparable percentage scale. Where effectiveness_pct is shown it is a different kind of number in each row -- a relative mortality reduction (row 2), a relative reduction in severe hearing loss (row 3), the authors' relative mortality reduction in a non-randomised study (row 5), vaccine efficacy or an incidence/death reduction (rows 6-10), or a carriage-eradication rate (rows 11-12) -- so the percentages must not be compared across rows. Rows 1-14 are REAL WORKING, evidence-positive (or guideline-mandated) interventions: rank 1 (immediate empiric antibiotics within the first hour, never delayed for imaging or lumbar puncture) is the practical top-line answer, followed by dexamethasone timed with the first antibiotic dose; row 15 is an honest evidence gap; rows 16-21 are documented REAL NEUTRAL or NEGATIVE findings reported specifically so they are not used instead of the working measures above them: do not rely on dexamethasone for benefit in advanced-HIV/low-income settings, treat the Listeria-dexamethasone question as unresolved, do not use glycerol, hypothermia, routine fluid restriction or activated protein C. Bacterial meningitis is an acute, curable infection with a real mortality and sequelae tail (see CURABILITY_NOTE) -- unlike the chronic neurological diseases in this knowledge base, the evidence here is about how fast and how correctly to treat, not how to manage indefinitely. The 2004 IDSA guideline is archived; regimens and doses were cross-checked against ESCMID 2016, the German 2023 guideline, the IDSA 2017 healthcare-associated guideline and WHO 2025.

amyotrophic_lateral_sclerosis.name: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
amyotrophic_lateral_sclerosis.icd11_hint: 8B60.0 Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (within 8B60 Motor neuron disease; related subcodes 8B60.1 Progressive bulbar palsy, 8B60.3 Progressive muscular atrophy, 8B60.4 Primary lateral sclerosis, 8B60.5 Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-Plus, 8B60.7 Madras type motor neuron disease); ICD-10-CM G12.21 Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (parent G12.2 Motor neuron disease)

definition.finding: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; also called motor neuron disease, MND) is a progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease of the human motor system characterised by degeneration of BOTH upper motor neurons (motor cortex and corticospinal tract) and lower motor neurons (brainstem motor nuclei and spinal anterior horn cells), leading to progressive muscle weakness and eventual paralysis. 'Amyotrophy' refers to atrophy of denervated muscle fibres with weakness and visible fasciculations; 'lateral sclerosis' refers to hardening (gliosis) of the lateral corticospinal tracts. ICD-11 (8B60.0 Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, under 8B60 Motor neuron disease) defines ALS as a progressive, fatal disorder in which progressive signs of LMN and UMN degeneration are seen within one or more of four regions: bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral. Recent imaging and neuropathology show that the non-motor neuraxis is also involved, so ALS is now regarded as a multisystem, clinically heterogeneous syndrome that lies on a continuum with frontotemporal dementia (see ALS-FTD spectrum below).
definition.source: Hardiman O et al., 'Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17071 (PMID 28980624); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, 'Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301; PMC2656493); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464; PMC10089700); WHO ICD-11 MMS 8B60.0 (icd.who.int; definition text consulted via a public mirror of the WHO ICD-11 MMS)
definition.confidence: high - consistent definition across review-level sources and the WHO classification

umn_and_lmn_degeneration_and_spread.finding: Pathology involves loss of upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex with corticospinal tract degeneration (myelin pallor and gliosis), and loss of ventral-horn and brainstem lower motor neurons (up to about 50% reduction of lower motor neurons at autopsy, with wide variation between cases and levels), with atrophic surviving neurons containing ubiquitinated/TDP-43-positive inclusions and Bunina bodies. Lower-motor-neuron pathology characteristically spares the Onuf nucleus (S2) and the oculomotor nuclei. Neuropathological staging of phosphorylated TDP-43 (pTDP-43) in 76 ALS autopsies proposed four sequential stages: stage 1 agranular motor cortex, brainstem motor nuclei (V, VII, X-XII) and spinal alpha-motoneurons; stage 2 prefrontal cortex, brainstem reticular formation, precerebellar nuclei and red nucleus; stage 3 prefrontal (gyrus rectus/orbital) then postcentral neocortex and striatum; stage 4 anteromedial temporal lobe including hippocampus - consistent with propagation of pTDP-43 along axonal pathways, and with the prefrontal involvement explaining executive deficits in ALS. Cases with C9orf72 expansion showed the same spreading pattern but a greater regional burden. Clinically, weakness spreads contiguously (85% of patients in one survey had focal onset in one body segment, then spread to the contralateral side and adjacent segments). A cortical-origin hypothesis ('dying-forward'), supported by transcranial magnetic stimulation evidence of presymptomatic cortical hyperexcitability (reduced short-interval intracortical inhibition), proposes that TDP-43 pathology begins in the cerebral cortex and spreads via corticofugal projections; this remains a hypothesis rather than settled fact.
umn_and_lmn_degeneration_and_spread.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Brettschneider J et al., 'Stages of pTDP-43 pathology in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', Ann Neurol 2013;74:20-38 (PMID 23686809); Eisen A et al., 'Cortical influences drive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2017;88:917-924 (PMID 28710326); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)
umn_and_lmn_degeneration_and_spread.confidence: high for the autopsy description and the staging proposal as reported; moderate for the cortical-origin (dying-forward) and prion-like spread interpretations, which are hypotheses

tdp43_proteinopathy.finding: Ubiquitinated, hyperphosphorylated and C-terminally cleaved TDP-43 (TAR DNA-binding protein 43) was identified in 2006 as the major disease protein in the ubiquitin-positive, tau- and alpha-synuclein-negative inclusions of ALS and of frontotemporal lobar degeneration with ubiquitin-positive inclusions. TDP-43 proteinopathy is an almost universal pathological hallmark of ALS: it is present in about 97% of ALS cases (and about 50% of FTD cases). The roughly 3% without TDP-43 pathology include SOD1-mutant familial ALS, whose inclusions are TDP-43-negative. Mutations in the TDP-43 gene TARDBP itself cause familial and some apparently sporadic ALS, which supports a pathophysiological role for TDP-43 dysfunction and not only a marker role.
tdp43_proteinopathy.source: Neumann M et al., Science 2006;314:130-133 (PMID 17023659); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464; ~97% of ALS and ~50% of FTD); Sreedharan J et al., Science 2008;319:1668-1672 (PMID 18309045); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)

glutamate_excitotoxicity.finding: Excitotoxicity is a long-standing mechanistic theory: post-mortem tissue from 13 ALS patients showed a disease-, region- and chemical-specific defect in high-affinity glutamate transport (maximal velocity reduced 59% in spinal cord and 70% in motor cortex, but not in visual cortex, striatum or hippocampus), and the astroglial glutamate transporter GLT-1 (EAAT2) protein was decreased by about 71% in ALS motor cortex (and about 90% in roughly a quarter of specimens) and in spinal cord. Reduced clearance of synaptic glutamate is proposed to overstimulate motor neurons. Honest limits: these are small autopsy series in sporadic ALS; whether GLT-1 loss is primary or secondary is unresolved in the original paper, and excitotoxicity is only one of several converging mechanisms.
glutamate_excitotoxicity.source: Rothstein JD, Martin LJ, Kuncl RW, N Engl J Med 1992;326:1464-1468 (PMID 1349424); Rothstein JD et al., Ann Neurol 1995;38:73-84 (PMID 7611729)
glutamate_excitotoxicity.confidence: high for the measurements; moderate for the causal interpretation

oxidative_stress_and_sod1_toxic_gain_of_.finding: SOD1 (Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase) mutations were the first ALS gene finding (11 missense mutations in 13 familial ALS families, 1993). Transgenic mice expressing mutant human SOD1 (G93A) develop motor neuron disease despite little change in enzyme activity, showing that dominant gain-of-function mutations contribute to pathogenesis rather than simple loss of antioxidant activity. Elevated markers of oxidative damage are found in ALS spinal cord and CSF, and oxidative stress is considered a central contributor, but the precise mechanism by which mutant SOD1 kills motor neurons is undefined, the trigger of oxidative stress in non-SOD1 ALS is unclear, and antioxidant clinical trials have so far been disappointing.
oxidative_stress_and_sod1_toxic_gain_of_.source: Rosen DR et al., Nature 1993;362:59-62 (PMID 8446170); Gurney ME et al., Science 1994;264:1772-1775 (PMID 8209258); Barber SC & Shaw PJ, Free Radic Biol Med 2010;48:629-641 (PMID 19969067)
oxidative_stress_and_sod1_toxic_gain_of_.confidence: high for the genetic and transgenic findings; moderate for the extent to which oxidative stress drives sporadic disease

protein_aggregation_rna_metabolism_and_p.finding: Current genetic and cell-biology evidence converges on disrupted RNA metabolism and protein homeostasis: defects in nucleocytoplasmic trafficking, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and impaired dynamics of ribonucleoprotein (RNA-granule) bodies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation. TDP-43, FUS/TLS, ubiquilin-2, VCP and the C9orf72 GGGGCC repeat expansion all feed into these pathways; it is proposed that perturbation of either RNA or protein homeostasis drives further deviation of both through a feed-forward loop that includes cell-to-cell prion-like spread, which may underlie relentless progression. FUS mutations cause mislocalisation of FUS to the neuronal cytoplasm, and C9orf72 expansions cause loss of one alternatively spliced transcript and formation of nuclear RNA foci, i.e. multiple parallel mechanisms.
protein_aggregation_rna_metabolism_and_p.source: Taylor JP, Brown RH, Cleveland DW, 'Decoding ALS: from genes to mechanism', Nature 2016;539:197-206 (PMID 27830784); Ling SC, Polymenidou M, Cleveland DW, Neuron 2013;79:416-438 (PMID 23931993); Kwiatkowski TJ et al., Science 2009;323:1205-1208 (PMID 19251627); DeJesus-Hernandez M et al., Neuron 2011;72:245-256 (PMID 21944778)
protein_aggregation_rna_metabolism_and_p.confidence: high that these pathways are implicated; moderate on which is primary, and no single mechanism explains all ALS

multistep_model_of_onset.finding: In five population registers (6,274 cases; Ireland, Netherlands, Italy, Scotland, England), the log of ALS incidence rose linearly with the log of age (combined slope 4.8, 95% CI 4.5-5.0), which is consistent with a multistep disease model and suggested ALS is a six-step process. Practical meaning: onset probably needs an accumulation of several genetic and environmental 'hits', which fits the small effect sizes of individual environmental risk factors and the fact that even known monogenic mutations are not fully penetrant.
multistep_model_of_onset.source: Al-Chalabi A et al., Lancet Neurol 2014;13:1108-1113 (PMID 25300936)
multistep_model_of_onset.confidence: moderate - a statistical modelling inference, not direct biological proof of six steps

genetics_by_gene.finding: Over 40 ALS-associated genes are known; the most common and penetrant are C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP and FUS. Approximate frequencies (percent of familial ALS / percent of sporadic ALS) in the tabulated genotype-phenotype summary: C9orf72 40 / 7; SOD1 12 / 1-2; TARDBP 4 / 1; FUS 4 / 1. Primary data: (1) C9orf72 GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat expansion (identified in 2011) is the most common genetic cause of both ALS and FTD; in a screen of 4,448 ALS patients from 17 regions it was found in 7.0% of sporadic ALS (236/3,377 white patients) and 39.3% of familial ALS (217/552 white patients), with 6.0% of sporadic and 24.8% of familial FTD; in Finland it explains 46.0% of familial and 21.1% of sporadic ALS. It was NOT found in 360 sporadic ALS patients from Asia/Pacific in that study; penetrance is nil below age 35, about 50% by age 58 and almost complete by age 80. (2) SOD1: about 20% of familial ALS in older series and 12% in the tabulated summary, with about 1-2% of apparently sporadic cases; SOD1 tends to present with prominent LMN features and cognitive impairment is very rare. (3) TARDBP (TDP-43): about 4% of familial and 1% of sporadic cases, typical ALS with FTD in some patients. (4) FUS: about 4% of familial and 1% of sporadic ALS, with typical or atypical ALS, juvenile or adult onset, and FTD/dementia in some patients. Frequencies vary with ancestry (see India-specific data in epidemiology).
genetics_by_gene.source: Goutman SA et al., 'Recent advances in the diagnosis and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', Lancet Neurol 2022;21:480-493 (PMID 35334233; Table 3, adapted from Chia R et al., Lancet Neurol 2018 and Goutman SA et al., Handb Clin Neurol 2018); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Majounie E et al., Lancet Neurol 2012;11:323-330 (PMID 22406228); DeJesus-Hernandez M et al., Neuron 2011;72:245-256 (PMID 21944778); Renton AE et al., Neuron 2011;72:257-268 (PMID 21944779); Rosen DR et al., Nature 1993;362:59-62 (PMID 8446170); Sreedharan J et al., Science 2008;319:1668-1672 (PMID 18309045); Kwiatkowski TJ et al., Science 2009;323:1205-1208 (PMID 19251627); Vance C et al., Science 2009;323:1208-1211 (PMID 19251628); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)
genetics_by_gene.confidence: high for the primary C9orf72 screening data (European-ancestry weighted); moderate for the tabulated percentages because they vary by ancestry, ascertainment and era (older series quote SOD1 at about 20% of familial ALS)

familial_versus_sporadic_split.finding: Estimates of the familial fraction differ by source and era and should be quoted as a range: ICD-11 and older reviews give familial ALS (mostly autosomal dominant) as about 5-10% of cases (Wijesekera & Leigh: about 5% with a family history in one place, 5-10% in the abstract); the 2022 Lancet seminar gives 10-15% of cases as familial (about 70% of these carry a mutation in a known ALS gene) and notes that familial ALS may be under-reported and closer to 20% because of low-penetrance mutations, small families and incomplete family history. About 15% of 'sporadic' ALS patients carry private pathogenic variants in known ALS genes, so a negative family history does not exclude a genetic cause. Familial ALS starts about a decade earlier than sporadic ALS on average, affects men and women equally, and has shorter survival in older series. In a prospective UK specialist-clinic series of 100 consecutive ALS patients, 21% carried a pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, and 93% of those had no family history of ALS.
familial_versus_sporadic_split.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); WHO ICD-11 MMS 8B60.0 (5-10% familial; C9orf72 and SOD1 account for 50-60% of familial cases); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Shepheard SR et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2021;92:510-518 (PMID 33589474)
familial_versus_sporadic_split.confidence: moderate - the honest answer is a range (5-10% classic, 10-15% recent, up to about 20% if under-ascertainment is corrected)

als_ftd_spectrum_overlap.finding: ALS and FTD are two ends of one disease continuum: they share TDP-43 pathology and the C9orf72 expansion, and cognitive/behavioural change is now recognised in 35-50% of ALS patients, while about 15% of ALS patients meet criteria for frontotemporal dementia (FTD); conversely, a subset of FTD patients develop motor neuron disease. In a consecutive series of 279 sporadic ALS patients with neuropsychological testing, 51% had cognitive impairment on non-motor tests (versus 5% of controls; 49% intact, 32% mild, 13% moderate, 6% severe) and 41 patients (15%) met FTD criteria; memory loss typical of Alzheimer disease was rare. The 2017 consensus (Strong criteria) defines the ALS-FTSD spectrum: ALS with cognitive impairment (ALSci), ALS with behavioural impairment (ALSbi), both combined, and ALS-FTD, with neuropsychological deficits affecting over 50% of persons with ALS and adversely affecting survival. Older reviews quote lower figures (frontal-executive dysfunction in 20-40% and overt FTD in about 5%), which reflects earlier, less sensitive testing.
als_ftd_spectrum_overlap.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Ringholz GM et al., 'Prevalence and patterns of cognitive impairment in sporadic ALS', Neurology 2005;65:586-590 (PMID 16116120); Strong MJ et al., ALS-FTSD revised diagnostic criteria, Amyotroph Lateral Scler Frontotemporal Degener 2017;18:153-174 (PMID 28054827); Burrell JR et al., 'The frontotemporal dementia-motor neuron disease continuum', Lancet 2016;388:919-931 (PMID 26987909); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)
als_ftd_spectrum_overlap.confidence: high that ALS-FTD overlap is real and common; moderate on the exact percentages, which depend on test battery and cohort (about 15% FTD, 35-50%+ any impairment)

diagnosis_is_clinical_no_confirmatory_bi.finding: ALS is diagnosed clinically: progressive UMN plus LMN signs that spread within or between body regions, supported by electrodiagnostic studies and by exclusion of mimics. No test or tool has replaced clinical history and examination for confirming the diagnosis, even with greater use of genetic testing. Serology is normal in ALS except for mildly raised creatine kinase in some cases; other abnormal serology should prompt reconsideration. Features that do not support ALS include prominent sensory, sphincter or autonomic dysfunction and anterior visual pathway abnormalities. Additional clues favouring ALS are unexplained weight loss, pseudobulbar affect, cognitive/executive change and a family history of ALS or other neurodegenerative disease.
diagnosis_is_clinical_no_confirmatory_bi.source: Goutman SA et al., Lancet Neurol 2022;21:480-493 (PMID 35334233); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)

revised_el_escorial_criteria.framework: The revised El Escorial (Airlie House) research criteria (World Federation of Neurology) require: (1) evidence of LMN degeneration by clinical, electrophysiological or neuropathological examination, (2) evidence of UMN degeneration by clinical examination, and (3) progressive spread of symptoms or signs within a region or to other regions, together with the ABSENCE of electrophysiological/pathological evidence of another disease that could explain the signs and of neuroimaging evidence of another disease process. Four regions are counted: bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral. UMN signs: clonus, Babinski sign, absent abdominal skin reflexes, hypertonia, loss of dexterity. LMN signs: atrophy, weakness (if only fasciculations, search with EMG for active denervation).
categories: Definite ALS: UMN and LMN signs in 3 regions
Probable ALS: UMN and LMN signs in 2 regions, with at least some UMN signs rostral to the LMN signs
Probable ALS, laboratory-supported: UMN signs in 1 or more regions and LMN signs defined by EMG in at least 2 regions (category rendered obsolete by the Awaji consensus)
Possible ALS: UMN and LMN signs in 1 region together, OR UMN signs in 2 or more regions, OR UMN and LMN signs in 2 regions with no UMN signs rostral to LMN signs
revised_el_escorial_criteria.performance_note: El Escorial was built for research/trial entry, is complex and prone to error, and most neurologists still use it to sub-classify ALS. Among the criteria sets, El Escorial is the most specific and Gold Coast the most sensitive. In a 506-patient retrospective series, sensitivity was 88.6% for revised El Escorial, 90.3% for Awaji and 92% for Gold Coast.
revised_el_escorial_criteria.source: Brooks BR, Miller RG, Swash M, Munsat TL, 'El Escorial revisited: revised criteria for the diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', ALS Other Motor Neuron Disord 2000;1:293-299 (PMID 11464847; category table as summarised in Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3, PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Hannaford A et al., Ann Neurol 2021;89:979-986 (PMID 33565111)

awaji_electrodiagnostic_criteria.framework: The Awaji-shima consensus (2006; published 2008) affirmed the utility of needle EMG and nerve conduction studies and recommended that electrophysiological evidence of chronic neurogenic change be taken as equivalent to clinical LMN signs when recognising involvement of individual muscles; in the context of suspected ALS, fasciculation potentials are taken as equivalent to fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves as evidence of active denervation. This made the 'Probable, laboratory-supported' El Escorial category obsolete. Methods for detecting UMN abnormality were judged promising but needing more study.
awaji_electrodiagnostic_criteria.source: de Carvalho M, Dengler R, Eisen A et al., 'Electrodiagnostic criteria for diagnosis of ALS', Clin Neurophysiol 2008;119:497-503 (PMID 18164242)

gold_coast_criteria.framework: The Gold Coast criteria (Shefner et al. 2020) simplify diagnosis to ALS or not-ALS (no certainty categories). Requirements: (1) progressive motor impairment documented by history or repeated clinical assessment, preceded by normal motor function; AND (2) UMN and LMN dysfunction in at least ONE body region (UMN and LMN in the same region if only one region is involved) OR LMN dysfunction in at least TWO body regions; AND (3) investigations excluding other disease processes. A region counts as LMN-involved if there are abnormalities in two limb muscles innervated by different roots and nerves, or one bulbar muscle, or one thoracic muscle, by examination or EMG; UMN dysfunction requires at least one of increased deep tendon reflexes (including a reflex in a weak, wasted muscle or spread to adjacent muscles), pathological reflexes (Hoffmann, Babinski, crossed adductor, snout), or increased velocity-dependent tone (spasticity). Body regions are bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral. Importantly, ALS can be diagnosed without any UMN sign if LMN dysfunction is present in two regions.
gold_coast_criteria.performance_note: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (9 studies, n=9,656, all from ALS referral centres) found Gold Coast sensitivity of about 95% versus 59% (revised El Escorial) and 54% (Awaji) at the 'Probable+' level, and 84% and 85% at the 'Possible+' level; specificity was lower for Gold Coast (66%) than El Escorial (94% Probable+, 77% Possible+) or Awaji (94%, 82%). The authors caution that lower specificity matters in low-prevalence (unselected) settings and that applicability outside referral centres is uncertain.
gold_coast_criteria.source: Shefner JM et al., 'A proposal for new diagnostic criteria for ALS', Clin Neurophysiol 2020;131:1975-1978 (PMID 32387049; criteria wording as reproduced in Turner MR, 'Diagnosing ALS: the Gold Coast criteria and the role of EMG', Pract Neurol 2022;22:176-178, PMID 34992096); von Quednow E et al., Clin Neurophysiol 2025;179:2111005 (PMID 40975951); Hannaford A et al., Ann Neurol 2021;89:979-986 (PMID 33565111)
gold_coast_criteria.confidence: high for the criteria text; moderate for real-world accuracy because sensitivity/specificity data come from referral-centre cohorts

emg_and_nerve_conduction_studies_role.finding: Electrodiagnosis has two jobs: (a) primarily to document lower motor neuron dysfunction (active denervation with fibrillation potentials/positive sharp waves/fasciculation potentials and chronic reinnervation with large, long-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials) in clinically involved AND clinically uninvolved regions, and (b) secondarily to exclude other disease processes. Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies are required to define or exclude disorders of nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle that mimic ALS - notably sensory neuropathy and motor conduction block (multifocal motor neuropathy). Sampling distal muscles and muscles in the clinically involved segment gives the highest sensitivity. Limits: EMG is operator-dependent and far from 100% sensitive, most often missing UMN-predominant and bulbar-onset ALS (typically women over 70) where tongue and limb EMG may show little denervation early; and suggestive EMG abnormalities alone cannot establish ALS without clinical support.
emg_and_nerve_conduction_studies_role.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Turner MR, Pract Neurol 2022;22:176-178 (PMID 34992096); de Carvalho M et al., Clin Neurophysiol 2008;119:497-503 (PMID 18164242)

neuroimaging_role.finding: MRI of brain and spine is used to EXCLUDE structural mimics (cervical spondylotic myelopathy, foramen magnum or intrinsic cord lesions, syringomyelia, conus/lumbosacral lesions, skull-base lesions), especially in clinically probable or possible ALS. Corticospinal tract hyperintensity on T2, proton-density or FLAIR MRI is the most characteristic MRI finding in ALS, but imaging cannot confirm the diagnosis. The WFN revised criteria state that imaging is not required in clinically definite bulbar or pseudobulbar-onset disease because structural lesions are unlikely to mimic it. Advanced imaging, neurofilament assays and other biomarkers are still mainly research tools.
neuroimaging_role.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Goutman SA et al., Lancet Neurol 2022;21:480-493 (PMID 35334233)
neuroimaging_role.confidence: high for the exclusion role; imaging cannot confirm ALS

diagnostic_delay.finding: In a review of 21 studies (1990-2020; US, Canada, Japan, Egypt, South America and Europe), the typical time from first symptom to diagnosis was 10-16 months. Points of delay include multiple specialist referrals and misdiagnoses that often lead to unnecessary procedures and surgeries; bulbar onset significantly shortens time to diagnosis. Reasons: rarity, unfamiliarity, incomplete recognition of symptoms, and commoner conditions being investigated first. A related caution: some mimics are diagnosed even later (Kennedy disease had an average delay of over 5 years from onset of weakness to diagnosis in one 57-patient series). No dedicated Indian diagnostic-delay study was found; Indian hospital cohorts report only a mean duration of illness at first evaluation (about 11 months in a 30-patient South Indian tertiary series; 17.7 months in a 1,153-patient series), which is not the same measure.
diagnostic_delay.source: Richards D, Morren JA, Pioro EP, 'Time to diagnosis and factors affecting diagnostic delay in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis', J Neurol Sci 2020;417:117054 (PMID 32763509); Goutman SA et al., Lancet Neurol 2022;21:480-493 (PMID 35334233); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Rhodes LE et al., Brain 2009;132:3242-3251 (PMID 19846582); Thomas PT et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler Frontotemporal Degener 2018;19:606-610 (PMID 30039719); Nalini A et al., J Neurol Sci 2008;272:60-70 (PMID 18550082)
diagnostic_delay.confidence: high for the 10-16 month figure (pooled over studies from mostly high-income settings); low for India, where no direct data exist

genetic_testing_indications.finding: Genetic testing is increasingly used to explain disease cause, predict family risk and identify patients eligible for gene-specific trials/therapies (e.g. SOD1 antisense oligonucleotide trials). Because a family history is absent in most carriers (93% of pathogenic-variant carriers in the Sheffield series had none), the 2023 Neurology Clinical Practice review states that genetic testing is increasingly recommended to be offered to ALL persons with ALS/FTD as part of routine neurological care, with pre- and post-test counselling; however, offer of testing is not yet formally 'standard of care' in every clinic, and specialist ALS centres are advised to perform it to avoid over- or under-calling genetic ALS (variants of uncertain significance are common: an additional 21% of patients in the Sheffield series carried a VUS, and 13% carried more than one variant). The most common and penetrant genes are C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP and FUS, and testing may still miss rare pathogenic variants (allele frequency below 1%); in the Sheffield series 15% of patients met inclusion criteria for a current ALS genetic-therapy trial. In the Indian cohort of 761 ALS patients, overall diagnostic yield of pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants was 15.9% (36.95% in familial, 12.96% in sporadic) with SOD1 dominant.
