genetic_testing_indications.source: Roggenbuck J, Quick A, Kolb SJ, Genet Med 2017;19:267-274 (PMID 27537704); Roggenbuck J & Fong JC, Clin Lab Med 2020;40:271-287 (PMID 32718499); Chambers C et al., Neurol Clin Pract 2023;13:e200201 (PMID 37736067); Shepheard SR et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2021;92:510-518 (PMID 33589474); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Kotambail A et al., J Neurol 2026;273:435 (PMID 42384233)
genetic_testing_indications.confidence: high that testing is increasingly advised for all patients; moderate on universality because guidance is expert consensus rather than a formal guideline, and availability in India is limited

need_to_exclude_mimics.finding: In the population-based Irish ALS Register, 32 of 437 referrals (7.3%) were re-diagnosed with a condition other than ALS between 1993 and 1997; multifocal motor neuropathy was the most common mimic (7 cases, 22%) followed by Kennedy disease (4 cases, 13%); 84% fulfilled only 'suspected' or 'possible' El Escorial ALS. Factors that led to diagnostic revision were evolution of atypical symptoms, results of specific investigations, and failure of symptoms to progress. Since some mimics are treatable, exclusion is part of the diagnostic definition. See differential_diagnosis for the individual conditions.
need_to_exclude_mimics.source: Traynor BJ et al., 'Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis mimic syndromes: a population-based study', Arch Neurol 2000;57:109-113 (PMID 10634456); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

core.name: Upper motor neuron (UMN) signs - spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski/Hoffmann signs
core.note: UMN degeneration produces loss of dexterity, stiffness, pathologically brisk tendon reflexes that are symmetrical and may spread beyond the stimulated muscle group (including finger jerks and a crossed adductor reflex), Hoffmann sign, an extensor plantar response, clonus and a supinator or patellar 'catch' (increased tone); in bulbar disease the jaw jerk may be brisk. Spasticity becomes evident in weakened, atrophic limbs and affects manual dexterity and gait; flexor spasms may appear late. Diagnostic sign lists for ALS use clonus, Babinski sign, absent abdominal skin reflexes, hypertonia and loss of dexterity as UMN signs. A brisk reflex in a weak, wasted muscle is itself a UMN sign under the Gold Coast criteria.
core.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Shefner JM et al., Clin Neurophysiol 2020;131:1975-1978 (PMID 32387049) as reproduced in Turner MR, Pract Neurol 2022;22:176-178 (PMID 34992096)

core.name: Lower motor neuron (LMN) signs - weakness, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, cramps
core.note: LMN degeneration produces focal weakness and wasting, most often in the hand, forearm and shoulder muscles in the arms and proximal thigh or distal foot muscles in the legs, with visible fasciculations usually present in more than one muscle group. Fasciculations or cramps can precede weakness by months to years but are rarely the presenting complaint. Weakness is insidious, usually asymmetrical at onset, may be worse in cold weather, and spreads to other limbs sooner or later. Tone and reflexes may be reduced in a wasted limb where LMN loss predominates (e.g. flail arm or flail leg presentations). Sensory examination is almost always unremarkable.
core.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

core.name: Limb (spinal)-onset ALS
core.note: About two thirds of patients with typical ALS have limb onset with asymmetric focal weakness and wasting that may start distally or proximally in the arms or legs; onset in one body segment is followed by spread to the contralateral side and then adjacent segments. The 2022 Lancet seminar describes bulbar and spinal (cervical/lumbar) onset as the two most common presentations, each roughly a quarter to a third of cases, so the exact limb-onset share depends on how phenotypes are counted. Neck-extensor weakness (dropped head) is uncommon: in a 683-patient Indian ALS series it occurred in 9 patients (1.3%), usually as an early feature within one to two years of onset, in the setting of diffuse UMN and LMN signs. Limb-onset carries a longer median survival than bulbar onset (see natural_history).
core.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Gourie-Devi M, Nalini A, Sandhya S, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:683-686 (PMID 12700323)

core.name: Bulbar-onset ALS - dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue wasting, sialorrhoea
core.note: Bulbar onset presents with slurred, slow or nasal speech (dysarthria; sometimes first noticed after a small amount of alcohol), dysphagia for solids and/or liquids, tongue atrophy and fasciculations, and jaw/facial weakness; almost all patients with bulbar symptoms develop drooling from difficulty swallowing saliva, plus mild UMN-type lower facial weakness. Limb symptoms usually follow within 1-2 years. Bulbar onset is more common in women and older patients: in one summary 43% of patients over 70 presented with bulbar symptoms versus 15% of those under 30. It accounts for about a quarter to a third of cases (35.9% in a German registry versus 22.8% in a Chinese registry). Dysarthria can be LMN (tongue/bulbar) or pseudobulbar (UMN) in origin.
core.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

core.name: Dysphagia progression, weight loss and malnutrition
core.note: Dysphagia is common in ALS and leads to aspiration risk, malnutrition, weight loss and dehydration; malnutrition can also arise with severe upper-limb weakness because meal preparation and eating become slow or impossible. ALS is a hypermetabolic state, so patients need more calories, and unexplained weight loss is itself a clue to ALS. Most guidelines suggest considering enteral feeding when body weight falls by more than 10% of pre-diagnostic weight. EFNS guidance advises placing a gastrostomy BEFORE respiratory insufficiency develops. In a survey of 130 bereaved Indian caregivers only 25.4% of patients had a PEG, and bulbar onset was significantly associated with assisted feeding (p=0.002).
core.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Andersen PM et al., EFNS guidelines, Eur J Neurol 2012;19:360-375 (PMID 21914052); Chikktimmegowda D et al., Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2026;29:386-391 (PMID 42241188)

core.name: Respiratory muscle weakness - the usual cause of death
core.note: About 5% of patients present with respiratory weakness without significant limb or bulbar symptoms; they present with type 2 respiratory failure or nocturnal hypoventilation: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, disturbed sleep, morning headaches, excessive daytime somnolence, anorexia, poor concentration and irritability or mood change. Neuromuscular respiratory failure is the most common cause of death, usually within two to five years of onset. In a prospective French study of 302 patients, 77% died of respiratory failure (terminal respiratory insufficiency 58%, pneumonia 14%, asphyxia from a foreign body 3%, pulmonary embolism 2%), and 10% died of other causes (post-surgical/traumatic 5%, cardiac 3.4%, suicide 1.3%); at death only 33% were on non-invasive ventilation. In an Indian caregiver survey (n=130), breathlessness was the most common terminal symptom (79.2%), followed by excessive oral secretions (54.6%) and anxiety/restlessness (44.6%); only 20% had received bilevel positive airway pressure and 29.2% experienced sudden death.
core.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Radunovic A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;10:CD004427 (PMID 28982219); Gil J et al., Eur J Neurol 2008;15:1245-1251 (PMID 18973614); Chikktimmegowda D et al., Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2026;29:386-391 (PMID 42241188)

core.name: Pseudobulbar affect (emotional lability) and other mood/behavioural symptoms
core.note: Pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - involuntary, disproportionate episodes of crying and/or laughing - reflects UMN bulbar involvement. In a population-based incident registry cohort in Apulia, Italy (132 sporadic ALS patients), PBA was present on neurological examination in 26% and on the CNS-LS questionnaire (score >=13) in 34% at diagnosis, and was associated with bulbar UMN involvement, bulbar onset and markers of a more severe phenotype. Excessive yawning is also seen. Depression, anxiety and sleep disruption also occur in ALS, and ALS is associated with neuropsychiatric illness including psychosis and suicidal ideation, so mood and suicide risk deserve direct enquiry. In a small Indian study of 20 patients (single site), 25% expressed a death wish (mainly from lack of financial support in 3 of 5), 30% had mild-moderate depression and 5% suicidal ideation.
core.source: Tortelli R et al., J Neurol 2016;263:316-321 (PMID 26588919); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Gourie-Devi M et al., Neurol India 2017;65:46-51 (PMID 28084237)

core.name: Cognitive and behavioural change (executive dysfunction, language impairment, apathy, disinhibition) and FTD
core.note: Cognitive and behavioural change can occur early and is now recognised in 35-50% of ALS patients; typical deficits are executive function, language and fluency, with long-term memory and spatial domains relatively intact; behaviours include apathy, irritability, disregard for hygiene and eating changes. About 15% meet criteria for FTD (Ringholz 2005: 15%, with 51% showing some cognitive impairment). In 146 patients, cognition worsened in 30% after 6 months, even among those initially normal, and decliners progressed faster and survived shorter. In a 70-couple clinic study, caregivers reported neurobehavioural abnormalities in 48.6% of patients (apathy 55.7%, executive dysfunction 45.7%, disinhibition 25.7%), which were linked to bulbar symptoms and to greater caregiver burden and depression. An Indian cohort of 60 ALS-spectrum patients found 11 (18%) with ALS-FTD and 28 (47%) with mild cognitive/behavioural deficits. Behavioural change affects consent, adherence and end-of-life decisions.
core.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Ringholz GM et al., Neurology 2005;65:586-590 (PMID 16116120); Strong MJ et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler Frontotemporal Degener 2017;18:153-174 (PMID 28054827); Chio A et al., Eur J Neurol 2010;17:1298-1303 (PMID 20402747); Srivastava K et al., Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2024;53:310-320 (PMID 39068922)

core.name: Functions classically spared until late - extraocular movements, sphincters, sensation
core.note: Sphincter and extraocular muscles are classically spared. Pathologically, the Onuf nucleus (S2) motoneuron group is remarkably preserved (X group of Onuf in all five cases studied), consistent with bladder and rectal sphincter function often being intact until the latest stage, and the oculomotor nuclei are relatively spared. Sensation is almost always normal. Honest nuance: 'spared' is relative, not absolute - autonomic dysfunction such as urinary urgency and incontinence is increasingly recognised, video-oculography detects subtle eye-movement abnormalities (executive antisaccade errors and, in more advanced cases, gaze palsy and disturbed pursuit) in 68 ALS patients, and in tracheostomy-ventilated survivors a 'totally locked-in state' with oculomotor impairment can develop. Practical rule: prominent early sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction, ophthalmoplegia or ptosis argues against ALS and prompts a search for a mimic.
core.source: Mannen T et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1977;40:464-469 (PMID 894318); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Gorges M et al., PLoS One 2015;10:e0142546 (PMID 26559944)

classic_symptoms_and_progression.finding: ALS is relentlessly progressive with contiguous spread of weakness. Typical sequence in limb-onset disease: focal asymmetric weakness and wasting, then other limbs, then bulbar symptoms and eventually respiratory symptoms (though not necessarily in that order). Progression rate differs greatly between individuals: rate of ALSFRS-R decline, forced vital capacity, age, site of onset, time to diagnosis, definite El Escorial category, FTD and C9orf72 expansion are the eight independent predictors in the ENCALS survival model (see natural_history). Late complications include dysphagia and aspiration, malnutrition, hypoventilation, sialorrhoea, communication loss, and in a small proportion of ventilated survivors a totally locked-in state.
classic_symptoms_and_progression.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Westeneng HJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:423-433 (PMID 29598923); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

motor_neuron_disease_variants.framework: Motor neuron disease is a spectrum: pure LMN (progressive muscular atrophy), mixed UMN+LMN (classic ALS), pure UMN (primary lateral sclerosis), regional variants (flail arm, flail leg) and bulbar/respiratory presentations. Opinion is divided on whether PLS and PMA are distinct diseases or the ends of the ALS spectrum; the 2022 Lancet seminar treats them as phenotypes on the ALS spectrum. Terms 'bulbar-onset ALS' and 'spinal-onset ALS' have largely replaced 'progressive bulbar palsy' and 'Charcot ALS'. ICD-11 8B60 lists ALS, progressive bulbar palsy, progressive pseudobulbar palsy, progressive muscular atrophy, primary lateral sclerosis, ALS-plus, monomelic amyotrophy and Madras-type motor neuron disease as separate 8B60 subcodes. In a population-based Italian study of 1,332 phenotyped incident cases, best outcomes were in pure UMN, pyramidal, pure LMN and flail-arm phenotypes and worst in respiratory and bulbar phenotypes; age at onset was lowest in pyramidal/pure LMN/pure UMN phenotypes and highest in bulbar.
motor_neuron_disease_variants.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Chio A et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:740-746 (PMID 21402743); WHO ICD-11 MMS 8B60 (icd.who.int; subcode list consulted via a public mirror)

variants.features: Slowly progressive pure UMN syndrome (spasticity, hyperreflexia, no or minimal LMN signs) that cannot be attributed to another disease; diagnosis is clinical after exclusion of structural, neurodegenerative and metabolic mimics (hereditary spastic paraplegia, primary progressive MS are the main confusions). It is difficult to separate from UMN-predominant ALS early, because many patients later develop LMN signs. In a 39-patient study, 13 of 29 patients with initial UMN-only signs later acquired denervation on EMG (at about 3.2 years) or on examination (at about 3.7 years) and were reclassified as UMN-dominant ALS, while 16 stayed clinically pure PLS (mean follow-up 8.7 years); the authors defined clinically pure PLS as isolated UMN signs 4 years after symptom onset. 2020 consensus criteria were proposed to shorten the diagnostic delay.
variants.prognosis: Considerably better than typical ALS: survival was longer in PLS than in ALS (p=0.027) and UMN-dominant ALS had similar disability to ALS but slower progression.
variants.source: Gordon PH et al., Neurology 2006;66:647-653 (PMID 16534101); Turner MR et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2020;91:373-377 (PMID 32029539); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

variants.features: Pure LMN syndrome (weakness, wasting, fasciculations without UMN signs); accounts for about 5-10% of MND patients, almost always limb-onset, with swallowing problems possible later. In a 962-patient comparison (91 PMA, 871 ALS), PMA patients were more often male, older and lived longer (p=0.01), UMN signs developed in 22% within 61 months of diagnosis, and shorter survival was predicted by the same factors as in ALS (more body regions affected, lower FVC, lower ALSFRS-R). Older reviews quote up to 50% eventually developing UMN signs.
variants.prognosis: Tends to live longer than classic ALS on average but is relentlessly progressive; the authors argue PMA should be considered a form of ALS. Non-invasive ventilation and gastrostomy were frequently needed.
variants.source: Kim WK et al., Neurology 2009;73:1686-1692 (PMID 19917992); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)

variants.variant: Progressive bulbar palsy (PBP) - isolated bulbar presentation
variants.features: Isolated bulbar onset (dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue involvement). In a review of 392 ALS clinic records, patients with isolated PBP were split into normal limb EMG (n=15) and limb denervation on EMG (n=17); 87% of those with normal limb EMG progressed to definite ALS, and the two groups did not differ in course.
variants.prognosis: Median survival was 35 months (normal limb EMG) and 40 months (limb denervation on EMG); all patients with FTD died within 40 months of onset. Practical implication: an isolated bulbar palsy should be treated as ALS-until-proven-otherwise, not as a benign variant.
variants.source: Karam C, Scelsa SN, Macgowan DJ, Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2010;11:364-368 (PMID 20132084); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)

variants.variant: Flail arm (Vulpian-Bernhardt, brachial amyotrophic diplegia) and flail leg (pseudopolyneuritic) variants
variants.features: Regional LMN-predominant presentations: flail arm shows symmetric proximal upper-limb weakness and wasting with the arms hanging flaccidly and depressed/absent arm reflexes, with the legs strong for some years; flail leg starts distally in both legs symmetrically with hypotonia and depressed reflexes and usually no pyramidal signs. Swallowing and diaphragmatic weakness are usually late. The unusual picture and lack of EMG denervation in other regions can cause considerable diagnostic delay.
variants.prognosis: Characteristically slower progression than typical ALS (flail arm had among the better outcomes in a population-based Italian series).
variants.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Chio A et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:740-746 (PMID 21402743)

variants.features: Onset with respiratory muscle weakness (about 5% of cases) - dyspnoea, orthopnoea, nocturnal hypoventilation - before significant limb or bulbar involvement. Male excess and older onset are reported.
variants.prognosis: Among the worst outcomes of all ALS phenotypes in a population-based Italian series (together with bulbar).
variants.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Chio A et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:740-746 (PMID 21402743)

variants.variant: Madras motor neuron disease (South India variant)
variants.features: A geographically distinct motor neuron syndrome reported predominantly from southern India: onset in youth (mean age 15.8 years in 116 patients seen over 36 years), weakness and wasting of limbs, multiple lower cranial nerve palsies, sensorineural hearing loss and pyramidal dysfunction; a variant also has optic atrophy, and familial forms exist.
variants.prognosis: Overall mean survival 334.9 months in that series, i.e. far longer than ALS; cause remains unknown.
variants.source: Nalini A et al., 'Madras motor neuron disease (MMND)', J Neurol Sci 2008;269:65-73 (PMID 18261745); WHO ICD-11 MMS 8B60.7 (via public mirror)

differential_diagnosis.framework: Diagnosis requires exclusion of ALS mimics because several are treatable. The conditions that most commonly mimic ALS are multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, axonal motor-predominant CIDP, spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) and inclusion body myositis; cervical root/cord compression is another classic error. In the population-based Irish register, 7.3% of referrals were re-diagnosed as mimics (MMN 22% and Kennedy disease 13% of them).
differential_diagnosis.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Traynor BJ et al., Arch Neurol 2000;57:109-113 (PMID 10634456); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301, Table 3)

conditions.condition: Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) with conduction block - the important treatable mimic
conditions.how_it_mimics: Slowly progressive, asymmetric, distal weakness of one or more limbs, usually the arms, with no objective sensory loss and no UMN signs (a pure LMN syndrome).
conditions.distinguishing_features: Focal asymmetrical onset, often in the upper limb; pure LMN syndrome; may stabilise for months or years; male:female about 4:1; weakness often out of proportion to wasting; motor nerve conduction block at non-compressible sites on nerve conduction studies (with other minor demyelinating features); anti-GM1 IgM antibodies are raised in fewer than half of patients (so a negative titre does not exclude MMN); nerve MRI/ultrasound may show non-uniform nerve enlargement. Steroids and plasma exchange usually do not help.
conditions.treatable: Yes - immunoglobulin. Cochrane 2022 (6 crossover RCTs, 90 participants): low-certainty evidence that IVIg improves strength (78% versus 4% of IVIg-naive participants improved in the strength outcome) and may improve disability (39% versus 11%, wide confidence interval); most responders deteriorate after withdrawal. Older reviews quote improvement with IVIg in about 70% of patients. Muscle strength often slowly declines long-term even with maintenance IVIg.
conditions.source: Traynor BJ et al., Arch Neurol 2000;57:109-113 (PMID 10634456); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Claytor B et al., Muscle Nerve 2025;71:512-534 (PMID 39936246); Keddie S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;1:CD004429 (PMID 35015296); EFNS/PNS joint task force MMN guideline, J Peripher Nerv Syst 2010;15:295-301 (PMID 21199100); Lawson V & Robbins NM, US Neurol 2018;14:102-107 (PMID 41583971)
conditions.confidence: high for the clinical/electrodiagnostic picture; moderate for treatment effect size (small RCTs)

conditions.condition: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy / radiculomyelopathy (and other cervical cord or foramen magnum lesions, syringomyelia)
conditions.how_it_mimics: Simultaneous cervical root and cord compression gives LMN signs (weakness, wasting, occasional fasciculations) in the arms with UMN signs in the legs, i.e. a 'combined UMN/LMN' picture, and can be misdiagnosed as classic ALS.
conditions.distinguishing_features: Asymmetrical onset, combined UMN and LMN signs in the arm(s) (occasionally with fasciculations), root-distribution pain (may be mild or brief), often progression followed by stabilisation, NO bulbar involvement, MRI evidence of cord and root compression, and no widespread chronic partial denervation on EMG in regions outside the compressed segments (patients may have coexisting lumbosacral radiculopathy). Syringomyelia typically gives LMN signs with dissociated sensory loss; foramen magnum and high cervical lesions may give C8/T1 wasting with cerebellar or sensory involvement.
conditions.treatable: Structural lesions are potentially treatable, which is why MRI of the cervical spine is part of the work-up in probable/possible ALS.
conditions.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301, Table 3); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

conditions.condition: Kennedy disease - spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA)
conditions.how_it_mimics: Slowly progressive proximal limb and bulbar weakness with wasting and fasciculations in a man.
conditions.distinguishing_features: X-linked, so males are symptomatic and there is a family history; caused by a CAG-repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene (identified 1991; positive DNA test is diagnostic); perioral/facial fasciculations, gynaecomastia and other signs of androgen insensitivity; proximal symmetric weakness in addition to foot drop; sensory involvement (sensory nerve action potentials reduced in nearly all of 57 genetically confirmed patients); slowly progressive. Diagnostic delay averaged over 5 years from onset of weakness. In 223 Japanese patients, hand tremor appeared at a median 33 years, weakness at 44, dysarthria at 50, dysphagia at 54, wheelchair use at 61; pneumonia and respiratory failure were the most common causes of death (median age 65 in the 15 who died).
conditions.treatable: No curative therapy exists (Atsuta 2006). Distinguishing it matters for prognosis (a much slower course than ALS: weakness first noticed at a median 44 years and deaths at a median 65 years in the Japanese series) and for genetic counselling.
conditions.source: La Spada AR et al., Nature 1991;352:77-79 (PMID 2062380); Rhodes LE et al., Brain 2009;132:3242-3251 (PMID 19846582); Atsuta N et al., Brain 2006;129:1446-1455 (PMID 16621916); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301, Table 3)

conditions.condition: Myasthenia gravis (MG), including MuSK-antibody MG - cross-reference: see the 'myasthenia_gravis' entry in this knowledge base
conditions.how_it_mimics: Bulbar-onset MG causes dysarthria and dysphagia and, in MuSK-antibody MG, predominant bulbar involvement with muscle atrophy, which can be mistaken for bulbar-onset ALS.
conditions.distinguishing_features: Ocular symptoms (ptosis, diplopia), clinical improvement or slow progression, absence of UMN signs, and AChR/MuSK antibody testing point to MG (full MG features are in the myasthenia_gravis entry). In four MuSK MG patients initially misdiagnosed as ALS, clues for changing the diagnosis were slow progression, clinical improvement, development of diplopia and absence of UMN signs; no MuSK antibodies were found in 256 Dutch bulbar-onset ALS patients, so true mis-diagnosis is rare. In a comparison of 70 ALS and 37 MG patients, speech-swallow dissociation in velopharyngeal closure on laryngoscopy was seen in 33% of ALS versus 3% of MG (odds ratio 26.6). MG and ALS can also coexist (42 reported cases in a systematic review): new ptosis or diplopia in an ALS patient should prompt consideration of a second diagnosis, a positive AChR antibody alone is insufficient to diagnose MG when ALS coexists, and repetitive nerve stimulation may be less sensitive in patients with ALS.
conditions.treatable: Yes - MG is treatable (see the myasthenia_gravis entry).
conditions.source: Huijbers MG et al., Neuromuscul Disord 2016;26:350-353 (PMID 27133662); Yaguchi H et al., Auris Nasus Larynx 2025;52:239-242 (PMID 40215589); Nashwan AJ et al., Med Princ Pract 2025;34:432-442 (PMID 40209696); Statland JM et al., Neurol Clin 2015;33:735-748 (PMID 26515618)
conditions.confidence: high for the distinguishing pattern; the overlap-syndrome evidence is case-report level

conditions.how_it_mimics: Progressive weakness with wasting, sometimes with bulbar symptoms and occasionally respiratory muscle weakness.
conditions.distinguishing_features: Characteristic weakness and wasting of the deep finger flexors and quadriceps femoris; EMG shows evidence of myopathy; muscle biopsy is the definitive test (rimmed vacuoles), and IBM pathology features invasion of myofibres by cytotoxic T cells.
conditions.treatable: No established effective disease-modifying treatment (relatively treatment-refractory autoimmune-T-cell myositis); distinguishing it matters for prognosis and avoiding unhelpful ALS labelling.
conditions.source: Greenberg SA, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2019;15:257-272 (PMID 30837708); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301, Table 3)
conditions.confidence: high for the clinical pattern; treatment statement reflects the review's description of IBM as relatively treatment-refractory

conditions.condition: Axonal motor-predominant chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) and other immune neuropathies/neuronopathies
conditions.how_it_mimics: Progressive motor weakness with wasting and reduced reflexes and, at times, fasciculations.
conditions.distinguishing_features: Nerve conduction studies are needed to identify demyelinating features, conduction block or sensory involvement; abnormal serology also calls the ALS diagnosis into question. Listed by the 2022 Lancet seminar among the most common mimics, and stressed as potentially treatable.
conditions.treatable: Some are treatable, hence the need for exclusion.
conditions.confidence: moderate - stated at review level without quantitative detail

conditions.condition: Lumbosacral radiculopathy / conus lesions, skull-base and focal cerebral lesions, cramp-fasciculation syndromes
conditions.how_it_mimics: Mixed UMN+LMN patterns (conus/radiculopathy), isolated lower cranial nerve signs (skull base) or cramps/fasciculations without weakness.
conditions.distinguishing_features: Conus and lumbosacral lesions usually have sensory symptoms or signs and bladder involvement, with radiculopathy on EMG and MRI; skull-base lesions cause asymmetric tongue wasting and lower cranial nerve signs without limb denervation on EMG; cramp/fasciculation/myokymia syndromes (Isaacs, peripheral nerve hyperexcitability) show myokymia on EMG, about 30% have voltage-gated potassium channel antibodies and about 20% are associated with thymoma or lung cancer.
conditions.source: Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301, Table 3)
conditions.confidence: moderate - single review table, adapted from Kato et al.

conditions.condition: UMN-dominant presentations: hereditary spastic paraplegia and primary progressive multiple sclerosis; rare metabolic causes
conditions.how_it_mimics: Pure UMN spasticity resembling PLS or UMN-dominant ALS.
conditions.distinguishing_features: UMN-dominant ALS or PLS may be confused with hereditary spastic paraplegia or primary progressive MS; rare mimics are hyperparathyroidism and hexosaminidase A/B deficiency.
conditions.treatable: The seminar notes that some of these mimics are treatable, which is why they must be excluded.
conditions.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Turner MR et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2020;91:373-377 (PMID 32029539)

red_flags: Respiratory failure symptoms in a patient with known or suspected ALS: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, disturbed sleep, morning headaches, excessive daytime somnolence, poor concentration or mood change indicate nocturnal hypoventilation/hypercapnia and need urgent respiratory assessment (vital capacity, maximal inspiratory pressure, overnight oximetry, blood gas/bicarbonate) - respiratory failure is the usual cause of death and non-invasive ventilation improves survival (best in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction). About 5% of patients present with respiratory weakness alone.

Bulbar decompensation: choking, aspiration episodes, pneumonia, inability to manage secretions, or weight loss of more than 10% of baseline - these need swallowing assessment and nutrition/gastrostomy planning (EFNS advises gastrostomy before respiratory insufficiency develops). In a French death series, pneumonia caused 14% and asphyxia from a foreign body 3% of deaths.

Features that argue against ALS and should trigger a search for a mimic: prominent sensory loss, sphincter or autonomic dysfunction, anterior visual pathway abnormalities, ophthalmoplegia/ptosis or fluctuating fatigable weakness, root-distribution pain, weakness that stabilises or fails to progress, isolated distal upper-limb weakness with conduction block, a family history with gynaecomastia in a man (Kennedy disease).
Multifocal motor neuropathy has to be excluded early because it is treatable (immunoglobulin) and is the most common mimic in population data (22% of mimics in the Irish register).

Pure UMN or pure LMN presentations: diagnose PLS only after about 4 years of isolated UMN signs (before that many patients develop LMN signs), and treat isolated progressive bulbar palsy as evolving ALS (87% progressed to definite ALS in one series).

New cognitive or behavioural change (apathy, disinhibition, executive or language decline) - about 15% meet FTD criteria and 35-50% have some impairment; behavioural impairment carries the strongest evidence for caregiver burden and affects consent and end-of-life planning.

Depression, hopelessness, suicidal ideation or a wish to die - ALS is associated with psychosis and suicidal ideation; in a 20-patient Indian study 25% expressed a death wish (mainly financial-support related) and 30% had mild-moderate depression.

Unexplained weight loss, pseudobulbar affect, and any UMN + LMN combination in an adult should prompt early neurology referral (the ALS Association 'thinkALS' tool is cited for a low threshold for referral) because the average time to diagnosis is 10-16 months.

real_risk_factors.note: Incidence rises from the 40s to a peak in the 60s-70s and then falls sharply. In a dose-response meta-analysis of 41 incidence studies, peak incidence in Europe and North America was 6.98-8.17 per 100,000 person-years at ages 71.6-77.4 years, with a lower peak (2.20 per 100,000 at about 75 years) in Eastern Asia; the 2022 Lancet seminar gives the highest incidence around 60-79 years. Mean onset of sporadic ALS is 55-65 years (median 64); only about 5% start before age 30. Familial ALS starts about a decade earlier. Indian hospital series report a much younger onset (mean 46.2 years), which may partly reflect referral patterns in tertiary centres rather than true biology.
real_risk_factors.source: Marin B et al., Eur J Epidemiol 2018;33:621-634 (PMID 29687175); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Nalini A et al., J Neurol Sci 2008;272:60-70 (PMID 18550082)

real_risk_factors.note: Male excess is one of the few replicable risk factors: standardised male:female incidence ratio 1.35 (2022 Lancet seminar); in a 2026 global meta-analysis of 142 studies the female:male incidence rate ratio was 0.74 (prevalence rate ratio 0.69), i.e. roughly 1.35:1 in men; in six European registers the incidence was 3.0 per 100,000 in men versus 2.4 in women, with a higher male incidence of spinal-onset ALS. The ratio is not constant: in a south-east England register the adjusted male:female ratio fell from 2.5 in the younger group to 1.4 in patients over 51 (prevalence data), and recent data suggest the sex gap may be narrowing. Hospital-based Indian data show a much larger male excess (M:F 3:1, n=1,153), but that is a referral cohort rather than population incidence.
real_risk_factors.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Liu RY et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2026 (PMID 42399099); Logroscino G et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2010;81:385-390 (PMID 19710046); Manjaly ZR et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2010;11:439-442 (PMID 20225930); Nalini A et al., J Neurol Sci 2008;272:60-70 (PMID 18550082)

real_risk_factors.note: About 5-10% (older) to 10-15% (recent estimate; possibly up to about 20%) of ALS is familial, mostly autosomal dominant; C9orf72 (about 40% of familial, 7% of sporadic ALS in European-ancestry cohorts), SOD1, TARDBP and FUS are the main genes; about 15% of apparently sporadic patients carry private pathogenic variants in known genes, so absence of family history does not exclude a genetic cause. The C9orf72 expansion is non-penetrant before age 35 and about 50% penetrant by age 58, nearly fully penetrant by 80. Heritability is higher in mother-daughter pairs, and the C9orf72 expansion lowers onset age in men versus women.
real_risk_factors.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Majounie E et al., Lancet Neurol 2012;11:323-330 (PMID 22406228); Goutman SA et al., Lancet Neurol 2022;21:480-493 (PMID 35334233); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)

real_risk_factors.note: In a pooled analysis of five large prospective cohorts (832 ALS cases among 562,804 men and 556,276 women), age- and sex-adjusted relative risk was 1.44 (95% CI 1.23-1.68) for former smokers and 1.42 (1.07-1.88) for current smokers versus never smokers; risk was higher with earlier age at smoking initiation, but there was no dose-response among ever smokers. Case-control estimates range from RR 0.8 to 1.67. In an umbrella review of 16 meta-analyses only one factor (chronic occupational lead exposure) reached 'convincing' evidence, so smoking is best described as a consistent but modest association whose causal status is not settled.
real_risk_factors.source: Wang H et al., Arch Neurol 2011;68:207-213 (PMID 21320987); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Belbasis L et al., Neuroepidemiology 2016;46:96-105 (PMID 26731747)

real_risk_factors.note: Among about 2.5 million eligible US Gulf War-era military personnel, 107 confirmed ALS cases were identified (0.43 per 100,000 per year); deployed personnel had RR 1.92 (95% CI 1.29-2.84), with an attributable risk associated with deployment of 18%. In the American Cancer Society's CPS-II cohort (over 500,000 men; 280 ALS deaths among 126,414 men who did not serve and 281,874 who did), men who served had RR 1.53 (1.12-2.09) for ALS mortality, largely independent of branch and period served. Evidence quality: observational cohorts; the responsible exposure is unidentified.
real_risk_factors.source: Horner RD et al., Neurology 2003;61:742-749 (PMID 14504315); Weisskopf MG et al., Neurology 2005;64:32-37 (PMID 15642900)

real_risk_factors.note: A meta-analysis of 16 studies found an association with head injury (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.21-1.74) that weakened when a time lag between injury and ALS diagnosis was imposed (OR 1.21 for lag of 1 year or more; OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.84-1.59, not significant, for 3 years or more), suggesting the risk has been somewhat overestimated and that reverse causation (latent ALS causing falls/injury) is possible. It does not deny an association.
real_risk_factors.source: Watanabe Y & Watanabe T, Eur J Epidemiol 2017;32:867-879 (PMID 29080013)

real_risk_factors.factor: Athletics and vigorous physical activity (e.g. professional football)
real_risk_factors.note: In a cohort of 7,325 male Italian professional footballers (1970-2001) five ALS cases were identified (mean onset 43.4 years; three bulbar) versus 0.77 expected, giving SMR 6.5 (95% CI 2.1-15.1) with a dose-response for years of play (over 5 years: SMR 15.2). Caveats: very small case numbers, a single-country cohort, and the study cannot separate head trauma from other exposures. The 2022 Lancet seminar notes that physical activity is supported as an ALS risk by several studies, though not settled.
real_risk_factors.source: Chio A et al., Brain 2005;128:472-476 (PMID 15634730); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

real_risk_factors.factor: Other environmental exposures (occupational lead, pollutants, metals, lifestyle)
real_risk_factors.note: Chronic occupational lead exposure is the only factor with 'convincing' evidence in an umbrella review (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.39-2.35). Plasma persistent organic pollutants and blood metals correlate with ALS risk and shorter survival in retrospective cohorts; higher cigarette pack-years, lower current BMI and lifetime alcohol consumption also associate with risk, sometimes depending on C9orf72 status (gene-environment interaction). High-quality population-based confirmation is lacking. Foci of higher ALS frequency in the Western Pacific (Guam, Kii peninsula, New Guinea) have declined over 40 years and their cause remains elusive.
real_risk_factors.source: Belbasis L et al., Neuroepidemiology 2016;46:96-105 (PMID 26731747); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)

global_incidence_prevalence.finding: A meta-analysis of 44 population-based studies (13,146 cases; 825 million person-years) gave a pooled worldwide crude ALS incidence of 1.75 per 100,000 person-years (1.68 standardised). A 2020 meta-analysis of 124 studies gave crude worldwide prevalence 4.42 per 100,000 and incidence 1.59 per 100,000 person-years; a 2026 meta-analysis of 142 studies gave incidence 1.65, prevalence 5.05 and mortality 1.26 per 100,000, with burden peaking at ages 70-79 and lower in females (IRR 0.74). Lifetime ALS risk is about 1 in 350 (1 in 400 by an older estimate) but limited life expectancy keeps prevalence low. Projection: cases worldwide were estimated to rise from 222,801 in 2015 to 376,674 in 2040 (+69%), mostly from population ageing, especially in developing nations.
global_incidence_prevalence.source: Marin B et al., Int J Epidemiol 2017;46:57-74 (PMID 27185810); Xu L et al., J Neurol 2020;267:944-953 (PMID 31797084); Liu RY et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2026 (PMID 42399099); Arthur KC et al., Nat Commun 2016;7:12408 (PMID 27510634); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301)
global_incidence_prevalence.confidence: high for pooled estimates; heterogeneity between studies is substantial

regional_and_ethnic_variation.finding: Standardised incidence is homogeneous across Europe, North America and New Zealand (pooled 1.81 per 100,000; North Europe 1.89) but lower in East Asia (0.83) and in the 'South Asia' sub-region (0.73). Important caveat: the South Asia value in that meta-analysis rested on Iranian data, not on India. In a European pooled register analysis the crude incidence was 2.16 per 100,000 with similar rates across registers. Across meta-analyses, incidence and prevalence are highest in Europe, North America and Oceania and lowest in Asia and South America, and lower in upper-middle and lower-middle-income than in high-income countries (which may partly reflect under-ascertainment). Survival appears longer in Asia (3.74 years in South Asia to 9.23 years in West Asia in one meta-analysis).
regional_and_ethnic_variation.source: Marin B et al., Int J Epidemiol 2017;46:57-74 (PMID 27185810); Logroscino G et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2010;81:385-390 (PMID 19710046); Liu RY et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2026 (PMID 42399099); Xu L et al., J Neurol 2020;267:944-953 (PMID 31797084)
regional_and_ethnic_variation.confidence: moderate - Asian and African data are sparse and mostly not population-based

india_specific.finding: No population-based ALS incidence or prevalence study for India was found in this search; published Indian data are hospital/tertiary-centre cohorts, which cannot give incidence and may carry referral and survivor bias. What exists: (1) 1,153 patients with classical sporadic ALS seen over 30 years in a single-institution experience from India: 74.2% men (M:F 3:1), mean age at onset 46.2 years (one third before age 40; bulbar-onset mean 52.8 versus limb-onset 43.7 years), mean duration of illness at evaluation 17.7 months, overall median survival 114.8 months (bulbar 55.9 versus limb 177.9 months) - i.e. younger onset, more male preponderance and longer survival than in Caucasian series. (2) A 159-patient North Indian cohort with whole-exome sequencing: bulbar-onset patients had older onset (59.7 versus 54 years) and shorter median survival (48 versus 60 months; HR 1.75 for bulbar onset), 6.3% survived more than 10 years, and male sex (HR 1.74) and rare genetic variants (HR 1.53) predicted mortality. (3) Genetics: in 761 Indian ALS patients diagnostic yield of pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants was 15.9% (familial 36.95%, sporadic 12.96%), with SOD1 dominating familial cases (53.85%) and OPTN, SOD1 and FIG4 prominent in sporadic cases; C9orf72 expansions were found in only 4% and ATXN2 repeats in 1.7%. In a related exome-sequenced series of 765 individuals from the same group (cohorts may overlap), SOD1-ALS accounted for 4.8% of all patients and 24.2% of familial cases, with mostly lower-limb-onset, LMN-predominant disease and a higher frequency of homozygous variants linked to earlier onset. (4) Regional entity: Madras motor neuron disease (see variants). (5) Asia overall holds over half the world population but ALS knowledge outside East Asia remains limited.
india_specific.source: Nalini A et al., J Neurol Sci 2008;272:60-70 (PMID 18550082); Khurana S et al., Brain Commun 2026;8:fcag003 (PMID 41574092); Kotambail A et al., J Neurol 2026;273:435 (PMID 42384233); Keerthipriya MS et al., J Neurol 2026;273:72 (PMID 41511639); Nalini A et al., J Neurol Sci 2008;269:65-73 (PMID 18261745); Shahrizaila N et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2016;87:821-830 (PMID 27093948)
india_specific.confidence: low-moderate for epidemiology (hospital-based only); high that the reported cohort figures are as published

median_survival_and_wide_variability.finding: ALS is uniformly fatal in its natural course. Median survival from symptom onset ranges from 20 to 48 months across studies (systematic review), i.e. about 2-4 years (2022 seminar); by onset site, about 2-3 years for bulbar onset and 3-5 years for limb onset. Clinic cohorts show 3-year and 5-year survival of about 48% and 24%, with about 4% surviving beyond 10 years; population-based 5-year survival is lower (4-30%). The 'about 10% long survivors' figure is source-dependent: 10-20% survive beyond 10 years in a systematic review, 4% (30 of 769) in the King's College database, and 6.3% (10 of 159) in a North Indian cohort. Long survivors tended to have younger onset and a predominance of pure UMN signs at presentation, but poor-prognosis features were also present in many, so individual survival is unpredictable. The European ENCALS model (11,475 patients, 14 centres) stratifies predicted median survival from about 17.7 months (very short-survival group) to 91.0 months (very long-survival group).
median_survival_and_wide_variability.source: Chio A et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2009;10:310-323 (PMID 19922118); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Turner MR et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:995-997 (PMID 12810805); Khurana S et al., Brain Commun 2026;8:fcag003 (PMID 41574092); Westeneng HJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:423-433 (PMID 29598923); Goutman SA et al., Lancet Neurol 2022;21:480-493 (PMID 35334233)
median_survival_and_wide_variability.confidence: high for the 2-4 year median and the wide spread; long-survivor percentage is 4-20% depending on source and setting

bulbar_versus_limb_onset_prognosis.finding: Older age and bulbar onset are consistently reported to worsen outcome. In the population-based Italian phenotype study, the best outcomes were in pure UMN, pyramidal, pure LMN and flail-arm phenotypes and the worst in respiratory and bulbar phenotypes. In the ENCALS development cohort, bulbar versus non-bulbar onset had a univariable HR of 1.71 (95% CI 1.63-1.79). Indian data agree: in 1,153 patients median survival was 55.9 months for bulbar versus 177.9 months for limb onset, and in 159 North Indian patients 48 versus 60 months (HR 1.75). Multidisciplinary clinic care extended prognosis of bulbar-onset patients by 9.6 months in an Irish register comparison.
bulbar_versus_limb_onset_prognosis.source: Chio A et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:740-746 (PMID 21402743); Westeneng HJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:423-433 (PMID 29598923); Chio A et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2009;10:310-323 (PMID 19922118); Nalini A et al., J Neurol Sci 2008;272:60-70 (PMID 18550082); Khurana S et al., Brain Commun 2026;8:fcag003 (PMID 41574092); Traynor BJ et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:1258-1261 (PMID 12933930)

prognostic_factors.finding: Eight independent predictors were retained in the ENCALS model (univariable HRs): bulbar onset 1.71, age at onset 1.03 per year, definite (versus probable/possible) El Escorial 1.47, diagnostic delay 0.52 (shorter delay means faster disease), forced vital capacity 0.99, progression rate 6.33, FTD 1.34, and C9orf72 expansion 1.45; external c-statistic 0.78. From the systematic review: older age and bulbar onset are consistently reported to worsen outcome, rate of symptom progression is an independent prognostic factor, and FTD, nutritional status, respiratory function and psychosocial factors are also related to outcome; evidence on sex, diagnostic delay and El Escorial category was conflicting; non-invasive ventilation improved survival. Genotype also matters: the SOD1 A4V (Ala4Val) mutation is associated with rapidly progressive familial ALS, DCTN1 mutations with slower progression; in an Indian SOD1 cohort survival was prolonged with H47R, V88M and I152N variants while juvenile onset had reduced survival.
prognostic_factors.source: Westeneng HJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:423-433 (PMID 29598923); Chio A et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2009;10:310-323 (PMID 19922118); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Rosen DR et al., Hum Mol Genet 1994;3:981-987 (PMID 7951249); Keerthipriya MS et al., J Neurol 2026;273:72 (PMID 41511639)
prognostic_factors.confidence: high for the model; predictions retain considerable uncertainty and should be used cautiously for individuals

respiratory_failure_as_cause_of_death.finding: Neuromuscular respiratory failure is the most common cause of death, usually within two to five years of onset. In the French prospective series (n=302), 77% of deaths were from respiratory failure; most died in a medical facility (63%), and only 55% were on riluzole, 33% on NIV, 3% tracheostomised and 37% had a gastrostomy at death. In an RCT (92 patients assessed, 41 randomised), non-invasive ventilation started when orthopnoea with MIP under 60% predicted or symptomatic hypercapnia developed improved survival and quality of life in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction (median survival benefit 205 days) but gave no survival benefit in those with severe bulbar impairment, though it improved sleep-related symptoms.
respiratory_failure_as_cause_of_death.source: Radunovic A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;10:CD004427 (PMID 28982219); Gil J et al., Eur J Neurol 2008;15:1245-1251 (PMID 18973614); Bourke SC et al., Lancet Neurol 2006;5:140-147 (PMID 16426990)

caregiver_burden.finding: Informal caregivers experience increasing burden as the disease progresses. Systematic review of 25 studies: high-quality evidence links caregiver burden to the patient's behavioural impairment; moderate-quality evidence to the caregiver's depression and the patient's physical functioning; other factors (bulbar, respiratory and motor function, cognition, disease duration) had low or very low evidence. Caregiver time rises with patient disability (70 patients, mean 2.0 caregivers each; the most time-consuming tasks were housekeeping, feeding and toileting, with growing reliance on paid caregivers) - a hidden cost. In an Indian study of 30 patient-caregiver pairs, worse function and quality of life correlated with higher caregiver burden (Zarit scale); in a survey of 130 bereaved Indian caregivers, most patients died at home (57.7%), 29.2% died suddenly, and the authors call for community-integrated palliative care and caregiver support.
caregiver_burden.source: de Wit J et al., Palliat Med 2018;32:231-245 (PMID 28671483); Chio A et al., Neurology 2006;67:902-904 (PMID 16966565); Chio A et al., Eur J Neurol 2010;17:1298-1303 (PMID 20402747); Thomas PT et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler Frontotemporal Degener 2018;19:606-610 (PMID 30039719); Chikktimmegowda D et al., Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2026;29:386-391 (PMID 42241188)
caregiver_burden.confidence: high for the association with behavioural impairment; Indian studies are small or single-centre

clinical_takeaway.point: Refer early: any adult with progressive weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia or unexplained UMN+LMN signs should see an experienced neurologist without delay, and a confirmed or strongly suspected ALS patient should be referred to a specialist multidisciplinary ALS clinic (a team including a consultant, physical and occupational therapists, speech pathologist, dietician and social worker, with respiratory and palliative-care input).
clinical_takeaway.why: Average time from first symptom to diagnosis is 10-16 months, delaying care. The AAN practice parameter recommends multidisciplinary clinic referral to optimise health-care delivery and prolong survival (Level B) and may enhance quality of life (Level C); the EFNS guideline advises assessment by an experienced neurologist as soon as possible, high-priority neurophysiology, and regular multidisciplinary team support. Evidence: in Ireland, median survival of clinic attenders was 7.5 months longer (attendance was an independent covariate of survival, HR 1.47), and in a later Republic of Ireland/Northern Ireland comparison clinic attendance carried HR 0.59; multidisciplinary care improved mental quality of life (SF-36) in a Dutch cross-sectional study. These are observational comparisons and the Irish clinic cohort was younger and more often on riluzole, so the survival effect size is uncertain, but the direction is consistent.
clinical_takeaway.source: Richards D et al., J Neurol Sci 2020;417:117054 (PMID 32763509); Miller RG et al., AAN practice parameter, Neurology 2009;73:1227-1233 (PMID 19822873); Andersen PM et al., EFNS guidelines, Eur J Neurol 2012;19:360-375 (PMID 21914052); Traynor BJ et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:1258-1261 (PMID 12933930); Rooney J et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2015;86:496-501 (PMID 25550416); Van den Berg JP et al., Neurology 2005;65:1264-1267 (PMID 16247055)

clinical_takeaway.point: Before labelling ALS, actively exclude treatable mimics: perform nerve conduction studies (motor conduction block, sensory involvement) with EMG, MRI of the cervical spine (and brain/whole spine as indicated), routine serology, anti-GM1 antibodies and other neuropathy work-up when a pure LMN pattern is present; consider AChR/MuSK antibody testing for bulbar presentations without UMN signs; and androgen-receptor CAG testing in men with slowly progressive bulbar/limb weakness and gynaecomastia.
clinical_takeaway.why: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, axonal CIDP, Kennedy disease, inclusion body myositis and cervical cord/root compression are the classic mimics; 7.3% of referrals to the Irish ALS register were re-diagnosed as mimics, with MMN the most common (22%). MMN is treatable with immunoglobulin, cervical compression is structurally treatable, and misdiagnosing them as ALS deprives the patient of treatment and imposes a wrong prognosis. Diagnosis remains clinical, and no single test confirms ALS.
clinical_takeaway.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Traynor BJ et al., Arch Neurol 2000;57:109-113 (PMID 10634456); Wijesekera LC & Leigh PN, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2009;4:3 (PMID 19192301); Keddie S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;1:CD004429 (PMID 35015296); Huijbers MG et al., Neuromuscul Disord 2016;26:350-353 (PMID 27133662)

clinical_takeaway.point: Monitor respiratory function from the outset and at every visit: ask about orthopnoea, dyspnoea, disturbed sleep, morning headaches and daytime somnolence, and measure vital capacity/maximal inspiratory pressure and, where needed, overnight oximetry and CO2/bicarbonate; offer non-invasive ventilation when criteria are met, and plan gastrostomy before respiratory insufficiency develops.
clinical_takeaway.why: Respiratory failure is the usual cause of death. In an RCT (92 patients assessed, 41 randomised), non-invasive ventilation improved survival and quality of life in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction (median survival benefit 205 days) and improved sleep-related symptoms in those with severe bulbar impairment. The AAN rates NIV to lengthen survival as Level B evidence. The Cochrane review notes the randomised evidence is thin (a single 41-patient study), and Indian data show that only 20% of decedents had received bilevel PAP.
clinical_takeaway.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Bourke SC et al., Lancet Neurol 2006;5:140-147 (PMID 16426990); Miller RG et al., AAN practice parameter, Neurology 2009;73:1218-1226 (PMID 19822872); Radunovic A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;10:CD004427 (PMID 28982219); Andersen PM et al., Eur J Neurol 2012;19:360-375 (PMID 21914052); Chikktimmegowda D et al., Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2026;29:386-391 (PMID 42241188)

clinical_takeaway.point: Have the advance-care-planning conversation early, while the patient has capacity, and screen cognition and behaviour at diagnosis.
clinical_takeaway.why: The EFNS guideline states that advance directives for palliative end-of-life care should be discussed early with the patient and carers, respecting their social and cultural background. Because 35-50% of patients have cognitive or behavioural change and about 15% have FTD, capacity and decision-making may be impaired later; the AAN recommends screening for cognitive and behavioural impairment (Level B). Cognitive/behavioural change also has direct consequences for caregiving and end-of-life decisions.
clinical_takeaway.source: Andersen PM et al., Eur J Neurol 2012;19:360-375 (PMID 21914052); Miller RG et al., Neurology 2009;73:1227-1233 (PMID 19822873); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Strong MJ et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler Frontotemporal Degener 2017;18:153-174 (PMID 28054827)

clinical_takeaway.point: Offer genetic testing and counselling through a specialist centre irrespective of family history (the most common and penetrant genes are C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP and FUS), and take a full family history including dementia and psychiatric illness.
clinical_takeaway.why: In a 100-patient prospective UK series, 21% carried a pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, 93% of them without a family history, and 15% qualified for a genetic-therapy trial. Genetic testing is increasingly recommended for all persons with ALS/FTD, although it is not yet universal standard of care. In India the diagnostic yield was 15.9% (SOD1 dominant), with C9orf72 rare (4%), so panels should reflect local genetics.
clinical_takeaway.source: Shepheard SR et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2021;92:510-518 (PMID 33589474); Chambers C et al., Neurol Clin Pract 2023;13:e200201 (PMID 37736067); Roggenbuck J & Fong JC, Clin Lab Med 2020;40:271-287 (PMID 32718499); Kotambail A et al., J Neurol 2026;273:435 (PMID 42384233)

clinical_takeaway.point: Give honest, individualised prognostic information and support the caregiver from the start.
clinical_takeaway.why: Median survival is only about 2-4 years, but individual survival varies widely (about 4-20% pass 10 years, depending on the source) and even the best prediction models retain uncertainty; the 2022 seminar advises teams to convey the anticipated course with the caveat that it varies by patient. Caregiver burden rises with disability and is most strongly associated with the patient's behavioural impairment.
clinical_takeaway.source: Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464); Westeneng HJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:423-433 (PMID 29598923); Chio A et al., Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2009;10:310-323 (PMID 19922118); de Wit J et al., Palliat Med 2018;32:231-245 (PMID 28671483)

clinical_takeaway.point: Scope note for this knowledge base: this entry covers diagnosis and clinical features only; disease-modifying and symptomatic drug therapy for ALS (for example riluzole) sits in the companion treatment entry for this disease, and any drug or device decision remains with the treating registered medical practitioner.
clinical_takeaway.why: ALS has no cure; the 2017 Primer notes two possible disease-modifying therapies that can slow progression, with patient management largely mediated by symptomatic therapies. The clinical first steps above are independent of drug choice.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hardiman O et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17071 (PMID 28980624); Feldman EL et al., Lancet 2022;400:1363-1380 (PMID 36116464)

amyotrophic_lateral_sclerosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is NOT curable, and this must be stated plainly rather than hedged. The underlying degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons continues under every treatment used today, and median survival is limited to about 3 years after disease onset, mostly because of respiratory failure (EAN guideline, Eur J Neurol 2024, PMID 38470068). That is the honest difference from stroke or epilepsy in this knowledge base, which carry a real curative-intent option; ALS has none, so no curative_option key is provided (same convention as Parkinson's disease, COPD and asthma). What the real evidence DOES show, in order of strength: (1) Supportive and multidisciplinary care has the strongest real evidence. Attending a specialist multidisciplinary ALS clinic was associated with a median survival 7.5 months longer than general neurology care in the Irish population register (p<0.0001; Traynor et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003, PMID 12933930) and a hazard ratio for death of 0.59 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.71) in a later 719-patient Irish/Northern Irish register comparison (Rooney et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2015, PMID 25550416); these are observational data, and the Cochrane overview of symptomatic treatments for MND found no randomised trial of multidisciplinary care (PMID 28072907). Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is the only supportive intervention with a randomised survival benefit: median survival 219 versus 171 days overall and 205 days longer in patients with normal to moderately impaired bulbar function, with maintained or improved quality of life (Bourke et al, Lancet Neurol 2006, PMID 16426990; Cochrane 2017, PMID 28982219). (2) Disease-modifying drugs give real but MODEST benefit. Riluzole, the one drug offered to all patients, probably prolongs median survival by about 2 to 3 months (Cochrane 2012, PMID 22419278). Edaravone showed a 2.49-point ALSFRS-R difference at 24 weeks in a small, tightly selected Japanese population (Lancet Neurol 2017, PMID 28522181), but a propensity-matched real-world cohort found no benefit (JAMA Neurol 2022, PMID 35006266), the European Medicines Agency application was withdrawn in 2019, and the 2024 EAN guideline does not recommend it outside clinical trials. Tofersen helps only the roughly 2 percent of patients with a SOD1 gene variant, and its US accelerated approval rests on a biomarker (plasma neurofilament light chain), not on a proven clinical benefit at the primary endpoint (VALOR, N Engl J Med 2022, PMID 36129998). (3) The sodium phenylbutyrate-taurursodiol (Relyvrio/AMX0035) story is a warning against overselling: a 137-patient phase 2 trial (CENTAUR) met its primary endpoint and the product was FDA-approved on 29 September 2022, but the 664-patient confirmatory phase 3 trial (PHOENIX) showed no difference from placebo at 48 weeks (p=0.667), the sponsor stopped marketing it, and FDA formally withdrew approval on 29 August 2025 (Federal Register 2025-16646). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has ALS: refer early to a specialist multidisciplinary ALS team; start riluzole at diagnosis; test for a SOD1 variant and, if present, discuss tofersen at a specialist centre; monitor respiratory function every 2 to 3 months and offer NIV and cough-assist techniques as soon as respiratory insufficiency appears; discuss gastrostomy early and before respiratory failure; treat drooling, cramps, spasticity, pseudobulbar affect, pain, low mood and anxiety actively; provide communication aids (AAC) and mobility equipment without delay; and hold advance-care-planning and palliative-care conversations early, at trigger points such as diagnosis, a fall in respiratory function, or the decision on gastrostomy or NIV.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine, procedure and device used for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), in the order: (1) multidisciplinary ALS clinic care, the single highest-value intervention category; (2) riluzole; (3) edaravone (intravenous and oral); (4) sodium phenylbutyrate-taurursodiol (Relyvrio/AMX0035), historical entry only because it was withdrawn from the market after the PHOENIX phase 3 trial failed; (5) tofersen for SOD1-ALS only, with the surrogate-endpoint nuance; (6) respiratory support: non-invasive ventilation, cough augmentation, invasive ventilation via tracheostomy, and the harmful diaphragm-pacing trial; (7) nutrition and gastrostomy, with the real timing controversy; (8) symptom management: sialorrhea, pseudobulbar affect, cramps, spasticity, and pain, mood, sleep and other symptoms; (9) communication aids (AAC) and mobility/rehabilitation equipment; (10) palliative care and advance care planning; (11) the honest record of failed or unproven treatments; (12) medical equipment and devices. ALS has NO curative option, so no curative_option key exists (see CURABILITY_NOTE). All keys are prefixed als_ to avoid collision with other entries. Every drug class carries real specific drug names per this project's standing rule (non-drug items and devices are labelled as such), and every entry names its actual trial, guideline or FDA label; where a number could not be retrieved from the primary source it is not stated. Note on guidelines: the 2024 European Academy of Neurology (EAN) guideline is the main current guideline used here; the 2009 American Academy of Neurology (AAN) practice parameter on drug, nutritional and respiratory therapies was formally retired by the AAN in 2026 (Neurology 2026, PMID 42060880) and is cited only as historical evidence.

als_multidisciplinary_clinic_care.name: Multidisciplinary ALS Clinic Care - the Single Highest-Value Intervention Category (Real Survival and Quality-of-Life Data)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - clinic-based team of neurologist, specialist nurse, pulmonologist, rehabilitation physician, dietitian, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech-language therapist, clinical psychologist, social care worker and palliative-care professional (team composition per the EAN 2024 guideline)
als_multidisciplinary_clinic_care.effectiveness: Irish ALS Register (Traynor et al, prospective population-based study, all ALS cases diagnosed over 5 years, 344 patients): 82 (24%) attended a multidisciplinary ALS clinic and 262 (76%) were followed in general neurology; median survival of the clinic cohort was 7.5 months longer (log-rank 15.4, p<0.0001), one-year mortality was decreased by 29.7%, bulbar-onset survival was extended by 9.6 months, and clinic attendance remained an independent covariate of survival on multivariate analysis (HR 1.47, p=0.02). Island-of-Ireland comparison (Rooney et al, 719 incident cases 2005-2010): survival benefit for patients attending the Republic of Ireland multidisciplinary clinic, HR 0.59 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.71, p<0.001), preserved after multivariate analysis, with a trend to better survival in Northern Ireland community-based care supported by a specialist care worker versus no clinic. Quality of life (Van den Berg et al, cross-sectional, 208 patients): mental quality of life on the SF-36 Mental Summary Score was better with multidisciplinary care (133 patients) than general care (75 patients) (p=0.01); adequate aids and appliances 93.1% versus 81.3% (p=0.008); no significant difference in the SF-36 Physical Summary Score or in caregiver quality of life. The former AAN 2009 practice parameter graded multidisciplinary clinic referral Level B for survival and Level C for quality of life. The 2024 EAN guideline recommends clinic-based specialist multidisciplinary care with a strong recommendation (++).
als_multidisciplinary_clinic_care.reason_why: ALS affects motor function, swallowing, speech, breathing, nutrition, cognition and mood at once, so no single specialist can manage it. A coordinated team reassesses the person regularly (EAN: usually every 3 to 6 months) using the ALSFRS-R, so that respiratory decline, weight loss, drooling, communication loss and caregiver strain are caught and acted on early instead of after a crisis. Traynor et al conclude that active and aggressive management enhances survival, particularly in bulbar-onset patients; Rooney et al propose that multiple decision-making processes within a multidisciplinary setting lead to an enriched set of clinical encounters that enhance outcome. In the Irish study 99% of clinic patients versus 61% of general-neurology patients received riluzole, and the clinic cohort was on average 5 years younger, so part of the association may reflect these differences.
als_multidisciplinary_clinic_care.important_caveat: The evidence is observational, not randomised: the Cochrane overview of symptomatic treatments for MND (2017) states there is no randomised-trial evidence in a Cochrane review to demonstrate benefit or harm for multidisciplinary care, and the clinic cohort in the Irish study differed from the comparison cohort in age and riluzole use. It is ranked first here because it is the intervention that organises every other one, it is recommended most strongly by the current EAN guideline, and the survival signal is consistent across two independent register studies, not because a randomised trial proved it.
als_multidisciplinary_clinic_care.real_working_solution: Refer every person with suspected or confirmed ALS to a specialist multidisciplinary ALS clinic at or soon after diagnosis (EAN strong recommendation). The team should include neurologist, specialist nurse, pulmonologist, rehabilitation specialist, dietitian, physiotherapist, clinical psychologist/neuropsychologist, social care worker, occupational therapist, speech therapist and a professional with palliative-care expertise, with access to specialist palliative care, a gastroenterologist or interventional radiologist, rehabilitation services, assistive mobility technology, AAC devices and community/home care teams; it should reassess symptoms and needs regularly, use the ALSFRS-R longitudinally, and offer remote or home-based visits to people who cannot attend. Where no dedicated ALS clinic exists nearby (availability of dedicated ALS multidisciplinary clinics in India was not verified in this research), the practical aim is to reproduce these team roles through the treating neurologist plus physiotherapy, speech-language therapy, dietetics, respiratory support and palliative-care input.
als_multidisciplinary_clinic_care.source: Traynor BJ et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:1258-61 (PMID 12933930); Rooney J et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2015;86:496-501 (PMID 25550416); Van den Berg JP et al, Neurology 2005;65:1264-7 (PMID 16247055); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 2, Neurology 2009;73:1227-33 (PMID 19822873); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline, Eur J Neurol 2024;31:e16264 (PMID 38470068); Ng L et al, Cochrane overview of symptomatic treatments for MND, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;1:CD011776 (PMID 28072907)

als_riluzole.name: Riluzole 50 mg Twice Daily - the Only Disease-Modifying Drug Offered to All Patients (Real Modest Survival Benefit)
specific_drugs: Riluzole tablets 50 mg (Rilutek and generic riluzole)
Riluzole oral suspension (Tiglutik) for people with swallowing difficulty or a gastrostomy tube
als_riluzole.effectiveness: Bensimon et al (ALS/Riluzole Study Group, 155 outpatients, 100 mg/day, median follow-up 573 days): 12-month survival 74% (57 of 77) with riluzole versus 58% (45 of 78) with placebo (p=0.014); at the end of the placebo-controlled period survival was 49% versus 37% (p=0.046); in bulbar-onset disease 12-month survival was 73% versus 35%; deterioration of muscle strength was slower on riluzole (p=0.028). Lacomblez et al (dose-ranging trial, 959 patients, median follow-up 18 months): alive without tracheostomy 56.8% on 100 mg/day versus 50.4% on placebo (unadjusted risk 0.79, p=0.076; adjusted risk 0.65, p=0.002); no functional scale discriminated between groups; 100 mg/day was judged to have the best benefit-to-risk ratio. Cochrane review (Miller et al 2012; four trials, 974 riluzole-treated and 503 placebo-treated patients): hazard ratio for tracheostomy-free survival 0.80 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.99) in the two homogeneous trials and 0.84 (95% CI 0.698 to 0.997) with the third trial added, representing a 9% gain in the probability of surviving one year (49% placebo versus 58% riluzole) and a median survival increase from 11.8 to 14.8 months; the authors conclude riluzole probably prolongs median survival by about 2 to 3 months. The FDA label reports a median-survival difference of about 90 days (study 1) and about 60 days (study 2) among patients who reached the tracheostomy-or-death end point, and states that measures of muscle strength and neurological function did not show a benefit. EAN 2024: offer lifelong riluzole to all people with ALS at diagnosis (strong recommendation ++), dose 50 mg twice daily.
als_riluzole.reason_why: The FDA label states that the mechanism by which riluzole exerts its therapeutic effect in ALS is unknown; the original 1994 trial described it as an antiglutamate agent, noting that some research suggests the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate may be involved in the pathogenesis of ALS.
als_riluzole.important_caveat: The benefit is real but modest: about 2 to 3 months of median survival, without a demonstrated improvement in muscle strength or function. FDA-label warnings include drug-induced liver injury (some fatal), neutropenia, interstitial lung disease and pancreatitis; the most common adverse reactions in the label are oral hypoesthesia, asthenia, nausea, decreased lung function, hypertension and abdominal pain. Riluzole is not a substitute for multidisciplinary care.
als_riluzole.real_working_solution: Start riluzole 50 mg twice daily at diagnosis (EAN strong recommendation), taken at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal (FDA label), and continue it alongside multidisciplinary care, NIV and the other supportive measures below, which carry larger real effects. Check serum aminotransferases before starting, every month for the first 3 months and periodically afterwards; advise patients to report any febrile illness (neutropenia); stop for interstitial lung disease or suspected pancreatitis (FDA label). If side effects occur, consider a dose reduction and re-evaluate, and consider stopping if they persist; if fatigue is judged to be a drug effect, pausing riluzole may be considered (EAN 2024). If swallowing becomes difficult the oral suspension can be given by mouth or through a PEG tube (Tiglutik label).
als_riluzole.source: Bensimon G et al, N Engl J Med 1994;330:585-91 (PMID 8302340); Lacomblez L et al, Lancet 1996;347:1425-31 (PMID 8676624); Miller RG et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;3:CD001447 (PMID 22419278); FDA Tiglutik (riluzole) label, DailyMed set id 75d68f19-4208-109e-e053-2991aa0ac857; Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline, Eur J Neurol 2024;31:e16264 (PMID 38470068)

als_riluzole.name: Riluzole Formulations and Real Indian Availability (Rilutor, Generic Tablets, Oral Suspension)
specific_drugs: Rilutor 50 mg tablets (Sun Pharmaceutical Industries; Indian brand of riluzole)
Tiglutik riluzole oral suspension 50 mg per 10 mL (FDA-labelled; not verified as marketed in India)
als_riluzole.effectiveness: The FDA label for Tiglutik documents that its efficacy is based on bioavailability studies comparing riluzole oral tablets with the oral suspension, and that the suspension may be given by mouth or through a PEG tube (both silicone and polyurethane tubes); the label dose is 50 mg (10 mL) twice daily. India: riluzole 50 mg is sold as an Indian generic brand, Rilutor, made by Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd, which appears on Indian drug-price directories (Medindia listing 'Rilutor (50mg)') and Indian marketplace listings; a Sun Pharma social-media post titled 'Advisory for patients in India taking Rilutor 50 mg (Riluzole)' was seen as a search result, but its content could not be retrieved and is not relied on. Indian pack prices vary widely between listings and were not treated as reliable, so no price is stated. The CDSCO approval document itself was not retrieved, so CDSCO approval status is not asserted.
als_riluzole.reason_why: Riluzole is a small molecule that is absorbed orally; the suspension exists so that people who can no longer swallow tablets, or who have a gastrostomy, can keep taking the drug.
als_riluzole.important_caveat: Indian availability rests on commercial drug-price directories and marketplace listings, not on a CDSCO regulatory document; liquid riluzole availability in India was not verified.
als_riluzole.real_working_solution: In India, prescribe the generic riluzole 50 mg tablet twice daily (for example the Sun Pharma brand Rilutor); ask the dispensing pharmacy to confirm current supply because stock varies between suppliers, and plan the switch to a liquid formulation or a crushed-tablet/PEG-tube strategy with the treating team before swallowing fails.
als_riluzole.source: FDA Tiglutik label, DailyMed set id 75d68f19-4208-109e-e053-2991aa0ac857; Medindia drug-price listing for Rilutor 50 mg (Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd), accessed via web search 2026-09-21; Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068) for the remark that formulations of riluzole may not be available in all countries

als_edaravone.name: Intravenous Edaravone (Radicava) - Real Trial Evidence in a Narrow Population, and the Real Generalizability Debate
als_edaravone.type: Intravenous free-radical scavenger (disease-modifying claim, small selected-population evidence)
specific_drugs: Edaravone (Radicava) 60 mg intravenous infusion over 60 minutes
Generic edaravone injection (for example the Zydus Lifesciences product reported to have received US FDA tentative approval for ALS; Indian ALS availability not verified)
als_edaravone.effectiveness: MCI186-19 (Edaravone ALS 19 Study Group, Lancet Neurol 2017): 137 Japanese patients randomised 1:1 (69 edaravone, 68 placebo) to 60 mg intravenous edaravone or saline for 6 cycles (14 days on then 14 days off in cycle 1, then 10 of 14 days on); change in ALSFRS-R at 24 weeks was -5.01 versus -7.50, least-squares mean difference 2.49 points (95% CI 0.99 to 3.98, p=0.0013); serious adverse events 16% versus 24%. The trial enrolled only a narrow group: Japan ALS Severity Classification grade 1 or 2, all 12 ALSFRS-R items scored 2 or more, forced vital capacity 80% or more, definite or probable ALS by revised El Escorial criteria, disease duration 2 years or less, and an ALSFRS-R fall of 1 to 4 points during a 12-week observation period; over 90% were also taking riluzole (FDA label). An earlier phase 3 study had shown no significant difference; the 2017 trial was designed after a post-hoc analysis of that study. FDA label: most common adverse reactions contusion 15% versus 9%, gait disturbance 13% versus 9%, headache 10% versus 6% (placebo).
