Real-world data (Witzel et al, German MND-NET, propensity-score-matched, 194 patients who started intravenous edaravone, 116 matched pairs analysed): ALSFRS-R decline -0.91 versus -0.85 points per month (p=0.37); no significant difference in survival, time to ventilation or subgroup outcomes, including patients who met the MCI186-19 criteria; the authors conclude no disease-modifying benefit was associated with long-term intravenous edaravone. European Medicines Agency: the marketing-authorisation application was withdrawn by the company on 24 May 2019 after the CHMP was of the provisional opinion that Radicava could not be approved because the study was small, there was not enough evidence of improvement in survival, breathing or muscle strength, there were group imbalances (more patients with less severe disease in the edaravone group), and 24 weeks was considered too short. EAN 2024 guideline: does not recommend intravenous or oral edaravone outside the context of a clinical trial (interim recommendation, strong negative).
als_edaravone.reason_why: The FDA label states that the mechanism by which edaravone exerts its therapeutic effect in ALS is unknown; the EMA summary describes it as thought to neutralise oxygen-containing free radicals linked to nerve damage.
als_edaravone.important_caveat: The trial-based benefit (2.49 ALSFRS-R points at 24 weeks) is about one-third of the placebo-arm decline over that period and comes from a single positive trial in a small selected population; regulators disagree (FDA approved; EMA application withdrawn); and the 2024 EAN guideline does not endorse it. Intravenous therapy also needs venous access and 10 to 14 infusion days per cycle.
als_edaravone.real_working_solution: Edaravone is an FDA-approved add-on (label: indicated for the treatment of ALS), but the honest position is that its benefit is unproven outside a narrow early-stage profile and is not supported by real-world data; the decision is a shared one between patient and specialist and should never displace multidisciplinary care, NIV, nutrition and riluzole, which carry stronger evidence. If chosen, follow the label schedule (initial cycle daily for 14 days, then 14 days off; later cycles 10 days of every 14 followed by 14 days off), watch for hypersensitivity and sulfite allergy (the product contains sodium bisulfite), and stop if there is no perceived benefit or if the infusion burden outweighs it.
als_edaravone.source: Edaravone (MCI-186) ALS 19 Study Group, Lancet Neurol 2017;16:505-512 (PMID 28522181); Witzel S et al, JAMA Neurol 2022;79:121-130 (PMID 35006266); EMA/293450/2019, Withdrawal of the marketing authorisation application for Radicava (edaravone), 29 May 2019; FDA Radicava/Radicava ORS label, DailyMed set id 0ce2c1c4-2a40-485c-b7cb-96a9b85d9d11; Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068); Medical Dialogues news report on Zydus Lifesciences US FDA tentative approval of edaravone injection

als_edaravone.name: Oral Edaravone (Radicava ORS) - FDA-Approved Oral Suspension Formulation (Approval Based on Bioavailability)
als_edaravone.type: Oral or feeding-tube suspension of edaravone
specific_drugs: Radicava ORS (edaravone oral suspension) 105 mg (5 mL) daily
als_edaravone.effectiveness: FDA approved Radicava ORS on 12 May 2022. The label states that the efficacy of the oral suspension is based on a bioavailability study comparing Radicava (intravenous) and Radicava ORS, and that the efficacy of intravenous Radicava rests on the single 6-month Japanese study described above. Dose: 105 mg (5 mL) taken orally or via feeding tube in the morning after overnight fasting, with no food for 1 hour afterwards except water, on the same cycle schedule as the intravenous product. In an open-label study of 185 patients treated with Radicava ORS for 6 months, fatigue was observed in 7.6% (FDA label). The current DailyMed label lists Shionogi Inc. as the labeller of Radicava and Radicava ORS. The 2024 EAN guideline does not recommend oral edaravone outside clinical trials (interim, pending the European phase 3 oral trial). Indian CDSCO approval or marketing of oral edaravone for ALS was searched and could not be verified, so it is not asserted.
als_edaravone.reason_why: Same active molecule as the intravenous product; the oral suspension avoids repeated intravenous infusions and can be given through a feeding tube.
als_edaravone.important_caveat: No randomised efficacy trial of the oral formulation was located; approval rests on pharmacokinetic bridging. India availability could not be verified.
als_edaravone.real_working_solution: If a patient and team decide to try edaravone, the oral suspension removes the need for infusion visits and can be given via feeding tube after gastrostomy; the label limits food intake for 1 hour afterwards. The same caution about limited and contested clinical benefit applies as for the intravenous form.
als_edaravone.source: FDA Radicava/Radicava ORS label, DailyMed set id 0ce2c1c4-2a40-485c-b7cb-96a9b85d9d11; FDA approval announcement of Radicava ORS, 12 May 2022 (Mitsubishi Tanabe press release and FDA Drug Information Update); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.name: Sodium Phenylbutyrate-Taurursodiol (Relyvrio/AMX0035; Albrioza in Canada) - Historical Entry Only: Positive CENTAUR, Failed PHOENIX, Withdrawn From the Market
als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.type: Oral combination (formerly FDA-approved; now withdrawn, do not start)
specific_drugs: Sodium phenylbutyrate 3 g plus taurursodiol 1 g per sachet (Relyvrio in the USA, Albrioza in Canada; AMX0035 in trials)
als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.effectiveness: CENTAUR (phase 2, Paganoni et al, N Engl J Med 2020): 137 adults with definite ALS and symptom onset within 18 months, randomised 2:1 to sodium phenylbutyrate-taurursodiol (89) or placebo (48); the rate of ALSFRS-R decline over 24 weeks was -1.24 versus -1.66 points per month (difference 0.42 points per month, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.81, p=0.03); secondary outcomes did not differ significantly and adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal. A later exploratory long-term survival analysis (Muscle Nerve 2021; vital status for 135 of 137; open-label extension available to all completers) reported median overall survival of 25.0 months for participants originally randomised to the drug versus 18.5 months for placebo (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.92, p=0.023). FDA approved Relyvrio on 29 September 2022 for the treatment of ALS in adults. PHOENIX (confirmatory phase 3; Amylyx topline announcement, 8 March 2024): 664 adults, 48-week randomised placebo-controlled trial; NO significant difference in ALSFRS-R total score change from baseline at week 48 (p=0.667) and no significant differences across secondary endpoints (quality of life, overall survival, slow vital capacity); no new safety signals. On 4 April 2024 Amylyx announced it had started a process with FDA and Health Canada to voluntarily discontinue the marketing authorisations, and that Relyvrio/Albrioza would no longer be available for new patients, with existing patients in the USA and Canada offered transition to a free drug programme. FDA Federal Register notice (29 August 2025): Amylyx reported on 30 April 2024 that PHOENIX did not meet its prespecified primary and secondary endpoints; it planned to discontinue marketing as of 31 October 2024; FDA requested a voluntary withdrawal letter on 31 October 2024; Amylyx asked for withdrawal of NDA 216660 on 28 February 2025; approval was withdrawn as of 29 August 2025. The 2024 EAN guideline (written before PHOENIX reported) already did not recommend AMX0035 outside clinical trials.
als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.reason_why: The CENTAUR paper states that the two compounds had been found to reduce neuronal death in experimental models; the large confirmatory trial shows that this laboratory rationale did not translate into a clinical effect on function.
als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.important_caveat: This is the clearest real example in ALS of a promising phase 2 result (single trial, 24 weeks, 137 patients, p=0.03) that did not survive a large confirmatory trial. The CENTAUR survival analysis was exploratory, came after placebo participants could cross over to the drug, and included sponsor-affiliated authors; it should not be used to justify the drug.
als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.real_working_solution: Do not start or seek this product: it is withdrawn in the USA and Canada because the confirmatory trial failed, and its Indian availability was not verified. For anyone who was taking it, the working plan is unchanged: riluzole from diagnosis, multidisciplinary clinic care, early respiratory and nutritional support, symptom control and advance care planning; tofersen if a SOD1 variant is present.
als_sodium_phenylbutyrate_taurursodiol_r.source: Paganoni S et al (CENTAUR), N Engl J Med 2020;383:919-930 (PMID 32877582); Paganoni S et al, Muscle Nerve 2021;63:31-39 (PMID 33063909); Amylyx Pharmaceuticals PHOENIX topline press release, 8 March 2024; Amylyx press release on intention to remove Relyvrio/Albrioza from the market, 4 April 2024; FDA, Federal Register 2025-16646 (90 FR 42251), 29 August 2025; Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.name: Tofersen (Qalsody) - Intrathecal Antisense Oligonucleotide for SOD1-ALS ONLY (Real VALOR Data, Biomarker Versus Clinical-Benefit Nuance)
als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.type: Intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide (gene-targeted, applies only to SOD1 variant carriers)
specific_drugs: Genetic testing for SOD1 pathogenic variant is required before use (about 2 percent of all ALS)
als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.effectiveness: VALOR (phase 3, Miller et al, N Engl J Med 2022): 108 adults with SOD1-ALS randomised 2:1 to tofersen 100 mg (72) or placebo (36) as 8 intrathecal doses over 24 weeks; primary end point, change in ALSFRS-R to week 28 in the 60 participants predicted to have faster progression: -6.98 tofersen versus -8.14 placebo, difference 1.2 points (95% CI -3.2 to 5.5, p=0.97) - the primary clinical end point was NOT met, and secondary clinical end points did not differ significantly. Biomarkers did move: plasma neurofilament light chain fell (adjusted geometric mean ratio to baseline 0.45 with tofersen versus 1.12 with placebo in the whole trial population, FDA label) and total CSF SOD1 protein fell 35% versus 2% (FDA label). Open-label extension at 52 weeks: ALSFRS-R change -6.0 in the early-start cohort versus -9.5 in the delayed-start cohort (difference 3.5 points, 95% CI 0.4 to 6.7, not adjusted for multiplicity). Integrated VALOR plus extension analysis (JAMA Neurol 2026, follow-up up to 192 to 276 weeks): over 148 weeks earlier initiation was associated with numerically less decline in ALSFRS-R (-9.9 versus -13.5 points), slow vital capacity (-13.8% versus -18.1%) and quality of life (ALSAQ-5 17.0 versus 22.5 points), and the authors report survival prolonged relative to the expected natural history of SOD1-ALS (a comparison against natural history, not a randomised comparison beyond week 28). Regulatory basis: FDA accelerated approval (25 April 2023) 'based on reduction in plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) observed in patients treated with QALSODY', with continued approval possibly contingent on verification of clinical benefit in confirmatory trial(s) (FDA label). European Commission authorisation under exceptional circumstances (EMA EPAR, authorised 29 May 2024) because comprehensive efficacy and safety data could not be obtained, as SOD1-ALS is found in about 2% of all ALS patients. EAN 2024: in progressive ALS caused by pathogenic SOD1 mutations, offer tofersen as first-line treatment (strong recommendation ++) and discuss that it may be associated with serious adverse events; in slow progression, discuss the balance of benefits and harms.
als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.reason_why: Tofersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that binds SOD1 mRNA and causes its degradation, reducing SOD1 protein synthesis (FDA label); it is used only in patients whose ALS is associated with a mutation in the SOD1 gene.
als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.important_caveat: Honest surrogate-endpoint nuance: the pre-specified 28-week clinical primary end point was not met; the accelerated approval is based on plasma NfL reduction, a biomarker judged 'reasonably likely' to predict benefit. The clinical benefit claim rests on the open-label extension and long-term natural-history comparison. Serious neurological adverse events (myelitis, radiculitis, aseptic meningitis, papilledema/raised intracranial pressure) occurred in about 7% of tofersen-treated trial participants (10 participants, 12 events); all but one event resolved and 3 led to discontinuation; lumbar-puncture-related adverse events were common.
als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.real_working_solution: Test every person with ALS for a SOD1 pathogenic variant (the EAN guideline notes a growing consensus to offer rapid gene testing to all people with ALS). If a SOD1 variant is found and the disease is progressing, discuss tofersen at a specialist centre: 100 mg intrathecal by lumbar puncture, 3 loading doses at 14-day intervals then a maintenance dose every 28 days, with about 10 mL of cerebrospinal fluid removed before each dose (FDA label). Earlier initiation was associated with less decline than delayed start in the extension analyses. Monitor for the label warnings (myelitis/radiculitis, papilledema/raised intracranial pressure, aseptic meningitis); Indian availability of tofersen was not verified.
als_tofersen_sod1_als_only.source: Miller TM et al (VALOR), N Engl J Med 2022;387:1099-1110 (PMID 36129998); Long-Term Tofersen in SOD1 Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (integrated VALOR and open-label extension analysis), JAMA Neurol 2026;83:115-125 (PMID 41661214); Lovett A et al, serious neurologic adverse events in tofersen clinical trials, Muscle Nerve 2025;71:1006-1015 (PMID 40017137); FDA Qalsody label, DailyMed set id 81356b45-1cb7-4eef-88ea-e44cc18b47c5; EMA Qalsody EPAR (authorised 29 May 2024); Biogen press release on FDA accelerated approval, 25 April 2023; Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.name: Non-Invasive Ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) - the Best-Evidenced Supportive Intervention (Only Randomised Survival and Quality-of-Life Benefit)
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.type: Bilevel positive-airway-pressure ventilatory support via nasal or face mask (device therapy)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - home bilevel (BiPAP-type) non-invasive ventilator with nasal or full-face mask, initially used at night and later also by day (see Medical Equipment/Devices)
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.effectiveness: Bourke et al (Lancet Neurol 2006; single-centre randomised trial, 41 patients randomised at orthopnoea with maximum inspiratory pressure less than 60% predicted or symptomatic hypercapnia; 22 NIV, 19 standard care): NIV improved survival and quality of life; median survival was 219 versus 171 days (48 days longer; Cochrane estimate 95% CI 12 to 91 days, p=0.0062); in patients with normal to moderately impaired bulbar function (n=20) median survival was 205 days longer (216 versus 11 days) with better quality-of-life measures; in patients with poor bulbar function (n=21) there was no survival or overall quality-of-life gain, but sleep-related symptoms improved (sleep apnoea quality-of-life index symptoms domain). The Cochrane review (2017) grades this moderate-quality evidence for survival and low-quality evidence for quality of life, notes it rests on a single 41-participant trial, and states that not offering NIV to a control group is no longer ethically justifiable. Early-NIV pilot (Jacobs et al, Neurology 2016; 54 patients not yet meeting guideline criteria, sham-controlled): the decline in forced vital capacity was slower with active NIV (difference 0.44 per month, p=0.049); survival and change in maximal inspiratory or expiratory pressure did not differ; mean use was 3.3 versus 2.0 hours per day (not significantly different). Guidelines: the former AAN 2009 parameter graded NIV Level B to lengthen survival and slow decline of forced vital capacity and Level C to improve quality of life; the 2024 EAN guideline recommends that NIV should be offered to all patients with ALS who have symptoms, signs or laboratory investigations supportive of respiratory insufficiency, and that every effort must be made to allow the use of NIV independently of bulbar function (strong ++). EFNS criteria as summarised by Dorst and Ludolph (2019): initiate NIV when at least one respiratory clinical symptom is present or one of these criteria is met - forced vital capacity below 80%, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure below 40 cm H2O, significant nocturnal desaturation, or pCO2 above 45 mmHg on morning blood gas; NICE recommends respiratory function tests (oxygen saturation, FVC, SNIP/MIP) every 2 to 3 months and nocturnal oximetry or a limited sleep study for sleep-related respiratory symptoms.
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.reason_why: Progressive weakness of the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles causes nocturnal hypoventilation first, then daytime hypercapnia, and respiratory failure is the usual cause of death in ALS. NIV supports ventilation and corrects hypoventilation, which addresses the sleep disturbance, daytime fatigue, cognitive impairment and depression that hypercapnia causes (Dorst and Ludolph review).
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.important_caveat: The randomised evidence is a single small unblinded trial (41 patients, 2006); a survival benefit was not shown in the poor-bulbar subgroup, and the Cochrane authors note that adverse effects of NIV were not systematically reported. Real NIV problems (mask discomfort, aerophagia and abdominal discomfort, secretion pooling) need active team management.
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.real_working_solution: Measure respiratory function every 2 to 3 months (FVC, SNIP or MIP, oxygen saturation) and ask about orthopnoea, morning headache, unrefreshing sleep and daytime sleepiness; refer promptly for NIV set-up when symptoms, signs or criteria appear, and start it early. Use room air with NIV, not oxygen alone: pure oxygen can reduce respiratory drive in neuromuscular disease and lead to carbon dioxide retention (Dorst and Ludolph review). Patients with poor bulbar function need extra effort with mask fit, secretion control and support, but should still be offered NIV because sleep-related symptoms improve. Introduce NIV before a gastrostomy if there is respiratory insufficiency (EAN).
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.source: Bourke SC et al, Lancet Neurol 2006;5:140-147 (PMID 16426990); Radunovic A et al, Cochrane review of mechanical ventilation for ALS/MND, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;10:CD004427 (PMID 28982219); Jacobs TL et al, Neurology 2016;87:1878-1883 (PMID 27581221); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 1, Neurology 2009;73:1218-1226 (PMID 19822872; retired 2026, PMID 42060880); EFNS Task Force, EFNS guideline, Eur J Neurol 2012;19:360-375 (PMID 21914052); Dorst J, Ludolph AC, Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2019 (PMID 31258624); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.name: Cough Augmentation and Secretion Management - Manual Assisted Cough, Breath Stacking, Mechanical Insufflation-Exsufflation, Suction, Mucolytics
specific_drugs: Not a drug (devices) - manual assisted cough, lung-volume-recruitment (breath-stacking) bag, mechanical cough-assist (insufflation-exsufflation) device, suction device
Drugs for thick mucus named in the EAN guideline: acetylcysteine, guaifenesin (mucolytics); propranolol, metoprolol (beta-blockers); saline nebuliser
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.effectiveness: EAN 2024 (adapted from NICE): offer cough augmentation techniques such as manual assisted cough to people with ALS who cannot cough effectively (strong ++); consider unassisted breath stacking and/or manual assisted cough as first-line (weak +); for bulbar dysfunction or ineffective unassisted breath stacking consider assisted breath stacking with a lung-volume recruitment bag (+); consider a mechanical cough-assist device if assisted breath stacking is not effective (+); consider adding a suction device (+). For thick mucus: review concomitant medications (especially treatments for drooling), advise on swallowing, posture, oral care, suctioning and hydration (++), and consider humidification, saline nebulisers, beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol) and mucolytics (acetylcysteine, guaifenesin) alone or combined (+). The former AAN 2009 parameter said insufflation-exsufflation may be considered to help clear secretions (Level C). No randomised trial effect size was retrieved for these techniques; the recommendations are guideline-level.
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.reason_why: Weak expiratory and bulbar muscles make coughing ineffective, so secretions pool and cause choking, infection and worsened respiratory failure; assisting inspiration (breath stacking) and then expiration (manual or mechanical assistance) restores an effective cough.
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.important_caveat: Recommendations are largely consensus and NICE-adapted; the EAN table lists these questions as 'adapt NICE recommendations' without randomised trials, so the certainty of benefit is lower than for NIV.
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.real_working_solution: Teach caregivers manual assisted cough and breath stacking early, escalate to a mechanical cough-assist device and suction when needed, and review anticholinergic drooling drugs if secretions become thick (see sialorrhea entry).
als_respiratory_support_niv_and_cough_au.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapters 5a and 5b (PMID 38470068); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 1, Neurology 2009;73:1218-1226 (PMID 19822872)

als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.name: Invasive Ventilation via Tracheostomy - Real Survival Data, Quality-of-Life Considerations and the Need for Advance Care Planning
als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.type: Invasive home mechanical ventilation (device therapy; personal-values decision)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - tracheostomy with home mechanical ventilator, suction and 24-hour trained care (see Medical Equipment/Devices)
als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.effectiveness: No randomised trial of tracheostomy-assisted ventilation exists: the Cochrane review of mechanical ventilation (2017) found randomised trials only of NIV, and the EAN 2024 guideline classes the invasive-ventilation question as an empty review with consensus-based recommendations. Danish 15-year cohort (Dreyer et al, 431 patients admitted to a referral respiratory care unit 1998-2012, all offered non-invasive and/or invasive home ventilation): average treatment time was 22.9 months with no treatment, 25.8 months with non-invasive home ventilation, 56.8 months with non-invasive followed by invasive (tracheostomy) ventilation, and 33.8 months with invasive ventilation from the outset; the authors conclude that non-invasive followed by invasive home ventilation is a possible treatment with a significant effect on survival (non-randomised, so selection and survivor bias apply). Rabkin et al (prospective study of 72 hospice-eligible ALS patients; 14 chose long-term mechanical ventilation and 58 died without it): those who chose it were younger, better educated, with higher household incomes and reported more optimism; after an average of 33 months on ventilation only about half retained high levels of optimism and enjoyment of daily life; caregivers reported substantial emotional burden although most spousal caregivers still expressed satisfaction; two patients expressed interest in hastening death but none asked to terminate ventilation; half identified future circumstances that would render life intolerable. Dorst and Ludolph review: invasive ventilation can end in complete paralysis and a locked-in state, many patients reject it because they do not regard that quality of life as acceptable, and patients who used NIV for more than 6 months were more likely to refuse tracheostomy. EAN 2024 (strong ++): find the right moment to discuss invasive ventilation with the person, family and carers as part of advance care planning; aim to avoid emergency invasive ventilation (for example an unplanned hospital admission); be sensitive about timing.
als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.reason_why: Tracheostomy ventilation replaces failing respiratory muscles completely, so it can prolong life beyond the point where NIV can compensate, but it does not treat the underlying motor-neuron disease; paralysis continues, so the person can end up ventilator-dependent with progressively less ability to move or communicate.
als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.important_caveat: All survival and quality-of-life data on tracheostomy ventilation in ALS are observational and from selected patients, so they cannot show how much of the longer survival is due to the ventilation itself; this is a values-based decision, not a purely medical one, and neither choosing nor declining it is medically wrong.
als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.real_working_solution: Raise the invasive-ventilation decision early and calmly, well before a respiratory crisis, and record the person's choice in an advance directive or plan; make sure the person and family understand the 24-hour care, equipment, cost and carer burden involved; if invasive ventilation is chosen, plan it (not an emergency intubation) and arrange trained home or facility care and an AAC system (eye-gaze or similar) so that communication is preserved; if it is declined, arrange palliative care for breathlessness (see palliative entry). Availability of home invasive-ventilation care in India was not verified.
als_invasive_ventilation_tracheostomy_an.source: Radunovic A et al, Cochrane review of mechanical ventilation for ALS/MND, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;10:CD004427 (PMID 28982219); Dreyer P et al, Amyotroph Lateral Scler Frontotemporal Degener 2014;15:62-67 (PMID 24067168); Rabkin JG et al, Amyotroph Lateral Scler 2006;7:86-95 (PMID 16753972); Dorst J, Ludolph AC, Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2019 (PMID 31258624); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 5c (PMID 38470068)

als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.name: Diaphragm Pacing (NeuRx RA/4 Diaphragm Pacing System) - Real DiPALS Randomised Trial Showed SHORTER Survival; Not Recommended
als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.type: Implanted diaphragm-pacing device (tested and found harmful)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - NeuRx RA/4 Diaphragm Pacing System (implanted electrodes with external stimulator)
als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.effectiveness: DiPALS (multicentre open-label randomised controlled trial in 7 UK centres; DiPALS Writing Committee, Lancet Neurol 2015): 74 participants randomised to NIV plus diaphragm pacing (37) or NIV alone (37); the Data Monitoring and Ethics Committee recommended suspending recruitment on the basis of survival figures and later advised discontinuing pacing in all patients; median survival was 11.0 months (95% CI 8.3 to 13.6) with pacing versus 22.5 months (13.6 to not reached) with NIV alone, adjusted hazard ratio 2.27 (95% CI 1.22 to 4.25, p=0.009); 28 (76%) versus 19 (51%) patients died; 162 adverse events (5.9 per person-year) in the pacing group versus 81 (2.5 per person-year). The device had US Humanitarian Device Exemption approval before this trial. EAN 2024: do not use diaphragmatic pacing for the treatment of ALS (strong negative).
als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.reason_why: Pacing stimulates the diaphragm through implanted electrodes to delay respiratory failure, but in ALS the phrenic motor neurons themselves are degenerating, and the trial found a survival disadvantage rather than an advantage.
als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.important_caveat: Open-label trial of 74 patients stopped early; the survival difference could be partly due to chance, but the direction and the EAN strong recommendation against use are clear.
als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.real_working_solution: Do not offer diaphragm pacing. The real working alternatives for respiratory failure in ALS are NIV started early, cough augmentation, an advance-care plan on invasive ventilation, and palliative measures for breathlessness.
als_diaphragm_pacing_real_harm_do_not_us.source: DiPALS Writing Committee (DiPALS), Lancet Neurol 2015;14:883-892 (PMID 26234554); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.name: Gastrostomy Feeding (PEG, Radiologically Inserted or Per-Oral Image-Guided) - Real Evidence, Timing and the Honest Controversy
specific_drugs: Not a drug - percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube, radiologically inserted gastrostomy (RIG) tube, or per-oral image-guided gastrostomy (PIG) tube with enteral feed
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.effectiveness: Cochrane review (2011): no randomised or quasi-randomised trials compare enteral tube feeding with continued oral feeding in ALS/MND; the best available (non-randomised) evidence suggests a survival advantage for some patients, but the authors call these conclusions tentative; evidence for improved nutrition is incomplete but tentatively favourable; quality of life needs more attention; surgical and radiological insertion approaches appear equivalent. ProGas (Lancet Neurol 2015; prospective cohort, 24 UK centres, 345 recruited, 330 had gastrostomy: 163 PEG, 121 RIG, 43 PIG, 3 surgical): 30-day mortality after gastrostomy was 4% (12 patients; 3% after PEG, 3% after RIG, 7% after PIG, p=0.46); 6% of procedures (21 of 344) could not be completed; the authors state that little evidence indicates the optimum method and timing. Guidelines: EFNS 2012 says PEG improves nutrition and quality of life and gastrostomy tubes should be placed before respiratory insufficiency develops; the former AAN 2009 parameter said PEG should be considered to stabilise weight and prolong survival (Level B) but that more studies are needed on the optimal time for PEG and on its impact on quality of life and survival; EAN 2024 (strong ++) says discuss gastrostomy at an early stage and at regular intervals as ALS progresses, take the person's preferences into account, explain the benefits of early placement and the risks of late placement (low critical body mass, respiratory complications, dehydration, higher risk of mortality and procedural complications), place the gastrostomy without delay once referred, and, if there is respiratory insufficiency, introduce NIV first and perform the gastrostomy with the patient established on NIV; nasogastric tube feeding may be considered while awaiting gastrostomy (+); parenteral feeding may be considered when gastrostomy is not feasible (+).
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.reason_why: Dysphagia, fatigue with eating and upper-limb weakness cause weight loss, which is a negative prognostic factor in ALS; a feeding tube secures calories, fluids and a route for drugs (riluzole suspension and oral edaravone can be given through the tube) when swallowing becomes unsafe or inadequate.
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.important_caveat: Real controversy: there is still no randomised trial showing that a gastrostomy prolongs life or improves quality of life, and the timing evidence is weak; the pro-early-placement position is a guideline consensus based on non-randomised data and on the risk of late procedures, not on trial proof. Late gastrostomy in patients with poor respiratory function carries higher procedural risk.
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.real_working_solution: Raise gastrostomy early, before weight loss is severe and before forced vital capacity has fallen to the point where the procedure becomes risky; decide together with the patient, accept that some people will decline, involve the dietitian and speech therapist early, and if respiratory function is already reduced establish NIV first. Continue to offer tastes and oral intake for pleasure as safety allows.
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.source: Katzberg HD et al, Cochrane review of enteral tube feeding for ALS/MND, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;1:CD004030 (PMID 21249659); ProGas Study Group, Lancet Neurol 2015;14:702-709 (PMID 26027943); EFNS Task Force, EFNS guideline, Eur J Neurol 2012;19:360-375 (PMID 21914052); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 1, Neurology 2009;73:1218-1226 (PMID 19822872; retired 2026, PMID 42060880); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 4 (PMID 38470068)

als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.name: Dietary Energy Supplementation - Hypercaloric Tube Feeds and High-Fat Diet (Real Small and Large Trials, Honest Negative Overall Result)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - high-carbohydrate hypercaloric enteral formula (Wills et al), high-caloric fatty diet supplement 405 kcal per day (LIPCAL-ALS), dietitian-directed food supplements
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.effectiveness: Wills et al (Lancet 2014; randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2, 24 enrolled, 20 started diet, all already receiving enteral nutrition): the high-carbohydrate hypercaloric diet had fewer serious adverse events than the isocaloric control diet (none versus 9, p=0.0005) and no deaths in 9 patients versus 3 deaths (43%) in 7 controls during 5 months of follow-up (log-rank p=0.03); the high-fat hypercaloric diet did not differ from control; the authors present this as preliminary evidence of safety and tolerability and call for larger trials. LIPCAL-ALS (Ludolph et al, Ann Neurol 2020; 1:1 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 201 patients on riluzole, high-caloric fatty diet 405 kcal per day versus placebo): survival probability at 28 months 0.37 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.49) versus 0.39 (0.27 to 0.51), hazard ratio 0.97 (p=0.44) - no life-prolonging effect for the whole ALS population; a post-hoc subgroup analysis suggested a survival benefit in fast-progressing patients (hypothesis-generating only). EAN 2024: identify causes of weight loss and reduced food and fluid intake (swallowing problems, respiratory insufficiency, depression, loss of appetite, muscle atrophy, upper-limb weakness) and consult the dietitian, speech therapist and/or occupational therapist on food composition, consistency, meal frequency, supplements, fluid intake, choking risk, utensils and positioning (strong ++).
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.reason_why: Weight loss and low body mass index are linked to worse survival in ALS, so energy supplementation was tested as a way to prevent malnutrition and possibly extend survival.
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.important_caveat: The Wills trial was tiny (20 patients started diet) and exploratory for survival; LIPCAL-ALS (201 patients) is the confirmatory-scale result and was negative overall.
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.real_working_solution: Have a dietitian assess weight, swallowing and intake at every clinic visit and tailor food consistency, supplements and meal pattern; treat reversible drivers of poor intake (drooling, depression, breathlessness, upper-limb weakness) and maintain weight, but do not promise survival benefit from high-fat supplements, since the large trial was negative overall.
als_nutrition_gastrostomy_peg_and_diet.source: Wills AM et al, Lancet 2014;383:2065-2072 (PMID 24582471); Ludolph AC et al (LIPCAL-ALS), Ann Neurol 2020;87:206-216 (PMID 31849093); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 4 (PMID 38470068)

als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.name: Sialorrhea (Drooling) - Anticholinergics, Botulinum Toxin, Radiotherapy and Dextromethorphan-Quinidine (Real Cochrane-Graded Evidence)
als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.type: Anticholinergic drugs, botulinum toxin injection and radiotherapy
specific_drugs: Glycopyrrolate (Cuvposa oral solution is FDA-labelled only for chronic severe drooling in patients aged 3 to 16 years with neurologic conditions, so use in adult ALS is off-label)
Amitriptyline, atropine, oxybutynin and scopolamine (hyoscine) are the other anticholinergics named by the EAN guideline
Rimabotulinumtoxin B (Myobloc, FDA-labelled for chronic sialorrhea in adults) injected into salivary glands
als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.effectiveness: Cochrane review (2022; four randomised trials, 110 participants with MND): botulinum toxin B injected into parotid and submandibular glands may give participant-reported improvement (6 of 9 versus 2 of 9; RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.81 to 11.08; low certainty) and probably reduces saliva production (mean difference -0.50 mL per 5 minutes, 95% CI -1.07 to 0.07; moderate certainty), with little to no effect on quality of life (low certainty); a small pilot of botulinum toxin A versus radiotherapy (20 participants) gave very low-certainty evidence; a crossover trial of dextromethorphan-quinidine 20/10 mg (60 participants) gave a slight improvement in the bulbar-function scale sialorrhea subscale (mean difference -1.52, 95% CI -2.52 to -0.52; moderate certainty); a scopolamine patch crossover trial (10 randomised) gave very low-certainty evidence; the authors conclude there is some low- or moderate-certainty evidence for botulinum toxin B and moderate-certainty evidence for dextromethorphan-quinidine. Cochrane overview (2017): a single session of botulinum toxin B probably improves sialorrhoea and quality of life at up to 4 weeks but not at 8 or 12 weeks (one placebo-controlled trial, 20 patients). Botulinum toxin meta-analysis (BMC Neurol 2025; 13 studies, 2 randomised and 11 quasi-experimental, 130 ALS patients): significant reduction in sialorrhea (risk difference 0.82, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.97), independent of toxin type, injection site or ultrasound guidance, but mostly observational data. The former AAN 2009 parameter said botulinum toxin B should be considered for refractory sialorrhea (Level B) and low-dose radiation to the salivary glands may be considered (Level C). EAN 2024: consider anticholinergics (amitriptyline, atropine, glycopyrrolate, oxybutynin, scopolamine) as first-line (weak +); consider dextromethorphan-quinidine particularly in people with emotional lability; consider botulinum toxin in severe sialorrhea when drugs fail or are not tolerated, given by a specialist centre; consider radiotherapy if these fail; surgery is not suggested.
als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.reason_why: In ALS, bulbar weakness impairs swallowing of saliva rather than increasing saliva production, so saliva pools; anticholinergics and botulinum toxin reduce salivary-gland secretion, and radiotherapy reduces gland function.
als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.important_caveat: The evidence base is small: four randomised trials in total (110 patients) in the Cochrane 2022 review, none of them of glycopyrrolate, so the first-line anticholinergic recommendation rests on consensus and clinical experience. Botulinum toxin carries a label warning of swallowing and breathing difficulty (deaths from severe dysphagia have been reported with botulinum toxin products), which matters in ALS.
als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.real_working_solution: Start with a bedside-appropriate anticholinergic chosen to fit other symptoms (for example amitriptyline where sleep or low mood is also a problem, which the EAN guideline notes), review swallowing, oral care and drink choices (sugary and acidic drinks, milk and juice may stimulate salivation), and escalate to specialist-delivered botulinum toxin injection or radiotherapy if drugs fail or are not tolerated. Watch for thick, tenacious secretions from over-treatment (see cough augmentation and secretion entry); the botulinum toxin label warns that swallowing or breathing difficulties can result, so use it under specialist supervision.
als_symptomatic_sialorrhea.source: James E et al, Cochrane review of treatment for sialorrhea in MND/ALS, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;5:CD006981 (PMID 35593746); Ng L et al, Cochrane overview, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;1:CD011776 (PMID 28072907); Huang J et al, botulinum toxin sialorrhea meta-analysis, BMC Neurol 2025;25:496 (PMID 41366746); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 2, Neurology 2009;73:1227-1233 (PMID 19822873); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 6e (PMID 38470068); FDA Cuvposa label, DailyMed set id d200bd44-9856-4104-a29e-a4cca3db6737; FDA Myobloc label, DailyMed set id 675cb354-9d13-482e-8ac2-22f709c58b4f

als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.name: Pseudobulbar Affect (Involuntary Crying/Laughing) - Dextromethorphan-Quinidine (Nuedexta; Real Randomised ALS Trial Data)
als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.type: Oral sigma-1 agonist/NMDA antagonist plus CYP2D6 inhibitor combination
specific_drugs: Dextromethorphan hydrobromide 20 mg plus quinidine sulfate 10 mg (Nuedexta)
SSRI or tricyclic antidepressants (the EAN guideline names the classes; amitriptyline is the tricyclic it names elsewhere for drooling)
als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.effectiveness: Brooks et al (Neurology 2004; randomised double-blind three-arm trial in ALS, 140 randomised, 28 days, dextromethorphan 30 mg plus quinidine 30 mg twice daily versus components): the combination produced 3.3-point greater improvement in Center for Neurologic Study Lability Scale (CNS-LS) than dextromethorphan alone (p=0.001) and 3.7 points greater than quinidine alone (p<0.001), with lower episode rates and better quality-of-life scores; treatment-related discontinuation was 24% with the combination versus 6% and 8% with the components. Pioro et al (Ann Neurol 2010; 12-week randomised double-blind trial, 326 patients with ALS or multiple sclerosis and CNS-LS at least 13): PBA-episode daily rate was 49.0% lower on dextromethorphan-quinidine 20/10 mg (p<0.0001) and 46.9% lower on 30/10 mg (p<0.0001) than on placebo; mean CNS-LS fell by 8.2 points on both doses versus 5.7 on placebo (p=0.0113 and p=0.0002); both doses were safe and well tolerated. FDA label (Nuedexta): indicated for pseudobulbar affect; dose one capsule (20/10 mg) daily for 7 days then one capsule every 12 hours. The former AAN 2009 parameter: dextromethorphan and quinidine should be considered for pseudobulbar affect (Level B). EAN 2024: consider SSRI antidepressants, tricyclic antidepressants or dextromethorphan-quinidine for emotional lability (weak +), differentiating it from depression and frontotemporal-dementia symptoms; dextromethorphan-quinidine may also improve bulbar function in some patients.
als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.reason_why: Pseudobulbar affect is a disorder of emotional expression from disrupted corticobulbar control; per the FDA label dextromethorphan acts as a sigma-1 receptor agonist and NMDA-receptor antagonist and quinidine inhibits CYP2D6 to raise dextromethorphan levels, but the label states that the mechanism by which dextromethorphan exerts its effect in PBA is unknown.
als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.important_caveat: FDA label contraindications include a prolonged QT interval, congenital long QT, a history suggestive of torsades de pointes or heart failure, complete AV block without a pacemaker, use with quinidine/quinine/mefloquine, MAOI use or use within 14 days, and concomitant CYP2D6-metabolised QT-prolonging drugs (thioridazine, pimozide); dizziness is a listed warning. The label dose (20/10 mg) is lower than the 30/30 mg dose used in the older ALS-only trial, where discontinuation from adverse effects reached 24%.
als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.real_working_solution: Confirm the diagnosis (episodes out of proportion to mood, brief and hard to control) and rule out depression and frontotemporal dementia, then use dextromethorphan-quinidine 20/10 mg daily for 7 days and then twice daily, after an ECG and medication review; an SSRI or tricyclic is a lower-cost alternative that also treats co-existing mood or drooling symptoms. Indian availability of Nuedexta was not verified.
als_symptomatic_pseudobulbar_affect.source: Brooks BR et al, Neurology 2004;63:1364-1370 (PMID 15505150); Pioro EP et al, Ann Neurol 2010;68:693-702 (PMID 20839238); FDA Nuedexta label, DailyMed set id c8cce784-8c5f-415b-8068-76e5d481d159; Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 2, Neurology 2009;73:1227-1233 (PMID 19822873); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 6f (PMID 38470068)

als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.name: Muscle Cramps - Mexiletine (Real Crossover Trial), Quinine Sulfate With Cardiac Monitoring, and Other Options
als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.type: Sodium-channel blocker and other antispasm drugs
specific_drugs: Quinine sulfate (start 100 to 200 mg per day with cardiac monitoring)
Baclofen, gabapentin, pregabalin, ranolazine and carbamazepine are the other options named by the EAN guideline
als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.effectiveness: Mexiletine (Oskarsson et al, Muscle Nerve 2018; multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 20 ALS patients requesting cramp treatment, 150 mg twice daily): cramp frequency fell from 5.3 per day on placebo to 3.5 per day on mexiletine (average reduction 1.8 per day), estimated reduction of cramp severity 15 units on a 100-unit scale (p=0.01) from a baseline average of 46, no effect on fasciculations; one patient discontinued for dizziness; no serious adverse event. Cochrane overview (2017; 13 randomised trials, N=4012 across cramp studies in MND): memantine and tetrahydrocannabinol are probably ineffective (moderate-quality evidence); vitamin E may have little or no effect (low-quality); effects of L-threonine, gabapentin, xaliproden, riluzole and baclofen are uncertain. EAN 2024: consider sodium-channel blockers (ranolazine, quinine sulfate, mexiletine, carbamazepine), gabapentin, pregabalin and baclofen for cramps (weak +); start quinine sulfate at low doses (100 to 200 mg per day) and monitor for cardiac adverse events before and after prescription (strong ++); if spasticity coexists consider baclofen first-line.
als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.reason_why: The EAN guideline groups ranolazine, quinine sulfate, mexiletine and carbamazepine as sodium-channel blockers used for cramps; the other listed options (gabapentin, pregabalin, baclofen) act through different pathways.
als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.important_caveat: The mexiletine trial was small (20 patients) and short; the Cochrane overview found that most other cramp drugs have uncertain evidence, and the EAN recommendation is weak. Quinine carries cardiac risk, which is why the guideline requires monitoring.
als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.real_working_solution: Ask specifically about cramps at each clinic visit, exclude reversible contributors (dehydration, medications), and offer mexiletine or another option guided by co-existing symptoms (the mexiletine prescribing information was not retrieved in this research, so check its cardiac contraindications before use); check ECG and interacting drugs before quinine, as the EAN guideline requires cardiac monitoring.
als_symptomatic_muscle_cramps.source: Oskarsson B et al, Muscle Nerve 2018 (PMID 29510461); Ng L et al, Cochrane overview, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;1:CD011776 (PMID 28072907); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 6b (PMID 38470068)

als_symptomatic_spasticity.name: Spasticity - Physical Therapy First, Then Baclofen, Tizanidine, Gabapentin or Cannabinoids (Honest Lack of ALS-Specific Trials)
specific_drugs: Baclofen (FDA-labelled for spasticity from multiple sclerosis and spinal cord disease; use in ALS is off-label)
Tizanidine (FDA-labelled for spasticity in adults; use in ALS is off-label)
als_symptomatic_spasticity.effectiveness: EAN 2024: consider non-pharmacological approaches such as physical therapy for spasticity (weak +); consider cannabinoids, baclofen, tizanidine or gabapentin to treat muscle stiffness, spasticity or increased tone (weak +); in focal spasticity consider botulinum toxin if these treatments are not effective, not tolerated or contraindicated (weak +). Cochrane overview (2017): the Cochrane review on spasticity in MND could not evaluate baclofen because no randomised trials were available; it is uncertain whether an endurance-based exercise programme improved spasticity or quality of life (one trial, 25 patients, very low-quality evidence). FDA baclofen label indications: alleviation of signs and symptoms of spasticity resulting from multiple sclerosis (also possibly of some value in spinal cord injury and other spinal cord disease); tizanidine label: treatment of spasticity in adults (monitoring of aminotransferase levels at baseline and 1 month after maximum dose).
als_symptomatic_spasticity.reason_why: Spasticity is a feature of upper motor neuron involvement in ALS; tizanidine is a central alpha-2-adrenergic agonist (FDA label), and the other listed drugs act through different pathways.
als_symptomatic_spasticity.important_caveat: No randomised trial of baclofen or tizanidine in ALS was found in the Cochrane review, so the recommendation is consensus-based; the doses must be titrated to effect and function.
als_symptomatic_spasticity.real_working_solution: Begin with a physiotherapy stretching and positioning programme and add baclofen, tizanidine or gabapentin at low doses, titrating to function, and reassess response and any effect on weakness at each clinic visit; the choice among agents follows co-existing problems (for example gabapentin if cramps or pain coexist, tizanidine with liver-function monitoring).
als_symptomatic_spasticity.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 6c (PMID 38470068); Ng L et al, Cochrane overview, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;1:CD011776 (PMID 28072907); FDA baclofen tablet label, DailyMed set id 00c6c924-ddfd-4a75-afd7-f6561ff9abbc; FDA tizanidine label, DailyMed set id d7d5dce0-f8a2-404d-9e87-e2235f5d3268

als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.name: Pain, Depression, Anxiety, Insomnia, Fatigue, Constipation and Laryngospasm - EAN 2024 Consensus-Based Symptom Management
als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.type: Symptom-directed drug and non-drug measures (consensus-level evidence)
specific_drugs: Antidepressants and anxiolytics - SSRIs, short-acting anxiolytics and SNRIs (EAN names these classes, not individual agents, for depression and anxiety)
Mirtazapine and quetiapine (named by the EAN guideline for insomnia with anxiety or depression), low-dose tricyclic antidepressants
als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.effectiveness: The EAN 2024 guideline systematic review found no randomised trials for constipation, hoarse voice and laryngospasm, insomnia, anxiety, depression and deep-vein-thrombosis prevention (empty reviews), so the recommendations are consensus statements. Pain: actively assess, identify and treat causes such as cramps, spasticity, malpositioning, frozen shoulder, stiff joints, pressure and restless-legs discomfort; advise positioning, mobilisation and physical therapy (for example to prevent frozen shoulder) and splinting; consider targeted steroid injections for joint pain; follow existing recommendations for neuropathic pain. Depression and anxiety: explore signs of depression and emotional distress and consider psychotherapy and/or pharmacotherapy; for anxiety identify and treat causes (breathing difficulty, fear of death, pain, loss of function, communication problems), consider psychological support, short-acting anxiolytics or SSRIs, SNRIs if those fail, and use pharmacotherapy as first-line in advanced disease or when psychotherapy is not possible. Insomnia: treat the underlying cause (anxiety, respiratory insufficiency, pain, cramps, immobility in sleep), consider relaxation techniques, then low-dose tricyclic antidepressants or hypnotics; mirtazapine or quetiapine if insomnia coexists with anxiety or depression. Fatigue: treat underlying causes and consider pausing riluzole if fatigue is judged a drug side effect. Constipation: identify causes (opioids, anticholinergics, NIV aerocolia, immobility, dehydration, low fibre, weak abdominal muscles), advise fibre and fluid, then laxatives. Laryngospasm: identify and avoid triggers, teach the multistep manoeuvre (upright posture, nose breathing, repeated swallowing, slow exhalation through lips), sublingual benzodiazepines for crises. Deep-vein thrombosis: non-drug measures (passive physiotherapy, limb elevation, compression stockings); there is insufficient evidence for primary prevention with anticoagulants. The Cochrane overview (2017) found no randomised-trial evidence in a Cochrane review for drug therapy of pain in MND.
als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.reason_why: The EAN guideline lists specific, identifiable causes for each of these symptoms (for example cramps, spasticity, malpositioning, respiratory insufficiency, anxiety, opioid or anticholinergic drugs, NIV aerocolia, immobility) and makes identifying and treating the cause the first step.
als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.important_caveat: Consensus-level evidence only; the guideline does not name individual drugs for depression and anxiety, and neither do the sources used here, so exact agent selection is a clinical judgement made by the treating team.
als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.real_working_solution: Ask about pain, mood, sleep, fatigue and bowels at every clinic visit, involve a clinical psychologist and social care worker early, and treat cause first, then use the class-level drug options above; in advanced disease do not wait for psychotherapy before starting drug treatment for anxiety or depression.
als_symptomatic_pain_mood_sleep_and_othe.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapters 6d, 6g, 6h, 6i, 6j, 7 and 8 (PMID 38470068); Ng L et al, Cochrane overview, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;1:CD011776 (PMID 28072907)

als_communication_aac_devices.name: Communication Support - Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) Devices, Voice Banking and Eye-Gaze Access
als_communication_aac_devices.type: Assistive communication technology (low- and high-technology aids)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - low-technology alphabet, word or picture boards
Not a drug - high-technology personal-computer or tablet-based voice-output communication aids
Not a drug - eye-gaze access systems with message and voice banking
als_communication_aac_devices.effectiveness: EAN 2024 (adapted from NICE; strong ++ for each point): have a speech and language therapist assess speech and communication needs without delay; provide AAC equipment that meets the person's needs without delay to maximise participation in daily activities and maintain quality of life; low-technology aids (alphabet, word or picture boards) and high-technology aids (personal computer or tablet-based voice-output communication aids) may both help; refer to a specialised AAC hub when complex high-technology equipment (message and voice banking, eye-gaze access) is needed or likely to be needed; involve occupational therapists so that AAC is integrated with environmental-control systems and personal computers or tablets; review communication needs and ability to use AAC regularly as ALS progresses; provide ongoing training and support for the person and carers. The EAN table lists this question as adapted from NICE recommendations rather than from randomised trials, and no randomised trial effect size was retrieved.
als_communication_aac_devices.reason_why: Bulbar involvement causes progressive loss of intelligible speech; AAC substitutes text, symbols or synthetic voice, and eye-gaze access allows control by eye movement when hand function is lost.
als_communication_aac_devices.important_caveat: The recommendation is consensus-based; the strength of the benefit is not quantified in trial data retrieved here. Cognitive and behavioural impairment (present in up to 50% of people with ALS per the EAN guideline) can change how AAC is used and should be assessed.
als_communication_aac_devices.real_working_solution: Refer to speech-language therapy at diagnosis, before speech is lost, so that message and voice banking can be done while the voice is still intelligible; introduce low-technology aids first, then tablet or eye-gaze systems as hand and speech function decline, and make sure an AAC system is available in hospital and at end of life. Availability of AAC hubs and eye-gaze equipment in India was not verified.
als_communication_aac_devices.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 3 (PMID 38470068)

als_mobility_aids_exercise_and_rehabilit.name: Mobility Aids, Orthoses, Exercise and Physiotherapy - Powered Wheelchair, Hoist, Riser-Recliner Chair and Tailored Exercise
specific_drugs: Not a drug - orthoses and splints
Not a drug - manual and powered wheelchairs and assistive mobility technology
Not a drug - hoist, riser-recliner chair, hospital bed and commode
als_mobility_aids_exercise_and_rehabilit.effectiveness: EAN 2024: consider an exercise programme (resistance, active-assisted or passive, tailored to function, posture and fatigue) to maintain joint range of movement, prevent contractures, reduce stiffness and discomfort and optimise function and quality of life (weak +); refer for orthoses without delay and provide them without delay (strong ++); give safe manual-handling advice to family and carers (strong ++); the multidisciplinary team should have access to assistive mobility technology; towards the end of life ensure prompt access to equipment such as syringe drivers, suction machines, riser-recliner chair, hospital bed, commode and hoist. For DVT risk from reduced mobility use passive physiotherapy, limb elevation, compression stockings and lymphatic drainage massage; insufficient evidence supports anticoagulants for primary prevention. Cochrane overview (2017): exercise may improve disability in MND at three months but not quality of life, compared with usual activities or usual care including stretching (two randomised trials, 43 patients, low-quality evidence); repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation is uncertain (three randomised trials, 50 patients, very low-quality evidence).
als_mobility_aids_exercise_and_rehabilit.reason_why: Progressive weakness and spasticity cause contractures, pain, falls and loss of independence; appropriate equipment and gentle tailored exercise slow these secondary problems and preserve independence and safety for patient and carer.
als_mobility_aids_exercise_and_rehabilit.important_caveat: Exercise evidence is low quality and the effect on quality of life was not shown; the exercise programme must be tailored to avoid over-exertion and fatigue.
als_mobility_aids_exercise_and_rehabilit.real_working_solution: Refer to physiotherapy and occupational therapy at diagnosis for a tailored, non-fatiguing exercise programme and an equipment plan (orthoses, wheelchair, hoist, bed and chair) that is ahead of, not behind, the disease; train carers in safe handling.
als_mobility_aids_exercise_and_rehabilit.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapters 6a, 8 and 9 (PMID 38470068); Ng L et al, Cochrane overview, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;1:CD011776 (PMID 28072907)

als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.name: Palliative Care and Advance Care Planning From Diagnosis - Breathlessness Relief, Anticipatory Medicines and Early End-of-Life Conversations
als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.type: Palliative-care approach (drugs, equipment and planning conversations)
specific_drugs: Opioids (for breathlessness when NIV or invasive ventilation is not tolerated, not accepted or no longer working, or in end-stage disease; specific agent not named in the EAN guideline)
Antimuscarinic medicines for problematic saliva and respiratory secretions in the last days (anticipatory prescribing)
als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.effectiveness: Bede et al (systematic analysis, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011): optimal ALS management requires a palliative approach from diagnosis with emphasis on autonomy, dignity and quality of life; late referral to palliative services is not uncommon and may impact negatively on quality of life of patients and caregivers; the authors state there is considerable evidence that palliative care intervention improves quality of life in patients and carers. Former AAN 2009 palliative-care recommendations concluded that strong evidence for many symptomatic and palliative strategies was lacking and called for more high-quality studies. Advance directives systematic review and meta-analysis (BMC Palliat Care 2024; 26 studies): advance directives were signed in 60.4% of patient records (1,629 of 2,696), falling from 78% (1999-2011) to 42% (2012-2024); the authors conclude advance care planning should be part of each individual support plan and include a discussion of the preferred place of death. EAN 2024 end-of-life recommendations (strong ++): offer the opportunity to discuss end-of-life preferences at trigger points - at diagnosis, when there is a significant change in respiratory function, or when interventions such as gastrostomy or NIV are needed; provide support and advice on advance care planning (what could happen at the end of life, anticipatory medicines, advance decisions to refuse treatment, do-not-attempt-resuscitation orders, lasting power of attorney or equivalent, when to involve specialist palliative care); discuss invasive ventilation, palliative sedation and withdrawal of treatment, and be prepared to discuss euthanasia and assisted suicide where legal; discuss advance care planning earlier if communication, cognition or capacity are expected to worsen; ensure prompt access towards the end of life to an AAC system, specialist palliative care, equipment (syringe drivers, suction machines, riser-recliner chair, hospital bed, commode, hoist) and anticipatory medicines including opioids and benzodiazepines for breathlessness and anxiety and antimuscarinics for saliva and secretions; offer bereavement support and attend to spiritual needs. EAN respiratory pharmacological recommendation (weak +): in patients who do not tolerate or accept NIV or invasive ventilation, in whom NIV is not or no longer working, or in end-stage disease, consider opioids for breathlessness, and benzodiazepines when breathlessness is worsened by anxiety.
als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.reason_why: ALS is progressive and life-limiting with median survival of about 3 years from onset; palliative care aims to relieve symptoms and support dignity at every stage, not only in the last days, and advance care planning ensures decisions about ventilation and feeding are made by the person while communication and capacity remain.
als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.important_caveat: Evidence for palliative-care effects is from reviews and observational data rather than large randomised trials; the EAN wording on euthanasia and assisted suicide reflects European legal frameworks and is not a recommendation for practice in India.
als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.real_working_solution: Involve palliative care at or soon after diagnosis; hold the first advance-care-planning conversation at diagnosis and revisit it at each trigger point (respiratory decline, gastrostomy, NIV); record advance decisions and a nominated decision-maker while the person can still communicate; prescribe anticipatory opioids, benzodiazepines and antimuscarinics for breathlessness, anxiety and secretions; and support carers and the family with respite and bereavement care. Legal status of assisted dying and the local legal form of advance directives vary by country and were not verified for India; follow local law.
als_palliative_care_and_advance_care_pla.source: Bede P et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:413-418 (PMID 21297150); Mangal AL et al, advance directives in ALS systematic review, BMC Palliat Care 2024;23:191 (PMID 39075493); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 2, Neurology 2009;73:1227-1233 (PMID 19822873); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapters 5c and 9 (PMID 38470068)

als_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Real Failed, Harmful or Unproven Disease-Modifying Attempts - Minocycline, Lithium, RIPK1 Inhibitor SAR443820, Cell-Based Therapies (Plus Cross-References)
specific_drugs: Minocycline (up to 400 mg/day) - harmful in a phase 3 trial
Lithium carbonate - no survival benefit in LiCALS
SAR443820 (oral RIPK1 inhibitor) - no benefit in HIMALAYA phase 2
als_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: Minocycline (Gordon et al, Lancet Neurol 2007; phase 3, 412 patients, up to 400 mg/day for 9 months): ALSFRS-R deteriorated faster on minocycline than placebo (-1.30 versus -1.04 units per month, 95% CI for difference -0.44 to -0.08, p=0.005), with non-significant tendencies towards faster decline in vital capacity and greater mortality (HR 1.32, p=0.23); the authors conclude minocycline has a harmful effect in ALS. Lithium (LiCALS, UKMND-LiCALS Study Group, Lancet Neurol 2013; 214 patients on riluzole, 18 months): 50% alive on lithium versus 59% on placebo, survival curves not significantly different (p=0.20; adjusted odds of survival 0.71, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.24); no evidence of benefit on survival and no safety concerns. SAR443820 (HIMALAYA, Lancet Neurol 2026; phase 2, 305 randomised, 24 weeks): ALSFRS-R change -6.73 versus -6.32 on placebo (difference -0.41, 95% CI -1.71 to 0.88); more adverse events (85% versus 78%) and treatment discontinuations (14% versus 5%), most commonly for elevated liver enzymes; the authors conclude that further development in ALS is not warranted. Cell-based therapies: the EAN 2024 guideline cannot recommend cell-based treatments outside clinical trials until positive phase 3 data are available (strong negative). Cross-references in this entry set: sodium phenylbutyrate-taurursodiol (withdrawn after PHOENIX), diaphragm pacing (shorter survival in DiPALS), oral or intravenous edaravone (not recommended outside trials by EAN 2024), and high-fat dietary supplementation (negative overall in LIPCAL-ALS).
als_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: Each of these was tested because a laboratory or small-pilot signal suggested benefit; the large randomised trials showed no benefit or harm.
als_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: The LiCALS authors' abstract notes that the lithium result differs from earlier smaller, less conventional studies; HIMALAYA was terminated early. These entries record real negative results so that unproven agents are not adopted.
als_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not use minocycline, lithium, RIPK1 inhibitors or unapproved stem-cell products outside a regulated clinical trial; put effort into what is proven - multidisciplinary care, riluzole, NIV, nutrition and symptom control - and offer enrolment in properly run ALS trials for people who want to contribute to research.
als_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Gordon PH et al, Lancet Neurol 2007;6:1045-1053 (PMID 17980667); UKMND-LiCALS Study Group (LiCALS), Lancet Neurol 2013;12:339-345 (PMID 23453347); Cudkowicz ME et al, HIMALAYA trial of SAR443820, Lancet Neurol 2026;25:900-910 (PMID 42716044); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapter 1c (PMID 38470068)

als_medical_devices_equipment.name: Home Non-Invasive Ventilator (Bilevel/BiPAP-Type) With Masks and Interface Supplies
specific_drugs: Not a drug - bilevel positive-airway-pressure home ventilator with nasal or full-face masks
als_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Device behind the only randomised NIV survival and quality-of-life benefit in ALS (Bourke 2006; Cochrane 2017: median survival 219 versus 171 days). Guidelines advise NIV for symptoms, signs or laboratory evidence of respiratory insufficiency, using room air rather than oxygen alone, monitoring with FVC, SNIP or MIP and oxygen saturation every 2 to 3 months, and nocturnal oximetry or a limited sleep study for sleep-related symptoms.
als_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Positive-pressure ventilation via mask supports breathing during sleep and later by day when respiratory muscles fail.
als_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Aerophagia, mask problems and secretion pooling are the practical obstacles; bulbar patients need extra support.
als_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Set up NIV early with a specialist respiratory team; provide mask-fitting support and troubleshooting for mask discomfort, aerophagia and secretion pooling.
als_medical_devices_equipment.source: Bourke SC et al, Lancet Neurol 2006;5:140-147 (PMID 16426990); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;10:CD004427 (PMID 28982219); Dorst J, Ludolph AC, Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2019 (PMID 31258624); Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

als_medical_devices_equipment.name: Cough-Assist (Mechanical Insufflation-Exsufflation) Device, Lung-Volume-Recruitment Bag and Suction Machine
specific_drugs: Not a drug - mechanical insufflation-exsufflation cough-assist device, lung-volume-recruitment (breath-stacking) bag, portable suction machine
als_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: EAN 2024 recommends cough augmentation (manual assisted cough and breath stacking first; assisted breath stacking with a lung-volume recruitment bag; a mechanical cough-assist device if these are ineffective; a suction device in addition) and lists a suction machine among end-of-life equipment. The former AAN 2009 parameter said insufflation-exsufflation may be considered to help clear secretions (Level C). Guideline-level evidence; no randomised trial effect size was retrieved.
als_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: These devices create the inspiratory and expiratory pressure swings that a weak cough can no longer produce, so secretions can be cleared.
als_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Guideline-level and consensus-based; the EAN notes that suction may increase saliva production.
als_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Introduce manual techniques and breath stacking early and add a cough-assist device and suction when cough is ineffective; train family carers.
als_medical_devices_equipment.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapters 5a and 9 (PMID 38470068); Miller RG et al, AAN practice parameter update part 1, Neurology 2009;73:1218-1226 (PMID 19822872)

als_medical_devices_equipment.name: Gastrostomy Tube, Enteral Feeding Pump and Consumables; Lumbar-Puncture Kit for Intrathecal Tofersen
als_medical_devices_equipment.type: Medical device - enteral access and intrathecal delivery
specific_drugs: Not a drug - PEG, RIG or PIG gastrostomy tube with enteral feed and pump
Not a drug - lumbar-puncture set for intrathecal tofersen administration
als_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Gastrostomy tube feeding (Cochrane 2011; ProGas 2015; EAN 2024) and intrathecal administration of tofersen by lumbar puncture (FDA label: 100 mg in 15 mL as an intrathecal bolus over 1 to 3 minutes after removing about 10 mL of cerebrospinal fluid) both depend on dedicated equipment; riluzole suspension and edaravone oral suspension can be given via the gastrostomy tube (FDA labels).
als_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: The tube provides a route for nutrition, fluids and drugs when swallowing fails; tofersen is administered intrathecally by lumbar puncture (FDA label).
als_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Procedure-related complications and a small periprocedural mortality (4% at 30 days in ProGas) must be discussed.
als_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Coordinate tube choice (endoscopic, radiological or per-oral image-guided) with the gastroenterology or interventional-radiology service and the respiratory team; for tofersen use a centre experienced in lumbar puncture.
als_medical_devices_equipment.source: Katzberg HD et al, Cochrane review of enteral tube feeding, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;1:CD004030 (PMID 21249659); ProGas Study Group, Lancet Neurol 2015;14:702-709 (PMID 26027943); FDA Qalsody label, DailyMed set id 81356b45-1cb7-4eef-88ea-e44cc18b47c5; FDA Tiglutik label, DailyMed set id 75d68f19-4208-109e-e053-2991aa0ac857

als_medical_devices_equipment.name: AAC Devices, Powered Wheelchairs, Hoists, Riser-Recliner Chairs, Hospital Beds and Orthoses
specific_drugs: Not a drug - voice-output and eye-gaze communication aids
Not a drug - manual or powered wheelchair, hoist, riser-recliner chair, hospital bed, commode, orthoses
als_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: EAN 2024 recommends AAC equipment provided without delay (strong ++), orthoses provided without delay (strong ++), safe manual-handling advice (strong ++), access to assistive mobility technology through the multidisciplinary team, and prompt access at the end of life to an AAC system and equipment such as riser-recliner chair, hospital bed, commode and hoist.
als_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Equipment substitutes for lost movement and speech, preserving independence, safety and participation.
als_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: Consensus-based; Indian supply and funding routes were not verified.
als_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Review equipment needs at every clinic visit and order items ahead of need; train carers in safe handling; assess funding and supply routes in India locally (not verified here).
als_medical_devices_equipment.source: Van Damme P et al, EAN guideline 2024, Chapters 3, 6a and 9 (PMID 38470068)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT end points (survival in months or days, hazard ratios, ALSFRS-R points, biomarker ratios, episode rates, cramp counts) in different populations (all ALS, bulbar or non-bulbar subgroups, SOD1-ALS only, and patients with ALS or MS for pseudobulbar affect), so the ordering is directional judgement (size of benefit on each option's own metric combined with the strength and quality of the evidence and the current EAN 2024 guideline), NOT a common-scale percentage ranking; effectiveness_pct appears only where a genuine percent exists (49.0% lower episode rate for dextromethorphan-quinidine) or where 0.0 records a documented negative or harmful result rather than a zero-quality drug. IMPORTANT: NO treatment in this table cures ALS or halts its progression; the disease-modifying drugs (riluzole, edaravone, tofersen for SOD1-ALS only) give real but modest and, for edaravone, contested benefit, and multidisciplinary care and NIV carry the strongest real evidence. The first-ranked multidisciplinary care evidence is observational, and rank 6 and rank 9 items are largely guideline consensus. Rows 12 to 15 record honest negative or harmful results: high-fat or hypercaloric supplementation (negative overall), the withdrawn AMX0035 (Relyvrio), lithium, minocycline and SAR443820, and diaphragm pacing, which shortened survival in the DiPALS randomised trial. See CURABILITY_NOTE.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tofersen (Qalsody) - SOD1-ALS ONLY (about 2% of ALS)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 55% reduction in plasma neurofilament light from baseline at 28 weeks with tofersen (geometric mean ratio 0.45) versus a 12% increase with placebo (ratio 1.12) - VALOR trial, full SOD1-ALS population; biomarker endpoint only: primary clinical endpoint (28-week ALSFRS-R) NOT met (difference 1.2 points, 95% CI -3.2 to 5.5, p=0.97); open-label extension early-versus-delayed-start difference 3.5 ALSFRS-R points at 52 weeks (not multiplicity-adjusted); FDA accelerated approval on the NfL surrogate; EAN 2024: offer as first-line in progressive SOD1-ALS.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Miller et al (VALOR), NEJM 2022 (PMID 36129998); JAMA Neurol 2026 (PMID 41661214); FDA Qalsody label; EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Dextromethorphan-quinidine (Nuedexta) for pseudobulbar affect
ranked_high_to_low.metric: PBA episode daily rate 49.0% lower than placebo on 20/10 mg (46.9% on 30/10 mg), p<0.0001; CNS-LS fall 8.2 versus 5.7 points, 12 weeks, 326 patients with ALS or MS
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pioro et al, Ann Neurol 2010 (PMID 20839238); Brooks et al, Neurology 2004 (PMID 15505150); FDA Nuedexta label

ranked_high_to_low.name: Gastrostomy feeding (PEG, RIG or PIG)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No randomised trial; tentative survival advantage and tentatively favourable nutrition in non-randomised data (Cochrane 2011); 30-day mortality 4% (12 of 330) and 6% incomplete procedures in ProGas; EAN 2024 strong recommendation to discuss early
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cochrane review 2011 (PMID 21249659); ProGas, Lancet Neurol 2015 (PMID 26027943); EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Botulinum toxin (type B) for drooling
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 66.7% (6 of 9) participant-reported improvement in drooling with botulinum toxin B versus 22.2% (2 of 9) placebo (computed responder proportions; RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.81 to 11.08, low-certainty evidence, small trial); saliva production reduced (mean difference -0.50 mL per 5 minutes, 95% CI -1.07 to 0.07); benefit lasts about 4 weeks after a single session; label warns of swallowing and breathing difficulty.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cochrane review 2022 (PMID 35593746); Cochrane overview 2017 (PMID 28072907); FDA Myobloc label

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cough augmentation and mechanical insufflation-exsufflation; AAC devices; mobility aids; palliative care and advance care planning
ranked_high_to_low.type: Supportive techniques, devices and care approach
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Guideline-level (EAN 2024 strong ++ for cough augmentation, AAC, orthoses, end-of-life planning); palliative care reported to improve quality of life of patients and carers (Bede review 2011); advance directives signed in 60.4% of records; no randomised effect sizes retrieved
ranked_high_to_low.source: EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068); Bede et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011 (PMID 21297150); BMC Palliat Care 2024 (PMID 39075493)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Invasive ventilation via tracheostomy
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No randomised trial; non-randomised Danish cohort average treatment time 56.8 months for NIV followed by tracheostomy versus 22.9 months with no ventilation; about half of long-term ventilated patients kept high optimism and enjoyment after an average of 33 months; substantial carer burden
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dreyer et al, ALS Frontotemporal Degener 2014 (PMID 24067168); Rabkin et al, ALS 2006 (PMID 16753972); EAN guideline 2024 (PMID 38470068)

rheumatoid_arthritis.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
rheumatoid_arthritis.icd11_hint: FA20 Rheumatoid arthritis (FA20.0 seropositive, FA20.1 seronegative, FA20.Z unspecified); ICD-10 M05 (seropositive), M06 (other rheumatoid arthritis)
rheumatoid_arthritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Rheumatoid arthritis is NOT curable, and this must be stated plainly: no drug, device or surgery in this entry eliminates the underlying autoimmune synovial inflammation described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry, and stopping treatment usually leads to relapse. What IS real is that REMISSION is a realistic, trial-proven treatment target, and modern treat-to-target care achieves it in a substantial share of patients.
