Real remission figures from the sources in this survey: in TICORA, intensive tight-control management gave remission (DAS <1.6) in 36/55 (65%) of patients versus 9/55 (16%) with routine care (Grigor C et al., Lancet 2004;364:263-269, PMID 15262104); in COMET (early moderate-severe RA) etanercept plus methotrexate produced clinical remission (DAS28 <2.6) in 132/265 (50%) versus 73/263 (28%) with methotrexate alone at 52 weeks (Emery P et al., Lancet 2008;372:375-382, PMID 18635256); in PREMIER, 49% of patients on adalimumab plus methotrexate were in DAS28 remission after 2 years, roughly twice the monotherapy rates (Breedveld FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:26-37, PMID 16385520); in C-EARLY, sustained remission at week 52 was 28.9% with certolizumab plus methotrexate versus 15.0% with methotrexate plus placebo (Emery P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:96-104, PMID 27165179); and in FUNCTION, DAS28-ESR remission at week 24 was 45% with tocilizumab plus methotrexate versus 15% with methotrexate (Burmester GR et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:1081-1091, PMID 26511996). DRUG-FREE remission - being off all DMARDs with no disease activity - is the real but MINORITY outcome: sustained DMARD-free remission was reached by 68/454 (15.0%) of the Leiden early-arthritis cohort and 84/895 (9.4%) of the ERAS cohort (van der Woude D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:2262-2271, PMID 19644846); it becomes more achievable with earlier methotrexate and DAS-steered treatment (adjusted HR 3.72, 95% CI 1.60-8.62; Ajeganova S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:867-873, PMID 25972519); and in a 2025 analysis 37% of patients who never used a biologic reached sustained DMARD-free remission at 5 years in one cohort and 15% at 3 years in tREACH, whereas none who used a biologic did (Heutz JW et al., Lancet Rheumatol 2025;7:e252-e260, PMID 39718182 - a comparison confounded by disease severity, not proof that biologics prevent it). Stopping treatment is where the honest limits show: after remission on etanercept plus methotrexate in PRESERVE, low disease activity at week 88 was 82.6% with continued full-dose etanercept and 79.1% with half-dose, but only 42.6% after etanercept was withdrawn (Smolen JS et al., Lancet 2013;381:918-929, PMID 23332236); 84.0% of patients who stopped tocilizumab after sustained remission flared, though they responded when it was restarted (Huizinga TW et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:35-43, PMID 25169728); and in routine care fewer than 50% of patients in remission were still in remission one year later (Prince FHM et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2012;14:R68, PMID 22429277). EULAR 2022 states that with sustained remission DMARDs may be tapered but should not be stopped (Smolen JS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18, PMID 36357155). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has RA: (1) start methotrexate (with folic acid) at diagnosis together with a short, tapered glucocorticoid bridge, and measure disease activity with a composite score every 1-3 months against a remission target (treat-to-target); (2) if the target is missed at 3-6 months, escalate to triple conventional therapy (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, non-inferior to etanercept plus methotrexate in RACAT) or add a biologic or - after weighing the ORAL Surveillance cardiovascular/cancer/thrombosis signal - a JAK inhibitor, choosing a different mechanism of action if a first biologic fails; (3) screen for TB, hepatitis B/C and update vaccines before any biologic or JAK inhibitor - a particular priority in TB-endemic India; (4) add exercise, occupational therapy/hand exercises, education, smoking cessation and weight management to drug therapy; (5) refer for surgery only when structural joint destruction or cervical instability leaves a joint or the spinal cord at risk; and (6) once in sustained remission, taper carefully rather than stop. 'No cure' does not mean 'nothing works': remission, not cure, is the achievable and evidence-based goal, and in India the conventional-drug ladder plus approved biosimilars and generics makes the target reachable for many patients, though exact costs were not verified in this survey.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for rheumatoid arthritis (RA): the treat-to-target strategy, conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) and triple therapy, glucocorticoids, TNF inhibitors, IL-6 receptor blockers, abatacept, rituximab, JAK inhibitors with the real ORAL Surveillance safety signal, NSAIDs/coxibs as symptomatic-only drugs, biosimilars and India availability, tapering and drug-free remission, non-drug care (exercise, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, education, lifestyle), surgery, pre-treatment safety screening, pregnancy, an honest list of failed/unproven treatments, and devices. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial, meta-analysis or guideline abstract; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms, diagnostic criteria and classification are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Doses named are the trial arm doses quoted in the cited abstracts, not prescribing instructions - dosing is a treating-rheumatologist decision.

ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.name: Treat-to-Target Tight-Control Strategy (TICORA, CAMERA, CAMERA-II, tREACH, BeSt) and Guideline Framework (EULAR 2022/2025, ACR 2021)
ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.type: Treatment strategy (frequent measured reassessment with protocolised escalation - not a single drug)
specific_drugs: Sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine added to methotrexate (triple therapy)
Adalimumab, etanercept or infliximab as biologic escalation
ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.effectiveness: TICORA (111 patients, 2 hospitals, single-blind RCT): intensive tight-control management gave remission (DAS <1.6) in 36/55 (65%) versus 9/55 (16%) with routine care (OR 9.7, 95% CI 3.9-23.9); good response in 45/55 (82%) versus 24/55 (44%); mean fall in DAS -3.5 versus -1.9. CAMERA (299 early-RA patients, open label): at least one remission period in 76 (50%) with computer-assisted monthly MTX adjustment versus 55 (37%) with conventional care (p=0.03). CAMERA-II (236 patients): adding prednisone 10 mg/day to the MTX tight-control strategy reduced erosive damage at 2 years and increased sustained remission versus MTX + placebo (the abstract gives no percentages). tREACH: initial triple DMARD therapy (MTX+SSZ+HCQ) gave 40% fewer treatment intensifications after 3 months than MTX + glucocorticoid; radiographic progression at 1 year was 21%, 24% and 23% in the three arms (no difference). BeSt (508 patients, four strategies): initial combination therapy including prednisone or infliximab gave earlier functional improvement (D-HAQ 0.6 versus 1.0 at 3 months) and less 1-year radiographic progression (median Sharp increase 1.0 and 0.5 versus 2.0 and 2.5). A systematic review update found that 5 of 6 included studies showed superiority of a target-oriented approach over routine care. EULAR 2022 and 2025 recommendations: start methotrexate ideally with short-term glucocorticoid; if there is insufficient response at 3-6 months add a biologic DMARD (JAK inhibitor only after careful risk consideration); the ACR 2021 guideline contains 44 recommendations (7 strong, 37 conditional).
ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.reason_why: RA joint damage and disability accumulate while synovitis remains uncontrolled. A strategy that measures disease activity with a composite score including joint counts every 1-3 months and escalates therapy against a predefined target removes the drift and inertia of routine care; the benefit in these trials came from the strategy itself, not from a new molecule.
ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.important_caveat: TICORA was single-blind with 111 patients; CAMERA was open label; CAMERA-II itself lists as a limitation that tight control implies monthly clinic visits, which is not always feasible. tREACH showed faster attainment of goals with initial triple therapy but no difference in radiographic progression at 1 year.
ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.real_working_solution: Set the target as remission (low disease activity as the alternative goal in long-standing disease), measure a composite index with joint counts at every visit (1-3 monthly while active), and escalate on a fixed schedule (MTX first, add glucocorticoid bridge, add SSZ+HCQ or a biologic/targeted DMARD at 3-6 months if the target is missed). This is the most cost-effective real improvement available in RA, including in resource-limited settings where conventional DMARDs are the mainstay.
ra_strategy_treat_to_target_and_guidelin.source: Grigor C et al. (CAMERA), Ann Rheum Dis 2007;66:1443-1449 (PMID 17519278); Bakker MF et al. (CAMERA-II), Ann Intern Med 2012;156:329-339 (PMID 22393128); de Jong PHP et al. (tREACH), Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1331-1339 (PMID 24788619); Goekoop-Ruiterman YPM et al. ra_csdmard_methotrexate.name: Methotrexate - the Anchor Conventional DMARD (Cochrane Placebo Data, Network Meta-Analysis, Subcutaneous vs Oral)
ra_csdmard_methotrexate.effectiveness: Cochrane review of methotrexate versus placebo (7 trials, 732 patients, previously failed other DMARDs): ACR50 at 52 weeks RR 3.0 (95% CI 1.5-6.0), absolute benefit 15 percentage points (NNT 7); physical function improved (mean difference -0.27 on a 0-3 scale); radiographic progression (erosion score rise >3 units) was less likely (RR 0.31). In a 158-trial network meta-analysis the estimated probability of ACR50 response with oral methotrexate in methotrexate-naive patients was 41%, against 56-67% for triple therapy, several biologics and tofacitinib. In a 6-month RCT of 375 MTX-naive patients (15 mg/week), subcutaneous methotrexate beat oral: ACR20 78% versus 70% and ACR70 41% versus 33%; changing non-responders from oral to SC gave ACR20 in 30%. The original 1985 double-blind crossover trial (28 refractory patients) showed significant falls in tender joints, morning stiffness and disease activity. Safety over 12+ years: transaminase elevation >2x ULN in about 13% and permanent stopping for liver toxicity in 3.7%; a meta-analysis estimated fibrosis incidence of 2.7% at 4 years; methotrexate does not appear to raise the risk of serious infection and may lower cardiovascular mortality; withdrawal for toxicity is lower than for sulfasalazine, gold and penicillamine and higher than for hydroxychloroquine.
ra_csdmard_methotrexate.reason_why: Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent purine/pyrimidine metabolism and increases extracellular adenosine, which dampens T-cell and macrophage activation in the synovium; weekly low-dose use is an anti-inflammatory, not a cytotoxic, regimen.
ra_csdmard_methotrexate.important_caveat: Methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped before conception (see the pregnancy entry); pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity and cytopenias require baseline and periodic monitoring. The Cochrane placebo comparison used older, small trials (12-52 weeks). Radiographic benefit of add-on strategies was, in the network meta-analysis, below the minimal clinically important difference for most regimens.
ra_csdmard_methotrexate.real_working_solution: Start methotrexate at diagnosis (EULAR 2022/2025: first-line with short-term glucocorticoid), give it with folic acid, escalate dose as tolerated toward target, and switch to the subcutaneous route if oral response is inadequate or GI side effects limit the dose before declaring methotrexate failure. It remains the anchor drug to which biologics and JAK inhibitors are added, and in India it is an inexpensive off-patent generic (exact rupee price not verified here).
ra_csdmard_methotrexate.source: Lopez-Olivo MA et al., 'Methotrexate for treating rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(6):CD000957 (PMID 24916606); Hazlewood GS et al., 'Methotrexate monotherapy and methotrexate combination therapy with traditional and biologic DMARDs for rheumatoid arthritis: abridged Cochrane systematic review and network meta-analysis', BMJ 2016;353:i1777 (PMID 27102806); Braun J et al., 'Comparison of the clinical efficacy and safety of subcutaneous versus oral administration of methotrexate in patients with active rheumatoid arthritis', Arthritis Rheum 2008;58:73-81 (PMID 18163521); Weinblatt ME et al., 'Efficacy of low-dose methotrexate in rheumatoid arthritis', N Engl J Med 1985;312:818-822 (PMID 3883172); Salliot C, van der Heijde D, 'Long-term safety of methotrexate monotherapy in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: a systematic literature research', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:1100-1104 (PMID 19060002); Visser K et al., 'Multinational evidence-based recommendations for the use of methotrexate in rheumatic disorders', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:1086-1093 (PMID 19033291); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biological DMARDs: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18 (PMID 36357155)

ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.name: Folic/Folinic Acid Supplementation and Monitoring with Methotrexate (Cochrane Evidence)
ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.type: Supportive vitamin supplement and laboratory monitoring protocol
specific_drugs: Folic acid (low-dose, given with weekly methotrexate)
Folinic acid (leucovorin/calcium folinate) as the alternative form
ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.effectiveness: Cochrane (6 trials, 624 patients, low-dose folic/folinic acid, starting dose <=7 mg weekly): gastrointestinal side effects RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.59-0.92; 26% relative, 9% absolute risk reduction); abnormal transaminase elevation RR 0.23 (95% CI 0.15-0.34; 76.9% relative, 16% absolute reduction); withdrawal from methotrexate for any reason RR 0.39 (95% CI 0.28-0.53; 60.8% relative, 15.2% absolute reduction). Stomatitis showed a non-significant trend (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.49-1.06). Folate did not significantly reduce methotrexate efficacy on RA disease-activity measures. In the leflunomide-versus-methotrexate trial (999 patients) 21 methotrexate patients were withdrawn for raised liver enzymes over 2 years against 8 on leflunomide, and two drug-related pulmonary deaths occurred on methotrexate; the authors noted this toxicity must be weighed when methotrexate is used without folate. The 10 multinational recommendations for methotrexate cover work-up before starting, dose and route, folic acid, monitoring and management of hepatotoxicity.
ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.reason_why: Methotrexate depletes the intracellular folate pool; replacing folate protects rapidly dividing mucosal and hepatic cells from the toxic effect without abolishing the anti-inflammatory effect.
ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.important_caveat: The Cochrane pooled analysis could not draw firm conclusions on haematological toxicity because of few events and poor reporting.
ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.real_working_solution: Prescribe folic acid with every methotrexate course and keep a scheduled blood-count and liver-enzyme monitoring plan; folate makes methotrexate more likely to be continued, which is what protects disease control.
ra_methotrexate_folate_and_safety_monito.source: Shea B et al., 'Folic acid and folinic acid for reducing side effects in patients receiving methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(5):CD000951 (PMID 23728635); Emery P et al., 'A comparison of the efficacy and safety of leflunomide and methotrexate for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2000;39:655-665 (PMID 10888712); Visser K et al., 'Multinational evidence-based recommendations for the use of methotrexate in rheumatic disorders', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:1086-1093 (PMID 19033291)

ra_csdmard_leflunomide.name: Leflunomide - Pyrimidine-Synthesis Inhibitor with Equivalent ACR20 Response to Methotrexate
specific_drugs: Leflunomide (loading 100 mg/day for 3 days then 20 mg/day in the trials)
Teriflunomide is its active metabolite (not a separate RA drug)
ra_csdmard_leflunomide.effectiveness: In the North American trial (482 patients) ACR20 response was 52% with leflunomide, 46% with methotrexate and 26% with placebo (p<0.001 for both actives versus placebo; the two actives were statistically equivalent); ACR success rates 41%, 35% and 19%; radiographic progression was less with leflunomide (p=0.001) and methotrexate (p=0.02). In the sulfasalazine-controlled trial ACR20 at week 24 was 55% with leflunomide versus 29% with placebo (p=0.0001) and 56% with sulfasalazine. A Cochrane meta-analysis of 6 trials found an absolute ACR20 improvement of 28% (95% CI 21-35%) versus placebo (232/413 versus 89/311) with no ACR20 difference from sulfasalazine or methotrexate at 6 and 12 months. In the 999-patient head-to-head trial methotrexate had some clinical advantage at 1 year and significantly less radiographic progression at 2 years. Asymptomatic transaminase rises led to discontinuation in 7.1% on leflunomide (1.7% placebo, 3.3% methotrexate); withdrawals due to adverse events were 10 percentage points higher than placebo (70/416 versus 18/311).
ra_csdmard_leflunomide.reason_why: Leflunomide's active metabolite inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, blocking de novo pyrimidine synthesis in activated, rapidly dividing lymphocytes.
ra_csdmard_leflunomide.important_caveat: Diarrhoea, nausea, alopecia, rash and raised liver enzymes were the commonest adverse events in the trials.
ra_csdmard_leflunomide.real_working_solution: Use leflunomide when methotrexate is contraindicated or not tolerated, or as a methotrexate partner; check liver enzymes regularly, and plan pregnancy separately (leflunomide requires discontinuation before planned pregnancy because fetal safety data are insufficient).
ra_csdmard_leflunomide.source: Strand V et al., 'Treatment of active rheumatoid arthritis with leflunomide compared with placebo and methotrexate', Arch Intern Med 1999;159:2542-2550 (PMID 10573044); Smolen JS et al., 'Efficacy and safety of the new DMARD leflunomide: comparison to placebo and sulfasalazine in active rheumatoid arthritis', Scand J Rheumatol Suppl 1999;112:15-21 (PMID 10668523); Osiri M et al., 'Leflunomide for treating rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2003;(1):CD002047 (PMID 12535423); Emery P et al., 'A comparison of the efficacy and safety of leflunomide and methotrexate for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2000;39:655-665 (PMID 10888712); Götestam Skorpen C et al., 'The EULAR points to consider for use of antirheumatic drugs before pregnancy, and during pregnancy and lactation', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:795-810 (PMID 26888948)

ra_csdmard_sulfasalazine.name: Sulfasalazine - Older Conventional DMARD, Low Cost, Pregnancy-Compatible
specific_drugs: Sulfasalazine (2 g/day in COBRA; 500 mg twice daily in O'Dell 1996)
ra_csdmard_sulfasalazine.effectiveness: Cochrane (6 trials, 468 patients versus placebo): significant benefit for tender and swollen joint scores (standardised difference -0.49), pain (-0.42) and ESR (-17.6 mm); withdrawals for adverse reactions were three times higher (OR 3.0) and placebo patients were four times more likely to stop for lack of efficacy. In the leflunomide comparison trial sulfasalazine reached ACR20 in 56% at week 24. In O'Dell 1996, sulfasalazine plus hydroxychloroquine achieved the primary endpoint (>=50% improvement maintained for 2 years without major toxicity) in 14/35 patients (40%) compared with 12/36 (33%) on methotrexate alone and 24/31 (77%) on all three drugs. EULAR pregnancy guidance lists sulfasalazine as compatible with pregnancy and lactation.
ra_csdmard_sulfasalazine.reason_why: Sulfasalazine is cleaved in the colon to sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid; its anti-rheumatic effect is systemic and not fully explained.
ra_csdmard_sulfasalazine.important_caveat: Cochrane concluded effects on overall health status and radiological progression are not clear and appear modest; the Cochrane review's evidence is old (searched to 1997). Sulfa allergy and GI intolerance are common reasons for stopping.
ra_csdmard_sulfasalazine.real_working_solution: Use sulfasalazine as part of triple therapy, as a methotrexate alternative when methotrexate is contraindicated, or in patients planning pregnancy; effects on radiographic progression are modest per Cochrane.
ra_csdmard_sulfasalazine.source: Suarez-Almazor ME et al., 'Sulfasalazine for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 1998;(2):CD000958 (PMID 10796400); Smolen JS et al., 'Efficacy and safety of the new DMARD leflunomide: comparison to placebo and sulfasalazine in active rheumatoid arthritis', Scand J Rheumatol Suppl 1999;112:15-21 (PMID 10668523); O'Dell JR et al., 'Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate alone, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine, or a combination of all three medications', N Engl J Med 1996;334:1287-1291 (PMID 8609945); Rüegg L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:910-926 (PMID 40287311)

ra_csdmard_hydroxychloroquine.name: Hydroxychloroquine - Mild DMARD, Best Tolerated; Retinal Screening Required
specific_drugs: Hydroxychloroquine (200 mg twice daily in O'Dell 1996; keep <=5.0 mg/kg real body weight/day for retinal safety)
Chloroquine (older antimalarial, more retinal risk, not preferred)
ra_csdmard_hydroxychloroquine.effectiveness: Cochrane (4 trials, 300 hydroxychloroquine versus 292 placebo patients): significant benefit versus placebo with standardised mean differences -0.33 to -0.52 for joint counts, pain and global assessments, and lower ESR; more placebo patients withdrew for lack of efficacy and no difference in withdrawals for toxicity - effect described as moderate with a low toxicity profile. In the randomised placebo-controlled trial by Clark et al., hydroxychloroquine gave 20% greater mean improvement in joint score with 10% more patients improved by >50%, and 40% greater mean improvement in pain with 19% more patients improved by >50%; side effects were mild and no patient stopped. Retinal safety: at recommended doses the risk of toxicity is under 1% up to 5 years and under 2% up to 10 years but rises to almost 20% after 20 years (AAO 2016); overall prevalence 7.5% in long-term users with OR 5.67 for >5.0 mg/kg/day and OR 2.08 for kidney disease (Melles & Marmor 2014). An observational study reported fewer incident cardiovascular events with hydroxychloroquine in RA.
ra_csdmard_hydroxychloroquine.reason_why: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in lysosomes, raising their pH and interfering with antigen processing and toll-like-receptor signalling; its effect is modulating rather than strongly suppressive.
ra_csdmard_hydroxychloroquine.important_caveat: Hydroxychloroquine alone is weak for active RA (a moderate effect per Cochrane). Retinopathy is irreversible and no treatment exists; the cardiovascular association is observational only.
ra_csdmard_hydroxychloroquine.real_working_solution: Use hydroxychloroquine as an add-on to methotrexate and in triple therapy, keep dose <=5.0 mg/kg real weight, do a baseline fundus exam, and start annual screening after 5 years (visual fields plus spectral-domain OCT) or earlier if kidney disease or tamoxifen are present.
ra_csdmard_hydroxychloroquine.source: Suarez-Almazor ME et al., 'Antimalarials for treating rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2000;(4):CD000959 (PMID 11034691); Clark P et al., 'Hydroxychloroquine compared with placebo in rheumatoid arthritis. A randomized controlled trial', Ann Intern Med 1993;119:1067-1071 (PMID 8239224); Marmor MF et al., 'Recommendations on screening for chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine retinopathy (2016 revision)', Ophthalmology 2016;123:1386-1394 (PMID 26992838); Melles RB, Marmor MF, 'The risk of toxic retinopathy in patients on long-term hydroxychloroquine therapy', JAMA Ophthalmol 2014;132:1453-1460 (PMID 25275721); Sharma TS et al., 'Hydroxychloroquine use is associated with decreased incident cardiovascular events in rheumatoid arthritis patients', J Am Heart Assoc 2016;5 (PMID 26727968)

ra_csdmard_triple_therapy.name: Triple Conventional Therapy (Methotrexate + Sulfasalazine + Hydroxychloroquine) - O'Dell 1996, RACAT, TEAR, SWEFOT
ra_csdmard_triple_therapy.effectiveness: O'Dell 1996 (102 patients, 2-year double-blind): >=50% improvement maintained at 2 years without major toxicity in 24/31 patients (77%) on all three drugs versus 12/36 (33%) on methotrexate alone (p<0.001) and 14/35 (40%) on sulfasalazine+hydroxychloroquine (p=0.003). RACAT (353 patients with active RA despite methotrexate, 48-week double-blind non-inferiority): DAS28 change -2.1 with triple therapy versus -2.3 with etanercept+methotrexate (upper confidence limit 0.41 below the 0.6 margin); 27% in each group needed a switch at 24 weeks; no significant difference in radiographic progression, pain or major adverse events. TEAR: oral triple therapy and etanercept+methotrexate had no significant DAS28 difference over 102 weeks, but radiographic change from baseline was 0.64 with etanercept+MTX versus 1.69 with triple therapy (p=0.047). SWEFOT: adding infliximab rather than SSZ+HCQ to methotrexate gave the primary outcome in 50/128 (39%) versus 32/130 (25%) (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.10-2.30). Network meta-analysis: after methotrexate inadequate response the probability of ACR50 was 61% with triple therapy (27-70% for other combinations), and triple therapy had fewer withdrawals for adverse events than methotrexate plus infliximab.
ra_csdmard_triple_therapy.reason_why: Three agents with different immunomodulatory mechanisms (antimetabolite, sulfa-derived anti-inflammatory, lysosomotropic antimalarial) have additive effects on synovitis without the cost or infection burden of biologics.
ra_csdmard_triple_therapy.important_caveat: TEAR and SWEFOT show the biologic-containing arms were somewhat better on radiographic progression (TEAR) or on the primary outcome (SWEFOT) than triple therapy; O'Dell 1996 was a small single-network trial of patients with previous DMARD failure.
ra_csdmard_triple_therapy.real_working_solution: When methotrexate alone fails (or as initial therapy in poor-prognosis disease), add sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine before or instead of a biologic; RACAT showed this was clinically non-inferior to etanercept+methotrexate, which makes it a conventional-drug option that avoids biologic cost. Escalate to a biologic or JAK inhibitor if the target is still missed at 3-6 months.
ra_csdmard_triple_therapy.source: O'Dell JR et al., 'Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate alone, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine, or a combination of all three medications', N Engl J Med 1996;334:1287-1291 (PMID 8609945); O'Dell JR et al. (RACAT), 'Therapies for active rheumatoid arthritis after methotrexate failure', N Engl J Med 2013;369:307-318 (PMID 23755969); Moreland LW et al. (TEAR), Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:2824-2835 (PMID 22508468); van Vollenhoven RF et al. (SWEFOT), Lancet 2009;374:459-466 (PMID 19665644); Hazlewood GS et al., 'Methotrexate monotherapy and methotrexate combination therapy with traditional and biologic DMARDs for rheumatoid arthritis: abridged Cochrane systematic review and network meta-analysis', BMJ 2016;353:i1777 (PMID 27102806)

ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.name: Glucocorticoid Bridging Therapy (COBRA, COBRA-light, CAMERA-II, Kirwan 1995, Wassenberg 2005)
ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.type: Corticosteroid, oral step-down (or intramuscular) bridge to slower DMARD onset
specific_drugs: Prednisolone (COBRA step-down from 60 mg/day to 7.5 mg/day, stopped after 28 weeks)
ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.effectiveness: COBRA (155 early-RA patients): combined step-down prednisolone + methotrexate + sulfasalazine versus sulfasalazine alone - improved by ACR criteria at week 28 in 55/76 (72%) versus 39/79 (49%); radiographic damage increase at week 28 was a median 1 versus 4 (p<0.0001), still lower at week 56 (2 versus 6) and week 80 (4 versus 12); withdrawals 8% versus 29%; the clinical advantage faded once prednisolone was stopped but the radiographic advantage persisted. COBRA-light (attenuated regimen) was non-inferior: DAS44 <1.6 reached in 49% (COBRA) and 41% (COBRA-light) at 6 months. CAMERA-II showed MTX + prednisone 10 mg/day reduced erosive damage and increased sustained remission versus MTX + placebo. Kirwan 1995 (low-dose prednisolone, 2 years): hands acquiring new erosions 15/68 (22.1%) versus 36/79 (45.6%) with placebo, a 51.5% relative reduction (23.5/45.6), and Larsen score rise 0.72 versus 5.37 (p=0.004). Wassenberg 2005 (very low-dose prednisolone): significantly less radiographic progression at 24 months (Ratingen score difference 3.14, p=0.006). Cochrane (15 studies, 1,414 patients): standardised mean difference in radiographic progression 0.40 (95% CI 0.27-0.54) favouring glucocorticoids when combined with other DMARDs. In trials most patients starting GC bridging stopped within 12 months (22% still on GC) to 24 months (10% still on GC); equal 2-year efficacy of 30 mg/day versus 60 mg/day starting doses.
ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.reason_why: Glucocorticoids suppress cytokine transcription broadly and quickly, covering the 6-12 weeks before slower csDMARDs act, and directly limit erosion formation.
ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.important_caveat: Safety risks scale with dose and duration (osteoporotic fractures, serious infections, diabetes, mortality - see the low-dose GLORIA/safety entry). In COBRA the clinical advantage over sulfasalazine alone decreased after prednisolone was stopped.
ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.real_working_solution: Bridge with a short, tapered glucocorticoid course (about 3-6 months) alongside methotrexate at treatment start, tapering to zero on a set schedule; EULAR 2022/2025 recommend methotrexate plus short-term glucocorticoid as the initial regimen.
ra_glucocorticoid_bridging_cobra.source: Boers M et al. (COBRA), 'Randomised comparison of combined step-down prednisolone, methotrexate and sulphasalazine with sulphasalazine alone in early rheumatoid arthritis', Lancet 1997;350:309-318 (PMID 9251634); den Uyl D et al. (COBRA-light), Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1071-1078 (PMID 23606682); Bakker MF et al. (CAMERA-II), Ann Intern Med 2012;156:329-339 (PMID 22393128); Kirwan JR et al. (ARC Low-Dose Glucocorticoid Study Group), 'The effect of glucocorticoids on joint destruction in rheumatoid arthritis', N Engl J Med 1995;333:142-146 (PMID 7791815); Wassenberg S et al., 'Very low-dose prednisolone in early rheumatoid arthritis retards radiographic progression over two years', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:3371-3380 (PMID 16255011); Kirwan JR et al., 'Effects of glucocorticoids on radiological progression in rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;(1):CD006356 (PMID 17253590); Bergstra SA et al., 'Efficacy, duration of use and safety of glucocorticoids: a systematic literature review informing the 2022 update of the EULAR recommendations for RA', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:81-94 (PMID 36410794); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic DMARDs: 2025 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2026;85:991-1009 (PMID 41826212)

ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.name: Long-Term Low-Dose Prednisolone (GLORIA) and Glucocorticoid Safety / Bone Protection
ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.type: Corticosteroid, long-term low dose (add-on) with safety management
specific_drugs: Alendronate/zoledronic acid, denosumab or parathyroid hormone analogues for glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (ACR 2022)
ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.effectiveness: GLORIA (451 patients aged 65+ with established RA, mean age 72, disease duration 11 years, 2-year double-blind): prednisolone 5 mg/day lowered DAS28 by 0.37 points versus placebo (p<0.0001) and slowed joint damage progression by 1.7 Sharp units (p=0.003); the harm outcome (at least one adverse event of special interest) occurred in 60% versus 49% (adjusted RR 1.24, one-sided 95% CL 1.04, p=0.02), driven mainly by mostly non-severe infections; other GC-specific events were rare; authors concluded a favourable balance in seniors. EULAR systematic review: safety risks increase with dose and duration (fractures, serious infections, diabetes, mortality) and no clearly safe dose was established. Wassenberg 2005 low-dose trial reported more weight gain (4 v 0), hypertension (6 v 2), glaucoma (3 v 0), Cushing's (5 v 0) and gastric distress (9 v 4). ACR 2022 glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis guideline: for adults on >3 months of glucocorticoids, strongly recommends early fracture-risk assessment (clinical, bone density with vertebral fracture assessment, FRAX if >=40 years) and strongly recommends pharmacologic treatment in medium, high or very-high fracture risk.
ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.reason_why: Chronic low-dose glucocorticoid retains a disease-modifying anti-erosive effect, while long-term exposure causes bone loss, infection risk and metabolic effects proportional to cumulative dose.
ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.important_caveat: GLORIA was a pragmatic trial in patients 65+ (79% on DMARDs, 14% on biologics) and used one-sided testing with 95% confidence limits; the results should not be over-extended to younger patients. EULAR's own review found conflicting evidence on which dose is safe.
ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.real_working_solution: If low-dose prednisolone is used long term (for example 5 mg/day in an older patient with established disease not controlled otherwise), weigh it explicitly against the 24% higher adverse-event risk seen in GLORIA, document fracture-risk assessment at the start, treat osteoporosis when indicated, and re-attempt tapering as disease allows.
ra_glucocorticoid_low_dose_gloria_and_sa.source: Boers M et al. (GLORIA), 'Low dose, add-on prednisolone in patients with rheumatoid arthritis aged 65+', Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:925-936 (PMID 35641125); Bergstra SA et al., 'Efficacy, duration of use and safety of glucocorticoids: a systematic literature review informing the 2022 update of the EULAR recommendations for RA', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:81-94 (PMID 36410794); Wassenberg S et al., 'Very low-dose prednisolone in early rheumatoid arthritis retards radiographic progression over two years', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:3371-3380 (PMID 16255011); Humphrey MB et al., '2022 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Prevention and Treatment of Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteoporosis', Arthritis Rheumatol 2023;75:2088-2102 (PMID 37845798)

ra_tnf_adalimumab.name: Adalimumab (TNF Inhibitor) - ARMADA, DE019, PREMIER; Indian Biosimilar Exemptia/Adfrar
ra_tnf_adalimumab.type: Biologic DMARD, fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Adalimumab (40 mg every other week in the trials)
ra_tnf_adalimumab.effectiveness: ARMADA (adalimumab + methotrexate, 24 weeks): ACR20 67.2% (40 mg) versus 14.5% placebo+MTX; ACR50 55.2% versus 8.1%; ACR70 26.9% versus 4.8%. DE019 (adalimumab + MTX, 52 weeks): ACR20 at week 24 63% (40 mg every other week) versus 30% placebo, and at week 52 59% versus 24%; radiographic progression (TSS) at week 52 was 0.1 versus 2.7 with placebo (p<=0.001). PREMIER (early aggressive RA): at year 1 ACR50 was 62% with adalimumab + MTX versus 46% (MTX alone) and 41% (adalimumab alone); after 2 years 49% of combination patients were in DAS28 remission (<2.6) and 49% had an ACR70 response for >=6 continuous months, about twice the monotherapy rates; Sharp-score progression 1.3 and 1.9 (years 1-2) with combination versus 5.7 and 10.4 with MTX. Indian real-life ASPIRE registry (biosimilar adalimumab ZRC-3197, 73 analysable patients, 24 weeks): ACR20/50/70 48%/48%/34% (as reported), no new safety signals.
ra_tnf_adalimumab.reason_why: Adalimumab neutralises soluble and membrane TNF-alpha, a central cytokine in synovial inflammation and osteoclast activation.
ra_tnf_adalimumab.important_caveat: TNF inhibitors raise the risk of tuberculosis reactivation and other serious infections; the ASPIRE registry data are an uncontrolled observational report with 73 analysable patients, so they show tolerability, not comparative efficacy.
ra_tnf_adalimumab.real_working_solution: For patients who miss the target on methotrexate (or triple therapy), add adalimumab (originator or an approved biosimilar such as the Indian brands) to methotrexate; the combination outperformed either alone in PREMIER. Screen for TB and hepatitis B first (see the screening entry).
ra_tnf_adalimumab.source: Weinblatt ME et al. (ARMADA), Arthritis Rheum 2003;48:35-45 (PMID 12528101); Keystone EC et al. (DE019), Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:1400-1411 (PMID 15146409); Breedveld FC et al. (PREMIER), Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:26-37 (PMID 16385520); Kapoor S et al., 'Real-life tolerability and effectiveness of adalimumab biosimilar in rheumatoid arthritis: ASPIRE registry data from India', Rheumatol Ther 2019;6:451-459 (PMID 31254222); GaBI Online, 'Similar biologics approved and marketed in India' (https://www.gabionline.net/biosimilars/general/Similar-biologics-approved-and-marketed-in-India)

ra_tnf_etanercept.name: Etanercept (TNF Receptor-Fc Fusion) - Moreland 1999, ERA, TEMPO, COMET
ra_tnf_etanercept.type: Biologic DMARD, soluble TNF receptor fusion protein, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Etanercept (25 mg in the pivotal trials)
Etanercept biosimilars Intacept (Intas, India 2015) and Etacept (Cipla, India 2013)
ra_tnf_etanercept.effectiveness: Moreland 1999 (monotherapy, 6 months): ACR20 59% (25 mg) versus 11% placebo; ACR50 40% versus 5%; mean fall in tender joints 56% versus 6%. ERA (early RA versus methotrexate): more etanercept 25 mg patients had ACR20/50/70 responses in the first 6 months (p<0.05), erosion score rose 0.47 versus 1.03 over 12 months (p=0.002), and 72% versus 60% had no increase in erosion score. TEMPO (682 patients): ACR-N area under the curve at 24 weeks 18.3%-years for etanercept + methotrexate versus 14.7 for etanercept alone and 12.2 for methotrexate alone; mean total Sharp score change -0.54 versus +2.80 for methotrexate alone. COMET (early moderate-severe RA): clinical remission (DAS28 <2.6) in 132/265 (50%) with etanercept + MTX versus 73/263 (28%) with MTX alone at 52 weeks; radiographic non-progression 80% versus 59%; serious adverse events similar.
ra_tnf_etanercept.reason_why: Etanercept is a dimeric soluble TNF receptor fused to IgG1 Fc that binds and inactivates TNF (and lymphotoxin-alpha) before it reaches its cellular receptor.
ra_tnf_etanercept.important_caveat: TB/serious infection risk applies to all TNF inhibitors. The Indian brand and year data come from the GaBI listing; formulation and price were not verified.
ra_tnf_etanercept.real_working_solution: Etanercept is a real option for patients who miss the target on methotrexate/triple therapy, and works alone (unlike infliximab) if methotrexate cannot be used, though the TEMPO combination was better. Indian biosimilars exist (see the biosimilars entry); TB/hepatitis B screening first.
ra_tnf_etanercept.source: Moreland LW et al., 'Etanercept therapy in rheumatoid arthritis. A randomized, controlled trial', Ann Intern Med 1999;130:478-486 (PMID 10075615); Bathon JM et al., 'A comparison of etanercept and methotrexate in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis', N Engl J Med 2000;343:1586-1593 (PMID 11096165); Klareskog L et al. (TEMPO), Lancet 2004;363:675-681 (PMID 15001324); Emery P et al. (COMET), Lancet 2008;372:375-382 (PMID 18635256); GaBI Online, 'Similar biologics approved and marketed in India' (https://www.gabionline.net/biosimilars/general/Similar-biologics-approved-and-marketed-in-India)

ra_tnf_infliximab.name: Infliximab (Chimeric Anti-TNF Antibody) - ATTRACT, ASPIRE, SWEFOT; TB Signal
ra_tnf_infliximab.type: Biologic DMARD, chimeric anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, intravenous infusion
specific_drugs: Infliximab (3 mg/kg in the ATTRACT/ASPIRE trials, always with methotrexate)
ra_tnf_infliximab.effectiveness: ATTRACT (methotrexate-inadequate responders, 30 weeks): ACR20 in 53%, 50%, 58% and 52% across the four infliximab regimens versus 20% with placebo+MTX (p<0.001); ACR50 26-31% versus 5%. ASPIRE (early RA): median ACR-N 38.9% (3 mg/kg) and 46.7% (6 mg/kg) versus 26.4% with MTX + placebo at week 54; Sharp-score change 0.4 and 0.5 versus 3.7 (p<0.001); more serious infections, especially pneumonia. In SWEFOT infliximab add-on gave the primary outcome in 39% versus 25% with SSZ+HCQ. NOR-SWITCH (482 patients, 77 with RA): disease worsening in 26% (originator) versus 30% (CT-P13 biosimilar), adjusted difference -4.4% (95% CI -12.7 to 3.9), i.e. no evidence of worse outcomes after switching to the biosimilar. The original TB report described 70 cases of TB after infliximab, median 12 weeks, 40 extrapulmonary and 17 disseminated.
ra_tnf_infliximab.reason_why: Infliximab binds soluble and transmembrane TNF; concomitant methotrexate reduces anti-drug antibodies and adds efficacy.
ra_tnf_infliximab.important_caveat: ASPIRE and ATTRACT showed higher serious-infection rates with infliximab; TB risk is real and dominant in TB-endemic countries such as India (see the screening entry).
ra_tnf_infliximab.real_working_solution: Use infliximab only with methotrexate; because it is an infusion with a documented early TB signal, screen for latent TB (IGRA/TST plus chest X-ray) before the first dose and treat latent TB first.
ra_tnf_infliximab.source: Maini R et al. (ATTRACT), Lancet 1999;354:1932-1939 (PMID 10622295); St Clair EW et al. (ASPIRE), Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:3432-3443 (PMID 15529377); van Vollenhoven RF et al. (SWEFOT), Lancet 2009;374:459-466 (PMID 19665644); Keane J et al., 'Tuberculosis associated with infliximab, a tumor necrosis factor alpha-neutralizing agent', N Engl J Med 2001;345:1098-1104 (PMID 11596589); Jørgensen KK et al. (NOR-SWITCH), Lancet 2017;389:2304-2316 (PMID 28502609); GaBI Online, 'Similar biologics approved and marketed in India' (https://www.gabionline.net/biosimilars/general/Similar-biologics-approved-and-marketed-in-India)

ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.name: Certolizumab Pegol (PEGylated Fab' Anti-TNF) - RAPID 1/2, C-EARLY
ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.type: Biologic DMARD, PEGylated anti-TNF antibody fragment, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Certolizumab pegol (200 mg and 400 mg arms in RAPID)
ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.effectiveness: RAPID 1 (24 weeks, with MTX): ACR20 58.8% (200 mg) and 60.8% (400 mg) versus 13.6% placebo; Sharp-score change at week 52 was 0.4 and 0.2 versus 2.8. RAPID 2: ACR20 57.3% and 57.6% versus 8.7%; mTSS change 0.2 and -0.4 versus 1.2; five patients developed tuberculosis. C-EARLY (879 DMARD-naive early RA with poor prognostic factors): sustained remission at week 52 in 28.9% versus 15.0% (p<0.001) and sustained low disease activity 43.8% versus 28.6%; mTSS non-progressors 70.3% versus 49.7%; serious infection rate 3.3 versus 3.7 per 100 patient-years.
ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.reason_why: Certolizumab is a TNF-binding Fab' fragment lacking an Fc region, which is PEGylated for a long half-life; it neutralises TNF like other anti-TNFs.
ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.important_caveat: As with all TNFi, TB screening is mandatory; RAPID 2 recorded 5 TB cases.
ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.real_working_solution: Certolizumab is a TNF-inhibitor option with C-EARLY evidence of higher sustained remission when combined with dose-optimised methotrexate in early poor-prognosis disease; for pregnancy planning see the pregnancy entry (the cited EULAR abstract says all TNF inhibitors can be used throughout pregnancy after individual assessment).
ra_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.source: Keystone E et al. (RAPID 1), Arthritis Rheum 2008;58:3319-3329 (PMID 18975346); Smolen J et al. (RAPID 2), Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:797-804 (PMID 19015207); Emery P et al. (C-EARLY), Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:96-104 (PMID 27165179)

ra_tnf_golimumab.name: Golimumab (Human Anti-TNF, Monthly Subcutaneous) - GO-FORWARD, GO-BEFORE
ra_tnf_golimumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous every 4 weeks
specific_drugs: Golimumab (50 mg or 100 mg monthly in the trials)
ra_tnf_golimumab.effectiveness: GO-FORWARD (MTX-inadequate responders): ACR20 at week 14 was 55.1% (50 mg + MTX, p=0.001) and 56.2% (100 mg + MTX, p<0.001) versus 33.1% with placebo + MTX; golimumab 100 mg alone 44.4% (p=0.059); HAQ-DI improvement 0.38 and 0.50 versus 0.13; serious infections to week 16 were 0.8% with placebo + MTX, 2.2% with golimumab 50 mg + MTX and 5.6% with 100 mg + MTX. GO-BEFORE (MTX-naive): ACR50 at week 24 was 38.4% (combined golimumab+MTX group) versus 29.4% for MTX alone (p=0.053, not significant on the primary ITT analysis) and 38.5% versus 29.4% on a post hoc modified ITT (p=0.049).
ra_tnf_golimumab.reason_why: Golimumab neutralises TNF as a monoclonal antibody with a dosing interval of 4 weeks.
ra_tnf_golimumab.important_caveat: GO-BEFORE's primary intention-to-treat comparison was not statistically significant (p=0.053); only a post hoc modified analysis reached p=0.049. Higher serious infection rate at the 100 mg dose in GO-FORWARD.
ra_tnf_golimumab.real_working_solution: Golimumab is an alternative anti-TNF for patients who prefer monthly dosing; note that in methotrexate-naive early RA (GO-BEFORE) the primary ITT analysis did not reach significance, so it is used mainly after methotrexate failure.
ra_tnf_golimumab.source: Keystone EC et al. (GO-FORWARD), Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:789-796 (PMID 19066176); Emery P et al. (GO-BEFORE), Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:2272-2283 (PMID 19644849)

ra_il6_tocilizumab.name: Tocilizumab (Anti-IL-6 Receptor) - OPTION, AMBITION, ADACTA, FUNCTION, ACT-RAY
ra_il6_tocilizumab.type: Biologic DMARD, humanised anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, intravenous or subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Tocilizumab (4 mg/kg and 8 mg/kg in the trials)
Tocilizumab monotherapy (when methotrexate cannot be used)
ra_il6_tocilizumab.effectiveness: OPTION (622 MTX-inadequate responders, 24 weeks): ACR20 59% (8 mg/kg), 48% (4 mg/kg), 26% (placebo) (OR 4.0 for 8 mg/kg). AMBITION (tocilizumab monotherapy versus methotrexate monotherapy): ACR20 69.9% versus 52.5% (p<0.001) and DAS28 <2.6 in 33.6% versus 12.1% at week 24; grade 3 neutropenia 3.1% versus 0.4%, total cholesterol >=240 mg/dl in 13.2% versus 0.4%, serious infections 1.4% versus 0.7%. ADACTA (325 patients, both drugs as monotherapy): DAS28 change -3.3 with tocilizumab versus -1.8 with adalimumab (difference -1.5, 95% CI -1.8 to -1.1, p<0.0001), serious adverse events 12% versus 10%. FUNCTION (1,157 early progressive RA): DAS28-ESR remission at week 24 was 45% with tocilizumab 8 mg/kg + MTX and 39% with tocilizumab alone versus 15% with placebo + MTX; mTSS change 0.08 versus 1.14 at week 52 (p=0.0001); withdrawals for adverse events 20% in the combination arm. ACT-RAY (556 patients): of those entering year 2, 50.4% discontinued tocilizumab after sustained remission, 5.9% reached drug-free remission, and 84.0% of those who stopped flared but responded to reintroduction.
ra_il6_tocilizumab.reason_why: Interleukin-6 drives hepatic acute-phase response, B-cell differentiation and osteoclast activation; blocking its receptor gives rapid CRP normalisation and also works as monotherapy, which is a distinctive advantage.
ra_il6_tocilizumab.important_caveat: AMBITION recorded higher neutropenia and cholesterol; ADACTA had more LDL rise, ALT rise and neutrophil/platelet reduction with tocilizumab. Indian availability of a tocilizumab biosimilar was not verified in the sources searched (the GaBI India listing does not include it).
ra_il6_tocilizumab.real_working_solution: Tocilizumab is the natural biologic when methotrexate must be avoided (monotherapy beat methotrexate in AMBITION and adalimumab in ADACTA); monitor neutrophils, liver enzymes and lipids (the AMBITION and ADACTA abnormalities above).
ra_il6_tocilizumab.source: Smolen JS et al. (OPTION), Lancet 2008;371:987-997 (PMID 18358926); Jones G et al. (AMBITION), Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:88-96 (PMID 19297346); Gabay C et al. (ADACTA), Lancet 2013;381:1541-1550 (PMID 23515142); Burmester GR et al. (FUNCTION), Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:1081-1091 (PMID 26511996); Huizinga TW et al. (ACT-RAY 2-year), Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:35-43 (PMID 25169728)

ra_il6_sarilumab.name: Sarilumab (Anti-IL-6 Receptor) - MOBILITY and MONARCH
ra_il6_sarilumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Sarilumab (150 mg and 200 mg in MOBILITY)
ra_il6_sarilumab.effectiveness: MOBILITY (MTX-inadequate responders): ACR20 at week 24 was 58.0% (150 mg), 66.4% (200 mg) versus 33.4% placebo (p<0.0001); mean mTSS change at week 52 was 0.90, 0.25 versus 2.78; ALT >3x upper limit in 9.5%, 8.0% versus 2.1%; neutrophils 0.5 to <1.0x10^9/L in 5.1%, 7.8% (none with placebo); serious infections 2.6%, 4.0% versus 2.3%. MONARCH (monotherapy versus adalimumab monotherapy, 24 weeks): DAS28-ESR change -3.28 versus -2.20 (p<0.0001); ACR20/50/70 71.7%/45.7%/23.4% versus 58.4%/29.7%/11.9%; CDAI remission 7.1% versus 2.7% (nominal p=0.0468); serious infections 1.1% in both arms.
ra_il6_sarilumab.reason_why: Same mechanism as tocilizumab: blockade of IL-6 receptor signalling, reducing acute-phase inflammation and bone erosion drivers.
ra_il6_sarilumab.important_caveat: Cytopenias and transaminase rises were dose-related in MOBILITY; the sarilumab-versus-adalimumab CDAI remission difference is labelled nominal in the MONARCH abstract. Indian commercial availability was not verified.
ra_il6_sarilumab.real_working_solution: Sarilumab is a second IL-6-blocking option, especially where monotherapy is needed; monitor neutrophils, ALT and lipids as in MOBILITY.
ra_il6_sarilumab.source: Genovese MC et al. (MOBILITY), Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:1424-1437 (PMID 25733246); Burmester GR et al. (MONARCH), Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:840-847 (PMID 27856432)

ra_abatacept.name: Abatacept (T-Cell Co-Stimulation Modulator) - AIM, ATTAIN, AGREE, AMPLE
ra_abatacept.type: Biologic DMARD, CTLA4-Ig fusion protein, intravenous or subcutaneous
ra_abatacept.effectiveness: AIM (652 MTX-resistant patients): ACR20/50/70 at 6 months 67.9%/39.9%/19.8% versus 39.7%/16.8%/6.5%; at 1 year 73.1%/48.3%/28.8% versus 39.7%/18.2%/6.1% (p<0.001); improvement in physical function 63.7% versus 39.3%; radiographic progression slowed; adverse events 87.3% versus 84.0%. ATTAIN (TNF-inadequate responders): ACR20 50.4% versus 19.5%, ACR50 20.3% versus 3.8%, ACR70 10.2% versus 1.5%; serious infections 2.3% in both groups. AGREE (early MTX-naive, poor-prognosis RA): remission 41.4% versus 23.3% at year 1 (p<0.001) and less radiographic progression (mean TS change 0.63 versus 1.06, p=0.040). AMPLE (646 patients, SC abatacept versus SC adalimumab, both with MTX): year-2 ACR20/50/70 59.7%/44.7%/31.1% versus 60.1%/46.6%/29.3%; serious infections 3.8% versus 5.8%; discontinuation for adverse events 3.8% versus 9.5%; injection-site reactions 4.1% versus 10.4%. In the ROC trial (300 anti-TNF-failure patients), a non-TNF-targeted biologic gave EULAR good/moderate response in 69% versus 52% with a second anti-TNF (OR 2.06).
ra_abatacept.reason_why: Abatacept binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells and blocks the CD28 co-stimulatory signal that fully activates T cells, acting earlier in the immune cascade than cytokine blockers.
ra_abatacept.important_caveat: AMPLE showed equivalent efficacy, not superiority; the ROC comparison is from a single French randomised trial of non-TNF biologics as a group. Indian availability and price were not verified.
ra_abatacept.real_working_solution: Abatacept is a well-tolerated biologic with equal efficacy to adalimumab in AMPLE and fewer serious infections/discontinuations; it is a strong choice after anti-TNF failure and in patients where infection risk is a concern.
ra_abatacept.source: Kremer JM et al. (AIM), Ann Intern Med 2006;144:865-876 (PMID 16785475); Kremer JM et al., 'Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis by selective inhibition of T-cell activation with fusion protein CTLA4Ig', N Engl J Med 2003;349:1907-1915 (PMID 14614165); Genovese MC et al. (ATTAIN), N Engl J Med 2005;353:1114-1123 (PMID 16162882); Westhovens R et al. (AGREE), Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:1870-1877 (PMID 19124524); Schiff M et al. (AMPLE), Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:86-94 (PMID 23962455); Gottenberg JE et al. (ROC), JAMA 2016;316:1172-1180 (PMID 27654603)

ra_rituximab.name: Rituximab (Anti-CD20 B-Cell Depletion) - Edwards 2004, REFLEX, IMAGE; Low-Dose Biosimilar Use
ra_rituximab.type: Biologic DMARD, chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, intravenous
specific_drugs: Rituximab 2 x 1000 mg + methotrexate (approved regimen per Cochrane)
Rituximab biosimilars Reditux (Dr Reddy's, India 2007), MabTas (Intas, 2013), RituxiRel (Reliance, 2015)
ra_rituximab.effectiveness: Edwards 2004 (rituximab+MTX or +cyclophosphamide versus MTX): ACR50 at week 24 was 43% and 41% versus 13% (p=0.005); ACR20 65-76% versus 38%. REFLEX (520 TNF-inadequate responders): ACR20 51% versus 18%, ACR50 27% versus 5%, ACR70 12% versus 1% (p<0.0001), EULAR response 65% versus 22%; serious infections 5.2 versus 3.7 per 100 patient-years. IMAGE (early MTX-naive): ACR50 65% (2x1000 mg + MTX) and 59% (2x500 mg + MTX) versus 42% with MTX alone at week 52; mTSS change 0.359 versus 1.079 (p=0.0004, 1000 mg dose only). Cochrane (8 studies, 2,720 patients): ACR50 at 24 weeks in 29% versus 9% (RR 3.3, NNT 6) and DAS28 remission at 52 weeks in 22% versus 11% (RR 2.4). A prospective single-centre real-world study (75 seropositive biologic-naive patients failing triple csDMARDs, biosimilar rituximab 500 mg x 2) reported DAS28-ESR remission of 50.7% at week 24 with all patients stopping corticosteroids.
ra_rituximab.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells, which contribute to autoantibody production and antigen presentation in seropositive RA.
ra_rituximab.important_caveat: The low-dose study is uncontrolled and single-centre (the country is not stated in the abstract); the 2 x 500 mg IMAGE arm did not significantly reduce radiographic progression. In REFLEX serious infections were 5.2 versus 3.7 per 100 patient-years, and most adverse events occurred with the first infusion.
ra_rituximab.real_working_solution: Rituximab is an established option after TNF failure and, as a biosimilar available in India since 2007, is a lower-cost biologic for seropositive patients; establish hepatitis B status before starting (EULAR 2022). Observational low-dose (500 mg x 2) data are encouraging but are not randomised evidence.
ra_rituximab.source: Edwards JCW et al., N Engl J Med 2004;350:2572-2581 (PMID 15201414); Cohen SB et al. (REFLEX), Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2793-2806 (PMID 16947627); Tak PP et al. (IMAGE), Ann Rheum Dis 2011;70:39-46 (PMID 20937671); Lopez-Olivo MA et al., 'Rituximab for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(1):CD007356 (PMID 25603545); Parrey A et al., 'Upfront low-dose biosimilar rituximab as first biologic therapy after triple csDMARD failure in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis', Clin Rheumatol 2026;45:4187-4196 (PMID 42287541); GaBI Online, 'Similar biologics approved and marketed in India' (https://www.gabionline.net/biosimilars/general/Similar-biologics-approved-and-marketed-in-India)

ra_jak_tofacitinib.name: Tofacitinib (JAK1/3 Inhibitor) - ORAL Standard, Solo, Step, Start, Strategy; Generic in India
ra_jak_tofacitinib.type: Targeted synthetic DMARD, oral Janus kinase inhibitor
specific_drugs: Tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily (10 mg twice daily was also studied)
ra_jak_tofacitinib.effectiveness: ORAL Standard: ACR20 at month 6 was 51.5% (5 mg) and 52.6% (10 mg) versus 47.2% with adalimumab and 28.3% with placebo. ORAL Solo (monotherapy): ACR20 at month 3 was 59.8% and 65.7% versus 26.7%; DAS28 <2.6 was not significantly different (5.6%, 8.7% versus 4.4%). ORAL Step (TNF-inadequate responders + MTX): ACR20 at month 3 41.7% (5 mg) and 48.1% (10 mg) versus 24.4%. ORAL Start (MTX-naive): ACR70 at month 6 25.5% and 37.7% versus 12.0% with MTX; mTSS change 0.2 and <0.1 versus 0.8; herpes zoster 4.0% (31/770) versus 1.1% (2/186). ORAL Strategy (1,146 patients): ACR50 at month 6 38% (tofacitinib alone), 46% (tofacitinib + MTX) and 44% (adalimumab + MTX); tofacitinib + MTX was non-inferior to adalimumab + MTX (difference 2%, 98.34% CI -6 to 11) but tofacitinib alone was not. Indian real-world single-centre report of generic tofacitinib (102 patients, mean RA duration 146 months): significant improvement in disease activity, no serious adverse events, 4 patients developed tuberculosis, and clinical failure occurred in 25.
ra_jak_tofacitinib.reason_why: Tofacitinib inhibits Janus kinases, blocking signalling of multiple cytokines (interferon, several interleukins) inside the cell instead of neutralising one cytokine outside it.
ra_jak_tofacitinib.important_caveat: ORAL Solo did not show a significant DAS28 <2.6 advantage; herpes zoster and TB (2 pulmonary TB cases at 10 mg in ORAL Standard) are recognised risks. The Indian data are a retrospective single-centre analysis.
ra_jak_tofacitinib.real_working_solution: Tofacitinib is an oral option with efficacy similar to adalimumab (in combination with methotrexate) but, after ORAL Surveillance, its use is restricted by regulators (see the JAK safety entry): the FDA limits use to patients who failed or cannot take a TNF blocker, and the EMA advises use in patients aged 65+, smokers, and those at cardiovascular or cancer risk only if no suitable alternative exists; screen for TB first.
ra_jak_tofacitinib.source: van Vollenhoven RF et al. (ORAL Standard), N Engl J Med 2012;367:508-519 (PMID 22873531); Fleischmann R et al. (ORAL Solo), N Engl J Med 2012;367:495-507 (PMID 22873530); Burmester GR et al. (ORAL Step), Lancet 2013;381:451-460 (PMID 23294500); Lee EB et al. (ORAL Start), N Engl J Med 2014;370:2377-2386 (PMID 24941177); Fleischmann R et al. (ORAL Strategy), Lancet 2017;390:457-468 (PMID 28629665); Phatak S et al., 'Real-world evidence of the effectiveness and safety of generic tofacitinib in rheumatoid arthritis patients: a retrospective, single-centre analysis from Western India', Clin Rheumatol 2022;41:2961-2966 (PMID 35596818)

ra_jak_baricitinib.name: Baricitinib (JAK1/2 Inhibitor) - RA-BEAM, RA-BEGIN, RA-BEACON, RA-BUILD
ra_jak_baricitinib.type: Targeted synthetic DMARD, oral Janus kinase inhibitor
specific_drugs: Baricitinib 4 mg once daily (2 mg also studied)
Olumiant (baricitinib, Eli Lilly India, launched October 2018 in 2 mg and 4 mg)
ra_jak_baricitinib.effectiveness: RA-BEAM (MTX-inadequate responders): ACR20 at week 12 70% versus 40% placebo (p<0.001) and versus 61% with adalimumab (p=0.014); mTSS change 0.41 versus 0.90; cancers 2 (baricitinib) versus 3 (placebo). RA-BEGIN (MTX-naive, 24 weeks): baricitinib monotherapy ACR20 77% versus 62% with MTX (p<=0.01). RA-BEACON (TNF-inadequate responders): ACR20 at week 12 55% (4 mg) versus 27% (p<0.001); serious adverse events in 4%, 10% and 7% across the three groups (the abstract does not state which figure belongs to placebo, 2 mg or 4 mg); two nonmelanoma skin cancers and two major adverse cardiovascular events (including a fatal stroke) occurred in the 4 mg group. RA-BUILD (csDMARD-inadequate responders): ACR20 62% versus 39% (p<=0.001) and small reductions in neutrophils with increases in LDL and HDL cholesterol.
ra_jak_baricitinib.reason_why: Baricitinib inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, blocking intracellular cytokine signalling including interferon, IL-6 family and GM-CSF pathways.
ra_jak_baricitinib.important_caveat: In RA-BEACON the 4 mg arm had two MACE (one fatal stroke) and two nonmelanoma skin cancers in a 24-week trial; ORAL Surveillance shows the long-term signal for the class member tofacitinib.
ra_jak_baricitinib.real_working_solution: Baricitinib is an oral option superior to adalimumab on ACR20 in RA-BEAM; apply the same risk-based restriction as other JAK inhibitors (see the JAK safety entry) and confirm TB/HBV screening.
ra_jak_baricitinib.source: Taylor PC et al. (RA-BEAM), N Engl J Med 2017;376:652-662 (PMID 28199814); Fleischmann R et al. (RA-BEGIN), Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:506-517 (PMID 27723271); Genovese MC et al. (RA-BEACON), N Engl J Med 2016;374:1243-1252 (PMID 27028914); Dougados M et al. (RA-BUILD), Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:88-95 (PMID 27689735); Lilly India launch of Olumiant (baricitinib), October 2018, BioSpectrum Asia (https://biospectrumasia.com/news/49/11862/lilly-india-enters-the-autoimmune-segment-with-olumiant.html)

ra_jak_upadacitinib.name: Upadacitinib (Selective JAK1 Inhibitor) - SELECT-COMPARE, SELECT-EARLY, SELECT-NEXT, SELECT-BEYOND
ra_jak_upadacitinib.type: Targeted synthetic DMARD, oral selective JAK1 inhibitor
specific_drugs: Upadacitinib 15 mg once daily (30 mg also studied)
ra_jak_upadacitinib.effectiveness: SELECT-COMPARE (1,629 MTX-inadequate responders): ACR20 at week 12 71% versus 36% placebo; DAS28-CRP <2.6 in 29% versus 6%; superior to adalimumab on ACR50, DAS28-CRP <=3.2, pain and HAQ-DI; radiographic progression inhibited; herpes zoster and CPK elevations highest with upadacitinib; 3 malignancies, 5 MACE and 4 deaths in the trial occurred in none of the upadacitinib patients. SELECT-EARLY (MTX-naive): ACR50 at week 12 was 52% (15 mg) and 56% (30 mg) versus 28% for MTX; DAS28-CRP <2.6 at week 24 in 48% and 50% versus 19%; no radiographic progression in 88% and 89% versus 78%. SELECT-NEXT (661 csDMARD-inadequate responders): ACR20 at week 12 64% (15 mg) and 66% (30 mg) versus 36%; DAS28-CRP <=3.2 in 48% versus 17%. SELECT-BEYOND (499 patients refractory to biologics): ACR20 65% (15 mg) and 56% (30 mg) versus 28%; DAS28-CRP <=3.2 in 43%, 42% versus 14%; more adverse events with 30 mg.
ra_jak_upadacitinib.reason_why: Upadacitinib preferentially inhibits JAK1, the kinase shared by IL-6, interferon and gamma-chain cytokine receptors.
ra_jak_upadacitinib.important_caveat: Zoster and CPK elevation were higher than with adalimumab; the SELECT trials are short (12-26 weeks for the cited endpoints) and were not powered for the cardiovascular/cancer signal seen with tofacitinib in ORAL Surveillance; the FDA extended the class boxed warning to upadacitinib.
ra_jak_upadacitinib.real_working_solution: Upadacitinib was superior to adalimumab on several endpoints in SELECT-COMPARE and effective in biologic-refractory RA (SELECT-BEYOND), and can be used after careful risk assessment per EULAR/regulators; commercial availability in India was not verified in the sources searched.
ra_jak_upadacitinib.source: Fleischmann R et al. (SELECT-COMPARE), Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:1788-1800 (PMID 31287230); van Vollenhoven R et al. (SELECT-EARLY), Arthritis Rheumatol 2020;72:1607-1620 (PMID 32638504); Burmester GR et al. (SELECT-NEXT), Lancet 2018;391:2503-2512 (PMID 29908669); Genovese MC et al. (SELECT-BEYOND), Lancet 2018;391:2513-2524 (PMID 29908670)

ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.name: JAK-Inhibitor Class Safety - ORAL Surveillance, FDA Boxed Warning (2021) and EMA Restrictions (2022)
ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.type: Drug-safety evidence and regulatory risk-management framework
specific_drugs: Filgotinib (in the EULAR list; India availability not verified)
ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.effectiveness: ORAL Surveillance (randomised safety trial, 4,362 RA patients; tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily n=1,455, 10 mg twice daily n=1,456, TNF inhibitor n=1,451; median follow-up 4.0 years): major adverse cardiovascular events 3.4% (98 patients) versus 2.5% (37), HR 1.33 (95% CI 0.91-1.94); cancers 4.2% (122) versus 2.9% (42), HR 1.48 (95% CI 1.04-2.09); non-inferiority of tofacitinib was not shown; opportunistic infections (including zoster and TB), all herpes zoster and nonmelanoma skin cancer were higher with tofacitinib; efficacy was similar in all arms. The EULAR safety review noted venous thromboembolism was higher with tofacitinib 10 mg than with TNF inhibitors, herpes zoster was more common with JAK inhibitors than with csDMARDs (adjusted HR 3.66) and bDMARDs (adjusted HR 1.9-2.3), while observational data showed malignancy and MACE risks similar between tofacitinib and bDMARDs (few studies). Regulators: on 1 September 2021 the FDA required boxed warnings on tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib for serious heart-related events, cancer, blood clots and death, and limited all approved uses to patients who have not responded to or cannot tolerate one or more TNF blockers. On 28 October 2022 the EMA safety committee recommended that JAK inhibitors be used in patients aged 65+, those at increased cardiovascular risk, current/long-term former smokers, and those at increased cancer risk only if no suitable alternatives exist, with caution in patients with risk factors for blood clots in the lungs and deep veins, and with dose reductions for patients at elevated risk of blood clots, cancer or serious cardiovascular events.
ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.reason_why: JAK inhibition suppresses signalling of many cytokines at once, which explains both high efficacy and the additional risks of viral reactivation (zoster), thrombosis, lipid change and possibly malignancy.
ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.important_caveat: ORAL Surveillance tested tofacitinib only; the FDA extended the boxed warning to baricitinib and upadacitinib without a head-to-head safety trial of those drugs (direct comparative safety trials have not been conducted for them). ORAL Surveillance enrolled patients with cardiovascular risk factors (per the EULAR safety review), so absolute risks in low-risk patients may differ.
ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.real_working_solution: Position JAK inhibitors after methotrexate failure and, per EULAR 2022/2025, only after careful consideration of MACE, malignancy and thromboembolism risks; prefer a biologic first in patients over 65, smokers, and those with prior cardiovascular events or cancer; use the lowest effective dose; screen for TB/HBV and offer herpes zoster vaccination.
ra_jak_oral_surveillance_safety_signal_a.source: Ytterberg SR et al. (ORAL Surveillance), 'Cardiovascular and cancer risk with tofacitinib in rheumatoid arthritis', N Engl J Med 2022;386:316-326 (PMID 35081280); Sepriano A et al., 'Safety of synthetic and biological DMARDs: a systematic literature review informing the 2022 update of the EULAR recommendations for RA', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:107-118 (PMID 36376026); US FDA Drug Safety Communication, 1 September 2021, 'FDA requires warnings about increased risk of serious heart-related events, cancer, blood clots, and death for JAK inhibitors that treat certain chronic inflammatory conditions' (https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-requires-warnings-about-increased-risk-serious-heart-related-events-cancer-blood-clots-and-death); European Medicines Agency, 'EMA recommends measures to minimise risk of serious side effects with Janus kinase inhibitors for chronic inflammatory disorders', 28 October 2022 (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/news/ema-recommends-measures-minimise-risk-serious-side-effects-janus-kinase-inhibitors-chronic-inflammatory-disorders); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biological DMARDs: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18 (PMID 36357155); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic DMARDs: 2025 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2026;85:991-1009 (PMID 41826212)

ra_difficult_to_treat_and_switching_stra.name: Difficult-to-Treat RA (EULAR Definition) and Choosing the Next Drug After Failure (ROC Trial, EULAR)
specific_drugs: Abatacept, tocilizumab or rituximab after a first anti-TNF failure
A second TNF inhibitor (adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab, infliximab)
JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) after risk review
ra_difficult_to_treat_and_switching_stra.effectiveness: EULAR definition of difficult-to-treat RA requires (1) treatment per EULAR recommendations and failure of >=2 biologic/targeted synthetic DMARDs with different mechanisms of action after failing conventional therapy, (2) at least one of: moderate disease activity, signs/symptoms of active disease, inability to taper glucocorticoids, rapid radiographic progression, or symptoms reducing quality of life, and (3) management perceived as problematic by rheumatologist or patient. In the ROC randomised trial (300 patients with insufficient response to a first anti-TNF), a non-TNF-targeted biologic gave a good or moderate EULAR response at week 24 in 101/146 (69%) versus 76 (52%) with a second anti-TNF (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.27-3.37, p=0.004); low disease activity 45% versus 28% at week 24 and 41% versus 23% at week 52. EULAR 2022/2025: if the first biologic or targeted DMARD fails, any other bDMARD (same or other class) or JAK inhibitor (considering risks) is recommended. Upadacitinib in SELECT-BEYOND gave ACR20 65% versus 28% in biologic-refractory RA.
ra_difficult_to_treat_and_switching_stra.reason_why: After a TNF-inhibitor failure a different pathway (T-cell co-stimulation, IL-6, B cells or JAK signalling) is often driving disease, so switching mechanism of action tends to outperform cycling within the class.
ra_difficult_to_treat_and_switching_stra.important_caveat: ROC compared a group of non-TNF biologics against a second anti-TNF; it does not rank individual non-TNF drugs against each other.
ra_difficult_to_treat_and_switching_stra.real_working_solution: Apply the EULAR criteria before labelling a patient difficult-to-treat (failure of at least two b/tsDMARDs of different mechanisms with problematic management), then switch to a different mechanism of action (abatacept, tocilizumab, rituximab, or a JAK inhibitor after risk review) rather than repeating a TNF inhibitor.
ra_difficult_to_treat_and_switching_stra.source: Nagy G et al., 'EULAR definition of difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:31-35 (PMID 33004335); Gottenberg JE et al. (ROC), JAMA 2016;316:1172-1180 (PMID 27654603); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biological DMARDs: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18 (PMID 36357155); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic DMARDs: 2025 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2026;85:991-1009 (PMID 41826212); Genovese MC et al. (SELECT-BEYOND), Lancet 2018;391:2513-2524 (PMID 29908670)

ra_nsaids_coxibs_symptomatic_only.name: NSAIDs and Coxibs - Symptom Relief Only (Not DMARDs); Cardiovascular and GI Risk Data
specific_drugs: Celecoxib or etoricoxib (coxibs) with a proton-pump inhibitor where risk factors exist
ra_nsaids_coxibs_symptomatic_only.effectiveness: The trials of DMARDs, biologics and JAK inhibitors in this survey measure disease control; none of the NSAID evidence found here shows disease-modifying effect. Cochrane review (4 crossover trials, 121 patients, 1968-1982): NSAIDs were preferred to paracetamol (20/54 patients preferred ibuprofen versus 7/54 paracetamol) but the trials were weak and no firm conclusion could be drawn. Individual-participant meta-analysis of NSAID trials (CNT Collaboration): major vascular events rate ratio 1.37 for coxibs and 1.41 for diclofenac; naproxen 0.93 (not significant); major coronary events increased with coxibs (RR 1.76), diclofenac (1.70) and ibuprofen (2.22); heart failure risk roughly doubled by all NSAIDs; upper GI complications increased with coxibs (RR 1.81), diclofenac (1.89), ibuprofen (3.97) and naproxen (4.22); of 1,000 patients on a coxib or diclofenac for a year, three more had major vascular events (one fatal). EULAR glucocorticoid recommendations address concomitant NSAID use, gastroprotection and COX-2 selective inhibitors.
ra_nsaids_coxibs_symptomatic_only.reason_why: NSAIDs and coxibs block cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin production, reducing pain and swelling but not the immune process that erodes joints.
ra_nsaids_coxibs_symptomatic_only.important_caveat: The CNT meta-analysis pooled NSAID trials in mixed conditions (not RA-specific). The Cochrane RA review of paracetamol versus NSAIDs used old, methodologically weak crossover trials.
ra_nsaids_coxibs_symptomatic_only.real_working_solution: Use an NSAID/coxib only as the lowest effective dose for the shortest time as a bridge while the DMARD takes effect, choose the agent by cardiovascular and GI risk (naproxen had no significant vascular increase in the CNT analysis but the highest GI complication ratio), add gastroprotection where indicated, and avoid using them as a substitute for a DMARD.
ra_nsaids_coxibs_symptomatic_only.source: Coxib and traditional NSAID Trialists' (CNT) Collaboration, Bhala N et al., Lancet 2013;382:769-779 (PMID 23726390); Wienecke T, Gøtzsche PC, 'Paracetamol versus nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004;(1):CD003789 (PMID 14974037); Hoes JN et al., 'EULAR evidence-based recommendations on the management of systemic glucocorticoid therapy in rheumatic diseases', Ann Rheum Dis 2007;66:1560-1567 (PMID 17660219)

ra_biosimilars_and_india_availability_co.name: Biosimilars and Honest India Availability/Cost (Adalimumab, Etanercept, Infliximab, Rituximab, Generic Tofacitinib, Baricitinib)
specific_drugs: Adalimumab biosimilars Exemptia (Zydus Cadila, 2014) and Adfrar (Torrent, 2016)
Infliximab biosimilar Infimab (2014 listing), rituximab biosimilars Reditux (Dr Reddy's, 2007), MabTas (Intas, 2013), RituxiRel (Reliance, 2015)
Generic tofacitinib; Olumiant (baricitinib, Eli Lilly India, October 2018)
ra_biosimilars_and_india_availability_co.effectiveness: GaBI's listing of similar biologics approved and marketed in India includes adalimumab (Exemptia 2014, Adfrar 2016), etanercept (Etacept 2013, Intacept 2015), infliximab (Infimab 2014) and rituximab (Reditux 2007, MabTas 2013, RituxiRel 2015); tocilizumab and abatacept were not in that listing. Exemptia was launched in December 2014 at about 20% of the price paid for Humira in the United States. In the Indian ASPIRE registry (149 patients, 73 analysable at 24 weeks) the adalimumab biosimilar gave ACR20/50/70 of 48%/48%/34% (as reported) with no new safety signals. NOR-SWITCH (482 patients, 77 with RA) showed disease worsening in 26% (originator infliximab) versus 30% (CT-P13 biosimilar), adjusted difference -4.4% (95% CI -12.7 to 3.9), and similar adverse events. Generic tofacitinib had been available in India for over a year by 2022 and was widely used; in a 102-patient Mumbai series disease activity improved significantly at mean 186 days and no serious adverse events occurred. Olumiant (baricitinib) was launched in India in October 2018 (2 mg and 4 mg).
ra_biosimilars_and_india_availability_co.reason_why: A biosimilar is a highly similar version of an originator biologic; equivalent efficacy is shown by comparative trials, and lower price widens access.
ra_biosimilars_and_india_availability_co.important_caveat: Cost-effectiveness and rupee prices were not independently verified; the ASPIRE data are an uncontrolled registry; commercial availability of upadacitinib and of a tocilizumab biosimilar in India could not be confirmed from the sources searched and is left unverified.
ra_biosimilars_and_india_availability_co.real_working_solution: In India, the practical ladder is: generic csDMARDs (methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) and triple therapy first; then an approved Indian biosimilar TNF inhibitor or rituximab, or generic tofacitinib after risk review, where insurance or access allows. Exact rupee prices for these products were not verified in the sources searched and should be confirmed locally.
ra_biosimilars_and_india_availability_co.source: GaBI Online, 'Similar biologics approved and marketed in India' (https://www.gabionline.net/biosimilars/general/Similar-biologics-approved-and-marketed-in-India); Rheumatology Live, 'Adalimumab biosimilar launched for 1/5 Humira price (in India)', 10 December 2014 (https://www.rheum-live.com/view/adalimumab-biosimilar-launched-15-humira-price-india); Kapoor S et al. (ASPIRE registry), Rheumatol Ther 2019;6:451-459 (PMID 31254222); Jørgensen KK et al. (NOR-SWITCH), Lancet 2017;389:2304-2316 (PMID 28502609); Phatak S et al., 'Real-world evidence of the effectiveness and safety of generic tofacitinib in rheumatoid arthritis patients: a retrospective, single-centre analysis from Western India', Clin Rheumatol 2022;41:2961-2966 (PMID 35596818); Lilly India launch of Olumiant (baricitinib), October 2018, BioSpectrum Asia (https://biospectrumasia.com/news/49/11862/lilly-india-enters-the-autoimmune-segment-with-olumiant.html)

ra_drug_free_remission_and_tapering.name: Sustained Remission, Tapering and Drug-Free Remission (PRESERVE, Cochrane TNFi Tapering, ACT-RAY, Leiden/ERAS Cohorts)
specific_drugs: Etanercept (full dose, half dose or stopped after remission - PRESERVE)
Methotrexate (backbone kept in most tapering studies)
ra_drug_free_remission_and_tapering.effectiveness: PRESERVE (834 patients with moderate RA entered open-label etanercept 50 mg + MTX; 604 eligible patients were randomised double-blind): at week 88 low disease activity in 166/201 (82.6%) with continued 50 mg etanercept + MTX, 159/201 (79.1%) with 25 mg etanercept + MTX, versus 84/197 (42.6%) after withdrawal of etanercept to placebo + MTX (differences 40.8% and 35.9%). Cochrane 2019 (14 studies, 3,315 participants): anti-TNF dose reduction made little or no difference to DAS28 (MD 0.06, high-certainty), discontinuation raised DAS28 (MD 0.96) with persistent remission RR 0.16-0.77 and more radiographic progression (RR 1.69), while disease-activity-guided tapering kept persistent remission (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.75-1.06). ACT-RAY: of patients who stopped tocilizumab after sustained remission 84.0% flared but responded when it was restarted; 5.9% reached drug-free remission. Sustained DMARD-free remission (drug-free and remission for a sustained period) was achieved in 15.0% (68/454, Leiden EAC) and 9.4% (84/895, ERAS) of early-arthritis cohort patients, predicted by acute onset, short symptom duration, non-smoking, little baseline radiographic damage and absence of IgM-RF and shared-epitope alleles; in a longitudinal inception cohort the adjusted HR for sustained DMARD-free remission rose from 1.13 (1996-98) to 3.72 (early MTX plus DAS-steered therapy, 2005-2011), with the HAQ at general-population level at remission. In a 2025 two-cohort analysis 37% (5 years, Leiden EAC) and 15% (3 years, tREACH) of patients who never used a biologic achieved sustained DMARD-free remission, while none of those who used a biologic did (this comparison is confounded by disease severity). In routine-care BRASS data <50% of patients in remission were still in remission 1 year later (median remission survival 1 year). EULAR 2022: with sustained remission DMARDs may be tapered but should not be stopped; EULAR 2025: caution is required as stopping often leads to flare.
ra_drug_free_remission_and_tapering.reason_why: Long-standing remission may permit lower drug exposure, but the underlying autoimmunity persists; withdrawing the drug removes the control that produced remission, so flares are common.
