ra_drug_free_remission_and_tapering.important_caveat: Cohort DFR rates come from historic early-arthritis cohorts and depend on the remission definition; PRESERVE and Cochrane data are mainly for etanercept and adalimumab; the 'no biologic-treated patient reached DFR' finding reflects who needs biologics rather than a proven biologic effect.
ra_drug_free_remission_and_tapering.real_working_solution: Once in sustained remission (and after glucocorticoids are off) taper stepwise: reduce the biologic/JAK dose or lengthen the interval first while keeping methotrexate, monitor disease activity closely, and re-escalate immediately at flare; drug-free remission is real but occurs in a minority (about 10-15% in early-arthritis cohorts) and is most likely in patients with acute onset, short symptom duration, non-smokers and seronegative disease.
ra_drug_free_remission_and_tapering.source: Smolen JS et al. (PRESERVE), Lancet 2013;381:918-929 (PMID 23332236); Verhoef LM et al., 'Down-titration and discontinuation strategies of tumour necrosis factor-blocking agents for rheumatoid arthritis in patients with low disease activity', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;(5):CD010455 (PMID 31125448); Huizinga TW et al. (ACT-RAY 2-year), Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:35-43 (PMID 25169728); van der Woude D et al., 'Prevalence of and predictive factors for sustained disease-modifying antirheumatic drug-free remission in rheumatoid arthritis', Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:2262-2271 (PMID 19644846); Ajeganova S et al., 'Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug-free sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis: an increasingly achievable outcome with subsidence of disease symptoms', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:867-873 (PMID 25972519); Heutz JW et al., 'Sustained DMARD-free remission in subgroups of patients with rheumatoid arthritis: an analysis of two prospective cohorts', Lancet Rheumatol 2025;7:e252-e260 (PMID 39718182); Prince FHM et al., 'Sustained rheumatoid arthritis remission is uncommon in clinical practice', Arthritis Res Ther 2012;14:R68 (PMID 22429277); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biological DMARDs: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18 (PMID 36357155); Smolen JS et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic DMARDs: 2025 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2026;85:991-1009 (PMID 41826212)

ra_nondrug_exercise_and_physiotherapy.name: Exercise and Physiotherapy - Aerobic, Strength and Fatigue-Directed Activity (Cochrane and Meta-Analyses)
ra_nondrug_exercise_and_physiotherapy.effectiveness: Cochrane (8 studies, dynamic exercise): short-term land-based aerobic training pooled effect size 0.99 (95% CI 0.29-1.68) on aerobic capacity (moderate evidence); aerobic plus strength training improved aerobic capacity and muscle strength (effect size 0.47, 95% CI 0.01-0.93); no deleterious effects in any included study. Meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (1,040 patients): aerobic exercise improved quality of life (SMD 0.39, p<0.0001), HAQ (SMD 0.24) and pain VAS (SMD 0.31) with DAS28 and joint counts unchanged between groups, i.e. safe. Cochrane on fatigue (24 studies, 2,882 patients): physical activity reduced fatigue (SMD -0.36, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.10; 14.4 points lower on a 100-point scale; NNTB 7, 95% CI 4-26).
ra_nondrug_exercise_and_physiotherapy.reason_why: Exercise improves aerobic capacity and muscle strength (Cochrane) and did not worsen disease activity or joint counts in the meta-analysis.
ra_nondrug_exercise_and_physiotherapy.important_caveat: Older Cochrane exercise review (search 2009) with small studies; effect on fatigue is small (NNTB 7); exercise complements but does not replace DMARD therapy.
ra_nondrug_exercise_and_physiotherapy.real_working_solution: Prescribe supervised exercise (aerobic and muscle strengthening) for every patient with RA in stable or controlled disease, with physiotherapy input for joint-specific problems and gradual progression during flares; it is safe and improves function, pain, quality of life and fatigue.
ra_nondrug_exercise_and_physiotherapy.source: Hurkmans E et al., 'Dynamic exercise programs (aerobic capacity and/or muscle strength training) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(4):CD006853 (PMID 19821388); Baillet A et al., 'Efficacy of cardiorespiratory aerobic exercise in rheumatoid arthritis: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials', Arthritis Care Res 2010;62:984-992 (PMID 20589690); Cramp F et al., 'Non-pharmacological interventions for fatigue in rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(8):CD008322 (PMID 23975674)

ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.name: Occupational Therapy, Joint Protection and Tailored Hand Exercises (Cochrane, SARAH Trial)
ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.type: Non-drug: occupational therapy / hand rehabilitation / splinting
ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.effectiveness: Cochrane (38 occupational therapy studies): strong evidence for instruction on joint protection (absolute benefit 17.5-22.5, relative benefit 100%), limited evidence for comprehensive occupational therapy improving function (absolute benefit 8.7, relative benefit 20%), and indicative evidence that provision of splints decreases pain (absolute benefit 1.0, relative benefit 19%). SARAH (490 participants, 12-month follow-up): overall hand function improved 7.9 points with tailored exercises versus 3.6 with usual care (mean difference 4.3, 95% CI 1.5-7.1, p=0.0028); no serious adverse events; cost per person GBP 156 and cost per QALY GBP 9,549 (EQ-5D).
ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.reason_why: Joint protection and hand exercises reduce mechanical load on inflamed joints and maintain grip and dexterity, which drug therapy alone does not restore once structural change has occurred.
ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.important_caveat: The Cochrane OT review's 'relative benefit' figures come from a 2004 synthesis of small trials with heterogeneous outcomes; SARAH is a single UK trial (pain, drug use and healthcare use were unchanged).
ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.real_working_solution: Refer every patient with hand involvement to occupational therapy for joint-protection education, a home hand-exercise programme and splints where needed; this is inexpensive and safe.
ra_nondrug_occupational_therapy_and_hand.source: Steultjens EMJ et al., 'Occupational therapy for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004;(1):CD003114 (PMID 14974005); Lamb SE et al. (SARAH), 'Exercises to improve function of the rheumatoid hand', Lancet 2015;385:421-429 (PMID 25308290)

ra_nondrug_patient_education_and_self_ma.name: Patient Education and Psychosocial/Self-Management Programmes (Cochrane)
specific_drugs: Shared decision-making counselling on target and drug options
ra_nondrug_patient_education_and_self_ma.effectiveness: Cochrane patient-education review (31 studies): significant effects at first follow-up on disability, joint counts, patient global assessment, psychological status and depression, with a trend favouring education for pain; no significant effects on anxiety or disease activity; at final follow-up no significant effects remained, with a trend towards benefit for disability. Cochrane fatigue review: psychosocial interventions reduced fatigue (SMD -0.24, 95% CI -0.40 to -0.07; 9.6 points lower on a 100-point scale; NNTB 10, 95% CI 6-33).
ra_nondrug_patient_education_and_self_ma.reason_why: Understanding the disease, drug timing and monitoring plans improves adherence to DMARDs and coping with chronic pain, fatigue and mood, which are outcomes not fully captured by joint counts.
ra_nondrug_patient_education_and_self_ma.important_caveat: Effects of education faded by final follow-up in the Cochrane review; the trials are heterogeneous.
ra_nondrug_patient_education_and_self_ma.real_working_solution: Give every patient structured education about early DMARD use, monitoring visits and flare plans, and refer to psychosocial/self-management programmes for fatigue and mood; expect short-term rather than durable effects and repeat education over time.
ra_nondrug_patient_education_and_self_ma.source: Riemsma RP et al., 'Patient education for adults with rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2003;(2):CD003688 (PMID 12804484); Cramp F et al., 'Non-pharmacological interventions for fatigue in rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(8):CD008322 (PMID 23975674); Smolen JS et al., 'Treating rheumatoid arthritis to target: 2014 update of the recommendations of an international task force', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:3-15 (PMID 25969430)

ra_nondrug_lifestyle_smoking_weight_diet.name: Lifestyle: Smoking, Body Weight and Diet - Real Predictors and Honest Diet Evidence
specific_drugs: Smoking-cessation support (behavioural counselling, nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline)
ra_nondrug_lifestyle_smoking_weight_diet.effectiveness: In SWEFOT, current smoking was an independent predictor of 1-year radiographic progression (adjusted OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.06-4.45) after adjusting for treatment strategy. In the same trial obesity predicted non-remission at 24 months (adjusted OR 5.2, 95% CI 1.8-15.2) and smoking also predicted non-remission (aOR 2.6, 95% CI 1.1-6.3). Cochrane dietary review (14 RCTs and 1 CCT, 837 patients): no overall effect could be calculated; single trials of fasting followed by a vegetarian diet (pain MD -1.89 on a 0-10 scale) and a 12-week Cretan Mediterranean diet (pain MD -14.00 on a 0-100 scale) reduced pain but not function or morning stiffness; dropout was 10% higher and weight loss 3.23 kg greater in diet groups.
ra_nondrug_lifestyle_smoking_weight_diet.reason_why: In the SWEFOT cohort, smoking predicted radiographic progression and obesity and smoking predicted non-remission; whether stopping smoking or losing weight reverses this was not tested in these trials.
ra_nondrug_lifestyle_smoking_weight_diet.important_caveat: The smoking and obesity data are predictive associations from trial cohorts, not proof that stopping smoking or losing weight reverses disease; the diet trials are small single-trial results.
ra_nondrug_lifestyle_smoking_weight_diet.real_working_solution: Advise smoking cessation and weight management as part of every RA plan because both predict worse outcomes; offer a Mediterranean-style diet as a low-risk supportive measure while being honest that dietary evidence is limited and does not replace DMARDs.
ra_nondrug_lifestyle_smoking_weight_diet.source: Saevarsdottir S et al. (SWEFOT smoking analysis), Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1509-1514 (PMID 24706006); Levitsky A et al. (SWEFOT obesity analysis), RMD Open 2017;3:e000458 (PMID 28879052); Hagen KB et al., 'Dietary interventions for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(1):CD006400 (PMID 19160281)

ra_surgery_synovectomy_joint_replacement.name: Surgery: Synovectomy, Radiosynovectomy, Joint Replacement and Atlantoaxial/Cervical Spine Fusion
specific_drugs: Total knee arthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty
C1-C2 fusion, occipitocervical fusion and subaxial instrumentation for rheumatoid cervical instability
ra_surgery_synovectomy_joint_replacement.effectiveness: Surgical rates: in California RA patients aged 40-59, knee surgery rates in 2003-2007 were 19% lower (adjusted rate ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.74-0.87) and hip surgery rates 40% lower than in 1983-1987, but did not fall in patients aged >=60. In two UK inception cohorts 29% of patients (770) had orthopaedic surgery over up to 25 years, 25-year cumulative incidence of major interventions was 21.7%, and the decline was in hand/foot procedures not large-joint replacement. Synovectomy at the time of TKA in RA (retrospective series): worse Knee Society score (80.2 versus 89.1, p=0.02), lower flexion (102 versus 130 degrees), more transfusions (23.3% versus 16.6%), longer stay, and 15-year survivorship 81% versus 95% without synovectomy - i.e. synovectomy at arthroplasty was not beneficial. P-32 radiation synovectomy in 31 patients with resistant knee monoarthritis (uncontrolled): pain, effusion and range of motion improved through 6 months, no serious infection or necrosis, but 51.6% and 54.8% had pain/swelling at the injection site and 19.4% and 16.1% worsened in week 1. Cervical spine: a systematic review (no RCTs; 25 observational studies) found neurological deterioration rare in Ranawat I-II patients after surgery, Ranawat III patients did not fully recover, 10-year survival was 77%, 63%, 47% and 30% for Ranawat I, II, IIIA, IIIB after surgery, and among 185 conservatively managed patients deterioration was almost inevitable in Ranawat II-III with 10-year survival 40%; a 2026 review states C1-C2 fusion, occipitocervical fusion and subaxial instrumentation generally yield pain relief, neurologic improvement and durable fusion but carry meaningful perioperative risk, and modern DMARD/biologic regimens reduce but do not abolish cervical progression. The 2017 ACR/AAHKS guideline gives 7 conditional recommendations on continuing or withholding DMARDs, biologics and tofacitinib and dosing glucocorticoids around elective THA/TKA.
ra_surgery_synovectomy_joint_replacement.reason_why: Once cartilage and bone destruction is established, drugs cannot restore the joint; replacement removes the damaged surfaces, and fusion stabilises unstable cervical segments that threaten the spinal cord.
ra_surgery_synovectomy_joint_replacement.important_caveat: There are no randomised trials for cervical-spine surgery in RA and all included studies were at high risk of bias; the synovectomy-at-TKA data are retrospective; the phosphorus-32 study is uncontrolled. No randomised or systematic-review evidence for isolated surgical synovectomy was found in the sources searched (unverified); surgical need in India was not quantified.
ra_surgery_synovectomy_joint_replacement.real_working_solution: Refer early for surgical opinion when a joint is structurally destroyed with pain and disability despite good disease control, and refer urgently for cervical instability or myelopathy given the poor outcome of Ranawat III disease; coordinate holding and restarting DMARDs/biologics around arthroplasty per the ACR/AAHKS guidance.
ra_surgery_synovectomy_joint_replacement.source: Louie GH, Ward MM, Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:868-871 (PMID 19581279); Nikiphorou E et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2014;66:1081-1089 (PMID 24782174); Hernigou P et al., 'Is synovectomy still of benefit today in total knee arthroplasty with rheumatoid arthritis?', Int Orthop 2025;49:641-646 (PMID 39932578); Zayeni H et al., 'The effect of radiation synovectomy with phosphorus-32 on the pain and swelling in 31 RA patients with resistant monoarthritis of the knee', Clin Rheumatol 2024;43:2791-2798 (PMID 38995432); Wolfs JFC et al., 'Neurologic outcome of surgical and conservative treatment of rheumatoid cervical spine subluxation: a systematic review', Arthritis Rheum 2009;61:1743-1752 (PMID 19950322); Song J et al., 'Rheumatoid arthritis in the cervical spine: an updated review', Spine Surg Relat Res 2026;10:331-342 (PMID 42292559); Goodman SM et al., '2017 ACR/AAHKS Guideline for the Perioperative Management of Antirheumatic Medication in Patients With Rheumatic Diseases Undergoing Elective Total Hip or Total Knee Arthroplasty', Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:1538-1551 (PMID 28620948)

ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.name: Pre-Treatment Safety Screening: Tuberculosis, Hepatitis B/C, Vaccinations, Baseline Monitoring (EULAR 2022 Infection and 2019 Vaccination Recommendations, India-Specific Algorithms)
ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.type: Screening and prophylaxis protocol (tests and vaccines)
specific_drugs: Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA, e.g. QuantiFERON-TB) or tuberculin skin test plus chest X-ray
Hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-HBc, hepatitis C RNA
Isoniazid (or isoniazid with rifampicin) for latent TB treatment
Influenza, pneumococcal, tetanus, hepatitis A/B and herpes zoster vaccines as indicated
ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.effectiveness: EULAR 2022 infection recommendations (4 overarching principles, 8 recommendations): latent TB screening should be performed before biologic/targeted synthetic DMARDs and could be considered before csDMARDs, glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants; IGRA is preferred over tuberculin skin test where available; hepatitis B antiviral treatment should be guided by HBV status determined before starting antirheumatic drugs; all hepatitis-C-RNA-positive patients should be referred for antiviral treatment; VZV non-immune patients should be told about post-exposure prophylaxis; Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis appears beneficial with prednisolone >15-30 mg/day for >2-4 weeks. The original infliximab TB report found 70 cases at a median of 12 weeks, 40 extrapulmonary. For India, an evidence-based algorithm (history, tuberculin skin test, IGRA, chest radiograph, isoniazid or isoniazid + rifampicin for latent TB) has been proposed as no national consensus existed, and INASL published hepatitis B management guidelines for patients on biologicals, immunosuppressants and corticosteroids because none previously existed. EULAR 2019 vaccination update: annual vaccination-status review, non-live vaccines can be given regardless of therapy, live-attenuated vaccines only with caution, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines strongly considered for most patients, tetanus and HPV as for the general population, hepatitis A, hepatitis B and herpes zoster vaccination for at-risk patients, ideally during quiescent disease and before immunosuppression. Methotrexate work-up, hydroxychloroquine baseline fundus examination and annual screening after 5 years are covered in the respective drug entries.
ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.reason_why: Immunosuppression can reactivate latent TB (the infliximab TB signal in the source above) and hepatitis B; identifying and treating them beforehand is the preventable part of the risk.
ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.important_caveat: The Indian algorithm was suggested in a 2017 review because no national consensus existed at that time; whether a later Indian consensus has been issued was not verified. Guideline recommendations are largely conditional/low-evidence.
ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.real_working_solution: Before starting a biologic or JAK inhibitor (EULAR 2022 says TB screening could also be considered before csDMARDs and glucocorticoids, which matters in TB-endemic India): screen for latent TB (IGRA or TST with chest X-ray), test for HBsAg/anti-HBc and HCV, treat latent TB or start HBV prophylaxis as required, and update non-live vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B, tetanus) ideally before immunosuppression.
ra_pretreatment_safety_screening_tb_hbv_.source: Fragoulis GE et al., '2022 EULAR recommendations for screening and prophylaxis of chronic and opportunistic infections in adults with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:742-753 (PMID 36328476); Keane J et al., 'Tuberculosis associated with infliximab, a tumor necrosis factor alpha-neutralizing agent', N Engl J Med 2001;345:1098-1104 (PMID 11596589); Handa R et al., 'Tuberculosis and biologics in rheumatology: a special situation', Int J Rheum Dis 2017;20:1313-1325 (PMID 28730751); Arora A et al., 'INASL guidelines on management of hepatitis B virus infection in patients receiving chemotherapy, biologicals, immunosuppressants, or corticosteroids', J Clin Exp Hepatol 2018;8:403-431 (PMID 30568345); Furer V et al., '2019 update of EULAR recommendations for vaccination in adult patients with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases', Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:39-52 (PMID 31413005)

ra_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.name: Pregnancy, Lactation and Reproductive Planning with RA Drugs (EULAR 2016/2024, ACR 2020)
specific_drugs: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab pegol, golimumab, infliximab) used through pregnancy after individual assessment
ra_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.effectiveness: EULAR 2024 update (5 overarching principles, 12 recommendations): csDMARDs compatible with pregnancy include antimalarials, azathioprine, colchicine, ciclosporin, sulfasalazine and tacrolimus; NSAIDs and glucocorticoids call for a more restrictive approach in pregnancy; all TNF inhibitors can be used throughout pregnancy after individualised risk-benefit assessment and non-TNF biologics may be used if needed; all bDMARDs are considered compatible with breastfeeding; for men, compatible options include methotrexate and leflunomide. EULAR 2016: methotrexate, mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide require discontinuation before conception due to proven teratogenicity; insufficient fetal-safety documentation implies discontinuing leflunomide, tofacitinib, abatacept, rituximab, tocilizumab and anakinra before a planned pregnancy. The 2020 ACR reproductive-health guideline (12 good-practice statements, 131 graded recommendations) emphasises safe contraception, pre-pregnancy counselling to conceive during quiescent disease on pregnancy-compatible drugs, and rheumatology-obstetrics collaboration.
ra_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.reason_why: Methotrexate, mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide are proven teratogens and several other drugs lack fetal-safety data (EULAR 2016), so planning lets disease be controlled with compatible drugs before conception.
ra_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.important_caveat: Recommendations are based on registry and observational exposure data; the 2016 and 2024 documents differ in detail and the more recent 2024 update supersedes on conflicting points.
ra_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.real_working_solution: Counsel every woman of childbearing potential before treatment: use reliable contraception on methotrexate/leflunomide, plan conception during remission on hydroxychloroquine/sulfasalazine or a TNF inhibitor, and involve rheumatology and obstetrics together.
ra_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.source: Rüegg L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:910-926 (PMID 40287311); Götestam Skorpen C et al., 'The EULAR points to consider for use of antirheumatic drugs before pregnancy, and during pregnancy and lactation', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:795-810 (PMID 26888948); Sammaritano LR et al., '2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Reproductive Health in Rheumatic and Musculoskeletal Diseases', Arthritis Rheumatol 2020;72:529-556 (PMID 32090480)

ra_failed_or_unproven_treatments.name: Failed, Modest or Unproven Treatments - Anakinra, Secukinumab, Fostamatinib, Herbals (GLA, Tripterygium), Acupuncture
specific_drugs: Gamma-linolenic acid (evening primrose/borage/blackcurrant oil) and Tripterygium wilfordii (thunder god vine)
ra_failed_or_unproven_treatments.effectiveness: Anakinra (Cochrane, 5 trials, 2,876 patients): ACR20 38% versus 23% (a 15% increase, 'clinically meaningful though modest'), ACR50 18% versus 7%, ACR70 7% versus 2%; injection-site reactions 71% versus 28%; serious infections 1.8% versus 0.6% (not statistically different). Secukinumab (phase III, active-comparator and placebo-controlled): ACR20 at week 24 30.7% (150 mg, p=0.0305) and 28.3% (75 mg, p=0.0916, not significant) versus 42.8% with abatacept and 18.1% with placebo; ACR50 and HAQ-DI improvements not significant. Fostamatinib phase 2: ACR20 67% (100 mg twice daily) and 57% versus 35% at 6 months, ACR50 43% and 32% versus 19%, but hypertension (23% versus 7% needed antihypertensive change), diarrhoea and neutropenia. Herbal Cochrane review (22 studies): GLA-containing oils reduced pain (mean difference -32.83 on a 100-point scale) and disability (-15.75%), with more adverse events (20% versus 3%, not significant); Tripterygium wilfordii improved some outcomes and one study reported serious side effects. Acupuncture Cochrane review (2 studies, 84 people): no significant difference in ESR, CRP, joint counts or disease activity for acupuncture; electroacupuncture reduced knee pain (WMD -2.0).
ra_failed_or_unproven_treatments.reason_why: Each was tested in randomised trials as a possible RA therapy; the results above show modest, non-significant or safety-limited benefit compared with the established drug classes.
ra_failed_or_unproven_treatments.important_caveat: Anakinra and Tripterygium data are from older or small studies; fostamatinib's regulatory status for RA and secukinumab's status were not verified in this survey and neither drug is among those listed in the EULAR 2022/2025 RA recommendations.
ra_failed_or_unproven_treatments.real_working_solution: Do not substitute any of these for methotrexate-based DMARD therapy; anakinra is a modest option only when other biologics are unsuitable, and herbals/acupuncture may be discussed for symptoms only with the toxicity and evidence limits above. The proven options are the DMARD ladder, glucocorticoid bridging, biologics/JAK inhibitors and non-drug care in the other entries.
ra_failed_or_unproven_treatments.source: Mertens M, Singh JA, 'Anakinra for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(1):CD005121 (PMID 19160248); Blanco FJ et al., 'Secukinumab in active rheumatoid arthritis: a phase III randomized, double-blind, active comparator- and placebo-controlled study', Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:1144-1153 (PMID 28217871); Weinblatt ME et al., 'An oral spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis', N Engl J Med 2010;363:1303-1312 (PMID 20879879); Cameron M, Chrubasik S, 'Herbal therapy for treating rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(2):CD002948 (PMID 21328257); Casimiro L et al., 'Acupuncture and electroacupuncture for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(4):CD003788 (PMID 16235342)

ra_medical_devices_equipment.name: Devices and Equipment - Implantable Vagus-Nerve Neurostimulator (SetPoint), Retinal Screening Devices, Bone Densitometry, Splints and Joint Prostheses
ra_medical_devices_equipment.type: Medical devices supporting or delivering RA care
specific_drugs: Spectral-domain OCT and automated visual-field perimetry for hydroxychloroquine retinal screening
DXA bone densitometry for glucocorticoid fracture-risk assessment
Wrist/hand resting and working splints; total knee/hip prostheses
ra_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: RESET-RA (242 patients with inadequate response/intolerance to biologic or targeted synthetic DMARDs, double-blind sham-controlled): ACR20 at 3 months 35.2% with active stimulation versus 24.2% sham (p=0.0209), rising in open-label to 50.0% at 6 months and 52.8% at 12 months (completers); adverse events similar in both arms, related serious adverse events 1.6%, all perioperative and resolved; the FDA approved the SetPoint System on 31 July 2025 (implanted neurostimulator delivering 60 seconds of vagus stimulation once daily), with a subgroup with one prior biologic/DMARD exposure showing ACR20 44.2% versus 19%. Hydroxychloroquine screening uses baseline fundus examination and, after 5 years, annual automated visual fields plus spectral-domain OCT, with multifocal ERG and fundus autofluorescence as corroboration. DXA with vertebral fracture assessment is part of the ACR 2022 glucocorticoid-osteoporosis assessment. Splints show indicative evidence of pain reduction (Cochrane OT review). Joint replacement data are in the surgery entry.
ra_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: The vagus-nerve device modulates the inflammatory reflex that regulates cytokine production; the other devices detect toxicity or risk early or offload/replace damaged joints.
ra_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: The RESET-RA primary benefit over sham was 11 percentage points at 3 months and the 6/12-month rates are open-label, uncontrolled; the FDA approval date comes from a news report (Healio) rather than the FDA document, and the device's availability in India was not verified.
ra_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: The vagus-nerve stimulator is a new, FDA-approved non-drug option for patients who have failed biologic/targeted DMARDs (the trial's primary 3-month benefit over sham was modest, 11 percentage points), and screening devices (OCT/visual fields, DXA) should be used as the drug-safety protocols above require.
ra_medical_devices_equipment.source: Tesser J et al. (RESET-RA), 'Vagus nerve-mediated neuroimmune modulation for rheumatoid arthritis: a pivotal randomized controlled trial', Nat Med 2026;32:369-378 (PMID 41429981); Healio Rheumatology, 'FDA approves vagus nerve stimulator for rheumatoid arthritis', 31 July 2025 (https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology/20250731/fda-approves-vagus-nerve-stimulator-for-rheumatoid-arthritis); Marmor MF et al., 'Recommendations on screening for chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine retinopathy (2016 revision)', Ophthalmology 2016;123:1386-1394 (PMID 26992838); Humphrey MB et al., '2022 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Prevention and Treatment of Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteoporosis', Arthritis Rheumatol 2023;75:2088-2102 (PMID 37845798); Steultjens EMJ et al., 'Occupational therapy for rheumatoid arthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004;(1):CD003114 (PMID 14974005)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Triple therapy (MTX + SSZ + HCQ) vs methotrexate alone - O'Dell 1996
ranked_high_to_low.metric: >=50% improvement maintained for 2 years without major toxicity in 24/31 = 77.4% of triple-therapy patients versus 12/36 = 33.3% on methotrexate alone and 14/35 = 40.0% on SSZ + HCQ (n=102, previously DMARD-failed)
ranked_high_to_low.source: O'Dell JR et al., 'Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate alone, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine, or a combination of all three medications', N Engl J Med 1996;334:1287-1291 (PMID 8609945)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Baricitinib monotherapy (RA-BEGIN, MTX-naive)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: ACR20 response at week 24 in 77% with baricitinib monotherapy versus 62% with methotrexate monotherapy (p<=0.01)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fleischmann R et al. (RA-BEGIN), Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:506-517 (PMID 27723271)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Abatacept + methotrexate (AIM, MTX-resistant, 1 year)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: ACR20 at 1 year 73.1% with abatacept versus 39.7% with placebo (both with methotrexate; difference 33.4 percentage points, n=652)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kremer JM et al. (AIM), Ann Intern Med 2006;144:865-876 (PMID 16785475)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combination therapy including prednisolone (COBRA)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Patients improved by ACR criteria at week 28: 55/76 = 72.4% with step-down prednisolone + MTX + SSZ versus 39/79 = 49.4% with sulfasalazine alone (n=155)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Boers M et al. (COBRA), 'Randomised comparison of combined step-down prednisolone, methotrexate and sulphasalazine with sulphasalazine alone in early rheumatoid arthritis', Lancet 1997;350:309-318 (PMID 9251634)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: IMPORTANT - how to read this table: effectiveness_pct is the single real percentage reported by the cited trial or meta-analysis for the endpoint named in each row's metric, and rows are ordered strictly by that number. It is NOT a head-to-head efficacy ranking. The rows measure DIFFERENT things (ACR20 response, ACR50 response, DAS28 remission, sustained remission, a strategy's remission rate, a relative reduction in erosions, an absolute benefit over placebo, or a toxicity-reduction percentage) in DIFFERENT trials, populations (methotrexate-naive, methotrexate-inadequate, TNF-inadequate) and time points (12 weeks to 5 years), with placebo, methotrexate or an active biologic as comparator, so a higher number does not mean a better drug. ACR20 is a lenient threshold (20% improvement) and ACR50/remission rows are stricter; the table therefore favours rows reported as ACR20. Read the metric and the comparator arm in each row: the placebo or methotrexate result is stated there so the real treatment effect (the difference) can be seen. Old trials with small samples (O'Dell 1996, n=102) sit near the top on raw percentage. Rows near the bottom (anakinra, secukinumab, hydroxychloroquine, exercise, vagus stimulation) are documented modest effects and are reported honestly so they are not mistaken for first-line options. Survey entries without a reliable single disease-control percentage - patient education, occupational therapy/joint protection, hand exercises, lifestyle/diet, surgery, pre-treatment screening, pregnancy planning, NSAIDs, glucocorticoid safety (GLORIA), and the tapering/drug-free-remission and folic-acid-toxicity-reduction figures (79.1% low disease activity with half-dose etanercept in PRESERVE, 15.0% and 9.4% sustained drug-free remission, 76.9% relative reduction of transaminase elevation with folate) - are described in the survey entries and CURABILITY_NOTE instead of being forced into this ranking. NSAIDs and coxibs are symptom-only drugs and do not alter the disease course; all csDMARD, biologic and JAK rows are genuinely disease-modifying - see CURABILITY_NOTE.

definition.finding: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic, inflammatory autoimmune disease characterised by persistent synovitis, systemic inflammation and autoantibodies (particularly rheumatoid factor and antibodies to citrullinated peptides). Uncontrolled active RA causes joint damage, disability, reduced quality of life and cardiovascular and other comorbidities. About 50% of the risk of developing RA is attributed to genetic factors and smoking is the main environmental risk factor.
definition.source: Scott DL, Wolfe F, Huizinga TW, 'Rheumatoid arthritis', Lancet 2010;376:1094-1108 (PMID 20870100); Smolen JS et al., 'Rheumatoid arthritis', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4:18001 (PMID 29417936)
definition.confidence: high - two major review articles agree on the definition; the genetic-attributable-risk figure varies by study (see hla_drb1_shared_epitope_and_genetics)

synovitis_and_synovial_pathology.finding: Most evidence (genetics, tissue analyses, models, clinical studies) points to an immune-mediated aetiology associated with dysregulation of stromal tissue, which together propagate chronic synovial inflammation and articular destruction. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) are not a uniform population; they acquire an autonomous, aggressive phenotype that persists for months after removal from the patient, and release matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), TIMPs, cytokines and chemokines that drive matrix remodelling and cartilage damage. Clinical onset comprises synovitis plus systemic comorbidity affecting the vasculature, metabolism and bone.
synovitis_and_synovial_pathology.source: Firestein GS, McInnes IB, 'Immunopathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis', Immunity 2017;46:183-196 (PMID 28228278; full text PMC5385708)
synovitis_and_synovial_pathology.confidence: high for the general model; individual cellular details are from a review summary and should be read as the current consensus model, not settled mechanism

citrullination_and_autoantibodies.finding: Peptidylarginine deiminase (PADI) enzymes convert arginine to citrulline and create new potential autoantigens (a PADI4 variant is reported to increase RA risk up to about 2-fold). Autoantibodies to citrulline-containing peptides (ACPA, measured clinically as anti-CCP) were shown in 1998 to be present in 76% of RA sera at 96% specificity, to be present early in disease and even before other manifestations occur, in contrast to rheumatoid factor (RF), which is 'not very specific for RA'. ACPA are described as not especially pathogenic on their own (they do not cause arthritis when injected into normal mice) but can exacerbate existing arthritis and bind directly to osteoclasts to promote their differentiation. Firestein 2017 states ACPA are present in roughly 80-90% of RA patients, which is higher than the 67% pooled diagnostic sensitivity in the Nishimura meta-analysis (see diagnostic_framework); the difference reflects differing populations, assays and disease duration, and a clinician should use the pooled diagnostic figure, not the higher review estimate, for pre-test reasoning.
citrullination_and_autoantibodies.source: Schellekens GAJ et al., J Clin Invest 1998;101:273-281 (PMID 9421490); Firestein GS, McInnes IB, Immunity 2017;46:183-196 (PMID 28228278; PMC5385708); Nishimura K et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;146:797-808 (PMID 17548411)
citrullination_and_autoantibodies.confidence: moderate-high - the mechanism is well supported; the PADI4 risk magnitude and the 80-90% ACPA figure come from a review and were not independently re-derived

hla_drb1_shared_epitope_and_genetics.finding: The HLA-DRB1 'shared epitope' hypothesis (Gregersen 1987) proposed that a shared amino-acid motif in HLA-DR beta chains underlies susceptibility to RA. In a fine-mapping study of 5,018 seropositive RA cases and 14,974 controls, three amino-acid positions (11, 71 and 74) in HLA-DR beta-1, plus single amino-acid polymorphisms at position 9 of HLA-B and position 9 of HLA-DP beta-1, almost completely explained the MHC association with seropositive RA; all lie in peptide-binding grooves. A trans-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (29,880 RA cases, 73,758 controls; European and Asian ancestries) brought the total to 101 RA risk loci and showed that 98 biological candidate genes at these loci include targets of already-approved RA drugs. Twin-based heritability was estimated at 65% (95% CI 50-77) in Finnish and 53% (95% CI 40-65) in UK twin data, i.e. about 60% of variation in liability. Gene-environment interaction: the shared-epitope alleles were a risk factor only for anti-citrulline-positive RA, and the combination of smoking history plus double copies of HLA-DR shared-epitope genes raised risk 21-fold compared with non-smokers carrying no shared-epitope genes.
hla_drb1_shared_epitope_and_genetics.source: Gregersen PK et al., Arthritis Rheum 1987;30:1205-1213 (PMID 2446635); Raychaudhuri S et al., Nat Genet 2012;44:291-296 (PMID 22286218); Okada Y et al., Nature 2014;506:376-381 (PMID 24390342); MacGregor AJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:30-37 (PMID 10643697); Klareskog L et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:38-46 (PMID 16385494)
hla_drb1_shared_epitope_and_genetics.confidence: high for the fine-mapping, GWAS and twin figures (primary publications, abstracts read); the 21-fold figure is a single Swedish case-control estimate and is specific to double-copy shared epitope plus smoking in ACPA-positive RA

hla_drb1_india_note.finding: Indian-specific HLA data retrieved in this pass are old: a 1992 serological (pre-molecular) HLA-typing study found HLA-DR4 significantly increased in both northern and southern Indian RA patients versus controls, with DR4-DQw8 but not DR4-DQw7 haplotypes seen. No modern allele-level Indian shared-epitope study was retrieved and verified, so no Indian shared-epitope odds ratio is quoted here.
hla_drb1_india_note.source: Taneja V et al., 'HLA-DR4-DQw8, but not DR4-DQw7 haplotypes occur in Indian patients with rheumatoid arthritis', Rheumatol Int 1992;11:251-255 (PMID 1579806)
hla_drb1_india_note.confidence: moderate for direction of association (DR4 increased); low for anything more specific because the study used serological typing and modern Indian genotyping data were not verified

cytokine_axis_tnf_il6_il1.finding: TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6 are the cytokines identified as promoting synovial inflammation. IL-6 and TNF (and probably GM-CSF) are considered of central importance 'as defined by the clear therapeutic benefits achieved upon their inhibition'; IL-1, TNF and IL-17 are particularly relevant to bone and cartilage damage. IL-17 is an instructive negative result: despite strong evidence in mouse models, IL-17A and IL-17 receptor inhibitors have so far not been particularly effective in established RA trials, so a cytokine implicated in the model is not automatically a treatment target in the patient.
cytokine_axis_tnf_il6_il1.source: Kay J et al., 'ACR/EULAR 2010 rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2012;51 Suppl 6:vi5-9 (PMID 23221588); Firestein GS, McInnes IB, Immunity 2017;46:183-196 (PMID 28228278; PMC5385708)
cytokine_axis_tnf_il6_il1.confidence: high for TNF/IL-6 (validated by therapeutic response); moderate for IL-1 and IL-17 roles

pannus_and_bone_erosion.finding: Bone erosion is a central feature of RA, is associated with disease severity and poor functional outcome, and results from excessive local bone resorption together with inadequate bone formation. The main triggers are synovitis (with proinflammatory cytokines and RANKL, the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand) and antibodies to citrullinated proteins, both of which stimulate differentiation of bone-resorbing osteoclasts. RANKL protein has been shown to be expressed at the pannus-bone interface at sites of articular bone erosion, and synovial tissue in RA is a source of osteoclast differentiation factor. Current antirheumatic therapy inhibits both erosion and inflammation, but repair of existing erosions occurs rarely, partly because proinflammatory cytokines actively suppress bone formation.
pannus_and_bone_erosion.source: Schett G, Gravallese E, 'Bone erosion in rheumatoid arthritis: mechanisms, diagnosis and treatment', Nat Rev Rheumatol 2012;8:656-664 (PMID 23007741); Pettit AR et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2006;45:1068-1076 (PMID 16490750, title-level finding); Gravallese EM et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:250-258 (PMID 10693863, title-level finding)

preclinical_phase.finding: RA has a preclinical phase that can last months to years during which circulating autoantibodies, cytokines and chemokines rise before clinical synovitis. In blood-donor studies, 83 individuals who later developed RA had donated blood a median of 2.5 years (IQR 1.1-4.7) before symptoms: anti-CCP was present in 33.7%, IgM-RF in 19.3% and IgA-RF in 33.7%, with anti-CCP sensitivity of 25% when sampled more than 1.5 years before onset and 52% within 1.5 years. In a second serial-sample study of 79 patients, 49% (39 of 79) were IgM-RF and/or anti-CCP positive on at least one occasion, a median of 4.5 years (range 0.1-13.8) before symptom onset, whereas only 1.1% (IgM-RF) and 0.6% (anti-CCP) of 2,138 control samples were positive. EULAR recommends describing at-risk individuals by combinations of genetic risk factors, environmental risk factors, systemic autoimmunity, symptoms without clinical arthritis, and unclassified arthritis; 'clinically suspect arthralgia' is a subgroup of the symptoms-without-arthritis phase. EULAR/ACR published risk-stratification criteria for the arthralgia stage in 2025 (details not extracted in this pass). Practical limit: an asymptomatic person with a positive anti-CCP has a raised risk of RA, but there is no established preventive treatment to offer on antibody status alone from the sources reviewed here.
preclinical_phase.source: Rantapaa-Dahlqvist S et al., Arthritis Rheum 2003;48:2741-2749 (PMID 14558078); Nielen MM et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:380-386 (PMID 14872479); Gerlag DM et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:638-641 (PMID 22387728); Raza K, Clin Ther 2019;41:1279-1285 (PMID 31196657); Firestein GS, McInnes IB, Immunity 2017;46:183-196 (PMID 28228278); van Steenbergen HW et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:1445-1457 (PMID 40447498, title only)
preclinical_phase.confidence: high for the antibody-precedes-symptoms findings (two independent cohorts); the final sentence on prevention is an honest statement of what this pass did not verify, not a claim that prevention is impossible

diagnosis_vs_classification.finding: RA is diagnosed clinically by a rheumatologist; the ACR/EULAR criteria are classification criteria written to standardise study populations. A meta-analysis of the 2010 criteria concluded that they 'have classificative and not diagnostic function', with good sensitivity, lower specificity and overall moderate diagnostic accuracy. The criteria are meant to be applied only to patients with at least one joint with definite clinical synovitis (swelling) that is not better explained by another disease.
diagnosis_vs_classification.source: Sakellariou G et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e56528 (PMID 23437156); Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241)

acr_eular_2010_criteria.finding: 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria: 'definite RA' requires confirmed synovitis in at least one joint, absence of an alternative diagnosis that better explains the synovitis, and a total score of 6 or more (of a possible 10) across four domains. (A) Joint involvement: 1 large joint = 0; 2-10 large joints = 1; 1-3 small joints (with or without large joints) = 2; 4-10 small joints = 3; more than 10 joints (at least 1 small joint) = 5. (B) Serology: negative RF and negative ACPA = 0; low-positive RF or low-positive ACPA (above the upper limit of normal but not more than 3x ULN) = 2; high-positive RF or ACPA (more than 3x ULN) = 3. (C) Acute-phase reactants: normal CRP and ESR = 0; abnormal CRP or ESR = 1. (D) Duration of symptoms: under 6 weeks = 0; 6 weeks or more = 1. Large joints are shoulders, elbows, hips, knees and ankles; small joints are MCPs, PIPs, 2nd-5th MTPs, thumb IPs and wrists; DIPs, first CMC joints and first MTP joints are excluded. Patients with typical bone erosions can be classified as RA regardless of score. The system was designed to identify, among patients newly presenting with undifferentiated inflammatory synovitis, those at high risk of persistent and/or erosive disease, and to shift attention to earlier disease than the 1987 criteria.
acr_eular_2010_criteria.source: Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241) and Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:2569-2581 (PMID 20872595) for the four-domain structure, ranges and threshold of 6; item-level point values, joint definitions and erosion rule read from published reproductions of the criteria table: Sakellariou G et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e56528 (PMC3577909) and Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMC3711368, PMID 22945499)
acr_eular_2010_criteria.confidence: high - the primary abstract confirms structure, ranges and threshold; the individual point values were checked in two independent open-access reproductions rather than in the paywalled primary table

seronegative_arithmetic_of_the_2010_scor.finding: Derived from the score table above (not a separately published claim): a seronegative patient scores 0 in the serology domain, so the maximum they can reach is 5 (joints) + 1 (acute-phase) + 1 (duration) = 7; reaching the threshold of 6 therefore effectively requires involvement of more than 10 joints (at least one small) or, at 3 points for 4-10 small joints, cannot be reached at all (3 + 1 + 1 = 5). This explains why seronegative patients classified under the 2010 criteria have more joints involved and higher inflammatory activity at presentation.
seronegative_arithmetic_of_the_2010_scor.source: Arithmetic on Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241) score table; consistent with the explanation offered by Nordberg LB et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:341-345 (PMID 27094444)
seronegative_arithmetic_of_the_2010_scor.confidence: high for the arithmetic; the clinical inference (seronegative early RA can be missed by the criteria when fewer joints are involved) is reasoning from the table, not a trial result

criteria_performance.finding: Meta-analysis of 17 full articles (6,816 patients): 2010 criteria pooled sensitivity 0.82 (95% CI 0.79-0.84) and specificity 0.61 (0.59-0.64) against various reference standards (for methotrexate initiation as reference: sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.52; for expert opinion: 0.88 and 0.48). Compared directly with the 1987 criteria in 8 studies, the 2010 criteria gave +0.11 higher sensitivity at the cost of -0.04 lower specificity. A separate meta-analysis with methotrexate as reference found sensitivity 0.80 (0.74-0.85), specificity 0.61 (0.56-0.67), positive likelihood ratio 2.11 and negative likelihood ratio 0.31. In a Norfolk primary-care inception register the 2010 criteria at baseline identified a similar number of RA patients as the 1987 criteria did cumulatively over up to 5 years, while about 20% of inflammatory arthritis patients satisfied neither set over 5 years. Practical reading: a patient who meets the 2010 criteria is reasonably likely to need DMARD therapy, but a positive score is not proof of RA (specificity around 0.5-0.6), and a patient who does not meet them may still have early RA or another arthritis that needs treatment.
criteria_performance.source: Radner H et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:114-123 (PMID 23592710); Sakellariou G et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e56528 (PMID 23437156); Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMID 22945499)
criteria_performance.confidence: high - two independent meta-analyses agree; reference standards (DMARD/methotrexate start, expert opinion) are imperfect by construction

acr_1987_criteria_context.finding: The 1987 ARA criteria were derived from 262 RA patients and 262 non-RA rheumatic-disease controls. RA is defined by 4 or more of 7 criteria: (1) morning stiffness in and around joints lasting at least 1 hour before maximal improvement; (2) soft-tissue swelling (arthritis) of 3 or more joint areas observed by a physician; (3) swelling of the PIP, MCP or wrist joints; (4) symmetric swelling; (5) rheumatoid nodules; (6) rheumatoid factor; (7) radiographic erosions and/or periarticular osteopenia in hand and/or wrist joints. Criteria 1-4 must have been present for at least 6 weeks. Reported sensitivity was 91-94% and specificity 89% versus non-RA rheumatic disease controls. Because the criteria rely on late features such as nodules, erosions and rheumatoid factor, they were criticised for lack of sensitivity in early disease, which was the stated reason for developing the 2010 criteria.
acr_1987_criteria_context.source: Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241)

anti_ccp_and_rf_accuracy.finding: Meta-analysis of 37 studies of anti-CCP and 50 of RF: anti-CCP pooled sensitivity 67% (95% CI 62-72%), specificity 95% (94-97%), positive likelihood ratio 12.46 (9.72-15.98), negative likelihood ratio 0.36 (0.31-0.42). IgM-RF pooled sensitivity 69% (65-73%), specificity 85% (82-88%), positive likelihood ratio 4.86 (3.95-5.97), negative likelihood ratio 0.38 (0.33-0.44). Results in early RA were similar to all studies; 3 of 4 studies found greater risk of radiographic progression with anti-CCP positivity than with IgM-RF positivity. Many studies had methodological limitations and RF studies were heterogeneous. Practical reading: a positive anti-CCP is a strong rule-in test for RA (likelihood ratio above 10) and is more specific than RF; a negative anti-CCP or RF does not exclude RA (negative likelihood ratios 0.36-0.38), which is why seronegative RA exists as a substantial subgroup. Under the 2010 criteria, serology scores 2 (low-positive) or 3 (high-positive, above 3x ULN).
anti_ccp_and_rf_accuracy.source: Nishimura K et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;146:797-808 (PMID 17548411); Schellekens GAJ et al., J Clin Invest 1998;101:273-281 (PMID 9421490) for the original 76% sensitivity / 96% specificity ACPA finding
anti_ccp_and_rf_accuracy.confidence: high - large meta-analysis; older data (literature to 2006) and heterogeneity acknowledged by the authors; assay generations have since changed

esr_crp_and_normal_labs_pitfall.finding: ESR and CRP contribute 1 point to the 2010 score if either is abnormal, but they are frequently normal in genuine RA. In two consecutive-patient databases (1,892 patients in Finland and 478 in the USA, seen 1980-2004), ESR was below 28 mm/h at presentation in 45% and 47%, CRP was normal in 44% and 58%, all RF tests were negative in 38% and 37%, both ESR and CRP were normal in 33% and 42%, and all three tests were normal in 15% and 14%. In the CORRONA registry, of 9,135 patients with active RA (CDAI above 2.8), 58% had neither ESR nor CRP elevated, 16% had both, and 26% had one of the two; the authors recommend obtaining both ESR and CRP at the initial visit. Practical takeaway: normal ESR/CRP and negative RF do not exclude RA and must not be used to dismiss a patient with clinically evident synovitis; use joint counts and clinical examination as the primary measure.
esr_crp_and_normal_labs_pitfall.source: Sokka T et al., J Rheumatol 2009;36:1387-1390 (PMID 19411389); Kay J et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2014;16:R40 (PMID 24485007)
esr_crp_and_normal_labs_pitfall.confidence: high - two large independent datasets show the same pattern; note the Finnish/US data pre-date modern early-treatment practice

radiographic_erosions.finding: In prospective studies of early RA, approximately 75% of patients have joint erosions, and the majority develop their first erosions during the first 2 years of disease; the rate of progression is highest in the early years and joints of the feet erode earlier and in greater number than those of the hands (the fifth MTP joint is typically among the first eroded). Radiographs of the feet should therefore be included with hands when looking for damage. For patients who score below 6 on the 2010 criteria, EULAR proposed a highly specific definition of erosive disease: a cortical break (erosion) in at least 3 separate joints among PIP, MCP, wrist (counted as one joint) and MTP joints on radiographs of both hands and feet. Absence of erosions on a plain film does not exclude RA (roughly a quarter of early-RA patients in the reviewed cohorts had no erosions); ultrasound and MRI can show synovitis and erosions when plain films are normal (see next entry).
radiographic_erosions.source: van der Heijde DM, Br J Rheumatol 1995;34 Suppl 2:74-78 (PMID 8535653); Hulsmans HM et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:1927-1940 (PMID 11014342); van der Heijde D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:479-481 (PMID 23378540)
radiographic_erosions.confidence: high for the natural-history statements; these are from pre-modern-therapy cohorts, so current erosion rates under early treatment are lower (see natural_history)

ultrasound_and_mri.finding: The 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria refer to possible use of ultrasound 'for confirmation of the clinical findings'. In 109 patients with musculoskeletal symptoms for 3 years or less, sensitivity/specificity for identifying patients who needed methotrexate within 1 year were 58.5%/79.4% for clinical synovitis, 78.0%/79.4% for ultrasound synovitis with a grey-scale score of 1 or more, and 56.1%/93.7% for grey-scale 2 or more or power-Doppler 1 or more; ultrasound improved criteria accuracy (preliminary, single-cohort data). For MRI, in 84 patients with RA of under 1 year duration, baseline MRI bone-marrow oedema (score above 2 RAMRIS units) independently predicted radiographic progression (odds ratio 2.77, 95% CI 1.06-7.21), and 48% had erosive progression by conventional radiography at 1 year versus 66% by MRI; in another 55 early-RA patients MRI synovitis and bone-marrow oedema independently predicted 3-year radiographic progression. EULAR issued 10 recommendations on imaging (radiography, ultrasound, MRI and others) for diagnosis, detecting inflammation and damage, predicting outcome and monitoring, from a review of 199 studies. Practical reading: ultrasound and MRI can detect subclinical synovitis and help prognosis, but the source studies are small and imaging is an adjunct to, not a replacement for, clinical examination.
ultrasound_and_mri.source: Nakagomi D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:890-898 (PMID 23334942); Haavardsholm EA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:794-800 (PMID 17981915); Boyesen P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2011;70:428-433 (PMID 20810395); Colebatch AN et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:804-814 (PMID 23520036)
ultrasound_and_mri.confidence: moderate-high - consistent direction across studies; sample sizes small (55-109) and specific numbers should be read as study-specific

seronegative_ra.finding: About 15% of early RA patients classified by the 2010 criteria are seronegative (RF-negative and ACPA-negative): 36 of 234 (15.4%) in a DMARD-naive inception cohort, and 34 of 230 (15%) in the ARCTIC treat-to-target trial. At presentation seronegative patients had higher inflammatory activity than seropositive ones (median ultrasound joint score 55 vs 25, median swollen joints 17 vs 8, mean DAS 3.9 vs 3.4), probably because the criteria require many involved joints in the absence of serology. Over 24 months in a treat-to-target setting, disease activity, radiographic progression and remission rates were similar between groups, although the initial treatment response was slower in seronegative patients. Takeaway: seronegative RA is not a mild form of RA and needs the same intensive treat-to-target therapy. Seronegative polyarthritis in India and other endemic regions should also prompt consideration of chikungunya and other viral arthritis (see differential_diagnosis).
seronegative_ra.source: Nordberg LB et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:341-345 (PMID 27094444); Nordberg LB et al., RMD Open 2018;4:e000752 (PMID 30564452)
seronegative_ra.confidence: high for the Norwegian cohort findings (two publications, same trial family); the 15% proportion is specific to criteria-classified early RA in a Norwegian setting and may differ elsewhere

early_recognition_referral_rule.finding: An evidence-based referral guide for primary-care doctors suggests rapid referral to a rheumatologist when RA is suspected and any of the following is present: 3 or more swollen joints, involvement of the metatarsophalangeal and/or metacarpophalangeal joints, or morning stiffness of 30 minutes or more.
early_recognition_referral_rule.source: Emery P et al., 'Early referral recommendation for newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis: evidence based development of a clinical guide', Ann Rheum Dis 2002;61:290-297 (PMID 11874828)
early_recognition_referral_rule.confidence: moderate-high - a consensus-based clinical guide built on a literature review; a referral trigger, not a diagnostic test

general_principle.finding: Composite indices that include joint counts are recommended for follow-up of RA (they integrate several facets of disease). Swollen joint counts correlate with joint-damage progression and tender joint counts with physical function. The SDAI and CDAI are easy to calculate and correlate with damage and function; their remission criteria are stringent, usually associated with a halt in damage progression and optimal function, and are still achieved in about 1 in 4 clinic patients and up to one-third of patients in trials of early arthritis.
general_principle.source: Smolen JS et al., 'Scores for all seasons: SDAI and CDAI', Clin Exp Rheumatol 2014;32(5 Suppl 85):S75-79 (PMID 25365093); Smolen JS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:3-15 (PMID 25969430)

das28.finding: DAS28 = (0.56 x sqrt of tender joint count 28) + (0.28 x sqrt of swollen joint count 28) + (0.70 x ln ESR) + (0.014 x patient global assessment in mm); a CRP-based version (DAS28-CRP) also exists. Range 0-9.4. ACR-recommended DAS28 categories: remission below 2.6; low disease activity 2.6 to below 3.2; moderate 3.2 to 5.1; high above 5.1. A DAS28 below 2.6 corresponds to fulfilment of the older ARA preliminary clinical-remission criteria (optimal ROC cut-off 2.66). Note that other DAS28 cut-off sets exist: an expert-rating-based derivation proposed 2.4 / 3.6 / 5.5 for remission / low / moderate boundaries, so the numbers depend on which convention a clinic or trial uses.
das28.source: Prevoo ML et al., Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:44-48 (PMID 7818570) for development; formula as given in Aletaha D et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2005;7:R796-R806 (PMID 15987481); categories: Anderson J et al., Arthritis Care Res 2012;64:640-647 (PMID 22473918; Table 3, PMC4028066); Fransen J et al., Rheumatology 2004;43:1252-1255 (PMID 15238643); Aletaha D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:2625-2636 (PMID 16142705)
das28.confidence: high for the formula and the ACR-recommended cut-offs; moderate on 'which cut-off set is universally used' because more than one derivation exists

cdai.finding: Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) = tender joint count (28) + swollen joint count (28) + patient global assessment (0-10 cm) + evaluator global assessment (0-10 cm); range 0-76. It is the only composite index that does not need an acute-phase reactant, so it can be calculated at the point of care at any visit. Categories: remission 2.8 or below; low disease activity above 2.8 to 10; moderate above 10 to 22; high above 22. In two cohorts, CDAI correlated strongly with DAS28 (R = 0.89-0.90), comparable to the SDAI-DAS28 correlation (R = 0.90-0.91); acute-phase reactants accounted for only about 5% of the SDAI and 15% of the DAS28.
cdai.source: Aletaha D et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2005;7:R796-R806 (PMID 15987481); Aletaha D et al., Clin Exp Rheumatol 2005;23(5 Suppl 39):S100-108 (PMID 16273793); categories: Anderson J et al., Arthritis Care Res 2012;64:640-647 (PMID 22473918)

sdai.finding: Simplified Disease Activity Index (SDAI) = swollen joint count (28) + tender joint count (28) + patient global (0-10 cm) + evaluator global (0-10 cm) + CRP (mg/dL); range 0-86. Categories: remission 3.3 or below; low above 3.3 to 11; moderate above 11 to 26; high above 26. These SDAI thresholds (3.3, 11, 26) were derived by mapping scores to the classification of 35 rheumatology experts, and validated in a 767-patient routine cohort (weighted kappa 0.70) and a 91-patient inception cohort, where they discriminated ACR20 responders from non-responders and patients with and without radiographic progression.
sdai.source: Aletaha D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:2625-2636 (PMID 16142705); formula: Aletaha D et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2005;7:R796-R806 (PMID 15987481); categories: Anderson J et al., Arthritis Care Res 2012;64:640-647 (PMID 22473918)

acr_eular_remission_definitions.finding: The 2011 ACR/EULAR remission definition (for trials) has two forms: a Boolean definition in which tender joint count, swollen joint count, CRP (mg/dL) and patient global assessment (0-10) must each be 1 or below, or an index-based definition of SDAI 3.3 or below (a CRP-free alternative uses CDAI 2.8 or below). A 2022 revision tested a patient-global threshold of 2 cm or below (Boolean 2.0) in 2,048 trial participants (1,101 early RA; 947 established RA): at 6 months, more patients qualified for remission, rising from 14.8% to 20.6% in early RA and 4.2% to 6.0% in established RA; Boolean 2.0, SDAI and CDAI remission had similar positive likelihood ratios (3.8-4.3) for predicting radiographic non-progression and good function (HAQ 0.5 or below). Practical reading: even with the relaxed threshold, remission at 6 months was reached by only about 1 in 5 early-RA and about 1 in 17 established-RA patients in these trial datasets.
acr_eular_remission_definitions.source: Felson DT et al., Arthritis Rheum 2011;63:573-586 and Ann Rheum Dis 2011;70:404-413 (PMIDs 21294106, 21292833) as summarised in the text of Studenic P et al., 'ACR/EULAR remission criteria for RA: 2022 revision', Arthritis Rheumatol 2023;75:15-22 (PMID 36274193; PMC10092655)
acr_eular_remission_definitions.confidence: high for the 2022 revision figures (abstract and full text read); the 2011 definition is described from the 2022 paper's background rather than the 2011 paper itself

core.name: Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis - MCP, PIP and wrist joints (plus MTP joints)
core.note: The classic presentation is persistent, symmetric swelling and tenderness of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and wrist joints, with the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints of the feet commonly involved as well. The 1987 criteria required arthritis of PIP, MCP or wrist joints, symmetric swelling, and soft-tissue swelling in 3 or more joint areas, each present for at least 6 weeks; the 2010 criteria score small-joint involvement (MCP, PIP, 2nd-5th MTP, thumb IP, wrist) higher than large-joint involvement and exclude DIP, first CMC and first MTP joints. In a Norfolk register of newly presenting inflammatory polyarthritis (n = 260, not all ultimately RA; percentages as printed in the open-access baseline table), 83% had arthritis of hand joints, 70% had symmetric arthritis, 66% had arthritis of 3 or more joint areas and 57% had more than 10 joints involved at first assessment. Feet are affected early: MTP joints erode earlier than hand joints and the fifth MTP is often the first eroded.
core.source: Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMC3711368; PMID 22945499) baseline table; Emery P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2002;61:290-297 (PMID 11874828); Hulsmans HM et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:1927-1940 (PMID 11014342)

core.name: Morning stiffness lasting an hour or more
core.note: Prolonged early-morning joint stiffness (at least 1 hour before maximal improvement) is criterion 1 of the 1987 criteria; 66% of the Norfolk early inflammatory polyarthritis cohort reported morning stiffness of 60 minutes or more. For primary-care referral the threshold is lower: 30 minutes or more, together with 3 or more swollen joints or MCP/MTP involvement. Duration of morning stiffness is not by itself specific to RA - the EULAR/ACR polymyalgia rheumatica criteria also score morning stiffness (over 45 minutes) - so it supports an inflammatory rather than mechanical cause but does not identify the specific disease.
core.source: Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); Emery P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2002;61:290-297 (PMID 11874828); Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMC3711368); Dasgupta B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:484-492 (PMID 22388996)

core.name: Fatigue
core.note: Fatigue is very common in RA: on a visual-analogue scale it was present in 88-98% of 1,488 rheumatic-disease patients, and clinically important fatigue (2.0 or more on the scale) was present in more than 41% of RA patients (and 76% of fibromyalgia patients). In multivariable analysis in RA the strongest independent predictors were pain, sleep disturbance and depression, and no independent association with the inflammatory process (ESR, joint count, grip strength) could be found; a later systematic review likewise found an unclear relationship with inflammatory activity and that being female was related to higher fatigue, with the strongest evidence for links to pain, physical functioning and depression. Patients describe RA fatigue as overwhelming, unresolving and different from normal tiredness, and often feel it is dismissed by clinicians. Practical reading: fatigue is not a reliable marker of joint inflammation, it should be asked about and managed as its own problem (pain, sleep and mood), and it should not be read as evidence that the disease is or is not active.
core.source: Wolfe F et al., J Rheumatol 1996;23:1407-1417 (PMID 8856621); Nikolaus S et al., Arthritis Care Res 2013;65:1128-1146 (PMID 23335492); Hewlett S et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;53:697-702 (PMID 16208668)

core.name: Persistent (6 weeks or more) inflammatory synovitis rather than a transient episode
core.note: Persistence matters for both classification sets: symptom duration of 6 weeks or more scores 1 point in the 2010 criteria, and criteria 1-4 of the 1987 set had to be present for at least 6 weeks. This is what separates early RA from self-limiting viral or reactive arthritis, which is why a short-lived polyarthritis after a viral illness should be re-examined at 6 weeks and again at 3 months before RA is declared.
core.source: Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241); Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); the re-examination interval is clinical reasoning from these duration thresholds, not a separately published rule

core.name: Rheumatoid nodules and other late or systemic signs at presentation
core.note: Subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules were present in 7% of the Norfolk early inflammatory polyarthritis cohort at first assessment; nodules are a 1987 criterion but are a later and less frequent feature than joint swelling, and the incidence of nodules has fallen over time (see extra_articular_disease). Radiographic erosions and periarticular osteopenia of hand or wrist are the 1987 radiographic criterion; such late features are often absent at first presentation, which is the reason the 2010 criteria were developed.
core.source: Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMC3711368); Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796)

extra_articular_disease.name: Overall burden of extra-articular RA (ExRA)
extra_articular_disease.note: In a community cohort of 609 RA patients in Olmsted County, Minnesota (diagnosed 1955-94), ExRA occurred in 247 (40.6%), and 78 (12.8%) had severe ExRA (defined in that study as vasculitis, pericarditis, pleuritis and/or Felty's syndrome). Independent predictors of severe ExRA were smoking at RA diagnosis (risk ratio 2.94, 95% CI 1.68-5.13) and early disability (risk ratio 2.45, 95% CI 1.51-4.00). Virtually all the excess mortality in RA in an earlier analysis of 424 patients occurred in the severe ExRA subgroup (incidence 1.04 per 100 person-years). In a later inception cohort of 907 patients (1985-2014), the 10-year cumulative incidence of any ExRA fell from 45.1% (1985-99) to 31.6% (2000-14); mortality remained increased with nonsevere (HR 1.83, 95% CI 1.18-2.85) and severe ExRA (HR 3.05, 95% CI 1.44-6.49); RF positivity (HR 2.02) and current smoking (HR 1.61) were risk factors.
extra_articular_disease.source: Turesson C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2003;62:722-727 (PMID 12860726); Turesson C et al., J Rheumatol 2002;29:62-67 (PMID 11824973); Kimbrough BA et al., Arthritis Care Res 2024;76:454-462 (PMID 37691141)

extra_articular_disease.name: Rheumatoid nodules
extra_articular_disease.note: In a population-based inception cohort (907 patients, 1985-2014), 10-year cumulative incidence of subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules fell from 30.9% (RA diagnosed 1985-99) to 15.8% (2000-14), the main driver of the fall in overall ExRA. In a Norfolk early inflammatory polyarthritis cohort 7% had nodules at first assessment. RF positivity and current smoking were risk factors for any ExRA in that cohort (the paper's risk factors are for ExRA overall, not nodule-specific).
extra_articular_disease.source: Kimbrough BA et al., Arthritis Care Res 2024;76:454-462 (PMID 37691141); Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMC3711368)

extra_articular_disease.name: Interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD)
extra_articular_disease.note: In a population-based incidence cohort (582 RA patients, mean follow-up 16.4 years) the lifetime risk of ILD was 7.7% in RA versus 0.9% in non-RA subjects (hazard ratio 8.96, 95% CI 4.02-19.94); risk was higher with older age at RA onset, male sex and more severe RA; ILD carried a hazard ratio of 2.86 (95% CI 1.98-4.12) for death, median survival after ILD diagnosis was only 2.6 years, and ILD accounted for about 13% of the excess mortality of RA. US death-certificate data (1988-2004) found RA-ILD in 6.6% of RA-associated deaths and estimated clinically significant RA-ILD in nearly 10% of the RA population; RA-ILD mortality rose 28.3% in women while overall RA mortality fell. A UK multicentre study (230 RA-ILD patients) found anti-CCP titre the single strongest predictor, usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) the commonest HRCT pattern, and UIP and extensive disease associated with higher mortality; baseline gas transfer (DLCO) is a useful screening test, and the authors cite a prevalence of about 5% for ILD in RA. Estimates therefore range about 5-10% depending on case definition and cohort.
extra_articular_disease.source: Bongartz T et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1583-1591 (PMID 20155830); Olson AL et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;183:372-378 (PMID 20851924); Kelly CA et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2014;53:1676-1682 (PMID 24758887)

extra_articular_disease.name: Rheumatoid vasculitis
extra_articular_disease.note: Rheumatoid vasculitis is described as the most serious extra-articular complication of RA, rare but with high morbidity and mortality despite aggressive treatment. Its incidence has fallen markedly: in the Norfolk vasculitis register the mean annual incidence for 2001-10 was 3.9 per million population, with 1-year mortality 12% and 5-year mortality 60% (18 patients, median age at diagnosis 72, average RA duration 15.6 years); in US veterans the prevalence dropped 53% in inpatients and 31% in outpatients between 2000 and 2001. Hydroxychloroquine and low-dose aspirin may be protective, and the role of newer biologics (prevention, treatment or trigger) is debated. Skin infarcts and nodules are typical cutaneous manifestations.
extra_articular_disease.source: Makol A et al., Curr Opin Rheumatol 2015;27:63-70 (PMID 25405822); Ntatsaki E et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2014;53:145-152 (PMID 24108586); Bartels C et al., Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:2553-2557 (PMID 19714622)

extra_articular_disease.name: Secondary Sjogren's syndrome and sicca symptoms
extra_articular_disease.note: In 636 RA patients from an unselected county register, ocular sicca symptoms were reported by 38%, oral sicca symptoms by 50% and both by 27%; reduced tear production was found in 29% and reduced saliva production in 17%; the minimum frequency of secondary Sjogren's syndrome was 7%. Symptoms, tear production and saliva production were only weakly inter-correlated, and high disease activity was an independent predictor of reduced saliva production. Practical reading: dry eyes and dry mouth are frequent in RA, but formal secondary Sjogren's syndrome is a much smaller subset than symptom prevalence suggests.
extra_articular_disease.source: Uhlig T et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1999;58:415-422 (PMID 10381485)

extra_articular_disease.name: Anaemia (anaemia of chronic disease and iron deficiency)
extra_articular_disease.note: A systematic review of 10 prevalence studies found mild anaemia in 33-60% of RA patients, with anaemia associated with more severe joint disease, and symptom improvement correlating with resolution of anaemia. In an Indian series of 214 RA patients (183 women; anaemia defined as haemoglobin 11 g/dL or below in women and 12 g/dL or below in men), 70.6% were anaemic: 51.6% of those had anaemia of chronic disease and 48.4% iron-deficiency anaemia (ferritin 50 or below), with higher DAS28 in anaemic (5.23) than non-anaemic (3.83) patients. Practical reading: in this Indian series nearly half of anaemic RA patients had biochemical iron deficiency, so iron status should be checked rather than assuming anaemia of chronic disease alone; only 37.74% of anaemic patients had recovered at 1 year.
extra_articular_disease.source: Wilson A et al., Am J Med 2004;116 Suppl 7A:50S-57S (PMID 15050886); Agrawal S et al., Rheumatol Int 2006;26:1091-1095 (PMID 16673131)

extra_articular_disease.name: Felty's syndrome
extra_articular_disease.note: Felty's syndrome is the triad of RA, neutropenia and splenomegaly, occurring in less than 1% of RA patients. It is typically seen with severe joint destruction and severe extra-articular disease (frequent nodules, lymphadenopathy, hepatopathy, vasculitis, leg ulcers). More than 95% of patients are RF-positive, 47-100% are ANA-positive and 78% carry HLA-DR4*0401; about 30% have large granular lymphocyte expansion. Recurrent bacterial infections from the neutropenia raise mortality; neutropenia can respond to DMARDs (widest experience with methotrexate), and splenectomy corrects neutropenia in 80% but infection risk falls less.
extra_articular_disease.source: Balint GP, Balint PV, Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2004;18:631-645 (PMID 15454123)

extra_articular_disease.name: Cardiovascular disease
extra_articular_disease.note: A meta-analysis of 24 studies (111,758 RA patients) found cardiovascular mortality about 50% higher than in the general population (meta-SMR 1.50, 95% CI 1.39-1.61), with ischaemic heart disease 1.59 and cerebrovascular disease 1.52; a second meta-analysis of 14 studies (41,490 patients) found incident cardiovascular disease increased 48% (pooled RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.36-1.62), myocardial infarction RR 1.68 (1.40-2.03), stroke RR 1.41 (1.14-1.74) and heart failure RR 1.87 (1.47-2.39, from a single study). Neutral finding: inception-cohort subgroups did not show a significant excess (meta-SMR 1.19, 95% CI 0.86-1.68 for CVD mortality; RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.97-1.65 for incident CVD), and both meta-analyses had significant heterogeneity, so the excess risk may be smaller in newly diagnosed, treated patients than in long-standing disease.
extra_articular_disease.source: Avina-Zubieta JA et al., Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1690-1697 (PMID 19035419); Avina-Zubieta JA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:1524-1529 (PMID 22425941)

extra_articular_disease.name: India-specific extra-articular data (single-centre, small)
extra_articular_disease.note: A prospective study of 140 RA patients from southern India found at least one ExRA in 36 (25.7%): interstitial lung disease 9.29%, neuropathy 8.57% (12 patients), eye involvement in 5, cutaneous vasculitis in 3, rheumatoid nodules in 4, and amyloidosis in 1. The authors note Indian patients had been considered to have a low prevalence of ExRA and that patients with ExRA were older, had longer disease duration and more deformities. This is one centre with a small sample, so it should be treated as suggestive that ILD and neuropathy are not rare in Indian RA, not as a national prevalence.
extra_articular_disease.source: Bharadwaj A et al., Med Sci Monit 2005;11:CR498-CR502 (PMID 16192902); Handa R et al., Int J Rheum Dis 2016;19:440-451 (PMID 26171649) for the general caution about Indian study quality

osteoarthritis.finding: Hand osteoarthritis (OA) is classified by hard-tissue (bony) enlargement of at least 2 of 10 selected joints (2nd and 3rd DIP, 2nd and 3rd PIP, and first carpometacarpal joints of both hands), fewer than 3 swollen MCP joints, and either at least 2 enlarged DIP joints or deformity of at least 1 of the 10 joints; the criteria were 92% sensitive and 98% specific against a control group that included RA and spondyloarthropathy. So in a patient with hand pain, DIP-predominant bony enlargement with few swollen MCP joints favours OA, whereas 3 or more swollen MCP, PIP and wrist joints with soft-tissue (synovial) swelling and prolonged morning stiffness favour RA. OA and RA can coexist in the same patient.
osteoarthritis.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1990;33:1601-1610 (PMID 2242058); Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); coexistence statement is general clinical knowledge not derived from these papers
osteoarthritis.confidence: high for the criteria contrast; the coexistence statement is uncited clinical knowledge

psoriatic_arthritis.finding: The CASPAR criteria classify psoriatic arthritis as established inflammatory articular disease plus at least 3 points from: current psoriasis (2 points), history of psoriasis, family history of psoriasis, dactylitis, juxta-articular new bone formation, rheumatoid-factor negativity and nail dystrophy (1 point each). Sensitivity was 0.914 and specificity 0.987 in a derivation study of 588 cases and 536 controls that included 384 RA patients.
