Practical pointers for a polyarthritis that looks like RA: look for psoriasis (skin, scalp, natal cleft, nails), dactylitis and new bone formation on radiographs, and note that RF negativity is itself a scored feature of psoriatic arthritis. Anti-CCP or high-titre RF positivity makes psoriatic arthritis less likely, although overlap is possible.
psoriatic_arthritis.source: Taylor W et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665-2673 (PMID 16871531); last sentence (anti-CCP/RF positivity makes PsA less likely) is inference from RF negativity being a CASPAR-scored feature, not a directly cited result
psoriatic_arthritis.confidence: high for CASPAR figures; moderate for the practical inference

systemic_lupus_erythematosus.finding: The 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE classification criteria require a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) at least once as the entry criterion, then weighted (2-10 points) criteria across seven clinical domains (constitutional, haematological, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) and three immunological domains (antiphospholipid antibodies, complement proteins, SLE-specific antibodies); 10 points or more classifies SLE (sensitivity 96.1%, specificity 93.4% in validation). Joint symptoms are common in SLE (musculoskeletal is one of the scored domains; the symmetric small-joint pattern is general clinical knowledge), so in a young woman with polyarthritis, ask for and examine for rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, serositis, cytopenias and proteinuria, and check ANA plus dsDNA, complement and urinalysis before labelling RA.
systemic_lupus_erythematosus.source: Aringer M et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); the clinical advice on what to ask and check is derived from the criteria domains rather than a specific trial
systemic_lupus_erythematosus.confidence: high for criteria structure and performance; moderate for the practical advice

gout_and_cppd.finding: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease are crystal arthritides that can mimic inflammatory arthritis, and the discriminating test is synovial fluid analysis. In the 2015 ACR/EULAR gout criteria, monosodium urate crystals in a symptomatic joint/bursa or a tophus are sufficient for classification (criteria sensitivity 92%, specificity 89%); additional domains include pattern of joint involvement, serum urate, double-contour sign on ultrasound or urate on dual-energy CT, and gout-related erosion. In the 2023 ACR/EULAR CPPD criteria, crowned dens syndrome or calcium pyrophosphate crystals in synovial fluid are sufficient; otherwise a weighted score above 56 is used (validation sensitivity 99.2%, specificity 92.5%). Practical point: a hot, swollen joint in a patient with RA still needs aspiration for both crystals and culture. See the gout entry in this knowledge base for the full crystal-arthritis picture.
gout_and_cppd.source: Neogi T et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-1798 (PMID 26359487); Abhishek A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:1248-1257 (PMID 37495237)
gout_and_cppd.confidence: high for both sets of criteria; the practical advice follows from the sufficiency of crystal findings and from the septic-arthritis risk in RA (see red_flags)

chikungunya_and_other_viral_arthritis_in.finding: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is a key India-relevant RA mimic. After acute infection a proportion of patients develop chronic inflammatory polyarthritis of small and large joints that can be erosive and can meet the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria: 8 of 10 US travellers infected in Haiti developed persistent symmetric polyarthritis meeting the 2010 criteria for seronegative RA, with T-cell phenotypes similar to untreated RA. In an Indian series (Ganu et al.), 16 chikungunya IgM-positive patients with arthritis for more than 3 months had erosive, rarely deforming polyarthritis of hands and feet, RF-negative but anti-CCP positive in the majority, non-granulomatous chronic synovitis on biopsy with no viral RNA, and chronic inflammatory arthritis is reported to occur in some (5.6%) after acute chikungunya infection; sulfasalazine with or without methotrexate was reported effective. A 2025 meta-analysis of 16 studies (2,879 patients) found RA diagnosed in a pooled 13.7% (95% CI 6.12-27.87%) after chikungunya infection, with very high heterogeneity (I-squared 96%) due to differing diagnostic criteria and populations. Discriminating steps are a history of outbreak-area exposure and an acute febrile illness (clinical reasoning) and virological or serological confirmation (molecular detection early, immune response later, per the 2018 review); but note that positive anti-CCP in the Indian series shows that anti-CCP positivity does not by itself exclude post-chikungunya arthritis, and there was no published guideline for its management as of the 2018 review. Other viral and infectious mimics of RA include parvovirus B19, hepatitis B and C, HIV, other alphaviruses, tuberculous arthritis and Poncet's disease, leprosy, brucellosis and Lyme disease; clues include travel, fever, rash, genital ulcers, urethral discharge, unpasteurised-milk intake, lymphadenopathy, tenosynovitis, low platelets and a positive Mantoux test. Most viral arthritis is self-limiting, and immunosuppression can worsen an underlying infection, so infection should be excluded before immunosuppressive DMARDs are escalated.
chikungunya_and_other_viral_arthritis_in.source: Miner JJ et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:1214-1220 (PMID 25605621); Ganu MA et al., J Assoc Physicians India 2011;59:83-86 (PMID 21751641); Amaral JK et al., Trop Med Infect Dis 2025;10 (PMID 39998058); Sharma SK et al., Int J Rheum Dis 2018;21:584-601 (PMID 29431292); Sharma V et al., Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2022;36:101736 (PMID 34974970)
chikungunya_and_other_viral_arthritis_in.confidence: moderate-high - the mimicry is well documented; the Indian series is small (16 patients) and single-centre; the 13.7% meta-analytic incidence has very high heterogeneity and should be read as 'a substantial minority', not a precise rate

polymyalgia_rheumatica.finding: The 2012 provisional EULAR/ACR PMR criteria apply to patients aged 50 or more with bilateral shoulder pain not better explained by another pathology, with elevated CRP and/or ESR, and score morning stiffness over 45 minutes (2 points), hip pain or limited range of motion (1), absence of RF and/or ACPA (2) and absence of peripheral joint pain (1); a score of 4 or more gave 68% sensitivity and 78% specificity, with specificity of only 65% for discriminating RA from PMR (88% versus shoulder conditions). This honest overlap matters: elderly-onset RA can present with shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, and PMR can have some peripheral joint involvement; seronegativity, absence of small-joint synovitis and rapid steroid response point to PMR, whereas MCP/PIP/wrist synovitis, erosions and positive anti-CCP point to RA. The criteria are not meant for diagnosis.
polymyalgia_rheumatica.source: Dasgupta B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:484-492 (PMID 22388996); the clinical contrast between features is derived from the criteria's scored items, and rapid steroid response is general clinical knowledge not established in this source
polymyalgia_rheumatica.confidence: moderate-high - criteria figures are primary; the PMR-versus-RA overlap is explicit in the paper

reactive_arthritis.finding: Reactive arthritis is sterile inflammatory arthritis following a remote infection, often gastrointestinal or urogenital, and is diagnosed mainly clinically as acute oligoarticular (large-joint) arthritis developing within 2-4 weeks of the preceding infection; annual incidence in population studies is 0.6-27 per 100,000. No generally agreed diagnostic criteria exist, and HLA-B27 should not be used as a diagnostic tool for acute reactive arthritis. Compared with RA, reactive arthritis is typically asymmetric, oligoarticular and post-infectious rather than symmetric small-joint polyarthritis, and the infection history (diarrhoea, urethritis, conjunctivitis) and its triggering organism matter.
reactive_arthritis.source: Hannu T, Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2011;25:347-357 (PMID 22100285); the contrast with RA distribution (asymmetric versus symmetric) is drawn from the described clinical pattern
reactive_arthritis.confidence: moderate-high - diagnostic uncertainty is acknowledged in the source

practical_discriminating_workup.finding: For any new inflammatory polyarthritis, a reasonable first-line set of tests derived from the differentials above is: ESR and CRP, RF and anti-CCP, ANA (with dsDNA and complement if positive), serum urate, hepatitis B and C serology and (in outbreak/endemic settings) chikungunya IgM/IgG, plain radiographs of hands and feet, and arthrocentesis with crystal analysis and culture for any hot or effusion-dominant joint. This is a synthesis of the source-specific findings in this section (crystal analysis for gout/CPPD; ANA entry for SLE; viral serology and Mantoux for infectious mimics; RF/anti-CCP and erosions for RA) rather than a single published algorithm.
practical_discriminating_workup.source: Synthesis of Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241); Aringer M et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); Neogi T et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-1798 (PMID 26359487); Sharma V et al., Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2022;36:101736 (PMID 34974970)
practical_discriminating_workup.confidence: moderate - reasoned synthesis; not itself a validated pathway

red_flags: Hot, swollen, painful joint (especially a single joint or a joint out of proportion to the rest) or fever in a patient with RA: treat as septic arthritis until proven otherwise. RA carries a strongly raised risk of septic arthritis - odds ratio 4.0 (95% CI 1.9-8.3) in a prospective clinic study, with joint prosthesis (OR 15), skin infection (OR 27.2) and joint surgery (OR 5.1) adding risk; in UK primary-care data the incidence rate of septic arthritis was 12.9 times higher in RA than in matched controls, and prednisolone (incidence rate ratio 2.94), sulfasalazine (1.74) and penicillamine (2.51) were associated with higher incidence while methotrexate was not. A flare and an infection can look identical, so aspirate and culture before attributing to a flare (the aspiration advice is clinical inference from these risk figures). [Source: Kaandorp CJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1819-1825 (PMID 8849354); Edwards CJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;57:1151-1157 (PMID 17907232)]

Chronic neck pain or any neurological deficit (myelopathy) in a patient with RA: possible cervical spine instability (atlantoaxial subluxation, atlantoaxial impaction or subaxial subluxation) with impending myelopathy. More than half of RA patients develop cervical spine involvement during the first 10 years, and the proportion with subluxation rises steeply with duration; although neurological injury is relatively uncommon, MRI is indicated when neurological deficit occurs or when plain films show atlantoaxial subluxation with a posterior atlantodental interval of 14 mm or less, any atlantoaxial impaction, or subaxial canal diameter of 14 mm or less, and surgery is considered for progressive deficit, atlantoaxial impaction or cord stenosis. Relevance before anaesthesia: in a single-centre record review of 217 surgeries in RA patients, 92 patients receiving airway management had cervical radiographs; 20% of those showed cervical spine abnormality but only 8% had a complete series adequate to assess atlantoaxial subluxation, and the findings did not change airway technique - so flag RA when intubation or neck manipulation is planned. [Source: van der Heijde DM, Br J Rheumatol 1995;34 Suppl 2:74-78 (PMID 8535653); Kim DH et al., J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2005;13:463-474 (PMID 16272271); Lopez-Olivo MA et al., J Clin Rheumatol 2012;18:61-66 (PMID 22334269)]

Rheumatoid vasculitis: new skin infarcts or unexplained systemic symptoms in a patient with long-standing RA (average RA duration 15.6 years in the UK series), particularly in smokers. It is rare (about 3.9 per million per year in a UK register) but 5-year mortality was 60% and 1-year mortality 12% despite modern immunosuppression, and smoking at diagnosis was the strongest predictor of severe extra-articular disease (RR 2.94). Urgent specialist assessment. [Source: Ntatsaki E et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2014;53:145-152 (PMID 24108586); Makol A et al., Curr Opin Rheumatol 2015;27:63-70 (PMID 25405822); Turesson C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2003;62:722-727 (PMID 12860726)]

New or progressive exertional breathlessness or dry cough in a patient with RA: consider RA-associated interstitial lung disease (ILD) rather than attributing it to age, smoking or anaemia. Median survival after ILD diagnosis was only 2.6 years in a population cohort, and the risk is higher in men, older-onset disease, smokers, anti-CCP-high and severe RA; baseline gas transfer and HRCT chest are the screening and characterisation tools cited; UIP pattern and extensive disease predict worse survival. Remember drug causes and infection also need consideration (not derived from these sources). [Source: Bongartz T et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1583-1591 (PMID 20155830); Kelly CA et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2014;53:1676-1682 (PMID 24758887)]

Before starting biologic or targeted synthetic DMARDs (and, per EULAR, considered before conventional DMARDs and glucocorticoids too): screen for latent tuberculosis, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and check vaccination and infection history. EULAR 2022: screen for latent TB before biologic/targeted synthetic DMARDs (interferon-gamma release assay preferred over tuberculin skin test where available); define hepatitis B status before starting antirheumatic drugs and guide antiviral treatment by it; refer all hepatitis-C-RNA-positive patients for antiviral therapy; Pneumocystis prophylaxis is suggested for prednisolone over 15-30 mg/day for over 2-4 weeks. Tuberculosis after infliximab: 70 reports (FDA MedWatch), median 12 weeks after starting, 48 after 3 or fewer infusions, 40 extrapulmonary (17 disseminated); 64 of 70 came from low-TB-incidence countries, and a 2017 review describes biologic-related TB as an area of potential concern for TB-endemic nations like India. For India there is no national consensus on latent TB screening and treatment in rheumatic patients (as of the 2017 review, which proposes a step-wise algorithm using history, tuberculin skin test, IGRA, chest radiograph and isoniazid preventive therapy). [Source: Fragoulis GE et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:742-753 (PMID 36328476); Keane J et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1098-1104 (PMID 11596589); Handa R et al., Int J Rheum Dis 2017;20:1313-1325 (PMID 28730751)]

RA with low neutrophil count, splenomegaly and recurrent bacterial infections, leg ulcers or severe joint destruction: Felty's syndrome (less than 1% of RA) - infection risk from neutropenia raises mortality and needs specialist management (DMARDs such as methotrexate, G-CSF, or splenectomy in selected cases). [Source: Balint GP, Balint PV, Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2004;18:631-645 (PMID 15454123)]

Delay is itself a red flag: 3 or more swollen joints, MCP/MTP involvement or morning stiffness of 30 minutes or more should trigger early referral, and in a Leiden early-arthritis cohort only 31% of RA patients were assessed within 12 weeks of symptom onset (median total delay 13.7 weeks; RA and spondyloarthritis had the longest delay at 18 weeks). Assessment after 12 or more weeks was associated with a hazard ratio 1.87 for not achieving DMARD-free remission and 1.3 times the rate of joint destruction. [Source: Emery P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2002;61:290-297 (PMID 11874828); van der Linden MP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:3537-3546 (PMID 20722031)]
symptoms.red_flags_source: Sources are given inline for each red flag above: Kaandorp 1995 (PMID 8849354); Edwards 2007 (PMID 17907232); van der Heijde 1995 (PMID 8535653); Kim 2005 (PMID 16272271); Lopez-Olivo 2012 (PMID 22334269); Ntatsaki 2014 (PMID 24108586); Makol 2015 (PMID 25405822); Turesson 2003 (PMID 12860726); Bongartz 2010 (PMID 20155830); Kelly 2014 (PMID 24758887); Fragoulis 2023 (PMID 36328476); Keane 2001 (PMID 11596589); Handa 2017 (PMID 28730751); Balint 2004 (PMID 15454123); Emery 2002 (PMID 11874828); van der Linden 2010 (PMID 20722031)

real_risk_factors.note: RA is more common in women: in the GBD 2021 analysis the age-standardised female-to-male prevalence ratio was 2.45 (95% CI 2.40-2.47), and a Lancet review states the disorder is most typical in women and elderly people. In a Norfolk primary-care register the incidence at baseline under the 2010 criteria was 54 per 100,000 in women and 25 per 100,000 in men (about 2.2 to 1). Male sex was however a risk factor for RA-associated ILD (see extra_articular_disease).
real_risk_factors.source: GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e594-e610 (PMID 37795020); Scott DL et al., Lancet 2010;376:1094-1108 (PMID 20870100); Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMID 22945499)

real_risk_factors.factor: Genetics - HLA-DRB1 shared epitope, other risk loci, family history
real_risk_factors.note: About 50% of RA risk is genetic (twin heritability 53-65%); 101 risk loci have been identified and HLA-DR beta-1 amino-acid positions 11, 71 and 74 explain most of the MHC association with seropositive RA. Shared-epitope alleles are a risk factor for anti-citrulline-positive but not anti-citrulline-negative RA. See definition_and_pathophysiology for the numbers and for the limited Indian HLA data.
real_risk_factors.source: Raychaudhuri S et al., Nat Genet 2012;44:291-296 (PMID 22286218); Okada Y et al., Nature 2014;506:376-381 (PMID 24390342); MacGregor AJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:30-37 (PMID 10643697); Klareskog L et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:38-46 (PMID 16385494)

real_risk_factors.note: Smoking is the strongest established modifiable environmental risk factor. Meta-analysis of 16 observational studies (odds ratios): men - ever-smokers 1.89 (95% CI 1.56-2.28), current 1.87 (1.49-2.34), past 1.76 (1.33-2.31); for RF-positive RA in men, ever 3.02 (2.35-3.88) and current 3.91 (2.78-5.50); 20 or more pack-years 2.31 (1.55-3.41) in men and 1.75 (1.52-2.02) in women. Women - ever 1.27 (1.12-1.44), current 1.31 (1.12-1.54), past 1.22 (1.06-1.40); for RF-positive RA in women the association was not statistically significant (ever OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.99-1.80). A Swedish population case-control study found increased risk only for seropositive, not seronegative, RA (ever-smokers OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2-2.3 in women and 1.9, 95% CI 1.0-3.5 in men), apparent only after 20 or more years of smoking, evident even at 6-9 cigarettes per day, and persisting for 10-19 years after cessation. Smoking plus double-copy HLA-DR shared epitope raised the risk of ACPA-positive RA 21-fold versus non-smokers without shared-epitope genes; smoking is thought to trigger citrullination in the lung (citrullinated proteins seen in bronchoalveolar lavage cells of smokers, not non-smokers). Smoking accounts for 7.1% (95% UI 3.6-10.3) of RA DALYs in the GBD 2021 estimate. Smoking at RA diagnosis also predicted severe extra-articular disease (RR 2.94). Practical point: smoking cessation lowers a modifiable risk but risk persists for many years after quitting.
real_risk_factors.source: Sugiyama D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:70-81 (PMID 19174392); Stolt P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2003;62:835-841 (PMID 12922955); Klareskog L et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:38-46 (PMID 16385494); GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e594-e610 (PMID 37795020); Turesson C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2003;62:722-727 (PMID 12860726)

real_risk_factors.note: In the Swedish EIRA study (276 male cases and 276 male controls), silica-exposed men had an odds ratio for RA of 2.2 (95% CI 1.2-3.9), 3.0 (95% CI 1.2-7.6) for rock drilling or stone crushing, not explained by smoking. In a larger male study (577 cases, 659 controls), silica exposure raised the risk of ACPA-positive RA (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.13-2.48) but not ACPA-negative RA (OR 0.98), and silica-exposed current smokers had an odds ratio of 7.36 (95% CI 3.31-16.38), exceeding the sum of the separate effects (attributable proportion due to interaction 0.60). Both studies are Swedish, male-only and self-reported exposure; no Indian silica-RA study (stone quarry, mining, construction workers) was retrieved, so the Indian relevance is inferred, not shown.
real_risk_factors.source: Stolt P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2005;64:582-586 (PMID 15319232); Stolt P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1072-1076 (PMID 19966090)

real_risk_factors.note: Meta-analysis of 21 studies: periodontitis was more common in RA than in healthy controls (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04-1.23) but this difference was not replicated when RA was compared with OA controls, so the association is weak and may partly reflect shared inflammatory or behavioural factors. In the Swedish EIRA study, antibodies to the P. gingivalis virulence factor RgpB were associated with RA (OR 2.96, 95% CI 2.00-4.37), more strongly than smoking (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07-1.74), with interactions with smoking and the shared epitope in ACPA-positive RA. Honest reading: P. gingivalis is a credible candidate trigger in a subset, but causality is not proven and no periodontal treatment has been shown here to prevent RA.
real_risk_factors.source: Fuggle NR et al., Front Immunol 2016;7:80 (PMID 26973655); Kharlamova N et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2016;68:604-613 (PMID 26554752)

real_risk_factors.note: Dose-response meta-analysis of 11 studies: obese individuals had a relative risk of RA of 1.31 (95% CI 1.12-1.53) versus normal weight and overweight 1.15 (95% CI 1.03-1.29); versus BMI under 30, obesity RR 1.25 (95% CI 1.07-1.45); non-linear association; substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 63-70%) and limited adjustment for confounders, so this is a modest association of uncertain independence.
real_risk_factors.source: Qin B et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:86 (PMID 25890172)

real_risk_factors.note: A meta-analysis of 16 studies found RA diagnosed in a pooled 13.7% (95% CI 6.12-27.87%) of people after chikungunya infection, with I-squared 96%. Because chronic post-chikungunya arthritis can itself meet RA classification criteria (see differential_diagnosis), this figure mixes true new-onset RA with chikungunya arthritis that mimics it, and cannot be read as a clean risk factor.
real_risk_factors.source: Amaral JK et al., Trop Med Infect Dis 2025;10 (PMID 39998058); Miner JJ et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:1214-1220 (PMID 25605621)

global.finding: Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis (204 countries, 98 prevalence and 25 incidence studies): an estimated 17.6 million people (95% uncertainty interval 15.8-20.3 million) had RA worldwide in 2020; age-standardised prevalence 208.8 per 100,000 (186.8-241.1), a 14.1% increase since 1990; 38,300 deaths (age-standardised death rate 0.47 per 100,000, a 23.8% decrease since 1990); 3.06 million DALYs, of which 76.4% was years lived with disability; prevalence forecast to rise to 31.7 million by 2050. Other estimates differ by method and era: 0.24% (GBD 2010, ACR 1987 case definition, unchanged 1990-2010); 0.46% (95% CI 0.39-0.54%; 95% prediction interval 0.06-1.27%) in a 2021 meta-analysis of 67 population studies; 0.5-1.0% of adults in industrialised countries; and about 5 per 1000 in a 2018 JAMA review. The spread of 0.24% to about 0.5-1% is driven by case definition, data source and geography, not by real disagreement about disease occurrence.
global.source: GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e594-e610 (PMID 37795020); Cross M et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1316-1322 (PMID 24550173); Almutairi K et al., Rheumatol Int 2021;41:863-877 (PMID 33175207); Scott DL et al., Lancet 2010;376:1094-1108 (PMID 20870100); Aletaha D et al., JAMA 2018;320:1360-1372 (PMID 30285183)
global.confidence: high for the GBD 2021 figures (primary abstract); moderate-high for cross-study comparison because case definitions differ

incidence_and_sex_ratio.finding: Incidence in industrialised countries is about 5-50 new cases per 100,000 per year. In the Norfolk Arthritis Register (2010 criteria at baseline visit) incidence was 54 per 100,000 in women and 25 per 100,000 in men. The age-standardised female-to-male prevalence ratio globally was 2.45. RA is most typical in women and elderly people, so it is not only a young-adult disease.
incidence_and_sex_ratio.source: Scott DL et al., Lancet 2010;376:1094-1108 (PMID 20870100); Humphreys JH et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:1315-1320 (PMID 22945499); GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e594-e610 (PMID 37795020)
incidence_and_sex_ratio.confidence: high - but incidence is from Norfolk (UK), not India

prevalence_varies_by_method_and_setting.finding: In a systematic review of 60 population-based studies the reported RA point prevalence ranged from 0.00% to 2.70% (mean 0.56%); prevalence was higher in urban than in rural settings in that review, though the authors caution that this may reflect poor case finding in areas with less healthcare access, and studies using linked databases with rheumatologist-validated diagnoses gave the highest and most consistent estimates. Practical takeaway: any single quoted prevalence should be read together with its case definition and data source.
prevalence_varies_by_method_and_setting.source: Almutairi KB et al., J Rheumatol 2021;48:669-676 (PMID 33060323)
prevalence_varies_by_method_and_setting.confidence: high for the review's own findings

india_specific.finding: Indian data come from a small number of community surveys and clinic studies, not a national registry. (1) A house-to-house survey of a rural population near Delhi (44,551 adults over 16; response 89.5%; 299 met the 1987 ARA criteria) gave a prevalence of 0.75%, which the authors projected to about 7 million patients in India at that time (a 1993 projection, not a current count). (2) The WHO-ILAR COPCORD survey in Bhigwan, a rural village in Pune district (1996; 4,092 adults; response 89%) found RA prevalence of 0.5% (95% CI 0.3-0.7) by ACR criteria, described as the highest reported in an Asian rural COPCORD study, plus 0.9% unclassifiable inflammatory arthritis. (3) A later urban Pune COPCORD survey (8,145 adults) found age-sex-standardised RA prevalence of 0.2% versus 0.5% in rural Bhigwan, with rural rates of most musculoskeletal disorders significantly higher than urban - the opposite direction to the pattern seen in the global review. Taken together, the retrieved Indian community estimates are about 0.2-0.75%, broadly comparable to Western figures, but these come from two regions (the Delhi periphery and Pune district) and surveys done between 1993 and 2009, and cannot be extrapolated to all of India. A 2016 literature review of RA in India (28 observational studies, 1985-2012; only 7 on descriptive epidemiology) found the studies to have small sample sizes, cross-sectional designs and/or clinic settings that may not be representative, and concluded that conclusions for the entire Indian RA population cannot be drawn.
india_specific.source: Malaviya AN et al., Rheumatol Int 1993;13:131-134 (PMID 8310203); Chopra A et al., J Assoc Physicians India 2001;49:240-246 (PMID 11225138); Joshi VL et al., J Rheumatol 2009;36:614-622 (PMID 19208598); Handa R et al., Int J Rheum Dis 2016;19:440-451 (PMID 26171649)
india_specific.confidence: moderate - primary Indian surveys were read, but they are old (1993-2009), regional and use different case definitions; no GBD India-specific figure was retrieved and verified in this pass

india_registry_status.finding: No national population-based RA registry and no nationwide incidence estimate for India was identified in this literature search (PubMed and web search), and the 2016 review of Indian RA literature points to the same limitation (small, cross-sectional, clinic-based or regional studies). Drug-specific registries exist (for example, the ASPIRE registry of an adalimumab biosimilar in RA), but these describe treated patients on a specific product, not population incidence or prevalence. 'None identified in this search' is stated, not 'none exists'; a web search for an Indian Rheumatology Association RA registry did not surface one either.
india_registry_status.source: Handa R et al., Int J Rheum Dis 2016;19:440-451 (PMID 26171649); Kapoor S et al., Rheumatol Ther 2019;6:451-459 (PMID 31254222, title-level); search outcome (absence of evidence) is reported by the researcher, not a published source
india_registry_status.confidence: moderate - an absence claim can only be as strong as the search; stated as such

erosions_and_radiographic_progression.finding: Historical data: in prospective studies of early RA about 75% of patients develop joint erosions, most first erosions appearing within the first 2 years, and the rate of progression is highest in the early years. In 502 patients with RA of under 1 year at entry (enrolled in a trial of three treatment strategies), radiographic damage progressed at a stable mean rate of 8.6 modified Sharp/van der Heijde units per year (erosion score 5.4, narrowing 3.2 per year) over up to 6 years. Modern data show that intensive early treatment slows this substantially: in the BeSt trial (508 early-RA patients), the median one-year increase in total Sharp/van der Heijde score was 2.0 and 2.5 with sequential monotherapy and step-up combination therapy, versus 1.0 with initial combination therapy including tapered prednisone and 0.5 with initial combination therapy including infliximab; a review states that early diagnosis and treatment can avert or substantially slow progression of joint damage in up to 90% of patients. These figures come from different cohorts, eras and summary statistics (mean over years versus median at 1 year) and should not be treated as a strict before/after comparison.
erosions_and_radiographic_progression.source: van der Heijde DM, Br J Rheumatol 1995;34 Suppl 2:74-78 (PMID 8535653); Hulsmans HM et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:1927-1940 (PMID 11014342); Goekoop-Ruiterman YP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:3381-3390 (PMID 16258899); Aletaha D et al., JAMA 2018;320:1360-1372 (PMID 30285183)
erosions_and_radiographic_progression.confidence: high for direction (damage is early and treatment slows it); moderate for cross-study numeric comparison

window_of_opportunity_for_early_treatmen.finding: A systematic review of 18 cohort studies and trials (10 high quality) found strong evidence for an association between longer symptom duration at treatment start and greater radiographic progression, and a meta-analysis showed symptom duration was independently associated with DMARD-free sustained remission (hazard ratio 0.989 per week of additional symptom duration, 95% CI 0.983-0.995), with moderate evidence for other remission outcomes; the authors conclude the data may support a therapeutic window of opportunity. In the Leiden Early Arthritis Clinic cohort (598 RA patients), assessment 12 or more weeks after symptom onset was associated with a hazard ratio of 1.87 for not achieving DMARD-free remission and a 1.3 times higher rate of joint destruction over 6 years, yet only 31% of RA patients were assessed within 12 weeks. In an Italian real-world study of 1,795 early arthritis patients (711 with RA), DAS28 remission at 12 months was 34.3% and ACR remission 15.2%; the only two independent predictors of remission were being 'very early RA' (under 12 weeks of symptoms at first treatment) and being on a DMARD within 3 months of onset. A small case-control study (20 very-early vs 20 late-early RA patients; median 3 vs 12 months to first DMARD) found greater DAS28 improvement (2.8 vs 1.7) and less Larsen-score progression over 36 months in the very-early group. Honest limits: apart from selected trials these are observational, and delay is correlated with patient characteristics (in Leiden, older age, female sex, gradual onset, small-joint involvement, lower CRP and autoantibody positivity were associated with longer delay), so some of the association may reflect disease type rather than timing alone.
window_of_opportunity_for_early_treatmen.source: van Nies JA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:861-870 (PMID 23572339); van der Linden MP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:3537-3546 (PMID 20722031); Gremese E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:858-862 (PMID 22798566); Nell VP et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2004;43:906-914 (PMID 15113999)
window_of_opportunity_for_early_treatmen.confidence: moderate-high - consistent across four independent designs; residual confounding acknowledged

remission_and_flares.finding: Remission is achievable but not universal or durable. In a review, methotrexate plus glucocorticoids brings 40-50% of patients to remission or at least low disease activity, and sequential targeted therapy (TNF, IL-6 or JAK inhibitors) allows up to 75% of patients to reach the target over time. In the TICORA trial (111 patients), intensive treat-to-target management gave remission (DAS below 1.6) in 65% versus 16% with routine care (odds ratio 9.7, 95% CI 3.9-23.9). In real-world clinics remission is lower: 34.3% by DAS28 and 15.2% by ACR criteria at 12 months in an Italian early-arthritis cohort; SDAI/CDAI remission in about 1 in 4 clinic patients and up to one-third of early-arthritis trial patients; and, in the ACR/EULAR remission revision, 14.8-20.6% of early-RA and 4.2-6.0% of established-RA trial participants at 6 months. Sustained remission is uncommon: in the BRASS registry (871 patients with 2 or more years of follow-up), fewer than 50% of patients in remission at a visit were still in remission 1 year later (median remission survival 1 year). The 2025 EULAR update states that with sustained remission DMARDs may be tapered but caution is required because stopping often leads to a flare.
remission_and_flares.source: Aletaha D et al., JAMA 2018;320:1360-1372 (PMID 30285183); Grigor C et al., Lancet 2004;364:263-269 (PMID 15262104); Gremese E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:858-862 (PMID 22798566); Smolen JS et al., Clin Exp Rheumatol 2014;32(5 Suppl 85):S75-79 (PMID 25365093); Studenic P et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2023;75:15-22 (PMID 36274193); Prince FH et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2012;14:R68 (PMID 22429277); Smolen JS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2026;85:991-1009 (PMID 41826212)
remission_and_flares.confidence: high that remission is achievable in a substantial minority and often not sustained; exact percentages vary widely by remission definition, setting and population

disability_and_work.finding: In a Finnish cohort of 82 patients with early RA who were gainfully employed at onset (treated with a 'sawtooth' DMARD strategy; published in 1999, so pre-biologic era), 19% were retired wholly or partly because of RA at 2 years and 44% (36 of 82) at an average of 9.9 years, though 51% were still gainfully employed; physically heavy work at baseline was the strongest independent predictor of permanent work disability. The authors conclude working capacity is in danger from the very start of RA. These figures pre-date modern early biologic and treat-to-target practice; a current-era work-disability estimate was not retrieved and verified in this pass, so the 44% should be read as a historical upper benchmark rather than a present-day expected outcome.
disability_and_work.source: Sokka T et al., J Rheumatol 1999;26:1681-1685 (PMID 10451062)
disability_and_work.confidence: moderate - small single-centre, older cohort; direction is well accepted but the number is dated

prognostic_factors.finding: Factors linked to worse outcomes in the sources reviewed: presence of autoantibodies, high disease activity and early erosions (EULAR 2022 uses autoantibodies, high disease activity, early erosions or failure of two conventional DMARDs as poor prognostic factors to justify adding a biologic); anti-CCP positivity (anti-CCP predicted radiographic progression better than IgM-RF in 3 of 4 studies in a meta-analysis); smoking and early disability (for severe extra-articular disease); longer symptom duration before treatment; and, for RA-ILD, older age, male sex and severe RA. Neutral finding: seronegative RA is not a mild disease, with similar radiographic progression and 24-month remission rates to seropositive RA under treat-to-target, though the initial response is slower.
prognostic_factors.source: Smolen JS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18 (PMID 36357155); Nishimura K et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;146:797-808 (PMID 17548411); Turesson C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2003;62:722-727 (PMID 12860726); Nordberg LB et al., RMD Open 2018;4:e000752 (PMID 30564452); Bongartz T et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1583-1591 (PMID 20155830)
prognostic_factors.confidence: moderate-high - each factor comes from a separate study; the list is a summary, not a validated prediction model

mortality_and_life_expectancy.finding: RA carries excess mortality that has fallen over time but not vanished. A meta-analysis of 11 inception-cohort studies (1955-1995 enrolment; 51,819 patients) found a mean incidence mortality rate of 2.7 per 100 person-years, declining 2.3% per year, but the pooled standardised mortality ratio remained 1.47 (95% CI 1.19-1.83) with no decline over time. In the Minnesota community cohort virtually all excess mortality occurred in patients with severe extra-articular disease (vasculitis, pericarditis, pleuritis, Felty's syndrome). ILD contributed about 13% of the excess mortality in a population cohort. GBD 2021 estimated 38,300 RA deaths globally in 2020 with age-standardised death rate down 23.8% since 1990. An estimate of years of life lost was not retrieved and verified, so none is quoted.
mortality_and_life_expectancy.source: Dadoun S et al., Joint Bone Spine 2013;80:29-33 (PMID 22459416); Turesson C et al., J Rheumatol 2002;29:62-67 (PMID 11824973); Bongartz T et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1583-1591 (PMID 20155830); GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e594-e610 (PMID 37795020)
mortality_and_life_expectancy.confidence: moderate-high - the SMR meta-analysis covers cohorts up to 1995, before modern treat-to-target

cardiovascular_risk.finding: Cardiovascular mortality in RA is about 50% higher than in the general population (meta-SMR 1.50, 95% CI 1.39-1.61; ischaemic heart disease 1.59; cerebrovascular 1.52), and incident cardiovascular disease is increased 48% (pooled RR 1.48; myocardial infarction 1.68; stroke 1.41; heart failure 1.87 from a single study). In inception-cohort subgroups the excess was not statistically significant (mortality meta-SMR 1.19, 95% CI 0.86-1.68; incident CVD RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.97-1.65), suggesting the excess may be smaller in newly diagnosed patients and may accumulate with duration and inflammation - but these subgroups were small and heterogeneity was high, so they should not be read as proof that early RA carries no cardiovascular risk. Practical takeaway: assess and treat conventional cardiovascular risk factors in every RA patient.
cardiovascular_risk.source: Avina-Zubieta JA et al., Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1690-1697 (PMID 19035419); Avina-Zubieta JA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:1524-1529 (PMID 22425941)
cardiovascular_risk.confidence: moderate-high - two meta-analyses in agreement; the practical takeaway is the researcher's reading, not stated as a guideline in these abstracts

clinical_takeaway.point: Suspect and refer early: 3 or more swollen joints, MCP/MTP involvement, or morning stiffness of 30 minutes or more should prompt rapid rheumatology referral, and a normal ESR/CRP or negative RF must not delay it.
clinical_takeaway.why: About 35-45% of RA patients have normal ESR, CRP or RF at presentation, and 58% of active-RA patients in a large registry had neither ESR nor CRP elevated, so laboratory normality does not exclude disease; the clinical referral rule is built on joint findings and stiffness. In Leiden, only 31% of RA patients were assessed within 12 weeks. A 2013 real-world study quotes the EULAR early-arthritis recommendation to refer arthritis of more than one joint to be seen by a rheumatologist, ideally within 6 weeks of symptom onset; the exact wording of the 2016 EULAR update was not retrievable (paywalled), so this quotation is second-hand.
clinical_takeaway.source: Emery P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2002;61:290-297 (PMID 11874828); Sokka T et al., J Rheumatol 2009;36:1387-1390 (PMID 19411389); Kay J et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2014;16:R40 (PMID 24485007); van der Linden MP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:3537-3546 (PMID 20722031); Gremese E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:858-862 (PMID 22798566, quoting the EULAR early-arthritis recommendation)

clinical_takeaway.point: Start DMARD therapy early - the observed benefit window is within about 3 months of symptom onset (and the 3-month mark also applies to reassessing response) - and do not wait for erosions or high-titre serology.
clinical_takeaway.why: Time to first DMARD is associated with radiographic progression and with DMARD-free remission (HR 0.989 per additional week; 12 weeks or more delay HR 1.87 for not achieving DMARD-free remission; being on a DMARD within 3 months of onset independently predicted remission in a real-world cohort). Erosions typically appear within the first 2 years, so treatment after erosions appear has already missed part of the window. Honest limit: the '3 months' figure is a study-derived window from observational data, not a randomised-trial threshold, and delay is partly confounded by disease type. The current EULAR recommendations (2022 update; 2025 update published 2026) lead with methotrexate, ideally with short-term glucocorticoids, with escalation to a biologic or JAK inhibitor if the response is insufficient after 3-6 months.
clinical_takeaway.source: van Nies JA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:861-870 (PMID 23572339); van der Linden MP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:3537-3546 (PMID 20722031); Gremese E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2013;72:858-862 (PMID 22798566); Nell VP et al., Rheumatology 2004;43:906-914 (PMID 15113999); van der Heijde DM, Br J Rheumatol 1995;34 Suppl 2:74-78 (PMID 8535653); Smolen JS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:3-18 (PMID 36357155) and 2026;85:991-1009 (PMID 41826212)

clinical_takeaway.point: Treat to target with a composite score that includes joint counts (CDAI, SDAI or DAS28): aim for remission (or at least low disease activity in long-standing disease), reassess every 1-3 months while active, and change therapy if the target is not reached - not by ESR/CRP alone.
clinical_takeaway.why: The international treat-to-target task force recommends remission (low disease activity as an alternative in long-standing disease), follow-up every 1-3 months during active disease with therapy adapted to reach the target, and composite measures that include joint counts. A review of the evidence recommends at least 50% improvement in disease activity within 3 months and remission or low disease activity within 6 months. TICORA showed 65% remission with intensive tight control versus 16% with routine care. Thresholds: CDAI remission 2.8 or below, low 10 or below, moderate 22 or below; SDAI 3.3, 11, 26; DAS28 2.6, 3.2, 5.1.
clinical_takeaway.source: Smolen JS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:3-15 (PMID 25969430); Aletaha D et al., JAMA 2018;320:1360-1372 (PMID 30285183); Grigor C et al., Lancet 2004;364:263-269 (PMID 15262104); Anderson J et al., Arthritis Care Res 2012;64:640-647 (PMID 22473918)

clinical_takeaway.point: Before any biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD - and considered before conventional DMARDs and glucocorticoids - screen for latent TB (IGRA preferred where available), hepatitis B (define status, guide antiviral treatment) and hepatitis C (refer RNA-positive patients for antivirals); in India, give latent-TB screening particular attention.
clinical_takeaway.why: EULAR 2022 recommendations on screening and prophylaxis of chronic and opportunistic infections. Tuberculosis has been reported soon after starting anti-TNF therapy (median 12 weeks with infliximab in a pharmacovigilance series, many extrapulmonary or disseminated), and a 2017 review describes biologic-related TB as an area of potential concern for TB-endemic nations like India and notes there was no Indian consensus on latent TB screening and treatment. The emphasis on India is the researcher's practical reading of the EULAR recommendation plus the Indian TB burden, not the wording of a guideline.
clinical_takeaway.source: Fragoulis GE et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:742-753 (PMID 36328476); Keane J et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1098-1104 (PMID 11596589); Handa R et al., Int J Rheum Dis 2017;20:1313-1325 (PMID 28730751)

clinical_takeaway.point: In India, before labelling a new symmetric polyarthritis as RA, actively consider chikungunya (and other viral) arthritis, and confirm the diagnosis with history, serology and follow-up rather than the 2010 criteria alone.
clinical_takeaway.why: Chronic post-chikungunya arthritis can be erosive, can meet 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria (8 of 10 travellers in one series), can be RF-negative yet anti-CCP-positive (Indian series), and is not treated as an emergency but may need DMARDs. Escalating immunosuppression in an unrecognised infectious arthritis carries its own risk.
clinical_takeaway.source: Miner JJ et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:1214-1220 (PMID 25605621); Ganu MA et al., J Assoc Physicians India 2011;59:83-86 (PMID 21751641); Sharma V et al., Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2022;36:101736 (PMID 34974970)

clinical_takeaway.point: Treat seronegative RA as seriously as seropositive RA, and assess and manage cardiovascular risk, lung disease and infection risk in every RA patient.
clinical_takeaway.why: Seronegative early RA had more inflammatory activity at presentation and, once treated to target, similar radiographic progression and remission rates at 24 months. Cardiovascular mortality is about 50% higher, RA-ILD carries a median survival of 2.6 years after diagnosis, and septic arthritis risk is about 13-fold higher than in controls.
clinical_takeaway.source: Nordberg LB et al., RMD Open 2018;4:e000752 (PMID 30564452); Avina-Zubieta JA et al., Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1690-1697 (PMID 19035419); Bongartz T et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1583-1591 (PMID 20155830); Edwards CJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;57:1151-1157 (PMID 17907232)

clinical_takeaway.point: A hot, swollen joint in a patient with RA - aspirate and culture before assuming it is a flare; and flag RA before anaesthesia because of possible cervical spine instability.
clinical_takeaway.why: Septic arthritis incidence is 12.9-fold higher in RA, and steroid and some DMARD exposure raises it further; cervical spine involvement affects over half of RA patients within 10 years, while only a minority of RA patients in one surgical series had a complete cervical radiographic series to assess atlantoaxial subluxation before anaesthesia.
clinical_takeaway.source: Edwards CJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;57:1151-1157 (PMID 17907232); van der Heijde DM, Br J Rheumatol 1995;34 Suppl 2:74-78 (PMID 8535653); Kim DH et al., J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2005;13:463-474 (PMID 16272271); Lopez-Olivo MA et al., J Clin Rheumatol 2012;18:61-66 (PMID 22334269)

gout.name: Gout
gout.icd11_hint: FA25 Gout (WHO ICD-11 MMS; FA25.0 primary, FA25.1 secondary, FA25.2 unspecified); legacy ICD-10 M10
gout.CURABILITY_NOTE: Gout is NOT curable in the sense of removing its underlying cause, but it is the rare chronic arthritis in which a genuine near-cure state is real and trial-proven: sustained lowering of serum urate to below 6 mg/dL (below 5 mg/dL in tophaceous disease) dissolves monosodium urate crystals and, in patients who stay on therapy, ends flares and shrinks or removes tophi. The evidence: (a) crystal dissolution - in 18 of 18 asymptomatic joints, monosodium urate crystals disappeared from synovial fluid after serum urate was normalised, in 3-33 months (longer in longer-standing gout; Pascual 2007); tophus shrinkage speed rises linearly as serum urate falls (Perez-Ruiz 2002); (b) flare cessation - patients reaching a mean serum urate below 6 mg/dL had a flare in 27% (91 of 343) between months 12 and 24 versus 64% (156 of 245) of those who did not (adjusted OR 0.29; Stamp 2022), and in the 5-year febuxostat FOCUS extension 93% of remaining subjects held serum urate below 6.0 mg/dL with flares nearly abolished and baseline tophi resolved in 69% (18 of 26; half the enrolled subjects had dropped out, so this is a completer figure); (c) attainable in routine care - nurse-led treat-to-target care brought 95% of patients to serum urate below 6 mg/dL at 2 years versus 30% under usual care (Doherty 2018, 517 patients). What is NOT cured: the hyperuricaemia itself (renal urate under-excretion and/or over-production, obesity, diuretics, diet) is still there; the 2020 ACR guideline conditionally recommends continuing urate-lowering therapy indefinitely, and in one prospective cohort (Perez-Ruiz 2011, 211 patients) that withdrew therapy after 5 years of control, recurrence was independently related to serum urate during and after therapy, with no crystal-proven recurrence in patients whose serum urate after withdrawal stayed below 7 mg/dL - so intermittent therapy may be possible in selected patients but is not the default. The near-cure also depends on adherence and on actually reaching the target - fixed-dose allopurinol 300 mg often fails (22% at target in APEX versus 69% with dose escalation in Stamp 2017), and the first 3-6 months of treatment need anti-inflammatory prophylaxis because flares transiently increase as crystals mobilise (Borstad 2004: 0.52 versus 2.91 flares). Acute-flare drugs (NSAIDs, colchicine, glucocorticoids, IL-1 inhibitors) treat only the inflammation and do not remove crystals. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has gout: (1) treat the flare promptly with an NSAID, low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg then 0.6 mg, not 4.8 mg) or oral prednisolone 30-35 mg for 4-5 days, whichever suits the patient's comorbidities (IL-1 blockade only when all three are unsuitable); (2) if there are tophi, frequent flares, radiographic damage, or two or more flares a year, start urate-lowering therapy - allopurinol from 100 mg/day (lower in CKD), escalated until serum urate is below 6 mg/dL (below 5 if tophi), with HLA-B*58:01 testing in Southeast Asian and African American patients; febuxostat, benzbromarone or probenecid if allopurinol fails or is not tolerated, and pegloticase (with methotrexate) for refractory gout; (3) cover the first 3-6 months with colchicine or another anti-inflammatory; (4) monitor serum urate until the target is reached and then keep it there, ideally through a structured nurse-led programme; and (5) support with weight loss, less beer, spirits and sugar-sweetened drinks, and (if hypertensive) losartan or a calcium channel blocker in place of a thiazide. Serum-urate-lowering therapy is not indicated for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia (ACR 2020, conditional), and allopurinol was neutral for heart and kidney outcomes in people without gout (ALL-HEART, CKD-FIX).

curative_option.name: Sustained Treat-to-Target Urate-Lowering Therapy (Serum Urate <6 mg/dL, <5 mg/dL if Tophaceous) - Real Crystal Dissolution and Flare Cessation in Adherent Patients; NOT a Cure of the Underlying Hyperuricaemia, Lifelong Therapy Usually Needed
curative_option.note: This is the real special case in gout treatment. Keeping serum urate below the tissue saturation threshold does more than relieve flares: it dissolves the monosodium urate crystal deposits that cause them, so in patients who reach and hold the target flares and tophi can stop. It is described here as a near-cure (crystal-depleted, flare-free, tophus-free state) and NOT as a cure, because the metabolic cause of hyperuricaemia remains, urate-lowering therapy is conditionally recommended to continue indefinitely (2020 ACR), and the only withdrawal data are observational, in selected patients, with recurrence tracking how high serum urate rose afterwards.

real_trial_data.crystal_dissolution: Pascual 2007 (prospective, 18 patients with MSU crystal-proven gout on successful urate-lowering therapy; arthrocentesis of an asymptomatic knee or first MTP joint every 3 months): MSU crystals disappeared from synovial fluid in all 18 (100%) joints once serum urate was normal; time to disappearance 3-33 months and correlated with gout duration (rs 0.71, p<0.01); median crystals per 400x field 7.5 at baseline falling to 3 at 3 months.
real_trial_data.tophus_shrinkage: Perez-Ruiz 2002 (63 patients with crystal-confirmed tophaceous gout on allopurinol, benzbromarone or both): the velocity of tophus size reduction was linearly related to mean serum urate during therapy - the lower the serum urate, the faster the tophus shrank; benzbromarone or combined therapy was faster than allopurinol alone; allopurinol and benzbromarone were equally effective when the same serum urate was reached.
real_trial_data.flare_cessation_at_target: Stamp 2022 (pooled individual data from two RCTs, 588 patients): between months 12 and 24, 91 of 343 (27%) serum-urate responders (mean urate <6 mg/dL) had a flare versus 156 of 245 (64%) non-responders; adjusted OR 0.29 (95% CI 0.17-0.51); mean flares per participant per month lower by 1.41 (1.04-1.77), independent of the randomised treatment.
real_trial_data.five_year_durability: FOCUS 5-year febuxostat extension (Schumacher 2009): 93% (54 of 58 remaining) had serum urate <6.0 mg/dL at 5 years; sustained reduction was associated with nearly complete elimination of flares; tophus resolution in 69% (18 of 26) of subjects with a baseline tophus; 50% of the 116 enrolled discontinued (38 in year 1), so these are completer figures.
real_trial_data.attainable_in_routine_care: Nottingham Gout Treatment Trial (Doherty 2018; 517 patients): serum urate <6 mg/dL at 2 years in 95% with nurse-led treat-to-target care versus 30% with GP-led usual care (RR 3.18, 95% CI 2.42-4.18); all secondary outcomes (flares in year 2, tophi, quality of life) favoured nurse-led care.
real_trial_data.withdrawal_and_recurrence: Perez-Ruiz 2011 (prospective cohort of 211 patients whose therapy was withdrawn after 5 years of control): no patient whose average serum urate after withdrawal stayed below 7 mg/dL had a crystal-proven recurrence; weight loss and losartan or fenofibrate use predicted staying below 7 mg/dL, diuretic use predicted failing. Perez-Ruiz 2006: symptom-free interval was longest (>4 years) when mean serum urate was <5.05 mg/dL on therapy and <8.75 mg/dL after withdrawal.
real_trial_data.guideline_position: 2020 ACR: strongly recommends a treat-to-target strategy with a serum urate target <6 mg/dL (high evidence) and conditionally recommends continuing urate-lowering therapy indefinitely over stopping; 2016 EULAR: target <6 mg/dL and <5 mg/dL in severe gout.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect: crystals dissolve, flares stop, tophi shrink or resolve while the serum urate target is held. Not curative: the hyperuricaemia and its causes persist; stopping therapy risks recurrence, which in one cohort tracked how high serum urate rose after withdrawal; symptoms and crystals return if the patient stops taking the drug or dose creep lets urate rise above target.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients who do not reach the target (fixed-dose allopurinol 300 mg fails in most: 22% at target in APEX versus 69% with dose escalation), patients with allopurinol intolerance or a positive HLA-B*58:01 who then need an alternative drug, and patients with refractory tophaceous disease who need pegloticase (42% pooled responders alone, 71.0% with methotrexate). There is no evidence that lowering urate in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia prevents gout enough to justify drug treatment (ACR 2020 conditionally recommends against it).
curative_option.important_caveat: The near-cure state requires achieving the target and staying on treatment; FOCUS and Doherty are the strongest sustained-target data but FOCUS has 50% dropout (completer bias) and the 95%/30% Doherty result is from one UK trial. Flares typically increase in the first months of therapy, so anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for at least 3-6 months is needed to keep patients on therapy.
curative_option.source: Pascual E, Sivera F, 'Time required for disappearance of urate crystals from synovial fluid after successful hypouricaemic treatment relates to the duration of gout', Ann Rheum Dis 2007;66:1056-1058 (PMID 17223663); Perez-Ruiz F et al., 'Effect of urate-lowering therapy on the velocity of size reduction of tophi in chronic gout', Arthritis Rheum 2002;47:356-360 (PMID 12209479); Stamp LK et al., 'Association between serum urate and flares in people with gout and evidence for surrogate status: a secondary analysis of two randomised controlled trials', Lancet Rheumatol 2022;4:e53-e60 (PMID 38288731); Schumacher HR Jr et al. (FOCUS), 'Febuxostat in the treatment of gout: 5-yr findings of the FOCUS efficacy and safety study', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2009;48:188-194 (PMID 19141576); Doherty M et al. (Nottingham Gout Treatment Trial), 'Efficacy and cost-effectiveness of nurse-led care involving education and engagement of patients and a treat-to-target urate-lowering strategy versus usual care for gout', Lancet 2018;392:1403-1412 (PMID 30343856); Perez-Ruiz F et al., 'A two-stage approach to the treatment of hyperuricemia in gout: the dirty dish hypothesis', Arthritis Rheum 2011;63:4002-4006 (PMID 21898351); Perez-Ruiz F et al., 'Using serum urate levels to determine the period free of gouty symptoms after withdrawal of long-term urate-lowering therapy: a prospective study', Arthritis Rheum 2006;55:786-790 (PMID 17013833); FitzGerald JD et al., '2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout', Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934); Richette P et al., '2016 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the management of gout', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:29-42 (PMID 27457514); Schumacher HR Jr et al. (APEX), 'Effects of febuxostat versus allopurinol and placebo in reducing serum urate in subjects with hyperuricemia and gout: a 28-week, phase III trial', Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1540-1548 (PMID 18975369); Stamp LK et al., 'A randomised controlled trial of the efficacy and safety of allopurinol dose escalation to achieve target serum urate in people with gout', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:1522-1528 (PMID 28314755)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for gout: acute flare treatment (NSAIDs, colchicine, glucocorticoids, IL-1 inhibitors, ice), urate-lowering therapy (treat-to-target strategy, allopurinol, febuxostat, uricosurics, pegloticase and its methotrexate co-therapy, and investigational agents), flare prophylaxis when starting urate-lowering therapy, diet and lifestyle with honest effect sizes and evidence quality, comorbidity and drug-interaction management, diagnostic/monitoring tools, tophus care including surgery, India availability notes, and negative/neutral evidence. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial, guideline, label or meta-analysis; derived percentages show their arithmetic.

gout_acute_flare_nsaids.name: NSAIDs for the Acute Flare (Naproxen, Indomethacin, Etoricoxib) - Equal to Low-Dose Colchicine and Oral Prednisolone; Pick by Comorbidity and Side-Effect Profile
gout_acute_flare_nsaids.type: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (non-selective and COX-2 selective), short oral course
specific_drugs: Naproxen 750 mg once then 250 mg every 8 hours for 7 days (CONTACT regimen)
Indomethacin 50 mg three times daily (regimen in the etoricoxib comparator trials)
Etoricoxib 120 mg once daily for up to 8 days (regimen in Schumacher 2002 and Rubin 2004; COX-2 selective)
gout_acute_flare_nsaids.effectiveness: Cochrane 2021 (28 trials, 3,406 participants): the only placebo-controlled NSAID trial (30 participants, low-certainty evidence) found >=50% pain reduction at 24 hours in 11 of 15 (73%) with NSAIDs versus 4 of 15 (27%) with placebo (RR 2.7, 95% CI 1.1-6.7). NSAIDs versus glucocorticoids (5 trials, 712 participants, moderate certainty): treatment success RR 0.9 (0.7-1.2), i.e. no meaningful difference. COX-2 versus non-selective NSAIDs (6 trials, 1,244 participants): equal pain relief, but non-selective NSAIDs caused more withdrawals for adverse events (RR 2.3, 1.3-4.1) and more total adverse events (RR 1.9, 1.4-2.8). Etoricoxib 120 mg versus indomethacin 50 mg three times daily (Schumacher 2002, 150 patients): mean pain change on a 0-4 Likert scale -1.72 versus -1.83 (comparable); drug-related adverse events 22.7% versus 46.7% (p=0.003). CONTACT (399 primary-care patients, naproxen versus low-dose colchicine 500 mcg three times daily for 4 days): mean pain-change difference -0.18 (95% CI -0.53 to 0.17) on a 0-10 scale over days 1-7, no significant difference; diarrhoea 45.9% with colchicine versus 20.0% with naproxen.
gout_acute_flare_nsaids.reason_why: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase, lowering the prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation, swelling and nociceptor sensitisation that follow monosodium urate crystal-triggered inflammation in the joint.
gout_acute_flare_nsaids.important_caveat: The placebo-controlled NSAID evidence rests on a single 30-patient trial (low certainty), so the strong recommendation rests mainly on active-comparator equivalence and guideline consensus. The choice among NSAID, colchicine and glucocorticoid is individualised to comorbidity (2020 ACR guideline, 2016 EULAR recommendations).
gout_acute_flare_nsaids.real_working_solution: For a patient with no NSAID contraindication, an NSAID at full anti-inflammatory dose started at the first sign of a flare is a first-line, equally effective option alongside low-dose colchicine and oral prednisolone (CONTACT authors: naproxen first-line in primary care 'in the absence of contraindications'); a COX-2 inhibitor such as etoricoxib gives the same relief with fewer adverse events than indomethacin.
gout_acute_flare_nsaids.source: van Durme CM et al., 'Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD010120 (PMID 34882311); Schumacher HR Jr et al., 'Randomised double blind trial of etoricoxib and indometacin in treatment of acute gouty arthritis', BMJ 2002;324:1488-1492 (PMID 12077033); Rubin BR et al., 'Efficacy and safety profile of treatment with etoricoxib 120 mg once daily compared with indomethacin 50 mg three times daily in acute gout', Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:598-606 (PMID 14872504); Roddy E et al. (CONTACT), Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:276-284 (PMID 31666237); FitzGerald JD et al., '2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout', Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934)

gout_acute_flare_colchicine.name: Low-Dose Colchicine (1.2 mg Then 0.6 mg One Hour Later) - AGREE Trial: Same Efficacy as 4.8 mg With Far Less Diarrhoea
gout_acute_flare_colchicine.type: Oral microtubule-inhibiting anti-inflammatory (alkaloid), given early in the flare
specific_drugs: Colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later (Colcrys label regimen; AGREE 'low-dose' arm, 1.8 mg over 1 hour)
Colchicine 0.5 mg tablets (the strength marketed in India, e.g. Zycolchin 0.5 mg)
Colchicine 500 mcg three times daily for 4 days (CONTACT trial regimen)
gout_acute_flare_colchicine.effectiveness: AGREE (184 intention-to-treat patients, early flare): >=50% pain reduction at 24 hours without rescue medication in 28 of 74 (37.8%) with low-dose colchicine (1.8 mg over 1 hour), 17 of 52 (32.7%) with high-dose (4.8 mg over 6 hours), and 9 of 58 (15.5%) with placebo (p=0.005 and p=0.034 versus placebo). Rescue medication within 24 hours: 31.1% low-dose, 34.6% high-dose, 50.0% placebo. Diarrhoea: 76.9% with high-dose (severe 19.2%, vomiting 17.3%) versus 23.0% with low-dose (no severe diarrhoea, no vomiting) and a low-dose adverse-event profile indistinguishable from placebo (OR 1.5, 0.7-3.2). Cochrane 2021 (4 trials, 803 participants): low-quality evidence that low-dose colchicine may improve outcome versus placebo without a meaningful excess of adverse events, and benefits may be similar to NSAIDs; no trial compared colchicine with glucocorticoids.
gout_acute_flare_colchicine.reason_why: Colchicine blocks microtubule-dependent neutrophil migration and activation, interrupting the neutrophil influx that drives monosodium-urate-crystal flares; the 1.2 mg + 0.6 mg regimen reaches peak plasma concentrations comparable to the 4.8 mg regimen, which is why the higher dose adds toxicity without added benefit.
gout_acute_flare_colchicine.important_caveat: In patients with renal or hepatic impairment, colchicine must not be given with P-glycoprotein or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (life-threatening and fatal toxicity reported in therapeutic doses; Colcrys label). Statins can add a myopathy/rhabdomyolysis interaction (same label). Indian tablets are 0.5 mg rather than 0.6 mg; no India-strength-adjusted regimen was verified, so the prescriber must adapt the trial regimen.
gout_acute_flare_colchicine.real_working_solution: Use the low-dose regimen only (1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later), taken at the first sign of the flare; do not use the 4.8 mg schedule - it did not work better and caused diarrhoea in about three of four patients. The label states the safety and efficacy of repeat flare treatment has not been evaluated.
gout_acute_flare_colchicine.source: Terkeltaub RA et al. (AGREE), 'High versus low dosing of oral colchicine for early acute gout flare', Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1060-1068 (PMID 20131255); McKenzie BJ et al., 'Colchicine for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;8:CD006190 (PMID 34438469); Roddy E et al. (CONTACT), Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:276-284 (PMID 31666237); FDA, Colcrys (colchicine) prescribing information, sections 2.1, 4, 7 (openFDA drug label API, label effective 2022-10-01, accessed 2026-09-21); Retail listings for Zycolchin (colchicine 0.5 mg) and other Indian colchicine 0.5 mg brands (medibuddy.in, medplusmart.com, accessed 2026-09-21)

gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.name: Oral Prednisolone 30-35 mg Daily for 4-5 Days - Real Equivalence to Naproxen and Indomethacin in Four Randomised Trials
specific_drugs: Prednisolone 35 mg once daily for 5 days (Janssens 2008 regimen)
Prednisolone 30-35 mg/day (dose range across the RCTs pooled by Yu 2018)
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.effectiveness: Janssens 2008 (120 primary-care patients, prednisolone 35 mg versus naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 5 days): pain reduction at 90 hours 44.7 mm versus 46.0 mm on a 100-mm scale (difference 1.3 mm, 95% CI -9.8 to 7.1), meeting the 10-mm equivalence margin. Rainer 2016 (416 patients, 4 Hong Kong emergency departments, prednisolone versus indomethacin): equivalent pain reduction (about 25 mm at rest and 45 mm on activity over days 1-14); minor adverse events in the ED 19% with indomethacin versus 6% with prednisolone (p<0.001). Man 2007 (90 patients): adverse events 29 of 46 with indomethacin versus 12 of 44 with prednisolone, with gastrointestinal bleeding in 5 (11%) indomethacin patients and none on prednisolone. Xu 2016 (113 patients, open-label, prednisolone 35 mg for 4 days): patient global response 'good' or 'very good' in 27 of 33 (81.8%) prednisolone, 38 of 44 (86.4%) etoricoxib and 30 of 36 (83.3%) indomethacin (p=0.743); total adverse events 6.1%, 6.8% and 30.6%. Cochrane 2021: glucocorticoids and NSAIDs equal for pain and treatment success (RR 0.9, 0.7-1.2). Meta-analysis of three RCTs (584 patients): prednisolone comparable for pain and reduced withdrawals for adverse events (RR 0.127) but raised skin rash risk (RR 4.05, 1.24-13.16).
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.reason_why: A short high-dose glucocorticoid course suppresses the cytokine-driven inflammatory cascade (including IL-1 and neutrophil recruitment) provoked by urate crystals without cyclo-oxygenase-related gastric and renal effects.
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.important_caveat: Cochrane 2008 found no placebo-controlled trials of systemic glucocorticoids in acute gout and rated the trials of low-to-moderate quality; the evidence is head-to-head equivalence, not placebo superiority. Xu 2016 was open-label and small; its percentages are patient global-response categories, not a pain threshold.
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.real_working_solution: Oral prednisolone about 30-35 mg daily for 4-5 days is a first-line option, particularly when NSAIDs are unsuitable (peptic ulcer, chronic kidney disease, anticoagulation) or colchicine interacts with the patient's medicines; trials show pain relief equal to naproxen or indomethacin with fewer adverse events.
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.source: Janssens HJ et al., 'Use of oral prednisolone or naproxen for the treatment of gout arthritis: a double-blind, randomised equivalence trial', Lancet 2008;371:1854-1860 (PMID 18514729); Rainer TH et al., 'Oral prednisolone in the treatment of acute gout: a pragmatic, multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial', Ann Intern Med 2016;164:464-471 (PMID 26903390); Man CY et al., 'Comparison of oral prednisolone/paracetamol and oral indomethacin/paracetamol combination therapy in the treatment of acute goutlike arthritis', Ann Emerg Med 2007;49:670-677 (PMID 17276548); Xu L et al., 'Comparison of prednisolone, etoricoxib, and indomethacin in treatment of acute gouty arthritis: an open-label, randomized, controlled trial', Med Sci Monit 2016;22:810-817 (PMID 26965791; PMC4791088); van Durme CM et al., 'Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD010120 (PMID 34882311); Yu J et al., 'Oral prednisolone versus non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in the treatment of acute gout: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials', Inflammopharmacology 2018;26:717-723 (PMID 29357007); FitzGerald JD et al., '2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout', Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934)

gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.name: Intra-Articular or Intramuscular Glucocorticoid (Triamcinolone Acetonide, Methylprednisolone) - Strongly Guideline-Recommended, No Dedicated Randomised Trial for the Intra-Articular Route
specific_drugs: Triamcinolone acetonide (intra-articular, or a 40 mg single injection as used as the control arm in the canakinumab and anakinra trials)
Methylprednisolone (intra-articular or parenteral; guideline-listed injectable glucocorticoid route)
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.effectiveness: Cochrane 2013: no randomised or quasi-randomised trial of intra-articular glucocorticoid for acute gout was identified, so there is no trial evidence for or against it. The 2020 ACR guideline nonetheless strongly recommends glucocorticoids given orally, intra-articularly or intramuscularly as first-line flare treatment, and IM, IV or intra-articular glucocorticoids for patients who cannot take oral medication. Triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg as a single injection, the comparator in the anaGO trial, produced a mean pain reduction of -39.4 points on a 0-100 scale from baseline to 24-72 hours, i.e. a clinically meaningful effect.
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.reason_why: A depot glucocorticoid delivered directly into the inflamed joint (or systemically by injection) suppresses local synovial inflammation for days from a single administration, useful when the patient cannot swallow tablets or one joint is involved.
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.important_caveat: The intra-articular recommendation is expert-consensus/extrapolated (Cochrane found no RCT); it is reported here honestly rather than as trial-proven.
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.real_working_solution: For a single hot joint or a patient who cannot take oral tablets, a single intra-articular (or IM) triamcinolone injection is a guideline-supported first-line option; confirm the diagnosis by crystal identification first, because monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid establish gout (2015 ACR/EULAR classification criteria).
gout_acute_flare_glucocorticoids.source: Wechalekar MD et al., 'Intra-articular glucocorticoids for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;CD009920 (PMID 23633379); FitzGerald JD et al., '2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout', Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934); Saag KG et al. (anaGO), 'A randomized, phase II study evaluating the efficacy and safety of anakinra in the treatment of gout flares', Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1533-1542 (PMID 33605029); Neogi T et al., '2015 gout classification criteria: an American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism collaborative initiative', Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2557-2568 (PMID 26352873)

gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.name: Canakinumab (Ilaris) 150 mg Single Subcutaneous Dose - Better Pain Relief and 62% Fewer New Flares Than Triamcinolone in Patients With Limited Options
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.type: Human monoclonal anti-interleukin-1 beta antibody, single subcutaneous injection
specific_drugs: Rilonacept (IL-1 trap; not effective versus indomethacin, see negative-evidence category)
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.effectiveness: Phase II dose-ranging (So 2010; 143 canakinumab versus 57 triamcinolone 40 mg IM): canakinumab 150 mg reduced pain more than triamcinolone by 11.5 mm at 24 h (p=0.04), 18.2 mm at 48 h (p=0.002) and 19.2 mm at 72 h (p<0.001) on a 100-mm scale; relative risk reduction of recurrent flares 94% versus triamcinolone; overall adverse events 41% versus 42%. Phase III beta-RELIEVED/beta-RELIEVED II (Schlesinger 2012, patients with limited treatment options): mean 72-hour pain 25.0 versus 35.7 mm (difference -10.7 mm, 95% CI -15.4 to -6.0; p<0.0001); risk of new flares reduced by 62% versus triamcinolone (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.26-0.57) over the core studies and by 56% (HR 0.44, 0.32-0.60) over 24 weeks; adverse events 66.2% versus 52.8% and serious adverse events 8.0% versus 3.5% (infections, low neutrophil and platelet counts more frequent). Cochrane 2014 rated the canakinumab-versus-triamcinolone evidence moderate quality, noted canakinumab cost is over 5,000 times that of triamcinolone acetonide, and found no comparison against NSAIDs or colchicine. The current FDA label lists gout flares in adults in whom NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated, not tolerated or inadequate, and in whom repeated corticosteroid courses are not appropriate. 2016 EULAR: consider an IL-1 blocker in frequent flares with contraindications to colchicine, NSAIDs and steroids.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.reason_why: Monosodium urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, releasing IL-1 beta, the master upstream cytokine of the flare; neutralising IL-1 beta switches off the cascade at its source and also lowers early recurrence.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.important_caveat: It is a second-line, high-cost agent with more infections and cytopenias than triamcinolone; it does not lower serum urate and does not replace urate-lowering therapy. India availability of canakinumab for gout could not be verified.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Reserve canakinumab for the small group with frequent flares in whom NSAIDs, colchicine and repeated steroid courses are all contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated; in that group it gives faster pain relief and markedly fewer new flares than triamcinolone.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.source: So A et al., 'Canakinumab for the treatment of acute flares in difficult-to-treat gouty arthritis: results of a multicenter, phase II, dose-ranging study', Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:3064-3076 (PMID 20533546); Schlesinger N et al. (beta-RELIEVED and beta-RELIEVED II), 'Canakinumab for acute gouty arthritis in patients with limited treatment options', Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:1839-1848 (PMID 22586173); Sivera F et al., 'Interleukin-1 inhibitors for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;CD009993 (PMID 25177840); FDA, Ilaris (canakinumab) prescribing information, indications section 1.3 (openFDA drug label API, label effective 2026-06-08, accessed 2026-09-21); Richette P et al., '2016 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the management of gout', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:29-42 (PMID 27457514)

gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.name: Anakinra (Off-Label) 100-200 mg Daily for 3-5 Days - Comparable to Triamcinolone in the anaGO Phase II Trial; Not FDA-Labelled for Gout
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.type: Recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist, daily subcutaneous injection
specific_drugs: Anakinra 200 mg subcutaneous daily (upper anaGO dose)
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.effectiveness: anaGO phase II RCT (165 patients: 110 anakinra 100 or 200 mg/day for 5 days versus 55 triamcinolone 40 mg single injection; patients for whom NSAIDs and colchicine were unsuitable): mean pain decline from baseline to 24-72 hours -41.2 points (anakinra) versus -39.4 (triamcinolone), p=0.688 - not superior but comparable, and favoured on most secondary end points. Retrospective series of 40 patients who had failed or could not take conventional drugs (Ottaviani 2013): 36 (90%) good response, median pain 73.5 falling to 25.0 mm, relapse in 13 patients after a median 15 days, and 7 infections mostly with long-term use. 31 patients with stage 4-5 chronic kidney disease or kidney transplant (Loustau 2018): effective in all with one serious infection. Open-label pilot (So 2007): all 10 patients responded to 100 mg daily for 3 days. The Kineret label lists rheumatoid arthritis, CAPS/NOMID and DIRA - gout is not a labelled indication.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.reason_why: Anakinra competitively blocks the IL-1 receptor, preventing both IL-1 alpha and beta from driving the crystal-triggered inflammatory cascade; its short half-life allows a brief 3-5 day course.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.important_caveat: Off-label use; the evidence is one phase II RCT plus retrospective series; long-term use is limited by infections. India availability for gout could not be verified.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.real_working_solution: For a gout flare in a patient who cannot take NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids (including advanced kidney disease or transplant), a short anakinra course is a trial-supported off-label option; check for active infection first and limit the course.
gout_acute_flare_il1_inhibitors.source: Saag KG et al. (anaGO), 'A randomized, phase II study evaluating the efficacy and safety of anakinra in the treatment of gout flares', Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1533-1542 (PMID 33605029); Ottaviani S et al., 'Efficacy of anakinra in gouty arthritis: a retrospective study of 40 cases', Arthritis Res Ther 2013;15:R123 (PMID 24432362); Loustau C et al., 'Effectiveness and safety of anakinra in gout patients with stage 4-5 chronic kidney disease or kidney transplantation', Joint Bone Spine 2018;85:755-760 (PMID 29654950); So A et al., 'A pilot study of IL-1 inhibition by anakinra in acute gout', Arthritis Res Ther 2007;9:R28 (PMID 17352828); FDA, Kineret (anakinra) prescribing information, indications (openFDA drug label API, label effective 2026-04-03, accessed 2026-09-21)
