gout_negative_or_neutral_evidence.effectiveness: Cochrane 2014 (IL-1 inhibitors for acute gout): low-quality evidence that rilonacept 320 mg provided less pain relief than maximum-dose indomethacin (mean difference 2.52, 95% CI 0.29-4.75, i.e. 25% less improvement), with similar adverse events (36% versus 30%; RR 1.2) and withdrawals due to adverse events 1 of 75 versus 2 of 76.
gout_negative_or_neutral_evidence.reason_why: Rilonacept traps IL-1 alpha and beta but did not outperform an NSAID in this single trial.
gout_negative_or_neutral_evidence.real_working_solution: Do not choose rilonacept over an NSAID, colchicine or a glucocorticoid for an acute flare; canakinumab (and off-label anakinra) are the IL-1 options with positive controlled data.
gout_negative_or_neutral_evidence.source: Sivera F et al., 'Interleukin-1 inhibitors for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;CD009993 (PMID 25177840)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pascual crystal-dissolution cohort - sustained normalisation of serum urate
ranked_high_to_low.type: Monosodium urate crystal clearance from synovial fluid
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% (18 of 18) of asymptomatic gouty joints (11 knees, 7 first MTP joints) cleared monosodium urate crystals from synovial fluid after successful serum-urate lowering; time to clearance 3-33 months and longer with longer gout duration (rs 0.71). Prospective, n=18, no control arm.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pascual E, Sivera F, 'Time required for disappearance of urate crystals from synovial fluid after successful hypouricaemic treatment relates to the duration of gout', Ann Rheum Dis 2007;66:1056-1058 (PMID 17223663)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Treat-to-target nurse-led care (Nottingham Gout Treatment Trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 95% of nurse-led patients had serum urate <360 umol/L (6 mg/dL) at 2 years versus 30% with GP-led usual care (RR 3.18, 95% CI 2.42-4.18; 517 patients, RCT).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Doherty M et al. (Nottingham Gout Treatment Trial), 'Efficacy and cost-effectiveness of nurse-led care involving education and engagement of patients and a treat-to-target urate-lowering strategy versus usual care for gout', Lancet 2018;392:1403-1412 (PMID 30343856)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Febuxostat 80-120 mg long-term (FOCUS 5-year)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 93.1% (54 of 58 remaining subjects) had serum urate <6.0 mg/dL at 5 years, with flares nearly abolished and baseline tophi resolved in 69% (18/26); 50% of the 116 enrolled discontinued, so this is a completer figure.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Schumacher HR Jr et al. (FOCUS), 'Febuxostat in the treatment of gout: 5-yr findings of the FOCUS efficacy and safety study', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2009;48:188-194 (PMID 19141576)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Benzbromarone 200 mg/day after allopurinol failure
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 91.7% (22 of 24) reached serum urate <=5.0 mg/dL (0.30 mmol/L) after 2 months versus 64.5% (20 of 31) with probenecid 2 g/day (p=0.03) in patients who failed or could not take allopurinol; RCT stage 2.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Reinders MK et al., 'Efficacy and tolerability of urate-lowering drugs in gout: a randomised controlled trial of benzbromarone versus probenecid after failure of allopurinol', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:51-56 (PMID 18250112)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Anakinra (off-label) for gout flare
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 90% (36 of 40) of patients who had failed or could not take conventional drugs showed a good response; median pain fell from 73.5 to 25.0 mm; retrospective multicentre series (the phase II RCT anaGO found equal pain relief to triamcinolone: -41.2 versus -39.4 points on a 0-100 scale, no responder percentage reported).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ottaviani S et al., 'Efficacy of anakinra in gouty arthritis: a retrospective study of 40 cases', Arthritis Res Ther 2013;15:R123 (PMID 24432362); Saag KG et al. (anaGO), 'A randomized, phase II study evaluating the efficacy and safety of anakinra in the treatment of gout flares', Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1533-1542 (PMID 33605029)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Etoricoxib 120 mg daily (4 days, acute flare)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 86.4% (38 of 44; 52.3% very good plus 34.1% good) patient-rated 'good' or 'very good' global response at end of 4 days; open-label RCT, no significant difference from prednisolone or indomethacin (p=0.743).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Xu L et al., 'Comparison of prednisolone, etoricoxib, and indomethacin in treatment of acute gouty arthritis: an open-label, randomized, controlled trial', Med Sci Monit 2016;22:810-817 (PMID 26965791; PMC4791088)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Indomethacin 50 mg three times daily (acute flare)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 83.3% (30 of 36; 44.4% very good plus 38.9% good) patient-rated 'good' or 'very good' global response at 4 days; same open-label RCT; total adverse events 30.6% versus 6.1-6.8% with prednisolone/etoricoxib.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Xu L et al., 'Comparison of prednisolone, etoricoxib, and indomethacin in treatment of acute gouty arthritis: an open-label, randomized, controlled trial', Med Sci Monit 2016;22:810-817 (PMID 26965791; PMC4791088)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Colchicine prophylaxis 0.6 mg twice daily when starting allopurinol
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 82.1% fewer flares over 6 months (mean 0.52 versus 2.91 flares per patient, p=0.008; computed (2.91-0.52)/2.91) in 43 patients, double-blind RCT; flares months 3-6: 0 versus 1.05.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Borstad GC et al., 'Colchicine for prophylaxis of acute flares when initiating allopurinol for chronic gouty arthritis', J Rheumatol 2004;31:2429-2432 (PMID 15570646)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral prednisolone 35 mg daily (acute flare)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 81.8% (27 of 33; 48.5% very good plus 33.3% good) patient-rated 'good' or 'very good' global response at 4 days (open-label RCT, n=113 across 3 arms); larger RCTs (Janssens n=120, Rainer n=416) found pain relief equivalent to naproxen or indomethacin.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Xu L et al., 'Comparison of prednisolone, etoricoxib, and indomethacin in treatment of acute gouty arthritis: an open-label, randomized, controlled trial', Med Sci Monit 2016;22:810-817 (PMID 26965791; PMC4791088); Janssens HJ et al., 'Use of oral prednisolone or naproxen for the treatment of gout arthritis: a double-blind, randomised equivalence trial', Lancet 2008;371:1854-1860 (PMID 18514729); Rainer TH et al., 'Oral prednisolone in the treatment of acute gout: a pragmatic, multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial', Ann Intern Med 2016;164:464-471 (PMID 26903390)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sustained serum urate <6 mg/dL (treat-to-target achievers)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 73.5% (252 of 343) of patients whose average serum urate reached <6 mg/dL had no flare between months 12 and 24 versus 36% (89 of 245) of non-responders; adjusted OR for a flare 0.29 (95% CI 0.17-0.51); pooled secondary analysis of two RCTs.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Stamp LK et al., 'Association between serum urate and flares in people with gout and evidence for surrogate status: a secondary analysis of two randomised controlled trials', Lancet Rheumatol 2022;4:e53-e60 (PMID 38288731)

ranked_high_to_low.name: NSAIDs versus placebo (acute flare)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 73.3% (11 of 15) had >=50% pain reduction at 24 hours with NSAIDs versus 26.7% (4 of 15) with placebo (RR 2.7, 95% CI 1.1-6.7); single 30-patient placebo-controlled trial, low-certainty evidence (Cochrane).
ranked_high_to_low.source: van Durme CM et al., 'Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for acute gout', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD010120 (PMID 34882311)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Weight-loss diet (13-man pilot)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 71.4% fewer monthly attacks (median 2.1 to 0.6 per month, computed (2.1-0.6)/2.1) after a mean 7.7 kg weight loss over 16 weeks; uncontrolled pilot of 13 men; serum urate normalised in 7 of 12 (58%). Low-quality evidence.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dessein PH et al., 'Beneficial effects of weight loss associated with moderate calorie/carbohydrate restriction, and increased proportional intake of protein and unsaturated fat on serum urate and lipoprotein levels in gout: a pilot study', Ann Rheum Dis 2000;59:539-543 (PMID 10873964)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pegloticase plus methotrexate (MIRROR RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 71.0% (71 of 100) responders (serum urate <6 mg/dL for >=80% of month 6) versus 38.5% (20 of 52) with pegloticase plus placebo (difference 32.3%, 95% CI 16.3-48.3); 12-month response 60.0% versus 30.8%.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Botson JK et al. (MIRROR RCT), 'A randomized, placebo-controlled study of methotrexate to increase response rates in patients with uncontrolled gout receiving pegloticase: primary efficacy and safety findings', Arthritis Rheumatol 2023;75:293-304 (PMID 36099211); Botson JK et al. (MIRROR RCT), '12-month findings', ACR Open Rheumatol 2023;5:407-418 (PMID 37385296)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pozdeutinurad 75 mg (investigational, REDUCE 2 topline)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 69.2% had serum urate <6 mg/dL at month 6 versus 8.1% placebo (50 mg: 56.6%); company topline press release, not peer-reviewed; not a prescribing option.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sobi, 'Positive topline results from the pivotal Phase 3 REDUCE 2 study of pozdeutinurad in gout', press release 21 May 2026 (sobi.com, accessed 2026-09-21)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Allopurinol with dose escalation to target
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 69% of the dose-escalation group had serum urate <6 mg/dL at 12 months versus 32% with dose continued (183 participants, RCT); 52% had creatinine clearance <60 mL/min.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Stamp LK et al., 'A randomised controlled trial of the efficacy and safety of allopurinol dose escalation to achieve target serum urate in people with gout', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:1522-1528 (PMID 28314755)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Probenecid 2 g/day after allopurinol failure
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 64.5% (20 of 31) reached serum urate <=5.0 mg/dL after 2 months versus 91.7% with benzbromarone (p=0.03); RCT stage 2.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Reinders MK et al., 'Efficacy and tolerability of urate-lowering drugs in gout: a randomised controlled trial of benzbromarone versus probenecid after failure of allopurinol', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:51-56 (PMID 18250112)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Canakinumab 150 mg (limited-option acute flares)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 62% lower risk of new flares versus triamcinolone (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.26-0.57; computed 1-0.38) in beta-RELIEVED I/II core studies; 56% lower over 24 weeks (HR 0.44); 72-hour pain 25.0 versus 35.7 mm.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Schlesinger N et al. (beta-RELIEVED and beta-RELIEVED II), 'Canakinumab for acute gouty arthritis in patients with limited treatment options', Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:1839-1848 (PMID 22586173)

ranked_high_to_low.name: SEL-212 (investigational, DISSOLVE I)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 56% responders (serum urate <6 mg/dL for >=80% of month 6) at 0.15 mg/kg versus 4% placebo (DISSOLVE I; DISSOLVE II 47% versus 12%); company press release; not a prescribing option.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sobi, 'Phase 3 DISSOLVE program of SEL-212 in chronic refractory gout meets primary endpoint', press release 21 March 2023 (sobi.com, accessed 2026-09-21)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lesinurad 200 mg plus allopurinol (CLEAR 1; no longer marketed in the US)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 54.2% reached serum urate <6.0 mg/dL at month 6 versus 27.9% with allopurinol alone (p<0.0001; 603 patients); no significant flare or tophus-resolution benefit.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Saag KG et al. (CLEAR 1), 'Lesinurad combined with allopurinol: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in gout patients with an inadequate response to standard-of-care allopurinol (a US-based study)', Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:203-212 (PMID 27564409)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Febuxostat 80 mg daily
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 48% had the last three monthly serum urate values <6.0 mg/dL at 28 weeks versus 22% allopurinol 300 mg (65% at 120 mg); APEX RCT, 1,072 subjects.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Schumacher HR Jr et al. (APEX), 'Effects of febuxostat versus allopurinol and placebo in reducing serum urate in subjects with hyperuricemia and gout: a 28-week, phase III trial', Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1540-1548 (PMID 18975369)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Fenofibrate (FIELD post-hoc, type 2 diabetes)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 46% lower risk of a first gout event over 5 years (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.41-0.70; computed 1-0.54; 81 versus 151 events); plasma uric acid 20.1% lower; post-hoc analysis.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Waldman B et al., 'Effect of fenofibrate on uric acid and gout in type 2 diabetes: a post-hoc analysis of the randomised, controlled FIELD study', Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2018;6:310-318 (PMID 29496472)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pegloticase 8 mg every 2 weeks alone (GOUT1/GOUT2)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 42.4% (36 of 85; reported as 42%) pooled responders (plasma uric acid <6.0 mg/dL in months 3 and 6) versus 0% (0 of 43) with placebo.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sundy JS et al. (GOUT1/GOUT2, C0405/C0406), 'Efficacy and tolerability of pegloticase for the treatment of chronic gout in patients refractory to conventional treatment: two randomized controlled trials', JAMA 2011;306:711-720 (PMID 21846852)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from DIFFERENT trials with DIFFERENT endpoints (serum urate below target at a timepoint, pain or global response in an acute flare, relative reduction in flares or gout events, crystal clearance, and cohort risk reductions), different comparators and very different evidence quality (RCT, retrospective series, observational cohort, company press release), so the ordering is purely by the numeric value shown and is NOT a like-for-like effectiveness league table; the metric column states what each number measures and derived percentages show their arithmetic. Rows are grouped in reality into three separate clinical questions: (1) getting rid of the acute flare (NSAIDs, colchicine, prednisolone, canakinumab, anakinra), (2) removing urate for good (allopurinol titration, febuxostat, uricosurics, pegloticase with methotrexate, sustained treat-to-target), and (3) supportive and comorbidity measures (weight loss, diet, losartan, fenofibrate, SGLT2 inhibitors). The crystal-clearance, treat-to-target, febuxostat-5-year and sustained-target rows are outcome or endpoint-attainment figures that anchor the curative argument in CURABILITY_NOTE. Pozdeutinurad and SEL-212 are investigational and company-reported, not prescribing options; lesinurad is no longer marketed in the US. Interventions with real evidence but no retrievable responder percentage are documented in the survey but deliberately not ranked here rather than given an invented number: intra-articular/intramuscular glucocorticoid (Cochrane 2013 found no RCT), topical ice (pain-scale difference only, n=19), HLA-B*58:01 screening (safety strategy: 0 of 2,339 screen-negative patients versus 7 expected severe cutaneous reactions, historical comparator) and dotinurad (no peer-reviewed responder rate retrieved). The single fixed-dose-allopurinol row (22%) is deliberately included so it is not mistaken for the real working allopurinol regimen (titrated to target, 69%).

definition.finding: Gout is a chronic disease caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in articular and non-articular structures. Sustained hyperuricaemia (serum urate above the solubility limit of about 6.8 mg/dL) is the most important risk factor. Clinically it typically presents as an acute, self-limiting inflammatory monoarthritis of the lower limb, but it remains a chronic disease between flares. It is the most common inflammatory arthritis. Long-term urate-lowering therapy dissolves MSU crystals and can prevent flares and tophi, so gout is a treatable and potentially curable crystal-deposition disease.
definition.source: Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Lancet 2021 (PMID 33798500); Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019 (PMID 31558729); Dehlin M et al., Global epidemiology of gout: prevalence, incidence, treatment patterns and risk factors, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 32541923)

purine_metabolism_and_uricase_loss.finding: In humans uric acid is the final product of purine catabolism: purine nucleotides are degraded to hypoxanthine, then xanthine, then uric acid by xanthine oxidase. Most mammals further convert urate to the more soluble allantoin using uricase; humans and some higher primates lack a functional uricase (in the human urate oxidase gene two nonsense mutations were found, and the enzyme 'has been lost by some unknown mechanism'), so uric acid is the end product and human serum urate (about 200-500 umol/L) is far higher than in most other mammals (3-120 umol/L). About two-thirds of urate elimination is renal (normal uricosuria about 620 mg/day in adults) and most of the remainder is thought to be excreted through the gastrointestinal tract; Vitart et al. give about 70% renal disposal and state that impaired renal excretion causes hyperuricaemia in 5-25% of the human population.
purine_metabolism_and_uricase_loss.source: Wu XW et al., Urate oxidase: primary structure and evolutionary implications, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 1989;86:9412-6 (PMID 2594778); Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633); Vitart V et al., SLC2A9 is a newly identified urate transporter influencing serum urate concentration, urate excretion and gout, Nat Genet 2008;40:437-42 (PMID 18327257)

urate_solubility_threshold_6_8_mg_dl.finding: Uric acid is a weak diprotic acid (aqueous pKa1 5.4, pKa2 9.8), so at physiological pH 98-99% exists as the urate anion. The solubility of urate at physiological pH is generally given as 6.8 mg/dL (about 400 umol/L; 416 umol/L is also quoted); hyperuricaemia is commonly defined as serum urate >6.8 mg/dL on this basis, above which MSU crystals may form or grow. Because typical laboratory reference ranges (about 3.5-7.2 mg/dL in men, 2.6-6.0 mg/dL in premenopausal women) reach or exceed the saturation point, a 'normal' upper limit can itself lie above the precipitation threshold. Alternative definitions of hyperuricaemia are in use (for example >7.0 mg/dL in men and >5.7 mg/dL in women in the US NHANES analysis), which must be considered when comparing prevalence figures. The solubility of MSU is temperature dependent (Loeb, 1972).
urate_solubility_threshold_6_8_mg_dl.source: Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633); FitzGerald JD et al., Gout, Ann Intern Med 2025;178:ITC33-ITC48 (PMID 40063960); Chen-Xu M et al., Contemporary Prevalence of Gout and Hyperuricemia in the United States and Decadal Trends: NHANES 2007-2016, Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:991-999 (PMID 30618180); Loeb JN, The influence of temperature on the solubility of monosodium urate, Arthritis Rheum 1972;15:189-92 (PMID 5027604)
urate_solubility_threshold_6_8_mg_dl.confidence: high for the 6.8 mg/dL figure as a conventional solubility limit; the temperature-dependence statement rests on the title of Loeb 1972 (abstract not available) so is moderate

urate_transporters_urat1_glut9_abcg2.finding: Serum urate is regulated by renal and gut urate transporters, particularly URAT1 (SLC22A12), GLUT9 (SLC2A9) and ABCG2. URAT1 is the renal urate-anion exchanger that reabsorbs urate and is the target of uricosuric and antiuricosuric agents; loss-of-function defects cause idiopathic renal hypouricaemia. GLUT9 variants explain 1.7-5.3% of variance in serum urate and are associated with low fractional excretion of urate and/or gout; GLUT9 also transports fructose and has strong urate transport activity. ABCG2 is a high-capacity urate exporter (renal proximal tubule secretion and intestinal excretion); the common Q141K variant (rs2231142) reduces urate transport by 53%, raises gout risk (adjusted OR 1.68 per risk allele) and is estimated to account for at least 10% of gout cases in whites; the nonfunctional Q126X variant carries an OR of 5.97 for gout and 10% of Japanese gout patients (16/159) had genotype combinations causing >75% loss of ABCG2 function (OR 25.8). ABCG2 dysfunction also causes hyperuricaemia through decreased extra-renal (gut) urate excretion, so the older 'overproducer' label is better described as 'renal overload'.
urate_transporters_urat1_glut9_abcg2.source: Enomoto A et al., Nature 2002;417:447-52 (PMID 12024214); Vitart V et al., Nat Genet 2008;40:437-42 (PMID 18327257); Woodward OM et al., PNAS 2009 (PMID 19506252); Matsuo H et al., Sci Transl Med 2009;1:5ra11 (PMID 20368174); Ichida K et al., Nat Commun 2012 (PMID 22473008); So A, Thorens B, J Clin Invest 2010;120:1791-9 (PMID 20516647); Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Lancet 2021 (PMID 33798500)

genetics_gwas.finding: Gout and serum urate are strongly heritable and polygenic. The first GWAS found SLC2A9 (GLUT9), ABCG2 and SLC17A3 associated with urate and gout (gout OR 0.59 per T allele for rs16890979 in SLC2A9; 1.74 per risk allele for rs2231142 in ABCG2; an additive score of risk alleles gave graded gout frequencies of 1-18% in ARIC whites). A later meta-analysis of >140,000 people identified 28 genome-wide significant urate loci. A 2024 GWAS of 2.6 million people (120,295 with prevalent gout) detected 377 loci and prioritised genes involved in epigenetic remodelling, cell osmolarity and regulation of NLRP3 inflammasome activity, and Mendelian randomisation supported a causal role of clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential in gout.
genetics_gwas.source: Dehghan A et al., Lancet 2008 (PMID 18834626); Kottgen A et al., Nat Genet 2013 (PMID 23263486); Major TJ et al., A genome-wide association analysis reveals new pathogenic pathways in gout, Nat Genet 2024;56:2392-2406 (PMID 39406924)

msu_crystal_formation_and_local_factors.finding: Hyperuricaemia is necessary but not sufficient for MSU crystal formation. The reason the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint is preferentially involved is not proven; Simkin proposed that crystals form in resolving synovial effusions because water leaves the joint space about twice as fast as urate, so urate concentration transiently rises above solubility; podagra correlates with degenerative joint disease of the toe, often follows abuse of the feet, and classically starts in the middle of the night. MSU crystals persist in joints between flares: they are found in synovial fluid in 12.5-90% of gout patients during otherwise asymptomatic phases, and urate-lowering treatment that dissolves them progressively eliminates chronic inflammation.
msu_crystal_formation_and_local_factors.source: Simkin PA, The pathogenesis of podagra, Ann Intern Med 1977;86:230-3 (PMID 319726); Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633)
msu_crystal_formation_and_local_factors.confidence: moderate (the Simkin mechanism is an explicitly stated hypothesis, not a demonstrated fact)

nlrp3_inflammasome_and_il1b_flare_initia.finding: MSU (and calcium pyrophosphate, CPPD) crystals engage the caspase-1-activating NALP3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, producing active IL-1beta and IL-18; mice lacking caspase-1, ASC, NALP3 or the IL-1 receptor have impaired neutrophil influx in crystal-induced peritonitis. Crystals alone are not sufficient in humans: MSU had no effect on PBMCs from healthy subjects, whereas the free fatty acid C18:0 plus MSU induced large amounts of IL-1beta via Toll-like receptor 2 (an ASC/caspase-1-dependent pathway that in that model was, surprisingly, NALP3-independent), offering a mechanism by which food/metabolic events trigger flares and explaining why patients with large tophi do not necessarily flare. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome with IL-1beta release is now considered central to flare initiation, which is the rationale for IL-1 blockade in flares (the 2016 EULAR recommendations advise an IL-1 blocker for frequent flares when colchicine, NSAIDs and corticosteroids are contraindicated).
nlrp3_inflammasome_and_il1b_flare_initia.source: Martinon F et al., Gout-associated uric acid crystals activate the NALP3 inflammasome, Nature 2006;440:237-41 (PMID 16407889); Joosten LA et al., Engagement of fatty acids with Toll-like receptor 2 drives interleukin-1beta production via the ASC/caspase 1 pathway in monosodium urate monohydrate crystal-induced gouty arthritis, Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:3237-48 (PMID 20662061); Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Lancet 2021 (PMID 33798500); Richette P et al., 2016 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the management of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:29-42 (PMID 27457514)
nlrp3_inflammasome_and_il1b_flare_initia.confidence: high for MSU-induced NLRP3/IL-1beta activation; moderate for the fatty-acid/TLR2 co-trigger model (mostly in vitro and mouse)

spontaneous_flare_resolution_and_nets.finding: A gout flare resolves spontaneously within a few days even though MSU crystals remain in the joint. Recruited neutrophils undergo oxidative burst and form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); at high neutrophil density the NETs aggregate and degrade cytokines and chemokines via serine proteases, promoting resolution. Tophi share characteristics with aggregated NETs, and individuals with impaired NETosis have uncontrolled inflammatory mediator production and persistent inflammation.
spontaneous_flare_resolution_and_nets.source: Schauer C et al., Aggregated neutrophil extracellular traps limit inflammation by degrading cytokines and chemokines, Nat Med 2014;20:511-7 (PMID 24784231); Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Lancet 2021 (PMID 33798500)
spontaneous_flare_resolution_and_nets.confidence: high (mechanistic; largely mouse and in vitro data plus human neutrophil work)

why_only_a_minority_of_hyperuricaemic_pe.finding: Most hyperuricaemic people never develop clinical gout, and even very high urate does not guarantee it. Vitart et al. cite about 10% of people with hyperuricaemia developing gout. In the Normative Aging Study (2,046 initially healthy men, mean 14.9 years, 30,147 person-years) the annual incidence of gouty arthritis was 4.9% for urate >=9 mg/dL, 0.5% for 7.0-8.9 mg/dL and 0.1% for <7.0 mg/dL, with a 22% cumulative incidence at 5 years for urate >=9 mg/dL. Pooled individual-participant data from four US cohorts (18,889 gout-free participants, 212,363 patient-years) showed 15-year cumulative incidence rising from 1.1% for urate <6 mg/dL to 49% for >=10 mg/dL, with adjusted hazard ratios of 2.7 (6.0-6.9), 6.6 (7.0-7.9), 15 (8.0-8.9), 30 (9.0-9.9) and 64 (>=10 mg/dL) versus <6; only about half of those with urate >=10 mg/dL developed clinical gout in 15 years. In the Malmo Preventive Project (33,346 people, mean follow-up 28.2 years) 3.8% developed gout overall, but among those with hyperuricaemia (>405 umol/L) 14.7% of men and 19.5% of women did. Dual-energy CT found urate deposits in 24% (6/25) of people with asymptomatic hyperuricaemia (urate >=540 umol/L) versus 79% of early gout and 84% of late gout, with lower deposit volume in the asymptomatic group, suggesting a threshold volume of crystal deposition may be needed before symptoms. Duration and degree of hyperuricaemia, plus co-factors (see real_risk_factors, genetics, and the fatty acid/TLR2 second signal above), determine who flares. It is not possible to predict accurately which hyperuricaemic individuals will go on to develop gout.
why_only_a_minority_of_hyperuricaemic_pe.source: Vitart V et al., Nat Genet 2008 (PMID 18327257); Campion EW et al., Asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Risks and consequences in the Normative Aging Study, Am J Med 1987 (PMID 3826098); Dalbeth N et al., Relationship between serum urate concentration and clinically evident incident gout: an individual participant data analysis, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:1048-1052 (PMID 29463518); Kapetanovic MC et al., The risk of clinically diagnosed gout by serum urate levels: results from 30 years follow-up of the Malmo Preventive Project cohort in southern Sweden, Arthritis Res Ther 2018;20:190 (PMID 30157929); Dalbeth N et al., Urate crystal deposition in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and symptomatic gout: a dual energy CT study, Ann Rheum Dis 2015 (PMID 25637002); Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633)

clinical_diagnosis_features.finding: Features that support a clinical diagnosis of gout (EULAR 2018): monoarticular involvement of a foot or ankle joint (especially the first MTP joint); previous episodes of similar acute arthritis; rapid onset of severe pain and swelling; erythema; male sex; associated cardiovascular disease; hyperuricaemia. A diagnosis of gout should not be based on hyperuricaemia alone. In the earlier EULAR 2006 evidence review, classic podagra had a positive likelihood ratio (LR) of 30.64 (95% CI 20.51-45.77) and clinically evident tophi 39.95 (21.06-75.79) for gout; hyperuricaemia defined by the local normal range had LR 9.74 (7.45-12.72).
clinical_diagnosis_features.source: Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758); Zhang W et al., EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1301-11 (PMID 16707533)

synovial_fluid_msu_crystals_gold_standar.finding: Demonstration of MSU crystals in synovial fluid (or a tophus aspirate) is the gold standard and gives a definite diagnosis; EULAR 2018 recommends a search for crystals in every person with suspected gout. Crystals are needle-shaped, preferably intracellular, with bright negative birefringence under compensated polarised light microscopy. In the EULAR 2006 review, crystal identification was very likely to be positive in symptomatic gout (LR 567, 95% CI 35.5-9053) but varies with observer skill. Crystals can be found even between flares: in 101 gout patients, arthrocentesis of previously inflamed but currently asymptomatic knees and first MTP joints yielded fluid in 91 of 101; all 43 patients not receiving urate-lowering drugs had MSU crystals, versus 34 of 48 on urate-lowering therapy, and in 90% of positive samples crystals were seen in the first five microscope fields. The 1977 ARA preliminary criteria likewise classified gout by urate crystals in joint fluid or a tophus proved to contain urate crystals. Practical point: aspirate the joint even when asymptomatic if the diagnosis is uncertain.
synovial_fluid_msu_crystals_gold_standar.source: Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758); Zhang W et al., EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1301-11 (PMID 16707533); Hainer BL et al., Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of gout, Am Fam Physician 2014;90:831-6 (PMID 25591183); Pascual E et al., Synovial fluid analysis for diagnosis of intercritical gout, Ann Intern Med 1999;131:756-9 (PMID 10577299); Wallace SL et al., Preliminary criteria for the classification of the acute arthritis of primary gout, Arthritis Rheum 1977;20:895-900 (PMID 856219)

acr_eular_2015_classification_criteria.finding: Entry criterion: at least one episode of swelling, pain or tenderness in a peripheral joint or bursa. Sufficient criterion: MSU crystals in a symptomatic joint/bursa (synovial fluid) or in a tophus classify as gout without further scoring. Otherwise score and classify as gout at a threshold of >=8 (maximum possible 23). Clinical domain: pattern of joint/bursa involvement (ankle or mid-foot, without first MTP = 1; first MTP involvement = 2); characteristics of episodes (erythema, cannot bear touch/pressure, great difficulty walking; 1, 2 or 3 points for one, two or three characteristics); time course (>=2 of: time to maximal pain <24 h, resolution in <=14 days, complete resolution between episodes; one typical episode = 1, recurrent = 2); clinical tophus = 4. Laboratory domain: serum urate (uricase method, ideally >4 weeks after a flare and off urate-lowering therapy): <4 mg/dL = -4, 4 to <6 = 0, 6 to <8 = 2, 8 to <10 = 3, >=10 = 4; MSU-negative synovial fluid aspirate = -2. Imaging: urate deposition by ultrasound double-contour sign or dual-energy CT = 4; gout-related radiographic erosion in hands/feet = 4. Performance in the validation data set (n=330): sensitivity 0.92 and specificity 0.89 for the full criteria; 0.85 and 0.78 using clinical parameters only (no crystal or imaging results). These are classification criteria for research; they are not designed as a stand-alone diagnostic test.
acr_eular_2015_classification_criteria.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275)

dual_energy_ct.finding: DECT colour-codes urate deposits. Against a combined reference standard of synovial fluid polarising and electron microscopy (40 active gout, 41 other joint disease), DECT sensitivity was 0.90 (95% CI 0.76-0.97) and specificity 0.83 (0.68-0.93); all false negatives were in acute/recent-onset gout and all false positives had advanced knee osteoarthritis. In patients with inflammatory arthritis and gout risk factors but negative synovial fluid microscopy, DECT showed urate deposition in 14/30 (46.7%). A meta-analysis of 28 studies gave pooled DECT sensitivity 0.89 and specificity 0.91; in early disease (<=2 years) 0.75 and 0.85. DECT is therefore most useful when crystals cannot be obtained or microscopy is negative, and a negative scan does not exclude early gout.
dual_energy_ct.source: Bongartz T et al., Dual-energy CT for the diagnosis of gout: an accuracy and diagnostic yield study, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1072-7 (PMID 24671771); Shang J et al., Diagnostic Performance of Dual-energy CT Versus Ultrasonography in Gout: A Meta-analysis, Acad Radiol 2022;29:56-68 (PMID 32980243)

ultrasound_double_contour_sign.finding: Ultrasound can show the double-contour sign (hyperechoic band over cartilage surface) and tophi. A meta-analysis of 11 studies (938 gout patients, 788 non-gout inflammatory arthritis controls) gave pooled sensitivity 65.1% and specificity 89.0% for ultrasound signs; individual signs were specific but insensitive (tophus sensitivity 54.3%, specificity 93.2%). A separate 28-study meta-analysis gave double-contour sensitivity 0.70 and specificity 0.95, tophus 0.57 and 0.99, and overall ultrasound signs 0.84 and 0.84 (early disease: 0.93 and 0.80). EULAR 2018 recommends imaging, particularly ultrasound for double-contour sign and tophi, when crystal identification is not possible in an atypical presentation.
ultrasound_double_contour_sign.source: Lee YH, Song GG, Diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound in patients with gout: A meta-analysis, Semin Arthritis Rheum 2018;47:703-709 (PMID 29054295); Shang J et al., Acad Radiol 2022 (PMID 32980243); Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758)

serum_urate_limitations_during_a_flare.finding: Serum urate is unreliable during an acute flare. In pooled data from two acute-gout trials (339 patients) only 14% had a 'true' normal urate (<=6 mg/dL) and 32% had urate <=8 mg/dL at the time of the attack, and attacks occurred despite urate below the 6.8 mg/dL saturation level; a normal level at presentation does not exclude gout. The 2015 ACR/EULAR criteria specify scoring urate ideally at a time when the patient was not on urate-lowering therapy and >4 weeks from a flare, and a value <4 mg/dL subtracts 4 points; EULAR 2006 noted some gouty patients have normal urate at the time of investigation, and EULAR 2018 states hyperuricaemia alone must not establish the diagnosis. Practical takeaway: neither a normal nor a high urate confirms or refutes a flare; confirm with crystals and repeat urate during the intercritical period.
serum_urate_limitations_during_a_flare.source: Schlesinger N, Norquist JM, Watson DJ, Serum urate during acute gout, J Rheumatol 2009;36:1287-9 (PMID 19369457); Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Zhang W et al., EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1301-11 (PMID 16707533); Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758)

radiographs.finding: Plain radiographs have little role in early diagnosis. In late or severe gout, asymmetrical swelling (LR 4.13) and subcortical cysts without erosion (LR 6.39) help distinguish chronic gout from other joint disease. The ACR/EULAR criteria define a gout-related erosion as a cortical break with sclerotic margin and overhanging edge on hand/foot radiographs.
radiographs.source: Zhang W et al., EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1301-11 (PMID 16707533); Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275)

comorbidity_assessment_at_diagnosis.finding: EULAR 2018 gives a strong recommendation that all people with gout are systematically assessed for associated comorbidities and cardiovascular risk factors, as well as risk factors for chronic hyperuricaemia.
comorbidity_assessment_at_diagnosis.source: Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758)

framework_note.finding: Gout is conventionally described in four stages: asymptomatic hyperuricaemia (with or without silent MSU deposition), acute flares, the intercritical period, and chronic tophaceous (and erosive) gout. This is a descriptive framework rather than a strictly sequential one: the review literature describes progression from hyperuricaemia to crystal deposition, flares and advanced disease with tophi, and not every hyperuricaemic person progresses.
framework_note.source: Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633); Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Lancet 2021 (PMID 33798500); Kapetanovic MC et al., The risk of clinically diagnosed gout by serum urate levels: results from 30 years follow-up of the Malmo Preventive Project cohort in southern Sweden, Arthritis Res Ther 2018;20:190 (PMID 30157929)
framework_note.confidence: high for the staging concept; the timing between stages is not quantified here (see natural_history)

stage_1_asymptomatic_hyperuricaemia.finding: Serum urate above about 6.8 mg/dL without a flare or tophus. Silent urate deposits on DECT occur in about one in four (24%) of people with urate >=540 umol/L. Absolute risk of a first flare rises steeply with urate level (see why_only_a_minority above). The 2020 ACR guideline conditionally recommends against starting pharmacological urate-lowering therapy in patients with serum urate >6.8 mg/dL who have had no flares and have no tophi.
stage_1_asymptomatic_hyperuricaemia.source: Dalbeth N et al., Urate crystal deposition in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and symptomatic gout: a dual energy CT study, Ann Rheum Dis 2015 (PMID 25637002); Dalbeth N et al., Relationship between serum urate concentration and clinically evident incident gout: an individual participant data analysis, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:1048-1052 (PMID 29463518); FitzGerald JD et al., 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934)

stage_2_acute_flare.finding: Sudden severe joint pain, swelling and erythema. Per the ACR/EULAR criteria, typical episodes reach maximal pain in <24 hours and resolve in <=14 days (even without treatment) with complete return to baseline between attacks; the widely quoted 'peak within 12-24 hours' is consistent with the <24 h criterion but the criteria do not specify a 12 h lower bound. Flares resolve spontaneously within days through NET-mediated cytokine degradation. Common precipitants include alcohol, purine-rich meals, diuretics and low-dose aspirin (see real_risk_factors). Onset is classically nocturnal for podagra.
stage_2_acute_flare.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Schauer C et al., Aggregated neutrophil extracellular traps limit inflammation by degrading cytokines and chemokines, Nat Med 2014;20:511-7 (PMID 24784231); Simkin PA, The pathogenesis of podagra, Ann Intern Med 1977;86:230-3 (PMID 319726)

stage_3_intercritical_period.finding: The symptom-free interval between flares. The disease is not dormant: MSU crystals were present in the synovial fluid of asymptomatic previously inflamed joints in all 43 patients not receiving urate-lowering drugs in one series (34/48 on urate-lowering drugs), and are reported in 12.5-90% of gout patients during asymptomatic phases, reflecting ongoing low-grade inflammation and progressive deposition. Anti-inflammatory treatment of flares alone does not alter crystal deposition, so tophi and joint damage can progress unnoticed.
stage_3_intercritical_period.source: Pascual E et al., Synovial fluid analysis for diagnosis of intercritical gout, Ann Intern Med 1999;131:756-9 (PMID 10577299); Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633)

stage_4_chronic_tophaceous_gout.finding: Persistent MSU deposition with subcutaneous tophi (draining or chalk-like nodules, often with overlying vascularity, typically at joints, ears, olecranon bursae, finger pads and tendons such as the Achilles), chronic arthropathy and radiographic erosions. Gout can progress to chronic tophaceous or chronic erosive gout, or both. DECT urate deposits are present in 84% of late gout. Tophus rupture can allow secondary wound infection and septic arthritis (the commonest route of infection in a series of concomitant septic and gouty arthritis). Course can be accelerated in transplant recipients (see natural_history).
stage_4_chronic_tophaceous_gout.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590); Dalbeth N et al., Urate crystal deposition in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and symptomatic gout: a dual energy CT study, Ann Rheum Dis 2015 (PMID 25637002); Yu KH et al., Concomitant septic and gouty arthritis - an analysis of 30 cases, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2003;42:1062-6 (PMID 12730521)

core.name: Podagra - acute arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
core.note: Classic podagra has an LR of 30.64 (95% CI 20.51-45.77) for gout, and the first MTP is the joint most commonly affected in gout. Monoarticular involvement of a foot or ankle joint, especially the first MTP, is a key clinical feature in EULAR 2018. A precise percentage of first attacks involving the first MTP joint was not verified from a primary source in this research pass and is deliberately not quoted.
core.source: Zhang W et al., EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1301-11 (PMID 16707533); Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758); Hainer BL et al., Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of gout, Am Fam Physician 2014;90:831-6 (PMID 25591183)

core.name: Acute, rapid-onset monoarthritis peaking within a day (often nocturnal)
core.note: Rapid onset of severe pain and swelling, with time to maximal pain <24 h as an ACR/EULAR criterion; podagra classically begins in the middle of the night. Pain is severe enough that ACR/EULAR scoring includes inability to bear touch/pressure on the joint and great difficulty walking.
core.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758); Simkin PA, The pathogenesis of podagra, Ann Intern Med 1977;86:230-3 (PMID 319726)

core.name: Local inflammatory signs: erythema, warmth, swelling, exquisite tenderness
core.note: Erythema overlying the joint, inability to bear touch or pressure, and great difficulty using the joint are the characteristics scored in the ACR/EULAR criteria; erythema is a suggestive feature in EULAR 2018. Because erythema mimics cellulitis and septic arthritis, these signs do not distinguish gout from infection.
core.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758)

core.name: Other joints: ankle, mid-foot, knee, oligoarticular or polyarticular flares
core.note: Ankle or mid-foot involvement (without the first MTP) scores in the ACR/EULAR criteria. First MTP, ankle or mid-foot involvement as part of a polyarticular presentation is not specific for gout because the same pattern is common in rheumatoid arthritis. Oligoarticular forms reduced diagnostic precision of referring physicians in a 248-patient cohort of urate crystal arthropathy.
core.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Perez Ruiz F et al., Influence of the natural history of disease on a previous diagnosis in patients with gout, Reumatol Clin 2009;5:248-51 (PMID 21794624)

core.name: Self-limiting course with complete resolution between early flares
core.note: Typical episodes resolve within <=14 days and, in early disease, return completely to baseline between attacks; flares resolve spontaneously through NET-mediated cytokine degradation even while crystals persist.
core.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Schauer C et al., Aggregated neutrophil extracellular traps limit inflammation by degrading cytokines and chemokines, Nat Med 2014;20:511-7 (PMID 24784231)

core.name: Tophi
core.note: Draining or chalk-like subcutaneous nodules under transparent skin, often with overlying vascularity, in typical locations (joints, ears, olecranon bursae, finger pads, tendons such as the Achilles). Clinically evident tophi have an LR of 39.95 (21.06-75.79) for gout and score 4 points in the ACR/EULAR criteria; aspirated tophus material showing MSU crystals is by itself sufficient to classify gout. A verified prevalence of tophi and typical time-to-tophi from a primary source was not obtained (see natural_history).
core.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Zhang W et al., EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1301-11 (PMID 16707533)

core.name: Chronic gouty arthropathy with joint erosions
core.note: Chronic inflammation and deposition lead to chronic erosive arthropathy (gout-related erosions on hand/foot radiographs are scored 4 points in ACR/EULAR criteria); in the GBD 2021 gout paper the disease is described as progressing to chronic tophaceous or chronic erosive gout, or both.
core.source: Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590)

core.name: Kidney stones (uric acid and calcium nephrolithiasis)
core.note: In NHANES III, 13.9% of people with gout reported prior kidney stones; the fully adjusted OR for stones in gout was 1.49 (95% CI 1.04-2.14) after adjusting for sex, race, BMI and hypertension. In a meta-analysis (17 studies) the pooled prevalence of self-reported lifetime nephrolithiasis in gout was 14% (95% CI 12-17%) and gout was associated with nephrolithiasis (pooled adjusted OR 1.77, 1.43-2.19).
core.source: Kramer HM, Curhan G, The association between gout and nephrolithiasis: NHANES III 1988-1994, Am J Kidney Dis 2002;40:37-42 (PMID 12087559); Roughley MJ et al., Gout and risk of chronic kidney disease and nephrolithiasis: meta-analysis of observational studies, Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:90 (PMID 25889144)

core.name: Chronic kidney disease (association with gout in both directions)
core.note: In the same meta-analysis the pooled prevalence of CKD stage >=3 in people with gout was 24% (19-28%) and gout was associated with CKD (pooled adjusted OR 2.41, 1.86-3.11). Causality runs both ways: in MRFIT, CKD raised the risk of incident gout (adjusted HR 1.61; each standard-deviation fall in eGFR HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.35-1.51), and proteinuria and haematuria were independently associated with gout. The GBD 2021 analysis attributes 11.8% of gout YLDs to kidney dysfunction. Whether urate crystals or hyperuricaemia themselves cause primary 'urate nephropathy' in gout is not resolved by these data and should be judged with the CKD entry.
core.source: Roughley MJ et al., Gout and risk of chronic kidney disease and nephrolithiasis: meta-analysis of observational studies, Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:90 (PMID 25889144); Krishnan E, Chronic kidney disease and the risk of incident gout among middle-aged men: a seven-year prospective observational study, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:3271-8 (PMID 23982888); GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590)

atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.name: Oligoarticular, polyarticular or chronic forms are frequently misdiagnosed
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.note: Clinical diagnostic precision was best in monoarticular forms and worsened with oligoarticular involvement; chronic and severe forms were frequently wrongly evaluated, and the presence of tophi did not improve diagnostic precision. Practical implication: a low threshold for arthrocentesis in atypical presentations.
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.source: Perez Ruiz F et al., Reumatol Clin 2009;5:248-51 (PMID 21794624)

atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.name: Normouricaemic flare
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.note: Only 14% of patients in two acute-gout trials had urate <=6 mg/dL during the attack, but attacks did occur with urate below the 6.8 mg/dL saturation point, attributed possibly to persistence of tophi and an increased body urate pool. A normal urate does not exclude gout.
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.source: Schlesinger N et al., J Rheumatol 2009;36:1287-9 (PMID 19369457)

atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.name: Gout in solid-organ transplant recipients
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.note: Hyperuricaemia occurs in 5-84% and gout in 1.7-28% of solid-organ transplant recipients; ciclosporin is an additional risk factor. In 196 heart or heart/lung transplant recipients on ciclosporin, hyperuricaemia occurred in 72% of men and 81% of women, and 14 (8%) developed definite gout a mean of 17 months after transplant; polyarticular arthritis and/or tophi developed in 6 of these 14 (43%) within a mean of 31 months, i.e. a frequently accelerated course. In Medicare kidney transplant recipients the cumulative incidence of new-onset gout was 7.6% at 3 years (Neoral vs tacrolimus adjusted HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.07-1.47) and new-onset gout was associated with worse patient survival (AHR 1.26, 1.08-1.47) and graft loss.
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.source: Stamp L et al., Gout in solid organ transplantation: a challenging clinical problem, Drugs 2005;65:2593-611 (PMID 16392875); Burack DA et al., Hyperuricemia and gout among heart transplant recipients receiving cyclosporine, Am J Med 1992;92:141-6 (PMID 1543197); Abbott KC et al., New-onset gout after kidney transplantation: incidence, risk factors and implications, Transplantation 2005;80:1383-91 (PMID 16340779)

atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.name: Gout complicated by septic arthritis
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.note: In 30 patients with concomitant septic and gouty arthritis one-third were afebrile, 30% had a normal blood leucocyte count and 10% had synovial fluid leucocytes <6,000/mm3; most had long-standing disease with tophi, and rupture of subcutaneous tophi with wound infection was the commonest route (Staphylococcus aureus in 16, 7 oxacillin-resistant). Two died. Culture of aspirated fluid is warranted in a gouty attack even when white cell count is low or Gram stain is negative.
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.source: Yu KH et al., Concomitant septic and gouty arthritis - an analysis of 30 cases, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2003;42:1062-6 (PMID 12730521)

atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.name: Chronic tophaceous gout mimicking rheumatoid arthritis
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.note: Chronic tophaceous gout may fulfil the older ARA criteria for RA, and tophaceous granulomas can histologically resemble rheumatoid nodules or rheumatoid synovitis; MSU crystals may be visible only on compensated polarised light of properly fixed (formalin/alcohol) material. True coexistence of chronic tophaceous gout and RA is extremely rare (only 6 genuine cases in one 1981 report).
atypical_presentations_and_special_setti.source: Atdjian M et al., Coexistence of chronic tophaceous gout and rheumatoid arthritis, J Rheumatol 1981;8:989-92 (PMID 7328573)

septic_arthritis_must_be_excluded.finding: Septic arthritis is the diagnosis that must not be missed in any acute hot joint. Risk factors that significantly raise the probability of septic arthritis include age, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, joint surgery, hip or knee prosthesis, skin infection and HIV infection. Symptoms are weak discriminators: joint pain (sensitivity 85%), history of joint swelling (78%) and fever (57%) were the only findings in >50% of septic arthritis, sweats 27% and rigors 19%, so absence of fever does not exclude infection. Synovial fluid WBC is the most powerful readily available test: LR 0.32 for <25,000/uL, 2.9 for >=25,000, 7.7 for >50,000 and 28 for >100,000/uL. Crystals do not exclude infection: among 265 crystal-positive aspirates in a tertiary centre, 4 (1.5%) had positive cultures, all with synovial WBC >50,000/uL and significant comorbidity (mean WBC in those four 113,000/uL versus 23,200/uL overall). Concomitant septic and gouty arthritis presents diagnostic difficulty; culture is warranted even with low WBC or negative Gram stain.
septic_arthritis_must_be_excluded.source: Margaretten ME et al., Does this adult patient have septic arthritis?, JAMA 2007;297:1478-88 (PMID 17405973); Shah K et al., Does the presence of crystal arthritis rule out septic arthritis?, J Emerg Med 2007;32:23-6 (PMID 17239729); Yu KH et al., Concomitant septic and gouty arthritis - an analysis of 30 cases, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2003;42:1062-6 (PMID 12730521)

cppd_pseudogout.finding: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease is the crystal-arthritis differential. Definitive diagnosis relies on identifying CPP crystals in synovial fluid; rapid-onset inflammatory symptoms are suggestive but not definitive. EULAR 2011 recognised risk factors: ageing, osteoarthritis, primary hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis and hypomagnesaemia (familial forms are rare); radiographic chondrocalcinosis is neither highly sensitive nor specific, and ultrasound is more useful (LR 24.2). CPP crystals in synovial fluid are typically rod or rhomboid in shape (67% rods, 33% rhomboids in one series) and often weakly birefringent, in contrast to needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent MSU crystals. Both crystal types activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, so flares can look identical. The 2023 ACR/EULAR CPPD classification criteria treat crowned dens syndrome or CPP crystals in synovial fluid as sufficient, otherwise a score >56; sensitivity/specificity 92.2%/87.9% in the derivation cohort and 99.2%/92.5% in the validation cohort. Of 265 crystal-positive aspirates in one series, 69.0% were gout, 30.6% pseudogout and 0.4% both, so the two can coexist. Practical point: CPPD tends to occur in older adults with osteoarthritis or a metabolic cause, but only polarised microscopy of synovial fluid reliably separates the two.
cppd_pseudogout.source: Zhang W et al., EULAR recommendations for calcium pyrophosphate deposition. Part I: terminology and diagnosis, Ann Rheum Dis 2011;70:563-70 (PMID 21216817); Abhishek A et al., The 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for CPPD disease, Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:1248-1257 (PMID 37495237); Zell M et al., Calcium pyrophosphate crystal size and characteristics, Osteoarthr Cartil Open 2021;3 (PMID 34386778); Hainer BL et al., Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of gout, Am Fam Physician 2014;90:831-6 (PMID 25591183); Martinon F et al., Gout-associated uric acid crystals activate the NALP3 inflammasome, Nature 2006;440:237-41 (PMID 16407889); Shah K et al., Does the presence of crystal arthritis rule out septic arthritis?, J Emerg Med 2007;32:23-6 (PMID 17239729)
cppd_pseudogout.confidence: high for the diagnostic framework; moderate for the birefringence contrast, which is stated from standard microscopy teaching plus the Hainer (MSU) and Zell (CPP shape, weak birefringence) sources

rheumatoid_arthritis.finding: RA is classified under the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria (definite RA: synovitis in >=1 joint, no better alternative diagnosis, total score >=6 of 10 from joint involvement, serology, acute-phase reactants and duration). Distinguishing features from gout: RA is scored on persistent synovitis, serological abnormality (rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP), acute-phase reactants and symptom duration, whereas gout is recurrent self-limiting attacks with complete resolution between episodes and crystal-proven monosodium urate; but early gout with polyarticular foot involvement and chronic tophaceous gout can mimic RA, and first MTP/ankle/mid-foot involvement within a polyarticular pattern is not specific for gout because it is common in RA. True coexistence is rare. See the rheumatoid arthritis entry in this knowledge base for RA clinical detail.
rheumatoid_arthritis.source: Aletaha D et al., 2010 rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria, Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-8 (PMID 20699241); Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Atdjian M et al., J Rheumatol 1981;8:989-92 (PMID 7328573)

cellulitis.finding: An acute gout attack is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis, and the reverse. In a single-centre study of 184 acute gout attacks and 183 lower-limb cellulitis cases, the delta neutrophil index (immature granulocyte fraction) was lower in gout (0.6% vs 2.8%; cut-off 1.7% to predict cellulitis; OR 9.7), including in patients without MSU confirmation and with normouricaemia. This is a single-centre finding and not a validated bedside rule; joint aspiration for crystals and culture remains the discriminating test when a joint effusion is present.
cellulitis.source: Pyo JY et al., Delta neutrophil index contributes to the differential diagnosis between acute gout attack and cellulitis within 24 hours after hospitalization, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2017;56:795-801 (PMID 28115599)

reactive_arthritis.finding: Reactive arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis: additive or migratory oligoarthritis (large-joint oligoarthritis in the Reiter's-syndrome subtype) with inflammatory back pain and extra-articular features (uveitis, urogenital, skin), following a gastrointestinal or urogenital infection by about 1-6 weeks; it typically affects young adults, is associated with HLA-B27, and cultures of synovial fluid are negative. It differs from septic arthritis (fever, systemic infection signs, monoarthritis) and from gout by the antecedent infection, extra-articular signs and absence of crystals.
reactive_arthritis.source: Selmi C, Gershwin ME, Diagnosis and classification of reactive arthritis, Autoimmun Rev 2014;13:546-9 (PMID 24418301)

trauma.finding: Acute trauma or fracture can present as a hot, swollen, painful joint; however, gout, especially podagra, often follows abuse or minor injury of the foot, so a history of trauma does not exclude gout. A dedicated primary study of discriminating features between traumatic arthritis and gout was not obtained in this research pass, so no quantitative discriminator is quoted; imaging and synovial fluid analysis (crystals, blood, culture) are the practical tools.
trauma.source: Simkin PA, The pathogenesis of podagra, Ann Intern Med 1977;86:230-3 (PMID 319726)
trauma.confidence: moderate (mechanism stated as hypothesis; no quantitative trauma-versus-gout data verified)

red_flags: Fever, rigors or systemic toxicity with a hot swollen joint: septic arthritis must be excluded by joint aspiration with cell count, Gram stain and culture before attributing the episode to gout; fever occurs in only about 57% of septic arthritis, so its absence does not reassure (Margaretten ME et al., JAMA 2007;297:1478-88, PMID 17405973).

Crystals seen in synovial fluid do not exclude infection: 1.5% of crystal-positive aspirates in one 265-aspirate series grew bacteria, and all had synovial WBC >50,000/uL and significant comorbidity; in 30 cases of concomitant septic and gouty arthritis one-third were afebrile, 30% had normal blood leucocyte count and 10% had synovial WBC <6,000/mm3, so send fluid for culture regardless (Shah K et al., J Emerg Med 2007, PMID 17239729; Yu KH et al., Rheumatology 2003, PMID 12730521).

Immunosuppression, diabetes, prosthetic joint, recent joint surgery, skin infection (including a ruptured or ulcerated tophus) or HIV: these raise the probability of septic arthritis and, in a gouty patient, tophus rupture with wound infection is the commonest route of infection in concomitant septic-gouty arthritis (Margaretten 2007; Yu 2003).

Polyarticular flare or rapid evolution to polyarticular arthritis and/or tophi in a transplant recipient on ciclosporin: in one series 43% of post-transplant-onset definite gout developed polyarticular disease and/or tophi within a mean 31 months, so gout in transplant patients is often accelerated and its treatment is complicated by renal insufficiency and drug interactions (Burack DA et al., Am J Med 1992;92:141-6, PMID 1543197; Stamp L et al., Drugs 2005;65:2593-611, PMID 16392875).

Monoarthritis without a clear pattern, or any atypical presentation where crystals cannot be identified: EULAR 2018 recommends imaging (ultrasound double-contour sign/tophi) rather than assuming gout, and a diagnosis must not rest on hyperuricaemia alone (Richette P et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38, PMID 31167758).

Flare in a patient with reduced eGFR, prior cardiovascular disease or on low-dose aspirin/diuretics: treatment choices (NSAIDs, colchicine dose) and cardiovascular risk need review; a recent flare was associated with a transient increase in myocardial infarction or stroke (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.57-2.38 within 0-60 days) (Cipolletta E et al., JAMA 2022;328:440-450, PMID 35916846).

Mono- or oligoarthritis after infection with inflammatory back pain, uveitis or urogenital symptoms suggests reactive arthritis or another spondyloarthritis rather than gout (Selmi C, Gershwin ME, Autoimmun Rev 2014;13:546-9, PMID 24418301).

real_risk_factors.factor: Serum urate level and duration of hyperuricaemia (strongest single predictor)
real_risk_factors.note: Risk is steeply concentration-dependent: 15-year cumulative incidence 1.1% at urate <6 mg/dL rising to 49% at >=10 mg/dL (adjusted HR 64 vs <6). The Normative Aging Study showed annual gout incidence of 4.9% at urate >=9 mg/dL versus 0.1% at <7.0 mg/dL; when urate was in the model, age, BMI, hypertension, cholesterol and alcohol lost independent predictive power, i.e. they act largely through urate.
real_risk_factors.source: Dalbeth N et al., Relationship between serum urate concentration and clinically evident incident gout: an individual participant data analysis, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:1048-1052 (PMID 29463518); Campion EW et al., Asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Risks and consequences in the Normative Aging Study, Am J Med 1987 (PMID 3826098)

real_risk_factors.factor: Male sex; age; menopause in women
real_risk_factors.note: GBD 2021: 2020 prevalence 3.26 times higher in males than females (95% UI 3.11-3.39) and increasing with age. In the Nurses' Health Study (92,535 women, 1,703 incident cases over 16 years) incidence rose from 0.6 per 1000 person-years in women <45 to 2.5 in women >=75; postmenopausal women had RR 1.26 (95% CI 1.03-1.55) vs premenopausal, RR 1.62 (1.12-2.33) with menopause before age 45 versus 50-54, and postmenopausal hormone use RR 0.82 (0.70-0.96).
real_risk_factors.source: GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590); Hak AE et al., Menopause, postmenopausal hormone use and risk of incident gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1305-9 (PMID 19592386)

real_risk_factors.note: In 47,150 men (730 incident cases), relative risk versus BMI 21-22.9 was 1.95 (BMI 25-29.9), 2.33 (30-34.9) and 2.97 (>=35); weight gain of >=30 lb since age 21 RR 1.99; weight loss of >=10 lb RR 0.61 (0.40-0.92). Meta-analysis: BMI >=30 adjusted RR 2.24 (1.76-2.86). GBD 2021: high BMI accounted for 34.3% of gout YLDs.
real_risk_factors.source: Choi HK et al., Arch Intern Med 2005;165:742-8 (PMID 15824292); Evans PL et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2018;20:136 (PMID 29976236); GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590)

real_risk_factors.note: Incident gout in men (RR versus abstainers): 1.32 (10.0-14.9 g/day), 1.49 (15.0-29.9), 1.96 (30.0-49.9), 2.53 (>=50 g/day); per 12-oz beer/day RR 1.49 (1.32-1.70); spirits per drink 1.15 (1.04-1.28); wine per 4-oz 1.04 (0.88-1.22, not significant). For flares in existing gout, >1-2 drinks in the prior 24 h raised attack risk 1.36 (1.00-1.88) and >2-4 drinks 1.51 (1.09-2.09), with wine, beer and liquor each associated.
real_risk_factors.source: Choi HK et al., Alcohol intake and risk of incident gout in men, Lancet 2004;363:1277-81 (PMID 15094272); Neogi T et al., Am J Med 2014;127:311-8 (PMID 24440541)

real_risk_factors.note: Men consuming >=2 servings/day of sugar-sweetened soft drinks had RR 1.85 (1.08-3.16) versus <1/month; top fifth of fructose intake RR 2.02 (1.49-2.75); fructose-rich fruit juice and fruits (apples, oranges) were also associated with higher risk, while diet soft drinks were not associated.
real_risk_factors.source: Choi HK, Curhan G, BMJ 2008;336:309-12 (PMID 18244959)

real_risk_factors.factor: Purine-rich foods (meat, seafood); dairy is protective
real_risk_factors.note: Highest versus lowest quintile RR of incident gout: meat 1.41 (1.07-1.86), seafood 1.51 (1.17-1.95); dairy 0.56 (0.42-0.74); purine-rich vegetables and total protein were not associated. In people with gout, acute purine intake over a 2-day window raised recurrent-attack risk with OR up to 4.76 for the top vs lowest quintile (animal-source purine OR 2.41, plant-source 1.39).
real_risk_factors.source: Choi HK et al., N Engl J Med 2004;350:1093-103 (PMID 15014182); Zhang Y et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:1448-53 (PMID 22648933)

real_risk_factors.factor: Diuretics (thiazide and loop) and other antihypertensives
real_risk_factors.note: In hypertensive patients, current diuretic use RR of incident gout 2.36 (2.21-2.52), beta-blockers 1.48 (1.40-1.57), ACE inhibitors 1.24 (1.17-1.32), non-losartan ARBs 1.29 (1.16-1.43); calcium-channel blockers 0.87 (0.82-0.93) and losartan 0.81 (0.70-0.94) were associated with lower risk. Meta-analysis: diuretic use adjusted RR 2.39 (1.57-3.65). Recent diuretic use within 48 h was associated with OR 3.6 (1.4-9.7) for recurrent attacks in an online case-crossover study of 197 people.
real_risk_factors.source: Choi HK et al., BMJ 2012;344:d8190 (PMID 22240117); Evans PL et al., 2018 (PMID 29976236); Hunter DJ et al., J Rheumatol 2006;33:1341-5 (PMID 16758506)

real_risk_factors.note: In 724 people with gout, aspirin <=325 mg/day on two consecutive days raised the odds of a gout attack (OR 1.81, 1.30-2.51; OR 1.91, 1.32-2.85 for <=100 mg), including in subgroups by renal function; concomitant allopurinol nullified the effect. Practical: cardioprotective aspirin should not be stopped reflexively; urate monitoring and adequate urate-lowering matter.
real_risk_factors.source: Zhang Y et al., Low-dose aspirin use and recurrent gout attacks, Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:385-90 (PMID 23345599)

real_risk_factors.factor: Chronic kidney disease (reduced eGFR, proteinuria, haematuria)
real_risk_factors.note: In MRFIT, CKD carried adjusted HR 1.61 for incident gout and each SD fall in eGFR HR 1.43 (1.35-1.51), independent of serum urate. See the chronic_kidney_disease entry.
real_risk_factors.source: Krishnan E, Chronic kidney disease and the risk of incident gout among middle-aged men: a seven-year prospective observational study, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:3271-8 (PMID 23982888)

real_risk_factors.note: Hypertension: incident-gout adjusted HR 1.64 (1.34-2.01) and RR 2.11 (1.64-2.72) in meta-analysis; in men RR 2.31 (1.96-2.72) independent of diuretics. Metabolic syndrome was present in 62.8% (51.9-73.6) of US adults with gout versus 25.4% (23.5-27.3) without (age-sex adjusted OR 3.05, 2.01-4.61). See hypertension and obesity_metabolic_syndrome entries.
real_risk_factors.source: Evans PL et al., 2018 (PMID 29976236); Choi HK et al., 2005 (PMID 15824292); Choi HK et al., Prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in patients with gout: NHANES III, Arthritis Rheum 2007;57:109-15 (PMID 17266099)

real_risk_factors.note: ABCG2 Q141K: adjusted gout OR 1.68 per risk allele, at least 10% of gout cases in whites attributable; ABCG2 Q126X OR 5.97; SLC2A9 rs16890979 T allele protective (OR 0.59); 2024 GWAS identified 377 loci including NLRP3-regulating genes. Genetic risk scores show graded gout frequency (1-18% across score categories in ARIC whites). Genetics explains why only some hyperuricaemic people flare and why gout runs in families.
real_risk_factors.source: Woodward OM et al., PNAS 2009 (PMID 19506252); Matsuo H et al., 2009 (PMID 20368174); Dehghan A et al., Lancet 2008 (PMID 18834626); Major TJ et al., Nat Genet 2024 (PMID 39406924)

real_risk_factors.note: Ciclosporin is an independent risk factor for gout after transplantation; new-onset gout in 7.6% of Medicare kidney recipients at 3 years (Neoral vs tacrolimus HR 1.25); diabetes was associated with lower risk of new-onset gout.
real_risk_factors.source: Abbott KC et al., New-onset gout after kidney transplantation: incidence, risk factors and implications, Transplantation 2005;80:1383-91 (PMID 16340779); Stamp L et al., Gout in solid organ transplantation: a challenging clinical problem, Drugs 2005;65:2593-611 (PMID 16392875)

real_risk_factors.factor: Diabetes as a paradoxical protective factor
real_risk_factors.note: In a UK nested case-control study of 24,768 incident gout cases, diabetes was associated with RR 0.67 (0.63-0.71) for future gout (0.81, 0.67 and 0.52 for duration 0-3, 4-9 and >=10 years; type 1 0.33 vs type 2 0.69), attributed in the paper to glycosuria's uricosuric effect or impaired inflammatory response. This is an inverse risk association, not a recommendation; gout nevertheless predicts later type 2 diabetes (see comorbidities).
real_risk_factors.source: Rodriguez G, Soriano LC, Choi HK, Impact of diabetes against the future risk of developing gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:2090-4 (PMID 20570836)

association_strength.finding: Allopurinol is a frequent cause of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR: DRESS/hypersensitivity syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis). In Han Chinese, HLA-B*58:01 was present in 100% of 51 allopurinol-SCAR patients versus 15% of 135 allopurinol-tolerant patients (OR 580.3, 95% CI 34.4-9780.9) and 20% of 93 healthy controls (OR 393.5). In Thai patients all 27 allopurinol SJS/TEN cases (100%) carried HLA-B*58:01 versus 12.96% of tolerant controls (OR 348.3, 19.2-6336.9); sensitivity 100%, specificity 87%, and at an assumed 0.2% SJS/TEN prevalence a positive predictive value of only 1.52% and negative predictive value of 100%. A meta-analysis gave pooled ORs of 96.60 (24.49-381.00) with matched controls (4 studies, 55 cases) and 79.28 (41.51-151.35) with population controls (5 studies, 69 cases) with similar findings in Asian and non-Asian populations; a later 21-study meta-analysis of cutaneous adverse reactions gave sensitivity 0.93 and specificity 0.89 for HLA-B*58:01. Note that most carriers never develop SCAR (low positive predictive value), while non-carriers are very unlikely to.
association_strength.source: Hung SI et al., HLA-B*5801 allele as a genetic marker for severe cutaneous adverse reactions caused by allopurinol, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2005;102:4134-9 (PMID 15743917); Tassaneeyakul W et al., Strong association between HLA-B*5801 and allopurinol-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in a Thai population, Pharmacogenet Genomics 2009;19:704-9 (PMID 19696695); Somkrua R et al., Association of HLA-B*5801 allele and allopurinol-induced Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis, BMC Med Genet 2011;12:118 (PMID 21906289); Wu R et al., Impact of HLA-B*58:01 allele and allopurinol-induced cutaneous adverse drug reactions: evidence from 21 pharmacogenetic studies, Oncotarget 2016 (PMID 27835909; full text PMC5348437)
association_strength.confidence: high (associations are very strong; absolute risk in any one carrier remains low)

prospective_screening_evidence.finding: In a Taiwanese national prospective cohort (2,926 Han Chinese with an indication for allopurinol, 2,910 genotyped), 19.6% (571) were HLA-B*58:01 positive and were advised to avoid allopurinol; 2,339 negatives were given allopurinol and none developed SCAR, whereas 7 cases were expected from the historical incidence (0.30% per year, 95% CI 0.28-0.31%); mild transient rash occurred in 97 (3%). Prospective screening with an alternative for carriers therefore significantly reduced allopurinol-induced SCAR.
prospective_screening_evidence.source: Ko TM et al., Use of HLA-B*58:01 genotyping to prevent allopurinol induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions in Taiwan: national prospective cohort study, BMJ 2015;351:h4848 (PMID 26399967)
prospective_screening_evidence.confidence: high (single national cohort, historical comparator rather than randomised)

allele_frequency_and_population_relevanc.finding: HLA-B*58:01 frequency in control groups was about 20% in Han Chinese (Hung 2005), 12.96% in Thai tolerant controls (Tassaneeyakul 2009) and 19.6% in Han Chinese Taiwanese with a gout/hyperuricaemia indication (Ko 2015). For India, a single molecular typing study of healthy unrelated North Indians found HLA-B*58:01 as the only B-locus allele with a frequency of about 15%. The 2020 ACR guideline text recommends HLA-B*58:01 testing before allopurinol for patients of Southeast Asian descent (for example Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) and African American patients, and recommends against testing in other ethnic groups; the CPIC guideline (2013, updated 2016) provides genotype-based allopurinol guidance. South Asian (Indian) ancestry is not named in the ACR wording as retrieved.
allele_frequency_and_population_relevanc.source: Hung SI et al., HLA-B*5801 allele as a genetic marker for severe cutaneous adverse reactions caused by allopurinol, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2005;102:4134-9 (PMID 15743917); Tassaneeyakul W et al., Strong association between HLA-B*5801 and allopurinol-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in a Thai population, Pharmacogenet Genomics 2009;19:704-9 (PMID 19696695); Ko TM et al., Use of HLA-B*58:01 genotyping to prevent allopurinol induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions in Taiwan: national prospective cohort study, BMJ 2015;351:h4848 (PMID 26399967); Rani R et al., Molecular diversity of HLA-A, -B and -C alleles in a North Indian population as determined by PCR-SSOP, Int J Immunogenet 2007;34:201-8 (PMID 17504510); FitzGerald JD et al., 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934); Hershfield MS et al., Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium guidelines for HLA-B genotype and allopurinol dosing, Clin Pharmacol Ther 2013;93:153-8 (PMID 23232549); Saito Y et al., CPIC update, Clin Pharmacol Ther 2016;99:36-7 (PMID 26094938)
allele_frequency_and_population_relevanc.confidence: high for the Han Chinese/Thai/Taiwan figures; moderate for the Indian frequency (single North Indian study, sample size not verified, India is genetically heterogeneous)

india_specific_gap.finding: No Indian study of allopurinol-induced SCAR genotype association (case-control or prospective screening) was found in this research pass. Because the reported North Indian HLA-B*58:01 frequency (about 15%) is of similar order to that in Han Chinese and Thai controls, the risk in Indian patients is plausibly comparable, but this is an inference from allele frequency, not a measured Indian risk estimate. Whether to genotype an Indian patient before allopurinol is therefore a clinician decision rather than a guideline-mandated step in the sources retrieved; with tophaceous/CKD patients needing allopurinol, low starting dose with slow titration is the ACR 2020 recommendation.
india_specific_gap.source: Rani R et al., Molecular diversity of HLA-A, -B and -C alleles in a North Indian population as determined by PCR-SSOP, Int J Immunogenet 2007;34:201-8 (PMID 17504510); FitzGerald JD et al., 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934)

cross_references.finding: This entry cross-references, rather than duplicates, the following knowledge-base entries: chronic_kidney_disease (bidirectional link with gout, urate handling and drug dosing), hypertension (risk factor for gout and drug-induced hyperuricaemia), obesity_metabolic_syndrome (dominant modifiable driver of gout; high BMI accounts for 34.3% of gout YLDs), diabetes_mellitus (gout predicts type 2 diabetes yet diabetes lowers incident gout risk) and, for the differential, rheumatoid_arthritis.
