cross_references.source: GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590); Roughley MJ et al., Gout and risk of chronic kidney disease and nephrolithiasis: meta-analysis of observational studies, Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:90 (PMID 25889144)

cardiovascular_disease.finding: Gout is associated with an excess of myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death. MRFIT (12,866 men, mean 6.5 years): gout associated with acute MI, adjusted OR 1.26 (1.14-1.40), independent of renal function, metabolic syndrome, diuretics and traditional risk factors; hyperuricaemia OR 1.11 (1.08-1.15). Health Professionals Follow-Up Study (51,297 men, 12 years): gout RR 1.38 (1.15-1.66) for CVD death, 1.55 (1.24-1.93) for fatal CHD and 1.59 (1.04-2.41) for nonfatal MI. English record-linkage (202,033 hospital patients with gout): RR of MI 1.82 (1.78-1.85), of stroke 1.71 (1.68-1.75); associations stronger in younger age groups. Meta-analysis (6 papers, 223,448 patients): adjusted pooled HR 1.29 (1.14-1.44) for CVD mortality and 1.42 (1.22-1.63) for CHD mortality, but no significant association with MI mortality. Cardiovascular events cluster after flares: the odds of a flare 0-60 days before an MI/stroke were 1.93 (1.57-2.38) and 61-120 days 1.57 (1.26-1.96), with no association at 121-180 days (OR 1.06).
cardiovascular_disease.source: Krishnan E et al., Gout and the risk of acute myocardial infarction, Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2688-96 (PMID 16871533); Choi HK, Curhan G, Circulation 2007;116:894-900 (PMID 17698728); Seminog OO, Goldacre MJ, Rheumatology 2013;52:2251-9 (PMID 24046469); Clarson LE et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2015;22:335-43 (PMID 24281251); Cipolletta E et al., JAMA 2022;328:440-450 (PMID 35916846)
cardiovascular_disease.confidence: high for association; causality of gout per se versus shared risk factors is not settled (the MRFIT and HPFS analyses adjust extensively, but residual confounding cannot be excluded)

all_cause_mortality.finding: Gout, more than asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, is linked with higher mortality. Health-screening cohort of 61,527 people in Taiwan: adjusted all-cause mortality HR 1.46 (1.12-1.91) and CV mortality HR 1.97 (1.08-3.59) for gout, but not for hyperuricaemia alone (HR 1.07, 0.94-1.22), and unchanged when limited to eGFR >60. NHANES III (15,773 participants, follow-up to 2006): gout HR 1.42 (1.12-1.82) for total and 1.58 (1.13-2.19) for CV mortality; each 1 mg/dL rise in urate HR 1.16 (1.10-1.22). HPFS: total mortality RR 1.28 (1.15-1.41) in men with gout.
all_cause_mortality.source: Kuo CF et al., Gout: an independent risk factor for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, Rheumatology 2010;49:141-6 (PMID 19933595); Stack AG et al., QJM 2013;106:647-58 (PMID 23564632); Choi HK, Curhan G, Circulation 2007 (PMID 17698728)

chronic_kidney_disease_and_nephrolithias.finding: Meta-analysis of 17 studies: pooled prevalence of CKD stage >=3 in gout 24% (19-28%); gout associated with CKD (pooled adjusted OR 2.41, 1.86-3.11) and with lifetime nephrolithiasis (14% prevalence; OR 1.77, 1.43-2.19). CKD also raises incident gout risk (MRFIT adjusted HR 1.61; each SD lower eGFR HR 1.43). Kidney dysfunction accounts for 11.8% of gout YLDs globally. Patients with gout should be actively screened for CKD and its consequences.
chronic_kidney_disease_and_nephrolithias.source: Roughley MJ et al., Gout and risk of chronic kidney disease and nephrolithiasis: meta-analysis of observational studies, Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:90 (PMID 25889144); Krishnan E, Chronic kidney disease and the risk of incident gout among middle-aged men: a seven-year prospective observational study, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:3271-8 (PMID 23982888); GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590)

hypertension.finding: Hypertension increases incident gout (meta-analysis adjusted HR 1.64, 1.34-2.01, RR 2.11, 1.64-2.72; HPFS RR 2.31), and antihypertensive choice matters (diuretics RR 2.36 and beta-blockers 1.48 raise gout risk; losartan RR 0.81 and calcium-channel blockers 0.87 lower it). In the Normative Aging Study, hypertensive men had about three times the incidence of gouty arthritis of normotensive men. Cross-reference: hypertension entry.
hypertension.source: Evans PL et al., 2018 (PMID 29976236); Choi HK et al., BMJ 2012;344:d8190 (PMID 22240117); Campion EW et al., Am J Med 1987 (PMID 3826098)

metabolic_syndrome_and_obesity.finding: Metabolic syndrome by revised NCEP ATP III criteria was found in 62.8% of NHANES III adults with gout versus 25.4% without (age-sex adjusted OR 3.05, 2.01-4.61). Obesity is the strongest modifiable risk factor for incident gout (BMI >=30 RR 2.24; weight loss of >=10 lb RR 0.61). Cross-reference: obesity_metabolic_syndrome entry.
metabolic_syndrome_and_obesity.source: Choi HK et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;57:109-15 (PMID 17266099); Evans PL et al., 2018 (PMID 29976236); Choi HK et al., 2005 (PMID 15824292)

diabetes_mellitus.finding: Two-way and partly paradoxical: in MRFIT (11,351 men, 6 years) gout was associated with incident type 2 diabetes (adjusted RR 1.34, 1.09-1.64; 1.26, 1.02-1.54 after adjusting for serum urate), whereas diabetes itself lowers the future risk of gout (RR 0.67, 0.63-0.71). Cross-reference: diabetes_mellitus entry.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Choi HK et al., Rheumatology 2008;47:1567-70 (PMID 18710901); Rodriguez G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:2090-4 (PMID 20570836)

other_associated_conditions.finding: A review of global gout epidemiology reports a firmly established increased risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease in gout, and novel associations with erectile dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, obstructive sleep apnoea, osteoporosis and venous thromboembolism, with discrete patterns of comorbidity clustering; rising obesity and comorbidity prevalence are likely to contribute substantially to the rising gout burden.
other_associated_conditions.source: Dehlin M et al., Global epidemiology of gout: prevalence, incidence, treatment patterns and risk factors, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 32541923)
other_associated_conditions.confidence: moderate (novel associations are less well established than CVD and CKD)

global.finding: GBD 2021: 55.8 million people (95% UI 44.4-69.8) had gout globally in 2020, age-standardised prevalence 659.3 per 100,000, up 22.5% since 1990; prevalence was 3.26 times higher in males and rises with age; cases are projected to reach 95.8 million in 2050 (an increase of more than 70%, mostly from population growth and ageing); age-standardised YLD rate 20.5 per 100,000; high BMI accounted for 34.3% and kidney dysfunction for 11.8% of YLDs. GBD authors note that in many low- and middle-income countries the estimates are modelled rather than primary data. A separate review reports gout prevalence from <1% to 6.8% and incidence of 0.58-2.89 per 1000 person-years in different populations, with only a third to half of patients on urate-lowering therapy and fewer than half adherent.
global.source: GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590); Dehlin M et al., Global epidemiology of gout: prevalence, incidence, treatment patterns and risk factors, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 32541923)

united_states.finding: NHANES 2015-2016: gout prevalence 3.9% of US adults (9.2 million), 5.2% in men and 2.7% in women; hyperuricaemia (>7.0 mg/dL men, >5.7 mg/dL women) about 20% in both sexes; prevalence stable 2007-2016; only 33% of gout patients were receiving urate-lowering therapy. A 2025 clinical review cites US gout prevalence of 5.1% (12.1 million adults).
united_states.source: Chen-Xu M et al., Contemporary Prevalence of Gout and Hyperuricemia in the United States and Decadal Trends: NHANES 2007-2016, Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:991-999 (PMID 30618180); FitzGerald JD et al., Gout, Ann Intern Med 2025;178:ITC33-ITC48 (PMID 40063960)
united_states.confidence: high (the two US estimates differ by survey period and method)

china_regional_comparator.finding: In a national cross-sectional survey of 78,130 adults in 31 Chinese provinces (2015-2017) weighted prevalence was 17.7% for hyperuricaemia and 3.2% for gout, with gout prevalence rising with age in both sexes.
china_regional_comparator.source: Song J et al., Prevalence and Risk Factors of Hyperuricemia and Gout: A Cross-sectional Survey from 31 Provinces in Mainland China, J Transl Int Med 2022;10:134-145 (PMID 35959454)

india_specific.finding: No national gout registry for India was identified in this research pass, and no nationally representative gout-specific survey was found; the national picture rests on community rheumatology surveys, modelled GBD estimates and hospital or health-camp hyperuricaemia series (the absence-of-registry statement means 'not found in this search', not proof that none exists). (1) Community COPCORD surveys with a rheumatologist examination found gout to be rare: 0.12% (5 of 4,092 adults) in rural Bhigwan, Pune district (1996 survey, published 2001); 0.06% urban Pune (8,145 adults) versus 0.1% rural in the later standardised comparison (2009); and 0.05% pooled across 12 sites (56,548 screened; 8 rural) in the 2025 COPCORD-BJD India analysis; the authors of the last note non-random site selection, clinical diagnosis and limited investigations, so these figures are probably conservative for true gout prevalence (my inference, not a statement in the papers). (2) GBD 2021 modelled figure for India: about 5.32 million prevalent gout cases and 164,153 YLDs in 2021, with age-standardised prevalence projected to rise in India through 2036; this modelled figure (roughly 0.4% of a ~1.4 billion population by simple division, my own arithmetic) is several-fold higher than the COPCORD point prevalences and the discrepancy is unresolved; GBD itself flags low- and middle-income estimates as modelled. (3) Hyperuricaemia is common and metabolically clustered: a retrospective screening study of 29,391 people attending Indian health-screening camps in 2017 found 25.8% with hyperuricaemia (33.6% of diabetics, 35.1% of hypertensives, 34.4% of diabetic hypertensives; point-of-care meter, not population-representative); a multicentre urban study of 1,528 hypertensive patients found 22.5% hyperuricaemia (12.2% Central to 29.6% East by region); in 316 patients at one tertiary hospital, metabolic syndrome was present in 35.4% of those with hyperuricaemia and uric acid correlated with central obesity, blood pressure and triglycerides. A clinical-profile series of Indian gout patients (tophi rate, delay to diagnosis, urate-lowering therapy use) and Indian national ULT-use data were not found and are not reported.
india_specific.source: Chopra A et al., Prevalence of rheumatic diseases in a rural population in western India: a WHO-ILAR COPCORD Study, J Assoc Physicians India 2001;49:240-6 (PMID 11225138); Joshi VL, Chopra A, Is there an urban-rural divide? Population surveys of rheumatic musculoskeletal disorders in the Pune region of India using the COPCORD Bhigwan model, J Rheumatol 2009;36:614-22 (PMID 19208598); Chopra A et al., Burden of Musculoskeletal (MSK) Pain and Arthritis in India: COPCORD-BJD India Project, Int J Rheum Dis 2025;28:e70163 (PMID 40051139); Mo Q et al., Burden, risk factors, and forecasts of gout in BRICS countries, 1990-2021, PLoS One 2025 (PMID 40991663); Billa G et al., Prevalence of Hyperuricemia in Indian Subjects attending Hyperuricemia Screening Programs, J Assoc Physicians India 2018;66:43-6 (PMID 30347952); Patni B et al., Prevalence of Hyperuricemia in Indian Population with Hypertension, J Assoc Physicians India 2023;71:45-48 (PMID 38716523); Rajadhyaksha A et al., A Clinical Profile of Patients with Hyperuricemia and the Relationship between Hyperuricemia and Metabolic Syndrome, J Assoc Physicians India 2022;70:11-12 (PMID 35598135); GBD 2021 Gout Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of gout, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, Lancet Rheumatol 2024;6:e507-e517 (PMID 38996590)
india_specific.confidence: moderate (real, peer-reviewed data, but no national registry; community surveys likely under-ascertain gout, GBD India figure is modelled, and hyperuricaemia series are convenience samples)

progression_from_hyperuricaemia.finding: Risk of a first flare rises steeply and non-linearly with serum urate and time: 15-year cumulative incidence 1.1% (<6 mg/dL) to 49% (>=10 mg/dL); annual incidence 4.9% at >=9 mg/dL, 0.5% at 7.0-8.9 and 0.1% at <7.0 mg/dL in men; long-term (28 years) Swedish cohort showed 14.7% of hyperuricaemic men and 19.5% of hyperuricaemic women developed gout, with the sex-by-urate interaction significant (higher hazard ratios in women). Practical takeaway: prolonged high urate is the driver, but most hyperuricaemic people do not get clinical gout.
progression_from_hyperuricaemia.source: Dalbeth N et al., Relationship between serum urate concentration and clinically evident incident gout: an individual participant data analysis, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:1048-1052 (PMID 29463518); Campion EW et al., Asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Risks and consequences in the Normative Aging Study, Am J Med 1987 (PMID 3826098); Kapetanovic MC et al., The risk of clinically diagnosed gout by serum urate levels: results from 30 years follow-up of the Malmo Preventive Project cohort in southern Sweden, Arthritis Res Ther 2018;20:190 (PMID 30157929)

flare_recurrence_rates_not_verified.finding: Exact recurrence percentages in untreated gout (the proportion of people with a second flare within 1, 2 and 10 years, and mean time to first tophus), which are widely quoted from mid-20th-century clinical series, could not be verified from a reachable primary text in this research pass (the primary article was paywalled) and are therefore deliberately not quoted here. What is verified: flares recur in people with sustained hyperuricaemia; MSU crystals remain in joints between flares (present in 43 of 43 sampled intercritical joints of patients not on urate-lowering drugs); and lowering urate reduces flares, tophi and deposit volume (long-term urate-lowering therapy dissolves crystals, preventing flares and tophi). Frequency of flares (>=2 per year) is used by the 2020 ACR guideline as a strong indication for urate-lowering therapy.
flare_recurrence_rates_not_verified.source: Pascual E et al., Synovial fluid analysis for diagnosis of intercritical gout, Ann Intern Med 1999;131:756-9 (PMID 10577299); Dalbeth N et al., Gout, Lancet 2021 (PMID 33798500); FitzGerald JD et al., 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934)
flare_recurrence_rates_not_verified.confidence: moderate (explicit verification gap for recurrence percentages)

progression_of_crystal_burden.finding: Dual-energy CT urate deposits were present in 24% of asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, 79% of early gout (<=3 years) and 84% of late gout, with similar volumes in early and late gout in that cross-sectional study, implying substantial deposition can accumulate before or early in clinical disease. Anti-inflammatory treatment of flares alone does not alter deposition, so patients may be unaware of progressive tophus formation and cartilage/bone destruction.
progression_of_crystal_burden.source: Dalbeth N et al., Urate crystal deposition in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and symptomatic gout: a dual energy CT study, Ann Rheum Dis 2015 (PMID 25637002); Benn CL et al., Physiology of Hyperuricemia and Urate-Lowering Treatments, Front Med (Lausanne) 2018;5:160 (PMID 29904633)

accelerated_course_in_transplant_and_ckd.finding: In ciclosporin-treated heart or heart/lung transplant recipients, gout began about 17 months post-transplant and 43% of definite post-transplant gout became polyarticular and/or tophaceous within about 31 months, i.e. an accelerated course; in kidney transplant recipients new-onset gout was independently associated with decreased patient survival (AHR 1.26, 1.08-1.47) and death-censored graft survival.
accelerated_course_in_transplant_and_ckd.source: Burack DA et al., Hyperuricemia and gout among heart transplant recipients receiving cyclosporine, Am J Med 1992;92:141-6 (PMID 1543197); Abbott KC et al., New-onset gout after kidney transplantation: incidence, risk factors and implications, Transplantation 2005;80:1383-91 (PMID 16340779)

mortality_and_cardiovascular_risk.finding: Gout carries excess all-cause and cardiovascular mortality independent of traditional risk factors in several cohorts (all-cause HR 1.28-1.46; CVD mortality HR/RR 1.29-1.97 depending on cohort; see comorbidities), with a transient rise in MI/stroke after flares. Hyperuricaemia alone in one large screening cohort did not raise mortality once adjusted, while gout did, suggesting inflammation and comorbidity burden rather than urate per se may drive the excess in gout.
mortality_and_cardiovascular_risk.source: Choi HK, Curhan G, Circulation 2007 (PMID 17698728); Kuo CF et al., Rheumatology 2010 (PMID 19933595); Stack AG et al., QJM 2013 (PMID 23564632); Clarson LE et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2015 (PMID 24281251); Cipolletta E et al., JAMA 2022 (PMID 35916846)
mortality_and_cardiovascular_risk.confidence: high for association; the causal interpretation in the final sentence is an inference

treatment_gap_shapes_natural_history.finding: Only about a third to a half of patients with gout receive urate-lowering therapy and fewer than half adhere (only 33% in NHANES 2007-2014), so real-world natural history includes avoidable progression; sustained lowering of urate below the saturation threshold is the primary method to prevent flares, tophi, chronic inflammatory arthritis and joint damage.
treatment_gap_shapes_natural_history.source: Dehlin M et al., Global epidemiology of gout: prevalence, incidence, treatment patterns and risk factors, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 32541923); Chen-Xu M et al., Contemporary Prevalence of Gout and Hyperuricemia in the United States and Decadal Trends: NHANES 2007-2016, Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:991-999 (PMID 30618180); FitzGerald JD et al., Gout, Ann Intern Med 2025;178:ITC33-ITC48 (PMID 40063960)

clinical_takeaway.point: Confirm gout with MSU crystals whenever possible: aspirate the joint (or a tophus) and look for needle-shaped, negatively birefringent intracellular crystals; aspirate previously inflamed joints even between flares if the diagnosis is uncertain.
clinical_takeaway.why: EULAR 2018 recommends a crystal search in every person with suspected gout because crystals allow a definite diagnosis; in one series all 43 patients not on urate-lowering drugs had crystals in asymptomatic previously inflamed joints. Ultrasound (double-contour sign, tophi) or dual-energy CT can support the diagnosis when crystals cannot be obtained, but DECT is less sensitive in early disease.
clinical_takeaway.source: Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758); Pascual E et al., Synovial fluid analysis for diagnosis of intercritical gout, Ann Intern Med 1999;131:756-9 (PMID 10577299); Bongartz T et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1072-7 (PMID 24671771)

clinical_takeaway.point: Always exclude septic arthritis in an acute hot joint, especially with fever, immunosuppression, diabetes, prosthesis or skin breakdown; send fluid for Gram stain and culture even if crystals are seen.
clinical_takeaway.why: Crystals and infection coexist (1.5% of crystal-positive aspirates in one series; 30 cases in another), one-third of concomitant cases were afebrile, and fever is present in only about 57% of septic arthritis; synovial WBC >50,000/uL has LR 7.7 and >100,000/uL LR 28.
clinical_takeaway.source: Margaretten ME et al., Does this adult patient have septic arthritis?, JAMA 2007;297:1478-88 (PMID 17405973); Shah K et al., Does the presence of crystal arthritis rule out septic arthritis?, J Emerg Med 2007;32:23-6 (PMID 17239729); Yu KH et al., Concomitant septic and gouty arthritis - an analysis of 30 cases, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2003;42:1062-6 (PMID 12730521)

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not use serum urate to confirm or exclude a flare; a normal level during an attack is common. Measure urate >4 weeks after the flare, off urate-lowering therapy, to guide long-term management.
clinical_takeaway.why: Only 14% of acute-gout trial participants had urate <=6 mg/dL during the flare, yet flares occurred below the 6.8 mg/dL saturation point; the ACR/EULAR criteria specify timing of urate measurement and EULAR states hyperuricaemia alone is not a diagnosis.
clinical_takeaway.source: Schlesinger N et al., J Rheumatol 2009;36:1287-9 (PMID 19369457); Neogi T et al., 2015 Gout Classification Criteria: an ACR/EULAR collaborative initiative, Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-98 (PMID 26359487; full text PMC4602275); Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758)

clinical_takeaway.point: At diagnosis assess kidney function (eGFR, proteinuria, stones) and cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, lipids, glucose, weight, smoking), and review provoking drugs (diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin).
clinical_takeaway.why: EULAR 2018 gives a strong recommendation for systematic comorbidity and cardiovascular risk assessment; 24% of people with gout have CKD stage >=3 and 14% have had kidney stones; gout is associated with excess MI, stroke and CV death, and the odds of MI/stroke are increased in the 60-120 days after a flare. Cross-reference: chronic_kidney_disease, hypertension, obesity_metabolic_syndrome and diabetes_mellitus entries.
clinical_takeaway.source: Richette P et al., 2018 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:31-38 (PMID 31167758); Roughley MJ et al., Gout and risk of chronic kidney disease and nephrolithiasis: meta-analysis of observational studies, Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:90 (PMID 25889144); Cipolletta E et al., JAMA 2022;328:440-450 (PMID 35916846)

clinical_takeaway.point: Urate-lowering therapy (ULT) indications: start ULT in patients with >=1 subcutaneous tophus, radiographic damage attributable to gout, or frequent flares (>=2 per year); conditionally in those with infrequent flares (>1 previous flare, <2/year) and, at a first flare, if CKD stage >=3, serum urate >9 mg/dL or urolithiasis; conditionally do not start pharmacological ULT for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia. Target serum urate <6 mg/dL (EULAR: <5 mg/dL in severe gout); start allopurinol low (<=100 mg/day, lower in CKD) and titrate. EULAR 2016 advises considering ULT from first presentation.
clinical_takeaway.why: These are the stated ACR 2020 and EULAR 2016 recommendations; ULT dissolves crystals, prevents flares and tophi, and is the definitive treatment; details of drugs and dosing sit in the treatment section of this entry. Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia has only low absolute risk of progression (14.7% of hyperuricaemic men over 28 years in the Malmo cohort).
clinical_takeaway.source: FitzGerald JD et al., 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934); Richette P et al., 2016 updated EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the management of gout, Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:29-42 (PMID 27457514); Kapetanovic MC et al., The risk of clinically diagnosed gout by serum urate levels: results from 30 years follow-up of the Malmo Preventive Project cohort in southern Sweden, Arthritis Res Ther 2018;20:190 (PMID 30157929)

clinical_takeaway.point: Before starting allopurinol consider HLA-B*58:01 status, particularly in patients of Southeast Asian or African American descent per ACR 2020; note the Indian evidence gap (a single North Indian typing study reports about 15% allele frequency, but no Indian SCAR-association or screening study was found).
clinical_takeaway.why: HLA-B*58:01 has OR ~80-100 for allopurinol SCAR in meta-analyses, and prospective screening in Taiwan prevented SCAR (none in 2,339 screen-negative patients versus 7 expected); positive predictive value of the allele is low (1.52% in the Thai analysis), so screening enables an alternative drug rather than implying certain reaction.
clinical_takeaway.source: Somkrua R et al., Association of HLA-B*5801 allele and allopurinol-induced Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis, BMC Med Genet 2011;12:118 (PMID 21906289); Ko TM et al., Use of HLA-B*58:01 genotyping to prevent allopurinol induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions in Taiwan: national prospective cohort study, BMJ 2015;351:h4848 (PMID 26399967); Tassaneeyakul W et al., Strong association between HLA-B*5801 and allopurinol-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in a Thai population, Pharmacogenet Genomics 2009;19:704-9 (PMID 19696695); Rani R et al., Molecular diversity of HLA-A, -B and -C alleles in a North Indian population as determined by PCR-SSOP, Int J Immunogenet 2007;34:201-8 (PMID 17504510); FitzGerald JD et al., 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020;72:744-760 (PMID 32391934)

clinical_takeaway.point: For an atypical or polyarticular presentation, or gout in a transplant recipient, keep a low threshold to aspirate and to involve a rheumatologist early.
clinical_takeaway.why: Oligo/polyarticular and chronic forms are misdiagnosed more often; gout after transplantation is often accelerated with polyarticular disease and tophi, and drug interactions with immunosuppressants complicate treatment.
clinical_takeaway.source: Perez Ruiz F et al., Reumatol Clin 2009;5:248-51 (PMID 21794624); Burack DA et al., Hyperuricemia and gout among heart transplant recipients receiving cyclosporine, Am J Med 1992;92:141-6 (PMID 1543197); Stamp L et al., Gout in solid organ transplantation: a challenging clinical problem, Drugs 2005;65:2593-611 (PMID 16392875)

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.icd11_hint: FA00 Osteoarthritis (WHO ICD-11 MMS; FA00 Primary osteoarthritis, FA01 Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of specified joint, FA02 Osteoarthritis due to other disorder, FA0Z unspecified); legacy ICD-10 M15-M19 (M15 polyosteoarthritis, M16 osteoarthritis of hip, M17 osteoarthritis of knee)

definition.finding: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint disease, not a disease of cartilage alone: it involves progressive breakdown of articular cartilage together with subchondral bone remodelling (sclerosis, cysts, marrow lesions), osteophyte (bony spur) formation at the joint margins, and low-grade synovial inflammation (synovitis), affecting the joint capsule, ligaments and periarticular muscle as well. This is explicitly framed as 'a disease of the joint as an organ' rather than a disease of one tissue.
definition.source: Loeser RF et al., 'Osteoarthritis: a disease of the joint as an organ', Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:1697-1707 (PMID 22392533); Glyn-Jones S et al., 'Osteoarthritis', Lancet 2015;386:376-387 (PMID 25748615); Hunter DJ, Bierma-Zeinstra S, 'Osteoarthritis', Lancet 2019;393:1745-1759 (PMID 31034380)
definition.confidence: high - concept is stated consistently across three independent major reviews/seminars

old_mechanical_wear_model_vs_current_mod.finding: OA was historically conceptualised as passive, purely mechanical 'wear and tear' of cartilage from cumulative use. The current model, built on tissue and imaging studies, treats OA as an active biological process: chondrocytes and synovial cells release matrix-degrading enzymes and inflammatory mediators, subchondral bone undergoes reactive remodelling that itself drives pain and further cartilage loss, and synovitis (detectable on MRI and by imaging-independent clinical signs) contributes to both pain and structural progression rather than being a late, incidental finding. The Lancet 2019 seminar explicitly states that recent research has clarified the mechanisms underlying pain in OA and that clinical evaluation, not imaging, should guide diagnosis because structural (radiographic) severity correlates poorly with pain - evidence against a purely mechanical, structure-equals-symptom model.
old_mechanical_wear_model_vs_current_mod.source: Loeser RF et al., Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:1697-1707 (PMID 22392533); Hunter DJ, Bierma-Zeinstra S, Lancet 2019;393:1745-1759 (PMID 31034380); Glyn-Jones S et al., Lancet 2015;386:376-387 (PMID 25748615)

subchondral_bone_and_bone_marrow_lesions.finding: Subchondral bone is an active participant, not a passive scaffold: bone marrow lesions (BMLs) seen on MRI - areas of altered subchondral marrow signal - were present in 272 of 351 (77.5%) painful knees versus 15 of 50 (30%) pain-free knees (p<0.001), and large lesions were found almost exclusively in painful knees (35.9% vs 2%, p<0.001); the association with pain persisted after adjusting for radiographic severity, effusion, age and sex, though lesion size did not track pain severity among those with pain.
subchondral_bone_and_bone_marrow_lesions.source: Felson DT et al., 'The association of bone marrow lesions with pain in knee osteoarthritis', Ann Intern Med 2001;134:541-549 (PMID 11281736)

biomechanical_loading_and_malalignment_m.finding: Abnormal joint loading is a real, imageable mechanical driver that interacts with the biological process: varus (bow-legged) knee alignment increases medial compartment load and was associated with a roughly 4-fold increase in the odds of medial radiographic progression (OR 4.09, 95% CI 2.20-7.62) over 18 months, while valgus alignment increased lateral compartment load and progression odds nearly 5-fold (OR 4.89, 95% CI 2.13-11.20); greater malalignment burden also predicted greater functional decline. This shows structural (mechanical) and biological disease drivers act together within the same joint.
biomechanical_loading_and_malalignment_m.source: Sharma L et al., 'The role of knee alignment in disease progression and functional decline in knee osteoarthritis', JAMA 2001;286:188-195 (PMID 11448282)

acr_clinical_classification_criteria_kne.finding: 1986 ACR (American Rheumatism Association) clinical classification criteria for knee OA: clinical criteria alone classify a patient as knee OA if knee pain is present plus at least 3 of 6 of: age over 50 years; morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes; crepitus on active motion; bony tenderness; bony enlargement on examination; and no palpable warmth of the synovium. A combined clinical-and-radiographic criteria set classifies knee OA if knee pain is present plus osteophytes on radiograph plus at least 1 of 3 of: age over 50, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, or crepitus on active motion.
acr_clinical_classification_criteria_kne.source: Altman R et al., 'Development of criteria for the classification and reporting of osteoarthritis. Classification of osteoarthritis of the knee', Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515)

acr_clinical_classification_criteria_hip.finding: 1991 ACR criteria for hip OA were derived from a multicentre comparison of 201 patients with hip pain from OA against patients with hip pain from other causes including rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthropathy. A clinical-and-laboratory-and-radiographic classification tree classifies hip OA using hip pain together with either radiographic femoral and/or acetabular osteophytes, or an ESR of 20 mm/hour or less together with radiographic axial joint-space narrowing.
acr_clinical_classification_criteria_hip.source: Altman R et al., 'The American College of Rheumatology criteria for the classification and reporting of osteoarthritis of the hip', Arthritis Rheum 1991;34:505-514 (PMID 2025304)

kellgren_lawrence_radiographic_grading.finding: The Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) system, the original systematic radiographic grading scheme for OA, grades severity 0-4: Grade 0 - no radiographic features of OA; Grade 1 - doubtful joint-space narrowing with possible osteophyte lipping; Grade 2 - definite osteophytes with possible joint-space narrowing; Grade 3 - multiple moderate osteophytes, definite joint-space narrowing, some subchondral sclerosis and possible bony-end deformity; Grade 4 - large osteophytes, marked joint-space narrowing, severe subchondral sclerosis and definite bony-end deformity. It remains the most widely used radiographic classification for OA severity despite being over 65 years old.
kellgren_lawrence_radiographic_grading.source: Kellgren JH, Lawrence JS, 'Radiological assessment of osteo-arthrosis', Ann Rheum Dis 1957;16:494-502 (PMID 13498604)

imaging_versus_clinical_diagnosis.finding: NICE (UK) guidance states that OA can and should be diagnosed clinically, without imaging, in adults aged 45 or over who have activity-related joint pain and either no morning joint-related stiffness or morning stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes; NICE explicitly advises not to routinely image to diagnose OA unless atypical features are present (for example recent trauma, prolonged morning stiffness, rapid symptom worsening, joint deformity, a hot swollen joint, or features suggesting infection or malignancy) that suggest an alternative or additional diagnosis. This is reinforced by the broader clinical literature: conventional radiographs detect only structural change and correlate poorly with pain, so imaging is reserved for atypical presentations or pre-surgical planning rather than routine diagnosis.
imaging_versus_clinical_diagnosis.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 'Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management', NICE guideline NG226 (2022, updated 2023), nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226; Hunter DJ, Bierma-Zeinstra S, Lancet 2019;393:1745-1759 (PMID 31034380); Glyn-Jones S et al., Lancet 2015;386:376-387 (PMID 25748615)
imaging_versus_clinical_diagnosis.confidence: high for the clinical-diagnosis rule (directly read from the NICE guidance page); NICE guidance is a policy/guideline document, not a PubMed-indexed trial, so no PMID exists for it

mri_findings_and_semiquantitative_scorin.finding: On MRI, OA shows cartilage loss/damage, bone marrow lesions, osteophytes, meniscal damage and extrusion, and synovitis/effusion (including Hoffa-fat-pad synovitis); the MRI Osteoarthritis Knee Score (MOAKS) was developed as a semiquantitative whole-organ scoring system that sub-regionally grades bone marrow lesions and cartilage and refines meniscal-morphology scoring, and has since been used across multiple OA cohort studies and trials, with inter/intra-reader reliability for cartilage, synovium, bone marrow and meniscal scoring in the moderate-to-excellent range (intraclass correlation coefficients approximately 0.77-0.94 across 9 OA studies). Bone marrow lesions specifically are the MRI feature most consistently linked to pain (see definition_and_pathophysiology).
mri_findings_and_semiquantitative_scorin.source: Hunter DJ et al., 'Evolution of semi-quantitative whole joint assessment of knee OA: MOAKS (MRI Osteoarthritis Knee Score)', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2011;19:990-1002 (PMID 21645627); Felson DT et al., Ann Intern Med 2001;134:541-549 (PMID 11281736)
mri_findings_and_semiquantitative_scorin.confidence: moderate-high - MOAKS structure and reliability figures are as reported; the reliability range is drawn from a pooled description across several MOAKS-using studies rather than a single trial

rheumatoid_arthritis.finding: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and OA are distinguished mainly by pattern and tempo. RA classification (1987 ACR criteria) requires morning stiffness of at least 1 hour, symmetric small-joint (MCP/PIP/wrist) polyarthritis, and often systemic serology (rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP) and elevated acute-phase reactants (2010 ACR/EULAR criteria); OA's clinical criteria specify morning stiffness under 30 minutes, no palpable synovial warmth, and a large-joint, often asymmetric or single-joint pattern (knee, hip, hand DIP/first CMC) with normal inflammatory markers. RA is an autoimmune, serology-positive-in-most, systemic inflammatory disease; OA is a mechanically and metabolically driven whole-joint disease without a systemic autoimmune serology. Coexistence is possible (nodal hand OA and RA can overlap in older women), so joint distribution, symmetry, stiffness duration, warmth and serology together - not any single feature - separate the two. See the rheumatoid_arthritis entry in this knowledge base for full RA diagnostic detail.
rheumatoid_arthritis.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515); Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); Aletaha D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1580-1588 (PMID 20699241)

gout_and_cppd.finding: Gout (monosodium urate crystal arthritis) and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD, 'pseudogout') are the crystal-arthritis differentials for OA and can also coexist with it. CPPD in particular is strongly age- and OA-associated: recognised EULAR 2011 risk factors for CPPD include ageing and pre-existing osteoarthritis itself, and radiographic chondrocalcinosis (a CPPD marker) is frequently found within osteoarthritic joints, so an acute flare of pain and swelling in a chronically osteoarthritic joint should prompt consideration of superimposed CPPD or gout rather than being assumed to be an OA flare; definitive separation requires synovial fluid crystal identification (CPP crystals typically rod/rhomboid and weakly birefringent versus urate's needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals). Gout itself is a recurrent, self-limiting, crystal-proven inflammatory monoarthritis, mechanistically distinct from OA's chronic mechanical/degenerative course, though both increase in prevalence with age and share risk factors such as obesity. See the gout entry in this knowledge base (differential_diagnosis.cppd_pseudogout) for the full crystal-arthritis diagnostic detail.
gout_and_cppd.source: Zhang W et al., 'EULAR recommendations for calcium pyrophosphate deposition. Part I: terminology and diagnosis', Ann Rheum Dis 2011;70:563-570 (PMID 21216817); Abhishek A et al., 'The 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for CPPD disease', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:1248-1257 (PMID 37495237)

septic_arthritis.finding: A hot, swollen, acutely painful joint - even in a patient with known chronic OA - must not be assumed to be an OA flare until septic arthritis is excluded, because clinical findings alone are weak discriminators (fever present in only about 57% of septic arthritis) and synovial fluid analysis is the key test: white cell count likelihood ratios rise from 0.32 for counts under 25,000/uL to 28 for counts over 100,000/uL. This is particularly relevant after intra-articular corticosteroid injection into an osteoarthritic joint, or in a joint with a prosthesis, both recognised risk contexts for septic arthritis. Onset is typically acute (hours to a day or two) with systemic illness, unlike OA's chronic, activity-related course.
septic_arthritis.source: Margaretten ME et al., 'Does this adult patient have septic arthritis?', JAMA 2007;297:1478-1488 (PMID 17405973)

avascular_necrosis.finding: Avascular necrosis (AVN, osteonecrosis) of the femoral head is an important hip-pain differential, especially in patients under about 40-50 years old or with risk factors such as corticosteroid exposure, alcohol excess, sickle cell disease or trauma. The 2019 revised ARCO staging system defines Stage I as a normal plain radiograph with a positive MRI or bone scan - the opposite of typical early OA, where radiographic change (osteophytes, joint-space narrowing) is what defines the disease. AVN can progress rapidly (weeks to months) to subchondral fracture (Stage III) and then to secondary osteoarthritic change with joint-space narrowing and acetabular involvement (Stage IV), at which point it can become radiographically indistinguishable from primary hip OA; MRI at an earlier stage is what allows AVN to be identified before this convergence occurs.
avascular_necrosis.source: Yoon BH et al., 'The 2019 Revised Version of Association Research Circulation Osseous Staging System of Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head', J Arthroplasty 2020;35:933-940 (PMID 31866252)

classic_symptoms.name: Activity-related (mechanical) joint pain
classic_symptoms.note: Pain that is worsened by joint use/loading and improved by rest is the cardinal OA symptom and is required by both the 1986 knee and 1991 hip ACR clinical classification criteria as the entry criterion before any other feature is scored. As disease advances, pain can also occur at rest and at night, but the activity-related pattern is what distinguishes it early from purely inflammatory arthritides.
classic_symptoms.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515); Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1991;34:505-514 (PMID 2025304)

classic_symptoms.name: Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes
classic_symptoms.note: Short-duration morning stiffness (under 30 minutes) is one of the six ACR clinical criterion items for knee OA and is the real, guideline-cited distinguishing feature from rheumatoid arthritis, whose 1987 classification criterion requires morning stiffness of at least 1 hour; NICE likewise uses stiffness of 30 minutes or less (or none) as one of the two clinical features sufficient, together with age 45+ and activity-related pain, to diagnose OA without imaging.
classic_symptoms.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515); Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NICE guideline NG226 (2022, updated 2023)

classic_symptoms.name: Crepitus on active motion
classic_symptoms.note: A palpable or audible grating/crackling sensation on moving the joint through range of motion is scored in both the ACR clinical-only and clinical-plus-radiographic knee OA criteria, reflecting irregular cartilage and bony surfaces articulating against each other.
classic_symptoms.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515)

classic_symptoms.name: Joint-line and bony tenderness with bony enlargement
classic_symptoms.note: Bony tenderness on palpation and visible/palpable bony enlargement (from osteophyte formation) are two of the six ACR knee OA clinical criterion items, and the absence of palpable synovial warmth is a seventh, used to help separate OA's mild low-grade inflammation from the warmer, more inflamed joints of RA or crystal arthritis.
classic_symptoms.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515)

classic_symptoms.name: Progressive functional limitation
classic_symptoms.note: As OA progresses, pain and joint dysfunction increasingly limit walking, stair use and other activities of daily living; in the IDEA trial's overweight/obese knee OA population (baseline WOMAC-scale pain and function scores measured, 18-month follow-up), function and pain both improved substantially only with sustained weight loss (see clinical_takeaway and natural_history), illustrating that functional decline in OA is not fixed and tracks modifiable mechanical load. Functional trajectory, not radiographic grade alone, is what patients and clinicians should track over time.
classic_symptoms.source: Messier SP et al., 'Effects of intensive diet and exercise on knee joint loads, inflammation, and clinical outcomes among overweight and obese adults with knee osteoarthritis: the IDEA randomized clinical trial', JAMA 2013;310:1263-1273 (PMID 24065013)

risk_factors.note: Age over 50 is embedded directly in the ACR knee OA clinical criteria and age 45+ in the NICE clinical-diagnosis rule, reflecting the real, steep rise in OA prevalence with age seen in every population-level dataset reviewed here (GBD 2021 and the India-specific GBD analysis both show prevalence rising with age).
risk_factors.source: Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515); GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e508-e522 (PMID 37675071)

risk_factors.note: A dose-response meta-analysis (12 studies) found a significant nonlinear relationship between BMI and knee OA risk relative to a BMI of 22.5 kg/m^2: relative risk 1.59 (95% CI 1.34-1.81) at BMI 25, 3.55 (95% CI 2.51-5.11) at BMI 30, and 7.45 (95% CI 4.19-13.13) at BMI 35 - risk rises almost exponentially with BMI. GBD 2021 separately estimated that high BMI accounts for 20.4% (95% UI -1.7 to 36.6) of the global OA burden. This is the single most quantified, modifiable OA risk factor.
risk_factors.source: Zhou J et al., 'Body mass index and knee osteoarthritis risk: a dose-response meta-analysis', Obesity (Silver Spring) 2014;22:2180-2185 (PMID 24990315); GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e508-e522 (PMID 37675071)

risk_factors.note: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 53 studies (roughly 1 million participants, including 185,219 with ACL injury and 83,267 with meniscal injury) found the odds of developing knee OA were 4.2-fold (95% CI 2.2-8.0) after ACL injury, 6.3-fold (95% CI 3.8-10.5) after meniscal injury, and 6.4-fold (95% CI 4.9-8.3) after combined ACL-plus-meniscal injury, compared with an uninjured knee - among the largest single relative-risk effects of any OA risk factor, though the authors note substantial heterogeneity (I^2 62-95%) and call for higher-quality future studies.
risk_factors.source: Snoeker B et al., 'Risk of Knee OA is Increased 4-6 Fold After Knee Injury - a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis', Br J Sports Med 2020;54:725-730 (PMID 31072840)

risk_factors.note: Coggon's case-control study (518 knee OA surgical patients vs 518 matched controls) found, after adjustment for BMI, knee injury history and Heberden's nodes, an odds ratio of 1.9 (95% CI 1.3-2.8) for prolonged occupational kneeling or squatting, 1.9 (95% CI 1.4-2.8) for walking more than 2 miles/day at work, and 1.7 (95% CI 1.2-2.6) for regularly lifting loads of 25 kg or more; critically, obese workers (BMI >=30) who also knelt/squatted at work had an OR of 14.7 (95% CI 7.2-30.2) versus non-obese, non-kneeling/squatting workers - a real multiplicative interaction between an occupational and a metabolic risk factor. A later meta-analysis of 51 studies (526,343 subjects) found an overall OR of 1.61 (95% CI 1.45-1.78) for occupational physical activities and knee OA.
risk_factors.source: Coggon D et al., 'Occupational physical activities and osteoarthritis of the knee', Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:1443-1449 (PMID 10902744); McWilliams DF et al., 'Occupational risk factors for osteoarthritis of the knee: a meta-analysis', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2011;19:829-839 (PMID 21382500)

risk_factors.note: OA prevalence, incidence and disease burden (DALYs) are consistently higher in women than men; in the India-specific GBD 1990-2019 analysis, prevalence, incidence and DALYs for OA and knee OA specifically were all consistently higher in females than males across the study period. Global GBD 2021 data likewise show a sex-differential burden, contributing to the overall disease pattern.
risk_factors.source: Kundu B et al. (GBD India), 'Burden of osteoarthritis in India and its states, 1990-2019: findings from the Global Burden of disease study 2019', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2022;30:1521-1533 (PMID 35598766); GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e508-e522 (PMID 37675071)

risk_factors.note: A classic twin study of 130 identical and 120 non-identical female twins (aged 48-70) found intraclass correlation for total radiographic OA score of 0.64 in identical versus 0.38 in non-identical pairs, giving an estimated genetic variance of 0.54 (95% CI 0.43-0.65) for overall OA and 0.39-0.65 across individual hand and knee sites, independent of known environmental/demographic confounders - the first clear demonstration of a genetic contribution to radiographic hand and knee OA in women.
risk_factors.source: Spector TD et al., 'Genetic influences on osteoarthritis in women: a twin study', BMJ 1996;312:940-943 (PMID 8616305)

risk_factors.note: In a prospective cohort of 237 people with knee OA followed 18 months, baseline varus alignment carried a roughly 4-fold increase in odds of medial compartment radiographic progression (OR 4.09, 95% CI 2.20-7.62), and baseline valgus alignment carried a nearly 5-fold increase in odds of lateral compartment progression (OR 4.89, 95% CI 2.13-11.20); greater malalignment also predicted greater functional decline. Malalignment is both a risk factor for progression and a real, radiographically measurable, mechanistic link between biomechanics and disease course.
risk_factors.source: Sharma L et al., 'The role of knee alignment in disease progression and functional decline in knee osteoarthritis', JAMA 2001;286:188-195 (PMID 11448282)

global.finding: GBD 2021 estimated that 595 million people worldwide had osteoarthritis in 2020 (7.6% of the global population), a 132.2% increase in absolute case count since 1990 (driven mainly by population growth and ageing, not necessarily rising per-person risk). The global age-standardised prevalence in 2020 ranged from 5,677.4 per 100,000 in southeast Asia to 8,632.7 per 100,000 in high-income Asia Pacific. The global age-standardised YLD (years lived with disability) rate was 255.0 per 100,000 (95% UI 119.7-557.2) in 2020, a 9.5% increase from 1990; for adults aged 70 and older, OA was the seventh-ranked cause of YLDs. High BMI was estimated to account for 20.4% (95% UI -1.7 to 36.6) of the OA burden. Cases are projected to keep rising to 2050: +74.9% for knee OA, +48.6% for hand OA, +78.6% for hip OA and +95.1% for other/other-joint OA compared with 2020.
global.source: GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators, 'Global, regional, and national burden of osteoarthritis, 1990-2020 and projections to 2050: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021', Lancet Rheumatol 2023;5:e508-e522 (PMID 37675071)

india_specific.finding: GBD 2019 modelled data for India: prevalent OA cases rose from about 23.46 million in 1990 to 62.35 million in 2019; age-standardised prevalence rose from 4,895 per 100,000 (95% UI 4,420-5,447) to 5,313 per 100,000 (95% UI 4,799-5,898); DALYs rose from about 0.79 million (95% UI 0.40-1.55) to 2.12 million (95% UI 1.07-4.23), with the age-standardised DALY rate rising from 164 per 100,000 (95% UI 83-325) to 180 per 100,000 (95% UI 91-361); OA's rank among all causes of YLDs in India rose from 23rd (1.25% of all YLDs) in 1990 to 20th (1.48% of all YLDs) in 2019; prevalence, incidence and DALYs were consistently higher in females than males. Separately, a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 Indian community studies estimated a pooled knee OA prevalence of 20.24% (95% CI 11.90-30.13), with wide state-to-state variation in the underlying studies (for example Agra 35.5%, Kolkata 33.7%, Bangalore 26.6%, Dehradun 27.2%, Pune 21.7%, and outlying figures such as rural Haryana 65.6% and mixed Gujarat 56%); advancing age, female sex, lower socioeconomic status, less education and prior knee injury were the risk factors most consistently identified across the pooled studies. No dedicated national OA registry for India was identified in this research pass - the national picture rests on GBD modelling and pooled community/state-level surveys, not a prospective national registry (absence of a registry in this search is not proof that none exists).
india_specific.source: Kundu B et al. (GBD India Collaborators), 'Burden of osteoarthritis in India and its states, 1990-2019: findings from the Global Burden of disease study 2019', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2022;30:1521-1533 (PMID 35598766); Hazra S et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of knee osteoarthritis prevalence in India, Indian J Orthop 2025 (PMID 41245277)
india_specific.confidence: moderate-high - GBD figures are modelled estimates (acknowledged by GBD authors as less reliable in lower-data-availability settings); the pooled Indian prevalence carries a wide confidence interval (11.90-30.13%) reflecting high between-study heterogeneity

typical_progression_is_usually_slow.finding: Most people with knee OA do not follow a rapid downhill course: in an Osteoarthritis Initiative analysis of 7,691 knees (4,165 participants, 58% female, 60% without radiographic OA or KL grade 0-1 at baseline), over 80% of knees that eventually reached criteria for end-stage knee OA (esKOA) got there primarily through worsening knee symptom severity rather than worsening radiographic severity, i.e. symptomatic progression outpaces structural progression for most people, and esKOA defined this way is potentially reversible with effective treatment rather than a fixed one-way endpoint.
typical_progression_is_usually_slow.source: Wang N et al., 'The natural history of end-stage knee osteoarthritis: data from the osteoarthritis initiative', Semin Arthritis Rheum 2023;58:152140 (PMID 36516483)

accelerated_osteoarthritis_subgroup.finding: A real minority phenotype exists: about 1 in 7 people with incident knee OA develop accelerated knee OA, an abrupt progression to advanced-stage radiographic disease, often within 12 months, frequently preceded 1-2 years earlier by rapid cartilage loss, enlarging bone marrow lesions, meniscal damage (classically a destabilising meniscal tear) and reduced mobility, with risk flagged 2-4 years beforehand by older age, higher BMI, altered joint alignment, contralateral OA and greater pre-radiographic disease burden. Among people who develop this accelerated phenotype, about 1 in 7 undergo knee replacement within 9 years, and the median time from any increase in radiographic severity to knee replacement is only 2.3 years - substantially faster than typical OA. This subgroup is the real-world explanation for why some patients seem to 'suddenly' need a joint replacement despite a long quiet history.
accelerated_osteoarthritis_subgroup.source: Driban JB et al., 'Risk factors and the natural history of accelerated knee osteoarthritis: a narrative review', BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2020;21:332 (PMID 32471412)
accelerated_osteoarthritis_subgroup.confidence: moderate-high - a narrative review synthesis of multiple cohort analyses (mainly Osteoarthritis Initiative-derived), not a single prospective trial

disability_burden.finding: OA is a real, major, and rising global cause of disability rather than a minor 'ageing nuisance': 595 million people were affected in 2020, the age-standardised global YLD rate rose 9.5% from 1990 to 2020, and among adults aged 70 and older OA was the seventh-ranked cause of years lived with disability worldwide. Rising case counts (projected +74.9% to +95.1% by 2050 depending on joint site) mean rising demand for joint replacement and other health-system resources, which GBD authors warn could widen health inequities without stronger prevention efforts (chiefly around obesity, the largest single modifiable contributor).

clinical_takeaway.point: Diagnose most patients clinically, without imaging: in anyone aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and morning stiffness of 30 minutes or less (or none), OA can be diagnosed on history and examination alone using the ACR clinical criteria (knee: 3 of age>50/stiffness<30min/crepitus/bony tenderness/bony enlargement/no synovial warmth, plus pain; hip: pain plus osteophytes or ESR<=20 with joint-space narrowing).
clinical_takeaway.why: NICE explicitly advises against routine imaging for OA diagnosis in typical presentations, and the Lancet 2019 seminar notes structural severity on imaging correlates poorly with pain, so imaging should be reserved for atypical features (recent trauma, prolonged stiffness, rapid worsening, deformity, a hot swollen joint, or suspicion of infection/malignancy/an alternative diagnosis) rather than used to confirm a typical presentation.
clinical_takeaway.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NICE guideline NG226 (2022, updated 2023); Hunter DJ, Bierma-Zeinstra S, Lancet 2019;393:1745-1759 (PMID 31034380); Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:1039-1049 (PMID 3741515); Altman R et al., Arthritis Rheum 1991;34:505-514 (PMID 2025304)

clinical_takeaway.point: Start weight and activity-modification counselling early, at diagnosis, in every overweight or obese patient with OA, rather than waiting for symptoms to worsen.
clinical_takeaway.why: In the IDEA randomised trial, 18 months of diet-induced weight loss (with or without exercise) in overweight/obese knee OA patients produced the largest weight loss (10.6 kg, 11.4% of body weight, with combined diet+exercise), the lowest knee compressive loads (2,487 N vs 2,687 N with exercise alone, p=.007), the lowest inflammatory marker IL-6 (2.7 pg/mL vs 3.1 pg/mL, p=.006-.007) and the best pain (3.6) and function (14.1) scores compared with diet-only or exercise-only groups; the dose-response obesity data (RR up to 7.45 at BMI 35) mean this is a modifiable, quantifiable risk, and the Lancet 2019 seminar lists self-management, education, exercise and weight management as the recommended first-line, personalised core treatment before drugs or surgery.
clinical_takeaway.source: Messier SP et al., JAMA 2013;310:1263-1273 (PMID 24065013); Zhou J et al., Obesity (Silver Spring) 2014;22:2180-2185 (PMID 24990315); Hunter DJ, Bierma-Zeinstra S, Lancet 2019;393:1745-1759 (PMID 31034380)

clinical_takeaway.point: Keep a low threshold to reconsider the diagnosis - and to investigate - when the presentation is atypical: age under 45, short symptom duration with rapid onset, a hot/acutely swollen joint, systemic symptoms, or prominent synovial warmth.
clinical_takeaway.why: These features point away from OA and toward its real differentials with different urgent management needs: rheumatoid arthritis (symmetric small-joint polyarthritis, morning stiffness >=1 hour), gout or CPPD (crystal-proven recurrent or acute inflammatory arthritis, sometimes superimposed on an OA joint), septic arthritis (a joint emergency needing synovial fluid Gram stain/culture, especially after intra-articular injection or with a prosthesis), or avascular necrosis (younger patients, corticosteroid/alcohol history, MRI-positive with a normal early X-ray).
clinical_takeaway.source: Margaretten ME et al., JAMA 2007;297:1478-1488 (PMID 17405973); Zhang W et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2011;70:563-570 (PMID 21216817); Yoon BH et al., J Arthroplasty 2020;35:933-940 (PMID 31866252); Arnett FC et al., Arthritis Rheum 1988;31:315-324 (PMID 3358796)

clinical_takeaway.point: Screen for and counsel on the real, quantified modifiable risk factors at every OA visit: weight (dose-response BMI effect), occupational kneeling/squatting/heavy lifting exposure, and prior joint injury, and refer promptly for physiotherapy/rehabilitation after any significant knee injury.
clinical_takeaway.why: The effect sizes are large and real: BMI 35 carries up to a 7.45-fold risk versus BMI 22.5; ACL/meniscal injury carries a 4.2- to 6.4-fold odds increase for later knee OA; occupational kneeling/squatting carries an OR of 1.9 alone but 14.7 when combined with obesity - each of these is independently actionable (weight loss, ergonomic/occupational modification, injury rehabilitation) and the combined-risk data show that addressing more than one factor at once (for example weight plus occupational exposure) yields disproportionate benefit.
clinical_takeaway.source: Zhou J et al., Obesity (Silver Spring) 2014;22:2180-2185 (PMID 24990315); Snoeker B et al., Br J Sports Med 2020;54:725-730 (PMID 31072840); Coggon D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2000;43:1443-1449 (PMID 10902744)

clinical_takeaway.point: Recognise the accelerated-OA phenotype early - rapid symptom and/or radiographic worsening within about 12 months, especially after a destabilising meniscal tear or in a patient with high pre-existing risk (older age, high BMI, malalignment, contralateral OA) - and refer for orthopaedic assessment sooner rather than on the usual slow-OA timeline.
clinical_takeaway.why: About 1 in 7 people with incident knee OA develop this accelerated course, and among them about 1 in 7 need a knee replacement within 9 years, with a median time from any radiographic worsening to replacement of only 2.3 years - far faster than the typical, mostly symptom-driven and often reversible course seen in most OA patients (Osteoarthritis Initiative data). Missing this phenotype means missing the window for more intensive conservative management or timely surgical planning.
clinical_takeaway.source: Driban JB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2020;21:332 (PMID 32471412); Wang N et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2023;58:152140 (PMID 36516483)

osteoarthritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Osteoarthritis (OA) is NOT curable: no medicine has ever been shown to reverse or reliably halt the loss of articular cartilage and the joint remodelling (osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, meniscal extrusion) that define the disease. This is a real, documented structural difference from gout (where urate can be pharmacologically normalised to dissolve crystals) or even rheumatoid arthritis (where drug-induced remission is a real, achievable target) - it is not an unresearched gap. OA drug development has a real, well-documented graveyard of genuine disease-modifying OA drug (DMOAD) trials that failed to translate structural change into clinical benefit, or failed outright: sprifermin (recombinant FGF18) produced a real, statistically significant MRI cartilage-thickness gain sustained to 5 years (100 microg every 6 months vs placebo: 0.05 mm mean difference in total femorotibial cartilage thickness, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.10, p=0.015) in the FORWARD trial - the longest DMOAD trial reported to date - yet WOMAC pain improved by roughly the same ~50% from baseline in EVERY treatment arm INCLUDING placebo, and no patient in the top-dose group needed a knee replacement, so the real structural signal never became a differential clinical benefit (Eckstein F et al., 'Long-term structural and symptomatic effects of intra-articular sprifermin in patients with knee osteoarthritis: 5-year results from the FORWARD study', Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:1062-1069, PMID 33962962); lorecivivint, an intra-articular CLK/DYRK1A Wnt-pathway inhibitor, failed its primary week-12 pain endpoint in BOTH of its 2025 phase 3 trials - OA-10 (498 patients; no significant treatment difference) and OA-11 (513 patients; LOR -2.24 vs placebo -2.49, p=0.185) (Yazici Y et al., Clin Exp Rheumatol 2025;43:847-853, PMID 39808288; Yazici Y et al., Clin Exp Rheumatol 2025;43:854-860, PMID 39808286); the ADAMTS-5 inhibitor S201086/GLPG1972 showed no significant slowing of cartilage loss at any of three doses and no symptom benefit in the 932-patient phase 2 ROCCELLA trial despite enrolling patients selected for rapid cartilage loss (Schnitzer T et al., Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2023;31:985-994, PMID 37059327); and tanezumab, an anti-nerve-growth-factor antibody, WAS genuinely efficacious for pain in phase 3 trials but caused a real, dose-related excess of rapidly progressive osteoarthritis, subchondral insufficiency fracture and joint destruction requiring total joint replacement, leading the FDA's joint Arthritis Advisory Committee and Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee to vote 19-1 in March 2021 that its risk-benefit balance did not support approval even with proposed risk-mitigation measures. What DOES have real, strong evidence: land-based therapeutic exercise gives a moderate, real reduction in pain (12 points/100, 95% CI 10-15) and improvement in function (10 points/100, 95% CI 8-13) sustained for 2-6 months after formal treatment stops (Fransen M et al., Cochrane review, Br J Sports Med 2015;49:1554-1557, PMID 26405113); and in overweight/obese patients, intensive combined diet-induced weight loss plus exercise produces a real 11.4% mean body-weight loss and significantly less pain (3.6 vs 4.7 on a 0-20 scale, p=0.004) and better function than exercise alone at 18 months, an effect size that is comparable to or better than many oral drugs without their systemic risk (Messier SP et al. (IDEA trial), JAMA 2013;310:1263-1273, PMID 24065013). When structural disease is advanced, total joint replacement is one of the most successful operations in all of surgery: pooled national-registry data show about 82% of total knee replacements (95% CI 81.3-83.2) and about 58-78% of total hip replacements are still functioning at 25 years (registry data more reliable than case series, which run higher), and a randomised trial versus nonsurgical treatment alone showed significantly greater pain and function improvement with knee replacement at 12 months (KOOS4 improvement 32.5 vs 16.0, adjusted difference 15.8, 95% CI 10.0-21.5), at the real cost of more serious adverse events (24 vs 6 events, p=0.005) (Evans JT et al., Lancet 2019;393:655-663, PMID 30782341; Evans JT et al., Lancet 2019;393:647-654, PMID 30782340; Skou ST et al., N Engl J Med 2015;373:1597-1606, PMID 26488691). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has OA: (1) start with patient education plus a structured, supervised exercise programme, and in overweight/obese patients an intensive diet-plus-exercise weight-loss programme targeting at least 10% body-weight loss - OARSI 2019 designates this the Core Treatment that comes before any drug for every patient; (2) add topical NSAID gel first for knee OA (OARSI Level 1A, and the largest network meta-analysis to date recommends topical diclofenac as first-line pharmacological treatment) before escalating to oral NSAIDs/coxibs, which should be reserved for inadequate response, used at the lowest effective dose, and avoided or used cautiously in cardiovascular, renal or GI comorbidity; (3) do not rely on paracetamol (modern network meta-analysis: effect size -0.17 versus a minimal clinically important difference of -0.37 - real but not clinically meaningful) or glucosamine/chondroitin (GAIT trial and a 3,803-patient network meta-analysis: effect below the minimal clinically important difference, no effect on joint-space narrowing); (4) use intra-articular corticosteroid only as an occasional short-window measure, not a repeated long-term one, given real trial evidence of greater cartilage-volume loss with repeated triamcinolone versus saline and no added pain benefit by 2 years, and be aware that most current guidelines recommend AGAINST routine hyaluronic acid/viscosupplementation because the pooled effect does not reach clinical importance; (5) consider duloxetine for OA pain with a central-sensitisation component (meta-analysis: 50% pain responders 69% more likely than placebo, RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.27-2.25); (6) do not use opioids - the largest network meta-analysis to date (192 trials, 102,829 patients) found the clinical benefit of opioid treatment, at any dose or preparation, does not outweigh its harm, with all opioids having 53% or less probability of a clinically relevant pain benefit versus at least 99% for the best oral NSAIDs, and up to 89.5% of opioid regimens carrying an increased risk of any adverse event; (7) refer for total joint replacement once conservative measures fail and structural damage is advanced - it reliably restores function and lasts decades in the large majority of patients. 'No cure' does not mean 'nothing works': slowing structural progression is not achievable with any medicine that has ever completed a trial, but real, substantial, evidence-based control of pain and disability - through weight loss, exercise, topical/oral drugs used correctly, and ultimately joint replacement - is genuinely available.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for osteoarthritis (OA): the OARSI 2019 core-treatment/guideline framework, topical NSAIDs, oral NSAIDs/coxibs with real efficacy and cardiovascular/GI/renal safety trade-offs, paracetamol's honest lack of clinically important benefit, duloxetine, intra-articular corticosteroid (with the real cartilage-volume-loss safety signal), intra-articular hyaluronic acid/viscosupplementation (honestly controversial, most guidelines now against routine use), platelet-rich plasma (mixed/controversial evidence), the real disease-modifying OA drug (DMOAD) graveyard (sprifermin, tanezumab, lorecivivint, the ADAMTS-5 inhibitor GLPG1972/S201086), glucosamine/chondroitin (largely negative), exercise therapy, diet-induced weight loss, total joint replacement, bracing, and an honest opioid entry. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial, meta-analysis or guideline abstract; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms, diagnostic criteria and classification are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here.

oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.name: OARSI 2019 Guidelines for Non-Surgical Management of Knee, Hip and Polyarticular OA - Core Treatment Framework
oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.type: Treatment strategy / guideline framework (not a single drug)
specific_drugs: No drug is 'Core' - Core Treatment is patient education plus structured land-based exercise, with dietary weight management added for knee OA
Topical NSAIDs (Level 1A, knee OA) as first pharmacological step
Oral NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, intra-articular corticosteroid and intra-articular hyaluronic acid as conditional, comorbidity-dependent options
oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.effectiveness: 60 interventions were evaluated by a multidisciplinary panel using GRADE evidence profiles and meta-analyses. Core Treatments for Knee OA were arthritis education and structured land-based exercise with or without dietary weight management; Core Treatments for Hip and Polyarticular OA were education and exercise. Topical NSAIDs were strongly recommended for Knee OA (Level 1A). For patients with GI comorbidities, COX-2 inhibitors were Level 1B and NSAIDs plus a proton pump inhibitor were Level 2. For patients with cardiovascular comorbidity or frailty, use of any oral NSAID was NOT recommended. Intra-articular corticosteroid, intra-articular hyaluronic acid and aquatic exercise were Level 1B/2 for Knee OA only (comorbidity-dependent) and were NOT recommended for Hip or Polyarticular OA. Acetaminophen/paracetamol was conditionally NOT recommended (Level 4A/4B). Oral and transdermal opioids were strongly NOT recommended (Level 5).
oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.reason_why: OA has no drug that reverses the underlying joint damage, so the guideline places the two interventions with the best real evidence for both safety and durable benefit - education/exercise and, where relevant, weight loss - ahead of every drug, and explicitly downgrades drugs whose real risk-benefit ratio is unfavourable (opioids, paracetamol, oral NSAIDs in comorbid patients).
oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.important_caveat: This is a 2019 guideline; individual trial data behind each recommendation is given in this survey's own entries below, and some rated to a lower level of evidence than OARSI's still show a real, non-zero effect (e.g. hyaluronic acid, PRP) - the guideline's grading reflects a risk-benefit judgement, not a claim that the drug has zero effect.
oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.real_working_solution: Use this framework as the real order of operations: education + exercise (+ weight loss in overweight/obese knee OA) for everyone; topical NSAID first for knee OA; oral NSAID/coxib only if needed and only after weighing cardiovascular/GI/renal comorbidity; corticosteroid/hyaluronic acid injections only in the specific comorbidity contexts the guideline allows; avoid paracetamol and opioids as primary therapy.
oa_guideline_framework_oarsi2019.source: Bannuru RR et al., 'OARSI guidelines for the non-surgical management of knee, hip, and polyarticular osteoarthritis', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2019;27:1578-1589 (PMID 31278997)

oa_topical_nsaids.name: Topical NSAIDs (Diclofenac Gel/Solution, Ketoprofen Gel) - First-Line Pharmacological Treatment
oa_topical_nsaids.type: Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (gel, solution or patch)
specific_drugs: Diclofenac sodium topical gel 1% / topical solution 1.5-2%
Ibuprofen gel (less trial evidence quoted in the cited reviews than diclofenac/ketoprofen)
oa_topical_nsaids.effectiveness: Cochrane review (Derry S et al., 61 studies, over 3000 participants on active gel/solution): with diclofenac or ketoprofen gel, about 6 in 10 people with knee osteoarthritis had much-reduced pain at 6-12 weeks compared with about 5 in 10 on topical placebo gel; the number needed to treat (NNT) for an additional patient achieving at least 50% pain relief over 8-12 weeks was 11 for gel formulations. Skin reactions (mostly mild) were more common with topical diclofenac (about 20 in 100) than topical placebo (about 5 in 100). In the 2021 BMJ network meta-analysis (192 trials, 102,829 patients), topical diclofenac 70-81 mg/day had at least 92.3% probability of exceeding the minimal clinically important pain reduction, versus at least 99% for the best oral NSAIDs, but with a 0% increased risk of dropout or any adverse event across topical NSAID regimens (versus 18.5% and 29.8% respectively for oral NSAIDs).
oa_topical_nsaids.reason_why: Topical application achieves therapeutic drug concentration in the joint capsule and periarticular tissue while producing only a small fraction of the systemic drug exposure of an oral dose, giving comparable local anti-inflammatory/analgesic action with far less systemic GI, cardiovascular or renal COX inhibition - the mechanism is the same as oral NSAIDs (COX-1/COX-2 inhibition, reduced prostaglandin-driven inflammation and pain sensitisation), only the route differs.
oa_topical_nsaids.important_caveat: An NNT of 11 means most patients using a topical NSAID do not get an extra 50%-plus pain response beyond what the placebo gel itself already gives (via massage, evaporative cooling and expectation); the evidence is strongest for superficial knee/hand OA and weakest for hip OA, where the joint is too deep for meaningful drug penetration.
oa_topical_nsaids.real_working_solution: Use topical diclofenac or ketoprofen gel as the first pharmacological step for knee (and hand) OA, per OARSI's strong Level 1A recommendation and the 2021 BMJ network meta-analysis's conclusion that topical diclofenac should be considered first-line pharmacological treatment for knee OA; it avoids the systemic risk of oral NSAIDs almost entirely and is a real option even in patients with cardiovascular, renal or GI comorbidity where oral NSAIDs are contraindicated.
oa_topical_nsaids.source: Derry S et al., 'Topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(4):CD007400 (PMID 27103611); da Costa BR et al., 'Effectiveness and safety of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and opioid treatment for knee and hip osteoarthritis: network meta-analysis', BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179); Bannuru RR et al., OARSI 2019 guidelines, Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2019;27:1578-1589 (PMID 31278997)

oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.name: Oral NSAIDs and COX-2 Inhibitors (Etoricoxib, Diclofenac, Celecoxib, Naproxen) - Network Meta-Analysis Efficacy
oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.type: Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug / selective COX-2 inhibitor
oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.effectiveness: da Costa BR et al. 2021 BMJ network meta-analysis (192 trials, 102,829 participants, 90 active preparations/doses: 68 NSAID, 19 opioid, 3 paracetamol): five oral preparations - diclofenac 150 mg/day, etoricoxib 60 and 90 mg/day, and rofecoxib 25 and 50 mg/day (withdrawn from market in 2004 for cardiovascular toxicity, evidence only) - had at least 99% probability of a treatment effect exceeding the minimal clinically important pain reduction versus placebo. Etoricoxib 60 mg/day and diclofenac 150 mg/day were the most effective oral NSAIDs for pain and function. Across all evaluated oral NSAID regimens, 18.5% had an increased risk of dropout due to adverse events and 29.8% had an increased risk of any adverse event; diclofenac 150 mg/day specifically showed an increased dropout risk.
oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.reason_why: Oral NSAIDs achieve systemic COX-1/COX-2 inhibition, reducing prostaglandin-mediated joint inflammation and peripheral/central pain sensitisation more potently and more consistently across joints (including hip) than the topical route, at the cost of the same COX inhibition acting systemically on gastric mucosa, renal perfusion and platelet/vascular function.
oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.important_caveat: Rofecoxib (Vioxx) was withdrawn worldwide in 2004 after the APPROVe trial showed increased cardiovascular risk and is cited here only as historical trial evidence, never as a prescribing option.
oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.real_working_solution: Reserve oral NSAIDs/coxibs for patients whose pain is inadequately controlled by topical NSAIDs plus exercise/weight loss, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, and choose naproxen preferentially in patients with cardiovascular risk (see the safety entry below) - the 2021 BMJ network meta-analysis's own conclusion is that etoricoxib 60 mg/day and diclofenac 150 mg/day are 'probably not appropriate for patients with comorbidities or for long-term use'.
oa_oral_nsaids_coxibs_efficacy.source: da Costa BR et al., 'Effectiveness and safety of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and opioid treatment for knee and hip osteoarthritis: network meta-analysis', BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179)

oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.name: Oral NSAID/Coxib Cardiovascular, Gastrointestinal and Renal Risk - CNT Collaboration Meta-Analysis and PRECISION Trial
oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.type: Safety data governing oral NSAID/coxib choice (not a separate drug)
specific_drugs: Naproxen (lowest cardiovascular risk of the NSAIDs studied)
Diclofenac and ibuprofen (higher-dose cardiovascular risk comparable to coxibs)
oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.effectiveness: Coxib and traditional NSAID Trialists' (CNT) Collaboration individual-participant meta-analysis (280 placebo-controlled trials, 124,513 participants; 474 head-to-head trials, 229,296 participants): major vascular events were increased about a third by a coxib (rate ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.14-1.66) or diclofenac (1.41, 1.12-1.78), driven by major coronary events (coxibs 1.76; diclofenac 1.70); ibuprofen significantly increased major coronary events (2.22) but not overall major vascular events; naproxen did NOT significantly increase major vascular events (0.93, 95% CI 0.69-1.27). Heart failure risk was roughly doubled by all NSAID classes. All regimens increased upper GI complications (coxibs 1.81-fold, diclofenac 1.89-fold, ibuprofen 3.97-fold, naproxen 4.22-fold vs placebo). The PRECISION trial (24,081 arthritis patients with elevated cardiovascular risk, comparing celecoxib, ibuprofen and naproxen) found a pre-specified cardiorenal composite outcome (renal event, heart-failure hospitalisation or hypertension hospitalisation) in 1.76% overall, with celecoxib carrying significantly lower risk than ibuprofen (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.85) and a trend to lower risk than naproxen (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.61-1.00).
