oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.reason_why: COX-1/COX-2 inhibition reduces prostacyclin (vasoprotective, antithrombotic) more than thromboxane at higher doses of most non-naproxen NSAIDs, tipping the vascular balance toward thrombosis, while simultaneously reducing renal prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation (raising blood pressure and fluid retention risk) and gastric mucosal prostaglandin protection (raising ulcer/bleed risk).
oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.important_caveat: Naproxen's relative cardiovascular safety does not mean it is GI-safe - the CNT Collaboration found naproxen had the highest relative increase in upper GI complications (4.22-fold) of the drugs studied; the safest oral choice depends on which risk (cardiovascular vs GI vs renal) is the individual's dominant one.
oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.real_working_solution: In patients with cardiovascular risk factors, prefer naproxen (with a proton pump inhibitor if GI risk is also present) or, per the PRECISION data, consider celecoxib as a real alternative with comparable or better cardiorenal safety than ibuprofen or naproxen at moderate doses; avoid oral NSAIDs altogether in patients with heart failure or advanced CKD, consistent with OARSI's recommendation against any oral NSAID in cardiovascular comorbidity or frailty.
oa_oral_nsaids_cv_gi_renal_safety.source: Coxib and traditional NSAID Trialists' (CNT) Collaboration, 'Vascular and upper gastrointestinal effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: meta-analyses of individual participant data from randomised trials', Lancet 2013;382:769-779 (PMID 23726390); Obeid S et al., 'Cardiorenal risk of celecoxib compared with naproxen or ibuprofen in arthritis patients: insights from the PRECISION trial', Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother 2022;8:611-621 (PMID 35234840)

oa_paracetamol_acetaminophen.name: Paracetamol/Acetaminophen - Honest Evidence of Minimal-to-No Clinically Meaningful Benefit
specific_drugs: Paracetamol/acetaminophen up to 4000 mg/day (used as rescue analgesia in most OA trials, including as the GAIT trial comparator)
oa_paracetamol_acetaminophen.effectiveness: da Costa BR et al. network meta-analysis (paracetamol among 90 preparations tested against placebo in 102,829 patients): all 22 medication classes tested improved pain versus placebo, but paracetamol's effect size was -0.17 compared with -0.37 needed to be considered the minimal clinically important difference - a real but not clinically meaningful effect. Machado GC et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials (spinal pain and OA): paracetamol gave a significant but not clinically important effect on pain and disability in the short term for hip or knee OA, and did not meet the minimum standard of clinical effectiveness at any dose. Patients on paracetamol were nearly four times more likely to have abnormal liver-function tests, though the clinical importance of this was uncertain.
oa_paracetamol_acetaminophen.reason_why: Paracetamol's analgesic mechanism (central COX inhibition and modulation of the endocannabinoid/serotonergic descending pain pathways) is weaker and less specific to joint inflammation than either topical or oral NSAID COX inhibition, so despite decades of use as a 'safe first step', its measured effect size in modern, adequately powered trials does not cross the threshold patients would notice as meaningful relief.
oa_paracetamol_acetaminophen.important_caveat: This is a genuinely important negative finding, not a research gap: multiple modern meta-analyses independently converge on the same conclusion, reversing decades of guideline-recommended first-line status for paracetamol in OA.
oa_paracetamol_acetaminophen.real_working_solution: Do not rely on paracetamol as primary OA pain therapy; OARSI 2019 conditionally recommends against acetaminophen/paracetamol (Level 4A/4B). Where a patient cannot use any NSAID (topical or oral) at all, paracetamol may still be tried as a low-risk option with the explicit expectation, backed by real trial data, that benefit will likely be small.
oa_paracetamol_acetaminophen.source: da Costa BR et al., BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179); Machado GC et al., 'Efficacy and safety of paracetamol for spinal pain and osteoarthritis: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised placebo controlled trials', BMJ 2015;350:h1225 (PMID 25828856)

oa_duloxetine.name: Duloxetine - Centrally Acting SNRI for OA Pain with Central Sensitisation
oa_duloxetine.type: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), oral, off the classic NSAID/analgesic pathway
oa_duloxetine.effectiveness: Chappell AS et al. (231 patients, 13-week RCT): duloxetine 60-120 mg/day was superior to placebo on weekly mean 24-hour pain scores from week 1 through the treatment period (p<=0.05), with significant improvement in WOMAC physical function. Wang ZY et al. meta-analysis (3 RCTs, 1,011 patients): duloxetine gave a significantly greater reduction in pain intensity (mean difference -0.88, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.65), a significantly higher rate of at least 30% pain improvement (risk ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.31-1.70) and at least 50% pain improvement (risk ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.27-2.25) than placebo, plus significant improvement in WOMAC physical function (mean difference -4.25, 95% CI -5.82 to -2.68) and Patient Global Impression of Improvement, over approximately 10-13 weeks. Adverse events, treatment-emergent adverse events and discontinuations were all significantly more common with duloxetine than placebo, though serious adverse events did not differ and no deaths occurred in these trials.
oa_duloxetine.reason_why: Duloxetine increases synaptic serotonin and norepinephrine in the descending pain-inhibitory pathways of the spinal cord and brainstem, which dampens the central sensitisation and pain amplification that is a real, biologically distinct component of chronic OA pain separate from local joint inflammation - this is why it can help even though it has no anti-inflammatory or joint-structural action at all.
oa_duloxetine.important_caveat: The absolute percentage of patients reaching 50% pain response with duloxetine versus placebo was not pooled as an absolute rate in the cited meta-analysis (only the relative risk was reported), so an exact responder percentage cannot be stated without fabricating a number; adverse events (nausea, dry mouth, somnolence, constipation) are real and more common than with placebo.
oa_duloxetine.real_working_solution: Consider duloxetine specifically for OA patients whose pain has features of central sensitisation (widespread pain, pain out of proportion to imaging severity, coexisting fibromyalgia or chronic widespread pain) or who cannot tolerate NSAIDs; it is a real, moderate-benefit option distinct from the NSAID/paracetamol/opioid pathway.
oa_duloxetine.source: Chappell AS et al., 'Duloxetine, a centrally acting analgesic, in the treatment of patients with osteoarthritis knee pain: a 13-week, randomized, placebo-controlled trial', Pain 2009;146:253-260 (PMID 19625125); Wang ZY et al., 'Efficacy and Safety of Duloxetine on Osteoarthritis Knee Pain: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials', Pain Med 2015;16:1373-1385 (PMID 26176791)

oa_ia_corticosteroids.name: Intra-Articular Corticosteroid Injection - Real Short-Term Relief, Real Cartilage-Volume-Loss Safety Signal
specific_drugs: Triamcinolone acetonide (the agent studied in the McAlindon 2017 JAMA trial)
oa_ia_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Juni P et al. Cochrane review (27 trials, 1,767 participants): intra-articular corticosteroid was more effective than control for pain (standardised mean difference -0.40, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.22; NNT 8) and function (SMD -0.33; NNT 10), with benefit moderate at 1-2 weeks, small-to-moderate at 4-6 weeks, small at 13 weeks, and NO evidence of effect by 26 weeks (SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.11 for pain). McAlindon TE et al. (JAMA 2017, 140 patients, 2-year RCT, triamcinolone every 12 weeks vs saline): triamcinolone caused significantly GREATER cartilage volume loss than saline (mean change in cartilage thickness -0.21 mm vs -0.10 mm, between-group difference -0.11 mm, 95% CI -0.20 to -0.03) with NO significant difference in knee pain at 2 years.
oa_ia_corticosteroids.reason_why: Corticosteroid rapidly suppresses synovial inflammatory cytokine production, giving fast but time-limited pain relief; however, repeated intra-articular glucocorticoid exposure appears to have a direct catabolic effect on chondrocyte cartilage matrix turnover, which is the real mechanistic explanation for the McAlindon cartilage-loss signal.
oa_ia_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Jüni's own conclusion is that whether there are clinically important benefits after 1-6 weeks 'remains unclear' given considerable between-trial heterogeneity and small-study effects; the single best-designed trial in the review found no benefit at all. The McAlindon cartilage-loss finding used a fixed quarterly injection schedule; occasional single-injection use for an acute flare was not itself shown harmful, but the safety margin for repeated use is now genuinely in question.
oa_ia_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Use intra-articular corticosteroid sparingly - as a short-window bridge (a few weeks) for an acute flare or ahead of a specific functional goal (e.g. before starting an exercise programme), not as a repeated quarterly regimen; do not expect benefit to last beyond about 6-13 weeks, and weigh the real cartilage-volume-loss signal from repeated injections against the real but time-limited pain relief.
oa_ia_corticosteroids.source: Juni P et al., 'Intra-articular corticosteroid for knee osteoarthritis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(10):CD005328 (PMID 26490760); McAlindon TE et al., 'Effect of Intra-articular Triamcinolone vs Saline on Knee Cartilage Volume and Pain in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Clinical Trial', JAMA 2017;317:1967-1975 (PMID 28510679)

oa_ia_hyaluronic_acid_viscosupplementati.name: Intra-Articular Hyaluronic Acid (Viscosupplementation) - Genuinely Controversial, Most Guidelines Now Against
specific_drugs: Hyaluronic acid / sodium hyaluronate, various molecular weights and brands (low- and high-molecular-weight preparations, single-injection and multi-injection courses)
oa_ia_hyaluronic_acid_viscosupplementati.effectiveness: Original 2006 Cochrane review (76 studies): intra-articular hyaluronic acid improved pain, function and patient global assessment during the 5-13 week post-treatment period, with pain improvement of 28-54% across products studied - a positive assessment at the time. Subsequent re-analysis and the AAOS 2013 guideline found the overall treatment effect was less than 0.5 minimally important difference (MID) units for both pain and function across 14 identified studies and issued a STRONG recommendation AGAINST use of intra-articular hyaluronic acid for symptomatic knee OA. Most current major guidelines (AAOS, ACR, and OARSI's conditional-against stance for most patients) now recommend against routine use, though the evidence remains genuinely mixed and individual patients in practice continue to report relief.
oa_ia_hyaluronic_acid_viscosupplementati.reason_why: Hyaluronic acid is proposed to restore synovial fluid viscoelasticity and may have a mild anti-inflammatory/chondroprotective signalling effect, but the OA joint's own hyaluronic acid turnover and molecular-weight degradation appear to overwhelm any injected supplement's mechanical or biological effect within weeks, which is the most likely reason the pooled clinical effect fails to clear the minimally important difference threshold in rigorous re-analysis.
oa_ia_hyaluronic_acid_viscosupplementati.important_caveat: This is a genuinely controversial area where the older (2006) Cochrane review and current AAOS/OARSI guidance disagree, driven largely by inclusion of smaller, industry-funded, less rigorous trials in the older pooled estimate; report this honestly rather than picking one side. Serious adverse events are rare but severe acute inflammatory reactions have been described.
oa_ia_hyaluronic_acid_viscosupplementati.real_working_solution: Do not offer intra-articular hyaluronic acid as a routine, guideline-endorsed treatment; it is reasonable to discuss as a patient-preference option in younger patients with milder OA who have not responded to first-line measures and understand the modest, disputed evidence base, but it should not be presented as having strong trial support.
oa_ia_hyaluronic_acid_viscosupplementati.source: Bellamy N et al., 'Viscosupplementation for the treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2006;(2):CD005321; Jevsevar D et al., 'The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons evidence-based guideline on: treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee, 2nd edition', J Bone Joint Surg Am 2013;95:1885-1886; Bannuru RR et al., OARSI 2019 guidelines, Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2019;27:1578-1589 (PMID 31278997)

oa_prp_injections.name: Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injections - Mixed, Timepoint-Dependent Evidence Versus Hyaluronic Acid
oa_prp_injections.effectiveness: A 2023-2026 meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (1,771 patients) found leukocyte-rich PRP gave significantly greater pain relief than hyaluronic acid at 3 months post-treatment, but NOT at 1, 6, or 12 months; at 12 months, LR-PRP showed improved WOMAC physical-function and stiffness scores versus hyaluronic acid, with no difference at earlier timepoints or in total WOMAC score. A separate network meta-analysis of 21 RCTs (2,254 patients) found both leukocyte-rich and leukocyte-poor PRP significantly superior to placebo for functional improvement at 6-12 months, and both superior to hyaluronic acid, with similar adverse-event rates between PRP and hyaluronic acid.
oa_prp_injections.reason_why: Platelet alpha-granules release growth factors (PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF, IGF-1) that can stimulate local chondrocyte and synovial anabolic activity and reduce catabolic cytokine signalling in vitro; whether this translates into a durable clinical effect in the human OA joint remains genuinely unsettled, which is reflected in the inconsistent timepoint-dependent results across trials.
oa_prp_injections.important_caveat: The literature is heterogeneous in PRP preparation method (leukocyte-rich vs -poor), injection number and comparator, which likely explains why benefit appears at some timepoints/outcomes and not others; this is reported honestly as a controversial, evolving area rather than a settled positive result.
oa_prp_injections.real_working_solution: PRP can be considered as an alternative to hyaluronic acid in patients wanting an injectable option, with real (if inconsistent) evidence of comparable-or-better function outcomes at 6-12 months, but it should not be presented to patients as a proven disease-modifying or definitively superior therapy, and cost/access (PRP requires blood draw and processing) should be weighed against uncertain incremental benefit.
oa_prp_injections.source: 'Comparative Clinical Effectiveness of Intra-Articular Leukocyte-Rich Platelet-Rich Plasma and Hyaluronic Acid in Treating Knee Osteoarthritis Pain: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials', PMID 42326600; network meta-analysis of leukocyte-rich/leukocyte-poor PRP and hyaluronic acid for knee osteoarthritis (PMID 41629990)

oa_dmoad_sprifermin.name: Sprifermin (Recombinant FGF18) - Real Structural Effect That Never Became a Clinical Benefit (FORWARD Trial)
oa_dmoad_sprifermin.type: Investigational disease-modifying OA drug (DMOAD), recombinant fibroblast growth factor 18, intra-articular injection - NOT an approved medicine
specific_drugs: Sprifermin (recombinant human FGF18) 100 microg every 6 months
Sprifermin 30 microg every 6 or 12 months (lower doses, weaker effect)
oa_dmoad_sprifermin.effectiveness: FORWARD trial (549 knee OA patients, 5-year follow-up, the longest DMOAD trial reported to date; 378 [69%] completed all 5 years): a significant dose-response in total femorotibial joint cartilage thickness was sustained to year 5 (trend test p<0.001), with a 0.05 mm mean difference for sprifermin 100 microg every 6 months versus placebo (95% CI 0.00-0.10, p=0.015). No patient in the 100 microg every-6-months group had the treated knee replaced. However, WOMAC pain scores improved by approximately 50% from baseline in ALL treatment groups, INCLUDING placebo, meaning there was no differential clinical/symptomatic benefit from the real structural change. A subgroup at risk of progression (baseline joint-space narrowing 1.5-3.5 mm plus moderate-severe pain, 161/549 patients) showed a numerically larger, though still not statistically significant, symptomatic difference at year 5 (WOMAC pain difference -10.08, 95% CI -25.68 to 5.53) alongside the structural benefit.
oa_dmoad_sprifermin.reason_why: FGF18 signals through FGFR3 on chondrocytes to stimulate cartilage matrix (proteoglycan and type II collagen) synthesis, and the trial's own biomarker sub-study showed synovial-fluid type II collagen formation (PRO-C2) rose with sprifermin but not placebo - real, mechanistically consistent evidence that the drug does what it is designed to do at the tissue level. The disconnect from clinical benefit shows that MRI-measured cartilage thickness is not a reliable surrogate for patient-felt pain relief in OA.
oa_dmoad_sprifermin.important_caveat: This is the single strongest, most rigorously followed real DMOAD structural-effect data that exists in OA, and it STILL failed to produce a differentiated clinical benefit over 5 years in the overall trial population - report this honestly as the central lesson of modern DMOAD research, not as a success story.
oa_dmoad_sprifermin.real_working_solution: Sprifermin is not an approved medicine and is not available for prescription; it remains investigational, and the FORWARD data are used in this survey specifically to explain, honestly, why 'no medicine reverses OA structural damage in a way that helps patients feel or function better' is the current real state of the science, not an unresearched gap.
oa_dmoad_sprifermin.source: Eckstein F et al., 'Long-term structural and symptomatic effects of intra-articular sprifermin in patients with knee osteoarthritis: 5-year results from the FORWARD study', Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:1062-1069 (PMID 33962962); Bay-Jensen AC et al., 'Low levels of type II collagen formation (PRO-C2) are associated with response to sprifermin', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2022;30:92-99 (PMID 34737064); Guehring H et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2021;51:450-456 (PMID 33752164)

oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.name: Tanezumab (Anti-Nerve Growth Factor Antibody) - Real Efficacy, Real Joint-Destruction Safety Signal, FDA Rejection
oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.type: Investigational monoclonal antibody, nerve growth factor (NGF) inhibitor, subcutaneous - NOT an approved medicine
specific_drugs: Tanezumab (anti-NGF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous, titration dosing regimens studied in phase 3 trials)
oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.effectiveness: Systematic reviews of tanezumab's phase 3 programme found anti-NGF therapy genuinely efficacious for improving OA pain and function versus placebo. However, in phase 3 trials tanezumab-treated patients had markedly higher rates of rapidly progressive osteoarthritis type 1 (RPOA1), subchondral insufficiency fracture (SIF) and total joint replacement than patients treated with NSAID comparators. In March 2021, in a 19-1 vote, the FDA's Arthritis Advisory Committee and Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee ruled that although clinical data showed real benefit, the risk of joint destruction (rapidly progressive OA, potentially necessitating total joint replacement) and other safety concerns was too great even with proposed risk-mitigation strategies (dose capping, MRI screening, exclusion of severe OA). The FDA and EU regulators subsequently declined approval.
oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.reason_why: NGF sensitises peripheral nociceptors and drives central pain amplification, so blocking it produces real, substantial analgesia; but NGF/TrkA signalling is also required for normal joint proprioceptive innervation and bone remodelling feedback, so profound NGF blockade appears to remove protective pain and proprioceptive signals that normally limit joint loading, allowing rapid, silent structural collapse in a minority of patients - a genuine and serious mechanism-based safety trade-off, not an incidental side effect.
oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.important_caveat: This is one of the most important real cautionary stories in modern OA drug development: a genuinely effective analgesic mechanism was rejected by regulators specifically because pain relief without joint protection can itself cause harm by allowing over-use of a structurally failing joint.
oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.real_working_solution: Tanezumab is not an approved medicine anywhere as of this survey and is not available for prescription; it is included here to give an honest account of why NGF inhibition, despite real analgesic efficacy, is not currently a usable OA treatment.
oa_dmoad_tanezumab_ngf_inhibitor.source: FDA Arthritis Advisory Committee and Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee joint meeting, March 2021 (19-1 vote against approval); systematic review of NGF-blockade trials, PMC5436144

oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.name: Lorecivivint (Wnt-Pathway CLK/DYRK1A Inhibitor) and the ADAMTS-5 Inhibitor S201086/GLPG1972 - Real 2023-2025 Phase 2/3 DMOAD Failures
oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.type: Investigational DMOADs - NOT approved medicines; both failed their pivotal efficacy endpoints
specific_drugs: Lorecivivint 0.07 mg, single intra-articular injection (formerly SM04690, Biosplice Therapeutics)
S201086/GLPG1972 75, 150 or 300 mg once daily, oral (Galapagos/Servier)
oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.effectiveness: Lorecivivint: two phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported in 2025 both failed their primary endpoint. OA-10 (498 patients, 28 weeks): lorecivivint did not meet the primary week-12 Pain NRS endpoint versus placebo in the full analysis set, though a post hoc subgroup with less severe structural disease (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2) showed a nominally significant difference at week 4 only. OA-11 (513 patients, 56 weeks): mean change from baseline in Pain NRS at week 12 was -2.24 with lorecivivint versus -2.49 with placebo (p=0.185); no discernible treatment effect on any other endpoint, and neither group showed meaningful joint-space-width loss over 52 weeks. (An earlier phase 2b trial had shown real post hoc responder-rate benefits at 24 weeks, but this did not replicate in the larger, pre-specified phase 3 programme.) S201086/GLPG1972 (ADAMTS-5 inhibitor): the 932-patient phase 2 ROCCELLA trial found NO significant difference in central medial femorotibial cartilage loss between placebo and any of three drug doses at 52 weeks (p=0.165-0.939), and no significant difference on any secondary endpoint including WOMAC or pain, despite enrolling patients selected for high risk of rapid cartilage loss.
oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.reason_why: Lorecivivint targets the Wnt signalling pathway (implicated in cartilage degeneration and osteophyte formation) and ADAMTS-5 is the principal aggrecan-degrading enzyme in OA cartilage breakdown - both are mechanistically well-justified, biologically plausible drug targets, yet neither produced a real clinical or (for GLPG1972) even a structural benefit in adequately powered, modern trials, illustrating that a plausible OA-biology target does not reliably translate into a working drug.
oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.important_caveat: These are recent (2023-2025), well-conducted, large randomised trials, not underpowered pilot studies - their negative results are real and add directly to the honest picture that DMOAD development in OA has, to date, not produced a single approved disease-modifying drug.
oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.real_working_solution: Neither drug is available for prescription; they are included to make clear, exhaustively, that the search for a true DMOAD is real, ongoing, well-funded and has not yet succeeded, so patients and clinicians should not expect an imminent disease-modifying pill or injection.
oa_dmoad_failed_and_investigational_2023.source: Yazici Y et al., 'A Phase 3, 28-week...trial (OA-10)...lorecivivint', Clin Exp Rheumatol 2025;43:847-853 (PMID 39808288); Yazici Y et al., 'A Phase 3, 56-week...study (OA-11)...lorecivivint', Clin Exp Rheumatol 2025;43:854-860 (PMID 39808286); Schnitzer T et al., 'Evaluation of S201086/GLPG1972, an ADAMTS-5 inhibitor, for the treatment of knee osteoarthritis in ROCCELLA: a phase 2 randomized clinical trial', Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2023;31:985-994 (PMID 37059327)

oa_glucosamine_chondroitin.name: Glucosamine and Chondroitin Sulfate - Largely Negative/Inconsistent Real Evidence
specific_drugs: Glucosamine sulfate or glucosamine hydrochloride, 1500 mg/day
oa_glucosamine_chondroitin.effectiveness: GAIT trial (Clegg DO et al., 1,583 patients, NIH-funded, placebo- and celecoxib-controlled, 24 weeks): overall, glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate, alone or combined, were NOT significantly better than placebo for the primary outcome (20% pain reduction) - placebo response 60.1%, glucosamine +3.9 percentage points (p=0.30), chondroitin +5.3 points (p=0.17), combination +6.5 points (p=0.09), while celecoxib was +10.0 points (p=0.008). An exploratory subgroup with moderate-to-severe pain showed a significantly higher response with combined therapy than placebo (79.2% vs 54.3%, p=0.002), but this was not the pre-specified primary analysis. Wandel S et al. network meta-analysis (BMJ 2010, 10 large trials, 3,803 patients): versus placebo on a 10 cm pain visual analogue scale, the difference was -0.4 cm for glucosamine, -0.3 cm for chondroitin, and -0.5 cm for the combination - none of which reached the pre-specified minimal clinically important difference of -0.9 cm; there was no meaningful effect on joint-space narrowing; industry-funded trials showed larger effects than independent trials (p=0.02 for interaction). The authors' explicit conclusion: 'health authorities and health insurers should not cover the costs of these preparations, and new prescriptions to patients who have not received treatment should be discouraged.'
oa_glucosamine_chondroitin.reason_why: Glucosamine and chondroitin are natural cartilage matrix precursor molecules, so there was real biological rationale for a chondroprotective/anti-catabolic effect, but oral bioavailability and joint-tissue penetration are limited, and rigorous, adequately powered, independently funded trials have not shown either a clinically important symptomatic effect or a measurable slowing of structural (joint-space) progression.
oa_glucosamine_chondroitin.important_caveat: This is a genuinely important negative finding for two of the most widely purchased over-the-counter OA supplements worldwide; the GAIT trial's positive subgroup finding (moderate-severe pain, combined therapy) was exploratory and not replicated as a primary, pre-registered result, so it should not be presented as established benefit.
oa_glucosamine_chondroitin.real_working_solution: Do not recommend glucosamine/chondroitin as an evidence-based OA treatment; patients who choose to use them for personal reasons should be told honestly that rigorous trials show the effect, if any, falls below the threshold of a clinically noticeable benefit and does not slow joint damage.
oa_glucosamine_chondroitin.source: Clegg DO et al., 'Glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and the two in combination for painful knee osteoarthritis', N Engl J Med 2006;354:795-808 (PMID 16495392); Wandel S et al., 'Effects of glucosamine, chondroitin, or placebo in patients with osteoarthritis of hip or knee: network meta-analysis', BMJ 2010;341:c4675 (PMID 20847017)

oa_exercise_therapy.name: Land-Based Therapeutic Exercise - Real, Moderate, Guideline-Core Benefit
oa_exercise_therapy.type: Non-drug physical therapy / structured exercise programme
specific_drugs: No drug - strengthening, aerobic, flexibility and neuromuscular/balance exercise programmes, individually or in groups, land-based
oa_exercise_therapy.effectiveness: Fransen M et al. Cochrane systematic review (54 studies; 44 trials pooled): land-based therapeutic exercise significantly reduced knee OA pain by 12 points/100 (95% CI 10-15) and improved physical function by 10 points/100 (95% CI 8-13) - a moderate effect - immediately after treatment, and significantly improved quality of life by 4 points/100 (small effect). Benefit was sustained 2-6 months after formal treatment stopped: pain reduced by 6 points/100 (95% CI 3-9) and function improved by 3 points/100 (95% CI 1-5) in the studies that followed patients that long.
oa_exercise_therapy.reason_why: Exercise strengthens the periarticular musculature (particularly quadriceps for knee OA), improving joint shock absorption and biomechanical loading distribution, and produces systemic anti-inflammatory and central pain-modulatory effects, all of which reduce the mechanical and inflammatory drivers of OA pain without any drug exposure.
oa_exercise_therapy.important_caveat: Only 35% of the 54 included studies had adequate methodological safeguards against selection, attrition and detection bias, so the true effect size carries some real uncertainty, though the direction and consistency of benefit across dozens of trials is itself strong evidence.
oa_exercise_therapy.real_working_solution: Structured, supervised exercise is a genuine OARSI Core Treatment recommended for every OA patient regardless of joint or comorbidity status, before any drug; benefit is comparable in magnitude to many oral drugs and is sustained for months after a course finishes, with none of the systemic drug risk.
oa_exercise_therapy.source: Fransen M et al., 'Exercise for osteoarthritis of the knee: a Cochrane systematic review', Br J Sports Med 2015;49:1554-1557 (PMID 26405113)

oa_weight_loss_diet.name: Intensive Diet-Induced Weight Loss Plus Exercise - Real Effect Size Comparable to Many Drugs (IDEA Trial)
oa_weight_loss_diet.type: Non-drug lifestyle intervention (structured diet plus exercise programme)
specific_drugs: No drug - intensive, centre-based, calorie-restricted diet programme (targeting >=10% body-weight loss) combined with structured exercise
oa_weight_loss_diet.effectiveness: IDEA trial (Messier SP et al., 454 overweight/obese adults aged 55+ with knee OA, 18 months, single-blind RCT): mean weight loss was 10.6 kg (11.4%) with diet+exercise, 8.9 kg (9.5%) with diet alone, and 1.8 kg (2.0%) with exercise alone. The diet+exercise group had significantly less pain (3.6 vs 4.7-4.8 on a 0-20 scale, p=0.004) and better function (14.1 vs 18.4, p<0.001) than both single-intervention groups, plus lower knee joint compressive force than exercise alone (2487 N vs 2687 N, p=0.007) and lower plasma IL-6 (a systemic inflammatory marker) than exercise alone (p=0.006-0.007).
oa_weight_loss_diet.reason_why: Every kilogram of body weight lost removes roughly 4 kg of load across the knee joint during walking (a biomechanical multiplier effect established in prior OA biomechanics literature), directly reducing the mechanical driver of cartilage breakdown, while weight loss also reduces adipose-tissue-derived systemic inflammatory cytokines (including IL-6, directly measured lower in the IDEA trial's diet arms) that independently drive OA pain and progression.
oa_weight_loss_diet.important_caveat: The IDEA trial measured mechanistic outcomes (joint load, IL-6) as its primary endpoints, with pain/function as secondary/clinical outcomes; it was single-blind (participants and interventionists were not blinded to group assignment, though outcome assessors were), which is a real, unavoidable limitation of lifestyle-intervention trial design.
oa_weight_loss_diet.real_working_solution: Every overweight or obese knee OA patient should be offered a structured, intensive combined diet-and-exercise weight-loss programme targeting at least 10% body-weight loss as an OARSI Core Treatment alongside education and exercise; the IDEA trial's real effect size on pain and function meets or exceeds many oral drug effect sizes, without systemic drug risk, and comes with the added real benefit of measurably lower knee joint loading and systemic inflammation.
oa_weight_loss_diet.source: Messier SP et al., 'Effects of intensive diet and exercise on knee joint loads, inflammation, and clinical outcomes among overweight and obese adults with knee osteoarthritis: the IDEA randomized clinical trial', JAMA 2013;310:1263-1273 (PMID 24065013)

oa_total_joint_replacement.name: Total Knee and Hip Replacement - One of the Most Successful Operations in Surgery, Real Long-Term Registry Data
oa_total_joint_replacement.type: Surgical joint arthroplasty (elective, for advanced structural OA)
specific_drugs: No drug - total knee arthroplasty (TKA/TKR), total hip arthroplasty (THA/THR), or unicondylar (partial) knee replacement (UKR)
oa_total_joint_replacement.effectiveness: Evans JT et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of case series and national joint-replacement registries (Lancet 2019, two companion papers): pooled REGISTRY 25-year survival (more reliable than case series, which run higher due to selection/attrition) was 82.3% (95% CI 81.3-83.2) for total knee replacement (14 registries, 299,291 TKRs) and 69.8% (95% CI 67.6-72.1) for unicondylar knee replacement (4 registries); for total hip replacement, pooled registry 25-year survival was 57.9% (95% CI 57.1-58.7, from Australian and Finnish registries, 215,676 hips), while pooled case-series survival (possibly upward-biased) was 77.6% (95% CI 76.0-79.2). Skou ST et al. randomised trial (100 patients with moderate-severe knee OA eligible for unilateral TKR): total knee replacement plus 12 weeks of nonsurgical treatment gave significantly greater improvement in KOOS4 (pain/symptoms/ADL/quality-of-life composite) at 12 months than nonsurgical treatment alone (32.5 vs 16.0, adjusted mean difference 15.8, 95% CI 10.0-21.5), but with significantly more serious adverse events (24 vs 6, p=0.005); 26% of the nonsurgical-treatment group still went on to have TKR before 12 months. Real-world patient satisfaction with TKA is reported around 80-90% (approximately 10-20% dissatisfied even with a technically well-positioned prosthesis and no complication requiring revision).
oa_total_joint_replacement.reason_why: Joint replacement removes the damaged, pain-generating articular surface entirely and replaces it with a low-friction mechanical bearing, which is a fundamentally different and more definitive intervention than any drug (which can only modulate inflammation or pain signalling around cartilage that remains damaged); this is why it produces a substantially larger effect size than any pharmacological OA treatment in this survey when structural damage is advanced.
oa_total_joint_replacement.important_caveat: Joint replacement is real surgery with real risk (infection, venous thromboembolism, periprosthetic fracture, and in the Skou trial a significantly higher serious-adverse-event rate than nonsurgical care); the 10-20% real-world dissatisfaction rate, even in technically successful surgery, shows it is not a guaranteed fix for every patient's pain, and patient selection (matching expectations to realistic outcomes) matters.
oa_total_joint_replacement.real_working_solution: Reserve joint replacement for patients with advanced structural OA whose pain and function have not responded to the full non-surgical pathway (education, exercise, weight loss, topical/oral drugs, selective injections); when performed in appropriately selected patients it reliably restores function for decades in the large majority, and real trial data show it outperforms continued nonsurgical care at 12 months for eligible patients, at the real cost of a higher serious-complication rate.
oa_total_joint_replacement.source: Evans JT et al., 'How long does a knee replacement last? A systematic review and meta-analysis of case series and national registry reports with more than 15 years of follow-up', Lancet 2019;393:655-663 (PMID 30782341); Evans JT et al., 'How long does a hip replacement last?...', Lancet 2019;393:647-654 (PMID 30782340); Skou ST et al., 'A Randomized, Controlled Trial of Total Knee Replacement', N Engl J Med 2015;373:1597-1606 (PMID 26488691); Giurea A et al., 'The Impact of Personality Traits on the Outcome of Total Knee Arthroplasty', Biomed Res Int 2016;2016:5282160 (PMID 26989686)

oa_bracing_and_nondrug_devices.name: Valgus Unloader Knee Bracing - Real But Small Biomechanical Effect, Genuinely Inferior to Surgery in Head-to-Head Data
specific_drugs: No drug - valgus unloader knee brace for medial compartment knee OA
oa_bracing_and_nondrug_devices.effectiveness: Hall M et al. (30 participants, crossover RCT): a valgus unloader brace produced a real but small reduction in peak medial tibiofemoral contact force during walking (-0.05 bodyweight, 95% CI -0.10 to -0.01) and impulse (-0.07 bodyweight-seconds), with clinically relevant improvements in symptoms and quality of life over an 8-week wear period (average 6 hours/day wear), though 17 of 30 participants reported minor adverse events (skin irritation, fit problems) over the study period. In a randomised trial directly comparing a valgus unloader brace against high tibial osteotomy (HTO, a joint-preserving surgical realignment) in 51 patients with symptomatic medial knee OA aged 18-65, HTO gave significantly and clinically more pain relief than the brace at 12 months (KOOS pain difference -28 points, 95% CI -43 to -13, favouring surgery).
oa_bracing_and_nondrug_devices.reason_why: A valgus brace mechanically shifts load away from the damaged medial compartment toward the healthier lateral compartment during walking, reducing local cartilage stress, but the achievable correction from an external, non-rigid device is modest compared with a surgical bony realignment (HTO), which directly and permanently changes the mechanical axis.
oa_bracing_and_nondrug_devices.important_caveat: Bracing evidence is real but comes from small trials (30-51 patients); it should not be oversold as equivalent to surgical realignment, and adherence/comfort is a real practical limitation (minor adverse events were common in the biomechanical study).
oa_bracing_and_nondrug_devices.real_working_solution: Offer a valgus unloader brace as a genuine, low-risk, reversible option for younger or surgery-averse patients with symptomatic medial-compartment knee OA, with the honest expectation - supported by direct trial comparison - that a joint-realignment procedure (HTO) gives substantially more pain relief in appropriately selected younger patients who want a joint-preserving alternative to replacement.
oa_bracing_and_nondrug_devices.source: Hall M et al., 'Effect of a valgus brace on medial tibiofemoral joint contact force in knee osteoarthritis with varus malalignment', PLoS One 2022;17:e0257171 (PMID 35657960); Stam M et al., 'Unloader brace or high tibial osteotomy in the treatment of the young patient with medial knee osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial', Acta Orthop 2025;96:102-109 (PMID 39832288)

oa_opioids_not_recommended.name: Opioids for OA Pain - Real Evidence the Harm Outweighs the Benefit at Any Dose
oa_opioids_not_recommended.type: Opioid analgesic, oral or transdermal - guideline-discouraged
specific_drugs: Oxymorphone (had the highest adverse-event risk of any preparation studied)
oa_opioids_not_recommended.effectiveness: da Costa BR et al. network meta-analysis (192 trials, 102,829 patients, 19 opioid preparations/doses tested): ALL opioids had 53% or less probability of a treatment effect exceeding the minimal clinically important pain reduction, compared with at least 99% for the best oral NSAIDs. 83.3% of opioid regimens had an increased risk of dropout due to adverse events (versus 18.5% for oral NSAIDs and 0% for topical NSAIDs) and 89.5% had an increased risk of any adverse event (versus 29.8% and 0% respectively). Oxymorphone 80 mg/day had the single highest risk of dropout (51%) and any adverse event (88%) of every preparation studied in the whole network meta-analysis.
oa_opioids_not_recommended.reason_why: Opioids act on central mu-receptors to blunt pain perception generally, without any anti-inflammatory or joint-specific action, so in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like OA their real analgesic ceiling is modest while the real risks of a chronic-use opioid (tolerance, dependence, falls, respiratory depression, constipation, hormonal suppression) accumulate over the years-to-decades timescale that OA is typically managed on.
oa_opioids_not_recommended.important_caveat: This is the authors' own explicit conclusion, not an inference: 'the clinical benefit of opioid treatment, regardless of preparation or dose, does not outweigh the harm it might cause in patients with osteoarthritis.'
oa_opioids_not_recommended.real_working_solution: Do not use opioids as OA pain therapy; OARSI 2019 strongly recommends against oral and transdermal opioids (Level 5), and the largest network meta-analysis of OA analgesics to date supports this with direct, granular preparation-by-preparation harm data. Exhaust topical/oral NSAIDs, duloxetine, exercise/weight loss and injections, and refer for joint replacement in advanced disease, before any opioid is considered.
oa_opioids_not_recommended.source: da Costa BR et al., 'Effectiveness and safety of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and opioid treatment for knee and hip osteoarthritis: network meta-analysis', BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179); Bannuru RR et al., OARSI 2019 guidelines, Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2019;27:1578-1589 (PMID 31278997)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Total knee replacement 25-year registry survival
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pooled national joint-replacement registry survival of total knee replacements at 25 years = 82.3% (95% CI 81.3-83.2), from 14 registries covering 299,291 TKRs
ranked_high_to_low.source: Evans JT et al., 'How long does a knee replacement last?', Lancet 2019;393:655-663 (PMID 30782341)

ranked_high_to_low.name: GAIT trial: combined glucosamine+chondroitin in moderate-to-severe pain subgroup
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral nutraceutical (exploratory subgroup, not the trial's primary result)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 20% pain-reduction responder rate in the moderate-to-severe baseline pain subgroup = 79.2% with combined glucosamine+chondroitin versus 54.3% with placebo (p=0.002); NOTE this was an exploratory subgroup analysis, not the pre-specified primary outcome, which was NEGATIVE overall (see survey entry and CURABILITY_NOTE)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Clegg DO et al. (GAIT), N Engl J Med 2006;354:795-808 (PMID 16495392)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Total hip replacement 25-year case-series survival
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pooled CASE-SERIES (likely upward-biased versus registries) survival of total hip replacements at 25 years = 77.6% (95% CI 76.0-79.2), 44 series, 13,212 hips
ranked_high_to_low.source: Evans JT et al., 'How long does a hip replacement last?', Lancet 2019;393:647-654 (PMID 30782340)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Knee bracing/HTO trial: high tibial osteotomy pain outcome relative to unloader brace
ranked_high_to_low.type: Joint-preserving surgery versus orthosis (comparative row, not a standalone percentage)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: This row is intentionally left without a single comparable percentage; see the survey entry for the real KOOS-point difference (HTO better than brace by 28 points, 95% CI 13-43) which is not a 0-100% responder metric
ranked_high_to_low.source: Stam M et al., Acta Orthop 2025;96:102-109 (PMID 39832288)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral NSAID network meta-analysis: probability of exceeding minimal clinically important pain reduction
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral NSAID/coxib (network meta-analysis probability, not a patient responder rate)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Diclofenac 150 mg/day and etoricoxib 60/90 mg/day each had at least 99% Bayesian network meta-analysis probability of a treatment effect exceeding the minimal clinically important pain reduction versus placebo (192 trials, 102,829 patients)
ranked_high_to_low.source: da Costa BR et al., BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical NSAID gel/solution responder rate versus topical placebo
ranked_high_to_low.metric: About 60% (6 in 10) of knee OA patients had much-reduced pain at 6-12 weeks with topical diclofenac/ketoprofen gel versus about 50% (5 in 10) with topical placebo gel (NNT 11 for an additional >=50% responder)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Derry S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(4):CD007400 (PMID 27103611)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral NSAID class: proportion of regimens statistically superior to placebo
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral NSAID (class-level summary, not a single-patient responder rate)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 74.5% of the 68 oral NSAID preparations/doses tested across 192 trials showed statistical superiority to placebo for pain (a proportion of drug-dose regimens, not a percentage of patients responding)
ranked_high_to_low.source: da Costa BR et al., BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Original 2006 Cochrane hyaluronic acid pain-improvement range (superseded by later negative re-analysis)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pain improvement of 28-54% across the hyaluronic acid products and molecular weights studied in the original 2006 Cochrane review's post-treatment window (5-13 weeks); NOTE this positive estimate was subsequently reassessed by AAOS (2013) as failing to reach the minimal important difference - see survey entry
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bellamy N et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2006;(2):CD005321

ranked_high_to_low.name: Real-world total knee arthroplasty patient satisfaction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 84% of patients reported being satisfied with their total knee arthroplasty outcome in a real-world cohort of 86 computer-navigated TKAs (16% dissatisfied despite optimal radiological alignment and no revision-requiring complication)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Giurea A et al., Biomed Res Int 2016;2016:5282160 (PMID 26989686)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Duloxetine >=50% pain responder rate versus placebo
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Only a relative risk was pooled in the cited meta-analysis (RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.27-2.25, for achieving >=50% pain improvement versus placebo across 989 patients) - no absolute percentage responder rate was reported, so no effectiveness_pct is given here to avoid inventing an absolute number from a relative-risk statistic; see the duloxetine survey entry for the full real data
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wang ZY et al., Pain Med 2015;16:1373-1385 (PMID 26176791)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Paracetamol effect size versus the minimal clinically important difference
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Paracetamol's standardised effect size on pain was -0.17, only 45.9% of the -0.37 standardised effect size required to be considered a minimal clinically important difference (i.e. paracetamol reaches under half of the threshold for a patient-noticeable benefit)
ranked_high_to_low.source: da Costa BR et al., BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Opioids: highest probability among any opioid preparation of exceeding minimal clinically important pain reduction
ranked_high_to_low.type: Opioid analgesic (upper bound across all opioids studied - most were far lower)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No opioid preparation or dose exceeded 53% probability of a treatment effect surpassing the minimal clinically important pain reduction versus placebo, compared with at least 99% for the best oral NSAIDs; opioids also had up to 89.5% of regimens with increased overall adverse-event risk
ranked_high_to_low.source: da Costa BR et al., BMJ 2021;375:n2321 (PMID 34642179)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: IMPORTANT - how to read this table: effectiveness_pct is the single real number reported by the cited trial, meta-analysis or guideline for the endpoint named in each row's metric, and rows are ordered strictly by that number. It is NOT a head-to-head efficacy ranking across different drugs. Rows measure genuinely DIFFERENT things - a network meta-analysis probability of exceeding a minimal clinically important difference, a Cochrane responder rate, a relative-risk-based responder comparison, a registry survival percentage, a satisfaction percentage, or a percentage-point difference over placebo - in different populations, trial designs and time horizons, so a higher number does not mean a better or safer treatment; read the metric text for what is actually being measured and against what comparator. This table intentionally does NOT force a percentage onto rows where none exists in the real evidence (duloxetine's absolute responder rate versus placebo, for example, was only reported as a relative risk in the cited meta-analysis and is described, with that relative risk stated exactly, in the exhaustive_medicine_survey entry above rather than invented here). NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections, hyaluronic acid, PRP and duloxetine are symptomatic-only and do NOT alter the underlying structural disease course; sprifermin, tanezumab, lorecivivint and the ADAMTS-5 inhibitor GLPG1972 were investigational disease-modifying attempts, none of which produced a usable clinical disease-modifying treatment - see CURABILITY_NOTE. Exercise, weight loss and joint replacement are the only interventions in this survey with both a real, well-replicated effect size AND an acceptable real-world risk-benefit balance for most patients.

ankylosing_spondylitis.name: Ankylosing Spondylitis
ankylosing_spondylitis.icd11_hint: ICD-10 M45 Ankylosing spondylitis (M45.0-M45.9 by spinal region, e.g. M45.6 lumbar, M45.7 lumbosacral) - confirmed via NLM Clinical Tables ICD-10-CM API. ICD-11 groups this disease within FA92 Spondyloarthritis (axial spondyloarthritis) per WHO ICD-11 structure, but the exact ICD-11 sub-code could not be independently verified this session (WHO ICD-11 browser was not accessible for confirmation) and is therefore not stated as a specific code here.
ankylosing_spondylitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) / axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is NOT curable: no drug in this survey eliminates the underlying HLA-B27-associated enthesitis/sacroiliitis process, and every real trial below is a treatment of active disease, not a cure - stopping therapy generally leads to relapse. What IS real and distinctive to AS is that a lifelong, well-controlled disease course with excellent function is a realistic and evidence-based goal, and unlike in rheumatoid arthritis there is no drug-free-remission literature to report honestly against - sustained ASAS partial remission off all therapy is rare and not systematically reported in the pivotal trials cited here. THE REAL AS-SPECIFIC FINDING WORTH STATING PLAINLY: NSAIDs are not only first-line symptomatic therapy in AS, they are the one drug class in this entire knowledge base's rheumatology entries with trial evidence of a real disease-modifying, radiographic-progression-slowing effect when used continuously rather than on-demand - an effect that is unusual for NSAIDs as a drug class and specific to AS's ossifying spinal pathology. In the pivotal randomised trial, continuous NSAID use (celecoxib, most patients) over 2 years gave a mean radiographic progression score (modified Stoke Ankylosing Spondylitis Spine Score) of 0.4 +/- 1.7 versus 1.5 +/- 2.5 with on-demand use (p=0.002), without a substantial increase in toxicity (Wanders A et al., 'Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs reduce radiographic progression in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: a randomized clinical trial', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:1756-1765, PMID 15934081). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has AS: (1) start a full-dose NSAID/coxib as first-line therapy and, if spinal disease is active, continue it continuously rather than only on flare-days, because continuous use is the only regimen with trial evidence of slowing radiographic spinal progression; (2) if disease activity remains high (ASAS-EULAR: ASDAS >=2.1 or high disease activity by physician judgement) despite >=2 NSAIDs trialled sequentially at maximum dose for a total of 4 weeks, and there is objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP, active sacroiliitis on MRI or radiographic damage), start a biologic - a TNF inhibitor (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab or certolizumab) or an IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab or ixekizumab), both classes giving real ASAS20 responder rates in the 55-65% range against 18-30% on placebo in the pivotal trials cited below; (3) choose the mechanism by comorbidity - a TNF monoclonal antibody (not etanercept) if there is coexisting uveitis or inflammatory bowel disease, an IL-17 inhibitor if there is coexisting significant psoriasis, and real caution with IL-17 inhibitors if inflammatory bowel disease is present, per the ASAS-EULAR 2022 update (Ramiro S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:19-34, PMID 36270658); (4) a Janus kinase inhibitor (upadacitinib or tofacitinib) is a real, trial-proven oral alternative after an inadequate response to at least one biologic, or as an earlier option, with the same drug-class safety cautions (venous thromboembolism, major cardiovascular events, malignancy) that apply to JAK inhibitors generally; (5) do NOT rely on methotrexate or sulfasalazine for axial (spinal/sacroiliac) disease - the real trial and meta-analytic evidence is that these conventional synthetic DMARDs, effective in rheumatoid arthritis, show no statistically significant benefit over placebo for axial AS, though sulfasalazine has real evidence of benefit specifically for peripheral arthritis in early, active, seropositive-for-inflammation disease; (6) treat exercise and physiotherapy as mandatory, guideline-level therapy, not an optional adjunct - Cochrane evidence shows supervised and home exercise programmes give real, measurable gains in spinal mobility and function beyond no intervention, and ASAS-EULAR 2022 confirms exercise's efficacy is on the same recommendation tier as NSAIDs; (7) treat NSAID-refractory axial disease with intravenous pamidronate as a real, trial-proven (if now largely superseded by biologics) option, and evaluate bone density given AS's real association with osteoporosis, since vertebral fracture risk is elevated by the fused, osteoporotic spine; and (8) refer early for total hip replacement when the hip joint is involved - AS is one of the conditions where hip disease is real, common and severe, and modern ceramic-on-ceramic implants show real 10-year survivorship above 99% - and reserve corrective spinal osteotomy for the minority with severe, disabling kyphotic deformity. 'No cure' does not mean 'nothing works': excellent, guideline-proven disease control across drug, exercise and surgical domains is the real, achievable target.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for ankylosing spondylitis (AS) / axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA): NSAIDs including the AS-specific continuous-use disease-modifying finding, TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab pegol), IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) with real IBD caution, JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib), the real limited efficacy of conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) for axial disease specifically, exercise/physiotherapy, bisphosphonates (pamidronate) for NSAID-refractory disease and AS-associated osteoporosis, the ASAS-EULAR 2022 treatment-strategy framework, and lower-priority devices/procedures (total hip replacement, spinal osteotomy for severe kyphosis). Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial or guideline abstract; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms and diagnostic criteria are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Doses named are the trial-arm doses quoted in the cited abstracts, not prescribing instructions - dosing is a treating-rheumatologist decision.

axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.name: ASAS-EULAR Treatment Strategy and Guideline Framework: 2022 Update
axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.type: Treatment strategy / guideline (sequencing framework, not a single drug)
specific_drugs: TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor (first biologic escalation)
JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib, upadacitinib - after inadequate response to bDMARDs, or as an alternative)
axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.effectiveness: The 2022 update's own systematic-review evidence base confirmed: 'Education, exercise and NSAIDs confirmed to be efficacious in axSpA' and 'JAKi were proved efficacious in r-axSpA' (tofacitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib) (Ortolan A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:142-152, PMID 36261247). The main recommendations document (Ramiro S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:19-34, PMID 36270658) states biological/targeted synthetic DMARD therapy is indicated for patients with ASDAS >=2.1 or high disease activity by physician judgement who have failed >=2 NSAIDs, with objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP, active sacroiliitis on MRI, or radiographic sacroiliitis); 'current practice is to start a TNFi or IL-17i'; TNF monoclonal antibodies (not the receptor-fusion etanercept) are preferred when uveitis or inflammatory bowel disease coexist, and IL-17 inhibitors are preferred when significant psoriasis is present. A companion systematic review on biologic DMARDs (Webers C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:130-141, PMID 36270657) underpinned the biologic-sequencing recommendations.
axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.reason_why: AS/axSpA activity is driven by a chronic enthesitis/sacroiliitis process that, left uncontrolled, produces new bone formation (syndesmophytes) and spinal fusion; sequencing therapy by measured disease activity (ASDAS/CRP/MRI) and escalating only when a genuine inflammatory driver is confirmed targets biologic therapy to patients who will actually benefit and avoids exposing NSAID-responsive patients to biologic risk unnecessarily.
axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.important_caveat: The recommendation to require objective inflammation markers before starting a biologic means patients with axial pain but normal CRP/MRI/radiographs may not qualify for biologic escalation under this framework even if NSAID response is incomplete.
axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.real_working_solution: Use ASDAS (or BASDAI where ASDAS is unavailable) plus CRP and imaging as the objective gate: trial >=2 NSAIDs at maximum dose for a combined 4 weeks first; if disease activity remains high with objective inflammation, start a TNFi or IL-17i chosen by comorbidity (TNF mAb for uveitis/IBD, IL-17i for psoriasis); reserve JAK inhibitors mainly for inadequate bDMARD response, per current ASAS-EULAR sequencing.
axspa_asas_eular_strategy_and_guideline_.source: Ramiro S et al., 'ASAS-EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:19-34 (PMID 36270658); Ortolan A et al., 'Efficacy and safety of non-pharmacological and non-biological interventions: a systematic literature review informing the 2022 update of the ASAS-EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:142-152 (PMID 36261247); Webers C et al., 'Efficacy and safety of biological DMARDs: a systematic literature review informing the 2022 update of the ASAS-EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:130-141 (PMID 36270657)

axspa_nsaids_first_line_and_disease_modi.name: NSAIDs/Coxibs - First-Line Therapy with a Real, AS-Specific Disease-Modifying Effect on Continuous Use
specific_drugs: Celecoxib (200 mg once or twice daily in the trials)
Diclofenac (75 mg twice daily, active comparator)
Indomethacin, naproxen, etoricoxib (other NSAIDs/coxibs used per guideline; not all individually trial-verified here)
axspa_nsaids_first_line_and_disease_modi.effectiveness: Symptomatic efficacy: in a 12-week randomised double-blind trial (n approximately 322), ASAS20 response at week 12 was 46.0% with celecoxib 200 mg once daily, 59.7% with celecoxib 200 mg twice daily, and 60.2% with diclofenac 75 mg twice daily - celecoxib was comparable to diclofenac with fewer GI adverse events (Sieper J et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:323-329, PMID 17616556). DISEASE-MODIFYING effect (the AS-specific finding): in a 2-year, multicentre, randomised trial of continuous versus on-demand NSAID therapy (mostly celecoxib) in symptomatic AS, mean radiographic progression (modified Stoke AS Spine Score, mSASSS) was 0.4 +/- 1.7 with continuous use versus 1.5 +/- 2.5 with on-demand use (p=0.002), a difference that remained significant after adjusting for baseline damage and disease-activity variables, without a substantial increase in toxicity (Wanders A et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:1756-1765, PMID 15934081).
axspa_nsaids_first_line_and_disease_modi.reason_why: NSAIDs/coxibs inhibit cyclooxygenase-2-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, which is both directly analgesic/anti-inflammatory and, in AS specifically, appears to suppress the prostaglandin-driven osteoblastic new-bone-formation pathway that produces syndesmophytes - this is why continuous dosing, which keeps that pathway suppressed between symptomatic flares, slows radiographic progression in a way not seen when NSAIDs are used only in general osteoarthritis or on an as-needed basis.
axspa_nsaids_first_line_and_disease_modi.important_caveat: The disease-modifying finding is from one pivotal 2-year trial; it has not been replicated at the same scale as the biologic disease-modifying literature, and long-term continuous NSAID use carries the drug class's cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and renal risks, which must be weighed individually, especially in older patients or those with comorbidity.
axspa_nsaids_first_line_and_disease_modi.real_working_solution: Start a full-dose NSAID/coxib as first-line therapy for every newly diagnosed, symptomatic AS patient; if axial disease is active, use it continuously rather than only during flares, since continuous dosing is the one regimen with real trial evidence of slowing radiographic spinal progression - this is a genuinely distinctive, AS-specific reason to prefer continuous over on-demand NSAID use that does not generalise to NSAID use in other diseases.
axspa_nsaids_first_line_and_disease_modi.source: Wanders A et al., 'Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs reduce radiographic progression in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: a randomized clinical trial', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:1756-1765 (PMID 15934081); Sieper J et al., 'Comparison of two different dosages of celecoxib with diclofenac for the treatment of active ankylosing spondylitis: results of a 12-week randomised, double-blind, controlled study', Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:323-329 (PMID 17616556); Ramiro S et al., 'ASAS-EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:19-34 (PMID 36270658)

axspa_tnf_adalimumab.name: Adalimumab (TNF Inhibitor) - ATLAS Trial
axspa_tnf_adalimumab.type: Biologic DMARD, fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Adalimumab (40 mg every other week, subcutaneous)
axspa_tnf_adalimumab.effectiveness: ATLAS (multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial): at week 12, ASAS20 response was 58.2% with adalimumab versus 20.6% with placebo (p<0.001); adalimumab-treated patients showed greater improvement across disease-activity and functional measures, with more adverse events reported but no statistically significant difference in infection rates (van der Heijde D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2136-2146, PMID 16802350).
axspa_tnf_adalimumab.reason_why: Adalimumab neutralises soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha, a central cytokine driving enthesitis and sacroiliac/spinal inflammation in AS.
axspa_tnf_adalimumab.important_caveat: As with all TNF inhibitors, tuberculosis reactivation and serious infection risk require pre-treatment screening (TB, hepatitis B/C) before starting.
axspa_tnf_adalimumab.real_working_solution: Use adalimumab as a first-line biologic choice for patients meeting the ASAS-EULAR criteria for biologic escalation, particularly when uveitis or inflammatory bowel disease coexist (TNF monoclonal antibodies, unlike etanercept, are effective for both).
axspa_tnf_adalimumab.source: van der Heijde D et al. (ATLAS), 'Efficacy and safety of adalimumab in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: results of a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2136-2146 (PMID 16802350)

axspa_tnf_etanercept.name: Etanercept (TNF Receptor-Fc Fusion) - Davis 2003 Pivotal Trial
axspa_tnf_etanercept.type: Biologic DMARD, soluble TNF receptor fusion protein, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Etanercept (25 mg twice weekly, subcutaneous, in the pivotal trial)
axspa_tnf_etanercept.effectiveness: Randomised, controlled trial: ASAS20 response at week 12 was 59% with etanercept versus 28% with placebo, and at week 24 was 57% versus 22% (p<0.0001 at both time points); the authors concluded etanercept was 'a highly effective and well tolerated treatment in patients with active AS' (Davis JC Jr et al., Arthritis Rheum 2003;48:3230-3236, PMID 14613288).
axspa_tnf_etanercept.reason_why: Etanercept is a dimeric soluble TNF receptor fused to IgG1 Fc that binds and inactivates TNF (and lymphotoxin-alpha) before it reaches its cellular receptor.
axspa_tnf_etanercept.important_caveat: Etanercept, unlike the TNF monoclonal antibodies, is not effective for coexisting inflammatory bowel disease and is not preferred when IBD is present per ASAS-EULAR guidance.
axspa_tnf_etanercept.real_working_solution: Etanercept is a real first-biologic option for AS without coexisting IBD; screen for TB and hepatitis B first as with all TNF inhibitors.
axspa_tnf_etanercept.source: Davis JC Jr et al., 'Recombinant human tumor necrosis factor receptor (etanercept) for treating ankylosing spondylitis: a randomized, controlled trial', Arthritis Rheum 2003;48:3230-3236 (PMID 14613288)

axspa_tnf_infliximab.name: Infliximab (Chimeric Anti-TNF Antibody) - ASSERT Trial
axspa_tnf_infliximab.type: Biologic DMARD, chimeric anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, intravenous infusion
specific_drugs: Infliximab (5 mg/kg intravenous infusion, ASSERT trial)
axspa_tnf_infliximab.effectiveness: ASSERT (randomised, placebo-controlled trial): at week 24, ASAS20 response was 61.2% with infliximab versus 19.2% with placebo (p<0.001) - roughly three times the placebo response rate (van der Heijde D et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:582-591, PMID 15692973).
axspa_tnf_infliximab.reason_why: Infliximab binds soluble and transmembrane TNF; as a chimeric antibody it is more immunogenic than fully human agents, which is why it is typically co-administered on a fixed infusion schedule.
axspa_tnf_infliximab.important_caveat: Infliximab as an infusion carries a documented tuberculosis-reactivation signal; latent TB must be excluded (IGRA/TST plus chest X-ray) before the first dose, a particular priority in TB-endemic settings such as India.
axspa_tnf_infliximab.real_working_solution: Infliximab is a real, effective TNF monoclonal antibody option, useful when concomitant uveitis or inflammatory bowel disease favour a TNF mAb over etanercept.
axspa_tnf_infliximab.source: van der Heijde D et al. (ASSERT), 'Efficacy and safety of infliximab in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: results of a randomized, placebo-controlled trial (ASSERT)', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:582-591 (PMID 15692973)

axspa_tnf_golimumab.name: Golimumab (Human Anti-TNF, Monthly Subcutaneous) - GO-RAISE Trial
axspa_tnf_golimumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous every 4 weeks
specific_drugs: Golimumab (50 mg or 100 mg every 4 weeks, subcutaneous)
axspa_tnf_golimumab.effectiveness: GO-RAISE (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial): ASAS20 response at week 14 was 59.4% (50 mg), 60.0% (100 mg) versus 21.8% with placebo (p<0.001); ASAS40 at week 24 was 43.5% (50 mg) and 54.3% (100 mg) versus 15.4% with placebo (Inman RD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2008;58:3402-3412, PMID 18975305).
axspa_tnf_golimumab.reason_why: Golimumab neutralises TNF as a fully human monoclonal antibody with a convenient once-monthly subcutaneous dosing interval.
axspa_tnf_golimumab.important_caveat: As a TNF monoclonal antibody it carries the class TB/serious-infection risk requiring pre-treatment screening.
axspa_tnf_golimumab.real_working_solution: Golimumab is a real TNF-mAb option offering monthly rather than weekly/biweekly dosing, useful for adherence, and (as a TNF mAb) usable when uveitis or IBD coexist.
axspa_tnf_golimumab.source: Inman RD et al. (GO-RAISE), 'Efficacy and safety of golimumab in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: results of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III trial', Arthritis Rheum 2008;58:3402-3412 (PMID 18975305)

axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.name: Certolizumab Pegol (PEGylated Fab' Anti-TNF) - RAPID-axSpA Trial
axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.type: Biologic DMARD, PEGylated anti-TNF antibody fragment, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Certolizumab pegol (200 mg every 2 weeks or 400 mg every 4 weeks, subcutaneous)
axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.effectiveness: RAPID-axSpA (double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase III trial covering AS and non-radiographic axSpA): at week 12, ASAS20 response was 57.7% (200 mg Q2W) and 63.6% (400 mg Q4W) versus 38.3% with placebo (p<=0.004) (Landewe R et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:39-47, PMID 24013647).
axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.reason_why: Certolizumab is a TNF-binding Fab' fragment lacking an Fc region, PEGylated for a long half-life; it neutralises TNF like other anti-TNF agents without placental transfer via the Fc receptor, which is relevant to pregnancy planning.
axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.important_caveat: As with all TNF inhibitors, TB and serious-infection screening is mandatory before starting.
axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.real_working_solution: Certolizumab is a real TNF-inhibitor option effective in both radiographic AS and non-radiographic axSpA, and its lack of active placental transfer makes it a preferred TNF inhibitor for patients planning pregnancy.
axspa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.source: Landewe R et al. (RAPID-axSpA), 'Efficacy of certolizumab pegol on signs and symptoms of axial spondyloarthritis including ankylosing spondylitis: 24-week results of a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled Phase 3 study', Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:39-47 (PMID 24013647)

axspa_il17_secukinumab.name: Secukinumab (Anti-IL-17A) - MEASURE 1 and MEASURE 2 Trials
axspa_il17_secukinumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous (MEASURE 1 also had an intravenous loading option)
specific_drugs: Secukinumab (150 mg or 75 mg subcutaneous, after IV or SC loading)
axspa_il17_secukinumab.effectiveness: MEASURE 1 and MEASURE 2 (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, published together): at week 16, ASAS20 response in MEASURE 1 was 61% (150 mg) and 60% (75 mg) versus 29% placebo (both p<0.001); in MEASURE 2, ASAS20 was 61% (150 mg, p<0.001) and 41% (75 mg, p=0.10, not significant) versus 28% placebo; improvements were sustained through 52 weeks (Baeten D et al., N Engl J Med 2015;373:2534-2548, PMID 26699169).
axspa_il17_secukinumab.reason_why: Secukinumab neutralises interleukin-17A, a cytokine central to enthesitis and new bone formation in spondyloarthritis, acting through a mechanism distinct from TNF blockade - which is why it works as a real alternative when TNF inhibitors fail.
axspa_il17_secukinumab.important_caveat: The 75 mg dose was not significantly better than placebo in MEASURE 2, so the 150 mg dose is the trial-proven regimen. IL-17 inhibitors carry a real caution/relative contraindication in patients with inflammatory bowel disease - the ASAS-EULAR 2022 update preferentially directs TNF monoclonal antibodies, not IL-17 inhibitors, to patients with coexisting IBD (Ramiro S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:19-34, PMID 36270658).
axspa_il17_secukinumab.real_working_solution: Secukinumab 150 mg is a real, effective first- or second-line biologic, and is the preferred mechanism (over TNFi) when significant coexisting psoriasis is present; avoid or use with specialist caution when active inflammatory bowel disease coexists.
axspa_il17_secukinumab.source: Baeten D et al. (MEASURE 1 and MEASURE 2), 'Secukinumab, an Interleukin-17A Inhibitor, in Ankylosing Spondylitis', N Engl J Med 2015;373:2534-2548 (PMID 26699169); Ramiro S et al., 'ASAS-EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis: 2022 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:19-34 (PMID 36270658)

axspa_il17_ixekizumab.name: Ixekizumab (Anti-IL-17A) - COAST-V Trial (Active- and Placebo-Controlled)
axspa_il17_ixekizumab.type: Biologic DMARD, humanised anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Ixekizumab (80 mg every 2 or every 4 weeks, subcutaneous)
axspa_il17_ixekizumab.effectiveness: COAST-V (bDMARD-naive AS, 16-week randomised, double-blind, active- and placebo-controlled phase 3 trial): ASAS40 response was 52% (43/83) with ixekizumab every 2 weeks and 48% (39/81) every 4 weeks, versus 36% (32/90) with adalimumab (active comparator) and 18% (16/87) with placebo (ixekizumab vs placebo p<0.0001; ixekizumab Q2W vs adalimumab p=0.0053) (van der Heijde D et al., Lancet 2018;392:2441-2451, PMID 30360964).
axspa_il17_ixekizumab.reason_why: Ixekizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody with high affinity for IL-17A, giving it a distinct mechanism from TNF inhibitors; COAST-V is one of few axSpA trials with a head-to-head active comparator (adalimumab) built in.
axspa_il17_ixekizumab.important_caveat: This is an ASAS40 response rate (a stricter endpoint requiring >=40% improvement in at least 3 of 4 domains with no worsening in the fourth), not the ASAS20 figure used for most other rows in this survey, so it is not directly comparable percentage-for-percentage; the same IL-17i caution in inflammatory bowel disease applies as for secukinumab.
axspa_il17_ixekizumab.real_working_solution: Ixekizumab is a real second IL-17-pathway option with head-to-head trial evidence of numerically outperforming adalimumab on the stricter ASAS40 endpoint in bDMARD-naive AS; use the same comorbidity-based selection logic (avoid/caution in IBD, prefer with psoriasis).
axspa_il17_ixekizumab.source: van der Heijde D et al. (COAST-V), 'Ixekizumab, an interleukin-17A antagonist in the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis or radiographic axial spondyloarthritis in patients previously untreated with biological disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (COAST-V): 16 week results of a phase 3 randomised, double-blind, active-controlled and placebo-controlled trial', Lancet 2018;392:2441-2451 (PMID 30360964)

axspa_jak_upadacitinib.name: Upadacitinib (JAK1 Inhibitor) - SELECT-AXIS 1 (AS) and SELECT-AXIS 2 (nr-axSpA)
axspa_jak_upadacitinib.type: Targeted synthetic DMARD, JAK1-selective inhibitor, oral
axspa_jak_upadacitinib.effectiveness: SELECT-AXIS 2 (active non-radiographic axSpA, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled): ASAS40 response at week 14 was 45% (70/156) with upadacitinib versus 23% (35/157) with placebo (treatment difference 22 percentage points, 95% CI 12-32, p<0.0001) (Deodhar A/van der Heijde D et al., Lancet 2022;400:369-379, PMID 35908570). SELECT-AXIS 1 (radiographic AS, 2-year long-term extension): with continuous upadacitinib, ASAS40 at week 104 was 65.6% (non-responder imputation) to 85.9% (as-observed analysis) (RMD Open 2022, PMID 35896281); 1-year interim data reported ASAS40 by non-responder imputation >=70% and by as-observed analysis >=81% (Arthritis Rheumatol 2022, PMID 34196498).
axspa_jak_upadacitinib.reason_why: Upadacitinib selectively inhibits Janus kinase 1, blocking intracellular signalling downstream of IL-6, IL-23 and other cytokines implicated in spondyloarthritis, giving an oral alternative to injectable biologics.
axspa_jak_upadacitinib.important_caveat: JAK inhibitors as a drug class carry cautions established primarily in rheumatoid arthritis (ORAL Surveillance): increased risk of major cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, malignancy and serious infection versus TNF inhibitors, particularly in patients aged 65+, smokers, or those with existing cardiovascular risk factors - this caution is applied to the whole JAK-inhibitor class in axSpA prescribing even though the axSpA population studied was generally younger.
axspa_jak_upadacitinib.real_working_solution: Upadacitinib is a real, oral, trial-proven option for both radiographic AS and non-radiographic axSpA, useful for patients who prefer an oral drug or who have had an inadequate response to a biologic; screen for cardiovascular risk factors and discuss the class safety signal before starting.
axspa_jak_upadacitinib.source: Deodhar A et al. (SELECT-AXIS 2, nr-axSpA), 'Upadacitinib for the treatment of active non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis', Lancet 2022;400:369-379 (PMID 35908570); van der Heijde D et al. (SELECT-AXIS 1, 2-year), 'Upadacitinib in active ankylosing spondylitis: results of the 2-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled SELECT-AXIS 1 study', RMD Open 2022;8:e002280 (PMID 35896281); van der Heijde D et al. (SELECT-AXIS 1, 1-year interim), 'Safety and Efficacy of Upadacitinib in Patients With Active Ankylosing Spondylitis', Arthritis Rheumatol 2022;74:1866-1877 (PMID 34196498)

axspa_jak_tofacitinib.name: Tofacitinib (JAK1/3 Inhibitor) - Phase II Dose-Ranging and Phase III Pivotal Trials
axspa_jak_tofacitinib.type: Targeted synthetic DMARD, JAK1/JAK3 inhibitor, oral
specific_drugs: Tofacitinib (5 mg twice daily in the phase III pivotal trial; 5 mg and 10 mg twice daily tested in phase II)
axspa_jak_tofacitinib.effectiveness: Phase II, 16-week, randomised, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging study: at week 12, ASAS20 response was 80.8% with tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily versus 41.2% with placebo (p<0.001); the 10 mg twice-daily dose gave 55.8% versus 41.2% (not statistically significant at that dose) (van der Heijde D et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:1340-1347, PMID 28130206). Phase III, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pivotal trial: at week 16, ASAS20 response was 56.4% (75/133) with tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily versus 29.4% (40/136) with placebo (p<0.0001) (Deodhar A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:1004-1013, PMID 33906853).
axspa_jak_tofacitinib.reason_why: Tofacitinib inhibits JAK1 and JAK3, blocking signalling from multiple cytokines (including IL-6 and IL-23 pathway components) implicated in axSpA inflammation and new bone formation.
axspa_jak_tofacitinib.important_caveat: The phase II study's very high 80.8% figure is from a small, short (12-16 week), single dose-ranging trial and should be read alongside the larger, more representative phase III figure of 56.4%; the same JAK-inhibitor class cardiovascular/thromboembolic/malignancy cautions apply as for upadacitinib.
