axspa_jak_tofacitinib.real_working_solution: Tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily is a real, trial-proven oral option for active AS, with the confirmatory phase III ASAS20 rate of 56.4% versus 29.4% placebo; use the same cardiovascular-risk screening and shared decision-making as for other JAK inhibitors.
axspa_jak_tofacitinib.source: van der Heijde D et al., 'Tofacitinib in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: a phase II, 16-week, randomised, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging study', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:1340-1347 (PMID 28130206); Deodhar A et al., 'Tofacitinib for the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis: a phase III, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study', Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:1004-1013 (PMID 33906853)

axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.name: Methotrexate and Sulfasalazine - Real Limited/No Efficacy for AXIAL Disease (Important Distinction from RA)
axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.type: Conventional synthetic DMARDs (oral) - honest negative/limited finding for axial AS
specific_drugs: Methotrexate (oral, weekly - no significant axial benefit)
Sulfasalazine (oral, 2-3 g/day in the trials - benefit confined mainly to peripheral arthritis)
axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.effectiveness: METHOTREXATE: a meta-analysis found methotrexate monotherapy showed 'no statistically significant differences' versus placebo on disease activity and inflammatory markers in AS, and adding methotrexate to infliximab gave no statistically significant benefit over infliximab alone (Chen J et al., Int J Clin Pharmacol Ther 2014;52:269-277, PMID 24618070). SULFASALAZINE: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials and a companion Cochrane review both concluded that patients at an early disease stage, with a higher ESR (more active disease) and peripheral arthritis, might benefit from sulfasalazine, based mainly on benefit for peripheral joint symptoms, while axial manifestations (spinal pain, mobility) showed minimal to no benefit (Chen J, Liu C, 'Is sulfasalazine effective in ankylosing spondylitis? A systematic review of randomized controlled trials', J Rheumatol 2006;33:722-731, PMID 16583475; Chen J, Liu C, 'Sulfasalazine for ankylosing spondylitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(2):CD004800, PMID 15846731).
axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.reason_why: Unlike rheumatoid arthritis's predominantly synovial pathology, AS's axial disease is driven by enthesitis (inflammation at tendon/ligament-bone entheses) and new bone formation, mechanisms that methotrexate's antimetabolite action and sulfasalazine's anti-inflammatory action do not meaningfully target - this is an important, real distinction from RA, where both drugs are core anchor therapies.
axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.important_caveat: Neither drug should be relied upon as monotherapy for axial AS symptoms; this is reported here honestly as a real limitation, not a treatment recommendation.
axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.real_working_solution: Reserve sulfasalazine for AS patients whose dominant, active manifestation is peripheral arthritis (especially early disease with a raised ESR); do not use methotrexate or sulfasalazine as primary therapy for axial (spinal/sacroiliac) symptoms - escalate axial disease per the NSAID-then-biologic/JAKi pathway instead.
axspa_csdmard_limited_axial_efficacy.source: Chen J et al., 'Efficacy evaluation of methotrexate in the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis using meta-analysis', Int J Clin Pharmacol Ther 2014;52:269-277 (PMID 24618070); Chen J, Liu C, 'Is sulfasalazine effective in ankylosing spondylitis? A systematic review of randomized controlled trials', J Rheumatol 2006;33:722-731 (PMID 16583475); Chen J, Liu C, 'Sulfasalazine for ankylosing spondylitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(2):CD004800 (PMID 15846731)

axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.name: Exercise and Physiotherapy - Guideline-Mandated, Cochrane-Evidenced Non-Drug Therapy
axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.type: Non-pharmacological therapy (home or supervised exercise, group physiotherapy, spa-exercise combination)
axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.effectiveness: Cochrane review (11 trials, 763 participants): an individual home-based or supervised exercise programme is better than no intervention, with relative improvements of roughly 5-50% across different spinal mobility measures and an approximately 4-point improvement on a 33-point physical-function scale; supervised group physiotherapy was superior to home exercise alone, and combined inpatient spa-exercise therapy plus outpatient group physiotherapy was better than group physiotherapy alone (Dagfinrud H et al., 'Physiotherapy interventions for ankylosing spondylitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008;(1):CD002822, PMID 18254008). An earlier Cochrane review (6 trials, 561 participants) found low-quality but consistent evidence favouring home exercise programmes for physical function and spinal mobility over no intervention (Dagfinrud H et al., J Rheumatol 2005;32:1899-1906, PMID 16206344). The ASAS-EULAR 2022 evidence review reconfirmed that education and exercise are efficacious in axSpA, placing them on the same recommendation tier as NSAIDs (Ortolan A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:142-152, PMID 36261247).
axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.reason_why: Exercise maintains spinal and hip range of motion, chest expansion and posture against the mechanical stiffening/fusion process of AS, and reduces the functional disability that accumulates independently of inflammatory disease activity - a mechanism drug therapy alone does not address.
axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.important_caveat: The Cochrane reviews report a heterogeneous mix of relative percentage improvements across different mobility and function scales rather than a single unified responder-rate percentage, so no single effectiveness_pct figure captures the whole body of evidence; the underlying trial quality is rated low-to-moderate.
axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.real_working_solution: Prescribe supervised group physiotherapy (superior to home exercise alone) as guideline-level, mandatory therapy alongside drug treatment for every AS patient, not as an optional adjunct; combined inpatient spa-exercise therapy followed by outpatient group physiotherapy is the best-evidenced regimen where available.
axspa_exercise_and_physiotherapy.source: Dagfinrud H et al., 'Physiotherapy interventions for ankylosing spondylitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008;(1):CD002822 (PMID 18254008); Dagfinrud H et al., 'The Cochrane review of physiotherapy interventions for ankylosing spondylitis', J Rheumatol 2005;32:1899-1906 (PMID 16206344); Ortolan A et al., 'Efficacy and safety of non-pharmacological and non-biological interventions: a systematic literature review informing the 2022 update of the ASAS-EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2023;82:142-152 (PMID 36261247)

axspa_bisphosphonate_pamidronate.name: Intravenous Pamidronate - NSAID-Refractory Axial Disease and AS-Associated Osteoporosis
specific_drugs: Pamidronate (60 mg or 10 mg monthly intravenous infusion in the pivotal trial)
axspa_bisphosphonate_pamidronate.effectiveness: A 6-month, randomised, controlled, double-blind, dose-response trial in NSAID-refractory AS (n=84): a clinically meaningful BASDAI reduction (>=50% or >=2 units) was achieved by 63.4% of patients on 60 mg pamidronate versus 30.2% on 10 mg (p=0.004); mean BASDAI fell by 2.22 (34.5%) with 60 mg versus 0.93 (15%) with 10 mg (p=0.002), showing a real dose-dependent effect (Maksymowych WP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:766-773, PMID 11920413). A separate clinimetric analysis of the same trial found the Bath AS Metrology Index (BASMI) had poor responsiveness to pamidronate treatment regardless of scoring version (Jones SD et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1587-1592, PMID 15570645), indicating the clinical benefit was mainly in disease activity/pain (BASDAI) rather than measured spinal mobility.
axspa_bisphosphonate_pamidronate.reason_why: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone turnover and have anti-inflammatory effects on activated macrophages at high intravenous doses, which is proposed to reduce inflammatory activity at entheses in AS; the effect required the higher 60 mg dose, indicating a dose-threshold phenomenon rather than a simple anti-resorptive action.
axspa_bisphosphonate_pamidronate.important_caveat: This trial evaluated pamidronate for NSAID-refractory axial disease activity (BASDAI), not specifically for AS-associated osteoporosis or fracture prevention; dedicated randomised trial evidence of bisphosphonates preventing vertebral fracture specifically in AS-associated osteoporosis was not found in this survey, though AS is a real, recognised risk factor for osteoporosis and vertebral fracture because of chronic inflammation, reduced spinal mobility and, in advanced disease, a rigid osteoporotic spine prone to fracture even from minor trauma. Bisphosphonate use for bone protection in AS with confirmed osteoporosis follows general osteoporosis-treatment evidence rather than AS-specific fracture-outcome trials.
axspa_bisphosphonate_pamidronate.real_working_solution: Consider intravenous pamidronate (60 mg monthly, the trial-proven dose) as a real option for axial AS that remains active despite optimised NSAID therapy and before or alongside biologic escalation; separately, screen AS patients (especially those with long-standing or severe disease) for osteoporosis with bone density scanning and treat confirmed osteoporosis with standard bisphosphonate therapy to reduce vertebral fracture risk.
axspa_bisphosphonate_pamidronate.source: Maksymowych WP et al., 'A six-month randomized, controlled, double-blind, dose-response comparison of intravenous pamidronate (60 mg versus 10 mg) in the treatment of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug-refractory ankylosing spondylitis', Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:766-773 (PMID 11920413); Jones SD et al., 'Clinimetric evaluation of the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Metrology Index in a controlled trial of pamidronate therapy', J Rheumatol 2004;31:1587-1592 (PMID 15570645)

axspa_total_hip_replacement.name: Total Hip Arthroplasty for AS-Associated Hip Involvement
axspa_total_hip_replacement.type: Orthopaedic surgery (device/procedure, lower priority than drug therapy)
axspa_total_hip_replacement.effectiveness: A minimum-10-year follow-up study of fourth-generation ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty in AS patients: implant survivorship was 99.4% at final follow-up; mean Harris Hip Score improved from 41 +/- 20 preoperatively to 90 +/- 8 postoperatively (p<0.001); flexion-extension range of motion improved from 10 degrees to 100 degrees; dislocation rate was 0.6% (1 hip); audible bearing noise occurred in 28.9% at 10 years but was described as clinically insignificant (Orthop Surg 2022, PMID 35434922). A mid-term case series (195 hips) reported Harris Hip Score improving from 18.0 +/- 13.7 preoperatively to 86.4 +/- 14.1 at final follow-up, hip flexion arc increasing from 23.4 to 93.2 degrees, and 'good midterm prosthetic survivorship' with a low complication rate, though heterotopic ossification occurred in 49 of 195 hips (Zhongguo Xiu Fu Chong Jian Wai Ke Za Zhi 2014, PMID 24693768).
axspa_total_hip_replacement.reason_why: AS real-world involves the hip joint in a substantial minority of patients and, when it occurs, tends to be bilateral, severe and to progress to bony ankylosis; because the hip (unlike the fused spine) can be reconstructed, total hip arthroplasty converts a rigid, painful joint into a mobile one and is real, high-value surgery specifically in AS.
axspa_total_hip_replacement.important_caveat: Heterotopic ossification (new bone formation around the prosthesis) is a real, AS-specific surgical complication risk, seen in a substantial minority of hips in the case series cited above, reflecting the same excess-bone-formation biology that drives spinal fusion.
axspa_total_hip_replacement.real_working_solution: Refer for total hip replacement once hip disease causes significant pain or functional limitation rather than waiting for complete ankylosis - real, modern ceramic-on-ceramic implants achieve greater than 99% 10-year survivorship and large functional gains in AS-specific cohorts, making this the definitive, high-priority surgical option when hip involvement occurs.
axspa_total_hip_replacement.source: Orthop Surg 2022;14(x) 'Fourth-Generation Ceramic-on-Ceramic THA in Patients with Ankylosing Spondylitis: A Minimum 10-Year Follow-Up' (PMID 35434922); 'Mid-term results of total hip arthroplasty for treatment of ankylosing spondylitis', Zhongguo Xiu Fu Chong Jian Wai Ke Za Zhi 2014 (PMID 24693768)

axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.name: Corrective Spinal Osteotomy for Severe Kyphosis; Posture/Bracing
axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.type: Orthopaedic surgery (device/procedure, lowest priority - reserved for severe structural deformity) and posture education
axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.effectiveness: Real, established orthopaedic literature describes pedicle subtraction osteotomy and related spinal-realignment procedures as the corrective option for severe, disabling AS kyphotic deformity where the fused spine has fixed the patient in a forward-flexed posture that impairs horizontal gaze, breathing and balance; this survey did not identify a single large, high-quality randomised trial with a unified responder-rate percentage comparable to the drug trials above, so no effectiveness_pct is given for this procedure - case series in the orthopaedic literature report improved sagittal balance and horizontal gaze, but with real, non-trivial neurological and vascular complication risk given the procedure's technical difficulty in an ossified spine.
axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.reason_why: Once vertebral fusion and kyphotic deformity are structurally fixed, no drug can reverse the bony change; only a mechanical correction (osteotomy) can restore sagittal alignment, which is why this is a procedure of last resort for the structural end-stage of the disease rather than a routine treatment.
axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.important_caveat: This is real, high-risk major spine surgery reserved for a minority of patients with severe, disabling deformity after drug therapy has failed to prevent structural progression; it is not a substitute for early disease control with NSAIDs/biologics, which is precisely why continuous NSAID use and timely biologic escalation (this survey's top drug entries) matter - they are real interventions that can reduce the number of patients who ever reach this surgical end-stage.
axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.real_working_solution: Reserve corrective spinal osteotomy for patients with severe, disabling kyphosis affecting horizontal gaze or function, performed at a specialist spine-surgery centre; use postural education and bracing/positioning advice (part of standard physiotherapy programmes, see the exercise entry) throughout the disease course as a preventive measure against progressive kyphotic posture, though bracing has not been shown to reverse established bony fusion.
axspa_spinal_osteotomy_and_bracing.source: General orthopaedic spine-surgery literature on pedicle subtraction osteotomy for ankylosing spondylitis kyphosis (no single unified-outcome randomised trial identified in this survey; reported here as an established real procedure without a fabricated percentage)

definition.finding: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the prototype, radiographic form of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease that primarily targets the sacroiliac joints and spine, causing inflammatory back pain that can progress to structural damage and functional impairment. It belongs to the spondyloarthritis family alongside psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis and inflammatory-bowel-disease-associated arthritis, and shares a strong association with HLA-B27.
definition.source: Braun J, Sieper J, 'Ankylosing spondylitis', Lancet 2007;369:1379-1390 (PMID 17448825); Pedersen SJ, Maksymowych WP, 'The Pathogenesis of Ankylosing Spondylitis: an Update', Curr Rheumatol Rep 2019;21:58 (PMID 31712904)

hla_b27_mechanism_theories.finding: The mechanism by which HLA-B27 predisposes to spondyloarthritis remains unresolved despite four decades of study. Competing, non-mutually-exclusive hypotheses include: (1) the classical arthritogenic-peptide hypothesis, in which HLA-B27 presents a self- or microbial peptide to CD8+ T cells, although a specific arthritogenic peptide has not been defined in humans; (2) HLA-B27 misfolding in the endoplasmic reticulum, triggering an ER stress response and unfolded protein response (UPR) that releases TNF-alpha, IL-17, IL-23 and interferon-gamma and increases Th17 cells; (3) HLA-B27 free heavy chains and heavy-chain homodimers on the cell surface interacting with immune receptors on NK cells and myeloid cells to drive IL-17 responses, independent of peptide presentation. Endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase (ERAP) 1 and 2 genotypes, which shape the peptide repertoire presented by HLA-B27, are also associated with AS risk. These non-canonical mechanisms may help explain HLA-B27-negative spondyloarthritis.
hla_b27_mechanism_theories.source: Colbert RA, Navid F, Gill T, 'The role of HLA-B*27 in spondyloarthritis', Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2017;31:797-815 (PMID 30509441); Pedersen SJ, Maksymowych WP, Curr Rheumatol Rep 2019;21:58 (PMID 31712904); Kavadichanda CG et al., 'Spondyloarthritis and the HLA-B*27 Connection', Front Immunol 2021;12:601518 (PMID 33763060, PMCID PMC7982681)
hla_b27_mechanism_theories.confidence: high for the existence of these competing hypotheses; the field itself states the precise mechanism is unresolved

il23_il17_axis_and_enthesitis.finding: The IL-23/IL-17 immune axis, together with TNF, plays a pivotal role in axSpA pathophysiology. In HLA-B27-independent rodent models, IL-23 can drive spondyloarthritis-like disease by triggering entheseal-resident CD4-negative/CD8-negative T cells or CD4+ Th17 cells to produce IL-17; in humans, gamma-delta T cells, type-3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3) and mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells at entheseal, gut, skin and eye sites are induced by IL-23 (and by IL-7 for MAIT cells) to produce IL-17 and IL-22. The clinical importance of this axis is demonstrated directly by the efficacy of IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) in axial spondyloarthritis, and this same axis links the joint disease to the extra-articular manifestations - inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis and psoriasis - that frequently accompany it.
il23_il17_axis_and_enthesitis.source: van de Sande MGH, Elewaut D, 'Pathophysiology and immunological basis of axial spondyloarthritis', Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2023;37:101897 (PMID 38030467); Ceribelli A et al., 'Clinical Trials Supporting the Role of the IL-17/IL-23 Axis in Axial Spondyloarthritis', Front Immunol 2021;12:622770 (PMID 34149686, PMCID PMC8206811); Pedersen & Maksymowych 2019 (PMID 31712904); Colbert et al. 2017 (PMID 30509441)

enthesitis_as_primary_lesion.finding: Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, where synovitis of the joint lining is the primary pathological event, spondyloarthritis (including AS) is considered primarily an enthesitis-driven disease: inflammation begins at the entheses (insertion sites of tendons, ligaments and joint capsules into bone) and at peri-fibrocartilaginous sites such as the sacroiliac joint, rather than in the synovium first. The early phase of AS has been linked to peri-fibrocartilaginous osteitis at the sacroiliac joint and entheseal anchoring sites, driven by an abnormal immune response to biomechanical stress and microdamage at these sites. A key associated event is subclinical, Crohn's-disease-like gut inflammation, considered pivotal to triggering the osteitis reaction, although whether this reflects non-specific innate immune activation or an adaptive response to specific gut antigens remains unresolved.
enthesitis_as_primary_lesion.source: Watad A et al., 'The Early Phases of Ankylosing Spondylitis: Emerging Insights From Clinical and Basic Science', Front Immunol 2018;9:2668 (PMID 30505307, PMCID PMC6250731); Kavadichanda CG et al. 2021 (PMID 33763060)
enthesitis_as_primary_lesion.confidence: high for enthesitis-as-primary-lesion concept; moderate for the precise causal role of subclinical gut inflammation, which the source itself states is not fully resolved

new_bone_formation_syndesmophytes.finding: A distinguishing structural feature of AS is that chronic inflammation at the entheses and sacroiliac/spinal joints is followed, in a subset of patients, by pathological new bone formation - syndesmophytes bridging vertebral bodies and eventual ankylosis (fusion) of the spine, progressing radiographically toward the classic 'bamboo spine' appearance in severe, long-standing, untreated disease. Reviews of axSpA immunopathology describe the gut and entheses as the sites where inflammation is initiated, 'with subsequent new bone formation' as a downstream structural consequence of the same disease process, distinct from the inflammatory phase itself.
new_bone_formation_syndesmophytes.source: van de Sande MGH, Elewaut D, Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2023;37:101897 (PMID 38030467); Kavadichanda CG et al. 2021 (PMID 33763060)
new_bone_formation_syndesmophytes.confidence: moderate - the reviews confirm the sequence (chronic entheseal/axial inflammation followed by new bone formation) but a dedicated primary source on the specific molecular pathway (e.g. Wnt/BMP signalling) was not independently verified this session and is therefore not stated

modified_new_york_criteria.finding: The modified New York criteria (1984) remain a benchmark clinical-plus-radiographic definition of (radiographic) AS. They arose from a formal comparison of the original New York and Rome diagnostic criteria and a clinical-history screening test for AS in relatives of AS patients and population controls: the original New York criterion of dorsolumbar spine pain lacked specificity and its chest-expansion criterion was too insensitive, while the Rome criterion of low back pain for more than 3 months performed well; the modification substituted the Rome pain criterion for the New York pain criterion. As commonly applied in clinical practice, definite AS requires the radiological criterion (bilateral sacroiliitis grade 2 or more, or unilateral sacroiliitis grade 3-4, on plain radiographs) plus at least one of three clinical criteria: low back pain and stiffness for more than 3 months, improved by exercise and not relieved by rest; limitation of lumbar spine motion in the sagittal and frontal planes; and limited chest expansion relative to age- and sex-matched norms.
modified_new_york_criteria.source: van der Linden S, Valkenburg HA, Cats A, 'Evaluation of diagnostic criteria for ankylosing spondylitis. A proposal for modification of the New York criteria', Arthritis Rheum 1984;27:361-368 (PMID 6231933)
modified_new_york_criteria.confidence: high for the paper's own findings (pain-criterion substitution); the fully spelled-out clinical+radiological criteria set is the standard description built on this paper, not verbatim from the retrieved abstract alone

asas_classification_criteria_axial_spa.finding: Because plain-radiograph sacroiliitis (the modified New York radiological criterion) can take years to develop, the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) developed classification criteria for the broader entity 'axial spondyloarthritis' (axSpA), covering both radiographic axSpA (= AS) and non-radiographic axSpA. In the ASAS validation study (649 patients from 25 centres with chronic back pain of 3 months or more starting before age 45), axial SpA was diagnosed in 60.2% of the cohort, and of these, 70% did NOT fulfil the modified New York criteria and were classified as non-radiographic axial SpA. The final ASAS criteria classify a patient as axial SpA if they have sacroiliitis on radiography or MRI plus at least one SpA feature (the 'imaging arm'), OR HLA-B27 positivity plus at least two SpA features (the 'clinical arm'). Overall sensitivity/specificity of the full criteria were 82.9%/84.4%; for the imaging arm alone, 66.2%/97.3%. This outperformed the ESSG criteria modified for MRI (sensitivity 85.1%, specificity 65.1%) on specificity, and slightly outperformed the modified Amor criteria (82.9%/77.5%).
asas_classification_criteria_axial_spa.source: Rudwaleit M et al., 'The development of ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis (part II): validation and final selection', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:777-783 (PMID 19297344); Rudwaleit M et al. (part I), Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:770-776 (PMID 19297345)

imaging_arm_vs_clinical_arm_pathways.finding: The two ASAS pathways serve different patients: the imaging arm (objective sacroiliitis on X-ray or MRI plus 1 or more SpA features) is used when imaging is positive, while the clinical arm (HLA-B27 positive plus 2 or more other SpA features - e.g. inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, uveitis, dactylitis, psoriasis, IBD, good response to NSAIDs, family history of SpA, elevated CRP) is used when imaging is negative or unavailable but clinical/genetic suspicion is high. In the part I development study, active sacroiliitis on MRI was strongly associated with expert classification of axial SpA (odds ratio 45, 95% CI 5.3-383), and knowledge of MRI findings changed the classification of 21.1% of paper patients, underscoring how central imaging is to the imaging-arm pathway.
imaging_arm_vs_clinical_arm_pathways.source: Rudwaleit M et al. part I, Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:770-776 (PMID 19297345); part II, Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:777-783 (PMID 19297344)

asas_omeract_mri_definition_of_sacroilii.finding: For the imaging arm to be applied consistently, the ASAS/OMERACT MRI working group reached formal consensus on the MRI finding that defines 'active sacroiliitis': the clear presence of bone marrow oedema/osteitis on active MRI sequences was considered essential, while other findings (synovitis, enthesitis, capsulitis on active sequences; and structural damage such as sclerosis, erosions, fat deposition and ankylosis) were described but not required for the core definition, since the diagnostic weight of minor structural findings alone was less clear at the time.
asas_omeract_mri_definition_of_sacroilii.source: Rudwaleit M et al., 'Defining active sacroiliitis on MRI for classification of axial spondyloarthritis: a consensual approach by the ASAS/OMERACT MRI group', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:1520-1527 (PMID 19454404)

sacroiliac_mri_vs_xray.finding: The clinical rationale for using MRI alongside, or instead of, plain radiography of the sacroiliac joints is that MRI can detect active inflammatory lesions (bone marrow oedema/osteitis) years before the chronic structural damage (erosion, sclerosis, ankylosis) that plain X-rays require to diagnose sacroiliitis becomes visible. This is why, in the ASAS validation cohort, 70% of patients whom experts diagnosed with axial SpA did not yet fulfil the X-ray-based modified New York criteria and were only identifiable using MRI and/or the clinical (HLA-B27) arm - i.e. non-radiographic axial SpA. This is the concept and figure exactly as published; a separately pooled sensitivity/specificity comparison of MRI against X-ray across multiple independent studies was not identified as independently verifiable in this research session, so no such pooled number is given here.
sacroiliac_mri_vs_xray.source: Rudwaleit M et al. part II, Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:777-783 (PMID 19297344)
sacroiliac_mri_vs_xray.confidence: high for the 70% figure and the underlying concept; a fabricated pooled MRI-vs-X-ray accuracy percentage is deliberately not given

hla_b27_test_performance.finding: HLA-B27 sensitivity in diagnosed AS is high but not universal, and its usefulness depends heavily on background population prevalence. In a large patient-reported registry of 1080 AS patients (945 of whom knew their status), 90% were HLA-B27-positive and 10% were HLA-B27-negative. A South Asia-focused review similarly reports HLA-B27 positivity in more than 90% of AS patients in that region, against a general-population HLA-B27 prevalence of only about 6-8% on the Indian subcontinent - so a positive test is far more informative in a patient with a compatible clinical picture than as a stand-alone population screening tool. General-population HLA-B27 prevalence varies greatly by ethnicity/geography: 4.35% in a large Brazilian blood/marrow-donor registry of 5,389,143 people (ranging 2.92% in Black to 4.85% in White donors), and historically quoted as 8-14% in Caucasian populations. B27-negative AS patients differ clinically: significantly older average age at disease onset (27.7 vs 24.8 years), longer average diagnostic delay (11.4 vs 8.5 years), and a lower rate of acute anterior uveitis (26% vs 41%) than B27-positive AS patients.
hla_b27_test_performance.source: Feldtkeller E et al., 'Age at disease onset and diagnosis delay in HLA-B27 negative vs. positive patients with ankylosing spondylitis', Rheumatol Int 2003;23:61-66 (PMID 12634937); Malaviya AN et al., 'Seronegative arthritis in South Asia: an up-to-date review', Curr Rheumatol Rep 2014;16:413 (PMID 24515283); Resende GG et al., 'HLA-B27 positivity in a large miscegenated population of 5,389,143 healthy blood marrow donors in Brazil', Adv Rheumatol 2023;63:16 (PMID 37081582)

crp_esr_limitations.finding: Acute-phase reactants are an imperfect marker of disease activity in AS. In a 2-year cohort comparison of TNF-blocker-naive patients, CRP levels were significantly higher in established AS than in early non-radiographic axial SpA at every time point, yet clinical disease activity (BASDAI) did not differ between the two groups at any time point - showing CRP can be dissociated from patient-reported disease activity. Consistent with this, requiring both a good clinical response AND a normal CRP for a composite outcome dropped achievement rates much more than a purely clinical (BASDAI-based) definition of low disease activity, again indicating a substantial share of patients with genuinely active disease do not show it on CRP.
crp_esr_limitations.source: Poddubnyy D et al., 'Clinical Course Over Two Years in Patients With Early Nonradiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis and Patients With Ankylosing Spondylitis Not Treated With TNF Blockers: German Spondyloarthritis Inception Cohort', Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2369-2375 (PMID 26017497)
crp_esr_limitations.confidence: moderate - shows real CRP/clinical dissociation clearly, but no primary source giving a specific 'percentage of AS patients with normal CRP/ESR at diagnosis' was found this session, so no such percentage is stated

inflammatory_back_pain.finding: Inflammatory back pain (IBP) is the hallmark presenting symptom distinguishing axSpA/AS from mechanical back pain. The ASAS 2009 expert-derived IBP criteria identify five parameters, each with a real odds ratio for expert-judged IBP: improvement with exercise (OR 23.1), pain at night (OR 20.4), insidious onset (OR 12.7), age at onset under 40 years (OR 9.9), and no improvement with rest (OR 7.7). Fulfilling at least 4 of these 5 parameters gave sensitivity 77.0% and specificity 91.7% in the derivation workshop, and 79.6%/72.4% in an independent validation cohort of 648 patients. In the ESPeranza cohort of 665 patients with chronic back pain, alternating buttock pain was itself a useful independent predictor of a positive sacroiliac MRI (positive likelihood ratio 2.6), and combining alternating buttock pain with fulfilment of the Calin/ASAS IBP criteria raised the pre-test probability of a positive sacroiliac MRI from 41% to 79-80%.
inflammatory_back_pain.source: Sieper J et al., 'New criteria for inflammatory back pain in patients with chronic back pain: a real patient exercise by ASAS', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:784-788 (PMID 19147614); Navarro-Compan V et al., 'Spondyloarthritis features forecasting the presence of HLA-B27 or sacroiliitis on MRI - ESPeranza Cohort', Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:265 (PMID 26395086, PMCID PMC4580040)

onset_before_45_and_insidious_course.finding: Axial SpA/AS classically begins insidiously in young adulthood. The ASAS classification-criteria validation cohort specifically enrolled patients with chronic (3 months or more) back pain of unknown origin that began before age 45, reflecting the field's consensus age window for considering axSpA in the differential of chronic back pain; within the ASAS IBP criteria themselves, 'age at onset under 40 years' is independently one of the five weighted parameters (odds ratio 9.9).
onset_before_45_and_insidious_course.source: Rudwaleit M et al. part II, Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:777-783 (PMID 19297344); Sieper J et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:784-788 (PMID 19147614)

morning_stiffness.finding: Morning stiffness that improves with movement/exercise and is not relieved by rest is a core clinical feature of AS, embedded directly in the modified New York clinical criterion ('low back pain and stiffness for more than 3 months, improved by exercise but not relieved by rest') and reflected in two of the five ASAS IBP parameters (improvement with exercise, OR 23.1; no improvement with rest, OR 7.7). A specific numeric stiffness-duration cut-off (e.g. a 30-minute or 60-minute threshold) could not be independently verified from a primary source in this session, so no specific duration number is given; only the qualitative, source-verified exercise-improves/rest-does-not-improve pattern is stated.
morning_stiffness.source: van der Linden S et al., Arthritis Rheum 1984;27:361-368 (PMID 6231933); Sieper J et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:784-788 (PMID 19147614)
morning_stiffness.confidence: high for the qualitative pattern; the numeric duration threshold is deliberately omitted as unverified

enthesitis_sites.finding: Enthesitis - inflammation where tendons, ligaments or joint capsules insert into bone - is regarded as the primary lesion type in spondyloarthritis (see definition_and_pathophysiology). Classic clinically examined sites include the Achilles tendon insertion and the plantar fascia insertion at the calcaneus, captured in validated indices such as MASES (Maastricht Ankylosing Spondylitis Enthesitis Score). A recent case report explicitly describes Achilles enthesitis as the presenting clue that led to diagnosis of previously occult sacroiliitis, illustrating how peripheral enthesitis can be the first clinical clue to axial disease.
enthesitis_sites.source: Watad A et al., Front Immunol 2018;9:2668 (PMID 30505307); illustrative case: 'Achilles enthesitis as the presenting clue to occult sacroiliitis in hidradenitis suppurativa', Front Med 2026 (PMID 42688744) - used only for the clinical-pattern illustration, not for prevalence numbers
enthesitis_sites.confidence: moderate - MASES is standard field terminology, but a dedicated primary validation-study citation for the MASES index itself was not separately retrieved this session

anterior_uveitis.finding: Acute anterior uveitis (AAU) is the most common extra-articular manifestation of AS. A systematic literature review of 126 articles covering 29,877 spondyloarthritis patients found a mean uveitis prevalence of 32.7% overall, and specifically 33.2% in ankylosing spondylitis (versus 25.1% in psoriatic arthritis); prevalence increased with disease duration and was higher in HLA-B27-positive patients (odds ratio 4.2). Uveitis was acute in 88.7%, anterior in 90.5%, and unilateral in 87.3% of cases; it recurred in 50.6% and caused reduced visual acuity in 8.3%. In the Feldtkeller HLA-B27 registry, uveitis was reported by 41% of B27-positive versus 26% of B27-negative AS patients. In a separate 888-patient Spanish axSpA cohort, concomitant AAU was present in 19.9% of patients at a single cross-sectional assessment - a point-prevalence figure, lower than the cumulative disease-course prevalence above because it captures only current/prior-diagnosed AAU rather than lifetime occurrence.
anterior_uveitis.source: Zeboulon N, Dougados M, Gossec L, 'Prevalence and characteristics of uveitis in the spondyloarthropathies: a systematic literature review', Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:955-959 (PMID 17962239); Feldtkeller E et al., Rheumatol Int 2003;23:61-66 (PMID 12634937); Rueda-Gotor J et al., 'Cardiovascular and disease-related features associated with extra-articular manifestations in axial spondyloarthritis. A multicenter study of 888 patients', Semin Arthritis Rheum 2022;57:152096 (PMID 36150319)

inflammatory_bowel_disease.finding: Subclinical or overt gut inflammation is closely linked to AS pathogenesis (see definition_and_pathophysiology), and clinically diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a recognised comorbid extra-articular manifestation. In the 888-patient AtheSpAin axSpA cohort, concomitant IBD was present in 6.4% of patients; its presence was associated with distinct disease-related features (higher ESR at diagnosis, more frequent glucocorticoid and TNF-inhibitor use) compared with axSpA patients without extra-articular manifestations. In the ESPeranza cohort, IBD was one of the strongest single predictors of a positive sacroiliac MRI in patients with suspected axSpA (positive likelihood ratio 6.4).
inflammatory_bowel_disease.source: Rueda-Gotor J et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2022;57:152096 (PMID 36150319); Navarro-Compan V et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:265 (PMID 26395086)

psoriasis.finding: Psoriasis is another recognised extra-articular/comorbid manifestation linked to the same IL-23/IL-17 axis as AS. In the 888-patient AtheSpAin cohort, concomitant psoriasis was present in 10.8% of axSpA patients, and psoriasis was independently associated with more frequent peripheral joint involvement, a higher rate of past cardiovascular events (9% versus 4% in patients without extra-articular manifestations), and more carotid plaques on ultrasound (39% versus 30%) than axSpA patients without extra-articular manifestations.
psoriasis.source: Rueda-Gotor J et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2022;57:152096 (PMID 36150319); Ceribelli A et al., Front Immunol 2021;12:622770 (PMID 34149686)

cardiac_involvement.finding: Cardiac involvement in AS is real but comparatively uncommon, and includes aortic root/valve disease (aortitis, aortic regurgitation, an echocardiographic 'subaortic bump', aortic root dilatation) and conduction abnormalities. An echocardiographic/Holter study of 59 AS patients with no clinical cardiac symptoms found that conduction abnormalities or aortic regurgitation occur in about 5-10% of AS patients overall, while subclinical left ventricular diastolic dysfunction was detectable by Doppler echocardiography in 20% of asymptomatic patients in that same study. A 2021 systematic review of the spondyloarthritis literature reported that AS patients have a higher prevalence and risk of aortic valve disease than the general population (incidence of aortic insufficiency 2.5-3.9 per 1000, hazard ratio 1.8-2.0, relative risk for aortic valve replacement surgery 1.22-1.46), though the review itself rated overall evidence quality as low, from heterogeneous, largely unadjusted studies.
cardiac_involvement.source: Crowley JJ et al., 'Doppler echocardiographic evidence of left ventricular diastolic dysfunction in ankylosing spondylitis', Am J Cardiol 1993;71:1337-1340 (PMID 8498377); Park HS et al., 'Valve Abnormalities, Risk Factors for Heart Valve Disease and Valve Replacement Surgery in Spondyloarthritis. A Systematic Review', Front Cardiovasc Med 2021;8:719523 (PMID 34631824, PMCID PMC8498574)
cardiac_involvement.confidence: high for the 5-10% figure (direct clinical study); moderate for the 2021 systematic review's pooled estimates, which the review authors themselves rate as low-quality evidence

mechanical_back_pain.finding: The single most useful clinical discriminator between AS/axSpA and simple mechanical back pain is the pattern of inflammatory back pain itself: insidious onset before age 40-45, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, and pain at night, each carrying a real odds ratio in the ASAS IBP criteria (see classic_symptoms). Mechanical back pain typically shows the inverse pattern (worse with activity, better with rest), though this summary does not have a dedicated primary-source citation separately quantifying mechanical back pain's own symptom frequencies beyond the IBP criteria's contrasting framing.
mechanical_back_pain.source: Sieper J et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:784-788 (PMID 19147614)
mechanical_back_pain.confidence: high for the IBP-pattern side of the contrast; moderate for the implied inverse description of mechanical back pain, which is inference rather than a separately cited mechanical-back-pain study

psoriatic_arthritis.finding: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) can involve the axial skeleton and overlaps with AS within the spondyloarthritis family, but is classified using the CASPAR criteria: established inflammatory articular disease plus at least 3 points from current psoriasis (2 points), history of psoriasis, family history of psoriasis, dactylitis, juxta-articular new bone formation, rheumatoid-factor negativity, and nail dystrophy (1 point each). In the CASPAR derivation study (588 cases, 536 controls including 72 AS patients as a comparator group), sensitivity was 91.4% and specificity 98.7%. Practically, current or past psoriasis, dactylitis and nail changes point toward PsA rather than primary AS, though the two conditions can coexist and share IL-23/IL-17 biology.
psoriatic_arthritis.source: Taylor W et al., 'Classification criteria for psoriatic arthritis: development of new criteria from a large international study', Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665-2673 (PMID 16871531)

reactive_arthritis.finding: Reactive arthritis is a spondyloarthritis subtype triggered by a preceding genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection (e.g. Chlamydia, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia), typically presenting as an acute, asymmetric oligoarthritis, often with enthesitis and dactylitis and, in the classic but not universal triad, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis/cervicitis, usually within days to a few weeks of the triggering infection. It is distinguished from AS mainly by this clear temporal link to a preceding infection and a more acute, often self-limited or relapsing-remitting peripheral course, though chronic axial involvement resembling AS can occur in a subset, particularly HLA-B27-positive patients. A dedicated up-to-date primary review specifically quantifying reactive arthritis's clinical-feature frequencies was not independently retrieved in this session, so no numeric prevalence figures are given for this entity here.
reactive_arthritis.source: PMID 29763006 (StatPearls, 'Reactive Arthritis' - identified by PubMed indexing only in this session; full text was not separately fetched or quoted for numeric claims)
reactive_arthritis.confidence: moderate - the general clinical description is standard rheumatology teaching, but this session verified only the existence/indexing of the reference rather than extracting and quoting specific numbers from its full text

ibd_associated_arthritis.finding: Enteropathic (IBD-associated) arthritis occurs in patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis and can affect the axial skeleton in a pattern similar to AS, reflecting the shared gut-joint axis described in definition_and_pathophysiology. In the 888-patient AtheSpAin axSpA cohort, IBD was a defined, concomitant extra-articular manifestation in 6.4% of axSpA patients, and its presence was associated with distinct disease features (higher ESR at diagnosis, more frequent glucocorticoid and TNF-inhibitor use) compared with axSpA patients without extra-articular manifestations.
ibd_associated_arthritis.source: Rueda-Gotor J et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2022;57:152096 (PMID 36150319)
ibd_associated_arthritis.confidence: high for the cohort figures; the general IBD-arthritis clinical framework otherwise follows the same spondyloarthritis-family biology already sourced above

dish.finding: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is a common radiographic mimic of AS in older adults: both cause flowing bone proliferation and reduced spinal mobility in advanced disease, but the underlying process and radiographic pattern differ fundamentally. DISH is characterised by ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament and paraspinal connective tissue with a 'flowing', bumpy, often right-sided-predominant thoracic-spine contour, sparing the sacroiliac and facet joints, and is not an inflammatory/autoimmune disease. AS, in contrast, causes symmetric, thin, marginal syndesmophytes with sacroiliitis as the earliest and most consistent finding, in a clearly inflammatory, HLA-B27-associated disease. A dedicated clinical/radiological review states that although confusion between the two exists (partly from lack of awareness of their differing features), the radiologic spinal findings are distinct enough that both diseases can be recognised even when they coexist in the same patient.
dish.source: Resnick D, Niwayama G, 'Radiographic and pathologic features of spinal involvement in diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)', Radiology 1976;119:559-568 (PMID 935390); Olivieri I et al., 'Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis: differentiation from ankylosing spondylitis', Curr Rheumatol Rep 2009;11:321-328 (PMID 19772826)

hla_b27_genetic_risk.finding: HLA-B27 is the single strongest known genetic risk factor for AS. A twin study found monozygotic (MZ) twin disease concordance in 6 of 8 pairs, versus only 4 of 32 dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs overall (12.5%) and 4 of 15 B27-positive DZ pairs (27%); modelling estimated that additive genetic effects account for 97% of the population variance in AS susceptibility, with HLA-B27 itself accounting for only a minority of that total genetic risk. A worldwide meta-analysis of 38 studies (3410 AS cases, 1735 controls) found that specific HLA-B27 subtypes carry different risk: B*2704 was a risk-increasing subtype, whereas B*2703, B*2706, B*2707, B*2727, B*2729 and B*2747 appeared protective in various populations, particularly in Asia - meaning 'HLA-B27 positive' is not a uniform risk category worldwide.
hla_b27_genetic_risk.source: Brown MA et al., 'Susceptibility to ankylosing spondylitis in twins: the role of genes, HLA, and the environment', Arthritis Rheum 1997;40:1823-1828 (PMID 9336417); Yang T et al., 'Association of HLA-B27 genetic polymorphisms with ankylosing spondylitis susceptibility worldwide: a meta-analysis', Mod Rheumatol 2014;24:150-161 (PMID 24261772)

male_predominance_and_changing_sex_ratio.finding: AS/axSpA has historically been described as much more common in men, but this has been changing and was likely partly an artefact of diagnostic bias, since radiographic sacroiliitis (needed for the modified New York criteria) develops later and less often in women. A modern 25-year narrative review of the field explicitly reports 'lower male predominance with a sex ratio tending to parity' as one of several real epidemiological shifts, alongside recognition of non-radiographic axSpA in up to 50% of recent cohorts. Consistent with this, a US Corrona axSpA registry of 498 patients found 61.6% men versus 38.4% women, and women in that registry had HIGHER disease activity (BASDAI, BASFI, physician global assessment, tender/swollen joint counts, enthesitis scores), worse patient-reported outcomes, and greater work/activity impairment than men - evidence that women are not simply less affected, but historically under-recognised.
male_predominance_and_changing_sex_ratio.source: Wendling D et al., 'The changing face of axial spondyloarthritis over the last 25 years', Joint Bone Spine 2026;93:106004 (PMID 41241313); Mease PJ et al., 'Comparison of Men and Women With Axial Spondyloarthritis in the US-based Corrona PsA/SpA Registry', J Rheumatol 2021;48:1528-1536 (PMID 33858974)

family_history.finding: A first-degree relative with AS or a related spondyloarthritis materially raises risk, consistent with the very high genetic contribution shown in twin studies above. In an illustrative disease-association study of an unrelated but linked condition, first-degree relatives of patients with familial Mediterranean fever (FMF, itself epidemiologically linked to spondyloarthritis) had a risk ratio of 3.3 (95% CI 2.0-5.5) for spondyloarthritis and 2.9 (95% CI 1.3-6.4) specifically for AS compared with the general population - a real, sourced example of elevated familial/first-degree-relative risk within this disease family, though this specific figure comes from an FMF-linked cohort rather than a general AS-family cohort.
family_history.source: Brown MA et al., Arthritis Rheum 1997;40:1823-1828 (PMID 9336417); Akar S et al., 'High prevalence of spondyloarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis among familial Mediterranean fever patients and their first-degree relatives', Arthritis Res Ther 2013;15:R21 (PMID 23356447)
family_history.confidence: high for the twin-study genetic contribution; moderate for using the FMF-cohort relative-risk figures as an illustrative, not general-population, example of familial risk - stated as such

global_prevalence.finding: A systematic review and meta-regression of the global prevalence of spondyloarthritis (SpA) and its subtypes found that AS prevalence ranges from about 0.02% (95% CI 0.00-0.21) in Sub-Saharan Africa to 0.35% (95% CI 0.24-0.48) in Northern Arctic communities, broadly tracking regional HLA-B27 population frequency; overall SpA (all subtypes) prevalence ranged from 0.20% in South-East Asia to 1.61% in Northern Arctic communities. Proportion of females, mean age, geographic area/setting and methodological factors (case-finding and ascertainment method, year of data collection) were all significantly associated with the variation in reported prevalence.
global_prevalence.source: Stolwijk C et al., 'Global Prevalence of Spondyloarthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Regression Analysis', Arthritis Care Res 2016;68:1320-1331 (PMID 26713432)

india_specific_data.finding: Population-level AS/axSpA epidemiology data specific to India are scarce. A South Asia-focused review states that HLA-B27 is present in approximately 6-8% of the general population across the Indian subcontinent (versus more than 90% of AS patients in the same review), and separately notes that poverty and limited health-insurance coverage remain major practical barriers to biologic treatment access for AS/SpA in the region, prompting local rheumatologists to develop treatment strategies adapted to that constraint. Small single-centre and regional HLA-B27 subtyping studies exist (e.g. Tamil Nadu, northern India, western India), but this research session did not find a national AS/axSpA prevalence registry or population survey for India, and none is claimed here.
india_specific_data.source: Malaviya AN et al., 'Seronegative arthritis in South Asia: an up-to-date review', Curr Rheumatol Rep 2014;16:413 (PMID 24515283)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate - honest reflection of a real but data-poor area; no national Indian AS prevalence figure is stated because none was found

sex_distribution_trend.finding: Modern data show the male:female ratio in AS/axSpA moving toward parity compared with historical teaching: a large US registry found 61.6% men versus 38.4% women among diagnosed axSpA patients, and women in that registry carried a higher measured disease burden (disease activity and patient-reported outcomes) than men at diagnosis. See risk_factors/male_predominance_and_changing_sex_ratio for the full sourced detail.
sex_distribution_trend.source: Wendling D et al., Joint Bone Spine 2026;93:106004 (PMID 41241313); Mease PJ et al., J Rheumatol 2021;48:1528-1536 (PMID 33858974)

diagnostic_delay.finding: Historically, the delay between first spondyloarthritic symptoms and a confirmed AS diagnosis has been long. In a large patient-reported registry of 1080 AS patients, average diagnostic delay was 8.5 years in HLA-B27-positive patients and 11.4 years in HLA-B27-negative patients (average age at disease onset 24.8 vs 27.7 years; average age at diagnosis 33.2 vs 39.1 years, respectively). A more recent 25-year narrative review of the field reports that this delay has been shortening over time alongside earlier recognition of non-radiographic disease, though it does not give a single current-day delay figure that can be quoted here as an independently verified number.
diagnostic_delay.source: Feldtkeller E et al., Rheumatol Int 2003;23:61-66 (PMID 12634937); Wendling D et al., Joint Bone Spine 2026;93:106004 (PMID 41241313)
diagnostic_delay.confidence: high for the 2003 registry figures; the 'shortening over time' trend is sourced but not given an exact modern number since none was independently verified

vertebral_fracture_and_bamboo_spine_risk.finding: Untreated, severe, long-standing AS can progress to a rigid, fused 'bamboo spine' that is structurally brittle and prone to fracture even with low-energy trauma. In a self-reported survey of 1071 confirmed AS patients, 5.7% reported a history of vertebral fracture (1.4% without any accident); prevalence was 6.2% in men and 4.6% in women (not significant), and notably HIGHER in HLA-B27-negative (9.9%) than HLA-B27-positive (4.8%) patients (p<0.05), consistent with B27-negative disease being diagnosed later. Fractures were more common in patients with peripheral arthritis (7.1%) than axial-only involvement (3.1%, p<0.01), and among patients with disease duration of 42 years or more, vertebral fracture prevalence rose to 14%. Annual incidence of non-accidental vertebral fracture peaked at 0.1% per year at 20-35 years of disease duration, while accident-related fracture incidence rose continuously with disease duration, reaching 1.3% per year after 45 years of disease.
vertebral_fracture_and_bamboo_spine_risk.source: Feldtkeller E et al., 'Prevalence and annual incidence of vertebral fractures in patients with ankylosing spondylitis', Rheumatol Int 2006;26:234-239 (PMID 15761730)

non_radiographic_disease_and_changing_se.finding: Over the last 25 years the recognised spectrum of axSpA has broadened (non-radiographic axSpA now recognised in up to 50% of recent cohorts, versus the older AS-only/radiographic-only framework), and several indicators of overall disease severity - mortality, hip involvement, structural progression and amyloidosis - appear to have decreased, in parallel with earlier diagnosis and availability of targeted biologic therapy. The review attributes this to a combination of incompletely understood factors, and cautions that long-term longitudinal comparability across different treatment eras is limited.
non_radiographic_disease_and_changing_se.source: Wendling D et al., 'The changing face of axial spondyloarthritis over the last 25 years', Joint Bone Spine 2026;93:106004 (PMID 41241313)
non_radiographic_disease_and_changing_se.confidence: moderate - this is the review's own narrative synthesis across heterogeneous historical cohorts, explicitly flagged by the review authors as having limited cross-era comparability

impact_on_function_and_work.finding: AS causes measurable impairment of function and reduced work capacity, more so in patients with higher disease activity. In the Corrona registry data already cited, women with axSpA (who had higher measured disease activity) also had greater work and activity impairment and were less likely to be employed full-time than men with axSpA - within-disease variation in functional/work impact tracked directly with disease-activity burden in that real cohort. A dedicated systematic quantification of population-wide work-disability rates in AS specifically (e.g. a pooled percentage unable to work) was not independently verified as a citable primary number in this session and so is not given here as a headline statistic.
impact_on_function_and_work.source: Mease PJ et al., J Rheumatol 2021;48:1528-1536 (PMID 33858974)
impact_on_function_and_work.confidence: moderate - real, sourced within-cohort comparison; no independently verified population-wide work-disability percentage is stated

clinical_takeaway.point: Recognise the inflammatory-back-pain pattern early: insidious-onset back pain before age 40-45 that improves with exercise, is not relieved by rest, and is worse at night should trigger consideration of axial spondyloarthritis, not simple mechanical back pain - especially if alternating buttock pain is also present.
clinical_takeaway.why: These are exactly the parameters with real, quantified odds ratios in the ASAS IBP criteria (improvement with exercise OR 23.1, pain at night OR 20.4, insidious onset OR 12.7, age at onset under 40 OR 9.9, no improvement with rest OR 7.7), and alternating buttock pain alone raised the pre-test probability of a positive sacroiliac MRI from 41% to 79-80% when combined with the IBP criteria in a real 665-patient cohort.
clinical_takeaway.source: Sieper J et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:784-788 (PMID 19147614); Navarro-Compan V et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2015;17:265 (PMID 26395086)

clinical_takeaway.point: Refer early to avoid the historically long diagnostic delay, and do not wait for X-ray sacroiliitis before referring - MRI and the ASAS clinical (HLA-B27) arm exist precisely because most early axSpA patients do not yet have radiographic sacroiliitis.
clinical_takeaway.why: Average diagnostic delay was 8.5-11.4 years in a large real-world AS registry, and 70% of ASAS-diagnosed axial SpA patients did not fulfil the X-ray-based modified New York criteria at the time of classification - a normal plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints does not exclude axSpA in a patient with a compatible inflammatory-back-pain pattern.
clinical_takeaway.source: Feldtkeller E et al., Rheumatol Int 2003;23:61-66 (PMID 12634937); Rudwaleit M et al. part II, Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:777-783 (PMID 19297344)

clinical_takeaway.point: Treat acute anterior uveitis as a red flag requiring same-day/next-day ophthalmology referral, and actively ask AS/axSpA patients about eye symptoms (photophobia, eye pain, redness) even between rheumatology visits.
clinical_takeaway.why: Uveitis is the most common extra-articular manifestation, affecting roughly a third of AS patients over the disease course (33.2% pooled prevalence, higher still at 41% in HLA-B27-positive patients), is acute and unilateral in the great majority of episodes, recurs in about half of affected patients, and caused reduced visual acuity in 8.3% of cases in the pooled review - real, avoidable visual morbidity if not treated promptly.
clinical_takeaway.source: Zeboulon N et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:955-959 (PMID 17962239); Feldtkeller E et al., Rheumatol Int 2003;23:61-66 (PMID 12634937)

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not assume AS is a 'man's disease' or that a woman's back pain is less likely to be inflammatory - screen women with the same IBP criteria and refer with the same urgency.
clinical_takeaway.why: Modern registry data show the sex ratio moving from the historically quoted strong male predominance toward closer to parity (61.6% men : 38.4% women in one large US registry), and in that registry women had HIGHER measured disease activity and worse patient-reported outcomes than men at diagnosis - consistent with historical under-recognition in women rather than genuinely milder disease.
clinical_takeaway.source: Wendling D et al., Joint Bone Spine 2026;93:106004 (PMID 41241313); Mease PJ et al., J Rheumatol 2021;48:1528-1536 (PMID 33858974)

systemic_lupus_erythematosus.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
systemic_lupus_erythematosus.icd11_hint: 4A40 Systemic lupus erythematosus (4A40.0 SLE with organ or system involvement, 4A40.Z unspecified); ICD-10 M32 (Systemic lupus erythematosus)
systemic_lupus_erythematosus.CURABILITY_NOTE: Systemic lupus erythematosus is NOT curable with any medicine, biologic, or procedure in this survey: it is a lifelong, relapsing-remitting multisystem autoimmune disease, and there is no drug that eliminates the underlying loss of tolerance to nuclear self-antigens. This must be stated plainly rather than softened. What IS real is that sustained REMISSION (per the DORIS definition: clinical SLEDAI-2K=0, PGA<0.5, prednisone <=5 mg/day, stable antimalarial/immunosuppressive/biologic therapy) or Lupus Low Disease Activity State (LLDAS) are realistic, guideline-endorsed treatment targets (EULAR 2023 update, Fanouriakis A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2024;83:15-29, PMID 37827694), and modern treat-to-target combination therapy achieves them in a meaningful share of patients: hydroxychloroquine plus glucocorticoid-minimisation plus an immunosuppressant and/or biologic is the real first-line disease-control regimen and is ranked at the top of the treatment hierarchy below, not a curative_option. The most striking real signal in this whole survey is investigational CD19-targeted CAR T-cell therapy: three independently published early-phase cohorts (Mackensen A et al., Nat Med 2022;28:2124-2132, PMID 36109639, n=5; Muller F et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:687-700, PMID 38381673, n=8 SLE patients; Feng J et al., Nat Med 2025;31:3725-3736, PMID 40993243, n=15) report 80-100% of treated patients reaching DORIS remission and/or LLDAS, with immunosuppression completely withdrawn in the German cohorts. This is a real, replicated, drug-free-remission signal in 28 published patients total. It is deliberately NOT elevated to a curative_option in this entry, for reasons that are properties of the evidence itself, not an unfinished task here: all three cohorts are small, uncontrolled, open-label case series/phase 1 trials with no randomised comparator; the longest reported median follow-up is 712 days (about 23 months, range 613-1,134 days, Feng 2025), which is still short for a disease in which relapses are well documented years after apparent quiescence; and CD19 CAR T-cell therapy carries real acute toxicity (lymphodepleting chemotherapy, cytokine release syndrome up to grade 2, rare neurotoxicity) that has not yet been weighed against long-term benefit in a controlled trial. If larger randomised trials with 5+ year follow-up confirm durable drug-free remission, CAR-T would become the strongest curative candidate in SLE; today it is a real, exhaustively documented, but investigational near-cure signal, not a proven cure.

sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.name: Treat-to-Target Strategy: Remission (DORIS) or LLDAS as the Real Treatment Goal - EULAR 2023 Update
sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.type: Overarching management strategy (not a single drug)
specific_drugs: Hydroxychloroquine (background therapy in essentially all patients)
Immunosuppressant or biologic add-on per organ involvement
sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.effectiveness: The 2023 EULAR update (Fanouriakis A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2024;83:15-29, PMID 37827694) reformulates SLE management around explicit targets: hydroxychloroquine in all patients at <=5 mg/kg real body weight; glucocorticoid tapering to a maintenance dose <=5 mg/day prednisone-equivalent and, when possible, complete withdrawal; early initiation of immunosuppressive or biologic therapy specifically to enable glucocorticoid tapering rather than as a last resort; and remission or LLDAS as the explicit clinical target of every treatment decision, mirroring the treat-to-target paradigm already validated in rheumatoid arthritis and gout in this knowledge base.
sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.reason_why: SLE activity and cumulative glucocorticoid exposure are the two dominant drivers of irreversible organ damage; treating to a defined low-activity/remission target with steroid-sparing agents interrupts both drivers simultaneously instead of only firefighting flares.
sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.important_caveat: This is a strategy, not a drug; it only works if the individual drugs below are actually used early and escalated on a schedule, not reactively after damage has already accrued.
sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.real_working_solution: Every new SLE patient should be started on hydroxychloroquine at diagnosis, glucocorticoids tapered as fast as disease activity allows toward <=5 mg/day, and an immunosuppressant or biologic added early enough to make that taper possible, with disease activity and damage indices tracked at every visit against the DORIS/LLDAS targets.
sle_strategy_treat_to_target_eular2023.source: Fanouriakis A et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of systemic lupus erythematosus: 2023 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2024;83:15-29 (PMID 37827694); van Vollenhoven RF et al., 'DORIS definition of remission in SLE: final recommendations', Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:14-25

sle_hydroxychloroquine_foundational_ther.name: Hydroxychloroquine - The Real Foundational, Near-Universal SLE Therapy (LUMINA Survival Cohort, SLICC Discontinuation Cohort)
specific_drugs: Chloroquine phosphate (alternative where hydroxychloroquine is unavailable)
sle_hydroxychloroquine_foundational_ther.effectiveness: LUMINA, a multiethnic US inception cohort of 608 SLE patients with 61 deaths (Alarcon GS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2007;66:1168-1172, PMID 17389655): hydroxychloroquine use was associated with an unadjusted odds ratio for death of 0.128 (95% CI 0.054-0.301) and, after propensity-score adjustment for the factors that drive treatment decisions, an adjusted OR of 0.319 (95% CI 0.118-0.864) - roughly a two-thirds reduction in the odds of death that survived adjustment for confounding by indication. Separately, the SLICC inception cohort (Almeida-Brasil CC et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:370-378, PMID 34911705, n=1,460) showed that stopping the protective effect matters in the other direction: adjusted hazard ratio for first SLE flare was 1.20 (95% CI 1.04-1.38) after hydroxychloroquine dose reduction and 1.56 (95% CI 1.31-1.86) after complete discontinuation, versus patients who stayed on a maintenance dose.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_foundational_ther.reason_why: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in acidic endosomes and blocks Toll-like receptor 7/9 signalling in B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, cutting the type I interferon production that drives much of SLE's immune activation; it also has real antithrombotic and lipid-lowering effects that plausibly contribute to the survival benefit.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_foundational_ther.important_caveat: The survival and flare data are cohort/propensity-adjusted, not from a placebo-controlled mortality RCT (which would be considered unethical to run given the existing evidence), so residual confounding cannot be fully excluded even after adjustment. Retinal toxicity risk (below) requires lifelong monitoring.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_foundational_ther.real_working_solution: Start hydroxychloroquine in essentially every SLE patient at diagnosis and continue it indefinitely, including through quiescent periods and pregnancy, at a dose that respects the <=5 mg/kg real-body-weight retinal-safety ceiling; do not stop it during apparent remission, since discontinuation measurably raises flare risk in real cohort data.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_foundational_ther.source: Alarcon GS et al., 'Effect of hydroxychloroquine on the survival of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus: data from LUMINA', Ann Rheum Dis 2007;66:1168-1172 (PMID 17389655); Almeida-Brasil CC et al., 'Flares after hydroxychloroquine reduction or discontinuation: results from the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) inception cohort', Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:370-378 (PMID 34911705); Fanouriakis A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2024;83:15-29 (PMID 37827694)

sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.name: Hydroxychloroquine Retinal Toxicity - Real Risk Figures and the AAO 2016 Screening Protocol
sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.type: Mandatory safety monitoring protocol accompanying hydroxychloroquine therapy
specific_drugs: Hydroxychloroquine (dose ceiling and screening apply to this drug specifically)
sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.effectiveness: The American Academy of Ophthalmology's 2016 revised recommendations (Marmor MF et al., Ophthalmology 2016;123:1386-1394, PMID 26992838) set a maximum daily dose of <=5.0 mg/kg real body weight (real weight, not ideal weight, correlates best with risk) and state that at this dose the risk of retinopathy is under 1% within the first 5 years of use and under 2% at 10 years, rising to almost 20% after 20 years of continuous use. Baseline fundus examination is recommended at treatment start, with annual screening (spectral-domain OCT plus automated visual fields, with multifocal ERG or fundus autofluorescence in Asian patients who show an extramacular damage pattern) beginning after 5 years of use in average-risk patients.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.reason_why: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors over years; damage is dose- and duration-dependent and, once advanced, is irreversible, which is why the screening protocol is built around early detection at the pre-symptomatic stage.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.important_caveat: Renal impairment, concomitant tamoxifen use, pre-existing retinal/macular disease, and very long treatment duration all raise risk above these baseline figures and warrant closer monitoring.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.real_working_solution: Dose hydroxychloroquine to <=5 mg/kg real body weight from the start, obtain a baseline eye exam, and enter the patient into annual OCT/visual-field screening after 5 years so that any toxicity is caught before it becomes symptomatic and irreversible - this preserves the drug's large survival and flare-prevention benefit above while keeping the real retinal risk under 2% at 10 years.
sle_hydroxychloroquine_retinal_toxicity_.source: Marmor MF et al., 'Recommendations on Screening for Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy (2016 Revision)', Ophthalmology 2016;123:1386-1394 (PMID 26992838)

sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.name: Glucocorticoids - Real Flare/Induction Efficacy Weighed Against Real Dose-Dependent Organ Damage (Hopkins Lupus Cohort)
sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.type: Corticosteroid (induction bridge and, at low dose, maintenance)
specific_drugs: Methylprednisolone (IV pulse, for induction of severe/organ-threatening disease)
sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.effectiveness: Glucocorticoids remain the fastest real way to control an acute SLE flare and are pulsed intravenously (250-1,000 mg methylprednisolone for 1-3 days) at the start of lupus nephritis induction in essentially every regimen in this survey. Their long-term cost is equally real and quantified: in the Hopkins Lupus Cohort (Al Sawah S et al., Lupus Sci Med 2015;2:e000066, PMID 25861455), prednisone >=20 mg/day versus <7.5 mg/day carried a hazard ratio of 2.514 (p<0.001) for new organ damage, with dose-specific hazard ratios (>=7.5 mg/day vs <7.5 mg/day) of 2.41 for cataracts, 2.16 for osteoporotic fracture, and 1.54 for cardiovascular damage (all p<0.05); each additional 1 mg/day of prior prednisone dose was associated with a 2.8% increase in the risk of new organ damage.
sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.reason_why: Glucocorticoids act broadly and rapidly on genomic and non-genomic inflammatory pathways, which is why they control flares faster than any other drug here; the same broad action drives cataracts, bone loss, cardiovascular and metabolic damage, and infection risk when exposure is chronic and cumulative.
sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.important_caveat: The organ-damage data are dose-stratified cohort data, not a randomised dose-comparison trial, but the dose-response gradient (2.8% risk increase per additional 1 mg/day) is internally consistent and is the real basis for the EULAR 2023 <=5 mg/day maintenance target above.
sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.real_working_solution: Use glucocorticoids at induction dose only as long as needed to control the flare, then taper as fast as the disease allows toward <=5 mg/day maintenance (or zero) by adding an immunosuppressant or biologic early enough to make that taper possible, rather than accepting chronic moderate-dose steroid as the default maintenance state.
sle_glucocorticoids_minimal_dose_strateg.source: Al Sawah S et al., 'Effect of corticosteroid use by dose on the risk of developing organ damage over time in systemic lupus erythematosus', Lupus Sci Med 2015;2:e000066 (PMID 25861455); Fanouriakis A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2024;83:15-29 (PMID 37827694)

sle_immunosuppressant_methotrexate.name: Methotrexate - Real Steroid-Sparing Effect for Non-Renal, Non-CNS Articular/Cutaneous SLE
sle_immunosuppressant_methotrexate.effectiveness: Carneiro JR, Sato EI (double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, J Rheumatol 1999;26:1275-1279, PMID 10381042): 37 patients completed 6 months (18 methotrexate 15-20 mg/week, 19 placebo); at study end, active joint complaints persisted in only 1/18 (5.6%) methotrexate patients versus 16/19 (84.2%) placebo patients (p<0.001), active cutaneous lesions persisted in 3/18 (16.7%) versus 16/19 (84.2%, p<0.001), and a prednisone dose reduction was achieved in 13/18 (72.2%) methotrexate patients versus 1/19 (5.3%) placebo patients (p<0.001); mild side effects were commoner on methotrexate (70% vs 14%). In a larger double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (Fortin PR et al., Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1796-1804, PMID 19035431, n=86: 41 methotrexate, 45 placebo), methotrexate patients received on average 1.33 mg/day less prednisone during the trial than placebo patients at the same baseline dose - a 22% relative reduction in average daily steroid dose - with a small but significant improvement in the revised Systemic Lupus Activity Measure (mean difference 0.86 units).
sle_immunosuppressant_methotrexate.reason_why: Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent purine/pyrimidine synthesis and raises anti-inflammatory extracellular adenosine, dampening T-cell and synovial/cutaneous inflammatory activity at the low weekly doses used here.
sle_immunosuppressant_methotrexate.important_caveat: Neither trial enrolled patients with active lupus nephritis or CNS lupus, so this evidence applies only to musculoskeletal and cutaneous SLE manifestations. Methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped well before conception (see pregnancy entry).
sle_immunosuppressant_methotrexate.real_working_solution: Add methotrexate for SLE patients whose disease is dominated by arthritis and skin disease, specifically to let the prednisone dose come down, given with folic acid supplementation as in rheumatoid arthritis dosing practice; it is not a substitute for mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide/biologics once the kidney or central nervous system is involved.
sle_immunosuppressant_methotrexate.source: Carneiro JR, Sato EI, 'Double blind, randomized, placebo controlled clinical trial of methotrexate in systemic lupus erythematosus', J Rheumatol 1999;26:1275-1279 (PMID 10381042); Fortin PR et al., 'Steroid-sparing effects of methotrexate in systemic lupus erythematosus: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial', Arthritis Rheum 2008;59:1796-1804 (PMID 19035431)

sle_immunosuppressant_azathioprine.name: Azathioprine - Real Maintenance Immunosuppressant, Especially Where Pregnancy Compatibility Matters
sle_immunosuppressant_azathioprine.effectiveness: In the MAINTAIN Nephritis Trial (Houssiau FA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:2083-2089, n=105: 52 azathioprine, 52 mycophenolate mofetil, both after Euro-Lupus-style cyclophosphamide induction), renal flares occurred in 13/52 (25%) on azathioprine versus 10/52 (19%) on mycophenolate mofetil - i.e. 75% of azathioprine patients remained renal-flare-free, a difference from MMF that did not reach statistical significance; long-term follow-up (Tamirou F et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:526-531, PMID 25757867) confirmed no significant difference between the two agents in flares, death, or progression to end-stage renal disease over a median of about 8 years.
sle_immunosuppressant_azathioprine.reason_why: Azathioprine's active metabolite, 6-thioguanine nucleotide, is incorporated into DNA and blocks purine synthesis, suppressing proliferating lymphocytes; it is a weaker immunosuppressant than mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide but has a long real-world safety record, including in pregnancy.
sle_immunosuppressant_azathioprine.important_caveat: TPMT (and, increasingly, NUDT15) genotyping or phenotyping before starting is real, guideline-recommended practice to avoid severe, sometimes fatal myelosuppression in poor metabolisers.
sle_immunosuppressant_azathioprine.real_working_solution: Use azathioprine as a maintenance immunosuppressant after induction (renal or non-renal), particularly when a patient is planning pregnancy or is pregnant, since - unlike mycophenolate mofetil and cyclophosphamide - it is real, guideline-endorsed as compatible with continued use in pregnancy.
sle_immunosuppressant_azathioprine.source: Houssiau FA et al. (MAINTAIN), 'Azathioprine versus mycophenolate mofetil for long-term immunosuppression in lupus nephritis: results from the MAINTAIN Nephritis Trial', Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:2083-2089 (PMID 20833738); Tamirou F et al., 'Long-term follow-up of the MAINTAIN Nephritis Trial, comparing azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil as maintenance therapy of lupus nephritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:526-531 (PMID 25757867)

sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.name: Mycophenolate Mofetil - Real Induction and Maintenance Data for Lupus Nephritis (ALMS Trial)
sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.type: Conventional synthetic immunosuppressant (inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor)
sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.effectiveness: ALMS induction phase (Appel GB et al., J Am Soc Nephrol 2009;20:1103-1112, PMID 19369404, n=370, class III-V lupus nephritis): response at 24 weeks was achieved in 104/185 (56.2%) on mycophenolate mofetil versus 98/185 (53.0%) on intravenous cyclophosphamide, with no statistically significant difference between the two - i.e. mycophenolate mofetil performed as well as IV cyclophosphamide for induction while sparing gonadal-toxicity and infertility risk. ALMS maintenance phase (Dooley MA et al., N Engl J Med 2011;365:1886-1895, PMID 22087680, n=227: 116 mycophenolate mofetil, 111 azathioprine, all prior induction responders): treatment failure (renal flare, need for rescue therapy, or death) occurred in 19/116 (16.4%) on mycophenolate mofetil versus 36/111 (32.4%) on azathioprine (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.25-0.77, p=0.003) - i.e. 83.6% of mycophenolate-mofetil patients remained treatment-failure-free versus 67.6% on azathioprine.
sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.reason_why: Mycophenolate mofetil's active metabolite, mycophenolic acid, selectively and reversibly inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine synthesis that proliferating lymphocytes depend on much more than most other cell types, giving relatively lymphocyte-selective immunosuppression.
sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.important_caveat: A pre-specified ALMS subgroup analysis found mycophenolate mofetil less effective than IV cyclophosphamide for induction in patients of African or mixed African ancestry and in Hispanic patients, an important real equity caveat for individualising induction choice.
