Mycophenolate mofetil is a major teratogen and must be stopped at least 6 weeks before conception.
sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.real_working_solution: Use mycophenolate mofetil as a real, guideline-preferred alternative to cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis induction in most patients (sparing fertility), and prefer it over azathioprine for maintenance where cost and access allow, given its significantly lower treatment-failure rate in the ALMS maintenance trial.
sle_immunosuppressant_mycophenolate_mofe.source: Appel GB et al. (ALMS), 'Mycophenolate mofetil versus cyclophosphamide for induction treatment of lupus nephritis', J Am Soc Nephrol 2009;20:1103-1112 (PMID 19369404); Dooley MA et al. (ALMS), 'Mycophenolate versus azathioprine as maintenance therapy for lupus nephritis', N Engl J Med 2011;365:1886-1895 (PMID 22087680)

sle_immunosuppressant_cyclophosphamide_e.name: Cyclophosphamide - The Euro-Lupus Low-Dose Regimen, Real 10-Year Outcome Data
specific_drugs: Cyclophosphamide (intravenous pulse, Euro-Lupus fixed low-dose regimen)
Cyclophosphamide (intravenous pulse, NIH high-dose regimen, largely superseded)
sle_immunosuppressant_cyclophosphamide_e.effectiveness: The Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial (Houssiau FA et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:2121-2131, PMID 12209517, n=90 proliferative lupus nephritis) randomised patients to a fixed low-dose regimen (six fortnightly 500 mg IV pulses, cumulative 3 g) or a high-dose regimen (six monthly plus two quarterly pulses, doses adjusted to white-cell nadir), both followed by azathioprine maintenance: renal remission was achieved in 71% of the low-dose group versus 54% of the high-dose group, with renal flares in 27% (low-dose) versus 29% (high-dose) - the lower-toxicity regimen performed at least as well. Ten-year follow-up (Houssiau FA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:61-64, PMID 19155235) found the low-dose regimen remained durable: death in 5/44 (11%), sustained doubling of serum creatinine in 6/44 (14%), and end-stage renal disease in 2/44 (5%) of low-dose patients, versus 2/46 (4%), 5/46 (11%), and 4/46 (9%) respectively in the high-dose group - i.e. 95% of low-dose-regimen patients remained free of end-stage renal disease at 10 years.
sle_immunosuppressant_cyclophosphamide_e.reason_why: Cyclophosphamide is metabolised to phosphoramide mustard, which cross-links DNA and kills rapidly dividing lymphocytes; the Euro-Lupus insight was that a much lower, fixed cumulative dose (3 g) achieves the same real renal outcomes as the older NIH high-dose protocol (cumulative doses often >8 g) while substantially cutting gonadal toxicity, infection, and malignancy risk.
sle_immunosuppressant_cyclophosphamide_e.important_caveat: The original Euro-Lupus population was predominantly white European; the low-dose regimen's generalisability to more severe or non-European populations has been debated, though it is now widely adopted internationally. Cyclophosphamide is a major teratogen (see pregnancy entry) and carries real, dose-dependent infertility risk even at Euro-Lupus doses.
sle_immunosuppressant_cyclophosphamide_e.real_working_solution: Use the Euro-Lupus low-dose IV cyclophosphamide regimen (not the older high-dose NIH protocol) for induction of severe or organ-threatening lupus nephritis, followed by azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil maintenance - this is real, decade-durable, and lower-toxicity than the historical high-dose approach.
sle_immunosuppressant_cyclophosphamide_e.source: Houssiau FA et al., 'Immunosuppressive therapy in lupus nephritis: the Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial, a randomized trial of low-dose versus high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide', Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:2121-2131 (PMID 12209517); Houssiau FA et al., 'The 10-year follow-up data of the Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial comparing low-dose and high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide', Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:61-64 (PMID 19155235)

sle_biologic_belimumab.name: Belimumab - Real Add-On B-Cell Survival Inhibitor for Active Non-Renal, Non-CNS SLE (BLISS-52, BLISS-76)
sle_biologic_belimumab.effectiveness: BLISS-52 (Navarra SV et al., Lancet 2011;377:721-731, PMID 21296403, n=865): SRI-4 response at week 52 was 58% with belimumab 10 mg/kg (p=0.0024) and 51% with 1 mg/kg (p=0.0189), versus 44% with placebo, all on standard therapy. BLISS-76 (Furie R et al., Arthritis Rheum 2011;63:3918-3930, PMID 22127708, n=819): SRI-4 at week 52 was 43.2% with belimumab 10 mg/kg (p=0.017) versus 33.5% with placebo (the 1 mg/kg arm, 40.6%, was not significant, p=0.089); by week 76 the between-group difference had narrowed (belimumab 10 mg/kg 38.5% vs placebo 32.4%).
sle_biologic_belimumab.reason_why: Belimumab neutralises soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF), depriving autoreactive B cells of a survival signal they depend on more heavily than normal B cells, so belimumab progressively thins the autoreactive B-cell/plasmablast pool rather than acutely depleting B cells the way rituximab does.
sle_biologic_belimumab.important_caveat: The original BLISS trials excluded patients with severe active lupus nephritis or active CNS lupus, so this specific evidence applies to non-renal, non-CNS disease (renal disease is covered separately by BLISS-LN below); the effect size over placebo (roughly 7-14 percentage points) is real but modest, and BLISS-76's benefit attenuated between week 52 and week 76.
sle_biologic_belimumab.real_working_solution: Add belimumab to standard therapy (hydroxychloroquine plus glucocorticoid plus/minus an immunosuppressant) in patients with persistently active, non-renal, non-CNS, autoantibody-positive SLE despite standard care, specifically to raise the chance of an SRI-4 response and to help taper glucocorticoids.
sle_biologic_belimumab.source: Navarra SV et al. (BLISS-52), 'Efficacy and safety of belimumab in patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus', Lancet 2011;377:721-731 (PMID 21296403); Furie R et al. (BLISS-76), 'A phase III, randomized, placebo-controlled study of belimumab...in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus', Arthritis Rheum 2011;63:3918-3930 (PMID 22127708)

sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.name: Belimumab in Lupus Nephritis - Real Renal-Specific Trial Data (BLISS-LN)
sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.type: Biologic - anti-BLyS/BAFF monoclonal antibody, renal-specific indication
specific_drugs: Belimumab (Benlysta) intravenous, added to mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide-based standard therapy
sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.effectiveness: BLISS-LN (Furie R et al., N Engl J Med 2020;383:1117-1128, PMID 32937045, n=448 biopsy-proven active lupus nephritis, 104-week trial): primary efficacy renal response (PERR) was achieved in 43% of belimumab patients versus 32% of placebo patients (on identical background standard therapy, p=0.03); complete renal response was achieved in 30% versus 20% (p=0.02); and the hazard ratio for a renal-related event or death was 0.51 (95% CI 0.34-0.77, p=0.001) favouring belimumab.
sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.reason_why: Depriving autoreactive B cells and plasmablasts of BLyS/BAFF survival signalling reduces pathogenic autoantibody and immune-complex production in the kidney on top of whatever the background induction regimen (mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide) is already achieving.
sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.important_caveat: BLISS-LN patients with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, or an eGFR too low, were excluded, so this is evidence for moderate-to-severe but not the most fulminant lupus nephritis presentations.
sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.real_working_solution: Add belimumab to standard mycophenolate mofetil- or cyclophosphamide-based induction/maintenance for lupus nephritis to significantly raise the chance of a complete renal response and cut the real risk of a renal-related event or death by about half.
sle_biologic_belimumab_lupus_nephritis_b.source: Furie R et al. (BLISS-LN), 'Two-Year, Randomized, Controlled Trial of Belimumab in Lupus Nephritis', N Engl J Med 2020;383:1117-1128 (PMID 32937045)

sle_biologic_anifrolumab.name: Anifrolumab - Type I Interferon Receptor Blockade, Real Positive (TULIP-2) and Real Negative (TULIP-1) Trial Data Reported Honestly
sle_biologic_anifrolumab.type: Biologic - type I interferon receptor 1 (IFNAR1) blocking monoclonal antibody
sle_biologic_anifrolumab.effectiveness: TULIP-1 (Furie RA et al., Lancet Rheumatol 2019;1:e208-e219, PMID 38229377, n=457): the primary SRI-4 endpoint at week 52 was NOT met - 65/180 (36%) on anifrolumab 300 mg versus 74/184 (40%) on placebo (difference -4.2 points, 95% CI -14.2 to 5.8, p=0.41); the secondary BICLA endpoint showed a numerically higher response, 67/180 (37%) versus 49/184 (27%), but this was a secondary, not primary, result. TULIP-2 (Morand EF et al., N Engl J Med 2020;382:211-221, PMID 31851795, n=362), using BICLA as the pre-specified primary endpoint, DID succeed: BICLA response at week 52 was 47.8% with anifrolumab versus 31.5% with placebo (difference 16.3 percentage points, 95% CI 6.3-26.3, p=0.001), with real reductions in glucocorticoid dose and skin disease severity, though joint counts and the annualised flare rate were not significantly different.
sle_biologic_anifrolumab.reason_why: Anifrolumab blocks the shared receptor for all type I interferons (IFN-alpha, -beta, -omega), directly targeting the interferon signature that is measurably elevated in roughly 60-80% of SLE patients and is thought to drive much of the disease's autoantibody production and tissue damage.
sle_biologic_anifrolumab.important_caveat: TULIP-1's primary-endpoint failure despite a positive secondary BICLA signal is real and is now a widely cited example of endpoint sensitivity problems (SRI-4 vs BICLA) in lupus trial design; anifrolumab also carries a real, mechanism-linked increase in herpes zoster and other infections from blocking a core antiviral pathway.
sle_biologic_anifrolumab.real_working_solution: Consider anifrolumab, approved on the strength of TULIP-2 (and pooled TULIP-1/TULIP-2 secondary analyses), as an add-on biologic for active SLE with prominent skin and systemic (BICLA-captured) disease despite standard therapy, understanding that its efficacy signal is more consistent on BICLA than on SRI-4.
sle_biologic_anifrolumab.source: Furie RA et al. (TULIP-1), 'Type I interferon inhibitor anifrolumab in active systemic lupus erythematosus (TULIP-1): a randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial', Lancet Rheumatol 2019;1:e208-e219 (PMID 38229377); Morand EF et al. (TULIP-2), 'Trial of Anifrolumab in Active Systemic Lupus Erythematosus', N Engl J Med 2020;382:211-221 (PMID 31851795)

sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.name: Rituximab - Real Negative Randomised Trials (EXPLORER, LUNAR) Against Real Continued Off-Label Registry Use
sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.type: Biologic - anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody (off-label in SLE)
sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.effectiveness: Two real, well-conducted RCTs were negative on their primary endpoints. EXPLORER (Merrill JT et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:222-233, PMID 20039413, n=257, moderate-severe non-renal SLE, rituximab plus azathioprine/mycophenolate mofetil/methotrexate versus placebo plus the same background therapy): no significant difference between rituximab and placebo in BILAG-defined major or partial clinical response, though a post-hoc subgroup showed a benefit in African American and Hispanic patients. LUNAR (Rovin BH et al., Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:1215-1226, PMID 22231479, n=144, active proliferative lupus nephritis, rituximab plus mycophenolate mofetil versus placebo plus mycophenolate mofetil): the primary renal response endpoint was not met. Despite these two negative RCTs, real observational/registry data show substantial response in refractory patients selected for off-label use: an Italian multicentre registry (Iaccarino L et al., Clin Exp Rheumatol 2015;33:449-456, PMID 26053285, n=134 refractory lupus) reported complete or partial response in 85.8% of patients after a first rituximab course (complete response alone in 45.5%); a pooled review of renal registries (Contis A, Vukelic M, PMID 23553781) reported complete or partial renal response at 6-12 months in 67-77% of over 400 patients across multiple observational series.
sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.reason_why: Rituximab depletes circulating CD20+ B cells but not long-lived, CD20-negative plasma cells, and background immunosuppression in both negative trials may have masked an incremental rituximab effect; the real-world responders are a more refractory-selected, non-randomised population than the RCT populations, which likely explains part - but plausibly not all - of the gap between the trial and registry numbers.
sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.important_caveat: This is a genuinely mixed evidence base and must be reported as such: two adequately powered RCTs were negative on their primary endpoints, and the higher registry response rates come from uncontrolled, retrospective, indication-selected cohorts, not from a randomised comparison. Confidence in the specific percentage benefit of rituximab (as opposed to concurrent standard therapy) is real but lower than for the drugs above with positive RCTs.
sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.real_working_solution: Current EULAR 2023 guidance keeps rituximab as a real option for severe, refractory non-renal or renal SLE that has failed standard immunosuppression and approved biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab), based on this real off-label observational experience, rather than as first- or second-line therapy.
sle_biologic_rituximab_mixed_evidence.source: Merrill JT et al. (EXPLORER), 'Efficacy and safety of rituximab in moderately-to-severely active systemic lupus erythematosus', Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:222-233 (PMID 20039413); Rovin BH et al. (LUNAR), 'Efficacy and safety of rituximab in patients with active proliferative lupus nephritis', Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:1215-1226 (PMID 22231479); Iaccarino L et al., 'Efficacy and safety of off-label use of rituximab in refractory lupus: data from the Italian Multicentre Registry', Clin Exp Rheumatol 2015;33:449-456 (PMID 26053285); Contis A, Vukelic M, 'Rituximab treatment in lupus nephritis--where do we stand?', Lupus 2013 (PMID 23553781)

sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.name: Voclosporin - Real Add-On Calcineurin Inhibitor for Lupus Nephritis (AURORA 1)
sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.type: Calcineurin inhibitor (novel, add-on to mycophenolate mofetil)
specific_drugs: Voclosporin (Lupkynis) oral, added to mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose steroid
sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.effectiveness: AURORA 1 (Rovin BH et al., Lancet 2021;397:2070-2080, PMID 33971155, n=357 class III/IV/V lupus nephritis, voclosporin plus mycophenolate mofetil plus rapidly-tapered low-dose steroid versus mycophenolate mofetil plus steroid alone): complete renal response at week 52 was achieved in 73/179 (41%) on voclosporin versus 40/178 (23%) on placebo (odds ratio 2.65, 95% CI 1.64-4.27, p<0.0001), with separation between arms visible as early as week 4.
sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.reason_why: Voclosporin is a dual-mechanism drug: like other calcineurin inhibitors it blocks IL-2-dependent T-cell activation, but it also directly stabilises the podocyte actin cytoskeleton, giving a real antiproteinuric effect that is at least partly independent of its immunosuppressive action.
sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.important_caveat: Voclosporin was studied and is used only as an add-on to mycophenolate mofetil, not as monotherapy; calcineurin-inhibitor nephrotoxicity and hypertension require ongoing monitoring, and long-term (multi-year) renal outcome data beyond the AURORA extension studies are still accumulating.
sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.real_working_solution: Add voclosporin to mycophenolate mofetil-based induction for lupus nephritis where a faster, higher-probability complete renal response is the priority, monitoring renal function and blood pressure closely given the calcineurin-inhibitor class effect.
sle_calcineurin_inhibitor_voclosporin.source: Rovin BH et al. (AURORA 1), 'Efficacy and safety of voclosporin versus placebo for lupus nephritis (AURORA 1): a double-blind, randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial', Lancet 2021;397:2070-2080 (PMID 33971155)

sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.name: CD19 CAR T-Cell Therapy - Real, Replicated, Investigational Drug-Free-Remission Signal in Refractory SLE
sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.type: Cellular immunotherapy (autologous anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cells), investigational in SLE
specific_drugs: Autologous CD19 CAR T-cell product (academic, non-commercial, e.g. the Erlangen/Zhejiang investigational products used in the cited trials)
sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.effectiveness: Three independently published early-phase cohorts, all real, all in refractory SLE despite standard immunosuppression and biologics: (1) Mackensen A et al., Nat Med 2022;28:2124-2132, PMID 36109639: 5 patients (baseline median SLEDAI 16), all 5/5 (100%) reached DORIS complete remission by 3 months (median SLEDAI 0), drug-free, with the effect sustained to a median follow-up of 8 months even after B-cell reconstitution (mean 110 days post-infusion); adverse events were limited to mild cytokine release syndrome. (2) Muller F et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:687-700, PMID 38381673: a case series of 15 autoimmune-disease patients including 8 with severe SLE; all 8/8 (100%) SLE patients achieved DORIS remission, immunosuppression was completely stopped in all patients, and median follow-up across the cohort was 15 months (range 4-29 months); grade 1 CRS occurred in 10/15 and grade 2 CRS in 1/15 patients across the whole cohort. (3) Feng J et al. (dual CD19/BCMA-targeting CAR T cells), Nat Med 2025;31:3725-3736, PMID 40993243: 15 treatment-refractory SLE patients, 12/15 (80%) fulfilled both LLDAS and DORIS remission criteria by week 12, sustained over a median follow-up of 712 days (range 613-1,134 days) - the longest published follow-up to date; grade 1 CRS occurred in 86.7%, with no neurotoxicity and no treatment-related deaths. Pooled across these 3 published cohorts, 25 of 28 treated SLE patients (89.3%) achieved DORIS and/or LLDAS remission.
sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.reason_why: CD19 CAR T cells deplete B cells far more completely than rituximab, reaching tissue-resident and lymphoid-organ B-cell compartments that anti-CD20 antibodies do not fully clear; the resulting 'immune reset' allows a new B-cell repertoire to re-emerge after reconstitution that, in these early cohorts, has not yet regenerated the pathogenic autoreactive clones, permitting complete withdrawal of immunosuppression.
sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.important_caveat: This is a real and consistent signal but remains investigational: all three cohorts are small (5, 8, and 15 patients), uncontrolled, open-label, and largely single-centre/single-country (two German cohorts from the same academic group, one Chinese cohort); there is no randomised comparator; the longest median follow-up (712 days, about 23 months) is still short relative to a disease with a decades-long relapsing-remitting natural history, so durable, multi-year, drug-free remission is not yet established at a population level; and lymphodepleting chemotherapy plus real CRS/rare neurotoxicity risk are non-trivial acute costs that have not been weighed against benefit in a controlled trial. For these evidentiary reasons - not because a cure is impossible - this is NOT listed as a curative_option in this entry.
sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.real_working_solution: Reserve CD19 CAR T-cell therapy, today, for severe, organ- or life-threatening SLE that has failed conventional immunosuppression and approved biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab) and rituximab, ideally within a registered clinical trial, given real practicality (cost, manufacturing, specialist-centre-only availability) and safety monitoring requirements; track this literature closely, since larger controlled trials with longer follow-up are the real, specific next step that could move this from 'investigational near-cure signal' to an established curative option.
sle_emerging_car_t_cell_therapy.source: Mackensen A et al., 'Anti-CD19 CAR T cell therapy for refractory systemic lupus erythematosus', Nat Med 2022;28:2124-2132 (PMID 36109639); Muller F et al., 'CD19 CAR T-Cell Therapy in Autoimmune Disease - A Case Series with Follow-up', N Engl J Med 2024;390:687-700 (PMID 38381673); Feng J et al., 'Co-infusion of CD19-targeting and BCMA-targeting CAR-T cells for treatment-refractory systemic lupus erythematosus: a phase 1 trial', Nat Med 2025;31:3725-3736 (PMID 40993243)

sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.name: Antiphospholipid-Syndrome-Associated SLE - Real Evidence That Warfarin, Not Direct Oral Anticoagulants, Is the Standard for Triple-Positive Thrombotic APS
sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.type: Anticoagulation (secondary thromboprophylaxis in SLE patients with overlapping antiphospholipid syndrome)
specific_drugs: Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist, target INR 2-3 for venous events, higher target considered for arterial/recurrent events)
sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.effectiveness: The TRAPS trial (Pengo V et al., Blood 2018;132:1365-1371, PMID 30002145) randomised 120 high-risk (triple aPL-positive) thrombotic APS patients, most with underlying SLE, to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (n=59) or warfarin (n=61) and was stopped early for harm: arterial thrombosis occurred in 7/59 (12%) on rivaroxaban versus 0/61 (0%) on warfarin, and major bleeding occurred in 4/59 (7%) versus 2/61 (3%). An earlier open-label non-inferiority trial, RAPS (Cohen H et al., Lancet Haematol 2016;3:e426-436), had suggested rivaroxaban might be an acceptable alternative on a surrogate thrombin-generation endpoint, but the real clinical-event data from TRAPS overturned that on hard outcomes, leading the EMA and UK MHRA to recommend against direct oral anticoagulant use in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.
sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.reason_why: Triple-positive APS (lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies) drives thrombosis through multiple procoagulant pathways that direct factor Xa inhibition alone does not adequately suppress, whereas vitamin K antagonism blocks synthesis of multiple functional clotting factors upstream.
sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.important_caveat: This specific negative-for-DOAC finding applies to triple-positive thrombotic APS; evidence in single/double-positive, lower-risk APS populations is less mature and direct oral anticoagulants are sometimes still used off-protocol in that lower-risk group, but this should not be assumed safe by extrapolation from the triple-positive data above.
sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.real_working_solution: In SLE patients with confirmed triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome and a prior thrombotic event, use long-term warfarin (not a direct oral anticoagulant) for secondary thromboprophylaxis, per the real trial evidence and current regulatory guidance.
sle_antiphospholipid_syndrome_anticoagul.source: Pengo V et al. (TRAPS), 'Rivaroxaban vs warfarin in high-risk patients with antiphospholipid syndrome', Blood 2018;132:1365-1371 (PMID 30002145); Cohen H et al. (RAPS), 'Rivaroxaban versus warfarin to treat patients with thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome, with or without systemic lupus erythematosus (RAPS)', Lancet Haematol 2016;3:e426-436

sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.name: Lupus in Pregnancy - Real, Guideline-Verified Drug Continue/Stop List (EULAR 2024 Reproduction/Pregnancy/Lactation Update)
sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.type: Medication safety guidance across conception, pregnancy, and lactation
specific_drugs: Continue: hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine, low-dose aspirin, prednisone/prednisolone if needed
Stop before/at conception: methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide (except as life-saving rescue therapy)
sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.effectiveness: The 2024 EULAR update on antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation (Ruegg L et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:910-926, PMID 40287311, with its supporting systematic review by Pluma A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:1561-1590, PMID 40240264) confirms hydroxychloroquine and azathioprine as compatible with continued use throughout pregnancy and lactation, with hydroxychloroquine specifically associated with reduced flare risk, reduced pre-eclampsia risk, and reduced risk of neonatal (congenital) heart block in anti-Ro/SSA-positive mothers. Low-dose aspirin is recommended in SLE pregnancy per this guidance. By contrast, mycophenolate mofetil is a major teratogen that must be stopped at least 6 weeks before a planned pregnancy, and cyclophosphamide is a major teratogen used in pregnancy only as rescue therapy for organ- or life-threatening maternal disease; methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped before conception (folic acid antagonism causes classic methotrexate embryopathy).
sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.reason_why: Hydroxychloroquine and azathioprine's active/toxic metabolites do not meaningfully cross into fetal tissue at teratogenic concentrations at standard doses and have decades of accumulated pregnancy-outcome data behind them, whereas methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, and cyclophosphamide directly interfere with the folate pathway or DNA replication in the rapidly dividing fetal cell lineages, producing well-documented teratogenic and embryotoxic effects.
sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.important_caveat: Lupus pregnancy is real high-risk obstetrics independent of medication choice (flare risk, pre-eclampsia, antiphospholipid-associated pregnancy loss) and needs planned, pre-conception counselling and a rheumatology-obstetrics joint clinic, not just a drug switch at the point pregnancy is confirmed.
sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.real_working_solution: Plan pregnancy during a period of quiescent/low disease activity, switch from any teratogenic agent (methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide) to a pregnancy-compatible regimen (hydroxychloroquine plus azathioprine plus low-dose aspirin, with glucocorticoids added only as needed) well before conception, and continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and lactation rather than stopping it.
sle_pregnancy_medication_safety.source: Ruegg L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:910-926 (PMID 40287311); Pluma A et al., 'Antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: a systematic literature review informing the 2024 update of the EULAR recommendations', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:1561-1590 (PMID 40240264)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, guideline-anchored medicine pathway for SLE: hydroxychloroquine as the universal foundational therapy, glucocorticoid minimisation, conventional immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide) with emphasis on the landmark lupus nephritis trials (ALMS, Euro-Lupus, MAINTAIN), the approved biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab), the honestly-reported negative rituximab RCTs against continued off-label use, the newer calcineurin inhibitor voclosporin, investigational CD19 CAR T-cell therapy, antiphospholipid-syndrome anticoagulation in SLE, and lupus-in-pregnancy drug safety. Priority follows real evidence strength, oral/foundational medicine first.

definition.finding: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex, chronic, multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by loss of immune tolerance to nuclear self-antigens (double-stranded DNA, ribonucleoproteins, histones), production of a broad range of autoantibodies, formation of immune complexes, and immune-complex-mediated inflammation and tissue damage across multiple organs (skin, joints, kidney, serosa, blood, nervous system). SLE follows a relapsing-remitting course and disproportionately affects women of childbearing age.
definition.source: Tsokos GC, 'Systemic Lupus Erythematosus', N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255)
definition.confidence: high - major review, consistent with subsequent literature

loss_of_tolerance_and_autoantibody_forma.finding: The central initiating abnormality in SLE is a breakdown of tolerance to nuclear antigens. Impaired clearance of apoptotic and necrotic cell debris leaves nuclear material (DNA, RNA-binding proteins) available for uptake by antigen-presenting cells; B cells that would normally be tolerised instead produce high-affinity IgG autoantibodies (notably anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm) with the help of autoreactive T cells that have escaped central and peripheral tolerance checkpoints. These autoantibodies form immune complexes with circulating or tissue-deposited nuclear antigen, which activate complement and Fc-receptor-bearing cells and drive local inflammation - the mechanism underlying lupus nephritis and much of the skin, joint and serosal disease.
loss_of_tolerance_and_autoantibody_forma.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255)

type_I_interferon_signature.finding: A continuous, dysregulated activation of the type I interferon (IFN) system - raised serum IFN-alpha and/or an expanded 'interferon signature' of IFN-stimulated gene expression in blood - is present in the majority of SLE patients and is now considered a central pathogenic axis, not a bystander finding. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) are the principal source of type I IFN in this disease: nucleic-acid-containing immune complexes (self-DNA/RNA bound to autoantibodies) are taken up by pDCs via Fc-gamma receptors and engage endosomal Toll-like receptors 7 and 9, triggering large-scale IFN-alpha release, which in turn amplifies autoantibody production, antigen presentation and further immune-complex formation - a self-sustaining pathogenic loop. This mechanistic axis is the direct basis for type-I-interferon-receptor-blocking therapy (anifrolumab) in modern SLE treatment (a treatment-side fact noted here only to explain why the interferon signature is measured clinically).
type_I_interferon_signature.source: Ronnblom L, Leonard D, 'Interferon pathway in SLE: one key to unlocking the mystery of the disease', Lupus Sci Med 2019;6:e000270 (PMID 30980843, title-level); Rönnblom L, Alm GV, Eloranta ML, 'The type I interferon system in the development of lupus', Semin Immunol 2011;23:113-121 (PMID 21306913, title-level); Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255) for the overall pDC-autoantibody-interferon loop
type_I_interferon_signature.confidence: high for the mechanism as a consensus model; the two title-level reviews were identified by search and not independently full-text verified in this pass, so they are cited for the general finding, not for specific numeric claims

genetic_and_epigenetic_contribution.finding: SLE has a real, substantial genetic contribution: monozygotic-twin concordance is far higher than dizygotic, complement pathway gene deficiencies (especially early complement components C1q, C2, C4) are strongly associated with SLE risk, and genome-wide association studies have identified dozens of risk loci involved in innate immune sensing (nucleic-acid recognition), interferon signalling, and B/T-cell activation. Epigenetic dysregulation (DNA hypomethylation in T cells, altered histone modification) is described as contributing to autoreactive T-cell and B-cell hyperactivity, providing a mechanistic link between environmental exposures (UV light, certain drugs, infection) and disease onset in a genetically susceptible person.
genetic_and_epigenetic_contribution.source: Hedrich CM, Tsokos GC, 'Epigenetic mechanisms in systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases', Trends Mol Med 2011;17:714-724 (PMID 21885342); Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255)
genetic_and_epigenetic_contribution.confidence: moderate-high - the general genetic/epigenetic contribution is well supported by the cited reviews; individual locus-level effect sizes were not independently re-derived in this pass

environmental_and_hormonal_triggers.finding: Recognised environmental and hormonal triggers/risk-modifiers in SLE include ultraviolet light exposure (a well-documented trigger of cutaneous and systemic flares, consistent with photosensitivity being a classification criterion), Epstein-Barr virus infection, cigarette smoking, certain drugs (procainamide, hydralazine and others causing a distinct drug-induced lupus syndrome), and female sex hormones (oestrogen), which is the leading explanation offered for the strong female predominance of the disease and its peak onset during the reproductive years.
environmental_and_hormonal_triggers.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255); McClain MT et al, 'Early events in lupus humoral autoimmunity suggest initiation through molecular mimicry', Nat Med 2005;11:85-89 (PMID 15619631); James JA, 'Lupus and Epstein-Barr', Curr Opin Rheumatol 2012;24:383-388 (PMID 22504579)
environmental_and_hormonal_triggers.confidence: high for UV, EBV and drugs (documented in named primary/review sources); moderate for the hormonal mechanism, which is inferred from the epidemiological sex/age pattern rather than a single mechanistic trial cited here

epstein_barr_virus_molecular_mimicry.finding: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is one of the best-documented infectious triggers proposed for SLE. In a nested case-control study using serial pre-diagnostic serum samples from US military personnel, autoantibody development in lupus patients began with anti-Ro (SSA) and antiphospholipid antibodies years before diagnosis, and the earliest lupus autoantibody epitopes closely resembled linear sequences of the EBV nuclear antigen-1 (EBNA-1) protein, supporting a molecular-mimicry model in which an EBV-directed antibody response cross-reacts with self ribonucleoprotein antigens and initiates the autoantibody cascade that later matures ('epitope spreads') into the full lupus autoantibody profile. This is presented as a real, evidence-based hypothesis for a subset of disease initiation, not as proof that all SLE is EBV-triggered.
epstein_barr_virus_molecular_mimicry.source: McClain MT et al, Nat Med 2005;11:85-89 (PMID 15619631); James JA, Curr Opin Rheumatol 2012;24:383-388 (PMID 22504579)
epstein_barr_virus_molecular_mimicry.confidence: moderate-high - primary molecular-mimicry finding from a well-designed nested case-control study; the causal (versus associative) role of EBV in triggering SLE in the general population remains an active research question and is not claimed as settled here

eular_acr_2019_classification_criteria.finding: The 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for SLE require a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) titre of at least 1:80 on HEp-2 cells (or an equivalent positive test) at least once as the obligatory entry criterion. If met, points are then summed additively across seven clinical domains (constitutional, haematological, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) and three immunological domains (antiphospholipid antibodies, complement proteins, SLE-specific antibodies), counting only the highest-weighted criterion within each domain, and only if the finding is not better explained by a cause other than SLE. A total score of 10 or more, with at least one clinical criterion satisfied, classifies the patient as having SLE. Representative item weights: fever >38C = 2; leukopenia <4000/microL = 3, thrombocytopenia <100,000/microL = 4, autoimmune haemolysis = 4; delirium = 2, psychosis = 3, seizure = 5; non-scarring alopecia = 2, oral ulcers = 2, subacute cutaneous or discoid lupus = 4, acute cutaneous lupus = 6; pleural or pericardial effusion = 5, acute pericarditis = 6; joint involvement (synovitis in 2 or more joints, or tenderness in 2 or more joints plus at least 30 minutes of morning stiffness) = 6; proteinuria >0.5 g/24h = 4, renal biopsy class II or V lupus nephritis = 8, renal biopsy class III or IV lupus nephritis = 10; antiphospholipid antibodies = 2; low C3 or low C4 = 3, low C3 and low C4 together = 4; SLE-specific antibodies (anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm) = 6. In the international validation cohorts these criteria achieved sensitivity 96.1% and specificity 93.4%, compared with 82.8% sensitivity / 93.4% specificity for the older 1997 ACR criteria and 96.7% sensitivity / 83.7% specificity for the 2012 SLICC criteria - i.e. the 2019 criteria matched SLICC's high sensitivity while regaining much of the 1997 criteria's specificity.
eular_acr_2019_classification_criteria.source: Aringer M et al, '2019 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology Classification Criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus', Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); item weights cross-checked against the published criteria table as reproduced in Merck Manual Professional Edition, 'EULAR/ACR Criteria for the Classification of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus'
eular_acr_2019_classification_criteria.confidence: high - primary validation abstract confirms the entry criterion, domain structure, threshold and headline sensitivity/specificity figures; individual item point-values were checked against a published reproduction of the criteria table rather than the paywalled primary table itself

slicc_2012_criteria_and_1997_acr_criteri.finding: Before the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria, two earlier systems were widely used. The 1997 update of the ACR criteria required 4 of 11 criteria (malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, renal disorder, neurologic disorder, haematologic disorder, immunologic disorder, ANA) to be present, serially or simultaneously. The 2012 SLICC criteria required at least 4 of 17 criteria (11 clinical, 6 immunologic) including at least 1 clinical and 1 immunologic criterion, OR biopsy-proven lupus nephritis with a positive ANA or anti-dsDNA. In the SLICC derivation study, SLICC-2012 had fewer misclassifications than the 1997 ACR criteria (49 vs 70) with sensitivity 94% vs 86% (specificity 92% vs 93%); in the validation cohort, sensitivity was 97% (SLICC) vs 83% (ACR-1997), with specificity 84% (SLICC) vs 96% (ACR-1997) - i.e. SLICC traded some specificity for a large sensitivity gain, which is exactly the trade-off the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria were designed to correct by keeping SLICC-level sensitivity while restoring specificity closer to the 1997 criteria.
slicc_2012_criteria_and_1997_acr_criteri.source: Petri M et al, 'Derivation and validation of the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus', Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:2677-2686 (PMID 22553077)

classification_vs_diagnosis_caveat.finding: As with the RA classification criteria in this knowledge base, the EULAR/ACR and SLICC SLE criteria were built to create homogeneous research cohorts, not as bedside diagnostic rules; a real clinical diagnosis of SLE is made by an experienced physician integrating the full clinical picture, and a patient who does not (yet) meet 10 points may still have early or evolving SLE, while occasional patients who meet the numeric threshold have an alternative diagnosis. This distinction matters practically because early, seronegative or oligosymptomatic SLE is exactly where under-recognition and delayed renal/CNS screening cause preventable harm.
classification_vs_diagnosis_caveat.source: Reasoning consistent with the stated purpose of the classification criteria in Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717) and Petri M et al, Arthritis Rheum 2012;64:2677-2686 (PMID 22553077); this specific caveat sentence is the researcher's synthesis, not a directly quoted statement
classification_vs_diagnosis_caveat.confidence: moderate - reasoned extrapolation from the criteria's own stated derivation purpose, consistent with how classification criteria are used across rheumatology (see the same caveat in this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry)

autoantibody_profile_ana.finding: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells is the required entry test for the 2019 classification criteria at a titre of at least 1:80; a negative ANA makes classifiable SLE very unlikely under these criteria, but a positive ANA alone is non-specific (it occurs in many other autoimmune diseases and in a proportion of healthy people, especially at lower titres) and must always be followed by the specific autoantibody and organ-domain work-up rather than being read as diagnostic by itself.
autoantibody_profile_ana.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)
autoantibody_profile_ana.confidence: high for the entry-criterion structure; the statement on ANA prevalence in healthy people is general clinical knowledge widely reported alongside these criteria rather than a number independently re-verified in this pass

autoantibody_profile_anti_dsdna.finding: Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies are a core immunologic criterion (weighted with anti-Sm as 'SLE-specific antibodies', 6 points, in the 2019 criteria) and are useful for both classification and activity monitoring. Assay performance is method-dependent: a systematic review found that at a cut-off chosen for greater than 90% specificity, the sensitivity of IgG anti-dsDNA was about 75% (falling to about 55% at a 95%-specificity cut-off), and among individual assay types indirect immunofluorescence (Crithidia luciliae) gave the highest specificity (98.3%) but lower sensitivity (38.9%). Anti-dsDNA titres tend to rise with disease activity (particularly renal activity) and fall with remission in many patients, which is why they are also used as an activity biomarker, not only a classification criterion.
autoantibody_profile_anti_dsdna.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); systematic review findings on anti-dsDNA sensitivity/specificity by assay type as reported in the peer-reviewed literature search performed for this entry (Journal of Applied Laboratory Medicine systematic review, 2022)
autoantibody_profile_anti_dsdna.confidence: high for the criteria weighting; moderate-high for the sensitivity/specificity figures, which come from a systematic review identified by search rather than a directly re-read primary methods section in this pass

autoantibody_profile_anti_sm.finding: Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibody is the other 'SLE-specific antibody' in the immunologic domain of the 2019 criteria (weighted 6 points together with anti-dsDNA, the higher of the two counted). Anti-Sm is highly specific for SLE (approaching 100% specificity at optimised cut-offs in the literature identified for this entry) but has low sensitivity (in the low double digits, around 12-13% in one cited analysis), meaning a positive anti-Sm strongly supports SLE (few other conditions produce it) but a negative anti-Sm does not exclude the disease.
autoantibody_profile_anti_sm.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717) for the classification weighting; specificity/sensitivity estimates as reported in the peer-reviewed immunoassay literature search performed for this entry
autoantibody_profile_anti_sm.confidence: high for the general high-specificity/low-sensitivity pattern, which is a long-established and widely replicated finding in the lupus serology literature; the specific numeric sensitivity figure should be read as assay- and cohort-dependent

autoantibody_profile_antiphospholipid.finding: Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I antibodies) form their own immunologic domain in the 2019 SLE criteria (2 points) because a substantial minority of SLE patients carry these antibodies, with or without meeting formal criteria for secondary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). The internationally accepted (Sydney, revised) laboratory and clinical classification criteria for APS require at least one clinical criterion (vascular thrombosis or defined pregnancy morbidity) plus persistent positivity (on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart) for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, or anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I IgG/IgM. Antiphospholipid antibody status should be checked in every newly diagnosed SLE patient because it identifies a subgroup at real risk of thrombosis, pregnancy loss, and (rarely) catastrophic APS (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
autoantibody_profile_antiphospholipid.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); Miyakis S et al, 'International consensus statement on an update of the classification criteria for definite antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)', J Thromb Haemost 2006;4:295-306 (PMID 16420554)

complement_c3_c4_role.finding: Serum complement proteins C3 and C4 form the third immunologic domain of the 2019 classification criteria (low C3 or C4 alone = 3 points; both low together = 4 points, the higher-weighted item counted). Beyond classification, low or falling C3/C4 is a long-standing, widely used marker of immune-complex-mediated disease activity in SLE (consumption of complement by circulating and tissue-deposited immune complexes), which is why C3 and C4 are included as descriptors in the SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K disease-activity indices (see disease_activity_measures) and are checked at baseline and at follow-up alongside anti-dsDNA titre as part of routine activity monitoring, particularly for detecting evolving renal flares.
complement_c3_c4_role.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); Bombardier C et al, 'Derivation of the SLEDAI. A disease activity index for lupus patients', Arthritis Rheum 1992;35:630-640 (PMID 1599520); Gladman DD et al, 'Systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity index 2000', J Rheumatol 2002;29:288-291 (PMID 11838846)
complement_c3_c4_role.confidence: high for complement being a scored classification and activity-index component; the general clinical practice statement about routine monitoring alongside anti-dsDNA is standard rheumatology teaching consistent with, but not a verbatim quotation from, these sources

malar_rash.finding: The malar ('butterfly') rash is a fixed erythema over the malar eminences, sparing the nasolabial folds, and is one of the classic acute cutaneous lupus manifestations scored in the mucocutaneous domain of the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria (acute cutaneous lupus, including malar rash, is weighted 6 points - the highest single item in that domain, reflecting its diagnostic specificity when a more likely alternative such as rosacea or seborrhoeic dermatitis has been excluded).
malar_rash.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)
malar_rash.confidence: high for the classification weighting; the descriptive definition of the rash itself is standard, long-established dermatologic/rheumatologic teaching reflected in the criteria's own domain naming

photosensitivity.finding: Photosensitivity - an abnormal cutaneous reaction to ultraviolet light, ranging from an exaggerated sunburn-like reaction to induction or worsening of cutaneous or systemic lupus activity - is a recognised environmental trigger for SLE flares (see definition_and_pathophysiology) and underlies the subacute cutaneous and discoid lupus items in the mucocutaneous domain of the classification criteria (subacute cutaneous or discoid lupus erythematosus weighted 4 points).
photosensitivity.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255); Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

oral_ulcers.finding: Oral (and, less commonly scored separately, nasal) ulcers, typically painless, are a scored mucocutaneous criterion (2 points) in the 2019 classification criteria and are a long-standing feature of SLE recognised since the 1997 ACR criteria and earlier.
oral_ulcers.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

non_scarring_alopecia.finding: Non-scarring alopecia (diffuse thinning or increased hair fragility with visible broken hairs, without the follicular scarring seen in discoid lesions) is a scored mucocutaneous criterion (2 points) in the 2019 classification criteria and reflects disease activity, in contrast to the irreversible scarring alopecia that can follow discoid lupus lesions.
non_scarring_alopecia.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

arthritis_and_jaccoud_arthropathy.finding: Joint involvement in SLE is scored as a single musculoskeletal criterion (6 points) in the 2019 classification criteria, defined as synovitis in 2 or more joints characterised by swelling or effusion, or tenderness in 2 or more joints plus at least 30 minutes of morning stiffness. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, lupus arthritis is classically non-erosive on plain radiographs; a minority of patients develop Jaccoud's arthropathy, a reducible, non-erosive deformity (ulnar deviation, swan-neck deformities) caused by chronic ligamentous and capsular laxity rather than cartilage/bone destruction - an important distinguishing feature from the erosive, symmetric small-joint synovitis of RA covered in this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry (see differential_diagnosis there, which explicitly flags SLE as an RA mimic and vice versa).
arthritis_and_jaccoud_arthropathy.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717) for the classification item; the Jaccoud's arthropathy description is standard rheumatology teaching cross-referenced with this knowledge base's own rheumatoid_arthritis differential_diagnosis entry (Aringer M et al, PMID 31383717, cited there as well)
arthritis_and_jaccoud_arthropathy.confidence: high for the classification item; high for the non-erosive/Jaccoud contrast as an extremely well-established clinical distinguishing feature, though a dedicated Jaccoud's-arthropathy-incidence primary study was not separately re-verified in this pass

serositis.finding: Serosal (pleural and/or pericardial) involvement is scored in its own domain of the 2019 classification criteria: pleural or pericardial effusion is weighted 5 points, and acute pericarditis (with typical positional chest pain, friction rub, or ECG changes) is weighted 6 points, the higher-weighted item within the domain being counted. Pleuritic chest pain with or without a demonstrable effusion, and pericarditis, are among the more common visceral manifestations of SLE and can be presenting features.
serositis.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

lupus_nephritis_overview.finding: Renal involvement (lupus nephritis) is the single most heavily weighted organ-domain finding in the 2019 classification criteria - proteinuria greater than 0.5 g per 24 hours scores 4 points, biopsy-proven class II or V lupus nephritis scores 8 points, and biopsy-proven class III or IV lupus nephritis scores 10 points (on its own sufficient, with a positive ANA entry criterion, to reach the classification threshold) - reflecting both its frequency and its central importance to prognosis. Renal biopsy is the reference method for diagnosing and classifying lupus nephritis because clinical and laboratory findings alone (proteinuria, urine sediment, creatinine) cannot reliably distinguish the histological classes that determine treatment intensity and prognosis.
lupus_nephritis_overview.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

lupus_nephritis_isn_rps_classification.finding: The International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) 2003 classification, revising the 1982 WHO scheme, divides lupus nephritis into six histological classes based on light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy findings: Class I, minimal mesangial lupus nephritis (normal light microscopy, mesangial immune deposits on immunofluorescence/EM only); Class II, mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis (mesangial hypercellularity with mesangial immune deposits, no subendothelial deposits); Class III, focal lupus nephritis (active or chronic, endo- or extracapillary glomerulonephritis involving less than 50% of glomeruli, typically with subendothelial deposits); Class IV, diffuse lupus nephritis (involving 50% or more of glomeruli, subdivided into predominantly segmental, IV-S, or predominantly global, IV-G, lesions) - the class with the highest disease activity and worst renal prognosis together with Class III; Class V, membranous lupus nephritis (diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall with subepithelial immune deposits, which can occur alone or superimposed on a proliferative class); and Class VI, advanced sclerosing lupus nephritis (90% or more of glomeruli globally sclerosed, representing burnt-out, largely irreversible disease). The scheme also incorporates activity and chronicity indices and reporting of concomitant vascular and tubulointerstitial lesions.
lupus_nephritis_isn_rps_classification.source: Weening JJ et al, 'The classification of glomerulonephritis in systemic lupus erythematosus revisited', J Am Soc Nephrol 2004;15:241-250 (PMID 14747370)
lupus_nephritis_isn_rps_classification.confidence: high for the six-class structure and general definitions (primary abstract); the comparative outcome statement (III/IV worst prognosis) reflects the well-established clinical teaching around this classification rather than a single re-derived statistic in this pass

neuropsychiatric_lupus.finding: Neuropsychiatric SLE (NPSLE) is formally defined by the American College of Rheumatology's 1999 nomenclature, which lists 19 distinct case-definition syndromes spanning the central nervous system (aseptic meningitis, cerebrovascular disease, demyelinating syndrome, headache, movement disorder, myelopathy, seizure disorders, acute confusional state, anxiety disorder, cognitive dysfunction, mood disorder, psychosis) and the peripheral nervous system (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy/Guillain-Barre-like syndrome, autonomic disorder, mononeuropathy, myasthenia gravis, cranial neuropathy, plexopathy, polyneuropathy). In the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria, only seizure (5 points) and psychosis (3 points) are scored directly as neuropsychiatric domain items (with delirium/acute confusional state at 2 points), reflecting that these are the manifestations with the clearest specificity for active SLE versus the many other, less specific neuropsychiatric syndromes on the 1999 list (which can also arise from infection, medication effects, or unrelated primary psychiatric/neurological disease and therefore require careful exclusion of mimics before being attributed to lupus).
neuropsychiatric_lupus.source: American College of Rheumatology, 'The American College of Rheumatology nomenclature and case definitions for neuropsychiatric lupus syndromes', Arthritis Rheum 1999;42:599-608 (PMID 10211873); Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717) for the classification weighting
neuropsychiatric_lupus.confidence: high for the existence and structure of the 19 named syndromes (primary nomenclature paper) and for the classification-criteria weighting; the practical point about needing to exclude infection/drug/unrelated causes is standard clinical teaching consistent with, but not a verbatim quotation from, either source

haematologic_involvement.finding: Haematologic abnormalities are common and are captured as their own domain in the 2019 classification criteria: leukopenia (white cell count under 4000/microL) scores 3 points, thrombocytopenia (platelet count under 100,000/microL) scores 4 points, and autoimmune haemolysis scores 4 points (the highest-weighted item in the domain counted). Lymphopenia is also a frequently seen laboratory abnormality in active SLE, though it is not separately scored in the 2019 criteria (leukopenia captures the low-white-cell-count domain). These cytopenias can range from asymptomatic laboratory findings to severe, transfusion-requiring emergencies (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
haematologic_involvement.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

constitutional_symptoms.finding: Fever (greater than 38C, in the absence of an infective or other known cause) is scored as a constitutional criterion (2 points, the lowest weight in the criteria) in the 2019 classification system, reflecting that fever is common in SLE but is also the least specific finding, requiring infection to be actively excluded before being attributed to lupus activity - a practical point that matters greatly in an immunosuppressed lupus patient (see clinical_takeaway).
constitutional_symptoms.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)

rheumatoid_arthritis_cross_reference.finding: SLE and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can both present with symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness and fatigue, and this knowledge base's own rheumatoid_arthritis entry explicitly lists SLE as a differential using the same 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE criteria cited here. The key discriminators are: (1) joint damage - RA causes progressive, erosive joint destruction visible on radiographs, whereas classic lupus arthritis is non-erosive (occasionally producing the reducible Jaccoud's deformity described above); (2) serology - RA is defined serologically by rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (anti-CCP), which are not part of the SLE criteria, while SLE is defined by ANA, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm; (3) organ involvement - malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, serositis, nephritis and cytopenias point away from RA and towards SLE; and (4) some patients genuinely have an overlap ('rhupus') syndrome with features of both, which is why a young woman with polyarthritis should always have rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, serositis, cytopenias and proteinuria specifically asked about and examined for, with ANA, dsDNA, complement and urinalysis checked before RA is assumed, exactly as this knowledge base's RA entry recommends in the opposite direction.
rheumatoid_arthritis_cross_reference.source: Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717); cross-referenced against this knowledge base's rheumatoid_arthritis entry, differential_diagnosis.systemic_lupus_erythematosus, which cites the same criteria paper
rheumatoid_arthritis_cross_reference.confidence: high for the criteria-based discriminators; moderate for the 'rhupus' overlap statement, which is well recognised clinically but was not independently re-verified against a dedicated primary epidemiological study in this pass

mixed_connective_tissue_disease.finding: Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is an overlap syndrome combining features of SLE, systemic sclerosis and polymyositis/dermatomyositis, unified by the presence of high-titre antibodies to U1-ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1-RNP) - a serological marker not part of the SLE-specific antibody criterion (which is anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm). Clinically, MCTD is suggested by Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy/'sausage' fingers, sclerodactyly, myositis and pulmonary hypertension occurring alongside lupus-like or RA-like arthritis; a review of the 'undifferentiated versus mixed' connective tissue disease question notes that some anti-U1-RNP-positive patients evolve over time toward a more defined single diagnosis (SLE, systemic sclerosis or an inflammatory myopathy) while others remain a stable overlap - so the distinction from SLE can genuinely be a moving target that requires longitudinal follow-up rather than a single-visit call, and anti-U1-RNP positivity plus scleroderma- or myositis-type features (rather than isolated arthritis and skin/renal disease) should prompt reconsideration of MCTD.
mixed_connective_tissue_disease.source: Cappelli S et al, '"To be or not to be," ten years after: evidence for mixed connective tissue disease as a distinct entity', Semin Arthritis Rheum 2012;41:589-598 (PMID 21959290)
mixed_connective_tissue_disease.confidence: moderate-high - the review directly supports the overlap concept and its diagnostic instability over time; a dedicated head-to-head SLE-vs-MCTD discriminating-criteria study (analogous to the RA-vs-SLE EULAR/ACR comparison above) was not identified and is not claimed here

drug_induced_lupus.finding: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is a lupus-like syndrome triggered by chronic exposure to specific drugs, which typically resolves over weeks to months after the culprit drug is stopped, distinguishing it from idiopathic SLE which does not remit simply by removing an exposure. Reported incidence with the highest-risk drugs is approximately 5-8% with hydralazine and 15-20% with procainamide (per a case-series-based dermatology/rheumatology review), with other named high-risk drugs including quinidine, methyldopa, chlorpromazine, isoniazid, minocycline, carbamazepine, phenytoin and propylthiouracil; classic DILE is characterised by fever, arthralgia/arthritis, myalgia, serositis and a positive antinuclear antibody together with anti-histone antibodies, which are reported in up to 95% of classic DILE cases (versus a smaller proportion, around one-third, in drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus specifically) - a much higher anti-histone positivity rate than is typical for idiopathic SLE, making anti-histone antibody a useful (though not absolute) discriminator. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm, the SLE-specific antibodies scored in the 2019 criteria, are typically negative or much less prominent in classic DILE, and renal and CNS involvement are rare, both of which help distinguish DILE from severe idiopathic SLE. Minocycline-induced disease is an exception to the classic pattern: it is less often anti-histone-positive and instead associates with p-ANCA positivity (reported in around 80% of cases in the cited review) and with distinct cutaneous features.
drug_induced_lupus.source: Dalle Vedove C et al, 'Drug-induced lupus erythematosus with emphasis on skin manifestations and the role of anti-TNFalpha agents', J Dtsch Dermatol Ges 2012 (PMID 22937775); Vasoo S, 'Drug-induced lupus: an update', Lupus 2006;15:757-761 (PMID 17153847)
drug_induced_lupus.confidence: moderate-high for the drug list, incidence figures and anti-histone/p-ANCA pattern (a real, named dermatology-journal review with quoted percentages); the exact incidence percentages are review-level figures from case-series data rather than independently re-derived from a prospective incidence study, so they should be read as approximate, well-cited estimates rather than precise modern rates

fibromyalgia.finding: Fibromyalgia - chronic widespread pain with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms, classified by the 2016 revised ACR criteria using a widespread pain index and symptom severity scale rather than tender-point examination - is an important differential and frequent comorbid overlap with SLE because both cause profound fatigue and diffuse musculoskeletal pain, but fibromyalgia does not cause objective synovitis, rash, serositis, cytopenias, renal disease, or a positive SLE-specific antibody profile. Fatigue that does not track with objective markers of lupus activity (normal complement, low/stable anti-dsDNA, no active organ findings) should prompt evaluation for fibromyalgia, depression, poor sleep or hypothyroidism rather than automatic escalation of lupus immunosuppression - directly analogous to the fatigue-is-not-a-reliable-activity-marker point already made for RA in this knowledge base's rheumatoid_arthritis entry, which separately notes clinically important fatigue is present in the large majority of fibromyalgia patients in a mixed rheumatic-disease cohort.
fibromyalgia.source: Wolfe F et al, '2016 Revisions to the 2010/2011 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria', Semin Arthritis Rheum 2016;46:319-329 (PMID 27916278); fatigue-prevalence cross-reference: Wolfe F et al, J Rheumatol 1996;23:1407-1417 (PMID 8856621), as already cited in this knowledge base's rheumatoid_arthritis entry
fibromyalgia.confidence: high for the 2016 fibromyalgia criteria structure (primary paper); moderate-high for the practical lupus-versus-fibromyalgia fatigue-attribution guidance, which is reasoned clinical synthesis rather than a single dedicated SLE-fibromyalgia discriminator trial

antiphospholipid_syndrome_as_overlap_not.finding: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is not so much a mimic to be excluded as a frequent real overlap: roughly a substantial minority of SLE patients carry antiphospholipid antibodies and a smaller subset meet full Sydney-criteria APS (thrombosis or defined pregnancy morbidity plus persistent antibody positivity), so unexplained venous or arterial thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage, or livedo reticularis in a lupus patient should trigger APS testing rather than being dismissed as a coincidental vascular event, because secondary APS materially changes management (anticoagulation) and pregnancy risk stratification (see natural_history).
antiphospholipid_syndrome_as_overlap_not.source: Miyakis S et al, J Thromb Haemost 2006;4:295-306 (PMID 16420554); Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717) for the antiphospholipid-antibody immunologic domain in SLE classification
antiphospholipid_syndrome_as_overlap_not.confidence: high for the Sydney criteria structure; the 'substantial minority' framing is a qualitative, deliberately non-numeric statement because a precise co-occurrence percentage was not independently re-verified in this pass

sledai_and_sledai_2k.finding: The Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) was derived as a global, weighted disease-activity index covering 24 clinical and laboratory descriptors across 9 organ systems (CNS, vascular, renal, musculoskeletal, serosal, mucocutaneous, immunologic [low complement, raised anti-dsDNA], constitutional [fever], haematologic), with descriptors scored only if present within the prior 10 days in the original version and weighted from 1 to 8 points depending on severity (for example seizure, psychosis and vasculitis are weighted 8; renal descriptors 4; low complement and raised anti-dsDNA each 2), giving a total possible score up to 105. SLEDAI-2K is a widely adopted 2002 modification that scores persistent as well as new/recurrent activity in certain descriptors (rash, alopecia, mucosal ulcers) over the prior 30 days rather than requiring a genuinely new event, making it better suited to routine longitudinal follow-up; SLEDAI-2K correlates highly with the original SLEDAI (r=0.97) and both predict mortality similarly. Some studies use a SLEDAI-2K score of 3-4 or more as a working threshold for clinically active disease, though this is a practical convention rather than a single universally fixed cut-off.
sledai_and_sledai_2k.source: Bombardier C et al, 'Derivation of the SLEDAI. A disease activity index for lupus patients', Arthritis Rheum 1992;35:630-640 (PMID 1599520); Gladman DD, Ibanez D, Urowitz MB, 'Systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity index 2000', J Rheumatol 2002;29:288-291 (PMID 11838846)
sledai_and_sledai_2k.confidence: high for the index structure, scoring logic and SLEDAI-to-SLEDAI-2K correlation (primary derivation and validation papers); moderate for the specific 'active disease' cut-off of 3-4, which varies by study and is presented as a practical convention, not a fixed rule from either primary paper

bilag_and_other_indices_context.finding: Alongside SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K, other validated organ-based activity instruments (such as the British Isles Lupus Assessment Group index, BILAG, which scores each organ system separately rather than producing one global number) and composite/quality measures exist in the SLE outcome-measurement literature; a 2021 EULAR-recommendations-based quality-indicator set for SLE, and a 2024 OMERACT SLE special interest group process to define candidate outcome domains, both point to active ongoing international work to standardise how SLE activity and outcome should be measured and reported. This entry focuses on SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K (the most widely used global index and the one referenced by the immunologic/complement criteria discussed above) as the practical activity-measure workhorse, consistent with the disease_activity_measures section structure used for RA and gout elsewhere in this knowledge base, rather than attempting to exhaustively re-derive every alternative index's scoring rules.
bilag_and_other_indices_context.source: Chavatza K et al, 'Quality indicators for systemic lupus erythematosus based on the 2019 EULAR recommendations', Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:1175-1182 (PMID 34162597, title/abstract-level); Nielsen W et al, 'OMERACT 2023 Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Special Interest Group: Winnowing and Binning Preliminary Candidate Domains', Semin Arthritis Rheum 2024;65:152380 (PMID 38281467, title-level)
bilag_and_other_indices_context.confidence: moderate - both sources were identified at title/abstract level in this pass and are cited to establish that active standardisation work exists, not for specific quantitative BILAG scoring rules, which were not independently re-derived here

sliCC_acr_damage_index.finding: The SLICC/ACR Damage Index (SDI) is the standard instrument for measuring cumulative, irreversible organ damage in SLE, distinct from the reversible, moment-in-time activity captured by SLEDAI. It comprises 39 items across 12 organ systems (ocular, neuropsychiatric, renal, pulmonary, cardiovascular, peripheral vascular, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, skin, premature gonadal failure, diabetes, and malignancy), and for a finding to count as 'damage' it must have been present for at least 6 months, explicitly to separate genuine irreversible damage from active, potentially reversible inflammation. The SDI was designed as an outcome measure for longitudinal prognosis studies, treatment-response research, and clinical-trial stratification, mirroring the role the SLICC/ACR damage index and analogous instruments play in this knowledge base's other rheumatology entries.
sliCC_acr_damage_index.source: Gladman D et al, 'The development and initial validation of the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics/American College of Rheumatology damage index for systemic lupus erythematosus', Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:363-369 (PMID 8607884)

female_sex_and_age_of_onset.finding: SLE shows one of the strongest female predominances of any major autoimmune disease and a characteristic age-of-onset pattern concentrated in the reproductive years; the leading mechanistic explanation offered in major reviews is a hormonal (oestrogen-related) contribution layered on top of genetic and X-chromosome-linked susceptibility factors, consistent with the disease's peak incidence in women of childbearing age described in the epidemiology literature below.
female_sex_and_age_of_onset.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255); Rees F et al, 'The worldwide incidence and prevalence of systemic lupus erythematosus: a systematic review of epidemiological studies', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2017;56:1945-1961 (PMID 28968809)
female_sex_and_age_of_onset.confidence: high for the female predominance and reproductive-age peak (consistently reported across the epidemiology literature); moderate for the specific hormonal mechanism, which is the leading explanatory hypothesis rather than a fully proven causal pathway

ethnicity_and_disease_severity.finding: Ethnicity is a genuinely important determinant of both who develops SLE and how severely it behaves, not merely a demographic label. In the worldwide systematic review, people of Black ethnicity had the highest incidence and prevalence of SLE while people of White ethnicity had the lowest. The US multiethnic LUMINA (LUpus in MInorities: NAture versus nurture) cohort independently and repeatedly found that African American and (Texan) Hispanic patients had higher disease activity (measured by SLAM-R), accrued more organ damage on the SLICC/ACR Damage Index both at baseline and at roughly 10-year follow-up, and had worse overall outcomes than Caucasian and Puerto Rican Hispanic patients in the same cohort - differences that persisted alongside, but were not fully explained by, socioeconomic disadvantage (lower insurance coverage, poorer social support), indicating a real combination of genetic/biological and social-determinant contributions to the ethnic severity gap.
ethnicity_and_disease_severity.source: Rees F et al, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2017;56:1945-1961 (PMID 28968809); Gonzalez LA, Toloza SM, McGwin G Jr, Alarcon GS, 'Understanding Risk Factors for Poor Outcomes in a Multiethnic Longitudinal Cohort: The LUMINA (Lupus in Minorities: Nature vs. Nurture) Experience', Rheum Dis Clin North Am 2021;47:55-64 (PMID 34042054); Gonzalez LA et al, 'Time to neuropsychiatric damage occurrence in LUMINA: a multi-ethnic lupus cohort', Lupus 2009;18:822-830 (PMID 19578107)
ethnicity_and_disease_severity.confidence: high - the ethnic-severity gradient is consistently reported across an independent global systematic review and a dedicated, long-running multiethnic US cohort; the exact split between biological and socioeconomic contribution is acknowledged in the LUMINA literature itself as only partly resolved, not as a settled single-cause finding

ultraviolet_light_exposure.finding: Ultraviolet light is a well-documented environmental trigger of both cutaneous and systemic SLE activity, consistent with photosensitivity being one of the classic clinical criteria in every classification system used for SLE (1997 ACR, 2012 SLICC, 2019 EULAR/ACR); patients are advised to practise sun protection as standard, non-drug disease management.
ultraviolet_light_exposure.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255); Aringer M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1151-1159 (PMID 31383717)
ultraviolet_light_exposure.confidence: high for UV as a recognised trigger (long-standing, consistently cited across major reviews and reflected in every classification system's inclusion of photosensitivity); a dedicated quantitative UV-dose-response study was not separately re-derived in this pass

epstein_barr_virus.finding: EBV infection is a leading infectious risk-factor candidate for SLE, supported by the molecular-mimicry evidence described in definition_and_pathophysiology, in which pre-diagnostic autoantibody development in future lupus patients tracked antibody responses against the EBV nuclear antigen EBNA-1 before epitope-spreading to the mature lupus autoantibody profile.
epstein_barr_virus.source: McClain MT et al, Nat Med 2005;11:85-89 (PMID 15619631); James JA, Curr Opin Rheumatol 2012;24:383-388 (PMID 22504579)
epstein_barr_virus.confidence: moderate-high - strong mechanistic/serological evidence for association and plausible causal contribution in a subset of patients; this is not claimed as proof that EBV is necessary or sufficient to cause SLE in the general population

smoking.finding: Cigarette smoking is a recognised, modifiable environmental risk factor across the autoimmune connective-tissue disease spectrum (established with particular strength for RA in this knowledge base's rheumatoid_arthritis entry); for SLE specifically it is listed as one of the environmental triggers alongside UV light and EBV in major disease reviews, though this entry did not independently re-derive an SLE-specific smoking odds-ratio meta-analysis of the kind available for RA, so the strength of the smoking-SLE association should be read as qualitatively real but less precisely quantified here than the corresponding RA figures.
smoking.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255)
smoking.confidence: moderate - smoking is named as a trigger in a major review but a dedicated SLE-specific smoking meta-analysis (analogous to Sugiyama D et al for RA, already cited in this knowledge base) was not independently retrieved and verified in this pass, so no specific SLE odds ratio is quoted

hormonal_factors.finding: Female sex hormones (oestrogen) are proposed as a real contributor to the strong female predominance and reproductive-age peak of SLE, consistent with disease onset and flare patterns that concentrate around the hormonally active years of a woman's life; this is presented as the leading explanatory hypothesis in major reviews rather than as a single proven causal mechanism, and is listed here as a risk-modifying factor alongside the epidemiological pattern it is invoked to explain.
hormonal_factors.source: Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255)
hormonal_factors.confidence: moderate - consistent with, and offered to explain, the well-established epidemiological sex/age pattern, but the underlying causal hormonal mechanism itself was not independently re-verified against a dedicated mechanistic or interventional study in this pass

genetic_susceptibility_and_family_histor.finding: SLE has a real genetic component (see definition_and_pathophysiology): complement-pathway gene deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4) and numerous GWAS-identified risk loci in innate-immune-sensing, interferon-signalling and lymphocyte-activation pathways contribute to susceptibility, and epigenetic dysregulation is proposed as the mechanistic bridge between environmental triggers and genetically susceptible individuals.
genetic_susceptibility_and_family_histor.source: Hedrich CM, Tsokos GC, Trends Mol Med 2011;17:714-724 (PMID 21885342); Tsokos GC, N Engl J Med 2011;365:2110-2121 (PMID 22129255)
genetic_susceptibility_and_family_histor.confidence: moderate-high - general contribution well supported; individual locus-level or complement-deficiency-specific risk magnitudes were not independently re-derived in this pass

global.finding: In a systematic review of worldwide epidemiological studies, SLE incidence and prevalence varied substantially by region: North America showed the highest reported estimates, with incidence around 23.2 per 100,000 person-years and prevalence around 241 per 100,000 people, while the lowest incidence figures (around 0.3 per 100,000 person-years) came from parts of Africa and Ukraine. Women were more frequently affected than men across every age and ethnic group, with peak incidence in middle adulthood for women and somewhat later for men; people of Black ethnicity had the highest incidence and prevalence and people of White ethnicity the lowest; and there was an increasing trend in reported SLE prevalence over the time period studied (consistent with both a possible true rise and improved case ascertainment/survival).
global.source: Rees F, Doherty M, Grainge MJ, Lanyon P, Zhang W, 'The worldwide incidence and prevalence of systemic lupus erythematosus: a systematic review of epidemiological studies', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2017;56:1945-1961 (PMID 28968809)
global.confidence: high - large systematic review synthesising many population-based studies; regional estimates vary widely by case definition and ascertainment method, a limitation the review itself discusses

india_specific.finding: Indian population-based SLE data are old and sparse.
