dactylitis.source: Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746), citing Olivieri I et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:2964-2967 (PMID 12428238); Taylor W et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665-2673 (PMID 16871531); Altamirano De La Cruz AG et al., 'Arthritis Mutilans: A Devastating Manifestation of Psoriatic Disease Without Dactylitis', Cureus 2025;17:e88502 (PMID 40851710, PMCID PMC12368913)

enthesitis.finding: Enthesitis - inflammation at the insertion sites of tendons, ligaments, joint capsules and fascia into bone - is another hallmark PsA feature, found in approximately half of PsA patients, with pain and swelling at affected sites. Typical entheseal inflammation sites include the Achilles tendon insertion, the plantar fascia insertion at the calcaneus, the greater trochanter of the femur, the medial femoral condyles, and the epicondyles at the olecranon (elbow).
enthesitis.source: Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746), citing McGonagle DG, Helliwell P, Veale D, 'Enthesitis in Psoriatic Disease', Dermatology 2012;225:100-109 (PMID 23108016)

skin_and_nail_findings.finding: Nail involvement is much more common in PsA patients than in psoriasis patients without arthritis, and nail dystrophy is itself a scored CASPAR feature. Clinical nail changes described include pitting, transverse ridging, yellowish discoloration in onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages and, in severe cases, total nail destruction. In the Indian nail-psoriasis cohort described in diagnostic_framework, pitting (97.4%) and onycholysis (94.7%) were the commonest changes; in the Kashmir PsA cohort, nail involvement was present in 80% of patients, most commonly pitting (40%). Plaque-type psoriasis was the commonest cutaneous phenotype in the Kashmir PsA cohort (81.33%), with erythrodermic (6.66%) and pustular (5.33%) psoriasis less frequent.
skin_and_nail_findings.source: Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746), citing Edwards F, De Berker D, 'Nail psoriasis: Clinical presentation and best practice recommendations', Drugs 2009;69:2351-2361 (PMID 19911853); Daulatabad D et al., Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2017;83:650-655 (PMID 28656915); Rather S et al., N Am J Med Sci 2015;7:356-361 (PMID 26417558)

extra_articular_associations_uveitis_ibd.finding: Extra-articular manifestations (EAM) of PsA are more common than previously thought and are associated with axial disease. The first study focused exclusively on EAM in PsA found a prevalence of 49% in a retrospective analysis of 387 PsA patients, most commonly in male patients with axial disease and significantly longer disease duration. The most commonly affected systems and example manifestations are: ocular (uveitis, conjunctivitis); gastrointestinal (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, non-specific colitis); cardiovascular (bundle-branch blocks, intraventricular conduction blocks, increased arterial stiffness, increased carotid intima-media thickness); and urogenital (urethritis, prostatitis, balanitis, cervicitis, vaginitis). These associations mirror the extra-articular pattern seen in ankylosing spondylitis (see this knowledge base's ankylosing spondylitis symptoms entry for uveitis, IBD and cardiac-involvement sourcing in that related disease), consistent with PsA and AS sharing the same spondyloarthritis-family, IL-23/IL-17-driven biology.
extra_articular_associations_uveitis_ibd.source: Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746), citing Peluso R et al., 'Extra-articular manifestations in psoriatic arthritis patients', Clin Rheumatol 2015;34:745-753 (PMID 24803233)
extra_articular_associations_uveitis_ibd.confidence: high for the EAM prevalence and manifestation list from the cited primary study; the cross-reference to the AS entry's shared biology is this knowledge base's own synthesis

axial_psoriatic_arthritis.finding: In Moll and Wright's fifth pattern, PsA can present with axial (spondylitis-predominant) disease, with typical features including asymmetrical sacroiliitis, non-marginal and asymmetrical syndesmophytes, paravertebral ossification and cervical-spine involvement, which can present with a broad variety of symptoms. A 2015 review of axial PsA (axPsA) states that its definition and measurement remain problematic because no consensus or definitive data have yet been published on the best diagnostic approach, though radiographic assessment with validated instruments is a useful tool for detecting typical axPsA findings, while the role of MRI is still being evaluated.
axial_psoriatic_arthritis.source: Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746); Lubrano E et al., 'The Definition and Measurement of Axial Psoriatic Arthritis', J Rheumatol Suppl 2015;93:40-42 (PMID 26523055)
axial_psoriatic_arthritis.confidence: moderate-high - the clinical feature list is sourced from the 2016 review; the 2015 axPsA-specific review itself states that consensus on definition and measurement is still lacking

rheumatoid_arthritis.finding: PsA and RA can both cause a symmetric polyarthritis (Moll and Wright's polyarticular PsA pattern resembles RA), but they are distinguished by rheumatoid-factor status (RF negativity is a scored point favouring PsA in the CASPAR criteria; RA is frequently RF- and/or anti-CCP-positive - see this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry, anti_ccp_and_rf_accuracy), by DIP joint involvement (a Moll-and-Wright PsA pattern, but explicitly excluded from RA's 2010 ACR/EULAR joint-count scoring - see this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry, acr_eular_2010_criteria), and by dactylitis, enthesitis and nail dystrophy, all of which are CASPAR-scored PsA features not typical of RA. In the CASPAR derivation study, 384 of the 536 non-PsA controls were RA patients, and the criteria achieved 98.7% specificity against this and other control groups combined.
rheumatoid_arthritis.source: Taylor W et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665-2673 (PMID 16871531); this knowledge base's own rheumatoid arthritis symptoms entry (acr_eular_2010_criteria, anti_ccp_and_rf_accuracy and its own psoriatic_arthritis differential-diagnosis sub-key, which cites the same Taylor 2006 CASPAR paper)

gout.finding: Gout, like PsA, can cause an asymmetric mono- or oligoarthritis and (in chronic tophaceous disease) can involve DIP joints, overlapping with PsA's classic presenting patterns. The discriminating test is synovial fluid analysis for monosodium urate crystals, which is sufficient on its own for classification under the 2015 ACR/EULAR gout criteria (sensitivity 92%, specificity 89% in that study); additional discriminating domains in those criteria include serum urate level, the double-contour sign on ultrasound, and gout-specific erosion pattern on imaging, as already detailed in this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry.
gout.source: Neogi T et al., '2015 Gout Classification Criteria: An American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism Collaborative Initiative', Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1789-1798 (PMID 26359487), as already cited in this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry (gout_and_cppd)
gout.confidence: high for the gout criteria themselves; the PsA-versus-gout overlap statement is clinical reasoning built on the shared DIP/oligoarticular pattern rather than a dedicated PsA-versus-gout discriminating study

osteoarthritis.finding: Hand osteoarthritis (OA) can mimic DIP-predominant PsA because both preferentially involve the DIP joints, but the underlying process differs: hand OA classification requires hard-tissue (bony) enlargement of at least 2 of 10 selected joints with few swollen MCP joints (92% sensitive, 98% specific against controls including inflammatory arthritis in the derivation study), reflecting a degenerative, non-inflammatory bony process, whereas PsA's DIP involvement is inflammatory (soft-tissue swelling, often with adjacent nail dystrophy in the same digit - the 'DIP joint plus diseased nail' association is a recognised clinical pattern) and can show pencil-in-cup erosive change rather than osteophytic bony enlargement on imaging (see diagnostic_framework).
osteoarthritis.source: Altman R et al., 'The American College of Rheumatology criteria for the classification and reporting of osteoarthritis of the hand', Arthritis Rheum 1990;33:1601-1610 (PMID 2242058), as already cited in this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis entry; Laasonen L et al., Acta Radiol Open 2015;4:2058460115588098 (PMID 26346445) for the PsA-side imaging contrast
osteoarthritis.confidence: high for the OA criteria; moderate for the specific 'DIP joint plus diseased nail' clinical teaching point, which is standard rheumatology reasoning built on the sourced nail-disease association rather than a single dedicated comparison study

ankylosing_spondylitis_and_axial_spa.finding: Axial PsA (Moll and Wright's fifth pattern) overlaps clinically with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) within the spondyloarthritis family and shares the IL-23/IL-17/TNF axis (see definition_and_pathophysiology), but the CASPAR derivation study specifically used 72 AS patients as a comparator group when validating PsA classification, and axial PsA is described as having distinguishing radiographic features - asymmetrical sacroiliitis and non-marginal, asymmetrical syndesmophytes with paravertebral ossification - contrasting with the typically symmetrical sacroiliitis and thin, marginal, symmetrical syndesmophytes of AS (see this knowledge base's ankylosing spondylitis symptoms entry, which cross-references PsA/CASPAR for the same distinction from the AS side). Peripheral psoriasis, current or past, dactylitis and nail dystrophy favour a PsA-family axial disease over primary AS, though the two can coexist.
ankylosing_spondylitis_and_axial_spa.source: Taylor W et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665-2673 (PMID 16871531); Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746); Lubrano E et al., J Rheumatol Suppl 2015;93:40-42 (PMID 26523055); this knowledge base's own ankylosing spondylitis symptoms entry (differential_diagnosis/psoriatic_arthritis sub-key)
ankylosing_spondylitis_and_axial_spa.confidence: high for the CASPAR/AS comparator numbers and the radiographic contrast; moderate for the practical coexistence statement, which follows from the shared spondyloarthritis-family biology rather than a single dedicated overlap study

psoriasis_severity_and_extent.finding: Greater psoriasis skin severity is associated with higher risk of developing PsA. In a Cox regression analysis of 943 dermatologist-diagnosed psoriasis patients (Utah Psoriasis Initiative), higher worst-ever body-surface-area (BSA) involvement with psoriasis independently predicted PsA (odds ratio 1.01 per unit increase, p=0.04), alongside younger age at psoriasis onset (OR 0.98, p<0.01), female sex (OR 1.45, p=0.01), the Koebner phenomenon (OR 1.59, p<0.01) and nail involvement (OR 1.76, p<0.01); current BMI and family history of psoriasis were not independently significant once these other variables were controlled for. PsA prevalence itself is highest in dermatology-clinic populations with established, more severe psoriasis: 30% (95% CI 27-33%) among 949 psoriasis patients across 34 European/North American dermatology centres, rheumatologist-confirmed - see epidemiology for the full range across settings.
psoriasis_severity_and_extent.source: Soltani-Arabshahi R et al., 'Obesity in early adulthood as a risk factor for psoriatic arthritis', Arch Dermatol 2010;146:721-726 (PMID 20644032); Mease PJ et al., 'Prevalence of rheumatologist-diagnosed psoriatic arthritis in patients with psoriasis in European/North American dermatology clinics', J Am Acad Dermatol 2013;69:729-735 (PMID 23981683)

family_history.finding: A family history of psoriasis or PsA substantially raises PsA risk, reflecting a strong heritable component. In a study of 100 consecutive PsA patients and 289 of their available first-degree relatives (73% participation among available relatives), the prevalence of PsA among first-degree relatives was 7.6% (versus an assumed 0.25% population prevalence used for the calculation) and of psoriasis was 15.2% (versus an assumed 2% population prevalence); the resulting recurrence risk ratio (lambda) was 30.4 for PsA and 7.6 for psoriasis among all first-degree relatives, and 30.8 (PsA) and 8.8 (psoriasis) specifically among siblings. Family history of PsA is also explicitly listed as one of only a small number of PsA risk factors (alongside obesity and injury/trauma) that has been replicated across multiple independent studies, per a dedicated epidemiology review.
family_history.source: Chandran V et al., 'Familial aggregation of psoriatic arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:664-667 (PMID 18524791); Ogdie A, Weiss P, 'The Epidemiology of Psoriatic Arthritis', Rheum Dis Clin North Am 2015;41:545-568 (PMID 26476218, PMCID PMC4610151, cross-checked via direct retrieval of the full-text article)

obesity.finding: Obesity, particularly in early adulthood, is a replicated independent risk factor for PsA. In the 943-patient Utah Psoriasis Initiative cohort, body mass index (BMI) at age 18 years (not current BMI) independently predicted later PsA (odds ratio 1.06 per unit, p<0.01) after controlling for age at psoriasis onset, sex, family history, worst-ever BSA involvement, Koebner phenomenon and nail involvement; the authors interpret this as adiposity-associated chronic inflammatory cytokine exposure increasing PsA risk in predisposed individuals, and note that prevention and early treatment of obesity may reduce risk. A separate review states obesity is one of only a few PsA risk factors that has been replicated across independent studies, and proposes a second, complementary mechanical-stress mechanism: greater body weight increases mechanical loading on entheseal structures, which - per the entheseal-disease model (see definition_and_pathophysiology) - may itself help trigger PsA in predisposed people.
obesity.source: Soltani-Arabshahi R et al., Arch Dermatol 2010;146:721-726 (PMID 20644032); Ogdie A, Weiss P, Rheum Dis Clin North Am 2015;41:545-568 (PMID 26476218); Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746)

trauma_and_the_deep_koebner_phenomenon.finding: Physical trauma - particularly to bone and joints - is a replicated risk factor for PsA in patients who already have psoriasis, a phenomenon sometimes termed the 'deep Koebner' effect (by analogy with the cutaneous Koebner phenomenon, in which new psoriasis plaques form at sites of skin trauma). In a UK matched cohort study (The Health Improvement Network) of 15,416 psoriasis patients exposed to physical trauma and 55,230 matched unexposed psoriasis controls, followed for 425,120 person-years (1,010 incident PsA cases), trauma exposure was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.32 (95% CI 1.13-1.54) for developing PsA; on subgroup analysis, bone trauma carried an HR of 1.46 (95% CI 1.04-2.04) and joint trauma an HR of 1.50 (95% CI 1.19-1.90), while nerve and skin trauma showed no statistically significant association. As a specificity check, the same trauma exposure in the same database showed no increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis (HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.99-1.10), supporting a mechanism specific to the entheseal/joint biology of PsA rather than a generic effect of trauma on any arthritis. Separately, in the Utah cohort, self-reported cutaneous Koebner phenomenon (new psoriasis at trauma sites) itself independently predicted PsA (odds ratio 1.59, p<0.01).
trauma_and_the_deep_koebner_phenomenon.source: Thorarensen SM et al., 'Physical trauma recorded in primary care is associated with the onset of psoriatic arthritis among patients with psoriasis', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:521-525 (PMID 27457510); Soltani-Arabshahi R et al., Arch Dermatol 2010;146:721-726 (PMID 20644032)

prevalence_among_psoriasis_patients.finding: The proportion of psoriasis patients who have PsA varies considerably by case definition, population and care setting. The largest and most recent systematic review and meta-analysis (266 studies, 976,408 psoriasis patients) found a pooled proportion of PsA among psoriasis patients of 19.7% (95% CI 18.5-20.9%) overall, rising to 23.8% (95% CI 20.1-27.6%) in the subset of studies that specifically applied the CASPAR classification criteria; by region, pooled prevalence was 22.7% in Europe, 21.5% in South America, 19.5% in North America, 15.5% in Africa (very wide CI) and 14.0% in Asia, and only 3.3% in children/adolescents under 18. An earlier narrative review quotes a wider range of 6% to 41% depending on diagnostic definition. In dermatology-clinic-based, rheumatologist-confirmed studies the figure runs higher: 30% (95% CI 27-33%) across 34 European/North American dermatology centres, of whom 41% had not been previously diagnosed with PsA; and a smaller UK primary-care-derived estimate of 13.8% (95% CI 7.1-24.1%), which the authors themselves flagged as a likely overestimate due to misclassification and response bias. Taken together, the real evidence-based headline figure for 'about 1 in 4 to 1 in 5 psoriasis patients have PsA' (matching this knowledge base's task brief of approximately 20-30%) is well supported, while the true figure in any individual population depends heavily on how PsA was ascertained.
prevalence_among_psoriasis_patients.source: Alinaghi F et al., 'Prevalence of psoriatic arthritis in patients with psoriasis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational and clinical studies', J Am Acad Dermatol 2019;80:251-265 (PMID 29928910); Ogdie A, Weiss P, Rheum Dis Clin North Am 2015;41:545-568 (PMID 26476218); Mease PJ et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2013;69:729-735 (PMID 23981683); Ibrahim G et al., 'The prevalence of psoriatic arthritis in people with psoriasis', Arthritis Rheum 2009;61:1373-1378 (PMID 19790120)
prevalence_among_psoriasis_patients.confidence: high - the headline 19.7-23.8% figure comes from a very large, recent, primary-abstract-verified meta-analysis; the wider 6-41% range and clinic-specific figures are also each independently primary-sourced

prevalence_in_general_population.finding: PsA's prevalence in the general adult population (not conditioned on having psoriasis) is far lower than its prevalence within psoriasis patients. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (30 studies: 13 population-based studies covering more than 92,000 adults, plus 17 health-administrative-data studies covering more than 180 million adults) estimated a worldwide PsA prevalence of 112 per 100,000 adults (0.112%), with continent-specific population-based estimates of 207 per 100,000 in Europe, 64 per 100,000 in North America and 37 per 100,000 in Asia; health-administrative data gave a global prevalence of 109 per 100,000, higher in Europe (175) and North America (147) than Asia (78) or South America (17). An earlier expert review had quoted a similar 0.3% to 1% general-population range as an approximation of PsA's 'exact prevalence, which is unknown'.
prevalence_in_general_population.source: Lembke S, Macfarlane GJ, Jones GT, 'The worldwide prevalence of psoriatic arthritis - a systematic review and meta-analysis', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2024;63:3211-3220 (PMID 38530786, PMCID PMC11637478); Gladman DD et al., 'Psoriatic arthritis: epidemiology, clinical features, course, and outcome', Ann Rheum Dis 2005;64(Suppl 2):ii14-ii17 (PMID 15708927, PMCID PMC1766874)

india_specific_data.finding: No national, population-based PsA prevalence registry or survey specific to India was identified in this research pass (this session's literature search returned only regional, hospital-based clinical cohorts, not community population surveys, in contrast to this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis entries, which at least found regional COPCORD-type community surveys). Available Indian data are clinic-based: a 6-year prospective hospital cohort of 150 PsA patients from Kashmir (northern India) characterised clinical phenotype (see classic_symptoms and definition_and_pathophysiology for its pattern and timeline data) but did not estimate population prevalence; and a 38-patient Delhi cross-sectional nail-psoriasis cohort found PsA in 23.7% of patients specifically recruited for nail disease (a severity-enriched, non-representative sample). 'None identified in this session's search' is stated honestly as an absence-of-evidence finding, not as proof that no such Indian data exist anywhere.
india_specific_data.source: Rather S et al., N Am J Med Sci 2015;7:356-361 (PMID 26417558, PMCID PMC4561441); Daulatabad D et al., Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2017;83:650-655 (PMID 28656915); absence-of-evidence statement is the researcher's own search-outcome report, not a published source
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate - an absence claim can only be as strong as the search performed; stated as such, following the same honesty convention as this knowledge base's rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis india_registry_status/india_specific entries

erosive_and_destructive_joint_damage_ris.finding: Untreated or inadequately controlled PsA carries a real risk of erosive, destructive and even mutilating joint damage, challenging any assumption that PsA is inherently a mild disease. In a detailed 220-patient Toronto cohort, 40% had deforming, erosive arthropathy overall, 17% had five or more deformed joints, 28% had reached ARA radiological stage 3 and 14% stage 4 damage, and 11% had ARA class III or IV functional impairment - the authors explicitly state these findings 'challenge the concept of psoriatic arthritis as a benign arthropathy'. In a separate prospective early-arthritis cohort comparing psoriatic spondylarthropathy (PsS, n=82) with undifferentiated spondylarthropathy (uSpA, n=59) and reactive arthritis (ReA, n=16), baseline radiographic erosions were already present in 28% of PsS patients (versus 5% of uSpA) and rose to 45% by 2 years (versus 25% in uSpA); 2-year clinical remission was reached in only 14% of PsS patients, compared with 61% of ReA and 63% of uSpA patients - PsS had the most aggressive clinical course and poorest functional/radiological outcome of the three spondylarthropathy subgroups studied. The most severe Moll-and-Wright pattern, arthritis mutilans, can progress to digital shortening from bone osteolysis and pencil-in-cup deformity if not identified and treated early (see diagnostic_framework).
erosive_and_destructive_joint_damage_ris.source: Gladman DD et al., 'Psoriatic arthritis (PSA)--an analysis of 220 patients', Q J Med 1987;62:127-141 (PMID 3659255); Stafford L, Kane D, Murphy E, Duffy T, Lassere M, Youssef PP, Bresnihan B, Fitzgerald O, 'Psoriasis predicts a poor short-term outcome in patients with spondylarthropathy', Arthritis Rheum 2001;45:485-493 (PMID 11762682)

cardiometabolic_comorbidity_burden.finding: PsA carries a real, elevated cardiometabolic comorbidity burden. A UK population-based cohort study (The Health Improvement Network, 1994-2010; 8,706 PsA, 41,752 RA, 138,424 psoriasis-without-PsA patients and 81,573 unexposed matched controls) found that, after adjustment for traditional cardiovascular risk factors, PsA patients not prescribed a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) had an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) versus the general population (hazard ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.03-1.49) - a smaller but real excess compared with RA patients (HR 1.39-1.58 depending on DMARD use) and psoriasis-without-PsA patients (HR 1.08-1.42 depending on severity/DMARD use). Beyond cardiovascular events specifically, PsA is associated with an increased prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors themselves - obesity, hypertension, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia - through what is described as a shared inflammatory pathway between metabolic syndrome and PsA; a large UK cohort study found increased diabetes incidence in PsA (partly attributable to obesity/lifestyle factors), and metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance were found to be highly prevalent in PsA and strongly associated with the severity of the underlying inflammatory disease. Thyroid autoimmunity (raised anti-thyroid-peroxidase antibodies and a hypoechoic thyroid on ultrasound) is also increased in PsA, especially in women.
cardiometabolic_comorbidity_burden.source: Ogdie A et al., 'Risk of major cardiovascular events in patients with psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis: a population-based cohort study', Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:326-332 (PMID 25351522, PMCID PMC4341911); Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746), citing Dubreuil M et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2014;53:346-352 (PMID 24185762), Haroon M et al., J Rheumatol 2014;41:1357-1365 (PMID 24931949) and Antonelli A et al., J Rheumatol 2006;33:2026-2028 (PMID 17014017)

quality_of_life_impact.finding: PsA reduces health-related quality of life (QOL), with a distinct pattern from RA rather than simply a milder version of it. In a direct comparison of 107 PsA and 43 RA patients (SF-36 and Health Assessment Questionnaire), both groups had lower physical health than the general population; RA patients had more objectively active inflammatory disease at assessment, yet after adjusting for clinical/demographic differences, PsA patients reported higher vitality than RA patients but also more role limitation from emotional problems and more bodily pain - the authors conclude there may be unique disabilities specifically associated with the psoriasis (skin) dimension of PsA, not just the joint disease. Consistent with a real skin-driven QOL burden, a German cross-sectional study of 2,009 psoriasis patients found that having the hands, arms, genitals or nails affected by psoriasis were among the strongest independent predictors of reduced Dermatology Life Quality Index scores, even though these are individually small body-surface areas.
quality_of_life_impact.source: Husted JA, Gladman DD, Farewell VT, Cook RJ, 'Health-related quality of life of patients with psoriatic arthritis: a comparison with patients with rheumatoid arthritis', Arthritis Rheum 2001;45:151-158 (PMID 11324779); Augustin M et al., Br J Dermatol 2019;181:358-365 (PMID 30430557)

clinical_takeaway.point: Every patient with psoriasis should be actively screened for joint, entheseal and nail symptoms - do not wait for the patient to volunteer joint complaints, and do not assume absent visible psoriasis rules out PsA.
clinical_takeaway.why: Up to 30% of psoriasis patients seen in dermatology clinics have rheumatologist-confirmed PsA, and 41% of those confirmed cases had not been previously diagnosed; conversely, in 15-20% of all PsA patients (and up to 20% in an Indian cohort) arthritis is the first or simultaneous manifestation, appearing before or alongside visible skin disease rather than clearly after it.
clinical_takeaway.source: Mease PJ et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2013;69:729-735 (PMID 23981683); Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746); Rather S et al., N Am J Med Sci 2015;7:356-361 (PMID 26417558)

clinical_takeaway.point: Use a validated screening tool such as PEST (Psoriasis Epidemiology Screening Tool) in dermatology settings to flag psoriasis patients for rheumatology referral, since informal history-taking alone under-detects PsA.
clinical_takeaway.why: The PEST questionnaire (5 simple questions covering swollen joints, history of arthritis, heel pain, nail pitting and dactylitis) had sensitivity 92% and specificity 78% in its validation study, an improvement on the earlier Swedish Alenius tool (sensitivity 63%, specificity 72%); yet a 2023 GRAPPA member survey found that while 81% of dermatologists reported using PsA-specific screening instruments, rheumatologists reported that only 26.8% of patients referred to them from all sources had actually been assessed with a screening tool before referral - a real, current gap between recommended and actual practice.
clinical_takeaway.source: Ibrahim GH et al., 'Evaluation of an existing screening tool for psoriatic arthritis in people with psoriasis and the development of a new instrument: the Psoriasis Epidemiology Screening Tool (PEST) questionnaire', Clin Exp Rheumatol 2009;27:469-474 (PMID 19604440); Song K et al., 'Screening and Referral Strategies for the Early Recognition of Psoriatic Arthritis Among Patients With Psoriasis: Results of a GRAPPA Survey', J Rheumatol 2023;50:1439-1445 (PMID 37582554)

clinical_takeaway.point: Establish early, structured dermatology-rheumatology co-referral pathways rather than relying on ad hoc referral, since both specialties independently identify this coordination gap as a priority unmet need.
clinical_takeaway.why: In the same GRAPPA survey, dermatologists reported that a mean of 67% of the PsA cases they suspected were subsequently confirmed by rheumatologists, while rheumatologists themselves confirmed only a mean of 47.9% of referred cases - a discrepancy the survey's authors attribute partly to inconsistent use of screening tools before referral; both specialties identified educating primary-care physicians and dermatologists, and combining patient-reported screening with physician-confirmed findings, as the top priorities for improving early PsA recognition.
clinical_takeaway.source: Song K et al., J Rheumatol 2023;50:1439-1445 (PMID 37582554)

clinical_takeaway.point: Treat unexplained dactylitis ('sausage digit'), enthesitis (especially Achilles or plantar-fascia pain), DIP-joint swelling with an adjacent diseased nail, or a family history of PsA/psoriasis as red flags warranting prompt rheumatology assessment, even before radiographic erosions appear.
clinical_takeaway.why: These are the CASPAR-scored, PsA-specific clinical features (dactylitis, enthesitis at classic sites in about half of patients, DIP predominance, nail dystrophy, family history) that distinguish PsA from RA, gout and OA (see differential_diagnosis); delay matters because a psoriatic spondylarthropathy cohort followed prospectively had erosions in 28% of patients already at presentation, rising to 45% by 2 years, with only 14% reaching 2-year remission - a substantially worse early trajectory than the reactive-arthritis/undifferentiated-spondylarthropathy comparators in the same study (61-63% remission).
clinical_takeaway.source: Taylor W et al., Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665-2673 (PMID 16871531); Stafford L et al., Arthritis Rheum 2001;45:485-493 (PMID 11762682)

clinical_takeaway.point: Screen every PsA patient for cardiometabolic comorbidity (weight, blood pressure, glucose, lipids) alongside joint disease management, not as an afterthought.
clinical_takeaway.why: PsA carries a real, independent excess risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (adjusted hazard ratio 1.24 even without a DMARD prescribed), and obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia and thyroid autoimmunity are all more prevalent in PsA than in the general population, sharing inflammatory pathways with the joint disease itself and, per the entheseal-mechanical-stress hypothesis, potentially contributing directly to disease onset and severity.
clinical_takeaway.source: Ogdie A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:326-332 (PMID 25351522); Kerschbaumer A et al., Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746)

psoriatic_arthritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is NOT curable with any medicine in this survey: no conventional DMARD, biologic, small molecule or procedure removes the underlying IL-23/IL-17/TNF-driven entheseal and synovial inflammation described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry, and treatment withdrawal is followed by relapse in most patients. What IS real and close to a cure-tier outcome is SKIN clearance: with the newest biologics, complete clearance of psoriasis plaques (PASI100, 0% body-surface involvement) is achieved in a majority of patients, a genuinely near-100% result for that one disease domain even though the joints do not fully normalise. Concretely: in BE OPTIMAL/BE COMPLETE (bimekizumab, dual IL-17A/F inhibitor), among PsA patients with baseline plaque psoriasis and nail disease, PASI100 was reached by 60.9% (biologic-naive) and 63.8% (TNF-inhibitor-inadequate-responder) of bimekizumab-treated patients at week 52, sustained from week 16 (Thaci D et al., Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026;16:953-976, PMID 41381988); in SPIRIT-H2H, ixekizumab gave PASI100 in 59.2% of PsA patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis versus 25.5% with adalimumab through week 52 (Reich K et al., Dermatol Pract Concept 2022;12:e2022104, PMID 35646453); and in BE COMPLETE, 69% of TNF-inadequate-responder patients reached PASI90 (near-complete clearance) with bimekizumab versus 7% on placebo at week 16 (Merola JF et al., Lancet 2023;401:38-48, PMID 36495881). For the JOINTS the evidence is real but more modest: ACR20 (at least 20% improvement, not remission) is achieved in roughly 50-78% of patients across pivotal trials of TNF, IL-17, IL-12/23, IL-23 and JAK-inhibitor drugs, each roughly double the 13-33% placebo rate, and minimal disease activity (a multi-domain near-remission state) is reached by a minority - for example 35.9% with etanercept and 35.7% with etanercept+methotrexate versus 22.9% with methotrexate alone at week 24 in SEAM-PsA (Mease PJ et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:1112-1124, PMID 30747501). Methotrexate, the anchor drug of rheumatoid arthritis, has NO significant placebo-controlled benefit on PsA joint disease: in the MIPA trial (221 patients, 6 months), methotrexate 15 mg/week showed no significant effect on PsARC (OR 1.77), ACR20 (OR 2.00) or DAS-28 versus placebo, with benefit confined to skin and global scores (Kingsley GH et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2012;51:1368-1377, PMID 22344575) - this must be stated plainly because methotrexate is often assumed effective for PsA joints by extrapolation from RA, and the trial evidence says otherwise. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has PsA: (1) classify which domains are active - peripheral arthritis, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin, nails - because GRAPPA/EULAR base drug choice on this profile, not on joints alone; (2) start an NSAID and/or local glucocorticoid injection for mild, oligoarticular disease without poor prognostic factors; (3) for polyarthritis or oligoarthritis with poor prognostic factors (dactylitis, joint damage, elevated inflammatory markers), start a conventional DMARD - sulfasalazine or leflunomide have real placebo-controlled joint benefit, methotrexate is reasonable mainly for concurrent skin disease; (4) if the target is not met, move to a biologic chosen by domain - a TNF, IL-17A(/F) or IL-12/23 inhibitor for peripheral+skin disease, a TNF or IL-17A inhibitor preferentially if axial disease predominates, an IL-23 inhibitor if TB risk or IBD risk make IL-17 blockade unattractive; (5) reserve JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) for after bDMARD failure given the real ORAL Surveillance cardiovascular/malignancy/VTE signal that led to a class-wide FDA boxed warning; (6) use apremilast (oral, non-injectable) for patients wanting to avoid injections or with milder, non-erosive disease; (7) if skin clearance is the dominant goal, bimekizumab or ixekizumab have the highest real PASI100 rates in PsA trials; and (8) add exercise/physiotherapy, and refer for joint replacement only for erosive, mechanically destroyed joints. 'No cure' does not mean 'nothing works': for the skin, near-complete clearance is now a realistic, trial-proven target with the newest biologics; for the joints, meaningful, though partial, control is achievable in the majority of patients who are matched to the right drug class for their disease domains.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for psoriatic arthritis (PsA): the GRAPPA 2021 and EULAR 2019 domain-based treatment strategy and the TICOPA treat-to-target trial, NSAIDs, conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate - including the real MIPA negative trial - leflunomide, sulfasalazine), apremilast, TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab pegol), the IL-12/23 inhibitor ustekinumab, IL-17A(/F) inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) with the real near-complete skin-clearance (PASI100) finding, IL-23-specific inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) with the real ORAL Surveillance-derived safety signal, glucocorticoid injections, biosimilars and India availability, non-drug care, surgery, TB/IL-23 safety screening, pregnancy, and an honest list of failed/limited-evidence treatments. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review abstract; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms, diagnostic criteria and classification are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Doses named are the trial arm doses quoted in the cited abstracts, not prescribing instructions - dosing is a treating-rheumatologist/dermatologist decision.

psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.name: Domain-Based Treat-to-Target Strategy - TICOPA Trial, GRAPPA 2021 and EULAR 2019 Recommendations
psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.type: Treatment strategy (domain classification plus frequent measured reassessment with protocolised escalation - not a single drug)
specific_drugs: Methotrexate, sulfasalazine or leflunomide as first-line conventional DMARDs
NSAIDs and intra-articular glucocorticoids for mild disease
TNF, IL-17A(/F) or IL-12/23-inhibitor biologics as escalation, chosen by which domains (peripheral joints, axial, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin, nails) are active
JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) after bDMARD failure
Apremilast (oral PDE4 inhibitor) for milder disease or when injectables are inappropriate
psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.effectiveness: TICOPA (206 early, DMARD-naive PsA patients, UK multicentre, open-label RCT): the odds of achieving ACR20 at 48 weeks were higher with tight control (4-weekly review, treatment escalated until minimal disease activity was met) than standard care (12-weekly review) - odds ratio 1.91 (95% CI 1.03-3.55, p=0.0392); serious adverse events occurred in 14% (tight control) versus 6% (standard care), with no unexpected serious adverse events (Coates LC et al., Lancet 2015;386:2489-2498, PMID 26433318). GRAPPA 2021 (Coates LC et al., Nat Rev Rheumatol 2022;18:465-479, PMID 35761070) provides domain-based recommendations across peripheral arthritis, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin, nails and associated conditions (uveitis, IBD), each graded by an international rheumatology-dermatology-patient taskforce. EULAR 2019 update (Gossec L et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:700-712, PMID 32434812; 28 international taskforce members): 6 overarching principles and 12 recommendations - NSAIDs and local glucocorticoid injections as initial therapy; rapid initiation of a conventional synthetic DMARD for polyarthritis or oligo/monoarthritis with poor prognostic factors (dactylitis, joint damage); a TNF, IL-17A or IL-12/23 inhibitor bDMARD if the target is not met, accounting for skin involvement; a TNF or IL-17A inhibitor preferred first-line if axial disease predominates; JAK inhibitors addressed primarily after bDMARD failure; PDE4 inhibition (apremilast) proposed when other drugs are inappropriate, generally in milder disease.
psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.reason_why: PsA is not one disease process but several (synovitis, enthesitis, dactylitis, axial inflammation, skin and nail disease) that respond differently to the same drug; matching drug class to the dominant active domain, and reassessing against a defined target on a fixed schedule (as TICOPA did), removes the treatment inertia of unstructured routine care.
psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.important_caveat: TICOPA was open-label (not blinded to patients/clinicians), and serious adverse events were numerically more frequent in the tight-control arm, reflecting more drug exposure and escalation, not treatment failure. EULAR and GRAPPA recommendations are consensus-graded on trial evidence, not new trials themselves, and treatment choice still requires individual comorbidity and access assessment (cost/availability were not verified for India in this survey).
psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.real_working_solution: Classify the patient's active domains at diagnosis, start conventional therapy appropriate to the dominant domain, review on a fixed short interval (TICOPA used 4-weekly for tight control) against a defined target such as minimal disease activity, and escalate promptly to a biologic matched to the active domains (skin-heavy: IL-17A(/F) or IL-12/23/23-specific inhibitors; axial-predominant: TNF or IL-17A inhibitor) if the target is missed.
psa_strategy_ticopa_grappa_eular.source: Coates LC et al. (TICOPA), 'Effect of tight control of inflammation in early psoriatic arthritis', Lancet 2015;386:2489-2498 (PMID 26433318); Coates LC, Helliwell PS, 'Treating to target in psoriatic arthritis: how to implement in clinical practice', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:640-643 (PMID 26672066); Coates LC et al., 'GRAPPA: updated treatment recommendations for psoriatic arthritis 2021', Nat Rev Rheumatol 2022;18:465-479 (PMID 35761070); Gossec L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of psoriatic arthritis with pharmacological therapies: 2019 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:700-712 (PMID 32434812)

psa_nsaids_symptomatic.name: NSAIDs / COX-2 Inhibitors - Celecoxib Randomised Trial
specific_drugs: Naproxen, diclofenac, ibuprofen (other NSAIDs used in practice, not separately trialled in this survey)
psa_nsaids_symptomatic.effectiveness: In a 12-week, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of PsA in flare (n=608), ACR20 at week 12 was reached by about 50% of patients in every group (celecoxib 400 mg, 200 mg and placebo) with no statistically significant difference; at the earlier week-2 timepoint ACR20 was significantly higher with celecoxib 400 mg (49%) and 200 mg (39%) than placebo (28%, p<0.001 and p=0.016) (Kivitz AJ et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2007;37:164-173, PMID 17570469).
psa_nsaids_symptomatic.reason_why: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, reducing pain and inflammation in joints and entheses, but do not modify the IL-23/IL-17/TNF-driven immune process that drives PsA progression.
psa_nsaids_symptomatic.important_caveat: The celecoxib trial's own conclusion notes a high placebo response and no difference from placebo by week 12, i.e. real symptomatic but not disease-modifying benefit, concentrated in the first weeks of treatment. NSAIDs alone do not prevent radiographic or entheseal progression and are recommended only for mild disease.
psa_nsaids_symptomatic.real_working_solution: Use an NSAID as initial therapy for mild, oligoarticular PsA without poor prognostic factors, or as an adjunct for pain/stiffness alongside a DMARD or biologic; do not rely on an NSAID alone once dactylitis, polyarthritis or joint damage are present - move to a conventional DMARD per EULAR 2019.
psa_nsaids_symptomatic.source: Kivitz AJ et al., 'A comparison of the efficacy and safety of celecoxib 200 mg and celecoxib 400 mg once daily in treating the signs and symptoms of psoriatic arthritis', Semin Arthritis Rheum 2007;37:164-173 (PMID 17570469); Gossec L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of psoriatic arthritis with pharmacological therapies: 2019 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:700-712 (PMID 32434812)

psa_csdmard_methotrexate_negative_trial.name: Methotrexate - the Real Negative Placebo-Controlled Trial (MIPA) and the SEAM-PsA Comparison
specific_drugs: Methotrexate oral tablets (15 mg/week in MIPA; 20 mg/week in SEAM-PsA)
Methotrexate subcutaneous injection (used in practice, not separately trialled here for PsA)
psa_csdmard_methotrexate_negative_trial.effectiveness: MIPA (221 patients, 6-month double-blind RCT, the first large placebo-controlled PsA methotrexate trial): no significant effect of methotrexate 15 mg/week versus placebo on PsARC (OR 1.77, 95% CI 0.97-3.23), ACR20 (OR 2.00, 95% CI 0.65-6.22) or DAS-28 (OR 1.70, 95% CI 0.90-3.17); the only significant benefits were on patient/assessor global scores and skin scores (Kingsley GH et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2012;51:1368-1377, PMID 22344575). SEAM-PsA (851 patients, 24-week double-blind, 3-arm): methotrexate monotherapy gave ACR20 50.7% and MDA 22.9%, both significantly lower than etanercept monotherapy (ACR20 60.9%, p=0.029; MDA 35.9%, p=0.005) and etanercept+methotrexate combination (ACR20 65.0%, p=0.005; MDA 35.7%, p=0.005); adding methotrexate to etanercept did not improve on etanercept alone except on some skin endpoints (Mease PJ et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:1112-1124, PMID 30747501).
psa_csdmard_methotrexate_negative_trial.reason_why: Methotrexate's anti-inflammatory mechanism (adenosine-mediated dampening of T-cell/macrophage activity) is well proven in rheumatoid synovitis, but PsA's IL-23/IL-17-axis-driven entheseal and synovial inflammation responds less consistently, which the MIPA trial's null result on joint outcomes demonstrates directly.
psa_csdmard_methotrexate_negative_trial.important_caveat: This must be stated plainly: methotrexate has no confirmed placebo-controlled benefit for PsA joint disease, unlike its central, proven role in rheumatoid arthritis. It remains reasonable when skin psoriasis is a significant concurrent problem (real benefit on skin/global scores in MIPA) or as a partner drug ahead of biologic step-up, but it should not be assumed effective for arthritis by extrapolation from RA.
psa_csdmard_methotrexate_negative_trial.real_working_solution: Do not rely on methotrexate alone to control PsA joint disease; use it mainly when concurrent plaque psoriasis needs treatment, or as background therapy when starting a TNF inhibitor if additional skin benefit or reduced immunogenicity is desired - move to etanercept or another biologic promptly if joint disease does not respond, as SEAM-PsA demonstrated the clear real superiority of etanercept-containing regimens over methotrexate monotherapy.
psa_csdmard_methotrexate_negative_trial.source: Kingsley GH et al., 'A randomized placebo-controlled trial of methotrexate in psoriatic arthritis', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2012;51:1368-1377 (PMID 22344575); Mease PJ et al. (SEAM-PsA), 'Etanercept and methotrexate as monotherapy or in combination for psoriatic arthritis: primary results from a randomized, controlled phase III trial', Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:1112-1124 (PMID 30747501)

psa_csdmard_leflunomide.name: Leflunomide - Real Joint and Skin Benefit (TOPAS Trial)
specific_drugs: Leflunomide (100 mg/day loading dose for 3 days, then 20 mg/day)
psa_csdmard_leflunomide.effectiveness: TOPAS (190 patients with plaque psoriasis and active PsA, 24-week double-blind RCT): PsA Response Criteria (PsARC) response was significantly higher with leflunomide than placebo (58.9% vs 29.7%, p<0.0001); PASI50 skin response 30.4% vs 18.9% (p=0.05); target lesion response 46.4% vs 25.3% (p=0.0048); combined skin-and-joint response 27.2% vs 8.9% (p<0.0001) (Nash P et al., Dermatology 2006;212:238-249, PMID 16549920).
psa_csdmard_leflunomide.reason_why: Leflunomide's active metabolite blocks dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, limiting pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing activated lymphocytes in both joint synovium and psoriatic skin, giving it, unlike methotrexate in the MIPA trial, a real placebo-controlled joint response in PsA.
psa_csdmard_leflunomide.important_caveat: TOPAS's primary joint outcome (PsARC 58.9% vs 29.7%) has not been replicated in a comparably sized independent placebo-controlled trial; diarrhoea, nausea, alopecia, rash and raised liver enzymes are the commonest adverse events, as in RA use.
psa_csdmard_leflunomide.real_working_solution: Leflunomide is a real evidence-based conventional DMARD option for PsA joint and skin disease when methotrexate is not used or not effective; monitor liver enzymes regularly and avoid in patients planning pregnancy (teratogenic, requires washout before conception).
psa_csdmard_leflunomide.source: Nash P et al., 'Leflunomide improves psoriasis in patients with psoriatic arthritis: an in-depth analysis of data from the TOPAS study', Dermatology 2006;212:238-249 (PMID 16549920)

psa_csdmard_sulfasalazine.name: Sulfasalazine - Modest Real Benefit (VA Cooperative Study)
psa_csdmard_sulfasalazine.effectiveness: VA Cooperative Study (221 patients with active, NSAID-resistant PsA, double-blind RCT, 36 weeks): response rate 57.8% with sulfasalazine versus 44.6% with placebo (p=0.05); ESR fell significantly more with sulfasalazine (p<0.0001); longitudinal analysis showed only a trend favouring sulfasalazine (p=0.13) (Clegg DO et al., Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2013-2020, PMID 8961906).
psa_csdmard_sulfasalazine.reason_why: Sulfasalazine's anti-rheumatic mechanism (via its sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid metabolites) is systemic and incompletely defined, giving a real but modest joint benefit over placebo.
psa_csdmard_sulfasalazine.important_caveat: The effect size (13 percentage points at the primary endpoint, marginal p=0.05) is smaller than for leflunomide or biologics; the trial is now nearly 30 years old and used older response criteria.
psa_csdmard_sulfasalazine.real_working_solution: Use sulfasalazine as a low-cost conventional DMARD option, particularly for peripheral (not axial) PsA and in patients planning pregnancy, where it is considered compatible.
psa_csdmard_sulfasalazine.source: Clegg DO et al., 'Comparison of sulfasalazine and placebo in the treatment of psoriatic arthritis. A Department of Veterans Affairs Cooperative Study', Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2013-2020 (PMID 8961906)

psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.name: Apremilast (Otezla) - Oral PDE4 Inhibitor (PALACE 1)
psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.type: Targeted synthetic small molecule, oral phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor
psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.effectiveness: PALACE 1 (504 patients with active PsA despite prior DMARD/biologic therapy, 24-week placebo-controlled phase): ACR20 at week 16 was 31% (20 mg BID) and 40% (30 mg BID) versus 19% with placebo (p<0.001); significant improvements also seen in physical function and psoriasis (Kavanaugh A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1020-1026, PMID 24595547). Adverse events were mostly gastrointestinal, self-limiting and early, with no imbalance in major cardiac events, serious infections or malignancies.
psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.reason_why: Apremilast inhibits phosphodiesterase-4, raising intracellular cyclic AMP in immune cells and reducing production of TNF, IL-17, IL-23 and other inflammatory mediators, without the immunosuppression profile of biologics or the monitoring burden of methotrexate/leflunomide.
psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.important_caveat: Apremilast's ACR20 rates (31-40%) are lower than most TNF and IL-17 biologics (58-78% in their pivotal trials); it is not an injectable and does not require TB/hepatitis screening, but is generally reserved for milder disease or when biologics/JAK inhibitors are inappropriate per EULAR 2019.
psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.real_working_solution: Apremilast is a real oral, non-injectable option for patients with milder PsA, needle aversion, or contraindications to biologics/JAK inhibitors, and it needs no baseline TB/hepatitis screening; step up to a biologic if the target is not met.
psa_apremilast_oral_pde4_inhibitor.source: Kavanaugh A et al. (PALACE 1), 'Treatment of psoriatic arthritis in a phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled trial with apremilast, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor', Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1020-1026 (PMID 24595547)

psa_tnf_adalimumab.name: Adalimumab (TNF Inhibitor) - ADEPT Trial
psa_tnf_adalimumab.type: Biologic DMARD, fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Adalimumab biosimilars Exemptia (Zydus Cadila, India) and Adfrar (Torrent, India)
psa_tnf_adalimumab.effectiveness: ADEPT (313 patients with moderately-to-severely active PsA, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 at week 12 was 58% (87/151) with adalimumab versus 14% (23/162) with placebo (p<0.001); at week 24 the mean change in modified total Sharp score was -0.2 (adalimumab) versus +1.0 (placebo) (p<0.001); PASI75 skin response was 59% versus 1% (p<0.001) (Mease PJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:3279-3289, PMID 16200601).
psa_tnf_adalimumab.reason_why: Adalimumab neutralises soluble and membrane TNF-alpha, a central driver of both synovial/entheseal inflammation and psoriatic skin plaques.
psa_tnf_adalimumab.important_caveat: TNF inhibitors carry a real risk of TB reactivation and serious infection, particularly relevant in TB-endemic India; TB and hepatitis B/C screening is required before starting.
psa_tnf_adalimumab.real_working_solution: Adalimumab is a first-line real biologic option for PsA with both joint and skin involvement, with the same Indian biosimilars available as for rheumatoid arthritis (Exemptia, Adfrar); screen for TB/hepatitis B first.
psa_tnf_adalimumab.source: Mease PJ et al. (ADEPT), 'Adalimumab for the treatment of patients with moderately to severely active psoriatic arthritis: results of a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:3279-3289 (PMID 16200601)

psa_tnf_etanercept.name: Etanercept (TNF Receptor-Fc Fusion) - Mease 2000 Pivotal Trial and SEAM-PsA
psa_tnf_etanercept.type: Biologic DMARD, soluble TNF receptor fusion protein, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Etanercept 25 mg twice weekly (pivotal trial) or 50 mg once weekly (SEAM-PsA)
Etanercept biosimilars Intacept (Intas, India) and Etacept (Cipla, India)
psa_tnf_etanercept.effectiveness: Mease 2000 (60 patients with PsA and psoriasis, 12-week double-blind RCT, the first PsA biologic trial): PsARC response 87% (26/30) with etanercept versus 23% (7/30) with placebo; ACR20 73% (22/30) versus 13% (4/30); PASI75 skin response 26% versus 0% (p=0.015) (Mease PJ et al., Lancet 2000;356:385-390, PMID 10972371). SEAM-PsA (851 patients, 24 weeks): etanercept monotherapy ACR20 60.9% and MDA 35.9%, both significantly greater than methotrexate monotherapy (ACR20 50.7%, p=0.029; MDA 22.9%, p=0.005); etanercept+methotrexate combination ACR20 65.0%, MDA 35.7% - combining did not clearly outperform etanercept alone except on some skin outcomes; less radiographic progression at week 48 in both etanercept arms versus methotrexate monotherapy (Mease PJ et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:1112-1124, PMID 30747501).
psa_tnf_etanercept.reason_why: Etanercept is a dimeric soluble TNF receptor fused to IgG1 Fc that binds and inactivates TNF before it reaches its cellular receptor.
psa_tnf_etanercept.important_caveat: TB/serious infection risk applies to all TNF inhibitors. The original 2000 trial was small (60 patients); its very high ACR20 (73%) reflects the small early-phase sample.
psa_tnf_etanercept.real_working_solution: Etanercept monotherapy is a real, evidence-strong option for PsA joints and skin, does not require concomitant methotrexate (unlike infliximab), and Indian biosimilars exist (Intacept, Etacept); screen for TB/hepatitis B first.
psa_tnf_etanercept.source: Mease PJ et al., 'Etanercept in the treatment of psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis: a randomised trial', Lancet 2000;356:385-390 (PMID 10972371); Mease PJ et al. (SEAM-PsA), Arthritis Rheumatol 2019;71:1112-1124 (PMID 30747501)

psa_tnf_infliximab.name: Infliximab (Chimeric Anti-TNF Antibody) - IMPACT Trials
psa_tnf_infliximab.type: Biologic DMARD, chimeric anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, intravenous infusion
specific_drugs: Infliximab 5 mg/kg at weeks 0, 2, 6, 14 and every 8 weeks thereafter (always with or without methotrexate background)
Infliximab biosimilars (e.g. CT-P13; India-marketed biosimilar Infimab)
psa_tnf_infliximab.effectiveness: IMPACT radiographic follow-up (104 patients randomised, 72 with paired radiographs): ACR20 was 65% with infliximab versus 10% with placebo at week 16 (p<0.001), maintained at 69% at week 50; infliximab inhibited radiographic progression through week 50, with 84-85% of patients showing no worsening of the total modified van der Heijde-Sharp score (Kavanaugh A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1038-1043, PMID 16439444).
psa_tnf_infliximab.reason_why: Infliximab binds soluble and transmembrane TNF; being an infusion, it reliably achieves high, sustained drug levels.
psa_tnf_infliximab.important_caveat: As an infusion with a well-documented early TB reactivation signal from RA/PsA/Crohn's data, latent TB screening (IGRA/TST plus chest X-ray) is mandatory before the first dose, particularly important in India.
psa_tnf_infliximab.real_working_solution: Use infliximab, generally with methotrexate to reduce anti-drug antibody formation, for patients needing an infusion-based option or with axial/erosive disease; screen for latent TB and hepatitis B first.
psa_tnf_infliximab.source: Kavanaugh A et al., 'The Infliximab Multinational Psoriatic Arthritis Controlled Trial (IMPACT): results of radiographic analyses after 1 year', Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:1038-1043 (PMID 16439444)

psa_tnf_golimumab.name: Golimumab (Human Anti-TNF, Monthly Subcutaneous) - GO-REVEAL
psa_tnf_golimumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous every 4 weeks
psa_tnf_golimumab.effectiveness: GO-REVEAL (405 patients with active PsA despite NSAID/DMARD therapy, 24-week double-blind RCT): significantly more golimumab-treated than placebo-treated patients achieved ACR20 at week 14 and week 24, with improvements in physical function, quality of life and radiographic progression versus placebo (McInnes IB et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2009 [reported as the GO-REVEAL 24-week efficacy and safety results], PMID 19333944).
psa_tnf_golimumab.reason_why: Golimumab is a human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody with a monthly subcutaneous dosing schedule, offering a lower-frequency injection alternative to adalimumab/etanercept.
psa_tnf_golimumab.important_caveat: TB and serious infection risk applies as with all TNF inhibitors; exact ACR20 percentage figures for GO-REVEAL were not extractable from the abstract text retrieved in this survey and so are not quoted numerically here to avoid inaccuracy.
psa_tnf_golimumab.real_working_solution: Golimumab is a real monthly-dosing TNF-inhibitor alternative for patients who prefer less frequent injections; screen for TB/hepatitis B first.
psa_tnf_golimumab.source: Kavanaugh A et al. (GO-REVEAL), 'Golimumab, a new human tumor necrosis factor alpha antibody, administered every four weeks as a subcutaneous injection in psoriatic arthritis: twenty-four-week efficacy and safety results of a randomized, placebo-controlled study', Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:976-986 (PMID 19333944)

psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.name: Certolizumab Pegol (PEGylated Fab' Anti-TNF) - RAPID-PsA
psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.type: Biologic DMARD, PEGylated anti-TNF antibody fragment, subcutaneous
psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.effectiveness: RAPID-PsA (409 patients, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 at week 12 was 58.0% (200 mg Q2W) and 51.9% (400 mg Q4W) versus 24.3% with placebo (p<0.001), with improvement observed by week 1; PsARC response at week 24 was 78.3% and 77.0% versus 33.1% (p<0.001); HAQ-DI improved -0.50 versus -0.19 (p<0.001) (Mease PJ et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:48-55, PMID 23942868). Long-term extension to week 216 (273 patients from baseline): 79.7% (with background DMARD) and 83.3% (without) maintained ACR20, with dactylitis resolution in over 91% and enthesitis resolution in 74-88% (Walsh JA et al., Clin Rheumatol 2018;37:3285-3296, PMID 30191421).
psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.reason_why: Certolizumab is a TNF-binding Fab' fragment lacking an Fc region, PEGylated for a long half-life, giving rapid TNF neutralisation without transplacental transfer (relevant to pregnancy planning).
psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.important_caveat: TB screening is mandatory as with all TNF inhibitors; the very high week-216 real-world-style response rates come from an open-label extension without a placebo comparator after week 24.
psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.real_working_solution: Certolizumab is a real TNF-inhibitor option with strong dactylitis/enthesitis resolution data and can be used throughout pregnancy after individual risk assessment per EULAR reproductive guidance, unlike most other biologics.
psa_tnf_certolizumab_pegol.source: Mease PJ et al. (RAPID-PsA), 'Effect of certolizumab pegol on signs and symptoms in patients with psoriatic arthritis: 24-week results of a Phase 3 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled study', Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:48-55 (PMID 23942868); Walsh JA et al., 'Efficacy of certolizumab pegol with and without concomitant use of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs over 4 years in psoriatic arthritis patients: results from the RAPID-PsA randomized controlled trial', Clin Rheumatol 2018;37:3285-3296 (PMID 30191421)

psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.name: Ustekinumab (IL-12/23 p40 Inhibitor) - PSUMMIT 1 and PSUMMIT 2
psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-IL-12/IL-23 p40 monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous every 12 weeks
specific_drugs: Ustekinumab 45 mg or 90 mg at weeks 0, 4 and every 12 weeks
psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.effectiveness: PSUMMIT 1 (615 patients, biologic-naive or conventional-DMARD-inadequate, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 at week 24 was 42.4% (45 mg) and 49.5% (90 mg) versus 22.8% with placebo (p<0.0001 for both) (McInnes IB et al., Lancet 2013;382:780-789, PMID 23769296). PSUMMIT 2 (312 patients, including prior anti-TNF-exposed): overall ACR20 43.8% (combined ustekinumab) versus 20.2% placebo (p<0.001); in the anti-TNF-inadequate-responder subgroup, ACR20 was 35.6% versus 14.5% and PASI75 47.1% versus 2.0% at week 24, sustained to week 52 (ACR20 38.9%, PASI75 43.4%) (Ritchlin C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:990-999, PMID 24482301). Integrated radiographic analysis of both trials: total Sharp score change at week 24 was 0.4 (ustekinumab, either dose) versus 1.0 (placebo, p<0.02), an effect maintained to week 52 (Kavanaugh A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1000-1006, PMID 24553909).
psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.reason_why: Ustekinumab blocks the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23, interrupting the Th1/Th17 differentiation pathway that drives both psoriatic skin plaques and joint/entheseal inflammation, giving it real efficacy even after prior anti-TNF failure.
psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.important_caveat: PSUMMIT 2's anti-TNF-experienced subgroup response rates (35.6% ACR20) are meaningfully lower than the biologic-naive PSUMMIT 1 rates (42-50%), consistent with reduced response after a prior biologic failure across drug classes.
psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.real_working_solution: Ustekinumab is a real option after TNF-inhibitor failure or intolerance, given every 12 weeks (least frequent dosing among the biologics in this survey), with real radiographic-progression inhibition data; useful when skin disease (PASI75 up to 47% even in TNF-experienced patients) is a major driver alongside joints.
psa_il12_23_ustekinumab.source: McInnes IB et al. (PSUMMIT 1), Lancet 2013;382:780-789 (PMID 23769296); Ritchlin C et al. (PSUMMIT 2), 'Efficacy and safety of the anti-IL-12/23 p40 monoclonal antibody, ustekinumab, in patients with active psoriatic arthritis despite conventional non-biological and biological anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy', Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:990-999 (PMID 24482301); Kavanaugh A et al., 'Ustekinumab...inhibits radiographic progression in patients with active psoriatic arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:1000-1006 (PMID 24553909)

psa_il17_secukinumab.name: Secukinumab (IL-17A Inhibitor) - FUTURE 2 and Pooled FUTURE 2-5 Analysis
psa_il17_secukinumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
psa_il17_secukinumab.effectiveness: FUTURE 2 (397 patients, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 at week 24 was 54% (300 mg), 51% (150 mg) and 29% (75 mg) versus 15% with placebo (odds ratios 6.81, 6.52 and 2.32 respectively, all p<0.04) (McInnes IB et al., Lancet 2015;386:1137-1146, PMID 26135703). Pooled individual-patient meta-analysis of FUTURE 2-5 (2049 patients): both 300 mg and 150 mg doses showed greater treatment effect than placebo on higher-hurdle endpoints at week 16, with 300 mg generally outperforming 150 mg (Gottlieb AB et al., J Clin Rheumatol 2021;27:239-247, PMID 32015257).
psa_il17_secukinumab.reason_why: Secukinumab neutralises IL-17A, a key effector cytokine downstream of the IL-23/Th17 axis in both entheseal/synovial inflammation and psoriatic skin plaques.
psa_il17_secukinumab.important_caveat: IL-17 inhibitors must be used cautiously in patients with, or at high risk of, inflammatory bowel disease, since IL-17 blockade can worsen or unmask IBD (per the GRAPPA 2021 IBD/uveitis review, PMID 36455946).
psa_il17_secukinumab.real_working_solution: Secukinumab 300 mg is a real first-line biologic option, particularly when skin disease is prominent or axial disease predominates (EULAR 2019 lists IL-17A inhibitors alongside TNF inhibitors as axial-preferred); screen for IBD history before starting.
psa_il17_secukinumab.source: McInnes IB et al. (FUTURE 2), 'Secukinumab, a human anti-interleukin-17A monoclonal antibody, in patients with psoriatic arthritis (FUTURE 2): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial', Lancet 2015;386:1137-1146 (PMID 26135703); Gottlieb AB et al., 'Secukinumab Efficacy in Psoriatic Arthritis: Machine Learning and Meta-analysis of Four Phase 3 Trials', J Clin Rheumatol 2021;27:239-247 (PMID 32015257)

psa_il17_ixekizumab.name: Ixekizumab (IL-17A Inhibitor) - SPIRIT-P1 and SPIRIT-H2H Head-to-Head vs Adalimumab
psa_il17_ixekizumab.type: Biologic DMARD, humanised anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Ixekizumab 80 mg every 2 weeks (after a 160 mg starting dose)
psa_il17_ixekizumab.effectiveness: SPIRIT-P1 (417 biologic-naive patients, 24-week double-blind, placebo- and adalimumab-controlled): ACR20 was 62.1% (every-2-week) and 57.9% (every-4-week) with ixekizumab versus 30.2% with placebo (p<=0.001); adalimumab (active reference) also showed significant improvement versus placebo (Mease PJ et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:79-87, PMID 27553214). SPIRIT-H2H (566 biologic-naive patients with active PsA and moderate-to-severe psoriasis, 52-week randomised, open-label, assessor-blinded head-to-head trial): simultaneous ACR50 and PASI100 achievement was significantly higher with ixekizumab than adalimumab at week 24 (40.8% vs 17.6%, p=0.015) and week 52 (38.8% vs 17.6%, p=0.026); PASI100 alone through week 52 was 59.2% (ixekizumab) versus 25.5% (adalimumab, p=0.001); PASI90 was 81.6% versus 60.8% (p=0.028) (Reich K et al., Dermatol Pract Concept 2022;12:e2022104, PMID 35646453).
psa_il17_ixekizumab.reason_why: Ixekizumab is a high-affinity humanised anti-IL-17A antibody; the SPIRIT-H2H head-to-head design (rather than a placebo comparison) directly demonstrates real superiority over a TNF inhibitor for simultaneous joint-and-complete-skin-clearance outcomes.
psa_il17_ixekizumab.important_caveat: SPIRIT-H2H was open-label (not blinded to treatment assignment, though outcome assessors were blinded), and, as with secukinumab, IL-17 inhibition carries a real risk of worsening inflammatory bowel disease.
psa_il17_ixekizumab.real_working_solution: Ixekizumab is a real evidence-strong choice when the goal is simultaneous joint control and complete (PASI100) skin clearance, having shown real superiority over adalimumab on this combined outcome in a head-to-head trial - not just versus placebo.
psa_il17_ixekizumab.source: Mease PJ et al. (SPIRIT-P1), 'Ixekizumab, an interleukin-17A specific monoclonal antibody, for the treatment of biologic-naive patients with active psoriatic arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:79-87 (PMID 27553214); Reich K et al. (SPIRIT-H2H), 'Efficacy and Safety of Ixekizumab Versus Adalimumab in Biologic-naive Patients With Active Psoriatic Arthritis and Moderate-to-severe Psoriasis: 52-week Results', Dermatol Pract Concept 2022;12:e2022104 (PMID 35646453)

psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.name: Bimekizumab (Dual IL-17A/IL-17F Inhibitor) - BE OPTIMAL, BE COMPLETE, and the Real Near-Complete Skin Clearance (PASI100) Finding
psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.type: Biologic DMARD, humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody selectively inhibiting both IL-17A and IL-17F, subcutaneous
psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.effectiveness: BE OPTIMAL (852 biologic-naive patients, 52-week RCT with adalimumab reference): ACR50 at week 16 was 44% (189/431) with bimekizumab versus 10% (28/281) with placebo (odds ratio 7.1, 95% CI 4.6-10.9, p<0.0001); adalimumab reference arm reached 46% (McInnes IB et al., Lancet 2023;401:25-37, PMID 36493791). BE COMPLETE (400 patients with prior inadequate response/intolerance to TNF inhibitors, 16-week RCT): ACR50 43% (116/267) with bimekizumab versus 7% (9/133) with placebo (adjusted OR 11.1, 95% CI 5.4-23.0, p<0.0001); PASI90 (near-complete skin clearance) was reached by 69% (121/176) versus 7% (6/88) with placebo (adjusted OR 30.2, 95% CI 12.4-73.9, p<0.0001) (Merola JF et al., Lancet 2023;401:38-48, PMID 36495881). THE REAL NEAR-COMPLETE-CLEARANCE FINDING: in a pooled 52-week post hoc analysis of PsA patients with baseline plaque psoriasis (>=3% body surface area) and nail involvement across both trials, complete skin clearance (PASI100, i.e. 100% improvement / 0% visible psoriasis) was sustained in 60.9% of biologic-naive and 63.8% of TNF-inhibitor-experienced bimekizumab-treated patients, alongside ACR50 in 65.4% and 61.0% respectively, and complete nail clearance (mNAPSI=0) in 68.4% and 70.5% (Thaci D et al., Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026;16:953-976, PMID 41381988).
psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.reason_why: Bimekizumab blocks both IL-17A and IL-17F (rather than IL-17A alone), and IL-17F is independently pathogenic in psoriatic skin and joint tissue; dual blockade produces a materially deeper and more durable skin response than single-cytokine IL-17A inhibition, which is the real mechanistic basis for the higher PASI100 rates seen here relative to secukinumab/ixekizumab.
psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.important_caveat: This is a genuinely close-to-100% outcome for the SKIN domain only (60-64% of a specific pre-selected subgroup with baseline moderate psoriasis and nail disease reaching complete clearance) - it is not a cure and does not mean the joints are fully normalised (ACR50, not ACR100/remission, was the concurrent joint outcome at 61-65%). Bimekizumab carries a real, mechanism-based increase in oral/vaginal candidiasis (fungal infection) risk, consistent across its phase 3 programme, because IL-17 is also protective at mucosal barriers against Candida.
psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.real_working_solution: For a patient whose skin disease is the dominant burden, bimekizumab is the real, trial-verified biologic with the highest reported PASI100 (complete clearance) rate among the drugs surveyed here (approximately 61-64% sustained to 1 year), while also giving real ACR50 joint responses in roughly two-thirds of patients; monitor for oral/genital candidiasis.
psa_il17af_bimekizumab_and_pasi100_findi.source: McInnes IB et al. (BE OPTIMAL), Lancet 2023;401:25-37 (PMID 36493791); Merola JF et al. (BE COMPLETE), Lancet 2023;401:38-48 (PMID 36495881); Thaci D et al., 'Bimekizumab Efficacy and Safety in Patients with Psoriatic Arthritis with Substantial Skin and Nail Psoriasis to 1 Year', Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026;16:953-976 (PMID 41381988)

psa_il23_guselkumab.name: Guselkumab (IL-23 p19 Inhibitor) - DISCOVER-2
psa_il23_guselkumab.type: Biologic DMARD, human anti-IL-23 (p19 subunit) monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Guselkumab 100 mg at weeks 0, 4, then every 8 weeks
psa_il23_guselkumab.effectiveness: DISCOVER-2 (741 biologic-naive patients, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 at week 24 was 64% (156/245) with every-4-week dosing and 64% (159/248) with every-8-week dosing versus 33% (81/246) with placebo (percentage differences 31 points for both regimens, p<0.0001 for both) (Mease PJ et al., Lancet 2020;395:1126-1136, PMID 32178766).
psa_il23_guselkumab.reason_why: Guselkumab selectively blocks the p19 subunit of IL-23 (upstream of IL-17), interrupting Th17 cell maintenance without blocking IL-12, giving high real efficacy with a serious-infection rate (1-3%) similar to placebo in this trial.
psa_il23_guselkumab.important_caveat: IL-23-specific inhibitors have a real, actively monitored TB-reactivation question in TB-endemic regions, though a large systematic review found no LTBI reactivation in 33 of 34 IL-23i psoriasis studies and none in 8 PsA studies reviewed (see the TB-screening entry).
psa_il23_guselkumab.real_working_solution: Guselkumab is a real, high-efficacy every-8-week-dosing option (least frequent among the drugs surveyed except ustekinumab) with a favourable early safety profile in biologic-naive PsA.
psa_il23_guselkumab.source: Mease PJ et al. (DISCOVER-2), 'Guselkumab in biologic-naive patients with active psoriatic arthritis (DISCOVER-2): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial', Lancet 2020;395:1126-1136 (PMID 32178766)

psa_il23_risankizumab.name: Risankizumab (IL-23 p19 Inhibitor) - KEEPsAKE 1 and KEEPsAKE 2
psa_il23_risankizumab.type: Biologic DMARD, humanised anti-IL-23 (p19 subunit) monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous
psa_il23_risankizumab.effectiveness: KEEPsAKE 1 (964 csDMARD-inadequate-responder patients, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% with risankizumab versus 33.5% with placebo (p<0.001); serious infections were similar between groups (1.0% vs 1.2%) (Kristensen LE et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:225-231, PMID 34911706). KEEPsAKE 2 (444 patients with prior biologic and/or csDMARD inadequate response, 24-week double-blind RCT): ACR20 51.3% versus 26.5% with placebo (p<0.001), including 46.5% of the population who were biologic-inadequate-responders (Ostor A et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:351-358, PMID 34815219).
psa_il23_risankizumab.reason_why: Like guselkumab, risankizumab selectively blocks IL-23 p19, giving durable joint and skin responses with infrequent (every-12-week maintenance) dosing and a real efficacy signal even in biologic-experienced patients.
psa_il23_risankizumab.important_caveat: As with all IL-23 inhibitors, TB screening practice is still debated; the KEEPsAKE trials themselves report only short-term (24-week) safety data in the abstracts reviewed here.
psa_il23_risankizumab.real_working_solution: Risankizumab is a real option after conventional-DMARD or prior-biologic failure, with meaningful (51%) ACR20 response even in the biologic-experienced KEEPsAKE 2 population.
psa_il23_risankizumab.source: Kristensen LE et al. (KEEPsAKE 1), Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:225-231 (PMID 34911706); Ostor A et al. (KEEPsAKE 2), Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:351-358 (PMID 34815219)

psa_jak_tofacitinib.name: Tofacitinib (Oral JAK Inhibitor) - OPAL Broaden (with Adalimumab Active Reference)
psa_jak_tofacitinib.type: Targeted synthetic small molecule, oral pan-JAK inhibitor
psa_jak_tofacitinib.effectiveness: OPAL Broaden (422 csDMARD-inadequate-responder patients, 12-month double-blind, placebo- and adalimumab-controlled): ACR20 at month 3 was 50% (5 mg) and 61% (10 mg) versus 33% with placebo (p=0.01 and p<0.001); adalimumab reference arm reached 52%; HAQ-DI improved -0.35 and -0.40 versus -0.18 with placebo (p=0.006, p<0.001) (Mease P et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:1537-1550, PMID 29045212). Adverse events through month 12 were more frequent with tofacitinib (66-71%) than placebo (64-69%), including 4 cancers, 3 serious infections and 4 herpes zoster cases across the tofacitinib arms.
psa_jak_tofacitinib.reason_why: Tofacitinib inhibits Janus kinases 1/3 (and to a lesser extent JAK2), blocking intracellular signalling downstream of multiple cytokine receptors including IL-23 and IL-6, giving oral efficacy comparable to a TNF inhibitor (adalimumab) in this trial.
psa_jak_tofacitinib.important_caveat: The ORAL Surveillance trial in rheumatoid arthritis (an older, cardiovascular-risk-enriched population) found tofacitinib not non-inferior to TNF inhibitors for major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism and malignancy, leading the US FDA to issue a class-wide boxed warning for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib across inflammatory arthritis indications including PsA (Misra DP et al., Clin Rheumatol 2023;42:621-632, PMID 36264400); analyses of tofacitinib trials specifically in psoriasis/PsA/spondyloarthritis suggest an overall similar MACE/VTE risk to TNF inhibitors in these generally younger populations, but risk is considerably heightened in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular risk factors.
psa_jak_tofacitinib.real_working_solution: Reserve tofacitinib for patients who have failed or cannot use a biologic, after individually assessing cardiovascular, VTE and malignancy risk factors per the FDA boxed warning; it is a real oral alternative with adalimumab-comparable efficacy in OPAL Broaden.
psa_jak_tofacitinib.source: Mease P et al. (OPAL Broaden), 'Tofacitinib or Adalimumab versus Placebo for Psoriatic Arthritis', N Engl J Med 2017;377:1537-1550 (PMID 29045212); Misra DP et al., 'Cardiovascular risks associated with Janus kinase inhibitors: peering outside the black box', Clin Rheumatol 2023;42:621-632 (PMID 36264400)

psa_jak_upadacitinib.name: Upadacitinib (Oral JAK1-Selective Inhibitor) - SELECT-PsA 1
psa_jak_upadacitinib.type: Targeted synthetic small molecule, oral JAK1-selective inhibitor
psa_jak_upadacitinib.effectiveness: SELECT-PsA 1 (1705 csDMARD-inadequate-responder patients, 24-week double-blind, placebo- and adalimumab-controlled): ACR20 at week 12 was 70.6% (15 mg) and 78.5% (30 mg) versus 36.2% with placebo (p<0.001 for both) and 65.0% with adalimumab; the 30 mg (but not 15 mg) dose was statistically superior to adalimumab (difference 13.5 percentage points, 95% CI 7.5-19.4) (McInnes IB et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384:1227-1239, PMID 33789011). Hepatic disorders occurred in 9.1% (15 mg) and 12.3% (30 mg) of patients, though grade 3 transaminase rises stayed under 2% in all groups.
psa_jak_upadacitinib.reason_why: Upadacitinib selectively inhibits JAK1, sparing JAK2/3 relative to tofacitinib, and blocks signalling from IL-23, IL-6 and interferon-gamma pathways implicated in PsA.
psa_jak_upadacitinib.important_caveat: Upadacitinib carries the same FDA class-wide boxed warning (MACE, VTE, malignancy, serious infection) derived from ORAL Surveillance as tofacitinib and baricitinib, even though direct upadacitinib cardiovascular outcome trial data in the PsA population itself were not separately available in this survey.
psa_jak_upadacitinib.real_working_solution: Upadacitinib 15 mg (the approved PsA dose) is a real oral option, with the 30 mg dose showing real statistical superiority to adalimumab on ACR20 in SELECT-PsA 1, reserved for patients who have had an inadequate response to a biologic or in whom biologic therapy is not appropriate, after individualised cardiovascular/VTE/malignancy risk assessment.
