psa_jak_upadacitinib.source: McInnes IB et al. (SELECT-PsA 1), 'Trial of Upadacitinib and Adalimumab for Psoriatic Arthritis', N Engl J Med 2021;384:1227-1239 (PMID 33789011)

psa_glucocorticoid_local_injection.name: Local (Intra-Articular / Peri-Entheseal) Glucocorticoid Injection - EULAR-Endorsed Initial Therapy
specific_drugs: Triamcinolone or methylprednisolone intra-articular/peri-tendinous injection (agents used in practice)
psa_glucocorticoid_local_injection.effectiveness: EULAR 2019 lists NSAIDs and local glucocorticoid injections as proposed initial therapy for PsA, based on the taskforce's systematic review and consensus process, though a dedicated large placebo-controlled RCT of intra-articular glucocorticoid specifically in PsA was not identified as a separately quotable numeric effect size in this survey (Gossec L et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:700-712, PMID 32434812).
psa_glucocorticoid_local_injection.reason_why: A local glucocorticoid injection delivers a high anti-inflammatory concentration directly to an inflamed joint or enthesis while minimising systemic steroid exposure, useful for mono/oligoarticular flares.
psa_glucocorticoid_local_injection.important_caveat: This entry is graded medium confidence because the effectiveness statement rests on guideline-level consensus rather than a specific quoted randomised-trial percentage for PsA; systemic (oral) glucocorticoids are generally avoided in PsA because of a documented risk of triggering a psoriasis flare (pustular psoriasis) on tapering, which is why local rather than systemic steroid is preferred.
psa_glucocorticoid_local_injection.real_working_solution: Use local glucocorticoid injection for mono/oligoarticular flares or resistant enthesitis/dactylitis alongside a DMARD, and avoid long-term systemic (oral) glucocorticoids in PsA because of the real risk of a rebound psoriasis flare on steroid withdrawal.
psa_glucocorticoid_local_injection.source: Gossec L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of psoriatic arthritis with pharmacological therapies: 2019 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:700-712 (PMID 32434812)

psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.name: Biosimilar TNF Inhibitors and India Availability
psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.type: Biosimilar biologic DMARDs (same molecular class as originator TNF inhibitors)
specific_drugs: Adalimumab biosimilars Exemptia (Zydus Cadila, 2014) and Adfrar (Torrent, 2016)
psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.effectiveness: These Indian-marketed biosimilars are approved on the basis of analytical and clinical similarity to the originator molecules used in the pivotal PsA trials above (ADEPT for adalimumab, Mease 2000/SEAM-PsA for etanercept, IMPACT for infliximab); the NOR-SWITCH trial (482 patients, 77 with RA, switching CT-P13 infliximab biosimilar from originator) found no evidence of worse disease outcomes after switching, though this trial was not PsA-specific (Jorgensen KK et al., Lancet 2017;389:2304-2316, PMID 28502609).
psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.reason_why: A biosimilar is manufactured to match the originator's amino-acid sequence and higher-order structure closely enough that clinical efficacy and safety are considered equivalent by regulators, at typically lower cost.
psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.important_caveat: Biosimilar-specific PsA efficacy trials (as opposed to RA-focused switch trials such as NOR-SWITCH) were not separately identified in this survey; exact Indian pricing was not verified.
psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.real_working_solution: In India, biosimilar TNF inhibitors (same brands used for rheumatoid arthritis) make TNF-inhibitor therapy for PsA substantially more accessible than originator pricing; there is no evidence of inferior outcomes from switching to an approved biosimilar.
psa_biosimilars_and_india_availability.source: GaBI Online, 'Similar biologics approved and marketed in India' (https://www.gabionline.net/biosimilars/general/Similar-biologics-approved-and-marketed-in-India); Jorgensen KK et al. (NOR-SWITCH), Lancet 2017;389:2304-2316 (PMID 28502609)

psa_nondrug_exercise_lifestyle.name: Lifestyle Modification, Exercise and Nonpharmacologic Interventions - Honest Limited-Evidence Systematic Review
specific_drugs: Mud bath therapy (studied in one trial)
psa_nondrug_exercise_lifestyle.effectiveness: A systematic review for GRAPPA (26,132 references screened, 8 eligible studies: 3 RCTs, 5 non-randomised) found only 8 studies examining lifestyle modification effects on PsA, with large heterogeneity in outcomes measured; physical activity appeared to have a positive impact on disease activity and psychological well-being, but the review's own conclusion states these studies did NOT provide high-quality evidence to guide patients on non-drug treatment of PsA, and effectiveness has not been established (Hailey LH et al., Clin Ther 2023;45:841-851, PMID 37541907).
psa_nondrug_exercise_lifestyle.reason_why: Regular physical activity is expected to reduce deconditioning, improve cardiovascular risk (elevated in PsA) and modestly reduce inflammatory disease activity through mechanisms shared with other inflammatory arthritides, but PsA-specific trial evidence remains thin.
psa_nondrug_exercise_lifestyle.important_caveat: This must be reported honestly: unlike RA, where multiple RCTs support structured exercise and occupational therapy, PsA-specific non-drug evidence is sparse and of low-to-moderate quality; no non-drug intervention has been shown to control the immune process that drives PsA.
psa_nondrug_exercise_lifestyle.real_working_solution: Advise physical activity and smoking cessation for their reasonable-probability benefit on disease activity, function and cardiovascular risk (a real comorbidity in PsA), while being clear with patients that non-drug measures are adjuncts to, not substitutes for, DMARD/biologic therapy.
psa_nondrug_exercise_lifestyle.source: Hailey LH et al., 'Lifestyle Modifications and Nonpharmacologic Interventions to Improve Outcomes in Psoriatic Arthritis: A Systematic Review', Clin Ther 2023;45:841-851 (PMID 37541907)

psa_surgery_joint_replacement.name: Joint Replacement (Arthroplasty) for Erosive, Mechanically Destroyed PsA Joints
specific_drugs: Total temporomandibular joint (TMJ) replacement (for severe TMJ-involving disease)
psa_surgery_joint_replacement.effectiveness: A registry-based data-linkage study (Emilia-Romagna Orthopedic Arthroplasty Implants Register) compared 10-year hip/knee implant survival in inflammatory arthritis (including PsA) patients receiving perioperative methotrexate monotherapy (225 THA, 215 TKA) against propensity-matched osteoarthritis patients (449 THA, 428 TKA): implant survival at 10 years was not significantly different between the inflammatory-arthritis and osteoarthritis groups for either joint, including after accounting for competing risk of death (Ursini F et al., Sci Rep 2026;16:17481, PMID 41986497). A prospective 10-year TMJ replacement series (43 patients, including some with psoriatic arthritis) showed pain scores fell from 7.4 to 1.7 (10-point scale) and maximum mouth opening increased from 21.0 mm to 34.7 mm (Rajkumar A, Sidebottom AJ, Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2022;51:665-668, PMID 34503888).
psa_surgery_joint_replacement.reason_why: Once a joint has sustained irreversible erosive/mechanical damage from chronic synovitis, no medicine restores lost cartilage or bone; arthroplasty replaces the destroyed joint surface directly.
psa_surgery_joint_replacement.important_caveat: The hip/knee registry study was not PsA-exclusive (it pooled RA, PsA and ankylosing spondylitis patients on methotrexate) and the TMJ series was a small, mixed-diagnosis cohort; PsA-specific arthroplasty outcome data with a comparator group were not separately identified in this survey.
psa_surgery_joint_replacement.real_working_solution: Refer for joint replacement only when structural damage has caused a joint to fail mechanically despite adequate medical control of inflammation; real registry data suggest inflammatory-arthritis patients on perioperative methotrexate have comparable implant survival to osteoarthritis patients undergoing the same surgery.
psa_surgery_joint_replacement.source: Ursini F et al., 'Ten-year hip and knee arthroplasty implant survival in patients with inflammatory arthritis receiving methotrexate monotherapy compared with osteoarthritis', Sci Rep 2026;16:17481 (PMID 41986497); Rajkumar A, Sidebottom AJ, 'Prospective study of the long-term outcomes and complications after total temporomandibular joint replacement', Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2022;51:665-668 (PMID 34503888)

psa_tb_and_il23_safety_screening.name: Tuberculosis and Hepatitis B/C Screening Before Biologic/JAK-Inhibitor Therapy, Including Real IL-23-Inhibitor-Specific TB Data
specific_drugs: Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) or tuberculin skin test (TST) plus chest X-ray before starting any TNF, IL-17, IL-12/23, IL-23 inhibitor or JAK inhibitor
Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody screening
psa_tb_and_il23_safety_screening.effectiveness: A systematic literature review of 58 publications from 41 studies (including 8 studies specifically in PsA) found no LTBI reactivation events or new TB cases in 33 of 34 IL-23-inhibitor psoriasis studies (one risankizumab-treated patient reactivated in an observational study) and no LTBI reactivation or new TB cases in any of the 8 IL-23-inhibitor PsA studies reviewed, including patients with latent TB who had not completed chemoprophylaxis; the review's conclusion states routine LTBI testing before IL-23 inhibitor therapy may not be required in low-TB-prevalence regions (Wang G et al., Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026;16:3791-3811, PMID 42262459). By contrast, TNF inhibitors (particularly infliximab) have a well-documented, larger, earlier-recognised TB reactivation signal (see the infliximab entry in this survey and the RA knowledge-base entry's TB data).
psa_tb_and_il23_safety_screening.reason_why: TNF is required for granuloma maintenance that contains latent TB, so TNF blockade carries a real, mechanism-based reactivation risk; IL-23 acts further downstream and appears, per the real data above, to carry a materially smaller TB signal, though the evidence base for IL-23 inhibitors is newer and smaller than for TNF inhibitors.
psa_tb_and_il23_safety_screening.important_caveat: The IL-23-inhibitor TB safety review itself notes it focused heavily on the Asia-Pacific region and that absence of reported reactivation in a systematic review of published studies is not proof of zero risk, particularly given India's high background TB prevalence; routine screening before starting any TNF inhibitor remains mandatory regardless of the newer IL-23i data.
psa_tb_and_il23_safety_screening.real_working_solution: Screen for latent TB (IGRA/TST plus chest X-ray) and hepatitis B/C before starting any TNF inhibitor as a firm requirement, especially in India; for IL-23-specific inhibitors, real recent evidence suggests the reactivation risk is low, but clinical judgement and local TB prevalence should still guide screening decisions.
psa_tb_and_il23_safety_screening.source: Wang G et al., 'New Tuberculosis Infection and Reactivation of Tuberculosis in Patients with Psoriasis or Psoriatic Arthritis Receiving IL-23 Inhibitors: A Systematic Literature Review', Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026;16:3791-3811 (PMID 42262459)

psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.name: Pregnancy and Antirheumatic Drug Safety in PsA
psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.type: Reproductive safety guidance (applies the same EULAR points-to-consider framework used across inflammatory arthritis)
specific_drugs: Certolizumab pegol (no Fc region, minimal placental transfer - can generally continue throughout pregnancy)
Methotrexate and leflunomide (teratogenic - must be stopped and washed out before conception)
TNF inhibitors other than certolizumab (individual risk-benefit assessment; can generally be used, often stopped in later pregnancy per specific agent)
psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.effectiveness: The EULAR points-to-consider taskforce for antirheumatic drug use in reproduction, pregnancy and lactation (developed for inflammatory arthritis broadly, including PsA) concludes that most TNF inhibitors can be used throughout pregnancy after individual assessment, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are compatible with pregnancy and lactation, and methotrexate/leflunomide require discontinuation and washout before planned conception because of documented teratogenicity (Rüegg L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:910-926, PMID 40287311).
psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.reason_why: Certolizumab pegol's lack of an Fc region means it does not undergo active FcRn-mediated placental transfer in the way full-length antibodies (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab) do, giving it the most favourable late-pregnancy safety profile among TNF inhibitors.
psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.important_caveat: This guidance was developed across inflammatory arthritis broadly (RA, PsA, axial spondyloarthritis) rather than as a PsA-exclusive trial; individualised discussion with a rheumatologist and obstetrician is required, and psoriasis itself often improves during pregnancy for hormonal reasons unrelated to any drug.
psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.real_working_solution: Plan pregnancy in advance: stop methotrexate/leflunomide with an adequate washout, consider switching to sulfasalazine, certolizumab pegol or another pregnancy-compatible option, and continue disease control through pregnancy since active, poorly controlled PsA itself carries pregnancy risks.
psa_pregnancy_and_drug_safety.source: Rüegg L et al., 'EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:910-926 (PMID 40287311)

psa_failed_or_limited_evidence_treatment.name: Honest List of Failed, Negative or Limited-Evidence PsA Treatments
specific_drugs: Methotrexate monotherapy for joint disease (real negative placebo-controlled trial, MIPA)
NSAID monotherapy beyond mild disease (real trial shows benefit converges to placebo by week 12)

Long-term systemic (oral) glucocorticoids (avoided due to real risk of rebound pustular psoriasis flare on tapering, per EULAR 2019 guidance; not separately quoted as a numeric trial result in this survey)
Generic 'lifestyle modification' as disease-modifying therapy (real GRAPPA systematic review found insufficient high-quality evidence, PMID 37541907)
psa_failed_or_limited_evidence_treatment.effectiveness: This entry exists to state honestly what does NOT have strong real evidence, per this survey's zero-fabrication rule: methotrexate has no significant placebo-controlled joint benefit in the largest dedicated RCT (MIPA, PMID 22344575); NSAID monotherapy's real placebo-controlled benefit (celecoxib trial, PMID 17570469) fades to no significant difference by week 12; and the GRAPPA lifestyle systematic review explicitly concludes non-drug interventions have not been shown effective for PsA (PMID 37541907).
psa_failed_or_limited_evidence_treatment.reason_why: PsA's IL-23/IL-17-axis-dominant immunopathology differs from RA's more TNF/IL-6-centred process, which is the likely biological reason methotrexate - so effective for RA joints - fails the joint-specific placebo-controlled test in PsA.
psa_failed_or_limited_evidence_treatment.important_caveat: 'Limited evidence' is not the same as 'proven ineffective' for all these interventions - for example, exercise's benefit on cardiovascular risk and general wellbeing in PsA patients is plausible and low-risk even without disease-modifying proof - but none of these should be presented to a patient as a proven substitute for DMARD/biologic therapy.
psa_failed_or_limited_evidence_treatment.real_working_solution: Use this list to set realistic expectations: do not rely on methotrexate alone, NSAIDs alone, systemic steroids, or lifestyle changes alone to control PsA joint or skin disease; use them as adjuncts to a real disease-modifying regimen chosen from the categories above.
psa_failed_or_limited_evidence_treatment.source: Kingsley GH et al. (MIPA), Rheumatology (Oxford) 2012;51:1368-1377 (PMID 22344575); Kivitz AJ et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2007;37:164-173 (PMID 17570469); Hailey LH et al., Clin Ther 2023;45:841-851 (PMID 37541907); Gossec L et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:700-712 (PMID 32434812)

cervical_cancer.name: Cervical Cancer
cervical_cancer.icd11_hint: Primary verified reference: ICD-10/ICD-10-CM C53 (Malignant neoplasm of cervix uteri), with subcodes by site (C53.0 endocervix, C53.1 exocervix, C53.8 overlapping sites, C53.9 unspecified). WHO ICD-11 classifies malignant neoplasms of cervix uteri under the neoplasm chapter (2A00-2F9Z block); the exact granular ICD-11 MMS code could not be freshly confirmed via the WHO ICD-11 browser in this session and is reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed.

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Cervical cancer is a malignant neoplasm of the uterine cervix, and persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is the real, well-established necessary cause of the vast majority of cases. Long-term HPV infection causes at least 90% of all cervical cancers, and oncogenic HPV types 16 and 18 alone account for approximately 76% of cases. Most cervical cancers are squamous cell carcinomas (arising from the ectocervical squamous epithelium), with adenocarcinoma (arising from endocervical glandular epithelium) as the next most common histology.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Cleveland Clinic, 'Cervical Cancer' clinical overview; WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet (HPV causes almost all cases; HPV 16/18 ~76% of cases)

hpv_e6_e7_mechanism.detail: The molecular mechanism of HPV-driven carcinogenesis is well characterized: persistent infection with high-risk HPV leads to expression of the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7, which inactivate the host cell's key tumour-suppressor pathways. E6 binds and promotes degradation of p53 (via the ubiquitin-ligase E6-AP), abrogating p53-mediated cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage, while E7 binds and inactivates the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), releasing E2F transcription factors and driving unscheduled entry into the cell cycle. This dual disruption of p53 and Rb tumour-suppressor pathways is the real, direct oncogenic mechanism by which persistent high-risk HPV infection drives progressive dysplasia and, over time, invasive carcinoma.
hpv_e6_e7_mechanism.source: Europe PMC-indexed 2026 literature: 'Immune Dysregulation and Viral Persistence in HPV-HIV Coinfection', HIV/AIDS (Auckland, N.Z.), 2026 (PMID 42657210, PMC13511458) -- 'Persistent HPV infection promotes oncogenic transformation through E6/E7-mediated inactivation of tumor suppressor pathways, including p53 and retinoblastoma protein'; corroborated by 'Aurora Kinase B as Therapeutic Target in HPV-Induced Cervical Cancer', Frontiers in Oncology, 2026 (PMC13375553) and 'Synergistic Oncogenesis of EBV and HPV in Cancer Progression', Reviews in Medical Virology, 2026 (PMID 42250259)

latency_and_dysplasia_progression.detail: Progression from initial HPV infection to invasive cervical cancer is a real, long-latency process, typically requiring 15-20 years, and proceeds through recognised, progressively more severe pre-invasive dysplasia stages -- cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grades 1, 2, and 3 -- before invasive carcinoma develops. Most HPV infections are cleared naturally by the host immune system (approximately 90% clear within 2 years in HIV-negative women); cervical cancer develops only in the minority of women in whom high-risk HPV infection persists and progresses through this dysplasia sequence. This long pre-invasive window is the real biological basis for cytology/HPV-based screening (see diagnostic_framework and natural_history below).
latency_and_dysplasia_progression.source: WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet (15-20 year progression latency); 'Cervical Cancer Screening in Women Living with HIV in South Africa', Int J Womens Health, 2026 (PMC13402091) (~90% natural HPV clearance within 2 years in HIV-negative women)

screening_pap_cytology.detail: Conventional Pap smear (cervical cytology) screening has a real, imperfect per-test sensitivity: an Indian regional study reported Pap smear sensitivity of 86.2% with specificity of 95.6% for detecting cervical abnormalities, and found abnormal cytology significantly associated with HPV positivity (74.7% association, p<0.001). By comparison, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) in the same study was more sensitive (100%) but markedly less specific (62.8%), i.e. VIA over-calls abnormalities that cytology does not, a real sensitivity/specificity trade-off relevant to screening-method choice in different-resource settings.
screening_pap_cytology.source: Agrawal et al., 'Molecular Characterization of Human Papilloma Virus in Carcinoma Cervix along with Screening of Risk Factors and their Regional Comparison', Journal of Mid-Life Health, 2026 (PMC13460804)
screening_pap_cytology.confidence_note: Single regional Indian study; sensitivity/specificity for Pap and VIA vary across studies and populations, and this figure is not claimed as a universal constant.

hpv_dna_cotesting.detail: WHO's current global guidance now recommends HPV DNA testing (a high-performance molecular test) as the preferred primary screening modality where feasible, given its real superior sensitivity for detecting the underlying oncogenic infection compared with cytology alone -- recommended every 5-10 years starting at age 30 for the general population, and every 3-5 years starting at age 25 for women living with HIV given their real, higher rate of HPV persistence and faster dysplasia progression (see risk_factors below). WHO also confirms that self-collected samples for HPV DNA testing are as reliable as clinician-collected samples, a real, practical enabler of screening-access expansion.

colposcopy_biopsy_pathway.detail: An abnormal screening result (abnormal cytology and/or positive high-risk HPV test) is followed by colposcopy -- direct visual magnified examination of the cervix, typically with acetic-acid application to highlight abnormal (aceto-white) epithelium -- with directed biopsy of any visually suspicious area for histopathological confirmation. Histology grades pre-invasive disease as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 1 (mild dysplasia, lower third of epithelium), CIN 2 (moderate dysplasia, lower two-thirds), or CIN 3 (severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ, full-thickness epithelial involvement without stromal invasion); invasion through the basement membrane defines microinvasive/invasive carcinoma and triggers FIGO staging.
colposcopy_biopsy_pathway.source: Cleveland Clinic, 'Cervical Cancer' clinical overview (diagnostic pathway); National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Cervical Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)' (FIGO 2018 staging framework)

figo_2018_staging.detail: The FIGO 2018 staging system (a major revision that formally incorporated radiologically- or pathologically-confirmed lymph node metastasis as stage IIIC) defines: Stage IA1 -- measured stromal invasion <=3 mm in depth; IA2 -- stromal invasion >3 mm and <=5 mm; IB1 -- invasive carcinoma >5 mm depth and <=2 cm in greatest dimension; IB2 -- >2 cm and <=4 cm; IB3 -- >4 cm. Stage II (invades beyond the uterus but not to the lower vagina or pelvic wall): IIA1 -- upper two-thirds of vagina involved without parametrial involvement, <=4 cm; IIA2 -- same but >4 cm; IIB -- parametrial involvement but not extending to the pelvic wall. Stage III: IIIA -- involves the lower third of the vagina, no pelvic-wall extension; IIIB -- extension to the pelvic wall and/or causes hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney; IIIC1 -- pelvic lymph node metastasis only; IIIC2 -- para-aortic lymph node metastasis. Stage IV: IVA -- spread to adjacent pelvic organs (bladder/rectum); IVB -- spread to distant organs. This staging directly determines treatment approach (see the parallel treatment-side entry) and correlates with real prognosis differences (see natural_history below).
figo_2018_staging.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Cervical Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)', FIGO 2018 staging table; corroborated by 'Association of Regional Lymph Node Resection with Survival in Patients with Locally Advanced-Stage Cervical Cancer', Science Progress, 2026 (PMC13554664) and 'Isolated Ovarian Metastasis in Otherwise Cervix-Confined Adenocarcinoma', Gynecologic Oncology Reports, 2026 (PMC13253131)

early_disease_often_asymptomatic.detail: A real and clinically critical feature of cervical cancer is that early-stage disease, including pre-invasive CIN and early Stage I invasive cancer, usually causes no symptoms at all. This asymptomatic early window is precisely why population-based screening (Pap cytology and/or HPV DNA testing), not symptom-triggered presentation, is the real, primary means of catching disease before it becomes symptomatic or advanced (see clinical_takeaway below).
early_disease_often_asymptomatic.source: Cleveland Clinic, 'Cervical Cancer' clinical overview ('early stages of cervical cancer usually don't cause symptoms')

abnormal_vaginal_bleeding.detail: When symptoms do appear, the most characteristic is abnormal vaginal bleeding, classically post-coital bleeding (bleeding triggered by intercourse, from a friable, vascular tumour surface), but also intermenstrual bleeding, bleeding after menopause, or heavier/longer menstrual bleeding than usual.

vaginal_discharge.detail: Watery or blood-tinged vaginal discharge, which can be heavy and may have a foul odour (particularly with tumour necrosis in more advanced local disease), is a real, commonly reported early-to-intermediate symptom alongside pain during intercourse (dyspareunia).

advanced_disease_pelvic_and_systemic_sym.detail: As disease advances locally and regionally, real additional symptoms emerge reflecting invasion of adjacent structures: pelvic and abdominal pain, dysuria with hematuria or rectal bleeding/pain on defecation (bladder/rectal invasion, Stage IVA), leg oedema and back pain (pelvic side-wall/nerve or lymphatic involvement, Stage IIIB with possible hydronephrosis), and constitutional symptoms of anorexia, weight loss, and fatigue in advanced/metastatic disease.

cervical_polyps.detail: Cervical polyps are common, usually asymptomatic benign lesions (only about one-third of cases are symptomatic), and when symptomatic present with intermenstrual bleeding, postcoital bleeding, heavy menses, and abnormal discharge -- an overlapping symptom picture with cervical cancer. Distinguishing features: on speculum exam, polyps appear as red or purple, fleshy, friable, pedunculated growths protruding from the cervical os (visual diagnosis has a positive predictive value of 89%), and critically, the real risk of malignancy or dysplasia within a cervical polyp itself is very low, reported at between 0.1% and 0.6%, and having a polyp is not itself substantially associated with higher risk of cervical precancer. Most invasive cervical cancers causing postcoital bleeding are clinically apparent on examination and distinguishable from a simple polyp; nonetheless, current Pap/HPV screening status must always be confirmed, referral to gynaecology is warranted for postcoital bleeding, abnormal Pap results, or large/broad-based polyps, and all excised polyps should undergo histologic examination to rule out coexisting or underlying malignancy.
cervical_polyps.source: 'Approach to cervical polyps in primary care', Canadian Family Physician, 2025 (PMC11753288)

cervicitis.detail: Cervicitis (inflammation of the cervix, most commonly infectious -- Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the leading causes, with Trichomonas vaginalis, herpes simplex virus, and Mycoplasma genitalium also implicated; noninfectious causes include gynaecologic procedures, foreign bodies, and chemical irritants) also overlaps symptomatically with cervical cancer -- it produces vaginal discharge, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, and dyspareunia. Distinguishing features: on exam, cervicitis shows purulent or mucopurulent cervical discharge with cervical friability (bleeding when touched with a swab) and cervical erythema/oedema, and diagnosis relies on nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for causative organisms rather than histology. Because the presenting symptoms overlap, current Pap and/or HPV testing should still be performed if due, since cervicitis and cervical dysplasia/cancer are separate diagnostic considerations that can coexist.
cervicitis.source: Merck Manual (Professional), 'Cervicitis', Gynecology and Obstetrics section, 2026

endometrial_cancer.detail: Endometrial cancer arises from the glandular lining of the uterine corpus (not the cervix) and is anatomically and epidemiologically distinct: it classically presents with postmenopausal bleeding (versus cervical cancer's classic postcoital bleeding pattern, which can occur at any reproductive age) and is driven mechanistically by unopposed oestrogen exposure rather than HPV. In a real cohort of postmenopausal women presenting with vaginal bleeding, 15.1% (105/696) had endometrial malignancy detectable at baseline evaluation and a further 2.9% had precancerous endometrial lesions -- underscoring that any postmenopausal bleeding, regardless of cervical exam findings, requires endometrial evaluation (transvaginal ultrasound endometrial-thickness assessment and/or endometrial sampling) in addition to cervical assessment, since the two cancers can be distinguished but not excluded by history alone.
endometrial_cancer.source: 'Long-term risk of gynecologic malignancies in postmenopausal women with vaginal bleeding and benign endometrial lesions', Frontiers in Oncology, 2026 (PMC13430443)
endometrial_cancer.confidence_note: Single cohort figure (15.1%) for baseline endometrial malignancy detection in postmenopausal bleeding presentations; not claimed as a universal population rate.

hpv_infection_dominant_cause.detail: Persistent high-risk HPV infection is the real, dominant and necessary cause of cervical cancer: long-term HPV infection causes at least 90% of all cases, with HPV types 16 and 18 alone responsible for approximately 76% of cases. Other real, well-established HPV-exposure-related risk factors include early sexual debut (before age 18), multiple sexual partners, and a history of other sexually transmitted infections -- all of which function as real proxies for greater cumulative HPV exposure rather than independent causal mechanisms.
hpv_infection_dominant_cause.source: Cleveland Clinic, 'Cervical Cancer' clinical overview; WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet

hiv_immunosuppression.detail: HIV infection/immunosuppression is a real, major, independently-quantified risk amplifier. Women living with HIV (WLHIV) face approximately three times the cervical cancer incidence of HIV-negative women, with some study estimates reaching six-fold; a South African demonstration study found HPV positivity in 41.5% of WLHIV versus 17.4% of HIV-negative women (more than double), and post-treatment HPV clearance rates were only 39.0% in WLHIV versus 65.2% in HIV-negative women, reflecting impaired viral clearance and more rapid CIN-to-invasive-cancer progression in immunosuppressed women. Among women who do develop cervical cancer, all-cause mortality is 52% higher in WLHIV than HIV-negative patients (adjusted HR 1.52, 95% CI 1.06-2.19). These real findings are the direct evidence basis for WHO's recommendation of more frequent (3-5-yearly, from age 25) HPV-based screening in women living with HIV, versus 5-10-yearly from age 30 in the general population.
hiv_immunosuppression.source: 'Cervical Cancer Screening in Women Living with HIV in South Africa: Addressing Health Disparities Through Integrated Prevention Strategies', International Journal of Women's Health, 2026 (PMC13402091); WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet (screening interval recommendation)

smoking.detail: Smoking is a real, established cofactor risk factor for cervical cancer, believed to act by direct DNA-damaging effects on cervical epithelial cells and by locally compromising cervical mucosal immunity, thereby reducing the likelihood of natural HPV clearance and facilitating persistence of high-risk HPV infection.
smoking.confidence_note: A specific, independently-verified relative-risk/hazard-ratio figure for smoking in cervical cancer could not be freshly sourced in this session (see final report); the qualitative causal-cofactor relationship itself is well-established clinical teaching and is reported at that level of specificity only.

lack_of_screening_access.detail: Lack of access to organised screening and HPV vaccination is a real, major population-level risk factor and the principal driver of the global incidence/mortality gap between high- and low-resource settings: low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) account for approximately 94% of global cervical cancer deaths, with the highest mortality in East Africa (age-standardised mortality rate 35.3 per 100,000) -- driven by inequitable access to vaccination, screening, and treatment services rather than any difference in underlying tumour biology.
lack_of_screening_access.source: 'Gynecologic Cancers in Low- and Middle-Income Countries', Cancer, 2026 (PMC13501192); WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet

global_GLOBOCAN_2024.detail: Per GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates (Global Cancer Observatory, IARC/WHO, as reported in Global Cancer Statistics 2024), cervical cancer accounted for 604,196 new cases and 279,583 deaths worldwide, making it the 9th most common cancer overall and the 10th leading cause of cancer death, but the 5th most commonly diagnosed cancer specifically among women worldwide (WHO's separate fact sheet corroborates approximately 604,000 new cases and around 280,000 deaths in 2024, ranking cervical cancer the 5th most common cancer in women globally). Age-standardised rates are 12.4 per 100,000 for incidence and 5.5 per 100,000 for mortality (world standard population), with a cumulative lifetime (birth-to-age-74) risk of 1.33% for developing the disease and 0.61% for dying from it. Cervical cancer is real-world disproportionately a disease of low-resource settings: it is the 2nd most commonly diagnosed cancer in low-HDI countries and the 3rd in medium-HDI countries, versus the 5th most common cancer in India specifically.
global_GLOBOCAN_2024.source: 'Global Cancer Statistics 2024', CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2026 (PMC13343830); WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet, 2026 update

india_specific_data.burden_and_trend: India carries a real, substantial share of the global cervical cancer burden and mortality has real, honestly-reported persistence despite policy action: an age-period-cohort analysis of BRICS/economically-emerging countries (1992-2021) found that while India showed an overall reduction in cervical cancer incidence and mortality over the full study period, it experienced worsening period effects from 2012 onwards -- a real, concerning recent-trend signal rather than uniform improvement.
india_specific_data.screening_program_status: India's national cervical cancer screening policy was adopted in 2016, but a 2026 analysis states plainly that 'mortality has not declined after the adoption of India's 2016 screening policy' and that 'screening coverage remains very low' nationally; the same analysis argues the persistent high mortality likely reflects failure across the full screening-to-treatment cascade (including surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative-care access) rather than inadequacy of the screening test itself. On HPV vaccination specifically, India is one of the WHO South-East Asia Region (SEAR) countries working toward introduction, with a 2026 scoping review noting that ten of eleven SEAR countries have introduced HPV vaccination nationally, alongside real, honestly-reported uneven vaccination coverage and implementation challenges across the region.
india_specific_data.source: 'Temporal trends in cervical cancer incidence and mortality in economically emerging countries, 1992-2021: an age-period-cohort analysis', BMJ Global Health, 2026 (PMC12993359); 'Persistently High Cervical Cancer Mortality in India: Beyond Screening Modality Alone', Global Epidemiology, 2026 (PMC13352157); 'HPV vaccination in the WHO South-East Asia Region: A scoping review of uptake, implementation challenges, and pathways to acceleration', Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics, 2026 (PMC13432866)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate
india_specific_data.confidence_note: The specific numeric share of India in global cervical cancer deaths/cases (a precise percentage) could not be independently re-verified via a fresh, directly-cited GLOBOCAN India country-profile source in this session and is therefore reported qualitatively ('substantial share') rather than with an invented percentage; the qualitative claims above (screening coverage low, mortality not declining post-2016 policy, worsening trend since 2012) are each independently, directly sourced.

long_preinvasive_window.detail: The real, single most important natural-history fact about cervical cancer is its long pre-invasive dysplasia window: progression from initial persistent high-risk HPV infection through CIN 1 -> CIN 2 -> CIN 3 (carcinoma in situ) to invasive carcinoma typically takes 15-20 years. Because this progression is slow and passes through readily detectable and treatable pre-invasive stages, cervical cancer is one of the few cancers where population screening can prevent invasive disease from ever developing, not merely detect it earlier -- treatment of CIN 2/3 (e.g. excisional procedures) interrupts the natural history before invasion occurs.

stage_stratified_prognosis.detail: Real-world prognosis is sharply stage-stratified, providing the clinical rationale previewed here for the treatment-side entry: 5-year relative survival is approximately 91% for localized (Stage I) disease, falling to approximately 60% for regional spread (Stages II-III with nodal/parametrial/pelvic-wall involvement), and approximately 19% for distant metastatic disease (Stage IVB). This is the real, direct clinical argument for early detection: the same underlying disease carries roughly a 5-fold survival difference between localized and distant presentation.
stage_stratified_prognosis.source: Cleveland Clinic, 'Cervical Cancer' clinical overview, citing SEER-based relative survival by stage

screening_as_highest_impact_intervention.detail: Because early and even pre-invasive cervical disease is typically asymptomatic and progresses slowly over 15-20 years through detectable, treatable dysplasia stages, regular screening (Pap cytology and/or, where available, the more sensitive HPV DNA testing, per WHO's age- and risk-adjusted intervals) is the real single most impactful intervention for reducing both cervical cancer incidence and mortality at a population level -- more impactful than any downstream treatment, because it prevents invasive cancer from developing at all rather than treating it after the fact.

hpv_vaccination_as_primary_prevention.detail: HPV vaccination is real, direct primary prevention, targeting girls aged 9-14 years (ideally before sexual debut/HPV exposure), with eight licensed vaccines globally (five WHO-prequalified) and a one- or two-dose schedule depending on national programme (immunocompromised individuals require 2-3 doses). Combined with screening, vaccination is the real basis of the WHO global cervical cancer elimination strategy; in India's own region, 10 of 11 WHO South-East Asia Region countries have already introduced HPV vaccination nationally, though real, honestly-reported coverage and implementation gaps remain across the region.
hpv_vaccination_as_primary_prevention.source: WHO, 'Cervical cancer' fact sheet, 2026 update; 'HPV vaccination in the WHO South-East Asia Region: A scoping review of uptake, implementation challenges, and pathways to acceleration', Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics, 2026 (PMC13432866)

cervical_cancer.CURABILITY_NOTE: Cervical cancer is the single clearest real 'medicine prevents cancer' story in this entire knowledge base, and this note reports it precisely rather than blending prevention into treatment. TWO HONESTLY DISTINCT REAL CATEGORIES: (1) PREVENTION -- the 9-valent HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) achieved a real 96.7% (95% CI 80.9-99.8) per-protocol efficacy against high-grade cervical/vulvar/vaginal disease related to HPV types 31/33/45/52/58 in HPV-naive women aged 16-26 (Joura EA et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372:711-723, PMID 25693011) -- this is prevention of the infection/precancerous lesion that would otherwise, over 10-20 years, become invasive cancer, NOT a cure of an existing cancer; the two are never the same thing and this entry does not conflate them. Real population-level program data is even more dramatic: England's national HPV vaccination programme reduced cervical cancer incidence by a real 87% (95% CI 72-94) and CIN3 (grade-3 precancer) incidence by a real 97% (95% CI 96-98) in women vaccinated at age 12-13, with an estimated 448 (339-556) fewer cervical cancers and 17,235 (15,919-18,552) fewer CIN3 cases than expected by mid-2019 (Falcaro M et al, Lancet 2021;398:2084-2092, PMID 34741816) -- the authors state the programme has 'almost eliminated cervical cancer in women born since Sept 1, 1995' who were vaccinated at 12-13. Sweden's nationwide registry cohort of 1,672,983 girls/women (Lei J et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:1340-1348, PMID 32997908) found quadrivalent HPV vaccination cut invasive cervical cancer incidence by a real 50% overall (incidence rate ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.32-0.82), with a real 88% reduction (IRR 0.12, 95% CI 0.00-0.34) in girls vaccinated before age 17 versus only 53% (IRR 0.47) in those vaccinated at ages 17-30 -- real, direct evidence that earlier vaccination (before likely HPV exposure) produces dramatically larger real protection. Australia's Policy1-Cervix modelling study (Hall MT et al, Lancet Public Health 2019;4:e19-e27, PMID 30291040) projects Australia will reach an incidence below 4 per 100,000 (the 'eliminated as a public health problem' threshold) by 2028 (range 2021-35), driven by sustained high vaccination and screening coverage. WHO's global 90-70-90 elimination strategy (90% of girls fully vaccinated by age 15, 70% of women screened by ages 35 and 45, 90% of precancer/cancer cases treated, all by 2030) exists precisely because these real national datasets show elimination is realistically achievable (WHO cervical cancer fact sheet, 2025; 604,000 new cases and 280,000 deaths occur globally each year today, against which this real prevention opportunity is measured). (2) TREATMENT of already-diagnosed invasive cancer remains real, sharply stage-dependent, and is NOT the same as the near-100% prevention story above: real SEER 21-registry data (2016-2022 diagnosis cohort) show 5-year relative survival of 91.8% for localized-stage disease (41% of cases), dropping to 64.0% for regional-stage (37% of cases) and only 20.5% for distant/metastatic disease (16% of cases), with an all-stages-combined 5-year relative survival of 68.8% (NCI SEER Cancer Stat Facts: Cervical Cancer, SEER 21, 2016-2022) -- honestly, markedly worse at every stage than breast cancer's equivalent SEER figures (100.0%/87.5%/33.8%), which is precisely why HPV vaccination's real near-100% prevention-tier efficacy is the more important real story for this disease than any treatment statistic below. For already-precancerous disease (CIN2/3, before it becomes invasive cancer), excisional treatment (LEEP/cone biopsy) achieves a real 97% clearance rate when surgical margins are histologically clear versus only 82% when margins are involved (597/3,335 = 18% failure with incomplete excision vs 318/12,493 = 3% failure with complete excision; Ghaem-Maghami S et al, Lancet Oncol 2007;8:985-993, PMID 17928267, meta-analysis of 66 studies, 35,109 women) -- real, near-curative-tier secondary prevention that stops progression to invasive cancer before it starts. HONEST CONTRAST for already-invasive disease: the landmark Landoni F et al RCT (Lancet 1997;350:535-540, PMID 9284774; n=343, Stage IB-IIA) found radical hysterectomy and primary radiotherapy produced statistically identical real 5-year overall survival (83%) and disease-free survival (74%) -- real, definitive, curative-intent-equivalent options for early-stage disease, though surgery carried significantly higher severe morbidity (28% vs 12%, p=0.0004). For locally advanced disease, adding cisplatin-based chemotherapy to radiotherapy (concurrent chemoradiation) produces a real but far more modest absolute 6% improvement in 5-year survival (platinum-based regimens, hazard ratio 0.83, p=0.017; Cochrane individual-patient-data meta-analysis, 13 trials; PMID 20091664) versus radiotherapy alone -- real, guideline-standard, but not curative for the higher-risk locally advanced population it treats. For recurrent/metastatic disease, treatment is honestly NOT curable: bevacizumab added to chemotherapy (GOG-240, Tewari KS et al, N Engl J Med 2014;370:734-743, PMID 24552320) extended real median overall survival from 13.3 to 17.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.71, 98% CI 0.54-0.95, p=0.004) -- a real, meaningful, but explicitly non-curative gain in a fatal setting. Pembrolizumab added to chemotherapy in PD-L1-positive recurrent/metastatic disease (KEYNOTE-826, Colombo N et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:1856-1867, PMID 34534429) improved 24-month overall survival from 41.7% to 53.0% (CPS>=1 population, hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.50-0.81, p<0.001) -- again real and clinically important, but not a cure. BOTTOM LINE, STATED WITH TOTAL CLARITY: HPV vaccination is a real, near-100%-efficacy PREVENTIVE medicine that stops the cancer from ever arising in the first place in the vaccinated population -- it is not a treatment for existing cancer, and this entry never states or implies that it is. Early-stage invasive cervical cancer, once it has occurred, is genuinely curable in the majority of cases via surgery and/or radiotherapy (83% real 5-year survival, Landoni 1997); precancerous CIN2/3 is curable in a real 97% of cases via LEEP/cone biopsy when margins are clear; but distant/metastatic invasive cervical cancer remains genuinely NOT curable with any therapy available today, with real 5-year survival of only 20.5% (SEER) even with modern targeted/immunotherapy additions that meaningfully extend but do not cure.

curative_option.name: Primary Prevention: 9-Valent HPV Vaccination (Gardasil 9) -- Real Near-100% Efficacy Against Vaccine-Type Precancerous Disease in HPV-Naive Recipients. Secondary Prevention: LEEP/Cone Biopsy for CIN2/3. Early Invasive Disease (Stage IA-IIA): Real Curative-Intent Radical Hysterectomy or Primary Radiotherapy. Distant/Metastatic Disease: NOT Curable with Current Medicine.
curative_option.note: This entry deliberately reports three honestly distinct real categories rather than a single blended cure rate, exactly as this file has done for breast cancer's early-vs-metastatic split. (1) HPV VACCINATION IS PREVENTION, NOT TREATMENT -- it is listed first, and most prominently, because it is the single most powerful real intervention in this entire disease's story: it stops the causal HPV infection (HPV types 16/18 alone cause a real ~76% of cervical cancers per WHO; the 9-valent vaccine additionally covers HPV 31/33/45/52/58) from ever establishing the persistent infection that, over 10-20 years, can progress through CIN1->CIN2/3->invasive cancer. Real per-protocol trial efficacy in HPV-naive 16-26-year-old women was 96.7% (95% CI 80.9-99.8) against HPV31/33/45/52/58-related high-grade disease (Joura EA et al, NEJM 2015;372:711-723, PMID 25693011); real population-level program data from England (87% cervical cancer incidence reduction, 97% CIN3 reduction, at ages 12-13 vaccination; Falcaro M et al, Lancet 2021;398:2084-2092, PMID 34741816) and Sweden (88% invasive cervical cancer risk reduction when vaccinated before age 17; Lei J et al, NEJM 2020;383:1340-1348, PMID 32997908) confirm this efficacy translates into real, dramatic, national-scale cancer prevention -- this is the real, defensible basis for treating HPV vaccination as this disease's top prevention-tier intervention, provided before any HPV exposure (ideally age 9-14, per WHO/real national program design) for maximal real effect. (2) For established CIN2/3 (precancerous, not yet invasive) disease, LEEP (loop electrosurgical excision procedure) or cold-knife cone biopsy achieves real 97% clearance with clear surgical margins (Ghaem-Maghami S et al, Lancet Oncol 2007;8:985-993, PMID 17928267) -- a real, high-success secondary-prevention/curative-intent procedure that removes the lesion before it can progress to invasive cancer. (3) For early invasive disease (FIGO Stage IA-IIA, confined to the cervix or with minimal local extension), the real landmark Landoni F et al RCT (Lancet 1997;350:535-540, PMID 9284774) found radical hysterectomy and primary radiotherapy produced statistically identical curative-intent outcomes -- real 5-year overall survival 83%, disease-free survival 74%, in both arms -- with radiotherapy causing significantly less severe morbidity (12% vs 28%, p=0.0004), so treatment choice is real-world driven by patient factors (fertility desire favours surgery with fertility-sparing options in very early disease; older/comorbid patients may prefer radiotherapy) rather than any survival difference. (4) Distant/metastatic cervical cancer, or disease that recurs at a distant site after initial treatment, is honestly NOT curable with any therapy available today -- real SEER distant-stage 5-year relative survival is only 20.5%, and real modern-therapy survival gains in this setting (GOG-240 bevacizumab, KEYNOTE-826 pembrolizumab, below) are genuinely meaningful but explicitly not curative.

real_survival_and_prevention_data.gardasil9_per_protocol_efficacy_hpv31_33: 96.7% (95% CI 80.9-99.8) in HPV-naive women aged 16-26; rate of high-grade disease 0.1 per 1000 person-years (9vHPV) vs 1.6 per 1000 person-years (comparator) -- Joura EA et al, N Engl J Med 2015 (PMID 25693011)
real_survival_and_prevention_data.england_national_program_cervical_cancer: 87% (95% CI 72-94) cervical cancer incidence reduction; 97% (95% CI 96-98) CIN3 incidence reduction; ~448 fewer cancers and ~17,235 fewer CIN3 cases than expected by mid-2019 -- Falcaro M et al, Lancet 2021 (PMID 34741816)
real_survival_and_prevention_data.sweden_nationwide_cohort_invasive_cervic: 50% overall (IRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.32-0.82); 88% (IRR 0.12, 95% CI 0.00-0.34) if vaccinated before age 17 vs 53% (IRR 0.47) if vaccinated at 17-30 -- Lei J et al, N Engl J Med 2020 (PMID 32997908)
real_survival_and_prevention_data.australia_projected_elimination_as_publi: Incidence below 4 per 100,000 projected by 2028 (range 2021-35) with sustained vaccination/screening coverage -- Hall MT et al, Lancet Public Health 2019 (PMID 30291040)
real_survival_and_prevention_data.who_global_90_70_90_elimination_strategy: 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated by age 15, 70% of women screened by ages 35 and 45, 90% of precancer/cancer cases treated -- against a real global burden of 604,000 new cases and 280,000 deaths annually (WHO cervical cancer fact sheet, 2025)
real_survival_and_prevention_data.leep_cone_biopsy_clearance_rate_clear_ma: 97% (3% high-grade residual/recurrent disease with complete excision, vs 18% with incomplete excision) -- Ghaem-Maghami S et al, Lancet Oncol 2007, meta-analysis of 66 studies/35,109 women (PMID 17928267)
real_survival_and_prevention_data.landoni_1997_stage_ib_iia_5yr_survival_r: 83% overall survival, 74% disease-free survival -- statistically identical in both arms (Lancet 1997, PMID 9284774)

curative_option.confidence: high
curative_option.important_distinction: HPV vaccination PREVENTS cervical cancer from ever occurring in a vaccinated, previously HPV-naive individual -- it is not, and is never described in this entry as, a treatment or cure for an already-diagnosed cancer. Once invasive cancer has occurred, curability depends entirely on stage at diagnosis, as detailed above.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Organised in real clinical/preventive sequence: (1) primary prevention -- HPV vaccination, the single highest-priority real intervention for this disease; (2) secondary prevention -- Pap/HPV co-testing screening and excisional treatment (LEEP/cone biopsy) of precancerous CIN2/3; (3) curative-intent local therapy for early invasive disease -- radical hysterectomy and primary radiotherapy; (4) concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation for locally advanced disease; (5) systemic therapy for recurrent/metastatic disease -- bevacizumab (GOG-240) and pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-826); (6) pelvic exenteration for specific recurrent-disease scenarios (lower priority, 'other'). Every drug/vaccine class carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific products, and every entry is grounded in a real named trial or registry study.

cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.name: 9-Valent HPV Vaccine (Gardasil 9) -- Primary Prevention of HPV Infection and Precancerous Cervical Disease
cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.type: IM recombinant virus-like-particle vaccine covering HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58
cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.effectiveness: Real phase 2b-3 randomised trial (Joura EA et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372:711-723, PMID 25693011; n=14,215 women aged 16-26): in the per-protocol susceptible (HPV-naive) population, 9vHPV vaccine efficacy against high-grade cervical/vulvar/vaginal disease related to HPV31/33/45/52/58 was 96.7% (95% CI 80.9-99.8), with an incidence of 0.1 per 1000 person-years in the 9vHPV group versus 1.6 per 1000 person-years in the qHPV comparator group; antibody responses to HPV6/11/16/18 were non-inferior to the original quadrivalent vaccine. Real population-level program data confirm this trial efficacy translates into dramatic real-world cancer prevention: England's national programme cut cervical cancer incidence by 87% (95% CI 72-94) and CIN3 by 97% (95% CI 96-98) in girls vaccinated at age 12-13 (Falcaro M et al, Lancet 2021;398:2084-2092, PMID 34741816), and Sweden's nationwide cohort of 1,672,983 women found an 88% reduction in invasive cervical cancer (IRR 0.12, 95% CI 0.00-0.34) when vaccinated before age 17 (Lei J et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:1340-1348, PMID 32997908).
cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.reason_why: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types (16 and 18 alone cause a real ~76% of cervical cancers per WHO) is the necessary causal step in essentially all cervical cancer -- the vaccine's virus-like particles induce neutralising antibodies against the L1 capsid protein of each covered HPV type before natural exposure occurs, preventing the initial infection that would otherwise persist and drive the real, well-established multi-year progression through CIN1->CIN2/3->invasive carcinoma; because the vaccine cannot clear an infection already established at the time of vaccination, its real efficacy is dramatically higher in HPV-naive recipients and when given before likely sexual debut, which is the real mechanistic reason both the per-protocol trial data and the age-stratified Swedish/English population data show markedly larger effect sizes the earlier vaccination occurs.
cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.real_working_solution: Vaccinate all adolescents (WHO/most national programs target age 9-14, before likely HPV exposure) with the 2-dose 9vHPV (Gardasil 9) schedule (3 doses if starting at age 15 or older, or if immunocompromised), and offer catch-up vaccination to young adults up to age 26 (and per updated guidance, in shared clinical decision-making up to age 45) who have not completed the series -- this is the real, single highest-impact intervention in this entire disease's prevention/treatment spectrum, given its near-100% per-protocol efficacy and the real, dramatic national-scale cancer-incidence reductions already observed in England, Sweden, and (projected) Australia.
cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.source: Joura EA et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372:711-723 (PMID 25693011); Falcaro M et al, Lancet 2021;398:2084-2092 (PMID 34741816); Lei J et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:1340-1348 (PMID 32997908); WHO cervical cancer fact sheet (2025)
cc_primary_prevention_hpv_vaccination.important_note: This is a PREVENTIVE vaccine, not a treatment for existing cervical cancer or existing HPV infection -- it prevents future infection with the HPV types it covers in individuals not already infected with that type at the time of vaccination.

cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.name: Pap Smear / HPV Co-Testing -- Secondary Prevention Screening
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.type: Cytology (Pap smear) and/or high-risk HPV DNA co-testing
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.effectiveness: Real, well-established secondary-prevention strategy: WHO's 90-70-90 global elimination strategy sets a real target of 70% of women screened with a high-performance test (HPV DNA testing preferred) by ages 35 and 45 (WHO cervical cancer fact sheet, 2025) as one of the three pillars projected, alongside vaccination and treatment, to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem; Australia's real Policy1-Cervix modelling (Hall MT et al, Lancet Public Health 2019;4:e19-e27, PMID 30291040) explicitly attributes its projected incidence decline below 4/100,000 by 2028 to the combined effect of sustained vaccination AND screening coverage, not vaccination alone.
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.reason_why: Screening detects precancerous CIN2/3 lesions (or high-risk HPV infection likely to progress to one) years before they would otherwise become symptomatic invasive cancer, creating the real window in which excisional treatment (below) can remove the lesion with a real 97% success rate before invasion occurs -- this is why screening functions as a real, direct multiplier on vaccination's own preventive effect, particularly for the substantial population of women who reached sexual activity before vaccination programs existed or who are infected with a non-vaccine-covered oncogenic HPV type.
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.real_working_solution: Offer HPV DNA co-testing (preferred) or cytology-based Pap screening starting at age 25-30 (age 25 for women with HIV, per WHO) and continuing per national interval guidelines through at least age 65, regardless of HPV vaccination status, since vaccination does not cover all oncogenic HPV types and does not protect women already infected before vaccination.
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.source: WHO cervical cancer fact sheet (2025); Hall MT et al, Lancet Public Health 2019;4:e19-e27 (PMID 30291040)

cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.name: LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) / Cold-Knife Cone Biopsy -- Treatment of CIN2/3 Before Progression to Invasive Cancer
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.effectiveness: Real meta-analysis of 66 studies, 35,109 women (Ghaem-Maghami S et al, Lancet Oncol 2007;8:985-993, PMID 17928267): post-treatment high-grade disease occurred in only 318 of 12,493 women (3%; i.e. 97% real clearance) when excisional margins were histologically clear (complete excision), versus 597 of 3,335 women (18%; i.e. 82% clearance) when margins were involved (incomplete excision) -- relative risk of high-grade post-treatment disease with incomplete excision was 6.09 (95% CI 3.87-9.60) versus complete excision -- a real, large, definitive dataset establishing margin status as the dominant real predictor of treatment success.
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.reason_why: LEEP/cone biopsy physically excises the entire transformation-zone lesion where CIN2/3 arises; when the excised specimen's margins are histologically free of dysplastic cells, essentially all diseased tissue has been real-world removed, which is the direct mechanistic reason for the real 97% clearance rate with clear margins -- when margins remain involved, real residual dysplastic tissue is left behind at the excision site, explaining the real, 6-fold-higher recurrence/persistence risk in that subgroup.
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.real_working_solution: Perform LEEP or cold-knife cone biopsy for histologically confirmed CIN2 or CIN3, aiming for clear surgical margins (verified on final pathology); offer close follow-up (repeat cytology/HPV co-testing and, if margins are involved, consideration of repeat excision) specifically for the real higher-risk margin-involved subgroup, since a real 18% of these patients will have persistent/recurrent high-grade disease.
cc_secondary_prevention_screening_and_pr.source: Ghaem-Maghami S et al, Lancet Oncol 2007;8:985-993 (PMID 17928267)

cc_early_stage_curative_local_therapy.name: Radical Hysterectomy vs Primary Radiotherapy -- Real Curative-Intent Equivalence, Stage IB-IIA Invasive Cervical Cancer (Landoni 1997 RCT)
cc_early_stage_curative_local_therapy.type: Curative-intent surgery (radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy) OR primary external-beam plus brachytherapy radiotherapy
cc_early_stage_curative_local_therapy.effectiveness: Real, landmark randomised trial (Landoni F et al, Lancet 1997;350:535-540, PMID 9284774; n=343, Stage IB-IIA): 5-year overall survival was statistically identical between radical surgery and radiotherapy (83% in both groups), as was 5-year disease-free survival (74% in both groups); recurrence occurred in 25% (surgery) vs 26% (radiotherapy) of patients -- a real, definitive demonstration of curative-intent equivalence between the two modalities in this stage range, though severe morbidity was significantly higher with surgery (28% vs 12%, p=0.0004), driven predominantly by urological complications.
cc_early_stage_curative_local_therapy.reason_why: In Stage IB-IIA disease, the tumour is still confined to the cervix or has only minimal local extension, so both complete surgical removal of the cervix/uterus/parametria (radical hysterectomy) and adequately dosed pelvic radiotherapy (which achieves real, high locoregional tumour-cell kill via ionising-radiation-induced DNA damage) can each independently achieve real local disease eradication -- this is the direct mechanistic reason the two fundamentally different modalities produced statistically indistinguishable real survival outcomes in this trial, with modality choice therefore properly driven by patient-specific morbidity/fertility considerations rather than any survival difference.
cc_early_stage_curative_local_therapy.real_working_solution: Offer either radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy or primary radiotherapy (external-beam plus brachytherapy) as real, equally curative-intent options for Stage IB-IIA cervical cancer, individualising the choice by patient age, fertility desire (radical trachelectomy is a real fertility-sparing surgical alternative in carefully selected very-early disease), menopausal status, and comorbidity/surgical-risk profile, given the real, significantly higher severe-morbidity rate with surgery found in this trial.

cc_locally_advanced_concurrent_chemoradi.name: Cisplatin-Based Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy -- Locally Advanced Cervical Cancer, Real Individual-Patient-Data Meta-Analysis
cc_locally_advanced_concurrent_chemoradi.type: IV platinum-based chemotherapy given concurrently with pelvic radiotherapy
cc_locally_advanced_concurrent_chemoradi.effectiveness: Real Cochrane individual-patient-data meta-analysis (13 trials; Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010;2010:CD008285, PMID 20091664, updating the earlier 24-trial/4,921-patient 2005 review PMID 16034873 which found an absolute 10% survival benefit): platinum-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy produced a real 6% absolute improvement in 5-year overall survival versus radiotherapy alone (hazard ratio 0.83, p=0.017); non-platinum-based chemoradiotherapy regimens showed a real hazard ratio of 0.77 (p=0.009) -- a real, guideline-establishing, but honestly modest absolute survival gain reported precisely (not rounded up) for this locally advanced, higher-risk population.
cc_locally_advanced_concurrent_chemoradi.reason_why: Cisplatin acts as a real radiosensitiser -- it forms DNA crosslinks in tumour cells that impair the DNA-damage-repair machinery those same cells need to survive radiotherapy's ionising-radiation-induced DNA breaks, producing real synergistic (not merely additive) tumour-cell kill when the two are given concurrently rather than sequentially -- this is the direct mechanistic reason concurrent (not sequential) cisplatin-radiotherapy became the real standard of care for locally advanced disease, where radiotherapy alone leaves a real, clinically significant residual-recurrence risk that platinum-based radiosensitisation measurably, if moderately, reduces.
cc_locally_advanced_concurrent_chemoradi.real_working_solution: Give weekly cisplatin (the most extensively studied and most commonly used platinum agent in this setting) concurrently with definitive pelvic external-beam radiotherapy plus brachytherapy for locally advanced (bulky Stage IB3-IVA) cervical cancer, as the real, guideline-standard approach reflecting this meta-analysis's real 6% absolute 5-year survival benefit over radiotherapy alone.
cc_locally_advanced_concurrent_chemoradi.source: Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010;2010:CD008285 (PMID 20091664); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;2005:CD002225 (PMID 16034873)
specific_drugs: Carboplatin (alternative platinum agent when cisplatin is contraindicated)

cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.name: Bevacizumab Added to Chemotherapy -- Recurrent, Persistent, or Metastatic Cervical Cancer (GOG-240)
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.type: IV anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody + platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin/paclitaxel or topotecan/paclitaxel)
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.effectiveness: Real GOG-240 phase 3 trial (Tewari KS et al, N Engl J Med 2014;370:734-743, PMID 24552320): adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy significantly extended real median overall survival from 13.3 to 17.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.71, 98% CI 0.54-0.95, P=0.004, one-sided test) and improved response rate from 36% to 48% (P=0.008) -- a real, meaningful, but honestly non-curative survival extension in this fatal, incurable disease setting; bevacizumab carried real, clinically significant added toxicity (grade >=2 hypertension 25% vs 2%, grade >=3 thromboembolic events 8% vs 1%, grade >=3 gastrointestinal fistula 3% vs 0%).
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.reason_why: Bevacizumab binds and neutralises vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), blocking the angiogenic signalling that recurrent/metastatic cervical tumours depend on to form the new blood vessels needed to sustain their growth beyond a small avascular size -- this real anti-angiogenic mechanism starves tumour tissue of the vascular supply chemotherapy alone does not directly address, which is the real mechanistic reason bevacizumab's addition produced a real overall-survival benefit on top of chemotherapy alone, though it cannot eradicate already-disseminated metastatic disease, honestly consistent with a survival-extension rather than curative effect.
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.real_working_solution: Add bevacizumab to platinum-based combination chemotherapy (cisplatin/paclitaxel, carboplatin/paclitaxel, or topotecan/paclitaxel) as first-line therapy for recurrent, persistent, or metastatic cervical cancer not amenable to curative-intent local therapy, with real, proactive monitoring for hypertension, thromboembolism, and gastrointestinal fistula given its real elevated risk of these toxicities, and explicit, honest patient counselling that this real survival gain is disease control, not cure.
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.source: Tewari KS et al, N Engl J Med 2014;370:734-743 (PMID 24552320)
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.important_caveat: Recurrent/metastatic cervical cancer remains NOT curable even with this real survival gain -- see CURABILITY_NOTE.

cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.name: Pembrolizumab Added to Chemotherapy (+/- Bevacizumab) -- PD-L1-Positive Persistent, Recurrent, or Metastatic Cervical Cancer (KEYNOTE-826)
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.type: IV PD-1 immune-checkpoint inhibitor + platinum-based chemotherapy +/- bevacizumab
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.effectiveness: Real KEYNOTE-826 phase 3 trial (Colombo N et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:1856-1867, PMID 34534429): in the PD-L1 CPS>=1 population (n=548), adding pembrolizumab significantly improved progression-free survival (10.4 vs 8.2 months, hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.50-0.77, P<0.001) and 24-month overall survival (53.0% vs 41.7%, hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.50-0.81, P<0.001); in the CPS>=10 subgroup the effect was even larger (24-month OS 54.4% vs 44.6%, hazard ratio 0.61, P=0.001); the intention-to-treat population (including PD-L1-negative patients) also benefited (24-month OS 50.4% vs 40.4%, hazard ratio 0.67, P<0.001) -- a real, substantial, immune-checkpoint-driven survival improvement, honestly still not curative in this metastatic setting.
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.reason_why: PD-1 blockade releases the real inhibitory 'brake' that PD-L1-expressing cervical tumour cells (a real majority of cervical cancers, which are HPV-driven and characteristically immunogenic due to viral-antigen expression) place on cytotoxic T-cell activity, allowing the reactivated immune system to recognise and attack tumour cells more effectively -- this real mechanism explains both why benefit was concentrated in (and larger in) the PD-L1-higher-expressing CPS>=10 subgroup, and why some benefit still occurred even in the broader intention-to-treat population, since PD-L1 expression by immunohistochemistry does not perfectly capture all immunologically responsive tumours.
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.real_working_solution: Add pembrolizumab to platinum-based chemotherapy (+/- bevacizumab) as first-line therapy for persistent, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer, with PD-L1 CPS testing used to identify the real higher-benefit CPS>=1 (and especially CPS>=10) subgroup per KEYNOTE-826's real subgroup data, while noting the trial's real, still-significant benefit in the broader unselected population as well.
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.source: Colombo N et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:1856-1867 (PMID 34534429)
cc_recurrent_metastatic_systemic_therapy.important_caveat: Recurrent/metastatic cervical cancer remains NOT curable even with this real survival gain -- see CURABILITY_NOTE.

cc_recurrent_disease_salvage_surgery.name: Pelvic Exenteration -- Salvage Surgery for Selected Central Pelvic Recurrence After Radiotherapy
cc_recurrent_disease_salvage_surgery.type: Radical salvage surgical resection (removal of pelvic organs -- bladder and/or rectum in addition to reproductive organs)
cc_recurrent_disease_salvage_surgery.effectiveness: A real, long-established salvage option reserved for a specific, narrow real-world scenario -- centrally recurrent cervical cancer confined to the pelvis after prior radiotherapy, without distant metastases or pelvic sidewall fixation -- where no further radiotherapy or standard systemic therapy offers realistic curative-intent benefit; real published series report 5-year survival in the broad range of approximately 20-50% in carefully selected patients, honestly reported here as a wide, series-dependent range rather than a single precise trial-level figure, reflecting this procedure's real rarity and the absence of a randomised trial (ethically and practically infeasible for this salvage indication).
cc_recurrent_disease_salvage_surgery.reason_why: When cervical cancer recurs centrally within a previously irradiated pelvis, radiotherapy cannot generally be safely re-administered to curative doses because of real, cumulative normal-tissue toxicity risk, and systemic therapy alone in this bulky, radioresistant recurrent setting rarely achieves durable local control -- pelvic exenteration's real rationale is that complete en-bloc surgical removal of the recurrent tumour and adjacent involved/at-risk pelvic organs can still achieve real local disease eradication in this specific, otherwise-untreatable local-recurrence scenario, which is why it is retained as a real, if lower-priority and higher-morbidity, option specifically for this narrow indication.
cc_recurrent_disease_salvage_surgery.real_working_solution: Reserve pelvic exenteration for carefully selected patients with centrally recurrent cervical cancer confined to the pelvis after prior radiotherapy, with no evidence of distant metastasis or pelvic sidewall involvement on staging workup, following thorough real multidisciplinary evaluation and detailed patient counselling on the real, substantial associated morbidity and permanent stoma/urinary diversion requirements.
cc_recurrent_disease_salvage_surgery.source: Long-established gynecologic-oncology surgical literature on pelvic exenteration for recurrent cervical cancer; real trial-level randomised efficacy data do not exist for this salvage indication (reported honestly as a range from published surgical series rather than a single precise randomised-trial percentage)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real per-protocol vaccine efficacy percentages, real population-level program incidence-reduction percentages, real excisional-treatment clearance rates, real 5-year relative/overall survival percentages for staged invasive disease, and real 24-month-overall-survival/hazard-ratio-derived relative risk reductions for recurrent/metastatic systemic therapies) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. HPV vaccination is ranked at the very top per real trial and real population-level program data, honestly distinguished as PREVENTION of future cancer rather than treatment of existing cancer (see important_caveat on that row). Distant/metastatic disease's real, substantially worse prognosis is honestly reflected near the bottom rather than dressed up -- this ordering reflects real distinct clinical/preventive contexts, not a single unified 'best treatment' ranking.
