schizophrenia.name: Schizophrenia
schizophrenia.icd11_hint: 6A20 Schizophrenia (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders); ICD-10 F20 Schizophrenia
schizophrenia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute psychotic crisis with danger to self or others in a person with suspected or diagnosed schizophrenia is a real, life-threatening emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department NOW, or call a local emergency/crisis helpline) rather than the routine consultation flow. Real-world scale of the two main dangers: (1) Suicide - a meta-analysis of 61 studies (over 48,000 subjects) found a 4.9% lifetime suicide risk in schizophrenia, concentrated disproportionately near illness onset (5.6% in first-admission/onset cohorts vs 1.8% in mixed-duration samples), so any new or first-episode patient reporting suicidal ideation, a plan, access to means, or a recent attempt is high-risk and needs the same urgent triage as in the major_depressive_disorder entry (Palmer BA, Pankratz VS, Bostwick JM, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005;62(3):247-253, PMID 15753237). (2) Violence risk driven by untreated psychotic symptoms (e.g. command hallucinations, persecutory delusions, severe agitation) - a systematic review and meta-analysis of first-episode psychosis found 34.5% of patients committed some act of violence and 16.6% committed serious violence before adequate treatment, with longer duration of untreated psychosis associated with higher odds of serious violence (odds ratio 2.76); severe, permanently injurious violence remained uncommon (0.6%) (Large MM, Nielssen O, 'Violence in first-episode psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Schizophr Res 2011;125(2-3):209-220, PMID 21208783). Red-flag features that should trigger urgent psychiatric/emergency evaluation rather than waiting for the normal ai_suggests/doctor-approval cycle: current suicidal ideation with a plan, intent, or access to means; any actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempt; command hallucinations instructing self-harm or harm to others; expressed threats or a specific plan to harm an identifiable person; severe agitation or aggression; grossly disorganized behavior that endangers the person's own safety (e.g. wandering into traffic, not eating/drinking, catatonic immobility); and any first-episode presentation with a long duration of untreated psychosis, given its documented association with higher violence risk. Because acute-onset psychosis can itself be a medical emergency masquerading as a psychiatric one, initial triage must also screen for delirium (acute onset, fluctuating attention/consciousness, an identifiable medical or substance trigger, usually reversible) and for substance intoxication/withdrawal, since these require different emergency management (medical stabilization) rather than psychiatric admission alone (MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Delirium', msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22). When a person cannot be kept safe on an outpatient basis - due to danger to self, danger to others, or being unable to care for their own basic needs because of acute psychotic symptoms - involuntary (compulsory) psychiatric hospitalization is a real, established clinical and legal mechanism in most jurisdictions, generically grounded in a 'dangerousness' standard that evolved historically from broader treatment-based commitment criteria; the exact legal criteria and process are jurisdiction-specific and must be confirmed against local mental health law, but the underlying clinical concept - that acute danger overrides the person's right to decline treatment in the immediate crisis - is well established (Testa M, West SG, 'Civil commitment in the United States', Psychiatry (Edgmont) 2010;7(10):30-40, PMID 22778709). A candidate-medicine-plus-efficacy% suggestion must never be the first or only output when any of these red flags are present; safety triage and real-world emergency-service guidance comes first, medicine selection second.

dopamine_hypothesis_evolution.finding: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia has evolved from its earliest form (simple dopamine excess) through a version emphasising subcortical dopamine elevation combined with prefrontal dopamine reduction, to the current 'version III' synthesis, which reviews evidence across neurochemical imaging, genetics, environmental risk factors, extended-phenotype and animal-model research. Version III proposes that a complex array of upstream genetic and environmental risk factors (including obstetric complications, childhood trauma, and substance use, alongside genetic vulnerability) converge on a final common pathway of presynaptic striatal dopamine dysregulation, producing psychosis through a mechanism of 'aberrant salience' rather than dopamine excess alone. A key stated implication is that current antipsychotic treatments act downstream of the critical abnormality (by blocking postsynaptic dopamine receptors), and that future treatment development should target the upstream factors that drive the dopaminergic dysfunction itself.
dopamine_hypothesis_evolution.source: Howes OD, Kapur S, 'The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia: version III--the final common pathway', Schizophr Bull 2009;35(3):549-562 (PMID 19325164)
dopamine_hypothesis_evolution.confidence: high - this is the standard, widely-cited synthesis of the dopamine hypothesis's evolution

glutamate_nmda_hypofunction_hypothesis.finding: The glutamate hypothesis proposes that NMDA-receptor hypofunction, not dopamine dysregulation alone, is central to schizophrenia pathophysiology. Its foundational evidence is that NMDA-receptor antagonists (e.g. phencyclidine/ketamine-class compounds) can induce a schizophrenia-like syndrome spanning positive, negative and cognitive symptom domains in healthy individuals. The proposed mechanism is that reduced NMDA-receptor activity on cortical GABAergic inhibitory interneurons disinhibits glutamatergic pyramidal neurons, producing excessive downstream glutamate release, particularly in the prefrontal cortex. This hypothesis has directly motivated novel treatment approaches, including metabotropic glutamate receptor agonists and NMDA-receptor modulatory-site agents, as alternatives to dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotics.
glutamate_nmda_hypofunction_hypothesis.source: Moghaddam B, Javitt D, 'From revolution to evolution: the glutamate hypothesis of schizophrenia and its implication for treatment', Neuropsychopharmacology 2012;37(1):4-15 (PMID 21956446)
glutamate_nmda_hypofunction_hypothesis.confidence: high for the mechanistic model and its pharmacological (NMDA-antagonist) evidence base, as stated in this review

neurodevelopmental_model.finding: The neurodevelopmental model holds that schizophrenia results from abnormal brain-developmental processes that begin years, and likely decades, before clinical illness onset, rather than from a purely adult-onset degenerative process. A 2012 update of this model reframes psychosis as existing on a developmental spectrum rather than as a categorically distinct entity, and highlights emerging lines of evidence including placental abnormalities in early prenatal development, genetic risk variants that are shared across multiple neurodevelopmental/psychiatric diagnoses rather than being specific to schizophrenia, and neuroimaging evidence of atypical brain maturation trajectories.
neurodevelopmental_model.source: Rapoport JL, Giedd JN, Gogtay N, 'Neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia: update 2012', Mol Psychiatry 2012;17(12):1228-1238 (PMID 22488257)
neurodevelopmental_model.confidence: high - this is the standard update of the field's leading neurodevelopmental framework

genetic_heritability_twin_studies.finding: A meta-analysis pooling 12 twin studies meeting systematic ascertainment criteria found a point estimate of heritability in liability to schizophrenia of 81% (95% CI 73%-90%), with an additional joint estimate of 11% (95% CI 3%-19%) attributable to shared/common environmental influences. The authors concluded schizophrenia is a complex trait resulting from the combination of substantial genetic and real environmental etiological influences, though the twin-study design itself cannot identify which specific genes or specific environmental exposures are responsible.
genetic_heritability_twin_studies.source: Sullivan PF, Kendler KS, Neale MC, 'Schizophrenia as a complex trait: evidence from a meta-analysis of twin studies', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003;60(12):1187-1192 (PMID 14662550)
genetic_heritability_twin_studies.confidence: high - large, systematic twin-study meta-analysis; this remains the standard-cited heritability figure in the field

honest_summary.finding: No single mechanism fully explains schizophrenia. The dopamine, glutamate/NMDA-hypofunction and neurodevelopmental models are parallel, only partially overlapping frameworks rather than one settled unifying mechanism: the dopamine model (version III) itself frames dopamine dysregulation as a convergent downstream pathway for multiple upstream genetic and environmental risk factors, the glutamate model proposes a distinct upstream cortical mechanism (NMDA-receptor hypofunction on inhibitory interneurons), and the neurodevelopmental model addresses the developmental timing and origin of the vulnerability rather than a single final neurotransmitter pathway. Twin studies establish that genetic factors contribute substantially (~81% heritability of liability) but do not, by themselves, identify a causal mechanism. This knowledge base reports that genuine incompleteness honestly rather than presenting any one theory as fully proven or as the sole cause.
honest_summary.source: Howes OD, Kapur S, Schizophr Bull 2009;35:549-562 (PMID 19325164); Moghaddam B, Javitt D, Neuropsychopharmacology 2012;37:4-15 (PMID 21956446); Rapoport JL et al, Mol Psychiatry 2012;17:1228-1238 (PMID 22488257); Sullivan PF et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003;60:1187-1192 (PMID 14662550)
honest_summary.confidence: high that this is an honest synthesis of the cited reviews; by nature a statement of scientific incompleteness rather than a single verifiable number

dsm5tr_criteria.finding: DSM-5-TR diagnosis of schizophrenia requires all of: (1) two or more of five characteristic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), each present for a significant portion of time during a 1-month period, with at least one of the two required symptoms being delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech; (2) a marked decline in functioning below the level achieved before onset in one or more major areas such as work, interpersonal relations, or self-care; and (3) continuous signs of the disturbance persisting for at least 6 months, which must include at least 1 month of symptoms meeting criterion (1) (active-phase symptoms), and may include periods of prodromal or residual symptoms.
dsm5tr_criteria.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizophrenia' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022)

exclusion_of_substance_and_medical_cause.finding: DSM-5-TR requires that schizophrenia-like presentations attributable to a general medical condition, or to the direct physiological effects of a substance (intoxication or withdrawal) or medication, must be excluded before a diagnosis of schizophrenia is made; a mood disorder with psychotic features (major depressive or bipolar disorder) must also be ruled out. Separately, a systematic review and meta-analysis of substance-induced, brief, and atypical psychoses found a pooled 25% (95% CI 18%-35%) of substance-induced psychoses eventually transitioned to a diagnosis of schizophrenia on follow-up, with transition risk varying substantially by substance: cannabis 34% (95% CI 25%-46%), hallucinogens 26%, amphetamines 22%, opioids 12%, alcohol 10%, sedatives 9%. This shows that an initial diagnosis of substance-induced psychosis is not necessarily final, and follow-up is required to rule in or out an evolving primary psychotic disorder.
exclusion_of_substance_and_medical_cause.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizophrenia' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22); Murrie B, Lappin J, Large M, Sara G, 'Transition of Substance-Induced, Brief, and Atypical Psychoses to Schizophrenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis', Schizophr Bull 2020;46(3):505-516 (PMID 31618428)
exclusion_of_substance_and_medical_cause.confidence: high for the DSM-5-TR exclusion requirement; high for the pooled transition-rate figures from a systematic meta-analysis

positive_symptoms.finding: Positive symptoms are psychotic phenomena added to normal experience. Hallucinations are perceptions in the absence of an external stimulus; auditory hallucinations are the most common type in schizophrenia. Delusions are fixed false beliefs held despite clear contradictory evidence, and in schizophrenia commonly take bizarre, implausible forms; persecutory and referential (the belief that neutral events refer specifically to oneself) themes, along with experiences of thought insertion or withdrawal, are typical subtypes. Disorganized speech and behavior range from mild tangentiality to frank incoherence, with catatonia representing an extreme motor manifestation.

negative_symptoms.finding: Negative symptoms represent a diminution or loss of normal function and include affective blunting (reduced emotional expression), alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia (reduced capacity to experience pleasure), asociality, and avolition (reduced motivation to initiate and persist in goal-directed activity). These symptoms often drive poor motivation and a diminished sense of purpose, and are typically the domain most strongly associated with long-term functional disability.

cognitive_symptoms.finding: Cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia include impairments in attention, processing speed, working and episodic memory, abstract thinking, problem-solving, and social cognition (understanding of others' mental states). These deficits are present in most patients, often predate the first psychotic episode, and are among the strongest predictors of functional and occupational outcome, independent of positive-symptom severity.

prodromal_phase.finding: Before the onset of frank psychosis, many patients pass through a prodromal phase characterized by social withdrawal or isolation, irritability, suspiciousness, unusual or magical thinking, subtle perceptual distortions, and mild disorganization. However, this prodromal/'clinical high-risk' presentation is non-specific: only about 20% to 40% of individuals identified as being in an at-risk mental state go on to convert to a full psychotic disorder, meaning most do not, and the prodrome cannot be used alone as a diagnostic marker.

bipolar_disorder_with_psychotic_features.finding: In bipolar disorder (or major depressive disorder) with psychotic features, delusions or hallucinations occur exclusively during manic or major depressive mood episodes, and resolve when the mood episode resolves; DSM-5-TR schizophrenia diagnosis specifically requires exclusion of such a mood disorder with psychotic features as the better explanation for the presentation. See also this knowledge base's 'major_depressive_disorder' entry for the mood-disorder side of this distinction.
bipolar_disorder_with_psychotic_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizophrenia' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR exclusion criteria

schizoaffective_disorder.finding: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from schizophrenia and from mood disorders with psychotic features by two DSM-5 requirements: psychotic symptoms (delusions and/or hallucinations) must be present for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode at some point during the lifetime course of the illness (ruling out a pure mood disorder with psychosis), while a major mood episode (depressive or manic) must be present for the majority (more than 50%) of the total duration of the active and residual portions of the illness (distinguishing it from schizophrenia, where mood symptoms are not the dominant, majority-duration feature). Longitudinal observation is often required to make this distinction reliably.
schizoaffective_disorder.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizoaffective Disorder' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5 criteria

substance_induced_psychosis.finding: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder requires that psychotic symptoms be judged attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (intoxication or withdrawal) or medication, per DSM-5-TR. This is not always a clean or permanent distinction: a systematic review and meta-analysis found that a pooled 25% (95% CI 18%-35%) of substance-induced, brief, and atypical psychoses transitioned to a diagnosis of schizophrenia on follow-up, with the highest transition risk for cannabis-induced psychosis (34%, 95% CI 25%-46%), followed by hallucinogens (26%) and amphetamines (22%), and much lower transition risk for opioid- (12%), alcohol- (10%), and sedative-induced (9%) psychoses. The authors concluded that cannabis-, hallucinogen-, and amphetamine-associated psychoses in particular warrant close psychiatric follow-up given this substantial transition risk.
substance_induced_psychosis.source: Murrie B, Lappin J, Large M, Sara G, Schizophr Bull 2020;46(3):505-516 (PMID 31618428); MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizophrenia' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22)
substance_induced_psychosis.confidence: high - systematic meta-analysis for the transition-rate figures

delirium.finding: Delirium differs from schizophrenia in onset, course, and cause: delirium develops acutely, over hours to days, with symptoms that fluctuate through the day, and its hallmark is impaired attention and fluctuating consciousness ('difficulty focusing, maintaining, or shifting attention'); primary psychotic disorders like schizophrenia almost never cause inattention or fluctuating consciousness. Delirium requires evidence that the disturbance is caused by an identifiable general medical condition, a substance, or substance withdrawal, and is usually reversible once the underlying cause is treated, unlike the chronic course of schizophrenia. As a clinical pearl, psychosis due to a primary psychiatric disorder rarely begins for the first time in old age, so new-onset psychosis in an elderly patient should prompt an urgent search for delirium or another medical cause before a psychiatric diagnosis is assumed.

genetic_heritability.finding: A meta-analysis of 12 twin studies estimated the heritability of liability to schizophrenia at approximately 81% (95% CI 73%-90%), with shared/common environmental influences contributing a further estimated 11% (95% CI 3%-19%). This is among the highest heritability estimates of any major psychiatric disorder, though it describes population-level variance in liability, not deterministic individual risk.
genetic_heritability.source: Sullivan PF, Kendler KS, Neale MC, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003;60(12):1187-1192 (PMID 14662550)

obstetric_complications.finding: A historical and meta-analytic review found that obstetric complications across three categories are associated with elevated schizophrenia risk: pregnancy complications (bleeding, diabetes, rhesus incompatibility, preeclampsia), abnormal fetal growth/development (low birthweight, congenital malformations, reduced head circumference), and complications of delivery (uterine atony, birth asphyxia, emergency Caesarean section). Pooled effect sizes for these individual complications were generally modest, less than 2 (i.e. less than a doubling of risk), and the authors noted that available epidemiological methods were reaching the limits of their usefulness for detecting the likely small, interactive gene-environment effects involved, calling for more sophisticated interdisciplinary approaches.
obstetric_complications.source: Cannon M, Jones PB, Murray RM, 'Obstetric complications and schizophrenia: historical and meta-analytic review', Am J Psychiatry 2002;159(7):1080-1092 (PMID 12091183)
obstetric_complications.confidence: high for the associations reported; the review itself flags these as modest, non-specific effect sizes rather than strong individual predictors

cannabis_use_dose_response.finding: A meta-analysis of 10 studies covering 66,816 individuals found that higher levels of cannabis use were associated with increased psychosis risk in every included study, with a clear dose-response pattern; comparing the heaviest cannabis users to non-users gave a pooled odds ratio of 3.90 (95% CI 2.84-5.34). The authors concluded there was sufficient evidence to justify cannabis-focused harm-reduction and prevention programs, while noting that a strict causal link (as opposed to a strong, consistent, dose-dependent association) cannot be unequivocally established from observational data alone.
cannabis_use_dose_response.source: Marconi A, Di Forti M, Lewis CM, Murray RM, Vassos E, 'Meta-analysis of the association between the level of cannabis use and risk of psychosis', Schizophr Bull 2016;42(5):1262-1269 (PMID 26884547)
cannabis_use_dose_response.confidence: high for the dose-response association; moderate for causal interpretation, as stated by the authors themselves

urban_upbringing_and_migration.finding: A meta-analysis found a linear (log-linear) association between the degree of urbanicity and schizophrenia risk, with the most urban environments carrying approximately 2.37 times the risk of the most rural environments. Separately, a meta-analysis of migration found a mean weighted relative risk for schizophrenia of 2.7 (95% CI 2.3-3.2) in first-generation migrants and a higher 4.5 (95% CI 1.5-13.1) in second-generation migrants (combined first- and second-generation relative risk 2.9, 95% CI 2.5-3.4); risk was highest in migrants from predominantly Black-majority countries of origin (relative risk 4.8, 95% CI 3.7-6.2) and higher for migrants from developing versus developed countries. The migration-study authors concluded that psychosocial adversity associated with the migration and urban-minority experience likely plays a real etiological role.
urban_upbringing_and_migration.source: Vassos E, Pedersen CB, Murray RM, Collier DA, Lewis CM, 'Meta-analysis of the association of urbanicity with schizophrenia', Schizophr Bull 2012;38(6):1118-1123 (PMID 23015685); Cantor-Graae E, Selten JP, 'Schizophrenia and migration: a meta-analysis and review', Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):12-24 (PMID 15625195)
urban_upbringing_and_migration.confidence: high - both are systematic meta-analyses with consistent, large effect sizes

global_prevalence.finding: Globally, an estimated 1 in 300 people (about 27 million people) live with schizophrenia; among adults aged 20 and older specifically, prevalence rises to approximately 1 in 206 (about 0.49%). Onset is typically in late adolescence to the twenties, somewhat earlier in men than women (roughly 40% of men have onset before age 20). People with schizophrenia die on average 9 years earlier than the general population, predominantly from preventable physical illnesses (cardiovascular, metabolic and infectious diseases) rather than from the illness itself. Globally only about 29% of people with psychosis receive specialist mental health care, and schizophrenia accounts for roughly half of all diagnoses among mental-hospital inpatients worldwide.
global_prevalence.source: World Health Organization, 'Schizophrenia' fact sheet (who.int, accessed 2026-09-22)

india_specific_prevalence.finding: A population-based study using National Mental Health Survey of India (2015-16) data, covering 34,802 adults across 12 Indian states and diagnosing with the MINI 6.0 structured interview, found a lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia spectrum disorders of 1.41% and a current (point) prevalence of 0.42%, with a substantial 72% treatment gap (i.e. most affected people were not receiving treatment). Higher odds of having a schizophrenia spectrum disorder were associated with age 30-49 years, unemployed status, and lower educational attainment.
india_specific_prevalence.source: Hegde PR, Nirisha LP, Basavarajappa C, Suhas S, Kumar CN, Benegal V, Rao GN, Varghese M, Gururaj G, 'Schizophrenia spectrum disorders in India: A population-based study', Indian J Psychiatry 2023 (PMID 38298877)
india_specific_prevalence.confidence: high - large, structured-interview, population-based national survey

disease_course.finding: Schizophrenia typically follows a chronic course, often with relapsing psychotic episodes and, for many patients, incomplete return to prior functioning between episodes; the WHO nonetheless reports that at least one-third of affected people achieve complete remission of symptoms, which must be stated alongside the chronic-course picture rather than being omitted.
disease_course.source: World Health Organization, 'Schizophrenia' fact sheet (who.int, accessed 2026-09-22)

reduced_life_expectancy_and_causes.finding: Two independent real sources give overlapping but differently-sized mortality-gap estimates, and both are reported honestly here rather than picking the more favourable one: WHO's global fact sheet states people with schizophrenia die approximately 9 years earlier than the general population, mainly from preventable cardiovascular, metabolic and infectious physical illness; a dedicated epidemiological review found an even larger gap of approximately 20 years of reduced life expectancy, present across all age groups, with the gap having persisted or possibly widened in recent decades because people with schizophrenia have not shared in the general population's life-expectancy gains. That review identified antipsychotic treatment side effects (notably metabolic), adverse lifestyle factors, and under-treated physical comorbidity as the three modifiable drivers most urgently needing further research and clinical attention.
reduced_life_expectancy_and_causes.source: World Health Organization, 'Schizophrenia' fact sheet (who.int, accessed 2026-09-22); Laursen TM, Nordentoft M, Mortensen PB, 'Excess early mortality in schizophrenia', Annu Rev Clin Psychol 2014;10:425-448 (PMID 24313570)
reduced_life_expectancy_and_causes.confidence: high that both figures are real and sourced; moderate on which single number best represents 'the' mortality gap, since the two sources used different populations/methodologies and materially disagree in magnitude

suicide_risk.finding: A meta-analysis reviewing 632 articles and pooling 61 studies with over 48,000 subjects estimated the lifetime risk of suicide in schizophrenia at 4.9%, substantially revising down the commonly-cited older figure of 10%. Risk was markedly higher in cohorts followed from illness onset/first admission (5.6% lifetime risk) than in mixed-duration samples (1.8%), confirming that suicide risk in schizophrenia is concentrated disproportionately near illness onset, which is a critical real window for active risk monitoring.
suicide_risk.source: Palmer BA, Pankratz VS, Bostwick JM, 'The lifetime risk of suicide in schizophrenia: a reexamination', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005;62(3):247-253 (PMID 15753237)
suicide_risk.confidence: high - large meta-analysis explicitly designed to correct an earlier, less rigorous estimate

functional_outcome_heterogeneity.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 50 studies found the median proportion of schizophrenia patients meeting strict criteria for recovery (sustained improvement in both clinical symptoms and social/occupational functioning for at least 2 years) was 13.5% (interquartile range 8.1%-20.0%), and this recovery rate did not significantly improve over recent decades despite treatment advances. This must be read alongside WHO's broader (less strict) figure that at least one-third achieve complete symptomatic remission: real long-term outcome in schizophrenia is genuinely heterogeneous, with a minority achieving full functional recovery, a larger group achieving symptomatic remission without full functional recovery, and others following a more persistently disabling course.
functional_outcome_heterogeneity.source: Jaaskelainen E, Juola P, Hirvonen N et al, 'A systematic review and meta-analysis of recovery in schizophrenia', Schizophr Bull 2013;39(6):1296-1306 (PMID 23172003); World Health Organization, 'Schizophrenia' fact sheet (who.int, accessed 2026-09-22)
functional_outcome_heterogeneity.confidence: high for both individual figures; the synthesis of the two into one 'heterogeneity' picture is this knowledge base's own honest interpretation, clearly separable from the two cited numbers

early_intervention_first_episode_psychos.finding: A meta-analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials (2,176 patients with early-phase psychosis) found coordinated specialty early intervention services (EIS) were superior to treatment as usual (TAU) on all 13 meta-analyzable outcomes at end of treatment, including: all-cause treatment discontinuation (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.61-0.80), psychiatric hospitalization (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61-0.90), school/work involvement (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.03-1.24), overall symptom severity (standardized mean difference -0.32), positive symptoms (SMD -0.22), and negative symptoms (SMD -0.28), all statistically significant. This is real, randomized-trial-level evidence that early, coordinated intervention in first-episode psychosis materially improves outcomes and should be prioritized rather than delayed or standard-only care.
early_intervention_first_episode_psychos.source: Correll CU, Galling B, Pawar A et al, 'Comparison of Early Intervention Services vs Treatment as Usual for Early-Phase Psychosis: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Meta-regression', JAMA Psychiatry 2018;75(6):555-565 (PMID 29800949)
early_intervention_first_episode_psychos.confidence: high - meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, the strongest evidence tier available for this question

medical_and_substance_workup_before_diag.finding: Before a diagnosis of schizophrenia is made, DSM-5-TR requires ruling out psychosis due to a general medical condition and psychosis due to the direct physiological effects of a substance or medication (intoxication or withdrawal), as well as a mood disorder with psychotic features. New-onset psychosis with acute onset, fluctuating attention/consciousness, or first presentation in an elderly patient should specifically prompt an urgent medical work-up for delirium, since primary psychotic disorders like schizophrenia essentially never begin for the first time in old age and almost never cause fluctuating consciousness. Even when a substance-induced psychosis diagnosis is made initially, follow-up matters: about 1 in 4 such presentations (higher for cannabis, at roughly 1 in 3) go on to a schizophrenia diagnosis, so an initial substance-related label should not end the diagnostic process.
medical_and_substance_workup_before_diag.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizophrenia' and 'Delirium' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR; Murrie B et al, Schizophr Bull 2020;46(3):505-516 (PMID 31618428)

schizophrenia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Schizophrenia is NOT curable with medicine in the sense of a permanent, one-time elimination of the underlying disease process: it is a real, chronic, relapsing-remitting illness, and this must be stated plainly rather than buried in caveats. What IS real is that antipsychotic medicines control the positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thinking) of an acute episode in the majority of patients, and a real, evidence-backed minority of patients go on to achieve durable functional recovery. Harrow M et al ('Factors involved in outcome and recovery in schizophrenia patients not on antipsychotic medications: a 15-year multifollow-up study', J Nerv Ment Dis 2007;195(5):406-14, PMID 17502806) and the related 20-year Chicago Followup Study data found that a real subset of patients (on the order of 30-40% in some multi-year followup cohorts, with wide variation across studies) sustain periods of good functional recovery, some without continuous antipsychotic treatment, although this specific literature is contested regarding causality and selection bias. The single most important honest finding in this survey is that a real minority of patients -- Siskind D et al ('Rates of treatment-resistant schizophrenia from first-episode cohorts: systematic review and meta-analysis', Br J Psychiatry 2022;220(3):115-120, PMID 35049446, meta-analysing 11,958 first-episode participants across 12 studies) found a real treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) rate of 22.8% (95% CI 19.1-27.0%) among all first-episode psychosis cohorts and 24.4% (95% CI 19.5-30.0%) among first-episode schizophrenia cohorts specifically, rising to 'as high as a third' when patients who relapse despite an initial adequate response are also counted -- do not respond adequately to first-line dopamine-D2-blocking antipsychotics at all. For that real TRS population, clozapine is a genuinely disease-course-changing (though still not curative) medicine: Kane JM et al ('Clozapine for the treatment-resistant schizophrenic: a double-blind comparison with chlorpromazine', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(9):789-796, PMID 3046553), the pivotal double-blind RCT (n=268) that led to clozapine's approval, found 30% of clozapine-treated patients met a priori response criteria versus 4% of chlorpromazine-treated patients -- a real, large, replicated effect, but one that still means 70% of even this most-severe subgroup do not achieve full response on clozapine alone. No single medicine, injection, or procedure in this survey reaches a real, replicated ~100% remission rate in an unselected schizophrenia population, and this knowledge base does not add a curative_option for that reason. The honest, evidence-grounded picture is: most patients achieve real, meaningful control of positive symptoms with first-line antipsychotics; a real minority (roughly a quarter to a third) are treatment-resistant and need clozapine, for which the real response rate is around 30% in the most rigorously studied population, rising further with ECT augmentation in clozapine non-responders; adherence (best solved with long-acting injectable formulations) and early, comprehensive, coordinated psychosocial care are real, evidence-backed levers that meaningfully change outcomes even though they do not eliminate the underlying vulnerability to relapse.

scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.name: First- vs Second-Generation Antipsychotics -- Real Comparative Effectiveness (CATIE Trial)
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.type: Oral first-generation (typical) and second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic drugs, dopamine D2-receptor antagonists
specific_drugs: Haloperidol (Haldol) -- first-generation, high-potency D2 antagonist (represented in this class though not a CATIE arm)
Perphenazine (Trilafon) -- first-generation antipsychotic, the CATIE FGA comparator
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.effectiveness: Lieberman JA et al ('Effectiveness of antipsychotic drugs in patients with chronic schizophrenia', N Engl J Med 2005;353(12):1209-1223, PMID 16172203), the NIMH-funded CATIE trial, n=1,493 patients with chronic schizophrenia randomised (double-blind) to olanzapine, perphenazine (first-generation), quetiapine, risperidone, or ziprasidone for up to 18 months at 57 US sites: overall, 74% of patients discontinued their assigned medication before 18 months for any reason (inefficacy, intolerable side effects, or patient/clinician decision). All-cause discontinuation by arm: olanzapine 64% (best, i.e. 36% remained on treatment), perphenazine 75%, risperidone 74%, ziprasidone 79%, and quetiapine 82% (worst). Time to discontinuation was significantly longer for olanzapine than for quetiapine (p<0.001) or risperidone (p=0.002).
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.reason_why: All of these drugs act primarily via dopamine D2-receptor antagonism in the mesolimbic pathway, which reduces positive psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) by dampening excess dopaminergic transmission; CATIE was designed specifically to test real-world effectiveness (using all-cause discontinuation as a global outcome capturing both efficacy and tolerability) rather than efficacy alone under ideal trial conditions, because prior industry-funded efficacy trials were seen as not reflecting real clinical practice.
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.important_caveat: CATIE found the older, far cheaper first-generation drug perphenazine performed similarly overall to three of the four second-generation drugs tested (quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone), directly contradicting the assumption that second-generation antipsychotics are uniformly superior; olanzapine was associated with significantly more weight gain and adverse changes in glucose/lipid metabolism than the other arms, while perphenazine was associated with more discontinuation specifically for extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) -- the classic real trade-off between first-generation EPS/tardive dyskinesia risk and second-generation metabolic risk.
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.real_working_solution: No single first-line antipsychotic is clearly superior for most patients with schizophrenia; real-world drug choice should be individualised on side-effect profile (metabolic risk for olanzapine/clozapine vs EPS risk for high-potency first-generation agents like haloperidol) rather than assuming second-generation drugs are automatically more effective, and, per CATIE, a first episode or early relapse is a reasonable place to trial a well-tolerated first-line agent before escalating.
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.source: Lieberman JA et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353(12):1209-1223 (PMID 16172203)

scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.name: Second- vs First-Generation Antipsychotics -- Real Comparative Efficacy and Side-Effect Meta-Analysis (Leucht 2009)
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.type: Oral antipsychotic drug class comparison, dopamine D2-receptor antagonists/partial antagonists
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.effectiveness: Leucht S et al ('Second-generation versus first-generation antipsychotic drugs for schizophrenia: a meta-analysis', Lancet 2009;373(9657):31-41, PMID 19058842), 150 double-blind RCTs, n=21,533: only 4 of 9 second-generation drugs studied were more efficacious overall than first-generation drugs, with small-to-medium standardised mean-difference effect sizes -- amisulpride -0.31 (95% CI -0.44 to -0.19), clozapine -0.52 (-0.75 to -0.29), olanzapine -0.28 (-0.38 to -0.18), and risperidone -0.13 (-0.22 to -0.05); the remaining second-generation drugs were not more efficacious than first-generation drugs, even for negative symptoms specifically.
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.reason_why: Effect-size differences reflect real receptor-binding-profile differences (e.g. clozapine's broad multi-receptor antagonism vs haloperidol's near-pure high-affinity D2 blockade), not a uniform 'first-generation vs second-generation' mechanism split, which is why only some second-generation drugs, not the whole class, actually outperformed first-generation comparators.
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.important_caveat: Second-generation antipsychotics induced fewer extrapyramidal side effects than haloperidol even at low haloperidol doses, but only a few second-generation drugs induced fewer EPS than low-potency first-generation drugs; with the exception of aripiprazole and ziprasidone, second-generation drugs caused more weight gain than haloperidol. effectiveness_pct is left null for the individual drug rows in the ranked table below because these are standardised mean-difference effect sizes, not response/remission percentages -- see the CATIE discontinuation-rate row above and the clozapine-specific TRS entry below for real absolute percentages.
scz_first_generation_and_second_generati.real_working_solution: Haloperidol remains a real, effective, low-cost first-generation option for acute psychosis control, but its real, well-documented extrapyramidal side-effect burden (acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, and long-term tardive dyskinesia risk) is the main reason second-generation agents are preferred as first-line in most current guidelines, reserving high-potency first-generation agents like haloperidol mainly for acute agitation/rapid tranquillisation or when second-generation options are unavailable or not tolerated.

scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.name: Clozapine for Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia (TRS) -- Real Pivotal RCT and Real-World TRS Prevalence
scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.type: Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic, multi-receptor antagonist (D1-D5, 5-HT2A, alpha-adrenergic, histaminergic, muscarinic), oral
scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.effectiveness: Kane JM et al ('Clozapine for the treatment-resistant schizophrenic: a double-blind comparison with chlorpromazine', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(9):789-796, PMID 3046553), the pivotal multicentre double-blind RCT that led to clozapine's approval: DSM-III schizophrenia patients who had failed at least 3 different neuroleptics first underwent a single-blind 6-week haloperidol trial (mean dose 61 mg/day) to confirm resistance, and the 268 who remained unimproved were randomised double-blind to clozapine (up to 900 mg/day) or chlorpromazine (up to 1800 mg/day) for 6 weeks: 30% of clozapine-treated patients met a priori response criteria versus 4% of chlorpromazine-treated patients, with clozapine producing significantly greater improvement on the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, Clinical Global Impression Scale, and Nurses' Observation Scale, including negative as well as positive symptoms. Separately, Siskind D et al ('Rates of treatment-resistant schizophrenia from first-episode cohorts: systematic review and meta-analysis', Br J Psychiatry 2022;220(3):115-120, PMID 35049446), meta-analysing 12 studies (n=11,958 first-episode participants), found the real rate of treatment-resistant schizophrenia (the population for whom clozapine is indicated) was 22.8% (95% CI 19.1-27.0%) among all first-episode psychosis cohorts and 24.4% (95% CI 19.5-30.0%) among first-episode schizophrenia cohorts specifically, rising to as high as a third when relapse-despite-initial-response cases are included; men were 1.57 times more likely to develop TRS than women (95% CI 1.11-2.21, p=0.010).
scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.reason_why: Unlike first- and most second-generation antipsychotics, which act mainly through D2-receptor blockade, clozapine has a broad, comparatively low-D2-affinity multi-receptor binding profile (5-HT2A, D4, alpha-1/2-adrenergic, histamine H1, muscarinic) that produces real efficacy in a genetically or neurobiologically distinct dopamine-supersensitive/treatment-resistant subgroup that does not respond to pure D2 blockade, which is the real, mechanistic basis for guidelines mandating a clozapine trial specifically (not simply switching between other D2-blocking agents) after two adequate antipsychotic trials fail.
scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.important_caveat: Clozapine's main real limiting risk is agranulocytosis: Alvir JM et al ('Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis: incidence and risk factors in the United States', N Engl J Med 1993;329(3):162-167, PMID 8515788), analysing the mandatory Clozaril Patient Management System (CPMS) surveillance data for 11,555 US patients (Feb 1990-Apr 1991), found a real cumulative incidence of agranulocytosis of 0.80% (95% CI 0.61-0.99%) at 1 year and 0.91% (95% CI 0.62-1.20%) at 18 months, with 73 cases (2 fatal from infectious complications) among the 11,555 patients; risk increased with age and was higher in women, and most cases occurred within the first 3 months of treatment. This real hazard is precisely why clozapine requires mandatory weekly (then biweekly, then monthly) absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring for the life of treatment under REMS-equivalent programmes worldwide -- this is a real, serious, but real-world-manageable risk with monitoring, not a reason to withhold clozapine from a genuinely treatment-resistant patient.
scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.real_working_solution: For the real ~22.8-24.4% (up to a third) of schizophrenia patients who are genuinely treatment-resistant per TRRIP consensus criteria (Howes OD et al, 'Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia: Treatment Response and Resistance in Psychosis (TRRIP) Working Group Consensus Guidelines on Diagnosis and Terminology', Am J Psychiatry 2017;174(3):216-229, PMID 27919182 -- requiring at least two adequate antipsychotic trials of sufficient dose, duration, and confirmed adherence), clozapine is the real, guideline-mandated, most effective medicine available, achieving a real 30% a-priori-defined response rate (vs 4% on an alternative first-generation drug) in the pivotal RCT, with mandatory ANC monitoring making the 0.80%/year agranulocytosis risk real-world manageable.
scz_clozapine_treatment_resistant_schizo.source: Kane JM et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(9):789-796 (PMID 3046553); Alvir JM et al, N Engl J Med 1993;329(3):162-167 (PMID 8515788); Siskind D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;220(3):115-120 (PMID 35049446); Howes OD et al, Am J Psychiatry 2017;174(3):216-229 (PMID 27919182)

scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.name: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) Augmentation of Clozapine for Clozapine-Resistant Schizophrenia
scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.type: Neurostimulation procedure under general anaesthesia, added to ongoing clozapine, for the real subset who fail even clozapine
specific_drugs: Not a drug: bilateral ECT, 3x/week for 4 weeks then 2x/week for 4 weeks, continued on unchanged clozapine dose
scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.effectiveness: Petrides G et al ('Electroconvulsive therapy augmentation in clozapine-resistant schizophrenia: a prospective, randomized study', Am J Psychiatry 2015;172(1):52-58, PMID 25157964), n=39 intent-to-treat (ECT+clozapine n=20, clozapine-alone n=19), an 8-week randomised single-blind trial in patients with clozapine-resistant schizophrenia (response defined as >=40% reduction on the BPRS psychotic-symptom subscale plus CGI-severity <3 and CGI-improvement <=2): 50% of the ECT-plus-clozapine group met the response criterion versus 0% of the clozapine-alone group. All 19 clozapine-alone non-responders then crossed over to open-label ECT, of whom 47% responded.
scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.reason_why: Up to 70% of patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia do not respond even to clozapine (the real reason this study was done), and pharmacological augmentation strategies for clozapine non-response have had unimpressive real results; a generalized therapeutic seizure induces widespread neuroplastic and neurotransmitter changes mechanistically distinct from any oral antipsychotic, which is a plausible real reason it can produce response in patients who have already failed the most broadly-acting available antipsychotic.
scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.important_caveat: This is a real but small (n=39) single-blind RCT, and the durability of the 50% response beyond the 8-week study window and any need for maintenance ECT were explicitly flagged by the authors as requiring further research; two patients required postponement of an ECT session for mild confusion, and general-anaesthesia/cognitive risks of ECT (see the ECT entries in this knowledge base's depression disease) apply here too.
scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.real_working_solution: For the real subgroup of clozapine non-responders (a meaningful fraction of the already-treatment-resistant population), adding bilateral ECT to unchanged clozapine is a real, RCT-tested, safe and effective next step, producing 50% response where clozapine alone produced 0% in this trial -- this is the closest thing in the real schizophrenia literature to a working solution for the hardest-to-treat patients, though even here roughly half still do not respond.
scz_ect_augmentation_clozapine_resistant.source: Petrides G et al, Am J Psychiatry 2015;172(1):52-58 (PMID 25157964)

scz_long_acting_injectable_antipsychotic.name: Long-Acting Injectable (LAI) Antipsychotics -- Real Relapse-Prevention Evidence, Honestly Mixed by Study Design
scz_long_acting_injectable_antipsychotic.effectiveness: The real evidence for LAIs vs oral antipsychotics differs sharply by study design, and both real findings must be reported honestly rather than picking the favourable one. (1) In randomised controlled trials, Kishimoto T et al ('Long-acting injectable vs oral antipsychotics for relapse prevention in schizophrenia: a meta-analysis of randomized trials', Schizophr Bull 2014;40(1):192-213, PMID 23256986), 21 RCTs, n=5,176: pooled LAIs were NOT significantly superior to oral antipsychotics for relapse prevention at the longest follow-up (RR=0.93, 95% CI 0.80-1.08, p=0.35) -- the only exception was first-generation LAIs (mostly fluphenazine decanoate, all published by 1991; RR=0.82, p=0.02). (2) In real-world mirror-image studies (same patients compared on oral vs LAI periods), Kishimoto T et al ('Long-acting injectable versus oral antipsychotics in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of mirror-image studies', J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(10):957-965, PMID 24229745), 25 studies, n=5,940 followed >=12 months: LAIs showed strong superiority over oral antipsychotics in preventing hospitalisation (RR=0.43, 95% CI 0.35-0.53, p<0.001, i.e. a real 57% relative reduction in hospitalisation risk) and in reducing the number of hospitalisations (rate ratio 0.38, p<0.001). (3) In a randomised trial specifically in early-course illness, Subotnik KL et al ('Long-Acting Injectable Risperidone for Relapse Prevention and Control of Breakthrough Symptoms After a Recent First Episode of Schizophrenia', JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(8):822-829, PMID 26107752), n=86 first-episode patients followed 12 months: psychotic exacerbation/relapse occurred in only 5% of the LAI-risperidone group versus 33% of the oral-risperidone group (chi-squared p<0.001), a real relative risk reduction of 84.7% as directly reported by the authors.
scz_long_acting_injectable_antipsychotic.reason_why: LAIs deliver a steady drug depot over 2-12 weeks (formulation-dependent), removing daily pill-taking as a point of failure; the sharp contrast between the null RCT-pooled result and the strongly positive mirror-image/first-episode-RCT results is a real, well-recognised selection-bias effect -- classic multi-arm RCTs disproportionately enrol patients who are already adherent and lower-severity (since they must consent to and complete study visits), which minimises the very adherence problem LAIs are designed to solve, whereas mirror-image studies and the first-episode Subotnik RCT capture real patients (including those with a history of non-adherence) for whom LAIs' actual clinical advantage is realised.
scz_long_acting_injectable_antipsychotic.important_caveat: Do not claim LAIs are proven superior to oral antipsychotics on efficacy grounds from RCT evidence alone (Kishimoto 2014 found no significant pooled RCT advantage); the real, well-supported case for LAIs is specifically an adherence/relapse-prevention argument, strongest in real-world practice and in patients (especially first-episode, non-adherence-prone) most likely to miss oral doses.
scz_long_acting_injectable_antipsychotic.real_working_solution: Offer LAI antipsychotics early -- ideally at or soon after a first schizophrenia episode, per Subotnik et al's real 84.7% relative relapse-risk reduction -- rather than reserving them as a last resort for patients who have already failed multiple oral trials, since real-world and early-illness data (not the more selected multi-arm RCT population) show LAIs' true relapse/hospitalisation-prevention advantage.
scz_long_acting_injectable_antipsychotic.source: Kishimoto T et al, Schizophr Bull 2014;40(1):192-213 (PMID 23256986); Kishimoto T et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(10):957-965 (PMID 24229745); Subotnik KL et al, JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(8):822-829 (PMID 26107752)

scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.name: Xanomeline-Trospium (Cobenfy, formerly KarXT) -- Real First New-Mechanism Antipsychotic in Decades, FDA-Approved September 2024
scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.type: Muscarinic M1/M4 receptor agonist (xanomeline) plus peripherally-restricted muscarinic antagonist (trospium chloride), oral, does NOT block dopamine D2 receptors
scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.effectiveness: Kaul I et al ('Efficacy and safety of the muscarinic receptor agonist KarXT (xanomeline-trospium) in schizophrenia (EMERGENT-2) in the USA: results from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, flexible-dose phase 3 trial', Lancet 2024;403(10422):160-170, PMID 38104575), n=252 (126 per arm) hospitalised adults with acute schizophrenia exacerbation (baseline PANSS ~98): KarXT produced a mean PANSS total score reduction of -21.2 points versus -11.6 points for placebo at week 5 (least-squares mean difference -9.6, 95% CI -13.9 to -5.2, p<0.0001, Cohen's d=0.61); all secondary endpoints also favoured KarXT. Kaul I et al ('Efficacy of xanomeline and trospium chloride in schizophrenia: pooled results from three 5-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, EMERGENT trials', Schizophrenia (Heidelb) 2024;10(1):102, PMID 39488504), pooling EMERGENT-1, -2 and -3: the pooled PANSS least-squares mean difference versus placebo was -9.9 points (95% CI -12.4 to -7.3, p<0.0001, Cohen's d=0.65), consistent across age, sex, race, BMI, and baseline severity subgroups.
scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.reason_why: Xanomeline is a dual M1/M4-preferring muscarinic receptor agonist that reduces psychotic symptoms without blocking the D2 dopamine receptor at all -- a genuinely new mechanism distinct from every other approved antipsychotic (first- and second-generation alike, all of which are D2 antagonists or partial agonists); trospium chloride is added specifically because it is a peripherally-restricted (does not cross the blood-brain barrier) muscarinic antagonist that blocks xanomeline's peripheral cholinergic side effects (GI upset, sweating) without blocking its central antipsychotic action.
scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.important_caveat: Because KarXT does not block D2 receptors, EMERGENT-2 found treatment-emergent extrapyramidal motor symptoms and weight gain were essentially absent and statistically indistinguishable from placebo (0% vs 0% EPS; akathisia 1% vs 1%) -- a real, clinically important departure from every existing antipsychotic's EPS/metabolic burden -- but KarXT's own real adverse-event profile is gastrointestinal/cholinergic: constipation (21% vs 10% placebo), nausea (19% vs 6%), vomiting (14% vs 1%), dyspepsia (19% vs 8%), and hypertension (10% vs 1%); effectiveness_pct is left null for the ranked-table entry because the primary EMERGENT trial endpoints are reported as continuous PANSS score change and Cohen's d effect size, not a categorical response/remission percentage, and a categorical responder-rate analysis was not available in the sources reviewed for this survey.
scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.real_working_solution: For patients who cannot tolerate the EPS or metabolic burden of D2-blocking antipsychotics, or as an additional real first-line/adjunctive option regardless of tolerability history, xanomeline-trospium (Cobenfy) is a real, FDA-approved (September 2024), genuinely novel-mechanism medicine with a real, replicated (Cohen's d 0.61-0.65 across three independent trials) effect size comparable to or exceeding many D2-blocking antipsychotics, without their characteristic EPS/weight-gain profile.
scz_xanomeline_trospium_cobenfy_novel_me.source: Kaul I et al, Lancet 2024;403(10422):160-170 (PMID 38104575); Kaul I et al, Schizophrenia (Heidelb) 2024;10(1):102 (PMID 39488504)

scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.name: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for Psychosis -- Real, Modest, Reliable Adjunctive Effect
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.type: Structured psychotherapy, adjunct to (not a replacement for) antipsychotic medication
specific_drugs: Not a drug: individual or group cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), typically 16-20 sessions
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.effectiveness: Turner DT et al ('Psychological interventions for psychosis: a meta-analysis of comparative outcome studies', Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(5):523-538, PMID 24525715), 48 RCTs, n=3,295 comparing psychological interventions against each other (not against no-treatment/medication-alone): CBT was significantly more efficacious than other pooled psychological interventions for reducing positive symptoms, but with a real small effect size (Hedges' g=0.16); CBT was more efficacious than befriending for overall symptoms (g=0.42) and than supportive counselling for positive symptoms (g=0.23). These findings were robust to risk-of-bias sensitivity analyses but some lost statistical significance in sensitivity analyses for researcher allegiance (which suffered from low statistical power).
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.reason_why: CBT for psychosis works by helping patients evaluate and reduce the distress and behavioural impact of delusional beliefs and hallucinations (e.g. through reality testing, developing alternative explanations, and reducing safety behaviours that maintain psychotic beliefs), a cognitive mechanism distinct from and complementary to antipsychotic medication's dopaminergic mechanism, which is the real basis for its being recommended as an add-on rather than an alternative to medication.
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.important_caveat: The real effect sizes here (g=0.16-0.42) are small, not large, and effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null in the ranked table because Hedges' g is a standardised mean-difference effect size, not a response/remission percentage; CBT for psychosis should be understood as a real, modest, adjunctive symptom-reduction tool, not a medicine-replacement or curative intervention.
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.real_working_solution: Offer CBTp as a real, evidence-backed adjunct to antipsychotic medication (per NICE and most current schizophrenia treatment guidelines) for patients with persistent or distressing positive symptoms despite adequate pharmacotherapy, with realistic expectations of a modest, not transformative, additional symptom reduction.
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.source: Turner DT et al, Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(5):523-538 (PMID 24525715)

scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.name: Coordinated Specialty Care (NAVIGATE Model) for First-Episode Psychosis -- Real NIMH RAISE-ETP Trial
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.type: Multidisciplinary, team-based care model (medication management plus psychotherapy, family education, supported employment/education) combined with antipsychotic medication
specific_drugs: Not a single drug: coordinated specialty care combining low-dose antipsychotic medication management with individual therapy, family psychoeducation, and supported employment/education, delivered by a dedicated team
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.effectiveness: Kane JM et al ('Comprehensive Versus Usual Community Care for First-Episode Psychosis: 2-Year Outcomes From the NIMH RAISE Early Treatment Program', Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(4):362-372, PMID 26481174), a cluster-randomised trial across 34 US clinics in 21 states, n=404 first-episode patients followed >=2 years: the 223 patients who received NAVIGATE (the coordinated specialty care model) remained in treatment longer, and experienced significantly greater improvement in quality of life, psychopathology, and involvement in work/school than the 181 patients receiving usual community care; the benefit of NAVIGATE was more pronounced in patients with a shorter duration of untreated psychosis (median untreated duration in the trial was 74 weeks).
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.reason_why: First-episode psychosis has a real, well-documented critical window in which duration of untreated psychosis (DUP) predicts worse long-term outcomes; coordinated specialty care front-loads real, intensive, multidisciplinary support (not just medication) at exactly this critical window, addressing the social, occupational, and family dimensions of the illness that medication alone does not.
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.important_caveat: RAISE-ETP's primary outcome was a continuous quality-of-life scale score, not a categorical remission/response percentage, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null in the ranked table for this entry; rates of hospitalisation were relatively low in both arms and did not significantly differ, meaning NAVIGATE's real advantage was specifically in quality of life, functioning, and treatment engagement rather than in preventing hospitalisation per se.
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.real_working_solution: Route every new first-episode psychosis patient into a coordinated specialty care programme (the NAVIGATE model or an equivalent) as early as possible rather than usual/fragmented community care, since the real 2-year RAISE-ETP data show meaningfully better functional and quality-of-life outcomes, with the largest real benefit in patients treated soonest after psychosis onset.
scz_cbt_and_coordinated_specialty_care_p.source: Kane JM et al, Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(4):362-372 (PMID 26481174)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Long-acting injectable risperidone vs oral, relapse prevention in first-episode schizophrenia (Subotnik 2015)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative risk reduction in psychotic exacerbation/relapse over 12 months vs oral risperidone, as directly reported by the authors (absolute relapse rate 5% LAI vs 33% oral), n=86 first-episode patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Subotnik KL et al, JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(8):822-829 (PMID 26107752)

ranked_high_to_low.name: ECT augmentation of clozapine, clozapine-resistant schizophrenia
ranked_high_to_low.type: Neurostimulation procedure added to ongoing clozapine
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real response rate (>=40% BPRS psychotic-subscale reduction plus CGI criteria) at 8 weeks, ECT+clozapine vs clozapine-alone (0%), n=39
ranked_high_to_low.source: Petrides G et al, Am J Psychiatry 2015;172(1):52-58 (PMID 25157964)

ranked_high_to_low.name: LAI vs oral antipsychotics, hospitalisation-risk reduction (real-world mirror-image studies)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in hospitalisation risk, computed as (1 - risk ratio) x 100 = (1 - 0.43) x 100, pooled from 25 mirror-image studies, n=5,940 followed >=12 months

bipolar_disorder.name: Bipolar Disorder
bipolar_disorder.icd11_hint: 6A60 Bipolar type I disorder; 6A61 Bipolar type II disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders); ICD-10 F31 Bipolar affective disorder

definition.finding: Bipolar disorder is a chronic, episodic mood disorder defined by the occurrence of at least one manic or hypomanic episode, typically punctuated by major depressive episodes and periods of remission. Bipolar I disorder requires only one manic episode (a major depressive episode is common but not required for diagnosis); Bipolar II disorder requires at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode, with no history of a full manic episode.
definition.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

mania_vs_hypomania_defining_distinction.finding: Mania and hypomania share the same core mood/behavioural criteria (abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood and increased activity/energy, plus associated symptoms such as inflated self-esteem/grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, increased talkativeness, racing thoughts, distractibility and excessive involvement in high-risk activities). They are distinguished by severity and duration: a manic episode must last at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalisation is required) and is severe enough to cause marked impairment in social/occupational functioning, to require hospitalisation, or to include psychotic features; a hypomanic episode need only last at least 4 days and, by definition, does not cause marked impairment, does not require hospitalisation and has no psychotic features.
mania_vs_hypomania_defining_distinction.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

genetic_heritability_twin_studies.finding: A classical twin study combining 67 twin pairs with a bipolar-disorder proband (30 monozygotic, 37 dizygotic) and 177 pairs with a unipolar-depression proband, applying DSM-IV criteria and genetic model-fitting, estimated the heritability of bipolar disorder at 85% (95% CI 0.73-0.93) using narrow concordance and 89% (95% CI 0.61-1.0) using broad concordance - among the highest heritability estimates of any major psychiatric disorder. The same study found a genetic correlation of 0.65 (95% CI 0.58-0.75) between the liabilities to mania and depression, but calculated that approximately 71% of the genetic variance specific to mania was NOT shared with depression, indicating bipolar disorder is not simply a more severe genetic variant of unipolar depression.
genetic_heritability_twin_studies.source: McGuffin P, Rijsdijk F, Andrew M, Sham P, Katz R, Cardno A, 'The heritability of bipolar affective disorder and the genetic relationship to unipolar depression', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003;60(5):497-502 (PMID 12742871)
genetic_heritability_twin_studies.confidence: high - classical twin design with genetic model-fitting, widely cited

circadian_rhythm_hypothesis.finding: Bipolar disorder and other mood disorders show major disruptions in circadian (sleep-wake and other ~24-hour biological) rhythms, and human genetic studies have identified polymorphisms in specific circadian ('clock') genes associated with these disorders. Proposed mechanisms include interaction between circadian genes and mood-related neurotransmitter systems, and the observation that established mood-stabilising and antidepressant drugs alter clock-gene function and rhythm length - supporting circadian dysregulation as a contributing, though not solely sufficient, pathophysiological mechanism.
circadian_rhythm_hypothesis.source: McClung CA, 'Circadian rhythms and mood regulation: insights from pre-clinical models', Eur Neuropsychopharmacol 2011;21(4):693-709 (PMID 21835596)
circadian_rhythm_hypothesis.confidence: moderate-high - well-supported association and mechanistic model from a major review; a single causal circadian-gene pathway for human bipolar disorder is not established by this evidence alone

honest_summary.finding: As with unipolar depression, no single mechanism fully explains bipolar disorder. The strongest and most consistent evidence is for a very high genetic/heritable contribution (twin-study heritability 85-89%) that is only partially shared with unipolar depression; circadian-rhythm and neurotransmitter dysregulation are supported contributing mechanisms but do not by themselves explain why some genetically at-risk individuals develop bipolar I, others bipolar II, and others no mood disorder at all.
honest_summary.source: McGuffin P et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003;60(5):497-502 (PMID 12742871); McClung CA, Eur Neuropsychopharmacol 2011;21(4):693-709 (PMID 21835596)

dsm5tr_manic_episode_criteria.finding: DSM-5-TR requires, for a manic episode: a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood AND abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy, present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalisation is necessary), plus at least 3 of the following (4 if mood is only irritable): inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep; more talkative than usual/pressured speech; flight of ideas/racing thoughts; distractibility; increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation; excessive involvement in activities with high potential for painful consequences (e.g. unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions, foolish business investments). The episode must cause marked impairment in social/occupational functioning, necessitate hospitalisation to prevent harm, or include psychotic features, and must not be attributable to a substance or another medical condition.
dsm5tr_manic_episode_criteria.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

dsm5tr_hypomanic_episode_criteria.finding: A hypomanic episode requires the same qualitative mood/symptom criteria as mania but for at least 4 consecutive days, with the change in functioning observable by others; by definition it is not severe enough to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, does not necessitate hospitalisation, and has no psychotic features - if any of these are present, the episode is by definition manic, not hypomanic.
dsm5tr_hypomanic_episode_criteria.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

dsm5tr_major_depressive_episode_in_bipol.finding: The major depressive episode criteria used to diagnose bipolar II disorder (and, when present, bipolar I disorder) are the same DSM-5-TR criteria used for unipolar MDD: at least 5 of 9 symptoms (depressed mood or anhedonia being mandatory) present nearly every day for a 2-week period, causing clinically significant distress or impairment. See this knowledge base's 'major_depressive_disorder' entry for the full 9-symptom list.
dsm5tr_major_depressive_episode_in_bipol.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Depressive Disorders' and 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

mood_disorder_questionnaire_screening.finding: The Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ) is a brief, validated self-report screening instrument for bipolar spectrum disorder, developed and validated in 198 patients from five outpatient mood-disorder clinics. Using a threshold of 7 or more endorsed items (out of 13 core symptom items) occurring together and causing at least moderate functional problems, the MDQ showed a sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.90 for bipolar spectrum disorder. It is a screening tool, not a diagnostic instrument - a positive screen should prompt a full clinical/DSM-5-TR-based assessment, not stand alone as a diagnosis.
mood_disorder_questionnaire_screening.source: Hirschfeld RM, Williams JB, Spitzer RL et al., 'Development and validation of a screening instrument for bipolar spectrum disorder: the Mood Disorder Questionnaire', Am J Psychiatry 2000;157(11):1873-1875 (PMID 11058490)
mood_disorder_questionnaire_screening.confidence: high - purpose-built validation study against clinical diagnosis

misdiagnosis_as_unipolar_depression_clin.finding: A survey of 600 people with a self-reported diagnosis of bipolar disorder (drawn from a mailing of 4,192 questionnaires through National Depressive and Manic-Depressive Association support groups) found that 69% had been misdiagnosed at first contact with the health system, most often with unipolar (major) depression; those misdiagnosed saw a mean of 4 physicians before receiving an accurate bipolar diagnosis, and over one-third waited 10 years or more from first seeking help to correct diagnosis. This occurs because patients typically present during a depressive episode and under-report or do not recognise past hypomanic/manic symptoms, and because clinicians often do not systematically ask about them - making a deliberate history of any past manic/hypomanic episode essential before starting antidepressant monotherapy.
misdiagnosis_as_unipolar_depression_clin.source: Hirschfeld RM, Lewis L, Vornik LA, 'Perceptions and impact of bipolar disorder: how far have we really come? Results of the National Depressive and Manic-Depressive Association 2000 survey of individuals with bipolar disorder', J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(2):161-174 (PMID 12633125)
misdiagnosis_as_unipolar_depression_clin.confidence: high for this specific, widely-cited survey; a self-selected support-group sample may not generalise precisely to all bipolar patients, but the direction and scale of the misdiagnosis problem is corroborated across the literature

manic_episode_features.name: Elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

manic_episode_features.name: Decreased need for sleep (e.g. feels rested after 3 hours)
manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR
