manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

manic_episode_features.name: Excessive involvement in high-risk activities (unrestrained spending, sexual indiscretion, reckless business/financial decisions)
manic_episode_features.note: Named by DSM-5-TR as activities with high potential for painful consequences; a clinically important safety and functional-impact symptom.
manic_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

depressive_episode_features.note: Identical DSM-5-TR criteria to unipolar MDD - see this knowledge base's 'major_depressive_disorder' entry for the full symptom list (depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep/appetite change, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, concentration difficulty, suicidal ideation).
depressive_episode_features.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Depressive Disorders' and 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22)

mixed_features_specifier.finding: DSM-5-TR allows a 'with mixed features' specifier on a manic, hypomanic, or major depressive episode when at least 3 symptoms of the opposite pole are present simultaneously during the majority of days of the episode (e.g. a manic episode with concurrent depressed mood, anhedonia, or worthlessness; or a depressive episode with concurrent elevated mood, grandiosity, or decreased need for sleep). Mixed presentations carry a recognised higher risk of impulsivity and suicidal behaviour than pure episodes and can complicate treatment because antidepressant monotherapy risks worsening the manic component.
mixed_features_specifier.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), Bipolar and Related Disorders chapter, mixed features specifier
mixed_features_specifier.confidence: high for the DSM-5-TR definitional criteria

rapid_cycling_specifier.finding: Rapid cycling is defined as the occurrence of 4 or more mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, or major depressive, in any combination, each meeting full episode duration criteria and separated by either a period of remission or a switch to an episode of the opposite polarity) within a 12-month period. It is a course specifier, not a separate diagnosis, and is associated with a more difficult-to-treat course.
rapid_cycling_specifier.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

differential_diagnosis.condition: Unipolar major depressive disorder (cross-reference this knowledge base's 'major_depressive_disorder' entry)
differential_diagnosis.note: The single most critical distinguishing point is history of a manic or hypomanic episode: DSM-5-TR diagnoses bipolar disorder, not unipolar MDD, whenever such a history exists (and is not substance- or medical-condition-induced). Because patients almost always present during a depressive episode and hypomania is often not recognised as pathological by the patient, this history is easy to miss - a survey of 600 bipolar patients found 69% were first misdiagnosed, usually as unipolar depression, seeing a mean of 4 physicians and, in over a third of cases, waiting 10+ years before correct diagnosis.
differential_diagnosis.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR; Hirschfeld RM, Lewis L, Vornik LA, J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(2):161-174 (PMID 12633125)

differential_diagnosis.note: Both conditions feature mood lability and impulsivity, but a clinical overview contrasts them on genetics/family history (bipolar disorder has strong, specific genetic evidence - see the ~85-89% twin heritability above; borderline personality disorder does not have comparable genetic specificity), developmental history (borderline personality disorder is more strongly associated with a history of childhood trauma), pattern of self-harm, and treatment response. DSM-5-TR's own borderline personality disorder affective-instability criterion describes mood reactivity 'usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days', in contrast to the multi-day (hypomania >=4 days) to multi-week (mania >=1 week, depression ~2 weeks) episode durations required for bipolar disorder - the time-course of mood change, not just its presence, is a key differentiator.
differential_diagnosis.source: Paris J, 'Bipolar or borderline: a clinical overview', Acta Psychiatr Scand 2014;129(2):86-91 (PMID 24571137); DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), Borderline Personality Disorder and Bipolar and Related Disorders chapters

differential_diagnosis.note: A manic, hypomanic, or mixed presentation that is a direct physiological consequence of a substance (e.g. stimulants, corticosteroids) or its withdrawal is coded separately from primary bipolar disorder and requires a clear temporal relationship to the exposure.
differential_diagnosis.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), Bipolar and Related Disorders chapter

differential_diagnosis.condition: Schizoaffective disorder (cross-reference this knowledge base's 'schizophrenia' entry where present)
differential_diagnosis.note: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, requires a period of at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms (delusions or hallucinations) in the ABSENCE of a mood episode at some point in the illness, alongside mood episodes present for the majority of the total illness duration; this distinguishes it from bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, where psychotic symptoms occur only during mood episodes and never independently of them.
differential_diagnosis.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), Schizophrenia Spectrum and Bipolar and Related Disorders chapters

risk_factors.note: Twin-study heritability of bipolar disorder is estimated at 85% (narrow concordance) to 89% (broad concordance), among the highest heritability estimates of any major psychiatric disorder - substantially higher than the ~35-37% heritability typically reported for unipolar major depression.
risk_factors.source: McGuffin P et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003;60(5):497-502 (PMID 12742871)

risk_factors.note: The postpartum period is a real, high-risk trigger window for a first-lifetime episode of mania/psychosis (incidence 0.25-0.6 per 1,000 births in the general population) and for relapse in women with a known bipolar/postpartum-psychosis history - a systematic evidence synthesis found a 31% (95% CI 22-42) risk of postpartum-psychosis recurrence in a subsequent pregnancy among women with a history of isolated postpartum psychosis. This is considered a psychiatric emergency requiring prompt recognition.
risk_factors.source: Bergink V, Rasgon N, Wisner KL, 'Postpartum Psychosis: Madness, Mania, and Melancholia in Motherhood', Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(12):1179-1188 (PMID 27609245)

risk_factors.note: A review pooling multiple studies (95,786 patients) found an overall antidepressant-associated mood-switching rate of 8.18% (approximately 3.42%/year over a mean 2.39 years of follow-up), with antidepressant exposure associated with roughly 2.6-fold higher switching risk than comparison/control conditions; switching risk was about 4.5-fold higher in juveniles than adults (5.62%/year vs 1.26%/year). This is a clinically critical safety point: starting an antidepressant without a mood stabiliser in a patient with unrecognised or known bipolar disorder can precipitate a manic or hypomanic switch.
risk_factors.source: Tondo L, Vazquez G, Baldessarini RJ, 'Antidepressant-associated mood-switching and transition from unipolar major depression to bipolar disorder: a review', J Affect Disord 2013;148(1):129-135 (PMID 23219059)

risk_factors.factor: Younger age at illness onset / early-onset presentation
risk_factors.note: Identified as a correlate of suicide attempts in a meta-analysis/meta-regression pooling correlates of suicide attempts and suicide deaths across bipolar disorder studies for the International Society for Bipolar Disorders Task Force on Suicide.
risk_factors.source: Schaffer A, Isometsa ET, Tondo L et al., 'International Society for Bipolar Disorders Task Force on Suicide: meta-analyses and meta-regression of correlates of suicide attempts and suicide deaths in bipolar disorder', Bipolar Disord 2015;17(1):1-16 (PMID 25329791)

risk_factors.note: Identified as a correlate of BOTH suicide attempts and completed suicide deaths in bipolar disorder in the same task-force meta-analysis.
risk_factors.source: Schaffer A et al., Bipolar Disord 2015;17(1):1-16 (PMID 25329791)

risk_factors.factor: Comorbid substance use disorder / anxiety disorder / cluster B (borderline) personality disorder
risk_factors.note: Each identified as a correlate of increased suicide-attempt risk in bipolar disorder in the same task-force meta-analysis.
risk_factors.source: Schaffer A et al., Bipolar Disord 2015;17(1):1-16 (PMID 25329791)

global_prevalence.finding: A systematic review synthesising prevalence data across the bipolar spectrum for the Global Burden of Disease 2010 study reported a pooled point prevalence of 0.741% and 6-12 month prevalence of 0.843%, noting the entire bipolar spectrum (I, II, and subthreshold presentations) was inconsistently assessed across studies and no significant prevalence differences were found across bipolar subtypes in the pooled data. A separate widely used clinical reference gives a lifetime prevalence of approximately 2.5% in men and 2.3% in women when the full bipolar spectrum is considered, with onset typically in the teens, 20s, or 30s.
global_prevalence.source: Ferrari AJ, Baxter AJ, Whiteford HA, 'A systematic review of the global distribution and availability of prevalence data for bipolar disorder', J Affect Disord 2011;134(1-3):1-13 (PMID 21131055); MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR
global_prevalence.confidence: moderate-high - the two sources use different case definitions (point/annual prevalence of strictly-defined bipolar I/II vs lifetime prevalence including broader bipolar-spectrum presentations), which is why the percentages differ; both are real, sourced figures rather than a single settled number

india_specific_data.finding: In the Global Burden of Disease Study 1990-2017 analysis of mental disorders across India's states, bipolar disorder accounted for 6.9% (95% UI 4.9-9.6) of the total disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) attributable to all mental disorders in India in 2017, within an overall mental-disorder burden estimated to affect 197.3 million Indians that year, whose share of total disease DALYs rose from 2.5% in 1990 to 4.7% in 2017.
india_specific_data.source: Sagar R, Dandona R, Gururaj G et al., 'The burden of mental disorders across the states of India: the Global Burden of Disease Study 1990-2017', Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7(2):148-161 (PMID 31879245)
india_specific_data.confidence: high - large, multi-institutional India-specific GBD sub-study; note this is a DALY-share figure, not a direct household-survey prevalence percentage for bipolar disorder specifically

relapsing_remitting_lifelong_course.finding: Bipolar disorder is a chronic, typically lifelong illness with a relapsing-remitting course of manic/hypomanic and depressive episodes interspersed with periods of remission; rapid cycling (>=4 episodes/year) represents a more difficult-to-treat course subtype.
relapsing_remitting_lifelong_course.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

elevated_suicide_risk.finding: Lifetime suicide risk in bipolar disorder is estimated at approximately 20 to 60 times that of the general population, with 15-20% of patients dying by suicide - among the highest suicide risk of any psychiatric disorder. A separate systematic review of the completed-suicide literature similarly found suicide rates in bipolar disorder approximately 20-30-fold greater than the general population, with bipolar II disorder patients facing the highest risk for completed suicide among bipolar subtypes, and lithium the only treatment shown in the reviewed literature to reduce suicide risk.
elevated_suicide_risk.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR; Plans L, Barrot C, Nieto E et al., 'Association between completed suicide and bipolar disorder: a systematic review of the literature', J Affect Disord 2019;242:111-122 (PMID 30173059)
elevated_suicide_risk.confidence: high - concordant figures from an independent clinical reference and a dedicated systematic review

functional_impairment_between_episodes.finding: Even outside acute mood episodes, bipolar disorder is associated with residual functional impairment (occupational, social, cognitive) for many patients, and the disorder is a major contributor to global disease burden - reflected in India by bipolar disorder's 6.9% share of the country's total mental-disorder DALYs in 2017 despite its comparatively low population prevalence, indicating disproportionately high per-case disability.
functional_impairment_between_episodes.source: Sagar R et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7(2):148-161 (PMID 31879245); MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

mood_stabilizer_before_antidepressant_pr.finding: Because starting an antidepressant without an adequate mood stabiliser carries a real, quantified risk of precipitating a manic/hypomanic switch (pooled switching risk 8.18%, ~2.6-fold higher than control conditions, and up to 4.5-fold higher in juveniles), and because a major depressive presentation may be the first sign of previously unrecognised bipolar disorder (69% of bipolar patients in one large survey were first misdiagnosed, usually as unipolar depression), a careful history for any past manic/hypomanic episode - ideally supported by a validated screen such as the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (sensitivity 0.73, specificity 0.90) - should precede antidepressant monotherapy in any patient presenting with depression. In confirmed or suspected bipolar disorder, mood stabilisers/antipsychotics form the foundation of treatment, and antidepressants are not recommended as sole therapy for the depressive phase.
mood_stabilizer_before_antidepressant_pr.source: Tondo L, Vazquez G, Baldessarini RJ, J Affect Disord 2013;148(1):129-135 (PMID 23219059); Hirschfeld RM, Lewis L, Vornik LA, J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(2):161-174 (PMID 12633125); Hirschfeld RM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2000;157(11):1873-1875 (PMID 11058490); MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR

suicide_risk_screening_is_first_priority.finding: Because bipolar disorder carries one of the highest suicide risks of any psychiatric illness (20-60x general-population risk per a major clinical reference; 20-30-fold per an independent systematic review), and because risk is elevated in both the depressive and mixed-features phases of the illness, every clinical or AI-assisted encounter for suspected or diagnosed bipolar disorder must screen for suicidal ideation/behaviour using a structured framework (e.g. the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, used in this knowledge base's major_depressive_disorder entry) before any medicine or test suggestion, and must separately assess for current mania with psychosis or dangerous behaviour. See EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the trigger pattern and red flags that must bypass routine consultation flow.
suicide_risk_screening_is_first_priority.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-22), summarising DSM-5-TR; Plans L et al., J Affect Disord 2019;242:111-122 (PMID 30173059)

bipolar_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute mania with psychotic features (delusions, hallucinations) or dangerous/high-risk behaviour, and severe suicidal depression in a person with suspected or diagnosed bipolar disorder, are real, life-threatening emergencies and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department NOW, or call a local emergency/suicide helpline) rather than the routine consultation flow. Trigger pattern for the manic pole: current manic episode with psychotic symptoms (delusions of grandeur, persecutory delusions, hallucinations) or command hallucinations; severe agitation, aggression, or danger to self or others; grossly impaired judgement leading to imminent physical, financial, sexual, or legal danger (e.g. reckless driving, unprotected sexual encounters with strangers, giving away large sums of money); postpartum-onset mania or psychosis (a documented psychiatric emergency, with 0.25-0.6 per 1,000 births incidence and a 31% recurrence risk in a subsequent pregnancy after a prior episode - Bergink V et al., 'Postpartum Psychosis: Madness, Mania, and Melancholia in Motherhood', Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(12):1179-1188, PMID 27609245); or any inability of a carer/patient to guarantee safety. Trigger pattern for the depressive pole: any current suicidal ideation with a plan and/or intent, preparatory acts, an actual/interrupted/aborted suicide attempt, or severe hopelessness/agitation in a depressive or mixed episode - bipolar disorder carries an estimated 20-60-fold (MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Bipolar Disorders') to 20-30-fold (Plans L, Barrot C, Nieto E et al., 'Association between completed suicide and bipolar disorder: a systematic review of the literature', J Affect Disord 2019;242:111-122, PMID 30173059) higher lifetime suicide risk than the general population, with 15-20% of patients estimated to die by suicide - among the highest of any psychiatric disorder - and mixed-features episodes (simultaneous manic and depressive symptoms) carry a recognised higher risk of impulsive suicidal behaviour than pure depressive episodes. A candidate-medicine-plus-efficacy% suggestion must never be the first or only output when any of these red flags are present; safety triage and real-world emergency-service guidance comes first, medicine selection second. Additionally, because starting an antidepressant alone in undiagnosed or inadequately mood-stabilised bipolar disorder carries a real risk of precipitating a manic switch (pooled switching risk 8.18%, ~2.6-fold higher than control - Tondo L, Vazquez G, Baldessarini RJ, J Affect Disord 2013;148(1):129-135, PMID 23219059), any patient reporting depressive symptoms plus a history of even brief unusual elevated/irritable mood, decreased sleep need, or reckless behaviour should be flagged for mood-stabiliser-first management rather than antidepressant monotherapy before any medicine suggestion is finalised.
bipolar_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bipolar disorder is NOT curable by medicine: it is a real, lifelong, relapsing-remitting condition, and no drug or regimen found in this survey approaches a real, replicated ~100% relapse-prevention rate in an unselected population -- so no curative_option is listed here, because claiming one would misrepresent the evidence. What IS real and genuinely important is that mood stabilizers achieve substantial, evidence-backed episode control and relapse-risk reduction in a majority of patients, and that lithium in particular has a real, distinctive, and clinically important anti-suicide effect not clearly shared by other psychiatric drugs. Geddes JR et al. (Am J Psychiatry 2004;161(2):217-222, PMID 14754766), a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (n=770), found long-term lithium reduced all relapses by a real relative risk of 0.65 (95% CI 0.50-0.84, an approximately 35% relative risk reduction) and manic relapses specifically by RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.40-0.95, approximately 38% reduction); the protective effect on depressive relapse was smaller and not statistically robust (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.49-1.07). Separately -- and this is the single most distinctive real finding for lithium among all psychiatric medicines -- Cipriani A et al. (BMJ 2013;346:f3646, PMID 23814104), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (n=6,674), found lithium reduced completed suicide by odds ratio 0.13 (95% CI 0.03-0.66) versus placebo, an approximately 87% relative reduction in the odds of suicide, and reduced all-cause mortality (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.15-0.95, approximately 62% reduction). No other mood stabilizer or antipsychotic in psychiatry has this specific, replicated, meta-analytic anti-suicide signal, which is why lithium requires routine serum-level monitoring (narrow therapeutic index, target typically 0.6-1.0 mEq/L) but remains the real gold-standard first-line agent. Even the best-performing real regimen identified in this survey -- lithium plus valproate combination therapy in the BALANCE trial (Geddes JR et al., Lancet 2010;375(9712):385-395, PMID 20092882, n=330, up to 24 months) -- still saw 54% of patients require a new intervention for an emergent mood episode (versus 59% on lithium alone and 69% on valproate alone); i.e. even the most effective real combination did not prevent relapse in the majority of the cohort over the long term, and no single medicine or regimen in the real literature reaches an unselected ~100% relapse-free outcome. The honest picture: managing bipolar disorder is a real, genuinely solvable engineering problem of matching the right mood stabilizer (or combination) to the individual patient's dominant relapse pole (manic vs depressive) and monitoring closely -- not a disease that medicine cures outright.

bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.name: Lithium -- Real Gold-Standard Maintenance Mood Stabilizer (Long-Term Relapse Prevention)
bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.type: Mood stabilizer, first-line, alkali metal salt
bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.effectiveness: Geddes JR et al. (Am J Psychiatry 2004;161(2):217-222, PMID 14754766), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (n=770) comparing lithium with placebo, found lithium significantly reduced all relapses (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.84 -- approximately 35% relative risk reduction) and manic relapses specifically (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40-0.95 -- approximately 38% reduction). The protective effect on depressive relapse was smaller and not statistically robust (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.49-1.07). This was independently corroborated in the pooled 18-month lamotrigine/lithium/placebo maintenance dataset (Goodwin GM et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2004;65(3):432-441, PMID 15096085, n=638), where lithium's median time-to-any-mood-intervention was 184 days versus 86 days on placebo, and lithium (not lamotrigine) was the treatment specifically superior to placebo for delaying manic episodes.
bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.reason_why: Lithium's exact mechanism is incompletely understood but includes inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3beta (GSK-3beta) and inositol monophosphatase, effects on neurotrophic (BDNF) signalling and circadian rhythm stabilization, which together dampen the amplitude of manic swings more robustly than depressive swings -- the real, physiological basis for its asymmetric efficacy (stronger for mania than depression).
bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.important_caveat: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (target serum level typically 0.6-1.0 mEq/L) requiring routine blood, renal and thyroid monitoring; abrupt discontinuation is associated with rebound relapse risk, which some experts argue may have inflated apparent placebo relapse rates in older discontinuation-design trials. It is not curative -- some real patients still relapse on lithium, particularly with depressive episodes.
bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.real_working_solution: Lithium remains real first-line maintenance therapy for bipolar I disorder, especially when the dominant relapse risk is mania; routine serum-level and renal/thyroid monitoring is required, and it should never be abruptly stopped.
bd_lithium_maintenance_relapse_preventio.source: Geddes JR et al., Am J Psychiatry 2004;161(2):217-222 (PMID 14754766); Goodwin GM et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2004;65(3):432-441 (PMID 15096085)

bd_lithium_anti_suicide_effect.name: Lithium -- Real, Distinctive Anti-Suicide Effect (Unique Among Psychiatric Medicines)
bd_lithium_anti_suicide_effect.effectiveness: Cipriani A et al. (BMJ 2013;346:f3646, PMID 23814104), an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (n=6,674 participants with mood disorders including bipolar disorder), found lithium significantly reduced completed suicide versus placebo (odds ratio 0.13, 95% CI 0.03-0.66 -- an approximately 87% relative reduction in the odds of suicide) and reduced death from any cause (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.15-0.95 -- approximately 62% reduction). No clear benefit was found for deliberate self-harm specifically (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.27-1.32, not statistically significant).
bd_lithium_anti_suicide_effect.reason_why: The authors note lithium's anti-suicidal effect may work partly through relapse prevention of the underlying mood disorder, but propose additional real mechanisms: lithium has documented effects on reducing aggression and impulsivity independent of mood-episode control, which may explain why its anti-suicide signal appears larger and more specific than mood-stabilization alone would predict.
bd_lithium_anti_suicide_effect.important_caveat: This is a real, replicated, and clinically important finding, but it rests on relatively few completed-suicide events across the pooled trials (suicide is a rare outcome even in high-risk populations), so the confidence interval is wide (0.03-0.66) -- interpret as a strong real signal, not a precise point estimate.
bd_lithium_anti_suicide_effect.real_working_solution: In bipolar patients with significant suicide risk, lithium should be considered specifically for its distinctive real anti-suicide property, not only for mood-episode control -- this is one of the only medicines in all of psychiatry with a real, meta-analytically supported, specific anti-suicide effect.

bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.name: Valproate/Divalproex Sodium -- Real Efficacy for Acute Mania
bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.type: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer, first-line for acute mania
bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.effectiveness: Bowden CL et al. (JAMA 1994;271(12):918-924, PMID 8120960), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=179 hospitalized acutely manic patients, ~half previously lithium-nonresponsive), found 48% of divalproex-treated patients achieved >=50% improvement on the Mania Rating Scale versus 25% on placebo (p=.004); lithium achieved 49% response in the same trial (p=.025 vs placebo). Divalproex was as effective in rapid-cycling manic patients as in others, and its efficacy was independent of prior lithium non-response.
bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.reason_why: Valproate increases GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, dampening the cortical/limbic hyperexcitability thought to underlie acute manic states; its real efficacy in patients who had already failed lithium suggests a distinct, non-overlapping mechanism of antimanic action.
bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.important_caveat: Valproate carries a real, serious teratogenicity risk: the EURAP pregnancy registry (Tomson T et al., Lancet Neurol 2011;10(7):609-617, PMID 21652013; 1,010 valproic-acid-exposed pregnancies) found major congenital malformation rates significantly higher with valproic acid than with lamotrigine at every dose studied, in a clear dose-dependent pattern, with lamotrigine <300 mg/day carrying the lowest rate (2.0%). This is a real, important reason valproate is generally avoided, or used only with strict contraception counselling, in women of childbearing potential. Separately, in a 52-week randomized maintenance trial (Bowden CL et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):481-489, PMID 10807488, n=372), divalproex did NOT differ significantly from placebo on the primary outcome (time to any mood recurrence) -- an honest negative finding for long-term maintenance monotherapy, even though divalproex is real and effective for the acute manic episode itself.
bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.real_working_solution: Valproate/divalproex is a real, effective first-line option for acute mania (response rate comparable to lithium, ~48-49% vs 25% placebo), but its long-term maintenance benefit is less proven than lithium's, and it should be avoided in women of childbearing potential wherever a safer alternative exists because of real, dose-dependent teratogenic risk.
bd_valproate_divalproex_acute_mania.source: Bowden CL et al., JAMA 1994;271(12):918-924 (PMID 8120960); Bowden CL et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):481-489 (PMID 10807488); Tomson T et al., Lancet Neurol 2011;10(7):609-617 (PMID 21652013)

bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.name: Lamotrigine -- Real, Specific Efficacy for Bipolar DEPRESSION and Maintenance (NOT Acute Mania)
bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.type: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer, distinct depression-predominant profile
bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.effectiveness: Goodwin GM et al. (J Clin Psychiatry 2004;65(3):432-441, PMID 15096085), a pooled analysis of 2 placebo-controlled 18-month maintenance trials (n=638 bipolar I patients), found lamotrigine significantly delayed time to intervention for a mood episode versus placebo (median survival 197 days vs 86 days) and was specifically superior to placebo for delaying depressive episodes, whereas lithium (not lamotrigine) was the treatment specifically superior to placebo for delaying manic episodes in the same analysis.
bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.reason_why: Lamotrigine inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and reduces glutamate release, but its real clinical profile is distinctively depression-weighted rather than antimanic -- consistent with trial data showing it has no meaningful efficacy for treating or preventing acute mania, in real contrast to lithium, valproate, and the antipsychotics; this is an important, genuine, clinically distinguishing feature.
bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.important_caveat: Lamotrigine is NOT an effective acute antimanic agent and should never be used as monotherapy for an active manic episode. It also carries a real risk of serious rash (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome), which is why it must be started at a very low dose and up-titrated slowly over weeks -- a real practical limitation on how quickly it can help an acutely depressed bipolar patient.
bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.real_working_solution: Lamotrigine is the real, evidence-preferred mood stabilizer specifically for bipolar depression prevention and maintenance therapy in patients whose dominant real risk is depressive (not manic) relapse, always titrated slowly to avoid rash.
bd_lamotrigine_bipolar_depression_and_ma.source: Goodwin GM et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2004;65(3):432-441 (PMID 15096085)

bd_carbamazepine_acute_mania.name: Carbamazepine (Extended-Release) -- Real Efficacy for Acute Mania
bd_carbamazepine_acute_mania.effectiveness: Weisler RH et al. (J Clin Psychiatry 2005;66(3):323-330, PMID 15766298), a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=239 hospitalized bipolar I patients with manic/mixed episodes), found extended-release carbamazepine produced significantly greater improvement in Young Mania Rating Scale and CGI scores than placebo, with significant separation from placebo beginning as early as day 7; a significantly greater proportion of placebo patients discontinued for lack of efficacy (p<.001).
bd_carbamazepine_acute_mania.reason_why: Carbamazepine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels similarly to valproate and lamotrigine, reducing neuronal hyperexcitability, and its real antimanic efficacy was confirmed in this large placebo-controlled trial after decades of prior open-label clinical use.
bd_carbamazepine_acute_mania.important_caveat: Carbamazepine induces its own hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4) and has extensive real drug-drug interactions, a major practical limitation especially in patients on multiple medications; it is generally considered a lower-priority option than lithium or valproate for first-line use (Akiskal HS et al., CNS Spectr 2005;10(6 Suppl 1):1-15, PMID 16041864). The pivotal trial's published abstract reported YMRS/CGI score changes rather than a plain categorical responder percentage, so effectiveness_pct for this entry is intentionally left null in the ranked table below rather than estimated.
bd_carbamazepine_acute_mania.real_working_solution: Carbamazepine ER is a real, effective option for acute mania, particularly useful as a second/third-line agent for patients unable to tolerate or who fail lithium/valproate, with the caveat of significant real drug-interaction risk requiring careful medication reconciliation.
bd_carbamazepine_acute_mania.source: Weisler RH et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2005;66(3):323-330 (PMID 15766298)

bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.name: Quetiapine -- Real Dual Efficacy for BOTH Manic AND Depressive Episodes
bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.type: Atypical antipsychotic, unique dual-phase real efficacy
bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.effectiveness: Weisler RH et al. (J Clin Psychiatry 2008;69(5):769-782, PMID 18452345), a post hoc pooled analysis of the BOLDER I and II randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (n=694 bipolar I depression patients), found quetiapine (300 or 600 mg/day) produced significantly greater MADRS score reduction than placebo at week 8 (-19.4 and -19.6 vs -12.6, p<.001 for each dose), with large effect sizes of 0.78 and 0.80. Thase ME et al. (J Clin Psychopharmacol 2006;26(6):600-609, PMID 17110817, the original BOLDER II trial, n=509) independently confirmed significant MADRS/HAM-D improvement and significantly higher MADRS response/remission rates than placebo, with a LOWER incidence of treatment-emergent mania/hypomania on quetiapine than placebo. Quetiapine also has real, separately established antimanic efficacy, confirmed in the Perlis RH et al. meta-analysis of atypical antipsychotics for acute mania (J Clin Psychiatry 2006;67(4):509-516, PMID 16669715, 12 monotherapy + 6 adjunctive placebo-controlled trials, n=4,304).
bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.reason_why: Quetiapine's active metabolite norquetiapine has meaningful norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and partial 5-HT1A agonism in addition to D2/5-HT2A antagonism, giving it a real pharmacological basis for antidepressant activity that most other antipsychotics used in mania lack -- the real, distinctive reason it is one of very few agents genuinely effective across BOTH poles of bipolar illness.
bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.important_caveat: The pooled BOLDER analysis reported effect sizes and MADRS score change rather than a plain categorical responder percentage in the accessible abstract text, so effectiveness_pct for the depression indication is intentionally left null in the ranked table below (with the reason stated) rather than estimated; the effect sizes (0.78-0.80) are nonetheless large by conventional psychiatric-trial standards. Sedation, weight gain and metabolic effects are common real adverse effects requiring monitoring.
bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.real_working_solution: Quetiapine is a real, evidence-strong choice specifically when a bipolar patient needs one medicine effective for both current-episode polarities (depression now, mania risk later), which is not true of most other single agents in this survey.
bd_quetiapine_bipolar_depression_and_man.source: Weisler RH et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2008;69(5):769-782 (PMID 18452345); Thase ME et al., J Clin Psychopharmacol 2006;26(6):600-609 (PMID 17110817); Perlis RH et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2006;67(4):509-516 (PMID 16669715)

bd_atypical_antipsychotics_comparative_a.name: Atypical Antipsychotics for Acute Mania -- Real Comparative Efficacy (Aripiprazole, Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Risperidone, Ziprasidone)
bd_atypical_antipsychotics_comparative_a.effectiveness: Perlis RH et al. (J Clin Psychiatry 2006;67(4):509-516, PMID 16669715), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 placebo-controlled monotherapy and 6 placebo-controlled adjunctive trials (n=4,304, including 1,750 placebo-treated), found aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, and ziprasidone all demonstrated significant efficacy over placebo for acute mania, with no statistically significant pairwise differences among them after adjustment for multiple comparisons -- i.e. real efficacy is broadly comparable across this drug class for the manic pole.
bd_atypical_antipsychotics_comparative_a.reason_why: All five agents share D2 dopamine receptor antagonism as their core antimanic mechanism, which explains why their acute antimanic efficacy clusters together despite differing 5-HT and other receptor profiles that differentiate them on other axes (e.g. depression efficacy, metabolic risk).
bd_atypical_antipsychotics_comparative_a.important_caveat: Because efficacy is broadly comparable, real-world drug choice is usually driven by side-effect profile (metabolic risk with olanzapine/quetiapine, akathisia with aripiprazole, prolactin elevation with risperidone) rather than differential antimanic potency.
bd_atypical_antipsychotics_comparative_a.real_working_solution: Any of these five atypical antipsychotics is a real, evidence-supported choice for acute mania; selection should be individualized on tolerability rather than an assumed superior efficacy of one over another.
bd_atypical_antipsychotics_comparative_a.source: Perlis RH et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2006;67(4):509-516 (PMID 16669715)

bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.name: Aripiprazole Monotherapy -- Real Head-to-Head Trial vs Lithium and Placebo for Acute Mania
bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.type: Atypical antipsychotic (dopamine D2/D3 partial agonist), acute and continuation mania treatment
bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.effectiveness: Keck PE et al. (J Affect Disord 2009;112(1-3):36-49, PMID 18835043), a randomized, double-blind, placebo- and lithium-controlled trial (n=480 acute bipolar I mania patients), found response rates at week 3 of 46.8% for aripiprazole and 45.8% for lithium versus 34.4% for placebo (both p<0.05); response increased by week 12 to 56.5% for aripiprazole and 49.0% for lithium, with aripiprazole showing significant separation from placebo as early as day 2.
bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.reason_why: Aripiprazole's partial dopamine D2/D3 agonism produces a stabilizing rather than purely blocking effect on dopaminergic tone, giving real antimanic efficacy typically with less sedation and metabolic burden than full D2 antagonists like olanzapine or quetiapine.
bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.important_caveat: Aripiprazole's real efficacy magnitude in this head-to-head trial was statistically similar to, not superior to, lithium -- it should be considered a real alternative with a different side-effect profile (akathisia is common), not a more powerful antimanic agent.
bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.real_working_solution: Aripiprazole is a real, effective, metabolically well-tolerated first-line option for acute and continuation-phase mania, with efficacy statistically comparable to lithium in a direct randomized comparison.
bd_aripiprazole_mania_head_to_head_trial.source: Keck PE et al., J Affect Disord 2009;112(1-3):36-49 (PMID 18835043)

bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.name: Lurasidone -- Real, FDA-Approved Efficacy Specifically for Bipolar Depression (PREVAIL-1)
bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.type: Atypical antipsychotic, FDA-approved specifically for bipolar I depression (monotherapy and adjunctive)
bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.effectiveness: Loebel A et al. (Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(2):160-168, PMID 24170180), the pivotal PREVAIL-1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=505 bipolar I depression patients), found lurasidone monotherapy significantly reduced MADRS scores at week 6 for both the 20-60 mg/day group (-15.4, effect size 0.51) and 80-120 mg/day group (-15.4, effect size 0.51) versus placebo (-10.7); CGI-BP depression severity also improved significantly (effect sizes 0.61 and 0.50). Discontinuation due to adverse events was low and similar across groups (5.9-6.6%), and minimal metabolic/weight changes were seen.
bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.reason_why: Lurasidone has high-affinity antagonism at 5-HT7 receptors (a real, distinguishing pharmacological feature versus most other antipsychotics) alongside D2/5-HT2A antagonism and partial 5-HT1A agonism, a receptor profile specifically implicated in its real antidepressant activity in bipolar depression.
bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.important_caveat: Lurasidone was studied and is FDA-approved specifically for the bipolar DEPRESSION indication, not for acute mania; it also has a real, favorable metabolic profile (minimal weight/lipid/glucose change) compared with olanzapine or quetiapine, an important real differentiator for long-term use. The pivotal trial reported effect sizes/score change, not a categorical responder percentage in the accessible abstract, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null in the ranked table below.
bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.real_working_solution: Lurasidone is a real, well-tolerated, metabolically favorable evidence-based choice specifically for bipolar I depression, as monotherapy or added to lithium/valproate.
bd_lurasidone_bipolar_depression.source: Loebel A et al., Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(2):160-168 (PMID 24170180)

bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.name: Cariprazine -- Real, FDA-Approved Efficacy Specifically for Bipolar Depression
bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.type: Atypical antipsychotic (D3-preferring D3/D2 partial agonist), FDA-approved for bipolar depression and mania
bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.effectiveness: Earley W et al. (Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(6):439-448, PMID 30845817), a phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=480 bipolar I depression patients), found both cariprazine 1.5 mg/day and 3.0 mg/day significantly reduced MADRS scores versus placebo (least-squares mean difference -2.5 and -3.0 respectively). This was independently supported in a second phase 3 trial (Earley WR et al., Bipolar Disord 2020;22(4):372-384, PMID 31628698, n=493), where cariprazine 1.5 mg/day significantly reduced MADRS scores versus placebo (LSMD -2.5, adjusted p=.0417), although the 3.0 mg/day dose did not reach significance in that second trial.
bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.reason_why: Cariprazine's preferential partial agonism at dopamine D3 (over D2) receptors, combined with 5-HT1A partial agonism and 5-HT2A antagonism, is proposed to underlie its real efficacy across both the depressive and manic poles of bipolar disorder -- a genuinely distinguishing dual-indication FDA approval shared with quetiapine among antipsychotics.
bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.important_caveat: The lower 1.5 mg/day dose showed more consistent efficacy across both pivotal trials than the 3.0 mg/day dose, an important real dose-response nuance -- more is not necessarily better with cariprazine for the depression indication. Akathisia and restlessness are the most common real adverse effects. Both pivotal trials reported only continuous MADRS/CGI-S score differences, not a categorical responder percentage, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null in the ranked table below.
bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.real_working_solution: Cariprazine 1.5 mg/day is the real, more consistently evidence-supported starting dose for bipolar I depression, with cautious titration if needed.
bd_cariprazine_bipolar_depression.source: Earley W et al., Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(6):439-448 (PMID 30845817); Earley WR et al., Bipolar Disord 2020;22(4):372-384 (PMID 31628698)

bd_lithium_valproate_combination_therapy.name: Lithium Plus Valproate Combination Therapy -- Real Best-in-Survey Relapse Prevention (BALANCE Trial)
bd_lithium_valproate_combination_therapy.effectiveness: Geddes JR et al. (Lancet 2010;375(9712):385-395, PMID 20092882), the BALANCE randomized, open-label trial (n=330 bipolar I patients, up to 24 months), found 54% of the combination-therapy group required a new intervention for an emergent mood episode versus 59% on lithium monotherapy and 69% on valproate monotherapy. Combination therapy was significantly better than valproate monotherapy (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42-0.83, p=.0023 -- approximately 41% relative risk reduction) and lithium alone was significantly better than valproate alone (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51-1.00, p=.0472 -- approximately 29% reduction); the trial could not reliably confirm or refute a benefit of combination therapy over lithium monotherapy alone (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.58-1.17, p=.27).
bd_lithium_valproate_combination_therapy.reason_why: Combining an agent with strong antimanic bias (lithium) with one thought to add anti-recurrence benefit (valproate) targets a broader range of relapse mechanisms than either drug alone, the real rationale tested (and partially supported) by BALANCE.
bd_lithium_valproate_combination_therapy.important_caveat: Even the best-performing real regimen in this trial (combination therapy) still saw 54% of patients require a new intervention within 2 years -- i.e. no regimen in this real trial came close to preventing relapse in the majority of patients over the long term, an important honest limitation to state plainly rather than oversell.
bd_lithium_valproate_combination_therapy.real_working_solution: Lithium plus valproate combination therapy is a real, evidence-supported option when either monotherapy alone is inadequate, with the strongest real advantage demonstrated over valproate monotherapy specifically.

bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.name: Antidepressants in Bipolar Depression -- Real Controversial, Limited Evidence and Real Manic-Switch Risk
bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.type: SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, bupropion -- adjunctive-use caution, not primary/monotherapy recommendation
bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.effectiveness: Pacchiarotti I et al. (Am J Psychiatry 2013;170(11):1249-1262, PMID 24030475), the International Society for Bipolar Disorders (ISBD) task force consensus report, concluded there is a 'striking incongruity between the wide use of and the weak evidence base' for antidepressants in bipolar disorder, with insufficient evidence for treatment benefit when combined with mood stabilizers; the task force could not make broad statements endorsing antidepressant use, though individual patients may benefit.
bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.reason_why: Antidepressants (particularly tricyclics and SNRIs) can precipitate a switch into mania/hypomania in vulnerable bipolar patients, a real risk documented directly in a bipolar population: Truman CJ et al. (J Clin Psychiatry 2007;68(10):1472-1479, PMID 17960960), using STEP-BD data (n=338 with prior antidepressant treatment), found 44% reported at least one manic/hypomanic switch episode associated with antidepressant use, with markedly higher odds for tricyclics (OR 7.80, 95% CI 1.56-28.9) and SSRIs (OR 3.73, 95% CI 1.98-7.05) than for electroconvulsive therapy or MAOIs, which were associated with less switch.
bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.important_caveat: This is a real, important prescribing caution, not a blanket prohibition: the ISBD task force specifically recommends that in bipolar I patients, antidepressants should be used only as an ADJUNCT to a mood-stabilizing medication, never as monotherapy, and that real switch risk is higher in bipolar I than bipolar II.
bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.real_working_solution: If an antidepressant is used at all in bipolar depression, real guideline-concordant practice is to add it on top of an existing mood stabilizer or antipsychotic (never alone), favoring agents with lower real switch risk (SSRIs, bupropion) over tricyclics or venlafaxine, and monitoring closely for emergent hypomania/mania.
bd_antidepressants_bipolar_depression_ca.source: Pacchiarotti I et al., Am J Psychiatry 2013;170(11):1249-1262 (PMID 24030475); Truman CJ et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2007;68(10):1472-1479 (PMID 17960960)

bd_electroconvulsive_therapy.name: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) -- Real Option for Severe/Treatment-Resistant Bipolar Mania or Depression
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), bilateral or unilateral electrode placement
bd_electroconvulsive_therapy.effectiveness: The UK ECT Review Group (Lancet 2003;361(9360):799-808, PMID 12642045), a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in depressive disorders (a population including bipolar depression), found real ECT was significantly more effective than simulated (sham) ECT (6 trials, 256 patients, standardised effect size -0.91, 95% CI -1.27 to -0.54) and significantly more effective than pharmacotherapy (18 trials, 1,144 participants, SES -0.80, 95% CI -1.29 to -0.29); bilateral ECT was more effective than unilateral ECT (22 trials, 1,408 participants, SES -0.32).
bd_electroconvulsive_therapy.reason_why: ECT induces a generalized seizure under controlled, anaesthetized conditions, producing rapid, broad neurochemical and neuroplastic changes (including profound but transient effects on monoamine systems and neurotrophic signalling) that can resolve severe mood-episode symptoms faster than pharmacotherapy in many real patients -- why it remains a real option for the most severe or medication-resistant presentations of either pole of bipolar illness.
bd_electroconvulsive_therapy.important_caveat: This meta-analysis pooled depressive disorders broadly rather than isolating bipolar depression specifically, so the effect sizes should be read as real evidence for depressive-episode treatment in general; bipolar-specific ECT literature (smaller trials and case series) supports similar real benefit in both severe bipolar mania and bipolar depression, but with less large-trial bipolar-specific quantification than for lithium or the antipsychotics in this survey, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null in the ranked table below rather than transposed from the general-depression effect sizes. Real, transient cognitive side effects (anterograde/retrograde memory impairment) are the main practical limitation.
bd_electroconvulsive_therapy.real_working_solution: ECT is a real, effective, fast-acting option that should be considered for severe, treatment-resistant, or life-threatening (e.g. actively suicidal, catatonic, or severely psychotic) episodes of either bipolar mania or bipolar depression, not withheld as a last resort beyond reasonable clinical need.
