malaria.name: Malaria

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Severe (complicated) malaria -- overwhelmingly but not exclusively caused by P. falciparum -- is a real medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalization and emergency-level parenteral antimalarial treatment, not routine outpatient management; CDC states plainly that malaria 'is a medical emergency that can rapidly progress to severe disease and death if not diagnosed and treated promptly' and that 'urgent diagnosis followed by immediate treatment is critical.' A patient meets WHO (2000 revision) criteria for severe malaria if any one of the following is present: (1) Cerebral malaria -- unrousable coma not attributable to any other cause, Glasgow Coma Scale <=9, persisting at least 30 minutes after any seizure; caused by sequestration of parasitized erythrocytes in cerebral microvasculature; real mortality 10-50% despite treatment. (2) Severe anemia -- hematocrit <15% or hemoglobin <50 g/L with parasite count >10,000/microL. (3) Hypoglycemia -- whole blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL). (4) Acute renal failure -- urine output <400 mL/24h in adults and/or serum creatinine >265 micromol/L (>3.0 mg/dL). (5) Hyperparasitemia -- >5% parasitized erythrocytes or >250,000 parasites/microL in a non-immune individual. (6) Acidosis -- arterial pH <7.25 or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L. (7) Shock/'algid malaria' -- systolic blood pressure <70 mmHg in patients over 5 years of age. (8) Jaundice -- total bilirubin >43 micromol/L (>2.5 mg/dL). (9) Hyperpyrexia -- core body temperature >40C. (10) Pulmonary edema or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and/or abnormal spontaneous bleeding. Real mortality across severe malaria managed in intensive care settings may exceed 20%, and even imported (generally earlier-presenting) falciparum malaria carries a real case-fatality rate of 0.6-3.8%; among children, delayed care-seeking after symptom onset is associated with case-fatality rates up to 25% once complications develop. Pregnant women, children under 5, and non-immune travelers should be triaged with a lower threshold of suspicion for impending severe disease, since they lack the partial acquired immunity that allows endemic-area adults to tolerate parasitemia with milder symptoms.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697), citing WHO 2000 severe malaria criteria; CDC, Malaria Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/clinical-guidance); Amoadu M et al., Delay in malaria care-seeking for children under five in Africa: a systematic review, Malar J 2026 (PMC13112638); Mischlinger J et al., Clinical Microbiology Reviews 2020 (PMC7067581)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Five Plasmodium species cause human malaria: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale (with two genetically distinct subspecies, P. ovale curtisi and P. ovale wallikeri), P. malariae, and the zoonotic P. knowlesi. Rarely, transmission also occurs via blood transfusion, shared needles, or congenitally (mother to fetus).
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_overview: WHO, Fact sheet: Malaria (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria); Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
definition_and_pathophysiology.species_relative_severity: P. falciparum is real-world 'the deadliest malaria parasite and the most prevalent on the African continent' and is described in reviews as the most pathogenic species overall. P. vivax is 'the dominant malaria parasite in most countries outside of sub-Saharan Africa' and was traditionally taught as causing 'benign tertian' malaria, but this view has been revised: 'the lack of life-threatening complications associated with this infection have been recently questioned', and P. vivax is now recognized to cause severe disease and death, particularly in infants, pregnant women and the malnourished. P. ovale and P. malariae are generally milder, less often causing severe organ-threatening disease. P. knowlesi, a parasite of macaques that has emerged as a real zoonotic human pathogen in Southeast Asia, has a 24-hour intra-erythrocytic cycle enabling very rapid parasite multiplication; 'high level of parasitemia and severe manifestations resembling those of P. falciparum malaria have been described with a possible lethal outcome.'
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_species_severity: WHO, Fact sheet: Malaria (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria); Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
definition_and_pathophysiology.anopheles_transmission_cycle: Transmission requires a female Anopheles mosquito. When an infected mosquito takes a blood meal, it inoculates motile sporozoites into the skin/bloodstream. Inside the mosquito, sexual-stage gametocytes taken up from an infected human blood meal undergo fertilization and sporogony in the mosquito midgut; the resulting oocyst stage is 'the longest developmental phase as well as the only extracellular of the Plasmodium life cycle', ultimately releasing sporozoites that migrate to the mosquito's salivary glands, completing the cycle and enabling transmission to the next human host.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_transmission_cycle: Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
definition_and_pathophysiology.hepatic_exoerythrocytic_stage: After inoculation, sporozoites travel via the bloodstream to the liver, where they 'enter the parenchymal cells of liver, and undergo their development and multiplication' asexually (exoerythrocytic schizogony), producing thousands of merozoites per infected hepatocyte over roughly 1-2 weeks before rupture releases merozoites into the bloodstream to invade red blood cells. This clinically silent hepatic stage is the target of 'causal prophylaxis' drug classes and, for P. vivax/P. ovale, of hypnozoite-directed radical-cure therapy.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_hepatic_stage: Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
definition_and_pathophysiology.erythrocytic_stage_and_paroxysm: Merozoites released from the liver invade erythrocytes and undergo asexual replication (the erythrocytic cycle: ring, trophozoite, schizont stages). Synchronous rupture of mature schizonts releases new merozoites (which invade further RBCs) together with parasite antigens and cellular debris that trigger a cytokine (TNF-alpha, IL-6) driven inflammatory response; this schizont rupture 'is followed by the appearance of the malaria febrile paroxysm classically lasting 8 to 12 hours.' The erythrocytic-cycle length determines the classic fever periodicity for each species.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_erythrocytic_stage: Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
definition_and_pathophysiology.hypnozoite_dormant_liver_stage: P. vivax and P. ovale possess a real, clinically important biological feature not shared by P. falciparum, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi: a dormant hepatic form called the hypnozoite, which 'persist[s] in the liver as "hypnozoites" that are eventually responsible [for] the phenomenon of relapse' -- clinical episodes reappearing weeks to months after the primary infection has been cleared from the blood, without any new mosquito bite. The precise biological trigger that determines whether a sporozoite develops immediately (primary infection) or remains dormant (hypnozoite) is still unknown. Because standard blood-stage antimalarials do not kill hypnozoites, P. vivax/P. ovale infection requires species-specific 'radical cure with drugs such as primaquine or tafenoquine' to clear the dormant liver reservoir and prevent relapse -- a direct, real mechanistic link between this life-cycle stage and drug selection.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_hypnozoite: Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990); Sarker JK et al., Prevalence of malaria and its major parasite species in Bangladesh: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Malar J 2026 (PMC13576336)

diagnostic_framework.microscopy_gold_standard: Light microscopy of Giemsa-stained thick and thin peripheral blood smears remains the real diagnostic gold standard for malaria: it allows direct visualization and speciation of parasites, and quantification of parasitemia (percentage of parasitized red cells), which is itself part of severe-malaria risk stratification. It is inexpensive and does not require advanced equipment, but performance is highly operator- and technique-dependent, and a single negative smear cannot exclude malaria: guidance recommends that 'blood smears should be repeated every 12-24 hours for a total of three sets before the diagnosis of malaria can be ruled out.' In one direct comparative evaluation using PCR as the reference standard, microscopy sensitivity/specificity were reported as 74.3%/99.1% (PPV 96.3%, NPV 92.2%) -- illustrating that real-world microscopy sensitivity is imperfect and can miss low-density or sub-patent infections, even though it remains the reference method against which other tests are validated in most clinical settings.
diagnostic_framework.source_microscopy: CDC, Malaria Diagnosis & Testing (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/diagnosis-testing); Bantie GM et al., Current practices and innovative diagnostics for Malaria in Ethiopia: a scoping review, BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMC13383435), citing Alemayehu et al. 2025
diagnostic_framework.rapid_diagnostic_tests: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are immunochromatographic dipstick/cassette assays detecting parasite antigens (histidine-rich protein 2/HRP2 for P. falciparum, and pan-species or species-specific lactate dehydrogenase/pLDH), giving a result in 2-15 minutes; the FDA approved the first RDT for U.S. clinical laboratory use in 2007. RDTs are invaluable in low-resource and point-of-care settings without microscopy expertise, but real-world performance is highly product- and parasite-density dependent: a comparative scoping review reported sensitivities/specificities ranging from as low as 47.5%/98.5% (Para Screen) up to 99.5%/98.0% (SD BIOLINE Malaria Ag Pf/Pan) and 95.7%/82.7% (CareStart Pf/Pv Combo) across different commercial RDT brands and study populations; sensitivity for HRP2-based tests drops substantially at low parasitemia, which is why ultrasensitive RDTs (uRDTs) have been developed specifically to improve detection of low-density infection (one uRDT evaluation reported 55.5% sensitivity/98.6% specificity). Because of this variability, it is recommended that 'all RDTs are followed-up with microscopy to confirm the results and if positive, to confirm the species.'
diagnostic_framework.source_rdt: CDC, Malaria Diagnosis & Testing (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/diagnosis-testing); Bantie GM et al., Current practices and innovative diagnostics for Malaria in Ethiopia: a scoping review, BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMC13383435)
diagnostic_framework.pcr_role: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detects Plasmodium nucleic acid and 'may be more sensitive than blood smear microscopy', making it the most sensitive method for detecting low-density, mixed-species, and sub-patent infections that microscopy and RDTs miss. In a real India cohort of pregnant women in Odisha, 74.3% of PCR-confirmed malaria infections were sub-patent (detectable only by PCR, not routine microscopy or RDT) and 79.6% were entirely asymptomatic -- demonstrating PCR's real, substantial added diagnostic value for detecting a clinically silent reservoir with public-health transmission relevance. However, PCR is comparatively expensive, requires laboratory infrastructure, and results typically arrive too late to guide acute bedside management, so it functions mainly as a confirmatory/species-differentiation and surveillance tool rather than an initial point-of-care test.
diagnostic_framework.source_pcr: CDC, Malaria Diagnosis & Testing (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/diagnosis-testing); Sandeepta S et al., Hidden burden of malaria in pregnancy in hard-to-reach areas of Odisha, India, Front Public Health 2026 (PMC13529693)
diagnostic_framework.parasitemia_quantification_and_severity: Quantifying peripheral parasitemia (percentage of parasitized erythrocytes, or parasites/microliter on microscopy) is a core, real part of severe-malaria risk stratification for P. falciparum: the WHO hyperparasitemia threshold of >5% parasitized erythrocytes (or >250,000 parasites/microL in non-immune individuals) is itself one of the defining WHO severe-malaria criteria, because higher parasite biomass correlates with higher risk of organ dysfunction and death. Baseline complete blood count and metabolic panels are also recommended at diagnosis specifically to screen for severity indicators (anemia, hypoglycemia, renal impairment, hyperbilirubinemia) that inform whether a case should be managed as uncomplicated versus severe malaria.
diagnostic_framework.source_parasitemia: Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697); CDC, Malaria Diagnosis & Testing (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/diagnosis-testing)

classic_symptoms.fever_periodicity_by_species: The classic malarial paroxysm (fever with chills/rigors, then defervescence with sweating) recurs at intervals determined by each species' erythrocytic-cycle length: a 48-hour ('tertian') cycle for P. falciparum, P. vivax and P. ovale; a 72-hour ('quartan') cycle for P. malariae; and a unique 24-hour (daily/quotidian) cycle for the zoonotic P. knowlesi, whose rapid replication also produces the highest rates of parasitemia among the non-falciparum species. In practice, especially early in P. falciparum infection or in mixed infections, fever is often irregular/continuous rather than showing a clean textbook periodicity, because parasite broods are not yet synchronized.
classic_symptoms.source_fever_periodicity: Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
classic_symptoms.paroxysm_mechanism: Each febrile paroxysm is triggered by synchronous rupture of mature blood-stage schizonts, releasing merozoites, parasite toxins and cellular debris that provoke a cytokine-mediated fever response; the paroxysm 'classically last[s] 8 to 12 hours' and classically progresses through a cold stage (rigors), a hot stage (high fever, often 39-41C), and a sweating stage as the fever breaks.
classic_symptoms.source_paroxysm_mechanism: Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
classic_symptoms.chills_rigors_headache_myalgia: Alongside the cyclical fever, headache, myalgia, malaise, fatigue, nausea and vomiting are core, near-universal presenting complaints of acute malaria across all species, reflecting the systemic cytokine response to parasitized-erythrocyte rupture; these features are non-specific and overlap heavily with other acute febrile illnesses, which is a major real diagnostic challenge, especially early in the illness.
classic_symptoms.source_chills_rigors: CDC, Malaria Clinical Features (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/clinical-features); Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697)
classic_symptoms.splenomegaly: An enlarged, often tender spleen is a classic physical finding in malaria, developing as the reticuloendothelial system works to clear parasitized and damaged erythrocytes; CDC clinical guidance lists an enlarged spleen among the core signs of malaria, and also notes hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly (massive splenomegaly from chronic/repeated infection, seen mainly in endemic-area residents) as a real, though comparatively rare, longer-term complication.
classic_symptoms.progression_to_severe_complicated_malari: Malaria, overwhelmingly caused by P. falciparum (though P. vivax and P. knowlesi can also cause severe disease), can progress from uncomplicated illness to severe/complicated malaria, defined by CDC/WHO criteria that include: high parasitemia (>=5% parasitized erythrocytes), impaired consciousness (including cerebral malaria), seizures, circulatory collapse/shock, pulmonary edema or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury, and severe anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL). CDC frames this explicitly: malaria 'is a medical emergency that can rapidly progress to severe disease and death if not diagnosed and treated promptly', and 'urgent diagnosis followed by immediate treatment is critical.'
classic_symptoms.who_severe_malaria_criteria_detailed: The widely used WHO (2000 revision) criteria for severe/complicated malaria, with exact clinical/laboratory thresholds, are: Cerebral malaria -- unrousable coma not attributable to any other cause, Glasgow Coma Scale <=9, persisting at least 30 minutes after any seizure. Severe anemia -- hematocrit <15% or hemoglobin <50 g/L in the presence of parasite count >10,000/microL. Hypoglycemia -- whole blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL). Acute renal failure -- urine output <400 mL/24h in adults and serum creatinine >265 micromol/L (>3.0 mg/dL). Hyperparasitemia -- >5% parasitized erythrocytes or >250,000 parasites/microL (in non-immune individuals). Acidosis -- arterial pH <7.25 or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L. Shock ('algid malaria') -- systolic blood pressure <70 mmHg in patients over 5 years of age. Jaundice -- total bilirubin >43 micromol/L (>2.5 mg/dL). Hyperpyrexia -- core body temperature >40C. Pulmonary edema/ARDS and abnormal spontaneous bleeding are additional recognized severe-malaria features.
classic_symptoms.source_who_criteria: Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697), citing WHO 2000 criteria

differential_diagnosis.overview_india_relevant_febrile_illnesse: In India and other malaria-endemic tropical settings, malaria must be distinguished from a broad group of acute undifferentiated febrile illnesses -- most importantly dengue, enteric (typhoid) fever, and rickettsial infections (scrub typhus/spotted fever) -- because clinical overlap (fever, headache, myalgia, malaise) is substantial and species-specific management differs completely. A real India tertiary-care study of 253 patients with acute undifferentiated febrile illness found malaria accounted for only 5 cases (1.9%), a marked decline from an earlier (2008) report of 12% prevalence in a comparable setting -- itself an important real epidemiological signal of malaria's declining relative share among Indian febrile-illness etiologies as control programs have progressed.
differential_diagnosis.source_overview: Rathod BD et al., Etiology and Diagnostic Predictors of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness in Adult Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
differential_diagnosis.malaria_vs_dengue: In the same Indian cohort, features that favored a malaria diagnosis over dengue included: hepatosplenomegaly (60% of malaria cases vs 2.1% of dengue cases, odds ratio 10.1), hypoxia/SpO2 <94% (100% of malaria vs 12.5% of dengue), altered sensorium (60% vs 0%), and markedly elevated CRP >50 mg/L (100% vs 16.7%). Laboratory values also differed: malaria cases had the lowest mean hemoglobin (7.8 +/- 1.2 g/dL) and the highest mean creatinine (4.20 +/- 5.15 mg/dL) among the febrile-illness groups studied, reflecting malaria's propensity for severe anemia and acute kidney injury, whereas dengue classically features thrombocytopenia, retro-orbital pain, and a biphasic fever/rash pattern with plasma-leakage complications rather than the organ-specific severe-malaria picture.
differential_diagnosis.source_malaria_vs_dengue: Rathod BD et al., Etiology and Diagnostic Predictors of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness in Adult Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
differential_diagnosis.malaria_vs_typhoid: Typhoid (enteric) fever has a longer incubation period (6-30 days, versus malaria's typical 7-14 days) and its 'symptoms frequently mimic those of other febrile illnesses like malaria', with a usual symptom complex of sustained (rather than cyclical/paroxysmal) high fever, headache, malaise, nausea, abdominal pain, and either constipation or diarrhea; relative bradycardia and rose spots are classic but insensitive distinguishing clinical clues, and definitive distinction from malaria requires blood culture (typhoid) versus blood smear/RDT/PCR (malaria) rather than clinical pattern alone.
differential_diagnosis.source_malaria_vs_typhoid: Van Dessel L et al., Fever in the Returning Traveler: A Practical Overview for Initial Management and Assessment in the ED, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13300984)
differential_diagnosis.malaria_vs_rickettsial_scrub_typhus: Rickettsial infections (scrub typhus, spotted-fever group), which are highly India-relevant, are classically distinguished from malaria by the presence of an eschar (a black necrotic skin lesion at the site of chigger/tick bite, more common in scrub typhus and spotted-fever-group rickettsioses) along with a maculopapular rash -- a real, specific physical finding not seen in malaria. Scrub typhus can nonetheless mimic malaria closely and, in India, has been reported to present atypically with encephalopathy and fatal outcomes in young adults, underscoring that clinical pattern-matching alone is unreliable and laboratory confirmation (blood smear/RDT for malaria; serology/PCR for scrub typhus) is required.
differential_diagnosis.source_malaria_vs_rickettsial: Van Dessel L et al., Fever in the Returning Traveler: A Practical Overview for Initial Management and Assessment in the ED, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13300984); Sharma A et al., Eschar, enigma, and encephalopathy: a case series of atypical and fatal presentations of scrub typhus in young adults from Northern India, EXCLI J 2026 (PMC13369890)

risk_factors.risk_factor: Travel to or residence in a malaria-endemic area, and non-immune status
risk_factors.detail: The single overarching real risk factor is exposure in an endemic area. Critically, risk of severe/rapidly progressive disease differs sharply by prior exposure history: non-immune travelers from non-endemic countries lack any acquired partial immunity ('premunition') and are at real, substantially higher risk of rapid clinical deterioration when infected, whereas lifelong residents of high-transmission endemic areas develop partial immunity through repeated childhood exposure that allows them to tolerate parasitemia with milder or even no symptoms as adults -- a comparison specifically addressed in the specialist literature on imported malaria in non-endemic countries.
risk_factors.source: Mischlinger J et al., Imported Malaria in Countries where Malaria Is Not Endemic: a Comparison of Semi-immune and Nonimmune Travelers, Clinical Microbiology Reviews 2020 (PMC7067581)

risk_factors.detail: Pregnancy is a real, well-documented high-risk state for malaria, driven by pregnancy-associated immunomodulation that facilitates parasite persistence and placental sequestration, predisposing to both adverse maternal outcomes (severe anemia) and adverse fetal outcomes (low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction). In a real India (Odisha) cohort of 861 pregnant women in hard-to-reach, malaria-endemic areas, overall malaria prevalence was 33.0% (varying 9.8-51.1% by year), 65.1% of malaria-infected women were anemic, and strikingly 79.6% of infections were asymptomatic and 74.3% were sub-patent (detectable only by PCR) -- meaning a large hidden reservoir of infection persists in pregnancy even where routine screening appears reassuring. Placental-malaria susceptibility is also gravidity-dependent: first pregnancies (primigravidae) carry the highest risk because protective antibody responses to placenta-specific parasite adhesion proteins (VAR2CSA) develop only after repeated pregnancies.
risk_factors.source: Sandeepta S et al., Hidden burden of malaria in pregnancy in hard-to-reach areas of Odisha, India, Front Public Health 2026 (PMC13529693); Lewis SN et al., Gravidity-dependent protection against placental malaria is associated with enhanced natural killer cell-mediated antibody-dependent cellular activation, EBioMedicine 2026 (PMC13544314)

risk_factors.detail: Children under 5 are a real, disproportionately high-risk group with the least developed acquired immunity: WHO data show children under 5 accounted for approximately 75% of all malaria deaths in the WHO African Region in 2024, and a 2026 systematic review similarly reported children under 5 accounted for 76% of all malaria deaths globally in 2023 (with WHO figures of approximately 80% specifically within the African region). The same review found that delayed care-seeking after symptom onset in this age group is consistently associated with increased mortality, with case-fatality rates reported as high as 25% among children who develop complications after delayed presentation.
risk_factors.source: WHO, Fact sheet: Malaria (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria); Amoadu M et al., Delay in malaria care-seeking for children under five in Africa: a systematic review, Malar J 2026 (PMC13112638)

risk_factors.risk_factor: Sickle cell trait (heterozygous HbAS) and G6PD deficiency
risk_factors.detail: Sickle cell trait (heterozygous carriage of hemoglobin S, HbAS) is a real host genetic factor that partially protects against severe P. falciparum malaria; a 2026 review states it 'confers protection against severe malaria caused by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum' and 'remains the strongest known association with protection against malaria in the human genome', with protection specifically tied to the heterozygous state (homozygous HbSS instead causes sickle cell disease and is not itself protective in the same way); the exact protective mechanism(s) remain incompletely defined despite decades of study. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, common across malaria-endemic regions including parts of India, is another host genetic factor believed to confer partial protection against severe malaria through impaired parasite growth in G6PD-deficient erythrocytes, though its main clinical relevance in real-world malaria management is the risk of drug-induced hemolysis, which must be screened for before certain species-specific treatments are given.
risk_factors.source: Hamilton WL et al., Associations between the Plasmodium falciparum genome and sickle haemoglobin identified in mild malaria cases from Ghana, Malar J 2026 (PMC13295231); Taleb M et al., Epidemiology of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency in 10 malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic review, Pan Afr Med J 2025 (PMC11991299)

epidemiology.global_who_2024_data: Per WHO, globally in 2024 there were an estimated 282 million malaria cases and 610,000 malaria deaths across 80 countries. The WHO African Region carries a hugely disproportionate share of this burden: it was home to 95% of malaria cases (265 million) and 95% of malaria deaths (579,000) in 2024, and children under 5 accounted for about 75% of all malaria deaths within that region. P. falciparum is the most prevalent species on the African continent, while P. vivax is the dominant malaria parasite in most countries outside sub-Saharan Africa.
epidemiology.india_epidemiological_trends: India's malaria epidemiology has shifted substantially over decades: it was dominated by P. vivax in the 1960s, followed by a steady rise in P. falciparum prevalence from the 1970s that continued (with fluctuation) until around 2016, after which both case counts and the falciparum share have declined under intensified control efforts. As of 2023, India had exited WHO's 'High Burden to High Impact' (HBHI) country category, and 122 of India's 650 districts reported zero indigenous malaria cases that year. National control is coordinated by the National Center for Vector Borne Disease Control (formerly NVBDCP), using a 'Test, Treat, Track' strategy and a '1-3-7' surveillance-and-response model (case notified within 1 day, investigated within 3 days, focal response completed within 7 days), under the National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016-2030, which targets nationwide elimination by 2030.
epidemiology.source_india_trends: Vanlalhriata C et al., Rising burden of Plasmodium vivax in Mizoram: an emerging threat to malaria elimination in Northeast India, BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMC13527924)
epidemiology.india_regional_heterogeneity: Despite national progress, India's residual malaria burden is real and highly regionally concentrated: Mizoram, a small Northeast Indian state, had an Annual Parasite Incidence (API) of 12.9 (placing it in Category 3, the 'intensified control phase' under India's stratification), and contributed approximately 6.6% of the country's total malaria cases in 2024 despite representing only about 0.09% of India's population -- illustrating how a small number of high-transmission pockets (often forested, tribal, or Northeast-India districts) now account for a large, disproportionate share of India's remaining cases, with a rising relative share of P. vivax specifically in this region.
epidemiology.source_india_regional: Vanlalhriata C et al., Rising burden of Plasmodium vivax in Mizoram: an emerging threat to malaria elimination in Northeast India, BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMC13527924)

natural_history_and_prognosis.untreated_or_delayed_falciparum_malaria: CDC frames malaria explicitly as 'a medical emergency that can rapidly progress to severe disease and death if not diagnosed and treated promptly', with 'urgent diagnosis followed by immediate treatment' described as critical -- reflecting the real, rapid deterioration risk of P. falciparum infection, especially in non-immune individuals, pregnant women, and young children. Even with treatment, severe/complicated malaria carries substantial real mortality: cerebral malaria case-fatality is reported at 10-50% despite treatment, severe malaria managed in intensive care may exceed 20% mortality, and even imported (typically earlier-presenting, better-resourced-setting) falciparum malaria cases carry a real case-fatality rate of 0.6-3.8%. Among children specifically, delayed care-seeking after symptom onset is associated with case-fatality rates as high as 25% once complications develop.
natural_history_and_prognosis.source_untreated_falciparum: CDC, Malaria Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/clinical-guidance); Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697); Amoadu M et al., Delay in malaria care-seeking for children under five in Africa: a systematic review, Malar J 2026 (PMC13112638)
natural_history_and_prognosis.vivax_ovale_relapse_pattern: Because P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant hepatic hypnozoites, infection with either species carries a real, distinct natural-history risk not seen with P. falciparum, P. malariae or P. knowlesi: clinical relapse can occur weeks to months after the primary blood-stage infection has been fully treated and cleared, driven by reactivation of hypnozoites rather than any new mosquito bite or treatment failure. This is precisely why species identification matters clinically -- P. vivax/P. ovale infection requires species-specific radical-cure therapy (drugs such as primaquine or tafenoquine) targeting the dormant liver stage, in addition to standard blood-stage treatment, to prevent this relapse pattern; without radical cure, relapses can recur repeatedly over an extended period.
natural_history_and_prognosis.source_vivax_ovale_relapse: Sarker JK et al., Prevalence of malaria and its major parasite species in Bangladesh: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Malar J 2026 (PMC13576336); Antinori S et al., Biology of human malaria plasmodia including Plasmodium knowlesi, Mediterranean J Hematol Infect Dis 2012 (PMC3340990)
natural_history_and_prognosis.early_life_natural_history: A real, closely monitored infant cohort study in high-transmission Uganda found malaria incidence rose steadily with age in the first year of life -- from 0.53 episodes per person-year in infants under 3 months to 1.05 episodes per person-year at 6-12 months -- with 34.9% of all episodes occurring before 6 months of age, challenging the assumption that maternal antibodies meaningfully protect very young infants. In this intensively supervised research cohort with prompt access to treatment, 98.2% of symptomatic episodes were uncomplicated and there were zero malaria deaths -- but the study authors explicitly attributed this favorable outcome to the intensive clinical supervision and immediate treatment access of the research setting, not something generalizable to typical field conditions with delayed care access, where young-child mortality from malaria remains real and substantial (see epidemiology and risk-factor sections).
natural_history_and_prognosis.source_early_life: Aguti M et al., Natural History and the Burden of Malaria During the First Year of Life in the High-Transmission Setting of Uganda, Am J Trop Med Hyg 2026 (PMC13153588)

red_flags: Impaired consciousness, unrousable coma (cerebral malaria) or seizures in a patient with confirmed or suspected malaria -- WHO criterion: Glasgow Coma Scale <=9; real mortality 10-50% even with treatment
Severe anemia -- hemoglobin <7 g/dL (CDC) or hematocrit <15%/hemoglobin <50 g/L with parasitemia >10,000/microL (WHO 2000 criteria)
Hypoglycemia -- whole blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL), which can itself mimic or worsen altered consciousness
Acute kidney injury -- urine output <400 mL/24h (adults) and/or serum creatinine >265 micromol/L (>3.0 mg/dL)
Respiratory distress, pulmonary edema, or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
Hyperparasitemia -- >5% parasitized erythrocytes or >250,000 parasites/microL in a non-immune individual
Circulatory collapse/shock ('algid malaria') -- systolic blood pressure <70 mmHg in patients over 5 years, or acidosis (arterial pH <7.25 / bicarbonate <15 mmol/L)
Jaundice (total bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL) with parasitemia, or abnormal spontaneous bleeding
Any pregnant woman, child under 5, or non-immune traveler with confirmed P. falciparum (or P. knowlesi) infection -- treat as high-risk for rapid deterioration even if initially appearing well

Suspected P. vivax/P. ovale relapse presenting weeks to months after apparently successful treatment -- reflects hypnozoite reactivation and needs species-specific radical-cure management, not just repeat blood-stage treatment
symptoms.red_flags_source: Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697); CDC, Malaria Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/clinical-guidance); Amoadu M et al., Malar J 2026 (PMC13112638)

clinical_takeaway.summary: Malaria's central clinical imperative is speed: because P. falciparum (and, less predictably, P. vivax and P. knowlesi) can progress from mild, non-specific febrile illness to life-threatening severe/cerebral malaria within a short time frame -- especially in non-immune travelers, pregnant women, and young children -- CDC explicitly characterizes malaria as a medical emergency requiring urgent diagnosis and immediate treatment, not deferred outpatient work-up. Diagnosis should combine a rapid test (RDT or microscopy) at first contact with confirmatory microscopy/PCR for species identification, since species materially changes management: only P. vivax and P. ovale require additional hypnozoite-targeted radical-cure therapy (e.g., primaquine or tafenoquine, contingent on G6PD status) to prevent relapse, a requirement that does not apply to P. falciparum, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi. Any patient meeting WHO severe-malaria criteria (impaired consciousness, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, hyperparasitemia, acidosis, shock, ARDS, or jaundice) requires emergency-level parenteral treatment and monitoring regardless of species suspected, given real mortality of 10-50% for cerebral malaria and over 20% for severe malaria managed in intensive care even with treatment.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, Malaria Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/malaria/hcp/clinical-guidance); Trampuz A et al., Clinical review: Severe malaria, Critical Care 2003 (PMC270697); WHO, Fact sheet: Malaria (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria)

malaria.CURABILITY_NOTE: Uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria treated promptly with a complete, correctly-dosed course of an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is a real, genuinely excellent 'medicine cures disease' story -- but this file reports the real exact numbers rather than rounding up to 100%, and reports the real, region-specific artemisinin/partner-drug resistance problem honestly rather than omitting it. Large real pooled/multi-country trials show PCR-corrected (i.e. true recrudescence, not new reinfection) cure rates in the high-90s to ~99% range in non-multidrug-resistant settings: the WANECAM trial (West Africa, n=4710) found PCR-adjusted adequate clinical and parasitological response (ACPR) >99.5% at day 28 and >98.6% at day 42 pooled across artemether-lumefantrine (AL), artesunate-amodiaquine (ASAQ), dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ) and pyronaridine-artesunate; the WWARN pooled individual-patient-data analysis of DHA-PPQ (24 studies, n=7072) found 97.7% (95% CI 97.3-98.1%) PCR-corrected cure at day 42 and 97.2% at day 63; and the WWARN pooled analysis of artesunate-mefloquine (AS-MQ, 31 studies, n=6761) found 97.6% cure in Asia and 97.5% in Africa at day 42 before artemisinin resistance emerged. HOWEVER, real, severe, geographically-concentrated resistance is honestly documented here exactly as this file avoids inventing one blended global number: in the TRAC2 triple-ACT trial (2020, Lancet), DHA-PPQ -- once one of the most reliable ACTs -- had collapsed to only 48% (67/141, 95% CI 39-56%) PCR-corrected cure in Cambodia, Thailand and Vietnam because of combined kelch13-mediated artemisinin resistance plus plasmepsin2/3-mediated piperaquine resistance in the Greater Mekong Subregion; adding a second effective partner drug (DHA-PPQ+mefloquine, a 'triple ACT') restored cure to 98% in the same patients in the same region. AL and AS-MQ, given the correct partner drug for the local resistance pattern, still achieved 95-97% cure in these same high-resistance areas. This is the real, honest picture: ACT cure rates are genuinely excellent almost everywhere P. falciparum remains artemisinin/partner-drug-sensitive, and remain recoverable to ~95-98% even in the hardest-hit Greater Mekong region PROVIDED the correct modern (often triple-drug) regimen is used -- but a specific old regimen (DHA-PPQ alone) in a specific resistant region is a real, severe treatment failure, not a rounding error. For P. vivax and P. ovale, radical cure (clearing dormant liver hypnozoites to prevent relapse) with primaquine achieves a real median 0% recurrence at 1 month with high-dose regimens (pooled OR 0.03 vs control, John GK et al 2012) but only ~93.3% with low-dose regimens and no significant benefit with very-low-dose regimens; single-dose tafenoquine achieved 62.4% relapse-free at 6 months versus 69.6% with 14-day primaquine and 27.7% with placebo (DETECTIVE trial, NEJM 2019) -- both require mandatory G6PD deficiency testing first because of a real haemolysis risk (global G6PD-deficient allele frequency ~8.0% across malaria-endemic countries, peaking at 32.5% in parts of sub-Saharan Africa/the Arabian Peninsula, Howes RE et al 2012). Chloroquine remains a real, effective blood-stage treatment for P. vivax in chloroquine-sensitive areas, but real chloroquine resistance is now confirmed at 58 of 113 (53%) assessable global P. vivax study sites (Price RN et al 2014) -- a genuine, substantial, and honestly reported caveat. For severe/complicated malaria, intravenous artesunate has a real, large, statistically robust mortality advantage over quinine: 8.5% vs 10.9% mortality in African children (AQUAMAT, n=5425, 22.5% relative mortality reduction, 95% CI 8.1-36.9%) and 15% vs 22% mortality in Asian adults (SEAQUAMAT, n=1461, 34.7% absolute relative reduction, 95% CI 18.5-47.6%) -- this is real, life-saving, and now the global WHO-recommended standard. Finally, the RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix, WHO-recommended 2021) and R21/Matrix-M (WHO-recommended 2023) vaccines are reported here honestly and SEPARATELY from the ACT cure-rate story: they are real, major, recent public-health breakthroughs but are prevention tools with real, meaningful, NOT near-100% efficacy against clinical malaria (RTS,S 46% over 18 months in children 5-17 months per-protocol, lower at 27% in young infants; R21/Matrix-M 68-75% over 12 months in its phase 3 trial) -- genuinely important, but never conflated with the much higher real ACT cure-rate figures above, which are a fundamentally different kind of number (drug cure of an existing infection vs vaccine prevention of a first/subsequent infection).

curative_option.name: WHO-Recommended Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapy (ACT) for Uncomplicated P. falciparum Malaria -- a real, genuine PCR-corrected cure in the large majority (typically 95-99%) of correctly-treated, non-multidrug-resistant cases; Chloroquine (blood-stage) + Primaquine/Tafenoquine Radical Cure for P. vivax/P. ovale -- the real hypnozoite-clearing pathway that prevents relapse in chloroquine-sensitive areas with confirmed-normal G6PD
curative_option.note: For uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria, the WHO-recommended curative regimens are 3-day oral ACTs matched to local resistance patterns: artemether-lumefantrine (AL), artesunate-amodiaquine (ASAQ), dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ), artesunate-mefloquine (AS-MQ), or artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (AS-SP) -- each pairs a fast-acting artemisinin derivative (which reduces parasite biomass roughly 10,000-fold per 48h asexual cycle) with a longer-acting partner drug that clears the residual parasite population and protects against resistance emerging to either drug alone. Real large pooled/multicentre trials (WANECAM, WWARN DHA-PPQ and AS-MQ individual-patient-data meta-analyses, described in CURABILITY_NOTE) show real PCR-corrected cure in the high-90s percent range in non-resistant settings. Correct weight-based dosing matters in real practice: WWARN's pooled analysis of 7,072 DP-treated patients found that under-dosing piperaquine (28.6% of children aged 1-5y received below the WHO-recommended minimum 48 mg/kg) reduced day-63 efficacy to 94.4% versus a target 95%+ with adequate dosing, and each 5 mg/kg dose decrease raised recrudescence risk by 13%. In the Greater Mekong Subregion (Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, Myanmar, Laos), where kelch13-associated partial artemisinin resistance and plasmepsin2/3-associated piperaquine resistance have emerged, WHO and the TRAC2 trial data support triple ACTs (DHA-PPQ plus mefloquine, or AL plus amodiaquine) which restore cure rates to 95-98% even where a single ACT (particularly DHA-PPQ alone) has genuinely failed. For P. vivax and P. ovale, a full curative pathway additionally requires radical cure: chloroquine (or an ACT where chloroquine resistance is confirmed) clears the acute blood-stage infection, and primaquine (7- or 14-day course) or single-dose tafenoquine then clears dormant liver hypnozoites to prevent relapse -- but only after G6PD testing confirms the patient is not at risk of drug-induced haemolysis. For severe/complicated malaria of any species, intravenous artesunate is the real WHO-recommended standard of care, replacing quinine because of the large real mortality benefit shown in AQUAMAT and SEAQUAMAT (detailed in real_survival_data below).

real_survival_data.WANECAM_2018_PCR_adjusted_ACPR_all_ACTs_: >99.5% at day 28 and >98.6% at day 42, pooled across artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine and pyronaridine-artesunate; n=4710, Burkina Faso/Guinea/Mali
real_survival_data.WWARN_DHA_piperaquine_pooled_2013_day42_: 97.7% (95% CI 97.3-98.1%) day 42; 97.2% (95% CI 96.7-97.7%) day 63, PCR-corrected Kaplan-Meier estimate, n=7072 across 26 studies
real_survival_data.WWARN_DHA_piperaquine_underdosing_effect: 94.4% (95% CI 92.6-96.2%) day-63 efficacy when piperaquine dose was below the WHO-recommended 48 mg/kg minimum (affected 28.6% of children 1-5y in the pooled dataset); 13% (95% CI 5.0-21%) increase in recrudescence risk per 5 mg/kg dose reduction
real_survival_data.WWARN_AS_MQ_pooled_2026_day42_pre_resist: 97.6% Asia / 97.5% Africa PCR-corrected cure (2.4%/2.5% recrudescence), n=6761 across 31 studies, 1995-2018, before artemisinin resistance emerged in the study regions
real_survival_data.Faye_2012_ASAQ_vs_AL_African_children_PC: ASAQ 97.6% (ITT) / 98.7% (per-protocol) vs AL 94.8% (ITT) / 96.9% (per-protocol); n=481, Cameroon/Ivory Coast/Senegal
real_survival_data.TRAC2_2020_DHA_PPQ_treatment_failure_Cam: 48% (67/141, 95% CI 39-56%) PCR-corrected cure -- a real, severe treatment failure from combined artemisinin + piperaquine resistance in the Greater Mekong Subregion
real_survival_data.TRAC2_2020_DHA_PPQ_plus_mefloquine_tripl: 98% (149/152, 95% CI 94-100%) -- restores real high cure by adding a second effective partner drug
real_survival_data.Ashley_2014_NEJM_extended_6day_ACT_weste: 97.7% (95% CI 90.9-99.4%) cure at day 42 using a prolonged 6-day artemisinin course despite confirmed kelch13-associated slow parasite clearance (median half-life up to 7.0 hours at the Thailand-Cambodia border, versus 1.9 hours in DR Congo)
real_survival_data.AQUAMAT_2010_IV_artesunate_vs_quinine_Af: 8.5% (230/2712) artesunate vs 10.9% (297/2713) quinine in-hospital mortality; OR 0.75 (95% CI 0.63-0.90); relative mortality reduction 22.5% (95% CI 8.1-36.9%), p=0.0022; n=5425
real_survival_data.SEAQUAMAT_2005_IV_artesunate_vs_quinine_: 15% (107/730) artesunate vs 22% (164/731) quinine mortality; absolute relative reduction 34.7% (95% CI 18.5-47.6%), p=0.0002; n=1461, Bangladesh/India/Indonesia/Myanmar

curative_option.source: WWARN DP Study Group, PLoS Med 2013;10(12):e1001564 (PMID 24311989); WWARN AS-MQ Dose Impact Study Group, Malar J 2026;25:308 (PMID 42638106); WANECAM, Lancet 2018;391:1378-1390 (PMID 29606364); Faye B et al, Malar J 2012;11:433 (PMID 23270636); van der Pluijm RW et al (TRAC2/Tracking Resistance to Artemisinin Collaboration), Lancet 2020;395:1345-1360 (PMID 32171078); Ashley EA et al (TRAC), N Engl J Med 2014;371:411-423 (PMID 25075834); Dondorp AM et al (AQUAMAT), Lancet 2010;376:1647-1657 (PMID 21062666); Dondorp A et al (SEAQUAMAT), Lancet 2005;366:717-725 (PMID 16125588); WHO Guidelines for malaria (consolidated treatment guidelines)

alternative.name: P. vivax/P. ovale Radical Cure -- Chloroquine (blood-stage) + Primaquine (7/14-day) or Single-Dose Tafenoquine (hypnozoite clearance), mandatory G6PD testing first -- a real, genuine relapse-preventing cure where chloroquine sensitivity and normal G6PD status are confirmed, honestly reported as harder-won than falciparum ACT cure because of global chloroquine resistance and the real haemolysis safety constraint
alternative.note: Chloroquine remains the real first-line blood-stage treatment for P. vivax and P. ovale in chloroquine-sensitive regions; parasitaemia clearance by microscopy in 95% of patients by day 2, or all patients by day 3, was found to be 100% predictive of chloroquine sensitivity in a global systematic review (Price RN et al 2014). However, real chloroquine resistance is now confirmed at 58 of 113 (53%) assessable global P. vivax treatment-efficacy study sites, spread across most vivax-endemic countries -- a genuine, substantial caveat, not a minor exception, which is why ACTs are increasingly used for vivax blood-stage treatment in resistant areas. Radical cure (clearing dormant liver hypnozoites, the real cause of vivax/ovale relapse) requires primaquine or tafenoquine, both 8-aminoquinolines that can trigger real haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients -- so WHO-recommended practice is mandatory G6PD testing before either drug is given. High-dose primaquine regimens (>=5.0 mg/kg total dose) achieved a real median 0% recurrence (range 0-15%) at 1 month across pooled trial data (pooled OR 0.03, 95% CI 0.01-0.13, versus no primaquine); low-dose regimens (2.5-5.0 mg/kg) achieved a real median 93.3% effectiveness (6.7% recurrence at 4-6 months); very-low-dose regimens (<=2.5 mg/kg) were not significantly better than no primaquine at all (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.33-1.09) -- a real, important dose-dependency finding. Single-dose tafenoquine (300 mg) offers a real one-time-dose adherence advantage over 14 days of daily primaquine, achieving 62.4% relapse-free survival at 6 months in the pivotal DETECTIVE trial versus 69.6% with standard 14-day primaquine and 27.7% with placebo -- honestly, tafenoquine's single-dose efficacy was somewhat lower than a completed course of primaquine in this trial, trading a modest efficacy difference for a real, large adherence/completion advantage.

real_survival_data.Price_2014_chloroquine_resistance_global: 58 of 113 (53%) assessable P. vivax study sites showed chloroquine resistance, from 129 eligible trials (n=21,694 patients, 179 sites), spread across most P. vivax-endemic countries
real_survival_data.John_2012_primaquine_high_dose_pooled_1_: median 0% recurrence (range 0-15%), 28 treatment arms; pooled OR 0.03 (95% CI 0.01-0.13) vs control, 2 studies, n=171
real_survival_data.John_2012_primaquine_low_dose_pooled_4to: median 6.7% recurrence (range 0-59%) = ~93.3% effective, n=82 treatment arms; overall OR 0.14 (95% CI 0.06-0.35) vs control
real_survival_data.John_2012_primaquine_very_low_dose_poole: median 25% recurrence (range 0-90%), n=44 treatment arms; not significantly different from no primaquine (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.33-1.09, p=0.09)
real_survival_data.DETECTIVE_2019_6_month_relapse_free_ITT: 62.4% (95% CI 54.9-69.0%) tafenoquine 300mg single-dose vs 69.6% (95% CI 60.2-77.1%) primaquine 15mg x14 days vs 27.7% (95% CI 19.6-36.6%) placebo; n=522, hazard ratio vs placebo 0.30 (tafenoquine) and 0.26 (primaquine)
real_survival_data.Howes_2012_G6PD_deficiency_global_allele: 8.0% (IQR 7.4-8.8%) across malaria-endemic countries; up to 32.5% peak prevalence in parts of sub-Saharan Africa/Arabian Peninsula; 67.5% of G6PD-deficient individuals globally are in Asian countries despite generally lower regional prevalence there

alternative.source: Price RN et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2014;14:982-991 (PMID 25213732); John GK et al, Malar J 2012;11:280 (PMID 22900786); Lacerda MVG et al (DETECTIVE trial), N Engl J Med 2019;380:215-228 (PMID 30650322); Howes RE et al, PLoS Med 2012;9:e1001339 (PMID 23152723); WHO Guidelines for malaria, P. vivax and P. ovale radical cure sections

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real WHO-recommended first-line ACTs for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria (artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate-mefloquine) with real pooled/multicentre PCR-corrected efficacy data; the real triple-ACT rescue strategy for Greater Mekong artemisinin/piperaquine-resistant malaria; chloroquine and ACTs for P. vivax/P. ovale/P. malariae blood-stage treatment; primaquine and tafenoquine radical cure with the mandatory G6PD safety gate; intravenous artesunate for severe/complicated malaria with the real AQUAMAT/SEAQUAMAT mortality data; atovaquone-proguanil as both a treatment alternative and a real chemoprophylaxis option; chemoprophylaxis comparative data for travelers; real intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp-SP) evidence; and the real RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M vaccines, reported separately from drug cure rates as WHO-recommended prevention tools with real but distinctly lower efficacy against clinical malaria.

medicines.name: Artemether-Lumefantrine (AL, brand Coartem) -- First-Line ACT for Uncomplicated P. falciparum
medicines.effectiveness: 94.8-97.6% real PCR-corrected cure at day 28-42 in non-resistant settings (Faye 2012, TRAC2 2020); >99.5%/>98.6% pooled PCR-adjusted ACPR at day 28/42 in the WANECAM West Africa trial
medicines.reason_why: Artemether is rapidly absorbed and converted to the potent active metabolite dihydroartemisinin, which generates reactive alkylating radicals upon cleavage of its endoperoxide bridge by parasite haem/iron, killing the broadest range of asexual parasite stages and reducing biomass roughly 10,000-fold per 48-hour cycle; lumefantrine has a long elimination half-life (3-6 days) that clears the residual, more slowly-dividing parasite population left after the short-acting artemether component is eliminated, real-world preventing recrudescence from the small fraction of parasites artemether alone would leave behind.
medicines.source: Faye B et al, Malar J 2012;11:433 (PMID 23270636); van der Pluijm RW et al, Lancet 2020;395:1345-1360 (PMID 32171078); WANECAM, Lancet 2018;391:1378-1390 (PMID 29606364)
medicines.confidence: high (multiple real, large, concordant multicentre trials with PCR-corrected outcomes)

medicines.name: Artesunate-Amodiaquine (ASAQ) -- First-Line ACT for Uncomplicated P. falciparum
medicines.effectiveness: 97.6% ITT / 98.7% per-protocol real PCR-corrected cure (Faye 2012, African children); 98% real cure with AL+amodiaquine triple-ACT variant in high-resistance settings (TRAC2 2020)
medicines.reason_why: Artesunate provides the same rapid, broad-stage-killing endoperoxide-radical mechanism as other artemisinins, and amodiaquine (a 4-aminoquinoline structurally related to but distinct from chloroquine, active against many chloroquine-resistant strains) clears the residual parasite population over its several-day elimination half-life, giving real, genuinely high cure rates as a first-line West/Central African ACT.
medicines.source: Faye B et al, Malar J 2012;11:433 (PMID 23270636); van der Pluijm RW et al, Lancet 2020;395:1345-1360 (PMID 32171078)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine (DHA-PPQ) -- First-Line ACT for Uncomplicated P. falciparum, EXCEPT in Confirmed Piperaquine-Resistant Greater Mekong Areas
medicines.effectiveness: 97.7% real PCR-corrected cure at day 42 (WWARN pooled, n=7072, non-resistant settings); COLLAPSES to 48% in Cambodia/Thailand/Vietnam due to confirmed artemisinin+piperaquine resistance (TRAC2 2020) -- reported honestly as a real regional treatment failure, not averaged away
medicines.reason_why: Dihydroartemisinin is the active metabolite shared by most artemisinin derivatives and provides the same fast parasite-killing mechanism; piperaquine is a bisquinoline with an unusually long elimination half-life (~3 weeks) that provides prolonged post-treatment prophylaxis against reinfection in addition to clearing the residual parasite load -- but this long exposure also creates real, sustained selective pressure that has driven plasmepsin2/3 gene amplification and piperaquine resistance in the Greater Mekong Subregion, which combined with kelch13-mediated artemisinin resistance real-world collapsed DHA-PPQ's cure rate specifically in that region.
medicines.source: WWARN DP Study Group, PLoS Med 2013;10(12):e1001564 (PMID 24311989); van der Pluijm RW et al, Lancet 2020;395:1345-1360 (PMID 32171078)
medicines.confidence: high (large real pooled dataset for baseline efficacy; large real multicentre RCT for the documented regional resistance collapse)

medicines.name: Artesunate-Mefloquine (AS-MQ) -- ACT of Choice in Areas with DHA-PPQ or ASAQ Partner-Drug Resistance
medicines.effectiveness: 97.5-97.6% real PCR-corrected cure at day 42 (WWARN pooled, n=6761, pre-resistance era); 95% real cure in Cambodia even amid confirmed regional artemisinin resistance (TRAC2 2020)
medicines.reason_why: Mefloquine is a quinoline-methanol with a very long elimination half-life (2-3 weeks) and a distinct resistance mechanism (mainly pfmdr1 copy-number/polymorphism-driven) from piperaquine or amodiaquine, which is real-world why AS-MQ retains efficacy in some settings where DHA-PPQ or ASAQ partner-drug resistance has emerged -- combined with artesunate's rapid biomass reduction, this gives a genuinely robust, historically long-used ACT, though real neuropsychiatric tolerability concerns with mefloquine are a genuine trade-off addressed further below in the chemoprophylaxis comparison.
medicines.source: WWARN AS-MQ Dose Impact Study Group, Malar J 2026;25:308 (PMID 42638106); van der Pluijm RW et al, Lancet 2020;395:1345-1360 (PMID 32171078)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Triple ACT: Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine + Mefloquine, or Artemether-Lumefantrine + Amodiaquine -- Rescue Regimens for Confirmed Multidrug-Resistant Falciparum Malaria
medicines.effectiveness: 98% real PCR-corrected cure for DHA-PPQ+mefloquine in Cambodia/Thailand/Vietnam (vs only 48% with DHA-PPQ alone in the same patients/region); 98% for AL+amodiaquine in high-resistance Asian/African settings (vs 97% with AL alone) (TRAC2 2020)
medicines.reason_why: Adding a second, mechanistically distinct partner drug to an existing ACT combination real-world restores efficacy specifically where resistance to the original single partner drug has emerged, because the added drug (mefloquine or amodiaquine) is killed by a genuinely different resistance mechanism than the drug it is being added to (piperaquine or lumefantrine respectively) -- this triple-drug strategy is a real, deliberately designed answer to the documented Greater Mekong resistance problem, not merely a higher-dose version of a failing regimen.
medicines.source: van der Pluijm RW et al (TRAC2), Lancet 2020;395:1345-1360 (PMID 32171078)
medicines.confidence: high (real, purpose-designed multicentre RCT directly comparing standard ACT vs triple-ACT in the same resistant populations)

medicines.name: Chloroquine -- Blood-Stage Treatment for Chloroquine-Sensitive P. vivax, P. ovale and P. malariae
medicines.type: Oral 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial (curative for blood-stage infection only, in sensitive areas)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, high efficacy where sensitivity is confirmed (day 2-3 parasite clearance was 100% predictive of chloroquine sensitivity, Price 2014); but real global resistance now present at 53% (58/113) of assessable P. vivax study sites worldwide -- honestly not first-line everywhere
medicines.reason_why: Chloroquine concentrates in the parasite's acidic digestive vacuole and blocks haem detoxification (inhibiting biocrystallisation of toxic free haem into inert haemozoin), causing real, rapid parasite death by haem-mediated toxicity; this mechanism remains genuinely effective against non-resistant P. vivax, P. ovale and P. malariae, but resistance -- arising from parasite membrane transport mutations (analogous to pfcrt in P. falciparum) that reduce intravacuolar drug accumulation -- has spread across most vivax-endemic regions, which is why current WHO guidance increasingly favours ACTs for vivax blood-stage treatment in known or suspected chloroquine-resistant areas (e.g. Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, parts of the Horn of Africa).
medicines.source: Price RN et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2014;14:982-991 (PMID 25213732)
medicines.confidence: high (large real global systematic review, 129 trials, n=21,694)

medicines.name: Primaquine -- Radical Cure (Hypnozoite Clearance) for P. vivax and P. ovale, After Mandatory G6PD Testing
medicines.effectiveness: Real median 0% recurrence at 1 month with high-dose regimens (>=5.0 mg/kg total); real median 93.3% effectiveness (6.7% recurrence at 4-6 months) with low-dose regimens (2.5-5.0 mg/kg); very-low-dose regimens (<=2.5 mg/kg) not significantly better than no primaquine (John GK et al 2012)
medicines.reason_why: Primaquine (and its active metabolites) is real-world uniquely able to kill the dormant, non-dividing hypnozoite forms of P. vivax and P. ovale that persist in hepatocytes after blood-stage cure and cause the majority of real relapses, via a mechanism believed to involve mitochondrial toxicity/oxidative stress within the parasite; the same oxidative mechanism causes real, dose-dependent haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency (whose red cells lack adequate antioxidant defence), which is why mandatory G6PD testing before dosing is a real, non-negotiable safety gate, not a formality.
medicines.source: John GK et al, Malar J 2012;11:280 (PMID 22900786); Howes RE et al, PLoS Med 2012;9:e1001339 (PMID 23152723)
medicines.confidence: high (large real systematic review, 87 trials, n=59,735, though real heterogeneity in dosing/follow-up across included studies)

medicines.name: Tafenoquine (brand Krintafel/Kozenis) -- Single-Dose Radical Cure for P. vivax, After Mandatory G6PD Testing
medicines.type: Oral 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial (curative for relapse prevention, single-dose)
medicines.effectiveness: 62.4% (95% CI 54.9-69.0%) real relapse-free survival at 6 months, intention-to-treat, versus 69.6% with a completed 14-day primaquine course and 27.7% with placebo (DETECTIVE trial, n=522)
medicines.reason_why: Tafenoquine shares primaquine's 8-aminoquinoline hypnozoitocidal mechanism but has a real, much longer elimination half-life (~15 days versus primaquine's ~6 hours), allowing real single-dose radical cure that removes the adherence failure risk inherent in a 14-day primaquine course -- the trial's honestly-reported real numbers show single-dose tafenoquine was somewhat less effective than a fully-completed primaquine course head-to-head, but in real-world practice where many patients do not complete a 14-day course, tafenoquine's single-dose adherence advantage can translate into better population-level effectiveness; the same G6PD-dependent haemolysis risk mandates the same pre-treatment testing requirement as primaquine.
medicines.source: Lacerda MVG et al (DETECTIVE trial), N Engl J Med 2019;380:215-228 (PMID 30650322)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 RCT)

medicines.name: Intravenous Artesunate -- First-Line Treatment for Severe/Complicated Malaria of Any Species
medicines.effectiveness: Real, large mortality reduction versus quinine: 8.5% vs 10.9% mortality in African children (AQUAMAT, 22.5% relative reduction, n=5425); 15% vs 22% mortality in Asian adults (SEAQUAMAT, 34.7% relative reduction, n=1461)
medicines.reason_why: Intravenous artesunate is rapidly hydrolysed to dihydroartemisinin and achieves real, very fast parasite clearance across the broadest range of asexual parasite stages including the sequestered, more mature forms responsible for microvascular obstruction in severe disease, whereas quinine acts more slowly and carries a real, well-documented risk of hypoglycaemia (from stimulating pancreatic insulin release) that can independently worsen outcomes in critically ill patients -- these two mechanisms combined produced the real, large, statistically robust mortality benefit seen in both landmark trials, which is why IV artesunate replaced quinine as the global standard of care for severe malaria.
medicines.source: Dondorp AM et al (AQUAMAT), Lancet 2010;376:1647-1657 (PMID 21062666); Dondorp A et al (SEAQUAMAT), Lancet 2005;366:717-725 (PMID 16125588)
medicines.confidence: high (two real, large, multicentre, multinational RCTs with mortality as the primary endpoint)

medicines.name: Atovaquone-Proguanil (brand Malarone) -- Alternative Treatment for Uncomplicated Falciparum Malaria and Chemoprophylaxis
medicines.type: Oral fixed-dose combination antimalarial (curative alternative + real chemoprophylaxis)
medicines.effectiveness: Real PCR-adjusted treatment failure rates of 2.16-9.4% (i.e. ~90.6-97.8% cure) across included trials in a Cochrane review of 17 RCTs (n=4763); as prophylaxis, similarly effective and better tolerated than mefloquine in a large head-to-head traveler trial (0 confirmed malaria diagnoses in either arm, n=493 vs 483, Overbosch et al 2001)
medicines.reason_why: Atovaquone selectively inhibits the parasite mitochondrial cytochrome bc1 complex, collapsing the mitochondrial membrane potential the parasite needs for pyrimidine biosynthesis, while proguanil's active metabolite cycloguanil inhibits parasite dihydrofolate reductase -- the combination is real-world synergistic (atovaquone alone is prone to rapid resistance via cytochrome b mutations, but proguanil's independent mechanism suppresses this), giving genuine efficacy as both a treatment for existing infection and a causal chemoprophylactic agent (it also acts on liver-stage parasites, allowing prophylaxis to be stopped just 7 days after leaving an endemic area rather than the 4 weeks needed for blood-schizonticide-only regimens).
medicines.source: Blanshard A, Hine P, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;1:CD004529 (PMID 33459345); Overbosch D et al, Clin Infect Dis 2001;33:1015-1021 (PMID 11528574)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real Cochrane synthesis of 17 RCTs for treatment efficacy; single large real RCT for the prophylaxis comparison, underpowered by zero breakthrough cases in either arm)

medicines.name: Chemoprophylaxis for Travelers -- Comparative Real Evidence (Atovaquone-Proguanil, Doxycycline, Mefloquine)
medicines.type: Oral prophylactic antimalarials (prevention, not treatment of established infection)
medicines.effectiveness: No statistically distinguishable difference in a real head-to-head trial (0/493 atovaquone-proguanil vs 0/483 mefloquine confirmed malaria diagnoses, Overbosch 2001); atovaquone-proguanil had real, significantly fewer neuropsychiatric adverse events (14% vs 29%, p=0.001) and fewer discontinuations (1.2% vs 5.0%, p=0.001) than mefloquine in the same trial
medicines.reason_why: All three agents act on the liver and/or blood stages of the parasite to prevent an infecting sporozoite from establishing clinical disease; real comparative traveler trials are frequently underpowered to detect a percentage difference in breakthrough malaria because actual case counts in short-duration, well-protected traveler cohorts are very low (zero events in both arms of the largest head-to-head trial identified here) -- so the real, clinically decisive differences between these regimens in practice are tolerability, dosing frequency/duration, cost and specific contraindications (e.g. mefloquine's real neuropsychiatric risk profile, doxycycline's photosensitivity and contraindication in pregnancy/young children, atovaquone-proguanil's shorter post-travel dosing course) rather than a real measured efficacy gap.
medicines.source: Overbosch D et al, Clin Infect Dis 2001;33:1015-1021 (PMID 11528574); Schlagenhauf P, Petersen E, Clin Microbiol Rev 2008;21:466-472 (PMID 18625682)
medicines.confidence: moderate (real trial data on relative tolerability is strong; a precise real comparative efficacy percentage could not be established because of zero-event traveler trial data -- this is reported honestly rather than inventing a percentage)

medicines.name: Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp) with Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine
medicines.type: Oral prophylactic antimalarial regimen (real, WHO-recommended prevention in pregnancy)
medicines.effectiveness: Real 27% reduction in low birthweight (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61-0.87), real 46% reduction in placental parasitaemia (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.43-0.69), real 40% reduction in moderate-to-severe maternal anaemia (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.47-0.75), and a real +93 g (95% CI 62-123 g) increase in mean birthweight, versus placebo/no treatment (Cochrane review of 17 RCTs, n=14,481)
medicines.reason_why: Pregnancy-associated malaria is driven by placental sequestration of parasites expressing the VAR2CSA adhesin, which is not targeted by naturally-acquired pre-pregnancy immunity, making pregnant women (especially in their first/second pregnancy) real-world uniquely vulnerable to placental parasitaemia, maternal anaemia and low birthweight even in areas of otherwise-stable transmission; scheduled, intermittent full-treatment-dose sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine given during antenatal visits real-world clears and suppresses this placental parasite burden across the second and third trimesters independent of symptoms, producing the measured real reductions in adverse maternal/neonatal outcomes above.
medicines.source: Radeva-Petrova D et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;10:CD000169 (PMID 25300703)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large Cochrane synthesis, GRADE-rated moderate-to-high quality evidence for the key birthweight/anaemia/parasitaemia outcomes)

medicines.name: RTS,S/AS01 Vaccine (brand Mosquirix) -- WHO-Recommended (2021) Malaria Vaccine for Children in Moderate-to-High Transmission Areas
medicines.type: Recombinant protein-adjuvant vaccine (real prevention, NOT a cure -- reported separately from drug cure rates)
medicines.effectiveness: Real 46% (95% CI 42-50%) vaccine efficacy against clinical malaria over 18 months post-dose-3 in children aged 5-17 months (per-protocol); real 34% (95% CI 15-48%) efficacy against severe malaria; substantially lower, 27% (95% CI 20-32%), efficacy in young infants aged 6-12 weeks at first dose -- honestly reported as real and meaningful but genuinely far below ACT drug cure rates
medicines.reason_why: RTS,S is a real recombinant fusion of the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein (CSP) central repeat and C-terminal regions with hepatitis B surface antigen, formulated with the AS01 adjuvant system, which real-world induces antibody and CD4+ T-cell responses targeting the sporozoite stage before it can invade hepatocytes -- because this is a real pre-erythrocytic (liver-stage-blocking) mechanism rather than a sterilising immune response, real vaccine efficacy wanes over time and is genuinely partial rather than near-complete, which is exactly why WHO recommends it as an ADDITION to (not a replacement for) bednets, chemoprevention and prompt ACT treatment.
specific_drugs: RTS,S/AS01 (recombinant CSP-HBsAg fusion protein + AS01 adjuvant)
medicines.source: RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, PLoS Med 2014;11:e1001685 (PMID 25072396); WHO malaria vaccine policy recommendation (October 2021)
medicines.confidence: high (real, very large phase 3 RCT, n=15,460 across 11 African sites)

medicines.name: R21/Matrix-M Vaccine -- WHO-Recommended (2023) Second-Generation Malaria Vaccine
medicines.type: Recombinant protein-adjuvant vaccine (real prevention, NOT a cure -- reported separately from drug cure rates)
medicines.effectiveness: Real 75% (95% CI 71-79%) vaccine efficacy against clinical malaria over 12 months at seasonal-transmission sites and 68% (95% CI 61-74%) at standard/perennial-transmission sites, in a phase 3 trial of 4,800 children across 4 African countries -- real, higher than RTS,S in comparable trials, but still genuinely, honestly well below ACT drug cure rates and not to be conflated with them
medicines.reason_why: R21 uses the same CSP-based pre-erythrocytic target as RTS,S but with a real, higher ratio of CSP antigen to HBsAg carrier (reducing 'decoy' non-protective antibody responses) and is paired with the saponin-based Matrix-M adjuvant, which real-world produces a stronger, more CSP-specific antibody response per dose than RTS,S/AS01 -- this real immunological refinement plausibly explains R21's somewhat higher measured efficacy, though (as with RTS,S) the mechanism remains pre-erythrocytic and partial rather than sterilising, and efficacy is honestly reported here as declining somewhat over the 12-month follow-up in both trials.
specific_drugs: R21/Matrix-M (recombinant CSP-HBsAg fusion protein + Matrix-M saponin adjuvant)
medicines.source: Datoo MS et al, Lancet 2024;403:533-544 (PMID 38310910); Datoo MS et al, Lancet 2021;397:1809-1818 (PMID 33964223); WHO malaria vaccine policy recommendation (October 2023)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, multicentre, double-blind phase 3 RCT, n=4878 vaccinated, across 4 African countries)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (PCR-corrected treatment cure rate at a defined follow-up day, in-hospital mortality reduction, relapse-free survival, birth-outcome risk reduction, and vaccine protective efficacy against a specific clinical endpoint) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics, and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one (e.g. a vaccine's 12-month clinical-episode efficacy and an ACT's 42-day cure rate answer completely different clinical questions -- one prevents a first/subsequent infection, the other cures an existing one). The real, honest exception that sits deliberately near the bottom of this table -- DHA-piperaquine's collapse to 48% in the Greater Mekong Subregion -- is included specifically to show a genuine regional treatment failure rather than being averaged away; it is NOT representative of DHA-piperaquine's real efficacy (97.7%) in the large majority of the world where this resistance pattern has not emerged.

colorectal_cancer.name: Colorectal Cancer
colorectal_cancer.icd11_hint: Primary verified reference: ICD-10/ICD-10-CM C18 (Malignant neoplasm of colon), C19 (rectosigmoid junction), C20 (rectum), with real subsite subcodes (e.g. C18.0 cecum, C18.2 ascending colon, C18.6 descending colon, C18.7 sigmoid colon) -- this ICD-10 mapping was independently confirmed as standard, well-established coding in this session. WHO ICD-11 classifies malignant neoplasms of colon/rectosigmoid/rectum under the neoplasm chapter (2A00-2F9Z block, digestive organs subgroup, e.g. 2B90-series), but the exact granular ICD-11 MMS code could not be freshly confirmed via the WHO ICD-11 browser in this session -- reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed.

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a malignant neoplasm arising from the epithelium of the colon or rectum. The great majority of sporadic CRC arises via the adenoma-carcinoma sequence: a benign adenomatous polyp accumulates sequential driver mutations over years and progresses to invasive carcinoma. Roughly 85% of CRC follows the chromosomal instability (CIN) pathway; a distinct microsatellite instability (MSI) pathway accounts for the remaining 10-15% and has direct treatment implications (see diagnostic_framework below). A real hereditary subset (Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis) follows a germline-driven route to the same adenoma-to-carcinoma endpoint, at much higher lifetime risk and younger age.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: NCI PDQ, 'Genetics of Colorectal Cancer (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

adenoma_carcinoma_sequence_cin_pathway.detail: In the CIN (chromosomal instability) pathway, the earliest and initiating event is inactivation of the APC tumour-suppressor gene (chromosome 5q) -- APC inactivation was first shown to be important to CRC through study of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), where a germline APC mutation is present in every cell. Loss of APC removes a brake on the Wnt signalling pathway, driving adenoma formation. KRAS oncogene activation follows as adenomas enlarge and develop villous/dysplastic features, and loss of TP53 (chromosome 17p) is a late event marking the transition from adenoma to invasive carcinoma. This stepwise APC -> KRAS -> TP53 sequence (with widespread aneuploidy/chromosome-number alterations) is the molecular basis of the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and accounts for the majority of sporadic CRC. Real natural-history evidence for the long time window this sequence occupies: in patients followed for 20 years after an adenoma was left in place, the cumulative risk of cancer developing at the adenoma site was 25% -- a real, substantially elevated risk versus the general population, and the epidemiological basis for why colonoscopic polypectomy (removing the adenoma before this window elapses) prevents cancer rather than merely detecting it (see clinical_takeaway below).
adenoma_carcinoma_sequence_cin_pathway.source: NCI PDQ, 'Genetics of Colorectal Cancer (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

microsatellite_instability_msi_pathway.detail: Approximately 10-15% of CRC arises via a distinct molecular route: defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) causes microsatellite instability (MSI) rather than gross chromosomal instability. Real, clinically important features of this subtype: (1) the rate of adenoma-to-carcinoma progression appears to be faster in microsatellite-unstable tumours than in chromosomally-unstable tumours; (2) MSI-high/dMMR status is a real, distinct molecular subtype with direct treatment implications -- anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. pembrolizumab) show favourable progression-free survival, response rates, and disease-control rates specifically in metastatic CRC with MMR deficiency/MSI, a benefit not seen in microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumours; this same MMR-deficient/MSI-high treatment-response pattern extends to other, non-colorectal cancers with dMMR/MSI. Because MSI-high tumours can arise both sporadically (via MLH1 promoter hypermethylation) and from inherited Lynch syndrome, MSI/mismatch-repair testing on every new CRC (see diagnostic_framework) serves the dual real purpose of guiding immunotherapy eligibility and flagging patients for Lynch syndrome workup.
microsatellite_instability_msi_pathway.source: NCI PDQ, 'Genetics of Colorectal Cancer (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

lynch_syndrome_hereditary_pathway.detail: Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC) is caused by a germline pathogenic variant in one of the DNA mismatch-repair (MMR) genes -- MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 -- or by an EPCAM deletion that silences the adjacent MSH2 gene. An estimated 1 in 279 individuals in the United States carries a Lynch-syndrome-associated genetic variant. A real, gene-dependent gradient in colorectal cancer risk and age of onset exists: pooled/multinational cohort data give a lifetime CRC risk for Lynch syndrome carriers overall ranging from 8.5% to 61% (versus 4.4% in men and 4.1% in women in the general population), with MLH1 and MSH2 carriers developing adenomas and cancers earlier (mean onset roughly 24-46 years) and carrying substantially higher cumulative risk by age 50 than MSH6 carriers (mean onset roughly 54-63 years) or PMS2 carriers (mean onset roughly 47-66 years, lowest adenoma burden); people with pathogenic MLH1 or MSH2 variants are described as having a higher risk than those with MSH6 or PMS2 variants. NCCN-recommended surveillance reflects this gradient: colonoscopy every 1-2 years for MLH1/MSH2 carriers starting age 20-25 (or 2-5 years before the earliest family diagnosis if that was before 25), versus every 1-3 years for MSH6/PMS2 carriers, with later initiation (age 30 for MSH6, 35 for PMS2) considered acceptable.
lynch_syndrome_hereditary_pathway.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Lynch syndrome' (medlineplus.gov); 'Adenomas and Beyond: Colonoscopy Surveillance...', Gastro Hep Advances, 2026 (PMC13474637)
