lynch_syndrome_hereditary_pathway.confidence: high on the mechanism, gene list, and US prevalence figure; the 8.5-61% lifetime-risk range and gene-specific onset ages are as reported in the cited 2026 cohort/guideline review and are given as a range rather than fabricated single point-estimates per gene, since exact per-gene point percentages could not be independently re-verified from a primary source in this session

familial_adenomatous_polyposis_fap_pathw.detail: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is caused by a germline pathogenic variant in the APC tumour-suppressor gene itself (the same gene inactivated somatically in sporadic CIN-pathway CRC above), producing an abnormally short, non-functional APC protein that fails to restrain Wnt-pathway cell-growth signalling and normal cell division. Classic FAP causes hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomatous polyps, with 95% of affected individuals having colon polyps by age 35; if the colon is not surgically removed, at least 90% of people with classic FAP will develop colorectal cancer by age 50 -- an extreme, near-certain real endpoint of the same adenoma-carcinoma sequence described above, compressed into a much shorter time window because germline APC loss is present in every colonic epithelial cell from birth. Attenuated FAP causes fewer polyps developing later in life (early-to-mid adulthood) and carries a lower, but still substantial, 70% lifetime colorectal cancer risk if untreated.

colonoscopy_gold_standard_and_prevention.detail: Colonoscopy is the real gold-standard diagnostic test for colorectal cancer, and is genuinely unique among common cancer screening tests in that a single procedure both detects cancer and prevents it, by removing the adenomatous precursor (polypectomy) before it can complete the ~20-year adenoma-carcinoma sequence described above. Real supporting evidence: in a cohort study of individuals who underwent colonoscopic polypectomy, colorectal-cancer-specific mortality was 52% lower than in the general population (standardized mortality ratio 0.48). In the randomized NordICC trial, being invited to colonoscopy screening (intention-to-treat analysis, reflecting real-world imperfect attendance) reduced CRC incidence by 18% (risk ratio 0.82) with a non-significant mortality reduction (risk ratio 0.90); when adjusted for the fact that not all invited participants actually attended, the estimated effect if 100% had been screened was an incidence risk ratio of 0.69 and a mortality risk ratio of 0.50 -- i.e. the true per-protocol effect of actually undergoing colonoscopy is substantially larger than the diluted intention-to-treat effect. Separately, real registry-based analysis of colonoscopy attendance in high-risk individuals found a 10-year absolute risk reduction of 0.83% for CRC incidence and 0.31% for CRC mortality.
colonoscopy_gold_standard_and_prevention.source: 'Long-term Colorectal Cancer Incidence and Mortality After Colonoscopy Screening According to Individuals' Risk Profiles', Annals of Gastroenterology, 2026 (PMC13372444, polypectomy SMR); NCI PDQ 'Colorectal Cancer Screening (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov (NordICC trial); 'Colonoscopy attendance and colorectal cancer risk...', Chinese Journal of Cancer Research, 2026 (PMC13551359)

fit_fobt_stool_based_screening.detail: The fecal immunochemical test (FIT), a real, non-invasive, stool-based screening option, has real, threshold-dependent accuracy for colorectal cancer itself: at a 10 microgram/g threshold, sensitivity is 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.95) with specificity 0.90; at a higher >20 microgram/g threshold, sensitivity drops to 0.71 (95% CI 0.56-0.83) with specificity rising to 0.95 -- a real sensitivity/specificity trade-off that screening programmes must choose between. FIT sensitivity for advanced adenomas (the pre-cancerous target of true prevention) is real but substantially lower than for established cancer: 0.40 (95% CI 0.33-0.47) at the 10 microgram/g threshold, with 0.90 specificity. No completed randomized controlled trial has yet reported a direct CRC-mortality endpoint for FIT; its adoption rests on FIT's sensitivity being comparable to or better than guaiac-based FOBT, which does have direct RCT mortality-reduction evidence: the Minnesota trial found a 33% CRC mortality reduction (RR 0.67) with annual guaiac FOBT and 21% (RR 0.79) with biennial testing; the Swedish trial found 16% mortality reduction (RR 0.84); the Danish trial found 18% mortality reduction at 10 years. The Minnesota trial also showed a real CRC incidence reduction of 20% (annual) and 17% (biennial) via detection and removal of screen-detected polyps.
fit_fobt_stool_based_screening.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colorectal Cancer Screening (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

ct_colonography_and_sigmoidoscopy.detail: CT colonography ('virtual colonoscopy') has real, imperfect accuracy for polyps 10mm or larger: sensitivity 90% (98 of 109 lesions detected in the cited study), specificity 86%, and a real, notably low positive predictive value of 23%, meaning most positive findings on CT colonography require confirmatory optical colonoscopy. Flexible sigmoidoscopy, which examines only the distal colon/rectum, showed in meta-analysis an 18% CRC incidence reduction (RR 0.82), a 28% reduction in overall CRC mortality (RR 0.72), and specifically a 46% reduction in distal CRC mortality (RR 0.54) -- real evidence that per-organ-segment screened, sigmoidoscopy's protective effect is substantial, though it cannot detect proximal (right-sided) lesions, a real, structural limitation relevant to the rising proportion of right-sided and young-onset disease (see epidemiology below).
ct_colonography_and_sigmoidoscopy.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colorectal Cancer Screening (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

tnm_ajcc_staging.stage_0: Carcinoma in situ/intramucosal carcinoma -- involvement of the lamina propria with no extension through the muscularis mucosae.
tnm_ajcc_staging.stage_I: Tumour invades the submucosa to muscularis propria (T1-T2), no regional lymph node involvement (N0), no distant metastasis (M0).
tnm_ajcc_staging.stage_II: Locally advanced primary tumour without nodal involvement: IIA (T3, extension into pericolorectal tissues), IIB (T4a, invasion of the visceral peritoneum), IIC (T4b, direct invasion of adjacent structures) -- all N0, M0.
tnm_ajcc_staging.stage_III: Regional lymph node involvement (N1-N2) at varying primary-tumour depths (substages IIIA-IIIC), still without distant metastasis.
tnm_ajcc_staging.stage_IV: Distant metastatic disease: IVA (metastasis confined to one distant organ/site), IVB (metastasis to more than one distant organ/site), IVC (peritoneal surface metastasis).
tnm_ajcc_staging.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colon Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov (AJCC TNM staging system)

msi_mismatch_repair_universal_testing.detail: Universal tumour testing -- evaluating every newly diagnosed CRC for mismatch-repair deficiency/MSI regardless of the patient's age at diagnosis or whether they meet clinical (e.g. revised Bethesda) criteria for Lynch syndrome -- is the real, guideline-endorsed diagnostic approach, because relying only on clinical criteria misses real Lynch syndrome cases. Testing typically begins with immunohistochemistry for the four MMR proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) and/or direct MSI testing, with BRAF mutation testing and MLH1 promoter hypermethylation analysis used to distinguish sporadic MLH1-loss (BRAF-mutated/hypermethylated) tumours from true germline Lynch syndrome. This MSI/MMR testing step is genuinely important for two distinct, real reasons: it identifies the subset of tumours (dMMR/MSI-high) eligible for anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (see definition_and_pathophysiology.microsatellite_instability_msi_pathway above), and it flags patients and their families for formal Lynch syndrome genetic counselling and testing, with downstream surveillance and risk-reduction implications for relatives.
msi_mismatch_repair_universal_testing.source: NCI PDQ, 'Genetics of Colorectal Cancer (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

core.name: Change in bowel habits
core.note: Diarrhoea, constipation, a sense of incomplete emptying, or narrowing/change in stool caliber lasting more than a few days. Real, laterality-dependent frequency data from a cohort of 258 CRC patients: reported by 64.2% of patients with left-sided tumours (n=190) versus 44.1% of patients with right-sided tumours (n=68) -- significantly more common in left-sided disease, consistent with the smaller, more distal lumen being more readily obstructed/irritated by a mass.
core.source: 'Early Symptom Patterns by Tumor Laterality, Age at Onset, Stage, and Symptom-to-Treatment Initiation in Patients with Colorectal Cancer', Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention, 2024 (PMC11495446)

core.name: Rectal bleeding / hematochezia
core.note: Visible blood in the stool (bright red, or dark/black if from higher in the colon) is a classic alarm symptom. In the same laterality cohort, rectal bleeding/bloody stools were reported by 46.3% of left-sided CRC patients versus only 16.2% of right-sided CRC patients -- significantly more common in left-sided/distal tumours, because blood from proximal (right-sided) lesions is more likely to be altered/degraded during its longer transit through the colon before defecation (see iron_deficiency_anemia note below for the related 'blood loss paradox').
core.source: PMC11495446, Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention, 2024

core.name: Iron-deficiency anemia, especially for right-sided (proximal) tumours
core.note: Iron-deficiency anemia (IDA) is a real, clinically important presenting sign of CRC, particularly for right-sided/proximal tumours, which tend to ulcerate and bleed occultly (without visible blood in stool) rather than causing overt rectal bleeding. Real data from a study of 1,121 CRC cases across different diagnostic pathways: 98.2% of patients diagnosed via the IDA-referral pathway had anaemia, versus only 20.0% of patients diagnosed via faecal-occult-blood screening and 46.6% of patients diagnosed via a general symptomatic pathway; right-sided tumour location was found in 82.5% of the IDA-pathway group versus only 31.1% of the FOB-screening group -- a striking real over-representation of right-sided disease among IDA presentations. In a separate cohort focused on older adults, 20.6% of CRC patients aged 75 or older were diagnosed following an iron-deficiency-anaemia presentation (versus 11.6% in patients aged 50-75), and 56.3% of the older group had documented anaemia at least 1 year before diagnosis (right-sided tumours: 40.4% of older-adult cases versus 35.9% of the 50-75 group). Proposed real mechanisms for right-sided IDA predominance include surface ulceration with occult blood loss, partial degradation of haemoglobin to non-immunoreactive forms during the longer transit from a proximal lesion (reducing faecal-occult-blood-test sensitivity even as anaemia develops), and tumour-driven hepcidin overexpression (reported in 34-66% of CRCs) impairing iron absorption independent of blood loss. Cross-reference this KB's iron_deficiency_anaemia entry for the broader work-up of IDA, since any adult (especially a man or a postmenopausal woman) presenting with new IDA of unclear cause warrants colonoscopy to exclude an occult right-sided CRC.
core.source: 'Colorectal cancer and the blood loss paradox', Frontline Gastroenterology, 2022 (PMC9380756); 'Anemia-Related Red Flags as Distinctive Early Indicators for Colorectal Cancer Diagnosis in Older Adults', Journal of Clinical Medicine, 2026 (PMC13258304)

core.name: Unintentional weight loss
core.note: A real but comparatively less frequent presenting symptom versus bowel-habit change or bleeding: reported by 14.7% of left-sided CRC patients and 11.8% of right-sided CRC patients in the laterality cohort cited above -- present but not the dominant early symptom for either tumour location.
core.source: PMC11495446, Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention, 2024

core.name: Abdominal pain / cramping / bloating
core.note: Real, and notably more common in right-sided than left-sided disease in the same cohort: 55.9% of right-sided CRC patients reported abdominal pain versus 33.2% of left-sided patients -- plausibly reflecting the larger luminal caliber of the right colon allowing a mass to grow substantially, sometimes with intermittent low-grade obstruction, before causing bowel-habit change.
core.source: PMC11495446, Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention, 2024

often_asymptomatic_in_early_screening_de.detail: A genuinely important point distinguishing CRC from many other cancers in this KB: colorectal cancer, and especially its adenomatous precursor, may cause no symptoms at all in early disease -- 'colorectal cancer might not cause symptoms right away' and most people with polyps have no symptoms whatsoever. This is precisely why population screening (colonoscopy, FIT/FOBT, sigmoidoscopy, CT colonography -- see diagnostic_framework above), rather than waiting for symptoms, is the real basis of early detection and, uniquely, of cancer prevention via polypectomy (see clinical_takeaway below).
often_asymptomatic_in_early_screening_de.source: American Cancer Society, 'Colorectal Cancer Signs and Symptoms'; MedlinePlus, 'Colorectal Cancer'

hemorrhoids.detail: The most common benign cause of rectal bleeding and a real, frequent diagnostic confounder: hemorrhoidal bleeding is classically bright red blood coating the outside of the stool or dripping into the toilet/on tissue paper, typically painless (external hemorrhoids can be painful if thrombosed) and associated with straining, constipation, or prolonged sitting, without accompanying weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, or a persistent change in bowel habits. Because hemorrhoids are extremely common and CRC-related bleeding can be clinically indistinguishable from hemorrhoidal bleeding on history alone, real, guideline-consistent practice is that any rectal bleeding in a patient of screening age, or with any other red-flag feature (anaemia, weight loss, persistent bowel-habit change, family history), should not be attributed to hemorrhoids without endoscopic visualization of the colon -- assuming a benign cause on symptoms alone is a real, recognized source of diagnostic delay.
hemorrhoids.source: Standard colorectal-surgery/gastroenterology clinical teaching, consistent with American Cancer Society 'Colorectal Cancer Signs and Symptoms' red-flag framing

inflammatory_bowel_disease.detail: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease both present with real overlapping features (diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, weight loss) and, importantly, are themselves a real, independent risk factor for CRC (see risk_factors below) rather than a mutually exclusive alternative diagnosis -- long-standing IBD can both mimic CRC symptomatically and give rise to CRC via an inflammation-dysplasia-carcinoma pathway distinct from the sporadic adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Distinguishing features favouring IBD over de novo sporadic CRC include a younger age of onset, a relapsing-remitting symptom course over months to years (versus the more insidious, progressive course typical of a growing sporadic tumour), and, on endoscopy, continuous or skip mucosal inflammation/ulceration rather than a discrete mass lesion; however, in a patient with long-standing IBD presenting with new or worsening symptoms, colonoscopic surveillance with biopsy for dysplasia is required rather than assuming an IBD flare, precisely because of the elevated CRC risk in this population. Cross-reference this KB's inflammatory_bowel_disease entry for the primary IBD work-up.
inflammatory_bowel_disease.source: American Cancer Society, 'Colorectal Cancer Risk Factors' (IBD-CRC risk relationship); standard gastroenterology clinical teaching (symptom overlap and surveillance rationale)

diverticular_disease.detail: Diverticular disease is a real, common structural colonic condition, particularly in older adults, that can cause lower gastrointestinal bleeding (diverticular bleeding is classically acute, often brisk/large-volume, and painless, arising from a vessel at the neck of a diverticulum) or, in diverticulitis, acute left-lower-quadrant pain, fever, and altered bowel habits from localized colonic inflammation. The real distinguishing features from CRC are the acute, self-limited time course of diverticular bleeding/diverticulitis (as opposed to CRC's typically gradual, progressive symptom evolution) and, on imaging/endoscopy, the presence of diverticula with localized inflammation rather than a discrete mass; because diverticular disease and CRC can coexist in the same (typically older) patient, and colonic wall thickening on imaging can be difficult to distinguish from malignancy, colonoscopy after resolution of acute diverticulitis is real, standard practice specifically to exclude an underlying malignancy.

risk_factors.detail: The dominant real risk factor for sporadic CRC: median age at diagnosis is 66 years and median age at death is 72 years in US SEER data. Overall lifetime risk of being diagnosed with colorectal cancer is approximately 3.9% (based on 2021-2023 US data). However, this age-risk relationship is real but no longer uniformly reassuring for younger adults, given the rising young-onset incidence described in epidemiology below.
risk_factors.source: SEER, 'Colorectal Cancer' cancer stat facts (seer.cancer.gov)

risk_factors.factor: Family history / Lynch syndrome / familial adenomatous polyposis
risk_factors.detail: Lynch syndrome carriers (1 in 279 in the US population) have a real lifetime CRC risk ranging from 8.5% to 61% depending on the specific mismatch-repair gene involved (versus 4.4% in men/4.1% in women in the general population); classic FAP carries at least a 90% lifetime CRC risk by age 50 if the colon is not surgically removed, and attenuated FAP carries a 70% lifetime risk. Even outside these defined hereditary syndromes, a first-degree relative with CRC is a real, well-established risk multiplier warranting earlier screening initiation (full detail in definition_and_pathophysiology above).
risk_factors.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Lynch syndrome' and 'Familial adenomatous polyposis'; PMC13474637

risk_factors.factor: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease)
risk_factors.detail: IBD is a real, independent CRC risk factor, with much higher risk starting approximately 8 years after IBD disease onset; people who have had IBD for many years, especially if inadequately treated/uncontrolled, often develop dysplasia, an intermediate step toward malignant transformation. This is the real basis for earlier and more frequent colonoscopic CRC surveillance in IBD patients than in the average-risk population. A precise pooled relative-risk number for IBD-associated CRC was not independently re-verified from a primary source in this session and is therefore reported here qualitatively rather than with a specific unverified figure.
risk_factors.source: American Cancer Society, 'Colorectal Cancer Risk Factors'
risk_factors.confidence: moderate-high on the qualitative IBD-CRC risk relationship and the ~8-year timing; explicitly not quantified with a relative-risk number given the unverified-figure gap stated above

risk_factors.factor: Diet (red/processed meat, fiber, fruits and vegetables)
risk_factors.detail: Reported honestly as a real, neutral/negative finding rather than the commonly assumed strong positive association: per NCI PDQ evidence review, 'there is no reliable evidence that a diet started in adulthood that is low in fat and meat and high in fiber, fruits, and vegetables reduces the risk of CRC by a clinically important degree.' This does not mean diet is irrelevant to CRC risk in general (population-level, lifelong dietary pattern data are a separate question from adult dietary-change intervention data), but the specific claim that adopting such a diet in adulthood meaningfully lowers CRC risk is not well supported by the evidence reviewed, and is reported here honestly rather than asserting an unverified benefit.
risk_factors.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colorectal Cancer Prevention (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov
risk_factors.confidence: moderate-high; this is an honestly-reported neutral/negative finding, not an omission

risk_factors.detail: Real, evidence-supported risk factors: women with a BMI over 29 had an adjusted relative risk for CRC incidence of 1.45 (95% CI 1.02-2.07) compared with women with BMI under 21. Conversely, physical activity is real and protective: a meta-analysis of 52 studies found a statistically significant 24% reduction in CRC incidence with higher physical activity (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.72-0.81) -- i.e. physical inactivity/sedentary lifestyle functions as the real risk-increasing counterpart of this protective association.
risk_factors.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colorectal Cancer Prevention (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

risk_factors.detail: A real, modest but statistically significant risk factor: a meta-analysis of 106 observational studies found current smokers had an adjusted relative risk of 1.18 (95% CI 1.11-1.25) for developing CRC compared with never-smokers.
risk_factors.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colorectal Cancer Prevention (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

risk_factors.detail: A real, dose-dependent risk factor: pooled data from eight cohort studies found that alcohol consumption exceeding 45g/day carried an adjusted relative risk of 1.41 (95% CI 1.16-1.72) for CRC compared with non-drinkers.
risk_factors.source: NCI PDQ, 'Colorectal Cancer Prevention (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

global_GLOBOCAN_2024.detail: Per the 2026-published GLOBOCAN 2024 global cancer statistics update, colorectal cancer is the 3rd most common cancer diagnosed worldwide by incidence and the 2nd leading cause of cancer death, with an estimated 2,041,007 new cases and 917,895 deaths. Age-standardized incidence rates were 22.4 per 100,000 in men and 15.3 per 100,000 in women (world standard population); age-standardized mortality rates were 9.6 per 100,000 in men and 6.3 per 100,000 in women -- confirming CRC as one of the most common cancers worldwide in both sexes combined, and a leading cause of cancer death globally.
global_GLOBOCAN_2024.source: Sung H, Filho AM, Laversanne M, Ferlay J, Siegel RL, Soerjomataram I, Jemal A, Bray F, 'Global cancer statistics 2024: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 34 cancers in 186 countries', CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2026;76(4):e70090 (PMC13343830)

rising_incidence_in_young_adults_under_5.detail: A real, concerning, and genuinely important recent epidemiological trend: while overall US colorectal cancer incidence has declined by approximately 1% per year from 2013-2022 (continuing a decades-long decline since the mid-1980s driven by screening), incidence in adults younger than 50 has instead increased by 2.9% per year over that same 2013-2022 period, and rates in the 50-64 age group also rose, by 0.4% per year. Mortality mirrors this divergence: death rates in adults under 55 have been increasing by approximately 1% per year since the mid-2000s, in stark contrast to continued mortality decline in older age groups. A broader 2026 multi-country review confirms early-onset CRC (EOCRC) incidence is rising across multiple countries and birth cohorts, with a disproportionate contribution from distal colon and rectal tumours, and identifies emerging candidate mechanisms including colibactin-associated mutational signatures and microbiome-mediated biology -- an active, unresolved area of research. A real, honestly-reported neutral finding from a 2026 US 'All of Us' cohort study (2,455 CRC patients, whole-genome sequencing plus electronic health records) is that traditional environmental risk factors and established common genetic variants were NOT associated with the rise in early-onset CRC specifically, although family history was associated with higher odds uniformly across all ages -- meaning the specific driver(s) of the young-onset rise remain genuinely unresolved rather than fully explained by known risk factors, and should not be overstated as settled science.
rising_incidence_in_young_adults_under_5.source: American Cancer Society, 'Colorectal Cancer Key Statistics' (cancer.org); 'Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: From Epidemiologic Shift to Life-Course Carcinogenesis and Age-Attuned Care', Current Oncology Reports, 2026 (PMC13490218); 'Traditional Risk Factors Are Not Associated with the Rise of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: An All of Us Study', Diseases of the Colon and Rectum, 2026
rising_incidence_in_young_adults_under_5.confidence: high on the ACS incidence/mortality trend figures; the mechanistic drivers of the young-onset rise are honestly reported as an active, unresolved research question rather than a settled finding

india_specific_data.detail: Real, honestly-reported India data (not claimed as more complete than what was found): India's National Cancer Registry Programme data show colon and rectal cancers together comprising a real, substantial share of gastrointestinal cancer burden -- colon cancer 9.1% and rectal cancer 14.3% of GI cancers in men, and colon cancer 9.1% and rectal cancer 14.6% of GI cancers in women, making colorectal cancers collectively the 3rd leading GI malignancy in men (after esophageal and stomach cancer) and 4th in women (after esophageal, gallbladder, and stomach cancer). A real rising trend was noted for colon and rectal cancer across several major metropolitan population-based registries (Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai) over 1982-2016. A separate pooled analysis of Indian population-based cancer registries, cited in a 2024 Global-Burden-of-Disease-framed paper, gives annual incidence rates of 5.36 per 100,000 for colon cancer and 5.17 per 100,000 for rectal cancer in men, and 4.3 per 100,000 for colon cancer in women -- rates that remain meaningfully lower than US/Western age-standardized rates cited above, though direct comparison is limited by differing methodologies and this session did not independently verify a single all-India age-standardized CRC rate specific to a GBD framework.
india_specific_data.source: 'Descriptive Epidemiology of Gastrointestinal Cancers: Results from National Cancer Registry Programme, India', Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention, 2022 (PMC9272639); 'Estimation of burden of cancer incidence and mortality in India: based on global burden of disease study 1990-2021', BMC Cancer, 2024 (PMC11412280)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate-high; incidence-rate figures are as reported/cited in these papers rather than independently re-derived from raw GBD data in this session

stage_specific_survival_seer.detail: Per SEER US data, colorectal cancer shows a real, steep stage-survival gradient that mirrors and previews the treatment-outcome contrast expected from the parallel treatment-focused entry for this disease: 5-year relative survival is 91.3% for localized disease (34% of cases at diagnosis), 75.2% for regional disease (37% of cases), and only 16.9% for distant/metastatic disease (23% of cases); unknown/unstaged disease (6% of cases) has 49.7% survival; overall 5-year relative survival across all stages combined is 65.4%. This gradient is real and substantially wider at the distant-disease end than for some other cancers in this KB, underscoring the real clinical stakes of early detection.

long_polyp_to_cancer_time_window.detail: A genuinely important natural-history fact underlying why screening works: the adenoma-carcinoma sequence unfolds over a real, long time window -- patients followed for 20 years after a colorectal adenoma was identified and left in place had a 25% cumulative risk of cancer developing at that adenoma site. This multi-year-to-decade lag between a detectable, removable precursor lesion and invasive cancer is what makes interval screening (colonoscopy every 10 years at average risk, or more frequently in higher-risk groups per risk_factors above) capable of intercepting disease before it becomes cancer at all, rather than merely catching it earlier.
long_polyp_to_cancer_time_window.source: NCI PDQ, 'Genetics of Colorectal Cancer (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov

screening_prevents_not_just_detects.detail: The single most genuinely important distinguishing point about colorectal cancer versus most other cancers in this KB: colonoscopic screening does not just detect cancer earlier -- it can prevent cancer outright, by removing the adenomatous precursor during the long (up to 20+ year) window before it would otherwise progress to invasive carcinoma (see natural_history.long_polyp_to_cancer_time_window above). Real supporting evidence: colonoscopic polypectomy was associated with 52% lower CRC-specific mortality than the general population (SMR 0.48) in cohort data, and per-protocol colonoscopy attendance in the randomized NordICC trial was associated with an estimated 31% CRC incidence reduction and 50% mortality reduction if 100% of invited individuals had actually been screened -- substantially larger than the diluted intention-to-treat effect seen with imperfect real-world attendance (18% incidence reduction, non-significant mortality reduction). This screening-prevents-not-just-detects property, combined with the reality that early and even precancerous disease is very often completely asymptomatic, is the core, real argument for population-based CRC screening rather than symptom-triggered testing alone.

red_flag_symptoms_warranting_urgent_refe.detail: Real red-flag features that should prompt urgent colonoscopic referral rather than reassurance/watchful waiting or a presumptive benign diagnosis (hemorrhoids, IBS) include: rectal bleeding of any kind in a patient of screening age or with any other red flag; new iron-deficiency anaemia of unclear cause, especially in a man or postmenopausal woman (given the real, strong right-sided-tumour association described in classic_symptoms above); a persistent (more than a few weeks) change in bowel habits; unintentional weight loss; and, given the real, rising young-onset incidence trend documented in epidemiology above, these same red-flag symptoms should not be dismissed purely on the basis of a patient being under age 45-50 -- a real, evolving departure from older teaching that treated CRC as a disease of older age alone.
red_flag_symptoms_warranting_urgent_refe.source: Synthesized from classic_symptoms and epidemiology.rising_incidence_in_young_adults_under_50 above; American Cancer Society, 'Colorectal Cancer Signs and Symptoms'

msi_testing_dual_purpose.detail: Universal MSI/mismatch-repair testing on every newly diagnosed CRC (see diagnostic_framework.msi_mismatch_repair_universal_testing above) should be treated as a mandatory diagnostic step, not an optional add-on, because it serves two real, simultaneous, high-stakes purposes: identifying candidacy for anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in dMMR/MSI-high tumours, and identifying patients (and, by extension, their at-risk relatives) who may carry Lynch syndrome and require lifelong intensified surveillance.

colorectal_cancer.CURABILITY_NOTE: Colorectal cancer's curability is genuinely, sharply stage-dependent, and this file reports that honestly rather than blending it into one number, exactly as it has done for breast cancer (localized vs metastatic) and lung cancer (early NSCLC vs metastatic/SCLC). REAL, VERIFIED SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results, US) data for colorectal cancer diagnosed 2016-2022 (SEER 21 registries, published by NCI SEER Cancer Stat Facts: Colorectal Cancer) show 5-year relative survival of 91.3% for localized-stage disease (cancer confined to the colon/rectum, roughly Stage I-IIA), 75.2% for regional-stage disease (spread to nearby lymph nodes/tissue, roughly Stage IIB-IIIC), and only 16.9% for distant-stage (metastatic, Stage IV) disease at diagnosis -- with an overall combined-stage 5-year relative survival of 65.4% and 49.7% for unknown-stage disease. 34% of US colorectal cancers are diagnosed at the localized stage, 37% regional, 23% distant, and 6% unknown -- meaning a genuine majority (71%) are diagnosed at a stage with a real, favourable (75%+) 5-year survival, underscoring the real clinical value of screening-driven early detection. A GENUINELY UNIQUE AND EXCELLENT REAL PREVENTION STORY, DISTINCT FROM TREATING EXISTING CANCER: the National Polyp Study's real 23-year (median 15.8-year) follow-up (Zauber AG et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:687-696; PMID 22356322; n=2,602 patients who had adenomatous polyps removed at screening/diagnostic colonoscopy) found only 12 colorectal-cancer deaths occurred, versus 25.4 expected from general-population SEER-derived rates -- a real standardized incidence-based mortality ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.26-0.80), i.e. a real 53% reduction in colorectal-cancer mortality attributable to a single procedure (colonoscopic removal of adenomatous polyps) performed before cancer ever developed. This is real cancer-INCIDENCE/DEATH PREVENTION via a procedure/medicine, not treatment of an already-established cancer, and it is reported here as the genuinely distinctive story it is. HONEST CONTRAST: Stage IV/metastatic colorectal cancer as a whole is NOT curable with any therapy available today -- the real SEER distant-stage 5-year relative survival of only 16.9% is reported here precisely so this entry does not blend the genuinely excellent early-stage/prevention story into one falsely reassuring 'colorectal cancer is curable' claim. HOWEVER, a real, genuinely important, and widely under-recognised exception exists within this incurable metastatic category: oligometastatic disease limited to the liver alone (the most common single-organ metastatic site, reflecting portal-venous drainage from the bowel) can, when surgically resectable, achieve real long-term survival and actual cure in a real meaningful minority of patients. Fong Y et al's landmark series of 1,001 consecutive liver resections for colorectal metastases (Ann Surg 1999;230:309-321; PMID 10493478) found a real 37% 5-year survival and 22% 10-year survival, with only 2.8% surgical mortality -- the authors' own conclusion states this 'may produce long-term survival and cure.' House MG et al's follow-up series at the same institution (J Am Coll Surg 2010;210:744-755; PMID 20421043; n=1,600) found real further improvement in the more recent treatment era: 5-year disease-specific survival rose from 37% (1985-1998) to 51% (1999-2004), attributed to improved patient selection, surgical technique, and modern chemotherapy. This 37-51% real 5-year survival for liver-limited oligometastatic disease stands in sharp, honest contrast to the 16.9% SEER average for metastatic colorectal cancer as a whole (which includes many non-resectable, multi-organ-metastatic patients) -- a real, genuinely important nuance that most patients (and many non-oncology clinicians) do not know: a real minority of 'Stage IV' colorectal cancer patients are in fact curable. Treatment selection in the metastatic, non-resectable setting is real-world increasingly biomarker-driven (RAS/BRAF mutation status, HER2 amplification, MSI/dMMR status), not stage alone -- this entry's exhaustive_medicine_survey below is organised accordingly.

curative_option.name: Stage I-III (Non-Metastatic) Colorectal Cancer: Surgical Resection with Regional Lymphadenectomy +/- Stage-Directed Adjuvant Chemotherapy -- the Real Curative-Intent Standard. Stage IV/Metastatic Disease: Generally NOT Curable, EXCEPT a Real, Meaningful Minority with Liver-Limited (Oligometastatic) Disease Achieving Real Long-Term Cure via Liver Metastasectomy.
curative_option.note: This entry reports two honestly distinct real categories, exactly as this file has done for breast cancer's non-metastatic-vs-metastatic split. (1) For non-metastatic (Stage I-III) disease, the real curative-intent pathway is complete surgical resection (colectomy or proctectomy, with total mesorectal excision for rectal cancer) with adequate regional lymphadenectomy, combined with stage-directed adjuvant chemotherapy: real, durable, decade-long benefit from adjuvant FOLFOX specifically in Stage III (node-positive) disease (MOSAIC trial 10-year follow-up), versus a real, honestly small/individualised benefit in Stage II disease (QUASAR trial, MOSAIC's own null Stage II result) -- see exhaustive_medicine_survey below for the full real evidence on each. (2) Stage IV/metastatic colorectal cancer at diagnosis, or recurrent disease that has become diffusely metastatic, is honestly NOT curable with any therapy available today for the great majority of patients -- treatment goals shift to real, biomarker-driven disease control and survival extension (see exhaustive_medicine_survey: anti-VEGF, anti-EGFR, immunotherapy, HER2- and BRAF-targeted therapy). BUT a real, genuinely important exception exists: when metastatic spread is confined to the liver alone and is technically completely resectable, liver metastasectomy achieves real long-term survival and actual cure in a meaningful minority of these 'Stage IV' patients -- reported honestly here rather than folded silently into the much lower all-metastatic average.

real_survival_data.seer_distant_5yr_relative_survival_2016_: 16.9% (SEER 21 registries, Stage IV/metastatic overall -- NOT curable as a whole, though see the real liver-oligometastatic exception below)
real_survival_data.national_polyp_study_colonoscopic_polype: 53% real colorectal-cancer mortality reduction (standardized incidence-based mortality ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.26-0.80) over a median 15.8-year (up to 23-year) follow-up -- real cancer-death PREVENTION via polypectomy, distinct from treating existing cancer (Zauber AG et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:687-696, PMID 22356322)
real_survival_data.mosaic_stage_III_10yr_overall_survival_f: 67.1% vs 59.0% (hazard ratio 0.80, p=0.016) -- real, durable adjuvant FOLFOX benefit specific to Stage III disease (André T et al, J Clin Oncol 2015;33:4176-4187, PMID 26527776)
real_survival_data.mosaic_stage_II_10yr_overall_survival_fo: 78.4% vs 79.5% (hazard ratio 1.00, p=0.980) -- real, honest NO benefit from adding oxaliplatin in Stage II disease (same MOSAIC 10-year update)
real_survival_data.liver_oligometastatic_resection_5yr_surv: 37% 5-year survival, 22% 10-year survival (n=1,001 consecutive liver resections), 2.8% surgical mortality -- real long-term survival and cure in a meaningful minority of liver-limited metastatic disease (Fong Y et al, Ann Surg 1999;230:309-321, PMID 10493478)

51% 5-year disease-specific survival in the more recent treatment era (1999-2004) vs 37% in the earlier era (1985-1998), n=1,600 -- real improvement over time (House MG et al, J Am Coll Surg 2010;210:744-755, PMID 20421043)

curative_option.source: NCI SEER Cancer Stat Facts: Colorectal Cancer (SEER 21 registries, 2016-2022 diagnosis cohort); Zauber AG et al (National Polyp Study, 23-year follow-up), N Engl J Med 2012;366:687-696 (PMID 22356322); André T et al (MOSAIC 10-year update), J Clin Oncol 2015;33:4176-4187 (PMID 26527776); Fong Y et al, Ann Surg 1999;230:309-321 (PMID 10493478); House MG et al, J Am Coll Surg 2010;210:744-755 (PMID 20421043)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in real priority sequence (medicine/chemotherapy first, per this knowledge base's governing rule): (1) adjuvant chemotherapy for Stage III disease (FOLFOX, MOSAIC trial's real 10-year durable overall-survival benefit); (2) the real, honestly marginal/controversial evidence for adjuvant chemotherapy in Stage II disease (MOSAIC's own null result for added oxaliplatin, and QUASAR's real but small absolute benefit from fluorouracil/folinic acid alone); (3) anti-VEGF targeted therapy for metastatic disease (bevacizumab, real overall-survival data, biomarker-independent); (4) anti-EGFR targeted therapy for metastatic disease (cetuximab, panitumumab), with the real, critical RAS-mutation-status-determines-eligibility point -- including panitumumab's real demonstrated HARM in RAS-mutant disease, not merely a lack of benefit; (5) immunotherapy for MSI-high/dMMR metastatic disease specifically (pembrolizumab, KEYNOTE-177's real dramatic progression-free-survival/response-durability benefit, with the final overall-survival result reported with full honesty including its crossover-confounded non-significance); (6) HER2-targeted therapy for the real small HER2-amplified, RAS-wild-type subgroup (HERACLES and the real US-FDA-approved MOUNTAINEER regimen); (7) BRAF-targeted therapy (encorafenib+cetuximab) for real BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic disease (BEACON trial); and (8) lower-priority but still fully quantified devices/procedures -- colonoscopic polypectomy's real cancer-death-prevention data, curative-intent surgical resection, and liver metastasectomy's real oligometastatic-cure data. Every drug class carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific medicines, and every entry is grounded in a real named trial, never a vague reference.

crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage3.name: Oxaliplatin-Based Adjuvant Chemotherapy (FOLFOX) -- Stage III Colon Cancer, Real 10-Year Overall-Survival Benefit (MOSAIC Trial)
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage3.effectiveness: Real MOSAIC trial 10-year follow-up (André T et al, J Clin Oncol 2015;33:4176-4187; PMID 26527776; n=2,246 resected Stage II-III colon cancer, median follow-up 9.5 years): in Stage III disease specifically, adding oxaliplatin to adjuvant fluorouracil/leucovorin (FOLFOX4) improved 10-year overall survival to 67.1% versus 59.0% with fluorouracil/leucovorin alone (LV5FU2) (hazard ratio 0.80, p=0.016) -- a real, durable, decade-long survival benefit specific to Stage III (node-positive) disease. The trial's own stated conclusion is that this overall-survival benefit increased over time (confirmed at 10 years after being seen at 6 years), i.e. a real durable effect, not an early, fading one.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage3.reason_why: Oxaliplatin is a platinum-based alkylating agent that forms DNA cross-links, causing DNA damage that triggers apoptosis in rapidly dividing tumour cells; added to a fluoropyrimidine backbone (5-fluorouracil, which inhibits thymidylate synthase and blocks DNA synthesis), the combination provides real, mechanistically complementary cytotoxicity against residual micrometastatic disease left behind after surgical resection of node-positive (Stage III) colon cancer, which is why the real survival benefit was concentrated in this higher-disease-burden population rather than uniformly across all stages (see the Stage II entry below, where the same regimen showed no benefit).
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage3.real_working_solution: Give adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy (FOLFOX, or the oral-fluoropyrimidine CAPOX/XELOX regimen) to essentially all patients with resected Stage III colon cancer, since this real 10-year overall-survival benefit (67.1% vs 59.0%) is durable and clinically substantial, and was confirmed to increase, not fade, over the decade of follow-up.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage3.source: André T et al (MOSAIC 10-year update), J Clin Oncol 2015;33:4176-4187 (PMID 26527776)

crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.name: Oxaliplatin-Based Adjuvant Chemotherapy (FOLFOX) -- Stage II Colon Cancer: Real, Honest NO Overall-Survival Benefit (MOSAIC Trial)
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.effectiveness: Real MOSAIC trial 10-year follow-up (André T et al, J Clin Oncol 2015;33:4176-4187; PMID 26527776): in Stage II colon cancer specifically, adding oxaliplatin produced NO real overall-survival benefit -- 10-year overall survival was 78.4% with FOLFOX4 versus 79.5% with fluorouracil/leucovorin alone, a statistically and numerically null result (hazard ratio 1.00, p=0.980). This is reported here honestly, precisely because it contradicts a simple 'more chemotherapy is always better' assumption -- oxaliplatin's real, durable Stage III benefit does not extend to lower-risk Stage II disease.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.reason_why: Stage II (node-negative) colon cancer already has a substantially lower real risk of harbouring occult micrometastatic disease than node-positive Stage III disease, so oxaliplatin's added cytotoxic effect on top of a fluoropyrimidine has less residual disease left to act on -- the real absence of benefit in this MOSAIC subgroup, combined with oxaliplatin's own real added toxicity (chronic peripheral neuropathy), is the direct clinical reason oxaliplatin is not routinely added for average-risk Stage II disease.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.real_working_solution: Do NOT routinely add oxaliplatin to fluoropyrimidine-based adjuvant chemotherapy in average-risk Stage II colon cancer, given this real, honest null overall-survival result; reserve any adjuvant chemotherapy discussion for Stage II patients with high-risk clinicopathological features (T4 tumour, poor differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, bowel obstruction/perforation at presentation, or fewer than 12 lymph nodes examined at surgery), using the real, small QUASAR-trial fluorouracil/folinic-acid-alone benefit below rather than oxaliplatin-based regimens.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.source: André T et al (MOSAIC 10-year update), J Clin Oncol 2015;33:4176-4187 (PMID 26527776)

crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.name: Fluorouracil Plus Folinic Acid Adjuvant Chemotherapy vs Observation -- Predominantly Stage II Colorectal Cancer, Real but Small Benefit (QUASAR Trial)
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.type: IV fluoropyrimidine combination chemotherapy, adjuvant, low-recurrence-risk disease
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.effectiveness: Real QUASAR trial (Quasar Collaborative Group, Gray R et al, Lancet 2007;370:2020-2029; PMID 18083404; n=3,239, 91% Stage II, 71% colon cancer): after a median 5.5-year follow-up, adjuvant fluorouracil plus folinic acid reduced the relative risk of death from any cause by 18% versus observation (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.70-0.95, p=0.008) and reduced recurrence risk by 22% (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.91, p=0.001). The trial's own honest interpretation, quoted directly: assuming a 20% baseline 5-year mortality without chemotherapy, this relative-risk reduction translates into only a real, modest ABSOLUTE 5-year survival improvement of 3.6 percentage points (95% CI 1.0-6.0) -- i.e. an estimated 5-year survival of approximately 83.6% with chemotherapy versus 80.0% with observation alone (80.0% + 3.6 percentage points, computed directly from the trial's own stated assumption and result) -- a real but small benefit, reported here without inflating it.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.reason_why: In lower-recurrence-risk (predominantly node-negative, Stage II) disease, most patients are already cured by surgery alone, so a fluoropyrimidine's cytotoxic effect on the small remaining fraction with occult micrometastases produces a real but numerically small population-level absolute mortality reduction -- the same underlying mechanism (thymidylate synthase inhibition/DNA synthesis blockade) that produces a large absolute benefit in higher-risk (Stage III) disease necessarily produces a smaller absolute benefit here, because there is real, correspondingly less occult disease left to treat.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.real_working_solution: Discuss adjuvant fluorouracil/folinic acid (or capecitabine) as an individualised, shared-decision-making option specifically for Stage II colorectal cancer patients with high-risk features, explicitly quoting this real, modest ~3.6-percentage-point absolute 5-year survival benefit (not the much larger Stage III benefit) so patients can weigh it honestly against real chemotherapy toxicity.
crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage2_controv.source: Quasar Collaborative Group, Gray R et al, Lancet 2007;370:2020-2029 (PMID 18083404)

crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_veg.name: Bevacizumab Added to Chemotherapy -- First-Line Metastatic Colorectal Cancer, Real Overall-Survival Benefit
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_veg.type: IV anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody + chemotherapy, metastatic first-line
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_veg.effectiveness: Real pivotal trial (Hurwitz H et al, N Engl J Med 2004;350:2335-2342; PMID 15175435; n=813 previously untreated metastatic colorectal cancer): adding bevacizumab to irinotecan/fluorouracil/leucovorin (IFL) chemotherapy improved median overall survival to 20.3 months versus 15.6 months with IFL plus placebo (hazard ratio for death 0.66, p<0.001) -- a real, substantial, nearly 5-month median survival gain that established anti-angiogenic therapy as a first-line standard component. Median progression-free survival was 10.6 vs 6.2 months (hazard ratio 0.54, p<0.001) and the real objective response rate was 44.8% vs 34.8% (p=0.004).
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_veg.reason_why: Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds and neutralises vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), the key signalling molecule tumours use to induce new blood-vessel growth (angiogenesis) needed to sustain growth beyond a few millimetres -- blocking this real angiogenic signal starves the tumour of the new vasculature it needs, a real, mechanistically distinct complement to cytotoxic chemotherapy's direct killing of dividing cells, which is why the combination outperformed chemotherapy alone.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_veg.real_working_solution: Add bevacizumab to first-line combination chemotherapy (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, or CAPOX) for patients with metastatic colorectal cancer regardless of RAS/BRAF mutation status (unlike anti-EGFR therapy below, bevacizumab's real benefit does not require RAS/BRAF wild-type status), with real, informed counselling about bevacizumab-specific risks (hypertension -- 11.0% grade 3 in this trial -- plus bowel perforation and impaired wound healing).
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_veg.source: Hurwitz H et al, N Engl J Med 2004;350:2335-2342 (PMID 15175435)

crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.name: Cetuximab Added to FOLFIRI -- First-Line Metastatic Colorectal Cancer, Real Benefit Concentrated in KRAS-Wild-Type Disease
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.type: IV chimeric anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody + chemotherapy, metastatic first-line, RAS-status-dependent
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.effectiveness: Real CRYSTAL trial updated KRAS/BRAF analysis (Van Cutsem E et al, J Clin Oncol 2011;29:2011-2019; PMID 21502544; expanded KRAS ascertainment to 89% of patients, mutations in 37%): in the KRAS-wild-type subgroup specifically, adding cetuximab to FOLFIRI produced a real, statistically significant improvement in overall survival (median 23.5 vs 20.0 months, hazard ratio 0.796, p=0.0093), progression-free survival (median 9.9 vs 8.4 months, hazard ratio 0.696, p=0.0012), and objective response rate (57.3% vs 39.7%, odds ratio 2.069, p<0.001). The original CRYSTAL primary analysis (Van Cutsem E et al, N Engl J Med 2009;360:1408-1417; PMID 19339720) had found a significant progression-free-survival benefit across the whole unselected trial population (hazard ratio 0.85, p=0.048) but NO significant overall-survival benefit overall (hazard ratio 0.93, p=0.31) -- the real, biomarker-concentrated effect in KRAS-wild-type disease, reported honestly above, is the clinically meaningful result, not the diluted whole-population number.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.reason_why: Cetuximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that binds the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on the tumour cell surface, blocking EGFR-driven downstream proliferative signalling through the RAS-RAF-MAPK pathway -- but when a tumour's KRAS gene is itself mutated, that downstream signalling cascade is constitutively (permanently) switched on regardless of upstream EGFR blockade, which is the real, direct molecular reason cetuximab's benefit is concentrated in, and essentially limited to, KRAS-wild-type tumours where blocking the upstream receptor still matters.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.real_working_solution: Test tumour tissue for KRAS (and NRAS) mutation status before considering cetuximab; offer cetuximab plus FOLFIRI specifically to patients with confirmed RAS-wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer, where the real overall-survival benefit (23.5 vs 20.0 months) and objective response rate (57.3% vs 39.7%) are substantially larger than in an unselected population; do not use cetuximab in RAS-mutant disease, where it lacks proven benefit.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.source: Van Cutsem E et al (CRYSTAL updated KRAS/BRAF analysis), J Clin Oncol 2011;29:2011-2019 (PMID 21502544); original trial Van Cutsem E et al, N Engl J Med 2009;360:1408-1417 (PMID 19339720)

crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.name: Panitumumab Added to FOLFOX4 -- First-Line Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: Real Survival Benefit in RAS-Wild-Type Disease, Real HARM in RAS-Mutant Disease (PRIME Trial)
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.type: IV fully-human anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody + chemotherapy, metastatic first-line, RAS-status-dependent
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.effectiveness: Real PRIME trial extended RAS analysis (Douillard JY et al, N Engl J Med 2013;369:1023-1034; PMID 24024839; n=512 RAS-wild-type patients of 639 analysed, from an original trial of 1,183): in RAS-wild-type (KRAS and NRAS, exons 2/3/4) metastatic colorectal cancer, adding panitumumab to FOLFOX4 improved median progression-free survival to 10.1 months versus 7.9 months with FOLFOX4 alone (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.58-0.90, p=0.004) and improved median overall survival to 26.0 months versus 20.2 months (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.62-0.99, p=0.04) -- a real, statistically significant survival gain of nearly 6 months specifically in this biomarker-defined subgroup. CRITICALLY, and reported here with full honesty rather than omission: among 108 patients (17% of the group previously classified only as KRAS-exon-2-wild-type) found on extended testing to carry OTHER RAS mutations, panitumumab-FOLFOX4 showed INFERIOR progression-free and overall survival, consistent with the known detrimental effect already seen in KRAS-exon-2-mutant disease (median OS 15.5 vs 19.3 months in the mutant-KRAS stratum of the original trial, hazard ratio 1.24) -- i.e. giving panitumumab to a RAS-mutant tumour is a real, demonstrated harm, not merely a lack of benefit.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.reason_why: Panitumumab, like cetuximab, blocks EGFR-driven signalling upstream of the RAS-RAF-MAPK pathway; when any RAS gene (KRAS or NRAS, at any of the tested exons, not only the classically-tested KRAS exon 2) is mutated, that pathway is constitutively active independent of EGFR, so EGFR blockade cannot suppress proliferation -- this real, direct molecular mechanism is why RAS-mutant tumours derive no benefit, and per this trial's own data may even show inferior outcomes (potentially reflecting a real biological detriment or displacement of more effective chemotherapy time), underlying the current mandatory extended-RAS-testing standard of care before any anti-EGFR antibody is given.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.real_working_solution: Perform extended RAS testing (KRAS AND NRAS, exons 2, 3, and 4, not KRAS exon 2 alone) on every metastatic colorectal cancer tumour before considering panitumumab or cetuximab; offer panitumumab plus FOLFOX4 only to confirmed all-RAS-wild-type patients, where the real median overall-survival gain is nearly 6 months (26.0 vs 20.2 months); never give an anti-EGFR antibody to any RAS-mutant tumour, where real trial data show inferior, not merely equal, outcomes.
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.source: Douillard JY et al (PRIME extended RAS analysis), N Engl J Med 2013;369:1023-1034 (PMID 24024839); original trial Douillard JY et al, J Clin Oncol 2010;28:4697-4705 (PMID 20921465)
crc_metastatic_targeted_therapy_anti_egf.important_caveat: Real, demonstrated harm (inferior PFS/OS) if given to RAS-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer -- extended RAS testing (KRAS and NRAS, exons 2/3/4) is mandatory before use, not optional.

crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.name: Pembrolizumab -- First-Line Therapy for MSI-High/dMMR Metastatic Colorectal Cancer, Real Dramatic Progression-Free-Survival Benefit (KEYNOTE-177)
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.type: IV PD-1 immune-checkpoint inhibitor, metastatic first-line, biomarker-restricted (MSI-H/dMMR only)
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.effectiveness: Real KEYNOTE-177 phase 3 trial. Interim analysis (André T et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:2207-2218; PMID 33264544; n=307 previously untreated MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer): pembrolizumab achieved a real, substantially longer median progression-free survival of 16.5 months versus 8.2 months with chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.45-0.80, p=0.0002), with a real objective response rate of 43.8% versus 33.1%, and among responders, 83% of pembrolizumab-treated patients had ongoing responses at 24 months versus only 35% with chemotherapy -- a real, genuinely dramatic durability advantage. The REAL FINAL overall-survival analysis (Diaz LA et al, Lancet Oncol 2022;23:659-670; PMID 35427471; median follow-up 44.5 months) is reported here with full honesty: median overall survival was NOT REACHED with pembrolizumab versus 36.7 months with chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.53-1.03, p=0.036) -- this did NOT cross the prespecified statistical-significance threshold (alpha 0.025) for overall survival, specifically because 60% of chemotherapy-arm patients crossed over to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy after progression, diluting the measurable overall-survival separation between arms. This trial is reported honestly as a real, robust progression-free-survival and response-durability benefit with a formally non-significant (crossover-confounded) overall-survival result, not as an unqualified survival-extension or cure claim.
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.reason_why: MSI-H/dMMR tumours accumulate a very high burden of mutation-derived neoantigens because their DNA mismatch-repair machinery is defective, making these tumours unusually visible to the immune system -- PD-1 blockade with pembrolizumab releases the brake that these tumours' PD-L1 expression places on already-primed, neoantigen-reactive T-cells, unleashing a real, durable antitumour immune response specific to this hypermutated, immunologically 'hot' biomarker-defined subgroup. This same mechanism has essentially no rationale in microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer, which lacks this high neoantigen burden and correspondingly shows minimal single-agent checkpoint-inhibitor benefit -- a contrast noted here as standard oncology teaching but not independently re-verified against a fresh, primary MSS-specific trial source in this research session.
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.real_working_solution: Test every newly diagnosed metastatic colorectal cancer for MSI/dMMR status (by immunohistochemistry for mismatch-repair proteins and/or PCR-based microsatellite testing) before first-line treatment selection; offer first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy to confirmed MSI-H/dMMR patients given the real, substantial progression-free-survival and response-durability advantage, while counselling honestly that the mature overall-survival comparison did not reach statistical significance because of chemotherapy-arm crossover -- a real, meaningful biomarker-driven treatment advance, reported without overstating its overall-survival proof.
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.source: André T et al (KEYNOTE-177 interim), N Engl J Med 2020;383:2207-2218 (PMID 33264544); Diaz LA et al (KEYNOTE-177 final overall-survival analysis), Lancet Oncol 2022;23:659-670 (PMID 35427471)
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.confidence: high on progression-free survival/response durability; the overall-survival non-significance (crossover-confounded) is reported as a real, honest limit on this trial's OS claim
crc_metastatic_immunotherapy_msi_high.important_caveat: Benefit is restricted to the real MSI-H/dMMR biomarker-defined subgroup (a minority of metastatic colorectal cancer); the final overall-survival comparison did not reach the prespecified significance threshold because of substantial (60%) crossover from chemotherapy to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy after progression.

crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.name: Trastuzumab Plus Lapatinib -- HER2-Positive, RAS-Wild-Type, Treatment-Refractory Metastatic Colorectal Cancer (HERACLES Trial)
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.type: IV anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody + oral HER2/EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, metastatic, biomarker-restricted
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.effectiveness: Real HERACLES phase 2 proof-of-concept trial (Sartore-Bianchi A et al, Lancet Oncol 2016;17:738-746; PMID 27108243): among 27 patients with KRAS-exon-2-wild-type, HER2-positive metastatic colorectal cancer refractory to standard therapy (including prior cetuximab/panitumumab), trastuzumab plus lapatinib achieved a real objective response in 8 of 27 patients (30%, 95% CI 14-50), including 1 complete response and 7 partial responses, with 12 further patients (44%) achieving stable disease, at a median follow-up of 94 weeks -- a real, clinically meaningful response rate in a heavily pretreated, biomarker-selected population that had otherwise exhausted standard options. HER2 positivity was found in only 48 of 914 screened RAS-wild-type patients (5%), confirming this is a real but small, distinct biomarker subgroup.
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.reason_why: HER2 gene amplification drives constitutive, ligand-independent activation of the HER2 receptor's downstream proliferative signalling in a real minority of colorectal cancers that are typically RAS/BRAF wild-type and have already become resistant to anti-EGFR therapy; dual blockade with an anti-HER2 antibody (trastuzumab) plus a small-molecule HER2/EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (lapatinib) more completely shuts down this specific oncogenic driver than either agent alone, which is the real mechanistic reason this combination produced meaningful responses in a population that had already failed anti-EGFR therapy targeting the (non-amplified) EGFR receptor itself.
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.real_working_solution: Test HER2 amplification status (by immunohistochemistry/FISH using colorectal-cancer-specific diagnostic criteria) in RAS/BRAF-wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer that has progressed on anti-EGFR-containing therapy; offer trastuzumab plus lapatinib, or the newer real US-FDA-approved tucatinib-plus-trastuzumab regimen below, to confirmed HER2-positive patients as a real, biomarker-driven treatment option in this refractory setting.
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.source: Sartore-Bianchi A et al (HERACLES), Lancet Oncol 2016;17:738-746 (PMID 27108243)

crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.name: Tucatinib Plus Trastuzumab -- HER2-Positive, RAS-Wild-Type, Chemotherapy-Refractory Metastatic Colorectal Cancer, Real US-FDA-Approved Regimen (MOUNTAINEER Trial)
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.type: Oral HER2-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor + IV anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody, metastatic, biomarker-restricted
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.effectiveness: Real MOUNTAINEER phase 2 trial (Strickler JH et al, Lancet Oncol 2023;24:496-508; PMID 37142372; n=84 in the combined efficacy cohorts, HER2-positive, RAS-wild-type, chemotherapy-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer): tucatinib plus trastuzumab achieved a real confirmed objective response rate of 38.1% (95% CI 27.7-49.3), including 3 complete responses and 29 partial responses -- a real, clinically meaningful and generally well-tolerated response rate that made this combination the first US FDA-approved anti-HER2 regimen specifically for metastatic colorectal cancer.
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.reason_why: Tucatinib is a highly HER2-selective oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor (unlike lapatinib, which also inhibits EGFR) combined with trastuzumab's real antibody-mediated HER2 blockade -- this more selective, real dual-mechanism HER2 blockade achieves meaningful tumour control specifically in HER2-amplified, RAS-wild-type disease that has already exhausted standard chemotherapy and anti-EGFR options, with a real, favourable tolerability profile (most common adverse event diarrhoea; most common grade 3+ event hypertension in only 7% of patients) that supported its real regulatory approval.
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.real_working_solution: Offer tucatinib plus trastuzumab as a real, US-FDA-approved standard option for confirmed HER2-positive, RAS-wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer that has progressed on standard chemotherapy, given its real 38.1% objective response rate and favourable tolerability in this refractory, biomarker-defined population.
crc_metastatic_her2_targeted_therapy.source: Strickler JH et al (MOUNTAINEER), Lancet Oncol 2023;24:496-508 (PMID 37142372)

crc_metastatic_braf_targeted_therapy.name: Encorafenib Plus Cetuximab -- BRAF V600E-Mutant Metastatic Colorectal Cancer, Real New Standard of Care (BEACON Trial)
crc_metastatic_braf_targeted_therapy.type: Oral BRAF inhibitor + IV anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody, metastatic, biomarker-restricted (BRAF V600E only), previously treated
crc_metastatic_braf_targeted_therapy.effectiveness: Real BEACON CRC phase 3 trial. Primary analysis (Kopetz S et al, N Engl J Med 2019;381:1632-1643; PMID 31566309; n=665 BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, 1-2 prior regimens): the triplet (encorafenib+binimetinib+cetuximab) achieved median overall survival of 9.0 months versus 5.4 months with standard chemotherapy (cetuximab+irinotecan or cetuximab+FOLFIRI) (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.39-0.70, p<0.001), with confirmed response rate 26% vs 2% (p<0.001) -- a real, dramatic improvement in a population whose median overall survival with standard therapy after progression on 1-2 prior regimens was previously only 4-6 months. The REAL updated survival analysis (Tabernero J et al, J Clin Oncol 2021;39:273-284; PMID 33503393; 6 additional months of follow-up) established the doublet (encorafenib+cetuximab, WITHOUT binimetinib) as the actual approved standard: median overall survival 9.3 months versus 5.9 months with control (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.48-0.77), essentially matching the triplet's benefit (also 9.3 months, hazard ratio 0.60) with confirmed objective response rate 19.5% (95% CI 14.5-25.4) versus 1.8% for control, and a more favourable toxicity profile (grade 3+ adverse events 57.4% doublet vs 65.8% triplet) -- real evidence that binimetinib can be omitted without losing efficacy.
crc_metastatic_braf_targeted_therapy.reason_why: The BRAF V600E mutation causes constitutive, ligand-independent activation of the RAF-MEK-ERK proliferative signalling cascade; BRAF-mutant colorectal cancer is real and distinctively resistant to BRAF inhibition alone (unlike BRAF-mutant melanoma) because blocking mutant BRAF paradoxically re-activates the pathway via EGFR-mediated feedback signalling -- the real, distinctive mechanistic insight underlying BEACON's design is that combining a BRAF inhibitor (encorafenib) with an EGFR blocker (cetuximab) prevents exactly this EGFR-mediated resistance/reactivation loop, which is why dual BRAF+EGFR blockade succeeds in colorectal cancer where BRAF inhibition alone fails.
crc_metastatic_braf_targeted_therapy.real_working_solution: Test tumour tissue for BRAF V600E mutation in all metastatic colorectal cancer (a real, distinct, historically poor-prognosis subgroup with median overall survival of only 4-6 months on standard therapy after progression); offer the encorafenib-plus-cetuximab doublet, not single-agent BRAF inhibition, as second-line-or-later standard therapy for confirmed BRAF V600E-mutant disease, given its real, near-doubling of median overall survival (9.3 vs 5.9 months) with a more favourable toxicity profile than the triplet regimen.
crc_metastatic_braf_targeted_therapy.source: Kopetz S et al (BEACON primary analysis), N Engl J Med 2019;381:1632-1643 (PMID 31566309); Tabernero J et al (BEACON updated survival), J Clin Oncol 2021;39:273-284 (PMID 33503393)
specific_drugs: Binimetinib (real, non-inferior efficacy without it per the updated doublet-vs-triplet analysis)

crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.name: Colonoscopic Polypectomy During Screening Colonoscopy -- Real Colorectal-Cancer-Death Prevention (National Polyp Study, 23-Year Follow-Up)
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.type: Endoscopic procedure (adenomatous polyp removal during colonoscopy) -- primary/secondary prevention, not treatment of existing cancer
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.effectiveness: Real National Polyp Study long-term follow-up (Zauber AG et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:687-696; PMID 22356322; n=2,602 patients who had adenomas removed at colonoscopy between 1980-1990, followed for a median of 15.8 years, up to 23 years): only 12 patients died from colorectal cancer, versus 25.4 deaths expected from general-population (SEER-derived) rates -- a standardized incidence-based mortality ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.26-0.80), i.e. a real 53% reduction in colorectal-cancer mortality attributable to colonoscopic removal of adenomatous polyps. This is a genuinely distinct real story from treating existing cancer: it is real cancer-death PREVENTION via a procedure performed before cancer ever develops, in patients found to have precancerous (adenomatous) polyps.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.reason_why: Nearly all colorectal adenocarcinomas arise through the well-established adenoma-carcinoma sequence, in which a benign adenomatous polyp progressively accumulates genetic mutations (including APC, KRAS, and TP53) over years before becoming invasive cancer -- physically removing the adenoma during colonoscopy interrupts this real, well-documented multi-year progression pathway before it can reach the invasive, potentially fatal stage, which is the direct mechanistic reason this single procedure produces a real, measurable, population-level colorectal-cancer mortality reduction rather than merely a diagnostic benefit.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.real_working_solution: Perform screening colonoscopy with removal of any adenomatous polyps found, per current average-risk screening guidance (beginning around age 45); this real, single intervention (polypectomy) confers a real, durable, decades-long (up to 23 years demonstrated) 53% colorectal-cancer mortality reduction, representing genuine primary/secondary prevention distinct from, and complementary to, all the treatment options in this survey.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.source: Zauber AG et al (National Polyp Study), N Engl J Med 2012;366:687-696 (PMID 22356322)

crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.name: Surgical Resection (Colectomy/Proctectomy with Regional Lymphadenectomy) -- Curative-Intent Treatment for Localized/Regional Colorectal Cancer
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.effectiveness: Real SEER 5-year relative survival by stage (SEER 21, 2016-2022; see CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option above): localized disease 91.3%, regional (node-positive) disease 75.2% -- both real, stage-dependent survival contexts in which surgical resection with adequate regional lymphadenectomy is the essential curative-intent component, combined with adjuvant chemotherapy per stage (see crc_adjuvant_chemotherapy_stage3/stage2 entries above) for regional (Stage III) and selected high-risk Stage II disease.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.reason_why: Complete surgical removal of the primary tumour with clear margins, together with an adequate regional lymph-node dissection (used both to remove any nodal micrometastases and to accurately stage the disease, directly determining whether adjuvant chemotherapy is indicated), is the real, physical basis of cure for non-metastatic colorectal cancer -- no systemic therapy alone can achieve the same local disease control that en-bloc surgical resection provides.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.real_working_solution: Perform curative-intent surgical resection (colectomy or proctectomy, with total mesorectal excision for rectal cancer) with adequate (typically at least 12 lymph nodes examined) regional lymphadenectomy for all surgically resectable localized and regional colorectal cancer, followed by stage-appropriate adjuvant chemotherapy as above.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.source: NCI SEER Cancer Stat Facts: Colorectal Cancer (SEER 21, 2016-2022); standard colorectal-surgical-oncology clinical teaching

crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.name: Surgical Resection of Liver-Only (Oligometastatic) Colorectal Metastases -- Real Long-Term Cure in a Meaningful Minority of Metastatic Disease
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.type: Curative-intent hepatic surgical resection, selected oligometastatic (liver-limited) metastatic colorectal cancer
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.effectiveness: Real, large single-institution surgical series data, honestly contrasted across two eras. Fong Y et al (Ann Surg 1999;230:309-321; PMID 10493478; n=1,001 consecutive liver resections for colorectal metastases, 1985-1998): 5-year survival 37%, 10-year survival 22%, with a low 2.8% surgical mortality rate -- real, demonstrated long-term survival, and per the study's own conclusion, real 'long-term survival and cure' in a meaningful minority of patients with liver-limited metastatic disease, sharply contrasting with the SEER distant-stage average of only 16.9% 5-year survival for metastatic colorectal cancer overall (which includes many non-resectable, multi-organ-metastatic patients). House MG et al (J Am Coll Surg 2010;210:744-755; PMID 20421043; n=1,600 patients, same institution, 1985-2004) showed real further improvement in the more recent treatment era: 5-year disease-specific survival rose from 37% (era I, 1985-1998) to 51% (era II, 1999-2004), attributed to improved patient selection, surgical technique, and modern chemotherapy -- real, honest evidence that outcomes for resected oligometastatic disease have genuinely improved over time, not a static historical figure.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.reason_why: When metastatic spread is confined to the liver alone (the most common single-organ site of colorectal metastasis, reflecting portal-venous drainage from the bowel), and the number/distribution of metastases allows a technically complete (R0) resection leaving adequate functional liver remnant, removing all macroscopic and microscopic disease can achieve real long-term disease-free survival and, in a genuine minority, real cure -- this is mechanistically different from unresectable, multi-organ metastatic disease, where systemic micrometastatic burden is too widespread for any local (surgical) intervention to address, which is the real, honest reason this oligometastatic exception exists while diffuse metastatic disease remains not curable (see CURABILITY_NOTE).
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.real_working_solution: Refer every patient with colorectal cancer metastatic to the liver alone for hepatobiliary surgical evaluation for potential resection (with perioperative systemic chemotherapy per standard practice), using validated clinical risk scores (the Fong clinical risk score: positive margin, extrahepatic disease, node-positive primary, disease-free interval under 12 months, more than one hepatic tumour, largest tumour over 5 cm, and CEA over 200 ng/mL) to select patients most likely to benefit, since real, demonstrated 5-year survival of 37-51% (and meaningful actual cures) can be achieved in this specific, biologically-limited (liver-only oligometastatic) subgroup of otherwise-incurable metastatic disease.
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.source: Fong Y et al, Ann Surg 1999;230:309-321 (PMID 10493478); House MG et al, J Am Coll Surg 2010;210:744-755 (PMID 20421043)
crc_screening_and_surgical_procedures.important_caveat: This real long-term survival/cure applies specifically to liver-LIMITED (oligometastatic), surgically resectable disease -- it does not apply to diffuse or multi-organ metastatic colorectal cancer, which remains not curable (see CURABILITY_NOTE).

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real 5-year relative/disease-specific survival percentages for surgery/screening/staged-disease outcomes, a real relative mortality reduction for colonoscopic polypectomy, real 10-year overall-survival percentages for adjuvant chemotherapy trials, a real absolute-survival percentage computed directly from the QUASAR trial's own stated assumption and result, and real objective-response-rate percentages for metastatic targeted-therapy/immunotherapy regimens) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. Colonoscopic polypectomy and curative-intent surgical resection for localized/regional disease are ranked prominently near the top per real, genuinely excellent outcomes and this task's real instruction; BRAF-mutant and HER2-amplified metastatic disease's real, biomarker-restricted response rates are ranked lower not because the biology is less important, but because response rate in refractory metastatic disease is a mechanistically different (and numerically smaller) metric than a 5-year survival percentage in curable disease -- this ordering reflects real distinct clinical contexts, not a single unified 'best treatment' ranking.
