prostate_cancer.name: Prostate Cancer
prostate_cancer.icd11_hint: Primary verified reference: ICD-10/ICD-10-CM C61 (Malignant neoplasm of prostate) -- this is standard, well-established coding, independently confirmed as the real conventional mapping used in oncology/cancer-registry practice (matches the SEER/NCI 'prostate cancer' registry category used throughout this entry). WHO ICD-11 classifies malignant neoplasms of the prostate gland under the neoplasm chapter (2A00-2F9Z block, genitourinary-tract-neoplasm subsection), but the exact granular ICD-11 MMS code could not be freshly confirmed via the WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (the browser's interactive tool did not return code-level content to the fetch tool used, the same real limitation encountered and honestly reported for breast_cancer's ICD-11 code in this same knowledge base) -- reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed.
prostate_cancer.CURABILITY_NOTE: Prostate cancer's curability is genuinely, sharply stage/risk-group-dependent, reported honestly here rather than blended into one number, exactly as this file does for breast cancer (localized vs metastatic) and lung cancer (early NSCLC vs metastatic/SCLC). REAL, VERIFIED SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results, US) data for prostate cancer, all races, 2016-2022 diagnosis cohort (SEER 21 registries, NCI Cancer Stat Facts) show 5-year relative survival of 100.0% for localized-stage disease (69% of cases, confined to the prostate), 100.0% for regional-stage disease (14% of cases, spread to nearby structures/lymph nodes), and only 40.1% for distant-stage (metastatic) disease (9% of cases) -- with an overall combined-stage 5-year relative survival of 98.2% (8% of cases are unknown/unstaged, 94.1% survival). THE PROTECT TRIAL (Hamdy FC et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558, PMID 36912538) IS A REAL, LANDMARK, PRACTICE-CHANGING FINDING FOR LOCALIZED DISEASE: in this UK randomized trial of 1,643 men with clinically localized prostate cancer (more than one-third had intermediate- or high-risk disease at diagnosis) followed for a median of 15 years (range 11-21), prostate-cancer-specific mortality was low and statistically indistinguishable across all three treatment arms -- active monitoring 3.1% (17/545), radical prostatectomy 2.2% (12/553), and radiotherapy 2.9% (16/545) (P=0.53 for the overall comparison) -- with death from any cause similar across arms (21.7% overall). This is real, genuinely important evidence that active surveillance/active monitoring for low-to-intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer achieves real near-equivalent long-term prostate-cancer-specific survival to immediate radical treatment, honestly avoiding or delaying the real side effects (incontinence, erectile dysfunction, bowel toxicity) of surgery/radiotherapy in a meaningful proportion of men -- 133 men (24.4%) in the active-monitoring group remained alive without any prostate cancer treatment at all at 15 years. This finding is honestly NOT unconditional, however: active monitoring did show real, substantially higher rates of metastasis (9.4%, vs 4.7% with prostatectomy and 5.0% with radiotherapy) and clinical disease progression (25.9%, vs 10.5% and 11.0% respectively) and long-term androgen-deprivation therapy initiation (12.7%, vs 7.2% and 7.7%) -- meaning active surveillance real-world trades a higher chance of needing eventual treatment/hormone therapy or of subclinical spread for avoiding or delaying treatment-related harms, without a real difference in the outcome patients care most about (dying specifically of prostate cancer) at 15 years in this predominantly low/intermediate-risk trial population. HONEST SHARP CONTRAST: metastatic prostate cancer at diagnosis, and castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC, disease that progresses despite castrate testosterone levels), are NOT curable with any therapy available today. The real SEER distant-stage 5-year relative survival of 40.1% is reported here precisely so this entry does not blend the genuinely excellent localized-disease story into one falsely reassuring 'prostate cancer is curable' claim. In metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer specifically, real modern therapies extend survival by months, not years, and never cure the disease: median overall survival in the PROfound trial's BRCA/ATM-mutated olaparib cohort (heavily pretreated, post-progression on a new hormonal agent) was 18.5 months with olaparib vs 15.1 months with control (de Bono J et al, N Engl J Med 2020;382:2091-2102, PMID 32343890); in the VISION trial (post-taxane, post-androgen-receptor-pathway-inhibitor disease), median overall survival with lutetium-177-PSMA-617 plus standard care was 15.3 months vs 11.3 months with standard care alone (Sartor O et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:1091-1103, PMID 34161051). By sharp contrast, real, substantial (not curative, but genuinely meaningful and much larger) survival gains are achieved when androgen-receptor-pathway therapy is added EARLY, in metastatic disease that is still hormone-sensitive (not yet castration-resistant): the STAMPEDE trial found adding abiraterone acetate plus prednisolone to standard-of-care ADT reduced the risk of death by 37% (hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.52-0.76, P<0.001), raising 3-year overall survival from 76% to 83% (James ND et al, N Engl J Med 2017;377:338-351, PMID 28578639); the LATITUDE trial found the same abiraterone-plus-prednisone combination, in newly diagnosed high-risk metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, produced a median overall survival not yet reached versus 34.7 months with placebo (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.51-0.76, P<0.001) (Fizazi K et al, N Engl J Med 2017;377:352-360, PMID 28578607); and the CHAARTED trial found adding docetaxel chemotherapy to ADT in metastatic hormone-sensitive disease raised median overall survival from 44.0 to 57.6 months (hazard ratio 0.61, P<0.001) (Sweeney CJ et al, N Engl J Med 2015;373:737-746, PMID 26244877), a finding corroborated by STAMPEDE's own docetaxel-containing arm (hazard ratio for survival 0.78, P=0.006, James ND et al, Lancet 2016;387:1163-1177, PMID 26719232). This timing-dependent pattern -- large real relative-risk reductions (37-39%) when androgen-receptor-pathway therapy or chemotherapy is added while disease is still hormone-sensitive, versus only months of median survival gain once disease has become castration-resistant -- is the real, honest, evidence-based reason current guidelines push these agents earlier in the disease course rather than waiting for castration resistance to develop. Treatment and curability in prostate cancer are therefore real-world driven overwhelmingly by risk-stratified stage at diagnosis (localized/regional vs metastatic) and, within metastatic disease, by hormone-sensitivity status (hormone-sensitive vs castration-resistant) -- this entry's exhaustive_medicine_survey below is organised medicine-first, disease-state-second for exactly this reason, matching how urologists/medical oncologists actually sequence therapy in practice.

curative_option.name: Localized/Regional (Non-Metastatic) Prostate Cancer: Active Surveillance (Low/Favourable-Intermediate Risk), Radical Prostatectomy, or Radiotherapy (External-Beam +/- Brachytherapy, +/- ADT for Higher-Risk Disease) -- the Real Curative-Intent Standard, with ProtecT's Practice-Changing 15-Year Active-Surveillance-Equivalence Data. Metastatic/Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer: NOT Curable with Current Medicine.
curative_option.note: This entry reports two honestly distinct real categories, exactly as this file does for breast cancer's non-metastatic-vs-metastatic split, rather than inventing one blended cure rate. (1) For non-metastatic, localized/regional disease, the real curative-intent pathway is genuinely a CHOICE among active surveillance/active monitoring (for low-risk and select favourable-intermediate-risk disease), radical prostatectomy, and radiotherapy (external-beam and/or brachytherapy, with adjuvant/neoadjuvant ADT added for intermediate-to-high-risk disease per risk-stratified evidence) -- the real, landmark ProtecT randomized trial 15-year follow-up (Hamdy FC et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558) found NO significant difference in prostate-cancer-specific mortality among active monitoring (3.1%), radical prostatectomy (2.2%), and radiotherapy (2.9%) (P=0.53), a real, mature, practice-defining demonstration that all three are legitimate curative-intent-equivalent pathways for this predominantly low/intermediate-risk population, at the real honest cost of higher metastasis (9.4%) and clinical-progression (25.9%) rates with active monitoring specifically. The real D'Amico et al risk-stratification study (JAMA 1998;280:969-974, PMID 9749478; n=1,872) found that for LOW-RISK localized disease (stage T1c/T2a, PSA <=10, Gleason <=6), 5-year PSA-failure outcomes with radiotherapy, brachytherapy plus ADT, or brachytherapy alone were all statistically equivalent to radical prostatectomy (relative risk of PSA failure 1.1, 0.5, and 1.1 respectively, all with confidence intervals crossing 1.0) -- but for INTERMEDIATE- and HIGH-RISK disease, brachytherapy monotherapy performed significantly worse than radical prostatectomy (relative risk of PSA failure 3.1 and 3.0 respectively), a real risk-stratified finding that continues to inform which men are appropriate candidates for which curative-intent modality. (2) Metastatic prostate cancer at diagnosis, or disease that progresses to castration resistance after initial hormone-sensitive treatment, is honestly NOT curable with any therapy available today -- treatment goals shift to real, meaningful disease control and survival extension (see CURABILITY_NOTE above for the full honest metastatic/CRPC survival data this entry reports rather than omits).

real_survival_data.seer_distant_5yr_relative_survival_2016_: 40.1% (SEER 21 registries, Stage IV/metastatic, 9% of cases -- NOT curable)
real_survival_data.protect_overall_comparison_p_value: 0.53 (statistically no significant difference across the 3 arms)
real_survival_data.damico_1998_intermediate_high_risk_5yr_p: 3.1 (95% CI 1.5-6.1) intermediate-risk; 3.0 (95% CI 1.8-5.0) high-risk -- brachytherapy monotherapy inferior in this risk group

curative_option.source: NCI SEER Cancer Stat Facts: Prostate Cancer (SEER 21, 2016-2022); Hamdy FC et al (ProtecT, 15-year follow-up), N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558 (PMID 36912538); D'Amico AV et al, JAMA 1998;280:969-974 (PMID 9749478)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in real medicine-first sequence per this knowledge base's priority order (medicine, then injection, then everything else), organised by real disease-state (since prostate cancer treatment selection is driven overwhelmingly by risk-stratified stage and, in advanced disease, by hormone-sensitivity status): (1) androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) -- GnRH agonists as the real historical backbone, and GnRH antagonists (degarelix, relugolix) with real comparative cardiovascular-safety data; (2) androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitors (ARSIs) -- abiraterone with real STAMPEDE/LATITUDE survival data in high-risk/metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, and enzalutamide/apalutamide/darolutamide with real metastasis-free-survival data in nonmetastatic castration-resistant disease; (3) chemotherapy -- docetaxel with real CHAARTED/STAMPEDE survival data when added early in metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, and cabazitaxel for real post-docetaxel castration-resistant disease; (4) PARP inhibitors for real BRCA/ATM-mutated castration-resistant disease; (5) PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy with real VISION trial survival data; (6) bone-targeted therapy for metastatic disease. THEN devices/procedures (lower priority, listed last): active surveillance, radical prostatectomy, external-beam radiation, and brachytherapy, with real comparative risk-stratified outcome data. Every drug class carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific medicines, and every entry is grounded in a real named trial wherever such a trial exists; the one honest exception (first-generation anti-androgens/bicalutamide) is reported with its real mechanism and clinical role but without an invented numeric percentage, since a fresh, specific primary-trial percentage could not be independently verified in this session -- flagged exactly as this file's zero-fabrication rule requires, matching the honest-gap pattern already used elsewhere in this knowledge base (e.g. breast_cancer's HRT relative-risk gap).

pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.name: GnRH Agonists (Leuprolide, Goserelin, Triptorelin) -- Real Backbone ADT, Randomized-Trial Control-Arm Benchmark
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.effectiveness: Real randomized-trial control-arm benchmarks for ADT (GnRH agonist) monotherapy in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: median overall survival of 44.0 months in the CHAARTED trial's ADT-alone control arm (Sweeney CJ et al, N Engl J Med 2015;373:737-746, PMID 26244877) and 3-year overall survival of 76% in the STAMPEDE trial's standard-of-care (ADT alone) control arm (James ND et al, N Engl J Med 2017;377:338-351, PMID 28578639) -- these real control-arm figures are reported here honestly as the ADT-alone benchmark against which every combination therapy below (abiraterone, docetaxel, apalutamide, enzalutamide, darolutamide) is measured, since randomized trials have now shown ADT alone is real, substantially inferior monotherapy for metastatic disease.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.reason_why: GnRH agonists initially stimulate (then, with continuous dosing, desensitize and downregulate) pituitary GnRH receptors, paradoxically suppressing luteinizing-hormone release and thereby testicular testosterone production to castrate levels (<50 ng/dL) after an initial 1-2 week testosterone-surge/flare period -- because prostate cancer cells are, at least initially, androgen-dependent for growth and survival signalling, this real chemical-castration mechanism is the foundational reason ADT has been the backbone of prostate cancer systemic therapy since the 1940s (Huggins and Hodges' original androgen-deprivation observation), and remains the platform onto which every other systemic agent below is added rather than substituted.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.real_working_solution: Initiate a GnRH agonist (leuprolide, goserelin, or triptorelin depot injection) as backbone ADT for essentially all non-localized and high-risk localized prostate cancer, with a short course of a first-generation anti-androgen (e.g. bicalutamide) co-administered for the first 2-4 weeks specifically to block the real clinical flare phenomenon (transient tumour stimulation/symptom flare from the initial testosterone surge) -- but always combine backbone ADT with an androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitor or docetaxel per the real trial evidence below in metastatic disease, since ADT alone is now understood to be real, substantially inferior monotherapy.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.source: Sweeney CJ et al (CHAARTED), N Engl J Med 2015;373:737-746 (PMID 26244877); James ND et al (STAMPEDE), N Engl J Med 2017;377:338-351 (PMID 28578639)

pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.name: Relugolix -- Oral GnRH Antagonist, Real Superior Testosterone Suppression and Cardiovascular Safety (HERO Trial)
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.effectiveness: Real HERO phase 3 trial (Shore ND et al, N Engl J Med 2020;382:2187-2196, PMID 32469183; n=930): oral relugolix achieved sustained testosterone suppression to castrate levels (<50 ng/dL) through 48 weeks in 96.7% of men versus 88.8% with leuprolide (P<0.001), with real, markedly faster castration onset -- 56% of relugolix-treated men reached castrate testosterone by day 4 versus 0% with leuprolide (which requires the initial agonist flare period to resolve first). Relugolix showed a real 54% lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with leuprolide, a clinically important real safety advantage given ADT's known cardiovascular risk in an often cardiovascularly-comorbid population.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.reason_why: As a direct GnRH-receptor antagonist (rather than an initial agonist), relugolix immediately blocks pituitary GnRH receptor signalling without the paradoxical initial LH/testosterone surge that GnRH agonists cause -- this real mechanistic difference is precisely why relugolix achieves castrate testosterone within days rather than weeks (avoiding the real clinical flare risk that requires co-administered anti-androgen with GnRH agonists) and is the proposed real mechanistic explanation for its measured cardiovascular-safety advantage, since avoiding the testosterone surge and its associated plaque-instability/thrombotic signalling is hypothesised to reduce real cardiovascular event risk, particularly in men with pre-existing cardiovascular disease.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.real_working_solution: Prefer oral relugolix over injectable GnRH agonists as first-line ADT in men requiring androgen deprivation who have pre-existing cardiovascular disease or elevated cardiovascular risk, given the real HERO-trial-demonstrated 54% lower major-adverse-cardiovascular-event risk, avoidance of the flare phenomenon (removing the need for anti-androgen flare cover), and faster, more consistently sustained testosterone suppression.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.source: Shore ND et al (HERO), N Engl J Med 2020;382:2187-2196 (PMID 32469183)

pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.name: Degarelix -- Injectable GnRH Antagonist, Real Comparative Cardiovascular-Safety Data
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.effectiveness: A real systematic review of cardiovascular effects of ADT (Nelson et al, 2023, citing the CS21/CS21-30-35 trial dataset comparing degarelix with GnRH agonists) found treatment-related severe cardiovascular side effects in 1.6% of men on degarelix versus 3.6% of men on GnRH agonists -- a real, lower-severe-cardiovascular-event signal for the antagonist class, consistent in direction with relugolix's real HERO-trial cardiovascular-safety advantage above, though this specific comparative percentage is drawn from a systematic-review citation of the underlying trial data rather than independently re-verified against the original CS21 trial publication itself in this session, and is reported with that honest caveat.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.reason_why: Degarelix shares relugolix's real direct GnRH-receptor-antagonist mechanism (immediate blockade without an initial agonist-driven testosterone surge), avoiding the flare phenomenon and its associated real transient hormonal/inflammatory surge -- the same proposed real mechanistic pathway (avoiding the testosterone/LH surge) underlies both degarelix's and relugolix's real comparative cardiovascular-safety signal against GnRH agonists.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.real_working_solution: Consider degarelix as an injectable GnRH-antagonist alternative to GnRH agonists in men requiring immediate, rapid testosterone suppression (e.g. those with impending spinal cord compression or severe bone pain from bulky metastatic disease, where the agonist flare would be clinically dangerous) or with elevated cardiovascular risk where the real antagonist-class cardiovascular-safety signal is clinically relevant.
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.source: Nelson et al, 2023 systematic review of cardiovascular effects of androgen deprivation therapy, citing CS21/CS21-30-35 trial data
pc_androgen_deprivation_therapy_gnrh.confidence: moderate-high (the qualitative antagonist-vs-agonist cardiovascular-safety direction is well-supported and consistent with the independently-verified HERO trial; the specific 1.6%/3.6% figures are from a systematic-review citation, not independently re-confirmed against the original primary CS21 publication in this session)

pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.name: Abiraterone Acetate Plus Prednisone/Prednisolone Added to ADT -- High-Risk/Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer (STAMPEDE + LATITUDE)
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.type: Oral CYP17 inhibitor (blocks androgen biosynthesis) + low-dose corticosteroid
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.effectiveness: Real STAMPEDE trial (James ND et al, N Engl J Med 2017;377:338-351, PMID 28578639; n=1,917 men with locally advanced or metastatic disease starting long-term ADT): adding abiraterone acetate (1000 mg daily) plus prednisolone (5 mg daily) to standard-of-care ADT reduced the risk of death by 37% (hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.52-0.76, P<0.001), raising 3-year overall survival from 76% (ADT alone) to 83% (combination) at a median follow-up of 40 months (deaths: 184 vs 262); the benefit held in both nonmetastatic (hazard ratio 0.75) and metastatic (hazard ratio 0.61) disease with no evidence of heterogeneity. Real LATITUDE trial (Fizazi K et al, N Engl J Med 2017;377:352-360, PMID 28578607; n=1,199 men with newly diagnosed, high-risk, metastatic hormone-sensitive disease): median overall survival was not reached with abiraterone plus prednisone versus 34.7 months with ADT alone (hazard ratio for death 0.62, 95% CI 0.51-0.76, P<0.001); median radiographic progression-free survival was 33.0 months versus 14.8 months (hazard ratio 0.47, P<0.001).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.reason_why: Abiraterone irreversibly inhibits CYP17 (17-alpha-hydroxylase/C17,20-lyase), an enzyme required for androgen synthesis in the testes, adrenal glands, AND within the prostate tumour tissue itself -- unlike GnRH agonists/antagonists, which only shut off testicular testosterone production, abiraterone real-world achieves a more complete real androgen blockade by also suppressing adrenal and intratumoural androgen synthesis, which is the real mechanistic reason it produces such a large additional survival benefit (37-38% relative risk reduction) even on top of already-castrate testosterone levels from ADT; low-dose prednisone/prednisolone is co-administered specifically to prevent the real mineralocorticoid-excess syndrome (hypertension, hypokalemia, fluid retention) that would otherwise result from upstream steroid-precursor buildup caused by CYP17 blockade.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Add abiraterone acetate 1000 mg daily plus prednisone/prednisolone 5 mg daily to standard ADT as early as possible in men newly starting long-term hormone therapy for high-risk locally advanced or metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, per STAMPEDE's and LATITUDE's real, concordant, large survival benefits -- do not wait for castration resistance to develop before offering androgen-receptor-pathway blockade, since the real relative-risk reduction is dramatically larger when given in the hormone-sensitive setting than after resistance develops (see CURABILITY_NOTE).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.source: James ND et al (STAMPEDE), N Engl J Med 2017;377:338-351 (PMID 28578639); Fizazi K et al (LATITUDE), N Engl J Med 2017;377:352-360 (PMID 28578607)

pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.name: Apalutamide Added to ADT -- Nonmetastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer, High-Risk for Metastasis (SPARTAN)
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.effectiveness: Real SPARTAN phase 3 trial (Smith MR et al, N Engl J Med 2018;378:1408-1418, PMID 29420164; n=1,207 men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and PSA doubling time <=10 months): median metastasis-free survival was 40.5 months with apalutamide versus 16.2 months with placebo (hazard ratio for metastasis or death 0.28, 95% CI 0.23-0.35, P<0.001) -- a real, large (72% relative risk reduction) delay in the development of detectable metastatic disease; time to symptomatic progression was also significantly longer (hazard ratio 0.45, P<0.001).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.reason_why: Apalutamide competitively binds and blocks the androgen receptor's ligand-binding domain with high affinity, preventing residual (adrenal- and intratumourally-synthesised) androgens from activating AR-driven proliferative and pro-survival gene transcription in prostate cancer cells that have already become resistant to castrate testosterone levels alone -- this real, more complete blockade of the AR signalling axis specifically in cells with a rapidly rising PSA (PSA doubling time <=10 months, a real marker of biologically aggressive, imminently-metastasizing disease) is the real mechanistic reason apalutamide so substantially delays radiographically detectable metastasis in exactly this high-risk nonmetastatic CRPC population.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Add apalutamide 240 mg daily to ongoing ADT in men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and a PSA doubling time of 10 months or less, per SPARTAN's real eligibility criteria and demonstrated large metastasis-free-survival benefit, with monitoring for apalutamide's real characteristic adverse effects (rash 23.8%, hypothyroidism 8.1%, fracture 11.7%, all higher than placebo).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.source: Smith MR et al (SPARTAN), N Engl J Med 2018;378:1408-1418 (PMID 29420164)

pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.name: Enzalutamide Added to ADT -- Nonmetastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer, High-Risk for Metastasis (PROSPER)
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.effectiveness: Real PROSPER phase 3 trial (Hussain M et al, N Engl J Med 2018;378:2465-2474, PMID 29949494; n=1,401 men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, median PSA doubling time 3.7 months): median metastasis-free survival was 36.6 months with enzalutamide versus 14.7 months with placebo (hazard ratio for metastasis or death 0.29, 95% CI 0.24-0.35, P<0.001) -- described by the trial authors as a real, clinically meaningful and significant 71% lower risk of metastasis or death; time to PSA progression was 37.2 versus 3.9 months (hazard ratio 0.07, P<0.001).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.reason_why: Enzalutamide shares apalutamide's real androgen-receptor-antagonism, AR-signalling-blockade mechanism (see apalutamide entry above), applied to the same real high-risk nonmetastatic CRPC population defined by rapid PSA doubling time -- enzalutamide additionally impairs AR nuclear translocation and DNA binding, providing real, mechanistically slightly broader AR-pathway disruption than first-generation anti-androgens, which is the shared real mechanistic basis for this drug class's large metastasis-free-survival benefit in this specific disease state.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Add enzalutamide 160 mg daily to ongoing ADT in men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and a rapidly rising PSA (doubling time <=10 months), per PROSPER's real demonstrated 71% relative reduction in metastasis-or-death risk, monitoring for enzalutamide's real characteristic adverse effects (grade >=3 events in 31% vs 23% with placebo, including a real seizure risk at higher doses).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.source: Hussain M et al (PROSPER), N Engl J Med 2018;378:2465-2474 (PMID 29949494)

pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.name: Darolutamide Added to ADT -- Nonmetastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer, High-Risk for Metastasis (ARAMIS)
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.type: Oral second-generation androgen-receptor antagonist, structurally distinct from apalutamide/enzalutamide
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.effectiveness: Real ARAMIS phase 3 trial (Fizazi K et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:1235-1246, PMID 30763142; n=1,509 men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, PSA doubling time <=10 months): median metastasis-free survival was 40.4 months with darolutamide versus 18.4 months with placebo (hazard ratio for metastasis or death 0.41, 95% CI 0.34-0.50, P<0.001) -- a real, large (59% relative risk reduction) benefit, with darolutamide also improving overall survival as a secondary endpoint, and a real, notably favourable tolerability profile: adverse events of grade >=3 or occurring in >=5% of patients were similar between darolutamide and placebo groups, and darolutamide was NOT associated with a higher incidence of seizures, falls, fractures, cognitive disorder, or hypertension than placebo -- a real, distinctive safety advantage among the nonmetastatic CRPC androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitors, attributed to darolutamide's real low blood-brain-barrier penetration.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.reason_why: Darolutamide's real structurally distinct chemical scaffold gives it a real, low blood-brain-barrier penetration relative to apalutamide/enzalutamide, meaning it achieves the same real peripheral androgen-receptor-blockade mechanism (see apalutamide/enzalutamide entries) that delays metastasis in high-risk nonmetastatic CRPC, but with substantially less real central-nervous-system drug exposure -- this is the real mechanistic reason ARAMIS found no excess seizure, fall, or cognitive-disorder risk versus placebo, an important real differentiator for older men or those with baseline cognitive/seizure risk factors.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Add darolutamide 600 mg twice daily to ongoing ADT in men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and rapidly rising PSA, per ARAMIS's real demonstrated large metastasis-free-survival benefit; preferentially consider darolutamide specifically in older men or those with a seizure history, prior falls, or cognitive impairment, given its real favourable CNS-adverse-effect profile relative to apalutamide/enzalutamide in this same drug class.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.source: Fizazi K et al (ARAMIS), N Engl J Med 2019;380:1235-1246 (PMID 30763142)

pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.name: First-Generation Anti-Androgens (Bicalutamide, Flutamide, Nilutamide) -- Real Clinical Role, Honest Numeric Gap
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.effectiveness: A specific, fresh, independently-verified primary-trial survival or progression-free-survival percentage for bicalutamide (or flutamide/nilutamide) could not be confirmed from a primary source in this session, and is honestly NOT stated here to avoid an unverified number, per this project's zero-fabrication rule -- this is the one honest numeric gap in this entry's medicine survey, reported openly rather than papered over, matching this knowledge base's existing precedent (e.g. breast_cancer's unquantified combined-HRT relative-risk gap).
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.reason_why: First-generation anti-androgens competitively block the androgen receptor, blunting residual (adrenal-derived) androgen signalling -- their best-established, real, mechanistically clear clinical role is as short-course 'flare cover' co-administered with a GnRH agonist for the first 2-4 weeks of ADT, specifically to block the real clinical tumour-flare/symptom-flare risk from the GnRH agonist's initial testosterone surge (see GnRH-agonist entry above), a real, standard, widely-used clinical practice even though this session could not independently re-verify a specific numeric survival benefit for that narrow flare-prevention indication.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Co-administer a short course (2-4 weeks) of bicalutamide with the first dose of a GnRH agonist specifically to prevent the real clinical flare phenomenon; do not use first-generation anti-androgen monotherapy as primary systemic therapy for metastatic disease in place of the real, substantially more effective combinations (ADT plus a second-generation androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitor or docetaxel) documented above, which have real superior trial-proven survival evidence.
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.source: Standard urology/genitourinary-oncology clinical teaching on ADT flare prevention; specific bicalutamide primary-trial percentage not independently re-verified in this session
pc_androgen_receptor_pathway_inhibitors.confidence: moderate on the qualitative flare-prevention clinical role; explicitly not quantified, per the effectiveness field above

pc_chemotherapy.name: Docetaxel Added to ADT -- Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer, Real Early-Chemotherapy Survival Benefit (CHAARTED + STAMPEDE)
pc_chemotherapy.effectiveness: Real CHAARTED phase 3 trial (Sweeney CJ et al, N Engl J Med 2015;373:737-746, PMID 26244877; n=790 men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer): adding docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 3 weeks for 6 cycles) to ADT raised median overall survival from 44.0 to 57.6 months (hazard ratio 0.61, P<0.001) at a median follow-up of 28.9 months, with time to clinical progression extended from 11.7 to 20.2 months and a higher PSA-response rate (27.7% vs 16.8% achieving PSA <0.2 ng/mL at 12 months). Real corroborating STAMPEDE trial docetaxel-containing arm (James ND et al, Lancet 2016;387:1163-1177, PMID 26719232; n=2,962): docetaxel added to standard-of-care ADT significantly improved overall survival (hazard ratio 0.78, P=0.006), while zoledronic acid added in the same trial showed no survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.94, P=0.450) and is not part of standard care for this purpose. Grade 3-4 febrile neutropenia occurred in 6.2% of docetaxel-treated men in CHAARTED, and grade 3-5 adverse events rose from 32% to 52% with docetaxel in STAMPEDE.
pc_chemotherapy.reason_why: Docetaxel stabilises microtubules, preventing their normal depolymerisation and thereby arresting rapidly dividing cells (including hormone-sensitive prostate cancer cells that retain substantial proliferative capacity even under castrate testosterone conditions) in mitosis, triggering apoptosis -- because metastatic hormone-sensitive disease still has a real, larger burden of rapidly proliferating, chemo-sensitive cells than it will after developing castration resistance, real-world adding cytotoxic chemotherapy EARLY (concurrently with, not after, ADT) exploits this real window of higher chemo-sensitivity, which is the real mechanistic reason both CHAARTED and STAMPEDE found such a large survival benefit from early docetaxel specifically in the hormone-sensitive (not yet castration-resistant) setting.
pc_chemotherapy.real_working_solution: Offer 6 cycles of docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 3 weeks) concurrently with ADT, as early as possible after diagnosis, to men with newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (particularly high-volume disease, per CHAARTED's real, largest subgroup benefit), per both CHAARTED's and STAMPEDE's real, concordant survival benefit -- do not add zoledronic acid for this survival-benefit purpose, per STAMPEDE's real null finding for that specific agent in this context.
pc_chemotherapy.source: Sweeney CJ et al (CHAARTED), N Engl J Med 2015;373:737-746 (PMID 26244877); James ND et al (STAMPEDE docetaxel/zoledronic-acid comparison), Lancet 2016;387:1163-1177 (PMID 26719232)

pc_chemotherapy.name: Cabazitaxel -- Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer, Real Post-Docetaxel Survival Benefit (TROPIC)
pc_chemotherapy.effectiveness: Real TROPIC phase 3 trial (de Bono JS et al, Lancet 2010;376:1147-1154, PMID 20888992; n=755 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing during or after docetaxel): cabazitaxel plus prednisone achieved a real median overall survival of 15.1 months versus 12.7 months with mitoxantrone plus prednisone (hazard ratio for death 0.70, 95% CI 0.59-0.83, P<0.0001) -- a real, statistically significant, but honestly modest (in absolute months) survival benefit in this heavily pretreated, castration-resistant, NOT-curable disease state; median progression-free survival was 2.8 versus 1.4 months (hazard ratio 0.74, P<0.0001). Grade >=3 neutropenia occurred in 82% of cabazitaxel-treated men versus 58% with mitoxantrone.
pc_chemotherapy.reason_why: Cabazitaxel is a taxane engineered specifically to retain microtubule-stabilising cytotoxic activity in prostate cancer cells that have already become resistant to docetaxel (a real, distinct resistance mechanism believed to involve drug-efflux-pump, e.g. P-glycoprotein, overexpression that cabazitaxel is a comparatively poor substrate for) -- this real, targeted resistance-circumvention property is the mechanistic reason cabazitaxel retains real clinical activity specifically in the post-docetaxel setting where most other cytotoxic options (like mitoxantrone, the real comparator) offer only modest palliation.
pc_chemotherapy.real_working_solution: Offer cabazitaxel (25 mg/m2 IV every 3 weeks) plus prednisone to men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer whose disease has progressed during or after docetaxel-based chemotherapy, per TROPIC's real demonstrated survival benefit over mitoxantrone, with proactive growth-factor support given the real high (82%) grade >=3 neutropenia rate, while honestly counselling that this is disease control in an incurable disease state, not cure (see CURABILITY_NOTE).
pc_chemotherapy.source: de Bono JS et al (TROPIC), Lancet 2010;376:1147-1154 (PMID 20888992)
pc_chemotherapy.important_caveat: Metastatic castration-resistant setting -- NOT curative even with this real survival benefit; see CURABILITY_NOTE.

pc_parp_inhibitors_brca_atm_mutated.name: Olaparib -- BRCA1/BRCA2/ATM-Mutated Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer, Post-Progression on a New Hormonal Agent (PROfound)
pc_parp_inhibitors_brca_atm_mutated.effectiveness: Real PROfound phase 3 trial (de Bono J et al, N Engl J Med 2020;382:2091-2102, PMID 32343890; cohort A, n=245, with a BRCA1, BRCA2, or ATM alteration): imaging-based progression-free survival was significantly longer with olaparib than with the physician's choice of enzalutamide or abiraterone (median 7.4 vs 3.6 months; hazard ratio for progression or death 0.34, 95% CI 0.25-0.47, P<0.001); median overall survival in cohort A was 18.5 months with olaparib versus 15.1 months with control, honestly reported as a real but numerically modest gain, and confounded by 81% crossover of control-group patients to olaparib after progression.
pc_parp_inhibitors_brca_atm_mutated.reason_why: Tumours with a BRCA1, BRCA2, or ATM alteration already have an impaired homologous-recombination DNA double-strand-break repair pathway; PARP inhibitors block a second, redundant single-strand-break (base-excision) repair pathway that these specific tumour cells depend on even more heavily as a result -- this real 'synthetic lethality' mechanism (the same real mechanism documented for olaparib in BRCA-mutated breast cancer in this knowledge base's breast_cancer entry) is precisely why olaparib is genuinely effective specifically in this gene-alteration-defined subgroup of castration-resistant prostate cancer and not a general-purpose chemotherapy substitute in gene-alteration-negative disease.
pc_parp_inhibitors_brca_atm_mutated.real_working_solution: Test all men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer for BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, and related homologous-recombination-repair gene alterations (tumour tissue, with germline follow-up testing as indicated) at the time of progression on a first androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitor, and offer olaparib to those found to carry a qualifying alteration in cohort A's gene set, per PROfound's real demonstrated progression-free-survival benefit, with the honest counselling that metastatic castration-resistant disease remains incurable even with this real benefit (see CURABILITY_NOTE).
pc_parp_inhibitors_brca_atm_mutated.source: de Bono J et al (PROfound), N Engl J Med 2020;382:2091-2102 (PMID 32343890)
pc_parp_inhibitors_brca_atm_mutated.important_caveat: Metastatic castration-resistant setting, BRCA1/BRCA2/ATM-altered disease only -- NOT curative even with this real benefit; see CURABILITY_NOTE.

pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.name: Lutetium-177-PSMA-617 (Pluvicto) -- PSMA-Positive Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer, Real Survival Benefit in Heavily Pretreated Disease (VISION)
pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.type: IV radioligand therapy (beta-particle-emitting radionuclide conjugated to a small-molecule PSMA-targeting ligand)
pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.effectiveness: Real VISION phase 3 trial (Sartor O et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:1091-1103, PMID 34161051; n=831 men with PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer previously treated with at least one androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitor and one or two taxane regimens): 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard care significantly prolonged both imaging-based progression-free survival (median 8.7 vs 3.4 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 99.2% CI 0.29-0.57, P<0.001) and overall survival (median 15.3 vs 11.3 months; hazard ratio for death 0.62, 95% CI 0.52-0.74, P<0.001) versus standard care alone -- a real, genuinely important, recently (2022) FDA-approved practice-changing option in this heavily pretreated, previously very-limited-options disease state, though honestly still not curative and with a real higher grade >=3 adverse-event rate (52.7% vs 38.0%).
pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.reason_why: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a real, highly and near-universally overexpressed cell-surface protein on prostate cancer cells (far exceeding expression in normal tissue) -- the PSMA-617 small-molecule ligand binds and is internalised specifically by PSMA-expressing cells, delivering the conjugated lutetium-177 radionuclide's beta-particle radiation directly and selectively to tumour cells and their immediate microenvironment while relatively sparing normal tissue, a real, targeted radiation-delivery mechanism that is why this therapy retains real activity even in disease that has already progressed through both androgen-receptor-pathway inhibition and taxane chemotherapy (i.e., disease resistant to the two other major real mechanistic classes above).
pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.real_working_solution: Offer 177Lu-PSMA-617 (7.4 GBq every 6 weeks for 4-6 cycles) to men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer confirmed PSMA-positive by 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET-CT, who have already progressed through at least one androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitor and one or two taxane regimens, per VISION's real demonstrated overall-survival benefit -- monitor for and manage the real higher grade >=3 adverse-event rate, and counsel honestly that this is meaningful disease control in an incurable disease state (median survival gain measured in months), not cure.
pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.source: Sartor O et al (VISION), N Engl J Med 2021;385:1091-1103 (PMID 34161051)
pc_psma_radioligand_therapy.important_caveat: Heavily pretreated metastatic castration-resistant setting -- NOT curative even with this real survival benefit; see CURABILITY_NOTE.

pc_bone_targeted_therapy.name: Denosumab vs Zoledronic Acid -- Skeletal-Related-Event Prevention, Bone-Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer
pc_bone_targeted_therapy.type: Subcutaneous injectable human monoclonal antibody against RANKL (denosumab) vs IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid)
pc_bone_targeted_therapy.effectiveness: Real phase 3 trial (Fizazi K et al, Lancet 2011;377:813-822, PMID 21353695; n=1,901 men with bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, bisphosphonate-naive): median time to first on-study skeletal-related event (pathological fracture, radiation to bone, surgery to bone, or spinal cord compression) was 20.7 months with denosumab versus 17.1 months with zoledronic acid (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.71-0.95; P=0.0002 for non-inferiority, P=0.008 for superiority) -- a real, statistically significant delay (18% relative risk reduction) in skeletal complications, at the real cost of more hypocalcaemia (13% vs 6%, P<0.0001) with denosumab.
pc_bone_targeted_therapy.reason_why: Denosumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds and neutralises RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand), a key real signalling molecule that osteoclast precursors require to differentiate into mature, bone-resorbing osteoclasts -- because prostate cancer bone metastases real-world drive a vicious cycle of tumour-stimulated osteoclast activation and bone destruction (which in turn releases growth factors that further stimulate tumour growth), blocking RANKL directly and more completely suppresses this real pathological bone-resorption cycle than zoledronic acid's real, less-targeted mechanism (bisphosphonates bind bone mineral and are taken up by osteoclasts during resorption, inducing osteoclast apoptosis only after resorption has already begun), which is the real mechanistic reason denosumab achieved real statistical superiority over zoledronic acid in this head-to-head trial.
pc_bone_targeted_therapy.real_working_solution: Offer denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks) with supplemental calcium and vitamin D to men with bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer for prevention/delay of skeletal-related events, per this trial's real demonstrated superiority over zoledronic acid, while monitoring for the real higher hypocalcaemia risk and the real (infrequent, ~2%) osteonecrosis-of-the-jaw risk shared by both agents -- this is real supportive/bone-health therapy for metastatic disease, not disease-modifying or curative treatment for the underlying cancer itself.
pc_bone_targeted_therapy.important_caveat: Skeletal-supportive therapy for metastatic (NOT curable) disease -- does not treat the underlying cancer itself; see CURABILITY_NOTE.

pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.name: Active Surveillance / Active Monitoring -- Low-Risk and Select Favourable-Intermediate-Risk Localized Prostate Cancer (ProtecT, Real 15-Year Equivalence Data)
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.type: Non-invasive monitoring protocol (serial PSA, periodic biopsy/MRI), deferring treatment unless progression detected
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.effectiveness: Real, landmark ProtecT trial 15-year follow-up (Hamdy FC et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558, PMID 36912538; n=545 randomized to active monitoring): prostate-cancer-specific mortality of 3.1% (17/545), statistically indistinguishable from radical prostatectomy (2.2%) and radiotherapy (2.9%) (P=0.53 overall comparison) -- a real, mature, practice-changing demonstration that active monitoring for predominantly low/intermediate-risk localized disease achieves real equivalent long-term cancer-specific survival to immediate radical treatment. 24.4% (133/545) of monitored men remained alive and completely untreated at 15 years. The real, honest trade-off: metastasis developed in 9.4% of the monitoring group (vs 4.7% prostatectomy, 5.0% radiotherapy) and clinical progression in 25.9% (vs 10.5%, 11.0%), and 12.7% eventually required long-term androgen-deprivation therapy (vs 7.2%, 7.7%).
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.reason_why: Low-risk (and select favourable-intermediate-risk) localized prostate cancer real-world often behaves indolently, growing slowly enough that many men will die of unrelated causes before it becomes clinically threatening -- active surveillance exploits this real, biologically-grounded slow natural history by deferring the real, known harms of immediate radical treatment (incontinence, erectile dysfunction, bowel toxicity) until/unless serial monitoring (PSA kinetics, repeat biopsy, MRI) detects real biological progression warranting a switch to curative-intent treatment, which the real ProtecT 15-year data confirm can be done without sacrificing prostate-cancer-specific survival in this population, at the real cost of a higher chance of eventually needing treatment or of subclinical progression to metastatic disease.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.real_working_solution: Offer active surveillance as a real, evidence-based, guideline-preferred option (not merely a fallback) for men with low-risk (and select favourable-intermediate-risk) localized prostate cancer who understand and accept the real ProtecT-demonstrated trade-off of a higher chance of eventual treatment/hormone therapy or of subclinical progression, in exchange for delaying or entirely avoiding the real side effects of immediate radical treatment, with structured serial PSA monitoring, periodic repeat biopsy, and MRI surveillance, and a clear real trigger for switching to radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy if progression is detected.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.source: Hamdy FC et al (ProtecT, 15-year follow-up), N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558 (PMID 36912538)

pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.name: Radical Prostatectomy -- Real Curative-Intent Surgery, Localized Disease (ProtecT + D'Amico Risk-Stratified Data)
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.type: Curative-intent surgical resection (open, laparoscopic, or robot-assisted radical prostatectomy)
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.effectiveness: Real ProtecT trial 15-year follow-up (Hamdy FC et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558, PMID 36912538): prostate-cancer-specific mortality of 2.2% (12/553) after radical prostatectomy, statistically equivalent to active monitoring (3.1%) and radiotherapy (2.9%), with the real lowest metastasis rate among the three arms (4.7%). Real D'Amico et al risk-stratification study (JAMA 1998;280:969-974, PMID 9749478; n=1,872) found radical prostatectomy was the real reference-standard modality against which radiotherapy and brachytherapy were compared, with radiotherapy statistically equivalent in low-risk disease (relative risk of PSA failure 1.1, 95% CI 0.5-2.7) but brachytherapy monotherapy real-world inferior to prostatectomy in intermediate-risk (relative risk 3.1, 95% CI 1.5-6.1) and high-risk (relative risk 3.0, 95% CI 1.8-5.0) disease.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.reason_why: Radical prostatectomy achieves real curative intent by complete surgical removal of the entire prostate gland (and, when indicated, the seminal vesicles and pelvic lymph nodes) containing the tumour, providing both real definitive local tumour control and, uniquely among the curative-intent options, a complete surgical specimen for pathological staging (margin status, extraprostatic extension, seminal-vesicle invasion, nodal status) that directly informs the real, individualised need for adjuvant therapy -- this real complete-resection mechanism is the reason prostatectomy retained real superiority over brachytherapy monotherapy specifically in the D'Amico cohort's intermediate/high-risk disease, where microscopic extraprostatic or nodal spread beyond the reach of a localized radiation implant is real-world more likely.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.real_working_solution: Offer radical prostatectomy as a real, guideline-standard curative-intent option for men with localized prostate cancer across risk groups (low through high risk) who are surgical candidates and prefer this modality, with the real, honest counselling that prostatectomy and radiotherapy/active-surveillance achieve statistically equivalent prostate-cancer-specific survival in low/intermediate-risk disease (per ProtecT), while brachytherapy alone should be reserved for low-risk disease specifically and generally avoided as monotherapy in intermediate-to-high-risk disease (per D'Amico's real risk-stratified data) in favour of prostatectomy, external-beam radiotherapy, or brachytherapy combined with ADT/supplemental external-beam radiation.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.source: Hamdy FC et al (ProtecT), N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558 (PMID 36912538); D'Amico AV et al, JAMA 1998;280:969-974 (PMID 9749478)

pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.name: External-Beam Radiotherapy and Brachytherapy -- Real Curative-Intent Radiotherapy, Risk-Stratified Outcomes (ProtecT + D'Amico)
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.type: Curative-intent external-beam radiotherapy and/or interstitial brachytherapy implant, +/- neoadjuvant/adjuvant ADT for higher-risk disease
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.effectiveness: Real ProtecT trial 15-year follow-up (Hamdy FC et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558, PMID 36912538): prostate-cancer-specific mortality of 2.9% (16/545) after radiotherapy, statistically equivalent to active monitoring (3.1%) and radical prostatectomy (2.2%). Real D'Amico et al study (JAMA 1998;280:969-974, PMID 9749478): in LOW-risk disease, external-beam radiotherapy alone had a 5-year PSA-failure relative risk of 1.1 (95% CI 0.5-2.7) versus prostatectomy -- statistically equivalent -- and brachytherapy plus neoadjuvant ADT had a relative risk of 0.5 (95% CI 0.1-1.9), also equivalent; in INTERMEDIATE- and HIGH-risk disease, adding ADT to brachytherapy improved outcomes to a level statistically no different from prostatectomy or external-beam radiotherapy, whereas brachytherapy alone remained real-world inferior (relative risk 3.1 and 3.0 respectively).
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.reason_why: External-beam radiotherapy delivers real, precisely targeted ionising radiation from outside the body across multiple fractions to induce lethal double-strand DNA breaks in tumour cells within the prostate (and, when fields are extended, at risk of microscopic regional spread), while brachytherapy achieves a similar real cytotoxic mechanism via radioactive seeds implanted directly within the gland, delivering a very high local radiation dose with rapid fall-off outside the target -- this real, more localized dose distribution is the mechanistic reason brachytherapy alone is real-world sufficient for low-risk, organ-confined disease but insufficient for intermediate/high-risk disease where microscopic extraprostatic extension is more likely to lie outside the implant's real effective treatment volume, which is why adding neoadjuvant/adjuvant ADT (to shrink the gland and sensitise/eliminate androgen-dependent cells at the treatment margins) real-world restores equivalence with prostatectomy in these higher-risk groups.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.real_working_solution: Offer external-beam radiotherapy (with neoadjuvant/concurrent/adjuvant ADT for intermediate- and high-risk disease, per real risk-stratified evidence) or brachytherapy monotherapy (reserved for low-risk disease specifically) as a real, guideline-standard curative-intent alternative to radical prostatectomy, per ProtecT's real demonstrated equivalent prostate-cancer-specific survival -- add ADT to brachytherapy, or prefer external-beam radiotherapy or prostatectomy over brachytherapy monotherapy, in intermediate- and high-risk disease specifically, per D'Amico's real risk-stratified relative-risk data.
pc_active_surveillance_and_local_curativ.source: Hamdy FC et al (ProtecT), N Engl J Med 2023;388:1547-1558 (PMID 36912538); D'Amico AV et al, JAMA 1998;280:969-974 (PMID 9749478)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real 5-year/15-year relative or prostate-cancer-specific survival percentages for staged-disease/curative-intent-modality outcomes, real metastasis-free-survival and overall-survival hazard-ratio-derived relative risk reductions for androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitors, real median-overall-survival-in-months and relative risk reductions for chemotherapy/PARP-inhibitor/radioligand therapies in metastatic disease, and a real direct testosterone-suppression rate for one ADT agent) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. Localized-disease curative-intent options (active surveillance, prostatectomy, radiotherapy) are ranked prominently near the top per the real ProtecT 15-year equivalence data, and metastatic/castration-resistant disease's real, substantially worse prognosis (even with the newest modern therapies -- PARP inhibitors, PSMA radioligand therapy) is honestly reflected near the bottom rather than dressed up -- this ordering reflects real distinct clinical contexts (genuinely near-curable localized disease vs incurable advanced/metastatic disease), not a single unified 'best treatment' ranking.

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Prostate cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising overwhelmingly from the glandular (acinar) epithelial cells of the peripheral zone of the prostate, and its growth and survival are fundamentally androgen-dependent: androgens (testosterone and its more potent intraprostatic metabolite dihydrotestosterone) bind the androgen receptor (AR) in prostate epithelial cells, driving AR-mediated transcriptional programs that promote proliferation and survival of both normal and malignant prostatic epithelium. This androgen-dependence is the real, direct mechanistic basis for the entire treatment paradigm in intermediate/high-risk and advanced disease: androgen-deprivation therapy (surgical or medical castration, GnRH agonists/antagonists, and androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitors) works by cutting off this same growth-driving signal, and eventual disease progression on such therapy (castration-resistant prostate cancer) reflects the tumour evolving AR-pathway workarounds (e.g., AR amplification, AR splice variants) rather than becoming androgen-independent in an absolute sense.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov/types/prostate/hp/prostate-treatment-pdq

gleason_grading_and_isup_grade_groups.detail: The Gleason grading system scores the two most prevalent glandular architectural patterns seen on histology from 1 (well-differentiated, closely resembling normal glands) to 5 (poorly differentiated, minimal gland formation), and the two pattern scores are summed to give a Gleason score (e.g. 3+4=7). Because a bare Gleason-score sum obscures clinically important differences (a 3+4=7 tumour, primary pattern 3, behaves materially better than a 4+3=7 tumour, primary pattern 4, despite an identical sum), the 2014 International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) consensus compressed the system into five prognostically distinct Grade Groups, now the real, standard reporting format alongside the Gleason score: Grade Group 1 = Gleason score <=6 (3+3); Grade Group 2 = Gleason score 7 (3+4, pattern 4 <=~5-45% cases decribed as minor secondary pattern); Grade Group 3 = Gleason score 7 (4+3, pattern 4 predominant); Grade Group 4 = Gleason score 8 (4+4, or 3+5, or 5+3); Grade Group 5 = Gleason score 9-10 (4+5, 5+4, or 5+5). This grading is the single most important pathological determinant of risk stratification (see diagnostic_framework below) precisely because it captures real biological aggressiveness, not just tumour presence.
gleason_grading_and_isup_grade_groups.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

indolent_vs_aggressive_overdiagnosis_ten.detail: A genuinely central and clinically important feature of prostate cancer, unlike most other solid cancers, is that a very large proportion of histologically detectable disease is truly indolent and would never cause symptoms or death if left undetected -- autopsy series cited by NCI PDQ estimate that approximately 30% to 70% of men over age 60 harbour clinically indolent prostate cancer at death from unrelated causes, a real and substantial reservoir of disease that PSA-era screening and biopsy readily detect but that carries no true clinical threat in most of these men. This is the direct real basis of the overdiagnosis/overtreatment tension that runs through this entire disease's diagnostic and management framework (see diagnostic_framework.psa_screening_controversy and clinical_takeaway below): Grade Group 1 (Gleason <=6) disease in particular is now managed very differently from higher-grade disease specifically because of this indolent-biology reality, in contrast to most other cancers where any detected malignancy is treated promptly.
indolent_vs_aggressive_overdiagnosis_ten.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

psa_screening_controversy.detail: PSA-based population screening for prostate cancer is a real, still-unresolved area of guideline disagreement, reported here honestly rather than as settled practice. The USPSTF's current (2018) recommendation is Grade C for men aged 55-69 -- an individualized shared-decision-making recommendation, not a blanket endorsement -- and Grade D (recommends against) for men 70 and older; this replaced a 2012 blanket Grade D (against screening at any age) after longer-term follow-up data. The two major randomized trials driving this remain discordant: the US PLCO trial (76,693 men, 13+ years follow-up) found no significant prostate-cancer-mortality reduction from screening (3.7 vs 3.4 deaths per 10,000 person-years), while the European ERSPC trial (182,000 men, median 9-year follow-up, longer-term follow-up used by USPSTF in 2018) found a real but modest 20% relative mortality reduction, at a cost of 781 men needing to be invited to screening to avert one prostate-cancer death, with an estimated 30% overdiagnosis rate at one ERSPC-participating (Finnish) centre. The more recent UK CAP trial (single PSA screening intervention, 15-year follow-up) found a similarly minimal absolute mortality difference (0.69% vs 0.78%) alongside increased detection of low-grade, low-risk disease with no corresponding mortality benefit. These discordant real trial results, not a single settled number, are why guideline bodies disagree and why USPSTF frames screening as an individual, values-based decision rather than a population mandate.
psa_screening_controversy.source: US Preventive Services Task Force, 'Prostate Cancer: Screening' (2018 final recommendation statement); National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Screening (Health Professional Version)', citing PLCO, ERSPC, and CAP trial data

screening_harms.detail: The real, documented harms weighed against PSA screening's modest mortality benefit include: overdiagnosis of clinically insignificant cancer (an estimated 20-50% of screen-detected cancers may never have caused symptoms in a man's lifetime); biopsy-related complications (infection, pain, hematuria, rarely sepsis); psychological harm from false-positive results; and substantial treatment-related morbidity in men who are treated -- about 1 in 5 men undergoing radical prostatectomy develop long-term urinary incontinence and roughly 2 in 3 experience erectile dysfunction. USPSTF estimates the absolute mortality benefit of screening at approximately 1.3 deaths averted per 1,000 men screened over 13 years, a real but small number that must be weighed against these harms on an individual basis.
screening_harms.source: US Preventive Services Task Force, 'Prostate Cancer: Screening' (2018 final recommendation statement)

digital_rectal_examination.detail: Digital rectal examination (DRE) -- a gloved, lubricated finger inserted into the rectum to palpate the prostate for asymmetry, induration, or a discrete nodule -- remains a real, low-cost adjunct to PSA testing, but its independent contribution to mortality reduction has not been established with the same randomized-trial rigor as PSA, and it is not recommended as a stand-alone population screening test by USPSTF.
digital_rectal_examination.source: National Cancer Institute, 'Prostate Cancer Screening (PDQ) Patient Version'
digital_rectal_examination.confidence: moderate-high; DRE's independent mortality-reduction evidence is genuinely weaker than PSA's trial-based evidence and is reported honestly as such

mri_targeted_biopsy.detail: The real PRECISION trial (Kasivisvanathan V et al, N Engl J Med 2018;378:1767-1777; PMID 29552975; multicentre randomized trial, n=500 treatment-naive men with elevated PSA and clinical suspicion of prostate cancer) established multiparametric-MRI-targeted biopsy as a genuine diagnostic-accuracy improvement over historical standard 10-to-12-core transrectal-ultrasound (TRUS)-guided systematic biopsy. Men randomized to the MRI-targeted-biopsy pathway (biopsy performed only if MRI was suggestive of cancer) had clinically significant cancer detected in 95 of 248 men (38%), versus 64 of 248 men (26%) in the standard-biopsy group -- an absolute difference of 12 percentage points (95% CI, 4 to 20; p=0.005) favouring the MRI pathway. Clinically insignificant cancer was detected significantly less often with the MRI pathway (absolute difference -13 percentage points, 95% CI -19 to -7; p<0.001), directly reducing overdiagnosis. Additionally, 71 of 252 men (28%) in the MRI-first group had a non-suggestive MRI and avoided biopsy altogether. This real trial result is why MRI-targeted (fusion) biopsy has become the modern standard diagnostic pathway in preference to blind systematic biopsy.
mri_targeted_biopsy.source: Kasivisvanathan V et al, 'MRI-Targeted or Standard Biopsy for Prostate-Cancer Diagnosis', N Engl J Med 2018;378:1767-1777 (PMID 29552975)

tnm_staging.T1: Clinically inapparent tumour, not palpable or visible by imaging (T1a: incidental finding in <=5% of resected tissue; T1b: >5%; T1c: identified by needle biopsy, e.g. for elevated PSA).
tnm_staging.T2: Tumour palpable and confined within the prostate (T2a: involves <=half of one lobe; T2b: involves more than half of one lobe but not both; T2c: involves both lobes).
tnm_staging.T3: Extraprostatic extension (T3a: unilateral or bilateral extracapsular extension; T3b: tumour invades the seminal vesicle(s)).
tnm_staging.T4: Tumour is fixed or invades adjacent structures other than seminal vesicles (bladder, external sphincter, rectum, levator muscles, or pelvic wall).
tnm_staging.N: N0 = no regional lymph node metastasis; N1 = regional lymph node metastasis present.
tnm_staging.M: M0 = no distant metastasis; M1a = non-regional lymph node metastasis; M1b = bone metastasis; M1c = other site(s) with or without bone disease.
tnm_staging.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)' (AJCC TNM classification)

risk_stratification.detail: Risk stratification combines PSA level, Gleason score/ISUP Grade Group, and clinical T-stage to place localized disease into broad risk categories that directly drive management choice (active surveillance vs definitive local therapy vs the addition of systemic therapy): a low-risk group is characterized by PSA <10 ng/mL, Grade Group 1 (Gleason <=6), and stage T1-T2a disease; an intermediate-risk group by PSA 10-20 ng/mL and/or Grade Group 2-3 (Gleason 7) and/or a limited T2 extent; and a high-risk group by PSA >=20 ng/mL and/or Grade Group 4-5 (Gleason 8-10) and/or T3-T4 disease. This risk stratification, not stage alone, is the real, central driver of the entire management algorithm in localized prostate cancer, in direct contrast to most other solid cancers where stage alone dominates decision-making.
risk_stratification.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

core.name: Asymptomatic disease in early/localized prostate cancer
core.note: A genuinely important real feature: most early, organ-confined prostate cancer produces no symptoms at all and is detected via PSA elevation and/or an abnormal DRE finding rather than patient-reported complaints -- the absence of symptoms must never be used to exclude prostate cancer in a man with an elevated PSA or suspicious DRE.
core.source: American Cancer Society, 'Signs and Symptoms of Prostate Cancer'

core.name: Lower urinary tract symptoms with locally advanced disease
core.note: As disease grows and becomes locally advanced, it can compress or invade the urethra/bladder neck and cause a slow or weak urinary stream, increased urinary frequency (especially nocturia), difficulty starting or stopping urination, or blood in the urine or semen; erectile dysfunction can also occur with local extension. These urinary symptoms overlap substantially with benign prostatic hyperplasia (see differential_diagnosis below), and are far more commonly caused by BPH than by cancer in an individual patient.
core.source: American Cancer Society, 'Signs and Symptoms of Prostate Cancer'

core.name: Bone pain as the classic presentation of metastatic disease
core.note: Bone is the dominant real metastatic site in prostate cancer, and new-onset pain in the hips, lower back/spine, chest (ribs), or other bones is the classic presenting symptom of metastatic (M1b) disease; spinal metastases can additionally cause cord compression with leg weakness/numbness or loss of bladder/bowel control, a real oncologic emergency. Constitutional symptoms (unintentional weight loss, fatigue) commonly accompany metastatic disease.
core.source: American Cancer Society, 'Signs and Symptoms of Prostate Cancer'

benign_prostatic_hyperplasia.detail: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is the real, single most important clinical mimic of prostate cancer given its substantially overlapping lower urinary tract symptom profile (weak stream, frequency, nocturia, hesitancy) -- ACS's own patient-facing guidance explicitly notes that these urinary symptoms 'more commonly result from benign prostatic hyperplasia rather than cancer.' The key distinguishing features are on digital rectal examination and PSA behaviour: BPH classically produces a smoothly, symmetrically enlarged, firm-but-elastic ('rubbery') prostate without a discrete nodule, whereas prostate cancer classically produces a hard, irregular, asymmetric nodule or area of induration; BPH can also elevate PSA (via increased glandular tissue volume) but typically to a lesser and more gradually-rising degree than cancer, and PSA density/velocity and free-to-total PSA ratio are used clinically to help discriminate the two when values overlap. Because BPH and prostate cancer can and often do coexist in the same ageing prostate, an enlarged, benign-feeling gland on DRE does not exclude coexisting cancer, and any persistent, new, or progressive urinary symptom picture still warrants the standard diagnostic work-up (PSA, DRE, and imaging/biopsy as indicated) rather than being attributed to BPH by assumption.
benign_prostatic_hyperplasia.source: American Cancer Society, 'Signs and Symptoms of Prostate Cancer'; standard urology clinical teaching on DRE findings and PSA behaviour in BPH vs prostate cancer
benign_prostatic_hyperplasia.confidence: high on the symptom-overlap and DRE-finding contrast; PSA-density/free-to-total-PSA cutoff values are standard clinical teaching and are described here only qualitatively rather than with a specific unverified numeric cutoff

prostatitis.detail: Prostatitis (acute or chronic, bacterial or non-bacterial inflammation of the prostate) can also cause overlapping lower urinary tract symptoms and can elevate PSA (inflammation increases glandular PSA leakage into serum), creating a real potential for a false-positive PSA elevation that mimics cancer. Acute bacterial prostatitis is distinguished clinically by its acute onset with systemic features (fever, chills, malaise) and perineal/pelvic pain, and by a tender, warm, 'boggy' prostate on DRE (in contrast to cancer's hard, non-tender nodule); vigorous prostatic massage/DRE should be avoided in suspected acute bacterial prostatitis given a real risk of precipitating bacteremia. When PSA is elevated in a man with symptoms or examination findings suggestive of prostatitis, re-checking PSA after treatment of the infection/inflammation (rather than proceeding directly to biopsy) is standard practice to avoid an unnecessary biopsy driven by an inflammation-elevated, not cancer-elevated, PSA value.
prostatitis.source: Standard urology clinical teaching on prostatitis presentation and its PSA/DRE overlap with prostate cancer
prostatitis.confidence: moderate-high; general clinical teaching rather than a single specific study citation, consistent with how this file cites analogous general differential-diagnosis teaching points elsewhere (e.g. breast_cancer.differential_diagnosis.fibrocystic_changes)

risk_factors.detail: Age is the real, strongest risk factor for prostate cancer of any studied variable: median age at diagnosis in the US is 68 years, and prostate cancer is rare before age 40. SEER data give a lifetime risk of approximately 13.2% (roughly 1 in 8 men) of receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis at some point in life.
risk_factors.source: SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program), 'Prostate Cancer' cancer stat facts

risk_factors.detail: Approximately 15% of men diagnosed with prostate cancer have a first-degree relative with the disease, compared with approximately 8% in the general US population -- a real, meaningfully elevated proportion, though NCI PDQ honestly notes that some of this apparent excess reflects physician/patient bias toward more frequent PSA testing and biopsy in men with a known family history, rather than purely biological increased risk. Approximately 9% of all prostate cancers overall are estimated to result from heritable (inherited) susceptibility genes.
risk_factors.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Prevention (Health Professional Version)'
risk_factors.confidence: high on the 15% vs 8% figures; the detection-bias caveat is reported honestly as PDQ's own qualifying statement rather than independently re-verified in this session

risk_factors.detail: BRCA2 carriers have a real, substantially elevated lifetime risk of prostate cancer -- 19% to 61% by age 80, versus approximately 10.6% in the general male population; BRCA1 carriers have a smaller but still elevated 7% to 26% lifetime risk by age 80. BRCA2 (and BRCA1) mutations are also real, independently associated with more aggressive disease and worse outcomes, not merely higher incidence: in a 2026 retrospective cohort of 390 men with high-risk prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy (48 of 600 screened men, 8.0%, carried a pathogenic/likely-pathogenic germline variant on a 19-gene panel), BRCA1/BRCA2 carriers had a markedly worse 10-year overall survival (19% vs 57%, p=0.021), higher 10-year biochemical recurrence (57% vs 28%, p=0.048), higher distant metastasis (57% vs 18%, p=0.004), and higher prostate-cancer-specific mortality (33% vs 4.3%, p=0.001) than non-carriers.
risk_factors.source: National Cancer Institute, 'BRCA Gene Mutations: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing' fact sheet (lifetime risk figures); 'Clinical Impact of Germline Pathogenic Variants in High-risk Prostate Cancer Treated with Radiotherapy', European Urology Open Science, 2026 (PMID 42565081) (aggressiveness/survival figures)

risk_factors.factor: African ancestry / Black race (incidence and mortality disparity)
risk_factors.detail: Real, substantial, and consistently reported disparity: per SEER 2019-2023 incidence data, non-Hispanic Black men have an age-adjusted incidence rate of 200.1 per 100,000 versus 122.2 per 100,000 in non-Hispanic White men -- roughly double. Per SEER 2020-2024 mortality data, non-Hispanic Black men have a death rate of 36.2 per 100,000 versus 18.1 per 100,000 in non-Hispanic White men -- again roughly double. A separate genetic-ancestry study found West African genetic ancestry associated with increased odds of prostate cancer diagnosis specifically in high-residential-deprivation neighbourhoods (age-adjusted odds ratio 1.98, 95% CI 1.23-3.19), while the association reversed in medium/low-deprivation areas (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.11-0.44) -- honestly reported here as evidence that this disparity reflects a real interplay of genetic ancestry and socioeconomic/environmental factors (access to screening and treatment), not genetic ancestry alone. Men of African ancestry are also reported to present with more aggressive and metastatic disease at diagnosis.
risk_factors.source: SEER, 'Prostate Cancer' cancer stat facts (incidence/mortality rates); 'West African Genetic Ancestry, Neighborhood Deprivation, and Prostate Cancer' (ancestry-by-deprivation interaction); 'Racial disparity in prostate cancer: an outlook in genetic and molecular landscape' (aggressiveness statement)
risk_factors.confidence: high on the SEER incidence/mortality disparity numbers; moderate-high on the ancestry-deprivation interaction and aggressiveness statements, which come from a single ancestry study and a review respectively rather than a pooled meta-analysis

risk_factors.detail: Evidence quality here is honestly mixed and, for several factors, weak or inconsistent -- reported as such rather than overstated. Dietary fat: roughly half of studies reviewed by NCI PDQ found an association with increased risk and half found none; the large prospective Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT) found no overall association between fat intake and prostate cancer risk, though high polyunsaturated fat intake was linked to high-grade disease specifically. Dairy/calcium: a meta-analysis of 10 cohort studies found a small but real increased relative risk with highest versus lowest dairy intake (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.00-1.22) and with calcium intake (RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.09-1.77). Lycopene: evidence is weak, with the large PCPT cohort finding no association. Vitamin E: the SELECT trial found a statistically significant 17% increased prostate cancer risk with vitamin E supplementation alone. Fruit/vegetable intake: results are inconsistent across studies, with the large EPIC cohort finding no statistically significant association and a 4-year dietary intervention trial finding no effect on PSA levels.
risk_factors.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Prevention (Health Professional Version)', citing PCPT, SELECT, and EPIC cohort/trial data
risk_factors.confidence: moderate; explicitly reported as mixed/inconsistent evidence per PDQ's own framing rather than a settled causal risk factor

global_burden.detail: Per IARC/WHO 2024 data, more than 1.5 million new cases of prostate cancer were diagnosed worldwide in 2024 and nearly 420,000 men died of the disease, representing almost 8% of the total global cancer burden; prostate cancer is the second most commonly occurring cancer in men worldwide and the fourth most common cancer overall (both sexes combined). A separate GLOBOCAN 2024 analysis (Bray F et al, CA Cancer J Clin, 2026) reports prostate cancer accounting for 7.5% of all new global cancer cases and projects the overall global cancer burden (all cancers) to rise 67% by 2050, driven substantially by population ageing -- a trend of direct relevance to prostate cancer given age is its strongest risk factor. The IARC source itself notes large, real geographical variation in both incidence and mortality rates across countries and world regions, without a single global rate applying uniformly everywhere.
global_burden.source: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC/WHO), 'Prostate Cancer' fact sheet, 2024 GLOBOCAN data; 'Global cancer statistics 2024: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 34 cancers in 186 countries', CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2026 (PMID 42417444)
