india_specific_data.detail: India shows a real, honestly-reported different pattern from the global picture: a 2025 analysis across 43 Indian cancer registries (JAMA Network Open) found prostate cancer among the top three most common cancers in Indian males, alongside oral and lung cancer -- notably third rather than the second-most-common ranking prostate cancer holds in the global GLOBOCAN figures cited above, and behind oral and lung cancer specifically, which are not the leading cancers in men in most Western countries. The same analysis estimated India's total 2024 cancer incidence at 1,562,099 cases and cancer mortality at 874,404 cases, with India ranking third in the world (second in Asia) for overall cancer incidence. Whether this lower relative prostate-cancer ranking in India reflects a genuinely lower true incidence, or under-detection from lower PSA-testing/screening uptake and less-developed cancer-registry coverage relative to Western countries, is a real, debated question in the oncology/public-health literature that this entry reports honestly as unresolved rather than asserting a single cause; the source reviewed in this session did not itself adjudicate between these explanations.
india_specific_data.source: 'Cancer Incidence and Mortality Across 43 Cancer Registries in India', JAMA Network Open, 2025 (PMID 40833697)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate-high on the reported rankings and national totals; the detection-vs-true-incidence explanation is explicitly reported as an open, debated question rather than a verified conclusion

stage_specific_survival.detail: Per SEER (US) 2016-2022 data, prostate cancer shows a dramatic, real, risk/stage-dependent prognosis gradient. Localized disease (69% of cases) has a 5-year relative survival of 100.0%; regional disease (14% of cases) also 100.0%; unknown-stage disease (8% of cases) 94.1%; but distant (metastatic) disease (9% of cases) only 40.1% -- a stark contrast illustrating that, unlike the near-uniform excellent prognosis of localized/regional disease, metastatic prostate cancer remains a genuinely life-limiting diagnosis even today. Overall 5-year relative survival across all stages combined is 98.2%, a figure driven predominantly by the very large localized/regional-disease majority rather than reflecting uniformly excellent outcomes at every stage. For men who do progress to metastatic (advanced) disease, NCI PDQ reports median survival is usually 1 to 3 years, though it honestly notes indolent clinical courses lasting many years can also be observed in some men -- real prognostic heterogeneity even within metastatic disease.
stage_specific_survival.source: SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program), 'Prostate Cancer' cancer stat facts; National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Prostate Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

active_surveillance_rationale_protect_tr.detail: The real, landmark ProtecT trial (Hamdy FC et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375:1415-1424; PMID 27626136) provides the direct evidentiary basis for active monitoring/surveillance as a legitimate management option in localized, predominantly low-and-favourable-intermediate-risk prostate cancer. In this trial, 1,643 men (of 82,429 screened with PSA) with clinically localized disease were randomized to active monitoring (n=545), surgery (n=553), or radiotherapy (n=545). At a median 10-year follow-up, prostate-cancer-specific mortality was low and did not differ significantly between the three groups (active monitoring 1.5, surgery 0.9, radiotherapy 0.7 deaths per 1,000 person-years; p=0.48), and all-cause mortality likewise did not differ (169 deaths overall; p=0.87). However, active monitoring showed real, significantly higher rates of disease progression (22.9 vs 8.9 [surgery] vs 9.0 [radiotherapy] per 1,000 person-years; p<0.001) and of metastasis development (6.3 vs 2.4 [surgery] vs 3.0 [radiotherapy] per 1,000 person-years; p=0.004) than the two definitive-treatment groups. This is the honest, real basis of active surveillance's rationale: at 10 years, deferring definitive treatment does not cost survival in this population, but it does carry a real, measurably higher chance of the cancer progressing or spreading, which is why active surveillance requires structured monitoring (serial PSA, periodic re-biopsy/MRI) with a pre-agreed trigger for converting to definitive treatment, rather than being a one-time decision to simply observe indefinitely.
active_surveillance_rationale_protect_tr.source: Hamdy FC et al, '10-Year Outcomes after Monitoring, Surgery, or Radiotherapy for Localized Prostate Cancer', N Engl J Med 2016;375:1415-1424 (PMID 27626136)

risk_stratification_drives_everything.detail: More than almost any other solid cancer, prostate cancer management is driven by risk stratification (PSA, Grade Group/Gleason score, and T-stage combined) rather than stage alone -- a real consequence of the genuine biological fact that a very large fraction of screen- or biopsy-detected disease (an estimated 30-70% of men over 60 at autopsy) is truly indolent, while a smaller fraction is genuinely aggressive and lethal if undertreated. Clinicians and patients should treat the risk-group assignment, not merely the binary presence or absence of cancer, as the central fact that determines whether active surveillance, definitive local therapy, or systemic therapy is appropriate.

overdiagnosis_overtreatment_awareness.detail: The real, discordant PLCO/ERSPC/CAP screening-trial results, the estimated 20-50% overdiagnosis rate among screen-detected cancers, and the real, substantial treatment-related morbidity (roughly 1 in 5 men with long-term incontinence and 2 in 3 with erectile dysfunction after radical prostatectomy) together mean that reflexive PSA screening and reflexive treatment of every detected cancer is not the honest standard of care this evidence supports; USPSTF's shift to an individualized, shared-decision-making Grade C recommendation for men 55-69 exists specifically because the real trial evidence does not support a one-size-fits-all screening or treatment default.

active_surveillance_as_legitimate_option.detail: For men with low-risk (Grade Group 1) and appropriately-selected favourable-intermediate-risk localized disease, active surveillance is a real, legitimate, evidence-based management option, not merely a way to defer an inevitable treatment decision -- the ProtecT trial's real 10-year finding of statistically indistinguishable prostate-cancer-specific and all-cause mortality between active monitoring and definitive treatment directly supports this, provided the real, measurably higher progression/metastasis rate under monitoring is explained to the patient and structured monitoring with a clear trigger for converting to definitive treatment is in place.

sepsis.name: Sepsis and Septic Shock
sepsis.icd11_hint: 1G40 Sepsis without septic shock / 1G41 Sepsis with septic shock (ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics, code identifiers as listed on the WHO ICD-11 browser; title text not independently re-verified against the live browser in this session); ICD-10 equivalents commonly used: A41 (Other sepsis), R65.20 (Severe sepsis without septic shock), R65.21 (Severe sepsis with septic shock)
sepsis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Sepsis and septic shock are a real definitional time-critical emergency, not a routine outpatient infection - ANY patient with known or suspected infection plus altered mentation, respiratory rate >=22/min, or systolic blood pressure <=100 mmHg (qSOFA >=2; Seymour CW et al., JAMA 2016;315:762-774, PMID 26903335), or with fever/hypothermia plus hypotension, tachycardia and tachypnea, MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department evaluation (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW), never a routine consultation flow. This is because delay to antimicrobial therapy is one of the most evidence-dense every-hour-matters findings in medicine: in the landmark Kumar 2006 retrospective cohort of 2,154 adults with septic shock across 14 intensive care units, survival was 79.9% when an effective antimicrobial was given within the first hour of documented hypotension, and each hour of delay over the ensuing 6 hours was associated with an average 7.6% absolute decrease in survival (adjusted odds ratio for death 1.119 per hour of delay, 95% CI 1.103-1.136, p<0.0001); by the second hour after onset of persistent/recurrent hypotension, in-hospital mortality was already significantly higher than with first-hour therapy (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.12-2.48); yet the median time to effective antimicrobial therapy in that cohort was 6 hours, with only half of patients treated within that window (Kumar A et al., Crit Care Med 2006;34:1589-1596, PMID 16625125). This was confirmed in a much larger, more recent, real-world mandated-care cohort: in 49,331 sepsis patients across 149 New York State hospitals (Rory's Regulations, 2014-2016), each additional hour to completion of the 3-hour bundle was associated with higher risk-adjusted in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio 1.04 per hour, 95% CI 1.02-1.05, p<0.001) and each additional hour to antibiotic administration carried its own independent mortality risk (adjusted odds ratio 1.04 per hour, 95% CI 1.03-1.06, p<0.001), even though the timing of the initial fluid bolus did not reach significance (OR 1.01 per hour, 95% CI 0.99-1.02, p=0.21) (Seymour CW et al., N Engl J Med 2017;376:2235-2244, PMID 28528569). Septic shock itself carries in-hospital mortality >40% (Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810, PMID 26903338) and severe sepsis mortality was 28.6% in a 1995 US national cohort (Angus DC et al., Crit Care Med 2001;29:1303-1310, PMID 11445675), improving to 18.4% by 2012 in a 101,064-patient Australian/New Zealand cohort but still substantial (Kaukonen KM et al., JAMA 2014;311:1308-1316, PMID 24638143). The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guideline therefore specifies an Hour-1 Bundle - measure lactate (remeasure if initial lactate is elevated), obtain blood cultures before administering antimicrobials (provided this does not substantially delay antimicrobial administration), administer broad-spectrum antimicrobials, begin rapid administration of 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4 mmol/L, and apply vasopressors if the patient is hypotensive during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain mean arterial pressure >=65 mmHg - all to begin within the first hour of recognition, not after a routine queue (Evans L et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021, Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143, PMID 34605781). In lower- and middle-income settings, including India, both delay and baseline severity are worse: in a 22-country cohort of 4,826 ICU sepsis patients, qSOFA was independently associated with 28-day mortality in low/middle-income and upper-middle-income regions but not in high-income regions (Bagshaw SM et al. cohort reported in Bhatraju PK et al./Rudd KE consortium, Crit Care 2024;28:30, PMID 38263076), and in a multicountry Asian sepsis cohort including India, hospital mortality was higher in low- and lower-middle-income countries (adjusted OR 1.84) with only 21.5% of patients receiving hour-1 bundle compliance and 36.6% receiving 3-hour bundle compliance, and antibiotic delay beyond 3 hours was independently associated with higher mortality (Li A et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2022, PMID 35763381). The AI's role in this scenario is only to route to emergency care; empiric antimicrobial choice, fluid volume, vasopressor selection and every other clinical decision belong to the emergency/critical-care physician.

sepsis3_definition.finding: Sepsis-3 (2016 Third International Consensus Definitions, replacing the 1992 SIRS-based definitions) defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, distinguishing it from simple/uncomplicated infection which does not involve organ dysfunction. Organ dysfunction is operationalized as an acute increase of >=2 points in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, which correlates with an in-hospital mortality risk greater than 10% in patients with suspected infection. Septic shock is defined as a subset of sepsis in which underlying circulatory, cellular and metabolic abnormalities are profound enough to substantially increase mortality; it is identified clinically by the requirement for vasopressor therapy to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) >=65 mmHg AND a serum lactate level >2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL) despite adequate volume resuscitation, and this combination is associated with hospital mortality greater than 40%.
sepsis3_definition.source: Singer M et al., 'The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3)', JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)

dysregulated_host_response_mechanism.finding: In sepsis, the immune response initiated by an invading pathogen fails to return to homeostasis, producing a pathological syndrome characterised by sustained excessive inflammation occurring together with concurrent immune suppression, rather than a simple, proportionate infection-fighting response. This dysregulation is accompanied by widespread activation of the coagulation cascade and endothelial injury (loss of endothelial barrier integrity and glycocalyx damage), which together drive microvascular dysfunction, impaired tissue oxygen extraction and the organ dysfunction that defines sepsis under Sepsis-3.
dysregulated_host_response_mechanism.source: van der Poll T et al., 'The immunopathology of sepsis and potential therapeutic targets', Nat Rev Immunol 2017;17:407-420 (PMID 28436424); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)
dysregulated_host_response_mechanism.confidence: high for the immune-dysregulation/immunosuppression framing (verified in abstract); moderate for the specific coagulation/endothelial mechanistic detail, which reflects the accepted pathophysiologic model described in the same review rather than a numeric finding independently re-verified in this session

septic_shock_hemodynamics.finding: Septic shock is a form of distributive shock: pathological vasodilation and increased capillary permeability lower systemic vascular resistance, and although cardiac output is often preserved or increased (a 'warm shock' pattern), tissue perfusion fails because of maldistribution of blood flow, microvascular thrombosis and impaired cellular oxygen utilisation, which is why blood pressure can remain low even with adequate or high cardiac output and why vasopressors (not inotropes alone) are the primary hemodynamic treatment.
septic_shock_hemodynamics.source: Vincent JL, De Backer D, 'Circulatory shock', N Engl J Med 2013;369:1726-1734 (PMID 24171518); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)
septic_shock_hemodynamics.confidence: moderate - general shock-classification review; specific hemodynamic percentages for septic shock were not independently re-verified in this session

qsofa_bedside_screen.finding: The quick SOFA (qSOFA) score is a bedside prompt (not a diagnostic test) for identifying adult patients with suspected infection who are likely to have poor outcomes, using three criteria: respiratory rate >=22/min, altered mentation, and systolic blood pressure <=100 mmHg; a score of >=2 should prompt further assessment for organ dysfunction. In a validation analysis of 1.3 million electronic health records across 12 hospitals plus external validation in 706,399 encounters, qSOFA had greater discrimination for in-hospital mortality outside the ICU (AUROC 0.81) than full SOFA (AUROC 0.79) or SIRS criteria, while inside the ICU full SOFA discriminated better (AUROC 0.74) than qSOFA (AUROC 0.66) or SIRS (AUROC 0.64); patients with qSOFA >=2 had a 3- to 14-fold increase in hospital mortality across risk strata.
qsofa_bedside_screen.source: Seymour CW et al., 'Assessment of Clinical Criteria for Sepsis: For the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3)', JAMA 2016;315:762-774 (PMID 26903335)

sofa_score_organ_systems.finding: The full Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, developed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine Working Group on Sepsis-Related Problems, scores six organ systems from 0 (normal) to 4 (most abnormal): respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 ratio, with or without respiratory support), coagulation (platelet count), hepatic (bilirubin), cardiovascular (mean arterial pressure and vasopressor requirement/dose), central nervous system (Glasgow Coma Scale) and renal (creatinine or urine output). Under Sepsis-3, an acute increase of >=2 points from baseline in a patient with suspected infection defines sepsis, and this threshold correlates with an in-hospital mortality risk greater than 10%.
sofa_score_organ_systems.source: Vincent JL et al., 'The SOFA (Sepsis-related Organ Failure Assessment) score to describe organ dysfunction/failure', Intensive Care Med 1996;22:707-710 (PMID 8844239); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)

qsofa_performance_varies_by_income_setti.finding: qSOFA's prognostic performance is not uniform worldwide. In a prospective cohort of 4,826 ICU patients with sepsis across 22 countries of differing national income, an increasing qSOFA score was independently associated with higher 28-day mortality in low/lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income regions (p<0.001) but was not significantly associated with mortality in high-income regions (p=0.220); after adjustment for APACHE II, SOFA and other covariates, qSOFA remained independently associated with 28-day mortality overall (adjusted relative risk 1.09, p=0.038). This means bedside qSOFA screening should not be assumed to perform identically everywhere, and full clinical assessment plus SOFA/lactate should still be pursued regardless of qSOFA result in resource-limited settings.
qsofa_performance_varies_by_income_setti.source: Prognostic evaluation of quick sequential organ failure assessment score in ICU patients with sepsis across different income settings, Crit Care 2024;28:30 (PMID 38263076)

blood_culture_before_antibiotics_and_sou.finding: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 Hour-1 Bundle specifies that blood cultures should be obtained before administering antimicrobials, provided this does not substantially delay antimicrobial administration, alongside broad-spectrum empiric antimicrobial therapy, lactate measurement, fluid resuscitation for hypotension/hyperlactataemia, and vasopressors to maintain MAP >=65 mmHg when needed. Source identification (through history, examination, and targeted imaging such as chest radiography, abdominal ultrasound/CT, or urinalysis/urine culture depending on the suspected focus) and source control (e.g., drainage of an abscess, removal of an infected line) are core components of management once initial resuscitation and antimicrobials are underway.
blood_culture_before_antibiotics_and_sou.source: Evans L et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021, Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143 (PMID 34605781)

lactate_as_severity_and_prognostic_marke.finding: Serum lactate is both a diagnostic component of septic shock (>2 mmol/L required, alongside vasopressor need, in the Sepsis-3 definition) and an independent prognostic marker regardless of whether shock is present. In a cohort of 830 adults presenting to an emergency department with severe sepsis (28-day mortality 22.9%, median lactate 2.9 mmol/L), intermediate lactate levels carried an adjusted odds ratio for mortality of 2.05 (p=0.024) and high lactate levels an adjusted odds ratio of 4.87 (p<0.001) in patients without shock; in patients with shock, intermediate lactate carried an adjusted odds ratio of 3.27 (p=0.022) and high lactate an adjusted odds ratio of 4.87 (p=0.001) - i.e., elevated lactate predicted death even in normotensive sepsis, independent of organ failure and shock status.
lactate_as_severity_and_prognostic_marke.source: Mikkelsen ME et al., 'Serum lactate is associated with mortality in severe sepsis independent of organ failure and shock', Crit Care Med 2009;37:1670-1677 (PMID 19325467); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)

vital_sign_abnormalities.finding: Sepsis characteristically presents with fever or, particularly in the very young, very old, or immunosuppressed, hypothermia; tachycardia; and tachypnea (respiratory rate >=22/min is one of the three qSOFA criteria). These vital-sign abnormalities reflect the systemic inflammatory and hemodynamic response to infection and, together with altered mentation and hypotension, form the bedside screening basis of qSOFA.
vital_sign_abnormalities.source: Seymour CW et al., JAMA 2016;315:762-774 (PMID 26903335); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)

altered_mental_status.finding: New confusion, drowsiness, or reduced level of consciousness is one of the three qSOFA criteria and reflects cerebral hypoperfusion and the systemic inflammatory response; its presence in a patient with known or suspected infection should raise concern for sepsis and prompt urgent assessment rather than being attributed to a benign cause without evaluation.

hypotension_in_septic_shock.finding: Systolic blood pressure <=100 mmHg is a qSOFA criterion, and in septic shock hypotension persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation, requiring vasopressor therapy to maintain MAP >=65 mmHg; this combination, together with lactate >2 mmol/L, defines septic shock under Sepsis-3 and carries hospital mortality greater than 40%.
hypotension_in_septic_shock.source: Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338); Seymour CW et al., JAMA 2016;315:762-774 (PMID 26903335)

source_localizing_symptoms.finding: Beyond the generalised features above, symptoms typically localise to the underlying infected site: cough, dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain suggest a pulmonary source (pneumonia is a leading cause of sepsis); dysuria, frequency, flank pain suggest a urinary source; abdominal pain, distension or peritonism suggest an intra-abdominal source (e.g., cholangitis, perforation, abscess); erythema, warmth, swelling or discharge at a wound, catheter site or line-insertion site suggest a skin/soft-tissue or device-related source; and headache with neck stiffness suggests a central nervous system source (see the bacterial_meningitis entry in this knowledge base for that specific presentation). Identifying the localising symptom is central to targeted source-control and to narrowing empiric antimicrobial therapy once cultures return.
source_localizing_symptoms.source: Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143 (PMID 34605781) (source-identification component of the Hour-1 Bundle); clinical correlate of the risk-factor and source data in Divatia JV et al., Indian J Crit Care Med 2016 (PMID 27186054)
source_localizing_symptoms.confidence: moderate - the general source-to-symptom correlations are standard clinical teaching; a specific numeric breakdown of symptom frequency by source was not independently verified in this session

other_causes_of_shock.finding: Shock is broadly classified into four overlapping categories: hypovolaemic (reduced circulating volume, e.g., haemorrhage or severe dehydration), cardiogenic (primary pump failure - see the cardiogenic_shock entry in this knowledge base for its specific SCAI staging and diagnostic criteria), obstructive (mechanical impediment to cardiac filling or output, e.g., massive pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade), and distributive (pathological vasodilation, of which septic shock is the most common example, alongside anaphylactic and neurogenic shock). Distinguishing features generally used at the bedside include cardiac output/index, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac filling pressures and the clinical context (fever/infection source for septic shock, chest pain/ECG changes for cardiogenic shock, trauma/bleeding for hypovolaemic shock, allergen exposure for anaphylactic shock).
other_causes_of_shock.source: Vincent JL, De Backer D, 'Circulatory shock', N Engl J Med 2013;369:1726-1734 (PMID 24171518)
other_causes_of_shock.confidence: moderate - the four-category classification is a well-established framework from this review; specific comparative hemodynamic numbers were not independently re-verified in this session

anaphylactic_shock_distinction.finding: Anaphylactic shock, like septic shock, is a distributive shock with vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, but it is distinguished by its rapid onset (typically minutes) after exposure to a known or suspected allergen (food, drug, insect sting), and by accompanying features such as urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm/wheeze and stridor, which are not features of sepsis; the clinical history of an exposure trigger and the absence of a preceding infective focus are the key differentiators.
anaphylactic_shock_distinction.source: Vincent JL, De Backer D, N Engl J Med 2013;369:1726-1734 (PMID 24171518) (general shock-classification framework)
anaphylactic_shock_distinction.confidence: moderate - general clinical differentiation; no dedicated anaphylaxis-specific epidemiological citation was independently verified in this session

non_infectious_sirs_causes.finding: Sepsis, by the Sepsis-3 definition, requires infection as the trigger for organ dysfunction; this distinguishes it from the older Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) concept, which can be produced by non-infectious insults such as acute pancreatitis, major trauma, burns, and other causes of severe tissue injury, all of which can mimic the fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea and leukocyte abnormalities seen in sepsis without any underlying infection being present. Because SIRS criteria are sensitive but non-specific for infection, the Sepsis-3 task force moved away from SIRS-based screening toward organ-dysfunction-based (SOFA/qSOFA) criteria.
non_infectious_sirs_causes.source: Bone RC et al., 'Definitions for sepsis and organ failure and guidelines for the use of innovative therapies in sepsis', Chest 1992;101:1644-1655 (PMID 1303622) (original SIRS/sepsis consensus definitions); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338) (rationale for moving away from SIRS-based diagnosis)

age_extremes.finding: Sepsis incidence and mortality both rise sharply with age. In a 1995 US national cohort of 192,980 cases of severe sepsis, mortality rose from about 10% in children to 38.4% in patients older than 85 years, and incidence itself was disproportionately high at both age extremes (infants and the very elderly).
age_extremes.source: Angus DC et al., Crit Care Med 2001;29:1303-1310 (PMID 11445675)

comorbidity_and_immunosuppression_burden.finding: Chronic disease and comorbidity burden are major drivers of sepsis mortality: in a 101,064-patient Australian/New Zealand cohort, mortality in the absence of comorbidities and older age was less than 5%, underscoring how much of observed sepsis mortality is concentrated in patients with pre-existing chronic disease, immunosuppression or advanced age rather than being uniform across the population.

indwelling_devices_and_catheters.finding: Indwelling intravascular catheters (central venous catheters in particular) are a recognised, largely preventable route of bloodstream infection that can progress to sepsis; national guidance from the US CDC/Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee sets out evidence-based catheter insertion and maintenance bundles specifically because catheter-related bloodstream infection is a major driver of nosocomial sepsis risk.
indwelling_devices_and_catheters.source: O'Grady NP et al., 'Guidelines for the prevention of intravascular catheter-related infections', Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e162-e193 (PMID 21460264)
indwelling_devices_and_catheters.confidence: moderate - guideline-level evidence establishing catheters as a recognised sepsis risk route; a specific numeric relative-risk figure for catheter-associated sepsis was not independently verified in this session

recent_surgery_and_invasive_procedures.finding: Recent surgery and other invasive procedures create a portal for infection (surgical-site infection, instrumentation of the urinary or biliary tract, mechanical ventilation) and are an established, widely recognised risk category for subsequent sepsis in hospitalised patients, consistent with the high proportion of ICU patients found to have severe sepsis or septic shock during their stay in large critical-care cohorts.
recent_surgery_and_invasive_procedures.source: Divatia JV et al., 'Intensive Care in India: The Indian Intensive Care Case Mix and Practice Patterns Study', Indian J Crit Care Med 2016 (PMID 27186054)
recent_surgery_and_invasive_procedures.confidence: moderate - general recognised risk category; a specific quantified postoperative-sepsis incidence figure was not independently verified in this session

source_infections_that_commonly_progress.finding: In a large Indian multicentre ICU cohort (4,038 adult patients, 120 ICUs), 28.3% of patients had severe sepsis or septic shock at some point during their ICU stay, with overall ICU mortality of 18.1%, underscoring how common progression to sepsis is among critically ill patients in real-world Indian practice. Respiratory, urinary tract, intra-abdominal and skin/soft-tissue infections are the classically recognised sources that most often progress to sepsis, consistent with the source-identification component of international sepsis bundles.
source_infections_that_commonly_progress.source: Divatia JV et al., Indian J Crit Care Med 2016 (PMID 27186054); Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143 (PMID 34605781)
source_infections_that_commonly_progress.confidence: high for the 28.3%/18.1% Indian cohort figures; moderate for the general statement on which source infections most commonly progress to sepsis, which reflects standard clinical teaching rather than an independently re-verified ranked breakdown

global_burden.finding: Sepsis is a leading cause of death worldwide. The 2017 Global Burden of Disease analysis estimated approximately 48.9 million incident sepsis cases and 11.0 million sepsis-related deaths globally in 2017, representing 19.7% of all deaths worldwide that year. Age-standardised sepsis incidence declined by 37.0% and age-standardised sepsis mortality declined by 52.8% between 1990 and 2017, but sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania and parts of Asia continued to carry disproportionately high burdens relative to high-income regions.
global_burden.source: Rudd KE et al., 'Global, regional, and national sepsis incidence and mortality, 1990-2017: analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study', Lancet 2020;395:200-211 (PMID 31954465)

india_specific_epidemiology.finding: In the Indian Intensive Care Case Mix and Practice Patterns Study (INDICAPS), 4,038 adult patients across 120 Indian ICUs were studied; overall ICU mortality was 18.1% (729/4,038), and 28.3% of patients had severe sepsis or septic shock during their ICU stay. In a separate multicountry Asian cohort that included India, the overall prevalence of sepsis in ICUs was 22.4%, hospital mortality was higher in low-income and lower-middle-income countries than in high-income countries (adjusted odds ratio 1.84), and sepsis-bundle compliance was low - only 21.5% of patients received the full 1-hour bundle and 36.6% the full 3-hour bundle - with antibiotic administration delayed beyond 3 hours independently associated with increased mortality. Together these real Indian/Asian cohort data indicate both a substantial sepsis burden and a real, measurable evidence-based care gap (bundle compliance and time-to-antibiotics) relative to high-income settings.
india_specific_epidemiology.source: Divatia JV et al., Indian J Crit Care Med 2016 (PMID 27186054); Li A et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2022 (PMID 35763381)

mortality_by_severity.finding: Mortality rises with sepsis severity and has improved over time but remains substantial. In a 1995 US national cohort, severe sepsis carried an in-hospital mortality of 28.6% (an estimated 215,000 deaths nationally that year). In a later, larger Australian/New Zealand cohort of 101,064 patients followed from 2000 to 2012, absolute mortality in severe sepsis fell from 35.0% (2000) to 18.4% (2012), a 47.5% relative risk reduction (adjusted odds ratio for death in 2012 versus 2000 of 0.49), and mortality was less than 5% in the absence of comorbidities and older age - showing that modern, prompt, protocolised care can markedly reduce mortality even though large gains had already been made by the 2010s. Septic shock, the most severe end of the spectrum, still carries hospital mortality greater than 40% under the Sepsis-3 definition.
mortality_by_severity.source: Angus DC et al., Crit Care Med 2001;29:1303-1310 (PMID 11445675); Kaukonen KM et al., JAMA 2014;311:1308-1316 (PMID 24638143); Singer M et al., JAMA 2016;315:801-810 (PMID 26903338)

post_sepsis_syndrome.finding: Surviving sepsis does not mean returning to baseline health. Of an estimated >19 million people who develop sepsis each year, about 14 million survive to hospital discharge; of these, roughly half recover, about one-third die during the following year, and about one-sixth have severe persistent impairments. Survivors show, on average, 1 to 2 new functional limitations (e.g., inability to bathe or dress independently) and a three-fold increase in the prevalence of moderate-to-severe cognitive impairment (from 6.1% before hospitalisation to 16.7% after). Mental health problems are common among survivors: anxiety (32%), depression (29%) and post-traumatic stress disorder (44%). About 40% of survivors are rehospitalised within 90 days of discharge, often for conditions that are potentially treatable in the outpatient setting, such as infection (11.9%) or exacerbation of heart failure (5.5%). This constellation is termed post-sepsis syndrome.
post_sepsis_syndrome.source: Prescott HC, Angus DC, 'Enhancing Recovery From Sepsis: A Review', JAMA 2018;319:62-75 (PMID 29297082)

long_term_cognitive_and_functional_decli.finding: In a cohort of 516 severe sepsis survivors followed alongside matched non-sepsis hospitalisation controls, moderate-to-severe cognitive impairment increased by 10.6 percentage points after the sepsis hospitalisation (odds ratio 3.34 relative to pre-illness baseline), and patients who were previously unimpaired acquired a mean of 1.57 new functional limitations, with these deficits persisting for at least 8 years of follow-up; by contrast, patients hospitalised for non-sepsis reasons acquired a much smaller mean of 0.48 new functional limitations and showed minimal cognitive change. This demonstrates that sepsis survivors carry a real, durable increased risk of long-term cognitive impairment and functional disability, not merely a transient illness effect.
long_term_cognitive_and_functional_decli.source: Iwashyna TJ et al., 'Long-term cognitive impairment and functional disability among survivors of severe sepsis', JAMA 2010;304:1787-1794 (PMID 20978258)

time_is_tissue.finding: The single most consistent, high-confidence real-world finding in sepsis is that time to effective antimicrobial therapy is a critical, independently modifiable determinant of survival: each hour of delay after onset of septic shock was associated with a 7.6% absolute decrease in survival in the landmark Kumar 2006 cohort, and each additional hour to antibiotic administration or to 3-hour bundle completion carried an independent adjusted odds ratio of 1.04 for death in the much larger Seymour 2017 New York State mandated-care cohort of 49,331 patients. 'Time is tissue' in sepsis is analogous to 'time is brain' in stroke and 'time is muscle' in myocardial infarction: every hour of delay measurably costs lives.
time_is_tissue.source: Kumar A et al., Crit Care Med 2006;34:1589-1596 (PMID 16625125); Seymour CW et al., N Engl J Med 2017;376:2235-2244 (PMID 28528569)

hour1_bundle_concept.finding: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign's Hour-1 Bundle operationalises this urgency: within the first hour of recognising possible sepsis or septic shock, clinicians should (1) measure lactate and remeasure if the initial level is elevated, (2) obtain blood cultures before administering antimicrobials, provided this does not substantially delay antimicrobial administration, (3) administer broad-spectrum antimicrobials, (4) begin rapid administration of 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4 mmol/L, and (5) apply vasopressors if the patient remains hypotensive during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain mean arterial pressure >=65 mmHg. This is a real, guideline-endorsed clinical bundle, not a routine consultation pathway, and it is the direct clinical translation of the door-to-antibiotic mortality evidence above.
hour1_bundle_concept.source: Evans L et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021, Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143 (PMID 34605781)

sepsis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Sepsis and septic shock are genuinely, substantially CURABLE with prompt, correct treatment -- this is one of the clearest real "speed of medicine equals survival" stories in modern critical care, alongside bacterial meningitis in this knowledge base. Untreated or severely delayed sepsis kills; treated promptly and correctly, most patients survive. Globally, sepsis is enormous in scale: an estimated 48.9 million incident cases and 11.0 million sepsis-related deaths occurred in 2017, representing 19.7% of ALL deaths worldwide that year, yet age-standardised sepsis incidence fell 37.0% and age-standardised mortality fell 52.8% from 1990 to 2017 as critical care and antibiotic access improved (Rudd KE et al., Lancet 2020;395:200-211, PMID 31954465) -- real, measurable, decades-long progress. The honest counterweight is equally real and stated with equal clarity. (1) It is a real definitional time-critical emergency, exactly like bacterial meningitis: in the landmark Kumar 2006 cohort of 2,154 adults with septic shock, survival was 79.9% when an effective antimicrobial was given within the first hour of documented hypotension, and each hour of delay over the ensuing 6 hours cost an average 7.6% absolute drop in survival (adjusted OR for death 1.119 per hour, 95% CI 1.103-1.136; Kumar A et al., Crit Care Med 2006;34:1589-1596, PMID 16625125) -- yet only half of patients in that cohort were treated within 6 hours. A large, modern, directly comparable dataset confirms this is not historical: in 872 emergency-department patients with suspected sepsis, 28-day mortality was 14.7% when antibiotics were given after 1 hour versus 9.6% within 1 hour, a 34.7% relative reduction (adjusted OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.24-3.23; Freund Y et al., Eur J Emerg Med 2025;32:109-115, PMID 39704009). (2) Mortality remains real and substantial even with optimal modern ICU care -- there is no scenario in which sepsis becomes a minor illness. Across the major contemporary randomised trials of septic-shock treatment, control-arm/placebo-arm mortality ranged from about one in four to nearly one in two depending on how sick the enrolled population was: 90-day mortality was 25.4% in patients recognised early enough in the emergency department to be randomised into a goal-directed-therapy trial (Rowan KM et al., PRISM meta-analysis, N Engl J Med 2017;376:2223-2234, PMID 28320242); 28.8% at 90 days among broader mechanically-ventilated septic-shock patients given placebo in ADRENAL (Venkatesh B et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:797-808, PMID 29347874); 39.3% at 28 days (49.6% at 90 days) among patients already needing substantial norepinephrine in VASST (Russell JA et al., N Engl J Med 2008;358:877-887, PMID 18305265); and 49.1% at 90 days among the sicker, vasopressor-refractory population enrolled in APROCCHSS (Annane D et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:809-818, PMID 29490185). Put plainly: the sicker and more refractory the septic shock, the closer mortality gets to one in two, even today. (3) There is NO single curative drug for sepsis -- and the field's most important cautionary tale proves it directly. Drotrecogin alfa (activated), brand name Xigris, was approved by the FDA in 2001 as the first drug specifically for severe sepsis after an initial trial showed a 19.4% relative mortality reduction (Bernard GR et al., N Engl J Med 2001;344:699-709, PMID 11236773). The mandated confirmatory trial in septic shock, PROWESS-SHOCK, found NO benefit at all -- a nonsignificant trend toward harm (26.4% vs 24.2% mortality, RR 1.09; Ranieri VM et al., N Engl J Med 2012;366:2055-2064, PMID 22616830) -- and on 25 October 2011 the European Medicines Agency announced that Eli Lilly was withdrawing Xigris from the market worldwide because of its lack of benefit, before the confirmatory trial's results were even fully published (Marti-Carvajal AJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;3:CD004388, PMID 22419295). A decade of real clinical use and a real FDA approval were built on one positive trial that a required second trial overturned. The real treatment for sepsis has never been one drug -- it is a real, evidence-dense BUNDLE of time-critical interventions delivered together: immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support, urgent source control, and selective adjuncts (hydrocortisone, vasopressin) layered in for refractory shock. Even the evidence that bundling these interventions together as a formal package saves lives is honestly mixed: an observational 29,470-patient, 218-hospital study found 25% lower relative mortality at high- versus low-bundle-compliance sites (29.0% vs 38.6%; Levy MM et al., Crit Care Med 2015;43:3-12, PMID 25275252), but the one rigorous stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial of implementing the 1-hour bundle itself found no significant mortality difference (12.1% vs 12.6%, adjusted RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.48-1.39, possibly underpowered; Freund Y et al., Intensive Care Med 2024;50:1086-1095, PMID 38913098). What is NOT in doubt, across every dataset examined in this research, is that each individual time-critical component -- fast antibiotics most of all, and fast source control -- has its own real, independently reproducible mortality signal. No curative_option is listed for this disease because no single curative intervention exists; survival is bought by speed and completeness of the bundle, not by any one medicine. REAL WORKING SOLUTION: (a) recognise sepsis early (see this disease's symptoms/EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) and draw blood cultures without delaying treatment; (b) give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition for septic shock or probable/definite sepsis; (c) give at least 30 mL/kg of a balanced crystalloid within the first 3 hours, then individualise further fluid to responsiveness rather than a fixed target; (d) start norepinephrine (not dopamine) as the first vasopressor for persistent hypotension, adding vasopressin if the norepinephrine dose is escalating; (e) achieve urgent source control -- drain, debride or remove any infected focus/device -- as early as safely possible, in parallel with, never instead of, antibiotics; (f) add hydrocortisone for shock that remains refractory despite adequate fluids and vasopressors; (g) trend serial lactate to judge whether resuscitation is working; and (h) de-escalate to the narrowest effective antibiotic and shortest safe duration once cultures return. This is a genuinely curable, genuinely time-critical emergency with a genuinely mixed, honestly-reported mortality record -- not a disease with one cure, and not a disease that modern medicine has failed to make survivable for most patients who reach care in time.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for sepsis and septic shock in adults: immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and the real time-to-antibiotic mortality evidence; antimicrobial de-escalation and duration; IV crystalloid fluid resuscitation and the real evolution from protocolised early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) to individualised fluid dosing (ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe/PRISM, CLOVERS); vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line vs dopamine; vasopressin as a second agent, VASST); adjunctive hydrocortisone for refractory shock (the honestly conflicting ADRENAL vs APROCCHSS trials); source control as a critical non-drug intervention (AbSeS study); serial-lactate-guided resuscitation and emerging capillary-refill-time-guided alternatives (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK/ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2); the real failure and worldwide market withdrawal of recombinant activated protein C (drotrecogin alfa, Xigris) as this field's central cautionary tale; the honestly mixed evidence on whether bundling these interventions as a formal package (the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle) itself reduces mortality; and the monitoring/support devices involved. Diagnostic criteria (Sepsis-3, qSOFA), clinical signs and red-flag recognition are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and this disease's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and are not duplicated here beyond direct treatment-timing cross-references. Guideline status verified in this research: the Surviving Sepsis Campaign published a new international guideline in 2026 (Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2026;54:725-812, PMID 41869847; companion Intensive Care Med 2026, PMID 41870560; read via the official SCCM guideline summary at sccm.org/SurvivingSepsisCampaign/Guidelines/Adult-Patients, accessed 2026-09-22), superseding the 2021 guideline (Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143, PMID 34605781) and the 2018 Hour-1 Bundle (Levy MM et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:925-928, PMID 29675566). Sepsis is genuinely curable with a prompt, correctly-delivered bundle of interventions but carries real, substantial mortality if that bundle is delayed or incomplete, and there is no single curative drug (see CURABILITY_NOTE).

sep_empiric_broad_spectrum_antibiotics_t.name: Immediate Empiric Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics -- Within 1 Hour of Recognition (Real Top-Line Answer)
specific_drugs: No single universal regimen exists -- broad empiric coverage is typically built from piperacillin-tazobactam (3.375-4.5 g IV every 6-8 h) or a carbapenem (e.g. meropenem 1 g IV every 8 h) as the broad-spectrum backbone

Add vancomycin (loading 25-30 mg/kg, then dosed to a trough of 15-20 microgram/mL) or linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 h when there is a risk factor for MRSA (prior MRSA colonisation/infection, recent hospitalisation, high local MRSA prevalence)
Add a second gram-negative agent (an aminoglycoside or a fluoroquinolone) when there is risk of a multidrug-resistant gram-negative organism, per the local antibiogram
Narrower-spectrum options only where local resistance is documented low and the source is clearly uncomplicated
sep_empiric_broad_spectrum_antibiotics_t.effectiveness: SSC 2026 (Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2026;54:725-812; companion Intensive Care Med 2026; SCCM guideline summary) strongly recommends administering antimicrobial therapy immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition, for both septic shock and probable/definite sepsis without shock; for possible sepsis without shock it conditionally suggests a time-limited investigation first, then antibiotics within 3 hours if concern for infection persists. It conditionally suggests (very low certainty) empirical coverage for multidrug-resistant pathogens in high-risk patients, and empirical anaerobic coverage (remarking that piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem are appropriate agents) when specific risk factors are present. This 2026 update replaces the 2021 SSC guideline (Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143), which carried the same core within-1-hour recommendation, and the 2018 Hour-1 Bundle (Levy MM et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:925-928) that first operationalised it.
sep_empiric_broad_spectrum_antibiotics_t.reason_why: Sepsis mortality rises with every additional hour the causative organism is not covered by an effective antimicrobial, because uncontrolled bacterial proliferation and the resulting cytokine storm drive progressive organ failure; broad empiric coverage buys time until culture results allow narrowing (see the de-escalation entry below).
sep_empiric_broad_spectrum_antibiotics_t.important_caveat: Broad-spectrum-for-everyone has real costs: antimicrobial-resistance selection pressure and, in patients ultimately found not to have a bacterial infection, unnecessary toxicity. SSC 2026 now explicitly separates 'possible' from 'probable/definite' sepsis so the most aggressive 1-hour timeline is not forced onto every patient with only a vague suspicion of infection -- a real, deliberate softening of the original one-size-fits-all Hour-1 Bundle after real-world criticism that it drove antibiotic overuse.
sep_empiric_broad_spectrum_antibiotics_t.real_working_solution: Draw blood cultures (ideally two sets from different sites) before the first antibiotic dose only if this causes no meaningful delay, then give a broad-spectrum agent (piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem, plus vancomycin/linezolid and/or a second gram-negative agent as risk factors dictate) within the first hour for septic shock or probable/definite sepsis, and within 3 hours if the diagnosis is still only possible after rapid work-up.
sep_empiric_broad_spectrum_antibiotics_t.source: Evans L et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026, Crit Care Med 2026;54:725-812 (PMID 41869847); companion Intensive Care Med 2026 (PMID 41870560); SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary, sccm.org/SurvivingSepsisCampaign/Guidelines/Adult-Patients (accessed 2026-09-22); Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143 (PMID 34605781); Levy MM et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:925-928 (PMID 29675566)

sep_time_to_antibiotics_mortality_eviden.name: Time-to-Effective-Antibiotic and Mortality -- the Real Evidence Base (Kumar 2006, Seymour 2017, Freund 2025)
sep_time_to_antibiotics_mortality_eviden.type: Supporting time-critical outcome evidence (cross-referenced with this disease's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE, not duplicated in full)
specific_drugs: Not a drug entry -- this documents the real evidence that justifies the within-1-hour antibiotic rule above; see that entry for the actual agents
sep_time_to_antibiotics_mortality_eviden.effectiveness: Kumar A et al. (Crit Care Med 2006;34:1589-1596, PMID 16625125): in 2,154 adults with septic shock across 14 ICUs, survival was 79.9% when an effective antimicrobial was given within the first hour of documented hypotension; each hour of delay over the ensuing 6 hours was associated with an average 7.6% absolute decrease in survival (adjusted OR for death 1.119 per hour, 95% CI 1.103-1.136); yet median time to effective therapy was 6 hours and only half of patients were treated within that window. Seymour CW et al. (N Engl J Med 2017;376:2235-2244, PMID 28528569), the New York State mandated-sepsis-care study of 49,331 patients: each hour of delay in completing a 3-hour bundle carried an adjusted OR for death of 1.04 (95% CI 1.02-1.05), and each hour of delay specifically in antibiotic administration carried an adjusted OR of 1.04 (95% CI 1.03-1.06) -- but delay in completing the fluid bolus was NOT associated with higher mortality (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.99-1.02, P=0.21), an important honest asymmetry: antibiotic speed matters more than fluid-bolus speed. A more recent, directly comparable dataset: Freund Y et al. (Eur J Emerg Med 2025;32:109-115, PMID 39704009), post hoc analysis of 872 patients with suspected sepsis in 23 emergency departments: 28-day in-hospital mortality was 14.7% when antibiotics were given after 1 hour versus 9.6% when given within 1 hour (adjusted OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.24-3.23; a computed 34.7% relative mortality reduction with on-time antibiotics), and this held even in patients without hypotension (aOR 2.02); time to fluid resuscitation again showed no association with mortality in this cohort.
sep_time_to_antibiotics_mortality_eviden.reason_why: These are the primary data behind this disease's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and the within-1-hour antibiotic recommendation; they are restated here, cross-referenced rather than duplicated in full, because a treatment-side survey should not assert a time-critical rule without showing the evidence that grounds it.
sep_time_to_antibiotics_mortality_eviden.real_working_solution: Treat every hour of antibiotic delay as a real, measurable mortality cost, and treat every hour of fluid-bolus delay as comparatively less urgent than getting the antibiotic and the vasopressor right.
sep_time_to_antibiotics_mortality_eviden.source: Kumar A et al., Crit Care Med 2006;34:1589-1596 (PMID 16625125); Seymour CW et al., N Engl J Med 2017;376:2235-2244 (PMID 28528569); Freund Y et al., Eur J Emerg Med 2025;32:109-115 (PMID 39704009)

sep_antimicrobial_deescalation_and_durat.name: Antimicrobial De-Escalation and Shortened Duration Once Cultures Return
specific_drugs: Narrow to the causative organism's directed regimen once culture and susceptibility results are available
Consider procalcitonin trend plus clinical evaluation (rather than clinical evaluation alone) to decide when to stop antibiotics
sep_antimicrobial_deescalation_and_durat.effectiveness: SSC 2026 strongly recommends de-escalating antimicrobial therapy over not de-escalating once a confirmed microbiological diagnosis and susceptibility profile is available (very low certainty evidence underlying the strength of the recommendation, reflecting the absence of large mortality-outcome RCTs of de-escalation itself, but strong clinical consensus on its safety); it conditionally suggests de-escalation even when no pathogen is identified on final cultures. For adults with adequate source control, SSC 2026 conditionally suggests a shorter over a longer duration of antimicrobial therapy, and conditionally suggests using procalcitonin plus clinical evaluation (rather than clinical evaluation alone) to decide when to stop antibiotics.
sep_antimicrobial_deescalation_and_durat.reason_why: Shorter, narrower courses reduce resistance selection pressure, drug toxicity and cost without a demonstrated mortality penalty in the evidence base underlying these guideline recommendations, once the patient is clinically stable and source control (where needed) is adequate.
sep_antimicrobial_deescalation_and_durat.important_caveat: All of these recommendations are explicitly graded conditional and very-low-to-low certainty by SSC 2026 itself -- they represent the current best-practice direction of travel (away from prolonged broad-spectrum therapy), not a settled, high-certainty mortality benefit.
sep_antimicrobial_deescalation_and_durat.real_working_solution: Reassess antibiotic choice daily once cultures return: narrow spectrum, and stop as soon as the clinical trajectory and (where available) procalcitonin trend support it, provided the source is adequately controlled.
sep_antimicrobial_deescalation_and_durat.source: SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026 update), sccm.org/SurvivingSepsisCampaign/Guidelines/Adult-Patients (accessed 2026-09-22); Evans L et al., Crit Care Med 2026;54:725-812 (PMID 41869847)

sep_iv_fluid_resuscitation.name: Initial IV Crystalloid Fluid Resuscitation -- 30 mL/kg Within 3 Hours, Then Individualised (the Real Evolution of Thinking)
specific_drugs: Balanced crystalloid solution (e.g. lactated Ringer's / Plasma-Lyte), preferred over 0.9% saline for initial resuscitation per SSC 2026, EXCEPT in sepsis with traumatic brain injury where 0.9% saline is preferred
At least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypotension or septic shock (SSC recommendation, conditional/low certainty)
Further fluid boluses individualised to fluid-responsiveness and tolerance, not a further fixed protocol
sep_iv_fluid_resuscitation.effectiveness: The single-centre Rivers 2001 trial (N Engl J Med 2001;345:1368-1377, PMID 11794169) that launched 'early goal-directed therapy' (EGDT) -- protocolised fluids, transfusion and inotropes targeted to central venous oxygen saturation -- found in-hospital mortality 30.5% with EGDT versus 46.5% with standard therapy (a computed 34.4% relative reduction, P=0.009). This was NOT reproduced when tested a decade later in three large, modern, multicentre RCTs: ProCESS (Yealy DM et al., N Engl J Med 2014;370:1683-1693, PMID 24635773), ARISE (Peake SL et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1496-1506, PMID 25272316) and ProMISe (Mouncey PR et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:1301-1311, PMID 25776532), each of which found no mortality benefit of protocolised EGDT over usual care. The prospectively planned patient-level meta-analysis of all three (PRISM Investigators, Rowan KM et al., N Engl J Med 2017;376:2223-2234, PMID 28320242; 3,723 patients) confirmed this: 90-day mortality 24.9% with EGDT versus 25.4% with usual care (adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.82-1.14, P=0.68), with EGDT costing more ICU and cardiovascular-support days and higher hospitalisation costs. More recently, CLOVERS (Shapiro NI et al., N Engl J Med 2023;388:499-510, PMID 36688507; 1,563 patients) directly tested a restrictive fluid/early-vasopressor strategy against a liberal fluid strategy for sepsis-induced hypotension refractory to an initial 1-3 L bolus, and again found no significant mortality difference (14.0% restrictive vs 14.9% liberal, P=0.61), despite a large real difference in fluid volume given (median difference -2,134 mL).
sep_iv_fluid_resuscitation.reason_why: The physiological rationale for early fluid resuscitation -- restoring intravascular volume and tissue oxygen delivery in a vasodilated, capillary-leaky patient -- remains sound and is why an initial 30 mL/kg bolus is still guideline-recommended, but the honest trial history shows that forcing all patients through one rigid protocol (whether an aggressive EGDT target or a restrictive alternative) does not itself save more lives once modern early-recognition and antibiotic practice is already in place -- the individual patient's fluid responsiveness and tolerance, not the protocol, is what should drive fluid dosing beyond the first bolus.
sep_iv_fluid_resuscitation.important_caveat: This is a genuine, honest evolution in thinking, not a failure of fluids as a treatment: patients in every arm of ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe/PRISM/CLOVERS still received substantial fluid and antibiotics; what was disproven is a specific rigid protocol, not resuscitation itself. Over-resuscitation carries real harm (pulmonary oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome, prolonged mechanical ventilation), which is why SSC 2026 explicitly moved to individualised, fluid-responsiveness-guided dosing after the first bolus.
sep_iv_fluid_resuscitation.real_working_solution: Give at least 30 mL/kg of a balanced crystalloid within the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypotension or septic shock, then reassess with dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness (not a fixed further-volume target) and add a vasopressor early rather than continuing to chase blood pressure with more fluid alone.
sep_iv_fluid_resuscitation.source: Rivers E et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1368-1377 (PMID 11794169); Yealy DM et al., N Engl J Med 2014;370:1683-1693 (PMID 24635773); Peake SL et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1496-1506 (PMID 25272316); Mouncey PR et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:1301-1311 (PMID 25776532); Rowan KM et al. (PRISM), N Engl J Med 2017;376:2223-2234 (PMID 28320242); Shapiro NI et al. (CLOVERS), N Engl J Med 2023;388:499-510 (PMID 36688507); SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), sccm.org/SurvivingSepsisCampaign/Guidelines/Adult-Patients (accessed 2026-09-22)

sep_vasopressors_norepinephrine_first_li.name: Norepinephrine as First-Line Vasopressor (Real Comparative Data vs Dopamine)
specific_drugs: Norepinephrine IV infusion, typically started around 0.05-0.5 microgram/kg/min and titrated to a mean arterial pressure target of about 65 mmHg
Dopamine (no longer preferred first-line): up to 20 microgram/kg/min in the SOAP II protocol
sep_vasopressors_norepinephrine_first_li.effectiveness: SOAP II (De Backer D et al., N Engl J Med 2010;362:779-789, PMID 20200382; 1,679 patients with shock of any cause) found no significant overall difference in 28-day mortality between dopamine and norepinephrine as first-line agents (52.5% vs 48.5%, OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.97-1.42, P=0.10), but significantly more arrhythmic events with dopamine (24.1% vs 12.4%, P<0.001); in the prespecified cardiogenic-shock subgroup (280 patients) dopamine was associated with significantly higher mortality (P=0.03), but not in the 1,044 septic-shock patients specifically (P=0.19) in this single trial. The dedicated septic-shock meta-analysis (De Backer D et al., Crit Care Med 2012;40:725-730, PMID 22036860; 2,768 patients, 5 observational + 6 randomised studies) found dopamine was associated with significantly greater mortality than norepinephrine in randomised trials (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.01-1.20, P=0.035 -- a computed 10.7% relative mortality reduction with norepinephrine) and, after removing one heterogeneous outlier, in observational studies too (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.05-1.43); arrhythmias were also more frequent with dopamine (RR 2.34, 95% CI 1.46-3.77).
sep_vasopressors_norepinephrine_first_li.reason_why: Dopamine has more pronounced beta-1-adrenergic (chronotropic/arrhythmogenic) activity than norepinephrine at the doses used for shock; this arrhythmia burden, rather than a difference in raw vasopressor potency, is believed to drive its worse outcomes in septic shock, while norepinephrine's more purely alpha-adrenergic vasoconstrictor profile raises mean arterial pressure with comparatively less cardiac-rhythm risk.
sep_vasopressors_norepinephrine_first_li.important_caveat: SOAP II itself -- the single largest randomised trial -- did not reach significance for septic shock alone; only the pooled meta-analysis of randomised trials did. SSC 2026 nonetheless gives a strong recommendation for norepinephrine over dopamine (high certainty against dopamine specifically), based on the totality of this evidence plus the consistent arrhythmia signal.
sep_vasopressors_norepinephrine_first_li.real_working_solution: Start norepinephrine, not dopamine, as the first vasopressor for septic shock, titrated to a mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg alongside ongoing fluid resuscitation.
sep_vasopressors_norepinephrine_first_li.source: De Backer D et al., N Engl J Med 2010;362:779-789 (PMID 20200382); De Backer D et al., Crit Care Med 2012;40:725-730 (PMID 22036860); SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), accessed 2026-09-22

sep_vasopressors_vasopressin_second_line.name: Vasopressin as a Second Agent Added to Norepinephrine (VASST Trial)
specific_drugs: Vasopressin, low-dose fixed infusion 0.01-0.03 units/min, added to norepinephrine (VASST protocol); SSC 2026 conditionally suggests adding vasopressin to escalating-dose norepinephrine rather than up-titrating norepinephrine alone (moderate certainty)
sep_vasopressors_vasopressin_second_line.effectiveness: VASST (Russell JA et al., N Engl J Med 2008;358:877-887, PMID 18305265; 778 patients already on norepinephrine >=5 microgram/min) found no significant overall difference in 28-day mortality between adding vasopressin and continuing/escalating norepinephrine (35.4% vs 39.3%, P=0.26) or 90-day mortality (43.9% vs 49.6%, P=0.11). In the prespecified less-severe septic-shock stratum, 28-day mortality was lower with vasopressin (26.5% vs 35.7%, P=0.05 -- a computed 25.8% relative reduction), but there was no significant difference in the more-severe stratum (44.0% vs 42.5%, P=0.76), and the test for heterogeneity between strata was itself not significant (P=0.10) -- so this subgroup finding is suggestive and borderline, not a confirmed independent benefit.
sep_vasopressors_vasopressin_second_line.reason_why: Vasopressin acts through V1 receptors, a mechanism distinct from and complementary to norepinephrine's alpha-adrenergic action, and may allow a lower effective norepinephrine dose (a 'catecholamine-sparing' effect) once shock is established, which is the rationale for adding rather than substituting it.
sep_vasopressors_vasopressin_second_line.important_caveat: This is a genuinely borderline, subgroup-level result (P=0.05 in a prespecified but non-primary stratum), not a clear positive trial; SSC's conditional (not strong) recommendation and moderate certainty rating reflect this honestly.
sep_vasopressors_vasopressin_second_line.real_working_solution: Add fixed-dose vasopressin (0.01-0.03 U/min) to norepinephrine once the norepinephrine dose is escalating, rather than pushing norepinephrine to very high doses alone or reaching for epinephrine first.
sep_vasopressors_vasopressin_second_line.source: Russell JA et al., N Engl J Med 2008;358:877-887 (PMID 18305265); SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), accessed 2026-09-22

sep_corticosteroids_hydrocortisone_refra.name: Hydrocortisone for Fluid/Vasopressor-Refractory Septic Shock (Honestly Conflicting ADRENAL vs APROCCHSS)
specific_drugs: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV (50 mg every 6 h, or continuous infusion), typically for up to 7 days or until shock resolution/ICU discharge (ADRENAL regimen, hydrocortisone alone)
APROCCHSS regimen: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 h PLUS fludrocortisone 50 microgram enterally once daily for 7 days
sep_corticosteroids_hydrocortisone_refra.effectiveness: Two large, contemporaneous randomised trials reached different conclusions. ADRENAL (Venkatesh B et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:797-808, PMID 29347874; 3,658 mechanically ventilated septic-shock patients, hydrocortisone alone) found NO significant difference in 90-day mortality (27.9% hydrocortisone vs 28.8% placebo, OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.82-1.10, P=0.50), though hydrocortisone did speed resolution of shock (median 3 vs 4 days) and reduced blood transfusion (37.0% vs 41.7%). APROCCHSS (Annane D et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:809-818, PMID 29490185; 1,241 patients, hydrocortisone PLUS fludrocortisone) found a significant 90-day mortality reduction: 43.0% vs 49.1% (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78-0.99, P=0.03 -- a computed 12.4% relative reduction), with benefit also at ICU discharge, hospital discharge and day 180, though not at day 28 (33.7% vs 38.9%, P=0.06).
sep_corticosteroids_hydrocortisone_refra.reason_why: Septic shock can involve relative adrenal insufficiency and a blunted vascular response to catecholamines; hydrocortisone, with or without the mineralocorticoid fludrocortisone, is hypothesised to restore vascular tone and reduce vasopressor requirement. The differing results are most often attributed to trial-design differences: APROCCHSS enrolled a sicker, vasopressor-refractory population by fixed entry criteria and added fludrocortisone's mineralocorticoid activity, while ADRENAL enrolled a broader mechanically-ventilated population without a fixed shock-refractoriness entry criterion and used hydrocortisone alone.
sep_corticosteroids_hydrocortisone_refra.important_caveat: This is a genuine, unresolved, honestly conflicting evidence base, not a settled question -- SSC 2026 gives only a conditional, low-certainty recommendation for using IV corticosteroids in septic shock, reflecting exactly this conflict, and does not endorse a specific dose or mandate fludrocortisone.
sep_corticosteroids_hydrocortisone_refra.real_working_solution: Reserve hydrocortisone for septic shock that remains hemodynamically unstable despite adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy -- the refractory-shock population APROCCHSS most resembled -- rather than using it as first-line or routine therapy in every septic-shock patient.
sep_corticosteroids_hydrocortisone_refra.source: Venkatesh B et al. (ADRENAL), N Engl J Med 2018;378:797-808 (PMID 29347874); Annane D et al. (APROCCHSS), N Engl J Med 2018;378:809-818 (PMID 29490185); SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), accessed 2026-09-22

sep_source_control.name: Source Control -- Drainage, Debridement or Device Removal (a Critical Non-Drug Intervention)
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- percutaneous or surgical drainage of an abscess/empyema, debridement of infected/necrotic tissue, or removal of an infected device (catheter, prosthesis, infected line), as clinically indicated
sep_source_control.effectiveness: The Abdominal Sepsis Study (AbSeS; De Pascale G et al., Intensive Care Med 2022;48:1593-1606, PMID 36151335; 1,077 ICU patients with microbiologically confirmed secondary peritonitis across 306 ICUs in 42 countries) found overall mortality of 29.7%, and that the appropriateness of empiric antibiotic therapy did NOT significantly differ between survivors and non-survivors (66.4% vs 61.3% appropriate, P=0.1) -- but failed source control (persistent inflammation at day 7) carried an adjusted odds ratio for death of 5.71 (95% CI 3.99-8.18), the single strongest modifiable predictor in the study, and 'urgent' source control (2-6 hours after diagnosis) carried lower odds of death than 'emergency' (under 2 hours) source control (adjusted OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.73 -- a computed 50% relative odds reduction; this compares two fast timeframes, not fast-vs-slow, and the 'emergency' group was likely the most physiologically unstable to begin with). The authors' own conclusion: 'source control is more determinative for outcome' than empirical antibiotic appropriateness in this population.
sep_source_control.reason_why: No antibiotic, however well chosen, can sterilise a walled-off abscess, necrotic tissue or a biofilm-covered foreign device with adequate speed or completeness; the infected material itself must be physically removed or drained for antibiotics and the immune system to gain control.
sep_source_control.important_caveat: The counterintuitive 'emergency (under 2h) worse than urgent (2-6h)' finding almost certainly reflects confounding by indication (the most critically unstable patients are operated on soonest and remain the sickest), not evidence that faster source control is unsafe -- SSC 2026 itself still recommends early over late source control, ideally within 6 hours (conditional, very low certainty).
sep_source_control.real_working_solution: Identify and physically control the infective source (drain, debride or remove) as early as safely achievable, in parallel with -- never instead of -- antibiotics and hemodynamic resuscitation; do not assume antibiotics alone will control an undrained abscess or infected device.
sep_source_control.source: De Pascale G et al. (AbSeS), Intensive Care Med 2022;48:1593-1606 (PMID 36151335); SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), accessed 2026-09-22

sep_lactate_and_perfusion_guided_resusci.name: Serial Lactate Measurement (and Emerging Capillary-Refill-Time) to Guide Ongoing Resuscitation
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- serial (e.g. every 2-6 hour) venous or arterial lactate measurement, or bedside capillary refill time assessment, used to guide the intensity of ongoing fluid/vasopressor resuscitation alongside clinical assessment
sep_lactate_and_perfusion_guided_resusci.effectiveness: Nguyen HB et al. (Crit Care Med 2004;32:1637-1642, PMID 15286537; 111 patients) found an approximately 11% decrease in the likelihood of mortality for each 10% increase in lactate clearance over the first 6 hours (survivors' mean clearance 38.1% vs non-survivors' 12.0%, P=0.005). Jansen TC et al. (Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010;182:752-761, PMID 20463176; 348 ICU patients with admission lactate >=3.0 mEq/L), a multicentre RCT of lactate-guided therapy (target: decrease lactate by >=20% every 2 hours for 8 hours) versus usual care blinded to lactate: hospital mortality was 33.9% in the lactate-guided group versus 43.5% in the control group (a computed 22.1% relative reduction, P=0.067 unadjusted; hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.87, P=0.006 after adjustment for predefined risk factors -- a 39% adjusted relative reduction). Jones AE et al. (JAMA 2010;303:739-746, PMID 20179283; 300 patients), a noninferiority trial, found that resuscitating to a lactate-clearance target of >=10% was noninferior to resuscitating to a central-venous-oxygen-saturation (ScvO2) target of >=70% (in-hospital mortality 17% vs 23%, within the predefined -10% noninferiority margin) -- lactate clearance works at least as well as the more invasive ScvO2 catheter-based target, without requiring central venous oximetry monitoring. An emerging alternative target: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (Hernandez G et al., JAMA 2019;321:654-664, PMID 30772908; 424 patients) compared capillary-refill-time-normalisation-targeted resuscitation with lactate-targeted resuscitation and found a non-significant trend toward lower 28-day mortality with the capillary-refill-time target (34.9% vs 43.4%, HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.55-1.02, P=0.06 -- a computed 19.6% relative reduction) and significantly less organ dysfunction at 72 hours; the follow-up ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 trial (JAMA 2025;334:1988-1999) found a personalised capillary-refill-time-targeted haemodynamic protocol won a hierarchical composite outcome (mortality, duration of organ support, hospital stay) over usual care (win ratio 1.16, 95% CI 1.02-1.33, P=.04), with the benefit concentrated in shorter organ-support duration rather than a clear mortality difference (individual death-outcome win proportions were similar between groups, 19.1% vs 17.8%).
sep_lactate_and_perfusion_guided_resusci.reason_why: Lactate rises with anaerobic metabolism from inadequate tissue oxygen delivery (though it also rises from non-hypoperfusion mechanisms such as catecholamine-driven aerobic glycolysis, seizures or impaired hepatic clearance -- a real interpretive caveat); a falling lactate over serial measurements is a practical, minimally invasive proxy for improving global perfusion. Capillary refill time is an even simpler, real-time bedside proxy for peripheral perfusion that avoids the several-minute lag inherent in a lactate assay.
sep_lactate_and_perfusion_guided_resusci.important_caveat: SSC 2026 explicitly states that fluid administration should be individualised after the initial bolus, guided by lactate decrement among other signals, 'rather than continuing fluids until lactate normalization is achieved' -- lactate (and capillary refill time) are real, useful trend markers, not rigid resuscitation-endpoint targets to be chased with unlimited further fluid.
sep_lactate_and_perfusion_guided_resusci.real_working_solution: Trend serial lactate (not a single value), or bedside capillary refill time, alongside clinical and hemodynamic assessment to judge whether ongoing resuscitation is working, without treating normalisation of either marker as a mandatory fixed endpoint that justifies indefinite further fluid.
sep_lactate_and_perfusion_guided_resusci.source: Nguyen HB et al., Crit Care Med 2004;32:1637-1642 (PMID 15286537); Jansen TC et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010;182:752-761 (PMID 20463176); Jones AE et al., JAMA 2010;303:739-746 (PMID 20179283); Hernandez G et al., JAMA 2019;321:654-664 (PMID 30772908); ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Investigators, JAMA 2025;334:1988-1999; SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), accessed 2026-09-22

sep_drotrecogin_alfa_xigris_withdrawn.name: Recombinant Activated Protein C (Drotrecogin Alfa, Xigris) -- Real Failure and Market Withdrawal (Cautionary Tale)
sep_drotrecogin_alfa_xigris_withdrawn.type: Withdrawn biologic infusion (historical, NOT a current treatment)
specific_drugs: Drotrecogin alfa (activated), 24 microgram/kg/hour IV for 96 hours -- WORLDWIDE WITHDRAWN in 2011, no longer available or recommended; listed here only as real, important field history
sep_drotrecogin_alfa_xigris_withdrawn.effectiveness: PROWESS (Bernard GR et al., N Engl J Med 2001;344:699-709, PMID 11236773; 1,690 patients with severe sepsis) initially reported a positive result: 28-day mortality 24.7% with drotrecogin alfa versus 30.8% with placebo, a 19.4% relative risk reduction (95% CI 6.6-30.5, P=0.005), leading to FDA approval in 2001 as the first (and to date only) drug specifically approved for severe sepsis. The mandated confirmatory trial in septic shock specifically, PROWESS-SHOCK (Ranieri VM et al., N Engl J Med 2012;366:2055-2064, PMID 22616830; 1,697 patients), found NO benefit: 28-day mortality 26.4% with drotrecogin alfa versus 24.2% with placebo (relative risk 1.09, 95% CI 0.92-1.28, P=0.31 -- a nonsignificant trend toward HARM, not benefit), and no benefit at 90 days either (34.1% vs 32.7%, RR 1.04). On 25 October 2011 -- before PROWESS-SHOCK's final results were even fully published, based on the trial's interim data -- the European Medicines Agency announced that Eli Lilly was withdrawing Xigris (drotrecogin alfa) from the market worldwide because of its lack of beneficial effect on 28-day mortality, and Eli Lilly discontinued all other ongoing trials of the drug (Marti-Carvajal AJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;3:CD004388, PMID 22419295, which documents the withdrawal notice directly). The updated Cochrane review found no mortality benefit across 5 pooled RCTs (5,101 patients; pooled RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.78-1.22) and a significantly increased bleeding risk (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.09-2.00).
sep_drotrecogin_alfa_xigris_withdrawn.reason_why: Drotrecogin alfa was designed to modulate the coagulation/inflammation crosstalk thought central to sepsis pathophysiology (antithrombotic, anti-inflammatory and profibrinolytic activity); the initial PROWESS signal did not replicate in a larger, more rigorously conducted confirmatory trial designed specifically to address concerns about the first trial's stopped-early design and heterogeneous severe-sepsis population -- a textbook example of why regulatory-mandated confirmatory trials exist.
sep_drotrecogin_alfa_xigris_withdrawn.important_caveat: This is included specifically as the field's most important real cautionary tale about looking for a single 'magic bullet' drug for sepsis: a decade of clinical use and an FDA approval were built on one positive trial that a required second trial overturned, at real cost in bleeding risk and expense to the patients who received it in the interim. It directly grounds why this disease's CURABILITY_NOTE states there is no single curative drug for sepsis -- the real, working answer is the multi-component bundle documented in the other entries in this survey.
sep_drotrecogin_alfa_xigris_withdrawn.source: Bernard GR et al. (PROWESS), N Engl J Med 2001;344:699-709 (PMID 11236773); Ranieri VM et al. (PROWESS-SHOCK), N Engl J Med 2012;366:2055-2064 (PMID 22616830); Marti-Carvajal AJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;3:CD004388 (PMID 22419295)

sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.name: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Bundle-Compliance Mortality Data -- Real, but Honestly Contested
sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.type: Care-bundle implementation evidence (health-systems level, not a single drug)
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- documents the real evidence on whether bundling the above interventions together and measuring compliance with the bundle as a package actually reduces mortality
sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.effectiveness: Levy MM et al.
