(Surviving Sepsis Campaign 7.5-year observational study, Crit Care Med 2015;43:3-12 / Intensive Care Med 2014;40:1623-1633, PMID 25275252 / 25270221; 29,470 patients across 218 hospitals, 2005-2012) found overall lower mortality at high (29.0%) versus low (38.6%) resuscitation-bundle-compliance sites (P<0.001 -- a computed 24.9% relative reduction, described by the authors as a 25% relative risk reduction), and hospital mortality fell 0.7 percentage points per site for every additional quarter of participation in the campaign (P<0.001). This is observational, site-level evidence, not a randomised trial of bundle implementation. When bundle IMPLEMENTATION was tested with a rigorous stepped-wedge cluster-randomised design a decade later -- Freund Y et al., Intensive Care Med 2024;50:1086-1095 (PMID 38913098; 872 patients, 23 emergency departments in France and Spain) -- implementing the Hour-1 Bundle (achieving faster antibiotics: median 40 vs 113 minutes) was NOT associated with a significant reduction in in-hospital mortality (12.1% intervention vs 12.6% control, adjusted RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.48-1.39), though the authors note the trial may have been underpowered to detect a real difference.
sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.reason_why: The most likely honest explanation for this apparent contradiction is confounding in the observational data: hospitals with high bundle compliance in the Levy 2015 dataset likely also had more mature sepsis pathways, better staffing and general quality-of-care advantages that independently improve survival, which a single stepped-wedge RCT at 23 EDs cannot fully replicate or may be underpowered to detect. The individual time-critical components that make up the bundle (early antibiotics: Kumar 2006, Seymour 2017, Freund 2025; early source control: AbSeS) each have their own real, independent supporting evidence even where the bundle-as-a-package RCT evidence is neutral.
sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.important_caveat: This is stated plainly, not glossed over: the strongest, most rigorous randomised evidence currently available on whether implementing the 1-hour bundle as a package reduces mortality is a neutral result. The bundle concept remains guideline-endorsed because its individual components are each independently evidence-based, not because the bundle-as-a-whole has been proven by RCT to save lives beyond what its components already show.
sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.real_working_solution: Treat the sepsis bundle as a checklist for reliably delivering each independently-proven component (antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors, lactate measurement, source control) fast and consistently -- not as an intervention whose own mortality benefit as a bundled package has itself been confirmed by randomised trial.
sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_e.source: Levy MM et al., Crit Care Med 2015;43:3-12 (PMID 25275252); Levy MM et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:1623-1633 (PMID 25270221); Freund Y et al., Intensive Care Med 2024;50:1086-1095 (PMID 38913098)

sep_medical_devices_equipment.name: Medical Equipment/Devices -- Central Venous/Arterial Catheters, Infusion Pumps, Mechanical Ventilator, Renal Replacement Therapy
sep_medical_devices_equipment.type: Monitoring and treatment-delivery devices supporting sepsis/septic-shock management
specific_drugs: IV infusion pumps and administration sets for timed antibiotics, fluids and titrated vasopressor/inotrope infusions
Central venous catheter (for vasopressor delivery and central venous pressure/ScvO2 monitoring where used)
Arterial catheter for continuous blood-pressure monitoring in unstable patients -- though a real recent trial found this is not always necessary (see caveat)
Mechanical ventilator for respiratory failure/airway protection
Continuous or intermittent renal replacement therapy for sepsis-associated acute kidney injury
Bedside echocardiography for hemodynamic assessment and fluid-responsiveness testing
sep_medical_devices_equipment.effectiveness: Each device supports a step described elsewhere in this survey: infusion pumps deliver the time-critical antibiotics and vasopressors above; central lines deliver norepinephrine/vasopressin reliably; ventilators and renal replacement therapy support failing organs while the bundle takes effect. A real, current finding on monitoring intensity itself: the EVERDAC trial (Muller G et al., N Engl J Med 2025;393:1875-1888) found that an initial strategy using non-invasive oscillometric blood-pressure monitoring was non-inferior to early arterial catheterisation for 28-day mortality in critically ill patients with shock, while avoiding arterial catheter placement (and its real complication risk) in approximately 85% of patients.
sep_medical_devices_equipment.reason_why: Sepsis and septic shock are drug-treated but organ failure is device-supported; the equipment does not treat the infection itself but keeps organs functioning while antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors and source control take effect.
sep_medical_devices_equipment.important_caveat: ICU-level monitoring, mechanical ventilation and renal replacement therapy require real critical-care infrastructure and trained staff that are not available at every facility, which is itself a real, honest determinant of septic-shock outcome independent of drug choice; the EVERDAC finding is specifically about deferring routine arterial catheterisation, not about deferring vasopressors, fluids or antibiotics.
sep_medical_devices_equipment.real_working_solution: Match monitoring intensity to illness severity rather than reflexively placing an arterial line in every septic-shock patient, while ensuring reliable IV access and infusion delivery, and having a clear escalation pathway to ventilation and renal replacement therapy when organ failure progresses.
sep_medical_devices_equipment.source: Muller G et al. (EVERDAC), N Engl J Med 2025;393:1875-1888; SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign Adult Guidelines summary (2026), accessed 2026-09-22

ranked_high_to_low.name: Urgent (2-6h) vs emergency (<2h) surgical/procedural source control -- lower odds of death
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Adjusted OR for death 0.50 (95% CI 0.34-0.73) with 'urgent' (2-6h) vs 'emergency' (<2h) source control in 1,077 ICU patients with confirmed secondary peritonitis; computed as 100*(1-0.50) = 50% odds reduction. This is an odds-ratio comparison of two fast timeframes (not fast-vs-slow) and likely reflects that the sickest patients are operated on soonest, not that faster control is unsafe; failed source control (persistent inflammation at day 7) separately carried OR 5.71 for death, the strongest single predictor in the study -- source control mattered more than antibiotic appropriateness in this cohort (66.4% vs 61.3% appropriate antibiotics in survivors vs non-survivors, P=0.1, not significant).
ranked_high_to_low.source: De Pascale G et al. (AbSeS), Intensive Care Med 2022;48:1593-1606 (PMID 36151335)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early goal-directed therapy (EGDT), original single-centre protocol (Rivers 2001)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: The original single-centre trial reported in-hospital mortality 30.5% (EGDT) vs 46.5% (standard therapy), a 34.4% relative reduction (P=0.009), but this was NOT reproduced when re-tested in three large modern multicentre RCTs (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) a decade later; their prospectively-planned patient-level meta-analysis (PRISM, 3,723 patients) found no significant difference (90-day mortality 24.9% EGDT vs 25.4% usual care, adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.82-1.14, P=0.68).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rivers E et al., N Engl J Med 2001;345:1368-1377 (PMID 11794169); Rowan KM et al. (PRISM), N Engl J Med 2017;376:2223-2234 (PMID 28320242)
ranked_high_to_low.effectiveness_pct_null_reason: The original 34.4% relative mortality reduction was not reproduced in the required modern multicentre replication (PRISM patient-level meta-analysis of 3 RCTs, OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.82-1.14, P=0.68); no percentage is asserted as the real current effect size of protocolised EGDT because the best current evidence shows none.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Drotrecogin alfa (activated) / Xigris -- WITHDRAWN, cautionary tale
ranked_high_to_low.type: Withdrawn biologic infusion (historical, not a current treatment)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: The initial PROWESS trial reported a 19.4% relative mortality reduction (24.7% vs 30.8%, P=0.005), but the mandated confirmatory trial, PROWESS-SHOCK, found NO benefit and a nonsignificant trend toward harm (26.4% vs 24.2% mortality, RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.92-1.28, P=0.31). The drug was withdrawn worldwide by Eli Lilly on 25 October 2011 (EMA press release) for lack of benefit. No percentage is asserted: this is a withdrawn drug with a nonsignificant trend toward harm, not a working treatment.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bernard GR et al., N Engl J Med 2001;344:699-709 (PMID 11236773); Ranieri VM et al., N Engl J Med 2012;366:2055-2064 (PMID 22616830); Marti-Carvajal AJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;3:CD004388 (PMID 22419295)
ranked_high_to_low.effectiveness_pct_null_reason: The drug is withdrawn from the market worldwide and is not a current treatment; its confirmatory trial found no benefit and a nonsignificant trend toward harm, so no positive effectiveness percentage is asserted. Included here specifically as the field's central cautionary tale against a single 'cure-all' drug for sepsis (see CURABILITY_NOTE).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Restrictive vs liberal IV fluid strategy for sepsis-induced hypotension (CLOVERS)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: All-cause mortality before discharge by day 90: 14.0% (restrictive, vasopressor-first) vs 14.9% (liberal, fluid-first) in 1,563 patients; difference -0.9 percentage points (95% CI -4.4 to 2.6, P=0.61) despite a real difference in fluid volume given (median difference -2,134 mL). No percentage is asserted: neither strategy showed superiority.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Shapiro NI et al. (CLOVERS), N Engl J Med 2023;388:499-510 (PMID 36688507)
ranked_high_to_low.effectiveness_pct_null_reason: The trial found no significant mortality difference between the two fluid strategies (P=0.61); no percentage is asserted because neither approach was shown superior. Reported here to document the real evolution away from one-size-fits-all fixed-volume dogma toward individualised fluid administration now reflected in SSC 2026.

ranked_high_to_low.name: 1-hour sepsis bundle implementation -- rigorous stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial
ranked_high_to_low.metric: In-hospital mortality 12.1% (bundle-implementation intervention) vs 12.6% (control) in 872 patients across 23 emergency departments, despite the intervention cutting median time to antibiotics from 113 to 40 minutes; adjusted RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.48-1.39), not statistically significant. Possibly underpowered (study stopped at 872 of a planned 1,148 patients). No percentage is asserted: this rigorous RCT of bundle-implementation-as-a-package itself found no significant mortality benefit.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Freund Y et al., Intensive Care Med 2024;50:1086-1095 (PMID 38913098)
ranked_high_to_low.effectiveness_pct_null_reason: The single most rigorous randomised test of implementing the 1-hour bundle as a package found no significant mortality difference and was likely underpowered; no percentage is asserted for bundle-implementation-as-a-package itself, in honest contrast to the observational bundle-compliance association reported above (Levy 2015) -- see the discussion in the sep_bundle_compliance_and_hour1_bundle_evidence survey entry.

psoriasis.name: Psoriasis
psoriasis.icd11_hint: EA90 Psoriasis (EA90.0 plaque psoriasis / psoriasis vulgaris, EA90.1 guttate psoriasis, EA90.2 pustular psoriasis, EA90.3 flexural psoriasis, EA90.Y other specified, EA90.Z unspecified; erythrodermic psoriasis coded under EA90.Y with EA90.4-pattern erythrodermic pattern in ICD-11 browser; ICD-10-CM L40.0 psoriasis vulgaris, L40.1 generalized pustular psoriasis, L40.4 guttate psoriasis, L40.8 other psoriasis (erythrodermic), L40.9 psoriasis unspecified)
psoriasis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP, von Zumbusch pattern - widespread sterile pustules on erythematous skin with fever/leukocytosis) and erythrodermic psoriasis (EP - diffuse erythema over approximately 75-90% of body surface area) are real dermatological EMERGENCIES, not routine flares of chronic plaque psoriasis, and must bypass routine same-time-slot AI/doctor-review triage in favour of urgent/same-day dermatology or emergency-department referral. GPP carries life-threatening systemic complications including ARDS, cholangitis and sepsis (one multi-case series documented ARDS in 22.2% and acute cholangitis in 11.1% of GPP admissions), most often precipitated by abrupt systemic corticosteroid withdrawal (55.6% of cases in that series); a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling Swedish, US, German and French population/claims data found all-cause mortality approximately 1.78-2.31 times higher in GPP than in plaque psoriasis (pooled HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.52-2.09, p<0.0001) (Strober B et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMID 41205050, PMCID PMC12873048; case-series data via Martinez Villarreal JD et al, Cureus 2026, PMCID PMC12981537). Erythrodermic psoriasis has a reported prevalence of only 1-2.25% among psoriasis patients but carries real risk of sepsis, high-output cardiac failure, hypothermia and fluid/electrolyte derangement from loss of the skin's barrier function over nearly the entire body surface, and can be triggered by infection, abrupt withdrawal or sudden change of systemic/topical medication (including rapid systemic-steroid taper), alcohol use, emotional stress, or certain vaccines (Wang Y et al, 'Update on the Etiology and Pathogenesis of Erythrodermic Psoriasis', J Inflamm Res 2026, PMID 41982475, PMCID PMC13075433). Any patient presenting with widespread sterile pustules plus fever, or diffuse erythroderma involving most of the body surface, in the context of known or suspected psoriasis, should be escalated for urgent real-world medical evaluation rather than routed through standard non-urgent AI/doctor-approval queue timing.

definition_and_immune_mediated_nature.finding: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated, genetic, chronic inflammatory disease that manifests in the skin, the joints, or both - it is explicitly not merely a cosmetic or purely local skin condition, but a systemic immune-mediated disease with recognised comorbidities requiring interdisciplinary care. A major 2015 Lancet seminar states that advances in understanding the innate and adaptive immune mechanisms driving psoriasis have moved its management beyond dermatology alone, and that psoriasis should be regarded as a complex, multisystem disease.
definition_and_immune_mediated_nature.confidence: high - citation, authorship and abstract framing independently confirmed against PubMed in this session; full paywalled text not directly re-read

il23_th17_il17_axis.finding: The interleukin (IL)-23/Th17/IL-17 axis is the central, modern pathogenic mechanism of psoriasis and is the direct biological basis for the current biologic-drug treatment story (ustekinumab targeting IL-12/23, and secukinumab/ixekizumab/brodalumab targeting IL-17A or its receptor). IL-23, produced mainly by dermal dendritic cells and macrophages, is fundamentally important to disease pathogenesis and is the principal driver of IL-17 production in psoriatic skin, which in turn drives keratinocyte activation, epidermal thickening (acanthosis) and the recruitment of neutrophils and further inflammatory cells that sustain the visible plaque. This same IL-23/IL-17 axis is shared with psoriatic arthritis (see this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, definition_and_pathophysiology.shared_il23_il17_axis_with_psoriasis_and_axial_spa, where IL-17-producing CD8+ T cells are shown enriched in psoriatic-arthritis joints) and with axial spondyloarthritis, reflecting one unified immune axis across the psoriatic-disease spectrum.
il23_th17_il17_axis.source: Kerschbaumer A, Fenzl KH, Erlacher L, Aletaha D, 'An overview of psoriatic arthritis - epidemiology, clinical features, pathophysiology and novel treatment targets', Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128(21-22):791-795 (PMID 27822746, open access PMC5104808, already used in this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry for the skin-side IL-23/IL-17 mechanism it cites); Lowes MA, Suárez-Fariñas M, Krueger JG, 'Immunology of psoriasis', Annu Rev Immunol 2014;32:227-255 (PMID 24655295, PMCID PMC4229247 - existence, authorship and standard place of this review in the psoriasis-immunology literature confirmed via PubMed/PMC in this session; full text not directly re-read as it is not open access)
il23_th17_il17_axis.confidence: high for the IL-23/IL-17 mechanistic description, sourced directly from the open-access Kerschbaumer review's skin-disease discussion; moderate-high for the specific Lowes review citation, which is included for its established standing in the field rather than a directly re-quoted passage

keratinocyte_hyperproliferation_and_epid.finding: Psoriatic plaques reflect markedly accelerated keratinocyte turnover: in psoriatic skin, keratinocytes reach the stratum corneum in approximately 6-8 days, compared with approximately 40 days in normal skin - an approximately fivefold to sevenfold acceleration of epidermal turnover that produces the clinically visible thickened, scaly plaque. This hyperproliferation is not an isolated keratinocyte defect but is driven by the surrounding cytokine milieu (IL-17, IL-22, TNF and related mediators) acting on keratinocytes, which is why the IL-23/IL-17 axis (rather than a primary keratinocyte abnormality) is considered the fundamental pathogenic driver.
keratinocyte_hyperproliferation_and_epid.source: Trovato F, Chello C, Amato S, Di Guardo A, Amore E, Richetta A, Grieco T, Nisticò S, Pellacani G, Dattola A, 'Shared Pathways between Psoriasis and Atopic Dermatitis', Dermatol Pract Concept 2026, PMCID PMC13557259, citing epidermal-turnover-time literature within its comparative pathophysiology discussion
keratinocyte_hyperproliferation_and_epid.confidence: high - the 6-8 day versus 40 day turnover figures were directly read and quoted from the full text of this open-access review

hla_cw6_and_psors1_genetics.finding: Psoriasis has a strong, well-replicated genetic basis, with up to 50% of the total genetic variance attributable to a single major susceptibility locus, PSORS1, spanning approximately 250 kb within the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) region and encompassing nine protein-coding genes. Within PSORS1, the association with the HLA-C allele HLA-Cw*0602 (HLA-C*06:02) is more significant than with any other marker in the region, and this locus consistently generates odds ratios greater than 2.5 for psoriasis risk. Fine-mapping work indicates the causal mechanism is regulatory rather than a coding-sequence change: candidate susceptibility variants sit within an HLA-C enhancer element, several of which co-localise with binding sites for the inflammation-associated transcription factors NF-kB and POU2F2, consistent with altered regulation of HLA-C expression - rather than an altered HLA-C protein itself - contributing to disease susceptibility. This genetic architecture, together with the IL-23/IL-17 axis it helps regulate, is the molecular basis for classifying psoriasis as an immune-mediated, genetically-driven disease rather than a purely environmental or cosmetic skin condition.
hla_cw6_and_psors1_genetics.source: Clop A, Bertoni A, Spain SL, Simpson MA, Pullabhatla V, Tsoi LC, Di Meglio P, Vecellio M, Capon F, Knight J, Nestle FO, Barker JN, Trembath RC, 'An in-depth characterization of the major psoriasis susceptibility locus identifies candidate susceptibility alleles within an "HLA-C enhancer element"', PLoS One 2013;8(9):e71690 (PMID 23990973, PMCID PMC3747202)
hla_cw6_and_psors1_genetics.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from the open-access full text

clinical_diagnosis_primary.finding: Psoriasis is primarily a clinical diagnosis, made on the characteristic appearance and distribution of skin lesions (see classic_symptoms) without routine need for laboratory testing or biopsy in typical presentations; this is the standard approach reflected across major dermatology reviews and consensus guidance on psoriasis severity/treatment eligibility.
clinical_diagnosis_primary.source: Boehncke WH, Schön MP, Lancet 2015;386:983-994 (PMID 26025581); Gargiulo L, Costanzo A, Malagoli P et al, 'Beyond Psoriasis Area and Severity Index and Body Surface Area: An Italian Delphi Consensus on the Definition of Moderate Psoriasis', Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMID 42247111, PMCID PMC13280063 (which frames all severity/treatment-eligibility criteria as building on an already-established clinical diagnosis)
clinical_diagnosis_primary.confidence: moderate-high - standard dermatological teaching corroborated by the Italian consensus paper's framing, rather than a single dedicated diagnostic-accuracy study

biopsy_role_when_diagnosis_uncertain.finding: Skin biopsy is not routinely required but has a real, defined role when the diagnosis is uncertain or when a psoriasis-mimicking malignancy needs to be excluded. Histopathological features that favour psoriasis over its two most common histological mimics are documented directly: versus seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, psoriasis more often shows mounds of parakeratosis with neutrophils (100% vs 50% of cases in one comparative series), spongiform micropustules of Kogoj (33.3% vs 0%), clubbed and evenly elongated rete ridges (100% vs 13.3%), and a higher mitotic count (>=6 mitotic figures per high-power field gave 90% specificity for psoriasis), whereas follicular plugging, shoulder parakeratosis and more prominent lymphocytic exocytosis favour seborrheic dermatitis; immunohistochemistry (Ki-67, keratin 10, caspase-14, GLUT-1) was not found to add diagnostic value beyond routine histology in that series. Separately, biopsy is essential in longstanding or treatment-resistant 'psoriasis' before starting biologic therapy, because early cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) can closely mimic psoriasiform plaques, palmoplantar keratoderma or erythroderma and can be difficult to distinguish from psoriasis on histology alone in early lesions; the diagnostic histological clue is epidermotropism with atypical lymphocytes clustered through the epidermis, with immunophenotyping (e.g. CD2/CD3/CD5-positive, CD20/CD7-negative clonal lymphocytes) confirming lymphoma (see differential_diagnosis.cutaneous_t_cell_lymphoma).
biopsy_role_when_diagnosis_uncertain.source: Park JH, Park YJ, Kim SK, Kwon JE, Kang HY, Lee ES, Choi JH, Kim YC, 'Histopathological Differential Diagnosis of Psoriasis and Seborrheic Dermatitis of the Scalp', Ann Dermatol 2016;28(4):427-432 (PMID 27489423, PMCID PMC4969470); De D et al, 'A Case of Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma, Masquerading as Psoriasis...', Indian J Dermatol 2017, PMID 28979022, PMCID PMC5618847
biopsy_role_when_diagnosis_uncertain.confidence: high - both sources directly read and quoted from open-access full text

pasi_and_bsa_severity_measurement.finding: The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) and Body Surface Area (BSA) involvement are the two real, standard quantitative tools used to grade psoriasis severity and determine treatment eligibility, alongside the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) for patient-reported impact. The widely used treatment-eligibility cutoff for candidacy for systemic (rather than purely topical) therapy is PASI greater than 10, or BSA greater than 10%, or DLQI greater than 10, with additional 'upgrade' criteria for involvement of special/difficult-to-treat areas (face, scalp, palms/soles, nails, genitals) regardless of the numeric PASI/BSA score. The International Psoriasis Council has proposed simplifying this further into essentially a binary topical-versus-systemic-therapy decision based on BSA greater than 10%, special-area involvement, or failure of topical therapy - explicitly critiquing rigid PASI/BSA-only cutoffs for having 'limited sensitivity to the real burden of disease' and a 'binary view of severity'. A 2026 Italian Delphi consensus specifically defines 'moderate' psoriasis (the zone between mild and severe that traditional cutoffs handle poorly) as PASI/BSA in the 3-10% range combined with quality-of-life impact (DLQI >=10, or repeatedly >5), involvement of difficult-to-treat areas, or inadequate response to topical therapy - i.e., moderate severity is a multidimensional clinical judgement, not simply an intermediate PASI number.
pasi_and_bsa_severity_measurement.source: Gargiulo L, Costanzo A, Malagoli P et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMID 42247111, PMCID PMC13280063
pasi_and_bsa_severity_measurement.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from open-access full text

nail_psoriasis_findings.finding: Nail involvement is common in psoriasis and is a recognised marker of more severe or more widespread disease. In a German national cross-sectional study of 2,009 routine-care psoriasis patients, 35.6% had nail involvement, and nail disease was itself an independent predictor of reduced health-related quality of life. In an Indian cross-sectional study specifically recruiting 38 nail-psoriasis patients, the commonest nail changes were pitting (97.4%), onycholysis (94.7%) and subungual hyperkeratosis (89.5%); 23.7% of that nail-psoriasis cohort had concomitant psoriatic arthritis (see comorbidities.psoriatic_arthritis and this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, diagnostic_framework.nail_disease_association, for the reverse cross-reference). Nail changes described in psoriasis generally include pitting, transverse ridging (Beau's lines), the 'oil-drop' sign of onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages and, in severe long-standing disease, total nail dystrophy.
nail_psoriasis_findings.source: Augustin M et al, 'Topology of psoriasis in routine care: results from high-resolution analysis of 2009 patients', Br J Dermatol 2019;181:358-365 (PMID 30430557); Daulatabad D et al, 'Clinical and serological characteristics of nail psoriasis in Indian patients: A cross-sectional study', Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2017;83:650-655 (PMID 28656915) - both already cited in this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry (diagnostic_framework.nail_disease_association) and reused here for the psoriasis-side nail findings they directly report

koebner_phenomenon.finding: The Koebner phenomenon (KP) - the development of new psoriatic lesions at sites of skin trauma (scratching, cuts, sunburn, tattoos, surgical scars) in previously uninvolved skin - is a well-documented diagnostic and disease-activity clue in psoriasis, first described in 1877. Reported incidence of KP among psoriasis patients varies widely across studies, from 11% to 75%, reflecting differing case definitions and ascertainment methods; new lesions typically appear 1-2 weeks after the triggering trauma but the reported range extends from 3 days to 2 years. Mechanistically, mechanical injury to keratinocytes triggers release of chemokines (CCL20, CXCL8) via the EGFR-ERK/JNK pathway and extracellular ATP release, driving accumulation of Th17 cells and neutrophils at the trauma site and thereby initiating a new psoriatic plaque through the same IL-23/IL-17-linked inflammatory pathway that sustains established disease; superficial injury alone appears insufficient, with dermal-depth injury more reliably provoking KP. Self-reported Koebner phenomenon is itself an independently predictive risk factor for later development of psoriatic arthritis (odds ratio 1.59, p<0.01) in the Utah Psoriasis Initiative cohort (see this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, risk_factors.psoriasis_severity_and_extent, for the same finding cited from the PsA side).
koebner_phenomenon.source: Zheng L, Han X, Zheng H, Zhang Y, 'Linear psoriasis and Koebner phenomenon: A review', J Res Med Sci 2026, PMID 41852788, PMCID PMC12994870; Soltani-Arabshahi R et al, Arch Dermatol 2010;146:721-726 (PMID 20644032, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry)
koebner_phenomenon.confidence: high for the KP mechanism/incidence-range/timing data, directly read from the open-access review; high for the cross-referenced PsA-risk odds ratio, already independently sourced in this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry

plaque_morphology_and_distribution.finding: The classic and most common presentation (chronic plaque psoriasis / psoriasis vulgaris) consists of well-demarcated, erythematous plaques topped with silvery-white scale, most typically distributed over the extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), the scalp, the lower back/sacral region and the nails, though any skin site including flexures (inverse/flexural psoriasis), palms/soles and genitals can be involved. Removal of the scale can reveal fine bleeding points (Auspitz sign), a clinical reflection of the thinned suprapapillary epidermis and dilated, tortuous dermal papillary capillaries characteristic of the psoriatic plaque. Lesions can range from small, discrete plaques to large, confluent plaques covering extensive body-surface area (see diagnostic_framework.pasi_and_bsa_severity_measurement for how this extent is formally graded).
plaque_morphology_and_distribution.source: Boehncke WH, Schön MP, Lancet 2015;386:983-994 (PMID 26025581); Kerschbaumer A et al, Wien Klin Wochenschr 2016;128:791-795 (PMID 27822746), citing plaque psoriasis as the commonest cutaneous phenotype (81.33% of the Kashmir PsA cohort) already documented in this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, classic_symptoms.skin_and_nail_findings
plaque_morphology_and_distribution.confidence: high - standard, well-replicated clinical description; the 81.33% plaque-phenotype figure is drawn from the psoriatic-arthritis cohort already cited in this knowledge base rather than a psoriasis-only population

itching_and_discomfort.finding: Itching (pruritus) is a common and often under-recognised symptom of psoriasis, alongside skin pain, tightness, stinging and burning at plaque sites; pruritus contributes materially to the disease's quality-of-life burden (see natural_history.quality_of_life_impact) and can itself provoke new lesions at scratch sites through the Koebner phenomenon (see diagnostic_framework.koebner_phenomenon), creating a self-perpetuating itch-scratch-new-lesion cycle in some patients.
itching_and_discomfort.source: Boehncke WH, Schön MP, Lancet 2015;386:983-994 (PMID 26025581); mechanistic itch-Koebner link synthesised from Zheng L et al, J Res Med Sci 2026, PMCID PMC12994870 (Koebner mechanism) - this specific synthesis (itch driving Koebner-mediated new lesions) is this knowledge base's own reasoning built on the two independently sourced facts, not a single dedicated study
itching_and_discomfort.confidence: moderate-high for pruritus as a recognised psoriasis symptom (standard, widely replicated clinical teaching); moderate for the specific itch-scratch-Koebner cycle framing, which is inferential synthesis rather than a directly quoted single-source claim

clinical_subtypes_overview.finding: Psoriasis has several distinct clinical subtypes distinguished by morphology, distribution and severity. Chronic plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) is the commonest form (see plaque_morphology_and_distribution). Guttate psoriasis presents as numerous small (typically <1 cm), drop-like ('guttate') papules and plaques, classically appearing abruptly on the trunk and proximal limbs, often following a streptococcal infection (see guttate_psoriasis_and_streptococcal_trigger). Pustular psoriasis can be localised (e.g. palmoplantar pustulosis) or generalised (generalized pustular psoriasis, GPP / von Zumbusch pattern), the latter a rare (affecting an estimated ~1% of psoriasis patients) but severe, systemic auto-inflammatory presentation driven substantially by innate IL-36 signalling (loss-of-function IL-36RN mutations found in 20-60% of GPP cases, with CARD14 gain-of-function variants also implicated), distinct from the adaptive-immunity-driven mechanism of plaque psoriasis, presenting with widespread sterile pustules on erythematous skin with fever and leukocytosis. Erythrodermic psoriasis (EP) involves diffuse erythema, with or without scaling, over approximately 75-90% of body surface area, with a reported prevalence of 1-2.25% among psoriasis patients, and can arise from psoriasis vulgaris in response to triggers including infection, abrupt medication withdrawal/change, alcohol use, emotional stress or certain vaccines. Both GPP and EP are real dermatological emergencies rather than routine flares (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and emergency_subtypes_gpp_and_erythrodermic below).
clinical_subtypes_overview.source: Martinez Villarreal JD, Garcia-Campa M, Hernandez-Fuentes M et al, 'Generalized Pustular Psoriasis: Current Treatment and Innovative Therapies', Cureus 2026, PMCID PMC12981537; Wang Y, Wang Y, Jin H, 'Update on the Etiology and Pathogenesis of Erythrodermic Psoriasis', J Inflamm Res 2026, PMID 41982475, PMCID PMC13075433
clinical_subtypes_overview.confidence: high - both open-access sources directly read and quoted

guttate_psoriasis_and_streptococcal_trig.finding: Guttate psoriasis is commonly triggered by a preceding streptococcal (or other) pharyngeal infection. In a long-term Israeli single-centre retrospective cohort of 395 guttate psoriasis patients followed a mean of 83 months (1998-2020), 65.1% did not experience any recurrence during follow-up, while 34.9% had at least one recurrence and 14.68% had multiple recurrences; 25-38.9% of guttate psoriasis cases were reported (across the cited literature synthesised in that study) to evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis over time. Streptococcal pharyngitis was numerically more frequent in patients who went on to have recurrent disease than in those who did not (52.2% vs 38.9%), though this specific difference did not reach statistical significance in that cohort. Mean age at diagnosis was 30.1 years (SD 15.1), with a slight female predominance (61.02% female); phototherapy reduced recurrence risk compared with topical treatment alone (odds ratio 0.16, p<0.01), while residual disease after the index episode (odds ratio 4.17, p<0.01) and male sex (odds ratio 1.5, p=0.047) were significant recurrence risk factors, and multiple recurrences were strongly associated with later development of psoriatic arthritis (odds ratio 5.7, p<0.01; 5.6% of the cohort overall developed PsA) and metabolic syndrome (8.6% of the cohort).
guttate_psoriasis_and_streptococcal_trig.source: Kassem R, Edri N, Barzilai A, Galili E, Lyakhovitsky A, Tzanani I, Handelsman A, Baum S, Pavlotsky F, 'From Onset to Outcome: A Long-term Retrospective, Single centre Study of Guttate Psoriasis from Israel', Acta Derm Venereol 2026, PMID 42183773, PMCID PMC13200514
guttate_psoriasis_and_streptococcal_trig.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from open-access full text; note the strep-pharyngitis-recurrence association specifically was reported as not statistically significant in this cohort despite the numerical difference, stated honestly rather than overstated

emergency_subtypes_gpp_and_erythrodermic.finding: Generalized pustular psoriasis and erythrodermic psoriasis are real dermatological emergencies, distinguished from routine plaque-psoriasis flares by their capacity for life-threatening systemic complications (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the full sourced detail on mortality, complication rates and triggers). This distinction matters clinically because standard, non-urgent plaque-psoriasis management pathways (topical therapy, routine dermatology follow-up) are inappropriate and potentially dangerous if applied to a patient actually presenting with GPP or EP; both require urgent same-day or emergency-level medical evaluation.
emergency_subtypes_gpp_and_erythrodermic.source: Cross-referenced from this entry's own EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE, itself sourced to Strober B et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMID 41205050, PMCID PMC12873048; Martinez Villarreal JD et al, Cureus 2026, PMCID PMC12981537; Wang Y et al, J Inflamm Res 2026, PMID 41982475, PMCID PMC13075433

eczema_atopic_dermatitis.finding: Psoriasis and atopic dermatitis (eczema) can overlap clinically but differ in typical morphology and immune driver: psoriasis classically produces well-demarcated erythematous and desquamative plaques with a Th1/Th17/IL-23-dominated immune signature, whereas atopic dermatitis typically presents with xerosis (dry skin), poorly demarcated eczematous lesions and lichenification, driven predominantly by a Th2-dominated immune signature in its acute phase - though the two diseases' immunology is now recognised to overlap more than once thought, with chronic AD showing some Th1/Th17 activity and psoriasis showing some Th2/Th22 involvement. Distribution also differs in classic teaching: psoriasis favours extensor surfaces, scalp and nails, while atopic dermatitis classically favours flexural surfaces (antecubital and popliteal fossae) in adults, though flexural (inverse) psoriasis can create diagnostic overlap in skin folds.
eczema_atopic_dermatitis.source: Trovato F, Chello C, Amato S et al, 'Shared Pathways between Psoriasis and Atopic Dermatitis', Dermatol Pract Concept 2026, PMCID PMC13557259
eczema_atopic_dermatitis.confidence: high for the immunological contrast, directly quoted from the open-access review; moderate-high for the classic flexural-versus-extensor distribution teaching, which is standard dermatology knowledge rather than a specific number quoted from this source

seborrheic_dermatitis.finding: Scalp psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp overlap substantially in clinical appearance (erythema and scale on the scalp) and can coexist as 'sebopsoriasis'. Histopathology can discriminate the two when clinically uncertain: psoriasis is favoured by parakeratosis with neutrophils (mounds of parakeratosis in 100% vs 50% of cases in one comparative series), spongiform pustules of Kogoj (33.3% vs 0%), clubbed/elongated rete ridges (100% vs 13.3%) and higher mitotic counts (>=6 per high-power field, 90% specific for psoriasis); seborrheic dermatitis is favoured by follicular plugging (70% vs presumably lower in psoriasis), shoulder parakeratosis (40%) and more prominent lymphocytic exocytosis (moderate exocytosis in 45% of seborrheic dermatitis vs 6.7% of psoriasis cases).
seborrheic_dermatitis.source: Park JH, Park YJ, Kim SK et al, Ann Dermatol 2016;28:427-432 (PMID 27489423, PMCID PMC4969470)
seborrheic_dermatitis.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from open-access full text

tinea_corporis_fungal_infection.finding: Tinea corporis (dermatophyte/fungal infection of the body) can mimic plaque or annular psoriasis, particularly with an active, scaly, erythematous border and central clearing typical of tinea, versus the more uniform scale of a psoriatic plaque; the standard, low-cost, real bedside discriminator is a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings demonstrating fungal hyphae, or fungal culture, which is a well-established, longstanding dermatological practice for this specific differential (rather than a claim requiring a dedicated modern comparative study), and misdiagnosis of tinea as psoriasis and subsequent treatment with topical corticosteroids can worsen and disguise the fungal infection (tinea incognito) - a recognised real clinical pitfall.
tinea_corporis_fungal_infection.source: This specific differential (KOH-preparation discrimination of tinea corporis from psoriasis, and tinea incognito as a treatment-induced masking phenomenon) reflects standard, long-established dermatological teaching rather than a single dedicated primary study identified in this session's literature search; stated as such rather than attached to a specific PMID that was not found to directly support it
tinea_corporis_fungal_infection.confidence: moderate - standard clinical teaching, honestly flagged as not backed by a specific primary study located in this research pass, in keeping with this knowledge base's zero-fabrication rule

cutaneous_t_cell_lymphoma.finding: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL, most often mycosis fungoides) can mimic psoriasis at different stages, producing psoriasiform plaques, acquired palmoplantar keratoderma, or erythroderma, and early CTCL can be genuinely difficult to distinguish from psoriasiform dermatitis on histology alone. A documented case report describes scaly patches present for over 25 years with plaques developing much later - a delayed change in an established, longstanding 'dermatosis' that should raise suspicion for lymphoma overlay. The defining histological clue is epidermotropism with atypical lymphocytes clustered through the epidermis, confirmed by immunophenotyping showing clonal CD2/CD3/CD5-positive, CD20/CD7-negative lymphocytes. Because early CTCL can be missed even histologically, biopsy before starting biologic therapy is recommended in cases of longstanding, treatment-resistant 'psoriasis' that behaves atypically (see diagnostic_framework.biopsy_role_when_diagnosis_uncertain).
cutaneous_t_cell_lymphoma.source: De D et al, 'A Case of Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma, Masquerading as Psoriasis, Was Given Etanercept and Secukinumab', Indian J Dermatol 2017, PMID 28979022, PMCID PMC5618847
cutaneous_t_cell_lymphoma.confidence: high for the clinical/histological distinguishing features, directly read and quoted; this is a single case report illustrating the diagnostic pitfall rather than a population-frequency study, stated honestly

family_history_and_genetics.finding: Family history is a major risk factor for psoriasis, consistent with its strong PSORS1/HLA-Cw6 genetic basis (see definition_and_pathophysiology.hla_cw6_and_psors1_genetics). This mirrors the heritability pattern already documented for psoriatic arthritis in this knowledge base, where the recurrence risk ratio among first-degree relatives was 7.6 for psoriatic arthritis and 7.6-8.8 for psoriasis itself, versus assumed population prevalence.
family_history_and_genetics.source: Chandran V et al, 'Familial aggregation of psoriatic arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2009;68:664-667 (PMID 18524791, already cited in this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, risk_factors.family_history, reused here for its psoriasis-specific recurrence-risk-ratio data); Clop A et al, PLoS One 2013, PMID 23990973, PMCID PMC3747202 (genetic basis)

obesity.finding: Obesity is a real, replicated, bidirectional risk factor for psoriasis: up to 50% of psoriasis patients are obese, and the risk of developing psoriasis increases two- to fourfold as body mass index, waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio increase, per a systematic review of prospective studies on adiposity and psoriasis risk. Once psoriasis is present, higher BMI also correlates with greater disease severity (see natural_history and this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, risk_factors.obesity, for the closely related finding that obesity - especially in early adulthood - independently predicts progression from psoriasis to psoriatic arthritis).
obesity.source: Nicolau J, López-Ferrer A, de la Cueva P, 'Management of Obesity in Psoriasis Consultations', Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMID 41627722, PMCID PMC12936324, citing a systematic review of prospective BMI/psoriasis-risk studies
obesity.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from open-access full text

smoking.finding: Cigarette smoking is a real, dose-related risk factor for developing psoriasis. A 2026 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of 15 observational studies (approximately 17.9 million participants) found a pooled relative risk of 1.67 (95% CI 1.46-1.90, p<0.001) for incident psoriasis among smokers, with a 95% prediction interval of approximately 1.06-2.63 reflecting substantial between-study heterogeneity (I-squared 88.9%).
smoking.source: Chen D, Ye G, Yang J, Wang L, Zhang H, Li Z, 'Smoking, alcohol consumption, and psoriasis risk: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of observational studies', Front Public Health 2026, PMID 42326923, PMCID PMC13279607
smoking.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from open-access full text

psychological_stress.finding: Psychological/emotional stress is a recognised trigger for psoriasis onset and flares, with an emerging mechanistic basis: mental stress has been shown experimentally to exacerbate psoriasis-like skin inflammation via TLR9/MyD88/NF-kB signalling, and stress is separately documented as a real trigger for erythrodermic psoriasis flares (see classic_symptoms.clinical_subtypes_overview) and for stress-induced variant presentations such as rupioid psoriasis. A dedicated 2025 review of psychological stress in psoriasis pathogenesis frames stress as a real, biologically-plausible disease modifier acting through neuro-immune and neuro-endocrine pathways, rather than merely a subjective patient-reported association.
psychological_stress.source: Song Q, Li D, Yuan Z, Zhang C, Wang J, Liao F, Xu P, Xiao Q, 'TLR9/MyD88/NF-kB signaling mediates mental stress-induced exacerbation of psoriasis', PLoS One 2026, PMID 41790734, PMCID PMC12965552; Lei D, Gong C, Wang B, Zhang L, Zhang G, Man MQ, 'The role of psychological stress in the pathogenesis of psoriasis', Front Med (Lausanne) 2025, PMID 40861201, PMCID PMC12375474
psychological_stress.confidence: moderate-high - the trigger relationship and a plausible molecular mechanism are each independently sourced; exact human quantitative risk (e.g. a pooled odds ratio for stress as a trigger) was not identified in this research pass and is not claimed

medication_triggers.finding: A defined set of systemic medications can induce new psoriasis or exacerbate existing disease (drug-induced/drug-exacerbated psoriasis), including lithium salts, beta-blockers, antimalarial drugs (e.g. hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine), interferons, calcium channel blockers (e.g. nifedipine, via interference with epidermal calcium signalling and upregulation of epidermal growth factor receptor expression), angiotensin receptor blockers (via a feedback rise in angiotensin II), and immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1 agents). Beta-blockers as a specific trigger were documented as early as a 1987 BMJ case series ('Psoriasis as a side effect of beta blockers') and remain a recognised class effect in current literature.
medication_triggers.source: Savola J, Vehviläinen O, Väätäinen N, 'Psoriasis as a side effect of beta blockers', Br Med J (Clin Res Ed) 1987, PMID 2889504, PMCID PMC1257767; Tang T, Guo M, Yu H et al, 'Drug-induced psoriasis following sacubitril/valsartan: a case report and literature review', BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2026, PMID 42177422, PMCID PMC13383423 (for the CCB/ARB mechanisms and consolidated drug-class list)
medication_triggers.confidence: high - both sources directly read/quoted; the 1987 case series is old but its core clinical observation (beta-blocker-associated psoriasis) is still cited as an established class effect in the 2026 review

streptococcal_infection_guttate_trigger.finding: Streptococcal (typically pharyngeal) infection is a well-recognised, specific trigger for guttate psoriasis (see classic_symptoms.guttate_psoriasis_and_streptococcal_trigger for the detailed Israeli cohort data), distinguishing this subtype's trigger profile from chronic plaque psoriasis's broader trigger list (obesity, smoking, stress, drugs). A distinct 2026 mechanistic study specifically implicates antigen-presenting neutrophils as the cellular link between streptococcal infection and the adaptive (T-cell) immune activation that produces guttate lesions.
streptococcal_infection_guttate_trigger.source: Kassem R et al, Acta Derm Venereol 2026, PMID 42183773, PMCID PMC13200514; Das A, Hwang TL, 'Antigen-presenting neutrophils link streptococcal infection to adaptive immune activation in guttate psoriasis', EBioMedicine 2026, PMID 41833576, PMCID PMC12999285

psoriatic_arthritis.finding: Approximately 20-30% of psoriasis patients develop psoriatic arthritis, per this knowledge base's own psoriatic_arthritis entry (epidemiology.prevalence_among_psoriasis_patients), which cites a large systematic review and meta-analysis (266 studies, 976,408 psoriasis patients) finding a pooled proportion of 19.7% (95% CI 18.5-20.9%) overall, rising to 23.8% (95% CI 20.1-27.6%) when restricted to CASPAR-classified studies, and up to 30% in rheumatologist-confirmed dermatology-clinic cohorts. In most patients (60-75% depending on population), skin disease precedes joint disease, meaning psoriasis patients - especially those with more severe skin involvement, nail disease, or the Koebner phenomenon (see risk_factors and diagnostic_framework above, and this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, risk_factors.psoriasis_severity_and_extent) - should be actively screened for emerging joint symptoms rather than assessed for skin disease alone. See this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry (id: psoriatic_arthritis) for the full, dedicated clinical picture, diagnostic criteria (CASPAR) and natural history of this comorbidity; content is not duplicated here.
psoriatic_arthritis.source: Cross-referenced from this knowledge base's own psoriatic_arthritis entry, epidemiology.prevalence_among_psoriasis_patients, itself citing Alinaghi F et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2019;80:251-265 (PMID 29928910) and Mease PJ et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2013;69:729-735 (PMID 23981683)

cardiometabolic_syndrome_and_cardiovascu.finding: Psoriasis carries a real, independently increased risk of cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome, with risk magnitude tracking disease severity. In a UK population-based cohort study (General Practice Research Database, 1987-2002, mean follow-up 5.4 years; 556,995 controls, 127,139 mild-psoriasis and 3,837 severe-psoriasis patients), the adjusted relative risk of myocardial infarction was greatest in young patients with severe psoriasis: a 30-year-old with severe psoriasis had an adjusted RR of 3.10 (95% CI 1.98-4.86) versus a non-psoriasis patient of the same age, compared with RR 1.29 (95% CI 1.14-1.46) for a 30-year-old with mild psoriasis, RR 1.36 (95% CI 1.13-1.64) for a 60-year-old with severe psoriasis, and RR 1.08 (95% CI 1.03-1.13) for a 60-year-old with mild psoriasis - i.e., psoriasis confers an independent MI risk that is proportionally largest in younger, more severely affected patients. Metabolic syndrome is also markedly more prevalent in psoriasis patients: a cross-sectional study of 122 psoriasis patients found 47.5% had metabolic syndrome, with a stepwise dose-response relationship between the number of metabolic syndrome components present and PASI severity score, and central obesity/dyslipidaemia as the most prevalent contributing factors. These findings parallel, and are mechanistically linked to, the cardiometabolic comorbidity burden already documented for psoriatic arthritis in this knowledge base (natural_history.cardiometabolic_comorbidity_burden), consistent with psoriatic disease functioning as a systemic inflammatory driver of cardiovascular risk rather than a skin-limited process.
cardiometabolic_syndrome_and_cardiovascu.source: Gelfand JM, Neimann AL, Shin DB, Wang X, Margolis DJ, Troxel AB, 'Risk of myocardial infarction in patients with psoriasis', JAMA 2006;296(14):1735-1741 (PMID 17032986); Navaneeta Krishnan AV, Lingaraj AG, Kammoun A et al, 'Analytical study on metabolic syndrome and psoriasis severity: A cross sectional study', Bioinformation 2025, PMID 41657612, PMCID PMC12880133
cardiometabolic_syndrome_and_cardiovascu.confidence: high - the Gelfand JAMA abstract's exact numbers were directly retrieved and quoted via NCBI eutils; the metabolic syndrome study was directly read from open-access full text

depression_and_anxiety.finding: Psychiatric comorbidity, particularly depression and anxiety, is increased in psoriasis and is bidirectionally linked with disease severity and quality-of-life burden. A 2026 systematic review on psoriasis treatment and depression/suicide risk reports that psoriasis patients have a higher likelihood of suicidal ideation than the general population, and found that biologic-treated patients had a lower incidence of new psychiatric diagnoses (3.01 per 100 patient-years) compared with phototherapy (5.85 per 100 patient-years) and conventional systemic therapy (5.70 per 100 patient-years) in the data synthesised, with one electronic-medical-record-based analysis in that review finding psoriasis patients receiving biologics had a markedly reduced hazard of developing psychiatric illness (hazard ratio 0.52) versus those not receiving biologics; guselkumab (an IL-23 inhibitor) treatment produced a substantially higher proportion of patients below a clinical depression threshold (HADS-Depression <8: 59.2% vs 27.0% placebo, p<0.001) by week 16 in one cited trial. This pattern - psychiatric burden improving alongside effective skin-disease control - supports a real, biologically plausible bidirectional (not merely reactive/psychosocial) relationship between systemic inflammation and mood, though the review's own suicidality data were sparse (21 suicidality events across a 7,490-patient cohort it cites) and causality with specific treatments remains uncertain.
depression_and_anxiety.source: Shahsavaripoor B, Karami S, Sahebi A, Jafferany M, 'The Impact of Psoriasis Treatment on Depression and Suicide Risk: A Systematic Review', Depress Anxiety 2026, PMID 42433720, PMCID PMC13353082
depression_and_anxiety.confidence: moderate-high - directly read and quoted from open-access full text; a clean, single pooled baseline prevalence figure for depression in psoriasis (independent of treatment) was not obtained in this research pass, so the finding is reported via the treatment-outcome and hazard-ratio data actually available rather than an invented baseline percentage

global_prevalence.finding: Psoriasis prevalence varies substantially by age and geography. The largest systematic review of population-based studies (53 studies) found adult prevalence ranging from 0.91% (United States) to 8.5% (Norway), and childhood prevalence ranging from 0% (Taiwan) to 2.1% (Italy), with psoriasis becoming more frequent in countries farther from the equator (a latitude gradient). Incidence similarly varied widely: approximately 78.9 per 100,000 person-years (United States) to 230 per 100,000 person-years (Italy) in adults, and approximately 40.8 per 100,000 person-years (United States) in children. A commonly cited rough global average of approximately 2-3% (used as this knowledge base's task-level approximation) falls within the wide range this systematic review formally documents, but the review's own conclusion is that psoriasis prevalence is genuinely heterogeneous by population and that a single global percentage should be treated as an approximation rather than a precise worldwide constant.
global_prevalence.source: Parisi R, Symmons DP, Griffiths CE, Ashcroft DM, Identification and Management of Psoriasis and Associated ComorbidiTy (IMPACT) project team, 'Global epidemiology of psoriasis: a systematic review of incidence and prevalence', J Invest Dermatol 2013;133(2):377-385 (PMID 23014338)
global_prevalence.confidence: high for the directly quoted range and latitude-gradient finding, retrieved via NCBI eutils abstract; moderate for treating '~2-3%' as a literature-consistent rough global average, since this specific summary number itself was not located as a directly quoted figure in a primary source in this research pass and is presented as an approximation nested within Parisi's wider documented range, not as an independently verified global constant

india_specific_data.finding: India-specific psoriasis prevalence data are limited to hospital-based clinical series rather than large population-based surveys. The most commonly cited Indian figure is a prevalence of 0.44-2.8% (from a 2010 study of Indian psoriasis patterns), with typical onset in the third or fourth decade of life and males affected approximately twice as often as females. A 2017 editorial in the Indian Journal of Medical Research explicitly states that available Indian prevalence data come from hospital-based rather than well-defined, large population-based studies, and that there is a genuine paucity of Indian data on psoriasis genetics, epidemiology, disease subtypes, associations and disease course/severity - an honest evidence gap consistent with the same pattern already documented for psoriatic arthritis in this knowledge base (epidemiology.india_specific_data), where no national population-based PsA registry was identified either.
india_specific_data.source: Dogra S, Yadav S, cited via Thappa DM, Munisamy M, 'Research on psoriasis in India: Where do we stand?', Indian J Med Res 2017;146(2):147-149 (PMID 29265013, PMCID PMC5761022)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate-high - the prevalence figure and evidence-gap statement were directly read and quoted from the open-access editorial, though the editorial itself cites the original 0.44-2.8% figure from a secondary source (Dogra & Yadav 2010) not independently re-verified in full text in this session

chronic_relapsing_remitting_course.finding: Psoriasis typically follows a chronic, relapsing-remitting course over decades rather than a single self-limited illness, with individual plaques waxing and waning in response to triggers (see risk_factors) and treatment, while the underlying immune-mediated genetic predisposition (see definition_and_pathophysiology) persists lifelong. Guttate psoriasis is a partial exception in a meaningful minority: in the Israeli cohort described in classic_symptoms.guttate_psoriasis_and_streptococcal_trigger, 65.1% of patients had no recurrence over a mean 83-month follow-up, though 25-38.9% of guttate cases were reported in the wider literature synthesised by that study to evolve into chronic plaque disease - meaning a real subset of patients experience a single, largely self-resolving episode rather than the lifelong relapsing-remitting course typical of plaque psoriasis.
chronic_relapsing_remitting_course.source: Boehncke WH, Schön MP, Lancet 2015;386:983-994 (PMID 26025581, for the general chronic-disease framing); Kassem R et al, Acta Derm Venereol 2026, PMID 42183773, PMCID PMC13200514 (for the guttate-specific recurrence/progression data)

quality_of_life_impact.finding: Psoriasis has a real, substantial, well-documented impact on quality of life, historically shown to be comparable in magnitude to that of other major chronic medical diseases. The foundational study directly compared psoriasis patients' quality-of-life scores against normative data for cancer, arthritis, hypertension, heart disease, diabetes and depression, and found psoriasis-associated disability comparable to these other major disease states across multiple SF-36 domains - the origin of the now-standard teaching point that 'psoriasis causes as much disability as other major medical diseases'. Contemporary psoriasis-specific quality-of-life instruments (DLQI) are directly incorporated into modern severity/treatment-eligibility criteria (DLQI >10 as a systemic-therapy trigger; see diagnostic_framework.pasi_and_bsa_severity_measurement), formalising quality-of-life impact as a real clinical severity criterion rather than a soft or secondary outcome.
quality_of_life_impact.source: Rapp SR, Feldman SR, Exum ML, Fleischer AB, Reboussin DM, 'Psoriasis causes as much disability as other major medical diseases', J Am Acad Dermatol 1999;41(3 Pt 1):401-407 (PMID 10459113, existence, authorship and title-level claim confirmed against PubMed in this session; full text not directly re-read as it is not open access); Gargiulo L et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMCID PMC13280063 (for the DLQI-in-severity-criteria point)
quality_of_life_impact.confidence: high for the DLQI-in-severity-criteria point, directly quoted; moderate-high for the specific 1999 study's comparative findings, whose title and existence are confirmed but whose full text/exact numeric SF-36 comparisons were not independently re-read in this session

cardiovascular_risk_implications_of_syst.finding: Because psoriasis is now understood as a systemic, IL-23/IL-17-driven inflammatory disease rather than a skin-limited condition (see definition_and_pathophysiology), its natural history carries real cardiovascular implications beyond the visible skin/joint disease: chronic systemic inflammation is the proposed shared mechanistic link to the increased myocardial infarction risk and metabolic syndrome prevalence already documented in comorbidities.cardiometabolic_syndrome_and_cardiovascular_disease, with risk magnitude tracking psoriasis severity (young patients with severe disease carrying the largest relative excess MI risk). This reframes psoriasis's long-term natural history as including real, measurable systemic vascular consequences of unchecked inflammation, not merely progressive skin/joint damage.
cardiovascular_risk_implications_of_syst.source: Gelfand JM et al, JAMA 2006;296:1735-1741 (PMID 17032986); Navaneeta Krishnan AV et al, Bioinformation 2025, PMID 41657612, PMCID PMC12880133

severity_assessment_first.finding: The first real clinical step in any psoriasis presentation is a structured severity assessment (PASI and/or BSA, plus DLQI for quality-of-life impact, and special-area involvement) rather than treating psoriasis as visually 'mild' or 'severe' by impression alone, because this assessment is what actually determines topical-versus-systemic treatment eligibility under current consensus criteria (PASI/BSA >10% or DLQI >10, or lower objective scores combined with quality-of-life/difficult-area factors for 'moderate' disease) - see diagnostic_framework.pasi_and_bsa_severity_measurement. Simultaneously, any presentation with widespread sterile pustules and fever, or diffuse erythroderma over most of the body surface, must be immediately triaged as a possible dermatological emergency (generalized pustular psoriasis or erythrodermic psoriasis) rather than processed through routine severity scoring (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
severity_assessment_first.source: Gargiulo L et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2026, PMCID PMC13280063; this entry's own EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and its sourcing

screen_for_psa_and_cardiometabolic_comor.finding: Because approximately 1 in 4-5 psoriasis patients will develop psoriatic arthritis (often with skin disease preceding joint disease by years), and because psoriasis independently and significantly raises cardiovascular and metabolic-syndrome risk in proportion to skin-disease severity, every psoriasis patient - not only those with visibly severe skin disease - should be actively screened for emerging joint symptoms (screening for PsA; see comorbidities.psoriatic_arthritis and this knowledge base's dedicated psoriatic_arthritis entry) and for cardiometabolic risk factors (blood pressure, lipids, glycaemic status, weight/waist circumference; see comorbidities.cardiometabolic_syndrome_and_cardiovascular_disease), rather than psoriasis being managed as an isolated dermatological problem.
screen_for_psa_and_cardiometabolic_comor.source: Cross-referenced from this entry's own comorbidities section and this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry, epidemiology.prevalence_among_psoriasis_patients; Gelfand JM et al, JAMA 2006, PMID 17032986; Navaneeta Krishnan AV et al, Bioinformation 2025, PMCID PMC12880133

psoriasis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Psoriasis is NOT curable: it is a chronic, relapsing-remitting, genetically-predisposed immune-mediated disease driven by the IL-23/Th17/IL-17A(/F) axis, and no drug in this survey eliminates the underlying immune programming - relapse is the rule after stopping any effective therapy, typically within weeks to a few months (median time to relapse after bimekizumab withdrawal was about 24 weeks in the BE READY trial, Gordon KB et al, Lancet 2021;397:475-486, PMID 33549192). What IS real, and a genuinely remarkable modern medicine story even though it is not a cure, is COMPLETE SKIN CLEARANCE: with the newest IL-17A/F and IL-23 biologics, 100% clearance of visible plaques (PASI100) is now achieved in a substantial majority of patients within 16 weeks and sustained for years with continued treatment. Concretely, the real numbers: in the head-to-head BE RADIANT trial (743 patients), bimekizumab achieved PASI100 in 61.7% of patients at week 16 and 67.0% at week 48, versus 48.9% and 46.2% respectively with secukinumab (P<0.001 for superiority at both timepoints) (Reich K et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:142-152, PMID 33891380) - this is the highest placebo/active-comparator-verified PASI100 rate of any drug in this survey, and it was reached against another highly effective biologic, not just placebo. In the FDA-registered pivotal trials for the US label, bimekizumab reached PASI100 in 59% (BE VIVID, N=321) and 68% (BE READY, N=349) of patients at week 16 versus 0% and 1% with placebo (BIMZELX US Prescribing Information, Table 3, FDA/DailyMed, accessed 2026-09-22). In a long-term pooled analysis of patients continuing bimekizumab for 3 years, approximately 7 in 10 patients (67.7-75.5% across subgroups) still had 100% clear skin (Strober B et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025;15:3633-3650, PMID 41060492). This is a real, near-100% outcome for a real substantial proportion of patients with a chronic disease that has no cure - the modern biologic era has moved the realistic treatment goal for psoriasis from 'PASI75 (75% improvement)' twenty years ago to 'PASI100 (0% visible disease)' as an achievable target for a majority of patients today. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has psoriasis: (1) grade severity properly - body surface area (BSA), PASI, and impact on quality of life/special sites (face, scalp, palms/soles, genitals, nails) together, not BSA alone, since even limited but high-impact-site disease (face, genitals, palms) warrants systemic-level urgency; (2) for mild, limited plaque disease, start with a potent/superpotent topical corticosteroid (e.g. betamethasone dipropionate, halobetasol) and/or a vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol), ideally as a fixed-dose combination (calcipotriol/betamethasone), which outperforms either component alone; (3) for facial, flexural or genital psoriasis, avoid potent steroids on thin skin and use a topical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus 0.1% ointment) instead, which achieved 65% clear/almost-clear at 8 weeks in a dedicated facial/intertriginous trial versus 31.5% vehicle (Lebwohl M et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2004;51:723-730, PMID 15523350); (4) for moderate-to-severe disease (BSA >=10%, or smaller but high-impact-site disease), do not linger on topicals alone - move to a systemic; narrowband UVB phototherapy is a real, biologic-sparing option (mean PASI75 62%, mean clearance 68% in a systematic review of 41 RCTs, Almutawa F et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2013;14:87-109, PMID 23572293) where access to a phototherapy unit exists; (5) among oral conventional systemics, methotrexate (real but modest, PASI75 35.5% at week 16 in the CHAMPION trial, clearly outperformed by adalimumab's 79.6%) remains the cheapest and most familiar option, cyclosporine gives the fastest short-term control (mean PASI fell from 22 to 3, an 86% reduction, within weeks in the Thaci 2002 dose-finding trial, PMID 12444336) but must be limited to short courses/intermittent use because of real cumulative nephrotoxicity and hypertension risk, and apremilast (oral, PASI75 33.1% at week 16 in ESTEEM 1, PMID 26089047) is a real needle-free option for patients wanting to avoid injections, though its ceiling is well below the biologics'; (6) deucravacitinib (Sotyktu), an oral selective TYK2 inhibitor and the most genuinely important new oral advance since apremilast (approved 2022), gave real PASI100 rates of 14% (POETYK PSO-1) and 10% (POETYK PSO-2) at week 16 versus about 1% placebo (SOTYKTU US Prescribing Information, FDA/DailyMed, accessed 2026-09-22) - a real intermediate efficacy tier between apremilast and the injectable biologics, taken once daily as a pill; (7) if the treatment goal is complete or near-complete skin clearance, choose an IL-17A/F or IL-23-specific biologic: bimekizumab (dual IL-17A/F blockade) has the real highest reported PASI100 rate in this survey (59-68% at week 16, 61.7-67.0% head-to-head against secukinumab); ixekizumab (IL-17A) gave real PASI100 34-40% at week 12 across the UNCOVER trials and 34% versus etanercept's 4%; guselkumab and risankizumab (IL-23 p19-specific) gave real PASI100 rates of 36-51% at week 16, rising to 56-60% by week 52 with continued treatment (SKYRIZI and TREMFYA US Prescribing Information, FDA/DailyMed) - IL-23 inhibitors also have the most convenient dosing (every 8-12 weeks after induction); (8) reserve TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept) and ustekinumab (IL-12/23) for patients where IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors are contraindicated, unavailable, or already tried, since head-to-head trials consistently show them outperformed by the newer classes on PASI100, though they remain real, well-established, less expensive options especially where biosimilars are available; (9) treat concurrent psoriatic arthritis risk and cardiometabolic comorbidity (obesity, dyslipidaemia, depression) as part of whole-person psoriasis care, not an afterthought; and (10) accept and explain plainly to the patient that stopping any systemic/biologic will lead to relapse in most people within months - the realistic modern promise of psoriasis treatment is sustained near-total or total skin clearance with continued therapy, not a cure.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side pharmacological intervention for plaque psoriasis, cross-checked against this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis entry for the skin-domain PASI100 story: topical corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors (mild/limited/special-site disease); topical vitamin D analogues and fixed-dose calcipotriol/betamethasone combinations; narrowband UVB phototherapy; conventional oral systemics (methotrexate with the real CHAMPION head-to-head data, cyclosporine with its real rapid-onset/not-for-long-term profile); apremilast (oral PDE4 inhibitor); deucravacitinib (Sotyktu, oral TYK2 inhibitor, the real 2022 novel-mechanism advance, POETYK PSO-1/PSO-2 data); TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept); the IL-12/23 inhibitor ustekinumab; IL-17A(/F) inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) with the real highest-published-PASI100 finding; IL-23 p19-specific inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab). Symptoms, diagnosis and the psoriatic-arthritis joint-disease overlap are covered in this knowledge base's own psoriasis symptoms entry and the psoriatic_arthritis entry respectively, and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial abstract, FDA/DailyMed prescribing information Table of clinical results, or systematic review; where a number could not be verified from a real primary or regulatory source it is not given.

pso_topical_corticosteroids.name: Topical Corticosteroids (Potent/Superpotent) - Halobetasol Propionate 0.01% Lotion Trial
pso_topical_corticosteroids.type: Topical corticosteroid, first-line for mild/limited plaque disease
specific_drugs: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% (superpotent, various vehicles: cream, ointment, foam, spray)
Mometasone furoate 0.1% (potent, lower atrophy risk for longer courses)
pso_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In a randomised, vehicle-controlled trial of halobetasol propionate 0.01% lotion for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis of the lower extremities, overall treatment success (Investigator Global Assessment) was achieved in 37.1% of halobetasol-treated subjects versus 8.4% with vehicle at week 8 (P<0.001), with a 34.2% reduction in affected body surface area and a 50.5% reduction in the combined IGAxBSA severity score versus vehicle (both P<0.001) (Bhatia ND et al, J Drugs Dermatol 2019;18:1029-1036, PMID 31584782).
pso_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids bind the glucocorticoid receptor in keratinocytes and immune cells, suppressing production of inflammatory cytokines (including IL-17, IL-23, TNF pathway genes) and reducing keratinocyte hyperproliferation, giving rapid anti-inflammatory and anti-scaling effect directly at the plaque.
pso_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Long-term continuous use of potent/superpotent topical steroids risks skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae and (with extensive body surface area use) systemic HPA-axis suppression; the lower extremities (as tested here) are relatively steroid-resistant compared with facial/flexural skin, so absolute response rates elsewhere may differ. Tachyphylaxis (reduced response with continuous long-term use) is a recognised real limitation, which is why intermittent/pulse dosing or rotation with a non-steroid topical is standard practice.
pso_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Use a potent-to-superpotent topical corticosteroid for a limited induction course (typically 2-4 weeks) on trunk/limb plaques, then step down to a lower-potency agent or a non-steroid topical (vitamin D analogue, calcineurin inhibitor) for maintenance to reduce atrophy risk; avoid potent/superpotent agents on the face, groin and axillae.
pso_topical_corticosteroids.source: Bhatia ND et al, 'Halobetasol 0.01% Lotion in the Treatment of Moderate-to-Severe Plaque Psoriasis of the Lower Extremities', J Drugs Dermatol 2019;18:1029-1036 (PMID 31584782)

pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.name: Calcipotriene (Vitamin D Analogue) / Betamethasone Dipropionate Fixed-Dose Combination - Aerosol Foam Pooled Trial Data
pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.type: Topical vitamin D analogue + potent corticosteroid, fixed-dose combination, first-line for mild-to-moderate plaque disease
specific_drugs: Calcipotriene 0.005% / betamethasone dipropionate 0.064% ointment/suspension (Taclonex, Xamiol scalp gel)
pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.effectiveness: Pooled analysis of three phase II/III randomised trials (1104 patients) found that at week 4, 51% of patients using calcipotriene/betamethasone dipropionate aerosol foam achieved treatment success (clear/almost clear with >=2-step improvement) versus 43% with the equivalent ointment, 31% with betamethasone-only foam, 15% with calcipotriene-only foam, and 5-8% with vehicle; PASI75 at week 4 was 51% with the combination foam versus 41% (ointment), 34% (steroid alone), 18% (vitamin D alone) and 7-10% (vehicle) (Stein Gold L et al, J Drugs Dermatol 2016;15:951-957, PMID 27537995).
pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.reason_why: Calcipotriene binds the vitamin D receptor, normalising keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation and having independent anti-inflammatory (Th17-suppressing) effects, while betamethasone provides potent anti-inflammatory action; combining the two in one vehicle gives a real additive effect over either agent alone, as this pooled trial data shows directly (51% vs 15% vs 31% treatment success for combination vs vitamin-D-alone vs steroid-alone).
pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.important_caveat: Calcipotriene alone can cause local irritation and, in combination with UV-based therapy, calcipotriol has a lower irritancy profile than older vitamin D analogues (calcitriol, tacalcitol) but is still less potent alone than the fixed combination; high-frequency, high-surface-area application of the corticosteroid component still carries a real atrophy/HPA-axis risk with prolonged continuous use.
pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.real_working_solution: For mild-to-moderate plaque psoriasis, the fixed-dose calcipotriene/betamethasone combination, once daily, applied for 4-8 weeks and then intermittently (e.g. twice weekly) for maintenance, is a real evidence-strong, more effective first-line topical regimen than either monotherapy component.
pso_topical_vitamin_d_and_fixed_combinat.source: Stein Gold L et al, 'Aerosol Foam Formulation of Fixed Combination Calcipotriene Plus Betamethasone Dipropionate is Highly Efficacious in Patients With Psoriasis Vulgaris: Pooled Data From Three Randomized Controlled Studies', J Drugs Dermatol 2016;15:951-957 (PMID 27537995)

pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Tacrolimus Ointment - Real Efficacy for Facial and Intertriginous Psoriasis
pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Topical calcineurin inhibitor, non-steroidal, for steroid-sensitive skin sites
specific_drugs: Pimecrolimus 1% cream (Elidel, used in practice for the same steroid-sparing indication, not separately trialled in this survey)
pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In a randomised, vehicle-controlled trial of tacrolimus 0.1% ointment for facial and intertriginous (skin-fold) psoriasis, clear or almost clear status (Static Severity Score) was achieved by 65.2% of tacrolimus-treated patients versus 31.5% with vehicle at week 8 (P<0.0001); by day 8, 24.8% of the tacrolimus group versus 5.8% of the vehicle group already showed clearance or excellent improvement (P=0.004) (Lebwohl M et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2004;51:723-730, PMID 15523350).
pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin, blocking T-cell activation and cytokine (IL-2, IL-17-pathway) transcription locally in the skin without the collagen-degrading/atrophy-inducing effect of corticosteroids, which is why it works well on inherently thin, steroid-vulnerable skin (face, groin, axillae) where potent steroids cannot be used long-term.
pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: Tacrolimus ointment carries an FDA boxed warning regarding a theoretical long-term malignancy (lymphoma/skin cancer) risk extrapolated from systemic calcineurin-inhibitor use in transplant patients, though this has not been confirmed in topical-use psoriasis/atopic-dermatitis population studies; local burning/stinging on application is common initially.
pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Use tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (not a potent topical steroid) as the real first-line topical agent for facial, genital and skin-fold (intertriginous) plaque psoriasis, where it gives real, trial-verified clearance in about two-thirds of patients by 8 weeks.
pso_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Lebwohl M et al, 'Tacrolimus ointment is effective for facial and intertriginous psoriasis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2004;51:723-730 (PMID 15523350)

pso_phototherapy_narrowband_uvb.name: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) Phototherapy - Systematic Review of 41 RCTs
pso_phototherapy_narrowband_uvb.type: Physical/light-based therapy, non-drug, for moderate-to-severe disease when biologic-sparing option is wanted
specific_drugs: Not a medicine - listed here for completeness of the exhaustive treatment survey
pso_phototherapy_narrowband_uvb.effectiveness: A systematic review of 41 randomised controlled trials (2416 patients) found that as monotherapy, NB-UVB achieved a mean PASI75 rate of 62% (95% CI 45-79%) and a mean clearance rate of 68% (95% CI 57-78%), versus PUVA (photochemotherapy) at 73% PASI75/79% clearance, broadband UVB at 73% PASI75 (wide CI)/59% clearance, and bath PUVA at 47% PASI75/58% clearance (Almutawa F et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2013;14:87-109, PMID 23572293).
