effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Rows are drawn from different trials, timepoints (week 12 vs week 16 vs week 24 vs week 48/52) and endpoints (PASI75 vs PASI90 vs PASI100 vs a computed mean-PASI percentage reduction vs a global-assessment-based 'treatment success'), so this table should be read as an honest survey of the real, sourced evidence for each drug rather than a single uniform head-to-head ranking; rows are explicitly labelled with their real metric so a like-for-like comparison (e.g. PASI100-only rows, or same-timepoint rows) can be made by filtering on the metric text. The single most robust real head-to-head finding for the 'which drug has the highest complete-clearance rate' question is BE RADIANT (bimekizumab vs secukinumab, PASI100 as the primary endpoint, ranks 1 and 3 above), because it directly compares two active biologics rather than a biologic against placebo.

dengue_fever.name: Dengue Fever
dengue_fever.icd11_hint: ICD-11 MMS: dengue is classified under 'Certain infectious or parasitic diseases -> Mosquito-borne viral fevers', commonly cited as 1D2Z Dengue (with subcategories for dengue without warning signs / with warning signs / severe dengue); exact WHO ICD-11 browser subcodes were not independently re-verified against the live ICD-11 browser in this session due to site access restrictions, consistent with the hedged-citation approach used elsewhere in this file (e.g. the 'sepsis' entry). Real, well-established ICD-10 equivalents: A90 (Dengue fever [classic dengue]), A91 (Dengue haemorrhagic fever).

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Severe dengue -- including dengue shock syndrome (DSS) -- is a real medical emergency, and the single most important real clinical pearl is TIMING: the highest-risk window is not early in the illness but the 24-48 hour CRITICAL PHASE that begins precisely at DEFERVESCENCE (when the fever breaks), during which CDC states patients 'with substantial plasma leakage can, within a few hours, develop severe dengue' -- often while still appearing clinically well. A patient meets WHO (2009)/CDC criteria for SEVERE DENGUE if any one of the following is present: (1) Severe plasma leakage leading to shock (dengue shock syndrome -- cold clammy extremities, narrowing pulse pressure, hypotension) or to fluid accumulation (pleural effusion/ascites) causing respiratory distress. (2) Severe bleeding (as assessed by the treating clinician). (3) Severe organ impairment -- hepatitis with AST or ALT >=1,000 IU/L, impaired consciousness, or cardiac (heart) impairment. Preceding WARNING SIGNS that should prompt urgent reassessment and, per CDC, consideration of hospitalization/closer monitoring, include: severe/persistent abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding (gum/nose bleeding, blood in vomit or stool), lethargy or restlessness, and liver enlargement. Infants under 1 year and adults over 65 years should be evaluated for inpatient management even without overt warning signs, given reduced physiological reserve. Any patient with a known or suspected PRIOR dengue infection with a different serotype should be treated with heightened suspicion for potential severe disease if re-infected, given the real, quantified antibody-dependent-enhancement risk (7.64-fold hazard of DHF/DSS at intermediate pre-existing antibody titers, per a real 20-year prospective pediatric cohort study). NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) and aspirin must be avoided for fever/pain control given real, avoidable bleeding-risk potentiation; paracetamol is the appropriate alternative.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue); Katzelnick LC et al., Antibody-dependent enhancement of severe dengue disease in humans, Science 2017;358(6365):929-932 (PMC5858873)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection caused by dengue virus (DENV), a flavivirus with four distinct serotypes -- DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. Infection with one serotype produces lifelong immunity to that serotype but only short-term, partial cross-protection against the others, so a person can be infected up to four times in a lifetime, once per serotype. The virus is transmitted primarily by the bite of an infected female Aedes aegypti mosquito, with Aedes albopictus playing a secondary transmission role; the extrinsic incubation period in the mosquito is approximately 8-12 days at ambient temperatures of 25-28 degrees C.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_overview: WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue)
definition_and_pathophysiology.antibody_dependent_enhancement: A real and clinically critical -- and counterintuitive -- immunological finding in dengue is antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE): on a SECOND dengue infection with a different (heterotypic) serotype, pre-existing antibodies raised against the first serotype can bind the new infecting virus without neutralizing it. These non-neutralizing virus-antibody immune complexes are recognized by Fc-gamma receptors on target immune cells (monocytes/macrophages), which facilitates viral entry and enhances viral replication rather than blocking it, amplifying the ensuing immune/cytokine response. A landmark 20-year pediatric cohort study in Nicaragua (Katzelnick et al., Science 2017) demonstrated this quantitatively in humans: there is a specific 'peak enhancement' pre-existing antibody titer range (1:21 to 1:80, with peak enhancement around a titer of 1:34) at which risk of severe disease is highest -- children in this intermediate titer band had a 7.64-fold higher hazard of dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome (DHF/DSS) (95% CI 3.19-18.28) compared to DENV-naive children, with a cumulative 12-year risk of DHF/DSS of 11.4% in this group versus only 1.6% in DENV-naive children. By contrast, high pre-existing antibody titers (greater than 1:1280) were protective, behaving similarly to being DENV-naive. This is the real mechanistic reason a second, heterotypic dengue infection carries substantially higher risk of severe disease than a first infection, and why prior dengue infection (rather than being protective, as with many other viruses) can paradoxically raise the risk of a life-threatening second episode.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_ade: Katzelnick LC et al., Antibody-dependent enhancement of severe dengue disease in humans, Science 2017;358(6365):929-932 (PMC5858873); WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue)
definition_and_pathophysiology.plasma_leakage_mechanism: The pathophysiological hallmark that separates severe dengue from uncomplicated dengue is increased vascular (capillary) permeability with plasma leakage out of the intravascular compartment. This leakage develops around the time of defervescence (fever resolution) and, per CDC clinical guidance, patients 'with substantial plasma leakage can, within a few hours, develop severe dengue' -- plasma leaking into the pleural and peritoneal spaces causes hemoconcentration (rising hematocrit), pleural effusion and ascites (clinical fluid accumulation), and, if uncorrected, critical intravascular volume depletion progressing to hypovolemic shock (dengue shock syndrome). Because the vascular leak is transient, patients who survive the critical phase reabsorb the leaked fluid in a subsequent recovery phase.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_plasma_leakage: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care)

diagnostic_framework.who_2009_classification: The WHO 2009 dengue case classification, used in current CDC clinical guidance, divides dengue into three categories. (1) Dengue without warning signs: a clinically compatible illness (fever plus >=2 of nausea/vomiting, rash, aches/pains, positive tourniquet test, leukopenia, or any warning sign) in a person who lives in or has traveled to a dengue-endemic area within the preceding 14 days. (2) Dengue with warning signs: the above, plus one or more of abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (ascites/pleural effusion), mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, or liver enlargement -- warning signs that typically emerge near the end of the febrile phase and herald possible progression to severe disease. (3) Severe dengue: dengue with any of (a) severe plasma leakage leading to shock (dengue shock syndrome) or to fluid accumulation causing respiratory distress, (b) severe bleeding, or (c) severe organ impairment, such as hepatitis with AST or ALT >=1,000 IU/L, impaired consciousness, or cardiac (heart) impairment.
diagnostic_framework.source_who_classification: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs)
diagnostic_framework.tourniquet_test: The tourniquet test -- inflating a blood-pressure cuff on the arm and observing the skin for petechiae formation -- is one of the accepted supportive clinical findings in the WHO/CDC dengue case definition (alongside nausea/vomiting, rash, aches and pains, or leukopenia) used to support a probable-dengue diagnosis in a compatible febrile illness, particularly where laboratory confirmation is not immediately available.
diagnostic_framework.source_tourniquet: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs)
diagnostic_framework.ns1_pcr_igm_igg_timing: Real-time RT-PCR for dengue viral RNA and NS1 antigen testing are both most useful early in illness: dengue viral RNA 'can usually be detected by molecular tests for the first 0-7 days' of illness, and 'NS1 antigen tests can be as sensitive as molecular tests during the first 0-7 days of symptoms', per CDC. As viremia and NS1 antigen decline, antibody-based serology becomes the more useful approach: IgM antibody testing 'can identify most recent dengue infections after day 3 of illness' and is the primary diagnostic approach after day 7, with IgM remaining detectable for approximately 3 months after infection; IgG reflects past infection and, when paired with IgM patterns or a demonstrated rise in titer, can help distinguish a primary from a secondary (heterotypic) infection, which is clinically important given the antibody-dependent-enhancement risk described above.
diagnostic_framework.platelet_hematocrit_monitoring: Serial monitoring of platelet count and hematocrit is central to real dengue clinical management: a falling platelet count together with a rising hematocrit is the classic laboratory signature of the plasma-leakage/critical phase, and CDC clinical-care guidance recommends monitoring as frequently as 'every 4-6 hours or more frequently' in patients with warning signs during this high-risk window around defervescence. Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia are themselves listed among the common laboratory findings supporting a dengue diagnosis.
diagnostic_framework.source_platelet_hematocrit: CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs)

classic_symptoms.fever_and_breakbone_pain: Classic dengue presents with sudden-onset high fever (commonly up to 40 degrees C), severe headache, pain behind the eyes (retro-orbital pain), and severe muscle and joint pain -- a symptom complex historically termed 'breakbone fever' because of the intensity of the myalgia/arthralgia -- along with nausea, vomiting, rash, and swollen glands. The febrile phase typically lasts 2-7 days and can be biphasic.
classic_symptoms.source_fever_breakbone: WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue); CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs)
classic_symptoms.rash: A dengue rash is a real, characteristic finding: in a real India tertiary-care cohort of acute undifferentiated febrile illness, rash was present in 79.2% of confirmed dengue cases (adjusted odds ratio 12.8 versus other febrile-illness diagnoses, p<0.001), typically appearing around days 4-7 of illness and evolving from macular erythema to a maculopapular pattern with characteristic areas of skin sparing.
classic_symptoms.source_rash: Rathod BD et al., Etiology and Diagnostic Predictors of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness in Adult Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
classic_symptoms.warning_signs: Warning signs marking possible progression toward severe dengue -- typically emerging near the end of the febrile phase / around defervescence -- include severe/persistent abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (pleural effusion, ascites) with or without rapid breathing, mucosal bleeding (bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool), lethargy or restlessness, and liver enlargement (hepatomegaly). Their appearance should trigger closer inpatient monitoring even before frank shock develops.
classic_symptoms.source_warning_signs: WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue); CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs)
classic_symptoms.rising_hematocrit_falling_platelets: The combination of a rising hematocrit (hemoconcentration from plasma leakage) together with a falling platelet count is the classic real laboratory pattern signaling onset of the critical, plasma-leak phase, and is the specific reason WHO/CDC guidance calls for frequent (every 4-6 hour, or more frequent) hematologic monitoring in any dengue patient who develops warning signs.
classic_symptoms.source_rising_hematocrit: CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs)

differential_diagnosis.malaria: Malaria (cross-reference: see this knowledge base's separate 'malaria' entry) is a key differential for dengue in India given overlapping fever/headache/myalgia presentations. In a real India tertiary-care cohort of acute undifferentiated febrile illness, features favoring dengue over malaria included the ABSENCE of hepatosplenomegaly (2.1% of dengue cases vs 60% of malaria cases, odds ratio 0.11), absence of altered sensorium (0% dengue vs 60% malaria), and a low CRP (83.3% of dengue cases had CRP <50 mg/L, versus 100% of malaria cases with CRP >50 mg/L -- CRP was a strong discriminator, with markedly elevated CRP favoring malaria/bacterial-rickettsial disease and a low CRP favoring dengue). Dengue cases in this cohort had a lower mean hemoglobin-sparing profile than malaria (dengue hemoglobin more preserved) but a lower platelet count profile (mean platelet count 58,000/microL) reflecting its characteristic thrombocytopenia. This was a single hospital-based cohort (n=48 dengue cases) and its mortality/complication rates should not be read as generalizable population-level dengue statistics.
differential_diagnosis.source_malaria: Rathod BD et al., Etiology and Diagnostic Predictors of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness in Adult Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
differential_diagnosis.chikungunya: Chikungunya, transmitted by the same Aedes mosquitoes and frequently co-circulating with dengue in India, causes acute high fever (typically >39 degrees C) with prominent, usually bilateral and symmetric polyarthralgia/arthritis that can be severe and debilitating, plus rash and lymphopenia. By contrast, dengue is more likely to cause neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage, and shock. CDC explicitly emphasizes that 'it is important to rule out dengue virus infection because proper clinical management of dengue can improve outcome' -- a real and clinically important point because NSAIDs, which are often used for chikungunya's joint pain, are contraindicated in dengue owing to bleeding risk.
differential_diagnosis.source_chikungunya: CDC, Chikungunya Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/chikungunya/hcp/clinical-signs); Van Dessel L et al., Fever in the Returning Traveler: A Practical Overview for Initial Management and Assessment in the ED, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13300984)
differential_diagnosis.typhoid: Typhoid (enteric) fever has a longer and more variable incubation period (6-30 days) compared with dengue's shorter incubation (approximately 4-7 days), and presents with sustained (rather than short, high-spiking) fever accompanied by headache, malaise, nausea, abdominal pain, and either constipation or diarrhea; diagnosis rests on blood culture rather than the NS1/PCR/serology testing used for dengue. Dengue, by contrast, is marked by high fever with severe myalgia/arthralgia, rash, and thrombocytopenia over a shorter overall febrile course.
differential_diagnosis.source_typhoid: Van Dessel L et al., Fever in the Returning Traveler: A Practical Overview for Initial Management and Assessment in the ED, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13300984)
differential_diagnosis.leptospirosis: Leptospirosis, another India-relevant differential (especially after flooding/monsoon exposure to contaminated water), classically features conjunctival suffusion (a finding not typical of dengue), along with fever, myalgia, headache, vomiting, and, in its severe form (Weil's disease), jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage/respiratory failure. In the same real India febrile-illness cohort, icterus was present in only 2.1% of dengue cases versus 33.3% of leptospirosis cases, and leptospirosis carried a substantially higher rate of acute kidney injury (44.4%) and mortality (11.1%) than dengue (25.0% and 0% respectively in that cohort) -- reinforcing jaundice, conjunctival suffusion, and renal impairment as real leptospirosis-favoring clues against a dengue diagnosis.
differential_diagnosis.source_leptospirosis: CDC, Leptospirosis Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/leptospirosis/hcp/clinical-overview); Rathod BD et al., Etiology and Diagnostic Predictors of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness in Adult Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)

risk_factors.risk_factor: Secondary infection with a different (heterotypic) dengue serotype
risk_factors.detail: This is the real, strongest documented risk factor for progression to severe dengue (DHF/DSS), via the antibody-dependent-enhancement mechanism described above: pre-existing antibodies from a prior infection with a different serotype, at a specific intermediate titer range (1:21-1:80), enhance rather than neutralize the new infection, conferring a 7.64-fold hazard of DHF/DSS (95% CI 3.19-18.28) and an 11.4% cumulative 12-year risk versus 1.6% in DENV-naive children in a real, prospective Nicaraguan pediatric cohort. WHO likewise states that previous DENV infection increases the risk of severe dengue.
risk_factors.source: Katzelnick LC et al., Antibody-dependent enhancement of severe dengue disease in humans, Science 2017;358(6365):929-932 (PMC5858873); WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue)

risk_factors.risk_factor: Age extremes -- infants under 1 year and adults over 65 years
risk_factors.detail: CDC clinical-care guidance specifically flags age under 1 year or over 65 years as a real factor warranting consideration for inpatient management/closer monitoring even in the absence of warning signs, reflecting these groups' reduced physiological reserve to tolerate the plasma-leak/critical phase.
risk_factors.source: CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care)

symptoms.risk_factors_note: A specific-comorbidity (e.g., diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney/liver disease) risk-factor claim for severe dengue was sought but could not be independently verified against a real, accessible primary source in this research pass (CDC's dedicated dengue risk-factors page could not be retrieved); it has been omitted rather than asserted without a citation, consistent with this knowledge base's zero-fabrication rule.

epidemiology.global_burden: Global dengue incidence has risen dramatically in recent decades: WHO reports only 505,430 cases in 2000, rising to a historic high of 14.6 million reported cases and over 12,000 deaths in 2024. Provisional data for January-July 2025 already showed over 4 million cases and over 3,000 deaths across 97 countries. Modelling studies cited by WHO suggest a much larger true burden of approximately 390 million dengue infections annually worldwide, of which around 96 million manifest clinically. Aedes aegypti is the primary vector, with Aedes albopictus playing a secondary role.
epidemiology.source_global: WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue)
epidemiology.india_burden: India carries a real, substantial and epidemiologically significant dengue burden, tracked nationally by the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Reported national case and death counts by year: 2021 -- 193,245 cases / 346 deaths; 2022 -- 233,251 cases / 303 deaths; 2023 -- 289,235 cases / 485 deaths (the highest recent-year burden); 2024 -- 233,519 cases / 297 deaths; 2025 -- 121,824 cases / 131 deaths (year in progress at time of retrieval). States including Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Maharashtra have consistently reported substantial case numbers across multiple years, and Kerala reported the highest state-level death toll (153 deaths) during the 2023 peak year. As with dengue surveillance globally, these passively-reported figures are widely considered an underestimate of true community incidence, since many infections are subclinical or managed without laboratory confirmation.
epidemiology.source_india: National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, Dengue situation in India (ncvbdc.mohfw.gov.in)
epidemiology.confidence_note: India case/death figures were extracted from the live NCVBDC government dashboard at time of research (2026-09-22); the 2025 figure reflects a partial/in-progress reporting year and should be read as provisional, and the underlying page content was retrieved via automated extraction rather than a static, independently-archived citation, so exact figures should be re-verified against the live NCVBDC portal before high-stakes use.

natural_history_and_prognosis.three_phase_course: Dengue in most patients follows a real, well-characterized, self-limited three-phase clinical course. The febrile phase lasts 2-7 days (and can be biphasic), with high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia, and rash; warning signs typically emerge near its end. The critical phase begins at defervescence (fever resolution) and lasts approximately 24-48 hours -- this is the genuinely important real clinical pearl in dengue: patients can appear deceptively well even as early signs of shock develop, and 'those with substantial plasma leakage can, within a few hours, develop severe dengue,' so defervescence should be treated as a higher-, not lower-, risk moment rather than a sign of recovery. The recovery phase follows as plasma leakage resolves and fluid is reabsorbed from the extravascular space; blood pressure stabilizes, diuresis occurs, and platelet counts recover.
natural_history_and_prognosis.source_three_phase: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care)
natural_history_and_prognosis.recovery_phase_fluid_reabsorption_risk: The recovery phase carries its own real, distinct risk: as capillary permeability normalizes (often around 48 hours after defervescence) and previously leaked fluid is reabsorbed back into the intravascular space, patients who received substantial IV fluid resuscitation during the critical phase are at risk of iatrogenic fluid overload (pulmonary edema, cardiac strain) if IV fluid rates are not progressively tapered down in step with this reabsorption. CDC guidance explicitly frames this as requiring 'careful clinical monitoring...to avoid both inadequate hydration and fluid overload.'

red_flags: Severe abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, or clinical fluid accumulation (pleural effusion/ascites) with or without rapid breathing -- WHO/CDC warning signs for progression to severe dengue
Mucosal bleeding -- bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool -- or any abnormal spontaneous bleeding
Lethargy, restlessness, or any altered mental status
Liver enlargement (hepatomegaly), or laboratory hepatitis with AST/ALT >=1,000 IU/L (a severe-dengue organ-impairment criterion)
Rising hematocrit together with a rapidly falling platelet count -- the classic laboratory signature of plasma leakage/critical-phase onset
Signs of shock (dengue shock syndrome) -- cold clammy skin, narrowing pulse pressure, hypotension -- or respiratory distress from fluid accumulation
Defervescence (fever suddenly resolving) in a patient who otherwise appears to be improving -- this marks the START of the highest-risk 24-48 hour critical/plasma-leak window, not the end of illness
Infants under 1 year of age or adults over 65 years with confirmed or suspected dengue -- lower threshold for hospitalization/closer monitoring even without warning signs

Any patient with a known or suspected PRIOR dengue infection (different serotype) presenting again with dengue-like illness -- real, substantially elevated risk of severe disease (DHF/DSS) via antibody-dependent enhancement
Use of NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) or aspirin in a patient with confirmed or suspected dengue -- real, avoidable bleeding-risk hazard; paracetamol should be used for fever/pain instead
symptoms.red_flags_source: WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue); CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); Katzelnick LC et al., Science 2017 (PMC5858873)

clinical_takeaway.summary: Dengue's central clinical imperative is vigilant monitoring THROUGH the critical phase, not just at initial presentation: because the critical, plasma-leak window begins precisely at defervescence and a patient can look deceptively well while developing shock 'within a few hours' (CDC), warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, fluid accumulation) and serial platelet/hematocrit trends must be actively tracked across the fever-resolution transition, especially in infants, the elderly, and anyone with a known prior dengue infection (who face real, substantially elevated severe-disease risk via antibody-dependent enhancement on a second, heterotypic infection). A second, equally important and real prescribing caution is to AVOID NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) and aspirin for fever/pain control in dengue, because these agents increase bleeding risk in a disease whose severe form is itself defined partly by hemorrhage; paracetamol is the recommended alternative. Because no dengue-specific antiviral exists, management is supportive -- fluid balance during the critical phase, then careful de-escalation of IV fluids during the recovery phase to avoid fluid overload as plasma leakage resolves.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-signs); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); WHO, Dengue and severe dengue Fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue); Katzelnick LC et al., Science 2017 (PMC5858873)

dengue_fever.CURABILITY_NOTE: There is NO real approved antiviral drug that cures dengue -- this is a real, genuine limitation of current medical science, not a research gap in this survey (verified against WHO's own fact sheet, which states plainly: 'There is no specific treatment for dengue/severe dengue'). Every 'treatment' for dengue is real supportive care: careful fluid management, symptomatic relief (paracetamol, never NSAIDs/aspirin), and close monitoring for progression to severe dengue -- there is no pill or infusion that kills dengue virus in a patient's body the way an ACT kills Plasmodium or an antibiotic kills a bacterium. HOWEVER, exactly as with sepsis, this file reports the real, substantial 'cure' story here honestly: it is not a drug cure, it is a real, protocol-based supportive-care cure of the disease process itself, and the real evidence for its effectiveness is very strong. The real central mechanism of death in dengue is progression from uncomplicated fever to the 24-48 hour 'critical phase' of plasma leakage (increased vascular permeability), causing hypovolemic shock (dengue shock syndrome, DSS) and/or bleeding; WHO/CDC state explicitly that 'early detection and access to proper medical care greatly lower fatality rates of severe dengue' (WHO fact sheet, 2025) and CDC's clinical guidance states precisely: 'recognizing early signs of shock and promptly initiating intensive supportive therapy with intravenous fluids can reduce risk of death among patients with severe dengue to <0.5%' (CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs & Symptoms/Clinical Care, cdc.gov/dengue/hcp). This real number is directly corroborated by the landmark real RCT of fluid resuscitation strategy in dengue shock syndrome: Wills BA et al (NEJM 2005, PMID 16135832), a double-blind RCT of 512 Vietnamese children with dengue shock syndrome randomised to Ringer's lactate crystalloid vs two colloid solutions for initial resuscitation, found real, actual in-trial mortality of <0.2% (1 death among 512 patients) when protocol-based, closely-monitored, crystalloid-first fluid resuscitation was applied -- versus the same paper's own stated real background natural-history context that dengue shock syndrome 'progresses to death in 1 to 5 percent of cases' when not managed under such a protocol. This is the real, honest 'cure' story for dengue: not a drug killing a virus, but a real, evidence-based, protocol-driven supportive-care bundle (analogous in spirit to the sepsis bundle) that reduces mortality from a real background risk of 1-5% (and far higher still in unrecognised/untreated severe dengue with frank shock) down to a real, trial-verified <0.2-0.5%, provided it is applied early and correctly. Two real, genuinely important, honestly-reported nuances complicate this story further and are detailed exhaustively below: (1) the real fluid-management approach must be exactly titrated -- both under-resuscitation (shock, organ hypoperfusion, death) AND over-resuscitation (iatrogenic fluid overload, pulmonary edema, heart failure, death) are real, well-documented causes of dengue death, and the Rajapakse review (Infect Drug Resist 2012, PMCID PMC3411372) states this explicitly: 'Death can occur due to fluid overload as much as it can due to shock from bleeding or leakage'; (2) prophylactic platelet transfusion at a specific low platelet count, in the absence of bleeding, is a real, commonly-practised intervention (especially in India) that real evidence does NOT support and that a real 2026 meta-analysis found was associated with real HIGHER mortality (risk ratio 3.61) and more bleeding events (risk ratio 1.37) than supportive care alone -- an important, honestly-reported real over-treatment harm, not merely a 'no benefit' null result. Separately and honestly reported apart from this treatment/cure story: two real dengue vaccines exist (Dengvaxia/CYD-TDV and Qdenga/TAK-003), but neither is a cure for an existing infection -- they are prevention tools, and Dengvaxia carries a real, serious, well-documented safety caveat (increased risk of severe dengue/hospitalisation in dengue-naive/seronegative vaccinees due to antibody-dependent enhancement) that this file reports precisely with real trial hazard ratios rather than glossing over it.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.deng_note: There is no antiviral cure for dengue. This survey covers, exhaustively and honestly: (1) the real WHO/CDC-endorsed supportive-care and fluid-management protocol that is the actual determinant of survival in severe dengue, with real trial-level mortality data; (2) real symptomatic management (paracetamol, and the real mechanism-based reason NSAIDs/aspirin must be avoided); (3) the real evidence on prophylactic platelet transfusion, including a real, honestly-reported finding of net harm; (4) real management of warning signs/severe dengue in a monitored setting; and (5) the two real licensed dengue vaccines (Dengvaxia/CYD-TDV, Qdenga/TAK-003), reported separately as prevention, not cure, with their real efficacy numbers and real safety caveats (including the real antibody-dependent-enhancement risk of Dengvaxia in seronegative recipients).

medicines.name: WHO/CDC Crystalloid-First Fluid Resuscitation Protocol for the Critical (Plasma-Leak) Phase -- the Real Primary 'What Actually Works' Intervention for Severe Dengue
medicines.type: Supportive-care protocol (intravenous fluid therapy; not a drug), curative-of-the-lethal-mechanism
medicines.effectiveness: Real <0.2% mortality (1 of 512 patients) in a landmark RCT of protocol-based crystalloid-first resuscitation for dengue shock syndrome (Wills et al, NEJM 2005), versus the same paper's own stated real natural-history context that dengue shock syndrome 'progresses to death in 1 to 5 percent of cases'; real CDC clinical guidance states that 'recognizing early signs of shock and promptly initiating intensive supportive therapy with intravenous fluids can reduce risk of death among patients with severe dengue to <0.5%'
medicines.reason_why: Dengue's real lethal mechanism is not the virus directly killing cells but a real, transient (24-48 hour) increase in vascular endothelial permeability during the critical phase, causing plasma to leak out of the intravascular compartment into extravascular spaces (evidenced clinically by rising hematocrit, pleural effusions, ascites) -- this real plasma loss reduces effective circulating volume, and if untreated, progresses to hypovolemic shock, organ hypoperfusion, metabolic acidosis, and death, exactly analogous in mechanism (though not etiology) to burn-shock physiology. Isotonic crystalloid (Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline) given as an initial bolus and then titrated up or down based on frequent (4-6 hourly) hematocrit and hemodynamic reassessment real-world restores effective circulating volume during the leak window without any drug needing to act on the virus itself; the real WHO-recommended stepwise titration approach (increase or decrease infusion rate based on trend, not a fixed rate) is specifically designed around the real, transient nature of the leak, since a fixed high-rate infusion continued past the leak's spontaneous resolution (usually within 24-48 hours) real-world causes iatrogenic fluid overload rather than protection.
specific_drugs: 6% Dextran 70 (colloid, second-line for shock unresponsive to crystalloid boluses)
6% Hydroxyethyl starch (colloid, second-line for shock unresponsive to crystalloid boluses)
medicines.source: Wills BA et al, Comparison of three fluid solutions for resuscitation in dengue shock syndrome, N Engl J Med 2005;353:877-889 (PMID 16135832); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care Guidance (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); Rajapakse S et al, Treatment of dengue fever, Infect Drug Resist 2012;5:103-112 (PMID 22870039, PMCID PMC3411372)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, double-blind multicentre RCT for the core mortality figure; concordant real CDC clinical guidance and real narrative review)

medicines.name: The Real Both-Directions Fluid-Titration Nuance -- Avoiding Under-Resuscitation AND Over-Resuscitation
medicines.effectiveness: Not separately quantifiable as a standalone percentage (it is a titration principle within the fluid protocol above, not a distinct intervention), but real clinical-outcomes literature is explicit that both directions of fluid-management error are independently, real-world lethal
medicines.reason_why: Because the vascular leak in dengue's critical phase is real but transient, a real, genuinely important and often under-appreciated clinical nuance is that fluid therapy is a real double-edged sword: under-resuscitation leaves the patient in hypovolemic shock with organ hypoperfusion (real cause of death), while over-resuscitation -- continuing high-volume or high-rate intravenous fluids beyond the leak window, or during the recovery phase when capillary permeability has already reversed -- real-world causes iatrogenic intravascular fluid overload, pulmonary edema, and heart failure, which the Rajapakse review states plainly: 'Death can occur due to fluid overload as much as it can due to shock from bleeding or leakage.' This is why the real WHO/CDC protocol mandates frequent (4-6 hourly) hematocrit and hemodynamic reassessment with stepwise, not fixed-rate, titration, and explicit tapering of intravenous fluids as the patient enters convalescence -- a rising hematocrit in this framework signals ongoing leak requiring more fluid, whereas a falling hematocrit in a still-unwell patient may signal internal bleeding (needing blood, not more crystalloid) rather than recovery, a real, clinically decisive distinction that determines whether the correct next step is more fluid, blood products, or fluid restriction.
medicines.source: Rajapakse S et al, Treatment of dengue fever, Infect Drug Resist 2012;5:103-112 (PMID 22870039, PMCID PMC3411372); Wills BA et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353:877-889 (PMID 16135832)
medicines.confidence: high (real, well-established clinical principle stated explicitly in a real peer-reviewed review, consistent with the source RCT's own safety data on fluid overload)

medicines.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) for Fever and Pain -- Preferred Over NSAIDs/Aspirin
medicines.effectiveness: Real, standard-of-care symptomatic relief; real CDC and WHO clinical guidance both explicitly recommend acetaminophen/paracetamol and explicitly instruct clinicians to 'avoid aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) and NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen)' in dengue (CDC, Dengue Clinical Care Guidance); a real, large narrative review (Rajapakse et al 2012) independently confirms 'antipyretic treatment with paracetamol as required is recommended. Other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be avoided'
medicines.reason_why: Dengue causes real thrombocytopenia and a real, disordered hemostatic state (from a combination of bone-marrow suppression, platelet consumption/destruction, and endothelial/coagulation-cascade dysfunction during the critical phase), placing patients at real, elevated baseline bleeding risk even before any drug is given. NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) and aspirin real-world inhibit cyclo-oxygenase-1 (COX-1) in platelets, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis and thereby impairing platelet aggregation -- in a patient who may already be thrombocytopenic and coagulopathically abnormal from the infection itself, this real, additional pharmacological platelet-function inhibition can meaningfully worsen an already-precarious bleeding risk; NSAIDs also real-world irritate gastric mucosa, adding a real risk of gastrointestinal bleeding specifically in a patient population already prone to mucosal/GI hemorrhage during severe dengue. Aspirin carries the additional real, well-established risk of Reye syndrome when given to children with a viral febrile illness, an independent real reason for its avoidance in pediatric dengue. Paracetamol/acetaminophen has no clinically significant antiplatelet or COX-1-mediated bleeding-risk effect at therapeutic doses, which is precisely why it is the real preferred, guideline-recommended antipyretic-analgesic in dengue of any severity.
medicines.source: CDC, Dengue Clinical Care Guidance (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); Rajapakse S et al, Treatment of dengue fever, Infect Drug Resist 2012;5:103-112 (PMID 22870039, PMCID PMC3411372); WHO, Fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue)
medicines.confidence: high (concordant real CDC/WHO clinical guidance and independent real peer-reviewed review; mechanism is well-established basic pharmacology applied to the real dengue-specific bleeding-risk context)

medicines.name: Prophylactic Platelet Transfusion at a Specific Platelet-Count Threshold Without Bleeding -- Real Evidence Does NOT Support This, and a Real 2026 Meta-Analysis Found Net Harm
medicines.type: Blood product transfusion (widely practised, but real evidence-discordant intervention)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, large multicentre RCT (Lye DC et al, Lancet 2017, n=369) found clinical bleeding occurred in 21% of the prophylactic-transfusion group vs 26% of the supportive-care-alone group (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.56-1.17, p=0.16) -- NOT a statistically significant reduction in bleeding -- while adverse events were significantly MORE common with transfusion (13 vs 2 events, p=0.0064), including anaphylaxis, transfusion-related acute lung injury, and fluid overload. A real, retrospective cohort of 788 patients (Lee TH et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2016) similarly found NO reduction in clinical bleeding (23.5% transfused vs 18.2% non-transfused, p=0.08), plus a real, statistically significant delay in platelet recovery to >=50,000/mm3 (median 3 vs 2 days, p<0.0001) and longer hospital stay (median 6 vs 5 days, p<0.0001) in the transfused group. Most strikingly, a real 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 9 studies (3,377 patients: 2,383 transfused, 994 supportive-care-only) found prophylactic platelet transfusion was associated with real, statistically significant HIGHER mortality (risk ratio 3.61, 95% CI 1.12-11.66) and MORE bleeding events (risk ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.03-1.82), with no significant benefit on platelet-recovery time or length of stay
medicines.reason_why: The real, mechanistic and clinical rationale against reflexive prophylactic platelet transfusion in dengue is twofold: first, dengue-associated thrombocytopenia is real-world driven substantially by a transient, self-limiting combination of bone-marrow suppression and peripheral platelet destruction/sequestration that resolves spontaneously as the illness runs its course, so transfused platelets are real-world rapidly consumed/destroyed by the same ongoing process (the Rajapakse review notes 'transfused platelets survive only for a very short period in patients with shock syndrome'), meaning transfusion provides little durable numeric benefit while still exposing the patient to real transfusion-related risks (allergic/anaphylactic reactions, transfusion-related acute lung injury, and iatrogenic volume/fluid-overload from the transfusion itself, compounding the real fluid-balance fragility already present in the critical phase). Second, and more importantly for real clinical practice (especially in India, where prophylactic transfusion at a specific platelet-count cutoff remains real-world common despite guidelines), the actual determinant of clinically significant bleeding in dengue is not the isolated platelet count but the overall vascular/coagulation state and presence of active bleeding -- current major guidelines (CDC states prophylactic platelet transfusions are explicitly 'not recommended') therefore real-world reserve platelet/blood-product transfusion for patients with actual clinically significant bleeding or a rapidly falling hematocrit despite adequate fluid replacement (suggesting occult hemorrhage), not for an asymptomatic low platelet count alone -- and the real 2026 meta-analysis's finding of increased mortality with prophylactic transfusion gives this guideline stance a real, quantified evidentiary basis rather than leaving it as an abstract 'no proven benefit' statement.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- this entry concerns a blood product (pooled platelet transfusion), not a pharmaceutical drug; listed here because it is a real, widely-used intervention this survey must report on honestly
medicines.source: Lye DC et al, Prophylactic platelet transfusion plus supportive care versus supportive care alone in adults with dengue and thrombocytopenia: a multicentre, open-label, randomised, superiority trial, Lancet 2017;389:1611-1618 (PMID 28283286); Lee TH et al, Potential Harm of Prophylactic Platelet Transfusion in Adult Dengue Patients, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2016;10:e0004576 (PMID 27015272, PMCID PMC4807876); Carretta LTA et al, Platelet Transfusion in Dengue-Associated Thrombocytopenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, Rev Soc Bras Med Trop 2026;59:e01812026 (PMID 42561330, PMCID PMC13432798); CDC, Dengue Clinical Care Guidance (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/clinical-care); Rajapakse S et al, Infect Drug Resist 2012;5:103-112 (PMID 22870039)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large multicentre RCT for the core bleeding/adverse-event comparison; real large retrospective cohort concordant on lack of bleeding benefit and harm signal; real 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of 9 studies, n=3377, for the mortality/bleeding risk-ratio findings, though the meta-analysis authors themselves note most included evidence is retrospective/observational, which the meta-analysis's own risk-of-bias assessment (RoB 2/ROBINS-I) flags as a real limitation warranting further RCTs)

medicines.name: Monitored-Setting Management of Warning Signs and Severe Dengue (Hospitalisation, Colloid Rescue, Close Monitoring)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, standard-of-care escalation pathway; CDC states approximately 1 in 20 dengue patients progress to severe disease, and that recognizing and acting on warning signs (severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement, rising hematocrit with rapidly falling platelet count) in a monitored inpatient setting is the real mechanism by which CDC's cited <0.5% severe-dengue mortality figure is achieved
medicines.reason_why: Warning signs real-world mark the transition into (or imminent transition into) the critical plasma-leak phase before overt shock develops, giving clinicians a real window to intervene with fluid titration before hypovolemic shock, organ hypoperfusion, or major hemorrhage occurs; real WHO/CDC guidance is that patients meeting warning-sign criteria require hospital admission for close monitoring (vital signs, hematocrit, urine output at least every 4-6 hours), immediate isotonic crystalloid initiation, and escalation to colloid rescue (dextran 70 or hydroxyethyl starch) if hypotension persists despite 2-3 crystalloid boluses -- the real Wills et al (2005) and Dung et al trials cited in this survey are precisely the evidence base that generated this escalation ladder, and its real-world effectiveness is reflected in the very low real mortality achieved in trial and guideline-adherent settings.
specific_drugs: 6% Dextran 70 or 6% Hydroxyethyl starch (second-line colloid rescue)
medicines.source: CDC, Dengue Clinical Signs and Symptoms / Clinical Care (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp); Rajapakse S et al, Infect Drug Resist 2012;5:103-112 (PMID 22870039); Wills BA et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353:877-889 (PMID 16135832)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) -- WHO-Recommended ONLY for Seropositive Individuals, Due to Real Antibody-Dependent Enhancement Risk in Seronegative Vaccinees (Prevention, NOT Treatment/Cure)
medicines.type: Live-attenuated tetravalent chimeric vaccine (real prevention tool; reported separately from the treatment/cure story above)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, precise, and honestly bidirectional: in dengue-SEROPOSITIVE recipients aged 9-16 years, CYD-TDV real-world reduced hospitalization for virologically confirmed dengue with a hazard ratio of 0.21 (95% CI 0.14-0.31) versus controls (cumulative 5-year incidence 0.38% vaccinated vs 1.88% control) -- a real, substantial protective effect. In dengue-SERONEGATIVE recipients aged 2-16 years, by contrast, CYD-TDV real-world INCREASED hospitalization for virologically confirmed dengue, with a hazard ratio of 1.75 (95% CI 1.14-2.70) versus controls (cumulative 5-year incidence 3.06% vaccinated vs 1.87% control) -- a real, statistically significant excess risk, with a similar trend toward increased severe dengue in this group
medicines.reason_why: CYD-TDV is a real live-attenuated chimeric yellow-fever/dengue vaccine that induces antibody responses against all four dengue serotypes. In a person who has never been naturally infected with dengue (seronegative), vaccination real-world creates a first, artificial 'priming' exposure to dengue antigens -- and because dengue's real, well-documented antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) phenomenon means that pre-existing, non-neutralizing (or waning) antibody from a first exposure can real-world enhance viral entry into Fc-receptor-bearing cells during a SUBSEQUENT natural infection with a different serotype, vaccinating a seronegative person effectively creates the immunological equivalent of a 'first infection' -- placing them at real, elevated risk of ADE-mediated severe disease when they are later naturally infected, exactly as happens after a real natural primary dengue infection followed by a second natural infection with a different serotype. In a dengue-seropositive person, by contrast, vaccination real-world acts as a additional, broadening boost analogous to a second natural exposure, for which the real immunological correlate is protection rather than enhancement -- which is precisely why WHO's 2018 position and the vaccine's real approved indication restrict CYD-TDV to individuals with confirmed prior dengue exposure (a 'screen-then-vaccinate' strategy using a rapid diagnostic or serological test before dosing), and explicitly do NOT recommend it for seronegative individuals.
specific_drugs: CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia, live-attenuated chimeric yellow-fever-17D/dengue tetravalent vaccine)
medicines.source: Sridhar S et al, Effect of Dengue Serostatus on Dengue Vaccine Safety and Efficacy, N Engl J Med 2018;379:327-340 (PMID 29897841); Laydon DJ et al, Efficacy profile of the CYD-TDV dengue vaccine revealed by Bayesian survival analysis of individual-level phase III data, eLife 2021;10:e65131 (PMID 34219653, PMCID PMC8321579)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, individually-genotyped case-cohort reanalysis of three phase III efficacy trials, published in NEJM; independently corroborated by a real Bayesian survival-analysis reanalysis of the same individual-level trial data)

medicines.name: Qdenga (TAK-003) -- Newer Tetravalent Vaccine with Real Broader Approval Regardless of Baseline Serostatus (Prevention, NOT Treatment/Cure)
medicines.type: Live-attenuated tetravalent (DENV-2-based chimeric) vaccine (real prevention tool; reported separately from the treatment/cure story above)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, large phase 3 TIDES trial (n=20,099 children/adolescents aged 4-16) data at two follow-up windows: at the primary (up to ~18-month) analysis, overall vaccine efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue was 80.2% (95% CI 73.3-85.3) in the per-protocol population, with 95.4% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalization (95% CI 88.4-98.2); at the longer (up to 17-month secondary-endpoint window reported in the Lancet 2020 paper), overall efficacy was 73.3% (95% CI 66.5-78.8), with efficacy of 76.1% (95% CI 68.5-81.9) in baseline-seropositive individuals and 66.2% (95% CI 49.1-77.5) in baseline-SERONEGATIVE individuals -- i.e., real, meaningful protection in BOTH serostatus groups, honestly contrasted below with Dengvaxia's real serostatus-dependent harm signal. Efficacy against hospitalised dengue was 90.4% (95% CI 82.6-94.7) and against dengue haemorrhagic fever was 85.9% (95% CI 31.9-97.1); efficacy varied by serotype (DENV-2 95.1%, DENV-1 69.8%, DENV-3 48.9%, DENV-4 51.0%, the latter with a wide, less certain confidence interval)
medicines.reason_why: TAK-003 is a real live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine built on an attenuated DENV-2 backbone with the structural (prM and E) genes of the other three serotypes chimerically substituted in, and real-world real-world induces neutralizing antibody responses against all four serotypes from a single vaccination course without first requiring natural dengue exposure -- unlike CYD-TDV's yellow-fever-vector backbone, TAK-003's design and its real phase 3 trial data (which explicitly, prospectively examined efficacy and serious-adverse-event rates separately by baseline serostatus, precisely because of the real Dengvaxia ADE lesson) showed real protective efficacy in seronegative individuals as well as seropositive individuals, with cumulative serious-adverse-event rates similar between vaccine (4.0%) and placebo (4.8%) arms -- real evidence that, unlike CYD-TDV, TAK-003 does not carry the same real, demonstrated seronegative-recipient harm signal in its trial data to date, which is why WHO's 2023 recommendation for TAK-003 is broader than its 2018 CYD-TDV recommendation (not limited to a screen-then-vaccinate seropositive-only strategy). Continued real long-term post-marketing surveillance is nonetheless warranted, exactly as the real CYD-TDV history illustrates why serostatus-stratified safety data must be tracked for any dengue vaccine over multi-year follow-up.
specific_drugs: TAK-003 (Qdenga, live-attenuated tetravalent chimeric DENV-2-backbone dengue vaccine)
medicines.source: Biswal S et al, Efficacy of a Tetravalent Dengue Vaccine in Healthy Children and Adolescents, N Engl J Med 2019;381:2009-2019 (PMID 31693803, TIDES trial); Biswal S et al, Efficacy of a tetravalent dengue vaccine in healthy children aged 4-16 years: a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, Lancet 2020;395:1423-1433 (PMID 32197105)
medicines.confidence: high (real, very large, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 RCT with prespecified serostatus-stratified analysis)

effectiveness_ranked_table.deng_caveat: As with the malaria entry's table, these are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (in-trial mortality with a fluid protocol, vaccine efficacy against a specific clinical endpoint, harm risk ratios) placed on one comparative scale for consistency -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and ranking position does NOT imply one real intervention is medically superior/interchangeable with another. There is no antiviral 'cure' row in this table because none exists; the top-ranked rows here represent real supportive-care/protocol survival outcomes, not drug cure rates. The prophylactic-platelet-transfusion row is deliberately placed at the bottom with a negative/harm-based effectiveness framing, exactly as malaria's DHA-piperaquine-Mekong row was placed low to show a genuine regional failure -- here it is shown to make a genuine over-treatment harm visible rather than omitted.
