atopic_dermatitis.name: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
atopic_dermatitis.icd11_hint: EA80 Atopic eczema (EA80.0 atopic eczema in remission / EA80.Z unspecified; ICD-10-CM L20 Atopic dermatitis, L20.8 Other atopic dermatitis, L20.9 Atopic dermatitis, unspecified)

skin_barrier_dysfunction_and_filaggrin.finding: Atopic dermatitis (AD) pathogenesis begins with impairment of epidermal barrier function - for example owing to deficiency in the structural protein filaggrin (FLG) - which promotes cutaneous inflammation and T-cell infiltration. Filaggrin is a key structural protein for the stratum corneum's cornified envelope and natural-moisturising-factor generation; loss-of-function FLG null mutations (such as 2282del4 and R501X) are carried by about 8-10% of the general European population and are associated with earlier onset and greater persistence of AD into adulthood, though the relationship is probabilistic rather than deterministic - a hospital-clinic and birth-cohort study found that filaggrin-null homozygous/compound-heterozygous individuals made up only 0.3% of a general adult population sample versus 3% of dermatitis-clinic patients, and that roughly one in nine such adults and one in three such children had never developed dermatitis at all, with year-long complete remission observed in half of the affected hospital patients studied.
skin_barrier_dysfunction_and_filaggrin.source: Weidinger S, Beck LA, Bieber T, Kabashima K, Irvine AD, 'Atopic dermatitis', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Thyssen JP et al, 'Individuals who are homozygous for the 2282del4 and R501X filaggrin null mutations do not always develop dermatitis and complete long-term remission is possible', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2012;26(3):386-389 (PMID 21501248)
skin_barrier_dysfunction_and_filaggrin.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved and quoted via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session

th2_skewed_immune_dysregulation_il4_il13.finding: The immune response in AD is skewed towards T-helper-2 (Th2) cell-mediated pathways, which can in turn favour further epidermal barrier disruption, creating a self-reinforcing barrier-immune cycle. A 2020 Lancet seminar states the disease's pathophysiology 'involves a strong genetic predisposition, epidermal dysfunction, and T-cell driven inflammation, and although type-2 mechanisms are dominant, there is increasing evidence that the disorder involves multiple immune pathways.' This Th2/type-2 axis - centred on the cytokines IL-4 and IL-13 - is genuinely important because it is the direct mechanistic basis for the modern biologic-drug story in AD (e.g., IL-4Ralpha- and IL-13-targeted biologics), mirroring how the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 axis underlies the biologic story in this knowledge base's psoriasis entry.
th2_skewed_immune_dysregulation_il4_il13.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Langan SM, Irvine AD, Weidinger S, 'Atopic dermatitis', Lancet 2020;396(10247):345-360 (PMID 32738956)
th2_skewed_immune_dysregulation_il4_il13.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

other_contributing_mechanisms.finding: Beyond barrier dysfunction and Th2 skewing, other mechanisms contribute to AD onset and clinical manifestations: dysbiosis of the skin microbiota (in particular overgrowth of Staphylococcus aureus), systemic immune responses including IgE-mediated sensitisation, and neuroinflammation, which is directly involved in generating the disease's hallmark itch. A 2026 update of the same primer series further notes AD is associated with other immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (alopecia areata, vitiligo, inflammatory bowel disease) and that understanding has advanced toward 'the complex interplay between the skin barrier, cutaneous and systemic immune pathways, cutaneous microbiome and neural networks.'
other_contributing_mechanisms.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Weidinger S, Aoki V, Dhar S et al, 'Atopic dermatitis', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026;12(1):36 (PMID 42243136)
other_contributing_mechanisms.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

atopic_march_concept.finding: The 'atopic march' describes the increased occurrence of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or both, following AD onset in some patients, historically framed as a sequential progression from skin disease to respiratory allergic disease. Proposed mechanisms include an impaired cutaneous barrier facilitating cutaneous allergen sensitisation, and a systemic Th2-dominant immune response to cutaneous inflammation amplifying the association in susceptible individuals. However, a 2019 review in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology honestly notes these associations 'might merely involve shared genetic loci and environmental triggers...with the temporal sequence reflecting tissue-specific peak time of occurrence of each disease, suggesting more of a clustering of disorders than a march' - i.e., the strict sequential 'march' framing is itself debated in the current literature, and risk factors for developing multiple atopic comorbidities include disease severity and persistence, age of onset, parental atopic history, filaggrin mutations, polysensitisation, and a non-rural environment. A 2022 comparison of paediatric versus adult AD similarly notes that 'most [atopic comorbidities] do not temporally have the atopic march.'
atopic_march_concept.source: Paller AS, Spergel JM, Mina-Osorio P, Irvine AD, 'The atopic march and atopic multimorbidity: Many trajectories, many pathways', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2019;143(1):46-55 (PMID 30458183); Ramirez-Marin HA, Silverberg JI, 'Differences between pediatric and adult atopic dermatitis', Pediatr Dermatol 2022;39(3):345-353 (PMID 35297082)
atopic_march_concept.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the 'march is debated/more a clustering' nuance is a direct quote, not this knowledge base's own interpretation

hanifin_rajka_and_uk_working_party_clini.finding: AD is diagnosed clinically - there is no single confirmatory laboratory test. A 2009 review states that although numerous diagnostic-criteria sets have been proposed, 'at present the two most reliable are the 2003 revision by the American Academy of Dermatology of the Hanifin-Rajka criteria, and those by Williams revised in 2005.' The original UK Working Party diagnostic criteria (Williams HC et al) were independently validated in a 1994 British Journal of Dermatology hospital-validation study, requiring an itchy skin condition (or parental report of scratching/rubbing in a child) plus three or more of: history of flexural involvement, personal history of asthma or hay fever (or atopic disease in a first-degree relative in children under 4), a history of generally dry skin in the last year, visible flexural eczema (or eczema affecting cheeks/forehead and outer limbs in children under 4), and onset before age 2 (this last criterion not used if the child is under 4).
hanifin_rajka_and_uk_working_party_clini.source: Ricci G, Dondi A, Patrizi A, 'Useful tools for the management of atopic dermatitis', Am J Clin Dermatol 2009;10(5):287-300 (PMID 19658441); Williams HC et al, 'The U.K. Working Party's Diagnostic Criteria for Atopic Dermatitis. III. Independent hospital validation', Br J Dermatol 1994;131(3):406-416 (PMID 7918017)
hanifin_rajka_and_uk_working_party_clini.confidence: high for the Ricci review's direct quote on the two most-reliable criteria sets and validated severity tools, retrieved via PubMed/eutils; moderate-high for the specific listed UK Working Party criteria items, which reflect this knowledge base's standard recall of the well-established Williams criteria content rather than a directly re-quoted checklist from the abstract itself (the abstract confirms the paper's existence, authorship, journal, year and its role as an independent hospital validation of these criteria)

easi_and_scorad_severity_scoring_tools.finding: To date, roughly 20 different clinical severity scores have been published for AD; the same 2009 review states that 'only the EASI (Eczema Area and Severity Index), the SCORAD (SCORing Atopic Dermatitis), and the POEM (Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure) seem to have been adequately validated and are recommended for use in clinical practice and trials.' These tools quantify extent and intensity of eczematous lesions (EASI, SCORAD) or patient-reported symptom burden (POEM) and are used both to grade severity (mild/moderate/severe) and to track treatment response over time.
easi_and_scorad_severity_scoring_tools.source: Ricci G, Dondi A, Patrizi A, Am J Clin Dermatol 2009;10(5):287-300 (PMID 19658441)
easi_and_scorad_severity_scoring_tools.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; this knowledge base was not able to independently verify the exact numeric severity-band cutoffs (e.g., specific EASI/SCORAD score ranges defining mild vs moderate vs severe) against a primary source in this research pass, and that specific cutoff-number detail is therefore omitted rather than asserted

allergy_and_patch_testing_role.finding: Diagnostic work-up to identify associated allergy or sensitisation - relevant to differentiating AD from, or identifying co-existing, allergic contact dermatitis - includes skin-prick tests, measurement of specific IgE in serum, and atopy patch tests; a food challenge may be required when food allergy is specifically suspected. These allergy-focused tests are adjuncts used when sensitisation or a contact-allergic contributor is suspected, not primary diagnostic criteria for AD itself, since AD remains a clinical diagnosis made on history and morphology.
allergy_and_patch_testing_role.source: Ricci G, Dondi A, Patrizi A, Am J Clin Dermatol 2009;10(5):287-300 (PMID 19658441)
allergy_and_patch_testing_role.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

intense_pruritus_as_hallmark.finding: Intense, chronic pruritus (itch) is the cardinal, defining symptom of AD across all phenotypes and severities, driving a repetitive itch-scratch cycle. AD is characterised by 'intense itch, recurrent eczematous lesions and a fluctuating course.' A 2026 review on the itch-scratch cycle notes this cycle 'can be worsened or triggered by stress' and involves both peripheral neuroimmune sensitisation and central brain circuits (with the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex shown to be overactive while regulating the itch-scratch circuit in AD patients on neuroimaging), such that some patients continue scratching despite clinical improvement on conventional treatment.
intense_pruritus_as_hallmark.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Steinhoff M, Yosipovitch G, Canchy L et al, 'Breaking the Itch-Scratch Cycle: An Integrative Approach for Atopic Dermatitis', Dermatitis 2026;37(4):541-553 (PMID 40813061)
intense_pruritus_as_hallmark.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

age_dependent_distribution_pattern.finding: AD's lesion distribution changes systematically with age, per a 2026 pediatric review directly read in full text. In infancy (0-2 years): 'lesions mostly appear on the cheeks and scalp and may extend to the trunk and extensor surfaces of the extremities during disease flares,' with facial involvement and 'relative sparing of the diaper area' considered diagnostically helpful (diaper-area sparing helps distinguish AD from irritant/contact diaper dermatitis). In childhood (2-12 years): 'lesions most frequently involve flexural areas, particularly the antecubital fossae, popliteal fossae, wrists, ankles, and neck.' In adolescence (12 years and older): distribution 'most commonly involves flexural areas such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae as well as the neck and periocular regions.' A 2022 comparison of paediatric versus adult AD confirms flexural involvement, atopy and xerosis as core features shared across ages, while noting adults show more chronic-disease signs, a higher prevalence and different pattern of hand eczema, and a stronger link between disease activity and emotional factors; children more often show exudative lesions, perifollicular accentuation, pityriasis alba, Dennie-Morgan folds, and a seborrheic-dermatitis-like presentation.
age_dependent_distribution_pattern.source: Ture Avci B, Cetinarslan T, Turel Ermertcan A, Folster-Holst R, 'Atopic Dermatitis in Children: Differential Diagnosis and Mimickers', Children (Basel) 2026;13(5):690 (PMID 42194216, PMCID PMC13204710, open-access full text directly read in this session); Ramirez-Marin HA, Silverberg JI, Pediatr Dermatol 2022;39(3):345-353 (PMID 35297082)
age_dependent_distribution_pattern.confidence: high - the age-band distribution quotes were directly read from the open-access full-text article (not just the abstract), and the paediatric-vs-adult contrast is directly quoted from the second abstract

xerosis_dry_skin.finding: Generalised xerosis (dry skin) is a near-universal, core feature of AD across the age spectrum, reflecting the underlying epidermal barrier/filaggrin defect, and is one of the shared core features present in both children and adults with AD.
xerosis_dry_skin.source: Ramirez-Marin HA, Silverberg JI, Pediatr Dermatol 2022;39(3):345-353 (PMID 35297082); Ture Avci B et al, Children (Basel) 2026;13(5):690 (PMID 42194216)
xerosis_dry_skin.confidence: high - directly supported by both sources retrieved in this session

chronic_scratching_and_lichenification.finding: Repeated, chronic scratching in response to persistent pruritus drives lichenification (thickened, leathery skin with accentuated skin markings), a hallmark feature of chronic-phase AD lesions, as part of the self-perpetuating itch-scratch cycle described in the 2026 integrative-management review of AD itch mechanisms.
chronic_scratching_and_lichenification.confidence: high for the itch-scratch-to-lichenification mechanism, drawn from the directly retrieved abstract; the specific term 'lichenification' as the classic morphological descriptor of chronic AD is standard, well-established dermatology terminology consistent with this source's described mechanism rather than a term directly quoted verbatim from this specific abstract

acute_versus_chronic_phase_morphology.finding: AD has a fluctuating course with acute flares (more exudative, oedematous, erythematous lesions, especially prominent in children per the paediatric-vs-adult comparison above) alternating with a chronic phase (drier, thickened, lichenified plaques, more prominent in adults and in long-standing disease), consistent with the disease being described as having 'a fluctuating course' with a chronic relapsing-remitting pattern overall.
acute_versus_chronic_phase_morphology.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Ramirez-Marin HA, Silverberg JI, Pediatr Dermatol 2022;39(3):345-353 (PMID 35297082)
acute_versus_chronic_phase_morphology.confidence: moderate-high - the fluctuating/relapsing-remitting course and the paediatric (more exudative) versus adult (more chronic-signs) contrast are each directly sourced; the general acute-versus-chronic morphological framing itself is standard dermatology teaching consistent with, though not a single verbatim quote from, these sources

psoriasis.finding: Psoriasis can mimic AD, particularly in infancy and in flexural (inverse) presentations, but the two differ in typical morphology and immune driver: this knowledge base's own psoriasis entry documents psoriasis as classically producing well-demarcated erythematous, desquamative plaques on extensor surfaces/scalp/nails, driven predominantly by the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 axis, versus AD's poorly demarcated, pruritic, xerotic, eczematous lesions with lichenification, driven predominantly by Th2/IL-4/IL-13 pathways (see this entry's own definition_and_pathophysiology and this knowledge base's psoriasis entry, differential_diagnosis.eczema_atopic_dermatitis, for the reciprocal cross-reference). A 2006 review on childhood AD differential diagnosis specifically lists psoriasis among diseases mimicking AD in infancy.
psoriasis.source: Cross-reference to this knowledge base's own psoriasis entry (differential_diagnosis.eczema_atopic_dermatitis, sourced there to Trovato F et al, Dermatol Pract Concept 2026, PMCID PMC13557259); Krol A, Krafchik B, 'The differential diagnosis of atopic dermatitis in childhood', Dermatol Ther 2006;19(2):73-82 (PMID 16669989)
psoriasis.confidence: high - both the cross-referenced existing knowledge-base content and the Krol/Krafchik abstract were directly checked in this session

seborrheic_dermatitis.finding: Seborrheic dermatitis is an important AD mimicker, especially in infancy, and the two can be distinguished clinically: per a 2026 open-access review, 'seborrheic dermatitis is usually characterized by oilier scales and minimal pruritus, whereas AD typically presents with marked pruritus and xerosis,' and seborrheic dermatitis 'commonly affects intertriginous areas and the diaper region, which are typically spared in infantile AD' - i.e., diaper-area involvement favours seborrheic dermatitis (or irritant contact/diaper dermatitis) over AD, while marked itch and dryness favour AD.
seborrheic_dermatitis.source: Ture Avci B et al, Children (Basel) 2026;13(5):690 (PMID 42194216, PMCID PMC13204710, open-access full text directly read in this session)
seborrheic_dermatitis.confidence: high - directly quoted from the open-access full text

contact_dermatitis_allergic_and_irritant.finding: Both irritant and allergic contact dermatitis can mimic AD. Per the same 2026 review, contact dermatitis 'usually presents as localized reactions associated with irritants - most notably diaper dermatitis - or allergens,' whereas 'AD usually spares the diaper region and presents as pruritic eczematous lesions on other body sites' - making anatomic distribution (localised-to-contact-site vs. widespread pruritic/flexural) and a history of a specific triggering exposure the key discriminators. When allergic contact dermatitis is specifically suspected as a co-existing or confounding diagnosis, patch testing (see this entry's diagnostic_framework.allergy_and_patch_testing_role) is the standard confirmatory test.
contact_dermatitis_allergic_and_irritant.source: Ture Avci B et al, Children (Basel) 2026;13(5):690 (PMID 42194216, PMCID PMC13204710, open-access full text directly read in this session); Ricci G et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2009;10(5):287-300 (PMID 19658441)
contact_dermatitis_allergic_and_irritant.confidence: high - both sources directly retrieved in this session

scabies.finding: Scabies is a key mimicker to actively exclude, since missing it delays appropriate antiparasitic treatment and risks household spread. Per the same 2026 review, scabies should be suspected 'when pruritus is severe or when lesions involve the palms, soles, or axillary folds,' and key distinguishing features include a 'history of pruritus affecting other household members and the nocturnal exacerbation of itching' - features not typical of AD itself.
scabies.source: Ture Avci B et al, Children (Basel) 2026;13(5):690 (PMID 42194216, PMCID PMC13204710, open-access full text directly read in this session)
scabies.confidence: high - directly quoted from the open-access full text

family_history_of_atopy.finding: A personal or family (first-degree relative) history of atopic disease - AD, asthma, or allergic rhinitis/hay fever - is a core risk factor and is explicitly embedded in the UK Working Party diagnostic criteria as a major criterion. AD has 'a strong heritability component and is closely related to and commonly co-occurs with other atopic diseases.'
family_history_of_atopy.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Williams HC et al, Br J Dermatol 1994;131(3):406-416 (PMID 7918017)
family_history_of_atopy.confidence: high - directly supported by the retrieved Weidinger abstract; the specific UK Working Party criterion content reflects this knowledge base's standard recall of the well-established Williams criteria rather than a verbatim quote from the abstract itself

filaggrin_gene_mutations.finding: Loss-of-function filaggrin (FLG) gene null mutations are carried by about 8-10% of the general European population and are associated with earlier-onset and more persistent AD, though - as detailed in this entry's definition_and_pathophysiology - the genotype is neither necessary nor sufficient: not all carriers develop dermatitis, and long-term complete remission is possible even in those who do.
filaggrin_gene_mutations.source: Thyssen JP et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2012;26(3):386-389 (PMID 21501248)
filaggrin_gene_mutations.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

urban_and_non_rural_environment.finding: A non-rural (urban) environment is identified as a risk factor for developing atopic comorbidities in children with AD in the 2019 atopic-march review, consistent with a broader, long-debated literature link between Western/urbanised lifestyle and rising allergic-disease prevalence. A 2015 global epidemiology review notes AD prevalence is still increasing, especially in low-income countries, and frames disease development as requiring the interaction of a genetically dysfunctional epidermal barrier with 'harmful effects of environmental agents' rather than genetics alone.
urban_and_non_rural_environment.source: Paller AS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2019;143(1):46-55 (PMID 30458183); Nutten S, 'Atopic dermatitis: global epidemiology and risk factors', Ann Nutr Metab 2015;66(Suppl 1):8-16 (PMID 25925336)
urban_and_non_rural_environment.confidence: high for the specific 'non-rural environment' risk-factor finding, directly quoted from Paller et al; moderate for the broader Western-lifestyle association framing, which the Nutten review supports in general terms (rising prevalence, environmental-agent interaction) without stating a specific quantified urban-versus-rural effect size

early_life_factors_debated.finding: This knowledge base could not locate, in this research pass, a specific primary source directly quantifying which early-life factors (e.g., mode of delivery, early antibiotic exposure, timing of complementary feeding, early skin-barrier interventions) causally alter AD risk with a verified effect size; the Nutten 2015 review frames this honestly at a mechanistic level only, stating that genetic mutations alone are insufficient and that the disease results from a dysfunctional epidermal barrier in genetically predisposed individuals interacting with environmental exposures, without giving a specific quantified early-life risk factor. This item is therefore reported as a general, literature-acknowledged area of interaction/debate rather than a specific proven early-life causal factor, and no specific unverified percentage is asserted.
early_life_factors_debated.confidence: moderate - the general gene-environment interaction framing is directly quoted; a specific early-life causal risk factor with an effect size could not be independently verified in this session and is deliberately not asserted

asthma_and_allergic_rhinitis.finding: AD is closely related to and commonly co-occurs with asthma and allergic rhinitis, historically framed under the 'atopic march' (see definition_and_pathophysiology.atopic_march_concept for the honest nuance that current literature increasingly describes this as clustering of shared-risk conditions rather than a strict sequential march in every patient).
asthma_and_allergic_rhinitis.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Paller AS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2019;143(1):46-55 (PMID 30458183)
asthma_and_allergic_rhinitis.confidence: high - directly supported by both retrieved abstracts

food_allergy.finding: Food allergy is a recognised AD comorbidity within the broader 'atopic multimorbidity' spectrum; a 2026 update of the disease-primer literature lists food allergy, asthma, allergic rhinitis and eosinophilic oesophagitis together as comorbidities 'mainly driven by type 2 immune responses,' the same Th2/IL-4/IL-13 axis underlying AD's own skin pathophysiology.
food_allergy.source: Weidinger S, Aoki V, Dhar S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026;12(1):36 (PMID 42243136)
food_allergy.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

mental_health_and_sleep_disruption.finding: Chronic pruritus and inflammation in AD lead to sleep disturbances and mental-health symptoms, which are not mutually exclusive of each other. A 2017 review found persons with AD at higher risk of multiple neuropsychiatric disorders, including depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, childhood speech disorders, headaches, and seizures, alongside a multifactorial association with osteoporosis, injuries and fractures. A 2026 disease-primer update separately lists 'mental health disorders' and 'disordered bone health' among AD's recognised comorbidities, and AD now 'carries the highest disability-adjusted life-years burden [of skin diseases], ranking 15th among all non-fatal diseases globally.'
mental_health_and_sleep_disruption.source: Silverberg JI, 'Selected comorbidities of atopic dermatitis: Atopy, neuropsychiatric, and musculoskeletal disorders', Clin Dermatol 2017;35(4):360-366 (PMID 28709566, PMCID PMC5512438); Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026;12(1):36 (PMID 42243136)
mental_health_and_sleep_disruption.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved and quoted via PubMed/eutils in this session

global_prevalence.finding: Reported global AD prevalence varies substantially depending on whether lifetime or point prevalence is measured, and by methodology. Lifetime-prevalence estimates are markedly higher: a 2018 Nature Reviews Disease Primers article states AD has 'a lifetime prevalence of up to 20%,' and a 2015 review similarly states AD 'affects up to 20% of children and up to 3% of adults,' with prevalence still increasing, especially in low-income countries. By contrast, a 2023 Bayesian hierarchical modelling study synthesising 344 studies across four databases estimated a global point prevalence of AD of only 2.6% (95% uncertainty interval 1.9-3.5%), affecting an estimated 204.05 million people worldwide - 4.0% of children (102.78 million) and 2.0% of adults (101.27 million) - and found AD point prevalence somewhat higher in females (2.8%) than males (2.4%). This knowledge base reports both figures honestly rather than collapsing them into one number, since the difference reflects real methodological divergence (lifetime-ever-diagnosed vs. point-in-time prevalence), not a contradiction in the underlying disease burden; both sources agree AD is among the most common chronic skin diseases, especially in children, and is 'the leading cause of the global burden from skin disease.'
global_prevalence.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Nutten S, Ann Nutr Metab 2015;66(Suppl 1):8-16 (PMID 25925336); Tian J, Zhang D, Yang Y et al, 'Global epidemiology of atopic dermatitis: a comprehensive systematic analysis and modelling study', Br J Dermatol 2023;190(1):55-61 (PMID 37705227); Langan SM et al, Lancet 2020;396(10247):345-360 (PMID 32738956)
global_prevalence.confidence: high - all figures directly quoted from abstracts retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the lifetime-vs-point-prevalence discrepancy is flagged explicitly rather than silently resolved

india_specific_data.finding: India-specific AD epidemiological data are limited and non-nationally-representative. A 2023 systematic literature review (De A et al, including 11 studies published 2011-2021) found reported AD prevalence ranging from 3.1% to 7.21% among the paediatric population (up to 16 years of age), and from 0.98% to 9.2% when studies including both paediatric and adult patients were considered; the review explicitly notes 'there is a lack of comprehensive understanding of the disease burden of AD in India' and that 'none of the current studies covers the entire country.' Cost of medications was reported as the major contributor to economic burden, and mental illnesses (depression, anxiety) were frequently reported in association with AD in the Indian studies reviewed.
india_specific_data.source: De A, Karekar S, Adhav C, 'Current Burden of Atopic Dermatitis in India: A Systematic Literature Review', Indian J Dermatol 2023;68(4):487 (PMID 37822382, PMCID PMC10564215)
india_specific_data.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the review's own honest limitation (no nationally representative Indian data exists) is reported as-is rather than smoothed over

chronic_relapsing_remitting_course.finding: AD follows a chronic, relapsing-remitting course with a fluctuating pattern of flares and quiescent periods rather than a single linear progression, and most often starts in the first 2 years of life, though onset can occur at any life stage (onset after age 60 is described as 'increasingly common' in a 2026 update).
chronic_relapsing_remitting_course.source: Ricci G et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2009;10(5):287-300 (PMID 19658441); Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242); Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026;12(1):36 (PMID 42243136)
chronic_relapsing_remitting_course.confidence: high - directly supported by all three retrieved abstracts

childhood_remission_and_the_important_pr.finding: A substantial proportion of children with early AD go into remission during childhood - an important, genuinely reassuring prognostic point for affected families. A German birth-cohort study following 1,314 children from birth to age 7 found the cumulative prevalence of AD in the first 2 years of life was 21.5%; of these children with early AD, 43.2% were in complete remission by age 3 years, 38.3% had an intermittent disease pattern, and 18.7% had symptoms every year, with greater initial severity and atopic sensitisation being the major determinants of a worse (more persistent) prognosis. This knowledge base could not independently verify, in this research pass, a single specific percentage figure for remission specifically 'by adolescence' from a directly retrieved primary source (the widely repeated claim that 'most children outgrow AD by adolescence' is broadly consistent with, but not identical to, this age-3 remission data), and that specific adolescence-cutoff percentage is therefore not asserted as a verified number.
childhood_remission_and_the_important_pr.source: Illi S, von Mutius E, Lau S et al; Multicenter Allergy Study Group, 'The natural course of atopic dermatitis from birth to age 7 years and the association with asthma', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2004;113(5):925-931 (PMID 15131576)
childhood_remission_and_the_important_pr.confidence: high for the directly quoted age-3 remission figures from the Illi et al birth-cohort study; the broader popular claim of a specific 'outgrown by adolescence' percentage is explicitly flagged as not independently verified in this session rather than asserted

adult_persistent_and_adult_onset_disease.finding: A distinct subset of patients has AD that persists into, or begins in, adulthood. A study of 725 adolescent and adult AD patients found 607 could be classified into disease-course subtypes, with the largest differences in sensitisation patterns and total serum IgE seen between patients with early-onset AD that persists chronically into adulthood versus those with late-onset AD starting after age 20, supporting genuine clinical heterogeneity within 'adult AD' rather than a single uniform adult phenotype. Separately, filaggrin-null genotype carriers who do develop dermatitis are not condemned to lifelong disease: complete long-term remission was observed in half of the filaggrin-null hospital dermatitis patients in the Thyssen et al cohort described in this entry's definition_and_pathophysiology and risk_factors sections.
adult_persistent_and_adult_onset_disease.source: Garmhausen D, Hagemann T, Bieber T et al, 'Characterization of different courses of atopic dermatitis in adolescent and adult patients', Allergy 2013;68(4):498-506 (PMID 23452057, PMCID PMC7159470); Thyssen JP et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2012;26(3):386-389 (PMID 21501248)
adult_persistent_and_adult_onset_disease.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

skin_barrier_repair_first_with_emollient.finding: Because AD's pathophysiology begins with epidermal barrier dysfunction (filaggrin deficiency and related defects) that permits both irritant/allergen penetration and downstream Th2-driven inflammation, restoring the skin barrier is the foundational clinical principle underlying AD management, with topical moisturisers/emollients listed as a current, standard treatment component alongside anti-inflammatory agents in the major disease-primer literature. This principle - fix the barrier first, because the barrier defect is mechanistically upstream of the inflammation - is the direct clinical corollary of this entry's definition_and_pathophysiology.skin_barrier_dysfunction_and_filaggrin finding.
skin_barrier_repair_first_with_emollient.source: Weidinger S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2018;4(1):1 (PMID 29930242)
skin_barrier_repair_first_with_emollient.confidence: high - directly supported by the retrieved abstract, which explicitly lists 'topical moisturizers' alongside anti-inflammatory agents as current AD treatment

breaking_the_itch_scratch_cycle_is_clini.finding: Because chronic scratching itself perpetuates and worsens AD (driving lichenification and further barrier damage, and because neural sensitisation can make patients continue scratching even after clinical improvement on conventional treatment), interrupting the itch-scratch cycle is a distinct, clinically important management goal in its own right, not merely a byproduct of treating inflammation. A 2026 review frames this as requiring attention to both peripheral neuroimmune itch pathways and central/psychological drivers (e.g., stress), supporting an integrative, multidisciplinary approach as an adjunct to standard pharmacological treatment.
breaking_the_itch_scratch_cycle_is_clini.source: Steinhoff M, Yosipovitch G, Canchy L et al, Dermatitis 2026;37(4):541-553 (PMID 40813061)
breaking_the_itch_scratch_cycle_is_clini.confidence: high - directly supported by the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

atopic_dermatitis.CURABILITY_NOTE:
Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is NOT cured by any medicine in adults with persistent/adult-onset disease: it is a chronic, relapsing-remitting, genetically-predisposed (filaggrin/skin-barrier-defect-associated) immune-mediated disease driven predominantly by Type 2/Th2 inflammation (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, IL-22, TSLP), and no drug in this survey eliminates the underlying immune/barrier predisposition - relapse is the rule after stopping any effective systemic therapy. What IS real, and a genuinely important natural-history fact that is NOT a medicine cure, is that a real substantial proportion of children with early-onset AD spontaneously outgrow it: in the German MAS (Multicenter Allergy Study) population-based birth cohort followed from birth to age 30 (1,314 recruited; 529 with AD onset in the first 5 years of life), 459 of 529 (87%) reported no AD symptoms at age 20 and 30 years, though remission was less likely in females, those with onset before age 2, those with early allergen sensitization, and those with allergic comorbidities (Hung CW et al, 'Incidence and Remission of Atopic Dermatitis' JAMA Netw Open 2025, PMID 41359337). This is a real, natural spontaneous-remission story specific to early-childhood-onset disease, not something any drug produces, and it does not apply reliably to adult-onset or persistent adult AD, which typically remains chronic.

What modern medicine has genuinely achieved, even though it is not a cure, is a substantial improvement in the realistic treatment ceiling: from 'EASI75 (75% improvement)' as the historical treatment-success bar to real EASI90/EASI100 (near-complete/complete clearance) now being reported for a meaningful minority-to-substantial proportion of patients with the newest oral and injectable systemic therapies. Concretely, the real highest published complete-clearance (EASI100) number found in this survey belongs to the oral JAK1 inhibitor upadacitinib (Rinvoq) 30 mg once daily: in a pooled secondary analysis of the pivotal Measure Up 1 and Measure Up 2 trials (n=1,683), EASI100 at week 16 was reached by 42.4% of patients on 30 mg upadacitinib versus 9.0% with placebo (Simpson EL et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025, PMID 40457140, a secondary analysis of data from Guttman-Yassky E et al, Lancet 2021, PMID 34023008) - this is a real, striking number for a disease with no drug-induced cure, though it comes from a secondary/pooled-analysis publication rather than the original 2021 pivotal paper's own abstract, which reported only EASI75 (70-80% with 15/30mg vs 16% placebo across the two trials) and vIGA-AD 0/1 (48-62% vs 5-8%) as its coprimary endpoints. Among the IL-13/IL-4 biologics, lebrikizumab (Ebglyss) also has a real, PMID-verified EASI100 figure, but only in an enriched subgroup: among patients who were already week-16 responders and continued treatment, EASI100 rose from approximately 20-21% at week 16 to approximately 40-41% by week 104 (2 years) (Simpson E et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2026, PMID 41814921) - a real deep-response number, but drawn from a responder-enriched population followed long-term, not directly comparable on a like-for-like basis to upadacitinib's week-16, all-comers 42.4%. Dupilumab (Dupixent) and tralokinumab (Adbry), the two other major biologics, do not publish an EASI100 percentage at all in their pivotal trials or FDA labels - they report EASI75/EASI90/IGA-0-or-1 as their standard deep-response cut, so no real EASI100 comparison number exists for them; this is a genuine gap in what those two drugs' own trial programmes have published, not evidence that they cannot achieve complete clearance. So, on the real, verifiable, like-for-like (week-16, all-comers trial population) evidence available, an oral JAK1 inhibitor (upadacitinib) currently has the real highest published complete-clearance rate in atopic dermatitis.

REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has atopic dermatitis: (1) foundational skin care - liberal daily emollient/moisturizer use (300-500g/week in adults) is the universal foundation of AD management at every severity, applied especially after bathing ('soak and smear'), to support the defective skin barrier and reduce topical-steroid burden between flares; however, be honest that two large, rigorous, adequately-powered randomised trials (BEEP, Chalmers JR et al, Lancet 2020, PMID 32087126; PreventADALL, Skjerven HO et al, Lancet 2020, PMID 32087121) found daily emollient use in high-risk newborns does NOT prevent AD onset - BEEP even showed increased skin infections in the emollient arm - so emollients should be used and recommended as management of existing AD, not marketed as a primary-prevention strategy in infants; (2) for active flares, potency-tiered topical corticosteroids (TCS) remain first-line - low potency (hydrocortisone 1%) for face/eyelids/genitals/flexures, mid-to-potent agents for trunk/limbs, short courses of potent/superpotent agents only on thick skin - with a real, quantifiable barrier to adherence: 'steroid phobia' (mean TOPICOP phobia scores of approximately 48-51% in recent validated-scale studies, PMID 41952605, PMID 41509933) that clinicians should proactively address with direct education rather than dismiss; (3) for facial, periocular, flexural or genital AD, or for long-term proactive maintenance, use a topical calcineurin inhibitor instead of continued steroids to avoid atrophy risk - a real, large head-to-head trial (Paller AS et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2005, PMID 15858471, n=1,065) showed tacrolimus ointment is significantly more effective than pimecrolimus cream (EASI improvement 54.1% vs 34.9% in adults, P<.0001; 67.2% vs 56.4% in children with moderate/severe disease, P=.04), so tacrolimus is preferred for moderate-severe sensitive-area disease while pimecrolimus may suit milder/facial disease; (4) crisaborole (Eucrisa, topical PDE4 inhibitor) and ruxolitinib cream (Opzelura, topical JAK1/2 inhibitor) are real non-steroidal options for mild-to-moderate disease - crisaborole gave a real but modest ISGA treatment-success rate of 31-33% versus 18-25% vehicle at day 29 (FDA label, Reference ID 4027634; Paller AS et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2016, PMID 27417017), while ruxolitinib cream gave a real, larger effect on IGA treatment success (51.3-53.8% versus 7.6-15.1% vehicle at week 8, Papp K et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021, PMID 33957195) plus rapid within-12-hour itch relief, though it carries the class-wide topical JAK-inhibitor label restriction to <=20% BSA and <=60g/week; (5) for moderate-to-severe disease not controlled by topicals, move to a systemic - dupilumab (Dupixent, IL-4Rα blocker, blocking both IL-4 and IL-13) is the original, most broadly age-approved (6 months and older) and most extensively real-world-validated biologic, with real EASI75 rates of 44-51% (SOLO 1/2 monotherapy, PMID 27690741) rising to 69% with background topical corticosteroids (CHRONOS trial) and 75% in children 6-11 years with background TCS; tralokinumab (Adbry, IL-13-specific) and lebrikizumab (Ebglyss, IL-13-specific, newer, approved 2024) are real alternatives, with lebrikizumab showing numerically higher EASI75 rates in its own pivotal trials (52-59% versus tralokinumab's 25-33%, though this is a cross-trial, not head-to-head, comparison so cannot be stated as proven superiority); (6) if the treatment goal is the deepest possible skin clearance and the patient can tolerate an oral small molecule, upadacitinib (Rinvoq, oral JAK1 inhibitor) has the real highest published EASI90 (56.5% pooled) and EASI100 (42.4% pooled) rates of any drug in this survey, with abrocitinib (Cibinqo, also oral JAK1 inhibitor) a real close alternative (EASI75 61-70.3%, EASI90 23.9-37.7%, and in the real head-to-head JADE COMPARE trial, abrocitinib 200mg significantly outperformed dupilumab on EASI75 at week 12: 70.3% vs 58.1%, PMID 33761207); (7) both oral JAK inhibitors carry the FDA class-wide boxed warning (serious infections, mortality, malignancy, MACE, thrombosis - extrapolated from the tofacitinib ORAL Surveillance rheumatoid-arthritis safety trial) and should be reserved for patients whose disease is not adequately controlled by other systemics/biologics, or when those are inadvisable, per their FDA labels; (8) oral cyclosporine remains a real, rapid-onset rescue option for severe flares (pooled relative effectiveness approximately 55% at 6-8 weeks, Schmitt J et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2007, PMID 17447974) but is limited to short, monitored courses because of real nephrotoxicity and hypertension risk with continuous use, the same trade-off that limits it in psoriasis; and (9) accept and explain plainly to the adult patient that stopping any effective systemic/biologic will typically lead to relapse, while for a child with early-onset AD there is a real, substantial (87% in the MAS cohort) chance of natural, drug-independent remission by early adulthood - two genuinely different honest messages for two different patients.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side pharmacological intervention for atopic dermatitis (eczema): emollients/moisturizers as foundational first-line skin-barrier therapy (with the real, honest negative evidence for primary prevention in high-risk infants); topical corticosteroids (TCS) potency-tiered by body site, including real, quantified 'steroid phobia' data; topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) for sensitive-area and maintenance therapy; crisaborole (topical PDE4 inhibitor) and ruxolitinib cream (topical JAK1/2 inhibitor) as newer non-steroidal topical options; the IL-4Rα biologic dupilumab (the landmark, most broadly age-approved AD biologic, including real pediatric/adolescent data down to 6 months of age); the IL-13-specific biologics tralokinumab and lebrikizumab; the oral JAK1 inhibitors upadacitinib and abrocitinib, one of which (upadacitinib) has the real highest published EASI100 (complete-clearance) rate in this survey; and oral cyclosporine as an older, rapid-onset but not-for-long-term-continuous-use systemic option. Symptoms and diagnosis are covered in this knowledge base's own atopic_dermatitis symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial abstract, FDA/DailyMed prescribing information, or systematic review; where a number could not be verified from a real primary or regulatory source it is explicitly marked as not found rather than estimated.

ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.name: Emollients/Moisturizers - Foundational Barrier Therapy (Real Negative Evidence for Primary Prevention)
ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.type: Barrier repair/skin hydration, foundational adjunct at all AD severities; not proven as primary prevention
specific_drugs: Bath oils / 'soak and smear' occlusive emollient technique
ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.effectiveness: Two large, adequately powered randomised controlled trials found daily emollient use in high-risk newborns does NOT prevent AD onset: the BEEP trial (1,394 term newborns with a family history of atopic disease, randomised to daily emollient from the first 3 weeks of life plus standard skin care vs standard care alone) found eczema at age 2 years in 23% of the emollient group versus 25% of controls - not a significant reduction - and skin infections were increased in the emollient group (Chalmers JR et al, Lancet 2020;395:962-972, PMID 32087126). The PreventADALL factorial trial (1,171 infants, skin emollient from 2 weeks of age vs no intervention) found AD by 12 months in 8% (48/596) of the no-intervention group versus 11% (64/575) of the emollient-intervention group - the emollient arm trended worse, not better (Skjerven HO et al, Lancet 2020;395:951-961, PMID 32087121). A specific quantified flare-frequency-reduction percentage for emollient use in patients who ALREADY have established AD (as distinct from prevention in unaffected infants) could not be verified from a single real RCT in this survey; emollients remain a guideline-consensus (AAD, NICE) foundational adjunct for established disease based on mechanism and steroid-sparing effect, not on a single quantified real percentage found here.
ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.reason_why: Restoring the stratum corneum lipid barrier and epidermal hydration reduces transepidermal water loss and irritant/allergen penetration in already-inflamed or barrier-defective skin.
ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.important_caveat: The totality of the more rigorous, adequately powered evidence (BEEP and PreventADALL, both Lancet 2020) is genuinely negative for using emollients as a primary-prevention strategy in high-risk newborns, directly contradicting older, smaller pilot studies that had suggested a preventive benefit; BEEP additionally found increased skin infections in the treated infants. This must be reported honestly rather than marketed as 'emollients prevent eczema.'
ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.real_working_solution: Use emollients liberally (300-500 g/week in adults) as foundational maintenance therapy in patients who already have AD, applied especially after bathing ('soak and smear'), to reduce topical-steroid burden and support barrier function between flares - but do not use or recommend emollients specifically as a primary-prevention strategy in high-risk newborns, since the two definitive RCTs do not support that specific use.
ad_eczema_emollients_moisturizers.source: Chalmers JR et al, 'Daily emollient during infancy for prevention of eczema: the BEEP randomised controlled trial', Lancet 2020;395(10228):962-972 (PMID 32087126); Skjerven HO et al, 'Skin emollient and early complementary feeding to prevent infant atopic dermatitis (PreventADALL)', Lancet 2020;395(10228):951-961 (PMID 32087121)

ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.name: Topical Corticosteroids (TCS) - Potency-Tiered First-Line for Active Flares, With Real Quantified 'Steroid Phobia' Data
ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.type: Anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid receptor agonist, first-line for active AD flares, potency selected by body site
ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In a real head-to-head active-comparator trial in adults with moderate-to-severe AD, 0.1% tacrolimus ointment (a calcineurin inhibitor) performed similarly to mid-potency 0.1% hydrocortisone butyrate ointment, while a lower-potency 1% hydrocortisone acetate was outperformed by tacrolimus in a separate pediatric trial (mean residual disease after treatment was higher with 1% hydrocortisone than with tacrolimus) (Reitamo S et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;110:539-546, PMID 11898004; Reitamo S et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;110:547-555, PMID 11898005) - real evidence that potency selection materially changes outcome, though a placebo/vehicle-controlled trial of a potent TCS reporting an exact EASI75/IGA-success percentage could not be independently verified in this survey. Real, current data on the barrier to adherence: in a 2026 study of 117 parents of children with AD, the mean TOPICOP (TOPICal Corticosteroid Phobia) score was 48.2% (SD 15.1%), with the 'Fear' subdomain highest at 53.7%, and higher phobia correlated with greater disease severity (PMID 41952605); a separate 2025 validation study in 123 dermatology patients found a mean global TOPICOP score of 50.74% (SD 21.06%) (PMID 41509933).
ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: TCS bind the glucocorticoid receptor in keratinocytes and immune cells, suppressing NF-kB/AP-1-driven inflammatory cytokine transcription and reducing erythema, pruritus and epidermal hyperplasia.
ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Potency must be matched to body site: low potency for face/eyelids/genitals/flexures, mid-to-potent for trunk/limbs, and only short courses of potent/super-potent agents on thick skin (palms/soles), to avoid atrophy, telangiectasia, striae and (rarely, with prolonged high-potency use over large body surface area) HPA-axis suppression. 'Steroid phobia', quantified above at TOPICOP scores of approximately 48-51%, is a real and common barrier to adherence, not a fringe concern, and directly undermines otherwise-effective treatment.
ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Apply potency-appropriate TCS once or twice daily during active flares (typically 1-2 weeks for potent agents), then step down to a lower-potency agent or transition to 'proactive' twice-weekly maintenance dosing on previously affected sites, or to a steroid-sparing non-steroid topical (calcineurin inhibitor, crisaborole, ruxolitinib) for maintenance and sensitive sites - combined with direct patient/caregiver education (e.g. using a TOPICOP-style tool) to address steroid phobia and improve real-world adherence.
ad_eczema_topical_corticosteroids.source: Reitamo S et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;110(3):539-546 (PMID 11898004) and 547-555 (PMID 11898005); Starbek Zorko M et al, Dermatol Res Pract 2026 (PMID 41952605); Ağaoğlu E et al, Turk J Med Sci 2025 (PMID 41509933)

ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors - Tacrolimus vs Pimecrolimus, Real Head-to-Head Data, Non-Steroidal Sensitive-Area Option
ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Calcineurin/NFAT-pathway inhibitor, suppresses T-cell activation; steroid-sparing, non-atrophogenic, for sensitive areas and maintenance
ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In 3 randomised, investigator-blinded, 6-week multicentre trials (1,065 patients total), tacrolimus ointment gave significantly greater EASI score improvement than pimecrolimus cream: adults 54.1% vs 34.9% (P<.0001); children with moderate/severe disease 67.2% vs 56.4% (P=.04); combined analysis 52.8% vs 39.1% (P<.0001); children with mild disease at week 1, 39.2% vs 31.2% (P=.04). More pimecrolimus patients withdrew for lack of efficacy (P<=.03) (Paller AS et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2005;52:810-822, PMID 15858471).
ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Calcineurin inhibition blocks dephosphorylation of NFAT, preventing transcription of IL-2 and other T-cell cytokines central to the AD inflammatory cascade, without the collagen-synthesis suppression that causes steroid-induced skin atrophy.
ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: No skin atrophy risk, making TCIs the preferred steroid-sparing option for face, eyelids, flexures and genital skin, and for long-term proactive maintenance. FDA carries a boxed warning for a theoretical malignancy risk based on animal/case-report data, not a proven human causal signal from these trials; transient burning/stinging on application is common, more so with tacrolimus than pimecrolimus.
ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Use as first-line for sensitive-area AD (face, eyelids, flexures, genitals) where steroid atrophy risk is a specific concern, and for proactive twice-weekly maintenance after a TCS-induced flare has cleared; tacrolimus (more potent per the head-to-head data above) is preferred for moderate-severe disease, while pimecrolimus may suit milder/facial disease.
ad_eczema_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Paller AS et al, 'Tacrolimus ointment is more effective than pimecrolimus cream with a similar safety profile in the treatment of atopic dermatitis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2005;52(5):810-822 (PMID 15858471)

ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.name: Crisaborole (Eucrisa) - Topical PDE4 Inhibitor, Non-Steroidal, Mild-to-Moderate Disease
ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.type: Topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor, non-steroidal, approved 2016 for mild-to-moderate AD age 2 years and older
ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.effectiveness: In two identically-designed, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials (ISCLA-1 and ISCLA-2, total N=1,522, ages 2-79 years, twice daily for 28 days), the primary endpoint (ISGA success = Clear/Almost Clear with >=2-grade improvement at Day 29) was reached by 32.8% with crisaborole vs 25.4% with vehicle in Trial 1 (N=503 vs N=256), and 31.4% vs 18.0% in Trial 2 (N=513 vs N=250) (FDA prescribing information, Reference ID 4027634, Clinical Studies Table 2; Paller AS et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2016;75:494-503, PMID 27417017).
ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.reason_why: PDE4 inhibition raises intracellular cAMP in keratinocytes and immune cells, dampening downstream pro-inflammatory cytokine production (including TNF-alpha, IL-4) implicated in AD.
ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.important_caveat: Modest absolute effect size - even the treated arm plateaus around 31-33% success at day 29, only about 7-14 percentage points above vehicle. Most common adverse reaction is application-site pain/burning (4% vs 1% vehicle). No skin atrophy or major systemic safety signal identified over the 28-day trial period, but not a substitute for TCS in more severe disease.
ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.real_working_solution: Apply a thin layer twice daily to affected mild-to-moderate AD skin, ages 2 and older; particularly useful for chronic, steroid-sparing maintenance on sensitive sites (face, skin folds) given its non-steroidal mechanism, accepting a real but modest efficacy relative to potent TCS.
ad_eczema_topical_pde4_crisaborole.source: FDA prescribing information, EUCRISA (crisaborole) ointment 2%, Reference ID 4027634 (accessdata.fda.gov, accessed 2026-09-22); Paller AS et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2016;75(3):494-503 (PMID 27417017)

ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.name: Ruxolitinib Cream (Opzelura) - Topical JAK1/JAK2 Inhibitor, Rapid Itch Relief, Mild-to-Moderate Disease
ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.type: Topical JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, approved 2021 for mild-to-moderate AD (non-immunocompromised, age 12 years and older)
specific_drugs: Ruxolitinib cream 1.5% (Opzelura) - the only marketed strength
ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.effectiveness: In two identical phase 3, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials (TRuE-AD1, N=631, and TRuE-AD2, N=618; patients >=12 years, IGA 2/3, 3-20% BSA, twice daily for 8 weeks), the primary endpoint IGA treatment success (IGA 0/1 with >=2-grade improvement) at week 8 for the marketed 1.5% dose was 53.8% (136/253) vs 15.1% (19/126) vehicle in Trial 1 (treatment difference 38.9%, 95% CI 30.3-47.4%), and 51.3% (117/228) vs 7.6% (9/118) vehicle in Trial 2 (treatment difference 44.1%, 95% CI 36.2-52.0%), P<.0001 for both (FDA prescribing information, Reference ID 4871457; Papp K et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85:863-872, PMID 33957195). A key secondary endpoint, itch NRS >=4-point reduction, was reached by 52.2% vs 15.4% (Trial 1) and 50.7% vs 16.3% (Trial 2), with itch improvement reported within 12 hours of first application. An exact EASI75 percentage could not be verified: neither the pivotal-trial abstract nor the FDA label reports EASI75 for the approved 1.5% dose - only IGA treatment success and itch-NRS outcomes are given in these primary sources.
ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.reason_why: JAK1/2 inhibition blocks signal transduction downstream of multiple AD-relevant cytokines (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, IL-22, TSLP, IFN-gamma) that all signal through the JAK-STAT pathway, giving broader cytokine coverage than a single-pathway topical agent, with rapid antipruritic onset.
ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.important_caveat: FDA label carries the class-wide JAK-inhibitor boxed warning (serious infections, malignancy/lymphoma, major adverse cardiovascular events, thrombosis, all-cause mortality - extrapolated largely from oral JAK-inhibitor data) despite low systemic absorption with topical use; label explicitly restricts treatment to <=60 g/week and short-term/non-continuous use over <=20% BSA.
ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.real_working_solution: Apply a thin layer twice daily to <=20% BSA, for short-term/non-continuous use capped at 60 g/week, in patients 12 years and older with mild-to-moderate AD not adequately controlled by or unsuitable for other topical prescription therapies; particularly valued for rapid itch relief (within 12 hours) and steroid-sparing maintenance.
ad_eczema_topical_jak_ruxolitinib.source: FDA prescribing information OPZELURA (ruxolitinib) cream 1.5%, Reference ID 4871457 (accessdata.fda.gov, accessed 2026-09-22); Papp K et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):863-872 (PMID 33957195)

ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.name: Dupilumab (Dupixent) - IL-4Ralpha Blocker (Dual IL-4/IL-13 Blockade), the Landmark AD Biologic, Broadest Age Approval (6 Months+)
ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.type: Biologic, fully human monoclonal antibody against IL-4 receptor alpha, blocking both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Dupilumab (Dupixent) 300 mg every 2 weeks, adults (after 600 mg loading dose)
Dupilumab weight-tiered dosing for pediatric patients 6 months and older
ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.effectiveness: Per the pivotal SOLO 1 and SOLO 2 trials (Simpson EL et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2335-2348, PMID 27690741, cross-verified against FDA label Table 2/17, Reference ID 5781952) at week 16, dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks vs placebo: SOLO 1 - IGA 0/1 38% vs 10%, EASI75 51% vs 15%, EASI90 36% vs 8% (P<0.001 for all); SOLO 2 - IGA 0/1 36% vs 9%, EASI75 44% vs 12%, EASI90 30% vs 7% (P<0.001 for all). With background topical corticosteroids (CHRONOS trial, week 16): IGA 0/1 39% vs 12%, EASI75 69% vs 23%, EASI90 40% vs 11%. Pediatric data (FDA label Section 14.1): adolescents 12-17 years (AD-1526) - IGA 0/1 24% vs 2%, EASI75 42% vs 8%; children 6-11 years with background TCS (AD-1652) - EASI75 75% vs 26-28% (both weight strata); children 6 months-5 years with background TCS (AD-1539, n=162) - IGA 0/1 28% vs 4%, EASI75 53% vs 11%, EASI90 25% vs 3%. An exact EASI100 percentage could not be verified: neither the pivotal trial abstracts nor the current FDA label report an EASI100 figure for dupilumab in any age group - this is a genuine reporting gap in the drug's own publications, not evidence it cannot achieve complete clearance.
ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.reason_why: Dupilumab binds IL-4Ralpha, the shared receptor subunit for both the Type I (mainly immune-cell) and Type II (epithelial/keratinocyte) receptor complexes, so blocking it inhibits signaling of both IL-4 and IL-13 - the two central Th2 cytokines driving the epidermal barrier defect, itch and Th2 skewing in AD.
ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.important_caveat: Conjunctivitis and keratitis occur more frequently with dupilumab than placebo: in pooled 16-week monotherapy trials, conjunctivitis 10% (dupilumab) vs 2% (placebo), blepharitis 2% vs <1%; in the 52-week +TCS trial, keratitis 4% (dupilumab+TCS) vs 0% (placebo+TCS). Injection site reactions 10% vs 5%; oral herpes 4% vs 2%.
ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.real_working_solution: First-line biologic for moderate-to-severe AD inadequately controlled by topical therapy, across the widest approved age range (6 months and older) of any AD biologic, often chosen first because of this age range and the most mature long-term safety/real-world dataset; can be used with or without background topical corticosteroids.
ad_eczema_il4ra_dupilumab.source: Simpson EL et al, 'Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis', N Engl J Med 2016;375(24):2335-2348 (PMID 27690741); FDA Dupixent Prescribing Information, current label (accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/761055s082lbl.pdf, Reference ID 5781952, accessed 2026-09-22)

ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.name: Tralokinumab (Adbry) - IL-13-Specific Biologic (ECZTRA 1/2)
ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.type: Biologic, fully human IgG4 monoclonal antibody specifically neutralising IL-13, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Tralokinumab (Adbry/Adtralza) 300 mg every 2 weeks (after 600 mg loading dose); can extend to every 4 weeks after week 16 in clear/almost-clear responders
ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.effectiveness: In the pivotal ECZTRA 1 and ECZTRA 2 trials (Wollenberg A et al, Br J Dermatol 2021;184:437-449, PMID 33000465), at week 16, tralokinumab 300 mg every 2 weeks vs placebo: ECZTRA 1 - IGA 0/1 15.8% vs 7.1% (P=0.002), EASI75 25.0% vs 12.7% (P<0.001); ECZTRA 2 - IGA 0/1 22.2% vs 10.9% (P<0.001), EASI75 33.2% vs 11.4% (P<0.001); FDA/DailyMed label figures are closely consistent (ECZTRA 1 n=601 vs n=197, IGA 0/1 16% vs 7%, EASI75 25% vs 13%; ECZTRA 2 n=577 vs n=193, IGA 0/1 21% vs 9%, EASI75 33% vs 10%). An exact numeric EASI90 or EASI100 percentage could not be verified: the Adbry label states qualitatively that a higher proportion of tralokinumab-treated subjects achieved EASI90 versus placebo across the pivotal trials, but does not give a numeric EASI90 or EASI100 figure, and none could be found in the pivotal publication either - a genuine reporting gap, tralokinumab publishes less granular deep-response data than lebrikizumab.
ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.reason_why: Tralokinumab neutralises IL-13 only, sparing IL-4 signaling; IL-13 is argued to be the dominant cytokine in AD skin lesions specifically, so IL-13-selective blockade aims for comparable skin efficacy with a narrower immunologic footprint than dual IL-4/13 blockade, though no head-to-head trial has proven a clinical advantage over dupilumab.
ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.important_caveat: Conjunctivitis 7.5% (tralokinumab) vs 3.1% (placebo) in the first 16 weeks; injection site reactions 7.4% vs 0.8%; eosinophilia also listed among common adverse reactions.
ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.real_working_solution: Used in adults and adolescents (12 years and older) with moderate-to-severe AD not controlled by topicals; positioned by some prescribers as a second-line option after dupilumab, including in real-world reports of dupilumab non-responders or dupilumab-associated conjunctivitis/facial dermatitis switching to tralokinumab.
ad_eczema_il13_tralokinumab.source: Wollenberg A et al, 'Tralokinumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: results from ECZTRA 1 and ECZTRA 2', Br J Dermatol 2021;184(3):437-449 (PMID 33000465); FDA Adbry Prescribing Information via DailyMed, accessed 2026-09-22

ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.name: Lebrikizumab (Ebglyss) - IL-13-Specific Biologic, Newer (Approved 2024), Real Long-Term EASI100 Data
ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.type: Biologic, humanised IgG4 monoclonal antibody targeting IL-13, blocking formation of the IL-4Ralpha/IL-13Ralpha1 signaling complex, subcutaneous
specific_drugs: Lebrikizumab (Ebglyss) 250 mg every 2 weeks through week 16 (after 500 mg loading dose), then 250 mg every 4 weeks maintenance in responders
ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.effectiveness: In the pivotal ADvocate 1 and ADvocate 2 trials (Silverberg JI et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1080-1091, PMID 36920778), at week 16, lebrikizumab 250 mg every 2 weeks vs placebo: ADvocate 1 (n=283 vs n=141) - IGA 0/1 43.1% vs 12.7% (P<0.001), EASI75 58.8% vs 16.2% (P<0.001), EASI90 38% vs 9% (FDA label); ADvocate 2 (n=281 vs n=146) - IGA 0/1 33.2% vs 10.8% (P<0.001), EASI75 52.1% vs 18.1% (P<0.001), EASI90 31% vs 10% (FDA label). Week-52 maintenance in week-16 responders re-randomised to continued dosing: IGA 0/1 maintained in 65-81% (every-4-week arm) and 74-76% (every-2-week arm) versus 47-50% after withdrawal to placebo. A real, PMID-verified EASI100 figure exists but only in an enriched subgroup: among patients who were already week-16 responders and continued lebrikizumab, IGA-0 (completely clear) rose from approximately 30-34% at week 16 to approximately 45-52% by week 104, and EASI100 rose from approximately 20-21% at week 16 to approximately 40-41% by week 104 (2 years) (Simpson E et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2026, PMID 41814921) - these are approximate ranges as extracted from the abstract, and the population is responder-enriched, not the all-comers ITT population, so it is not directly comparable to upadacitinib's week-16 all-comers EASI100 of 42.4%.
ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.reason_why: Same IL-13-selective rationale as tralokinumab (sparing IL-4), with a claimed (mechanistic/PK, not proven-superior) higher-affinity/slower-off-rate binding epitope; lebrikizumab's higher raw EASI75 rates versus tralokinumab's in their respective pivotal trials are a real, striking cross-trial difference, but cross-trial comparisons (different placebo response rates, different populations) cannot be read as proof of head-to-head superiority - only indirect/matching-adjusted analyses have attempted this comparison, with contested conclusions in the literature.
ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.important_caveat: Conjunctivitis 10% (lebrikizumab monotherapy) vs 3% (placebo) in the 16-week monotherapy trials - numerically the highest conjunctivitis rate of the three biologics by label-reported percentage. Herpes zoster is also listed among common adverse reactions specifically for lebrikizumab.
ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.real_working_solution: Newest approved option (2024) for adults/adolescents 12 years and older weighing at least 40 kg; positioned as a monotherapy-oriented IL-13 biologic with a maintenance every-4-week option for responders (dosing-convenience advantage), including real-world use as a switch option after dupilumab.
ad_eczema_il13_lebrikizumab.source: Silverberg JI et al, 'Two Phase 3 Trials of Lebrikizumab for Moderate-to-Severe Atopic Dermatitis', N Engl J Med 2023;388(12):1080-1091 (PMID 36920778); FDA Ebglyss Prescribing Information via DailyMed, accessed 2026-09-22; long-term EASI100 data: Simpson E et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2026 (PMID 41814921, abstract only)

ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.name: Upadacitinib (Rinvoq) - Oral JAK1 Inhibitor, the Real Highest Published EASI100 (Complete Clearance) Rate in This Survey (Measure Up 1/2, AD Up)
ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.type: Oral, selective JAK1 inhibitor, once-daily tablet, reserved for disease not adequately controlled by other systemics/biologics
ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.effectiveness: In the pivotal Measure Up 1 and Measure Up 2 monotherapy trials (Guttman-Yassky E et al, Lancet 2021, PMID 34023008; n=847 and n=836), at week 16, 30 mg vs placebo: Measure Up 1 - EASI75 80% (227/285) vs 16% (46/281), vIGA-AD 0/1 62% (177/285) vs 8% (24/281); Measure Up 2 - EASI75 73% (206/282) vs 13% (37/278), vIGA-AD 0/1 52% (147/282) vs 5% (13/278); 15 mg gave EASI75 60-70% vs the same placebo arms (all P<0.0001). With background topical corticosteroids (AD Up trial, Reich K et al, Lancet 2021, PMID 34023009, n=901): 30 mg+TCS EASI75 77% (229/297) vs placebo+TCS 26% (80/304), adjusted difference 50.6%, P<0.0001; vIGA-AD 0/1 59% (174/297) vs 11% (33/304). Deep-response secondary endpoints (pooled Measure Up 1+2, n=1,683, from a 2025 secondary-analysis publication, Simpson EL et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025, PMID 40457140 - NOT reported in the original 2021 Lancet abstract itself): EASI90 at week 16 - 15 mg 41.9%, 30 mg 56.5%, placebo 11.5%; EASI100 (complete clearance) at week 16 - 15 mg 29.1%, 30 mg 42.4%, placebo 9.0%. This 42.4% is the real highest published EASI100 rate found in this entire survey, though it should be read with the caveat that it comes from a secondary/pooled-analysis paper rather than the pivotal trial's own primary publication.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.reason_why: JAK1 inhibition blocks intracellular signaling downstream of IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, IL-22, TSLP and other type-2/pruritogenic cytokine receptors that all signal through JAK1, giving broader suppression of the itch-scratch and inflammatory cascade than a single-cytokine biologic.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.important_caveat: FDA boxed warning (verified from DailyMed SPL, RINVOQ, setid 2966aec7-2ef0-923c-d8ff-fe1a957bf095): 'SERIOUS INFECTIONS, MORTALITY, MALIGNANCY, MAJOR ADVERSE CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS (MACE), AND THROMBOSIS' - class labeling extrapolated from the tofacitinib ORAL Surveillance rheumatoid-arthritis safety trial (patients >=50 with a cardiovascular risk factor), applied across the JAK-inhibitor class including upadacitinib in AD.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.real_working_solution: FDA-approved only for refractory moderate-to-severe AD (age 12 and older) not adequately controlled by other systemic drug products, including biologics, or when those therapies are inadvisable, per the RINVOQ label; start at 15 mg once daily, may increase to 30 mg if inadequate response (fixed 15 mg in patients 65 years and older). For a patient whose primary goal is the deepest possible skin clearance, upadacitinib 30 mg has the real highest published EASI100 rate among all AD treatments surveyed here.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_upadacitinib_highest_.source: Guttman-Yassky E et al, 'Once-daily upadacitinib versus placebo... (Measure Up 1 and Measure Up 2)', Lancet 2021 (PMID 34023008); Reich K et al, 'Safety and efficacy of upadacitinib in combination with topical corticosteroids... (AD Up)', Lancet 2021 (PMID 34023009); Simpson EL et al, 'Rapid Itch Improvement and Skin Clearance with Upadacitinib Versus Placebo (Measure Up 1 and Measure Up 2) and Versus Dupilumab (Heads Up)', Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025 (PMID 40457140); DailyMed SPL setid 2966aec7-2ef0-923c-d8ff-fe1a957bf095 (RINVOQ label, accessed 2026-09-22)

ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.name: Abrocitinib (Cibinqo) - Oral JAK1 Inhibitor, Real Head-to-Head Superiority Over Dupilumab on EASI75 (JADE COMPARE)
ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.type: Oral, selective JAK1 inhibitor, once-daily tablet, reserved for disease not adequately controlled by other systemics/biologics
ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.effectiveness: In JADE MONO-1 (Simpson EL et al, Lancet 2020, PMID 32711801, n=387, week 12): IGA response 200 mg 44% (67/153) vs placebo 8% (6/76), P<0.0001; EASI75 200 mg 63% (96/153) vs placebo 12% (9/76), P<0.0001. In JADE MONO-2 (Silverberg JI et al, JAMA Dermatol 2020, PMID 32492087, week 12): 200 mg - IGA 0/1 38.1%, EASI75 61.0%, EASI90 37.7% (vs placebo IGA 0/1 9.1%, EASI75 10.4%, EASI90 3.9%); 100 mg - EASI75 44.5%, EASI90 23.9%. In the real head-to-head JADE COMPARE trial against dupilumab and placebo, all with background TCS (Bieber T et al, N Engl J Med 2021, PMID 33761207, n=838, week 12): IGA 0/1 - 200 mg 48.4%, 100 mg 36.6%, dupilumab 36.5%, placebo 14.0%; EASI75 - 200 mg 70.3%, 100 mg 58.7%, dupilumab 58.1%, placebo 27.1% (P<0.001 for both abrocitinib doses vs placebo); at week 2, abrocitinib 200 mg (but not 100 mg) was statistically superior to dupilumab on itch response. No EASI100 percentage could be verified for abrocitinib in any of the three pivotal-trial abstracts (JADE MONO-1, JADE MONO-2, JADE COMPARE) - none reported EASI100 as a stated endpoint in the primary sources checked, so a direct abrocitinib-vs-upadacitinib EASI100 comparison could not be made; this is a real gap, not evidence abrocitinib cannot reach complete clearance.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.reason_why: Same mechanism class as upadacitinib - oral, JAK1-selective inhibition blocking IL-4/IL-13/IL-31/TSLP/IL-22 signaling.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.important_caveat: FDA boxed warning verified from DailyMed SPL (CIBINQO, setid 3f6d6fcd-e9f9-42c8-bfa2-bb2cfc9ed258): same class warning as upadacitinib (serious infections including tuberculosis, mortality, malignancy/lymphoma, MACE, thrombosis), extrapolated from the tofacitinib ORAL Surveillance trial. Adverse events in JADE COMPARE: nausea 11.1% (200 mg) vs 4.2% (100 mg); acne 6.6% (200 mg) vs 2.9% (100 mg).
ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.real_working_solution: Reserved for refractory moderate-to-severe AD after inadequate response/intolerance to other systemics including biologics, the same positioning as upadacitinib. The 200 mg dose gives the fastest itch relief and highest response rates, including real head-to-head superiority over dupilumab on EASI75 at week 12 (70.3% vs 58.1%), but carries more nausea/acne; 100 mg is the lower-intensity option.
ad_eczema_oral_jak_abrocitinib.source: Simpson EL et al, 'JADE MONO-1', Lancet 2020;396:255-266 (PMID 32711801); Silverberg JI et al, 'JADE MONO-2', JAMA Dermatol 2020;156(8):863-873 (PMID 32492087); Bieber T et al, 'Abrocitinib versus Placebo or Dupilumab for Atopic Dermatitis (JADE COMPARE)', N Engl J Med 2021;384:1101-1112 (PMID 33761207); DailyMed SPL setid 3f6d6fcd-e9f9-42c8-bfa2-bb2cfc9ed258 (CIBINQO label, accessed 2026-09-22)

ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.name: Oral Cyclosporine - Older Conventional Systemic, Rapid Onset, Not for Long-Term Continuous Use
ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.type: Calcineurin inhibitor, broad T-cell-directed immunosuppressant (not AD-pathway-selective), oral, off-label use in AD
ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.effectiveness: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies (602 patients) found pooled mean disease-severity decrease of 22% (95% CI 8-36%) at low dose (3 mg/kg/day) and 40% (95% CI 29-51%) at >=4 mg/kg/day by 2 weeks, rising to a pooled relative effectiveness of 55% (95% CI 48-62%) at 6-8 weeks (Schmitt J et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2007;21:606-619, PMID 17447974). The authors themselves cautioned that evidence of publication bias means the quantitative results should be interpreted with caution, and flagged a lack of long-term safety/efficacy data - this is an older (2007), smaller-study meta-analysis, not a modern large RCT.
ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.reason_why: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, inhibiting calcineurin and blocking IL-2 transcription, broadly suppressing T-cell activation - mechanistically non-selective compared with JAK inhibitors or biologics, which is why response can be faster in some patients but the drug is not disease-pathway-targeted.
ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.important_caveat: Cyclosporine's approved dermatology indication is psoriasis, not AD (AD use is off-label). It causes dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity (afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction reducing GFR, interstitial fibrosis with prolonged use) and hypertension, the same trade-off that limits its use in psoriasis, which is why continuous treatment is conventionally kept to short, defined courses with regular renal-function and blood-pressure monitoring rather than open-ended use.
ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.real_working_solution: Use as a rapid-onset bridge/rescue systemic for severe AD flares (faster onset than biologics/JAK inhibitors in some patients) or when biologics/JAK inhibitors are unavailable or contraindicated, for short, defined courses with monitored tapering and regular renal function/blood pressure checks, given the nephrotoxicity/hypertension ceiling on continuous use.
ad_eczema_oral_cyclosporine.source: Schmitt J, Schmitt N, Meurer M, 'Cyclosporin in the treatment of patients with atopic eczema - a systematic review and meta-analysis', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2007;21(5):606-619 (PMID 17447974)
