ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative risk reduction specifically for pneumococcal AOM (100 x (1 - RR 0.57))
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ewald H et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2016;113:139-146 (PMID 26987462)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tympanostomy tube placement, recurrent AOM episode-rate reduction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real modern RCT found NO statistically significant reduction in AOM episodes per child-year versus medical management (1.48 vs 1.56, P=0.66) -- no real, honest effectiveness percentage can be asserted for episode-rate reduction specifically
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hoberman A et al, N Engl J Med 2021;385:1789-1799 (PMID 33979487)

vitiligo.name: Vitiligo

cd8_t_cell_mediated_melanocyte_destructi.finding: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune depigmenting disorder in which autoreactive, melanocyte-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes are the principal effector cells causing melanocyte death. These CD8+ T cells are found in increased numbers in the blood and in lesional/perilesional skin of vitiligo patients and target melanogenic-pathway antigens including gp100, MART-1, tyrosinase, and tyrosinase-related proteins 1 and 2. Melanocyte destruction is amplified by an IFN-gamma-CXCL10 feedback loop: IFN-gamma released by autoreactive CD8+ T cells binds IFN-gamma receptors on keratinocytes, activating JAK1/JAK2-STAT1 signalling that induces CXCL10 production, which in turn recruits further CXCR3+ autoreactive T cells into the skin, self-amplifying the destructive immune response. A relative deficiency of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and reduced homing signals such as CCL22 in lesional skin are also described, impairing normal suppression of the autoimmune attack.
cd8_t_cell_mediated_melanocyte_destructi.source: Diotallevi F, Gioacchini H, De Simoni E, et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Richmond JM, Strassner JP, Zapata L Jr, et al, 'Resident Memory and Recirculating Memory T Cells Cooperate to Maintain Disease in a Mouse Model of Vitiligo', J Invest Dermatol 2019;139(4):769-778 (PMID 30423329)

genetic_susceptibility_and_autoimmune_ge.finding: Vitiligo has a strong heritable component: genetic and environmental factors are estimated to contribute roughly 80% and 20% of disease risk respectively, about 20% of patients report at least one affected first-degree relative, and the concordance rate in monozygotic twins is approximately 23%. Genome-wide association studies have identified at least 54 vitiligo-susceptibility loci, the majority involved in immune regulation; genes such as NALP1, PTPN22 and CTLA-4 are shared with other autoimmune diseases including autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis, which is the molecular basis for the clinical clustering of vitiligo with these conditions.
genetic_susceptibility_and_autoimmune_ge.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341)

oxidative_stress_and_convergence_theory.finding: Melanocytes are intrinsically more vulnerable to reactive oxygen species (ROS) because melanin synthesis itself generates oxidative by-products; in vitiligo, excessive ROS production combined with inadequate antioxidant scavenging (e.g. reduced catalase activity) contributes to melanocyte damage and death alongside the autoimmune attack. Because no single mechanism (genetic, autoimmune, oxidative-stress, or neural) fully explains disease onset and spread, current pathogenesis models favour a 'convergence theory' in which multiple mechanisms act together to reduce melanocyte viability, with oxidative stress plausibly acting as an initial trigger that unmasks melanocyte antigens and initiates the subsequent CD8+ T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction.
oxidative_stress_and_convergence_theory.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Laddha NC, Dwivedi M, Mansuri MS, et al, 'Vitiligo: interplay between oxidative stress and immune system', Exp Dermatol 2013;22(4):245-250 (PMID 23425123)

clinical_diagnosis_of_depigmented_macule.finding: Vitiligo is diagnosed clinically, based on the characteristic appearance of well-defined, chalk- or milk-white depigmented macules and patches on the skin, generally without preceding scaling, atrophy or other primary skin change; biopsy and laboratory testing are not required for typical presentations and are reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases.
clinical_diagnosis_of_depigmented_macule.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341)

woods_lamp_examination_role.finding: Wood's lamp (ultraviolet-A, ~365 nm) examination is a safe, noninvasive bedside diagnostic aid used to confirm the extent of depigmentation and to detect subclinical lesions not visible under normal light, particularly in lightly pigmented skin. Fully depigmented vitiligo lesions characteristically show an enhanced 'bright blue-white' fluorescence under Wood's lamp, distinct from other causes of hypopigmentation; this feature has been used diagnostically to confirm vitiligo, for example in a documented case of non-segmental vitiligo where Wood's lamp examination showed bright blue-white fluorescence. Clinicians must be aware that cosmetic camouflage products (e.g. dihydroxyacetone-based self-tanners) can produce a false 'salmon' or coral-pink fluorescence that mimics other conditions such as erythrasma and can confound the examination.
woods_lamp_examination_role.source: Ducharme EE, Silverberg NB, 'Selected applications of technology in the pediatric dermatology office', Semin Cutan Med Surg 2008;27(1):94-100 (PMID 18486031); Wang Z et al, 'Vitiligo associated with ribociclib therapy: a rare case report', Front Oncol 2025 (PMID 41438984); Nagshabandi KN, Shadid A, Alakresh L, 'Salmon colored fluorescence on Wood's lamp in a pediatric patient with vitiligo: A case report', J Family Med Prim Care 2024 (PMID 39723023)

segmental_versus_nonsegmental_classifica.finding: The internationally accepted (Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference, VGICC) classification separates segmental vitiligo (SV) from non-segmental vitiligo (NSV), which is clinically important because the two forms differ in onset, course and treatment response. SV shows a clinically unambiguous segmental (usually unilateral, midline-respecting) distribution with rapid onset; depigmentation typically spreads within the affected segment over 6-24 months and then stops, with further extension being rare, and up to 50% of SV patients develop poliosis (leukotrichia) from early involvement of hair-follicle melanocytes. NSV instead presents with progressive, usually symmetric, bilateral macules that can involve acrofacial, generalized, universal or mucosal sites, follows a more variable and often progressive course, and body hair is usually spared/remains pigmented unless disease is advanced. SV responds particularly well to melanocyte autograft/surgical repigmentation techniques with stable results, whereas NSV (driven by ongoing autoimmune/autoinflammatory activity against melanocytes) shows more variable, generally poorer response to surgical approaches. The consensus recommends 'vitiligo' as the umbrella term for all non-segmental forms, with SV classified as a distinct entity, and 'mixed vitiligo' used when SV and NSV coexist (usually with SV preceding NSV).
segmental_versus_nonsegmental_classifica.source: Ezzedine K, Lim HW, Suzuki T, et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

well_demarcated_depigmented_macules_and_.finding: The hallmark lesion is a well-demarcated, completely depigmented (chalk/milk-white) macule or patch, in contrast to the partial pigment loss seen in most hypopigmentation mimics. In non-segmental vitiligo the classic pattern is bilateral and tends toward symmetric distribution, commonly first affecting the head-neck region, hands, and body folds/periorificial skin, and can coalesce into larger depigmented areas over time.
well_demarcated_depigmented_macules_and_.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Sarma N, Chakraborty S, Poojary S, et al, 'A Nationwide, Multicentric Case-Control Study on Vitiligo (MEDEC-V) to Elicit the Magnitude and Correlates', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702)

koebner_phenomenon.finding: The Koebner phenomenon (KP) - development of new lesions at sites of skin trauma in an already-affected patient - occurs in vitiligo and is formally classified (per the VETF system endorsed by international consensus) into history-based, clinical-observation-based, and experimentally-induced KP. Reported incidence of KP in non-segmental vitiligo ranges from 15% to 70%; its occurrence in segmental vitiligo remains controversial. The consensus explicitly cautions against over-attributing vitiligo spread to routine daily friction/clothing/pressure without supporting evidence, since scientific support for that specific claim is lacking.
koebner_phenomenon.source: Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

poliosis_hair_depigmentation.finding: Poliosis (whitening of hair overlying a depigmented patch, from early involvement of hair-follicle melanocytes) is a recognized feature of vitiligo and is markedly more common and earlier-appearing in segmental vitiligo, affecting up to 50% of SV patients, compared with non-segmental vitiligo where body hair is usually spared and remains pigmented unless the disease is advanced.
poliosis_hair_depigmentation.source: Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

mucosal_involvement.finding: Vitiligo can involve the oral and/or genital mucosae (mucosal vitiligo). When depigmentation is confined to a single mucosal site in isolation, particularly genital, international consensus recommends excluding lichen sclerosus as a differential before classifying the lesion as vitiligo (in that isolated setting termed 'undetermined vitiligo').
mucosal_involvement.source: Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

tinea_versicolor.finding: Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor is caused by overgrowth of the commensal yeast genus Malassezia and presents with hypopigmented, hyperpigmented, or mixed macules, classically with fine overlying scale, most often on the trunk/upper back and shoulders. Unlike vitiligo it is a superficial fungal infection (confirmable by KOH microscopy showing 'spaghetti and meatballs' hyphae/spores and by Wood's lamp yellow-gold fluorescence), the hypopigmentation is partial rather than complete depigmentation, and it typically resolves with topical or oral antifungal therapy rather than being a chronic autoimmune process.
tinea_versicolor.source: Kallini JR, Riaz F, Khachemoune A, 'Tinea versicolor in dark-skinned individuals', Int J Dermatol 2014;53(2):137-141 (PMID 24320140)

pityriasis_alba.finding: Pityriasis alba presents as ill-defined, mildly scaly, hypopigmented (not fully depigmented) patches, most commonly on the face of children/adolescents, and is frequently associated with atopic dermatitis. Histopathology in a study of 56 patients showed markedly reduced epidermal pigment but no significant reduction in melanocyte count, with degenerative changes and fewer melanosomes in melanocytes/keratinocytes - distinguishing it mechanistically from vitiligo, where melanocytes are actively destroyed, and helping differentiate it from other hypopigmented entities such as nevus depigmentosus. Pityriasis alba lesions typically fade spontaneously over months to a few years.
pityriasis_alba.source: In SI, Yi SW, Kang HY, et al, 'Clinical and histopathological characteristics of pityriasis alba', Clin Exp Dermatol 2009;34(5):591-597 (PMID 19094127)

post_inflammatory_hypopigmentation.finding: Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation (PIH) is an acquired partial or total loss of skin pigmentation occurring as a sequela of preceding cutaneous inflammation, an inflammatory/infectious dermatosis, or a dermatologic procedure. It is distinguished from vitiligo by: (1) a clear history of an antecedent inflammatory trigger at the same site, which vitiligo does not require; (2) typically ill-defined, round-to-oval borders rather than vitiligo's sharp demarcation; (3) usually partial rather than complete pigment loss; and (4) a favourable natural course, with most cases resolving spontaneously over time, unlike vitiligo's typically chronic, often progressive course.
post_inflammatory_hypopigmentation.source: Rao M, Young K, Jackson-Cowan L, et al, 'Post-Inflammatory Hypopigmentation: Review of the Etiology, Clinical Manifestations, and Treatment Options', J Clin Med 2023;12(3):1243 (PMC9917556, PMID 36769891)

chemical_leukoderma.finding: Chemical (occupational/contact) leukoderma is depigmentation clinically resembling vitiligo but caused by cutaneous exposure to specific phenolic/catecholic industrial and cosmetic chemicals, notably 4-tert-butylphenol (4-TBP), monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH) and the cosmetic skin-lightening agent rhododendrol. Mechanistically these compounds are converted by tyrosinase into toxic ortho-quinones that bind cellular proteins and generate reactive oxygen species, directly damaging melanocytes - a chemically-triggered route to melanocyte loss rather than primary autoimmune attack. A distinguishing clue is a temporal and spatial relationship to occupational or cosmetic-product exposure (e.g., a case of proton-pump-inhibitor-induced vitiligo following airborne occupational sensitization, and a documented case of T-cell responses specifically against 4-tert-butylphenol-exposed pigmented cells in a patient with occupational vitiligo), though once triggered the resulting depigmentation can clinically and immunologically overlap with autoimmune vitiligo.
chemical_leukoderma.source: Watanabe F, Kawakami R, Hozumi H, et al (National Institute of Health Sciences Japan), leukoderma caused by 4-alkyl/aryl-substituted phenols and rhododendrol, Kokuritsu Iyakuhin Shokuhin Eisei Kenkyusho Hokoku 2015 (PMID 26821466); van Geel N et al, 'T-cell responses against 4-tert-butylphenol-exposed pigmented cells in a patient with occupational vitiligo', Br J Dermatol 2019 (PMID 30719700); Kim D et al, 'Proton pump inhibitor-induced vitiligo following airborne occupational sensitization', Contact Dermatitis 2021;85(5):595-596 (PMID 34153133)

autoimmune_thyroid_disease.finding: Autoimmune thyroid disease is the single most important comorbidity to screen for in vitiligo. In one series, 19.4% of vitiligo patients over age 20 reported a personal history of autoimmune thyroid disease, an approximately eight-fold increase over the general population frequency of 2.39%. In a separate large Indian nationwide case-control study (MEDEC-V, n=3,968 cases), hypothyroidism was present in 10.52% of vitiligo cases versus 5.35% of matched controls, and anti-thyroglobulin antibody positivity was significantly more common in vitiligo patients than controls - concordant evidence across populations for a real, clinically significant thyroid-autoimmunity link, cross-referenced with this knowledge base's thyroid_disorders entry.
autoimmune_thyroid_disease.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Sarma N et al, 'A Nationwide, Multicentric Case-Control Study on Vitiligo (MEDEC-V) to Elicit the Magnitude and Correlates', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702)

other_autoimmune_associations.finding: Beyond thyroid disease, vitiligo shares GWAS-identified susceptibility genes (e.g. NALP1, PTPN22, CTLA-4) with type 1 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis, reflecting a common immune-regulatory basis for clustering of these autoimmune conditions in vitiligo patients and their families. International consensus explicitly recommends that vitiligo patients be screened periodically for other concomitant autoimmune diseases given this elevated risk, rather than treating vitiligo as a purely dermatologic/cosmetic condition.
other_autoimmune_associations.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

family_history_and_genetics.finding: Family history is a major risk factor: about 20% of vitiligo patients report at least one affected first-degree relative, monozygotic twin concordance is approximately 23%, and genetic factors are estimated to account for roughly 80% of overall disease risk, with at least 54 GWAS-identified susceptibility loci, most involved in immune regulation.
family_history_and_genetics.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341)

other_autoimmune_disease.finding: A personal or family history of another autoimmune disease, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, is a recognized risk factor/association for vitiligo, reflecting shared genetic susceptibility loci across these conditions; this underlies the consensus recommendation for periodic autoimmune-disease screening in vitiligo patients.
other_autoimmune_disease.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Sarma N et al, 'A Nationwide, Multicentric Case-Control Study on Vitiligo (MEDEC-V)', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702)

koebner_triggering_skin_trauma.finding: Skin trauma at a site can trigger new depigmented lesions via the Koebner phenomenon, reported in 15-70% of non-segmental vitiligo patients under formal (history-based/clinical-observation-based/experimentally-induced) classification; however, the international consensus specifically cautions against attributing ordinary daily friction, clothing contact, or pressure as a proven trigger, since rigorous evidence for that specific causal claim is lacking.
koebner_triggering_skin_trauma.source: Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

global_prevalence.finding: Vitiligo affects approximately 0.5-2% of the global population, making it the most common disorder of acquired depigmentation, and can begin at any age though onset is frequently before age 20-30.
global_prevalence.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341)

india_specific_data_and_psychosocial_bur.finding: A large Indian nationwide, multicentric hospital-based case-control study (MEDEC-V) found an institutional vitiligo prevalence of 0.89% (0.86% in males, 0.93% in females), mean age at onset 25.14 +/- 7.48 years, with more than 46% of cases having onset before age 20; non-segmental vitiligo accounted for 67.89% of cases versus 6.49% segmental, and 77% of cases were clinically unstable within the preceding year. The same study found a feeling of depressed mood among vitiligo patients aged 10 and above was three times more common than in controls, and a validated India-developed instrument (the Vitiligo Impact Scale) was specifically created because vitiligo carries a disproportionately large psychosocial burden and social stigma in the Indian context, independent of physical disease extent; a separate multi-country study (including India) similarly documented significant adverse effects of vitiligo on quality of life, social participation and productivity.
india_specific_data_and_psychosocial_bur.source: Sarma N, Chakraborty S, Poojary S, et al, 'A Nationwide, Multicentric Case-Control Study on Vitiligo (MEDEC-V) to Elicit the Magnitude and Correlates', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702); Krishna GS, Ramam M, Mehta M, et al, 'Vitiligo impact scale: an instrument to assess the psychosocial burden of vitiligo', Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2013;79(2):205-210 (PMID 23442459); Kurosky SK et al, 'Social determinants of health, quality of life, and productivity outcomes among adults with vitiligo in Brazil, China, India, and South Africa', J Dermatolog Treat 2025;36(1):2555198 (PMID 40916214)

unpredictable_course_and_relapse_risk.finding: The clinical course of vitiligo is genuinely unpredictable: some patients experience periods of spontaneous partial repigmentation, but progression to involve additional body sites is common in others, and disease activity often fluctuates over years. Even after successful repigmentation with treatment, relapse risk is substantial, estimated at around 40% within the first year. In the Indian MEDEC-V cohort, 77% of cases were unstable (actively spreading) within the preceding year, while only about 11% showed both stability and signs of repigmentation, illustrating that spontaneous, durable remission is the minority outcome rather than the expected course.
unpredictable_course_and_relapse_risk.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Sarma N et al, 'A Nationwide, Multicentric Case-Control Study on Vitiligo (MEDEC-V)', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702)

psychosocial_impact_disproportionate_to_.finding: Despite being asymptomatic and non-life-threatening from a purely physical standpoint, vitiligo carries a psychosocial and quality-of-life burden that is disproportionately large relative to its physical severity - documented as significantly increased depressed mood (threefold higher than controls in the Indian MEDEC-V cohort), the specific development of a dedicated psychosocial-burden instrument (the Vitiligo Impact Scale) in India because of the disease's social stigma there, and documented adverse effects on quality of life and productivity across multiple countries including India. This clinical point is important because management decisions should account for psychosocial impact, not physical extent of depigmentation alone.
psychosocial_impact_disproportionate_to_.source: Sarma N et al, 'A Nationwide, Multicentric Case-Control Study on Vitiligo (MEDEC-V)', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702); Krishna GS et al, 'Vitiligo impact scale: an instrument to assess the psychosocial burden of vitiligo', Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2013;79(2):205-210 (PMID 23442459); Kurosky SK et al, 'Social determinants of health, quality of life, and productivity outcomes among adults with vitiligo in Brazil, China, India, and South Africa', J Dermatolog Treat 2025;36(1):2555198 (PMID 40916214)

screen_for_comorbid_autoimmune_thyroid_d.finding: Every newly diagnosed vitiligo patient should be evaluated for autoimmune thyroid disease (and periodically re-screened), given an approximately eight-fold increase in personal history of autoimmune thyroid disease reported in vitiligo patients (19.4% vs 2.39% general population) and a significantly higher hypothyroidism/anti-thyroglobulin-antibody prevalence confirmed in a large Indian case-control cohort (10.52% vs 5.35% in controls); international consensus explicitly recommends this periodic screening.
screen_for_comorbid_autoimmune_thyroid_d.source: Diotallevi F et al, 'Vitiligo, from Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Advances: State of the Art', Int J Mol Sci 2023;24(5):4910 (PMC10003418, PMID 36902341); Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114); Sarma N et al, 'MEDEC-V', Indian J Dermatol 2020;65(6):473-482 (PMID 33487702)

segmental_vs_nonsegmental_classification.finding: Correctly classifying segmental versus non-segmental vitiligo at presentation meaningfully changes treatment-response expectations and counselling: segmental vitiligo tends to stabilize within 6-24 months of onset and responds particularly well to surgical/melanocyte-transplantation techniques, whereas non-segmental vitiligo follows a more variable, often progressive autoimmune-driven course with generally less predictable surgical response, making this classification a clinically important first step rather than a purely academic distinction.
segmental_vs_nonsegmental_classification.source: Ezzedine K et al, 'Revised classification/nomenclature of vitiligo and related issues: the Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference', Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2012;25(3):E1-13 (PMC3511780, PMID 22417114)

vitiligo.CURABILITY_NOTE: Vitiligo is NOT curable: it is a chronic autoimmune depigmenting disease in which cytotoxic CD8+ T cells progressively destroy epidermal melanocytes, and no drug in this survey reverses the underlying autoimmune predisposition or guarantees a permanent, drug-free result - relapse/progression is a real risk after stopping effective therapy, and even patients who achieve near-complete facial repigmentation on treatment generally see far poorer response on acral skin (hands, feet, lips) and in areas with white hair (poliosis), because there are no residual perifollicular melanocyte reservoirs left to repopulate the epidermis there. What IS real, and a genuinely important recent medicine story, is FDA-approved topical drug-induced REPIGMENTATION: ruxolitinib cream 1.5% (Opzelura), approved by the US FDA in July 2022 specifically for non-segmental vitiligo repigmentation - the first medicine ever FDA-approved for this specific indication - achieved real, vehicle-controlled F-VASI75 (>=75% improvement in the Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index) in 29.8% of patients in TRuE-V1 and 30.9% in TRuE-V2 at week 24, versus only 7.4% and 11.4% respectively with vehicle cream (P<0.001 both trials, n=674 pooled) (Rosmarin D et al, N Engl J Med 2022;387:1445-1455, PMID 36260792). With continued treatment to week 52 (after vehicle-arm patients crossed over to ruxolitinib), pooled F-VASI75 rose to 50.3% among patients who used ruxolitinib continuously throughout, versus 28.2% among those who crossed over late (Ren H et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025;15:1227-1238, PMID 40156697) - a real, roughly-doubled response with sustained use, though facial disease still responds far better than whole-body disease in these same trials. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has vitiligo: (1) confirm non-segmental vs segmental subtype and disease activity/stability first, since this changes treatment choice - surgical options are reserved for STABLE, especially segmental, disease, while active/spreading disease needs anti-inflammatory control first; (2) for active, rapidly spreading non-segmental vitiligo, use a short course of oral mini-pulse (OMP) corticosteroid (betamethasone or dexamethasone on two consecutive days per week) - a real, decades-old, well-evidenced way to arrest progression: 89% of patients had progression arrested and 80% went on to spontaneous repigmentation within a few months in the original Pasricha & Khaitan cohort (Int J Dermatol 1993;32:753-757, PMID 8225724), and a 2021 systematic review of 246 patients across 4 RCTs found up to 32% achieved >75% repigmentation on OMP monotherapy (Chavez-Alvarez S et al, Int J Dermatol 2021;60:794-801, PMID 33729554) - OMP's real job is to stop the disease spreading, with repigmentation a real but secondary benefit; (3) for limited, especially facial/non-acral disease, start a topical agent: potent topical corticosteroids (e.g. clobetasol propionate 0.05%) are a real, effective, cheap first-line option (49.3% mean repigmentation in a head-to-head paediatric trial) but must be limited to short courses given real atrophy/striae risk, especially on facial skin; topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment is nearly as effective (41.3% mean repigmentation in the same head-to-head trial, Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585, PMID 12756094) without the atrophy risk, making it the real preferred first-line agent specifically for facial and periorbital/perioral vitiligo; (4) for the single best evidence-based drug purpose-built for vitiligo repigmentation, use topical ruxolitinib 1.5% cream twice daily for at least 24 weeks (see headline TRuE-V data above), continuing to 52 weeks or beyond for the best chance of a real F-VASI75 response, understanding it works far better on the face than the whole body; (5) combine any topical (tacrolimus, corticosteroid, or ruxolitinib) with narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy wherever access exists, because real, replicated evidence shows combination therapy meaningfully outperforms either component alone - in the UK HI-Light randomised trial, treatment success was seen in 17% with topical corticosteroid alone, 22% with NB-UVB alone, and 27% with the combination (adjusted risk difference +10.9 points over corticosteroid alone, P=0.032, Batchelor JM et al, Health Technol Assess 2020;24(64):1-128, PMID 33245043), and a dedicated meta-analysis found tacrolimus+NB-UVB gave a real 34% relative improvement in achieving >75% repigmentation over NB-UVB alone (RR 1.34, P=0.02, PMID 31267534); (6) for widespread or treatment-refractory active disease, real emerging oral JAK inhibitors now have real, positive phase 3 data: upadacitinib 15 mg once daily achieved real F-VASI75 in 25% and 23% of patients (vs 6-7% placebo, P<0.001) and T-VASI50 (whole-body improvement) in 19-21% (vs 6% placebo) at week 48 across the two Viti-Up phase 3 trials, only recently published (Lancet 2026;408:636-648, PMID 42594914) - a genuine new whole-body efficacy signal, still below the face-only ruxolitinib numbers but a real systemic option; oral ritlecitinib gave a real, statistically significant mean percentage reduction in F-VASI of -21.2% (50 mg with loading dose) versus +2.1% (worsening) with placebo at week 24 in its phase 2b trial (Ezzedine K et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2023;88:395-403, PMID 36370907) and is now in phase 3 (Tranquillo) trials for vitiligo, though as of this survey it remains FDA-approved only for alopecia areata, not vitiligo; (7) for STABLE (non-progressing for at least 1 year) segmental or focal vitiligo unresponsive to medical therapy, autologous non-cultured epidermal cell (melanocyte-keratinocyte) transplantation is a real, effective surgical option, achieving >75% repigmentation in 69-73% of treated patches in a real comparative trial (Dev A et al, J Cosmet Dermatol 2022;21:1234-1241, PMID 34133823) - the closest thing to a definitive local fix for stable, localised disease, though it does not address the underlying autoimmune process or prevent new lesions elsewhere; (8) for extensive (generally >50% body surface area), treatment-refractory vitiligo where the realistic goal shifts from repigmentation to uniformity, monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (monobenzone) permanent depigmentation of the remaining normally-pigmented skin is a real, described-as-effective-and-safe-in-the-medium-term option in a retrospective cohort of 53 patients (Tan ES, Sarkany R, Br J Dermatol 2015, PMID 25556887) - a genuinely last-resort, irreversible option that treats the cosmetic mismatch rather than the disease; (9) camouflage cosmetics (corrective make-up, dihydroxyacetone-based self-tanning products) are a real, non-disease-modifying but genuinely quality-of-life-improving adjunct at every stage, and should be offered alongside medical treatment, not only as a last resort; and (10) set realistic expectations throughout: no medicine in this survey reverses vitiligo permanently, acral and white-hair (poliosis) areas are real, biologically-grounded poor responders to every therapy here, and the realistic modern promise of vitiligo treatment - genuinely new since 2022 - is real, meaningful, drug-induced facial repigmentation in roughly 3 in 10 patients by 6 months and roughly 5 in 10 by a year with ruxolitinib, not a cure.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for non-segmental (and, where specifically noted, segmental/stable) vitiligo: topical corticosteroids; topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus); topical ruxolitinib cream (the real 2022 FDA-approved repigmentation-drug breakthrough, TRuE-V1/TRuE-V2 data); oral mini-pulse (OMP) corticosteroids for halting active/progressive disease; emerging oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib phase 3 Viti-Up 2026 data, ritlecitinib phase 2b data); narrowband UVB phototherapy with its real combination-therapy advantage; 308-nm excimer laser; autologous melanocyte-keratinocyte (non-cultured epidermal cell) transplantation for stable segmental/focal disease; and camouflage cosmetics/permanent monobenzone depigmentation as adjunct/last-resort options. Symptoms and diagnosis are covered in this knowledge base's own vitiligo symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial abstract, systematic review, or regulatory prescribing information; where a number could not be verified from a real primary source it is not given.

vit_topical_corticosteroids.name: Topical Corticosteroids (Potent/Superpotent) - Real Head-to-Head Repigmentation Data vs Tacrolimus (Childhood Vitiligo)
vit_topical_corticosteroids.type: Topical corticosteroid, first-line for limited/localized non-segmental vitiligo
vit_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In a double-blind randomized trial comparing tacrolimus 0.1% ointment versus clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream in 20 children with vitiligo (18 completing with repigmentation outcomes), mean repigmentation was 49.3% with clobetasol propionate versus 41.3% with tacrolimus over the treatment period (Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585, PMID 12756094). In the UK HI-Light Vitiligo randomised trial, topical corticosteroid (mometasone furoate 0.1%) monotherapy achieved treatment success in 17% (20/119) of participants at 9 months (Batchelor JM et al, Health Technol Assess 2020;24(64):1-128, PMID 33245043).
vit_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids suppress the cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of epidermal melanocytes by binding the glucocorticoid receptor and reducing local production of interferon-gamma and other pro-inflammatory cytokines implicated in melanocyte killing, allowing residual/follicular melanocyte reservoirs to repopulate the epidermis.
vit_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Potent/superpotent topical corticosteroids carry a real risk of skin atrophy, telangiectasia and striae with continuous use beyond 2-3 months, particularly on facial and periorbital skin, and current practice limits continuous use to defined courses with breaks or step-down to a non-steroid agent; response is also visibly poorer on acral skin (hands, feet), consistent with every other therapy in this survey.
vit_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Use a potent-to-superpotent topical corticosteroid once daily for a defined course (commonly 2-4 months, then reassess) on trunk/limb lesions in non-segmental vitiligo, and prefer tacrolimus over steroids on the face/periorbital/perioral area from the outset given its near-equal efficacy without atrophy risk.
vit_topical_corticosteroids.source: Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585 (PMID 12756094); Batchelor JM et al, Health Technol Assess 2020;24(64):1-128 (PMID 33245043)

vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Tacrolimus Ointment - Real Preferred First-Line for Facial Vitiligo, Near-Steroid Efficacy Without Atrophy
vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Topical calcineurin inhibitor, non-steroidal, preferred for facial/periorbital/perioral disease
specific_drugs: Pimecrolimus 1% cream (Elidel, used in practice for the same steroid-sparing indication)
vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In the same head-to-head paediatric trial cited above, tacrolimus 0.1% ointment achieved 41.3% mean repigmentation versus 49.3% with clobetasol propionate 0.05% (Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585, PMID 12756094) - a real, near-equivalent effect without steroid-associated atrophy. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies (814 patients), tacrolimus combined with narrowband UVB improved the rate of achieving >75% repigmentation by a real relative 34% over NB-UVB alone (risk ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.05-1.71, P=0.02), while tacrolimus and topical steroids showed similar potency for >75% repigmentation head-to-head (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.19-5.51, P=0.98) (Arora CJ et al, Australas J Dermatol 2020;61:e1-e9, PMID 31267534).
vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin, blocking T-cell activation and local cytokine (interferon-gamma, IL-15) transcription that drives melanocyte-directed cytotoxicity, without the collagen/dermal-thinning effect of corticosteroids - which is why it is the real preferred agent for thin, steroid-vulnerable facial and genital skin.
vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: Tacrolimus ointment carries an FDA boxed warning for a theoretical long-term malignancy risk extrapolated from systemic use in transplant patients, not confirmed in topical-use vitiligo/dermatitis population studies; local burning/stinging on application is common initially, and, like steroids, response is poorer on acral skin.
vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Use tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (0.03% in children) as the real first-line topical agent for facial, periorbital, perioral and genital vitiligo, ideally combined with NB-UVB phototherapy where accessible, which gives a real, meta-analysis-verified 34% relative improvement in achieving substantial repigmentation over either alone.
vit_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585 (PMID 12756094); Arora CJ et al, Australas J Dermatol 2020;61:e1-e9 (PMID 31267534)

vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.name: Ruxolitinib Cream 1.5% (Opzelura) - Real FDA-Approved (2022) Repigmentation Drug, TRuE-V1/TRuE-V2 Phase 3 Trials
vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.type: Topical Janus kinase (JAK1/JAK2) inhibitor, first and only FDA-approved medicine specifically for vitiligo repigmentation
specific_drugs: Ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (Opzelura), applied twice daily to affected areas up to 10% body surface area
vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.effectiveness: In two identically designed phase 3, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials (TRuE-V1, n=330; TRuE-V2, n=344; total 674 patients with non-segmental vitiligo affecting <=10% BSA, randomized 2:1 to ruxolitinib cream or vehicle twice daily), the primary endpoint F-VASI75 (>=75% improvement in Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index) at week 24 was achieved by 29.8% with ruxolitinib versus 7.4% with vehicle in TRuE-V1 (relative risk approximately 4.0, P<0.001), and by 30.9% versus 11.4% in TRuE-V2 (relative risk approximately 2.7, P<0.001) (Rosmarin D et al, N Engl J Med 2022;387:1445-1455, PMID 36260792). After all patients received open-label ruxolitinib from week 24-52, a pooled descriptive analysis found F-VASI75 in 50.3% (176/350) of patients who applied ruxolitinib continuously throughout versus 28.2% (46/163) of those who crossed over late from vehicle at week 52 (Ren H et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025;15:1227-1238, PMID 40156697). Most common adverse events over 52 weeks were application-site acne (6.3-6.6%), nasopharyngitis (5.4-6.1%) and application-site pruritus (5.3-5.4%).
vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.reason_why: Ruxolitinib inhibits JAK1/JAK2, blocking interferon-gamma-driven JAK-STAT signalling in and around vitiligo lesions - interferon-gamma and its downstream chemokines CXCL9/CXCL10 are the specific, now well-characterised molecular drivers that recruit and sustain the cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that kill melanocytes in vitiligo, making JAK1/2 blockade a real, mechanistically targeted treatment rather than a repurposed generic anti-inflammatory.
vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.important_caveat: Facial disease (F-VASI) responds far better than whole-body disease (T-VASI) in these same trials - the headline numbers above are specifically facial outcomes; approved use is capped at <=10% body surface area; long-term (beyond 52 weeks) real-world repigmentation durability data are still accumulating.
vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.real_working_solution: Apply ruxolitinib 1.5% cream twice daily to facial and other affected areas for at least 24 weeks before judging response, and continue to 52 weeks or longer if any improvement is seen, since continuous use roughly doubles the F-VASI75 response rate (50.3%) compared with late-starting or interrupted use (28.2%) in the real pooled trial data - this is the single most evidence-backed medicine in this survey purpose-built for vitiligo repigmentation.
vit_topical_jak_inhibitor_ruxolitinib.source: Rosmarin D et al (TRuE-V1/TRuE-V2), N Engl J Med 2022;387:1445-1455 (PMID 36260792); Ren H et al (pooled subgroup analysis), Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025;15:1227-1238 (PMID 40156697)

vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.name: Oral Mini-Pulse (OMP) Corticosteroid Therapy - Real Evidence for Halting Progression of Active/Fast-Spreading Vitiligo
vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.type: Systemic (oral) corticosteroid, pulsed/intermittent dosing, for active or rapidly progressive non-segmental vitiligo
specific_drugs: Betamethasone 5 mg on two consecutive days per week (oral mini-pulse)
Dexamethasone 2.5-5 mg on two consecutive days per week (oral mini-pulse)
vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In the original oral mini-pulse cohort of 40 patients with extensive or fast-spreading vitiligo (36 with active disease), progression was arrested in 89% of the 36 active-disease patients within 1-3 months, and 80% of patients went on to show spontaneous repigmentation within 2-4 months of starting therapy (Pasricha JS, Khaitan BK, Int J Dermatol 1993;32:753-757, PMID 8225724). A 2021 systematic review pooling 246 patients across 4 randomised controlled trials found up to 32% of patients achieved >75% repigmentation with OMP used as monotherapy, with no significant difference between OMP and other active treatments specifically for arresting disease activity (Chavez-Alvarez S et al, Int J Dermatol 2021;60:794-801, PMID 33729554). A separate paediatric/adolescent cohort found OMP led to disease stabilization in 63.6% of cases, though 25.3% relapsed after discontinuation (Kumaran MS et al, Int J Dermatol 2025;64:2292-2298, PMID 40716114).
vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.reason_why: Pulsed oral corticosteroids produce a brief but real systemic immunosuppressive effect on the circulating cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell population driving active melanocyte destruction, sufficient to halt an acute autoimmune flare, while the intermittent (two-days-per-week) dosing schedule is specifically designed to minimise the cumulative systemic steroid exposure of daily continuous corticosteroid use.
vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.important_caveat: OMP's real, well-evidenced job is arresting disease progression - repigmentation is a real but secondary and more variable benefit, and relapse after stopping OMP occurs in a meaningful minority (25.3% in the paediatric cohort above); OMP is not intended as, and should not be used as, long-term continuous therapy given cumulative systemic corticosteroid risk (weight gain, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, HPA-axis suppression with prolonged use).
vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Use a short course (typically 3-6 months) of oral mini-pulse betamethasone or dexamethasone on two consecutive days per week for any patient with active, rapidly spreading non-segmental vitiligo, to arrest progression before or alongside starting a topical/phototherapy repigmentation regimen; do not use OMP as an indefinite maintenance therapy.
vit_oral_mini_pulse_corticosteroids.source: Pasricha JS, Khaitan BK, Int J Dermatol 1993;32:753-757 (PMID 8225724); Chavez-Alvarez S et al, Int J Dermatol 2021;60:794-801 (PMID 33729554); Kumaran MS et al, Int J Dermatol 2025;64:2292-2298 (PMID 40716114)

vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.name: Emerging Oral JAK Inhibitors - Upadacitinib (Viti-Up Phase 3, 2026) and Ritlecitinib (Phase 2b Complete, Phase 3 In Progress)
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.type: Targeted oral small molecules, JAK1-selective (upadacitinib) and JAK3/TEC-family-selective (ritlecitinib), for widespread or treatment-refractory non-segmental vitiligo
specific_drugs: Upadacitinib 15 mg once daily (Rinvoq; not yet FDA-approved for vitiligo as of this survey, phase 3 data below)

Ritlecitinib 50 mg once daily with optional loading dose (Litfulo; FDA-approved for alopecia areata, phase 2b vitiligo data below and phase 3 vitiligo trials in progress, not yet approved for vitiligo)
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.effectiveness: Upadacitinib: in two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (Viti-Up-1, n=308; Viti-Up-2, n=306; upadacitinib 15 mg once daily vs placebo, 2:1), at week 48 F-VASI75 was achieved by 25% vs 6% (Viti-Up-1) and 23% vs 7% (Viti-Up-2), and T-VASI50 (>=50% whole-body improvement) by 19% vs 6% and 21% vs 6% respectively (all P<0.001) (Lancet 2026;408:636-648, PMID 42594914). Ritlecitinib: in a phase 2b randomised, placebo-controlled trial, the 50 mg-with-loading-dose group had a mean percentage change in F-VASI of -21.2% versus +2.1% (worsening) with placebo at week 24 (P<0.001); 50 mg without loading dose gave -18.5% vs 2.1% (P<0.001), and 30 mg gave -14.6% vs 2.1% (P=0.01) (Ezzedine K et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2023;88:395-403, PMID 36370907), with the trial's own conclusion stating ritlecitinib was 'effective and well tolerated over 48 weeks'.
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.reason_why: Both drugs block Janus kinase signalling required downstream of interferon-gamma (upadacitinib, via JAK1) or the specific kinase pathways sustaining resident cytotoxic and tissue-resident memory T cells in vitiligo skin (ritlecitinib, via JAK3/TEC-family kinases important to T-cell receptor signalling), giving systemic (whole-body, not just facial) reach that topical ruxolitinib cannot achieve at scale for extensive disease.
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.important_caveat: Neither drug is FDA-approved specifically for vitiligo as of this survey (upadacitinib phase 3 data was only published in 2026 and ritlecitinib is in ongoing phase 3 Tranquillo trials for vitiligo); both carry JAK-inhibitor class boxed-warning risks (malignancy, major cardiovascular events, thrombosis, serious infection) from their approved indications in other diseases. Whole-body (T-VASI) response rates for upadacitinib (19-21%) remain well below topical ruxolitinib's facial (F-VASI) response rates, showing even the newest oral option has not closed the gap to a majority-response drug for total-body vitiligo.
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.real_working_solution: Consider oral upadacitinib or ritlecitinib (where access, cost and JAK-inhibitor safety screening allow) for patients with widespread non-segmental vitiligo beyond the reach of topical therapy, setting a realistic expectation of roughly 1 in 4-5 patients reaching a substantial (F-VASI75/T-VASI50) response at 48 weeks - a real, genuinely new, but still partial systemic option rather than a reliable whole-body cure.
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.source: Upadacitinib: Viti-Up phase 3 trials, Lancet 2026;408:636-648 (PMID 42594914); Ritlecitinib: Ezzedine K et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2023;88:395-403 (PMID 36370907)
vit_oral_jak_inhibitors_emerging.confidence: high for the upadacitinib phase 3 percentages and ritlecitinib phase 2b percentages, both directly retrieved from PubMed abstract text; moderate for exact current regulatory-approval status of each drug specifically for vitiligo, which was assessed from trial-publication dates and general prescribing-information knowledge rather than a dedicated live regulatory-database check on 2026-09-22

vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.name: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) Phototherapy - Real Standalone and Combination-Therapy Evidence (UK HI-Light Trial)
vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.type: Physical/light-based therapy, non-drug, standard adjunct/backbone for moderate-to-extensive non-segmental vitiligo
specific_drugs: Narrowband UVB (311-313 nm) phototherapy, 2-3 sessions/week, in-clinic or home-based unit
Not a medicine - listed here for completeness of the exhaustive treatment survey
vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.effectiveness: In the UK HI-Light Vitiligo randomised controlled trial (n=370, adults and children with vitiligo of the face and/or body), treatment success at 9 months was achieved by 27% (34/128) with combined NB-UVB plus topical corticosteroid, versus 22% (27/123) with NB-UVB alone and 17% (20/119) with topical corticosteroid alone; the combination was statistically superior to corticosteroid alone (adjusted risk difference 10.9 percentage points, P=0.032), while NB-UVB alone was not statistically superior to corticosteroid alone (P=0.29) (Batchelor JM et al, Health Technol Assess 2020;24(64):1-128, PMID 33245043). A Cochrane systematic review found NB-UVB showed a non-significant 60% relative increase in repigmentation versus PUVA (RR 1.60, 95% CI 0.74-3.45) and noted individual trials in which oral corticosteroid plus NB-UVB outperformed corticosteroid alone (Whitton ME et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;2015(2):CD003263, PMID 25710794).
vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.reason_why: Narrowband UVB (311-313 nm) suppresses the cytotoxic T-cell infiltrate in vitiligo skin via induction of T-cell apoptosis and local immunomodulation, while separately stimulating proliferation and migration of residual melanocyte precursors from the hair-follicle bulge - a dual mechanism that explains why it performs best combined with an anti-inflammatory topical that further suppresses the autoimmune attack while NB-UVB drives melanocyte repopulation.
vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.important_caveat: This is a real, systemic-drug-free option but requires 2-3 clinic (or supervised home-unit) sessions per week for many months, a genuine access/adherence burden, and carries a real, though generally low, long-term cumulative skin-cancer risk with extensive lifetime UV exposure; response, as with every other therapy in this survey, is poorer on acral (hand/foot) skin.
vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.real_working_solution: Use NB-UVB as a real, evidence-backed combination-therapy backbone alongside a topical corticosteroid, tacrolimus, or (increasingly) ruxolitinib cream rather than as monotherapy, since the real, replicated UK trial evidence shows combination therapy is what achieves a statistically real advantage over any single agent.
vit_phototherapy_nbuvb.source: Batchelor JM et al, Health Technol Assess 2020;24(64):1-128 (PMID 33245043); Whitton ME et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;2015(2):CD003263 (PMID 25710794)

vit_excimer_laser.name: 308-nm Excimer Laser - Real Network Meta-Analysis of Combination Therapy
vit_excimer_laser.type: Targeted physical/light-based therapy, non-drug, for localized/limited vitiligo lesions
specific_drugs: 308-nm excimer laser or excimer lamp monotherapy, 2 sessions/week
Not a medicine - listed here for completeness of the exhaustive treatment survey
vit_excimer_laser.effectiveness: A 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis of 38 studies (1841 participants) found that combining 308-nm excimer light with a topical corticosteroid improved the relative risk of achieving >=50% repigmentation by 1.65-fold and of achieving 100% repigmentation by 2.31-fold versus excimer monotherapy; combining excimer with a topical calcineurin inhibitor gave a 1.47-fold relative improvement for >=50% repigmentation and a 1.60-fold improvement for 100% repigmentation versus excimer monotherapy (Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2026, PMID 41564112).
vit_excimer_laser.reason_why: The 308-nm excimer wavelength is within the narrowband UVB range and works through the same T-cell-apoptosis/melanocyte-precursor-stimulation mechanism as NB-UVB, but is delivered as a targeted beam that can treat individual lesions at a higher, more precisely titrated fluence than a full-body NB-UVB cabinet, making it particularly suited to limited/localized lesions rather than widespread disease.
vit_excimer_laser.important_caveat: This network meta-analysis reports relative risks (improvement multiples) rather than absolute monotherapy response percentages in the retrievable abstract, so an exact standalone excimer-laser responder percentage is not given here as a single number; excimer laser is impractical for extensive body-surface-area disease given its lesion-by-lesion, per-session treatment approach, and access to the device is a real limiting factor outside specialist dermatology centres.
vit_excimer_laser.real_working_solution: Use 308-nm excimer laser/lamp for limited, localized non-segmental or stable segmental lesions (face, neck, limited trunk/limb patches), combined with a topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor from the outset, since the real network meta-analysis evidence shows this combination meaningfully outperforms excimer monotherapy for both partial and complete repigmentation.
vit_excimer_laser.source: Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2026, PMID 41564112 (308-nm excimer light network meta-analysis, 38 studies, 1841 participants)
vit_excimer_laser.confidence: moderate-high - relative-risk figures directly retrieved from the abstract; absolute monotherapy responder percentage was not available from the abstract text retrieved in this research pass, stated honestly rather than estimated

vit_melanocyte_transplantation.name: Autologous Non-Cultured Epidermal Cell (Melanocyte-Keratinocyte) Transplantation - Real Surgical Option for Stable Segmental/Focal Vitiligo
vit_melanocyte_transplantation.type: Surgical/cellular-grafting procedure, for stable (non-progressing >=1 year) segmental or focal vitiligo unresponsive to medical therapy
specific_drugs: Not a medicine - autologous non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (NCES) / melanocyte-keratinocyte transplantation procedure (MKTP), harvested from the patient's own unaffected skin via dermabrasion or suction blister and applied to dermabraded/laser-ablated recipient vitiligo patches
vit_melanocyte_transplantation.effectiveness: In a comparative trial of 26 patients (dermabrasion technique variants for recipient-site preparation before non-cultured epidermal cell suspension transplantation), >75% repigmentation was observed in 69.3% of patches prepared by manual dermabrasion and 73.1% of patches prepared by electrofulguration-assisted dermabrasion (Dev A et al, J Cosmet Dermatol 2022;21:1234-1241, PMID 34133823). A related technique-comparison trial (30 patients, 41 matched lesion pairs) found >=90% ('excellent') repigmentation in 34-37% of patches and >=75% ('good') repigmentation in 68-71% of patches, depending on cell-suspension preparation method (Mrigpuri S et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2019, PMID 30176093).
vit_melanocyte_transplantation.reason_why: This procedure physically transplants a patient's own healthy, pigment-producing melanocytes (together with keratinocytes, which support melanocyte survival and function) directly into the depigmented patch after ablating the recipient epidermis, bypassing the need for residual melanocyte reservoirs or drug-induced melanocyte stimulation - which is why it works specifically well in STABLE disease with no ongoing autoimmune destruction, but does not address or prevent new lesions from the underlying autoimmune process elsewhere on the body.
vit_melanocyte_transplantation.important_caveat: Strict patient selection is essential: the procedure is only appropriate for disease that has been stable (no new lesions or spread) for at least 1 year, most classically segmental vitiligo, since transplanting melanocytes into a still-actively-inflamed patch risks the graft itself being attacked; it requires a specialist dermatosurgery setup, carries real risks of scarring, cobblestoning or patchy/uneven repigmentation at the recipient site, and does not treat or prevent disease elsewhere on the body.
vit_melanocyte_transplantation.real_working_solution: Offer autologous non-cultured epidermal cell transplantation to patients with stable (>=1 year non-progressing), especially segmental, vitiligo who have not achieved adequate repigmentation with 6-12 months of medical therapy (topical/phototherapy) - real trial data shows a substantial majority (69-73%) of treated patches reach >75% repigmentation, the strongest localized-clearance number of any option in this survey.
vit_melanocyte_transplantation.source: Dev A et al, J Cosmet Dermatol 2022;21:1234-1241 (PMID 34133823); Mrigpuri S et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2019 (PMID 30176093)

vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.name: Camouflage Cosmetics and Permanent Depigmentation (Monobenzone) - Adjunct and Last-Resort Options for Extensive/Refractory Disease
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.type: Non-pharmacological cosmetic adjunct (camouflage) and irreversible chemical depigmentation (monobenzone), not disease-modifying
specific_drugs: Monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (monobenzone) 20% cream, for permanent depigmentation of remaining pigmented skin in extensive/refractory disease
Camouflage cosmetics: corrective make-up, dihydroxyacetone (DHA)-based self-tanning/staining products - not medicines, listed for completeness
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.effectiveness: Topical monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone was described as 'an effective and safe treatment for depigmentation of extensive vitiligo in the medium term' in a retrospective cohort of 53 patients (Tan ES, Sarkany R, Br J Dermatol 2015, PMID 25556887); this was published as a short communication/letter without a structured abstract, so an exact quantitative success percentage could not be independently retrieved in this research pass and is not stated as a number here. Camouflage cosmetics are separately documented to produce real, substantial quality-of-life improvement in visible dermatological conditions generally (Children's/Family Dermatology Life Quality Index improving from a mean of 6.1-6.8 at baseline to 2.1-4.7 after camouflage teaching, across cohorts that included pigmentary conditions; PMID 26162859, PMID 25218434), though these specific cohorts were not vitiligo-only populations.
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.reason_why: Monobenzone is directly melanocytotoxic - it selectively destroys the remaining functioning melanocytes in still-pigmented skin, permanently equalising skin tone in patients with extensive depigmentation, rather than restoring lost pigment; camouflage cosmetics work purely optically, masking visible contrast without any biological effect on melanocytes.
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.important_caveat: Monobenzone depigmentation is irreversible and permanent - it eliminates the patient's remaining natural pigmentation and confers resulting lifelong photosensitivity requiring strict sun protection, and unpredictable repigmentation after stopping has itself been separately documented in case reports; this is a genuinely last-resort option appropriate only for extensive (generally >50% body surface area), treatment-refractory disease where achieving pigmentary uniformity (rather than repigmentation) becomes the realistic goal, and requires extensive patient counselling and informed consent given its permanence. Camouflage cosmetics do not treat vitiligo at all and their real benefit here (quality of life) was documented in cohorts that were not vitiligo-specific, stated honestly rather than extrapolated as a vitiligo-specific number.
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.real_working_solution: Offer camouflage cosmetics as a real, immediately available, non-invasive quality-of-life adjunct at every stage of vitiligo, regardless of disease extent or treatment choice; reserve monobenzone permanent depigmentation strictly for extensive, medically refractory disease after exhausting repigmentation-directed therapy (topical, phototherapy, oral JAK inhibitors, surgical options above), with thorough counselling on its irreversibility.
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.source: Tan ES, Sarkany R, Br J Dermatol 2015 (PMID 25556887); camouflage quality-of-life data: PMID 26162859, PMID 25218434 (general dermatology camouflage cohorts, not vitiligo-specific)
vit_camouflage_and_depigmentation.confidence: moderate - the monobenzone effectiveness claim is qualitative (author-stated 'effective and safe') rather than a specific quantitative percentage, honestly flagged as not retrievable from this letter-format publication's abstract; the camouflage quality-of-life data is real but drawn from general dermatology cohorts rather than vitiligo-specific studies

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral mini-pulse corticosteroid, progression arrest in active disease (Pasricha & Khaitan cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Disease progression arrested in 89% of 36 patients with active vitiligo within 1-3 months (n=36 active-disease patients of 40 total cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pasricha JS, Khaitan BK, Int J Dermatol 1993;32:753-757 (PMID 8225724)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral mini-pulse corticosteroid, spontaneous repigmentation after arrest (Pasricha & Khaitan cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 80% of patients showed spontaneous repigmentation within 2-4 months of starting therapy, following disease arrest
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pasricha JS, Khaitan BK, Int J Dermatol 1993;32:753-757 (PMID 8225724)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Melanocyte-keratinocyte transplantation, electrofulguration-assisted dermabrasion, >75% repigmentation
ranked_high_to_low.metric: >75% repigmentation achieved in 73.1% of treated patches (n=26 patients, comparative technique trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dev A et al, J Cosmet Dermatol 2022;21:1234-1241 (PMID 34133823)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Melanocyte-keratinocyte transplantation, manual dermabrasion, >75% repigmentation
ranked_high_to_low.metric: >75% repigmentation achieved in 69.3% of treated patches (n=26 patients, comparative technique trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dev A et al, J Cosmet Dermatol 2022;21:1234-1241 (PMID 34133823)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral mini-pulse corticosteroid, disease stabilization (paediatric/adolescent real-world cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Disease stabilization achieved in 63.6% of cases (25.3% subsequently relapsed after discontinuation)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kumaran MS et al, Int J Dermatol 2025;64:2292-2298 (PMID 40716114)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ruxolitinib cream, continuous use, F-VASI75 at week 52 (pooled TRuE-V subgroup analysis)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: F-VASI75 in 50.3% (176/350) of patients applying ruxolitinib cream continuously through week 52
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ren H et al, Dermatol Ther (Heidelb) 2025;15:1227-1238 (PMID 40156697)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Mean repigmentation 49.3% over the treatment period (n=18 completers, double-blind randomised trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585 (PMID 12756094)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Mean repigmentation 41.3% over the treatment period (n=18 completers, double-blind randomised trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lepe V et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139:581-585 (PMID 12756094)
