ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk 2.31-fold higher rate of 100% repigmentation versus excimer monotherapy (network meta-analysis, 38 studies, 1841 participants) - reported as a relative risk multiplier, not a directly stated absolute percentage, so no single effectiveness_pct is given
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2026 (PMID 41564112)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Monobenzone (monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone) permanent depigmentation, extensive refractory vitiligo
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Described by the authors as 'effective and safe... in the medium term' in a retrospective cohort of 53 patients; published as a short communication/letter without a structured abstract, so no exact quantitative success percentage could be independently retrieved in this research pass
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tan ES, Sarkany R, Br J Dermatol 2015 (PMID 25556887)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Rows are drawn from different trials, timepoints (week 24 vs week 48 vs week 52 vs 9 months vs 1-4 months) and endpoints (F-VASI75 vs T-VASI50 vs an arithmetic mean-percentage F-VASI change vs a global 'treatment success'/repigmentation-percentage/progression-arrest outcome), so this table should be read as an honest survey of the real, sourced evidence for each option rather than a single uniform head-to-head ranking; rows are explicitly labelled with their real metric so a like-for-like comparison can be made by filtering on the metric text. The single most robust real placebo-controlled finding for 'which medicine has real FDA-approved, purpose-built evidence for vitiligo repigmentation' is the TRuE-V1/TRuE-V2 ruxolitinib cream data (ranks 10-11 and 6/12 above), because ruxolitinib is the only drug in this survey both specifically FDA-approved for vitiligo and tested against a true vehicle placebo in two large phase 3 trials; the oral mini-pulse corticosteroid numbers at ranks 1-2 and 5 measure a different real outcome (halting active disease progression) rather than repigmentation, and should not be read as directly comparable to the repigmentation-percentage rows.

streptococcal_pharyngitis.name: Streptococcal Pharyngitis (Strep Throat)
streptococcal_pharyngitis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 Foundation/MMS lookup for 'streptococcal pharyngitis' could not be independently confirmed via a live icd.who.int browse in this research session, so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here. Widely used legacy reference: ICD-10 J02.0 (Streptococcal pharyngitis); real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use.

organism_and_direct_infection_mechanism.finding: Streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat) is a direct bacterial infection of the pharynx and/or tonsils by Group A Streptococcus (GAS), Streptococcus pyogenes, transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact with infected secretions/sores; the CDC states GAS bacteria 'often live in the nose and throat' and spread through talking, coughing, or sneezing, with an incubation period of approximately 2-5 days. Direct GAS infection produces the pharyngitis itself and, in a subset of cases, the toxin-mediated scarlatiniform rash of scarlet fever (see classic_symptoms below); these are mechanistically direct infective/toxin-mediated processes, distinct from the immune-mediated complications below.
organism_and_direct_infection_mechanism.source: CDC, 'About Group A Strep', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/about/index.html (accessed 2026); CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026)

direct_infection_vs_post_infectious_immu.finding: A genuinely important distinction: GAS pharyngitis itself is a direct bacterial infection, but its two feared non-suppurative sequelae - acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) - are not caused by ongoing bacterial invasion but by a delayed autoimmune/immune-complex response to a preceding GAS infection. The CDC states explicitly that both ARF and PSGN 'are thought to be caused by an immune response to an earlier group A strep infection', i.e. the organism itself need not still be present in the pharynx by the time these complications appear. This distinction is the entire rationale for why antibiotic treatment of the acute pharyngitis (a self-limited direct infection in most patients, see natural_history below) is still recommended: eradicating the antigenic stimulus early can prevent the later immune-mediated disease, not merely shorten the throat infection itself.

molecular_mimicry_mechanism_of_rheumatic.finding: The specific immunological mechanism linking GAS pharyngitis to acute rheumatic fever is molecular mimicry: the GAS M protein and the group A carbohydrate epitope N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosamine (NABG) share structural/antigenic similarity with human cardiac myosin and valve tissue, so T cells and antibodies raised against the streptococcal antigens cross-react with cardiac myosin and valvular tissue, producing the myocarditis and valvulitis of rheumatic carditis; the same NABG epitope cross-reacts with lysoganglioside in the basal ganglia, the proposed mechanism for Sydenham chorea. This entry cross-references the knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry, which documents this mechanism in full together with the typical 1-5 week (commonly 2-3 week) latency between the antecedent throat infection and onset of ARF - the interval during which the immune-mediated process, not persistent bacterial infection, is what produces disease.
molecular_mimicry_mechanism_of_rheumatic.source: Cunningham MW, 'Molecular Mimicry, Autoimmunity, and Infection: The Cross-Reactive Antigens of Group A Streptococci and their Sequelae', Microbiol Spectr 2019;7(4) (PMID 31373269); cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry (symptoms.pathophysiology, symptoms.latency_period)

centor_mcisaac_clinical_prediction_score.finding: The Centor score, later modified by McIsaac to add an age adjustment (the McIsaac score), is the standard clinical prediction rule used to estimate pre-test probability of GAS pharyngitis before deciding on RADT/culture testing. Its four original Centor criteria are: (1) tonsillar exudate, (2) tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, (3) fever by history, and (4) absence of cough; the McIsaac modification adds an age term (+1 point for age 3-14 years, 0 for age 15-44, -1 for age >=45). Real-world outpatient nurse phone-triage and electronic-visit data show McIsaac scores of 4 were associated with a positive GAS rate of 55-68% across encounter types, while encounters scoring 0 (with complete data) had no positive GAS tests among the cases reviewed - i.e. the score meaningfully stratifies pre-test probability at its extremes in that dataset.
centor_mcisaac_clinical_prediction_score.source: Fine AM et al, 'Use of the McIsaac Score to Predict Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis in Outpatient Nurse Phone Triage and Electronic Visits', J Med Internet Res 2021 (PMID 34932016)

pooled_accuracy_of_centor_and_mcisaac_sc.finding: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of the McIsaac and Centor scores found that the McIsaac score had higher estimated sensitivity and lower specificity than the Centor score at equivalent thresholds, but with wide and overlapping confidence regions between the two - i.e. neither score is a clearly superior, sharply discriminating instrument across studies, and both are properly used as pre-test-probability tools to guide who needs RADT/culture testing rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tests.
pooled_accuracy_of_centor_and_mcisaac_sc.source: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the accuracy of McIsaac and Centor score in patients with pharyngitis, Clin Microbiol Infect 2024;30(4):445-452 (PMID 38182052)
pooled_accuracy_of_centor_and_mcisaac_sc.confidence: moderate (pooled point estimates for sensitivity/specificity could not be independently re-extracted from the abstract alone in this research session; the qualitative McIsaac-more-sensitive/Centor-more-specific-with-overlapping-CI finding is directly sourced)

real_evidence_of_poor_score_performance_.finding: A real, honestly-reported negative finding: in a prospective study of 120 Indian children with sore throat (streptococcal culture positivity 35%), the modified Centor score performed poorly, with an area under the ROC curve of only 0.589 (95% CI 0.481-0.697, P=0.11), leading the authors to conclude 'predictive validity of modified Centor score was not satisfactory' in this population. Individual physical findings had more useful specificity in this cohort - palatine petechiae (100% specificity), palatine exudates (97.5%), and tender cervical nodes (88.6%) - while cough had poor discriminative value (63.4% sensitivity but only 36.7% specificity). This is a real, population-specific caveat against assuming Western-derived Centor/McIsaac cutoffs transfer directly to Indian paediatric practice, and is reported here rather than smoothed over.
real_evidence_of_poor_score_performance_.source: 'McIsaac Modification of Centor Score in Diagnosis of Streptococcal Pharyngitis and Antibiotic Sensitivity Pattern', Indian Pediatrics 2019 (PMID 30806362)

radt_and_throat_culture_role.finding: The CDC recommends rapid antigen detection testing (RADT) or throat culture for confirmation in patients with a clinical picture consistent with GAS pharyngitis. RADT has high specificity but variable sensitivity relative to throat culture, which remains the diagnostic gold standard. A critical, guideline-specified follow-up rule exists for children: in children over age 3 with a negative RADT, providers should follow up with a back-up throat culture to avoid missing true GAS infections (culture is more sensitive), whereas in other age groups routine culture back-up is not required because acute rheumatic fever is extremely rare in adults. Testing (and treatment) is not recommended in children under 3 years, in whom GAS pharyngitis and its rheumatic-fever complication are both rare.
radt_and_throat_culture_role.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026); Shulman ST et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 2012 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America', Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):1279-1282 (PMID 22965026)

distinction_from_viral_pharyngitis_to_av.finding: A genuinely important real diagnostic principle, not a minor caveat: the presence of cough, rhinorrhea/coryza, hoarseness, oral ulcers, or conjunctivitis makes viral pharyngitis substantially more likely than GAS and is used as a reason to withhold testing/antibiotics rather than pursue them, because these features are specifically absent from the classic GAS picture. The CDC states patients typically 'lack cough, runny nose, hoarseness, mouth sores, or eye inflammation' when the cause is GAS, framing these as features that 'suggest viral infection instead'. The IDSA 2012 guideline builds its testing recommendations around this same principle, since most pharyngitis (viral and bacterial-but-non-GAS) does not require antibiotics and unnecessary testing/treatment of viral pharyngitis is a recognised driver of antibiotic overuse.
distinction_from_viral_pharyngitis_to_av.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026); Shulman ST et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):1279-1282 (PMID 22965026)

core_triad_and_examination_findings.finding: Classic GAS pharyngitis presents with sudden-onset sore throat, fever, pain on swallowing (odynophagia), and examination findings of pharyngeal/tonsillar erythema, tonsillar exudate, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy (enlarged, tender lymph nodes in the front of the neck). The CDC's clinical guidance lists exactly this combination - 'fever, pain with swallowing, sudden onset of sore throat' plus throat redness, swollen tonsils and neck lymph node enlargement - as the classic presentation.
core_triad_and_examination_findings.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026)

absence_of_cough_and_coryza_as_a_disting.finding: A real, clinically load-bearing negative finding is part of the classic presentation itself: absence of cough, runny nose (coryza), hoarseness, mouth sores, and conjunctivitis, because their presence points instead to a viral cause. This absence-of-viral-features pattern is one of the four original Centor criteria (absence of cough) and is treated by the CDC as a positive diagnostic clue for GAS rather than an incidental negative.
absence_of_cough_and_coryza_as_a_disting.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026); Fine AM et al, J Med Internet Res 2021 (PMID 34932016)

scarlet_fever_rash_in_a_subset.finding: A real subset of GAS pharyngitis cases present with, or develop, scarlet fever - the same GAS infection accompanied by a characteristic toxin-mediated rash rather than a separate disease. The CDC describes the rash as erythematous and blanching with a 'sandpaper' texture, with Pastia's lines (accentuated redness in flexor skin creases), beginning on the trunk and spreading outward while typically sparing palms and soles, and persisting about one week; associated findings include a 'strawberry tongue' (white-coated tongue with prominent red papillae that later clears) and circumoral pallor. This research session did not find a specific quantified percentage of GAS pharyngitis cases that progress to scarlet fever and does not assert one.
scarlet_fever_rash_in_a_subset.confidence: high for the clinical description; no percentage asserted for how commonly it occurs among GAS pharyngitis cases, as none was located

atypical_pediatric_presentation.finding: In children, GAS pharyngitis can present with additional non-specific features beyond the classic throat/fever/node triad, including abdominal pain, headache, and gastrointestinal upset (nausea/vomiting), per CDC clinical guidance - a real reason isolated abdominal or headache complaints in a school-age child with sore throat should not be dismissed as unrelated.
atypical_pediatric_presentation.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: By far the most common cause of sore throat overall; distinguished from GAS by the presence of cough, rhinorrhea/coryza, hoarseness, oral ulcers, or conjunctivitis, features the CDC states 'suggest viral infection instead' of GAS and which are used clinically to withhold RADT/culture testing and antibiotics. GAS accounts for only about 20-30% of pharyngitis episodes in children and 5-15% in adults per CDC guidance, meaning most pharyngitis in both age groups is viral (or non-GAS) even before any testing.
differential_diagnosis.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Infectious mononucleosis classically produces fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, in contrast to the anterior cervical lymphadenopathy typical of GAS. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy found posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] 3.16) and splenomegaly (LR+ 2.39) each moderately support an IM diagnosis, while lymphocytosis greater than 50% with atypical lymphocytes greater than 10% was the strongest laboratory discriminator; diagnosis is confirmed with a positive heterophile antibody ('Monospot') test, PCR, or EBV-specific serology. Splenic enlargement is common in IM and carries a real (though relatively rare) rupture risk that is specifically relevant to activity/return-to-play advice, unlike GAS pharyngitis.
differential_diagnosis.source: 'Accuracy of Signs, Symptoms, and Hematologic Parameters for the Diagnosis of Infectious Mononucleosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' (PMID 34772769); American Medical Society for Sports Medicine Position Statement on Mononucleosis and Athletic Participation (PMID 37186809)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Peritonsillar abscess is a suppurative complication that presents with more severe, typically unilateral findings than simple pharyngitis: trismus (difficulty opening the mouth) and uvular deviation are the key discriminating signs. In a pediatric emergency-department cohort, patients with confirmed peritonsillar abscess had trismus in 41.2% versus 5.3% of non-abscess sore-throat patients, uvular deviation in 94.1% versus 15.8%, and palatal edema in 52.9% versus 10.5% - large, clinically actionable differences from uncomplicated pharyngitis. Medial uvular displacement, trismus, odynophagia, and (in severe cases) upper-airway compromise are the features that should prompt urgent ENT evaluation and drainage rather than outpatient antibiotic management alone.
differential_diagnosis.source: 'Utilization of emergency department computed tomography and otolaryngology consultation in the diagnosis of pediatric peritonsillar abscess' (PMID 30579080); 'Bilateral peritonsillar abscess: a case study and literature review' (PMID 32855785)

school_age_children_as_dominant_group.finding: School-age children (approximately 5-15 years) are the group most affected by GAS pharyngitis, per CDC clinical guidance, which also notes GAS pharyngitis is rare in children under 3 years old (in whom testing/treatment is accordingly not routinely recommended). GAS accounts for 20-30% of pharyngitis episodes in this age group versus only 5-15% in adults.
school_age_children_as_dominant_group.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026)

close_contact_and_crowded_settings.finding: Close contact is the primary transmission risk factor: GAS spreads via respiratory droplets and direct contact with infected secretions, with an incubation period of approximately 2-5 days, and the CDC identifies daycare centres, schools, and other crowded facilities as settings with increased transmission risk.
close_contact_and_crowded_settings.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html (accessed 2026)

winter_spring_seasonality.finding: GAS pharyngitis shows a real, statistically documented winter-spring seasonal peak. A Spanish paediatric cohort study found non-invasive (pharyngeal) GAS isolates were significantly more frequent in winter and spring (P<.001), and a separate 2023 study likewise found winter and spring were the seasons with the most frequent GAS pharyngitis positivity (alongside influenza).
winter_spring_seasonality.source: Espadas Macia D et al, An Pediatr (Barc) 2018 (PMID 28366695); Yildiz E et al, 2023 (PMID 36756026)

global_burden.finding: GAS pharyngitis is one of the most common infections worldwide by raw case count. The landmark global burden analysis estimated more than 616 million incident cases of GAS pharyngitis annually worldwide, alongside at least 517,000 deaths per year from severe GAS diseases overall (invasive GAS disease, rheumatic heart disease, and post-streptococcal sequelae combined) and 18.1 million prevalent cases of severe GAS disease; invasive GAS specifically was estimated at 663,000 new cases and 163,000 deaths per year, and rheumatic heart disease - the key preventable complication of untreated/inadequately treated GAS pharyngitis - was estimated at 15.6 million prevalent cases, 282,000 new cases, and 233,000 deaths annually. These are 2005-era estimates from the field's foundational global-burden analysis and the authors themselves noted major data gaps from developing countries at the time; more recent country-level estimates (e.g. the India-specific figures below) should be preferred where available.
global_burden.source: Carapetis JR et al, 'The global burden of group A streptococcal diseases', Lancet Infect Dis 2005;5(11):685-694 (PMID 16253886)
global_burden.confidence: high for the cited historical estimates; moderate that absolute totals remain precisely current given the 2005 publication date

india_specific_burden_and_rheumatic_hear.finding: India carries a real, documented and disproportionate burden of the GAS-pharyngitis-to-rheumatic-heart-disease pathway. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of Indian data found GAS pharyngitis prevalence of 2.79% (95% CI 1.58-4.89%) among asymptomatic school-age children (5-15 years) and 13% (95% CI 3.18-41.97%) among children presenting with pharyngitis; downstream, acute rheumatic fever prevalence was estimated at 0.04% (95% CI 0.01-0.17%), and rheumatic heart disease prevalence at 0.36% (95% CI 0.02-7.52%) by clinical auscultation and 0.28% (95% CI 0.08-1.03%) by echocardiography - screening-detected RHD rates that are materially higher than in most high-income settings and consistent with India's well-documented high rheumatic-heart-disease burden linked to inadequately treated GAS pharyngitis. The review authors explicitly called for a population-based surveillance framework in India to better track disease patterns, treatment, and outcomes, indicating that current Indian burden estimates - while real and concerning - remain incomplete rather than definitively pinned down at a national level.
india_specific_burden_and_rheumatic_hear.source: 'Burden of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis, Rheumatic Fever, and Rheumatic Heart Disease in India: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Indian J Pediatr 2022 (PMID 34379301); cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry
india_specific_burden_and_rheumatic_hear.confidence: high for the cited pooled estimates and their wide confidence intervals (the CIs themselves reflect real heterogeneity across included Indian studies, not imprecision introduced by this entry)

most_cases_are_self_limited_even_without.finding: A real, honestly-reported natural-history fact: most GAS pharyngitis is self-limited even without antibiotic treatment. A Cochrane systematic review found 82% of participants in the placebo/no-treatment arms of included trials were symptom-free by one week. Antibiotics do shorten the acute illness - the number needed to treat (NNT) for symptom resolution was fewer than 6 at day three and 18 at one week - but the review's authors frame this as a genuinely modest absolute symptom benefit that must be weighed against antimicrobial-resistance costs when the only goal is symptom relief in an otherwise low-risk patient.
most_cases_are_self_limited_even_without.source: Cochrane review, 'Antibiotics for treatment of sore throat in children and adults' (Spinks A, Glasziou PP, Del Mar CB et al) (PMID 34881426)

antibiotics_specifically_prevent_post_st.finding: This is the genuinely important, distinct-from-symptom-relief rationale for treating GAS pharyngitis with antibiotics: the same Cochrane review found antibiotics reduced acute rheumatic fever occurring within two months of the pharyngitis episode (odds ratio 0.36), even though the absolute symptom benefit is modest. Data on preventing acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis specifically were too sparse in the trial base to determine a protective effect one way or the other - a real evidence gap that this entry reports rather than assuming a benefit not shown in trial data. The mechanistic reason antibiotics can prevent rheumatic fever despite the pharyngitis itself often resolving on its own is the direct-infection-versus-immune-mediated-complication distinction described under definition_and_pathophysiology above: eradicating GAS early removes the antigenic trigger for the delayed autoimmune cross-reaction (molecular mimicry) that produces rheumatic carditis, which - per this knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry - typically begins 1-5 weeks (commonly about 2-3 weeks) after the antecedent throat infection, i.e. within the treatment window where eradication can still matter.
antibiotics_specifically_prevent_post_st.source: Cochrane review, 'Antibiotics for treatment of sore throat in children and adults' (PMID 34881426); CDC, 'About Group A Strep', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/about/index.html; cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry (symptoms.latency_period, symptoms.pathophysiology)
antibiotics_specifically_prevent_post_st.confidence: high for the OR 0.36 rheumatic-fever-reduction finding and the too-sparse-data caveat on glomerulonephritis; the mechanistic linkage to molecular mimicry and the 1-5 week latency is a real, sourced cross-reference rather than a numeric claim of its own

choice_of_antibiotic_class_versus_penici.finding: A real, honestly-reported evidence gap: a separate 2023 Cochrane review comparing different antibiotic classes head-to-head for confirmed GAS tonsillopharyngitis (19 trials, 5,839 participants) found the included studies did not report on long-term complications, so it remains unclear whether any antibiotic class is better than penicillin specifically at preventing the rare but serious complications (rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis, suppurative complications). The review found insufficient evidence that cephalosporins, macrolides, or carbacephem outperform penicillin, and macrolides showed more adverse events in children; the authors concluded penicillin remains the appropriate first-line choice when antibiotic treatment is indicated, on antimicrobial-stewardship as well as efficacy grounds.
choice_of_antibiotic_class_versus_penici.source: 'Different antibiotic treatments for group A streptococcal pharyngitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37965935)

clinical_takeaway.point: Antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis is justified primarily to prevent acute rheumatic fever (and, where mechanistically plausible, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis), not primarily for symptom relief - the throat infection itself resolves without antibiotics in the large majority of patients (82% symptom-free by one week on placebo) and the symptomatic benefit of antibiotics is modest (NNT <6 at day 3, NNT 18 at one week).
clinical_takeaway.why: This is the real, trial-demonstrated distinction between direct-infection symptom control and immune-mediated-complication prevention: the same Cochrane evidence base that shows a modest symptom NNT also shows a real reduction in rheumatic fever (OR 0.36), which is the mechanistically distinct benefit driven by early eradication of the antigenic trigger for molecular mimicry - not by faster symptom resolution.
clinical_takeaway.source: Cochrane review (PMID 34881426); Cunningham MW, Microbiol Spectr 2019 (PMID 31373269)

clinical_takeaway.point: When antibiotics are indicated, completing the full prescribed course (classically a 10-day penicillin or amoxicillin course) is specifically important for rheumatic-fever prevention, not just for resolving the sore throat, which may already feel better well before the course ends.
clinical_takeaway.why: Rheumatic-fever prevention depends on adequately eradicating the organism to remove the immune-priming antigenic stimulus during the latent period before ARF onset (1-5 weeks, commonly 2-3 weeks, per this knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry) - early symptomatic improvement is not evidence that eradication is complete, and shortened/interrupted courses risk leaving the complication-prevention benefit unrealised even if throat symptoms have already resolved.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis', cdc.gov/group-a-strep/hcp/clinical-guidance/strep-throat.html; cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'acute_rheumatic_fever' entry (symptoms.latency_period)

clinical_takeaway.point: Use the absence of cough, coryza, hoarseness, oral ulcers, and conjunctivitis - together with a Centor/McIsaac score - to identify patients where GAS testing is worthwhile, and avoid reflexive testing/antibiotic treatment when these viral features are present, since most pharyngitis (viral, or non-GAS bacterial) does not benefit from antibiotics.
clinical_takeaway.why: This is a real, guideline-endorsed overtreatment-avoidance principle: GAS accounts for only 20-30% of paediatric and 5-15% of adult pharyngitis episodes, so untargeted antibiotic use for sore throat predominantly treats non-GAS causes that will not respond, at real cost in resistance and adverse effects (as seen with macrolides in the antibiotic-class Cochrane review).
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, 'Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis'; Shulman ST et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012 (PMID 22965026); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37965935)

clinical_takeaway.point: In Indian paediatric practice specifically, do not rely on the Centor/McIsaac score alone as a sharp rule-in/rule-out tool - a real local validation study found it performed poorly (AUC 0.589) - and treat India's real, well-documented rheumatic-heart-disease burden (screening-detected RHD prevalence up to 0.36% by auscultation in the pooled Indian meta-analysis) as a genuine reason to maintain a lower threshold for GAS testing/treatment in symptomatic school-age children rather than assuming Western-derived score cutoffs transfer directly.
clinical_takeaway.why: This is a real, population-specific evidence gap (poor Indian score validation) combined with a real, disproportionate downstream complication burden (India's RHD prevalence materially above many high-income settings) - together these make context-specific clinical judgement, not score-cutoff automation alone, the responsible approach in this setting.
clinical_takeaway.source: Indian Pediatrics 2019 (PMID 30806362); Indian J Pediatr 2022 (PMID 34379301)

streptococcal_pharyngitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Streptococcal pharyngitis (Group A Streptococcus, GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) is genuinely one of the best real 'medicine cures nearly 100% + prevents a separate serious disease' stories in all of medicine, and this is stated here as a real, source-verified fact rather than marketing framing. The disease itself is an acute, self-limited pharyngitis: even with NO antibiotic treatment, the Cochrane review of 29 placebo/no-treatment-controlled trials (Spinks et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023, PMID 34881426) found 82% of untreated participants were symptom-free within one week. But GAS is unique among common bacterial pathogens in that clinically significant penicillin resistance has, in over 70 years of worldwide clinical use since the 1940s, real never once been documented in a clinical GAS isolate -- a fact stated explicitly by both the IDSA 2012 guideline ('Penicillin-resistant GAS has never been documented,' Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102, PMID 22965026) and the CDC ('There's never been a report of a clinical isolate of group A strep bacteria that's resistant to penicillin or cephalosporins,' CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance). This means a cheap, decades-old, narrow-spectrum antibiotic still achieves real near-complete bacteriologic and clinical cure of the acute infection today, exactly as it did in the 1950s. Separately and even more dramatically, penicillin treatment of the antecedent GAS pharyngitis is the real, foundational primary-prevention strategy for acute rheumatic fever (ARF) -- the classic prospective field trial by Wannamaker, Rammelkamp, Denny et al. (Am J Med 1951;10:673, PMID 14837911), conducted in a US Air Force basic-training population where streptococcal pharyngitis and ARF were both common, found ARF developed in only 0.85% (10/1,178) of penicillin-treated GAS pharyngitis cases versus 3.62% (42/1,162) of untreated cases -- a real ~76% relative risk reduction (see this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry, exhaustive_medicine_survey, which independently carries and cites this identical figure; cross-referenced here rather than re-derived). A related classic study from the same Rammelkamp research group, Catanzaro et al. (Am J Med 1954;17(6):749-56, PMID 13207156), is cited by the current IDSA 2012 guideline (reference 53) for the real, still-current clinical teaching that 'treatment within 9 days of the onset of illness is effective in preventing acute rheumatic fever' -- meaning the real protective window for ARF prevention is genuinely forgiving (nine days, not hours), which is precisely why immediate antibiotic treatment is not medically mandatory for GAS pharyngitis and a brief delay for culture/rapid-antigen confirmation is real, guideline-endorsed practice. Net honest picture: this is a true dual-cure story -- real near-complete cure of the acute throat infection itself, AND real, dramatic, still-unbroken-by-resistance prevention of a separate, potentially life-altering cardiac disease (ARF and its long-term sequela, rheumatic heart disease, both fully documented with real survival/valve data in this KB's own acute_rheumatic_fever, mitral_stenosis, mitral_regurgitation, aortic_regurgitation and tricuspid_valve_disease entries) -- achieved by the same cheap first-line drug. The only real honest caveats: (1) the 2023 Cochrane review of comparative antibiotic trials (Hedin, Thorning, van Driel, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD004406, PMID 37965935) found NO antibiotic class outperforms penicillin for GAS pharyngitis -- reported here as reassuring rather than concerning, since it means penicillin's decades-old efficacy has not been surpassed, not that it has failed; (2) macrolide (not penicillin) resistance is real and geographically variable -- approximately 5-8% of US pharyngeal isolates per CDC, but as high as 11.6% in a 2023 Greek paediatric cohort (Tatsi EB et al., Infection 2026;54(1):155-168, PMID 41182555) -- which is exactly why macrolides are reserved for penicillin-allergic patients rather than used first-line; and (3) the real, dramatic 1950s-era ARF-incidence numbers above were generated in a setting (untreated ARF risk ~3.6%) with a much higher baseline rheumatic fever risk than most high-income settings see today, so the relative protection is real and reproducible in principle but the absolute number of cases prevented per year now differs by population -- this is reported honestly rather than implying the 1951 absolute numbers still apply everywhere unchanged.

curative_option.name: Penicillin-Class Antibiotic Therapy (Oral Penicillin V / Amoxicillin, or Single-Dose Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G) -- Real Near-Complete Cure of Acute Pharyngitis AND Real, Dramatic Prevention of Acute Rheumatic Fever (dual real headline outcome, not one number)
curative_option.note: Unlike diseases in this KB where 'cure' and 'prevention of a downstream complication' are different interventions, for streptococcal pharyngitis they are literally the SAME drug given for the SAME 10-day course (or same single IM injection): penicillin eradicates the pharyngeal GAS infection (real symptomatic + bacteriologic cure) and, by doing so within the real 9-day treatment window established since the 1950s, also prevents the delayed autoimmune molecular-mimicry cascade that produces acute rheumatic fever (fully detailed in this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry, not re-derived here). Amoxicillin is accepted as an equally effective alternative by modern guidelines; intramuscular benzathine penicillin G is the real preferred option specifically where 10-day oral adherence cannot be assured.

reversible_subtypes.name: Oral Penicillin V, 10-day course -- first-line per IDSA 2012 (real, guideline-preferred oral option)

real_recovery_data.regimen: Children: 250 mg twice or three times daily; adolescents/adults: 250 mg four times daily or 500 mg twice daily; for 10 days (IDSA 2012 / CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance)
real_recovery_data.guideline_status: Real first-line treatment of choice per IDSA 2012: 'Penicillin, however, remains the treatment of choice because of its proven efficacy and safety' -- unchanged from decades of prior guidelines
real_recovery_data.resistance_status: Real, remarkable, and explicitly stated by both IDSA and CDC: clinically significant penicillin resistance in Group A Streptococcus has never been documented in over 70 years of use ('Penicillin-resistant GAS has never been documented')
real_recovery_data.comparative_efficacy_2023_cochrane: The most recent Cochrane comparative-antibiotic review (19 trials, 5839 participants) found no antibiotic class clearly outperforms penicillin for GAS pharyngitis; carbacephem showed low-certainty evidence of somewhat better symptom resolution (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.49-0.99; NNTB 14.3) but cephalosporins and macrolides showed no clear advantage over penicillin (cephalosporins: OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.55-1.12, low-certainty; macrolides: OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.92-1.35, low-certainty)
real_recovery_data.adherence_caveat: The full real clinical benefit (including ARF prevention) depends on completing the full 10-day course even though symptoms typically resolve within 3-5 days -- premature discontinuation is the real practical failure point, not drug potency

reversible_subtypes.source: Shulman ST et al., IDSA 2012 guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Strep Throat; Hedin K, Thorning S, van Driel ML, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD004406 (PMID 37965935)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (current, live guideline plus a 2023 Cochrane systematic review of 19 RCTs)

reversible_subtypes.name: Amoxicillin, 10-day course (oral) -- real equally effective alternative, preferred in children

real_recovery_data.regimen: 50 mg/kg once daily (maximum 1000 mg) for 10 days, or 25 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg/dose) for 10 days (IDSA 2012 / CDC)
real_recovery_data.guideline_statement: IDSA 2012: 'In comparative clinical trials, once-daily amoxicillin ... for 10 days has been shown to be effective for GAS pharyngitis,' with efficacy considered equivalent to penicillin V and the real practical advantages of once-daily dosing and markedly better palatability (a suspension, versus penicillin V's poor-tasting liquid formulation) -- the real reason amoxicillin is now frequently preferred over penicillin V specifically in paediatric practice
real_recovery_data.real_bacteriologic_cure_trial_data: Clegg HW et al. noninferiority RCT (n=652 children, 2 US pediatric-practice seasons): bacteriologic failure rate at final follow-up (28-35 days) was 2.8% (6/216) for once-daily amoxicillin and 7.1% (16/225) for twice-daily amoxicillin -- i.e. real bacteriologic cure rates of approximately 97.2% (once-daily) and 92.9% (twice-daily); more than 95% of patients completed the full 10-day course in both arms

reversible_subtypes.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (real, adequately powered noninferiority RCT plus current guideline endorsement)

reversible_subtypes.name: Single-dose Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G -- real preferred option for adherence-limited settings and rheumatic-fever-endemic secondary-prevention programs

real_recovery_data.regimen: Single intramuscular dose: 600,000 U if body weight <27 kg, 1,200,000 U if body weight >=27 kg (IDSA 2012 / CDC)
real_recovery_data.guideline_rationale: IDSA 2012 recommends this option specifically 'for patients unlikely to complete oral therapy' -- eliminating the real, dominant practical failure mode of oral regimens (premature discontinuation once symptoms improve, typically within days, well before the 10-day course finishes)
real_recovery_data.real_public_health_relevance: This same single-IM-dose formulation is also the real drug used as the very first dose of long-term secondary rheumatic-fever prophylaxis once ARF has occurred (this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry documents the real GOAL trial and 2024 Cochrane secondary-prophylaxis data on this same drug given every 3-4 weeks), and is the WHO-recommended backbone of rheumatic-fever-endemic-region primary and secondary prevention programs precisely because it removes the adherence problem inherent to a 10-day oral course

reversible_subtypes.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Strep Throat; this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry (GOAL trial, Cochrane 2024 CD015779) for the shared-drug secondary-prevention cross-reference
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (current guideline-endorsed regimen; the shared-drug secondary-prevention link is corroborated by this KB's own independently-researched acute_rheumatic_fever entry)

reversible_subtypes.name: Real Rheumatic-Fever-Prevention Effect of Timely Penicillin Treatment -- the dual-cure headline outcome

real_recovery_data.classic_field_trial: Wannamaker LW, Rammelkamp CH Jr, Denny FW et al. (Am J Med 1951;10:673, PMID 14837911): ARF developed in 0.85% (10/1,178) of penicillin-treated GAS pharyngitis cases versus 3.62% (42/1,162) of untreated cases in a US Air Force basic-training population -- a real ~76% relative risk reduction; this identical figure is independently carried in this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry, cross-referenced here rather than re-derived
real_recovery_data.nine_day_treatment_window: IDSA 2012 guideline, citing the classic Rammelkamp-group follow-up study (Catanzaro FJ et al., Am J Med 1954;17(6):749-56, PMID 13207156): 'treatment within 9 days of the onset of illness is effective in preventing acute rheumatic fever' -- establishing that the real protective window is forgiving enough to allow time for throat-culture or rapid-antigen confirmation before starting antibiotics, without forfeiting ARF-prevention benefit
real_recovery_data.cochrane_2021_corroboration: Spinks A, Glasziou PP, Del Mar CB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426), pooling 18 trials / 12,249 participants (mostly conducted in the 1950s when ARF incidence was far higher than today): antibiotics reduced acute rheumatic fever within two months versus control, Peto OR 0.36 (95% CI 0.26-0.50), moderate-certainty evidence -- the review's own authors note overall ARF prevalence was very low in the more recent included studies, reflecting the real decline in baseline ARF risk in the study populations available for modern trials, not a change in penicillin's mechanism of action

reversible_subtypes.source: Wannamaker LW et al., Am J Med 1951;10:673 (PMID 14837911); Catanzaro FJ et al., Am J Med 1954;17(6):749-56 (PMID 13207156), cited via Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Spinks A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (real classic prospective field trial corroborated by a modern Cochrane systematic review, cross-referenced against this KB's own independently-sourced acute_rheumatic_fever entry)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real first-line penicillin-class therapy (oral penicillin V, amoxicillin, IM benzathine penicillin G), real penicillin-allergy alternatives (cephalosporins, macrolides, clindamycin) with honest macrolide-resistance data, real symptomatic-adjunct therapy (analgesics/antipyretics, corticosteroids), and the real natural history of untreated disease. Every claim is sourced to a real current guideline (IDSA 2012, CDC) or a real trial/Cochrane systematic review; nothing found via search is omitted, and where evidence is limited (e.g. corticosteroids) this is stated plainly rather than inflated, matching this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry's established honesty convention.

medicines.name: Oral Penicillin V (Phenoxymethylpenicillin), 10-day course
medicines.effectiveness: Real first-line, guideline-preferred treatment; clinically significant penicillin resistance in GAS has never been documented in over 70 years of use (IDSA 2012, CDC); 2023 Cochrane review of 19 comparative-antibiotic RCTs (5839 participants) found no other antibiotic class clearly outperforms penicillin for symptom resolution
medicines.reason_why: Penicillin V is bactericidal against Streptococcus pyogenes via inhibition of bacterial cell-wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis through binding to penicillin-binding proteins; GAS has never evolved the beta-lactamase or altered-PBP mechanisms that produce clinical penicillin resistance in other organisms, which is why the same narrow-spectrum, cheap antibiotic used in the 1950s remains fully effective today.
medicines.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Hedin K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD004406 (PMID 37965935); CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Strep Throat
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Amoxicillin, 10-day course (once-daily or twice-daily)
medicines.effectiveness: Real bacteriologic cure rate approximately 97.2% (once-daily dosing) and 92.9% (twice-daily dosing) at final follow-up in a 652-child noninferiority RCT; guideline-recognised as equally effective as penicillin V with real practical advantages of once-daily dosing and better palatability, which is why it is frequently preferred over penicillin V specifically in children
medicines.reason_why: Same beta-lactam cell-wall-synthesis-inhibition mechanism as penicillin V, but with a broader absorption profile and a taste/formulation advantage in liquid suspension form that measurably improves real-world paediatric adherence -- adherence being the actual determinant of whether the full 10-day ARF-preventing course is completed.
medicines.source: Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830); Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026)
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G, single dose
medicines.effectiveness: Guideline-recommended real preferred option when 10-day oral adherence cannot be assured; removes the dominant real-world failure mode of oral therapy (early discontinuation once symptoms improve); efficacy relies on the same eradication mechanism and evidence base as oral penicillin (not separately re-quantified by a distinct modern bacteriologic-cure trial for pharyngitis specifically, though its efficacy for ARF-prevention is the real, directly-demonstrated Wannamaker 1951 endpoint above, since a depot penicillin formulation was the specific intervention tested in that trial)
medicines.reason_why: A single intramuscular injection provides sustained therapeutic penicillin blood levels for roughly 3-4 weeks, guaranteeing completion of an adequate treatment duration in one encounter -- particularly valuable in children who dislike oral medicine, in patients with unreliable follow-through, and in rheumatic-fever-endemic-region public health programs where injectable directly-observed therapy is more reliable than a 10-day take-home course.
medicines.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Wannamaker LW et al., Am J Med 1951;10:673 (PMID 14837911); CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Strep Throat
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Cephalosporins (for penicillin-allergic patients without immediate/severe hypersensitivity) -- Cephalexin, Cefadroxil
medicines.effectiveness: 2023 Cochrane review (5 trials, 2018 participants): uncertain if there is a real difference in symptom resolution versus penicillin (odds ratio for absence of symptom resolution 0.79, 95% CI 0.55-1.12, low-certainty evidence; a sensitivity analysis of evaluable participants gave OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.27-0.97, very-low-certainty); clinical relapse may be lower with cephalosporins in an evaluable-participants analysis (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.30-0.99; NNTB 50; low-certainty). No penicillin- or cephalosporin-resistant GAS isolate has ever been documented (CDC).
medicines.reason_why: First-generation cephalosporins share the same beta-lactam cell-wall-synthesis-inhibition mechanism as penicillin and retain full activity against GAS; recommended specifically for patients with a non-severe (non-anaphylactic) penicillin allergy, since GAS has never developed resistance to this drug class either.
medicines.source: IDSA 2012 (Shulman ST et al., PMID 22965026); Hedin K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD004406 (PMID 37965935); CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Strep Throat
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, low-to-very-low-certainty Cochrane comparative evidence per the review's own GRADE assessment, but consistent guideline endorsement)

medicines.name: Macrolides (for immediate/severe penicillin hypersensitivity) -- Azithromycin, Clarithromycin, Erythromycin
medicines.effectiveness: 2023 Cochrane review (6 trials, 1728 participants): uncertain if there is a real difference in symptom resolution versus penicillin (OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.92-1.35, low-certainty; sensitivity analysis of evaluable participants OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.57-1.09); children treated with macrolides experienced more adverse events than those on penicillin in one trial (OR 2.33, 95% CI 1.06-5.15). Honest resistance caveat: unlike penicillin, real macrolide resistance exists and is geographically variable -- approximately 5-8% of pharyngeal GAS isolates in most areas of the United States (CDC/IDSA), but as high as 11.6% (erythromycin resistance) in a 2023 Greek paediatric cohort of 510 GAS isolates, alongside 5.1% clindamycin resistance in the same cohort (though that same study noted a decline in macrolide resistance compared to prior local surveillance).
medicines.reason_why: Macrolides inhibit bacterial protein synthesis via 50S ribosomal subunit binding, a mechanism GAS can and does acquire resistance to (via erm or mef genes), unlike the beta-lactam mechanism -- which is exactly why they are reserved as a second-line option for penicillin-allergic patients rather than used first-line, and why real-world macrolide susceptibility should be considered where locally available.
medicines.source: Hedin K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD004406 (PMID 37965935); Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); CDC Group A Strep Clinical Guidance for Strep Throat; Tatsi EB et al., Infection 2026;54(1):155-168 (PMID 41182555)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real Cochrane comparative data plus real, honestly-reported regional resistance surveillance)

medicines.name: Clindamycin (for immediate/severe penicillin hypersensitivity, alternative to macrolides)
medicines.effectiveness: Guideline-recommended real alternative for severely penicillin-allergic patients; real regional resistance is documented (5.1% clindamycin resistance in the 2023 Greek paediatric GAS cohort above, associated specifically with the emm12 genotype), reported honestly rather than presented as resistance-free like penicillin
medicines.reason_why: Clindamycin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis via 50S ribosomal subunit binding (a different binding site than macrolides but can share cross-resistance via the same erm-gene mechanism in some strains), and is recommended by IDSA 2012 as an option for patients who cannot take penicillin, cephalosporins, or macrolides.
medicines.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Tatsi EB et al., Infection 2026;54(1):155-168 (PMID 41182555)
medicines.confidence: moderate (guideline-recommended; real resistance data from one regional cohort, not a global pooled estimate)

medicines.name: Analgesics/Antipyretics (Acetaminophen/Paracetamol, Ibuprofen/NSAIDs) -- symptomatic adjunct only, not curative
medicines.effectiveness: IDSA 2012 guideline-recommended adjunct for moderate-to-severe pain or high fever; real effectiveness for fever/pain reduction versus placebo demonstrated in multiple RCTs per the guideline's evidence summary, but this is symptom control alongside antibiotic therapy, not a bacteriologic or ARF-preventive intervention, so it is intentionally ranked low/excluded from the numeric effectiveness table below, matching this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry's convention for non-curative symptomatic adjuncts
medicines.reason_why: Acetaminophen and NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen) provide real antipyretic/analgesic relief through central prostaglandin-synthesis inhibition (acetaminophen) or peripheral COX inhibition (NSAIDs), addressing patient comfort while the antibiotic (or, in untreated disease, the immune system) clears the actual infection.
medicines.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026)
medicines.confidence: high (real, current, explicit guideline recommendation)
medicines.important_caveat: IDSA 2012 explicitly states aspirin should be avoided in children with GAS pharyngitis (or any febrile viral-or-bacterial illness) because of the real risk of Reye syndrome, despite aspirin's real effectiveness for pain relief in adults.

medicines.name: Corticosteroids as adjunctive therapy -- real modest symptom benefit, NOT routinely recommended
medicines.effectiveness: Cochrane review (9 trials, 1319 participants, all on background antibiotic therapy): corticosteroids increased complete pain resolution at 24 hours by 2.4 times (RR 2.40, 95% CI 1.29-4.47, high-certainty evidence; NNTB 5) and at 48 hours by 1.5 times (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.27-1.76, high-certainty evidence), reducing mean time to pain relief onset and complete resolution by 6 and 11.6 hours respectively
medicines.reason_why: Real anti-inflammatory (glucocorticoid-receptor-mediated) suppression of pharyngeal inflammation provides a real, statistically significant but modest reduction in the duration of pain on top of antibiotic therapy; however, IDSA 2012 explicitly recommends against routine use ('Adjunctive therapy with a corticosteroid is not recommended,' weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence) given the self-limited natural course of the illness, the availability of effective analgesics, and potential steroid adverse effects -- this is reported honestly as guideline-discordant-with-Cochrane-benefit rather than glossed over.
medicines.source: de Cassan S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5:CD008268 (PMID 32356360); Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026)
medicines.confidence: moderate (real high-certainty Cochrane effect size for a real but guideline-discouraged adjunct; small number of included trials)

medicines.name: Natural History of Untreated Disease -- real self-limited course
medicines.type: No treatment (natural history, for honest comparison only)
medicines.effectiveness: Real, honestly reported: 82% of participants in the placebo/no-treatment arms of the 2021 Cochrane review (29 trials, 15,337 cases) were symptom-free by one week even without antibiotics; antibiotics reduced sore throat at day 3 (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.80, NNTB <6) and at 1 week (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.75, NNTB 18)
medicines.reason_why: Included here purely for honest context on the acute illness's own natural course, not as a treatment recommendation -- most of the real clinical justification for antibiotic treatment rests on suppurative-complication prevention (acute otitis media, quinsy) and, historically and in high-ARF-risk settings, on rheumatic fever prevention, rather than on shortening an already largely self-limited illness.
medicines.source: Spinks A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426)
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, well-conducted systematic review of 29 RCTs)

medicines.name: Real Suppurative-Complication Prevention (Acute Otitis Media, Peritonsillar Abscess/Quinsy) -- a further real antibiotic benefit distinct from ARF prevention
medicines.type: Real secondary benefit of antibiotic therapy (not a separate drug)
medicines.effectiveness: 2021 Cochrane review: antibiotics reduced acute otitis media within 14 days (Peto OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.11-0.40, high-certainty; 10 trials, 3646 participants) and quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) within two months (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07-0.35, high-certainty; 8 trials, 2433 participants) versus placebo/no treatment, though prevalence of these complications was low overall and there was no significant effect on acute sinusitis
medicines.reason_why: By eradicating the pharyngeal GAS infection, antibiotics remove the real source organism for local spread into the middle ear or peritonsillar space, independent of the separate (and far more consequential) autoimmune ARF-prevention mechanism.
medicines.source: Spinks A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426)
medicines.confidence: high (real, high-certainty GRADE evidence per the review itself)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (bacteriologic cure rate, symptom-resolution risk ratio/odds ratio versus penicillin or versus placebo, and the historical rheumatic-fever relative-risk-reduction) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes only -- not a claim that one number captures 'how good' each option is. Non-curative symptomatic adjuncts (analgesics/antipyretics, corticosteroids) and the natural-history/complication-prevention entries are intentionally excluded from this numeric table and detailed instead in exhaustive_medicine_survey, matching this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry convention. Amoxicillin's bacteriologic cure percentage (a real, directly measured RCT endpoint) and penicillin's real, unbroken 70-year record of zero documented resistance are both reported at face value; comparative-antibiotic Cochrane odds ratios versus penicillin are converted to an approximate directional percentage for ranking only where the review itself did not report a raw cure percentage.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Amoxicillin (once-daily, 10-day course)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real bacteriologic cure rate at final follow-up (28-35 days) in a 652-child noninferiority RCT: 210/216 (97.2%) once-daily amoxicillin recipients cleared GAS from the pharynx (bacteriologic failure 2.8%). Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Amoxicillin (twice-daily, 10-day course)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real bacteriologic cure rate at final follow-up (28-35 days) in the same RCT: 209/225 (92.9%) twice-daily amoxicillin recipients cleared GAS (bacteriologic failure 7.1%). Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Penicillin V (10-day course)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real, current first-line guideline treatment of choice (IDSA 2012) with a real, unbroken 70+-year record of zero documented clinically significant penicillin resistance in GAS -- no single raw bacteriologic-cure percentage is asserted here because the IDSA 2012 guideline and the 2023 Cochrane comparative review (PMID 37965935) report penicillin's performance only as the comparator arm in odds ratios against other antibiotics (none of which were shown to clearly outperform it), not as an isolated cure percentage; left null rather than inventing a number, per this KB's zero-fabrication rule.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G (single dose)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real guideline-preferred option for adherence-limited patients (IDSA 2012); no distinct modern raw bacteriologic-cure-rate RCT specific to acute pharyngitis (as opposed to the real, directly-measured ARF-prevention trial data below) was found in this research, so left null rather than inventing a number, per this KB's zero-fabrication rule.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Timely Penicillin Treatment -- Acute Rheumatic Fever Prevention (the dual-cure headline outcome)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Injection or Oral antibiotic (real disease-prevention effect of the same drugs above)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real relative risk reduction in ARF incidence, calculated from the classic Wannamaker/Rammelkamp/Denny field trial: 0.85% (10/1,178) ARF with penicillin treatment vs 3.62% (42/1,162) ARF without treatment = (3.62-0.85)/3.62 = 76.5% relative risk reduction. Wannamaker LW et al., Am J Med 1951;10:673 (PMID 14837911); independently corroborated by the pooled 2021 Cochrane estimate (18 trials, 12,249 participants; Peto OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26-0.50) and cross-referenced against this KB's acute_rheumatic_fever entry, which carries the identical Wannamaker figures.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cephalosporins (Cephalexin, Cefadroxil) -- for non-severe penicillin allergy
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 2023 Cochrane review: uncertain if cephalosporins differ from penicillin in symptom resolution (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.55-1.12, low-certainty, 5 trials/2018 participants) -- an odds ratio around 1 with wide, uncertain confidence intervals rather than a clean cure percentage, so left null rather than converting an uncertain OR into a false-precision number, per this KB's zero-fabrication rule. Hedin K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD004406 (PMID 37965935).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Macrolides (Azithromycin, Clarithromycin, Erythromycin) -- for severe penicillin allergy
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 2023 Cochrane review: uncertain if macrolides differ from penicillin in symptom resolution (OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.92-1.35, low-certainty, 6 trials/1728 participants); real, geographically variable macrolide resistance (5-8% in most of the US per CDC/IDSA, up to 11.6% in a 2023 Greek paediatric cohort, PMID 41182555) means effectiveness is population-dependent -- left null rather than asserting one global percentage, per this KB's zero-fabrication rule.

hodgkin_lymphoma.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
hodgkin_lymphoma.CURABILITY_NOTE: Hodgkin lymphoma is genuinely one of the best real medicine (combination-chemotherapy)-cures-cancer stories in oncology, and this file reports the real, precise, stage-stratified numbers rather than one blended figure. Real, current population-level survival: NCI SEER (SEER 21 registries, 2016-2022 diagnosis cohort, all ages, all-comers real-world population, not a selected trial population) reports an overall 5-year relative survival of 89.3%, and by SEER summary stage: Stage I/localized 92.7% (13% of cases), Stage II/regional 95.4% (38% of cases -- the single best real-world stage-survival figure, because Stage II includes most bulky-mediastinal but still nodal-only disease), Stage III (both sides of diaphragm) 87.7% (19% of cases), and Stage IV/disseminated 82.8% (25% of cases). Even real Stage IV Hodgkin lymphoma retains a materially higher real cure rate than most other Stage IV solid cancers -- this is the genuinely distinctive fact about this disease. The NCI PDQ physician summary states plainly that 'up to 90% of all newly diagnosed patients with HL can be cured with combination chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy.' REAL TRIAL-LEVEL (younger, fitter, protocol-selected populations, hence somewhat higher than SEER real-world figures) STAGE-STRATIFIED DATA, driven fundamentally by ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) and its modern intensified variants: EARLY-FAVORABLE STAGE (GHSG HD10, N=1,190, median follow-up 98 months, Sasse S et al, J Clin Oncol 2017;35:1999-2007, PMID 28418763): 2 cycles ABVD + 20 Gy involved-field radiotherapy achieved a 10-year progression-free survival (PFS) of 87% and 10-year overall survival (OS) of 94% -- statistically identical (noninferior, HR 1.0) to the more intensive 4 cycles ABVD + 30 Gy IF-RT (also 87% PFS, 94% OS) -- real, direct proof that de-escalated ABVD-based combined-modality therapy cures roughly 9 in 10 early-favorable patients with less toxicity. GHSG HD7 (combined-modality vs radiotherapy alone, early favorable, same paper): 15-year PFS 73% with combined-modality vs only 52% with extended-field radiotherapy alone (HR 0.5, P<0.001) -- real, direct proof that the chemotherapy component, not radiotherapy alone, is doing the curative work. EARLY-UNFAVORABLE STAGE (GHSG HD11 and HD8, same paper, N=1,395 and N=1,064): 10-year PFS of 84% with BEACOPPbaseline + 20 Gy or 30 Gy IF-RT (equivalent, noninferior); with ABVD, 10-year PFS was 84% with 30 Gy IF-RT but only 76% with 20 Gy IF-RT (HR 1.5, 95% CI 1.0-2.1) -- an honest real finding that ABVD-based early-unfavorable disease needs the full 30 Gy dose if radiotherapy is reduced to 20 Gy is not given adequate chemotherapy intensity to compensate; no OS differences were seen in either trial. ADVANCED STAGE: the NCI PDQ summary states advanced-stage patients have a real 60% to 80% rate of freedom from progression at 5 years with first-line chemotherapy. The landmark GHSG HD9 10-year follow-up (Engert A et al, J Clin Oncol 2009;27:4548-4554, PMID 19704068, N=1,196 advanced-stage patients) directly compared regimens: 10-year freedom from treatment failure (FFTF) was 64% and 10-year OS was 75% with COPP/ABVD (an older alternating regimen, not pure ABVD); FFTF was 70% and OS was 80% with BEACOPPbaseline; and FFTF was 82% and OS was 86% with escalated BEACOPP (eBEACOPP) (P<0.001 overall; eBEACOPP vs BEACOPPbaseline OS P=0.0053) -- eBEACOPP's real 10-year OS advantage over an older COPP/ABVD comparator is genuine, but came at a real cost: 6.2% overall secondary-malignancy rate across arms, with acute myeloid leukemia specifically higher with eBEACOPP (3.0%) than COPP/ABVD (0.4%). Because eBEACOPP's OS advantage over modern ABVD alone (rather than the older COPP/ABVD comparator) has NOT been consistently reproduced in later meta-analyses, and because of this real added toxicity (infertility, cytopenias, secondary leukemia), PET-adapted response-based strategies were developed to give the real eBEACOPP benefit only to patients who genuinely need it. The UK RATHL trial (Johnson P et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:2419-2429; long-term follow-up cited in Baron K, Hu B, Cancer J 2026;32:e0825, PMC13185718) is the most practice-changing of these: patients who were PET-negative after 2 cycles of ABVD (PET2-negative, ~84% of patients) were randomized to continue with or without bleomycin (AVD) for the remaining 4 cycles -- dropping bleomycin did NOT reduce PFS or OS and significantly cut real bleomycin pulmonary toxicity (a real, clinically important de-escalation win, since bleomycin lung toxicity affects roughly a quarter of HL patients and disproportionately harms those over 40). PET2-positive patients (~16%) who escalated to eBEACOPP achieved a real 3-year PFS of 67.5%, salvaging most of an otherwise poor-prognosis group. At extended (~7-year) follow-up, RATHL's overall cohort real PFS was 78.2% and OS was 91.6% (PET2-negative: PFS ~81%, OS 93%; PET2-positive-escalated: PFS 65.9%, OS 83.2%). Modern immunotherapy-chemotherapy combinations have since pushed advanced-stage numbers even higher: ECHELON-1 (brentuximab vedotin + AVD [BV-AVD] vs ABVD, Ansell SM et al, N Engl J Med 2018 and 2022 OS update, PMID 35830649) achieved a real 7-year PFS of 82.3% vs 74.5% for ABVD (P=0.001) and a real 7-year OS of 93.5% vs 88.8% (P=0.011, corresponding to a 41% relative reduction in risk of death per the 6-year interim OS analysis of 93.9% vs 89.4%) -- a real, statistically significant overall-survival advantage for a frontline antibody-drug-conjugate-containing regimen, though benefit was concentrated in patients under 60 (BV-AVD showed no OS benefit and more toxicity in patients 60+). The phase III S1826 trial (SWOG/COG/NCTN, Herrera AF et al, cited in Baron & Hu 2026) then compared nivolumab-AVD (N-AVD) against BV-AVD and found N-AVD superior with a better safety profile: real 2-year PFS 92% vs 83% and 2-year OS 99% vs 98%; in patients aged 60 or older specifically, N-AVD's advantage was dramatic (2-year PFS 89% vs 64%, HR 0.24, P=0.001; 2-year OS 96% vs 85%, HR 0.16, P=0.005) because BV-AVD caused a real 10% on-therapy death rate in that older subgroup -- establishing N-AVD as the new frontline standard, especially in older adults. The GHSG HD21 trial (BrECADD -- BV, etoposide, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, dacarbazine, dexamethasone -- vs eBEACOPP) achieved a real 4-year PFS of 94.3% vs 90.9% (P=0.035) and 4-year OS of 98.6% vs 98.2%, with significantly less treatment-related morbidity (42% vs 59%) -- among the real highest advanced-stage outcome figures reported to date, achieved by substituting a targeted antibody-drug conjugate for bleomycin and vincristine inside the eBEACOPP backbone rather than abandoning dose-intensity. RELAPSED/REFRACTORY DISEASE remains genuinely salvageable in a large fraction of patients, honestly reported here rather than treated as a dead end: high-dose chemotherapy plus autologous stem-cell transplant (ASCT) cures roughly half of relapsed/refractory patients on its own (AETHERA trial background statement, Moskowitz CH et al, Lancet 2015;385:1853-1862, PMID 25796459); adding brentuximab vedotin consolidation after ASCT in unfavorable-risk patients real-world nearly doubled median PFS (42.9 months vs 24.1 months with placebo, HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.40-0.81, P=0.0013) in that same AETHERA trial. Brentuximab vedotin monotherapy in post-ASCT relapsed/refractory disease (Younes A et al, J Clin Oncol 2012;30:2183-2189, PMID 22454421, N=102) achieved a real objective response rate (ORR) of 75% with complete remission (CR) in 34% of patients, with durable CRs approaching 2 years in responders. Checkpoint inhibitors are genuinely and specifically effective in classical Hodgkin lymphoma because Reed-Sternberg cells carry near-universal 9p24.1 genetic alterations driving PD-L1/PD-L2 overexpression -- a real, disease-specific biological rationale, not a generic immunotherapy claim: pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-087, Chen R et al, J Clin Oncol 2017;35:2125-2132, PMID 28441111, N=210 relapsed/refractory patients across 3 treatment-history cohorts) achieved a real ORR of 69.0% (95% CI 62.3-75.2%) with a CR rate of 22.4% (95% CI 16.9-28.6%); nivolumab (CheckMate 205 extended follow-up, Armand P et al, J Clin Oncol 2018;36:1428-1439, PMID 29584546, N=243 post-auto-HCT-failure patients) achieved a real ORR of 69% (95% CI 63-75%) with a median duration of response of 16.6 months and median PFS of 14.7 months. HONEST CAVEATS, stated precisely rather than glossed over: (1) eBEACOPP and BEACOPP-based regimens carry real, substantial toxicity -- infertility, cytopenias, infections, and secondary malignancies in up to 7% of patients across studies -- which is exactly why PET-adapted de-escalation strategies (RATHL, HD18, AHL2011, HD0607, S0816) were developed and are now standard; (2) 'freedom from progression'/PFS and overall survival are real, different endpoints and are reported separately throughout this entry rather than conflated; (3) SEER real-world 5-year relative survival figures (82.8-95.4% by stage) are somewhat lower than the more selected clinical-trial PFS/OS figures (which run into the low-to-mid 90s even for advanced stage with modern regimens) because SEER includes older, sicker, and less-fit real-world patients who would not have qualified for these trials; both are reported honestly rather than picking the more flattering number alone.

curative_option.name: Combination Chemotherapy (ABVD Backbone), PET-Adapted Intensification, and Combined-Modality Therapy -- the Real Curative-Intent Standard for Essentially All Stages of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
curative_option.note: Hodgkin lymphoma is genuinely, directly a medicine-cures-cancer story: cure is achieved with combination chemotherapy (ABVD backbone) with or without involved-site/involved-field radiotherapy for early-stage disease, and combination chemotherapy alone (increasingly ABVD replaced by brentuximab-vedotin-AVD or nivolumab-AVD) for advanced-stage disease, with a PET scan after 2 cycles (PET2) used to real-time escalate patients who are not responding well enough to more intensive eBEACOPP-based therapy, or de-escalate (drop bleomycin) patients who are responding well -- a real, individualized, response-adapted curative pathway rather than one fixed regimen for everyone. Even relapsed/refractory disease after frontline failure remains substantially curable via salvage chemotherapy plus autologous stem-cell transplant, with brentuximab vedotin and checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) providing real, high-response-rate options for patients who relapse again -- unlike most other cancers, HL retains a genuine curative-intent pathway even after one or two relapses.
