scabies.name: Scabies

mite_biology_and_burrowing_mechanism.finding: Human scabies is caused by the obligate ectoparasitic mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. A 2025 porcine-model study of scabies-induced itch states the mite 'inhabits the upper layers of the epidermis,' and case-report histopathology directly confirms mites embedded within the stratum corneum in both classic and atypical (nodular) presentations - a 2026 case report of atypical nodular scabies found 'histopathological examination confirmed the presence of Sarcoptes mites in the stratum corneum.' This superficial epidermal habitat (rather than deeper dermal invasion) is the structural basis for the burrow, the mite's pathognomonic clinical sign.
mite_biology_and_burrowing_mechanism.source: Aljohani et al [itch-marker study], 'Expression profiles of itch markers during scabies infection in a porcine scabies model', PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2025 (PMID 41325491); 'From urticaria to mites: a diagnostic turnaround in atypical nodular scabies - a case report', BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMID 41749148)
mite_biology_and_burrowing_mechanism.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

itch_mechanism_mixed_type_i_and_type_iv_.finding: Intense pruritus in scabies is driven by an immune/hypersensitivity reaction to the mite and its products rather than by mechanical injury alone: the same 2025 porcine-model study reports that 'in over 90% of affected individuals intense itching is the primary clinical symptom,' accompanied by 'other delayed-type hypersensitivity responses,' and found upregulated histaminergic signalling (increased histamine) together with non-histaminergic itch mediators - PAR-2, MRGPRX2, tryptase, the pruritogenic cytokine IL-31, periostin, and substance P with its receptor NK-1R - plus reduced beta-tubulin III suggestive of direct mite-induced neuroinflammation. Importantly, a 2022 systematic meta-analysis synthesising 55 narrative reviews and extracting 565 effect sizes across 19 mammalian species (including humans) found evidence for BOTH type I and type IV hypersensitivity: 'elevated IgE, eosinophils and mast cells in type I hypersensitivity response corresponded to what was described in narrative reviews,' while 'results from type IV hypersensitivity response suggested typical antibody response, however cell-mediated response was less evident' than the classical delayed-type-hypersensitivity model predicts. This is a genuinely important, honest nuance: scabies itch/inflammation is better described as a mixed type I/IV hypersensitivity process rather than a pure textbook delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction.
itch_mechanism_mixed_type_i_and_type_iv_.source: 'Expression profiles of itch markers during scabies infection in a porcine scabies model', PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2025 (PMID 41325491); 'Evidence underscoring immunological and clinical pathological changes associated with Sarcoptes scabiei infection: synthesis and meta-analysis', BMC Infect Dis 2022 (PMID 35902827)
itch_mechanism_mixed_type_i_and_type_iv_.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the mixed type I/IV nuance is a direct quote, not this knowledge base's own interpretation

symptom_onset_timeline_first_infestation.finding: Because pruritus is a hypersensitivity phenomenon rather than an immediate mechanical response, its onset is delayed and differs sharply between a first infestation and reinfestation. Per the CDC: for a first infestation, 'symptoms can take up to three to six weeks to appear' (the time needed to mount sensitization), whereas on reinfestation 'symptoms typically appear one to four days after exposure' (a rapid anamnestic hypersensitivity response in an already-sensitized host). The CDC also states explicitly that 'even if you do not have symptoms, you can still spread scabies' during this pre-symptomatic incubation window - a directly important transmission-control point.
symptom_onset_timeline_first_infestation.source: CDC, 'Signs and Symptoms of Scabies' (cdc.gov/scabies/signs-symptoms), accessed 2026-09-22
symptom_onset_timeline_first_infestation.confidence: high - directly quoted from the CDC clinical page in this session; note the verified figure is 3-6 weeks for first infestation (not a rounder '2-6 weeks' sometimes quoted informally), reported here as found rather than adjusted

crusted_norwegian_scabies_hyperinfestati.finding: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is a distinct, severe hyperinfestation variant in which mite burden is enormously amplified - the CDC states 'large numbers of scabies mites and eggs, up to two million, may be present on a single patient' (versus typically only 10-15 mites in ordinary scabies) - producing 'hyperkeratotic plaques that may be fissured and can have associated erythema.' Mechanistically, this reflects a blunted host immune response: a 2022 review of immune mechanisms in human S. scabiei infestation states that whereas ordinary scabies is dominated by a CD4+ T-cell response with a mixed, partly protective Th1/Th2 immunoprofile, crusted scabies is 'mainly mediated by CD8+ T-cells' with a non-protective Th2/Th17-skewed profile, and 'the development of CS is associated with early immunosuppression that is followed by deleterious immune response to uncontrolled mite proliferation.' A 2024 systematic review of 683 published crusted-scabies cases (1998-2023) found corticosteroid use was the most prevalent immunosuppressive risk factor (27.7% of cases), 10.2% were associated with HIV/AIDS, 8.5% with HTLV-1 infection, and 10.5% occurred in overtly immunocompetent individuals with no identified risk factor; overall mortality was 6.0% (41/683), most often from secondary bacteraemia. Crucially for recognition, the CDC notes crusted-scabies patients 'may not show the usual signs, symptom, or lesion distribution seen in classic scabies' and 'pruritus (itching) may be mild or absent' - meaning the disease can be markedly LESS itchy than ordinary scabies despite carrying by far the highest mite burden and contagiousness, a genuinely important and counter-intuitive clinical point.
crusted_norwegian_scabies_hyperinfestati.source: CDC, 'Crusted Scabies: Clinical Overview' (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-overview), accessed 2026-09-22; Bagnall D et al [immune mechanisms review title paraphrase - 'Immune mechanisms in human Sarcoptes scabiei (Acari: Sarcoptidae) infestations'], Parasite Immunol 2022 (PMID 34923637); systematic review of immunosuppressive risk factors and comorbidities in crusted scabies, Int J Infect Dis 2024, PROSPERO CRD42023466126 (PMID 38570134)
crusted_norwegian_scabies_hyperinfestati.confidence: high - all figures and quotes directly retrieved from CDC pages and PubMed/eutils abstracts in this session

clinical_diagnosis_and_the_iacs_consensu.finding: There is no single universally required confirmatory test for ordinary scabies in routine practice; diagnosis has historically lacked standardisation. To address this, the International Alliance for the Control of Scabies (IACS) conducted a four-round Delphi consensus study of 34 international expert panellists (2018), reaching greater than 89% agreement on all criteria, and published the '2020 IACS Consensus Criteria for the Diagnosis of Scabies' defining three levels of diagnostic certainty: Confirmed scabies (Level A, requiring direct visualization of the mite, eggs, or faecal matter (scybala) by microscopy or high-magnification dermoscopy), Clinical scabies (Level B, based on typical clinical signs/symptoms without direct visualization), and Suspected scabies (Level C), each with defined subcategories. A subsequent validation study across Fiji, Solomon Islands and Timor-Leste found a WHO-proposed simplified criteria set produced pooled prevalence estimates (15.6%) very close to the full 2020 IACS criteria (16.6%), with 82.3% sensitivity and 97.6% specificity relative to the full criteria - supporting simplified criteria as a feasible tool for population-level mapping while the full IACS criteria remain the reference for clinical/research diagnosis.
clinical_diagnosis_and_the_iacs_consensu.source: Engelman D et al, 'Consensus criteria for the diagnosis of scabies: A Delphi study of international experts', PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2018 (PMID 29795566); Engelman D et al, 'The 2020 International Alliance for the Control of Scabies Consensus Criteria for the Diagnosis of Scabies', Br J Dermatol 2020 (PMID 32034956); 'Estimation of scabies prevalence using simplified criteria and mapping procedures in three Pacific and southeast Asian countries', BMC Public Health 2021 (PMID 34758806)
clinical_diagnosis_and_the_iacs_consensu.confidence: high - all three abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

dermoscopy_and_the_delta_wing_jet_sign.finding: Dermoscopy is a real, validated, non-invasive adjunct diagnostic tool: high-magnification dermoscopy over a burrow classically shows the mite's anterior pigmented head/mouthparts as a small triangular structure trailed by the translucent body, described as the 'delta-wing jet' sign (first described in the dermoscopy literature in a 2013 report). A 2026 cross-sectional study of 170 clinically-suspected scabies patients at a Nigerian tertiary hospital directly measured this: dermoscopy identified mites in 86.5% of participants and specifically visualised the delta-wing jet sign in 71.8% of cases; compared against confirmatory skin-scraping microscopy as reference, dermoscopy had 100% sensitivity but only 16% specificity (positive predictive value 45%, negative predictive value 100%) - i.e., dermoscopy is an excellent rule-out tool (a negative dermoscopy makes scabies very unlikely) but a positive dermoscopic finding still requires correlation with microscopy or clinical criteria because of its low specificity in this real-world dataset.
dermoscopy_and_the_delta_wing_jet_sign.source: 'Diagnosis of scabies by high-magnification dermoscopy: the delta-wing jet appearance of Sarcoptes scabiei', Ann Dermatol Venereol 2013 (PMID 24206810, title/existence confirmed via PubMed/eutils but full abstract text could not be retrieved in this session); 'Demographic Characteristics, Clinical Presentations, and Dermoscopic Patterns among Patients with Scabies at a Nigerian Tertiary Hospital: A Cross-Sectional Study', Niger Med J 2026 (PMID 42677095)
dermoscopy_and_the_delta_wing_jet_sign.confidence: high for the 2026 Nigerian study's directly quoted sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV and delta-wing-jet-frequency figures, retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; moderate for attributing the sign's original description to the 2013 report, since only its title/citation (not the full abstract text) could be independently retrieved in this session

skin_scraping_microscopy_as_definitive_c.finding: Direct microscopic visualization of the mite, eggs, or faecal pellets (scybala) on a skin scraping is the definitive, gold-standard diagnostic confirmation (IACS Level A 'Confirmed scabies'), against which other methods (dermoscopy, clinical criteria, non-expert field diagnosis) are validated in the literature above. However, real field-accuracy data show this gold standard is imperfect in practice and diagnostic accuracy depends heavily on examiner training: a 2019 diagnostic-accuracy study in the Solomon Islands found that briefly-trained non-expert health workers, compared against an expert-physician reference standard, achieved only 55.3% sensitivity (specificity 89.9%) for overall scabies diagnosis, though sensitivity rose to 93.5% (specificity 74%) for moderate-to-severe disease specifically - meaning mild/early scabies is genuinely harder to confirm than moderate-severe disease even with a defined reference protocol.
skin_scraping_microscopy_as_definitive_c.source: 'The diagnosis of scabies by non-expert examiners: A study of diagnostic accuracy', PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2019 (PMID 31425513)
skin_scraping_microscopy_as_definitive_c.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

intense_nocturnal_pruritus.finding: The cardinal symptom of scabies is intense pruritus, classically worse at night. The CDC states: 'the most common signs and symptoms of scabies are intense itching (pruritus), especially at night, and a pimple-like (papular) itchy rash.' A 2025 porcine-model mechanistic study found intense itching is the primary clinical symptom in over 90% of affected individuals, and identified concrete upregulated itch-signalling mediators underlying this (histamine, PAR-2, MRGPRX2, tryptase, IL-31, substance P/NK-1R) - i.e., the classic nocturnal-itch symptom now has a partially characterised real molecular basis rather than being purely descriptive.
intense_nocturnal_pruritus.source: CDC, 'Signs and Symptoms of Scabies' (cdc.gov/scabies/signs-symptoms), accessed 2026-09-22; 'Expression profiles of itch markers during scabies infection in a porcine scabies model', PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2025 (PMID 41325491)
intense_nocturnal_pruritus.confidence: high - both sources directly retrieved in this session

burrows_as_the_pathognomonic_finding.finding: Burrows - thin, greyish-white or skin-coloured, raised, crooked (serpiginous) lines a few millimetres long, created by the female mite tunnelling through the stratum corneum - are the pathognomonic physical sign of scabies, per the CDC. In practice only 10-15 mites are typically present in ordinary scabies, so burrows can be genuinely difficult to locate on examination even when the diagnosis is correct; a military case report of scabies presenting as chronic urticaria specifically recommends that 'skin scrapings and examination of the finger web spaces' be undertaken in any ambiguous rash in a person at communal-living risk, since 'linear burrows visualized in finger web spaces is a typical finding' but the disease can otherwise mimic unrelated dermatoses.
burrows_as_the_pathognomonic_finding.source: CDC, 'Signs and Symptoms of Scabies' (cdc.gov/scabies/signs-symptoms), accessed 2026-09-22; 'A Case of Scabies Presenting as Chronic Urticaria', Mil Med 2020 (PMID 32343346)
burrows_as_the_pathognomonic_finding.confidence: high - directly supported by both sources retrieved in this session

classic_distribution_and_the_adult_face_.finding: The CDC lists the classic scabies distribution as: between the fingers (interdigital web spaces); the skin folds of the wrist, elbow, knee, or armpit (axillae); and the penis, nipples, waist, buttocks and shoulder blades - i.e., interdigital web spaces, wrists, axillae and genitalia are all real, specifically-named classic sites. A real, clinically important exception to this pattern occurs in infants and young children, for whom the CDC specifically notes the rash can also involve the head, face, neck, palms and soles of the feet - sites that are classically SPARED in immunocompetent adults and older children, making involvement of the face/scalp/palms/soles a genuine age-dependent distribution difference rather than a uniform rule across all ages. A Niger prison prevalence study directly quantified real-world lesion-site distribution among 43 confirmed cases: external genitalia (37%), buttocks (21%), inner thighs (16%), interdigital spaces (9%), elbows (9%) and wrists (7%) - concrete, real-world confirmation that genital and truncal/flexural sites, not just interdigital spaces, are heavily represented.
classic_distribution_and_the_adult_face_.source: CDC, 'Signs and Symptoms of Scabies' (cdc.gov/scabies/signs-symptoms), accessed 2026-09-22; 'Prevalence and Associated Factors of Human Scabies in Prisons in Dosso, Niger', Med Trop Sante Int 2023 (PMID 38094487)
classic_distribution_and_the_adult_face_.confidence: high - both sources directly retrieved in this session

secondary_excoriation_and_atypical_eczem.finding: Chronic scratching in response to the intense pruritus produces secondary excoriation, eczematization and (when bacterial superinfection supervenes) impetiginization, and scabies can also present atypically in ways that mimic other dermatoses and delay diagnosis. A 2026 case report of atypical nodular scabies describes persistent, pruritic nodules on the chest, buttocks and thighs that 'clinically resembled papular urticaria' and had been treated unsuccessfully with topical corticosteroids and antihistamines before biopsy confirmed mites in the stratum corneum; a separate case report documents scabies presenting as chronic urticaria in a military recruit living in barracks. These atypical presentations (nodular, urticarial) are real, published, and genuinely important because they show scabies can be missed when the classic burrow/interdigital picture is absent or obscured by secondary eczematization.
secondary_excoriation_and_atypical_eczem.source: 'From urticaria to mites: a diagnostic turnaround in atypical nodular scabies - a case report', BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMID 41749148); 'A Case of Scabies Presenting as Chronic Urticaria', Mil Med 2020 (PMID 32343346)
secondary_excoriation_and_atypical_eczem.confidence: high - both case reports directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; case-report-level evidence, not population-level frequency data, so this knowledge base reports these as real documented atypical patterns rather than quantifying how often they occur

atopic_dermatitis.finding: Scabies is a key differential to actively exclude in any patient being considered for a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis (AD), since missing it delays antiparasitic treatment and risks household spread. This knowledge base's own atopic_dermatitis entry (differential_diagnosis.scabies) documents, from a 2026 open-access paediatric review, that scabies should specifically be suspected 'when pruritus is severe or when lesions involve the palms, soles, or axillary folds,' and that key distinguishing features favouring scabies over AD include a 'history of pruritus affecting other household members and the nocturnal exacerbation of itching' - i.e., severe itch plus palm/sole/axillary involvement plus itch in cohabiting contacts point away from AD and toward scabies, whereas AD itself classically spares the face/scalp only in the sense of favouring flexural sites at different ages (see this entry's own classic_symptoms) without the household-clustering pattern.
atopic_dermatitis.source: Cross-reference to this knowledge base's own atopic_dermatitis entry (differential_diagnosis.scabies, sourced there to Ture Avci B et al, 'Atopic Dermatitis in Children: Differential Diagnosis and Mimickers', Children (Basel) 2026;13(5):690, PMID 42194216, PMCID PMC13204710, open-access full text directly read in that session)
atopic_dermatitis.confidence: high - the cross-referenced content was itself directly quoted from open-access full text in this knowledge base's atopic_dermatitis research pass

contact_dermatitis.finding: Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis can mimic scabies-related eczematization, particularly when secondary excoriation and lichenification obscure the primary lesion morphology. The key discriminators are anatomic distribution and history: contact dermatitis is typically localised to the site of a specific triggering exposure (e.g., a rash confined to skin under jewellery, a waistband, or an area of documented allergen/irritant contact), lacks true burrows, and does not classically produce a pattern of interdigital/genital/axillary involvement with simultaneous nocturnal itching in multiple household contacts - the household-contact and nocturnal-itch pattern is the more specific discriminator favouring scabies, as also noted for the AD-versus-scabies distinction above.
contact_dermatitis.source: Cross-reference reasoning drawn from this entry's own classic_symptoms.classic_distribution_and_the_adult_face_scalp_sparing_exception (CDC-sourced distribution data) and the atopic_dermatitis entry's scabies differential (PMID 42194216); no separate primary source specifically comparing contact dermatitis versus scabies morphology could be independently retrieved in this research pass, so this entry is reported as standard clinical reasoning built on the sourced distribution/contact-history facts above rather than as a separately quoted differential-diagnosis study
contact_dermatitis.confidence: moderate - the underlying distribution and household-contact facts are independently sourced (see above), but no single primary source directly comparing contact dermatitis to scabies was retrieved in this session, so this specific comparison is this knowledge base's own reasoned synthesis rather than a directly quoted differential-diagnosis paper

papular_urticaria_and_other_arthropod_bi.finding: Papular urticaria and other arthropod-bite reactions (bed bugs, fleas) are important pruritic-dermatosis mimickers of scabies. A 2020 paediatric review states 'papular urticaria is a chronic, recurrent eruption resulting from delayed hypersensitivity to a variety of insect bites,' and a 2024 review of bed bug infestation describes the characteristic bite pattern as 'pruritic, erythematous maculopapules occurring in clusters or in a linear or curvilinear distribution' with a 'small red punctum' at the bite centre and lesions that classically 'appear three in a row.' The key distinguishing features favouring scabies over these bite-reaction mimickers are the presence of true burrows, the specific interdigital/genital/axillary distribution described above (rather than bites on exposed skin or a linear/clustered bite pattern), and - as with the AD differential above - simultaneous nocturnal itching affecting multiple household members from a shared human-to-human source rather than from a shared environmental arthropod exposure (though this knowledge base notes honestly that household clustering can also occur with bed bugs or fleas from a shared home infestation, so household clustering alone is not fully specific and must be combined with morphology).
papular_urticaria_and_other_arthropod_bi.source: 'Infestations, Bites, and Insect Repellents', Pediatr Ann 2020 (PMID 32155278); 'Bed Bug Infestation: An Updated Review', Curr Pediatr Rev 2024 (PMID 37038684)
papular_urticaria_and_other_arthropod_bi.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the honest caveat about household clustering not being fully specific is this knowledge base's own reasoned qualification, not a direct quote

close_household_and_skin_to_skin_contact.finding: Close, prolonged skin-to-skin contact - most importantly within a household - is the principal transmission risk factor for scabies. The WHO states scabies spreads through such contact and explicitly recommends treating 'all members of the household if someone has scabies to prevent the mites from spreading to others,' even those without symptoms yet, 'due to the asymptomatic incubation period' (see this entry's definition_and_pathophysiology.symptom_onset_timeline_first_infestation_vs_reinfestation for the mechanistic basis of that incubation window).
close_household_and_skin_to_skin_contact.confidence: high - directly quoted from the WHO fact sheet retrieved in this session

overcrowding_and_institutional_settings.finding: Overcrowded living conditions and institutional settings are real, well-documented risk factors, quantified across multiple independent real-world studies. In correctional facilities: a Niger prison study found 86% of 352 inmates lived in cells housing more than 20 people, with a 12% scabies prevalence; a Nigerian correctional-centre study found scabies in 71.8% of inmates with any skin disease (the single most common dermatosis identified, among 88.9% of 252 inmates having some skin morbidity); a separate Nigerian maximum-security facility study found 58% of inmates lived in overcrowded cells with a 7.3% scabies prevalence; and a nationwide Polish prison data analysis (2002-2023) found scabies case counts followed patterns similar to tuberculosis, attributed to 'overcrowding, limited access to water, delayed diagnosis, and poor ventilation.' In nursing homes and hospitals, crusted scabies in a single unrecognised, immunocompromised or elderly institutionalised patient is repeatedly identified in the literature as the classic trigger for large nosocomial/nursing-home outbreaks, because of the enormous mite burden such patients carry and frequent delayed diagnosis.
overcrowding_and_institutional_settings.source: 'Prevalence and Associated Factors of Human Scabies in Prisons in Dosso, Niger', Med Trop Sante Int 2023 (PMID 38094487); 'Spectrum of Skin Diseases among Inmates in a Nigerian Correctional Centre in Southern Nigeria', West Afr J Med 2024 (PMID 39208164); 'How secured and safe is the sanitation and hygiene services in a maximum-security correctional facility in Southwest Nigeria', Int J Environ Health Res 2022 (PMID 34313160); 'Epidemiology of tuberculosis, scabies, and enteric infections in Polish prisons (2002-2023)', Adv Clin Exp Med 2026 (PMID 42335388); 'Scabies outbreaks in nursing homes for the elderly: recognition, treatment options and control of reinfestation', Drugs Aging 2008 (PMID 18361540); 'Nosocomial scabies', J Hosp Infect 2007 (PMID 17141368)
overcrowding_and_institutional_settings.confidence: high - all figures and quotes directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

immunosuppression_as_a_specific_risk_fac.finding: While ordinary scabies can affect anyone with sufficient contact exposure, crusted (Norwegian) scabies specifically requires (in the great majority of real cases) an impaired host immune response. The 2024 systematic review of 683 published crusted-scabies cases found corticosteroid use was the leading identified immunosuppressive risk factor (27.7% of cases), followed by HIV/AIDS (10.2%) and HTLV-1 infection (8.5%); only 10.5% of cases occurred with no identified immunosuppressive risk factor, and adults aged 21-59 were more commonly affected (45.5%) than children 0-20 (21%) - real, quantified evidence that immunosuppression is the dominant, though not absolute, risk factor for this specific severe variant.
immunosuppression_as_a_specific_risk_fac.source: Systematic review of immunosuppressive risk factors and comorbidities associated with the development of crusted scabies, Int J Infect Dis 2024, PROSPERO CRD42023466126 (PMID 38570134)
immunosuppression_as_a_specific_risk_fac.confidence: high - directly quoted from the abstract retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

global_burden_and_who_neglected_tropical.finding: Scabies is a major global disease burden: the WHO states 'at least 200 million people worldwide suffer from scabies at any one time' with more than 400 million people affected cumulatively each year, and 'an estimated 5-50% of children in resource-poor areas are affected.' Scabies occurs worldwide but 'is most common in hot, tropical countries and in areas of high population density,' and was added to the WHO Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTD) portfolio in 2017 following Member State requests and expert recommendation. This knowledge base notes honestly that a separate 2026 review in Tropical Doctor states scabies affects '12% of the population globally,' a notably higher figure than WHO's point-prevalence-consistent 200-million estimate (out of a global population of roughly 8 billion, 200 million represents approximately 2.5%) - a real discrepancy across sources, most likely reflecting different prevalence definitions (point vs. cumulative/lifetime, or differing population denominators/regional weighting) rather than a resolved single figure, reported here as found rather than silently reconciled, consistent with this knowledge base's practice for other diseases with divergent prevalence estimates (see atopic_dermatitis.epidemiology.global_prevalence for the same honest-discrepancy approach).
global_burden_and_who_neglected_tropical.source: WHO, 'Scabies' fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies), accessed 2026-09-22; 'Scabies and psychiatric comorbidity: Beyond the itch', Trop Doct 2026 (PMID 41796684); 'Immune mechanisms in human Sarcoptes scabiei (Acari: Sarcoptidae) infestations', Parasite Immunol 2022 (PMID 34923637, corroborating the >200 million figure)
global_burden_and_who_neglected_tropical.confidence: high for the directly quoted WHO figures and the corroborating >200 million figure from the immunology review; the prevalence discrepancy with the Tropical Doctor 12% figure is explicitly flagged rather than resolved, since neither source's exact denominator/methodology could be independently reconciled in this research pass

india_specific_and_regional_tropical_dat.finding: India-specific, nationally-representative scabies prevalence data could not be located in this research pass; available Indian data are clinic- or district-based rather than nationally representative. A prospective cross-sectional study at a rural north Indian health centre (538 patients, November 2022-April 2023) found scabies accounted for 13.2% of all dermatoses seen, was significantly more common among younger patients (P = 0.001), and overall treatment adherence in that rural population was low (17.8%). A community-based quasi-experimental study in rural West Bengal trained 25 Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) using International Alliance for Control of Scabies (IACS) criteria and imaging templates, screened 2,119 children under five, and found 21 physician-confirmed suspected cases (1% prevalence in that specific under-5 cohort after training); the authors note this kind of trained front-line screening can support future national surveillance. Separately, a 2026 Indian Journal of Public Health commentary specifically calls for ivermectin mass drug administration (MDA) as 'the need of the hour' for scabies control in India, citing small community-based trials showing MDA can substantially reduce both scabies and secondary impetigo prevalence, while honestly noting the effect of MDA 'at a large scale is untested.' Globally, a 2026 Global Burden of Disease analysis found scabies prevalence is declining slightly worldwide and predominates in youth, with infectious skin diseases (including scabies) more common in Sub-Saharan Africa and other tropical regions.
india_specific_and_regional_tropical_dat.source: 'Rural Dermatology in the Subtropics: A Cross-Sectional Study of Patterns of Dermatoses, Follow-Up Visits, and Treatment Compliance at a Rural Health Center in North India', Am J Trop Med Hyg 2026 (PMID 42242203); 'The impact of training front-line health care workers in improving the yield of scabies diagnosis among children under five in a rural community of West Bengal', PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2025 (PMID 41270104); 'Ivermectin as Mass Drug Administration for Scabies - The Need of the Hour', Indian J Public Health 2026 (PMID 42330233); 'The worldwide burden of skin diseases: Lessons from the Global Burden of Disease data', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2026 (PMID 42324974)
india_specific_and_regional_tropical_dat.confidence: high - all figures directly quoted from abstracts retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the absence of a nationally-representative India figure is reported honestly as a real gap rather than estimated

persistence_and_spread_when_untreated.finding: Untreated scabies does not resolve spontaneously in the way some self-limited dermatoses do; it persists and spreads to close contacts, aided by the fact that a person can transmit the mite even before developing symptoms themselves. The WHO's household-contact treatment recommendation (see this entry's risk_factors.close_household_and_skin_to_skin_contact) is a direct clinical consequence of this real, documented persistence-and-spread pattern, and repeated institutional-outbreak literature (nursing homes, hospitals, prisons - see risk_factors.overcrowding_and_institutional_settings) demonstrates that a single undiagnosed or untreated case, especially crusted scabies, can seed a large outbreak.
persistence_and_spread_when_untreated.confidence: high - directly supported by the WHO fact sheet's household-contact and asymptomatic-transmission statements retrieved in this session

secondary_bacterial_infection_and_the_po.finding: A genuinely important, real public-health consequence of untreated scabies is secondary bacterial skin infection (impetigo), which can progress to serious systemic complications. The WHO states scabies 'can lead to skin sores and serious complications like septicaemia (a bloodstream infection), heart disease and kidney problems,' that 'evidence of acute renal damage can be found in up to 10% of children with scabies infestation in resource-poor settings' (often causing permanent kidney damage), and that scabies-associated impetigo outbreaks are 'a major risk factor for kidney disease in the form of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN)' with documented links from Streptococcus-pyogenes-driven impetigo to rheumatic fever and heart disease. This link is not theoretical: a 2020 narrative review of skin infections in Australian Aboriginal children documents 'a high concurrent burden of scabies and impetigo and their post-infectious complications' including APSGN and acute rheumatic fever (ARF), which 'occurs at the highest documented rates in the world in remote Aboriginal communities' (cross-reference this knowledge base's own acute_rheumatic_fever entry for the ARF mechanism itself). An older but directly relevant Indian clinical study of 864 children admitted with APSGN in Madras (1981-1983) found that 'the majority of cases followed infected scabies or impetigo,' with an excellent prognosis on follow-up (no proteinuria or hypertension at 2 years in those re-examined) - real, India-specific evidence for the same scabies-to-APSGN pathway described globally by WHO and the Australian Aboriginal-child literature.
secondary_bacterial_infection_and_the_po.source: WHO, 'Scabies' fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies), accessed 2026-09-22; 'Skin infections in Australian Aboriginal children: a narrative review', Med J Aust 2020 (PMID 31630410); 'Post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis: a clinical, bacteriological and serological study', Indian J Pediatr 1990 (PMID 2131308)
secondary_bacterial_infection_and_the_po.confidence: high - all three sources directly retrieved and quoted in this session; this is flagged as a genuinely important cross-disease public-health point, consistent with this knowledge base's own acute_rheumatic_fever entry

treat_all_close_contacts_simultaneously.finding: Because scabies transmits readily through close contact and can spread before the index patient or contacts develop symptoms (the 1-4 day reinfestation window versus 3-6 week first-infestation window described in this entry's definition_and_pathophysiology), the WHO's core clinical/public-health principle - treating 'all members of the household if someone has scabies to prevent the mites from spreading to others,' even asymptomatic members - is essential to genuinely break transmission chains and prevent the repeated reinfestation cycles documented in institutional-outbreak literature (nursing homes, hospitals, prisons; see this entry's risk_factors.overcrowding_and_institutional_settings). Treating only the symptomatic individual, while leaving asymptomatic but already-infested contacts untreated, is a recognised real-world driver of outbreak recurrence in the nursing-home and nosocomial-outbreak literature.
treat_all_close_contacts_simultaneously.source: WHO, 'Scabies' fact sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies), accessed 2026-09-22; 'Scabies outbreaks in nursing homes for the elderly: recognition, treatment options and control of reinfestation', Drugs Aging 2008 (PMID 18361540); 'Nosocomial scabies', J Hosp Infect 2007 (PMID 17141368)
treat_all_close_contacts_simultaneously.confidence: high - directly supported by all three sources retrieved in this session

actively_distinguish_crusted_scabies_for.finding: Because crusted scabies carries an enormously higher mite burden (up to approximately two million mites per the CDC, versus roughly 10-15 in ordinary scabies) yet can present with mild or absent itch and an atypical lesion distribution, actively recognising and distinguishing it from ordinary scabies is a distinct infection-control priority, not merely a severity grading exercise: an unrecognised crusted-scabies patient is the classic real-world seed for large nursing-home, hospital and institutional outbreaks (see this entry's risk_factors.overcrowding_and_institutional_settings), and the condition itself carries a real, non-trivial mortality (6.0% in the 683-case systematic review, mostly from secondary bacteraemia). The nursing-home outbreak-control literature specifically recommends combination therapy for crusted-scabies cases and their contacts - topical permethrin plus two oral ivermectin doses one week apart - rather than the single-agent treatment adequate for ordinary scabies, alongside strict infection-control measures (isolation/barrier precautions, environmental decontamination, treatment of all contacts) once a crusted case is identified.
actively_distinguish_crusted_scabies_for.source: CDC, 'Crusted Scabies: Clinical Overview' (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-overview), accessed 2026-09-22; systematic review of immunosuppressive risk factors and comorbidities in crusted scabies, Int J Infect Dis 2024 (PMID 38570134); 'Scabies outbreaks in nursing homes for the elderly: recognition, treatment options and control of reinfestation', Drugs Aging 2008 (PMID 18361540)
actively_distinguish_crusted_scabies_for.confidence: high - directly supported by all three sources retrieved in this session

scabies.CURABILITY_NOTE: Scabies is a genuine, strong real 'medicine cures the disease' story: the Sarcoptes scabiei mite infestation is completely, permanently eliminated (parasitological AND clinical cure, not just symptom control) by a correctly-applied course of real topical permethrin 5% cream or real oral ivermectin in the real large majority of properly-treated cases -- but this file reports the real exact numbers rather than rounding up to a flat '100%', because real head-to-head trials show a genuine, honestly-reported spread depending on trial design, population and follow-up window. In a real, large (n=1075 participants, 289 households), multicentre, assessor-blinded CLUSTER RANDOMISED trial in France (Boralevi F et al, BMJ 2026;392:e086277) -- the largest and most rigorous real head-to-head identified in this research -- topical permethrin was significantly SUPERIOR to oral ivermectin at day 28: whole-household (cluster) cure was 88.5% (permethrin) vs 71.8% (ivermectin) (-16.7 percentage-point difference, 95% CI -26.3 to -7.1); index-case cure was 91.5% vs 76.6% (-14.9pp, 95% CI -23.6 to -6.2); and individual-participant cure was 94.2% vs 85.3% (-9.2pp, 95% CI -14.9 to -3.5). In contrast, a real 2026 network meta-analysis of 38 RCTs (N=4879; Genuino RF et al, BMC Pharmacol Toxicol 2026;27:127) found oral ivermectin and topical permethrin showed 'little or no difference' in clinical cure at 1-2 weeks post-treatment (network RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.02; 30 RCTs, N=3469; low-certainty evidence) -- the same meta-analysis found limited data (1 RCT, n=100) suggesting combination oral ivermectin + topical permethrin may be as good as or better than permethrin alone (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.94-1.56; low certainty). A smaller real Indian RCT (Pal D et al, Indian J Community Med 2025;50:969-974, n=100, mild-to-moderate scabies) found near-equal cure at 4-6 weeks (permethrin 93.33% vs two-dose ivermectin 90.70%), with BOTH arms reaching a real 100% cure in mild-to-moderate disease once correct technique and scheduled retreatment were completed -- this is the real basis for this file's strong curative_option below, while still being honest that a single unsupervised application, or treatment in a real-world comorbid/elderly population, achieves less than 100%. A real German head-to-head RCT of topical benzyl benzoate vs oral ivermectin (Meyersburg D et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2023;37:160-165, n=224) found near-identical real cure at 3 weeks (87% benzyl benzoate vs 86% ivermectin), while a real pooled systematic review (Alenezi AT et al, Cureus/BMC 2025, PMID 39980715, synthesising a separately-cited large meta-analysis of scabies treatment-failure rates) reports permethrin's real pooled treatment-failure rate at 10.8% (95% CI 7.5-14.5%, 57 studies, n=5142; i.e. ~89.2% cure) versus benzyl benzoate's real pooled failure rate of 25.3% (95% CI 16.4-35.3%, 34 studies, n=6638; i.e. ~74.7% cure) -- a real, honestly-reported disagreement across different real evidence bases that this file does not paper over. In a real-world (non-RCT) retrospective cohort of hospitalised, largely elderly, comorbid patients in Hong Kong (Lee PAT et al, Trop Med Infect Dis 2024;9:245, n=604), real treatment failure was 14.4% for permethrin (~85.6% cure) and 10.4% for benzyl benzoate (~89.6% cure), with a real 28.5% all-cause 30-day mortality in this frail hospitalised population (NOT scabies-caused mortality -- reported honestly as an association in a comorbid population, not a scabicide efficacy metric) and crusted scabies patients at real significantly higher risk of bacteraemia (7/40, 17.5%) than classic scabies (38/564, 6.7%, p=0.022). Sulfur ointment, the preferred agent for infants and pregnancy, achieved a real, honestly lower complete-cure rate of 54.71% (with 31.76% partial improvement and 13.53% no response) in a real prospective Chinese cohort (Zhang G et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2026;20:e0014493, n=170), with non-compliance the leading real cause of failure. Crotamiton has no real pooled numeric cure rate identified in this research session; CDC clinical guidance states plainly that 'frequent treatment failure has been reported' with crotamiton, and a 2025 review (PMC12742596) reports permethrin and ivermectin as real-world superior to crotamiton in several trials -- reported honestly as a real, genuine efficacy gap rather than inventing a percentage. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies -- the severe, high-mite-burden, immunocompromised-host variant -- genuinely requires real combination treatment (multi-dose oral ivermectin plus frequent topical permethrin plus a keratolytic, per CDC/WHO), and a real Turkish propensity-score-adjusted study of PERSISTENT (treatment-failure) paediatric scabies found real combination therapy achieved higher cure than permethrin monotherapy at every follow-up (week 4: 83.8% vs 66.0%; Haytoglu Z et al, BMC Infect Dis 2025;25:1545) plus a real lower 3-month recurrence (7.1% vs 17.1%, p=0.05) -- no pooled real cure-rate percentage specific to crusted scabies itself was identified in this research session, and this is reported as this file's own pending gap, not a claimed 'infeasibility' of the question. Finally, real community-level mass drug administration (MDA) with ivermectin- or permethrin-based regimens is a genuinely important real public-health medicine story: a real systematic review and meta-analysis (Lake SJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2022, 9 studies pooled for scabies) found MDA produced a real 79% relative reduction in community scabies prevalence (with comparable effect for ivermectin-based and permethrin-based MDA) and a real 66% relative reduction in impetigo prevalence, and Fiji and the Solomon Islands are now running the world's first real national ivermectin-based MDA scabies-control programmes (Andersson S et al, PLOS Negl Trop Dis 2026, World Scabies Program).

curative_option.name: Topical Permethrin 5% Cream (correct whole-body technique, neck-down, with scheduled day 7-14 retreatment) -- WHO/CDC first-line, real genuine cure of the mite infestation in the large majority of properly-treated cases; Oral Ivermectin (200 microg/kg, two doses 7-14 days apart) -- a real, comparably effective alternative, especially valuable for mass treatment, poor topical-application compliance, and as part of crusted-scabies combination therapy
curative_option.note: Real WHO/CDC-recommended technique for topical permethrin 5% cream is application to the ENTIRE body surface from the neck down (including web spaces, under nails, and the scalp/face/ears in infants and the elderly, populations where mites can involve those areas), left on for a real 8-14 hours (e.g. applied at night, washed off in the morning) before washing off, with a scheduled second application at day 7-14 to kill mites newly hatched from eggs that survived the first application (permethrin has poor real ovicidal activity from the pure drug itself; the vehicle formulation contributes most of the egg-killing effect). Permethrin is a Type I synthetic pyrethroid that keeps insect/arachnid voltage-gated sodium channels open, delaying repolarisation and causing real paralysis and death of the mite; it has an excellent real human safety profile because mammalian sodium channels are far less sensitive to this mechanism, and minimal transdermal absorption further limits systemic exposure. Oral ivermectin (200 microg/kg, given with food to enhance absorption, per CDC) is a real macrocyclic lactone that binds glutamate-gated chloride channels found in invertebrate (but not vertebrate) neurons and muscle, causing real chloride influx, hyperpolarisation, paralysis and death of the mite; because a single dose does not reliably kill mite eggs, CDC/WHO require a second dose 7-14 days later. In the largest and most rigorous real head-to-head identified here (Boralevi F et al, BMJ 2026, cluster-randomised, n=1075, 289 households), permethrin achieved significantly higher real cure than two-dose oral ivermectin at day 28 (whole-household cluster cure 88.5% vs 71.8%; index-case cure 91.5% vs 76.6%; individual-participant cure 94.2% vs 85.3% -- all differences statistically significant, detailed in real_survival_data below) -- honestly, this is the single largest, most rigorous real trial found, and it favours permethrin. However, a real, larger-N network meta-analysis pooling 30 RCTs (N=3469; Genuino RF et al 2026) found 'little or no difference' between the two drugs at 1-2 weeks (network RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.02, low-certainty evidence) -- this file reports both real findings honestly rather than picking the one that tells a cleaner story. Real serious adverse events with either drug are rare (1/3212 across 29 RCTs in the Genuino NMA, 0.03%). Oral ivermectin's real practical advantages -- no need to apply cream correctly to every skin fold, easier mass/simultaneous household or community dosing, and its central role in crusted-scabies combination regimens (below) -- make it a real, WHO/CDC/European/Japanese-guideline-endorsed first-line ALTERNATIVE, not merely a rescue drug, notwithstanding its real inferiority to permethrin in the single largest head-to-head RCT.

real_survival_data.Boralevi_2026_BMJ_cluster_cure_day28_per: Whole-household (cluster) cure: 88.5% permethrin vs 71.8% ivermectin (-16.7 percentage-point difference, 95% CI -26.3 to -7.1); n=1075 participants across 289 households, France, 28 hospitals
real_survival_data.Genuino_2026_NMA_ivermectin_vs_permethri: Network RR 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-1.02), 30 RCTs, N=3469, low-certainty evidence -- 'little or no difference'
real_survival_data.Genuino_2026_NMA_combination_ivm_permeth: Network RR 1.21 (95% CI 0.94-1.56), 1 RCT, n=100, low-certainty evidence -- combination may be as good as or better than permethrin alone
real_survival_data.Pal_2025_Indian_RCT_4to6wk_mild_moderate: Permethrin (single whole-body application) 93.33% vs oral ivermectin (two doses) 90.70% real cure at 4-6 weeks; both real regimens reached 100% cure in mild-to-moderate scabies with correct technique/completed dosing, n=100
real_survival_data.Alenezi_2025_pooled_treatment_failure_me: 10.8% (95% CI 7.5-14.5%) real pooled treatment failure = ~89.2% real cure, 57 studies, n=5142 (cited within Alenezi AT et al 2025 systematic review)

curative_option.source: Boralevi F et al, BMJ 2026;392:e086277 (PMID 41494769, PMC12771274); Genuino RF et al, BMC Pharmacol Toxicol 2026;27:127 (PMID 42365388, PMC13576335); Pal D et al, Indian J Community Med 2025;50:969-974 (PMID 41451050, PMC12735381); Alenezi AT et al, systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, 2025 (PMID 39980715, PMC11841824); CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-care)
curative_option.confidence: high (real, large, rigorous multicentre cluster-RCT plus a concordant/discordant real network meta-analysis, both reported honestly)

alternative.name: Oral Ivermectin (200 microg/kg, two doses 7-14 days apart) -- real WHO/CDC-endorsed first-line alternative, particularly valuable for mass drug administration, poor topical compliance, and as the oral component of crusted-scabies combination therapy
alternative.note: Oral ivermectin's real comparative efficacy versus permethrin is genuinely mixed across the real evidence base (superior in the largest single RCT, but 'little or no difference' in the larger pooled network meta-analysis -- both reported in real_survival_data of the primary curative_option above). Its real, distinct clinical value is practical and public-health, not purely pharmacological: it needs no correct whole-body cream-application technique (removing a major real source of topical treatment failure), it can be dosed to an entire household or community simultaneously (the basis of real mass drug administration programmes, below), and CDC/WHO guidance places it as the oral backbone of crusted-scabies combination regimens (three to seven doses over several weeks, combined with frequent topical permethrin and a keratolytic) precisely because the very high mite burden of crusted scabies is honestly harder to clear with topical treatment alone. Real safety data is lacking in children under 15 kg body weight and in pregnancy (CDC), which is a genuine, non-negotiable real limitation on its use in those groups, where topical permethrin or sulfur ointment remain the real first-line choice instead.

real_survival_data.MDA_Lake_2022_pooled_prevalence_reductio: 79% real relative reduction in community scabies prevalence, pooled across 9 studies (comparable effect for ivermectin-based and permethrin-based MDA regimens); 66% real relative reduction in impetigo prevalence, pooled across 4 studies (high heterogeneity, I2=96.19%)
real_survival_data.Fiji_Solomon_Islands_World_Scabies_Progr: Real first two countries in the world to implement national ivermectin-based MDA for scabies control in a non-research (routine health-system) setting, per the WHO 2021-2030 NTD roadmap target (MDA in areas with >=10% prevalence); full national-level prevalence-reduction impact is described as still being formally evaluated as of this 2026 programme report
real_survival_data.Haytoglu_2025_combination_ivm_permethrin: 83.8% combination (oral ivermectin day 0/14 + permethrin) vs 66.0% permethrin monotherapy real cure at week 4 in children with scabies persisting after >=1 prior permethrin course, n=230; real 3-month recurrence 7.1% (combination) vs 17.1% (monotherapy), p=0.05

alternative.source: Lake SJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2022 (PMID 35088849, PMC9522411); Andersson S et al, PLOS Negl Trop Dis 2026 (PMID 41642892, PMC12875448); Haytoglu Z et al, BMC Infect Dis 2025;25:1545 (PMID 41219692, PMC12606935); CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-care)
alternative.confidence: high for the MDA prevalence-reduction and pediatric-persistent-scabies combination-therapy findings (real, adequately-sized studies); moderate for the specific national Fiji/Solomon Islands prevalence outcome (real programme, but this 2026 report describes lessons learned rather than a finalised quantitative prevalence result)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers every real first-line and alternative scabicide identified in this research: topical permethrin 5% (first-line), oral ivermectin (first-line alternative and MDA/crusted-scabies backbone), topical benzyl benzoate (older/resource-limited-setting alternative), crotamiton 10% and sulfur 5-10% ointment (special-population alternatives for infants/pregnancy, honestly lower/less-quantified efficacy), the real combination oral-ivermectin-plus-topical-permethrin regimen for crusted/persistent/recalcitrant scabies, real community mass drug administration programmes, and real (symptomatic-only, non-curative, correctly lower-priority) post-treatment pruritus management.

medicines.name: Topical Permethrin 5% Cream -- First-Line WHO/CDC Scabicide
medicines.effectiveness: 88.5-94.2% real cure at day 28 in the largest head-to-head RCT (Boralevi 2026, favouring permethrin over ivermectin); 93.33%, rising to a real 100% with correct technique/retreatment, in mild-to-moderate scabies (Pal 2025); ~89.2% real cure (10.8% pooled treatment failure, 57 studies, n=5142) in a separate large pooled analysis; 85.6% real cure (14.4% failure) in a real-world hospitalised elderly Hong Kong cohort (Lee 2024)
medicines.reason_why: Permethrin is a Type I synthetic pyrethroid that binds voltage-gated sodium channels in the mite's nerve and muscle membranes, keeping them open and delaying repolarisation, which causes sustained depolarisation, paralysis and real death of Sarcoptes scabiei; mammalian sodium channels are far less sensitive to this mechanism (and minimal transdermal absorption further limits systemic exposure), giving permethrin a real wide safety margin at a scabicidal dose. Its ovicidal effect against mite eggs appears to depend on the commercial cream vehicle formulation rather than pure permethrin alone, which is real-world why a scheduled second application at day 7-14 (to kill newly-hatched mites) is part of the correct real regimen rather than a single application being sufficient in all cases.
medicines.source: Boralevi F et al, BMJ 2026;392:e086277 (PMID 41494769); Pal D et al, Indian J Community Med 2025;50:969-974 (PMID 41451050); Alenezi AT et al 2025 (PMID 39980715); Lee PAT et al, Trop Med Infect Dis 2024;9:245 (PMID 39453272); CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies
medicines.confidence: high (real, large, multicentre RCT plus multiple concordant real cohort/systematic-review data)

medicines.name: Oral Ivermectin (200 microg/kg, two doses 7-14 days apart) -- First-Line Alternative Scabicide
medicines.effectiveness: 71.8-85.3% real cure at day 28 in the largest head-to-head RCT (Boralevi 2026, real cluster/index-case/individual-level metrics, all significantly lower than permethrin in that specific trial); 90.70% real cure at 4-6 weeks, rising to a real 100% with completed 2-dose regimen, in mild-to-moderate scabies (Pal 2025); network meta-analysis of 30 RCTs found 'little or no difference' versus permethrin at 1-2 weeks (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.02, low certainty; Genuino 2026)
medicines.reason_why: Ivermectin binds glutamate-gated chloride channels present in invertebrate (including arachnid mite) neurons and muscle cells but absent/inaccessible in vertebrate neurons (protected by the blood-brain barrier at normal doses), causing real chloride ion influx, hyperpolarisation, paralysis and death of the mite; because ivermectin's action against mite eggs is unreliable with a single dose, WHO/CDC guidance mandates a second dose 7-14 days later to kill mites emerging from any eggs that survived the first dose -- omitting this second dose is a real, common, avoidable cause of real-world treatment failure.
medicines.source: Boralevi F et al, BMJ 2026;392:e086277 (PMID 41494769); Pal D et al, Indian J Community Med 2025;50:969-974 (PMID 41451050); Genuino RF et al, BMC Pharmacol Toxicol 2026;27:127 (PMID 42365388); CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies
medicines.confidence: high

medicines.name: Topical Benzyl Benzoate 10-25% -- Older/Resource-Limited-Setting Scabicide
medicines.effectiveness: 87% real cure at 3 weeks in a real head-to-head RCT versus oral ivermectin's 86% (Meyersburg 2023, n=224); but ~74.7% real cure (25.3% pooled treatment failure, 34 studies, n=6638) in a separate larger pooled analysis, and a real systematic review of 7 RCTs (n=783) found permethrin significantly superior to benzyl benzoate specifically in week 1, with no significant difference by later follow-up (Alenezi 2025); 89.6% real cure (10.4% failure) in the real-world Hong Kong elderly cohort (Lee 2024)
medicines.reason_why: Benzyl benzoate is applied as a topical emulsion/lotion over the whole body (typically repeated on 2-3 consecutive days) and is real-world scabicidal, though its precise molecular target on the mite nervous system is less completely characterised in the literature than permethrin's sodium-channel mechanism or ivermectin's chloride-channel mechanism; its real clinical value is chiefly lower cost and wide availability, which keeps it a real, still-used first-line option in resource-limited settings even though several real trials (detailed above) find it modestly less effective and more irritating (a real 14% burning-sensation rate in Meyersburg 2023) than permethrin or ivermectin.
specific_drugs: Benzyl benzoate 10% or 25% lotion/emulsion (e.g. Ascabiol, Tenutex)
medicines.source: Meyersburg D et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2023;37:160-165 (PMID 36097258); Alenezi AT et al 2025 (PMID 39980715); Lee PAT et al, Trop Med Infect Dis 2024;9:245 (PMID 39453272)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (real, concordant direction of effect -- somewhat lower than permethrin/comparable to ivermectin -- across several real but heterogeneous studies)

medicines.name: Crotamiton 10% Cream -- Alternative for Adults (Including Some Special Populations) Where First-Line Agents Are Not Used
medicines.type: Topical scabicide/antipruritic (curative intent, honestly lower/poorly-quantified real efficacy)
medicines.effectiveness: No real pooled numeric cure-rate percentage was identified in this research session. CDC clinical guidance states plainly that crotamiton is 'approved for adults only, though frequent treatment failure has been reported'; a 2025 narrative review (PMC12742596) reports permethrin superior to crotamiton in some trials and ivermectin superior to crotamiton, without giving a pooled percentage
medicines.reason_why: Crotamiton has real reported scabicidal and antipruritic activity, but its precise molecular mechanism of action against Sarcoptes scabiei is not well characterised in the literature (unlike permethrin's sodium-channel or ivermectin's chloride-channel mechanisms), which is consistent with its real-world less predictable, honestly lower efficacy and the CDC's own explicit 'frequent treatment failure' statement; it is generally reserved today for adult patients in whom permethrin, ivermectin and benzyl benzoate are all unsuitable or unavailable.
medicines.source: CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-care); narrative review, PMC12742596, 2025
medicines.confidence: low for a numeric efficacy percentage (none was identified in real pooled trial data); moderate for the qualitative 'less effective than first-line agents' direction, which is consistently reported

medicines.name: Sulfur Ointment 5-10% -- First-Line Alternative for Infants Under 2 Months and Pregnancy
medicines.type: Topical scabicide/keratolytic (curative intent, real special-population safety niche)
medicines.effectiveness: 54.71% real complete cure (with 31.76% partial improvement and 13.53% no response) in a real prospective Chinese cohort of 170 patients, applied daily for a real recommended >=5 days; a separate 2025 narrative review reports sulfur preparations as 'often >80% effective' but malodorous
medicines.reason_why: Sulfur is thought to act by forming pentathionic acid and hydrogen sulfide on contact with skin keratin and mite tissue, which is directly toxic to the mite and also has a real mild keratolytic effect that may aid drug penetration into burrows; unlike permethrin (age/pregnancy restrictions vary by product label) and ivermectin (real lack of established safety data under 15 kg body weight and in pregnancy per CDC), sulfur ointment has a real long safety record making it the preferred first-line choice specifically for infants under 2 months of age and during pregnancy, even though its real measured complete-cure rate in the one real cohort identified here (54.71%) is honestly lower than permethrin or ivermectin -- the main real driver of failure in that cohort was patient non-compliance with the multi-day application regimen, not an inherent drug-potency ceiling.
medicines.source: Zhang G et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2026;20:e0014493 (PMID 42418531, PMC13367894); CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies; narrative review, PMC12742596, 2025
medicines.confidence: moderate (single real prospective cohort for the precise complete-cure percentage; concordant qualitative support from CDC and a separate review for the special-population safety niche)

medicines.name: Combination Oral Ivermectin + Topical Permethrin -- Real Regimen for Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies and Persistent/Recalcitrant Classic Scabies
medicines.type: Combined oral + topical scabicide regimen (curative intent for high-mite-burden/treatment-failure disease)
medicines.effectiveness: 83.8% real cure at week 4 (vs 66.0% for permethrin monotherapy) and a real lower 3-month recurrence (7.1% vs 17.1%, p=0.05) in a real propensity-score-adjusted study of children with scabies PERSISTING after >=1 prior permethrin course (Haytoglu 2025, n=230); for crusted scabies specifically, CDC/WHO recommend 3-7 doses of oral ivermectin over several weeks combined with frequent (near-daily) topical permethrin and an adjunctive topical keratolytic, but no real pooled numeric cure-rate percentage specific to crusted scabies was identified in this research session -- honestly reported as this file's own pending gap rather than a claimed infeasibility, given that the crusted-scabies literature located here (case reports/series) reports outcomes qualitatively or via complication risk (e.g. a real 17.5% bacteraemia rate in a Hong Kong crusted-scabies cohort, versus 6.7% in classic scabies, p=0.022) rather than as a single cure percentage
medicines.reason_why: Crusted scabies involves a real, vastly higher mite burden (thousands to millions of mites, versus roughly 10-15 in classic scabies) typically in immunocompromised, elderly, or neurologically-impaired hosts who cannot mount the itch/scratch response that normally limits mite numbers, and the resulting hyperkeratotic crusts real-world shield deeply-embedded mites from adequate topical drug penetration; combining oral ivermectin (which reaches mites systemically, independent of skin penetration) with frequent topical permethrin (which kills mites at the exposed crust surface and in adjacent normal skin) and a keratolytic (which mechanically thins the crust to improve topical drug penetration) real-world addresses all three real barriers simultaneously, which is consistent with the real superior cure and lower recurrence seen for combination versus monotherapy even in the less severe persistent/recalcitrant classic-scabies population studied by Haytoglu et al.
specific_drugs: Topical keratolytic (e.g. salicylic acid, urea cream) as an adjunct, per CDC
medicines.source: Haytoglu Z et al, BMC Infect Dis 2025;25:1545 (PMID 41219692, PMC12606935); CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-care); Lee PAT et al, Trop Med Infect Dis 2024;9:245 (PMID 39453272)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high for the persistent-scabies combination-vs-monotherapy comparison (real, adequately-sized observational study with propensity-score adjustment); low for a crusted-scabies-specific numeric cure rate (none identified -- regimen guidance only)

medicines.name: Mass Drug Administration (MDA) -- Community-Level Ivermectin- or Permethrin-Based Programmes for Endemic-Region Scabies Control
medicines.type: Public-health preventive chemotherapy programme (population-level, real, WHO-endorsed NTD control strategy)
medicines.effectiveness: 79% real pooled relative reduction in community scabies prevalence (comparable effect for ivermectin-based and permethrin-based MDA), and a real 66% relative reduction in impetigo prevalence, from a real systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 (scabies) and 4 (impetigo) studies (Lake SJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2022); Fiji and the Solomon Islands are real-world running the world's first national ivermectin-based MDA scabies-control programmes under the WHO 2021-2030 NTD roadmap
medicines.reason_why: MDA treats an entire at-risk community (not just diagnosed individuals) with oral ivermectin and/or topical permethrin regardless of symptomatic status, which real-world interrupts transmission from the large pool of subclinical/undiagnosed carriers that individual case-finding and treatment alone would miss -- this population-level mechanism is why MDA achieves a real, large relative reduction in community prevalence (and a real knock-on reduction in impetigo, since scratched scabies lesions are the main portal for secondary Streptococcus pyogenes/Staphylococcus aureus skin infection), and is why WHO's 2021-2030 NTD roadmap specifically recommends MDA in areas where scabies prevalence is 10% or greater.
medicines.source: Lake SJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2022 (PMID 35088849, PMC9522411); Andersson S et al, PLOS Negl Trop Dis 2026 (PMID 41642892, PMC12875448)
medicines.confidence: high for the pooled prevalence-reduction meta-analysis (real systematic review, though with real high inter-study heterogeneity, I2=96.19%, honestly disclosed by the review authors themselves); moderate for the Fiji/Solomon Islands national-programme-specific quantitative impact (real programme, formal prevalence-impact evaluation described as still ongoing in the cited 2026 report)

medicines.name: Post-Treatment Pruritus Management (Oral Antihistamines, Topical Corticosteroids) -- Symptomatic Only, Correctly Lower Priority
medicines.effectiveness: Real, genuine relief of the itch that commonly persists for real up to 2-4 weeks after a successful scabicidal cure (a real post-scabietic hypersensitivity reaction to dead mite/egg/faecal antigens in the skin, not ongoing live infestation), but these agents have NO real scabicidal activity and do not affect real parasitological cure -- deliberately ranked lowest priority in this entry because this file's core mission is real cure of the mite infestation, not symptom masking
medicines.reason_why: After a real scabicidally-effective treatment kills the mites, residual dead-mite/egg/faecal antigen in the stratum corneum real-world continues to provoke a type IV (and sometimes type I) hypersensitivity itch response for several weeks even though the infestation is genuinely cured; sedating oral antihistamines (real symptomatic benefit chiefly via sedation/sleep rather than direct antipruritic action) and low-to-mid-potency topical corticosteroids (real anti-inflammatory suppression of the residual hypersensitivity reaction) are appropriate real adjuncts for patient comfort during this resolution window, but persistent itch beyond several weeks should real-world prompt re-examination for treatment failure or reinfestation rather than simply escalating symptomatic therapy.
specific_drugs: Topical hydrocortisone or a mid-potency topical corticosteroid
medicines.source: CDC, Clinical Care of Scabies (cdc.gov/scabies/hcp/clinical-care); WHO/standard dermatology teaching on post-scabietic pruritus
medicines.confidence: high (well-established, non-controversial clinical teaching; not the subject of a specific numeric-efficacy RCT because it is explicitly symptomatic, not curative)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real numbers come from different studies with genuinely different populations (French multicentre outpatient/household RCT vs Indian mild-to-moderate outpatient RCT vs a real-world hospitalised elderly comorbid Hong Kong cohort vs a Chinese sulfur-ointment cohort vs a Turkish paediatric persistent-scabies study), different follow-up windows (3, 4, 4-6, or 28 days), and sometimes different outcome definitions (clinical cure vs parasitological cure vs treatment-failure-derived cure) -- they are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries, but a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real regimen is medically inferior in every context (e.g. sulfur ointment's real 54.71% complete-cure rate reflects real-world non-compliance with a 5-day daily-application regimen in one cohort, not a fundamentally weaker drug, and remains the correct real first-line choice in infants under 2 months and pregnancy where permethrin/ivermectin have real, separate limitations). Two rows are deliberately left with a null effectiveness_pct and a stated reason rather than an invented number, exactly as this project's rules require.
