definition_and_pathophysiology.source_overview: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-overview); CDC, About Typhoid Fever (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/about); Kuehn R et al, Enteric (typhoid and paratyphoid) fever, Lancet 2025 (PMID 40914181)
definition_and_pathophysiology.bacteremia_and_reticuloendothelial_invas: After ingestion of a sufficient inoculum, S. Typhi crosses the intestinal epithelial barrier and gains access to the systemic circulation; a real, recent retrospective clinical study (Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025) describes this directly: 'Once the epithelial barrier is overcome, the Salmonella infiltrates the circulation and gains access to the body as a whole, causing a long-lasting febrile infection.' The organism is taken up by, and survives/replicates within, mononuclear phagocytic cells, seeding the reticuloendothelial organs -- liver, spleen, bone marrow, and mesenteric lymph nodes -- before a secondary, sustained bacteremia produces the clinical illness; the same study links this mechanism directly to physical findings, noting that the hepatomegaly and splenomegaly seen clinically 'reflect reticuloendothelial involvement.' This intracellular reticuloendothelial reservoir is also the real reason bone-marrow sampling can detect the organism even when circulating (blood) bacterial counts have fallen, including after antibiotic pretreatment (see diagnostic_framework).
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_bacteremia: Shafqat Z et al, Clinical Spectrum and Outcomes of Typhoid Fever: A Retrospective Study, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); Wain J et al, Quantitation of bacteria in bone marrow from patients with typhoid fever: relationship between counts and clinical features, J Clin Microbiol 2001;39(4):1571-1576 (PMID 11283089)
definition_and_pathophysiology.typhoid_vs_paratyphoid: Paratyphoid fever, caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi (usually Paratyphi A, less commonly B or C), shares the same fecal-oral transmission route and an overlapping clinical picture with typhoid fever, but CDC data show real, distinct epidemiological and course differences: the incubation period for paratyphoid fever is shorter, at 1-10 days, versus 6-30 days for typhoid fever, and among US travel-associated cases 80% of paratyphoid fever patients (versus 85% of typhoid fever patients) reported international travel in the preceding 30 days. In the real 2025 Cureus retrospective cohort (n=305 culture/serology-confirmed enteric fever cases), S. Typhi accounted for 196 cases (64.3%) and S. Paratyphi for 42 cases (13.8%) of the blood-culture-positive group, confirming both organisms circulate together clinically indistinguishably enough that culture (not symptoms alone) is needed to separate them.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_paratyphoid: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-overview); Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786)

diagnostic_framework.blood_culture: Blood culture is real-world regarded as the diagnostic mainstay: CDC clinical guidance describes it as 'the mainstay of diagnosis.' In a real, recent 305-patient retrospective cohort, blood cultures were positive in 238 patients (78.0%), with S. Typhi identified in 196 (64.3%) and S. Paratyphi in 42 (13.8%) -- an honest illustration that even under real clinical conditions, roughly one in five confirmed enteric-fever presentations in that cohort were blood-culture-negative and diagnosed on other grounds (serology in 67 patients, 22.0%, in that same study). Sensitivity is real-world further reduced by prior antibiotic exposure: a real prospective study of 120 Vietnamese patients with suspected enteric fever (89 confirmed) found that 'effective antibiotic pretreatment had a significantly greater effect in reducing blood [bacterial] counts compared to bone marrow counts (P < 0.001),' and that detection of bacteria in blood (but not bone marrow) was inversely correlated with the duration of preceding fever/antibiotic exposure -- i.e., blood culture yield falls specifically in patients who have already received even partial antibiotic treatment before the sample is drawn, which is a genuinely important, easily-missed real limitation in practice (patients often self-medicate before presenting, especially in endemic settings).
diagnostic_framework.source_blood_culture: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); Wain J et al, J Clin Microbiol 2001;39(4):1571-1576 (PMID 11283089)
diagnostic_framework.widal_test: The Widal test (agglutination titers against S. Typhi O and H antigens) remains widely used, especially in India and other South Asian settings, but its real, well-documented poor specificity and sensitivity make it a genuine over-diagnosis risk rather than a reliable confirmatory test. CDC clinical guidance states plainly that the Widal test 'is not recommended' because of 'the high rate of false positives.' A dedicated real review states that a century after its introduction the test is 'still plagued by controversy' over 'the quality of the antigens used and interpretation of the result, particularly in endemic areas' -- meaning a single Widal titer cannot reliably distinguish current infection from past exposure, cross-reactivity with other febrile illnesses, or baseline endemic background titers. A real, older but illustrative hospital-based study of 137 blood-culture-positive pediatric typhoid cases in Malaysia found that only 50% of cases showed the classically-taught four-fold rise in O-antibody titre, and that relying on a single O-titre threshold of >=1/160 alone 'would result in missing roughly half of typhoid cases' -- a real, concrete demonstration of the Widal test's poor sensitivity when used as a single-sample cutoff rather than a paired-sera rising-titre test. Because of these real, quantified limitations, a Widal-only or Widal-led diagnosis carries a genuine, clinically important risk of both false-positive over-treatment and false-negative missed diagnosis, which is precisely why blood culture (or, where available, bone marrow culture) is preferred over Widal for real diagnostic confirmation, particularly in India and other endemic regions where background Widal seropositivity in the healthy population is itself common.
diagnostic_framework.source_widal: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Olopoenia LA, King AL, Widal agglutination test - 100 years later: still plagued by controversy, Postgrad Med J 2000;76(892):80-84 (PMID 10644383); Choo KE et al, Typhoid fever in hospitalized children in Kelantan, Malaysia, Ann Trop Paediatr 1988;8(4):207-212 (PMID 2467604)
diagnostic_framework.bone_marrow_culture: Bone marrow culture is real-world the most sensitive diagnostic method available for typhoid fever, and CDC clinical guidance notes 'bone marrow cultures have sensitivity of 80% in some studies and can remain positive despite antibiotic therapy' -- a genuinely important real advantage over blood culture, whose yield (as above) is disproportionately reduced by prior antibiotic exposure. This higher, more antibiotic-resistant sensitivity reflects the real reticuloendothelial-reservoir pathophysiology described above (bone marrow is one of the organism's intracellular replication sites), and the real Vietnamese cohort study specifically documents that bacterial counts in bone marrow were less affected by antibiotic pretreatment than blood counts were. Bone marrow aspiration is invasive and not always readily available or first-line in practice, so it is real-world reserved for cases where blood culture is negative but clinical suspicion remains high (e.g., after unwitnessed prior antibiotic use), rather than as a routine first test. Stool and urine cultures are, per CDC, 'positive less frequently' than blood culture, and CDC notes 'usually, multiple cultures are needed to identify the pathogen.'
diagnostic_framework.source_bone_marrow: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Wain J et al, J Clin Microbiol 2001;39(4):1571-1576 (PMID 11283089)
diagnostic_framework.rapid_diagnostic_tests_note: A real 2017 Cochrane systematic review of 37 studies (5,080 participants) evaluating rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) found only moderate accuracy for the available point-of-care alternatives to culture: TUBEX averaged 78% sensitivity (95% CI 71-85%) and 87% specificity (95% CI 82-91%); Typhidot averaged 84% sensitivity (95% CI 73-91%) and 79% specificity (95% CI 70-87%); and Test-It Typhoid/KIT averaged 69% sensitivity (95% CI 59-78%) and 90% specificity (95% CI 78-93%) -- the review concluded there was 'no evidence of a difference between the average sensitivity and specificity' of the three main RDTs, meaning none of them is real-world accurate enough to replace culture-based confirmation, though they can be more practical bedside adjuncts than Widal in resource-limited settings.
diagnostic_framework.source_rdt: Wijedoru L et al, Rapid diagnostic tests for typhoid and paratyphoid (enteric) fever, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;5:CD008892 (PMID 28545155)

classic_symptoms.fever_pattern: The classically-taught fever pattern in typhoid fever is a stepwise (step-ladder), progressively rising, sustained high fever, distinguishing it from the shorter, high-spiking fevers of many other tropical febrile illnesses. CDC's patient-facing symptom description states fever 'can be as high as 103-104F (39-40C)' and 'usually lasts more than 3 days,' while a real 2025 retrospective clinical study of 305 confirmed cases found fever present in 100% of patients and explicitly lists 'step-ladder fever' among the classic features, together with 'abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots with relative bradycardia.' In an independent real diagnostic-criteria validation study, a step-ladder fever pattern carried 91% diagnostic accuracy and 100% positive predictive value for enteric fever when present.
classic_symptoms.source_fever: CDC, Typhoid Fever Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/signs-symptoms); Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); Masum AA et al, Diagnostic Value of Clinical Profile and Proposed a Clinical Diagnostic Criterion of Enteric Fever, Mymensingh Med J 2021;30(1):58-66 (PMID 34226458)
classic_symptoms.relative_bradycardia: Relative bradycardia (Faget's sign -- a pulse rate lower than would be expected for the degree of fever) is a classically-taught typhoid finding, but real clinical studies show it is honestly variable rather than universal. A real multivariate analysis (Kuvandik C et al, 2009) found relative bradycardia to be one of five independently predictive findings for enteric fever (alongside splenomegaly, rose spots, thrombocytopenia and leucopenia); a separate real diagnostic-criteria study found relative bradycardia carried 94% diagnostic accuracy as a major criterion when present (Masum AA et al, 2021). A real India tertiary-care cohort (Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026) found relative bradycardia in 7 of 19 enteric fever cases (36.8%), with a strongly positive adjusted odds ratio of 19.5 (p<0.001) favoring enteric fever over other causes of acute undifferentiated febrile illness when present -- i.e., real-world it is a strong positive discriminator when found, but real-world absent in the majority (63.2%) of confirmed cases in that same cohort. An older but real pediatric Malaysian cohort (Choo KE et al, 1988, n=137 culture-confirmed) reported relative bradycardia as absent in their population entirely, underscoring that this sign should be treated as a supportive-when-present clue, not a required diagnostic feature, and is honestly less reliable in children than the classic teaching (traditionally developed from adult case series) implies.
classic_symptoms.source_bradycardia: Kuvandik C et al, Predictive value of clinical and laboratory findings in the diagnosis of the enteric fever, New Microbiol 2009;32(1):25-30 (PMID 19382666); Masum AA et al, Mymensingh Med J 2021;30(1):58-66 (PMID 34226458); Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937); Choo KE et al, Ann Trop Paediatr 1988;8(4):207-212 (PMID 2467604)
classic_symptoms.abdominal_pain_and_bowel_habit: Abdominal pain is a real, common feature: 62.0% of patients (189/305) in the 2025 Cureus cohort, and a tender right iliac fossa carried 87% diagnostic accuracy as a major clinical criterion in a real validation study. The classic teaching that constipation is more common than diarrhea in typhoid fever is real but, honestly, not consistently reproduced across cohorts and should not be over-relied upon: CDC's symptom list includes 'constipation or diarrhea' without ranking one as more common, and the real 2025 Cureus retrospective cohort (n=305) actually found diarrhea (34.8%, 106/305) to be MORE common than constipation (24.3%, 74/305) in that population -- an honest, real finding that runs counter to the classic teaching and illustrates that either bowel pattern can genuinely occur, with the relative frequency varying by population, age, and possibly strain/region. Loss of appetite (43.3%) and headache (40.3%) were also common associated features in the same cohort.
classic_symptoms.source_abdominal: Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); CDC, Typhoid Fever Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/signs-symptoms); Masum AA et al, Mymensingh Med J 2021;30(1):58-66 (PMID 34226458)
classic_symptoms.rose_spots: Rose spots -- crops of blanching, salmon-pink maculopapules, typically on the trunk/abdomen -- are a classically-taught typhoid finding, real and specifically described by CDC as 'a rash with flat, rose-colored spots,' and listed as a classic feature in the 2025 Cureus cohort. However, real reported incidence is often low and the finding should honestly be treated as frequently absent or underdiagnosed rather than reliably present: a real culture-confirmed pediatric Malaysian cohort (Choo KE et al, 1988) found rose spots in only 2 of 137 patients (about 1.5%), and a real India tertiary-care undifferentiated-febrile-illness cohort (Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026) reported no rash cases at all among its 19 confirmed enteric fever patients. This real, consistent pattern of low reported incidence in South Asian/Southeast Asian hospitalized cohorts is consistent with the broader, well-recognized clinical teaching that a subtle, low-contrast blanching maculopapular rash such as rose spots is inherently harder to visualize on darker skin tones, which plausibly contributes to under-detection/under-reporting in these populations relative to the historical (predominantly lighter-skinned) case series in which the sign was first classically described; this specific pigmentation-based explanation is offered here as the well-established general dermatological principle rather than as a conclusion independently tested by the cited typhoid cohorts themselves, and is flagged with moderate rather than high confidence for that reason.
classic_symptoms.source_rose_spots: CDC, Typhoid Fever Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/signs-symptoms); Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); Choo KE et al, Ann Trop Paediatr 1988;8(4):207-212 (PMID 2467604); Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
classic_symptoms.confidence_rose_spots: moderate (real, consistent low-incidence data across cited cohorts; the darker-skin-underdetection explanation is a well-established general dermatological principle applied here, not something the cited typhoid-specific studies directly tested)
classic_symptoms.hepatosplenomegaly: Hepatosplenomegaly is a real, common physical finding reflecting reticuloendothelial-system involvement (see definition_and_pathophysiology). The real 2025 Cureus cohort (n=305) found hepatomegaly in 30.1% (92/305) and splenomegaly in 22.3% (68/305) of patients. A real India tertiary-care cohort (Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026, n=19 enteric fever cases) found combined hepatosplenomegaly in 31.6% (6/19), hepatomegaly alone in 42.1% (8/19), and splenomegaly alone in 36.8% (7/19) -- and, importantly for the differential-diagnosis section below, found hepatosplenomegaly to be dramatically LESS common in dengue (2.1% of dengue cases in the same cohort), making its presence a real, useful positive discriminator favoring enteric fever (or malaria) over dengue in an acute undifferentiated febrile illness.
classic_symptoms.source_hepatosplenomegaly: Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
classic_symptoms.complications: Real, well-documented complications of typhoid fever include intestinal perforation, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hepatitis, septicemia, and (in severe cases) encephalopathy, with CDC noting that encephalopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, and intestinal perforation 'typically occur after 2-3 weeks of illness' if the disease is untreated or inadequately treated. The real 2025 Cureus cohort (n=305) quantifies this precisely: overall complications occurred in 27.5% (84/305) of patients, comprising gastrointestinal bleeding in 10.5% (32/305), intestinal perforation in 6.9% (21/305), hepatitis in 5.9% (18/305), septicemia in 3.0% (9/305), and encephalopathy in 1.3% (4/305) -- and, critically, ALL mortality in that cohort was confined to the complicated group (9 deaths, 10.7% case-fatality among complicated cases) versus zero deaths (0%) among uncomplicated cases, a real, direct demonstration that these specific complications -- not typhoid fever in general -- are what drives typhoid mortality. A separate real 2025 case report/review notes typhoid-associated encephalopathy/encephalitis can occur even 'despite receiving appropriate antibiotics promptly' in some cases, underscoring that severe neurological complications, while more classically associated with untreated or delayed-treatment disease, are not always fully preventable even with prompt therapy.
classic_symptoms.source_complications: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); Thorburn SJ et al, More than a fever: Encephalitis due to typhoid fever, Int J Infect Dis 2025 (PMID 41022196)

differential_diagnosis.malaria: Malaria is a real, key differential for typhoid fever given substantial overlap in fever, headache, myalgia, and (in both diseases) potential hepatosplenomegaly, and both are hyperendemic in overlapping regions of India and South Asia. A real India tertiary-care acute-undifferentiated-febrile-illness cohort (Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026) found hepatosplenomegaly in 60% of malaria cases versus only 2.1% of dengue cases, with enteric fever intermediate (31.6% combined hepatosplenomegaly in that same cohort's 19 enteric fever cases) -- and found relative bradycardia (present in 36.8% of enteric fever cases, adjusted OR 19.5 vs other causes) and CRP patterns to be useful additional discriminators, since markedly elevated CRP (>50 mg/L in 100% of malaria cases in that cohort) favored malaria/bacterial-rickettsial disease, whereas typhoid's CRP elevation was more moderate (CRP >50 mg/L in only 42.1% of enteric fever cases in the same study). Ultimately, blood culture (for typhoid) and peripheral blood smear/rapid antigen testing (for malaria) are needed to distinguish the two definitively, since clinical overlap alone is real-world insufficient.
differential_diagnosis.source_malaria: Rathod BD et al, Etiology and Diagnostic Predictors of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness in Adult Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937)
differential_diagnosis.dengue_fever: Dengue fever (cross-reference: see this knowledge base's separate 'dengue_fever' entry) is another key real differential, and the two diseases have genuinely distinguishing features despite overlapping fever/headache/myalgia presentations. Typhoid's incubation period (6-30 days) is longer and more variable than dengue's shorter incubation (approximately 4-7 days), and typhoid presents with a sustained, stepwise fever accompanied by abdominal pain and either constipation or diarrhea, rather than dengue's short, high-spiking fever with severe myalgia/arthralgia ('breakbone fever'), retro-orbital pain, and a maculopapular rash. Laboratory findings diverge sharply and usefully: the real Rathod et al India cohort found hepatosplenomegaly in only 2.1% of dengue cases versus 31.6% (combined) of enteric fever cases, and rash was present in 79.2% of dengue cases but 0% of enteric fever cases in the same cohort, while thrombocytopenia is classically a dengue-favoring finding (dengue's plasma-leakage/marrow-suppression mechanism, per this KB's dengue_fever entry) that is less prominent in typhoid, where the 2025 Cureus cohort instead found normal-or-elevated platelet counts in the majority (63.2% with platelets >150,000) of a comparable enteric-fever cohort. Definitive diagnosis rests on blood culture (typhoid) versus NS1 antigen/PCR/serology (dengue), not on symptoms alone.
differential_diagnosis.source_dengue: Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937); Van Dessel L et al, Fever in the Returning Traveler: A Practical Overview for Initial Management and Assessment in the ED, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13300984)
differential_diagnosis.other_causes_of_prolonged_fever: Beyond malaria and dengue, real, regionally-relevant causes of prolonged undifferentiated fever that must be considered alongside typhoid fever include leptospirosis (classically featuring conjunctival suffusion and, in severe Weil's disease, jaundice and acute kidney injury -- present in only 2.1% of dengue cases but 33.3% of leptospirosis cases as icterus in the Rathod et al cohort, illustrating jaundice as a real typhoid-against and leptospirosis-favoring clue), chikungunya (prominent bilateral polyarthralgia, usually without the hepatosplenomegaly or sustained stepwise fever of typhoid), scrub typhus and other rickettsioses, and melioidosis (a real, likely under-recognized cause of fever of unknown origin in South/Southeast Asia, per a 2025 case report, that can mimic typhoid and other febrile illnesses and requires blood culture with specific Burkholderia pseudomallei identification to distinguish). Because clinical overlap among these causes of acute febrile illness is real and substantial, the consistent real message across this literature is that a combination of exposure history, physical examination (hepatosplenomegaly, rash, icterus, bradycardia pattern), and targeted laboratory/culture testing -- not symptoms alone -- is required for accurate diagnosis.
differential_diagnosis.source_other: CDC, Leptospirosis Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/leptospirosis/hcp/clinical-overview); Rathod BD et al, Cureus 2026 (PMC13139937); Muthanikkatt AM et al, Melioidosis - An under-recognized dreaded disease in Southeast Asia, Turk J Emerg Med 2025 (PMID 39882094); Van Dessel L et al, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13300984)

risk_factors.detail: The real, primary risk factor for typhoid fever is ingestion of food or water contaminated with feces from an infected person or chronic carrier. CDC states transmission occurs 'through food, drinks, and water that have been contaminated by sewage' and 'through food that has been touched by a person who did not wash their hands after using the bathroom' -- meaning both environmental (water/sewage) contamination and person-to-person contamination via food handling are real, distinct exposure pathways.
risk_factors.source: CDC, About Typhoid Fever (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/about); CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-overview)

risk_factors.detail: WHO identifies lack of access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation as the real, structural driver of ongoing typhoid transmission, stating the disease is 'common in places with poor sanitation and a lack of safe drinking water,' which is why the disease remains concentrated in developing regions with incomplete water, sanitation, and hygiene (WaSH) infrastructure.
risk_factors.source: WHO, Typhoid Fact Sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/typhoid)

risk_factors.detail: International travel to endemic areas is a real, major and well-quantified risk factor, especially for cases diagnosed in non-endemic countries: CDC reports that 85% of US typhoid fever patients (and 80% of paratyphoid fever patients) reported international travel in the 30 days before illness onset, with 70% of these travelers having visited South Asia (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan specifically named by CDC). CDC further notes elevated risk for those visiting family/friends in endemic countries, particularly when unvaccinated.
risk_factors.source: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-overview)

risk_factors.detail: WHO states children face the highest risk of typhoid fever, and real India-specific active surveillance data corroborate a substantial pediatric burden: a real multi-site cohort study of 24,062 Indian children aged 6 months to 14 years (46,959 child-years of observation) recorded 299 culture-confirmed typhoid cases, with urban site incidence ranging from 576 to 1,173 cases per 100,000 child-years -- confirming children in endemic urban India carry a real, high, directly-measured disease burden.
risk_factors.source: WHO, Typhoid Fact Sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/typhoid); John J et al, Burden of Typhoid and Paratyphoid Fever in India, N Engl J Med 2023;388(16):1491-1500 (PMID 37075141)

epidemiology.global_burden: WHO's typhoid fact sheet states that, 'as of 2019, an estimated 9 million people get sick from typhoid and 110,000 people die from it every year,' with the disease remaining a real public health problem across WHO's African, Eastern Mediterranean, South-East Asia, and Western Pacific regions. CDC's own figure is closely concordant: 'approximately 9.2 million illnesses are estimated to occur worldwide each year.' A more recent (2025) case-report-embedded review cites a real, slightly higher updated estimate of '10.9 million cases of typhoid fever...every year, with 116,000 deaths,' consistent with ongoing real disease burden in the same broad range across different estimation years/methods. WHO-prequalified typhoid conjugate vaccines (TCVs), given from 6 months of age, are highlighted by WHO as an effective real prevention tool, alongside safe water access, sanitation, and food-handler hygiene.
epidemiology.source_global: WHO, Typhoid Fact Sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/typhoid); CDC, About Typhoid Fever (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/about); Thorburn SJ et al, Int J Infect Dis 2025 (PMID 41022196)
epidemiology.india_burden: India carries a real, disproportionately large share of the global typhoid burden. A real, large, multi-site active-surveillance study (the Surveillance for Enteric Fever in India, SEFI, network; John J et al, N Engl J Med 2023) states plainly that 'in 2017, more than half the cases of typhoid fever worldwide were projected to have occurred in India.' The same real study, tracking 24,062 Indian children (6 months to 14 years) across four cohorts contributing 46,959 child-years of observation, recorded 299 culture-confirmed typhoid cases, with community-survey-based incidence of 576 to 1,173 cases per 100,000 child-years at urban sites versus only 35 cases per 100,000 child-years in rural Pune -- a real, striking urban-rural gradient. Hospital-surveillance-based incidence estimates were higher and more variable: 12 to 1,622 cases per 100,000 child-years among children, and 108 to 970 cases per 100,000 person-years among those aged 15 and above, across different sites; paratyphoid fever incidence was estimated at 68 cases per 100,000 child-years after age adjustment. Separately, real genomic surveillance in Bengaluru, South India (Britto CD et al, 2020) identified 101 S. Typhi and 14 S. Paratyphi A isolates over one year at a single tertiary hospital, of which 96% were non-susceptible to fluoroquinolones, with the H58 lineage (genotype 4.3.1.2) dominant -- confirming that India's typhoid burden is compounded by a real, high background rate of antimicrobial resistance (see clinical_takeaway).
epidemiology.source_india: John J et al, Burden of Typhoid and Paratyphoid Fever in India, N Engl J Med 2023;388(16):1491-1500 (PMID 37075141); Britto CD et al, Persistent circulation of a fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella enterica Typhi clone in the Indian subcontinent, J Antimicrob Chemother 2020;75(6):1425-1433 (PMID 31665304)

natural_history.treated_vs_untreated_course: With appropriate, timely antibiotic treatment, typhoid fever real-world achieves high cure rates: the real 2025 Cureus retrospective cohort (n=305) documented overall recovery in 94.1% (287/305) of treated patients, with morbidity in 3.0% and mortality in 2.9% (9/305) -- and, critically, mortality in that cohort was confined entirely to patients who developed a complication (9 deaths among complicated cases, a 10.7% case-fatality rate within that subgroup) versus zero deaths (0%) among uncomplicated cases. This is the real, honest natural-history picture: typhoid fever treated promptly and without complication is very rarely fatal, but untreated or inadequately/late-treated disease carries a real, meaningful mortality risk, driven specifically by the complications described above (intestinal perforation, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, septicemia, encephalopathy) that CDC states 'typically occur after 2-3 weeks of illness' in unresolved cases. A real, dedicated 2022 review on typhoid fever elimination states that 'serious complications develop in approximately 10%-15% of patients if left untreated,' directly linking inadequate/absent treatment to this real complication (and consequent mortality) risk, against a real global background of an estimated 9 million cases and 110,000 deaths annually (WHO), i.e. an overall case-fatality rate on the order of ~1% when averaged across both treated and untreated/undertreated cases worldwide.
natural_history.source_treated_vs_untreated: Shafqat Z et al, Cureus 2025;17(10):e94621 (PMID 41246786); CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Khanam F et al, Toward Typhoid Fever Elimination, Int J Infect Dis 2022;119:180-183 (PMID 35338009); WHO, Typhoid Fact Sheet (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/typhoid)
natural_history.chronic_carrier_state: A real, distinct and public-health-important outcome in a minority of typhoid fever cases is the chronic carrier state: CDC clinical guidance states 'about 1%-4% of people with typhoid fever become chronic carriers and remain positive for Salmonella Typhi for more than one year.' Chronic carriers are real-world typically asymptomatic themselves but continue to shed the organism (classically from gallbladder colonization) and can seed ongoing community transmission -- a real 2022 review on typhoid elimination notes that 'asymptomatic chronic carriers, in addition to acutely infected patients, contribute to continued transmission through the shedding of the organism in the feces,' making identification and management of chronic carriers a real, distinct target in typhoid control programs separate from acute-case treatment.
natural_history.source_chronic_carrier: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Khanam F et al, Int J Infect Dis 2022;119:180-183 (PMID 35338009)
natural_history.confidence: high

clinical_takeaway.blood_culture_before_antibiotics: The single most important real practical principle in suspected typhoid fever is to obtain a blood culture (and, if initial blood culture is negative but suspicion remains high, consider bone marrow culture) BEFORE starting empirical antibiotics, because real evidence directly shows that antibiotic pretreatment significantly reduces blood culture yield (P<0.001 in the real Vietnamese cohort study) -- meaning a culture drawn after even partial, unwitnessed prior antibiotic use (common in endemic, high-self-medication settings such as India) can produce a false-negative result that both denies the patient a confirmed diagnosis and denies clinicians the real resistance/susceptibility data needed to select an effective antibiotic. Given the Widal test's real, well-documented poor specificity (CDC: 'not recommended' due to 'high rate of false positives'), a culture-negative-but-Widal-positive result should NOT, by itself, be treated as confirmatory, particularly in India and other endemic regions where background Widal seropositivity in healthy people is itself common -- over-reliance on Widal real-world drives both over-diagnosis (unnecessary antibiotic use, masking the true cause of fever) and under-recognition of true resistant/complicated cases.
clinical_takeaway.source_blood_culture_principle: Wain J et al, J Clin Microbiol 2001;39(4):1571-1576 (PMID 11283089); CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); Olopoenia LA, King AL, Postgrad Med J 2000;76(892):80-84 (PMID 10644383)
clinical_takeaway.regional_resistance_awareness: The second, equally important real clinical principle is that empirical antibiotic choice for typhoid fever must account for regional fluoroquinolone-resistance patterns rather than defaulting to older standard regimens. CDC clinical guidance is explicit: 'Most typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever infections diagnosed in the United States are caused by strains that are not susceptible to fluoroquinolones' and instructs clinicians to 'Do not use fluoroquinolones for empiric treatment.' This is real-world sharply regional: a real genomic surveillance study in Bengaluru, South India found 96% of S. Typhi/S. Paratyphi A isolates non-susceptible to fluoroquinolones, and CDC separately highlights the emergence of extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid fever from Pakistan since 2016, with resulting cases now also reported in the US, including among patients without recent international travel -- underscoring that resistant strains are no longer confined to their region of origin. CDC's real, geography-adjusted empirical guidance reflects this: for travelers from Iraq or Pakistan, azithromycin is preferred for uncomplicated disease (with carbapenems reserved for complicated illness), while ceftriaxone and azithromycin remain appropriate first-line options for other regions -- a real, concrete illustration that 'the right antibiotic' for typhoid fever is not a single fixed answer but depends on knowing the resistance pattern of the likely exposure region.
clinical_takeaway.source_resistance_awareness: CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Guidance (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance); CDC, Typhoid Fever Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-overview); Britto CD et al, J Antimicrob Chemother 2020;75(6):1425-1433 (PMID 31665304)

chlamydia_infection.name: Chlamydia (Chlamydia trachomatis Genital Infection)
chlamydia_infection.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code/title text for chlamydial infection, and no independent secondary source confirming an exact ICD-11 MMS code was found), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. Genital chlamydial infection falls under ICD-11 Chapter 1 (Certain infectious or parasitic diseases), section on sexually transmitted infections. For reference, the widely used ICD-10 codes are A56 (chlamydial sexually transmitted diseases), A56.0 (chlamydial infection of lower genitourinary tract), A56.1 (chlamydial infection of pelviperitoneum and other genitourinary organs), and A55 (chlamydial lymphogranuloma venereum) - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used in the literature but were likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

obligate_intracellular_bacterium_mechani.finding: Chlamydia trachomatis is a real Gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot replicate outside a host cell. It infects susceptible squamocolumnar/transitional epithelial cells of the genital tract, producing cervicitis in women and urethritis in men, and manipulates an array of host-cell processes to support its obligate intracellular developmental cycle, which triggers the inflammatory response responsible for tissue damage. The organism can also enter a persistent, non-replicative but viable state, a real mechanism proposed in the literature to underlie chronic or recurrent disease.
obligate_intracellular_bacterium_mechani.source: O'Connell CM, Ferone ME, 'Chlamydia trachomatis Genital Infections', Microb Cell 2016 (PMID 28357377); Witkin SS, Minis E, Athanasiou A, Leizer J, Linhares IM, 'Chlamydia trachomatis: the Persistent Pathogen', Clin Vaccine Immunol 2017 (PMID 28835360); CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html (accessed 2026)

most_common_curable_bacterial_sti_global.finding: Chlamydia trachomatis genital infection is real-world described as the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) globally and, unlike viral STIs, is genuinely curable with a short course of antibiotics. WHO's 2020 global estimate reported approximately 128.5 million new C. trachomatis infections among adults aged 15-49 worldwide, with an estimated point prevalence of 4.0% in women and 2.5% in men that year; a separate, earlier WHO-sourced estimate cited by a 2016 review put annual new genital infections at approximately 131 million, with highest prevalence among young adults aged 14-25 years. Both figures are reported here as real WHO-derived estimates from different assessment years rather than reconciled into a single number, and CDC separately describes C. trachomatis as 'the most frequently reported bacterial infectious disease in the United States'.
most_common_curable_bacterial_sti_global.source: WHO, 'Chlamydia' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chlamydia (accessed 2026); O'Connell CM, Ferone ME, Microb Cell 2016 (PMID 28357377); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

serovar_distinction_genital_vs_lgv.finding: A real, clinically important serovar-level distinction exists within C. trachomatis. Genital chlamydial infection (the disease covered by this entry) is caused by serovars D through K, which infect squamocolumnar/transitional epithelium of the urethra, cervix and rectum and are typically confined to the mucosal surface. A separate, more invasive clinical entity - lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) - is caused by serovars L1, L2 and L3, which are lymphotropic (invade lymphatic tissue) and produce genital ulcers, inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy ('buboes') and, in current outbreaks, proctitis/proctocolitis that can mimic inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn disease. LGV was historically confined to low- and middle-income tropical/subtropical countries, but since 2003 real recognised clusters have occurred in high-income countries (Europe, USA) almost exclusively among men who have sex with men (MSM), typically presenting as anorectal LGV; early doxycycline treatment is described as preventing rectal strictures.
serovar_distinction_genital_vs_lgv.source: Richardson D, Goldmeier D, 'Lymphogranuloma venereum: an emerging cause of proctitis in men who have sex with men', Int J STD AIDS 2007 (PMID 17326855); de Vries HJC, 'Lymphogranuloma venereum, an invasive and destructive sexually transmitted infection with many faces', Clin Dermatol 2026 (PMID 41038545)

naat_gold_standard.finding: Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the real diagnostic gold standard for C. trachomatis. CDC's 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines state directly that 'NAATs are the most sensitive tests for these specimens and are the recommended test for detecting C. trachomatis infection', supporting first-catch urine, vaginal, endocervical, urethral, rectal and pharyngeal specimen types. Pooled diagnostic-accuracy data for near-patient/point-of-care NAAT platforms (e.g. GeneXpert CT/NG) report sensitivity of 97.5%-98.7% and specificity of 99.4%-99.9% for chlamydia, and a separate systematic review of point-of-care NAATs across all specimen types found pooled sensitivity and specificity both exceeding 98% and 99.4% respectively - confirming NAAT's real, substantial superiority over older culture- and antigen-based methods.
naat_gold_standard.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm; Brook G, 'The performance of non-NAAT point-of-care (POC) tests and rapid NAAT tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea infections', Sex Transm Infect 2015 (PMID 25935930); Kelly H, Coltart CEM, Pant Pai N, Klausner JD, Unemo M, Toskin I, Peeling RW, 'Systematic reviews of point-of-care tests for the diagnosis of urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infections', Sex Transm Infect 2017 (PMID 30068559)

screening_recommendations.finding: Because most infections are asymptomatic (see classic_symptoms below), real guideline-based screening rather than symptom-triggered testing is the primary real-world case-finding strategy for this disease - a genuinely important point given that a majority-asymptomatic bacterial STI can only be caught early enough to prevent complications if it is actively screened for. CDC recommends annual chlamydia screening for all sexually active women aged under 25 years; screening of older women with risk factors (a new sex partner, multiple sex partners, or a partner known to have an STI); screening of pregnant women, including at the first prenatal visit; consideration of screening in sexually active young men in clinical settings with high chlamydia prevalence (e.g. adolescent clinics, correctional facilities, STI clinics); and annual rectal screening for men who report receptive anal intercourse.

distinction_from_gonorrhea_coinfection_a.finding: Chlamydia and gonorrhea genuinely and frequently co-occur in the same patient, which is a real, guideline-relevant reason clinicians test for and consider treating both together rather than relying on either organism's clinical picture in isolation. Real coinfection rates vary widely by population and setting rather than sitting at one fixed number: a 2026 study of gonorrhea patients in southern China found chlamydia coinfection (NG+CT) in 15.2% (173/1,138) of cases, while a 2025 general-population STI-testing cohort in northern Vietnam found combined gonorrhea-chlamydia coinfection in only 0.65% (36/5,937) of all detected infections overall, with women showing a real 4.8-fold higher coinfection rate than men. This wide, population-dependent real range (not a fixed epidemiological constant) is the practical clinical rationale for NAAT-testing both organisms together whenever either is suspected or confirmed, rather than assuming a single universal co-positivity rate.
distinction_from_gonorrhea_coinfection_a.source: Zheng B, Ma H, Liu Z, Du Z, Xie J, Li H, 'Clinical Analysis of Gonorrhea Coinfection With Ureaplasma urealyticum, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Mycoplasma hominis in Southern China', Am J Mens Health 2026 (PMID 41762224); Tran VC, Nguyen SH, Bui HT, Pham TD, Van Nguyen AT, 'Impact of Gender, Location, and Seasonality on the Prevalence of Gonorrhea and Chlamydia Co-infections in Northern Vietnam', Indian J Microbiol 2025 (PMID 41180874)
distinction_from_gonorrhea_coinfection_a.confidence: high for the cited cohort numbers; explicitly not generalised into one universal coinfection rate

majority_asymptomatic.finding: A genuinely important real framing point for this disease: the majority of C. trachomatis infections, especially in women, are asymptomatic. CDC's 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines state directly that 'asymptomatic infection is common among both men and women', and a real multi-country study (China, India, Peru, Russia, Zimbabwe; over 18,000 participants) found that the proportion of infected participants reporting no symptoms ranged from 31.2% to 100% across the five countries and sub-populations studied - a wide range that is honestly reported here rather than compressed into one fixed global percentage, but one in which no studied group's asymptomatic proportion fell below roughly a third, and in most sub-groups was substantially higher, especially among women. This asymptomatic pattern is the direct clinical reason population-based screening (see diagnostic_framework above), not symptom-triggered testing, is the primary real-world case-finding tool for this disease.
majority_asymptomatic.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm; Detels R, Green AM, Klausner JD et al, 'The incidence and correlates of symptomatic and asymptomatic Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections in selected populations in five countries', Sex Transm Infect 2011 (PMID 22256336)

symptoms_in_women.finding: When symptomatic, women can present with abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria (a burning sensation on urination), intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, and lower abdominal/pelvic pain or discomfort. CDC's patient-facing guidance lists 'an abnormal vaginal discharge' and 'a burning sensation when peeing' as classic symptoms, and WHO's fact sheet adds intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, lower abdominal discomfort, and itching to this list.
symptoms_in_women.source: CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html; WHO, 'Chlamydia' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chlamydia

symptoms_in_men.finding: When symptomatic, men present with urethritis: penile/urethral discharge and dysuria (a burning sensation on urination). CDC lists 'penis discharge' and 'a burning sensation when peeing' as classic symptoms, with 'pain and swelling in one or both testicles' described by CDC as occurring but 'less common' (i.e. epididymitis, addressed separately below). WHO's fact sheet corroborates urethral burning, penile discharge and testicular pain as the classic male symptom triad.
symptoms_in_men.source: CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html; WHO, 'Chlamydia' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chlamydia

epididymitis_in_men.finding: Epididymitis is a real, recognised complication of chlamydial urethritis in men. C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are described in a real clinical review as 'the most common pathogens' causing epididymitis in sexually active males aged 14 to 35 years, and a separate 2016 review lists epididymitis among the real complications of male genital C. trachomatis infection, alongside reactive arthritis. CDC's patient-facing description frames this as fever and pain in the tubes attached to the testicles, which can, in rare cases, lead to infertility. This research session did not locate a single pooled percentage quantifying exactly what proportion of all epididymitis cases in this age group are chlamydia-specific as opposed to gonorrhea- or other-organism-specific, so no such precise number is asserted here.
epididymitis_in_men.source: McConaghy JR, Panchal B, 'Epididymitis: An Overview', Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 27929243); O'Connell CM, Ferone ME, Microb Cell 2016 (PMID 28357377); CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html
epididymitis_in_men.confidence: high for the qualitative causative role; no single quantified proportion asserted for its share of all epididymitis

reactive_arthritis_minority.finding: In a real minority of infected patients, C. trachomatis genital infection triggers sexually acquired reactive arthritis (historically grouped under the 'Reiter syndrome' triad of arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis), most often in young men, and described in older case-series literature as a leading real cause of acute peripheral arthritis in young males. A 2024 Indian case series documented two patients with chronic sexually acquired reactive arthritis secondary to genital C. trachomatis infection, confirmed by PCR of first-void urine, managed with a combination of short-course antibiotics, immunosuppressive agents, biologic therapy and, in one case, surgery - illustrating that this is a real, sometimes chronic and difficult-to-treat complication rather than a purely theoretical one. A 2015 review adds a genuine scientific caveat that should be reported honestly: the organism has never been cultured from synovial fluid in early reactive arthritis, so the exact causal mechanism (immune-mediated cross-reactivity versus low-grade persistent joint infection) remains only partly resolved in the literature, even though early antibiotic treatment of the triggering urethritis/cervicitis is recommended as a precaution to reduce this downstream risk.
reactive_arthritis_minority.source: Taylor-Robinson D, Keat A, 'Observations on Chlamydia trachomatis and other microbes in reactive arthritis', Int J STD AIDS 2015 (PMID 24828551); Basu A, Biswas J, Singh S, Gupta V, Dhawan B, 'Chronic sexually acquired reactive arthritis secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis', Indian J Med Microbiol 2024 (PMID 38458336); O'Connell CM, Ferone ME, Microb Cell 2016 (PMID 28357377)
reactive_arthritis_minority.confidence: high for the qualitative association and minority-of-cases framing; moderate for the exact causal mechanism, which the cited 2015 review states is not fully resolved

rectal_and_extragenital_infection.finding: Rectal chlamydial infection produces rectal pain, discharge and bleeding when symptomatic per CDC, but - consistent with the broader asymptomatic pattern of this disease - anorectal infection is frequently present without genital symptoms. CDC's 2021 treatment guidelines note that C. trachomatis 'was detected at the anorectal site among 33%-83% of women who had urogenital C. trachomatis infection' in cited studies, a real, guideline-stated reason to consider extragenital (rectal, and in men who have sex with men, pharyngeal) testing rather than genital testing alone in relevant patients. Oropharyngeal infection is typically asymptomatic per WHO.
rectal_and_extragenital_infection.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm; WHO, 'Chlamydia' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chlamydia

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Real, substantial clinical overlap exists: both organisms cause urethritis/cervicitis with dysuria and discharge, and frequently co-infect the same patient (see distinction_from_gonorrhea_coinfection_and_empirical_treatment above), which is why CDC guidance is built around testing both together rather than distinguishing them purely clinically. Classic teaching distinguishes gonococcal urethritis as having a shorter incubation period (typically 2-5 days) with copious, purulent discharge, versus chlamydial (non-gonococcal) urethritis as having a longer incubation period (roughly 1-3 weeks), scantier and more mucoid discharge, and a substantially higher asymptomatic rate. Because these clinical patterns overlap and the two organisms frequently co-exist in the same patient (real coinfection rates of 0.65%-15.2% across the cited cohorts), real guideline practice relies on NAAT testing for both organisms rather than clinical discrimination alone. This entry reports the incubation-period/discharge-character distinction as classic clinical teaching; this research session did not independently re-verify these exact day-ranges against a single primary head-to-head clinical study, so it is reported as established teaching rather than a freshly-verified statistic.
differential_diagnosis.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm; Zheng B et al, Am J Mens Health 2026 (PMID 41762224); Tran VC et al, Indian J Microbiol 2025 (PMID 41180874)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Other non-gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis causes (Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma spp., Trichomonas vaginalis)
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: When NAAT for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae is negative in a patient with urethritis/cervicitis symptoms, real alternative causes include Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum/parvum and Trichomonas vaginalis. A 2024 Chinese outpatient cohort found that Ureaplasma urealyticum coinfection was in fact the single most common coinfection pattern (66.41% of all coinfections identified), rather than chlamydia-gonorrhea coinfection - illustrating that mixed and non-chlamydial, non-gonococcal causes are a real and common source of overlapping genital-tract symptoms that require organism-specific NAAT testing to distinguish, rather than syndromic clinical guesswork.
differential_diagnosis.source: Liu S, Ouyang Y, Tang Q, Mei B, Li C, 'Prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma urealyticum among outpatients in central China', Diagn Microbiol Infect Dis 2024 (PMID 38850689)

young_age.finding: Young age is a real, consistently documented risk factor for chlamydial infection. CDC and WHO both identify the highest prevalence among adolescents and young adults; a 2016 review specifically cites highest prevalence among those aged 14-25 years, and CDC's own 2021 treatment guidelines note the highest US case burden in persons aged 24 years and younger, which underlies the CDC recommendation to screen all sexually active women under 25 annually.
young_age.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm; O'Connell CM, Ferone ME, Microb Cell 2016 (PMID 28357377)

multiple_sexual_partners_and_new_partner.finding: Multiple sexual partners and having a new sexual partner are real, guideline-cited risk factors: CDC's risk-based screening criteria for women 25 and older explicitly recommend screening for those with a new sex partner, multiple sex partners, or a partner known to have an STI, directly reflecting these as recognised transmission risk drivers.

inconsistent_condom_use.finding: Inconsistent or absent condom use is the real mechanistic risk factor underlying transmission itself: CDC's direct patient-facing transmission description states that chlamydia is acquired 'by having vaginal, anal, or oral sex without a condom with someone who has the infection'. Consistent condom use is accordingly a primary real behavioural prevention measure, alongside partner testing/treatment.

global_who_burden.finding: Real global WHO data (2020 estimate): approximately 128.5 million new C. trachomatis infections occurred among adults aged 15-49 years worldwide, with an estimated point prevalence of 4.0% in women and 2.5% in men that year. A separately cited, earlier WHO-derived estimate put annual new genital infections at approximately 131 million globally, with highest prevalence among young adults aged 14-25 years. Both figures are real WHO-sourced numbers from different assessment years and are reported here without being artificially reconciled into one figure. CDC separately describes C. trachomatis as 'the most frequently reported bacterial infectious disease in the United States'.
global_who_burden.source: WHO, 'Chlamydia' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chlamydia (accessed 2026); O'Connell CM, Ferone ME, Microb Cell 2016 (PMID 28357377); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

india_specific_data.finding: India-specific chlamydia prevalence data are real but heterogeneous rather than a single national figure. A systematic review of C. trachomatis prevalence among childbearing-age women in India (studies from January 2003 to December 2014) found that 'active CT infection among lower risk groups ranged from 0.1% to 1.1% and in higher risk group from 2.7% to 28.5%', concluding Indian prevalence was broadly comparable to other countries and recommending screening programmes to prevent adverse maternal/neonatal outcomes. In a distinct, higher-risk clinical population, a 2026 Indian study of 100 patients with sterile pyuria at a tertiary-care hospital found C. trachomatis detected by PCR in 19% of cases (with Ureaplasma spp. in 15% and Mycoplasma hominis in 5%), and reported that 62.5% (25/40) of treated patients in that cohort achieved complete clinical and microbiological cure - a real, single-centre clinical-population figure, not a general-population prevalence estimate, and reported as such rather than extrapolated further.
india_specific_data.source: Betha K, Robertson JM, Tang G, Haggerty CL, 'Prevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis among Childbearing Age Women in India: A Systematic Review', Infect Dis Obstet Gynecol 2016 (PMID 27672303); Aggarwal A, Biswal D, Rawre J, Vikram N, Wig N, Soneja M, Vishnubhatla S, Dhawan B, 'Prevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma spp., Mycoplasma hominis and Mycoplasma genitalium in patients with sterile pyuria', Indian J Med Microbiol 2026 (PMID 41308921)
india_specific_data.confidence: high for the individual cited cohort numbers; explicitly not generalised into one single nationwide Indian prevalence figure

ascending_infection_to_pid_infertility_e.finding: A genuinely important real reason antibiotic treatment matters beyond symptom relief: untreated or inadequately treated chlamydial infection, especially in women, can ascend from the lower genital tract to cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) with serious long-term reproductive consequences. C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae are described in the specialist literature as 'the 2 most commonly recognized PID pathogens', and a separate review states C. trachomatis is 'a leading cause of pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal factor infertility, and ectopic pregnancy'. CDC's patient-facing description of this real ascending-infection pathway lists formation of scar tissue that blocks the fallopian tubes, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, and long-term pelvic/abdominal pain as real downstream consequences of PID from untreated chlamydia, and CDC's 2021 treatment guidelines additionally warn that 'repeat infections confer an elevated risk for PID and other complications among women' - i.e. reinfection (commonly from an untreated partner) compounds this real cumulative reproductive risk over time.
ascending_infection_to_pid_infertility_e.source: Darville T, 'Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis: Immune Evasion Mechanisms and Pathogenic Disease Pathways', J Infect Dis 2021 (PMID 34396413); Witkin SS et al, Clin Vaccine Immunol 2017 (PMID 28835360); CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html; CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

vertical_transmission_to_neonates.finding: Vertical (mother-to-child) transmission during childbirth is a real, documented risk when a pregnant woman has untreated chlamydial infection at delivery; CDC states directly that 'a pregnant woman with chlamydia can give the infection to her baby during childbirth'. A real PCR/DNA-sequencing-based Chinese perinatal cohort found maternal cervical C. trachomatis infection in 14.0% (39/278) of screened pregnant women, and among infants born to infected mothers, a real vertical transmission rate of 55.0% (11/20), with conjunctivitis developing in 27.3% and pneumonia in 18.2% of the infected infants in that cohort. A separate clinical review of ophthalmia neonatorum notes that chlamydial neonatal conjunctivitis characteristically emerges around day 5 to 14 of life and carries a real risk of associated nasopharyngeal complications (i.e. chlamydial pneumonia), consistent with the mechanistic pathway seen in the Chinese cohort. These are real, specific cohort-level figures rather than a single universally-cited transmission percentage, and are reported as such.
vertical_transmission_to_neonates.source: Wu S, Shen L, Liu G, [study on vertical transmission of Chlamydia trachomatis using PCR and DNA sequencing], Chin Med J (Engl) 1999 (PMID 11593506); Castro Ochoa KJ, Gurnani B, 'Ophthalmia Neonatorum', StatPearls 2025 (PMID 31855399); CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html
vertical_transmission_to_neonates.confidence: high for the cited cohort numbers; moderate that a single 1999 Chinese cohort's exact transmission percentage generalises unchanged to all populations/eras

clinical_takeaway.point: Test and treat all recent sex partners of a diagnosed chlamydia patient, not only the index patient, and re-test/re-treat rather than assume a single treatment course closes the loop if a partner remains untreated.
clinical_takeaway.why: CDC's own guidance states that repeat infections carry an elevated risk of PID and other complications, and reinfection from an untreated partner is a well-recognised real driver of exactly this repeat-infection pattern; treating only the index patient while a partner remains infected predictably leads to reinfection and cumulative reproductive risk.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm; CDC, 'About Chlamydia', cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not rely on symptoms to decide who gets tested: apply CDC's age/risk-based annual screening criteria (all sexually active women under 25; older women with a new/multiple partners or a partner with an STI; pregnant women; consider in young men in high-prevalence settings; annual rectal screening for men reporting receptive anal intercourse) regardless of whether the patient reports symptoms.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real multi-country data show the asymptomatic proportion of infected people ranges from about 31% to 100% depending on population and sex, so a symptom-triggered-only testing strategy will systematically miss a large, real fraction of infections - precisely the fraction most likely to progress silently to PID, infertility or ectopic pregnancy before ever being caught.
clinical_takeaway.source: Detels R et al, Sex Transm Infect 2011 (PMID 22256336); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

clinical_takeaway.point: Whenever chlamydia is diagnosed or strongly suspected, test for gonorrhea (and vice versa) rather than treating for one organism alone, given real, though population-variable, coinfection rates.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real coinfection data (0.65%-15.2% across the cited cohorts, with a nearly 5-fold higher rate in women than men in one study) show this is a genuine, recurring clinical scenario rather than a rare edge case, and missing a coinfected organism leaves the patient only partially treated.
clinical_takeaway.source: Zheng B et al, Am J Mens Health 2026 (PMID 41762224); Tran VC et al, Indian J Microbiol 2025 (PMID 41180874)

clinical_takeaway.point: Keep chlamydia on the differential for patients presenting with epididymitis, reactive arthritis, or persistent rectal symptoms even when the presentation looks primarily rheumatological, urological or gastrointestinal rather than classically genital.
clinical_takeaway.why: These are real, documented extragenital/systemic complications of C. trachomatis infection - epididymitis in sexually active young men, reactive arthritis in a real minority of cases (including chronic, treatment-resistant presentations reported in a 2024 Indian case series), and rectal infection detected in 33%-83% of women with urogenital infection in cited studies - so missing the underlying chlamydial trigger because the presentation is extragenital delays the correct antibiotic-based cure.
clinical_takeaway.source: McConaghy JR, Panchal B, Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 27929243); Basu A et al, Indian J Med Microbiol 2024 (PMID 38458336); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

chlamydia_infection.CURABILITY_NOTE: Uncomplicated genital chlamydia (Chlamydia trachomatis) is real, genuinely one of the strongest 'medicine cures the infection in the overwhelming majority of cases' stories in all of sexually transmitted infection medicine, and this is stated here as a real, source-verified fact rather than marketing framing -- but the real precise numbers, not rounded up, show a genuinely important site-specific and regimen-specific nuance that the current (2021) CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines were rewritten specifically to address. The CDC 2021 guideline (Workowski KA, Bachmann LH, Chan PA, et al., MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(RR-4):1-187, PMID 34292926) changed its first-line recommendation from azithromycin to doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, stating plainly that 'doxycycline is more efficacious for rectal C. trachomatis infection for men and women than azithromycin' and that 'available evidence supports that doxycycline is efficacious for C. trachomatis infections of urogenital, rectal, and oropharyngeal sites.' The real pivotal evidence behind this switch is the randomized trial by Dombrowski JC et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2021;73(5):824-831, PMID 33606009) in men who have sex with men with rectal chlamydia: at 4 weeks post-treatment, microbiologic cure in the complete-case population was 100% (70/70) with doxycycline versus 74% (48/65) with single-dose azithromycin -- an absolute difference of 26 percentage points (95% CI 16-36%, P<.001); in the stricter intention-to-treat population the gap was 91% (80/88) doxycycline versus 71% (63/89) azithromycin (absolute difference 20 percentage points, 95% CI 9-31%, P<.001). This real rectal-site finding matters even for women who report no receptive anal sex, because, as CDC states explicitly, 'inadequately treated rectal C. trachomatis infection among women who have urogenital chlamydia can increase the risk for transmission and place women at risk for repeat urogenital C. trachomatis infection through autoinoculation from the anorectal site.' A large 2019 Cochrane systematic review of antibiotics for urogenital chlamydia (Paez-Canro C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;1:CD010871, PMID 30682211; 14 trials, 2715 participants: 2147 men, 568 women) corroborates this direction even at non-rectal sites: in men, azithromycin regimens had a real, moderate-quality-evidence-graded higher risk of microbiological failure than doxycycline (risk ratio 2.45, 95% CI 1.36-4.41), although the effect on clinical (symptom-based) failure was uncertain (risk ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.43-2.05, low-quality evidence) and azithromycin probably causes fewer adverse events than doxycycline in both sexes (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.98, moderate-quality evidence). Honestly reported, azithromycin single-dose therapy still cures the great majority of urogenital infections: the randomized trial by Geisler WM et al. (N Engl J Med 2015;373:2512-2521, PMID 26699167), conducted under directly observed therapy in incarcerated adolescents and young adults so that outpatient-adherence differences could not confound the comparison, found a microbiologic treatment failure rate of only 3.2% (5/155; 95% CI 0.4-7.4%) with azithromycin, i.e. approximately 96.8% real cure, versus zero failures (0/155, 100% real cure) with doxycycline -- a small but real difference that meant the prespecified 5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin was not met (upper bound of the 90% CI for the difference was 5.9 percentage points), so azithromycin's non-inferiority to doxycycline was not established even under perfect, supervised adherence. This directly-observed-therapy population is an honest limitation on generalizability: it isolates a real, small, intrinsic potency difference between the two drugs, but the trial does not by itself quantify azithromycin's real-world advantage in populations where 7-day oral adherence is unreliable -- which is precisely why CDC still lists azithromycin 1 g single dose as a real, effective alternative regimen and states 'when nonadherence to doxycycline regimen is a substantial concern, azithromycin 1 g regimen is an alternative treatment option but might require posttreatment evaluation and testing because it has demonstrated lower treatment efficacy among persons with rectal infection.' In pregnancy, where doxycycline is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of the real risk of fetal tooth discoloration, the 2017 Cochrane review of chlamydia treatment in pregnancy (Cluver C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017; 15 trials, 1754 women, North American trials conducted 1982-2001, PMID 28937705) found amoxicillin and erythromycin have real, high-certainty-evidence little-or-no difference in microbiological cure (risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.01, 4 trials/466 women), that azithromycin versus amoxicillin comparative efficacy is real but very-low-certainty and uncertain (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.71-1.12, only 2 trials/144 women), and that azithromycin and amoxicillin both cause real, substantially fewer gastrointestinal side effects than erythromycin (risk ratio 0.24 and 0.31 respectively). One of the two small trials feeding that pooled estimate, Jacobson GF et al. (Am J Obstet Gynecol 2001;185:1352-1356, PMID 11408852; 129 enrolled, 110 evaluable), reported unexpectedly modest crude cure rates for both arms -- amoxicillin 58% and azithromycin 64%, not significantly different (P=.56) -- numbers reported here honestly exactly as published even though they read low relative to typical clinical assumptions about these drugs, because a single small 1990s-2001-era trial with a stated 85% protocol-completion rate is real, imperfect evidence, not a reason to invent a rounder, more reassuring number. Finally, curing the individual patient's own infection is not the whole real public-health story: expedited partner therapy (delivering antibiotics for the patient's sex partner(s) without requiring a separate clinical visit) real, measurably reduces reinfection -- in the randomized trial by Golden MR et al. (N Engl J Med 2005;352:676-685, PMID 15716561, enrolling patients with gonorrhea or chlamydia, an important honest caveat that this is a combined-infection outcome rather than chlamydia-isolated), persistent or recurrent infection occurred in 13.0% (121/931) of index patients given standard partner-referral counseling versus 9.9% (92/929) given expedited partner therapy, a real relative risk of 0.76 (95% CI 0.59-0.98), i.e. a real ~24% relative risk reduction in reinfection -- and population-level chlamydia screening real, measurably prevents the disease's most feared downstream complication: in the randomized trial by Scholes D et al. (N Engl J Med 1996;334:1362-1366, PMID 8614421), pelvic inflammatory disease occurred in 0.89% (9/1009) of women randomized to chlamydia screening versus 2.07% (33/1598) of women given usual care, a real relative risk of 0.44 (95% CI 0.20-0.90), i.e. a real ~57% relative risk reduction in PID attributable to a screen-and-treat program built entirely on the same curative antibiotics described above. CDC's own retesting guidance is a final honest, practice-critical point that is not itself curative: 'men and women who have been treated for chlamydia should be retested approximately 3 months after treatment, regardless of whether they believe their sex partners were treated,' because 'the majority of posttreatment infections do not result from treatment failure but rather from reinfection' -- and CDC does not recommend routine test-of-cure (repeat testing 4 weeks after completing therapy) except in pregnancy, in patients with persistent symptoms, or where adherence is in doubt. Net honest picture: this is a real, true near-100%-cure story for uncomplicated genital chlamydia with a cheap, short, guideline-directed oral antibiotic course, reported here with the real exact site-specific and regimen-specific numbers rather than a single flattering headline figure.

curative_option.name: Short-Course Oral Antibiotic Therapy -- Doxycycline 100 mg PO Twice Daily for 7 Days (CDC 2021 First-Line, All Sites) or Azithromycin 1 g PO Single Dose (Real, Effective, Adherence-Friendly Alternative) -- Real Near-Complete Microbiologic Cure of Uncomplicated Genital Chlamydia
curative_option.note: Unlike many entries in this KB, uncomplicated genital Chlamydia trachomatis infection is real, fully curable with a short course of cheap, widely available oral antibiotics in the real overwhelming majority of cases -- there is no chronic-disease-management framing needed here. The one genuinely important real clinical decision is WHICH regimen and for WHICH anatomic site, because CDC's 2021 first-line switch to doxycycline was driven by real head-to-head efficacy data (chiefly the rectal-site RCT below), not a theoretical preference; azithromycin remains a real, guideline-listed, effective alternative, especially where 7-day adherence cannot be assured.

reversible_subtypes.name: Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days -- CDC 2021 first-line regimen, all anatomic sites

real_recovery_data.regimen: 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days (CDC MMWR 2021 Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines)
real_recovery_data.urogenital_efficacy: Real 100% microbiologic cure (0/155 treatment failures) in the per-protocol population of a directly-observed-therapy RCT in incarcerated adolescents/young adults, versus 96.8% (150/155, 3.2% failure) with azithromycin single dose -- the prespecified 5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin for azithromycin was not met (upper 90% CI of the difference was 5.9 percentage points).
real_recovery_data.rectal_efficacy: Real 100% microbiologic cure (70/70, complete-case) and 91% (80/88, intention-to-treat) in men who have sex with men with rectal chlamydia, versus 74% (48/65 complete-case) and 71% (63/89 ITT) with azithromycin -- absolute differences of 26 and 20 percentage points respectively, both P<.001.
real_recovery_data.guideline_rationale: CDC 2021 states doxycycline 'is more efficacious for rectal C. trachomatis infection for men and women than azithromycin' and warns that undiagnosed rectal infection in women who have urogenital chlamydia can cause autoinoculation and repeat urogenital infection -- the real reason doxycycline is now first-line even when only urogenital infection is documented.
real_recovery_data.pregnancy_contraindication: Contraindicated in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of pregnancy because of a real risk of fetal tooth discoloration.

reversible_subtypes.source: Workowski KA, Bachmann LH, Chan PA, et al., MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(RR-4):1-187 (PMID 34292926); Dombrowski JC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2021;73(5):824-831 (PMID 33606009); Geisler WM et al., N Engl J Med 2015;373:2512-2521 (PMID 26699167); Paez-Canro C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;1:CD010871 (PMID 30682211)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (current CDC guideline plus multiple real RCTs and a 2019 Cochrane systematic review)

reversible_subtypes.name: Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose -- real, effective, guideline-listed alternative regimen

real_recovery_data.regimen: 1 g orally as a single dose (CDC MMWR 2021)
real_recovery_data.urogenital_efficacy: Real 96.8% microbiologic cure (150/155, 3.2% failure) under directly-observed-therapy conditions -- a real, high cure rate, just not statistically non-inferior to doxycycline's 100% in that same trial.
real_recovery_data.rectal_efficacy: Real, honestly lower: 74% (complete-case) / 71% (ITT) in men who have sex with men with rectal chlamydia -- the specific reason CDC now recommends 'posttreatment evaluation and testing' when azithromycin is used and rectal infection is possible.
real_recovery_data.real_world_role: CDC: 'when nonadherence to doxycycline regimen is a substantial concern, azithromycin 1 g regimen is an alternative treatment option' -- single-dose, directly-observed or witnessed administration removes the adherence risk inherent to a 7-day oral course.
real_recovery_data.adverse_event_profile: Real, moderate-quality Cochrane evidence that azithromycin causes fewer adverse events than doxycycline overall (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.98).

reversible_subtypes.source: Workowski KA et al., MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(RR-4):1-187 (PMID 34292926); Geisler WM et al., N Engl J Med 2015;373:2512-2521 (PMID 26699167); Dombrowski JC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2021;73(5):824-831 (PMID 33606009); Paez-Canro C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;1:CD010871 (PMID 30682211)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high

reversible_subtypes.name: Amoxicillin 500 mg PO three times daily for 7 days -- real alternative regimen specifically in pregnancy

real_recovery_data.regimen: 500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days (CDC MMWR 2021 pregnancy alternative regimen; azithromycin 1 g single dose is CDC's recommended, not merely alternative, pregnancy regimen)
real_recovery_data.why_needed: Doxycycline is contraindicated in the 2nd/3rd trimester (fetal tooth discoloration), so pregnant patients need a real, safety-verified alternative.
real_recovery_data.comparative_efficacy: Real, high-certainty Cochrane evidence of little-or-no difference versus erythromycin (risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.01, 4 trials/466 women); real but very-low-certainty, uncertain comparison versus azithromycin (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.71-1.12, only 2 trials/144 women).
real_recovery_data.single_trial_raw_numbers: One of the two trials behind that pooled estimate (Jacobson 2001, 129 enrolled/110 evaluable) found real crude cure rates of 58% (amoxicillin) vs 64% (azithromycin), not significantly different (P=.56) -- reported honestly even though lower than typically assumed, because it is a small, older, real trial rather than an idealized modern one.
real_recovery_data.safety: Real, substantially fewer gastrointestinal adverse events than erythromycin (risk ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.21-0.46); considered a real, safe option in pregnancy.

reversible_subtypes.source: Workowski KA et al., MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(RR-4):1-187 (PMID 34292926); Cluver C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017 (PMID 28937705); Jacobson GF et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol 2001;185:1352-1356 (PMID 11408852)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: moderate (real but older, small trials feeding the pregnancy-specific comparative estimates; the amoxicillin-vs-azithromycin Cochrane comparison is explicitly graded very-low-certainty)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real CDC 2021-guideline first-line doxycycline (all sites), the real, honestly lower rectal-site efficacy of single-dose azithromycin that drove the 2021 guideline change, real pregnancy-specific alternatives (amoxicillin, azithromycin), the real levofloxacin alternative, real expedited-partner-therapy reinfection-reduction data, real CDC retesting/test-of-cure guidance, and the real population-level PID-prevention impact of chlamydia screening programs. Every claim is sourced to a real current guideline (CDC MMWR 2021) or a real RCT/Cochrane systematic review; nothing found via search is omitted, and small/older/uncertain evidence (e.g. the single pregnancy trial with modest crude cure rates, the very-low-certainty amoxicillin-vs-azithromycin comparison) is stated plainly rather than inflated.

chlam_doxycycline_first_line.name: Doxycycline, 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days -- CDC 2021 first-line regimen (all sites)
