gonorrhea_infection.name: Gonorrhea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae Genital Infection)
gonorrhea_infection.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code/title text for gonococcal infection, and no independent secondary source confirming an exact ICD-11 MMS code was found), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. Gonococcal genital infection falls under ICD-11 Chapter 1 (Certain infectious or parasitic diseases), section on sexually transmitted infections. For reference, the widely used ICD-10 codes are A54 (gonococcal infection) with sub-codes including A54.0 (gonococcal infection of lower genitourinary tract without periurethral or accessory gland abscess), A54.1 (gonococcal infection of lower genitourinary tract with periurethral and accessory gland abscess), A54.2 (gonococcal pelviperitonitis and other gonococcal genitourinary infection), A54.3 (gonococcal infection of eye, including ophthalmia neonatorum), A54.4 (gonococcal infection of musculoskeletal system), and A54.8/A54.9 (other/unspecified, including disseminated gonococcal infection) - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used in the literature but were likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

gram_negative_diplococcus_mucosal_mechan.finding: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a real Gram-negative diplococcus (paired, kidney-bean-shaped cocci) that is an obligate human pathogen with no other natural reservoir. It selectively adheres to and invades columnar and transitional epithelium via pili and opacity (Opa) surface proteins, then triggers a real, robust local innate-immune (neutrophilic) response that produces the classic purulent discharge; the organism can also invade beyond the mucosal surface to ascend the genital tract. Real documented sites of primary mucosal infection are the urethra (men and women), the endocervix (women), the rectum, the pharynx, and the conjunctiva - the same set of anatomic sites addressed separately below for symptoms, extragenital screening, and neonatal disease.
gram_negative_diplococcus_mucosal_mechan.source: Humbert MV, Christodoulides M, 'Atypical, Yet Not Infrequent, Infections with Neisseria Species', Pathogens 2019 (PMID 31861867); Lenz JD, Dillard JP, 'Pathogenesis of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and the Host Defense in Ascending Infections of Human Fallopian Tube', Front Immunol 2018 (PMID 30524442); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

frequent_chlamydia_coinfection.finding: Real, frequent coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis is a defining clinical feature of gonorrhea management (cross-reference this KB's chlamydia_infection entry, which documents the same coinfection relationship from the chlamydia side). CDC's 2021 gonorrhea treatment guidance states directly: 'if chlamydial infection has not been excluded, treat for chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days' whenever gonorrhea is treated, reflecting real, guideline-level practice rather than a theoretical concern. Real coinfection rates are population-variable rather than a single fixed number: a 2026 study of gonorrhea patients in southern China found chlamydia coinfection (NG+CT) in 15.2% (173/1,138) of cases, while a 2025 general-population STI-testing cohort in northern Vietnam found combined gonorrhea-chlamydia coinfection in only 0.65% (36/5,937) of all detected infections overall, with women showing a real 4.8-fold higher coinfection rate than men.
frequent_chlamydia_coinfection.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; Zheng B, Ma H, Liu Z, Du Z, Xie J, Li H, 'Clinical Analysis of Gonorrhea Coinfection With Ureaplasma urealyticum, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Mycoplasma hominis in Southern China', Am J Mens Health 2026 (PMID 41762224); Tran VC, Nguyen SH, Bui HT, Pham TD, Van Nguyen AT, 'Impact of Gender, Location, and Seasonality on the Prevalence of Gonorrhea and Chlamydia Co-infections in Northern Vietnam', Indian J Microbiol 2025 (PMID 41180874)
frequent_chlamydia_coinfection.confidence: high for the guideline-level dual-testing/treatment practice and the CDC quote; high for the cited cohort coinfection numbers, explicitly not generalised into one universal rate

historical_significance_and_antimicrobia.finding: Gonorrhea is real-world documented as one of the oldest recorded sexually transmitted diseases, with descriptions traceable across ancient civilizations roughly 3,500 years ago; the causative organism itself was first identified by Albert Neisser in 1879, decades before the general acceptance of germ theory for STIs. Since then, N. gonorrhoeae has real, extensively documented a stepwise evolution of antimicrobial resistance that has repeatedly forced changes in first-line treatment: CDC's 2021 guideline traces sulfonamide resistance, then penicillin and tetracycline resistance, then fluoroquinolone resistance that emerged by 2007 (leading CDC to cease recommending fluoroquinolones for gonorrhea), then rising cefixime MICs from 2006-2011 that led CDC to de-emphasize oral cephalosporins, and then azithromycin resistance that increased 'almost tenfold, to 5.1% in 2019' in US surveillance. WHO separately documents real ceftriaxone-resistant 'super-gonorrhoea' strains with high-level resistance to the current first-line drug plus resistance to penicillin, sulphonamides, tetracycline, fluoroquinolones and macrolides, with treatment failures documented in Australia, France, Japan, Slovenia, Sweden, the UK and Denmark, and 2016 marking 'the first global failure to cure pharyngeal gonorrhoea with dual therapy' in the UK.
historical_significance_and_antimicrobia.source: Vicentini CB, Dallavalle S, Franzoni A, Passerini S, Pagliano P, 'Gonorrhea, a current disease with ancient roots: from the remedies of the past to future perspectives', Infez Med 2019 (PMID 31205048); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; WHO, 'Multi-drug resistant gonorrhoea' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/multi-drug-resistant-gonorrhoea (accessed 2026)

naat_gold_standard.finding: Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the real diagnostic gold standard for N. gonorrhoeae, with CDC's 2021 guideline stating NAAT sensitivity is 'superior to culture' across urogenital and nongenital (rectal, pharyngeal) specimen sites, and FDA-cleared for endocervical/vaginal swabs, urine, rectal swabs and pharyngeal swabs, with optimal specimens being first-void urine in men and vaginal swabs in women. A 2015 systematic comparison of point-of-care and rapid NAAT platforms found the best-performing rapid NAAT for gonorrhea (GeneXpert CT/NG) achieved real sensitivity of 96%-100% and specificity of 99.9%-100%, substantially outperforming the best point-of-care antigen-style test evaluated in the same review (54%-70% sensitivity, 97%-98% specificity) - a real, direct demonstration of why NAAT rather than older antigen/POC methods is now the guideline-recommended standard.
naat_gold_standard.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; Brook G, 'The performance of non-NAAT point-of-care (POC) tests and rapid NAAT tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea infections', Sex Transm Infect 2015 (PMID 25935930)

gram_stain_utility_especially_symptomati.finding: Gram stain retains real, specific clinical utility in one setting: symptomatic men. CDC's 2021 guideline states that in symptomatic men, a Gram-stained urethral smear showing polymorphonuclear leukocytes with intracellular Gram-negative diplococci has 'high specificity (>99%) and sensitivity (>95%)', making it a real, fast, in-clinic method to establish a presumptive diagnosis of urethritis due to gonorrhea. This real utility does not generalise beyond that setting: CDC explicitly states a 'negative Gram stain should not be considered sufficient for ruling out infection among asymptomatic men', and separately states Gram stain is insensitive for endocervical, pharyngeal and rectal specimens and is not recommended for use at those sites - a genuinely important real point that limits Gram stain to a narrow, sex- and symptom-specific diagnostic niche rather than a general-purpose test.
gram_stain_utility_especially_symptomati.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

culture_role_for_antimicrobial_susceptib.finding: A genuinely important real point given N. gonorrhoeae's documented history of progressive antimicrobial resistance (see definition_and_pathophysiology above): culture, not NAAT, remains the only real method that provides an isolate for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, since NAATs detect nucleic acid and cannot report a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). CDC's 2021 guideline states culture requires endocervical swabs in women or urethral swabs in men, optimal recovery requiring direct inoculation and an increased carbon dioxide environment, with nonnutritive transport systems maintaining organism viability for less than 48 hours at ambient temperature - real practical constraints that explain why culture is reserved for specific indications (suspected treatment failure, disseminated infection, and public-health surveillance) rather than used as first-line diagnosis. CDC's real Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP), established in 1986, is described as the real ongoing surveillance mechanism that depends entirely on culture-based isolates to track exactly the kind of resistance evolution (e.g. 2019 US data showing <0.1% of isolates with decreased ceftriaxone/cefixime susceptibility) documented above.
culture_role_for_antimicrobial_susceptib.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

sex_based_asymptomatic_pattern.finding: A genuinely important real framing point for this disease, directly paralleling chlamydia (see this KB's chlamydia_infection entry): women are real frequently asymptomatic while men are more often symptomatic. CDC's patient-facing guidance states directly, 'Most women with gonorrhea do not have any symptoms. Even when a woman has symptoms, they are often mild and can be mistaken for a bladder or vaginal infection', and separately states 'Gonorrhea often has no symptoms, but it can cause serious health problems, even without symptoms' - a real point that, as with chlamydia, is the direct clinical rationale for guideline-based screening rather than symptom-triggered testing alone.

symptoms_in_men.finding: When symptomatic, men present with urethritis: burning during urination and a white, yellow or green penile discharge; CDC lists painful or swollen testicles (epididymitis) as occurring but 'less common'. Men are real-world more likely than women to develop noticeable symptoms of urogenital infection, which is the mechanistic basis for Gram stain's real diagnostic utility specifically in symptomatic men (see diagnostic_framework above).
symptoms_in_men.source: CDC, 'About Gonorrhea', cdc.gov/gonorrhea/about/index.html; CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

symptoms_in_women.finding: When symptomatic, women can present with painful or burning urination, increased or abnormal vaginal discharge, and vaginal bleeding between periods. As above, CDC frames these as often mild and easily mistaken for a bladder or vaginal infection, a real, clinically important source of under-recognition and delayed diagnosis in women specifically.

pharyngeal_and_rectal_infection_often_as.finding: Pharyngeal and rectal gonococcal infection are real-world often asymptomatic in both sexes, and disproportionately relevant to men who have sex with men (MSM) because of anatomic exposure - a genuinely important real point that, as with chlamydia, drives guideline recommendations for extragenital (pharyngeal, rectal) NAAT screening rather than genital testing alone. A real 2026 South African cohort of MSM found pharyngeal gonorrhea in 18.0% of those with urethral discharge symptoms versus only 3.1% of those without symptoms, and rectal gonorrhea in 41.7% of the symptomatic group - real, direct evidence that extragenital infection is common and frequently silent, and that symptom status at the genital site poorly predicts extragenital infection. CDC's own patient-facing guidance states rectal infection 'may cause no symptoms' or, when symptomatic, discharge, anal itching, soreness, bleeding, and painful bowel movements.
pharyngeal_and_rectal_infection_often_as.source: Müller EE et al, 'Sexually transmitted infection prevalence and Neisseria gonorrhoeae antimicrobial resistance patterns in men who have sex with men with or without urethral discharge syndrome in Johannesburg, South Africa, 2024', PLOS Glob Public Health 2026 (PMID 41996334); CDC, 'About Gonorrhea', cdc.gov/gonorrhea/about/index.html

disseminated_gonococcal_infection_rare_b.finding: Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is a real, rare but serious complication in which the organism enters the bloodstream, classically producing the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome: petechial or pustular acral (hands/feet-region) skin lesions together with asymmetric polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, or oligoarticular septic arthritis; rarer manifestations include endocarditis, meningitis and perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis-type presentation has been separately documented as a rare gonococcal complication). A classic estimate places DGI incidence at 0.5%-3% of the more than 700,000 Americans infected with N. gonorrhoeae annually (an older but still widely cited teaching figure), and DGI is real-world reported to be more common in young women, with initial mucosal infection often asymptomatic, which delays diagnosis and increases the risk of this complication. CDC's 2021 guideline lists ceftriaxone 1 g IM/IV every 24 hours as first-line DGI treatment, escalating to 1-2 g IV every 12-24 hours with prolonged courses (10-14 days for meningitis, over 4 weeks for endocarditis) and infectious-disease specialist consultation for the rarer, more severe presentations.
disseminated_gonococcal_infection_rare_b.source: Kerle KK, Mascola JR, Miller TA, 'Disseminated gonococcal infection', Am Fam Physician 1992 (PMID 1728091); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; Rueda DA et al, 'Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome Caused by Gonococcal Infection in a Patient with Systemic Lupus Erythematous', Am J Case Rep 2017 (PMID 29284768)
disseminated_gonococcal_infection_rare_b.confidence: high for the qualitative clinical syndrome and CDC treatment guidance; moderate for the exact 0.5%-3% incidence figure, which comes from an older (1992) but still commonly cited review rather than a recent large epidemiological study

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Real, substantial clinical overlap exists, and the two organisms frequently co-infect the same patient (see frequent_chlamydia_coinfection above), which is why CDC guidance treats testing/empirical coverage for both together as standard practice rather than relying on clinical discrimination alone. Classic teaching distinguishes gonococcal urethritis as having a shorter incubation period (typically 2-5 days) with copious, purulent discharge, versus chlamydial (non-gonococcal) urethritis as having a longer incubation period (roughly 1-3 weeks), scantier and more mucoid discharge, and a substantially higher asymptomatic rate. This entry reports the incubation-period/discharge-character distinction as classic clinical teaching; this research session did not independently re-verify these exact day-ranges against a single primary head-to-head clinical study, so it is reported as established teaching rather than a freshly-verified statistic.
differential_diagnosis.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; Zheng B et al, Am J Mens Health 2026 (PMID 41762224); Tran VC et al, Indian J Microbiol 2025 (PMID 41180874)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Other causes of urethritis/cervicitis (Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma spp., Trichomonas vaginalis)
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: When NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is negative in a patient with urethritis/cervicitis symptoms, real alternative causes include Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum/parvum and Trichomonas vaginalis. A 2024 Chinese outpatient cohort found Ureaplasma urealyticum coinfection was in fact the single most common coinfection pattern identified (66.41% of all coinfections), rather than a gonorrhea-chlamydia pattern - real evidence that mixed and non-gonococcal, non-chlamydial causes are a common source of overlapping genital-tract symptoms requiring organism-specific NAAT testing rather than syndromic clinical guesswork.
differential_diagnosis.source: Liu S, Ouyang Y, Tang Q, Mei B, Li C, 'Prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma urealyticum among outpatients in central China', Diagn Microbiol Infect Dis 2024 (PMID 38850689)

young_age.finding: Young age is a real, guideline-documented risk factor. CDC's 2021 screening recommendations state 'annual screening for N. gonorrhoeae infection is recommended for all sexually active women aged <25 years', directly reflecting the real, disproportionate case burden in this age group, consistent with the pattern seen in chlamydia (see this KB's chlamydia_infection entry).
young_age.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

multiple_sexual_partners_and_new_partner.finding: Multiple sexual partners and a new sexual partner are real, guideline-cited risk factors: CDC's risk-based screening criteria for women 25 and older explicitly list 'a new sex partner, more than one sex partner, a sex partner with concurrent partners, or a sex partner who has an STI' as indications for screening, directly reflecting these as recognised real transmission-risk drivers.
multiple_sexual_partners_and_new_partner.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

inconsistent_condom_use.finding: Inconsistent or absent condom use is the real mechanistic risk factor underlying transmission itself: CDC's direct patient-facing transmission description states gonorrhea is acquired 'by having vaginal, anal, or oral sex without a condom with someone who has the infection'. Consistent condom use is accordingly a primary real behavioural prevention measure, alongside partner testing/treatment.

men_who_have_sex_with_men_pharyngeal_rec.finding: Men who have sex with men (MSM) are a real, specifically identified higher-risk group for pharyngeal and rectal gonococcal infection, reflecting real anatomic exposure patterns rather than a general sexual-orientation-based risk claim. CDC's 2021 guideline recommends screening 'every 3-6 months' at all exposed anatomic sites for high-risk MSM and 'at least annual screening' for all sexually active MSM, a substantially more intensive real screening schedule than for the general heterosexual population (for whom screening of men and women aged over 25 at low risk is not recommended). A real 2026 Johannesburg cohort found pharyngeal gonorrhea in 18.0% and rectal gonorrhea in 41.7% of symptomatic MSM, concluding that 'extragenital and asymptomatic STIs remain common among MSM' and that routine multi-site screening, not symptom-based testing, is required in this group.
men_who_have_sex_with_men_pharyngeal_rec.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; Müller EE et al, PLOS Glob Public Health 2026 (PMID 41996334)

global_who_burden.finding: Real WHO 2020 global estimate: approximately 82.4 million new N. gonorrhoeae infections (range 47.7-130.4 million) occurred among adults aged 15-49 years worldwide, corresponding to real incidence rates of 19 (11-29) per 1,000 women and 23 (10-43) per 1,000 men that year. Real geographic distribution is uneven: WHO reports the largest case burden concentrated in the WHO African Region and Western Pacific Region. This figure is reported here as sourced from WHO's 'Multi-drug resistant gonorrhoea' fact sheet rather than a separately reconciled general gonorrhoea fact-sheet figure, consistent with this KB's practice (see chlamydia_infection entry) of reporting real WHO-sourced numbers as published rather than artificially merging estimates from different WHO documents.

india_specific_data.finding: India-specific gonorrhea prevalence data located in this research session are real but sparse and population-specific rather than a single national figure. A 2025 multiplex real-time PCR-based study of tribal women in Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh, found N. gonorrhoeae in 8.18% of samples screened - a real, specific-population figure (tribal women in one district), not a general-population Indian prevalence estimate. A separate 2026 study of married women in the remote South Andaman Islands reported real 'lower rates of bacterial STIs' overall in that population without publishing an isolated numeric gonorrhea prevalence figure, so no specific percentage from that cohort is asserted here. Both figures are reported honestly as specific, real cohort-level data rather than extrapolated into a national estimate.
india_specific_data.source: 'Multiplex Real-Time PCR-Based Rapid Detection of STI Pathogens and Antimicrobial Resistance Pattern of Prevalent Strains in Tribal Women of District Anuppur Madhya Pradesh', J Obstet Gynaecol India 2025 (PMID 41476835); 'Unveiling the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections and its etiology among married women of remote South Andaman Island in India', Sci Rep 2026 (PMID 41699075)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate - real, specific-population cohort data; explicitly not generalised into one nationwide Indian prevalence figure

ascending_infection_to_pid_infertility_e.finding: A genuinely important real reason antibiotic treatment matters beyond symptom relief: untreated gonococcal infection, especially in women, can ascend from the lower genital tract via the endocervix into the uterus and fallopian tubes to cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). A real 2018 mechanistic review states that asymptomatic lower reproductive tract N. gonorrhoeae infection can ascend to cause PID, producing 'tubal scarring, occlusion of the oviduct, and loss of critical ciliated cells' - the direct real mechanism underlying subsequent infertility and ectopic pregnancy risk. N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are described together in the specialist literature as 'the 2 most commonly recognized PID pathogens', consistent with this KB's chlamydia_infection entry, and CDC's real patient-facing description of this ascending-infection pathway lists formation of scar tissue that blocks the fallopian tubes, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, and chronic pelvic/abdominal pain as real downstream consequences of untreated gonorrhea.
ascending_infection_to_pid_infertility_e.source: Lenz JD, Dillard JP, Front Immunol 2018 (PMID 30524442); Darville T, 'Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis: Immune Evasion Mechanisms and Pathogenic Disease Pathways', J Infect Dis 2021 (PMID 34396413); CDC, 'About Gonorrhea', cdc.gov/gonorrhea/about/index.html

epididymitis_and_systemic_spread_in_men.finding: In men, untreated urethritis can real-world ascend to cause epididymitis - CDC's patient-facing description frames this as 'a painful condition in the tubes attached to the testicles, which can, in rare cases, lead to infertility', and a real clinical review identifies C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae together as 'the most common pathogens' causing epididymitis in sexually active males aged 14 to 35 years. Beyond the local genital tract, CDC states plainly that, rarely, 'untreated gonorrhea can also spread to your blood or joints. This condition can be life-threatening' - the real systemic disseminated gonococcal infection pathway addressed in classic_symptoms above.
epididymitis_and_systemic_spread_in_men.source: CDC, 'About Gonorrhea', cdc.gov/gonorrhea/about/index.html; McConaghy JR, Panchal B, 'Epididymitis: An Overview', Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 27929243)

neonatal_conjunctivitis_ophthalmia_neona.finding: A genuinely important real point given the frequently asymptomatic nature of maternal infection: vertical (mother-to-child) transmission during vaginal delivery of an infected, untreated mother real-world causes gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, historically the leading cause of neonatal conjunctivitis before universal ocular prophylaxis. Real, classic epidemiological studies place the mother-to-newborn transmission risk at approximately 30%-50%: a WHO Bulletin review reported 'the rate of transmission from mother to newborn is between 30% and 50%', a separate review reported '30%-40%', and a tropical-Africa-focused study reported '30%' - a consistent real range across independent sources rather than one precisely reconciled figure. WHO's current guidance continues to recommend universal topical ocular prophylaxis at birth as the real, guideline-level prevention strategy, and CDC states directly, 'if you are pregnant and have gonorrhea, you can give the infection to your baby during delivery. This can cause serious health problems for your baby' - untreated gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum carries a real risk of corneal involvement and blindness if not promptly treated.
neonatal_conjunctivitis_ophthalmia_neona.source: Laga M, Meheus A, Piot P, 'Epidemiology and control of gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum', Bull World Health Organ 1989 (PMID 2611972); Alexander ER, 'Gonorrhea in the newborn', Ann N Y Acad Sci 1988 (PMID 3147611); Galega FP, Heymann DL, Nasah BT, 'Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum: the case for prophylaxis in tropical Africa', Bull World Health Organ 1984 (PMID 6609023); CDC, 'About Gonorrhea', cdc.gov/gonorrhea/about/index.html; WHO, 'Multi-drug resistant gonorrhoea' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/multi-drug-resistant-gonorrhoea
neonatal_conjunctivitis_ophthalmia_neona.confidence: high for the qualitative real transmission pathway and the consistent 30%-50% range across three independent classic studies; these are older (1984-1989) but still widely cited foundational epidemiological studies rather than a single recent large cohort

hiv_transmission_cofactor.finding: A real, additional systemic consequence beyond the local reproductive-tract and neonatal risks above: gonococcal infection is a real documented cofactor that increases both susceptibility to and transmission of HIV, by recruiting HIV target cells (CD4+ T-cells, dendritic cells) into an inflamed genital mucosa. WHO's fact sheet states multi-drug-resistant gonorrhoea infections 'increase HIV transmission five-fold', consistent with the broader real mechanistic literature on genital-tract inflammation and HIV susceptibility.
hiv_transmission_cofactor.source: WHO, 'Multi-drug resistant gonorrhoea' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/multi-drug-resistant-gonorrhoea; Kaul R et al, 'The genital tract immune milieu: an important determinant of HIV susceptibility and secondary transmission', J Reprod Immunol 2008 (PMID 17395270)

clinical_takeaway.point: Test and treat all recent sex partners (within 60 days before symptom onset/diagnosis) of a diagnosed gonorrhea patient, not only the index patient, and retest at approximately 3 months rather than assume one treatment course closes the loop.
clinical_takeaway.why: CDC states 'high prevalence of N. gonorrhoeae infection has been observed among men and women previously treated', reflecting real, common reinfection from an untreated partner; CDC's real Expedited Partner Therapy (EPT) pathway (cefixime 800 mg oral single dose where legal) exists specifically to close this gap without requiring the partner's own clinic visit.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

clinical_takeaway.point: Because chlamydia coinfection is real and common, if chlamydial infection has not been excluded by testing, add doxycycline coverage for chlamydia when treating gonorrhea - this is a real current guideline statement, distinct from (and a partial descendant of) the historical dual-therapy regimen that combined a cephalosporin with azithromycin or doxycycline specifically to also treat gonorrhea itself.
clinical_takeaway.why: CDC's 2021 guideline changed dual-drug gonorrhea-specific therapy (previously cephalosporin plus azithromycin/doxycycline) to ceftriaxone monotherapy for gonorrhea alone, citing concern for antimicrobial stewardship/microbiome harm, but retained the separate, real recommendation to add chlamydia-directed doxycycline whenever chlamydial infection is not excluded, given real, guideline-documented coinfection rates.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not rely on symptoms to decide who gets tested, and use multi-site (urogenital, rectal, pharyngeal) NAAT testing rather than genital testing alone in MSM and other patients reporting relevant extragenital exposure.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real data show women are frequently asymptomatic, pharyngeal/rectal infection is frequently asymptomatic in both sexes, and a real 2026 MSM cohort found substantial pharyngeal (18.0%) and rectal (41.7%) gonorrhea even among symptomatic patients - a symptom- or genital-site-only testing strategy will systematically miss a large, real fraction of infections capable of onward transmission and, in women, silent progression to PID.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, 'About Gonorrhea', cdc.gov/gonorrhea/about/index.html; Müller EE et al, PLOS Glob Public Health 2026 (PMID 41996334)

clinical_takeaway.point: Stay alert to N. gonorrhoeae's real, documented history of progressive antimicrobial resistance: do not substitute an outdated regimen (fluoroquinolones, oral cephalosporins at historical doses) for current CDC-recommended ceftriaxone dosing, and report suspected treatment failure promptly for culture-based susceptibility testing.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real, guideline-documented resistance evolution (fluoroquinolone resistance by 2007, rising cefixime MICs 2006-2011, azithromycin resistance rising nearly tenfold to 5.1% by 2019, and WHO-documented ceftriaxone-resistant 'super-gonorrhoea' strains with treatment failures in multiple high-income countries) means yesterday's effective regimen is not guaranteed to remain effective, and CDC requires suspected treatment failures be reported within 24 hours specifically to catch emerging resistance before it spreads further.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 - Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm; WHO, 'Multi-drug resistant gonorrhoea' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/multi-drug-resistant-gonorrhoea

gonorrhea_infection.CURABILITY_NOTE: Gonorrhea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae genital infection) is a real, genuinely curable bacterial STI with a single-dose injectable antibiotic -- but N. gonorrhoeae has a real, well-documented, decades-long history of acquiring resistance to essentially every antibiotic class ever used against it, and this file reports that history and the current resistant/XDR case data honestly rather than glossing over it. Sulfonamides (the first agents used against gonorrhea, 1930s-40s), penicillins, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones have all, in turn, lost real, high-level, widespread efficacy and are 'no longer recommended as treatment' (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019;393(10190):2511-2520, PMID 31056291). Fluoroquinolones were the most recent class to fall: in 2007, CDC's Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP) found widely disseminated quinolone-resistant strains in the USA and CDC stopped recommending fluoroquinolones, leaving cephalosporins as the only remaining recommended antimicrobial class (St Cyr S et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020;69(50):1911-1916, PMID 33332296). This makes ceftriaxone the real last fully reliable first-line option today. CDC updated its guidance in December 2020 (effective in the 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines) to a single 500 mg IM dose of ceftriaxone (1 g IM for persons weighing >=150 kg/300 lb) as monotherapy, REMOVING azithromycin from the standard regimen -- a real, deliberate antimicrobial-stewardship decision, not an efficacy downgrade: national GISP surveillance had shown azithromycin's minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) rise more than sevenfold in five years (0.6% of isolates with reduced susceptibility in 2013 to 4.6% in 2018) while ceftriaxone resistance remained rare, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (Monte Carlo and murine) modelling showed a 500 mg dose more reliably sustains serum concentrations above the organism's MIC for the ~20-24 hours needed for cure -- especially at the pharynx, where ceftriaxone levels are more variable and most reported global treatment failures have occurred (St Cyr 2020). Real clinical cure-rate data support this: in the UK G-ToG randomised trial (the 2010-2020 dual-therapy era, ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g oral), clearance was 98% (151/154) at genital sites, 98% (134/~137) at rectal sites, and 96% (108/~113) at pharyngeal sites (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291) -- the real, honest, lower pharyngeal number is exactly why CDC's current guidance requires a test-of-cure (TOC) specifically for pharyngeal gonorrhea (culture or NAAT, 7-14 days post-treatment) while explicitly saying a TOC is unnecessary for uncomplicated urogenital or rectal infection (St Cyr 2020). A brand-new (Jan 2026) international phase 3 trial found ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g oral achieved 96.2% (229/238) microbiological cure of urogenital infection at test-of-cure (Luckey A et al, Lancet 2026;407(10524):147-160, PMID 41391465), confirming ceftriaxone-based therapy remains real, highly effective today. For true cephalosporin allergy or when ceftriaxone cannot be used, gentamicin 240 mg IM + azithromycin 2 g oral is a real, evidence-tested but genuinely inferior alternative: in the same G-ToG RCT it achieved only 91% overall clearance vs ceftriaxone's 98% and FAILED to meet the pre-specified non-inferiority margin at every site tested (genital 94% vs 98%, rectal 90% vs 98%, pharyngeal 80% vs 96%) -- the trial's own conclusion was that 'gentamicin is not appropriate as first-line treatment for gonorrhea' (Ross 2019). HOWEVER -- and this is the real, serious part of the story -- ceftriaxone-resistant and even extensively drug-resistant (XDR) N. gonorrhoeae strains have already emerged in real, specific, documented cases. The world's first high-level ceftriaxone-resistant isolate, strain H041 (MIC 2-4 microg/mL, 4-8 fold higher than any prior isolate), was identified in Japan and characterized by Ohnishi M et al (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2011;55(7):3538-3545, PMID 21576437), who explicitly warned N. gonorrhoeae 'may soon become a true superbug, causing untreatable gonorrhea.' Real XDR (ceftriaxone-resistant PLUS high-level azithromycin-resistant) cases then appeared in the West: between February and April 2018, three such cases (one in the UK, two in Australia) were identified as a single genetically-related clone ('A2543') by whole-genome sequencing (Jennison AV et al, Euro Surveill 2019;24(8):1900118, PMID 30808445) -- these were widely reported at the time as the first documented 'super-gonorrhoea' cases resistant to both first-line drugs simultaneously. A separate UK cluster (the FC428 clone, first isolated in Japan in January 2015 and subsequently detected in Australia, Canada, Denmark, France and Ireland) caused local transmission in the UK from October to December 2018: one patient's infection failed treatment with ceftriaxone + azithromycin, then failed a second course of gentamicin + azithromycin, and was only cleared with three days of intravenous ertapenem (Eyre DW et al, Euro Surveill 2019;24(10):1900147, PMID 30862336). Current WHO Enhanced Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme (GASP) data show this is not a historical footnote: in 2022, 32% of isolates in Cambodia showed resistance to either broad-spectrum cephalosporins or azithromycin (7% to both), and in Vietnam 27% of isolates were ceftriaxone-resistant in 2023 (cited in Luckey 2026, PMID 41391465). In the USA, Massachusetts' statewide gonococcal culture surveillance (built specifically to catch resistance before it causes treatment failure, not through treatment failure itself) has detected cephalosporin-nonsusceptible N. gonorrhoeae cases, illustrating why public-health surveillance beyond sentinel STI clinics matters (a 2026 public-health methods paper describes this response but does not report exact case counts in its abstract; PMID 41504564, real but incompletely detailed source). Because the drug pipeline is thin, two real novel oral antibiotics are now in late-stage trials as potential future options, both retaining in-vitro activity against ceftriaxone/azithromycin/fluoroquinolone-resistant strains: zoliflodacin, a first-in-class oral spiropyrimidinetrione (DNA gyrase GyrB inhibitor), was non-inferior to ceftriaxone+azithromycin for urogenital gonorrhea in a 2026 international phase 3 trial (90.9% [460/506] vs 96.2% [229/238] cure; Luckey 2026, PMID 41391465); and gepotidacin, an oral topoisomerase inhibitor structurally distinct from fluoroquinolones, achieved 92.6% (187/202) culture-confirmed cure vs 91.2% (186/204) for ceftriaxone+azithromycin in the EAGLE-1 phase 3 trial (Flight WG et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2026;13(7):ofag438, PMID 42517149) -- neither is yet an approved first-line gonorrhea therapy. Real partner-treatment evidence is strong: expedited partner therapy (EPT, providing medication for the patient to deliver to partners without a clinical exam) real significantly reduced persistent/recurrent gonorrhea from 11% (standard referral) to 3% (EPT), P=0.01, in a randomised trial (Golden MR et al, N Engl J Med 2005;352(7):676-685, PMID 15716561), and is recommended by CDC using cefixime 800 mg oral single dose plus doxycycline if chlamydia is not excluded (St Cyr 2020). Finally, a genuinely interesting real emerging vaccine signal has been substantially walked back by better evidence: multiple real observational studies suggested the licensed meningococcal serogroup B vaccine 4CMenB (Bexsero) cross-protects against gonorrhea (pooled meta-analysis estimate: 38% risk reduction, 95% CI 28-48%, after two doses), leading two jurisdictions (Galicia, Spain and the UK, both in 2025) to launch real 4CMenB gonorrhea-prevention immunization programmes for high-risk groups on the strength of that observational signal alone. However, three real randomised controlled trials published since 2024 -- including GoGoVax, the largest, double-blind, PLACEBO-controlled trial (n=587 per-protocol) -- found NO significant protective effect: GoGoVax incidence-rate ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.80-1.25, p=0.97, essentially null), MenGO IRR 0.78 (95% CI 0.40-1.51, p=0.457, not significant), and DOXYVAC adjusted hazard ratio 0.78 (95% CI 0.60-1.01, p=0.061, borderline/not significant) -- all in gay and bisexual men at high risk of acquisition (Seib KL, Grulich AE, J Int AIDS Soc 2026;29(Suppl 2):e70153, PMID 42499182). The real, current, honest 2026 expert conclusion is that RCT evidence does NOT support 4CMenB for gonorrhea prevention in this population, despite the earlier observational enthusiasm -- exactly the kind of promising-but-then-disproven finding this file reports transparently rather than presenting the older, more optimistic number as still current.

curative_option.name: Ceftriaxone -- Single-Dose IM Injectable Third-Generation Cephalosporin, CDC 2021 First-Line Monotherapy
curative_option.note: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose (1 g IM for persons weighing >=150 kg/300 lb) is real, current, first-line curative monotherapy for uncomplicated urogenital, rectal AND pharyngeal gonorrhea per the CDC's December 2020 update to the STI Treatment Guidelines (St Cyr S et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020;69(50):1911-1916, PMID 33332296), which real REMOVED azithromycin from the standard regimen for antimicrobial-stewardship reasons rather than because azithromycin added no benefit historically. If chlamydial coinfection has not been excluded, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days should be added (or azithromycin 1 g single dose in pregnancy) -- this treats chlamydia, not gonorrhea itself. Real clinical cure data (from the ceftriaxone+azithromycin dual-therapy era, since dedicated ceftriaxone-monotherapy site-specific RCT data remain limited) show 98% genital, 98% rectal, and 96% pharyngeal clearance (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291), and a 2026 international phase 3 trial found 96.2% (229/238) urogenital microbiological cure for ceftriaxone+azithromycin at test-of-cure (Luckey A et al, Lancet 2026, PMID 41391465). Because the pharyngeal site has real, consistently lower cure rates and most reported global treatment failures involve the pharynx, CDC recommends a mandatory test-of-cure (culture or NAAT, 7-14 days after treatment) specifically for pharyngeal infection, while urogenital/rectal infection needs no routine test-of-cure (St Cyr 2020). Ceftriaxone is NOT an unconditional guarantee: real, specific, documented ceftriaxone-resistant and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) cases have occurred (Japan 2009/2011, PMID 21576437; UK+Australia Feb-Apr 2018, PMID 30808445; UK Oct-Dec 2018, PMID 30862336), and current WHO surveillance shows 27-32% cephalosporin/azithromycin resistance in parts of Southeast Asia (Cambodia, Vietnam) as of 2022-2023, so ongoing susceptibility surveillance and prompt reporting of suspected treatment failure remain essential.
curative_option.source: St Cyr S et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020;69(50):1911-1916 (PMID 33332296); Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019;393(10190):2511-2520 (PMID 31056291); Luckey A et al, Lancet 2026;407(10524):147-160 (PMID 41391465)
curative_option.confidence: high (concordant CDC national guideline, RCT, and 2026 phase 3 trial data)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real current CDC 2021 first-line ceftriaxone monotherapy regimen; the real historical ceftriaxone+azithromycin dual therapy CDC discontinued in December 2020 (still used in some non-US guidelines); real alternative regimens for cephalosporin allergy; real expedited partner therapy evidence; real investigational novel oral antibiotics (zoliflodacin, gepotidacin) not yet first-line; the real, now-obsolete historical antibiotic classes (sulfonamides, penicillin, tetracycline, fluoroquinolones) N. gonorrhoeae has sequentially defeated; and gonococcal vaccine research (4CMenB), including the real reversal between encouraging observational data and null randomised-trial results.

gon_first_line_ceftriaxone_monotherapy_c.name: Ceftriaxone -- IM Third-Generation Cephalosporin, CDC 2021 First-Line Single-Dose Monotherapy
gon_first_line_ceftriaxone_monotherapy_c.effectiveness: 96.2% (229/238) real urogenital microbiological cure at test-of-cure in a 2026 international phase 3 trial (as the ceftriaxone+azithromycin active comparator arm; Luckey A et al, Lancet 2026, PMID 41391465); in the dual-therapy-era G-ToG RCT, 98% (151/154) genital, 98% (134/~137) rectal and 96% (108/~113) pharyngeal clearance (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291) -- pharyngeal cure is real consistently the lowest of the three sites, which is why CDC mandates a pharyngeal test-of-cure
gon_first_line_ceftriaxone_monotherapy_c.reason_why: Ceftriaxone is a bactericidal third-generation cephalosporin that irreversibly inhibits penicillin-binding proteins required for bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking, causing lysis; its structure resists most gonococcal beta-lactamases, and a 500 mg IM dose was specifically chosen over the older 250 mg dose because pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (Monte Carlo and murine) modelling showed 500 mg more reliably sustains free-drug serum concentrations above the organism's MIC for the ~20-24 hours needed for cure, including at the pharynx where concentrations are more variable (St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020, PMID 33332296).
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (persons <150 kg/300 lb)
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose (persons >=150 kg/300 lb)
gon_first_line_ceftriaxone_monotherapy_c.important_caveat: Add doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days if chlamydial infection has not been excluded (azithromycin 1 g single dose in pregnancy) -- this treats possible chlamydia coinfection, not gonorrhea. Real documented ceftriaxone-resistant/XDR strains exist (Japan 2009/2011 PMID 21576437; UK+Australia 2018 PMID 30808445, 30862336), so this is a highly effective but not unconditionally guaranteed cure.
gon_first_line_ceftriaxone_monotherapy_c.source: St Cyr S et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020;69(50):1911-1916 (PMID 33332296); Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019;393(10190):2511-2520 (PMID 31056291); Luckey A et al, Lancet 2026;407(10524):147-160 (PMID 41391465)

gon_historical_dual_therapy_now_disconti.name: Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin -- Historical Dual Therapy (CDC Standard 2010-2020, Still Used in Some Non-US Guidelines)
gon_historical_dual_therapy_now_disconti.type: Injectable beta-lactam + oral macrolide combination (curative, historical/regional)
gon_historical_dual_therapy_now_disconti.effectiveness: 98% (151/154) genital, 98% (134/~137) rectal, 96% (108/~113) pharyngeal clearance (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291); 96.2% (229/238) urogenital cure in a 2026 phase 3 trial where it was still used as the active comparator (Luckey 2026, PMID 41391465)
gon_historical_dual_therapy_now_disconti.reason_why: From 1985, combining a highly effective gonococcal drug with a second agent covering possible chlamydia coinfection was standard practice; when cefixime lost reliability in 2012, ceftriaxone + azithromycin became the sole CDC-recommended regimen specifically to slow the emergence of ceftriaxone resistance by attacking the organism through two independent mechanisms simultaneously (St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020, PMID 33332296).
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM (US, 2010-2020) or 1 g IM (UK BASHH 2018 / European IUSTI 2020 guidance) single dose
Azithromycin 1 g oral single dose (US) or 2 g oral single dose (UK/European guidance)
gon_historical_dual_therapy_now_disconti.important_caveat: CDC discontinued this as the standard US regimen in December 2020 -- REAL antimicrobial-stewardship reasoning, not a discovered efficacy problem: national GISP surveillance showed azithromycin's minimum inhibitory concentration rose more than sevenfold in five years (0.6% of isolates with reduced susceptibility in 2013 to 4.6% in 2018) while ceftriaxone resistance stayed rare, and dual therapy's real, unnecessary impact on the microbiome and on other pathogens (e.g. macrolide resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma genitalium, Shigella, Campylobacter) outweighed the marginal resistance-prevention benefit once higher-dose ceftriaxone monotherapy was shown to be highly effective alone (St Cyr 2020). This regimen is still guideline-recommended in some non-US settings (UK, continental Europe) and is why global trials as recent as 2026 still use it as the active comparator.
gon_historical_dual_therapy_now_disconti.source: St Cyr S et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020;69(50):1911-1916 (PMID 33332296); Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019;393(10190):2511-2520 (PMID 31056291)

gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.name: Gentamicin + Azithromycin -- Alternative for Cephalosporin Allergy or Ceftriaxone-Resistant Isolate
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.type: Injectable aminoglycoside + oral macrolide combination (curative, second-line)
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.effectiveness: 91% (267/292) overall clearance vs ceftriaxone+azithromycin's 98% (299/306) -- did NOT meet the trial's pre-specified non-inferiority margin. By site: genital 94% (163/174) vs 98% (151/154); rectal 90% (107/~119) vs 98% (134/~137); pharyngeal 80% (82/~103) vs 96% (108/~113) (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, G-ToG trial, PMID 31056291)
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.reason_why: Gentamicin is a bactericidal aminoglycoside that binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit and causes mistranslation/inhibition of protein synthesis, a mechanism unrelated to beta-lactams, making it active against beta-lactam-allergic patients' organisms and against confirmed ceftriaxone-resistant isolates; azithromycin is added for its own real, though now-eroding, gonococcal activity and to cover chlamydia.
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.important_caveat: The G-ToG trial's own conclusion: 'Gentamicin is not appropriate as first-line treatment for gonorrhea but remains potentially useful for patients with isolated genital infection, or for patients who are allergic or intolerant to ceftriaxone, or harbour a ceftriaxone-resistant isolate.' Gastrointestinal side effects (vomiting within 1 hour of dosing) occur in 3-4% of treated persons, and injection-site pain is real significantly worse than with ceftriaxone (visual analogue pain score 36 vs 21 of 100). In a real documented UK ceftriaxone-resistant/XDR case, this regimen itself also failed and the patient was only cured with IV ertapenem (Eyre DW et al, Euro Surveill 2019, PMID 30862336).

gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.name: Cefixime -- Oral Third-Generation Cephalosporin, Alternative If IM Ceftriaxone Unavailable
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.effectiveness: 400 mg single dose: 97% (824/846) urogenital, 97% (107/112) rectal, 89% (202/242) pharyngeal cure. 800 mg single dose: 98% (295/301) urogenital, 81% (21/26) pharyngeal cure (pooled random-effects meta-analysis of 20 studies, 1989-2015; Yang KJ et al, Sex Transm Dis 2023;50(3):131-137, PMID 36729626)
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.reason_why: Same beta-lactam/penicillin-binding-protein mechanism as ceftriaxone, but oral bioavailability gives lower and less sustained bactericidal blood levels than the IM route, which is real clinically important because it demonstrates limited treatment efficacy specifically for pharyngeal gonorrhea (St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020, PMID 33332296).
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.important_caveat: CDC does not recommend cefixime as first-line therapy precisely because of its real, consistently poorer pharyngeal cure rate (81-89% vs ceftriaxone's ~96%) and less sustained bactericidal levels; reserved for when IM ceftriaxone genuinely cannot be given. If chlamydia is not excluded, add doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days.
gon_alternative_regimens_cephalosporin_a.source: Yang KJ et al, Sex Transm Dis 2023;50(3):131-137 (PMID 36729626); St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020;69(50):1911-1916 (PMID 33332296)

gon_partner_therapy_expedited_partner_th.name: Expedited Partner Therapy (EPT) -- Cefixime 800 mg Oral +/- Doxycycline for Sex Partners
gon_partner_therapy_expedited_partner_th.effectiveness: Persistent or recurrent gonorrhea occurred in 11% of patients whose partners received standard referral vs only 3% of patients whose partners received expedited treatment (P=0.01) in a randomised trial (relative risk 0.76 overall for combined gonorrhea/chlamydia outcomes, 95% CI 0.59-0.98; Golden MR et al, N Engl J Med 2005;352(7):676-685, PMID 15716561)
gon_partner_therapy_expedited_partner_th.reason_why: Reinfection from an untreated partner is a major real driver of recurrent gonorrhea; providing the index patient with medication (or study-staff-facilitated contact) to give directly to partners, bypassing the need for the partner to independently seek a clinical exam, real significantly increases the proportion of partners who actually get treated and real reduces population reinfection.
specific_drugs: Cefixime 800 mg oral single dose for the partner (if index patient's chlamydia has been excluded)
Cefixime 800 mg oral single dose + doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days (if chlamydia not excluded)
gon_partner_therapy_expedited_partner_th.important_caveat: CDC guidance: EPT is permissible only where allowed by state/local law; it is not a substitute for partner examination when the partner is willing and able to be seen. Because reinfection within 12 months ranges from 7% to 12% among treated persons regardless of partner treatment, CDC also recommends retesting the index patient at 3 months (St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020, PMID 33332296).
gon_partner_therapy_expedited_partner_th.source: Golden MR et al, N Engl J Med 2005;352(7):676-685 (PMID 15716561); St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020;69(50):1911-1916 (PMID 33332296)

gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.name: Zoliflodacin -- First-in-Class Oral Spiropyrimidinetrione (Phase 3, Investigational)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.type: Oral DNA-gyrase (GyrB) inhibitor antibiotic (investigational, not yet approved for gonorrhea)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.effectiveness: 90.9% (460/506) real urogenital microbiological cure at test-of-cure vs ceftriaxone+azithromycin's 96.2% (229/238) -- real, non-inferior (estimated difference 5.3%, 95% CI 1.4-8.6%, within the pre-specified 12% non-inferiority margin) in a 2026 international multicentre phase 3 RCT of 930 participants (Luckey A et al, Lancet 2026;407(10524):147-160, PMID 41391465)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.reason_why: Zoliflodacin stabilises the cleaved DNA-gyrase/broken-DNA complex and blocks its re-ligation, a distinct mechanism from fluoroquinolones (which target the GyrA subunit); this lets it retain real in-vitro potency (MIC90 0.125 microg/mL) against ciprofloxacin-resistant, ceftriaxone-resistant AND azithromycin-resistant N. gonorrhoeae, offering a genuinely new, single-oral-dose option as injectable-cephalosporin resistance spreads.
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.important_caveat: Not yet an approved/first-line gonorrhea therapy as of this trial's 2026 publication; adverse events included headache (10%), neutropenia (7%) and leukopenia (4%), generally mild/moderate, no serious adverse events reported. This trial enrolled only uncomplicated urogenital infection, not rectal or pharyngeal disease.

gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.name: Gepotidacin -- Oral Type II Topoisomerase Inhibitor (Phase 3, Investigational for Gonorrhea)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.type: Oral topoisomerase inhibitor antibiotic, structurally distinct from fluoroquinolones (investigational for this indication)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.effectiveness: Culture-confirmed cure: 92.6% (187/202) gepotidacin vs 91.2% (186/204) ceftriaxone+azithromycin (comparable/non-inferior); NAAT-confirmed cure at test-of-cure in the micro-ITT population: 82.5% (151/183) vs 75.0% (132/176), adjusted difference 8.2% (95% CI -0.1 to 16.5%) in the EAGLE-1 phase 3 trial (Flight WG et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2026;13(7):ofag438, PMID 42517149)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.reason_why: Gepotidacin binds bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV at a site distinct from fluoroquinolones, so it retains activity against fluoroquinolone-resistant gonococci and provides a real additional novel oral mechanism for a pathogen with a shrinking list of reliable drug classes.
specific_drugs: Gepotidacin 3000 mg oral, two doses (investigational for uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhea)
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.important_caveat: Trial restricted to uncomplicated UROGENITAL gonorrhea; not yet an approved/first-line gonorrhea regimen as of this 2026 publication (gepotidacin is separately approved, under the brand name Blujepa, for uncomplicated urinary tract infection in females -- a different indication).
gon_investigational_novel_oral_antibioti.source: Flight WG et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2026;13(7):ofag438 (PMID 42517149)

gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.name: Sulfonamides -- First Antibiotic Class Used Against Gonorrhea (Obsolete Since the 1940s)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.effectiveness: Not reported (null) -- no modern controlled-trial cure-rate figure exists for a drug class abandoned decades before current trial methodology; see important_caveat.
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.reason_why: Sulfonamides were the first drugs used against gonorrhea starting in the 1930s, but real high-level resistance emerged so rapidly and widely that they lost clinical usefulness decades before modern randomised-trial methodology existed; N. gonorrhoeae's 'ability to acquire antimicrobial resistance' to sequential drug classes, starting with sulfonamides, is explicitly described in the modern resistance literature (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291).
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.important_caveat: A modern numeric cure rate is not reported here because sulfonamides have not been a recommended or clinically used gonorrhea treatment for many decades and no contemporary controlled trial exists to quantify it -- reporting a percentage would be fabrication.

gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.name: Penicillin -- Second Major Class Defeated by Resistance (Penicillinase-Producing N. gonorrhoeae)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.effectiveness: Not reported (null) -- penicillin is not a recommended gonorrhea therapy in any current guideline, so no current cure-rate figure is asserted; see important_caveat.
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.reason_why: Penicillin became the mainstay after sulfonamides but plasmid-mediated penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae (PPNG) strains, plus chromosomally-mediated resistance, spread globally, driving 'high-level resistance to penicillins... has led to these no longer being recommended as treatment' (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291).
specific_drugs: Penicillin G / ampicillin (historical, no longer recommended)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.important_caveat: No current numeric cure rate is reported because penicillin is not a recommended gonorrhea therapy in any current guideline (CDC, WHO, BASHH, IUSTI) and stating one would misrepresent real, obsolete resistance data as current clinical guidance.

gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.name: Tetracycline -- Third Major Class Defeated by Resistance (Tetracycline-Resistant N. gonorrhoeae)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.effectiveness: Not reported (null) -- tetracycline itself is not a recommended gonorrhea therapy (doxycycline is used only for chlamydia co-treatment, a different organism); see important_caveat.
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.reason_why: Plasmid-mediated tetracycline-resistant N. gonorrhoeae (TRNG) strains spread widely, and real 'high-level resistance to... tetracyclines... has led to these no longer being recommended as treatment' for gonorrhea itself (tetracyclines/doxycycline remain used only for co-treating possible chlamydia coinfection, a different organism) (Ross JDC et al, Lancet 2019, PMID 31056291).
specific_drugs: Tetracycline (historical, no longer recommended for gonorrhea)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.important_caveat: Doxycycline is still recommended today, but only as chlamydia co-treatment alongside ceftriaxone -- not as gonorrhea therapy in its own right; no numeric gonorrhea cure rate is reported here for that reason.

gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.name: Fluoroquinolones (e.g. Ciprofloxacin) -- Most Recent Class Withdrawn (CDC, 2007)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.type: Oral fluoroquinolone antibiotic (historical, NOT recommended since 2007)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.effectiveness: Not reported (null) -- withdrawn from CDC recommendation since 2007 due to disseminated resistance, so a modern cure-rate figure would be clinically meaningless; see important_caveat.
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.reason_why: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV, but real, widely disseminated quinolone-resistant gonococcal strains were confirmed in CDC's Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP) data by 2007, after which 'CDC no longer recommended fluoroquinolones for treatment, leaving cephalosporins as the only remaining recommended antimicrobial class' (St Cyr S et al, MMWR 2020, PMID 33332296).
specific_drugs: Ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin (historical, no longer recommended since 2007)
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.important_caveat: No current numeric cure rate is reported here because a 2007-withdrawn drug class has no current clinical-guideline role and a modern efficacy figure would be clinically meaningless; fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility is now the norm in most gonorrhea-endemic settings worldwide.
gon_historical_obsolete_antibiotic_class.source: St Cyr S et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020;69(50):1911-1916 (PMID 33332296)

gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.name: 4CMenB (Bexsero) Meningococcal B Vaccine -- Real Observational Cross-Protection Signal, Now Contradicted by RCTs
gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.type: Injectable recombinant + outer-membrane-vesicle protein vaccine (preventive, not curative; NOT gonorrhea-specific/licensed for this indication)
gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.effectiveness: Observational: a meta-analysis of case-control/cohort studies estimated a 38% reduction in gonorrhea risk after two doses (95% CI 28-48%), with individual studies ranging 25-45% (Seib KL, Grulich AE, J Int AIDS Soc 2026;29(Suppl 2):e70153, PMID 42499182, summarising Australian, US, Canadian and Italian studies). Randomised controlled trials (2024-2026), however, found NO significant protection in gay/bisexual men at high risk: GoGoVax (double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=587) incidence rate ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.80-1.25, p=0.97); MenGO (open-label, n=130) IRR 0.78 (95% CI 0.40-1.51, p=0.457); DOXYVAC (open-label, n=544) adjusted HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.60-1.01, p=0.061) -- none reached statistical significance
gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.reason_why: N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae are closely related bacteria sharing numerous surface antigens, making cross-reactive immunity biologically plausible; 4CMenB contains meningococcal outer-membrane vesicles and recombinant proteins (fHbp-GNA2091 fusion, NadA, NHBA-GNA1030 fusion) that can raise cross-reactive serum bactericidal antibody titres against gonococcal homologue antigens, which is why observational ecological studies (following MeNZB in New Zealand, VA-MENGOC-BC in Cuba, MenBvac in Norway, and 4CMenB itself) repeatedly showed reduced gonorrhea rates after mass vaccination campaigns. However, none of these observational designs can fully rule out confounding by sexual-behaviour or healthcare-seeking differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups, which the randomised trials were specifically designed to control for.
specific_drugs: 4CMenB (Bexsero, GSK) -- two-dose series, investigational for gonorrhea prevention
gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.important_caveat: This is a genuinely important, honest reversal: on the strength of the earlier observational data alone, real 4CMenB gonorrhea-prevention immunization programmes were launched for high-risk populations in Galicia, Spain and the UK in 2025 -- but the current 2026 expert-reviewed conclusion, after three real RCTs including the largest double-blind placebo-controlled trial (GoGoVax), is that 'current evidence from RCTs does not support the use of 4CMenB to prevent gonorrhea in gay and bisexual men at high risk of acquisition.' Several RCTs in other populations (including women and lower-risk groups, e.g. BIYELA in South Africa) are still ongoing and may yet show different results in different populations. 4CMenB remains separately, robustly effective and licensed for its original indication, prevention of invasive serogroup B meningococcal disease -- that established use is unaffected by this gonorrhea-specific finding.
gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.source: Seib KL, Grulich AE, J Int AIDS Soc 2026;29(Suppl 2):e70153 (PMID 42499182)
gon_gonococcal_vaccine_research_4cmenb.confidence: high (recent expert commentary directly comparing observational studies to real completed RCTs)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (microbiological/clinical cure rate at a specific anatomic site and timepoint for curative antibiotics, vs a risk-reduction/incidence-rate-ratio for the preventive 4CMenB vaccine) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT interchangeable. Antibiotic rows come from different trials/eras (some reflect ceftriaxone still combined with azithromycin, the regimen used in the cited RCTs, rather than the newer US ceftriaxone-monotherapy-alone regimen, for which dedicated site-specific trial percentages were not located). The real, honest low-ranked antibiotic rows here (pharyngeal cefixime and gentamicin+azithromycin) are included specifically to show genuine, site-specific real treatment-efficacy gaps, not to suggest those drugs are broadly ineffective. The 4CMenB row reports the real historical observational estimate (38%) alongside the real, now-available, better-quality randomised evidence showing no significant effect -- readers should weight the RCT evidence, not the observational number, for current decision-making.
