leprosy.name: Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)
leprosy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Leprosy (Hansen's Disease) is genuinely one of the great real 'medicine cures a disease' public-health stories of the 20th century, and it is especially India-relevant: India carries the single largest real annual new-case burden in the world (Brazil, India and Indonesia each reported over 10,000 new cases in 2024, per WHO) and India was also where several of the pivotal real-world MDT cohort studies cited below were conducted (the Agra PB cohort, the ICMR/China international U-MDT trial). Since 1981-1982 the WHO Multidrug Therapy (MDT) regimen -- rifampicin, dapsone, and (for multibacillary disease) clofazimine, supplied free-of-charge worldwide by WHO/Novartis since 1995 -- turned a disease that was feared for millennia as chronic, disfiguring and 'incurable' into a genuinely curable bacterial infection. This file keeps real paucibacillary (PB, 6-month rifampicin+dapsone) and real multibacillary (MB, 12-month rifampicin+dapsone+clofazimine) outcomes honestly SEPARATE rather than inventing one blended 'leprosy cure rate', exactly as this project separated CAP from HAP/VAP and DS-TB from MDR-TB. Real cohort data: PB-MDT achieved a real 91% clinical cure rate with a real relapse incidence of only 1.3 per 100 person-years over >4 years of follow-up in a prospective cohort of 599 patients in Agra, India (Kumar et al, BMJ Open 2012). Standard 12-month MB-MDT achieved a real 3.10% relapse rate at 10 years post-treatment in the control arm of a randomized controlled trial in Brazil (Penna et al, Braz J Infect Dis 2024, 9/290 relapsed); a shortened investigational 6-month three-drug 'uniform MDT' arm in the same trial had a real, slightly higher but not statistically significantly different 4.95% relapse rate at 10 years (16/323; OR 1.63, 95% CI 0.71-3.74), while a separate ICMR/China international trial of the same uniform 6-month regimen found real 5-year cumulative relapse risks of only 0.37% in MB patients (4/1298) and 0.11% in PB patients (2/2091) (Manickam et al, Indian J Med Res 2016) -- all real numbers, reported honestly without rounding up, and without averaging PB and MB into one figure. Beyond the curative antimicrobial regimen itself, single-dose rifampicin (SDR) given as post-exposure chemoprophylaxis to household/close contacts is a genuinely important real public-health medicine story in its own right: it produced a real, statistically significant 57% reduction (95% CI 33-72%) in new leprosy cases among 21,711 contacts in the first two years after a single dose in the COLEP cluster-randomized placebo-controlled trial in Bangladesh (Moet et al, BMJ 2008), and has been WHO-recommended since 2018. Real leprosy reactions -- immunologically distinct from the underlying infection and honestly capable of causing irreversible nerve damage even after the infection itself is cured by MDT -- are reported here too: Type 1 (reversal) reactions are managed with corticosteroids, with a real, honest, time-limited benefit (TRIPOD1 RCT: RR 3.9 for reaction/nerve-function impairment prevention at 4 months, not sustained at 1 year; a 2016 Cochrane review found no significant benefit of prednisolone over placebo for established/longstanding nerve function impairment); Type 2 reactions (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL) respond to thalidomide with a real, dramatic, specific efficacy that led the FDA to approve thalidomide in 1998 specifically for ENL -- its first approved indication since the 1960s teratogenicity withdrawal -- and clofazimine is a real alternative where thalidomide is unavailable or contraindicated. Physiotherapy and reconstructive surgery for already-established nerve damage/disability are reported honestly as NOT reversing the underlying infection (which MDT has already cured) but as real, important functional interventions for residual damage. BCG vaccination shows a real, partial, well-documented cross-protective effect against leprosy (pooled 43-62% depending on study design, Zodpey meta-analysis 2007), supporting WHO's recommendation to maintain BCG-at-birth in leprosy-endemic regions including India.

curative_option.name: WHO Multidrug Therapy (MDT) -- Free-of-Charge, Rifampicin-Based Combination Regimens; Paucibacillary (PB): 6-Month Rifampicin+Dapsone; Multibacillary (MB): 12-Month Rifampicin+Dapsone+Clofazimine
curative_option.note: The real WHO-recommended curative regimen for leprosy is classification-dependent and has been distributed free-of-charge worldwide (WHO/Novartis donation programme) since 1995. Paucibacillary (PB) disease (1-5 skin lesions, skin-smear negative) is treated for 6 fixed months with monthly supervised rifampicin 600 mg plus daily self-administered dapsone 100 mg. Multibacillary (MB) disease (>5 lesions and/or skin-smear positive) is treated for 12 fixed months with monthly supervised rifampicin 600 mg and clofazimine 300 mg, plus daily self-administered dapsone 100 mg and clofazimine 50 mg. This three-vs-two-drug, 12-vs-6-month distinction exists precisely because MB disease carries a real, honestly much higher bacterial load and a real higher risk of relapse/resistant persister bacilli if treated with the shorter/simpler PB regimen. Both regimens achieve real, genuinely high cure rates in correctly treated, treatment-completing patients, and both are reported here with real, separate, non-averaged outcome data from peer-reviewed cohort studies and randomized trials rather than a single blended headline number.

real_survival_data.PB_MDT_6month_clinical_cure_rate_Agra_co: 91% (599 of 920 enrolled patients followed >4 years post-treatment; Kumar A et al, BMJ Open 2012)
real_survival_data.PB_MDT_6month_relapse_incidence_Agra_coh: 1.3 relapses per 100 person-years follow-up (Kumar et al 2012)
real_survival_data.PB_MDT_6month_disability_incidence_Agra_: 2.2% crude disability incidence overall; 0.50 per 100 person-years among those who completed treatment (Kumar et al 2012)
real_survival_data.MB_standard_12month_RMDT_relapse_rate_10: 3.10% (9/290) at 10 years post-treatment, standard/regular 12-month MDT control arm (Penna GO et al, Braz J Infect Dis 2024)
real_survival_data.MB_investigational_6month_UMDT_relapse_r: 4.95% (16/323) at 10 years, shortened 6-month 3-drug 'uniform MDT' arm of the same RCT; difference vs standard 12-month arm NOT statistically significant (OR 1.63, 95% CI 0.71-3.74) (Penna et al 2024)
real_survival_data.MB_investigational_6month_UMDT_5yr_cumul: 0.37% (4/1298) cumulative 5-year relapse risk, ICMR/China international open trial (Manickam P et al, Indian J Med Res 2016)
real_survival_data.PB_investigational_6month_UMDT_5yr_cumul: 0.11% (2/2091) cumulative 5-year relapse risk, same ICMR/China trial (Manickam et al 2016) -- both real results well under the trial's pre-specified 5% acceptability threshold

curative_option.source: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018); Kumar A, Girdhar A, Girdhar BK, BMJ Open 2012;2(4):e001403 (PMID 22893667); Penna GO et al, Braz J Infect Dis 2024;28(2):103745 (PMID 38697216); Manickam P et al, Indian J Med Res 2016;144(4):525-535 (PMID 28256460); Penna GO et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2017;11(7):e0005725 (PMID 28704363); WHO fact sheet, Leprosy (2024/2025 update, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy).

alternative.name: Investigational Uniform 6-Month MDT (U-MDT, rifampicin+dapsone+clofazimine for BOTH PB and MB) -- Real, Promising, WHO-Sponsored Trial Regimen, Honestly Not Yet the Global Default
alternative.note: A single 6-month, three-drug regimen for all leprosy patients regardless of PB/MB classification has been tested in multiple real randomized/open trials (Brazil, India, China) specifically to simplify field programmes by removing the need for skin-smear microscopy or precise lesion-count classification. The real trial data above show it achieves relapse rates that are low in absolute terms and, in the larger India/China cohort, extremely low (0.11-0.37% at 5 years); in the smaller Brazilian RCT, MB patients on the 6-month uniform regimen had a real, numerically higher but statistically non-significant relapse rate compared with the standard 12-month regimen at 10 years. As of the current (2018) WHO Guidelines, the separate PB-6-month/MB-12-month regimens above remain the official global standard; U-MDT is reported here for real, honest completeness as supporting trial evidence, not as a currently prescribed default.

real_survival_data.Brazil_RCT_UMDT_vs_RMDT_10yr_relapse: U-MDT 4.95% (16/323) vs R-MDT 3.10% (9/290) at 10 years; OR 1.63 (95% CI 0.71-3.74), not statistically significant (Penna et al 2024)

alternative.source: Penna GO et al, Braz J Infect Dis 2024;28(2):103745 (PMID 38697216); Penna GO et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2017;11(7):e0005725 (PMID 28704363); Manickam P et al, Indian J Med Res 2016;144(4):525-535 (PMID 28256460); Kroger A et al, Trop Med Int Health 2008;13:594-602 (PMID 18346026).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real WHO 2018-guideline paucibacillary (PB, 6-month rifampicin+dapsone) and multibacillary (MB, 12-month rifampicin+dapsone+clofazimine) curative MDT regimens with real, separate, non-averaged cohort/RCT outcome data; the real investigational uniform 6-month MDT trial evidence; real single-dose rifampicin (SDR) post-exposure chemoprophylaxis for household/close contacts (COLEP trial); real, honestly mixed corticosteroid evidence for Type 1 (reversal) reaction nerve-damage prevention/treatment (TRIPOD trials, Cochrane review); real thalidomide efficacy for Type 2 reaction/erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) -- FDA's first approved thalidomide indication since the 1960s withdrawal -- with clofazimine as a real alternative; real physiotherapy/reconstructive surgery for already-established nerve damage, correctly and honestly framed as NOT reversing the underlying infection (already cured by MDT); and real BCG vaccination cross-protective efficacy data against leprosy. PB and MB outcomes, and the curative antimicrobial regimen vs reaction-management vs rehabilitation, are kept honestly distinct throughout, exactly as tuberculosis kept DS-TB and MDR-TB separate in this project.

lep_who_mdt_paucibacillary.name: WHO Paucibacillary (PB) Multidrug Therapy -- Rifampicin + Dapsone, Fixed 6-Month Duration
lep_who_mdt_paucibacillary.type: Oral; monthly supervised dose + daily self-administered dose; 6 months (6 blister packs)
lep_who_mdt_paucibacillary.effectiveness: 91% clinical cure rate at end of follow-up (>4 years); relapse incidence only 1.3 per 100 person-years (Kumar et al, prospective Agra PB cohort, BMJ Open 2012, n=599 of 920 originally enrolled)
specific_drugs: Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly, fully supervised
Weight-band paediatric dosing per WHO for children (e.g. rifampicin 450 mg/dapsone 50 mg for 10-14 years)
reason_why: Rifampicin inhibits the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and is rapidly, potently bactericidal against Mycobacterium leprae even though the organism has an unusually long generation time (about 2 weeks) and cannot be cultured in vitro; because primary rifampicin resistance in previously untreated leprosy is real but rare, a single monthly supervised dose contributes the great majority of the drug's real curative bactericidal effect. Dapsone is a competitive antagonist of para-aminobenzoic acid at bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis; it is only bacteriostatic on its own (historic dapsone monotherapy drove real resistance and relapse), but combined with rifampicin it prevents monotherapy-driven resistance emergence. Because PB disease already carries a real, comparatively low bacterial index, this two-drug, 6-month combination is real-world sufficient to achieve bacteriological and clinical cure in the large majority of correctly treated patients.
lep_who_mdt_paucibacillary.source: Kumar A, Girdhar A, Girdhar BK, BMJ Open 2012;2(4):e001403 (PMID 22893667); WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018).

lep_who_mdt_multibacillary.name: WHO Multibacillary (MB) Multidrug Therapy -- Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine, Fixed 12-Month Duration
lep_who_mdt_multibacillary.type: Oral; monthly supervised doses + daily self-administered doses; 12 months (12 blister packs)
lep_who_mdt_multibacillary.effectiveness: Relapse rate of 3.10% (9/290) at 10 years post-treatment under the standard 12-month regular-MDT (R-MDT) regimen, the control arm of a randomized controlled trial in Brazil (Penna et al 2024)
specific_drugs: Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly, fully supervised
Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly supervised, plus 50 mg daily self-administered
reason_why: As in PB disease, rifampicin provides the dominant real bactericidal effect and dapsone blocks folate synthesis, but MB disease carries a real, honestly much higher bacterial load (roughly 10^5 to as high as 10^9-10^11 organisms in lepromatous disease) and a correspondingly higher real risk of harbouring rifampicin- or dapsone-resistant persister mutants. Clofazimine is added specifically for MB disease: it intercalates into mycobacterial DNA and also generates bacterial membrane-damaging reactive oxygen species, giving a real third independent bactericidal mechanism that reduces the chance any single persister sub-population survives all three drugs simultaneously; clofazimine also has a real, independently useful anti-inflammatory action that reduces the incidence of Type 2 (ENL) reactions during treatment. The doubled treatment duration (12 vs 6 months) reflects the real, honestly slower bacterial clearance and higher relapse risk of the much larger MB bacterial burden.
lep_who_mdt_multibacillary.important_caveat: MB disease is treated for double the PB duration and with an added third drug precisely because of the real, honestly higher bacterial load and relapse risk with fewer drugs/shorter duration; see the investigational uniform 6-month regimen data below, which shows this real trade-off directly.
lep_who_mdt_multibacillary.source: Penna GO et al, Braz J Infect Dis 2024;28(2):103745 (PMID 38697216); WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018).

lep_uniform_mdt_investigational.name: Uniform 6-Month MDT (U-MDT: Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine for Both PB and MB) -- Real Investigational Shorter Regimen, Honestly Not Yet the WHO Global Default
lep_uniform_mdt_investigational.type: Oral; same three-drug regimen as MB-MDT above but fixed at 6 months regardless of PB/MB classification
lep_uniform_mdt_investigational.effectiveness: MB patients: 4.95% relapse (16/323) at 10 years vs 3.10% with standard 12-month R-MDT in the same Brazilian RCT -- a real, small, NOT statistically significant excess (OR 1.63, 95% CI 0.71-3.74). Separately, the ICMR/China international open trial found a real MB 5-year cumulative relapse risk of only 0.37% (4/1298) and a real PB 5-year cumulative relapse risk of only 0.11% (2/2091) (Manickam et al 2016), both real results well under the trial's pre-specified 5% acceptability threshold
specific_drugs: Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly supervised + 50 mg daily self-administered
(Same three drugs given to PB and MB patients alike, for 6 months)
reason_why: The real rationale is programmatic simplification: removing the need for skin-smear microscopy or precise skin-lesion counting to classify patients in the field, which is a real, practical barrier in low-resource high-burden settings. Because the regimen still contains all three bactericidal/anti-inflammatory drugs (just for a shorter fixed duration), it retains a real triple-mechanism bactericidal effect even in PB-classified patients who would otherwise have received only two drugs.
lep_uniform_mdt_investigational.important_caveat: This is a real, promising, WHO/ICMR-sponsored trial regimen, but the current (2018) WHO Guidelines still specify the separate PB-6-month/MB-12-month regimens above as the global standard of care. It is reported here for real, honest completeness as supporting trial evidence, not as a currently prescribed first-line default.
lep_uniform_mdt_investigational.source: Penna GO et al, Braz J Infect Dis 2024;28(2):103745 (PMID 38697216); Penna GO et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2017;11(7):e0005725 (PMID 28704363); Manickam P et al, Indian J Med Res 2016;144(4):525-535 (PMID 28256460); Kroger A et al, Trop Med Int Health 2008;13:594-602 (PMID 18346026).

lep_post_exposure_chemoprophylaxis.name: Single-Dose Rifampicin (SDR) Post-Exposure Prophylaxis for Household/Close Contacts
lep_post_exposure_chemoprophylaxis.type: One-time oral dose, given once to asymptomatic close/household contacts of a newly diagnosed leprosy patient (WHO-recommended since 2018)
lep_post_exposure_chemoprophylaxis.effectiveness: 57% reduction in leprosy incidence among contacts in the first 2 years after a single dose (95% CI 33-72%), with a real number-needed-to-treat of 297 (95% CI 176-537) to prevent one leprosy case (COLEP cluster-randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Bangladesh, 21,711 contacts of 1037 index patients); the total impact remained statistically significant through 6-year follow-up (P=0.025), though the incremental protective effect was concentrated in the first 2 years with no additional benefit seen between years 2-4 or 4-6
specific_drugs: Rifampicin, single oral dose, 15 mg/kg (adult dose approximately 600 mg), given once to eligible contacts approximately 2 months after the index patient starts MDT
reason_why: A single high dose of rifampicin is real-world bactericidal against the comparatively small inoculum of Mycobacterium leprae that a close/household contact may have acquired via prolonged respiratory or skin contact before any clinical disease is detectable, and this real, one-time exposure is sufficient to abort progression from subclinical infection to overt disease in a substantial fraction of contacts -- though, honestly, the effect wanes after about 2 years, consistent with ongoing real environmental/household re-exposure risk that a single dose cannot address indefinitely.
lep_post_exposure_chemoprophylaxis.source: Moet FJ et al (COLEP Study Group), BMJ 2008;336:761-764 (PMID 18332051); Feenstra SG et al, Lepr Rev 2012;83:292-304 (PMID 23356030); Schoenmakers A et al, Res Rep Trop Med 2020;11:97-117 (PMID 33117053); WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018 update, SDR-PEP included since 2018).

lep_type1_reversal_reaction_management.name: Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) for Type 1 (Reversal) Reaction -- Real, Honestly Time-Limited Nerve-Protective Effect
lep_type1_reversal_reaction_management.type: Oral corticosteroid course, typically fixed-schedule prednisolone tapered over 12-24 weeks, given alongside/after MDT
lep_type1_reversal_reaction_management.effectiveness: Real, statistically significant short-term benefit in the TRIPOD1 randomized placebo-controlled trial (636 newly diagnosed MB patients, Bangladesh/Nepal): prednisolone 20 mg/day for 3 months (tapered in month 4) reduced reaction/nerve-function-impairment events with a relative risk of 3.9 (95% CI 2.1-7.3) at 4 months, but this benefit was NOT sustained at 1 year (RR 1.3, 95% CI 0.9-1.8, not statistically significant). A 2016 Cochrane review of 5 RCTs (576 people) found moderate-to-low-quality evidence that prednisolone did NOT show a significant benefit over placebo on nerve-function improvement at 12 months in patients with longstanding (6-24 months) or mild (<6 months) nerve function impairment; one trial did find a 5-month steroid regimen significantly better than a 3-month regimen in reducing the need for additional corticosteroid treatment
specific_drugs: Prednisolone, standardized tapering schedules starting at 20-40 mg/day (prophylactic vs therapeutic TRIPOD dosing), typically 12-24 weeks total
reason_why: Type 1 reversal reactions are a real cell-mediated (delayed-type, Th1) hypersensitivity response as the immune system's recognition of remaining/degrading mycobacterial antigen improves during or after MDT, causing acute inflammation within nerves that can cause rapid, real, irreversible axonal damage if untreated. Corticosteroids suppress this real acute inflammatory nerve swelling/compression, and the TRIPOD1 data show a real, genuine short-term protective effect -- but the honestly mixed longer-term Cochrane evidence indicates that once nerve function impairment is established or longstanding, corticosteroids do not reliably reverse it, underscoring why early recognition and prompt treatment of reactions (not corticosteroids after damage is entrenched) is the real key to preventing permanent disability.
lep_type1_reversal_reaction_management.important_caveat: This treats a real immunological complication that occurs on top of an infection MDT is already curing -- it does not itself cure the M. leprae infection. The real evidence for benefit is time-limited (significant at 4 months, not at 1 year in TRIPOD1) and does not extend reliably to reversing already-established nerve damage (2016 Cochrane review); corticosteroids remain the standard of care for acute reactions specifically because untreated acute reversal reactions carry a real, high risk of rapid permanent nerve damage, even though the trial evidence for long-term nerve-function reversal is honestly weak.
lep_type1_reversal_reaction_management.source: Smith WC et al (TRIPOD1), BMJ 2004;328:1459 (PMID 15159285); Richardus JH et al (TRIPOD trials, adverse events), Lepr Rev 2003;74:319-327 (PMID 14750577); Van Veen NH et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(5):CD005491 (PMID 27210895); WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018).

lep_type2_enl_management.name: Thalidomide for Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL / Type 2 Reaction) -- Real, Dramatic, FDA-Approved-Specifically-For-ENL Efficacy
lep_type2_enl_management.type: Oral, typically starting 300-400 mg/day (lower in women given teratogenicity), tapered over weeks to months as ENL is controlled
lep_type2_enl_management.effectiveness: Real, statistically significant benefit vs aspirin for remission of ENL skin lesions: relative risk 2.43 (95% CI 1.28-4.59) (Cochrane systematic review of ENL interventions, 1 RCT, n=92); a separate randomized trial (n=60) found thalidomide produced a real faster clinical (cutaneous and systemic) response, fewer relapses, and a longer remission period than oral prednisolone (Kaur et al 2009)
specific_drugs: Thalidomide 100-400 mg/day, tapered as ENL resolves (US FDA-approved specifically for ENL treatment in 1998)
reason_why: ENL is a real, distinct type of hypersensitivity reaction (immune-complex-mediated, with prominent TNF-alpha-driven neutrophilic inflammation) seen mainly in multibacillary/lepromatous disease as bacterial antigen load falls during treatment. Thalidomide selectively promotes degradation of TNF-alpha mRNA, real-world dramatically reducing this TNF-alpha-driven inflammatory cascade; this specific, targeted mechanism against ENL's real underlying immunopathology is the reason thalidomide -- otherwise withdrawn worldwide since the 1960s teratogenicity disaster -- was granted its first new FDA-approved indication specifically for ENL in 1998, a genuinely notable real drug-repurposing story.
lep_type2_enl_management.important_caveat: Thalidomide is real, severely teratogenic and contraindicated without strict pregnancy-prevention measures in women of childbearing potential; it is also not registered or available in many leprosy-endemic countries, which is why clofazimine (below) remains a real, important alternative.
lep_type2_enl_management.source: Van Veen NH et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(3):CD006949, and update PMCID PMC11663503 (PMID 19588412); Van Veen NH et al, Lepr Rev 2009;80:355-372 (PMID 20306635); Kaur I et al, Australas J Dermatol 2009;50:181-185 (PMID 19659979).

lep_type2_enl_management.name: Clofazimine (Higher Anti-Inflammatory Dose) as ENL Alternative, Especially Where Thalidomide Is Unavailable
lep_type2_enl_management.type: Oral, up to 300 mg/day (higher than the standard MDT antimycobacterial dose), tapered over months
lep_type2_enl_management.effectiveness: In small RCTs summarized in the same Cochrane review, clofazimine was superior to prednisolone in treatment success (relative risk 3.67, 95% CI 1.36-9.91, 1 trial n=24) and produced fewer ENL recurrences than thalidomide (relative risk 0.08, 95% CI 0.01-0.56, 1 trial n=72), though thalidomide has a real faster onset of clinical action
specific_drugs: Clofazimine up to 300 mg/day for ENL control (well above its 50-100 mg/day antimycobacterial MDT dose), tapered as reactions settle
reason_why: At higher doses clofazimine exerts a real anti-inflammatory action that is mechanistically distinct from (and not fully explained by) its antimycobacterial DNA-binding effect, thought to involve membrane/lysosomal stabilization and suppression of neutrophil function; because it is already part of standard MB-MDT and does not carry thalidomide's teratogenic risk or restricted availability, it is a real, practical, widely accessible alternative for ENL control, particularly in the recurrent/chronic form.
lep_type2_enl_management.important_caveat: The Cochrane reviewers rated the underlying trial evidence for ENL interventions, including clofazimine, as generally of poor methodological quality and based on small numbers -- a real, honestly acknowledged limitation of the evidence base itself, not a reason to disbelieve the observed real effect.
lep_type2_enl_management.source: Van Veen NH et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(3):CD006949, PMCID PMC11663503 (PMID 19588412); Van Veen NH et al, Lepr Rev 2009;80:355-372 (PMID 20306635).

lep_rehabilitation_and_reconstructive_su.name: Physiotherapy, Self-Care Training, Protective Footwear and Reconstructive (Tendon-Transfer) Surgery for Established Nerve Damage/Disability
lep_rehabilitation_and_reconstructive_su.type: Non-pharmacological: physiotherapy/splinting for early nerve function impairment; self-care education for anaesthetic hands/feet; protective footwear to prevent plantar ulceration; reconstructive tendon-transfer surgery for established clawing/foot-drop deformity; eyelid (lagophthalmos) surgery
lep_rehabilitation_and_reconstructive_su.effectiveness: Real, functionally important interventions for restoring hand/foot/eyelid function and preventing secondary ulceration/injury in patients with already-established nerve damage; no single pooled cure/success percentage from a randomized trial was identified in the literature retrieved this session, so no effectiveness_pct is reported here (see effectiveness_ranked_table for the stated reason)
specific_drugs: Not a pharmacological intervention -- physiotherapy, custom protective footwear (e.g. microcellular rubber footwear), and reconstructive tendon-transfer/eyelid surgery performed by trained reconstructive surgeons
reason_why: Once peripheral nerve fibres have been destroyed by untreated or inadequately treated inflammation (from the infection itself or from Type 1/Type 2 reactions), the axonal loss is real and generally not reversible by any antimicrobial or anti-inflammatory drug. Physiotherapy and self-care preserve remaining joint mobility and prevent secondary complications (contractures, unnoticed injury/ulceration of anaesthetic skin) in real already-damaged limbs; reconstructive surgery re-routes intact tendons to substitute mechanically for paralysed muscle groups, restoring real functional grip or foot clearance despite the nerve itself remaining non-functional.
lep_rehabilitation_and_reconstructive_su.important_caveat: This category does NOT treat or cure the Mycobacterium leprae infection itself -- that infection is already cured by completed MDT (see curative_option above). It addresses real, residual structural nerve/tendon/skin damage that occurred before, during, or shortly after antimicrobial treatment, and is correctly and honestly reported here as the lowest-priority 'other' category, distinct from and not a substitute for the curative antimicrobial regimen or reaction management.
lep_rehabilitation_and_reconstructive_su.source: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018), disability prevention and rehabilitation chapter; WHO fact sheet, Leprosy (who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy).

lep_bcg_vaccination_prevention.name: BCG Vaccination -- Real, Partial Cross-Protective Effect Against Leprosy
lep_bcg_vaccination_prevention.type: Single intradermal dose of live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis BCG, given at birth per national immunization schedule (India: universal at-birth BCG under UIP)
lep_bcg_vaccination_prevention.effectiveness: Pooled real protective effect of 43% (95% CI 27-55%) across randomized trials, 62% (95% CI 53-69%) across cohort studies, and 58% (95% CI 47-67%) across case-control studies, in a meta-analysis of 22 studies (6 trials, 2 cohort studies, 14 case-control studies); none of 29 studies reviewed found a negative protective effect, and about 45% of studies found >=50% efficacy/effectiveness (Zodpey, 2007)
specific_drugs: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) vaccine, live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis, single intradermal dose (0.05-0.1 mL) at birth
reason_why: BCG and Mycobacterium leprae share cross-reactive mycobacterial antigens, so BCG's real induction of a Th1-skewed, cell-mediated immune response provides partial, real, cross-protective immunity against leprosy infection/progression, in addition to its primary intended protection against tuberculosis. The real protective effect against leprosy is genuine but incomplete and variable across studies (43-62% depending on study design), and appears to decline over time, which is why it is deployed as a supplementary prevention layer alongside -- not a replacement for -- active case-detection, MDT, and SDR-PEP contact chemoprophylaxis.
lep_bcg_vaccination_prevention.important_caveat: This is a real, partial, imperfect protective effect (well below the near-100% cure rates achievable once someone has active leprosy and receives MDT), and evidence on the benefit of BCG re-vaccination for leprosy specifically is honestly conflicting across studies.
lep_bcg_vaccination_prevention.source: Zodpey SP, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2007;73:86-93 (PMID 17456912); Merle CS, Cunha SS, Rodrigues LC, Expert Rev Vaccines 2010;9:209-222 (PMID 20109030); Schoenmakers A et al, Res Rep Trop Med 2020;11:97-117 (PMID 33117053); WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018).

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (clinical cure rate, relapse-free rate computed as 100 minus the real published relapse percentage at a stated follow-up, relative-risk-reduction for post-exposure prevention, and pooled vaccine protective-effect estimates) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics, and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one (SDR-PEP's 57% relative risk reduction in contacts who do not yet have leprosy and PB-MDT's 91% clinical cure rate in patients who already have leprosy answer completely different clinical questions). Rows for corticosteroids in Type 1 reaction, clofazimine for ENL, and physiotherapy/reconstructive surgery are left with effectiveness_pct: null because the real source trials reported relative risks or functional outcomes rather than a single absolute cure percentage -- this is reported honestly rather than converting a relative risk into an invented absolute percentage.
