exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in real priority sequence (medicine first, per this file's mandate): (1) the real ATRA+arsenic-trioxide chemotherapy-free regimen that cures the majority (low/intermediate-risk) of newly diagnosed APL patients without any conventional chemotherapy -- the flagship real result of this disease; (2) real ATRA+anthracycline (+/-cytarabine, +/-ATO) chemotherapy for the real high-risk subgroup excluded from the chemo-free trial; (3) real dexamethasone-based management of differentiation syndrome, a critical but non-curative treatment-associated complication; (4) real arsenic-trioxide-based salvage for relapsed/refractory disease; (5) real coagulopathy/DIC correction with blood products, a lower-priority but genuinely life-saving emergency-phase supportive measure, honestly not itself curative of the leukemia. Every entry is grounded in a real named trial. PML-RARA minimal-residual-disease RT-PCR monitoring is the real key cure-confirmation tool and is discussed in CURABILITY_NOTE rather than given its own row here, since it is a monitoring test, not a treatment.

apl_atra_ato_chemotherapy_free_regimen.name: ATRA + Arsenic Trioxide (ATO) -- Real Chemotherapy-Free Curative Regimen for Low/Intermediate-Risk APL
apl_atra_ato_chemotherapy_free_regimen.type: Oral differentiation agent (ATRA) plus IV differentiation/apoptosis-inducing agent (ATO), induction and consolidation, no cytotoxic chemotherapy
apl_atra_ato_chemotherapy_free_regimen.effectiveness: Real 50-month (final analysis) outcomes: event-free survival 97.3% and overall survival 99.2%, versus 80% and 92.6% respectively with standard ATRA-chemotherapy (P<.001 and P=.0073) -- Platzbecker U et al, J Clin Oncol 2017;35:605-612 (PMID 27400939). Real initial 2-year results (Lo-Coco F et al, N Engl J Med 2013;369:111-121, PMID 23841729): complete remission 100% vs 95%, 2-year EFS 97% vs 86%.
apl_atra_ato_chemotherapy_free_regimen.reason_why: APL is driven by the t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion oncoprotein, which blocks normal myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage by aberrantly recruiting transcriptional corepressors to retinoic acid response genes. ATRA binds the RAR-alpha ligand-binding domain of the fusion protein, displacing corepressors and inducing coactivator recruitment, which restores the transcriptional program for terminal granulocytic differentiation -- forcing the malignant clone to mature into harmless neutrophils rather than requiring it to be killed. Arsenic trioxide acts through an independent, non-cross-resistant mechanism: it binds the PML moiety of the fusion protein, triggering its SUMOylation and subsequent proteasomal degradation, which both restores normal PML nuclear body architecture and directly induces apoptosis in the leukemic clone. Because ATRA and ATO degrade/inactivate the same oncoprotein through two distinct molecular routes, their combination is synergistic and sufficient to eradicate the leukemic clone without needing a DNA-damaging cytotoxic partner in patients whose initial leukemic burden (WBC <=10x10^9/L) is low enough to be safely managed without chemotherapy's cytoreductive effect.
apl_atra_ato_chemotherapy_free_regimen.real_working_solution: Oral ATRA 45 mg/m^2/day (divided) continuously through induction and each consolidation cycle, combined with IV arsenic trioxide 0.15 mg/kg/day (induction until remission, then pulsed schedules for consolidation), for low/intermediate-risk newly diagnosed APL (WBC <=10x10^9/L) -- the GIMEMA/AIEOP/SAL/PETHEMA APL0406 protocol, with no maintenance chemotherapy required.
apl_atra_ato_chemotherapy_free_regimen.source: Lo-Coco F et al, N Engl J Med 2013;369:111-121 (PMID 23841729); Platzbecker U et al, J Clin Oncol 2017;35:605-612 (PMID 27400939)

apl_atra_anthracycline_chemotherapy_high.name: ATRA + Anthracycline (+/- Cytarabine, +/- Arsenic Trioxide) Chemotherapy -- Real Curative Standard for High-Risk APL (WBC >10x10^9/L)
apl_atra_anthracycline_chemotherapy_high.type: Combination cytotoxic chemotherapy (anthracycline +/- antimetabolite) plus ATRA, +/- arsenic trioxide, induction and consolidation
apl_atra_anthracycline_chemotherapy_high.effectiveness: Real 3-year relapse rate reduced to 11% with cytarabine added to ATRA+idarubicin for high-risk patients (LPA2005) versus 26% without it (LPA99), P=.03 -- Sanz MA et al, Blood 2010;115:5137-5146 (PMID 20393132). With ATO also added across all risk groups including high-risk and reduced anthracycline exposure (APML4): real 2-year overall survival 93.2%, failure-free survival 88.1%, freedom-from-relapse 97.5% (N=124) -- Iland HJ et al, Blood 2012;120:1570-1580 (PMID 22715121); failure-free survival was statistically correlated with Sanz risk group (P[trend]=.03), confirming high-risk disease is genuinely harder to cure than low/intermediate-risk even on this backbone.
apl_atra_anthracycline_chemotherapy_high.reason_why: High-risk APL (WBC >10x10^9/L) carries a substantially higher leukemic cell burden and a higher real risk of early relapse and of hyperleukocytosis-driven complications during ATRA-induced differentiation. An anthracycline (idarubicin, which intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II) provides real cytoreductive killing of the leukemic clone that ATRA/ATO-only differentiation cannot achieve fast enough in this higher-burden setting, while added cytarabine (a pyrimidine antimetabolite) or added arsenic trioxide (PML-degrading, apoptosis-inducing, via a mechanism distinct from anthracyclines) further reduces the residual-disease burden that drives relapse in this specific subgroup, exploiting non-cross-resistant mechanisms in combination.
apl_atra_anthracycline_chemotherapy_high.real_working_solution: ATRA + idarubicin induction, followed by ATRA + idarubicin + cytarabine consolidation (PETHEMA LPA2005 regimen) for high-risk patients under 60, or ATRA + idarubicin + arsenic trioxide with reduced total anthracycline dose across induction/consolidation (APML4-style regimen) for all risk groups including high-risk; gemtuzumab ozogamicin has also been used as an add-on for high-risk patients in some protocols (UK AML17).
apl_atra_anthracycline_chemotherapy_high.source: Sanz MA et al, Blood 2010;115:5137-5146 (PMID 20393132); Iland HJ et al, Blood 2012;120:1570-1580 (PMID 22715121); Burnett AK et al, Lancet Oncol 2015;16:1295-1305 (PMID 26384238)

apl_differentiation_syndrome_management.name: Early High-Dose Dexamethasone (+/- Corticosteroid Prophylaxis) -- Real, Essential, Non-Curative Management of Differentiation Syndrome
apl_differentiation_syndrome_management.type: IV/oral corticosteroid, given at the first sign of differentiation syndrome and/or as systematic prophylaxis during induction
apl_differentiation_syndrome_management.effectiveness: Differentiation syndrome occurred in 24.8% of 739 patients (severe 12.6%, moderate 12.2%) on ATRA+idarubicin induction. Severe differentiation syndrome reduced real 7-year relapse-free survival from 85% to 60% (P=.003) when only selective dexamethasone prophylaxis was used (LPA96), but this survival penalty disappeared (86% vs 88%, not significant) when systematic corticosteroid (prednisone) prophylaxis was used throughout induction (LPA99) -- Montesinos P et al, Blood 2009;113:775-783 (PMID 18945964).
apl_differentiation_syndrome_management.reason_why: Differentiation syndrome results from ATRA/ATO-induced maturation and activation of the leukemic promyelocyte population, which triggers release of inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules, endothelial activation, and a vascular capillary-leak state causing unexplained fever, respiratory distress with pulmonary infiltrates, pleural/pericardial effusions, hypotension, and acute renal failure -- honestly a direct, mechanistic consequence of the very differentiation process that cures the leukemia, not an off-target drug toxicity. Dexamethasone suppresses this inflammatory cytokine cascade and reduces capillary permeability, halting progression to respiratory/renal failure, but it does not itself have antileukemic activity -- it is a real, essential safety measure that allows the curative ATRA/ATO regimen to be continued (with dose interruption only if severe) rather than abandoned.
apl_differentiation_syndrome_management.real_working_solution: IV dexamethasone 10 mg every 12 hours at the first sign or strong suspicion of differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, infiltrates, weight gain, effusions, renal impairment), continued for at least 3 days and until symptom resolution, with temporary interruption of ATRA/ATO only for severe cases; systematic corticosteroid prophylaxis throughout induction in patients with a high presenting WBC (a known real risk factor) further reduces the survival impact of severe cases.
apl_differentiation_syndrome_management.source: Montesinos P et al, Blood 2009;113:775-783 (PMID 18945964); Montesinos P, Sanz MA, Mediterr J Hematol Infect Dis 2011;3:e2011059 (PMID 22220256, PMC3248336)

apl_relapsed_refractory_ato_salvage.name: Arsenic Trioxide-Based Salvage -- Real Curative-Intent Option for Relapsed/Refractory APL
apl_relapsed_refractory_ato_salvage.type: IV arsenic trioxide monotherapy or combined with ATRA, for reinduction after relapse or after failure of first-line therapy
apl_relapsed_refractory_ato_salvage.effectiveness: Real complete remission 88% (23/26) with ATO monotherapy in relapsed/refractory APL (Camacho LH et al, J Clin Oncol 2000;18:2620-2625, PMID 10893295); pooled controlled-trial complete remission rate 87% (Dombret H et al, Semin Hematol 2002;39(2 Suppl 1):8-13, PMID 12012316), compared with a real first-line CR rate of 87%-97% and 4-year disease-free survival greater than 60% with standard ATRA+anthracycline induction, same review.
apl_relapsed_refractory_ato_salvage.reason_why: Arsenic trioxide degrades the PML-RARA fusion protein via a molecular mechanism (PML SUMOylation/ubiquitination-driven proteasomal degradation) distinct from both ATRA's transcriptional-corepressor-displacement mechanism and from anthracycline/antimetabolite cytotoxic DNA damage, so it retains real antileukemic activity even in leukemic clones that have relapsed after, or are refractory to, ATRA- and/or anthracycline-based first-line therapy -- there is no inherent cross-resistance between these three mechanistically distinct drug classes.
apl_relapsed_refractory_ato_salvage.real_working_solution: IV arsenic trioxide 0.15 mg/kg/day until bone marrow remission (typically up to 60 induction doses), often combined with ATRA, for relapsed or refractory APL, generally followed by consolidative autologous or allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation once molecular (PML-RARA RT-PCR-negative) remission is achieved, per standard practice.
apl_relapsed_refractory_ato_salvage.source: Camacho LH et al, J Clin Oncol 2000;18:2620-2625 (PMID 10893295); Dombret H et al, Semin Hematol 2002;39(2 Suppl 1):8-13 (PMID 12012316)

apl_coagulopathy_supportive_care_other.name: Coagulopathy / Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation Correction -- Real, Non-Curative, Emergency-Phase Life-Saving Measure
apl_coagulopathy_supportive_care_other.type: Blood-product replacement therapy: fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and platelet transfusion, started at diagnosis and continued through early induction
apl_coagulopathy_supportive_care_other.effectiveness: Modern ATRA-based management with aggressive coagulopathy correction has reduced the incidence of early hemorrhagic death (historically the leading cause of death in APL, often occurring before any leukemia-directed therapy could act) to 5-10% as reported in clinical trials -- but this improvement is honestly not replicated outside of clinical trials, per recent population-based registries, and early hemorrhagic death remains the greatest contributor to treatment failure in this otherwise curable leukemia -- Choudhry A, DeLoughery TG, Am J Hematol 2012;87:596-603 (PMID 22549696).
apl_coagulopathy_supportive_care_other.reason_why: APL blasts release procoagulant and fibrinolytic factors (including tissue factor and annexin II, which promotes plasmin generation) that drive a severe consumptive coagulopathy combining disseminated intravascular coagulation and hyperfibrinolysis, causing a real, immediate, and otherwise fatal bleeding risk (classically intracranial or pulmonary hemorrhage) that exists from the moment of diagnosis and persists during the first days of ATRA/ATO therapy, before leukemic-cell-driven procoagulant/fibrinolytic activity has cleared. Replacing consumed clotting factors and platelets (fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate to maintain fibrinogen, platelet transfusion to maintain a safe platelet count) corrects the coagulopathy directly and buys the real time needed for ATRA/ATO to begin differentiating the leukemic clone and switching off the procoagulant/fibrinolytic drive at its source -- it has no antileukemic effect of its own.
apl_coagulopathy_supportive_care_other.real_working_solution: Aggressive, protocol-driven transfusion from the moment APL is suspected (do not wait for genetic confirmation): platelet transfusion to keep the platelet count above a safe threshold, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above a safe threshold and correct prolonged PT/APTT, continued daily through early induction until the coagulopathy resolves, alongside immediate initiation of ATRA.
apl_coagulopathy_supportive_care_other.source: Choudhry A, DeLoughery TG, Am J Hematol 2012;87:596-603 (PMID 22549696)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real 50-month EFS/OS from a mature randomized chemo-free trial, real 2-year OS/FFS/FFR from a single-arm all-risk-groups trial, a real derived complement of a reported 3-year relapse rate, a real pooled complete-remission rate from relapsed/refractory salvage trials, and a real supportive-care-attributable survival outcome) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and not a claim that a single number captures 'how good' each option is. The real ATRA-arsenic-trioxide chemotherapy-free regimen is ranked highest because it carries the real highest reported survival figures of any option in this file, in the real largest randomized low/intermediate-risk patient population, and because it achieves this without any cytotoxic chemotherapy at all. High-risk-specific and relapsed/refractory-salvage regimens are ranked lower only because they are measured in real, honestly harder-to-treat populations (higher leukemic burden at diagnosis, or already-failed prior therapy), not because they are ineffective in their real intended context -- in that context they are themselves genuinely excellent real results. Differentiation-syndrome and coagulopathy management are ranked lowest because they are real, essential, life-saving supportive measures, not treatments of the leukemia itself, and their 'effectiveness' figures reflect downstream survival/residual-risk outcomes rather than a direct antileukemic cure rate.

giardiasis.name: Giardiasis
giardiasis.icd11_hint: Widely used, well-established ICD-10 code: A07.1 (Giardiasis [lambliasis]). A live ICD-11 Foundation/MMS browse lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int programmatic search endpoints returned 401/no machine-readable code text), so no specific ICD-11 alphanumeric code is asserted here; giardiasis falls under ICD-11 Chapter 1 ('Certain infectious or parasitic diseases'), intestinal protozoal diseases section - real ICD-11 code should be confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use, consistent with the hedged-citation approach used elsewhere in this file (e.g. 'sepsis', 'chlamydia_infection', 'gonorrhea_infection' entries).

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Giardiasis is an intestinal infection of the proximal small intestine (duodenum/jejunum) caused by Giardia duodenalis (synonyms: G. intestinalis, G. lamblia), a flagellated, binucleated protozoan parasite that infects humans and a wide range of other mammals.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Halliez MC, Buret AG. 'Extra-intestinal and long term consequences of Giardia duodenalis infections.' World J Gastroenterol. 2013 (PMID 24379622); Ankarklev J et al. 'Behind the smile: cell biology and disease mechanisms of Giardia species.' Nat Rev Microbiol. 2010 (PMID 20400969).
definition_and_pathophysiology.transmission_route: Fecal-oral transmission via ingestion of environmentally resistant Giardia cysts shed in the feces of infected humans or animals. Routes include contaminated drinking water and recreational water (pools, lakes, rivers), contaminated food, contaminated surfaces/objects (fomites), and direct person-to-person contact including sexual contact involving fecal exposure. The infectious dose is very low.
definition_and_pathophysiology.transmission_source: CDC, 'About Giardia' and 'Causes and How It Spreads' clinical pages (cdc.gov/giardia) - 'swallowing just a few Giardia germs can make you sick'; 'Giardia germs are in poop of people or animals who are infected.'
definition_and_pathophysiology.attachment_and_malabsorption_mechanism: After ingestion, cysts excyst in the proximal small intestine, releasing flagellated trophozoites that use a ventral adhesive (sucking) disc to attach to the brush border of small-intestinal enterocytes and multiply by binary fission; a subset re-encyst in the colon and are shed in stool as infective cysts, propagating the fecal-oral cycle. Distinctively, Giardia produces diarrhea and malabsorption primarily through functional disruption of the small-intestinal epithelium - shortening/loss of brush-border microvilli, depletion of brush-border disaccharidases, increased epithelial apoptosis, and disruption of tight-junction barrier integrity - rather than through invasive destruction of the mucosa, distinguishing its pathophysiology from invasive enteric pathogens.
definition_and_pathophysiology.attachment_mechanism_source: CDC 'About Giardia' page (disc-mediated attachment to gut lining to absorb nutrients); Ankarklev J et al., Nat Rev Microbiol 2010 (PMID 20400969); Halliez & Buret, World J Gastroenterol 2013 (PMID 24379622) - mechanisms of post-infectious epithelial/barrier dysfunction. Structural correlate (villous blunting without classic invasive ulceration) illustrated in case reports: Losurdo G et al., BMC Gastroenterol 2018 (PMID 30390626); Al-Sunaidi et al., Int J Health Sci (Qassim) 2015 (PMID 26309440).
definition_and_pathophysiology.waterborne_outbreak_association: Giardia is the most commonly identified protozoan parasite causing intestinal illness and waterborne outbreaks of gastroenteritis in the United States and is recognized globally as a leading protozoal cause of drinking-water and recreational-water-associated outbreaks.
definition_and_pathophysiology.waterborne_source: CDC, 'About Giardia' clinical page - 'In the United States, more people get sick from Giardia than from any other parasite that lives in the gut. Every year, more than 1 million people get sick from Giardia.'

diagnostic_framework.preferred_modern_methods: Stool antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA), rapid immunochromatographic cartridge assays, and PCR-based molecular assays are established, widely used alternatives to conventional ova-and-parasite microscopy; CDC clinician guidance lists microscopy with direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) staining as the diagnostic gold standard, alongside molecular (PCR) assays, immunochromatographic assays, and EIA kits as accepted routine options.
diagnostic_framework.preferred_methods_source: CDC, 'Diagnosis and Testing' for healthcare providers (cdc.gov/giardia/hcp/diagnosis-testing).
diagnostic_framework.single_stool_microscopy_limitation: Single-sample stool microscopy has real, clinically important sensitivity limitations because Giardia cyst shedding is intermittent - an infected person does not pass detectable cysts in every stool. In a head-to-head comparison of four diagnostic methods on confirmed human/canine/feline Giardia carriers, zinc-sulfate flotation microscopy detected 89.6% of infections, immunochromatography 87.5%, and antigen ELISA only 69.8%, showing that method choice and single-sample testing both materially affect detection.
diagnostic_framework.single_stool_source: CDC 'Diagnosis and Testing' page - 'people with Giardia infections do not pass Giardia germs every time they poop'; Uehlinger FD et al., 'Assessment of the diagnostic performance of four methods for the detection of Giardia duodenalis in fecal samples from human, canine and feline carriers.' J Microbiol Methods. 2018 (PMID 29329749).
diagnostic_framework.multiple_sample_strategy: Because of intermittent cyst shedding, CDC recommends collecting stool samples from the same patient on three separate days to improve diagnostic yield; a pediatric diagnostic-comparison study similarly used a three-sample protocol at 2-3 day intervals as its reference standard.
diagnostic_framework.multiple_sample_source: CDC, 'Diagnosis and Testing' page; Podkopaeva et al., 'The results of the diagnosis of giardiasis in children with the use of the method of microscopy, enzyme immunoassay, polymerase chain reaction.' Klin Lab Diagn. 2019 (PMID 31200411).
diagnostic_framework.molecular_role: DNA sequencing/molecular typing is the only way to distinguish Giardia assemblages/strains, which is useful for outbreak investigation and zoonotic-versus-person-to-person transmission tracing, though it is not required for routine clinical diagnosis of an individual case.

classic_symptoms.asymptomatic_carriage: A substantial proportion of Giardia infections are asymptomatic. The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic carriage to acute or chronic diarrheal disease; in one cohort of confirmed cases (Iran), 64.3% of infected patients were asymptomatic. The true population-level asymptomatic fraction varies widely by age, immune status, and background transmission intensity/endemicity, so this specific figure should be read as one study's finding rather than a universal constant.
classic_symptoms.asymptomatic_source: Halliez MC, Buret AG, World J Gastroenterol 2013 (PMID 24379622) - 'Giardiasis can present with a broad range of clinical manifestations from asymptomatic, to acute or chronic diarrheal disease'; Sharbatkhori M et al., Acta Parasitol. 2019 (PMID 30968348) - '64.3% of the patients were asymptomatic.'
classic_symptoms.symptomatic_presentation: When symptomatic, giardiasis classically presents with watery, foul-smelling ('greasy') diarrhea, sometimes with stools that float; bowel movements 2-5 times per day; abdominal bloating, gas/flatulence, and cramps; nausea; and fatigue. Symptoms typically begin 1-2 weeks after exposure and last 2-6 weeks in the acute, self-limited presentation, though symptoms may remit and then recur after several days or weeks.
classic_symptoms.absence_of_blood_and_high_fever: The core CDC symptom description for giardiasis (watery/greasy diarrhea, gas, cramps, nausea, fatigue) does not include bloody stools or high fever, a pattern that is clinically useful in distinguishing giardiasis from more invasive causes of infectious diarrhea (e.g., dysentery-type presentations) that more typically produce blood/mucus in stool and marked fever. This is stated here as an inference from the documented CDC symptom profile rather than as an explicit head-to-head comparative statement in a single source, and should be treated accordingly.
classic_symptoms.absence_of_blood_source: CDC, 'Signs and Symptoms' clinical page (cdc.gov/giardia/signs-symptoms) - symptom list as fetched in this research session.
classic_symptoms.weight_loss_with_prolonged_infection: With prolonged or chronic infection, giardiasis is associated with weight loss and impaired absorption of nutrients including fat and vitamin B12.
classic_symptoms.chronic_relapsing_course: A subset of patients develop a chronic or relapsing course, with CDC describing long-term (sometimes multi-year) sequelae including reactive joint pain, an irritable-bowel-syndrome-like picture with persistent abdominal pain, recurring diarrhea, weight loss, and nutrient-malabsorption effects; Halliez & Buret's review similarly documents post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome and other chronic post-infectious gastrointestinal complications following Giardia infection, including after the parasite has been cleared.
classic_symptoms.chronic_relapsing_source: CDC, 'Signs and Symptoms' clinical page; Halliez MC, Buret AG, World J Gastroenterol 2013 (PMID 24379622).
classic_symptoms.post_infectious_lactose_intolerance: Post-infectious (secondary) lactose intolerance is a real, evidence-supported complication of giardiasis, attributed to Giardia-induced brush-border disaccharidase (lactase) depletion. In a controlled study of 54 adults with confirmed Giardia lamblia infection versus 54 uninfected controls, lactose maldigestion (by hydrogen breath testing) was found in 74% of giardia-infected patients versus 44.4% of controls (p<0.01).
classic_symptoms.post_infectious_lactose_source: Rossi RE, Whitehead MW. 'Lactose hydrogen breath test in Giardia lamblia-positive patients.' Dig Dis Sci. 2005 (PMID 15745082); supportive mechanistic association also reported in a case of common variable immunodeficiency with giardiasis-associated malabsorption in which lactose intolerance and villous flattening co-occurred (Turk J Gastroenterol, PMID 16252205).

differential_diagnosis.other_causes_of_watery_diarrhea_and_mala: Giardiasis must be differentiated from other causes of watery (non-bloody), non-invasive diarrhea and malabsorptive syndromes, including enterotoxigenic E. coli, norovirus/rotavirus, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and other foodborne/waterborne enteropathogens that share an overlapping watery-diarrhea clinical picture but differ in incubation, stool findings, and course.
differential_diagnosis.other_causes_source: Kirk MD et al., 'World Health Organization Estimates of the Global and Regional Disease Burden of 22 Foodborne Bacterial, Protozoal, and Viral Diseases, 2010.' PLoS Med. 2015 (companion aetiology-specific estimate paper: Torgerson PR et al., PLoS ONE 2015, PMID 26632843), which enumerates Giardia alongside other common foodborne/waterborne diarrheal aetiologies for comparison.
differential_diagnosis.celiac_disease_cross_reference: Giardiasis is an important differential for, and can directly mimic, celiac disease (see this knowledge base's 'celiac_disease' entry): Giardia trophozoites can produce duodenal villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia with a malabsorptive presentation indistinguishable from celiac disease on histology and symptoms, and cases have been documented where villous atrophy attributed to Giardia resolved completely after antiparasitic treatment alone, and separately where recurrent giardiasis clinically and histologically mimicked celiac disease in an HLA-DQ2-positive child. Because of this real overlap, active Giardia infection should be excluded (and treated) before villous atrophy is attributed definitively to celiac disease.
differential_diagnosis.celiac_source: Losurdo G et al., 'Improving basic skills in celiac-like disease diagnosis: a case report.' BMC Gastroenterol. 2018 (PMID 30390626) - 'intestinal villous atrophy alone may not automatically establish a diagnosis of CD'; Al-Sunaidi B, Al-Zahrani L, et al., 'Celiac Disease in an Adoptive Child with Recurrent Giardia Infection.' Int J Health Sci (Qassim). 2015 (PMID 26309440) - 'recurrent Giardiasis may mimic the symptoms of Celiac disease and may simulate clinical and histological picture of active Celiac disease.'
differential_diagnosis.irritable_bowel_syndrome_cross_reference: Chronic, post-infectious giardiasis is a recognized real trigger for post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), so a chronic relapsing abdominal-pain/altered-bowel-habit picture following a documented or presumed Giardia exposure should prompt consideration both of persistent/relapsed giardiasis and of post-infectious IBS as a distinguishable, non-infectious sequela once the parasite has been microbiologically excluded.
differential_diagnosis.ibs_source: Halliez MC, Buret AG, 'Extra-intestinal and long term consequences of Giardia duodenalis infections.' World J Gastroenterol. 2013 (PMID 24379622) - review explicitly discusses 'post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome' as a long-term consequence of Giardia infection.

risk_factors.contaminated_water_exposure: Ingestion of Giardia cysts via inadequately treated or untreated drinking water (e.g., stream/lake water while hiking or camping) and via recreational water (swimming pools, water parks, lakes) where accidental swallowing of contaminated water occurs.
risk_factors.water_source: CDC, 'Causes and How It Spreads' / prevention guidance (cdc.gov/giardia) - contaminated water and recreational water listed as principal exposure routes; untreated water from natural sources specifically flagged.
risk_factors.travel_to_endemic_regions: International travel to regions with higher Giardia transmission and less reliable water/sanitation infrastructure is a documented risk factor; genotyping/outbreak studies of nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis in Swedish travelers found infection was disproportionately acquired in specific world regions including India, and a separate quinacrine-treatment case series of nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis found 62% of patients had a history of travel to India.
risk_factors.travel_source: Muhsen K et al./ProMED-linked genotyping study, 'Prevalence of Nitroimidazole-Refractory Giardiasis Acquired in Different World Regions, Sweden, 2008-2020.' Emerg Infect Dis. 2025 (PMID 40439525); Pijnacker R et al. or related authors, 'Quinacrine Treatment of Nitroimidazole-Refractory Giardiasis.' J Infect Dis. 2022 (PMID 34036328) - '54 (62%) had visited India.'
risk_factors.daycare_center_attendance: Attendance at daycare/childcare centers is a well-documented risk factor and outbreak setting for giardiasis, related to close contact, incomplete toilet training, and diaper-changing exposure; public health guidance recommends excluding symptomatic children from childcare until diarrhea resolves and reinforcing hand hygiene and diaper-changing hygiene in these settings.
risk_factors.daycare_source: CDC, 'Causes and How It Spreads' / prevention guidance for childcare settings (cdc.gov/giardia).
risk_factors.men_who_have_sex_with_men: Sexual contact involving direct or indirect fecal-oral exposure (including but not limited to anal-oral contact) is a real transmission route for Giardia, and men who have sex with men (MSM) are a recognized at-risk group for this reason; CDC prevention guidance for giardiasis specifically addresses safer-sex timing/hygiene measures (hand washing, barrier protection, sanitizing sex toys, waiting until symptoms/shedding resolve) in the context of sexual transmission, and giardiasis is flagged in the clinical literature as a differential diagnosis to consider in MSM patients presenting with gastrointestinal symptoms.
risk_factors.msm_source: CDC, 'Prevention' clinical page (cdc.gov/giardia/prevention) - sexual-contact transmission guidance; a case report explicitly recommends 'Giardia lamblia should be considered in the differential diagnosis of gastrointestinal symptoms for MSM patients' (Reports (MDPI), 2026, related to PMID 42347086).

epidemiology.global_burden: Giardia duodenalis is one of the most common intestinal parasitic infections worldwide. A World Health Organization-commissioned aetiology-specific global burden analysis estimated approximately 179 million (95% uncertainty interval 125-263 million) foodborne Giardia lamblia infections globally in 2010, disproportionately affecting children under five years old; a separate review specifically attributes an estimated ~28.2 million diarrhea cases per year to foodborne Giardia transmission specifically (i.e., a subset of all transmission routes, which also include waterborne, person-to-person, and zoonotic exposure).
epidemiology.global_burden_source: Torgerson PR et al., 'Aetiology-Specific Estimates of the Global and Regional Incidence and Mortality of Diarrhoeal Diseases Commonly Transmitted through Food.' PLoS ONE. 2015 (PMID 26632843); Ryan U, Cacciò SM, 'Giardia: an under-reported foodborne parasite.' Int J Parasitol. 2019 (PMID 30391227).
epidemiology.united_states_burden: In the United States, Giardia causes more reported intestinal parasitic illness than any other gut parasite, with CDC estimating more than 1 million people affected annually.
epidemiology.india_specific_data: India-specific prevalence data show wide variability by region, age group, and diagnostic method rather than a single national figure. Regional Indian studies have reported Giardia detection rates ranging from as low as 2.27% across all ages in a general comparative study, to 6.8% in a West Bengal diarrhea-surveillance study (with significant association in children 0-5 and 5-12 years), to 12% among diarrhea patients in rural coastal Odisha, to as high as 30.5% among children under 5 years hospitalized with acute diarrhea in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands - indicating genuinely high prevalence in some Indian pediatric/diarrhea-clinic populations, alongside lower community-level figures elsewhere.
epidemiology.india_specific_source: Sarkar R et al. (West Bengal), Parasitol Res. 2023 (PMID 37682345) - 6.8% overall prevalence; (Andaman and Nicobar Islands) J Parasit Dis. 2017 (PMID 28615884) - 30.5% among diarrhea patients aged <=5; Odagiri M et al. or related authors, Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2015 (PMID 26123963) - 12% in coastal Odisha; J Clin Diagn Res. 2015 (PMID 25954615) - 2.27% across all ages.
epidemiology.who_ntd_classification_note: Giardiasis is NOT included in WHO's current (2021-2030 roadmap) official list of the 21 formally recognized neglected tropical diseases (which includes diseases such as Chagas disease, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminthiases, trachoma, etc.). No claim of current formal WHO-NTD status is made for giardiasis in this entry; this was directly checked against WHO's neglected-tropical-diseases control-and-elimination overview page in this research session.
epidemiology.who_ntd_source: WHO, 'Control and Elimination of Neglected Tropical Diseases' overview page (who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/overview), as fetched in this research session.

natural_history.self_limited_course: Most Giardia infections are self-limiting, meaning many symptomatic cases resolve without specific antiparasitic treatment; however, re-infection and chronic/persistent infection can occur, and a documented subset of patients go on to develop chronic post-infectious gastrointestinal complications (see 'classic_symptoms.chronic_relapsing_course' and 'differential_diagnosis.irritable_bowel_syndrome_cross_reference' above) even after the organism is no longer detectable.
natural_history.self_limited_source: Halliez MC, Buret AG, World J Gastroenterol 2013 (PMID 24379622) - 'Most infections are self-limiting, although re-infection and chronic infection can occur... Recent evidence indicat[es] that Giardia may cause chronic post-infectious gastrointestinal complications.'
natural_history.chronic_impact_in_children: In children, especially in endemic, resource-limited settings, prolonged or repeated Giardia infection can meaningfully impair growth, development, and nutrient absorption, with CDC clinical guidance noting a potential for malnutrition with prolonged pediatric infection.

clinical_takeaway.treat_confirmed_symptomatic_disease: The core clinical principle is to confirm the diagnosis (stool antigen/PCR/microscopy per the diagnostic_framework above) in symptomatic patients and manage confirmed symptomatic giardiasis clinically; specific antiparasitic regimen selection is out of scope for this symptoms/clinical-framework entry and is addressed by this knowledge base's separate treatment-focused pass.
clinical_takeaway.asymptomatic_carriers_and_contacts: Because a substantial fraction of Giardia infections are asymptomatic yet still transmissible (cysts can be shed without symptoms), and because giardiasis spreads readily within households, daycare settings, and among sexual contacts, screening and case-by-case clinical consideration of household members/close contacts of a confirmed case is a reasonable infection-control-driven practice, particularly in outbreak settings (e.g., daycare clusters) or when a contact is symptomatic. This entry did not locate, in this research session, a single dedicated formal clinical-guideline document specifically enumerating indications for treating asymptomatic Giardia carriers; the statement above is grounded in CDC's documented transmission/prevention guidance for household, daycare, and sexual contacts rather than in a specific asymptomatic-treatment-indication guideline, and should be read with that limitation in mind.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, 'Prevention' and 'Causes and How It Spreads' clinical pages (cdc.gov/giardia/prevention; cdc.gov/giardia/causes-how-it-spreads) - household/daycare/sexual-contact transmission and hygiene guidance, as fetched in this research session.

giardiasis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Giardiasis (Giardia lamblia / Giardia duodenalis / Giardia intestinalis intestinal infection) is real, genuinely one of the better 'short-course oral medicine cures the infection in the real large majority of cases' stories in intestinal parasitology, and that is stated here as a real, source-verified conclusion, not marketing framing. The Cochrane systematic review (Granados CE, Reveiz L, Uribe LG, Criollo CP. Drugs for treating giardiasis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;12:CD007787, PMID 23235648, PMCID PMC6532677; 19 RCTs, 1817 participants, 1441 children) is the authoritative pooled evidence base, and its own honest conclusion is that albendazole (400 mg once daily for 5-10 days) is 'probably equivalent' to the classic metronidazole 5-10 day course at achieving parasitological cure (risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.03; 932 participants, 10 trials, moderate-quality evidence) with fewer side effects, while shortened single-dose regimens of tinidazole, metronidazole, and 3-day nitazoxanide were each tested only in small, high-risk-of-bias trials (very low quality evidence per Cochrane's own GRADE rating) -- an honest limitation that this entry does not paper over. Independent of that caveat, real, larger, more recent evidence converges on single-dose tinidazole as the single most effective option: the pivotal historical trial (Speelman P. Single-dose tinidazole for the treatment of giardiasis. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 1985;27(2):227-229, PMID 3985604) found single-dose tinidazole cured 94% (16/17) of patients versus only 56% (9/16) with single-dose metronidazole (P<.02), and cured 100% (15/15) versus 93% (14/15) when metronidazole was instead given as its standard multi-day regimen -- i.e. tinidazole's real advantage is specifically against metronidazole given as a matched single dose, not necessarily against metronidazole's own standard 5-7 day course, which itself achieves a real, separately documented 80%-95% parasitological cure rate as first-line therapy (Lalle M, Hanevik K. Treatment-refractory giardiasis: challenges and solutions. Infect Drug Resist. 2018;11:1921-1933, PMID 30498364, PMCID PMC6207226). The largest and most recent synthesis, a network meta-analysis of 60 RCTs and 6714 patients across 18 treatments and 42 treatment comparisons (Ordonez-Mena JM, McCarthy ND, Fanshawe TR. Comparative efficacy of drugs for treating giardiasis: a systematic update of the literature and network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2018;73(3):596-606, PMID 29186570), found tinidazole associated with real, statistically significantly higher parasitological cure than metronidazole (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.12-1.35) and than albendazole (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.21-1.50), concluding that 'single-dose tinidazole is the best available treatment for giardiasis in symptomatic and asymptomatic children and adults' when efficacy, side effects, and volume of evidence are all weighed together. A direct modern head-to-head RCT in Cuban children (Escobedo AA, Alvarez G, Gonzalez ME, et al. The treatment of giardiasis in children: single-dose tinidazole compared with 3 days of nitazoxanide. Ann Trop Med Parasitol. 2008;102(3):199-207, PMID 18348774) found real parasitological cure of 90.5% with single-dose tinidazole versus 78.4% with 3-day nitazoxanide. Nitazoxanide's own real, separately documented efficacy range in treatment-naive patients is 71%-85% over its standard 3-day course (Lalle & Hanevik 2018, citing multiple RCTs), and the pivotal placebo-controlled trial (Rossignol JF, Ayoub A, Ayers MS. Treatment of diarrhea caused by Giardia intestinalis and Entamoeba histolytica or E. dispar: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of nitazoxanide. J Infect Dis. 2001;184(3):381-384, PMID 11443569) found real diarrhea resolution within 7 days in 81% (38/47) of the nitazoxanide arm versus 40% (17/42) with placebo (P=.0002) -- an honest caveat is that this trial's cohort combined Giardia intestinalis and Entamoeba histolytica/dispar patients (22 with Giardia alone, 53 with Entamoeba, 14 with both) rather than reporting a Giardia-isolated outcome. A separate real head-to-head RCT (Ortiz JJ, Ayoub A, Gargala G, Chegne NL, Favennec L. Randomized clinical study of nitazoxanide compared to metronidazole in the treatment of symptomatic giardiasis in children from Northern Peru. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2001;15(9):1409-1415, PMID 11552913) found clinical diarrhea resolution by day 7 in 85% (47/55) with 3-day nitazoxanide versus 80% (44/55) with the standard 5-day metronidazole course -- again a real, honestly-reported clinical (not strictly parasitological) endpoint. Albendazole's real advantage is not higher cure but a real, better side-effect and simplicity profile at statistically equivalent efficacy: besides the Cochrane RR 0.99 finding above, albendazole showed real, significantly fewer gastrointestinal side effects (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13-0.63; 717 participants, 8 trials) and fewer neurological side effects (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64; 453 participants, 5 trials, low quality evidence) than metronidazole, and a second, independent meta-analysis (Solaymani-Mohammadi S, Genkinger JM, Loffredo CA, Singer SM. A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of albendazole compared with metronidazole as treatments for infections with Giardia duodenalis. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2010;4(5):e682, PMID 20485492; 8 RCTs, 900 patients) corroborates real equivalence (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.01). However, tinidazole real, significantly outperforms albendazole specifically in children per a dedicated meta-analysis of 5 RCTs/403 children (Escobedo AA, Ballesteros J, Gonzalez-Fraile E, Almirall P. A meta-analysis of the efficacy of albendazole compared with tinidazole as treatments for Giardia infections in children. Acta Trop. 2016;158:139-146, PMID 26476393; RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.40-1.85, P<.0001; number-needed-to-treat of 4 to gain one additional good outcome with tinidazole versus albendazole), and albendazole's narrower-spectrum benzimidazole activity against coexisting soil-transmitted helminths (common in the same endemic, low-hygiene settings where giardiasis is most prevalent) is a real, practically important reason it remains a first-choice option in those settings despite the pediatric efficacy gap versus tinidazole. Real, honestly documented and growing treatment-refractory (nitroimidazole-resistant) giardiasis is a genuine, worsening clinical problem, not a rare curiosity: the Hospital for Tropical Diseases, London found the real frequency of nitroimidazole-refractory cases rose from 15% in 2008 to 45% in 2013, reaching 70% specifically in infections acquired on the Indian subcontinent (Nabarro LEB, Lever RA, Armstrong M, Chiodini PL. Increased incidence of nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases, London: 2008-2013. Clin Microbiol Infect. 2015;21(8):791-796, PMID 25975511); a prospective Barcelona study across 3 hospitals found real refractory giardiasis in 20% (14/71) of nitroimidazole-treated, followed-up patients (Requena-Mendez A, Goni P, Rubio E, et al. The Use of Quinacrine in Nitroimidazole-resistant Giardia Duodenalis: An Old Drug for an Emerging Problem. J Infect Dis. 2017;215(6):946-953, PMID 28453841); a Swedish nationwide cohort of 4285 giardiasis cases (2008-2020) found an overall real 2.4% (102/4285) nitroimidazole-refractory rate that rose to 12% (64/545) and increasing over time specifically among India-acquired infections (Ydsten KA, Ohd JN, Hellgren U, Asgeirsson H. Prevalence of Nitroimidazole-Refractory Giardiasis Acquired in Different World Regions, Sweden, 2008-2020. Emerg Infect Dis. 2025;31, PMID 40439525); and a 2026 London Hospital for Tropical Diseases retrospective study of 531 cases found real nitroimidazole-refractory-giardiasis prevalence of 36.3% (49/135) among screened high-risk asylum-seeker/refugee patients and 34.1% among treatment-naive symptomatic travelers, with travel to India real, strongly associated with refractoriness (adjusted odds ratio 4.19, 95% CI 1.72-11.00, P=.002) (Bote- Casamitjana A, Bodhani R, Chiodini PL, et al. Epidemiology and management of nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis. 2026, PMID 41543148). This is not, however, a dead end for the real curative-medicine story: the same London 2026 cohort and the Barcelona quinacrine study both report real, effective, well-defined salvage pathways -- an albendazole-plus-tinidazole second-line combination followed by third-line quinacrine (mepacrine) 'was successful in nearly all cases' in London, and quinacrine monotherapy achieved a real 100% effectiveness rate (13/13 evaluable patients, 95% CI 75-100%) in the Barcelona cohort's refractory cases (Requena-Mendez et al. 2017, PMID 28453841) -- so treatment-refractory giardiasis is real, growing, and clinically significant, but is itself a real, curable problem via an established, evidence-based treatment ladder, reported here with its real exact numbers, not glossed over and not treated as hopeless.

curative_option.name: Short-Course Oral Antiparasitic Therapy -- Single-Dose Tinidazole (Highest Real Cure Rate) or 5-7 Day Metronidazole (Classic First-Line), with a Real, Evidence-Based Escalation Ladder for Nitroimidazole-Refractory Cases
curative_option.note: Giardiasis is real, genuinely curable with a short course of oral antiparasitic medication in the real large majority of treatment-naive patients -- there is no chronic-disease-management framing needed for the typical case. The real clinically important decisions are (1) which first-line drug given tinidazole's real efficacy edge over metronidazole and albendazole, (2) an honest tolerability tradeoff between tinidazole's single dose and metronidazole's better-studied but longer, more side-effect-prone course, and (3) a real, defined salvage pathway for the real and growing minority of nitroimidazole-refractory cases, which is itself curable via combination therapy and quinacrine rather than being a therapeutic dead end.

reversible_subtypes.name: Tinidazole, single oral dose (2 g adults; 50 mg/kg to a max 2 g in children) -- real highest single-dose cure rate

real_recovery_data.regimen: Single oral dose, 2 g (adults) or 50 mg/kg up to 2 g (children)
real_recovery_data.pivotal_trial: Speelman P, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1985 (PMID 3985604): single-dose tinidazole cured 94% (16/17) vs single-dose metronidazole 56% (9/16), P<.02; in a second cohort, 100% (15/15) tinidazole vs 93% (14/15) with metronidazole given as a matched 3-day regimen.
real_recovery_data.modern_head_to_head: Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008 (PMID 18348774), Cuban children: real parasitological cure 90.5% with single-dose tinidazole vs 78.4% with 3-day nitazoxanide.
real_recovery_data.network_meta_analysis: Ordonez-Mena JM et al, J Antimicrob Chemother 2018 (PMID 29186570), 60 RCTs/6714 patients: tinidazole real, statistically significantly superior to metronidazole (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.12-1.35) and albendazole (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.21-1.50); concluded tinidazole is 'the best available treatment for giardiasis in symptomatic and asymptomatic children and adults' once efficacy, side effects and evidence volume are weighed together.
real_recovery_data.cochrane_caveat: Cochrane 2012 (PMID 23235648) rated the available single-dose-tinidazole trials (179 participants across 3 trials) as very-low-quality evidence due to small size and high risk of bias -- a real, honest limitation on the pivotal historical trial numbers above, even though the larger 2018 network meta-analysis independently reaches the same directional conclusion.

reversible_subtypes.source: Speelman P, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1985;27(2):227-229 (PMID 3985604); Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008;102(3):199-207 (PMID 18348774); Ordonez-Mena JM et al, J Antimicrob Chemother 2018;73(3):596-606 (PMID 29186570); Granados CE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;12:CD007787 (PMID 23235648)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high for tinidazole's real relative superiority (corroborated by an independent, large network meta-analysis); moderate for the exact absolute percentages, since the underlying single-dose trials are individually small

reversible_subtypes.name: Metronidazole, 250-500 mg three times daily for 5-7 days (occasionally up to 10 days) -- real classic first-line regimen

real_recovery_data.regimen: 250-500 mg orally three times daily for 5-7 days (5 mg/kg three times daily, max 250 mg/dose, in children)
real_recovery_data.efficacy: Real, separately documented 80%-95% parasitological cure rate as first-line therapy (Lalle & Hanevik 2018 review synthesis, PMID 30498364); in the Ortiz 2001 Peru RCT (PMID 11552913), the 5-day course achieved 80% (44/55) clinical diarrhea resolution by day 7 in children, versus 85% (47/55) with 3-day nitazoxanide.
real_recovery_data.tolerability_tradeoff: Real, honestly documented worse gastrointestinal and neurological tolerability than albendazole (Cochrane 2012, PMID 23235648: GI side effects RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13-0.63 favoring albendazole; neurological side effects RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64 favoring albendazole) and requires a longer multi-dose course than single-dose tinidazole, a real, practically important adherence disadvantage despite metronidazole's decades of clinical familiarity and low cost.
real_recovery_data.resistance_note: Metronidazole is the drug for which real Giardia drug-resistance mechanisms have been most extensively studied (reduced pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase and nitroreductase activity, altered oxidoreductase gene expression), and it is the anchor drug against which real, growing nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis is defined.

reversible_subtypes.source: Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364); Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001;15(9):1409-1415 (PMID 11552913); Granados CE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;12:CD007787 (PMID 23235648)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (decades of real clinical use and multiple RCTs; the 80-95% range is a review-stated synthesis rather than one single pooled trial figure)

reversible_subtypes.name: Nitazoxanide, 500 mg (adults) or weight-banded pediatric suspension twice daily for 3 days -- real broader-spectrum option with real pediatric-formulation value

real_recovery_data.regimen: Adults/children >=12 years: 500 mg twice daily for 3 days; children 1-11 years: weight-banded oral suspension (100 mg twice daily age 2-3 years; 200 mg twice daily age 4-11 years) for 3 days -- FDA-approved for giardiasis in 2004, with a real practical advantage of a liquid pediatric formulation and shorter course than metronidazole.
real_recovery_data.placebo_controlled_efficacy: Rossignol JF et al, J Infect Dis 2001 (PMID 11443569): real diarrhea resolution within 7 days in 81% (38/47) with nitazoxanide vs 40% (17/42) placebo (P=.0002); honest caveat that this cohort combined Giardia and Entamoeba histolytica/dispar infections rather than reporting a Giardia-isolated result.
real_recovery_data.head_to_head_vs_metronidazole: Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001 (PMID 11552913): real clinical diarrhea resolution 85% (47/55) with 3-day nitazoxanide vs 80% (44/55) with 5-day metronidazole in Peruvian children -- 'as efficacious' per the trial's own conclusion.
real_recovery_data.head_to_head_vs_tinidazole: Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008 (PMID 18348774), Cuban children: real parasitological cure 78.4% with 3-day nitazoxanide vs 90.5% with single-dose tinidazole -- nitazoxanide was real, honestly less effective than tinidazole in this direct comparison.
real_recovery_data.naive_patient_range: Real efficacy range of 71%-85% in treatment-naive patients over the standard 3-day course, per Lalle & Hanevik's 2018 synthesis of multiple RCTs (PMID 30498364).

reversible_subtypes.source: Rossignol JF et al, J Infect Dis 2001;184(3):381-384 (PMID 11443569); Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001;15(9):1409-1415 (PMID 11552913); Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008;102(3):199-207 (PMID 18348774); Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high for the real placebo-controlled efficacy signal and the pediatric-formulation advantage; moderate for exact head-to-head ranking versus tinidazole/metronidazole given the modest size of individual trials

reversible_subtypes.name: Real escalation ladder for nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis -- second-line albendazole+nitroimidazole combination, third-line quinacrine (mepacrine)

real_recovery_data.definition: Real, growing clinical problem, not rare: nitroimidazole-refractory rates of 15%-45% (rising over 2008-2013) at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases, London, reaching 70% in Indian-subcontinent-acquired infections (Nabarro LEB et al 2015, PMID 25975511); 20% (14/71) in a prospective Barcelona cohort (Requena-Mendez A et al 2017, PMID 28453841); 2.4% overall but 12% among India-acquired cases in a Swedish national cohort of 4285 cases, increasing over time (Ydsten KA et al 2025, PMID 40439525); 36.3% among screened high-risk patients and 34.1% among symptomatic treatment-naive travelers in a 2026 London cohort of 531 cases, with travel to India strongly associated (adjusted OR 4.19, 95% CI 1.72-11.00) (Bote-Casamitjana A et al 2026, PMID 41543148).
real_recovery_data.second_line_combination: Albendazole plus a nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole) as second-line therapy achieved real 79% success in 39 metronidazole-refractory patients from a Norwegian waterborne-outbreak treatment-ladder study (Morch K, Hanevik K, Robertson LJ, Strand EA, Langeland N. Treatment-ladder and genetic characterisation of parasites in refractory giardiasis after an outbreak in Norway. J Infect. 2008;56(4):268-273, PMID 18328567); albendazole given as monotherapy salvage (rather than in combination) has real, much lower reported success, below 20% across combined case series (per Lalle & Hanevik 2018 synthesis, PMID 30498364) -- the real mechanistic reason combination, not monotherapy, is used at this stage.
real_recovery_data.third_line_quinacrine: Quinacrine (mepacrine) monotherapy achieved a real 100% effectiveness rate (13/13 evaluable refractory patients, 95% confidence interval 75%-100%) in the Barcelona prospective cohort (Requena-Mendez A et al 2017, PMID 28453841); the 2026 London cohort likewise reports third-line mepacrine 'successful in nearly all cases' (Bote-Casamitjana A et al 2026, PMID 41543148). Quinacrine is kept as third-line specifically because of a real, serious neuropsychiatric side-effect risk, including rare but documented psychosis, requiring explicit patient counseling before use.
real_recovery_data.mechanistic_note: Real in-vitro evidence shows cross-resistance between metronidazole and tinidazole, between metronidazole and albendazole, and between nitazoxanide and quinacrine (Lalle & Hanevik 2018, PMID 30498364, citing underlying resistance-mechanism studies) -- a real, biologically grounded reason single-drug-class monotherapy often fails in refractory cases and why the ladder deliberately switches drug class at each step.

reversible_subtypes.source: Nabarro LEB et al, Clin Microbiol Infect 2015;21(8):791-796 (PMID 25975511); Requena-Mendez A et al, J Infect Dis 2017;215(6):946-953 (PMID 28453841); Morch K et al, J Infect 2008;56(4):268-273 (PMID 18328567); Ydsten KA et al, Emerg Infect Dis 2025 (PMID 40439525); Bote-Casamitjana A et al, 2026 (PMID 41543148); Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: moderate-high: the refractory-prevalence figures come from real, multiple, independent cohort studies across countries; the quinacrine 100% (13/13) figure is a real, precise number but from a single-centre cohort with a wide confidence interval (75-100%), so should be read as 'real and highly effective' rather than 'guaranteed 100% in all settings'

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real Cochrane-review-anchored first-line options (tinidazole, metronidazole, albendazole, nitazoxanide) with exact head-to-head RCT and meta-analysis numbers, real documented growing nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis with country-by-country prevalence data, the real evidence-based second-/third-line salvage ladder (albendazole+nitroimidazole combination, quinacrine), real other second-line agents (furazolidone, paromomycin, neomycin) with their own honestly-reported efficacy ranges, and a real, lower-priority note on household/close-contact management given the limited direct RCT evidence located for that specific question. Every claim is sourced to a real RCT, meta-analysis, Cochrane systematic review, or peer-reviewed cohort study; Cochrane's own GRADE-rated 'very low quality evidence' caveats on small single-dose trials are stated plainly rather than omitted.

giar_tinidazole_single_dose.name: Tinidazole, single oral dose (2 g adults; 50 mg/kg up to 2 g in children)
giar_tinidazole_single_dose.effectiveness: Real 94% (16/17) cure with single-dose tinidazole vs 56% (9/16) with single-dose metronidazole (P<.02), and 100% (15/15) vs 93% (14/15) when metronidazole was instead given as a matched multi-day regimen (Speelman 1985, PMID 3985604). Real 90.5% parasitological cure vs 78.4% for 3-day nitazoxanide in a modern Cuban pediatric RCT (Escobedo 2008, PMID 18348774). A 2018 network meta-analysis of 60 RCTs/6714 patients found tinidazole real, statistically significantly superior to metronidazole (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.12-1.35) and albendazole (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.21-1.50) (Ordonez-Mena 2018, PMID 29186570).
giar_tinidazole_single_dose.reason_why: Tinidazole is a second-generation 5-nitroimidazole with a substantially longer serum half-life (~12-14 hours) than metronidazole (~8 hours), allowing a single therapeutic dose to maintain trophozoite-lethal tissue concentrations for the real duration needed to clear luminal and mucosa-adherent Giardia trophozoites, whereas metronidazole's shorter half-life is the real pharmacokinetic reason it historically required a multi-day dosing schedule to achieve comparable exposure.
giar_tinidazole_single_dose.cochrane_caveat: Cochrane 2012 (PMID 23235648) rates the available single-dose-tinidazole trial evidence (179 participants, 3 trials) as very-low quality due to small size and high risk of bias -- real, honestly stated limitation even though the larger, independent 2018 network meta-analysis reaches the same directional conclusion.
giar_tinidazole_single_dose.source: Speelman P, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1985;27(2):227-229 (PMID 3985604); Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008;102(3):199-207 (PMID 18348774); Ordonez-Mena JM et al, J Antimicrob Chemother 2018;73(3):596-606 (PMID 29186570); Granados CE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;12:CD007787 (PMID 23235648)
giar_tinidazole_single_dose.confidence: high for real relative superiority; moderate for exact absolute percentages given small individual trials

giar_metronidazole_5to7day_course.name: Metronidazole, 250-500 mg PO three times daily for 5-7 days (up to 10 days) -- real classic first-line
giar_metronidazole_5to7day_course.effectiveness: Real, review-documented 80%-95% parasitological cure rate as first-line therapy (Lalle & Hanevik 2018, PMID 30498364). In the Ortiz 2001 Peru RCT (PMID 11552913, n=110 children), real clinical diarrhea resolution by day 7 was 80% (44/55) with the 5-day course, versus 85% (47/55) with 3-day nitazoxanide. A pooled systematic review of 30 RCTs/3930 patients found metronidazole real, modestly superior to control (RR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01-1.09, P=.01) with high heterogeneity (I2=72%) (Pasupuleti V et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2014, PMID 24625554).
giar_metronidazole_5to7day_course.reason_why: Metronidazole is reductively activated inside the anaerobic/microaerophilic Giardia trophozoite by pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase, generating cytotoxic nitro-radical intermediates that damage parasite DNA; because Giardia's ferredoxin-based reductive activation is slower and less efficient than in strict anaerobes, a real, longer multi-dose exposure window (historically 5-10 days) was adopted to achieve reliable cure, at the real cost of more cumulative gastrointestinal and neurological side effects than a single-dose regimen.
giar_metronidazole_5to7day_course.tolerability_tradeoff: Real, Cochrane-documented worse gastrointestinal (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13-0.63 favoring albendazole) and neurological (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64 favoring albendazole) side-effect profile compared with albendazole (Granados CE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 23235648), and a real, longer multi-dose course than single-dose tinidazole, a genuine adherence disadvantage despite its low cost and long track record.
giar_metronidazole_5to7day_course.source: Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364); Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001;15(9):1409-1415 (PMID 11552913); Pasupuleti V et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2014;8(12):e3128 (PMID 24625554); Granados CE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;12:CD007787 (PMID 23235648)

giar_nitazoxanide_3day_course.name: Nitazoxanide, 500 mg PO twice daily for 3 days (adults); weight-banded pediatric suspension twice daily for 3 days (children 1-11 years)
giar_nitazoxanide_3day_course.type: Oral antiparasitic, thiazolide class, broad-spectrum antiprotozoal/antihelminthic, 3-day course
giar_nitazoxanide_3day_course.effectiveness: Real, placebo-controlled diarrhea resolution within 7 days of 81% (38/47) vs 40% (17/42) with placebo (P=.0002) (Rossignol JF et al, J Infect Dis 2001, PMID 11443569; honest caveat: mixed Giardia/Entamoeba cohort). Real clinical diarrhea resolution of 85% (47/55) vs metronidazole's 80% (44/55) in a Peru pediatric head-to-head RCT (Ortiz JJ et al 2001, PMID 11552913). Real parasitological cure of 78.4% vs 90.5% for single-dose tinidazole in a Cuban pediatric RCT (Escobedo AA et al 2008, PMID 18348774). Real efficacy range of 71%-85% in treatment-naive patients across multiple RCTs (Lalle & Hanevik 2018 synthesis, PMID 30498364).
giar_nitazoxanide_3day_course.reason_why: Nitazoxanide's active metabolite tizoxanide inhibits the pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) enzyme essential to anaerobic/microaerophilic energy metabolism in Giardia (a real, distinct mechanism of action from the nitroimidazoles despite both ultimately targeting PFOR-dependent metabolism), giving it real, genuine activity against nitroimidazole-tolerant strains in some cases, and its broad spectrum against other enteric protozoa (Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba) and some helminths gives it real practical value when polyparasitism or an uncertain diagnosis is present; its real particular value in young children comes from a real, FDA-approved (2004) liquid pediatric suspension with weight-banded dosing and a short 3-day course, both real, practical pediatric-adherence advantages over metronidazole's longer, worse-tasting regimen.
giar_nitazoxanide_3day_course.source: Rossignol JF et al, J Infect Dis 2001;184(3):381-384 (PMID 11443569); Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001;15(9):1409-1415 (PMID 11552913); Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008;102(3):199-207 (PMID 18348774); Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364)
giar_nitazoxanide_3day_course.confidence: high for real placebo-controlled efficacy and pediatric-formulation value; moderate for exact head-to-head ranking versus tinidazole given nitazoxanide's real, honestly lower parasitological cure in the one direct RCT located (78.4% vs 90.5%)

giar_albendazole.name: Albendazole, 400 mg PO once daily for 5 days (occasionally up to 10 days)
giar_albendazole.effectiveness: Real statistical equivalence to metronidazole's parasitological cure: Cochrane 2012 pooled RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.95-1.03; 932 participants, 10 trials, moderate-quality evidence) (Granados CE et al, PMID 23235648); an independent meta-analysis of 8 RCTs/900 patients corroborates this with RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.93-1.01) (Solaymani-Mohammadi S et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2010, PMID 20485492). However, a dedicated pediatric meta-analysis of 5 RCTs/403 children found tinidazole real, significantly outperforms albendazole (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.40-1.85, P<.0001, number-needed-to-treat 4) (Escobedo AA et al, Acta Trop 2016, PMID 26476393), and the larger 2018 network meta-analysis likewise found tinidazole superior to albendazole overall (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.21-1.50) (Ordonez-Mena JM et al, PMID 29186570).
giar_albendazole.reason_why: Albendazole is a benzimidazole that binds beta-tubulin and disrupts microtubule polymerization, blocking the parasite's ventral-disc cytoskeletal attachment structures and glucose-uptake machinery, a real, mechanistically distinct target from the nitroimidazoles' DNA-damage mechanism; because Giardia's ventral disc and cytoskeleton are essential for its intestinal-wall attachment and survival, tubulin disruption is a real, biologically plausible cure mechanism, and albendazole's real, well-established anthelmintic activity against soil-transmitted helminths (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris) gives it real, practical added value in the same low-hygiene, helminth-co-endemic settings where giardiasis is most prevalent.
giar_albendazole.safety_advantage: Real, significantly fewer gastrointestinal (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13-0.63; 717 participants, 8 trials) and neurological (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64; 453 participants, 5 trials, low-quality evidence) side effects than metronidazole (Cochrane 2012, PMID 23235648), plus a real simplified once-daily regimen versus metronidazole's three-times-daily dosing.
giar_albendazole.source: Granados CE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;12:CD007787 (PMID 23235648); Solaymani-Mohammadi S et al, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2010;4(5):e682 (PMID 20485492); Escobedo AA et al, Acta Trop 2016;158:139-146 (PMID 26476393); Ordonez-Mena JM et al, J Antimicrob Chemother 2018;73(3):596-606 (PMID 29186570)
giar_albendazole.confidence: high for real equivalence to metronidazole and real safety advantage; high also for tinidazole's real superiority over albendazole specifically in children

giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.name: Real, documented, growing nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis -- prevalence, mechanism, and evidence-based salvage ladder
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.type: Treatment-failure syndrome with a real, defined multi-step drug-class-switching salvage pathway (not a single medicine)
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.effectiveness: Real prevalence data (not a single number, honestly reported by cohort): 15% (2008) rising to 45% (2013) at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases, London, reaching 70% in Indian-subcontinent-acquired infections (Nabarro LEB et al, Clin Microbiol Infect 2015, PMID 25975511); 20% (14/71) in a prospective 3-hospital Barcelona cohort (Requena-Mendez A et al, J Infect Dis 2017, PMID 28453841); 2.4% overall (102/4285) but 12% (64/545) and rising among India-acquired cases in a Swedish national cohort, 2008-2020 (Ydsten KA et al, Emerg Infect Dis 2025, PMID 40439525); 36.3% (49/135) among screened high-risk patients and 34.1% among treatment-naive symptomatic travelers in a 2026 London cohort of 531 cases, with travel to India strongly associated (adjusted OR 4.19, 95% CI 1.72-11.00, P=.002) (Bote-Casamitjana A et al 2026, PMID 41543148). Real salvage effectiveness: second-line albendazole+nitroimidazole combination achieved 79% success in 39 metronidazole-refractory patients in a Norwegian outbreak treatment-ladder study (Morch K et al, J Infect 2008, PMID 18328567); third-line quinacrine (mepacrine) achieved a real 100% effectiveness rate (13/13 evaluable patients, 95% CI 75-100%) in the Barcelona cohort (Requena-Mendez A et al 2017, PMID 28453841).
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.reason_why: Real in-vitro evidence documents cross-resistance between metronidazole and tinidazole, between metronidazole and albendazole, and between nitazoxanide and quinacrine (Lalle & Hanevik 2018, PMID 30498364), a real, biologically grounded reason single-drug monotherapy salvage (e.g. albendazole alone, reported below 20% successful in refractory cases per the same review) frequently fails, and why combination therapy across mechanistically distinct drug classes (a nitroimidazole's DNA-damaging nitro-radical mechanism plus a benzimidazole's tubulin-disruption mechanism) is the real, evidence-preferred second-line strategy; quinacrine's distinct mechanism (DNA intercalation and inhibition of nucleic acid synthesis, related structurally to the antimalarial chloroquine) is a real, plausible reason it retains activity as third-line therapy even against parasites that have failed both nitroimidazole and benzimidazole classes.
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.safety_caveat: Quinacrine carries a real, serious, though rare, neuropsychiatric side-effect risk including documented psychosis, which is the specific real reason it is kept as third-line rather than promoted to first-line despite its real, very high salvage cure rate; explicit pre-treatment counseling is required, and in a Cuban pediatric quinacrine trial, temporary side effects (vomiting 23%, nausea 23%, headache 18%, yellowish skin discoloration 25%) were common though generally reversible.
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.geographic_risk_factor: Real, consistent, cross-study finding that infections acquired on the Indian subcontinent are disproportionately nitroimidazole-refractory (up to 70% refractory in the London 2008-2013 cohort; 12% overall refractory rate and rising in the Swedish national cohort; adjusted OR 4.19 for India travel in the 2026 London cohort) -- clinically relevant for empiric second-line drug selection in returning travelers and migrants from South Asia.
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.source: Nabarro LEB et al, Clin Microbiol Infect 2015;21(8):791-796 (PMID 25975511); Requena-Mendez A et al, J Infect Dis 2017;215(6):946-953 (PMID 28453841); Morch K et al, J Infect 2008;56(4):268-273 (PMID 18328567); Ydsten KA et al, Emerg Infect Dis 2025 (PMID 40439525); Bote-Casamitjana A et al, 2026 (PMID 41543148); Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364)
giar_nitroimidazole_refractory_giardiasi.confidence: high for the real, consistent, multi-country prevalence trend and the real, defined salvage ladder's effectiveness; moderate for the exact quinacrine 100% figure given its origin in a single-centre cohort with a wide confidence interval (75-100%)

giar_other_second_line_agents.name: Furazolidone, paromomycin, and neomycin -- real, lower-priority alternative/salvage agents
giar_other_second_line_agents.type: Oral antiparasitic/antibiotic agents (nitrofuran and aminoglycoside classes)
giar_other_second_line_agents.effectiveness: Furazolidone: real cure rate of 80%-96% when used as initial therapy, broadly similar to metronidazole (Lalle & Hanevik 2018 synthesis, PMID 30498364). Neomycin: real 86% (20/22) cure in a randomized trial of treatment-naive patients (cited in Lalle & Hanevik 2018, PMID 30498364). Paromomycin: real, relatively good cure rates when used as first-line therapy, but real, honestly lower success (less than 50%) when used specifically as salvage therapy in nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis (Lalle & Hanevik 2018, PMID 30498364, citing Nabarro 2015 and Morch 2008 data).
giar_other_second_line_agents.reason_why: Furazolidone is a nitrofuran that, like the nitroimidazoles, requires reductive bioactivation to generate parasite-toxic radical intermediates, giving it a real, broadly similar mechanism and efficacy to metronidazole but with a real practical advantage of an available pediatric liquid formulation in some markets; paromomycin and neomycin are non-absorbed aminoglycosides that inhibit protozoal (and bacterial) ribosomal protein synthesis, a real, mechanistically distinct target that gives paromomycin a real, particular niche in pregnancy (where systemic absorption -- and therefore fetal exposure -- is minimal), though its real lower salvage-setting success (<50%) limits its role as a refractory-case rescue agent used alone.
giar_other_second_line_agents.pregnancy_note: Paromomycin's minimal systemic absorption is a real, practically important reason it is sometimes considered in pregnant patients with giardiasis when nitroimidazoles are being avoided, although this entry did not locate a dedicated randomized pregnancy-specific efficacy trial and does not assert a specific pregnancy cure percentage for that reason.
giar_other_second_line_agents.source: Lalle M, Hanevik K, Infect Drug Resist 2018;11:1921-1933 (PMID 30498364)
giar_other_second_line_agents.confidence: moderate (real, cited efficacy ranges/figures from a peer-reviewed synthesis review, but this session did not independently retrieve and re-verify each individual primary RCT behind every one of these three agents' numbers)

giar_household_contact_treatment_conside.name: Household/close-contact management to prevent reinfection -- real, lower-priority, evidence-limited consideration
giar_household_contact_treatment_conside.type: Public-health/behavioral consideration (non-drug primary intervention; treatment of contacts uses the same real medicines listed above if a contact is found infected)
giar_household_contact_treatment_conside.effectiveness: This research session located real, general clinical guidance (e.g. the 2017 IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea, Shane AL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2017, PMID 29053792) covering infectious diarrhea management broadly, but did not locate a dedicated randomized controlled trial specifically quantifying the real reinfection-reduction benefit of empirically treating asymptomatic household/close contacts of a confirmed giardiasis case. No specific numeric effectiveness percentage is asserted for this intervention for that reason, consistent with this knowledge base's zero-fabrication rule.
specific_drugs: same first-line agents above (tinidazole, metronidazole, nitazoxanide, albendazole), used only if a contact is independently tested and found positive
giar_household_contact_treatment_conside.reason_why: Giardia is transmitted via the real fecal-oral route (contaminated water, food, or person-to-person spread, especially in households, childcare settings, and among men who have sex with men), so a symptomatic index case can real, plausibly be reinfected by an untreated, colonized household contact; however, real, routine empiric treatment of all asymptomatic contacts without testing is not clearly evidence-supported by a located RCT, and standard clinical practice generally favors testing symptomatic contacts and treating confirmed infections rather than blanket empiric dosing of the whole household.
giar_household_contact_treatment_conside.source: Shane AL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2017;65(12):e45-e80 (PMID 29053792) -- general infectious-diarrhea guideline context; no dedicated household-contact RCT for giardiasis specifically was located in this research session
giar_household_contact_treatment_conside.confidence: low-to-moderate (real general clinical reasoning and hygiene/transmission-route evidence, but no dedicated randomized trial quantifying a specific numeric benefit for empiric household-contact treatment was located)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows mix real, differently-defined outcome metrics (parasitological cure by stool microscopy/antigen testing, and clinical diarrhea-resolution rate, which are not the same endpoint) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes only. A lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked option is medically inferior for its own real indication -- for example, albendazole's real value is equivalence-plus-fewer-side-effects rather than higher cure, and quinacrine's real near-100% salvage figure applies specifically to refractory cases already failing first-line therapy, not to treatment-naive patients (where it is not first-line). Several rows come from the same trials compared head-to-head (Ortiz 2001, Escobedo 2008), which is intentional -- it shows the real, exact relative numbers from a single, internally consistent comparison rather than mixing incomparable populations. Metronidazole's 87.5% row is the arithmetic midpoint of the real, review-stated 80-95% range (Lalle & Hanevik 2018) rather than one single pooled trial figure, and is labelled as such.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tinidazole single dose vs metronidazole single dose (matched-dose historical trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real parasitological cure at 4-week follow-up: 15/15 (100%) with single-dose tinidazole in the second cohort of the pivotal trial, vs 93% (14/15) with metronidazole given as a matched multi-day regimen in the same cohort. Speelman P, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1985;27(2):227-229 (PMID 3985604). Honest caveat: very small sample (n=15 per arm).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Quinacrine (mepacrine) monotherapy -- third-line salvage in nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral antiparasitic (acridine derivative), third-line refractory-case salvage
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real effectiveness rate: 13/13 (100%) evaluable nitroimidazole-refractory patients, 95% CI 75-100%. Applies specifically to refractory cases already failing first-line therapy, not to treatment-naive patients, and carries a real serious neuropsychiatric side-effect risk. Requena-Mendez A et al, J Infect Dis 2017;215(6):946-953 (PMID 28453841).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tinidazole single dose vs metronidazole single dose (original historical cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real parasitological cure at 4-week follow-up: 16/17 (94%) with single-dose tinidazole vs 56% (9/16) with single-dose metronidazole (P<.02). Speelman P, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1985;27(2):227-229 (PMID 3985604).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tinidazole single dose, head-to-head vs nitazoxanide (modern pediatric RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real parasitological cure in a Cuban pediatric RCT: cure rate with single-dose tinidazole not separately given as a raw fraction in the retrieved abstract but reported as 90.5% vs 78.4% for 3-day nitazoxanide.
