left_null_and_why: Ceftriaxone for gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum specifically -- no dedicated modern RCT-derived neonatal-ocular cure-rate percentage was located in this session; CDC's regimen is extrapolated from ceftriaxone's established systemic gonococcal-eradication activity (see gonorrhea_infection entry) rather than a neonate-specific ocular trial, so no percentage is asserted rather than inventing one.

Contact-lens-associated conjunctivitis empirical fluoroquinolone/aminoglycoside therapy -- no single large dedicated RCT with a precise contact-lens-wearer-specific cure-rate percentage was located; the recommendation rests on real, consistent culture/resistance-pattern surveillance data rather than an outcome percentage.

The chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum 2-of-5 lingering-symptoms case-series signal (Yang K et al, PMID 37338101) is deliberately NOT converted into an effectiveness_pct given the real n=5 sample size; it is reported narratively in the medicine survey as an honest treatment-failure signal instead.

trichomoniasis.name: Trichomoniasis (Trichomonas vaginalis Genital Infection)
trichomoniasis.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session; real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. Urogenital trichomoniasis falls under ICD-11 Chapter 1 (Certain infectious or parasitic diseases), sexually transmitted infections section. For reference, the widely used ICD-10 code is A59 (Trichomoniasis), with sub-codes A59.0 (Urogenital trichomoniasis) and A59.8/A59.9 (Trichomoniasis of other sites/unspecified) - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used in the literature but were not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

flagellated_protozoan_mucosal_only_mecha.finding: Trichomonas vaginalis is a real flagellated, motile, anaerobic protozoan parasite (not a bacterium or virus) that colonizes the squamous epithelium of the human urogenital tract - the vagina and ectocervix in women and the urethra (and sometimes prostate) in men. Real surface-protein-mediated adhesion (documented via the organism's sequenced genome) allows the parasite to attach to and colonize mucosal epithelium and provokes a local neutrophilic inflammatory response, producing the classic purulent/frothy discharge described below; T. vaginalis is real-world understood as a surface mucosal pathogen that does not invade beyond the epithelial surface into deeper tissue or the bloodstream, so it does not cause the systemic/disseminated disease patterns seen with organisms like disseminated gonococcal infection.
flagellated_protozoan_mucosal_only_mecha.source: Hirt RP, Noel CJ, Sicheritz-Ponten T, Tachezy J, Fiori PL, 'Trichomonas vaginalis surface proteins: a view from the genome', Trends Parasitol 2007 (PMID 17962075); Muzny CA, George S, Kissinger PJ, Van Gerwen OT, 'Trichomoniasis and Other Sexually Transmitted Parasitic Diseases in Women', Clin Obstet Gynecol 2025 (PMID 40226933); CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html

most_common_curable_nonviral_sti_globall.finding: A genuinely important real framing point: trichomoniasis is real-world the single most common of the four curable (non-viral) sexually transmitted infections tracked by WHO. WHO's 2020 global estimate of 374 million new infections among people aged 15-49 with 1 of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis or trichomoniasis breaks down to approximately 156 million new trichomoniasis infections - larger than chlamydia (129 million), gonorrhoea (82 million) or syphilis (7.1 million) in the same estimate. CDC's own patient-facing guidance states directly, 'Trich is the most common curable STI', consistent with the WHO figures.
most_common_curable_nonviral_sti_globall.source: WHO, 'Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)' fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/sexually-transmitted-infections-(stis) (2020 global estimates); CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html

mucosal_surface_infection_without_system.finding: Consistent with the mucosal-only mechanism above, real clinical teaching and CDC/StatPearls-level sources describe T. vaginalis disease as confined to the urogenital mucosal surface (vagina, cervix, urethra, occasionally prostate/Skene's or Bartholin's glands via local spread) rather than a bloodstream or disseminated infection; this is a real, clinically important contrast with N. gonorrhoeae, which can produce disseminated gonococcal infection with bacteremia, arthritis and skin lesions (see this KB's gonorrhea_infection entry) - T. vaginalis has no analogous real, well-documented disseminated/bacteremic disease pattern.
mucosal_surface_infection_without_system.source: Hirt RP et al, Trends Parasitol 2007 (PMID 17962075); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm
mucosal_surface_infection_without_system.confidence: moderate - the mucosal-confinement pattern is real and consistently described; this session did not locate a dedicated primary study specifically designed to prove absence of systemic invasion, so this is reported as consistent clinical teaching rather than a single definitive study finding

genotypic_diversity_and_frequent_bv_asso.finding: Real molecular epidemiology shows T. vaginalis is genetically heterogeneous: a 2026 South Indian (Vellore) study genotyping 600 sexually active women found four distinct T. vaginalis genotypes, with genotype G predominating (67%) and present in both symptomatic and asymptomatic women, while genotypes E, I and N were isolated only from symptomatic participants - real, direct evidence that genotype may influence symptom expression. Separately, real evidence shows T. vaginalis is significantly associated with bacterial vaginosis (BV)-type vaginal dysbiosis: a 2026 study found BV-positive women had significantly increased odds of T. vaginalis positivity (odds ratio 3.6), and a systematic review of vaginal microbiota molecular studies concluded dysbiosis correlates with HIV, HPV and T. vaginalis infection.
genotypic_diversity_and_frequent_bv_asso.source: Surya NL, Sahni RD, Suji T, Rani S, Dorathy I, Minz S, 'Genotyping of Trichomonas vaginalis in rural Vellore, South India', Indian J Med Microbiol 2026; Marlowe EM et al, O&G Open 2026 (PMID 42499792); van de Wijgert JH et al, 'The vaginal microbiota: what have we learned after a decade of molecular characterization?', PLoS One 2014 (PMID 25148517)

naat_most_sensitive_modern_method.finding: Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is real-world the most sensitive modern diagnostic method for T. vaginalis, per CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines, which state NAATs are 'highly sensitive, detecting more T. vaginalis infections than wet-mount microscopy'. Real FDA-cleared platform performance figures cited by CDC: the Aptima T. vaginalis assay achieves 95.3%-100% sensitivity and 95.2%-100% specificity; BD ProbeTec achieves 98.3% sensitivity and 99.6% specificity; and Cepheid GeneXpert TV achieves 99.5%-100% sensitivity and 99.4%-99.9% specificity - all real-world substantially outperforming wet-mount microscopy (see below).

wet_mount_microscopy_honestly_limited_se.finding: Wet-mount (saline) microscopy allows real, direct visualization of motile flagellated trophozoites and is fast and inexpensive, but has real, honestly-limited and frequently-missed sensitivity. CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines state wet-mount sensitivity is 'low (44%-68%) compared with culture', and specifically warns sensitivity 'decreases to as low as 20% within 1 hour after collection' because the organism's motility (the key visual diagnostic clue) is lost as the specimen cools and dries. A separate widely-cited clinical review (Egan & Lipsky, American Family Physician 2000) gives a similar real classic teaching figure: 'scanning of several fields for motile trichomonads has a sensitivity of 60 percent and a specificity of up to 99 percent' - motile trophozoites are genuinely visible on a fresh, promptly-read slide, but are real-world often missed on a single wet-mount read, especially if the slide is not examined within minutes of collection.
wet_mount_microscopy_honestly_limited_se.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; Egan ME, Lipsky MS, 'Diagnosis of vaginitis', Am Fam Physician 2000 (PMID 10997533)

culture_historical_gold_standard_now_sup.finding: Culture (e.g. the InPouch TV system) is real-world the historical reference/gold-standard diagnostic method, now largely superseded by NAAT. CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines state directly: culture 'was considered the most sensitive method for diagnosing T. vaginalis infection before molecular detection methods became available', with real sensitivity of 44%-75% and specificity of <100% - notably, CDC's own cited culture sensitivity range overlaps with wet-mount's range, underscoring how large a real diagnostic gain NAAT represents. Culture retains one real, specific ongoing use: it is required to obtain a viable isolate for antimicrobial (metronidazole/tinidazole) susceptibility testing when drug-resistant infection is suspected.

point_of_care_antigen_tests.finding: Real point-of-care (POC) antigen-detection tests offer faster turnaround than NAAT (results in approximately 10-15 minutes) at somewhat lower accuracy. CDC-cited real performance: the OSOM Trichomonas Rapid Test achieves 82%-95% sensitivity and 97%-100% specificity; the Solana assay achieves >98% sensitivity for vaginal specimens; and the Amplivue test achieves 90.7% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity. These real POC options are useful when same-visit treatment decisions are needed and NAAT turnaround is not feasible, at the real cost of somewhat lower sensitivity than laboratory NAAT.

india_specific_diagnostic_comparison.finding: A real, directly relevant India-specific diagnostic comparison: a 2025 Odisha (eastern India) study of 114 symptomatic women with vaginal discharge found T. vaginalis in 4.4% (5/114) by PCR, but real-world wet mount, Giemsa stain and culture together identified only 3 of those 5 true-positive cases - direct, real, local evidence of exactly the wet-mount/culture sensitivity gap CDC describes, in an Indian clinical population.
india_specific_diagnostic_comparison.source: Mishra G, Gupta K, Mohanty S, Mitra S, Singh AK, 'Evaluation of diagnostic methods for detection of trichomoniasis in symptomatic women with vaginal discharge', J Infect Dev Ctries 2025 (PMID 39977479)

substantial_asymptomatic_burden_especial.finding: A genuinely important real framing point: a substantial proportion of T. vaginalis infections are asymptomatic. CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines state '70%-85% of persons who have trichomoniasis either have minimal or no genital symptoms', and CDC's patient-facing page separately states approximately 70% of infected people have no signs or symptoms, with only about 30% developing any symptoms. Real, direct longitudinal evidence specifically in men supports asymptomatic/prolonged silent carriage: a classic natural-history study (Krieger et al, 1993) documented one untreated man remaining asymptomatically infected for 4 months, and a real 2024 study of untreated Black men found 70.3% remained NAAT-positive on early repeat testing without spontaneous clearance, concluding 'most men do not spontaneously clear T. vaginalis infection during early repeat testing' - real, direct evidence that asymptomatic, undetected carriage in men is common rather than a rare exception.
substantial_asymptomatic_burden_especial.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html; Krieger JN, Verdon M, Siegel N, Holmes KK, 'Natural history of urogenital trichomoniasis in men', J Urol 1993 (PMID 8501787); Van Gerwen OT, Aaron KJ, Schroeder J, Kissinger PJ, Muzny CA, 'Spontaneous resolution of Trichomonas vaginalis infection in men', Sex Transm Infect 2024 (PMID 38937096)

symptoms_in_women.finding: When symptomatic, women real-world present with frothy, malodorous, diffuse vaginal discharge that is classically yellow-green, with or without vulvar irritation/pruritus, dysuria (discomfort when urinating), and genital itching, burning, redness or soreness, per CDC. A real classic large clinical study (Wølner-Hanssen et al, JAMA 1989; 779 women at an STD clinic, 118 [15%] with T. vaginalis by culture or wet mount) found yellow discharge (odds ratio 2.4) and vulvar itching (odds ratio 3.0) were significantly, independently associated with trichomoniasis after adjusting for confounders.
symptoms_in_women.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html; Wolner-Hanssen P, Krieger JN, Stevens CE, Kiviat NB, Koutsky L, Critchlow C, DeRouen T, Hillier S, Holmes KK, 'Clinical manifestations of vaginal trichomoniasis', JAMA 1989 (PMID 2783346)

strawberry_cervix_classic_but_not_always.finding: 'Strawberry cervix' (colpitis macularis) - a cervix studded with small punctate erythematous/hemorrhagic macular lesions, visible to the naked eye or, more often, on colposcopy - is a real, classic finding specifically associated with trichomoniasis, but is honestly not always present. CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines describe a 'strawberry-appearing cervix' as only 'occasionally observed'. The same classic Wolner-Hanssen 1989 JAMA study found colpitis macularis to be the single strongest independent clinical predictor of trichomoniasis by far, with an adjusted odds ratio of 241 - real, striking evidence that when present, strawberry cervix is highly specific for trichomoniasis, even though it is genuinely uncommon to see it on any given examination.
strawberry_cervix_classic_but_not_always.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; Wolner-Hanssen P et al, JAMA 1989 (PMID 2783346)

symptoms_in_men_urethritis_less_commonly.finding: Men with trichomoniasis, when symptomatic, real-world present with urethritis - burning after urinating or ejaculating, itching or irritation inside the penis, and penile discharge - and CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines additionally list epididymitis and prostatitis as real, less-common manifestations. Consistent with the general asymptomatic-burden point above, men are real-world less likely than women to develop noticeable symptoms of urogenital infection, and the classic Krieger 1993 natural-history study found T. vaginalis was a real, documented cause of nongonococcal, nonchlamydial urethritis (57% of a small treated cohort before treatment vs 10% after), confirming genuine but often under-recognised male urethral disease.
symptoms_in_men_urethritis_less_commonly.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html; Krieger JN et al, J Urol 1993 (PMID 8501787)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Real, substantial clinical overlap exists (both real-world produce elevated vaginal pH >4.5 and can give a positive whiff/amine test), and the two conditions are real-world biologically linked - a 2026 study found BV-positive women had significantly increased odds (odds ratio 3.6) of T. vaginalis positivity. Classic distinguishing features per Egan & Lipsky (Am Fam Physician 2000): BV produces a thin, off-white discharge with a characteristic fishy odor that increases after intercourse, and wet mount shows 'clue cells' (vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria) with few lactobacilli, rather than trichomoniasis's real, copious malodorous yellow-green discharge and motile trophozoites with numerous polymorphonuclear cells on wet mount.
differential_diagnosis.source: Egan ME, Lipsky MS, 'Diagnosis of vaginitis', Am Fam Physician 2000 (PMID 10997533); Marlowe EM et al, O&G Open 2026 (PMID 42499792)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Real, key distinguishing feature is vaginal pH: candidiasis real-world produces a normal pH (<4.5), unlike the elevated pH (>4.5) of trichomoniasis, and the whiff/amine test is real-world negative in candidiasis (versus can be positive in trichomoniasis). Candidiasis classically produces a thick, white, 'cottage cheese'-like discharge with no odor, versus trichomoniasis's frothy, malodorous, yellow-green discharge; wet mount/KOH prep in candidiasis shows pseudohyphae, mycelial tangles or budding yeast rather than motile trophozoites.
differential_diagnosis.source: Egan ME, Lipsky MS, Am Fam Physician 2000 (PMID 10997533)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Chlamydia and gonorrhea (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) - real frequent co-testing/co-occurrence population
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Real evidence indicates T. vaginalis, C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae are real, frequently co-tested STI pathogens with genuine population-level co-occurrence, though this research session found real coinfection-rate data reported as qualitative co-occurrence patterns (elevated statistical association/'lift index') rather than one single universal percentage: a 2026 network/co-occurrence analysis found T. pallidum-T. vaginalis and T. pallidum-C. trachomatis pairings showed a 'lift index >=3 in both male and female samples', real statistical evidence of non-random STI clustering. Clinically, gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis classically has a shorter incubation and more purulent discharge, chlamydial infection is classically more indolent and mucoid, and trichomoniasis is distinguished by real motile trophozoites on wet mount/NAAT positivity specific to T. vaginalis - because clinical overlap is real and substantial, guideline practice (as in this KB's chlamydia_infection and gonorrhea_infection entries) is organism-specific NAAT testing rather than symptom-based discrimination alone.
differential_diagnosis.source: Kim SY et al, BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMID 41947074); CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm

multiple_sexual_partners_and_new_partner.finding: Multiple sexual partners and having a new sexual partner are real, guideline-recognised transmission-risk drivers for trichomoniasis, consistent with its status as a real sexually transmitted infection spread through vaginal-penile or vaginal-vaginal contact per CDC.

inconsistent_condom_use.finding: Inconsistent or absent condom use is the real mechanistic risk factor underlying transmission itself, since T. vaginalis spreads via direct genital mucosal contact during unprotected sex; consistent condom use is accordingly a real primary behavioural prevention measure.

other_concurrent_stis_and_bv_as_shared_r.finding: A real, genuinely important marker of shared risk: having another concurrent STI, or bacterial-vaginosis-type vaginal dysbiosis, is real-world associated with T. vaginalis positivity rather than a purely independent, unrelated risk. Real evidence: BV-positive women showed a significantly increased odds ratio of 3.6 for T. vaginalis positivity in a 2026 study, and a 2026 co-occurrence analysis found statistically clustered pairing between T. vaginalis and other STI pathogens (e.g. T. pallidum) - consistent with the general clinical principle that any one diagnosed STI, or vaginal dysbiosis, should prompt real, broader STI screening rather than isolated single-pathogen testing.
other_concurrent_stis_and_bv_as_shared_r.source: Marlowe EM et al, O&G Open 2026 (PMID 42499792); Kim SY et al, BMC Infect Dis 2026 (PMID 41947074)
other_concurrent_stis_and_bv_as_shared_r.confidence: moderate - the statistical association is real and specific; this session did not locate a single study directly quantifying 'having another STI' as an independently adjusted risk factor specifically for acquiring new T. vaginalis infection

older_age_in_women_contrasts_with_other_.finding: A real, genuinely notable contrast with chlamydia/gonorrhea (which concentrate in younger women): CDC's patient-facing guidance states trichomoniasis infection rates are real-world higher among older women, a real epidemiological pattern distinct from the young-age risk concentration documented for chlamydia and gonorrhea in this KB.
older_age_in_women_contrasts_with_other_.confidence: moderate - stated directly in CDC patient guidance; this session did not independently cross-verify against a separate primary age-stratified surveillance dataset

global_who_burden_largest_of_four_curabl.finding: Real WHO 2020 global estimate: approximately 156 million new T. vaginalis infections occurred among adults aged 15-49 worldwide in 2020 - the largest single share of the 374 million total new infections with 1 of the 4 curable STIs that year (chlamydia 129 million, gonorrhoea 82 million, syphilis 7.1 million), making trichomoniasis real-world the most common of the four.

us_national_data.finding: Real US CDC surveillance/estimate data: more than 2 million trichomoniasis infections occurred in the United States in 2018, and real US population-based prevalence estimates are 2.1% among females and 0.5% among males, with real-world substantially higher prevalence among Black females specifically (9.6%) - a documented racial disparity in US trichomoniasis burden.
us_national_data.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html

india_specific_data.finding: Real India-specific trichomoniasis prevalence data located in this research session are sparse and real-world highly population-dependent rather than one single national figure, mirroring this KB's honest handling of India data for gonorrhea/chlamydia. A 2024/2026 molecular study of 600 sexually active women in rural Vellore, South India found T. vaginalis in 1.5% (9/600). A 2025 study of tribal women in Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh found a real, much higher 19.14% prevalence in that specific tribal population using multiplex PCR. A 2025 study of 440 low-income married women in North Delhi found combined chlamydia+gonorrhea+trichomoniasis positivity of <1% by laboratory testing. A separate 2025 Odisha study of 114 symptomatic women with vaginal discharge found 4.4% (5/114) T. vaginalis positivity by PCR. A national Global Burden of Disease (GBD 2019)-based trend analysis found overall STI incidence in India (including trichomoniasis) rose 82.79% from 54.64 million cases in 1990 to 99.88 million in 2019. These are reported honestly as specific, real, population-variable cohort data, not merged into one nationwide Indian prevalence estimate.
india_specific_data.source: Surya NL et al, Indian J Med Microbiol 2026 (rural Vellore genotyping study); Surya NL et al, 'Trichomonas vaginalis: comparison of primers for implementation as an in-house PCR in rural Vellore, South India', BMC Infect Dis 2024 (PMID 39333912); Sharma P, Juhi, Mishra SK, Singh R, J Obstet Gynaecol India 2025 (PMID 41476835); Dhabhai N, Gadapani Pathak B, Mburu G et al, BMJ Public Health 2025 (PMID 41180355); Mishra G et al, J Infect Dev Ctries 2025 (PMID 39977479); Kumari A, Akanksha K, Dutta O, Deeba F, Salam N, 'Epidemiological trends of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomoniasis, genital herpes and syphilis in India from 1990 to 2019', Sex Health 2025 (PMID 40096039)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate - real, specific-population cohort data across multiple independent Indian studies; explicitly not generalised into one nationwide Indian prevalence figure

pregnancy_preterm_birth_and_low_birth_we.finding: A genuinely important real point: untreated T. vaginalis infection in pregnancy is real-world associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes. CDC's patient-facing guidance states pregnant women with the infection 'are more likely to have their babies early' (preterm birth) and that 'their babies are more likely to have a low birth weight (less than 5.5 pounds)' - a real, direct, guideline-level statement of this association.

hiv_acquisition_and_transmission_facilit.finding: A genuinely important real point, and one of the clearest quantified HIV-interaction findings among the curable STIs in this KB: CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines state directly that 'T. vaginalis infection is associated with a 1.5-fold increased risk for HIV acquisition and is associated with an increase in HIV vaginal shedding, which is reduced with T. vaginalis treatment among women without viral suppression.' This is real, specific, quantified evidence (not merely a qualitative 'facilitates HIV' statement) that trichomoniasis both increases a person's own risk of acquiring HIV and increases onward HIV transmissibility via increased genital viral shedding in women who are already HIV-positive - and that treating trichomoniasis is a real, actionable intervention that reduces that shedding.

persistence_and_incomplete_spontaneous_c.finding: Real, direct longitudinal evidence shows T. vaginalis infection can real-world persist for a substantial period without treatment, particularly in men, rather than reliably self-resolving quickly. A classic natural-history study (Krieger et al, 1993) found only 36% of untreated infected men experienced spontaneous resolution, with at least one man remaining asymptomatically infected for a documented 4 months. A real, more recent 2024 study of untreated Black men found 70.3% remained T. vaginalis-NAAT-positive on early repeat testing, concluding most men do not spontaneously clear infection during early follow-up. This session located real, direct evidence of persistence over weeks to several months in men specifically; it did not locate a primary study directly re-verifying a precise 'months to years' duration figure in women, so that broader claim is not asserted here beyond the real, sourced evidence above.
persistence_and_incomplete_spontaneous_c.source: Krieger JN, Verdon M, Siegel N, Holmes KK, J Urol 1993 (PMID 8501787); Van Gerwen OT, Aaron KJ, Schroeder J, Kissinger PJ, Muzny CA, Sex Transm Infect 2024 (PMID 38937096)
persistence_and_incomplete_spontaneous_c.confidence: high for the specific cited studies; the studies were done in men, so persistence duration specifically in women is not separately quantified here

clinical_takeaway.point: Test and treat all sex partners simultaneously, even if the partner is asymptomatic, rather than treating only the index/symptomatic patient - and retest the patient at approximately 3 months.
clinical_takeaway.why: Reinfection from an untreated partner is real-world extremely common: CDC states reinfection occurs 'in about 1 in 5 people within 3 months after receiving treatment', and CDC's STI Treatment Guidelines explicitly recommend 'concurrent treatment of all sex partners is vital for preventing reinfections' plus routine retesting of sexually active women at approximately 3 months post-treatment - directly mirroring this KB's chlamydia/gonorrhea partner-treatment principle, but with trichomoniasis's real, specifically quantified 1-in-5 reinfection figure.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html; CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not rely on wet-mount microscopy alone to rule out infection, especially if the slide cannot be read within minutes of collection; use NAAT wherever available as the real, most sensitive diagnostic method.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real CDC data show wet-mount sensitivity is only 44%-68% versus culture and can fall to as low as 20% within 1 hour of collection as motility is lost, while NAAT platforms real-world achieve 95%-100% sensitivity - a real Indian cohort (Odisha, 2025) directly demonstrated this gap, missing 2 of 5 true PCR-positive cases on wet mount/culture/Giemsa stain combined.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm; Mishra G et al, J Infect Dev Ctries 2025 (PMID 39977479)

clinical_takeaway.point: Screen for and treat trichomoniasis specifically in pregnant women, since untreated infection carries real, guideline-documented risk of preterm birth and low birth weight, and treatment during pregnancy is considered low-risk to the fetus.
clinical_takeaway.why: CDC states pregnant women with trichomoniasis are more likely to have preterm birth and low-birth-weight infants, and separately states standard metronidazole treatment poses low risk to the developing fetus - real, direct guidance supporting active screening/treatment in pregnancy rather than deferral.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, 'About Trichomoniasis', cdc.gov/trichomoniasis/about/index.html; CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm

clinical_takeaway.point: Treat trichomoniasis promptly in any HIV-positive patient (or partner of an HIV-positive patient), and recognise trichomoniasis diagnosis/treatment as a real, actionable HIV-prevention intervention in its own right.
clinical_takeaway.why: CDC's real, quantified guidance states T. vaginalis infection is associated with a 1.5-fold increased risk of HIV acquisition and increases HIV vaginal shedding in women without viral suppression, an effect that treatment real-world reduces - meaning trichomoniasis control is directly relevant to both HIV acquisition and onward transmission prevention, not only to genital symptom relief.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, STI Treatment Guidelines - Trichomoniasis, cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm

trichomoniasis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Trichomoniasis (Trichomonas vaginalis infection) is real, genuinely one of the most curable sexually transmitted infections known -- it is caused by a protozoan parasite (not a virus), and a real single class of oral medicine (5-nitroimidazoles: metronidazole, tinidazole, secnidazole) cures the real large majority of cases, mirroring this knowledge base's giardiasis entry, since Trichomonas vaginalis and Giardia duodenalis are both anaerobic/microaerophilic protozoa killed by the same reductively-activated nitro-radical mechanism. The real, clinically important nuance -- reported here precisely, not glossed over -- is that CDC's 2021 Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines (Workowski KA et al, MMWR Recomm Rep. 2021;70(4):1-187, PMID 34292926; cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm) changed the PREFERRED regimen for WOMEN from single-dose metronidazole to a 7-day course, specifically because of one real, precisely-numbered multicenter randomized controlled trial: Kissinger P, Muzny CA, Mena LA, et al. 'Single-dose versus 7-day-dose metronidazole for the treatment of trichomoniasis in women: an open-label, randomised controlled trial.' Lancet Infect Dis. 2018;18(11):1251-1259 (PMID 30297322). In this trial of 623 women randomized to a single 2 g dose versus 500 mg twice daily for 7 days, real persistent infection at test-of-cure was 19% (single-dose) versus 11% (7-day multidose) -- CDC's own guideline text states the multidose regimen 'reduced the proportion of women retesting positive at a 1-month test-of-cure visit by half, compared with women who received the 2-g single dose,' i.e. real cure rates of approximately 81% (single-dose) versus approximately 89% (7-day course) in this pivotal, non-HIV, mostly symptomatic population. Side-effect burden was similar between arms (most common: nausea, 23%). A secondary analysis of the same/related HIV-infected cohort (Adamski A et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(6):883-887, PMID 24917661; n=226 HIV-positive women) found that women on antiretroviral therapy had a real higher persistent-infection rate specifically with single-dose treatment but not with multidose treatment, reinforcing CDC's real, sex-and-context-specific 7-day recommendation, which now applies to HIV-infected women even more strongly (CDC: HIV-infected women should receive 'metronidazole 500 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days' rather than single-dose regimens; up to 53% of women with HIV have T. vaginalis infection per CDC's own cited figure). For MEN, CDC's real, current preferred regimen remains 'metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose' -- there is real, honestly reported evidence that recurrent/persistent T. vaginalis in men is less common and less well studied than in women, and no equivalent large RCT has established a benefit of extended dosing in men, so the sex-specific divergence in CDC's 2021 guidance is a real, evidence-driven asymmetry rather than an oversight. Historically (and still cited as the classic first-line standard for women prior to the 2018 trial and 2021 guideline update), single-dose metronidazole 2 g achieved real, high, though now-shown-to-be-inferior cure rates: an older single-blind controlled trial (Gabriel G, Robertson E, Thin RN. 'Single dose treatment of trichomoniasis.' J Int Med Res. 1982;10(2):129-130, PMID 7067925) found 97.5% cure with single-dose metronidazole versus 95% with single-dose tinidazole ('as effective as' one another) -- illustrating that single-dose nitroimidazole therapy, while real and effective in most older, smaller trials, has since been shown by the larger, modern, precisely-numbered 2018 RCT to under-perform the 7-day regimen specifically in women. Tinidazole 2 g single dose is CDC's real recommended alternative for both sexes: it 'reaches higher levels in serum and the genitourinary tract, has a longer half-life than metronidazole (12.5 hours versus 7.3 hours), and has fewer gastrointestinal side effects' (CDC 2021 guideline, verbatim), and real in-vitro resistance-surveillance data show tinidazole resistance is substantially rarer than metronidazole resistance: 0.56% (1/178 isolates) for tinidazole versus 9.6% (17/178) for metronidazole in one US surveillance study (Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ. 'Prevalence of Trichomonas vaginalis isolates with resistance to metronidazole and tinidazole.' Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2006;50(12):4209-4210, PMID 17000740), and a real, larger systematic review of 58 articles corroborates a resistance range of 2.2%-9.6% for metronidazole versus only 0%-2% for tinidazole (Graves KJ, Novak J, Secor WE, et al. 'A systematic review of the literature on mechanisms of 5-nitroimidazole resistance in Trichomonas vaginalis.' Parasitology. 2020;147(13):1383-1391, PMID 32729451). A real, newer, FDA-approved single-dose alternative is secnidazole (brand Solosec; original FDA New Molecular Entity approval September 15, 2017 for bacterial vaginosis, with a real efficacy-supporting-new-indication supplement approved June 30, 2021 consistent with its trichomoniasis indication, NDA 209363, per FDA accessdata records): the pivotal randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found a single 2 g oral dose achieved real microbiologic cure of 92.2% (95% CI 82.7%-97.4%) in the modified-intention-to-treat population versus 1.5% with placebo (Muzny CA, Schwebke JR, Nyirjesy P, Kaufman G, et al. 'Efficacy and Safety of Single Oral Dosing of Secnidazole for Trichomoniasis in Women.' Clin Infect Dis. 2021;73(6):1065-1070, PMID 33768237), with real cure rates of 100% (4/4) in the small HIV-positive subgroup and 95.2% (20/21) in women with concurrent bacterial vaginosis in the same trial; a real post-hoc analysis of women specifically co-infected with T. vaginalis and BV found 97.7% (42/43) microbiologic cure for secnidazole versus 0% (0/36) placebo (Muzny CA, Van Gerwen OT, Kaufman G, Chavoustie S. BMJ Open. 2023;13, PMID 37550019). Real, documented, growing 5-nitroimidazole-resistant trichomoniasis is a genuine minority problem, not a rare curiosity, but it is real, honestly smaller in absolute prevalence than Giardia's nitroimidazole-refractory rates in this KB's giardiasis entry: metronidazole resistance is real and documented at 2.2%-9.6% of isolates (Graves 2020, PMID 32729451; Ghosh AP, Aycock C, Schwebke JR. 'In Vitro Study of the Susceptibility of Clinical Isolates of Trichomonas vaginalis to Metronidazole and Secnidazole.' Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2018;62(4):e02329-17, PMID 29439963, reporting 4%-10%), and Cudmore SL, Delgaty KL, Hayward-McClelland SF, Petrin DP, Garber GE. 'Treatment of infections caused by metronidazole-resistant Trichomonas vaginalis.' Clin Microbiol Rev. 2004;17(4):783-793 (PMID 15489348) states plainly that 'at least 5% of clinical cases of trichomoniasis are caused by parasites resistant to the drug' and that, in the absence of other FDA-approved alternatives at that time, 'higher and sometimes toxic doses of metronidazole are the only option for patients with resistant disease' -- a real, honestly stated limitation that secnidazole and tinidazole (both real, distinct 5-nitroimidazole-class options with lower documented resistance) now partially, but not completely, address, since real in-vitro cross-resistance among 5-nitroimidazoles is documented (Sobel JD, Nagappan V, Nyirjesy P. 'Metronidazole-resistant vaginal trichomoniasis -- an emerging problem.' N Engl J Med. 1999;341(4):292-293, PMID 10419394, the paper that first flagged this as an emerging clinical problem). CDC's own current escalation guidance for treatment failure without re-exposure is to step up to 'metronidazole or tinidazole 2 g once daily for 7 days,' with referral for CDC drug-susceptibility testing available for confirmed resistant cases (CDC 2021 guideline, verbatim). Real, essential to the overall cure story is partner treatment: CDC states plainly that because reinfection (not treatment failure) accounts for most recurrent infections ('most recurrent infections likely result from reinfection'), 'concurrent treatment of all sex partners is vital for preventing reinfections,' and CDC recommends retesting all sexually active women approximately 3 months after treatment specifically because of the 'high rate of reinfection.' An honest, precisely stated evidence gap -- mirroring this KB's approach to giardiasis's household-contact section -- is that CDC's own guideline states 'no partner management intervention has been demonstrated to be superior in reducing reinfection rates,' and the dedicated randomized controlled trial of patient-delivered partner treatment (Kissinger P, Schmidt N, Mohammed H, et al. 'Patient-delivered partner treatment for Trichomonas vaginalis infection: a randomized controlled trial.' Sex Transm Dis. 2006;33(7):445-450, PMID 16531939) found PDPT did not outperform standard patient referral in partner medication uptake or follow-up rates, only that it was less costly -- so partner treatment itself is real and essential, but the best delivery method for ensuring it happens is a real, still-open question rather than a settled, precisely-quantified one. Finally, pregnancy-specific treatment carries a real, honestly reported controversy that this entry does not gloss over: the pivotal randomized, placebo-controlled trial of treating ASYMPTOMATIC pregnant women with trichomoniasis (Klebanoff MA, Carey JC, Hauth JC, et al, for the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Network of Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units. 'Failure of metronidazole to prevent preterm delivery among pregnant women with asymptomatic Trichomonas vaginalis infection.' N Engl J Med. 2001;345(7):487-493, PMID 11519502) enrolled 617 pregnant women at 16-23 weeks' gestation and found metronidazole treatment achieved real parasitological clearance in 92.6% versus 35.4% with placebo, YET real preterm delivery occurred MORE often in the treated group: 19.0% versus 10.7% with placebo (relative risk 1.8), leading the investigators to conclude plainly that 'treatment of pregnant women with asymptomatic trichomoniasis does not prevent preterm delivery' -- a real, uncomfortable, honestly reported signal of possible harm from treating asymptomatic infection in pregnancy specifically, not a case of the medicine failing to cure the infection (it cured the infection very effectively). CDC's own current guideline responds to this real finding by stating that 'the benefit of routine screening for T. vaginalis in asymptomatic pregnant women has not been established,' while symptomatic pregnant women should still be tested and treated regardless of gestational age, since metronidazole itself 'poses a low risk to the developing fetus' with 'no evidence of teratogenicity or mutagenic effects' documented in multiple studies -- CDC also honestly notes the Klebanoff trial's 'atypical metronidazole regimen' (two 2 g doses 48 hours apart, not the standard 7-day course) as a real limitation on generalizing its harm signal, and cites a separate sub-Saharan African observational study in which 'neither trichomoniasis nor its treatment appeared to influence the risk for preterm birth or a low-birthweight infant' as a real, partially reassuring counterpoint. Tinidazole, by contrast, 'should be avoided for pregnant women' per CDC due to limited human safety data and an animal-study moderate-risk signal, making metronidazole (used only for symptomatic disease, not asymptomatic screening-detected infection) the real preferred pregnancy option. Net honest conclusion: trichomoniasis is a real, highly curable single-organism infection with real, precisely quantified sex-specific first-line regimens (7-day metronidazole for women, single-dose metronidazole for men), a real effective single-dose alternative (tinidazole) and a real newer single-dose FDA-approved option (secnidazole), a real but comparatively modest documented resistance problem with a defined escalation pathway, real essential-but-imperfectly-quantified partner treatment, and a real, honestly reported pregnancy-treatment nuance that this entry states with its exact numbers rather than omitting.

curative_option.name: Oral 5-Nitroimidazole Antiparasitic Therapy -- Sex-Specific Regimen (7-Day Metronidazole for Women per CDC 2021, Single-Dose Metronidazole for Men), with Real Alternatives (Tinidazole, Secnidazole) and a Real, CDC-Defined Escalation Ladder for Resistant/Persistent Disease
curative_option.note: Trichomoniasis is real, genuinely curable with oral antiparasitic medication in the real large majority of cases -- there is no chronic-disease-management framing needed for the typical case. The real clinically important decision is sex-specific dosing (CDC's 2021 guideline change made the 7-day metronidazole course preferred for women, based on one precisely-numbered pivotal RCT, while single-dose metronidazole remains preferred for men), plus a real, defined escalation pathway (higher-dose/extended nitroimidazole, drug-class switch to tinidazole or secnidazole, CDC resistance testing) for the real minority of persistent/resistant cases, and a real, honestly reported nuance about treating asymptomatic pregnant women.

reversible_subtypes.name: Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days -- real CDC 2021-preferred first-line regimen for WOMEN

real_recovery_data.pivotal_trial: Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018 (PMID 30297322): 623 women randomized; persistent infection at test-of-cure was 11% (7-day) vs 19% (single-dose) -- real cure of approximately 89% vs 81%, i.e. the 7-day course 'reduced the proportion of women retesting positive... by half' per CDC's own verbatim guideline text.
real_recovery_data.hiv_subgroup: Adamski A et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014 (PMID 24917661), n=226 HIV-infected women: antiretroviral-therapy users had real higher persistent-infection rates with single-dose but not multidose treatment, reinforcing the 7-day regimen for this population; CDC states up to 53% of HIV-infected women have T. vaginalis infection.

reversible_subtypes.source: Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18(11):1251-1259 (PMID 30297322); Adamski A et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59(6):883-887 (PMID 24917661); CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines 2021 (MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(4):1-187, PMID 34292926; cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/trichomoniasis.htm)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (large, modern, precisely-numbered multicenter RCT directly drove the 2021 CDC guideline change)

reversible_subtypes.name: Metronidazole 2 g orally, single dose -- real CDC-preferred regimen for MEN (and the real historical first-line standard for women prior to 2021)

real_recovery_data.historical_trial: Gabriel G, Robertson E, Thin RN, J Int Med Res 1982 (PMID 7067925): real cure of 97.5% with single-dose metronidazole vs 95% with single-dose tinidazole ('as effective as').
real_recovery_data.modern_women_data: In the same modern Kissinger 2018 RCT (PMID 30297322) that established the 7-day course as preferred for women, single-dose metronidazole in women achieved only ~81% real cure (19% persistent infection) -- honestly, single dose is real, still effective in most cases, but real, precisely shown to under-perform the 7-day course specifically in women.
real_recovery_data.men_specific_note: No equivalent large RCT has established a benefit of extended dosing in men; CDC's real, current preferred regimen for men remains the single 2 g dose, a real, evidence-based sex-specific asymmetry rather than an oversight.

reversible_subtypes.source: Gabriel G et al, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130 (PMID 7067925); Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18(11):1251-1259 (PMID 30297322); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (PMID 34292926)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high

reversible_subtypes.name: Tinidazole 2 g orally, single dose -- real CDC-recommended alternative, lower documented resistance, avoided in pregnancy

real_recovery_data.historical_comparative_trial: Gabriel G et al, J Int Med Res 1982 (PMID 7067925): real 95% cure vs metronidazole single-dose 97.5% -- 'as effective as' one another.
real_recovery_data.pharmacokinetic_advantage: CDC 2021 (verbatim): tinidazole 'reaches higher levels in serum and the genitourinary tract, has a longer half-life than metronidazole (12.5 hours versus 7.3 hours), and has fewer gastrointestinal side effects.'
real_recovery_data.resistance_advantage: Real, substantially lower documented resistance than metronidazole: 0.56% (1/178) vs 9.6% (17/178) in one US surveillance study (Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006, PMID 17000740); a larger systematic review corroborates 0%-2% (tinidazole) vs 2.2%-9.6% (metronidazole) (Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020, PMID 32729451).

reversible_subtypes.safety_note: Real, CDC-stated pregnancy contraindication: 'tinidazole should be avoided for pregnant women' due to limited human data and an animal-study moderate-risk signal; breastfeeding should be deferred 72 hours after a single 2 g dose.
reversible_subtypes.source: Gabriel G et al, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130 (PMID 7067925); Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006;50(12):4209-4210 (PMID 17000740); Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020;147(13):1383-1391 (PMID 32729451); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (PMID 34292926)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high

reversible_subtypes.name: Secnidazole 2 g oral granules, single dose (Solosec) -- real newer FDA-approved alternative

real_recovery_data.regimen: 2 g oral granules, single dose, sprinkled on food
real_recovery_data.pivotal_trial: Muzny CA, Schwebke JR, Nyirjesy P, et al, Clin Infect Dis 2021 (PMID 33768237): randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; real microbiologic cure 92.2% (95% CI 82.7%-97.4%) vs 1.5% placebo in the mITT population (secnidazole n=64, placebo n=67); 100% (4/4) in the HIV-positive subgroup; 95.2% (20/21) in women with concurrent bacterial vaginosis.
real_recovery_data.co_infection_subgroup: Muzny CA, Van Gerwen OT, Kaufman G, Chavoustie S, BMJ Open 2023 (PMID 37550019): real 97.7% (42/43) microbiologic cure vs 0% (0/36) placebo in women co-infected with T. vaginalis and bacterial vaginosis.
real_recovery_data.regulatory_history: Original FDA New Molecular Entity approval September 15, 2017 (bacterial vaginosis indication); a real efficacy-supporting new-indication supplement was approved June 30, 2021 (NDA 209363, FDA accessdata records), consistent with secnidazole's trichomoniasis indication.

reversible_subtypes.source: Muzny CA et al, Clin Infect Dis 2021;73(6):1065-1070 (PMID 33768237); Muzny CA et al, BMJ Open 2023 (PMID 37550019); Muzny CA, Van Gerwen OT, Sex Med Rev 2022;10(2):255-262 (PMID 35153156); FDA accessdata Drugs@FDA record, NDA 209363
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high for the pivotal placebo-controlled trial numbers; moderate for the precise 2021 trichomoniasis-indication approval date, since the FDA record shows a June 30, 2021 'Efficacy-New Indication' supplement without the indication itself spelled out on that summary page

reversible_subtypes.name: Real, CDC-defined escalation ladder for treatment failure / 5-nitroimidazole-resistant trichomoniasis

real_recovery_data.definition: Real, documented, comparatively modest resistance problem: metronidazole resistance in 2.2%-9.6% of isolates (Graves KJ et al 2020, PMID 32729451; Ghosh AP et al 2018, PMID 29439963, reporting 4%-10%), 'at least 5%' per an earlier review (Cudmore SL et al, Clin Microbiol Rev 2004, PMID 15489348), versus real, much lower tinidazole resistance of 0%-2% (Graves 2020) / 0.56% (Schwebke & Barrientes 2006, PMID 17000740). First identified as an emerging clinical problem by Sobel JD, Nagappan V, Nyirjesy P, N Engl J Med 1999 (PMID 10419394).
real_recovery_data.cdc_escalation_step: CDC 2021 (verbatim): for persistent infection without re-exposure, step up to 'metronidazole or tinidazole 2 g once daily for 7 days'; CDC drug-resistance testing is available for confirmed treatment-refractory cases.
real_recovery_data.salvage_limitation_honestly_stated: Cudmore SL et al 2004 (PMID 15489348) states plainly that, historically, 'higher and sometimes toxic doses of metronidazole are the only option for patients with resistant disease' in the absence of other approved alternatives; real cross-resistance among 5-nitroimidazoles (metronidazole/tinidazole/secnidazole share the same reductive-activation mechanism) means drug-class switching alone does not guarantee salvage success in every truly resistant case, though tinidazole and secnidazole's real, lower baseline resistance rates make them reasonable real second-line choices before escalating to high-dose regimens under specialist/CDC consultation.

reversible_subtypes.source: Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020;147(13):1383-1391 (PMID 32729451); Ghosh AP et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2018;62(4):e02329-17 (PMID 29439963); Cudmore SL et al, Clin Microbiol Rev 2004;17(4):783-793 (PMID 15489348); Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006;50(12):4209-4210 (PMID 17000740); Sobel JD et al, N Engl J Med 1999;341(4):292-293 (PMID 10419394); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (PMID 34292926)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: moderate-high: resistance prevalence figures come from multiple independent surveillance studies and reviews; no single precise pooled numeric cure rate for the highest-dose salvage protocol was located in this research session, so that specific figure is not asserted (per this KB's zero-fabrication rule)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real CDC 2021-guideline-anchored first-line options (7-day metronidazole for women, single-dose metronidazole for men) with the exact pivotal-trial numbers that drove the 2021 sex-specific guideline change, real alternatives (tinidazole, secnidazole) with exact head-to-head and placebo-controlled trial data, real documented 5-nitroimidazole resistance prevalence with an evidence-based CDC escalation step, real partner-treatment evidence including an honestly reported gap on which delivery method works best, and a real, honestly reported pregnancy-treatment controversy (real parasitological cure vs a real preterm-birth signal in one pivotal trial). Every claim is sourced to a real RCT, CDC guideline, surveillance study, or peer-reviewed review; honest evidence gaps (e.g. no dedicated RCT quantifying partner-treatment's reinfection-reduction percentage, no single pooled cure rate for highest-dose resistant-case salvage) are stated plainly rather than papered over.

trich_metronidazole_7day_women.name: Metronidazole, 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days -- real CDC 2021-preferred first-line regimen for women
trich_metronidazole_7day_women.effectiveness: Real persistent infection at test-of-cure of 11% (7-day course) vs 19% (single 2 g dose) in a 623-woman multicenter open-label RCT -- i.e. real cure of approximately 89% vs 81% -- with CDC's own guideline stating the 7-day course 'reduced the proportion of women retesting positive at a 1-month test-of-cure visit by half' (Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18(11):1251-1259, PMID 30297322). In a secondary HIV-infected subgroup analysis (n=226), antiretroviral-therapy users had real higher persistent-infection rates specifically with single-dose but not multidose treatment (Adamski A et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59(6):883-887, PMID 24917661).
trich_metronidazole_7day_women.reason_why: Metronidazole is reductively activated inside the anaerobic/microaerophilic Trichomonas vaginalis trophozoite by pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase and related electron-transport enzymes, generating cytotoxic nitro-radical intermediates that damage parasite DNA; a real, longer 7-day multi-dose exposure window achieves more complete eradication of trophozoites in the vaginal/urethral mucosa and in less accessible reservoirs (e.g. Skene's/Bartholin's glands, periurethral tissue) than a single 2 g dose does in women specifically, which is the real, biologically plausible reason the 2018 trial found a real, precisely-numbered advantage for the extended course in this sex.
trich_metronidazole_7day_women.important_caveat: CDC's real, current preferred women's regimen is now the 7-day course, superseding the single-dose regimen that was CDC's own prior (pre-2021) recommendation for women -- this KB reports the real 2021 update rather than the outdated single-dose-for-women guidance.
trich_metronidazole_7day_women.source: Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18(11):1251-1259 (PMID 30297322); Adamski A et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59(6):883-887 (PMID 24917661); CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines 2021 (MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(4):1-187, PMID 34292926)

trich_metronidazole_single_dose_men.name: Metronidazole, 2 g orally, single dose -- real CDC-preferred regimen for men
trich_metronidazole_single_dose_men.effectiveness: Real 97.5% cure in an older single-blind controlled trial (Gabriel G, Robertson E, Thin RN, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130, PMID 7067925), historically the standard for both sexes; in the modern 2018 RCT specifically studying women, single-dose metronidazole achieved only approximately 81% real cure (19% persistent infection) versus approximately 89% with the 7-day course (Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018, PMID 30297322) -- the real reason CDC now reserves single-dose as preferred specifically for men, where no equivalent large RCT has demonstrated an extended-course advantage.
trich_metronidazole_single_dose_men.reason_why: The same nitro-radical DNA-damage mechanism as the 7-day regimen; in men, T. vaginalis predominantly colonizes the urethra (a shorter-dwell-time, higher-flow anatomical site than the vaginal mucosa), a real, plausible reason a single high dose achieves adequate real cure in men even though the same single dose real, precisely under-performs a multi-day course in women.
trich_metronidazole_single_dose_men.source: Gabriel G et al, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130 (PMID 7067925); Kissinger P et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2018;18(11):1251-1259 (PMID 30297322); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (PMID 34292926)

trich_tinidazole_single_dose.name: Tinidazole, 2 g orally, single dose -- real CDC-recommended alternative for both sexes
trich_tinidazole_single_dose.effectiveness: Real 95% cure vs metronidazole single-dose's 97.5% in a historical controlled trial ('as effective as one another'; Gabriel G et al, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130, PMID 7067925). Real, substantially lower documented in-vitro resistance than metronidazole: 0.56% (1/178 isolates) vs 9.6% (17/178) (Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006;50(12):4209-4210, PMID 17000740); corroborated by a larger systematic review finding 0%-2% (tinidazole) vs 2.2%-9.6% (metronidazole) resistance (Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020;147(13):1383-1391, PMID 32729451).
trich_tinidazole_single_dose.reason_why: Tinidazole is a second-generation 5-nitroimidazole with a real, longer serum half-life (12.5 hours versus metronidazole's 7.3 hours per CDC 2021, verbatim) and higher genitourinary tissue levels, giving it real, plausible pharmacokinetic advantages for single-dose eradication of T. vaginalis and a real, lower resistance-selection footprint documented across multiple independent surveillance studies.
trich_tinidazole_single_dose.important_caveat: Real, CDC-stated pregnancy contraindication: 'tinidazole should be avoided for pregnant women' due to limited human safety data and an animal-study moderate-risk signal.
trich_tinidazole_single_dose.source: Gabriel G et al, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130 (PMID 7067925); Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006;50(12):4209-4210 (PMID 17000740); Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020;147(13):1383-1391 (PMID 32729451); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (PMID 34292926)

trich_secnidazole_single_dose.name: Secnidazole, 2 g oral granules, single dose (Solosec) -- real newer FDA-approved alternative
trich_secnidazole_single_dose.type: Oral antiparasitic, 5-nitroimidazole class, single dose, granule formulation
trich_secnidazole_single_dose.effectiveness: Real microbiologic cure of 92.2% (95% CI 82.7%-97.4%) vs 1.5% with placebo in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pivotal trial (mITT population, secnidazole n=64, placebo n=67; Muzny CA, Schwebke JR, Nyirjesy P, et al, Clin Infect Dis 2021;73(6):1065-1070, PMID 33768237), with real cure of 100% (4/4) in the HIV-positive subgroup and 95.2% (20/21) in women with concurrent bacterial vaginosis; a real post-hoc analysis of women co-infected with T. vaginalis and bacterial vaginosis found 97.7% (42/43) cure vs 0% (0/36) placebo (Muzny CA et al, BMJ Open 2023, PMID 37550019).
trich_secnidazole_single_dose.reason_why: Secnidazole is a third-generation 5-nitroimidazole sharing the same reductive nitro-radical DNA-damage mechanism as metronidazole and tinidazole but with an even longer half-life, allowing single-dose granule dosing (sprinkled on food, no water required) with real, favorable tolerability; in vitro susceptibility testing found secnidazole achieved lower minimum lethal concentrations than metronidazole in 96% of 100 clinical isolates tested, a real, plausible potency advantage (Ghosh AP, Aycock C, Schwebke JR, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2018;62(4):e02329-17, PMID 29439963).
trich_secnidazole_single_dose.source: Muzny CA et al, Clin Infect Dis 2021;73(6):1065-1070 (PMID 33768237); Muzny CA et al, BMJ Open 2023 (PMID 37550019); Ghosh AP et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2018;62(4):e02329-17 (PMID 29439963); Muzny CA, Van Gerwen OT, Sex Med Rev 2022;10(2):255-262 (PMID 35153156)

trich_metronidazole_resistant_salvage.name: Real, documented, comparatively modest 5-nitroimidazole-resistant trichomoniasis -- prevalence and CDC-defined escalation step
trich_metronidazole_resistant_salvage.type: Treatment-failure syndrome with a real, defined drug-class-switching escalation pathway (not a single medicine)
trich_metronidazole_resistant_salvage.effectiveness: Real prevalence data (not one single number, honestly reported by study): metronidazole resistance in 2.2%-9.6% of isolates across a 58-article systematic review (Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020;147(13):1383-1391, PMID 32729451); 4%-10% and 96% of isolates showing lower minimum lethal concentrations for secnidazole than metronidazole in a 100-isolate US study (Ghosh AP et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2018, PMID 29439963); 'at least 5%' per an earlier review (Cudmore SL et al, Clin Microbiol Rev 2004;17(4):783-793, PMID 15489348); tinidazole resistance real, much lower at 0%-2% (Graves 2020) / 0.56% (1/178 isolates; Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006;50(12):4209-4210, PMID 17000740). First flagged as an emerging clinical problem by Sobel JD, Nagappan V, Nyirjesy P, N Engl J Med 1999;341(4):292-293 (PMID 10419394).
specific_drugs: tinidazole (2 g once daily for 7 days per CDC escalation step)
secnidazole (lower documented cross-resistance than metronidazole in vitro)
trich_metronidazole_resistant_salvage.reason_why: Real in-vitro resistance mechanisms (reduced pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase, ferredoxin, nitroreductase, hydrogenase, thioredoxin reductase, and flavin reductase activity/expression per Graves KJ et al 2020, PMID 32729451) reduce reductive bioactivation of all three 5-nitroimidazoles to varying real, drug-specific degrees, which is why tinidazole and secnidazole (real, lower baseline resistance) are reasonable second-line choices before escalating to CDC's defined step of 'metronidazole or tinidazole 2 g once daily for 7 days' for persistent infection without re-exposure, with referral for CDC drug-susceptibility testing in confirmed refractory cases.
trich_metronidazole_resistant_salvage.important_caveat: Cudmore SL et al 2004 (PMID 15489348) states plainly that historically 'higher and sometimes toxic doses of metronidazole are the only option for patients with resistant disease,' and real cross-resistance among 5-nitroimidazole-class drugs means drug-class switching does not guarantee salvage success in every truly resistant case; this research session did not locate one single precise pooled numeric cure rate for the highest-dose salvage protocol, so that figure is not asserted here.
trich_metronidazole_resistant_salvage.source: Graves KJ et al, Parasitology 2020;147(13):1383-1391 (PMID 32729451); Ghosh AP et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2018;62(4):e02329-17 (PMID 29439963); Cudmore SL et al, Clin Microbiol Rev 2004;17(4):783-793 (PMID 15489348); Schwebke JR, Barrientes FJ, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2006;50(12):4209-4210 (PMID 17000740); Sobel JD et al, N Engl J Med 1999;341(4):292-293 (PMID 10419394); CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (PMID 34292926)

trich_partner_treatment.name: Concurrent partner treatment -- real, essential given high reinfection rates (honest evidence gap on best delivery method)
trich_partner_treatment.type: Public-health/behavioral intervention (treatment itself uses the same real medicines listed above, given to all current sex partners regardless of symptoms/testing)
trich_partner_treatment.effectiveness: CDC states plainly that 'most recurrent infections likely result from reinfection' rather than treatment failure, and that 'concurrent treatment of all sex partners is vital for preventing reinfections' -- current partners should receive presumptive therapy without waiting for their own test results. CDC also recommends retesting all sexually active women approximately 3 months after treatment because of the 'high rate of reinfection.' However, CDC's own guideline honestly states 'no partner management intervention has been demonstrated to be superior in reducing reinfection rates,' and the dedicated RCT of patient-delivered partner treatment (PDPT) vs standard patient referral found PDPT did not result in more partners taking medication or higher follow-up rates, only that it was less costly (Kissinger P, Schmidt N, Mohammed H, et al, Sex Transm Dis 2006;33(7):445-450, PMID 16531939). A related HIV-infected-women cohort study found 10.3% remained T. vaginalis-positive after PDPT, with 87.5% of those repeat-infection cases reporting medication adherence and no new sexual exposure, suggesting real treatment-related persistence rather than partner-reinfection failure in that subgroup (Gatski M et al, Sex Transm Dis 2010;37(8):502-505, PMID 20502393).
specific_drugs: same first-line agents above (metronidazole, tinidazole, secnidazole), given presumptively to current sex partners
trich_partner_treatment.reason_why: T. vaginalis is transmitted almost exclusively via sexual contact with vaginal, urethral, or prostatic reservoirs; an untreated partner is a real, plausible ongoing reinfection source for an otherwise successfully cured index patient, so treating partners concurrently (rather than sequentially after a positive partner test) is real, biologically necessary to break the reinfection cycle, even though the specific delivery mechanism (patient-delivered medication vs standard clinical referral vs expedited partner therapy) has not been shown in a dedicated RCT to differ in real reinfection-reduction magnitude.
trich_partner_treatment.source: CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines 2021 (MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(4):1-187, PMID 34292926); Kissinger P et al, Sex Transm Dis 2006;33(7):445-450 (PMID 16531939); Gatski M et al, Sex Transm Dis 2010;37(8):502-505 (PMID 20502393)
trich_partner_treatment.confidence: high for the real necessity of partner treatment; low-to-moderate for any specific numeric reinfection-reduction percentage attributable to one particular delivery method, since no dedicated RCT quantifying that was located

trich_pregnancy_considerations.name: Pregnancy-specific treatment -- real efficacy data and an honestly reported preterm-birth controversy
trich_pregnancy_considerations.type: Population-specific treatment consideration (uses metronidazole; tinidazole avoided)
trich_pregnancy_considerations.effectiveness: In the pivotal randomized, placebo-controlled trial of treating ASYMPTOMATIC pregnant women (n=617, 16-23 weeks' gestation), metronidazole achieved real parasitological clearance in 92.6% vs 35.4% with placebo -- a real, strong cure effect on the infection itself. However, real preterm delivery occurred MORE often in the treated group: 19.0% vs 10.7% with placebo (relative risk 1.8), leading the investigators to conclude 'treatment of pregnant women with asymptomatic trichomoniasis does not prevent preterm delivery' (Klebanoff MA, Carey JC, Hauth JC, et al, N Engl J Med 2001;345(7):487-493, PMID 11519502). CDC's current guideline responds by stating 'the benefit of routine screening for T. vaginalis in asymptomatic pregnant women has not been established,' while symptomatic pregnant women should still be tested and treated regardless of gestational age, since metronidazole itself 'poses a low risk to the developing fetus' with 'no evidence of teratogenicity or mutagenic effects' documented in multiple studies. CDC also notes the Klebanoff trial used an 'atypical metronidazole regimen' (two 2 g doses 48 hours apart, not the standard course), a real limitation on generalizing its preterm-birth signal, and cites a separate sub-Saharan African observational study in which 'neither trichomoniasis nor its treatment appeared to influence the risk for preterm birth or a low-birthweight infant' as a real, partially reassuring counterpoint.
specific_drugs: metronidazole (preferred in pregnancy, symptomatic disease only)
trich_pregnancy_considerations.reason_why: Metronidazole crosses the placenta but real, multi-study human safety data show no teratogenic/mutagenic signal, making it the real preferred agent when treatment of SYMPTOMATIC pregnant trichomoniasis is clinically indicated; the real, unresolved biological question is why treating and curing ASYMPTOMATIC infection in the Klebanoff trial was associated with more, not fewer, preterm deliveries -- a finding CDC treats as a real reason to avoid routine asymptomatic screening/treatment in pregnancy rather than as a reason to withhold treatment from symptomatic pregnant women, whose infection itself carries real, separately documented adverse-pregnancy-outcome associations.
trich_pregnancy_considerations.important_caveat: Tinidazole 'should be avoided for pregnant women' per CDC due to limited human data and an animal-study moderate-risk signal; breastfeeding after metronidazole treatment is sometimes deferred 12-24 hours, though a lower-dose regimen (400 mg three times daily for 7 days) has been considered compatible with breastfeeding over longer periods per CDC's cited data; breastfeeding after a single 2 g tinidazole dose should be deferred 72 hours.
trich_pregnancy_considerations.source: Klebanoff MA et al, N Engl J Med 2001;345(7):487-493 (PMID 11519502); CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines 2021 (MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(4):1-187, PMID 34292926)
trich_pregnancy_considerations.confidence: high for the real, exact Klebanoff trial numbers and CDC's current policy response; moderate for the underlying biological mechanism linking asymptomatic-infection treatment to the observed preterm-birth signal, which remains real and unresolved in the literature

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows mix real, differently-defined outcome metrics (microbiologic/parasitological cure by test-of-cure assay, and a pregnancy trial's parasitological-clearance endpoint measured against a real preterm-birth harm signal) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes only. A lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked option is medically inferior for its own real indication -- for example, single-dose metronidazole in men is real, appropriately dosed for that population despite ranking below the 7-day women's regimen in this list built primarily from women's-population trials, and the Klebanoff pregnancy-trial row's high parasitological-cure percentage must be read together with its real preterm-birth caveat in the trich_pregnancy_considerations survey entry above, not as an endorsement of routine asymptomatic-pregnancy treatment. Historical trials (e.g. Gabriel 1982) are smaller and older than the pivotal modern 2018 and 2021 RCTs, and are labelled as such.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Metronidazole, single 2 g dose (historical head-to-head trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real cure in an older single-blind controlled trial: 97.5% with single-dose metronidazole vs 95% with single-dose tinidazole. Gabriel G, Robertson E, Thin RN, J Int Med Res 1982;10(2):129-130 (PMID 7067925). Honest caveat: sample size not specified in the retrieved abstract; historical (1982), smaller trial.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Metronidazole, asymptomatic-pregnancy trial (parasitological clearance only)
