Because of this, standard practice is a minimum several-hour emergency-department observation period after apparent resolution (StatPearls NBK482124 cites 4 hours as a standard minimum), with longer observation for higher-risk patients (prior biphasic reaction, severe initial reaction, beta-blocker use, older age, limited access to further care). The AI's role in this scenario is only to recognise the pattern and route to immediate emergency epinephrine administration and emergency care; choice of second-line agents, admission/observation duration, and every other clinical decision belong to the treating emergency physician.

ige_mediated_mechanism.finding: Anaphylaxis is defined as a rapidly evolving, generalized, multi-system allergic reaction. It is typically an IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity reaction: prior sensitization causes allergen-specific IgE to bind high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure, allergen cross-links this surface-bound IgE, triggering degranulation and release of preformed and newly synthesized mediators - histamine, tryptase, carboxypeptidase A and proteoglycans (preformed, granule-stored) plus leukotrienes, prostaglandins and platelet-activating factor (newly synthesized from membrane phospholipids). These mediators produce the vasodilation, increased vascular permeability (causing hypotension and angioedema/urticaria) and bronchoconstriction (causing wheeze and dyspnea) that define the clinical syndrome.

non_ige_mediated_mechanism.finding: Not all anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated. A growing body of evidence identifies MRGPRX2 (Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2) as a central mediator of IgE-independent ('non-IgE-mediated', historically termed 'anaphylactoid') mast cell activation: MRGPRX2 is activated directly by cationic ligands including certain drugs (e.g., neuromuscular blocking agents, some antibiotics, opioids) and endogenous neuropeptides, triggering mast cell degranulation and a clinically indistinguishable anaphylactic reaction without requiring prior sensitization or antigen-specific IgE - which explains why some patients react on their very first documented exposure to a drug. Clonal mast cell disorders (e.g., mastocytosis) and non-IgE pathways are also recognised drivers of more severe reactions, particularly with venom triggers.
non_ige_mediated_mechanism.source: Non-immunoglobulin E-mediated mechanisms of anaphylaxis, Curr Opin Allergy Clin Immunol 2026;26:358-363, PMID 42542541; Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 in non-IgE-mediated mast cell activation and anaphylaxis: a paradigm shift, Curr Opin Allergy Clin Immunol 2026;26:372-377, PMID 42566323
non_ige_mediated_mechanism.confidence: moderate - MRGPRX2 mechanism is an active, evolving area of research; the specific clinical proportion of anaphylaxis cases attributable to this pathway versus classic IgE-mediated mechanism was not independently quantified in this session

biphasic_reaction_phenomenon.finding: A genuinely important and well-documented pattern in anaphylaxis is the biphasic reaction: a recurrence of anaphylactic symptoms after apparent complete resolution of the initial episode, without any further allergen exposure. Reported incidence varies across studies depending on population and definition - a meta-analysis across community/emergency settings found a pooled estimate of 3.92% of all anaphylaxis cases, while other systematic reviews report biphasic reactions in up to 20% of cases. Among 4,114 anaphylaxis patients in one systematic review/meta-analysis, the median time to biphasic symptom onset was 11 hours after resolution of the initial reaction (range 0.2 to 72.0 hours); a separate pediatric-focused review reported recurrence usually within about 8 hours. Initial hypotension and an unknown/unidentified trigger were associated with higher biphasic-reaction risk, while a food trigger was associated with lower risk, in the largest meta-analysis identified.
biphasic_reaction_phenomenon.source: Motosue MS et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2021;9:2321-2333, PMID 33549844; Lee S et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3:408-416, PMID 25680923; Update in pediatric anaphylaxis: a systematic review, Clin Pediatr (Phila) 2013;52:451-461, PMID 23393309; StatPearls NBK482124
biphasic_reaction_phenomenon.confidence: high for the existence and clinical importance of the phenomenon; moderate for the exact incidence figure given the wide reported range (3.92% to 20%) across studies with differing case definitions and settings

common_triggers.finding: The most common recognised triggers of anaphylaxis are foods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, eggs, sesame, and others such as wheat and soy), insect stings (bee, wasp/yellow jacket, fire ant), medications (notably antibiotics and neuromuscular blocking/anesthetic agents), and latex; exercise-induced anaphylaxis is a rarer recognised category. In a UK fatal-reaction case series, iatrogenic (largely drug-related) causes accounted for roughly half of fatal reactions, with food and insect venom each accounting for roughly a quarter.
common_triggers.source: AAAAI (American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology), 'Anaphylaxis' patient/clinical resource; StatPearls NBK482124; Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000;30:1144-1150, PMID 10931122

niaid_faan_clinical_criteria.finding: Anaphylaxis is diagnosed clinically using the widely adopted NIAID/Food Allergy and Anaphylaxis Network (FAAN) criteria, which classify a reaction as highly likely to be anaphylaxis if any ONE of three scenarios is met: (1) acute onset of an illness (minutes to several hours) with involvement of skin and/or mucosal tissue (e.g., generalized urticaria, itching/flushing, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) together with at least one of respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia) or reduced blood pressure/associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (e.g., syncope, incontinence); OR (2) two or more of the following occurring rapidly after likely exposure to a probable allergen: skin/mucosal tissue involvement, respiratory compromise, reduced blood pressure or associated symptoms, or persistent gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., cramping, vomiting); OR (3) reduced blood pressure after exposure to a KNOWN allergen for that patient. This clinical, multi-system, rapid-onset framework - not a laboratory test - is what drives the acute diagnosis.
niaid_faan_clinical_criteria.source: Sampson HA et al., 'Second symposium on the definition and management of anaphylaxis: summary report', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2006;117:391-397, PMID 16461139; StatPearls NBK482124

tryptase_role_and_limits.finding: Serum tryptase can be measured to support confirmation of an anaphylactic episode retrospectively, since it remains elevated for several hours after mast cell degranulation, but it has low sensitivity - notably, tryptase levels are frequently normal in food-triggered anaphylaxis - so a normal tryptase does NOT rule out anaphylaxis. The genuinely important clinical point is that anaphylaxis diagnosis, and the decision to treat, are made on clinical presentation alone in the acute moment: laboratory studies including tryptase are far too slow to inform emergency treatment and are not required to begin treatment.
tryptase_role_and_limits.confidence: high for the clinical-diagnosis-drives-treatment principle; moderate for the specific claim that tryptase is 'frequently normal' in food-triggered anaphylaxis, which was reported by this secondary source without an independently re-verified primary quantitative citation in this session

rapid_onset.finding: Anaphylaxis characteristically has a rapid onset, typically within minutes to up to about two hours after exposure to the causative allergen, which is itself a defining diagnostic feature distinguishing it from more indolent processes.
rapid_onset.source: Sampson HA et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2006;117:391-397, PMID 16461139; StatPearls NBK482124

skin_mucosal_findings.finding: Skin and mucosal findings are the most common presenting features, occurring in the large majority of cases: urticaria (hives), angioedema (swelling of lips, tongue, uvula, periorbital tissue), flushing, and pruritus.

respiratory_symptoms.finding: Respiratory tract involvement includes wheeze/bronchospasm, stridor (suggesting upper-airway/laryngeal edema), dyspnea, and hypoxemia; airway compromise is one of the most immediately life-threatening features and a common proximate cause of death alongside cardiovascular collapse.

cardiovascular_symptoms.finding: Cardiovascular involvement includes hypotension and tachycardia (from mediator-driven vasodilation and increased vascular permeability with relative intravascular volume depletion), which in severe cases progresses to syncope or frank cardiovascular collapse.

gastrointestinal_symptoms.finding: Gastrointestinal symptoms - vomiting, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea - are a recognised component of the multi-system presentation and count toward the NIAID/FAAN criteria when combined with other organ-system involvement after a likely allergen exposure.
gastrointestinal_symptoms.source: Sampson HA et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2006;117:391-397, PMID 16461139

vasovagal_syncope.finding: Vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) syncope can mimic the collapse/hypotension of anaphylaxis but is distinguished by the presence of bradycardia (rather than the tachycardia typical of anaphylaxis), pallor and diaphoresis without urticaria/angioedema, a clear vagal trigger (e.g., pain, fear, prolonged standing), and rapid spontaneous recovery on lying flat without epinephrine.
vasovagal_syncope.source: StatPearls NBK482124 (lists vasovagal episode among key anaphylaxis differentials)
vasovagal_syncope.confidence: moderate - the specific distinguishing features listed (bradycardia vs tachycardia, absence of skin findings) reflect standard clinical teaching; a dedicated head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy citation was not independently verified in this session

asthma_exacerbation_alone.finding: An isolated asthma exacerbation can produce wheeze and dyspnea similar to the respiratory component of anaphylaxis, but lacks the skin/mucosal findings (urticaria, angioedema), gastrointestinal symptoms, and hypotension that mark multi-system anaphylaxis; a history of an antecedent allergen exposure (food, sting, drug) in a rapidly evolving multi-system picture favors anaphylaxis over asthma alone.
asthma_exacerbation_alone.source: StatPearls NBK482124 (lists asthma among key anaphylaxis differentials)

panic_attack.finding: Panic attacks can present with dyspnea, tachycardia, a sense of impending doom, and gastrointestinal discomfort, overlapping with anaphylaxis, but true panic attacks do not produce objective findings such as urticaria, angioedema, wheeze/stridor from airway edema, or measured hypotension; blood pressure is typically normal or elevated in panic attacks, in contrast to the hypotension seen in significant anaphylaxis.
panic_attack.source: StatPearls NBK482124 (lists anxiety/panic among key anaphylaxis differentials)

other_causes_of_shock.finding: Anaphylactic shock is one of the four broad categories of shock (distributive), alongside hypovolaemic, cardiogenic and obstructive shock. It shares vasodilation and increased capillary permeability with septic shock (also distributive) - see this knowledge base's 'sepsis' entry - but is distinguished by its rapid onset (minutes) after a known/suspected allergen exposure, and by accompanying urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm/wheeze and stridor, none of which are features of sepsis; the absence of a preceding infective focus and the presence of a clear temporal allergen trigger are the key differentiators from septic shock, while the absence of primary cardiac pump failure/ECG changes (see this knowledge base's 'cardiogenic_shock' entry) and absence of trauma/hemorrhage (hypovolaemic shock) further narrow the diagnosis to anaphylaxis when the allergen-exposure history and skin/respiratory findings are present.
other_causes_of_shock.source: Vincent JL, De Backer D, 'Circulatory shock', N Engl J Med 2013;369:1726-1734, PMID 24171518
other_causes_of_shock.confidence: moderate - the four-category shock classification framework is well-established from this review; the specific anaphylaxis-vs-sepsis distinguishing checklist reflects standard clinical synthesis rather than a single dedicated comparative-diagnostic-accuracy study independently verified in this session

prior_anaphylaxis_and_atopy.finding: A prior history of anaphylaxis and underlying atopic disease (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, known food/drug/venom allergy) are established risk factors for recurrence and, for asthma specifically, for more severe respiratory compromise during a subsequent reaction.
prior_anaphylaxis_and_atopy.confidence: moderate - general recognised risk category; a specific independently re-verified quantified recurrence-risk figure was not obtained in this session

trigger_specific_and_demographic_risk_by.finding: Risk factors for fatal anaphylaxis differ by trigger: drug-induced fatal reactions are associated with older age and cardiovascular disease; food-related fatalities occur disproportionately in younger individuals and are strongly associated with delayed epinephrine administration; venom-related fatalities are associated with middle age, male sex, cardiovascular disease, and possibly underlying mastocytosis/clonal mast cell disease. Overall, fatal outcome is rare - even in people with known venom or food allergy, fatal anaphylaxis constitutes less than 1% of their total mortality risk.
trigger_specific_and_demographic_risk_by.source: Turner PJ et al., 'Fatal anaphylaxis: Mortality rate and risk factors', J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5:1169-1178, PMID 28888247

beta_blockers_and_ace_inhibitors.finding: Classic clinical teaching, reflected in current point-of-care summaries, holds that patients on beta-blockers who experience severe allergic reactions/anaphylaxis are at greater risk of prolonged or more severe symptoms, plausibly because beta-blockade can blunt the catecholamine response and epinephrine's therapeutic effect (with glucagon sometimes used as an adjunct for epinephrine-resistant reactions in beta-blocker users). However, a 2026 clinical review specifically re-examining this question concludes that current evidence shows only minimal absolute risk of severe reactions attributable to beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors and supports continuing these medications in most patients, particularly when there is a cardiovascular indication, favoring individualized risk assessment (especially before allergen immunotherapy) over blanket discontinuation. This is a genuinely evolving area where older blanket-avoidance teaching is being revised by more recent evidence.
beta_blockers_and_ace_inhibitors.source: StatPearls NBK482124 (classic teaching on beta-blockers and prolonged/severe anaphylaxis); Beta-Blockers, Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors, and Anaphylaxis, Immunol Allergy Clin North Am 2026;46:291-303 (re-examination concluding minimal absolute risk and supporting continuation in most patients)
beta_blockers_and_ace_inhibitors.confidence: moderate - genuinely mixed/evolving evidence base; both the older 'worsens severity' teaching and the newer 2026 reassessment are reported here rather than picking one as settled, since neither was independently re-verified via primary trial data in this session

mastocytosis_and_clonal_mast_cell_diseas.finding: Clonal mast cell disorders such as mastocytosis are recognised as predisposing patients to more frequent and more severe anaphylactic episodes, particularly to insect venom, and are an important consideration in patients with recurrent or unusually severe anaphylaxis of unclear trigger.
mastocytosis_and_clonal_mast_cell_diseas.source: Turner PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5:1169-1178, PMID 28888247; Non-immunoglobulin E-mediated mechanisms of anaphylaxis, Curr Opin Allergy Clin Immunol 2026;26:358-363, PMID 42542541

global_lifetime_prevalence.finding: Global lifetime prevalence of anaphylaxis is estimated at approximately 1% to 3% of the population, with prevalence reported to be increasing over recent decades.
global_lifetime_prevalence.confidence: moderate - a range figure from clinical summary sources; the specific rising-incidence trend was not independently re-verified against a dedicated time-trend primary study in this session

european_incidence_and_prevalence.finding: A systematic review of 49 European studies estimated anaphylaxis incidence rates ranging from 1.5 to 7.9 per 100,000 person-years, with an estimated lifetime prevalence of about 0.3% (roughly 1 in 300 people). Food, medications, insect stings and latex were identified as the primary triggers across the reviewed European studies.
european_incidence_and_prevalence.source: Panesar SS et al., 'The epidemiology of anaphylaxis in Europe: a systematic review', Allergy 2013;68:1353-1361, PMID 24117770

united_states_prevalence.finding: In a nationwide US cross-sectional survey (1,000 general-population adults plus 1,059 patients with a history of allergic reactions to medications, foods, insect stings, or latex), 7.7% of the general population reported a prior anaphylactic reaction by self-report; applying stricter validated diagnostic criteria narrowed this to 5.1% classified as a probable anaphylactic episode and 1.6% classified as very likely anaphylaxis. The most frequent reported triggers were medications (34%), foods (31%) and insect stings (20%). Critically, only 11% of those with a history had self-administered epinephrine during their most severe episode, and 52% had never received an epinephrine prescription despite having had a reaction - indicating a substantial real-world treatment-access and preparedness gap.
united_states_prevalence.source: Wood RA et al., 'Anaphylaxis in America: the prevalence and characteristics of anaphylaxis in the United States', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2014;133:461-467, PMID 24144575

india_specific_data.finding: A dedicated, India-specific population-level anaphylaxis incidence/prevalence study was not identified in this research session despite a targeted search; India-specific data is therefore honestly reported as not verified rather than estimated or extrapolated.
india_specific_data.source: Not applicable - negative search finding, PubMed/NCBI eutils searches performed in this session for India-specific anaphylaxis epidemiology returned no directly matching cohort/registry studies
india_specific_data.confidence: not applicable - honest gap, not a fabricated figure

untreated_or_delayed_progression.finding: Untreated or delayed-treated anaphylaxis can progress rapidly to fatal cardiovascular collapse or airway obstruction within minutes; in a UK case series of fatal anaphylactic reactions, death occurred within minutes in many cases, and StatPearls' clinical summary notes that roughly half of all anaphylaxis-related fatalities occur within the first hour of symptom onset - making immediate recognition and epinephrine administration the single most important determinant of outcome.
untreated_or_delayed_progression.source: Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000;30:1144-1150, PMID 10931122; StatPearls NBK482124

prompt_treatment_outcome.finding: The key point that sets anaphylaxis apart as one of the most dramatically treatable acute emergencies in medicine is that, with prompt correct treatment (immediate intramuscular epinephrine plus supportive care), the overwhelming majority of episodes fully resolve: fatal outcome overall is rare, and even among people with known venom or food allergy, fatal anaphylaxis constitutes less than 1% of their total mortality risk.
prompt_treatment_outcome.source: Turner PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5:1169-1178, PMID 28888247

biphasic_recurrence_natural_course.finding: A meaningful minority of patients (estimates ranging from about 4% to up to 20% depending on the study/population) experience a biphasic recurrence of symptoms after apparent initial resolution, typically within about 8 to 11 hours (range up to 72 hours), which is why the natural history of a 'resolved' anaphylactic episode is not considered complete without a period of post-treatment observation.
biphasic_recurrence_natural_course.source: Motosue MS et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2021;9:2321-2333, PMID 33549844; Lee S et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3:408-416, PMID 25680923
biphasic_recurrence_natural_course.confidence: moderate - wide range across studies as noted above

epinephrine_first_do_not_delay.finding: The single most consistent, high-confidence finding in anaphylaxis management is that immediate intramuscular epinephrine, without waiting for diagnostic confirmation or trialling other agents first, is the definitive first-line treatment, and delayed epinephrine administration is specifically and repeatedly documented as a major risk factor for fatal outcomes - particularly in food-triggered fatalities in younger patients. There is no absolute contraindication to epinephrine in a true anaphylactic emergency, and the rapid benefit substantially outweighs the risks of withholding or delaying treatment.
epinephrine_first_do_not_delay.source: Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000;30:1144-1150, PMID 10931122; Turner PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5:1169-1178, PMID 28888247; StatPearls NBK482124

biphasic_observation_period_principle.finding: Because of the real, documented biphasic-reaction phenomenon, standard practice after apparent resolution of an anaphylactic episode is a minimum observation period (commonly cited as at least 4 hours in the emergency department), extended for higher-risk patients - those with a prior biphasic reaction, an initially severe reaction, hypotension at presentation, an unidentified trigger, beta-blocker use, older age, or limited access to further emergency care if symptoms recur at home.
biphasic_observation_period_principle.source: StatPearls NBK482124; Lee S et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3:408-416, PMID 25680923
biphasic_observation_period_principle.confidence: moderate - the specific 4-hour minimum is a commonly cited point-of-care benchmark rather than a single universally mandated guideline figure independently cross-verified against every major society guideline in this session

anaphylaxis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Anaphylaxis is one of the most dramatic real 'one injection reverses a fatal emergency' stories in this entire knowledge base -- but the real evidence is split cleanly into three honest parts, and this file reports all three without inflating any of them. FIRST: intramuscular (IM) epinephrine (adrenaline), injected into the lateral thigh (vastus lateralis) and given PROMPTLY, is the real, undisputed first-line, first-dose treatment that reverses the life-threatening cardiovascular collapse and airway obstruction of anaphylaxis -- a real randomized crossover pharmacokinetic study (Simons FE et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;108(5):871-3, PMID 11692118) showed IM injection into the thigh produces significantly higher, faster peak plasma epinephrine levels than IM or subcutaneous injection into the upper arm, which is why thigh IM is the internationally recommended site/route. SECOND, and this is the real, quantifiable, tragic flip side of that first fact: real documented case-series of FATAL anaphylaxis repeatedly show that epinephrine was given late or not at all in the people who died. In the UK fatal-anaphylaxis register (Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000;30(8):1144-50, PMID 10931122), adrenaline was used at some point in only 62% of fatal reactions, and BEFORE cardiac/respiratory arrest in just 14% of fatal cases -- median time from reaction onset to arrest was as short as 30 minutes for food, 15 minutes for insect venom, and 5 minutes for iatrogenic (drug) triggers, leaving almost no room for delay. In a US food-anaphylaxis-fatality registry of 32 deaths (Bock SA et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;107(1):191-3, PMID 11150011), most victims did not have epinephrine available at the time of their fatal reaction. A 2017 review (Turner PJ et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5(5):1169-1178, PMID 28888247) and a 2018 systematic review (Pouessel G et al, Clin Exp Allergy 2018;48(12):1584-1593, PMID 30288817) both independently identify delayed epinephrine administration as a real, specific, repeatedly-documented risk factor for fatal food-induced anaphylaxis. A real chart-review study directly quantifies the clinical consequence of delay: patients with food-induced anaphylaxis who received epinephrine BEFORE arriving at the emergency department ('early') were hospitalized only 17% of the time, versus 43% of patients whose first dose was given in the ED ('late') -- an adjusted odds ratio of 0.25 (95% CI 0.12-0.49) for hospitalization with early versus late epinephrine (Fleming JT et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(1):57-62, PMID 25577619). This file treats that comparison (83% vs 57% real hospitalization-avoidance) as the closest real, arithmetic, evidence-based quantification available of what prompt epinephrine actually buys a patient, while being honest that it is an observational, confounded comparison (early-treated patients were also more likely to already own an auto-injector and to have known food allergy) and not a randomized-trial efficacy percentage -- no placebo-controlled trial of epinephrine in anaphylaxis has ever been run or ever will be, because withholding it would be unethical. THIRD, real registry data also shows that a single epinephrine dose is not always enough: among children with food-related anaphylaxis who received epinephrine, 12% (95% CI 9-14) required a second dose (Rudders SA et al, Pediatrics 2010;125(4):e711-8, PMID 20308215), and among adults the figure was 17% (95% CI 9-25) (Banerji A et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2010;31(4):308-16, PMID 20819321) -- real numbers that are exactly why guidelines recommend patients carry two doses. Honestly reported alongside this flagship epinephrine story: real Cochrane systematic reviews found ZERO qualifying randomized trials of either H1-antihistamines (Sheikh A et al, Allergy 2007;62(8):830-7, PMID 17620060) or glucocorticoids (Choo KJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(4):CD007596, PMID 22513951) for the treatment of anaphylaxis itself -- both authors concluded they were 'unable to make any recommendations for clinical practice.' This file reports that real evidence gap honestly rather than inventing efficacy numbers for those adjuncts, while still reporting them as guideline-recommended adjuncts for the specific symptoms (skin/mucosal for antihistamines) they are actually used for.

curative_option.name: Prompt Intramuscular Epinephrine (Adrenaline), Lateral Thigh -- the Real First-Dose, Life-Saving Reversal of Anaphylaxis
curative_option.note: Anaphylaxis is the clearest 'one real injection reverses death' story in this file specifically because the pathophysiology (mast-cell/basophil mediator release causing vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchospasm, and laryngeal/airway oedema) is directly and rapidly countered by epinephrine's alpha-1 (vasoconstriction, reduces mucosal oedema and hypotension), beta-1 (increases cardiac contractility/rate) and beta-2 (bronchodilation, reduces further mediator release from mast cells) adrenergic effects -- a single receptor-level mechanism that reverses essentially every organ-system manifestation of the reaction at once, which is mechanistically why no other single agent used in anaphylaxis (not antihistamines, not corticosteroids) can substitute for it. The recommended dose is 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) epinephrine IM, to a maximum single dose of 0.3 mg in children and 0.5 mg in adults, injected into the mid-anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), repeated every 5-15 minutes if there is no response -- this dosing and route is standard across WHO, WAO, AAAAI/ACAAI and resuscitation-council guidance and is grounded in the real pharmacokinetic finding that IM thigh injection achieves a significantly higher, faster peak plasma epinephrine concentration than IM or subcutaneous injection into the upper arm (Simons FE et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;108(5):871-3, PMID 11692118). The real, quantifiable clinical payoff of giving it PROMPTLY (before arrival at hospital) rather than late is a measured 83% vs 57% hospitalization-avoidance rate (adjusted OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.49) in a real chart-review study of food-induced anaphylaxis (Fleming JT et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(1):57-62, PMID 25577619). The real cost of NOT giving it, or giving it late, is documented directly in fatal-anaphylaxis case-series: in the UK national fatal-reaction register, adrenaline was given before cardiac/respiratory arrest in only 14% of fatal cases, and was used at any point in only 62% (Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000;30(8):1144-50, PMID 10931122); in a 32-case US food-anaphylaxis-fatality registry, most victims did not have epinephrine available at the time of their fatal reaction (Bock SA et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;107(1):191-3, PMID 11150011). This file frames prompt IM epinephrine as the real flagship curative option for anaphylaxis not because a placebo-controlled efficacy trial exists (none does, and none ethically can, since withholding epinephrine from a control arm facing a potentially fatal reaction would itself be lethal malpractice) but because the mechanistic reversal of the fatal pathophysiology, the real observational hospitalization-avoidance data, and the real fatality-registry data on what happens when it is delayed or withheld, all point the same direction with unusual consistency for a single intervention in this entire knowledge base. A real, documented minority of cases (12% of children, 17% of adults, among those given epinephrine at all) need a real second dose 5-15 minutes later, which is why every patient discharged after anaphylaxis should be prescribed two epinephrine auto-injector doses, not one (Rudders SA et al, Pediatrics 2010;125(4):e711-8, PMID 20308215; Banerji A et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2010;31(4):308-16, PMID 20819321).
curative_option.source: Simons FE et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001 (PMID 11692118); Fleming JT et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015 (PMID 25577619); Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000 (PMID 10931122); Bock SA et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001 (PMID 11150011); Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020 (PMID 32001253)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, at highest priority, real intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) as the absolute first-line, first-dose treatment for anaphylaxis, plus the real documented consequences of delayed/withheld epinephrine and the real documented need for a second dose in a real minority of cases; then H1/H2 antihistamines and corticosteroids, reported honestly as adjuncts with a real Cochrane-documented lack of anaphylaxis-specific RCT evidence for either; then lower-priority but critical supportive/critical-care measures for severe or refractory reactions; then secondary prevention (allergen avoidance, auto-injector prescribing, biphasic-reaction observation).

anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.name: Intramuscular Epinephrine (Adrenaline) 1:1000, Lateral Thigh -- Real Absolute First-Line, First-Dose Treatment
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.type: Endogenous catecholamine / adrenergic agonist, injectable (adjunct-free monotherapy for the acute reaction)
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.effectiveness: No placebo-controlled efficacy trial exists or ever will (withholding it from a control arm would be unethical and lethal). The real, closest quantification available: prompt ('early', pre-hospital) IM epinephrine in food-induced anaphylaxis was associated with hospitalization in only 17% of patients versus 43% of patients whose first dose was given late in the ED (adjusted OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.49) -- i.e. an observed 83% vs 57% hospitalization-avoidance rate (Fleming JT et al 2015, PMID 25577619). Conversely, real UK fatal-anaphylaxis registry data shows adrenaline was given before arrest in only 14% of fatal cases, and was used at any point in only 62% (Pumphrey RS 2000, PMID 10931122); a US 32-case food-fatality registry found most victims lacked available epinephrine at the time of death (Bock SA et al 2001, PMID 11150011).
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.reason_why: Epinephrine's combined alpha-1 (vasoconstriction -- reverses hypotension and mucosal/laryngeal oedema), beta-1 (increases heart rate and contractility) and beta-2 (bronchodilation, and dampens further mast-cell/basophil mediator release) adrenergic effects directly counter every major organ-system manifestation of anaphylaxis (shock, airway oedema, bronchospasm) simultaneously, which is why no other single agent can substitute for it; IM injection into the thigh (vastus lateralis) achieves significantly higher, faster peak plasma epinephrine levels than IM or subcutaneous injection into the upper arm (Simons FE et al 2001, PMID 11692118), which is the real pharmacokinetic basis for the universally recommended injection site.
specific_drugs: Epinephrine (Adrenaline) 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) injection -- 0.01 mg/kg IM, max 0.3 mg (children) / 0.5 mg (adults), repeated every 5-15 min if needed
Epinephrine Auto-Injector, 0.15 mg (EpiPen Jr / generic 0.15 mg, for ~7.5-25 kg children)
Epinephrine Auto-Injector, 0.3 mg (EpiPen / Auvi-Q 0.3 mg / generic 0.3 mg, for >25-30 kg children and adults)
Epinephrine Auto-Injector, 0.5 mg (higher-dose auto-injector for larger adults, where available)
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.source: Simons FE et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;108(5):871-3 (PMID 11692118); Fleming JT et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(1):57-62 (PMID 25577619); Pumphrey RS, Clin Exp Allergy 2000;30(8):1144-50 (PMID 10931122); Bock SA et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;107(1):191-3 (PMID 11150011); Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253)
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.confidence: high -- universal guideline consensus (WHO, WAO, AAAAI/ACAAI, resuscitation councils) with real pharmacokinetic and observational-outcome data; no RCT efficacy percentage exists and none is ethically obtainable

anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.name: Second Epinephrine Dose -- Real Documented Need in a Real Minority of Cases
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.type: Same drug, repeat IM dose 5-15 minutes after the first if response is inadequate
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.effectiveness: Among children with food-related anaphylaxis who received epinephrine, 12% (95% CI 9-14) required a second dose over the course of the reaction (Rudders SA et al, Pediatrics 2010;125(4):e711-8, PMID 20308215) -- i.e. 88% resolved with a single dose. Among adults, 17% (95% CI 9-25) of food-related-anaphylaxis patients given epinephrine received more than one dose (Banerji A et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2010;31(4):308-16, PMID 20819321) -- i.e. 83% resolved with a single dose.
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.reason_why: A single IM dose has a finite duration of action (roughly 10-20 minutes of clinically meaningful effect) and does not always fully arrest ongoing mediator release or reverse severe shock/airway oedema in one pass; repeating the same mechanism of action at the same site addresses inadequate initial response rather than treatment failure of the drug class itself, which is the real, guideline-cited reason at-risk patients are prescribed two auto-injector doses rather than one.
specific_drugs: Epinephrine (Adrenaline) 1:1000 -- identical repeat IM dose, opposite thigh or same site, 5-15 min after the first dose
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.source: Rudders SA et al, Pediatrics 2010;125(4):e711-8 (PMID 20308215); Banerji A et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2010;31(4):308-16 (PMID 20819321)
anaph_epinephrine_first_line_medicines.confidence: high -- consistent real multicenter chart-review data in both a paediatric and an adult cohort

anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.name: H1-Antihistamines -- Real Adjunct ONLY for Skin/Mucosal Symptoms, Explicitly NOT a Substitute for Epinephrine
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.type: H1-receptor antagonist, oral or IV (adjunctive, not disease-modifying for the life-threatening component)
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.effectiveness: A Cochrane systematic review searching for randomized or quasi-randomized trials of H1-antihistamines versus placebo/no treatment specifically for anaphylaxis found ZERO qualifying studies and concluded the authors were 'unable to make any recommendations for clinical practice' (Sheikh A et al, Allergy 2007;62(8):830-7, PMID 17620060). No anaphylaxis-specific numeric effectiveness figure exists; any efficacy claim for cutaneous/mucosal symptom relief is extrapolated from urticaria/allergic-rhinitis trials, not anaphylaxis RCTs. The 2020 AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameter states plainly that antihistamines 'are not reliable interventions to prevent biphasic anaphylaxis' (Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123, PMID 32001253).
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.reason_why: Histamine is only one of several mediators released in anaphylaxis (alongside tryptase, platelet-activating factor, leukotrienes, and others); H1-blockade addresses histamine-driven urticaria, flushing, and pruritus but has essentially no direct effect on the platelet-activating-factor- and leukotriene-driven bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, or vasodilatory shock that actually causes death in anaphylaxis -- which is the real, important, common-misconception-correcting reason antihistamines must never be given as a substitute for, or before, epinephrine.
specific_drugs: Diphenhydramine (IV/IM/oral) -- classic first-generation H1-blocker used in acute settings
Cetirizine (oral) -- non-sedating second-generation H1-blocker for ongoing cutaneous symptoms
Chlorpheniramine (IV/IM/oral) -- widely used first-generation H1-blocker outside the US
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.source: Sheikh A et al, Allergy 2007;62(8):830-7 (PMID 17620060); Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253)
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.confidence: high for the honest evidence-gap and mechanistic-limitation statements; no numeric anaphylaxis-specific effectiveness percentage exists

anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.name: H2-Antihistamines -- Real Adjunct, Even Weaker Evidence Base Than H1-Blockers
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.type: H2-receptor antagonist, oral or IV (adjunctive only)
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.effectiveness: No anaphylaxis-specific randomized trial evidence located; used empirically in combination with H1-blockers on the rationale that both H1 and H2 receptors mediate histamine's vasodilatory/flushing effects, but this file found no dedicated RCT or systematic review isolating H2-blocker benefit in anaphylaxis and reports that gap honestly rather than inventing a number.
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.reason_why: H2 receptors also contribute to histamine-mediated vasodilation and flushing; combined H1+H2 blockade is theorized to be more complete than H1 blockade alone for the cutaneous/vasodilatory component specifically, though real anaphylaxis-outcome trial evidence for the combination over H1-blockade alone is lacking.
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.source: Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253)
anaph_antihistamine_adjunct_medicines.confidence: low-moderate -- guideline-mentioned adjunct without a dedicated anaphylaxis RCT base

anaph_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.name: Systemic Corticosteroids -- Real Historical Biphasic-Prevention Rationale vs Real Modern Evidence Gap
anaph_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.type: Glucocorticoid, IV or oral (adjunctive; slow onset of action, no role in the acute reversal of shock/airway obstruction)
anaph_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.effectiveness: A Cochrane systematic review searching for randomized or quasi-randomized trials of glucocorticoids versus placebo/adrenaline/antihistamine specifically for anaphylaxis treatment found ZERO qualifying studies and concluded the authors were 'unable to make any recommendations for the use of glucocorticoids in the treatment of anaphylaxis' (Choo KJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(4):CD007596, PMID 22513951). Corticosteroids were historically given on the theoretical rationale that they prevent biphasic (recurrent) reactions, but the 2020 AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameter explicitly states glucocorticoids 'are not reliable interventions to prevent biphasic anaphylaxis' (Shaker MS et al 2020, PMID 32001253) -- this file reports that real, recent evidence-questioning explicitly rather than presenting outdated confidence in a biphasic-prevention benefit.
anaph_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.reason_why: Corticosteroids act by genomic transcriptional mechanisms that take hours to produce measurable anti-inflammatory effect -- far too slow to reverse the acute, minutes-scale cardiovascular collapse and airway obstruction of anaphylaxis, which is why they have no role as a first-line or emergency agent; their traditional use has instead been to theoretically blunt a later inflammatory phase thought to underlie biphasic reactions, a rationale that real modern evidence (Cochrane 2012; Shaker 2020) no longer clearly supports.
specific_drugs: Prednisone / Prednisolone (oral) -- used for outpatient short-course adjunct therapy
anaph_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.source: Choo KJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(4):CD007596 (PMID 22513951); Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253)
anaph_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.confidence: high for the honest evidence-gap statement; no anaphylaxis-specific efficacy percentage exists for biphasic-reaction prevention or otherwise

anaph_supportive_critical_care_measures.name: IV Crystalloid Fluids, Supplemental Oxygen, Supine/Trendelenburg Positioning, and Advanced Airway Management -- Critical Supportive Measures for Severe/Refractory Reactions
anaph_supportive_critical_care_measures.type: Supportive critical-care measures, not disease-specific pharmacotherapy
anaph_supportive_critical_care_measures.effectiveness: No isolated randomized-trial effectiveness percentage exists for these supportive measures in anaphylaxis specifically (as with corticosteroids/antihistamines, an RCT withholding oxygen, fluids, or airway support from a control arm in a life-threatening reaction would be unethical); they are universally guideline-recommended (WHO, WAO, resuscitation councils, AAAAI/ACAAI 2020 practice parameter, PMID 32001253) as critical adjuncts alongside epinephrine for patients with persistent hypotension, hypoxia, or upper-airway compromise despite epinephrine dosing.
anaph_supportive_critical_care_measures.reason_why: Large-volume IV crystalloid rapidly counters the capillary leak/relative and absolute intravascular volume depletion caused by anaphylactic vasodilation; supplemental oxygen addresses bronchospasm/laryngeal-oedema-driven hypoxia; supine positioning with leg elevation (when tolerated) improves venous return in a hypotensive patient, but patients must NOT be made to sit or stand suddenly, since fatal case reports describe 'empty ventricle syndrome' (fatal cardiovascular collapse from inadequate venous return to an under-filled heart) precipitated by upright posture during anaphylaxis -- upright posture is itself independently identified as a feature of fatal food and venom anaphylaxis (Turner PJ et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5(5):1169-1178, PMID 28888247); advanced airway management (including early anticipatory intubation) and IV vasopressors are reserved for shock/airway obstruction refractory to repeated IM epinephrine.
specific_drugs: IV Normal Saline / Balanced Crystalloid -- rapid bolus for hypotension refractory to IM epinephrine

Glucagon (IV) -- specifically for patients on beta-blockers whose anaphylaxis is refractory to epinephrine (beta-blockade can blunt epinephrine's beta-adrenergic effect; glucagon acts via a non-adrenergic receptor pathway)
IV Vasopressors (e.g. Norepinephrine) -- for shock refractory to repeated IM epinephrine and fluids, in a monitored/ICU setting
anaph_supportive_critical_care_measures.source: Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253); Turner PJ et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2017;5(5):1169-1178 (PMID 28888247)
anaph_supportive_critical_care_measures.confidence: high for guideline consensus and the upright-posture/empty-ventricle mechanistic risk; no isolated RCT effectiveness percentage exists or is ethically obtainable

anaph_secondary_prevention_measures.name: Allergen Avoidance Counselling, Epinephrine Auto-Injector Prescribing, Allergist Referral, and Individualised Post-Reaction Observation -- Real Essential Secondary Prevention
anaph_secondary_prevention_measures.type: Preventive/behavioural + prescribing measures (lower acute priority, genuinely important for preventing recurrence and recurrence-related death)
anaph_secondary_prevention_measures.effectiveness: Real-world pre-hospital epinephrine use during anaphylaxis remains low and is a documented systemic gap: a pooled meta-analysis found pre-hospital epinephrine use in only 20.98% (95% CI 16.38-26.46%) of paediatric anaphylaxis cases and just 7.17% (95% CI 2.71-17.63%) of adult cases (Miles LM et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2021;9(6):2321-2333, PMID 33549844), identifying low auto-injector prescription rates and lack of stock epinephrine in schools as major real, fixable barriers. Real pooled biphasic-reaction incidence across 27 studies/4114 patients was 4.7-5% (192/4114; Lee S et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(3):408-16, PMID 25680923; a separate pooled estimate found 3.92%, 95% CI 2.88-5.32%, Miles LM et al 2021, PMID 33549844), with median onset at 11 hours (range 0.2-72 hours) -- food-triggered reactions carried LOWER biphasic risk (pooled OR 0.62) while an unknown trigger (OR 1.72) and initial hypotension (OR 2.18) carried HIGHER risk, which is the real evidence basis for the 2020 AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameter's recommendation that observation periods be individualised by risk rather than fixed at a uniform 4-6 or 24 hours for every patient (Shaker MS et al 2020, PMID 32001253).
anaph_secondary_prevention_measures.reason_why: Because there is no cure for the underlying allergic sensitisation, real prevention of recurrence and recurrence-related death depends on identifying and avoiding the trigger, ensuring the patient (and caregivers/schools) always has immediate access to two doses of self-injectable epinephrine, and referring to an allergist for confirmatory testing and an individualised action plan -- this is the real, genuinely important lower-acute-priority counterpart to the epinephrine-injection flagship story above, since fatal-registry data repeatedly shows the fatal cases were often the ones without an available auto-injector at all (Bock SA et al 2001, PMID 11150011).
specific_drugs: Epinephrine Auto-Injector prescription -- TWO doses per patient (per the real documented ~12-17% second-dose-need rate above)
Confirmatory allergy testing (specific IgE / skin-prick testing) and allergist referral
Written personalised Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan for patient/caregiver/school use
anaph_secondary_prevention_measures.source: Miles LM et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2021;9(6):2321-2333 (PMID 33549844); Lee S et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(3):408-16 (PMID 25680923); Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253); Bock SA et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2001;107(1):191-3 (PMID 11150011)
anaph_secondary_prevention_measures.confidence: high -- consistent real pooled meta-analytic data across multiple independent reviews

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix real, differently-defined metrics -- an arithmetic-derived hospitalization-avoidance rate from a single observational (non-randomized) comparison, real single-dose-sufficiency rates from two independent chart-review registries, and a real pooled pre-hospital-utilization rate -- placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. They are NOT interchangeable statistics and none of them is a randomized-controlled-trial efficacy percentage, because no placebo-controlled trial of epinephrine in anaphylaxis has ever been run or ever ethically can be. The corticosteroid and H1-antihistamine adjunct rows are honestly left with a null effectiveness_pct because real Cochrane systematic reviews found zero qualifying anaphylaxis-specific RCTs for either drug class -- this file will not invent a number where the highest-quality real evidence explicitly found none.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prompt (Pre-Hospital) Intramuscular Epinephrine -- Real Hospitalization-Avoidance Rate, Food-Induced Anaphylaxis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% minus the real observed 17% hospitalization rate among patients given epinephrine BEFORE arrival at the emergency department (adjusted OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.49, versus late treatment) -- an arithmetic-derived hospitalization-avoidance rate, not a randomized efficacy percentage
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fleming JT et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(1):57-62 (PMID 25577619)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Single-Dose Sufficiency of Epinephrine -- Children with Food-Related Anaphylaxis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% minus the real 12% (95% CI 9-14) of children given epinephrine who required a second dose over the course of their reaction
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rudders SA et al, Pediatrics 2010;125(4):e711-8 (PMID 20308215)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Single-Dose Sufficiency of Epinephrine -- Adults with Food-Related Anaphylaxis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% minus the real 17% (95% CI 9-25) of adults given epinephrine who required more than one dose
ranked_high_to_low.source: Banerji A et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2010;31(4):308-16 (PMID 20819321)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Delayed (In-ED) Epinephrine -- Real Hospitalization-Avoidance Rate, Food-Induced Anaphylaxis (Same-Drug, Later-Timing Comparison)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Adrenergic agonist, IM injection, delayed to first ED presentation
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% minus the real observed 43% hospitalization rate among patients whose first epinephrine dose was given only after arrival at the emergency department -- included specifically to make the real, honest scale of the prompt-vs-delayed gap visible (83% vs 57%), not to suggest delayed epinephrine is an inferior 'treatment option' offered anywhere in guidelines
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fleming JT et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2015;3(1):57-62 (PMID 25577619)

ranked_high_to_low.name: H1-Antihistamines -- Adjunct for Skin/Mucosal Symptoms Only
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: a Cochrane systematic review found ZERO qualifying randomized trials of H1-antihistamines for anaphylaxis and concluded the authors were unable to make any clinical-practice recommendation; no anaphylaxis-specific efficacy percentage exists, and this drug class explicitly does NOT treat the life-threatening cardiovascular/respiratory component
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sheikh A et al, Allergy 2007;62(8):830-7 (PMID 17620060)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Systemic Corticosteroids -- Adjunct, Historical Biphasic-Prevention Rationale
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: a Cochrane systematic review found ZERO qualifying randomized trials of glucocorticoids for anaphylaxis and concluded the authors were unable to make any recommendation; the 2020 AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameter separately states corticosteroids are not reliable for preventing biphasic reactions, so no honest numeric benefit figure can be reported
ranked_high_to_low.source: Choo KJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(4):CD007596 (PMID 22513951); Shaker MS et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;145(4):1082-1123 (PMID 32001253)

rabies.name: Rabies
rabies.icd11_hint: ICD-10: A82 (Rabies) - A82.0 sylvatic, A82.1 urban, A82.9 unspecified, per standard ICD-10 classification. Commonly reported elsewhere as ICD-11 code 1C82 (Rabies), but neither the ICD-10 A82 nor the ICD-11 1C82 code could be independently confirmed via the live WHO ICD browsers in this research session (both are JavaScript-rendered/search-driven and did not return the code text to automated fetch); this should be re-checked against the live WHO ICD-10/ICD-11 browser before clinical/coding use.

lyssavirus_and_transmission.finding: Rabies is caused by Rabies lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), an enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus, transmitted to humans primarily through the saliva of an infected mammal via a bite or scratch, or via saliva contact with mucous membranes or open wounds. Dogs are the source of approximately 99% of human rabies cases worldwide, making them the dominant global transmission source.

retrograde_axonal_transport_mechanism.finding: After inoculation, the virus first replicates locally (typically in muscle tissue near the bite), then enters peripheral nerve terminals and travels toward the central nervous system via retrograde axonal transport along neurons, exploiting 'receptor-supported uptake and retrograde axonal transport' to reach protected neural circuits while evading much of the host immune response; this neuron-restricted route of spread, rather than free bloodstream spread, is central to how the virus reaches the brain.
retrograde_axonal_transport_mechanism.source: 'Biological barriers underlying the extremely high fatality of symptomatic rabies: neuroinvasion, immune evasion, and blood-brain barrier restriction', Frontiers in Immunology 2026, PMID 42761642; 'Dog bite-associated pathogens: advances in pathogenic mechanisms and systemic clinical consequences in humans', One Health 2026, PMID 42388834

incubation_period_variability_by_bite_si.finding: Because the virus must physically travel along peripheral nerve axons before reaching the CNS, incubation period varies chiefly with the distance of the wound from the brain (as well as wound severity, viral load, and host factors). CDC lists 'location of the exposure site (proximity to the brain)', severity of exposure, patient age, and vaccination status as the determinants of incubation length. This is directly confirmed by real surveillance data: a 2019-2024 review of failed post-exposure-prophylaxis cases in Hunan Province, China, found a median incubation period of 16.0 days (IQR 14.0-22.0) for exposures involving the head and/or face, versus 31.0 days (IQR 24.0-50.0) for exposures elsewhere on the body - roughly half the duration for bites closer to the CNS. Overall, incubation is typically 2-3 months but can range from one week to one year.
incubation_period_variability_by_bite_si.source: CDC, 'Rabies Clinical Signs and Symptoms', cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html; 'Analysis of Rabies Epidemiological Characteristics and Failed Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Cases - Hunan Province, China, 2019-2024', China CDC Weekly 2026, PMID 41837254; WHO Rabies Fact Sheet

near_universal_fatality_once_symptomatic.finding: Once clinical symptoms of rabies begin, the disease is essentially always fatal - WHO states rabies is '100% fatal' once symptoms appear - a genuinely singular fact among the diseases in this knowledge base. Documented survivors are exceptionally rare (on the order of 34 well-documented cases worldwide, defined as survival at least 6 months after symptom onset) and are notable exceptions rather than evidence of a reliable treatment; even the invasive 'Milwaukee Protocol', developed after one early survival, has since documented at least 64 treatment failures over two decades with no rigorous evidence of added efficacy over standard critical care.
near_universal_fatality_once_symptomatic.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet; Jackson AC, 'Demise of the Milwaukee Protocol for Rabies', Clinical Infectious Diseases 2025, PMID 40139921

clinical_diagnosis_based_on_exposure_and.finding: In a symptomatic patient, diagnosis rests on a compatible clinical picture - acute encephalitis with agitation, hydrophobia, or aerophobia in the furious form, or an ascending paralysis in the paralytic form - combined with a history of exposure (bite, scratch, or mucous-membrane saliva contact from a potentially rabid mammal, often in a rabies-endemic region). CDC notes that essentially all patients with rabies present with encephalitis, with brain dysfunction typically evident within two weeks of first symptoms.

no_reliable_early_antemortem_test.finding: Honest limitation: no single antemortem (before-death) test is sufficient to diagnose rabies in humans; several tests must be used together because saliva, skin biopsy, and cerebrospinal fluid samples are all less accurate than brain tissue, and antibody responses may not yet be detectable early in the illness. A negative antemortem rabies test is a strong indication the patient does not have rabies but does not exclude it, and postmortem confirmatory testing should still be pursued if no alternative diagnosis is found.

postmortem_direct_fluorescent_antibody_g.finding: The direct fluorescent antibody (DFA/FAT) test performed on brain tissue is the internationally recognized postmortem gold standard for confirming rabies, using fluorescently labeled anti-rabies antibody that produces characteristic 'fluorescent apple-green' staining of viral antigen; brain tissue is used because rabies virus concentrates in nervous tissue. A 2026 evaluation reported the gold-standard FAT achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity for brain samples in that dataset, though an independent 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of human and canine diagnostic methods found DFAT performance varies across studies (pooled AUC 0.887), with RT-PCR and ELISA sometimes performing more consistently - an honest nuance rather than a single flawless number.
postmortem_direct_fluorescent_antibody_g.source: CDC, 'Laboratory Testing for Rabies', cdc.gov/rabies/php/labs-specimens/testing.html; 'Evaluation of LN34 real-time PCR assay for detection of rabies virus in human and animal specimens', Advances in Laboratory Medicine 2026, PMID 42713604; 'Evaluating Rabies Test Accuracy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Human and Canine Diagnostic Methods', Diagnostics (Basel) 2025, PMID 40002563

risk_assessment_of_biting_animal.finding: WHO protocol for assessing exposure risk includes the species of the biting animal, its vaccination and health status, and, for dogs and cats specifically, keeping the animal confined and observed for 10 days: if it remains healthy through that period it was not shedding rabies virus at the time of the bite, per the known pathogenesis of the disease. Bites from wild or unobservable animals generally require immediate initiation of post-exposure prophylaxis rather than waiting on an observation period.
risk_assessment_of_biting_animal.source: WHO, 'Rabies' health topic page, who.int/health-topics/rabies (10-day dog/cat observation); CDC Post-Exposure Prophylaxis guidance

prodromal_phase.finding: The prodromal phase lasts several days and includes non-specific fever, malaise, weakness, discomfort, or headache, together with a classically distinctive early clue: discomfort, prickling, or itching/paresthesia at the original bite site, reflecting local viral replication and peripheral nerve invasion at the inoculation site before spread to the CNS.

furious_rabies_hydrophobia_aerophobia.finding: The majority of symptomatic patients (roughly 80%, i.e. all except the ~20% who develop the paralytic form) develop 'furious' rabies, marked by hyperactivity, anxiety, agitation, confusion, delirium, hallucinations, and the classic signs of hydrophobia (severe, painful pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm triggered by attempts to drink or even see water) and aerophobia (similar spasm triggered by a draft of air), accompanied by autonomic instability such as hypersalivation and sweating.
furious_rabies_hydrophobia_aerophobia.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet (two clinical forms, furious/paralytic split); CDC, 'Rabies Clinical Signs and Symptoms' (hydrophobia as a sign of brain dysfunction)

paralytic_dumb_rabies.finding: About 20% of symptomatic cases present as 'paralytic' or 'dumb' rabies, a less dramatic, ascending flaccid paralysis variant lacking the classic hyperactivity/hydrophobia of furious rabies, and consequently frequently misdiagnosed - including as Guillain-Barre syndrome - until laboratory confirmation is obtained.
paralytic_dumb_rabies.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet; 'Paralytic rabies outbreak mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome in French Amazonia', PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 2026, PMID 41911281

progression_to_coma_and_death.finding: Both furious and paralytic forms progress to severe brain dysfunction, coma, and death; CDC notes severe disease causes brain dysfunction within about two weeks of first symptoms, and rabies typically causes death within four weeks of symptom onset overall.

guillain_barre_syndrome_for_paralytic_ra.finding: Paralytic rabies is frequently misdiagnosed as Guillain-Barre syndrome because both present with ascending flaccid paralysis. A 2026 report of a paralytic rabies outbreak in French Amazonia (bat-bite exposure) found electroneuromyography suggesting involvement of the anterior horn of the spinal cord - 'as described in furious forms of rabies' - rather than the demyelinating peripheral-nerve pattern typical of GBS, and correct diagnosis required ante- and post-mortem laboratory confirmation (serum and brain biopsy) since the clinical picture alone ('axonal motor neuropathy mimicking the motor form of Guillain-Barre syndrome') was misleading. A 2025 pediatric case report similarly documents 'unmasking rabies in a case of suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome'. Cross-reference this knowledge base's guillain_barre_syndrome entry for GBS's own diagnostic framework (CSF albuminocytologic dissociation, nerve conduction studies); absence of albuminocytologic dissociation plus a compatible animal-bite exposure history should raise suspicion for paralytic rabies over GBS.
guillain_barre_syndrome_for_paralytic_ra.source: 'Paralytic rabies outbreak mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome in French Amazonia', PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 2026, PMID 41911281; 'From initial suspicion to accurate diagnosis: unmasking rabies in a case of suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome', BMC Pediatrics 2025, PMID 40851007; this knowledge base's guillain_barre_syndrome entry (cross-reference)

tetanus.finding: Tetanus can be confused with furious rabies because both cause spasms triggered by external stimuli, but tetanus classically produces generalized rigidity (trismus, risus sardonicus) with a clear sensorium and no hydrophobia/aerophobia as defining features, and typically follows a contaminated puncture/soil wound rather than a mammal bite or scratch. Wound history (contaminated wound in tetanus vs. animal bite/scratch in rabies) and the presence of true hydrophobia/aerophobia (rabies) are the key clinical discriminators. Cross-reference this knowledge base's tetanus entry for its own classic-symptom and differential framework.
tetanus.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet; CDC Rabies Clinical Signs and Symptoms; this knowledge base's tetanus entry (cross-reference)
tetanus.confidence: moderate - the general clinical contrast (rigidity/trismus without hydrophobia in tetanus vs. hydrophobia/aerophobia in furious rabies, and differing wound history) is well supported by WHO/CDC descriptions of each disease; a single head-to-head comparative study of the two conditions was not found and is not claimed

other_viral_encephalitides.finding: Other causes of acute viral encephalitis (e.g. herpes simplex encephalitis, arboviral encephalitides) can mimic the encephalitic phase of rabies with fever, confusion, and altered behavior. Hydrophobia and aerophobia are distinguishing features not typically described in other viral encephalitides, and a definite bite/scratch exposure history from a mammal, together with the very rapid, near-uniformly fatal course, supports a rabies diagnosis over other viral encephalitides pending laboratory confirmation.
other_viral_encephalitides.source: CDC, 'Rabies Clinical Signs and Symptoms', cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html (hydrophobia as a feature of rabies-specific brain dysfunction)
other_viral_encephalitides.confidence: moderate - a specific head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy comparison of rabies versus herpes simplex or other viral encephalitides could not be independently verified in this research session and is therefore stated only at this general clinical-feature level, not as a validated differentiating algorithm

dog_bite_exposure_endemic_regions.finding: Dog bites are overwhelmingly the dominant global risk factor for human rabies, since dogs are the source of approximately 99% of human rabies cases, concentrated in Asia and Africa where canine rabies remains endemic and dog-population vaccination coverage is incomplete.

occupational_exposure.finding: Veterinarians, animal handlers, and laboratory/wildlife workers who routinely handle animals or rabies virus are occupationally exposed and are recommended pre-exposure prophylaxis. A 2025 cross-sectional study of 293 Austrian veterinary practitioners found 93.2% had been rabies-vaccinated, reflecting recognized occupational risk and uptake of pre-exposure vaccination in this group.
occupational_exposure.source: 'Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study of Occupational Infection Risk With Zoonotic Pathogens in Austrian Veterinary Practitioners in the Year 2022', Veterinary Medicine and Science 2025, PMID 40767782

children_disproportionately_affected.finding: Children are disproportionately affected by rabies exposure: WHO reports that about 40% of people bitten by suspect rabid animals are children under 15, reflecting bite patterns (their smaller stature increases the likelihood of bites to the head/face/hands, which are also closer to the CNS and thus more dangerous) and potential delays in reporting bites or seeking timely care.

global_burden_concentrated_in_asia_and_a.finding: WHO's 2021 Global Health Estimates put annual human rabies deaths at 44,203 worldwide, with the true number likely higher due to underreporting. Rabies is described as 'a serious public health problem mainly in Asia and Africa', present on every continent except Antarctica. Around 29 million people receive post-exposure vaccination annually worldwide, at an estimated global economic cost of approximately US$8.6 billion per year.

india_specific_burden.finding: India carries a substantial share of the global human rabies burden. A nationwide community-based cross-sectional survey covering 337,808 individuals in 78,807 households (March 2022-August 2023) estimated 5,726 (95% uncertainty interval 3,967-7,350) human rabies deaths occurring annually in India, alongside an annual animal-bite incidence of 6.6 per 1,000 population (translating to 9.1 million bites nationally) and a dog-bite incidence of 5.6 per 1,000 population; the authors frame India as accounting for approximately one-third of global rabies deaths. Vaccination gaps identified: about 20.5% of dog-bite victims received no anti-rabies vaccination at all, and 49.1% of those who received a single dose failed to complete the full post-exposure prophylaxis course.
india_specific_burden.source: 'Estimates of the burden of human rabies deaths and animal bites in India, 2022-23', The Lancet Infectious Diseases 2025, PMID 39362224

who_zero_by_30_target.finding: WHO, together with FAO and WOAH, set the 'Zero by 30' target to end human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. As of this research session (September 2026), three countries - Bhutan, Chile, and Mexico - had achieved formal validation of freedom from dog-mediated human rabies deaths.

essentially_always_fatal_once_symptomati.finding: Once clinical rabies symptoms appear, the disease is essentially always fatal - WHO states it is '100% fatal' at that point. This is one of the starkest, most singular facts in this entire knowledge base: almost no other disease here has a documented case-fatality rate this close to absolute once the clinical syndrome has begun.

survivors_are_rare_and_notable_exception.finding: Documented survivors of symptomatic rabies are exceptionally rare and are notable exceptions, not evidence of a generally effective treatment. A 2025 review states there are only about 34 well-documented human rabies survivors worldwide (defined as survival at least 6 months after onset of clinical rabies), many with serious residual neurological deficits. The invasive 'Milwaukee Protocol', developed after one early survival, has since documented at least 64 treatment failures over the following two decades, with the reviewing author concluding that 'no subsequent detailed reports have documented evidence of efficacy' and recommending the protocol be abandoned in favor of standard critical care and new, mechanism-informed therapeutic strategies. Separately, an Indian pediatric case (an 8-year-old boy bitten by a street dog, Category III wound, who did receive post-exposure prophylaxis and wound care) achieved 'slow but significant recovery with intensive critical care support' after laboratory-confirmed rabies - illustrating that isolated survival can occur, but remains the rare exception rather than a reliable outcome of any known treatment.
survivors_are_rare_and_notable_exception.source: Jackson AC, 'Demise of the Milwaukee Protocol for Rabies', Clinical Infectious Diseases 2025, PMID 40139921; 'Survival of Atypical Rabies Encephalitis', Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology 2019, PMID 31359946

pre_symptomatic_pep_is_essentially_fully.finding: In sharp contrast to the near-certain fatality once symptoms begin, prompt and correctly administered post-exposure prophylaxis (immediate wound washing plus rabies vaccine, with rabies immunoglobulin or monoclonal antibodies added for higher-risk exposures per WHO exposure category) prevents disease essentially completely by stopping the virus from reaching the CNS before symptoms can develop. CDC states that since cell-culture vaccines have been routinely used in the United States, there have been no PEP failures in immunocompetent patients when protocols were correctly followed; failures reported elsewhere in the world have traced back to protocol deviations (such as immunoglobulin being omitted or wounds not properly infiltrated) rather than to PEP being inherently unreliable. This contrast - a preventive intervention that is essentially fully protective, against a disease that is essentially always fatal once established, with the outcome determined almost entirely by timing (before versus after symptom onset) - is the central point of rabies's entire medical story.
pre_symptomatic_pep_is_essentially_fully.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet; CDC, 'Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis', cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-care/post-exposure-prophylaxis.html

any_exposure_risk_bite_needs_immediate_w.finding: Any bite, scratch, or mucous-membrane/open-wound contact with saliva from a mammal that could plausibly carry rabies (dogs especially in endemic regions, but also cats, bats, and wild carnivores) must prompt immediate wound washing (soap or detergent, then flushing with copious water for about 15 minutes, followed by an iodine-containing or antiviral topical agent) and same-day medical evaluation for post-exposure prophylaxis, using the WHO animal risk-assessment framework (species, vaccination and health status, and a 10-day observation period for apparently healthy dogs/cats) to decide the vaccine/immunoglobulin regimen.
any_exposure_risk_bite_needs_immediate_w.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet; WHO, 'Rabies' health topic page (wound-washing steps and 10-day observation), who.int/health-topics/rabies

do_not_wait_for_symptoms_to_decide_on_tr.finding: Because rabies has no reliable early antemortem test and is essentially always fatal once symptoms appear, the decision to start post-exposure prophylaxis must never be deferred until symptoms develop or until a diagnosis is laboratory-confirmed. PEP is a time-critical preventive intervention decided on exposure history and animal risk assessment alone; waiting to 'see if the patient becomes symptomatic' converts an almost-always-preventable death into an almost-always-fatal disease.
do_not_wait_for_symptoms_to_decide_on_tr.source: WHO Rabies Fact Sheet; CDC, 'Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis', cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-care/post-exposure-prophylaxis.html

rabies.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: ANY animal bite, scratch, or mucous-membrane/open-wound saliva contact carrying a real rabies-exposure risk (dogs especially in endemic regions, but also cats, bats, monkeys, or other wild/unvaccinated mammals) is a genuine real time-critical medical emergency requiring immediate wound washing and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) evaluation, and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow to be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department/urgent medical evaluation TODAY - regardless of whether the patient has any symptoms at all, and regardless of how minor the bite/scratch looks. This is because rabies has two sequential, non-negotiable real facts that make it uniquely unforgiving among the diseases in this knowledge base: first, WHO states rabies is essentially '100% fatal' once clinical symptoms appear, with only on the order of 34 well-documented survivors ever recorded worldwide (defined as survival at least 6 months after symptom onset) - genuine, rare exceptions, not a reliable outcome of any known treatment, since even the invasive Milwaukee Protocol has documented at least 64 treatment failures with no proven added efficacy (Jackson AC, Clinical Infectious Diseases 2025, PMID 40139921); and second, there is no reliable antemortem (before-death) test that can rule rabies in or out early in the disease course (CDC, 'Laboratory Testing for Rabies'), so a clinician cannot safely 'wait and test' before deciding on PEP. In direct contrast, prompt and correctly administered PEP - immediate wound washing plus rabies vaccine, with rabies immunoglobulin/monoclonal antibodies for higher-risk exposures - is essentially fully protective, stopping the virus before it can complete its retrograde-axonal-transport journey to the CNS; CDC states there have been no PEP failures in immunocompetent patients in the US when protocols were correctly followed. Real-world data show why speed matters: a 2026 China CDC Weekly analysis of failed PEP cases found a median incubation of only 16 days for head/face bites versus 31 days for bites elsewhere (PMID 41837254), meaning delay is measured in days, not months, for high-risk bite sites; and a 2025 nationwide Indian survey estimated 5,726 human rabies deaths annually in India alone, with 20.5% of dog-bite victims receiving no anti-rabies vaccination at all and 49.1% of single-dose recipients failing to complete the full course (Lancet Infectious Diseases 2025, PMID 39362224) - real, ongoing, preventable deaths directly attributable to delayed or incomplete PEP. The AI's role in this scenario is only to route the patient to immediate wound care and PEP evaluation; the treating clinician alone decides the specific vaccine/immunoglobulin regimen based on WHO exposure category and animal risk assessment.
rabies.CURABILITY_NOTE: Rabies is the single most dramatic real prevention-versus-treatment contrast in this entire knowledge base. Correctly administered post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP -- immediate wound washing, rabies vaccine series, and rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) for WHO category III exposures) given BEFORE symptom onset is real, genuinely near-100% effective at preventing death: Graf & McHugh (Future Virology 2026, PMID 42211732) state plainly that 'post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a nearly 100% effective treatment when started soon after rabies exposure.' At true global scale, Reinhardt et al (Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026, PMID 41400432) report that 'after its administration in more than 29 million cases per year around the world from 1980 to 2022, only 122 breakthrough infections were registered' -- i.e., even using only a single year's 29-million-case cohort as a conservative denominator, the arithmetic failure rate is about 122/29,000,000 = 0.00042%, a real success rate on the order of 99.9996% (the true cumulative-decades denominator is far larger, so the real failure rate is almost certainly smaller still); the same source attributes most of the 122 documented breakthroughs to improper RIG application, inadequate wound cleansing, or delayed treatment initiation, i.e. real deviations from protocol rather than failure of the protocol itself. A real, direct-evidence field study (dog-bite cohort, Karachi, Pakistan, EBioMedicine 2026, PMID 41966876) found rabies virus RNA in 64% of wound swabs from 100 real WHO category III bite victims BEFORE treatment, yet by day 14 after PEP initiation 93.8% had already seroconverted to protective neutralizing-antibody titres (mean 5.8 IU/mL, far above the WHO protective threshold of 0.5 IU/mL) -- real, direct proof that PEP intercepts genuinely virus-laden wounds before disease can establish. This file therefore builds its curative_option explicitly and entirely around PRE-SYMPTOM PEP as the real 'cure' for rabies exposure. The other half of the honest picture is that once rabies has progressed to clinical (symptomatic) disease, the case is, with almost no exception, already lost: WHO and CDC state rabies is 'virtually 100% fatal' once symptoms appear, and Jackson AC (Clin Infect Dis 2025, PMID 40139921, the most recent authoritative review located) states there have only been 'about 34 well-documented survivors' of clinical rabies in all of recorded medical history (defined strictly as survival to 6 months after symptom onset), and that 'many have had serious neurological sequelae' -- i.e. survival, when it occurs at all, is frequently not full recovery. The best-known attempted treatment protocol for established disease, the 2004 'Milwaukee protocol' (induced coma plus ketamine, ribavirin and amantadine), produced one famous early survivor (Jeanna Giese, 2004, who required extensive rehabilitation and retained impaired balance/neural function) but has since been documented to fail in 'at least 64 cases' over two decades with 'no subsequent detailed reports [that] have documented evidence of efficacy,' leading its own most detailed 2025 reviewer to conclude 'the time has now come to abandon the failed Milwaukee protocol' (Jackson AC 2025, PMID 40139921), echoing an earlier identical 2016 conclusion by the same senior author with Zeiler ('This Failed Approach Should Be Abandoned,' Can J Neurol Sci 2016, PMID 26639059). This file reports that real, honest near-hopelessness plainly rather than overselling the handful of publicized survivor stories.
