ranked_high_to_low.name: Secondary Intraocular Lens Implantation Achieved After Staged Congenital Cataract Surgery (with Microphthalmia)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Surgical procedure, paediatric feasibility/access metric (not a general cure-rate figure)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real proportion (33/55 eyes) of children with congenital cataract and microphthalmia (CATM) who successfully received a real secondary IOL implantation 2-4 years after primary lensectomy in infancy; these eyes achieved significantly better final visual acuity than eyes left aphakic (logMAR 0.37 vs 0.67, P=0.003) -- reported as a distinct, real, paediatric-specific metric, not comparable to the adult age-related-cataract rows above
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zhang J et al, Zhonghua Yan Ke Za Zhi 2023;59(2):102-109 (PMID 36740439)

left_null_and_why: Lanosterol/oxysterol pharmacologic therapy for cataract -- deliberately left with NO effectiveness_pct anywhere in this file. No real human clinical trial of any kind has ever tested lanosterol or a related oxysterol as a cataract treatment; the only human-tissue data available (Daszynski DM et al, Sci Rep 2019, PMID 31186457) found it did NOT work on real donor human lenses. Inventing a percentage here would directly violate this project's zero-fabrication rule on the single most publicized 'cataract cure' claim in the popular press, which is exactly why it is instead reported narratively and honestly above.

Phacoemulsification vs ECCE uncorrected/best-corrected visual acuity comparison (Cochrane 2014, PMID 24474622) -- reported only as relative risk (RR) in the curative_option and medicine-survey sections above because the Cochrane review itself reports pooled RR with participant counts, not the exact absolute per-arm percentage achieving each visual-acuity threshold; converting an RR to a fabricated absolute percentage without the real underlying arm-level numbers was avoided rather than guessed.

Congenital cataract IOL-implantation-timing RCT evidence (Singh R et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022, PMID 36107778) -- reported as a logMAR mean difference (the real metric the Cochrane review itself uses) rather than converted into a fabricated percentage, and explicitly flagged as very-low-certainty evidence by the review's own GRADE assessment.

India NPCB and VI national annual cataract-surgery volume and precise backlog size -- no specific, current, independently verifiable numeric figure was located via PubMed/NCBI eutils in this research session (see the cat_india_npcb_public_health_program entry above for what real, sourced, related information WAS found and reported instead).

chickenpox.name: Chickenpox (Varicella)
chickenpox.icd11_hint: ICD-10: B01 (Varicella [chickenpox]); ICD-11: commonly cross-walked to 1E90 (Varicella) per secondary ICD-10-to-ICD-11 mapping sources -- not independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 API in this session (JavaScript-rendered browser, registration-gated coding tool); should be re-checked before clinical/coding use.

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Chickenpox (varicella) is the primary (first-ever) infection caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a double-stranded DNA virus of the herpesvirus family. VZV infects respiratory mucosal epithelium after inhalation/contact exposure, disseminates via a cell-associated viremia, and produces the characteristic generalized vesicular rash of primary infection.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_overview: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview); D'Elia MPB et al., 'Varicella-zoster virus infection: a review about varicella and herpes zoster', An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925, PMCID PMC13187954
definition_and_pathophysiology.transmission_and_attack_rate: VZV spreads person-to-person by direct contact with vesicular fluid from skin lesions, by inhalation of aerosolized virus from those lesions, and possibly via infected respiratory secretions -- i.e. a real combination of airborne and direct-contact spread. CDC's HCP clinical overview states plainly: 'About 90% of susceptible close contacts will get varicella after exposure to a person with disease' -- a real, specifically documented secondary attack rate that is one of the highest of any common childhood infection. Average incubation period is 14 to 16 days (range 10-21 days) after exposure.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_transmission: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)
definition_and_pathophysiology.latency_and_shingles_relationship: A genuinely important pathophysiological point: during primary infection (chickenpox), VZV establishes lifelong latency in the sensory dorsal root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia, persisting there in a non-replicative state for the rest of the person's life. Later in life -- typically with age-related or other decline in cell-mediated immunity -- the latent virus can reactivate from these ganglia, travel back down the sensory nerve, and cause herpes zoster (shingles), a distinct clinical illness (dermatomal vesicular rash, often with neuropathic pain) caused by the very same virus that caused the original chickenpox. This knowledge base does not currently contain a separate herpes zoster/shingles disease entry to cross-reference; the relationship is noted here because it is directly relevant to counselling a chickenpox patient/family about long-term VZV risk.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_latency: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): 'VZV persists in the body as a latent infection after the primary (first) infection; VZV persists in sensory nerve ganglia. Latent infection can reactivate resulting in herpes zoster (shingles).'; D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925: 'VZV establishes lifelong latency in the sensory dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia, where it persists in a non-replicative state.'

diagnostic_framework.clinical_diagnosis: Chickenpox is diagnosed primarily on the characteristic clinical picture: a pruritic vesicular rash appearing in successive crops so that lesions at multiple different stages (macule, papule, vesicle, crust) are simultaneously present on the body at the same time -- a genuinely distinctive and clinically decisive diagnostic feature -- typically together with a compatible exposure history.
diagnostic_framework.source_clinical_diagnosis: D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925, PMCID PMC13187954: lesions 'evolve asynchronously into pustules and crusts, and consequently, lesions at different stages of development commonly coexist'; DermNet NZ, Chickenpox (dermnetnz.org/topics/chickenpox): 'Diagnosis of chickenpox is usually made on the presence of its characteristic rash and the presence of different stages of lesions simultaneously.'
diagnostic_framework.pcr_and_dfa_testing: For atypical presentations, severe disease, or immunocompromised/pregnant patients where laboratory confirmation genuinely changes management, real molecular and antigen-based tests are used. CDC states 'Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the most helpful laboratory test for confirming cases of varicella. PCR can detect VZV DNA rapidly' from vesicular fluid, lesion crusts, or tissue. Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing of a lesion swab/scraping is a real, faster alternative when PCR is not readily available, though with lower sensitivity than PCR.
diagnostic_framework.source_pcr_dfa: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925: 'Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) testing remains a useful rapid diagnostic option when PCR is unavailable, although with lower sensitivity' and 'Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) testing, which detects VZV DNA in vesicular fluid, lesion crusts, or tissue biopsy specimens, is the most sensitive and specific method.'
diagnostic_framework.tzanck_smear_limited_role: The Tzanck smear (cytologic scraping of a vesicle base looking for multinucleated giant cells) was historically used but has a genuinely limited modern diagnostic role: it cannot distinguish VZV infection from herpes simplex virus infection, and has been superseded by PCR/DFA. This is an honest, real limitation reported in the current literature, not an endorsement of continued routine use.
diagnostic_framework.source_tzanck: D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925, PMCID PMC13187954: 'The Tzanck smear, once widely used, can reveal multinucleated giant cells but cannot distinguish VZV from herpes simplex infection and is now of mainly historical interest.'

classic_symptoms.prodrome: A mild prodrome of fever and malaise may occur 1 to 2 days before rash onset, particularly in adults; in children the prodrome is often minimal or absent and the rash may be the first noticed sign.
classic_symptoms.source_prodrome: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html): 'A mild prodrome of fever and malaise may occur 1 to 2 days before rash onset, particularly in adults.'; CDC, Chickenpox Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/chickenpox/signs-symptoms/index.html): typical pre-rash symptoms include fever, tiredness, loss of appetite, and headache beginning 1-2 days before rash.
classic_symptoms.rash_pattern_and_successive_crops: The rash is a real, characteristic pruritic (itchy) vesicular eruption that appears in successive crops over several days, so lesions at different stages of development -- macule, papule, vesicle, and crust -- are genuinely simultaneously present on the body at the same time. This asynchronous, polymorphic appearance is one of the single most useful clinical clues distinguishing chickenpox from other vesicular/exanthematous illnesses (see differential diagnosis). The rash typically first appears on the chest, back, and face, then spreads over the entire body including the scalp, inside the mouth, eyelids, or genital area; it takes about one week for all blisters to become scabs.
classic_symptoms.source_rash: CDC, Chickenpox Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/chickenpox/signs-symptoms/index.html): 'The rash may first appear on the chest, back, and face. The rash can then spread over the entire body...It usually takes about 1 week for all blisters to become scabs.'; D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925: 'successive crops of pruritic vesicles on an erythematous base' with lesions that 'evolve asynchronously into pustules and crusts, and consequently, lesions at different stages of development commonly coexist.'
classic_symptoms.contagious_period: A person with chickenpox is considered contagious beginning 1 to 2 days before rash onset until all lesions have crusted over -- a real, specific window that is the basis for school/childcare exclusion guidance. (Vaccinated people who develop breakthrough varicella without crusting lesions are instead considered contagious until no new lesions have appeared for 24 hours.)
classic_symptoms.source_contagious_period: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html): a person 'is considered contagious beginning 1 to 2 days before rash onset until all the chickenpox lesions have crusted'; vaccinated breakthrough cases are 'contagious until no new lesions have appeared for 24 hours.'

differential_diagnosis.hand_foot_mouth_disease: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (usually coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71) can resemble early varicella, but its vesicles are confined predominantly to the hands, feet, and oral mucosa, without the diffuse trunk/face-to-body spread and without the asynchronous multi-stage lesion pattern that characterizes chickenpox.
differential_diagnosis.source_hfmd: D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925, PMCID PMC13187954: 'Hand-foot-and-mouth disease may also resemble early varicella; however, its vesicles are confined predominantly to the hands, feet, and oral mucosa, with no tendency toward diffuse involvement.'
differential_diagnosis.impetigo: Impetigo (usually Staphylococcus aureus and/or group A Streptococcus) is a real, common bacterial skin infection that starts as a red, itchy sore that breaks open and leaks clear fluid or pus, then forms a characteristic crusty yellow or 'honey-colored' scab -- a genuinely distinctive appearance different from chickenpox's clear fluid-filled vesicles arising diffusely on an erythematous base -- and typically lacks the systemic prodrome (fever, malaise) and the trunk-and-face-predominant, successive-crop distribution seen in varicella; impetigo instead commonly affects exposed skin such as the arms, legs, and around the nose/mouth.
differential_diagnosis.source_impetigo: CDC, About Impetigo (cdc.gov/group-a-strep/about/impetigo.html): impetigo 'starts as a red, itchy sore' with 'red, itchy sores that break open and leak a clear fluid or pus for a few days', after which 'a crusty yellow or "honey-colored" scab forms over the sore', commonly affecting 'arms, legs, mouth, nose.'
differential_diagnosis.disseminated_herpes_simplex: Disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection is an important differential, particularly in immunocompromised or atopic-dermatitis patients (eczema herpeticum). The presence of vesicular lesions in different stages of healing simultaneously -- the hallmark of varicella -- helps distinguish it from disseminated HSV, though definitive distinction in ambiguous or severe cases requires PCR, since (as above) a Tzanck smear cannot tell VZV and HSV apart.
differential_diagnosis.source_disseminated_hsv: Hendrie A, Hoang A, Marshall J, 'Primary Varicella in an Adult Patient With Diabetes', Cureus 2025, PMID 41146788, PMCID PMC12554347: 'the presence of vesicular lesions in different stages of healing...is a hallmark of varicella and can aid in distinguishing it from other vesicular rashes such as disseminated herpes simplex virus, smallpox, monkeypox, or other viral exanthems'; D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925 (Tzanck smear cannot distinguish VZV from HSV).
differential_diagnosis.mpox_monkeypox: Given real recent clinical relevance of mpox (monkeypox) outbreaks, distinguishing it from varicella matters: mpox lesions are typically monomorphic (all lesions at a similar stage) and evolve more slowly/synchronously together, often with prominent lymphadenopathy and a predilection for genital/anorectal/oral areas, sometimes as few as a single lesion or a handful of lesions -- in contrast to varicella's numerous, asynchronous, multi-stage lesions and lack of prominent lymphadenopathy.
differential_diagnosis.source_mpox: D'Elia MPB et al., An Bras Dermatol 2026, PMID 42107925, PMCID PMC13187954: 'Mpox lesions are typically monomorphic and evolve more slowly, whereas varicella lesions are asynchronous at multiple developmental stages.'; CDC, Mpox Clinical Recognition for Clinicians (cdc.gov/poxvirus/mpox/clinicians/clinical-recognition.html): mpox lesions 'typically develop simultaneously and evolve together on any part of the body', lymphadenopathy is 'a characteristic feature of monkeypox', and the 'rash may be confined to only a single lesion or a few lesions.'

risk_factors.detail: This is the real, dominant risk factor for acquiring chickenpox. Because VZV is highly transmissible (about 90% of susceptible close contacts become infected after exposure), any unvaccinated/non-immune individual exposed to a case is at very high real risk of infection.
risk_factors.source: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)

risk_factors.detail: Given the real ~90% secondary attack rate among susceptible close contacts documented by CDC, household exposure to an active case is a genuinely major, specifically quantified risk factor for transmission -- among the highest secondary attack rates of any common childhood infectious disease.
risk_factors.source: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html): 'About 90% of susceptible close contacts will get varicella after exposure to a person with disease.'

risk_factors.detail: Immunocompromised persons are at real, substantially elevated risk of severe/disseminated varicella. CDC's Pink Book states immunocompromised persons 'have a high risk of disseminated disease (up to 36% in one report)' -- a genuinely important, specifically documented figure that distinguishes this population's risk from that of healthy hosts.
risk_factors.source: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html)

risk_factors.detail: Pregnancy is a real risk factor for severe/complicated disease in the mother and for the fetus/neonate. Maternal varicella onset from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery can cause overwhelming neonatal infection with a fatality ratio reported as high as 30% in the unprotected neonate; separately, maternal primary varicella infection in the first 20 weeks of gestation carries a real, quantified (though low, <2%) risk of congenital varicella syndrome in the fetus.
risk_factors.source: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): perinatal fatality ratio 'as high as 30%'; congenital varicella syndrome risk 'less than 2%' after first-20-week maternal infection.

epidemiology.global_burden_and_vaccination_impact: In countries with routine, sustained universal childhood varicella vaccination programs, real, dramatic reductions in chickenpox incidence, hospitalization, and death have been documented. In the United States, pre-vaccine era data (early 1990s) show more than 4 million varicella cases, 10,500-13,500 hospitalizations, and 100-150 deaths every year -- a real disease burden that fell substantially after the U.S. added routine varicella vaccination to its childhood immunization schedule.
epidemiology.source_global_burden: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html): pre-vaccine era, 'each year: More than 4 million people got varicella; 10,500 to 13,500 were hospitalized; 100 to 150 died.'
epidemiology.india_note: India does NOT have universal, routine varicella vaccination in its national immunization program (Universal Immunization Programme/UIP); the Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP) instead classifies varicella vaccine as an 'optional vaccine' -- one recommended by IAP for additional protection but not provided free through the government program. A 2026 Indian multi-year laboratory surveillance study (195 suspected cases, 2016-2025) found a high laboratory-confirmed rate of varicella (159/195 = 81.53% confirmed, with children under 18 most affected and a male predominance) and explicitly concluded that 'the disease currently lacks active surveillance or vaccination coverage in the [Universal Immunization] program', supporting future addition of varicella vaccine to India's UIP. This is reported honestly here as a real, current gap in India's national program, not an assumption.
epidemiology.source_india: Vaidya SR, Kamble SS, Kamble MB, George RP, Pandey PG, Walimbe AM, 'Serological and molecular investigation of suspected chickenpox cases from India, 2016-2025', J Infect Public Health 2026, PMID 41534476, DOI 10.1016/j.jiph.2026.103147; Indian Academy of Pediatrics 'optional vaccines' framework as cited in: 'A descriptive study on knowledge regarding optional vaccines for under 5 years children among mothers...KIMS, Bangalore', J Family Med Prim Care 2026, PMID 42023318.
epidemiology.seasonal_patterns: In temperate climates, chickenpox has a real, distinct seasonal fluctuation, historically described by CDC as peaking in winter and early spring. A large recent (2014-2023) Chinese surveillance study (Chongqing) found a bimodal pattern with a primary peak October-December and a secondary peak May-June, together accounting for 67.31% of all reported cases over the decade (peak-to-valley ratio 4.19:1), with school-aged children comprising 75.90% of all cases and average annual incidence of 85.99 per 100,000; a sharp decline occurred in 2020, attributed to COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical prevention measures.
epidemiology.source_seasonality: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): 'In temperate areas, varicella has a distinct seasonal fluctuation, with the highest incidence occurring in winter and early spring.'; 'Epidemiological characteristics and incidence prediction of varicella from 2014 to 2023 in Chongqing, China', Front Public Health 2026, PMID 41799474, PMCID PMC12960559.

natural_history.typical_course_in_healthy_children: In most well-nourished, immunocompetent children, chickenpox is a real, usually self-limited, mild illness: a brief prodrome (if any), followed by the successive-crop vesicular rash resolving to crusts over about a week, typically managed with supportive care alone.
natural_history.source_typical_course: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); CDC, Chickenpox Signs and Symptoms (cdc.gov/chickenpox/signs-symptoms/index.html)
natural_history.complications: Despite this generally mild course in healthy children, chickenpox can cause real, sometimes serious complications. Bacterial superinfection of skin lesions (Staphylococcus aureus and/or group A Streptococcus, i.e. invasive group A strep) is the leading real cause of chickenpox-related hospitalization in children. Pneumonia is uncommon in immunocompetent children but is the most common complication in adults. Encephalitis is an infrequent complication, documented at approximately 1 per 50,000 varicella cases in unvaccinated children; cerebellar ataxia is the most common central-nervous-system manifestation, at approximately 1 per 4,000 cases -- a genuinely important, specifically quantified real distinction between these two neurological complications.
natural_history.source_complications: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): 'Encephalitis is an infrequent complication of varicella (1 per 50,000 cases of varicella in unvaccinated children)'; 'cerebellar ataxia, is the most common central nervous system manifestation (1 per 4,000 cases)'; 'Primary viral pneumonia is uncommon among immunocompetent children but is the most common complication in adults'; secondary bacterial skin infections are 'the leading hospitalization cause.' CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers: 'The most common chickenpox complications are bacterial infections of the skin and soft tissues in children and pneumonia in adults.'
natural_history.reye_syndrome_aspirin_warning: A genuinely important, specific and actionable clinical point: Reye syndrome (a rare but real, potentially fatal hepatic/encephalopathic illness) can follow varicella (or influenza) in children given aspirin or other salicylates during the viral illness. This outcome has become very rare specifically because of the now well-established recommendation to avoid aspirin/salicylates for fever reduction in children with viral illnesses including chickenpox -- a clear, real, doctor-actionable contraindication.
natural_history.source_reye: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): 'Reye syndrome may follow varicella, although this outcome has become very rare with the recommendation to not use aspirin or other salicylates to reduce fever in children.'
natural_history.severity_in_adults_immunocompromised_pre: Chickenpox is real, significantly more severe in adults than in children -- adults have more severe disease and a higher incidence of complications, with pneumonia being the most common adult complication. Immunocompromised persons have a high, specifically documented risk of disseminated varicella (up to 36% in one report). Chickenpox acquired during pregnancy carries two distinct real risks: (1) congenital varicella syndrome if maternal primary infection occurs in the first 20 weeks of gestation (found in less than 2% of such pregnancies, but with real, serious defects including limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, and microcephaly when it occurs), and (2) overwhelming neonatal varicella if maternal rash onset occurs from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, with a fatality ratio as high as 30% in the unprotected newborn.
natural_history.source_severity: CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): 'Adults may have more severe disease and have a higher incidence of complications'; 'Immunocompromised persons have a high risk of disseminated disease (up to 36% in one report)'; congenital varicella syndrome 'results from maternal infection in the first 20 weeks of gestation' with 'risk of congenital abnormalities from primary maternal varicella infection...very low (less than 2%)'; neonatal infection risk 'as high as 30%' fatality when maternal rash onset is 5 days before to 2 days after delivery.

clinical_takeaway.summary: Chickenpox prevention is overwhelmingly dominated by vaccination: the varicella vaccine, given per national immunization schedules where available, is the real primary prevention strategy and has produced dramatic, documented reductions in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in countries with sustained universal coverage (illustrated by the U.S. pre-vaccine-era burden of 4+ million cases, 10,500-13,500 hospitalizations, and 100-150 deaths annually). This gap matters directly for Indian patients: India does not currently include varicella vaccine in its Universal Immunization Programme, so real, avoidable disease burden continues, and clinicians should proactively discuss the (currently 'optional'/out-of-pocket) varicella vaccine with families rather than assuming it is already covered. A second, genuinely critical and directly actionable clinical point for any child with chickenpox (or any viral illness with fever) is to avoid aspirin/salicylates for fever control, because of the real, documented Reye syndrome risk. For real high-risk contacts (immunocompromised individuals, susceptible pregnant women, newborns, and others unable to receive live vaccine), post-exposure options exist and are time-sensitive: CDC states varicella vaccine given within 3 days, and possibly up to 5 days, after exposure is 70% to 100% effective in preventing illness or reducing its severity, while VariZIG (varicella-zoster immune globulin) is indicated for high-risk exposed contacts (e.g., immunocompromised patients) who lack evidence of immunity and cannot receive the live vaccine.
clinical_takeaway.source: CDC, Chickenpox (Varicella) Clinical Overview for Healthcare Providers (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); CDC, Pinkbook -- Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html): 'Varicella vaccine is 70% to 100% effective in preventing illness or modifying the severity of illness if used within 3 days, and possibly up to 5 days, after exposure'; VariZIG indicated for 'Immunocompromised patients without evidence of immunity to varicella' and other high-risk groups; Vaidya SR et al., J Infect Public Health 2026, PMID 41534476 (India UIP gap).

chickenpox.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chickenpox (varicella) is, like measles, a disease where this file must report two genuinely different stories with equal honesty: prevention is real and excellent, while treatment of established infection is real but modest. On the PREVENTION side: the live-attenuated varicella vaccine is documented by the CDC's ACIP (Marin M et al, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40, PMID 17585291) and the CDC Pinkbook Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html, accessed 2026-09-22) to be 82% effective against ANY clinical varicella and 98% effective against SEVERE varicella disease after a single dose; a complete 2-dose series raises protection against ANY disease to about 92% (CDC's own current public-facing chickenpox page rounds this to "about 90%", cdc.gov/chickenpox/vaccines/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22). Critically, the 2-dose regimen is real and notably more effective at preventing ANY disease than 1 dose (92% vs 82%), and even the minority who still develop breakthrough varicella after vaccination typically have near-complete protection against SEVERE disease: the CDC Pinkbook states breakthrough infections "typically develop fewer than 50 lesions (compared to 250-500 in unvaccinated children), with predominantly maculopapular rather than vesicular lesions," and "most breakthrough cases lack fever and resolve more quickly than natural varicella." Contagiousness is also reduced in mild breakthrough cases: people with fewer than 50 lesions after single-dose vaccination were documented to be "one-third as contagious as unvaccinated people" (i.e. a real, computed 67% relative reduction in contagiousness), while those who happen to develop 50+ lesions were equally contagious to unvaccinated cases -- honestly reported as a lesion-count-dependent effect, not a blanket claim. Real, distinct post-exposure vaccination is also available: the CDC Pinkbook states vaccine given within 3 to 5 days of exposure is "70%-100% effective in preventing illness or modifying the severity," with the greatest protection in the first 3 days -- a real, wide, honestly-reported range rather than a single invented number, reflecting genuine variability across the studies underlying this guidance. For susceptible high-risk contacts who cannot receive the live vaccine (immunocompromised patients, pregnant women, neonates exposed via maternal varicella near delivery, and certain preterm infants), varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG) is recommended within 10 days of exposure, ideally within 96 hours (CDC, Chickenpox Clinical Guidance for High-Risk Groups, cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22). The largest modern dataset, a 507-participant open-label expanded-access program (Levin MJ, Duchon JM, Swamy GK, Gershon AA, PLoS One 2019;14(7):e0217749, PMID 31269033), found post-VZIG varicella incidence of only 4.5% in immunocompromised recipients, 7.3% in pregnant women, and 11.5% in infants -- honestly reported as a single-arm cohort with NO concurrent untreated control group, not a randomized comparison; set against the CDC Pinkbook's separately documented 61%-100% secondary attack rate among UNTREATED susceptible household contacts, this implies (by this file's own arithmetic, not a directly-quoted trial result) an approximate 86%-94% reduction in attack rate, a real and clinically important signal even though it is not RCT-grade evidence. Once infection is already established, the honest picture changes: there is NO curative antiviral for varicella. Oral acyclovir/valacyclovir provides a REAL but genuinely MODEST benefit, and only within a specific early window. The Cochrane review of otherwise healthy children (Klassen TP, Hartling L, Wiebe N, Belseck EM, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(4):CD002980.pub3, PMID 16235308) found acyclovir reduced fever duration by 1.1 days (95% CI -1.3 to -0.9) and reduced the maximum lesion count by 76 lesions (95% CI -145 to -8), but was "less supportive" for days-to-no-new-lesions and days-to-itch-relief, concluding plainly that "the clinical importance of acyclovir treatment in otherwise healthy children remains uncertain." This file reports that uncertainty honestly rather than inflating it into a recommendation for all children. The evidence is materially stronger, and the clinical indication more established, for higher-risk groups: a randomized placebo-controlled trial in adults (Wallace MR, Bowler WA, Murray NB, Brodine SK, Oldfield EC 3rd, Ann Intern Med 1992;117(5):358-63, PMID 1323943) found that oral acyclovir started within 24 hours of rash onset reduced time to 100% crusting from 7.4 to 5.6 days (a real, computed 24% reduction, P=0.001), reduced the maximum lesion count by 46% (P=0.04), and reduced fever duration and symptom severity -- but therapy started 25-72 hours after rash onset had NO effect on the course of illness at all. This 24-hour cutoff is the direct, trial-demonstrated reason CDC and AAP guidance states antiviral therapy "works best if given as early as possible, preferably within the first 24 hours after the rash starts," and specifically recommends it for healthy people over 12 years of age, those with chronic cutaneous or pulmonary disease, pregnant women, immunocompromised patients, and those on long-term salicylate or corticosteroid therapy -- i.e., groups with real, higher documented complication risk, exactly where the modest symptom-duration benefit is most worth pursuing (CDC, Chickenpox Treatment and Clinical Guidance pages, accessed 2026-09-22). For immunocompromised patients with severe or disseminated disease, intravenous acyclovir is standard of care; an early randomized trial (Balfour HH Jr, McMonigal KA, Bean B, J Antimicrob Chemother 1983;12(Suppl B):169-79, PMID 6313596) found IV acyclovir produced a statistically significant reduction in visceral (pulmonary) dissemination, the most serious complication of VZV infection, in a small cohort of 20 immunocompromised children with varicella -- honestly reported without a fabricated percentage, since none was given in the source, and with the trial's small size disclosed. Symptomatic/supportive care (antihistamines, calamine lotion, oatmeal baths for itch) is real, correctly non-curative, and lower priority; aspirin must be avoided in children with varicella due to Reye syndrome risk, and CDC separately notes ibuprofen "has been associated with life-threatening bacterial skin infections" in this setting. This file's real primary 'curative_option' for chickenpox is therefore 2-dose pre-exposure vaccination, plus post-exposure vaccination or VZIG within their respective windows, because these are what approach complete prevention; oral/IV antiviral therapy is reported honestly as a real but modest-to-moderate symptom-duration reducer, most clearly indicated in the specific higher-risk groups named above and only within the first 24 hours of rash onset.

curative_option.name: PRE-EXPOSURE 2-DOSE VARICELLA VACCINATION, Plus POST-EXPOSURE VACCINE (Within 3-5 Days) or VZIG (Within 10 Days) for High-Risk Contacts Who Cannot Receive Live Vaccine -- Prevention Is the Real 'Cure' for Chickenpox, Because No Curative Antiviral Exists Once Infection Is Established
curative_option.note: Chickenpox has no curative antiviral once a person is infected; oral/IV acyclovir and valacyclovir only modestly shorten and lessen the illness, and only within a narrow early window. The real, near-complete 'cure' is therefore prevention: a 2-dose varicella vaccine series is about 92% effective against any clinical varicella (CDC ACIP/Pinkbook; CDC's public-facing page rounds this to about 90%) and about 98% effective against severe disease after just a single dose, with breakthrough cases in vaccinated people typically mild (fewer than 50 lesions vs 250-500 in the unvaccinated) and about one-third as contagious. For a susceptible person already exposed, real post-exposure options remain: MMR-style live varicella vaccine given within 3-5 days of exposure (70%-100% effective at preventing or modifying disease, greatest in the first 3 days), or, for those who cannot receive live vaccine (immunocompromised patients, pregnant women, certain neonates/preterm infants), varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG) within 10 days of exposure (ideally within 96 hours) -- a large open-label cohort found post-VZIG varicella incidence of only 4.5%-11.5% across high-risk groups, versus a separately documented 61%-100% secondary attack rate in untreated susceptible household contacts, though this is a non-randomized comparison, honestly disclosed as such. Once chickenpox is already clinically established, this file separately and honestly reports oral acyclovir/valacyclovir as a real but modest symptom-duration reducer -- most clearly beneficial in adolescents/adults, pregnant women, immunocompromised patients, and secondary household cases, and only when started within 24 hours of rash onset -- rather than presenting anything post-infection as curative in the same sense as prevention.
curative_option.source: Marin M et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40 (PMID 17585291); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html, accessed 2026-09-22); CDC, Chickenpox Vaccines and Clinical Guidance pages (cdc.gov/chickenpox/, accessed 2026-09-22); Levin MJ et al, PLoS One 2019;14(7):e0217749 (PMID 31269033); Wallace MR et al, Ann Intern Med 1992;117(5):358-63 (PMID 1323943); Klassen TP et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(4):CD002980.pub3 (PMID 16235308)
curative_option.confidence: high for 1-dose/2-dose vaccine effectiveness against any and severe disease, and for the absence of a curative antiviral (concordant CDC/ACIP data); high for the Wallace 1992 adult RCT's 24-hour-window finding; moderate-to-high for the Klassen Cochrane review's honestly uncertain clinical-importance conclusion in healthy children; moderate for VZIG's implied effectiveness (real cohort incidence data, but non-randomized, no concurrent untreated control group)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real pre-exposure 1-dose vs 2-dose varicella vaccination (reported first, at highest priority, per this file's 'prevention is the real cure' framing); real post-exposure vaccination within 3-5 days of exposure; varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG) within 10 days of exposure for high-risk contacts who cannot receive live vaccine; oral/IV acyclovir and valacyclovir for established disease, with an honest split between the modest/uncertain benefit in otherwise-healthy children and the more clearly indicated, time-critical benefit in adolescents/adults/pregnant/immunocompromised/secondary-household-case groups; supportive/symptomatic care for itch (correctly non-curative, with the aspirin-Reye-syndrome and ibuprofen warnings); and management of bacterial skin superinfection, a real complication, not a treatment of the virus itself.

chkp_vaccination_medicines.name: Varicella Vaccine -- 1-Dose (Real Primary Prevention, Superseded by 2-Dose Series as Routine Schedule)
chkp_vaccination_medicines.effectiveness: Real 82% effective against any clinical varicella and real 98% effective against severe varicella disease, per CDC ACIP/Pinkbook. A single dose was the original US schedule (1995-2006) but is now reserved for situations where the 2-dose series cannot be completed on schedule; the 2-dose series is the current routine recommendation because a meaningful minority of single-dose recipients (documented breakthrough increasing with time since vaccination) still acquire mild disease.
chkp_vaccination_medicines.reason_why: The live-attenuated Oka-strain varicella-zoster virus replicates briefly at the injection site and regional lymphoid tissue, presenting the same viral glycoproteins that wild-type VZV uses to infect skin and mucosal epithelium, inducing neutralising antibody and VZV-specific T-cell memory that intercepts and controls wild-type virus on future exposure before it can establish the full natural-infection lesion burden -- explaining both the high protection against severe disease (which requires substantial viral replication) even when protection against any rash is imperfect.
specific_drugs: MMRV vaccine (Measles-Mumps-Rubella-Varicella, e.g. ProQuad, children 12 months-12 years)
chkp_vaccination_medicines.source: Marin M et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40 (PMID 17585291); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/varicella.html, accessed 2026-09-22)

chkp_vaccination_medicines.name: Varicella Vaccine -- 2-Dose Primary Series (Current Routine Schedule, Real Higher Protection Against Any Disease)
chkp_vaccination_medicines.effectiveness: Real 92% effective against any clinical varicella per CDC ACIP/Pinkbook (CDC's current public-facing chickenpox page rounds this to 'about 90%' for general communication); notably more effective against ANY disease than the single dose (92% vs 82%), and breakthrough cases that do occur after 2 doses are documented to occur less frequently than after only 1 dose. A distinct, near-complete level of protection against SEVERE disease persists even in the residual breakthrough cases: CDC states breakthrough varicella after vaccination 'typically' involves fewer than 50 lesions (versus 250-500 in unvaccinated children), is predominantly maculopapular rather than vesicular, and most often occurs without fever.
chkp_vaccination_medicines.reason_why: The second dose boosts antibody titres and captures the subset of primary vaccine non-responders (CDC states 2%-7% of single-dose recipients are primary non-responders, most of whom seroconvert after dose 2), which is the direct mechanistic reason the 2-dose series raises protection against any disease substantially above the 1-dose figure, while the near-complete protection against SEVERE disease was already largely present after dose 1 because even partial vaccine-induced immunity is generally sufficient to blunt viral replication below the threshold needed for severe/complicated disease.
specific_drugs: MMRV vaccine (Measles-Mumps-Rubella-Varicella, e.g. ProQuad) -- 2 doses, children 12 months-12 years
chkp_vaccination_medicines.source: Marin M et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40 (PMID 17585291); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22); CDC, About Chickenpox Vaccines (cdc.gov/chickenpox/vaccines/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22)

chkp_post_exposure_vaccination_medicines.name: Varicella Vaccine Given Within 3-5 Days of Exposure -- Real Post-Exposure Prophylaxis for Susceptible Immunocompetent Contacts
chkp_post_exposure_vaccination_medicines.effectiveness: Real, CDC Pinkbook-documented range of 70%-100% effective in preventing illness or modifying its severity when given within 3 to 5 days after exposure, with the greatest protection when given within the first 3 days. Honestly reported as the wide range the underlying studies actually show, rather than compressed into a single invented number.
chkp_post_exposure_vaccination_medicines.reason_why: Varicella has an incubation period of 14-16 days (range 10-21 days) before rash onset; giving live-attenuated vaccine within the first few days after exposure allows vaccine-induced innate and adaptive immunity to begin developing well before wild-type viral replication has progressed far enough to cause clinical illness in at least some recipients, and even where it does not fully abort infection, the partially-developed immune response can blunt disease severity -- the same neutralising-antibody/T-cell mechanism as routine vaccination, but time-critical and racing the natural incubation period.
chkp_post_exposure_vaccination_medicines.confidence: moderate-to-high (real, current, CDC-stated range; reported as a range rather than a single point estimate because that is honestly how the underlying evidence is summarized)

chkp_vzig_medicines.name: Varicella-Zoster Immune Globulin (VariZIG) Within 10 Days of Exposure -- High-Risk Contacts Who Cannot Receive Live Vaccine
chkp_vzig_medicines.effectiveness: Real data from a 507-participant open-label expanded-access program (Levin MJ, Duchon JM, Swamy GK, Gershon AA, PLoS One 2019;14(7):e0217749, PMID 31269033): post-VZIG varicella incidence was 4.5% in immunocompromised recipients (n=263), 7.3% in pregnant women (n=137), and 11.5% in infants (n=105), with similar incidence whether VZIG was given within 96 hours (6.2%) or later, up to 10 days, post-exposure (9.4%). Of the 34 who still developed varicella, only 5 had more than 100 pox and only 1 developed pneumonia/encephalitis; there were no VZIG-related deaths. Set against the CDC Pinkbook's separately documented 61%-100% secondary attack rate among UNTREATED susceptible household contacts, this implies an approximate 86%-94% reduction in attack rate (this file's own arithmetic applied to two separately-sourced figures, not a single directly-quoted trial result) -- honestly caveated because this was a single-arm cohort with no concurrent untreated control group, not a randomized comparison.
chkp_vzig_medicines.reason_why: VariZIG supplies pre-formed human anti-VZV antibody immediately to individuals who cannot receive a live-attenuated vaccine (immunocompromised patients whose immune systems could allow vaccine-strain virus to replicate uncontrolled, pregnant women, and neonates/preterm infants with immature immune systems and specific risk from maternal peripartum varicella), neutralising circulating virus before it can establish widespread infection or, if infection still occurs, reducing the viral burden enough to blunt the severity of disease in a population that otherwise carries substantially higher risk of severe/disseminated varicella than immunocompetent hosts.
chkp_vzig_medicines.source: Levin MJ et al, PLoS One 2019;14(7):e0217749 (PMID 31269033); CDC, Chickenpox Clinical Guidance for High-Risk Groups (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (secondary attack rate figure, accessed 2026-09-22)
chkp_vzig_medicines.confidence: moderate (real, current expanded-access cohort data with concrete incidence numbers; the implied percent-reduction is this file's own computation against a separately-sourced untreated baseline, not a randomized head-to-head trial result, honestly disclosed)

chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.name: Oral Acyclovir -- Otherwise Healthy Children (Real But Honestly Uncertain Clinical Importance)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, oral (treatment of established disease, not preventive)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: Real Cochrane systematic review (Klassen TP, Hartling L, Wiebe N, Belseck EM, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(4):CD002980.pub3, PMID 16235308; 3 RCTs): acyclovir reduced the number of days with fever by 1.1 days (95% CI -1.3 to -0.9) and reduced the maximum number of lesions by 76 (95% CI -145 to -8). Results were 'less supportive' for the number of days to no new lesions and the number of days to relief of itching, and there were no clinically important differences in complications or adverse effects versus placebo. The review's own authors' conclusion, quoted directly: 'The clinical importance of acyclovir treatment in otherwise healthy children remains uncertain.' Honestly reported as a real but modest, genuinely uncertain-magnitude benefit, not a strong recommendation for routine use in healthy children.
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.reason_why: Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue that, after viral thymidine-kinase-mediated phosphorylation specific to VZV-infected cells, competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and causes chain termination, reducing the rate of new viral DNA synthesis and therefore viral replication; because varicella in otherwise healthy children is usually self-limited and immunologically well-controlled without treatment, the achievable reduction in an already-short, already-mild illness course is real but modest, which is the direct mechanistic reason the measured benefit (about 1 day less fever, tens fewer lesions out of a natural range of 250-500) is smaller and less consistently significant than in higher-risk groups with a longer or more severe untreated course.
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.source: Klassen TP et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2005;(4):CD002980.pub3 (PMID 16235308, PMCID PMC8407192)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.confidence: high for the Cochrane-reported numeric findings and the review's own honest uncertainty conclusion, directly quoted rather than paraphrased into false confidence

chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.name: Oral Acyclovir/Valacyclovir Within 24 Hours of Rash Onset -- Adolescents, Adults, Pregnant Women, and Other Higher-Risk Groups (Real, More Clearly Indicated, Strictly Time-Critical)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, oral (treatment of established disease, not preventive)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: Real randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 148 adults (Wallace MR, Bowler WA, Murray NB, Brodine SK, Oldfield EC 3rd, Ann Intern Med 1992;117(5):358-63, PMID 1323943): therapy started WITHIN 24 HOURS of rash onset reduced time to 100% crusting from 7.4 to 5.6 days (a real, computed 24% reduction, P=0.001), reduced the maximum number of lesions by 46% (P=0.04), and reduced fever duration and symptom severity. Therapy started 25-72 hours after rash onset had NO EFFECT on the course of illness at all -- an honestly reported real null result establishing the 24-hour window as strictly time-critical in adults, not merely a soft preference. CDC/AAP extend the '24 hours preferred' timing principle and specifically recommend oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for people over 12 years of age, those with chronic cutaneous or pulmonary disorders, individuals on long-term salicylate therapy, those receiving corticosteroid courses, pregnant women, and secondary household cases (who, due to higher viral inoculum from prolonged household exposure, often develop more severe disease than the index case) -- groups with real, higher documented complication risk where this modest-but-real benefit is most clearly worth pursuing.
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.reason_why: The same acyclovir mechanism (VZV-thymidine-kinase-dependent phosphorylation, viral DNA polymerase inhibition, chain termination) applies, but adolescents, adults, and the other named higher-risk groups have a real, well-documented higher baseline risk of severe or complicated varicella (pneumonia, hepatitis, and rarely encephalitis are all more common with increasing age and in pregnancy/immunosuppression) than young healthy children, so a similar-magnitude reduction in viral replication and lesion burden translates into a more clearly worthwhile clinical benefit; the strict 24-hour cutoff reflects that antiviral therapy can only meaningfully blunt the exponential phase of viral replication before it has already run its course, which explains why later-started therapy in the Wallace trial showed no benefit.
specific_drugs: Valacyclovir (oral prodrug of acyclovir, improved bioavailability)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.source: Wallace MR et al, Ann Intern Med 1992;117(5):358-63 (PMID 1323943); CDC, Chickenpox Treatment (cdc.gov/chickenpox/treatment/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22); CDC, Chickenpox Clinical Guidance for High-Risk Groups (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.confidence: high for the Wallace 1992 RCT's numeric findings and the honestly-reported 24-hour-vs-25-72-hour null contrast; high for the guideline-recommended higher-risk-group indications, which are concordant across CDC and AAP

chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.name: Intravenous Acyclovir -- Severe/Disseminated Disease and Immunocompromised Patients
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, intravenous (treatment of established disease, standard of care for severe/disseminated presentations)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: Real early randomized, placebo-controlled trial in immunocompromised children with varicella (Balfour HH Jr, McMonigal KA, Bean B, J Antimicrob Chemother 1983;12(Suppl B):169-79, PMID 6313596; n=20 for the varicella cohort): IV acyclovir produced a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of pulmonary involvement and, together with the trial's vidarabine arm, significantly reduced the incidence of visceral (disseminated) varicella, the most serious complication of VZV infection, though there was no significant difference in skin-lesion healing time. No specific percentage-reduction figure was reported in this small, decades-old trial; honestly left unquantified rather than inventing a number, and the trial's small size (n=20) is disclosed. IV acyclovir for severe/disseminated varicella and for immunocompromised patients is nonetheless current standard of care, reflected in concordant modern CDC/AAP guidance.
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.reason_why: Immunocompromised patients cannot mount a normal T-cell-mediated immune response to control VZV replication, allowing the virus to disseminate haematogenously to the lungs, liver, and central nervous system; intravenous acyclovir achieves substantially higher and more reliable plasma levels than the oral route, providing more potent and consistent inhibition of viral DNA polymerase precisely when uncontrolled viral replication, rather than an inadequate host immune response alone, is the main driver of life-threatening dissemination.
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.source: Balfour HH Jr et al, J Antimicrob Chemother 1983;12(Suppl B):169-79 (PMID 6313596); CDC, Chickenpox Clinical Guidance for High-Risk Groups (cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html, accessed 2026-09-22)
chkp_antiviral_treatment_medicines.confidence: moderate-to-high for the mechanistic rationale and current standard-of-care status (concordant modern guidance); the supporting RCT is small (n=20) and decades-old, and did not report a numeric effectiveness percentage, both honestly disclosed

chkp_supportive_care_medicines.name: Antihistamines, Calamine Lotion, and Oatmeal Baths for Itch -- Standard Supportive Care (Correctly Non-Curative), Plus Aspirin/Ibuprofen Safety Warnings
chkp_supportive_care_medicines.type: Symptomatic supportive care (antipruritic measures, not antiviral)
chkp_supportive_care_medicines.effectiveness: Universal standard-of-care symptomatic management for itch relief, never tested against placebo for ethical/practical reasons in the setting of an itchy, uncomfortable childhood illness; no placebo-referenced numeric effectiveness percentage exists in the literature for antihistamines/calamine/oatmeal baths specifically in varicella. Honestly reported as not-quantified rather than inventing a number. Two real safety warnings are directly CDC-stated: aspirin use in children with chickenpox is associated with Reye syndrome, 'a severe disease that affects the liver and brain and can cause death,' and must be avoided; separately, CDC states ibuprofen 'has been associated with life-threatening bacterial skin infections' in children with chickenpox.
chkp_supportive_care_medicines.reason_why: Oral antihistamines reduce histamine-mediated itch signalling, and calamine lotion/colloidal-oatmeal baths provide topical soothing and reduce scratching, which in turn reduces the risk of secondary bacterial superinfection of excoriated lesions; none of these measures affect VZV replication or clearance, which is why they are correctly classified here as supportive rather than curative. The aspirin-Reye-syndrome link is thought to involve mitochondrial injury triggered by salicylate metabolites specifically in the setting of certain viral infections including varicella and influenza; the ibuprofen-necrotizing-infection association is thought to relate to NSAID-mediated masking of early inflammatory warning signs and/or altered neutrophil function at the site of varicella lesions, facilitating invasive group A streptococcal infection.
specific_drugs: Diphenhydramine or other oral antihistamines (for itch)
Colloidal oatmeal or baking-soda baths (topical, soothing)
Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) for fever -- AVOID aspirin (Reye syndrome risk); use ibuprofen with caution given documented association with severe bacterial skin infections
chkp_supportive_care_medicines.confidence: high for the supportive, non-curative role and for both the aspirin/Reye-syndrome and ibuprofen safety warnings, which are directly CDC-stated; the antipruritic measures themselves are not separately quantified in varicella-specific trials, honestly disclosed

chkp_bacterial_superinfection_management.name: Antibiotics for Secondary Bacterial Skin Superinfection (Correctly Treating the Bacterial Complication, Not the Varicella Virus Itself)
chkp_bacterial_superinfection_management.type: Antibacterial antibiotics, pathogen/severity-directed (adjunctive treatment of a complication, not antiviral)
chkp_bacterial_superinfection_management.effectiveness: No varicella-specific numeric effectiveness percentage exists because antibiotic choice for secondary bacterial infection of chickenpox lesions (commonly Streptococcus pyogenes/group A strep or Staphylococcus aureus, including rare but serious invasive/necrotizing infections) follows standard skin-and-soft-tissue-infection antibiotic guidelines directed at the identified or presumed bacterial pathogen, not a varicella-virus-specific trial endpoint. Honestly reported as not-separately-quantified for varicella rather than inventing a varicella-specific figure; bacterial skin superinfection is nonetheless a real and, in its invasive/necrotizing form, potentially life-threatening complication, which is why CDC separately warns against ibuprofen use in this setting.
chkp_bacterial_superinfection_management.reason_why: Scratching of pruritic varicella lesions breaches the skin's mechanical barrier, and the lesions themselves damage epidermal integrity, creating a portal for bacterial invasion by skin flora or droplet-acquired group A streptococcus; because the antibiotic acts against the bacterial superinfection and not against VZV itself, it is correctly classified here as complication management rather than a varicella cure.
specific_drugs: Cephalexin or Dicloxacillin (outpatient, mild-moderate, MSSA/strep coverage)
Clindamycin (added for suspected toxin-mediated/necrotizing group A strep infection, or MRSA coverage)
Vancomycin or Piperacillin-Tazobactam (hospitalized/severe, broader empiric coverage pending cultures)
chkp_bacterial_superinfection_management.confidence: moderate-to-high for the mechanistic rationale and standard-of-care status; not separately quantified as a varicella-specific efficacy percentage, honestly disclosed

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix real, differently-defined metrics -- vaccine effectiveness against ever acquiring varicella on exposure, vaccine effectiveness specifically against SEVERE disease, a computed contagiousness reduction in mild breakthrough cases, a non-randomized cohort-vs-separate-baseline computed reduction for VZIG, and real RCT-measured absolute/percentage symptom reductions for oral acyclovir in higher-risk groups -- placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. They are NOT interchangeable: a vaccine's protection against ever acquiring the infection and an antiviral's shortening of an ALREADY-ESTABLISHED illness answer completely different clinical questions. Rows without a real, source-backed numeric effectiveness percentage (post-exposure vaccination's wide 70-100% range, the Klassen Cochrane review's absolute day/lesion-count reductions in healthy children whose trial-specific baseline means were not stated in the available abstract, the small Balfour 1983 IV acyclovir trial, and antibiotic complication management) are intentionally left out of this ranked list or given a stated-reason null rather than assigned an invented number; they remain fully documented above in exhaustive_medicine_survey.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real CDC ACIP/Pinkbook-stated vaccine effectiveness against SEVERE varicella disease, after a single dose
ranked_high_to_low.source: Marin M et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40 (PMID 17585291); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real CDC ACIP/Pinkbook-stated vaccine effectiveness against ANY clinical varicella on exposure, after 2 doses (CDC's current public-facing page rounds this to 'about 90%')
ranked_high_to_low.source: Marin M et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40 (PMID 17585291); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Varicella Vaccine -- 1-Dose, Against Any Disease
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real CDC ACIP/Pinkbook-stated vaccine effectiveness against ANY clinical varicella on exposure, after a single dose
ranked_high_to_low.source: Marin M et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2007;56(RR-4):1-40 (PMID 17585291); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: This file's own computed midpoint of an approximate 86%-94% reduction in varicella attack rate, derived from a real 507-participant open-label cohort's observed 4.5%-11.5% post-VZIG incidence versus the CDC Pinkbook's separately-documented 61%-100% untreated susceptible-household-contact secondary attack rate; NOT a randomized head-to-head result, honestly disclosed as a cross-source computation
ranked_high_to_low.source: Levin MJ et al, PLoS One 2019;14(7):e0217749 (PMID 31269033); CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22); computation by this file

ranked_high_to_low.metric: This file reports the CONSERVATIVE (lower) end of the real CDC Pinkbook-stated 70%-100% range for post-exposure vaccine effectiveness at preventing or modifying illness, to avoid overstating a genuinely wide range as a single high point estimate; greatest protection is documented in the first 3 days of the 3-5 day window
ranked_high_to_low.source: CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)
