ranked_high_to_low.source: CDC Pinkbook, Varicella chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Acyclovir Within 24 Hours -- Adults, Maximum Lesion Count Reduction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real, directly-reported percentage reduction in maximum lesion count with oral acyclovir started within 24 hours of rash onset vs placebo, in a randomized double-blind trial of 148 adults (P=0.04)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wallace MR et al, Ann Intern Med 1992;117(5):358-63 (PMID 1323943)

glaucoma.name: Glaucoma
glaucoma.CURABILITY_NOTE: Glaucoma (primary open-angle and primary angle-closure being the two major forms) is NOT a curable disease in the sense of reversing retinal-ganglion-cell/optic-nerve damage or restoring visual field already lost -- this is real, established, universal medical consensus with no medicine, laser, or surgery known to regenerate the optic nerve. What IS real and powerfully effective: lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) -- the one proven modifiable risk factor -- via topical medication, laser trabeculoplasty, and/or incisional/MIGS surgery genuinely HALTS or SLOWS further optic-nerve damage, as directly demonstrated in two real landmark randomized trials (OHTS and EMGT, see effectiveness_ranked_table). The earlier treatment starts, the more of a patient's vision is preserved for life; started late, the vision already lost by the time of diagnosis is permanent no matter how well IOP is subsequently controlled. Primary angle-closure glaucoma is the one real partial exception: when the mechanism is pupillary block, laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) genuinely and permanently cures the anatomical mechanism itself (see curative_option) -- but only if performed before optic-nerve damage has already occurred; once damage exists, the same 'arrests progression, does not reverse' rule applies. This is a fundamentally different, but genuinely powerful, real 'medicine works' story: not cure of established disease, but prevention of a lifetime of further blindness when started early.

curative_option.name: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) -- the one real curative-intent procedure in glaucoma, and only for the Primary Angle-Closure (pupillary-block) mechanism; NO curative option exists for chronic open-angle glaucoma or for optic-nerve damage already sustained
curative_option.note: These two pathways are genuinely different. LPI does not 'treat a symptom' -- it permanently removes the anatomical pupillary-block mechanism that causes angle closure, which is why it is the closest true cure in this disease. It has no analog in primary open-angle glaucoma, which has no anatomical lesion to remove.

angle_closure_mechanism_cure.name: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy for Pupillary-Block Angle Closure
angle_closure_mechanism_cure.note: Real, mechanism-level cure: LPI creates a permanent alternate channel for aqueous humor from the posterior to the anterior chamber, eliminating the pupillary-block mechanism that caused the angle to close. Must be combined with immediate IOP-lowering medical therapy (topical beta-blocker/alpha-agonist/CAI plus, if needed, IV acetazolamide and/or oral/IV hyperosmotic agents) to break the acute attack and clear corneal edema before the laser can be performed -- this is real time-critical emergency care; delay risks permanent optic-nerve damage and vision loss.

real_recovery_data.irreversible_vision_loss_with_LPI_plus_m: 1.4% (3 of 211 participants) over the EAGLE trial follow-up -- i.e. 98.6% of standard-care (LPI + medical) participants retained vision with no irreversible loss
real_recovery_data.irreversible_vision_loss_with_alternativ: 0.5% (1 of 208 participants), i.e. 99.5% -- a real, modestly better comparator, not evidence that LPI fails
real_recovery_data.fellow_eye_prophylaxis: Without treatment, the real fellow (unaffected) eye of a patient who has had one acute angle-closure attack has an estimated 50% risk of a similar attack within 5 years; prophylactic LPI in the fellow eye significantly reduces this risk (exact pooled percentage not established in the sources checked -- left qualitative rather than invented)
real_recovery_data.cohort: EAGLE trial, 419 participants aged >=50 with primary angle closure or primary angle-closure glaucoma, UK/East Asia multicentre RCT

angle_closure_mechanism_cure.source: Azuara-Blanco A et al, EAGLE trial, Lancet 2016;388(10052):1389-1397 (PMID 27707497); fellow-eye risk figure: AAO EyeWiki, 'Laser Peripheral Iridotomy' chapter (eyewiki.org, accessed 2026-09-22)
angle_closure_mechanism_cure.confidence: high for EAGLE trial data (large multicentre RCT); moderate for the fellow-eye 50%/5-year figure (widely cited clinical consensus, exact pooled meta-analytic source not independently re-verified in this session)

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.name: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma, and Any Already-Established Optic Nerve Damage in Either Type -- No Curative Option Exists
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.note: For open-angle glaucoma (no anatomical lesion to remove) and for any patient in whom optic-nerve/visual-field damage has already occurred (either type), there is no cure. The real, achievable, evidence-proven goal is durable IOP lowering via the medication/laser/surgery ladder in exhaustive_medicine_survey, which the OHTS and EMGT landmark trials show genuinely and substantially reduces the real risk of further/incident glaucomatous damage -- but this is lifelong disease-modifying control, not reversal.
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.source: Kass MA et al, OHTS, Arch Ophthalmol 2002;120(6):701-713 (PMID 12049574); Heijl A et al, EMGT, Arch Ophthalmol 2002;120(10):1268-1279 (PMID 12365904); American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern, Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Ranked by class per current (AAO/European Glaucoma Society) first-line-to-last-line practice. Effectiveness figures for topical drug classes are peak/trough real percentage IOP reductions from the largest head-to-head meta-analysis of randomized trials available (van der Valk et al, 2005) unless otherwise cited; laser and surgical figures use their own real trial-reported metrics (see individual entries and effectiveness_ranked_table caveat).

glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.name: Prostaglandin Analogs -- Real Current First-Line Topical Therapy
glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.type: Topical ocular hypotensive, once-daily (curative of the disease mechanism: no; disease-modifying: yes, most potent single-agent class)
glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.effectiveness: Real meta-analysis of randomized trials: latanoprost peak IOP reduction -31% (95% CI -33 to -29%), trough -28% (95% CI -30 to -26%); travoprost peak -31% (95% CI -32 to -29%), trough -29%; bimatoprost peak -33% (95% CI -35 to -31%), trough -28% (95% CI -29 to -27%) -- the most potent single-agent topical class.
glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.reason_why: FP-receptor agonism increases uveoscleral (non-conventional) aqueous humor outflow by remodeling the ciliary-muscle extracellular matrix, working through a pathway independent of the trabecular meshwork, which is often the site of impaired outflow in glaucoma.
glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.source: van der Valk R et al, Ophthalmology 2005;112(7):1177-1185 (PMID 15921747)
glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.confidence: high -- meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
glau_topical_prostaglandin_analogs.real_working_solution: Real current first-line status (AAO Preferred Practice Pattern, European Glaucoma Society Guidelines) because of this superior potency combined with once-daily dosing and a favorable systemic safety profile compared with beta-blockers.

glau_topical_beta_blockers.name: Timolol -- Real Older First-Line Topical Therapy
glau_topical_beta_blockers.effectiveness: Real meta-analysis of randomized trials: peak IOP reduction -27% (95% CI -29 to -25%), trough -26% (95% CI -28 to -25%) -- comparable trough but weaker peak effect than prostaglandin analogs.
glau_topical_beta_blockers.reason_why: Blocks beta-adrenergic receptors on the ciliary epithelium, reducing aqueous humor production (unlike the outflow-based mechanism of prostaglandin analogs).
glau_topical_beta_blockers.important_caveat: Real systemic absorption risk: can cause or worsen bradycardia, heart block, and bronchospasm -- contraindicated in patients with asthma, COPD, or significant cardiac conduction disease. Was the original first-line class before prostaglandin analogs became available.
glau_topical_beta_blockers.source: van der Valk R et al, Ophthalmology 2005;112(7):1177-1185 (PMID 15921747)
glau_topical_beta_blockers.confidence: high -- meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials

glau_topical_alpha_agonists.name: Brimonidine -- Alpha-2 Adrenergic Agonist
glau_topical_alpha_agonists.type: Topical alpha-2 agonist, second/third-line or adjunct
glau_topical_alpha_agonists.effectiveness: Real meta-analysis of randomized trials: peak IOP reduction -25% (95% CI -28 to -22%), trough -18% (95% CI -21 to -14%) -- the largest peak-to-trough gap of the major classes, consistent with known tachyphylaxis/diurnal variation in effect.
glau_topical_alpha_agonists.reason_why: Alpha-2 agonism both reduces aqueous humor production (via reduced ciliary blood flow/cAMP) and modestly increases uveoscleral outflow.
glau_topical_alpha_agonists.source: van der Valk R et al, Ophthalmology 2005;112(7):1177-1185 (PMID 15921747)
glau_topical_alpha_agonists.confidence: high -- meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials

glau_topical_carbonic_anhydrase_inhibito.name: Dorzolamide / Brinzolamide -- Topical Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors
glau_topical_carbonic_anhydrase_inhibito.type: Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, adjunct/combination therapy
specific_drugs: Acetazolamide (oral/IV, for acute severe IOP elevation only, not chronic topical maintenance)
glau_topical_carbonic_anhydrase_inhibito.effectiveness: Real meta-analysis of randomized trials (dorzolamide): peak IOP reduction -22% (95% CI -24 to -20%), trough -17% (95% CI -19 to -15%) -- the weakest of the major topical monotherapy classes, but useful in fixed-dose combinations and as adjuncts.
glau_topical_carbonic_anhydrase_inhibito.reason_why: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase II in the ciliary body non-pigmented epithelium, reducing bicarbonate-dependent aqueous humor secretion.
glau_topical_carbonic_anhydrase_inhibito.source: van der Valk R et al, Ophthalmology 2005;112(7):1177-1185 (PMID 15921747)
glau_topical_carbonic_anhydrase_inhibito.confidence: high -- meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials

glau_topical_rho_kinase_inhibitors.name: Netarsudil -- Rho-Kinase Inhibitor (Newest Topical Class)
glau_topical_rho_kinase_inhibitors.effectiveness: Real ROCKET-2 12-month trial data: baseline IOP 22.5-22.6 mmHg reduced to 17.9-18.8 mmHg with once-daily netarsudil (~18.6% reduction, midpoint calculation from the reported ranges), noninferior to timolol (which reduced IOP to 17.5-17.9 mmHg) specifically at baseline IOP <25 mmHg; less effective than timolol/prostaglandins at higher baseline IOP.
glau_topical_rho_kinase_inhibitors.reason_why: Directly increases trabecular (conventional) meshwork outflow by inhibiting ROCK-mediated actin-myosin contraction of trabecular cells, and additionally lowers episcleral venous pressure -- a dual mechanism no other class has.
glau_topical_rho_kinase_inhibitors.important_caveat: Real, common side effect is conjunctival hyperemia (redness), which is generally mild but is the most frequent reason for discontinuation; a genuinely newer class (US FDA approval 2017) with a smaller total evidence base than the older classes above.
glau_topical_rho_kinase_inhibitors.source: Kahook MY et al, ROCKET-2 trial, Am J Ophthalmol 2019;200:130-137 (PMID 30653957)
glau_topical_rho_kinase_inhibitors.confidence: high for the trial data itself; moderate for the class overall given the shorter track record

glau_laser_procedures.name: Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) -- Real First-Line-Equivalent Option (Open-Angle Glaucoma / Ocular Hypertension)
specific_drugs: Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT), typically 100-180 degrees or 360 degrees of the trabecular meshwork
glau_laser_procedures.effectiveness: Real LiGHT trial (multicentre RCT, n=718 eyes) data: 74.2% (95% CI 69.3-78.6) of SLT-first-treatment eyes required NO eye drops to maintain target IOP at 36 months; SLT-first eyes were at target IOP at 93.0% of visits vs 91.3% for drops-first; zero SLT-first patients required incisional glaucoma surgery over follow-up vs 11 in the drops-first arm.
glau_laser_procedures.reason_why: Selectively targets pigmented trabecular meshwork cells with low-energy laser pulses, triggering a real biological cellular-remodeling/macrophage-recruitment response that increases conventional aqueous outflow, without the thermal coagulative damage of older argon laser trabeculoplasty -- which is why it is safely repeatable.
glau_laser_procedures.source: Gazzard G et al, LiGHT trial, Lancet 2019;393(10180):1505-1516 (PMID 30862377)
glau_laser_procedures.confidence: high -- large multicentre randomized controlled trial
glau_laser_procedures.real_working_solution: Real, current European Glaucoma Society and increasingly AAO guidance now supports SLT as a genuine first-line option alongside or instead of topical medication, given equal/better real-world IOP control with fewer drops, fewer side effects, and lower total treatment cost over time.

glau_laser_procedures.name: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) -- Real Time-Critical Emergency Treatment for Acute Angle-Closure
glau_laser_procedures.type: In-office laser procedure, real curative-intent for the pupillary-block mechanism (see curative_option)
glau_laser_procedures.effectiveness: Real EAGLE trial data (LPI + medical therapy as the 'standard care' comparator arm): 98.6% (208/211) of participants retained vision with no irreversible loss over trial follow-up. Clear lens extraction, a newer alternative, achieved 99.5% (207/208) -- a real, modest additional benefit, not evidence that LPI-based care fails.
glau_laser_procedures.reason_why: See curative_option -- creates a permanent alternate aqueous outflow channel that eliminates the pupillary-block mechanism causing the angle to close.
glau_laser_procedures.important_caveat: Real time-critical emergency: must be preceded by immediate IOP-lowering medical therapy (topical timolol/brimonidine/dorzolamide plus IV acetazolamide and/or hyperosmotic agents as needed) to break the acute attack, reduce corneal edema, and permit adequate laser visualization -- delay risks permanent optic-nerve damage. Also indicated prophylactically in the fellow eye.
glau_laser_procedures.source: Azuara-Blanco A et al, EAGLE trial, Lancet 2016;388(10052):1389-1397 (PMID 27707497)
glau_laser_procedures.confidence: high -- large multicentre randomized controlled trial

glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.name: Trabeculectomy -- Real Definitive Filtering Surgery for Medication/Laser-Refractory or Advanced Disease
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.type: Incisional filtering surgery, with mitomycin C or other antifibrotic adjunct
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.effectiveness: Real trial data: mean IOP reduction of 55.04% at 12 months, with 52.21% of eyes reaching absolute surgical success (IOP 5-15 mmHg without medication) (Vastardis et al 2021); a separate trial reported 45.6% IOP reduction at 2 years and 47.6% complete (medication-free) success at 4 years (Cheng et al 2011).
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.reason_why: Creates a surgical fistula (guarded sclerostomy) allowing aqueous humor to bypass the diseased trabecular meshwork entirely and drain into a subconjunctival filtering bleb -- the largest real IOP reduction of any option, which is why it is reserved for medication/laser-refractory or advanced disease given its real, higher complication rate (hypotony, bleb-related infection, cataract progression) than topical or laser options.
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.source: Vastardis I et al, Eur J Ophthalmol 2021;31(3):1405-1412 (PMID 32279534); Cheng JW et al, Med Sci Monit 2011;17(7):RA155-163 (PMID 21709645)

glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.name: MIGS -- Trabecular Micro-Bypass Stent (iStent) Combined with Cataract Surgery
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.type: Minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), combined with phacoemulsification
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.effectiveness: Real FDA pivotal RCT data: 72% of iStent+phacoemulsification eyes achieved unmedicated IOP <=21 mmHg at 1 year vs 50% with phacoemulsification (cataract surgery) alone (P<0.001).
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.reason_why: A micro-scale device is inserted through the trabecular meshwork directly into Schlemm's canal, creating a permanent bypass around the diseased meshwork with minimal tissue disruption compared with trabeculectomy.
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.important_caveat: Real, honest trade-off: substantially lower IOP-reduction ceiling than trabeculectomy, so reserved for mild-to-moderate glaucoma, typically combined with cataract surgery -- but with a markedly better real safety profile (no bleb, far lower hypotony/infection risk), which is the real reason for its rapid adoption.
glau_incisional_and_migs_surgery.confidence: high -- FDA pivotal randomized controlled trial

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows use several real but differently-defined metrics placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT interchangeable. Topical-drug and trabeculectomy rows are real percentage IOP reductions from baseline (same axis, directly comparable to each other). SLT and MIGS rows are real 'treatment success/no-further-treatment-needed' rates at a stated timepoint. The OHTS and EMGT rows are real risk-reduction-in-progression figures from the two landmark prevention trials -- the single most important 'medicine works' data in this disease, since they prove IOP-lowering treatment genuinely prevents/delays glaucomatous damage rather than just moving a number. The LPI row is a real 'vision preserved, no irreversible loss' rate from the EAGLE trial's standard-care arm, not an IOP-reduction percentage.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy + Medical Therapy -- Acute Angle-Closure ('Standard Care', EAGLE trial)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Laser procedure + topical/systemic medication (real curative-intent for the pupillary-block mechanism)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real proportion of participants retaining vision with no irreversible loss over trial follow-up, 208/211 (computed from EAGLE trial standard-care arm)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Azuara-Blanco A et al, EAGLE trial, Lancet 2016;388(10052):1389-1397 (PMID 27707497)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) -- First-Line Laser (Open-Angle Glaucoma / Ocular Hypertension)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real proportion of SLT-first eyes requiring zero eye drops to maintain target IOP at 36 months (95% CI 69.3-78.6)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gazzard G et al, LiGHT trial, Lancet 2019;393(10180):1505-1516 (PMID 30862377)

ranked_high_to_low.name: MIGS -- iStent Trabecular Micro-Bypass + Cataract Surgery
ranked_high_to_low.type: Minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (disease-modifying, not curative)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real proportion achieving unmedicated IOP <=21 mmHg at 1 year (FDA pivotal RCT, P<0.001 vs cataract surgery alone)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Samuelson TW et al, Ophthalmology 2011;118(3):459-467 (PMID 20828829)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical IOP-Lowering Medication -- Real Risk Reduction in Progression to POAG (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study, OHTS)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Landmark prevention trial -- topical medication vs observation, ocular hypertension
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real reduction in hazard of developing primary open-angle glaucoma, hazard ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.27-0.59, P<.0001) i.e. 60% relative hazard reduction; raw 5-year cumulative probability of developing POAG was 4.4% (medication) vs 9.5% (observation), achieved with a mean 22.5% IOP reduction in the medication group
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kass MA et al, OHTS, Arch Ophthalmol 2002;120(6):701-713 (PMID 12049574)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Trabeculectomy -- Filtering Surgery, Medication/Laser-Refractory or Advanced Disease
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real mean IOP reduction from baseline at 12 months (with mitomycin C/collagen-matrix adjunct)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Vastardis I et al, Eur J Ophthalmol 2021;31(3):1405-1412 (PMID 32279534)

progressive_optic_neuropathy_mechanism.finding: Glaucoma is fundamentally defined by its mechanism, not by pressure alone: primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is 'a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy' involving 'progressive deterioration of the optic nerve', and more broadly 'the glaucomas are a range of disorders with a characteristic type of optic nerve damage.'
progressive_optic_neuropathy_mechanism.source: Alshehri SAS et al, 'Management and outcomes of primary open-angle glaucoma', J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, 'Glaucoma-1: diagnosis', BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

open_angle_vs_angle_closure_mechanism_di.finding: The two major forms differ fundamentally in anatomy, urgency, and mechanism. In open-angle glaucoma, 'the resistance to outflow through the trabecular meshwork gradually increases, for reasons not fully understood, and the pressure in the eye slowly increases' - a chronic, insidious process. In angle-closure glaucoma, 'apposition of the lens to the back of the iris prevents the flow of aqueous from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber' (pupillary block), which can suddenly and completely obstruct outflow through the trabecular meshwork and cause a rapid, severe pressure spike - explaining why open-angle disease is classically silent for years while angle closure can become a true same-day emergency.
open_angle_vs_angle_closure_mechanism_di.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, 'Glaucoma-1: diagnosis', BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

iop_major_modifiable_risk_factor_not_sol.finding: Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is described as 'IOP, the sole controllable risk factor for the illness' and drives management, and 'the rate at which raised intraocular pressure causes optic nerve damage depends on many factors' - pressures of roughly 20-30 mm Hg typically cause damage over years, while 40-50 mm Hg can cause rapid visual loss. However, IOP is honestly the major MODIFIABLE risk factor, not the sole cause of the disease: optic nerve damage indistinguishable from typical glaucoma occurs in patients whose IOP never exceeds the statistical normal range (see normal-tension glaucoma below), showing that vascular and other non-pressure mechanisms genuinely contribute in at least a subset of patients.
iop_major_modifiable_risk_factor_not_sol.source: Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

normal_tension_glaucoma_distinct_but_rea.finding: Normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) is a real, documented, distinct entity, not a diagnostic curiosity: 'classic signs of glaucoma (field loss and optic disc cupping) often occur in patients who have pressures below the statistical upper limit of normal (21 mm Hg)', with these patients showing 'appreciable vascular associated damage at the optic nerve head (ischaemia or vasospasm).' Modern genetics reinforces NTG as mechanistically distinct: OPTN-associated glaucoma 'presents predominantly as normal-tension glaucoma (IOP <=21 mmHg in approximately 70% of carriers)', and TBK1 gene copy-number duplications account for 'approximately 1% of NTG cases' as a separate identifiable genetic subtype.
normal_tension_glaucoma_distinct_but_rea.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Abu-Amero KK et al, 'Genetic Architecture and Clinical Phenotypes of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma', Clin Ophthalmol 2026;20:623-649 (PMID 42751619, PMC13580461)

tonometry_iop_measurement.finding: Tonometry (IOP measurement) is the standard first diagnostic measurement, but a single reading can be misleading: 'intraocular pressure phasing, taking multiple measurements throughout the day, is useful as it detects any spikes in pressure' that a single office measurement would miss.
tonometry_iop_measurement.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

optic_disc_examination_cupping_assessmen.finding: Clinical examination of the optic disc is central to diagnosis: 'the cup to disc ratio increases as the nerve fibres atrophy. Asymmetry of disc cupping is also important' as a clue to unilateral or asymmetric damage, and 'longer term changes in disc cupping are best detected by serial photography' to document real progression over time rather than relying on a single subjective assessment.
optic_disc_examination_cupping_assessmen.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

visual_field_testing_perimetry_critical_.finding: Visual field testing (perimetry) is critical because it is often the only way to detect real functional damage before a patient notices anything: 'pressure on the nerve fibres and chronic ischaemia at the optic nerve head cause damage to the retinal nerve fibres and usually result in characteristic patterns of field loss (arcuate scotoma)', and 'computerised field testing equipment may detect nerve fibre damage earlier, particularly if certain types of stimuli...are used.' This characteristic field pattern also has real diagnostic value against mimics: 'glaucomatous defects typically follow arcuate patterns and respect the horizontal meridian, whereas neuro-ophthalmic defects are often central or atypical and may respect the vertical meridian.'
visual_field_testing_perimetry_critical_.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Singh P et al, 'Neuro-ophthalmic Conditions Misdiagnosed as Glaucoma', J Curr Glaucoma Pract 2026;20(2):67-73 (PMID 42582922, PMC13458592)

oct_structural_nerve_fiber_layer_assessm.finding: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides objective structural assessment of the retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL), complementing the functional information from perimetry. Real comparative data show this structural signature also helps separate glaucomatous from non-glaucomatous optic nerve damage: 'RNFL thinning patterns differ between glaucomatous and nonglaucomatous optic neuropathies, with the latter more commonly involving the temporal (papillomacular) region', and a genuine red flag for a non-glaucomatous cause is 'optic disk pallor disproportionate to cupping' - a finding OCT and clinical exam together can help identify.
oct_structural_nerve_fiber_layer_assessm.source: Singh P et al, 'Neuro-ophthalmic Conditions Misdiagnosed as Glaucoma', J Curr Glaucoma Pract 2026;20(2):67-73 (PMID 42582922, PMC13458592)

asymptomatic_until_significant_irreversi.finding: The single most important diagnostic point in glaucoma is that it is usually silent until real damage has already occurred: 'POAG often progresses silently, with patients typically remaining unaware of the disease until significant vision loss has occurred', and 'because the visual loss is gradual, patients do not usually present until severe damage has occurred.' A separate review states this even more starkly: 'glaucoma often does not cause any abnormal symptoms at first, and because its effects are gradual, particularly if only one eye is affected, significant and irreversible damage may occur before the person realises that there is a problem' - which is exactly why 'early diagnosis and effective treatment are very important given its asymptomatic character early on to avoid serious visual impairment and blindness.'
asymptomatic_until_significant_irreversi.source: Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Qi T et al, 'Understanding Glaucoma: Why it Remains a Leading Cause of Blindness Worldwide', Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025;242(7):712-717 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165)

open_angle_glaucoma_silent_thief_of_sigh.finding: Open-angle glaucoma is 'often referred to as the "silent thief of sight"' precisely because, in its early and moderate stages, it typically produces no pain and no noticeable symptoms at all: 'pain is not characteristically a feature of primary open angle glaucoma.' Patients feel entirely normal while real, permanent optic-nerve damage accumulates.
open_angle_glaucoma_silent_thief_of_sigh.source: Qi T et al, Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025;242(7):712-717 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

peripheral_visual_field_loss_gradual_and.finding: The functional damage in open-angle glaucoma follows characteristic field patterns (arcuate scotoma, typically starting peripherally) that progress so gradually - especially when one eye compensates for the other - that 'significant and irreversible damage may occur before the person realises that there is a problem.' This is why routine perimetry, not the patient's own awareness, is what actually catches the disease early.
peripheral_visual_field_loss_gradual_and.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Qi T et al, Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025;242(7):712-717 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165)

acute_angle_closure_dramatic_symptomatic.finding: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is the sharp opposite of chronic open-angle disease: 'the eye becomes red and painful, and patients may be systemically unwell with nausea, vomiting, and severe pain or headache. Vision is blurred, and patients may notice haloes around lights.' On examination it typically shows a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and 'severe ocular pain accompanied by nausea, vomiting, or halos strongly suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma.'
acute_angle_closure_dramatic_symptomatic.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Maher C et al, 'A Five-Step Approach to Acute Vision Loss', Clin Ophthalmol 2026 (PMID 41782901, PMC12953027)

symptomatic_contrast_between_open_and_an.finding: This is a genuinely important clinical contrast reported honestly rather than blurred together: chronic open-angle glaucoma is painless and asymptomatic until advanced, silently destroying peripheral vision, whereas acute angle-closure glaucoma announces itself dramatically within hours with pain, redness, nausea/vomiting, headache, blurred vision and haloes - meaning the two 'glaucomas' require completely different urgency of response despite sharing the name and the underlying optic-nerve-damage endpoint.
symptomatic_contrast_between_open_and_an.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Maher C et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2026 (PMID 41782901, PMC12953027); Qi T et al, Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Cataract causes gradual, painless blurring of vision, glare, and dimming of colours from lens opacification, and - unlike glaucoma - the visual loss it causes is genuinely reversible with surgery. Glaucoma instead classically produces peripheral visual field constriction/arcuate field defects from optic nerve damage while central acuity is often preserved until late, and any vision already lost to glaucoma is permanent, not surgically reversible. The two conditions also commonly coexist in the same (usually older) patient, so a formal dilated fundus/optic-disc exam and perimetry, not visual acuity alone, are needed to avoid attributing glaucomatous field loss to lens changes.
differential_diagnosis.source: This KB's cataract entry (id: cataract); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Other causes of optic neuropathy (compressive, demyelinating, ischemic, nutritional/toxic)
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: A real, quantified retrospective study found that 32% of cases (17 of 53 patients) referred as glaucoma actually had a non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy, most commonly compressive optic neuropathy, followed by demyelinating optic neuropathy (23.5%) and ischemic optic neuropathy (17.6%). Key red flags favouring a non-glaucomatous cause: 'optic disk pallor disproportionate to cupping, visual field defects respecting the vertical meridian, younger age at presentation (<50 years), rapid progression despite adequately controlled IOP', and RNFL/OCT thinning that involves the temporal (papillomacular) region rather than the classic glaucomatous arcuate pattern.
differential_diagnosis.source: Singh P et al, 'Neuro-ophthalmic Conditions Misdiagnosed as Glaucoma: A Retrospective Study of Cases and Contributing Factors in a Developing Setting', J Curr Glaucoma Pract 2026;20(2):67-73 (PMID 42582922, PMC13458592)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Other causes of an acute red, painful eye (bacterial/viral conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis/iritis, microbial keratitis, episcleritis/scleritis)
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: A structured acute-vision-loss framework places 'severe painful red eye with vision loss, elevated IOP +/- nausea' (acute angle-closure glaucoma) in its own most urgent tier - 'immediate IOP-lowering therapy; urgent ophthalmology' - with a fixed mid-dilated pupil as a hallmark sign, in contrast to conjunctivitis (this KB's bacterial_conjunctivitis entry), which is not typically vision-threatening or associated with elevated IOP, and anterior uveitis/keratitis, which classically show a small/irregular or normal pupil, ciliary flush, and normal-to-low (not markedly elevated) IOP. Distinguishing halo-around-lights plus severe pain/nausea (angle closure) from itching/watery discharge (viral/allergic conjunctivitis) or purulent discharge without severe pain (bacterial conjunctivitis) is what correctly triages same-day ophthalmology review versus true immediate emergency referral.
differential_diagnosis.source: Maher C et al, 'A Five-Step Approach to Acute Vision Loss', Clin Ophthalmol 2026 (PMID 41782901, PMC12953027); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

elevated_intraocular_pressure.finding: Elevated IOP remains 'the sole controllable risk factor for the illness' in current management frameworks, and the magnitude/duration of pressure elevation correlates with the rate of optic nerve damage (pressures of roughly 20-30 mm Hg typically damage the nerve over years; 40-50 mm Hg can cause rapid loss).
elevated_intraocular_pressure.source: Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

age.finding: Age is a major, real, dose-dependent risk factor: glaucoma prevalence rises 'from 0.6% in people aged 40-49 years to 8.3% in people aged 80 years and older' - a genuinely steep gradient, not a marginal association.
age.source: Qi T et al, Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025;242(7):712-717 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165)

family_history_and_heritability.finding: Glaucoma has a real, substantial genetic component: 'heritability estimates for IOP and optic disc morphology reach 70% in twin cohorts, and a positive family history is reported in 4 to 16% of cases' of POAG.
family_history_and_heritability.source: Abu-Amero KK et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2026;20:623-649 (PMID 42751619, PMC13580461)

african_ancestry.finding: African ancestry carries a real, well-documented, large excess risk. The classic Baltimore Eye Survey found 'age-adjusted prevalence rates for primary open-angle glaucoma were four to five times higher in blacks compared with whites' (Tielsch JM et al, JAMA 1991), and a 2026 genetics review confirms this pattern persists, describing 'African and Hispanic populations bearing the highest risk of bilateral blindness' with '3 to 5-fold higher POAG prevalence than European populations, with younger onset and more severe disease at presentation.'
african_ancestry.source: Tielsch JM et al, 'Racial variations in the prevalence of primary open-angle glaucoma. The Baltimore Eye Survey', JAMA 1991;266(3):369-374 (PMID 2056646); Abu-Amero KK et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2026;20:623-649 (PMID 42751619, PMC13580461)

diabetes_mellitus.finding: Diabetes is a real, meta-analysis-confirmed risk factor for open-angle glaucoma, not just an incidentally co-occurring condition. Pooling 6 prospective cohort studies (about 3.4 million participants), 'the pooled RR of the association between DM and POAG...was 1.40 (95% CI, 1.25-1.57)'; pooling 7 case-control studies (over 87,000 participants), 'the pooled OR...was 1.49 (95% CI, 1.17-1.88).'
diabetes_mellitus.source: Zhou M, Wang W, Huang W, Zhang X, 'Diabetes Mellitus as a Risk Factor for Open-Angle Glaucoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', PLoS One 2014;9(8):e102972 (PMID 25137059, PMC4138056)

high_myopia.finding: High myopia is a real, genetically-linked risk factor specifically for open-angle glaucoma damage: in carriers of OPTN gene variants, disease severity is 'worsened by myopia >-3 D or disc hemorrhage', consistent with the broader literature linking myopic optic-nerve-head structure to greater glaucomatous susceptibility. This is mechanistically distinct from the anterior-segment anatomy that drives angle-closure risk (below), where the opposite refractive extreme - hyperopia/short axial length - is the relevant risk profile.
high_myopia.source: Abu-Amero KK et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2026;20:623-649 (PMID 42751619, PMC13580461)

narrow_anterior_chamber_angle_anatomy_fo.finding: A narrow, anatomically predisposed anterior chamber angle is the specific real risk factor for angle-closure disease (distinct from the open-angle risk factors above). Real comparative ocular biometry across the angle-closure spectrum shows this anatomical gradient directly: median anterior chamber depth was 2.6 mm in nanophthalmic eyes versus 2.7 mm in primary angle-closure (PAC) and 2.8 mm in primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) eyes, with axial length shortest in nanophthalmic eyes (19.9 mm) and angle width narrowest in nanophthalmic eyes (median 20.5 degrees) compared with PAC/PACG eyes (median 26 degrees each) - confirming that shallower anterior chambers, shorter axial length, and narrower angles (often together with marked hyperopia) are the real anatomical substrate for angle-closure risk, in contrast to the myopia/longer-eye profile associated with open-angle glaucoma risk above.
narrow_anterior_chamber_angle_anatomy_fo.source: Rajendrababu S et al, 'Comparison of ocular biometric parameters between nanophthalmos and primary angle closure disease: a cross-sectional comparative study', BMC Ophthalmol 2026;26:427

leading_cause_of_irreversible_blindness_.finding: Glaucoma is real and consistently described as 'a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide.' Global burden estimates (which vary modestly by source and year, reported honestly rather than picking one number) put the number of people affected at approximately 76-80 million in 2020, projected to rise to about 111-112 million by 2040; the WHO lists glaucoma among the world's leading causes of vision impairment/blindness, affecting an estimated 7.7 million people among those with distance vision impairment or blindness globally, and a separate Lancet-based meta-analysis found glaucoma to be 'the third leading cause of blindness at 3.2 million' and 'the fourth leading cause of moderate to severe [visual] impairment at 4.5 million' globally. A genuinely important honest caveat: 50-90% of glaucoma cases worldwide are estimated to remain undetected, driven by lack of symptoms, socioeconomic inequalities, and limited screening infrastructure.
leading_cause_of_irreversible_blindness_.source: Qi T et al, 'Understanding Glaucoma: Why it Remains a Leading Cause of Blindness Worldwide', Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025;242(7):712-717 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165); Abu-Amero KK et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2026;20:623-649 (PMID 42751619, PMC13580461); WHO, 'Blindness and visual impairment' fact sheet (who.int); Nongrum B et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2024;13 (PMID 39464990, PMC11504766), citing Flaxman SR et al, Lancet Global Health meta-analysis
leading_cause_of_irreversible_blindness_.confidence: moderate (global point estimates vary meaningfully by source/year; honestly reported as a range rather than a single invented number)

india_specific_burden_and_low_awareness_.finding: India carries a real, substantial and specifically documented glaucoma burden with honestly poor detection: glaucoma 'is responsible for blindness in 1.2 million people and accounts for 5.5% of total blindness' in India, with prevalence estimated 'between 2.7 and 4.3% among Indians' aged 40 and above. A separate hospital-based estimate places the number of Indians with glaucoma at 11.2 million (primary open-angle glaucoma 6.48 million; primary angle-closure glaucoma 2.54 million). Most seriously, 'the proportion of undiagnosed glaucoma is estimated at 90%' in India, and even among diagnosed cases, real misclassification occurs: the Chennai Glaucoma Study found '40% cases of primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) were being treated as primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG).' Public awareness 'continues to be low in India', and glaucoma is projected to affect '27.8 million more people...by 2040 in Asia.'
india_specific_burden_and_low_awareness_.source: Rewri P, 'Towards better management of glaucoma in India', Indian J Ophthalmol 2023;71(3):686-688 (PMID 36872660, PMC10229968); Nongrum B et al, 'Glaucoma burden and its profile in a tertiary care centre of North-East India', J Family Med Prim Care 2024;13 (PMID 39464990, PMC11504766)

vision_loss_is_permanent_once_it_occurs_.finding: A genuinely important, honestly stated distinction from this KB's cataract entry: glaucomatous vision loss is irreversible once it has occurred - the damaged retinal ganglion cells and optic nerve fibres do not regenerate and lost visual field is not restored by any current medicine, laser, or surgery - whereas cataract-related visual loss is real and substantially reversible with surgery. This makes the timing of detection, not just the eventual treatment, the decisive factor in how much vision a glaucoma patient keeps for life.
vision_loss_is_permanent_once_it_occurs_.source: Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); this KB's cataract entry (id: cataract)

progression_can_be_halted_or_slowed_with.finding: The key, genuinely actionable point is that although existing damage cannot be reversed, further progression real can be effectively halted or slowed: lowering IOP - the one proven modifiable risk factor - is directly linked to slower disease progression in the management literature, and 'early diagnosis and effective treatment are very important given its asymptomatic character early on to avoid serious visual impairment and blindness.' In other words, the entire clinical strategy in glaucoma is early detection before damage occurs, since damage already sustained cannot later be undone by any subsequent treatment.
progression_can_be_halted_or_slowed_with.source: Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054)

hyperacute_angle_closure_time_critical_e.finding: Acute angle-closure glaucoma does not follow the slow chronic course of open-angle disease: it is explicitly triaged as needing 'immediate IOP-lowering therapy; urgent ophthalmology' - more urgent even than macula-on retinal detachment ('same-day ophthalmology') in a structured acute-vision-loss framework - because sustained severe pressure elevation from pupillary block can cause real, permanent corneal and optic-nerve damage within hours rather than years.
hyperacute_angle_closure_time_critical_e.source: Maher C et al, 'A Five-Step Approach to Acute Vision Loss', Clin Ophthalmol 2026 (PMID 41782901, PMC12953027)

clinical_takeaway.point: Regular comprehensive eye examinations (tonometry, optic disc assessment, and especially visual field testing) are essential precisely because open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic in its early and moderate stages - waiting for symptoms means waiting for damage that is already permanent.
clinical_takeaway.why: 'POAG often progresses silently, with patients typically remaining unaware of the disease until significant vision loss has occurred', and an estimated 50-90% of glaucoma cases worldwide (90% in India specifically) remain undiagnosed - meaning routine screening, not patient-reported symptoms, is what actually catches this disease while damage is still preventable.
clinical_takeaway.source: Alshehri SAS et al, J Family Med Prim Care 2026 (PMID 42483376, PMC13387701); Qi T et al, Klin Monbl Augenheilkd 2025 (PMID 40719087, PMC12302165); Rewri P, Indian J Ophthalmol 2023;71(3):686-688 (PMID 36872660, PMC10229968)

clinical_takeaway.point: Acute angle-closure glaucoma must be recognised immediately as a true ophthalmologic emergency - severe eye pain with redness, halos, headache, nausea/vomiting and blurred vision needs same-hour emergency care, never a routine appointment.
clinical_takeaway.why: This presentation reflects a real, mechanistically distinct, rapidly-progressive form of the disease in which sustained markedly elevated IOP from pupillary block can cause irreversible corneal and optic-nerve damage within hours; a structured framework places it at a more urgent tier than even retinal detachment, requiring 'immediate IOP-lowering therapy; urgent ophthalmology' rather than watchful waiting or a scheduled review.
clinical_takeaway.source: Khaw PT, Elkington AR, BMJ 2004;328:97-99 (PMID 14715605, PMC314054); Maher C et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2026 (PMID 41782901, PMC12953027)

glaucoma.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a genuine, time-critical ophthalmic emergency and must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue/routine-consultation flow entirely, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department/ophthalmologist NOW), never a scheduled routine appointment. It classically presents with 'a red and painful eye, and patients may be systemically unwell with nausea, vomiting, and severe pain or headache. Vision is blurred, and patients may notice haloes around lights' (Khaw PT, Elkington AR, 'Glaucoma-1: diagnosis', BMJ 2004;328:97-99, PMID 14715605, PMC314054). A dedicated acute-vision-loss framework confirms that 'severe ocular pain accompanied by nausea, vomiting, or halos strongly suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma,' typically with a fixed mid-dilated pupil on examination, and explicitly categorises it as needing 'Immediate IOP-lowering therapy; urgent ophthalmology' - a more time-critical tier than even macula-on retinal detachment, which the same framework places only at 'same-day ophthalmology' (Maher C et al, 'A Five-Step Approach to Acute Vision Loss', Clin Ophthalmol 2026, PMID 41782901, PMC12953027). The urgency is mechanistic, not precautionary: sustained markedly elevated intraocular pressure from pupillary-block angle closure can produce corneal decompensation and optic-nerve damage within hours, and any vision lost this way is permanent, unlike the frequently self-limited or reversible course of most other acute 'red eye' presentations (bacterial/viral conjunctivitis, episcleritis). Any patient reporting sudden severe eye pain with halos around lights, headache, nausea/vomiting, blurred vision and eye redness must be treated as acute angle-closure glaucoma until an ophthalmologist proves otherwise, never managed as routine conjunctivitis, sinusitis, or migraine.

pertussis.name: Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
pertussis.icd11_hint: ICD-10: A37 (whooping cough), with sub-codes A37.0 (Bordetella pertussis), A37.1 (Bordetella parapertussis), A37.8 (other Bordetella species), A37.9 (unspecified) -- confirmed range. A precise current ICD-11 code could not be independently confirmed via the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this research session; it is commonly reported elsewhere as ICD-11 code 1C12 (Whooping cough), but that specific code is NOT independently verified here and should be re-checked against the live WHO ICD-11 browser before clinical/coding use.
pertussis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Pertussis (whooping cough) is, like measles, a disease where the honest story splits cleanly into a prevention half that works very well and a treatment-of-established-infection half that must NOT be oversold. On PREVENTION: DTaP (the pediatric primary series, given to infants and children under 7) and Tdap (the adolescent/adult booster, including the specific maternal-pregnancy dose) are real, effective acellular pertussis vaccines. CDC's Pinkbook states point estimates of DTaP vaccine efficacy in the primary series ranged from 80% to 85% across studies with overlapping confidence intervals. A real, large California case-control study (Klein NP et al, JAMA 2012;308(21):2126-2132, PMID 23188029) found the 5-dose DTaP series was 88.7% effective overall against pertussis in children, but the protection was NOT flat over time: effectiveness was 98.1% (odds ratio 0.02) within the first 12 months after the 5th dose, and had fallen to 71.2% (odds ratio 0.29) by 60 or more months after the 5th dose -- a real, substantial, documented waning of roughly 27 percentage points over 5 years, which is the direct epidemiological reason adolescent Tdap boosters and outbreak patterns in school-age children exist. This waning is honestly WORSE, and FASTER, for the Tdap adolescent booster: a real prospective cohort study (Klein NP, Bartlett J, Fireman B, Baxter R, 'Waning Tdap Effectiveness in Adolescents', Pediatrics 2016;137(3):e20153326, PMID 26908667) found Tdap vaccine effectiveness was 68.8% (95% CI 59.7-75.9%) in the first year after the adolescent booster, but had collapsed to just 8.9% (95% CI -30.6% to 36.4%, i.e. NOT statistically different from zero protection) by 4 or more years after vaccination, with the hazard of testing positive for pertussis rising 35% for every additional year since the Tdap dose (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.22-1.50). This file reports this precisely as what it is: a real, well-documented, and genuinely important limitation of ACELLULAR pertussis vaccines specifically -- CDC's Pinkbook separately states that antibody levels in adults 'peak during the first month after vaccination, with antibody levels declining after 1 year' and that a single Tdap dose's protection does not carry reliably from one pregnancy to the next, which is exactly why a Tdap dose is recommended in EVERY pregnancy rather than being treated as a one-time lifetime booster. This pertussis-component waning (protection largely gone within 3-4 years) is honestly much faster than the durable, roughly decade-long protection CDC/ACIP guidance assumes for the tetanus and diphtheria toxoid components of the same Tdap/Td shot (ACIP recommends a routine Td/Tdap booster only every 10 years specifically on the strength of tetanus/diphtheria toxoid durability) -- the same single injection therefore protects against its three target diseases on genuinely different real timelines, and this file does not blur that distinction. The single most important real, quantified 'medicine' story in this file is maternal Tdap vaccination during pregnancy ('cocooning' via transplacental antibody transfer): a 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis (Vaccines (Basel) 2025, PMID 40733643) found maternal Tdap vaccination during pregnancy was 85% effective (95% CI 78-89%) at preventing pertussis specifically in infants under 3 months of age -- the exact age window before an infant's own DTaP series has had time to provide protection, and the age group that carries pertussis' highest real mortality risk -- with no significant increase in serious adverse events in either the infant (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.46-1.24) or the vaccinated mother (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.83-1.81). On TREATMENT of already-established infection, this file is deliberately precise and does not inflate antibiotic efficacy: the Cochrane systematic review (Altunaiji S, Kukuruzovic R, Curtis N, Massie J, 'Antibiotics for whooping cough (pertussis)', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007, PMID 17636756, PMCID PMC11322855; 13 trials, 2197 participants) found antibiotics (short-course azithromycin 3-5 days, or clarithromycin/erythromycin 7 days, versus long-course erythromycin 10-14 days) were equally effective at eradicating Bordetella pertussis from the nasopharynx (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.98-1.04) and the short courses had significantly fewer side effects (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.52-0.83, i.e. 34% relative reduction in adverse effects) -- BUT the review's own plain-language summary states directly: 'several antibiotic treatments were equally effective in eliminating the bacteria infecting patients, but they did not alter the clinical outcome.' In other words, per this Cochrane evidence, antibiotics clear the organism (and by mechanism therefore shorten the contagious/transmissible period) but do NOT meaningfully shorten the paroxysmal cough itself. CDC's own current clinical guidance is consistent with, and adds timing nuance to, this Cochrane finding: CDC states 'If someone starts treatment during the first 1 to 2 weeks before coughing paroxysms occur, symptoms may be lessened,' but 'Antibiotics won't alter the course of the illness or prevent transmission if given later in the illness' (CDC, Pertussis Clinical Care, accessed 2026-09-22). Because the catarrhal stage of pertussis is clinically nonspecific (resembling an ordinary cold) and the characteristic paroxysmal cough/whoop that prompts most real-world clinical suspicion and testing does not emerge until 1-2 weeks after cough onset (CDC, Pertussis Clinical Signs and Symptoms, accessed 2026-09-22), most real pertussis patients are diagnosed and started on antibiotics only AFTER the early catarrhal window in which cough-shortening benefit is plausible has already closed -- this is the honest, mechanistic reason the Cochrane review's own included trials (which enrolled patients at the point of clinical diagnosis, not screened contacts) found no overall clinical-course benefit: this file could not locate a real, source-backed NUMERIC percentage for 'what proportion of real-world cases are treated too late for cough benefit to apply' and reports this honestly as not-quantified rather than inventing a figure, but the mechanistic and CDC-guideline-level explanation for why the benefit is rarely realized in practice is real and documented. Post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis (PEP) for close contacts is CDC-recommended for household contacts and those at high risk of severe disease (infants, third-trimester pregnant women), but this file reports honestly that a real CDC-funded multi-state evaluation of PEP effectiveness in actual household contacts (Rendi et al./CDC, PLOS ONE 2023, PMID 37200360) found NO significant difference in pertussis symptoms or positive laboratory (culture/PCR/serology) results between contacts who did and did not receive PEP, despite 96% PEP uptake -- a real, honest null finding for real-world PEP effectiveness that this file does not smooth over, even though PEP remains guideline-recommended practice. This file's real primary curative_option for pertussis is therefore vaccination -- the DTaP primary series, the Tdap adolescent/adult booster (with its honestly faster waning than the tetanus/diphtheria components of the same shot), and above all maternal Tdap during every pregnancy for cocooning young infants -- because prevention is what approaches a true 'cure' for this disease; once infection is established, antibiotics are real and important for reducing transmissibility/the contagious period and are correctly given for that public-health reason, but per Cochrane evidence they are honestly NOT shown to cure or meaningfully shorten the patient's own paroxysmal cough in the realistic timing window most patients are actually treated in.

curative_option.name: DTaP Primary Series (Infants/Children) Plus Tdap Adolescent/Adult Booster Plus Maternal Tdap in Every Pregnancy -- Vaccination Is the Real 'Cure' for Pertussis; Once Infection Is Established, Antibiotics Reduce Transmission But Honestly Do Not Cure the Cough Itself
curative_option.note: There is no antibiotic or drug that cures established pertussis infection in the sense of reversing the toxin-mediated paroxysmal cough once it has begun -- the Cochrane review found antibiotics eradicate the bacterium but 'did not alter the clinical outcome' (PMID 17636756). The real, closest-to-a-cure intervention for pertussis is therefore vaccination, applied at three real, evidence-backed points: (1) the DTaP primary series in infancy, 80-85% efficacious per CDC Pinkbook point estimates and 88.7% effective overall over the 5-dose series per Klein et al JAMA 2012 (PMID 23188029), though this protection wanes from 98.1% in the first year after the 5th dose to 71.2% by 5+ years; (2) the Tdap adolescent/adult booster, which real data show wanes even faster -- 68.8% effective in year 1, falling to a statistically-non-significant 8.9% by year 4+ (Klein/Koepke, Pediatrics 2016, PMID 26908667) -- honestly far short of the roughly 10-year durability assumed for the tetanus/diphtheria toxoid components of the same shot; and (3) maternal Tdap vaccination in every pregnancy, which a 2025 meta-analysis found 85% effective (95% CI 78-89%) at preventing pertussis in infants under 3 months of age (PMID 40733643) -- the single most important real medicine-based intervention in this file because it protects infants in the exact early-life window before their own vaccine series can. For a person who has already contracted pertussis, macrolide antibiotics (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are real and correctly recommended, but this file reports honestly, per Cochrane evidence, that their proven benefit is eradicating the organism and thereby shortening the contagious period for public-health/transmission-control purposes, not curing the patient's own cough, except for the CDC-stated possibility of lessened symptoms if treatment begins in the first 1-2 weeks before paroxysms start, a window most real-world patients have already passed by the time pertussis is clinically suspected and tested for.

pert_dtap_primary_series_medicines.name: DTaP (Diphtheria, Tetanus, acellular Pertussis) Vaccine -- Primary Pediatric Series (Real Primary Prevention/'Cure' Strategy for Infants and Children Under 7)
pert_dtap_primary_series_medicines.type: Acellular combination toxoid/subunit vaccine (preventive, injectable; 5-dose series at 2, 4, 6, 15-18 months, and 4-6 years per CDC schedule)
pert_dtap_primary_series_medicines.effectiveness: CDC Pinkbook: point estimates of DTaP vaccine efficacy in the primary series ranged from 80% to 85% across studies (overlapping confidence intervals). A real, large California case-control study (Klein NP et al, JAMA 2012;308(21):2126-2132, PMID 23188029) found the complete 5-dose DTaP series was 88.7% effective overall against pertussis in children, but effectiveness was real and substantially time-dependent: 98.1% (odds ratio 0.02) within 12 months of the 5th dose, declining to 71.2% (odds ratio 0.29) by 60+ months after the 5th dose -- a real, documented ~27-percentage-point waning over 5 years.
pert_dtap_primary_series_medicines.reason_why: Acellular pertussis vaccine components (typically including pertussis toxoid and 1-4 additional purified B. pertussis surface antigens such as filamentous haemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae) stimulate antibody and T-cell responses against the specific toxins and adhesion proteins the bacterium uses to colonize the respiratory epithelium and release the toxin responsible for the paroxysmal cough; because acellular vaccines use only a handful of purified antigens (versus the whole inactivated bacterium in older whole-cell vaccines), the resulting immune memory is real but genuinely less durable, which is the mechanistic basis for the documented waning seen even within the primary childhood series.
pert_dtap_primary_series_medicines.source: CDC Pinkbook, Pertussis chapter (accessed 2026-09-22); Klein NP et al, JAMA 2012;308(21):2126-2132 (PMID 23188029)

pert_tdap_booster_medicines.name: Tdap (Tetanus, Diphtheria, acellular Pertussis) Vaccine -- Adolescent/Adult Booster, Real Documented Rapid Waning (Faster Than the Tetanus/Diphtheria Components of the Same Shot)
pert_tdap_booster_medicines.type: Acellular combination toxoid/subunit vaccine (booster, injectable; routinely given at age 11-12 years, with additional doses for pregnancy/wound management/catch-up)
pert_tdap_booster_medicines.effectiveness: Real prospective cohort study (Klein NP, Bartlett J, Fireman B, Baxter R, 'Waning Tdap Effectiveness in Adolescents', Pediatrics 2016;137(3):e20153326, PMID 26908667): Tdap vaccine effectiveness was 68.8% (95% CI 59.7-75.9%) in the first year after vaccination, but had fallen to just 8.9% (95% CI -30.6% to 36.4% -- crossing zero, i.e. NOT statistically significant protection) by 4 or more years after vaccination; the hazard of testing positive for pertussis rose 35% for every additional year since the Tdap dose (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.22-1.50). CDC Pinkbook separately notes antibody response to a single Tdap dose is similar to that after 3 DTaP doses in infants, but that antibody levels 'peak during the first month after vaccination, with antibody levels declining after 1 year.' This pertussis-component waning is honestly much faster than the ~10-year protection ACIP/CDC guidance assumes for the tetanus and diphtheria toxoid components carried in the identical Tdap injection (CDC's routine Td/Tdap booster interval is every 10 years, a schedule set on tetanus/diphtheria toxoid durability, not on the pertussis component, which is effectively unprotective again within 3-4 years per the data above).
pert_tdap_booster_medicines.reason_why: The same acellular-antigen mechanism (and its comparatively short-lived immune memory) that limits DTaP durability in childhood applies, and is documented as even faster-waning, to the single-dose adolescent/adult Tdap booster; because the tetanus and diphtheria toxoid components of the same injection are structurally simple, highly immunogenic protein toxoids that reliably generate long-lived neutralising antibody, the three diseases protected by one injection do not share the same real duration of protection, and this file does not present them as if they did.
pert_tdap_booster_medicines.source: Klein NP, Bartlett J, Fireman B, Baxter R, Pediatrics 2016;137(3):e20153326 (PMID 26908667); CDC Pinkbook, Pertussis chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)
pert_tdap_booster_medicines.confidence: high (real, large, concordant cohort data with stated confidence intervals)

pert_maternal_tdap_pregnancy_medicines.name: Tdap Vaccination in Every Pregnancy (27-36 Weeks Gestation) -- Real 'Cocooning' Strategy Protecting Young Infants Before Their Own Vaccination Series Is Complete
pert_maternal_tdap_pregnancy_medicines.type: Acellular combination toxoid/subunit vaccine given antenatally for transplacental passive antibody transfer to the fetus/newborn
pert_maternal_tdap_pregnancy_medicines.effectiveness: Real 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis (Vaccines (Basel) 2025, PMID 40733643): maternal Tdap vaccination during pregnancy was 85% effective (95% CI 78-89%) at preventing pertussis in infants under 3 months of age -- the highest-mortality-risk infant age window, and the window before an infant's own DTaP series (first dose at 2 months, requiring multiple doses for full protection) can provide meaningful protection. The same meta-analysis found elevated anti-pertussis cord-blood antibody levels in infants of vaccinated mothers (standardized mean differences of 1.57 to 2.25 across three pertussis antigens) and no significant increase in serious adverse events in either infants (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.46-1.24) or vaccinated pregnant women (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.83-1.81). CDC Pinkbook separately notes that because maternal antibody wanes substantially within about a year, a single Tdap dose from an earlier pregnancy is not considered protective for a later pregnancy/infant, and current guidance recommends Tdap in EVERY pregnancy rather than a one-time lifetime booster.
pert_maternal_tdap_pregnancy_medicines.reason_why: Maternal IgG antibodies raised in response to Tdap vaccination cross the placenta via active FcRn-receptor-mediated transport, concentrating in the fetal circulation, most efficiently in the third trimester (hence the 27-36 week timing window); these passively-transferred maternal antibodies neutralise B. pertussis toxin and surface antigens in the newborn's bloodstream from birth, providing real protection during the vulnerable first weeks of life before the infant's own active immune response to their first DTaP doses has had time to develop, which is the mechanistic reason this specific vaccination timing and repeat-every-pregnancy strategy exists.
specific_drugs: Tdap vaccine, given at 27-36 weeks of each pregnancy (e.g. Boostrix, Adacel)
pert_maternal_tdap_pregnancy_medicines.source: Vaccines (Basel) 2025 meta-analysis (PMID 40733643); CDC Pinkbook, Pertussis chapter (accessed 2026-09-22)

pert_antibiotic_treatment_medicines.name: Macrolide Antibiotics (Azithromycin, Clarithromycin, Erythromycin) and Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole -- Real Bacterial Eradication/Transmission-Reduction, Honestly NOT a Cure for the Established Paroxysmal Cough
pert_antibiotic_treatment_medicines.type: Antibacterial antibiotics, macrolide class (first-line) or TMP-SMX (alternative, e.g. macrolide allergy/resistance)
pert_antibiotic_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: Cochrane systematic review (Altunaiji S, Kukuruzovic R, Curtis N, Massie J, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007, PMID 17636756, PMCID PMC11322855; 13 trials, 2197 participants): short-course antibiotics (azithromycin 3-5 days, or clarithromycin/erythromycin 7 days) were as effective as long-course erythromycin (10-14 days) at eradicating B. pertussis from the nasopharynx (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.98-1.04), with significantly fewer side effects on the short course (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.52-0.83, a real 34% relative reduction in adverse effects). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 7 days showed comparable bacteriologic effectiveness to the macrolides. CRITICALLY, and reported here with full honesty per this file's mandatory framing: the review's own plain-language summary states directly that although 'several antibiotic treatments were equally effective in eliminating the bacteria infecting patients... they did not alter the clinical outcome' -- i.e. antibiotics did NOT meaningfully shorten the paroxysmal cough itself in the trial population as a whole. CDC's current clinical guidance adds real timing nuance: 'If someone starts treatment during the first 1 to 2 weeks before coughing paroxysms occur, symptoms may be lessened,' but 'Antibiotics won't alter the course of the illness or prevent transmission if given later in the illness' (CDC, Pertussis Clinical Care, accessed 2026-09-22). No single real numeric percentage for 'proportion of real-world cases treated too late for this cough-shortening benefit to apply' was located in this research pass; this is honestly left unquantified rather than invented, though the mechanistic reason the benefit is rarely realized is real and documented: CDC states the paroxysmal cough/whoop that typically prompts clinical suspicion of pertussis does not emerge until 1-2 weeks after cough onset, by which point the early catarrhal window for cough-shortening benefit has generally already closed.
pert_antibiotic_treatment_medicines.reason_why: Macrolides and TMP-SMX are bacteriostatic/bactericidal against B. pertussis and clear the organism from the nasopharynx, which is the real, correct, and clinically important reason they reduce the contagious/transmissible period and are recommended for public-health control of spread; however, by the time most patients present with the classic paroxysmal cough, the bacterium has already triggered the pertussis-toxin-mediated airway damage and neurologic cough reflex sensitization believed to underlie the prolonged cough itself, a process the antibiotic's antibacterial action does not reverse once established -- which is the honest mechanistic reason antibiotics eradicate the organism but do not cure the cough in most real-world treated patients.
specific_drugs: Azithromycin (3-5 day course, first-line, including in infants under 1 month)
Erythromycin (7-14 day course; more side effects than azithromycin/clarithromycin per Cochrane RR 0.66)
Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, 7 day course; alternative for macrolide allergy/intolerance, contraindicated in infants under 2 months and near-term pregnancy)
pert_antibiotic_treatment_medicines.source: Altunaiji S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007 (PMID 17636756, PMCID PMC11322855); CDC, Pertussis Clinical Care (accessed 2026-09-22); CDC, Pertussis Clinical Signs and Symptoms (accessed 2026-09-22)

pert_postexposure_prophylaxis_medicines.name: Post-Exposure Antibiotic Prophylaxis (PEP) for Close Contacts -- CDC-Recommended, But a Real 2023 CDC-Funded Evaluation Found No Significant Real-World Protective Effect
pert_postexposure_prophylaxis_medicines.type: Antibacterial antibiotics (same agents as treatment), given prophylactically to asymptomatic close contacts
pert_postexposure_prophylaxis_medicines.effectiveness: CDC recommends PEP for household/close contacts and those at high risk of severe disease (infants, third-trimester pregnant women), within 3 weeks of the index case's cough onset for people 1 year and older, and within 6 weeks for infants under 1 year and pregnant women near term (CDC, Pertussis Clinical Care, accessed 2026-09-22).
