exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real Shingrix (recombinant zoster vaccine, RZV) pre-exposure vaccination in immunocompetent adults >=50 (reported first, at highest priority, per this file's 'prevention is the real cure' framing) and separately in immunocompromised adults (a real modern indication expansion); the older live-attenuated Zostavax (ZVL), now discontinued in the US, reported honestly as substantially less protective and faster-waning; oral valacyclovir/famciclovir/acyclovir for established disease within the strictly time-critical 72-hour window, with an honest Cochrane-sourced null finding on PHN-incidence prevention specifically and a real head-to-head valacyclovir-vs-acyclovir advantage on pain duration; IV acyclovir for disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients; oral corticosteroids as an acute-pain adjunct with honestly no proven PHN-prevention benefit; herpes zoster ophthalmicus as a distinct vision-threatening presentation needing urgent ophthalmology referral; and established PHN pain management (gabapentin/pregabalin/topical lidocaine), correctly symptomatic rather than curative of the underlying nerve damage.

hz_shingrix_recombinant_vaccine_medicine.name: Shingrix (Recombinant Zoster Vaccine, RZV) -- 2-Dose Series, Immunocompetent Adults >=50
hz_shingrix_recombinant_vaccine_medicine.type: Non-live recombinant subunit vaccine with AS01B adjuvant (preventive, intramuscular, 2 doses 2-6 months apart)
hz_shingrix_recombinant_vaccine_medicine.effectiveness: Real, landmark ZOE-50 trial (Lal H et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372(22):2087-2096, PMID 25916341; n=15,411 adults >=50, median 3.2 years follow-up): overall vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster of 97.2% (95% CI 93.7-99.0; P<0.001), with only 6 cases in vaccine recipients versus 210 in placebo; efficacy was 96.6% (95% CI 89.6-99.3) in ages 50-59 and 97.4% (95% CI 90.1-99.7) in ages 60-69. In the companion ZOE-70 trial (Cunningham AL et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375(11):1019-1032, PMID 27626517; adults >=70), efficacy in that trial alone was 89.8% (95% CI 84.2-93.7); pooling ZOE-50 and ZOE-70 participants aged >=70 gave 91.3% (95% CI 86.8-94.5). Durability was real and honestly reported as declining over time but remaining substantial: 97.6% (95% CI 90.9-99.8) in year 1 versus 84.7% (95% CI 69.0-93.4) across years 2-4 in the >=70 pooled analysis. Against postherpetic neuralgia specifically, efficacy was 91.2% (95% CI 75.9-97.7) in adults >=50 and 88.8% (95% CI 68.7-97.1) in adults >=70.
hz_shingrix_recombinant_vaccine_medicine.reason_why: Shingrix contains a non-live, recombinant varicella-zoster virus glycoprotein E (gE) antigen combined with the AS01B adjuvant system; gE is the most abundant VZV surface glycoprotein and a principal target of both neutralising antibody and CD4+ T-cell responses, while the AS01B adjuvant strongly boosts and prolongs both humoral and, critically, cell-mediated immunity -- the arm of the immune system that specifically wanes with age and whose decline is the central reason older adults lose control over latent VZV reactivation from dorsal root/cranial nerve ganglia in the first place. Because the vaccine is non-live, it can safely be given at a dose that drives a much larger, adjuvant-boosted immune response than a live-attenuated virus could safely achieve, which is the direct mechanistic reason its efficacy and durability substantially exceed the older live vaccine.
specific_drugs: Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), 2 doses intramuscular, 2-6 months apart
hz_shingrix_recombinant_vaccine_medicine.source: Lal H et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372(22):2087-2096 (PMID 25916341); Cunningham AL et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375(11):1019-1032 (PMID 27626517); Dooling KL et al, ACIP, MMWR Recomm Rep 2018;67(3):103-108; CDC ACIP Pinkbook, Chapter 23: Herpes Zoster (accessed 2026-09-23)
hz_shingrix_recombinant_vaccine_medicine.confidence: high (concordant NEJM pivotal RCT data and ACIP/CDC Pinkbook secondary summary, both directly fetched in this session)

hz_shingrix_immunocompromised_medicines.name: Shingrix (RZV) in Immunocompromised Adults -- Real Modern Indication Expansion Beyond the Original Pivotal Trials
hz_shingrix_immunocompromised_medicines.type: Non-live recombinant subunit vaccine with AS01B adjuvant (preventive, intramuscular, 2 doses)
hz_shingrix_immunocompromised_medicines.effectiveness: The pivotal ZOE-50/ZOE-70 trials excluded immunocompromised persons and those on moderate-to-high-dose immunosuppressive therapy, but dedicated real trials in these higher-risk groups, summarised in ACIP's 2022 immunocompromised-adults recommendation (Anderson TC et al, MMWR 2022;71(3):80-84), found vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster of 68.2% (95% CI 55.6-77.5) in autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients (Bastidas A et al, ZOE-HSCT Study Group, JAMA 2019;322(2):123-133, PMID 31287523), with 89% (95% CI 22-100) efficacy against postherpetic neuralgia and 85% (95% CI 32-97) efficacy against herpes-zoster-related hospitalisation in the same trial; 87.2% (95% CI 44.3-98.6) in patients with haematologic malignancies (Dagnew AF et al, Zoster-039 Study Group, Lancet Infect Dis 2019;19(9):988-1000, post hoc analysis); and 90.5% (95% CI 73.5-97.5) in adults with certain immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (Dagnew AF et al, ZOE-50/70 Study Group, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2021, pooled post hoc analysis). Honestly reported as real but mostly post hoc/pooled analyses rather than each population's own fully independent pivotal RCT, and with genuinely wide confidence intervals in the smaller HSCT-PHN and HSCT-hospitalisation endpoints (95% CI as wide as 22-100).
hz_shingrix_immunocompromised_medicines.reason_why: Immunocompromised patients (post-transplant, haematologic malignancy, or on immune-suppressing therapy for inflammatory disease) have impaired T-cell surveillance of latent VZV, which is the direct reason their baseline risk of zoster, and of severe/complicated zoster, is substantially higher than in immunocompetent adults; because Shingrix is a non-live antigen-plus-adjuvant vaccine rather than a live-attenuated virus, it can safely be given to these patients (unlike the live Zostavax, which is contraindicated in significant immunosuppression), and the AS01B adjuvant still drives a meaningful, if somewhat attenuated relative to immunocompetent hosts, boost in VZV-specific immunity sufficient to substantially reduce zoster reactivation risk in this real, higher-risk population.
specific_drugs: Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), 2 doses intramuscular, 1-2 months apart in immunocompromised adults per ACIP
hz_shingrix_immunocompromised_medicines.source: Anderson TC et al, ACIP, MMWR 2022;71(3):80-84; Bastidas A et al, JAMA 2019;322(2):123-133 (PMID 31287523); Dagnew AF et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2019;19(9):988-1000; Dagnew AF et al, Rheumatology (Oxford) 2021
hz_shingrix_immunocompromised_medicines.confidence: moderate-to-high (real trial-derived efficacy figures, but mostly post hoc/pooled analyses per ACIP's own characterisation, and some endpoints with wide confidence intervals, honestly disclosed)

hz_zostavax_live_vaccine_medicines.name: Zostavax (Zoster Vaccine Live, ZVL) -- Real Lower-Efficacy, Faster-Waning Predecessor, US Production Discontinued 2020
hz_zostavax_live_vaccine_medicines.type: Live-attenuated Oka-strain viral vaccine (preventive, subcutaneous, single dose)
hz_zostavax_live_vaccine_medicines.effectiveness: Zostavax was available in the US from 2006 until its production for US distribution was discontinued in 2020. CDC's current comparison states ZVL 'efficacy wanes substantially during the 4 years following receipt when compared to RZV' and 'has been shown to be less efficacious when administered at age 70 years or older,' giving as a concrete real example that ZVL efficacy among adults aged 70-79 years and adults aged 80 years and older was only 41% and 18% respectively, on average, during the first 3 years following vaccination. This file honestly notes that ZVL's original Shingles Prevention Study headline efficacy figures (commonly cited elsewhere as approximately 51% against herpes zoster and approximately 66.5% against postherpetic neuralgia, Oxman MN et al, N Engl J Med 2005;352(22):2271-2284) were NOT independently re-verified against the primary source in this session; only the CDC-stated waning/lower-efficacy comparison above was directly confirmed.
hz_zostavax_live_vaccine_medicines.reason_why: Zostavax uses the same live-attenuated Oka-strain VZV as the childhood varicella vaccine but at a much higher potency; because it is a live virus, its dose is safety-capped well below what would maximise immune stimulation, and it carries no adjuvant, so the T-cell boost it provides is smaller and less durable than Shingrix's adjuvanted non-live antigen approach -- directly explaining both its lower peak efficacy and its faster waning, and why it is contraindicated in significantly immunocompromised patients who cannot safely receive live vaccines.
specific_drugs: Zoster vaccine live (Zostavax) -- no longer produced for the US market as of 2020
hz_zostavax_live_vaccine_medicines.source: CDC, Shingles Vaccine Considerations (cdc.gov/shingles/hcp/vaccine-considerations/index.html, accessed 2026-09-23); CDC ACIP Pinkbook, Chapter 23: Herpes Zoster (accessed 2026-09-23)
hz_zostavax_live_vaccine_medicines.confidence: moderate-to-high for the CDC-stated waning/lower-efficacy comparison and discontinuation fact (directly fetched); the original 2005 Shingles Prevention Study headline percentages are reported as commonly-cited figures NOT independently re-verified against the primary source this session, honestly disclosed

hz_oral_antiviral_72hr_treatment_medicin.name: Oral Valacyclovir/Famciclovir/Acyclovir Within 72 Hours of Rash Onset -- Real, Strictly Time-Critical Treatment of Established Disease
hz_oral_antiviral_72hr_treatment_medicin.type: Nucleoside analogue antivirals, oral (treatment of established disease, not preventive)
hz_oral_antiviral_72hr_treatment_medicin.effectiveness: CDC states these antivirals are 'most effective within 72 hours of symptom onset,' where they accelerate resolution of lesions, reduce development of new lesions and viral shedding, and decrease the severity of acute pain (CDC, Shingles Clinical Overview, accessed 2026-09-23). Honestly, the Cochrane systematic review specifically addressing PHN PREVENTION (Li Q, Chen N, Yang J, et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(2):CD006866; 6 RCTs, 1,211 participants, 5 evaluating oral acyclovir and 1 evaluating famciclovir) found 'there was no significant difference between the oral acyclovir and control groups on the incidence of PHN' at 4 months (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.51-1.11; P=0.15) or 6 months (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87-1.27; P=0.62), concluding directly that 'oral acyclovir did not reduce the incidence of PHN significantly,' though there was some evidence for reduced acute pain at 4 weeks. In a real, separate head-to-head randomized trial (Beutner KR et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1995;39(7):1546-1553, PMID 7492102; n=1,141 immunocompetent adults >=50), valacyclovir 'significantly accelerated the resolution of herpes zoster-associated pain' compared with acyclovir: median pain duration was 38 days (valacyclovir x7 days) and 44 days (valacyclovir x14 days) versus 51 days (acyclovir x7 days), and the proportion of patients with pain persisting at 6 months was 19.3% with valacyclovir versus 25.7% with acyclovir -- a real, computed 24.9% relative reduction in 6-month pain persistence favouring valacyclovir over acyclovir specifically ((25.7-19.3)/25.7 = 24.9%, this file's own arithmetic applied to the trial's two directly-reported percentages).
hz_oral_antiviral_72hr_treatment_medicin.reason_why: All three drugs (acyclovir and its prodrug valacyclovir, and famciclovir, the prodrug of penciclovir) are guanosine analogues that, after phosphorylation specifically by VZV's own viral thymidine kinase in infected cells, competitively inhibit viral DNA polymerase and cause chain termination, reducing new VZV DNA synthesis; because established zoster reflects virus already reactivated and replicating along a sensory nerve and its dermatome, therapy can only meaningfully blunt further viral replication and its downstream inflammatory/neural damage while that replication is still ongoing (the acute 72-hour-to-a-few-day window), which is the direct mechanistic reason for the strict timing recommendation and why antivirals more reliably shorten and lessen the ACUTE illness than they prevent the separate, complex, centrally-mediated pain-sensitisation process underlying postherpetic neuralgia; valacyclovir's higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir achieves higher and more sustained plasma drug levels for a similar dosing burden, which is the likely mechanistic reason for its measured advantage over acyclovir on pain-duration outcomes specifically.
specific_drugs: Valacyclovir (oral prodrug of acyclovir, improved bioavailability)
hz_oral_antiviral_72hr_treatment_medicin.source: CDC, Shingles Clinical Overview (cdc.gov/shingles/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html, accessed 2026-09-23); Li Q et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(2):CD006866; Beutner KR et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1995;39(7):1546-1553 (PMID 7492102)
hz_oral_antiviral_72hr_treatment_medicin.confidence: high for the 72-hour CDC recommendation and its stated acute-illness benefits, and for the Cochrane PHN-prevention null finding (directly quoted); high for the Beutner 1995 valacyclovir-vs-acyclovir RCT's directly-reported percentages

hz_iv_acyclovir_disseminated_medicines.name: Intravenous Acyclovir -- Disseminated Zoster in Immunocompromised Patients
hz_iv_acyclovir_disseminated_medicines.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, intravenous (treatment of established disease, standard of care for disseminated/severe presentations)
hz_iv_acyclovir_disseminated_medicines.effectiveness: IV acyclovir is guideline-standard-of-care treatment for disseminated or visceral herpes zoster in immunocompromised patients. This file was unable to locate a clean randomized-trial numeric efficacy percentage for this specific indication in this session; the available literature located consisted of case reports/case series describing 'marked improvement' with IV acyclovir (10mg/kg every 8 hours) in disseminated VZV with visceral (bone marrow, gastrointestinal) involvement in immunocompromised hosts. Honestly reported as not-quantified rather than inventing a percentage; this is the same honest pattern this file's parallel chickenpox entry uses for IV acyclovir in disseminated varicella, where a similarly small, older trial found a statistically significant reduction in visceral dissemination without a reported percentage.
hz_iv_acyclovir_disseminated_medicines.reason_why: Immunocompromised patients cannot mount a normal T-cell-mediated immune response to contain VZV reactivation, allowing haematogenous dissemination to the lungs, liver, and other viscera; intravenous acyclovir achieves substantially higher and more reliable plasma drug levels than the oral route, providing more potent and consistent inhibition of viral DNA polymerase precisely when uncontrolled viral replication, rather than an adequate host immune response, is the main driver of life-threatening dissemination.
hz_iv_acyclovir_disseminated_medicines.source: CDC, Shingles Clinical Overview (accessed 2026-09-23); case reports of disseminated VZV managed with IV acyclovir (e.g. PMID 42472290, PMID 42005579) illustrating standard-of-care response, not a randomized efficacy trial
hz_iv_acyclovir_disseminated_medicines.confidence: moderate for standard-of-care status (concordant guideline recommendation); no numeric randomized-trial efficacy percentage located for this specific indication in this session, honestly disclosed

hz_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.name: Oral Corticosteroids as Acute-Pain Adjunct -- Real, Honestly No Proven Postherpetic-Neuralgia-Prevention Benefit
hz_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.type: Systemic corticosteroids, oral (adjunctive symptomatic treatment, not antiviral)
hz_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.effectiveness: The current Cochrane review (Jiang X, Li Y, Chen N, Zhou M, He L, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;12:CD005582) found 'the evidence is very uncertain about the effects of corticosteroids given orally during an acute herpes zoster infection in preventing postherpetic neuralgia six months after the onset of herpes' (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.45-1.99; 2 trials, 114 participants; very low-certainty evidence), with 'no observed differences in serious...or non-serious adverse events' versus placebo. Honestly reported: despite some researchers historically recommending corticosteroids to relieve acute zoster-associated pain, the current best evidence does NOT support a proven PHN-prevention benefit, and the review's authors call for longer-term follow-up in future trials rather than making a positive claim the data do not support.
hz_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.reason_why: Corticosteroids are anti-inflammatory and could plausibly reduce the acute neural inflammation and oedema associated with zoster, which underlies the historical rationale for their adjunctive use in acute pain; however, postherpetic neuralgia is now understood to arise from complex, only partly inflammation-driven peripheral and central neuroplastic/pain-sensitisation changes following nerve injury, which is the likely reason a purely anti-inflammatory intervention has not been shown to meaningfully alter the trajectory toward chronic PHN despite the small trials available.

hz_corticosteroid_adjunct_medicines.confidence: high for the Cochrane review's own very-low-certainty, no-significant-difference conclusion, directly quoted rather than paraphrased into false confidence

hz_ophthalmicus_management_medicines.name: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus -- Oral Antiviral Therapy Plus Urgent Ophthalmology Referral (Real Vision-Threatening Presentation)
hz_ophthalmicus_management_medicines.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, oral, plus mandatory specialist referral (treatment of a distinct anatomical presentation, not a separate drug class)
hz_ophthalmicus_management_medicines.effectiveness: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) is real and vision-threatening when it involves the cornea, uvea, or retina, warranting urgent ophthalmology referral. A randomized trial (Cobo LM, Foulks GN, Liesegang T, et al, Ophthalmology 1986;93(6):763-770) found a 10-day course of oral acyclovir 600mg five times daily 'significantly reduces the incidence and severity of the most common complications of herpes zoster ophthalmicus: dendritiform keratopathy, stromal keratitis, and uveitis.' Honestly, the same trial explicitly found acyclovir 'has no evident effect on either incidence, severity, or duration of post-herpetic neuralgia' -- i.e. the HZO-specific antiviral benefit is on real, vision-threatening ocular complications, a distinct and separately-earned benefit from PHN prevention. No numeric complication-reduction percentage was available from the located abstract; honestly left unquantified rather than inventing one.
hz_ophthalmicus_management_medicines.reason_why: HZO occurs when VZV reactivates in the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve, which supplies the cornea, conjunctiva, and structures around the eye; oral antiviral therapy suppresses viral replication in this nerve distribution by the same thymidine-kinase-dependent DNA-polymerase-inhibition mechanism as elsewhere, reducing direct viral damage to corneal and uveal tissue and the resulting inflammatory complications, but does not alter the separate, largely centrally-mediated pain-sensitisation process that underlies postherpetic neuralgia, explaining the trial's honestly-reported lack of effect on that specific outcome; urgent ophthalmology referral is required because vision loss from corneal scarring, uveitis, or (rarely) acute retinal necrosis can occur rapidly and needs specialist monitoring and topical/intraocular therapy beyond what oral antivirals alone provide.
hz_ophthalmicus_management_medicines.confidence: moderate-to-high for the qualitative ocular-complication-reduction and no-PHN-effect findings (both directly quoted); no numeric effectiveness percentage located in the available abstract, honestly disclosed; urgent-referral necessity is standard ophthalmology practice rather than a separately quantified trial endpoint

hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.name: Gabapentin -- Established Postherpetic Neuralgia (Real, Correctly Symptomatic, Not Curative)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.type: Gabapentinoid anticonvulsant/neuropathic-pain agent, oral (symptomatic pain management, not curative of nerve damage)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.effectiveness: Real Cochrane review (Moore RA, Wiffen PJ, Derry S, et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(4):CD007938, PMID 24771480): in postherpetic neuralgia trials, gabapentin at doses of 1200mg/day or more achieved at least 50% pain intensity reduction in 34% of patients versus 21% on placebo (NNT 8.0, 95% CI 6.0-12). The review's own authors note plainly that 'over half of those treated with gabapentin will not have worthwhile pain relief,' honestly reported rather than oversold.
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.reason_why: Gabapentin binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels on hyperexcitable, injured sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion and spinal dorsal horn, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release and dampening the abnormal, sensitised pain signalling that persists after the original VZV-induced nerve injury has otherwise healed; because this action modulates pain signalling rather than repairing the underlying nerve damage, it is correctly classified as symptomatic rather than curative.

hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.name: Pregabalin -- Established Postherpetic Neuralgia, Real Dose-Response Relationship (Real, Correctly Symptomatic, Not Curative)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.type: Gabapentinoid anticonvulsant/neuropathic-pain agent, oral (symptomatic pain management, not curative of nerve damage)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.effectiveness: Real Cochrane review (Derry S, Bell RF, Straube S, et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;(1):CD007076, PMID 30673120; 45 RCTs, 11,906 participants across neuropathic pain conditions): in postherpetic neuralgia specifically, at 300mg/day, 32% versus 13% of patients achieved >=50% pain reduction (RR 2.5, NNT 5.3), and at 600mg/day, 41% versus 15% achieved >=50% pain reduction (RR 2.7, NNT 3.9) -- a real, clearly dose-dependent effect. Somnolence rose from 5.5-5.8% (placebo) to 16-25% (pregabalin) and dizziness from 8.1-8.8% to 29-35%, honestly disclosed as a real tolerability trade-off that leads some patients to discontinue treatment.
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.reason_why: Pregabalin acts via the same alpha-2-delta voltage-gated-calcium-channel mechanism as gabapentin but with more predictable, linear (rather than saturable) oral absorption, which is the likely pharmacokinetic reason its dose-response relationship in PHN trials is more clearly demonstrable; it modulates pain signalling in already-injured sensory pathways rather than repairing the underlying VZV-induced nerve damage, so it is correctly classified as symptomatic, not curative.
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.source: Derry S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;(1):CD007076 (PMID 30673120)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.confidence: high (directly-quoted Cochrane numeric findings, including the real dose-response gradient)

hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.name: Topical Lidocaine -- Established Postherpetic Neuralgia (Real, Honestly Weak Evidence Base Despite Clinical Use)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.type: Topical local anaesthetic (sodium-channel blocker), applied over the affected dermatome (symptomatic pain management, not curative of nerve damage)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.effectiveness: Real Cochrane review (Derry S, Wiffen PJ, Moore RA, Quinlan J, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(7):CD010958, PMID 25058164; 12 studies, 508 participants, 6 specifically enrolling PHN patients) found 'no evidence from good quality randomised controlled studies to support the use of topical lidocaine to treat neuropathic pain,' although 'individual studies indicated that it was effective for relief of pain' in some patients; the PHN-specific evidence was rated third-tier (very low quality). No numeric effectiveness percentage or NNT is given in this file's ranked table for topical lidocaine because the Cochrane review itself found the evidence base too weak to support one, honestly disclosed rather than inventing a figure; some other pain-medicine consensus guides (e.g. Lawson et al, Pain Medicine 2026) separately describe lidocaine and capsaicin 8% as effective for PHN as part of a wider tiered-treatment consensus, a real but lower-certainty source than a Cochrane RCT synthesis, honestly distinguished here.
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.reason_why: Topical lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in cutaneous sensory nerve endings at the site of application, which could plausibly reduce peripherally-generated hyperexcitable pain signals arising from damaged nerve fibres in the PHN-affected dermatome; however, much of PHN's pain is thought to also involve central sensitisation beyond the reach of a topical peripheral agent, which is a plausible mechanistic reason the existing RCT evidence for topical lidocaine has not consistently demonstrated benefit despite its logical rationale and continued clinical use.
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.source: Derry S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(7):CD010958 (PMID 25058164)
hz_phn_pain_management_medicines.confidence: low-to-moderate; the Cochrane review's own conclusion is evidence-negative for good-quality RCT support, honestly reported rather than inflated on the strength of clinical experience alone

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix real, differently-defined metrics -- vaccine efficacy against ever acquiring herpes zoster on latent VZV reactivation, vaccine efficacy specifically against postherpetic neuralgia, vaccine efficacy in distinct immunocompromised sub-populations, a real head-to-head antiviral pain-duration comparison, and real RCT-measured proportions of PHN patients achieving >=50% pain relief on symptomatic agents -- placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. They are NOT interchangeable: a vaccine's protection against ever developing shingles, an antiviral's shortening of an ALREADY-ESTABLISHED acute illness, and a pain medicine's symptomatic relief of ALREADY-ESTABLISHED chronic PHN answer completely different clinical questions. Rows without a real, source-backed numeric effectiveness percentage (oral acyclovir's honestly-null Cochrane PHN-prevention finding, IV acyclovir for disseminated disease, the HZO-specific ocular-complication reduction whose trial abstract gave no percentage, corticosteroids' very-low-certainty null finding, topical lidocaine's evidence-negative Cochrane conclusion, Zostavax's original un-re-verified 2005 headline figures, and antibiotic-type complication management) are intentionally left out of this ranked list or given a stated-reason null rather than assigned an invented number; they remain fully documented above in exhaustive_medicine_survey.
