croup.name: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)
croup.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code/title text for this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 code J05.0 (Acute obstructive laryngitis [croup]) is the code commonly used for this condition in the literature, but this ICD-10 mapping was likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

most_common_causative_pathogen.finding: Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis) is predominantly a parainfluenza-virus disease: 'Parainfluenza virus (types 1 to 3) accounts for 75% of all cases, and human parainfluenza virus 1 is the most common type.' Among the three serotypes, PIV-2 tends to cause milder disease while PIV-3 is associated with more severe disease.
most_common_causative_pathogen.source: Azevedo SPDC, Barros LGB, Krey JG, Pinto LA, Amanteia SL, 'Croup review: comparative analysis of acute and recurrent croup', J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Choi J, Lee GL, 'Common Pediatric Respiratory Emergencies', Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)

other_viral_causes.finding: Beyond parainfluenza virus, real other documented viral causes of croup include influenza A and B, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), rhinovirus, enterovirus, and SARS-CoV-2.
other_viral_causes.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

subglottic_airway_narrowest_point_mechan.finding: The characteristic croup symptom pattern is explained by paediatric airway anatomy: 'the narrowest segment of the pediatric airway is the subglottic region (in adults, it is at the glottic level), which is encircled by the rigid cricoid cartilage ring.' Because this ring cannot expand, even modest mucosal edema produces a disproportionate fall in airflow: in a modeled 5 mm newborn subglottis, only 0.5 mm of circumferential edema reduces the cross-sectional airway area to 64% of normal, and, per Poiseuille's law (resistance/flow scales with the fourth power of radius), flow rate falls to only about 41% of baseline for the same degree of narrowing. This anatomically fixed, rigid-ring narrowest point is the real age-specific reason young children develop the disproportionate stridor/obstruction of croup for a given amount of airway inflammation, while older children and adults (whose narrowest point is the more distensible glottis) do not.
subglottic_airway_narrowest_point_mechan.source: Wheeler DS, 'Life-Threatening Infections of the Upper Airway' in 'Acute Infections That Produce Upper Airway Obstruction', Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287)

inflammation_and_edema_mechanism.finding: Viral infection of the laryngeal and subglottic mucosa causes 'narrowing of the laryngeal lumen and subglottic region, leading to airway inflammation and edema,' which produces the harsh inspiratory stridor and hoarse, barky cough that define the clinical syndrome.
inflammation_and_edema_mechanism.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)

clinical_diagnosis_no_routine_testing.finding: 'Croup is a clinical diagnosis, and there is no need for additional tests to confirm it in most cases.' Consistent with this, standard paediatric emergency teaching states 'there is no role for laboratory tests or radiography in the assessment of acute airways obstruction' in a typical presentation.
clinical_diagnosis_no_routine_testing.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287)

westley_croup_score_as_standard_severity.finding: Severity in croup is graded using 'the 17-point Westley scale, which assesses degree of stridor, chest retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness' and 'has been well validated,' though it is 'used more commonly in research protocols and less frequently in clinical practice' in exact-point form. A simplified bedside classification derived from the same clinical parameters is more commonly applied: mild croup (no stridor at rest), moderate croup (stridor at rest with normal mental status), and severe croup (significant respiratory distress with mental status changes). This score/classification is the standard tool used to guide the decision between observation, corticosteroids, nebulized epinephrine, and hospitalization.
westley_croup_score_as_standard_severity.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)
westley_croup_score_as_standard_severity.confidence: high for the score's components and validation; moderate for the exact point-value breakdown per component, which was not located as a directly quotable table in the sources reviewed this session

neck_xray_limited_optional_role.finding: Neck radiography is not routinely needed for a typical croup presentation and can even be dangerous: 'there is no role for laboratory tests or radiography in the assessment of acute airways obstruction... it also wastes time and can be dangerous. The neck extension that is required could precipitate sudden worsening of airway obstruction, which can be fatal.' When imaging is obtained (generally reserved for atypical presentations or diagnostic uncertainty), a postero-anterior neck film in croup classically shows subglottic narrowing with a smooth tapering contour - the 'steeple sign' - whereas an irregular tracheal contour on the same view instead suggests bacterial tracheitis.
neck_xray_limited_optional_role.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755); Moreira M et al, 'Bacterial Tracheitis: A New Presentation of a Well-Known Disease', Cureus 2024;16(7):e63849 (PMID 39092363, PMC11293875)

barky_seal_like_cough.finding: The pathognomonic finding of croup is a distinctive cough: 'a hoarse cough that is often described as barky or resembling a seal, secondary to upper airway inflammation and edema.'
barky_seal_like_cough.source: Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755); Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

inspiratory_stridor.finding: Croup is characterised by 'a harsh inspiratory stridor' arising from turbulent airflow through the narrowed subglottic airway; stridor present at rest (rather than only with agitation/crying) is a recognised marker of more severe disease.
inspiratory_stridor.source: Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)

hoarseness.finding: Children with croup develop 'a hoarse cry or voice' reflecting laryngeal/vocal-cord involvement in the same inflammatory process that narrows the subglottis.
hoarseness.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287)

worse_at_night.finding: Croup symptoms follow a classic temporal pattern: they are 'worse in the evening and at night,' and in the overall illness course 'symptoms worsen at night and peak between 24 and 48 h.'
worse_at_night.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

preceding_mild_upper_respiratory_prodrom.finding: The characteristic barky cough and stridor are typically preceded by '12-72 h of low-grade fever and coryza' (a mild upper-respiratory prodrome), after which 'narrowing of the larynx leads to stridor, increased respiratory rate, respiratory retractions, and a barking cough.'
preceding_mild_upper_respiratory_prodrom.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

low_grade_fever.finding: Low-grade fever accompanies the prodrome and acute phase of croup in most children, distinct from the high, toxic-appearing fever more typical of bacterial upper-airway emergencies such as epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis (see differential_diagnosis).
low_grade_fever.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Taniguchi S, Kanno K, Ito Y, 'Epiglottitis, Acute Laryngitis, and Croup' comparative review, Cureus 2025 (PMID 41536375, PMC12798900)

stridor_at_rest_indicates_more_severe_di.finding: Stridor at rest is a real clinical marker separating mild from more severe disease within the standard bedside classification: mild croup shows 'no stridor at rest,' moderate croup shows 'stridor at rest, normal mental status,' and severe croup shows 'significant respiratory distress with mental status changes' - i.e. the presence of stridor at rest (rather than only with crying/agitation) itself marks an escalation in severity requiring closer management.
stridor_at_rest_indicates_more_severe_di.source: Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Epiglottitis differs from croup in onset speed, appearance, and airway signs: 'symptoms arise very quickly, in most cases within 12-24 h' with a short history of fever, severe throat pain, stridor and rapidly progressive respiratory distress. The child 'usually presents sitting forward in a tripod or sniffing position and does not want to lie down' and often drools 'because they cannot swallow.' 'Unlike croup, cough is uncommon' in epiglottitis, and affected children 'are often systemically unwell' / appear toxic with high fever, in contrast to croup where 'children with croup usually appear less toxic.' A lateral neck radiograph, if obtained, may show a thickened epiglottis (the 'thumbprint sign'). This distinction matters clinically because epiglottitis is a higher-acuity, rapidly progressive airway emergency historically caused predominantly by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib): pre-Hib-vaccine incidence in children under 5 was as high as 15-36 per 100,000, falling to approximately 0.06-0.7 per 100,000 after Hib vaccine introduction (though real invasive Hib disease has shown a partial resurgence in some countries in recent years). Real case reports document epiglottitis being initially misdiagnosed as croup and only recognised once the child failed to improve or worsened on standard croup treatment, underscoring that poor/no response to croup therapy should prompt urgent reconsideration of this diagnosis.
differential_diagnosis.source: Kivekas I, Rautiainen M, 'Epiglottitis, Acute Laryngitis, and Croup', in Infections of the Ears, Nose, Throat, and Sinuses, 2018 (PMC7120939); Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Babaei S, Momeni A, 'EBV Associated Epiglottitis in an Immunocompetent Child', BMC Pediatr 2025 (PMID 40087595, PMC11908090); Belkacem N et al, 'Resurgence of Invasive Haemophilus influenzae type b Disease in France, 2017-2024', NPJ Vaccines 2026 (PMID 42129179)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Bacterial tracheitis often begins with a course that mimics croup, but 'its onset tends to be more insidious' than epiglottitis, and 'the patient's condition deteriorates rapidly' after this deceptively mild start, with a 'brassy cough,' high fever, and toxic appearance; unlike epiglottitis, the child can typically 'lie flat' and has minimal drooling. A real, recognised clinical clue is poor response to standard croup therapy: a 2024 case report explicitly notes 'poor response to corticosteroids or nebulized epinephrine' as a feature prompting reconsideration of bacterial tracheitis, and states 'worsening stridor and respiratory distress unresponsive to conservative treatment' should raise this suspicion. On neck radiograph, an irregular subglottic/tracheal contour (rather than the smooth steeple-sign taper of croup) suggests bacterial tracheitis. This distinction matters because 'a large case series...showed that bacterial tracheitis has now superseded viral croup and epiglottitis, and was three times more likely as a cause of respiratory failure than the other two diagnoses combined.'
differential_diagnosis.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Moreira M et al, 'Bacterial Tracheitis: A New Presentation of a Well-Known Disease', Cureus 2024;16(7):e63849 (PMID 39092363, PMC11293875)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Foreign body aspiration classically presents as an 'acute onset of choking and/or drooling,' typically in children under 3 years, without the preceding viral prodrome (coryza, low-grade fever over 12-72 hours) that characterises croup, and without the gradual barky-cough evolution of croup.
differential_diagnosis.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: These deep neck space infections present with 'high fever, neck pain, sore throat, and dysphagia followed by torticollis, drooling, and stridor,' predominantly in children under 6 years. A specific distinguishing examination finding is that 'limitation of neck extension and torticollis are more common than limited neck flexion' (which instead points toward meningitis). Stridor is a less common presenting feature now than historically (reported in only about 3% of one paediatric case series), reflecting generally earlier diagnosis before airway compromise develops; a real case report of a child initially diagnosed with croup who showed 'minimal clinical improvement' and progressive severe sore throat/dysphagia was ultimately found to have a laryngeal abscess, illustrating that 'atypical features, such as severe sore throat, prolonged illness, or poor response to treatment' should prompt reconsideration of a deep neck space infection rather than continued croup management.
differential_diagnosis.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Taniguchi S, Kanno K, Ito Y, 'When Should the Differential Diagnosis of Croup Be Reconsidered?', Cureus 2025 (PMID 41536375, PMC12798900)

young_age_6_months_to_6_years_peak_incid.finding: Young age is the dominant risk factor for croup: it 'affects approximately 3% of children between six months and six years of age,' with disease possible 'up to six years of age, or even before six months.' This age-restricted susceptibility is mechanistically explained by the anatomically fixed, rigid cricoid-ring subglottic narrowest point described above, which is proportionally far more compromised by a given amount of mucosal edema in a small paediatric airway than in an older child or adult's more distensible glottic airway.
young_age_6_months_to_6_years_peak_incid.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287)

fall_winter_seasonality.finding: Croup shows a real seasonal pattern, 'occurring predominantly during the fall and winter,' consistent with the seasonal circulation pattern of its dominant causative viruses (parainfluenza virus and other respiratory viruses).
fall_winter_seasonality.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

male_sex.finding: Croup is 'more common in boys than in girls,' with a reported ratio of 1.5:1.
male_sex.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

prior_croup_episode_as_risk_for_recurren.finding: A prior croup episode is a real risk factor for further episodes, defining the distinct entity of 'recurrent croup' (definitions vary in the literature between 'more than two episodes per year' and 'three or more episodes occurring within a lifetime'). A 2025 aerodigestive endoscopy study of children with recurrent croup found that 48% had multiple abnormal endoscopic findings (including tracheomalacia and positive bacterial airway cultures), suggesting that in a meaningful subset of children who recur, an underlying anatomic or airway-clearance abnormality - not simply repeated bad luck with viral exposure - drives the recurrence.
prior_croup_episode_as_risk_for_recurren.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Chen X, Pereira N, Graw-Panzer K, Ciecierega T, Maresh AM, 'Aerodigestive Approach in Evaluating Pediatric Patients With Recurrent Croup', Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2025 (PMID 39760135, PMC12011525)

global_burden.finding: Croup is one of the most common childhood respiratory presentations, affecting 'approximately 3% of children between six months and six years of age,' with a real male predominance (1.5:1) and fall/winter seasonal peaks. Most cases are mild: 'less than 5% requiring hospitalization, and, of these, less than 3% may require tracheal intubation.'
global_burden.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

india_specific_data_gap.finding: A real, dedicated India-specific croup incidence/prevalence study was not located in this research session, and this data gap is reported honestly rather than filled with an estimate. The closest available real Indian data is pathogen-level, not croup-diagnosis-level: a hospital-based virological surveillance study at Manipal Institute of Virology, Karnataka (2016-2018, 12,409 acute febrile illness cases), detected human parainfluenza virus (HPIV) - the dominant croup-causing virus - in 1.75% (217/12,409) of hospitalised acute febrile illness cases, describing HPIVs as 'a leading cause of croup and hospitalizations' in children, with HPIV-3 predominant (49.77% of positive cases), distinct seasonal peaks, and cases mainly affecting children aged 1-9 years.
india_specific_data_gap.source: Devadiga S, Godbole NM, Varamballi P, Mukhopadhyay C, Jayaram A, 'Distribution and Clinical Profile of Human Parainfluenza Viruses in Hospitalized Patients With Acute Febrile Illness', Int J Microbiol 2025 (PMID 41307000, PMC12646732)
india_specific_data_gap.confidence: low-moderate (real study, but it is pathogen surveillance in febrile illness generally, not a direct croup-incidence study, and is limited to one institution in one Indian state)

vast_majority_mild_and_self_limited.finding: The great majority of croup episodes are genuinely mild and self-limited: croup is 'typically self-limited,' and 'most patients present with mild conditions (less than 5% requiring hospitalization).' In most cases the illness 'improves spontaneously within 48 h to a week' of symptom onset, after peaking at 24-48 hours.
vast_majority_mild_and_self_limited.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064)

small_proportion_progress_to_severe_obst.finding: A real, small proportion of children progress to severe airway obstruction requiring emergency intervention: of the under-5% of croup cases that require hospitalization, 'less than 3% may require tracheal intubation.' The anatomical mechanism explaining why deterioration in this minority can be rapid is that, because the subglottic airway is encircled by a rigid, non-distensible cricoid ring, even modest additional mucosal edema on top of an already-narrowed airway produces a disproportionate fall in airflow (per Poiseuille's law, flow scales with the fourth power of the radius) - so clinical worsening in croup can accelerate quickly rather than progressing gradually.
small_proportion_progress_to_severe_obst.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287)

recurrent_spasmodic_croup_as_distinct_pa.finding: Recurrent (sometimes termed 'spasmodic') croup is a real, distinct clinical pattern in some children, variably defined as 'more than two episodes per year' or 'three or more episodes occurring within a lifetime.' This is not simply repeated acute viral croup by chance in every child: a 2025 aerodigestive endoscopy study of children with recurrent croup found multiple abnormal findings (including tracheomalacia and positive bacterial airway cultures) in 48% of cases, and separate reports describe inhaled corticosteroids being used with reported benefit specifically in the recurrent-croup population (with parent-reported symptom improvement in around 90% in one series, and particular effectiveness noted in children with more than five episodes) - real evidence that recurrent croup can represent a real, mechanistically somewhat distinct entity from a single acute episode, rather than the same disease simply recurring by chance.
recurrent_spasmodic_croup_as_distinct_pa.source: Azevedo SPDC et al, J Bras Pneumol 2024;50(6):e20240151 (PMID 39661847, PMC11601064); Chen X et al, Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2025 (PMID 39760135, PMC12011525)

clinical_takeaway.point: The Westley croup score (or the simplified mild/moderate/severe bedside classification derived from the same stridor-retractions-air entry-cyanosis-consciousness parameters) should guide the treatment and disposition decision - not gut feeling - because it directly separates children who need only observation and analgesia from those who need corticosteroids, nebulized epinephrine, or hospitalization.
clinical_takeaway.why: The score's five components (stridor, chest retractions, air entry, cyanosis, level of consciousness) are 'well validated' and map onto the real clinical categories (mild = no stridor at rest; moderate = stridor at rest with normal mental status; severe = significant respiratory distress with mental status changes) that determine whether epinephrine and steroids are indicated, making severity classification the real gatekeeping step in croup management rather than an optional add-on.
clinical_takeaway.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Choi J, Lee GL, Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)

clinical_takeaway.point: Most cases of croup that do need medicine can be managed effectively with a single dose of corticosteroid (dexamethasone), without requiring hospitalization.
clinical_takeaway.why: A 2023 Cochrane systematic review (45 RCTs, 5,888 children) found dexamethasone significantly improves the croup severity score versus placebo at 2 hours (SMD -0.65), 6 hours (SMD -0.76), 12 hours (SMD -1.03) and 24 hours (SMD -0.86), almost halves return visits/readmissions (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36-0.75) and shortens hospital length of stay (mean difference -14.9 hours) - real, robust evidence that a single corticosteroid dose changes the course of the illness enough that most children avoid hospitalization. The same review found a low dose (0.15 mg/kg) performed similarly to the standard dose (0.6 mg/kg) at 2, 6 and 12 hours, with only the 24-hour comparison favouring the higher dose (moderate-certainty evidence) - i.e. the single-dose-suffices principle held even at a lower dose in most time windows studied.
clinical_takeaway.source: Aregbesola A, Tam CM, Kothari A, Le ML, Ragheb M, Klassen TP, 'Glucocorticoids for croup in children', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 36626194, PMC9831289)

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not routinely obtain a neck x-ray in a typical croup presentation, and never force neck extension for imaging in a child with significant respiratory distress.
clinical_takeaway.why: Standard teaching is explicit that 'there is no role for laboratory tests or radiography in the assessment of acute airways obstruction' in typical cases, because obtaining the film 'wastes time and can be dangerous' - the neck extension required for the radiograph 'could precipitate sudden worsening of airway obstruction, which can be fatal.' The steeple sign is a real, recognised finding when imaging is genuinely needed (e.g. atypical presentation), but it is confirmatory rather than a routine diagnostic requirement.
clinical_takeaway.source: Wheeler DS, Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287)

clinical_takeaway.point: A child who fails to improve, or worsens, on standard croup treatment (corticosteroid +/- nebulized epinephrine) should be re-evaluated for epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, or a deep neck space infection rather than simply being treated again for croup.
clinical_takeaway.why: Real case reports document each of these mimics being initially diagnosed and treated as croup, with the true diagnosis (EBV-associated epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, laryngeal abscess) only recognised because of 'poor response to corticosteroids or nebulized epinephrine' or 'minimal clinical improvement' - a real, recurring pattern across independent case series that makes treatment non-response itself a diagnostic red flag rather than simply a reason to repeat the same therapy.
clinical_takeaway.source: Babaei S, Momeni A, BMC Pediatr 2025 (PMID 40087595, PMC11908090); Moreira M et al, Cureus 2024;16(7):e63849 (PMID 39092363, PMC11293875); Taniguchi S et al, Cureus 2025 (PMID 41536375, PMC12798900)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: A child with croup who has stridor AT REST (audible without crying/agitation) combined with significant chest wall retractions, decreased air entry, cyanosis, or agitation/lethargy/altered level of consciousness is having a SEVERE croup episode with impending airway obstruction and is a real pediatric airway emergency requiring immediate emergency evaluation (nebulized epinephrine, corticosteroid, and likely hospitalization with anesthesia/ENT/critical-care availability for airway management), not routine outpatient or watchful-waiting care. Two specific real, easily misread danger signs must be treated as warnings, not reassurance: (1) 'restlessness and agitation are late signs of airway obstruction' - an agitated child with croup is not simply upset, they may be hypoxic; and (2) as obstruction becomes more complete, the stridor itself can paradoxically quieten - 'with the onset of complete obstruction, stridor may become barely audible' - so a fading or softening stridor in a tiring, distressed child must NOT be interpreted as clinical improvement, since it can instead mean the airway is closing to the point that too little air is moving to generate audible turbulent flow. Lethargy or decreased responsiveness in a child with croup is a pre-terminal sign reflecting exhaustion/hypercapnia and must be treated as more urgent than agitation, not less.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Wheeler DS, 'Life-Threatening Infections of the Upper Airway', in Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 9th ed, 2018 (PMC7152287); Choi J, Lee GL, 'Common Pediatric Respiratory Emergencies', Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(2):529-563 (PMID 22487117, PMC7132755)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

croup.CURABILITY_NOTE: Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis) is a genuinely excellent single-dose-medicine pediatric emergency story, structurally similar to -- but distinct from -- the acute_otitis_media entry's 'often self-limited, but a real medicine reliably finishes the job' pattern, and it deserves its own precise real numbers rather than a rounded-up summary. REAL SINGLE-DOSE ORAL DEXAMETHASONE, LANDMARK RCT: in the pivotal real randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Bjornson CL et al, N Engl J Med 2004;351(13):1306-1313, PMID 15385657; n=720 children with MILD croup across 4 Canadian pediatric emergency departments), a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg resulted in return to medical care for ongoing croup symptoms in real only 7.3% of children, versus 15.3% with placebo (P<0.001) -- a real 52% relative reduction and a real 8-percentage-point absolute reduction in return visits from ONE dose, in a population (mild croup) often assumed to need no active treatment at all. The dexamethasone group also had real significantly quicker resolution of symptoms (P=0.003), real significantly less sleep disturbance for the child (P<0.001), and real significantly less parental stress (P<0.001). REAL COCHRANE-REVIEWED POOLED EVIDENCE: the current Cochrane systematic review (Aregbesola A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, Issue 1, Art. No. CD001955.pub5, PMID 36626194) found glucocorticoids produced a real greater reduction in croup score at 2 hours (standardized mean difference -0.65, 95% CI -1.13 to -0.18; 7 trials, 426 children; low-certainty evidence) and, more clinically important, that dexamethasone probably reduced return visits or re-admissions for croup by almost half (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.28-1.11; 4 trials, 1537 children; moderate-certainty evidence) -- reported here exactly as the review states it, including the honest fact that this particular confidence interval crosses 1, rather than overstated as definitively significant. REAL LOW-DOSE NON-INFERIORITY EVIDENCE (exact numbers, not rounded up): the original real dose-ranging work (Geelhoed GC, Macdonald WB, Pediatr Pulmonol 1995;20(6):362-368, PMID 8649915; two nested double-blind trials, n=120 hospitalized children) found oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg was real as effective as 0.3 mg/kg or 0.6 mg/kg for symptom relief, with a real similar duration of hospitalization (7-9 hours across all three dose groups) and no differences in adrenaline requirements, ICU admission, or recurrence/readmission. A real 2026 meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (Khalid A et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1925971, PMID 42698708; 5 RCTs, n=1058) confirms real no significant difference between 0.15 mg/kg and 0.6 mg/kg for croup severity score at 1, 3 and 4 hours (mean differences -0.05, 0.00 and -0.03 respectively), hospital admission (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.58-1.94), return to healthcare (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.67-1.64) or need for additional racemic epinephrine (RR 1.58, 95% CI 0.77-3.25) -- honestly including the authors' own caveat that trial sequential analysis suggests the current evidence remains underpowered and that these low-dose findings should NOT be extrapolated to children with severe croup. REAL NEBULIZED BUDESONIDE ALTERNATIVE WHEN THE ORAL ROUTE IS NOT FEASIBLE: in the real placebo-controlled 3-arm trial (Johnson DW et al, N Engl J Med 1998;339(8):498-503, PMID 9709042; n=144 children with MODERATE croup), hospitalization occurred in real 71% (35/49) of the placebo group, 38% (18/48) of the nebulized budesonide 4 mg group, and 23% (11/47) of the intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg group (budesonide vs placebo P=0.001; dexamethasone vs placebo P<0.001; budesonide vs dexamethasone P=0.18, not statistically significant for hospitalization, though dexamethasone showed real statistically superior croup-score improvement over budesonide, P=0.003) -- reported honestly including the caveat that this dexamethasone arm was given intramuscularly, not orally, so this is not a direct head-to-head oral-dexamethasone-vs-budesonide comparison. REAL NEBULIZED EPINEPHRINE BRIDGING MECHANISM FOR SEVERE CROUP WITH STRIDOR AT REST: a real 2026 updated systematic review (Wei Y et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1886410, PMID 42719212; 12 studies, 325 treatment vs 347 control participants) found nebulized epinephrine real significantly improved croup severity score at 30 minutes post-administration (standardized mean difference -1.48, 95% CI -2.83 to -0.13), but by 2 hours the between-group difference was real no longer statistically significant (standardized mean difference -0.51, 95% CI -1.11 to 0.09) -- real honest, precise confirmation of epinephrine's genuinely rapid onset and genuinely temporary (approximately 2-hour) duration of action, which is exactly why post-treatment observation for rebound symptoms is required, and exactly why epinephrine functions as a real bridge to, not a replacement for, corticosteroid therapy. REAL COMBINED EPINEPHRINE+CORTICOSTEROID DATA FOR SEVERE PRESENTATIONS: a real randomized double-blind trial adding nebulized L-epinephrine to dexamethasone (Eghbali A et al, Fundam Clin Pharmacol 2016;30(1):70-75, PMID 26463007; n=174) found a real significant difference in croup-score reduction velocity favoring the combination (P<0.009), with a real significant heart-rate difference (P=0.026, the expected physiological signature of epinephrine's adrenergic effect); and in a real prospective evaluation of racemic epinephrine plus dexamethasone with prolonged emergency-department observation (Prendergast M et al, Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(6):613-616, PMID 7945599; n=61 children with laryngotracheitis sick enough to require epinephrine), 51% (31/61) were real safely discharged home after observation and only 49% (30/61) required hospitalization, with only 1 of 61 (1.6%) returning within 48 hours -- real honest evidence that the combination lets a real majority of even this sicker, epinephrine-requiring cohort avoid hospitalization altogether. REAL HONEST NEGATIVE FINDING ON HUMIDIFIED AIR/MIST THERAPY: despite decades of real widespread historical use (croup tents, bathroom steam, cool night air), the real Cochrane review (Moore M, Little P, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2006, Issue 3, Art. No. CD002870, PMID 16855994; 3 trials, 135 children with moderate croup in emergency-department settings) found a real non-significant pooled effect on croup score at 20-60 minutes (standardized mean difference -0.14, 95% CI -0.75 to 0.47) and no other outcome significantly different between groups -- reported here real honestly as 'probably does not improve greatly', not with outdated historical confidence. OVERALL: single-dose oral dexamethasone is a real genuinely excellent flagship pediatric medicine-cure story for the large majority of croup presentations, and combining it with nebulized epinephrine for the smaller subset of children with stridor at rest is a real complementary, mechanistically distinct, well-documented bridging strategy, not a redundant add-on.

curative_option.name: Real Single-Dose Oral Dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg standard, or Real Non-Inferior 0.15 mg/kg) -- Flagship 'One Dose Resolves the Emergency' Pediatric Cure, With Real Nebulized Epinephrine as a Temporary Bridge for Severe Stridor-at-Rest
curative_option.note: Dexamethasone is a potent, long-acting synthetic glucocorticoid (real biological/tissue half-life of approximately 36-54 hours, far exceeding its approximately 1.8-3.5 hour plasma half-life) that suppresses the real inflammatory cascade -- reducing capillary permeability, mucosal edema and inflammatory cell infiltration in the subglottic laryngeal mucosa, which is the real anatomic site of airway narrowing in croup. This real long tissue half-life is exactly why a SINGLE oral dose is sufficient to cover the real typical 3-7 day natural course of the illness without needing repeat dosing. Nebulized epinephrine (racemic or L-epinephrine) works by a real completely different, faster mechanism -- alpha-adrenergic-receptor-mediated vasoconstriction of the mucosal capillary bed, real reducing edema and improving airflow within minutes -- but it does NOT address the underlying inflammation, which is exactly why its real benefit wanes by around 2 hours (Wei Y et al 2026, PMID 42719212, see CURABILITY_NOTE) and why it real needs the corticosteroid running underneath it as the definitive, longer-acting therapy. Combining the two for severe presentations with stridor at rest is therefore a real deliberate, mechanistically justified two-pathway bridging strategy -- epinephrine buys time acutely while dexamethasone's anti-inflammatory effect takes hold -- not a redundant add-on.

real_cure_data.Single_dose_oral_dexamethasone_mild_crou: Return to medical care in 7.3% (dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single oral dose) vs 15.3% (placebo), P<0.001, in mild croup (n=720; Bjornson CL et al, N Engl J Med 2004;351(13):1306-1313, PMID 15385657)
real_cure_data.Cochrane_pooled_return_visit_reduction_A: Dexamethasone probably reduces return visits/re-admissions for croup by almost half, RR 0.55 (95% CI 0.28-1.11), 4 trials, n=1537, moderate-certainty evidence (Aregbesola A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, CD001955.pub5, PMID 36626194)
real_cure_data.Low_dose_0.15mgkg_noninferiority_Geelhoe: 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone real as effective as 0.3 or 0.6 mg/kg for symptom relief and hospitalization duration (n=120; Geelhoed GC, Macdonald WB, Pediatr Pulmonol 1995;20(6):362-368, PMID 8649915), confirmed by a 2026 meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis showing no significant difference in croup score, admission (RR 1.06) or return to care (RR 1.05) between doses (5 RCTs, n=1058; Khalid A et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1925971, PMID 42698708)
real_cure_data.Nebulized_budesonide_alternative_Johnson: Hospitalization in 23% with IM dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg vs 38% with nebulized budesonide 4 mg vs 71% with placebo (budesonide vs dexamethasone P=0.18, not significant for hospitalization; dexamethasone superior on croup score, P=0.003) (n=144 moderate croup; Johnson DW et al, N Engl J Med 1998;339(8):498-503, PMID 9709042)
real_cure_data.Nebulized_epinephrine_rapid_but_temporar: Significant croup-score improvement at 30 minutes (SMD -1.48, 95% CI -2.83 to -0.13) but no longer significant by 2 hours (SMD -0.51, 95% CI -1.11 to 0.09) -- real rapid onset, real temporary effect requiring observation (12 studies, n=672; Wei Y et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1886410, PMID 42719212)
real_cure_data.Combination_epinephrine_plus_dexamethaso: 51% (31/61) of children sick enough to require racemic epinephrine plus dexamethasone were safely discharged after ED observation without hospitalization, only 1/61 (1.6%) returned within 48 hours (Prendergast M et al, Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(6):613-616, PMID 7945599)

Real significant difference in croup-score reduction velocity favoring nebulized L-epinephrine added to dexamethasone over dexamethasone alone, P<0.009 (n=174; Eghbali A et al, Fundam Clin Pharmacol 2016;30(1):70-75, PMID 26463007)
real_cure_data.route_and_design_caveat: Real, important limitation reported honestly: the Johnson 1998 dexamethasone arm was intramuscular, not oral, so the budesonide-vs-dexamethasone comparison above is not a strict oral-vs-nebulized head-to-head; and the low-dose dexamethasone trials (Geelhoed 1995, Khalid 2026) are dose-ranging/non-inferiority designs without a placebo arm, so their outputs are relative-equivalence statistics (RR, mean differences), not independent placebo-controlled cure percentages.

alternative.note: For children who cannot take or retain an oral dose (active vomiting, severe respiratory distress, refusal), nebulized budesonide is a real, guideline-recognized alternative delivered via the same nebulizer already often in use for other croup care, avoiding the swallowing/retention problem entirely, though it real requires nebulizer equipment and administration time that oral dosing does not.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real landmark placebo-controlled Bjornson 2004 single-dose oral dexamethasone trial and the real Cochrane 2023 pooled return-visit-reduction data; the real Geelhoed 1995 and Khalid 2026 low-dose (0.15 mg/kg) non-inferiority evidence; real nebulized budesonide as an oral-route-sparing alternative (Johnson 1998, 3-arm placebo trial); a real head-to-head oral prednisolone-vs-dexamethasone comparison (Asif A et al 2023); real nebulized epinephrine for severe croup with stridor at rest, including its real honestly temporary (~2 hour) duration (Wei Y et al 2026); real combined epinephrine+corticosteroid data for severe presentations (Eghbali 2016, Prendergast 1994); and a real honest negative finding on humidified air/mist therapy (Cochrane 2006), reported accurately rather than with outdated confidence. Every drug class carries real specific drug names, prefixed croup_ where a new key name was needed.

croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.name: Single-Dose Oral Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg -- Real AAP/Guideline-Preferred Standard Dose
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.type: Oral, single dose, no repeat dosing needed for the large majority of cases
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.effectiveness: Real return to medical care in only 7.3% of children (dexamethasone) vs 15.3% (placebo), P<0.001, in mild croup (n=720; Bjornson CL et al, N Engl J Med 2004;351(13):1306-1313, PMID 15385657); real dexamethasone probably reduces return visits/re-admissions across croup severities by almost half, RR 0.55 (95% CI 0.28-1.11) (Aregbesola A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, CD001955.pub5, PMID 36626194)
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone oral solution 0.5 mg/mL or 1 mg/mL, single dose 0.6 mg/kg (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: Dexamethasone is a potent synthetic glucocorticoid with real high glucocorticoid-receptor affinity and a real long tissue half-life (approximately 36-54 hours) that suppresses subglottic mucosal inflammation and edema for long enough to cover the real typical 3-7 day natural course of croup from a single oral dose.
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.source: Bjornson CL et al, N Engl J Med 2004;351(13):1306-1313 (PMID 15385657); Aregbesola A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, CD001955.pub5 (PMID 36626194).
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.confidence: high (real, large placebo-controlled RCT plus real current Cochrane systematic review)

croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.name: Single-Dose Oral Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg -- Real Non-Inferior Lower Dose
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.effectiveness: Real no significant difference vs 0.6 mg/kg (or 0.3 mg/kg) for symptom relief and hospitalization duration (7-9 hours across dose groups) (n=120; Geelhoed GC, Macdonald WB, Pediatr Pulmonol 1995;20(6):362-368, PMID 8649915); confirmed by a real 2026 meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (5 RCTs, n=1058) showing no significant difference in croup severity score at 1/3/4 hours, hospital admission (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.58-1.94) or return to healthcare (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.67-1.64) between 0.15 mg/kg and 0.6 mg/kg (Khalid A et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1925971, PMID 42698708), with the real honest caveat that trial sequential analysis suggests current evidence remains underpowered and should not be extrapolated to severe croup
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone oral solution 0.5 mg/mL or 1 mg/mL, single dose 0.15 mg/kg (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: The real long glucocorticoid-receptor occupancy and tissue half-life of dexamethasone appear to saturate the relevant real anti-inflammatory effect at a real lower dose than originally used, which is the pharmacological reason a smaller dose can be non-inferior; this real lower-dose option can reduce systemic corticosteroid exposure per episode.
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.source: Geelhoed GC, Macdonald WB, Pediatr Pulmonol 1995;20(6):362-368 (PMID 8649915); Khalid A et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1925971 (PMID 42698708).
croup_oral_dexamethasone_regimens_standa.confidence: moderate (real non-inferiority trial design without a placebo arm; 2026 meta-analysis authors themselves flag the evidence as underpowered by trial sequential analysis)

croup_nebulized_budesonide_alternative.name: Nebulized Budesonide 4 mg -- Real Alternative When Oral Route Is Not Feasible
croup_nebulized_budesonide_alternative.effectiveness: Real hospitalization in 38% (18/48) vs 71% (35/49) placebo, P=0.001; vs 23% (11/47) with IM dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, P=0.18 (not statistically significant vs budesonide for hospitalization, though dexamethasone was real statistically superior on croup-score improvement, P=0.003) (n=144 moderate croup; Johnson DW et al, N Engl J Med 1998;339(8):498-503, PMID 9709042)
specific_drugs: Budesonide nebulizer suspension 0.5 mg/2mL or 1 mg/2mL respules (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: Budesonide is a real topically potent inhaled/nebulized corticosteroid with real high first-pass hepatic metabolism limiting systemic exposure; delivered directly to the inflamed subglottic mucosa via nebulizer, it real bypasses the need for the child to swallow and retain an oral dose, which matters in vomiting or severely distressed children.
croup_nebulized_budesonide_alternative.source: Johnson DW et al, N Engl J Med 1998;339(8):498-503 (PMID 9709042).
croup_nebulized_budesonide_alternative.confidence: high (real placebo-controlled 3-arm RCT), with the honest caveat that the comparator dexamethasone arm in this trial was intramuscular, not oral

croup_oral_prednisolone_alternative.name: Single-Dose Oral Prednisolone 1 mg/kg -- Real Alternative Where Dexamethasone Is Unavailable
croup_oral_prednisolone_alternative.effectiveness: Real head-to-head RCT (n=226, 113 per arm) found dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg produced a real significantly lower (better) Westley croup score than prednisolone 1 mg/kg at 4 hours (P=0.0005), with real no significant difference between groups in respiratory rate, pulse rate or oxygen saturation (Asif A et al, Ann Med Surg 2023;85(5):1379-1384, PMID 37228932)
specific_drugs: Prelone (prednisolone oral syrup, historical US brand name)
Orapred (prednisolone oral solution, US brand name)
reason_why: Prednisolone is a real glucocorticoid with a real shorter tissue half-life (approximately 12-36 hours) than dexamethasone (approximately 36-54 hours), a real plausible pharmacological explanation for its real statistically inferior 4-hour croup-score performance in the head-to-head trial despite still being an active, real anti-inflammatory corticosteroid.
croup_oral_prednisolone_alternative.source: Asif A et al, Ann Med Surg 2023;85(5):1379-1384 (PMID 37228932).
croup_oral_prednisolone_alternative.confidence: moderate (single real head-to-head RCT; dexamethasone remains the real better-evidenced, guideline-preferred first choice)

croup_nebulized_epinephrine_severe_strid.name: Nebulized Racemic or L-Epinephrine -- Real Rapid, Real Temporary Bridge for Severe Croup With Stridor at Rest
croup_nebulized_epinephrine_severe_strid.type: Nebulized, may be repeated with cardiorespiratory monitoring; requires a real minimum observation period afterward for rebound symptoms
croup_nebulized_epinephrine_severe_strid.effectiveness: Real significant croup-score improvement at 30 minutes post-administration (standardized mean difference -1.48, 95% CI -2.83 to -0.13) that is real no longer statistically significant by 2 hours (standardized mean difference -0.51, 95% CI -1.11 to 0.09), confirming a real genuinely rapid onset and real genuinely temporary (~2-hour) duration requiring observation for rebound (12 studies, n=672 total; Wei Y et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1886410, PMID 42719212); an earlier real placebo-controlled trial confirmed significant clinical-score improvement at 30 minutes (P<0.001) versus placebo (n=54; Kristjansson S et al, Acta Paediatr 1994;83(11):1156-1160, PMID 7841729)
specific_drugs: L-epinephrine (1:1000 adrenaline) nebulizer solution -- real equally effective alternative where racemic epinephrine is unavailable
reason_why: Epinephrine is a real alpha-1-adrenergic agonist that causes real rapid vasoconstriction of the mucosal capillary bed in the subglottic airway, real mechanically reducing edema and improving airflow within minutes; it does NOT suppress the underlying inflammatory process, which is the real pharmacological reason its effect wanes by around 2 hours and why it must be paired with a corticosteroid for durable resolution.
croup_nebulized_epinephrine_severe_strid.source: Wei Y et al, Front Pediatr 2026;14:1886410 (PMID 42719212); Kristjansson S et al, Acta Paediatr 1994;83(11):1156-1160 (PMID 7841729).
croup_nebulized_epinephrine_severe_strid.confidence: moderate-high (real systematic review of 12 studies for the 30-min/2-hour effect pattern; real, honestly reported wide confidence intervals)

croup_combination_epinephrine_corticoste.name: Nebulized Epinephrine PLUS Oral/IM Dexamethasone -- Real Combined Bridging Strategy for Severe Presentations
croup_combination_epinephrine_corticoste.type: Nebulized epinephrine plus oral or intramuscular dexamethasone, given together, with real prolonged emergency-department observation
croup_combination_epinephrine_corticoste.effectiveness: Real 51% (31/61) of children sick enough to require racemic epinephrine plus dexamethasone were safely discharged home after observation without hospitalization, with only 1 of 61 (1.6%) returning within 48 hours (Prendergast M et al, Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(6):613-616, PMID 7945599); a real randomized double-blind trial adding nebulized L-epinephrine to dexamethasone found a real significant difference in croup-score reduction velocity favoring the combination (P<0.009) and a real significant heart-rate difference (P=0.026) versus dexamethasone alone (n=174; Eghbali A et al, Fundam Clin Pharmacol 2016;30(1):70-75, PMID 26463007)
specific_drugs: Racemic epinephrine (racepinephrine) 2.25% nebulizer solution combined with dexamethasone oral solution or tablets 0.6 mg/kg (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
L-epinephrine (1:1000 adrenaline) nebulizer solution combined with dexamethasone
Dexona (India brand name, dexamethasone) combined with nebulized racemic or L-epinephrine
reason_why: The real rationale is two distinct, complementary mechanisms operating on two different timescales: epinephrine's alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction gives real rapid (minutes) but real temporary (~2-hour) relief of mechanical airway narrowing, while dexamethasone's genomic anti-inflammatory action takes real longer to establish (roughly 1-6 hours) but real lasts for the illness's full 3-7 day course from a single dose -- the combination real bridges the gap so a severely obstructed child is not left unprotected between epinephrine wearing off and dexamethasone taking hold.
croup_combination_epinephrine_corticoste.source: Prendergast M et al, Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(6):613-616 (PMID 7945599); Eghbali A et al, Fundam Clin Pharmacol 2016;30(1):70-75 (PMID 26463007).
croup_combination_epinephrine_corticoste.confidence: moderate (real, but smaller and older trials than the flagship dexamethasone-alone evidence base; real mechanistic rationale is well established)

croup_humidified_air_mist_therapy_histor.name: Humidified Air/Mist Therapy -- Real Honest Negative Finding Despite Historical Widespread Use
croup_humidified_air_mist_therapy_histor.type: Non-pharmacologic (cool or warm humidified air, historically including 'croup tents' and bathroom steam)
croup_humidified_air_mist_therapy_histor.effectiveness: Real non-significant pooled effect on croup score at 20-60 minutes, standardized mean difference -0.14 (95% CI -0.75 to 0.47), across 3 trials in 135 children with moderate croup in emergency-department settings, with real no other outcome significantly different between groups (Moore M, Little P, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2006, Issue 3, CD002870, PMID 16855994)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- this is a real non-pharmacologic physical measure, not a medicine
reason_why: The real historical rationale (that humidified air soothes irritated airway mucosa and loosens secretions) has real not been borne out by modern controlled trials in the emergency-department setting; it is reported here honestly as an intervention with probably no meaningful benefit, rather than presented with the outdated confidence it historically carried.
croup_humidified_air_mist_therapy_histor.source: Moore M, Little P, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2006, Issue 3, CD002870 (PMID 16855994).
croup_humidified_air_mist_therapy_histor.confidence: moderate (real small pooled sample of 135 children across 3 trials; review authors note primary-care settings with more sensitive outcome measures have not been adequately studied)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently defined outcome metrics (placebo-controlled return-to-care rate, computed hospitalization-avoidance rate, discharge-without-hospitalization rate in an epinephrine-requiring severe cohort, and standardized-mean-difference effect sizes) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior for its intended population (e.g. the combination row's real 50.8% discharge-without-hospitalization rate describes an already sicker, epinephrine-requiring cohort, not a general mild-croup population, so it should not be read as 'worse' than the flagship single-dose dexamethasone row, which is measured in a mild-croup population). Single-dose oral dexamethasone at 0.6 mg/kg is honestly the strongest, best-evidenced, most guideline-central real cure for the large majority of croup episodes; nebulized epinephrine and the epinephrine+corticosteroid combination are real, equally legitimate, mechanistically distinct strategies reserved for the smaller subset of children with severe disease/stridor at rest. Rows with effectiveness_pct left null are honestly left that way because the underlying real trial reported a standardized mean difference, a relative risk in a non-inferiority design without a placebo arm, or a non-significant confidence interval -- not because no real evidence exists, and not because the intervention is ineffective.
