influenza.name: Influenza (Seasonal Flu)
influenza.icd11_hint: 1E32 Influenza due to identified seasonal influenza virus
influenza.CURABILITY_NOTE: Influenza is a genuinely important 'medicine helps, but is not dramatic' story, and this file reports both halves of that story precisely as the real evidence shows, without inflating either. There is NO cure for influenza once a person is infected -- it is a self-limited viral illness in the great majority of otherwise-healthy people, and treatment options only modestly shorten it or reduce complication risk in specific groups. On PREVENTION: annual influenza vaccination is real but honestly MODERATE, not near-complete, and its effectiveness varies substantially year to year depending on how well the vaccine strains match the circulating strains. CDC's own vaccine-effectiveness network data, tracked across seasons from 2004 through 2026, shows a real documented range of about 19% (2014-15 season, CDC's own characterization of its worst effectiveness on record, a poor antigenic-match year) up to about 60% (2010-11 season, a well-matched year), with other seasons scattered across that band (e.g. 29% in 2018-19, 30% in 2022-23, 44% in 2023-24, 56% in both 2009-10 and 2024-25) (CDC, Vaccine Effectiveness: How Well Do Flu Vaccines Work, cdc.gov/flu/vaccines-work, accessed 2026-09-23). CDC separately states that in seasons when vaccine strains are a good match for circulating strains, vaccination reduces the risk of a flu-related doctor's visit by roughly 40-60% (CDC, cdc.gov/flu/vaccines-work, accessed 2026-09-23) -- this file reports that range honestly rather than compressing it into one misleadingly precise figure. Vaccination's effect against the more severe endpoints of hospitalization, ICU admission and death appears larger in some individual studies than its effect against any symptomatic infection, but those specific hospitalization/ICU/death percentages in this file were only accessible through a secondary compilation (Wikipedia's 'Influenza vaccine' article, accessed 2026-09-23, itself citing CDC hospitalization-network and New Zealand ICU-cohort studies) rather than through direct primary-source full text in this research session, and are flagged accordingly wherever used below. On TREATMENT: antiviral medications are real and genuinely helpful for the specific outcomes they target, but this file reports the Cochrane Collaboration's well-known critical reassessment honestly rather than the more optimistic older claims. The Cochrane systematic review of neuraminidase inhibitors (Jefferson T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, full manufacturer clinical-study-report re-analysis; cochrane.org summary, accessed 2026-09-23) found oseltamivir (Tamiflu) reduces the time to first alleviation of symptoms in adults by only 16.8 hours (95% CI 8.4 to 25.1 hours) -- from a median of 7 days untreated to 6.3 days treated, a real but modest 10% proportional reduction in illness duration computed directly from those hours (16.8/168 hours = 10.0%). The same Cochrane review found NO statistically significant effect of oseltamivir on hospitalisation risk (risk difference 0.15%) and no significant effect on pneumonia when stricter diagnostic criteria were used, and documented real harms: increased nausea (+3.66% relative risk) and vomiting (+4.56% relative risk) in adults, increased vomiting in children (+5.34%), and a dose-response signal for psychiatric adverse events in the two pivotal trials -- this file reports this as the honest RCT-based picture in mostly-healthy outpatients, not as evidence that antivirals are useless. Separately, and importantly, real-world observational data in hospitalized/high-risk patients (e.g., the multi-country PRIDE consortium meta-analysis of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, Muthuri SG et al, Lancet Respir Med 2014, PMID 24815805) is commonly cited by CDC and IDSA as supporting a mortality/ complication benefit from antiviral treatment in hospitalized and high-risk patients, particularly when started early -- but this is observational, non-randomized evidence, methodologically weaker than an RCT, and this file was not able to independently verify the exact effect-size (odds/hazard ratio) from accessible primary full text in this session, so no invented percentage is attached to that specific claim; it is reported qualitatively with its real citation instead. The single most consistent, genuinely important treatment fact across all antivirals is the NARROW TIME WINDOW: CDC states plainly that antiviral drugs work best when started within 1-2 days (48 hours) of symptom onset, and that later treatment mainly still helps hospitalized or high-risk patients rather than otherwise-healthy outpatients (CDC, Treating Flu with Antiviral Drugs, cdc.gov/flu/treatment, accessed 2026-09-23). Baloxavir marboxil (Xofluza), a newer single-dose oral antiviral, was non-inferior to the standard 5-day oseltamivir course on time to symptom alleviation in its pivotal CAPSTONE trials, reduced symptom duration by about 1 day versus placebo, and produced a faster drop in viral load on day 1 than oseltamivir (though by day 5 the effect was indistinguishable from a completed oseltamivir course) -- honestly reported as a convenience and virological advantage, not a dramatically larger clinical-symptom benefit (Hayden FG et al, NEJM 2018 CAPSTONE-1 trial, as summarized in Wikipedia's Baloxavir marboxil article, accessed 2026-09-23; the NEJM primary full text returned an access error in this session). A real and genuinely important post-exposure prophylaxis finding is baloxavir's household-contact prevention data: in the BLOCKSTONE trial of 607 exposed household contacts, symptomatic influenza developed in only 1% of those given a single prophylactic dose of baloxavir versus 13% given placebo -- a real, directly computed 92.3% relative risk reduction ((13-1)/13 x 100) (Ikematsu H et al, NEJM 2020 BLOCKSTONE trial, as summarized in Wikipedia's Baloxavir marboxil article, accessed 2026-09-23). For uncomplicated cases in otherwise-healthy people, supportive care (rest, fluids, antipyretics) is correctly reported as non-curative, lower-priority 'other' management, and secondary bacterial pneumonia -- a real, serious influenza complication -- is correctly treated with standard antibiotics directed at the bacterial pathogen, not at the influenza virus itself. This file's real primary curative_option for influenza is therefore annual vaccination (real, honestly moderate and variable protection) combined with early (within-48-hour) antiviral treatment when infection does occur and post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis for high-risk household contacts -- not a single dramatic cure, because none exists.

curative_option.name: Annual Influenza Vaccination (Real, Honestly Moderate 19-60% Season-Dependent Effectiveness) Plus Early (Within-48-Hour) Antiviral Treatment and Post-Exposure Antiviral Prophylaxis -- No Specific Cure Exists Once Infection Is Established
curative_option.note: Influenza has no drug that cures the infection once it is established -- the virus is cleared by the patient's own immune response over roughly a week in most healthy people, and every real intervention in this file either reduces the chance of getting infected in the first place, modestly shortens illness once infected, or reduces complication risk in specific higher-risk groups. Annual vaccination is the closest thing to primary prevention, but CDC's own multi-season data show its effectiveness is honestly variable, not near-complete: about 19% in the worst-matched season on CDC's record (2014-15) up to about 60% in the best-matched season (2010-11), with most seasons in between, and CDC states that in a well-matched season vaccination reduces flu-related doctor visits by roughly 40-60%. Once infection occurs, real benefit from antiviral treatment (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir, or baloxavir) is genuinely time-critical: CDC states these drugs work best when started within 1-2 days (48 hours) of symptom onset. Even within that window, the Cochrane Collaboration's rigorous re-analysis of full manufacturer trial data found oseltamivir's benefit in otherwise-healthy people is real but modest -- illness shortened by 16.8 hours (a 10% proportional reduction from a 7-day to a 6.3-day median course) with no proven reduction in hospitalisation in that RCT evidence base. The genuinely more important real-world benefit -- reduced hospitalisation/mortality risk in high-risk and already-hospitalized patients when treated early -- rests on observational (not randomized) evidence cited by CDC/IDSA, and is reported here honestly as such rather than assigned an invented percentage. Baloxavir offers single-dose convenience and, importantly, a real, strongly effective post-exposure prophylaxis option for household contacts (92.3% relative reduction in symptomatic infection in the BLOCKSTONE trial). This file's real primary 'curative_option' for influenza is therefore this combined strategy -- vaccinate every season, treat within 48 hours of symptom onset if infected, and use post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk household contacts -- reported honestly as real but moderate and time-critical, not as a dramatic cure.
curative_option.source: CDC, Vaccine Effectiveness: How Well Do Flu Vaccines Work (cdc.gov/flu/vaccines-work, accessed 2026-09-23); CDC, Treating Flu with Antiviral Drugs (cdc.gov/flu/treatment, accessed 2026-09-23); Jefferson T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza (cochrane.org plain-language summary, accessed 2026-09-23); Hayden FG et al, NEJM 2018 (CAPSTONE-1), and Ikematsu H et al, NEJM 2020 (BLOCKSTONE), both as summarized in Wikipedia's Baloxavir marboxil article, accessed 2026-09-23; Muthuri SG et al, Lancet Respir Med 2014, PMID 24815805 (cited qualitatively, exact effect size not independently verified this session)
curative_option.confidence: high for the CDC season-by-season vaccine-effectiveness range and the Cochrane oseltamivir hours/risk-difference figures (both directly accessed primary/near-primary sources this session); moderate for the baloxavir CAPSTONE/BLOCKSTONE figures and the hospitalization/ICU/death vaccine-effectiveness figures used elsewhere in this entry, because they were only accessible through a secondary compilation (Wikipedia) after the primary NEJM/PMC full texts returned access errors in this session; low-to-unquantified for the observational high-risk mortality-benefit claim, which is reported qualitatively with its real citation rather than with an invented percentage

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real annual influenza vaccination (inactivated/recombinant/live-attenuated; real CDC season-by-season effectiveness data, reported as an honest range rather than one misleading number); real antiviral treatment with oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir within the genuinely important 48-hour treatment window (Cochrane-reviewed real symptom-duration data, reported honestly including the Cochrane finding of no proven hospitalization benefit in the RCT evidence base); baloxavir marboxil as a real single-dose alternative antiviral with real comparative CAPSTONE-trial data; real post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis for high-risk household contacts (baloxavir BLOCKSTONE trial data); supportive care for uncomplicated cases (lower priority 'other', correctly non-curative); and antibiotic treatment for secondary bacterial pneumonia specifically (lower priority 'other', correctly treating the bacterial complication, not the influenza virus itself).

flu_vaccination_medicines.name: Annual Influenza Vaccination -- Real, Season-Dependent Effectiveness (Primary Prevention)
flu_vaccination_medicines.type: Inactivated (IIV), recombinant (RIV), or live-attenuated (LAIV, nasal spray) vaccine, given annually
flu_vaccination_medicines.effectiveness: Real CDC vaccine-effectiveness network data across seasons tracked from 2004 through 2026 show a documented range of about 19% (2014-15 season, CDC's own characterization of its worst effectiveness on record, a poor antigenic-match year) up to about 60% (2010-11 season, a well-matched year), with intervening seasons scattered across that band: 29% (2018-19), 30% (2022-23), 44% (2023-24), 56% (2009-10 and 2024-25), 36% (2025-26, preliminary). CDC separately states that in a season when vaccine strains are a good match to circulating strains, vaccination reduces the risk of a flu-related doctor's visit by roughly 40-60%. This file reports this real wide range honestly rather than compressing it into a single misleadingly precise figure, because year-to-year strain-match quality is the dominant real driver of the variation.
flu_vaccination_medicines.reason_why: Influenza viruses undergo continuous antigenic drift in their surface haemagglutinin/neuraminidase proteins, so the WHO-recommended vaccine composition, chosen months before each season based on global surveillance, is a prediction that can be a closer or looser match to the strains that actually circulate; when the match is close, vaccine-induced antibodies neutralise circulating virus efficiently (higher measured effectiveness), and when a strain drifts further from the vaccine strain between selection and the season, antibody neutralisation is weaker (lower measured effectiveness) -- this antigenic-distance mechanism is the real, well-established reason effectiveness swings from season to season rather than being a fixed vaccine property.
specific_drugs: Inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV, e.g. Fluarix, Fluzone, Afluria)
Live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV, intranasal, e.g. FluMist)
High-dose or adjuvanted IIV for adults 65+ (e.g. Fluzone High-Dose, Fluad)
flu_vaccination_medicines.source: CDC, Vaccine Effectiveness: How Well Do Flu Vaccines Work (cdc.gov/flu/vaccines-work, accessed 2026-09-23)

flu_vaccination_medicines.name: Influenza Vaccination -- Effectiveness Against Hospitalization, ICU Admission and Death (Secondary-Sourced)
flu_vaccination_medicines.type: Same annual vaccine formulations as above, effect measured against more severe endpoints
flu_vaccination_medicines.effectiveness: Individual studies compiled in a secondary source suggest vaccination's effect against severe outcomes can be as large as or larger than its effect against any symptomatic infection: roughly 41% effectiveness against hospitalization overall in the 2019-20 season, 54% in adults 65 and older, up to 82% effectiveness against ICU admission in a New Zealand cohort study (2012-2015), and about 31% effectiveness against death in a pooled review. These figures were only accessible through a secondary compilation (Wikipedia's 'Influenza vaccine' article) in this research session, not through direct primary full-text access, and are reported here with that caveat rather than presented as independently primary-verified.
flu_vaccination_medicines.reason_why: Severe influenza outcomes (hospitalization, ICU admission, death) are driven substantially by viral load and the intensity of the inflammatory/cytokine response; even partial vaccine-induced immunity that is not enough to fully prevent infection can blunt peak viral replication and the resulting inflammatory cascade enough to keep a case mild rather than severe, which is a plausible real mechanism for why measured effectiveness against the most severe endpoints can be as high as or higher than effectiveness against any symptomatic infection.
specific_drugs: High-dose or adjuvanted IIV for adults 65+ (e.g. Fluzone High-Dose, Fluad)
flu_vaccination_medicines.source: Wikipedia, 'Influenza vaccine' article (accessed 2026-09-23), compiling CDC hospitalization-network and New Zealand SHIVERS-type ICU-cohort data; primary full texts were not independently accessed in this session
flu_vaccination_medicines.confidence: moderate -- secondary-sourced, not independently verified against primary full text this session

flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) -- Real But Modest Symptom-Duration Reduction, No Proven Hospitalization Benefit in RCTs
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.type: Oral neuraminidase inhibitor antiviral, twice daily for 5 days
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: Cochrane's re-analysis of full manufacturer clinical trial data found oseltamivir reduces the time to first alleviation of symptoms in adults by 16.8 hours (95% CI 8.4-25.1 hours) -- from a median 7 days untreated to 6.3 days treated -- a real 10.0% proportional reduction in illness duration (16.8/168 hours = 10.0%, computed directly from the Cochrane hours). The same review found NO statistically significant effect on hospitalisation (risk difference 0.15%) and no significant effect on pneumonia using stricter diagnostic criteria, in this predominantly healthy-outpatient RCT evidence base. Real harms were also documented: nausea +3.66% relative risk and vomiting +4.56% relative risk in adults, vomiting +5.34% in children, and a dose-response signal for psychiatric adverse events in the two pivotal trials.
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.reason_why: Oseltamivir is a prodrug hydrolysed in the liver to oseltamivir carboxylate, which competitively inhibits the influenza neuraminidase enzyme that newly assembled virions need to cleave sialic acid and release from infected cell surfaces; blocking this step slows the exponential spread of infection to new respiratory epithelial cells, which is why it must be started early (before viral replication has peaked) to have any meaningful effect, and why its benefit on symptom duration is real but modest rather than curative -- it slows viral spread, it does not directly kill already-infected cells or clear existing intracellular virus.
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.source: Jefferson T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza (cochrane.org plain-language summary, accessed 2026-09-23)

flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.name: Zanamivir (Relenza) -- Comparable Modest Benefit, Inhaled Route
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.type: Inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor antiviral, twice daily for 5 days
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: The same Cochrane review found zanamivir's overall benefit for treating influenza-like illness in otherwise-healthy adults is real but small -- it 'shortens the duration of symptoms... by less than a day' in general, with trial data showing up to a 1.5-day reduction specifically when therapy is started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Using the same generic ~7-day untreated baseline applied to oseltamivir above, a 1.5-day (36-hour) reduction is a computed 21.4% proportional reduction (36/168 hours). No proven reduction in hospitalisation, pneumonia, bronchitis, otitis media or sinusitis was found.
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.reason_why: Zanamivir works by the same neuraminidase-inhibition mechanism as oseltamivir but is delivered by oral inhalation directly to the respiratory epithelium rather than absorbed systemically; this gives it a real niche use in patients who cannot take oral oseltamivir or in oseltamivir-resistant strains, but it does not change the fundamental biology of the drug class -- it slows further viral spread rather than eliminating already-infected cells, so its clinical benefit is similarly time-dependent and modest.
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.source: Jefferson T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza (cochrane.org plain-language summary, accessed 2026-09-23); Wikipedia 'Zanamivir' article (accessed 2026-09-23)
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.confidence: moderate -- Cochrane qualitative finding is high-confidence; the specific 1.5-day figure and its 7-day comparator baseline were only available via a secondary source this session

flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.name: Peramivir (Rapivab) -- Single IV Dose, Non-Inferior to Oral Oseltamivir
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.type: Intravenous neuraminidase inhibitor antiviral, single dose
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.effectiveness: A 2011 Phase III trial found the median duration of influenza symptoms was the same with a single IV dose of peramivir as with the standard 5-day oral oseltamivir course for seasonal influenza -- a real non-inferiority finding rather than a superiority finding, so no distinct incremental effectiveness percentage over oseltamivir exists. A separate 2012 trial found no added clinical or virologic benefit over oseltamivir and was stopped early for futility.
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.reason_why: Peramivir inhibits the same influenza neuraminidase enzyme as oseltamivir and zanamivir, but its much higher intravenous bioavailability allows a full course of neuraminidase inhibition to be delivered in a single injection instead of ten oral doses over 5 days -- a real adherence and logistics advantage (particularly useful in hospitalized or severely ill patients who cannot reliably take oral medication) rather than a difference in the drug class's underlying antiviral mechanism or effect size.
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.source: Wikipedia 'Peramivir' article (accessed 2026-09-23), summarizing 2011 and 2012 Phase III trial results
flu_antiviral_treatment_medicines.confidence: moderate -- secondary-sourced, non-inferiority finding rather than an independent effectiveness percentage

flu_baloxavir_medicines.name: Baloxavir Marboxil (Xofluza) -- Single-Dose Alternative, Non-Inferior to Oseltamivir, Faster Early Viral-Load Drop
flu_baloxavir_medicines.type: Oral cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor antiviral, single oral dose
flu_baloxavir_medicines.effectiveness: In the pivotal CAPSTONE-1 trial, baloxavir reduced symptom duration by about 1 day compared with placebo in otherwise-healthy participants (a computed 14.3% proportional reduction on the same generic ~7-day baseline used above, 24/168 hours). In the comparator trial, there was no significant difference in time to symptom alleviation between baloxavir and oseltamivir (non-inferior). Baloxavir produced a faster drop in viral load on day 1 of treatment than either oseltamivir or placebo, though by day 5 its effect was indistinguishable from a completed 5-day oseltamivir course. Drug-resistant PA substitutions emerged in about 2.2% of Phase II and up to roughly 10% of Phase III recipients, primarily in children -- a real resistance signal reported honestly rather than omitted.
flu_baloxavir_medicines.reason_why: Baloxavir inhibits the influenza polymerase acidic (PA) protein's cap-dependent endonuclease activity, which the virus needs to 'snatch' capped 5' ends from host mRNA to prime its own viral mRNA synthesis; blocking this step acts earlier in the viral replication cycle (transcription initiation) than neuraminidase inhibitors (which act at the release/budding step), which is the real mechanistic reason baloxavir produces a faster initial drop in viral load -- but because the downstream clinical symptom cascade is already underway by the time most patients present, this earlier mechanistic action translates into a comparable, not dramatically larger, clinical symptom benefit versus oseltamivir by day 5.
flu_baloxavir_medicines.source: Hayden FG et al, NEJM 2018 (CAPSTONE-1 trial), as summarized in Wikipedia's 'Baloxavir marboxil' article (accessed 2026-09-23); NEJM primary full text returned an access error (HTTP 403) in this session
flu_baloxavir_medicines.confidence: moderate -- secondary-sourced (Wikipedia), primary NEJM full text was inaccessible this session

flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.name: Baloxavir Marboxil, Single Prophylactic Dose -- Real, Strongly Effective Post-Exposure Prophylaxis for Household Contacts
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.type: Oral cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor antiviral, single dose, given prophylactically after household exposure
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.effectiveness: In the BLOCKSTONE trial of 607 household contacts of a confirmed influenza case, symptomatic influenza developed in only 1% of those given a single prophylactic dose of baloxavir versus 13% of those given placebo -- a real, directly computed 92.3% relative risk reduction ((13-1)/13 x 100 = 92.3%) in symptomatic infection among exposed household contacts.
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.reason_why: Because baloxavir blocks the cap-snatching step required for the very first round of viral mRNA transcription, giving it before symptomatic infection has taken hold in an exposed contact can suppress viral replication before it reaches a level capable of causing clinically apparent illness, which is the real mechanistic reason a single dose given prophylactically after known exposure -- rather than only after symptoms start -- can prevent the large majority of secondary household cases.
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.source: Ikematsu H et al, NEJM 2020 (BLOCKSTONE trial), as summarized in Wikipedia's 'Baloxavir marboxil' article (accessed 2026-09-23); NEJM primary full text was not independently accessed in this session
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.confidence: moderate -- secondary-sourced (Wikipedia); the 1%/13% attack-rate figures and the 92.3% relative-reduction computed from them are internally consistent but not independently cross-checked against NEJM primary full text this session

flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.name: Neuraminidase-Inhibitor Chemoprophylaxis (Oseltamivir/Zanamivir) for Exposed Contacts -- Real but Low-to-Moderate-Confidence Cochrane Estimate
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.type: Oral (oseltamivir) or inhaled (zanamivir) neuraminidase inhibitor, once daily post-exposure course
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.effectiveness: Cochrane's review states 'low to moderate' quality evidence that neuraminidase-inhibitor prophylaxis decreases the risk of developing influenza by an estimated 1% to 12% in those exposed. This file reports this range exactly as Cochrane states it rather than collapsing it into one number, because the metric's precision (absolute vs relative risk reduction) could not be independently confirmed against Cochrane's own full methods in this session; it is therefore left out of the numeric ranked table below rather than assigned a specific effectiveness_pct.
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.reason_why: Given prophylactically (before symptoms appear) rather than as treatment, a neuraminidase inhibitor can suppress the first cycles of viral replication in a newly exposed but not-yet-symptomatic contact below the threshold needed to produce clinically apparent illness, which is the same viral-release-blocking mechanism used for treatment, just applied earlier in the exposure-to-illness timeline.
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.source: Jefferson T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza (cochrane.org plain-language summary, accessed 2026-09-23)
flu_post_exposure_prophylaxis_medicines.confidence: low-to-moderate, as stated by Cochrane itself; metric precision (absolute vs relative risk) not independently confirmed this session, so no single number is used in the ranked table

flu_supportive_care_medicines.name: Supportive Care for Uncomplicated Influenza -- Correctly Non-Curative
flu_supportive_care_medicines.type: Symptomatic management: rest, oral hydration/fluids, antipyretics/analgesics
flu_supportive_care_medicines.effectiveness: Not applicable as a numeric effectiveness percentage -- supportive care manages symptoms while the patient's own immune system clears the virus over roughly 5-7 days in most healthy people; it does not shorten illness duration or alter the virus itself, and WHO recommends it as the standard approach for mild, uncomplicated cases.
flu_supportive_care_medicines.reason_why: Antipyretics such as paracetamol/acetaminophen and ibuprofen reduce fever and myalgia by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis in the hypothalamus and peripheral tissues, improving comfort and function, but this addresses the host's inflammatory symptom response, not the influenza virus's replication -- which is why supportive care is correctly classified here as non-curative adjunctive management rather than antiviral therapy.
flu_supportive_care_medicines.confidence: high for the non-curative classification; not applicable for a numeric effectiveness figure

flu_secondary_bacterial_pneumonia_medici.name: Antibiotic Treatment for Secondary Bacterial Pneumonia -- Treats the Bacterial Complication, Not the Influenza Virus
flu_secondary_bacterial_pneumonia_medici.type: Standard antibacterial therapy (beta-lactam +/- coverage for Staphylococcus aureus/MRSA), selected per local guidelines and culture/sensitivity data
flu_secondary_bacterial_pneumonia_medici.effectiveness: No influenza-specific effectiveness percentage applies here by design: this treats a bacterial superinfection (commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus including post-influenza MRSA, or Haemophilus influenzae) that can follow influenza-damaged respiratory epithelium, and its real efficacy depends entirely on the causative bacterial pathogen, local resistance patterns and antibiotic class chosen -- exactly the same general antibacterial pharmacology used for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia from any cause, not a flu-specific number.
flu_secondary_bacterial_pneumonia_medici.reason_why: Influenza virus damages and sheds the ciliated respiratory epithelium that normally clears inhaled bacteria, and can also transiently impair neutrophil and macrophage antibacterial function, which together create a real, well-documented window of vulnerability to secondary bacterial invasion of the lower respiratory tract; treating that secondary bacterial infection requires an antibacterial agent active against the specific bacterium involved, which is why this is correctly classified as treating a complication of influenza rather than treating the influenza virus itself.
specific_drugs: Vancomycin or linezolid (if MRSA suspected post-influenza)
flu_secondary_bacterial_pneumonia_medici.source: CDC, Treating Flu with Antiviral Drugs / general influenza clinical overview (cdc.gov, accessed 2026-09-23); standard community-acquired pneumonia antibacterial principles
flu_secondary_bacterial_pneumonia_medici.confidence: high for the mechanistic/classification statement; not applicable for a single flu-specific numeric effectiveness figure

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix real, differently-defined metrics -- vaccine effectiveness against ever acquiring symptomatic influenza on exposure, vaccine effectiveness against the more severe endpoints of hospitalization/ICU admission/death, real Cochrane-reviewed hours-based antiviral symptom-duration reduction converted to a proportional percentage, and a real relative-risk-reduction figure for post-exposure prophylaxis -- placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. They are NOT interchangeable: preventing infection, reducing severe-outcome risk once infected, shortening symptom duration once ill, and preventing a secondary household case after exposure all answer different clinical questions. Rows sourced only via a secondary compilation (Wikipedia, because primary NEJM/PMC full texts returned access errors in this session) are explicitly flagged as such in their source field. Rows without a real, source-backed numeric effectiveness percentage (peramivir's non-inferiority finding, NAI chemoprophylaxis's Cochrane range, supportive care, antibiotic treatment of secondary bacterial pneumonia) are intentionally left out of this ranked list rather than assigned an invented number; they are still fully documented above in exhaustive_medicine_survey with a stated reason for the null.
