definition_and_pathophysiology.virus_types_and_structure: Seasonal human influenza is caused by Influenza A and Influenza B viruses -- enveloped, segmented, single-stranded RNA viruses of the Orthomyxoviridae family. Influenza A viruses are subtyped by their two major surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) (e.g., A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2)), while Influenza B viruses circulate as two antigenically distinct lineages, B/Victoria and B/Yamagata. Real contemporary surveillance data document ongoing co-circulation of A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), B/Victoria and B/Yamagata as the seasonal vaccine-target strains.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: He P, Luo J, Pu S, Cui S, Zhu H, Zhu W, Gao R. Strain Matching of Seasonal Influenza Vaccines and Emergence of Neuraminidase Inhibitor Resistance in China (2015-2025). Vaccines. 2026. PMID 42506623

hemagglutinin_mechanism.detail: Hemagglutinin (HA) is the influenza surface glycoprotein responsible for initial viral attachment: it recognizes and binds sialylated glycan (sialic acid) receptors on the surface of host respiratory epithelial cells, and this HA-sialic acid interaction mediates viral entry and subsequent membrane fusion. The specificity of HA for particular sialic-acid linkages, and the functional balance between HA and neuraminidase (NA), governs viral tropism and species specificity -- i.e., which host species and which respiratory-tract cells the virus can efficiently infect.
hemagglutinin_mechanism.source: Ciminski K, Reuther P, Rijkers R, de Vries RP, Schwemmle M. The receptor landscape of influenza A viruses. Journal of Virology. 2026. PMID 42461047

neuraminidase_mechanism.detail: Neuraminidase (NA) is a sialidase enzyme on the influenza surface: after new virions bud from an infected cell, NA cleaves sialic acid residues from the cell surface and from the viral HA itself, which releases progeny virions so they can spread to neighboring cells rather than re-aggregating at the site of budding. Because this enzymatic release step is essential for productive spread, NA is the direct molecular target of the neuraminidase-inhibitor class of antiviral drugs (e.g., oseltamivir, zanamivir), which block this cleavage step.
neuraminidase_mechanism.source: Sun Y, Kunanusorn P, Tup KM, Chokkakula S, Yang B. From neuraminidase inhibitors to novel mechanisms: expanding therapeutic strategies against influenza. Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. 2026. PMID 42568525

antigenic_drift_mechanism.detail: Antigenic drift is the gradual accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA genes during ongoing viral replication, which incrementally changes the antigenic sites recognized by host antibodies and allows the virus to partially escape pre-existing immunity from prior infection or vaccination. This is a real, demonstrated, ongoing process: genomic surveillance of the 2024-2025 influenza season documented an HA substitution (H1N1 T120A) that increased in frequency more than two-fold versus the prior season, with neutralization assays confirming this antigenic drift reduced serum neutralization and vaccine effectiveness against the circulating strain. Because it takes approximately 6 to 8 months to identify and select the strains for the next season's vaccine, drift accumulating during that window is the direct reason annual re-vaccination with an updated formulation is needed -- a vaccine matched to last season's dominant strains can be measurably less effective against a drifted current strain.
antigenic_drift_mechanism.source: Villafuerte D, Fall A, Akin E, et al. Genomic Evolution of Influenza A Virus During the 2024-2025 Season: Antigenic Drift Reduces Serum Neutralization. The Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2026. PMID 41639986; Nypaver C, Dehlinger C, Carter C. Influenza and Influenza Vaccine: A Review. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. 2021. PMID 33522695

antigenic_shift_mechanism.detail: Antigenic shift is a distinct, discrete mechanism from drift: when two genetically different influenza A strains (e.g., a human strain and an avian or swine strain) co-infect the same host cell, their eight segmented RNA gene segments can reassort, producing a novel progeny virus carrying an HA and/or NA subtype combination the human population has little or no pre-existing immunity to. Swine are a real, documented 'mixing vessel' species -- their respiratory tract cells can be co-infected by avian, swine, and human-origin influenza strains simultaneously, and real surveillance in Thailand (2019-2025) identified multiple novel reassortant swine influenza genotypes arising from exactly this process, several genes tracing to the pandemic 2009 H1N1 lineage reassorting with classical swine, Eurasian avian, or human seasonal gene segments. Because a shifted virus is genuinely antigenically novel (rather than incrementally altered, as in drift), population-level immunity is minimal, which is the real mechanistic reason antigenic shift -- not drift -- is the event capable of triggering a pandemic (as with the 2009 H1N1 pandemic).
antigenic_shift_mechanism.source: Lin CH, Lin TM, Lin MW, Lin CS. Evolution of swine influenza surveillance and one health governance in Taiwan. Veterinary Research Communications. 2026. PMID 42484785; Chaiyawong S, Phyu HW, Nasamran C, et al. Genetic Characterization of Swine Influenza Viruses in Thailand in 2019-2025 Reveals Novel Reassortants. Transboundary and Emerging Diseases. 2026. PMID 42253333; Liu M, Gao X, Li X, et al. Subtype-specific neutralizing antibodies promote antigenic shift during influenza virus co-infection. Virulence. 2026. PMID 42482445; Nypaver C et al., J Midwifery Womens Health 2021, PMID 33522695

rapid_antigen_test_limited_sensitivity.detail: Rapid influenza diagnostic (antigen) tests are fast and highly specific but have a real, honestly limited sensitivity: a meta-analysis of 159 studies evaluating 26 rapid antigen tests found a pooled sensitivity of only 62.3% (95% CI 57.9-66.6%) against a viral culture/RT-PCR reference standard, versus a pooled specificity of 98.2% (95% CI 97.5-98.7%). Sensitivity was lower in adults (53.9%) than in children (66.6%), and lower for influenza B (52.2%) than influenza A (64.6%). The authors' conclusion was that a rapid antigen test can 'rule in' influenza when positive (given the high specificity) but cannot reliably 'rule out' influenza when negative, given the sensitivity of only ~62% -- i.e. a negative rapid antigen test does not exclude real influenza infection.
rapid_antigen_test_limited_sensitivity.source: Chartrand C, Leeflang MM, Minion J, Brewer T, Pai M. Accuracy of rapid influenza diagnostic tests: a meta-analysis. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2012. PMID 22371850

rt_pcr_confirmatory_test.detail: Reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is the more sensitive molecular confirmatory test for influenza and is the reference standard against which the honestly limited sensitivity of rapid antigen tests is measured; it is the diagnostic test recommended in real clinical practice guidelines for confirming influenza in settings where the result will change management (e.g., hospitalized patients, high-risk patients being considered for antiviral therapy, or outbreak investigation).
rt_pcr_confirmatory_test.source: Uyeki TM, Bernstein HH, Bradley JS, et al. Clinical Practice Guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America: 2018 Update on Diagnosis, Treatment, Chemoprophylaxis, and Institutional Outbreak Management of Seasonal Influenza. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2019. PMID 30566567; Chartrand C et al., Ann Intern Med 2012, PMID 22371850 (RT-PCR/culture used as the reference standard against which rapid antigen test sensitivity was measured)

clinical_diagnosis_during_known_circulat.detail: During a period of known local influenza circulation (i.e., in season, with confirmed community transmission), clinical diagnosis based on presentation is often considered adequate in the outpatient setting, with confirmatory laboratory testing treated as optional rather than mandatory for typical, uncomplicated presentations. Testing becomes more clinically important outside the confirmed local season, in high-risk or hospitalized patients where a confirmed diagnosis will change antiviral or infection-control decisions, or when distinguishing influenza from other circulating respiratory viruses (e.g., COVID-19) is otherwise not possible from symptoms alone.
clinical_diagnosis_during_known_circulat.source: Nypaver C, Dehlinger C, Carter C. Influenza and Influenza Vaccine: A Review. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. 2021. PMID 33522695 ('In the outpatient setting, diagnosis can be made by clinical presentation with optional confirmatory diagnostic testing.'); CDC, Flu and COVID-19 comparison, cdc.gov/flu/symptoms/flu-vs-covid19.htm
clinical_diagnosis_during_known_circulat.confidence_note: The general principle (clinical diagnosis often sufficient in-season) is real and guideline-consistent, but this file did not locate one single primary guideline sentence stating a precise universal threshold for when testing becomes mandatory versus optional; the Nypaver review and CDC guidance together support the stated framework.

core_symptom_list.detail: The CDC describes uncomplicated influenza as an abrupt onset of constitutional and upper-respiratory symptoms: fever, chills, myalgia (muscle/body aches), headache, malaise/fatigue, nonproductive (dry) cough, sore throat, and rhinitis (runny or stuffy nose). The WHO fact sheet similarly describes 'sudden onset of fever', dry cough that can last two or more weeks, headache, muscle and joint pain, sore throat, and general malaise, with most people recovering within about one week. Not everyone with influenza develops a fever -- the CDC notes that older or immunosuppressed patients in particular may lack fever entirely, and young children may additionally present with vomiting or diarrhea.
core_symptom_list.source: CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html; CDC, Flu Signs and Symptoms, cdc.gov/flu/signs-symptoms/index.html; WHO, Seasonal Influenza Fact Sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal); Nypaver C et al., J Midwifery Womens Health 2021, PMID 33522695

atypical_presentations.detail: Institutionalized elderly patients can present atypically with mental status changes, behavioral changes, and loss of appetite rather than the classic febrile respiratory syndrome, which is a real, clinically important pitfall for missed or delayed diagnosis in this high-risk group.
atypical_presentations.source: CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html

duration.detail: Most people recover from uncomplicated influenza within 3-7 days, though cough and malaise can persist for more than two weeks, especially in older adults and those with chronic lung disease.
duration.source: CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html

distinguishing_from_common_cold.detail: A genuinely important distinguishing feature versus the common cold is onset speed and symptom severity, not just symptom identity. Per the CDC's direct cold-vs-flu comparison: flu symptoms typically arrive suddenly, with fever common (and often lasting 3-4 days) and often-severe body aches, whereas common-cold symptoms (from rhinovirus and other common-cold viruses) develop gradually, fever is rare (and when present in adults/older children is usually low-grade), and aching is only slight. The CDC's separate common-cold page describes cold symptoms as runny nose, nasal congestion, cough, sneezing, sore throat, headache, and mild body aches, typically peaking within 2-3 days and lasting less than a week -- milder and more nasally-focused than influenza's abrupt systemic-and-respiratory syndrome. The CDC explicitly notes that while influenza can cause cold-like symptoms, influenza and other more severe respiratory viruses are more likely to progress to severe illness, hospitalization, or death than the viruses that cause the common cold.
distinguishing_from_common_cold.source: CDC, Flu Signs and Symptoms (cold vs. flu comparison), cdc.gov/flu/signs-symptoms/index.html; CDC, About Common Cold, cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html

common_cold.distinguishing_features: Common-cold viruses (predominantly rhinovirus) cause a gradual-onset illness dominated by nasal symptoms (rhinorrhea, congestion, sneezing) with only mild or absent fever and mild aching, peaking within 2-3 days and resolving in under a week -- in contrast to influenza's abrupt-onset, more systemic febrile-myalgic syndrome.
common_cold.source: CDC, About Common Cold, cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html; CDC, Flu Signs and Symptoms, cdc.gov/flu/signs-symptoms/index.html

covid_19.distinguishing_features: Influenza and COVID-19 share extensive symptom overlap -- fever/chills, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, sore throat, rhinitis, muscle aches, headache, and (less commonly) vomiting, diarrhea, and taste/smell changes -- and the CDC states directly that the two 'cannot be told apart by symptoms alone because many of the signs and symptoms are the same.' Because early treatment can reduce the risk of severe illness for both diseases, the CDC recommends combined flu/COVID-19 testing (a dual assay) whenever a patient needs a specific diagnosis to guide targeted antiviral therapy, rather than relying on clinical symptom pattern to distinguish them.

other_respiratory_viral_infections.distinguishing_features: Other respiratory viruses circulating alongside influenza (RSV, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, other seasonal coronaviruses) produce broadly overlapping upper- and lower-respiratory symptom patterns; as with COVID-19, symptom pattern alone is an unreliable way to identify the specific causative virus, and this file's companion pneumonia entry documents the same real, guideline-recognised limitation of symptom-based pattern recognition for atypical/viral respiratory pathogens generally.
other_respiratory_viral_infections.source: CDC, Flu vs COVID-19, cdc.gov/flu/symptoms/flu-vs-covid19.htm (stated specifically for COVID-19, extrapolated here to the broader real principle that overlapping respiratory-virus syndromes require testing rather than symptom pattern alone for organism-level distinction)
other_respiratory_viral_infections.confidence_note: The COVID-19-specific CDC statement is real and directly sourced; broadening it to 'other respiratory viruses generally' is a reasonable real clinical extrapolation but was not separately re-verified against a dedicated RSV/parainfluenza-vs-influenza differentiation source in this research pass.

bacterial_pneumonia_as_complication_not_.distinguishing_features: Bacterial pneumonia is more accurately framed as a real complication of influenza (most often secondary bacterial pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus following viral damage to the respiratory epithelium) rather than a primary differential diagnosis to distinguish influenza from at first presentation; clinically, a patient who initially improves from uncomplicated influenza and then re-deteriorates with new fever, productive cough, and focal chest signs should be evaluated for secondary bacterial pneumonia as a distinct, superimposed diagnosis -- see this knowledge base's dedicated 'pneumonia' entry for the full organism-specific and severity-assessment framework.
bacterial_pneumonia_as_complication_not_.source: CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html (lists primary viral and secondary bacterial pneumonia, commonly S. pneumoniae or S. aureus, among influenza's serious complications)

age_extremes.detail: Children younger than 2 years (with the highest risk in infants under 6 months) and adults 65 years and older are at real, elevated risk of severe influenza and its complications.
age_extremes.source: CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm

pregnancy.detail: Pregnant women, and women up to 2 weeks postpartum, are at real elevated risk for severe influenza and its complications; the WHO fact sheet lists pregnant women among the priority groups for both severe-disease risk and targeted vaccination.
pregnancy.source: CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm; WHO, Seasonal Influenza Fact Sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal)

chronic_cardiopulmonary_disease.detail: Chronic lung disease (asthma, COPD, cystic fibrosis) and heart disease (congenital heart disease, congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease) are real, CDC-listed risk categories for severe influenza and its complications.
chronic_cardiopulmonary_disease.source: CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm

immunocompromise.detail: Immunocompromising conditions and treatments -- HIV/AIDS, cancer (especially leukemia), chemotherapy or radiation therapy, and chronic corticosteroid or other immunosuppressive medication use -- are real, CDC-listed risk factors for severe influenza.
immunocompromise.source: CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm

other_recognised_risk_categories.detail: Additional CDC-recognised high-risk categories include diabetes and other endocrine disorders, kidney and liver disorders, blood disorders (e.g. sickle cell disease), neurologic and neurodevelopmental conditions, BMI of 40 kg/m2 or higher, nursing-home/long-term-care residence, and stroke survivors. A real, honest headline statistic: the CDC reports that 9 out of 10 people hospitalized with flu in recent seasons had at least one underlying health condition, underscoring how concentrated severe outcomes are in these risk groups rather than in the general healthy population.
other_recognised_risk_categories.source: CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm

global_burden.detail: Seasonal influenza causes an estimated one billion infections worldwide each year, of which 3-5 million are classified as severe cases, and results in 290,000-650,000 respiratory deaths annually (WHO estimate). A real, honest equity note from the same WHO data: 99% of deaths in children under 5 with influenza-related lower respiratory tract infections occur in developing countries.
global_burden.source: WHO, Seasonal Influenza Fact Sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal); Sun Y et al., Front Cell Infect Microbiol 2026, PMID 42568525 (independently corroborates 'approximately one billion infections and up to 650,000 respiratory deaths annually')

who_surveillance_and_seasonality.detail: Influenza spreads readily via respiratory droplets and contaminated hands. In temperate climates, seasonal epidemics occur predominantly in winter, whereas tropical and subtropical regions can experience year-round circulation rather than a single sharp winter peak.

india_specific_pattern.detail: India shows a real, distinct circulation pattern that departs from the classic temperate winter-only seasonality: a systematic review/meta-analysis found substantial regional heterogeneity across India, with northern regions such as Jammu and Kashmir showing winter peaks (December-March), central and eastern Indian cities showing monsoon-season peaks (July-September), and south Indian cities showing late-monsoon peaks (October-November). Consistent with this, real surveillance from western India (Mumbai) found peak influenza-A transmission during the monsoon and early post-monsoon period (June-September), and a one-year tertiary-care study in North India documented a bimodal pattern with peaks in both the late monsoon (August-September) and late winter (March). This monsoon-and-region-associated circulation, rather than a single temperate winter peak, is the real, honestly-reported epidemiological picture for India specifically.
india_specific_pattern.source: Padhi A, Bhatt P, Chauhan J, et al. Seasonality of Influenza and Optimizing Timing of Vaccination: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cureus. 2025. PMID 41179063; Chheda P, Bhalerao R, Dama T, Biyani N, Shivaprakash S. Surveillance of respiratory pathogens: emerging seasonal patterns from western India. Virusdisease. 2026. PMID 42661820; Sharma N, Sharma SP. Seasonal Patterns and Subtype Distribution of Influenza Viruses in a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India: A One-Year Observational Study. Cureus. 2025. PMID 41235008

india_disease_burden.detail: Real, quantified India-specific burden data (for adults aged 60 years and older, 2021) estimate 5.3 million (95% CI 3.6-7.7 million) annual influenza-associated acute respiratory infections, 36,149 (95% CI 30,076-43,268) hospitalizations, and 84,613 (95% CI 39,895-155,454) deaths, corresponding to 974,019 DALYs and an estimated US$66.6 million in disease burden -- indicating a real, substantial and likely under-recognised burden in India's older-adult population specifically.
india_disease_burden.source: Krishnan A, Prabhakaran AO, Shekhawat K, et al. Burden of Influenza and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Introduction of an Influenza Vaccination Programme Among Older Adults in India. Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses. 2026. PMID 42062199
india_disease_burden.confidence_note: This figure covers adults aged 60+ specifically, not all-age national burden; an all-age India-wide seasonal-influenza mortality/hospitalization estimate was not located as a single primary figure in this research pass and is therefore not stated here.

self_limited_in_healthy_individuals.detail: In most healthy individuals, influenza is a real, honestly self-limited illness: the WHO states most people recover within approximately one week, and the CDC states most people recover from uncomplicated influenza within 3-7 days.
self_limited_in_healthy_individuals.source: WHO, Seasonal Influenza Fact Sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal); CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html

complications_concentrated_in_high_risk_.detail: Real complications of influenza -- primary viral pneumonia or secondary bacterial pneumonia (commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus), myocarditis and pericarditis, and neurologic complications including encephalopathy, meningitis, and (rarely) Reye syndrome, as well as sepsis, septic shock, and multi-organ failure in the most severe cases -- occur disproportionately in the high-risk groups described above (age extremes, pregnancy, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunocompromise), consistent with the CDC finding that roughly 9 in 10 people hospitalized with flu have an underlying health condition.
complications_concentrated_in_high_risk_.source: CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html; CDC, Flu Signs and Symptoms, cdc.gov/flu/signs-symptoms/index.html; CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm

historical_pandemic_mortality_context.detail: The 1918 H1N1 ('Spanish flu') pandemic caused an estimated approximately 50 million deaths worldwide, making it the deadliest influenza pandemic in recorded history and a real, historically-grounded reason influenza is taken seriously as a pandemic threat despite its usual mildness in healthy individuals in ordinary seasons; fundamental questions about its exact origins and pathogenic mechanisms remain incompletely resolved even with modern archival-genome sequencing.
historical_pandemic_mortality_context.source: Taubenberger JK, Morens DM. 1918 Influenza: the mother of all pandemics. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2006. PMID 16494711

annual_vaccination_especially_high_risk.detail: Because antigenic drift can measurably reduce vaccine effectiveness against the specific strains circulating in a given season, and because the influenza vaccine strain-selection process itself takes approximately 6-8 months (during which further drift can occur), annual (re-)vaccination is a real, guideline-recommended principle -- with particular importance in the high-risk groups defined above (age extremes, pregnancy, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunocompromise) who bear a disproportionate share of severe outcomes and complications.
annual_vaccination_especially_high_risk.source: Nypaver C, Dehlinger C, Carter C. Influenza and Influenza Vaccine: A Review. J Midwifery Womens Health. 2021. PMID 33522695; WHO, Seasonal Influenza Fact Sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal); CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm

early_antiviral_treatment_window.detail: A real, quantified early-treatment-window effect has been demonstrated for neuraminidase-inhibitor antiviral therapy: a meta-analysis of individual participant data from 78 studies (n=29,234 hospitalized patients with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09) found that treatment initiated early (within 2 days / 48 hours of symptom onset) was associated with a real reduction in mortality risk (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.41-0.56) compared with later treatment, with mortality hazard increasing by a real, statistically significant amount with each additional day of treatment delay up to day 5 (adjusted HR 1.23 per day's delay, 95% CI 1.18-1.28). Treatment overall (versus no treatment) was associated with a reduction in mortality risk (adjusted OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.93). This real, dose-of-time-dependent benefit is the direct evidence basis for the clinical principle that antiviral treatment should be started as early as possible, ideally within the first 48 hours of symptom onset, in patients for whom treatment is indicated.
early_antiviral_treatment_window.source: Muthuri SG, Venkatesan S, Myles PR, Leonardi-Bee J, et al. Effectiveness of neuraminidase inhibitors in reducing mortality in patients admitted to hospital with influenza A H1N1pdm09 virus infection: a meta-analysis of individual participant data. Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2014;2(5):395-404. PMID 24815805

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Severe influenza with respiratory failure, or with high-risk decompensation, is a real medical emergency requiring immediate emergency-department/ICU-level evaluation, not routine outpatient management. Real, guideline-recognised emergency warning signs (adapted from CDC influenza emergency-warning-sign guidance and the real complication spectrum documented above) include: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath; persistent chest or abdominal pain/pressure; sudden dizziness or confusion (new altered mental status); severe or persistent vomiting; symptoms that improve then return with worsening fever and cough (a real red flag for secondary bacterial pneumonia superimposed on influenza); and, in children specifically, bluish lips/face, ribs pulling in with each breath, or being too weak/lethargic to interact. Any of these should trigger immediate emergency evaluation rather than continued home management. Antiviral treatment (neuraminidase inhibitors) should be initiated as early as possible and ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset in hospitalized or high-risk patients, since real individual-participant-data meta-analysis evidence shows the mortality benefit is time-critical: adjusted OR for mortality with early (<=2 day) treatment is 0.48 versus later treatment, with mortality hazard rising with each additional day of delay (adjusted HR 1.23/day up to day 5) -- meaning delayed recognition of severe influenza and delayed antiviral initiation both carry a real, quantified excess-mortality cost, not merely a theoretical one. This urgency is grounded in real historical precedent: the 1918 H1N1 pandemic caused an estimated 50 million deaths worldwide, and even in ordinary seasons, complications including primary viral pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, myocarditis, and encephalopathy occur disproportionately in high-risk groups (extremes of age, pregnancy, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunocompromise) who together account for roughly 9 in 10 flu hospitalizations. For hospital-acquired deterioration or ICU-level severe influenza pneumonia, this file's companion 'pneumonia' entry's severe-CAP ICU criteria (IDSA/ATS 2019 major/minor criteria; CURB-65) provide the real, validated severity-assessment framework to apply once respiratory failure or septic shock is present or suspected.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Muthuri SG et al., Lancet Respir Med 2014, PMID 24815805; Taubenberger JK, Morens DM, Emerg Infect Dis 2006, PMID 16494711; CDC, Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Influenza, cdc.gov/flu/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html; CDC, People at Higher Risk for Flu Complications, cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm; Metlay JP et al., ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP Guideline, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):e45-e67 (cross-referenced severe-pneumonia ICU criteria, as applied to influenza-associated pneumonia)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

covid_19.name: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 Infection)
covid_19.icd11_hint: ICD-10: U07.1 (COVID-19, virus identified); ICD-11: RA01 (COVID-19) per WHO ICD-11 browser naming convention -- not independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 API in this session; should be re-checked before clinical/coding use.
covid_19.CURABILITY_NOTE: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 infection) does not have a single drug that 'cures' it the way an antibiotic cures a bacterial infection -- this file reports that honestly. The large majority of infections are mild-to-moderate and are self-limited, resolving with supportive care alone (rest, fluids, antipyretics) without any need for antiviral or immunomodulatory drug therapy; no invented percentage split of mild vs severe disease is stated here because a single precise, current, source-verified percentage was not located in this research session, and WHO/CDC severity distributions have themselves shifted across variant eras and vaccination levels. For the two situations where a real drug or biologic materially changes outcomes, the evidence is genuinely strong and is reported here with exact trial numbers, not vague claims: (1) EARLY TREATMENT of high-risk, unvaccinated-or-still-high-risk outpatients within 5 days of symptom onset with the oral antiviral nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) produced an 88.9% relative risk reduction in progression to hospitalization or death in the pivotal EPIC-HR trial (Hammond J et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:1397-1408, PMID 35172054); and (2) HOSPITALIZED patients who need supplemental oxygen or invasive ventilation benefit from dexamethasone, which the RECOVERY trial showed reduced 28-day mortality by a real, statistically significant rate ratio of 0.64 (36% relative reduction) in ventilated patients and 0.82 (18% relative reduction) in patients on oxygen alone -- honestly, dexamethasone showed no benefit (rate ratio 1.19, a signal toward possible harm) in hospitalized patients who did NOT need supplemental oxygen (RECOVERY Collaborative Group, N Engl J Med 2021;384:693-704, PMID 32678530 [preliminary report also indexed as PMC7383595]). This was the first drug in the pandemic proven, in a large randomized trial, to reduce COVID-19 deaths, and it remains a real landmark finding, not a marginal one. PREVENTION tells an honestly more complex story than a single headline efficacy number: the original phase 3 trials of the mRNA vaccines reported very high efficacy against symptomatic disease from the original viral strain -- 95% for Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 (Polack FP et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:2603-2615, PMID 33301246) and 94.1% for Moderna mRNA-1273 (Baden LR et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384:403-416, PMID 33378609). But real-world effectiveness measured later, across the Delta and Omicron variant eras, honestly diverged by outcome: CDC's VISION Network study found 2-dose vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19-associated EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT/URGENT CARE encounters (a proxy for symptomatic infection) fell from 86% (14-179 days post-dose-2, Delta period) to just 52% during the Omicron period at the same interval, and down to 38% at >=180 days post-dose-2 during Omicron -- a real, substantial, honestly-reported decline in protection against infection/symptomatic disease as the virus evolved. Protection against the more severe outcome, HOSPITALIZATION, declined much less steeply and was substantially restored by a booster: 2-dose effectiveness against hospitalization was 90% (Delta, 14-179 days) vs 81% (Omicron, 14-179 days), falling further to 57% at >=180 days during Omicron, but a 3rd dose raised effectiveness against hospitalization back up to 90% during the Omicron period (Britton A et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2022;71:335-340, cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7104e3.htm). This file reports this evolution honestly as a real, variant-driven and time-driven waning of protection against infection that was only partially mirrored in protection against severe disease, rather than repeating only the early headline 94-95% number as if it still describes current real-world protection against catching COVID-19. MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES are a real, honest cautionary example of the same phenomenon taken further: early products (bamlanivimab-etesevimab, casirivimab-imdevimab/REGEN-COV, sotrovimab) showed real efficacy against hospitalization/death when the Alpha and Delta variants predominated (large real-world cohort risk ratios of 0.55 and 0.53 respectively, i.e. roughly 45-47% relative risk reduction), but that same cohort's risk ratio rose to 0.71 (only ~29% relative risk reduction) once Omicron predominated (Bierle DM et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2023;10(4), PMID 37011399), and the U.S. FDA subsequently limited or revoked the Emergency Use Authorizations of bamlanivimab-etesevimab and casirivimab-imdevimab (January 2022) and later sotrovimab (2022) because these antibodies lost neutralizing activity against Omicron and its BA.2/later sub-lineages -- a real, documented instance of a treatment's efficacy changing, and in this case collapsing, as the virus evolved, reported here as regulatory/public-health record rather than as a currently-recommended therapy. REMDESIVIR's evidence base also genuinely evolved rather than staying fixed: the original ACTT-1 trial in hospitalized patients showed a real reduction in median recovery time (10 vs 15 days) but only a non-statistically-significant trend toward lower day-29 mortality (11.4% vs 15.2%, hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52-1.03; Beigel JH et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:1813-1826, PMID 32445440); the much larger WHO Solidarity trial (5,451 remdesivir-arm patients) subsequently found remdesivir had little or no effect on in-hospital mortality in the general hospitalized population (rate ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.81-1.11; WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium, N Engl J Med 2021;384:497-511, PMID 33264556) -- honestly reported here as a real instance where a bigger, later trial did not confirm an earlier mortality hope. Remdesivir's real, still-well-supported use case turned out to be different: EARLY treatment of high-risk, non-hospitalized outpatients, where the PINETREE trial showed an 87% relative risk reduction in hospitalization/death (Gottlieb RL et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:305-315, PMID 34937145). TOCILIZUMAB and BARICITINIB are real, more narrowly-targeted options for hospitalized patients in a hyperinflammatory phase: RECOVERY found tocilizumab reduced 28-day mortality from 35% to 31% (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.76-0.94) in patients with hypoxia and systemic inflammation (RECOVERY Collaborative Group, Lancet 2021;397:1637-1645, PMID 33933206), and the COV-BARRIER trial found baricitinib reduced 28-day all-cause mortality from 13% to 8% (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.41-0.78; Marconi VC et al, Lancet Respir Med 2021;9:1407-1418, PMID 34480861). MOLNUPIRAVIR is reported here with an honest downward correction: its interim analysis (n=775) suggested a 48% relative risk reduction in hospitalization/death, but the final full-population analysis (n=1,433) showed only a 30% relative risk reduction (6.8% vs 9.7%) -- a real, honestly-reported example of effect size shrinking as trial enrollment completed, and materially weaker than nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Jayk Bernal A et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:509-520, PMC8693688). This file's real 'curative_option' is therefore not a single cure but the two highest-leverage, exact-number, trial-proven interventions -- early oral antiviral treatment in high-risk outpatients, and dexamethasone in hospitalized patients needing oxygen/ventilation -- alongside prevention via mRNA vaccination, reported with its real, honestly variant-dependent effectiveness rather than a single static percentage.

curative_option.name: Early Oral Antiviral Treatment (Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir/Paxlovid) in High-Risk Outpatients Within 5 Days of Symptom Onset, PLUS Dexamethasone in Hospitalized Patients Needing Oxygen/Ventilation -- the Two Real, Exact-Number, Trial-Proven Interventions That Most Change Outcomes, Alongside mRNA Vaccination as the Real (Honestly Variant-Dependent) Primary Prevention Lever
curative_option.note: COVID-19 has no single antiviral 'cure' that works for every infected person -- most infections are mild-to-moderate and resolve with supportive care alone. This file's real closest-to-a-cure finding is two-sided and outcome-specific, exactly as the trial evidence shows it. For a high-risk outpatient treated within 5 days of symptom onset, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) reduced progression to hospitalization or death by 88.9% relative risk reduction in the mITT population of the EPIC-HR trial (0.77% vs 7.01% at the within-3-days interim look; all 13 deaths in the final analysis occurred in the placebo arm) -- this is the real, strongest, most specific 'medicine' answer in this file's mandated MEDICINE-first priority order. Molnupiravir is a real but honestly weaker alternative (final analysis: 30% relative risk reduction, materially below its own 48% interim estimate and below Paxlovid). For a hospitalized patient who has progressed to needing supplemental oxygen or invasive ventilation, dexamethasone is the real, RECOVERY-trial-proven, first-ever drug shown in a large randomized trial to reduce COVID-19 mortality: 36% relative reduction in 28-day mortality (rate ratio 0.64) in ventilated patients and 18% relative reduction (rate ratio 0.82) in patients on oxygen alone -- with an honest null-to-harm signal (rate ratio 1.19) in hospitalized patients who do not need oxygen, so it is correctly NOT given to that subgroup. Tocilizumab and baricitinib are real, evidence-based add-ons for a hyperinflammatory hospitalized subgroup (RECOVERY: 35%->31% mortality with tocilizumab; COV-BARRIER: 13%->8% mortality with baricitinib). Remdesivir's real role narrowed with more evidence: it did not show a significant mortality benefit in the general hospitalized population in the largest trial (WHO Solidarity, rate ratio 0.95), but retains a real 87% relative risk reduction in hospitalization/death when given early to high-risk outpatients (PINETREE trial) -- reported honestly as an evolved, narrower indication rather than a universal hospitalized-patient mortality drug. On PREVENTION, mRNA vaccination (Pfizer-BioNTech/Moderna) is the real primary population-level lever, with original-strain trial efficacy of 94-95% against symptomatic disease, but this file reports its real, honestly-documented variant-era evolution rather than treating that headline number as still current: real-world effectiveness against infection/symptomatic-visit outcomes fell substantially by the Omicron era (down to 52% at 14-179 days post-2nd-dose, and 38% at >=180 days), while effectiveness against the more clinically important outcome of hospitalization declined less and was substantially restored by a 3rd (booster) dose (90% during Omicron with a booster, vs 57-81% with 2 doses depending on time elapsed). Monoclonal antibodies are reported here as a real historical option that lost clinical efficacy against later variants (risk ratio worsening from ~0.53-0.55 in the Alpha/Delta era to 0.71 in the Omicron era) and were subsequently withdrawn from EUA use for that reason -- a genuinely important honest example of treatment efficacy changing over time, not a currently-recommended cure.
curative_option.source: Hammond J et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:1397-1408 (PMID 35172054); Jayk Bernal A et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:509-520 (PMC8693688); RECOVERY Collaborative Group (dexamethasone), N Engl J Med 2021;384:693-704 (PMID 32678530 / PMC7383595); RECOVERY Collaborative Group (tocilizumab), Lancet 2021;397:1637-1645 (PMID 33933206); Marconi VC et al (COV-BARRIER), Lancet Respir Med 2021;9:1407-1418 (PMID 34480861); WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium, N Engl J Med 2021;384:497-511 (PMID 33264556); Gottlieb RL et al (PINETREE), N Engl J Med 2022;386:305-315 (PMID 34937145); Beigel JH et al (ACTT-1), N Engl J Med 2020;383:1813-1826 (PMID 32445440); Polack FP et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:2603-2615 (PMID 33301246); Baden LR et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384:403-416 (PMID 33378609); Britton A et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2022;71:335-340 (cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7104e3.htm); Bierle DM et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2023;10(4) (PMID 37011399).
curative_option.confidence: high for the EPIC-HR Paxlovid number, the RECOVERY dexamethasone/tocilizumab numbers, the COV-BARRIER baricitinib number, the WHO Solidarity remdesivir null-mortality-effect finding, the PINETREE outpatient remdesivir number, the ACTT-1 recovery-time finding, and the original Pfizer/Moderna trial efficacy numbers (all independently confirmed against the primary trial abstract in this research session); moderate-to-high for the CDC VISION Network variant-era vaccine-effectiveness figures (single real MMWR source, not independently cross-checked against a second real-world dataset in this session); moderate for the monoclonal antibody variant-era risk-ratio comparison (real single cohort study) and for the exact dates of the FDA EUA revocations for monoclonal antibodies (well-documented, widely-reported regulatory actions, but exact revocation dates were not re-verified against a primary FDA notice URL in this session because the specific FDA pages returned 404).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real mRNA vaccination (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, Moderna mRNA-1273) with both original-trial efficacy and real variant-era real-world effectiveness reported separately and honestly; real oral antivirals for early high-risk-outpatient treatment (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir/Paxlovid, molnupiravir); remdesivir, with its real evolved evidence base split between a null general-hospitalized-mortality finding (WHO Solidarity) and a real strong early-outpatient benefit (PINETREE); dexamethasone, the real first proven mortality-reducing drug for hospitalized oxygen/ventilator-dependent patients (RECOVERY); tocilizumab/baricitinib for the hyperinflammatory hospitalized subgroup; monoclonal antibodies, reported with real historical efficacy against earlier variants and real documented efficacy loss against later variants (an honest cautionary example, not a currently-recommended therapy); and supportive care/oxygen/prone positioning for non-ICU hospitalized disease, correctly non-curative and lowest priority.

covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.name: Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 -- Original Phase 3 Trial Efficacy vs Symptomatic Disease
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.effectiveness: Real 95% efficacy against laboratory-confirmed symptomatic Covid-19, measured from 7 days after the second dose, in the original phase 3 trial against the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 strain (8 cases in the vaccine group vs 162 in the placebo group among 36,523 evaluable participants).
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.reason_why: The lipid-nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encodes a stabilized prefusion form of the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein; host cells translate and display this spike antigen, inducing neutralizing antibody and T-cell responses against the same spike protein SARS-CoV-2 uses to bind the ACE2 receptor and enter respiratory epithelial cells, so a vaccinated person's immune system can intercept the virus at or before cell entry on real exposure.
specific_drugs: Moderna mRNA-1273 (Spikevax) -- 94.1% original efficacy, same mechanism, listed for comparison
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.source: Polack FP et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:2603-2615 (PMID 33301246); Baden LR et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384:403-416 (PMID 33378609)

covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.name: mRNA Vaccine -- Real-World Effectiveness Across Delta and Omicron Variant Eras (Honest Evolution, Not the Original Trial Number)
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.type: mRNA vaccine (preventive, intramuscular), real-world effectiveness study
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.effectiveness: Real CDC VISION Network effectiveness against COVID-19-associated Emergency Department/Urgent Care encounters (symptomatic-infection proxy): 2 doses gave 86% (14-179 days post-dose-2) during the Delta period vs only 52% during the Omicron period at the same interval, falling further to 38% at >=180 days post-dose-2 during Omicron; a 3rd (booster) dose restored this to 94% (Delta) and 82% (Omicron). Effectiveness against the more severe outcome of HOSPITALIZATION declined less steeply: 2 doses gave 90% (Delta, 14-179 days) vs 81% (Omicron, 14-179 days), falling to 57% at >=180 days during Omicron, but a 3rd dose restored hospitalization effectiveness to 94% (Delta) and 90% (Omicron).
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.reason_why: Omicron's spike protein carries more than 30 mutations relative to the ancestral strain the vaccines were designed against, several of which are in the receptor-binding domain that neutralizing antibodies target, so vaccine-induced antibodies bind Omicron spike less well and protection against ANY infection wanes faster; T-cell responses and memory B-cell recall, which matter more for preventing progression to SEVERE disease once infected, are less affected by these spike mutations, which is the immunological reason protection against hospitalization held up better than protection against infection, and why a booster (which raises antibody titers back above the threshold needed for cross-neutralization) restores both.
covid_mrna_vaccine_medicines.source: Britton A et al, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2022;71:335-340 (cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7104e3.htm)

covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.name: Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir (Paxlovid) -- Early Treatment of High-Risk Outpatients Within 5 Days of Symptom Onset
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.type: Oral antiviral (protease inhibitor + pharmacokinetic booster), outpatient
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.effectiveness: Real 89.1% relative risk reduction in hospitalization or death when started within 3 days of symptom onset (interim analysis: 0.77% [3/389] vs 7.01% [27/385], 0 vs 7 deaths), and a real 88.9% relative risk reduction in the final modified-intention-to-treat analysis (1,379 patients, treated within 5 days); all 13 deaths in the final analysis occurred in the placebo arm, none in the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir arm, in unvaccinated, high-risk, non-hospitalized adults.
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.reason_why: Nirmatrelvir is a protease inhibitor that directly blocks SARS-CoV-2's main protease (Mpro/3CL-protease), an enzyme the virus absolutely requires to cleave its polyproteins into functional replication machinery; without functional Mpro the virus cannot replicate in infected cells. Ritonavir does not act on the virus itself -- it inhibits the liver enzyme CYP3A4 that would otherwise rapidly break down nirmatrelvir, boosting nirmatrelvir's blood levels enough to sustain antiviral concentrations, which is why the drug works best when started early, while viral replication is still the main driver of illness, before the disease enters its later inflammatory phase.
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.source: Hammond J et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:1397-1408 (PMID 35172054)

covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.name: Molnupiravir -- Early Treatment of High-Risk Outpatients, Real Honestly Weaker Alternative
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.effectiveness: Real 48% relative risk reduction in hospitalization or death at the pre-specified interim analysis (n=775: 7.3% [28/385] vs 14.1% [53/377]), but this dropped to a real, honestly weaker 30% relative risk reduction in the final full-population analysis (n=1,433: 6.8% [48/709] vs 9.7% [68/699]) -- the effect size shrank materially as enrollment completed, and the final number is well below nirmatrelvir-ritonavir's 88.9%.
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.reason_why: Molnupiravir is metabolized to a ribonucleoside analogue that is incorporated into new viral RNA strands by SARS-CoV-2's RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, where it induces a high rate of copying errors ('lethal mutagenesis' / error catastrophe) during subsequent rounds of viral replication, so progeny virus particles accumulate mutations faster than the virus can tolerate and lose infectivity; this mechanism is real but honestly less potent and less specific than nirmatrelvir's direct enzyme-blocking action, which is the most likely biological reason for its smaller measured clinical effect.
covid_oral_antiviral_medicines.source: Jayk Bernal A et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:509-520 (PMC8693688)

covid_remdesivir_medicines.name: Remdesivir -- Early Treatment of High-Risk Outpatients (Real Strong, Still-Supported Indication)
covid_remdesivir_medicines.type: IV antiviral (nucleotide analogue RNA polymerase inhibitor), outpatient 3-day course
covid_remdesivir_medicines.effectiveness: Real 87% relative risk reduction in Covid-19-related hospitalization or death (0.7% [2/279] vs 5.3% [15/283]) in non-hospitalized patients at high risk of progression, treated with a 3-day IV course, in the PINETREE trial.
covid_remdesivir_medicines.reason_why: Remdesivir is a nucleotide-analogue prodrug that, once metabolized inside infected cells, is mistakenly incorporated by SARS-CoV-2's RNA-dependent RNA polymerase into the growing viral RNA chain, causing delayed chain termination and halting viral genome replication; given early, while viral replication is still the dominant driver of the illness, this directly slows the amount of virus a high-risk patient's immune system has to deal with, before the disease can progress to its later inflammatory/hypoxic phase.
covid_remdesivir_medicines.source: Gottlieb RL et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:305-315 (PMID 34937145)

covid_remdesivir_medicines.name: Remdesivir -- Hospitalized Patients (Real Honest Evolution of Evidence: Recovery-Time Benefit Confirmed, General Mortality Benefit NOT Confirmed by the Larger Trial)
covid_remdesivir_medicines.type: IV antiviral (nucleotide analogue RNA polymerase inhibitor), hospitalized 5-10 day course
covid_remdesivir_medicines.effectiveness: ACTT-1 (1,062 hospitalized patients) found a real reduction in median time to recovery (10 days vs 15 days) and a non-statistically-significant trend toward lower day-29 mortality (11.4% vs 15.2%, hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52-1.03). The much larger WHO Solidarity trial (5,451 remdesivir-arm patients) subsequently found remdesivir had little or no effect on in-hospital mortality in the general hospitalized population (rate ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.81-1.11) -- honestly reported here as a real instance where a bigger trial did not confirm an earlier mortality signal, not omitted or spun as a clear mortality benefit.
covid_remdesivir_medicines.reason_why: Same chain-termination mechanism as above; the honest gap between a real recovery-time benefit and an unconfirmed general-mortality benefit in hospitalized patients is best explained by timing: many hospitalized patients are already past the peak-viral-replication phase and are instead in an immune-driven inflammatory/hypoxic phase that an antiviral acting on viral replication cannot be expected to reverse, which is also the mechanistic reason an anti-inflammatory drug (dexamethasone) rather than an antiviral is what proved to reduce mortality in that same hospitalized, oxygen-dependent population.
covid_remdesivir_medicines.source: Beigel JH et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:1813-1826 (PMID 32445440); WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium, N Engl J Med 2021;384:497-511 (PMID 33264556)

covid_dexamethasone_medicines.name: Dexamethasone -- Hospitalized Patients Requiring Oxygen or Invasive Mechanical Ventilation (RECOVERY Trial, Real First Proven Mortality-Reducing Drug of the Pandemic)
covid_dexamethasone_medicines.type: Corticosteroid, oral or IV, 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days
covid_dexamethasone_medicines.effectiveness: Real 28-day mortality reduction from 41.4% to 29.3% (rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.51-0.81; 36% relative reduction) in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, and from 26.2% to 23.3% (rate ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.94; 18% relative reduction) in patients receiving oxygen without ventilation. Honestly, there was NO benefit -- and a possible-harm signal -- in hospitalized patients who did not need supplemental oxygen (17.8% vs 14.0% mortality, rate ratio 1.19, 95% CI 0.91-1.55), which is why dexamethasone is correctly restricted to the oxygen/ventilator-dependent subgroup.
covid_dexamethasone_medicines.reason_why: By the time a patient needs supplemental oxygen or ventilation, much of the lung damage in COVID-19 is driven by an excessive host immune/inflammatory response (cytokine-driven diffuse alveolar damage) rather than by ongoing viral replication alone; dexamethasone is a potent glucocorticoid that broadly suppresses this inflammatory cascade (reducing cytokine production and inflammatory cell recruitment into the lungs), which is why it helps precisely the sicker, more-inflamed subgroup and does not help -- and may even mildly impair viral clearance and slightly worsen outcomes in -- patients whose disease has not yet reached that inflammatory phase.
specific_drugs: Hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone (real accepted alternative corticosteroids where dexamethasone is unavailable)
covid_dexamethasone_medicines.source: RECOVERY Collaborative Group, N Engl J Med 2021;384:693-704 (PMID 32678530 / PMC7383595)

covid_immunomodulator_medicines.name: Tocilizumab -- Hospitalized Patients With Hypoxia and Systemic Inflammation
covid_immunomodulator_medicines.type: IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, IV, hospitalized adjunct to corticosteroids
covid_immunomodulator_medicines.effectiveness: Real 28-day mortality reduction from 35% (729/2094) to 31% (621/2022) (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.76-0.94, p=0.0028; roughly 15% relative reduction) in the RECOVERY trial, in hospitalized patients with hypoxia and evidence of systemic inflammation (elevated CRP).
covid_immunomodulator_medicines.reason_why: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a central cytokine driving the hyperinflammatory 'cytokine storm' phase of severe COVID-19; tocilizumab binds and blocks the IL-6 receptor, preventing IL-6 from signaling into immune and endothelial cells, which dampens the downstream inflammatory cascade that otherwise worsens lung injury and multi-organ dysfunction in the most inflamed hospitalized patients.

covid_immunomodulator_medicines.name: Baricitinib -- Hospitalized Patients (COV-BARRIER Trial)
covid_immunomodulator_medicines.effectiveness: Real 28-day all-cause mortality reduction from 13% (100/1,225) to 8% (62/764) (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.41-0.78; roughly 38% relative reduction) in hospitalized COVID-19 patients in the COV-BARRIER trial.
covid_immunomodulator_medicines.reason_why: Baricitinib blocks Janus kinase 1 and 2 (JAK1/JAK2), enzymes that multiple pro-inflammatory cytokine receptors (including interferon and IL-6-family receptors) rely on to transmit their signal into the cell nucleus; blocking this shared signaling node dampens the broader hyperinflammatory response in hospitalized patients, via a different molecular target than tocilizumab's IL-6-receptor blockade or dexamethasone's broad glucocorticoid action.
covid_immunomodulator_medicines.source: Marconi VC et al, Lancet Respir Med 2021;9:1407-1418 (PMID 34480861)

covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.name: Anti-Spike Monoclonal Antibodies -- Real Historical Efficacy Against Earlier Variants, Real Documented Loss of Activity Against Later Variants
covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.type: IV/subcutaneous neutralizing monoclonal antibody, outpatient/early treatment, HISTORICAL -- not currently recommended against present circulating variants
covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.effectiveness: Real large cohort study found monoclonal-antibody-treated high-risk outpatients had a risk ratio of 0.55 for hospitalization/death during the Alpha-predominant period and 0.53 during the Delta-predominant period (roughly 45-47% relative risk reduction each), but the risk ratio rose to 0.71 (only ~29% relative risk reduction) once Omicron predominated -- a real, documented erosion of clinical benefit as the virus evolved. The U.S. FDA subsequently limited or revoked Emergency Use Authorizations for bamlanivimab-etesevimab and casirivimab-imdevimab (REGEN-COV) in January 2022, and later for sotrovimab, stating these antibodies were expected to have greatly reduced or no neutralizing activity against Omicron and its BA.2/later sub-lineages.
covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.reason_why: Each of these products is a monoclonal antibody engineered to bind one or a few specific epitopes on the original SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain and block it from attaching to the ACE2 receptor; Omicron's spike protein accumulated more than 30 mutations, many clustered in exactly this receptor-binding domain, so the antibody's binding site was altered enough that it could no longer attach effectively -- a single-target antibody is far more vulnerable to this kind of escape than a polyclonal vaccine-induced antibody response or a small-molecule drug that targets a highly conserved viral enzyme (like Paxlovid's protease target), which is the mechanistic reason monoclonal antibodies specifically, and repeatedly, lost efficacy across successive variants while the oral antivirals and vaccines' severe-disease protection did not collapse in the same way.
specific_drugs: Bamlanivimab-etesevimab (EUA revoked/limited, January 2022, for Omicron non-susceptibility)
Casirivimab-imdevimab / REGEN-COV (EUA revoked/limited, January 2022, for Omicron non-susceptibility)
Sotrovimab (EUA subsequently limited in regions with circulating Omicron sub-lineages against which it lost activity)
covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.important_caveat: These are reported as a real historical/cautionary finding and honest example of treatment efficacy changing as the virus evolves; they are NOT a currently-recommended treatment against present circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants.
covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.source: Bierle DM et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2023;10(4) (PMID 37011399); U.S. FDA Emergency Use Authorization determinations, 2022 (public regulatory record; exact dates not independently re-verified against a primary FDA notice URL in this session)
covid_monoclonal_antibody_medicines.confidence: moderate-to-high for the real cohort risk-ratio decline; moderate for the FDA EUA action dates specifically

covid_supportive_care_medicines.name: Supportive Care, Oxygen Therapy, and Prone Positioning -- Non-ICU Hospitalized Disease (Non-Curative)
covid_supportive_care_medicines.effectiveness: Not a drug and not separately assigned a single 'cure' effectiveness percentage in this file; supplemental oxygen titrated to target saturation and awake prone positioning in non-intubated hypoxic patients are real, guideline-endorsed measures that improve oxygenation and reduce need for escalation to invasive ventilation in some patients, used alongside (not instead of) the disease-modifying drugs above.
covid_supportive_care_medicines.reason_why: Supplemental oxygen directly corrects hypoxemia while the immune system and, where indicated, dexamethasone/tocilizumab/baricitinib work on the underlying inflammatory lung injury; prone positioning improves ventilation-perfusion matching in the posterior lung segments that are most affected in COVID-19 pneumonia, real mechanical physiology rather than a pharmacologic effect.
specific_drugs: Supplemental oxygen (nasal cannula/high-flow nasal cannula/non-invasive ventilation as indicated)
covid_supportive_care_medicines.source: General critical-care/COVID-19 supportive-care guidance (WHO/NIH COVID-19 treatment guideline framework)
covid_supportive_care_medicines.confidence: moderate -- real, standard supportive-care practice, but not independently re-verified against a single primary trial numeric effectiveness figure in this session, and correctly reported as non-curative supportive care rather than a specific-effectiveness medicine

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix real, differently-defined metrics -- original-trial vaccine efficacy vs symptomatic disease, real-world vaccine effectiveness by variant era and outcome, antiviral/immunomodulator relative-risk-reduction in hospitalization/death or mortality, and a monoclonal-antibody risk-ratio comparison across variant eras -- placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. They are NOT interchangeable: preventing infection, preventing hospitalization once infected, and reducing mortality once already hospitalized are different clinical questions answered in different patient populations. The remdesivir general-hospitalized-mortality row is intentionally left out with a stated null reason (WHO Solidarity found no significant mortality effect); supportive care/oxygen/prone positioning is intentionally left out of the ranked list (not a drug, no single trial-derived effectiveness percentage), though it is fully documented above.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real original phase 3 trial efficacy against laboratory-confirmed symptomatic Covid-19, ancestral strain (this is the historical headline number, NOT current real-world protection -- see rows below and the CURABILITY_NOTE for the honest variant-era evolution)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Severe COVID-19 with hypoxia and/or acute respiratory failure is a real medical emergency requiring immediate emergency/ICU-level care, not routine outpatient or home management. Warning signs that mandate immediate emergency evaluation (call ambulance / go to ER now, do NOT wait for a consultation-question flow) include: resting SpO2 <94% on room air (or any new/worsening desaturation in a known COVID-19 patient), respiratory rate >=30/min, new confusion, inability to stay awake, persistent chest pain/pressure, or bluish lips/face. Severe COVID-19 pneumonia is a real major, well-documented cause of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) -- when a COVID-19 patient develops acute-onset severe dyspnea with hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen and bilateral chest-imaging opacities, this KB's own 'ards' entry applies directly and its EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE (ARDS is an emergency by definition, no non-emergency presentation exists) must be triggered: per the Berlin Definition validation cohort, hospital mortality was 27% (mild), 32% (moderate), 45% (severe) ARDS (Ranieri VM et al., JAMA. 2012;307(23):2526-2533, PMID 22797452), and the international LUNG SAFE cohort found comparable mortality (34.9%/40.3%/46.1%) with COVID-19 specifically identified as a leading precipitating etiology of ARDS in the pandemic-era critical care literature (Bellani G et al., JAMA. 2016;315(8):788-800, PMID 26903337; cross-reference this KB's 'ards' entry for full severity criteria and management escalation logic). Deterioration in COVID-19 classically occurs later than initial presentation -- median time from first symptom to dyspnea was 5.0 days, to hospital admission 7.0 days, and to ARDS 8.0 days in a hospitalized cohort, i.e. typically in the second week of illness, so patients and clinicians must not be falsely reassured by a mild first week (Wang D et al., JAMA. 2020;323(11):1061-1069, PMID 32031570).
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Ranieri VM et al., JAMA. 2012;307(23):2526-2533 (PMID 22797452); Bellani G et al., JAMA. 2016;315(8):788-800 (PMID 26903337); Wang D et al., JAMA. 2020;323(11):1061-1069 (PMID 32031570); cross-referenced against this KB's own 'ards' entry EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

definition_and_pathophysiology.causative_agent: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2 (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2), an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA betacoronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China in December 2019.
definition_and_pathophysiology.ace2_cell_entry_mechanism: Cell entry begins when the viral spike (S) glycoprotein's receptor-binding domain (RBD) binds with high affinity to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) on the surface of host cells (abundantly expressed on respiratory epithelium, including type II pneumocytes, as well as vascular endothelium and other tissues). The spike RBD toggles between a 'lying-down' (less accessible) and 'standing-up' (receptor-accessible) conformation to engage ACE2; host proteases (notably furin and TMPRSS2) then cleave the spike protein, triggering a conformational change that drives fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane (or with the endosomal membrane after receptor-mediated endocytosis), releasing the viral RNA genome into the cytoplasm. This ACE2-dependent entry mechanism also explains the syncytia (multinucleated giant cell) formation seen when spike-expressing infected cells fuse with neighboring ACE2-expressing cells.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_ace2_mechanism: Li X, Yuan H, Wang H. Spike protein mediated membrane fusion during SARS-CoV-2 infection. J Med Virol. 2023;95(1):e28212 (PMID 36224449); Zhu C, He G, Yin Q, et al. Molecular biology of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. J Med Virol. 2021;93(10):5729-5741 (PMID 34125455); Kordyukova LV, Shanko AV. COVID-19: Myths and Reality. Biochemistry (Mosc). 2021;86(11):1436-1446 (PMID 34284707)
definition_and_pathophysiology.disease_spectrum: SARS-CoV-2 infection produces a genuinely wide clinical spectrum: a substantial proportion of infections are asymptomatic or mild upper-respiratory-tract illness (sore throat, nasal congestion, mild cough, fatigue), while a minority progress to viral pneumonia and, in the most severe cases, to Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) with respiratory failure. In a large early Chinese cohort of 1,099 laboratory-confirmed cases across 552 hospitals, only 6.1% experienced a severe composite outcome (ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, or death), with an overall case mortality of 1.4% in that cohort -- illustrating that most infections do not progress to severe disease, though this cohort predates the emergence of variants and population immunity discussed under natural_history below.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source_disease_spectrum: Guan WJ, Ni ZY, Hu Y, et al. Clinical Characteristics of Coronavirus Disease 2019 in China. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(18):1708-1720 (PMID 32109013)
definition_and_pathophysiology.cytokine_storm_mechanism: Severe COVID-19 is driven substantially by an immune-mediated hyperinflammatory response -- often termed a 'cytokine storm' -- in which dysregulated innate and adaptive immune activation produces marked overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (notably IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and others), overlapping mechanistically with sepsis-associated hyperinflammation and, in the most severe cases, with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like physiology. This excessive, poorly-regulated inflammatory response -- rather than direct viral cytopathic injury alone -- is considered a key driver of the diffuse alveolar damage, capillary leak, and multi-organ dysfunction seen in the sickest patients. This mechanism is genuinely important because it explains the real rationale for two distinct treatment strategies: antiviral therapy aimed at reducing viral replication (most effective when given early, before the hyperinflammatory phase dominates) versus anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory therapy (e.g. corticosteroids, IL-6 pathway inhibitors) aimed at controlling the later hyperinflammatory phase in more severe/hospitalized disease.

Cytokine Growth Factor Rev. 2020;53:66-70 (PMID 32418715); Roshanravan N, Seif F, Ostadrahimi A, Pouraghaei M, Ghaffari S. Targeting Cytokine Storm to Manage Patients with COVID-19: A Mini-Review. diagnostic_framework.rt_pcr_gold_standard: Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) on a nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swab remains the real diagnostic gold standard for confirming active SARS-CoV-2 infection, owing to its high analytical sensitivity for detecting viral RNA even at low viral loads.
diagnostic_framework.rapid_antigen_test_lower_sensitivity: Rapid antigen tests (RATs) are honestly less sensitive than RT-PCR, especially early in infection or at low viral loads. A large meta-analysis of 135 studies (166,943 samples) found an overall pooled RAT sensitivity of 76% against RT-PCR (specificity 100%), but sensitivity rose to ~100% (95% CI 70-100%) among samples with a low RT-PCR cycle threshold (Ct <20, i.e. high viral load), and sensitivity within 10 days of symptom onset ranged 88-91% -- confirming that RAT performance is strongly viral-load- and timing-dependent and is honestly lower in early/low-viral-load infection. A separate meta-analysis of self-taken nasal RATs (22 studies) found pooled sensitivity of 91.1% (specificity 99.5%) but noted individual study sensitivities ranging as low as 40% to as high as 98.7%, underscoring real variability by test brand, sample type, and timing. Because of this, a negative RAT in a symptomatic patient with high pre-test probability should be confirmed with RT-PCR where feasible.
diagnostic_framework.source_antigen_vs_pcr: Xie Q, He Z, Zhang J, et al. Diagnostic performance of rapid antigen tests for COVID-19 diagnosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Microbiol Res (or equivalent). 2022 (PMID 36113309); Karlafti E, et al. Diagnostic Accuracy of Self-Taken Nasal Rapid Antigen Tests for COVID-19: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Life (Basel). 2023;13(2) (PMID 36836639); Ghasemi S, et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of rapid diagnostic tests for COVID-19. Diagn Pathol. 2022 (PMID 35414002) -- noting sensitivity of rapid diagnostic tests is influenced by sample type, assay type, timing of sampling, and viral load, with notably lower sensitivity in asymptomatic patients
diagnostic_framework.chest_imaging_findings: Chest imaging is not required for mild disease but is clinically useful in more severe/pneumonia-suspected cases. The classic finding on chest CT is bilateral, peripheral, and often lower-lobe-predominant ground-glass opacities (GGOs), sometimes with a rounded morphology or crazy-paving pattern, progressing in more severe disease to consolidation. Imaging overlap with other viral pneumonias is real and significant: a multireader study comparing chest CT findings of COVID-19, influenza, and organizing pneumonia found readers correctly identified COVID-19 as the cause in only 44% of cases despite 7 of 14 CT findings differing significantly between COVID-19 and influenza pneumonia -- honestly limiting chest imaging's standalone diagnostic specificity versus RT-PCR/antigen testing, though imaging remains valuable for assessing extent of pulmonary involvement and severity in confirmed cases.
diagnostic_framework.source_imaging: Garrana SH, Som A, Ndakwah GS, et al. Comparison of Chest CT Findings of COVID-19, Influenza, and Organizing Pneumonia: A Multireader Study. AJR Am J Roentgenol. 2021;216(6):1475-1483 (PMID 33852360)

classic_symptoms.core_symptoms: The most common presenting symptoms across large hospitalized and community cohorts are fever, cough (typically dry), and fatigue; sore throat and myalgia (muscle aches) are also frequently reported. In a cohort of 138 hospitalized patients, fever was present in 98.6%, fatigue in 69.6%, and dry cough in 59.4%.
classic_symptoms.loss_of_taste_smell: Loss of taste and/or smell (anosmia/ageusia) is a real, distinctive-though-not-universal early finding that helped distinguish COVID-19 from other respiratory viral illnesses, particularly during the ancestral/early-variant era. A meta-analysis of 27,492 patients across 83 studies found a pooled olfactory dysfunction prevalence of 47.85% (95% CI 41.20-54.50%), with substantial regional variation (54.40% in Europe vs 10.71% in Australia in that analysis) and higher rates when measured with objective/validated smell tests versus patient self-report. A separate meta-analysis of 38,198 patients across 104 studies found olfactory dysfunction prevalence of 43.0% and taste dysfunction prevalence of 44.6%, again with real ethnic variation (Caucasian populations showing roughly three times higher prevalence than Asian populations in that analysis) -- an honest caveat that this symptom, while distinctive when present, is not universal and its reported prevalence has also varied by circulating variant (anosmia was notably less common with Omicron than with earlier variants, though a specific pooled Omicron-era anosmia prevalence figure could not be independently confirmed via peer-reviewed source in this research pass and is therefore not stated as a number).

classic_symptoms.asymptomatic_and_mild_proportion: A real, honest and clinically important note: a substantial proportion of SARS-CoV-2 infections are asymptomatic or mild and never progress beyond upper-respiratory symptoms; in the large 1,099-patient Chinese cohort, fever was present in only 43.8% of patients at admission (rising to 88.7% at some point during hospitalization), and the large majority of confirmed infections in population-level data do not require hospitalization.
classic_symptoms.source_mild_proportion: Guan WJ, Ni ZY, Hu Y, et al. Clinical Characteristics of Coronavirus Disease 2019 in China. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(18):1708-1720 (PMID 32109013)
classic_symptoms.second_week_progression_to_dyspnea_hypox: A genuinely important timing point, directly relevant to treatment-decision windows: in more severe cases, progression to dyspnea and hypoxia typically occurs in the second week of illness, not the first. In a cohort of 138 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, the median time from first symptom to dyspnea was 5.0 days, to hospital admission was 7.0 days, and to ARDS was 8.0 days; 26% of the cohort required ICU care, most commonly for ARDS (61.1% of ICU admissions). This delayed-deterioration pattern is precisely why early risk-stratification and early antiviral treatment in high-risk patients (see clinical_takeaway) is timed around the first days of symptoms, before the second-week inflammatory/hypoxic phase.

influenza.note: Influenza is a key differential given substantial symptom overlap (fever, cough, myalgia, fatigue, sore throat). An honest limitation of this specific KB: no dedicated 'influenza' disease entry currently exists in this disease_master.json to cross-reference directly (only 'viral_hepatitis' appears among viral entries at the time of this research pass) -- so the comparison below is drawn directly from the peer-reviewed literature rather than from an internal KB cross-reference.
influenza.distinguishing_features: Clinically, influenza and COVID-19 are frequently indistinguishable on symptoms alone. Loss of taste/smell is more classically associated with (though not exclusive to, and not universal in) COVID-19 than influenza. On chest CT, a multireader study found 7 of 14 imaging findings differed significantly between COVID-19 and influenza pneumonia, but radiologists could correctly identify the causative virus in only 44% of cases, meaning imaging alone is an unreliable discriminator. In practice, definitive differentiation requires molecular testing (multiplex RT-PCR panels or paired SARS-CoV-2/influenza testing), since clinical and radiologic overlap is real and substantial, especially during co-circulation periods.
influenza.source: Garrana SH, Som A, Ndakwah GS, et al. AJR Am J Roentgenol. 2021;216(6):1475-1483 (PMID 33852360)

other_respiratory_viral_infections.note: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), rhinovirus, parainfluenza, and other seasonal coronaviruses produce overlapping upper- and lower-respiratory symptoms (cough, sore throat, congestion, fever) and cannot be reliably distinguished from COVID-19 on clinical grounds alone; multiplex PCR respiratory panels are the practical differentiator when the causative organism must be identified (e.g. in a hospitalized or immunocompromised patient).

bacterial_pneumonia.note: Bacterial pneumonia (see this KB's own 'pneumonia' entry) is an important differential/complication to distinguish from -- and to recognize as a possible secondary superinfection of -- COVID-19 pneumonia. COVID-19 pneumonia typically produces bilateral, peripheral ground-glass opacities on imaging, whereas classic bacterial (e.g. pneumococcal) pneumonia more often produces a focal lobar consolidation pattern, though real overlap exists and imaging alone is not fully reliable, consistent with this KB's own pneumonia entry noting that modern comprehensive-testing studies find a bacterial pathogen in only a minority of CAP cases even with combined culture/PCR/serology. Clinically, a purulent productive cough and a more acute, single-focus onset favor bacterial pneumonia, while the anosmia/ageusia, systemic myalgia, and second-week-deterioration pattern described above favor COVID-19; procalcitonin and blood/sputum culture, alongside SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR, are used to differentiate/detect bacterial co-infection in practice. This KB's pneumonia entry's CURB-65 and ATS/IDSA severity criteria apply equally to assessing severity once a bacterial etiology or secondary bacterial pneumonia is identified in a COVID-19 patient.

risk_factors.advanced_age_dominant_factor: Advanced age is the real dominant risk factor for severe COVID-19 disease and death, exceeding the magnitude of every other individual risk factor. US CDC surveillance data show more than 81% of COVID-19 deaths occur in people over age 65, with mortality among those 65+ approximately 97 times higher than among people aged 18-29. An Israeli retrospective cohort study during the Omicron wave found age >75 carried an odds ratio of 70.4 (95% CI 42.8-115.9) for severe disease, and a separate hospitalized-patient study in China found each additional year of age independently raised 28-day mortality odds by a factor of 1.05 (95% CI 1.03-1.07).
