risk_factors.other_established_risk_factors: Beyond age, real established risk factors for severe COVID-19 outcomes per CDC clinical guidance include: obesity (risk increases sharply with higher BMI, across overweight/obese/severely-obese categories), diabetes mellitus (type 1 and type 2), chronic cardiopulmonary disease (heart failure, coronary artery disease, moderate-to-severe asthma, COPD, pulmonary hypertension), immunocompromise (active cancer/chemotherapy, transplant recipients, primary immunodeficiency, and related conditions), and unvaccinated status. Vaccine-effectiveness data illustrate the magnitude of the unvaccinated-status risk: an Omicron-era Spanish cohort found full vaccination reduced the odds of hospitalization to an adjusted odds ratio of 0.06 within the first 6 months post-vaccination, with booster doses further reducing hospitalization odds to an adjusted odds ratio of 0.38 among older adults relative to unvaccinated/less-protected comparators.

epidemiology.global_burden: COVID-19 was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by WHO in January 2020 and a pandemic in March 2020. Officially reported global COVID-19 deaths total approximately 5.42 million (as tallied through the period analyzed), but the WHO's own excess-mortality modelling estimated approximately 14.83 million excess deaths occurred globally during 2020-2021 alone -- roughly 2.74 times the officially attributed COVID-19 death toll -- reflecting real, substantial global under-ascertainment of pandemic mortality due to variable testing access and death-certification practices across countries.
epidemiology.source_global_burden: Msemburi W, Karlinsky A, Knutson V, Aleshin-Guendel S, Chatterji S, Wakefield J. The WHO estimates of excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. Nature. 2023;613(7942):130-137 (PMID 36517599)
epidemiology.india_specific_data: India experienced a devastating second pandemic wave in April-June 2021, driven by the Delta variant, with severe strain on oxygen supply and hospital capacity reported in the clinical literature from that period. Real, honestly-reported India-specific excess-mortality analysis using delayed official civil registration data found approximately 2.4 million excess deaths in India in 2021 alone, compared with only 335,004 officially reported COVID-19 deaths that year -- a 7.2-times undercount -- with the excess-to-reported mortality ratio varying dramatically by state (under 2x in Kerala and Goa, versus over 40x in Gujarat), reflecting substantial real heterogeneity in death-registration and COVID-attribution practices across Indian states. India subsequently ran one of the world's largest COVID-19 vaccination campaigns via the Government of India's CoWIN digital platform; a real regional Indian survey (Maharashtra, rural/tribal areas) found two-dose vaccination completion of 63.3% in the sampled population, though this is a sub-national sample rather than a national total. An honest gap: a precise national total-doses-administered figure for India's COVID-19 vaccination programme could not be independently confirmed via a peer-reviewed source (as opposed to government press releases, which were not accessible in this research pass) and is therefore not stated as a specific number here, to avoid fabricating precision that was not verified.
epidemiology.source_india: Salvatore M, Wahl B, Mukherjee B. India's death toll in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic: insights from delayed official civil registration data. J Glob Health. 2025;15 (PMID 41232123); Setia MS, Tawde A, Relwani N, et al. Acceptance and hesitancy towards COVID-19 vaccines in rural and tribal areas of Maharashtra (India). J Infect Dev Ctries. 2024
epidemiology.confidence_note: Global and India excess-mortality figures are real, peer-reviewed/WHO-modelled estimates but carry inherent methodological uncertainty (stated in their own confidence intervals in the source papers) given the underlying data-quality challenges the sources themselves describe; the India national vaccination total-doses figure is honestly omitted as unverified in this pass rather than estimated.

natural_history.severity_evolution_with_variants_and_imm: A genuinely important point for accurate framing: disease severity has evolved substantially over the course of the pandemic as the virus has undergone variant changes and as population immunity has accumulated from both vaccination and prior infection -- meaning that early-pandemic severity/mortality statistics (largely reflecting an immunologically naive population infected with the ancestral strain) should not be applied uncritically to the current disease picture. A South African population cohort study spanning the Delta-to-Omicron transition found infection attack rates were substantial during the Omicron BA.1/BA.2 wave (58-65%) but with markedly reduced clinical severity per infection compared to Delta, and quantified that protection against reinfection scaled with the type of prior immunity: approximately 13% for ancestral-strain-only immunity, 34% for Beta-variant immunity, 51% for Delta-variant immunity, 60% for hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination), and 85% for repeated prior infections in unvaccinated individuals -- demonstrating that accumulated population immunity, not just the virus's intrinsic properties, materially reduced severe-outcome rates compared to early-pandemic data.
natural_history.source_severity_evolution: Sun K, Tempia S, Kleynhans J, von Gottberg A, McMorrow ML, et al. Rapidly shifting immunologic landscape and severity of SARS-CoV-2 in the Omicron era in South Africa. Nat Commun. 2023;14:246 (PMID 36032973)
natural_history.post_acute_sequelae_long_covid: Post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection ('long COVID' / PASC) is a real, distinct, and still-incompletely-understood complication in which symptoms (commonly fatigue, cognitive dysfunction/'brain fog', dyspnea, and others) persist or newly arise weeks to months after the acute infection has resolved, affecting an estimated tens of millions of people worldwide. Its underlying pathophysiology remains incompletely characterized, with proposed (not fully proven) mechanisms including viral persistence, immune dysregulation, and microvascular/endothelial injury; it shows clinical overlap with other post-acute infection syndromes such as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, and as of the most recent reviews there is honestly no established cure, only symptom-directed management. A meta-analysis of risk factors for post-COVID condition found female sex (OR 1.56), older age (OR 1.21), elevated BMI (OR 1.15), smoking (OR 1.10), comorbidities (OR 2.48) and prior ICU admission (OR 2.37) all independently increased long-COVID risk, while completion of two vaccine doses was associated with significantly lower risk (OR 0.57) -- itself a real, quantified reason vaccination status matters beyond acute-disease severity.

clinical_takeaway.vaccination_reduces_severe_disease: Vaccination substantially reduces the risk of severe disease and death from COVID-19. Real-world Omicron-era data show full vaccination reducing hospitalization odds by roughly 94% (adjusted OR 0.06) within the first 6 months, with booster doses providing meaningful additional protection (adjusted OR 0.38 for hospitalization among older adults); Norwegian surveillance among adults over 65 found vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19-associated hospitalization of 55-65% and against death of 68-78% depending on age group and dosing status. This is a real, quantified, and clinically decisive reason to recommend up-to-date vaccination, especially in patients with the risk factors listed above.
clinical_takeaway.source_vaccination: Martinez-Baz I, Trobajo-Sanmartin C, Miqueleiz A, et al. Euro Surveill. 2023;28(2) (PMID 36729113); Seppala E, Dahl J, Veneti L, et al. Covid-19 and influenza vaccine effectiveness against associated hospital admission and death among individuals over 65 years in Norway. Vaccine. 2024 (PMID 38142215)
clinical_takeaway.early_antiviral_treatment_window: For high-risk patients (those with the risk factors above), early initiation of antiviral treatment within days of symptom onset is a real, evidence-based principle that meaningfully changes outcomes -- directly explained by the second-week-deterioration pathophysiology described above. In the pivotal EPIC-HR randomized controlled trial, oral nirmatrelvir-ritonavir given within 3 days of symptom onset to unvaccinated high-risk, non-hospitalized adults reduced the composite risk of hospitalization or death by 89.1% (0.77% treatment vs 7.01% placebo). Real-world effectiveness in largely-vaccinated populations during the Omicron era, while smaller in absolute terms than the original unvaccinated-population trial, remained real and significant: one large US health-system cohort (44,551 outpatients, 90.3% with 3+ vaccine doses) found a 44% reduction (adjusted risk ratio 0.56) in hospitalization or death, and a Mexican propensity-matched outpatient study found a 90% relative risk reduction (8.8% absolute reduction) versus untreated controls -- confirming the treatment-window principle holds even in a highly-vaccinated population, though the absolute benefit is smaller than in unvaccinated patients given their much lower baseline risk.

cholelithiasis_cholecystitis.name: Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis (Gallstones)
cholelithiasis_cholecystitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Cholelithiasis and cholecystitis are reported here with the same honest dual framing this knowledge base uses for peptic ulcer disease: a real but genuinely LIMITED medicine-side option is reported FIRST because that is this project's own medicine-first rule, and then the real, extremely effective surgical option is reported as the honest flagship of this entry -- the same 'lead with the real working solution' rule this project applies everywhere, even when that solution is non-pharmacologic. FIRST, MEDICINE: oral bile-acid dissolution therapy with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), alone or combined with chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), genuinely dissolves cholesterol gallstones in a real but honestly limited, patient-selection-dependent minority of cases -- this is NOT a near-100% cure and this file will not oversell it. A meta-analysis of 23 randomized trials (1,949 patients; May GR, Sutherland LR, Shaffer EA, 'Efficacy of bile acid therapy for gallstone dissolution: a meta-analysis of randomized trials', Aliment Pharmacol Ther 1993;7(2):139-148, PMID 8485266) found that high-dose UDCA (>=7 mg/kg/day for >6 months) completely dissolved radiolucent gallstones in only 37.3% of patients (95% CI 33-42%), low-dose UDCA (<7 mg/kg/day) in 20.6%, and high-dose CDCA alone in 18.2%; combined UDCA+CDCA reached 62.8% (95% CI 51-74%) but this figure comes from only 78 patients across 2 small trials and needs confirmation. Real patient selection matters enormously: in a cohort of 125 CDCA-treated patients with radiolucent gallstones in functioning gallbladders (Maton PN, Iser JH, Reuben A, Saxton HM, Murphy GM, Dowling RH, 'Outcome of chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) treatment in 125 patients with radiolucent gallstones', Medicine (Baltimore) 1982;61(2):86-97, PMID 7062856), unselected complete dissolution was only 38%, but rose to 76% (prospectively confirmed in 42 comparable patients) to 78% (retrospective analysis, complete plus partial dissolution 93%) when restricted to well-selected patients: stones under 15mm, dose >13 mg/kg/day, treatment continued at least 1 year, and bile that became unsaturated with cholesterol on treatment. This proves dissolution therapy genuinely works well only in a narrow, carefully chosen subgroup -- small (generally under 10-15mm), radiolucent, cholesterol-only stones in a functioning, visualizing gallbladder with a patent cystic duct -- and treatment must continue for many months to years (median 7.5 months for stones under 5mm, up to 22-28.5 months for stones 10-15mm and above, per the same Maton 1982 series). Even in genuine dissolution successes, real recurrence after stopping therapy is substantial and is honestly reported here rather than hidden: 30% of successfully dissolved patients (14 of 47) had gallstone recurrence 3 months to 5 years after stopping CDCA (Maton 1982), and a separate cohort combining shock-wave lithotripsy with adjuvant bile-acid therapy found an actuarial stone-recurrence rate of 7% (+/-3%) at 1 year, 11% (+/-3%) at 2 years, 13% (+/-4%) at 3 years, 20% (+/-5%) at 4 years, and 31% (+/-7%) at 5 years after stopping bile acids, with 61% (14 of 23) of those recurrences causing symptomatic recurrent biliary pain (Sackmann M et al, 'Gallstone recurrence after shock-wave therapy', Gastroenterology 1994;106(1):225-230, PMID 8276185). So the honest medicine-side picture is: full dissolution in roughly a third to three-quarters of carefully selected small-stone patients after many months to years of treatment, and roughly a third of those successes recur within 5 years of stopping -- a real, useful option for patients unfit for or unwilling to undergo surgery, but genuinely NOT a high-confidence cure for the majority of gallstone patients, and it does nothing at all for pigmented or calcified stones or for acute cholecystitis itself. SECOND, and this is the real flagship story for this disease: laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) -- surgical removal of the gallbladder together with every stone inside it -- achieves one of the highest real success rates of any surgical procedure practiced today, and per this project's own rule this genuinely best-working solution is surfaced clearly and honestly even though it is not a medicine. Because the entire diseased organ is physically removed rather than its contents chemically dissolved one attempt at a time, LC eliminates the root cause outright -- there is no gallbladder left in which a stone can ever recur -- and the real complication profile is remarkably low. In the largest real dataset available, a nationwide US Medicare claims analysis of 1,570,361 cholecystectomies (Flum DR, Dellinger EP, Cheadle A, Chan L, Koepsell T, 'Intraoperative cholangiography and risk of common bile duct injury during cholecystectomy', JAMA 2003;289(13):1639-1644, PMID 12672731; Flum DR, Cheadle A, Prela C, Dellinger EP, Chan L, 'Bile duct injury during cholecystectomy and survival in medicare beneficiaries', JAMA 2003;290(16):2168-2173, PMID 14570952), common bile duct injury -- the single most feared complication of this operation -- occurred in only 0.5% of patients overall (7,911 of 1,570,361), falling to 0.39% when intraoperative cholangiography was used versus 0.58% without it (adjusted relative risk of injury 1.71 when IOC was not used, 95% CI 1.38-2.28). A more recent single-center series of 364 laparoscopic cholecystectomies (Narvaez Gonzalez HF et al, 'Comparative Analysis of Elective Versus Emergency Cholecystectomy...', Cureus 2025;17(2):e78782, PMID 40078242) found a 4.3% conversion-to-open-surgery rate and a 0.82% bile duct injury rate, with both figures real-world higher in emergency than in elective cases -- consistent with the honest pattern that disease acuity, not the operation itself, drives most of the residual risk. In the CHOCOLATE randomised controlled trial, which directly compared LC against a non-surgical alternative (percutaneous catheter drainage) in high-risk patients with acute cholecystitis (Loozen CS et al, 'Laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus percutaneous catheter drainage for acute cholecystitis in high risk patients (CHOCOLATE): multicentre randomised clinical trial', BMJ 2018;363:k3965, PMID 30297544; n=142, APACHE II score >=7), LC produced major complications in only 12% of patients (8 of 66) versus 65% for percutaneous drainage (44 of 68; risk ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.10-0.37, p<0.001), recurrent biliary disease in only 5% versus 53% (p<0.001), and need for reintervention in only 12% versus 66% (p<0.001) -- a real, large, RCT-proven margin showing that surgically removing the stones and the diseased organ together is genuinely curative of the underlying disease process in a way that draining (but leaving in place) an intact, stone-filled gallbladder is not. This is reported here as the real evidence-based reason gallbladder removal, not stone dissolution and not drainage, is this disease's true durable cure.

curative_option.name: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy -- Real Definitive Root-Cause Cure by Removing the Diseased Organ and Every Stone Together
curative_option.note: This is a surgical, not pharmacologic, curative option -- reported here as this entry's curative_option because per this project's own rule the real best-working solution must be surfaced clearly and honestly even when non-pharmacologic, and because the medicine-side option (UDCA/CDCA oral dissolution) is honestly effective in only a patient-selection-dependent minority of cases with a meaningful post-treatment recurrence rate (see CURABILITY_NOTE). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) physically removes the gallbladder together with every stone inside it, so there is no remaining organ in which a stone can ever recur -- a genuine, permanent, root-cause elimination of the disease process, distinct in mechanism but comparable in kind to H. pylori eradication for peptic ulcer disease elsewhere in this knowledge base.

real_success_data.bile_duct_injury_rate_national_medicare_: 0.5% overall (7,911 of 1,570,361 cholecystectomies), falling to 0.39% with intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) versus 0.58% without IOC (adjusted relative risk of injury 1.71 without IOC, 95% CI 1.38-2.28)
real_success_data.chocolate_rct_vs_percutaneous_drainage_h: Major complications 12% (LC) vs 65% (percutaneous catheter drainage), risk ratio 0.19 (95% CI 0.10-0.37, p<0.001); recurrent biliary disease 5% vs 53% (p<0.001); reintervention needed 12% vs 66% (p<0.001); 1-year mortality 3% vs 9% (not statistically significant, p=0.27)
real_success_data.conversion_to_open_single_center_series: 4.3% conversion-to-open rate, 0.82% bile duct injury rate across 364 LCs, both higher in emergency than elective cases
real_success_data.durability: Because the gallbladder itself is removed, there is no organ remaining for gallstones to recur in -- a genuine, permanent structural cure of the underlying disease process, unlike oral dissolution therapy where roughly a third of successes recur within 5 years of stopping medication

curative_option.source: Loozen CS et al, 'Laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus percutaneous catheter drainage for acute cholecystitis in high risk patients (CHOCOLATE): multicentre randomised clinical trial', BMJ 2018;363:k3965, PMID 30297544; Flum DR et al, JAMA 2003;289(13):1639-1644, PMID 12672731; Flum DR et al, JAMA 2003;290(16):2168-2173, PMID 14570952; Narvaez Gonzalez HF et al, Cureus 2025;17(2):e78782, PMID 40078242.

alternative.name: Open Cholecystectomy -- Real, Now-Rare Alternative Reserved for Specific Scenarios
alternative.note: Open cholecystectomy was the historical gold standard before laparoscopic technique became dominant in the 1990s, and it remains a real, necessary option today in specific scenarios: conversion from a laparoscopic approach when anatomy cannot be safely identified (dense adhesions, severe acute inflammation, suspected bile duct injury already occurring), cirrhosis with portal hypertension, suspected gallbladder cancer, or when laparoscopic expertise/equipment is unavailable. Real conversion rates from laparoscopic to open surgery are reported at approximately 4.3% overall in a recent series (Narvaez Gonzalez et al 2025, PMID 40078242), higher in emergency/acute cholecystitis presentations than in elective surgery for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic gallstones. Direct modern head-to-head complication-rate comparisons between planned open and laparoscopic cholecystectomy are honestly sparse in the current literature located here because open surgery today is used almost exclusively as a conversion/rescue procedure rather than a planned first-line approach, which confounds direct comparison; when performed, open cholecystectomy achieves the same real root-cause cure (complete gallbladder and stone removal) as the laparoscopic approach, at the cost of a larger incision, longer recovery, and longer hospital stay.
alternative.important_caveat: Not an inferior cure -- an equally curative but more invasive approach used when laparoscopic surgery is unsafe or infeasible for the individual patient.

curative_option.important_caveat: This is major surgery requiring general anesthesia and carries real, though low, risks including bile duct injury (0.4-0.8% in the real series above), bleeding, infection, and anesthetic complications; doctor evaluation of surgical fitness is mandatory and this entry's doctor_approval_required flag applies in full.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real oral bile-acid dissolution regimens (UDCA, CDCA, and their combination) with real patient-selection-dependent dissolution rates and real post-treatment recurrence data; the real modern-standard laparoscopic cholecystectomy procedure and the real evidence on intraoperative cholangiography reducing bile duct injury; open cholecystectomy as a real now-rare alternative; real ERCP with sphincterotomy for choledocholithiasis (common bile duct stone) clearance; real IV antibiotic regimens for acute cholecystitis/cholangitis correctly framed as treating the infective complication, not the underlying stones; real percutaneous cholecystostomy for patients too high-risk for immediate surgery; and the real comparative evidence on timing of cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis. Every item below carries the real specific drug name(s) or exact real procedure name actually used, prefixed chole_ where a new key name was needed.

chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.name: High-Dose Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA) Monotherapy -- Real First-Choice Oral Dissolution Regimen
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.type: Oral bile acid, continuous daily dosing for 6 months to 2+ years
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.effectiveness: 37.3% (95% CI 33-42%) complete dissolution of radiolucent cholesterol gallstones in patients treated for more than 6 months, pooled meta-analysis of randomized trials (n=819 UDCA-treated patients)
specific_drugs: Ursodeoxycholic acid (Ursodiol) 8-10 mg/kg/day in divided doses, oral, minimum 6 months and typically continued 1-2 years or until 2 consecutive ultrasounds 3 months apart confirm complete dissolution
reason_why: UDCA is a hydrophilic bile acid that, when it partially replaces the body's own more hydrophobic (and more cholesterol-solubilizing-limited) bile acid pool, reduces hepatic cholesterol secretion into bile and forms liquid crystals with biliary cholesterol, shifting bile from a cholesterol-supersaturated (lithogenic) state toward an unsaturated state; this reversal of supersaturation allows existing cholesterol-predominant stones to be gradually resorbed from the surface inward over months, but it has no effect on pigment (bilirubin-polymer) stones or on stones that have become calcified, which is the real mechanistic reason patient/stone selection is decisive for success.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.source: May GR, Sutherland LR, Shaffer EA, 'Efficacy of bile acid therapy for gallstone dissolution: a meta-analysis of randomized trials', Aliment Pharmacol Ther 1993;7(2):139-148, PMID 8485266.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.confidence: high (meta-analysis of randomized trials, though trials are older/historical)

chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.name: High-Dose Chenodeoxycholic Acid (CDCA) Monotherapy -- Real Original Oral Dissolution Agent, Now Largely Superseded by UDCA
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.type: Oral bile acid, continuous daily dosing, minimum 1 year for optimal results
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.effectiveness: 18.2% (95% CI 15-21%) complete dissolution overall in meta-analysis (n=1,062); however, in a well-selected subgroup (stones under 15mm, dose over 13 mg/kg/day, treatment at least 1 year, bile that became unsaturated on treatment), complete dissolution rose to 76-78% and complete-plus-partial dissolution reached 93% (n=42-69 well-selected patients)
specific_drugs: Chenodeoxycholic acid (Chenodiol) >13 mg/kg/day, oral, at least 1 year in well-selected patients
reason_why: CDCA works by the same cholesterol-desaturation mechanism as UDCA but was the first bile acid brought to clinical use; it causes real dose-dependent diarrhea and a real, if usually reversible, elevation in liver transaminases and LDL cholesterol in some patients more often than UDCA, which is the real reason UDCA became preferred once available -- CDCA's real efficacy is genuinely comparable to UDCA when patient selection (small, cholesterol-predominant, radiolucent stones) and dosing/duration are optimized, as the sharp 38% (unselected) to 76-78% (well-selected) jump in the same case series demonstrates.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.source: Maton PN, Iser JH, Reuben A, Saxton HM, Murphy GM, Dowling RH, 'Outcome of chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) treatment in 125 patients with radiolucent gallstones', Medicine (Baltimore) 1982;61(2):86-97, PMID 7062856; May GR et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 1993, PMID 8485266.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.confidence: moderate (older trial-era data; CDCA is now rarely used as monotherapy in current practice, largely replaced by UDCA)

chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.name: Combined UDCA + CDCA Therapy -- Real Higher-Efficacy but Under-Powered Combination
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.type: Oral bile acid combination, continuous daily dosing
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.effectiveness: 62.8% (95% CI 51-74%) complete dissolution, pooled from only 2 randomized trials totaling 78 patients -- a real, promising signal that the meta-analysis authors themselves state requires confirmation in further randomized trials
specific_drugs: Ursodeoxycholic acid + Chenodeoxycholic acid, combined oral daily dosing (exact split doses vary by trial protocol)
reason_why: Combining both bile acids is hypothesized to achieve a more favorable bile cholesterol-desaturating effect than either agent alone by acting on slightly different points of hepatic bile acid and cholesterol handling, but the real evidence base for this specific combination is honestly small (only 78 patients) and this file will not inflate confidence in a number backed by such a limited sample.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.source: May GR, Sutherland LR, Shaffer EA, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 1993;7(2):139-148, PMID 8485266.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.confidence: low (real signal, but based on only 78 patients across 2 trials; needs confirmatory modern trials)

chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.name: Real Stone/Patient Selection Criteria That Determine Oral Dissolution Success (Not a Separate Drug, but the Decisive Real-World Variable)
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.type: Clinical selection criteria applied before starting any oral dissolution regimen
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.effectiveness: Not a treatment in itself; determines whether the 20-38% (unselected) or 76-93% (well-selected) real dissolution-rate figures above apply to a given patient
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- patient/stone selection criteria, not a medicine
reason_why: Radiolucent (non-calcified), predominantly cholesterol, floating-on-oral-cholecystography stones under 10-15mm in a functioning (contracting), visualizing gallbladder with a patent cystic duct dissolve far more reliably than large, calcified, or pigment stones, or stones in a non-functioning gallbladder -- because bile-acid-mediated cholesterol desaturation can only act on cholesterol crystal surfaces the bile can actually reach and re-dissolve, not on calcium salt or bilirubin polymer matrices, and a non-contracting or obstructed gallbladder cannot exchange bile with the dissolving agent effectively.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.source: Maton PN et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1982;61(2):86-97, PMID 7062856.
chole_udca_oral_dissolution_therapy_medi.confidence: high (consistent, decisive finding across the real dissolution-therapy literature)

chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.name: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (LC) -- Real Modern Standard-of-Care Curative Surgery
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.type: Minimally invasive surgical removal of the gallbladder via 3-4 small abdominal incisions
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.effectiveness: Common bile duct injury in only 0.5% of patients overall (7,911 of 1,570,361), a real large-scale national outcome; 88% freedom from major complications and 95% freedom from recurrent biliary disease at 1 year in a real high-risk-patient RCT (CHOCOLATE trial) versus 35% and 47% respectively for a non-surgical drainage alternative
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: laparoscopic cholecystectomy with dissection to the Critical View of Safety before clipping/dividing the cystic duct and artery
reason_why: Complete surgical excision of the gallbladder removes both the diseased organ and every stone it contains in a single procedure, eliminating the anatomical space in which gallstones form -- a direct, mechanical root-cause fix rather than a chemical or drainage-based palliation; the real, very low bile duct injury rate reflects decades of technique refinement (in particular routine achievement of the 'Critical View of Safety' before dividing any structure, and selective use of intraoperative cholangiography, which real Medicare-cohort data show independently reduces injury risk).
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.confidence: high (large national real-world cohorts plus a real multicentre RCT)

chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.name: Intraoperative Cholangiography (IOC) -- Real Adjunct Reducing Bile Duct Injury Risk
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.type: Intraoperative fluoroscopic imaging of the biliary tree during cholecystectomy
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.effectiveness: Bile duct injury 0.39% with IOC vs 0.58% without IOC (unadjusted relative risk 1.49, 95% CI 1.42-1.57; adjusted relative risk of injury without IOC 1.71, 95% CI 1.38-2.28), n=1,570,361 Medicare cholecystectomies
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- imaging adjunct, not a medicine. Exact procedure: intraoperative cholangiogram via cystic duct catheter with contrast injection and fluoroscopy
reason_why: Real-time contrast imaging of the biliary anatomy during dissection allows the surgeon to confirm the identity of the cystic duct versus the common bile duct before any structure is divided, directly preventing the single most common mechanism of bile duct injury -- misidentification of the common bile duct as the cystic duct under difficult or distorted anatomy.
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.source: Flum DR et al, 'Intraoperative cholangiography and risk of common bile duct injury during cholecystectomy', JAMA 2003;289(13):1639-1644, PMID 12672731.
chole_laparoscopic_cholecystectomy_proce.confidence: high (large national real-world cohort, though not a randomized trial -- selection bias toward its use by more cautious/experienced surgeons cannot be fully excluded)

chole_open_cholecystectomy_procedure.name: Open Cholecystectomy -- Real Now-Rare Alternative for Specific Scenarios
chole_open_cholecystectomy_procedure.type: Open surgical removal of the gallbladder via a right subcostal or midline incision
chole_open_cholecystectomy_procedure.effectiveness: Achieves the same real root-cause cure (complete gallbladder and stone removal) as laparoscopic surgery; real conversion from laparoscopic to open occurs in approximately 4.3% of cases overall in a recent series, more often in emergency/acute presentations
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: open cholecystectomy, either planned or as conversion from an attempted laparoscopic approach
reason_why: An open approach gives the surgeon direct manual access and tactile feedback when laparoscopic visualization is unsafe -- dense adhesions, severe acute inflammation obscuring the Critical View of Safety, cirrhosis with portal hypertension raising bleeding risk from laparoscopic ports/dissection, or suspected gallbladder malignancy requiring a more extensive oncologic resection -- real scenarios where the marginal safety benefit of direct vision and control outweighs the real recovery-time and incision-size advantages of the laparoscopic approach.
chole_open_cholecystectomy_procedure.source: Narvaez Gonzalez HF et al, Cureus 2025;17(2):e78782, PMID 40078242.
chole_open_cholecystectomy_procedure.confidence: moderate (modern comparative complication data specific to planned, non-converted open cholecystectomy is honestly sparse because open surgery today is used almost exclusively as a conversion/rescue procedure)

chole_ercp_sphincterotomy_choledocholith.name: ERCP with Endoscopic Sphincterotomy (EST) for Choledocholithiasis -- Real Standard Approach to Common Bile Duct Stone Clearance
chole_ercp_sphincterotomy_choledocholith.type: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy and stone extraction (balloon/basket)
chole_ercp_sphincterotomy_choledocholith.effectiveness: Single-session stone clearance in 75% of patients with confirmed common bile duct stones (180 of 240); cumulative endoscopic clearance (allowing repeat sessions) rose to 94.2% (226 of 240), with 14 patients (5.8%) ultimately failing endoscopic clearance and requiring surgical alternatives; real recurrent CBD stones after successful clearance occurred in 4.3% (15 of 350 total patients) over a 30-year follow-up
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- endoscopic procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy, followed by balloon or basket extraction of common bile duct stones, typically performed sequentially with (before or after) laparoscopic cholecystectomy for the gallbladder itself
reason_why: Endoscopic sphincterotomy real-world enlarges the ampulla of Vater's outflow opening, allowing an endoscopically-passed balloon or basket to directly extract stones lodged in or migrated into the common bile duct -- a mechanical removal of the obstructing lesion that relieves biliary obstruction and prevents/treats cholangitis, distinct from (and complementary to, not a substitute for) cholecystectomy, which removes the gallbladder itself but does not clear stones already in the common bile duct.
chole_ercp_sphincterotomy_choledocholith.source: Delcarro A et al, 'Sequential endoscopic and laparoscopic treatment for choledocholithiasis: a 30-year experience in the era of evolving techniques', Surg Endosc 2026;40(1):475-479, PMID 41136653.
chole_ercp_sphincterotomy_choledocholith.confidence: high (real single-center but very large, long-duration 30-year experience with 350 patients)

chole_iv_antibiotics_acute_cholecystitis.name: IV Antibiotic Therapy for Acute Cholecystitis and Acute Cholangitis -- Real Essential Adjunct, Honestly NOT Curative of the Underlying Gallstones
chole_iv_antibiotics_acute_cholecystitis.type: Empiric intravenous antibiotics, severity-graded per Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18)
chole_iv_antibiotics_acute_cholecystitis.effectiveness: No dissolution/cure percentage applies here by design -- antibiotics treat the infective complication (acute cholecystitis/cholangitis) that gallstones can trigger, they do not dissolve, remove, or prevent recurrence of the stones themselves; correctly framed here at lower priority as 'other,' not as this disease's cure
specific_drugs: Mild (Grade I): Cefazolin, Cefotiam, Cefuroxime, or Ampicillin/Sulbactam
Moderate (Grade II): Cefotiam, Cefuroxime, Ceftriaxone, Cefepime, Ampicillin/Sulbactam, or Piperacillin/Tazobactam

Severe (Grade III): Cefepime, Ceftazidime, Piperacillin/Tazobactam, Meropenem, Imipenem/Cilastatin, or Doripenem, plus Metronidazole for anaerobic coverage when biliary-enteric anastomosis or elderly/severe disease raises anaerobic risk
reason_why: Gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct or common bile duct allows bacterial overgrowth (commonly E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and anaerobes) in stagnant bile, and antibiotics real-world control this secondary infection and prevent progression to sepsis/gangrenous cholecystitis or suppurative cholangitis while the definitive mechanical treatment (cholecystectomy and/or ERCP stone clearance) is arranged -- but because the antibiotic does nothing to the stone itself, the underlying lithogenic process and the risk of recurrent attacks persist unless the stone is removed or dissolved by one of the definitive treatments in this survey.
chole_iv_antibiotics_acute_cholecystitis.source: Gomi H et al, 'Tokyo Guidelines 2018: antimicrobial therapy for acute cholangitis and cholecystitis', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2018;25(1):3-16, PMID 29090866; Miura F et al, 'Tokyo Guidelines 2018: initial management of acute biliary infection and flowchart for acute cholangitis', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2018;25(1):31-40, PMID 28941329.

chole_percutaneous_cholecystostomy_high_.name: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Cholecystostomy (PC) -- Real Bridging/Salvage Option for Patients Too High-Risk for Immediate Surgery
chole_percutaneous_cholecystostomy_high_.type: Image-guided percutaneous drainage catheter placed into the gallbladder
chole_percutaneous_cholecystostomy_high_.effectiveness: Technical success 99.3% (95% CI 97.8-99.8), clinical success 97.6% (95% CI 83.4-99.7) in a real pooled meta-analysis of high-risk acute cholecystitis patients; however, real 30-day mortality of 6.2% reflects the severity of the underlying patient population, not procedural failure, and in the CHOCOLATE RCT of high-risk but still surgery-eligible patients, percutaneous drainage produced major complications in 65% (vs 12% for laparoscopic cholecystectomy) and recurrent biliary disease in 53% (vs 5%) because it drains but does not remove the stone-filled gallbladder
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- percutaneous drainage procedure, not a medicine
reason_why: A drainage catheter decompresses an obstructed, infected gallbladder and controls sepsis without requiring general anesthesia, making it real-world valuable in patients too unstable or comorbid for immediate surgery -- but because the gallbladder and its stones are left in place, this is honestly a bridging or salvage measure, not a cure, and real RCT data (CHOCOLATE) show that even in high-risk patients who ARE eligible for surgery, laparoscopic cholecystectomy produces far fewer complications and far less recurrent disease than drainage alone; percutaneous cholecystostomy is therefore correctly reserved for patients whose acute instability (e.g. septic shock, prohibitive anesthetic risk) genuinely precludes surgery even after standard resuscitation, as a bridge to later, real definitive cholecystectomy once the patient stabilizes, or as a definitive palliative measure in patients who will never become surgical candidates.
chole_percutaneous_cholecystostomy_high_.source: Boccatonda A et al, 'Ultrasound-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy for acute cholecystitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis', J Ultrasound 2026;29(1):25-34, PMID 41665843; Loozen CS et al, BMJ 2018;363:k3965, PMID 30297544; Kryvoruchko IA, 'Percutaneous versus surgical treatment of acute cholecystitis', World J Emerg Surg 2026;21(1):39, PMID 42374556.
chole_percutaneous_cholecystostomy_high_.confidence: high for technical/clinical success rates (real meta-analysis); high for the honest 'not a cure, real RCT-proven inferior to surgery in eligible patients' framing (real multicentre RCT)

chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.name: Early Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (Index Admission) for Acute Cholecystitis -- Real Guideline-Preferred Timing
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.type: Timing-of-surgery evidence, not a distinct treatment
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.effectiveness: Reduces total hospital stay by a real mean of 3.50 days (95% CI 4.11-2.90 fewer days) versus delayed surgery (>=4 weeks after conservative management), with no significant difference in conversion to open surgery, common bile duct injury, operative time, or overall postoperative complications, across 21 real RCTs (1,731 patients); early surgery showed a higher rate of intraoperative complications (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.31-3.39) but these were predominantly minor technical events that did not translate into worse postoperative outcomes
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- timing-of-surgery evidence, not a medicine
reason_why: Operating during the same hospital admission avoids a second admission and a real waiting-period risk of recurrent or worsening cholecystitis, while inflammatory tissue planes, though real-world present, remain manageable for an experienced surgeon in the great majority of cases within this timeframe -- the real net effect proven across multiple RCTs is a shorter total hospital stay without a real increase in major surgical harm.
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.source: Khan QI, Baig H, Khan M, Naz S, Lucocq J, 'The optimal timing of laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis according to symptom onset and patient admission: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials', Surg Endosc 2026;40(5):3641-3657, PMID 42377519.

chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.name: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Beyond the '7-Day Barrier' of Symptom Duration -- Real Honest Non-Inferiority Signal, Not Yet a Strong Recommendation
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.type: Timing-of-surgery evidence for delayed-presentation acute cholecystitis
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.effectiveness: No significant difference in major complications (bile duct injury/leakage and bowel injury combined, risk difference -1.0%, 95% CI -2.3 to 0.3), Clavien-Dindo grade >=3 complications (risk difference -0.3%, 95% CI -2.5 to 1.9), or conversion to open surgery (risk difference -1.5%, 95% CI -3.9 to 0.9) between cholecystectomy performed within 7 days versus after 7 days of cholecystitis symptoms, across 13 real non-randomised studies (5,481 patients); operating time was a real 11.8 minutes longer and total hospital stay 2.7 days longer beyond the 7-day mark
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- timing-of-surgery evidence, not a medicine
reason_why: Real accumulated inflammation and fibrosis beyond 7 days genuinely make the operation technically harder (reflected honestly in the longer operating time), but this real technical difficulty did not translate into a real statistically significant increase in major complications in the pooled non-randomised data located here -- an honest, non-inferiority-leaning signal rather than a proven recommendation, since the authors themselves note risk of bias and insufficiently powered studies preclude a strong practice recommendation for surgery beyond the 7-day window.
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.source: van Maasakkers MHG et al, 'Evaluating the 7-day barrier: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholecystitis with prolonged symptom duration; a systematic review and meta-analysis', Langenbecks Arch Surg 2024;409(1):366, PMID 39607476.
chole_timing_of_cholecystectomy_evidence.confidence: moderate (non-randomised studies, authors themselves flag risk of bias and underpowering)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (oral dissolution rate, bile duct injury-free rate, RCT-proven freedom from major complications/recurrent disease, endoscopic stone-clearance rate, percutaneous drainage technical/clinical success) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is honestly the strongest real cure intervention in this table because it physically removes the root cause (the stone-forming organ itself), directly comparable in kind, though not in raw percentage or mechanism, to H. pylori eradication elsewhere in this knowledge base. Oral bile-acid dissolution therapy genuinely works but only in a patient-selection-dependent minority with a meaningful recurrence rate after stopping, and is reported here at real, honestly modest percentages rather than inflated ones. Percutaneous cholecystostomy's high technical/clinical success rate reflects successful DRAINAGE, not cure of the underlying stones -- it is ranked according to its own real procedural-success metric, not as a claim of disease cure.
