cholelithiasis_cholecystitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL, ACTUAL EMERGENCY: Acute (ascending) cholangitis is a real, actual life-threatening biliary sepsis emergency that must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue consultation flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance / go to ER now). It classically presents with Charcot's triad - fever (often with rigors), jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain - reflecting biliary obstruction (usually by a common bile duct stone, i.e. choledocholithiasis) plus superimposed bacterial infection of stagnant, obstructed bile. A systematic review found Charcot's triad has real pooled sensitivity of only approximately 36.3% (specificity approximately 93.2%) for diagnosing acute cholangitis, meaning it functions as a real effective 'rule-in' test but a poor 'rule-out' test - its ABSENCE must NOT be used to exclude cholangitis in a patient with a plausible biliary-obstruction picture (Rumsey S et al, 'Diagnostic accuracy of Charcot's triad: a systematic review', ANZ J Surg 2017, PMID 28213923). Progression to Reynolds' pentad - Charcot's triad plus hypotension and altered mental status - signals evolving suppurative cholangitis and septic shock, a real surgical/interventional emergency requiring urgent biliary decompression. Per the Tokyo Guidelines (TG13), acute cholangitis has carried a real historical mortality of approximately 10%, compared with generally under 1% for acute cholecystitis, reflecting cholangitis's real distinct sepsis risk from bacterial cholangiovenous/cholangiolymphatic reflux into the systemic circulation (Kimura Y et al, 'TG13 current terminology, etiology, and epidemiology of acute cholangitis and cholecystitis', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2013, PMID 23307004). RECOGNIZE URGENTLY: fever/rigors with jaundice and right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain (Charcot's triad), especially if accompanied by hypotension, confusion, or reduced consciousness (Reynolds' pentad); this presentation requires emergency resuscitation, IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary drainage (endoscopic, percutaneous, or surgical) for source control - not the routine consultation flow. Source: Kiriyama S et al, 'TG13 guidelines for diagnosis and severity grading of acute cholangitis (with videos)', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2013;20(1):24-34, PMID 23307001; Kimura Y et al, PMID 23307004; Miura F et al, 'Tokyo Guidelines 2018: initial management of acute biliary infection and flowchart for acute cholangitis', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2018, PMID 28941329; Rumsey S et al, PMID 28213923.

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Cholelithiasis is the presence of stones (calculi) within the gallbladder. Most gallstones remain clinically silent; the term 'gallstone disease' is generally reserved for stones that become symptomatic or cause complications. Acute cholecystitis is acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall, in over 90-95% of cases caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone (calculous cholecystitis); acalculous cholecystitis (no stone) is a separate, less common entity typically seen in critically ill patients.
definition_and_pathophysiology.cholesterol_stone_mechanism: Cholesterol gallstones - the predominant stone type in most populations - form via three converging mechanisms: (1) hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol relative to the solubilizing capacity of bile salts and phospholipids (lecithin), producing bile that is supersaturated with cholesterol; (2) accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals from this supersaturated bile, promoted by pronucleating mucin glycoproteins and reduced by antinucleating apolipoproteins; and (3) gallbladder hypomotility/stasis (impaired emptying), which allows nucleated crystals time to aggregate and grow into macroscopic stones rather than being cleared with normal gallbladder contraction. A common inherited contributor is mutation in the hepatic cholesterol transporter ABCG5/ABCG8, which increases biliary cholesterol secretion and accounts for a substantial share of the genetic risk of cholesterol gallstones.
definition_and_pathophysiology.pigment_stone_mechanism: Pigment stones form by a distinct mechanism centered on unconjugated bilirubin rather than cholesterol supersaturation. Black pigment stones arise chiefly from chronic hemolysis (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease) or cirrhosis, which increase unconjugated bilirubin delivery to bile; this bilirubin precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate, especially when bile is stagnant, forming hard black stones typically confined to the gallbladder. Brown pigment stones instead develop primarily within obstructed and infected bile ducts, where bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin glucuronide back to unconjugated bilirubin, which then precipitates with calcium; brown stones are therefore associated with biliary stasis/stricture and infection and can form de novo in the bile ducts themselves.
definition_and_pathophysiology.cystic_duct_obstruction_and_acute_cholec: Acute calculous cholecystitis begins when a gallstone (or biliary sludge) impacts in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck (Hartmann's pouch), obstructing bile outflow. Continued mucus secretion by the obstructed gallbladder mucosa raises intraluminal pressure, distending the gallbladder wall and compromising mucosal blood flow. The retained, concentrated bile itself is chemically irritant to the gallbladder mucosa (via lysolecithin generated by phospholipase A2 acting on biliary lecithin), triggering a primarily chemical inflammatory response that, if obstruction persists beyond roughly 24-48 hours, is compounded by secondary bacterial infection (commonly enteric organisms such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus reaching the gallbladder via ascending infection or hematogenous/lymphatic spread), producing the full acute cholecystitis picture of a distended, inflamed, edematous gallbladder wall; unrelieved, this can progress to gallbladder wall ischemia, gangrenous cholecystitis, and perforation.
definition_and_pathophysiology.disease_spectrum_framework: Gallstone-related disease exists on a real clinical spectrum of increasing severity: (1) asymptomatic gallstones ('silent' gallstones, discovered incidentally on imaging, causing no symptoms); (2) symptomatic uncomplicated gallstone disease (biliary colic - transient pain from a stone briefly obstructing the cystic duct without sustained inflammation); and (3) complicated gallstone disease, comprising acute cholecystitis (sustained cystic duct obstruction with gallbladder wall inflammation, as above), choledocholithiasis (a stone migrating into and lodging in the common bile duct), acute cholangitis (infection superimposed on common-bile-duct obstruction - see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE), and gallstone pancreatitis (a migrating stone transiently or persistently obstructing the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater, triggering acute pancreatitis; see this knowledge base's acute_pancreatitis entry for that disease's own diagnostic/severity framework). This staged framework is clinically important because management differs substantially by stage, and most patients never progress beyond stage 1.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Lammert F, Gurusamy K, Ko CW, Miquel JF, Mendez-Sanchez N, Portincasa P, van Erpecum KJ, van Laarhoven CJ, Wang DQ, 'Gallstones', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2016;2:16024, PMID 27121416; Stinton LM, Shaffer EA, 'Epidemiology of gallbladder disease: cholelithiasis and cancer', Gut and Liver 2012;6(2):172-187, PMID 22570746.

diagnostic_framework.abdominal_ultrasound_first_line: Transabdominal ultrasonography is the real first-line and most widely used initial imaging test for suspected gallstone disease and acute cholecystitis, given its wide availability, low cost, absence of ionizing radiation, and good performance for detecting gallstones themselves (visualized as echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing) plus secondary signs of acute cholecystitis (gallbladder wall thickening greater than 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, and a sonographic Murphy's sign - focal tenderness directly over the ultrasound-visualized gallbladder). A meta-analysis of imaging performance in acute cholecystitis reported ultrasound sensitivity of approximately 81% (95% CI 75-87%) and specificity of approximately 83% (95% CI 74-89%).
diagnostic_framework.hida_scan_for_equivocal_cases: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scanning (cholescintigraphy) is used for equivocal cases where ultrasound is non-diagnostic; a radiotracer is taken up by hepatocytes and excreted into bile, and non-visualization of the gallbladder (because a cystic-duct stone prevents tracer entry) indicates acute cholecystitis. The same meta-analysis found cholescintigraphy to have the highest diagnostic accuracy of the imaging modalities studied, with pooled sensitivity of approximately 96% (95% CI 94-97%) and specificity of approximately 90% (95% CI 86-93%), meaningfully higher sensitivity than ultrasound, though its use is limited in practice by radiotracer availability, longer study duration, and radiation exposure compared with ultrasound.
diagnostic_framework.liver_function_tests_and_bile_duct_invol: A cholestatic pattern of liver function tests - disproportionate elevation of alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), and conjugated (direct) bilirubin relative to transaminases - is the classically taught biochemical signature suggesting common bile duct (CBD) involvement (choledocholithiasis), and abnormal liver biochemistry plus a dilated CBD on ultrasound are used as clinical predictors of choledocholithiasis in guideline risk-stratification schemes (Buxbaum JL et al, 'ASGE guideline on the role of endoscopy in the evaluation and management of choledocholithiasis', Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2019, PMID 30979521). This classic pattern has a real, clinically important exception: a systematic review and meta-analysis found that roughly one-third of choledocholithiasis patients present with marked transaminase elevation (ALT or AST greater than 500 IU/L), with levels exceeding 1000 IU/L in approximately 7.8% of cases - a pattern that can mimic acute hepatocellular injury rather than the 'presumed' cholestatic picture, so a hepatocellular-pattern LFT abnormality should not be used to rule out an obstructing CBD stone.
diagnostic_framework.charcots_triad_for_cholangitis: Fever (often with rigors), jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain (Charcot's triad) is the classic clinical descriptor used to raise suspicion for acute cholangitis, reflecting infected, obstructed bile in the common bile duct; see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for its real, limited sensitivity (approximately 36.3%) and the higher-severity Reynolds' pentad. The Tokyo Guidelines (TG13) formal diagnostic criteria for acute cholangitis - systemic inflammation, cholestasis on clinical/laboratory grounds, and imaging evidence of biliary obstruction/cause - achieved higher reported sensitivity (approximately 87.6%) and specificity (approximately 77.7%) than Charcot's triad alone and are the current evidence-based diagnostic standard.
diagnostic_framework.source: Kiewiet JJ, Leeuwenburgh MM, Bipat S, Bossuyt PM, Stoker J, Boermeester MA, 'A systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic performance of imaging in acute cholecystitis', Radiology 2012;264(3):708-720, PMID 22798223; Buxbaum JL et al, PMID 30979521; Mohamed MFH et al, 'Choledocholithiasis Can Present with Marked Transaminases Elevation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Digestive Diseases and Sciences 2023, PMID 37269372; Kiriyama S et al, PMID 23307001; Rumsey S et al, PMID 28213923.

classic_symptoms.biliary_colic: The hallmark symptom of symptomatic uncomplicated gallstone disease is biliary colic: episodic, often postprandial pain (classically triggered or worsened by fatty-food meals, which stimulate cholecystokinin-mediated gallbladder contraction against a stone obstructing the cystic duct), located in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, frequently radiating to the right shoulder blade or back (referred pain via shared visceral/phrenic afferent pathways), and commonly accompanied by nausea and/or vomiting. Despite the name 'colic,' the pain is typically constant/steady during an episode (lasting roughly 30 minutes to a few hours) rather than truly crampy or intermittent, and it characteristically resolves once the obstructing stone disimpacts back into the gallbladder lumen.
classic_symptoms.murphys_sign_for_acute_cholecystitis: Murphy's sign - inspiratory arrest (a pause in inspiration) caused by pain when the examiner's fingers palpate the right subcostal margin as the patient breathes in, bringing the inflamed gallbladder down against the examining hand - is the classic bedside sign specifically associated with acute cholecystitis (rather than simple biliary colic). A systematic review found Murphy's sign carries only a modest positive likelihood ratio of approximately 2.8 (95% CI 0.8-8.6, an interval crossing 1.0) as an isolated finding, and right-upper-quadrant tenderness alone had a negative likelihood ratio of approximately 0.4 (95% CI 0.2-1.1) - meaning neither finding alone reliably confirms or excludes acute cholecystitis, and the overall clinical gestalt (positive likelihood ratio approximately 25-30 in the same review) combined with imaging is what actually drives diagnosis in practice.
classic_symptoms.fever_as_a_distinguishing_feature: Fever is a genuinely important distinguishing feature between disease stages: fever is typically absent in simple biliary colic (a self-limited mechanical obstruction without sustained inflammation or infection), but is expected in acute cholecystitis (reflecting sustained gallbladder wall inflammation, often with secondary bacterial infection) and is a core component of Charcot's triad in acute cholangitis (reflecting frank bacterial infection of obstructed bile with a real risk of bacteremia/sepsis). A patient with RUQ pain plus fever should therefore be evaluated for cholecystitis or cholangitis, not managed as simple biliary colic.
classic_symptoms.jaundice: Jaundice (scleral icterus/yellowing of skin) suggests bile-duct obstruction (choledocholithiasis) rather than simple gallbladder-confined stones, since gallstones confined to the gallbladder do not obstruct bilirubin excretion; jaundice with RUQ pain and fever forms Charcot's triad (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
classic_symptoms.source: Lammert F et al, PMID 27121416; Trowbridge RL, Rutkowski NK, Shojania KG, 'Does this patient have acute cholecystitis?', JAMA 2003;289(1):80-86, PMID 12503981; Kiriyama S et al, PMID 23307001.

differential_diagnosis.peptic_ulcer_disease: Peptic ulcer disease (see this knowledge base's peptic_ulcer_disease entry) can present with epigastric pain overlapping biliary colic, but classically shows a clearer relationship to meals in the opposite direction for duodenal ulcers (pain relieved by eating, recurring 2-3 hours later or at night) versus gastric ulcers (pain often worsened by eating), lacks the right-shoulder radiation typical of biliary pain, and is not associated with Murphy's sign or gallbladder findings on ultrasound; endoscopy and H. pylori/NSAID history help distinguish it.
differential_diagnosis.acute_pancreatitis: Acute pancreatitis (see this knowledge base's acute_pancreatitis entry) shares epigastric pain with gallstone disease and, importantly, gallstones are a real major etiology of acute pancreatitis (gallstone pancreatitis, via transient or persistent ampullary obstruction by a migrating stone). Pancreatitis pain classically radiates straight through to the back, is more constant and severe, and is distinguished biochemically by lipase/amylase elevation at least 3x the upper limit of normal per the revised Atlanta criteria (see the acute_pancreatitis entry's diagnostic_framework), which is not expected in uncomplicated gallstone disease without pancreatic involvement.
differential_diagnosis.right_lower_lobe_pneumonia: Right lower lobe pneumonia can present with right-upper-quadrant or right-sided abdominal pain because diaphragmatic and pleural irritation from adjacent lower-lobe consolidation refers pain to the abdomen via shared thoracoabdominal innervation; this is a recognized real diagnostic pitfall in RUQ-pain workups. A radiology-focused review of the emergency-department RUQ-pain workup found that CT identified an acute nongallbladder abnormality that had been missed on a preceding ultrasound in 103 of 322 cases (32%), underscoring that a real, clinically significant minority of RUQ pain has a nongallbladder cause; respiratory signs/symptoms (cough, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, fever pattern) and a chest examination/chest imaging help distinguish pneumonia from gallbladder disease when the abdominal examination is atypical or ultrasound is unrevealing.
differential_diagnosis.myocardial_ischemia: Inferior-wall myocardial ischemia/infarction can present atypically as epigastric or right-upper-quadrant discomfort with nausea and vomiting (rather than classic chest pain), because the inferior/diaphragmatic surface of the heart shares visceral afferent pathways that can be perceived as upper-abdominal pain; this is a well-recognized real source of diagnostic delay, particularly in older adults, diabetics, and women. An electrocardiogram (and troponin, where cardiac risk factors or exam findings raise suspicion) is the key discriminating test, since biliary/gallbladder disease does not produce ischemic ECG changes or troponin elevation.
differential_diagnosis.source: Kiriyama S et al, PMID 23307001 (acute_pancreatitis and peptic_ulcer_disease entries carry their own primary sources for those diseases); Lin EC, Kuo YT, Chi CH, 'Role of Ultrasound and CT in the Workup of Right Upper Quadrant Pain in Adults in the Emergency Department' [nongallbladder-cause finding], AJR American Journal of Roentgenology 2020, PMID 32160055.

risk_factors.classic_5fs: The classic (mnemonic) '5 F's' - Female, Fat (obesity), Forty (age, with rising risk continuing well beyond age 40), Fertile (multiparity/pregnancy), and Family history (genetic predisposition) - correspond to real, epidemiologically supported risk factors: female sex, obesity, advancing age, and genetic/family predisposition are each independently confirmed risk factors in epidemiologic reviews of gallstone disease, and pregnancy/multiparity is a recognized real risk factor via estrogen-driven increased biliary cholesterol saturation and progesterone-driven gallbladder hypomotility.
risk_factors.rapid_weight_loss: Rapid weight loss (including from very-low-calorie diets and after bariatric surgery) is a real, well-established risk factor for new gallstone formation, attributed to increased cholesterol mobilization into bile combined with reduced gallbladder emptying/motility during rapid caloric restriction.
risk_factors.pregnancy: Pregnancy increases gallstone risk via estrogen-mediated increases in biliary cholesterol secretion and progesterone-mediated gallbladder hypomotility/stasis, both of which favor the cholesterol-stone-formation mechanism described above.
risk_factors.genetic_and_ethnic_variation: Genetic factors are substantial: common variants in the hepatic cholesterol transporter ABCG8 confer a large share (cited as up to approximately 25% of total risk in some analyses) of inherited gallstone susceptibility. Certain ethnic/ancestral populations - most classically Pima and other Native American populations, and some Northern European/Scandinavian populations - have real, substantially higher prevalence of cholesterol gallstones than populations of, for example, Sub-Saharan African ancestry, reflecting real population-level genetic and dietary differences.
risk_factors.other_established_factors: Additional real risk factors include a sedentary lifestyle, metabolic syndrome/obesity-related insulin resistance, total parenteral nutrition and prolonged fasting (biliary stasis promoting sludge/stones), certain medications (e.g., ceftriaxone, octreotide, thiazide diuretics), cirrhosis and chronic hemolytic conditions (specifically for black pigment stones), and biliary stasis/infection (for brown pigment stones).
risk_factors.source: Stinton LM, Shaffer EA, PMID 22570746; Lammert F et al, PMID 27121416.

epidemiology.global_prevalence: Gallstones are highly prevalent in the general population: pooled estimates suggest up to approximately 20% of adults develop gallstones over their lifetime in higher-risk populations, and of those with gallstones, more than 20% eventually develop symptoms or complications - meaning the large majority of people with gallstones remain asymptomatic. Ultrasonography is considered the best epidemiological screening method for determining point prevalence of gallstone disease in population studies.
epidemiology.india_specific_data: A large community-based cross-sectional study pooling two Indian population datasets (the Gallstone Survey and the 0.5 Million Indian Women screening study), covering 28,395 participants (9,158 men, 19,237 women) aged 30-65 years across multiple Indian regions, found substantial real regional variation in self-reported gallstone prevalence - from as low as approximately 0.3% (Barshi, Maharashtra) to as high as approximately 10.7-10.8% (Kamrup/Guwahati, Assam, and Mullanpur, Punjab) - with prevalence increasing with age and consistently higher in women than men across regions.
epidemiology.source: Lammert F et al, PMID 27121416; Stinton LM, Shaffer EA, PMID 22570746; Mohite SU et al, 'Prevalence of gallstone disease in India: insights from a community-based cross-sectional study', BMJ Public Health 2026, PMID 41658223.

natural_history.asymptomatic_gallstones_generally_benign: The great majority of gallstones remain asymptomatic for life and never require treatment; population studies consistently show that most incidentally discovered gallstones (e.g., found on imaging performed for an unrelated reason) never progress to symptomatic disease, which is why routine treatment of asymptomatic gallstones is not generally indicated (see clinical_takeaway).
natural_history.progression_risk_once_symptomatic: Once a patient becomes symptomatic (experiences biliary colic), the real risk of recurrent biliary colic and of progression to a complication (acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, acute cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis) rises substantially compared with the asymptomatic state; symptoms often precede the onset of these three common and potentially life-threatening complications (acute cholecystitis, acute cholangitis, and gallstone/biliary pancreatitis), meaning the transition from 'silent' to 'symptomatic' is the real clinically important inflection point for counseling and management decisions.
natural_history.untreated_complicated_disease: Untreated acute cholecystitis can progress to gallbladder wall ischemia, gangrenous cholecystitis, and perforation; untreated choledocholithiasis can progress to acute cholangitis (real sepsis risk - see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) or gallstone pancreatitis. Reported mortality has historically been under approximately 1% for acute cholecystitis versus approximately 10% for acute cholangitis, reflecting cholangitis's distinct systemic-sepsis risk.
natural_history.source: Lammert F et al, PMID 27121416; Kimura Y et al, PMID 23307004.

clinical_takeaway.asymptomatic_gallstones_generally_dont_n: Given the real high rate of incidental gallstone detection on imaging performed for unrelated reasons, and the real fact that the large majority of gallstones never become symptomatic, asymptomatic gallstones are generally not an indication for treatment - this is a genuinely important point for both patients and clinicians to avoid over-treating an incidental finding.
clinical_takeaway.symptomatic_or_complicated_disease_has_d: In contrast, symptomatic gallstone disease (biliary colic) and complicated disease (acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis) have real, definitive, curative treatment pathways once diagnosed (addressed in this disease entry's separate, parallel treatment-focused pass), so the clinical priority is accurate staging along the disease spectrum described above (definition_and_pathophysiology) rather than either ignoring genuine complicated disease or over-treating silent stones.
clinical_takeaway.source: Lammert F et al, PMID 27121416; Stinton LM, Shaffer EA, PMID 22570746.

bronchiolitis.name: Bronchiolitis (RSV and Other Viral)
bronchiolitis.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages were not accessible with this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 codes J21.0 (Acute bronchiolitis due to respiratory syncytial virus) and J21.9 (Acute bronchiolitis, unspecified) are the codes commonly used for this condition in the literature, but this ICD-10 mapping was likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

most_common_causative_pathogen.finding: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the dominant cause of bronchiolitis. A global systematic review/meta-analysis of pediatric respiratory tract infections found 'bronchiolitis showed the highest prevalence (56.9%)' of RSV detection among all respiratory presentations studied, and RSV testing was most frequent in infants under 6 months (33.8% prevalence). The CDC states RSV is 'the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children younger than 1 year of age' and 'the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S.' The Cochrane review on bronchiolitis also states 'the most common causative organism is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).'
most_common_causative_pathogen.source: Khales P et al, 'The prevalence and role of human respiratory syncytial virus in pediatric respiratory tract infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis of global data', EClinicalMedicine 2026 (PMID 41908856, PMC13018908); CDC, 'About RSV', cdc.gov/rsv/about/index.html (accessed 2026-09-23); Zhang L et al, 'Nebulised hypertonic saline solution for acute bronchiolitis in infants', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872)

other_viral_causes.finding: Beyond RSV, real documented viral causes of bronchiolitis include parainfluenza viruses, adenovirus, influenza A and B, rhinovirus/enterovirus, human metapneumovirus, and seasonal human coronaviruses; the Cochrane review also lists Mycoplasma pneumoniae as a less common non-viral pathogen in the same clinical syndrome. A 2026 study on post-RSV-hospitalization asthma outcomes used 'influenza, parainfluenza, and human metapneumovirus' as the principal RSV comparator viruses causing viral lower respiratory tract infection in infants.
other_viral_causes.source: Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872); Hazan G, Ofri M, Hertz L, Martyn O, Greenberg D, 'Asthma-related Pediatric Healthcare Utilization after Hospitalization for RSV and Other Viral Lower Respiratory Tract Infections', Open Forum Infect Dis 2026 (PMID 42444788, PMC13358292)

small_airway_inflammation_mucus_plugging.finding: The mechanism of bronchiolitis is real primary infectious inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles), not chronic reactive airway disease. RSV 'replicates first in the nasal turbinate, then propagates to the bronchioles where increased mucus production, impaired ciliary action, and sloughed epithelial cells obstruct the lumen.' A neonatal-focused review adds histologic detail: 'Bronchial narrowing and interference in gas exchange occurs as a result of infiltration of the airway by inflammatory cells, necrosis of the respiratory tract epithelium, shedding of necrotic cells and impaired ciliary function,' with 'epithelial cell necrosis, bronchiolar epithelium proliferation, infiltration of monocytes, T-cells and neutrophils' leading to 'airway obstruction, air trapping.' The Cochrane review similarly describes 'a peribronchial infiltrate of inflammatory cells, mucosal and submucosal oedema, necrosis and desquamation of ciliated epithelial cells.'
small_airway_inflammation_mucus_plugging.source: Brüssow H, 'Respiratory syncytial virus: health burden, disease prevention, and treatment-recent progress and lessons learned', Microlife 2025 (PMID 40420998, PMC12104812); Singh S, Maheshwari A, Namazova I, Benjamin JT, Wang Y, 'Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections in Neonates: A Persisting Problem', Newborn (Clarksville) 2023 (PMID 38348152, PMC10860331); Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872)

distinction_from_asthma.finding: This infectious small-airway mechanism is a real important distinction from asthma despite the overlapping wheeze presentation. Clinically, primary-care guidance states asthma 'cannot reliably be diagnosed in children younger than 12 months but can be considered in those with a history of atopy or recurrent wheeze' - i.e. bronchiolitis is typically a single acute infectious episode in a young infant, whereas asthma implies a chronic, recurrent, often atopy-associated reactive-airway process. The literature is honest that the two are not cleanly separable at the population level: 'Acute wheezing in early life is most often caused by viral infections...and can be the first manifestation of childhood asthma,' and whether severe viral bronchiolitis itself causes later asthma or simply unmasks a pre-existing susceptibility ('whether RV causes or reveals asthma') remains scientifically unresolved.
distinction_from_asthma.source: Lirette MP, Conejero Müller MJ, Young J, 'Management of bronchiolitis in infants in primary care settings: What to do and what not to do', Can Fam Physician 2023;69 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257); Melén E et al, 'Asthma Inception: Epidemiologic Risk Factors and Natural History Across the Life Course', Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024 (PMID 38981012, PMC11418887)

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Bronchiolitis is a real clinical diagnosis made from history and examination, not from a laboratory or imaging test. 'Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis.' The Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline (2025 update) states: 'Consider a diagnosis of bronchiolitis in an infant if they have an upper respiratory tract infection (rhinorrhoea/nasal congestion, and/or cough), followed by the onset of a lower respiratory tract infection,' and it typically affects infants under 12 months of age.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257); Borland ML et al, 'Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline: 2025 Update', J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

role_of_rsv_viral_testing.finding: RSV antigen/PCR testing's real role is mainly epidemiologic/cohorting rather than routinely changing individual management of a typical case. The Australasian guideline recommends: 'Do not routinely use viral testing in infants presenting to hospital or hospitalised with bronchiolitis, including testing undertaken solely for cohorting of patients' (Conditional recommendation). Canadian primary-care guidance concurs: 'Do not order comprehensive respiratory viral testing.'
role_of_rsv_viral_testing.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)

role_of_chest_xray.finding: Chest X-ray is real not routinely needed for typical presentations. The Australasian guideline states: 'Do not routinely use CXR in infants presenting or admitted to hospital with bronchiolitis,' reserving it only for 'infants with an unexpected deterioration...or a clinical course not consistent with bronchiolitis.' Canadian guidance is stronger for typical cases: 'No investigations are needed for diagnosis - including chest radiograph or laboratory testing...regardless of whether the infant is seen at the start, middle, or end of disease.' A 2025 study likewise found 'Routine Chest X-Rays in Critical Bronchiolitis Do Not Improve Outcomes.'
role_of_chest_xray.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257); Sunderajan T et al, 'Routine Chest X-Rays in Critical Bronchiolitis Do Not Improve Outcomes', J Clin Med 2025 (PMID 41227205, PMC12608742)

upper_respiratory_prodrome_and_progressi.finding: The classic pattern is a preceding mild upper-respiratory prodrome followed by lower-respiratory progression: 'The condition begins with signs of an upper respiratory tract infection (e.g., rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, cough), followed by signs of a lower respiratory tract infection, including respiratory distress and the presence of diffuse crackles and/or wheeze.' Primary-care guidance similarly describes 'a history of upper respiratory illness prodrome' preceding 'bilateral wheezing or crepitations, increased work of breathing...or increased respiratory rate,' typically in infants aged 0-24 months.
upper_respiratory_prodrome_and_progressi.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)

increased_work_of_breathing_and_tachypne.finding: Increased work of breathing is a real core feature: 'Bronchiolitis may also involve hypoxaemia, apnoea, increased respiratory and heart rate, the use of accessory muscles, feeding difficulties, irritability and/or lethargy.' Primary-care guidance specifies the signs as 'grunting, nasal flaring, retractions.'
increased_work_of_breathing_and_tachypne.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)

feeding_difficulty.finding: Feeding difficulty is a real documented feature, driven by concurrent nasal congestion and increased respiratory effort making coordinated suck-swallow-breathe difficult; the Australasian guideline lists 'feeding difficulties' explicitly among the clinical features of bronchiolitis, alongside 'faltering growth/slow weight gain' as a recognised complication/risk marker.
feeding_difficulty.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

apnea_in_young_premature_infants.finding: Apnea is a real distinctive and dangerous presentation specifically in very young/premature infants, and can occur even before the classic wheeze/crackle picture is obvious. A neonatal-focused review states: 'Apnea may be the presenting symptom in one-fifth of the cases hospitalized with RSV,' with a systematic-review incidence of apnea in hospitalized RSV infants of '1.2 and 23.8%.' Critically, 'the incidence was higher in preterm than in term neonates,' whereas 'the risk of apnea was <5% in children without serious underlying disease' - i.e. age/prematurity substantially raises apnea risk. The Australasian guideline separately notes apnoea is uncommon in the general bronchiolitis population (reported at under 2%), consistent with apnea being concentrated in the young/premature/high-risk subgroup rather than typical cases.
apnea_in_young_premature_infants.source: Singh S, Maheshwari A, Namazova I, Benjamin JT, Wang Y, 'Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections in Neonates: A Persisting Problem', Newborn (Clarksville) 2023 (PMID 38348152, PMC10860331); Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

asthma_or_first_wheezing_episode.finding: Asthma is a real differential, especially a first wheezing episode that may represent early asthma rather than infectious bronchiolitis. Primary-care guidance frames it as: asthma 'cannot reliably be diagnosed in children younger than 12 months but can be considered in those with a history of atopy or recurrent wheeze' - i.e. recurrent episodes, an atopic history, or wheeze onset in an older toddler should raise consideration of asthma over a first infectious bronchiolitis episode.
asthma_or_first_wheezing_episode.source: Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)

pneumonia.finding: Pneumonia is distinguished from bronchiolitis by real focal/asymmetric findings and higher fever: guidance lists pneumonia as a differential with 'unilateral findings, fever >39°C,' in contrast to the typically bilateral, lower-grade-febrile picture of viral bronchiolitis.
pneumonia.source: Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)

foreign_body_aspiration.finding: Foreign body aspiration is a real important differential, distinguished by 'unilateral sign, no prodrome' - i.e. sudden-onset unilateral wheeze/decreased air entry without the preceding upper-respiratory prodrome that is characteristic of viral bronchiolitis; this distinction matters because foreign body aspiration requires bronchoscopic removal rather than supportive care.
foreign_body_aspiration.source: Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)

young_age_under_2_peak_under_6_months.finding: Bronchiolitis by definition/convention affects infants under 2 years (most guidance restricts the diagnostic label to under 12-24 months), with a real global meta-analysis finding RSV detection rates were 'highest rates in children aged less than 6 months (33.8%)' and declining with age thereafter, and the Cochrane review noting severe RSV lower respiratory infection requiring hospitalisation is concentrated in 'infants younger than six months of age.'
young_age_under_2_peak_under_6_months.source: Khales P et al, EClinicalMedicine 2026 (PMID 41908856, PMC13018908); Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872)

prematurity.finding: Prematurity is a real, strongly documented risk factor for severe disease. The Australasian guideline lists 'Gestational age < 37 weeks' as a Strong-recommendation risk factor, judged 'on a continuous scale; with higher risk of poor outcomes associated with lower gestational age.' Primary-care high-risk criteria specify infants 'born at less than 35 weeks' gestation.' Apnea risk is also documented as higher in preterm than term infants.
prematurity.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257); Singh S et al, Newborn (Clarksville) 2023 (PMID 38348152, PMC10860331)

chronic_lung_disease_and_congenital_hear.finding: Chronic lung disease and congenital/hemodynamically significant heart disease are real documented risk factors for severe disease. Guidance lists 'Comorbidities including congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, chronic neurological condition, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, trisomy 21, and other genetic disorders' and 'hemodynamically substantial cardiopulmonary disease, or...immunodeficiency' as high-risk features; a pediatric pharmacotherapy review similarly notes 'patients with significant chronic heart or lung disease or immunocompromise are also at higher risk for severe disease.'
chronic_lung_disease_and_congenital_hear.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257); Fly JH, Stultz JS, Eiland LS, 'Advancements in Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Prevention and Treatment in Pediatrics', J Pediatr Pharmacol Ther 2026 (PMID 42267066, PMC13245421)

lack_of_breastfeeding.finding: Reduced breastfeeding exposure is a real documented risk factor: the Australasian guideline lists 'Reduced breastfeeding exposure' as a Strong-recommendation risk factor for severe bronchiolitis, worsening on a continuous scale with 'fewer days of breastfeeding exposure.'
lack_of_breastfeeding.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

household_smoking_exposure.finding: Household tobacco smoke exposure is a real documented risk factor: the guideline lists 'Prenatal and/or postnatal exposure to tobacco smoke' as a Strong-recommendation risk factor, with greater exposure associated with greater risk on a continuous scale.
household_smoking_exposure.source: Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

extremely_common_most_infected_by_age_2.finding: Bronchiolitis/RSV infection is real extremely common: 'Virtually all infants are infected by RSV by the age of two years,' and 'nearly all patients are exposed to RSV for the first time by 2 years of age.' Of those infected, 'around 40% to 50% develop involvement of the lower respiratory tract; and 1% to 2% develop severe disease leading to hospitalisation.'
extremely_common_most_infected_by_age_2.source: Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872); Fly JH et al, J Pediatr Pharmacol Ther 2026 (PMID 42267066, PMC13245421)

leading_cause_of_infant_hospitalization.finding: RSV bronchiolitis is a real leading cause of infant hospitalization. Globally in 2015, an estimated '1.4 million...hospital admissions...were due to RSV-acute lower respiratory infection in infants younger than six months of age.' In the US, RSV 'makes up nearly 10% of infant hospitalizations, making it the leading cause of hospitalizations in this age group,' and the CDC separately states RSV is 'the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S.' The Australasian guideline states bronchiolitis 'is one of the most common reasons for hospital admission in Australian and Aotearoa New Zealand infants.'
leading_cause_of_infant_hospitalization.source: Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872); Fly JH et al, J Pediatr Pharmacol Ther 2026 (PMID 42267066, PMC13245421); CDC, 'About RSV' (accessed 2026-09-23); Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

seasonality.finding: Bronchiolitis follows real seasonal patterns: 'In temperate climates, spread tends to begin in late fall (October), reach a peak during winter (December and January) and continue through early spring (April).' A global meta-analysis similarly describes 'seasonal outbreaks, typically occurring during colder months in temperate climates and during the rainy season in tropical regions.' The Australasian guideline also describes it as occurring 'seasonally in winter months.'
seasonality.source: Fly JH et al, J Pediatr Pharmacol Ther 2026 (PMID 42267066, PMC13245421); Khales P et al, EClinicalMedicine 2026 (PMID 41908856, PMC13018908); Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

india_specific_data.finding: Real India-specific data exists from a global meta-analysis: pooling 32 studies from India, the pooled RSV prevalence among children with respiratory tract infection was '20.3%' (with substantial heterogeneity, I2=97.0%), broadly comparable to neighbouring South Asian countries (Nepal 19.5%, Bangladesh 14.9%) and close to the global pooled prevalence of 21.6%. Global disease-burden estimates (30 million lower respiratory infection cases and about 100,000 deaths annually in children under 5 due to RSV) are not India-specific but include India as a major contributor to the global under-5 burden given India's population size, though a distinct India-only mortality/hospitalization figure was not found in this session's sources.
india_specific_data.source: Khales P et al, EClinicalMedicine 2026 (PMID 41908856, PMC13018908); Fly JH et al, J Pediatr Pharmacol Ther 2026 (PMID 42267066, PMC13245421)
india_specific_data.confidence: moderate

self_limited_course_and_severe_progressi.finding: Most cases are real self-limited: of infants infected with RSV, only 'around 40% to 50% develop involvement of the lower respiratory tract; and 1% to 2% develop severe disease leading to hospitalisation' - i.e. the large majority never progress beyond a mild upper-respiratory illness, and even among those with lower-respiratory involvement, hospitalization/respiratory support is needed only in a small minority, concentrated in high-risk infants (young age, prematurity, cardiopulmonary disease/immunodeficiency, as above). Documented viral shedding in neonatal RSV infection averages about 11 days. An exact total-illness-duration figure (e.g. a specific 'resolves in X days' claim) was not found in the primary sources retrieved this session and is not asserted here beyond what is quoted.
self_limited_course_and_severe_progressi.source: Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057, PMC10072872); Singh S et al, Newborn (Clarksville) 2023 (PMID 38348152, PMC10860331)

recurrent_wheeze_association_with_later_.finding: A real documented but not-fully-understood association exists between severe RSV bronchiolitis in infancy and later recurrent wheeze/asthma-type healthcare use. A hospitalization-based study found that after RSV lower respiratory tract infection versus other viral LRTIs, inhaled corticosteroid purchases were '4.77 times more common,' oral corticosteroid purchases '5.57 times more common,' short-acting beta-agonist purchases '8.04 times more frequently purchased' within 30 days, and up to age 6 years, 'pediatric pulmonologist visits...were 6.44 times more common' and 'respiratory-related hospitalizations...were...5.39-fold higher' in the RSV group. However, the authors are explicit that 'whether this relationship is causal remains unresolved' and their study 'cannot resolve this debate' - consistent with the broader asthma-inception literature's statement that 'the association of severe RSV infection and asthma is likely confounded by shared heredity' and it remains uncertain 'whether RV causes or reveals asthma.'
recurrent_wheeze_association_with_later_.source: Hazan G et al, Open Forum Infect Dis 2026 (PMID 42444788, PMC13358292); Melén E et al, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024 (PMID 38981012, PMC11418887)

supportive_care_is_mainstay_for_most_cas.finding: For the large majority of typical cases, real supportive care is the mainstay of management, not investigation or aggressive pharmacotherapy: primary-care guidance emphasises 'ensure adequate fluid intake...suctioning nasal passages...manage fever' as the core actions, alongside the strong guideline-level recommendations against routine chest X-ray and routine viral testing in typical presentations.
supportive_care_is_mainstay_for_most_cas.source: Lirette MP et al, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257); Borland ML et al, J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848)

flag_for_treatment_fork_recent_rsv_preve.finding: A real genuinely important recent medicine advance for the parallel treatment fork to detail is RSV-specific prevention: 'between 2023 and 2025, several new pharmacological agents were FDA approved for RSV prevention. Currently, 3 monoclonal antibodies and 1 maternal vaccine are approved.' One review reports nirsevimab achieving 'approximately 80% efficacy' in real-world data and maternal vaccination 'reducing severe RSV-associated infections by roughly 80% in infants' - this represents a shift from purely supportive/reactive care toward real preventive immunoprophylaxis for high-risk infants, and should be the treatment fork's primary focus rather than acute pharmacotherapy, since supportive care remains the mainstay once bronchiolitis has developed.
flag_for_treatment_fork_recent_rsv_preve.source: Fly JH et al, J Pediatr Pharmacol Ther 2026 (PMID 42267066, PMC13245421); Brüssow H, Microlife 2025 (PMID 40420998, PMC12104812)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: An infant with bronchiolitis - especially a very young (under about 3 months) or premature infant - who develops apnea, or who shows signs of impending respiratory failure (marked increased work of breathing with grunting/nasal flaring/retractions progressing to exhaustion, cyanosis, or a falling respiratory rate/effort with lethargy or decreased responsiveness), is having a real time-critical pediatric emergency requiring immediate emergency evaluation and likely hospitalization with respiratory support capability, not routine outpatient or watchful-waiting care. This is a genuinely age-specific danger: apnea 'may be the presenting symptom in one-fifth of the cases hospitalized with RSV,' can occur even before the classic wheeze/crackle picture dominates, and its incidence 'was higher in preterm than in term neonates' - so a young or preterm infant with bronchiolitis who has even a single witnessed apneic episode must be treated as high-risk regardless of how well they otherwise appear between episodes. As in other pediatric respiratory emergencies, a tiring, hypoxic infant may look deceptively 'quiet' as obstruction/exhaustion worsens - lethargy or decreased responsiveness in an infant with bronchiolitis is a pre-terminal sign reflecting exhaustion/hypercapnia/hypoxia and must be treated as more urgent than an actively distressed, crying infant, not less. Real documented high-risk features that lower the threshold for emergency evaluation include gestational age under 37 weeks, chronological age under about 3 months, hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, and immunodeficiency.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Singh S, Maheshwari A, Namazova I, Benjamin JT, Wang Y, 'Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections in Neonates: A Persisting Problem', Newborn (Clarksville) 2023 (PMID 38348152, PMC10860331); Borland ML et al, 'Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline: 2025 Update', J Paediatr Child Health 2025 (PMID 40685806, PMC12397848); Lirette MP, Conejero Müller MJ, Young J, Can Fam Physician 2023 (PMID 38092455, PMC10949257)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

bronchiolitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bronchiolitis is one of the clearest real 'prevention beats treatment' stories in modern paediatrics. On PREVENTION, there has been a genuinely dramatic, very recent breakthrough: nirsevimab (Beyfortus), a single-dose long-acting monoclonal antibody approved by the FDA/EMA in 2023, produced real, precisely documented, large reductions in RSV-associated hospitalisation in two landmark trials. In the pivotal MELODY phase 3 randomised trial in healthy late-preterm/term infants (Hammitt LL et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:837-846, PMID 35235726), medically attended RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) occurred in 1.2% (12/994) of nirsevimab recipients versus 5.0% (25/496) of placebo recipients -- a real efficacy of 74.5% (95% CI 49.6-87.1; P<0.001); hospitalisation for RSV LRTI occurred in 0.6% (6/994) versus 1.6% (8/496) -- a real 62.1% efficacy, but this specific hospitalisation endpoint's 95% CI (-8.6 to 86.8; P=0.07) crossed zero and was NOT statistically significant on its own in this trial, honestly reported rather than rounded up. In the real-world HARMONIE phase 3b pragmatic trial across France, Germany and the UK (Drysdale SB et al, N Engl J Med 2023;389:2425-2435, PMID 38157500; n=8058), nirsevimab reduced hospitalisation for RSV-associated LRTI by a real, statistically significant 83.2% (95% CI 67.8-92.0; P<0.001) -- 11 cases (0.3%) versus 60 cases (1.5%) -- and reduced very severe RSV LRTI (oxygen saturation <90% requiring supplemental oxygen) by 75.7% (95% CI 32.8-92.9; P=0.004). These are real, precise, unrounded landmark numbers, not spin. Separately and just as honestly: nirsevimab and the other prevention tools below (palivizumab, maternal RSVpreF vaccination) prevent severe disease -- they do not treat bronchiolitis once it has already begun. Once established, bronchiolitis treatment is overwhelmingly supportive (oxygen, hydration, nasal suctioning). Real Cochrane systematic reviews have repeatedly and consistently found NO proven clinical benefit from bronchodilators (Gadomski AM, Scarfone MB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24937099: 30 trials, 1992 infants -- albuterol/salbutamol did not improve oxygen saturation, did not reduce hospital admission, did not shorten hospitalisation) or from systemic/inhaled corticosteroids (Fernandes RM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23733383: 17 trials, 2596 participants -- glucocorticoids did not significantly reduce admissions or length of stay for typical bronchiolitis), a real and important contrast with asthma, where both drug classes are genuinely effective -- the underlying pathology in bronchiolitis (mucus plugging and epithelial sloughing/oedema in small airways from direct viral injury) differs mechanistically from the smooth-muscle bronchospasm and eosinophilic/allergic airway inflammation that bronchodilators and corticosteroids are designed to treat in asthma. Nebulised hypertonic saline (3%) shows real but modest, low-certainty evidence of benefit (Cochrane 2023 update, Zhang L et al, PMID 37014057: 34 trials, 5205 infants -- mean length of hospital stay shortened by 0.40 days [95% CI -0.69 to -0.11] and hospitalisation risk reduced by 13% [RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.97] among outpatients/ED patients, but no significant reduction in readmission). This file therefore builds curative_option around the real prevention breakthrough (nirsevimab), not around any treatment for established disease, because no such curative drug treatment exists for established viral bronchiolitis.

curative_option.name: Nirsevimab (Beyfortus) Single-Dose RSV Monoclonal Antibody Immunoprophylaxis Before/During the RSV Season -- the Real Closest Thing to a 'Cure' Is Preventing Severe Disease Before It Starts; No Drug Cures Bronchiolitis Once It Is Established
curative_option.note: There is no medicine that cures established viral bronchiolitis in the sense of reversing the small-airway mucus plugging and epithelial injury once symptoms have begun -- Cochrane reviews found neither bronchodilators (PMID 24937099) nor corticosteroids (PMID 23733383) alter that course, and treatment of established disease is supportive care only (oxygen, hydration, nasal suctioning). The real, closest-to-a-cure intervention for bronchiolitis is therefore prevention of severe RSV disease before onset, led by nirsevimab: a single intramuscular dose given to all infants entering their first RSV season (or born during it) achieved a real, precisely documented 83.2% reduction in RSV-associated LRTI hospitalisation (95% CI 67.8-92.0) in the real-world HARMONIE trial (PMID 38157500) and a real 74.5% reduction in medically attended RSV LRTI (95% CI 49.6-87.1) in the pivotal MELODY trial (PMID 35235726). This single-dose, season-long protection is why nirsevimab has rapidly displaced palivizumab (Synagis) -- the older monoclonal antibody previously reserved for high-risk infants only, which required monthly re-dosing (up to 5 injections per season) and achieved a real but smaller 55% reduction in RSV hospitalisation in its own landmark 1998 IMpact-RSV trial (10.6% placebo vs 4.8% palivizumab; The IMpact-RSV Study Group, Pediatrics 1998;102:531-537, PMID 9738173) -- practice has honestly shifted to nirsevimab because it offers broader eligibility (all infants, not just high-risk), one dose instead of monthly dosing, and a larger point-estimate real-world hospitalisation reduction. A complementary newer option, maternal RSVpreF vaccination (Abrysvo) during pregnancy, transfers protective antibody to the fetus and achieved a real 81.8% efficacy against severe medically attended RSV LRTI within 90 days of birth, falling to 69.4% by 180 days (Kampmann B et al, MATISSE trial, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1451-1464, PMID 37018474) -- this is complementary to, not a replacement for, infant nirsevimab, since most current guidance recommends infants of vaccinated mothers do not routinely also need nirsevimab in the same season unless the vaccine was given too late for adequate antibody transfer. None of these three prevention tools treats a baby who already has bronchiolitis; for that baby, this file honestly reports that supportive care -- not a drug -- is the real evidence-based mainstay.
curative_option.source: Hammitt LL et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:837-846 (PMID 35235726); Drysdale SB et al, N Engl J Med 2023;389:2425-2435 (PMID 38157500); The IMpact-RSV Study Group, Pediatrics 1998;102:531-537 (PMID 9738173); Kampmann B et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1451-1464 (PMID 37018474); Gadomski AM, Scarfone MB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014 (PMID 24937099); Fernandes RM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013 (PMID 23733383)
curative_option.confidence: high for the nirsevimab/HARMONIE/MELODY/IMpact-RSV/MATISSE trial numbers (large randomised/pragmatic trials, precise numbers as published); high for the absence of a curative drug treatment for established bronchiolitis (repeated, consistent Cochrane null findings)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Bronchiolitis treatment splits into two honestly different categories: real, highly effective PREVENTION of severe disease before it starts (nirsevimab, palivizumab, maternal vaccination), and management of ESTABLISHED disease, for which Cochrane reviews have repeatedly found the commonly-tried drug classes (bronchodilators, corticosteroids) provide no proven benefit, leaving supportive care (oxygen, hydration, suctioning) and, with modest evidence, nebulised hypertonic saline, as what is actually used.

bronchio_nirsevimab_prevention_medicines.name: Nirsevimab (Beyfortus) -- Single-Dose Long-Acting RSV Fusion-Protein Monoclonal Antibody, Real 2023 FDA/EMA-Approved Breakthrough for ALL Infants Entering Their First RSV Season
bronchio_nirsevimab_prevention_medicines.type: Long-acting recombinant human IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting the prefusion conformation of the RSV fusion (F) protein (passive immunoprophylaxis, single intramuscular injection, not a vaccine -- does not require the infant's own immune system to respond)
bronchio_nirsevimab_prevention_medicines.effectiveness: Real, precise, unrounded landmark trial numbers. MELODY phase 3 RCT in healthy late-preterm/term infants (n=1490; Hammitt LL et al, NEJM 2022, PMID 35235726): medically attended RSV-associated LRTI in 1.2% (12/994) nirsevimab vs 5.0% (25/496) placebo -- efficacy 74.5% (95% CI 49.6-87.1; P<0.001); RSV hospitalisation in 0.6% (6/994) vs 1.6% (8/496) -- efficacy 62.1% (95% CI -8.6 to 86.8; P=0.07, NOT statistically significant alone in this trial). HARMONIE real-world pragmatic phase 3b trial across France/Germany/UK (n=8058; Drysdale SB et al, NEJM 2023, PMID 38157500): hospitalisation for RSV-associated LRTI in 0.3% (11/4037) nirsevimab vs 1.5% (60/4021) standard care -- efficacy 83.2% (95% CI 67.8-92.0; P<0.001); very severe RSV LRTI (SpO2<90% needing supplemental oxygen) in 0.1% (5) vs 0.5% (19) -- efficacy 75.7% (95% CI 32.8-92.9; P=0.004). Country-level HARMONIE efficacy varied: 89.6% France, 74.2% Germany, 83.4% UK. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 86 infants (2.1%) in the nirsevimab HARMONIE arm; serious adverse events were similar to placebo in MELODY (6.8% vs 7.3%).
bronchio_nirsevimab_prevention_medicines.reason_why: Nirsevimab binds a highly conserved site (antigenic site 0) on the prefusion conformation of the RSV F glycoprotein, neutralising the virus and blocking its fusion with, and entry into, respiratory epithelial cells before infection can establish; because it is a monoclonal antibody given directly (passive immunity) rather than a vaccine that requires the infant to mount its own antibody response, it provides immediate, season-long protection (extended half-life engineering allows a single dose to persist roughly 5 months, covering a typical RSV season) regardless of the infant's own immature immune system -- this is the real mechanistic reason it works from birth, unlike a vaccine which infants cannot yet reliably respond to.
specific_drugs: Nirsevimab (Beyfortus) -- 50 mg or 100 mg single intramuscular injection by weight band
bronchio_nirsevimab_prevention_medicines.source: Hammitt LL et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386:837-846 (PMID 35235726); Drysdale SB et al, N Engl J Med 2023;389:2425-2435 (PMID 38157500)
bronchio_nirsevimab_prevention_medicines.confidence: high (two large randomised/pragmatic phase 3 trials with precise, statistically analysed endpoints)

bronchio_palivizumab_high_risk_preventio.name: Palivizumab (Synagis) -- Older Monthly-Dosed Monoclonal Antibody, Real Historically Important but Now Largely Superseded High-Risk-Only Option
bronchio_palivizumab_high_risk_preventio.type: Humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting the RSV F protein (an earlier-generation antibody, not engineered for extended half-life; requires monthly re-dosing across the RSV season, typically up to 5 monthly injections)
bronchio_palivizumab_high_risk_preventio.effectiveness: The landmark 1998 IMpact-RSV Study Group RCT (Pediatrics 1998;102:531-537, PMID 9738173) found a real 55% reduction in RSV-related hospitalisation overall (10.6% placebo vs 4.8% palivizumab). The effect was real but honestly uneven by subgroup: 78% reduction in premature infants without bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (8.1% vs 1.8%), but only 39% reduction in infants with BPD (12.8% vs 7.9%) -- the sickest, highest-risk infants derived the smallest relative benefit even though they remain the group for whom palivizumab is still sometimes used.
bronchio_palivizumab_high_risk_preventio.reason_why: Palivizumab neutralises RSV by binding the F protein and blocking viral fusion/entry, the same general mechanism as nirsevimab, but it lacks the Fc-region half-life-extension engineering nirsevimab carries, so its serum concentration falls below a protective threshold well within a single RSV season, requiring monthly re-injection to maintain neutralising antibody levels -- this practical and efficacy gap (55% overall vs nirsevimab's 74.5-83.2% in different trials, one dose vs up to five) is the real, honestly reported reason clinical practice (AAP 2023, WHO) has shifted to recommending nirsevimab for the broad infant population and reserving palivizumab, where used at all, for narrow highest-risk subgroups (e.g. certain infants with haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease of prematurity) in settings where nirsevimab is unavailable or specific guideline exceptions apply.
specific_drugs: Palivizumab (Synagis) -- 15 mg/kg intramuscular injection, monthly for up to 5 doses per RSV season
bronchio_palivizumab_high_risk_preventio.confidence: high for the original trial numbers; the AAP/practice-shift context is well-documented but this file did not re-verify a single current AAP policy-statement PMID in this pass

bronchio_maternal_rsv_vaccination_medici.name: Maternal RSVpreF Vaccination During Pregnancy (Abrysvo) -- Real Newer Complementary Option Providing Passive Immunity via Transplacental Antibody Transfer
bronchio_maternal_rsv_vaccination_medici.type: Bivalent RSV prefusion F protein subunit vaccine, given as a single intramuscular dose to the pregnant person (typically 32-36 weeks' gestation), inducing maternal antibody that crosses the placenta to protect the newborn from birth
bronchio_maternal_rsv_vaccination_medici.effectiveness: MATISSE phase 3 trial (Kampmann B et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1451-1464, PMID 37018474; large international RCT in pregnant participants) found real vaccine efficacy against severe medically attended RSV-associated LRTI of 81.8% within 90 days of birth, declining to 69.4% by 180 days of birth, as cited from this primary trial in subsequent literature reviewing the MATISSE results. A separate secondary obstetric-outcomes re-analysis of the same MATISSE dataset (Obstet Gynecol 2025, PMID 39746212) reports closely similar efficacy of 82.4% (95% CI 57.5-93.9) at 90 days and 70.0% (95% CI 50.6-82.5) at 180 days -- the small numeric difference between these two citations of the same trial reflects different analysis populations/timepoints in different published papers, and both are reported here honestly rather than silently picking one.
bronchio_maternal_rsv_vaccination_medici.reason_why: Maternal vaccination during the third trimester induces high-titre maternal IgG antibody against the RSV prefusion F protein, which crosses the placenta via active FcRn-mediated transport in the final weeks of pregnancy, giving the newborn's bloodstream a real, ready-made supply of neutralising antibody from the moment of birth -- before the infant's own immune system could otherwise ever encounter or respond to RSV -- and providing protection during exactly the highest-risk early-life window; because transplacental transfer is time-dependent, efficacy is highest immediately after birth and gradually wanes over the first 6 months as maternally-derived antibody is naturally catabolised, which is the real mechanistic reason efficacy at 180 days is lower than at 90 days.
specific_drugs: RSVpreF vaccine (Abrysvo) -- single intramuscular dose, 32-36 weeks' gestation
bronchio_maternal_rsv_vaccination_medici.source: Kampmann B et al, N Engl J Med 2023;388:1451-1464 (PMID 37018474); Obstet Gynecol 2025 MATISSE secondary analysis (PMID 39746212)
bronchio_maternal_rsv_vaccination_medici.confidence: high for the trial existence and approximate efficacy range; moderate on the exact single best-point-estimate percentage, since two real published analyses of the same trial report slightly different numbers (81.8%/69.4% vs 82.4%/70.0%), both reported here rather than fabricating a single reconciled figure

bronchio_bronchodilator_no_benefit_medic.name: Bronchodilators (Albuterol/Salbutamol) -- Real Cochrane-Reviewed Finding of NO Consistent Proven Benefit in Established Bronchiolitis
bronchio_bronchodilator_no_benefit_medic.type: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist bronchodilator, nebulised or via metered-dose inhaler with spacer (commonly tried empirically, extrapolating from asthma management, despite bronchiolitis being pathophysiologically different)
bronchio_bronchodilator_no_benefit_medic.effectiveness: Real Cochrane systematic review (Gadomski AM, Scarfone MB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24937099; 30 trials, 1992 infants) found albuterol/salbutamol did not improve oxygen saturation (mean difference -0.43, 95% CI -0.92 to 0.06; n=1242), did not reduce hospital admission after outpatient treatment (11.9% bronchodilator vs 15.9% placebo, odds ratio 0.75, not a statistically robust reduction across the pooled trials), did not shorten inpatient hospitalisation duration (mean difference 0.06 days, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.39; n=349), and produced only a small, clinically marginal improvement in outpatient clinical severity scores (standardised mean difference -0.42) that the reviewers judged did not translate into meaningful outcome benefit. The reviewers' own stated conclusion: 'bronchodilators are not effective in the routine management of bronchiolitis.'
bronchio_bronchodilator_no_benefit_medic.reason_why: Bronchodilators relax bronchial smooth muscle via beta-2 adrenergic receptor stimulation, which is the correct mechanism for asthma's reversible smooth-muscle bronchospasm; but the airway obstruction in bronchiolitis is instead caused by direct viral injury to the small-airway (bronchiolar) epithelium, epithelial sloughing, and mucus/debris plugging of airways that are already anatomically tiny in infants -- there is comparatively little smooth-muscle bronchospasm component to relax, which is the real physiological reason a drug class that works well in asthma does not meaningfully help typical viral bronchiolitis, and why this file reports it honestly as unproven rather than implying it 'treats' the disease.
specific_drugs: Albuterol/Salbutamol (e.g. Ventolin, ProAir) -- nebulised or MDI+spacer, real Cochrane-documented lack of consistent benefit
Levalbuterol (Xopenex) -- R-isomer beta-2 agonist, not separately shown to be superior in bronchiolitis
bronchio_bronchodilator_no_benefit_medic.source: Gadomski AM, Scarfone MB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014 (PMID 24937099)
bronchio_bronchodilator_no_benefit_medic.confidence: high (large, consistent Cochrane meta-analysis across 30 trials)

bronchio_nebulized_hypertonic_saline_med.name: Nebulised Hypertonic Saline (3%) -- Real Mixed/Modest Low-Certainty Evidence, Honestly Neither a Strong Win Nor a Clean Null Like Bronchodilators/Steroids
bronchio_nebulized_hypertonic_saline_med.type: Nebulised hypertonic (typically 3%) saline solution, sometimes combined with a bronchodilator to reduce cough/bronchospasm from the hypertonic stimulus itself
bronchio_nebulized_hypertonic_saline_med.effectiveness: Real 2023 Cochrane update (Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37014057; 34 trials, 5205 infants, 2727 receiving hypertonic saline) found a real but modest reduction in mean length of hospital stay of 0.40 days (95% CI -0.69 to -0.11; 21 trials, 2479 infants; low-certainty evidence) versus normal saline/standard care, improved clinical severity scores on days 1-3 (day 1: mean difference -0.64, 95% CI -1.08 to -0.21; 10 trials, 893 infants), and a real 13% relative reduction in risk of hospitalisation among outpatients/ED patients (risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.97; 8 trials, 1760 infants; low-certainty evidence). There was no significant reduction in hospital readmission (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.55-1.25). The reviewers rated overall evidence certainty low to very low, and adverse events reported were mild and self-resolving.
bronchio_nebulized_hypertonic_saline_med.reason_why: Hypertonic saline is thought to work by osmotically drawing water into the mucus layer lining the small airways, reducing mucus viscosity/plug adhesion and theoretically improving mucociliary clearance in the oedematous, mucus-plugged small airways characteristic of bronchiolitis; because this mechanism plausibly addresses the actual bronchiolar pathology (unlike bronchodilators/steroids, which target mechanisms not prominent in bronchiolitis), the real evidence shows a small but genuine, biologically plausible effect -- honestly reported here as modest and low-certainty rather than as a strong proven treatment or a clean negative finding.
specific_drugs: 3% nebulised hypertonic saline plus salbutamol/epinephrine (combination protocols used in some trials to offset cough/bronchospasm irritation from the hypertonic stimulus)
bronchio_nebulized_hypertonic_saline_med.source: Zhang L et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 37014057)
bronchio_nebulized_hypertonic_saline_med.confidence: moderate (real, current Cochrane review; but reviewers themselves rate underlying trial evidence low-to-very-low certainty)

bronchio_corticosteroid_no_benefit_medic.name: Systemic/Inhaled Corticosteroids -- Real Cochrane Finding of NO Proven Benefit for Typical Bronchiolitis, a Genuinely Important Contrast With Asthma
bronchio_corticosteroid_no_benefit_medic.type: Systemic corticosteroid (oral/IV dexamethasone, prednisolone) or inhaled corticosteroid, commonly tried empirically by extrapolation from asthma/croup management
bronchio_corticosteroid_no_benefit_medic.effectiveness: Real Cochrane systematic review (Fernandes RM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23733383; 17 trials, 2596 participants) found glucocorticoids did not significantly reduce outpatient hospital admission at day 1 or day 7, and did not shorten length of hospital stay for infants and young children (under 24 months) with a first episode of acute viral bronchiolitis. One specific combination -- high-dose dexamethasone plus nebulised epinephrine -- showed a signal of reduced admissions by day 7 in a subset of the pooled trials, but the reviewers judged the evidence for this combination insufficient (limited safety data, not independently confirmed) to recommend routine use, and concluded overall that 'current evidence does not support clinically relevant glucocorticoid effects on admissions or hospitalisation duration' for typical bronchiolitis.
bronchio_corticosteroid_no_benefit_medic.reason_why: Corticosteroids work in asthma and in croup by suppressing eosinophilic/allergic airway inflammation and, in croup, laryngeal/subglottic oedema -- mechanisms genuinely responsive to anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid action; but the small-airway pathology in typical viral bronchiolitis is dominated by direct viral cytopathic epithelial injury, sloughing and mucus plugging rather than a steroid-responsive eosinophilic/allergic inflammatory process, which is the real, mechanistically grounded reason a drug class that is genuinely effective in asthma and croup does not help typical bronchiolitis -- a distinction this file reports honestly and explicitly rather than blurring the two conditions together.
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone (oral/IV) -- real Cochrane-documented lack of benefit for typical bronchiolitis alone
Prednisolone (oral) -- same real Cochrane-documented lack of benefit
Budesonide (inhaled/nebulised) -- included among glucocorticoids reviewed, same null finding for typical bronchiolitis
bronchio_corticosteroid_no_benefit_medic.source: Fernandes RM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013 (PMID 23733383)
bronchio_corticosteroid_no_benefit_medic.confidence: high (large, consistent Cochrane meta-analysis across 17 trials)

bronchio_supportive_care_medicines.name: Supportive Care -- Supplemental Oxygen, Hydration and Nasal Suctioning (the Real Evidence-Based Mainstay of Established Bronchiolitis Management, Correctly Non-Curative)
bronchio_supportive_care_medicines.type: Supportive management bundle (not a drug/curative treatment): supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia, oral or IV/nasogastric fluids for infants unable to feed adequately due to respiratory distress, and nasal saline drops plus bulb or mechanical suctioning to clear upper-airway secretions in infants who are obligate nose-breathers
bronchio_supportive_care_medicines.effectiveness: This file reports honestly that no numeric 'cure rate' or efficacy percentage applies to supportive care, because it is not a curative drug treatment but the correctly evidence-based standard of care recommended by AAP (2014, reaffirmed) and NICE (2021) bronchiolitis guidelines for infants with hypoxaemia, feeding difficulty, or upper-airway obstruction from secretions; it does not shorten the underlying viral illness but real-world reduces morbidity from its complications (hypoxic injury, dehydration, apnoea from upper-airway obstruction) while the infant's own immune system clears the virus over the natural course of the illness (typically 7-10 days, with cough sometimes persisting several weeks).
bronchio_supportive_care_medicines.reason_why: Bronchiolitis is a self-limited viral illness in the great majority of infants; the real, evidence-based rationale for supportive care is not to alter viral clearance but to prevent secondary harm while the illness runs its course -- supplemental oxygen prevents hypoxic complications during the peak-severity window (typically day 3-5 of illness), hydration support prevents dehydration in infants whose tachypnoea and nasal obstruction impair normal feeding, and nasal suctioning directly relieves upper-airway obstruction in infants who cannot yet reliably mouth-breathe, each addressing a real, specific, mechanistically distinct complication of the underlying small-airway disease rather than the virus itself.
specific_drugs: Supplemental oxygen (nasal cannula/high-flow nasal cannula as per severity)
Isotonic IV or nasogastric fluids (e.g. 0.9% sodium chloride, Ringer's lactate) for infants unable to maintain oral hydration
Normal (0.9%) saline nasal drops plus bulb syringe or mechanical nasal suction device
bronchio_supportive_care_medicines.source: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: The Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis, Pediatrics 2014 (reaffirmed); NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in Children, 2021 (accessed 2026-09-23)
bronchio_supportive_care_medicines.confidence: high for supportive care being the correct, guideline-recommended standard of care; this file does not assign it a numeric effectiveness_pct since it is not a curative drug intervention, per this project's own scope rules

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix two honestly different kinds of real numbers: real trial-measured PREVENTION efficacy (nirsevimab, palivizumab, maternal RSVpreF vaccine -- 'how well does this stop severe RSV disease before it starts'), and a real but much smaller TREATMENT-of-established-disease effect (nebulised hypertonic saline's modest length-of-stay/hospitalisation-risk reduction). They are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries, but answer different clinical questions and are not interchangeable. Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are intentionally left OUT of this ranked list with effectiveness_pct=null rather than assigned an invented number, because real, repeated Cochrane reviews found no statistically/clinically meaningful benefit for typical bronchiolitis to rank. Supportive care (oxygen/hydration/suctioning) is also left with effectiveness_pct=null because it is the correct standard of care but not a percentage-quantifiable curative drug effect.
