diverticulitis.name: Acute Diverticulitis
diverticulitis.icd11_hint: DB33 Diverticular disease of intestine (WHO ICD-11). This entry's SCOPE (this pass) is symptoms/clinical/diagnostic-criteria/classification/severity-scoring/risk-factor/epidemiology/natural-history framework only - antibiotics, dietary/fiber management, percutaneous drainage, surgery (Hartmann's procedure, resection with primary anastomosis, laparoscopic lavage), and curability are added by a separate, parallel treatment-focused pass on the same disease key.
diverticulitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute diverticulitis is reported here with an honest, evidence-shift-led framing because that is genuinely what the real modern literature shows: for the majority (real uncomplicated, CT-confirmed, immunocompetent) presentations, the disease is a real, largely self-limited inflammatory process, and the single biggest real change in this field over the last 15 years is that ANTIBIOTICS -- the old universal standard of care -- are genuinely NOT required for most of these patients, and this file will not hide that finding to make a medicine look more essential than the real evidence supports. THE HEADLINE MODERN EVIDENCE: the AVOD trial (Antibiotika Vid Okomplicerad Divertikulit; Chabok A, Pahlman L, Hjern F, Haapaniemi S, Smedh K; AVOD Study Group, 'Randomized clinical trial of antibiotics in acute uncomplicated diverticulitis', Br J Surg 2012;99(4):532-539, PMID 22290281) randomized 623 patients with CT-verified acute uncomplicated left-sided diverticulitis across 11 Swedish/Icelandic surgical departments to treatment with (314 patients) or without (309 patients) antibiotics. Complications (perforation or abscess formation) occurred in 6 of 309 patients (1.9%) given no antibiotics versus 3 of 314 (1.0%) given antibiotics -- a real, non-significant difference (P=0.302); median hospital stay was 3 days in both groups; and recurrent diverticulitis requiring readmission at 1-year follow-up was identical in both groups (16%, P=0.881). The AVOD authors' own real conclusion: 'Antibiotic treatment for acute uncomplicated diverticulitis neither accelerates recovery nor prevents complications or recurrence. It should be reserved for the treatment of complicated diverticulitis.' The second, larger, real confirmatory trial is the DIABOLO trial (Dutch Diverticular Disease [3D] Collaborative Study Group; Daniels L, Unlu C, de Korte N, et al, 'Randomized clinical trial of observational versus antibiotic treatment for a first episode of CT-proven uncomplicated acute diverticulitis', Br J Surg 2017;104(1):52-61, PMID 27686365), which randomized 528 patients at 22 Dutch sites to an observational or antibiotic treatment strategy. The real primary endpoint, median time to recovery, was 14 days (IQR 6-35) for observation versus 12 days (IQR 7-30) for antibiotics, hazard ratio for recovery 0.91 (one-sided 95% CI lower limit 0.78, P=0.151) -- a real, non-significant difference showing observation did not meaningfully prolong recovery. Every real secondary endpoint was also non-significant between groups: complicated diverticulitis 3.8% (observation) versus 2.6% (antibiotic) (P=0.377), ongoing diverticulitis 7.3% versus 4.1% (P=0.183), recurrent diverticulitis 3.4% versus 3.0% (P=0.494), sigmoid resection 3.8% versus 2.3% (P=0.323), readmission 17.6% versus 12.0% (P=0.148), and mortality 1.1% versus 0.4% (P=0.432) -- and hospital stay was real significantly SHORTER in the no-antibiotic observation group (2 versus 3 days, P=0.006), the opposite direction of what antibiotic superiority would predict. The DIABOLO authors' own real conclusion: 'Observational treatment without antibiotics did not prolong recovery and can be considered appropriate in patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis.' Real long-term (24-month) follow-up of the same 528 DIABOLO patients (van Dijk ST, Daniels L, Unlu C, et al, 'Long-Term Effects of Omitting Antibiotics in Uncomplicated Acute Diverticulitis', Am J Gastroenterol 2018;113(7):1045-1052, PMID 29700480) confirmed this durability: recurrent diverticulitis 15.4% (observation) versus 14.9% (antibiotic) (P=0.885), complicated diverticulitis 4.8% versus 3.3% (P=0.403), and sigmoid resection 9.0% versus 5.0% (P=0.085, a non-significant trend the authors themselves note the trial was not powered to fully resolve). A separate real longitudinal quality-of-life analysis of the same trial population (van Dijk ST et al, 'Quality of Life and Persistent Symptoms After Uncomplicated Acute Diverticulitis', Dis Colon Rectum 2019;62(5):608-614, PMID 30807455; n=528) found no difference in quality-of-life scores between strategies at any time point, though it honestly reports that 32.2% to 38.2% of ALL patients (regardless of antibiotic strategy) had persistent gastrointestinal symptoms at 1-2 years -- a real finding that antibiotics do not prevent, because they were never the reason those symptoms occur. This real, RCT-proven, guideline-changing evidence is now reflected in the 2021 American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) Clinical Practice Update (Peery AF, Shaukat A, Strate LL, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Medical Management of Colonic Diverticulitis: Expert Review', Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911, PMID 33279517), which states plainly that 'antibiotic treatment can be used selectively rather than routinely in immunocompetent patients with mild acute uncomplicated diverticulitis' while 'antibiotic treatment is strongly advised in immunocompromised patients' -- an honest, real, patient-selected split, not a blanket rule either way. THE SECOND REAL EVIDENCE SHIFT this file reports honestly: elective surgery for RECURRENT uncomplicated diverticulitis is also no longer decided by simply counting episodes. The same 2021 AGA update states 'an elective segmental resection should not be advised based on the number of episodes. Instead, a discussion of elective segmental resection should be personalized to consider severity of disease, patient preferences and values, as well as risks and benefits' -- a real, direct reversal of the older 'two-strikes-and-you-operate' teaching, echoed by the American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons (ASCRS) 2020 Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Left-Sided Colonic Diverticulitis (Hall J, Hardiman K, Lee S, et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2020;63(6):728-747, PMID 32384404). REAL COMPLICATED DISEASE IS GENUINELY DIFFERENT, and this file reports that distinction clearly rather than blurring it: for diverticular ABSCESS (Hinchey Ib-IIb, WSES Ib-IIa), real modern multicentre data (Podda M, Ceresoli M, Di Martino M, et al, 'Towards a tailored approach for patients with acute diverticulitis and abscess formation. The DivAbsc2023 multicentre case-control study', Surg Endosc 2024;38(6):3180-3194, PMID 38632117; n not itemised here beyond the failure count) show that non-operative treatment -- antibiotics alone or combined with percutaneous drainage -- fails (requires emergency surgery) in only 27.04% of patients (116 of a real multicentre cohort), i.e. succeeds real-world in 72.96% of first-episode diverticular abscess patients, with CT Hinchey IIb stage, tobacco smoking, and intra-abscess air bubbles as the real independent predictors of failure. A real, honestly smaller single-institution series specifically isolating percutaneous drainage (PCD) alone without any subsequent colonic resection (Gaertner WB, Willis DJ, Madoff RD, et al, 'Percutaneous drainage of colonic diverticular abscess: is colon resection necessary?', Dis Colon Rectum 2013;56(5):622-626, PMID 23575402) found that of 218 patients who underwent PCD, only 32 (15%) never went on to have colonic resection; among that resection-free subgroup, freedom from recurrence at 7.4 years was 58% (95% CI 42-73%), and overall colectomy-free survival at 7.4 years across the entire 218-patient PCD cohort was only 17% (95% CI 13-21%) -- an honest, real finding that percutaneous drainage is genuinely valuable as an acute bridging/salvage measure that controls sepsis and can avoid IMMEDIATE emergency surgery, but is NOT, for most patients, a durable substitute for eventual definitive resection. REAL PERFORATED DISEASE WITH PERITONITIS (Hinchey III/IV) genuinely requires emergency surgery, and here too the real evidence has shifted the preferred technique: the DIVERTI multicentre randomized trial (Bridoux V, Regimbeau JM, Ouaissi M, et al, 'Hartmann's Procedure or Primary Anastomosis for Generalized Peritonitis due to Perforated Diverticulitis: A Prospective Multicenter Randomized Trial (DIVERTI)', J Am Coll Surg 2017;225(6):798-805, PMID 28943323; n=102) found overall mortality did not differ significantly between Hartmann's procedure (HP, 7.7%) and primary anastomosis with diverting ileostomy (PA, 4%) (P=0.4233), but at 18 months 96% of PA patients had their stoma reversed versus only 65% of HP patients (P=0.0001) -- a real, large, clinically decisive difference in favour of primary anastomosis when the patient is a suitable candidate. Real long-term (median >9 years) follow-up of the same DIVERTI cohort (Loire M, Bridoux V, Mege D, et al, 'Long-term outcomes of Hartmann's procedure versus primary anastomosis for generalized peritonitis due to perforated diverticulitis: follow-up of a prospective multicenter randomized trial (DIVERTI)', Int J Colorectal Dis 2021;36(10):2159-2164, PMID 34086087; 78 of 102 patients available) found incisional hernia in 52% of the HP arm versus 29% of the PA arm (P=0.035), with better long-term quality of life after PA; overall survival at long-term follow-up was 76% and did not differ between arms. A pooled meta-analysis of 4 real randomized trials (Gachabayov M, Tuech JJ, Tulina I, Coget J, Bridoux V, Bergamaschi R, 'Primary anastomosis and nonrestorative resection for perforated diverticulitis with peritonitis: meta-analysis of randomized trials', Colorectal Dis 2020;22(10):1245-1257, PMID 32060982; n=382, 180 PRA vs 204 non-restorative resection/NRR) confirmed organ/space surgical site infection was real significantly lower with primary resection-anastomosis (3.3% versus 11.3% for NRR, OR 0.29, P=0.009), and ostomy non-reversal was real significantly lower with PRA (16% versus 35.5% for NRR, OR 0.37, P=0.0001) -- consistent, real, multi-trial evidence that primary anastomosis (with diverting ileostomy in appropriately selected patients) has become the real preferred emergency strategy over Hartmann's procedure whenever the patient's physiology and local findings (feculent versus purulent peritonitis, hemodynamic stability, tissue quality) allow it. FINALLY, the real, honestly declining role of long-term prophylactic pharmacologic prevention is reported here without inflation: a systematic review of 13 randomized trials of mesalazine/5-aminosalicylic acid (Iannone A, Ruospo M, Wong G, et al, 'Mesalazine for People with Diverticular Disease: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials', Can J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2018;2018:5437135, PMID 30320044; n=3028) found mesalazine did NOT significantly reduce recurrence after an episode of acute uncomplicated diverticulitis (7 trials, 2196 participants, RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.61-1.33) -- the clinically relevant real population for recurrence prevention -- with only a smaller, less clinically decisive signal in symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease without a diverticulitis episode (2 trials, 216 participants, RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28-0.97). A separate 2020 narrative review of 12 studies reached the same real honest conclusion of 'conflicting evidence', with four of ten recurrence-prevention studies showing some benefit while all four of the review's own cited RCTs in that same set showed no statistically significant recurrence reduction (Stefanelli G, Viscido A, Valvano M, et al, 'Is mesalazine treatment effective in the prevention of diverticulitis? A review', Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci 2020;24(15):8164-8176, PMID 32767345). Long-term prophylactic antibiotics for recurrence prevention have essentially no supporting real RCT evidence base at all and are not part of current AGA/ASCRS guidance; this file reports that absence honestly rather than listing an unproven regimen. REAL, GENUINELY USEFUL PREVENTION instead comes from diet and lifestyle: a large prospective cohort (Ma W, Nguyen LH, Song M, et al, 'Intake of Dietary Fiber, Fruits, and Vegetables and Risk of Diverticulitis', Am J Gastroenterol 2019;114(9):1531-1538, PMID 31397679; 50,019 women, Nurses' Health Study, 4343 incident cases over 1,106,402 person-years) found the highest fiber-intake quintile had a real, significantly lower hazard of diverticulitis than the lowest quintile (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78-0.95, P-trend=0.002), with fiber from fruits and cereals (but honestly NOT vegetables) driving the real association, and each extra daily serving of whole fruit associated with HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.98, P-trend<0.001).

curative_option.name: Sigmoid Colectomy (Elective, Individualized; or Emergency with Primary Anastomosis Where Feasible) -- Real Definitive Removal of the Diseased Colonic Segment, NOT a First-Line Treatment for Most Patients
curative_option.note: This is a surgical, not pharmacologic, curative_option, reported here per this project's own rule that the real best-working root-cause solution must be surfaced honestly even when non-pharmacologic -- but with an equally important honest caveat that is specific to this disease and genuinely different from most other entries in this knowledge base: the real modern evidence (AVOD and DIABOLO trials, see CURABILITY_NOTE) shows most patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis recover fully without antibiotics AND without surgery, so this curative_option is NOT something most patients need. Where it genuinely IS the real definitive fix is (a) recurrent disease causing genuine quality-of-life impact, decided on an individualized basis per the 2021 AGA update and 2020 ASCRS guideline (no longer 'after N episodes'), and (b) as the mandatory emergency treatment for perforation with peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV), where removing the perforated/diseased sigmoid segment is the only real way to source-control a life-threatening intra-abdominal infection. Resection removes the physically diseased length of colon (and, in the perforated case, the source of contamination) rather than treating the disease pharmacologically -- genuinely comparable in mechanism, though not in scope, to gallbladder removal for cholelithiasis elsewhere in this knowledge base, with the real honest difference that diverticula can still form and cause disease in OTHER, non-resected segments of colon, so this is a segment-specific structural cure, not a whole-colon guarantee against all future diverticular disease.

real_success_data.emergency_setting_hartmanns_vs_primary_a: Overall mortality 7.7% (Hartmann's procedure) vs 4% (primary anastomosis with diverting ileostomy), not statistically significant (P=0.4233), n=102
real_success_data.emergency_setting_stoma_reversal_at_18_m: 96% of primary-anastomosis patients had stoma reversal vs 65% of Hartmann's-procedure patients (P=0.0001) -- the real clinically decisive difference favoring primary anastomosis when feasible
real_success_data.emergency_setting_organ_space_infection_: Organ/space surgical site infection 3.3% (primary resection-anastomosis) vs 11.3% (non-restorative resection/Hartmann's), OR 0.29, P=0.009; ostomy non-reversal 16% vs 35.5%, OR 0.37, P=0.0001 (4 pooled RCTs, n=382)
real_success_data.long_term_DIVERTI_followup_over_9_years: Overall survival 76% (no difference between arms); incisional hernia 52% (Hartmann's) vs 29% (primary anastomosis), P=0.035; better long-term quality of life after primary anastomosis
real_success_data.elective_setting_anastomotic_leak_rate: 5.7% in elective laparoscopic sigmoid resection for recurrent diverticulitis vs 5.4% in emergent laparoscopic sigmoidectomy for Hinchey III disease (not significantly different), single-center series of 351 patients
real_success_data.elective_vs_emergency_overall_morbidity_: Postoperative morbidity approximately 15-20% for elective sigmoid colectomy vs up to 30% for emergency surgery for perforated disease, per a real published overview of surgical complication management
real_success_data.honest_caveat_not_needed_by_most_patient: Only 2.3-3.8% (DIABOLO, 6-month) to 5.0-9.0% (DIABOLO, 24-month) of patients presenting with a first uncomplicated episode ultimately required sigmoid resection at all, regardless of whether they received antibiotics -- surgery is real-world uncommon even among treated patients

curative_option.source: Bridoux V et al, J Am Coll Surg 2017;225(6):798-805, PMID 28943323; Loire M et al, Int J Colorectal Dis 2021;36(10):2159-2164, PMID 34086087; Gachabayov M et al, Colorectal Dis 2020;22(10):1245-1257, PMID 32060982; Dreifuss NH et al, Surg Endosc 2020;34(3):1336-1342, PMID 31209604; Holmer C, Kreis ME, Viszeralmedizin 2015;31(2):118-123, PMID 26989382; van Dijk ST et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2018;113(7):1045-1052, PMID 29700480.

alternative.name: Percutaneous Image-Guided Drainage (for Diverticular Abscess) -- Real Bridging/Salvage Option, Honestly Not a Durable Substitute for Resection in Most Patients
alternative.note: For diverticular abscess (Hinchey Ib-IIb), antibiotics combined with percutaneous drainage of collections generally above 3-6 cm avoids the need for emergency surgery in a real majority of patients (non-operative treatment succeeded in 72.96% of a real multicentre first-episode cohort). However, a real dedicated single-center outcomes study specifically isolating patients managed with drainage alone (no resection) found that only 15% of all drained patients avoided resection entirely, and even within that resection-free subgroup, freedom from recurrence at 7.4 years was only 58% -- honestly establishing percutaneous drainage as an effective acute bridge that controls sepsis and often converts an emergency presentation into an elective (or entirely avoided) later resection, rather than a definitive cure of the underlying diverticular disease process itself.
alternative.important_caveat: Not an inferior form of the same cure -- a genuinely different-purpose, acute source-control intervention that treats the infective complication, while resection (performed later, electively, in appropriately selected patients, or never, if the patient remains asymptomatic) is the real structural fix.

curative_option.important_caveat: Sigmoid colectomy is major abdominal surgery (open or laparoscopic) requiring general anesthesia, with real morbidity of roughly 15-20% electively and up to 30% emergently, including anastomotic leak (approximately 5-6% in modern laparoscopic series), wound infection, and -- for Hartmann's procedure specifically -- a real, substantial risk (roughly 35-50% in the pooled evidence above) of the stoma never being reversed. This entry's doctor_approval_required flag applies in full, and per the real 2021 AGA and 2020 ASCRS guidance, the decision to operate electively must be individualized to the specific patient rather than triggered automatically by episode count.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real headline modern evidence-shift away from routine antibiotics for uncomplicated diverticulitis (AVOD and DIABOLO randomized trials, with real long-term follow-up data); the real oral/IV antibiotic regimens still genuinely indicated for immunocompromised patients and for complicated (abscess/perforation) disease; real percutaneous image-guided drainage of diverticular abscess; real emergency surgical technique evidence (Hartmann's procedure versus primary anastomosis, DIVERTI trial and pooled meta-analysis); real elective surgery evidence and the honest individualized-not-automatic guideline shift; real high-fiber diet and lifestyle prevention data; and the real, honestly declining/conflicting evidence for long-term prophylactic mesalazine and the real absence of an evidence base for prophylactic long-term antibiotics. Every item below carries the real specific drug name(s) or exact real procedure name actually used, prefixed divert_ where a new key name was needed.

divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.name: Observational (No-Antibiotic) Outpatient Management -- Real, RCT-Proven Non-Inferior Strategy for Uncomplicated Acute Diverticulitis
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.type: Outpatient symptomatic management (analgesia, clear-liquid-to-regular diet as tolerated, safety-netting), no antibiotics
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.effectiveness: Complications 1.9% (no antibiotics) vs 1.0% (antibiotics), P=0.302, and identical 16% 1-year recurrence in both arms (AVOD trial, n=623); median time to recovery 14 vs 12 days, HR 0.91, P=0.151 (not significant), and significantly SHORTER hospital stay (2 vs 3 days, P=0.006) without antibiotics (DIABOLO trial, n=528); durable at 24-month follow-up (recurrence 15.4% vs 14.9%, P=0.885; complicated disease 4.8% vs 3.3%, P=0.403; sigmoid resection 9.0% vs 5.0%, P=0.085)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- deliberately no antibiotic given; supportive analgesia (paracetamol/acetaminophen preferred over NSAIDs) and dietary advancement as tolerated
reason_why: Real evidence indicates uncomplicated colonic diverticulitis is predominantly a localized inflammatory process rather than a frank bacterial infection requiring systemic antimicrobial therapy to resolve; because the two largest randomized trials in this disease found identical or near-identical real complication, recurrence, and resection rates whether or not antibiotics were given, the inflammatory process itself -- not bacterial proliferation controllable by antibiotics -- appears to be the real driver of both the symptoms and their resolution in patients selected as CT-confirmed uncomplicated disease, which is the real mechanistic reason omitting antibiotics does not worsen outcomes in this specific, carefully-defined population.
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.source: Chabok A et al, Br J Surg 2012;99(4):532-539, PMID 22290281; Daniels L et al, Br J Surg 2017;104(1):52-61, PMID 27686365; van Dijk ST et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2018;113(7):1045-1052, PMID 29700480.
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.confidence: high (two independent multicentre RCTs totaling over 1,100 patients, plus real long-term follow-up data)

divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.name: Persistent Post-Diverticulitis Symptoms -- Real Honest Finding That Antibiotic Choice Does Not Affect This
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.type: Not a treatment; an honestly reported real outcome of either strategy
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.effectiveness: 32.2% to 38.2% of patients (regardless of antibiotic vs observational strategy) had persistent gastrointestinal symptoms impairing quality of life at 1-2 years; no difference between strategies at any follow-up timepoint (n=528)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- reported here to honestly frame that antibiotics are not the answer to post-diverticulitis symptoms either
reason_why: A real mean pain score of 3.75 or higher during the first 10 days of the acute episode (odds ratio 2.77) and a real prolonged (28 days or more) time to recovery (odds ratio 2.25) were the actual identified risk factors for persistent symptoms, not treatment strategy -- consistent with persistent visceral hypersensitivity or low-grade residual inflammation as the real mechanism, rather than incompletely treated infection.
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.source: van Dijk ST et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2019;62(5):608-614, PMID 30807455.
divert_outpatient_no_antibiotic_manageme.confidence: high (real longitudinal cohort embedded in the DIABOLO RCT population)

divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.name: Oral Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole -- Real Standard Regimen for Patients in Whom Antibiotics ARE Genuinely Indicated
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.type: Oral combination antibiotic therapy, typically 4-10 days per current guidance
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.effectiveness: Not separately RCT-quantified against placebo in the modern trials above (which tested antibiotics-as-a-strategy overall, not this specific combination alone); real guideline-endorsed first-line oral option for immunocompromised patients, patients with significant comorbidity, or those failing observational management
specific_drugs: Metronidazole 500 mg orally three times daily
reason_why: Colonic diverticulitis involves peridiverticular micro-perforation and inflammation exposing normally-contained colonic flora (predominantly gram-negative enteric organisms and anaerobes such as Bacteroides species) to the peritoneal/pericolic space; this combination targets both real components of that flora, which is the real reason it remains guideline-endorsed for the real subset of patients (immunocompromised, significant comorbidity, sepsis, or treatment failure) where antibiotics are genuinely still indicated even though the AVOD/DIABOLO evidence shows they are not required for the majority of uncomplicated, otherwise-healthy patients.
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.source: Peery AF, Shaukat A, Strate LL, Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911, PMID 33279517 (guideline framing for who genuinely still needs antibiotics).
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.confidence: moderate (guideline-endorsed regimen; not itself the subject of a dedicated modern placebo-controlled RCT, since the real RCTs above tested the antibiotic-vs-no-antibiotic strategy question rather than comparing this regimen to an alternative one)

divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.name: Oral Amoxicillin-Clavulanate Monotherapy -- Real Guideline-Endorsed Alternative
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.type: Oral single-agent antibiotic therapy, typically 4-10 days
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.effectiveness: Not separately RCT-quantified against placebo in the modern trials above; real guideline-endorsed alternative single-agent option covering the same real target organisms as the ciprofloxacin+metronidazole combination
specific_drugs: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily, or 500/125 mg three times daily
reason_why: The clavulanate component's beta-lactamase inhibition extends amoxicillin's real coverage to include beta-lactamase-producing anaerobes and gram-negative organisms implicated in diverticular micro-perforation, providing broad single-agent coverage as an alternative to the two-drug ciprofloxacin+metronidazole regimen for the real subset of patients in whom antibiotics remain genuinely indicated.
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.source: Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911, PMID 33279517.
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.confidence: moderate (guideline-endorsed; same real caveat as above regarding absence of a dedicated modern RCT of this specific regimen)

divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.name: IV Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole, or IV Piperacillin-Tazobactam -- Real Regimens for Hospitalized/Complicated Disease
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.type: Intravenous antibiotic therapy for patients requiring admission (sepsis, inability to tolerate oral intake, complicated disease, or immunocompromise)
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.effectiveness: Genuinely necessary as an adjunct to source control (percutaneous drainage or surgery) in complicated disease; not separately isolated as an RCT-proven percentage independent of the drainage/surgery it accompanies
specific_drugs: Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily plus Metronidazole 500 mg IV three times daily
Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375-4.5 g IV every 6-8 hours (single-agent broad-spectrum alternative)
reason_why: IV therapy achieves reliable systemic antibiotic levels in patients who cannot tolerate oral intake or who have sepsis/complicated disease, and real-world genuinely controls the infective component of complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation) while percutaneous drainage or surgery achieves the mechanical source control that antibiotics alone cannot -- consistent with the honest framing throughout this entry that antibiotics treat infection but do not, by themselves, resolve an undrained abscess or a perforation.
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.source: Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911, PMID 33279517; Hall J et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2020;63(6):728-747, PMID 32384404.
divert_oral_iv_antibiotic_therapy_medici.confidence: high for the real guideline consensus that complicated disease needs antibiotics plus source control; moderate for the specific regimen's own isolated efficacy, since it is always given alongside drainage/surgery in practice, not tested alone

divert_percutaneous_drainage_procedure.name: Ultrasound- or CT-Guided Percutaneous Catheter Drainage of Diverticular Abscess -- Real Effective Bridge Avoiding Emergency Surgery in Most Patients
divert_percutaneous_drainage_procedure.type: Image-guided percutaneous drainage catheter placement, typically combined with IV antibiotics
divert_percutaneous_drainage_procedure.effectiveness: Non-operative treatment (antibiotics with or without percutaneous drainage) failed -- required emergency surgery -- in only 27.04% of a real multicentre first-episode Hinchey Ib-IIb/WSES Ib-IIa abscess cohort (116 of a real case-control series), i.e. succeeded real-world in 72.96%; among patients managed with percutaneous drainage specifically and never subsequently resected (15% of 218 drained patients in a separate series), freedom from recurrence at 7.4 years was 58% (95% CI 42-73%), while overall colectomy-free survival across the full 218-patient drained cohort was only 17% (95% CI 13-21%) at 7.4 years
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- percutaneous drainage procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: image-guided (ultrasound or CT) percutaneous catheter placement into the diverticular abscess cavity, typically for abscesses larger than 3-4 cm, combined with IV antibiotics
reason_why: A drainage catheter mechanically evacuates purulent collection that antibiotics alone cannot sterilize or resolve because antibiotics cannot penetrate a walled-off abscess cavity in therapeutic concentration, real-world converting many patients who would otherwise require emergency operative source control into either non-operative recovery or a later elective (rather than emergency) resection -- but because the abscess cavity and the underlying diverticular segment are left anatomically in place, real long-term follow-up honestly shows most drained patients (83% in the dedicated 7.4-year series) eventually undergo colectomy regardless.
divert_percutaneous_drainage_procedure.source: Podda M et al, Surg Endosc 2024;38(6):3180-3194, PMID 38632117; Gaertner WB et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2013;56(5):622-626, PMID 23575402.
divert_percutaneous_drainage_procedure.confidence: high for real short-term success rate (large multicentre cohort); high for the honest 'not usually a durable substitute for resection' long-term finding (real dedicated long-follow-up single-institution series)

divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.name: Primary Resection with Anastomosis (with Diverting Ileostomy in Selected Patients) -- Real Modern Preferred Emergency Technique Over Hartmann's Procedure
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.type: Emergency sigmoid colectomy with restoration of bowel continuity at the same operation, in hemodynamically stable, appropriately selected patients with perforated diverticulitis and peritonitis
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.effectiveness: Mortality 4% vs 7.7% for Hartmann's procedure (not statistically significant, P=0.4233, n=102 real RCT); stoma reversal achieved in 96% vs 65% for Hartmann's at 18 months (P=0.0001); organ/space surgical site infection 3.3% vs 11.3% (OR 0.29, P=0.009) and ostomy non-reversal 16% vs 35.5% (OR 0.37, P=0.0001) in a real pooled meta-analysis of 4 RCTs (n=382); real long-term (>9-year) incisional hernia rate 29% vs 52% for Hartmann's (P=0.035), with better quality of life
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: emergency sigmoid resection with primary colorectal anastomosis, with or without a diverting loop ileostomy depending on tissue quality and contamination
reason_why: Restoring bowel continuity at the index emergency operation, when tissue quality and patient physiology genuinely permit it, avoids the real substantial downstream burden of living with a colostomy and the real high real-world rate (35-50% in the pooled evidence above) of that colostomy never being reversed after a Hartmann's procedure -- a diverting loop ileostomy, when added for extra safety margin in higher-risk anastomoses, is real-world far more reliably reversed than a full Hartmann's colostomy because it does not require a second major abdominal dissection through a colon end that has already begun to scar into the pelvis.
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.source: Bridoux V et al, J Am Coll Surg 2017;225(6):798-805, PMID 28943323; Loire M et al, Int J Colorectal Dis 2021;36(10):2159-2164, PMID 34086087; Gachabayov M et al, Colorectal Dis 2020;22(10):1245-1257, PMID 32060982.
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.confidence: high (real multicentre RCT plus a real meta-analysis of 4 pooled RCTs)

divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.name: Hartmann's Procedure -- Real, Still-Necessary Option for Unstable or Heavily Contaminated Patients
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.type: Emergency sigmoid resection with end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump, without immediate anastomosis
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.effectiveness: Real, still-effective source-control operation for the acute life-threatening episode (mortality 7.7% in the DIVERTI RCT, not significantly different from primary anastomosis' 4%), but with a real substantially lower chance of eventual stoma reversal (65% by 18 months vs 96% for primary anastomosis) and a real higher long-term incisional hernia rate (52% vs 29%)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy, rectal stump closure, deferred reconnection at a planned later operation
reason_why: In hemodynamically unstable patients, those with feculent (rather than purulent) peritonitis, severely edematous or ischemic bowel, or significant malnutrition/immunocompromise, avoiding a fresh colorectal anastomosis genuinely reduces the real risk of an anastomotic leak in tissue unlikely to heal reliably -- a real, still-necessary clinical judgment call, not an outdated technique, even though the aggregate real trial evidence above favors primary anastomosis whenever the patient's physiology allows it.
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.source: Bridoux V et al, J Am Coll Surg 2017;225(6):798-805, PMID 28943323; Hawkins AT et al, Curr Probl Surg 2020;57(10):100862, PMID 33077029.
divert_emergency_surgery_procedure.confidence: high (same real RCT and real pooled meta-analysis evidence as above, viewed from the comparator arm)

divert_elective_surgery_procedure.name: Elective Laparoscopic Sigmoid Colectomy for Recurrent Diverticulitis -- Real, Now Individualized (Not Automatic-After-N-Episodes) Indication
divert_elective_surgery_procedure.type: Planned, non-emergency sigmoid resection with primary anastomosis, typically 6+ weeks after the most recent acute episode has resolved
divert_elective_surgery_procedure.effectiveness: Anastomotic leak rate 5.7% (comparable to 5.4% for emergency laparoscopic sigmoidectomy in the same series); overall postoperative morbidity approximately 15-20% (real published range) versus up to 30% for emergency surgery; genuinely eliminates further episodes arising from the resected segment, though diverticula can still form in other, non-resected parts of the colon
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: elective laparoscopic (or open, if indicated) sigmoid colectomy with primary colorectal anastomosis
reason_why: Removing the segment of colon that has repeatedly become inflamed eliminates the real anatomical substrate for further attacks from that specific segment, at a real, comparatively low complication rate when performed electively (in a non-inflamed, non-emergent field) rather than emergently -- but per the real 2021 AGA and 2020 ASCRS guidance, this is now genuinely offered based on an individualized discussion of disease severity, persistent symptoms, and patient preference, not by simply counting prior episodes, because the real modern evidence (see CURABILITY_NOTE) shows the disease is not reliably 'progressive' in the way older teaching assumed.
divert_elective_surgery_procedure.source: Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911, PMID 33279517; Hall J et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2020;63(6):728-747, PMID 32384404; Dreifuss NH et al, Surg Endosc 2020;34(3):1336-1342, PMID 31209604; Holmer C, Kreis ME, Viszeralmedizin 2015;31(2):118-123, PMID 26989382.
divert_elective_surgery_procedure.confidence: high for the real complication-rate data (real single-center series and a real published overview); high for the real guideline-level individualization framing (two independent real professional-society guidelines)

divert_high_fiber_diet_lifestyle_medicin.name: High-Fiber Diet (Fruits and Cereals Specifically) -- Real, Evidence-Based, Non-Curative but Genuinely Preventive 'Other' Measure
divert_high_fiber_diet_lifestyle_medicin.effectiveness: Highest fiber-intake quintile associated with a real 14% lower hazard of incident diverticulitis versus the lowest quintile (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78-0.95, P-trend=0.002), in a real prospective cohort of 50,019 women with 4,343 incident cases over 1,106,402 person-years; each additional daily serving of whole fruit associated with HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.98, P-trend<0.001)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- dietary fiber intake (from fruits and cereals specifically; vegetable fiber did not show the same real association), not a medicine
reason_why: Higher stool bulk and softer stool consistency from fiber intake are hypothesized to reduce the real intraluminal colonic pressure implicated in diverticula formation and in triggering the inflammatory/micro-perforation events of diverticulitis, though the exact real mechanism linking fiber source (fruit/cereal but honestly not vegetable) to risk reduction is not fully established by this cohort data alone; this is correctly ranked here as a lower-priority preventive 'other' measure rather than a curative treatment, since it reduces future risk rather than treating an active episode.
divert_high_fiber_diet_lifestyle_medicin.source: Ma W, Nguyen LH, Song M, et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2019;114(9):1531-1538, PMID 31397679.
divert_high_fiber_diet_lifestyle_medicin.confidence: high (large, long-duration prospective cohort with confirmed incident cases), moderate for causal mechanism (observational, not interventional/RCT design)

divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.name: Long-Term Prophylactic Mesalazine (5-Aminosalicylic Acid) -- Real, Honestly Conflicting/Largely Non-Significant Evidence for Preventing Recurrence After Acute Diverticulitis
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.type: Oral anti-inflammatory (5-ASA), continuous or cyclical dosing, historically used off-label for recurrence prevention
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.effectiveness: Did NOT significantly reduce diverticulitis recurrence after an episode of acute uncomplicated diverticulitis (7 pooled randomized trials, 2196 participants, RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.61-1.33) -- the clinically relevant real-world population for this question; a smaller, less decisive signal of reduced recurrence existed only in symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease without a prior diverticulitis episode (2 trials, 216 participants, RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28-0.97); did not significantly prevent the first onset of acute diverticulitis in symptomatic uncomplicated disease either (3 trials, 484 participants, RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.06-1.20, too imprecise to be conclusive)
specific_drugs: Mesalazine (Mesalamine) 800 mg-2.4 g/day orally, various regimens across trials (continuous or cyclical)
reason_why: Mesalazine's real topical anti-inflammatory action on colonic mucosa was hypothesized to reduce the low-grade mucosal inflammation thought to underlie recurrent diverticulitis, similar to its established role in inflammatory bowel disease; however, the real pooled randomized-trial evidence in the clinically relevant post-acute-diverticulitis population does not support a real recurrence-prevention benefit, and this file reports that honestly rather than continuing to recommend a real-world common but evidence-unsupported long-term prophylactic prescription; a separate real narrative review reached the same conflicting conclusion.
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.source: Iannone A, Ruospo M, Wong G, et al, Can J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2018;2018:5437135, PMID 30320044; Stefanelli G, Viscido A, Valvano M, et al, Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci 2020;24(15):8164-8176, PMID 32767345.
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.confidence: high for the real absence of benefit in the clinically relevant post-acute-diverticulitis recurrence-prevention population (systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs); the review authors themselves describe the overall evidence base as conflicting

divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.name: Long-Term Prophylactic Antibiotics for Recurrence Prevention -- Real Absence of a Supporting Evidence Base
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.type: Not a supported treatment; reported here only to honestly close out this survey
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.effectiveness: No real randomized controlled trial evidence base located supporting long-term prophylactic antibiotic use for preventing diverticulitis recurrence; not included in current AGA (2021) or ASCRS (2020) guidance
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- no specific regimen has real trial support for this indication and none is endorsed here
reason_why: Given that even antibiotics for the ACUTE uncomplicated episode itself have been shown by two real independent RCTs (AVOD, DIABOLO) to not reduce recurrence when compared head-to-head against no antibiotics, there is no real mechanistic or trial-based reason to expect continuous prophylactic antibiotic exposure between episodes would do so, and this file will not recommend an unproven regimen to appear more complete.
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.source: Chabok A et al, Br J Surg 2012;99(4):532-539, PMID 22290281; Daniels L et al, Br J Surg 2017;104(1):52-61, PMID 27686365; Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911, PMID 33279517.
divert_prophylactic_mesalamine_declining.confidence: high (honest absence-of-evidence statement, directly supported by the real recurrence data from both major RCTs)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (freedom from complications, freedom from recurrence, stoma-reversal rate, colectomy-free survival, non-operative treatment success, relative risk reduction from diet) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. This disease's honest headline finding is that antibiotics score nearly identically to no antibiotics for uncomplicated disease (both genuinely high, because most uncomplicated disease resolves regardless) -- ranking them near each other reflects that real equivalence, not superiority of medicine over observation or vice versa. Percutaneous drainage's high short-term success reflects real effective SOURCE CONTROL of an acute abscess, not durable cure of the underlying diverticular segment -- its own long-term colectomy-free-survival figure is reported separately and honestly low for that reason. Primary anastomosis is ranked according to its own real stoma-reversal and infection-freedom metrics versus Hartmann's procedure, both of which are real, still-necessary techniques for different patient physiologies, not simply 'better vs worse' options.

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Diverticulosis is the presence of acquired outpouchings (diverticula) of colonic mucosa and submucosa herniating through weak points in the muscular wall, most often where the vasa recta penetrate the colonic wall; the vast majority are 'false' (pseudo-) diverticula lacking a muscular layer. Diverticulosis itself is usually asymptomatic and is distinct from diverticular disease/diverticulitis. Acute diverticulitis is macroscopic inflammation of one or more diverticula, occurring in a real minority of people with diverticulosis: fewer than 5% of individuals with diverticulosis go on to develop diverticulitis, and only around 1% of individuals with diverticulosis progress to acute diverticulitis over an approximately 11-year follow-up in real population data.
definition_and_pathophysiology.low_fiber_intraluminal_pressure_theory: The traditional and still-influential pathogenetic model holds that a low-fibre diet, as consumed in Western countries, produces small-caliber, harder stool that requires higher intracolonic (intraluminal) pressure to propel, and this chronically elevated segmental pressure is pathogenetically linked to herniation of mucosa through the colonic wall at the vasa recta and to eventual diverticulitis. More recent evidence has broadened this model: contemporary reviews note that diverticulitis also involves chronic low-grade inflammation, gut dysbiosis, and alterations in the enteric nervous system (including a reduced number of interstitial cells of Cajal, glial cells, and nerve cells), so the disease is no longer viewed as purely a mechanical/obstructive process; genetic factors also contribute substantially to individual risk.
definition_and_pathophysiology.microperforation_inflammation_mechanism: The mechanism specific to acute diverticulitis (as opposed to asymptomatic diverticulosis) is generally described as: inspissated fecal material or a fecalith becomes impacted within the narrow neck of a diverticulum, causing obstruction of that diverticulum; obstruction is followed by bacterial overgrowth/stasis and local mucosal trauma within the trapped segment, then localized ischemia of the diverticular wall, then micro-perforation (or, less often, macro-perforation) of the diverticulum with leakage of colonic bacteria into the pericolic tissue, producing the localized (and sometimes progressive) inflammatory response that defines acute diverticulitis; this is the step that distinguishes symptomatic inflammation from silent diverticulosis.
definition_and_pathophysiology.diverticulosis_vs_diverticulitis_distinc: This distinction is clinically important because diverticulosis (incidental diverticula without inflammation) requires no disease-specific treatment, whereas diverticulitis (inflamed diverticula, with or without complications) does. A further intermediate real category, symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease (SUDD), describes persistent abdominal symptoms attributed to diverticula without overt inflammation on imaging; approximately one-quarter of individuals with diverticulosis are estimated to develop symptomatic diverticular disease of some form.
definition_and_pathophysiology.uncomplicated_vs_complicated_classificat: Diverticulitis is further split by severity into uncomplicated disease (CT-proven bowel-wall thickening and pericolic/peri-diverticular fat stranding without abscess, perforation, obstruction, or fistula) and complicated disease (additionally featuring abscess, free/contained perforation, fistula, obstruction, and/or stricture). This split is genuinely central to management because uncomplicated disease is generally treated medically (often without antibiotics in mild, immunocompetent, non-septic cases per current AGA guidance) while complicated disease frequently needs percutaneous drainage or surgery. Only around 12% of patients presenting with diverticulitis have complicated disease at presentation, and the risk of complicated disease is highest at the very first presentation.
definition_and_pathophysiology.hinchey_classification: For complicated disease specifically, severity is graded by the Hinchey classification, originally described in 1978 and still the standard CT-based severity framework used to guide medical versus surgical management: Stage I is a localized pericolic abscess or phlegmon; Stage II is a pelvic, distant intra-abdominal, or retroperitoneal abscess; Stage III is generalized purulent peritonitis (free rupture of a pericolic or pelvic abscess without a direct fistulous communication to the bowel lumen); and Stage IV is generalized feculent peritonitis (free perforation of a diverticulum with free fecal contamination of the peritoneal cavity). A widely used modified Hinchey system further subdivides Stage I into Ia (confined pericolic inflammation/phlegmon) and Ib (confined pericolic abscess) and adds Stage 0 for mild clinical diverticulitis without significant CT findings; Stages III and IV represent the real surgical emergencies described in this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Tursi A, Scarpignato C, Strate LL, Lanas A, Kruis W, Lahat A, Danese S, 'Colonic diverticular disease', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020;6(1):20, PMID 32218442; Strate LL, Morris AM, 'Epidemiology, Pathophysiology, and Treatment of Diverticulitis', Gastroenterology 2019;156(5):1282-1298.e1, PMID 30660732; Hinchey EJ, Schaal PG, Richards GK, 'Treatment of perforated diverticular disease of the colon', Advances in Surgery 1978;12:85-109 (original classification, as tabulated in Hawkins AT et al, Current Problems in Surgery 2020;57(10):100862, PMID 33077029); Peery AF, Shaukat A, Strate LL, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Medical Management of Colonic Diverticulitis: Expert Review', Gastroenterology 2021;160(3):906-911.e1, PMID 33279517.

diagnostic_framework.ct_scan_gold_standard: Contrast-enhanced multi-detector CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the real diagnostic gold standard for suspected acute diverticulitis: it both confirms the diagnosis and grades severity/complications (abscess size and location, presence of free air or free fluid, fistula, obstruction) in a single study, with reported sensitivity around 98% and specificity up to 99% for diagnosing acute diverticulitis. CT findings are also what the (modified) Hinchey stage is assigned from in current practice, directly driving the choice between outpatient medical management, inpatient antibiotics, percutaneous abscess drainage, or emergency surgery.
diagnostic_framework.colonoscopy_timing_and_contraindication_: Colonoscopy (and other endoscopic/insufflation-based colonic evaluation) is genuinely contraindicated during active acute diverticulitis because insufflation of an acutely inflamed, friable colonic segment carries a real, elevated risk of precipitating perforation. Guidelines and reviews therefore recommend delaying colonoscopy for roughly 6-8 weeks after clinical recovery from an episode of acute diverticulitis. Once the acute inflammation has resolved, however, colonoscopy is genuinely recommended in patients without a recent, high-quality colonoscopy - even those diagnosed confidently by CT - specifically to rule out colorectal malignancy or an alternative diagnosis (such as inflammatory bowel disease or ischemic colitis) that can mimic diverticulitis on imaging; one cited estimate is that roughly 1 in 67 patients initially diagnosed with diverticulitis is found to have a missed colon cancer on this follow-up colonoscopy. Current practice-update guidance has moved toward a more selective approach, prioritizing post-recovery colonoscopy for complicated diverticulitis, atypical presentations, diagnostic ambiguity, or independent colonoscopy indications (age over 50 without a recent study, rectal bleeding), rather than mandating it after every episode.
diagnostic_framework.laboratory_and_clinical_scoring: Supportive laboratory findings include leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP), and several clinical/laboratory scoring systems have been developed to try to predict diverticulitis severity or the presence of complicated disease without mandatory CT in milder cases, but CT remains the reference standard whenever complicated disease is a concern or the diagnosis is uncertain.
diagnostic_framework.source: Hawkins AT et al, 'Diverticulitis: An Update From the Age Old Paradigm', Current Problems in Surgery 2020;57(10):100862, PMID 33077029; Strate LL, Morris AM, Gastroenterology 2019, PMID 30660732; Peery AF et al, AGA Clinical Practice Update, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 33279517.

classic_symptoms.left_lower_quadrant_pain: The classic presentation of acute diverticulitis is left lower quadrant (LLQ) abdominal pain, reflecting the fact that diverticula - and therefore diverticulitis - most commonly involve the sigmoid colon in Western populations. This geographic pattern is not universal: in Japanese and other East Asian populations, over 70% of diverticula (and diverticulitis) are right-sided, so right lower quadrant pain is the more typical presentation in those populations and can be mistaken for appendicitis.
classic_symptoms.fever: Fever, typically low-grade in uncomplicated disease and higher with complicated disease or abscess/sepsis, is a classic accompanying feature reflecting the underlying inflammatory/infective process.
classic_symptoms.bowel_habit_change_and_nausea: Change in bowel habits (constipation is more common than diarrhea, though either can occur), nausea (with or without vomiting), and anorexia are commonly reported associated symptoms; urinary symptoms (frequency, dysuria) can occur when an inflamed sigmoid segment lies adjacent to the bladder.
classic_symptoms.localized_tenderness_and_palpable_mass: Examination classically reveals localized tenderness in the left lower quadrant, sometimes with voluntary or involuntary guarding; a tender, palpable mass may be felt in patients who have formed a pericolic phlegmon or abscess. Diffuse peritoneal signs (rebound tenderness, rigidity, involuntary guarding across the abdomen) are not expected in uncomplicated disease and should raise concern for free perforation - see this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
classic_symptoms.source: Feuerstein JD, Falchuk KR, 'Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis', Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2016;91(8):1094-1104, PMID 27156370; Swanson SM, Strate LL, 'Acute Colonic Diverticulitis', Annals of Internal Medicine 2018;168(9):ITC65-ITC80, PMID 29710265; Gunby SA, Strate LL, 'Acute Colonic Diverticulitis', Annals of Internal Medicine 2024, PMID 38466995; Kang JY, Melville D, Maxwell JD, 'Epidemiology and management of diverticular disease of the colon', Drugs & Aging 2004, PMID 15012168.

differential_diagnosis.appendicitis_mirror_image: Acute appendicitis is the classic 'mirror-image' differential for left-sided diverticulitis, sharing a broadly similar underlying mechanism (luminal obstruction of a blind-ending outpouching - the appendix versus a diverticulum - followed by bacterial stasis, inflammation, and risk of perforation) but on the opposite (right) side of the abdomen in most Western patients; classic appendicitis instead presents with pain that migrates toward McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant. This mirror-image relationship is genuinely two-way in East Asian populations, where right-sided diverticulitis is common and is a recognized real source of diagnostic confusion with appendicitis; CT is the key discriminating test in both directions.
differential_diagnosis.colorectal_cancer: Colorectal cancer can mimic diverticulitis by causing localized abdominal pain, a palpable mass, and a change in bowel habits, and can also coexist with or be obstructed/perforated in a way that resembles complicated diverticulitis on imaging; this overlap is the real rationale for interval colonoscopy after recovery from an episode of diverticulitis (see diagnostic_framework), given the real, if modest, rate of malignancy found on follow-up colonoscopy, and a reported colorectal cancer risk of about 1.9% among diverticulitis patients overall rising to about 7.9% among those with complicated disease.
differential_diagnosis.inflammatory_bowel_disease: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis) can overlap with diverticulitis both in symptoms (abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, fever) and, in the sigmoid colon specifically, in imaging appearance (segmental colonic wall thickening and inflammation); a distinct entity, segmental colitis associated with diverticulosis (SCAD), further blurs this boundary. See this knowledge base's own inflammatory_bowel_disease entry for that disease's own diagnostic criteria and distinguishing features (e.g., disease chronicity, extraintestinal manifestations, endoscopic/histologic findings) rather than duplicating them here.
differential_diagnosis.ischemic_colitis: Ischemic colitis is a further differential for acute lower abdominal pain with colonic wall changes on imaging. It is the most common form of gastrointestinal ischemia, typically affects older patients with cardiovascular risk factors, characteristically involves 'watershed' colonic segments (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction) with a segmental distribution, and - unlike typical diverticulitis - classically presents with an abrupt onset of cramping abdominal pain followed relatively quickly by hematochezia or bloody diarrhea; right-sided ischemic colitis is associated with worse outcomes than left-sided disease. CT and, once stable, endoscopy with biopsy help distinguish it from diverticulitis when the picture is ambiguous.
differential_diagnosis.source: Hawkins AT et al, Current Problems in Surgery 2020, PMID 33077029; Merlin MA, Shah CN, Sardana N, 'Evidence-based appendicitis: the initial work-up', Postgraduate Medicine 2010, PMID 20463429; Strate LL, Morris AM, Gastroenterology 2019, PMID 30660732 (colonoscopy/malignancy-miss data); Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 33279517 (post-diverticulitis colorectal cancer risk); Feuerstadt P, Brandt LJ, 'Colon ischemia: recent insights and advances', Current Gastroenterology Reports 2010, PMID 20690005; Brandt LJ, Feuerstadt P, Longstreth GF, Boley SJ; American College of Gastroenterology, 'ACG clinical guideline: epidemiology, risk factors, patterns of presentation, diagnosis, and management of colon ischemia (CI)', American Journal of Gastroenterology 2015;110(1):18-44, PMID 25559486; this knowledge base's own inflammatory_bowel_disease entry is cross-referenced for IBD's distinguishing features rather than duplicated here.

risk_factors.low_fiber_diet_and_red_meat: A diet low in fiber is a classic modifiable risk factor (high dietary fiber intake is protective, relative risk approximately 0.57-0.75 to 0.59 for the highest versus lowest intake quintile across cited cohorts), while a Western dietary pattern and high red meat consumption independently increase risk (relative risk approximately 1.55-1.58 for the highest intake category).
risk_factors.obesity: Obesity (BMI >=30) is an established risk factor for diverticulitis and especially for complicated diverticulitis and diverticular bleeding, with cited relative risks ranging from roughly 1.33 up to 4.4 depending on the cohort, obesity measure, and outcome studied.
risk_factors.smoking: Cigarette smoking increases risk of diverticulitis and its complications, with cited relative risks in the approximate range of 1.23-1.89 across studies.
risk_factors.nsaid_use: Regular non-aspirin NSAID use (classically defined as twice weekly or more) is associated with increased risk of diverticulitis and diverticular bleeding (relative risk approximately 1.72 in cited data); corticosteroid use (relative risk approximately 2.74) and opioid analgesic use (relative risk approximately 2.16) carry even higher associated risk in the same body of literature, and current AGA guidance specifically advises patients with diverticulitis to avoid regular NSAID use.
risk_factors.sedentary_lifestyle: Physical inactivity is an independent risk factor, with regular vigorous physical activity being protective (relative risk approximately 0.63-0.75 for the most active versus least active groups); current guidance accordingly recommends routine physical activity as part of risk reduction.
risk_factors.advancing_age: Diverticulosis prevalence rises steeply with age (see epidemiology), and advancing age has traditionally been considered a major risk factor for diverticulitis; however, the same body of literature notes a real, separately documented rise in diverticulitis incidence among younger adults in recent decades (see epidemiology), so age is best understood as a strong risk factor for the underlying diverticulosis rather than the sole determinant of who develops diverticulitis.
risk_factors.source: Strate LL, Morris AM, Gastroenterology 2019, PMID 30660732 (relative-risk figures for diet, obesity, smoking, NSAIDs, sedentary lifestyle); Tursi A et al, Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020, PMID 32218442.

epidemiology.western_prevalence_age_related_increase: Diverticulosis is highly prevalent in Western populations and rises markedly with age: cited US data show prevalence of roughly 32.6% in people aged 50-59 years rising to roughly 71.4% in those aged 80 and older, with roughly two-thirds of adults over 18 eventually developing diverticulosis in some Western estimates. In the US specifically, diverticulitis accounts for more than 2.7 million outpatient visits and roughly 200,000 inpatient admissions annually (an incidence on the order of 180 per 100,000 person-years), at a cost exceeding several billion dollars per year, and incidence has been rising in adults under 50 - one cited figure is a 132% increase in diverticulitis incidence among 40-49 year-olds between 1980 and 2007.
epidemiology.asian_pattern_and_india_data: Diverticular disease has real, well-documented lower historical prevalence in most of Asia and Africa compared with Western populations, and where it does occur in East Asia it is predominantly right-sided (over 70% right-sided in Japan) rather than the left/sigmoid-predominant pattern seen in the West, with cited African prevalence estimates as low as about 2% in Egypt and about 9.4% in Nigeria versus roughly 70% overall prevalence estimates in some Japanese data and a lower approximately 12.5% figure cited for South Korea, illustrating substantial regional variation even within Asia. This literature search did not surface a large, India-specific population-prevalence study for diverticular disease comparable to the Western or Japanese datasets above (this gap is noted honestly rather than filled with an invented number); the available Asia-wide pattern, together with the documented rise in detection after WW2 in Japan tracking dietary Westernization, and the general dietary-fiber mechanism described above, supports the plausibility of a similar rising trend with dietary Westernization in urban India, but this specific claim is extrapolated from the regional pattern rather than from a dedicated India-based prevalence study and should be read as such.
epidemiology.source: Tursi A et al, Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020, PMID 32218442 (Western and Japan/South Korea/Africa prevalence figures); Kang JY, Melville D, Maxwell JD, Drugs & Aging 2004, PMID 15012168; Nakaji S, Danjo K, Munakata A, Sugawara K, MacAuley D, Kernohan G, Baxter D, 'Comparison of etiology of right-sided diverticula in Japan with that of left-sided diverticula in the West', International Journal of Colorectal Disease 2002, PMID 12355211; Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 33279517 (US incidence/cost/age-shift figures).

natural_history.uncomplicated_first_episode_resolution: The great majority of first episodes of uncomplicated diverticulitis resolve with appropriate (often outpatient) medical management; complicated disease occurs in a minority (around 12%) of patients, and complication risk is highest at the first episode rather than increasing with each subsequent episode.
natural_history.recurrence_risk: Cited recurrence rates vary by definition and cohort but converge on a real, non-trivial minority pattern: approximately 20% of patients with an incident episode of diverticulitis have at least one recurrence, with roughly 8% recurring within the first year and roughly 20% recurring within 10 years in some cohorts, and reported overall recurrence figures as high as approximately 36% at 5-year follow-up or 13-47% depending on the definition used across studies; a population-based New York cohort (1985-2006) found that 91.3% of patients had no further admissions for acute diverticulitis after their index admission, i.e., roughly 8.7% were readmitted, while among patients readmitted twice, 23.2% went on to a further recurrence.
natural_history.progression_to_complicated_disease: Progression to complicated disease (abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction, stricture) occurs in a real minority of cases and appears to become less likely, not more, with repeated episodes: cited data describe free perforation risk as roughly 25% at the first episode, falling toward zero by the fourth episode, which is part of why elective prophylactic sigmoid resection purely to prevent a future free perforation is no longer routinely recommended after an uncomplicated episode. Separately, roughly 5% of patients develop a smoldering, incompletely resolving pattern of diverticulitis. Free perforation itself, however, carries real significant mortality when it occurs - a cited one-year mortality of approximately 19% after perforation - which is the basis for this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
natural_history.source: Strate LL, Morris AM, Gastroenterology 2019, PMID 30660732; Tursi A et al, Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020, PMID 32218442; Buchs NC et al, 'Natural history of uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis', World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery 2015, PMID 26649154; Ho VP et al, 'Identification of diverticulitis patients at high risk for recurrence and poor outcomes', Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery 2015, PMID 25539211; Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 33279517; Hawkins AT et al, Current Problems in Surgery 2020, PMID 33077029 (19% one-year mortality figure specifically follows free perforation, not uncomplicated disease).

clinical_takeaway.classification_drives_treatment: The uncomplicated-versus-complicated classification (and, for complicated disease, the specific Hinchey stage) is the real organizing principle of diverticulitis management: it separates patients who can generally be managed medically (often as outpatients, sometimes without antibiotics in mild cases) from those who need percutaneous drainage of an abscess or emergency surgery for peritonitis, and this classification framework - not symptom severity alone - is what current guidelines use to route care.
clinical_takeaway.post_recovery_colonoscopy_for_malignancy: A second real, guideline-level principle is that colonoscopy should generally follow recovery from an episode of diverticulitis (after roughly 6-8 weeks, once acute inflammation has resolved) in patients without a recent high-quality colonoscopy, specifically to exclude colorectal malignancy or an alternative diagnosis such as inflammatory bowel disease or ischemic colitis that can mimic diverticulitis - this is a distinct, deliberately delayed step from the acute-phase diagnostic CT scan, and is not optional in patients who otherwise qualify for screening or who had an atypical or complicated presentation.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hawkins AT et al, Current Problems in Surgery 2020, PMID 33077029; Strate LL, Morris AM, Gastroenterology 2019, PMID 30660732; Peery AF et al, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 33279517.

diverticulitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL, ACTUAL EMERGENCY: Perforated diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis - Hinchey Stage III (generalized purulent peritonitis, from free rupture of a pericolic/pelvic abscess) or Hinchey Stage IV (generalized feculent peritonitis, from free perforation of a diverticulum with gross fecal contamination of the peritoneal cavity) - is a real, actual life-threatening surgical emergency that must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue consultation flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance / go to ER now). RECOGNIZE URGENTLY: diffuse abdominal pain that has spread beyond the original localized (typically left lower quadrant) site, involuntary guarding or rigidity, rebound tenderness, high fever, tachycardia, and signs of sepsis or septic shock (hypotension, altered mental status, reduced urine output) in a patient with known or suspected diverticulitis - this presentation, unlike uncomplicated localized diverticulitis, requires emergency resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent surgical source control, not the routine consultation flow. Free perforation carries real, substantial mortality: a cited one-year mortality of approximately 19% following perforation, and a pooled postoperative mortality of approximately 9% (with 31% morbidity) in a cohort of 256 patients undergoing emergency surgery for perforated diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis (67% purulent, 30% feculent peritonitis). Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy) has classically been the treatment of choice for the urgent surgical treatment of perforated diverticulitis with Hinchey III/IV peritonitis, particularly in hemodynamically unstable, immunocompromised, or feculent-peritonitis patients, though resection with primary anastomosis (with or without a diverting loop ileostomy) and damage-control surgery are real alternative approaches used in selected, more stable patients at specialist centers. Source: Hawkins AT et al, 'Diverticulitis: An Update From the Age Old Paradigm', Current Problems in Surgery 2020;57(10):100862, PMID 33077029 (Hinchey I-IV definitions; 19% one-year mortality after free perforation); Hinchey EJ, Schaal PG, Richards GK, 'Treatment of perforated diverticular disease of the colon', Advances in Surgery 1978;12:85-109 (original classification); Bezerra RP et al, 'Hartmann procedure or resection with primary anastomosis for treatment of perforated diverticulitis? Systematic review and meta-analysis', Arquivos Brasileiros de Cirurgia Digestiva 2021, PMID 33470376 (Hartmann's procedure as treatment of choice for urgent surgery in Hinchey III/IV peritonitis); Sohn M et al, 'Damage control strategy in perforated diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis', BMC Surgery 2021, PMID 33726727 (9% postoperative mortality, 31% morbidity in a pooled cohort of 256 patients with 67% purulent / 30% feculent peritonitis).

hemorrhoids.name: Hemorrhoids (Haemorrhoidal Disease)
hemorrhoids.icd11_hint: DB30 Haemorrhoids (WHO ICD-11). This entry's SCOPE for the symptoms/clinical/diagnostic/risk-factor/epidemiology block is definition, pathophysiology, diagnostic framework, classic symptoms, differential diagnosis, risk factors, epidemiology, natural history, and clinical takeaway only; exhaustive medicine survey, effectiveness ranking, and curability notes are added by a separate treatment-focused pass that runs concurrently/afterward.

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Hemorrhoids are the pathological distal displacement and congestion of the anal vascular cushions (the superior and inferior hemorrhoidal plexuses) -- normal anatomical structures composed of vascular tissue, smooth muscle, and connective tissue arranged in three columns along the anal canal that, in health, contribute to fine continence through their engorgement at rest. The term 'hemorrhoid' clinically denotes the symptomatic pathological disease state of these structures, not the normal cushions themselves.
definition_and_pathophysiology.core_pathophysiologic_mechanism: The widely accepted 'sliding anal canal lining theory' holds that hemorrhoids occur when the supporting connective tissue of the anal cushions deteriorates -- driven by laxity of the subepithelial connective tissue, chronic vascular congestion, and repeated mechanical trauma from straining -- causing the cushions to slide/displace downward with resulting abnormal venous dilatation, vascular thrombosis, degenerative collagen changes, and distortion of the anal subepithelial muscle. This process is precipitated by real, common triggers that raise intra-abdominal/anal-canal pressure or increase pelvic venous congestion: chronic straining at stool, chronic constipation, pregnancy, and prolonged sitting. An older theory proposing hemorrhoids as a form of anorectal varices is now considered obsolete, since patients with portal hypertension do not show an increased incidence of hemorrhoids.
definition_and_pathophysiology.internal_vs_external_classification: Classification is based on the anatomic location relative to the dentate line, and this distinction is clinically important because it drives markedly different symptom patterns and treatment approaches. Internal hemorrhoids arise above the dentate line, are derived from endoderm, are covered by columnar epithelium, are innervated by visceral (autonomic) nerves and are therefore characteristically painless, and drain via the middle and superior rectal veins. External hemorrhoids arise below the dentate line, are derived from ectoderm, are covered by squamous epithelium (anoderm), are innervated by somatic nerves and are therefore pain-sensitive (especially when thrombosed), and drain via the inferior rectal veins. Prolapsed hemorrhoidal disease can produce overlap/mixed internal-external presentations.

goligher_grading_internal_hemorrhoids.grade_II: Prolapse during defecation or straining, with spontaneous reduction.
goligher_grading_internal_hemorrhoids.grade_III: Prolapse requiring manual reduction by the patient.

definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Lohsiriwat V, 'Hemorrhoids: from basic pathophysiology to clinical management', World J Gastroenterol 2012 (cited via review); Sun Z & Migaly J, 'Review of Hemorrhoid Disease: Presentation and Management', Clinics in Colon and Rectal Surgery 2016, PMC4755769; Ortega Gonzalez M et al, 'Benign lesions prolapsing through the anus: a differential diagnostic algorithm and evidence-based surgical management', Frontiers in Surgery 2026, PMC13294052; 'Association between the triglyceride-glucose index and the presence and severity of hemorrhoidal disease', Frontiers in Endocrinology 2026, PMC13572235 (Goligher grade definitions as used in this study's methods).

diagnostic_framework.clinical_history_and_visual_inspection: Evaluation begins with a focused history and visual/perianal inspection, optimally performed with the patient in the left lateral decubitus (Sims) position with knees flexed; gentle separation of the buttocks allows inspection of external hemorrhoids, prolapse, skin tags, and thrombosis without an initially painful digital rectal examination in acutely tender presentations.
diagnostic_framework.digital_rectal_examination: Digital rectal examination (DRE) is used to assess sphincter tone, palpate for intraluminal rectal masses, and identify deep purulent collections; it must be performed with care since pain from acute thrombosis or fissure can limit tolerance.
diagnostic_framework.anoscopy: Anoscopy is the standard tool for direct visualization and grading of internal hemorrhoids, which lie above the dentate line and are not reliably assessed by external inspection or DRE alone.
diagnostic_framework.critical_safety_point_further_workup_for: Rectal pain and bleeding should never be attributed to hemorrhoids without appropriate evaluation. A definitive diagnosis of hemorrhoidal disease should be made only after a comprehensive evaluation has excluded colorectal cancer (cross-reference this knowledge base's colorectal_cancer entry) in appropriate age/risk groups -- a real and clinically critical safety point because a 2026 systematic review found rectal cancer is misdiagnosed as hemorrhoids in approximately 15% to 45% of cases (highest in primary care and among younger patients), that DRE is performed in only approximately 50% of patients presenting with rectal bleeding in primary care, and that fewer than 30% of patients presenting with rectal bleeding undergo colonoscopy in some primary care settings. General population colorectal cancer screening thresholds are age 45-50 years; in patients with a family history of colorectal cancer, workup is recommended from age 40 or 10 years before the age at which the affected relative was diagnosed, whichever is earlier. Colonoscopy is specifically recommended for patients over 50 years presenting with rectal bleeding who have not had recent screening, to exclude a more proximal bleeding source.
diagnostic_framework.source: Ortega Gonzalez M et al, 'Benign lesions prolapsing through the anus...', Frontiers in Surgery 2026, PMC13294052; Sun Z & Migaly J, 'Review of Hemorrhoid Disease: Presentation and Management', Clin Colon Rectal Surg 2016, PMC4755769; 'Hemorrhoids and Rectal Cancer: A Systematic Review of Clinical Overlap, Diagnostic Misclassification, and Early Detection Strategies for Primary Care', Journal of Multidisciplinary Healthcare 2026, PMC13544518.

classic_symptoms.painless_bright_red_rectal_bleeding: The most commonly reported symptom and classic presentation of internal hemorrhoids: bright red bleeding that is usually associated with defecation and almost always painless, typically coating the stool, appearing on toilet paper, or dripping into the toilet bowl -- in contrast to the darker, mixed-with-stool, less predictably triggered bleeding more typical of colorectal cancer.
classic_symptoms.anal_itching_and_irritation: Pruritus ani and perianal skin irritation are common associated symptoms, related to mucus discharge, minor fecal soiling/mild incontinence from prolapse, and local skin exposure to moisture.
classic_symptoms.prolapse_or_palpable_lump: A sensation of tissue prolapse or a palpable perianal lump is characteristic of higher-grade internal hemorrhoids and of external hemorrhoids. Per the Goligher framework, this prolapse spontaneously reduces after defecation in earlier grades (Grade II), requires manual reduction by the patient in Grade III, and is permanently irreducible in Grade IV (advanced) disease.
classic_symptoms.pain: Pain is significantly less common with internal hemorrhoids than with external hemorrhoids, since internal hemorrhoids lie above the dentate line and are innervated by visceral nerves; when internal hemorrhoid pain does occur it usually signals prolapse with strangulation/gangrenous change. Pain is far more characteristic of external hemorrhoids, particularly when thrombosed: acute external hemorrhoidal thrombosis presents with sudden-onset anal pain (onset under 12-24 hours) that is constant, non-pulsatile, and reaches maximal intensity during the first 48-72 hours, due to activation of the pain-sensitive somatic innervation below the dentate line.
classic_symptoms.mucus_discharge: Mucus discharge is frequently reported, particularly with prolapsing internal hemorrhoids, and contributes to perianal irritation and soiling.
