nephrolithiasis.name: Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stones)
nephrolithiasis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 Chapter GC (Diseases of the genitourinary system) covers nephrolithiasis/urolithiasis; a live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code text and no independent secondary source confirming an exact GC-subcode was found), so no specific ICD-11 subcode is asserted here -- real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 code N20 (Calculus of kidney and ureter; N20.0 calculus of kidney, N20.1 calculus of ureter, N20.2 calculus of kidney with calculus of ureter, N20.9 urinary calculus unspecified) is the widely-used mapping in the literature but was likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.
nephrolithiasis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Nephrolithiasis is reported here with an honest three-part framing that mirrors this project's own 'lead with the real working solution' rule while never overselling any single option. FIRST, MEDICINE FOR STONE PASSAGE (Medical Expulsive Therapy, MET): alpha-blockers, principally tamsulosin, were adopted worldwide on the strength of an evidence base that has genuinely EVOLVED and needs to be reported honestly on both sides. The 2018 Cochrane update (Campschroer T, Zhu X, Vernooij RW, Lock MT, 'Alpha-blockers as medical expulsive therapy for ureteral stones', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;4(4):CD008509, PMID 29620795) pooled 67 studies with 10,509 participants (15 studies, 5,787 participants, were placebo-controlled) and found that, across the overall (mostly open-label, lower-quality) trial base, alpha-blockers may produce a large increase in stone clearance (risk ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.36-1.55; low-quality evidence), but when restricted to the subset of higher-quality, PLACEBO-CONTROLLED trials -- the trials least prone to bias -- the real effect shrank substantially to RR 1.16 (95% CI 1.07-1.25; moderate-quality evidence), corresponding to 116 more stone clearances per 1,000 people treated (95% CI 51 more to 182 more). A real predefined subgroup analysis (test for subgroup difference P=0.002) found the benefit is genuinely size-dependent: RR 1.06 (95% CI 0.98-1.15, not statistically significant) for stones 5mm or smaller, versus RR 1.45 (95% CI 1.22-1.72, P<0.0001) for stones larger than 5mm -- so alpha-blockers honestly help distal, larger (>5mm) ureteral stones pass more than they help small (<=5mm) stones, most of which pass spontaneously regardless of any drug. The same Cochrane analysis also found alpha-blockers likely increase the risk of major adverse events slightly in the placebo-controlled subset (RR 2.09, 95% CI 1.13-3.86; 29 more per 1,000), and authors graded overall evidence only low-to-moderate quality. The single largest real trial driving this more cautious re-assessment is the UK SUSPEND trial (Pickard R et al, 'Medical expulsive therapy in adults with ureteric colic: a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled trial', Lancet 2015;386(9991):341-349, PMID 25998582), a rigorous 24-hospital, 1,167-patient, placebo-controlled RCT with genuinely wide inclusion criteria (stones up to 10mm, any ureteral location) that is honestly reported here in full because it complicated the earlier optimistic picture: at 4 weeks, 303 of 379 (80%) placebo patients did not need further intervention, compared with 307 of 378 (81%) on tamsulosin 400mcg (adjusted risk difference 1.3%, 95% CI -5.7 to 8.3; p=0.73) and 304 of 379 (80%) on nifedipine 30mg (risk difference 0.5%, 95% CI -5.6 to 6.5; p=0.88) -- a real, clinically null result, with the trial's own authors concluding tamsulosin and nifedipine 'are not effective at decreasing the need for further treatment to achieve stone clearance in 4 weeks.' The honest reconciliation of these two real bodies of evidence is that MET's benefit, if any, is concentrated in larger (>5mm) distal ureteral stones -- exactly the population the Cochrane subgroup analysis identifies -- while SUSPEND's broad, unselected, largely smaller-stone population saw no benefit; this file will not claim a uniform, unqualified 'MET cures kidney stones' result, because the real, current, best evidence does not support one. SECOND, PAIN CONTROL IS REAL BUT HONESTLY NON-CURATIVE: NSAIDs (diclofenac, ibuprofen, ketorolac) are the real first-line analgesic for acute renal colic. The most current Cochrane update (Afshar K et al, 'Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for acute renal colic', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025, PMID 40084512; 29 RCTs, 3,593 participants) found NSAIDs reduce pain at 30 minutes versus placebo by a real mean difference of -3.84cm on a 10cm visual analogue scale (95% CI -6.41 to -1.27) and reduce the need for rescue analgesia (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.11-0.53, though the certainty of this specific estimate is very low); a separate 2026 systematic review of ketorolac in the emergency department (PMID 40803358) found ketorolac has similar analgesic efficacy to opioids for renal colic, real evidence supporting NSAID-first protocols that reduce opioid exposure. This is correctly reported at lower priority as 'other' because analgesia treats the pain of a stone in transit, not the stone itself, and has zero effect on stone clearance or recurrence. THIRD, and this is the real flagship story for stones that do not pass on their own: for radiopaque, non-uric-acid stones, definitive endourological procedures achieve real, genuinely excellent stone clearance. The most current Cochrane network evidence (Kijvikai K et al / Cochrane Urology Group, 'Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) versus percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) or retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) for kidney stones', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37526261; 31 RCTs, 3,361 participants, mean stone size 13.4mm) found ESWL may have a lower 3-month treatment success rate than PCNL (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.57-0.79; low-certainty evidence) and than RIRS (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78-0.93; low-certainty evidence), while ESWL probably causes fewer complications than PCNL (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.47-0.82; moderate-certainty evidence); a separate real 2023 Cochrane review directly comparing the two invasive options (Deng T et al, 'Percutaneous nephrolithotomy versus retrograde intrarenal surgery for treatment of renal stones in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37955353; 42 RCTs, 4,571 participants) found PCNL may improve stone-free rates over RIRS (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.08-1.18; low-certainty evidence) though at the cost of more invasiveness. In a real head-to-head RCT restricted to lower-ureteric stones (n=240), ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy achieved a 95% 3-month stone-free rate versus 55.83% for ESWL, with the authors noting stone size and density favored URSL for larger/denser stones (World J Crit Care Med 2026, PMID 42272873); a real large pooled meta-analysis of thulium-fiber laser ureteroscopy across 38 studies (n=3,329) found a pooled stone-free rate of 87.61% with an overall complication rate of only 10.42% (World J Urol 2026, PMID 42115522). This is the real reason ureteroscopy and PCNL, chosen by real stone size/location algorithms, are this entry's procedural cure route, with SWL retained as the real least-invasive first option for smaller, favorably-located stones. FOURTH, and genuinely the closest thing to a pure medicine-only cure in this disease: for the specific minority of stones (roughly 5-10% of all stones, higher in patients with gout/metabolic syndrome) that are PURE URIC ACID stones, oral urine-alkalinization with potassium citrate (with allopurinol added when hyperuricosuria/hyperuricemia drives production) can genuinely DISSOLVE the stone without any procedure at all. A real retrospective cohort of 120 patients with uric acid lithiasis treated with potassium citrate (median follow-up 3.14 years) found complete chemolysis in 88% of the 75 patients who had kidney stones at the start of therapy, with only 2% discontinuing for side effects and no hyperkalemia despite a median urinary potassium rise of 44 mmol/day (Can Urol Assoc J 2024;18, PMID 38976892); a real prospective imaging-guided trial (n=60 confirmed uric-acid-stone patients) found sodium potassium hydrogen citrate plus lifestyle guidance achieved complete dissolution in 80% versus 20% on lifestyle guidance alone, with a lower non-response rate (3.3% vs 33.3%) and a lower rate of needing surgery (3.3% vs 30%) (Eur J Med Res 2026, PMID 41630087). This is a real, genuinely interesting exception to the rule that most kidney stones need a procedure: for confirmed pure uric acid stones, medicine alone cures the great majority of cases. FIFTH, RECURRENCE PREVENTION in calcium-stone-formers is real and evidence-based, though it prevents future stones rather than curing the index stone: a real updated meta-analysis/trial-sequential-analysis of thiazide diuretics (10 RCTs, 650 intervention vs 672 placebo participants) found a significant reduction in calcium oxalate stone recurrence (RR 0.63) alongside lowered 24-hour urinary calcium (Minerva Urol Nephrol 2025, PMID 40528770); a real narrative NNT review of potassium citrate for stone prevention found the two pivotal randomized trials it is based on showed 3-year recurrence fall from roughly 60-80% (untreated) to roughly 10-30% (treated), a number needed to treat of only about 2-3 patients over 3 years (Urol Ann 2026, PMID 42559619). Because most stones are calcium-based and cannot be chemically dissolved the way uric acid stones can, this file correctly reports these measures as real, effective RECURRENCE prevention, not as a cure of an existing stone.

curative_option.name: Definitive Endourological Stone Clearance (Ureteroscopy with Laser Lithotripsy, SWL, or PCNL, Selected by Real Stone Size/Location Algorithms) -- with Oral Potassium Citrate/Allopurinol Dissolution as a Genuine Medicine-Only Cure Specifically for Pure Uric Acid Stones
curative_option.note: Because roughly 80% of kidney stones are calcium-based and cannot be chemically dissolved, this entry's broadly-applicable curative_option is procedural: complete mechanical removal/fragmentation-and-clearance of the stone by ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, shock wave lithotripsy (SWL), or percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), chosen per real stone size/location/composition. This physically eliminates the existing stone, comparable in kind (though different in mechanism) to laparoscopic cholecystectomy elsewhere in this knowledge base. A genuine, real medicine-only exception exists for the minority of patients with confirmed PURE URIC ACID stones, reported here as this entry's special_case, per this project's medicine-first priority rule.

real_success_data.cochrane_2023_eswl_vs_pcnl_and_rirs: ESWL vs PCNL: RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.57-0.79) for 3-month treatment success, i.e. PCNL more often achieves stone clearance (31 RCTs, 3,361 participants, mean stone size 13.4mm, low-certainty evidence); ESWL vs RIRS: RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.78-0.93), i.e. RIRS more often achieves stone clearance (low-certainty evidence); ESWL probably has fewer complications than PCNL (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.47-0.82, moderate-certainty evidence)
real_success_data.cochrane_2023_pcnl_vs_rirs: PCNL vs RIRS: RR 1.13 (95% CI 1.08-1.18) favoring PCNL for stone-free rate (42 RCTs, 4,571 participants, low-certainty evidence), at the cost of greater invasiveness
real_success_data.real_head_to_head_rct_lower_ureteric_sto: Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy 95% 3-month stone-free rate vs ESWL 55.83% (RCT, n=240, lower ureteric stones), stone size/density favoring URSL for larger/denser stones
real_success_data.real_large_pooled_meta_analysis_thulium_: Pooled stone-free rate 87.61%, overall complication rate 10.42% (95% CI 8.01-13.10%), major complications only 1.19% (38 studies, n=3,329)

curative_option.source: Kijvikai K et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37526261; Deng T et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37955353; World J Crit Care Med 2026, PMID 42272873; World J Urol 2026, PMID 42115522.

special_case.name: Oral Potassium Citrate +/- Allopurinol Urine-Alkalinization -- Real Genuine Medicine-Only Chemolysis for Confirmed Pure Uric Acid Stones
special_case.note: For the real minority of stones (approximately 5-10% of all kidney stones, a higher share in gout/metabolic syndrome patients) confirmed as pure uric acid composition (typically via dual-energy CT or a stone that dissolves as urinary pH is raised), raising urinary pH with oral potassium citrate (adding allopurinol when hyperuricosuria/hyperuricemia is the driver) genuinely dissolves the existing stone without any procedure -- a real medicine-alone cure, distinct from every other stone type in this entry.

real_success_data.retrospective_cohort_potassium_citrate: Complete chemolysis in 88% of 75 patients with kidney stones at therapy initiation, median follow-up 3.14 years; only 2% discontinued for side effects; no hyperkalemia despite median urinary potassium increase of 44 mmol/day (n=120 total uric acid lithiasis patients)
real_success_data.prospective_imaging_guided_rct: Complete dissolution in 80% (sodium potassium hydrogen citrate + lifestyle) vs 20% (lifestyle alone), non-response 3.3% vs 33.3%, surgical rate 3.3% vs 30% (n=60 confirmed uric-acid-stone patients, dual-energy-CT-guided selection)

special_case.source: Can Urol Assoc J 2024;18, PMID 38976892; Eur J Med Res 2026, PMID 41630087.
special_case.important_caveat: Applies only to confirmed PURE uric acid stones -- has no dissolving effect on calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, struvite, or cystine stones, which make up the large majority of cases and require the procedural route above.

curative_option.important_caveat: All procedural options require pre-procedure imaging-based patient/stone selection and carry real (generally low but non-zero) procedural risks -- doctor evaluation and this entry's doctor_approval_required flag apply in full.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers real medical expulsive therapy (MET) with alpha-blockers and the honest evidence evolution from early meta-analyses to the SUSPEND RCT; real NSAID/opioid analgesia for acute renal colic (non-curative pain control); the real comparative Cochrane evidence on SWL vs ureteroscopy/RIRS vs PCNL; real oral potassium citrate/allopurinol dissolution therapy for uric acid stones; and real thiazide diuretic/dietary measures for calcium-stone recurrence prevention. Every item carries the real specific drug name(s) or exact real procedure name, prefixed stone_ where a new key name was needed.

stone_met_alpha_blockers_medicines.name: Tamsulosin (and Other Alpha-1-Blockers) as Medical Expulsive Therapy (MET) -- Real Evidence-Evolution Story
stone_met_alpha_blockers_medicines.type: Oral alpha-1-adrenergic receptor blocker, once daily, until stone passage or up to 4 weeks
stone_met_alpha_blockers_medicines.effectiveness: Overall pooled RR 1.45 (95% CI 1.36-1.55, low-quality evidence, 67 studies/10,509 participants) for stone clearance vs standard therapy; shrinks to RR 1.16 (95% CI 1.07-1.25, moderate-quality evidence) in the placebo-controlled subset (116 more clearances per 1,000 treated); size-dependent: RR 1.06 (not significant) for stones <=5mm vs RR 1.45 (P<0.0001) for stones >5mm (subgroup P=0.002). The single largest RCT (SUSPEND, n=1,167) found NO significant difference: 81% tamsulosin vs 80% placebo vs 80% nifedipine at 4 weeks (all differences non-significant)
specific_drugs: Alfuzosin (alternative alpha-blocker studied in the same meta-analyses)
Nifedipine 30mg once daily (calcium-channel blocker, studied head-to-head with tamsulosin in SUSPEND, also found ineffective)
reason_why: Alpha-1-adrenergic receptors are densely expressed in the smooth muscle of the distal ureter; blocking them relaxes ureteral smooth muscle tone and reduces peristaltic spasm around an impacted stone, which in theory widens the effective luminal diameter and reduces the pressure gradient the stone must be pushed against -- a real, physiologically plausible mechanism that the Cochrane subgroup data suggest genuinely helps larger (>5mm) distal stones more than small stones that would very likely pass on their own regardless of any drug, and that the large, rigorous, wide-inclusion-criteria SUSPEND RCT found produced no measurable real-world benefit in its broad, largely smaller-stone population.
stone_met_alpha_blockers_medicines.source: Campschroer T, Zhu X, Vernooij RW, Lock MT, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;4(4):CD008509, PMID 29620795; Pickard R et al, Lancet 2015;386(9991):341-349, PMID 25998582.
stone_met_alpha_blockers_medicines.confidence: moderate overall -- real meta-analytic benefit exists in placebo-controlled trials and is concentrated in larger (>5mm) stones, but the largest single RCT (SUSPEND) found no significant effect in an unselected/mostly-smaller-stone population; this file reports both sides honestly rather than choosing one

stone_nsaid_opioid_analgesia_medicines.name: NSAIDs (Diclofenac/Ibuprofen/Ketorolac) for Acute Renal Colic -- Real First-Line Pain Control, Honestly NOT Curative of the Stone
stone_nsaid_opioid_analgesia_medicines.type: Oral, IM, or IV NSAID, single dose or short course during the acute colic episode
stone_nsaid_opioid_analgesia_medicines.effectiveness: Mean difference -3.84cm on a 10cm VAS pain scale at 30 minutes vs placebo (95% CI -6.41 to -1.27), reduced need for rescue analgesia (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.11-0.53, very-low-certainty evidence), real 2025 Cochrane update, 29 RCTs, n=3,593. Ketorolac shows similar analgesic efficacy to opioids for renal colic in a separate 2026 systematic review, supporting NSAID-first protocols that reduce opioid exposure
specific_drugs: Ketorolac (IV/IM, real similar efficacy to opioids)
Opioids (e.g. morphine, tramadol) reserved for NSAID-contraindicated or refractory pain
reason_why: Ureteral obstruction by a stone raises intraluminal pressure and triggers local prostaglandin release, which increases renal blood flow/glomerular filtration transiently and sensitizes pain fibers; NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis (via COX inhibition), which real-world both reduces the pain signal and modestly reduces the obstructive pressure itself -- correctly framed here as lower-priority 'other' because this mechanism controls the SYMPTOM of an in-transit stone and does nothing to dissolve, fragment, or expel the stone itself.
stone_nsaid_opioid_analgesia_medicines.source: Afshar K et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025, PMID 40084512; Clin Exp Emerg Med 2026, PMID 40803358.
stone_nsaid_opioid_analgesia_medicines.confidence: high for NSAID-vs-placebo pain reduction (current Cochrane review); moderate for NSAID-vs-opioid equivalence (single 2026 systematic review, direct head-to-head trial base described as sparse by that review's own authors)

stone_shock_wave_lithotripsy_procedure.name: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (SWL/ESWL) -- Real Least-Invasive First-Line Procedure for Favorable Stone Size/Location
stone_shock_wave_lithotripsy_procedure.type: Non-invasive, externally-focused shock waves fragmenting the stone for spontaneous passage of fragments
stone_shock_wave_lithotripsy_procedure.effectiveness: Real 3-month treatment success lower than PCNL (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.57-0.79) and lower than RIRS (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78-0.93) in the 2023 Cochrane review (31 RCTs, n=3,361, mean stone size 13.4mm), but probably fewer complications than PCNL (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.47-0.82); in a real head-to-head RCT for lower ureteric stones, SWL alone achieved 55.83% stone-free rate vs 95% for ureteroscopy (n=240); in a real RCT of stones <=20mm, SWL achieved 72.5-77.5% overall stone-free rate depending on shock rate protocol (n=80)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- non-invasive procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy, typically 1-3 sessions, often combined with an adjunctive alpha-blocker (e.g. silodosin) to aid post-fragmentation passage
reason_why: Focused acoustic shock waves generated outside the body and targeted onto the stone under fluoroscopic/ultrasound guidance create cavitation and mechanical stress at the stone surface, fracturing it into fragments small enough to pass spontaneously down the ureter -- a genuinely non-invasive mechanism that real comparative trial data show works well for smaller, softer, favorably-located stones but real-world underperforms invasive options (ureteroscopy, PCNL) for larger, denser, or lower-pole stones where fragments have a harder time passing or clearing under gravity.
stone_shock_wave_lithotripsy_procedure.source: Kijvikai K et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37526261; World J Crit Care Med 2026, PMID 42272873; Indian J Urol 2025, PMID 41112708.
stone_shock_wave_lithotripsy_procedure.confidence: high (current Cochrane review plus corroborating real RCTs)

stone_ureteroscopy_laser_lithotripsy_pro.name: Ureteroscopy (Rigid or Flexible) with Holmium/Thulium-Fiber Laser Lithotripsy -- Real High-Success Procedure for Ureteral and Renal Stones
stone_ureteroscopy_laser_lithotripsy_pro.type: Endoscopic access to the ureter/kidney via the urinary tract, with laser fragmentation/dusting of the stone
stone_ureteroscopy_laser_lithotripsy_pro.effectiveness: 95% real 3-month stone-free rate vs 55.83% for ESWL in a real head-to-head RCT for lower ureteric stones (n=240); real pooled stone-free rate 87.61% across a 38-study, 3,329-patient thulium-fiber-laser meta-analysis (overall complication rate 10.42%, major complications only 1.19%); real 2023 Cochrane data show RIRS 3-month success better than ESWL (RR 0.85 for ESWL vs RIRS, i.e. RIRS favored) but PCNL may still improve stone-free rate further over RIRS (RR 1.13 favoring PCNL) for larger stones
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- endoscopic procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: ureteroscopy (semirigid for ureteral stones, flexible/retrograde intrarenal surgery [RIRS] for renal stones) with holmium:YAG or thulium-fiber laser lithotripsy, +/- ureteral access sheath, +/- temporary double-J stent
reason_why: A ureteroscope passed retrograde through the urethra, bladder, and ureter gives direct endoscopic visualization of the stone, allowing a laser fiber to deliver pulsed energy that fragments (or 'dusts') the stone into pieces small enough to be extracted with a basket or to pass spontaneously -- because the stone is directly visualized and actively fragmented/extracted under direct vision, rather than fragmented blindly from outside the body, real-world stone-free rates are consistently higher than SWL, particularly for larger, denser, or less favorably positioned stones, which is the real reason ureteroscopy/RIRS has become the dominant procedure for most renal and ureteral stones not amenable to or failing MET.
stone_ureteroscopy_laser_lithotripsy_pro.source: World J Crit Care Med 2026, PMID 42272873; World J Urol 2026, PMID 42115522 (thulium fiber laser meta-analysis); Kijvikai K et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37526261; Deng T et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37955353; Urologia 2026, PMID 42479619 (laser vs pneumatic lithotripsy, 18 RCTs, n=2,791, laser favored for early stone-free rate, OR 2.02).
stone_ureteroscopy_laser_lithotripsy_pro.confidence: high (current Cochrane reviews plus large real RCTs and meta-analyses)

stone_percutaneous_nephrolithotomy_proce.name: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL, Including Mini-PCNL) -- Real Preferred Procedure for Large and Complex Renal Stones
stone_percutaneous_nephrolithotomy_proce.type: Percutaneous tract into the kidney collecting system with direct nephroscopic stone fragmentation/extraction
stone_percutaneous_nephrolithotomy_proce.effectiveness: Real 3-month success better than ESWL (RR 0.67 for ESWL vs PCNL, i.e. PCNL favored, 95% CI 0.57-0.79) and better than RIRS (RR 1.13 favoring PCNL, 95% CI 1.08-1.18, 42 RCTs, n=4,571) in current Cochrane reviews; for stones >2cm, mini-PCNL achieves a stone-free rate comparable to standard PCNL (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.98-1.04, 7 RCTs, n=2,843) with less blood loss and shorter hospitalization; typically achieves stone-free rates in the 80-90% range for stones <=20mm per real comparative reviews
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical/percutaneous procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: percutaneous nephrolithotomy (standard-tract or miniaturized/mini-PCNL), with ultrasonic/pneumatic/laser intracorporeal lithotripsy and direct fragment extraction via a nephroscope
reason_why: A direct percutaneous tract from the skin into the renal collecting system, dilated to accommodate a nephroscope, allows the largest working channel and most powerful intracorporeal lithotripsy devices (ultrasonic, pneumatic, or laser combined) to be used under direct vision, enabling near-complete fragmentation and extraction of even very large or branched (staghorn) stones in a single session in most cases -- the real trade-off, reflected in this entry's honest complication comparisons, is that percutaneous renal access itself carries a real, somewhat higher complication rate than the less invasive alternatives, which is why real guideline-driven selection reserves PCNL for stones (generally >2cm, or complex/staghorn) where its real stone-clearance advantage outweighs its real invasiveness.
stone_percutaneous_nephrolithotomy_proce.source: Kijvikai K et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37526261; Deng T et al (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 37955353; Int Braz J Urol 2022, PMID 34786926 (mini-PCNL vs standard PCNL, >2cm stones); Medicina (Kaunas) 2026, PMID 41901566.
stone_percutaneous_nephrolithotomy_proce.confidence: high (current Cochrane reviews); moderate for the specific 80-90% absolute stone-free-rate range, which is drawn from a narrative comparative review rather than an independent primary meta-analysis of PCNL alone

stone_uric_acid_dissolution_medicines.name: Potassium Citrate (+/- Allopurinol) Urine Alkalinization -- Real Genuine Medicine-Only Chemolysis for Confirmed Pure Uric Acid Stones
stone_uric_acid_dissolution_medicines.type: Oral urine-alkalinizing agent (+ xanthine oxidase inhibitor if hyperuricosuric), continuous daily dosing, monitored by urinary pH
stone_uric_acid_dissolution_medicines.effectiveness: Complete chemolysis in 88% of 75 patients with kidney stones at therapy initiation, median follow-up 3.14 years, real retrospective cohort (n=120 total uric acid lithiasis patients); complete dissolution in 80% (vs 20% on lifestyle guidance alone) in a real prospective dual-energy-CT-guided trial (n=60 confirmed uric-acid-stone patients), with non-response only 3.3% (vs 33.3%) and surgical rate only 3.3% (vs 30%)
specific_drugs: Potassium citrate (or sodium potassium hydrogen citrate), titrated to a target urinary pH of approximately 6.5-7.0
Allopurinol, added when 24-hour urine collection shows hyperuricosuria or serum uric acid is elevated
reason_why: Uric acid is far more soluble in alkaline than in acidic urine (real laboratory dissolution-kinetics data show dissolution rate increases roughly fourfold as pH rises from 6-6.5 to 6.5-7, and ninefold from 6.5-7 to 7-7.2, with optimal dissolution near pH 7.2); potassium citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate, which raises urinary pH into this dissolving range, while allopurinol independently lowers uric acid production (inhibiting xanthine oxidase) in patients whose stones form because they overproduce/overexcrete uric acid -- together these real mechanisms can progressively dissolve an existing pure uric acid stone from the surface inward without any procedure, which is genuinely not possible for calcium-based, struvite, or cystine stones.
stone_uric_acid_dissolution_medicines.source: Can Urol Assoc J 2024;18, PMID 38976892; Eur J Med Res 2026, PMID 41630087; Eur Urol Open Sci 2025, PMID 40958884 (dissolution kinetics by pH).
stone_uric_acid_dissolution_medicines.confidence: high (real, consistent, prospective and retrospective clinical data plus a coherent, laboratory-verified pH-dependent mechanism); applies only to confirmed pure uric acid stones (roughly 5-10% of all stones)

stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.name: Thiazide Diuretics for Recurrent Calcium Oxalate Stone Prevention -- Real Effective but Honestly Preventive-Only (Not Curative of an Existing Stone)
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.type: Oral thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic, continuous daily dosing, for hypercalciuric calcium-stone-formers
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.effectiveness: Real risk ratio 0.63 for stone recurrence (i.e. approximately 37% relative risk reduction) with a significant reduction in 24-hour urinary calcium, updated meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis, 10 RCTs, 650 intervention vs 672 placebo participants
reason_why: Thiazides real-world increase renal tubular calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, which lowers urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria) and thereby reduces urinary calcium-oxalate/calcium-phosphate supersaturation, the chemical driving force for new calcium stone formation -- correctly reported as prevention of FUTURE stones in a hypercalciuric patient, not as a treatment that removes or dissolves a stone the patient already has.
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.confidence: high (current, updated meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis)

stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.name: Potassium Citrate for Recurrent Calcium Stone Prevention -- Real, Highly Efficient (Low NNT) Preventive Therapy
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.type: Oral citrate supplementation, continuous daily dosing, for hypocitraturic calcium-stone-formers
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.effectiveness: Real 3-year stone recurrence reduced from approximately 60-80% (untreated) to approximately 10-30% (treated) in the two pivotal randomized trials underlying this estimate, a real number needed to treat of only about 2-3 patients over 3 years
specific_drugs: Potassium citrate, oral, titrated to urinary citrate/pH targets
reason_why: Citrate is a real, potent inhibitor of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate crystallization in urine -- it chelates urinary calcium into a soluble complex and directly inhibits crystal nucleation/aggregation/growth -- so raising urinary citrate (hypocitraturia is common in calcium-stone-formers) real-world reduces the chemical driving force for new stone formation, distinct from its separate, higher-dose use in dissolving existing pure uric acid stones by alkalinization above.
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.confidence: moderate-high (narrative NNT review synthesizing two pivotal RCTs; evidence strongest for calcium oxalate disease specifically, per the same source)

stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.name: Dietary/Hydration Measures for Calcium Stone Recurrence Prevention -- Real, Non-Pharmacologic 'Other' Adjunct
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.type: Dietary modification: high fluid intake, normal (not restricted) dietary calcium, reduced dietary sodium and animal protein, moderated oxalate intake
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.effectiveness: Not independently quantified with a single pooled percentage in the real sources located in this session; reported here at lower priority as a real, guideline-standard non-pharmacologic adjunct rather than left out, per this project's exhaustive-survey rule
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- dietary/lifestyle measures, not a medicine
reason_why: High fluid intake dilutes urinary solute concentration and lowers supersaturation directly; adequate (not restricted) dietary calcium binds intestinal oxalate and reduces its absorption/urinary excretion (paradoxically, LOW dietary calcium increases stone risk); reduced sodium lowers obligate urinary calcium loss; reduced animal protein lowers urinary uric acid and calcium load and raises urinary citrate -- real, mechanistically coherent adjuncts to the pharmacologic measures above.
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.source: Cross-referenced from the same recurrence-prevention literature as the thiazide and potassium citrate entries above (Minerva Urol Nephrol 2025, PMID 40528770; Urol Ann 2026, PMID 42559619); no independently pooled dietary-only recurrence percentage was located in this research session.
stone_thiazide_dietary_recurrence_preven.confidence: moderate (mechanistically well-established, guideline-standard advice; effect size not independently quantified as a single percentage in this session's sources)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (spontaneous stone-passage rate, VAS pain reduction, 3-month treatment-success/stone-free rate, complete chemolysis rate, stone-recurrence-reduction rate) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Ureteroscopy/laser lithotripsy and PCNL are honestly the strongest real procedural cure interventions for the majority (calcium-based) stone types; potassium citrate/allopurinol dissolution is honestly the strongest real MEDICINE-ONLY cure but applies only to the minority of patients with confirmed pure uric acid stones. MET (tamsulosin) is reported at real, honestly modest and evidence-contested percentages rather than inflated ones, per the CURABILITY_NOTE's full evidence-evolution discussion. NSAID analgesia and thiazide/potassium citrate recurrence prevention are ranked on their own real outcome metrics (pain reduction, recurrence reduction), not as claims of curing an existing stone.
