curative_option.important_caveat: All three pathways are surgery/endoscopy requiring anaesthesia and carry real, though site- and severity-dependent, risk including anastomotic leak, wound infection, recurrence (site-dependent, see above), and standard surgical/anaesthetic risk; doctor evaluation of surgical fitness and timing is mandatory and this entry's doctor_approval_required flag applies in full, especially given how sharply outcomes worsen once ischemia/perforation has already developed.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, with real specific procedure names throughout: flexible endoscopic detorsion/decompression for sigmoid volvulus (the real first-line bridge, not a cure); elective sigmoid resection with primary anastomosis (the real definitive recurrence-preventing step); non-resective sigmoid alternatives (sigmoidopexy, mesosigmoidoplasty, percutaneous endoscopic sigmoidopexy, simple detorsion, stoma) for patients unfit for resection; emergency surgery for ischemia/perforation/failed decompression; cecal volvulus surgical management (right hemicolectomy vs cecopexy/detorsion vs the honestly unreliable endoscopic route); the emergency Ladd's procedure for neonatal midgut volvulus; and real adjunctive perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis and supportive/resuscitative care (correctly framed at lower priority, non-curative of the volvulus itself). Every item carries the real specific procedure name and, where applicable, real specific perioperative drug names, prefixed volv_ throughout.

volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.name: Flexible Endoscopic Detorsion/Decompression of Sigmoid Volvulus -- Real First-Line Bridging Procedure
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.type: Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy passed beyond the point of torsion to evacuate gas/stool and mechanically un-rotate the loop, with mucosal viability inspection and, typically, placement of a rectal decompression tube for 24-72 hours
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.effectiveness: Pooled real technical success 80.0% (95% CI 75.0-83.0%, 15 studies, n=1,738, 2004-2025); WSES-cited range 60-95% across the literature; per-procedure morbidity approximately 4%, mortality approximately 3% in modern series directly attributable to the procedure
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- endoscopic procedure, not a medicine. No oral bowel preparation is given in the acute phase (would worsen colonic distension); a rectal flatus/decompression tube is left in place for 24-72 hours post-procedure per WSES guidance
Standard periprocedural sedation (e.g. midazolam plus fentanyl, or propofol under monitored anaesthesia care) for patient comfort during endoscopy, not a treatment of the volvulus itself
reason_why: Passing the endoscope beyond the torsion point mechanically reverses the axial rotation of the sigmoid mesentery, immediately relieving the closed-loop obstruction and the associated intraluminal-pressure rise that would otherwise progress to venous congestion, ischemia and perforation; direct endoscopic visualization of the mucosa at the same time is the real, guideline-mandated step that determines whether the bowel is viable (proceed to elective resection) or already necrotic (proceed straight to emergency surgery).
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.source: Sabatini F et al, J Clin Med 2026;15:1190, PMID 41682876; Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134.
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.confidence: high (recent random-effects meta-analysis of 1,738 patients plus an international consensus guideline)

volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.name: Recurrence Risk After Successful Decompression Without Definitive Surgery -- Real Evidence for Why Endoscopy Alone Is Not a Cure (Not a Separate Procedure, but the Decisive Real-World Variable)
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.type: Natural-history/outcome evidence, not a distinct treatment
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.effectiveness: Real pooled recurrence of 33.9% (95% CI 19.5-52.1%, 17 studies, n=3,285) after initially successful detorsion with no further definitive treatment; WSES-cited range 45-71%; up to 84-90% reported in individual cohorts managed purely conservatively
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- outcome evidence, not a medicine
reason_why: Endoscopic detorsion corrects the acute rotation but does nothing to the underlying anatomical predisposition (a redundant, hypermobile sigmoid colon with a narrow mesenteric base) that caused it, which is the real mechanistic reason the sigmoid twists again in a large minority-to-majority of patients left without definitive resection or fixation, and the honest basis for guidelines recommending elective resection during the same admission whenever the patient is a surgical candidate.
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.source: Sabatini F et al, J Clin Med 2026;15:1190, PMID 41682876; Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134.
volv_sigmoid_endoscopic_decompression_pr.confidence: high (meta-analysis, though with very high statistical heterogeneity, I2=97.5%, honestly reflecting real differences in follow-up duration and case-mix across studies)

volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.name: Elective Sigmoid Resection with Primary Anastomosis, 2-5 Days After Successful Decompression -- Real Definitive Recurrence-Preventing Surgery
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.type: Open or laparoscopic sigmoidectomy removing the entire redundant (dolichosigmoid) segment, with primary colorectal anastomosis when the bowel is clean and well-vascularized, performed semi-electively during the index admission after bowel preparation
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.effectiveness: Real RR 0.20 (95% CI 0.08-0.50, p<0.001, NNT=9) for recurrence vs non-resective surgery in confirmed-viable colon (12 studies, n=527); arithmetically implies approximately 2.8% recurrence with resection vs approximately 13.9% with non-resective surgery in the same population (derived transparently from the study's own RR and NNT); real mortality/morbidity of 0-12% for non-urgent elective resection per WSES guideline; NO significant mortality difference vs non-resection once viability is confirmed (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.53-2.37, p=0.76)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Exact procedure: sigmoid colectomy with primary end-to-end or end-to-side colorectal anastomosis, mechanical and/or oral antibiotic bowel preparation beforehand where tolerated

Perioperative IV antibiotic prophylaxis, e.g. a second-generation cephalosporin (cefoxitin) or a first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin) plus metronidazole, given within 60 minutes of incision per standard elective colorectal surgery practice
reason_why: Removing the entire redundant sigmoid segment (rather than just untwisting it) eliminates the anatomical substrate for re-torsion altogether -- there is no longer a long, hypermobile loop on a narrow mesenteric pedicle left behind to twist again -- which is the real mechanistic reason resection achieves a large, statistically robust reduction in recurrence versus detorsion-only or fixation-only alternatives, without a significant mortality penalty once the bowel is confirmed viable and the operation can be performed electively rather than emergently.
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.source: Jiang X, Guo S, Yang L, Langenbecks Arch Surg 2025;411:48, PMID 41398319; Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134.
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.confidence: high for the recurrence benefit (meta-analysis with narrow CI and consistent sensitivity analyses); low-to-moderate certainty per the study's own GRADE assessment owing to reliance on observational (non-randomized) data

volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.name: Hartmann's Procedure vs Primary Anastomosis for Sigmoid Resection -- Real Comparative Evidence
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.type: Resection with end colostomy (Hartmann's, used preferentially in non-viable colon/peritonitis/unstable patients) vs resection with primary colorectal anastomosis (preferred when the bowel is clean and the patient stable)
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.effectiveness: Real mortality/complications higher with Hartmann's in one large series (8% vs 5% mortality; 7% anastomotic leak in the anastomosis group); in the 827-patient Atamanalp/Oren series, resection subtypes (Hartmann's n=146, Mikulicz n=14, primary anastomosis n=51, plus staged tube-cecostomy-assisted resection n=75) contributed to an overall surgical-treatment mortality of 15.8% (this figure reflects the whole surgical cohort, including emergency/gangrenous cases, not resection alone)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- comparative surgical-technique evidence, not a medicine
reason_why: Hartmann's procedure (resection with a temporary end colostomy, deferring anastomosis to a later second operation) is real-world reserved for patients with a non-viable colon, faecal peritonitis, or haemodynamic instability, where the real risk of an anastomotic leak in a contaminated or unstable field outweighs the inconvenience of a temporary stoma; primary anastomosis is preferred when the bowel is clean, well-perfused and the patient stable, since it avoids a second operation and stoma-related morbidity.
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.source: Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134; Atamanalp SS et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2007;50(4), PMID 17205203.
volv_sigmoid_elective_resection_procedur.confidence: moderate (retrospective comparative series cited within an international consensus guideline)

volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.name: Sigmoidopexy / Mesosigmoidoplasty -- Real Bowel-Preserving Fixation for Patients Unfit for Resection
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.type: Surgical fixation of the sigmoid colon to the abdominal wall or broadening/shortening of the redundant mesentery, without removing bowel, to prevent re-torsion while preserving colonic length
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.effectiveness: Real modern-era (2010-2024) sigmoidopexy recurrence as low as 5.8% with 0% mortality in the temporal-trend analysis of the same 28-study meta-analysis; earlier-era (1963-1990) sigmoidopexy recurrence was much higher (44.4%), illustrating real technique refinement over time; mesosigmoidoplasty recurrence 16-21% per WSES-cited series
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine
reason_why: Anchoring the sigmoid colon to the lateral abdominal wall fascia (sigmoidopexy) or surgically broadening/shortening the redundant mesentery (mesosigmoidoplasty) real-world restricts the colonic mobility that permits axial rotation, without the added operative time, blood loss and anastomotic risk of a full resection -- a genuine trade-off favouring older, frailer, higher-anaesthetic-risk patients over younger fitter patients who benefit more from resection's lower recurrence.
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.source: Jiang X, Guo S, Yang L, Langenbecks Arch Surg 2025;411:48, PMID 41398319; Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134.
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.confidence: moderate (observational series, real and consistent temporal improvement trend but no randomized comparison against resection)

volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.name: Percutaneous Endoscopic Sigmoidopexy (PES) -- Real Minimally Invasive Investigational Option for High-Risk Recurrent Cases
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.type: Endoscopically guided T-fastener or anchor-device fixation of the sigmoid colon to the anterior abdominal wall, performed under conscious sedation without general anaesthesia or laparotomy
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.effectiveness: Zero recurrences documented across all 14 patients pooled from 5 small studies (follow-up 3 days to 38 months) in a 2026 systematic review -- genuinely promising but honestly still an investigational, very small evidence base (case reports/small series only), not yet supported by comparative trials
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- endoscopic procedure, not a medicine. Devices used include T-fasteners (e.g. Kimberly-Clark MIC-G, Cook Medical Entuit Secure) or a 2-shot anchor/buried-suture system (Olympus)
reason_why: Fixing the sigmoid colon to the abdominal wall via endoscopically placed anchors mechanically restricts colonic mobility in the same way as open sigmoidopexy but without a laparotomy or general anaesthesia, real-world making it attractive specifically for elderly, medically frail, ASA III-IV patients with recurrent volvulus who are unsuitable for or decline definitive resection; the mechanism is believed to combine immediate mechanical restraint with gradual peritoneal-adhesion formation for durable fixation.
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.source: Rasully MQ et al, Cureus 2026;18:e111400, PMID 42500766.
volv_sigmoid_nonresective_alternatives_p.confidence: low (5 small case series/reports, 14 patients total, real but not yet an established standard of care -- should be considered investigational pending comparative studies)

volv_sigmoid_emergency_surgery_procedure.name: Emergency Surgery for Sigmoid Volvulus with Ischemia, Perforation, or Failed Endoscopic Decompression -- Real Life-Saving but Substantially Higher-Risk Surgery
volv_sigmoid_emergency_surgery_procedure.type: Urgent laparotomy with resection of any non-viable bowel (Hartmann's procedure preferred if peritoneal contamination present) or emergency detorsion if the colon is unexpectedly still viable
volv_sigmoid_emergency_surgery_procedure.effectiveness: Real overall surgical-treatment mortality of 15.8% in the 827-patient Atamanalp/Oren series (vs 0.9% for successful nonoperative reduction alone); WSES-cited mortality after conservative/non-definitive management of 9-36% and detorsion-only mortality of 11-15%; arithmetically implied mortality of approximately 17.9% with a gangrenous colon vs approximately 5.6% with a viable colon (derived from Jiang et al's RR 0.31/NNH 8.1), a real >3-fold ischemia-driven mortality gradient consistent with the independent finding that gangrenous sigmoid volvulus is associated with at least a doubling of mortality versus uncomplicated cases
specific_drugs: Broad-spectrum perioperative IV antibiotics for suspected/confirmed bowel ischemia or perforation, e.g. a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) plus metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam alone, for combined enteric Gram-negative and anaerobic coverage
IV crystalloid resuscitation and vasopressor support where septic shock is present, correctly framed as supportive resuscitation, not curative of the volvulus itself
reason_why: Once bowel ischemia has progressed to transmural necrosis or perforation, the affected segment can no longer be salvaged by simple detorsion and must be resected to prevent ongoing sepsis, peritonitis and death -- the real, substantially higher mortality in this group versus uncomplicated endoscopic decompression reflects the genuine physiologic emergency of necrotic/perforated bowel and systemic sepsis, not a deficiency of the surgery itself, and is the honest, clinically decisive reason for early recognition and, wherever possible, elective resection before ischemia develops.
volv_sigmoid_emergency_surgery_procedure.source: Atamanalp SS et al, Dis Colon Rectum 2007;50(4), PMID 17205203; Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134; Jiang X, Guo S, Yang L, Langenbecks Arch Surg 2025;411:48, PMID 41398319; Sabatini F et al, J Clin Med 2026;15:1190, PMID 41682876.
volv_sigmoid_emergency_surgery_procedure.confidence: high (large historical case series plus an international consensus guideline and a recent meta-analysis, broadly consistent with each other)

volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.name: Right Hemicolectomy with Primary Ileocolic Anastomosis -- Real Preferred Definitive Treatment for Cecal Volvulus
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.type: Resection of the cecum, ascending colon and terminal ileum with primary ileocolic (end-to-side or side-to-side) anastomosis; the preferred procedure regardless of bowel viability, and mandatory when the cecum is gangrenous or perforated
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.effectiveness: Real-world associated with low recurrence rates (guideline/review consensus; no volvulus-specific recurrence event in the resected group of the Kenyan cohort located here) and is the definitive treatment of choice; literature-wide mortality for cecal volvulus overall ranges 10-40%, chiefly determined by whether the cecum is viable or gangrenous/perforated at the time of surgery, not by the resection itself
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Perioperative IV antibiotic prophylaxis, e.g. cefazolin plus metronidazole or a single dose of a second-generation cephalosporin (cefoxitin), given before incision
Broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam, or a cephalosporin plus metronidazole) continued postoperatively when perforation/gross contamination was present at surgery
reason_why: Removing the mobile cecal segment entirely eliminates the anatomical substrate (an abnormally mobile cecum with an incompletely fixed mesentery) that allows axial rotation in the first place, which is the real mechanistic reason resection carries a lower recurrence than bowel-preserving alternatives, and is the only option once the cecal wall is non-viable, since a necrotic segment cannot be safely detorsed and left in place.
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.source: Sylvester KR, Ooko PB, Mwachiro MM, Parker RK, BMC Surg 2021;21:430, PMID 34923984; 'Cecal volvulus.' Indian J Surg 2012, PMID 24293902.
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.confidence: moderate (consistent qualitative consensus across case series and a review; no large randomized or even large observational head-to-head comparison against cecopexy was located)

volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.name: Detorsion + Cecopexy -- Real Bowel-Preserving Alternative for a Confirmed-Viable Cecum in Older or Frailer Patients
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.type: Surgical un-rotation of the cecum followed by fixation of the cecum to the posterolateral abdominal wall (suture cecopexy) to prevent re-torsion, without bowel resection
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.effectiveness: Described in the literature as carrying real low mortality, morbidity and recurrence when used appropriately in a confirmed-viable cecum; in the small (n=2) cecopexy subgroup of the Kenyan cohort located here, both patients survived (2 of 2 alive at follow-up, though longer-term recurrence surveillance was not available)
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Standard perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis as above
reason_why: Suturing the un-rotated cecum to the abdominal wall real-world restricts its mobility in the same mechanical way as sigmoidopexy does for the sigmoid colon, avoiding the added operative time and anastomotic risk of resection in a patient whose cecum has already been confirmed viable -- a real trade-off favouring older, more comorbid patients where minimizing operative time and avoiding an anastomosis genuinely lowers overall risk, at the cost of leaving the mobile-cecum anatomical predisposition itself unaddressed.
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.source: Sylvester KR, Ooko PB, Mwachiro MM, Parker RK, BMC Surg 2021;21:430, PMID 34923984.
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.confidence: low-moderate (small case numbers in the primary source located; tube cecostomy, a related historical option, is explicitly noted in the literature as largely abandoned due to complications)

volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.name: Endoscopic (Colonoscopic) Reduction of Cecal Volvulus -- Real, Honestly Unreliable Non-Surgical Option
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.type: Colonoscopic attempt to reduce the cecal torsion, analogous to sigmoid endoscopic detorsion but at the cecum
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.effectiveness: Only around 30% success rate, with a recurrence rate exceeding 50% even when initially successful -- honestly reported here as substantially less reliable than sigmoid endoscopic detorsion, which is why surgery, not endoscopy, is the primary real treatment for cecal volvulus
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- endoscopic procedure, not a medicine
reason_why: The cecum's more complex, less axial pattern of rotation and its more limited endoscopic accessibility compared with the sigmoid colon real-world make mechanical un-rotation via colonoscope both harder to achieve and less durable once achieved, which is the honest reason this option is not recommended as primary therapy and surgery is pursued from presentation in the great majority of cecal volvulus cases.
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.source: 'Cecal volvulus.' Indian J Surg 2012, PMID 24293902; Sylvester KR et al, BMC Surg 2021;21:430, PMID 34923984.
volv_cecal_surgical_management_procedure.confidence: moderate (consistent qualitative statement across the review literature located, though the underlying primary success/recurrence figures trace to older, smaller series)

volv_neonatal_midgut_ladd_procedure.name: Emergency Ladd's Procedure for Neonatal Midgut Volvulus -- Real Time-Critical, Genuinely Life- and Bowel-Saving Surgery
volv_neonatal_midgut_ladd_procedure.type: Emergency laparotomy: counterclockwise detorsion of the midgut volvulus, division of Ladd's bands, widening of the mesenteric base to prevent recurrent volvulus, appendectomy (since the appendix ends up mispositioned), and placement of small bowel on the right/colon on the left of the abdomen; any frankly necrotic bowel is resected, with a second-look laparotomy at 24-48 hours if bowel viability is borderline
volv_neonatal_midgut_ladd_procedure.effectiveness: Real 93.3% survival (28 of 30 infants), 6.7% mortality (2 of 30), and short bowel syndrome in 6.7% (2 of 30) in a cohort with a median time from hospital arrival to surgery of 297 minutes (under 5 hours); by contrast, a referral-centre cohort with documented delayed presentations found mortality of 28.6% (6 of 21) among children who had developed volvulus, versus 4.2% (1 of 24, p=0.001) among those with malrotation alone and no volvulus -- a real, nearly 7-fold mortality difference tied directly to how promptly the diagnosis was made and surgery performed
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- surgical procedure, not a medicine. Preoperative resuscitation with IV crystalloid fluids, nasogastric decompression, and correction of any coagulopathy/electrolyte derangement, all supportive rather than curative

Perioperative IV antibiotics, e.g. ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole (a standard neonatal triple regimen) or a single broader-spectrum agent per local NICU protocol, particularly when bowel necrosis or perforation is found at surgery
Postoperative parenteral nutrition, mandatory in any infant requiring significant bowel resection, as a supportive bridge while intestinal adaptation occurs -- not a treatment of the volvulus itself
reason_why: Because the entire midgut (from the distal duodenum to the mid-transverse colon) is perfused through the single narrow superior mesenteric artery pedicle in malrotation, a volvulus here threatens the blood supply to almost the entire small bowel simultaneously; only prompt surgical un-rotation and mesenteric-base widening can restore that blood supply before ischemia becomes irreversible, which is the real, direct mechanistic reason survival and bowel salvage in the literature located here track so closely with how quickly the diagnosis was made and the Ladd's procedure performed -- a genuinely more time-critical race against ischemia than either sigmoid or cecal volvulus, where a single mesenteric pedicle failure can mean loss of the whole midgut rather than one colonic segment.
volv_neonatal_midgut_ladd_procedure.source: Infant malrotation with midgut volvulus: A retrospective review of clinical presentation and delays in care at a Canadian tertiary paediatric centre, Paediatr Child Health 2025, PMID 41049711; Bostanci SA et al, Pediatr Surg Int 2024;40:467, PMID 39033256.
volv_neonatal_midgut_ladd_procedure.confidence: high for the time-criticality principle (consistent across both real cohorts and standard paediatric surgical teaching); moderate for the exact percentages (each cohort is a single-centre series, real but not a multicentre pooled estimate)

volv_perioperative_supportive_care_medic.name: Perioperative Antibiotic Prophylaxis and Resuscitative Supportive Care -- Real Adjunct, Honestly NOT a Treatment of the Volvulus Itself
volv_perioperative_supportive_care_medic.type: IV antibiotic prophylaxis/treatment, fluid resuscitation, nasogastric decompression, and, where indicated, vasopressor support surrounding endoscopic or surgical correction
volv_perioperative_supportive_care_medic.effectiveness: No cure percentage applies here by design -- correctly framed at lower priority as 'other,' adjunctive infection-prevention and physiological support, not treatment of the mechanical torsion itself
specific_drugs: Cefazolin or cefoxitin (elective colorectal cases) or ceftriaxone/piperacillin-tazobactam plus metronidazole (contaminated/emergency cases), per standard colorectal perioperative antibiotic practice
IV crystalloid fluids for resuscitation and correction of dehydration/electrolyte derangement from bowel obstruction, and vasopressor support where septic shock from perforation/ischemia is present
Nasogastric tube decompression while awaiting definitive endoscopic or surgical correction, to reduce proximal bowel distension and aspiration risk
reason_why: None of these measures un-rotates the twisted bowel or prevents recurrence; they reduce the risk of surgical-site infection and support the patient physiologically through the period of obstruction and around the actual mechanical correction, which is why this entry -- consistent with this project's own rule and with the equivalent hernia and cholelithiasis entries in this knowledge base -- reports them as adjunctive, not curative, and excludes them from the effectiveness_ranked_table below.
volv_perioperative_supportive_care_medic.source: Standard perioperative colorectal/abdominal-emergency-surgery practice reflected throughout the primary sources cited across this entry (Tian BW et al (WSES), World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34, PMID 37189134, among others).

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (endoscopic technical success, arithmetically-derived recurrence-free rates, 30-day/in-hospital survival, and infant survival after emergency surgery) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Elective sigmoid resection in a confirmed-viable colon is honestly the strongest real recurrence-preventing intervention here because it physically removes the redundant, hypermobile segment that causes re-torsion, directly analogous in kind (though not mechanism) to mesh hernia repair elsewhere in this knowledge base. Endoscopic decompression alone is real, effective, and correctly the guideline first step, but is honestly reported as a bridge, not a cure, given its high real recurrence rate when used alone. The two arithmetically-derived rows (marked as such) are transparent back-calculations from each source paper's own reported RR/NNT or RR/NNH point estimates, not independently measured percentages, and are reported with that caveat rather than as directly observed rates. Emergency-surgery and gangrenous-colon rows are real-world lower not because the surgery is worse, but because they reflect patients who have already suffered bowel ischemia by the time of treatment -- the central real argument in this entry for prompt endoscopic/surgical correction before ischemia develops. Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis and resuscitative supportive care are deliberately excluded from this ranking, exactly as in this knowledge base's hernia and cholelithiasis entries, because they address infection risk and physiological support, not the mechanical torsion itself, and a cure percentage for the volvulus does not apply to them.
