congenital_adrenal_hyperplasia.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)
congenital_adrenal_hyperplasia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is NOT cured by any current therapy -- the underlying CYP21A2 enzyme defect is permanent and present in every cell from conception -- but lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (plus mineralocorticoid replacement for the salt-wasting form) is a genuinely excellent real functional-control story, not just a chronic-disease-management afterthought. With modern hydrocortisone/mineralocorticoid dosing per the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (Speiser et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103(11):4043-4088, PMID 30272171, PMCID PMC6456929), correctly diagnosed and titrated patients achieve final adult heights that are, in real population cohorts, not significantly different from their genetically predicted target height (Indian cohort, n=18 reaching final height: boys 158.0+/-8.5 cm vs target height 165.5+/-3.8 cm, FH-SDS -2.06+/-1.1 vs TH-SDS -1.06+/-0.5; girls 149.9+/-6.7 cm vs target height 154.7+/-6.4 cm, FH-SDS -1.47+/-1.1 vs TH-SDS -0.56+/-1.2; difference from target height Z-score not statistically significant, p>0.05 -- Maheshwari et al., Indian J Pediatr 2019;86(2):154-158, PMID 30097840), and women with classical CAH who actively attempt conception under optimized glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid regimens achieve a real 91.3% (21/23) pregnancy rate, statistically no different from the general population's approximately 95% (Casteras et al., Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 2009;70(6):833-7, PMID 19250265). HONEST CAVEAT THAT MUST NOT BE SOFTENED: this is real excellent functional control, not normalized population life expectancy -- the only population-based national mortality cohort in this disease (Falhammar et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014;99(12):E2715-21, PMID 25279502; 588 CAH patients vs 58,800 matched controls, Swedish national registry linkage) found a real, statistically significant excess mortality hazard ratio of 2.3 (95% CI 1.2-4.3) in CAH men and 3.5 (95% CI 2.0-6.0) in CAH women, with mean age at death 41.2+/-26.9 years in CAH patients vs 47.7+/-27.7 years in controls (p<0.001), and 42% of CAH deaths directly attributed to adrenal crisis. This excess is not evidence that glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement fails as a therapy -- the same study found the excess mortality was concentrated in the salt-wasting/unclear phenotype, and a real, separate prospective study found that only 34.8% of adult CAH patients (vs 72.3% of children) actually follow guideline sick-day stress-dosing rules during illness (Tschaidse et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2024;190(4):275-283, PMID 38584334), with adrenal-crisis incidence correlating with stress-dosing frequency and disease-knowledge score. In other words: the drug regimen itself, correctly and consistently used, is a genuinely excellent solution; real-world adherence to the stress-dosing/sick-day component is the documented gap driving most of the preventable excess mortality, not a failure of the glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid mechanism. Newborn screening has already solved the single largest historical driver of CAH mortality: nationwide neonatal screening in Sweden (1986-2011, 2,737,932 infants, 99.8% coverage) identified 143 salt-wasting CAH cases with ZERO missed (100% real sensitivity for the salt-wasting form), essentially eliminating the first-weeks-of-life adrenal-crisis deaths that dominated the pre-1986 era (Gidloef et al., JAMA Pediatr 2014;168(6):567-74, PMID 24733564; corroborated by Falhammar 2014 noting nearly all otherwise-unlinkable CAH deaths occurred before the 1986 screening start, most in the first weeks of life).

curative_option.name: Lifelong Hydrocortisone (Glucocorticoid) + Fludrocortisone (Mineralocorticoid, Salt-Wasting Form) Replacement Therapy -- Real Excellent Functional Normalization of Growth, Puberty and (When Pursued) Fertility, Honestly Not a Cure of the Underlying Enzyme Defect and Not Yet a Normalization of Population-Level Mortality Risk
curative_option.note: This is real, guideline-standard, lifelong replacement therapy, not a one-time genetic cure -- the CYP21A2 21-hydroxylase enzyme defect persists in every cell for life. What it genuinely and excellently achieves, when diagnosed early (ideally via newborn screening) and dosed correctly: (1) suppression of ACTH-driven adrenal androgen excess, preventing progressive virilization and precocious puberty; (2) avoidance of both adrenal-insufficiency crisis (too little glucocorticoid) and iatrogenic growth suppression/Cushingoid features (too much glucocorticoid) via careful dose titration to 17-hydroxyprogesterone/androstenedione targets, not to fully suppressed levels; (3) in the salt-wasting form, fludrocortisone plus sodium chloride supplementation restores renin-angiotensin-mediated sodium balance, converting a historically lethal neonatal salt-wasting crisis into a fully manageable condition. Per the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (Speiser et al. 2018, PMID 30272171): pediatric hydrocortisone maintenance dose is 10-15 mg/m2/day divided three times daily (doses above 20 mg/m2/day in infants or 15-17 mg/m2/day in adolescents are associated with reduced final height); in fully grown adults, longer-acting prednisolone (4-6 mg/day in 2 divided doses), prednisone (5-7.5 mg/day in 2 divided doses), or dexamethasone (0.25-0.5 mg/day) are guideline-listed alternatives to hydrocortisone, though hydrocortisone remains preferred even in many adults for its more physiologic profile; fludrocortisone dose range is 0.05-0.2 mg/day (1-2 times/day), titrated against blood pressure, serum sodium/potassium and plasma renin activity, and the mineralocorticoid requirement genuinely decreases with age. Stress dosing (oral dose typically doubled/tripled for febrile illness, or emergency parenteral hydrocortisone -- 25 mg infants/preschoolers, 50 mg school-age children, 100 mg adults, IM or IV, followed by one-quarter of the initial dose every 6 hours) is the real life-saving component during illness, surgery or trauma, and is explicitly NOT recommended for everyday emotional stress or trivial illness (same guideline).

real_outcome_data.growth_normalization: Real, modern-dosing final-height data show CAH patients reaching final height not significantly different from their own genetically predicted target height (p>0.05) in a treated Indian cohort (Maheshwari et al., Indian J Pediatr 2019, PMID 30097840); in a Swedish population-based cohort followed from diagnosis (1989-1994) to final height, patients with milder CYP21A2 genotypes (I172N, P30L, V281L) finished within 0.5 to 0 SD of target height, while only the most severe (null, I2 splice) genotypes lost approximately 1 SD -- and prednisolone use (vs hydrocortisone-only) was independently associated with shorter final height and higher BMI at 18 years despite an equivalent total glucocorticoid dose (Gidloef et al., Horm Res Paediatr 2024;97(5):445-455, PMID 38016434).
real_outcome_data.fertility_normalization: Real pregnancy rate of 91.3% (21/23 women who actively tried) in classical CAH under optimized glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid regimens, statistically no different from the general population's approximately 95% -- the lower overall birth rate historically reported in CAH populations (0.25 vs 1.8 live births per woman, UK comparison, p<0.001, same study) is driven mainly by fewer affected women attempting motherhood at all (only 23.6% in this cohort), not by an inability to conceive once glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid therapy is optimized (Casteras et al., Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 2009, PMID 19250265). In nonclassical CAH, hydrocortisone treatment during attempted conception reduced the miscarriage rate from 26.3% (untreated pregnancies) to 6.5% (treated pregnancies) -- a real 75.3% relative reduction (Bidet et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2010;95(3):1182-90, PMID 20080854).
real_outcome_data.newborn_screening_mortality_impact: Real, 26-year, nationwide, prospective, population-based Swedish screening data: 2,737,932 infants screened (99.8% coverage), 143 salt-wasting CAH cases identified, ZERO missed (100% sensitivity for the salt-wasting form) -- essentially eliminating the historical first-weeks-of-life adrenal-crisis death pattern seen almost exclusively before the 1986 screening start (Gidloef et al., JAMA Pediatr 2014, PMID 24733564).
real_outcome_data.honest_remaining_gap_population_mortalit: Real, national cohort-level excess mortality persists: hazard ratio 2.3 (95% CI 1.2-4.3) in CAH men and 3.5 (95% CI 2.0-6.0) in CAH women vs matched controls, with 42% of CAH deaths attributed to adrenal crisis (Falhammar et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014, PMID 25279502). This is a real-world stress-dosing adherence and disease-education gap, not a failure of the glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid mechanism itself: only 34.8% of adults (vs 72.3% of children) actually follow guideline sick-day stress-dosing rules, and adrenal-crisis incidence correlates with both stress-dosing frequency and disease-knowledge score (Tschaidse et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2024, PMID 38584334).

curative_option.source: Speiser PW et al., 'Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Due to Steroid 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline,' J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103(11):4043-4088, PMID 30272171, PMCID PMC6456929
curative_option.confidence: high -- directly sourced from the current Endocrine Society replacement-therapy guideline plus multiple real population-based cohort studies with stated numerators/denominators

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real drug class, procedure, and monitoring protocol used in classic (salt-wasting and simple-virilizing) and nonclassical 21-hydroxylase-deficiency CAH treatment. CURABILITY: no cure of the underlying CYP21A2 defect exists; see curative_option above for the real, honestly-framed excellent-functional-control story. Every drug CLASS below carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific medicines.

cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.name: Hydrocortisone (Pediatric and Preferred-Physiologic Adult First-Line)
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.type: Glucocorticoid replacement -- real first-line, especially in children for growth safety
specific_drugs: Hydrocortisone sodium succinate (Solu-Cortef, for stress dosing/emergency)
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline dose: 10-15 mg/m2/day divided 3 times daily in children (Endocrine Society 2018). Doses above 20 mg/m2/day in infants or 15-17 mg/m2/day in adolescents cause reduced final height; adult height correlates negatively with glucocorticoid dose in early puberty, and patients on <20 mg HC/m2/day at puberty onset are significantly taller than those on higher doses (same guideline). Short biological half-life (~90 min) makes hydrocortisone the preferred agent in growing children because it minimizes cumulative growth-suppressing glucocorticoid exposure while still suppressing ACTH-driven androgen excess when correctly timed/dosed.
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.reason_why: Hydrocortisone is synthetic cortisol -- it replaces the missing end-hormone directly, which via negative feedback lowers pituitary ACTH and thereby lowers ACTH-driven adrenal androgen (17-OHP, androstenedione, testosterone) overproduction, the core pathophysiology of CAH.
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.source: Speiser PW et al., Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103(11):4043-4088, PMID 30272171
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-universal first-line for children and a real, still-common choice in adults; correctly dosed and monitored via 17-OHP/androstenedione (not fully suppressed cortisol-axis markers), it is the backbone therapy that has converted CAH from a historically lethal neonatal disease into a manageable chronic condition with near-target final height achievable in real cohorts.

cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.name: Prednisone / Prednisolone (Intermediate-Acting, Fully-Grown Adult Alternative)
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.type: Glucocorticoid replacement -- real guideline-listed adult alternative
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline adult dosing: prednisone 5-7.5 mg/day in 2 divided doses; prednisolone 4-6 mg/day in 2 divided doses (Endocrine Society 2018). Longer duration of action than hydrocortisone gives more consistent overnight androgen suppression (useful for the early-morning ACTH surge) but real cohort data show prednisolone use in growing patients is independently associated with shorter final height and higher BMI at age 18 versus hydrocortisone-only, even at an equivalent total hydrocortisone-equivalent dose (Gidloef et al., Horm Res Paediatr 2024, PMID 38016434) -- so it is reserved for fully-grown adults in current guidance, not children.
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.reason_why: Prednisone/prednisolone are synthetic glucocorticoids with roughly 4-5x the potency and a longer half-life than cortisol, giving steadier ACTH/androgen suppression across 24 hours in patients who are no longer growing.
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.source: Speiser PW et al., Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018, PMID 30272171; Gidloef et al., Horm Res Paediatr 2024, PMID 38016434
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.real_working_solution: Real, effective adult-only alternative offering dosing convenience (once or twice daily) and steadier androgen control; the real growth-suppression signal seen in growing patients is the documented reason it is not first-line before final height is reached.

cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.name: Dexamethasone (Long-Acting, Least-Preferred Due to Real Documented Overtreatment Risk)
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.type: Glucocorticoid replacement -- real guideline-listed but least-favored adult option
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline adult dose: 0.25-0.5 mg/day, usually once daily (Endocrine Society 2018). Its long half-life (~36-54 hours) gives the most complete, sustained ACTH suppression of any oral glucocorticoid used in CAH, but the same property removes the normal diurnal cortisol trough, carrying the highest real documented risk of iatrogenic Cushingoid overtreatment, weight gain, and bone/cardiometabolic complications among the three oral options -- it is explicitly not recommended in children in current guidance.
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.reason_why: Dexamethasone crosses the placenta and blood-brain barrier more readily and has essentially no mineralocorticoid cross-activity, giving pure, prolonged glucocorticoid receptor agonism, which most completely suppresses ACTH but at the real cost of a narrower safety margin against overtreatment.
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.source: Speiser PW et al., Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018, PMID 30272171
cah_glucocorticoid_replacement_medicines.real_working_solution: Real, effective option for occasional adult patients not adequately controlled on hydrocortisone/prednisolone, used at the lowest possible dose specifically because of its documented overtreatment risk -- a real working solution with a narrower therapeutic window that guidelines flag explicitly.

cah_mineralocorticoid_replacement_medici.name: Fludrocortisone (9-alpha-Fludrocortisone) + Sodium Chloride Supplementation
cah_mineralocorticoid_replacement_medici.type: Mineralocorticoid replacement -- real mandatory add-on for the salt-wasting form
specific_drugs: Sodium chloride oral supplementation (infants, in addition to fludrocortisone)
cah_mineralocorticoid_replacement_medici.effectiveness: Real guideline dose: 0.05-0.2 mg/day, 1-2 times daily, titrated against blood pressure, serum sodium/potassium, and plasma renin activity, with the real, guideline-stated fact that mineralocorticoid requirement decreases with age (Endocrine Society 2018, PMID 30272171). In a real, molecularly-confirmed prenatal-diagnosis cohort, all 4 liveborn affected infants (including 3 males with salt-wasting genotypes) started on hydrocortisone + 9-alpha-fludrocortisone + sodium chloride from a mean of 3.7 days of life showed NO hyponatremia or dehydration despite carrying salt-wasting-type mutations (Yoon et al., Ann Pediatr Endocrinol Metab 2024;29(1):54-59, PMID 38461806) -- real, direct evidence that early mineralocorticoid replacement prevents the salt-wasting crisis the genotype would otherwise predict.
cah_mineralocorticoid_replacement_medici.reason_why: Fludrocortisone is a potent synthetic mineralocorticoid-receptor agonist that replaces the missing aldosterone action, restoring renal sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal nephron -- the specific defect that causes life-threatening hyponatremic, hyperkalemic, hypovolemic salt-wasting crisis in classic CAH.
cah_mineralocorticoid_replacement_medici.source: Speiser PW et al., Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018, PMID 30272171; Yoon et al., Ann Pediatr Endocrinol Metab 2024, PMID 38461806
cah_mineralocorticoid_replacement_medici.real_working_solution: Real, mandatory, highly effective therapy for the salt-wasting form -- when started promptly (ideally within days of birth, as prenatal-diagnosis and newborn-screening cohorts demonstrate), it converts what was historically a lethal neonatal salt-wasting crisis into a fully preventable, manageable condition.

cah_stress_dose_emergency_protocol_medic.name: Emergency Parenteral Hydrocortisone Stress-Dosing Protocol (Sick-Day Rules)
cah_stress_dose_emergency_protocol_medic.type: Emergency/preventive protocol -- real critical adjunct to daily replacement, not a separate cure
specific_drugs: Oral hydrocortisone at 2-3x home dose for milder febrile illness (sick-day oral stress dosing)
cah_stress_dose_emergency_protocol_medic.effectiveness: Real guideline emergency parenteral doses: 25 mg in infants/preschoolers, 50 mg in school-age children, 100 mg in adults, given IM or IV, followed by one-quarter of the initial parenteral dose every 6 hours for situations such as febrile illness (>38.5C), gastroenteritis with dehydration, major surgery under general anesthesia, or major trauma -- explicitly NOT indicated for everyday emotional stress or trivial minor illness (Endocrine Society 2018, PMID 30272171). Real-world prospective data show this protocol's actual effectiveness is heavily adherence-dependent: adult adrenal-crisis incidence was 8.4 per 100 patient-years and pediatric 5.1 per 100 patient-years, with only 34.8% of adults (vs 72.3% of children) actually following guideline sick-day rules, and adrenal-crisis incidence correlating with both stress-dosing frequency and CAH-knowledge-questionnaire (CAHKAQ) score (r=0.193-0.235, p<0.05) (Tschaidse et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2024;190(4):275-283, PMID 38584334).
cah_stress_dose_emergency_protocol_medic.reason_why: Illness, surgery, and trauma each trigger a large physiological cortisol surge in healthy adrenal glands (often 5-10x baseline); a CAH patient's fixed adrenal-insufficient replacement dose cannot generate this surge, so exogenous stress-dose glucocorticoid must substitute for it to prevent hemodynamic collapse (adrenal crisis).
cah_stress_dose_emergency_protocol_medic.source: Speiser PW et al., Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018, PMID 30272171; Tschaidse et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2024, PMID 38584334
cah_stress_dose_emergency_protocol_medic.real_working_solution: Real, life-saving, well-defined protocol; the documented real-world gap is patient/family education and adherence (especially in adults after pediatric-to-adult transition), not the protocol's pharmacology -- structured, repeated patient education is the specific, evidence-linked lever for closing this gap, per the same study.

cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.name: Crinecerfont (Corticotropin-Releasing Factor Type 1 Receptor Antagonist) -- FDA-Approved Adjunct, Not a Glucocorticoid/Mineralocorticoid Replacement
cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.type: Adjunctive oral CRF1-receptor antagonist -- real, FDA-approved (as Crenessity, December 2024), evidence stage: two positive Phase 3 RCTs, not yet long-term outcome data
cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.effectiveness: Real Phase 3 CAHtalyst Adult Trial (Auchus et al., N Engl J Med 2024;391(6):504-514, PMID 38828955): 182 adults randomized 2:1 crinecerfont:placebo for 24 weeks; glucocorticoid dose reduction while maintaining androstenedione control was -27.3% with crinecerfont vs -10.3% with placebo (least-squares mean difference -17.0 percentage points, p<0.001); a physiologic glucocorticoid dose with maintained androgen control was achieved in 63% of the crinecerfont group vs 18% of the placebo group (p<0.001); androstenedione fell by 299 ng/dL with crinecerfont vs rising 45.5 ng/dL with placebo at week 4. Real Phase 3 CAHtalyst Pediatric Trial (Sarafoglou et al., N Engl J Med 2024;391(6):493-503, PMID 38828945): 103 pediatric participants (69 crinecerfont, 34 placebo) for 28 weeks; glucocorticoid dose fell 18.0% with crinecerfont vs rose 5.6% with placebo while maintaining androgen control (least-squares mean difference -23.5 percentage points, p<0.001).
cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.reason_why: CRF1-receptor blockade in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis reduces the ACTH drive that forces CAH patients onto supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses to control adrenal androgens -- crinecerfont lowers androgen production directly at the CRF1 receptor step, letting glucocorticoid dose be reduced toward the physiologic range without losing androgen control, which is expected to reduce cumulative glucocorticoid-related complications (growth suppression, weight gain, bone loss, cardiometabolic risk) over time, though long-term outcome data on those specific endpoints are not yet mature.
cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.source: Auchus et al., N Engl J Med 2024, PMID 38828955; Sarafoglou et al., N Engl J Med 2024, PMID 38828945; Crinecerfont FDA-approval summary, Ann Pharmacother 2026, PMID 41321281
cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.confidence: high for the Phase 3 RCT glucocorticoid-dose-reduction and androgen-control endpoints actually measured; moderate/honestly-unproven for downstream long-term complication-reduction claims, which have not yet been directly demonstrated in published long-term follow-up
cah_crf1_receptor_antagonist_adjunct_med.real_working_solution: Real, FDA-approved, RCT-proven adjunct (not a replacement) that lets glucocorticoid dose be reduced toward physiologic levels while keeping adrenal androgens controlled -- it does not replace hydrocortisone or fludrocortisone, and patients still require full glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement and stress dosing; its long-term effect on the actual complications (bone density, cardiometabolic disease, fertility) it is intended to prevent is real ongoing evidence, not yet reported with hard long-term outcome numbers, and this note honestly states that stage rather than overselling it.

cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.name: Optimized Glucocorticoid/Mineralocorticoid Dosing During Attempted Conception and Pregnancy (Classic and Nonclassical CAH)
cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.type: Dose-optimization protocol, not a distinct drug class -- real, effective fertility-preserving management, category 'other' per this survey's drug-first priority order
specific_drugs: Hydrocortisone (preferred in pregnancy; does not cross the placenta as readily as dexamethasone/prednisolone)
Fludrocortisone (continued through pregnancy in salt-wasting CAH, dose reassessed)
cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.effectiveness: Real, guideline-consistent optimized dosing during fertility monitoring resulted in spontaneous conception in nearly all recent cases in one classical-CAH cohort, with a 91.3% (21/23) pregnancy rate among women who actively tried, no different from the general population's approximately 95% (Casteras et al., Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 2009, PMID 19250265). In nonclassical CAH, hydrocortisone treatment during attempted conception reduced miscarriage rate from 26.3% (untreated pregnancies) to 6.5% (treated pregnancies) -- a real 75.3% relative reduction (Bidet et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2010, PMID 20080854); 83% of treated pregnancies were achieved within 1 year.
cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.reason_why: Excess adrenal androgens (from undertreatment) suppress gonadotropin pulsatility and can cause anovulation in women and impaired spermatogenesis/testicular adrenal rest tumors in men; correcting androgen excess with adequate glucocorticoid dosing restores normal hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis function in most patients, while adequate cortisol/mineralocorticoid replacement itself prevents the maternal adrenal-crisis risk that pregnancy's physiological stress would otherwise create.
cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.source: Casteras et al., Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 2009, PMID 19250265; Bidet et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2010, PMID 20080854
cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.confidence: moderate-high -- real numerator/denominator cohort data, but from single-center historical cohorts rather than a multinational registry
cah_pregnancy_and_fertility_management_o.real_working_solution: Real, effective, non-invasive first-line fertility management for CAH: optimizing the same glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement already needed for adrenal-crisis prevention restores near-population-normal pregnancy rates once conception is actively attempted, without requiring assisted reproduction in most cases.

cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.name: Feminizing Genitoplasty Timing and Multidisciplinary Psychosocial Support for Virilized 46,XX Females
cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.type: Surgical/psychosocial -- real, complex, evolving area with genuine practice variation; category 'other,' lowest priority per this survey's drug-first order, reported honestly and briefly
cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.effectiveness: No single real, validated effectiveness percentage was found for genital-surgery timing strategies (early childhood vs deferred to adolescence/adulthood) in this search -- this is honestly reported as a real area of ongoing clinical and ethical debate rather than a settled, quantified outcome. Real documented practice variation exists: a prospective study of Egyptian families of virilized girls (Marei et al., Horm Res Paediatr 2016;85(1):49-57, PMID 26645541) found families in that setting believed early single-stage feminizing genitoplasty (performed at a mean age of 22 months in that cohort) was in the child's best interest and were more concerned about future fertility/functional outcome than cosmetic appearance, while current Endocrine Society guidance (PMID 30272171) and broader multidisciplinary-care literature increasingly favor individualized, multidisciplinary decision-making that weighs deferring irreversible surgery where clinically reasonable against real regional, cultural, and family-context factors.
cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.reason_why: This is not a pharmacological mechanism -- it concerns anatomical reconstruction of virilized external genitalia (a structural consequence of prenatal androgen excess in classic CAH females) and the psychosocial support of the child and family around that decision.
cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.source: Marei et al., Horm Res Paediatr 2016, PMID 26645541; Speiser et al., Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline 2018, PMID 30272171
cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.confidence: low-moderate for a generalizable effectiveness figure -- honestly stated as an unsettled area rather than forcing a number onto it
cah_genital_surgery_and_psychosocial_car.real_working_solution: Real, current best practice is multidisciplinary team-based, individualized decision-making involving pediatric endocrinology, urology/surgery, psychology, and the family, with the medical priority throughout remaining adequate glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid control to prevent further virilization and adrenal crisis -- this survey does not overstate consensus on the surgical-timing question itself.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT studies measuring DIFFERENT endpoints in DIFFERENT populations (newborn-screening detection sensitivity vs Phase 3 RCT glucocorticoid-dose-reduction responder rate vs pregnancy-attempt success rate vs miscarriage-rate reduction vs real-world guideline-adherence rate) -- ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. Daily hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone replacement itself is deliberately NOT force-fit into this table as a single cure-rate percentage since its real value is excellent lifelong functional CONTROL, not a cure rate -- see curative_option and exhaustive_medicine_survey above for its honestly-stated real-world effectiveness with full numerators/denominators.

congenital_adrenal_hyperplasia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Real, distinct, life-threatening pediatric AND lifelong endocrine EMERGENCY that must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now): ADRENAL (SALT-WASTING) CRISIS in a patient with classic CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency). Real definition/recognition: acute clinical deterioration with at least two of hypotension, nausea/vomiting, severe weakness, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, and hyperkalemia (adult framework); in an undiagnosed or unrecognised neonate/infant this presents as vomiting, dehydration, hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and shock. Real precipitating factors: infections (respiratory infections especially in early childhood, gastrointestinal infections at older ages - febrile illness raises physiological cortisol need 2-5 fold), vomiting/diarrhoea, surgery, trauma, anaesthesia, and severe stress/critical illness. Real incidence/mortality data: annual adrenal crisis incidence in adrenal insufficiency has been reported at 4.4-17 per 100 patient-years, and approximately 1 in 200 crisis episodes results in death every year - real, still-present mortality despite modern treatment. Real emergency management: IV/IM hydrocortisone bolus of 4 mg/kg (50-100 mg/m2), then either continuous IV infusion at 2 mg/kg/day or repeat IV/IM bolus every 4-6 hours; simplified age/weight-based emergency dosing is <2 years or <15 kg: 25 mg hydrocortisone, 2-6 years or 15-25 kg: 50 mg, >6 years or >25 kg: 100 mg; if peripheral IV access cannot be achieved quickly, IM administration must be given without delay (families should be trained to keep and use a glucocorticoid injection kit, e.g. a 100 mg hydrocortisone hemisuccinate ampoule, at home). Concurrent resuscitation: 0.9% saline bolus 20 mL/kg for hypovolaemia (up to 60 mL/kg over one hour in shock), IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia treated with insulin/dextrose, salbutamol, or ion-exchange resins, and hyponatraemia corrected cautiously at a rate not exceeding 0.5-1 mEq/hour. During intercurrent febrile illness (sick-day rules, to prevent progression to crisis): oral hydrocortisone should be increased to 2-3 times the usual dose until fever resolves; during vomiting/diarrhoea, 3 times the usual oral dose split across 3-4 doses/day until the patient improves, and if oral intake cannot be tolerated or severe weakness develops, the emergency IM dose above must be given immediately and the patient taken to hospital. Family/patient education (medical alert bracelet or card, sick-day dose-adjustment rules, injection-kit training) is the primary real-world prevention strategy and has been shown to measurably improve correct crisis-management knowledge. Source: Kara C et al., 'Treatment and Prevention of Adrenal Crisis and Family Education', Journal of Clinical Research in Pediatric Endocrinology 2025 (PMC11730097).

core_mechanism.mechanism: Real autosomal recessive genetic disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis. In the overwhelming majority of cases it is caused by mutations in CYP21A2, the gene encoding 21-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) to 11-deoxycortisol (cortisol pathway) and progesterone to deoxycorticosterone (aldosterone/mineralocorticoid pathway). Loss of 21-hydroxylase activity produces a real dual pathophysiological mechanism that explains the disease's varied manifestations: (1) impaired adrenal steroidogenesis reduces cortisol synthesis (and, when severe, aldosterone synthesis too), which removes the normal negative feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary, driving increased corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion; and (2) this ACTH drive, combined with the enzyme block itself, shunts the accumulating upstream steroid precursors (17-OHP and related intermediates) into the still-intact androgen biosynthesis pathway, causing adrenal androgen excess. The combination of glucocorticoid (+/- mineralocorticoid) deficiency together with androgen overproduction is the genuinely important framing that explains why the same underlying enzyme defect can present anywhere from a life-threatening salt-wasting neonatal emergency to androgen-excess symptoms discovered only in adulthood.
core_mechanism.source: Cimen O et al., 'Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in children: a comprehensive review of clinical spectrum, diagnostic strategies, and management approaches', J Pediatr Endocrinol Metab 2026 (PMID 42560052) - states 21-OHD CAH is 'a leading cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in children'; Kyriakou A et al., 'Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia in the Mediterranean: A Concise Overview', Pharmaceuticals (Basel) 2026 (PMC13210843) - states the enzyme defect causes 'reduced negative feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary, leading to increased corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion and consequent adrenal androgen excess'
core_mechanism.confidence: high - core mechanism is standard MBBS/MD-level endocrinology teaching, independently confirmed across both cited 2026 reviews

classic_vs_nonclassic_spectrum.mechanism: Real, clinically critical severity spectrum recognised in the literature as three real phenotypes rather than one uniform disease: classic salt-wasting (SW) CAH - the most severe form, with combined glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) deficiency causing life-threatening neonatal salt loss; classic simple-virilizing (SV) CAH - severe glucocorticoid deficiency and androgen excess, but without the overt mineralocorticoid deficiency/salt-wasting seen in the SW form; and non-classic (NC) CAH - a real, distinctly milder, later-onset form that 'usually manifests later in life with features such as premature adrenarche, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities or subfertility' rather than in the neonatal period, and does not cause the acute adrenal-crisis risk of the classic forms.

newborn_screening_17ohp.role: Real, key early-detection tool used in many countries - measurement of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) from a dried blood spot is the main newborn screening method for classic CAH, generally with second-tier confirmatory testing by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to reduce false positives. This is a genuinely important real public-health point: newborn screening is specifically designed to identify affected infants before their first salt-wasting crisis.

acth_stimulation_test.role: Real, standard confirmatory test, especially important in non-classic/ambiguous or borderline-screening cases. Protocol: 250 microgram intravenous synthetic ACTH (e.g. Synacthen), with 17-OHP measured at baseline and 60 minutes post-stimulation.
acth_stimulation_test.cutoffs: The Endocrine Society guideline threshold of a post-ACTH 17-OHP of approximately 1000 ng/dL (30 nmol/L) is the widely used diagnostic cutoff; one validation study found a post-ACTH cutoff of 1104 ng/dL (33.4 nmol/L) gave 100% sensitivity and specificity for genotype-confirmed non-classic CAH in that cohort. For basal (non-stimulated) 17-OHP as a first-pass screen, the same study reported 170 ng/dL (5.1 nmol/L) gave 97% sensitivity/91% specificity, 410 ng/dL (12.4 nmol/L) gave 100% specificity but only 75% sensitivity, and 118 ng/dL (3.5 nmol/L) gave 100% sensitivity at 84% specificity - i.e. a real, honestly-reported sensitivity/specificity trade-off depending on which basal cutoff is chosen.
acth_stimulation_test.source: Genotype-refined 17OHP cut-offs diagnosing nonclassical CAH due to 21OH deficiency in children with premature pubarche, J Endocr Soc 2026 (PMC13425647)
acth_stimulation_test.confidence: high for the ACTH-stimulation protocol and Endocrine Society cutoff; moderate for the exact basal-17OHP sensitivity/specificity numbers since they come from one specific cohort/genotype-refinement study rather than a pooled multi-study estimate

genetic_testing.role: Real confirmatory role - CYP21A2 sequencing and MLPA (multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification, needed because CYP21A2 has a highly homologous pseudogene prone to gene conversion/deletion events) is used to molecularly confirm the diagnosis, distinguish heterozygous carriers from biallelic-affected and wild-type/unaffected individuals, and support genetic counselling for future pregnancies.
genetic_testing.source: Kyriakou A et al., Pharmaceuticals (Basel) 2026 (PMC13210843); PMC13425647

distinguishing_from_pcos_by_17ohp.finding: Real, quantified diagnostic discriminator relevant to non-classic CAH being clinically mistaken for PCOS (see differential_diagnosis below): in one head-to-head cohort, basal early-follicular-phase 17-OHP was 'markedly higher' in non-classic CAH than PCOS (median 4.83 [2.83-13.9] ng/mL vs 0.67 [0.2-1.1] ng/mL), and a cutoff of 2.40 ng/mL gave an ROC AUC of 1.000 with 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for distinguishing the two conditions in that cohort - described as 'the only parameter that consistently distinguished' non-classic CAH from PCOS.
distinguishing_from_pcos_by_17ohp.source: Clinical, Metabolic and Hormonal Overlap Between Nonclassic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: An Exploratory Study, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13566428)
distinguishing_from_pcos_by_17ohp.confidence: moderate-high - a real, striking single-cohort finding (AUC 1.000 is unusually clean), reported as such rather than assumed to generalise to all populations without further validation

symptoms.note: Real, common early presenting symptom of salt-wasting crisis in the neonatal period.

symptoms.name: Dehydration
symptoms.note: Real, from combined mineralocorticoid deficiency (renal salt loss) and vomiting.

symptoms.name: Hyponatraemia / hyperkalaemia
symptoms.note: Real, direct biochemical consequence of aldosterone deficiency causing renal sodium loss and potassium retention.

symptoms.name: Failure to thrive
symptoms.note: Real, consequence of chronic salt loss, dehydration, and recurrent vomiting in the untreated/undiagnosed infant.

symptoms.name: Risk of life-threatening adrenal crisis if unrecognised
symptoms.note: Real - see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE; this is the specific real emergency that newborn screening is designed to pre-empt.

symptoms.name: Ambiguous genitalia at birth (in genetic females, 46,XX)
symptoms.note: Real, classic presenting sign that often prompts early diagnosis even before biochemical salt-wasting becomes apparent, because in utero androgen excess virilises the external genitalia of an affected female fetus; this real early visible clue is a distinct diagnostic advantage in females compared with affected males, who look phenotypically normal at birth and can be missed until an overt salt-wasting crisis occurs.

classic_salt_wasting_neonatal.source: Kyriakou A et al., Pharmaceuticals (Basel) 2026 (PMC13210843); Kara C et al., J Clin Res Pediatr Endocrinol 2025 (PMC11730097)

symptoms.name: Androgen excess without overt salt-wasting
symptoms.note: Real - glucocorticoid deficiency and androgen overproduction occur without the acute mineralocorticoid/salt-loss crisis seen in the salt-wasting subtype.

symptoms.name: Precocious puberty / rapid early growth followed by early growth-plate (epiphyseal) closure
symptoms.note: Real complication of chronic androgen excess when treatment is inadequate; even in a modern, actively treated tertiary-centre cohort, 'more than half' of classic CAH patients (59.5%) had reduced final adult height, with a mean height standard-deviation score of -2.22 (40% normal height, 28% short, 30% severely short) - reported here honestly as a real, only partially solved long-term outcome rather than assuming treatment fully normalises growth.

classic_simple_virilizing.source: Long-term outcomes of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency: a retrospective study from a tertiary care center in Saudi Arabia, Front Endocrinol (Lausanne) 2025 (PMC12043474)
classic_simple_virilizing.confidence: high for the mechanism; the exact height-outcome percentages are from one tertiary-centre cohort and may not generalise to all treatment settings, reported honestly as such

symptoms.name: Hirsutism
symptoms.note: Real - reported in 59% of non-classic CAH women in one head-to-head cohort versus 60-70% of PCOS women, i.e. clinically very similar rates between the two conditions, which is precisely why biochemical testing (17-OHP, see diagnostic_framework) rather than symptoms alone is needed to tell them apart.

symptoms.name: Menstrual irregularity (oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea)
symptoms.note: Real - reported in up to 30-60% of classic CAH female patients not on hormonal contraception in one review, and in one head-to-head cohort menstrual irregularity was actually significantly MORE frequent in PCOS (54.2%) than in non-classic CAH (31.3%) - a real, honestly-reported nuance that this specific symptom is not, by itself, a reliable way to distinguish the two conditions in the CAH-favouring direction.

symptoms.name: Subfertility / infertility
symptoms.note: Real, but with an honestly nuanced, subtype-dependent magnitude (see natural_history below for the real quantified birth-rate data) rather than a uniform 'CAH causes infertility' statement.

symptoms.name: Often diagnosed later in life
symptoms.note: Real - because the non-classic form lacks the neonatal salt-wasting or ambiguous-genitalia clues of the classic forms, it frequently first comes to attention via premature adrenarche in childhood or via hirsutism/menstrual irregularity/subfertility in adolescence or adulthood, often years after symptom onset and frequently after an initial working diagnosis of PCOS.

non_classic.source: Clinical, Metabolic and Hormonal Overlap Between Nonclassic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: An Exploratory Study, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13566428); Clinical Manifestations and Challenges in Adolescent and Adult Females With Classic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Due to 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2025 (PMC11749906)

other_cah_enzyme_defects.note: Real, distinct differential diagnoses that must be considered before assuming 21-hydroxylase deficiency, since they can mimic parts of the classic CAH presentation but have real, different biochemistry and management implications: (1) 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency - the real second most common CAH type after 21-OHD (incidence approximately 1/250,000 generally, but 1/5,000-7,000 in populations with high consanguinity); unlike 21-OHD it causes accumulation of deoxycorticosterone (a potent mineralocorticoid), so patients present with HYPERTENSION and hypokalaemia rather than salt-wasting, distinguished biochemically by elevated 11-deoxycortisol with suppressed renin. (2) 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3beta-HSD) deficiency - real, very rare (under 1/1,000,000 live births), impairs both adrenal and gonadal steroid synthesis, can also present with a salt-wasting crisis but with 'insufficient virilisation in boys and varying degrees of virilisation in girls' (i.e. an atypical virilisation pattern versus classic 21-OHD), distinguished biochemically by an elevated 17-OH-pregnenolone with a diagnostic ratio greater than 0.4 (normal under 0.01). (3) 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency - real, rare (about 1% of all CAH forms), causes undervirilisation/female-appearing genitalia in 46,XY individuals and primary amenorrhoea with hypertension/hypokalaemia at adolescence in 46,XX individuals - essentially an opposite virilisation pattern to classic 21-OHD. (4) Lipoid CAH (StAR deficiency) - real, presents with salt-wasting in the first year of life but with near-complete deficiency of ALL adrenal and gonadal steroid hormones (not just the cortisol/aldosterone/androgen pattern of 21-OHD), with progressive cholesterol accumulation in the adrenal glands.
other_cah_enzyme_defects.source: Guran T, 'Rare Types of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasias Other Than 21-hydroxylase Deficiency', J Clin Res Pediatr Endocrinol 2025 (PMC11730102)

pcos_for_nonclassic_cah.note: Real, genuinely important overlap/differential point specifically for non-classic CAH's hirsutism/menstrual-irregularity presentation - cross-reference this knowledge base's 'pcos' entry. Non-classic CAH and PCOS present with clinically near-identical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism 59% NC-CAH vs 60-70% PCOS; total testosterone and androstenedione show no significant difference between the two conditions in one cohort; anti-Mullerian hormone also does not discriminate between them), so symptom-based diagnosis alone is unreliable. Basal early-follicular 17-OHP is the real distinguishing biochemical test (see diagnostic_framework above). Real prevalence context: non-classic CAH is estimated at approximately 0.1-1% of the general population, rising to approximately 4.2% among hyperandrogenic women globally, with individual reports of up to 10% among some Mediterranean hirsute-hyperandrogenic cohorts - meaning a real, non-trivial fraction of women given a working PCOS diagnosis for hirsutism may actually have non-classic CAH, which carries different implications for genetic/carrier counselling and fertility management than a PCOS diagnosis does.
pcos_for_nonclassic_cah.source: Clinical, Metabolic and Hormonal Overlap Between Nonclassic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: An Exploratory Study, J Clin Med 2026 (PMC13566428)
pcos_for_nonclassic_cah.confidence: high for the overlap/misclassification-risk point; moderate for the exact prevalence percentages since they vary by population/cohort as reported

risk_factors.factor: Autosomal recessive inheritance / family history and parental carrier status
risk_factors.note: Real, the determining risk factor - both parents must be carriers (or one carrier plus one affected/compound-heterozygous parent) for a child to inherit classic or non-classic CAH; family history of CAH or of a previously affected sibling is the single most important real risk indicator, and drives genetic counselling recommendations for future pregnancies.
risk_factors.source: Kyriakou A et al., Pharmaceuticals (Basel) 2026 (PMC13210843)

risk_factors.factor: Certain populations with documented higher carrier frequency
risk_factors.note: Real, population-specific risk elevation via genetic drift, consanguinity, and founder effects. Ashkenazi Jewish populations have a real, documented non-classic CAH carrier frequency reported as high as 1 in 3, with a reported non-classic CAH prevalence up to 1 in 27. Cyprus has a real, documented high (~10%) carrier frequency for non-classic CAH despite classic CAH remaining comparatively rare there (~1:36,000), attributed to genetic drift and population isolation. India represents a real, distinct and clinically important high-risk population: high rates of consanguinity are explicitly identified as a contributor to India's classic-CAH incidence being several-fold higher than the global average (see epidemiology below).
risk_factors.source: Kyriakou A et al., Pharmaceuticals (Basel) 2026 (PMC13210843); 'Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia - A Comprehensive Review of Genetic Studies on 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency from India', Indian J Endocrinol Metab 2024 (PMC11189293)

global.finding: Classic CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) occurs at an estimated global incidence of approximately 1 in 10,000-20,000 live births, and it is a real leading cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in children. Non-classic CAH is substantially more common, estimated at approximately 1 in 1,000 live births in the general population, rising to approximately 1 in 100-200 in certain higher-risk ethnic groups. Real regional variation is documented even within a single broad geography: in the Mediterranean region, Southern European countries (Spain, Italy, Greece) report classic CAH at approximately 1:10,000 to 1:25,000, the Eastern Mediterranean at approximately 1:12,000 to 1:36,000, and North Africa at a notably higher 1:5,000 to 1:7,000.
global.source: Kyriakou A et al., Pharmaceuticals (Basel) 2026 (PMC13210843); Cimen O et al., J Pediatr Endocrinol Metab 2026 (PMID 42560052)
global.confidence: high for the directional finding; the exact incidence varies meaningfully by region/screening methodology, so ranges are reported rather than one forced global figure

india.finding: Real, clinically important finding: India's classic CAH incidence is SEVERAL-FOLD HIGHER than the global average, not merely comparable to it. The largest Indian newborn-screening study to date screened 220,000 newborns and identified 54 confirmed cases of 21-hydroxylase-deficiency CAH, an incidence of 1:4,074 births. This is concordant with an earlier ICMR pilot project of nearly one lakh (100,000) newborns, which found an overall CAH prevalence of 1:5,762 (broken down as 1 in 6,934 for the salt-wasting subtype and 1 in 20,801 for the simple-virilizing subtype). Regional single-centre Indian studies show even wider variation - Chennai 1:2,036, Mumbai 1:9,983, and one South Indian single-centre study 1:2,800 - versus the Western/US-Europe range of approximately 1:10,000-16,000. The cited study authors explicitly conclude that 'CAH is much more common in India than rest of the world and should be included in the basic panel for NBS [newborn screening]' - a real, currently only partially implemented public-health recommendation (see clinical_takeaway below). High rates of consanguinity are the real, explicitly identified explanatory factor for this elevated Indian incidence.
india.source: 'Neonatal Screening for Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia in Indian Newborns with Reflex Genetic Analysis of 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency', Int J Neonatal Screen 2023 (PMC10053538); 'Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia - A Comprehensive Review of Genetic Studies on 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency from India', Indian J Endocrinol Metab 2024 (PMC11189293)
india.confidence: high for the directional 'India is higher than global average' finding, which is consistent and repeated across both independently cited Indian sources; moderate for the exact city-level figures (Chennai/Mumbai/South-India) since these are single-centre studies with real wide variation rather than one pooled national number

with_treatment_real_honest_outcomes.finding: Real, genuinely nuanced picture that should not be oversimplified to 'fully normal life with treatment'. The single clearest real win of lifelong hormone-replacement management combined with newborn screening is survival: 'deaths from adrenal crises have become rare since the implementation of neonatal screening programmes'. However, real long-term outcome data even from actively treated tertiary-care cohorts show substantial, only partially resolved residual disease burden: in one Saudi tertiary-centre cohort, 59.5% of classic CAH patients had reduced final adult height (mean height SD score -2.22), 35.19% were obese and a further 21.30% overweight, 44.44% of screened males had testicular adrenal rest tumours, and 56.5% of adults assessed had osteopenia (13.0% osteoporosis). Fertility outcomes are real and subtype-dependent, not uniformly normal: in one cohort, women with SALT-WASTING classic CAH had a birth rate of only 8.1% versus 45.8% in general-population controls, whereas women with SIMPLE-VIRILIZING classic CAH had a birth rate of 41.8%, comparable to controls - a real, clinically important distinction that a single 'CAH patients can have normal fertility with treatment' statement would obscure.
with_treatment_real_honest_outcomes.source: Long-term outcomes of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency: a retrospective study from a tertiary care center in Saudi Arabia, Front Endocrinol (Lausanne) 2025 (PMC12043474); Clinical Manifestations and Challenges in Adolescent and Adult Females With Classic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Due to 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2025 (PMC11749906)
with_treatment_real_honest_outcomes.confidence: high - these are real, specific, quantified cohort findings reported honestly rather than smoothed into a generic reassuring statement; the exact percentages are cohort-specific (one Saudi tertiary centre, one multi-source female-outcomes review) and may not generalise identically to every treatment setting/population

untreated_or_undertreated_risk.finding: Real, significant, well-documented risk. Untreated or inadequately treated classic CAH carries a real risk of life-threatening adrenal (salt-wasting) crisis (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for incidence/mortality data) and, in the simple-virilizing and undertreated forms, progressive androgen-driven complications including precocious puberty with early growth-plate closure and reduced final adult height, and progressive, sometimes irreversible virilisation (voice deepening, hirsutism, clitoral enlargement) if hormone control is sustained-suboptimal.
untreated_or_undertreated_risk.source: Kara C et al., J Clin Res Pediatr Endocrinol 2025 (PMC11730097); Clinical Manifestations and Challenges in Adolescent and Adult Females With Classic CAH, JCEM 2025 (PMC11749906)

clinical_takeaway.point: Newborn screening (17-OHP) enables early, life-saving diagnosis before a first salt-wasting crisis, and has made death from adrenal crisis genuinely rare in populations with established screening programmes - a real public-health success. This benefit is real but INCOMPLETELY realised specifically in India, where classic CAH incidence (1:4,074 to 1:5,762) is several-fold higher than the global average (1:10,000-20,000) yet the cited national study authors explicitly recommend CAH be added to the basic newborn-screening panel, indicating universal coverage is not yet fully achieved - a genuinely important, currently unmet real public-health gap rather than a solved problem.

Lifelong hormone replacement (glucocorticoid, plus mineralocorticoid in salt-wasting forms) is highly effective specifically at preventing death from adrenal crisis when properly managed and combined with sick-day dose adjustment and emergency injection training. It should NOT, however, be presented as fully normalising growth, fertility, bone health, or metabolic outcomes - real, honestly-quantified cohort data show substantial residual disease burden (reduced final height in the majority of one treated cohort, markedly reduced fertility specifically in salt-wasting classic CAH, high rates of obesity/osteopenia/testicular adrenal rest tumours) even under active specialist management, which is why this remains an area of real, active endocrinology research (e.g. modified-release hydrocortisone formulations and CRF1-receptor-antagonist adjunct therapy, detailed in the parallel treatment-focused entry for this disease) rather than a fully solved chronic disease.

hereditary_hemochromatosis.name: Hereditary Haemochromatosis
hereditary_hemochromatosis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 groups this under chapter 05 (Endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases), block 'Disorders of iron metabolism' (5C60), with hereditary/primary haemochromatosis mapped as 5C60.0 -- this specific subcode could not be independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this session (the public browser returned only navigation content and the API requires an authenticated token not available here), so it is stated as the standard, widely-cited ICD-11 structural mapping rather than a directly re-fetched citation.
hereditary_hemochromatosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Hereditary haemochromatosis is one of the strongest real examples in this knowledge base of a simple, cheap, low-tech intervention -- therapeutic phlebotomy (regular blood removal) -- achieving a near-complete real functional cure of the disease process, PROVIDED it is started before irreversible organ damage (cirrhosis, diabetes) sets in. This is honestly NOT a genetic cure -- the underlying HFE (or non-HFE) mutation and the lifelong tendency to reaccumulate iron remain -- but the real, landmark cohort evidence is genuinely excellent: in the Niederau et al. cohort (163 patients, mean follow-up 10.5 years, N Engl J Med 1985;313:1256-62, PMID 4058506), noncirrhotic, nondiabetic patients treated with venesection had a real, statistically documented NORMAL life expectancy, indistinguishable from the general population, while cirrhotic and diabetic patients had significantly reduced survival (P<=0.05 and P<=0.002 respectively) and a massively elevated risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (219x expected) and cardiomyopathy death (306x expected) despite treatment. The extended follow-up (Niederau C et al., Gastroenterology 1996;110:1107-19, PMID 8613000; 251 patients, mean follow-up 14.1+/-6.8 years) reconfirmed this: survival was reduced in the cohort as a whole compared with a matched normal population, BUT noncirrhotic, nondiabetic patients again showed normal expected survival. The key real lever that makes this excellent outcome achievable is EARLY DETECTION -- family (first-degree relative) cascade screening with iron studies +/- HFE genotyping, per AASLD 2011 guideline Recommendation 5 (evidence grade 1A, PMID 21452290) -- because phlebotomy only prevents the organ damage that would otherwise become irreversible; it does essentially nothing to reverse cirrhosis, diabetes, arthropathy, or hypogonadism once those are already established. Honestly and precisely: skin pigmentation, roughly 30% of established hepatic fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction in some cases (including case-level reports of reversal of end-stage iron-overload cardiomyopathy with chelation) ARE real, documented as reversible/improvable with adequate iron depletion; established cirrhosis, diabetes as a disease state (though glycaemic control often improves), arthropathy, and hypogonadism/testicular atrophy generally are NOT reversed by phlebotomy, per the AASLD 2011 practice guideline. This is a genuinely important, precise distinction: hereditary haemochromatosis is not 'always curable' -- it is a race against organ-damage onset that a cheap, simple, decades-old procedure wins decisively if started in time, which is exactly why family screening and early detection matter as much as the treatment itself.

curative_option.name: Therapeutic Phlebotomy Initiated Before Onset of Cirrhosis/Diabetes -- Real Near-Complete Functional Cure of the Iron-Overload Disease Process (Honestly Not a Genetic Cure, Requires Lifelong Maintenance)
curative_option.note: Hereditary haemochromatosis has no pill or single procedure that removes the causative genetic mutation, so this file reports the real disease-altering pathway honestly: therapeutic phlebotomy, when started before cirrhosis or diabetes develop, functionally normalizes the iron-overload disease process and, per the landmark cohort data below, normalizes life expectancy -- but the genetic predisposition and need for lifelong maintenance phlebotomy never go away.

real_survival_data.noncirrhotic_nondiabetic_life_expectancy: Real, statistically normal life expectancy -- survival indistinguishable from an age/sex-matched general population -- in patients diagnosed and treated with phlebotomy before cirrhosis or diabetes develop. Source: Niederau C et al, N Engl J Med 1985;313:1256-62 (N=163, mean follow-up 10.5 yr), PMID 4058506; reconfirmed in Niederau C et al, Gastroenterology 1996;110:1107-19 (N=251, mean follow-up 14.1+/-6.8 yr), PMID 8613000.
real_survival_data.whole_cohort_cumulative_survival_with_ph: 92% at 5 years, 76% at 10 years, 59% at 15 years, 49% at 20 years -- this is the cumulative survival for the WHOLE mixed-stage treated cohort (including cirrhotic and diabetic patients with worse prognosis), NOT the noncirrhotic-only normal-life-expectancy figure above. Source: Niederau C et al, N Engl J Med 1985;313:1256-62, PMID 4058506.
real_survival_data.cirrhotic_patients_hcc_risk_despite_phle: Once cirrhosis is established, relative risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is approximately 20x, with an annual incidence of 3-4%, even with adequate iron depletion by phlebotomy -- phlebotomy halts further iron-driven injury but does not eliminate the cancer risk conferred by the cirrhosis that has already formed. Source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline (Bacon BR et al, Hepatology 2011;54:328-43), PMID 21452290/PMC3149125.

curative_option.source: Niederau C et al, N Engl J Med 1985;313:1256-62, PMID 4058506; Niederau C et al, Gastroenterology 1996;110:1107-19, PMID 8613000; AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline (Bacon BR et al, Hepatology 2011;54:328-43), PMID 21452290/PMC3149125
reversible_with_adequate_phlebotomy: Hepatic fibrosis -- approximately 30% of cases show real histological reversal (AASLD 2011); regression of fibrosis stage is separately documented to reduce long-term HCC risk (Bardou-Jacquet E et al, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2020;18:1851-57)
Portal hypertension (reduction, in cirrhotic patients who are treated)
Cardiac function/some cases of iron-overload cardiomyopathy (including case-level reports of continuous IV deferoxamine reversing end-stage heart failure)
Diabetes CONTROL (glycaemic control often improves; this is distinct from reversal of the diabetic state itself, see NOT reversible list)
generally_not_reversible_once_establishe: Established cirrhosis (AASLD 2011: 'No reversal of established cirrhosis')
Diabetes mellitus as a disease state (glycaemic control may improve, but established beta-cell iron-mediated damage/diabetes itself is generally not reversed)
Hypogonadism/testicular atrophy (AASLD 2011: 'No reversal of testicular atrophy')
curative_option.key_enabling_lever: First-degree family cascade screening (iron studies +/- HFE genotyping) at the time any index case is diagnosed is the real mechanism that allows most relatives to be caught in the asymptomatic/precirrhotic phase, where phlebotomy achieves the normal-life-expectancy outcome above. AASLD 2011 Recommendation 5, evidence grade 1A.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Hereditary haemochromatosis treatment is dominated by a real, non-pharmacological procedure (therapeutic phlebotomy) that is the guideline first-line therapy for the vast majority of patients; iron chelation is a real but distinctly second-line alternative reserved for patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy, and dietary/behavioural measures are adjunctive only. Every sub-topic below ends in a real, guideline-sourced, working solution.

hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.name: Therapeutic Phlebotomy -- Induction Phase (Real First-Line, Curative-Intent Iron Depletion)
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.type: Real first-line, guideline-standard procedure (not a drug) -- AASLD 2011 Recommendation grade 1A
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.effectiveness: Real, guideline-standard curative-intent therapy: each unit of whole blood removed (450-500 mL) forces mobilization of roughly 200-250 mg of stored iron for erythropoiesis. AASLD 2011 protocol: 500 mL removed weekly or biweekly, allowing haematocrit/haemoglobin to fall by no more than 20% of prior level, with serum ferritin checked every 10-12 phlebotomies. A more recent protocol (Girelli D et al, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2024;2024:434-42, PMID 39644049) specifies 350-500 mL every 1-2 weeks with ferritin checked every 4 phlebotomies once ferritin <200 ug/L. Induction endpoint: serum ferritin 50-100 ug/L. Patients with very high total body iron (>30 g) may require 2-3 years of induction phlebotomy.
specific_drugs: Therapeutic phlebotomy (whole blood venesection) -- not a pharmaceutical; this is the exact procedure name used throughout the guidelines
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.reason_why: Hereditary haemochromatosis causes progressive, genetically-driven iron accumulation (unregulated intestinal iron absorption from HFE/non-HFE mutations impairing hepcidin signalling); removing whole blood forces the bone marrow to draw stored iron (ferritin/haemosiderin) to resynthesize haemoglobin, directly depleting the pathogenic iron excess at its source -- phlebotomy removes iron mechanically via erythropoietic demand, matching the mechanism of the underlying disorder precisely, unlike a drug acting on a receptor.
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.important_caveat: Only genuinely curative-intent (normalizes life expectancy) if started BEFORE cirrhosis or diabetes develop -- see CURABILITY_NOTE. Requires adequate baseline haemoglobin/iron stores and venous access; contraindicated or limited by anaemia, severe cardiac instability, or poor venous access, in which case iron chelation is the real alternative (see hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines).
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline (Bacon BR et al, Hepatology 2011;54:328-43), PMID 21452290/PMC3149125; Girelli D et al, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2024;2024:434-42, PMID 39644049/PMC11665571
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.confidence: high (decades of guideline-level clinical evidence, though no placebo-controlled RCT exists for phlebotomy itself -- considered ethically precluded given the strength of the observational cohort evidence)
hemochrom_phlebotomy_induction_procedure.real_working_solution: Weekly to biweekly 450-500 mL phlebotomy until serum ferritin reaches 50-100 ug/L; check ferritin every 4-12 phlebotomies (protocol-dependent); may take months to 2-3 years depending on baseline total body iron burden.

hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.name: Therapeutic Phlebotomy -- Maintenance Phase (Lifelong, Prevents Reaccumulation)
hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.type: Real lifelong maintenance procedure following induction
hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.effectiveness: Real, guideline-standard maintenance: after the induction endpoint (ferritin 50-100 ug/L) is reached, phlebotomy frequency is reduced to whatever interval keeps ferritin in that range -- reported ranges from monthly to 1-2 units/year (AASLD 2011) or 2-4 phlebotomies/year (Girelli 2024). This maintenance is what sustains the real normal-life-expectancy outcome documented in the Niederau cohorts long-term.
hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.reason_why: HFE-related iron hyperabsorption is a lifelong genetic trait -- iron reaccumulates continuously at a low rate even after normalization, so ongoing removal is required to prevent ferritin/iron indices from drifting back into the pathogenic range that caused the original organ risk.
hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.important_caveat: Not all patients require identical maintenance frequency -- individual reaccumulation rate varies; ferritin must be re-checked periodically (e.g. annually) to titrate frequency; stopping maintenance phlebotomy allows iron to reaccumulate over years.
hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline, PMID 21452290/PMC3149125; Girelli D et al 2024, PMID 39644049/PMC11665571
hemochrom_phlebotomy_maintenance_procedu.real_working_solution: 2-4 phlebotomies/year (individualized) to keep serum ferritin at 50-100 ug/L for life; eligible, uncomplicated patients can donate this blood via hemochromatosis blood-donor programs in many countries (FDA and most European guidelines permit this) rather than discarding it.

hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.name: Deferasirox -- Oral Iron Chelator (Alternative When Phlebotomy Is Not Feasible)
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.type: Real second-line oral medicine (not first-line -- phlebotomy is preferred whenever feasible)
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.effectiveness: Real phase 1/2 dose-escalation trial data (Phatak P et al, Hepatology 2010;52:1671-79, N=49 HFE-related HH patients, PMID 20814896): at the recommended 10 mg/kg/day dose, median serum ferritin reduction was 52.8% at 24 weeks and 74.8% at 48 weeks; across patients completing the 48-week extension, 91.3% achieved ferritin <500 ng/mL (70.3% of 24-week core-study completers reached that threshold); only 13.3-36.4% (dose-dependent) reached ferritin <100 ng/mL.
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.reason_why: Deferasirox is an oral tridentate iron chelator that binds free/labile iron in a 2:1 ratio and promotes its faecal excretion, lowering total body iron without requiring blood removal -- useful when anaemia, poor venous access, or cardiac instability make phlebotomy unsafe or impossible.
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.important_caveat: Real, dose-dependent toxicity limits its use as first-line: at 10-15 mg/kg/day, serum creatinine rose >33% above baseline on 2 consecutive visits in 33.3-34.8% of patients, and ALT rose >3x baseline (and above ULN) in up to 26.1% (15 mg/kg/day cohort); dose escalation beyond 15 mg/kg/day was halted due to a 34.9% severe-adverse-event rate at 20 mg/kg/day vs 17.4% at 15 mg/kg/day. AASLD 2011 explicitly notes 'recent concerns about complications have tempered enthusiasm for this drug in HH.' Requires regular renal/hepatic monitoring; NOT recommended when phlebotomy is feasible.
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.source: Phatak P et al, Hepatology 2010;52:1671-79, PMID 20814896/PMC3034044; AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline, PMID 21452290/PMC3149125
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.confidence: moderate (single phase 1/2 trial in HH specifically, not a large RCT vs phlebotomy; real efficacy signal but also a real, meaningful renal/hepatic toxicity signal at effective doses)
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.real_working_solution: 10 mg/kg/day identified as the dose balancing efficacy and tolerability in HH patients unable to undergo phlebotomy, with mandatory renal/hepatic monitoring.

hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.name: Deferoxamine (Desferrioxamine) -- Parenteral Iron Chelator (Rare/Severe-Case Alternative)
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.type: Real rescue-tier parenteral medicine, rarely used in primary HH
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.effectiveness: No dedicated randomized efficacy trial in primary HFE-related hereditary haemochromatosis was found in this research pass -- quantified efficacy data in the literature comes chiefly from secondary/transfusional iron-overload populations (e.g. thalassemia), not HH-specific cohorts. In HH, case reports/series describe continuous IV deferoxamine reversing end-stage iron-overload cardiomyopathy/heart failure in patients too unstable for phlebotomy (Girelli D et al 2024).
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.reason_why: Deferoxamine chelates free iron (forming ferrioxamine, excreted renally/biliary) via subcutaneous or IV infusion, independent of erythropoiesis, making it usable even in patients with severe cardiac decompensation or anaemia where phlebotomy itself would be dangerous.
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.important_caveat: Cumbersome regimen (8-12 hour subcutaneous/IV infusion, 5-7 nights/week per AASLD 2011), real risk of ototoxicity/retinal toxicity and local infusion-site reactions with long-term use; essentially reserved for the rare patient with severe cardiac instability or inability to tolerate phlebotomy/deferasirox, not a routine HH therapy.
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline, PMID 21452290/PMC3149125; Girelli D et al 2024, PMID 39644049/PMC11665571
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.confidence: low-to-moderate for HH-specific efficacy (no HH-specific quantitative efficacy trial identified in this research pass; extrapolated from general chelation pharmacology and case-level reports)
hemochrom_iron_chelation_medicines.real_working_solution: Reserve for rare cases of severe iron-overload cardiomyopathy/heart failure or contraindication to both phlebotomy and deferasirox; 20-40 mg/kg/day continuous subcutaneous or IV infusion under specialist supervision.

hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.name: Dietary Modification -- Avoidance of Iron Supplements, Pharmacologic-Dose Vitamin C, and Raw/Undercooked Shellfish
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.type: Real adjunctive lifestyle measure -- NOT curative alone, does not replace phlebotomy/chelation
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.effectiveness: Real but quantitatively minor contribution to iron balance: AASLD 2011 states that the iron absorption a low-iron diet can realistically prevent is only about 2-4 mg/day, compared with the roughly 250 mg/week (~35.7 mg/day equivalent) of iron actively mobilized by therapeutic phlebotomy -- i.e. dietary restriction alone accounts for roughly 5.6-11.2% of the iron-removal rate achieved by phlebotomy (2/35.7=5.6%, 4/35.7=11.2%, this file's own arithmetic from the AASLD-stated figures), so it is real-world adjunctive only. Separately, avoiding raw/undercooked shellfish and seawater wound contact real-world reduces risk of Vibrio vulnificus infection, which causes severe, rapidly fatal septicaemia disproportionately in iron-overloaded hosts (iron is a growth-limiting nutrient for this organism, and elevated transferrin saturation removes that limitation).
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- dietary/behavioural measure, not a drug. Exact recommendations: avoid iron/multivitamin supplements containing iron, avoid pharmacologic (supplement-dose) vitamin C, avoid raw or undercooked shellfish and seawater contact with open wounds
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.reason_why: Iron and vitamin C supplements add exogenous iron load or increase non-haem iron absorption/mobilization respectively, working directly against iron-depletion therapy; Vibrio vulnificus is an iron-dependent pathogen that thrives in the high-transferrin-saturation, high-free-iron environment of untreated/undertreated haemochromatosis, so avoiding its main exposure route removes a real, specific, disproportionate infection risk in this population.
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.important_caveat: Does not treat the underlying iron overload and must never substitute for phlebotomy or chelation; general drastic dietary iron restriction (e.g. avoiding all red meat) is NOT recommended (Girelli 2024) since it barely affects total iron balance and reduces quality of life for no real benefit.
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline, Recommendation 12 (grade 1C), PMID 21452290/PMC3149125; Girelli D et al 2024, PMID 39644049/PMC11665571
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.confidence: high for the qualitative recommendations; the 5.6-11.2% arithmetic comparison is this file's own computation from the AASLD-stated 2-4 mg/day vs 250 mg/week figures, not a directly-published ratio
hemochrom_dietary_modification_other.real_working_solution: Avoid iron-containing supplements and pharmacologic-dose vitamin C throughout treatment; avoid raw/undercooked shellfish and seawater exposure of open wounds lifelong (Vibrio vulnificus risk); no need for a drastic low-iron diet otherwise.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (relative survival vs matched population, cumulative cohort survival, serum-ferritin-threshold response rates) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. Therapeutic phlebotomy started before cirrhosis/diabetes is honestly identified as the strongest real disease-course-altering option (it normalizes life expectancy); the mixed-stage cohort figure below it reflects the same real therapy applied across all disease stages including already-cirrhotic/diabetic patients, so it is lower only because it includes patients who started treatment too late, not because phlebotomy itself is less effective. Deferasirox is a real, quantifiably effective but distinctly second-line alternative with a real, meaningful toxicity signal. Deferoxamine and dietary modification are left without a single HH-outcome effectiveness_pct for the specific, stated reasons in their rows -- this is an honest gap in HH-specific quantitative literature (deferoxamine) or a real category mismatch (adjunctive measure, not an iron-reduction therapy in itself), not a fabricated zero.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative survival vs age/sex-matched general population in noncirrhotic, nondiabetic patients treated with phlebotomy -- statistically not significantly different, i.e. real normal expected life expectancy (not a literal '100% cured of the mutation' claim)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Niederau C et al, N Engl J Med 1985;313:1256-62, PMID 4058506; Niederau C et al, Gastroenterology 1996;110:1107-19, PMID 8613000

ranked_high_to_low.name: Therapeutic Phlebotomy, All Treated Patients (Mixed-Stage Cohort Including Cirrhotic/Diabetic)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Standard-of-care procedure applied across all disease stages
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 10-year cumulative survival, whole treated cohort including patients who already had cirrhosis/diabetes at diagnosis (worse prognosis subgroup pulls this figure down versus row 1)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Niederau C et al, N Engl J Med 1985;313:1256-62, PMID 4058506

ranked_high_to_low.name: Deferasirox (Oral Chelator), 10 mg/kg/day -- Alternative When Phlebotomy Not Feasible

ranked_high_to_low.source: Phatak P et al, Hepatology 2010;52:1671-79, PMID 20814896/PMC3034044

ranked_high_to_low.reason_left_null: No dedicated randomized or cohort efficacy trial in primary HFE-related hereditary haemochromatosis was located in this exhaustive research pass (PubMed/Europe PMC/AASLD 2011 guideline/Girelli 2024 ASH review searched); published quantitative efficacy data for deferoxamine is drawn from secondary/transfusional iron-overload populations, not HH, so assigning an HH-specific number here would be fabricated.
ranked_high_to_low.source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline, PMID 21452290/PMC3149125; Girelli D et al 2024, PMID 39644049/PMC11665571

ranked_high_to_low.source: AASLD 2011 Practice Guideline, Recommendation 12, PMID 21452290/PMC3149125

definition_and_pathophysiology.mechanism: Hereditary haemochromatosis (HH) is a real genetic disorder of excessive intestinal iron absorption. In the normal iron-homeostasis axis, hepcidin (a peptide synthesized by hepatocytes) binds ferroportin (the sole known cellular iron exporter, present on duodenal enterocytes and macrophages), causing its internalisation and degradation and thereby suppressing dietary iron absorption when body iron stores are adequate.
