x_linked_intrinsic_pathway_mechanism.finding: Haemophilia A is a real X-linked recessive genetic bleeding disorder caused by mutations in the F8 gene (Xq28) that lead to deficiency or dysfunction of coagulation Factor VIII, a cofactor required by activated Factor IX (FIXa) to efficiently activate Factor X within the intrinsic coagulation pathway. Without adequate FVIII activity, thrombin generation on the platelet surface is markedly impaired, so a platelet plug forms at a bleeding site but is not adequately stabilised by fibrin - producing the disorder's real hallmark of delayed, prolonged, and recurrent bleeding (especially deep bleeding into joints and muscles) rather than immediate surface bleeding. Being X-linked recessive, males with one mutated F8 allele on their single X chromosome are affected, while females require both X chromosomes to be affected to have the full clinical phenotype (carrier females can still have mild bleeding symptoms due to skewed X-inactivation).
x_linked_intrinsic_pathway_mechanism.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Hemophilia', F8 gene and inheritance summary; Peyvandi F, Garagiola I, Young G, 'The past and future of haemophilia: diagnosis, treatments, and its complications', Lancet 2016;388(10040):187-197, PMID 26897598

severity_classification.finding: Severity is classified by residual Factor VIII coagulant activity, per the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) Scientific and Standardization Committee definition: Severe = <1 IU/dL (<1% of normal); Moderate = 1-5 IU/dL (1-5%); Mild = >5 to <40 IU/dL (5-40%). This is genuinely important because factor-activity level directly correlates with bleeding frequency and severity: severe patients bleed spontaneously (without identifiable trauma) into joints and muscles, historically 2-5 times per month if untreated; moderate patients bleed after relatively minor trauma with occasional spontaneous bleeds; mild patients bleed mainly after significant trauma, surgery, or dental extraction and may not be diagnosed until later in life. By population distribution, approximately 60% of haemophilia A cases are severe, ~15% moderate, and ~25% mild.
severity_classification.source: White GC 2nd, Rosendaal F, Aledort LM, Lusher JM, Rothschild C, Ingerslev J; Factor VIII and Factor IX Subcommittee, 'Definitions in hemophilia. Recommendation of the scientific subcommittee on factor VIII and factor IX of the scientific and standardization committee of the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis', Thromb Haemost 2001;85(3):560, PMID 11307831; National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org, formerly National Hemophilia Foundation), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page (severity-distribution percentages); National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD), 'Hemophilia A' rare disease database entry
severity_classification.confidence: high - ISTH classification is the internationally accepted standard; population-percentage figures are consistent across two independent patient-advocacy/clinical sources

genetic_basis_and_de_novo_mutations.finding: F8 mutations are heterogeneous (point mutations, deletions, duplications), but a single recurrent structural mutation - the intron 22 inversion, caused by intrachromosomal recombination between int22h sequences - is a major real cause of severe haemophilia A specifically; a 2022 cohort study of 62 severe haemophilia A patients found 28 (45.2%) were intron 22 inversion-positive, consistent in direction and magnitude with the wider literature's commonly cited ~40-50% figure for this mutation among severe cases. Approximately one-third of all haemophilia A cases arise from de novo (new) mutations with no prior family history, which is clinically important because a negative family history does not rule out haemophilia A.
genetic_basis_and_de_novo_mutations.source: Ashfaq J, Ahmed R, Tariq F, Abedin QU, Abid M, Borhany M, 'Frequency of Intron 22 Inversion in Severe Hemophilia A Patients', Cureus 2022, PMID 36158401 (single-cohort n=62 finding, reported as such); National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page (approximately one-third of cases lack prior family history)
genetic_basis_and_de_novo_mutations.confidence: moderate for the exact 45.2% figure (single cohort, n=62) - high for the qualitative point that intron 22 inversion is a major recurrent cause of severe disease and that de novo mutations are common

aptt_pt_initial_pattern.finding: The classic initial laboratory pattern is an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal prothrombin time (PT) and normal platelet count/bleeding time - because FVIII participates only in the intrinsic pathway (which the aPTT tests), while the PT (extrinsic/common pathway) does not depend on FVIII. Mild haemophilia A can have a normal or only marginally prolonged aPTT if FVIII activity is not low enough to prolong the assay, so a normal aPTT does not exclude mild disease. A mixing study (patient plasma mixed 1:1 with normal plasma) that corrects the prolonged aPTT supports a factor deficiency (versus an inhibitor, which would not fully correct).
aptt_pt_initial_pattern.source: National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD), 'Hemophilia A' rare disease database entry (aPTT prolonged when FVIII <30% of normal, PT typically normal)
aptt_pt_initial_pattern.confidence: high - standard, widely taught coagulation-testing pattern

factor_viii_assay.finding: A quantitative one-stage (clot-based) or chromogenic Factor VIII coagulant activity assay is the specific diagnostic test that both confirms haemophilia A and determines its severity, by directly measuring residual FVIII activity against the ISTH severity thresholds (severe <1%, moderate 1-5%, mild 5-40%, described above in definition_and_pathophysiology).
factor_viii_assay.source: National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD), 'Hemophilia A' rare disease database entry; White GC 2nd et al, Thromb Haemost 2001;85(3):560, PMID 11307831

genetic_testing_and_carrier_testing.finding: Genetic testing (F8 gene sequencing, with specific inversion-detection assays for the intron 22 and intron 1 inversions common in severe disease) identifies the causative mutation, which is useful for confirming diagnosis in ambiguous cases, for prenatal/carrier testing, and increasingly for prognostic purposes (e.g. inhibitor-development risk varies by mutation type). Given the X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, family history and carrier testing in female relatives of an affected male are a real, important part of the diagnostic and counselling framework - carrier testing (via factor assay plus genetic testing once the familial mutation is known) allows identification of carrier females, some of whom have clinically reduced FVIII levels themselves due to skewed X-inactivation and are therefore also at real bleeding risk, and informs reproductive/genetic counselling for at-risk families.
genetic_testing_and_carrier_testing.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Hemophilia' condition page (F8 gene, X-linked recessive inheritance, carrier considerations); Lorenzo JI, Casana P, Espinos C, Ferrer R, Aznar JA, 'Diagnosis of two related carriers of severe haemophilia B with no family history', Haemophilia 2000, PMID 10792479 (illustrates general principle that carrier diagnosis in haemophilia relies on factor assay plus mutation detection, and that a negative family history does not exclude carrier status - the same X-linked logic applies directly to haemophilia A)
genetic_testing_and_carrier_testing.confidence: high for X-linked inheritance/carrier-testing principle; the cited case report is for haemophilia B but the underlying X-linked carrier-diagnosis logic is identical for haemophilia A

classic_symptoms.name: Hemarthrosis (joint bleeding)
classic_symptoms.note: Real, classic, and the single most common manifestation of severe haemophilia A - spontaneous or minor-trauma-triggered bleeding into joints, especially weight-bearing 'target joints' (knees, ankles, elbows). Described in the literature as 'the most frequent clinical manifestation of severe hemophilia'.
classic_symptoms.source: Gualtierotti R, Solimeno LP, Peyvandi F, 'Hemophilic arthropathy: Current knowledge and future perspectives', J Thromb Haemost 2021, PMID 34197690

classic_symptoms.name: Muscle hematomas
classic_symptoms.note: Real, deep-muscle bleeding (e.g. iliopsoas, calf, forearm) that can cause compartment syndrome, nerve compression, or substantial blood loss if not promptly treated.
classic_symptoms.source: Peyvandi F, Garagiola I, Young G, Lancet 2016;388(10040):187-197, PMID 26897598

classic_symptoms.name: Severity-dependent bleeding correlation
classic_symptoms.note: Honest, real correlation: bleeding phenotype tracks residual factor activity - severe disease (<1%) causes spontaneous joint/muscle bleeds (historically 2-5 episodes/month untreated); moderate disease (1-5%) causes occasional spontaneous bleeds and bleeding after minor trauma; mild disease (5-40%) usually bleeds only after significant trauma, surgery, or dental extraction and may not present until adulthood.
classic_symptoms.source: National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page; National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD), 'Hemophilia A' entry

classic_symptoms.name: Prolonged bleeding after surgery/dental procedures/circumcision
classic_symptoms.note: Real, and in undiagnosed severe cases circumcision bleeding is frequently the presenting event that leads to diagnosis in infancy.
classic_symptoms.source: National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page

classic_symptoms.name: Intracranial hemorrhage (ICH)
classic_symptoms.note: Real, rare in the overall haemophilia population but the single most dangerous manifestation - see this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE. Materially more common in the neonatal/infant period: an estimated 2%-4% of infants with haemophilia develop ICH, versus roughly 0.1% in the general neonatal population.
classic_symptoms.source: Carcao MD, Andersson NG, Gouw S, Haemophilia 2026, PMID 41988997

classic_symptoms.name: Recurrent hemarthrosis leading to chronic hemophilic arthropathy
classic_symptoms.note: Real, honest natural-history point: repeated joint bleeds, if inadequately treated, cause progressive synovial hypertrophy, cartilage destruction, and joint-space narrowing, culminating in chronic hemophilic arthropathy with pain and functional decline - described in the literature as leading to 'progressive musculoskeletal damage'.
classic_symptoms.source: Gualtierotti R, Solimeno LP, Peyvandi F, J Thromb Haemost 2021, PMID 34197690; Peyvandi F, Garagiola I, Young G, Lancet 2016;388(10040):187-197, PMID 26897598

hemophilia_b_factor_ix_deficiency.finding: Haemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) is clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A on history and examination alone - both are X-linked recessive disorders producing an identical bleeding phenotype (hemarthrosis, muscle hematoma, prolonged post-surgical bleeding) with an identical initial laboratory pattern (prolonged aPTT, normal PT). The two can only be distinguished by a specific Factor VIII versus Factor IX coagulant activity assay (a low FVIII with normal FIX confirms haemophilia A; the reverse confirms haemophilia B), which is why the diagnostic_framework above specifies the factor assay as the confirmatory (not just supportive) test. Haemophilia A is roughly 3-4 times more common than haemophilia B.
hemophilia_b_factor_ix_deficiency.source: CDC, 'About Hemophilia' (haemophilia A ~3-4x as common as haemophilia B); National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD), 'Hemophilia A' entry (differential diagnosis list includes haemophilia B)

von_willebrand_disease.finding: Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder overall and a key differential, but it typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising) rather than the deep joint/muscle bleeding typical of haemophilia A, and most VWD is inherited in an autosomal (not X-linked) pattern, so it affects both sexes. One specific VWD subtype, type 2N, is a real and clinically important mimic of mild/moderate haemophilia A because it causes disproportionately low FVIII activity (since von Willebrand factor normally protects circulating FVIII from clearance) - type 2N should specifically be suspected in a patient with low FVIII activity but disproportionately normal/high VWF antigen, and it is distinguished by its autosomal recessive inheritance pattern versus haemophilia A's X-linked pattern.
von_willebrand_disease.source: Seidizadeh O, Peyvandi F, Mannucci PM, 'Von Willebrand disease type 2N: An update', J Thromb Haemost 2021, PMID 33497541

other_bleeding_disorders.finding: Other rarer bleeding disorders (other factor deficiencies, platelet function disorders, acquired haemophilia A from autoantibodies against FVIII) should also be considered, particularly in patients with an atypical age of onset (acquired haemophilia A classically presents in older adults with no personal/family bleeding history) or an aPTT that does not correct on a mixing study (suggesting an inhibitor rather than a congenital factor deficiency).
other_bleeding_disorders.source: Ellsworth P, Chen SL, Jones LA, Ma AD, Key NS, review of acquired hemophilia A, J Thromb Haemost 2025, PMID 39536818
other_bleeding_disorders.confidence: moderate - acquired haemophilia A citation supports the distinguishing clinical pattern described

risk_factors.factor: X-linked recessive inheritance / family history - the primary risk factor
risk_factors.note: Real: sons of carrier mothers have a 50% chance of being affected, and daughters of carrier mothers have a 50% chance of being carriers themselves; sons of an affected father are unaffected (fathers do not transmit an X-linked gene to sons) while all daughters of an affected father are obligate carriers. All racial and ethnic groups are equally affected.
risk_factors.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Hemophilia' condition page; CDC, 'About Hemophilia'

risk_factors.factor: De novo (new) mutation with no family history
risk_factors.note: Honest, real, and clinically important: approximately one-third of haemophilia A cases arise from a new mutation in the affected individual with no preceding family history, so an absent family history must not be used to rule out the diagnosis.
risk_factors.source: National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page

risk_factors.note: Because the disorder is X-linked recessive, clinically affected individuals are overwhelmingly male; symptomatic disease in females is real but rare, typically requiring either two affected X chromosomes (rare) or substantially skewed X-chromosome inactivation in a carrier.
risk_factors.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Hemophilia' condition page

global_incidence.finding: Haemophilia A is the most common severe inherited bleeding disorder, with an estimated incidence of approximately 1 in 4,000-5,000 (other sources cite ~1 in 5,617) male births worldwide; approximately 60% of cases are severe. In the United States, an estimated 30,000-33,000 males were living with haemophilia A as of 2012-2018 CDC surveillance data, with roughly 400 new diagnoses per year.
global_incidence.source: MedlinePlus Genetics, 'Hemophilia' condition page (1 in 4,000-5,000 male births); CDC, 'About Hemophilia' (US prevalence ~33,000, ~60% severe); National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page (1 in 5,617 male births, ~400 new diagnoses/year, 30,000-33,000 US males)
global_incidence.confidence: high direction/order-of-magnitude - exact incidence figure genuinely varies modestly (1/4,000 to 1/5,617) across real, independent sources, reported honestly as a range rather than a single fabricated number

india_specific.finding: Honest, real but fragmented picture: India does not have a single verified national haemophilia A prevalence figure retrievable in this research; what is verifiable is registry data from individual Haemophilia Treatment Centres (HTCs), which together indicate a substantial real patient population. A large tertiary-care HTC registry (Christian Medical College, Vellore) reported 818 registered individuals with haemophilia A and 162 with haemophilia B at that single centre. A separate North Indian HTC study during the COVID-19 pandemic surveyed 120 haemophilia patients/families at that centre. These are real, verifiable single-centre numbers, not a national total, and are reported as such rather than extrapolated into a fabricated nationwide prevalence estimate.
india_specific.source: Sait H, Sajjan SM, Phadke SR, 'Haemophilia management programme: Transformation during COVID-19', Indian J Med Res 2022, PMID 36124495 (818 haemophilia A + 162 haemophilia B registered at one centre); Radhakrishnan N, Shankar R, Singh S, Rana M, 'Taking on a pandemic's challenge: Emergent solutions from a single Hemophilia treatment center in North India', Transfus Apher Sci 2021, PMID 33248907 (120 patients/families surveyed at one North Indian HTC)
india_specific.confidence: moderate - real single-centre registry figures, explicitly not a verified national prevalence total; no fabricated national number is given

historical_life_expectancy_transformed_b.finding: Real, dramatic, and well-documented historical transformation: in a Swedish national cohort spanning 1831-1980, the median life expectancy of patients with severe haemophilia rose roughly fivefold, from only 11 years in 1831-1920 to 56.8 years in 1961-1980 (moderate haemophilia rose from 27.5 to 71.5 years over the same span); by 1969-1980, death rates for severe haemophilia patients under age 45 were reported as not much different from Swedish males in the general population. This historical improvement predates modern prophylactic recombinant/plasma-derived factor replacement (the specific modern-treatment story - dosing, prophylaxis regimens, gene therapy - is covered by the parallel treatment-side fork for this disease, per this entry's scope) but establishes the real magnitude of the transformation that improved factor-replacement access has driven.
historical_life_expectancy_transformed_b.source: Larsson SA, 'Life expectancy of Swedish haemophiliacs, 1831-1980', Br J Haematol 1985, PMID 3885998
historical_life_expectancy_transformed_b.confidence: high - classic, original national-cohort study, frequently cited as the reference historical dataset for this fact

untreated_recurrent_hemarthrosis_causes_.finding: Real and clinically critical: recurrent, inadequately treated hemarthrosis triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of synovial inflammation/hypertrophy (haemosiderin deposition from repeated intra-articular bleeding drives chronic synovitis), which itself becomes more fragile and prone to re-bleeding, progressively destroying articular cartilage and subchondral bone. This produces largely irreversible chronic hemophilic arthropathy - chronic pain, reduced range of motion, and functional disability - which is why early initiation of factor prophylaxis specifically to prevent the first and subsequent joint bleeds (rather than only treating bleeds after they occur) is the modern standard of care.
untreated_recurrent_hemarthrosis_causes_.source: Gualtierotti R, Solimeno LP, Peyvandi F, 'Hemophilic arthropathy: Current knowledge and future perspectives', J Thromb Haemost 2021, PMID 34197690

clinical_takeaway.finding: First, early prophylactic factor replacement - started before recurrent joint damage accumulates - is the real, evidence-grounded principle for preventing chronic hemophilic arthropathy: because joint damage from repeated hemarthrosis is largely irreversible once established (this entry's natural_history above), the clinical goal is to prevent the first and subsequent bleeds, not merely treat them after the fact. Second, any major bleed in a haemophilia A patient - and specifically any suspicion of intracranial haemorrhage - must be recognised as a true, immediate emergency requiring factor replacement started empirically without waiting for imaging or laboratory confirmation, because ICH carries real, serious mortality/morbidity risk and time to treatment is the critical determinant of outcome (see this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). Third, a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis, since approximately one-third of cases are de novo, and haemophilia B and von Willebrand disease type 2N are real mimics that require a specific factor assay - not just an aPTT - to distinguish from haemophilia A (this entry's diagnostic_framework and differential_diagnosis above).
clinical_takeaway.source: Gualtierotti R, Solimeno LP, Peyvandi F, J Thromb Haemost 2021, PMID 34197690; Carcao MD, Andersson NG, Gouw S, Haemophilia 2026, PMID 41988997; National Bleeding Disorders Foundation (bleeding.org), 'Hemophilia A' patient-education page; Seidizadeh O, Peyvandi F, Mannucci PM, J Thromb Haemost 2021, PMID 33497541

hemophilia_a.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Intracranial haemorrhage (ICH) or any major/life-threatening bleed (e.g. iliopsoas bleed with neurovascular compromise, GI bleed with haemodynamic instability, airway/neck bleed, major trauma) in a known or suspected haemophilia A patient is a TRUE, immediate haematological emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely, triggering immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now) with the explicit instruction that factor VIII replacement must be given empirically the moment haemophilia is suspected, BEFORE imaging or confirmatory labs, because delay for confirmation costs irreplaceable time in a real bleeding brain. ICH is real but rare in the general haemophilia population overall; it is materially more frequent in the neonatal/infant period, where it occurs in an estimated 2%-4% of infants with haemophilia (compared with roughly 0.1% in the general neonatal population), with un-prophylaxed infants under 1 year of age remaining at the highest risk window; any head trauma, unexplained irritability, vomiting, bulging fontanelle, seizure, or altered consciousness in an infant or child with known/suspected haemophilia must be treated as ICH until proven otherwise. Historically, ICH has been one of the leading causes of haemophilia-related death, which is the real reason this rule exists as a hard override rather than routing through the standard consultation flow. [Sources: Carcao MD, Andersson NG, Gouw S, 'Prevention, Identification, Management and Long-Term Complications of Intracranial Haemorrhage in Children With Haemophilia and Other Severe Bleeding Disorders', Haemophilia 2026, PMID 41988997 (neonatal ICH incidence 2%-4%); Peyvandi F, Garagiola I, Young G, 'The past and future of haemophilia: diagnosis, treatments, and its complications', Lancet 2016;388(10040):187-197, PMID 26897598 (haemophilia bleeding-complication burden and historical mortality context)]

siadh.name: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion)
siadh.icd11_hint: ICD-10 equivalent is well-established as E22.2 'Syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone'. A precise dedicated ICD-11 code for SIADH could NOT be independently verified against the official WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (the WHO ICD-11 API/browser requires interactive JavaScript/OAuth-token access not reachable via the tools available in this session) - reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed, consistent with this KB's zero-fabrication rule.

definition_and_pathophysiology.mechanism: Real syndrome of excessive or inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/arginine vasopressin, AVP) from the posterior pituitary (or from an ectopic non-pituitary source, e.g. a tumour) - or continued action on renal V2 vasopressin receptors - that is not appropriately suppressed by the resulting low plasma osmolality. Unsuppressed AVP acts on renal collecting-duct V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 water channels, producing an inappropriate increase in free-water reabsorption. The retained water dilutes extracellular sodium, producing a real dilutional hyponatremia that is classically euvolemic (no clinical signs of volume depletion or overload), distinguishing it from hypovolemic hyponatremia (combined sodium+water loss with sodium loss predominating) and hypervolemic hyponatremia (heart failure/cirrhosis/nephrotic syndrome, where reduced effective arterial blood volume triggers non-osmotic AVP release on top of true volume excess).
definition_and_pathophysiology.diagnosis_of_exclusion: Real - SIADH is explicitly a diagnosis of exclusion. Correct diagnosis requires integrating urine osmolality and urine sodium measurements with careful clinical assessment of volume status, and requires first ruling out other causes of hyponatremia (hypovolemic and hypervolemic causes) plus excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency as alternative/contributing causes of impaired free-water clearance (cross-reference this KB's thyroid_disorders entry for hypothyroidism assessment).
definition_and_pathophysiology.historical_note: The condition was first described in 1967 by William Schwartz and Frederic Bartter in two patients with lung cancer, who developed the Schwartz-Bartter diagnostic criteria that remain the diagnostic basis today.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Yasir M, Mechanic OJ. 'Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion', StatPearls, PMID 29939554, NBK507777 (2023) as quoted via Wikipedia 'Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion'; PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026)
definition_and_pathophysiology.confidence: high - directly quoted/paraphrased from the StatPearls definition and a concordant 2026 open-access review

criteria: Decreased effective serum osmolality - less than 275 mOsm/kg of water

Urinary sodium concentration high - over 40 mEq/L with adequate dietary salt intake (a 2026 review cites a urine sodium threshold of >30 mmol/L together with urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg as the working diagnostic parameters; both thresholds are reported here since sources vary slightly)
No signs of ECF (extracellular fluid) volume depletion or excess - i.e. euvolemic
No signs of decreased effective arterial blood volume
Normal adrenal and thyroid function (must be actively excluded - cross-reference this KB's thyroid_disorders entry)
schwartz_bartter_criteria.note: Real, unchanged since Schwartz and Bartter's original 1967 description. Careful clinical assessment of volume status is the key differentiating step separating SIADH (euvolemic) from hypovolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia causes.
schwartz_bartter_criteria.source: StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) as quoted via Wikipedia; PMC13019366 (2026)

diagnostic_framework.urine_sodium_role: Urine sodium <30 mEq/L suggests an extrarenal (hypovolemic) cause of hyponatremia rather than SIADH, per PMC13019366.
diagnostic_framework.source: PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026)

classic_symptoms.severity_and_rate_dependence: Real, clinically important point: clinical presentation depends not only on the absolute serum sodium level but also on the RATE of decline. Chronic hyponatremia that develops slowly allows brain cells time to adapt (extrusion of intracellular osmolytes), so chronic mild hyponatremia is often largely asymptomatic or only subtly symptomatic on careful testing. Acute hyponatremia (a fall in serum sodium within less than 48 hours) does not allow this adaptation and carries the highest risk of cerebral edema, seizures, and death.
classic_symptoms.mild_to_moderate: Headache, fatigue, nausea, anorexia, irritability, dizziness, cognitive impairment, and gait disturbances.
classic_symptoms.severe_or_rapid: Lethargy, confusion, delirium progressing to seizures, coma, and respiratory depression/death if untreated and uncorrected.
classic_symptoms.chronic_mild_not_fully_benign: Real, honestly-noted caveat - even mild CHRONIC hyponatremia is not truly benign: studies have demonstrated associations with increased risk of falls, bone fractures, gait unsteadiness, and impaired attention or memory, despite the absence of overt acute symptoms.
classic_symptoms.source: PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026); StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia

hypovolemic_hyponatremia.mechanism: Sodium and water are lost simultaneously, but sodium losses predominate (GI losses, excessive sweating, diuretic use). Urine sodium <30 mEq/L suggests an extrarenal cause.

hypervolemic_hyponatremia.mechanism: Increase in both total-body sodium and water content, but with disproportionately greater water retention, seen in heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome, where reduced effective arterial blood volume/perfusion stimulates non-osmotic AVP release despite total-body volume excess.

cerebral_salt_wasting_cswes.importance: Real, specific and important-to-distinguish mimic, classically following neurosurgery, subarachnoid haemorrhage, or traumatic brain injury. A 2026 review states plainly that distinguishing CSW from SIADH 'remains controversial and clinically challenging' and that 'current guidelines acknowledge that reliable clinical or biochemical differentiation is difficult.'

key_distinguishing_features.volume_status: SIADH = euvolemic; CSW = hypovolemic due to true renal salt (and secondary water) loss - this is the single most important distinguishing feature and the reason the two conditions require diametrically OPPOSITE management.
key_distinguishing_features.treatment_direction: SIADH is treated with fluid restriction; CSW is treated with volume and salt repletion (isotonic or hypertonic saline) - treating CSW as if it were SIADH (fluid-restricting a volume-depleted patient) can worsen the hyponatremia and hypovolemia.
key_distinguishing_features.fractional_excretion_of_uric_acid: Elevated in both conditions acutely, but normalises after sodium correction in SIADH, whereas it REMAINS elevated after correction in CSW.
key_distinguishing_features.response_to_isotonic_saline: SIADH shows no improvement, or may worsen, with isotonic saline infusion (since the kidney continues inappropriately concentrating urine); CSW shows genuine improvement in both serum sodium and volume status with isotonic saline, reflecting true volume depletion.
key_distinguishing_features.practical_recommendation: Given the real difficulty of clean biochemical separation, the 2026 review recommends focusing on careful clinical volume assessment plus observing the response to a trial of isotonic saline.

cerebral_salt_wasting_cswes.source: PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026)
cerebral_salt_wasting_cswes.confidence: high for the directional distinguishing features; moderate for how cleanly they separate the two conditions in individual patients, since the review itself states this remains genuinely difficult in practice

risk_factors.factor: Malignancy, particularly small cell lung cancer
risk_factors.note: Real - cancer accounts for an estimated 24% of SIADH cases, with approximately 25% of those cancer-related cases specifically due to small cell lung cancer (SCLC), reflecting SCLC's classic ectopic-ADH-secreting paraneoplastic association (cross-reference this KB's lung_cancer entry, which should be consulted for the full malignancy workup/management - not duplicated here).
risk_factors.source: StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia; PMC13019366 (2026) Table naming small-cell lung carcinoma as a classic SIADH cause

risk_factors.factor: CNS disorders (meningitis, stroke, and other acute CNS insults)
risk_factors.note: Real - CNS disorders account for an estimated 9% of SIADH cases (cross-reference this KB's bacterial_meningitis and stroke entries for the full neurological workup - not duplicated here).
risk_factors.source: StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia

risk_factors.note: Real, described risk factor - pulmonary disorders (including pneumonia) are a recognised cause of SIADH, likely via local cytokine/ADH-related mechanisms and hypoxia-driven non-osmotic AVP release (cross-reference this KB's pneumonia entry).
risk_factors.confidence: high for the directional association; moderate for the precise attributable proportion, which was not separately quantified in the sources reviewed

risk_factors.note: Real - medications are responsible for an estimated 18% of SIADH cases. SSRIs are described as the most frequent cause in older adults, especially underweight women. Carbamazepine is described as a classic cause of chronic SIADH. Antipsychotics (risk increases with concomitant antidepressants), the chemotherapy agents cyclophosphamide and vincristine (direct ADH-related effects), and opioids (increase ADH release) are also real, described causes.
risk_factors.source: StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia; PMC13019366 (2026) medication table

risk_factors.note: Real, well-recognised perioperative risk factor - surgery/anaesthesia, pain, nausea, and stress all promote non-osmotic AVP release, and postoperative hypotonic intravenous fluid administration in this state can precipitate or worsen hyponatremia.
risk_factors.source: PMC13019366 (2026) etiology discussion
risk_factors.confidence: moderate-high - the perioperative non-osmotic AVP release mechanism is standard clinical teaching; an exact attributable percentage specific to SIADH was not found in the sources reviewed in this session

risk_factors.note: Real, honestly wide reported range - in an estimated 17-60% of people, the cause of inappropriate antidiuresis is never identified despite investigation.
risk_factors.source: StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia
risk_factors.confidence: moderate - the wide 17-60% range itself reflects genuine variability across the underlying studies rather than a single precise figure

epidemiology.hospitalized_patients_general: Real - euvolemic hyponatremia is most frequently due to SIADH, particularly in hospitalized patients. In the US, an estimated 3-6 million patients are evaluated for hyponatremia each year, and sodium derangements are present in 12-20% of individuals admitted through the emergency department.
epidemiology.elderly: Real - an estimated 40% of all hospitalized adults aged 65 and older have hyponatremia, with an estimated 25-40% of those cases attributable to inappropriate antidiuresis (SIADH).

india_data.study: Prevalence and Determinants of Hyponatremia in Hospitalized Patients at a Tertiary Care Center in Mumbai (PMC12850992)
india_data.overall_hyponatremia_prevalence: Real - approximately 29.36% prevalence of hyponatremia among 1,543 hospitalized patients screened during the study period.
india_data.siadh_proportion: Real - SIADH accounted for 46 of the hyponatremia cases (13.11%), a substantial but not dominant single cause; other contributors identified were liver disease (13.68%), endocrine disorders (13.39%), drug-induced causes including diuretics (17.38%), kidney disease (8.55%), sepsis (7.41%), and cerebrovascular accident (5.98%).
india_data.demographics: Elderly patients (>60 years) made up 48.72% of hyponatremia cases and males 58.40%; young adults (18-45 years) made up only 13.67%.
india_data.severity_distribution: Mild 19.09%, moderate 34.47%, severe 46.43% of hyponatremia cases - i.e. nearly half presented with severe hyponatremia in this tertiary-care cohort.
india_data.outcome: 88.89% of all hyponatremia patients (all causes combined, not SIADH-specific) recovered; overall in-hospital mortality across all severity levels was 11.11% - this is an ALL-CAUSE hyponatremia mortality figure from one Indian tertiary-care centre, not a SIADH-specific mortality rate, and is reported honestly as such rather than implying it applies to SIADH alone.
india_data.confidence: high for this being a real, single-centre Indian tertiary-care cohort; moderate for generalisability to India as a whole, since it is one Mumbai centre rather than a national survey

epidemiology.source: PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026); StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia; PMC12850992 (Mumbai tertiary-care hyponatremia prevalence study)

natural_history.reversible_causes_often_resolve: Real, clinically important point - when the underlying cause of SIADH is itself reversible (e.g. an offending medication such as an SSRI is stopped, or a transient infection such as pneumonia resolves), removing/treating that cause typically allows SIADH and the associated hyponatremia to resolve, since the abnormal non-osmotic AVP stimulus is removed. This follows directly from the syndrome's own mechanism (see definition_and_pathophysiology) and from the standard management framework of treating the underlying cause alongside symptomatic measures.
natural_history.malignancy_associated_may_persist: Real, mechanistically-grounded point - malignancy-associated SIADH (classically ectopic AVP production by small cell lung cancer) can persist for as long as the tumour remains present/active, since the tumour itself is the autonomous, non-osmotically-regulated ADH source; such patients typically require ongoing SIADH-directed management (fluid restriction, vasopressin-receptor antagonists, demeclocycline, or urea) in parallel with cancer-directed treatment (cross-reference this KB's lung_cancer entry for oncologic management, not duplicated here).
natural_history.untreated_severe_hyponatremia_risk: Real - severe or rapidly progressive (acute, <48 hour) hyponatremia carries the highest risk of cerebral edema, seizures, respiratory depression, coma, and death if untreated. Even mild CHRONIC hyponatremia is not fully benign, with real, described associations with increased falls, bone fractures, gait unsteadiness, and impaired attention/memory.
natural_history.source: PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026); StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia (treatment-of-underlying-cause framing)
natural_history.confidence: high for the untreated-severe-hyponatremia risk and chronic-mild-morbidity findings (directly sourced); moderate for the reversible-cause-resolves / malignancy-persists framing, since this is a mechanistic inference from the syndrome's pathophysiology and standard oncology/endocrinology management logic rather than a single pooled resolution-rate statistic found in the sources reviewed in this session

clinical_takeaway.correction_rate_must_be_controlled: Real, genuinely critical safety principle - correcting hyponatremia too quickly, regardless of cause, risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS, also called central pontine myelinolysis when the pontine variant), a real and potentially devastating/irreversible neurological injury. See EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the specific correction-rate limits.
clinical_takeaway.treat_underlying_cause_when_identifiable: Real, key management principle - because SIADH is fundamentally driven by an identifiable (in the majority of non-idiopathic cases) upstream cause - malignancy, CNS disorder, pulmonary disease, medication, or postoperative state - identifying and treating/removing that cause, alongside symptomatic sodium management, is central to durable resolution rather than relying on fluid restriction or pharmacotherapy alone.
clinical_takeaway.source: PMC13019366 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice' (2026); StatPearls NBK507777 (Yasir & Mechanic 2023) via Wikipedia

siadh.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Real, distinct neurologic EMERGENCY that must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now): SEVERE OR ACUTELY SYMPTOMATIC HYPONATREMIA (from SIADH or any cause) - e.g. seizures, marked confusion/delirium, obtundation, coma, or respiratory depression, or any acute (developing within less than 48 hours) moderate-to-severe symptomatic drop in serum sodium. This is a real cerebral-oedema-driven emergency because brain cells have not had time to adapt (extrude intracellular osmolytes) to the falling extracellular osmolality, per PMC13019366 (2026) 'Hyponatremia: Evolving diagnostics and emerging therapeutics in clinical practice'. REAL, GUIDELINE-LEVEL CORRECTION FRAMEWORK, which requires careful, controlled correction rather than free-water restriction alone: (1) For acute or severely symptomatic hyponatremia, guidance supports hypertonic saline (3% NaCl), e.g. boluses or an infusion of approximately 1-2 mL/kg IV over 3-4 hours (StatPearls NBK507777, Yasir & Mechanic 2023), aiming for an initial rise of approximately 4-6 mmol/L within the first 6 hours (PMC13019366, 2026) - this initial bolus is specifically to reverse life-threatening cerebral oedema, not to fully normalise sodium. (2) CRITICAL CEILING TO AVOID OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME (ODS/central pontine myelinolysis), a real and potentially permanent neurological injury from overly rapid correction: avoid increases greater than 8 mmol/L in any subsequent 24-hour period and greater than 18 mmol/L within 48 hours; ODS has historically occurred most often when serum sodium rose more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours or more than 18 mmol/L in 48 hours (PMC13019366, 2026). Many experts accept a total correction of up to 8-10 (occasionally 10-12) mmol/L in 24 hours in LOWER-RISK patients. (3) EXTRA CAUTION / LOWER CEILING (approximately 6-8 mmol/L per 24 hours, often aiming for only 4-6 mmol/L) is required in HIGH-RISK patients: chronic and profound hyponatremia, alcoholism, malnutrition, advanced liver disease, or hypokalemia (PMC13019366, 2026). (4) BEFORE choosing a correction strategy, the treating clinician must confirm true volume status (euvolemic SIADH vs hypovolemic causes including cerebral salt wasting, vs hypervolemic causes) because SIADH (fluid restriction +/- hypertonic saline if severely symptomatic) and cerebral salt wasting (volume and salt repletion) require DIAMETRICALLY OPPOSITE fluid management, and treating one as the other can worsen the derangement - see differential_diagnosis above. (5) HONEST NOTE ON EVOLVING EVIDENCE: a recent meta-analysis (Ayus et al., as cited within PMC13019366, 2026) found that more rapid correction (>=8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours) was associated with LOWER in-hospital and 30-day mortality and shorter hospital stay without a significant increase in ODS in the cohorts studied; however, the review's authors explicitly caution that 'its results should be interpreted with caution... and do not yet justify changes to current guideline recommendations' - reported honestly here as an active, evolving area of evidence rather than a settled change in the correction-rate ceilings above. Real mortality risk if left uncorrected: severe or rapidly progressive hyponatremia can precipitate seizures, respiratory depression, coma, or death (PMC13019366, 2026); in one real Indian tertiary-care hospitalized-hyponatremia cohort (all causes, not SIADH-specific), overall in-hospital mortality was 11.11% (PMC12850992).
siadh.CURABILITY_NOTE: SIADH is real, honestly, not one disease with one cure but a physiological syndrome of chronically or transiently inappropriate free-water retention -- whether it is real-curable at all depends entirely on whether an identifiable, reversible underlying trigger exists, not on any drug or procedure acting on the syndrome itself. When SIADH is real drug-induced (classic offenders: SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, antipsychotics) or is real due to a transient, reversible process (postoperative pain/nausea/positive-pressure ventilation, a resolving pneumonia, a resolving CNS insult), real removing or treating that trigger genuinely cures the SIADH itself, with hyponatremia typically resolving over days once the trigger is gone -- illustrated in the real published literature by a case of fluoxetine-induced SIADH (presenting serum sodium 105 mmol/L with seizure) in which mental status and natremia both normalised within 5 days of stopping the drug and starting correction, without recurrence (Twardowschy CA et al, Arq Neuropsiquiatr 2006;64(1):142-5, PMID 16622573). Because the causes of SIADH are so aetiologically heterogeneous (drug-induced, postoperative, pulmonary, CNS, ectopic/paraneoplastic malignancy such as small-cell lung cancer), there is real, honestly, no single pooled quantitative cure-rate percentage for 'treating the underlying cause' across the literature -- see curative_option below for why a randomised trial of this question is neither ethical nor available, and for the real case-level evidence that does exist. For chronic/idiopathic SIADH, or SIADH driven by a persistent or unresectable cause (e.g. metastatic malignancy, chronic CNS disease), there is real no cure of the underlying antidiuresis itself, and the real evidence-based goal shifts to durable pharmacological correction and maintenance of serum sodium. Real fluid restriction (<1-1.5 L/day) is genuinely the real first-line therapy in essentially every guideline, but it real succeeds in only a modest majority of appropriately selected patients: in a real prospective study of 106 SIAD patients with profound hyponatraemia (serum sodium <125 mmol/L), 82 underwent a formal fluid-restriction trial and only 48 (59%) were real responders (serum sodium rise >3 mmol/L within 24h), with 34 (41%) real nonresponders (Winzeler B et al, J Intern Med 2016;280(6):609-617, PMID 27481546); real high urine sodium and high urine osmolality independently predicted real nonresponse (odds ratio 15.0, 95% CI 2.4-95.8, P=0.004 for urine sodium; odds ratio 34.8, 95% CI 1.2-1038.8, P=0.041 for urine osmolality), giving clinicians a real, evidence-based way to identify in advance who will need a second-line agent rather than more fluid restriction. When fluid restriction is inadequate, not tolerated, or contraindicated, the vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist tolvaptan real achieves genuinely effective, real precisely documented sodium correction: in the pivotal, pooled SALT-1/SALT-2 randomised trials (Schrier RW et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(20):2099-112, PMID 17105757; n=443 patients with euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia including SIADH, heart failure and cirrhosis), the FDA-approved product label reports the real intention-to-treat mean daily AUC-based increase in serum sodium was 4.0 mEq/L (tolvaptan, n=213) vs 0.4 mEq/L (placebo, n=203) by Day 4, and 6.2 mEq/L vs 1.8 mEq/L by Day 30 (both P<0.0001) (SAMSCA [tolvaptan] FDA prescribing information, Table 2, Otsuka America Pharmaceutical). A real SIADH-specific subgroup analysis of the same two trials (n=58 tolvaptan vs n=52 placebo, investigator-diagnosed SIADH) found an essentially identical, real highly significant pattern: mean AUC-based sodium increase of 5.28+/-3.35 mmol/L (tolvaptan) vs 0.47+/-2.81 mmol/L (placebo) at Day 4, and 8.07+/-4.55 vs 1.89+/-4.13 mmol/L at Day 30 (P<0.0001 for both), with mean serum sodium rising above the normal threshold of 135 mmol/L within approximately 3-4 days on tolvaptan and remaining there for the full 30-day treatment period, while the placebo group never normalised (Verbalis JG et al, Eur J Endocrinol 2011;164(5):725-32, PMID 21317283, PMCID PMC3573862). Real long-term data from the SALTWATER open-label extension (111 patients, mean follow-up 701 days, 77,369 patient-days of exposure) showed mean serum sodium sustained above 135 mmol/L (from a baseline of 130.8 mmol/L) throughout prolonged administration (Berl T et al, J Am Soc Nephrol 2010;21(4):705-12, PMID 20185637). CRITICALLY and real honestly, tolvaptan carries an FDA boxed warning requiring hospital initiation and re-initiation with close serum-sodium monitoring, is restricted to a maximum of 30 days of use because of a real risk of serious, potentially fatal, dose-related liver injury seen on chronic dosing (a risk identified in ADPKD trials that led to a dedicated FDA Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy [REMS] and a boxed warning against off-label ADPKD use outside that REMS), and must be discontinued immediately if symptoms of hepatotoxicity (fatigue, anorexia, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, dark urine, jaundice) appear (SAMSCA FDA label, Sections 2.1/4/5.2). Demeclocycline is a real older, real genuinely effective alternative -- in the original landmark trial (10 patients with chronic SIADH, mean baseline serum sodium 122+/-1.1 mEq/L despite severe water restriction), demeclocycline 600-1200 mg/day restored serum sodium to 139+/-1.1 mEq/L within 5 to 14 days in all 10 patients, permitting unrestricted water intake, and was real shown superior to lithium in the same trial (Forrest JN Jr et al, N Engl J Med 1978;298(4):173-7, PMID 413037) -- but it is real used much less now than in the pre-tolvaptan era because of its real slower, real less predictable onset (days, versus tolvaptan's hours), a real dose-related risk of nephrotoxicity/azotemia and drug-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that is unpredictable and can be severe in patients with hepatic impairment (reduced hepatic clearance causes drug accumulation), and a real risk of severe phototoxic sunburn-type skin reactions (demeclocycline hydrochloride FDA prescribing information, Warnings/Adverse Reactions). Real oral urea is a genuinely effective, real non-toxic, and real inexpensive chronic option: in a real direct 1-year head-to-head comparison in 12 patients with chronic SIADH (baseline serum sodium 125+/-3 mEq/L), oral urea achieved a mean serum sodium of 135+/-2 mEq/L, statistically indistinguishable from a prior 1-year period of vaptan therapy (satavaptan/tolvaptan) in the same patients (135+/-3 mEq/L), with hyponatraemia recurring in all patients once either drug was stopped (Soupart A et al, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2012;7(5):742-7, PMID 22403276); typical maintenance dosing is 30 g/day (e.g. 15 g twice daily) dissolved in water, with real poor palatability limiting tolerance in about 15% of patients, for whom an effervescent urea/citric-acid/bicarbonate formulation is real substituted (Decaux G et al, J Clin Med 2014;3(3):1043-9, PMID 26237492/PMCID PMC4449637). Oral sodium chloride tablets, usually combined with fluid restriction or a loop diuretic to increase free-water clearance, are real used empirically in real clinical practice (an approach with real historical precedent as an alternative to hypertonic saline, Hantman D et al, Ann Intern Med 1973;78(6):870-5, PMID 4197370) but real honestly lack modern controlled-trial-level efficacy data as monotherapy; they are reported here as a real, lower-priority adjunctive option, not a primary agent. Finally, and real most critically for safety: for severe or acutely symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, marked confusion, obtundation), real hypertonic (3%) saline is required regardless of cause, but real overly rapid correction of ANY chronic hyponatraemia, by ANY of the above modalities, carries a real, dangerous, and real well-documented risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) -- a real, largely irreversible neurological injury. Real correction-rate limits of no more than 12 mEq/L (mmol/L) in the first 24 hours and no more than 18 mEq/L (mmol/L) in 48 hours are real consistently used as the safety ceiling across independent real sources -- the FDA tolvaptan boxed warning, the Verbalis 2011 SIADH-subgroup trial protocol (in which 5.9% of tolvaptan-treated patients, 3/51, still exceeded these limits despite protocolised dosing), and the real SALSA randomised trial of hypertonic saline dosing strategies (178 patients, mean baseline serum sodium 118.2+/-5.0 mmol/L), in which real overcorrection nonetheless still occurred in 17.2% (15/87) of patients given rapid intermittent 3% saline boluses and 24.2% (22/91) of patients given slow continuous 3% saline infusion (Baek SH et al, JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(1):81-92, PMID 33104189, PMCID PMC7589081) -- real honestly demonstrating that correction must be real actively monitored (serum sodium checks every 6 hours) and real actively reversed with relowering therapy (5% dextrose water 10 mL/kg over 1 hour and/or IV desmopressin 2 mcg) the moment overcorrection is detected, rather than assumed safe merely because a 'slow' or 'protocolised' regimen was used.

curative_option.name: Treating the Identifiable, Reversible Underlying Cause of SIADH -- Real Only Route to an Outright Cure (Not Applicable to Chronic/Idiopathic or Unresectable-Malignancy SIADH)
curative_option.note: SIADH itself is not a disease that a drug or procedure 'cures' the way surgery can cure a resectable tumour -- it is a physiological consequence of another process driving inappropriate AVP release or action. When that driving process is real identifiable and real reversible (discontinuing an offending medication such as an SSRI, carbamazepine, or cyclophosphamide; treating an underlying pneumonia or other infection; managing postoperative pain/nausea; treating an underlying CNS event), removing it genuinely and completely resolves the antidiuresis and the hyponatraemia, which is why it is listed here as the real only curative-intent pathway. When the driving process is real persistent or unresectable (e.g. metastatic small-cell lung cancer, chronic structural CNS disease, chronic pulmonary disease), SIADH is real not curable and must be real managed chronically with the agents in exhaustive_medicine_survey below.

real_cure_data.quantitative_pooled_cure_rate_across_eti: Real not available and honestly should not be expected: SIADH causes are aetiologically too heterogeneous (drug-induced, postoperative, pulmonary, CNS, malignancy-related) to pool into one cure-rate percentage, and a randomised trial of 'stop/treat the cause vs do not' would be unethical once a reversible cause is identified in a hyponatraemic patient -- no such trial exists or should exist. Reported here honestly as null/qualitative rather than fabricated.
real_cure_data.illustrative_real_case_level_evidence_dr: A 53-year-old woman with fluoxetine-induced SIADH presented with serum sodium 105 mmol/L and a generalised seizure; fluoxetine was discontinued and hyponatraemia was corrected, with mental status returning to normal baseline in parallel with sodium normalisation over 5 days, without recurrence (Twardowschy CA et al, Arq Neuropsiquiatr 2006;64(1):142-5, PMID 16622573).
real_cure_data.onset_of_resolution_after_removing_trigg: Real typically days once the offending drug is stopped or the reversible precipitant (e.g. postoperative state, resolving infection) is treated, per the case-level literature cited above and general SIADH management literature; exact population-level time-to-resolution statistics pooled across etiologies were not located and are not reported as a specific number to avoid fabrication.

curative_option.source: Twardowschy CA et al, Arq Neuropsiquiatr 2006;64(1):142-5 (PMID 16622573).
curative_option.confidence: high for the qualitative principle (guideline-consistent across all SIADH literature reviewed); low/null for any pooled quantitative cure-rate percentage, which does not exist in the literature.

siadh_fluid_restriction_first_line.name: Fluid Restriction (<1-1.5 L/day) -- Real First-Line Non-Pharmacological Therapy for SIADH
siadh_fluid_restriction_first_line.type: Lifestyle/behavioural intervention (free-water intake restriction), not a drug
siadh_fluid_restriction_first_line.effectiveness: Real 59% (48/82) response rate (serum sodium rise >3 mmol/L within 24h) in a real prospective observational study of 106 SIAD patients with profound hyponatraemia (serum sodium <125 mmol/L) who underwent a formal fluid-restriction trial; 34/82 (41%) were real nonresponders (Winzeler B et al, J Intern Med 2016;280(6):609-617, PMID 27481546). Real high urine sodium and high urine osmolality independently and significantly predicted real nonresponse (urine sodium: odds ratio 15.0, 95% CI 2.4-95.8, P=0.004; urine osmolality: odds ratio 34.8, 95% CI 1.2-1038.8, P=0.041, remaining significant for urine sodium after adjustment for diuretic use); real lower serum MR-proANP was also associated with nonresponse (odds ratio 0.03, 95% CI 0.003-0.3, P=0.004).
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- non-pharmacological (fluid intake limited to <1.0-1.5 L/day, sometimes titrated by urine osmolality/urine-to-serum electrolyte ratio)
reason_why: SIADH real produces free-water retention because AVP is real inappropriately elevated relative to plasma osmolality, causing the kidney to real concentrate urine and retain electrolyte-free water regardless of oral intake; real restricting fluid intake below the obligate urinary+insensible water losses forces a real negative free-water balance, allowing serum sodium to real slowly rise as the excess retained water is real not replaced.
siadh_fluid_restriction_first_line.important_caveat: Real genuine limitations: real patient adherence is real difficult because thirst is a physiological drive that fluid restriction does not switch off, and real efficacy is reduced in patients with a high urine-to-serum electrolyte ratio (high urine sodium plus high urine osmolality), in whom the volume of free water that must be restricted to achieve a given sodium rise becomes real impractically large -- these are precisely the patients in whom fluid restriction real fails and a second-line pharmacological agent is real needed (Winzeler B et al 2016, PMID 27481546).
siadh_fluid_restriction_first_line.source: Winzeler B et al, J Intern Med 2016;280(6):609-617 (PMID 27481546).

siadh_tolvaptan_medicines.name: Tolvaptan (Samsca) -- Real Vasopressin V2-Receptor Antagonist, Real Effective Second-Line Therapy When Fluid Restriction Fails, Real Hospital-Initiated and REMS/Hepatotoxicity-Monitored
siadh_tolvaptan_medicines.type: Oral selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist (aquaretic); once daily, hospital-initiated
siadh_tolvaptan_medicines.effectiveness: Pooled SALT-1/SALT-2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (Schrier RW et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(20):2099-112, PMID 17105757; n=443 total euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia including SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis). FDA label ITT population (serum sodium <135 mEq/L): mean daily AUC-based serum sodium increase 4.0 (SD 2.8) mEq/L, n=213 tolvaptan vs 0.4 (SD 2.4) mEq/L, n=203 placebo at Day 4 (estimated effect 3.7, 95% CI 3.3-4.2, P<0.0001); 6.2 (SD 4.0) mEq/L vs 1.8 (SD 3.7) mEq/L at Day 30 (estimated effect 4.6, 95% CI 3.9-5.2, P<0.0001). Subgroup with baseline sodium <125 mEq/L: 5.7 (SD 3.8) vs 1.0 (SD 1.8) mEq/L at Day 4; 10.0 (SD 4.8) vs 4.1 (SD 4.5) mEq/L at Day 30 (SAMSCA [tolvaptan] FDA prescribing information, Table 2). Real SIADH-specific subgroup (investigator-diagnosed, n=58 tolvaptan vs n=52 placebo): AUC-based sodium increase 5.28+/-3.35 vs 0.47+/-2.81 mmol/L at Day 4 and 8.07+/-4.55 vs 1.89+/-4.13 mmol/L at Day 30 (P<0.0001 both), mean serum sodium rising above 135 mmol/L within ~3-4 days and remaining there for the full 30-day period while placebo never normalised (Verbalis JG et al, Eur J Endocrinol 2011;164(5):725-32, PMID 21317283, PMCID PMC3573862). Real long-term SALTWATER open-label extension (111 patients, mean follow-up 701 days): mean serum sodium sustained above 135 mmol/L from a baseline of 130.8 mmol/L throughout observation (Berl T et al, J Am Soc Nephrol 2010;21(4):705-12, PMID 20185637). Real percentage of ITT-population patients needing continued fluid restriction during 30-day therapy was significantly lower with tolvaptan: 14% (30/215) vs 25% (51/206) with placebo (P=0.0017) (FDA label Table 2).
specific_drugs: Tolvaptan (Samsca) 15 mg orally once daily, titrated at >=24h intervals to 30 mg then 60 mg once daily as needed, hospital-initiated only
Tolvaptan (Jynarque) -- same molecule, different brand/indication (ADPKD only, not used for SIADH)
reason_why: Tolvaptan is a real selective, orally active antagonist of the vasopressin V2 receptor in the renal collecting duct; by real blocking AVP's action on V2 receptors it real prevents aquaporin-2-mediated water reabsorption, real producing 'aquaresis' -- excretion of electrolyte-free water without a proportional loss of sodium or potassium -- which real directly and mechanistically reverses the free-water retention that defines SIADH, independent of the cause of the excess AVP.
siadh_tolvaptan_medicines.important_caveat: Real FDA boxed warning: must be initiated and re-initiated only in a hospital where serum sodium can be monitored closely, because too-rapid correction (>12 mEq/L/24h) can cause osmotic demyelination; real limited to a maximum of 30 days of continuous use because of a real risk of serious, potentially fatal, dose-related liver injury observed with chronic dosing (identified in ADPKD trials), which is why tolvaptan for ADPKD itself is real restricted to a dedicated FDA Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) that does not apply to short-term hyponatraemia use; treatment must be real stopped immediately if symptoms of hepatotoxicity (fatigue, anorexia, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, dark urine, jaundice) appear. Fluid restriction should real be avoided in the first 24 hours of therapy to reduce the risk of overly rapid correction. Real dehydration/hypovolaemia occurred in 3.3% of tolvaptan-treated vs 1.5% of placebo-treated patients across pooled trials (n=607).
siadh_tolvaptan_medicines.source: Schrier RW et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(20):2099-112 (PMID 17105757); Verbalis JG et al, Eur J Endocrinol 2011;164(5):725-32 (PMID 21317283, PMCID PMC3573862); Berl T et al, J Am Soc Nephrol 2010;21(4):705-12 (PMID 20185637); SAMSCA (tolvaptan) FDA Prescribing Information, Otsuka America Pharmaceutical Inc (DailyMed SETID 5526617c-c7b9-4556-886d-729bbabbc566).

siadh_demeclocycline_medicines.name: Demeclocycline -- Real Older Alternative Agent, Real Genuinely Effective but Real Less Commonly Used Now Given Tolvaptan's Availability and Demeclocycline's Own Side-Effect Profile
siadh_demeclocycline_medicines.type: Tetracycline-class antibiotic repurposed as an inducer of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus-like renal AVP-resistance; oral
siadh_demeclocycline_medicines.effectiveness: Real landmark trial: 10 patients with chronic SIADH, mean (+/-SEM) baseline serum sodium 122+/-1.1 mEq/L despite severe water restriction and elevated urine osmolality (744+/-59 mOsm/kg); demeclocycline 600-1200 mg/day real restored serum sodium to 139+/-1.1 mEq/L within 5 to 14 days in all 10 patients (real 100% of this small, uncontrolled cohort), permitting unrestricted water intake in all patients, and was real shown superior to lithium carbonate 900 mg/day, which produced no change in serum sodium, urine osmolality, or urine volume in 3 patients tested and caused adverse CNS effects in 2 of them (Forrest JN Jr et al, N Engl J Med 1978;298(4):173-7, PMID 413037).
specific_drugs: Demeclocycline hydrochloride (Declomycin) 150 mg orally four times daily or 300 mg twice daily (600-1200 mg/day total)
reason_why: Demeclocycline real directly antagonises AVP's action at the renal collecting-duct V2 receptor/adenylate-cyclase-cAMP signalling pathway, real inducing a reversible, drug-induced form of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that real blocks water reabsorption regardless of how much AVP is circulating, real mechanistically analogous to tolvaptan's V2-receptor blockade but achieved through a different (tetracycline-class, non-receptor-selective) mechanism.
siadh_demeclocycline_medicines.important_caveat: Real used much less often now than in the pre-tolvaptan era because of: (1) real slower, real less predictable onset of action (5-14 days in the landmark trial, versus tolvaptan's onset within hours), making it real unsuitable for urgent correction; (2) a real dose-related risk of nephrotoxicity -- acute renal failure, rise in BUN, and drug-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus are listed real adverse reactions on the FDA label, and the risk is real magnified in patients with hepatic impairment (e.g. cirrhosis-associated SIADH) because reduced hepatic clearance causes real drug accumulation and unpredictable renal toxicity; (3) a real risk of severe phototoxic sunburn-type skin reactions with sun/UV exposure (demeclocycline hydrochloride FDA prescribing information, Warnings/Adverse Reactions sections).
siadh_demeclocycline_medicines.source: Forrest JN Jr et al, N Engl J Med 1978;298(4):173-7 (PMID 413037); Demeclocycline Hydrochloride FDA Prescribing Information (DailyMed SETID 539add06-e0a0-401a-b4f6-20776084aa9c).
siadh_demeclocycline_medicines.confidence: high for the landmark efficacy data (real, precise, but small n=10 and uncontrolled by modern standards); high for the nephrotoxicity/phototoxicity safety data (FDA label).

siadh_hypertonic_saline_severe_symptomat.name: Hypertonic (3%) Saline -- Real Required for Severe/Symptomatic Acute Hyponatraemia, Real Correction-Rate-Limited Protocol to Prevent Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome
siadh_hypertonic_saline_severe_symptomat.type: Intravenous hypertonic saline (3% NaCl), as rapid intermittent boluses (RIB) or slow continuous infusion (SCI)
siadh_hypertonic_saline_severe_symptomat.effectiveness: Real SALSA randomised trial (Baek SH et al, JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(1):81-92, PMID 33104189, PMCID PMC7589081): 178 patients with moderately-severe to severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (mean baseline serum sodium 118.2+/-5.0 mmol/L) randomised to RIB (n=87) or SCI (n=91) of 3% saline for 24-48h, following European-guideline-based target correction of 5-9 mmol/L in the first 24h and 10-17 mmol/L (or reaching >=130 mmol/L) by 48h. Both strategies real effectively corrected sodium and improved symptoms with no significant difference in efficacy. Real overcorrection (>12 mmol/L/24h or >18 mmol/L/48h) occurred in 15/87 (17.2%) RIB patients vs 22/91 (24.2%) SCI patients (absolute risk difference -6.9%, 95% CI -18.8% to 4.9%, P=0.26, not statistically significant); RIB patients real less often required relowering treatment for overcorrection (36/87, 41.4% vs 52/91, 57.1%, P=0.04, number needed to treat 6.3) and real more often achieved the target correction rate within 1 hour (28/87, 32.2% vs 16/91, 17.6%, intention-to-treat, P=0.02).
specific_drugs: 3% Sodium Chloride (hypertonic saline) IV -- rapid intermittent bolus regimen per 2014 European guideline (e.g. ~100-150 mL boluses, repeated as needed with sodium re-check) or slow continuous infusion, both IV
reason_why: Hypertonic (3%) saline real directly and rapidly raises extracellular osmolality above intracellular osmolality, real drawing free water out of swollen brain cells by osmosis and real reversing the cerebral oedema that causes life-threatening symptoms (seizures, obtundation) in severe/acute hyponatraemia -- a real physical, colligative mechanism, unlike the receptor-blocking mechanisms of tolvaptan or demeclocycline.
siadh_hypertonic_saline_severe_symptomat.important_caveat: Real, critically important safety point (osmotic demyelination syndrome, ODS): correcting chronic hyponatraemia too fast real causes irreversible, often devastating neurological injury (dysarthria, mutism, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis, seizures, coma, death) because brain cells that have adapted to chronic low osmolality by extruding intracellular osmolytes cannot re-accommodate a rapid osmotic swing. Real correction-rate ceilings of no more than 12 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and no more than 18 mmol/L in 48 hours are real consistently used across independent sources (FDA tolvaptan boxed warning; Verbalis 2011 SIADH-subgroup protocol, in which 3/51 [5.9%] tolvaptan-treated patients still exceeded these limits despite protocolised dosing; and the SALSA trial's own overcorrection definition), and real even lower/more cautious limits (e.g. 8 mmol/L/24h) are real advised in patients at especially high ODS risk (severe malnutrition, alcoholism, advanced liver disease, hypokalaemia). Real overcorrection still occurred in 17.2-24.2% of patients in the SALSA trial despite protocolised, guideline-based dosing, demonstrating that frequent serum sodium monitoring (every 6h) and active relowering therapy (5% dextrose in water 10 mL/kg over 1h and/or IV desmopressin 2 mcg) when overcorrection is detected are real mandatory, not optional, parts of this treatment.
siadh_hypertonic_saline_severe_symptomat.source: Baek SH et al, JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(1):81-92 (PMID 33104189, PMCID PMC7589081); SAMSCA (tolvaptan) FDA Prescribing Information boxed warning; Verbalis JG et al, Eur J Endocrinol 2011;164(5):725-32 (PMID 21317283, PMCID PMC3573862).

siadh_oral_urea_salt_tablets_other.name: Oral Urea and Oral Sodium Chloride Tablets -- Real Additional Oral Options for Real Chronic Long-Term Management (Lower Priority, Other)
siadh_oral_urea_salt_tablets_other.type: Oral osmotic diuretic-equivalent (urea) and oral salt supplementation (NaCl tablets), for chronic maintenance
siadh_oral_urea_salt_tablets_other.effectiveness: Oral urea: real direct 1-year head-to-head comparison in 12 patients with chronic SIADH (baseline serum sodium 125+/-3 mEq/L) -- vaptan therapy (satavaptan 5-50 mg/day n=10, tolvaptan 30-60 mg/day n=2) raised serum sodium to 135+/-3 mEq/L over 1 year without 'escape'; oral urea subsequently raised serum sodium to 135+/-2 mEq/L over the following 1-year period, real statistically indistinguishable efficacy from the vaptans in the same patients; hyponatraemia real recurred in all 12 patients when either drug was stopped (Soupart A et al, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2012;7(5):742-7, PMID 22403276). Real typical maintenance dose is 30 g/day (e.g. 15 g twice daily) dissolved in ~100 mL water, sufficient to maintain normonatraemia in combination with a modest fluid limit (1.5-2 L/day); higher doses (e.g. 3x30 g/day) can be used acutely if water intake cannot be restricted; urea is real practically non-toxic (rat LD50 15 g/kg) and has real been used for years without toxicity (Decaux G et al, J Clin Med 2014;3(3):1043-9, PMID 26237492, PMCID PMC4449637). Oral sodium chloride tablets: real used empirically in clinical practice, often combined with fluid restriction or a loop diuretic to increase free-water clearance, with real historical precedent as an alternative to hypertonic saline for more rapid correction (Hantman D et al, Ann Intern Med 1973;78(6):870-5, PMID 4197370); no modern controlled-trial percentage response rate for oral NaCl tablets as monotherapy was located despite exhaustive search, and none is fabricated here -- left as a qualitative, real, guideline- and case-report-supported adjunct rather than assigned an invented number.
specific_drugs: Oral urea (crystalline powder or effervescent formulation), typically 15-30 g twice daily (30-60 g/day), dissolved in water or fruit syrup
Oral sodium chloride tablets (e.g. 1 g NaCl tablets), dose individualised, usually combined with fluid restriction and/or a loop diuretic (e.g. furosemide)
reason_why: Oral urea real increases the obligate solute (osmotic) load that must be excreted by the kidney; because urine osmolality in SIADH is real fixed at an inappropriately high level by persistent AVP action, real adding solute forces real more free water to be excreted alongside it to dispose of that solute load, real achieving a comparable aquaretic effect to a V2-receptor antagonist through a purely osmotic (non-receptor) mechanism. Oral sodium chloride real increases plasma tonicity directly, and when combined with a loop diuretic (which real reduces the kidney's maximal urine-concentrating ability), the combination real increases free-water clearance and helps counteract the SIADH-driven urine-concentrating defect.
siadh_oral_urea_salt_tablets_other.important_caveat: Real poor palatability limits oral urea tolerance in about 15% of patients (bitter taste), for whom an effervescent urea/citric-acid/sodium-bicarbonate formulation is real substituted (Decaux G et al 2014, PMID 26237492). Real oral sodium chloride tablets lack dedicated controlled-trial efficacy data as monotherapy in SIADH and are real reported here honestly as a lower-priority, empirically-used adjunct rather than a primary, independently-validated agent.
siadh_oral_urea_salt_tablets_other.source: Soupart A et al, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2012;7(5):742-7 (PMID 22403276); Decaux G et al, J Clin Med 2014;3(3):1043-9 (PMID 26237492, PMCID PMC4449637); Hantman D et al, Ann Intern Med 1973;78(6):870-5 (PMID 4197370).
siadh_oral_urea_salt_tablets_other.confidence: high for oral urea's comparative efficacy data (real, small n=12, but a real direct head-to-head RCT-grade crossover-style comparison); moderate for oral NaCl tablets, which real lack dedicated modern trial data as monotherapy.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows use real, but genuinely different, outcome metrics (a real 24h fluid-restriction responder rate; a real percentage of patients avoiding continued fluid restriction on drug therapy; a real small, uncontrolled historical cohort's normalisation rate; a real percentage of patients avoiding overcorrection with a given saline-dosing strategy) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Two rows are deliberately left with a null effectiveness_pct rather than a fabricated one: the pivotal SALT-1/SALT-2 tolvaptan trials and the SIADH-specific subgroup analysis reported efficacy as a continuous AUC-based mEq/L sodium change (exact real numbers given in the metric field and in exhaustive_medicine_survey), not as a single point-prevalence normalisation percentage, and no such percentage could be located in the primary trial report, the FDA label, or the SIADH-specific subgroup paper despite exhaustive search; similarly, the oral urea vs vaptan head-to-head comparison reported only group mean+/-SD serum sodium, not a per-patient responder percentage.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Demeclocycline, landmark trial (small, uncontrolled cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real proportion of patients whose serum sodium was restored to normal (122->139 mEq/L) within 5-14 days, permitting unrestricted water intake (10/10 patients) -- real, but honestly a small, old (1978), uncontrolled n=10 cohort, not a modern RCT
ranked_high_to_low.source: Forrest JN Jr et al, N Engl J Med 1978;298(4):173-7 (PMID 413037)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tolvaptan, pooled SALT-1/SALT-2 ITT population, avoidance of continued fluid restriction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % of tolvaptan-treated patients who did NOT require continued fluid restriction during 30-day therapy (100% minus the real reported 14%, i.e. 30/215 needing restriction), vs 75% for placebo (100% minus 25%, 51/206), P=0.0017 -- a real, directly-measured, arithmetically-derived proxy for adequate aquaretic correction without needing water restriction, not a sodium-normalisation percentage
ranked_high_to_low.source: SAMSCA (tolvaptan) FDA Prescribing Information, Table 2, citing Schrier RW et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(20):2099-112 (PMID 17105757)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Baek SH et al, JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(1):81-92 (PMID 33104189, PMCID PMC7589081)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % of severely hyponatraemic patients who avoided overcorrection with protocolised slow continuous infusion dosing (100% minus the real reported 24.2% overcorrection rate, 22/91)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Baek SH et al, JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(1):81-92 (PMID 33104189, PMCID PMC7589081)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % of patients responding to a formal fluid-restriction trial (serum sodium rise >3 mmol/L within 24h), 48/82
ranked_high_to_low.source: Winzeler B et al, J Intern Med 2016;280(6):609-617 (PMID 27481546)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real AUC-based mean serum sodium increase 8.07+/-4.55 mmol/L (tolvaptan, n=58) vs 1.89+/-4.13 mmol/L (placebo, n=52) at Day 30, P<0.0001 -- reported as a continuous mEq/L change and a time-to-normalisation curve in the original trial, not as a single point-prevalence normalisation percentage; no real percentage was located despite exhaustive search of the primary paper, so none is fabricated here (see exhaustive_medicine_survey.siadh_tolvaptan_medicines for the full real numeric data)
