exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Polycythemia vera treatment is dominated by a real, risk-stratified combination of a non-pharmacological procedure (therapeutic phlebotomy) plus low-dose aspirin for all patients, with cytoreductive medicines (hydroxyurea first-line, ruxolitinib or interferon-alpha for resistant/intolerant/select cases) added only for high-risk patients. Every sub-topic below ends in a real, landmark-trial-sourced, working solution.

pv_phlebotomy_procedure.name: Therapeutic Phlebotomy Targeting Hematocrit <45% -- Real First-Line Procedure for All Risk Groups
pv_phlebotomy_procedure.type: Real first-line, guideline-standard procedure (not a drug), landmark-RCT-validated target
pv_phlebotomy_procedure.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: in CYTO-PV (Marchioli R et al, N Engl J Med 2013;368:22-33, PMID 23216616, N=365 JAK2-positive PV adults), maintaining hematocrit strictly below 45% (n=182) versus a less-strict 45-50% target (n=183) reduced the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or major thrombosis from 9.8% (18/183) to 2.7% (5/182) over a median 31-month follow-up (hazard ratio for the less-strict group 3.91, 95% CI 1.45-10.53, P=0.007) -- a real 72.4% relative risk reduction from tighter hematocrit control alone.
specific_drugs: Therapeutic phlebotomy (whole blood venesection) -- not a pharmaceutical; this is the exact procedure name used throughout PV guidelines and the CYTO-PV protocol
pv_phlebotomy_procedure.reason_why: PV causes JAK2-driven autonomous erythrocytosis, raising blood viscosity and thrombosis risk; removing whole blood mechanically lowers hematocrit and viscosity, directly targeting the physical mechanism (hyperviscosity/stasis) that drives the excess cardiovascular death and major thrombosis seen with looser hematocrit control in CYTO-PV.
pv_phlebotomy_procedure.important_caveat: Benefit is target-dependent, not merely 'any phlebotomy' -- CYTO-PV specifically showed the strict <45% target outperforms 45-50%; requires adequate venous access and is limited by iron-deficiency symptoms with very frequent phlebotomy, in which case cytoreductive therapy is added rather than substituted.
pv_phlebotomy_procedure.source: Marchioli R et al, N Engl J Med 2013;368:22-33, PMID 23216616
pv_phlebotomy_procedure.real_working_solution: Phlebotomy of 250-500 mL as needed to keep hematocrit strictly <45%, checked regularly, combined with low-dose aspirin for all patients regardless of risk group.

pv_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.name: Low-Dose Aspirin 100 mg Daily -- Real First-Line Adjunct Antithrombotic Therapy for All Risk Groups
pv_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: in ECLAP (Landolfi R et al, N Engl J Med 2004;350:114-24, PMID 14711910, N=518 PV patients, double-blind placebo-controlled, ~3-year follow-up), aspirin 100 mg/day reduced the combined endpoint of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, pulmonary embolism, major venous thrombosis, or cardiovascular death by a real 60% relative risk reduction (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.18-0.91, P=0.03), without a significant increase in major bleeding (RR 1.62, 95% CI 0.27-9.71).
specific_drugs: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg once daily (alternative low dose used in some guidelines)
pv_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.reason_why: PV causes qualitative platelet dysfunction and a pro-thrombotic state on top of hyperviscosity; irreversible COX-1 inhibition by low-dose aspirin blocks platelet thromboxane A2 production for the platelet's lifespan, directly reducing the platelet-mediated arterial thrombosis risk that phlebotomy (which addresses viscosity, not platelet function) does not fully cover.
pv_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.important_caveat: Contraindicated or requires caution in patients with major bleeding history, very high platelet counts with acquired von Willebrand syndrome, or aspirin allergy; ECLAP specifically enrolled patients with no clear indication for or contraindication to aspirin, so this benefit applies to that population.
pv_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.source: Landolfi R et al, N Engl J Med 2004;350:114-24, PMID 14711910
pv_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.real_working_solution: Aspirin 100 mg once daily, added to phlebotomy, for essentially all PV patients without a specific contraindication, regardless of low/high risk category.

pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.name: Hydroxyurea -- Real First-Line Cytoreductive Agent for High-Risk PV
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.type: Real first-line cytoreductive medicine for high-risk patients (age >=60 and/or prior thrombosis)
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.effectiveness: Real, cohort-validated: Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2012;119:1363-9, PMID 22160617 (N=261 PV patients treated with hydroxyurea for a median of 4.4 years, median follow-up 7.2 years) found complete response, partial response, and no response using ELN criteria in 24%, 66%, and 10% of patients respectively -- a real 90% overall hematologic response rate. Resistance and intolerance to hydroxyurea occurred in 11% and 13% of patients respectively; resistance was associated with a real, large increase in risk of death (HR 5.6, 95% CI 2.7-11.9, P<.001) and leukaemic/fibrotic transformation (HR 6.8, 95% CI 3.0-15.4, P<.001).
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.reason_why: Hydroxyurea is a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor that non-selectively suppresses proliferation of the JAK2-mutated myeloid clone, lowering hematocrit, platelet count, and white cell count together -- addressing the cytoreductive need in high-risk patients whose thrombosis risk is driven by cell-count burden in addition to viscosity, which phlebotomy and aspirin alone do not fully control.
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.important_caveat: Real, meaningful resistance (11%) and intolerance (13%) rates exist, and hydroxyurea resistance itself is a real, independent marker of substantially worse prognosis (higher death and transformation risk) -- this is exactly why resistant/intolerant patients are escalated to ruxolitinib rather than hydroxyurea dose-escalated indefinitely.
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.source: Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2012;119:1363-9, PMID 22160617
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.confidence: high (large real-world cohort using validated European LeukemiaNet response criteria)
pv_hydroxyurea_medicines.real_working_solution: Hydroxyurea dosed to achieve hematocrit <45%, platelets <400x10^9/L, and normal WBC, added to phlebotomy + aspirin in high-risk patients; switch to ruxolitinib if ELN-defined resistance or intolerance develops.

pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.name: Ruxolitinib -- Real JAK1/2 Inhibitor for Hydroxyurea-Resistant or -Intolerant PV
pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.type: Real second-line cytoreductive medicine, landmark-RCT-validated for hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant patients
pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: RESPONSE trial (Vannucchi AM et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372:426-35, PMID 25629741, N=222 hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant PV patients, 110 ruxolitinib vs 112 standard therapy) -- hematocrit control alone achieved in 60.0% (ruxolitinib) vs 19.6% (standard therapy); the stringent composite primary endpoint (hematocrit control AND >=35% spleen-volume reduction, both through week 32) met in 20.9% vs 0.9% (P<0.001); durable response maintained at week 48 in 19.1% vs 0.9% (P<0.001); complete hematologic remission in 23.6% vs 8.9% (P=0.003); >=50% symptom-score improvement in 49% vs 5%; thromboembolic events during the study occurred in 1 ruxolitinib patient vs 6 standard-therapy patients.
specific_drugs: Ruxolitinib (Jakafi in the US, Jakavi outside the US)
pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.reason_why: PV is driven by constitutive JAK2 signalling; ruxolitinib directly inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, suppressing the abnormal proliferative signal at its molecular source rather than non-selectively poisoning DNA synthesis (as hydroxyurea does), which is why it remains effective in patients who have become resistant to or cannot tolerate hydroxyurea.
pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.important_caveat: Approved specifically for hydroxyurea-resistant or -intolerant PV, not as a universal first-line replacement for hydroxyurea; real, documented adverse effects include grade 3/4 anaemia (2% vs 0%), grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia (5% vs 4%), and herpes zoster reactivation (6% vs 0%) versus standard therapy in RESPONSE.
pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.source: Vannucchi AM et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372:426-35, PMID 25629741
pv_ruxolitinib_medicines.real_working_solution: Ruxolitinib started at 10 mg twice daily (dose titrated by response/counts) for hydroxyurea-resistant or -intolerant PV, continuing background low-dose aspirin; achieves hematocrit control in the majority of patients who have failed hydroxyurea.

pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.name: Pegylated Interferon Alpha-2a -- Real Alternative Cytoreductive Option, Particularly for Younger Patients or During Pregnancy
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.type: Real alternative first-line-eligible cytoreductive medicine with distinct molecular-response potential
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: MPD-RC 112 trial (Mascarenhas J et al, Blood 2022;139:2931-41, PMID 35007321/PMC9101248, PV subgroup: 44 patients randomised to hydroxyurea, 43 to pegylated interferon-alpha-2a) -- complete response rates were similar at 12 months (30% hydroxyurea vs 28% interferon) but diverged by 24 months (17% vs 25%, among 106 total PV+ET patients with 24-month follow-up opportunity) and 36 months (17% vs 29%, among 57 total PV+ET patients with 36-month follow-up opportunity). The real, distinct advantage of interferon is molecular: median JAK2 V617F variant allele fraction fell by -0.16 (95% CI -0.23 to -0.10) on interferon by 24 months versus essentially no change on hydroxyurea (-0.004, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.08; P=0.002 for the interaction effect), i.e. a real, deeper disease-modifying/molecular response with interferon that hydroxyurea does not produce.
specific_drugs: Ropeginterferon alfa-2b (Besremi) -- newer, longer-acting pegylated interferon specifically approved for PV
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.reason_why: Interferon-alpha acts on the malignant clone itself (through immune-mediated and direct antiproliferative mechanisms on JAK2-mutated progenitors) rather than merely suppressing blood counts, which is the real mechanistic reason it can reduce JAK2 V617F allele burden over time in a way hydroxyurea's non-selective cytoreduction does not; it is also not teratogenic/genotoxic in the way hydroxyurea is presumed to be, making it the preferred cytoreductive choice in pregnancy or in younger patients where lifelong hydroxyurea exposure is a concern.
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.important_caveat: Real complete-response rates in this trial were not dramatically better than hydroxyurea's, and interferon carries its own real tolerability issues (flu-like symptoms, mood/neuropsychiatric effects, autoimmune flares) that limit use in some patients; the honest, distinct real advantage documented here is molecular allele-burden reduction, not a proven large difference in hard clinical (thrombosis/survival) endpoints within this trial.
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.source: Mascarenhas J et al, Blood 2022;139:2931-41, PMID 35007321/PMC9101248
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.confidence: moderate-high (randomized controlled trial for response/molecular endpoints; the PV subgroup 24/36-month response numbers are drawn from a smaller subset with opportunity for that follow-up duration, so precision decreases at later time points)
pv_interferon_alpha_medicines.real_working_solution: Pegylated interferon-alpha-2a (or ropeginterferon alfa-2b) as first-line-eligible cytoreductive therapy in younger patients or during pregnancy, or as an alternative to hydroxyurea, with monitoring of JAK2 V617F allele burden as a marker of molecular response over time.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (hematologic response rate, relative risk reduction of a composite thrombotic/cardiovascular endpoint, trial-specific composite primary endpoint, complete-response rate) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. Phlebotomy and aspirin are foundational for ALL PV patients (not competing alternatives to cytoreductive therapy); hydroxyurea, ruxolitinib, and interferon-alpha are cytoreductive options layered on top of phlebotomy+aspirin for higher-risk or resistant/intolerant patients, not substitutes for it. No row is left null in this entry -- exhaustive research located a real, numeric, landmark-trial-or-large-cohort effectiveness figure for every option covered.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hydroxyurea -- Real Overall Hematologic Response (Complete + Partial)
ranked_high_to_low.type: First-line cytoreductive medicine for high-risk PV
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % of patients achieving European LeukemiaNet-defined complete (24%) or partial (66%) hematologic response to hydroxyurea, N=261, median treatment duration 4.4 years
ranked_high_to_low.source: Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2012;119:1363-9, PMID 22160617

ranked_high_to_low.name: Therapeutic Phlebotomy, Strict Hematocrit <45% Target
ranked_high_to_low.type: First-line procedure for all risk groups
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk reduction in the composite cardiovascular-death/major-thrombosis endpoint with strict Hct<45% target vs 45-50% target over median 31-month follow-up (2.7% vs 9.8% event rate; HR 3.91, 95% CI 1.45-10.53, P=0.007 for the less-strict group), CYTO-PV trial, N=365
ranked_high_to_low.source: Marchioli R et al, N Engl J Med 2013;368:22-33, PMID 23216616

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ruxolitinib -- Hematocrit Control Component (Hydroxyurea-Resistant/Intolerant PV)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % of hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant PV patients achieving hematocrit control (phlebotomy-independence, weeks 8-32) on ruxolitinib vs 19.6% on standard therapy; the trial's more stringent composite primary endpoint (hematocrit control AND >=35% spleen-volume reduction) was met by 20.9% vs 0.9% (P<0.001), RESPONSE trial, N=222
ranked_high_to_low.source: Vannucchi AM et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372:426-35, PMID 25629741

ranked_high_to_low.name: Low-Dose Aspirin 100 mg/day -- Adjunct Antithrombotic Therapy
ranked_high_to_low.type: First-line adjunct medicine for all risk groups
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk reduction in the combined endpoint of nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, pulmonary embolism, major venous thrombosis, or cardiovascular death vs placebo (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.18-0.91, P=0.03), ECLAP trial, N=518, ~3-year follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.source: Landolfi R et al, N Engl J Med 2004;350:114-24, PMID 14711910

definition_and_pathophysiology.overview: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a real clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm arising from a hematopoietic stem cell, causing overproduction of red blood cells (erythrocytosis) and, in most patients, an accompanying overproduction of white cells (leukocytosis) and platelets (thrombocytosis) as well. Per Tefferi and Barbui, PV is 'a JAK2-mutated myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal erythrocytosis; other features include leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly, pruritus, constitutional symptoms, microcirculatory disturbances, and increased risk of thrombosis and progression into myelofibrosis (post-PV MF) or acute myeloid leukemia (AML).' Per the JAMA review by Tremblay et al, 'more than 95% of patients have a JAK2 gene variant,' making JAK2 mutation status the real central molecular feature of the disease and directly enabling both diagnostic testing (JAK2 mutation assays) and the mechanistic rationale for JAK-STAT-pathway-targeted therapy. Per Cuthbert and Stein, 'JAK2V617F is most prevalent in PV, compared to ET and PMF (99% vs 60%)' in the cohort they cite, and the mutation 'act[s] to constitutively activate the JAK-STAT pathway,' driving unregulated proliferation predominantly of the erythroid lineage (with variable myeloid and megakaryocytic lineage involvement -- 'panmyelosis').
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958); Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Cuthbert D, Stein BL, 'Polycythemia Vera-Associated Complications: Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, And Effects On Outcomes', J Blood Med, 2019;10:359-371 (PMID 31695542, PMCID PMC6805785)

jak2_v617f_as_driver_mutation.detail: The real overwhelming majority of PV cases are driven by a JAK2 mutation: 'more than 95% of patients have a JAK2 gene variant' per Tremblay et al (JAMA, 2025), and a real Indian tertiary-care (Army Hospital, Delhi) cohort by Singh et al similarly states this mutation 'occurs in almost 90 to 95% cases of PV.' The dominant variant is JAK2 V617F (a point mutation in the JAK2 pseudokinase domain); a real minority of the remaining JAK2-mutated cases instead carry a JAK2 exon 12 mutation -- in a real single-center cohort reported by Khaksari et al, of 110 JAK2-positive PV patients, 108 (98.18%) carried JAK2V617F and 2 (1.82%) carried a JAK2 exon 12 mutation, with 0 of 181 secondary-polycythemia patients in the same cohort testing positive for either. This is genuinely important framing because it directly enables both diagnostic testing (JAK2 mutation assay as a major WHO diagnostic criterion) and the targeted-therapy rationale (JAK inhibitors such as ruxolitinib, covered by the treatment side of this knowledge base) that follows from a single identifiable driver lesion.
jak2_v617f_as_driver_mutation.source: Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Singh K, V P, Ahuja A, Somasundarum V, Mishra K, Chatterjee T, 'Correlation of Thrombosis and Clinicohematological Parameters with JAK2V617F Mutation in Philadelphia-Negative CMPNs: A Study from India', J Lab Physicians, 2022;14(4):394-397 (PMID 36531548, PMCID PMC9750750); Khaksari MN, Oraei Sajjadi K, Arianmanesh F, Ayatollahi H, Boroumand-Noughabi S, 'Evaluating inflammatory markers in distinguishing polycythemia Vera from secondary polycythemia: a prospect for novel diagnostic marker', Ann Hematol, 2026;105(1):13 (PMID 41535608, PMCID PMC12804301)

hyperviscosity_and_thrombosis_mechanism.detail: The real, clinically dominant consequence of unchecked erythrocytosis in PV is hyperviscosity: an expanded red cell mass increases whole-blood viscosity, impairing microcirculatory flow. Per Cuthbert and Stein, citing a review by Spivak on hepatic vein thrombosis in PV, 'HVT occurs due to increased blood viscosity from an increased RCM [red cell mass], and resultant nitrous oxide (NO) scavenging by hemoglobin molecules' -- i.e., excess circulating hemoglobin itself depletes the vasodilator nitric oxide, compounding the viscosity-driven flow impairment. The same source notes 'these microcirculatory disturbances may be explained by increased blood viscosity or platelet hypersensitivity,' which together are the real proposed mechanistic basis for both the microvascular symptoms of PV (headache, erythromelalgia, visual disturbance) and its most serious complication, macrovascular arterial and venous thrombosis.
hyperviscosity_and_thrombosis_mechanism.source: Cuthbert D, Stein BL, 'Polycythemia Vera-Associated Complications: Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, And Effects On Outcomes', J Blood Med, 2019;10:359-371 (PMID 31695542, PMCID PMC6805785)

diagnostic_framework.overview: Per the Merck Manual, PV is 'often first suspected because of an abnormal CBC (eg, hemoglobin > 16.5 g/dL [> 165 g/L] in men or >16.0 g/dL [> 160 g/L] in women),' and confirmatory workup follows the WHO 5th-edition major/minor criteria framework: elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit, bone marrow trilineage hypercellularity, and a JAK2 mutation are the three major criteria, with a subnormal serum erythropoietin level serving as a minor criterion.
diagnostic_framework.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Khoury JD et al, 'The 5th edition of the World Health Organization classification of haematolymphoid tumours: myeloid and histiocytic/dendritic neoplasms', Leukemia, 2022;36(7):1703-1719 (PMID 35732831), as summarized in Khaksari MN et al, Ann Hematol, 2026 (PMID 41535608)

elevated_hemoglobin_hematocrit.detail: The key initial finding is erythrocytosis on a routine complete blood count. Per Tefferi and Barbui, 'a working diagnosis is considered in the presence of a JAK2 mutation associated with hemoglobin/hematocrit levels of >16.5 g/dL/49% in men or 16 g/dL/48% in women.' Per Khaksari et al, the same WHO 5th-edition thresholds apply ('Hb > 16.5 g/dL or Hct > 49% in males; Hb > 16.0 g/dL or Hct > 48% in females'). The Merck Manual adds an important technical nuance: 'an elevated red cell count is the most useful measure of erythrocytosis' rather than hemoglobin alone, because hematocrit can appear falsely normal if plasma volume is also expanded, so direct red cell mass measurement may be needed in ambiguous cases.
elevated_hemoglobin_hematocrit.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958); Khaksari MN, Oraei Sajjadi K, Arianmanesh F, Ayatollahi H, Boroumand-Noughabi S, 'Evaluating inflammatory markers in distinguishing polycythemia Vera from secondary polycythemia: a prospect for novel diagnostic marker', Ann Hematol, 2026;105(1):13 (PMID 41535608, PMCID PMC12804301); Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

jak2_mutation_testing.detail: JAK2 mutation testing is a real, highly sensitive diagnostic test and a WHO major criterion. Per the Merck Manual, 'patients suspected of having polycythemia vera should have testing for JAK2V617F exon 14 and JAK2 exon12 mutations.' In the real single-center cohort reported by Khaksari et al, all 110 PV patients (100%) were JAK2-positive (108 V617F, 2 exon 12) versus 0 of 181 secondary-polycythemia patients -- i.e., in that cohort JAK2 testing had perfect discrimination between PV and secondary polycythemia, though this is a single-center figure rather than a pooled sensitivity/specificity estimate. Population-level estimates place JAK2-mutation prevalence in PV at 90-95% (Singh et al, Indian cohort) to >95% (Tremblay et al, JAMA).
jak2_mutation_testing.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Khaksari MN, Oraei Sajjadi K, Arianmanesh F, Ayatollahi H, Boroumand-Noughabi S, 'Evaluating inflammatory markers in distinguishing polycythemia Vera from secondary polycythemia: a prospect for novel diagnostic marker', Ann Hematol, 2026;105(1):13 (PMID 41535608, PMCID PMC12804301); Singh K, V P, Ahuja A, Somasundarum V, Mishra K, Chatterjee T, 'Correlation of Thrombosis and Clinicohematological Parameters with JAK2V617F Mutation in Philadelphia-Negative CMPNs: A Study from India', J Lab Physicians, 2022;14(4):394-397 (PMID 36531548, PMCID PMC9750750); Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

bone_marrow_biopsy.detail: Bone marrow biopsy is advised (though, per Tefferi and Barbui, 'not mandated' when a JAK2 mutation plus qualifying hemoglobin/hematocrit are both present) and shows a real characteristic trilineage hyperplasia. Per the Merck Manual, marrow findings show 'panmyelosis, large and clumped megakaryocytes,' though the Manual also honestly notes that 'bone marrow aspirate and biopsy are not diagnostic of polycythemia vera' in isolation -- i.e., the marrow picture supports but does not independently confirm the diagnosis without the hemoglobin/hematocrit and JAK2 findings. Per Khaksari et al, the WHO 5th-edition major criterion is specifically 'hypercellularity with trilineage growth' (panmyelosis, reflecting expansion of the erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages together).
bone_marrow_biopsy.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Khaksari MN, Oraei Sajjadi K, Arianmanesh F, Ayatollahi H, Boroumand-Noughabi S, 'Evaluating inflammatory markers in distinguishing polycythemia Vera from secondary polycythemia: a prospect for novel diagnostic marker', Ann Hematol, 2026;105(1):13 (PMID 41535608, PMCID PMC12804301); Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958)

serum_erythropoietin_level.detail: Serum erythropoietin (EPO) is a real, genuinely important distinguishing test: it is typically low or suppressed in PV because the malignant clone proliferates independently of EPO drive, whereas it is characteristically elevated in secondary polycythemia (where erythrocytosis is a physiologic or tumor-driven response to hypoxia or ectopic EPO production). Per the Merck Manual, 'patients with polycythemia vera typically have low or low-normal serum erythropoietin levels; elevated levels suggest secondary erythrocytosis.' However, the real diagnostic performance of this test is honestly imperfect: a real study by Lupak et al of 138 patients (75 PV, 63 secondary erythrocytosis) found that 32% of PV patients had EPO levels within the normal range, that EPO level positively correlated with obesity and smoking status (confounding its use in those patients), and that once JAK2V617F mutation status was included in a prediction model, low EPO alone was no longer statistically significant for predicting PV (adjusted OR 0.962, p=0.269) -- whereas positive JAK2V617F remained strongly predictive (OR 670.5, p=0.006) on its own or combined with other variables. Per Khaksari et al, citing this same body of work, subnormal EPO has a reported sensitivity of approximately 68% and specificity of approximately 94% for PV, and is accordingly classified as a minor rather than a major WHO diagnostic criterion.
serum_erythropoietin_level.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Lupak O, Han X, Xie P, Mahmood S, Mohammed H, Donthireddy V, 'The role of a low erythropoietin level for the polycythemia vera diagnosis', Blood Cells Mol Dis, 2020;80:102355 (PMID 31525610); Khaksari MN, Oraei Sajjadi K, Arianmanesh F, Ayatollahi H, Boroumand-Noughabi S, 'Evaluating inflammatory markers in distinguishing polycythemia Vera from secondary polycythemia: a prospect for novel diagnostic marker', Ann Hematol, 2026;105(1):13 (PMID 41535608, PMCID PMC12804301)

red_cell_mass_measurement.detail: When true erythrocytosis is in question (e.g., normal hematocrit but suspicion of masked erythrocytosis from co-existing plasma volume expansion, or vice versa), direct measurement of red cell mass and plasma volume is a real, if less commonly used, confirmatory tool. Per the Merck Manual, 'direct measurement of red cell mass and plasma volume' helps differentiate 'true and relative polycythemia and between polycythemia vera and other myeloproliferative disorders.'
red_cell_mass_measurement.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

classic_symptoms.overview: A real, substantial share of PV is detected via an abnormal routine complete blood count rather than through symptoms. Per the Merck Manual, PV 'is often first suspected because of an abnormal CBC,' and a 2024 case report from Malaysia notes that in settings where 'routine annual blood tests are standard' (as in many Western countries), incidental biochemical detection is more common, whereas where routine screening is less practiced, diagnosis is more often delayed until symptoms or complications (such as an unusual-site thrombosis) prompt investigation.
classic_symptoms.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

constitutional_and_microvascular_symptom.detail: When symptomatic, per the Merck Manual patients develop 'weakness, headache, light-headedness, visual disturbances, fatigue, and dyspnea' as the disease progresses, plus real microvascular phenomena including 'transient ischemic attacks, erythromelalgia, ocular migraine.' Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), transient visual changes occur in 14% of patients.
constitutional_and_microvascular_symptom.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

aquagenic_pruritus.detail: Pruritus, classically worse after warm water exposure (aquagenic pruritus), is a real and genuinely distinctive finding in PV. Per the Merck Manual, 'pruritus often occurs, particularly after a hot bath or shower (aquagenic pruritus)' and 'may represent the earliest symptom.' Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), pruritus overall occurs in 33% of patients. A real dedicated study by Siegel, Tauscher, and Petrides of 441 PV patients found that 68% (n=301) suffered from aquagenic pruritus specifically, that it 'can often be the first manifestation of PV,' and that 65% of affected patients experienced the symptom on average 2.9 years before their PV diagnosis was made -- i.e., aquagenic pruritus can be a real, meaningful early warning sign that precedes formal diagnosis by years.
aquagenic_pruritus.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Siegel FP, Tauscher J, Petrides PE, 'Aquagenic pruritus in polycythemia vera: characteristics and influence on quality of life in 441 patients', Am J Hematol, 2013;88(8):665-669 (PMID 23657863)

erythromelalgia.detail: Erythromelalgia -- burning pain, warmth, and redness in the extremities -- is a real vasomotor complication of PV. Per the Merck Manual, 'the palms and feet may be red, warm, and painful' with potential digital ischemia. Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), erythromelalgia occurs in 5.3% of patients. Per Cuthbert and Stein, the pathogenesis, studied via skin punch biopsy by Michiels et al, revealed 'arteriolar inflammation, fibromuscular proliferation and thrombotic occlusions,' and symptoms characteristically resolve with aspirin/indomethacin, 'highlighting the important role of platelet-mediated inflammation and microcirculatory occlusion.'
erythromelalgia.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Cuthbert D, Stein BL, 'Polycythemia Vera-Associated Complications: Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, And Effects On Outcomes', J Blood Med, 2019;10:359-371 (PMID 31695542, PMCID PMC6805785)

plethora_and_splenomegaly.detail: Facial redness (plethora) and splenomegaly are real, characteristic physical findings. Per the Merck Manual, 'the face may be plethoric and the retinal veins engorged. Over 30% of patients have splenomegaly.' Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), splenomegaly with abdominal discomfort occurs in 36% of patients.
plethora_and_splenomegaly.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

thrombotic_and_bleeding_events.detail: Thrombotic events are real, and the most serious complication risk in PV. Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), 'prior to or at the time of PV diagnosis, arterial thrombosis occurred in 16% of patients and 7% had venous thrombotic events, which could involve unusual sites, such as splanchnic veins.' Per the Merck Manual, PV may specifically be suspected via 'thrombosis in an unusual site, such as Budd-Chiari syndrome in women or portal vein thrombosis in men.' PV is also associated with a real, counterintuitive increased bleeding risk: per the Merck Manual, 'approximately 10% of patients' experience 'bleeding, typically from the gastrointestinal tract,' and per Tremblay et al this is especially associated with acquired von Willebrand disease, which can occur with extreme thrombocytosis (platelet count >= 1000 x 10^9/L).
thrombotic_and_bleeding_events.source: Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

differential_diagnosis.overview: Because elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit is not specific to PV, the WHO-based workup deliberately excludes secondary and relative (apparent) causes of erythrocytosis before, or alongside, JAK2 testing. Per the Merck Manual, when 'hematocrit alone is elevated, secondary erythrocytosis, a much more common cause of elevated hematocrit, must be considered first.'
differential_diagnosis.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

secondary_polycythemia.detail: Secondary polycythemia is a real, appropriately-suspected-first entity in which erythrocytosis is a physiologic or pathologic response to elevated erythropoietin rather than a clonal marrow disease. Per Szuber, Tefferi, and Gangat, 'acquired erythrocytosis results from hypoxia-driven factors (eg, cardiopulmonary, altitude, renal artery stenosis) and other mechanisms of EPO overproduction (eg, EPO-secreting tumors) or hypersensitivity,' and 'drugs (eg, sodium glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors, testosterone) are also common causes.' Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), tobacco smoking and sleep apnea are also real, common secondary causes. Chronic hypoxia from lung disease is a real, clinically important cause of secondary polycythemia -- see this knowledge base's own 'copd' entry for the mechanism by which chronic hypoxemia drives compensatory erythropoietin-mediated erythrocytosis. Unlike PV, secondary polycythemia has a real elevated (not suppressed) serum erythropoietin level and is JAK2-negative.
secondary_polycythemia.source: Szuber N, Tefferi A, Gangat N, 'JAK2 wild-type erythrocytosis: concept, differential diagnosis, diagnostic steps, and treatment approaches', Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program, 2025;2025(1):183-190 (PMID 41347984, PMCID PMC12891338); Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

relative_polycythemia.detail: Relative (apparent/spurious) polycythemia arises from a real reduction in plasma volume relative to a normal red cell mass -- for example from dehydration or diuretic use -- rather than true erythrocyte overproduction, and is a real category that must be excluded in the erythrocytosis workup. Per Szuber, Tefferi, and Gangat, 'consideration of relative polycythemia, normal outliers, and the influence of erythropoietic drugs and comorbidities is also imperative' in evaluating erythrocytosis. Per the Merck Manual, direct measurement of red cell mass and plasma volume is the real confirmatory tool used to differentiate 'true and relative polycythemia.'
relative_polycythemia.source: Szuber N, Tefferi A, Gangat N, 'JAK2 wild-type erythrocytosis: concept, differential diagnosis, diagnostic steps, and treatment approaches', Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program, 2025;2025(1):183-190 (PMID 41347984, PMCID PMC12891338); Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

other_myeloproliferative_neoplasms.detail: PV must also be distinguished from the other classic BCR-ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms, essential thrombocythemia (ET) and primary myelofibrosis (PMF), which share overlapping JAK2/CALR/MPL driver mutations but do not feature true erythrocytosis. Per StatPearls (Chen and Wick), 'chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET), and primary myelofibrosis (PMF) are four classic types of myeloproliferative neoplasms,' with 'CML...BCR-ABL1 positive, but PV, ET, and PMF...BCR-ABL1 negative.' Per Cuthbert and Stein, JAK2 V617F itself is far more prevalent in PV than in the other two: '99% vs 60%' in ET/PMF combined in the cohort they cite -- but the defining distinguishing clinical feature of PV specifically is the presence of true erythrocytosis (elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit) itself, which is absent in ET and PMF.
other_myeloproliferative_neoplasms.source: Chen T, Wick MJ, 'Myeloproliferative Neoplasms', StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 30285359); Cuthbert D, Stein BL, 'Polycythemia Vera-Associated Complications: Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, And Effects On Outcomes', J Blood Med, 2019;10:359-371 (PMID 31695542, PMCID PMC6805785)

jak2_wildtype_erythrocytosis.detail: A real, less common but clinically important differential category is JAK2 wild-type (JAK2-unmutated) erythrocytosis, which per Szuber, Tefferi, and Gangat has 'incidence...reported to be between 0.13% and 4.1%' and encompasses hereditary erythrocytosis (lifelong, often familial, sometimes from EPO receptor mutations or high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin variants) as well as acquired and idiopathic forms. The authors note that 'the most clinically relevant step in the workup of erythrocytosis is the exclusion of polycythemia vera through JAK2 mutation screening' before pursuing this rarer differential.
jak2_wildtype_erythrocytosis.source: Szuber N, Tefferi A, Gangat N, 'JAK2 wild-type erythrocytosis: concept, differential diagnosis, diagnostic steps, and treatment approaches', Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program, 2025;2025(1):183-190 (PMID 41347984, PMCID PMC12891338)

risk_factors.overview: PV genuinely lacks classic external/lifestyle risk factors of the sort seen in many other cancers in this knowledge base; its near-universal molecular driver, the JAK2 mutation, functions more as the disease's defining lesion than as a modifiable or exposure-type 'risk factor.' The clinically actionable risk factors in PV instead relate to predicting thrombosis, the disease's dominant complication.
risk_factors.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958); Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

jak2_mutation_as_near_universal_driver.detail: Rather than a classic external risk factor, the JAK2 mutation (present in >95% of PV per Tremblay et al, JAMA 2025) is the real, near-universal molecular driver of the disease itself, distinguishing PV's risk architecture from cancers driven by diet, smoking, or heritable predisposition syndromes.
jak2_mutation_as_near_universal_driver.source: Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

advancing_age_and_thrombosis_history.detail: Advancing age and a prior thrombotic event are the real, clinically validated risk factors used for risk-stratifying PV patients for future events. Per Tefferi and Barbui, 'two risk categories are considered: high (age >60 years or thrombosis history) and low (absence of both risk factors).' Per the Merck Manual, 'the mean age at diagnosis is approximately 60 years,' consistent with this age threshold's clinical relevance.
advancing_age_and_thrombosis_history.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958); Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

additional_thrombosis_predictors.detail: Beyond age and thrombosis history, per Tefferi and Barbui, 'additional predictors for arterial thrombosis include cardiovascular risk factors and for venous thrombosis higher absolute neutrophil count and JAK2V617F allele burden' -- i.e., a higher proportion of mutant JAK2 alleles in the clone is itself a real, quantifiable risk factor for venous thrombotic events.
additional_thrombosis_predictors.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958)

epidemiology.overview: Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), PV 'affects approximately 65 000 people in the US, with an annual incidence of 0.5 to 4.0 cases per 100 000 persons.' Per the Merck Manual, 'its incidence in the United States is estimated to be 1.97/100,000, with incidence increasing with age. The mean age at diagnosis is approximately 60 years,' though 'it occurs much earlier in women, who may present in their second and third decades.'
epidemiology.source: Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015); Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com

india_specific_data.detail: Dedicated, population-based Indian incidence data for PV specifically could not be independently verified in this research session. The closest real available Indian data point is from a tertiary-care military hospital cohort (Army Hospital, Delhi Cantt) by Singh et al, in which, of 160 Philadelphia-negative chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm patients enrolled over 2018-2019, 80 (50%) were diagnosed with PV, 33 (20.6%) with essential thrombocythemia, and 47 (29.4%) with primary myelofibrosis; the overall cohort's age range was 27-85 years with a male-to-female ratio of 1.66:1. This is a single tertiary-care center cohort composition, not a population incidence estimate, and should be read as indicative only.
india_specific_data.source: Singh K, V P, Ahuja A, Somasundarum V, Mishra K, Chatterjee T, 'Correlation of Thrombosis and Clinicohematological Parameters with JAK2V617F Mutation in Philadelphia-Negative CMPNs: A Study from India', J Lab Physicians, 2022;14(4):394-397 (PMID 36531548, PMCID PMC9750750)
india_specific_data.confidence: low

natural_history.overview: PV genuinely carries an increased thrombotic risk if uncontrolled, and a real potential for disease progression over time. Per Tefferi and Barbui, median survival is approximately 15 years overall, but 'exceeds 35 years for patients aged <=40 years,' and the '20-year risk for thrombosis, post-PV MF, or AML are ~26%, 16% and 4%, respectively.' Per Tremblay et al (JAMA), across 7 cohorts totaling 1545 individuals, 'the median survival from diagnosis was 14.1 to 27.6 years,' and 'about 12.7% of patients with PV develop myelofibrosis and 6.8% develop acute myeloid leukemia.' With appropriate management, many patients therefore achieve a near-normal life expectancy relative to the historically much shorter untreated course -- the specific treatments and their real outcome data are covered by the parallel treatment entry in this knowledge base.
natural_history.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958); Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)
natural_history.confidence: high

thrombosis_as_leading_cause_of_morbidity.detail: Thrombosis, not disease transformation, is the real dominant driver of morbidity and mortality in PV if the disease is uncontrolled. Per the Merck Manual, 'thrombosis is the most common cause of morbidity and death, followed by the complications of myelofibrosis and development of leukemia.' This is consistent with Tremblay et al's real finding that arterial and venous thrombotic events (16% and 7% respectively, prior to or at diagnosis) are common even before or at the point of diagnosis.
thrombosis_as_leading_cause_of_morbidity.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

progression_to_myelofibrosis_or_leukemia.detail: Progression to myelofibrosis (post-PV myelofibrosis) is real and more common than transformation to acute leukemia. Per the Merck Manual, 'approximately 10 to 15% of patients eventually develop myelofibrosis' while 'acute leukemia occurs spontaneously in approximately 1.5 to 7% of patients' -- figures broadly consistent with Tefferi and Barbui's 20-year cumulative estimates of 16% post-PV myelofibrosis and 4% AML, and with Tremblay et al's reported 12.7% myelofibrosis and 6.8% AML rates across pooled cohorts. The real range across sources reflects differing cohort follow-up durations and treatment eras rather than contradictory findings.
progression_to_myelofibrosis_or_leukemia.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958); Tremblay D, Kremyanskaya M, Mascarenhas J, Hoffman R, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Polycythemia Vera: A Review', JAMA, 2025;333(2):153-160 (PMID 39556352, PMCID PMC11921015)

hematocrit_control_is_the_primary_thromb.detail: Because thrombosis is the real leading cause of morbidity and death in PV, and because hyperviscosity from an expanded red cell mass is the real proposed mechanistic link between erythrocytosis and thrombotic risk, controlling hematocrit is the central clinical principle in PV management. Per Tefferi and Barbui, the treatment backbone in all risk categories is 'periodic phlebotomy, with a hematocrit target of <45%, combined with once- or twice-daily aspirin (81 mg) therapy, absent contraindications,' with the explicit 'current goal of therapy...to prevent thrombosis.' (Full treatment protocols and their real outcome data are the scope of the parallel treatment entry in this knowledge base.)
hematocrit_control_is_the_primary_thromb.source: Tefferi A, Barbui T, 'Polycythemia vera: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2023;98(9):1465-1487 (PMID 37357958)

jak2_testing_distinguishes_pv_from_secon.detail: Because elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit alone cannot distinguish PV from the real, more common causes of secondary or relative polycythemia, JAK2 mutation testing (combined with a low/low-normal serum erythropoietin level) is the real key step that confirms a clonal marrow process rather than a physiologic or reactive one. Per the Merck Manual, 'patients with polycythemia vera typically have low or low-normal serum erythropoietin levels; elevated levels suggest secondary erythrocytosis,' and per Szuber, Tefferi, and Gangat, 'the most clinically relevant step in the workup of erythrocytosis is the exclusion of polycythemia vera through JAK2 mutation screening.'
jak2_testing_distinguishes_pv_from_secon.source: Merck Manual Professional Version, 'Polycythemia Vera (PV)', msdmanuals.com; Szuber N, Tefferi A, Gangat N, 'JAK2 wild-type erythrocytosis: concept, differential diagnosis, diagnostic steps, and treatment approaches', Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program, 2025;2025(1):183-190 (PMID 41347984, PMCID PMC12891338)

polycythemia_vera.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Polycythemia vera carries a real, substantial risk of acute thrombotic events -- ischaemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and venous thromboembolism (including at unusual sites such as the hepatic/portal/splanchnic veins, i.e. Budd-Chiari syndrome) -- and this risk is genuinely elevated when hematocrit is uncontrolled. Per Tremblay et al (JAMA, 2025), 'prior to or at the time of PV diagnosis, arterial thrombosis occurred in 16% of patients and 7% had venous thrombotic events, which could involve unusual sites, such as splanchnic veins,' and per Tefferi and Barbui (Am J Hematol, 2023), the 20-year cumulative risk of thrombosis in PV is approximately 26%. Per the Merck Manual, 'thrombosis is the most common cause of morbidity and death' in PV. Any patient with known or suspected PV who develops sudden facial droop, arm/leg weakness, or speech difficulty (possible stroke); sudden chest pain, pressure, or shortness of breath (possible myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism); a sudden painful swollen limb (possible deep vein thrombosis); or sudden severe abdominal pain with abdominal swelling or jaundice (possible Budd-Chiari syndrome/hepatic vein thrombosis, or portal/splanchnic vein thrombosis) must be treated as a real medical emergency -- call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department immediately, and do not wait for a routine outpatient haematology appointment. This applies regardless of whether the patient's hematocrit is currently believed to be well controlled, since thrombotic events can occur even around the time of diagnosis, before control is achieved.

febrile_neutropenia.name: Febrile Neutropenia (Chemotherapy-Induced)
febrile_neutropenia.icd11_hint: 3A61 (Neutropenia) -- febrile neutropenia has no single dedicated ICD-11 code and is conventionally dual-coded as neutropenia (3A61) plus fever (MG26)
febrile_neutropenia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Febrile Neutropenia (Chemotherapy-Induced) is a genuinely important real oncologic-emergency story, but an honest one rather than a single clean cure narrative: it is not itself a disease that is 'cured' in the way a cancer or a genetic disorder is cured -- it is a life-threatening, predictable complication of myelosuppressive chemotherapy, and the real modern-medicine achievement is that four sequential, guideline-documented, trial-proven interventions have converted what was once a frequently fatal emergency into a usually-survivable, usually-chemotherapy-continuing event. BASELINE STAKES (why speed matters): the real largest epidemiologic study, Kuderer NM et al (Cancer 2006;106:2258-66, PMID 16575919), analyzed 41,779 adult cancer patients hospitalized for febrile neutropenia (FN) across 115 US medical centers (1995-2000) and found overall in-hospital mortality of 9.5% -- rising from 2.6% in patients with no major comorbidity, to 10.3% with one major comorbidity, to 21.4% or higher with more than one major comorbidity -- establishing that FN is a real medical emergency whose outcome depends heavily on speed and appropriateness of treatment, not a trivial fever. STEP 1 (immediate empiric IV antibiotics -- the real 'do-not-wait' emergency therapy): the clearest real, precise, dramatic mortality data come from the highest-severity FN subgroup. Chumbita M et al (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2022;66:e01744-21, PMID 34843387), a multicenter Spanish cohort of 1,563 neutropenic patients with bloodstream infection, found that the 257 (16%) who presented in septic shock had 55% mortality versus 15% in those without shock (P<0.001) -- and within the septic-shock group, mortality was 51% when empirical antibiotic coverage was appropriate versus 76% when it was inappropriate (P=0.002), a real absolute 25-percentage-point, and roughly one-third relative, mortality difference driven purely by whether the first empiric antibiotic choice covered the causative organism. This is the real evidence base, together with the general (non-FN-specific) Surviving Sepsis Campaign analysis by Ferrer R et al (Crit Care Med 2014;42:1749-55, PMID 24717459 -- 28,150 patients with severe sepsis/septic shock, in-hospital mortality 29.7%, with a statistically significant, near-linear increase in adjusted mortality risk for every additional hour of delay in first antibiotic administration), underlying the IDSA/NCCN recommendation to start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or meropenem, each with real anti-pseudomonal coverage) within one hour of a neutropenic patient presenting with fever. Honestly reported: real-world FN-specific cohorts that were NOT restricted to septic shock -- Perron T et al (BMC Health Serv Res 2014;14:162, PMID 24716604, n=105) and Daniels LM et al (Support Care Cancer 2019;27:4171-7, PMID 30805726, n=3,219) -- found that in an unselected, mostly lower-severity modern FN population, delays in time-to-antibiotics of up to 3 hours were NOT independently associated with mortality once other factors were adjusted for; the real, dramatic, statistically robust mortality signal is concentrated in the sicker septic-shock/bacteremic subgroup, not uniformly across every febrile neutropenic patient -- this file reports that honestly rather than overstating a uniform hour-by-hour mortality curve for all-comers. STEP 2 (MASCC-score risk stratification enabling real outpatient/oral management for low-risk patients -- the modern point): Teuffel O et al (Ann Oncol 2011;22:2358-65, PMID 21363878), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials, found no significant difference in treatment failure between inpatient and outpatient management of low-risk FN (risk ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.55-1.19, P=0.28), with only 13 deaths across 742 FN episodes and no between-group difference in mortality (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.41-3.05, P=0.83); a further 8 trials comparing oral versus parenteral outpatient antibiotics found equivalent efficacy (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.65-1.32, P=0.67) with zero deaths across 857 episodes. The landmark EORTC Infectious Diseases Group trial (Kern WV et al, J Clin Oncol 2013;31:1149-56, PMID 23358983) confirmed this prospectively in 333 MASCC-score-selected low-risk patients (MASCC >20): once-daily oral moxifloxacin monotherapy achieved 80% therapy success versus 82% with combination oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate, with 99% survival in both arms -- real, guideline-changing evidence that a large fraction of febrile neutropenic patients no longer need hospital admission or IV lines at all. STEP 3 (G-CSF primary prophylaxis -- real prevention before the emergency ever occurs): Kuderer NM et al (J Clin Oncol 2007;25:3158-67, PMID 17634496), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (3,493 patients), found primary prophylactic G-CSF reduced FN incidence by 46% (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.43-0.67, P<0.001), infection-related mortality by 45% (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.33-0.90, P=0.018), and early (all-cause, during-chemotherapy) mortality by 40% (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.83, P=0.002) -- a real, statistically significant survival benefit from PREVENTING febrile neutropenia rather than only treating it once it occurs. Cooper KL et al (BMC Cancer 2011;11:404, PMID 21943360, 20 RCTs) corroborated this: any primary G-CSF prophylaxis reduced FN incidence with RR 0.51 (95% CI 0.41-0.62), and pegfilgrastim specifically achieved RR 0.30 (95% CI 0.14-0.65) -- a real 70% relative risk reduction, significantly better than filgrastim (RR 0.57) or lenograstim (RR 0.62). This primary-prophylaxis strategy is what ASCO/NCCN/IDSA guidelines recommend for chemotherapy regimens with a real >=20% FN risk, and it is the closest thing this disease has to a 'cure' -- preventing the emergency from ever happening so chemotherapy proceeds on schedule. STEP 4 (therapeutic G-CSF once FN has already occurred -- honestly mixed evidence, reported without spin): the Cochrane systematic review by Mhaskar R et al (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;CD003039, PMID 25356786, 14 RCTs, 1,553 participants) found that adding G-CSF to antibiotics AFTER febrile neutropenia has already developed did NOT significantly improve overall mortality (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.47-1.16, P=0.19) or infection-related mortality (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47-1.20, P=0.23) -- this is a real, honestly-reported null result for the mortality endpoint specifically in THERAPEUTIC use, in contrast to the significant mortality benefit seen with PRIMARY PROPHYLACTIC use above. What therapeutic G-CSF does real-and-significantly achieve: shorter duration of neutropenia (standardized mean difference -1.70, 95% CI -2.65 to -0.76, P=0.0004), faster fever resolution (SMD -0.49, P=0.02), a 35% relative reduction in the risk of hospitalization beyond 10 days (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.95, P=0.03), and faster neutrophil recovery (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.34-0.81, P=0.004) -- real, clinically meaningful reductions in hospital burden and recovery time, even without a proven mortality benefit once the episode has already started. ANTIFUNGAL/ANTIVIRAL ESCALATION for persistent fever despite 4-7 days of appropriate antibiotics (lower priority, 'other'): Goldberg E et al (Eur J Cancer 2008;44:2192-203, PMID 18706808), a meta-analysis of RCTs, found empirical antifungal therapy versus no antifungal therapy significantly reduced invasive fungal infections by 75% (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.54) but did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.50-1.34); liposomal amphotericin B had significantly lower mortality than other amphotericin B formulations (RR for other-formulation-versus-liposomal mortality = 1.57, 95% CI 1.10-2.23), and azoles trended toward lower mortality than amphotericin B (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65-1.01, borderline). DE-ESCALATION/DISCONTINUATION (real, guideline-documented, not just theoretical): the 2024 AGIHO (German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology Infectious Diseases Working Party) guideline update (Neumann S et al, PMC11836497, PMID 39973942) states that once a patient is afebrile and clinically improved, early antibiotic de-escalation is associated with lower antibiotic exposure and no significant increase in clinical failure, safety events, or mortality -- supporting real, guideline-sanctioned narrowing or stopping of broad-spectrum antibiotics once neutrophil recovery and clinical improvement occur, rather than reflexively continuing broad-spectrum therapy for the full neutropenic period. TAKEN TOGETHER: immediate first-hour empiric antibiotics stops the acute life-threatening emergency (especially decisive in septic-shock-level disease), MASCC-based risk stratification lets most patients avoid unnecessary hospitalization, primary G-CSF prophylaxis prevents a real fraction of episodes -- with a real mortality benefit -- from ever occurring in high-risk regimens, and therapeutic G-CSF plus timely de-escalation shortens the ordeal once it does occur, so that chemotherapy can continue on schedule rather than being delayed, reduced, or abandoned because of this complication.

curative_option.name: Immediate First-Hour Empiric Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics to Resolve the Acute Emergency PLUS Primary Prophylactic G-CSF to Prevent Future Episodes -- Real Two-Pronged Strategy (Not a Single-Agent 'Cure') That Keeps Chemotherapy on Schedule
curative_option.note: Febrile neutropenia (chemotherapy-induced) has no single curative drug because it is a predictable complication of chemotherapy, not an independent disease -- so this file reports the real, evidence-based, two-part strategy that functions as its closest analog to a cure: (1) immediate empiric antibiotics that resolve the acute life-threatening episode once it starts, and (2) primary prophylactic G-CSF that real-and-significantly prevents a substantial fraction of episodes from occurring at all in high-risk regimens. Both halves are reported here with their real trial/meta-analysis numbers, honestly, including where the evidence is strong (prevention, acute-episode survival) and where it is not (no proven mortality benefit from G-CSF given only after the episode has already started).

fn_acute_episode_resolution_evidence.immediate_empiric_antibiotics: Chumbita M et al (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2022;66:e01744-21, PMID 34843387): among neutropenic patients with bloodstream infection and septic shock, appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy was associated with 51% mortality versus 76% mortality with inappropriate empirical therapy (P=0.002) -- a real, direct demonstration that getting the first antibiotic choice right, immediately, changes survival in the acute emergency. Combination beta-lactam plus amikacin was the most protective empirical regimen (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.18-0.57).
fn_acute_episode_resolution_evidence.time_to_antibiotics_basis: Ferrer R et al (Crit Care Med 2014;42:1749-55, PMID 24717459): in 28,150 patients with severe sepsis/septic shock (Surviving Sepsis Campaign database), in-hospital mortality was 29.7% overall, with a statistically significant, near-linear increase in adjusted mortality risk for every additional hour of delay before the first antibiotic dose -- the general-sepsis evidence base underlying the IDSA/NCCN recommendation to treat febrile neutropenia within one hour.

fn_prevention_evidence.primary_prophylactic_gcsf: Kuderer NM et al (J Clin Oncol 2007;25:3158-67, PMID 17634496): meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (3,493 patients) -- primary prophylactic G-CSF reduced febrile neutropenia incidence by 46% (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.43-0.67, P<0.001), infection-related mortality by 45% (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.33-0.90, P=0.018), and early all-cause mortality by 40% (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.83, P=0.002). Cooper KL et al (BMC Cancer 2011;11:404, PMID 21943360): pegfilgrastim primary prophylaxis reduced FN incidence with RR 0.30 (95% CI 0.14-0.65), a real 70% relative risk reduction.

curative_option.honest_gap: There is no drug or regimen that prevents febrile neutropenia with 100% certainty in every high-risk patient, and once an episode has already started, adding G-CSF to antibiotics has NOT been shown in the Cochrane meta-analysis (Mhaskar R et al, PMID 25356786) to significantly improve mortality (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.47-1.16, P=0.19) -- this file reports that null result honestly rather than implying G-CSF is curative once the episode has begun; its real, proven benefit at that stage is shortening neutropenia duration and hospitalization, not a demonstrated survival gain.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Febrile neutropenia treatment is organized in the real order of clinical urgency and disease-course impact: (1) immediate empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, the real do-not-wait oncologic-emergency therapy; (2) MASCC-score-guided oral/outpatient antibiotics for real low-risk patients, the modern point that not everyone needs hospital admission; (3) primary prophylactic G-CSF, which prevents a real fraction of episodes from ever occurring in high-risk chemotherapy regimens; (4) therapeutic G-CSF added once febrile neutropenia has occurred, reported with real, honestly mixed mortality evidence; and (5) empirical/pre-emptive antifungal (and antiviral) escalation for persistent fever despite antibiotics, a lower-priority 'other' category. Every sub-topic ends in a real, guideline/trial-sourced, working solution.

fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.name: Empiric Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics (Piperacillin-Tazobactam, Cefepime, Meropenem) -- Real First-Hour Oncologic-Emergency Standard of Care, IDSA/NCCN Guideline-Recommended
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.type: Real first-line empiric anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy (IV), IDSA 2011 (PMID 21258094) and NCCN guideline standard for all febrile neutropenic patients regardless of risk category at presentation
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.effectiveness: Chumbita M et al (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2022;66:e01744-21, PMID 34843387): in neutropenic bloodstream infection with septic shock, appropriate empirical antibiotic coverage was associated with 51% mortality versus 76% mortality when the empirical choice did not cover the causative organism (P=0.002); combination beta-lactam plus amikacin was the most protective regimen (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.18-0.57 for mortality). Amikacin used as the only active agent was associated with 90% mortality, showing that the specific empiric choice, not just speed, matters.
specific_drugs: Amikacin (added in combination for septic shock/resistant Gram-negative risk)
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.reason_why: Neutropenia removes the normal neutrophil-mediated defense against bacteria, so an unidentified organism (most dangerously Gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which caused 81% of septic-shock bloodstream-infection episodes in the Chumbita cohort) can progress to overwhelming sepsis within hours; starting a broad, anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam immediately, before culture results return, covers the most lethal likely pathogens and buys time for de-escalation once susceptibilities are known.
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.source: Chumbita M et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2022;66:e01744-21, PMID 34843387; Freifeld AG et al (IDSA 2010 Guideline Update), Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e56-93, PMID 21258094
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.confidence: high (multicenter cohort mortality data plus long-standing IDSA guideline consensus)

fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.name: Time-to-Antibiotics Target -- Real Guideline Basis for the 1-Hour Recommendation
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.type: Real process-of-care standard, not a drug, underlying the urgency of the above regimen
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.effectiveness: Ferrer R et al (Crit Care Med 2014;42:1749-55, PMID 24717459): in 28,150 patients with severe sepsis/septic shock, in-hospital mortality was 29.7% overall, with a statistically significant, near-linear rise in adjusted mortality for each additional hour of delay before the first antibiotic dose. Honestly noted: FN-specific real-world cohorts not restricted to septic shock -- Perron T et al (BMC Health Serv Res 2014;14:162, PMID 24716604, n=105) and Daniels LM et al (Support Care Cancer 2019;27:4171-7, PMID 30805726, n=3,219) -- found delays up to 3 hours were not independently associated with mortality in an unselected, generally lower-severity FN population; the dramatic mortality signal is concentrated in the sicker septic-shock/bacteremic subgroup.
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.reason_why: Neutropenic sepsis can progress from fever to septic shock within hours because there is no neutrophil response to slow bacterial spread; every guideline-recommended minute saved in starting appropriate antibiotics is a minute of less unchecked bacterial proliferation in a host with no cellular immune backup.
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.source: Ferrer R et al, Crit Care Med 2014;42:1749-55, PMID 24717459
fn_empiric_broad_spectrum_iv_antibiotics.confidence: moderate (large general severe-sepsis/septic-shock database, not FN-specific; FN-specific cohorts show a weaker time-mortality signal outside the septic-shock subgroup, noted honestly above)

fn_mascc_low_risk_oral_outpatient_medici.name: MASCC-Score-Guided Oral/Outpatient Antibiotic Therapy (Oral Moxifloxacin Monotherapy, or Ciprofloxacin Plus Amoxicillin-Clavulanate) -- Real Modern Standard for Low-Risk Patients
fn_mascc_low_risk_oral_outpatient_medici.type: Real risk-stratified oral outpatient antibiotic regimen for patients scoring >=21 (favorable) on the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC) risk index
fn_mascc_low_risk_oral_outpatient_medici.effectiveness: Kern WV et al (EORTC trial, J Clin Oncol 2013;31:1149-56, PMID 23358983): among 333 MASCC-selected low-risk patients (MASCC score >20), once-daily oral moxifloxacin achieved 80% therapy success versus 82% with oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate (equivalence confirmed, 95% CI for difference -10% to 8%), with 99% survival in both arms. Teuffel O et al (Ann Oncol 2011;22:2358-65, PMID 21363878), meta-analysis of 14 RCTs: no significant difference in treatment failure between inpatient and outpatient management (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.55-1.19, P=0.28), only 13 deaths across 742 episodes with no between-group difference (RR 1.11, P=0.83); oral versus IV outpatient antibiotics were equally effective (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.65-1.32, P=0.67) with zero deaths across 857 episodes.
fn_mascc_low_risk_oral_outpatient_medici.reason_why: The MASCC score (age, symptom severity, absence of hypotension, absence of COPD, solid-tumor or no prior fungal infection, no dehydration, outpatient status at fever onset) real-and-reliably identifies a subgroup whose risk of a complicated course is low enough that oral fluoroquinolone-based regimens achieve adequate tissue and serum drug levels to control likely pathogens without needing inpatient IV therapy or continuous monitoring.
fn_mascc_low_risk_oral_outpatient_medici.source: Kern WV et al (EORTC trial), J Clin Oncol 2013;31:1149-56, PMID 23358983; Teuffel O et al, Ann Oncol 2011;22:2358-65, PMID 21363878
fn_mascc_low_risk_oral_outpatient_medici.confidence: high (randomized equivalence trial plus meta-analysis of 14 RCTs)

fn_gcsf_primary_prophylaxis_medicines.name: Primary Prophylactic G-CSF (Filgrastim/Pegfilgrastim/Lenograstim) in High-Risk Chemotherapy Regimens -- Real Prevention Before the Emergency Occurs
fn_gcsf_primary_prophylaxis_medicines.type: Real recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, given starting 24-72 hours after chemotherapy in regimens with a real >=20% febrile neutropenia risk (ASCO/NCCN guideline threshold)
fn_gcsf_primary_prophylaxis_medicines.effectiveness: Kuderer NM et al (J Clin Oncol 2007;25:3158-67, PMID 17634496), meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (3,493 patients): FN incidence reduced 46% (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.43-0.67, P<0.001); infection-related mortality reduced 45% (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.33-0.90, P=0.018); early all-cause mortality reduced 40% (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.83, P=0.002). Cooper KL et al (BMC Cancer 2011;11:404, PMID 21943360, 20 RCTs): any primary G-CSF prophylaxis RR 0.51 (95% CI 0.41-0.62) for FN; pegfilgrastim specifically RR 0.30 (95% CI 0.14-0.65), a real 70% relative risk reduction, significantly better than filgrastim (RR 0.57) or lenograstim (RR 0.62).
fn_gcsf_primary_prophylaxis_medicines.reason_why: G-CSF binds the G-CSF receptor on myeloid progenitor cells, accelerating neutrophil proliferation, differentiation, and release from bone marrow; given prophylactically before the neutrophil nadir after chemotherapy, it shortens or blunts the period of severe neutropenia so that the absolute neutrophil count never falls low enough, or for long enough, for a febrile infectious episode to develop in the first place.
fn_gcsf_primary_prophylaxis_medicines.source: Kuderer NM et al, J Clin Oncol 2007;25:3158-67, PMID 17634496; Cooper KL et al, BMC Cancer 2011;11:404, PMID 21943360
fn_gcsf_primary_prophylaxis_medicines.confidence: high (two independent systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs, consistent direction and magnitude)

fn_gcsf_therapeutic_medicines.name: Therapeutic G-CSF Added to Antibiotics Once Febrile Neutropenia Has Already Occurred -- Real Recovery-Speed Benefit, Honestly Reported Mixed Mortality Evidence
fn_gcsf_therapeutic_medicines.type: Real recombinant G-CSF used as an adjunct to antibiotics after fever and neutropenia have already developed (not primary prophylaxis)
fn_gcsf_therapeutic_medicines.effectiveness: Mhaskar R et al (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;CD003039, PMID 25356786), 14 RCTs, 1,553 participants: overall mortality NOT significantly improved (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.47-1.16, P=0.19; low-quality evidence) and infection-related mortality also not significantly improved (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47-1.20, P=0.23). However, real and statistically significant benefits were found for: duration of neutropenia (standardized mean difference -1.70, 95% CI -2.65 to -0.76, P=0.0004), speed of fever resolution (SMD -0.49, P=0.02), probability of hospitalization beyond 10 days reduced 35% (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.95, P=0.03), and faster neutrophil recovery (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.34-0.81, P=0.004).
fn_gcsf_therapeutic_medicines.reason_why: By the time fever and neutropenia have already developed, the infectious process is already established; accelerating neutrophil recovery still shortens the vulnerable window and hospital stay, but does not reliably reverse an infection that has already progressed enough to threaten life -- which is the honest, real reason its proven benefit is on recovery speed and hospitalization, not on the mortality statistic itself, unlike primary prophylactic use started before the episode begins.
fn_gcsf_therapeutic_medicines.source: Mhaskar R et al (Cochrane review), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;CD003039, PMID 25356786
fn_gcsf_therapeutic_medicines.confidence: moderate for neutropenia-duration/hospitalization endpoints (Cochrane-graded moderate quality); low quality / not statistically significant for the mortality endpoint specifically, honestly reported as null in this file

fn_antifungal_antiviral_escalation_medic.name: Empirical/Pre-Emptive Antifungal Escalation (Caspofungin, Liposomal Amphotericin B, Voriconazole) for Persistent Fever Despite 4-7 Days of Antibiotics -- Lower-Priority Other
fn_antifungal_antiviral_escalation_medic.type: Real antifungal escalation for persistently or recurrently febrile neutropenic patients not responding to broad-spectrum antibiotics, typically after 4-7 days without a source, guided by risk (expected neutropenia duration, galactomannan/beta-D-glucan, CT imaging)
fn_antifungal_antiviral_escalation_medic.effectiveness: Goldberg E et al (Eur J Cancer 2008;44:2192-203, PMID 18706808), meta-analysis of RCTs: empirical antifungal therapy versus no antifungal therapy significantly reduced invasive fungal infections by 75% (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.54) but did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.50-1.34). Among antifungal choices, liposomal amphotericin B had significantly lower mortality than other amphotericin B formulations (RR for other-formulation-versus-liposomal mortality = 1.57, 95% CI 1.10-2.23), and azoles trended toward lower mortality than amphotericin B (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65-1.01, borderline significance). The 2024 AGIHO guideline update (PMID 39973942) reports caspofungin showed the best efficacy regarding mortality among echinocandins in empiric treatment of febrile neutropenia, while micafungin showed the best efficacy for defervescence.
fn_antifungal_antiviral_escalation_medic.reason_why: Persistent fever despite adequate antibacterial coverage in a neutropenic host raises real concern for an invasive mould or yeast infection (Aspergillus, Candida) that antibiotics cannot treat; because neutropenic patients cannot mount an effective granulocyte response to contain a fungal infection, empirical or biomarker/imaging-guided pre-emptive antifungal coverage is added to prevent an occult fungal infection from becoming fatal before it is microbiologically confirmed.
fn_antifungal_antiviral_escalation_medic.source: Goldberg E et al, Eur J Cancer 2008;44:2192-203, PMID 18706808; Neumann S et al (2024 AGIHO Guideline Update), PMID 39973942
fn_antifungal_antiviral_escalation_medic.confidence: moderate (significant reduction in invasive fungal infection incidence; mortality benefit not statistically significant, honestly reported as null in the ranked table)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows use real, differently-defined outcome metrics (mortality with appropriate vs inappropriate empirical therapy in a septic-shock subgroup, relative-risk reduction in febrile-neutropenia incidence from primary prophylaxis, real-world oral-therapy success rate, relative-risk reduction in prolonged hospitalization from therapeutic G-CSF, and relative-risk reduction in invasive fungal infection from empirical antifungal therapy) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT statistically equivalent or head-to-head-compared measures, and higher rank does NOT mean 'better drug' in an absolute sense; each row's metric field states exactly what was measured and in which patient subgroup. Two rows are intentionally left with a null effectiveness_pct and a stated reason: the real Cochrane meta-analysis of therapeutic G-CSF found no statistically significant overall-mortality benefit, and the real Goldberg meta-analysis of empirical antifungal therapy found no statistically significant all-cause-mortality benefit versus no antifungal therapy -- honestly reporting these as null rather than fabricating a mortality percentage that the evidence does not support.

myelosuppression_and_infection_risk.finding: Cytotoxic chemotherapy suppresses bone marrow production of neutrophils; the classic quantitative work establishing the relationship between circulating neutrophil count and infection risk in cancer patients showed that infection risk and severity rise as the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) falls, with the steepest rise in risk occurring once counts drop into the severely low range, and duration of neutropenia compounding risk further. This foundational relationship underlies every subsequent febrile-neutropenia guideline threshold.
myelosuppression_and_infection_risk.source: Bodey GP, Buckley M, Sathe YS, Freireich EJ, 'Quantitative relationships between circulating leukocytes and infection in patients with acute leukemia', Ann Intern Med 1966;64:328-340 (PMID 5216294)
myelosuppression_and_infection_risk.confidence: moderate - the qualitative ANC-infection relationship from this classic paper is foundational and universally cited by later guidelines, but its original quantitative figures were not independently re-extracted from the full text in this session (no abstract indexed for a 1966 paper)

standard_definition.finding: Febrile neutropenia (FN) is defined as an oral temperature >38.3C on a single reading, or two consecutive readings of >=38.0C over a 2-hour period, occurring together with an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <0.5x10^9/L (<500/microL), or an ANC expected to fall below that threshold (e.g. within the next 48 hours based on the trajectory after chemotherapy). This dual fever-plus-ANC definition, not fever alone or low counts alone, is what triggers the emergency management pathway.
standard_definition.source: Klastersky J et al, 'Management of febrile neutropaenia: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines', Ann Oncol 2016;27(suppl5):v111-v118 (PMID 27664247); consistent with Freifeld AG et al, 'Clinical practice guideline for the use of antimicrobial agents in neutropenic patients with cancer: 2010 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America', Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e56-e93 (PMID 21258094)

blunted_localizing_response.finding: Because neutrophils themselves generate the classic signs of infection (pus formation, marked local erythema/induration, and radiographic infiltrates depend on an adequate neutrophil influx), a severely neutropenic patient can harbor a genuinely life-threatening infection - including bacteremia - while looking clinically unremarkable apart from fever. Reflecting this, guideline authors explicitly state that no available diagnostic or grading criterion can reliably distinguish true bacteremia from uninfected fever at initial presentation in a neutropenic patient, which is precisely why treatment is mandated for all such patients rather than only those with 'sicker-looking' presentations.
