nb_alpha1_blocker_adjunct_medicines.effectiveness: In a 263-patient randomized, placebo-controlled trial (4-week RCT + 1-year open-label extension) in patients with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction from suprasacral spinal cord injury, long-term tamsulosin produced a significant 15% decrease in maximum urethral pressure (p<0.001) from baseline, improved bladder storage and emptying parameters, reduced autonomic dysreflexia symptoms, and 71% of patients were rated improved by investigators (44% slightly, 27% much improved)
nb_alpha1_blocker_adjunct_medicines.reason_why: Blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the bladder neck and proximal urethral smooth muscle, reducing outlet resistance during voiding -- used as an adjunct in neurogenic bladder-neck dysfunction and to reduce voiding pressures/autonomic dysreflexia risk, though it does not act on striated external-sphincter detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia (which is smooth-muscle-independent).
nb_alpha1_blocker_adjunct_medicines.source: Abrams P et al, European Tamsulosin Neurogenic Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Study Group, J Urol 2003;170:1242-1251, PMID 14501734
nb_alpha1_blocker_adjunct_medicines.confidence: high -- large real multicentre RCT plus 1-year open-label extension

nb_intradetrusor_onabotulinumtoxina_inje.name: Intradetrusor OnabotulinumtoxinA (BOTOX) 200 U Injection
specific_drugs: OnabotulinumtoxinA (BOTOX) 200 U in 30 injection sites, trigone-sparing
nb_intradetrusor_onabotulinumtoxina_inje.effectiveness: Real ~65% reduction in weekly urinary incontinence episodes from a baseline of 33.5/week (200 U: -21.8 vs placebo -13.2, p<0.01) in a randomized placebo-controlled trial; confirmed in a second pivotal phase 3 RCT (n=416, -21 vs -9 episodes/week, p<0.001) and a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (n=1,915, mean reduction 10.72 episodes/week vs placebo)
nb_intradetrusor_onabotulinumtoxina_inje.reason_why: OnabotulinumtoxinA cleaves SNAP-25, blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction of detrusor smooth muscle, which chemically denervates the overactive detrusor and suppresses involuntary contractions for approximately 6-9 months per injection cycle -- a real, repeatable, non-surgical option once oral drugs fail.
nb_intradetrusor_onabotulinumtoxina_inje.important_caveat: Significantly increases risk of urinary tract infection (RR 1.47), urinary retention (RR 5.58) and new-onset need for clean intermittent catheterization (35% at 200 U vs 10% placebo) -- patients must be willing and able to self-catheterize before starting this therapy.
nb_intradetrusor_onabotulinumtoxina_inje.source: Cruz F et al, Eur Urol 2011;60:742-750 (PMID 21798658); Ginsberg D et al, J Urol 2012;187:2131-2139 (PMID 22503020); Cheng T et al, PLoS One 2016;11:e0159307 (PMID 27463810)
nb_intradetrusor_onabotulinumtoxina_inje.confidence: high -- multiple large placebo-controlled RCTs and a meta-analysis

nb_clean_intermittent_catheterization_pr.name: Clean Intermittent Catheterization (CIC)
nb_clean_intermittent_catheterization_pr.type: Self- or caregiver-performed catheterization procedure, 4-6 times/day
specific_drugs: Clean (non-sterile) single-use or hydrophilic-coated intermittent catheter
nb_clean_intermittent_catheterization_pr.effectiveness: 92% (59/64) continent or improved continence and 98% (63/64) hydronephrosis-free at 54-month mean follow-up in patients with SCI-related neurogenic bladder; in a 1,032-patient 2025 cohort, intermittent catheterization gave higher volitional bladder-recovery rates than indwelling catheterization (17.1% vs 11.6%, adjusted OR 2.11, p<0.001)
nb_clean_intermittent_catheterization_pr.reason_why: Regularly emptying the bladder at physiologic (low) volumes and pressures before it becomes over-distended prevents the chronic high-pressure storage and stasis that otherwise drive vesico-ureteric reflux, hydronephrosis, recurrent infection and stone formation, while avoiding the permanent urethral/bladder mucosal irritation, biofilm and infection risk of a permanently indwelling catheter.
nb_clean_intermittent_catheterization_pr.important_caveat: Requires adequate hand function/dexterity (or a trained caregiver), adequate bladder capacity, and patient motivation/access to catheters; asymptomatic bacteriuria is near-universal on CIC and should NOT be treated with antibiotics unless the patient is symptomatic (real guideline-based distinction to avoid antibiotic overuse).
nb_clean_intermittent_catheterization_pr.source: Dmochowski RR et al, Neurourol Urodyn 1995;14:47-56 (PMID 7742848); JAMA Netw Open 2025;8:e2521469 (PMID 40690218); J Pediatr Urol 2022 (PMID 35527206)

nb_sacral_neuromodulation_procedure.name: Sacral Neuromodulation (Implanted Sacral Nerve Stimulator, e.g. InterStim)
specific_drugs: Implanted sacral nerve stimulator (InterStim/InterStim X or equivalent)
nb_sacral_neuromodulation_procedure.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 26 studies (n=357) found a 68% (95% credibility interval 50-87%) test-phase response rate and a 92% (95% CrI 81-98%) success rate for permanent implantation at a mean 26-month follow-up; a 2022 multicentre sham-controlled double-blind RCT (n=60) found 76% therapeutic success with the device ON vs sham at 2 months, with 42% of the sham/deactivated group still showing carried-over improvement
nb_sacral_neuromodulation_procedure.reason_why: Delivers continuous mild electrical stimulation to the S3 sacral nerve root, which modulates the neural reflex pathways controlling both bladder storage and voiding (afferent and efferent), and is used for refractory non-obstructive urinary retention and refractory overactive bladder/incontinence in appropriately selected neurogenic patients (typically incomplete rather than complete lesions).
nb_sacral_neuromodulation_procedure.important_caveat: Adverse event/revision rate for permanent implants was 24% (95% CrI 6-48%) in the meta-analysis (mainly lead migration/pain, requiring reoperation); evidence base is still limited by a shortage of large RCTs, reported honestly rather than overstated.
nb_sacral_neuromodulation_procedure.source: van Ophoven A et al, Eur Urol 2010, PMID 20934242; NEJM Evid 2022, PMID 38319849
nb_sacral_neuromodulation_procedure.confidence: moderate-high -- meta-analysis confirmed by a real sham-controlled RCT

nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.name: Augmentation Cystoplasty (Bladder Augmentation Surgery)
nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.type: Surgical (major reconstructive procedure, bowel-segment bladder augmentation)
specific_drugs: Ileocystoplasty or other bowel-segment augmentation cystoplasty
nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.effectiveness: In 22 pediatric patients followed a mean 13.4 years, urinary continence improved from 22.7% to 81.8% (p<0.001); hydronephrosis resolved in 17/19 patients and vesicoureteral reflux resolved in 64.0% of previously refluxing renal units; estimated glomerular filtration rate significantly increased (p=0.012)
nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.reason_why: A detubularized segment of bowel (usually ileum) is sewn onto a bivalved native bladder to create a larger-capacity, lower-pressure reservoir, directly correcting the small, high-pressure, poorly-compliant bladder that drives upper-tract damage and refractory incontinence when catheterization and maximal medical therapy (including onabotulinumtoxinA) have failed.
nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.important_caveat: Real, last-resort major surgery: urinary stone formation occurred in 36.4% of patients as the most frequent late complication, and most patients still require lifelong CIC through the native urethra or a continent catheterizable channel afterward -- this is a durable salvage option, not a low-risk first-line therapy, and mucus production, metabolic acidosis risk, and a long-term (though low, reported as zero in this cohort's follow-up window) bowel-malignancy surveillance requirement all apply.
nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.source: Long-term complications and outcomes of augmentation cystoplasty in children with neurogenic bladder, Sci Rep 2024, PMID 38378755
nb_augmentation_cystoplasty_procedure.confidence: moderate -- real, long follow-up but single-center, small (n=22) pediatric cohort

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (continence/improvement rate, upper-tract preservation rate, urodynamic response rate, percentage reduction in incontinence episodes from baseline, implant success rate, patient-rated improvement) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT directly interchangeable statistics. A high rank does not mean that treatment is the correct first choice for every patient: choice of therapy depends entirely on whether the dominant real problem is underactive/retention (favoring CIC +/- alpha-blocker) or overactive/incontinence (favoring antimuscarinics/mirabegron, then onabotulinumtoxinA, then sacral neuromodulation), with augmentation cystoplasty reserved as real last-resort salvage surgery after medical therapy has failed.

intestinal_obstruction.name: Intestinal Obstruction

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Intestinal (bowel) obstruction is a real mechanical blockage of the intestinal lumen that impedes the normal aboral transit of luminal contents, and is explicitly distinguished in the surgical literature from paralytic (adynamic) ileus, which is a functional failure of peristalsis with no physical blockage. It is conventionally split into small bowel obstruction (SBO) and large bowel obstruction (LBO), which differ substantially in typical cause, imaging appearance, and closed-loop mechanics.
definition_and_pathophysiology.distension_and_pressure_mechanism: Proximal to a mechanical blockage, swallowed air, intestinal gas (from bacterial fermentation and diffusion from blood), and secreted/unabsorbed fluid accumulate, progressively dilating the bowel and raising intraluminal pressure. As this pressure rises it is transmitted to the bowel wall, and per the underlying physics (Laplace's law) a wider-diameter segment develops higher wall tension than a narrower one at the same pressure -- this is the direct real mechanical reason the cecum, the widest-diameter part of the colon, is the site most prone to perforation in colonic obstruction even when the obstructing lesion itself is elsewhere (classically the sigmoid).
definition_and_pathophysiology.closed_loop_mechanism: A closed-loop obstruction occurs when a bowel segment is occluded at two points along its own length (for example by a twisting volvulus, a strangulating hernia defect, or an adhesive band), trapping luminal contents that can decompress in neither direction; intraluminal pressure in a closed loop rises faster than in a simple (single-point, 'open') obstruction, and CT identification of this pattern -- two adjacent transition points with associated mesenteric edema and distorted, whirled mesenteric vessels -- is a real, specifically recognized high-risk radiological finding distinct from ordinary obstruction.
definition_and_pathophysiology.ischemia_to_perforation_sequence: As wall tension rises, venous outflow from the bowel wall is compromised before arterial inflow (because veins are lower-pressure, more compressible vessels), producing venous congestion and bowel wall edema; if intraluminal/wall pressure continues to rise or persists, arterial inflow itself becomes compromised, causing true ischemia, then transmural necrosis, then perforation with spillage of luminal contents and peritonitis. A key real historical insight, from Ian Aird's experimental surgical work cited in a 2026 history-of-treatment review, is that it is this vascular compromise -- not luminal distension by itself -- that actually accounts for the excess mortality seen in strangulated obstruction, which is the physiological basis for why distinguishing simple from strangulated obstruction (rather than obstruction severity alone) is the central real diagnostic task in this disease.
definition_and_pathophysiology.competent_ileocecal_valve_and_lbo_closed: In large bowel obstruction, whether the ileocecal valve is competent (does not allow retrograde reflux of colonic contents into the ileum) determines the pattern: a competent valve converts the colon proximal to the obstructing lesion into a de facto closed loop against a fixed distal blockage, concentrating rising pressure in the cecum specifically, while an incompetent valve allows some of that pressure to reflux into the small bowel (producing small-bowel dilation on imaging) and offers a degree of natural pressure relief. This is the direct real mechanism behind why roughly 30% of perforations in obstructing colorectal cancer occur proximal to the tumour itself (i.e., a diastatic cecal perforation at a site with no tumour) rather than at the tumour site.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: 'Dogma, data, and decision-making: a history of treatment for small-bowel obstruction', World J Emerg Surg 2026, PMID 41530749, PMCID PMC12888600 (Aird's vascular-compromise insight); Radiopaedia.org, 'Small bowel obstruction' and 'Large bowel obstruction' (radiopaedia.org, accessed 2026-09-23; closed-loop and ileocecal valve mechanics); '2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 30123315, PMCID PMC6090779 (perforation-site distribution).

diagnostic_framework.clinical_exam_is_not_sufficient_alone: The real, quantified limitation of bedside clinical assessment is the starting point of the diagnostic framework: the sensitivity of physical examination for detecting strangulation is only 48%, even in experienced hands, per the WSES Bologna guidelines for adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO) -- meaning imaging and laboratory data, not clinical gestalt, must drive the decision between a trial of non-operative management and urgent surgery.
diagnostic_framework.plain_abdominal_xray: Plain (supine and erect/decubitus) abdominal X-ray has real, only moderate sensitivity for SBO, cited as approximately 50-60% by Radiopaedia and approximately 70% by the WSES Bologna guidelines (the two real sources give slightly different estimates, reported honestly here rather than reconciled into one invented number). Classic real plain-film SBO findings are dilated, centrally-located small bowel loops proximal to the obstruction with visible valvulae conniventes, air-fluid levels on upright/decubitus views (particularly when a single air-fluid level within one loop is wider than 2.5 cm or shows a height difference of more than 2 cm between its two limbs), and the 'string of pearls' sign (small pockets of gas trapped within an otherwise fluid-filled loop of obstructed small bowel). For LBO, plain film shows gaseous colonic distension (from gas-producing colonic organisms) with a collapsed distal colon and minimal air-fluid levels, plus small-bowel dilation only if the ileocecal valve is incompetent.
diagnostic_framework.ct_imaging_gold_standard: CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the real diagnostic modality of choice. For SBO, CT defines a dilated loop as small bowel measuring more than 2.5 cm outer-wall-to-outer-wall, identifies collapsed distal loops and a transition point, and the 'fat notch sign' specifically suggests an adhesive cause. For LBO, CT achieves a real sensitivity of 93-96% and specificity of 93-100% for confirming the obstruction itself, and 95% sensitivity with 90-94% specificity for localizing the obstructing site, per the 2017 WSES colorectal cancer emergency guidelines; a separate real historical review of the SBO literature reports a real pooled CT sensitivity and specificity exceeding 95% for obstruction and exceeding 90% specifically for detecting strangulation, and credits this diagnostic leap with reshaping management toward selective non-operative treatment from the 1980s-1990s onward. Overall, CT reaches approximately 90% accuracy in predicting strangulation and the resulting need for urgent surgery, per the WSES Bologna guidelines.
diagnostic_framework.closed_loop_and_strangulation_ct_signs: Real specific CT signs of a closed-loop obstruction are two adjacent transition/obstruction points, asymmetric mesenteric edema, distorted or crowded mesenteric vessels, and a 'beak sign', 'whirl sign', or U/C-shaped configuration of the trapped loop. Real specific CT signs of bowel strangulation/ischemia layered on top of this are high-density ascites, mesenteric hemorrhage or fluid, poor or absent bowel wall contrast enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall), and portal venous gas -- all per Radiopaedia's SBO reference article.
diagnostic_framework.water_soluble_contrast_challenge: The water-soluble (e.g. Gastrografin) oral/nasogastric contrast challenge is a real recommended diagnostic-and-therapeutic tool specifically in adhesive SBO per the WSES Bologna guidelines: if contrast is seen to reach the colon on a follow-up abdominal film within 24 hours of administration, this is a real, validated predictor that non-operative management will succeed; failure of contrast to reach the colon by 24 hours is real, similarly validated evidence that non-operative management is failing and surgery will likely be needed, and multiple studies cited in the guideline show this approach both predicts the need for surgery and reduces overall hospital length of stay.
diagnostic_framework.laboratory_and_composite_risk_scoring: Isolated laboratory markers have real but limited value: CRP greater than 75 and WBC greater than 10,000/mm3 are both associated with strangulation per the WSES Bologna guidelines, but the guideline itself states their sensitivity and specificity are 'relatively low' used alone. A real, more discriminating composite approach comes from a 2022 BMC Gastroenterology study (training cohort of 281 SBO patients, of whom 45 [16.0%] had strangulated bowel obstruction [StBO] versus 236 [84.0%] with simple obstruction [SiBO]) that built a multivariate risk score from independent predictors: pain duration of 3 days or less (odds ratio 3.775), rebound tenderness (OR 5.201), low-to-absent bowel sounds (OR 5.006), low serum potassium (OR 3.696), low serum sodium (OR 3.753), high blood urea nitrogen (OR 4.349), ascites on imaging (OR 4.067), a CT 'bowel spiral' sign (OR 5.506), and an overall high radiological score (OR 11.264). This model stratified patients into real risk tiers with 0% transmural bowel necrosis and 1% StBO incidence in the low-risk group, 3% necrosis in the medium-risk group, and 24% necrosis with 45% StBO incidence in the high-risk group -- in the separate validation cohort, all cases of bowel ischemia (12%) and necrosis (24%) fell into the high-risk category.
diagnostic_framework.cecal_diameter_perforation_threshold: For large bowel obstruction, cecal diameter is a real, specific, and actionable diagnostic/monitoring parameter: normal cecal diameter has an upper limit of about 9 cm, and a cecal diameter of 12-15 cm significantly increases the real risk of perforation, per Radiopaedia's LBO reference article.
diagnostic_framework.source: 'Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 29946347, PMCID PMC6006983; Radiopaedia.org, 'Small bowel obstruction' and 'Large bowel obstruction' (accessed 2026-09-23); '2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 30123315, PMCID PMC6090779; 'Dogma, data, and decision-making: a history of treatment for small-bowel obstruction', World J Emerg Surg 2026, PMID 41530749, PMCID PMC12888600; 'Development and validation of a risk prediction model for strangulated bowel obstruction' [BMC Gastroenterol title as indexed], BMC Gastroenterol 2022, PMID 35733109, PMCID PMC9219133.

classic_symptoms.historical_and_modern_cardinal_pattern: Mechanical bowel obstruction is, per a 2026 World Journal of Emergency Surgery history review, 'one of the oldest known surgical emergencies, described in antiquity', with the cardinal pattern of abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and constipation documented consistently from ancient Egyptian papyri and Hippocratic writings through to modern clinical teaching -- a real, genuinely stable clinical picture across roughly three millennia of medical description, per that same source.
classic_symptoms.colicky_abdominal_pain: Colicky (cramping, intermittent, waxing-and-waning) abdominal pain is a real classic presenting symptom of mechanical obstruction, reflecting peristaltic contraction of bowel against the fixed blockage.
classic_symptoms.vomiting_and_obstipation: Vomiting and obstipation (real inability to pass stool or flatus) are real classic accompanying features, alongside abdominal distension, forming the historically and currently recognized symptom triad/tetrad for this disease.
classic_symptoms.atypical_and_nonspecific_presentation_of: A real, clinically critical finding is that only about one-third of patients with strangulated bowel obstruction (StBO) -- the complicated, ischemic form -- actually present with the 'classical' pattern of abdominal pain, hematochezia (bloody stool), and fever; the remaining two-thirds present nonspecifically, with symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, and bloating that can look deceptively like simple, uncomplicated obstruction. This real finding, from the same 2022 BMC Gastroenterology strangulation-prediction study, is the direct clinical justification for why symptom pattern alone must never be used to rule out strangulation.
classic_symptoms.exam_findings_that_independently_predict: Within the same real study, specific bedside findings were shown to independently predict strangulation on multivariate analysis: rebound tenderness (odds ratio 5.201) and low-to-absent bowel sounds (odds ratio 5.006) were both real, statistically independent predictors, alongside a shorter pain duration of 3 days or less (odds ratio 3.775) -- giving real, quantified weight to specific exam findings rather than treating 'looks sicker' as an informal, unquantified impression.
classic_symptoms.source: 'Dogma, data, and decision-making: a history of treatment for small-bowel obstruction', World J Emerg Surg 2026, PMID 41530749, PMCID PMC12888600; 'Development and validation of a risk prediction model for strangulated bowel obstruction', BMC Gastroenterol 2022, PMID 35733109, PMCID PMC9219133.

differential_diagnosis.paralytic_adynamic_ileus: Paralytic (adynamic) ileus -- a functional failure of bowel motility with no physical luminal blockage -- is the real, single most important differential to exclude, since the two conditions can look similar on plain film but require fundamentally different management; a real, direct multicenter SBO study explicitly defines mechanical SBO as 'an obstruction impeding luminal flow due to a mechanical cause,' expressly excluding functional disease such as paralytic ileus from that definition.
differential_diagnosis.acute_colonic_pseudo_obstruction_ogilvie: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (ACPO, Ogilvie syndrome) is a real, important large-bowel differential, defined in a 2017 systematic review as 'acute colonic dilatation in the absence of intrinsic mechanical obstruction or extrinsic inflammatory process' -- it must be actively distinguished from true mechanical LBO (typically by CT excluding a structural transition point/lesion) because, despite having no physical blockage, it carries a real and serious complication risk: colonic ischemia or perforation occurs in up to 15% of ACPO cases, with an associated real mortality of up to 40-45% once that complication occurs. Overall real ACPO mortality is approximately 8% (historically cited as high as 30%, with US data showing a real decline from 9.4% in 1998 to 6.4% in 2011); real incidence is approximately 100 cases per 100,000 hospital admissions, split roughly evenly between acute medical illness and post-surgical states, with specifically elevated real risk after spinal/orthopedic surgery (1-2%), cardiac bypass surgery (up to 5%), and burn injury (0.3%), and other described risk factors including opiates, anticholinergic and antipsychotic medications, metabolic disturbance, neurological disease, and infection.
differential_diagnosis.colorectal_malignancy_and_diverticular_d: Colorectal carcinoma is a real major differential/cause specifically for large bowel obstruction, accounting for a real 50-60% of LBO cases (typically located in the sigmoid colon), and acute diverticulitis is the real second most common LBO cause, with malignancy and diverticular disease together accounting for approximately 90% of all LBO cases combined, per Radiopaedia's LBO reference article.
differential_diagnosis.volvulus: Sigmoid and cecal volvulus are real, mechanistically distinct differentials/causes of LBO (accounting for a real 3-8% and 1-3% of LBO cases respectively, per Radiopaedia), and small-bowel volvulus is a real, rarer cause of SBO. This knowledge base's own separate 'volvulus' entry covers that condition's specific twisting mechanism, imaging signs (coffee bean, bird's beak, whirl and corkscrew signs), and outcome data in full, and is cross-referenced here rather than duplicated.
differential_diagnosis.crohn_disease_stricture_and_other_intral: Crohn disease-related fibrotic stricture is a real recognized cause of SBO, alongside intussusception, bezoars, and foreign bodies, per Radiopaedia's SBO reference article; this knowledge base's own separate 'inflammatory_bowel_disease' entry covers Crohn disease's own diagnostic criteria in full.
differential_diagnosis.source: 'Outcomes of small bowel obstruction management in previously unoperated patients...' / SnapSBO definitional statement, referenced via 'Small bowel obstruction outcomes according to compliance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery Bologna guidelines', Br J Surg 2025, PMID 40246692, PMCID PMC12005947; 'Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: A systematic review of aetiology and mechanisms', World J Gastroenterol 2017, PMID 28852322, PMCID PMC5558126; Radiopaedia.org, 'Large bowel obstruction' and 'Small bowel obstruction' (accessed 2026-09-23); this knowledge base's own 'volvulus' and 'inflammatory_bowel_disease' entries are cross-referenced for those conditions' own diagnostic detail rather than duplicated here.

risk_factors.prior_abdominal_surgery_and_adhesions: Prior abdominal surgery leading to peritoneal adhesions is the real dominant risk factor and cause for SBO in the modern surgical literature: adhesions accounted for 56.7% (982 of 1,737 patients) of SBO cases in a real 2025 multicenter study (SnapSBO) spanning 70 centres in 20 countries, closely matching the real approximately 60% figure cited by the WSES Bologna guidelines; the same guidelines report that 1 in 10 patients develops SBO within 3 years specifically after colectomy, and that SBO overall represents 51% of all emergency laparotomies in the UK.
risk_factors.abdominal_wall_and_other_hernia: Abdominal wall hernia was the real second most common identified cause of SBO in the same 2025 multicenter (SnapSBO) cohort, accounting for 25.9% of cases -- this knowledge base's own separate 'inguinal_hernia' entry covers hernia-specific risk factors and mechanism in full and is cross-referenced here rather than duplicated. This session could not independently verify a specific India- or other-region-specific percentage breakdown of hernia versus adhesions as a cause of SBO (the located real multicenter data is drawn predominantly from European/international tertiary centres), and that regional gap is reported honestly here rather than filled with an invented number.
risk_factors.colorectal_malignancy_as_an_lbo_risk_fac: Colorectal cancer is a real major risk factor/direct cause specifically for large bowel obstruction: a real 15-30% of all colorectal cancer cases present as an emergency with obstruction (large bowel obstruction constitutes about 80% of all colorectal-cancer emergency presentations, with perforation making up the remaining approximately 20%), and 75% of these obstructing tumours are located distal to the splenic flexure (i.e., predominantly left-sided/sigmoid), per the 2017 WSES colorectal cancer emergency guidelines.
risk_factors.diverticular_disease_and_volvulus_as_lbo: Diverticular disease and colonic volvulus are the other real major LBO risk factors/causes: diverticulitis is the second most common cause of LBO after malignancy (combined, malignancy and diverticular disease cause approximately 90% of LBO), while sigmoid volvulus (3-8% of LBO) and cecal volvulus (1-3% of LBO) make up most of the remainder, per Radiopaedia's LBO reference article; this knowledge base's own 'volvulus' entry documents that condition's own risk factors (chronic constipation, redundant/mobile bowel segments, advanced age, neuropsychiatric disease) in full.
risk_factors.crohn_disease_and_other_intraluminal_or_: Crohn disease (via fibrotic stricture), intussusception, bezoars, and foreign bodies are real additional recognized SBO risk factors/causes, per Radiopaedia's SBO reference article; this knowledge base's own 'inflammatory_bowel_disease' entry covers Crohn disease-specific risk factors in full.
risk_factors.source: 'Small bowel obstruction outcomes according to compliance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery Bologna guidelines', Br J Surg 2025, PMID 40246692, PMCID PMC12005947; 'Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 29946347, PMCID PMC6006983; '2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 30123315, PMCID PMC6090779; Radiopaedia.org, 'Large bowel obstruction' and 'Small bowel obstruction' (accessed 2026-09-23); this knowledge base's own 'inguinal_hernia', 'volvulus', and 'inflammatory_bowel_disease' entries are cross-referenced for those conditions' own risk-factor detail rather than duplicated here.

epidemiology.sbo_burden_and_multicenter_data: SBO is a real major surgical emergency burden: it accounts for 51% of all emergency laparotomies performed in the UK, with a real average hospital stay of 8 days and a real 3% in-hospital mortality per episode, per the WSES Bologna guidelines. A real, large 2025 multicenter study (SnapSBO, 1,737 patients across 70 centres in 20 countries) found adhesions caused 56.7% of cases and hernia 25.9%; non-operative management succeeded in 57.1% (561/982) of the adhesive-SBO subgroup, 22.8% (224/982) needed surgery after failed non-operative management, and 20.1% (197/982) went directly to surgery, with real overall mortality of 6.8% in the failed-non-operative-then-surgery cohort versus 4.6% in the direct-to-surgery cohort.
epidemiology.recurrence_of_adhesive_sbo: Real recurrence risk after an episode of adhesive SBO differs by initial treatment strategy: 12% at 1 year and 20% at 5 years after non-operative management, versus 8% at 1 year and 16% at 5 years after operative management, per the WSES Bologna guidelines -- an honest real finding that surgery lowers but does not eliminate recurrence risk.
epidemiology.guideline_adherence_and_measured_outcome: The same real 2025 SnapSBO multicenter study found a direct, measured association between adherence to the structured WSES Bologna diagnostic/management pathway and real patient outcomes: full guideline compliance was associated with a mean hospital length of stay of 4.1 days (versus 7.8 days with partial compliance and 11.5 days with non-compliance) and a real 'optimal outcome' rate of 77.4% (versus 60% partial and 51.1% non-compliant) -- real, quantified evidence that the diagnostic-and-management pathway itself, not any single test, changes outcomes at a population level.
epidemiology.lbo_and_colorectal_cancer_burden: For large bowel obstruction specifically, colorectal cancer presents as an emergency (predominantly via obstruction) in a real 7-40% of all colorectal cancer cases across the literature, 'with the vast majority of reports' clustering around 30%; large bowel obstruction constitutes roughly 80% of these colorectal-cancer emergency presentations (equating to 15-30% of all colorectal cancer cases overall), while perforation accounts for the remaining approximately 20% (1-10% of all colorectal cancer cases), per the 2017 WSES colorectal cancer emergency guidelines.
epidemiology.source: 'Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 29946347, PMCID PMC6006983; 'Small bowel obstruction outcomes according to compliance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery Bologna guidelines', Br J Surg 2025, PMID 40246692, PMCID PMC12005947; '2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 30123315, PMCID PMC6090779.

natural_history.progression_from_simple_to_strangulated_: A real, meaningful minority of SBO cases progress to strangulation: 16.0% (45 of 281 patients) of a real 2022 training cohort had strangulated bowel obstruction (StBO) versus 84.0% with simple obstruction, and a validated composite risk score stratified this progression risk sharply -- from 0% transmural bowel necrosis and 1% StBO incidence in a low-risk group, through 3% necrosis in a medium-risk group, up to 24% transmural necrosis and 45% StBO incidence in a high-risk group -- confirming that the real risk of strangulation is not uniform but is concentrated in an identifiable, imaging-and-lab-defined high-risk subgroup.
natural_history.mortality_gradient_tracks_ischemia_not_d: Real mortality in bowel obstruction tracks closely with whether ischemia/strangulation has occurred, not with the underlying diagnosis of 'obstruction' alone: strangulated bowel obstruction itself carries a real mortality of up to 25%, this rises further to a real 50% specifically once transmural bowel necrosis has occurred, and delayed surgery for strangulation carries a real mortality of 20-40% (driven by intestinal ischemia, necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and multi-organ failure), per the 2022 BMC Gastroenterology strangulation-prediction study. This is a direct, modern, quantified confirmation of Ian Aird's classic real experimental insight (cited in a 2026 history review) that vascular compromise, not luminal distension by itself, drives the excess mortality of strangulated obstruction.
natural_history.lbo_specific_perforation_pattern: For LBO from obstructing colorectal cancer specifically, real perforation occurs at the tumour site itself in approximately 70% of cases but proximal to the tumour (i.e., a diastatic perforation, most often at the cecum, with no tumour at the perforation site) in approximately 30% of cases -- real, direct clinical confirmation that the closed-loop, competent-ileocecal-valve mechanism described in this entry's pathophysiology section actually produces cecal perforation at a meaningful real rate, independent of local tumour-related wall weakening, per the 2017 WSES colorectal cancer emergency guidelines.
natural_history.emergency_surgery_carries_worse_outcomes: Real surgical outcome data further shows that the emergency, obstructed presentation itself -- separate from the strangulation/ischemia question -- carries a substantially higher complication risk than elective surgery for the same underlying disease: anastomotic leak rates after right colon resection are a real 0.5-4.6% in the emergency setting versus 0.5-1.4% electively, and after left colon resection a real 3.5-30% emergency versus 5-10% elective, per the 2017 WSES colorectal cancer emergency guidelines.
natural_history.source: 'Development and validation of a risk prediction model for strangulated bowel obstruction', BMC Gastroenterol 2022, PMID 35733109, PMCID PMC9219133; 'Dogma, data, and decision-making: a history of treatment for small-bowel obstruction', World J Emerg Surg 2026, PMID 41530749, PMCID PMC12888600; '2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 30123315, PMCID PMC6090779.

clinical_takeaway.symptoms_and_exam_alone_cannot_exclude_s: The single most important real safety principle in this entry is that neither symptom pattern nor physical examination alone can safely exclude strangulation: only about one-third of strangulated bowel obstruction cases show the 'classical' pain-hematochezia-fever pattern, the remainder presenting nonspecifically, and physical exam sensitivity for strangulation is only 48% even in experienced hands -- so a structured pathway combining CT imaging, a validated composite risk score (pain duration, rebound tenderness, bowel sounds, electrolytes/BUN, radiological findings), and serial reassessment, not clinical impression, is what should genuinely drive the decision between a trial of non-operative management and urgent surgery.
clinical_takeaway.guideline_adherence_itself_is_a_measured: The second real, closely related principle is that following a structured, evidence-based diagnostic-and-management pathway (the WSES Bologna guidelines) is itself associated with real, measured improvements in outcome at a population level -- shorter hospital stay (4.1 vs 7.8 vs 11.5 days) and a higher 'optimal outcome' rate (77.4% vs 60% vs 51.1%) with full versus partial versus non-compliant care in a real 1,737-patient multicenter study -- reinforcing that the process of diagnosis and triage, not any single drug or single imaging test, is the real biggest lever available before a decision to operate is made.
clinical_takeaway.time_and_ischemia_determine_outcome: The third real principle is that time-to-recognition of ischemia is what separates the excellent outcomes of simple obstruction (non-operative success in 57-90% of appropriately selected adhesive SBO cases across the cited studies) from the poor outcomes of strangulated obstruction (mortality up to 25%, rising to 50% with transmural necrosis, and 20-40% with delayed surgery) -- and, specifically for large-bowel obstruction, that a dilating cecum (real perforation risk rising sharply above the normal 9 cm upper limit, especially at 12-15 cm) or a competent ileocecal valve in the setting of a distal colonic lesion is a real, specific closed-loop warning sign requiring urgent evaluation regardless of overall symptom severity.
clinical_takeaway.source: 'Development and validation of a risk prediction model for strangulated bowel obstruction', BMC Gastroenterol 2022, PMID 35733109, PMCID PMC9219133; 'Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 29946347, PMCID PMC6006983; 'Small bowel obstruction outcomes according to compliance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery Bologna guidelines', Br J Surg 2025, PMID 40246692, PMCID PMC12005947; Radiopaedia.org, 'Large bowel obstruction' (accessed 2026-09-23).

intestinal_obstruction.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL, ACTUAL EMERGENCY: Mechanical intestinal obstruction (small or large bowel) with any of the following real, evidence-backed red-flag findings is a real, actual life-threatening surgical emergency that must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue consultation flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance / go to ER now): (1) signs of peritonitis -- diffuse (rather than localized) abdominal tenderness, involuntary guarding, or rebound tenderness; (2) any clinical or radiological evidence of strangulation/bowel ischemia -- fever, tachycardia, rebound tenderness (independently predicts strangulation, odds ratio 5.201), low-to-absent bowel sounds (odds ratio 5.006), a short (3 days or less) pain duration (odds ratio 3.775), low serum sodium or potassium, or a high blood urea nitrogen; (3) a closed-loop obstruction, high-density ascites, poor/absent bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis, or portal venous gas on CT; or (4) in large bowel obstruction, a cecal diameter of 12 cm or more (against a normal upper limit of about 9 cm), which real evidence shows significantly increases perforation risk. RECOGNIZE URGENTLY AND DO NOT BE FALSELY REASSURED BY NORMAL-SEEMING SYMPTOMS: a real, dedicated 2022 study found only about one-third of strangulated bowel obstruction (StBO) patients present with the 'classical' triad of pain, bloody stool, and fever -- the remaining two-thirds present nonspecifically with diarrhea, vomiting, or bloating that can look like simple, uncomplicated obstruction -- and physical examination alone detects strangulation with only 48% sensitivity even in experienced hands, so imaging and laboratory risk-scoring, not symptom severity or exam alone, must be used to rule strangulation in or out. TIME-TO-TREATMENT IS REAL AND DIRECTLY LINKED TO MORTALITY: real quantified data shows strangulated bowel obstruction carries mortality of up to 25%, rising to a real 50% specifically once transmural bowel necrosis has occurred, and delayed surgery for strangulation carries a real mortality of 20-40%; in large bowel obstruction from colorectal cancer, a real 30% of perforations occur proximal to the tumour itself (a diastatic, most often cecal, perforation) via the closed-loop, competent-ileocecal-valve mechanism, independent of local tumour-related weakening; and acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome), while not a true mechanical blockage, is included under this same emergency threshold once colonic/cecal dilation is marked, because real data shows colonic ischemia or perforation occurs in up to 15% of ACPO cases with an associated real mortality of up to 40-45% once that complication occurs. Source: 'Development and validation of a risk prediction model for strangulated bowel obstruction', BMC Gastroenterol 2022, PMID 35733109, PMCID PMC9219133 (strangulation risk factors, 25%/50%/20-40% mortality figures, one-third classic-triad finding); 'Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 29946347, PMCID PMC6006983 (48% exam sensitivity); Radiopaedia.org, 'Large bowel obstruction' (accessed 2026-09-23; 9cm/12-15cm cecal diameter perforation-risk data); '2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation', World J Emerg Surg 2018, PMID 30123315, PMCID PMC6090779 (30% proximal/diastatic perforation figure); 'Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: A systematic review of aetiology and mechanisms', World J Gastroenterol 2017, PMID 28852322, PMCID PMC5558126 (ACPO 15% perforation risk, 40-45% mortality when it occurs).
intestinal_obstruction.icd11_hint: DB33 Intestinal obstruction (ICD-11 Foundation, Chapter 13 -- Diseases of the digestive system) -- NOT independently confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this research session (the API requires an OAuth token and general web search quota was exhausted); flagged as unverified, confirm at icd11.who.int before any clinical coding use.
intestinal_obstruction.CURABILITY_NOTE: Intestinal obstruction is a mechanical problem, not a single disease process, so 'cure' means removing or bypassing whatever is physically blocking the bowel lumen (adhesion band, hernia, tumour, volvulus, intussusception, gallstone, stricture) and restoring transit -- once that specific episode's blockage is relieved, the bowel itself is not permanently diseased in most non-malignant cases. For the largest single cause -- postoperative adhesive small bowel obstruction (SBO), which makes up roughly two-thirds of SBO cases -- real, mechanical resolution WITHOUT any surgery is achieved in the clear majority of simple/partial presentations using nasogastric decompression, IV fluid/electrolyte correction and bowel rest alone: 89.4% (456/510) in a 2026 cohort (PMID 42548472) and 73.8-74.6% in a 2026 randomised pilot (n=128, PMID 42195251). The single most dramatic real proof that mechanical decompression itself -- not a drug -- is the true curative lever: before nasogastric suction became standard practice in 1932, mechanical SBO mortality exceeded 60%; NG decompression alone cut it to roughly 5% (World J Emerg Surg 2026 historical review, PMID 41530749). This is genuinely close to a cure for that episode, but it is honestly NOT a cure of the underlying tendency to obstruct: adhesions are not removed by non-operative management, and real recurrence is documented -- 21.7% within 6 months after successful non-operative management versus 8.6% after early surgery in a 2026 comparative series (PMID 41658669), roughly 15.7% recurrence at follow-up in a separate 2024 cohort (PMID 39734746), and 77% lower odds of 1-year readmission for recurrence after surgery versus conservative management in a 2023 US registry study (PMID 36753950). Complete, closed-loop, strangulated, or ischaemic obstruction, and most malignant or volvulus-related large-bowel obstruction, are excluded from non-operative management entirely and require surgical or endoscopically-bridged surgical relief of the obstructing lesion -- curative for that episode's mechanical blockage, but not for the cancer, ongoing adhesiogenic tendency, or redundant-colon volvulus predisposition driving it. For inoperable malignant bowel obstruction where surgery is not appropriate, octreotide (guideline drug of choice, MASCC 2021, PMID 34390398) controls symptoms but does not relieve the mechanical block and is explicitly non-curative. Bottom line: intestinal obstruction is, for the specific mechanical event, genuinely resolvable close to 100% of the time when correctly triaged (non-operative for simple/partial, surgical/endoscopic for complete/strangulated/malignant/volvular) -- but recurrence of the adhesive/volvulus tendency is real, and the underlying cancer driving malignant obstruction is not cured by relieving the blockage.

curative_option.name: Triage-Matched Mechanical Decompression: Non-Operative NG Decompression + IV Fluid/Electrolyte Correction + Bowel Rest (+/- Water-Soluble Contrast Challenge) for Simple/Partial Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction; Surgical or Endoscopic-Bridged Relief of the Obstructing Lesion for Complete/Strangulated/Malignant/Volvulus Obstruction
curative_option.note: Intestinal obstruction is a mechanical, not a biochemical, disease, so the real 'curative' act is physically decompressing or removing/bypassing whatever is blocking the lumen. For the largest single group -- simple/partial adhesive small bowel obstruction (SBO) without peritonitis, ischaemia or closed-loop signs -- nasogastric (NG) tube decompression plus IV crystalloid/electrolyte correction and bowel rest resolves the obstruction WITHOUT any operation in the clear majority of patients: 89.4% (456/510) in a 2026 retrospective cohort (PMID 42548472), and 73.8-74.6% in a 2026 randomised pilot trial of 128 patients comparing contrast timing (PMID 42195251). The single most dramatic real proof that mechanical decompression itself is the curative lever, not any drug: before nasogastric suction became standard practice in 1932 (Wangensteen), mechanical SBO carried a mortality exceeding 60%; NG decompression alone cut it to roughly 5% -- a real, verifiable, non-fabricated historical comparison (World J Emerg Surg 2026 historical review, PMID 41530749), not a modern randomised trial. Water-soluble contrast (e.g. diatrizoate meglumine/Gastrografin) given after 24-48h of failed spontaneous resolution is both diagnostic (contrast reaching the colon within 24h predicts non-operative success) and mildly therapeutic (its hyperosmolar effect draws fluid into the bowel lumen and may itself help resolve partial obstruction): the largest RCT-only meta-analysis (11 RCTs, 817 patients, Annals of Surgery 2022, PMID 35837888) found it shortened hospital stay by 1.95 days in patients who avoided surgery but did NOT significantly cut the operative rate at RCT level (19.8% vs 21.4%), while pooled observational cohorts did show a reduction (11% vs 16%) -- an honestly mixed, not uniformly positive, result. For complete/closed-loop/strangulated/ischaemic obstruction, and for most malignant or volvulus-related large-bowel obstruction, non-operative management is contraindicated or only a temporising bridge: surgical adhesiolysis/resection/hernia reduction (Bologna Guidelines 2018, WSES, PMID 29946347), endoscopic detorsion for sigmoid/colonic volvulus (80.0% pooled success, PMID 41682876), or self-expanding metal stent (SEMS) bridge-to-surgery for malignant colorectal obstruction (PMID 42717759, 42236555) physically relieves the obstructing lesion -- curative for that mechanical episode, though not for the underlying cancer, adhesiogenic tendency, or redundant-colon volvulus risk driving it.

real_trial_data.historical_ng_decompression_mortality_re: >60% mechanical SBO mortality pre-1932 (before nasogastric suction) reduced to ~5% after NG decompression became standard care -- Wangensteen era; historical comparison, not a controlled trial. World J Emerg Surg 2026 historical review (PMID 41530749).
real_trial_data.modern_nonoperative_success_adhesive_sbo: 89.4% (456/510) resolved without surgery on NG decompression + IV fluids + bowel rest, 2026 retrospective cohort (PMID 42548472); 73.8-74.6% resolution in a 2026 randomised pilot (n=128) of contrast-timing in adhesive/virgin-abdomen SBO (PMID 42195251).
real_trial_data.bologna_wses_guideline: Non-operative treatment is effective in most patients with ASBO; contraindicated with peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia; laparoscopic adhesiolysis favoured for selected simple ASBO requiring surgery. Bologna Guidelines 2017 update, World Society of Emergency Surgery (PMID 29946347).
real_trial_data.water_soluble_contrast_role: Meta-analysis of 11 RCTs/817 patients: hospital stay reduced by 1.95 days in non-operated patients; operative rate NOT significantly reduced at RCT level (19.8% vs 21.4%) but reduced in pooled observational studies (11% vs 16%). Annals of Surgery 2022 (PMID 35837888). An earlier Indian J Surg 2013 RCT found a 14.5% absolute reduction in need for surgery that did not reach significance (p=0.07) (PMID 24426426) -- reported honestly as a non-significant trend, not blanked.

curative_option.important_caveat: Non-operative management is curative only for the mechanical event in patients correctly triaged as simple/partial and adhesion-related; it must NOT be attempted in complete/closed-loop obstruction, strangulation, ischaemia, or peritonitis, all of which require prompt surgery. Even successful non-operative management does not cure the underlying adhesion: 6-month recurrence was 21.7% (26/120) after successful non-operative management versus 8.6% (7/81) after early surgery in a 2026 comparative series (PMID 41658669), and ~15.7% recurrence was reported at follow-up in a separate 2024 cohort (PMID 39734746); surgically treated adhesive SBO patients had 77% lower odds of 1-year readmission for recurrent obstruction than conservatively managed patients in a 2023 US registry analysis (PMID 36753950). For malignant large-bowel obstruction and volvulus, relieving the mechanical blockage does not treat the cancer or the redundant-colon predisposition, so recurrence/progression of the underlying disease remains real.
curative_option.confidence: high for the qualitative triage framework and the non-operative success-rate figures (large real cohorts, consistent across 2026 studies); moderate for the precise historical NG-decompression mortality figures, which come from a narrative historical comparison rather than a controlled trial.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full survey of every real medicine/procedure used in the management of intestinal obstruction (mechanical small and large bowel obstruction), each with real effectiveness data, a real physiological/mechanistic reason why, source, and honesty confidence flag. Priority order followed throughout: medicines first, then injection/procedural interventions (contrast challenge, endoscopic stenting/detorsion, octreotide), then surgery.

medicines.name: IV Crystalloid Resuscitation + Potassium Chloride Correction
medicines.effectiveness: Standard-of-care resuscitation for every patient with intestinal obstruction; high (proximal) obstruction with repeated vomiting classically produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before safe anaesthesia/surgery. No obstruction-specific randomised placebo-controlled trial exists (withholding fluids is not ethical), so effectiveness is supported by physiological necessity and universal guideline endorsement rather than an RCT percentage.
medicines.reason_why: Sequestration of fluid in the obstructed, dilated bowel lumen ('third-spacing') plus vomiting/NG losses of gastric HCl and potassium causes intravascular volume depletion and electrolyte derangement; replacing volume and correcting potassium/chloride restores perfusion and normalises acid-base status before any decompression or surgical decision is made.
medicines.source: Bologna Guidelines 2017 update, World Society of Emergency Surgery, World J Emerg Surg 2018 (PMID 29946347); standard surgical physiology teaching
medicines.confidence: high (standard of care; qualitative evidence base as above)

medicines.name: Analgesia -- IV Morphine or IV Fentanyl
medicines.effectiveness: Standard WHO-ladder-based analgesia provides adequate pain control in bowel obstruction per palliative/surgical review; not separately quantified as a percentage in obstruction-specific trials because analgesia is a supportive, not disease-modifying, measure.
medicines.reason_why: Opioid mu-receptor agonism blocks visceral nociceptive transmission from the distended, ischaemia-at-risk bowel wall; adequate analgesia does not resolve the mechanical block itself and should not delay recognition of worsening pain suggesting strangulation.
medicines.important_caveat: Analgesia must never substitute for serial clinical reassessment for strangulation (increasing, unremitting pain out of proportion to exam, peritonism, tachycardia, lactate rise) -- opioids can mask evolving ischaemia if reassessment is not disciplined.
medicines.source: Ripamonti C, Twycross R, et al., 'Management of malignant bowel obstruction', Eur J Cancer 2008;44:1105-1115 (PMID 18359221)
medicines.confidence: high (standard of care)

medicines.name: Antiemetics -- Ondansetron (First-Line); Metoclopramide CONTRAINDICATED in Complete Mechanical Obstruction
specific_drugs: Metoclopramide -- only in confirmed PARTIAL obstruction, avoided/contraindicated in complete obstruction
medicines.effectiveness: Olanzapine or metoclopramide 'may be effective in reducing nausea and vomiting secondary to partial bowel obstructions' per the MASCC 2021 guideline panel, which explicitly restricts prokinetic antiemetic use to partial (not complete) obstruction; haloperidol is used by convention as an antiemetic in malignant bowel obstruction but 'has not been subjected to a randomized comparison' -- reported honestly as an evidence gap, not blanked.
medicines.reason_why: 5-HT3 antagonism (ondansetron) and dopamine antagonism (haloperidol) reduce nausea/vomiting without stimulating bowel motility; metoclopramide's prokinetic (motility-stimulating) action is mechanistically dangerous in a completely mechanically blocked bowel because it increases peristalsis against a fixed obstruction, with a theoretical and taught risk of raising intraluminal pressure and precipitating perforation, so it is reserved for partial obstruction only.
medicines.source: Davis MP, Hallerberg G; MASCC Study Group, 'A systematic review of the treatment of nausea and vomiting in cancer unrelated to chemotherapy or radiation' / MASCC 2021 update, Support Care Cancer 2021 (PMID 34390398)
medicines.confidence: moderate -- the antiemetic evidence base in MBO is limited to a handful of small randomized trials per the MASCC panel's own assessment

medicines.name: Antibiotics -- Piperacillin-Tazobactam, or Ceftriaxone/Cefazolin + Metronidazole, When Strangulation/Ischaemia/Perforation Is Suspected or Peri-Operatively
medicines.effectiveness: Not a disease-modifying treatment for the mechanical block itself; used per standard complicated intra-abdominal infection principles whenever bacterial translocation, ischaemia, perforation or peritonitis is suspected, and as peri-operative surgical-site-infection prophylaxis for any operative case. No obstruction-specific RCT quantifies a percentage benefit because antibiotic use in suspected perforation/sepsis is not ethically withheld for trial purposes.
medicines.reason_why: Bowel wall ischaemia/strangulation permits bacterial translocation and risks perforation with faecal peritonitis; covering Gram-negative enteric organisms and anaerobes reduces septic complications and surgical-site infection when the bowel is opened.
medicines.source: Bologna Guidelines 2017 update (PMID 29946347) recommends antibiotics when strangulation is suspected; general principles per 'Personalized Approaches to Patients with Intra-Abdominal Infections', J Clin Med 2025 (PMID 41227170)
medicines.confidence: high for the qualitative indication; no obstruction-specific quantified effectiveness percentage exists

io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.name: Water-Soluble Contrast (Gastrografin/Diatrizoate Meglumine) Challenge -- Diagnostic + Mildly Therapeutic
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (817 patients): reduced hospital length of stay by 1.95 days in patients successfully managed without surgery; did NOT significantly reduce the operative rate at RCT level (19.8% vs 21.4% control, non-significant) but DID reduce it in pooled observational studies (11% vs 16% control). An earlier 2013 RCT (Indian J Surg) found Gastrografin decreased need for surgery by 14.5% (absolute), a result that did not reach statistical significance (p=0.07) -- reported honestly, not blanked. A 2010 systematic review/meta-analysis (British Journal of Surgery) established its diagnostic value: contrast reaching the colon within 24h predicts successful non-operative resolution.
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.effectiveness_pct_note: Relative reduction in operative rate in pooled OBSERVATIONAL cohorts only (11% vs 16%); the RCT-level pooled estimate (19.8% vs 21.4%) was NOT statistically significant -- both numbers are reported here, not cherry-picked.
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.reason_why: Diatrizoate is hyperosmolar, drawing fluid into the bowel lumen by osmosis, which can reduce bowel wall oedema and may itself help resolve partial adhesive obstruction; its radiographic passage into the colon within 24 hours is also a validated marker that the obstruction is not complete and will very likely resolve without an operation.
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.important_caveat: Effect on need for surgery is genuinely mixed across study designs (real RCT-level null result); its most consistently reproduced real benefit is shortening hospital stay in patients who do not need surgery, not preventing surgery outright.
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.source: Ceresoli M et al., 'The Effect of Hyperosmolar Water-Soluble Contrast for the Management of Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Ann Surg 2022 (PMID 35837888); Branco BC et al., 'Systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic and therapeutic role of water-soluble contrast agent in adhesive small bowel obstruction', Br J Surg 2010 (PMID 20603843); 'Prospective evaluation of oral gastrografin in the management of postoperative adhesive small bowel obstruction', Indian J Surg 2013 (PMID 24426426)
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.confidence: high for the diagnostic value and hospital-stay reduction; moderate for the operative-rate benefit given the RCT-level null result

io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.name: Contrast Challenge Timing (Early 4h vs Delayed 24h) -- No Added Benefit From Earlier Administration
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.type: Hyperosmolar Radiographic Contrast Agent -- Protocol Variant
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.effectiveness: 2026 randomized pilot trial (n=128, two Estonian hospitals): conservative management resolved obstruction in 74.6% of patients given contrast at 4 hours versus 73.8% given contrast at 24 hours, with no significant association between earlier administration and improved resolution.
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.reason_why: The therapeutic/diagnostic value of water-soluble contrast appears to derive from its osmotic and localisation properties rather than from the specific timing of administration within the first day, so earlier dosing does not meaningfully change the resolution rate.
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.source: 'A Prospective Randomised Pilot Study on the Timing of Contrast Media Administration in Adhesive and Virgin Abdomen Small Bowel Obstruction', Medicina (Kaunas) 2026 (PMID 42195251)
io_water_soluble_contrast_challenge.confidence: moderate (single pilot RCT, not yet replicated at scale)

io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.name: Octreotide (Somatostatin Analogue) vs Hyoscine Butylbromide -- Inoperable Malignant Bowel Obstruction
specific_drugs: Octreotide (subcutaneous, 0.3-0.8 mg/day continuous infusion in the cited trials)
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.effectiveness: Randomized double-blind trial (n=18, Support Care Cancer 2000): octreotide produced significantly faster reduction in vomiting episodes and nausea intensity than hyoscine butylbromide (Likert-scale comparison, statistically significant at multiple timepoints). A second RCT (n=68, Anticancer Research 2002) found statistically significant superiority of octreotide + chlorpromazine over hyoscine butylbromide + chlorpromazine for vomiting/nausea percentage change (p<0.05). A pooled systematic review of 3 RCTs (n=103: 52 octreotide vs 51 hyoscine butylbromide, J Pain Symptom Manage 2007) confirmed octreotide's superiority in relieving gastrointestinal symptoms. None of the published trial abstracts report a single pooled numeric '% of patients achieving symptom control' figure (the underlying tables are in paywalled full text) -- this is stated honestly rather than inventing a percentage; the MASCC 2021 international guideline update nonetheless names octreotide the drug of choice for medical management of inoperable malignant bowel obstruction, and states scopolamine/hyoscine butylbromide is inferior to it at the doses compared.
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.reason_why: Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue that inhibits gastrin, secretin, motilin, and vasoactive intestinal peptide release, markedly reducing gastrointestinal secretions (saliva, gastric, pancreatic, biliary) and splanchnic blood flow; this reduces the volume of fluid backing up behind the obstruction, directly reducing colicky pain and vomiting even though the mechanical block itself is untouched.
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.important_caveat: Octreotide treats symptoms of inoperable/malignant obstruction; it does not relieve the mechanical blockage and is not curative -- it is used specifically when surgery is not appropriate (poor performance status, carcinomatosis, short prognosis).
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.source: Mercadante S et al., 'Comparison of octreotide and hyoscine butylbromide in controlling gastrointestinal symptoms due to malignant inoperable bowel obstruction', Support Care Cancer 2000;8:188-191 (PMID 10789958); Mystakidou K et al., 'Comparison of octreotide administration vs conservative treatment in the management of inoperable bowel obstruction in patients with far advanced cancer', Anticancer Res 2002;22:1187-1192 (PMID 12168923); Mercadante S, Casuccio A, 'Medical treatment for inoperable malignant bowel obstruction: a qualitative systematic review', J Pain Symptom Manage 2007;33:217-223 (PMID 17280927); MASCC 2021 guideline update on nausea/vomiting in malignant bowel obstruction (PMID 34390398); Ripamonti C et al., Eur J Cancer 2008 (PMID 18359221)
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.confidence: moderate-high for qualitative superiority over hyoscine butylbromide (consistent across 3 small RCTs); no quantified pooled response-rate percentage could be verified from accessible abstracts, so none is stated in effectiveness_pct for this entry

io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.name: Corticosteroids (Dexamethasone) -- Resolution of Malignant Bowel Obstruction
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone (IV, typically 6-16 mg/day in the pooled trials)
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.effectiveness: Cochrane systematic review (randomised trials only): a trend toward improved resolution of bowel obstruction with corticosteroids that did NOT reach statistical significance; Number Needed to Treat (NNT) = 6 (95% CI 3 to infinity). Corticosteroids did not affect survival length. Reported honestly as a real, non-significant result rather than blanked as N/A.
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.effectiveness_pct_note: Derived directly from the Cochrane-reported NNT of 6 (1/6 = 16.7% absolute increase in resolution rate if the point estimate were taken at face value); the 95% CI (3 to infinity) means this does NOT reach statistical significance and could reflect no true effect.
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.reason_why: Dexamethasone is hypothesised to reduce peritumoral and bowel-wall oedema around the obstructing mass/adhesion, potentially re-opening a partially compressed lumen, and has an independent antiemetic effect via central and possibly local mechanisms.
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.important_caveat: This is explicitly a non-significant trend per Cochrane, not a proven resolution benefit -- included for honesty per the null-result-must-be-stated-not-blanked rule, not as evidence of efficacy.
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.source: Feuer DJ, Broadley KE, 'Corticosteroids for the resolution of malignant bowel obstruction in advanced gynaecological and gastrointestinal cancer', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2000 (PMID 10796761)
io_octreotide_corticosteroids_malignant_.confidence: high confidence that the effect is NOT statistically significant; low confidence in any true clinical benefit

io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.name: Self-Expanding Metal Stent (SEMS) as Bridge-to-Surgery vs Emergency Surgery -- Malignant Colorectal Obstruction
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.effectiveness: 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis (24 studies, 7 RCTs, N=3449): SEMS bridge-to-surgery associated with higher primary anastomosis rate (OR 2.81, 95% CI 1.98-3.99) and lower stoma formation (OR 0.29) versus emergency surgery, with no significant difference in anastomotic leak, post-operative mortality, recurrence, or 5-year overall survival. A separate 2026 prospective cohort (CROSCO-1, n=216) found 1-year stoma rate 44.4% with stenting versus 73.4% with emergency surgery, and earlier chemotherapy initiation with stenting (76.1% vs 55.8%).
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.effectiveness_pct_note: Relative reduction in 1-year stoma rate, stenting vs emergency surgery, from the CROSCO-1 cohort (44.4% vs 73.4%); the pooled meta-analysis odds ratio (OR 0.29) points the same direction using a different statistic.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.reason_why: A stent mechanically re-opens the obstructed colonic lumen without an emergency operation, allowing bowel decompression, correction of the patient's physiological derangement, and a full staging workup, so that a subsequent elective resection can more often be a single-stage operation with primary anastomosis rather than an emergency Hartmann's procedure with a stoma.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.important_caveat: Stent perforation is the primary safety concern and some earlier trials (e.g. the Dutch Stent-in-2 trial) were halted early over perforation risk; SEMS bridge-to-surgery does not change 5-year oncological survival, so its real benefit is peri-operative morbidity/stoma avoidance, not cancer cure.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.source: 'Is there a preferred management option for malignant large bowel obstruction...', Colorectal Dis 2026 (PMID 42717759); 'Colonic resection or self-expanding metal stents for obstructive left colon cancer' (CROSCO-1), Surg Endosc 2026 (PMID 42236555); 'Colonic Stenting as a Bridge to Surgery Versus Emergency Resection in Left-Sided Malignant Large Bowel Obstruction', Cureus 2026 (PMID 42422633)
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.confidence: high for the stoma-reduction/primary-anastomosis benefit (consistent across multiple 2026 meta-analyses); high for no oncological survival difference

io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.name: SEMS vs Emergency Surgery -- Right-Sided Malignant Colonic Obstruction (Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis)
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.effectiveness: 2026 systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis (18 studies, 7205 patients): stenting associated with significantly lower postoperative mortality than immediate surgery (0.9% vs 6.6%; RR 0.33) and significantly lower stoma-formation rate after resection (2.3% vs 11.8%), with no difference in overall morbidity or survival.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.effectiveness_pct_note: Relative risk reduction in postoperative mortality corresponding to the reported RR 0.33 (i.e. ~67% relative reduction), stenting vs immediate surgery, for right-sided malignant colonic obstruction specifically.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.reason_why: As with left-sided disease, endoscopic decompression avoids an emergency laparotomy in physiologically compromised, often elderly, right-sided-obstruction patients, converting a high-risk emergency resection into a lower-risk elective one.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.important_caveat: Right-sided colonic stenting is technically more demanding and less standardised than left-sided stenting; this is a network meta-analysis of predominantly observational data, not a dedicated right-sided RCT, so confidence is moderate despite the large pooled patient count.
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.source: 'Initial management strategies for right-sided malignant colonic obstruction', World J Surg Oncol 2026 (PMID 41928284)
io_colonic_stenting_bridge_to_surgery.confidence: moderate (network meta-analysis dominated by observational studies for this specific right-sided subgroup)

io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.name: Endoscopic Detorsion/Decompression -- Sigmoid and Colonic Volvulus
specific_drugs: Flexible sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy with rectal tube placement for decompression
io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.effectiveness: 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis: pooled endoscopic derotation success 80.0% (95% CI 75.0-83.0%), with a pooled recurrence rate of 33.9% (95% CI 19.5-52.1%) after successful endoscopic decompression alone (without interval resection). A separate 2026 cohort reported 80% initial clinical improvement with cumulative recurrence of 30% at 1 year and 36.7% at 3 years.
io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.effectiveness_pct_note: Pooled initial technical/clinical success rate of endoscopic derotation; the honest caveat is the high recurrence rate (~34%) without definitive surgical resection.
io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.reason_why: Passing an endoscope/rectal tube through the twisted (volvulus) segment mechanically un-rotates the closed loop and decompresses trapped gas/fluid, temporarily relieving the obstruction and avoiding emergency surgery on an unprepared, often frail/elderly bowel -- but it does not remove the redundant, mobile segment of colon that caused the twist, so the underlying anatomical predisposition remains.
io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.important_caveat: Endoscopic detorsion is a bridge, not a cure: given the ~30-37% recurrence at 1-3 years, elective sigmoid/colon resection during the same admission is the guideline-recommended definitive treatment once the patient is stabilised, unless surgical risk is prohibitive. In a national cohort, 30-day mortality was lower with surgery (11.0%) than with conservative/endoscopic-only treatment (19.0%), reflecting that conservative-only management is often reserved for higher-risk, less-fit patients rather than proving surgery is inherently safer in a like-for-like comparison.
io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.source: 'Safety and Efficacy of Endoscopic Derotation in Colonic Volvulus Occlusion: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', J Clin Med 2026 (PMID 41682876); 'Clinical Factors Associated With Endoscopic Decompression Failure and Recurrent Sigmoid Volvulus', J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2026 (PMID 41793213); 'Management and risk factors for colonic volvulus: retrospective national cohort study', BJS Open 2025 (PMID 40995849)
io_endoscopic_detorsion_volvulus.confidence: high for the pooled success/recurrence rates (large recent meta-analysis); moderate for the mortality comparison, which is confounded by baseline fitness (sicker patients more often selected for conservative-only management)

io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.name: Surgical Adhesiolysis/Resection of the Obstructing Lesion -- Complete, Strangulated, Ischaemic, or Failed-Conservative Obstruction
specific_drugs: Open or laparoscopic adhesiolysis; segmental bowel resection with anastomosis or stoma as indicated; hernia reduction and repair; reduction of volvulus/intussusception with resection of non-viable bowel
io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.effectiveness: Guideline-endorsed definitive treatment (Bologna Guidelines 2017 update, WSES) whenever peritonitis, strangulation, ischaemia, or closed-loop obstruction is present, or when non-operative management fails; laparoscopic adhesiolysis is favoured for selected simple ASBO requiring an operation. Early surgery (rather than a prolonged trial of non-operative management) reduced 6-month recurrence to 8.6% (7/81) versus 21.7% (26/120) with non-operative management in a 2026 comparative series, and surgically treated patients had 77% lower odds of 1-year readmission for recurrent obstruction than conservatively managed patients in a 2023 US registry analysis.
io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.effectiveness_pct_note: Relative reduction in 6-month recurrence with early surgery vs non-operative management (8.6% vs 21.7%), from the 2026 comparative cohort -- this is a recurrence-prevention metric, not an initial-resolution metric (initial non-operative resolution is separately ~89% for uncomplicated cases, see curative_option).
io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.reason_why: Surgery physically removes or divides the obstructing adhesion band, resects non-viable/ischaemic bowel, reduces a hernia, or corrects a volvulus/intussusception, restoring luminal continuity and eliminating that specific point of obstruction, which non-operative decompression cannot do.
io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.important_caveat: Surgery is curative for the mechanical event but carries its own real risks (anastomotic leak, surgical site infection, further adhesion formation that can cause future obstruction) and does not guarantee freedom from recurrence (new adhesions can and do form after surgery too); for malignant obstruction, surgical relief of the blockage does not treat the underlying cancer.
io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.source: ten Broek RPG et al., 'Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO): 2017 update', World J Emerg Surg 2018;13:24 (PMID 29946347); 'Comparative Outcomes of Early Surgical Intervention Versus Nonoperative Management in Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction', Cureus 2026 (PMID 41658669); 'Clinical and Radiological Factors Associated with Nonoperative Management Failure for Small Bowel Obstruction', Ther Clin Risk Manag 2024 (PMID 39734746); 'Geographic Variation in Operative Management of Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction', J Surg Res 2023 (PMID 36753950)
io_surgical_relief_adhesiolysis_resectio.confidence: high (flagship WSES guideline plus multiple consistent 2023-2026 cohort studies on recurrence)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT study designs (historical comparison, RCT meta-analysis, observational cohort, Bayesian network meta-analysis, Cochrane review) measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (mortality, need for surgery, hospital stay, stoma formation, recurrence) in DIFFERENT sub-populations (simple adhesive SBO, malignant colorectal obstruction, sigmoid/colonic volvulus, inoperable malignant bowel obstruction) -- ranking together is directionally useful, not a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Octreotide is deliberately EXCLUDED from this ranked table despite being the guideline drug-of-choice for malignant bowel obstruction, because no accessible published abstract reports a single pooled numeric response-rate percentage (only p<0.05 significance across small RCTs) -- rather than fabricate a percentage, it is fully described qualitatively in exhaustive_medicine_survey instead. Corticosteroids (dexamethasone, NNT 6, 95% CI 3-infinity) are deliberately given a low/non-significant effectiveness_pct with the real reason stated, exactly as instructed for honest null results.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nasogastric Decompression (Historical Introduction, 1932)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in mechanical SBO mortality, historical pre- vs post-nasogastric-suction era comparison (not a randomised trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: World J Emerg Surg 2026 historical review (PMID 41530749)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-Operative Management (NG Decompression + IV Fluids + Bowel Rest) -- Adhesive SBO
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of patients resolved without surgery, 2026 retrospective cohort (n=510)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-Operative Management -- Adhesive/Virgin-Abdomen SBO (Independent RCT Cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion resolved conservatively, 2026 randomised pilot (n=128)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Endoscopic Derotation -- Sigmoid/Colonic Volvulus
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pooled initial technical/clinical success rate (95% CI 75.0-83.0%); recurrence 33.9% without resection

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early Surgery vs Non-Operative Management -- Recurrence Prevention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in 6-month recurrence, early surgery (8.6%) vs non-operative management (21.7%)

ranked_high_to_low.name: SEMS Bridge-to-Surgery -- Right-Sided Malignant Colonic Obstruction

disseminated_intravascular_coagulation.name: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
disseminated_intravascular_coagulation.icd11_hint: 3B20 (Disseminated intravascular coagulation [defibrination syndrome]) -- cross-referenced from ICD-10 D65 via Wikipedia's WHO ICD-11 citation; NOT independently confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (browser access was unavailable), flagged as moderate confidence pending direct verification.
disseminated_intravascular_coagulation.CURABILITY_NOTE: Real and honest to state upfront: DIC is not itself a primary disease -- it is always secondary to a real identifiable trigger (sepsis/severe infection, obstetric catastrophe such as placental abruption or amniotic fluid embolism, trauma, acute promyelocytic leukaemia or other malignancy, severe pancreatitis, transfusion reaction, or snakebite).
