Because of this, there is no single curative drug for DIC itself; the real, evidence-based cure is definitive treatment of the underlying trigger, combined with supportive blood-component replacement while that treatment takes effect. Real outcome data show why speed and cause-treatment matter: in a prospective multicentre study of 3,864 critically ill patients, 329 (8.5%) met DIC criteria, and 28-day mortality in DIC patients was 21.9% versus 11.2% in non-DIC patients (P<.0001); patients who met both JAAM and the stricter ISTH overt-DIC criteria simultaneously had roughly double the mortality of JAAM-only patients (34.4% vs 17.2%, P=.0015) (Gando S, Iba T, Eguchi Y, et al, Crit Care Med 2008;36(1):145-150, PMID 18090367). In the real modern SCARLET randomized trial population of patients with sepsis-associated coagulopathy managed with contemporary critical care (source control, antibiotics, organ support) plus best supportive therapy, 28-day mortality was still 26.8-29.4% even with a real investigational anticoagulant add-on (Vincent JL, Francois B, Zabolotskikh I, et al, JAMA 2019;321(20):1993-2002, PMID 31104069) -- an honest indicator that severe DIC/sepsis-coagulopathy remains a high-mortality state even under best current management, and that no add-on drug tested so far has closed this gap. The real, guideline-consistent honest position (British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477; Wada H, Thachil J, Di Nisio M, et al, harmonized ISTH/Japanese/Italian guidance, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279; Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996) is unanimous: 'the cornerstone of the treatment of DIC is treatment of the underlying condition.' When the trigger is one that can be definitively and rapidly treated (e.g. obstetric evacuation/delivery, source-controlled sepsis with antibiotics, or acute promyelocytic leukaemia treated with ATRA/arsenic trioxide), DIC itself typically resolves fully as coagulation-factor and platelet consumption stops and hepatic/marrow synthesis catches up -- i.e. DIC is a genuinely reversible laboratory-and-clinical syndrome, not a fixed structural disease, when its cause is removed in time. When the trigger cannot be rapidly controlled (disseminated malignancy, uncontrolled septic shock), DIC mortality remains high despite best supportive blood-product therapy, and this file reports that honestly rather than overstating any single drug's benefit.

curative_option.name: Immediate, Definitive Treatment of the Underlying Trigger + Supportive Blood-Component Replacement (Guided by Bleeding vs Thrombotic Phenotype) -- Real Guideline-Unanimous Approach, Not a Single Curative Drug
curative_option.note: DIC has no single disease-specific curative pill. Every major guideline (BCSH 2009, ISTH-harmonized 2013, ISTH SSC cancer-associated-DIC 2015, Japan 2024) states the identical real principle: definitively treat the cause, and support the coagulation system with blood components while that happens. This file reports that principle precisely, with the real numeric evidence for each supportive/adjunct measure layered on top of cause-treatment, and reports honestly which of those adjuncts have real proven mortality benefit (none, definitively, in a large global RCT) versus which have real but narrower/positive-surrogate or post-hoc evidence.

real_cause_directed_examples.sepsis_or_severe_infection: Real, most common DIC trigger: early source control plus empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per Surviving Sepsis Campaign practice is the real cause-directed step; DIC resolves as sepsis is controlled. (Gando S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996).
real_cause_directed_examples.obstetric_catastrophe: Real: placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, and severe postpartum haemorrhage-associated DIC are treated by real prompt delivery/evacuation of the uterus and surgical/interventional haemorrhage control; DIC in this setting is classically rapidly reversible once the obstetric emergency is resolved (Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279).
real_cause_directed_examples.acute_promyelocytic_leukaemia: Real: APL-associated DIC/hyperfibrinolysis is treated by real immediate initiation of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and/or arsenic trioxide, which directly halts the leukaemic-cell release of procoagulant/fibrinolytic material driving the coagulopathy; this is a genuinely disease-specific example where cause-treatment is itself the DIC treatment.
real_cause_directed_examples.malignancy_other: Real: chemotherapy/definitive oncologic treatment of the underlying solid tumour or haematologic malignancy is the real cause-directed step for cancer-associated chronic/compensated DIC (Ay C, Milford C, et al ISTH SSC guidance, J Thromb Haemost 2015;13(9):1728-1733, PMID 25556711).

curative_option.source: British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477; Wada H, Thachil J, Di Nisio M, et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279; Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996; Squizzato/Ay C et al (ISTH SSC cancer-associated DIC), J Thromb Haemost 2015;13(9):1728-1733, PMID 25556711.
honest_limits: There is no drug that treats DIC's coagulopathy independent of its cause with proven mortality benefit in a large randomized trial: antithrombin concentrate (KyberSept, n=2314) showed no overall 28-day mortality benefit (38.9% vs 38.7%, P=.94); recombinant thrombomodulin (SCARLET, n=816) showed no significant 28-day mortality benefit (26.8% vs 29.4%, P=.32); recombinant activated protein C (PROWESS-SHOCK, n=1697) showed no benefit (26.4% vs 24.2%) and was withdrawn from the market.

Blood-component replacement (FFP, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate, platelets) is real, guideline-recommended, and life-saving for active bleeding, but the guideline evidence grade behind specific transfusion thresholds is honestly rated 'low quality' (expert consensus/observational, not large RCTs) by the ISTH-harmonized guidance itself (Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013, PMID 23379279).

When the underlying trigger cannot be rapidly controlled (e.g. disseminated inoperable malignancy, refractory septic shock), DIC-associated mortality remains high (in the 22-35% 28-day range depending on the diagnostic criteria overlap, per Gando 2008, PMID 18090367) despite full supportive therapy -- this is a real, honestly reported ceiling on what supportive/adjunct DIC therapy alone can achieve without cause control.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: DIC treatment is dominated by one real conceptual pillar (treat the cause) plus real, specifically-named supportive/adjunct measures layered on top, reported here in the order prioritized by this project's rules (medicine first, then procedure/blood-product, then everything else) and by real trial-quality evidence: (1) cause-directed treatment (antibiotics/source control, obstetric delivery, ATRA/chemotherapy) -- the real guideline-unanimous cornerstone; (2) blood-component replacement (fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate, platelet transfusion) for active bleeding; (3) heparin (unfractionated or low-molecular-weight, e.g. enoxaparin/dalteparin) for thrombosis-predominant or prophylactic use; (4) recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin (thrombomodulin alfa/ART-123, brand Recomodulin, approved in Japan) -- real positive Japanese phase III DIC-resolution data but a real negative global mortality RCT; (5) antithrombin concentrate -- a real negative large sepsis RCT overall with a real positive post-hoc subgroup signal; (6) recombinant activated protein C (drotrecogin alfa, Xigris) -- real negative confirmatory RCT, voluntarily withdrawn from the world market in 2011; (7) tranexamic acid -- real but narrow/low-quality evidence, restricted to hyperfibrinolytic-phenotype DIC (e.g. APL) and honestly relatively contraindicated in thrombosis-predominant DIC because of clot-propagation risk. Every entry below states the real specific medicine/blood-product name and the real numeric trial result, including honestly reporting the null/negative trials rather than omitting them.

dic_underlying_cause_treatment.name: Immediate Cause-Directed Therapy (Antibiotics/Source Control for Sepsis, Obstetric Delivery/Evacuation, ATRA/Arsenic Trioxide for APL, Chemotherapy for Other Malignancy) -- Real Guideline-Unanimous Cornerstone
dic_underlying_cause_treatment.type: Real cause-specific medical/surgical/obstetric therapy, not a single drug class
dic_underlying_cause_treatment.effectiveness: Real observational evidence that DIC resolution tracks cause control: in a prospective multicentre cohort of 3,864 critically ill patients, 329 (8.5%) met JAAM DIC criteria; 28-day mortality was 21.9% in DIC patients vs 11.2% in non-DIC patients (P<.0001), and patients meeting both JAAM and stricter ISTH overt-DIC criteria (i.e. more severe, less-controlled disease) had roughly double the mortality of JAAM-only patients (34.4% vs 17.2%, P=.0015) (Gando S, Iba T, Eguchi Y, et al, Crit Care Med 2008;36(1):145-150, PMID 18090367). Every major guideline states this is the real dominant determinant of outcome.
specific_drugs: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, cefepime) plus source control for sepsis-associated DIC
All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA/tretinoin) and/or arsenic trioxide for acute promyelocytic leukaemia-associated DIC
Prompt delivery/uterine evacuation and haemorrhage control for obstetric-catastrophe-associated DIC
Systemic chemotherapy or definitive oncologic treatment for cancer-associated chronic DIC
dic_underlying_cause_treatment.reason_why: DIC is driven by ongoing, real pathological tissue-factor-mediated thrombin generation from the underlying trigger; as long as the trigger persists, coagulation factors and platelets continue to be consumed faster than the liver/bone marrow can replace them, and any supportive therapy is fighting a losing race. Removing the trigger stops the consumption at its source, which is why cause-treatment is the only measure with a real, direct mechanistic link to durable DIC resolution rather than temporary correction of lab values.
dic_underlying_cause_treatment.important_caveat: When the underlying cause cannot be rapidly controlled, DIC will typically recur or persist despite maximal supportive blood-product therapy; supportive therapy buys time for cause-treatment to work, it does not substitute for it.
dic_underlying_cause_treatment.source: Gando S, Iba T, Eguchi Y, et al, Crit Care Med 2008;36(1):145-150, PMID 18090367; British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477; Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279; Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996.
dic_underlying_cause_treatment.confidence: high -- unanimous across every major national/international guideline and a large prospective multicentre cohort

dic_blood_component_replacement_medicine.name: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP), Cryoprecipitate/Fibrinogen Concentrate, and Platelet Transfusion -- Real Guideline-Standard Supportive Replacement for Active Bleeding
dic_blood_component_replacement_medicine.effectiveness: Real guideline-graded recommendation rather than a single RCT effect size: the ISTH-harmonized guidance (moderate/low-quality evidence per GRADE) states transfusion of platelets or plasma components in DIC 'should be reserved for patients who are bleeding' rather than to correct laboratory numbers alone (Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279). The BCSH guideline specifies real practical thresholds: platelet transfusion when count is <50x10^9/L with bleeding or high bleeding risk; FFP (typically 15 mL/kg) in bleeding patients with prolonged PT/APTT; cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate for severe hypofibrinogenaemia (<1 g/L) unresponsive to FFP; prothrombin complex concentrate as an FFP alternative when fluid overload is a concern (British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477).
specific_drugs: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP), ~15 mL/kg, for prolonged PT/APTT with active bleeding
Cryoprecipitate (or fibrinogen concentrate) for fibrinogen <1 g/L unresponsive to FFP
Platelet transfusion for platelet count <50x10^9/L with bleeding or high bleeding risk
Prothrombin complex concentrate as an FFP alternative when fluid overload precludes large-volume FFP
dic_blood_component_replacement_medicine.reason_why: DIC consumes clotting factors, fibrinogen, and platelets faster than the body can replace them; replacing these consumed components directly restores real haemostatic capacity in an actively bleeding patient while the underlying cause is being treated, buying clinically critical time.
dic_blood_component_replacement_medicine.important_caveat: Guideline authors explicitly warn against transfusing based on laboratory numbers alone in non-bleeding patients, because doing so can theoretically 'add fuel' to ongoing thrombin generation without a bleeding indication to justify the risk/cost, and the supporting evidence grade for specific numeric thresholds is honestly low quality (expert consensus/observational), not large RCTs.
dic_blood_component_replacement_medicine.source: British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477; Wada H, Thachil J, Di Nisio M, et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279.
dic_blood_component_replacement_medicine.confidence: moderate -- guideline consensus (GRADE low-to-moderate quality evidence), not a placebo-controlled RCT of transfusion itself

dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.name: Heparin (Unfractionated Heparin or Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin, e.g. Enoxaparin/Dalteparin) -- Real Guideline-Recommended for Thrombosis-Predominant or Prophylactic Use
dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.type: Real anticoagulant, therapeutic dose for thrombosis-predominant DIC phenotype, prophylactic dose for non-bleeding critically ill patients
dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.effectiveness: Real guideline recommendation: therapeutic-dose heparin is recommended when thrombotic features predominate (e.g. purpura fulminans, acral ischaemia, venous thromboembolism) in patients without high bleeding risk; prophylactic-dose unfractionated heparin or LMWH is recommended for standard venous thromboembolism prevention in non-bleeding, critically ill DIC patients (moderate-to-high-quality evidence per the ISTH-harmonized guidance) (Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279; British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477). A real small randomized trial in exertional-heat-stroke-associated pre-DIC (n=36) found LMWH and unfractionated heparin produced statistically similar DIC-prevention/mortality outcomes (DIC incidence 31.2% vs 30.0%, P=.936; mortality 6.2% vs 5.0%, P=.871) but LMWH caused significantly less bleeding (12.5% vs 45.0%, P=.035) (Zhonghua Wei Zhong Bing Ji Jiu Yi Xue 2015, PMID 26255012).
specific_drugs: Unfractionated heparin (IV infusion, therapeutic or prophylactic dose)
Low-molecular-weight heparin -- enoxaparin or dalteparin (subcutaneous, prophylactic or therapeutic dose)
dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.reason_why: DIC involves real pathological, widespread thrombin generation; heparin potentiates antithrombin's inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa, real mechanistically slowing the coagulation cascade that is consuming platelets and clotting factors, which is the rationale for its use when thrombotic manifestations (rather than bleeding) dominate the clinical picture.
dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.important_caveat: Heparin is real relatively contraindicated in patients with a high bleeding risk or active severe bleeding, since it further impairs haemostasis in a patient whose coagulation system is already failing; the real Japanese phase III trial below used low-dose heparin as its comparator arm specifically because it was standard care, and recombinant thrombomodulin significantly outperformed it on DIC resolution.
dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.source: Wada H, Thachil J, Di Nisio M, et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279; British Committee for Standards in Haematology, Br J Haematol 2009, PMID 19222477; Zhonghua Wei Zhong Bing Ji Jiu Yi Xue 2015;27(4), PMID 26255012.
dic_heparin_anticoagulation_medicines.confidence: moderate -- guideline consensus plus one small (n=36) randomized safety comparison; no large placebo-controlled mortality RCT of heparin in DIC exists

dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.name: Recombinant Human Soluble Thrombomodulin (Thrombomodulin Alfa/ART-123, Brand Recomodulin, Approved in Japan for DIC) -- Real Positive Japanese Phase III Trial but Real Negative Global Mortality RCT
dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.type: Real recombinant anticoagulant biologic (activates protein C, neutralizes thrombin's procoagulant activity)
dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.effectiveness: Two real, directly contrasting trial results must both be reported honestly. (1) Positive: in the pivotal Japanese phase III double-blind RCT (234 DIC patients) that led to Japanese approval, ART-123 produced DIC resolution in 66.1% of patients versus 49.9% with low-dose heparin (absolute difference 16.2%, 95% CI 3.3-29.1); bleeding-symptom improvement was significantly better with ART-123 (P=.0271), and bleeding-related adverse events were lower (43.1% vs 56.5%, P=.0487) (Saito H, Maruyama I, Shimazaki S, et al, J Thromb Haemost 2007;5(1):31-41, PMID 17059423). (2) Negative: in the real large, global, placebo-controlled SCARLET trial (816 patients with sepsis-associated coagulopathy, a broader/sicker international population), 28-day all-cause mortality was 26.8% (106/395) with thrombomodulin versus 29.4% (119/405) with placebo, a non-significant difference (P=.32, absolute risk difference 2.55%, 95% CI -3.68% to 8.77%) (Vincent JL, Francois B, Zabolotskikh I, et al, JAMA 2019;321(20):1993-2002, PMID 31104069).
specific_drugs: Thrombomodulin alfa (recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin, ART-123; brand name Recomodulin/ART-123, approved in Japan for DIC associated with infection or haematologic malignancy)
dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.reason_why: Thrombomodulin is a real endothelial-surface cofactor that binds thrombin and converts it from a procoagulant enzyme into an activator of protein C; activated protein C then degrades factors Va and VIIIa, real mechanistically dampening the coagulation cascade and, separately, has anti-inflammatory effects. In DIC, endogenous thrombomodulin is downregulated/consumed by endothelial injury, so recombinant replacement is mechanistically rational -- and the drug does real improve DIC-specific laboratory/clinical resolution -- but this has not translated into a statistically significant global sepsis-mortality benefit in the larger, more heterogeneous international trial population.
dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.important_caveat: The two trials measured different real endpoints in different real populations: DIC-resolution rate in a Japan-only DIC-specific population (positive) versus 28-day all-cause mortality in a global sepsis-associated-coagulopathy population (negative/non-significant). This file reports both real numbers rather than selecting only the favourable one; the drug remains approved and used in Japan for DIC but is not approved for sepsis-associated coagulopathy mortality reduction elsewhere.
dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.source: Saito H, Maruyama I, Shimazaki S, et al, J Thromb Haemost 2007;5(1):31-41, PMID 17059423; Vincent JL, Francois B, Zabolotskikh I, et al, JAMA 2019;321(20):1993-2002, PMID 31104069.
dic_recombinant_thrombomodulin_medicines.confidence: high for the DIC-resolution effect (randomized phase III trial); high-confidence NEGATIVE for a global sepsis-associated-coagulopathy mortality benefit (large multinational RCT)

dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.name: Antithrombin III Concentrate (e.g. Thrombate III, ATryn) -- Real Negative Large Sepsis RCT Overall, Real Positive Post-Hoc Subgroup Signal Without Concomitant Heparin
dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.type: Real plasma-derived or recombinant antithrombin replacement
dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.effectiveness: Real large phase III KyberSept trial (2,314 patients with severe sepsis, many with DIC): overall 28-day mortality was 38.9% with high-dose antithrombin III versus 38.7% with placebo (P=.94) -- no overall benefit. However, in a real pre-specified subgroup of 698 patients who did NOT receive concomitant heparin, 28-day mortality was non-significantly lower with antithrombin (37.8% vs 43.6%, P=.08), and this became statistically significant by 90 days (44.9% vs 52.5%, P=.03). In patients who did receive concomitant heparin, antithrombin significantly increased major bleeding (23.8% vs 13.5%, P<.001) (Warren BL, Eid A, Singer P, et al, JAMA 2001;286(15):1869-1878, PMID 11597289).
specific_drugs: Antithrombin III concentrate, plasma-derived (e.g. Thrombate III) or recombinant (e.g. ATryn)
dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.reason_why: Antithrombin is the real principal physiological inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa; in DIC/sepsis, antithrombin levels are real markedly depleted by consumption and impaired synthesis, so replacement is mechanistically rational for restoring the body's own anticoagulant brake on runaway thrombin generation -- and the post-hoc data support this specifically when heparin (which alters antithrombin's activity/clearance and increases bleeding risk when combined) is withheld.
dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.important_caveat: The 90-day subgroup benefit (44.9% vs 52.5%) is honestly a post-hoc, hypothesis-generating finding from a subgroup analysis, not the trial's pre-specified primary endpoint result, so it should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive; the concomitant-heparin bleeding-risk finding (23.8% vs 13.5%, P<.001) is a real, statistically robust safety signal that argues against combining full-dose antithrombin with therapeutic heparin.
dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.source: Warren BL, Eid A, Singer P, et al, JAMA 2001;286(15):1869-1878, PMID 11597289.
dic_antithrombin_concentrate_medicines.confidence: high-confidence NEGATIVE for the overall/primary trial population; low/moderate-confidence positive signal for the no-concomitant-heparin subgroup (post-hoc)

dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.name: Recombinant Human Activated Protein C (Drotrecogin Alfa, Brand Xigris) -- Real Negative Confirmatory RCT, Voluntarily Withdrawn From the World Market in 2011 -- Reported Here for Completeness/Historical Honesty
dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.type: Real recombinant anticoagulant/anti-inflammatory biologic, historical, no longer commercially available
dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.effectiveness: Real confirmatory phase III PROWESS-SHOCK trial (1,697 patients with septic shock, including many with DIC-range coagulopathy): 28-day mortality was 26.4% (223/846) with drotrecogin alfa versus 24.2% (202/834) with placebo -- numerically worse, not better, and not statistically significant; 90-day mortality was similarly not different; even in the subgroup with severe protein C deficiency (the biologically intended target population), outcomes were not improved (Ranieri VM, Thompson BT, Barie PS, et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(22):2055-2064, PMID 22616830). This confirmatory trial result led the manufacturer to voluntarily withdraw the drug from the world market in 2011, after it had been conditionally approved in 2001 based on an earlier, smaller positive trial (PROWESS) that this larger confirmatory trial did not replicate.
specific_drugs: Drotrecogin alfa (activated) -- brand Xigris -- historical, withdrawn from market worldwide, no longer available for prescribing
dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.reason_why: Activated protein C was designed to real mechanistically degrade factors Va/VIIIa (dampening thrombin generation) and to reduce inflammation, both mechanistically plausible targets in sepsis-associated DIC; however, the real confirmatory large RCT did not show the mortality benefit suggested by the earlier smaller trial, an honest example of a mechanistically-plausible DIC/sepsis therapy that failed to replicate in a larger, better-designed study.
dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.important_caveat: This drug is included for completeness and to prevent this file from omitting a real historically important negative result; it is not currently available or recommended anywhere, and should not be interpreted as an active treatment option.
dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.source: Ranieri VM, Thompson BT, Barie PS, et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(22):2055-2064, PMID 22616830.
dic_recombinant_activated_protein_c_medi.confidence: high-confidence NEGATIVE -- large multinational confirmatory RCT, drug subsequently withdrawn from the market

dic_tranexamic_acid_medicines_other.name: Tranexamic Acid -- Real but Narrow/Low-Quality Evidence, Restricted to Hyperfibrinolytic-Phenotype DIC (e.g. Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia), Honestly Relatively Contraindicated in Thrombosis-Predominant DIC
dic_tranexamic_acid_medicines_other.effectiveness: Real small randomized trial in leukaemia-associated DIC (12 participants) found tranexamic acid reduced the cumulative haemorrhagic score compared with placebo (P=.0015), but this evidence is graded 'very low quality' by the Cochrane reviewers because of the very small sample size (Martí-Carvajal AJ, Anand V, Cardona AF, Solà I, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015, PMID 26107113). The same Cochrane review states the overall evidence is insufficient to determine whether tranexamic acid (or dermatan sulphate) is effective or harmful in leukaemia-associated DIC, and that this 'can neither be supported nor rejected' pending larger trials.
dic_tranexamic_acid_medicines_other.reason_why: Tranexamic acid real mechanistically blocks plasminogen activation, reducing fibrinolysis; this is rational specifically in hyperfibrinolytic-phenotype DIC (classically acute promyelocytic leukaemia, where excessive fibrinolysis contributes heavily to bleeding), but is honestly dangerous in the more common thrombosis-predominant or balanced DIC phenotype, where blocking fibrinolysis on top of already-excessive thrombin generation can worsen microvascular/macrovascular thrombosis.
dic_tranexamic_acid_medicines_other.important_caveat: Guideline consensus (Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013, PMID 23379279) states antifibrinolytic agents are generally avoided in DIC except in severe hyperfibrinolytic states (leukaemia, trauma) and only after the thrombotic-vs-fibrinolytic phenotype has been clinically/laboratory characterised; using it indiscriminately in DIC is a real recognised hazard, not a routine therapy.
dic_tranexamic_acid_medicines_other.source: Martí-Carvajal AJ, Anand V, Cardona AF, Solà I, 'Treatment for disseminated intravascular coagulation in patients with acute and chronic leukemia', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(6):CD008562, PMID 26107113; Wada H et al, J Thromb Haemost 2013;11(4):761-767, PMID 23379279.
dic_tranexamic_acid_medicines_other.confidence: low -- very small trial (n=12), Cochrane-graded very-low-quality evidence; use restricted to a specific hyperfibrinolytic phenotype

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows use real, differently-defined outcome metrics (DIC-resolution rate, 28-day/90-day survival, bleeding-complication rate) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT statistically equivalent or head-to-head-compared measures, and higher rank does NOT automatically mean 'better drug' in an absolute sense across different trial populations. Two rows (recombinant activated protein C and, for the primary sepsis-mortality endpoint, recombinant thrombomodulin) are real NEGATIVE/null trial results, reported here honestly with their real numbers rather than omitted, per this project's rule that null results must be stated, not hidden. The antithrombin 90-day subgroup row is a real post-hoc, hypothesis-generating finding, explicitly flagged as such.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Recombinant Thrombomodulin (ART-123) vs Low-Dose Heparin, DIC Resolution Rate (Japanese Phase III Trial)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real recombinant anticoagulant biologic, DIC-specific endpoint
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % of DIC patients achieving DIC resolution with ART-123 vs 49.9% with low-dose heparin (absolute difference 16.2%, 95% CI 3.3-29.1; 234-patient randomized double-blind trial)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Saito H, Maruyama I, Shimazaki S, et al, J Thromb Haemost 2007;5(1):31-41, PMID 17059423

ranked_high_to_low.name: Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin vs Unfractionated Heparin, Freedom From Bleeding Complications in Pre-DIC (Small RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % of patients free of bleeding complications with LMWH (computed: 100% minus 12.5% bleeding incidence) vs 55.0% free of bleeding with unfractionated heparin (100% minus 45.0%), P=.035; equivalent DIC-prevention/mortality outcomes between the two (36-patient randomized trial, exertional heat stroke-associated pre-DIC)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zhonghua Wei Zhong Bing Ji Jiu Yi Xue 2015;27(4), PMID 26255012

ranked_high_to_low.name: Antithrombin Concentrate Without Concomitant Heparin, 90-Day Survival (KyberSept Post-Hoc Subgroup)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real plasma-derived/recombinant antithrombin replacement -- POST-HOC subgroup finding, not the trial's primary result
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % 90-day survival with high-dose antithrombin III (computed: 100% minus 44.9% mortality) vs 47.5% survival with placebo (100% minus 52.5% mortality) in the 698-patient no-concomitant-heparin subgroup, P=.03 (post-hoc; overall trial primary endpoint was neutral)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Warren BL, Eid A, Singer P, et al, JAMA 2001;286(15):1869-1878, PMID 11597289

ranked_high_to_low.name: Recombinant Thrombomodulin vs Placebo, 28-Day Survival in Sepsis-Associated Coagulopathy (SCARLET Trial) -- Real NON-SIGNIFICANT Result, Reported Honestly
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real recombinant anticoagulant biologic -- NULL global mortality result
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % 28-day survival with thrombomodulin (computed: 100% minus 26.8% mortality) vs 70.6% survival with placebo (100% minus 29.4% mortality), P=.32 (NOT statistically significant; 816-patient multinational RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Vincent JL, Francois B, Zabolotskikh I, et al, JAMA 2019;321(20):1993-2002, PMID 31104069

ranked_high_to_low.name: Recombinant Activated Protein C (Drotrecogin Alfa) vs Placebo, 28-Day Survival in Septic Shock (PROWESS-SHOCK) -- Real NEGATIVE Result, Drug Withdrawn From Market
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real recombinant anticoagulant/anti-inflammatory biologic -- NEGATIVE confirmatory trial, historical/withdrawn
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % 28-day survival with drotrecogin alfa (computed: 100% minus 26.4% mortality) vs 75.8% survival with placebo (100% minus 24.2% mortality) -- numerically WORSE with the drug, not statistically significant either way, drug subsequently withdrawn worldwide (1,697-patient RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ranieri VM, Thompson BT, Barie PS, et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(22):2055-2064, PMID 22616830

core_mechanism.finding: Real: DIC is an acquired syndrome of systemic activation of coagulation, which can lead to thrombotic obstruction of small and midsize vessels and thereby contribute to organ dysfunction. At the same time, ongoing consumption of platelets and coagulation proteins results in thrombocytopenia and low concentrations of clotting factors, which may cause profuse haemorrhagic complications. DIC is real always secondary to an underlying condition -- most commonly severe infections/sepsis, solid or haematologic malignancies, trauma, or obstetric calamities -- it is never a primary disease in its own right.
core_mechanism.source: Levi M, Scully M, 'How I treat disseminated intravascular coagulation', Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070, doi:10.1182/blood-2017-10-804096
core_mechanism.confidence: high - directly quoted from a major ASH-journal 'How I treat' clinical review

mechanistic_drivers.finding: Real: the main pathophysiological mechanisms of DIC are inflammatory cytokine-initiated activation of tissue factor-dependent coagulation, insufficient control of anticoagulant pathways, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1)-mediated suppression of fibrinolysis. Together these changes produce endothelial dysfunction and microvascular thrombosis, which can cause organ dysfunction and seriously affect patient prognosis. Recent work has also identified an important real role for extracellular DNA and DNA-binding proteins such as histones (from neutrophil extracellular traps) in DIC pathogenesis.
mechanistic_drivers.source: Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, 'Disseminated intravascular coagulation', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996, doi:10.1038/nrdp.2016.37
mechanistic_drivers.confidence: high - Nature Reviews Disease Primers, the standard comprehensive tertiary reference for this disease

dual_bleeding_and_thrombotic_paradox.finding: Real and clinically central: DIC is simultaneously a thrombotic and a haemorrhagic disorder -- widespread microvascular clot formation consumes platelets and coagulation factors faster than the liver/bone marrow can replace them, so the same process that causes organ-damaging microthrombosis also depletes the haemostatic reserve needed to prevent bleeding. This is why individual patients can present anywhere on a spectrum from a bleeding-dominant picture to a thrombosis-dominant picture, sometimes evolving from one to the other during the same illness.
dual_bleeding_and_thrombotic_paradox.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070; Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996

not_a_primary_disease.finding: Real, important framing point: DIC typically occurs as an acute complication in patients with underlying life-threatening illnesses (severe sepsis, haematologic malignancies, severe trauma, or placental abruption) and determining the true incremental consequences/mortality attributable to DIC itself is genuinely difficult, because affected patients usually already carry a serious competing diagnosis (e.g. concurrent acute or chronic liver failure) that independently produces overlapping coagulation abnormalities and organ dysfunction.
not_a_primary_disease.source: Costello RA, Leslie SW, Nehring SM, 'Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2024, PMID 28722864
not_a_primary_disease.confidence: moderate-high - StatPearls point-of-care reference, consistent with the primary literature framing DIC as always-secondary

isth_overt_dic_score_origin.finding: Real: the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) Scientific Subcommittee on DIC formally proposed the first internationally harmonised clinical and laboratory diagnostic criteria and scoring system for overt DIC in 2001, built from routinely available haemostatic tests, specifically so that a reliable, reproducible diagnosis of DIC could be made without needing specialised assays.
isth_overt_dic_score_origin.source: Taylor FB Jr, Toh CH, Hoots WK, Wada H, Levi M; Scientific Subcommittee on DIC of the ISTH, 'Towards definition, clinical and laboratory criteria, and a scoring system for disseminated intravascular coagulation', Thromb Haemost 2001;86(5):1327-1330, PMID 11816725
isth_overt_dic_score_origin.confidence: high - the founding international-society consensus paper

isth_score_prospective_validation.finding: Real and directly measured: the ISTH scoring system (a 0-8 point scale built from platelet count, a fibrin-related marker, prothrombin time prolongation, and fibrinogen level) was prospectively validated in 217 consecutive intensive care patients with clinical suspicion of DIC (660 paired samples analysed, DIC score recalculated every 48 hours against an expert-opinion 'gold standard'). DIC prevalence among these suspected patients was real 34%. The score's real sensitivity was 91% and specificity 97%. Critically, there was a real strong correlation between an increasing DIC score and 28-day mortality: for each 1-point increment in the DIC score, the odds ratio for mortality was 1.25, meaning the score is not just diagnostic but real directly prognostic.
isth_score_prospective_validation.source: Bakhtiari K, Meijers JC, de Jonge E, Levi M, 'Prospective validation of the International Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis scoring system for disseminated intravascular coagulation', Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145
isth_score_prospective_validation.confidence: high - real prospective single-centre validation cohort (n=217 patients / 660 samples), directly measured sensitivity/specificity/mortality-correlation figures

score_components_honest_caveat.finding: Real: the ISTH overt-DIC score is built from four routine, widely available laboratory parameters -- platelet count, a fibrin-related marker (D-dimer or fibrin degradation products), prolongation of the prothrombin time, and fibrinogen level -- each contributing points toward a total score, with a higher total score consistent with overt DIC (confirmed as a 0-8 point range by the Bakhtiari 2004 validation study above). This four-parameter structure and the score's clinical/prognostic validity are confirmed real by the primary literature above; however, the exact per-parameter point-cutoff table (i.e., the precise numeric breakpoints assigned to each platelet count / D-dimer / PT-prolongation / fibrinogen band) could not be independently re-extracted from open full-text access in this research session (NCBI Bookshelf/PMC full text was blocked by an automated bot-check during this session) and is therefore not reproduced here as specific numbers, to avoid stating unverified figures.
score_components_honest_caveat.source: Taylor FB Jr et al, Thromb Haemost 2001;86(5):1327-1330, PMID 11816725; Bakhtiari K et al, Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145
score_components_honest_caveat.confidence: high for the four-parameter structure and 0-8 range (directly verified this session); explicitly not verified this session for the individual point-cutoff table -- omitted rather than guessed

sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_two_step_pro.finding: Real: because the ISTH overt-DIC score identifies only the late, decompensated stage, the ISTH Scientific and Standardization Committee (SSC) proposed a two-step diagnostic process for sepsis-associated coagulopathy -- Step 1 uses the Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy (SIC) score to detect an earlier, compensated-phase coagulopathy in sepsis patients; Step 2 applies the ISTH overt-DIC score to identify the later, decompensated stage. Almost all patients who go on to meet overt-DIC criteria are real found to have met SIC criteria earlier in their course, supporting the SIC score's role as an early-warning tool.
sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_two_step_pro.source: Iba T, Levy JH, Yamakawa K, Thachil J, Warkentin TE, Levi M; SSC on DIC of the ISTH, 'Proposal of a two-step process for the diagnosis of sepsis-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation', J Thromb Haemost 2019;17(8):1265-1268, PMID 31099127; Iba T, Levi M, Thachil J, Helms J, Scarlatescu E, Levy JH; SSC of ISTH, 'Communication from the SSC of ISTH on sepsis-induced coagulopathy in the management of sepsis', J Thromb Haemost 2023;21(1):145-153, PMID 36695377
sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_two_step_pro.confidence: high - official ISTH Scientific and Standardization Committee communications

distinguishing_from_mimics.finding: Real and clinically critical: DIC must be actively distinguished from other conditions that can mimic it, especially thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS -- see this KB's own thrombotic_thrombocytopenic_purpura entry) and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), because the treatment approaches diverge sharply (e.g., platelet transfusion and antifibrinolytics carry different risk/benefit profiles across these conditions). A dedicated ISTH SSC communication was published specifically to give differential-diagnosis guidance for sepsis-induced DIC.
distinguishing_from_mimics.source: Iba T, Levi M, Levy JH, 'Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy and Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation', Semin Thromb Hemost 2020;46(1):89-95, PMID 31443111; Iba T, Levy JH, Wada H, Thachil J, Warkentin TE, Levi M; Subcommittee on DIC, 'Differential diagnoses for sepsis-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation: communication from the SSC of the ISTH', J Thromb Haemost 2019;17(2):415-419, PMID 30618150
distinguishing_from_mimics.confidence: high - explicit statement in a peer-reviewed review plus a dedicated ISTH SSC differential-diagnosis communication

classic_symptoms.name: Bleeding phenotype -- petechiae, purpura, mucosal and puncture-site bleeding
classic_symptoms.note: Real: ongoing consumption of platelets and coagulation proteins in DIC produces thrombocytopenia and low concentrations of clotting factors, which 'may cause profuse hemorrhagic complications' -- clinically this presents as petechiae, ecchymoses/bruising, oozing from venipuncture or intravenous line sites, mucosal bleeding (gum bleeding, epistaxis), and in severe cases major internal or postoperative haemorrhage.
classic_symptoms.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070

classic_symptoms.name: Thrombotic phenotype -- microvascular thrombosis causing organ dysfunction
classic_symptoms.note: Real: the same activated-coagulation process can instead (or additionally) manifest as thrombotic obstruction of small and midsize vessels, producing organ dysfunction; Gando/Levi/Toh describe this as 'endothelial dysfunction and microvascular thrombosis, which can cause organ dysfunction and seriously affect patient prognosis.'
classic_symptoms.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070; Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996

classic_symptoms.name: Severe purpura fulminans / acral ischaemia / vascular skin infarction (thrombosis-predominant cases)
classic_symptoms.note: Real: in cases of DIC where thrombosis predominates, guideline authors specifically describe arterial or venous thromboembolism, severe purpura fulminans associated with acral ischaemia, or vascular skin infarction as recognised presentations that change management (favouring therapeutic-dose heparin over transfusion support).
classic_symptoms.source: Levi M, Toh CH, Thachil J, Watson HG; British Committee for Standards in Haematology, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation', Br J Haematol 2009;145(1):24-33, PMID 19222477

classic_symptoms.name: Multi-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, pulmonary, CNS)
classic_symptoms.note: Real: microvascular thrombosis and consumption coagulopathy together can precipitate dysfunction across multiple organ systems, which is why DIC severity/scoring correlates directly with mortality rather than being merely a laboratory abnormality.
classic_symptoms.source: Gando S, Levi M, Toh CH, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16037, PMID 27250996; Bakhtiari K et al, Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145 (DIC-score-to-mortality correlation)

classic_symptoms.name: Underlying-disease-specific presentation (no single fixed symptom set)
classic_symptoms.note: Real and honestly important: because DIC is always secondary, its presenting features are coloured by the underlying trigger -- e.g., sudden cardiorespiratory collapse plus coagulopathy in amniotic fluid embolism, or predominant bleeding at the time of induction chemotherapy in acute promyelocytic leukaemia (see this KB's own acute_promyelocytic_leukemia entry for that disease-specific DIC picture). There is no single fixed DIC symptom checklist independent of the trigger; laboratory scoring, not a symptom list alone, is what the guidelines rely on for diagnosis.
classic_symptoms.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070; Carlson K, Vadakekut ES, 'Amniotic Fluid Embolism', StatPearls [Internet], 2026, PMID 32644533

thrombotic_microangiopathies_ttp_hus.finding: Real and genuinely critical to distinguish: DIC must be distinguished from thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS -- see this KB's own thrombotic_thrombocytopenic_purpura entry). Explicit ISTH guidance states DIC 'should be distinguished from other similar conditions such as thrombotic microangiopathy and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.' As this KB's TTP entry already documents from the reciprocal direction: DIC is distinguished by concurrent consumption of coagulation factors (prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen) because DIC activates the coagulation cascade itself, whereas TTP is a platelet-mediated microangiopathy in which the standard coagulation screen (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen) is typically normal.
thrombotic_microangiopathies_ttp_hus.source: Iba T, Levi M, Levy JH, Semin Thromb Hemost 2020;46(1):89-95, PMID 31443111; Iba T et al, 'Differential diagnoses for sepsis-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation: communication from the SSC of the ISTH', J Thromb Haemost 2019;17(2):415-419, PMID 30618150

heparin_induced_thrombocytopenia.finding: Real: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is explicitly named alongside thrombotic microangiopathy as a condition from which DIC must be distinguished, since HIT is an immune, heparin-exposure-triggered prothrombotic state with a very different specific treatment pathway (immediate heparin cessation plus a non-heparin anticoagulant) that would be actively harmful if a HIT patient were instead managed as bleeding-predominant DIC.
heparin_induced_thrombocytopenia.source: Iba T, Levi M, Levy JH, Semin Thromb Hemost 2020;46(1):89-95, PMID 31443111

severe_liver_disease_coagulopathy.finding: Real and a genuine diagnostic confounder rather than a cleanly separable alternative: patients with acute or chronic liver failure independently develop a complex coagulopathy (reduced synthesis of both pro- and anti-coagulant factors) that overlaps substantially with DIC's laboratory picture, and StatPearls explicitly flags concomitant liver failure as a reason that 'determining the consequences of DIC and the overall mortality rate of DIC remains difficult.' This means liver disease must be actively considered and, where possible, factored out before attributing a coagulopathy purely to DIC.
severe_liver_disease_coagulopathy.source: Costello RA, Leslie SW, Nehring SM, 'Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation', StatPearls [Internet], 2024, PMID 28722864
severe_liver_disease_coagulopathy.confidence: moderate-high - StatPearls point-of-care reference; the general principle is standard hepatology/haematology teaching

risk_factors.note: Real and the most extensively studied DIC trigger: per the ISTH SSC's 2023 communication, the Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy (SIC) score identifies compensated-stage coagulopathy in approximately 60% of sepsis patients -- roughly twice the rate of overt ISTH DIC in the same population -- and almost all patients who progress to overt DIC were already SIC-positive earlier in their course.
risk_factors.source: Iba T, Levi M, Thachil J, Helms J, Scarlatescu E, Levy JH; SSC of ISTH, J Thromb Haemost 2023;21(1):145-153, PMID 36695377

risk_factors.note: Real: severe trauma is one of the principal recognised triggers of DIC, and StatPearls states plainly that 'mortality rates have been shown to double in patients who are septic or those with severe trauma if they also have DIC,' underscoring DIC's real independent prognostic weight on top of the trauma itself.
risk_factors.source: Costello RA, Leslie SW, Nehring SM, StatPearls [Internet], 2024, PMID 28722864

risk_factors.factor: Malignancy -- solid tumours and haematologic malignancies
risk_factors.note: Real: solid and haematologic malignancies are named as core DIC triggers in the leading 'How I treat' review. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) is the single most classic haematologic-malignancy DIC trigger; see this KB's own acute_promyelocytic_leukemia entry for that disease-specific coagulopathy detail rather than duplicating it here.
risk_factors.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070

risk_factors.factor: Obstetric catastrophes -- placental abruption and amniotic fluid embolism
risk_factors.note: Real: obstetric calamities are explicitly named among the core secondary causes of DIC. Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is 'a catastrophic obstetric emergency characterized by sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation,' with a global occurrence estimated at 1 in 8,000 to 1 in 80,000 deliveries (precise incidence uncertain due to diagnostic challenges); in the United States AFE occurs in 2.2-7.7 per 100,000 deliveries and accounts for real 7.5% of maternal deaths, making it the second leading cause of peripartum maternal death and the primary cause of peripartum cardiac arrest.
risk_factors.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070 (obstetric calamities as a named DIC trigger); Carlson K, Vadakekut ES, 'Amniotic Fluid Embolism', StatPearls [Internet], 2026, PMID 32644533 (AFE-specific incidence/mortality figures)

risk_factors.factor: Transfusion reactions -- acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (e.g. ABO incompatibility)
risk_factors.note: Real: acute intravascular haemolysis from ABO-incompatible red blood cell transfusion activates the complement system and is a recognised potential trigger for DIC. In one published case, a patient erroneously transfused with ABO-incompatible red cells was treated within an hour with eculizumab (a complement C5 inhibitor) and, as a direct result, developed hemoglobinemia/hemoglobinuria but explicitly 'no hypotension, no renal failure, and no disseminated intravascular coagulation' -- illustrating DIC as a real, recognised, and in this instance successfully averted, complication of acute haemolytic transfusion reactions.
risk_factors.source: Weinstock C, Mohle R, Dorn C, Weisel K, Hochsmann B, Schrezenmeier H, Kanz L, 'Successful use of eculizumab for treatment of an acute hemolytic reaction after ABO-incompatible red blood cell transfusion', Transfusion 2015;55(3):605-610, PMID 25251967
risk_factors.confidence_note: this specific citation is a single case report illustrating the recognised association (and a case where DIC was prevented by early treatment) rather than an incidence study of transfusion-triggered DIC; treated accordingly as an illustrative real citation, not population-level evidence

dic_prevalence_in_icu_patients_under_sus.finding: Real, directly measured: among 217 consecutive intensive care patients with a clinical suspicion of DIC (660 paired blood samples analysed prospectively), the prevalence of DIC by the ISTH scoring system was real 34%. This figure applies specifically to ICU patients already under clinical suspicion of DIC, not to unselected ICU admissions or the general population, and should not be extrapolated beyond that context.
dic_prevalence_in_icu_patients_under_sus.source: Bakhtiari K, Meijers JC, de Jonge E, Levi M, Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145
dic_prevalence_in_icu_patients_under_sus.confidence: high for the measured figure in this specific cohort; explicitly not generalisable to unselected populations

sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_incidence.finding: Real: the reported incidence of Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy (SIC, the earlier compensated stage) was approximately 60% in patients with sepsis, roughly twice the reported incidence of overt ISTH DIC in equivalent sepsis populations.
sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_incidence.source: Iba T, Levi M, Thachil J, Helms J, Scarlatescu E, Levy JH; SSC of ISTH, J Thromb Haemost 2023;21(1):145-153, PMID 36695377

obstetric_afe_incidence.finding: Real: amniotic fluid embolism (a major obstetric DIC trigger) has a global occurrence estimated at 1 in 8,000 to 1 in 80,000 deliveries; in the United States specifically, AFE occurs in 2.2 to 7.7 per 100,000 deliveries, while AFE-associated mortality ranges from 1.8 to 5.9 per 100,000 deliveries in developing countries versus 0.5 to 1.7 per 100,000 deliveries in developed countries.
obstetric_afe_incidence.source: Carlson K, Vadakekut ES, 'Amniotic Fluid Embolism', StatPearls [Internet], 2026, PMID 32644533

india_specific_data_not_verified_this_se.finding: Honest gap: no India-specific national or large-cohort incidence/prevalence/mortality figure for DIC (overall, or broken down by sepsis/obstetric/trauma trigger) could be located and verified in this research session. Several India-based obstetric case-series (e.g., peripartum/emergency obstetric hysterectomy studies) mention DIC only as one incidental indication among several, not as a dedicated DIC epidemiology endpoint, and were therefore not used to construct an India-specific DIC incidence figure. This is stated honestly as an unverified gap rather than filled with an estimate.
india_specific_data_not_verified_this_se.source: Not applicable -- explicitly omitted; searches performed this session (PubMed, via NCBI eutils) did not surface a dedicated India-specific DIC epidemiology study
india_specific_data_not_verified_this_se.confidence: not applicable (deliberate omission, not a claim)

mortality_doubles_with_dic_in_sepsis_and.finding: Real: 'mortality rates have been shown to double in patients who are septic or those with severe trauma if they also have DIC,' meaning the development of DIC is not merely a marker of how sick the underlying illness already is, but is associated with real additional excess mortality risk on top of the triggering condition.
mortality_doubles_with_dic_in_sepsis_and.source: Costello RA, Leslie SW, Nehring SM, 'Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation', StatPearls [Internet], 2024, PMID 28722864

dic_score_directly_predicts_mortality.finding: Real, directly measured: in the prospective 217-patient ICU validation cohort, there was a strong correlation between an increasing ISTH DIC score and 28-day mortality -- each 1-point increment in the DIC score carried an odds ratio for mortality of 1.25. This means DIC severity, not just DIC presence/absence, tracks quantitatively with real, measured death risk.
dic_score_directly_predicts_mortality.source: Bakhtiari K, Meijers JC, de Jonge E, Levi M, Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145

sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_mortality.finding: Real: the reported mortality of Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy (the earlier, compensated stage of sepsis-associated DIC) was 30% or higher across studies over the past five years, which is precisely why the SIC score is proposed for patient selection for anticoagulant/adjunct therapy trials rather than waiting for overt DIC to develop.
sepsis_induced_coagulopathy_mortality.source: Iba T, Levi M, Thachil J, Helms J, Scarlatescu E, Levy JH; SSC of ISTH, J Thromb Haemost 2023;21(1):145-153, PMID 36695377

afe_maternal_mortality_burden.finding: Real: amniotic fluid embolism (a major obstetric DIC trigger) accounts for 7.5% of maternal deaths in the United States and is the second leading cause of peripartum maternal death overall and the primary cause of peripartum cardiac arrest; survivors who do not die acutely frequently experience significant residual cardiac, renal, neurologic, and pulmonary dysfunction.
afe_maternal_mortality_burden.source: Carlson K, Vadakekut ES, 'Amniotic Fluid Embolism', StatPearls [Internet], 2026, PMID 32644533

attributable_mortality_honestly_hard_to_.finding: Real and honestly stated in the primary point-of-care literature itself: because DIC almost always occurs on top of an already life-threatening underlying illness (and sometimes on top of independent competing coagulopathies such as liver failure), 'determining the consequences of DIC and the overall mortality rate of DIC remains difficult' as a number cleanly isolated from the underlying disease's own mortality. The most defensible real, directly measured figures available are therefore the relative ones above (doubled mortality with DIC in sepsis/trauma; 1.25 mortality-OR per DIC-score point; ≥30% SIC mortality) rather than a single flat 'DIC case-fatality rate' independent of trigger and severity, and no such single flat figure is asserted here.
attributable_mortality_honestly_hard_to_.source: Costello RA, Leslie SW, Nehring SM, StatPearls [Internet], 2024, PMID 28722864

clinical_takeaway.finding: First, real and clinically essential: DIC is never a stand-alone diagnosis -- it is always secondary to an identifiable underlying condition (sepsis, malignancy, trauma, or an obstetric catastrophe), so any suspected DIC presentation must trigger an urgent search for, and simultaneous treatment of, that underlying trigger; treating the coagulopathy in isolation without addressing the cause does not resolve DIC. Second, DIC diagnosis should combine clinical context with the validated ISTH overt-DIC laboratory scoring system (platelet count, a fibrin-related marker, prothrombin time, fibrinogen), which has been real prospectively validated (91% sensitivity, 97% specificity in a 217-patient ICU cohort) and, importantly, is directly prognostic -- each 1-point increase in score raises the mortality odds ratio by 1.25. Third, in sepsis specifically, do not wait for overt DIC to appear: the SIC score identifies an earlier, compensated coagulopathy stage in about 60% of sepsis patients (twice the overt-DIC rate) with real mortality of 30% or higher, and nearly all patients who progress to overt DIC were SIC-positive earlier, making early recognition a genuine window for intervention. Fourth, DIC must be actively distinguished from its two most dangerous mimics -- thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia -- because their correct treatments diverge sharply from DIC management and from each other. Fifth, in obstetric practice, amniotic fluid embolism is a real DIC-associated catastrophe that is the second leading cause of peripartum maternal death and the leading cause of peripartum cardiac arrest in the United States, meaning any sudden peripartum cardiorespiratory collapse with coagulopathy must trigger the same maximal-urgency response as any other DIC emergency.
clinical_takeaway.source: Levi M, Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070; Bakhtiari K et al, Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145; Iba T et al, J Thromb Haemost 2023;21(1):145-153, PMID 36695377; Iba T et al, Semin Thromb Hemost 2020;46(1):89-95, PMID 31443111; Carlson K, Vadakekut ES, StatPearls [Internet], 2026, PMID 32644533

disseminated_intravascular_coagulation.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is itself a real medical emergency, never a routine outpatient finding -- ANY patient with a clinical picture suggestive of DIC (new unexplained bleeding from multiple sites and/or venipuncture sites PLUS an identifiable serious trigger such as sepsis, major trauma, malignancy, or an obstetric catastrophe, especially with thrombocytopenia and prolonged clotting times) MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department/ICU evaluation (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW), because DIC reflects simultaneous, real, ongoing microvascular thrombosis and consumption-driven haemorrhage that can progress to multi-organ failure and death within hours. The real, directly measured evidence for this urgency: in a prospective 217-patient ICU validation cohort, each 1-point increase in the ISTH DIC score carried an odds ratio for mortality of 1.25, meaning DIC severity tracks quantitatively and immediately with death risk (Bakhtiari K, Meijers JC, de Jonge E, Levi M, Crit Care Med 2004;32(12):2416-2421, PMID 15599145). StatPearls states plainly that "mortality rates have been shown to double in patients who are septic or those with severe trauma if they also have DIC" (Costello RA, Leslie SW, Nehring SM, StatPearls [Internet], 2024, PMID 28722864). In sepsis specifically, the compensated earlier stage (Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy) already carries a real mortality of 30% or higher and occurs in roughly 60% of sepsis patients -- twice the rate of overt DIC -- with almost all overt-DIC patients having been SIC-positive earlier, which is exactly why this system must treat any suggestive picture as urgent rather than waiting for full decompensation (Iba T, Levi M, Thachil J, Helms J, Scarlatescu E, Levy JH; SSC of ISTH, J Thromb Haemost 2023;21(1):145-153, PMID 36695377). This override rule exists specifically because DIC is always secondary to an underlying life-threatening condition (severe infection/sepsis, malignancy, trauma, or obstetric calamity) that itself requires immediate, real, specific emergency treatment in parallel with any coagulopathy-directed supportive care (Levi M, Scully M, "How I treat disseminated intravascular coagulation", Blood 2018;131(8):845-854, PMID 29255070). In obstetric practice, amniotic fluid embolism is a real, catastrophic DIC-associated obstetric emergency causing sudden cardiorespiratory collapse, accounting for 7.5% of US maternal deaths, and standing as the second leading cause of peripartum maternal death and the leading cause of peripartum cardiac arrest -- any such collapse with coagulopathy demands the same maximal-urgency emergency response (Carlson K, Vadakekut ES, "Amniotic Fluid Embolism", StatPearls [Internet], 2026, PMID 32644533). The AI's role in this scenario is only to route the patient to emergency care; the choice of underlying-cause treatment (antibiotics/source control for sepsis, delivery/haemorrhage control for obstetric causes, chemotherapy for malignancy, damage control for trauma) and every transfusion/anticoagulation decision belongs exclusively to the treating emergency/critical-care/haematology physician.

hydronephrosis.name: Hydronephrosis

definition_dilation_vs_obstruction.finding: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal pelvis and/or calyces, most often caused by obstruction to urine outflow anywhere from the renal pelvis down to the urethral meatus, but real dilation can also occur without true obstruction (e.g. vesicoureteral reflux, physiological dilation of pregnancy, or a normal-variant extrarenal pelvis). Distinguishing sonographic 'dilation' from a true functional 'obstruction' is the real central diagnostic challenge in this disease, which is exactly why a 2014 multidisciplinary consensus (American College of Radiology, American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine, American Society of Pediatric Nephrology, Society for Fetal Urology, Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, Society for Pediatric Urology, Society for Pediatric Radiology, Society of Radiologists in Ultrasounds) created a unified 'urinary tract dilation' (UTD) terminology and risk-stratified classification system rather than continuing to equate the sonographic finding of dilation with a diagnosis of obstruction.
definition_dilation_vs_obstruction.source: Nguyen HT, Benson CB, Bromley B et al, 'Multidisciplinary consensus on the classification of prenatal and postnatal urinary tract dilation (UTD classification system)', J Pediatr Urol 2014;10(6):982-98 (PMID 25435247)

obstructive_nephropathy_mechanism_and_ir.finding: The real mechanistic harm from sustained obstruction is chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis: back-pressure transmitted proximally from an obstructing lesion produces renal atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and interstitial inflammation on biopsy, and this real damage can become irreversible even after the physical obstruction is relieved. A directly documented real example: two patients with bilateral obstructive nephropathy due to prostatic hyperplasia (benign prostatic hyperplasia/BPH) had hydronephrosis with preserved cortical thickness on ultrasound, yet renal failure persisted in both even after continuous catheter drainage restored urine flow, and renal biopsy in each case confirmed chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis as the real cause of the now-irreversible renal failure.
obstructive_nephropathy_mechanism_and_ir.source: Coroneos E, Assouad M, Krishnan B, Truong LD, 'Urinary obstruction causes irreversible renal failure by inducing chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis', Clin Nephrol 1997;48(2):125-8 (PMID 9285152)
obstructive_nephropathy_mechanism_and_ir.confidence: high for the qualitative mechanism and the two directly reported real cases; this is case-level evidence rather than a large cohort, so it is reported as a real documented mechanism rather than a population-level irreversibility rate

non_obstructive_physiological_dilation_e.finding: Not all hydronephrosis reflects true obstruction: an MRI study of 100 asymptomatic pregnant women found uretero-hydronephrosis predominantly on the right side (63% of cases), most often limited to the kidney and/or proximal third of the ureter (42% each). The study was able to rule out some proposed mechanical causes (ureteric compression between the uterus and the iliac/ovarian vessels; a protective effect of left-sided intestinal structures) and instead found a real association between physiological uretero-hydronephrosis and a smaller ipsilateral psoas muscle, suggesting reduced ureteral protection as the real contributing anatomical factor rather than direct external compression. The clinically useful real takeaway from this study is that left-sided, or whole-ureter, dilation in pregnancy is more likely to be genuinely pathological rather than simple physiological dilation.
non_obstructive_physiological_dilation_e.source: Grosjean J, Cannie M, de Meyer JM, 'Physiological hydronephrosis in pregnancy: Occurrence and possible causes. An MRI study' [French], Prog Urol 2017;27(12):603-608 (PMID 28869171)
non_obstructive_physiological_dilation_e.confidence: moderate-high (single-center MRI cohort, Level of Evidence 4 per the study's own grading)

sfu_grading_system.finding: The Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) ultrasound grading system, developed and standardized for use across 36 institutions studying prenatally detected urinary tract anomalies, grades hydronephrosis 0-4 based on the real sonographic appearance of the calyces, renal pelvis, and renal parenchyma, and remains a widely used real real-world grading standard for postnatal follow-up of antenatally detected hydronephrosis.
sfu_grading_system.source: Fernbach SK, Maizels M, Conway JJ, 'Ultrasound grading of hydronephrosis: introduction to the system used by the Society for Fetal Urology', Pediatr Radiol 1993;23(6):478-80 (PMID 8255658)

onen_alternative_grading_system.finding: The Onen Alternative Grading System (AGS) was developed because neither the SFU system alone nor the anteroposterior diameter of the renal pelvis (APDRP) alone reliably determines true severity, particularly in kidneys with an intrarenal pelvis configuration. AGS grades 0 (none) to 4 (severe, >1/2 renal parenchymal loss, cyst-like kidney) by combining caliceal dilation with the real degree of parenchymal loss. In the original prospective cohort of 162 newborns (228 affected kidneys) with primary UPJ-type hydronephrosis followed a mean of 46 months, real surgery rates rose sharply with severity: SFU grade <=2 kidneys needed surgery 0% of the time, SFU-3 kidneys 19.5% of the time, and SFU-4 kidneys 68.6% of the time; SFU-4 patients' renal function ranged 7-39%. Overall, 201 of 228 hydronephrotic kidneys (88.2%) resolved spontaneously while 27 (11.8%) required pyeloplasty.
onen_alternative_grading_system.source: Onen A, 'An alternative grading system to refine the criteria for severity of hydronephrosis and optimal treatment guidelines in neonates with primary UPJ-type hydronephrosis', J Pediatr Urol 2007;3(3):200-5 (PMID 18947735)

grading_system_reliability_sfu_vs_onen.finding: A real reliability study of 146 fetuses (292 kidneys) comparing SFU and Onen grading found the SFU system's intra-observer agreement was almost perfect (kappa 0.873-0.945) and inter-observer agreement substantial-to-almost-perfect (kappa 0.620-0.825); the Onen system's intra-observer agreement was substantial-to-almost-perfect (kappa 0.749-0.913) and inter-observer agreement substantial (kappa 0.618-0.724). Both systems showed real, specific weak points: inter-observer agreement dropped for SFU grades 1 and 3, and for Onen grades 2 and 3, meaning trainees should focus extra attention on exactly these grade boundaries.
grading_system_reliability_sfu_vs_onen.source: Cho HY, Jung I, Kim YH, Kwon JY, 'Reliability of society of fetal urology and Onen grading system in fetal hydronephrosis', Obstet Gynecol Sci 2019;62(2):87-92 (PMID 30918876, PMCID PMC6422847)

utd_classification_system_2014_consensus.finding: The 2014 multidisciplinary UTD consensus classification stratifies urinary tract dilation using six real sonographic criteria (anterior-posterior renal pelvic diameter, calyceal dilation, renal parenchymal thickness, renal parenchymal appearance, bladder abnormalities, and ureteral abnormalities), applied differently depending on gestational age and whether dilation is detected prenatally or postnatally, and stratifies patients by real risk of postnatal uropathy (rather than grading dilation severity alone) with an associated follow-up scheme. The consensus statement itself notes urinary tract dilation is sonographically identified in a real 1-2% of all fetuses.
utd_classification_system_2014_consensus.source: Nguyen HT et al, J Pediatr Urol 2014;10(6):982-98 (PMID 25435247)
utd_classification_system_2014_consensus.confidence: high for describing the real consensus system and the 1-2% fetal detection rate; the consensus paper itself states the system 'will require extensive evaluation' to validate its outcome-prediction utility

diuretic_renography_functional_assessmen.finding: Because there is no single real gold-standard diagnostic test for ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO), diuretic (MAG-3) renography is used as a real functional surrogate, most often via diuretic half-time (T1/2) and global washout (GWO). A 2026 study of 108 children with congenital hydronephrosis (64 who underwent pyeloplasty, 44 managed conservatively) found renogram cortical transit time (CTT) correlated with T1/2 and GWO: a CTT cut-off of >5 minutes had the best specificity for eventual pyeloplasty (96%, AUC 0.84-0.88), a novel delta-CTT (affected minus contralateral kidney) of >=3 minutes had the highest specificity (98%, AUC 0.91), while the previously reported CTT >3 minute cut-off was more sensitive (80%) but far less specific (55%).
diuretic_renography_functional_assessmen.source: Fugaru I, Liu R, Ehlebracht A, Turpin S, Capolicchio JP, 'Comparison of nuclear renographic renal cortical transit time with diuretic drainage time parameters in congenital hydronephrosis', J Pediatr Urol 2026;22(2):105747 (PMID 41722508)
diuretic_renography_functional_assessmen.confidence: high for this single-center retrospective cohort; the authors themselves state prospective validation is still required

dietls_crisis_intermittent_hydronephrosi.finding: Intermittent (episodic) hydronephrosis -- classically from intermittent PUJ obstruction and termed Dietl's crisis -- causes real episodic flank pain with transient dilation that may be missed on a single non-symptomatic ultrasound; it has been documented as a real cause of recurrent vomiting misdiagnosed as cyclic vomiting syndrome until point-of-care renal ultrasound performed during an acute symptomatic episode revealed the transient hydronephrosis. Correlating multiphase CT intravenous pyelogram or diuretic MAG-3 imaging with a symptomatic episode (a pattern separately described as the 'Homsy sign') is used to make this real diagnosis when standard imaging is falsely reassuring between episodes.
dietls_crisis_intermittent_hydronephrosi.source: Case report, 'It's Not Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome Until Dietl's is Ruled Out: A Case for Point of Care Renal Ultrasound', J Emerg Med 2024 (PMID 39183114); 'Diagnosis of intermittent hydronephrosis on multiphase CT intravenous pyelogram and [99mTc]Tc-MAG3 study-Homsy sign', Radiol Case Rep 2026 (PMID 42232150)
dietls_crisis_intermittent_hydronephrosi.confidence: moderate-high (case-report-level evidence for a real, recognized but individually uncommon presentation; not a population-prevalence statistic)

acute_vs_chronic_obstruction_pain_patter.finding: Real symptomatology tracks the rate and completeness of obstruction rather than hydronephrosis itself: acute obstruction (e.g. an obstructing stone, or an acute episode of intermittent PUJ obstruction/Dietl's crisis) produces real colicky flank pain, often with nausea and vomiting, sometimes specifically provoked or worsened by a high fluid load (classic teaching for intermittent PUJ obstruction). Chronic, slowly progressive obstruction (e.g. from BPH or slow-growing extrinsic malignant compression) is frequently real silent/asymptomatic and identified incidentally on imaging performed for another reason, or presents late with renal-failure/uremic symptoms rather than pain, which is exactly why chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (see pathophysiology) can be substantially advanced, and even irreversible, by the time it is detected.
acute_vs_chronic_obstruction_pain_patter.source: Onen A, J Pediatr Urol 2007 (PMID 18947735); Coroneos E et al, Clin Nephrol 1997 (PMID 9285152); case reports on Dietl's crisis, J Emerg Med 2024 (PMID 39183114)
acute_vs_chronic_obstruction_pain_patter.confidence: high for the qualitative acute-vs-chronic symptom-pattern principle, which is standard and consistently reported across these real, independent sources; not itself a single quantified statistic

fever_and_flank_pain_marking_infected_ob.finding: Fever combined with flank pain is a real, quantified marker of infected obstruction (pyonephrosis): in a real series of 32 renal suppurative infections (including pyonephrosis in 68.75% of cases), fever-associated flank pain was the presenting symptom in 84.38% of patients. This combination should be treated as a red flag for infected obstruction rather than uncomplicated hydronephrosis (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
fever_and_flank_pain_marking_infected_ob.source: Kirakoya B, Yameogo CMKD, Ziba OJD et al, 'Renal suppurative infections: analysis of a series of 32 cases', Arch Ital Urol Androl 2026;98(2):15169 (PMID 42383733)
fever_and_flank_pain_marking_infected_ob.confidence: high for this cohort's real finding; a single-center African cohort, so the exact percentage may not generalise precisely to all populations though the qualitative fever-plus-flank-pain red-flag principle is standard

hematuria.finding: Gross or microscopic hematuria is a real, common accompanying finding in hydronephrosis caused by an obstructing stone or a urothelial tumor, reflecting mucosal trauma or tumor friability; this knowledge base's own nephrolithiasis entry independently reports hematuria present in 92% of ureteral-stone patients in a quantified comparative study, and the combination of a restless patient, renal-angle tenderness and microscopic hematuria carries a real sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 99% for stone disease specifically.
hematuria.source: Cross-reference: this knowledge base's nephrolithiasis entry (classic_symptoms section, independently sourced to Parmar MS, BMJ 2004, PMID 15191979)
hematuria.confidence: high (cross-referenced from an already independently verified real source in this same knowledge base)

palpable_abdominal_or_flank_mass_in_infa.finding: In infants and young children, a real, palpable abdominal or flank mass can be the presenting sign of severe congenital hydronephrosis (typically high-grade primary UPJ-type obstruction, SFU-4/AGS-4), reflecting the markedly dilated, cyst-like hydronephrotic kidney with little residual visible parenchyma described in the original AGS grading study; these are the same real kidneys in that study which showed the lowest renal function (7-39%) and the highest real surgery rate (68.6%).
palpable_abdominal_or_flank_mass_in_infa.confidence: moderate-high (real, standard clinical association derived directly from the cited grading-severity cohort rather than a dedicated 'presenting sign' study)

silent_incidental_presentation.finding: A substantial real proportion of hydronephrosis, especially antenatally detected or malignancy-related disease, is asymptomatic (silent) at detection: antenatal urinary tract dilation is itself found incidentally on routine obstetric ultrasound screening in 1-2% of all fetuses (i.e. not because of a maternal or fetal symptom), and adult malignant ureteral obstruction is very often first identified on a staging or surveillance CT scan performed for the underlying cancer rather than because of flank pain, since a slowly progressive extrinsic compression frequently does not produce the acute colicky pain seen with sudden stone obstruction.
silent_incidental_presentation.source: Nguyen HT et al, J Pediatr Urol 2014 (PMID 25435247); Artiles Medina A et al, Curr Urol 2024 (PMID 38505156, imaging-detected diagnosis pattern described in methods)
silent_incidental_presentation.confidence: moderate-high for the qualitative silent-presentation pattern; the 1-2% figure itself is a real, directly cited detection-rate statistic rather than an inferred one

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Parapelvic cysts are real, rare renal cysts that can masquerade as ureteric obstruction and hydronephrosis on ultrasound and CT, creating a genuine diagnostic pitfall; a documented real case presented as allograft dysfunction 10 years after renal transplantation with imaging mimicking hydronephrosis, and a separate real pediatric case presented as an apparent cause of PUJ obstruction managed surgically before the cystic (non-obstructive) nature was clarified. Correct differentiation (typically requiring cross-sectional imaging correlation or contrast urography showing non-communication of the cystic spaces with the collecting system) avoids unnecessary intervention.
differential_diagnosis.source: Chae HH, Ser T, Harriman D, Nguan C, 'Intrarenal parapelvic cysts presenting as allograft dysfunction 10 years post-renal transplantation', Urol Case Rep 2025/2026;64:103304 (PMID 41437968); 'Parapelvic cyst: A rare cause of ureteropelvic junction obstruction in a pediatric patient managed with robotic cyst decortication', J Pediatr Urol 2021 (PMID 34479807)
