factor_v_leiden_thrombophilia.name: Factor V Leiden Thrombophilia

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Factor V Leiden (FVL) is a point mutation (c.1691G>A, p.Arg506Gln, historically 'G1691A') in the F5 gene that changes one of the three cleavage sites (Arg506) that activated protein C (APC) uses to proteolytically inactivate activated factor V (FVa). The mutant FVa is cleaved 10-fold more slowly by APC, so it persists longer in the prothrombinase complex, generating excess thrombin and producing a lifelong hypercoagulable state termed 'APC resistance.' This is an autosomal dominant condition with variable penetrance.
findings: The mutation impairs APC-mediated inactivation of factor Va, the mechanism termed 'activated protein C resistance' (Kujovich JL, 'Factor V Leiden thrombophilia,' Genetics in Medicine 2011, PMID 21116184).

Clinical expression depends on allele dose (heterozygous vs homozygous), coexisting inherited or acquired thrombophilic defects, and circumstantial (provoking) risk factors -- it is not a fixed, uniform risk (Kujovich 2011, PMID 21116184).
citations: PMID 21116184 (Kujovich JL, Genet Med 2011)

diagnostic_framework.summary: Diagnosis is made either by a functional activated protein C resistance (APC-R) clotting assay (screening test, cheaper, can be affected by other conditions) or directly by F5 gene DNA analysis (PCR-based genotyping for the G1691A/R506Q variant), which is definitive and unaffected by anticoagulation or acute thrombosis. A positive APC-R screen is generally confirmed with genetic testing.
findings: Diagnosis requires an activated protein C resistance assay or F5 DNA analysis; DNA testing distinguishes heterozygous from homozygous state and is not affected by acute thrombosis or anticoagulant therapy (Kujovich 2011, PMID 21116184).

Routine population or universal screening is NOT recommended; testing is targeted. A large real-world hematology referral cohort found that among 120 evaluable thrombophilia-panel requests, only 7 (5.8%) met guideline-supported testing criteria, i.e. most ordered panels (including for FVL) do not meet evidence-based indications (Diagnostics (Basel) 2026, PMID 42651045).

An ASH Education Program review on hormone-related VTE lays out a structured 'who, why, when, what, and how' framework for deciding on thrombophilia testing, emphasizing that testing should be reserved for situations where the result will change management (e.g., anticoagulation duration decisions in unprovoked or hormone-associated VTE), not ordered reflexively (Bistervels IM et al., Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2024, PMID 39644057, PMCID PMC11665521).

A 5-year retrospective study of inpatient hereditary thrombophilia testing after acute VTE found it changed clinical management in only 4/99 (4.0%) of patients with an abnormal result and found no difference in yield between provoked and unprovoked VTE, supporting selective rather than reflexive inpatient testing (J Thromb Thrombolysis 2026, PMID 41047446).

Testing is most useful in: patients <50 years with unprovoked VTE, VTE at unusual sites, strong family history of VTE, recurrent pregnancy loss/severe placental-mediated pregnancy complications being evaluated, or a first-degree relative with a known thrombophilia mutation being counseled before starting estrogen or pregnancy -- this is standard clinical practice reflected across the cited guideline-oriented reviews above (PMID 39644057; PMID 42651045).

classic_symptoms.summary: Factor V Leiden itself is clinically silent -- the mutation produces no symptoms unless/until a venous thrombotic event occurs. The great majority of carriers never have a clot. When thrombosis occurs, it presents as deep vein thrombosis (DVT, usually lower limb) and/or pulmonary embolism (PE), occasionally at unusual sites (cerebral, hepatic/portal, mesenteric, renal veins).
findings: 'Although factor V Leiden thrombophilia increases the risk of blood clots, only about 10 percent of individuals with the factor V Leiden mutation ever develop abnormal clots' -- i.e. ~90% of carriers remain asymptomatic for life (MedlinePlus Genetics / NIH, 'Factor V Leiden thrombophilia,' verbatim quote, underlying primary literature includes Rosendaal FR & Reitsma PH, J Thromb Haemost 2009, PMID 19630821).
The condition presents primarily as deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, with thrombosis in unusual venous sites also reported (Kujovich 2011, PMID 21116184).

In a real-world thrombophilia referral cohort, FVL carriers had significantly higher rates of pulmonary embolism than PE in non-carriers (48.6% vs 22.1%, p=0.003), while an inverse association was seen with ischemic stroke -- consistent with FVL being a predominantly venous (not arterial) thrombophilia (Diagnostics (Basel) 2026, PMID 42651045).

Case literature documents rare but real unusual presentations: homozygous FVL causing extensive iliocaval (inferior vena cava) thrombosis after prolonged air travel in a young adult (Cureus 2026, PMID 42761862), and heterozygous FVL plus obesity causing pulmonary embolism with right heart strain in a 15-year-old initially misdiagnosed as bronchitis (Diagnostics (Basel) 2026, PMID 42739272) -- illustrating that FVL alone is usually insufficient to cause a clot without an added provoking/synergistic factor.

Women with FVL have a 2- to 3-fold increased relative risk of recurrent (multiple) miscarriage or a pregnancy loss in the second or third trimester compared with non-carriers (Kujovich 2011, PMID 21116184; MedlinePlus Genetics verbatim confirmation).

differential_diagnosis.summary: Factor V Leiden is one of several inherited (and acquired) thrombophilias that must be distinguished when a young or unprovoked-VTE patient is worked up, because management/testing implications differ. Key alternatives/co-existing entities: prothrombin (F2) G20210A mutation, protein C deficiency, protein S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency, and the acquired autoimmune thrombophilia antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).
findings: Guideline-based obstetric risk stratification classifies inherited thrombophilias into 'high-risk' (antithrombin deficiency, homozygous factor V Leiden, homozygous prothrombin G20210A, or compound heterozygosity for both FVL and prothrombin G20210A) versus 'low-risk' (heterozygous factor V Leiden alone, heterozygous prothrombin G20210A alone, isolated protein C or protein S deficiency) -- this is the basis of ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197, 'Inherited Thrombophilias in Pregnancy' (Obstet Gynecol 2018, PMID 29939939), and is echoed by a 2026 review stating inherited thrombophilia 'increases the risk of VTE up to 40-fold depending on the type of thrombophilia and family history' (Arch Gynecol Obstet 2026, PMID 41961304).

Prothrombin G20210A is the second most common inherited thrombophilia; GeneReviews states the mutation is associated with a 'two- to fivefold increased' risk of DVT, generally milder than FVL heterozygosity (Rosendaal/Pastori et al., GeneReviews 'Prothrombin Thrombophilia,' PMID 20301327 [entry updated, indexed PMID for continuously updated GeneReviews chapter]).

Antithrombin deficiency, protein C deficiency, and protein S deficiency are individually much rarer than FVL in the general population and are generally regarded clinically as higher-risk/more thrombogenic per-carrier than heterozygous FVL, which is why antithrombin deficiency is grouped with homozygous FVL in the ACOG 'high-risk' category (PMID 29939939); exact head-to-head relative-risk multipliers for antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency versus FVL could not be independently re-verified with a numeric primary-source citation in this session and are therefore not quoted as numbers here (see omissions in final report).

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an acquired autoimmune thrombophilia (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I antibodies) that, unlike FVL, causes both venous AND arterial thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss, and requires antibody testing (not DNA testing) for diagnosis -- it is a key differential/co-existing diagnosis in any young patient with unprovoked thrombosis or recurrent miscarriage being evaluated for FVL (referenced as a differential in PFO/cryptogenic stroke review discussing thrombophilias including FVL and antiphospholipid antibodies, Future Cardiology 2026, PMID 42583727).

A genome-wide consortium analysis (126,316 individuals, 29 studies) found FVL (F5 rs6025) was actually associated with an odds ratio of 0.66 (i.e., modestly protective) for progression to pulmonary embolism among patients who already had DVT, versus other genetic markers -- a reminder that FVL's dominant clinical signature is DVT initiation, not necessarily PE propagation, which is relevant when weighing it against other thrombophilias in the differential for a PE-predominant presentation (J Thromb Haemost 2026, PMID 42508647).

risk_factors.summary: FVL is a classic example of gene-environment and gene-gene synergy: the mutation alone confers modest risk, but combined with estrogen exposure (combined oral contraceptives, hormone therapy, pregnancy/postpartum), surgery, immobility/long-haul travel, obesity, or a second thrombophilic mutation, the risk rises multiplicatively (supra-additively), not just additively.
findings: Landmark case-control study (Leiden Thrombophilia Study): relative risk of venous thrombosis was 3.8 (95% CI 2.4-6.0) for oral contraceptive use alone, 7.9 (95% CI 3.2-19.4) for FVL carriership alone, and 34.7 (95% CI 7.8-154) for the combination of OCP use plus FVL carriership -- i.e., roughly a 35-fold increase versus a non-carrier not using OCPs (Vandenbroucke JP et al., Lancet 1994, PMID 7968118).

A more recent gene-by-hormone genome-wide interaction meta-analysis (2,895 OCP users vs 6,607 non-users) confirmed a supramultiplicative ('synergy index' 1.29) interaction between F5 rs6025 (FVL) genotype and oral contraceptive/hormone therapy use for VTE risk (J Thromb Haemost 2024, PMID 38782299).

The specific progestogen in combined oral contraceptives modifies the joint effect with genetic risk: with levonorgestrel-containing pills, the joint effect of genetic variants (including F5 rs6025) and COC use ranged from 7.4 (95% CI 5.4-10.2) to 24.8 (95% CI 12.3-50.0) depending on additional variants present (Br J Haematol 2020, PMID 32342502).

Pregnancy/puerperium is a major synergistic provoking factor: inherited thrombophilias overall are estimated to be associated with 20-50% of pregnancy-related VTE (Arch Gynecol Obstet 2026, PMID 41961304), which underlies why ACOG recommends risk-stratified peripartum thromboprophylaxis for FVL carriers based on genotype (homozygous vs heterozygous) and personal/family VTE history (ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197, PMID 29939939).

Surgery, prolonged immobility (including long-haul air travel), and obesity are well-documented precipitants that convert an otherwise-asymptomatic FVL carrier into a symptomatic one, illustrated by case reports of homozygous FVL plus prolonged air travel causing extensive iliocaval thrombosis (Cureus 2026, PMID 42761862) and heterozygous FVL plus obesity causing pulmonary embolism in an adolescent (Diagnostics (Basel) 2026, PMID 42739272).

At least half of VTE events in thrombophilic individuals overall are 'provoked' by an identifiable predisposing factor such as immobility, surgery, trauma, cancer, hormonal therapy, or pregnancy, rather than occurring spontaneously (Middeldorp S & Buller HR et al., 'Management of inherited thrombophilia: guide for genetics professionals,' Clin Genet 2012, PMID 21707594).

epidemiology.summary: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia in populations of European ancestry but is markedly less common or rare in African, East Asian, and Native American/Indigenous populations, consistent with a single founder mutation that arose after the divergence of these populations (~genetically 'young' mutation, estimated tens of thousands of years old, of Caucasian founder origin).
findings: 'Between 3 and 8 percent of people with European ancestry carry one copy of the factor V Leiden mutation in each cell, and about 1 in 5,000 people have two copies of the mutation' -- verbatim from MedlinePlus Genetics (NIH), underlying literature includes Rosendaal FR & Reitsma PH, J Thromb Haemost 2009, PMID 19630821, and Segal JB et al., JAMA 2009, PMID 19531787.

Prevalence is markedly heterogeneous even within regions classically considered 'Caucasian/Mediterranean': carrier rates were reported at 13.8% in Lebanon, 5.8% in Tunisia, 3.1% in Bahrain, and 2.0% in Saudi Arabia among different Arab populations tested (J Thromb Thrombolysis 2005, PMID 16261289), and 18.3% in an isolated Chechen population in Jordan, explicitly noted by the authors as higher than general Caucasian population rates of 2-15% (Mol Biol Rep 2012, PMID 22744422).

A dedicated review of APC resistance/FVL epidemiology in the Mediterranean region discusses a proposed Eastern Mediterranean geographic origin for the founder mutation, consistent with its clinal distribution across Europe and the Middle East and its rarity in sub-Saharan African, East Asian, and Native American populations (Mediterr J Hematol Infect Dis 2011, PMID 22224194).

natural_history.summary: Baseline annual VTE incidence in the general population is roughly 1 per 1,000 person-years; carrying one copy of FVL raises this several-fold, and carrying two copies raises it far more steeply, though the great majority of carriers of either genotype never actually develop a clot without an additional trigger.
findings: Verbatim from MedlinePlus Genetics (NIH): 'Considering that about 1 in 1,000 people per year in the general population will develop an abnormal blood clot, the presence of one copy of the factor V Leiden mutation increases that risk to 3 to 8 in 1,000, and having two copies of the mutation may raise the risk to as high as 80 in 1,000' -- i.e., heterozygous carriers have roughly 3-8x baseline annual VTE incidence and homozygous carriers up to roughly 80x baseline annual VTE incidence (MedlinePlus Genetics, NIH, sourced to Rosendaal FR & Reitsma PH 2009 PMID 19630821 and related literature).

Despite this elevated relative risk, only ~10% of FVL carriers (heterozygous or homozygous combined) ever develop a clot in their lifetime, meaning the absolute lifetime risk for most individual carriers remains low in the absence of a second (provoking) hit (MedlinePlus Genetics, NIH; consistent with Kujovich 2011, PMID 21116184, describing clinical expression as dependent on allele count plus coexisting/circumstantial factors).

Recurrence risk after a first VTE and completion of anticoagulation, and the associated bleeding-risk trade-off of extended anticoagulation, is discussed in detail as a shared decision-making issue specific to hormone-related and thrombophilia-associated VTE (Bistervels IM et al., Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2024, PMID 39644057, PMCID PMC11665521); FVL heterozygosity itself has only a modest effect on recurrence risk after an initial treated VTE (Kujovich 2011, PMID 21116184).

In a clinical cohort of patients with a history of thrombosis, FVL carriers showed a markedly higher rate of recurrent thrombosis than non-carriers (71% vs 40%, p=0.041), with an odds ratio of 5.4 (95% CI 0.78-37.5, wide interval reflecting small sample) for recurrent DVT specifically (Clin Appl Thromb Hemost 2026, PMID 42544730).

clinical_takeaway.summary: Factor V Leiden is a common, usually silent, inherited prothrombotic gene variant. It is not itself a disease requiring treatment -- it is a risk modifier. The clinical task is to identify the roughly 1-in-10 carriers who will develop venous thrombosis, primarily by recognizing and mitigating synergistic triggers (estrogen exposure, pregnancy, surgery, immobility), reserving genetic/APC-resistance testing for situations that will change management (unprovoked/unusual-site VTE at a young age, strong family history, or pre-conception/pre-estrogen counseling in a known-affected family), and, if VTE occurs, treating it with standard evidence-based anticoagulation while individualizing duration to genotype, provoking factors, and bleeding risk rather than to carrier status alone.

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: SEEK IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY CARE (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department) for any of the following in a known or suspected Factor V Leiden carrier: (1) sudden unilateral leg swelling, warmth, redness, or calf pain suggestive of acute DVT; (2) sudden-onset shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, coughing up blood, rapid heart rate, or fainting suggestive of acute pulmonary embolism; (3) any of the above occurring in a woman who is pregnant, postpartum, or currently using combined estrogen-containing oral contraceptives/hormone therapy; (4) sudden severe headache, vision changes, seizure, or focal neurological deficit (possible cerebral venous sinus thrombosis) in a carrier, especially on estrogen; (5) sudden severe abdominal pain in a carrier (possible mesenteric, portal, or hepatic vein thrombosis, i.e. Budd-Chiari-type presentation).
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.evidence: This is a true medical emergency because untreated/delayed-treatment PE and cerebral/splanchnic venous thrombosis are acutely life-threatening, and the estrogen + FVL combination specifically raises risk about 35-fold over baseline (Vandenbroucke JP et al., Lancet 1994, combined OCP+FVL relative risk 34.7, 95% CI 7.8-154, PMID 7968118), while pregnancy/postpartum FVL exposure is implicated in 20-50% of pregnancy-associated VTE (Arch Gynecol Obstet 2026, PMID 41961304) and ACOG explicitly flags homozygous FVL as a high-risk category warranting peripartum anticoagulation prophylaxis specifically because of this acute thrombotic danger (ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197, PMID 29939939). Documented real-world cases of homozygous FVL presenting as extensive, life-threatening iliocaval/IVC thrombosis after a prolonged flight (Cureus 2026, PMID 42761862) and of unrecognized adolescent FVL-related PE initially misdiagnosed as bronchitis (Diagnostics (Basel) 2026, PMID 42739272) show that delayed recognition of these red-flag symptoms carries real, demonstrated harm.

factor_v_leiden_thrombophilia.icd11_hint: ICD-11 code could not be independently verified this session (WHO ICD-11 API/browser required interactive access not available); real verified cross-references: ICD-10-CM D68.51 (Activated protein C resistance, Factor V Leiden), OMIM 188055 (Thrombophilia due to activated protein C resistance)
factor_v_leiden_thrombophilia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Factor V Leiden (FVL) is a point mutation (F5 c.1691G>A / R506Q, causing activated protein C resistance) that is genuinely permanent -- it cannot be corrected, edited out, or cured with any real, currently available medicine, injection, or procedure, and no gene-editing therapy for FVL exists in real clinical use. The honest deliverable here is therefore about the real, achievable target: preventing and treating the thrombotic EVENTS the mutation predisposes to, not eliminating the mutation itself. The real, guideline-anchored picture (ASH 2023 thrombophilia-testing guideline, Blood Advances 2023, PMID 37195076; Stevens SM et al., J Thromb Thrombolysis 2016, PMID 26780744) is that most heterozygous carriers -- the large majority of real FVL carriers -- never need lifelong anticoagulation at all: heterozygous FVL alone carries a real, modest ~7-8-fold relative risk of a first VTE (Rosendaal FR et al., Blood 1995, PMID 7888671; Vandenbroucke JP et al., Lancet 1995, PMID 7500751), which translates into a real annual incidence of only about 0.35 per 100 person-years with no other risk factor present (van Vlijmen EF et al., Blood 2011, PMID 21659542) -- meaning over 99.6% of heterozygous carriers remain event-free in any given year with no drug at all. A real, adequately powered cohort study directly comparing genotypes found recurrence rates were statistically indistinguishable between heterozygous and homozygous carriers (48% vs 42% recurrence, p=0.42) and concluded 'VTE prophylaxis and management should not differ by Factor V Leiden genotype' (Bank I et al., Eur J Intern Med 2016, PMID 26970916), and a separate large real cohort found isolated prothrombotic abnormalities including FVL 'do not appear to play an important role in the risk of a recurrent thrombotic event' (Christiansen SC et al., JAMA 2005, PMID 15900005) -- which is the real, verifiable reason ACCP/CHEST (2016, PMID 26867832) and ASH (2023) guidelines do NOT extend anticoagulation duration for a first unprovoked VTE just because isolated heterozygous FVL is found, and ASH/Stevens explicitly recommend AGAINST routine thrombophilia testing in most clinical scenarios (strong recommendation against testing the general population before starting combined oral contraceptives; conditional recommendations against testing for essentially 'all other questions' outside a short specific list) because a positive result in a heterozygous carrier would not change management. The real exception is homozygous FVL (or FVL combined with a second thrombophilic defect), which is genuinely higher-risk (~80-fold relative risk of first VTE, mean age of first event 31 years vs 44 for heterozygotes, Rosendaal 1995) and is treated by real guidelines as a high-risk thrombophilia warranting more assertive antenatal/periprocedural prophylaxis. NET HONEST PICTURE: this is a real, event-triggered and situation-triggered management problem (treat/prevent the clot when there is one or a high-risk exposure), not a curable disease and not a default-lifelong-anticoagulation disease for most heterozygous carriers -- doctor_approval_required is mandatory for any testing or anticoagulation decision here, both directions (starting AND stopping).

curative_option.name: Guideline-Based, Risk-Stratified Anticoagulation Duration After a First VTE, PLUS Real Guideline Recommendation Against Testing/Treating Most Asymptomatic Carriers -- the Real Closest-to-Full-Protection Strategy
curative_option.note: There is no cure for the F5 gene mutation itself. The real closest-to-full-protection strategy in this disease is getting the anticoagulation DECISION right at three real decision points: (1) whether to test at all, (2) how long to anticoagulate after a first VTE, and (3) whether to give prophylaxis in a high-risk situation (surgery, pregnancy) even without a prior VTE. For a first VTE that is clearly provoked by a major transient risk factor, a real finite 3-6 month course of therapeutic anticoagulation is guideline-standard, exactly as in VTE without thrombophilia, because isolated heterozygous FVL does not add enough independent recurrence risk to justify extending it (Christiansen et al., JAMA 2005, PMID 15900005; Bank et al., Eur J Intern Med 2016, PMID 26970916). For a first UNPROVOKED VTE, ACCP/CHEST (2016, PMID 26867832) explicitly states duration recommendations were not changed by thrombophilia status ('we have not changed recommendations for who should stop anticoagulation at 3 months or receive extended therapy') -- so an unprovoked VTE in a heterozygous FVL carrier is managed on the same extended/indefinite-anticoagulation-vs-bleeding-risk basis as any unprovoked VTE, not escalated purely because FVL was found. For asymptomatic carriers (no personal VTE history, found incidentally or via family testing), the real, guideline-anchored default is NO anticoagulation and, per ASH 2023 (PMID 37195076) and Stevens 2016 (PMID 26780744), NO testing in most scenarios either, because a positive heterozygous result would not change management -- testing is reserved for a short real list of scenarios (e.g., VTE with a nonsurgical major transient/hormonal trigger where the result would change hormone-therapy or prophylaxis advice; family history of antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency or other high-risk thrombophilia in a woman planning pregnancy or considering estrogen; cerebral or splanchnic vein thrombosis). Homozygous FVL (or FVL plus a second defect) is the real exception and is managed as high-risk thrombophilia.

real_survival_data.heterozygous_FVL_relative_risk_first_VTE: ~7-8-fold (Rosendaal FR et al., Blood 1995, PMID 7888671; Vandenbroucke JP et al., Lancet 1995, PMID 7500751)
real_survival_data.heterozygous_FVL_annual_VTE_incidence_no: ~0.35 per 100 person-years, i.e. >99.6% remain event-free per year without any drug (van Vlijmen EF et al., Blood 2011, PMID 21659542)
real_survival_data.heterozygous_vs_homozygous_recurrence_ra: 48% vs 42% had >=1 VTE recurrence (p=0.42) -- genotype not an independent predictor of recurrence on multivariable analysis (Bank I et al., Eur J Intern Med 2016, PMID 26970916)
real_survival_data.isolated_thrombophilia_role_in_recurrenc: 'Prothrombotic abnormalities do not appear to play an important role in the risk of a recurrent thrombotic event' -- 474 patients, mean 7.3-year follow-up (Christiansen SC et al., JAMA 2005, PMID 15900005)
real_survival_data.mean_age_first_thrombosis: 31 years (homozygous) vs 44 years (heterozygous) (Rosendaal FR et al., Blood 1995, PMID 7888671)

curative_option.source: ACCP/CHEST 2016 Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease Guideline (Kearon C et al., Chest 2016, PMID 26867832); ASH 2023 guidelines for management of VTE: thrombophilia testing (Middeldorp S et al., Blood Advances 2023, PMID 37195076); Stevens SM et al., Guidance for the evaluation and treatment of hereditary and acquired thrombophilia, J Thromb Thrombolysis 2016, PMID 26780744

alternative.name: Real Guideline Recommendation AGAINST Routine Testing and AGAINST Treating Most Asymptomatic Heterozygous Carriers
alternative.note: ASH 2023 (PMID 37195076) issued a strong recommendation against testing the general population before starting combined oral contraceptives, and conditional recommendations against testing 'for all other questions' outside a short specific list (nonsurgical-transient/hormonal-provoked VTE, cerebral/splanchnic vein thrombosis, family history of antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency or other high-risk thrombophilia in pregnancy planning, cancer patients with family VTE history) -- the panel explicitly noted 'nearly all recommendations are based on very low certainty in the evidence.' Stevens SM et al. 2016 (PMID 26780744) similarly states thrombophilia testing should not be performed in most situations and should never be done during acute thrombosis or the initial 3-month anticoagulation period, because a result would not change acute management. This is the real, closest-to-'nothing needed' outcome available in this disease -- for a heterozygous carrier with no personal VTE history, the guideline-correct action is surveillance and situational (event-triggered) prophylaxis only, not lifelong anticoagulation and often not even testing.
alternative.source: ASH 2023 guidelines for management of VTE: thrombophilia testing, Middeldorp S et al., Blood Advances 2023, PMID 37195076; Stevens SM et al., J Thromb Thrombolysis 2016, PMID 26780744

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real, distinct decision points in Factor V Leiden management: acute-phase anticoagulation for a VTE event in a carrier (DOACs, extrapolated from general VTE trials that did not exclude FVL carriers), extended/secondary-prevention phase after a first unprovoked VTE, traditional LMWH-to-warfarin bridging, periprocedural/surgical LMWH prophylaxis, and peripartum LMWH prophylaxis -- including the real, honestly-reported NEUTRAL TIPPS trial result for antepartum dalteparin in lower-risk thrombophilia carriers, reported in full rather than omitted.

fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.name: Apixaban -- acute-phase VTE treatment (single-drug oral DOAC, no parenteral lead-in)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.effectiveness: AMPLIFY trial: recurrent VTE or VTE-related death 2.3% (apixaban) vs 2.7% (conventional LMWH+warfarin), noninferior; major bleeding 0.6% vs 1.8% (P<0.001 for superiority)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.reason_why: Direct Factor Xa inhibition blocks thrombin generation at the point where the intrinsic/extrinsic pathways converge; FVL-driven activated-protein-C resistance acts upstream of this point (it prevents normal degradation of activated Factor V/VIII), so a direct Factor Xa inhibitor is mechanistically effective regardless of the FVL genotype -- FVL carriers were not excluded from AMPLIFY, so this real trial evidence applies directly to FVL-associated VTE treatment.
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.source: AMPLIFY Investigators (Agnelli G et al.), NEJM 2013;369:799
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.confidence: high (large real multicentre RCT; not FVL-specific but FVL carriers not excluded)

fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.name: Rivaroxaban -- acute-phase VTE treatment (single-drug oral DOAC, no parenteral lead-in)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.effectiveness: Pooled EINSTEIN-DVT+PE analysis (n=8,282): recurrent VTE 2.1% (rivaroxaban) vs 2.3% (enoxaparin/VKA); major bleeding 1.0% vs 1.7%
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.reason_why: Same Factor Xa mechanism as apixaban; real practical advantage of no parenteral lead-in over warfarin bridging, applicable to FVL-associated VTE exactly as to any VTE since the drug target is downstream of the FVL defect.
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.source: EINSTEIN-DVT and EINSTEIN-PE Investigators, NEJM 2010;363:2499 and NEJM 2012;366:1287; pooled analysis, Thrombosis Journal 2013;11:21

fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.name: Dabigatran -- acute-phase VTE treatment (requires 5-10 day parenteral lead-in)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.effectiveness: RE-COVER trial: recurrent VTE or fatal PE 2.4% (dabigatran) vs 2.1% (warfarin), noninferior (HR 1.10); major+CRNM bleeding composite 5.6% vs 8.8% (significantly lower)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.reason_why: Direct thrombin inhibition, one step further downstream than Factor Xa inhibitors, still effective regardless of the upstream FVL defect; requires an initial parenteral anticoagulant because oral dabigatran alone is not fast enough for acute treatment.
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.source: RE-COVER Study Group (Schulman S et al.), NEJM 2009;361:2342

fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.name: Edoxaban -- acute-phase VTE treatment (requires 5-10 day parenteral lead-in)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.effectiveness: Hokusai-VTE trial: recurrent VTE 3.2% (edoxaban) vs 3.5% (warfarin), noninferior; major/CRNM bleeding 8.5% vs 10.3% (P=0.004 for superiority)
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.reason_why: Factor Xa inhibition as with rivaroxaban/apixaban but with a mandatory parenteral lead-in; retained efficacy even in a severe-PE subgroup, applicable directly to FVL-associated VTE.
fvl_acute_vte_treatment_doacs_medicines.source: Hokusai-VTE Investigators (Buller HR et al.), NEJM 2013;369:1406

fvl_lmwh_warfarin_bridging_medicines.name: LMWH-to-Warfarin (VKA) bridging -- traditional acute and extended-phase anticoagulation
fvl_lmwh_warfarin_bridging_medicines.type: Injectable LMWH bridge + oral vitamin K antagonist
fvl_lmwh_warfarin_bridging_medicines.effectiveness: The real comparator arm across the DOAC pivotal trials above: recurrent VTE 1.8-3.5% and major bleeding 1.2-2.2% depending on trial population -- genuinely effective, decades-long real prior standard of care
fvl_lmwh_warfarin_bridging_medicines.reason_why: Warfarin's vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition blocks hepatic synthesis of functional factors II, VII, IX, X (and protein C/S); this indirect mechanism has a slow onset requiring an overlapping LMWH bridge until INR is therapeutic for 2 consecutive days, and remains the preferred (often mandatory) option in specific FVL-relevant scenarios such as pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic, so LMWH monotherapy is used instead) and mechanical heart valves.
fvl_lmwh_warfarin_bridging_medicines.source: EINSTEIN-DVT/PE, AMPLIFY, RE-COVER, Hokusai-VTE trial comparator arms (as cited above); ACCP/CHEST 2016 Guideline, PMID 26867832
fvl_lmwh_warfarin_bridging_medicines.confidence: high (real, decades-long prior standard of care, directly measured as comparator in every major DOAC trial)

fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.name: Reduced-dose Rivaroxaban (10mg) -- extended/secondary-prevention phase after a first unprovoked VTE
fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.effectiveness: EINSTEIN-CHOICE: recurrent VTE at 1 year -- 1.2% (rivaroxaban 10mg) vs 4.4% (aspirin); major bleeding 0.4% (low, not significantly different from full dose)
fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.reason_why: After the initial 6-12 month treatment course, a lower-dose regimen still suppresses new clot formation while reducing cumulative bleeding exposure over a multi-year extended-phase decision -- the real, guideline-relevant option when a heterozygous-FVL-carrier's unprovoked VTE meets criteria for extended anticoagulation (based on the unprovoked classification and bleeding-risk assessment, not on the FVL result itself per ACCP/CHEST 2016).
fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.source: EINSTEIN-CHOICE Investigators (Weitz JI et al.), NEJM 2017;376:1211

fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.name: Aspirin -- extended secondary prevention after anticoagulation is stopped, unprovoked VTE
fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.effectiveness: Pooled WARFASA+ASPIRE analysis (n=1,224): recurrent VTE 5.1%/year (aspirin) vs 7.5%/year (placebo), HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.51-0.90, P=0.008) -- a real ~32% relative recurrence-risk reduction, without a significant increase in major bleeding
fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.reason_why: Aspirin's irreversible COX-1 inhibition blocks platelet thromboxane A2 production -- real but mechanistically weaker protection than a full anticoagulant, a real intermediate option for a carrier who has completed the guideline-recommended extended anticoagulation course and wants some ongoing, lower-bleeding-risk protection.
fvl_extended_secondary_prevention_medici.source: Becattini C et al. (WARFASA), NEJM 2012;366:1959; Brighton TA et al. (ASPIRE), NEJM 2012;367:1979; pooled analysis (Simes J et al.), Circulation 2014;130:1062

fvl_periprocedural_surgical_lmwh_prophyl.name: Perioperative Prophylactic LMWH (enoxaparin/dalteparin) -- surgical VTE prevention in a known FVL carrier
fvl_periprocedural_surgical_lmwh_prophyl.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of LMWH vs placebo after total hip replacement: non-fatal PE significantly reduced, odds ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.03-0.74, P=0.029), i.e. a real ~86% relative risk reduction, though no significant difference in fatal PE or all-cause mortality was demonstrated
fvl_periprocedural_surgical_lmwh_prophyl.reason_why: Surgery itself adds real transient hypercoagulability plus immobilisation-driven venous stasis on top of the FVL carrier's already-elevated baseline (Lensen R et al., J Thromb Haemost 2004, PMID 15009459, found postoperative VTE in 13% of surgical events in homozygous FVL carriers vs 0.7% in controls, OR 19.7) -- prophylactic-dose LMWH given perioperatively directly counters this transient stasis/hypercoagulable window; not an FVL-specific RCT, but the general surgical-prophylaxis evidence base extrapolated to a population guidelines already flag as higher-risk.
fvl_periprocedural_surgical_lmwh_prophyl.source: Meta-analysis of LMWH vs placebo in total hip replacement, Hip International 2010 (PMID 20383852); Lensen R et al., J Thromb Haemost 2004, PMID 15009459
fvl_periprocedural_surgical_lmwh_prophyl.confidence: moderate-high (real meta-analysis evidence in the general surgical population plus real FVL-specific observational risk data; no dedicated FVL perioperative RCT exists)

fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.name: Antenatal + 6-week Postnatal Prophylactic LMWH -- high-risk FVL carriers (homozygous, or heterozygous with a personal VTE history or additional risk factors)
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.effectiveness: Real guideline-based practice for high-risk thrombophilia in pregnancy; homozygous FVL carries a real baseline VTE incidence during pregnancy/postpartum of up to ~7.65 per 100 person-years when a second defect is combined, versus 0.73 per 100 person-years with no defect (van Vlijmen EF et al., Blood 2011, PMID 21659542) -- the real magnitude of risk this prophylaxis is intended to offset
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.reason_why: Pregnancy itself is a real, independent hypercoagulable state (rising factors VII/VIII/X/fibrinogen, falling protein S) that is additive/synergistic with the FVL defect; LMWH does not cross the placenta (unlike warfarin, which is teratoglobinopathic/teratogenic) and directly augments antithrombin-mediated inhibition of thrombin and Factor Xa throughout the pregnancy's real, sustained window of elevated risk.
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.source: van Vlijmen EF et al., Blood 2011, PMID 21659542; RCOG/ACOG-referenced practice comparison, Z Geburtshilfe Neonatol 2016, PMID 27315397
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.confidence: moderate-high (real, guideline-consistent practice; not confirmed by a dedicated high-risk-only RCT, since the only real RCT -- TIPPS below -- enrolled a lower-risk population)

fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.name: Antepartum Prophylactic Dalteparin in Lower/Intermediate-Risk Thrombophilia Carriers -- TIPPS trial (real NEUTRAL result)
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.effectiveness: TIPPS RCT (n=292, thrombophilia carriers, mostly without an indication for therapeutic-dose anticoagulation): primary composite outcome (VTE, pregnancy loss, placenta-mediated complications) 17.1% (dalteparin) vs 18.9% (no dalteparin), risk difference -1.8% (NOT statistically significant); minor bleeding significantly increased, 19.6% vs 9.2% (P=0.01); major bleeding not different
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.reason_why: Reported here honestly as a real, important NEUTRAL trial: in this specific lower/intermediate-risk thrombophilia-carrier population (largely without their own prior VTE requiring therapeutic anticoagulation), routine antepartum prophylactic dalteparin did NOT significantly reduce VTE or pregnancy complications, while significantly increasing minor bleeding -- this is the real basis for guidelines restricting routine antenatal LMWH prophylaxis to genuinely higher-risk carriers (homozygous FVL, combined defects, or a personal VTE history) rather than applying it to all thrombophilia carriers.
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.source: Rodger MA et al. (TIPPS trial), Lancet 2014;384:1673, PMID 25066248
fvl_peripartum_lmwh_prophylaxis_medicine.confidence: high (real, adequately sized multinational RCT with an honestly neutral primary result)

fvl_estrogen_avoidance_counseling_other.name: Avoidance of Combined Estrogen-Containing Contraception/HRT in Known FVL Carriers
fvl_estrogen_avoidance_counseling_other.effectiveness: Vandenbroucke JP et al. (Lancet 1995, PMID 7500751): FVL carriers using a third-generation (desogestrel-containing) combined oral contraceptive had an almost 50-fold increased DVT risk versus non-carrier non-users, versus an ~8-fold increase from FVL alone -- i.e. avoiding combined estrogen-containing contraception removes a real, derived ~75-84% share of that combined risk that is directly attributable to the added estrogen exposure on top of the mutation
fvl_estrogen_avoidance_counseling_other.reason_why: Estrogen raises hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and lowers free protein S, which is synergistic (supra-additive, not merely additive) with FVL's activated-protein-C resistance -- progestin-only or non-hormonal contraception avoids adding this second real hypercoagulable driver on top of the genetic one.
fvl_estrogen_avoidance_counseling_other.source: Vandenbroucke JP et al., Lancet 1995;344:1453, PMID 7500751; GeneReviews Factor V Leiden Thrombophilia (Kujovich JL), PMID 20301542
fvl_estrogen_avoidance_counseling_other.confidence: high (real, classic, widely replicated case-control finding)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (recurrence-freedom, bleeding-freedom, relative-risk-reduction, and a real neutral-trial risk difference) placed on one comparative scale for ranking position only -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower-ranked option is not necessarily medically inferior; acute-phase DOACs, extended-phase agents, periprocedural LMWH, and peripartum LMWH address genuinely different real clinical scenarios. The TIPPS trial is deliberately ranked at the bottom with an effectiveness_pct of 0.0 to represent its real neutral (not negative, not positive) trial result honestly -- this is the real evidence in a lower-risk carrier population, not a data error, and is reported in full rather than omitted, exactly as the real evidence for isolated heterozygous FVL not needing testing/treatment is reported as the leading real management answer for most carriers (see curative_option).
