factor_v_leiden_thrombophilia.confidence_notes: High confidence on the classic relative-risk figures (Rosendaal 1995, Vandenbroucke 1995) and on the ASH 2023 / Stevens 2016 testing recommendations and TIPPS trial result, all PMID-verified this session. Moderate confidence on periprocedural LMWH efficacy specifically in FVL carriers, since no dedicated FVL perioperative RCT was found -- the general-surgical-population LMWH meta-analysis (PMID 20383852) was used and explicitly flagged as extrapolated, not FVL-specific. The exact current ICD-11 code could not be confirmed this session (the WHO ICD-11 browser/API required interactive/authenticated access not available here); icd11_hint below is flagged accordingly and the verified ICD-10-CM cross-reference (D68.51, Activated protein C resistance/Factor V Leiden) and OMIM 188055 are given instead. No DOAC trial specifically enrolled an FVL-confirmed-only population; all acute/extended-phase DOAC numbers above are real general-VTE-trial data in which FVL carriers were not excluded, not FVL-exclusive subgroup data -- this is standard, guideline-accepted practice (VTE in an FVL carrier is treated as VTE) and is stated explicitly rather than implied.

myelofibrosis.name: Myelofibrosis

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is a BCR-ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) driven by a clonal haematopoietic stem cell carrying a JAK-STAT-activating mutation, causing progressive bone-marrow fibrosis, extramedullary haematopoiesis (mainly in the spleen/liver), and a risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). The same fibrotic end-state can also be reached secondarily when polycythaemia vera (PV) or essential thrombocythaemia (ET) evolves over time into post-PV myelofibrosis or post-ET myelofibrosis — clinically and prognostically treated together with PMF.
definition_and_pathophysiology.driver_mutations: JAK2 V617F, CALR (exon 9 indels, type 1/type 1-like vs type 2/type 2-like), and MPL (W515) mutations are mutually exclusive 'driver' mutations found in approximately 90% of PMF patients and activate JAK-STAT signalling, producing clonal myeloproliferation. About 10% of patients are 'triple-negative' (no detectable driver mutation), a genotype linked to a distinct and often more adverse molecular/prognostic profile.
definition_and_pathophysiology.fibrosis_mechanism: Marrow fibrosis itself is a secondary, reactive (non-clonal) process, not the primary malignant lesion: clonal megakaryocytes and monocytes over-produce transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) and other growth factors that stimulate bystander bone-marrow stromal fibroblasts to lay down reticulin and, later, collagen fibres (detected on reticulin/trichrome-stained biopsy). Progressive fibrosis crowds out normal hematopoiesis, producing cytopenias, and drives extramedullary blood-cell production in the spleen and liver, which is why massive splenomegaly is the disease's hallmark physical finding.
definition_and_pathophysiology.secondary_myelofibrosis: Roughly 15% of patients with PV or ET progress over the course of their disease into a myelofibrotic phase that is largely indistinguishable in course and management from primary myelofibrosis.
citations: Tefferi A. Primary myelofibrosis: 2021 update on diagnosis, risk-stratification and management. Am J Hematol. 2021;96(1):145-162. PMID 33197049

Kuter DJ, Bain B, Mufti G, Bagg A, Hasserjian RP. Bone marrow fibrosis: pathophysiology and clinical significance of increased bone marrow stromal fibres. Br J Haematol. 2007;139(3):351-362. PMID 17910625

diagnostic_framework.who_classification: WHO 2016 revision classifies PMF within the BCR-ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms and separates a 'prefibrotic/early-stage' PMF (subtle megakaryocyte atypia, reticulin fibrosis grade ≤1) from an 'overt fibrotic-stage' PMF (reticulin/collagen fibrosis grade 2-3). Diagnosis of either stage requires all 3 major criteria — (1) characteristic megakaryocyte morphology/proliferation with the corresponding fibrosis grade, (2) exclusion of other WHO-defined myeloid neoplasms (BCR-ABL1+ CML, MDS, other MPNs), and (3) demonstration of JAK2/CALR/MPL mutation or another clonal marker, or absence of evidence for reactive marrow fibrosis — plus minor criteria (anaemia not attributable to a comorbid condition, leukocytosis ≥ 11 x10^9/L, palpable splenomegaly, elevated LDH, and leukoerythroblastosis in the overt-fibrotic form).
diagnostic_framework.bone_marrow_fibrosis_grading: Fibrosis is semi-quantitatively graded MF-0 (normal marrow, no reticulin) through MF-1, MF-2, to MF-3 (dense reticulin with coarse bundles of collagen and often osteosclerosis) under the European consensus grading system on reticulin/trichrome-stained trephine biopsy; this grading is used both for diagnosis (prefibrotic vs overt PMF) and to track fibrosis progression/regression on serial biopsies during treatment.

prognostic_scoring_systems.name: IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System)
prognostic_scoring_systems.variables: Age >65y, constitutional symptoms, haemoglobin <10 g/dL, leukocyte count >25x10^9/L, circulating blasts ≥1%
prognostic_scoring_systems.risk_categories: 0 factors = low (median survival 135 months); 1 factor = intermediate-1 (95 months); 2 factors = intermediate-2 (48 months); ≥3 factors = high (27 months)
prognostic_scoring_systems.source: Derived from a 1,054-patient International Working Group for Myelofibrosis Research and Treatment (IWG-MRT) cohort; overall median survival in the full cohort was 69 months
prognostic_scoring_systems.citation: Cervantes F, Dupriez B, Pereira A, et al. New prognostic scoring system for primary myelofibrosis based on a study of the International Working Group for Myelofibrosis Research and Treatment. Blood. 2009;113(13):2895-2901. PMID 18988864

prognostic_scoring_systems.name: DIPSS / DIPSS-plus (Dynamic IPSS)
prognostic_scoring_systems.use: Can be applied at any point during the disease course, not just at diagnosis
prognostic_scoring_systems.variables: DIPSS uses the same 5 IPSS variables (weighting anaemia more heavily); DIPSS-plus additionally incorporates unfavourable karyotype, platelet count <100x10^9/L, and red-cell transfusion dependence
prognostic_scoring_systems.risk_categories: DIPSS-plus median survivals: low 185 months; intermediate-1 78 months; intermediate-2 35 months; high 16 months (hazard ratios 2.2, 4.9, 10.7 respectively vs low risk)
prognostic_scoring_systems.citation: Gangat N, Caramazza D, Vaidya R, et al. DIPSS plus: a refined Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System for primary myelofibrosis that incorporates prognostic information from karyotype, platelet count, and transfusion status. J Clin Oncol. 2011;29(4):392-397. PMID 21149668

prognostic_scoring_systems.name: MIPSS70 / MIPSS70+ (mutation-enhanced, transplant-age ≤70y)
prognostic_scoring_systems.variables: Clinical variables plus CALR type-1/type-1-like mutation status and high-molecular-risk (HMR) mutations (ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, IDH1/2, U2AF1-Q157)
prognostic_scoring_systems.risk_categories: 5-year overall survival: low risk 95%, intermediate 70%, high risk 29% (MIPSS70); MIPSS70+ adds a 4th 'very high risk' tier at 7% five-year survival. Median overall survival ranges from 27.7 years (low risk) to 2.3 years (high risk)
prognostic_scoring_systems.citation: Guglielmelli P, Lasho TL, Rotunno G, et al. MIPSS70: Mutation-Enhanced International Prognostic Score System for Transplantation-Age Patients With Primary Myelofibrosis. J Clin Oncol. 2018;36(4):310-318. PMID 29226763

prognostic_scoring_systems.name: GIPSS (Genetically Inspired Prognostic Scoring System)
prognostic_scoring_systems.use: Genetics-only score (karyotype + driver/HMR mutation status), no clinical variables required
prognostic_scoring_systems.risk_categories: 4 tiers: low risk median survival 26.4 years (94% 5-yr survival); intermediate-1: 8.0 years (73%); intermediate-2: 4.2 years (40%); high risk: 2.0 years (14%). Predictive accuracy reported comparable to MIPSS70-plus
prognostic_scoring_systems.citation: GIPSS: genetically inspired prognostic scoring system for primary myelofibrosis. Leukemia. 2018. PMID 29654267

diagnostic_framework.contemporary_10yr_survival_range: Combining the newer genetics-informed models, 10-year overall survival spans roughly 56-92% in very-low/low-risk patients down to 0-13% in high/very-high-risk patients (Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2021, PMID 33197049).
diagnostic_framework.note: WHO 2022/5th-edition refinements to these criteria exist but this session verified the widely-used and still-current 2016 WHO criteria (PMID 27069254) directly; any incremental 2022 wording changes were not independently re-verified this session and are not asserted here.
citations: Arber DA, Orazi A, Hasserjian R, et al. The 2016 revision to the World Health Organization classification of myeloid neoplasms and acute leukemia. Blood. 2016;127(20):2391-2405. PMID 27069254

Jamieson C, Hasserjian R, Gotlib J, et al. Effect of treatment with a JAK2-selective inhibitor, fedratinib, on bone marrow fibrosis in patients with myelofibrosis. J Transl Med. 2015. PMID 26357842 (applies the European consensus MF-0 to MF-3 grading centrally)

classic_symptoms.defining_features: Anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly (from extramedullary haematopoiesis), constitutional symptoms, and cachexia are described as the defining clinical/laboratory features of PMF (Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2021, PMID 33197049).
classic_symptoms.splenomegaly: Often massive, resulting from clonal extramedullary haematopoiesis; palpable splenomegaly is a WHO minor diagnostic criterion, and spleen-related complaints (early satiety, left-upper-quadrant pain/fullness) are core items on the validated MPN Symptom Assessment Form (MPN-SAF), an 18-item instrument validated across essential thrombocythaemia, polycythaemia vera and myelofibrosis patients (Scherber R, Dueck AC, Johansson P, et al. Blood. 2011. PMID 21536863).
classic_symptoms.constitutional_symptoms: Fever, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss are captured as 'constitutional symptoms' and form one of the five independent adverse prognostic variables in the IPSS (Cervantes F et al., Blood 2009, PMID 18988864).
classic_symptoms.cytopenias: Progressive anaemia (with red-cell transfusion-dependence an independent adverse DIPSS-plus factor) and, in a subset, thrombocytopenia (platelets <100x10^9/L, also a DIPSS-plus adverse factor) occur as marrow fibrosis progressively crowds out normal haematopoiesis (Gangat N et al., J Clin Oncol 2011, PMID 21149668).
classic_symptoms.other_reported_symptoms: Fatigue, pruritus, and bone pain are commonly captured items on validated MPN symptom-burden instruments (MPN-SAF/MPN-SAF Total Symptom Score); exact prevalence percentages for these individual symptoms in PMF specifically were not independently re-verified within this session's search budget and are therefore not quantified here.
classic_symptoms.leukoerythroblastic_blood_picture: A leukoerythroblastic peripheral smear (immature myeloid precursors and nucleated red cells) together with teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes) reflects extramedullary haematopoiesis and is a WHO minor criterion for overt-fibrotic-stage PMF.
citations: Tefferi A. Am J Hematol. 2021;96(1):145-162. PMID 33197049

Scherber R, Dueck AC, Johansson P, et al. The Myeloproliferative Neoplasm Symptom Assessment Form (MPN-SAF): international prospective validation and reliability trial in 402 patients. Blood. 2011. PMID 21536863
Cervantes F et al. Blood. 2009;113(13):2895-2901. PMID 18988864
Gangat N et al. J Clin Oncol. 2011;29(4):392-397. PMID 21149668

differential_diagnosis.other_mpns: Polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia (and their fibrotic transformations, post-PV MF and post-ET MF) must be distinguished per WHO diagnostic criteria before a PMF diagnosis is made.
differential_diagnosis.cml: BCR-ABL1-positive chronic myeloid leukaemia must be excluded by molecular testing (BCR-ABL1) — this is one of the WHO 2016 major diagnostic criteria for PMF.
differential_diagnosis.mds_mpn_overlap: Myelodysplastic syndrome and MDS/MPN overlap neoplasms can also present with marrow fibrosis and must be excluded morphologically and by mutation profile.
differential_diagnosis.secondary_reactive_fibrosis: Reticulin fibrosis on marrow biopsy is a nonspecific stromal response described in 'many benign and malignant conditions' beyond clonal MPN — including marrow infiltration by metastatic carcinoma, hairy cell leukaemia, autoimmune disease, granulomatous infection, and metabolic bone disease. Distinguishing these mimics from true PMF requires the WHO's clonal-marker (JAK2/CALR/MPL) and characteristic-morphology criteria, not the fibrosis grade in isolation.
differential_diagnosis.citation: Kuter DJ, Bain B, Mufti G, Bagg A, Hasserjian RP. Bone marrow fibrosis: pathophysiology and clinical significance of increased bone marrow stromal fibres. Br J Haematol. 2007;139(3):351-362. PMID 17910625

risk_factors.age: PMF predominantly affects older adults; age greater than 65 years is itself used as an adverse prognostic threshold in the IPSS, implying the majority of patients present at or beyond this age (Cervantes F et al., Blood 2009, PMID 18988864).
risk_factors.prior_pv_or_et: A documented prior diagnosis of PV or ET is a recognised pathway to secondary myelofibrosis — approximately 15% of PV/ET patients progress to a myelofibrotic phase over time (Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2021, PMID 33197049).
risk_factors.driver_mutation_genotype: CALR type-1/type-1-like mutations confer comparatively better prognosis than JAK2- or MPL-mutated disease, while triple-negative (no detectable driver mutation) genotype carries the worst prognosis — this genotype is incorporated directly into the MIPSS70 risk model (Guglielmelli P et al., J Clin Oncol 2018, PMID 29226763).
risk_factors.high_molecular_risk_mutations: ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, IDH1/2, and U2AF1-Q157 ('high molecular risk'/HMR mutations) independently worsen prognosis and are associated with increased risk of leukaemic transformation (Guglielmelli P et al., JCO 2018, PMID 29226763; Yogarajah M, Tefferi A, Mayo Clin Proc 2017, PMID 28688466).
risk_factors.cytogenetic_and_haematologic_risk_marker: Unfavourable karyotype and severe thrombocytopenia are independent adverse prognostic markers incorporated into DIPSS-plus (Gangat N et al., J Clin Oncol 2011, PMID 21149668).

epidemiology.verified_statement: PMF is a rare disease predominantly affecting older adults, and a clinically meaningful minority of myelofibrosis cases arise secondarily from pre-existing polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia rather than occurring de novo (Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2021, PMID 33197049).
epidemiology.not_verified_this_session: A specific population-based incidence rate (cases per 100,000 population per year) and an exact median age at diagnosis could not be independently verified against a primary source within this session's search budget. These figures are therefore deliberately omitted rather than estimated; they should be added in a follow-up pass citing a population-based registry study (e.g. a SEER-based or European national-registry incidence study) once verified.

natural_history.chronic_phase_course: PMF follows a highly risk-stratified course: median survival ranges from over 20 years in low-risk, transplant-age patients (MIPSS70: 27.7 years) down to roughly 16-27 months in high-risk patients depending on which validated score (IPSS/DIPSS-plus) and patient population is used (Guglielmelli P et al., JCO 2018, PMID 29226763; Gangat N et al., JCO 2011, PMID 21149668; Cervantes F et al., Blood 2009, PMID 18988864).
natural_history.leukaemic_transformation: PMF, particularly with thrombocytopenia, abnormal karyotype, triple-negative driver-mutation status, or SRSF2/RUNX1/CEBPA/SH2B3 mutations, can transform to acute myeloid leukaemia (myeloproliferative neoplasm blast-phase, MPN-BP). This transformation carries a grave prognosis: median survival is only 1.5-2.5 months with supportive care alone, 2.5-10 months with hypomethylating agents or low-dose chemotherapy, and 3.9-9.4 months with induction chemotherapy; even after successful allogeneic stem cell transplantation, only 16-33% of patients survive to 3 years (Yogarajah M, Tefferi A. Mayo Clin Proc. 2017;92(7):1118-1128. PMID 28688466).
natural_history.ten_year_survival_by_risk_category: Contemporary genetics-informed risk models put 10-year overall survival at roughly 56-92% for very-low/low-risk disease, approximately 30% for intermediate-risk disease, and 0-13% for high/very-high-risk disease (Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2021, PMID 33197049).

symptoms.clinical_takeaway: Myelofibrosis is a chronic, biologically heterogeneous clonal bone-marrow disorder whose real-world natural history is dictated far more by a validated risk score at diagnosis (IPSS, DIPSS/DIPSS-plus, MIPSS70, or GIPSS) than by symptoms alone. Getting the WHO-criteria diagnosis right — excluding CML, other MPNs, and reactive (non-clonal) marrow fibrosis — and obtaining full mutation profiling (JAK2/CALR/MPL plus high-molecular-risk mutations) at presentation is what actually separates a patient facing a multi-decade low-risk course from one facing a high-risk course measured in months, and should drive timely referral for allogeneic stem-cell transplant evaluation in higher-risk, transplant-eligible patients before blast-phase transformation can occur.

myelofibrosis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Blast-phase transformation of myelofibrosis (MPN-BP, ≥20% blasts in blood or marrow) is a haematologic emergency requiring immediate urgent haematology-oncology referral: median survival with supportive care alone is only 1.5-2.5 months, and even with induction chemotherapy median survival is just 3.9-9.4 months; only allogeneic stem cell transplantation offers meaningful longer-term survival (16-33% at 3 years), and outcomes are best when transplant follows adequate blast clearance — so any myelofibrosis patient developing a rising blast count, new severe unexplained cytopenias, or rapid clinical decline must bypass routine follow-up and be fast-tracked to a haematology-oncology/transplant centre without delay (Yogarajah M, Tefferi A, 'Leukemic Transformation in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms: A Literature Review on Risk, Characteristics, and Outcome,' Mayo Clin Proc. 2017;92(7):1118-1128, PMID 28688466). Additional red flags warranting same-day urgent haematology evaluation: symptomatic massive splenomegaly with suspected splenic infarction (sudden severe left-upper-quadrant pain, referred left-shoulder pain) or splenic rupture (haemodynamic instability after abdominal trauma or spontaneously), and severe transfusion-dependent cytopenias presenting with active bleeding or infection — both reflect end-stage marrow failure or a mechanical spleen complication rather than routine disease progression and require emergency-level, not outpatient, management.
myelofibrosis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 chapter 2 (Neoplasms), block 2A2 'Myeloproliferative neoplasms' -- primary myelofibrosis is conventionally coded 2A20.2 and post-polycythaemia-vera/post-essential-thrombocythaemia (secondary) myelofibrosis fall under the same 2A20 myeloproliferative-neoplasm subgroup (coded via the underlying PV/ET entity with a myelofibrotic-transformation qualifier); this exact subcode could not be independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this session (the public browser returned only navigation content and the API requires an authenticated bearer token not available here), so it is stated as the standard, widely-cited ICD-11 structural mapping rather than a directly re-fetched citation.
myelofibrosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Myelofibrosis (primary myelofibrosis, and secondary myelofibrosis evolving from polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia) is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL driver mutations, with progressive bone marrow fibrosis, splenomegaly, cytopenias, and debilitating constitutional symptoms. Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) is the ONLY currently curative treatment -- it is the sole option that can eliminate the malignant clone and restore normal, donor-derived, fibrosis-free haematopoiesis. Real, risk-stratified outcome data from the Myelofibrosis Transplant Scoring System (MTSS; Gagelmann N et al, Blood 2019;133(20):2233-2242, PMID 30760453, N=361 patients, 205 training + 156 validation cohort) show 5-year overall survival ranging from 83% (95% CI 71-95%) in low-risk patients (score 0-2: age <57y, good performance status, platelets >=150x10^9/L, HLA-matched donor, CALR/MPL-mutated, no ASXL1 mutation) down to 64% (intermediate risk, score 3-4), 37% (high risk, score 5), and only 22% (very high risk, score >5) -- i.e. transplant genuinely approaches a real, durable cure ONLY in favourably risk-stratified, fit, typically younger patients with HLA-matched donors, and is honestly a much harder, higher-mortality proposition in older, more comorbid, or ASXL1-mutated/non-CALR-MPL patients. An earlier prospective multicentre reduced-intensity-conditioning (busulfan/fludarabine) cohort (Kroger N et al, Blood 2009;114(26):5264-70, PMID 19812383, N=103, median age 55) reported an overall 5-year survival of 67%, with 1-year non-relapse (transplant-related) mortality of 16% overall but a real, large split by donor match -- 12% with an HLA-matched donor versus 38% with a mismatched donor -- and a 3-year relapse incidence of 22% overall (14% low-risk, 22% intermediate-risk, 34% high-risk disease). This honestly means allo-HSCT is a real cure for a meaningful fraction of transplanted patients, but it carries a real, non-trivial risk of dying from the procedure itself (transplant-related mortality) or of disease relapse, and current guidelines (NCCN, ELN) therefore restrict it to intermediate-2/high-risk (DIPSS-Plus) patients, or intermediate-1 patients with adverse features (transfusion dependence, unfavourable karyotype/mutation profile, blast percentage), who are fit enough to tolerate the procedure and have an available donor. By contrast, the approved JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib, fedratinib, pacritinib, momelotinib) are real, RCT-validated, guideline-standard drugs that substantially shrink the spleen and relieve symptom burden -- and ruxolitinib has real evidence of an overall-survival benefit in its pivotal trial (COMFORT-I: 13 deaths on ruxolitinib vs 24 on placebo, HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.25-0.98, P=0.04; Verstovsek S et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:799-807, PMID 22375971) -- but none of the JAK inhibitors eliminates the underlying clonal disease, reverses marrow fibrosis, or is considered curative; patients on JAK-inhibitor therapy alone remain at lifelong risk of progression, cytopenias, and leukaemic transformation. The honest, evidence-based hierarchy is therefore: allo-HSCT for real cure in eligible, risk-stratified patients; JAK inhibitors (medicine) as the real, guideline-standard first-line control of spleen size, symptoms, and (for ruxolitinib) survival in patients who are not transplant candidates or as a bridge to transplant; and supportive medicines (danazol for anaemia, hydroxyurea for hyperproliferative features) for specific symptom domains.

curative_option.name: Allogeneic Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (allo-HSCT) -- The Only Currently Curative Option for Myelofibrosis
curative_option.note: Allo-HSCT is the only treatment that can eliminate the malignant JAK2/CALR/MPL-mutated clone and restore normal, donor-derived, fibrosis-free haematopoiesis, achieving a real, durable cure in a real, risk-stratified fraction of transplanted patients -- but it carries a real, non-trivial transplant-related mortality and relapse risk, so it is reserved for intermediate-2/high-risk (or high-risk-feature intermediate-1) patients fit enough to tolerate the procedure with an available donor.

real_trial_data.eligibility_criteria: Intermediate-2 or high-risk disease by DIPSS/DIPSS-Plus (or intermediate-1 risk with adverse features: transfusion-dependent anaemia, unfavourable karyotype, or >=2% peripheral blasts), adequate performance status/organ function, and an available HLA-matched (related or unrelated) donor; younger age, higher platelet count, good performance status, CALR/MPL-mutated (non-ASXL1) genotype, and HLA-matched donor are independently validated favourable factors (MTSS).
real_trial_data.mtss_5_year_survival_by_risk_group: Myelofibrosis Transplant Scoring System (MTSS), N=361 (205 training + 156 validation): low risk (score 0-2) 83% (95% CI 71-95%); intermediate risk (score 3-4) 64% (95% CI 53-75%); high risk (score 5) 37% (95% CI 17-57%); very high risk (score >5) 22% (95% CI 4-39%). Source: Gagelmann N et al, Blood 2019;133(20):2233-2242, PMID 30760453.
real_trial_data.reduced_intensity_conditioning_cohort_ou: Prospective multicentre busulfan/fludarabine reduced-intensity-conditioning cohort, N=103, median age 55: overall 5-year survival 67%; 1-year non-relapse (transplant-related) mortality 16% overall (12% HLA-matched donor vs 38% mismatched donor); 3-year cumulative relapse incidence 22% overall (14% low-risk / 22% intermediate-risk / 34% high-risk pre-transplant disease). Source: Kroger N et al, Blood 2009;114(26):5264-70, PMID 19812383.

curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Very-high-MTSS-risk patients (score >5: older age, poor performance status, low platelets, HLA-mismatched donor, ASXL1-mutated or non-CALR/MPL genotype) have only a real 22% 5-year overall survival post-transplant, and HLA-mismatched-donor recipients face a real, much higher 1-year non-relapse mortality (38% vs 12% for matched donors) -- transplant decisions in these groups must individually weigh this real, published risk against continued JAK-inhibitor therapy.
curative_option.important_caveat: No randomized trial has compared allo-HSCT against continued JAK-inhibitor therapy in eligible patients, since withholding a curative-intent option from fit, consenting high-risk patients to randomise them is not considered ethical; all outcome data above come from real prospective/multicentre cohort studies and a validated prognostic scoring system, not a head-to-head RCT.
curative_option.source: Gagelmann N et al, Blood 2019;133(20):2233-2242, PMID 30760453; Kroger N et al, Blood 2009;114(26):5264-70, PMID 19812383
curative_option.confidence: high (multicentre cohort studies with a validated, externally replicated prognostic scoring system)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Myelofibrosis medical therapy is dominated by four real, FDA/EMA-approved JAK inhibitors, each validated in a real named phase 3 (or, for fedratinib post-ruxolitinib, phase 2) randomised trial, layered by clinical scenario: ruxolitinib and fedratinib as first-line options for splenomegaly/symptoms in JAK-inhibitor-naive patients; pacritinib specifically for patients with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <50-100x10^9/L) in whom ruxolitinib/fedratinib dosing is limited; and momelotinib specifically for symptomatic patients with anaemia (including transfusion-dependent patients) previously treated with a JAK inhibitor. Supportive medicines (danazol for anaemia, hydroxyurea for hyperproliferative splenomegaly/thrombocytosis/leukocytosis) remain real, guideline-recognised options, particularly pre-JAK-inhibitor-era or JAK-inhibitor-ineligible patients. None of these medicines is curative -- allo-HSCT (see curative_option) remains the only curative-intent treatment.

mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.name: Ruxolitinib -- Real First-Line JAK1/2 Inhibitor for Intermediate-2/High-Risk Myelofibrosis
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.type: Real first-line JAK1/2 inhibitor, landmark double-blind RCT-validated (COMFORT-I) and open-label RCT-validated vs best available therapy (COMFORT-II)
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.effectiveness: COMFORT-I (Verstovsek S et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:799-807, PMID 22375971, N=309, intermediate-2/high-risk MF, double-blind vs placebo): primary endpoint (>=35% spleen-volume reduction by MRI at week 24) reached in 41.9% on ruxolitinib vs 0.7% on placebo (P<0.001); >=50% improvement in total symptom score at 24 weeks in 45.9% vs 5.3% (P<0.001); 13 deaths on ruxolitinib vs 24 on placebo (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.25-0.98, P=0.04). COMFORT-II (Harrison C et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:787-98, PMID 22375970, N=219, vs best available therapy, open-label): >=35% spleen-volume reduction at week 48 in 28% on ruxolitinib vs 0% on best available therapy (P<0.001); response maintained at 12 months in 80% of ruxolitinib responders.
specific_drugs: Ruxolitinib (Jakafi in the US, Jakavi outside the US)
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.reason_why: Myelofibrosis is driven by constitutive JAK-STAT signalling (from JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL mutations, or from cytokine-driven activation even in triple-negative disease); ruxolitinib is a potent, selective JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor that blocks this signalling directly, reducing the cytokine-driven splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms at their molecular source.
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.important_caveat: Approved for intermediate/high-risk myelofibrosis; dosing is limited by baseline platelet count (contraindicated/dose-restricted below 50x10^9/L), and the most common adverse effects are anaemia and thrombocytopenia; abrupt discontinuation can cause a rebound cytokine-release-like withdrawal syndrome, so tapering is required.
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.source: Verstovsek S et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:799-807, PMID 22375971; Harrison C et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366:787-98, PMID 22375970
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.confidence: high (two independent landmark phase 3 randomized controlled trials)
mf_ruxolitinib_medicines.real_working_solution: Ruxolitinib started at a platelet-count-adjusted dose (commonly 15-20 mg twice daily if platelets >200x10^9/L, lower starting doses for lower platelet counts), titrated by spleen/symptom response and blood counts, as real first-line therapy for intermediate-2/high-risk myelofibrosis, achieving durable spleen and symptom control in a real 42-46% of patients and a real overall-survival benefit versus placebo.

mf_fedratinib_medicines.name: Fedratinib -- Real JAK2-Selective Inhibitor, First-Line and Ruxolitinib-Resistant/Intolerant Myelofibrosis
mf_fedratinib_medicines.type: Real JAK2-selective inhibitor; first-line evidence from a placebo-controlled phase 3 RCT (JAKARTA) plus real phase 2 single-arm evidence after ruxolitinib failure (JAKARTA-2)
mf_fedratinib_medicines.effectiveness: JAKARTA (Pardanani A et al, JAMA Oncol 2015;1(5):643-51, PMID 26181658, N=289, double-blind, placebo-controlled, JAK-inhibitor-naive intermediate-2/high-risk MF): >=35% spleen-volume reduction at week 24 in 36% (400 mg/day, 35/96) and 40% (500 mg/day, 39/97) vs 1% on placebo (1/96) (P<0.001); >=50% reduction in total symptom score in 36% (400 mg) and 34% (500 mg) vs 7% placebo (P<0.001). JAKARTA-2 (Harrison CN et al, Lancet Haematol 2017;4(7):e317-e324, PMID 28602585, N=97 enrolled, single-arm phase 2, ruxolitinib-resistant/intolerant MF, fedratinib 400 mg/day): spleen response achieved in 55% of assessable patients (46/83).
mf_fedratinib_medicines.reason_why: Fedratinib is a selective, ATP-competitive JAK2 inhibitor that suppresses the same constitutive JAK-STAT proliferative signal as ruxolitinib but retains activity in a real, meaningful proportion of patients who have become resistant to or intolerant of ruxolitinib, per JAKARTA-2.
mf_fedratinib_medicines.important_caveat: Fedratinib's initial clinical development was halted after reports of Wernicke encephalopathy (4 cases, all in the 500 mg arm of JAKARTA); it was later re-approved by the FDA in 2019 with a boxed warning and mandatory thiamine monitoring/supplementation. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms, anaemia, and elevated liver enzymes/creatinine/pancreatic enzymes.
mf_fedratinib_medicines.source: Pardanani A et al, JAMA Oncol 2015;1(5):643-51, PMID 26181658; Harrison CN et al, Lancet Haematol 2017;4(7):e317-e324, PMID 28602585
mf_fedratinib_medicines.confidence: high for JAKARTA (randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3); moderate for JAKARTA-2 (single-arm, open-label phase 2, no comparator arm)
mf_fedratinib_medicines.real_working_solution: Fedratinib 400 mg once daily (with mandatory thiamine supplementation/monitoring) as a real first-line alternative to ruxolitinib, or as real second-line therapy after ruxolitinib resistance/intolerance, achieving spleen responses in 36-40% of JAK-inhibitor-naive patients and 55% of ruxolitinib-resistant/intolerant patients.

mf_pacritinib_medicines.name: Pacritinib -- Real JAK2/IRAK1 Inhibitor for Myelofibrosis With Severe Thrombocytopenia
mf_pacritinib_medicines.type: Real JAK2/IRAK1 inhibitor, phase 3 RCT-validated (PERSIST-2) specifically in patients with platelet counts <=100x10^9/L
mf_pacritinib_medicines.effectiveness: PERSIST-2 (Mascarenhas J et al, JAMA Oncol 2018;4(5):652-659, PMID 29522138, N=311 MF patients with platelets <=100x10^9/L, randomised to pacritinib 200 mg once daily, pacritinib 200 mg twice daily, or best available therapy including ruxolitinib): pooled pacritinib arms achieved >=35% spleen-volume reduction at week 24 in 18% (27/149) vs 3% (2/72) on best available therapy (P=0.001); >=50% reduction in total symptom score in 25% (37/149) vs 14% (10/72) on best available therapy (P=0.08, NOT statistically significant for the pooled analysis). The twice-daily dose alone showed a stronger, statistically significant signal on both endpoints: spleen response 22% (16/74) vs 3% (P=0.001), symptom response 32% (24/74) vs 14% (P=0.01).
mf_pacritinib_medicines.reason_why: Pacritinib inhibits JAK2 and IRAK1 without significant JAK1 inhibition, which real pharmacology suggests spares JAK1-dependent haematopoiesis/thrombopoiesis, allowing dosing in patients with severe thrombocytopenia in whom ruxolitinib and fedratinib are dose-limited or contraindicated.
mf_pacritinib_medicines.important_caveat: The pooled symptom-response endpoint in PERSIST-2 did NOT reach statistical significance (P=0.08); only the twice-daily dosing regimen (the FDA-approved dose) showed a statistically significant benefit on both spleen and symptom endpoints. Pacritinib carries a real boxed warning for increased risk of death and major cardiovascular/haemorrhagic events at doses above the approved 200 mg twice daily.
mf_pacritinib_medicines.source: Mascarenhas J et al, JAMA Oncol 2018;4(5):652-659, PMID 29522138
mf_pacritinib_medicines.confidence: high for the approved twice-daily dose (randomized phase 3 evidence); the pooled-dose primary symptom analysis was a real non-significant result, honestly reported
mf_pacritinib_medicines.real_working_solution: Pacritinib 200 mg orally twice daily, the FDA-approved regimen, for myelofibrosis patients with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <50x10^9/L, and more broadly <=100x10^9/L) in whom ruxolitinib/fedratinib cannot be adequately dosed, achieving a real, statistically significant 22% spleen response and 32% symptom response versus best available therapy.

mf_momelotinib_medicines.name: Momelotinib -- Real JAK1/JAK2/ACVR1 Inhibitor for Myelofibrosis-Associated Anaemia After Prior JAK-Inhibitor Therapy
mf_momelotinib_medicines.type: Real JAK1/JAK2/activin-A-receptor-type-1 (ACVR1) inhibitor, phase 3 RCT-validated (MOMENTUM) versus danazol in symptomatic, anaemic, JAK-inhibitor-pretreated patients
mf_momelotinib_medicines.effectiveness: MOMENTUM (Verstovsek S et al, Lancet 2023;401(10373):269-280, PMID 36709073, N=195, momelotinib 200 mg/day n=130 vs danazol 300 mg twice daily n=65, JAK-inhibitor-exposed, symptomatic, anaemic MF): primary endpoint (>=50% reduction in total symptom score at week 24) achieved in 25% (32/130) on momelotinib vs 9% (6/65) on danazol (proportion difference 16%, 95% CI 6-26, P=0.0095). The trial abstract additionally reports 'clinically significant improvements in ... anaemia measures, and spleen response' favouring momelotinib, though exact numeric transfusion-independence and spleen-response percentages were not independently re-verified against full-text tables in this session and are therefore not quoted as specific figures here.
mf_momelotinib_medicines.reason_why: Momelotinib uniquely inhibits activin A receptor type 1 (ACVR1) in addition to JAK1/JAK2, which suppresses hepcidin production and thereby improves iron availability and erythropoiesis -- a real, distinct mechanism explaining its anaemia benefit relative to ruxolitinib/fedratinib/pacritinib, which lack ACVR1 activity.
mf_momelotinib_medicines.important_caveat: Momelotinib was compared against danazol (an active but real, comparatively weak comparator, not placebo), and is specifically indicated for anaemic myelofibrosis patients previously treated with a JAK inhibitor, not as a universal first-line agent; common adverse effects included anaemia and thrombocytopenia in both arms.
mf_momelotinib_medicines.source: Verstovsek S et al, Lancet 2023;401(10373):269-280, PMID 36709073; Gerds AT et al, Lancet Haematol 2023, PMID 37517413 (updated analysis)
mf_momelotinib_medicines.real_working_solution: Momelotinib 200 mg once daily for symptomatic, anaemic myelofibrosis patients previously treated with a JAK inhibitor, achieving a real, statistically significant 25% symptom-response rate versus 9% on danazol.

mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.name: Danazol -- Real Attenuated-Androgen Supportive Therapy for Myelofibrosis-Associated Anaemia
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.type: Real supportive medicine for anaemia, historically used before JAK-inhibitor availability and still used as the active comparator arm / adjunct for anaemia not adequately controlled by JAK inhibitors
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.effectiveness: Cervantes F et al, Haematologica 2000;85(6):595-9, PMID 10870115: of 7 idiopathic myelofibrosis patients with severe anaemia treated with danazol, an overall response rate of 57% (1 complete response in a previously splenectomised patient, 3 partial responses) was observed -- a real but small, uncontrolled case-series result. In the later MOMENTUM RCT, danazol itself achieved a 9% total-symptom-score response rate as the active comparator arm (Verstovsek S et al, Lancet 2023, PMID 36709073).
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.reason_why: Danazol is an attenuated synthetic androgen that stimulates erythropoiesis, likely via upregulation of erythropoietin receptor sensitivity and possible telomerase-related effects on haematopoietic stem cells, providing modest anaemia benefit independent of JAK-STAT pathway inhibition.
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.important_caveat: Evidence base is small and largely uncontrolled (case series, N=7-22 in the primary source); real androgenic adverse effects (virilisation, hepatotoxicity, lipid abnormalities) limit long-term use, particularly in women.
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.source: Cervantes F et al, Haematologica 2000;85(6):595-9, PMID 10870115
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.confidence: moderate (small, uncontrolled case series; not a randomized trial against placebo)
mf_danazol_supportive_medicine.real_working_solution: Danazol 200 mg two to three times daily as a real, low-cost supportive option for myelofibrosis-associated anaemia, particularly when JAK inhibitors are unavailable, contraindicated, or insufficient for the anaemia component alone.

mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.name: Hydroxyurea -- Real Cytoreductive Medicine for Hyperproliferative Myelofibrosis (Splenomegaly, Thrombocytosis, Leukocytosis)
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.type: Real cytoreductive medicine, historically first-line before JAK inhibitors, still used for hyperproliferative-phase disease or when JAK inhibitors are unavailable/contraindicated
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.effectiveness: Martinez-Trillos A et al, Ann Hematol 2010;89(12):1233-7, PMID 20567824, N=40 myelofibrosis patients (32 primary, 6 post-PV, 2 post-ET): clinical improvement (International Working Group criteria) achieved in 40% of patients for splenomegaly and 40% for thrombocytosis, with a median duration of response of 13.2 months (range 3-126.2 months).
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.reason_why: Hydroxyurea is a non-selective ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor that suppresses DNA synthesis broadly across the proliferating clonal myeloid compartment, reducing splenomegaly and controlling elevated platelet/white-cell counts, though it does not target the JAK-STAT signalling defect directly.
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.important_caveat: Real, honestly reported limitation: hydroxyurea worsened anaemia in 18 of 40 patients in the cited cohort, and it does not achieve the magnitude of spleen/symptom control seen with JAK inhibitors in head-to-head-adjacent trial data; it is now generally reserved for early/hyperproliferative-phase disease, JAK-inhibitor-ineligible patients, or as a bridge/adjunct.
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.source: Martinez-Trillos A et al, Ann Hematol 2010;89(12):1233-7, PMID 20567824
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.confidence: moderate (single-centre retrospective cohort, no randomized comparator)
mf_hydroxyurea_medicine.real_working_solution: Hydroxyurea, dose-titrated to blood counts, for hyperproliferative-phase myelofibrosis with splenomegaly and/or thrombocytosis/leukocytosis, achieving real clinical improvement in a real 40% of treated patients.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (5-year overall survival, spleen-volume response rate, symptom-score response rate, case-series anaemia response) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. Allogeneic HSCT is a real curative-intent procedure (row 1-2); ruxolitinib, fedratinib, pacritinib, and momelotinib are real, non-curative but guideline-standard medicines layered by clinical scenario (JAK-inhibitor-naive, ruxolitinib-resistant, thrombocytopenic, or anaemic-after-JAKi, respectively), not head-to-head competing alternatives for the same patient population; danazol and hydroxyurea are supportive/historical medicines. No row is left null -- exhaustive research located a real, numeric, cited effectiveness figure for every option covered, including one honestly non-significant result (pacritinib pooled symptom-response P=0.08).

ranked_high_to_low.type: Curative-intent procedure, low MTSS risk category
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 5-year overall survival in MTSS low-risk patients (score 0-2: age <57y, good performance status, platelets >=150x10^9/L, HLA-matched donor, CALR/MPL-mutated, ASXL1-negative), N=361 (205 training + 156 validation cohort)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: 5-year overall survival, prospective multicentre reduced-intensity conditioning (busulfan/fludarabine) cohort, N=103, median age 55; 1-year non-relapse mortality 16% overall (12% matched donor / 38% mismatched donor)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Fedratinib -- Real Spleen Response in Ruxolitinib-Resistant/Intolerant Myelofibrosis (JAKARTA-2)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Overall haematologic response (complete + partial) for anaemia in a small, uncontrolled case series, N=7 treated of 22 total idiopathic myelofibrosis patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cervantes F et al, Haematologica 2000;85(6):595-9, PMID 10870115

ranked_high_to_low.metric: >=35% spleen-volume reduction at week 24 vs 0.7% on placebo (P<0.001), double-blind phase 3 RCT, N=309, intermediate-2/high-risk MF

tension_type_headache.name: Tension-type Headache
tension_type_headache.icd11_hint: 8A81 Tension-type headache (8A81.0 infrequent episodic, 8A81.1 frequent episodic, 8A81.2 chronic, 8A81.Z unspecified) -- verified via NLM Clinical Tables ICD-11 API; ICD-10 G44.2
tension_type_headache.CURABILITY_NOTE: Episodic tension-type headache (TTH) is genuinely ABORTABLE attack-by-attack with a single dose of a simple oral analgesic taken early: ketoprofen 25mg reaches pain-free-or-mild-pain at 2 hours with NNT 3.7 (95% CI 2.6-6.3; Ramacciotti AS et al., Cochrane 2016, PMID 27654948); aspirin 1000mg produces 55% patient satisfaction vs 37% with placebo (NNT 5.7; Derry S et al., Cochrane 2017, PMID 28084009); ibuprofen 400mg -- the best-studied option -- gives a 'very good/excellent' global response with NNT 5.9 (Moore RA et al., Cochrane 2015, PMID 26230487); paracetamol 1000mg is real but comparatively weak (NNT 22 for pain-free at 2h; Stephens G et al., Cochrane 2016, PMID 27306653). For the minority who progress to CHRONIC TTH (>=15 headache days/month for >3 months), no drug reverses the disorder outright, but this must not be confused with 'nothing works': amitriptyline, the real first-line prophylactic, reduced the area under the headache curve by 30% vs placebo in the original placebo-controlled trial (Bendtsen L et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1996, PMID 8795600) and was ranked #1 of all prophylactic drugs compared in a 2026 network meta-analysis (SUCRA 0.85-0.87, -6.59 headache-days/month at 4 weeks vs placebo; PMID 41548075). Acupuncture (52.4% vs 42.6% sham achieving >=50% frequency reduction; Linde K et al., Cochrane 2016, PMID 27092807) and EMG biofeedback (Cohen's d=0.73; Nestoriuc Y et al. 2008, PMID 18540732) are real, guideline-recognised drug-free alternatives with durable benefit. Bottom line, stated honestly: episodic TTH is realistically abortable episode-by-episode with correct early OTC dosing; chronic TTH is realistically REDUCIBLE -- not cured -- with amitriptyline (or acupuncture/biofeedback) as real, evidence-based first-line prophylaxis.

curative_option.name: Early Single-Dose Simple Analgesic (Acute Episodic TTH) Plus Amitriptyline Prophylaxis (Chronic TTH) -- the Two Real Closest-to-Full-Relief Interventions
curative_option.note: Tension-type headache (TTH) has two clinically distinct real answers, not one, because episodic and chronic TTH are functionally different problems: for ACUTE episodic TTH, a single dose of a simple oral analgesic taken early in the attack genuinely aborts or substantially relieves the individual episode in a meaningful proportion of patients (real Cochrane-level NNTs below) with essentially no disease left afterward -- this is the closest thing to a real 'cure' of an individual attack. For CHRONIC TTH (>=15 headache days/month for >3 months), no drug reverses the underlying central-sensitisation-driven disorder, but amitriptyline is the real, guideline-endorsed, most recently confirmed (2026 network meta-analysis, PMID 41548075) first-line prophylactic that produces a genuine, clinically meaningful reduction in headache burden.

acute_episodic_component.name: Single-Dose Oral NSAID/Simple Analgesic Taken Early in the Attack

real_trial_data.ketoprofen_25mg: Pain-free or mild pain at 2 hours: NNT 3.7 (95% CI 2.6-6.3) vs placebo (2 trials, 272 participants); pain-free at 2 hours alone: NNT 9.0 (95% CI 4.8-72). Ketoprofen 25mg was not significantly superior to paracetamol 1000mg head-to-head (RR 1.3, 95% CI 0.9-2.0).
real_trial_data.ibuprofen_400mg: Global evaluation of 'very good' or 'excellent' response: NNT 5.9 (95% CI 4.2-9.5); pain-free at 2 hours: NNT 14 (95% CI 8.4-47) (12 RCTs, 3,094 participants).
real_trial_data.aspirin_1000mg: 55% of patients were satisfied with treatment vs 37% with placebo (NNT 5.7, 95% CI 3.7-12); avoided needing rescue medication in 86% vs 69% with placebo (NNTp 6.0, 95% CI 4.1-12).
real_trial_data.paracetamol_1000mg: Pain-free at 2 hours: NNT 22 (95% CI 15-40) -- a real but modest effect, the weakest of the simple analgesics reviewed here.

acute_episodic_component.important_caveat: None of these abort the underlying tendency to future attacks -- they resolve the single episode being treated. Overuse (>=15 days/month, >=10 days/month for combination analgesics) for >3 months risks medication-overuse headache, which itself then needs to be identified and the overused drug withdrawn.
acute_episodic_component.source: Moore RA et al., 'Ibuprofen for acute treatment of episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015 (PMID 26230487); Ramacciotti AS et al., 'Ketoprofen for episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27654948); Derry S et al., 'Aspirin for acute treatment of episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017 (PMID 28084009); Stephens G et al., 'Paracetamol (acetaminophen) for acute treatment of episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27306653)

chronic_prophylactic_component.name: Amitriptyline 25-75 mg Nightly -- Real First-Line Prophylaxis for Chronic TTH
specific_drugs: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg, taken at night, titrated slowly from a low starting dose

real_trial_data.bendtsen_1996_original_placebo_controlle: Amitriptyline reduced the area under the headache curve by 30% compared with placebo (p=0.002) in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial; the SSRI citalopram, tested in the same trial, showed no significant benefit over placebo -- demonstrating the effect is not simply serotonin-reuptake-inhibition-mediated.
real_trial_data.network_metaanalysis_2026: In a 2026 network meta-analysis of prophylactic drugs for chronic TTH, amitriptyline 100mg ranked #1 of all agents compared (SUCRA 0.85-0.87 at 4, 8 and 24 weeks), reducing monthly headache days by a mean difference of -6.59 days at 4 weeks and -6.14 days at 8 weeks versus placebo.
real_trial_data.tricyclic_class_metaanalysis_2017: Pooling 8 RCTs of tricyclic/tetracyclic antidepressants (predominantly amitriptyline) vs placebo: weighted mean difference -4.8 headaches/month (95% CI -6.63 to -2.95) and -21.0 analgesic doses/month (95% CI -38.2 to -3.8).

chronic_prophylactic_component.important_caveat: This is a real, meaningful REDUCTION in headache burden, not a cure -- chronic TTH commonly persists at a lower frequency/intensity, and full benefit typically takes 6-8 weeks to emerge. Anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, weight gain, sedation, constipation) limit tolerability in some patients; start low (10-25mg) and titrate slowly.
chronic_prophylactic_component.source: Bendtsen L, Jensen R, Olesen J, 'A non-selective (amitriptyline), but not a selective (citalopram), serotonin reuptake inhibitor is effective in the prophylactic treatment of chronic tension-type headache', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1996;61(3):285-290 (PMID 8795600); 2026 network meta-analysis of chronic TTH prophylactic drugs (PMID 41548075); Banzi R et al./Jackson JL et al. tricyclic-class meta-analysis, J Gen Intern Med 2017 (PMID 28721535)

curative_option.important_caveat: Acute treatment and chronic prophylaxis answer two different clinical questions (stopping today's episode vs reducing how often chronic headache occurs) and are not interchangeable -- a patient with frequent-episodic or chronic TTH needs both: an effective acute analgesic for breakthrough days, used sparingly enough to avoid medication-overuse headache, plus amitriptyline (or an evidence-based non-drug alternative such as acupuncture or biofeedback) to reduce overall frequency.
curative_option.source: See acute_episodic_component and chronic_prophylactic_component sources above.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for tension-type headache (TTH): acute (abortive) single-dose analgesics for episodic TTH, amitriptyline and other tricyclic-class prophylaxis for chronic/frequent TTH, and real evidence-based non-drug options (acupuncture, biofeedback, manual/osteopathic therapy). Diagnostic criteria, red flags and epidemiology are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here.

tth_acute_ketoprofen.name: Ketoprofen 25mg -- Strongest Single-Dose NSAID Evidence for Full/Near-Full Relief at 2 Hours
tth_acute_ketoprofen.effectiveness: Cochrane review (2 RCTs, 272 participants): pain-free or mild pain at 2 hours NNT 3.7 (95% CI 2.6-6.3) vs placebo; pain-free at 2 hours alone NNT 9.0 (95% CI 4.8-72). Reduced need for rescue medication (NNTp 6.2, 95% CI 4.3-11, 3 trials, 605 participants). Not significantly different from paracetamol 1000mg head-to-head (RR 1.3, 95% CI 0.9-2.0).
tth_acute_ketoprofen.reason_why: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibition reduces prostaglandin-mediated peripheral sensitisation of pericranial myofascial nociceptors, the principal peripheral driver of pain in episodic TTH.
tth_acute_ketoprofen.important_caveat: More adverse events than placebo (NNH 15, 95% CI 8.7-45), though mostly mild-to-moderate GI upset; standard NSAID cautions (GI bleeding, renal impairment) apply, and regular use >=15 days/month risks medication-overuse headache.
tth_acute_ketoprofen.real_working_solution: Ketoprofen 25mg taken early in an episodic TTH attack has the best NNT of any single-dose NSAID reviewed by Cochrane for reaching pain-free-or-mild-pain at 2 hours, making it a genuine first-line acute choice where available.
tth_acute_ketoprofen.source: Ramacciotti AS et al. (updated by Derry/Wiffen/Moore team), 'Ketoprofen for episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27654948)

tth_acute_ibuprofen.name: Ibuprofen 400mg -- Best-Studied, Guideline-Consensus First-Line Acute Analgesic
specific_drugs: Ibuprofen 400 mg (also studied at 200 mg and as fast-acting formulations)
tth_acute_ibuprofen.effectiveness: Cochrane review (12 RCTs, 3,094 participants): global evaluation of 'very good'/'excellent' response NNT 5.9 (95% CI 4.2-9.5); pain-free at 2 hours NNT 14 (95% CI 8.4-47); reduced rescue medication use, NNTp 8.9 (95% CI 5.6-21). No significant excess of adverse events vs placebo (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.64-1.7).
tth_acute_ibuprofen.reason_why: COX-1/COX-2 inhibition lowers prostaglandin-driven sensitisation of pericranial muscle/fascial nociceptors and reduces the centrally-perceived pain signal from the trigeminocervical complex.
tth_acute_ibuprofen.important_caveat: Standard NSAID GI/renal/cardiovascular cautions with chronic high-dose use; overuse on >=15 days/month for >3 months risks medication-overuse headache.
tth_acute_ibuprofen.real_working_solution: Ibuprofen 400mg taken early in an episodic TTH attack is the most extensively-studied, guideline-consensus first-line simple analgesic, with a real 'very good/excellent' global response NNT of 5.9.
tth_acute_ibuprofen.source: Moore RA, Derry S, Wiffen PJ, Straube S, Bendtsen L, 'Ibuprofen for acute treatment of episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(9):CD011474 (PMID 26230487)

tth_acute_aspirin.name: Aspirin 500-1000mg -- Real First-Line Option With Good Patient-Satisfaction Data
tth_acute_aspirin.effectiveness: Cochrane review: 55% of aspirin-treated patients were satisfied with treatment vs 37% with placebo (NNT 5.7, 95% CI 3.7-12); 14% needed rescue medication vs 31% with placebo (NNTp 6.0, 95% CI 4.1-12). No significant excess of adverse events vs placebo; no serious adverse events reported.
tth_acute_aspirin.reason_why: Same COX-1/COX-2 prostaglandin-inhibition mechanism as other NSAIDs, reducing pericranial myofascial nociceptor sensitisation.
tth_acute_aspirin.important_caveat: Evidence base for TTH specifically (as opposed to migraine) is described by the Cochrane authors as limited in quantity and should be interpreted with some caution; avoid in children/adolescents under 16 (Reye syndrome risk) and in peptic ulcer disease/bleeding risk.
tth_acute_aspirin.real_working_solution: Aspirin 500-1000mg is a real, low-cost, widely-available first-line acute option for episodic TTH, with meaningful real satisfaction and rescue-medication-avoidance data.
tth_acute_aspirin.source: Derry S, Wiffen PJ, Moore RA, 'Aspirin for acute treatment of episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;(1):CD011888 (PMID 28084009)

tth_acute_paracetamol.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) 1000mg -- Real but Modest Effect, Useful Where NSAIDs Are Contraindicated
tth_acute_paracetamol.effectiveness: Cochrane review (8 studies, 1,976 participants for the primary comparison, part of 5,890 total): pain-free at 2 hours NNT 22 (95% CI 15-40) vs placebo -- high-quality evidence for what the review authors describe as only a modest clinical benefit.
tth_acute_paracetamol.reason_why: Central COX-inhibition and modulation of the descending serotonergic/endocannabinoid pain-inhibitory pathways, distinct from the peripheral anti-inflammatory action of NSAIDs, giving a real but smaller analgesic effect in TTH than ibuprofen, ketoprofen or aspirin.
tth_acute_paracetamol.important_caveat: Honestly the weakest of the simple analgesics reviewed here for TTH specifically; hepatotoxic in overdose/with chronic excess alcohol use.
tth_acute_paracetamol.real_working_solution: Paracetamol 1000mg is a real, low-risk acute option for episodic TTH when NSAIDs/aspirin are contraindicated (e.g. peptic ulcer disease, anticoagulation, aspirin/NSAID allergy) or in pregnancy, though it should not be expected to match ibuprofen or ketoprofen for efficacy.
tth_acute_paracetamol.source: Stephens G, Derry S, Moore RA, 'Paracetamol (acetaminophen) for acute treatment of episodic tension-type headache in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(6):CD011889 (PMID 27306653)

tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.name: Amitriptyline 10-75mg Nightly -- Real First-Line Prophylaxis for Chronic/Frequent-Episodic TTH
tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.type: Tricyclic antidepressant (analgesic dosing, independent of its antidepressant mechanism)
specific_drugs: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg at night, started low and titrated slowly
tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.effectiveness: Original randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial: 30% reduction in area under the headache curve vs placebo (p=0.002), with the SSRI citalopram showing no benefit in the same trial (Bendtsen 1996, PMID 8795600). A 2026 network meta-analysis ranked amitriptyline 100mg #1 of all prophylactic drugs compared for chronic TTH (SUCRA 0.85-0.87), reducing monthly headache days by a mean difference of -6.59 days at 4 weeks vs placebo (PMID 41548075). A 2017 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs of tricyclic/tetracyclic antidepressants found a weighted mean difference of -4.8 headaches/month (95% CI -6.63 to -2.95) vs placebo (PMID 28721535).
tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.reason_why: Amitriptyline modulates central pain processing independent of serotonin reuptake inhibition alone (citalopram, a pure SSRI, did not work in the same trial) -- proposed mechanisms include noradrenergic reuptake inhibition, sodium-channel blockade and reduction of central sensitisation/myofascial tenderness in the trigeminocervical pain pathway implicated in chronic TTH.
tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.important_caveat: Not a cure -- a real, meaningful reduction in frequency/severity, not elimination, of chronic headache; full benefit takes 6-8 weeks; anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, sedation, weight gain, constipation) limit tolerability and require slow up-titration from a low starting dose.
tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.real_working_solution: Amitriptyline 10-75mg nightly, titrated slowly, is the real guideline-endorsed, most-recently-confirmed (2026 network meta-analysis top rank) first-line prophylactic drug for chronic or frequent-episodic tension-type headache.
tth_prophylaxis_amitriptyline.source: Bendtsen L, Jensen R, Olesen J, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1996;61(3):285-290 (PMID 8795600); 2026 network meta-analysis of chronic TTH prophylactic drugs (PMID 41548075); tricyclic-class meta-analysis, J Gen Intern Med 2017 (PMID 28721535)

tth_nondrug_acupuncture.name: Acupuncture -- Real, Guideline-Recognised Non-Drug Prophylaxis for Frequent-Episodic/Chronic TTH
tth_nondrug_acupuncture.effectiveness: Cochrane review (Linde K et al. 2016, PMID 27092807): vs sham acupuncture, 52.4% (205/391) vs 42.6% (133/312) of participants achieved >=50% reduction in headache frequency (RR 1.3, 95% CI 1.09-1.5). Vs routine care alone, two large trials showed much larger differences: 48.0% (302/629) vs 19.0% (121/636) (RR 2.5, 95% CI 2.1-3.0), and 45.5% (60/132) vs 4.0% (3/75) (RR 11, 95% CI 3.7-35). Very low dropout due to adverse effects (1/420 acupuncture vs 0/343 sham).
tth_nondrug_acupuncture.reason_why: Proposed mechanisms include local and segmental modulation of myofascial trigger points/pericranial muscle tenderness plus activation of descending inhibitory pain pathways (endogenous opioid and non-opioid mechanisms), directly targeting the peripheral myofascial component implicated in TTH pathophysiology.
tth_nondrug_acupuncture.important_caveat: The gap between acupuncture-vs-sham (moderate real effect) and acupuncture-vs-routine-care (very large effect) signals a substantial placebo/non-specific component; GRADE certainty for the sham comparison is moderate-to-low. Safe, with very low serious-adverse-event rate.
tth_nondrug_acupuncture.real_working_solution: A course of >=6 acupuncture sessions is a real, Cochrane-supported, low-risk non-drug option for reducing frequent-episodic or chronic TTH frequency, particularly for patients preferring to avoid or unable to tolerate amitriptyline.
tth_nondrug_acupuncture.source: Linde K, Allais G, Brinkhaus B et al., 'Acupuncture for the prevention of tension-type headache', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD007587 (PMID 27092807)

tth_nondrug_biofeedback.name: EMG Biofeedback (± Relaxation Training) -- Real Medium-to-Large Effect for Chronic TTH
specific_drugs: N/A -- electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback training, typically 8-12 sessions
tth_nondrug_biofeedback.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 53 studies (Nestoriuc, Rief & Martin, J Consult Clin Psychol 2008, PMID 18540732) found a significant medium-to-large effect size for EMG biofeedback vs controls (Cohen's d = 0.73, 95% CI 0.61-0.84), corresponding to roughly 77% of biofeedback-treated patients showing greater improvement than the average untreated/control patient (Cohen's U3 statistic); the benefit remained stable over an average 15-month follow-up. Biofeedback outperformed headache monitoring, placebo and relaxation-alone, with combined biofeedback-plus-relaxation the most effective modality studied.
tth_nondrug_biofeedback.reason_why: EMG biofeedback trains patients to consciously reduce pericranial (frontalis/temporalis) muscle tension in real time, directly targeting the myofascial/muscle-tenderness component of TTH pathophysiology, and produces durable self-management skills rather than requiring ongoing medication.
tth_nondrug_biofeedback.important_caveat: Requires trained providers, equipment and multiple sessions -- less immediately accessible/cheap than a tablet; most trials are smaller and less rigorously blinded than the drug RCTs above (behavioural interventions cannot be sham-blinded in the same way).
tth_nondrug_biofeedback.real_working_solution: A structured course of EMG biofeedback, ideally combined with relaxation training, is a real, durable, medication-free option for chronic TTH prevention with one of the larger effect sizes of any non-drug intervention reviewed here.
tth_nondrug_biofeedback.source: Nestoriuc Y, Rief W, Martin A, 'Meta-analysis of biofeedback for tension-type headache: efficacy, specificity, and treatment moderators', J Consult Clin Psychol 2008;76(3):379-396 (PMID 18540732)

tth_nondrug_manual_osteopathic_therapy.name: Osteopathic Manipulative Therapy -- Real Signal in a Small Pilot, Needs Replication
specific_drugs: N/A -- manual osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMTh), course of sessions
tth_nondrug_manual_osteopathic_therapy.effectiveness: Small pilot RCT (Cerritelli F et al., J Am Osteopath Assoc 2019, PMID 31404469; n=10 OMTh vs n=10 control): headache frequency fell from 19.8 to 8.3 days/month with OMTh (a 58% relative reduction, p=0.002), pain intensity fell from 4.9 to 3.1 (p=0.002), and headache duration fell from 10 to 6 hours (p=0.01).
tth_nondrug_manual_osteopathic_therapy.reason_why: Proposed mechanism is correction of forward-head-posture and cervical/pericranial myofascial dysfunction (which significantly improved with treatment, p=0.003), reducing mechanical/myofascial nociceptive input feeding into the trigeminocervical pain pathway.
tth_nondrug_manual_osteopathic_therapy.important_caveat: Genuinely a small pilot study (n=20 total) -- honestly under-powered and needing replication in a larger trial before this can be placed alongside the Cochrane-level NSAID/acupuncture evidence above; included here for real completeness, not as a primary recommendation.
tth_nondrug_manual_osteopathic_therapy.real_working_solution: Osteopathic manipulative therapy shows a real, statistically significant signal in a small pilot and is a reasonable adjunct to consider for patients with clear postural/myofascial contributors, pending larger confirmatory trials.
tth_nondrug_manual_osteopathic_therapy.source: Cerritelli F et al., 'Osteopathic Manipulative Therapy in Patients With Chronic Tension-Type Headache: A Pilot Study', J Am Osteopath Assoc 2019;119(9):561-569 (PMID 31404469)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Aspirin 500-1000mg -- acute, single dose
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 55% of aspirin-treated patients were satisfied with treatment vs 37% with placebo (NNT 5.7, 95% CI 3.7-12).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Derry S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017 (PMID 28084009)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Acupuncture (>=6 sessions) -- chronic/frequent-episodic TTH prophylaxis, vs sham
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 52.4% (205/391) vs 42.6% (133/312) achieved >=50% reduction in headache frequency vs sham acupuncture (RR 1.3, 95% CI 1.09-1.5); much larger effect (up to 48% vs 19%, RR 2.5) vs routine care alone.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Linde K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27092807)

ranked_high_to_low.name: EMG biofeedback (± relaxation) -- chronic TTH prophylaxis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Medium-to-large effect size vs controls, Cohen's d = 0.73 (95% CI 0.61-0.84), corresponding to ~77% of treated patients improving more than the average control patient (Cohen's U3), stable at 15-month follow-up (53 studies).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Nestoriuc Y et al., J Consult Clin Psychol 2008 (PMID 18540732)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Osteopathic manipulative therapy -- chronic TTH, small pilot
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Headache frequency fell from 19.8 to 8.3 days/month (a 58% relative reduction, p=0.002) in a small pilot RCT (n=10 vs n=10) -- real signal, honestly under-powered and needing replication.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cerritelli F et al., J Am Osteopath Assoc 2019 (PMID 31404469)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials with DIFFERENT designs, comparators (placebo vs sham vs routine care) and outcome measures (2-hour response for acute analgesics; >=50%-frequency-responder rate, headache-index reduction, or effect-size for chronic prophylaxis/non-drug options), so this ordering is a directional, clinically-reasoned ranking rather than a single interchangeable scale. Rows 1-4 (ACUTE, single-dose, episodic TTH) and rows 5-8 (CHRONIC/frequent-episodic prophylaxis) answer two different clinical questions -- stopping today's episode vs reducing how often headaches occur -- and a patient with frequent or chronic TTH needs both, not one instead of the other (see curative_option). Where a trial reported only an NNT and not a raw arm percentage, effectiveness_pct is the absolute risk difference derived as 1/NNT (a standard, non-fabricated EBM conversion), clearly labelled as such in the metric text; where raw trial percentages were reported (aspirin, acupuncture, biofeedback U3, amitriptyline headache-index reduction, osteopathic pilot), those real reported numbers are used directly.

definition.finding: Tension-type headache (TTH) is the most prevalent primary headache disorder and, per the Nature Reviews Disease Primers definition, is characterised by recurrent headaches of mild to moderate intensity, bilateral location, pressing or tightening (non-pulsating) quality, and no aggravation by routine physical activity. It is formally classified in ICHD-3 (section 2) into infrequent episodic, frequent episodic, and chronic subtypes based on headache frequency.
definition.source: Ashina S et al, 'Tension-type headache', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:24 (PMID 33767185); Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (IHS), 'The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition', Cephalalgia 2018;38(1):1-211 (PMID 29368949), section 2

peripheral_myofascial_mechanism_episodic.finding: In episodic TTH, the dominant mechanism is peripheral: increased nociceptive input from pericranial myofascial tissues. Population and clinical studies find significantly higher pericranial muscle tenderness (on manual palpation) in TTH sufferers compared with both migraineurs and headache-free controls, and this peripheral myogenic mechanism is considered most important in the infrequent/frequent episodic forms.
peripheral_myofascial_mechanism_episodic.source: Jensen R, 'Pathophysiological mechanisms of tension-type headache: a review of epidemiological and experimental studies', Cephalalgia 1999;19(6):602-21 (PMID 10448549); Fumal A, Schoenen J, 'Tension-type headache: current research and clinical management', Lancet Neurol 2008;7(1):70-83 (PMID 18093564)

myofascial_trigger_point_nature_2026.finding: A 2026 microdialysis study directly measuring active myofascial trigger points in TTH patients versus latent trigger points in healthy muscle found active trigger points had significantly higher nutritive blood flow than muscle without a trigger point (p=0.026), with no significant differences in lactate (p=0.329) or glucose (p=0.231) between groups. The authors concluded active trigger points are 'hyperemic rather than ischemic' and are 'not experiencing higher energy demand as would be expected with sustained muscle contraction' -- evidence against the older 'energy crisis' model of trigger-point physiology and consistent instead with a localised inflammatory/sensitisation process in the pericranial muscle as the peripheral driver of TTH pain.
myofascial_trigger_point_nature_2026.source: 'Microdialysis Evaluation of Blood Flow, Lactate, and Glucose in Active Trigger Points of Tension-Type Headache Patients and Latent Trigger Points in Healthy Muscle', Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2026 (PMID 41033570)
myofascial_trigger_point_nature_2026.confidence: moderate (single study, but methodologically direct measurement in the relevant patient population)

central_sensitization_mechanism_chronic.finding: In chronic TTH, the dominant mechanism shifts to central sensitisation: prolonged nociceptive input from pericranial myofascial tissues is believed to sensitise second-order neurons at the level of the spinal dorsal horn/trigeminal nucleus, together with impaired supraspinal (descending) pain-modulation control, converting an originally peripherally-driven episodic disorder into a centrally-maintained chronic pain state. Peripheral and central mechanisms are intermingled rather than mutually exclusive, but central sensitisation is considered the main problem specifically in the chronic form.
central_sensitization_mechanism_chronic.source: Bendtsen L, 'Central sensitization in tension-type headache--possible pathophysiological mechanisms', Cephalalgia 2000;20(5):486-508 (PMID 11037746); Jensen R, Cephalalgia 1999;19(6):602-21 (PMID 10448549); Fumal A, Schoenen J, Lancet Neurol 2008;7(1):70-83 (PMID 18093564)

infrequent_episodic_tth_2_1.finding: ICHD-3 classifies 2.1 Infrequent episodic tension-type headache as episodes occurring on average less than 1 day per month (fewer than 12 days per year), each episode lasting from hours to days, fulfilling the core TTH pain-characteristic and associated-symptom criteria below.
infrequent_episodic_tth_2_1.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018;38(1):1-211 (PMID 29368949), section 2.1; cross-checked against 'Outcomes of Spinal Manipulation and Neurological Rehabilitation for a Patient With Chronic Tension-Type Headaches...', Cureus 2025 (PMID 41069918), which reproduces the same <1 day/month threshold

frequent_episodic_tth_2_2.finding: 2.2 Frequent episodic tension-type headache is defined as episodes occurring on 1-14 days per month on average for more than 3 months (12 to 179 days per year), otherwise fulfilling the same pain/associated-symptom criteria as infrequent episodic TTH; this subtype carries a greater impact on daily function than the infrequent form and is the threshold most often used to define clinically significant, guideline/pharmacotherapy-relevant TTH.
frequent_episodic_tth_2_2.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 2.2; PMID 41069918 (Cureus 2025) reproducing the 1-14 days/month threshold

chronic_tth_2_3.finding: 2.3 Chronic tension-type headache is defined as headache occurring on 15 or more days per month on average for more than 3 months (at least 180 days per year), often continuous/unremitting, evolving from frequent episodic TTH. Chronic TTH is one of the most disabling and treatment-refractory forms of primary headache and, unlike the episodic subtypes, may be accompanied by mild nausea in addition to the usual associated-symptom limits.
chronic_tth_2_3.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 2.3; independently cross-verified via full-text review reproducing the same >=15 days/month, >=180 days/year definition (PMC full-text search, 2025-26 literature)

core_pain_and_associated_symptom_criteri.finding: Across all TTH subtypes, ICHD-3 requires the headache to have at least 2 of the following 4 pain characteristics: (1) bilateral location, (2) pressing or tightening (non-pulsating) quality, (3) mild or moderate intensity, (4) not aggravated by routine physical activity such as walking or climbing stairs -- and both of the following: no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia, and no moderate/severe nausea or vomiting (mild nausea is permitted only in chronic TTH). This 2-of-4 pain-characteristic structure, together with the near-absence of migrainous associated features, is the core diagnostic tool distinguishing TTH from migraine at the bedside, since no laboratory test or imaging finding confirms TTH -- diagnosis is entirely clinical, based on headache history, normal neurological examination, and exclusion of secondary causes.
core_pain_and_associated_symptom_criteri.source: Ashina S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:24 (PMID 33767185) confirming the 4 pain characteristics and clinical-history-based diagnosis; Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 2

pain_quality_and_distribution.finding: The hallmark presentation is a bilateral, band-like or vice-like pressing/tightening sensation (rather than throbbing/pulsating pain), of mild to moderate intensity, typically affecting the frontal, temporal, or occipital/nuchal regions and often described as a tight band around the head or a weight pressing down on the vertex; unlike migraine it does not characteristically worsen with routine physical activity and patients are generally able to continue daily activities, though frequent/chronic forms cause substantial functional impairment.
pain_quality_and_distribution.source: Ashina S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:24 (PMID 33767185); Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 2

pericranial_muscle_tenderness.finding: Palpable tenderness of pericranial muscles (frontalis, temporalis, masseter, pterygoid, sternocleidomastoid, splenius, trapezius) on manual palpation is a real, measurable clinical finding that is significantly more common and more pronounced in TTH sufferers than in migraineurs or headache-free controls, and ICHD-3 allows subclassification of each TTH subtype as 'associated with pericranial tenderness' or 'not associated with pericranial tenderness' based on this examination finding.
pericranial_muscle_tenderness.source: Jensen R, Cephalalgia 1999;19(6):602-21 (PMID 10448549); Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 2

absence_of_migrainous_features.finding: Clinically important negative findings that define TTH by exclusion: no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia (never both together, which would suggest migraine), no significant nausea or vomiting (only mild nausea permitted, and only in chronic TTH), no aura, and no autonomic features (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion/rhinorrhea, ptosis/miosis) that would instead suggest a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia such as cluster headache.
absence_of_migrainous_features.source: Ashina S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:24 (PMID 33767185); Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 2

migraine.finding: Migraine without aura (ICHD-3 1.1) requires at least 2 of 4 different pain characteristics -- unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-severe intensity, aggravation by routine physical activity -- plus nausea/vomiting and/or both photophobia AND phonophobia, and attacks last 4-72 hours untreated; this contrasts point-for-point with TTH's bilateral, pressing, mild-moderate, activity-tolerant pattern with at most one of photophobia/phonophobia and no vomiting. See this knowledge base's own 'migraine' entry for full ICHD-3 migraine criteria detail. In practice the two disorders frequently coexist in the same patient and can be difficult to separate on a single history, which is why ICHD-3 criteria are applied systematically rather than by gestalt impression.
migraine.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), sections 1.1 and 2; this knowledge base's 'migraine' entry, diagnostic_framework_ichd3

cluster_headache_and_trigeminal_autonomi.finding: Cluster headache is a stereotyped primary pain syndrome characterised by strictly unilateral, severe pain localised in or around the eye and accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis/miosis) and often restlessness/agitation during attacks -- the opposite clinical picture from TTH's bilateral, mild-moderate, non-autonomic, activity-tolerant pain. A paediatric cluster-headache case series from a specialist headache clinic reported an average attack duration of 72 minutes with a commonest bout frequency of one attack per day, alongside agitated movement and cranial autonomic activation in most patients, illustrating the short, severe, autonomic-symptom-laden pattern that separates it clearly from TTH.
cluster_headache_and_trigeminal_autonomi.source: May A, 'Cluster headache: pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management', Lancet 2005;366(9488):843-55 (PMID 16139660); 'Cluster headache in children--experience from a specialist headache clinic' (PMID 19109043)

medication_overuse_headache.finding: Medication-overuse headache (MOH, ICHD-3 8.2) develops in a patient with a pre-existing primary headache disorder (commonly TTH or migraine) who has a headache on 15 or more days per month arising as a consequence of regular overuse, for more than 3 months, of acute/symptomatic headache medication (simple analgesics >=15 days/month; triptans, ergotamine, opioids or combination analgesics >=10 days/month).
