MOH is a major, at-least-partially-reversible driver of the transition from frequent episodic to chronic TTH, and must be actively screened for (medication-use history) in any patient presenting with daily or near-daily headache, since continuing to treat it as simple chronic TTH without addressing the overused drug will not resolve it.
medication_overuse_headache.source: Ashina S et al, 'Medication overuse headache', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2023;9:5 (PMID 36732518); this knowledge base's 'migraine' entry, diagnostic_framework_ichd3.medication_overuse_headache_8_2, citing ICHD-3 section 8.2 (PMID 29368949) and Diener HC et al, Lancet Neurol 2019;18(9):891-902 (PMID 31174999)

secondary_headache_red_flags.finding: Before any headache is diagnosed as TTH, secondary (dangerous) causes must be excluded using the SNNOOP10 red/orange flag list, since TTH is a diagnosis of exclusion made on a normal neurological examination plus a headache history that fits ICHD-3 criteria -- see this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and this knowledge base's 'migraine' entry (red_flags_secondary_headache) for the full SNNOOP10 detail and specific urgent scenarios (thunderclap onset/subarachnoid haemorrhage, fever+neck stiffness/meningitis, papilledema/raised intracranial pressure, new headache in pregnancy/postpartum, new headache in immunocompromised patients, or a fundamentally changed headache pattern).
secondary_headache_red_flags.source: Do TP et al, 'Red and orange flags for secondary headaches in clinical practice: SNNOOP10 list', Neurology 2019;92(3):134-144 (PMID 30587518); this knowledge base's 'migraine' entry, red_flags_secondary_headache

pericranial_muscle_tenderness_and_muscle.finding: Increased pericranial myofascial tenderness/nociception is both a defining clinical sign and a mechanistic risk factor for TTH, more pronounced in TTH sufferers than migraineurs or controls and correlated with headache frequency/intensity in population studies.

psychiatric_comorbidity_anxiety_depressi.finding: Depression and anxiety are significantly more prevalent in chronic TTH than in episodic TTH: in a Chinese multicentre cross-sectional study of hospitalised primary headache patients, depression prevalence was 30.6% in chronic TTH versus 15.1% in episodic TTH, and anxiety prevalence was 20.1% versus 12.8% respectively -- indicating psychiatric comorbidity rises with, and is likely both a risk factor for and a consequence of, chronification.
psychiatric_comorbidity_anxiety_depressi.source: Jia Z et al, 'Depression and anxiety in Chinese patients hospitalized with primary headache: A cross-sectional multicenter study', Mol Pain 2025 (PMID 39921551)

poor_outcome_predictors_from_population_.finding: A 12-year Danish population-based follow-up study of headache patients identified specific predictors of a poor tension-type-headache outcome (i.e. progression to or persistence of chronic TTH): baseline chronic TTH (versus frequent episodic), coexisting migraine, not being married, and sleeping problems -- establishing sleep disturbance and psychosocial factors as real, population-verified risk factors for chronification rather than purely anecdotal associations.
poor_outcome_predictors_from_population_.source: Lyngberg AC et al, 'Prognosis of migraine and tension-type headache: a population-based follow-up study', Neurology 2005;65(4):580-5 (PMID 16116119)

medication_overuse.finding: Regular overuse of acute/symptomatic headache medication (per the drug-class-specific thresholds defining ICHD-3 8.2 medication-overuse headache) is a major, actively modifiable risk factor for transformation of episodic TTH into a chronic daily headache pattern.
medication_overuse.source: Ashina S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2023;9:5 (PMID 36732518); ICHD-3 section 8.2 (PMID 29368949)

most_common_headache_disorder_globally.finding: Tension-type headache is the most prevalent primary headache disorder and, per the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016, the third most prevalent condition of all causes studied by GBD in 2016, with a global age-standardised prevalence of 26.1% (95% UI 23.6-29.0) -- higher in women (30.8%) than men (21.4%) -- corresponding to an estimated 1.89 billion people affected globally, versus migraine's 1.04 billion. Despite its much higher prevalence than migraine, TTH causes far less disability: 7.2 million (95% UI 4.6-10.5) years lived with disability (YLDs) globally in 2016 versus migraine's 45.1 million YLDs, reflecting TTH's much lower per-case disability weight (0.037 versus migraine's 0.434).
most_common_headache_disorder_globally.source: GBD 2016 Headache Collaborators, 'Global, regional, and national burden of migraine and tension-type headache, 1990-2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016', Lancet Neurol 2018;17(11):954-976 (PMID 30353868)

lifetime_and_1_year_prevalence_variation.finding: Reported prevalence varies substantially by study methodology and population, and this variation is presented honestly rather than collapsed into one number: a Danish population study found lifetime prevalence of 88% in women and 69% in men (with prevalence decreasing with increasing age); a separate epidemiological review reported an overall lifetime prevalence of about 78% of adults; and the Eurolight population survey across Europe found a 1-year prevalence of 60% for TTH versus 15% for migraine. The GBD 2016 modelled global age-standardised 1-year prevalence of 26.1% is lower than these self-report population-survey figures, a well-recognised discrepancy in headache epidemiology attributable to differences in case ascertainment strictness (structured diagnostic interview vs modelled/registry-based estimation) rather than a real contradiction in the underlying biology.
lifetime_and_1_year_prevalence_variation.source: Rasmussen BK et al, 'Epidemiology of headache in a general population--a prevalence study', J Clin Epidemiol 1991;44:1147-57 (PMID 1941010); Jensen R, Cephalalgia 1999;19(6):602-21 (PMID 10448549); Stovner LJ et al, 'Prevalence of headache in Europe: a review for the Eurolight project', J Headache Pain 2010;11(4):289-99 (PMID 20473702); GBD 2016 Headache Collaborators, Lancet Neurol 2018;17(11):954-976 (PMID 30353868)
lifetime_and_1_year_prevalence_variation.confidence: high (qualitative variation is well established; no single 'true' prevalence number should be presented as definitive)

india_specific_data_not_verified.finding: No India-specific TTH prevalence figure could be independently verified in this research session; only the global (GBD), Danish, and European (Eurolight) figures above are reported, and an India-specific number is explicitly omitted rather than estimated or assumed.

episodic_to_chronic_progression_real_fol.finding: In the same 12-year Danish population-based follow-up study (146 subjects with frequent episodic TTH and 15 with chronic TTH at baseline, 81.6% follow-up participation), outcomes at follow-up were: 45% experienced remission (infrequent or no TTH), 39% remained at frequent episodic TTH, and 16% had a poor outcome (chronic TTH) -- i.e. the overall prognosis of TTH was favourable for the majority, but a real minority (about 1 in 6) progressed to or remained at the most disabling, chronic end of the spectrum. Poor outcome was independently associated with baseline chronic TTH, coexisting migraine, not being married, and sleeping problems.

chronic_tth_as_the_treatment_refractory_.finding: Chronic TTH, once established, is one of the most challenging headache disorders to treat, with preventive drug therapies showing only limited efficacy on average and combination drug plus non-drug management (relaxation training, stress management, physical therapy) generally recommended over pharmacotherapy alone -- reflecting the pathophysiological shift toward centrally-sensitised, less peripherally-reversible pain once chronification has occurred.
chronic_tth_as_the_treatment_refractory_.source: Fumal A, Schoenen J, Lancet Neurol 2008;7(1):70-83 (PMID 18093564)

exclude_danger_then_apply_ichd3_criteria.finding: The first clinical priority in any new headache presentation is to exclude secondary/dangerous causes using SNNOOP10 red flags (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) -- TTH is a diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory laboratory or imaging test. Once secondary causes are reasonably excluded and the neurological examination is normal, TTH is diagnosed clinically by applying the ICHD-3 frequency thresholds (infrequent episodic <1 day/month, frequent episodic 1-14 days/month, chronic >=15 days/month for >3 months) together with the 2-of-4 pain-characteristic rule (bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-moderate, activity-tolerant) and the associated-symptom limits (at most one of photophobia/phonophobia, no significant nausea/vomiting). Because chronic TTH is driven by a different (centrally sensitised) mechanism than the episodic forms and carries a real ~16% 12-year progression risk with a strong sleep/psychiatric-comorbidity/medication-overuse signal, screening every TTH patient for sleep disturbance, depression/anxiety, and acute-medication-overuse pattern at first presentation is a real, evidence-based opportunity to intervene before chronification rather than after it.
exclude_danger_then_apply_ichd3_criteria.source: Do TP et al, Neurology 2019 (PMID 30587518); Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949); Bendtsen L, Cephalalgia 2000 (PMID 11037746); Lyngberg AC et al, Neurology 2005 (PMID 16116119); Jia Z et al, Mol Pain 2025 (PMID 39921551)

tension_type_headache.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: A headache that is being assumed to be simple tension-type headache MUST be immediately escalated to emergency care (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW) rather than managed as routine TTH if any SNNOOP10 red/orange flag is present: thunderclap onset (pain reaching maximal intensity within seconds to about a minute -- classic warning sign of subarachnoid haemorrhage), Systemic symptoms including fever, Neoplasm history, Neurologic deficit or altered consciousness, Older age at onset (after 50-65 years), Pattern change or recent onset of a new/different headache type, Positional headache, Precipitated by sneezing/coughing/exercise/Valsalva, Papilledema, Progressive headache with atypical presentation, Pregnancy or puerperium, Painful eye with autonomic features, Post-traumatic onset, Pathology of the immune system (e.g. HIV/immunosuppression), or Painkiller/acute-medication overuse or a new drug at headache onset. True tension-type headache is, by ICHD-3 definition, a bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-to-moderate, non-disabling headache with no more than one of photophobia/phonophobia and no vomiting -- a headache that is unilateral-thunderclap, associated with fever/neck stiffness/altered consciousness, worsening/positional/Valsalva-provoked, new after age 50, or occurring with focal neurological signs is NOT tension-type headache and must never be treated as one; it requires urgent neuroimaging and/or lumbar puncture to rule out subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis/encephalitis, raised intracranial pressure (mass lesion, venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) or another dangerous secondary cause before any tension-type-headache management plan is applied.

cluster_headache.name: Cluster Headache

definition.finding: Cluster headache is a primary headache disorder within the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs, ICHD-3 group 3), classified as ICHD-3 code 3.1. It is characterised by attacks of severe or very severe, strictly unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes if untreated, accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features and/or a sense of restlessness/agitation, with attack frequency ranging from one every other day to eight per day.
definition.source: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (IHS), 'The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition', Cephalalgia 2018;38(1):1-211 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1

trigeminal_autonomic_reflex.finding: The ipsilateral cranial autonomic features of cluster headache (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion/rhinorrhoea, ptosis, miosis, eyelid oedema, facial sweating/flushing) are produced by the 'trigeminal-autonomic reflex': nociceptive trigeminal afferents activate second-order neurons in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, which have central connections to the superior salivatory nucleus in the pons; this drives parasympathetic outflow via the facial nerve (VII) and pterygopalatine (sphenopalatine) ganglion to the lacrimal gland, nasal mucosa and orbit, producing the autonomic signs synchronously with the pain on the same side.
trigeminal_autonomic_reflex.source: Burish MJ, Rozen TD, 'Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias', Neurol Clin 2019;37(4):847-869 (PMID 31563236); May A, Bahra A, Buchel C, Frackowiak RS, Goadsby PJ, 'Hypothalamic activation in cluster headache attacks', Lancet 1998;352(9124):275-8 (PMID 9690407)

hypothalamic_activation.finding: PET imaging of regional cerebral blood flow during nitroglycerin-induced acute cluster headache attacks (9 chronic cluster headache patients; 8 additional cluster headache patients studied out-of-bout as controls) showed activation specifically in the ipsilateral inferior hypothalamic grey matter that was present only during the pain state and absent in patients who were out of their cluster bout; activation was also seen in the contralateral ventroposterior thalamus, anterior cingulate cortex and bilateral insulae. This established central hypothalamic dysfunction, not a purely vascular process, as the likely primary driver ('primum movens') of cluster headache, and the authors proposed the condition be reclassified as a neurovascular rather than purely vascular headache.
hypothalamic_activation.source: May A, Bahra A, Buchel C, Frackowiak RS, Goadsby PJ, Lancet 1998;352(9124):275-8 (PMID 9690407)

circadian_circannual_periodicity.finding: Cluster headache attacks show a striking circadian pattern (frequent recurrence at the same clock time, often waking the patient in the early hours of the morning) and, in episodic cluster headache, circannual periodicity of bouts (cluster periods often recurring in the same season each year). The original PET study explicitly noted that this rhythmicity 'cannot be readily explained by the vascular hypothesis' and pointed to hypothalamic (near-suprachiasmatic-nucleus) involvement as the likely biological clock driving it; this periodicity is a classic clinical feature helping distinguish cluster headache from migraine, which lacks this degree of clock-time and seasonal regularity.
circadian_circannual_periodicity.source: May A et al., Lancet 1998 (PMID 9690407, as above); Burish MJ, 'Cluster Headache and Other Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias', Continuum (Minneap Minn) 2018;24(4):1137-1156 (PMID 30074553)

ichd3_cluster_headache_3_1.finding: ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for 3.1 Cluster headache: (A) At least 5 attacks fulfilling criteria B-D; (B) Severe or very severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes when untreated; (C) Either or both of the following: (1) at least one of the following ipsilateral symptoms/signs - conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation, nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, forehead and facial sweating, forehead and facial flushing, sensation of fullness in the ear, miosis and/or ptosis; and/or (2) a sense of restlessness or agitation; (D) Attacks have a frequency between one every other day and 8 per day; (E) Not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis.
ichd3_cluster_headache_3_1.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS, Cephalalgia 2018 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1

episodic_cluster_headache_3_1_1.finding: Episodic cluster headache (ICHD-3 3.1.1) is diagnosed when attacks meeting the 3.1 criteria occur in bouts ('cluster periods') lasting from 7 days to 1 year, separated by pain-free remission periods of 1 month or longer. This is the more common presentation; population-based data give an episodic-to-chronic cluster headache ratio of approximately 6:1.
episodic_cluster_headache_3_1_1.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1.1; Fischera M, Marziniak M, Gralow I, Evers S, 'The incidence and prevalence of cluster headache: a meta-analysis of population-based studies', Cephalalgia 2008;28(6):614-8 (PMID 18422717)

chronic_cluster_headache_3_1_2.finding: Chronic cluster headache (ICHD-3 3.1.2) is diagnosed when attacks meeting the 3.1 criteria recur for more than 1 year without remission, or with remission periods lasting less than 3 months. Chronic cluster headache can arise de novo or evolve from episodic cluster headache, and accounts for roughly 10-15% of all cluster headache cases (consistent with the ~6:1 episodic:chronic ratio reported by Fischera et al.).
chronic_cluster_headache_3_1_2.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1.2; Fischera M et al., Cephalalgia 2008 (PMID 18422717, as above)

diagnostic_delay.finding: In a prospective multicentre Korean cluster headache registry (445 patients), the mean diagnostic delay from symptom onset to correct diagnosis was 5.7 +/- 6.7 years (range 0-36 years). Delay was longer in younger patients (onset <20 years: 60% fell in the longest-delay tertile, i.e. >=7 years) than older patients (onset >40 years: only 9.0% in that tertile), and the proportion of patients with prolonged (>=7-year) delay fell sharply after diagnostic-criteria dissemination - from 74.7% (diagnosed before ICHD-2) to 0.5% (diagnosed after the ICHD-3-beta criteria were published) - and longer delay was independently associated with a worse (higher) HIT-6 headache-impact score (p=0.041).
diagnostic_delay.source: Kim BS, Chung PW, Kim BK, Lee MJ, Chu MK et al. (Korean Cluster Headache Registry), 'Diagnostic Delay and Its Predictors in Cluster Headache', Front Neurol 2022;13:820479 (PMID 35222255)

pain_characteristics.finding: Pain is strictly unilateral (side may switch between bouts but essentially never within an attack), centred on the orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal region, and described as excruciating - among the most severe pain syndromes known in clinical medicine, often characterised by patients as boring, burning, stabbing or drilling in quality, in contrast to migraine's more commonly pulsating quality.

cranial_autonomic_features.finding: Ipsilateral cranial autonomic features required for diagnosis (at least one, per criterion C1) are: conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation, nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, forehead/facial sweating or flushing, a sensation of fullness in the ear, and miosis and/or ptosis (partial Horner's syndrome can persist between attacks in some chronic patients).

restlessness_agitation_distinguishing_fe.finding: A hallmark clinical feature distinguishing cluster headache from migraine is behaviour during an attack: cluster headache patients are characteristically restless or agitated - pacing, rocking, banging their head, or unable to stay still - whereas migraineurs typically prefer to lie motionless in a dark, quiet room. ICHD-3 formally incorporates 'a sense of restlessness or agitation' as an alternative to (or in addition to) autonomic features under criterion C.
restlessness_agitation_distinguishing_fe.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1, criterion C2; Burish MJ, Rozen TD, Neurol Clin 2019 (PMID 31563236)

attack_pattern_and_triggers.finding: Attacks in a US survey of 1,134 cluster headache patients most commonly began between midnight and 3 am, with a right-sided predominance reported, and alcohol (particularly beer) was the most commonly identified trigger during an active bout (cluster headache is unusual among primary headaches in that alcohol reliably triggers attacks only during active bouts, not during remission). Diagnostic delay in this cohort was substantial, with a minority of patients receiving the correct diagnosis at first presentation.
attack_pattern_and_triggers.source: Rozen TD, Fishman RS, 'Cluster headache in the United States of America: demographics, clinical characteristics, triggers, suicidality, and personal burden', Headache 2012;52(1):99-113 (PMID 22077141)

migraine.finding: Migraine differs from cluster headache in: longer attack duration (4-72 hours vs 15-180 minutes); more often bilateral pain, pulsating quality; patients seeking stillness/quiet dark rooms rather than restlessness; associated nausea/vomiting and photophobia+phonophobia (rather than ipsilateral cranial autonomic signs) as the defining associated features; and a female predominance (roughly 3:1) in contrast to cluster headache's strong male predominance.

paroxysmal_hemicrania.finding: Paroxysmal hemicrania (ICHD-3 3.2) shares unilateral orbital/supraorbital/temporal pain and ipsilateral autonomic features with cluster headache, but attacks are shorter (2-30 minutes vs 15-180 minutes) and more frequent (classically more than 5 per day for more than half the time, versus cluster headache's up to 8/day), and - the defining diagnostic feature - attacks are completely abolished by therapeutic doses of indomethacin, which cluster headache is not reliably responsive to. An 'indomethacin trial' is therefore the practical way to distinguish the two when duration/frequency overlap.
paroxysmal_hemicrania.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.2; Burish MJ, Rozen TD, Neurol Clin 2019 (PMID 31563236)

sunct_suna.finding: SUNCT (short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing, ICHD-3 3.3.1) and SUNA (...with cranial autonomic symptoms, 3.3.2) produce much shorter, more frequent attacks than cluster headache: individual attacks last seconds to a few minutes (on the order of 1-600 seconds per ICHD-3, commonly cited as roughly 5-240 seconds in clinical series) and can recur up to several hundred times per day. SUNCT specifically requires both conjunctival injection AND lacrimation; SUNA is diagnosed when one or both of these two specific features are absent but other cranial autonomic symptoms are present. Both are markedly briefer and more frequent than the 15-180 minute, up-to-8/day pattern of cluster headache, and neither responds to indomethacin the way paroxysmal hemicrania does.
sunct_suna.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), sections 3.3.1-3.3.2; Burish MJ, Rozen TD, Neurol Clin 2019 (PMID 31563236)

trigeminal_neuralgia.finding: Classical trigeminal neuralgia (ICHD-3 13.1.1) causes paroxysms of unilateral facial pain confined to one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most often V2/V3, sparing the periorbital autonomic pattern of cluster headache), described as electric-shock-like, shooting, stabbing or sharp, lasting from a fraction of a second up to two minutes, and classically precipitated by innocuous stimuli in the trigger zone (light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, cold wind) - a precipitation pattern not seen in cluster headache. It lacks the prominent ipsilateral autonomic features and restlessness of cluster headache, and does not show cluster headache's circadian/circannual bout pattern.

secondary_cluster_headache_like_syndrome.finding: A structured literature review found that even attacks with a fully typical cluster-headache time pattern and typical treatment response can, uncommonly, be caused by an underlying structural lesion - most notably pituitary adenoma, but also vascular malformations and other lesions in the region of the cavernous sinus/pituitary fossa - so a symptomatic ('secondary') cluster-headache-like syndrome cannot be excluded on clinical grounds (typical phenotype/treatment response) alone.
secondary_cluster_headache_like_syndrome.source: Favier I, Haan J, Ferrari MD, 'Cluster headache: to scan or not to scan', Curr Pain Headache Rep 2008;12(2):122-7 (PMID 18474193)
secondary_cluster_headache_like_syndrome.confidence: moderate-high (real, cited finding; the review itself concludes that no firm scanning algorithm could be derived, reflecting genuine evidence-quality limits, not omission on our part)

male_predominance.finding: Cluster headache shows a strong male predominance, with an overall pooled male:female ratio of approximately 4.3:1 across population-based studies; the sex skew is even more pronounced in chronic cluster headache (male:female ratio ~15.0) than in episodic cluster headache (male:female ratio ~3.8), though some more recent series suggest the historical male preponderance may be narrowing over time.
male_predominance.source: Fischera M, Marziniak M, Gralow I, Evers S, Cephalalgia 2008;28(6):614-8 (PMID 18422717)

smoking_tobacco_exposure.finding: Tobacco exposure is strikingly common in cluster headache: in a US survey of 1,134 patients, 88% had a personal and/or childhood second-hand tobacco exposure history (83% personal smoking history among the exposed group). Tobacco-exposed patients had a significantly later mean age of onset (>40 years vs <=40 years in non-exposed patients), a higher rate of transition to chronic cluster headache (23% vs 14% in non-exposed patients), and higher reported suicidal ideation during attacks (57% vs 43% in non-exposed patients) - suggesting tobacco-exposed and non-exposed cluster headache may represent distinct clinical phenotypes rather than smoking being an incidental association.
smoking_tobacco_exposure.source: Rozen TD, 'Cluster Headache Clinical Phenotypes: Tobacco Nonexposed... versus Tobacco-Exposed: Results from the United States Cluster Headache Survey', Headache 2018;58(10):1552-1563 (PMID 29536529); Rozen TD, Fishman RS, Headache 2012 (PMID 22077141, describing the cohort as predominantly 'chronic heavy smokers')

family_history_genetics.finding: Cluster headache has a real, if modest-prevalence, familial/genetic component: in an Italian case-control study of 220 cluster headache patients, first-degree relatives of probands had a 39-fold significantly increased risk of cluster headache and second-degree relatives an eightfold increased risk, compared with the general population, although a positive family history was present in only a minority of probands overall - i.e. most cluster headache is sporadic, but when a family history exists, the relative risk to relatives is very high.
family_history_genetics.source: Leone M, Russell MB, Rigamonti A, Attanasio A, Grazzi L, D'Amico D, Usai S, Bussone G, 'Increased familial risk of cluster headache', Neurology 2001;56(9):1233-6 (PMID 11342697)
family_history_genetics.confidence: moderate-high (single case-control study; fold-risk figures are large and study-specific, quoted directly from the source abstract)

prevalence_incidence.finding: A meta-analysis of population-based studies estimated the lifetime prevalence of cluster headache at 124 per 100,000 (95% CI 101-151) and the 1-year prevalence at 53 per 100,000 (95% CI 26-95) - i.e. roughly 1 in 1,000 people lifetime, or a bit over 1 in 2,000 in a given year - making cluster headache far less common than migraine but still a real and likely under-diagnosed condition given the diagnostic-delay data above.
prevalence_incidence.source: Fischera M, Marziniak M, Gralow I, Evers S, Cephalalgia 2008;28(6):614-8 (PMID 18422717)

onset_age.finding: Cluster headache classically has an onset in early-to-middle adulthood, most commonly cited as the 20-40 year age range, though genuine onset outside this window (including in childhood/adolescence and after age 40, especially in tobacco-exposed patients as above) occurs and should not be used to exclude the diagnosis.
onset_age.source: Burish MJ, Continuum 2018 (PMID 30074553); Rozen TD, Headache 2018 (PMID 29536529, tobacco-exposed vs non-exposed onset-age comparison, as above)

episodic_course.finding: In episodic cluster headache (the majority presentation, roughly 80-90% of cases), bouts of daily or near-daily attacks lasting 7 days to 1 year (commonly weeks to a few months in practice) are separated by remission periods of a month or more, and bouts often recur with circannual (same-season) regularity; the disorder can remain purely episodic for life, though a subset of episodic patients transition to chronic cluster headache over time.
episodic_course.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1.1; May A et al., Lancet 1998 (PMID 9690407, circannual periodicity)

chronic_course_and_transition.finding: Chronic cluster headache (10-15% of cases) involves attacks recurring for over a year without remission, or with remissions under 3 months, and can either begin de novo (primary chronic) or evolve from previously episodic cluster headache (secondary chronic); population data giving an episodic:chronic ratio of about 6:1 imply that the chronic form, while a minority presentation, represents a meaningfully large absolute number of more severely and persistently affected patients given cluster headache's overall prevalence.
chronic_course_and_transition.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1.2; Fischera M et al., Cephalalgia 2008 (PMID 18422717, episodic:chronic ratio)

disease_duration_and_disability.finding: Longer cluster headache disease duration, higher headache-related disability, and greater depressive symptom burden (PHQ-9) were independently identified as predictors of higher suicidality (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) in a large Korean multicentre cohort, indicating that the natural history of unremitting/long-duration disease carries a real, quantified escalation in psychiatric risk over and above the pain itself.
disease_duration_and_disability.source: Lee MJ, Cho SJ, Park JW, Chu MK, Moon HS et al., 'Increased suicidality in patients with cluster headache', Cephalalgia 2019;39(10):1249-1256 (PMID 31018651)

clinical_takeaway.point: Diagnose cluster headache formally against ICHD-3 3.1 criteria (attack duration 15-180 minutes, ipsilateral autonomic features and/or restlessness, frequency up to 8/day) rather than as a severe migraine, and specifically ask about restlessness/agitation during attacks versus preference for stillness.
clinical_takeaway.why: Restlessness/agitation versus stillness is one of the most reliable bedside features separating cluster headache from migraine, and correct classification changes treatment entirely (oxygen/triptan/verapamil-based cluster protocols versus migraine-specific therapy).
clinical_takeaway.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), section 3.1

clinical_takeaway.point: Actively screen for suicidal ideation at every visit, especially during an active bout, in tobacco-exposed patients, and in those with longer disease duration or higher depression scores.
clinical_takeaway.why: Suicidal ideation is reported in over half of patients during attacks in independent US and Korean cohorts (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE), with quantified predictors (disease duration, disability, PHQ-9 score, tobacco exposure) that make risk stratification realistic and actionable rather than a vague concern.
clinical_takeaway.source: Rozen TD, Fishman RS, Headache 2012 (PMID 22077141); Lee MJ et al., Cephalalgia 2019 (PMID 31018651)

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not assume a typical clinical phenotype and typical treatment response rules out a secondary cause; obtain MRI (not CT) in atypical presentations, first presentation, abnormal neurological examination, or poor/atypical treatment response.
clinical_takeaway.why: Typical-appearing cluster headache, including typical treatment response, has been documented with an underlying pituitary or other structural lesion, so clinical typicality alone is not sufficient to exclude a secondary cause when other red flags are present.
clinical_takeaway.source: Favier I, Haan J, Ferrari MD, Curr Pain Headache Rep 2008 (PMID 18474193)

clinical_takeaway.point: Distinguish cluster headache from the other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias using attack duration/frequency and indomethacin response, not autonomic features alone (which overlap across all TACs).
clinical_takeaway.why: Paroxysmal hemicrania (2-30 min, indomethacin-responsive) and SUNCT/SUNA (seconds, very high frequency) are managed completely differently from cluster headache despite sharing the unilateral-pain-plus-autonomic-features phenotype; missing this distinction leads to ineffective treatment trials.
clinical_takeaway.source: ICHD-3 (PMID 29368949), sections 3.2-3.3; Burish MJ, Rozen TD, Neurol Clin 2019 (PMID 31563236)

cluster_headache.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Cluster headache is colloquially termed the 'suicide headache' for a real, quantified reason, not just because of pain severity: in a US survey of cluster headache patients, suicidal ideation was reported by approximately 55% overall, and in a separate prospective Korean multicentre cohort (173 patients), DURING attacks, passive suicidal ideation was reported by 64.2% and active suicidal ideation by 35.8% of patients, with 5.8% reporting suicide planning and 2.3% reporting an actual suicide attempt during an attack; these rates fell sharply between attacks (interictal: passive ideation 4.0%, active 3.5%) and were near zero during remission between bouts - i.e. suicidality in cluster headache is strongly attack-linked, not a constant baseline trait. Independent predictors of higher suicidality were longer disease duration, greater headache-related disability, and higher depressive symptom burden (PHQ-9); tobacco-exposed cluster headache patients report even higher suicidal ideation (57%) than non-tobacco-exposed patients (43%) in a separate US cohort. OPERATIONAL RULE: any cluster headache patient (or suspected cluster headache patient) who reports active suicidal ideation, a suicide plan, or a prior suicide attempt during a bout MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue/routine-consultation flow and receive immediate real-world emergency/crisis guidance (call local emergency services or a suicide/crisis helpline now, or go to the nearest emergency department), the same as any other acute suicide-risk presentation - this should never be minimised as 'just a bad headache.' RED FLAGS FOR A SECONDARY (NOT PRIMARY) CAUSE requiring urgent neuroimaging (MRI, not CT) rather than routine cluster-headache management: first-ever attack or atypical age of onset; abnormal findings on neurological examination (including any persistent, not just attack-related, cranial nerve or other focal deficit); poor or atypical response to standard cluster headache treatment (oxygen, triptans, verapamil); a fundamentally changed pattern in a previously typical cluster headache patient; and any systemic red flags (fever, unexplained weight loss, history of malignancy). A structured review found that even a fully typical cluster-headache time pattern and typical treatment response can, uncommonly, still be caused by an underlying structural lesion such as a pituitary adenoma, so typicality alone does not exclude a secondary cause when other red flags are present.
cluster_headache.icd11_hint: 8A83.0 Cluster headache (WHO ICD-11 MMS, listed under 8A83 Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias) -- this code is widely used in current (2024-2026) cluster-headache literature and guidelines, but could NOT be independently confirmed against a live WHO ICD-11 browser/API query in this research session (the WHO ICD API requires OAuth authentication not available here, and the public browser page is JavaScript-rendered). FLAGGED for independent verification against icd.who.int before clinical/coding use. Legacy ICD-10-CM: G44.0 Cluster headache syndrome.
cluster_headache.CURABILITY_NOTE: Cluster headache is NOT curable -- there is no treatment that removes the hypothalamic/trigeminal-autonomic mechanism that generates cluster bouts, and even after decades of remission the disease can return. But the disease has two real, evidence-based silver linings that deserve to lead: (1) individual attacks are highly abortable -- 78% of oxygen-treated attacks and 74% of sumatriptan-treated attacks resolve within 15 minutes in randomised placebo-controlled trials (Cohen 2009 JAMA, PMID 19996400; Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group 1991 NEJM, PMID 1647496), versus 20% and 26% respectively with placebo; and (2) about 80-85% of patients have the episodic form, in which cluster bouts are separated by genuine, treatment-free remission periods lasting months to years -- this is a real spontaneous 'remission,' not a cure, because a new bout can still start later (Coppola et al 2025, J Headache Pain, PMID 41039211). The remaining 15-20% develop chronic cluster headache (attacks for over a year without a remission of 3+ months), which is harder to control and did not respond to the one CGRP-antibody drug (galcanezumab) purpose-tested for it in a randomised trial (PMID 32050782). Verapamil, dosed to at least 240 mg/day with ECG monitoring, is the evidence-based first-line prophylactic agent for suppressing attacks during a bout in both forms (EFNS guideline, PMID 16987158; Leone 2000 RCT, PMID 10746617).

curative_option.name: Attack Abortion With High-Flow 100% Oxygen or Subcutaneous Sumatriptan Plus First-Line Verapamil Prophylaxis -- Real Near-Total Individual-Attack Control, Explicitly NOT a Cure of the Underlying Trigeminal-Autonomic/Hypothalamic Disorder
curative_option.note: Cluster headache (CH) has no known cure -- the hypothalamic/trigeminal-autonomic mechanism that generates cluster bouts is not reversed by any current therapy. But CH is one of the most abortable severe pains in medicine: within a single treated attack, roughly 3 in 4 to 4 in 5 patients become pain-free or reach adequate relief within 15 minutes using high-flow oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan, and about 4 in 5 patients started on adequate-dose verapamil during a bout have their remaining attacks in that bout suppressed. Episodic cluster headache (about 80-85% of all CH patients) also has a real, favourable natural history most patients are not told about: bouts are separated by genuine remission periods of months to years with zero attacks and no treatment needed.

real_trial_data.oxygen_abortion_rct: Cohen AS, Burns B, Goadsby PJ (2009), double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover trial, 109 adults (76 analysed: 57 episodic + 19 chronic CH), National Hospital for Neurology, London: 100% oxygen at 12 L/min via face mask for 15 min rendered patients pain-free/adequately relieved in 78% of 150 treated attacks (95% CI 71-85%) versus 20% of 148 air-placebo attacks (95% CI 14-26%), Wald chi(5)^2=66.7, p<0.001. JAMA 2009;302(22):2451-2457 (PMID 19996400; ISRCTN94092997).
real_trial_data.sumatriptan_abortion_rct: Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group (Ekbom K et al, 1991), double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover trial, 49 randomised / 39 fully evaluable patients: subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg reduced headache to no-pain-or-mild-pain in 74% of attacks within 15 min versus 26% with placebo (p<0.001); pain-free at 10 min in 36% vs 3% (p<0.001), at 15 min in 46% vs 10% (p<0.001); only 13% needed rescue oxygen versus 49% on placebo. N Engl J Med 1991;325(5):322-326 (PMID 1647496).
real_trial_data.verapamil_prophylaxis_rct: Leone M, D'Amico D, Frediani F et al (2000), double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled trial, 30 episodic-CH patients (5-day run-in, then 2 weeks verapamil 120 mg three times daily vs placebo): significant reduction in attack frequency and use of abortive medication on verapamil; a contemporaneous review of this trial reports 80% responders on verapamil versus none on placebo. Neurology 2000;54(6):1382-1385 (PMID 10746617). Verapamil >=240 mg/day is the EFNS Task Force's first-choice prophylactic agent for both episodic and chronic CH (May A et al, Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077, PMID 16987158).
real_trial_data.episodic_natural_remission: Approximately 80-85% of cluster headache patients have the episodic form: bouts (cluster periods) lasting weeks to months, separated by genuine attack-free remission periods that can last months to years without any treatment. Roughly 15-20% instead develop the chronic form (attacks continuing beyond 1 year without a remission of at least 3 months), which is harder to control and did not respond to galcanezumab in its dedicated RCT. Coppola G et al, 'Hallmarks of primary headache: part 3 - cluster headache', J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211; PMCID PMC12490097).

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Nothing here cures cluster headache -- these treatments abort an attack already under way (oxygen, sumatriptan) or suppress attacks for the duration they are taken (verapamil, corticosteroid bridging, monoclonal antibodies). What is real and close to complete control: 3 out of 4 (sumatriptan) to 4 out of 5 (oxygen) treated attacks resolve within 15 minutes, and roughly 4 out of 5 patients on adequate verapamil have the rest of that cluster bout suppressed. What is NOT cured: the tendency of the brain to generate a new cluster bout is untouched -- episodic patients will very likely have another bout in the future (though on their own biological timetable, often 1-2 bouts a year), and the 15-20% of patients with chronic CH have no true attack-free window at all without ongoing therapy.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Chronic cluster headache responds less reliably to verapamil than episodic CH and was NOT superior to placebo for galcanezumab in the one purpose-designed phase 3 RCT (mean weekly-attack-frequency reduction -5.4 galcanezumab vs -4.6 placebo, p=0.334; PMID 32050782). Triptans (sumatriptan, zolmitriptan) are contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, prior stroke/MI, and peripheral vascular disease because of their vasoconstrictive action. Verapamil at the high doses cluster headache requires (240-960 mg/day) needs baseline and serial ECGs because of dose-dependent PR-interval prolongation and heart block risk (Cohen AS, Matharu MS, Goadsby PJ, Neurology 2007;69:668-675).
curative_option.important_caveat: Oxygen and sumatriptan only abort the single attack being treated -- with up to 8 attacks a day in an active bout, both must be used repeatedly and neither shortens the bout itself. Injectable/nasal triptans are capped at a maximum of 2 doses per 24 hours and should not be used on more than a few days per week because of medication-overuse and cardiovascular-toxicity risk. Verapamil's prophylactic effect typically takes 1-3 weeks to build in, so a short course of oral corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone 60-100 mg/day tapering over 2-3 weeks) or a single suboccipital/greater-occipital-nerve corticosteroid injection is used as bridging ('transitional') therapy while verapamil is titrated up.
curative_option.source: Cohen AS et al, JAMA 2009;302(22):2451-2457 (PMID 19996400); Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group, N Engl J Med 1991;325(5):322-326 (PMID 1647496); Leone M et al, Neurology 2000;54(6):1382-1385 (PMID 10746617); May A et al (EFNS Task Force), Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077 (PMID 16987158); Dodick DW et al, Cephalalgia 2020;40(9):935-948 (PMID 32050782); Coppola G et al, J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for cluster headache (CH): acute attack abortion (high-flow oxygen, subcutaneous/nasal-spray triptans), first-line and alternative prophylaxis (verapamil, lithium, topiramate, galcanezumab and other CGRP-pathway monoclonal antibodies), transitional/bridging therapy (oral corticosteroids, suboccipital/greater-occipital-nerve corticosteroid injection), investigational agents (intranasal civamide), and honestly reported negative evidence (galcanezumab in chronic CH, fremanezumab in episodic CH). Diagnostic criteria and clinical features are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial, review or guideline.

ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.name: High-Flow 100% Oxygen -- First-Line Acute Abortive Treatment, Real Randomised-Trial-Proven, Zero Serious Adverse Events
ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.type: Inhaled gas therapy, non-rebreather/demand-valve face mask, acute attack treatment
specific_drugs: Medical-grade oxygen, 100%, delivered at 12-15 L/min via a non-rebreather face mask for 15 minutes at attack onset (EFNS guideline minimum: at least 7 L/min for 15 min)
ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.effectiveness: Cohen et al 2009 JAMA double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover RCT (109 adults, 76 analysed, National Hospital for Neurology, London): 78% of 150 oxygen-treated attacks were pain-free/adequately relieved at 15 minutes (95% CI 71-85%) versus 20% of 148 air-placebo attacks (95% CI 14-26%), p<0.001; no important adverse events in either arm. Older open reports (Kudrow 1981) had described 50-85% abortion rates at lower flows (7-10 L/min).
ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.reason_why: Hyperoxia is thought to normalise the elevated calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release and trigeminal-autonomic/parasympathetic reflex activation that drive the attack, and animal data show oxygen inhibits neuropeptide release and neuronal activation in the trigeminocervical complex.
ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.important_caveat: Requires a demand-valve or non-rebreather mask capable of 12-15 L/min (a standard low-flow nasal cannula/hospital wall oxygen at 2-4 L/min is not adequate and will not reproduce the trial results); portable cylinders and a home oxygen concentrator/prescription are needed for reliable acute-attack access, which is a real access barrier in many health systems including India.
ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.real_working_solution: Prescribe a home oxygen cylinder/regulator set (12-15 L/min capable) with a non-rebreather mask for every diagnosed CH patient in an active bout, to be used at the very first sign of an attack; combine with subcutaneous sumatriptan for attacks that do not fully resolve on oxygen alone.
ch_acute_high_flow_oxygen.source: Cohen AS, Burns B, Goadsby PJ, 'High-flow oxygen for treatment of cluster headache: a randomized trial', JAMA 2009;302(22):2451-2457 (PMID 19996400); May A et al, 'EFNS guidelines on the treatment of cluster headache and other trigeminal-autonomic cephalalgias', Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077 (PMID 16987158)

ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.name: Subcutaneous Sumatriptan 6 mg -- First-Line Injectable Acute Abortive, Real Randomised-Trial-Proven, Fastest Injectable Option
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.type: Selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist (triptan), subcutaneous autoinjector, acute attack treatment
specific_drugs: Sumatriptan succinate 6 mg subcutaneous autoinjector (Imigran/Imitrex injection; in India: Suminat injection, Sumo injection)
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.effectiveness: Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group (Ekbom K et al) 1991 NEJM double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover RCT (49 randomised, 39 evaluable): 74% of sumatriptan-treated attacks improved to no/mild pain within 15 minutes versus 26% with placebo (p<0.001); pain-free at 10 min in 36% vs 3%, at 15 min in 46% vs 10% (all p<0.001); only 13% needed rescue oxygen versus 49% on placebo. Numbers needed to treat for sc sumatriptan 6 mg across pooled RCTs: 3.3 (95% CI 2.4-5.0) and 2.4 (95% CI 1.9-3.2); pooled pain-free response at 15 min approximately 46-49% (63/131) (Cochrane review: Law S, Derry S, Moore RA, 'Triptans for acute cluster headache', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;CD008042).
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.reason_why: Sumatriptan is a selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonist that constricts dilated cranial/meningeal vessels and inhibits trigeminal nociceptive neurotransmission and CGRP release at the trigeminovascular synapse, the same pathway activated during a cluster attack.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.important_caveat: Contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, prior stroke/TIA, and peripheral vascular disease because of vasoconstrictive risk; maximum 2 doses (12 mg total) in 24 hours; frequent daily use (many patients need 1-2 injections/day in an active bout) raises real long-term cardiovascular and medication-overuse concerns that require physician oversight.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.real_working_solution: Self-administered subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg autoinjector at attack onset for patients without cardiovascular contraindications, reserved as the injectable option when oxygen alone is insufficient or unavailable.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.source: Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group (Ekbom K et al), 'Treatment of acute cluster headache with sumatriptan', N Engl J Med 1991;325(5):322-326 (PMID 1647496); Law S, Derry S, Moore RA, 'Triptans for acute cluster headache', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;CD008042; Coppola G et al, J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211)

ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.name: Intranasal Zolmitriptan 5-10 mg -- Real Non-Injectable Triptan Alternative for Needle-Averse Patients
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.type: Selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist (triptan), intranasal spray, acute attack treatment
specific_drugs: Zolmitriptan 5 mg nasal spray (Zomig nasal spray; in India, zolmitriptan is marketed mainly as oral tablets -- Zolmist, Zomig -- intranasal formulation availability is limited)
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.effectiveness: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of intranasal zolmitriptan in episodic CH: pain-free response at 30 minutes in 63% of participants on the 10 mg dose and 48% on the 5 mg dose; numbers needed to treat 4.9 (95% CI 3.3-9.2) for 10 mg and 11 (95% CI 6.4-49) for 5 mg. Only the 5 mg formulation is commercially available in most markets.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.reason_why: Same 5-HT1B/1D agonist mechanism as sumatriptan, absorbed transnasally to avoid injection; onset is slower than subcutaneous sumatriptan but faster than oral triptans.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.important_caveat: Same cardiovascular contraindications as all triptans; slower onset than subcutaneous sumatriptan, so less effective for the fastest-peaking cluster attacks (which can reach maximal pain within 5-10 minutes); the more effective 10 mg dose is not widely marketed.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.source: Cited via Coppola G et al, 'Hallmarks of primary headache: part 3 - cluster headache', J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211), reporting the original intranasal zolmitriptan RCTs in cluster headache

ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.name: Sumatriptan 20 mg Nasal Spray -- Real Non-Injectable Sumatriptan Option
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.type: Selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist (triptan), intranasal spray, acute attack treatment
specific_drugs: Sumatriptan 20 mg nasal spray (Imigran nasal spray; in India: Suminat nasal spray)
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.effectiveness: One randomised controlled trial of sumatriptan 20 mg nasal spray in cluster headache reported 47% of participants pain-free at 30 minutes (versus subcutaneous sumatriptan's 46% pain-free at 15 minutes and 74% attack-improvement at 15 minutes) -- effective, but slower-onset than the injectable form.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.reason_why: Same 5-HT1B/1D agonist mechanism as subcutaneous sumatriptan, delivered nasally; useful for patients who cannot or will not self-inject.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.important_caveat: Same triptan cardiovascular contraindications; nasal absorption is slower and less reliable than subcutaneous injection during a rapidly escalating cluster attack.
ch_acute_sumatriptan_and_triptans.source: Cited via Coppola G et al, J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211), reporting the original sumatriptan nasal-spray RCT in cluster headache

ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.name: Verapamil (High-Dose) -- Real First-Line Prophylactic Agent for Both Episodic and Chronic Cluster Headache
ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.type: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, oral, prophylactic (preventive) treatment
specific_drugs: Verapamil hydrochloride sustained-release tablets, titrated from 120-240 mg/day up to 240-960 mg/day in divided doses (Calaptin SR, Veramil, generic verapamil -- widely available in India)
ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.effectiveness: Leone M et al 2000 Neurology double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy RCT (30 episodic-CH patients, verapamil 120 mg three times daily for 2 weeks after a 5-day run-in): significant reduction in attack frequency and abortive-medication use versus placebo; approximately 80% of patients responded to verapamil versus none on placebo. Verapamil >=240 mg/day is the EFNS Task Force's Level-A/first-choice prophylactic recommendation for cluster headache (May A et al 2006).
ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.reason_why: Verapamil blocks L-type (Cav1.2) voltage-gated calcium channels expressed on trigeminal neurons and is thought to modulate CGRP release and circadian-rhythm-generating hypothalamic circuits implicated in cluster headache's clock-like attack pattern.
ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.important_caveat: Requires a baseline ECG and repeat ECGs at each dose increase because of dose-dependent PR-interval prolongation, bradycardia and atrioventricular block risk (Cohen AS, Matharu MS, Goadsby PJ, Neurology 2007;69:668-675); other side effects include constipation and gingival hyperplasia; onset of prophylactic benefit typically takes 1-3 weeks, so bridging therapy (corticosteroids or nerve block) is used in the interim.
ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.real_working_solution: Start verapamil at 80-120 mg/day, titrate upward every few days to a target of at least 240 mg/day (often 360-720 mg/day is needed) guided by attack frequency and serial ECGs, continued through the expected length of the cluster bout (or indefinitely in chronic CH); bridge the first 1-3 weeks with oral corticosteroids or a suboccipital nerve block.
ch_prophylaxis_verapamil.source: Leone M, D'Amico D, Frediani F et al, 'Verapamil in the prophylaxis of episodic cluster headache: a double-blind study versus placebo', Neurology 2000;54(6):1382-1385 (PMID 10746617); May A et al, 'EFNS guidelines on the treatment of cluster headache and other trigeminal-autonomic cephalalgias', Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077 (PMID 16987158); Bussone G, Leone M, Peccarisi C et al, 'Double blind comparison of lithium and verapamil in cluster headache prophylaxis', Headache 1990;30(7):411-417 (PMID 2205598)

ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.name: Lithium Carbonate -- Real Alternative First/Second-Line Prophylaxis, Especially for Chronic Cluster Headache
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.type: Mood-stabiliser drug repurposed as chronobiological prophylactic, oral, prophylactic treatment
specific_drugs: Lithium carbonate 600-1500 mg/day in divided doses, titrated to a serum level of about 0.6-1.2 mmol/L (Lithosun, generic lithium carbonate -- available in India)
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.effectiveness: Bussone G, Leone M, Peccarisi C et al 1990 double-blind, double-dummy, crossover trial comparing lithium with verapamil in chronic CH prophylaxis: both drugs were effective in preventing attacks, with no significant difference in efficacy, but verapamil caused fewer side effects and had a shorter latency to benefit than lithium. EFNS guideline (2006) recommends lithium as an alternative prophylactic, especially for chronic CH, when verapamil is insufficient or not tolerated.
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.reason_why: Lithium's mechanism in CH is not fully defined but is thought to act on circadian-rhythm-generating hypothalamic pathways (via inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 and modulation of the suprachiasmatic nucleus), consistent with cluster headache's clock-like, seasonally-timed attack pattern.
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.important_caveat: Narrow therapeutic window requires regular serum lithium, thyroid and renal function monitoring; toxicity (tremor, ataxia, renal and thyroid dysfunction) is a real risk; contraindicated with concurrent indomethacin, and caution needed with verapamil (can raise lithium levels).
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.source: Bussone G, Leone M, Peccarisi C et al, 'Double blind comparison of lithium and verapamil in cluster headache prophylaxis', Headache 1990;30(7):411-417 (PMID 2205598); May A et al, Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077 (PMID 16987158)

ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.name: Topiramate and Methysergide -- Real Second-Line/Alternative Prophylactic Agents
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.type: Anticonvulsant (topiramate) and ergot-derivative serotonin antagonist (methysergide), oral, prophylactic treatment
specific_drugs: Topiramate 50-200 mg/day (Topamac, generic topiramate -- available in India)
Methysergide (largely withdrawn from most markets, including India, because of retroperitoneal/pulmonary/cardiac fibrosis risk with prolonged use; historical alternative agent only)
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.effectiveness: EFNS Task Force guideline lists topiramate and methysergide as recommended alternative prophylactic treatments to verapamil and lithium, based on open-label series rather than large placebo-controlled RCTs specific to cluster headache; evidence quality is lower than for verapamil.
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.reason_why: Topiramate modulates voltage-gated sodium/calcium channels and GABA-A/AMPA-kainate glutamate receptors, dampening cortical and trigeminal neuronal excitability; methysergide is a serotonin (5-HT2) receptor antagonist thought to stabilise cranial vascular tone.
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.important_caveat: Methysergide requires drug holidays and monitoring for fibrotic complications and is not marketed in India or most countries today, making topiramate the practically available option in this pair; topiramate carries risk of cognitive slowing, paraesthesia, weight loss, kidney stones and teratogenicity.
ch_prophylaxis_alternatives.source: May A et al, 'EFNS guidelines on the treatment of cluster headache and other trigeminal-autonomic cephalalgias', Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077 (PMID 16987158)

ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.name: Galcanezumab 300 mg Monthly -- Real CGRP-Monoclonal-Antibody Prophylaxis, Proven Only for Episodic Cluster Headache
ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.type: Anti-CGRP humanised monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous injection, prophylactic treatment
specific_drugs: Galcanezumab 120 mg/mL subcutaneous autoinjector (Emgality), dosed as 300 mg (two 120 mg + one additional injection) at baseline and again at month 1 for episodic cluster headache -- a different, higher dose than the 120 mg/month used for migraine
ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.effectiveness: Goadsby PJ et al 2019 NEJM phase 3 RCT (106 patients with episodic CH, 49 galcanezumab / 57 placebo): mean reduction in weekly attack frequency across weeks 1-3 was 8.7 attacks with galcanezumab versus 5.2 with placebo (difference 3.5/week, 95% CI 0.2-6.7, p=0.04); 71% of galcanezumab patients had a >=50% reduction in weekly attack frequency at week 3 versus 53% on placebo. Injection-site pain occurred in 8% of galcanezumab-treated patients.
ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.reason_why: Galcanezumab binds and neutralises calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a neuropeptide released during cluster attacks that is central to trigeminal-autonomic activation; blocking it reduces attack frequency in the episodic (but not chronic) form.
ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.important_caveat: Critically, galcanezumab did NOT work for chronic cluster headache: a dedicated phase 3 RCT (Dodick DW et al 2020 Cephalalgia, 237 patients) found no significant benefit on its primary endpoint (mean weekly-attack reduction -5.4 galcanezumab vs -4.6 placebo, p=0.334) or key secondary endpoints, underscoring that episodic and chronic CH may have distinct underlying biology. It is FDA/EMA-approved only for episodic cluster headache prevention, not chronic.
ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.real_working_solution: Reserve galcanezumab 300 mg (baseline + month 1) for episodic cluster headache patients who cannot tolerate or do not adequately respond to verapamil; do not expect benefit in chronic cluster headache based on current trial evidence, though some real-world case series report benefit from higher off-label doses (240-360 mg monthly) in refractory chronic CH.
ch_cgrp_monoclonal_antibodies.source: Goadsby PJ, Dodick DW, Leone M et al, 'Trial of Galcanezumab in Prevention of Episodic Cluster Headache', N Engl J Med 2019;381(2):132-141 (PMID 31291515); Dodick DW, Goadsby PJ, Lucas C et al, 'Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled study of galcanezumab in patients with chronic cluster headache', Cephalalgia 2020;40(9):935-948 (PMID 32050782); Kudrow D et al, 'Treatment Outcomes in Patients Treated With Galcanezumab vs Placebo... Episodic Cluster Headache', Headache 2020;60(10):2254-2264 (PMID 33179263)

ch_transitional_corticosteroids.name: Oral or Intravenous Corticosteroids -- Real Bridging/Transitional Therapy While Verapamil Is Titrated
ch_transitional_corticosteroids.type: Systemic corticosteroid, oral or IV, transitional (bridging) treatment
specific_drugs: Prednisolone 60-100 mg/day orally, tapered over 2-3 weeks (widely available in India)
Methylprednisolone at least 100 mg/day orally, or up to 500 mg/day IV for 5 days then tapering (per EFNS guideline)
ch_transitional_corticosteroids.effectiveness: No class I/II placebo-controlled RCTs exist, but corticosteroids are considered clearly effective in clinical practice and are a formal EFNS Task Force recommendation for bridging therapy; a large proportion of patients become attack-free within days of starting an adequate steroid taper, though about 79% experience a recurrence of cluster attacks when the steroid is tapered down (necessitating verapamil or another prophylactic to be in place before the taper completes).
ch_transitional_corticosteroids.reason_why: Corticosteroids have broad anti-inflammatory and neuromodulatory effects, including suppression of neurogenic inflammation and CGRP-related trigeminal-autonomic activation, producing a fast (days) but non-durable suppression of attacks.
ch_transitional_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Corticosteroids are not intended for long-term/repeated use because of cumulative steroid toxicity (weight gain, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, adrenal suppression); they are a short bridge to a definitive prophylactic (verapamil, lithium) or to a suboccipital nerve block, not a standalone long-term therapy.
ch_transitional_corticosteroids.source: May A et al, 'EFNS guidelines on the treatment of cluster headache and other trigeminal-autonomic cephalalgias', Eur J Neurol 2006;13(10):1066-1077 (PMID 16987158); Coppola G et al, J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211)

ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.name: Suboccipital/Greater Occipital Nerve Corticosteroid Injection -- Real Randomised-Trial-Proven Transitional Procedure
ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.type: Local anaesthetic + corticosteroid injection around the greater occipital nerve, transitional/bridging procedure
specific_drugs: Cortivazol 3.75 mg (a rapid- and long-acting steroid mixture) injected suboccipitally, 2-3 injections 48-72 hours apart (as used in the Leroux 2011 RCT)
Betamethasone (rapid- + long-acting mixture) suboccipital injection, single dose (as used in the Ambrosini 2005 RCT)
Methylprednisolone plus lidocaine greater occipital nerve block (commonly used formulation in clinical practice)
ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.effectiveness: Two independent double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs confirm real efficacy: (1) Leroux E et al 2011 Lancet Neurology (43 patients with >2 attacks/day, add-on to oral verapamil): 95% (20/21) of patients receiving cortivazol had a mean of 2 or fewer daily attacks after three injections versus 55% (12/22) on placebo (odds ratio 14.5, 95% CI 1.8-116.9, p=0.012). (2) Ambrosini A et al 2005 Pain (23 patients, monotherapy): 85% (11/13) of patients receiving a single betamethasone suboccipital injection were attack-free within 1 week versus 0% (0/10) on placebo (p=0.0001); 62% (8/13) remained attack-free at 4 weeks (p=0.0026), with remission lasting 4-26 months in some. A separate open audit of single greater-occipital-nerve local anaesthetic + corticosteroid injections (Afridi SK et al 2006 Pain) reported complete or partial response in 59% (13/22) of cluster-headache injections, lasting a median of 21 days for partial responders.
ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.reason_why: The greater occipital nerve converges with trigeminal nociceptive afferents in the trigeminocervical complex in the upper cervical spinal cord/brainstem; local corticosteroid delivery near this nerve is thought to dampen this convergent nociceptive circuit well beyond the local anaesthetic's own duration of action, consistent with the multi-week benefit seen in trials.
ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.important_caveat: Most trial data are on it as add-on/transitional therapy alongside oral verapamil, not as a replacement for prophylaxis; effect can wane over weeks to months and injections may need to be repeated; local adverse effects include injection-site neck pain and, rarely, a small patch of localized alopecia.
ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.real_working_solution: Offer a suboccipital/greater occipital nerve corticosteroid injection as bridging therapy at the start of a cluster bout (alongside verapamil titration) for patients with frequent daily attacks, or as an added option when oral steroids are undesirable or contraindicated.
ch_procedure_occipital_nerve_injection.source: Leroux E, Valade D, Taifas I et al, 'Suboccipital steroid injections for transitional treatment of patients with more than two cluster headache attacks per day: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Lancet Neurol 2011;10(10):891-897 (PMID 21903477); Ambrosini A, Vandenheede M, Rossi P et al, 'Suboccipital injection with a mixture of rapid- and long-acting steroids in cluster headache: a double-blind placebo-controlled study', Pain 2005;118(1-2):92-96 (PMID 16202532); Afridi SK, Shields KG, Bhola R, Goadsby PJ, 'Greater occipital nerve injection in primary headache syndromes--prolonged effects from a single injection', Pain 2006;122(1-2):126-129 (PMID 16527404)

ch_investigational_civamide.name: Intranasal Civamide -- Real but Modest Investigational Prophylactic (Not FDA-Approved)
ch_investigational_civamide.type: Synthetic capsaicin analogue (TRPV1 desensitising agent), intranasal solution, investigational prophylactic treatment
specific_drugs: Civamide (cis-capsaicin) 0.025% intranasal solution, 100 microlitres to each nostril once daily for 7 days -- investigational, not an approved marketed product in the US, EU or India
ch_investigational_civamide.effectiveness: Saper JR et al 2002 Arch Neurology multicentre, double-blind, randomised, vehicle-controlled trial (28 episodic-CH patients, 18 civamide / 10 vehicle, 2:1 randomisation): civamide produced a significantly greater percent decrease in headache frequency from baseline during days 1-7 of treatment (-55.5% vs -25.9%, p=0.03), with a trend toward continued benefit in the following weeks (not statistically significant, likely underpowered).
ch_investigational_civamide.reason_why: Civamide desensitises TRPV1-expressing trigeminal sensory afferents in the nasal mucosa (the same afferents implicated in cluster headache's sphenopalatine/trigeminal-autonomic reflex arc), reducing neurogenic activation over repeated dosing.
ch_investigational_civamide.important_caveat: Small trial (n=28); not commercially available as an approved cluster-headache treatment in most countries including India; nasal burning is a common and expected adverse effect of the mechanism itself.
ch_investigational_civamide.source: Saper JR, Klapper J, Mathew NT, Rapoport A, Phillips SB, Bernstein JE, 'Intranasal civamide for the treatment of episodic cluster headaches', Arch Neurol 2002;59(6):990-994 (PMID 12056936)

ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.name: Fremanezumab (Anti-CGRP Monoclonal Antibody) -- Real Negative Trial in Episodic Cluster Headache
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.type: Anti-CGRP humanised monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous injection, tested but not proven effective
specific_drugs: Fremanezumab (Ajovy) -- tested in a placebo-controlled trial for episodic cluster headache prevention
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.effectiveness: Reported as ineffective versus placebo in a placebo-controlled trial in episodic cluster headache using a four-week primary endpoint, in contrast to galcanezumab's positive episodic-CH trial -- illustrating that not every CGRP-pathway antibody works for this indication even though the mechanism is shared.
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.reason_why: Not established why fremanezumab (which targets the CGRP ligand, like galcanezumab) failed where galcanezumab succeeded; possible explanations include differences in trial endpoint timing, dosing, or genuine molecule-specific pharmacodynamic differences in the trigeminal-autonomic system.
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.important_caveat: This is a secondary-sourced negative finding (via the cited 2025 review); the original primary trial report was not independently re-verified against its own PMID/registration in this survey and effectiveness data should be treated as a headline result only.
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.source: Cited via Coppola G et al, 'Hallmarks of primary headache: part 3 - cluster headache', J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211)

ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.name: Galcanezumab in Chronic Cluster Headache -- Real Negative Phase 3 Trial (Included Here for Honesty, Not as a Recommended Option)
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.type: Anti-CGRP humanised monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous injection, negative trial in this subtype
specific_drugs: Galcanezumab 300 mg monthly, subcutaneous (same drug/dose that is effective in episodic CH, tested separately in chronic CH)
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.effectiveness: Dodick DW et al 2020 Cephalalgia phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled RCT (237 chronic-CH patients, 117 galcanezumab / 120 placebo, 12-week double-blind period): primary endpoint (mean change in weekly attack frequency) was NOT met -- galcanezumab -5.4 vs placebo -4.6 (p=0.334); key secondary endpoints (>=50% responder rate, sustained response) also not met. Injection-site erythema was more common with galcanezumab.
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.reason_why: Suggests chronic cluster headache may have distinct underlying pathophysiology from episodic CH, in which the same drug and dose are effective; the trial authors explicitly note this points to a biological difference between the two subtypes rather than a dosing failure.
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.important_caveat: Included here so the ranked-treatment table and curative_option above do not overstate galcanezumab's evidence base; galcanezumab should not be presented to chronic-CH patients as proven effective.
ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence.source: Dodick DW, Goadsby PJ, Lucas C, Jensen R et al, 'Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled study of galcanezumab in patients with chronic cluster headache: Results from 3-month double-blind treatment', Cephalalgia 2020;40(9):935-948 (PMID 32050782)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Suboccipital cortivazol injection, add-on to oral verapamil (Leroux 2011 RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 95.2% (20/21) of patients receiving 3 suboccipital cortivazol injections (add-on to verapamil) had a mean of 2 or fewer daily attacks, versus 55% (12/22) on placebo add-on (OR 14.5, 95% CI 1.8-116.9, p=0.012); randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=43 (28 episodic + 15 chronic CH).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Leroux E, Valade D, Taifas I et al, Lancet Neurol 2011;10(10):891-897 (PMID 21903477)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Suboccipital betamethasone injection, monotherapy (Ambrosini 2005 RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 84.6% (11/13) of patients were attack-free within 1 week of a single suboccipital betamethasone injection versus 0% (0/10) on placebo (p=0.0001); 61.5% (8/13) remained attack-free at 4 weeks (p=0.0026). Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=23 (16 episodic + 7 chronic CH).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ambrosini A, Vandenheede M, Rossi P et al, Pain 2005;118(1-2):92-96 (PMID 16202532)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Verapamil (>=240 mg/day) prophylaxis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Approximately 80% of episodic-CH patients responded (significant reduction in attack frequency and abortive-medication use) to verapamil 120 mg three times daily versus 0% (no) responders on placebo. Double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled RCT, n=30.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Leone M, D'Amico D, Frediani F et al, Neurology 2000;54(6):1382-1385 (PMID 10746617)

ranked_high_to_low.name: High-flow 100% oxygen, 12 L/min for 15 min
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 78% (95% CI 71-85%) of 150 oxygen-treated attacks were pain-free/adequately relieved at 15 minutes versus 20% (95% CI 14-26%) of 148 air-placebo attacks (p<0.001). Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover RCT, n=76 analysed (109 randomised).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cohen AS, Burns B, Goadsby PJ, JAMA 2009;302(22):2451-2457 (PMID 19996400)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 74% of sumatriptan-treated attacks improved to no/mild pain within 15 minutes versus 26% with placebo (p<0.001); pain-free at 15 min in 46% vs 10%. Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover RCT, n=39 evaluable of 49 randomised. Pooled across RCTs, NNT 2.4-3.3 for pain relief; pooled 15-minute pain-free rate approximately 46-49%.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group (Ekbom K et al), N Engl J Med 1991;325(5):322-326 (PMID 1647496)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Galcanezumab 300 mg monthly (episodic cluster headache only)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 71% of galcanezumab-treated episodic-CH patients had a >=50% reduction in weekly attack frequency at week 3 versus 53% on placebo; mean reduction 8.7 vs 5.2 attacks/week (p=0.04). Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 RCT, n=106. NOT effective in chronic cluster headache (see negative-evidence entry).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Goadsby PJ, Dodick DW, Leone M et al, N Engl J Med 2019;381(2):132-141 (PMID 31291515)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intranasal zolmitriptan 10 mg
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 63% of participants were pain-free at 30 minutes with the 10 mg intranasal dose (NNT 4.9, 95% CI 3.3-9.2) in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; only the lower-efficacy 5 mg formulation (48% pain-free, NNT 11) is widely marketed.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cited via Coppola G et al, J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211), reporting the original intranasal zolmitriptan RCTs

ranked_high_to_low.name: Greater occipital nerve block, local anaesthetic + corticosteroid (open audit, single injection)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 59% (13/22) of cluster-headache greater-occipital-nerve injections yielded a complete or partial response, lasting a median of 21 days for partial responders. Open clinical audit (not placebo-controlled), n=22 injections in cluster-headache patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Afridi SK, Shields KG, Bhola R, Goadsby PJ, Pain 2006;122(1-2):126-129 (PMID 16527404)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intranasal civamide (investigational)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 55.5% reduction in cluster-headache frequency from baseline during days 1-7 of treatment, versus 25.9% reduction with vehicle (p=0.03). This is a percent-reduction-in-frequency metric, NOT a responder/pain-free rate, and is not directly comparable to the other rows. Randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trial, n=28 (18 civamide + 10 vehicle).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Saper JR, Klapper J, Mathew NT et al, Arch Neurol 2002;59(6):990-994 (PMID 12056936)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sumatriptan 20 mg nasal spray
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 47% of participants pain-free at 30 minutes in a randomised controlled trial -- effective but slower-onset than subcutaneous sumatriptan (46% pain-free at 15 minutes, 74% attack-improvement at 15 minutes).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cited via Coppola G et al, J Headache Pain 2025;26(1):196 (PMID 41039211), reporting the original sumatriptan nasal-spray RCT

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These effectiveness_pct figures come from different trial designs (double-blind RCT vs open audit), different endpoints (pain-free at 15/30 min vs >=50% attack-frequency responder vs percent reduction in frequency vs proportion attack-free at 1 week), and different cluster-headache subtypes (episodic vs chronic vs mixed) -- they are NOT a single head-to-head comparison and should not be read as a strict ranking of clinical superiority. Galcanezumab (rank 6) is proven only for episodic cluster headache and was NOT effective in chronic cluster headache in its dedicated RCT (PMID 32050782); fremanezumab was ineffective in episodic cluster headache and is excluded from this ranking as a negative result (see exhaustive_medicine_survey.ch_negative_and_neutral_evidence). In real-world practice, oxygen and subcutaneous sumatriptan are used together as first-line acute therapy, and verapamil is the default first-line prophylactic, with suboccipital nerve injection or oral corticosteroids as bridging therapy.

frontotemporal_dementia.name: Frontotemporal Dementia

definition.finding: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a clinical syndrome caused by frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) - a group of neurodegenerative diseases characterised by progressive atrophy of the frontal and/or temporal lobes. It presents either as behavioural-variant FTD (bvFTD, with progressive personality/behaviour change) or as one of the primary progressive aphasia (PPA) syndromes (progressive language decline). FTD is the second most common cause of early-onset dementia (typically manifesting before age 65), after Alzheimer's disease.
definition.source: Onyike CU, Diehl-Schmid J, 'The epidemiology of frontotemporal dementia', Int Rev Psychiatry 2013;25(2):130-137, PMID 23611343

ftld_tdp43_pathology.finding: Roughly half of FTLD cases show TDP-43 proteinopathy (FTLD-TDP, subtypes A-D based on the morphology/distribution of neuronal inclusions), the pathological substrate most strongly linked to GRN mutations and to the C9orf72 repeat expansion.
ftld_tdp43_pathology.source: Greaves CV, Rohrer JD, 'An update on genetic frontotemporal dementia', J Neurol 2019;266(8):2075-2086, PMID 31119452 (Europe PMC PMC6647117)

ftld_tau_pathology.finding: The remainder of sporadic FTLD cases (roughly the other half, alongside FTLD-TDP) show tauopathy (FTLD-tau: Pick's disease, corticobasal degeneration, progressive supranuclear palsy, or MAPT-mutation-associated tauopathy), and a smaller minority show FUS proteinopathy (FTLD-FUS). Overall, about 70% of all FTD is sporadic, split roughly evenly between TDP-43 and tau pathology, with a smaller number of FUS cases; the remaining ~30% is genetic.
ftld_tau_pathology.source: Greaves CV, Rohrer JD, J Neurol 2019;266(8):2075-2086, PMID 31119452

c9orf72_repeat_expansion.finding: A hexanucleotide (GGGGCC) repeat expansion in the non-coding region of C9orf72 is the single most common genetic cause of FTD worldwide, and also the most common known genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) - the same expansion causes both diseases, reflecting a shared TDP-43-driven pathological spectrum.
