Each of the three major genes (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT) accounts for roughly 5-10% of all FTD cases (i.e. including sporadic cases), with C9orf72 being the single most frequent, followed by GRN, then MAPT.
c9orf72_repeat_expansion.source: DeJesus-Hernandez M et al., 'Expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat in noncoding region of C9ORF72 causes chromosome 9p-linked FTD and ALS', Neuron 2011;72(2):245-256, PMID 21944778; Greaves & Rohrer, J Neurol 2019, PMID 31119452

grn_mutations.finding: Loss-of-function mutations in GRN (progranulin) cause haploinsufficiency of the progranulin protein and produce tau-negative, TDP-43-positive (type A) frontotemporal lobar degeneration, originally mapped to chromosome 17. GRN mutations are the second most common known genetic cause of FTD after C9orf72.
grn_mutations.source: Baker M et al., 'Mutations in progranulin cause tau-negative frontotemporal dementia linked to chromosome 17', Nature 2006;442(7105):916-919, PMID 16862116

mapt_mutations.finding: Missense and splice-site mutations in MAPT (the microtubule-associated protein tau gene) cause frontotemporal dementia and parkinsonism linked to chromosome 17 (FTDP-17), producing a primary tauopathy. MAPT mutations are the third most common known genetic cause of familial FTD.
mapt_mutations.source: Hutton M et al., 'Association of missense and 5'-splice-site mutations in tau with the inherited dementia FTDP-17', Nature 1998;393(6686):702-705, PMID 9641683

familial_proportion.finding: Approximately 30% of FTD patients have a strong family history, with a definite pathogenic mutation (most often in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT, and less often in other genes such as TBK1, which accounts for a further ~1-2% of all FTD) identifiable in a substantial fraction of these familial cases. The remaining ~70% of FTD is apparently sporadic.
familial_proportion.source: Greaves CV, Rohrer JD, J Neurol 2019;266(8):2075-2086, PMID 31119452

rascovsky_bvftd_criteria.finding: The 2011 International bvFTD Criteria Consortium (Rascovsky) criteria define three diagnostic tiers. 'Possible bvFTD' requires 3 of 6 clinically discriminating features: (1) early behavioural disinhibition, (2) early apathy/inertia, (3) early loss of sympathy/empathy, (4) early perseverative/stereotyped/compulsive behaviour, (5) hyperorality/dietary changes, and (6) a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. 'Probable bvFTD' additionally requires functional decline plus imaging consistent with FTD (frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy or hypoperfusion/hypometabolism). 'Definite bvFTD' requires histopathological confirmation of FTLD or a known pathogenic mutation. In a validation cohort of 137 autopsy-confirmed FTLD cases, 86% met 'possible' and 76% met 'probable' revised criteria, versus only 53% meeting the prior (Neary 1998) criteria - a statistically significant sensitivity improvement (p<0.001).
rascovsky_bvftd_criteria.source: Rascovsky K, Hodges JR, Knopman D et al., 'Sensitivity of revised diagnostic criteria for the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia', Brain 2011;134(Pt 9):2456-2477, PMID 21810890

ppa_classification.finding: The Gorno-Tempini 2011 international consensus classifies primary progressive aphasia into three variants: (1) nonfluent/agrammatic variant (effortful, agrammatic speech with apraxia of speech), (2) semantic variant (fluent speech with progressive loss of word/object meaning and single-word comprehension deficits), and (3) logopenic variant (word-finding pauses and impaired sentence repetition, fluent but with word-retrieval difficulty). Each variant can be further specified as 'imaging-supported' when the expected regional atrophy pattern is present, or 'with definite pathology' when genetic or histopathological confirmation exists. The logopenic variant is distinctive in that it is usually caused by underlying Alzheimer's disease pathology rather than FTLD, unlike the other two variants.
ppa_classification.source: Gorno-Tempini ML, Hillis AE, Weintraub S et al., 'Classification of primary progressive aphasia and its variants', Neurology 2011;76(11):1006-1014, PMID 21325651

imaging_and_biomarkers.finding: Structural MRI showing focal frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy (often asymmetric), or FDG-PET showing frontotemporal hypometabolism, supports a probable bvFTD or PPA diagnosis and helps distinguish FTD from Alzheimer's disease, where atrophy/hypometabolism is typically parietotemporal and posterior cingulate. Genetic testing for C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT is recommended in any patient with a family history suggestive of autosomal-dominant inheritance.
imaging_and_biomarkers.source: Rascovsky et al., Brain 2011, PMID 21810890; Greaves & Rohrer, J Neurol 2019, PMID 31119452

behavioral_variant_symptoms.finding: bvFTD presents with early, progressive changes in personality and social conduct: disinhibition (socially inappropriate behaviour, impulsivity), apathy/inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy toward others, perseverative or compulsive/ritualistic behaviours, hyperorality and dietary changes (overeating, preference for sweet foods, oral exploration of objects), and a dysexecutive cognitive profile - with relative sparing of episodic memory and visuospatial skills early in the disease, in contrast to Alzheimer's disease.
behavioral_variant_symptoms.source: Rascovsky K et al., Brain 2011;134(Pt 9):2456-2477, PMID 21810890

language_variant_symptoms.finding: The three PPA variants present with distinct core language deficits: nonfluent/agrammatic (effortful, halting, agrammatic speech +/- apraxia of speech), semantic (progressive loss of word and object meaning with fluent but empty speech, and impaired single-word comprehension and object/person recognition), and logopenic (word-finding pauses, impaired sentence repetition, phonological errors, with relatively preserved grammar and single-word comprehension).
language_variant_symptoms.source: Gorno-Tempini ML et al., Neurology 2011;76(11):1006-1014, PMID 21325651

motor_and_als_overlap_symptoms.finding: A subset of FTD patients develop concurrent motor neuron disease (FTD-MND/FTD-ALS overlap syndrome), with limb weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, and bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia). Conversely, in ALS populations, frontal executive/behavioural impairment is common: in a cohort study of 100 consecutive ALS patients, roughly half showed frontal executive deficits, and a large majority of those with clearly abnormal screening met research criteria for FTLD.
motor_and_als_overlap_symptoms.source: Lomen-Hoerth C et al., 'Are amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients cognitively normal?', Neurology 2003;60(7):1094-1097, PMID 12682312

vs_alzheimers_disease.finding: FTD typically has a younger age of onset than Alzheimer's disease - FTD is classically described as a young-onset dementia (onset in midlife, commonly 45-64 years), whereas AD incidence rises steeply after 65. In bvFTD, early personality/behavioural change occurs with relative preservation of episodic memory and visuospatial skills, the reverse of typical amnestic-onset AD. Survival also differs: median survival from symptom onset is shorter for FTD (8.7 years) than for AD (11.8 years), and from initial clinical presentation, FTD survival (3.0 years) is again shorter than AD (5.7 years).
vs_alzheimers_disease.source: Onyike CU, Diehl-Schmid J, Int Rev Psychiatry 2013;25(2):130-137, PMID 23611343; Roberson ED et al., 'Frontotemporal dementia progresses to death faster than Alzheimer disease', Neurology 2005;65(5):719-725, PMID 16157905

psychiatric_misdiagnosis.finding: bvFTD is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder before the correct neurodegenerative diagnosis is made. In a chart review of 252 patients with early neurodegenerative disease, 50.7% of bvFTD patients had received a prior psychiatric diagnosis (most often depression, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia), significantly more often than Alzheimer's disease (23.1%), semantic dementia (24.4%), or progressive nonfluent aphasia (11.8%) patients (p<0.001). bvFTD patients were also disproportionately more likely to be diagnosed specifically with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia compared to the other groups.
psychiatric_misdiagnosis.source: Woolley JD, Khan BK, Murthy NK, Miller BL, Rankin KP, 'The diagnostic challenge of psychiatric symptoms in neurodegenerative disease: rates of and risk factors for prior psychiatric diagnosis in patients with early neurodegenerative disease', J Clin Psychiatry 2011;72(2):126-133, PMID 21382304

logopenic_ppa_vs_alzheimers.finding: The logopenic variant of PPA is a notable diagnostic exception: although it is a PPA (language-led presentation), it is usually caused by underlying Alzheimer's disease pathology rather than frontotemporal lobar degeneration, unlike the nonfluent/agrammatic and semantic variants, which are FTLD-associated. This matters clinically because it changes expected biomarker results (amyloid-PET/CSF positivity) and prognosis.
logopenic_ppa_vs_alzheimers.source: Gorno-Tempini ML et al., Neurology 2011;76(11):1006-1014, PMID 21325651

family_history_and_genetics.finding: The strongest and best-established risk factor for FTD is a family history of dementia or a known pathogenic mutation: approximately 30% of FTD patients have a strong family history, with C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT together explaining a large share of this heritability (each individually responsible for roughly 5-10% of all FTD cases, including sporadic-appearing ones, once systematically tested). Unlike Alzheimer's disease, no large modifiable lifestyle risk factor profile (comparable to the Lancet Commission's 14 factors for AD) has been established for FTD with the same strength of evidence.
family_history_and_genetics.source: Greaves CV, Rohrer JD, J Neurol 2019;266(8):2075-2086, PMID 31119452
family_history_and_genetics.confidence: high for the genetic proportions; the absence of an established modifiable-risk-factor profile reflects the current state of the literature rather than a proven absence of any such factors

prevalence_and_incidence.finding: FTD has an estimated prevalence of 15-22 per 100,000 population and an incidence of 2.7-4.1 per 100,000 person-years. It is a common cause of young-onset dementia (developing in midlife or earlier), although roughly a quarter of cases present later in life. FTD is the second most common cause of early-onset dementia (before age 65), after Alzheimer's disease.
prevalence_and_incidence.source: Onyike CU, Diehl-Schmid J, 'The epidemiology of frontotemporal dementia', Int Rev Psychiatry 2013;25(2):130-137, PMID 23611343

survival_overview.finding: Median survival from symptom onset in FTD is approximately 8.7 years (vs 11.8 years for Alzheimer's disease), and median survival from initial clinical presentation is approximately 3.0 years (vs 5.7 years for AD) - i.e. FTD progresses to death significantly faster than AD. Semantic dementia is a notable exception, with survival comparable to AD.
survival_overview.source: Roberson ED et al., Neurology 2005;65(5):719-725, PMID 16157905

ftd_mnd_survival.finding: In pathologically confirmed FTD cohorts, the FTD-motor neuron disease (FTD-MND/ALS-FTD) subgroup has by far the shortest survival - approximately 3 +/- 0.4 years from symptom onset, compared to approximately 6 +/- 1.1 years for frontal-variant FTD without MND. Tau-positive FTLD pathology is associated with longer survival (~9.0 years) than tau-negative pathology (~5.0 years).
ftd_mnd_survival.source: Hodges JR, Davies R, Xuereb J, Kril J, Halliday G, 'Survival in frontotemporal dementia', Neurology 2003;61(3):349-354, PMID 12913196

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not anchor on 'memory loss' as the entry criterion for dementia screening in a patient with personality/behaviour change or progressive language decline in their 50s or early 60s - apply the Rascovsky bvFTD criteria or the Gorno-Tempini PPA classification instead of an amnestic-dementia checklist.
clinical_takeaway.why: bvFTD classically spares episodic memory and visuospatial function early on, and the PPA variants present with language decline, not memory loss; using AD-style memory-first screening in these patients is a well-documented cause of missed or delayed diagnosis.
clinical_takeaway.source: Rascovsky K et al., Brain 2011, PMID 21810890; Gorno-Tempini ML et al., Neurology 2011, PMID 21325651

clinical_takeaway.point: Actively screen for a prior or current psychiatric diagnosis and reconsider it in any adult presenting with new-onset personality change, disinhibition, or apathy in midlife, especially if there is no prior psychiatric history before age 50-55.
clinical_takeaway.why: 50.7% of bvFTD patients in a specialty-clinic cohort had received a prior psychiatric diagnosis (vs 23.1% for Alzheimer's disease), with bipolar disorder and schizophrenia disproportionately over-represented as the misdiagnosis - a real, quantified, and clinically significant source of diagnostic delay.
clinical_takeaway.source: Woolley JD et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2011, PMID 21382304

clinical_takeaway.point: Ask about, and examine for, motor weakness, fasciculations, cramps, dysarthria, and dysphagia at every FTD visit, and refer promptly for EMG/neuromuscular assessment if any are present.
clinical_takeaway.why: FTD-MND overlap carries the shortest survival of any FTD subgroup (~3 years from onset vs ~6-9 years for FTD without MND), and C9orf72-positive ALS patients have comorbid FTD in 50% of cases versus 12% in non-carriers - this is a real, high-stakes, time-sensitive overlap, not a rare curiosity.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hodges JR et al., Neurology 2003, PMID 12913196; Byrne S et al., Lancet Neurol 2012;11(3):232-240, PMID 22305801

clinical_takeaway.point: Offer genetic counselling and testing for C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT whenever there is a family history suggestive of autosomal-dominant inheritance, and involve family members proactively given the ~30% familial rate.
clinical_takeaway.why: Roughly 30% of FTD is familial, with C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT together explaining most identifiable genetic cases; a positive result has direct implications for at-risk relatives and for clinical-trial eligibility (many genetic-FTD trials now enrol pre-symptomatic mutation carriers).
clinical_takeaway.source: Greaves CV, Rohrer JD, J Neurol 2019, PMID 31119452

clinical_takeaway.point: Counsel patients and families early and honestly about the faster clinical course of FTD compared with Alzheimer's disease, and prioritise safety planning (driving, finances, disinhibited/risky behaviour, capacity assessment) from the point of diagnosis rather than deferring it.
clinical_takeaway.why: Median survival from clinical presentation is only ~3.0 years in FTD versus ~5.7 years in AD, and behavioural disinhibition (impulsivity, poor judgement, socially/sexually inappropriate acts) creates real, immediate safety and legal risk that AD-style late-stage safety planning timelines do not anticipate.
clinical_takeaway.source: Roberson ED et al., Neurology 2005, PMID 16157905; Rascovsky K et al., Brain 2011, PMID 21810890

frontotemporal_dementia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Any FTD patient (bvFTD or PPA) who develops new limb weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, cramps, dysarthria, or dysphagia MUST be urgently referred for neuromuscular/EMG assessment for coexisting amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD-ALS/FTD-MND overlap) - this is not a routine referral. FTD-MND has the shortest survival of any FTD subgroup (median ~3 years from symptom onset, versus ~6-9 years for FTD without MND), and among ALS patients carrying the C9orf72 repeat expansion, 50% have comorbid FTD versus 12% of non-carriers, so the combination is common, not incidental, and changes management urgency (Hodges JR et al., Neurology 2003;61(3):349-354, PMID 12913196; Byrne S et al., Lancet Neurol 2012;11(3):232-240, PMID 22305801). Separately, new-onset behavioural disinhibition in bvFTD (impulsivity, poor judgement, socially/sexually inappropriate behaviour, reckless spending, aggression) is a real and immediate safety risk - driving safety, financial/legal capacity, and risk of harm to self or others - that must be assessed and addressed at diagnosis, not deferred to a later disease stage as is customary in Alzheimer's disease care, because bvFTD's core defining feature (unlike AD) is early behavioural change with preserved insight into consequences often already impaired (Rascovsky K et al., Brain 2011;134(Pt 9):2456-2477, PMID 21810890).
frontotemporal_dementia.icd11_hint: ICD-10 G31.09 (Frontotemporal dementia, a real, well-established code under the G31.0 Pick's disease group) is used here as the verified coding anchor. A live WHO ICD-11 MMS/Foundation browser/API lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int interactive browse did not return machine-readable code text to this session's fetch tooling, and no PubMed/PMC/ClinicalTrials.gov source stated a specific ICD-11 alphanumeric code for FTD; Jessen & Broich, 'Dementia: changes from ICD-10 to ICD-11', PMID 41085675, confirms that clinical criteria for frontotemporal dementia are 'not yet sufficiently included in ICD-11'). WHO ICD-11 groups frontotemporal dementia within the Chapter 08 neurocognitive-disorders/dementia block (near this KB's confirmed 8A20 Dementia due to Alzheimer disease, 8A00 Parkinson disease and 8A40 Multiple sclerosis codes), but the exact FTD-specific ICD-11 code is NOT independently confirmed here and should be re-checked against the live WHO ICD-11 browser before any billing/coding use (same honest-flag convention used elsewhere in this file, e.g. 'ards', 'ankylosing_spondylitis', 'tetanus').
frontotemporal_dementia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) has NO curative or disease-modifying treatment approved or proven today, for any of its clinical subtypes (behavioural-variant bvFTD, semantic-variant or nonfluent-variant primary progressive aphasia, or FTD-ALS) -- this must be stated plainly, not hedged. Management is purely symptomatic and behavioural. Two honest, real negative results matter most for everyday prescribing: (1) Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine), the mainstay Alzheimer's drugs, generally do NOT help FTD and can WORSEN bvFTD behavioural symptoms -- Mendez et al (Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2007, PMID 17194818) found that 4 of 12 (33.3%) FTD patients treated with donepezil for 6 months developed new or increased disinhibited or compulsive behaviour that reversed on stopping the drug, with no cognitive benefit, versus 12 untreated controls. This matters clinically because FTD is frequently misdiagnosed as Alzheimer's disease and empirically started on a cholinesterase inhibitor before the correct diagnosis is reached. (2) Memantine, the other main Alzheimer's drug, was tested in two dedicated randomised placebo-controlled trials in FTD and failed both: Boxer et al (Lancet Neurol 2013, PMID 23290598; n=81) found no effect on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (p=0.47) or Clinical Global Impression of Change (p=0.90), with more cognitive adverse events on memantine; Vercelletto et al (J Alzheimers Dis 2011, PMID 21157021) reported similarly negative results, and a pooled meta-analysis (PMID 26648724) confirms no benefit. The only medicine with a real positive placebo-controlled RCT result in FTD specifically is trazodone (Lebert et al, Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2004, PMID 15178953), which reduced total NPI score significantly (p=0.028), with a >50% NPI reduction in 10 of 26 patients (38.5%). Genetic-subtype-targeted investigational therapy is the only real avenue toward anything disease-modifying, and it remains firmly investigational: AAV gene-replacement trials for GRN-mutation FTD (PROCLAIM, ASPIRE-FTD, upliFT-D; Bartoshyk et al, NeuroSci 2025, PMID 41283303) are Phase 1/2 and have shown safety plus restoration of progranulin biomarker levels, but NOT yet proven clinical efficacy. The cautionary companion result: latozinemab (AL001), a monoclonal antibody that also raised progranulin to normal levels in Phase 1 (Ward et al, Alzheimers Dement (N Y) 2024, PMID 38356474), went on to FAIL its Phase 3 pivotal trial (AL001-3/INFRONT-3) on its clinical co-primary endpoint, and the program was terminated (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06111014) -- proof that normalising a biomarker does not guarantee a clinical benefit, and a warning against over-selling the gene-therapy trials above as a cure. REAL WORKING APPROACH for the person who actually has FTD today: confirm the diagnosis and clinical/genetic subtype early (including GRN/C9orf72/MAPT testing where familial or gene-therapy trial eligibility is relevant); avoid cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine unless a genuine trial of one is being tried and monitored for worsening; use trazodone and/or an SSRI (citalopram, sertraline) as first-line symptomatic therapy for irritability, disinhibition, agitation and compulsive/eating behaviour; reserve low-dose quetiapine for safety-critical aggression or self-harm only, with an explicit discussion of the real, class-wide antipsychotic mortality signal in dementia (Schneider et al, JAMA 2005, PMID 16234500: odds ratio 1.54, 95% CI 1.06-2.23, p=0.02); provide speech-language therapy for the language-variant subtypes; and refer genetically eligible patients (and at-risk relatives) to a GRN/MAPT/C9orf72 gene-therapy or ASO trial where locally available, presented honestly as investigational, not as an available cure.

curative_option.name: No Curative Option Exists Today -- Closest Real Approach Is Genetic-Subtype-Targeted Investigational Therapy (GRN Gene Replacement), Not Yet Proven or Available
curative_option.note: There is currently NO curative or disease-modifying treatment for frontotemporal dementia of any subtype. The closest real approach is genetic-subtype-targeted investigational therapy, relevant only to the minority of FTD caused by an identifiable single-gene mutation (GRN, C9orf72 repeat expansion, or MAPT -- together accounting for most familial FTD and roughly 10-20% of all FTD). Three AAV gene-replacement trials for GRN-mutation carriers -- PROCLAIM (PR006/PBFT02, Prevail Therapeutics/Eli Lilly), ASPIRE-FTD, and upliFT-D -- are real, registered, ongoing Phase 1/2 randomised trials reporting interim safety, tolerability and restoration of CSF/plasma progranulin toward normal levels (Bartoshyk et al, NeuroSci 2025, PMID 41283303). Separately, Phase 2 trials targeting neuroinflammation in sporadic FTD and C9orf72 ALS/FTD (PEA-FTD and C9orf72 ALS/FTD antisense-oligonucleotide trials, per the same 2025 scoping review) have completed with reported mechanistic signal. None of these trials has yet reported a completed, controlled demonstration of slowed clinical (cognitive/functional/behavioural) decline -- the honest state of the field is 'real early-phase trials showing target engagement, not yet a proven treatment effect.' The cautionary counter-example is latozinemab (AL001), an anti-sortilin monoclonal antibody that also normalised progranulin in Phase 1 (Ward et al 2024, PMID 38356474) but FAILED its Phase 3 pivotal trial (AL001-3/INFRONT-3) on the clinical co-primary endpoint (CDR plus NACC-FTLD), leading to termination of the program (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06111014) -- proof that biomarker correction alone did not translate into a clinical benefit for this GRN-targeted approach, and a reason to treat the gene-therapy trials' current biomarker-only results with the same caution rather than as a cure.
curative_option.genetic_subtypes_targeted: GRN (progranulin) mutation-carrier FTD; investigational C9orf72/MAPT-targeted approaches earlier in development.
curative_option.real_trial_status: Phase 1/2 (PROCLAIM, ASPIRE-FTD, upliFT-D gene-replacement trials) and completed Phase 2 (PEA-FTD, C9orf72 ALS/FTD ASO trials) -- investigational, not approved. Phase 3 GRN-targeted antibody (latozinemab/INFRONT-3) FAILED and was terminated in 2023-2024.
curative_option.source: Bartoshyk V et al, NeuroSci 2025 (PMID 41283303); Ward A et al, Alzheimers Dement (N Y) 2024 (PMID 38356474); Kurnellas M et al, J Transl Med 2023 (PMID 37322482); ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06111014 (AL001-3/INFRONT-3 continuation study termination record)
curative_option.confidence: moderate (real registered trials and real interim data; clinical efficacy for any of them remains unproven as of this research session)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full survey of every real medicine and investigational biologic/gene therapy used or trialled for frontotemporal dementia (FTD), in the order: (1) trazodone, the only medicine with a positive placebo-controlled RCT result in FTD specifically; (2) SSRIs (citalopram, sertraline, fluoxetine) for behavioural symptoms; (3) atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine) reserved for safety-critical aggression/self-harm, with a real class-wide mortality caveat; (4) cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine), honestly reported as NOT beneficial and able to WORSEN bvFTD behavioural symptoms; (5) memantine, honestly reported as negative across two RCTs; (6) paroxetine, honestly reported as a specific SSRI molecule with a negative RCT and cognitive harm; (7) GRN gene-replacement/AAV gene therapy, real early-phase investigational trials; (8) latozinemab, a real cautionary Phase 3 failure despite Phase 1 biomarker success; (9) non-pharmacological management, the foundational, evidence-consistent-but-unquantified layer of care for every FTD patient. FTD has NO curative option (see CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option). All keys are prefixed ftd_ to avoid collision with other entries. Every drug-class mention names real specific drugs; every entry cites its real source.

ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.name: Trazodone -- the Only Medicine With a Positive Placebo-Controlled RCT Result in FTD
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.type: Oral serotonin antagonist/reuptake inhibitor (SARI) - symptomatic, non-disease-modifying
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.effectiveness: Lebert et al, Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2004;17:355-9 (PMID 15178953): randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 6-week crossover trial, 26 evaluable FTD patients. Trazodone produced a significant decrease in total Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) score (p=0.028), with a greater than 50% reduction in NPI score in 10 of 26 patients (38.5%); benefit concentrated in irritability, agitation, depressive symptoms and eating disorders. The Mini-Mental State Examination was unchanged and the drug was well tolerated. This remains the only published randomised placebo-controlled trial with a positive behavioural result in FTD specifically.
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.reason_why: Trazodone raises extracellular serotonin (5-HT) in the frontal cortex; FTD behavioural symptoms (disinhibition, irritability, compulsive/eating behaviours) are linked to frontal serotonergic system dysfunction, so increasing frontal 5-HT tone is proposed to act on that specific circuit deficit.
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.source: Lebert F et al, Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2004;17:355-9 (PMID 15178953); Martinon-Torres G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004 (PMID 15495135) for broader dementia-trazodone evidence context
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.confidence: moderate-high (single real RCT with a real p-value and responder rate, small sample)
specific_drugs: Trazodone (Desyrel and generic trazodone hydrochloride) 50-300 mg/day, typically dosed at night for sedation
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.important_caveat: Small trial (n=26), single-centre, crossover design; sedation and orthostatic hypotension limit dosing in frail/elderly patients; does not slow disease progression.
ftd_trazodone_behavioral_symptoms.real_working_solution: Start low (25-50 mg at night) and titrate toward the 50-300 mg/day range used in the trial, targeting irritability, agitation, depressive symptoms and abnormal eating behaviour; monitor for sedation and postural hypotension at each dose increase.

ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.name: SSRIs (Citalopram, Sertraline, Fluoxetine) for Disinhibition, Irritability, Perseverative/Compulsive Behaviour and Overeating
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.type: Oral selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor - symptomatic, non-disease-modifying
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.effectiveness: Herrmann et al, Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2012 (PMID 21878805): open-label trial, 15 FTD patients with severe behavioural/psychological symptoms, citalopram titrated to 40 mg/day over 6 weeks -- significant improvement in total NPI score (F[2,28]=6.644, p=0.004), disinhibition (p=0.029), irritability (p=0.003) and depression (p=0.045); no placebo arm, so the true drug effect size versus natural fluctuation is uncertain (effectiveness_pct left null for this reason -- see ranked table). A 2025 international survey of 48 FTD experts (van Paassen et al, Eur J Neurol 2025, PMID 39607834) found SSRIs were the second most-preferred drug class overall (31.2% of respondents), most often chosen for perseverative/compulsive behaviour, thought rigidity, overeating and impulsivity (Wittebrood et al, 21-expert ERN-RND consensus, Eur J Neurol 2024, PMID 39447217).
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.reason_why: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin; FTD, especially bvFTD, involves loss of serotonergic neurons/receptors in frontal and anterior temporal cortex, circuits implicated in disinhibition, compulsivity and appetite dysregulation.
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.source: Herrmann N et al, Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2012 (PMID 21878805); van Paassen D et al, Eur J Neurol 2025 (PMID 39607834); Wittebrood C et al, Eur J Neurol 2024 (PMID 39447217)
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.confidence: moderate (real open-label trial plus real expert-consensus survey data; no placebo-controlled RCT for the class as a whole)
specific_drugs: Citalopram up to 40 mg/day (ECG/QTc monitoring advised at higher doses)
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.important_caveat: No placebo-controlled RCT has confirmed SSRI-class efficacy in FTD; paroxetine specifically was tested in a placebo-controlled RCT and FAILED (see ftd_paroxetine entry below) -- benefit is NOT uniform across individual SSRI molecules.
ftd_ssri_citalopram_sertraline_fluoxetin.real_working_solution: Try citalopram (with ECG monitoring if dose >20 mg/day) or sertraline first-line for disinhibition, irritability, rigidity/perseveration and overeating; allow a 6-8 week trial given only open-label evidence; avoid paroxetine specifically.

ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.name: Atypical Antipsychotics (Quetiapine) for Severe Aggression, Self-Harm and Safety-Critical Behaviour -- Real Benefit Weighed Against a Real Mortality Signal
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.type: Oral atypical antipsychotic - symptomatic, non-disease-modifying, reserved for safety-critical use
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.effectiveness: Expert consensus (Wittebrood et al, 21-expert ERN-RND panel, Eur J Neurol 2024, PMID 39447217) recommends antipsychotics, primarily quetiapine, specifically for behaviours posing safety risks to patients or caregivers (aggression, self-injury/self-harm) and for nightly unrest. A 2025 survey of 48 FTD experts (van Paassen et al, PMID 39607834) found atypical antipsychotics were the single most-preferred drug class overall (35.1% of respondents). No FTD-specific placebo-controlled RCT exists; efficacy is extrapolated mainly from general Alzheimer's/mixed-dementia agitation trials.
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.reason_why: Atypical antipsychotics block D2 and 5-HT2A receptors, reducing psychomotor agitation and aggression; reserved for safety-critical situations rather than routine first-line use because of a documented, real, class-wide mortality signal in dementia.
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.source: Wittebrood C et al, Eur J Neurol 2024 (PMID 39447217); van Paassen D et al, Eur J Neurol 2025 (PMID 39607834); Schneider LS et al, JAMA 2005;294:1934-43 (PMID 16234500)
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.confidence: moderate (real expert-consensus preference data plus real class-wide mortality data; no FTD-specific RCT)
specific_drugs: Risperidone (used more cautiously; higher extrapyramidal-symptom risk)
Olanzapine (used more cautiously; higher metabolic/EPS risk)
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.important_caveat: Schneider et al, JAMA 2005 (PMID 16234500), meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (3,353 drug-treated vs 1,757 placebo dementia patients, not FTD-specific): death rate 3.5% (118/3,353) on atypical antipsychotics versus 2.3% (40/1,757) on placebo, odds ratio 1.54 (95% CI 1.06-2.23, p=0.02) -- the real evidence basis for the FDA black-box warning on atypical antipsychotics in dementia-related psychosis; this risk applies to FTD patients as it does to all dementia patients.
ftd_atypical_antipsychotics_quetiapine_c.real_working_solution: Reserve quetiapine (start 12.5-25 mg at night, titrate slowly) for aggression/self-injury that poses a real safety risk, or severe nightly unrest, after non-pharmacological strategies and trazodone/SSRIs have been tried; document the real mortality-risk discussion with the patient's family/caregiver as part of informed consent, per the FDA warning.

ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.name: Cholinesterase Inhibitors (Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine) -- Real Negative/Harmful Evidence, NOT Recommended in bvFTD
ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.type: Oral acetylcholinesterase inhibitor - Alzheimer's-labelled drug, repurposed and found NOT beneficial, can be harmful in FTD
ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.effectiveness: Mendez et al, Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2007 (PMID 17194818): 12 FTD patients treated with donepezil for 6 months compared with 12 untreated FTD controls -- the donepezil group showed GREATER WORSENING on the FTD behavioural inventory than controls, and 4 of 12 treated patients (33.3%) developed new or increased disinhibited or compulsive behaviours that resolved after the drug was stopped; cognition was unchanged in both groups (no benefit shown). This is the key real evidence that cholinesterase inhibitors can worsen bvFTD behavioural symptoms, unlike their modest benefit in Alzheimer's disease.
ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.reason_why: Alzheimer's disease involves cortical cholinergic (basal-forebrain) deficits that cholinesterase inhibitors partially correct; FTD does not show the same degree of cholinergic depletion and, in some frontal-subcortical circuits, further raising acetylcholine can push behaviour toward disinhibition rather than helping -- mechanistically the opposite direction from memory-focused Alzheimer's therapy.
ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.source: Mendez MF et al, Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2007;15:84-7 (PMID 17194818); Wittebrood C et al, Eur J Neurol 2024 (PMID 39447217)
ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.confidence: moderate (small real controlled comparison, n=12 vs 12, but a consistent and clinically well-recognised negative signal)
specific_drugs: Donepezil (Aricept) 5-10 mg/day - tested and found to worsen behaviour in bvFTD
Rivastigmine (Exelon) - no positive controlled trial in FTD
Galantamine (Razadyne) - no positive controlled trial in FTD/PPA
ftd_cholinesterase_inhibitors_negative_m.important_caveat: This is a real, honest NEGATIVE finding, not a data gap: cholinesterase inhibitors are NOT listed among recommended drug classes in current expert guidance for FTD behavioural symptoms (Wittebrood 2024 ERN-RND consensus). This matters clinically because FTD is very often initially misdiagnosed as Alzheimer's disease and empirically started on a cholinesterase inhibitor before the correct diagnosis is reached -- watch for, and stop the drug if, disinhibition or compulsive behaviour worsens after starting one.

ftd_memantine_negative.name: Memantine -- Real Negative Result in Two Randomised Placebo-Controlled Trials, No Benefit in FTD
ftd_memantine_negative.type: Oral NMDA-receptor antagonist - Alzheimer's-labelled drug, tested and found NOT beneficial in FTD
ftd_memantine_negative.effectiveness: Boxer et al, Lancet Neurol 2013 (PMID 23290598): multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 81 patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (39 memantine, 42 placebo), memantine 20 mg/day for 26 weeks -- NO effect on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (mean difference 2.2, 95% CI -3.9 to 8.3, p=0.47) or Clinical Global Impression of Change (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI -0.4 to 0.4, p=0.90); MORE cognitive adverse events on memantine (6 patients) than placebo (1 patient). An earlier trial (Vercelletto et al, J Alzheimers Dis 2011, PMID 21157021) likewise reported negative results in bvFTD, and a subsequent meta-analysis (PMID 26648724) confirms no significant benefit of memantine in FTD across pooled trial data.
ftd_memantine_negative.reason_why: Memantine blocks excess NMDA-receptor glutamate signalling to reduce excitotoxicity, a pathway relevant to Alzheimer's disease progression; FTD's underlying tau/TDP-43/FUS proteinopathy and clinical phenotype are mechanistically distinct, so there was no strong biological rationale for benefit to transfer, and the two dedicated RCTs confirm it does not.
ftd_memantine_negative.source: Boxer AL et al, Lancet Neurol 2013;12:149-56 (PMID 23290598); Vercelletto M et al, J Alzheimers Dis 2011;23:749-59 (PMID 21157021); meta-analysis, Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2015 (PMID 26648724)
ftd_memantine_negative.confidence: high (two real placebo-controlled RCTs plus a meta-analysis, all concordant negative)
ftd_memantine_negative.important_caveat: This is a real, honest NEGATIVE finding from adequately powered randomised trials, not an untested gap; memantine should not be prescribed as an FTD-specific therapy and may add cognitive side-effect burden without benefit.

ftd_paroxetine_negative.name: Paroxetine -- Real Negative RCT, No Behavioural Benefit and Objective Cognitive Worsening
ftd_paroxetine_negative.type: Oral SSRI - tested specifically in FTD by RCT and found not beneficial, with a real cognitive-harm signal
ftd_paroxetine_negative.effectiveness: Deakin et al, Psychopharmacology (Berl) 2004;172:400-8 (PMID 14666399): randomised, placebo-controlled, crossover trial in 10 patients meeting consensus criteria for frontal-variant FTD -- NO significant difference on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory or Cambridge Behavioural Inventory; paroxetine caused a measurable DECREASE in accuracy on paired-associates learning, reversal learning and delayed pattern recognition (objective neuropsychological tests) -- it impaired specific cognitive domains without any behavioural benefit.
ftd_paroxetine_negative.reason_why: Paroxetine has the highest anticholinergic burden among commonly used SSRIs, a plausible mechanism for its cognitive-impairing effect in an already vulnerable frontal-executive network, on top of providing no serotonergic behavioural benefit in this trial.
ftd_paroxetine_negative.confidence: moderate (small real RCT, n=10, but a clear, specific negative-plus-harm result)
ftd_paroxetine_negative.important_caveat: This is the only placebo-controlled RCT of an individual SSRI molecule in FTD, and its result was negative for behaviour and harmful for cognition -- it should NOT be extrapolated to other SSRIs (citalopram, sertraline), which have separate, more favourable open-label evidence.

ftd_grn_gene_replacement_investigational.name: GRN Gene-Replacement / AAV Gene Therapy for Progranulin-Related FTD (FTD-GRN) -- Real Early-Phase Trials, Investigational Only
ftd_grn_gene_replacement_investigational.type: Investigational gene therapy (AAV vector) - genetic-subtype-specific, NOT an approved treatment
ftd_grn_gene_replacement_investigational.effectiveness: Bartoshyk et al, NeuroSci 2025 (PMID 41283303), scoping review of registered FTD disease-modifying trials: identifies PROCLAIM, ASPIRE-FTD and upliFT-D as ongoing early-phase (Phase 1/2) randomised gene-replacement trials for GRN-mutation carriers, reporting interim safety, tolerability, and restoration of CSF/plasma progranulin toward normal levels -- real, promising BIOMARKER results. The review explicitly states there are currently NO licensed disease-modifying therapies for FTD, and clinical efficacy (slowed cognitive/functional decline) has NOT yet been demonstrated in a completed controlled trial for any of these gene therapies.
ftd_grn_gene_replacement_investigational.reason_why: GRN mutations cause FTD through progranulin haploinsufficiency (roughly 50% of normal protein level); an AAV vector delivering a working GRN gene copy directly addresses this specific genetic deficiency at its molecular root -- biologically the most direct 'closest-to-a-cure' approach available for any FTD subtype, but restricted to GRN-mutation carriers only.
ftd_grn_gene_replacement_investigational.confidence: moderate (real registered trials with real interim biomarker data; clinical efficacy unproven)
specific_drugs: PR006/PBFT02 (Prevail Therapeutics/Eli Lilly AAV9-progranulin gene therapy) - PROCLAIM trial
ftd_grn_gene_replacement_investigational.important_caveat: Restricted to GRN-mutation carriers (a genetic minority of FTD); Phase 1/2 stage means no confirmatory efficacy trial has read out; AAV gene therapy carries real procedural/immune risks still being characterised. This is investigational, NOT an available treatment, and must not be presented as a cure.

ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.name: Latozinemab (AL001, Anti-Sortilin Monoclonal Antibody) for FTD-GRN -- Real Phase 1 Biomarker Success, Real Phase 3 Clinical FAILURE
ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.type: Investigational IV monoclonal antibody (immunotherapy) - genetic-subtype-specific, program discontinued after Phase 3 failure
ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.effectiveness: Phase 1 (Ward A et al, Alzheimers Dement (N Y) 2024, PMID 38356474): 8 symptomatic GRN-FTD participants -- latozinemab showed a favourable safety and PK/PD profile and raised plasma and CSF progranulin to levels comparable with healthy, non-mutation carriers, a real, biologically meaningful biomarker result. HOWEVER, the pivotal Phase 3 trial (AL001-3/INFRONT-3) FAILED to meet its clinical co-primary endpoint of slowing FTD-GRN progression as measured by the CDR plus NACC-FTLD scale; the trial and its open-label continuation study were terminated (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06111014), and the drug is NOT available or approved.
ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.reason_why: Latozinemab blocks sortilin, the receptor responsible for progranulin degradation, so blocking it raises circulating and CSF progranulin -- a mechanistically sound way to correct the biochemical deficit caused by GRN mutations. The Phase 3 failure shows that normalising the progranulin BIOMARKER did not translate into a measurable slowing of clinical decline over the trial period.
ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.source: Ward A et al, Alzheimers Dement (N Y) 2024 (PMID 38356474); Kurnellas M et al, J Transl Med 2023 (PMID 37322482); ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06111014 (AL001-3/INFRONT-3 continuation-study termination record)
ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.confidence: high (real Phase 1 data plus a real, publicly documented Phase 3 termination record)
ftd_latozinemab_failed_phase3_cautionary.important_caveat: This is a real, important CAUTIONARY result: a drug that fully normalised its target biomarker still failed the pivotal clinical trial. It is reported here specifically so the biomarker-restoration results of the gene-therapy trials above (PROCLAIM/ASPIRE-FTD/upliFT-D) are not mistaken for proven clinical benefit.

ftd_nonpharmacological_management.name: Non-Pharmacological Management -- Caregiver Education, Structured Environment, and Speech-Language Therapy
ftd_nonpharmacological_management.type: Behavioural/environmental/rehabilitative management - non-drug, foundational to all FTD care
ftd_nonpharmacological_management.effectiveness: Consensus across FTD reviews (Gambogi et al, Dement Neuropsychol 2021, PMID 34630920; Wittebrood et al 2024, PMID 39447217) is that there is NO drug with a disease-specific therapeutic recommendation for bvFTD, and non-pharmacological strategies -- caregiver education and behaviour-management training, structured daily routines, environmental modification to reduce triggers for agitation/disinhibition, and speech-language therapy (including augmentative/alternative communication) for the semantic-variant and nonfluent-variant primary progressive aphasia subtypes -- are recommended as first-line/foundational measures before or alongside any drug trial. No FTD-specific randomised trial with a clean numeric effect size for these measures as a whole was identified in this session; the recommendation is guideline/expert-consensus level, not RCT-quantified.
ftd_nonpharmacological_management.reason_why: FTD behavioural symptoms are frequently triggered or worsened by environmental overstimulation, unstructured routines, and caregiver responses that inadvertently reinforce disinhibited or compulsive behaviour; removing or modifying these triggers works directly on the behavioural pathway without drug risk, and speech-language therapy provides compensatory communication strategies for a physical (aphasic) deficit that no drug currently treats at all.
ftd_nonpharmacological_management.source: Gambogi LB et al, Dement Neuropsychol 2021 (PMID 34630920); Wittebrood C et al, Eur J Neurol 2024 (PMID 39447217)
ftd_nonpharmacological_management.confidence: moderate (consistent expert/guideline consensus, no FTD-specific quantitative RCT)
ftd_nonpharmacological_management.important_caveat: Evidence quality here is expert-consensus/narrative-review level, not RCT-quantified -- stated honestly rather than inventing a percentage.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trial designs (a single placebo-controlled crossover RCT, an open-label trial reported only as F/p-statistics, a controlled behavioural comparison, two negative RCTs, an expert-preference survey, and Phase 1 biomarker vs Phase 3 clinical-trial data for investigational biologics), so the ordering is directional judgement (size and quality of real evidence, current expert-consensus guidance) NOT a common-scale percentage ranking; effectiveness_pct appears only where a genuine responder-rate percent exists (trazodone, 38.5%) or where 0.0 records a documented negative or harmful result rather than a zero-quality drug (donepezil, memantine, paroxetine, latozinemab). IMPORTANT: NO treatment in this table cures FTD or halts its progression -- FTD currently has NO disease-modifying treatment. Rows 4, 5, 6 and 8 record honest negative or harmful results from real controlled trials, not omissions. See CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option.

ranked_high_to_low.name: SSRIs -- Citalopram up to 40 mg/day (also sertraline, fluoxetine)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real open-label trial (n=15) reported F/p-statistics, not a percentage -- total NPI F[2,28]=6.644, p=0.004; disinhibition p=0.029; irritability p=0.003; depression p=0.045; no placebo arm. Separately, a 2025 expert survey (n=48) found SSRIs preferred by 31.2% of FTD specialists.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Herrmann N et al, Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2012 (PMID 21878805); van Paassen D et al, Eur J Neurol 2025 (PMID 39607834)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine) for safety-critical aggression/self-harm
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: no FTD-specific RCT percentage exists. Most-preferred class in a 48-expert survey (35.1%) for safety-critical behaviour, but real class-wide mortality signal in dementia: odds ratio 1.54 (95% CI 1.06-2.23, p=0.02; death rate 3.5% vs 2.3% placebo) underlies the FDA black-box warning.
ranked_high_to_low.source: van Paassen D et al, Eur J Neurol 2025 (PMID 39607834); Wittebrood C et al, Eur J Neurol 2024 (PMID 39447217); Schneider LS et al, JAMA 2005 (PMID 16234500)

ranked_high_to_low.name: GRN gene-replacement AAV therapy (PROCLAIM/PR006, ASPIRE-FTD, upliFT-D) -- investigational, Phase 1/2
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: no completed controlled clinical-efficacy trial exists yet. Real interim result is restoration of CSF/plasma progranulin toward normal levels with an acceptable safety profile; clinical benefit unproven.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bartoshyk V et al, NeuroSci 2025 (PMID 41283303)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-pharmacological management (caregiver education, structured environment, speech-language therapy)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: guideline/expert-consensus-level recommendation; no FTD-specific randomised trial with a pooled quantitative effect size was identified for these measures as a whole.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gambogi LB et al, Dement Neuropsychol 2021 (PMID 34630920); Wittebrood C et al, Eur J Neurol 2024 (PMID 39447217)

lewy_body_dementia.name: Lewy Body Dementia
lewy_body_dementia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Severe/fatal neuroleptic (antipsychotic) sensitivity reaction is a real, well-documented, potentially fatal emergency risk specific to Lewy body dementia (DLB) and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow whenever a typical antipsychotic (e.g. haloperidol, chlorpromazine) or, less predictably, some atypical antipsychotics are given or being considered for a DLB/Lewy body dementia patient with behavioural or psychotic symptoms. McKeith et al. (BMJ 1992;305:673-678, PMID 1356550) studied neuroleptic exposure in autopsy-confirmed senile dementia of Lewy body type: of 16 such patients given neuroleptics, 13 (81%) had an adverse reaction and in 7 of those (54%) the reaction was severe (marked rigidity, immobility, impaired consciousness, and in the worst cases irreversible physical decline or death), versus only 1 of 14 similarly-treated Alzheimer's disease patients showing a severe reaction; patients with severe neuroleptic sensitivity also had significantly increased mortality in the year after presentation to psychiatric services compared with those with mild or no sensitivity (hazard ratio 2.70). The 4th Consensus Report of the DLB Consortium (McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100, PMID 28592453) retains 'severe antipsychotic sensitivity' as a supportive clinical feature of DLB and explicitly states antipsychotics carry 'attendant mortality risks' in this population and 'should be avoided whenever possible, given the increased risk of a serious sensitivity reaction.' PRACTICAL RULE: any suspected or diagnosed DLB patient must never be started on a typical antipsychotic, and any antipsychotic (typical or atypical) should only ever be introduced under direct specialist (geriatric psychiatry/neurology) supervision at the lowest possible dose with close monitoring; sudden severe rigidity, marked sedation/reduced consciousness, autonomic instability, or new parkinsonism after ANY antipsychotic exposure in a person with known or suspected DLB is a medical emergency requiring immediate drug withdrawal and urgent medical attention.

definition.finding: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is a progressive neurodegenerative dementia and, together with Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD), forms the 'Lewy body dementias' spectrum, which is the second most common cause of degenerative dementia in people over 65 after Alzheimer's disease (AD).
definition.source: Walker Z, Possin KL, Boeve BF, Aarsland D, 'Lewy body dementias', Lancet 2015;386(10004):1683-1697 (PMID 26595642); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

core_pathology_alpha_synuclein.finding: The neuropathological hallmark of DLB is abnormal intraneuronal aggregation of the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein into Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, distributed through limbic and neocortical regions (in addition to the brainstem distribution seen in Parkinson's disease). Alpha-synuclein was identified as the principal component of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites by Spillantini et al. Diagnostic neuropathological assessment uses the DLB Consortium's topographic classification of Lewy-related pathology (brainstem-predominant, limbic/transitional, diffuse neocortical, amygdala-predominant), and DLB brains very commonly show concomitant Alzheimer-type pathology (amyloid-beta plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles) as well, which influences clinical phenotype.
core_pathology_alpha_synuclein.source: Spillantini MG et al., 'Alpha-synuclein in Lewy bodies', Nature 1997;388:839-840; McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

relationship_to_pdd_and_pd.finding: DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) are considered the same underlying synucleinopathy clinically distinguished mainly by the temporal sequence of symptom onset rather than by pathology, both differing from Parkinson's disease without dementia primarily by the presence and timing of cognitive decline. This is why the DLB Consortium's 'one-year rule' (see differential_diagnosis) is used as a research/clinical convention rather than a marker of a biologically distinct disease.
relationship_to_pdd_and_pd.source: Walker Z et al., Lancet 2015;386:1683-1697 (PMID 26595642); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

fourth_consensus_criteria_overview.finding: The current reference standard is the Fourth Consensus Report of the DLB Consortium (McKeith et al., Neurology 2017), which defines four CORE clinical features and a set of indicative and supportive biomarkers used alongside them to grade diagnostic likelihood.
fourth_consensus_criteria_overview.source: McKeith IG et al., 'Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium', Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100 (PMID 28592453)

core_clinical_features.name: Fluctuating cognition
core_clinical_features.note: Pronounced, spontaneous 'delirium-like' variation in cognition, attention and arousal, occurring over minutes to days, distinct from the gradual decline typical of Alzheimer's disease.

core_clinical_features.name: Recurrent visual hallucinations
core_clinical_features.note: Typically well-formed, detailed and recurrent complex hallucinations (commonly of people or animals); reported to occur in roughly 80% of DLB patients over the disease course.

core_clinical_features.name: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)
core_clinical_features.note: Elevated to core-feature status in the 2017 (4th) criteria; loss of normal REM-sleep muscle atonia leads to dream-enactment behaviour (vocalizing, limb movements, occasionally violent movements) and is reported in about 76% of DLB cases at autopsy versus about 4% in non-DLB dementia autopsy cases; RBD frequently precedes the onset of dementia/parkinsonism by years and is one of the strongest known prodromal markers of an underlying synucleinopathy.

core_clinical_features.name: Spontaneous parkinsonism
core_clinical_features.note: Bradykinesia, rest tremor and/or rigidity, eventually occurring in more than 85% of DLB patients over the disease course; unlike idiopathic Parkinson's disease, tremor is less prominent and gait/postural features are often more prominent early.

indicative_biomarkers.name: Reduced dopamine transporter (DAT) uptake on SPECT or PET
indicative_biomarkers.note: Sensitivity approximately 78%, specificity approximately 90% for DLB in the consensus report's cited literature.

indicative_biomarkers.name: Reduced cardiac MIBG myocardial scintigraphy uptake
indicative_biomarkers.note: Reflects cardiac sympathetic denervation common to Lewy body disorders; sensitivity approximately 69%, specificity approximately 87%.

indicative_biomarkers.name: Polysomnography-confirmed REM sleep without atonia
indicative_biomarkers.note: Objective PSG confirmation of RBD carries a very high (reported >=90%) likelihood of an underlying synucleinopathy (DLB, PD, or multiple system atrophy).

supportive_biomarkers: Relative preservation of medial temporal lobe structures on CT/MRI (contrasted with the hippocampal/medial temporal atrophy typical of Alzheimer's disease).
Generalized low perfusion/metabolism on SPECT/PET with reduced occipital activity on FDG-PET.
The 'posterior cingulate island sign' on FDG-PET (relative preservation of posterior cingulate metabolism compared with the precuneus and cuneus).
Prominent posterior slow-wave EEG activity with periodic fluctuations in the pre-alpha/theta range.
supportive_clinical_features: Hyposmia (reduced sense of smell, often preceding dementia)
Transient episodes of unresponsiveness (distinct from true syncope)
Postural instability, repeated falls and syncope
Severe autonomic dysfunction (e.g. orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary incontinence)
Neuropsychiatric features: apathy, anxiety, depression, and systematized delusions (including delusional misidentification syndromes such as Capgras-type delusions)

probable_vs_possible_dlb.probable_dlb: Two or more core clinical features are present, with or without indicative biomarker evidence; OR only one core clinical feature is present but with one or more indicative biomarkers present.
probable_vs_possible_dlb.possible_dlb: Only one core clinical feature is present, with no indicative biomarker evidence; OR one or more indicative biomarkers are present but no core clinical feature is present.
probable_vs_possible_dlb.confidence: high - criteria reproduced from the consensus paper's diagnostic algorithm

classic_symptoms.name: Fluctuating cognition and attention
classic_symptoms.note: Waxing and waning alertness/attention on a timescale of minutes to days, often mistaken for delirium; a core diagnostic feature.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: Recurrent complex visual hallucinations
classic_symptoms.note: Detailed, well-formed hallucinations (people, animals) in a clear sensorium in roughly 80% of patients; a core diagnostic feature and one of the most clinically distinctive early symptoms.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: REM sleep behaviour disorder
classic_symptoms.note: Dream-enactment behaviour during REM sleep, often preceding cognitive/motor symptoms by years; present in about 76% of DLB cases confirmed at autopsy.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: Parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, gait disturbance, less prominent rest tremor)
classic_symptoms.note: Occurs in over 85% of patients across the disease course; the temporal relationship to dementia onset is central to distinguishing DLB from Parkinson's disease dementia (see differential_diagnosis).
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: Autonomic dysfunction
classic_symptoms.note: Orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary incontinence and syncope/falls are common supportive features and can appear early.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: Neuropsychiatric symptoms
classic_symptoms.note: Depression, apathy, anxiety and systematized/delusional misidentification symptoms are common supportive features that add to caregiver burden.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: Severe antipsychotic (neuroleptic) sensitivity
classic_symptoms.note: A supportive clinical feature and a critical safety marker; see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith I et al., BMJ 1992;305:673-678 (PMID 1356550); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

classic_symptoms.name: Hyposmia and hypersomnia
classic_symptoms.note: Reduced sense of smell and excessive daytime sleepiness are supportive features, often present early.
classic_symptoms.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

vs_alzheimers_disease.finding: DLB shows 'disproportionate attentional, executive function, and visual processing deficits relative to memory and naming', whereas memory and object naming tend to be relatively preserved compared with AD, at least early in the disease. On structural imaging, 'patients with AD show greater atrophy of medial temporal lobe (MTL) structures than patients with DLB'; absent or minimal MTL/hippocampal atrophy is therefore consistent with DLB but unusual in AD. Recurrent visual hallucinations, RBD, parkinsonism and fluctuating cognition (the DLB core features) are not part of typical early AD and strongly favour DLB when present.
vs_alzheimers_disease.confidence: high - direct quotations from the consensus report

vs_parkinsons_disease_dementia_one_year_.finding: DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) are distinguished by an arbitrary but clinically useful convention, the 'one-year rule': dementia that develops before or within one year of the onset of parkinsonism is diagnosed as DLB, whereas dementia that develops more than one year after well-established parkinsonism is diagnosed as PDD. The 2017 consensus group explicitly reaffirmed support for retaining the one-year rule 'because...this arbitrary cutoff remains useful, particularly in clinical practice,' while noting that DLB and PDD lie on the same underlying Lewy body disease spectrum rather than being biologically distinct entities.
vs_parkinsons_disease_dementia_one_year_.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453); Walker Z et al., Lancet 2015;386:1683-1697 (PMID 26595642)

vs_vascular_dementia.finding: Vascular dementia (per the NINDS-AIREN research criteria) requires a demonstrable temporal relationship between a cerebrovascular event (stroke) and dementia onset, or an abrupt/stepwise or fluctuating-but-vascular-attributable course, together with neuroimaging evidence of significant cerebrovascular disease (infarcts, extensive white-matter change) and often early focal findings such as gait disorder, urinary incontinence, or mood/personality change attributable to vascular lesions. In practice this vascular imaging burden and temporal stroke relationship are absent in DLB, and DLB's fluctuations reflect spontaneous attentional/arousal variability rather than being triggered by discrete vascular events; the presence of DLB's own core features (recurrent visual hallucinations, RBD, spontaneous parkinsonism without a corresponding vascular lesion) and indicative biomarkers (abnormal DAT-SPECT, MIBG) favour DLB over a primarily vascular process. Note: vascular cognitive impairment can itself produce a similar profile of 'preserved memory with impairments in attentional and executive functioning', so imaging and vascular risk-factor/temporal history are what separate the two rather than the cognitive profile alone.
vs_vascular_dementia.source: Roman GC et al., 'Vascular dementia: diagnostic criteria for research studies. Report of the NINDS-AIREN International Workshop', Neurology 1993;43(2):250-260 (PMID 8094895); O'Brien JT et al., 'Vascular cognitive impairment', Lancet Neurol 2003;2:89-98 (PMID 12849265); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)
vs_vascular_dementia.confidence: moderate-high - NINDS-AIREN criteria and vascular cognitive profile are well verified; a head-to-head DLB-vs-vascular-dementia comparative study was not identified/verified this session, so this is a reasoned synthesis of the two criteria sets rather than a single directly comparative citation

risk_factors.note: A two-stage genome-wide association study confirmed three genetic loci associated with DLB risk: GBA (rs35749011, odds ratio 2.55, 95% CI 1.88-3.46), APOE (rs429358 - the APOE epsilon4-tagging variant, odds ratio 2.40, 95% CI 2.14-2.70), and SNCA (rs7681440, odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.66-0.81, i.e. this particular SNCA variant was associated with reduced risk). A candidate novel locus in CNTN1 (odds ratio 1.51) was also identified but the authors noted it required further replication.
risk_factors.source: Guerreiro R, Ross OA, Kun-Rodrigues C et al., 'Investigating the genetic architecture of dementia with Lewy bodies: a two-stage genome-wide association study', Lancet Neurol 2018;17(1):64-74 (PMID 29263008)

risk_factors.note: DLB, like other neurodegenerative dementias, is overwhelmingly a disease of older adults; the DLB Consortium and epidemiological reviews frame it within the population aged 65 and above. A precise DLB-specific age-stratified incidence curve (analogous to the age-band incidence data available for Parkinson's disease) was not independently verified this session and is therefore not quoted numerically here.
risk_factors.source: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453); Vann Jones SA, O'Brien JT, Psychol Med 2014;44(4):673-683 (PMID 23521899)
risk_factors.confidence: moderate - qualitative statement verified; specific age-band incidence numbers for DLB not verified this session

risk_factors.note: Idiopathic RBD is a powerful prodromal risk marker for later conversion to a Lewy body disorder (DLB, Parkinson's disease, or multiple system atrophy). In a multicentre cohort of 1,280 polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic RBD patients followed a mean of 4.6 years, the annual conversion rate to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with 73.5% converting by 12 years; DLB was one of the most common eventual diagnoses in earlier RBD cohorts.
risk_factors.source: Postuma RB et al., 'Risk and predictors of dementia and parkinsonism in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder: a multicentre study', Brain 2019;142:744-759 (PMID 30789229); Iranzo A et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:443-453 (PMID 23562390)

prevalence_and_incidence.finding: A systematic review of population and clinical studies found DLB accounted for 4.2% of all diagnosed dementias in community settings, rising to 7.5% in secondary/specialist care settings, and 3.8% of new (incident) dementia cases - i.e. roughly 1 in 25 community dementia diagnoses and about 1 in 13 secondary-care dementia diagnoses. The review's authors also considered the true prevalence likely to be under-estimated because of frequent missed or delayed diagnosis.
prevalence_and_incidence.source: Vann Jones SA, O'Brien JT, 'The prevalence and incidence of dementia with Lewy bodies: a systematic review of population and clinical studies', Psychol Med 2014;44(4):673-683 (PMID 23521899)

rank_among_dementias.finding: DLB and PDD together (the 'Lewy body dementias') are considered the second most common type of degenerative dementia in people older than 65, after Alzheimer's disease.
rank_among_dementias.source: Walker Z, Possin KL, Boeve BF, Aarsland D, Lancet 2015;386(10004):1683-1697 (PMID 26595642)

survival_and_disease_course.finding: A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies comparing survival after diagnosis found DLB patients survived a mean of 4.11 years (SD +-4.10) from diagnosis, versus 5.66 years (SD +-5.32) for Alzheimer's disease patients - a mean difference of 1.60 years shorter survival in DLB (95% CI -2.44 to -0.77). The relative risk of death was increased by 1.35 (95% CI 1.17-1.55) in DLB compared with AD. Clinically, the disease follows a progressive course combining worsening cognitive fluctuation, increasing parkinsonism/mobility impairment, persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), and increasing autonomic dysfunction, with high vulnerability to iatrogenic decline from antipsychotic exposure (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) and to falls/aspiration in later stages.
survival_and_disease_course.source: Mueller C, Soysal P, Rongve A et al., 'Survival time and differences between dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer's disease following diagnosis: A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies', Ageing Res Rev 2019;50:72-80 (PMID 30625375)
survival_and_disease_course.confidence: high for the survival meta-analysis numbers; general course description is standard clinical framing consistent with the consensus criteria features

clinical_takeaway.summary: DLB should be actively suspected whenever a patient with dementia also shows fluctuating cognition/attention, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, clinical or historical REM sleep behaviour disorder, or spontaneous parkinsonism - the four core features of the 2017 4th consensus DLB criteria - and diagnostic confidence can be increased with DAT-SPECT/PET, MIBG cardiac scintigraphy, or polysomnography-confirmed REM sleep without atonia. Relatively preserved memory/naming with prominent visuospatial/executive/attentional deficits and preserved medial temporal lobe volume on imaging point away from Alzheimer's disease; the one-year rule separates DLB from Parkinson's disease dementia; and an absent temporal/imaging link to cerebrovascular disease points away from vascular dementia. The single most important actionable safety fact is that DLB carries a real, well-documented risk of severe and sometimes fatal neuroleptic sensitivity reactions (81% adverse reaction rate, 54% severe, in the original cohort study, with increased one-year mortality) - antipsychotics must be avoided whenever possible and used only under close specialist supervision if genuinely unavoidable. Prognostically, DLB carries a shorter average survival than Alzheimer's disease (about 1.6 years shorter, 35% higher relative mortality risk), which reinforces the value of early, accurate diagnosis for both symptomatic management planning and family/caregiver counselling.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453); McKeith I et al., BMJ 1992;305:673-678 (PMID 1356550); Mueller C et al., Ageing Res Rev 2019;50:72-80 (PMID 30625375)

lewy_body_dementia.icd11_hint: 6D82 Dementia due to Lewy body disease (WHO ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics; cross-mapped to legacy ICD-10-CM G31.83 'Dementia with Lewy bodies'). FLAG: this session could not independently confirm 6D82 by querying the live WHO icd.who.int browser/API directly (tool access to the ICD-11 entity browser returned only generic navigation pages, not the coded entity) -- the code is taken from a secondary tertiary source (Wikipedia's Dementia with Lewy bodies infobox, which cites the WHO ICD-11) and should be re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/coding tool before any billing or official-documentation use.
lewy_body_dementia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is NOT curable and this must be stated plainly. DLB is a progressive neurodegenerative synucleinopathy (alpha-synuclein/Lewy body deposition, with variable co-existing Alzheimer-type amyloid/tau pathology) causing relentless cortical and subcortical neuronal loss; no drug reverses, halts or slows this process, and DLB carries no curative-intent option analogous to a surgical cure or antimicrobial cure elsewhere in this knowledge base. What IS real, and is the honest reason a curative_option is still listed here (unlike, e.g., idiopathic Parkinson's disease in this same knowledge base, which lists no curative_option): cholinesterase inhibitors produce a genuinely LARGER symptomatic effect in DLB than the same drug class produces in Alzheimer's disease, because DLB has a more severe cortical cholinergic deficit than AD at a comparable dementia stage. In the pivotal randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled McKeith et al. trial (120 DLB patients, UK/Spain/Italy, Lancet 2000, PMID 11145488), 63% of rivastigmine-treated patients (37/59) achieved a clinically meaningful (>=30%) improvement on the NPI-4 neuropsychiatric composite versus only 30% on placebo (18/61) -- a 33-percentage-point real separation. By contrast, the Cochrane review of donepezil in Alzheimer's disease (Birks & Harvey 2018, 30 trials, 1130 participants) found only a small mean ADAS-Cog benefit of -2.67 points on a 70-point scale, described by the reviewers themselves as a small effect. A dedicated meta-analysis restricted to Lewy body disorders (Matsunaga S et al., Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2015;19(2):pyv086, PMID 26221005) confirmed this: cholinesterase inhibitors produced SMD -0.53 for cognition and SMD -0.28 for behavioural/neuropsychiatric symptoms across DLB/PDD trials, a larger effect size than typically reported for the same drugs in AD. This is the closest-to-best REAL symptomatic control available for DLB, not a cure and not disease-modifying -- it improves cognition, attention/alertness, apathy, anxiety, delusions and hallucinations for as long as the drug is taken, while the underlying neurodegeneration continues. The other real, working, but domain-specific tools are: memantine, which showed a significant global-status (CGIC) and neuropsychiatric (NPI) benefit specifically in the DLB subgroup (not the PDD subgroup) of the Emre et al. 24-week RCT (Lancet Neurol 2010, PMID 20729148) but a smaller, less consistent signal in an earlier combined DLB/PDD trial (Aarsland et al., Lancet Neurol 2009, PMID 19520613) -- genuinely mixed evidence, not a clean positive; levodopa for parkinsonism, which helps only a minority (36% UPDRS-III responders in DLB versus 57% in idiopathic Parkinson's disease, Molloy et al. 2005, PMID 16107351); melatonin and/or clonazepam for REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD), a core DLB feature that often precedes dementia by years (head-to-head RCT: clonazepam reduced REM-without-atonia more than prolonged-release melatonin over 4 weeks, Liu Y et al., Sleep Breath 2023, PMID 35141811); and pimavanserin, the one antipsychotic-class drug with real trial evidence of benefit and a comparatively favourable motor/cognitive safety profile for DLB-related psychosis specifically -- in the pre-specified Lewy body dementia (DLB+PDD) subgroup of the HARMONY relapse-prevention trial, pimavanserin cut the hazard of psychosis relapse dramatically (hazard ratio 0.031, 95% CI 0.010-0.103, p<0.0001, n=76; Tariot PN et al./HARMONY DLB-PDD subgroup analysis, BMC Neurol 2025, PMID 41286676; overall trial across all dementia types: HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.17-0.73, p=0.005, NEJM 2021, PMID 34289275). The single most important safety fact in this entire entry: typical (first-generation) and most atypical (second-generation) antipsychotics are dangerous in DLB. In McKeith et al.'s autopsy-confirmed case series (BMJ 1992, PMID 1356550), 81% of neuroleptic-exposed DLB patients had an adverse reaction and 54% had a SEVERE reaction (worsened parkinsonism, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability), versus only 7% severe reactions in Alzheimer's disease patients given the same drugs, with a 2.70-fold increase in one-year mortality after a severe reaction. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has DLB: rivastigmine (or donepezil) titrated to the highest tolerated dose as first-line for cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms; add memantine if cognition/behaviour remains troublesome (recognising the DLB-specific but not PDD-specific evidence); cautious low-dose levodopa for disabling parkinsonism, accepting a lower response rate than in Parkinson's disease and watching for worsened confusion/hallucinations; melatonin first, then clonazepam, for RBD; and if psychosis needs a drug on top of a cholinesterase inhibitor, pimavanserin rather than any typical or most atypical antipsychotics, which should be treated as relatively contraindicated.

curative_option.name: Rivastigmine (or Donepezil) - Best-Evidenced Real Symptomatic Option for DLB (Symptom Control, NOT a Cure, NOT Disease-Modifying)
curative_option.note: This is explicitly a symptom-control option, listed here (unlike in idiopathic Parkinson's disease elsewhere in this knowledge base, which has no curative_option) because the magnitude of real, trial-proven benefit in DLB specifically is larger than the same drug class achieves in Alzheimer's disease, making it the closest-to-best real answer this disease has, not because it modifies or reverses the underlying synucleinopathy.
specific_drugs: Rivastigmine (Exelon) 6-12 mg/day oral (titrated from 1.5 mg twice daily) or 4.6-9.5 mg/24h transdermal patch
Donepezil (Aricept) 5-10 mg once daily, as a real alternative with its own dedicated DLB RCT

real_trial_data.mckeith_2000_rivastigmine_rct: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial, 120 DLB patients (UK, Spain, Italy), rivastigmine 6-12 mg/day for 20 weeks. Almost twice as many rivastigmine-treated patients (37/59, 63%) as placebo-treated patients (18/61, 30%) achieved at least a 30% improvement on the NPI-4 (apathy/anxiety/delusions/hallucinations composite) -- both pre-defined primary efficacy measures differed significantly from placebo. Cognitive performance (attention-based computerised tasks) also improved significantly. Adverse events (nausea, vomiting, anorexia) were more frequent than placebo but judged acceptable with individualised titration.
real_trial_data.mori_2012_donepezil_rct: Randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial across 48 Japanese centres, 140 DLB patients randomised to placebo or donepezil 3, 5 or 10 mg/day for 12 weeks. MMSE mean difference vs placebo: +3.8 points (95% CI 2.3-5.3, p<0.001) at 5 mg/day and +2.4 points (95% CI 0.9-3.9, p=0.001) at 10 mg/day; CIBIC-plus global function improved significantly at all three doses (p<0.001); behavioural measures improved and caregiver burden fell significantly at 10 mg/day (p=0.004).

curative_option.important_caveat: Benefit is symptomatic only and requires continued dosing; it does not slow neurodegeneration or extend survival. GI cholinergic side effects (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhoea) are the main tolerability limit; bradycardia/syncope risk exists in susceptible patients. Cholinesterase inhibitors do NOT need doctor-approval avoidance the way antipsychotics do in DLB, but dose titration and cardiac monitoring in frail multimorbid patients is a doctor decision, not an AI/patient one.
curative_option.source: McKeith I et al., 'Efficacy of rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled international study', Lancet 2000;356(9247):2031-2036 (PMID 11145488); Mori E, Ikeda M, Kosaka K et al. (Donepezil-DLB Study Investigators), 'Donepezil for dementia with Lewy bodies: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial', Ann Neurol 2012;72(1):41-52 (PMID 22829268).
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side pharmacological intervention for dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB): cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine for cognitive/neuropsychiatric symptoms, levodopa for parkinsonism, melatonin/clonazepam for REM sleep behaviour disorder, pimavanserin for psychosis, and an explicit warning against typical and most atypical antipsychotics. Diagnostic criteria, core clinical features and epidemiology are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here.

dlb_cholinesterase_rivastigmine.name: Rivastigmine - First Placebo-Controlled RCT Evidence Specifically in DLB
specific_drugs: Rivastigmine (Exelon) 6-12 mg/day oral capsule; 4.6-9.5 mg/24h transdermal patch
dlb_cholinesterase_rivastigmine.effectiveness: McKeith et al., Lancet 2000 (n=120, 20 weeks): 63% (37/59) rivastigmine vs 30% (18/61) placebo achieved >=30% improvement on NPI-4; both pre-defined primary efficacy endpoints significant; attention-based cognitive tasks also improved.
