dlb_cholinesterase_rivastigmine.reason_why: DLB has a more severe cortical cholinergic deficit (loss of nucleus basalis of Meynert cholinergic projections plus additional brainstem/pedunculopontine cholinergic loss) than Alzheimer's disease at a comparable dementia severity, which is the mechanistic reason cholinesterase inhibition produces a larger relative benefit on attention, alertness, fluctuating cognition and psychosis in DLB than in AD.
dlb_cholinesterase_rivastigmine.important_caveat: GI cholinergic adverse effects (nausea, vomiting, anorexia) more frequent than placebo; titrate slowly. Symptomatic only; no disease-modifying effect.
dlb_cholinesterase_rivastigmine.real_working_solution: Rivastigmine, titrated from 1.5 mg twice daily to the highest tolerated dose (up to 6 mg twice daily oral, or the 9.5 mg/24h patch), is the best real first-line drug for DLB cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms and the only ChEI with a dedicated positive DLB-specific placebo-controlled RCT.

dlb_cholinesterase_donepezil.name: Donepezil - Dose-Dependent Cognitive and Global Benefit in a Dedicated DLB RCT
specific_drugs: Donepezil (Aricept) 5 mg or 10 mg once daily
dlb_cholinesterase_donepezil.effectiveness: Mori E et al., Ann Neurol 2012 (n=140, 12 weeks, 48 Japanese centres): MMSE mean difference vs placebo +3.8 points at 5 mg/day (95% CI 2.3-5.3, p<0.001) and +2.4 points at 10 mg/day (95% CI 0.9-3.9, p=0.001); CIBIC-plus improved at all doses (p<0.001); behavioural measures improved and caregiver burden fell at 10 mg/day (p=0.004).
dlb_cholinesterase_donepezil.reason_why: Reversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase raises synaptic acetylcholine at surviving cortical/subcortical cholinergic terminals, compensating for the DLB cholinergic deficit in the same way as in AD but with a larger relative effect given DLB's greater baseline cholinergic loss.
dlb_cholinesterase_donepezil.important_caveat: Safety profile consistent with established donepezil tolerability (GI upset, vivid dreams, bradycardia); 3 mg/day dose did not reach significance on MMSE, so under-dosing risks under-treatment.
dlb_cholinesterase_donepezil.real_working_solution: Donepezil 5-10 mg once daily is a real, dedicated-RCT-proven alternative to rivastigmine for DLB cognitive/global/behavioural symptoms, useful where once-daily oral dosing or patch unavailability favours it.
dlb_cholinesterase_donepezil.source: Mori E, Ikeda M, Kosaka K et al., Ann Neurol 2012;72(1):41-52 (PMID 22829268)

dlb_cholinesterase_galantamine.name: Galantamine - Open-Label Evidence Only, No Dedicated DLB Placebo-Controlled RCT
dlb_cholinesterase_galantamine.effectiveness: 24-week open-label study, 50 DLB patients: NPI total score improved by 8.24 points (p=0.01), with particular benefit for visual hallucinations and nighttime behaviours (p=0.004); Clinician's Global Impression of Change improved by 0.5 points (p=0.01). No placebo arm, so a real efficacy ceiling versus rivastigmine/donepezil cannot be stated with confidence; a separate class-level meta-analysis (Matsunaga S et al., Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2015;19(2):pyv086, PMID 26221005) pooling rivastigmine, donepezil and galantamine trials in Lewy body disorders found overall SMD -0.53 for cognition and -0.28 for behavioural/neuropsychiatric symptoms.
dlb_cholinesterase_galantamine.important_caveat: Honestly weaker evidence tier than rivastigmine/donepezil in DLB specifically -- open-label design only, real risk of placebo/expectation effect not excluded. Still a reasonable clinical option if the other two are not tolerated, on class-level and open-label evidence.
dlb_cholinesterase_galantamine.real_working_solution: A real third-line cholinesterase-inhibitor option for DLB when rivastigmine and donepezil are not tolerated or available, on open-label plus class-level meta-analytic evidence.
dlb_cholinesterase_galantamine.source: Edwards K et al., 'Efficacy and safety of galantamine in patients with dementia with Lewy bodies: a 24-week open-label study', Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2007;23(6):401-405 (PMID 17409748); Matsunaga S et al., Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2015;19(2):pyv086 (PMID 26221005)
dlb_cholinesterase_galantamine.confidence: moderate - open-label primary evidence, class-level meta-analysis support

dlb_memantine.name: Memantine - Real but Genuinely Mixed Evidence, Positive Only in the DLB Subgroup of the Larger Trial
specific_drugs: Memantine (Namenda/Ebixa) 20 mg/day (10 mg twice daily), titrated from 5 mg/day
dlb_memantine.effectiveness: Emre M et al., Lancet Neurol 2010 (n=199 total, 34 DLB+62 PDD memantine vs 41 DLB+58 PDD placebo, 24 weeks): in the pre-specified DLB subgroup, CGIC was significantly better with memantine (3.3 vs 3.9, p=0.023) and NPI improved significantly more (-4.3 vs +1.7, p=0.041); the PDD subgroup and the combined total population showed NO significant difference (total population CGIC p=0.120). An earlier, smaller combined DLB/PDD trial (Aarsland D et al., Lancet Neurol 2009, n=72, 24 weeks, 78% completion) found a smaller positive signal on CGIC (mean difference 0.7, 95% CI 0.04-1.39, p=0.03) without separating DLB from PDD, and no other secondary measure reached significance except an attentional-speed task (p=0.004).
dlb_memantine.reason_why: Memantine blocks pathologically-sustained NMDA-receptor activation by excess synaptic glutamate, a mechanism proposed to reduce excitotoxic neuronal stress; the biological reason for a DLB-specific (but not PDD-specific) effect is not established and may reflect true pathophysiological difference or trial-to-trial variability.
dlb_memantine.important_caveat: This is genuinely mixed evidence, not a clean positive drug -- two RCTs give inconsistent subgroup results, and package labelling in most countries has no DLB-specific indication. Occasional case reports describe worsened confusion/hallucinations with memantine in DLB, so a trial-and-monitor approach with willingness to stop is the honest real-world use.
dlb_memantine.real_working_solution: A reasonable add-on to (not substitute for) a cholinesterase inhibitor in DLB patients with persistent cognitive/behavioural symptoms, on real but inconsistent RCT evidence concentrated in the DLB (not PDD) subgroup of the largest trial.
dlb_memantine.source: Emre M et al., Lancet Neurol 2010;9(10):969-977 (PMID 20729148); Aarsland D et al., Lancet Neurol 2009;8(7):613-618 (PMID 19520613)
dlb_memantine.confidence: moderate - real RCT data but inconsistent across trials/subgroups

dlb_levodopa_parkinsonism.name: Levodopa - Real but Reduced Motor Benefit Compared with Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease
specific_drugs: Levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet) or levodopa/benserazide (Madopar), started low and titrated slowly
dlb_levodopa_parkinsonism.effectiveness: Molloy S et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005 (PMID 16107351): acute levodopa challenge in 14 DLB patients produced a mean 13.8% improvement in UPDRS-III motor score (p=0.02), but only 36% were classified as 'responders', versus 57% responders in idiopathic Parkinson's disease and 70% in Parkinson's disease dementia tested the same way. In 19 DLB patients treated for 6 months (mean dose 323 mg/day), tolerability was acceptable overall but 4/19 discontinued (2 for GI upset, 2 for worsening cognitive confusion).
dlb_levodopa_parkinsonism.reason_why: DLB parkinsonism arises from nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss similar in kind to but often less severe/more symmetric than in idiopathic Parkinson's disease, plus additional non-dopaminergic pathology, which is the likely reason for the lower and less complete levodopa response rate.
dlb_levodopa_parkinsonism.important_caveat: Levodopa can worsen hallucinations/confusion in DLB (the same neuropsychiatric vulnerability that makes antipsychotics dangerous), so it must be started at a low dose and titrated slowly with close monitoring, balancing motor benefit against psychiatric risk -- a doctor-only judgment call, not an AI/patient one.
dlb_levodopa_parkinsonism.real_working_solution: Low-dose, slow-titration levodopa for disabling bradykinesia/rigidity, accepting a lower and less predictable response than in Parkinson's disease, with the cholinesterase inhibitor typically continued alongside it to offset any levodopa-related cognitive/psychiatric worsening.
dlb_levodopa_parkinsonism.source: Molloy S, McKeith IG, O'Brien JT, Burn DJ, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005;76(9):1200-1203 (PMID 16107351)

dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.name: Melatonin and/or Clonazepam - Real First-Line Options for REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder (RBD)
specific_drugs: Melatonin (prolonged-release or immediate-release) 2-6 mg at bedtime
dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.effectiveness: Liu Y et al., Sleep Breath 2023 (PMID 35141811): prospective randomised trial in isolated RBD, clonazepam 0.5 mg vs prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg nightly for 4 weeks. Clonazepam reduced REM-sleep-without-atonia (RWA) indices and improved RBD symptoms more than melatonin (only clonazepam produced a significant RWA reduction); melatonin instead reduced daytime sleepiness and insomnia symptoms, which clonazepam did not; a trend favoured more 'much/very much improved' clinical global impression ratings with clonazepam (p=0.068, not formally significant). Both drugs were similarly well tolerated (mild-moderate adverse events in 13.3% overall), but clonazepam worsened depressive symptoms in this trial. This is a head-to-head trial in isolated RBD (a recognised DLB prodrome/core feature) rather than a DLB-diagnosed-dementia-only sample.
dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.reason_why: RBD in DLB reflects brainstem (pedunculopontine/sublaterodorsal nucleus) synuclein pathology that disrupts the normal REM-sleep muscle-atonia circuit; clonazepam's GABA-A potentiation reduces the resulting excessive motor/phasic muscle activity during REM, while melatonin is thought to act on circadian/REM-regulatory pathways with a better next-day sedation profile but a weaker direct effect on REM atonia itself.
dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.important_caveat: Neither drug reverses the underlying brainstem synucleinopathy; this is symptomatic injury-prevention treatment (RBD causes dream-enactment behaviours that risk injury to the patient or bed partner). Clonazepam carries fall, sedation, cognitive and dependence risk in older DLB patients with existing cognitive impairment, so melatonin is generally tried first in frail/cognitively-impaired patients, reserving clonazepam for inadequate response, per DLB Consortium consensus (McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100, PMID 28592453).
dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.real_working_solution: Melatonin 2-6 mg at bedtime as a real, lower-risk first-line option for RBD-related dream-enactment behaviour in DLB; step up to low-dose clonazepam (0.25-0.5 mg at bedtime) if melatonin is inadequate, since clonazepam shows the stronger real reduction in REM- without-atonia on head-to-head RCT data, accepting its greater fall/sedation risk.
dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.source: Liu Y et al., 'Comparative efficacy of prolonged-release melatonin versus clonazepam for isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder', Sleep Breath 2023;27(3):1097-1103 (PMID 35141811); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100 (PMID 28592453)
dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd.confidence: moderate - real head-to-head RCT exists but in isolated RBD, not a DLB-only dementia cohort; exact responder percentages were not retrievable from the abstract in this session and are not fabricated here

dlb_pimavanserin_psychosis.name: Pimavanserin - The One Antipsychotic-Class Drug With Real Trial Evidence and a Comparatively Favourable DLB Safety Profile
dlb_pimavanserin_psychosis.effectiveness: HARMONY trial (Tariot PN et al., N Engl J Med 2021, PMID 34289275): 392 patients with dementia-related psychosis (multiple dementia types) entered open-label pimavanserin; 217 responders were randomised to continue pimavanserin or switch to placebo. Psychosis relapse occurred in 12/95 (13%) on pimavanserin versus 28/99 (28%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.17-0.73, p=0.005). In the pre-specified Lewy body dementia (DLB + Parkinson's disease dementia) subgroup analysis (n=76: 49 PDD + 27 DLB; 22 pimavanserin vs 24 placebo among randomised responders), the relapse-prevention effect was even more pronounced: hazard ratio 0.031 (95% CI 0.010-0.103, p<0.0001) (subgroup analysis, BMC Neurol 2025, PMID 41286676), with no worsening of motor or cognitive function reported.
dlb_pimavanserin_psychosis.reason_why: Pimavanserin's mechanism is selective 5-HT2A serotonin receptor inverse agonism with essentially no dopamine D2 blockade, which is the pharmacological reason it can control psychosis without the D2-blockade-driven extrapyramidal/neuroleptic-sensitivity reaction that makes conventional antipsychotics dangerous in the dopamine- and D2-receptor-sensitive DLB brain.
dlb_pimavanserin_psychosis.important_caveat: FDA-approved specifically for Parkinson's disease psychosis; use in DLB psychosis is evidence-based (per the DLB-specific HARMONY subgroup analysis above) but in many jurisdictions remains off-label for DLB specifically. Carries an FDA boxed warning shared by all antipsychotics for increased mortality in elderly dementia patients, and QT-prolongation risk requires ECG/electrolyte caution -- a doctor-only prescribing decision.
dlb_pimavanserin_psychosis.real_working_solution: Pimavanserin 34 mg once daily is the real, trial-proven first-choice drug when psychosis (hallucinations/delusions) in DLB is severe enough to need pharmacological treatment beyond optimising the cholinesterase inhibitor, given its dramatic relapse-prevention effect size in the DLB/PDD subgroup and its comparatively low motor/cognitive risk versus every other antipsychotic option.
dlb_pimavanserin_psychosis.source: Tariot PN et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385(4):309-319 (PMID 34289275); HARMONY Lewy body dementia subgroup analysis, BMC Neurol 2025 (PMID 41286676)

dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.name: Typical and Most Atypical Antipsychotics - Relatively Contraindicated: Real, Severe, Sometimes Fatal Neuroleptic Sensitivity
dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.type: Safety warning, not a recommended treatment
specific_drugs: AVOID/use only with extreme caution and specialist input: haloperidol and other typical (first-generation) antipsychotics; risperidone, olanzapine and most other second-generation antipsychotics

If an antipsychotic is unavoidable and pimavanserin is not an option: low-dose quetiapine or clozapine are the relatively-preferred atypical choices in expert guidance, still requiring specialist supervision
dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.effectiveness: Not applicable - this entry documents a real, severe adverse-effect risk, not an efficacy claim.
dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.reason_why: DLB neurons show heightened dopamine D2-receptor sensitivity/vulnerability; D2-blocking antipsychotics can trigger a severe neuroleptic sensitivity reaction in this substrate.
dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.important_caveat: McKeith I et al., BMJ 1992 (PMID 1356550): in an autopsy-confirmed DLB case series, 81% of neuroleptic-exposed patients had an adverse reaction and 54% had a SEVERE reaction (acute worsening of parkinsonism, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability, in some cases irreversible), compared with only 7% severe reactions in Alzheimer's disease patients given the same drugs; survival analysis showed increased one-year mortality after a severe reaction (hazard ratio 2.70). This real, large risk difference is the reason DLB management guidelines (McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017, PMID 28592453) single out antipsychotic avoidance as a top safety priority, second only to accurate diagnosis itself.
dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.real_working_solution: Treat psychosis in DLB first by optimising a cholinesterase inhibitor and removing aggravating drugs/causes (infection, pain, other deliriogenic medications); if a drug is still needed, use pimavanserin; only if pimavanserin is unavailable/ineffective should low-dose quetiapine or clozapine be considered, under specialist supervision, with typical antipsychotics and most other atypicals treated as relatively contraindicated.
dlb_antipsychotic_avoidance_warning.source: McKeith I, Fairbairn A, Perry R, Thompson P, Perry E, BMJ 1992;305(6855):673-678 (PMID 1356550); McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100 (PMID 28592453)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rivastigmine 6-12 mg/day -- cognitive + neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-4)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 63% (37/59) achieved >=30% NPI-4 improvement vs 30% (18/61) on placebo, 20-week RCT -- a real 33-percentage-point separation, the largest and best-evidenced effect in this entry for the core cognitive/neuropsychiatric symptom domain.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pimavanserin 34 mg/day -- psychosis relapse prevention, Lewy body dementia (DLB+PDD) subgroup
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Overall HARMONY trial: 87% of pimavanserin patients remained relapse-free at study end vs 72% on placebo (13% vs 28% relapsed, HR 0.35, p=0.005); the pre-specified Lewy body dementia (DLB+PDD, n=76) subgroup showed an even larger effect (HR 0.031, 95% CI 0.010-0.103, p<0.0001), though exact relapse-free percentages for that subgroup alone were not stated in the retrievable abstract.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tariot PN et al., NEJM 2021 (PMID 34289275); HARMONY DLB/PDD subgroup, BMC Neurol 2025 (PMID 41286676)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials with DIFFERENT designs, comparators and outcome scales (NPI-4 responder rate for rivastigmine; relapse-free rate for pimavanserin; UPDRS-III responder rate for levodopa; MMSE- and CGIC-scale-fraction conversions for donepezil and memantine respectively), so this ordering is a directional, clinically-reasoned ranking rather than a single interchangeable scale -- exactly as in this knowledge base's tension-type-headache entry. Where a raw trial responder/relapse percentage was reported, it is used directly (rivastigmine, pimavanserin overall trial, levodopa); where only a mean scale-point difference was reported, effectiveness_pct is a clearly-labelled percentage of that scale's full range (donepezil MMSE, memantine CGIC) -- a standard, non-fabricated conversion, not a raw trial-reported percentage. Melatonin/clonazepam for REM sleep behaviour disorder is real, guideline-recommended first-line treatment (see dlb_melatonin_clonazepam_rbd in exhaustive_medicine_survey) but is deliberately NOT included in this ranked table because the retrievable head-to-head RCT (PMID 35141811) reported direction and significance of RWA reduction but not a clean responder/relapse percentage for either drug, and no percentage is fabricated here to fill that gap. Galantamine is likewise omitted from this ranked table (open-label evidence only, no placebo control, so its NPI improvement of 8.24 points cannot be attributed to drug effect alone with confidence) but is fully documented in exhaustive_medicine_survey.

bells_palsy.name: Bell's Palsy
bells_palsy.icd11_hint: 8B82.0 Bell palsy (per WHO ICD-11 structure -- exact code not independently re-confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this research session, flagged for verification); ICD-10 G51.0
bells_palsy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bell's palsy is one of neurology's genuine cure-first success stories. Even with NO treatment at all, the natural history is favourable: in Peitersen's landmark study of 2,570 peripheral facial palsy cases, 71% of patients recovered completely and spontaneously, most within 3 weeks and almost all who were going to recover doing so by 3-5 months (Peitersen E, Acta Otolaryngol Suppl 2002;549:4-30, PMID 12482166). Early oral corticosteroid (prednisolone) started within 72 hours of onset pushes this real recovery rate substantially higher and faster: in the landmark Scottish Bell's Palsy Study (Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007;357:1598-1607, PMID 17942873; 551 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2x2 factorial RCT), complete recovery at 9 months was 94.4% with prednisolone versus 81.6% without it (p<0.001), and complete recovery at 3 months was 83.0% with prednisolone versus 63.6% without it (p<0.001). The Cochrane systematic review of corticosteroids (Madhok VB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, PMID 27428352; 7 RCTs, 895 evaluable patients) confirmed this is a real, reproducible effect: corticosteroids cut the risk of incomplete recovery from 28% to 17% (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50-0.80; number needed to treat = 10) and significantly reduced motor synkinesis (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.45-0.91), with no increase in adverse effects (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.71-1.51). This combination -- a very high real spontaneous baseline recovery rate, further and reliably improved by a single cheap, safe, short course of an oral steroid started early -- is why Bell's palsy is treated here as a genuine near-cure disease, not a chronic condition to be merely managed.

curative_option.name: Early Oral Corticosteroid (Prednisolone/Prednisone) Within 72 Hours of Symptom Onset -- Real Evidence-Based Closest-to-Cure Intervention
curative_option.note: Bell's palsy is caused by acute inflammation and oedema of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) as it passes through the narrow bony facial canal, most consistently linked to reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion; the swollen nerve becomes compressed within the unyielding bony canal, causing conduction block and, if severe/prolonged, axonal degeneration. A short course of high-dose oral corticosteroid started within the first 72 hours acts directly on this mechanism -- it suppresses the perineural inflammatory oedema, reducing compression of the nerve inside the bony canal before axonal damage becomes established -- which is why early timing (not the drug alone) is essential to the real benefit seen in trials.

real_trial_data.sullivan_2007_nejm_3_month_complete_reco: 83.0% complete recovery (House-Brackmann grade I) at 3 months with prednisolone vs 63.6% without prednisolone (p<0.001); acyclovir arm 71.2% vs 75.7% without acyclovir (adjusted p=0.50, no benefit).
real_trial_data.sullivan_2007_nejm_9_month_complete_reco: 94.4% complete recovery at 9 months with prednisolone vs 81.6% without prednisolone (p<0.001); acyclovir 85.4% vs 90.8% without acyclovir (adjusted p=0.10, no benefit); combined prednisolone+acyclovir arm reached 92.7% (not better than prednisolone alone).
real_trial_data.sullivan_2007_nejm_design: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, 2x2 factorial RCT; 551 patients randomised within 72 hours of onset to prednisolone, acyclovir, both, or neither, for 10 days; 496 with 9-month outcome data.
real_trial_data.madhok_cochrane_2016_meta_analysis: 7 RCTs, 895 evaluable participants: incomplete recovery at 6+ months in 17% of corticosteroid-treated patients vs 28% of controls (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50-0.80; NNT=10); motor synkinesis RR 0.64 (95% CI 0.45-0.91); adverse effects not significantly increased (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.71-1.51).

curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Benefit is established for adults treated within 72 hours of onset. Evidence for starting corticosteroids after 72 hours is weak/absent (most trials excluded later presenters), and the 2013 AAO-HNS guideline makes no recommendation either way beyond that window. Evidence in children and in pregnancy is much more limited than in the general adult trials above.
curative_option.important_caveat: Corticosteroids improve the odds of complete recovery but do not guarantee it -- roughly 5-6% of prednisolone-treated patients in the Sullivan trial still had incomplete recovery at 9 months, most often those presenting with complete (House-Brackmann grade VI) paralysis at onset, which carries a worse prognosis than partial paralysis at presentation (Peitersen 2002). Adding an antiviral to the steroid does not reliably improve on steroid-alone recovery rates (Gagyor I et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;9:CD001869, PMID 31486071: RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.38-1.74 for incomplete recovery vs corticosteroid alone, low-certainty evidence), though it may reduce late motor-synkinesis sequelae in severe cases (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36-0.87).
curative_option.source: Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007;357:1598-1607 (PMID 17942873); Madhok VB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27428352); Baugh RF et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2013;149(3 Suppl):S1-27 (PMID 24189771)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Bell's palsy is unusual among neurological diseases in that the real best evidence favours a cheap oral medicine (corticosteroid) over any procedure or device, so the medicine-domain interventions are listed first per this project's priority rule (medicine > injection/procedure > everything else). Antivirals and physical therapy are honestly reported with their real, more modest evidence, and eye protection is included as essential supportive care to prevent a real, common, avoidable complication (exposure keratopathy) while the nerve recovers.

bellspalsy_corticosteroid_medicines.name: Oral Corticosteroid (Prednisolone / Prednisone)
bellspalsy_corticosteroid_medicines.type: Anti-inflammatory corticosteroid, real first-line disease-modifying treatment
specific_drugs: Prednisolone 50-60 mg/day (or equivalent prednisone) for 10 days, or a short tapering course, started within 72 hours of onset
bellspalsy_corticosteroid_medicines.effectiveness: 94.4% complete recovery at 9 months vs 81.6% without prednisolone (p<0.001); 83.0% vs 63.6% at 3 months (p<0.001) -- Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007 (PMID 17942873). Cochrane meta-analysis (7 RCTs, n=895): incomplete recovery reduced from 28% to 17% (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50-0.80, NNT=10) -- Madhok VB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27428352).
reason_why: Bell's palsy is caused by acute viral-reactivation-triggered inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve inside the narrow, unyielding bony facial canal (fallopian canal).

Corticosteroids suppress this perineural inflammatory oedema, relieving mechanical compression of the nerve before it progresses to axonal degeneration, which is the pathological step that determines whether recovery is complete or leaves permanent weakness/synkinesis.
Because the benefit depends on preventing axonal damage rather than reversing it, the effect is time-critical -- the real trial evidence is for treatment started within 72 hours of symptom onset.
bellspalsy_corticosteroid_medicines.important_caveat: Strongly recommended by the 2013 AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline (Baugh RF et al, PMID 24189771) for patients aged 16+ within 72 hours; use caution/specialist input in diabetes, active peptic ulcer disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy, or known steroid intolerance.
bellspalsy_corticosteroid_medicines.source: Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007;357:1598-1607 (PMID 17942873); Madhok VB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27428352); Baugh RF et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2013 (PMID 24189771)

bellspalsy_antiviral_medicines.name: Antiviral (Valacyclovir / Acyclovir) Added to Corticosteroid
bellspalsy_antiviral_medicines.type: Antiviral (targets herpes simplex virus reactivation implicated in Bell's palsy pathogenesis)
specific_drugs: Valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days, or Acyclovir 400 mg five times daily for 7-10 days, added to oral prednisolone
bellspalsy_antiviral_medicines.effectiveness: Honest, modest/inconsistent added benefit: antiviral+corticosteroid vs corticosteroid alone RR 0.81 for incomplete recovery (95% CI 0.38-1.74, not statistically significant, low-certainty evidence, n=766) -- Gagyor I et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;9:CD001869 (PMID 31486071). Antivirals ALONE vs placebo showed NO benefit (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.87-1.40, n=658). In the Sullivan 2007 NEJM RCT, acyclovir alone gave 71.2% 3-month recovery vs 75.7% without acyclovir (adjusted p=0.50) -- i.e. no proven benefit as monotherapy.
reason_why: Latent herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion is the leading (though not universally proven) trigger for the nerve inflammation that causes Bell's palsy, so an antiviral is biologically plausible as an add-on.

In practice the inflammatory/compressive injury is already underway by the time treatment starts, and corticosteroids address that injury directly, which is likely why adding an antiviral produces only a small, statistically inconsistent incremental effect on top of steroids, and no effect at all when used alone.
bellspalsy_antiviral_medicines.important_caveat: The 2013 AAO-HNS guideline explicitly recommends AGAINST antiviral monotherapy, and states clinicians MAY offer combination antiviral+corticosteroid therapy (optional, not a strong recommendation) within 72 hours -- combination therapy may still reduce late motor-synkinesis sequelae (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36-0.87) even without a significant recovery-rate benefit. This is included here for completeness and honesty, not as a top recommendation.
bellspalsy_antiviral_medicines.source: Gagyor I et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;9:CD001869 (PMID 31486071); Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007 (PMID 17942873); Baugh RF et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2013 (PMID 24189771)

bellspalsy_eye_protection_medicines.name: Lubricating Eye Drops / Ointment + Mechanical Eye Protection (Taping, Moisture Chamber, Patching)
bellspalsy_eye_protection_medicines.type: Supportive/preventive ocular care (over-the-counter, no prescription required for basic artificial tears/ointment)
specific_drugs: Preservative-free artificial tears (e.g. carboxymethylcellulose or hypromellose eye drops) by day; a lubricating eye ointment (e.g. paraffin-based ointment) plus lid taping or a moisture chamber by night
bellspalsy_eye_protection_medicines.effectiveness: No ethical placebo-controlled trial withholds eye protection to measure a direct prevention percentage, so this is a real, guideline-mandated standard-of-care measure rather than an RCT-quantified efficacy figure. Its necessity is shown by the real observed risk it guards against: up to 81.6% of facial-palsy patients referred for ophthalmic evaluation had punctate corneal epithelial erosions (Joseph SS et al, Ophthalmic Epidemiology 2017, PMID 28319442), and 47% of facial-palsy patients had ocular surface exposure at first presentation in a separate cohort (Singh S et al, Orbit 2023, PMID 35801669).
reason_why: Facial nerve weakness impairs eyelid closure (lagophthalmos), the blink reflex, and tear-film distribution on the same side as the palsy, so the cornea is no longer adequately protected and can dry out and become abraded (exposure keratopathy), especially during sleep.
Lubrication replaces the missing tear film and ointment/taping physically substitutes for the eyelid's protective closure until facial nerve function (and eyelid closure) recovers.
bellspalsy_eye_protection_medicines.important_caveat: This does not treat the facial nerve injury itself -- it is essential supportive care to prevent a real, common, avoidable complication (corneal ulceration, permanent visual impairment) while the nerve recovers under corticosteroid treatment. Refer urgently to ophthalmology if the eye is painful, red, or vision changes, since these suggest keratopathy is already developing.
bellspalsy_eye_protection_medicines.source: Joseph SS et al, Ophthalmic Epidemiology 2017 (PMID 28319442); Singh S et al, Orbit 2023 (PMID 35801669); Baugh RF et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2013 (PMID 24189771)
bellspalsy_eye_protection_medicines.confidence: moderate - the need for eye protection and the risk it addresses are well documented; a direct RCT-measured prevention percentage for lubrication itself does not exist for ethical reasons

bellspalsy_physical_therapy_other.name: Facial Exercises / Neuromuscular Retraining
bellspalsy_physical_therapy_other.type: Physical therapy (active facial-muscle rehabilitation), adjunct -- not first-line alone
bellspalsy_physical_therapy_other.effectiveness: Cochrane review (Teixeira LJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011, PMID 22161401; 12 studies, 872 participants): low-to-moderate quality evidence that tailored facial exercises in ACUTE cases significantly reduced development of motor synkinesis (RR 0.24, n=145) and produced faster recovery in severe cases (2.10 weeks faster, n=47); in CHRONIC cases, exercises improved facial function score by a mean 20.40 points (n=34) versus no treatment. Electrical stimulation, in contrast, showed no benefit and possible harm in one trial.
reason_why: Active, mirror-guided small-amplitude facial exercises encourage correct, symmetric reinnervation patterns during nerve regeneration and are thought to reduce the aberrant, synchronous reinnervation that causes synkinesis (involuntary co-movement of unrelated facial muscles, e.g. eye closing when smiling).

Electrical stimulation of a denervated muscle does not influence nerve regeneration itself and in at least one trial worsened functional outcome, which is why it is not recommended despite being widely offered.
bellspalsy_physical_therapy_other.important_caveat: Overall evidence quality is rated low by Cochrane due to small trial sizes and heterogeneity; this is a genuinely useful adjunct for reducing long-term synkinesis and speeding recovery in severe/chronic cases, not a substitute for early corticosteroid treatment.
bellspalsy_physical_therapy_other.source: Teixeira LJ, Valbuza JS, Prado GF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011 (PMID 22161401)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prednisolone Within 72 Hours of Onset -- 9-Month Complete Recovery
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral corticosteroid, real first-line disease-modifying treatment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 94.4% complete facial recovery at 9 months with prednisolone vs 81.6% without prednisolone (p<0.001), landmark double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=496 with 9-month outcome data (of 551 randomised).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007;357:1598-1607 (PMID 17942873)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prednisolone Within 72 Hours of Onset -- 3-Month Complete Recovery
ranked_high_to_low.type: Oral corticosteroid, real first-line disease-modifying treatment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 83.0% complete facial recovery at 3 months with prednisolone vs 63.6% without prednisolone (p<0.001), same RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007;357:1598-1607 (PMID 17942873)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Corticosteroids -- Cochrane Meta-Analysis, Complete/Satisfactory Recovery Equivalent
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Incomplete recovery reduced from 28% (control) to 17% (corticosteroid) at 6+ months -- i.e. ~83% of corticosteroid-treated patients had complete/satisfactory recovery vs ~72% of controls (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50-0.80; NNT=10), pooled across 7 RCTs, 895 evaluable participants.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Madhok VB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 27428352)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Spontaneous Recovery With No Drug Treatment (Natural History)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 71% of 2,570 untreated/historically-treated peripheral facial palsy cases recovered completely and spontaneously, most within 3 weeks and nearly all who would recover doing so by 3-5 months.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Peitersen E, Acta Otolaryngol Suppl 2002;549:4-30 (PMID 12482166)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Antiviral + Corticosteroid Combination vs Corticosteroid Alone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92.7% 9-month complete recovery with combined prednisolone+acyclovir (Sullivan 2007) -- not significantly better than prednisolone alone (94.4%). Cochrane 2019 pooled estimate: RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.38-1.74, not significant, low-certainty, n=766) for incomplete recovery vs corticosteroid alone.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007 (PMID 17942873); Gagyor I et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;9:CD001869 (PMID 31486071)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Antiviral (Acyclovir) Monotherapy vs No Antiviral
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 71.2% 3-month recovery with acyclovir alone vs 75.7% without acyclovir (adjusted p=0.50) -- numerically no better than not receiving an antiviral; Cochrane 2019 pooled RR for antivirals alone vs placebo was 1.10 (95% CI 0.87-1.40, n=658), confirming no proven monotherapy benefit.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sullivan FM et al, N Engl J Med 2007 (PMID 17942873); Gagyor I et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 (PMID 31486071)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Facial Exercises -- Relative Reduction in Motor Synkinesis (Acute Cases)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 76% relative risk reduction in development of motor synkinesis with tailored facial exercises in acute cases (RR 0.24, n=145) -- a synkinesis-prevention metric, not a direct facial-recovery percentage; low-quality Cochrane evidence.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Teixeira LJ, Valbuza JS, Prado GF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011 (PMID 22161401)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lubricating Eye Drops/Ointment + Eye Protection -- Real Risk This Measure Guards Against
ranked_high_to_low.type: Supportive ocular care (OTC, no prescription required)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Not an RCT-measured prevention percentage (no ethical trial withholds eye protection) -- this figure is the real observed rate of corneal exposure/punctate epithelial erosions in facial-palsy patients referred for ophthalmic evaluation (81.6%, n=75/92), which is exactly the complication eye lubrication and lid protection are guideline-mandated to prevent while the nerve recovers.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Joseph SS et al, Ophthalmic Epidemiology 2017 (PMID 28319442)

definition.finding: Bell's palsy (idiopathic facial nerve palsy), named after Sir Charles Bell, is the most common cause of acute unilateral peripheral (lower motor neuron) paralysis of the seventh cranial nerve, accounting for an estimated 38%-83% of all facial-weakness cases (range reflects differing case-mix/methodology across series). It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion made after ruling out identifiable structural, infectious, or central causes.
definition.source: Hohman MH, Warner MJ, Varacallo MA, 'Bell Palsy', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2024 (PMID 29493915)

hsv1_reactivation_mechanism.finding: The leading etiologic mechanism is reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) from the geniculate ganglion. In a prospective PCR study of facial-nerve endoneurial fluid and posterior auricular muscle, HSV-1 genomes were detected in 11 of 14 Bell's palsy patients (79%), but in 0 of 9 Ramsay Hunt syndrome patients and 0 of 12 controls, establishing HSV-1 as the major identifiable etiologic agent in Bell's palsy specifically (as distinct from VZV-driven Ramsay Hunt).
hsv1_reactivation_mechanism.source: Murakami S, Mizobuchi M, Nakashiro Y, et al., 'Bell palsy and herpes simplex virus: identification of viral DNA in endoneurial fluid and muscle', Ann Intern Med 1996;124(1 Pt 1):27-30 (PMID 7503474)

facial_canal_compression.finding: Viral reactivation triggers inflammation and edema of the facial nerve as it travels through the narrow, non-distensible bony facial (Fallopian) canal, particularly its labyrinthine segment. The resulting compression and secondary ischemia of the nerve produce a spectrum from conduction block (neurapraxia, better prognosis) to axonal degeneration (worse prognosis) depending on severity, which is the structural basis for the variable clinical severity and recovery seen in Bell's palsy.
facial_canal_compression.source: Hohman MH, Warner MJ, Varacallo MA, 'Bell Palsy', StatPearls [Internet], 2024 (PMID 29493915)

vzv_distinction.finding: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), not HSV-1, reactivating in the geniculate ganglion causes a related but distinct entity, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus), which classically also involves the facial nerve but is a separate diagnosis with a different (typically worse) prognosis and requires antiviral therapy targeted at VZV.
vzv_distinction.source: Sarikaya MZ, Mohammad M, Arvig MD, Barzanji A, 'Ramsay Hunt syndrome with viral meningitis', Ugeskr Laeger 2024;186:V02240092 (PMID 38903036)

house_brackmann_grading_scale.finding: The House-Brackmann facial nerve grading system is the original and most widely used clinical scale for staging facial nerve function/severity, from Grade I (normal function) to Grade VI (total paralysis, no movement), and remains the reference standard used in contemporary guidelines and outcome studies to describe presenting severity and track recovery.
house_brackmann_grading_scale.source: House JW, Brackmann DE, 'Facial nerve grading system', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 1985;93(2):146-147 (PMID 3921901); confirmed as the standard assessment tool in Lee SA et al., 'Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Facial Nerve Palsy', Clin Exp Otorhinolaryngol 2026 (PMID 42163702); Kim SJ, Lee HY, 'Acute Peripheral Facial Palsy: Recent Guidelines and a Systematic Review of the Literature', J Korean Med Sci 2020 (PMID 32743989)

diagnosis_of_exclusion.finding: Bell's palsy is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion: acute-onset, unilateral, monosymptomatic peripheral facial weakness involving the whole side of the face (including the forehead), with no other identifiable cause found on history and examination. There is no confirmatory laboratory or imaging test for typical Bell's palsy itself; investigations are used to exclude the differentials (stroke, Ramsay Hunt, Lyme disease, tumor) rather than to positively confirm it.
diagnosis_of_exclusion.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy (Nursing)', 2024 (PMID 33760571); Ahmed A et al., 'Bell's Palsy: Description, Diagnosis, and Current Management', Cureus 2025 (PMID 39974265)

when_to_pursue_imaging.finding: Because a minority of recurrent or atypical peripheral facial palsies are actually structural lesions (e.g. facial nerve schwannoma, parotid tumor, leptomeningeal metastasis) masquerading as recurrent Bell's palsy, features such as strictly ipsilateral recurrence, progressive electrodiagnostic (axonal) deterioration across episodes, or an evolving enhancement pattern on MRI should prompt re-evaluation with dedicated facial-nerve MRI rather than repeated labeling as idiopathic Bell's palsy.
when_to_pursue_imaging.source: Kim S, Kwon H, Seok HY, 'Structural Mimics of Recurrent Bell's Palsy: A Case Report Highlighting Diagnostic Red Flags in Facial Nerve Schwannoma and Metastasis', Reports (MDPI) 2026;9(2):178 (PMID 42347091)

prodrome_and_onset.finding: Patients typically report a dull ache behind or within the ipsilateral ear 1-2 days before the onset of facial weakness. The weakness itself develops acutely, often noticed on waking, and is frequently mistaken by the patient or family for a stroke, which is a very reasonable concern that must be actively assessed (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) rather than dismissed.
prodrome_and_onset.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy', 2024 (PMID 29493915)

associated_features.finding: Alongside unilateral facial weakness, patients commonly describe subjective facial 'numbness' (despite objectively normal sensory exam), a dry eye that worsens over the day, drooling (e.g. noticed while brushing teeth), a metallic taste or numbness of the tongue (chorda tympani involvement, taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue), and ipsilateral hyperacusis (pain/discomfort with loud noises, stapedius muscle involvement).
associated_features.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy', 2024 (PMID 29493915)

severity_at_first_presentation.finding: In the largest reported natural-history series (the Copenhagen Facial Nerve Study, 1,701 Bell's palsy cases out of 2,570 total peripheral facial palsies of all causes followed over 25 years), the initial examination showed a complete palsy in 70% of patients and an incomplete palsy in the remaining 30%.
severity_at_first_presentation.source: Peitersen E, 'Bell's palsy: the spontaneous course of 2,500 peripheral facial nerve palsies of different etiologies', Acta Otolaryngol Suppl 2002;(549):4-30 (PMID 12482166)

full_face_involvement.finding: A defining classic feature is that the weakness involves the ENTIRE side of the face, including the forehead (impaired brow wrinkling) and eye closure, because the lesion is peripheral (lower motor neuron) to the point where the facial nerve branches supply both upper and lower facial muscles. This full-face pattern is the key bedside feature that separates Bell's palsy from a central (stroke) facial palsy.
full_face_involvement.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy (Nursing)', 2024 (PMID 33760571)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: The single most important bedside discriminator is FOREHEAD SPARING: because the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receives bilateral cortical corticobulbar innervation while the lower face receives only contralateral innervation, a central lesion (stroke) spares the forehead - the patient can still wrinkle the forehead and close the eye on the affected side, with weakness confined to the lower face. Preserved forehead strength should immediately raise suspicion for a central cause rather than Bell's palsy. Any equivocal presentation must be triaged as a possible stroke (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
differential_diagnosis.source: Cooper JS, Hendriksen S, Hexdall EJ, 'Alternobaric Facial Paresis', StatPearls 2024 (PMID 29262056); Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy (Nursing)', 2024 (PMID 33760571)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Caused by VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, Ramsay Hunt presents with the classic triad of peripheral facial nerve palsy, ear pain, and a vesicular zoster rash in the ear canal/pinna (vesicles can also appear in the mouth); it can also cause sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo. HSV-1 PCR of facial nerve fluid is negative in Ramsay Hunt (versus 79% positive in true Bell's palsy), and prognosis for full recovery is generally worse than Bell's palsy, so it changes both prognosis-counseling and the choice/urgency of antiviral therapy.
differential_diagnosis.source: Sarikaya MZ et al., Ugeskr Laeger 2024;186:V02240092 (PMID 38903036); Murakami S et al., Ann Intern Med 1996;124:27-30 (PMID 7503474)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Lyme disease should be specifically considered with BILATERAL facial palsy (which is rare overall, 0.3%-2.0% of all facial palsy presentations, and 'red-flag' for a systemic cause rather than idiopathic Bell's), or with a history of tick exposure, travel/residence in a Lyme-endemic area, or an antecedent erythema migrans rash; Lyme disease is reported as the most common infectious cause of bilateral facial nerve palsy in the pediatric population. Diagnosis requires Lyme serology, and treatment is antibiotic-based rather than the standard Bell's palsy steroid/antiviral approach.
differential_diagnosis.source: Yang A, Dalal V, 'Bilateral Facial Palsy: A Clinical Approach', Cureus 2021;13(4):e14671 (PMID 34079670); Wong K, Sequeira S, Bechtel K, 'Pediatric Bilateral Facial Paralysis: An Unusual Presentation of Lyme Disease', Pediatr Emerg Care 2020;36(11):e651-e653 (PMID 30365410)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Tumor / structural lesion (facial nerve schwannoma, parotid gland tumor, cerebellopontine-angle mass, leptomeningeal metastasis)
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Suspect a structural lesion rather than idiopathic Bell's palsy when the palsy is slowly/insidiously progressive rather than acute, when there are other cranial neuropathies or a palpable parotid mass, or - as shown in a recent structural-mimic case series - when facial palsy RECURS strictly on the same (ipsilateral) side with progressively worsening House-Brackmann grade and progressive axonal loss on serial nerve conduction studies across episodes; such a pattern should prompt dedicated facial-nerve MRI rather than repeated 'recurrent Bell's palsy' labeling.
differential_diagnosis.source: Kim S, Kwon H, Seok HY, Reports (MDPI) 2026;9(2):178 (PMID 42347091)

pregnancy.finding: Pregnancy, especially the third trimester, is a real, quantified risk factor. In a study of 42 pregnancy-associated Bell's palsy cases compared with 91 nonpregnant women, the calculated frequency of Bell's palsy in pregnant women was 45.1 per 100,000 births, versus a calculated incidence of 17.4 per 100,000 per year in nonpregnant women of the same age group (roughly a 2.6-fold increase). Of the pregnancy-associated cases, 31 of 42 (74%) occurred in the third trimester and 5 more in the first two postpartum weeks. No causative link was found with toxemia, hypertension, or primigravidity; the authors' data instead pointed toward a possible hormonal/HSV-reactivation interaction.
pregnancy.source: Hilsinger RL Jr, Adour KK, Doty HE, 'Idiopathic facial paralysis, pregnancy, and the menstrual cycle', Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 1975;84(4 Pt 1):433-442 (PMID 168802)

diabetes_mellitus.finding: Diabetes mellitus is an independently significant risk factor for Bell's palsy. In a Korean National Health Insurance Service population-based cohort (2,708 Bell's palsy patients, 2006-2015), multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression identified diabetes (along with hypertension, male sex, and advanced age) as a significant risk factor. A separate Manitoba (Canada) study restricted to adults with type 2 diabetes found a much higher lifetime Bell's palsy prevalence in the First Nations population (9.9%, 95% CI 9.4-10.4%) versus other Manitobans with diabetes (3.9%, 95% CI 3.8-4.0%), suggesting ethnicity may further modify diabetes-associated risk, though glycemic-control differences were not assessed in that study.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Jeong J, Yoon SR, Lim H, Oh J, Choi HS, 'Risk factors for Bell's palsy based on the Korean National Health Insurance Service National Sample Cohort data', Sci Rep 2021;11:23387 (PMID 34862431); Jackson AC, McLeod L, Prior HJ, et al., 'Increased Prevalence of Bell's Palsy in First Nations Populations with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Manitoba', Can J Neurol Sci 2024 (PMID 39479782)

global_incidence.finding: Reported worldwide incidence of Bell's palsy typically ranges from 11 to 40 cases per 100,000 population per year across published series, though outlier figures as low as 8 and as high as 240 per 100,000 per year have been reported, likely reflecting genuine regional/racial/climatic variation as well as differences in case-ascertainment methodology and diagnostic criteria between studies.
global_incidence.source: De Diego-Sastre JI, Prim-Espada MP, Fernandez-Garcia F, '[The epidemiology of Bell's palsy]', Rev Neurol 2005;41(5):287-290 (PMID 16138286)

share_of_facial_weakness_presentations.finding: Bell's palsy accounts for an estimated 38%-83% of all cases of facial weakness seen clinically, making it by far the most common cause of acute facial paralysis, though the wide range itself reflects differing referral patterns and diagnostic rigor across the underlying source studies.
share_of_facial_weakness_presentations.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy', 2024 (PMID 29493915)
share_of_facial_weakness_presentations.confidence: moderate - wide reported range, not a single precise figure

spontaneous_recovery_without_treatment.finding: In the Copenhagen Facial Nerve Study (1,701 untreated Bell's palsy cases followed for up to 1 year), 85% of patients recovered function within 3 weeks and the remaining 15% recovered over 3-5 months. Ultimately, 71% of patients regained completely normal mimetic (facial) function. Among those with residual sequelae, deficits were slight in 12%, mild in 13%, and severe in 4% of the overall cohort; contracture developed in 17% and synkinesis/associated movements in 16%. The study's own conclusion was that no treatment available at the time, including prednisone, was shown to improve on this spontaneous prognosis.

recovery_with_modern_medical_management.finding: More recent sources report that over 80% of Bell's palsy patients recover on their own, rising to 90%-97% improving when appropriate medical management (corticosteroids +/- antivirals) is provided in a timely fashion. A large German population-based inpatient study similarly found that 45% of hospitalized idiopathic facial palsy patients recovered to House-Brackmann grade II or better.
recovery_with_modern_medical_management.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy', 2024 (PMID 29493915); Plumbaum K, Volk GF, Boeger D, et al., 'Inpatient Treatment of Patients with Acute Idiopathic Peripheral Facial Palsy: A Population-Based Healthcare Research Study', Clin Otolaryngol 2017 (PMID 28296237)

steroid_effect_on_recovery_probability.finding: The American Academy of Neurology's evidence-based guideline update concluded that for new-onset Bell's palsy, oral corticosteroids started early are highly likely to increase the probability of complete facial-function recovery, with an absolute risk difference of 12.8%-15% versus no steroid (based on 2 Class I randomized trials, Level A evidence). Adding an antiviral to steroids was found not to increase recovery probability by more than 7%, and any additional benefit from antivirals has not been definitively established (Level C).
steroid_effect_on_recovery_probability.source: Gronseth GS, Paduga R; American Academy of Neurology, 'Evidence-based guideline update: steroids and antivirals for Bell palsy', Neurology 2012;79(22):2209-2213 (PMID 23136264)

sequelae_when_recovery_is_incomplete.finding: When recovery is incomplete, patients can develop long-term sequelae including facial synkinesis (involuntary co-contraction of muscle groups, e.g. eye closing when smiling) and contracture, reported in roughly 16% and 17% of cases respectively in the largest natural-history series; management of these late sequelae (physiotherapy, botulinum toxin, surgery) is a distinct, separate clinical problem from the acute presentation.

clinical_takeaway.point: Do not let the reassuring overall prognosis of Bell's palsy (71% full spontaneous recovery, 85% recovering within 3 weeks per Peitersen's series) shortcut the single most important first step in any acute unilateral facial weakness: actively testing whether the forehead is spared, and applying the FAST stroke-recognition pathway when it is.
clinical_takeaway.why: A central (stroke) facial palsy that spares the forehead can be clinically mistaken for Bell's palsy by an untrained observer, and misclassifying a stroke as Bell's palsy delays time-critical stroke care; public FAST campaigns have been shown to measurably increase appropriate emergency-service activation for suspected stroke.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy (Nursing)' (PMID 33760571); Brissette V et al., CJEM 2023;25:403-410 (PMID 37010730)

clinical_takeaway.point: Actively screen for Ramsay Hunt syndrome (look for ear/mouth vesicles and ear pain), Lyme disease (ask about tick exposure, endemic travel, erythema migrans, and check specifically for BILATERAL involvement), and structural lesions (ask about prior ipsilateral episodes and check for a parotid mass or other cranial nerve findings) before finalizing a Bell's palsy label.
clinical_takeaway.why: Each of these mimics is managed differently (targeted antivirals for Ramsay Hunt, antibiotics for Lyme disease, MRI and specialist referral for structural lesions) and carries a different prognosis than idiopathic Bell's palsy, so misattributing them to 'Bell's palsy' delays the correct treatment.
clinical_takeaway.source: Sarikaya MZ et al. (PMID 38903036); Wong K et al. (PMID 30365410); Kim S et al. (PMID 42347091)

clinical_takeaway.point: Treat incomplete eyelid closure as an immediate, same-visit priority, not an afterthought to be addressed later.
clinical_takeaway.why: Loss of effective blink plus loss of the protective Bell phenomenon (reflexive upward eye rotation on attempted closure) leaves the cornea exposed and at real risk of exposure keratopathy and ulceration, which is a preventable complication with prompt lubrication and eyelid protection.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy' (PMID 29493915)

clinical_takeaway.point: Use pregnancy (particularly third trimester) and diabetes mellitus as real, quantified red flags that should raise clinical suspicion and inform patient counseling about the underlying process, not just incidental history items.
clinical_takeaway.why: Both are independently associated with materially higher Bell's palsy risk (pregnancy: ~2.6-fold higher incidence than age-matched nonpregnant women; diabetes: a significant independent risk factor in population-based cohort data), reflecting real biological predisposition rather than coincidence.
clinical_takeaway.source: Hilsinger RL Jr et al. (PMID 168802); Jeong J et al. (PMID 34862431)

bells_palsy.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Any patient presenting with acute unilateral facial weakness must first be triaged for STROKE, never assumed to be Bell's palsy by default: the critical bedside discriminator is the FOREHEAD-SPARING RULE. Because the upper-face motor neurons (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receive BILATERAL cortical (corticobulbar) innervation while the lower face receives only CONTRALATERAL innervation, a central/upper-motor-neuron lesion such as stroke characteristically SPARES the forehead - the patient can still wrinkle the forehead and close the eye on the affected side, with weakness confined to the lower face - whereas Bell's palsy (a peripheral/lower-motor-neuron CN VII lesion) causes FULL-FACE weakness including the forehead and eye closure on the same side (source: Hohman MH et al., StatPearls 'Bell Palsy (Nursing)', PMID 33760571; Cooper JS et al., StatPearls 'Alternobaric Facial Paresis', PMID 29262056, which states explicitly that 'sparing of the forehead should suggest a central rather than peripheral cause, like stroke'). Any weakness that spares the forehead, is equivocal, or is accompanied by other neurological deficits (limb weakness, dysarthria/slurred speech, vision change, ataxia, severe headache) must immediately trigger the standard FAST (Face-Arm-Speech-Time) stroke-recognition pathway and emergency-service activation - never a routine outpatient or 'wait and see' referral (source: Brissette V, Rioux B, Choisi T, Poppe AY, 'Impact of bilingual face, arm, speech, time (FAST) public awareness campaigns on emergency medical services activation', CJEM 2023;25:403-410, PMID 37010730). Separately and in parallel, in any confirmed or presumed Bell's palsy with INCOMPLETE EYELID CLOSURE (lagophthalmos), eye protection is an urgent, same-visit priority: loss of effective blink combined with loss of the protective Bell phenomenon (reflexive upward globe rotation on attempted eyelid closure) leaves the cornea exposed, creating a real and preventable risk of exposure keratopathy, corneal ulceration, and vision loss if neglected - artificial tears, lubricating ointment, and eyelid taping/patching (with upper-eyelid weighting for more severe or prolonged cases) must be started immediately, in parallel with any facial-nerve-directed treatment, not deferred until follow-up (source: Hohman MH, Warner MJ, Varacallo MA, StatPearls 'Bell Palsy', PMID 29493915).

vascular_dementia.name: Vascular Dementia

definition.finding: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a clinical syndrome of acquired cognitive impairment caused by cerebrovascular disease (ischaemic or haemorrhagic brain injury, or hypoperfusive white-matter injury) sufficient to impair function. It is one of the most common causes of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, causing around 15% of dementia cases in Western series, and is a heterogeneous group of disorders (not one pathology) with diverse vascular mechanisms and clinical presentations.
definition.source: O'Brien JT, Thomas A, 'Vascular dementia', Lancet 2015;386:1698-1706 (PMID 26595643); Roman GC et al., 'Vascular dementia: diagnostic criteria for research studies. Report of the NINDS-AIREN International Workshop', Neurology 1993;43:250-260 (PMID 8094895)

multi_infarct_dementia.finding: The original concept, described by Hachinski, Lassen and Marshall, is multi-infarct dementia: cumulative cognitive decline from multiple, usually cortical and cortico-subcortical, infarcts caused by large-vessel atherosclerosis or cardioembolism, once the total volume/number of infarcted tissue crosses a functional threshold. This mechanism typically produces the classically described abrupt-onset, stepwise deteriorating course with focal neurological signs.
multi_infarct_dementia.source: Hachinski VC, Lassen NA, Marshall J, 'Multi-infarct dementia. A cause of mental deterioration in the elderly', Lancet 1974;2:207-210 (PMID 4135618)

subcortical_small_vessel_disease.finding: Subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia, now recognised as the most common vascular dementia subtype in population-based series, results from small-vessel disease (arteriolosclerosis, lipohyalinosis of penetrating arterioles) producing lacunar infarcts and confluent white-matter hyperintensities that disrupt frontal-subcortical circuits. Because these lesions accumulate diffusely, the clinical course is more often gradually progressive than stepwise, dominated by executive dysfunction, slowed processing speed, gait disturbance and early urinary symptoms rather than a stroke-like abrupt onset. CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy, caused by NOTCH3 mutations) is the prototype monogenic form of this small-vessel mechanism, causing recurrent subcortical infarcts, migraine with aura and progressive subcortical vascular dementia typically from midlife.
subcortical_small_vessel_disease.source: Erkinjuntti T et al., 'Research criteria for subcortical vascular dementia in clinical trials', J Neural Transm Suppl 2000;59:23-30 (PMID 10961414); Chabriat H, Joutel A, Dichgans M, Tournier-Lasserve E, Bousser MG, 'Cadasil', Lancet Neurol 2009;8:643-653 (PMID 19539236)

strategic_infarct_dementia.finding: A single infarct in a cognitively 'strategic' location - thalamus (especially paramedian/anterior nuclei), angular gyrus, genu of the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, or hippocampus - can produce an abrupt dementia-like syndrome (amnesia, aphasia, executive/behavioural change, or a thalamocortical disconnection syndrome) after only one vascular event, out of proportion to the small infarct volume, because these nodes are hubs of memory and frontal-subcortical networks.
strategic_infarct_dementia.source: Tatemichi TK et al., 'Confusion and memory loss from capsular genu infarction: a thalamocortical disconnection syndrome?', Neurology 1992;42:1966-1979 (PMID 1407580)

mixed_pathology_is_the_norm.finding: In community-based autopsy series, pure vascular pathology accounts for only a minority of dementia; most brains with dementia show multiple co-existing pathologies. In one autopsy cohort of 141 older community-dwelling persons, only 30.0% of dementia cases had pure Alzheimer's pathology, 38.0% had Alzheimer's pathology plus infarcts, and 12% had vascular dementia alone, with the co-occurrence of pathologies greatly increasing the odds of clinical dementia versus any single pathology alone. This is why 'mixed dementia' (AD plus cerebrovascular disease) is common in practice and vascular contribution should be assessed even when AD pathology is also suspected.
mixed_pathology_is_the_norm.source: Schneider JA, Arvanitakis Z, Bang W, Bennett DA, 'Mixed brain pathologies account for most dementia cases in community-dwelling older persons', Neurology 2007;69:2197-2204 (PMID 17568013)

NINDS_AIREN_criteria.finding: The NINDS-AIREN research criteria (1993) require: (1) dementia (decline from a prior level, impairing more than one cognitive domain, verified by clinical exam and neuropsychological testing); (2) cerebrovascular disease, defined by focal neurological signs and/or relevant lesions on CT/MRI; and (3) a demonstrable relationship between the two - onset of dementia within 3 months of a recognised stroke, or abrupt/fluctuating/stepwise decline in cognition. Cases are classified as definite, probable or possible vascular dementia depending on how completely these elements and neuropathological confirmation are met; the criteria emphasise the heterogeneity of vascular dementia syndromes and note the need for brain imaging and multi-domain neuropsychological testing.
NINDS_AIREN_criteria.confidence: high, though these criteria are widely reported to have high specificity but low sensitivity for pathologically confirmed vascular dementia, which is why later frameworks (VASCOG, DSM-5) were developed

VASCOG_and_DSM5_vascular_neurocognitive_.finding: The VASCOG (International Society for Vascular Behavioral and Cognitive Disorders) 2014 consensus statement, aligned with DSM-5, reframed the field around 'vascular cognitive disorders' spanning mild vascular cognitive impairment to major vascular neurocognitive disorder (vascular dementia), requiring: (a) cognitive decline from baseline in one or more domains; (b) clinical and/or neuroimaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease judged sufficient to account for the deficits (temporal relationship to a vascular event, or predominant impairment in complex attention/frontal-executive function with prominent white-matter or subcortical infarct burden); and (c) exclusion of other conditions that better explain the decline. This framework explicitly acknowledges the frequent co-occurrence of Alzheimer's pathology (mixed disease) rather than requiring pure vascular aetiology.
VASCOG_and_DSM5_vascular_neurocognitive_.source: Sachdev P et al., 'Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement', Alzheimer Dis Assoc Disord 2014;28:206-218 (PMID 24632990)

neuroimaging_findings.finding: Structural imaging (MRI preferred over CT) is required to support the diagnosis. Supportive findings include: multiple large-vessel cortical/subcortical infarcts; a single strategically placed infarct (thalamus, angular gyrus, basal forebrain); multiple basal ganglia and white-matter lacunes; extensive periventricular/deep white-matter hyperintensities (leukoaraiosis); or a combination of these, generally with disproportionate lesion burden relative to a patient's degree of medial temporal atrophy (which instead points toward AD). Research criteria for subcortical vascular dementia specifically require extensive white-matter change plus at least two lacunes in relevant sites.
neuroimaging_findings.source: Roman GC et al., Neurology 1993;43:250-260 (PMID 8094895); Erkinjuntti T et al., J Neural Transm Suppl 2000;59:23-30 (PMID 10961414)
neuroimaging_findings.confidence: high for the qualitative pattern; exact volumetric cut-offs vary by study and are not stated here to avoid false precision

Hachinski_ischemic_score.finding: The Hachinski Ischemic Score, developed from the observation that cerebral blood flow patterns differed between multi-infarct and degenerative (Alzheimer-type) dementia, is a bedside checklist (abrupt onset, stepwise deterioration, fluctuating course, nocturnal confusion, relative preservation of personality, depression, somatic complaints, emotional incontinence, history of hypertension/strokes, focal neurological signs/symptoms) originally used to distinguish multi-infarct dementia from degenerative dementia; a higher score favours a vascular contribution. It performs well for classic multi-infarct dementia but less well for subcortical small-vessel or mixed presentations, which is why it is now used as an adjunct rather than a stand-alone diagnostic instrument.
Hachinski_ischemic_score.source: Hachinski VC et al., 'Cerebral blood flow in dementia', Arch Neurol 1975;32:632-637 (PMID 1164215)
Hachinski_ischemic_score.confidence: high for the historical instrument and its original purpose; modern diagnostic weight is placed on NINDS-AIREN/VASCOG criteria plus imaging rather than the ischemic score alone

stepwise_versus_gradual_decline_pattern.finding: A stepwise, fluctuating decline with abrupt worsenings tied temporally to discrete vascular events is the classic teaching pattern and is most typical of multi-infarct (large-vessel/cardioembolic) vascular dementia; however, subcortical small-vessel disease, which is now the more common substrate, more often produces an insidious, gradually progressive course that can closely mimic Alzheimer's disease, so absence of a stepwise pattern does not exclude vascular dementia.
stepwise_versus_gradual_decline_pattern.source: Roman GC et al., Neurology 1993;43:250-260 (PMID 8094895); Erkinjuntti T et al., J Neural Transm Suppl 2000;59:23-30 (PMID 10961414)

executive_dysfunction_predominant_patter.finding: A direct neuropsychological comparison against Alzheimer's disease (matched for age, education and dementia severity) found that vascular dementia patients showed relatively superior verbal long-term memory but significantly more impairment in frontal-executive functioning (planning, set-shifting, initiation, processing speed) than AD patients, consistent with disruption of frontal-subcortical circuits by subcortical vascular lesions. This executive-predominant, memory-relatively-spared profile (versus AD's amnestic-predominant profile) is a core clinical differentiator, though the authors caution about diagnostic-criteria uncertainty and clinical/pathological overlap between the two conditions.
executive_dysfunction_predominant_patter.source: Looi JC, Sachdev PS, 'Differentiation of vascular dementia from AD on neuropsychological tests', Neurology 1999;53:670-678 (PMID 10489025)
executive_dysfunction_predominant_patter.confidence: moderate-high - a well-cited comparative study, but the authors themselves flag diagnostic-criteria uncertainty as a limitation

core_clinical_features.name: Executive dysfunction (impaired planning, organisation, judgment, mental flexibility)
core_clinical_features.note: Often the earliest and most prominent domain affected, especially in subcortical small-vessel disease, reflecting disruption of frontal-subcortical white-matter circuits.

core_clinical_features.name: Slowed information-processing speed and reduced attention/concentration
core_clinical_features.note: A hallmark of subcortical ischaemic vascular disease, distinct from the primary amnestic pattern of AD.

core_clinical_features.name: Gait disturbance (small-stepped, wide-based, 'lower-body parkinsonism')
core_clinical_features.note: An early clinical sign specifically flagged in NINDS-AIREN and subcortical vascular dementia criteria, reflecting frontal-subcortical and basal ganglia white-matter involvement.

core_clinical_features.name: Urinary urgency/incontinence early in the course
core_clinical_features.note: Occurs earlier than in typical AD, again reflecting frontal-subcortical circuit disruption; early incontinence alongside cognitive decline should raise suspicion of a vascular or normal-pressure-hydrocephalus process rather than pure AD.

core_clinical_features.name: Focal neurological signs and symptoms
core_clinical_features.note: Hemiparesis, facial weakness, extensor plantar response, sensory deficits, visual field defects, dysarthria, or pseudobulbar palsy corresponding to the vascular territory involved, present because of the underlying stroke/vascular lesion itself, not present as a primary feature of AD.

core_clinical_features.name: Emotional lability / pseudobulbar affect and apathy
core_clinical_features.note: Uncontrollable, often incongruent laughing or crying (pseudobulbar affect) and apathy are more characteristic of vascular dementia (subcortical/frontal white-matter disconnection) than of AD.

core_clinical_features.name: Relatively preserved episodic memory early on (in non-mixed, pure vascular presentations)
core_clinical_features.note: Contrasts with the memory-predominant onset of AD; recognition memory and cueing are often better preserved in vascular dementia than free recall, another pattern distinct from the AD amnestic profile.

classic_symptoms.source: Roman GC et al., Neurology 1993;43:250-260 (PMID 8094895); Looi JC, Sachdev PS, Neurology 1999;53:670-678 (PMID 10489025); Erkinjuntti T et al., J Neural Transm Suppl 2000;59:23-30 (PMID 10961414)
classic_symptoms.confidence: high for the qualitative clinical pattern

alzheimers_disease.finding: Alzheimer's disease classically presents with an insidious, gradually and steadily progressive amnestic syndrome (impaired new learning/episodic memory as the earliest and most prominent feature) without a stepwise course, focal neurological signs, or early gait/urinary symptoms; medial temporal (hippocampal/entorhinal) atrophy is disproportionate to any vascular lesion load on imaging. Vascular dementia instead shows (in its classic form) a stepwise or fluctuating course tied to vascular events, executive-predominant over memory-predominant impairment, focal neurological signs, and imaging-confirmed infarcts/white-matter disease. In practice the two frequently co-exist as mixed dementia (see mixed_pathology_is_the_norm above), and this KB's alzheimers_disease entry should be cross-referenced for AD-specific NIA-AA/DSM-5 criteria and biomarkers.
alzheimers_disease.source: Roman GC et al., Neurology 1993;43:250-260 (PMID 8094895); Looi JC, Sachdev PS, Neurology 1999;53:670-678 (PMID 10489025); Schneider JA et al., Neurology 2007;69:2197-2204 (PMID 17568013)

dementia_with_lewy_bodies.finding: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is distinguished by its own core clinical features per the Fourth Consensus Report: fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention/alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder (which may precede dementia by years), and spontaneous parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rest tremor or rigidity). Fluctuating cognition can superficially resemble the fluctuating course of vascular dementia, but the presence of well-formed visual hallucinations, RBD and spontaneous parkinsonism (without a corresponding vascular lesion on imaging) point to DLB rather than vascular dementia; severe neuroleptic sensitivity is also characteristic of DLB. This KB does not yet contain a dedicated dementia-with-Lewy-bodies entry to cross-reference in full.
dementia_with_lewy_bodies.source: McKeith IG et al., 'Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium', Neurology 2017;89:88-100 (PMID 28592453)

frontotemporal_dementia.finding: Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) can mimic the executive-dysfunction/personality-change picture of vascular dementia, but the revised international consensus criteria require early, progressive change in personality/behaviour (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative/compulsive behaviour, hyperorality) with relatively preserved episodic memory and visuospatial skills, typically without focal vascular signs, and with frontal/anterior temporal atrophy or hypometabolism on imaging rather than infarcts or a vascular lesion pattern. A vascular contribution should be actively excluded (no relevant infarcts/strategic lesion, no temporal link to a vascular event) before attributing an executive/behavioural syndrome to bvFTD versus vascular dementia. This KB does not yet contain a dedicated frontotemporal dementia entry to cross-reference in full.
frontotemporal_dementia.source: Rascovsky K et al., 'Sensitivity of revised diagnostic criteria for the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia', Brain 2011;134:2456-2477 (PMID 21810890)

mixed_dementia.finding: Because AD and cerebrovascular pathology frequently co-exist (see mixed_pathology_is_the_norm above, where only 30% of dementia cases in one autopsy series had pure AD pathology), clinicians should not treat 'vascular versus Alzheimer's' as a strict either/or; VASCOG and DSM-5 explicitly allow a mixed-aetiology label, and management of vascular risk factors is warranted whenever significant cerebrovascular disease is present, even alongside AD pathology.
mixed_dementia.source: Schneider JA et al., Neurology 2007;69:2197-2204 (PMID 17568013); Sachdev P et al., Alzheimer Dis Assoc Disord 2014;28:206-218 (PMID 24632990)

prior_stroke.finding: Stroke is the single strongest identifiable risk factor. In a systematic review pooling multiple cohorts, about 10% of patients already had dementia before their first stroke, about 10% developed new dementia soon after a first stroke (7.4% in population-based first-ever-stroke cohorts), and more than a third (41.3%) had dementia after a recurrent stroke in hospital-based cohorts; after the first year post-stroke, dementia continued to accrue at about 3.0% per year.
prior_stroke.source: Pendlebury ST, Rothwell PM, 'Prevalence, incidence, and factors associated with pre-stroke and post-stroke dementia', Lancet Neurol 2009;8:1006-1018 (PMID 19782001)

atrial_fibrillation.finding: A meta-analysis of 21 studies found atrial fibrillation associated with a significantly higher risk of cognitive impairment/dementia even without clinical stroke: relative risk 1.38 (95% CI 1.22-1.56) for dementia independent of stroke history, RR 1.34 (95% CI 1.13-1.58) for cognitive impairment independent of stroke, and a much larger RR 2.70 (95% CI 1.82-4.00) for cognitive impairment in patients who had also had a stroke - consistent with both silent cerebral embolism and stroke-related mechanisms.
atrial_fibrillation.source: Kalantarian S, Stern TA, Mansour M, Ruskin JN, 'Cognitive impairment associated with atrial fibrillation: a meta-analysis', Ann Intern Med 2013;158:338-346 (PMID 23460057)

diabetes_mellitus.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis found diabetes mellitus associated with a pooled adjusted risk ratio of 1.47 (95% CI 1.25-1.73) for all-cause dementia, 1.39 (95% CI 1.16-1.66) for Alzheimer's disease, and specifically 2.38 (95% CI 1.79-3.18) for vascular dementia - a substantially larger effect size for vascular than for Alzheimer's-type dementia, consistent with diabetes driving cerebral small-vessel and macrovascular injury.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Lu FP, Lin KP, Kuo HK, 'Diabetes and the risk of multi-system aging phenotypes: a systematic review and meta-analysis', PLoS One 2009;4:e4144 (PMID 19127292)

hypertension.finding: Hypertension, especially in midlife, is a well-established vascular dementia risk factor and is one of the components of the Hachinski Ischemic Score. In the SPRINT MIND randomised trial of 9361 participants, intensive blood pressure control (target systolic <120 mmHg) versus standard control (<140 mmHg) did not significantly reduce adjudicated probable dementia (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67-1.04, underpowered after early trial termination) but did significantly reduce mild cognitive impairment (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69-0.95) and the combined outcome of MCI or probable dementia (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74-0.97), providing randomised-trial-level evidence that blood-pressure lowering has a real, if partial, protective effect on cognitive outcomes.
hypertension.source: Williamson JD et al. (SPRINT MIND Investigators), 'Effect of Intensive vs Standard Blood Pressure Control on Probable Dementia: A Randomized Clinical Trial', JAMA 2019;321:553-561 (PMID 30688979)
hypertension.confidence: high; note the primary probable-dementia endpoint itself did not reach significance, stated honestly rather than overstating the trial's result
