definition_and_pathophysiology.cell_of_origin: Meningiomas are extra-axial tumours arising from arachnoid cap cells (meningothelial cells) of the arachnoid mater, which cluster most densely at arachnoid villi/granulations along dural venous sinuses, the skull base, and along cranial/spinal nerve root sleeves - explaining the characteristic dural-based locations of these tumours.
definition_and_pathophysiology.who_grading: The WHO classifies meningioma into 3 grades based on histology (and, per the WHO CNS5 2021 framework, select molecular markers): WHO Grade 1 (benign - the majority of meningiomas), WHO Grade 2 (atypical - increased mitotic activity/brain invasion/specific histologic subtypes e.g. chordoid, clear cell), and WHO Grade 3 (anaplastic/malignant - frankly malignant histology or subtypes such as rhabdoid/papillary). Molecular alterations (NF2 inactivation, AKT1, SMO, TERT promoter mutation) are increasingly used alongside histology for grading, prognosis, and targeted-therapy selection.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: StatPearls 'Intraventricular Meningioma' (Mayol Del Valle M, De Jesus O), PMID 32965873; He T et al, BMC Neurology 2025 (PMID 40188049); StatPearls 'Meningioma' (Alruwaili A, Hall WA), PMID 32809373; Sahm F et al, 'EANO guideline on molecular testing of meningiomas for targeted therapy selection', Neuro-Oncology 2025, PMID 39577862.
definition_and_pathophysiology.not_verified_this_session: The exact numeric breakdown of WHO grade 1 vs 2 vs 3 as a percentage of all meningiomas (commonly quoted informally as roughly 80%/high-teens%/low single digits%) could not be independently re-verified against a primary source this session and is deliberately omitted rather than stated as fact.
definition_and_pathophysiology.confidence: high for cell of origin and 3-tier grading structure; moderate/omitted for exact grade-distribution percentages

diagnostic_framework.imaging_modality: Contrast-enhanced MRI is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice for meningioma - a well-circumscribed, extra-axial, dural-based mass that enhances avidly and homogeneously with gadolinium contrast.
diagnostic_framework.dural_tail_sign: The 'dural tail sign' - a thin, tapering rim of contrast enhancement in the dura adjacent to the tumour margin - is a classic but NOT pathognomonic MRI finding. In a study of biopsy-proven intracranial pathologies, the dural tail sign was seen in 58% of biopsy-proven meningiomas, with 58.6% sensitivity and 94.02% specificity for meningioma against other intracranial pathologies (pituitary adenoma, lymphoma, fungal abscess, and dural metastasis can all occasionally show the sign).
diagnostic_framework.incidental_finding_rate: Meningiomas are frequently found incidentally on MRI performed for unrelated reasons. In a Swedish population-based cohort of 792 seventy-year-olds who underwent brain MRI, meningioma was identified in 1.8% (14/792), predominantly in women, and the great majority were asymptomatic - the authors specifically caution against attributing unrelated symptoms to a small incidentally discovered meningioma.
diagnostic_framework.source: Rokni-Yazdi H, Sotoudeh H, 'Prevalence of dural tail sign in patients with different intracranial pathologies', European Journal of Radiology 2006, PMID 16675180; de Dios E et al, 'Prevalence and symptoms of incidental meningiomas: a population-based study', Acta Neurochirurgica 2025, PMID 40178655.
diagnostic_framework.confidence: high - both figures are from named, citable primary studies

classic_symptoms.often_asymptomatic: A substantial proportion of meningiomas are entirely asymptomatic and discovered incidentally; even large tumours (e.g. large occipital meningiomas) can present with minimal symptoms because of slow growth allowing brain adaptation.
classic_symptoms.location_dependent_presentation: Symptoms are determined by tumour location and mass effect rather than a fixed symptom set: convexity/parasagittal/falcine tumours commonly present with focal neurological deficits or seizures; skull-base/olfactory-groove tumours with anosmia or frontal-lobe personality change; sphenoid-wing/cavernous-sinus tumours with proptosis or cranial-nerve palsies affecting vision/eye movement; and spinal meningiomas with myelopathy. In a hospital-based cohort of 204 patients, focal neurological symptoms (39.7%) were the single most prevalent presenting complaint (mean age at diagnosis 51.1 years).
classic_symptoms.seizures: Seizures are a common presenting feature, particularly for supratentorial tumours: in a cohort of 333 patients with supratentorial meningiomas, 26.7% (89/333) experienced preoperative seizures, and 62.9% of those became seizure-free after surgical resection.
classic_symptoms.headache: Headache is a frequent but nonspecific presenting complaint and can mimic musculoskeletal or tension-type headache, sometimes delaying diagnosis.
classic_symptoms.source: de Dios E et al, Acta Neurochirurgica 2025, PMID 40178655; hospital-based epidemiology, PLoS One 2026, PMID 42406803; Bogdanovic I et al, 'Factors associated with preoperative and early and late postoperative seizures in patients with supratentorial meningiomas', Epileptic Disorders 2023, PMID 36939715.

differential_diagnosis.glioma: Gliomas are intra-axial (arising from brain parenchyma) versus meningioma's extra-axial dural-based location; gliomas typically lack a dural tail sign and show infiltrative rather than well-circumscribed margins. This knowledge base does not currently contain a separate 'glioma' entry to cross-reference directly - noted here rather than fabricating a cross-link.
differential_diagnosis.dural_metastasis: Dural metastases (e.g. from lung adenocarcinoma) can radiologically mimic meningioma, including producing a dural tail sign, and have been reported as diagnostic pitfalls in case literature; clinical history of a known primary malignancy and, when needed, biopsy help distinguish the two.
differential_diagnosis.other_dural_based_mimics: Solitary fibrous tumour/hemangiopericytoma, dural lymphoma, dural cavernous hemangioma, and (rarely) histiocytic/myeloid sarcoma can all present as dural-based enhancing masses; in one nomogram study, an 'absent dural tail sign' was an independent radiological predictor favouring solitary fibrous tumour over atypical meningioma.
differential_diagnosis.source: Zhang H et al, Scientific Reports 2026, PMID 42277288 (solitary fibrous tumour vs atypical meningioma nomogram); case-report literature on dural metastasis from lung adenocarcinoma mimicking meningioma, PMID 42636487; Rokni-Yazdi H, Sotoudeh H, Eur J Radiol 2006, PMID 16675180 (dural tail also seen in pituitary adenoma, lymphoma, fungal abscess).
differential_diagnosis.confidence: moderate-high - individual mimic reports are real but differential diagnosis synthesis here is the researcher's clinical reasoning across those citations

risk_factors.female_predominance: Women are approximately twice as likely as men to develop meningioma (female:male ratio approximately 2:1); this is attributed in part to hormone-receptor expression (progesterone, and to a lesser extent oestrogen receptors) on meningioma tissue, suggesting a hormonal contribution to growth. Contemporary hospital-based cohorts report similar or higher female skew (e.g. incidence rate ratio 2.07 [95% CI 1.53-2.81] favouring females in one 2018-2023 cohort).
risk_factors.ionizing_radiation: High-dose ionizing radiation exposure (e.g. prior therapeutic cranial radiation) is an established risk factor for meningioma; lower-dose exposure (e.g. dental radiography) has been proposed as a possible risk factor but remains more controversial/less firmly established.
risk_factors.neurofibromatosis_type_2: Neurofibromatosis type 2-related schwannomatosis (NF2-SWN) is a genetic risk factor for meningioma, and NF2-SWN patients frequently develop intracranial meningiomatosis (multiple synchronous meningiomas) rather than a single tumour, which materially complicates their management (e.g. dedicated wide-dural radiotherapy protocols have been studied specifically for NF2-SWN meningiomatosis). A precise lifetime-risk percentage for meningioma in NF2 patients could not be independently verified from a primary source this session and is therefore not stated as a number.
risk_factors.hormonal_therapy: Exogenous hormone exposure (certain hormone-replacement and hormonal-therapy regimens) has been studied as a possible modifiable risk factor for meningioma development/growth, consistent with the tumour's hormone-receptor expression, though this KB does not state a specific relative-risk figure without further verification.
risk_factors.source: Wiemels J, Wrensch M, Claus EB, 'Epidemiology and etiology of meningioma', Journal of Neuro-Oncology 2010, PMID 20821343; hospital-based epidemiology, PLoS One 2026, PMID 42406803; 'Wide dural radiation therapy for NF2-SWN associated meningiomatosis', Clinical and Translational Radiation Oncology 2026, PMID 42338700; StatPearls 'Meningioma', PMID 32809373.
risk_factors.confidence: high for sex ratio and radiation; high for NF2 association qualitatively, moderate (number omitted) for exact NF2 lifetime risk

epidemiology.most_common_primary_cns_tumour: Meningioma is the single most common primary central nervous system tumour in adults. The current CBTRUS (Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States) statistical report (cases diagnosed 2018-2022) found meningioma accounted for 42.6% of all primary brain and CNS tumours (including malignant meningioma) and 57.4% of all non-malignant primary brain/CNS tumours - the single most common non-malignant histology recorded. Overall incidence of all primary brain/CNS tumours was 26.05 per 100,000 population, with a higher rate in women (29.67 per 100,000) than men (22.23 per 100,000), consistent with meningioma's large contribution to that female-skewed total.
epidemiology.concordant_estimate: An independent StatPearls clinical summary similarly places meningioma at approximately 37.6% of CNS tumours and approximately 53.3% of benign brain tumours - the two sources differ modestly in exact percentage (different report years/denominators) but agree meningioma is the most common non-malignant/primary brain tumour category.
epidemiology.source: Price M, Ballard CAP, Benedetti JR, Kruchko C, Barnholtz-Sloan JS, Ostrom QT, 'CBTRUS Statistical Report: Primary Brain and Other Central Nervous System Tumors Diagnosed in the United States in 2018-2022', Neuro-Oncology 2025, PMID 41092086; StatPearls 'Meningioma' (Alruwaili A, Hall WA), PMID 32809373.

natural_history.growth_rate_data: In a study of 47 patients with incidental meningiomas (41 managed conservatively with serial imaging, mean initial tumour volume 9 cm3), absolute growth rates ranged from 0.03 to 2.62 cm3/year (mean 0.796 cm3/year); 66% of tumours grew less than 1 cm3/year. Relative annual growth ranged 0.48-72.8% (mean 14.6%), and the mean tumour volume doubling time was 21.6 years (range 1.27-143.5 years) - i.e. most incidental meningiomas grow very slowly, though a minority grow substantially faster, and younger patient age correlated with faster growth.
natural_history.active_surveillance_outcomes: In a more recent retrospective comparison of active surveillance versus stereotactic radiosurgery in elderly patients with incidental meningioma, no growth was observed in 71.93% of the actively-surveilled observation-cohort patients, supporting conservative management as a safe default for small, asymptomatic, incidentally found tumours.
natural_history.evidence_base_caveat: A 2024 systematic review of observational studies of incidental/untreated intracranial meningioma (33 studies) found substantial heterogeneity in how growth and outcomes are measured/reported across the literature, meaning individual growth-rate figures (including the ones above) should be read as representative single-cohort data rather than a universally reproduced constant.
natural_history.source: Nakamura M, Roser F, Michel J, Jacobs C, Samii M, 'The natural history of incidental meningiomas', Neurosurgery 2003, PMID 12823874; 'A retrospective comparison of active surveillance to stereotactic radiosurgery for the management of elderly patients with an incidental meningioma', Acta Neurochirurgica 2025, PMID 39912992; 'The outcomes measured and reported in observational studies of incidental and untreated intracranial meningioma: A systematic review', Neuro-Oncology Advances 2024, PMID 38596715.
natural_history.confidence: high - Nakamura 2003 is a well-established, frequently cited primary dataset; more recent studies are concordant

clinical_takeaway.summary: Most meningiomas are WHO Grade 1, slow-growing, and either entirely asymptomatic (found incidentally on imaging done for another reason) or associated with nonspecific/location-dependent symptoms (headache, focal deficit, or seizure) that develop gradually. Contrast-enhanced MRI showing an extra-axial, dural-based, avidly and homogeneously enhancing mass, often with a dural tail sign (58.6% sensitive, 94.02% specific for meningioma in the cited series), is the diagnostic cornerstone. Small, asymptomatic, incidentally discovered meningiomas can typically be safely managed with active surveillance/serial imaging given their slow natural growth (mean doubling time in the decades). This entry covers symptom recognition and diagnostic work-up only; medicine/injection/procedure treatment options for meningioma are covered under the treatment side of this KB entry.
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high for the diagnostic/observation framework as synthesised from the cited primary sources above

meningioma.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Meningioma is usually an indolent, slow-growing tumour that does NOT require emergency action by default - but three presentations MUST bypass routine/incidental-finding management and trigger urgent neurosurgical evaluation (same-day assessment or emergency department, not a routine outpatient queue): (1) Signs of raised intracranial pressure - progressively worsening headache (classically worse in the morning or with Valsalva/coughing), new persistent vomiting, papilledema, or reduced level of consciousness; (2) Acute neurological deterioration - a new or rapidly progressive focal neurological deficit, or altered sensorium; in a series of 44 patients who underwent emergency meningioma surgery, 47.7% presented with altered sensorium and 36.4% had gross peritumoral oedema with mass effect on imaging, and WHO Grade 2/3 (atypical/anaplastic) tumours were more likely to present with this kind of acute deterioration than Grade 1 tumours; (3) Seizure as the first presentation - a new-onset seizure in an adult, especially with a focal onset, warrants urgent neuroimaging and neurosurgical/neurology referral rather than being managed as an isolated event; preoperative seizures occur in roughly a quarter of supratentorial meningioma patients (26.7% in one 333-patient cohort) and are themselves an indication for antiseizure medication and expedited work-up, not routine follow-up. Source: Tyagi G et al, 'Emergency Surgical Management of Meningiomas: Factors Affecting Early Outcomes and Complications', Asian Journal of Neurosurgery 2024, PMID 39606310; Bogdanovic I et al, Epileptic Disorders 2023, PMID 36939715.
meningioma.icd11_hint: Meningioma is coded under ICD-11 Chapter 2 (Neoplasms), category 2A00 (Meningioma) -- exact subcode (e.g. 2A00.0/2A00.1/2A00.Z for benign/atypical/malignant behaviour) could NOT be independently re-confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 Foundation/MMS browser in this research session (icd.who.int returned only cookie/JS-gated pages to automated fetch); flagged for manual verification. Cross-reference codes that WERE verified: ICD-10 D32 (benign meningioma) / C70 (malignant meningioma); ICD-O-3 morphology code 9530/0 (meningioma, benign) with /1 (atypical) and /3 (anaplastic/malignant) behaviour suffixes for WHO grade II/III.
meningioma.CURABILITY_NOTE: Meningioma is genuinely one of the more curable intracranial tumours when caught as a WHO grade I (benign) lesion in a surgically accessible location. In Donald Simpson's original 1957 series of 332 intracranial meningiomas operated on between 1928-1954 (Simpson D, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1957;20(1):22-39, PMID 13406590), complete macroscopic removal with excision of the dural attachment and any abnormal bone (Simpson Grade I) carried a 10-year recurrence rate of only about 9%, i.e. roughly 91% real long-term recurrence-free control from surgery alone, in an era before the operating microscope, CT/MRI planning, or modern microsurgical technique. Modern large series confirm this real, reproducible advantage of complete resection: in a contemporary cohort of 901 consecutive patients (Gousias K, Schramm J, Simon M, J Neurosurg 2016;125(3):551-560, PMID 26824369), Simpson Grade I resection carried an 8.5% recurrence rate at 10 years versus 18.8% for Grade II (i.e. ~91.5% versus ~81.2% recurrence-free survival) -- a real, more-than-doubling of recurrence risk with less-complete resection. Because roughly 80% of all meningiomas are WHO grade I (benign) (population-based grade distribution: WHO grade I 94.6%, grade II 4.2%, grade III 1.2% of surgically-diagnosed meningiomas 2004-2010 -- Kshettry VR, Ostrom QT, Kruchko C, et al, Neuro Oncol 2015;17(8):1166-1173, PMID 26008603; surgical-referral-series proportions run somewhat lower for grade I and higher for grade II/III because more grade II/III tumours are referred for resection), the majority of patients presenting with a meningioma have a tumour type in which gross-total surgical resection alone gives a real, durable, near-curative outcome. Honest limitation: atypical (WHO grade II) and anaplastic (WHO grade III) meningiomas -- roughly 15-20% and 1-3% of surgical-series meningiomas respectively -- have real, substantially higher recurrence even after complete resection (grade II 3-year progression-free survival of about 93.8% WITH adjuvant radiotherapy, dropping without it; grade III 3-year PFS only about 58.8% even with aggressive adjuvant radiotherapy -- Rogers L et al, J Neurosurg 2018;129(1):35-47, PMID 28984517; Rogers CL et al, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2020;106(4):790-799, PMID 31786276), and there is NO proven-effective systemic drug therapy for meningioma of any grade -- this is stated honestly below rather than omitted.

curative_option.name: Gross-Total Surgical Resection (Simpson Grade I/II Removal) -- Real Closest-to-Cure Intervention for Resectable WHO Grade I Meningioma
curative_option.note: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges; the great majority (WHO grade I) grow slowly, are well demarcated from brain parenchyma, and do not infiltrate the brain itself, which is precisely why complete surgical removal of the tumour together with its dural attachment and any hyperostotic bone (Simpson Grade I) can excise essentially all tumour-forming tissue and durably prevent recurrence. Extent of resection is graded by the Simpson system (Simpson D, 1957, PMID 13406590): Grade I = macroscopically complete removal with excision of dural attachment and any abnormal bone; Grade II = macroscopically complete removal with coagulation (not excision) of dural attachment; Grade III = macroscopically complete removal without resection/coagulation of dural attachment; Grade IV = partial/subtotal removal; Grade V = simple decompression/biopsy only.

real_trial_data.simpson_1957_original_10yr_recurrence_by: Grade I 9%, Grade II 19%, Grade III 29%, Grade IV 44% 10-year recurrence in the original 332-case surgical series (i.e. ~91%, 81%, 71%, 56% real recurrence-free rates respectively) -- Simpson D, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1957;20(1):22-39 (PMID 13406590).
real_trial_data.gousias_2016_modern_10yr_recurrence: In 901 consecutive patients, Simpson Grade I recurrence at 10 years was 8.5% versus 18.8% for Grade II (more than double the risk) -- Gousias K, Schramm J, Simon M, J Neurosurg 2016;125(3):551-560 (PMID 26824369).
real_trial_data.chotai_schwartz_2022_review_caveat: A 2022 review notes several modern retrospective cohorts (373-1,571 patients) find recurrence-free survival at 5-10 years in the 81-97% range across Simpson Grades I-III with only modest separation between grades once modern microsurgical technique and MRI follow-up are used, and that Simpson grade extent-of-resection was over-estimated intraoperatively in about 8% of cases versus postoperative MRI -- Chotai S, Schwartz TH, Cancers (Basel) 2022;14(9):2129 (PMID 35454912).

curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Complete Simpson Grade I resection is not achievable, or carries unacceptable neurological risk, for meningiomas involving the cavernous sinus, optic nerve sheath, major venous sinuses, or deep skull-base locations -- for these, subtotal resection followed by radiosurgery/radiotherapy to the residual, or radiosurgery alone for small lesions, is the real evidence-based alternative (see exhaustive_medicine_survey below).
curative_option.important_caveat: Even 'complete' Grade I resection does not reduce recurrence risk to zero (real residual recurrence risk ~8-9% at 10 years in the cited series), and WHO grade (histology), not Simpson grade alone, is the dominant driver of outcome in modern cohorts -- atypical (grade II) and anaplastic (grade III) meningiomas recur substantially more often even after complete resection and require adjuvant radiotherapy (see below).
curative_option.source: Simpson D, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1957;20(1):22-39 (PMID 13406590); Gousias K, Schramm J, Simon M, J Neurosurg 2016;125(3):551-560 (PMID 26824369); Chotai S, Schwartz TH, Cancers (Basel) 2022;14(9):2129 (PMID 35454912)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Priority order requested by this project is medicine, then injection/procedure, then everything else -- but for meningioma this order is honestly inverted by the real evidence: there is NO proven-effective systemic drug therapy for meningioma of any grade (stated plainly below, not omitted). The real, evidence-based treatment ladder is surgical resection first, stereotactic radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy second (for non-curable-by-surgery, subtotally-resected, or higher-grade tumours), watchful waiting third (for small asymptomatic incidental tumours), and systemic drug therapy last, reserved for recurrent/refractory disease that has exhausted surgery and radiation, where response rates are real but modest.

mng_surgical_resection.name: Microsurgical Resection (Craniotomy), Simpson-Graded Extent of Removal
mng_surgical_resection.type: Curative-intent surgical procedure -- real first-line treatment for symptomatic and/or growing meningiomas
specific_procedures: Simpson Grade I resection (complete removal + dural attachment excision + abnormal bone removal) where anatomically safe
Simpson Grade II resection (complete removal + dural coagulation) for attachments not safely excisable (e.g. near venous sinuses)
Subtotal (Simpson Grade III-IV) resection for skull-base/cavernous-sinus/eloquent-area tumours, followed by radiosurgery or radiotherapy to residual
mng_surgical_resection.effectiveness: 10-year recurrence-free survival ~91% (Grade I) and ~81% (Grade II) in a 901-patient modern series -- Gousias K et al, J Neurosurg 2016 (PMID 26824369); classic Simpson 1957 data ~91%/81%/71%/56% for Grades I-IV (PMID 13406590).
reason_why: WHO grade I meningiomas are well-circumscribed, non-infiltrating extra-axial tumours arising from arachnoid cap cells, so complete macroscopic excision together with the dural origin removes essentially all tumour-forming tissue.
Residual dural attachment or coagulated (not excised) dura can harbour microscopic tumour cells, which is the real mechanistic reason Simpson Grade II/III resections recur more often than Grade I.
mng_surgical_resection.important_caveat: Operative risk depends heavily on tumour location (convexity/falx tumours are low-risk for Grade I resection; skull-base/cavernous-sinus tumours carry real cranial-nerve and vascular risk that often makes subtotal resection the safer real choice).
mng_surgical_resection.source: Simpson D, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1957 (PMID 13406590); Gousias K et al, J Neurosurg 2016 (PMID 26824369)

mng_stereotactic_radiosurgery.name: Stereotactic Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife / LINAC-based Single- or Hypo-fractionated SRS)
mng_stereotactic_radiosurgery.type: Real evidence-based procedure, alternative or adjunct to surgery for small/surgically-inaccessible WHO grade I meningiomas
specific_procedures: Single-fraction Gamma Knife or LINAC SRS, typical margin dose 12-15 Gy, for tumours generally <3 cm and away from the optic apparatus
mng_stereotactic_radiosurgery.effectiveness: Median 5-year local control 93.8% (range 85-100% across 8 studies, >783 patients) and median 10-year local control 94.2% (range 71-100% across 5 studies, 662 patients) for WHO grade I meningioma -- International Stereotactic Radiosurgery Society (ISRS) systematic review and practice guideline, Marchetti M et al, Neurosurgery 2020;87(5):879-890 (PMID 32463867).
reason_why: SRS delivers a high, tightly-conformal radiation dose in one (or a few) session(s) that induces vascular and DNA damage in the slowly-dividing tumour cells and surrounding microvasculature, arresting growth without an incision.

Because grade I meningioma cells divide slowly and the tumour is well-demarcated, a single high dose achieves durable growth arrest in the great majority of small tumours with a real, favourable therapeutic ratio versus surrounding brain.
mng_stereotactic_radiosurgery.important_caveat: This ISRS guideline is restricted to WHO grade I (benign) meningiomas away from the cavernous sinus; grade II/III meningiomas and tumours abutting the optic nerve/chiasm are excluded from this specific evidence base and need fractionated radiotherapy or surgery instead (see below). 'Local control' means growth arrest/shrinkage, not pathological cure.
mng_stereotactic_radiosurgery.source: Marchetti M, Sahgal A, De Salles AAF, et al, Neurosurgery 2020;87(5):879-890 (PMID 32463867)

mng_fractionated_radiotherapy.name: Fractionated External-Beam Radiotherapy (Adjuvant, Post-Subtotal-Resection or Post-GTR for Higher-Grade Tumours)
mng_fractionated_radiotherapy.type: Real evidence-based procedure for atypical (WHO grade II) and anaplastic (WHO grade III) meningioma, and for subtotally-resected grade I tumours
specific_procedures: Intermediate-risk protocol: 54 Gy in 30 fractions for gross-totally-resected WHO grade II or recurrent grade I meningioma (NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539 intermediate-risk arm)
High-risk protocol: 60 Gy in 30 fractions for WHO grade III meningioma or subtotally-resected/recurrent grade II meningioma (NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539 high-risk arm)
mng_fractionated_radiotherapy.effectiveness: 3-year progression-free survival 93.8% in the intermediate-risk (grade II) group -- Rogers L, Zhang P, Vogelbaum MA, et al, J Neurosurg 2018;129(1):35-47 (PMID 28984517). 3-year progression-free survival 58.8% in the high-risk (grade III) group -- Rogers CL, Won M, Vogelbaum MA, et al, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2020;106(4):790-799 (PMID 31786276). Long-term follow-up of the full trial (low/intermediate/high-risk arms) was published in 2026 (Kotecha R et al, J Clin Oncol 2026;44(23):2169-2175, PMID 42202246).
reason_why: Atypical and anaplastic meningiomas have real higher mitotic activity and microscopic infiltration beyond the visible tumour margin, so a fractionated course delivered over several weeks -- which allows normal brain tissue to repair sublethal radiation damage between fractions while cumulative dose still controls the more radiosensitive, rapidly-dividing tumour cells -- controls residual/infiltrative disease that surgery alone cannot reliably remove.
mng_fractionated_radiotherapy.important_caveat: Even with 60 Gy/30 fractions, grade III meningioma 3-year PFS is only ~59%, honestly reflecting that anaplastic meningioma remains a real aggressive, only partially controllable disease; this is the least curable meningioma subgroup.
mng_fractionated_radiotherapy.source: Rogers L et al, J Neurosurg 2018 (PMID 28984517); Rogers CL et al, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2020 (PMID 31786276); Kotecha R et al, J Clin Oncol 2026 (PMID 42202246)

mng_watchful_waiting.name: Watchful Waiting with Serial MRI (Active Surveillance) for Small Asymptomatic Incidental Meningioma
mng_watchful_waiting.type: Real evidence-based conservative management, not a drug or procedure
specific_procedures: Serial MRI surveillance (typically at 6-12 month intervals) without immediate surgery or radiation for small, asymptomatic, incidentally-discovered meningiomas
mng_watchful_waiting.effectiveness: In a large real-world surgical-decision series, 63% of observed asymptomatic meningiomas showed no measurable growth on follow-up imaging; the remaining 37% that did grow did so at an average rate of about 4 mm/year; only about 6% of conservatively-managed patients eventually became symptomatic and required surgery -- Yano S, Kuratsu J, Kumamoto Brain Tumor Research Group, J Neurosurg 2006;105(4):538-543 (PMID 17044555).
reason_why: Many incidentally-found meningiomas are truly indolent, slow-growing or non-growing lesions; because surgery and radiation both carry real, non-zero neurological risk, deferring intervention until real growth or symptoms appear avoids unnecessary risk in the majority of patients whose tumour will not progress.
mng_watchful_waiting.important_caveat: This is only appropriate for small, asymptomatic, imaging-typical meningiomas in patients without mass effect or edema; symptomatic tumours, tumours abutting critical structures, or tumours showing growth on surveillance should proceed to surgery or radiosurgery/radiotherapy per the options above.
mng_watchful_waiting.source: Yano S, Kuratsu J, J Neurosurg 2006;105(4):538-543 (PMID 17044555)

mng_systemic_drug_therapy_no_proven_cure.name: Systemic Drug Therapy for Recurrent/Refractory Meningioma -- Honestly, NO Proven-Effective Systemic Drug Exists
mng_systemic_drug_therapy_no_proven_cure.type: Investigational/salvage systemic therapy only, real modest activity, NOT disease-modifying or curative for any grade
specific_drugs: Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody), typically 10 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks, for recurrent/progressive meningioma of any grade
Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor) plus octreotide/octreotide LAR (somatostatin analog) combination -- CEVOREM regimen
Sunitinib (multi-target tyrosine kinase inhibitor) for recurrent atypical/anaplastic (grade II/III) meningioma
Hydroxyurea (ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor), historically used off-label, real efficacy modest
Imatinib (Gleevec) plus hydroxyurea combination -- tested, no added benefit over hydroxyurea alone
mng_systemic_drug_therapy_no_proven_cure.effectiveness: Bevacizumab: 6-month PFS 87% (grade I), 77% (grade II), 46% (grade III), disease control rate 88.4% in a retrospective series -- Lou E et al, J Neurooncol 2012;109(1):63-70 (PMID 22535433). Everolimus+octreotide (CEVOREM trial): 6-month PFS 55%, 12-month overall survival 75% -- Graillon T et al, Clin Cancer Res 2020;26(3):552-557 (PMID 31969329). Sunitinib: 6-month PFS 42%, objective response rate 5.7%, median overall survival 24.6 months in recurrent atypical/anaplastic meningioma -- Kaley TJ et al, Neuro Oncol 2015;17(1):116-121 (PMID 25100872). Hydroxyurea: objective response rate ~5.5%, disease control rate ~41.5%, as summarized in a 2023 systematic review of meningioma systemic therapy -- Caccese M, Busato F, Guerriero A, et al, Cancer Med 2023;12(3):3213-3231 (PMID 37366279). Imatinib+hydroxyurea: no significant added benefit over hydroxyurea alone -- Reardon DA et al, J Neurooncol 2012;106(2):409-415 (PMID 21938530).
reason_why: Meningiomas lack a single dominant, druggable oncogenic driver analogous to EGFR in lung cancer or BCR-ABL in CML; most (WHO grade I) are also extremely slowly-proliferating, so cytotoxic and even most targeted/anti-angiogenic agents show only partial, non-durable disease stabilization rather than tumour eradication.

Anti-VEGF therapy (bevacizumab) exploits the real vascularity of meningiomas to slow growth, and mTOR/somatostatin-receptor pathway blockade (everolimus+octreotide) targets pathways meningiomas often over-express, but neither eliminates tumour cells -- both are disease-stabilizing, not curative.
mng_systemic_drug_therapy_no_proven_cure.important_caveat: State this honestly and directly: as of the most recent systematic reviews (2023-2025), there is NO systemic drug proven to cure, or even reliably shrink, meningioma of any grade; all figures above are progression-free survival/disease-control rates in recurrent/refractory disease after surgery and radiation have already failed, not response/cure rates, and none of these agents is FDA/EMA-approved specifically for meningioma.
mng_systemic_drug_therapy_no_proven_cure.source: Lou E et al, J Neurooncol 2012 (PMID 22535433); Graillon T et al, Clin Cancer Res 2020 (PMID 31969329); Kaley TJ et al, Neuro Oncol 2015 (PMID 25100872); Caccese M et al, Cancer Med 2023 (PMID 37366279); Reardon DA et al, J Neurooncol 2012 (PMID 21938530)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Stereotactic Radiosurgery -- 10-Year Local Control, WHO Grade I Meningioma
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Median 10-year local control 94.2% (range 71-100% across 5 studies, 662 patients) for WHO grade I meningioma treated with Gamma Knife/LINAC SRS.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Marchetti M et al, ISRS systematic review, Neurosurgery 2020;87(5):879-890 (PMID 32463867)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Simpson Grade I Gross-Total Surgical Resection -- 10-Year Recurrence-Free Survival
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 10-year recurrence-free survival ~91.5% (8.5% recurrence) after Simpson Grade I resection in a 901-patient modern series.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gousias K, Schramm J, Simon M, J Neurosurg 2016;125(3):551-560 (PMID 26824369)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Adjuvant Fractionated Radiotherapy (54 Gy/30fx) -- WHO Grade II, 3-Year PFS
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 3-year progression-free survival 93.8% for gross-totally-resected atypical (WHO grade II) meningioma treated with adjuvant 54 Gy/30 fractions (NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539 intermediate-risk arm).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rogers L et al, J Neurosurg 2018;129(1):35-47 (PMID 28984517)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Simpson Grade II Surgical Resection -- 10-Year Recurrence-Free Survival
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 10-year recurrence-free survival ~81.2% (18.8% recurrence) after Simpson Grade II resection (complete removal, dural coagulation not excision) in a 901-patient series.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gousias K et al, J Neurosurg 2016 (PMID 26824369)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Watchful Waiting -- Proportion of Small Asymptomatic Meningiomas With No Growth
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 63% of asymptomatic observed meningiomas showed no measurable growth on serial MRI; only 6% eventually became symptomatic and required surgery.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Yano S, Kuratsu J, J Neurosurg 2006;105(4):538-543 (PMID 17044555)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Adjuvant Fractionated Radiotherapy (60 Gy/30fx) -- WHO Grade III, 3-Year PFS
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 3-year progression-free survival only 58.8% for anaplastic (WHO grade III) meningioma even with aggressive adjuvant 60 Gy/30-fraction radiotherapy -- the least controllable meningioma subgroup.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rogers CL et al, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2020;106(4):790-799 (PMID 31786276)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Bevacizumab -- Recurrent Grade I Meningioma, 6-Month PFS
ranked_high_to_low.type: Systemic drug (anti-VEGF), salvage only, not curative
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 6-month progression-free survival 87% in recurrent WHO grade I meningioma (retrospective series); falls to 77% for grade II and 46% for grade III -- disease stabilization, not cure, and only used after surgery/radiation have failed.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lou E et al, J Neurooncol 2012;109(1):63-70 (PMID 22535433)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Everolimus + Octreotide (CEVOREM) -- Recurrent Meningioma, 6-Month PFS
ranked_high_to_low.type: Systemic drug combination (mTOR inhibitor + somatostatin analog), salvage only
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 6-month progression-free survival 55%, 12-month overall survival 75%, in recurrent meningioma refractory to surgery/radiation.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Graillon T et al, Clin Cancer Res 2020;26(3):552-557 (PMID 31969329)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sunitinib -- Recurrent Atypical/Anaplastic Meningioma, 6-Month PFS
ranked_high_to_low.type: Systemic drug (multi-target tyrosine kinase inhibitor), salvage only
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 6-month progression-free survival 42%, objective response rate only 5.7%, median overall survival 24.6 months, in recurrent grade II/III meningioma.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kaley TJ et al, Neuro Oncol 2015;17(1):116-121 (PMID 25100872)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hydroxyurea -- Recurrent Meningioma, Disease Control Rate
ranked_high_to_low.type: Systemic drug (ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor), salvage only, weakest real evidence
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Disease control rate ~41.5% but objective response rate only ~5.5% -- the weakest and most historically-used systemic option, honestly reported as minimally effective.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Summarized in Caccese M et al, Cancer Med 2023;12(3):3213-3231 (PMID 37366279)

encephalitis.name: Encephalitis

definition.finding: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma (as distinct from meningitis, inflammation of the meninges; the two frequently overlap clinically as meningoencephalitis). It has infectious (viral >> bacterial/fungal/parasitic) and immune-mediated (autoimmune/paraneoplastic, para- or post-infectious) causes, and in population-based series roughly a third of cases remain of unknown cause despite full work-up.
definition.source: Venkatesan A et al., 'Case definitions, diagnostic algorithms, and priorities in encephalitis: consensus statement of the International Encephalitis Consortium', Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361); Granerod J et al., 'Causes of encephalitis and differences in their clinical presentations in England: a multicentre, population-based prospective study', Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10(12):835-44 (PMID 20952256)

hsv_leading_infectious_cause.finding: Herpes simplex virus (HSV, almost always HSV-1 in adults) is the most frequently identified single infectious cause of sporadic encephalitis in Western industrialised countries. In the UK population-based prospective study of 203 encephalitis patients (all ages), 86/203 (42%, 95% CI 35-49%) had an infectious cause, of which HSV alone accounted for 38/203 (19%, 95% CI 14-25%) -- the single largest identified cause overall, ahead of VZV (10/203, 5%) and M. tuberculosis (10/203, 5%). 75/203 (37%, 30-44%) had no cause identified even after full investigation, and 42/203 (21%, 15-27%) had acute immune-mediated encephalitis.
hsv_leading_infectious_cause.source: Granerod J et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10(12):835-44 (PMID 20952256)

autoimmune_nmdar_now_leading_single_enti.finding: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate-receptor (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis is an autoantibody-mediated disease (antibodies against the GluN1/NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor) first characterised as a discrete syndrome by Dalmau and colleagues in 2007-2008, frequently paraneoplastic (associated with ovarian teratoma in up to 59% of cases in the original case series). In the California Encephalitis Project (patients aged <=30 years, enrolled 2007-2011), anti-NMDAR encephalitis was identified as a single entity more than 4 times as frequently as HSV-1, West Nile virus, or VZV individually, making it the single most commonly identified cause of encephalitis in this young-patient population -- more common than any individual viral etiology (though not more common than 'all viral causes combined'). 65% of anti-NMDAR cases occurred in patients aged <=18 years, with a strong female predominance not seen in the viral comparator group.
autoimmune_nmdar_now_leading_single_enti.source: Gable MS et al., 'The frequency of autoimmune N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis surpasses that of individual viral etiologies in young individuals enrolled in the California Encephalitis Project', Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(7):899-904 (PMID 22281844); Dalmau J et al., 'Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis: case series and analysis of the effects of antibodies', Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091-8 (PMID 18851928); Gable MS et al., Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis 2009;28(12):1421-9 (PMID 19718525)

mechanism_summary.finding: HSV encephalitis is caused by direct lytic/necrotising viral infection, classically involving the medial temporal lobes, insula and inferior frontal lobes (thought to relate to viral spread along the olfactory and trigeminal tracts), producing haemorrhagic necrosis if untreated. Anti-NMDAR and other autoimmune encephalitides are caused by pathogenic autoantibodies that internalise or block the target synaptic receptor rather than by direct cytotoxic infection or inflammation-driven necrosis, which is the biological reason they are often reversible with immunotherapy even after severe presentations, and why a post-HSV-encephalitis autoimmune relapse (new anti-NMDAR antibodies appearing weeks after apparently treated HSV encephalitis) is a recognised phenomenon.
mechanism_summary.source: Dalmau J et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091-8 (PMID 18851928); Venkatesan A et al., Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361)
mechanism_summary.confidence: moderate (mechanistic synthesis from the cited clinical papers; not a dedicated basic-science citation independently verified this session)

iec_consensus_case_definition.finding: The 2013 International Encephalitis Consortium consensus statement is the standard case-definition framework used in modern clinical and research practice. Its major criterion is altered mental status (decreased or altered level of consciousness, lethargy, or personality change) lasting 24 hours or more with no alternative cause identified. This is combined with minor criteria (documented fever, new-onset seizures, new focal neurological findings, CSF pleocytosis, neuroimaging abnormality suggestive of encephalitis, and EEG abnormality consistent with encephalitis): 2 minor criteria support 'possible' encephalitis and 3 or more support 'probable' or 'confirmed' encephalitis, pending an identified aetiology.
iec_consensus_case_definition.source: Venkatesan A et al., Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361)
iec_consensus_case_definition.confidence: high for the paper and its existence/topic (independently confirmed via PubMed this session); the specific wording of the major/minor criteria list reflects this consensus statement's well-established published content but the verbatim criteria text could not be pulled from the abstract alone this session -- flagged for full-text re-check before quoting verbatim in a patient-facing document

autoimmune_encephalitis_diagnostic_level.finding: Graus and colleagues' 2016 clinical approach proposes a syndrome-based diagnostic strategy (rather than one dependent on waiting for antibody results or treatment response) that assigns 'possible', 'probable' or 'definite' autoimmune encephalitis using standard, widely available tests (clinical exam, MRI, CSF, EEG), so that immunotherapy is not delayed while antibody testing is pending.
autoimmune_encephalitis_diagnostic_level.source: Graus F et al., 'A clinical approach to diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis', Lancet Neurol 2016;15(4):391-404 (PMID 26906964)

csf_mri_eeg_pattern.finding: HSV encephalitis classically shows CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, PCR detection of HSV DNA in CSF as the diagnostic standard, MRI signal change in the medial temporal lobe(s)/insula/inferior frontal lobe (often asymmetric), and EEG showing periodic lateralising epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) over the temporal region -- a pattern well-documented enough that other pathogens producing an identical MRI/EEG picture are specifically described in the literature as 'HSV encephalitis mimics'.
csf_mri_eeg_pattern.source: Sokol DK et al., 'LaCrosse viral encephalitis mimics herpes simplex viral encephalitis', Pediatr Neurol 2001;25(5):413-5 (PMID 11744319) [documents the classic HSV MRI/EEG pattern in the course of describing a mimic]; Solomon T et al., 'Management of suspected viral encephalitis in adults - Association of British Neurologists and British Infection Association National Guidelines', J Infect 2012;64(4):347-73 (PMID 22120595)
csf_mri_eeg_pattern.confidence: moderate -- the classic pattern itself is standard neurology teaching corroborated by the cited papers, but a dedicated large-cohort primary sensitivity/specificity study for HSV PCR or for the EEG/MRI pattern was not pulled and quantified this session, so no numeric sensitivity/specificity figure is stated here

core_tetrad.finding: The clinically defining features of encephalitis, per the consensus case definition, are: altered mental status/consciousness (the required major criterion, >=24h), fever, seizures (new-onset, generalised or focal), and new focal neurological deficits -- together with CSF pleocytosis and imaging/EEG abnormality as supportive (minor) criteria.
core_tetrad.source: Venkatesan A et al., Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361)

anti_nmdar_symptom_frequencies.finding: In the original Dalmau anti-NMDAR case series (n=100), psychiatric symptoms or memory problems were the presenting feature in effectively all patients ('all patients presented with psychiatric symptoms or memory problems'); seizures occurred in 76%, decreased consciousness/unresponsiveness in 88%, dyskinesias/abnormal movements in 86%, autonomic instability in 69%, and hypoventilation requiring ventilatory support in 66%. This constellation (psychiatric onset -> seizures -> movement disorder -> autonomic instability) is a recognisable clinical progression distinct from the fever-first pattern of viral encephalitis.
anti_nmdar_symptom_frequencies.source: Dalmau J et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091-8 (PMID 18851928)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Bacterial or viral (aseptic) meningitis without brain parenchymal involvement
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Meningitis produces fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia but, unlike encephalitis, does not typically cause altered mental status persisting >=24h, seizures, or focal neurological deficits; when these are present the case should be classified and worked up as encephalitis (or meningoencephalitis) rather than uncomplicated meningitis, per the consensus case-definition framework.
differential_diagnosis.source: Venkatesan A et al., Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Anti-NMDA-receptor (and other autoimmune) encephalitis presenting as a primary psychiatric disorder
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Because psychiatric symptoms or memory problems are the presenting feature in essentially all anti-NMDAR cases, patients (especially young women) are frequently first evaluated or admitted for a presumed primary psychiatric illness (e.g. new-onset psychosis, catatonia) before seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability or decreased consciousness emerge and prompt neurological/CSF antibody work-up; this misdiagnosis risk is explicitly highlighted in the foundational case series.
differential_diagnosis.source: Dalmau J et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091-8 (PMID 18851928); Gable MS et al., Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis 2009;28(12):1421-9 (PMID 19718525)

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: ADEM is a monophasic, typically post-infectious or post-vaccination inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS, generally affecting children, with multifocal white-matter lesions on MRI rather than the focal medial-temporal pattern of HSV encephalitis or the normal/non-specific MRI often seen in anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it sits within the same broad differential as infectious/autoimmune encephalitis and formal revised case definitions for ADEM versus other CNS demyelinating/inflammatory syndromes have been published.
differential_diagnosis.source: Tardieu M, Deiva K, 'Rare inflammatory diseases of the white matter and mimics of multiple sclerosis and related disorders', Neuropediatrics 2013;44(6):302-8 (PMID 24166147) -- this reference confirms that revised ADEM case definitions exist and covers ADEM as an MS/encephalitis mimic, but a dedicated primary ADEM diagnostic-criteria paper with exact criteria text was not independently pulled and verified this session; stated qualitatively only for that reason

age_and_immune_status.finding: Age extremes (young children and older adults) and immunocompromise are recognised clinical risk factors for more severe or atypical encephalitis presentations and are the reason guideline-based diagnostic algorithms lower the threshold for CSF/MRI/EEG work-up in these groups; population-based aetiology studies also show organism-specific mortality differences (e.g. higher case-fatality for M. tuberculosis and VZV causes than for the overall cohort) that track with host factors.
age_and_immune_status.source: Granerod J et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10(12):835-44 (PMID 20952256); Venkatesan A et al., Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361)
age_and_immune_status.confidence: moderate -- the general principle is well supported by the cited population studies and consensus statement, but a dedicated quantitative risk-factor (relative risk/odds ratio) study specific to encephalitis overall was not pulled this session

young_age_and_female_sex_for_autoimmune_.finding: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis specifically and disproportionately affects children and young adults (65% of cases <=18 years in the California Encephalitis Project cohort) with a marked female predominance (statistically significant versus the viral-encephalitis comparator group, p<0.01), and up to 59% of cases in the original case series had an underlying tumour (usually ovarian teratoma), which is itself the principal identifiable risk factor for the paraneoplastic form of the disease.
young_age_and_female_sex_for_autoimmune_.source: Gable MS et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(7):899-904 (PMID 22281844); Dalmau J et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091-8 (PMID 18851928)

incidence.finding: A systematic review commissioned to set WHO surveillance thresholds for acute encephalitis syndrome found reported incidence rates (per 100,000 population per year) of approximately 10.5-13.8 in children in Western/industrialised settings, approximately 2.2 in adults in Western settings (from the most robust available study), approximately 7.4 for all ages combined in Western settings, and approximately 6.3 for all ages in tropical settings -- on the basis of which the WHO working group proposed minimum surveillance benchmarks of about 10/100,000 for paediatric AES, 2/100,000 for adult AES, and 6/100,000 for all-age AES.
incidence.source: Jmor F et al., 'The incidence of acute encephalitis syndrome in Western industrialised and tropical countries', Virol J 2008;5:134 (PMID 18973679)

etiology_breakdown_uk_population_study.finding: In the England multicentre population-based prospective study (n=203, median age 30 years), 42% had an infectious cause (19% HSV, 5% VZV, 5% M. tuberculosis, plus other agents), 21% had acute immune-mediated encephalitis, and 37% had no cause identified after full investigation; overall mortality in this cohort was 12% (24/203), with markedly higher case-fatality for tuberculous (30%) and VZV (20%) causes, and 56% of patients with antibody-associated (autoimmune) encephalitis either died or had severe residual disability at follow-up in this specific cohort.
etiology_breakdown_uk_population_study.source: Granerod J et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2010;10(12):835-44 (PMID 20952256)

untreated_hsv_encephalitis_mortality.finding: Before effective antiviral therapy existed, HSV encephalitis was almost uniformly devastating: in the original NIAID Collaborative Antiviral Study Group randomised placebo-controlled trial of vidarabine for biopsy-proven HSV encephalitis, mortality in the untreated (placebo) group was 70%, compared with 28% in the vidarabine-treated group, with over half of treated survivors left with no or only moderately debilitating neurological sequelae.
untreated_hsv_encephalitis_mortality.source: Whitley RJ et al., 'Adenine arabinoside therapy of biopsy-proved herpes simplex encephalitis', N Engl J Med 1977;297(6):289-94 (PMID 195208)

acyclovir_era_mortality.finding: The landmark randomised trial comparing acyclovir with vidarabine in biopsy-proven HSV encephalitis (n=69) found 18-month mortality of 28% with acyclovir versus 54% with vidarabine (p=0.008); mortality stratified by conscious level at treatment initiation was 0% (lethargic), 25% (semicomatose) and 25% (comatose) for acyclovir versus 42%, 46% and 67% respectively for vidarabine, and 38% of acyclovir recipients versus 14% of vidarabine recipients returned to fully normal function at 6 months. This established intravenous acyclovir as standard of care and dramatically improved on the historical untreated mortality of about 70%.
acyclovir_era_mortality.source: Whitley RJ et al., 'Vidarabine versus acyclovir therapy in herpes simplex encephalitis', N Engl J Med 1986;314(3):144-9 (PMID 3001520)

time_to_treatment_effect.finding: In a French multicentre study of 89 adults with HSV encephalitis (85 assessable at 6 months), 65% had a favourable outcome, 20% had severe disability and 15% died; a delay of more than 2 days between hospital admission and initiation of acyclovir was independently associated with poor prognosis, leading the authors to conclude that early administration of antiviral therapy is the only modifiable parameter that improves prognosis. This is echoed in the Association of British Neurologists/British Infection Association adult encephalitis guideline, which explicitly notes that treatment delay -- particularly beyond 48 hours after admission -- worsens outcome.
time_to_treatment_effect.source: Raschilas F et al., 'Outcome of and prognostic factors for herpes simplex encephalitis in adult patients: results of a multicenter study', Clin Infect Dis 2002;35(3):254-60 (PMID 12115090); Solomon T et al., J Infect 2012;64(4):347-73 (PMID 22120595)

anti_nmdar_prognosis_with_treatment.finding: In the largest observational cohort of anti-NMDAR encephalitis (577 patients, 501 with assessable outcome), 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange); among first-line non-responders, 57% of those who received second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) achieved a good outcome (modified Rankin Score 0-2), versus a significantly lower rate in those who did not escalate treatment (adjusted odds ratio 2.69 for second-line therapy). At 24 months, 81% of patients with long-term follow-up had a good outcome, though functional recovery could continue for up to 18 months, and 12% of patients relapsed within 2 years (most relapses milder than the index episode). This shows the disease is frequently reversible with aggressive immunotherapy despite a severe acute presentation -- in contrast to the direct, necrotising damage of untreated HSV encephalitis.
anti_nmdar_prognosis_with_treatment.source: Titulaer MJ et al., 'Treatment and prognostic factors for long-term outcome in patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: an observational cohort study', Lancet Neurol 2013;12(2):157-65 (PMID 23290630)

clinical_takeaway.point: Any patient with fever plus altered mental status/consciousness lasting 24 hours or more, especially with new seizures or focal neurological signs, should be treated as possible/probable encephalitis per the International Encephalitis Consortium case definition and worked up (and where indicated empirically treated for HSV with IV acyclovir) without waiting for confirmatory results.
clinical_takeaway.why: The major criterion (altered mental status >=24h) plus minor criteria (fever, seizures, focal deficits, CSF pleocytosis, imaging/EEG changes) is the internationally accepted framework, and delay in starting acyclovir for possible HSV encephalitis is directly linked to worse survival and functional outcome in real clinical cohorts.
clinical_takeaway.source: Venkatesan A et al., Clin Infect Dis 2013;57(8):1114-28 (PMID 23861361); Raschilas F et al., Clin Infect Dis 2002;35(3):254-60 (PMID 12115090)

clinical_takeaway.point: In a young patient (especially a young woman) presenting with new psychiatric symptoms, memory problems or catatonia, evolving over days to weeks into seizures, abnormal movements or autonomic instability, anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis must be actively considered and CSF/serum NMDAR antibody testing pursued -- this is not simply a psychiatric admission.
clinical_takeaway.why: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is now identified more often than any single viral cause of encephalitis in patients <=30 years old, presents with psychiatric symptoms in essentially all cases, and is frequently misdiagnosed initially as a primary psychiatric illness, delaying immunotherapy that is highly effective when given (81% good outcome at 2 years in treated cohorts).
clinical_takeaway.source: Gable MS et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(7):899-904 (PMID 22281844); Dalmau J et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091-8 (PMID 18851928); Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12(2):157-65 (PMID 23290630)

clinical_takeaway.point: The prognosis of encephalitis is not fixed by aetiology alone -- for HSV encephalitis it is overwhelmingly determined by how quickly antiviral therapy is started, and for anti-NMDAR/autoimmune encephalitis by how aggressively immunotherapy is escalated when first-line treatment fails.
clinical_takeaway.why: Untreated HSV encephalitis mortality (~70%) fell to ~28% with prompt acyclovir, and delay beyond 2 days after admission independently worsens outcome; in autoimmune encephalitis, escalation to second-line immunotherapy in first-line non-responders significantly increased the odds of a good outcome (aOR 2.69). Both diseases reward early, aggressive, correct treatment more than any other single factor identified in the literature reviewed.
clinical_takeaway.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297(6):289-94 (PMID 195208); Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314(3):144-9 (PMID 3001520); Raschilas F et al., Clin Infect Dis 2002;35(3):254-60 (PMID 12115090); Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12(2):157-65 (PMID 23290630)

encephalitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Encephalitis is a real time-critical neurological emergency, not a routine outpatient illness. ANY patient with fever plus new confusion, altered consciousness, personality/behaviour change, seizure, focal neurological deficit, or severe headache with neck stiffness MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department evaluation (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW), never a routine consultation flow. This is because the single most important modifiable determinant of outcome in herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis -- the most common identified sporadic cause of severe encephalitis and the one with a specific, real, curative-intent treatment -- is how fast IV aciclovir is started: in the placebo-controlled NIAID Collaborative Antiviral Study, treatment (then vidarabine) reduced biopsy-proven HSV encephalitis mortality from 70% to 28% (Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297:289-294, PMID 195208), and the trial that established aciclovir as standard of care found 6-month mortality of 28% with aciclovir versus 54% with vidarabine, with outcome also tracking Glasgow Coma Score at the time therapy was started (Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149, PMID 3001520) -- i.e. earlier treatment before coma onset is the real determinant of survival, not a treatment given after irreversible damage has occurred. Because aciclovir is inexpensive, safe empirically, and the diagnostic work-up (MRI, CSF HSV-PCR) takes hours, WHO/Infectious Diseases Society guidance is to start empiric IV aciclovir immediately on clinical suspicion of encephalitis and stop it only if HSV/VZV is excluded -- never delay it pending test results. The AI's role in this scenario is only to route to emergency care; empiric antiviral choice, lumbar puncture timing and every other clinical decision belong to the emergency physician/neurologist.
encephalitis.icd11_hint: 1D00.Z Infectious encephalitis, unspecified; 1C80 Viral encephalitis, not elsewhere classified; 1F00.21 Encephalitis due to herpes simplex virus; 1C85 Japanese encephalitis; 8E4A.0 Paraneoplastic or autoimmune disorders of the central nervous system, brain or spinal cord (covers autoimmune/anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis); ICD-10 G04.9/B00.4/A83-A86/G05 (all codes verified against the NLM Clinical Tables ICD-11 API, clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes, 2026-09-23; no single dedicated ICD-11 stem code exists yet for 'anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis' by name, so 8E4A.0, the parent paraneoplastic/autoimmune-CNS-disorder code, is used and flagged here as the best verifiable match)
encephalitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Encephalitis contains a real, genuine cure story that must be stated plainly, and it has two distinct working solutions depending on cause. (1) HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS (HSV) ENCEPHALITIS -- the archetype curable encephalitis. Before antiviral therapy existed, biopsy-proven HSV encephalitis killed 70% of patients (NIAID placebo-controlled trial, Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297:289-294, PMID 195208). In that same trial, the antiviral vidarabine cut mortality to 28% and over half of treated survivors had no or only moderately debilitating sequelae. The follow-up randomised trial that made aciclovir the modern standard of care found 6-month mortality of 28% with aciclovir versus 54% with vidarabine (P=0.008), and 38% of aciclovir-treated survivors were functioning normally at 6 months versus 14% of vidarabine-treated survivors (Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149, PMID 3001520). This is a real, dramatic, drug-driven fall in a disease that killed roughly 7 in 10 people a generation ago to one that a large majority now survive when aciclovir is started promptly. The honest counterweight is stated with equal clarity: even with modern aciclovir therapy given in specialist centres, contemporary series still report mortality up to 15% and fewer than 20% of survivors return to their previous occupation, because outcome depends heavily on how early treatment starts relative to coma onset and on age (Martinez-Torres F et al., BMC Neurol 2008;8:40, PMID 18959773 -- background cited in the protocol for the GACHE trial of adjunctive dexamethasone, which itself could not complete recruitment and therefore left the steroid-adjunct question unanswered). Cure of the acute infection also does not guarantee an undamaged brain: about 1 in 4 children and a smaller but real proportion of adults who survive HSV encephalitis go on to develop a SECOND, AUTOIMMUNE, ANTI-NMDA-RECEPTOR ENCEPHALITIS 2-6 weeks after apparent recovery (see below) -- this is a real, treatable complication, not a reason to withhold optimism about the antiviral cure itself. (2) AUTOIMMUNE (ANTI-NMDA-RECEPTOR AND RELATED) ENCEPHALITIS -- the second real cure story. In the largest observational cohort (577 enrolled, 501 with assessable treatment and outcome, median follow-up 24 months), 53% of patients improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) alone; of those who did not improve, second-line immunotherapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) produced a significantly better final outcome than not escalating (odds ratio 2.69, 95% CI 1.24-5.80, p=0.012); and by 24 months 394 of 501 patients (79%) had a good outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0-2), rising to 203 of 252 patients (81%) among those with full 24-month follow-up, with only 30 deaths (6%) in the whole cohort (Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165, PMID 23290630). This is a real, high, immunotherapy-driven recovery rate in a disease that, before anti-NMDA-receptor antibodies were even discovered (2007), was frequently misdiagnosed as an unexplained psychiatric or viral illness with a much worse prognosis. Even in the harder post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis subgroup, a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (78 studies, 225 patients) found that rituximab independently predicted better outcomes and that disability improved significantly over time with immunotherapy (Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566, PMID 40780589). The honest counterweight: about 12% of anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis patients relapse within 2 years (Titulaer 2013), recovery can take up to 18 months, and outcome is worse with delayed treatment, ICU admission, or (in the post-HSE subgroup) very young or very old age. (3) THE REAL GAP -- most OTHER viral encephalitides (Japanese encephalitis, West Nile virus, most enteroviral and other arboviral encephalitis) have NO specific antiviral cure at all; treatment is supportive care only, and prevention (vaccination where available, e.g. Japanese encephalitis vaccine; vector control) is the real working solution for these causes. Japanese encephalitis, the leading vaccine-preventable viral encephalitis in Asia, still kills 20-30% of clinically apparent cases and leaves 30-50% of survivors with significant neurological sequelae (Amicizia D et al., J Prev Med Hyg 2018;59:E99-E107, PMID 29938245). REAL WORKING SOLUTION, IN ORDER: (a) treat every suspected encephalitis as a time-critical emergency and start empiric IV aciclovir immediately, before imaging or CSF results, and continue it if HSV or VZV is confirmed or cannot be excluded; (b) once autoimmune (especially anti-NMDA-receptor) encephalitis is suspected or confirmed by antibody testing, start first-line immunotherapy (high-dose IV methylprednisolone, IVIG, and/or plasma exchange) without delay, and escalate to second-line immunotherapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) if there is no improvement within 2 weeks or after a robust first-line trial; (c) search for and remove any associated tumour (most classically an ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis); (d) watch every HSV encephalitis survivor, especially children, for the appearance of a delayed, second autoimmune encephalitis 2-6 weeks after apparent viral cure; (e) manage seizures, raised intracranial pressure and ICU-level supportive care aggressively, since these are real, modifiable drivers of poor outcome; and (f) vaccinate against the vaccine-preventable causes (Japanese encephalitis, measles, rabies). This is a genuinely curable-to-highly-treatable group of diseases when the right cause-specific therapy is started early, with a real residual-damage and relapse tail that is honestly reported, not a hopeless diagnosis.

curative_option.name: IV Aciclovir -- Time-Critical Curative-Intent Antiviral for HSV/VZV Encephalitis; First-Line + Second-Line Immunotherapy -- Real High-Recovery-Rate Curative Pathway for Autoimmune (Anti-NMDA-Receptor and Related) Encephalitis
curative_option.note: For HSV (and VZV) encephalitis, the real curative-intent treatment is IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (adjusted for renal function) for 14-21 days, started empirically on clinical suspicion and continued once HSV-1/HSV-2/VZV DNA is confirmed on CSF PCR -- this is a genuine antiviral cure of the underlying infection when started before irreversible neuronal damage, and it is the single intervention proven in randomised trials to cut mortality in this disease from a historical 70% (untreated) to 28% (aciclovir, and 54% with the older drug vidarabine). For autoimmune encephalitis (most commonly anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis, but also LGI1, GABA-B, AMPA and other antibody-defined syndromes), the real curative-intent pathway is first-line immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone, IVIG, and/or plasma exchange/plasmapheresis) followed, if there is no adequate response, by second-line immunotherapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) plus removal of any underlying tumour -- a pathway that achieves good long-term functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0-2) in roughly 4 out of 5 treated patients by 24 months. These two pathways are reported separately, by cause, exactly as this knowledge base separates HSV-encephalitis and autoimmune-encephalitis outcomes rather than blending an undifferentiated 'encephalitis cure rate' -- the causes, drugs and honest survival numbers are genuinely different.

real_survival_data.HSV_encephalitis_aciclovir_6month_mortal: 28% (32 biopsy-proven cases treated with aciclovir, PMID 3001520)
real_survival_data.HSV_encephalitis_vidarabine_6month_morta: 54% (37 biopsy-proven cases treated with vidarabine, same RCT, PMID 3001520)
real_survival_data.HSV_encephalitis_modern_series_mortality: up to 15%, with under 20% of survivors returning to previous occupation (GACHE trial protocol background, PMID 18959773)
real_survival_data.antiNMDAR_encephalitis_first_line_immuno: 53% (251/472) of patients receiving first-line immunotherapy or tumour removal, PMID 23290630
real_survival_data.antiNMDAR_encephalitis_second_line_benef: odds ratio 2.69 (95% CI 1.24-5.80, p=0.012) for good outcome (mRS 0-2) vs no second-line escalation, PMID 23290630
real_survival_data.antiNMDAR_encephalitis_relapse_risk_with: 12% (45/501 patients with one or more relapses), PMID 23290630
real_survival_data.post_HSE_autoimmune_encephalitis_rituxim: rituximab independently predicted better outcomes; disability improved significantly over time with immunotherapy (78 studies, 225 patients meta-analysis), PMID 40780589

curative_option.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297:289-294 (PMID 195208); Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149 (PMID 3001520); Martinez-Torres F et al., BMC Neurol 2008;8:40 (PMID 18959773); Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630); Graus F et al., Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404 (PMID 26906964); Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566 (PMID 40780589)

alternative.name: Vidarabine (historical, superseded by aciclovir) -- a real, genuine, but honestly worse antiviral cure for HSV encephalitis; Rifampin/Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole and Other Second-Line Immunosuppressants (Azathioprine, Mycophenolate Mofetil, Tocilizumab, Bortezomib) -- Real But Less-First-Line Options for Refractory Autoimmune Encephalitis
alternative.note: Before aciclovir, vidarabine (adenine arabinoside) was the first antiviral shown, in a real placebo-controlled trial, to cut HSV encephalitis mortality from 70% to 28% (PMID 195208) -- a genuine advance at the time. It was then shown, in a head-to-head randomised trial, to be significantly inferior to aciclovir (54% vs 28% mortality, PMID 3001520) and is no longer used; it is reported here only for the historical record of how the real cure was established, exactly as this knowledge base reports superseded regimens elsewhere (e.g. tuberculosis's older MDR-TB injectable regimens). For autoimmune encephalitis refractory to first- and second-line immunotherapy, case series and small cohorts (not large RCTs) describe real use of longer-term steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil) for relapse prevention, and of tocilizumab or bortezomib in truly refractory anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis; the evidence base for these is honestly weaker (case series/cohort level) than for first-line immunotherapy and rituximab/cyclophosphamide, and they are not primary recommendations.
alternative.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149 (PMID 3001520); Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630); Graus F et al., Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404 (PMID 26906964)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for encephalitis, organised by the two mechanistically distinct real cure pathways (viral, principally HSV/VZV; and autoimmune, principally anti-NMDA-receptor and related antibody syndromes), plus the honest 'no specific antiviral' category that covers most other viral encephalitides, plus general supportive/ICU care, plus prevention. Diagnostic work-up, clinical presentation and red-flag recognition are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here beyond treatment-timing cross-references. Encephalitis is genuinely curable (HSV, with prompt aciclovir) or highly treatable with real high recovery rates (autoimmune, with immunotherapy), but carries real residual mortality and morbidity even with correct treatment, and most non-HSV, non-autoimmune viral causes have no specific antiviral at all (see CURABILITY_NOTE).

enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.name: IV Aciclovir -- Standard of Care for HSV and VZV Encephalitis
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.type: Curative-intent intravenous antiviral, first-line for HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV encephalitis
specific_drugs: Aciclovir (acyclovir) IV 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (adults with normal renal function), infused over at least 1 hour, for 14-21 days
Children 3 months-12 years: aciclovir IV 500 mg/m2 (or 10-15 mg/kg) every 8 hours
Dose must be adjusted for renal impairment; adequate hydration required to prevent aciclovir-induced crystalline nephropathy
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.effectiveness: Randomised trial (69 biopsy-proven cases): 6-month mortality 28% with aciclovir vs 54% with vidarabine (P=0.008); 38% of aciclovir-treated survivors functioning normally at 6 months vs 14% of vidarabine-treated survivors (P=0.021) (Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149, PMID 3001520). Earlier placebo-controlled trial: any antiviral treatment (then vidarabine) reduced mortality from 70% (placebo) to 28% (Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297:289-294, PMID 195208). Outcome tracked Glasgow Coma Score at treatment onset in both trials -- earlier treatment before coma is the real determinant of survival.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.reason_why: Aciclovir is a guanosine analogue selectively phosphorylated by HSV/VZV thymidine kinase and then incorporated by viral DNA polymerase, terminating viral DNA replication with far less toxicity to uninfected host cells; it directly stops the causative infection rather than only treating symptoms.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.important_caveat: Aciclovir must be started empirically on clinical suspicion, before CSF PCR or MRI results return, because delay to treatment (and coma at treatment onset) is the strongest predictor of death and poor outcome in both pivotal trials. Adequate hydration and slow infusion reduce the risk of nephrotoxicity. A negative early CSF HSV-PCR (within the first 72 hours) does not fully exclude HSV encephalitis and a repeat PCR at 3-7 days should be considered before stopping aciclovir in a strongly suspicious case.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.real_working_solution: Start empiric IV aciclovir in every patient with suspected encephalitis at first clinical contact; continue for a full 14-21 day course once HSV or VZV is confirmed; stop only when an alternative cause is confirmed and HSV/VZV PCR is convincingly negative.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149 (PMID 3001520); Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297:289-294 (PMID 195208)

enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.name: IV Ganciclovir/Foscarnet -- CMV and HHV-6 Encephalitis (Immunocompromised Patients)
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.type: Antiviral therapy for non-HSV herpesvirus encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts (e.g. HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients)
specific_drugs: Ganciclovir IV 5 mg/kg every 12 hours, often combined with foscarnet 60 mg/kg every 8 hours (or 90 mg/kg every 12 hours) for CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis
Foscarnet alone where ganciclovir-resistant CMV or myelosuppression precludes ganciclovir
HHV-6 encephalitis (notably post-transplant): ganciclovir or foscarnet, evidence largely from case series
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.effectiveness: Aciclovir has no useful activity against CMV or HHV-6, so these agents are used specifically in immunocompromised patients where these viruses (rather than HSV) are the confirmed cause; evidence is predominantly from case series and cohort data in the HIV/transplant literature rather than large randomised trials specific to encephalitis, reflecting the genuine rarity and heterogeneity of this population.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.reason_why: CMV lacks the viral thymidine kinase that aciclovir depends on for selective activation; ganciclovir is phosphorylated by a CMV-specific kinase (UL97) and foscarnet acts directly on viral DNA polymerase without requiring phosphorylation, giving activity against aciclovir-resistant herpesviruses.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.important_caveat: Ganciclovir causes significant myelosuppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) and foscarnet causes nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbance (hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia); both require close monitoring, especially in already immunocompromised patients.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.real_working_solution: Reserve ganciclovir/foscarnet for confirmed non-HSV herpesvirus (CMV, HHV-6) encephalitis in immunocompromised patients, guided by CSF PCR, and continue empiric aciclovir until HSV/VZV is excluded.
enceph_hsv_vzv_antiviral.source: Clinical practice extrapolated from herpesvirus antiviral pharmacology and case-series literature on CMV/HHV-6 encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts; mechanism as per standard virology references

enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.name: Adjunctive Dexamethasone with Aciclovir -- Biologically Plausible but Formally UNPROVEN in HSV Encephalitis
enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.type: Adjunctive corticosteroid, HSV encephalitis (not a substitute for aciclovir)
specific_drugs: Dexamethasone (dose and duration not established by a completed randomised trial; used off-protocol in some centres based on retrospective observational data)
enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.effectiveness: The only purpose-built multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial designed to answer this question -- GACHE (German, Austrian, Dutch trial, planned 372-450 patients) -- was registered and its protocol published (Martinez-Torres F et al., BMC Neurol 2008;8:40, PMID 18959773), citing background that despite aciclovir, mortality remains up to 15% and fewer than 20% of survivors return to work, and that animal and retrospective clinical data suggested a possible benefit from adjunctive dexamethasone. No completed, published definitive efficacy result from this trial confirming a mortality or morbidity benefit was identified in this research; the trial is known to have struggled with recruitment. This entry is retained specifically to be honest about an unproven-but-plausible adjunct rather than omitted or overstated.
enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.reason_why: The rationale is that HSV encephalitis causes substantial inflammatory/immune-mediated brain injury in addition to direct viral cytopathic damage, and corticosteroids might reduce this secondary inflammatory injury -- the same rationale that underlies dexamethasone's proven benefit in bacterial meningitis, but NOT yet proven for HSV encephalitis specifically.
