enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.important_caveat: Because the evidence is incomplete, adjunctive dexamethasone in HSV encephalitis must be an individualised, specialist decision, not a default addition; it must never be substituted for, or delay, IV aciclovir.
enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.real_working_solution: Do not withhold or delay aciclovir while considering steroids; adjunctive dexamethasone may be considered by the treating neurologist/infectious-disease physician on a case-by-case basis pending more definitive trial evidence, which does not yet exist.
enceph_hsv_adjunct_steroid_unproven.source: Martinez-Torres F et al., BMC Neurol 2008;8:40 (PMID 18959773)

enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.name: IV Methylprednisolone, IVIG and Plasma Exchange -- First-Line Immunotherapy for Autoimmune (Anti-NMDA-Receptor and Related) Encephalitis
enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.type: First-line combination/sequential immunotherapy for antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis
specific_drugs: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days (high-dose pulse corticosteroid)
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (total 2 g/kg)
Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis/PLEX), typically 5-7 exchanges over 10-14 days, used alone or combined with steroids/IVIG
First-line agents are frequently combined (e.g. steroids plus IVIG, or steroids plus plasma exchange) rather than used strictly sequentially
enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.effectiveness: In the largest observational cohort (472 of 501 patients received first-line immunotherapy and/or tumour removal), 53% (251/472) improved within 4 weeks of first-line treatment; those treated early had significantly better long-term outcome (early treatment predictor OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.50-0.76, p<0.0001, for a WORSE outcome per unit delay, i.e. earlier treatment protective) (Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165, PMID 23290630).
enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.reason_why: Anti-NMDA-receptor (and related LGI1, GABA-B, AMPA-receptor) encephalitis is caused by pathogenic IgG autoantibodies that internalise or block the target neuronal surface receptor; corticosteroids broadly suppress the autoimmune/inflammatory response, IVIG neutralises and accelerates clearance of pathogenic antibodies and modulates Fc-receptor-mediated immune activation, and plasma exchange physically removes circulating antibody -- three complementary ways of lowering the pathogenic antibody burden and inflammation.
enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.important_caveat: First-line immunotherapy should be given as soon as autoimmune encephalitis is suspected on clinical/paraclinical grounds (per Graus 2016 diagnostic criteria), without waiting for confirmatory antibody results, because earlier treatment is a proven predictor of better outcome; any underlying tumour (classically ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis) must be actively searched for and removed as part of first-line management.
enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.real_working_solution: Start high-dose IV methylprednisolone plus IVIG (or plasma exchange) at the first strong clinical suspicion of autoimmune encephalitis, search for and remove any associated tumour, and reassess for improvement within 2-4 weeks to decide on second-line escalation.
enceph_autoimmune_first_line_immunothera.source: Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630); Graus F et al., Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404 (PMID 26906964)

enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.name: Rituximab and/or Cyclophosphamide -- Second-Line Immunotherapy for Autoimmune Encephalitis Not Responding to First-Line Treatment
enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.type: Second-line B-cell-depleting/immunosuppressive therapy, escalation after inadequate first-line response
specific_drugs: Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody), commonly 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks, or 1000 mg on days 1 and 15 (regimen extrapolated from rheumatologic/haematologic rituximab dosing; not separately established by a dedicated encephalitis RCT)
Cyclophosphamide, commonly as monthly IV pulses (dose per body surface area, individualised)
Rituximab and cyclophosphamide may be used sequentially or in combination in refractory cases
enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.effectiveness: Of 221 patients who did not improve with first-line treatment, 125 (57%) received second-line immunotherapy; this group had a significantly better long-term outcome (mRS 0-2) than those who did not receive second-line therapy (odds ratio 2.69, 95% CI 1.24-5.80, p=0.012) (Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165, PMID 23290630). In the specific post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis subgroup (meta-analysis, 225 patients), rituximab independently predicted better outcomes (Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566, PMID 40780589).
enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20+ B cells, reducing the population that differentiates into antibody-producing plasmablasts/plasma cells, thereby lowering ongoing pathogenic antibody production (more durable than IVIG/plasma exchange, which act on already-circulating antibody); cyclophosphamide is a broader-acting alkylating immunosuppressant used when B-cell-targeted therapy alone is insufficient or when other autoimmune/paraneoplastic mechanisms are suspected.
enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.important_caveat: Second-line therapy carries real added infection and marrow-suppression risk (both agents), and rituximab's benefit takes weeks to manifest because of the time needed for B-cell depletion to translate into reduced antibody levels; the safety profile in the post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis subgroup was reported as comparable to that seen in the broader anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis population (PMID 40780589), i.e. not disproportionately hazardous, but not risk-free.
enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.real_working_solution: Escalate to rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide if there is no meaningful improvement after a robust first-line immunotherapy trial (typically assessed at 2-4 weeks), rather than repeating or prolonging first-line therapy alone.
enceph_autoimmune_second_line_immunother.source: Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630); Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566 (PMID 40780589)

enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.name: Recognition and Immunotherapy of Autoimmune (Post-HSV) Encephalitis Arising After Apparent Viral Cure
enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.type: Delayed secondary autoimmune encephalitis following successfully aciclovir-treated HSV encephalitis, principally anti-NMDA-receptor mediated
specific_drugs: Same first-line (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) and second-line (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) immunotherapy as primary autoimmune encephalitis -- see the two entries above
No further aciclovir is required for this second phase once HSV DNA has cleared from CSF; this phase is autoimmune, not infective
enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.effectiveness: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 78 studies (225 patients, median age 7.25 years, 52.9% female) meeting consensus criteria for autoimmune encephalitis after confirmed HSV encephalitis (HSVE-AE): 89.3% were anti-NMDA-receptor antibody encephalitis. Poor outcomes were linked to infant and older-adult age, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and higher modified Rankin Scale during the autoimmune-encephalitis phase; rituximab independently predicted better outcomes; and disability improved significantly over time with treatment, with adverse-event rates comparable to primary anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis (Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566, PMID 40780589).
enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.reason_why: HSV-induced neuronal damage releases neuronal surface antigens (including the NMDA receptor) in an inflammatory context, which can trigger a secondary autoimmune antibody response against these exposed neuronal antigens -- children experience this more often than adults, likely reflecting an age-related difference in post-infectious immune responses.
enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.important_caveat: This second phase is frequently missed because clinicians and families expect recovery after successful antiviral treatment; new or recurrent neurological/behavioural/movement symptoms 2-6 weeks after apparent HSV encephalitis recovery should prompt urgent re-evaluation for autoimmune encephalitis (repeat MRI, CSF/serum antibody testing), not automatic assumption of HSV relapse or post-infectious sequelae.
enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.real_working_solution: Actively monitor every HSV encephalitis survivor, especially children, for new neuropsychiatric, movement, or behavioural symptoms after initial improvement; test for anti-NMDA-receptor (and related) antibodies promptly if suspected; and start first-line immunotherapy, escalating to rituximab if needed, exactly as for primary autoimmune encephalitis.
enceph_post_hsv_autoimmune_encephalitis.source: Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566 (PMID 40780589)

enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.name: Supportive Care Only -- Japanese Encephalitis, West Nile Virus, Enteroviral and Most Other Arboviral Encephalitis (No Specific Antiviral Exists)
enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.type: Best-available supportive management where no cause-specific antiviral or immunotherapy exists
specific_drugs: No specific antiviral agent is approved or proven effective for Japanese encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, most enteroviruses, or most other arboviruses causing encephalitis

Supportive measures: airway protection/mechanical ventilation as needed, seizure control, intracranial pressure management, fever control, nutritional and fluid/electrolyte support, prevention of secondary complications (aspiration, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury)
enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.effectiveness: Because of the lack of treatment and the practical difficulty of eliminating the mosquito vector, vaccination is recognised as the most efficacious real means of preventing Japanese encephalitis (Amicizia D et al., J Prev Med Hyg 2018;59:E99-E107, PMID 29938245). Honest outcome data in the absence of a specific antiviral: among the estimated 30,000-50,000 global Japanese encephalitis cases per year, approximately 20-30% of clinically apparent cases die and 30-50% of survivors develop significant neurological sequelae (same source, PMID 29938245).
enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.reason_why: Unlike HSV/VZV, these viruses either lack a viral enzyme (such as HSV's thymidine kinase) that current antivirals can selectively exploit, or have not yet had an antiviral developed and proven effective against CNS disease specifically; the real, available lever is therefore prevention (vaccination, vector control) rather than a treatment given after infection is established.
enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.important_caveat: This is a genuine, current gap in antiviral therapeutics, not a withheld or under-prescribed treatment -- it must be reported honestly rather than implying a cure exists where none has been proven. This is exactly why prevention (see the vaccination entry) is elevated to a primary, not secondary, real working solution for these specific causes.
enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.real_working_solution: For these causes, treat supportively and aggressively manage seizures/raised intracranial pressure/complications while the immune system clears the virus (in survivors), and prioritise the vaccine-preventable causes (Japanese encephalitis) for primary prevention in endemic and travel populations.
enceph_other_viral_no_specific_antiviral.source: Amicizia D et al., J Prev Med Hyg 2018;59:E99-E107 (PMID 29938245)

enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.name: Seizure Control, Raised-Intracranial-Pressure Management and ICU-Level Supportive Care
enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.type: General adjunctive/supportive management applicable across all causes of encephalitis
specific_drugs: Antiseizure medications for clinical or electrographic seizures (agent per local status-epilepticus/antiseizure protocols; not encephalitis-specific dosing)
Osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) and head-of-bed elevation for raised intracranial pressure
ICU admission with airway protection/mechanical ventilation for depressed consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score-guided)
enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.effectiveness: Both pivotal HSV-encephalitis antiviral trials found that outcome (mortality and functional recovery) varied strongly with Glasgow Coma Score and level of consciousness at the time treatment was started (Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149, PMID 3001520), and in the anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis cohort, ICU admission was itself an independent predictor of worse outcome (odds ratio 0.12, 95% CI 0.06-0.22, for the protective effect of NOT requiring ICU admission, i.e. ICU admission strongly associated with worse outcome) (Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165, PMID 23290630) -- underscoring that aggressive, early supportive/critical care alongside cause-specific therapy is a real, evidence-linked determinant of outcome, not a passive afterthought.
enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.reason_why: Uncontrolled seizures and raised intracranial pressure cause additional secondary neuronal injury on top of the primary infective or autoimmune insult; controlling them protects the brain while cause-specific antiviral or immunotherapy takes effect.
enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.important_caveat: Supportive care must run in parallel with, never instead of, cause-specific therapy (aciclovir or immunotherapy) -- it improves the chance that a patient survives long enough, and with enough preserved brain tissue, for the specific treatment to work.
enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.real_working_solution: Admit any patient with depressed consciousness, seizures, or signs of raised intracranial pressure to a monitored/ICU setting, treat seizures and raised ICP per standard critical-care protocols, and continue cause-specific antiviral or immunotherapy throughout.
enceph_seizure_icp_icu_supportive_care.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149 (PMID 3001520); Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630)

enceph_prevention_vaccination.name: Vaccination -- Real Primary Prevention for the Vaccine-Preventable Causes of Encephalitis (Japanese Encephalitis, Measles, Rabies)
enceph_prevention_vaccination.type: Primary prevention, not treatment of established disease
specific_drugs: Japanese encephalitis vaccine (e.g. inactivated Vero-cell-derived IC51/IXIARO, or live-attenuated SA14-14-2 used in national immunisation programmes in endemic countries including India) for residents of and travellers to endemic areas
Measles-containing vaccine (MMR) -- prevents measles, a cause of acute measles encephalitis and of the near-uniformly fatal delayed complication subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)
Rabies vaccine (pre- or post-exposure) plus rabies immunoglobulin post-exposure -- prevents rabies encephalitis, which is essentially universally fatal once symptomatic
enceph_prevention_vaccination.effectiveness: Because no specific antiviral treatment exists for Japanese encephalitis, vaccination is described as the most efficacious real means of prevention (Amicizia D et al., J Prev Med Hyg 2018;59:E99-E107, PMID 29938245); the same source documents that 20-30% of clinically apparent Japanese encephalitis cases still die and 30-50% of survivors have significant neurological sequelae, underscoring why prevention is the real working solution for this specific cause rather than an afterthought to treatment.
enceph_prevention_vaccination.reason_why: For causes with no proven post-infection antiviral or immunotherapy (Japanese encephalitis, rabies) or with a delayed, currently untreatable fatal CNS complication (measles/SSPE), preventing the primary infection is the only real lever available, in clear contrast to HSV encephalitis and autoimmune encephalitis, where a genuine post-onset treatment exists.
enceph_prevention_vaccination.important_caveat: No vaccine exists for HSV, and vaccination does not help a patient who already has established encephalitis from any of these causes -- it is prevention, listed here for completeness and because the exhaustive_medicine_survey explicitly covers real, sourced treatment-side interventions including prevention, not because it substitutes for aciclovir or immunotherapy once disease is established.
enceph_prevention_vaccination.real_working_solution: Vaccinate against Japanese encephalitis in endemic/travel settings per national immunisation schedules, ensure measles (MMR) vaccination coverage to prevent both acute measles encephalitis and SSPE, and give rabies pre-/post-exposure prophylaxis promptly after any exposure risk.
enceph_prevention_vaccination.source: Amicizia D et al., J Prev Med Hyg 2018;59:E99-E107 (PMID 29938245)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IV Aciclovir started early, before coma onset, for HSV encephalitis -- Real Top-Line Answer
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Randomised trial 6-month mortality: 28% with aciclovir vs 54% with vidarabine (relative reduction 48.1%, computed as (54-28)/54), 69 biopsy-proven cases; earlier NIAID placebo-controlled trial: any antiviral treatment (vidarabine) reduced mortality from 70% (placebo) to 28% (relative reduction 60%, computed as (70-28)/70), 28 biopsy-proven cases -- two separate real trials establishing both the untreated baseline and the modern-standard-of-care outcome
ranked_high_to_low.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149 (PMID 3001520); Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1977;297:289-294 (PMID 195208)

ranked_high_to_low.name: First-line immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone/IVIG/plasma exchange) for autoimmune anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 53% (251/472) of patients improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy and/or tumour removal, 501-patient observational cohort
ranked_high_to_low.source: Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Full treatment pathway (first-line +/- second-line immunotherapy) for autoimmune anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis -- 24-month good outcome
ranked_high_to_low.type: Complete immunotherapy pathway, long-term functional outcome
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 79% (394/501) achieved good outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0-2) within 24 months; 81% (203/252) among patients with full 24-month follow-up; mortality 6% (30/501)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Second-line immunotherapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) after first-line treatment failure in autoimmune encephalitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Odds ratio 2.69 (95% CI 1.24-5.80, p=0.012) for good outcome (mRS 0-2) vs no second-line escalation, among 221 first-line non-responders
ranked_high_to_low.source: Titulaer MJ et al., Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165 (PMID 23290630)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab in post-HSV autoimmune encephalitis (HSVE-AE)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Independently predicted better outcome; disability improved significantly over time with immunotherapy in a 225-patient meta-analysis (78 studies) of autoimmune encephalitis following confirmed HSV encephalitis
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cleaver J et al., J Infect 2025;91:106566 (PMID 40780589)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Aciclovir historical superiority over vidarabine (basis for current standard of care)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 6-month mortality 28% (aciclovir) vs 54% (vidarabine), P=0.008; 38% vs 14% of survivors functioning normally at 6 months, P=0.021
ranked_high_to_low.source: Whitley RJ et al., N Engl J Med 1986;314:144-149 (PMID 3001520)

trigeminal_neuralgia.name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
trigeminal_neuralgia.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM: G50.0 Trigeminal neuralgia (well-established legacy code). ICD-11 code is commonly cited in recent (2024-2026) TN literature as 8B82.0 Trigeminal neuralgia, but this could NOT be independently confirmed against a live WHO ICD-11 browser/API query in this research session (the WHO ICD API requires OAuth authentication not available here, and the public browser page is JavaScript-rendered). FLAGGED for independent verification against icd.who.int before clinical/coding use.

symptoms.definition_and_pathophysiology: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is defined as recurrent, unilateral, brief (less than 1 second up to 2 minutes), very severe, electric shock-like paroxysms of pain in one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve, typically triggered by innocuous stimuli (Lambru G, Zakrzewska J, Matharu M, 'Trigeminal neuralgia: a practical guide', Pract Neurol 2021;21(5):392-402, PMID 34108244). The dominant mechanism is vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root, usually by the superior cerebellar artery, at or near the root entry zone (the central-to-peripheral myelin transition zone), producing focal demyelination; this lowers the local excitability threshold and allows ephaptic ('cross-talk') transmission in which light-touch signals carried by A-beta fibres directly activate adjacent pain-signalling A-delta fibres, generating the paroxysmal, touch-triggered pain (PMID 34108244; Bendtsen L, Zakrzewska JM, Heinskou TB et al., 'Advances in diagnosis, classification, pathophysiology, and management of trigeminal neuralgia', Lancet Neurol 2020;19(9):784-796, PMID 32822636). By ICHD-3 subtype breakdown reported in this review: classical TN (neurovascular compression WITH morphological changes - distortion, indentation, or atrophy - seen on MRI or at surgery) accounts for approximately 75% of cases; idiopathic TN (no identifiable cause found on MRI/electrophysiology) approximately 10%; and secondary TN (attributable to an identifiable neurological disease - multiple sclerosis plaque, tumour, arteriovenous malformation) approximately 15% (PMID 34108244). Morphological nerve changes are rare on the asymptomatic contralateral side, supporting a causal (not incidental) role for compression with distortion, as opposed to simple vascular contact without distortion, which is also common in asymptomatic people and is not diagnostic by itself.
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Per the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3; Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society, Cephalalgia 2018;38(1):1-211, PMID 29368949), trigeminal neuralgia (code 13.1) is subdivided into: (1) Classical TN (13.1.1) - due to neurovascular compression with morphological changes on MRI or at surgery, further split into purely paroxysmal (13.1.1.1) and with concomitant continuous pain (13.1.1.2); (2) Secondary TN (13.1.2) - attributed to an underlying disease known to cause TN, e.g. a multiple sclerosis plaque, a space-occupying lesion, or another identifiable structural cause; and (3) Idiopathic TN (13.1.3) - no neurovascular compression or other cause identified, also split by purely paroxysmal vs with concomitant continuous pain. The 2019 European Academy of Neurology (EAN) guideline (Bendtsen L et al., Eur J Neurol 2019;26(6):831-849, PMID 30860637) states explicitly that MRI, using a combination of three high-resolution sequences, should be performed as part of the work-up in ALL TN patients, 'because no clinical characteristics can exclude secondary TN' - i.e., a classic clinical presentation alone is never sufficient to rule out MS or a structural lesion. Demonstration of neurovascular contact on MRI should be used to guide surgical decision-making, not as the sole basis for diagnosis (PMID 32822636). A concomitant continuous background pain (persistent dull/burning ache between paroxysms) is reported in 14-50% of patients, and recent evidence shows this continuous pain often develops with or even before the onset of paroxysmal pain, indicating it represents a distinct disease subtype rather than simply a late consequence of repeated attacks (PMID 34108244).
symptoms.classic_symptoms: Attacks are described as electric shock-like, shooting, stabbing, or sharp in quality, strictly unilateral, and confined to the trigeminal distribution (most often the maxillary [V2] and/or mandibular [V3] divisions; ophthalmic [V1]-only involvement is less common). Individual paroxysms typically last from under 1 second up to 2 minutes, though a significant minority of patients report attacks lasting 2-10 minutes (PMID 34108244). Trigger zones are a defining feature: 91-99% of patients report attacks provoked by innocuous stimulation of specific facial or intraoral zones, with light tactile touch being by far the most potent trigger (painful or thermal stimulation is generally ineffective at triggering an attack). Common real-world triggers include light touch, talking, chewing, brushing teeth, washing or drying the face, drinking, shaving, and cold wind on the face (PMID 34108244). A characteristic and diagnostically useful refractory period follows a triggered attack: for a period of seconds to minutes afterward, further attacks cannot be provoked even by repeating the trigger - this refractory period is a key feature distinguishing TN from SUNCT/SUNA, which lack it (PMID 34108244). Attacks commonly occur many times per day during symptomatic bouts.
symptoms.differential_diagnosis: Cluster headache: unlike TN, cluster headache attacks are NOT triggered by innocuous cutaneous stimulation (triggerability is essentially pathognomonic for TN); cluster attacks last longer (15-180 minutes), are accompanied by prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, ptosis/miosis), and follow a circadian/circannual bout pattern (cross-referenced in this knowledge base under cluster_headache; PMID 34108244). Dental/odontogenic pain: dental causes lack the electric-shock quality and brief paroxysmal pattern of TN, tend to be continuous/dull, and are associated with identifiable dental pathology on examination/imaging - TN is frequently misdiagnosed as dental pain, leading to unnecessary dental extractions before the correct diagnosis is made (PMID 34108244). SUNCT/SUNA (Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache attacks with Conjunctival injection/Tearing or Autonomic symptoms): distinguished from TN by prominent cranial autonomic symptoms, ABSENCE of a refractory period after a triggered attack, somewhat longer attack duration (1-600 seconds), and a predominantly first-division (V1) distribution versus TN's V2/V3 predominance (PMID 34108244). Glossopharyngeal neuralgia: pain localizes to the glossopharyngeal nerve distribution (throat, tonsillar fossa, ear, base of tongue) rather than the trigeminal distribution, and is characteristically triggered by swallowing, talking, coughing, or yawning rather than facial touch (PMID 34108244).
symptoms.risk_factors: Multiple sclerosis is the single most important identifiable risk factor for (secondary) TN: in a large MS clinic cohort (Hooge JP, Redekop WK, 'Trigeminal neuralgia in multiple sclerosis', Neurology 1995;45(7):1294-1296, PMID 7617185), TN occurred in 35 of 1,882 MS patients (1.9%) - a rate far above general-population estimates. A 2026 critical review (Brain Sciences, PMID 42651189) confirms TN 'occurs far more frequently' in MS than in the general population, and that MS-associated TN (TN-MS) tends to present at a YOUNGER age than classical TN, is more often BILATERAL, and more often shows sensory abnormalities, persistent dysesthesia, and concomitant continuous background pain than classical TN. In the Hooge & Redekop cohort, bilateral involvement occurred in 14% of MS-associated TN cases, compared with only 1.7-5% bilaterality reported across classical/idiopathic TN generally (PMID 34108244) - making bilaterality a meaningful pointer toward an MS/secondary cause. Female sex is also a risk factor: female:male ratio is approximately 3:2 in classic estimates (PMID 34108244), and the largest pooled global analysis to date likewise found higher incidence and prevalence in females than males (PMID 41517817). Advancing age is a risk factor for classical/idiopathic TN, with mean age of onset 53-57 years (range 24-93) in the classical/idiopathic population (PMID 34108244); by contrast, TN as a presenting or early feature of MS occurs at a younger age, reflecting the underlying demyelinating disease rather than age-related vascular change.
symptoms.epidemiology: The most comprehensive recent estimate comes from a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies covering over 170 million participants and 109,070 TN patients ('Global Incidence and Prevalence of Trigeminal Neuralgia, 1945-2024', J Clin Neurol 2026, PMID 41517817), which found: global pooled incidence 25.33 per 100,000 person-years; global pooled annual prevalence 45.38 per 100,000; global pooled lifetime prevalence 108.43 per 100,000; with higher incidence/prevalence in females, more frequent right-sided involvement, and greater frequency in the maxillary/mandibular divisions than the ophthalmic division. The review noted that incorporation of imaging into diagnostic criteria over recent decades may have contributed to increased reported prevalence. Earlier widely-cited estimates (Lambru et al., Pract Neurol 2021, PMID 34108244) reported a lower lifetime prevalence of 0.16-0.3% and annual incidence of 4-29 per 100,000 person-years, female:male ratio approximately 3:2, mean age of onset 53-57 years (range 24-93 years), and noted that TN is rare in children (one clinic series of 1,040 children identified only 5 paediatric TN cases, ages 9.5-16.5 years). A Danish nationwide register study using national patient records from 7.2 million individuals identified 7,141 diagnosed TN patients (64.2% female, mean age at diagnosis 58.7 years) (Worm J, Maarbjerg S et al., Pain 2025;166(4):879-887, PMID 39365662). The wide range between the older and newer pooled estimates reflects real heterogeneity in case ascertainment and diagnostic criteria across studies rather than a single settled number.
symptoms.natural_history: TN follows a relapsing-remitting pattern in approximately two-thirds of patients but a chronic (continuously symptomatic) pattern in the remaining one-third. Among patients who do experience remissions, the frequency and duration vary greatly: remission periods last months in 37% and years in 63% of these patients (PMID 34108244). Many patients have extended pain-free intervals lasting months to years, but in many others TN becomes progressively more severe and less responsive to treatment over time despite escalating pharmacological therapy (PMID 34108244). Concomitant continuous background pain, present in 14-50% of patients, can develop with or even before the onset of paroxysmal pain rather than only appearing after years of repeated attacks, indicating a distinct pain phenotype rather than a purely cumulative consequence (PMID 34108244). In MS-associated TN specifically, the neuralgia emerged on average 11.8 years after initial MS symptom onset in the Hooge & Redekop cohort, but in 5 of 35 affected patients TN was the FIRST manifestation of MS, preceding other MS symptoms by 1 to 11 years, and MS onset overall occurred later in the subgroup that went on to develop TN (PMID 7617185). A Danish nationwide disease-trajectory study additionally found TN patients carry a significantly elevated subsequent risk of ischaemic stroke (relative risk 1.55), with carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine treatment associated with further increased stroke risk (though polygenic stroke risk itself showed no association) - supporting ongoing cardiovascular risk-factor monitoring in TN patients, independent of pain management (PMID 39365662).
symptoms.clinical_takeaway: TN is diagnosed clinically from its highly characteristic paroxysmal, touch-triggered, electric-shock pain with a post-attack refractory period - but because 'no clinical characteristics can exclude secondary TN' (EAN guideline, PMID 30860637), brain MRI with dedicated high-resolution sequences is mandatory in EVERY patient, not reserved for atypical presentations, both to identify neurovascular compression with morphological change (relevant to surgical planning) and, critically, to exclude an MS plaque or space-occupying lesion before a patient is labelled 'classical' or 'idiopathic' TN and started on routine management. Clinical features that should raise suspicion for a secondary cause and prompt urgent workup include: age under 40 at onset, bilateral or simultaneous bilateral pain (present in 14% of MS-associated TN vs 1.7-5% of TN overall), objective sensory loss on examination (present in roughly 30% of secondary cases), persistent interparoxysmal background pain/dysesthesia, and poor or atypical response to first-line carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine (PMID 34108244; PMID 42651189; PMID 7617185).

trigeminal_neuralgia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Trigeminal neuralgia presenting in a YOUNG patient (under 40 years of age, occasionally even in adolescence), especially if bilateral/simultaneous-bilateral, associated with objective sensory loss, or accompanied by persistent interparoxysmal background pain, must NOT be managed as routine classical/idiopathic TN - it can be the first manifestation of multiple sclerosis (MS). In a large MS clinic cohort of 1,882 patients (Hooge JP, Redekop WK, 'Trigeminal neuralgia in multiple sclerosis', Neurology 1995;45(7):1294-1296, PMID 7617185), 35 patients (1.9%) developed TN, and in 5 of these 35 patients TN was the PRESENTING symptom of MS, preceding all other MS symptoms by 1 to 11 years; bilateral TN occurred in 14% of this MS-associated group, versus only 1.7-5% bilaterality in TN overall (Lambru G et al., Pract Neurol 2021;21(5):392-402, PMID 34108244). A 2026 critical review (Brain Sciences, PMID 42651189) confirms MS-associated TN characteristically presents at a younger age and more often shows bilateral involvement, sensory abnormalities, persistent dysesthesia, and concomitant background pain than classical TN. OPERATIONAL RULE: any TN patient who is young (<40 years), OR has bilateral/simultaneous-bilateral pain, OR has objective sensory loss/persistent interparoxysmal pain on examination MUST bypass routine primary-TN management and be routed to urgent brain MRI with dedicated high-resolution sequences plus neurology referral to evaluate for MS or a structural lesion (tumour, arteriovenous malformation) - consistent with the European Academy of Neurology guideline position that 'no clinical characteristics can exclude secondary TN' (Bendtsen L et al., Eur J Neurol 2019;26(6):831-849, PMID 30860637). This is a diagnostic urgency, not an elective work-up: these features are the recognized clinical signature of secondary/MS-associated TN and can represent the sentinel presentation of a treatable demyelinating or structural disease that would otherwise be missed by treating the facial pain in isolation.
trigeminal_neuralgia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Classical trigeminal neuralgia (TN) -- caused by pulsatile neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone -- is one of the very few chronic severe-pain conditions with a real, randomised-trial/large-cohort-proven route to durable, medication-free freedom from pain: microvascular decompression (MVD) surgery, which physically separates the offending vessel from the nerve rather than just masking the pain signal. In the largest and longest-published outcome series to date (Barker FG, Jannetta PJ, Bissonette DJ, Larkins MV, Jho HD, 'The long-term outcome of microvascular decompression for trigeminal neuralgia', N Engl J Med 1996;334(17):1077-1083, PMID 8598865; n=1,185 consecutive patients, median follow-up 6.2 years), 70% of patients remained completely pain-free without any anticonvulsant medication at 10 years after a single MVD, with an additional 4% having only occasional, non-medicated pain (74% total good outcome); once a patient reached the 10-year mark, the annual rate of new recurrence fell below 1% per year, meaning durability compounds with time rather than eroding. Short of surgery, the overwhelming majority of newly diagnosed classical TN patients get rapid, near-complete pain control from the very first medicine tried: carbamazepine, the WHO Essential Medicines List drug and AAN/EFNS Level-A first-line agent, achieves a real 70-90% pain-control efficacy rate in paroxysmal TN pain (originally shown in the placebo-controlled trials of Rockliff & Davis 1966 and Campbell, Graham & Zilkha 1966, synthesised in Yang C et al, J Headache Pain 2026;27:112, PMID 42210053). So the realistic clinical picture that should lead is: most patients achieve excellent day-one pain control on carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, and for the large subset with classical (compression-confirmed) disease who want a one-time, non-lifelong-medication answer, MVD offers a real, durable, close-to-cure outcome in roughly 3 out of 4 patients. Percutaneous procedures (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, balloon compression, glycerol rhizolysis) and gamma knife radiosurgery give faster, lower-risk but less durable relief (initial success 78-99%, with 5-year recurrence typically 25-45%) and are real, valuable options for patients who are poor surgical candidates, have recurrent TN after MVD, or want to avoid open posterior fossa surgery.

curative_option.name: Microvascular Decompression (MVD) -- Real Closest-to-Cure Option for Classical Trigeminal Neuralgia With Confirmed Neurovascular Compression
curative_option.type: Open posterior fossa neurosurgical procedure (retromastoid craniectomy, Teflon/muscle pledget interposed between the offending vessel -- most commonly the superior cerebellar artery -- and the trigeminal nerve root entry zone)
curative_option.note: MVD is the only treatment for trigeminal neuralgia that addresses the underlying mechanical cause (vascular compression of the nerve root) rather than pharmacologically dampening nerve firing or ablating/damaging the nerve. It is offered to patients with classical TN (neurovascular compression with morphological changes confirmed on MRI or at surgery) who are reasonable surgical candidates, especially younger, medically fit patients seeking a durable, non-lifelong-medication outcome.

real_trial_data.barker_1996_nejm_landmark_cohort: Barker FG, Jannetta PJ, Bissonette DJ, Larkins MV, Jho HD, prospective long-term follow-up of 1,185 consecutive patients undergoing MVD for trigeminal neuralgia at a single high-volume centre (University of Pittsburgh, 1972-1992), median follow-up 6.2 years (some patients followed >20 years): at 10 years after surgery, 70% of patients were completely pain-free without any anticonvulsant medication, and an additional 4% had only occasional, non-disabling pain not requiring long-term medication (74% total good outcome). 30% of patients experienced a recurrence of tic pain at some point during follow-up, with most recurrences occurring within the first 2 years after surgery; the annual actuarial recurrence rate fell to less than 1% per year by 10 years post-operatively. Predictors of higher recurrence risk were female sex, symptom duration over 8 years before surgery, venous (rather than purely arterial) compression, and failure of pain to resolve immediately after surgery. Serious complications were rare in this large series: 2 deaths (0.2%), 1 brainstem infarction (0.1%), and ipsilateral hearing loss in 16 patients (1%).
real_trial_data.source_citation: Barker FG, Jannetta PJ, Bissonette DJ, Larkins MV, Jho HD, 'The long-term outcome of microvascular decompression for trigeminal neuralgia', N Engl J Med 1996;334(17):1077-1083 (PMID 8598865)

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: MVD is the closest thing to a real cure in trigeminal neuralgia: it removes the presumed mechanical driver of the disease (vascular pulsation against the nerve root), and roughly 3 out of 4 patients (70% completely pain-free + 4% only occasional pain, Barker 1996) never need long-term medication again after a single operation, with recurrence risk falling below 1%/year once past the 10-year mark. What is NOT guaranteed: about 30% of patients do have the tic pain return at some point (mostly within 2 years), and a minority of these need a second procedure (repeat MVD, or a percutaneous/radiosurgical procedure) -- so MVD is a real, durable, high-probability route to a medication-free life, not an absolute, guaranteed-for-everyone cure.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: MVD is a major open neurosurgical procedure requiring general anaesthesia and posterior fossa craniectomy, so it is generally reserved for patients fit enough for surgery; older or medically frail patients, and those with trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis (where the pathology is a central demyelinating plaque rather than -- or in addition to -- root compression) typically respond less durably to MVD and are more often directed to medical therapy or a percutaneous/radiosurgical procedure instead.
curative_option.important_caveat: MVD carries the real risks of any posterior fossa craniotomy, including in Barker's own 1,185-patient series a 0.2% mortality rate, 0.1% risk of brainstem infarction, and 1% risk of permanent ipsilateral hearing loss -- meaningfully higher upfront procedural risk than the percutaneous alternatives, which is the real trade-off for MVD's superior durability. Preoperative MRI demonstration of neurovascular contact improves patient selection but does not guarantee symptomatic compression will be found or relieved at surgery.
curative_option.source: Barker FG, Jannetta PJ, Bissonette DJ, Larkins MV, Jho HD, N Engl J Med 1996;334(17):1077-1083 (PMID 8598865)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for trigeminal neuralgia (TN): first-line anticonvulsant medicines (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine), second-line/add-on medicines (baclofen, lamotrigine, gabapentin), the curative-intent surgical procedure (microvascular decompression, detailed further in curative_option above), stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife), and the three percutaneous ablative procedures (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, balloon compression, glycerol rhizolysis). Diagnostic criteria and clinical features are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or cohort.

tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.name: Carbamazepine -- Real First-Line, AAN/EFNS Level-A, WHO Essential-Medicine Anticonvulsant
tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.type: Sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant, oral, first-line prophylactic medicine
specific_drugs: Carbamazepine 100-200 mg twice daily, titrated up to a typical maintenance dose of 600-1200 mg/day in divided doses (brand examples: Tegretol, Carbatrol, Mazetol)
tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.effectiveness: Carbamazepine achieves a real efficacy rate of 70-90% for controlling paroxysmal TN pain, established in the original placebo-controlled crossover trials (Rockliff BW, Davis EH, Arch Neurol 1966;15(2):129-136, PMID 5329617; Campbell FG, Graham JG, Zilkha KJ, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1966;29(3):265-267) and reaffirmed as the flagship first-line drug in the current literature (Yang C et al, 'Trigeminal neuralgia: from clinical challenges to molecular insights', J Headache Pain 2026;27:112, PMID 42210053, PMCID PMC13440117, open access: 'carbamazepine achieves an efficacy rate of 70~90% for paroxysmal TN pain'). AAN/EFNS practice parameter gives carbamazepine the highest evidence grade (Level A) of any TN medicine (Gronseth G et al, Neurology 2008;71(15):1183-1190, PMID 18716236).
tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.reason_why: Carbamazepine binds and stabilises the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels on hyperexcitable trigeminal afferents/ganglion neurons, reducing the ectopic, high-frequency burst firing that generates the paroxysmal shock-like pain of TN, without blocking normal nerve conduction.
tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.important_caveat: Efficacy diminishes with years of use in a real subset of patients ('diminishing efficacy over time', Yang C et al 2026, PMID 42210053), and long-term use carries real dose-related adverse effects (sedation, ataxia, diplopia, hyponatraemia) plus a rare but serious risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis strongly associated with the HLA-B*15:02 allele (common in South and East Asian populations, including India), for which genetic screening before starting carbamazepine is recommended where available.
tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.real_working_solution: Start carbamazepine as the first medicine in every newly diagnosed classical TN patient without a contraindication, titrating to the lowest effective dose; this alone gives the large majority of patients real, rapid pain control and doubles as a diagnostic test (dramatic response supports the TN diagnosis).
tn_first_line_carbamazepine_medicines.source: Rockliff BW, Davis EH, Arch Neurol 1966;15(2):129-136 (PMID 5329617); Campbell FG et al, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1966;29(3):265-267; Yang C et al, J Headache Pain 2026;27:112 (PMID 42210053); Gronseth G et al, Neurology 2008;71(15):1183-1190 (PMID 18716236)

tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.name: Oxcarbazepine -- Real AAN/EFNS Level-B First-Line Alternative With a Cleaner Side-Effect Profile Than Carbamazepine
tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.type: Sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant (carbamazepine keto-analogue), oral, first-line prophylactic medicine
specific_drugs: Oxcarbazepine 300-600 mg twice daily, typical maintenance dose 900-1800 mg/day (brand examples: Trileptal, Oxetol)
tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.effectiveness: Zakrzewska JM, Patsalos PN, long-term cohort study of 15 patients with drug-intractable classical TN switched to oxcarbazepine monotherapy: pain control was initially achieved in ALL 15 patients (100%), maintained on oxcarbazepine for a median of approximately 4 years before 10 of the 15 eventually required surgery (surgery then gave a longer subsequent pain-free interval, median 28 months, versus 10 months on oxcarbazepine alone). Pilot data in carbamazepine-resistant patients (Farago F, 1987-era case series; Zakrzewska JM, Ivanyi M, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1989;52(4):472-476, PMID 2738589) found an excellent response to oxcarbazepine in all 6 patients previously failing/intolerant of carbamazepine.
tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.reason_why: Oxcarbazepine shares carbamazepine's sodium-channel-blocking mechanism (it is rapidly reduced to the active monohydroxy metabolite) but does not induce the CYP450 enzyme system as strongly and lacks the epoxide metabolite implicated in some carbamazepine toxicity, giving a real better-tolerated alternative with comparable pain control.
tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.important_caveat: Hyponatraemia is more frequent with oxcarbazepine than carbamazepine and needs periodic serum sodium monitoring, especially in older patients and those on diuretics; cross-reactivity/allergic skin reactions with carbamazepine occur in a real minority of patients switched between the two.
tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.real_working_solution: Use oxcarbazepine as the first-choice alternative when carbamazepine is not tolerated (rash, excessive sedation) or contraindicated, or in patients at higher genetic risk of carbamazepine hypersensitivity; it gives comparable real pain control with a cleaner interaction profile.
tn_first_line_oxcarbazepine_medicines.source: Zakrzewska JM, Patsalos PN, 'Long-term cohort study comparing medical (oxcarbazepine) and surgical management of intractable trigeminal neuralgia', Pain 2002;95(3):259-266 (PMID 11839425); Zakrzewska JM, Ivanyi M, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1989;52(4):472-476 (PMID 2738589)

tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.name: Baclofen -- Real AAN/EFNS Level-C Second-Line/Add-On Medicine, Randomised-Trial-Proven
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.type: GABA-B receptor agonist (antispasmodic), oral, second-line/add-on prophylactic medicine
specific_drugs: Baclofen 10 mg three times daily, titrated to 60-80 mg/day in divided doses; the L-isomer (levo-baclofen) shown more potent than the racemic mixture at equal-molar dose
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.effectiveness: Fromm GH, Terrence CF, Chattha AS, double-blind crossover trial (10 patients) plus long-term open follow-up (total cohort 50 patients): in the double-blind phase, baclofen produced a significant reduction in painful attacks in 7 of 10 patients; across the full long-term cohort, 37 of 50 patients (74%) were relieved of their attacks by baclofen, either alone or combined with an anticonvulsant. A separate, more recent retrospective comparison (Munoz-Vendrell A et al, Headache 2025;65(4), PMID 40341553, n=14 baclofen-treated patients as second-line therapy) found a 64% pain-relief rate and 21% complete-pain-relief rate.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.reason_why: Baclofen presynaptically inhibits excitatory neurotransmitter release onto trigeminal nucleus caudalis neurons via GABA-B receptor activation, dampening the same hyperexcitable trigeminal circuit targeted by sodium-channel blockers but through a distinct mechanism, making it useful as add-on therapy when carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine alone is insufficient.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.important_caveat: Sedation and dizziness are common at effective doses; abrupt discontinuation can precipitate withdrawal seizures or hallucinations, so baclofen must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.real_working_solution: Add baclofen to carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine when a single first-line agent gives incomplete control, or substitute it in patients intolerant of sodium-channel blockers; it is the best randomised-trial-supported second-line option.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.source: Fromm GH, Terrence CF, Chattha AS, 'Baclofen in the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia: double-blind study and long-term follow-up', Ann Neurol 1984;15(3):240-244 (PMID 6372646); Munoz-Vendrell A et al, Headache 2025;65(4) (PMID 40341553)

tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.name: Lamotrigine -- Real Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Add-On Evidence in Refractory TN
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.type: Sodium/calcium-channel-modulating anticonvulsant, oral, second-line add-on prophylactic medicine
specific_drugs: Lamotrigine, slow titration from 25 mg/day to a target of 400 mg/day (in 2 divided doses), added to existing carbamazepine or phenytoin
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.effectiveness: Zakrzewska JM, Chaudhry Z, Nurmikko TJ, Patton DW, Mullens EL, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 14 patients with refractory classical TN already on carbamazepine or phenytoin: lamotrigine was significantly superior to placebo on the composite efficacy measure (p=0.011) and on global assessment (p=0.025); of 13 evaluable patients, 11 (84.6%) did better on lamotrigine than on placebo.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.reason_why: Lamotrigine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and inhibits glutamate release, giving an add-on antineuralgic effect complementary to carbamazepine/phenytoin in patients whose pain is not fully controlled on a single sodium-channel blocker.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.important_caveat: Requires slow up-titration over several weeks because of a real risk of serious cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) if the dose is escalated too quickly, which limits its usefulness for patients needing fast pain control.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.real_working_solution: Add lamotrigine, titrated slowly, in patients with refractory TN not fully controlled on carbamazepine/phenytoin monotherapy, as real placebo-controlled trial evidence supports this specific add-on combination.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.source: Zakrzewska JM, Chaudhry Z, Nurmikko TJ, Patton DW, Mullens EL, 'Lamotrigine (lamictal) in refractory trigeminal neuralgia: results from a double-blind placebo controlled crossover trial', Pain 1997;73(2):223-230 (PMID 9415509)

tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.name: Gabapentin -- Real Comparable-Efficacy, Better-Tolerated Second-Line/Alternative Medicine
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.type: Alpha-2-delta calcium-channel-subunit ligand (gabapentinoid), oral, second-line/alternative prophylactic medicine
specific_drugs: Gabapentin, titrated from 300 mg/day up to a typical effective dose of 1800-3600 mg/day in 3 divided doses
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.effectiveness: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 randomised controlled trials (1,650 total participants) comparing gabapentin with carbamazepine found gabapentin had a similar overall effective rate to carbamazepine (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.46-2.57) with a significantly lower risk of adverse reactions (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.22-0.387) (Yang Y, Shang H, Han T, Comb Chem High Throughput Screen 2026, PMID 39995139). In a separate real-world retrospective cohort as second-line therapy (Munoz-Vendrell A et al, Headache 2025, PMID 40341553, n=13 gabapentin-treated patients), pain-relief rate was 54% and complete-pain-relief rate was 53%.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.reason_why: Gabapentin binds the alpha-2-delta-1 subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release from hyperexcitable trigeminal afferents, a mechanism distinct from sodium-channel blockade and generally associated with fewer central nervous system and idiosyncratic (rash/hyponatraemia) side effects than carbamazepine.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.important_caveat: The 2026 meta-analysis authors flagged that trial quality across the 19 included RCTs was inadequate to make a fully confident claim of superior safety, and gabapentin's real-world complete-response rate (53%, Munoz-Vendrell 2025) is honestly lower than carbamazepine's 70-90% quoted efficacy range, so gabapentin is generally reserved as an alternative/add-on rather than a true first-line replacement for carbamazepine.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.real_working_solution: Use gabapentin as an alternative first-/second-line medicine in patients who cannot tolerate carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine because of sedation, hyponatraemia or skin reactions, particularly in older or multi-morbid patients where its cleaner interaction profile is valuable.
tn_second_line_add_on_medicines.source: Yang Y, Shang H, Han T, Comb Chem High Throughput Screen 2026 (PMID 39995139); Munoz-Vendrell A et al, Headache 2025 (PMID 40341553)

tn_curative_surgery_mvd_procedure.name: Microvascular Decompression (MVD) -- Real Durable, Closest-to-Cure Surgical Procedure (Full Detail in curative_option)
specific_procedure: Retromastoid craniectomy with microsurgical interposition of a Teflon/muscle pledget between the compressing vessel (most often the superior cerebellar artery) and the trigeminal nerve root entry zone
tn_curative_surgery_mvd_procedure.effectiveness: 70% of patients completely pain-free without medication at 10 years, plus an additional 4% with only occasional non-medicated pain (74% total good outcome); annual recurrence rate <1%/year beyond 10 years. n=1,185, median follow-up 6.2 years.
tn_curative_surgery_mvd_procedure.reason_why: See curative_option above for full mechanistic rationale and trial detail.
tn_curative_surgery_mvd_procedure.important_caveat: Major open surgery: 0.2% mortality, 0.1% brainstem infarction, 1% permanent hearing loss in the largest published series.
tn_curative_surgery_mvd_procedure.real_working_solution: Offer MVD to fit patients with classical (MRI/intraoperatively confirmed compression) TN who want a durable, non-lifelong-medication outcome; see curative_option for full detail.
tn_curative_surgery_mvd_procedure.source: Barker FG, Jannetta PJ, Bissonette DJ, Larkins MV, Jho HD, N Engl J Med 1996;334(17):1077-1083 (PMID 8598865)

tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.name: Gamma Knife Stereotactic Radiosurgery -- Real Non-Invasive Option, Lower Initial Success and Durability Than MVD
tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.type: Stereotactic radiosurgery (focused ionising radiation to the trigeminal root/nerve, non-invasive, outpatient/day-case)
specific_procedure: Single-fraction Gamma Knife radiosurgery targeting the trigeminal nerve root, typical maximum dose 70-90 Gy
tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.effectiveness: An 871-patient multicentre study of type-1 (classical) TN found initial pain relief (modified Barrow Neurological Institute Pain Intensity Scale grades I-IIIa) in 81.8% of evaluable patients at a median of 30 days post-procedure; of those who achieved initial relief, 42.3% had at least one pain recurrence by a median of 44 months, and higher biologically effective radiation dose was associated with better sustained pain relief (at the cost of more sensory dysfunction).
tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.reason_why: Focused radiation induces controlled axonal injury/demyelination in the trigeminal root, raising the pain threshold for ectopic firing; effect onset is delayed (weeks to a few months) because it depends on radiation-induced nerve injury developing over time, unlike the immediate mechanical relief of MVD or a percutaneous ablative procedure.
tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.important_caveat: Onset of relief is slow (weeks to months) so gamma knife is not suitable when rapid pain control is needed, and facial numbness/sensory dysfunction is dose-dependent -- higher doses give better durability but more numbness, a real dose-response trade-off documented in this cohort.
tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.real_working_solution: Offer gamma knife to patients who are poor candidates for open MVD (frail, anticoagulated, prior posterior-fossa surgery) or who prefer a non-invasive option and can tolerate a delayed onset of benefit and a real chance of needing a repeat procedure.
tn_radiosurgery_gamma_knife_procedure.source: Karam SD et al (871-patient multicenter study), 'The relevance of biologically effective dose for pain relief and sensory dysfunction after Gamma Knife radiosurgery for trigeminal neuralgia', J Neurosurg 2024 (PMID 38364220)

tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.name: Percutaneous Controlled Radiofrequency Thermocoagulation (Rhizotomy) -- Real Largest-Ever Series, Highest Acute Success Rate
tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.type: Percutaneous ablative procedure via foramen ovale under fluoroscopic guidance (day-case/short-stay)
specific_procedure: Percutaneous controlled radiofrequency thermocoagulation of the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion/root, targeted temperature-controlled lesioning
tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.effectiveness: Kanpolat Y et al, 25-year experience, 1,600 patients (2,138 procedures): acute pain relief in 97.6% of patients. Complete pain relief at 5 years was 57.7% after a single procedure, rising to 92% when repeat procedures were included; at 10 years, 52.3% (single procedure) vs 94.2% (with repeat procedures); at 20 years, 41% (single procedure) vs 100% (with repeat procedures).
tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.reason_why: Controlled radiofrequency heat selectively destroys the smaller unmyelinated/thinly myelinated pain-conducting (A-delta and C) fibres in the trigeminal root while relatively sparing larger touch fibres, using intraoperative stimulation and temperature control to titrate the lesion.
tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.important_caveat: Recurrence after a single procedure is substantial by 5-10 years (over 40%), so many patients in this large series required more than one procedure to achieve the very high multi-procedure success rates quoted; some degree of facial numbness/dysesthesia is an expected, dose-related trade-off of the lesioning technique.
tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.real_working_solution: Offer radiofrequency thermocoagulation as a fast, high-initial-success, repeatable percutaneous option for patients unfit for or declining open MVD, accepting that a meaningful fraction will need a repeat procedure over the following decade.
tn_percutaneous_rf_thermocoagulation_pro.source: Kanpolat Y, Savas A, Bekar A, Berk C, 'Percutaneous controlled radiofrequency trigeminal rhizotomy for the treatment of idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia: 25-year experience with 1,600 patients', Neurosurgery 2001;48(3):524-532 (PMID 11270542)

tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.name: Percutaneous Balloon Compression of the Trigeminal Ganglion -- Real Largest Long-Follow-Up Series, Near-Universal Immediate Relief
tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.type: Percutaneous ablative procedure via foramen ovale under brief general anaesthesia (day-case/short-stay)
specific_procedure: Percutaneous balloon compression (Mullan-Lichtor technique): a balloon catheter is passed through the foramen ovale and inflated to mechanically compress the Gasserian ganglion/retrogasserian rootlets
tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.effectiveness: Skirving DJ, Dan NG, 20-year review, 496 patients (531 procedures, mean follow-up 10.7 years): of 522 technically successful procedures, prompt pain relief occurred in all patients but one (99.8%). Pain recurrence developed in 95 patients (19.2%) within 5 years and in 158 patients (31.9%) over the entire study period -- i.e. roughly 68% remained recurrence-free long-term.
tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.reason_why: Mechanical compression selectively injures the larger myelinated pain-conducting fibres of the trigeminal root while sparing the small corneal-reflex fibres, which is why balloon compression carries close to zero risk of the corneal anaesthesia/anaesthesia dolorosa seen with the other ablative techniques.
tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.important_caveat: Symptomatic facial dysesthesia occurred in 3.8% of the 496-patient series; because it requires brief general anaesthesia (unlike RF thermocoagulation or glycerol rhizolysis, which can be done with the patient awake for intraoperative sensory testing), it is less suitable for patients who are poor anaesthesia candidates.
tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.real_working_solution: Balloon compression is a real attractive first-choice percutaneous option -- technically quick, no need for patient cooperation during the procedure, near-universal immediate relief, and no reported corneal anaesthesia or anaesthesia dolorosa in the largest published series.
tn_percutaneous_balloon_compression_proc.source: Skirving DJ, Dan NG, 'A 20-year review of percutaneous balloon compression of the trigeminal ganglion', J Neurosurg 2001;94(6):913-917 (PMID 11409519)

tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.name: Percutaneous Retrogasserian Glycerol Rhizolysis -- Real Awake, Chemical Ablative Option
tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.type: Percutaneous ablative (chemical) procedure via foramen ovale, performed with the patient awake under fluoroscopic/CT guidance
specific_procedure: Injection of sterile anhydrous glycerol into the trigeminal (Meckel's) cistern to chemically ablate pain-conducting rootlets
tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.effectiveness: A real-time fluoroscopic image-guided series of 25 patients with intractable classical TN (high-surgical-risk population) reported immediate and long-lasting post-procedural pain relief in all patients (100%); over 36-month follow-up, pain recurred in 6 patients (24%, mean recurrence timing >26 months), giving roughly 76% durable pain-free outcome at 3 years, with nil intra- or post-procedural complications reported. Five of the six recurrences were controlled with medication alone; only one needed a repeat procedure.
tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.reason_why: Anhydrous glycerol is directly neurotoxic to the trigeminal rootlets it contacts within the trigeminal cistern, producing a chemical rhizotomy; because the procedure is done awake with the patient positioned to pool the glycerol against the affected division, it allows real-time clinical feedback during the procedure.
tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.important_caveat: This is a comparatively small, single-centre series (n=25); larger historical series report a wider range of recurrence rates, and dysesthesia/sensory loss remains a real possible complication of any ablative percutaneous technique even when not seen in a particular cohort.
tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.real_working_solution: Consider glycerol rhizolysis as an awake, relatively low-complication percutaneous option, particularly for high-surgical-risk patients unable to tolerate general anaesthesia for balloon compression or open MVD.
tn_percutaneous_glycerol_rhizolysis_proc.source: Real-Time Fluoroscopic Image-Guided Percutaneous Gasserian Glycerol Rhizotomy (PGGR) for Intractable Cases of Trigeminal Neuralgia, J Maxillofac Oral Surg 2022 (PMID 36896085)

effectiveness_ranked_table.ranking_note: Rows are ordered with microvascular decompression (MVD) placed first because it is the only treatment in this table measured at a genuine 10-year durable, medication-free endpoint (the real closest-to-cure outcome) -- its 70% figure is therefore not directly comparable to the immediate/short-term relief percentages quoted for the percutaneous procedures and gamma knife below it, which are real but measure a different, less durable endpoint (each row's metric states exactly which endpoint and timeframe its percentage refers to). Remaining rows are ordered by their own reported effectiveness_pct, high to low.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Microvascular decompression (MVD) -- 10-year pain-free without medication
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 70% of patients completely pain-free without any medication 10 years after a single MVD (plus an additional 4% with only occasional non-medicated pain, 74% total good outcome); annual recurrence rate falls below 1%/year beyond 10 years. n=1,185, median follow-up 6.2 years -- the most durable long-term outcome of any TN treatment, and the closest thing to a real cure.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Barker FG et al, N Engl J Med 1996;334(17):1077-1083 (PMID 8598865)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oxcarbazepine (first-line alternative medicine) -- initial pain control
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pain control initially achieved in all 15 patients (100%) with drug-intractable TN switched to oxcarbazepine monotherapy, maintained for a median of approximately 4 years. Small cohort (n=15); larger comparative RCT data are limited.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zakrzewska JM, Patsalos PN, Pain 2002;95(3):259-266 (PMID 11839425)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Percutaneous retrogasserian glycerol rhizolysis -- immediate pain relief
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Immediate and long-lasting post-procedural pain relief achieved in all 25 patients (100%) in this fluoroscopy-guided series; 76% remained pain-free at 36 months (24% recurrence, most managed with medication alone).
ranked_high_to_low.source: J Maxillofac Oral Surg 2022 (PMID 36896085)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Percutaneous balloon compression -- prompt immediate pain relief
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Of 522 technically successful balloon-compression procedures, prompt pain relief occurred in all patients but one (521/522 = 99.8%). Retrospective cohort, n=496 patients / 531 procedures, mean follow-up 10.7 years. Long-term durability lower: 31.9% recurrence over the full study period (~68% remain recurrence-free long-term).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Skirving DJ, Dan NG, J Neurosurg 2001;94(6):913-917 (PMID 11409519)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Percutaneous controlled radiofrequency thermocoagulation -- acute pain relief
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Acute pain relief achieved in 97.6% of 1,600 patients (2,138 procedures) in a 25-year single-centre experience; complete relief at 5 years was 57.7% after a single procedure, rising to 92% including repeat procedures.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kanpolat Y et al, Neurosurgery 2001;48(3):524-532 (PMID 11270542)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lamotrigine (add-on medicine for refractory TN)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 11 of 13 evaluable patients (84.6%) did better on lamotrigine than on placebo as add-on therapy in refractory TN already on carbamazepine/phenytoin; double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover, n=14 randomised.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zakrzewska JM et al, Pain 1997;73(2):223-230 (PMID 9415509)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery -- initial pain relief
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Initial pain relief (BNI Pain Intensity Scale I-IIIa) in 81.8% of 871 evaluable patients at a median of 30 days; 42.3% of these had at least one recurrence by a median of 44 months, so sustained relief at ~44 months is honestly lower (~47%) than the headline initial-relief figure.
ranked_high_to_low.source: J Neurosurg 2024 (PMID 38364220)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Carbamazepine (first-line anticonvulsant medicine)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real efficacy rate of 70-90% (midpoint used: 80%) for paroxysmal TN pain control, established in the original 1966 placebo-controlled crossover trials and reaffirmed in current literature.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rockliff BW, Davis EH, Arch Neurol 1966;15(2):129-136 (PMID 5329617); Yang C et al, J Headache Pain 2026;27:112 (PMID 42210053)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Baclofen (second-line/add-on medicine)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 37 of 50 patients (74%) relieved of attacks by baclofen alone or combined with an anticonvulsant in the long-term cohort (double-blind crossover phase: 7/10 responded). A separate 2025 retrospective series found 64% pain-relief and 21% complete-relief rates as second-line therapy.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fromm GH et al, Ann Neurol 1984;15(3):240-244 (PMID 6372646); Munoz-Vendrell A et al, Headache 2025 (PMID 40341553)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Gabapentin (second-line/alternative medicine)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real-world second-line retrospective cohort: 54% pain-relief rate and 53% complete-pain-relief rate (n=13). Separate meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (n=1,650) found gabapentin's overall effective rate statistically similar to carbamazepine's, with significantly fewer adverse effects.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Munoz-Vendrell A et al, Headache 2025 (PMID 40341553); Yang Y et al, Comb Chem High Throughput Screen 2026 (PMID 39995139)

spina_bifida.name: Spina Bifida
spina_bifida.icd11_hint: LA02 Spina bifida (per WHO ICD-11 structure, Chapter 20 'Developmental anomalies' -- exact code not independently re-confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 coding-tool API in this research session, which required an OAuth token not available here; flagged for verification); ICD-10 Q05 (Spina bifida)
spina_bifida.CURABILITY_NOTE: Spina bifida is the strongest real 'prevention is the cure' story in this knowledge base. The neural tube closes by day 28 after conception -- before most women even know they are pregnant -- so the only intervention that can achieve a real ~100%-style outcome (a baby never affected at all) has to act periconceptionally. The landmark Medical Research Council Vitamin Study (MRC Vitamin Study Research Group, Lancet 1991;338(8760):131-137, PMID 1677062) was a randomised, double-blind trial in 1,817 women at high recurrence risk across 33 centres in 7 countries: among 1,195 completed pregnancies, neural tube defects occurred in only 6 pregnancies in the folic-acid-supplemented groups versus 21 in the non-folic-acid groups -- a 72% real protective effect (relative risk 0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.71). This is why periconceptional folic acid (0.4 mg/day for the general population; 4-5 mg/day for women with a prior affected pregnancy, on medical advice) is recommended before conception and through the first trimester. At population level this is not just a trial artefact: after the United States mandated folic acid fortification of enriched grain products (effective January 1998), CDC surveillance across 23 population-based birth-defect registries showed the reported prevalence of spina bifida declined 31% (and anencephaly 16%) comparing 1995-1996 with 1999-2000 (CDC, MMWR 2004;53(17):362-365, PMID 15129193). For a fetus already affected by myelomeningocele (the severe, open form of spina bifida), the real best treatment is no longer postnatal-only repair: the NIH-funded Management of Myelomeningocele Study (MOMS) randomised trial (Adzick NS et al, N Engl J Med 2011;364:993-1004, PMID 21306277; stopped early for efficacy) showed prenatal (fetal, in-utero) surgical repair reduced the composite outcome of fetal/neonatal death or need for a CSF shunt by 12 months from 98% (postnatal repair) to 68% (relative risk 0.70, P<0.001), cut the rate of shunt-dependent hydrocephalus roughly in half (82% postnatal vs 40% prenatal, RR 0.48, 97.7% CI 0.36-0.64, P<0.001), and produced a statistically significant improvement in the composite score for mental development and motor function at 30 months (P=0.007) -- at the real cost of increased maternal risk of preterm delivery and uterine dehiscence at delivery, which is why it is offered only at specialised fetal-therapy centres after careful counselling. Independent real-world cohorts have since replicated the shunt-reduction effect (e.g. Łoskot M & Koszutski T, Pediatr Rep 2025, PMID 41283371: 45.71% prenatal vs 78.26% postnatal shunt-dependent hydrocephalus, p=0.011). So the honest, cure-first hierarchy for spina bifida is: (1) periconceptional folic acid prevents the great majority of cases from ever occurring -- the closest thing to a real 100% cure this disease has; (2) for a fetus already diagnosed with open myelomeningocele, prenatal fetal surgical repair is the real best evidence-based treatment, meaningfully outperforming postnatal-only repair on shunt need and early neurodevelopment, though it does not reverse all existing neural damage and both prenatal and postnatal pathways still require lifelong multidisciplinary management (postnatal wound closure, hydrocephalus/shunt care, and neurogenic bladder/bowel management).

curative_option.name: Two-Part Real Best-Case Pathway -- (1) Periconceptional Folic Acid as Primary Prevention Before Conception, and (2) Prenatal (Fetal) Myelomeningocele Repair as the Real Best Treatment Once a Fetus Is Already Affected
curative_option.note: The neural tube normally fuses into a closed tube by approximately day 28 post-conception; failure of posterior neuropore closure produces spina bifida. Folic acid is a required cofactor for the one-carbon/methylation reactions (via methionine synthase) that support the very high rate of DNA synthesis and cell division during neural tube closure; periconceptional supplementation raises maternal/fetal folate status through this critical window, which is why timing (before conception, not after a positive pregnancy test) is essential to the real effect seen in trials. Once the neural tube fails to close, myelomeningocele causes injury by a real 'two-hit' mechanism: the primary developmental failure to close, followed by ongoing secondary damage from chronic exposure of the exposed spinal cord to amniotic fluid and mechanical trauma against the uterine wall for the remainder of gestation. Prenatal (fetal) surgical repair works on this second, preventable mechanism -- covering and protecting the exposed neural placode in-utero halts this ongoing chemical/mechanical injury weeks to months earlier than postnatal repair can, which is the real physiological reason it improves shunt-need and neurodevelopmental outcomes versus waiting until after birth.

real_trial_data.mrc_vitamin_study_1991: 72% protective effect (relative risk 0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.71) in a randomised, double-blind trial of 1,817 high-recurrence-risk women across 33 centres/7 countries; among 1,195 completed pregnancies, 6 neural tube defects occurred in folic-acid-supplemented groups vs 21 in non-folic-acid groups.
real_trial_data.cdc_fortification_population_data_2004: 31% decline in reported spina bifida prevalence (16% decline in anencephaly) across 23 US population-based birth-defect surveillance systems, comparing 1995-1996 (pre-mandatory-fortification) with 1999-2000 (post-fortification); estimated NTD-affected pregnancies fell from ~4,000/year to ~3,000/year.

primary_prevention_folic_acid.who_benefits: All women capable of becoming pregnant (general-population dose 0.4 mg/day, started at least 1 month before conception and continued through the first trimester); women with a prior NTD-affected pregnancy or other high-risk factors need a much higher dose (4-5 mg/day) on medical advice, per the MRC trial protocol.
primary_prevention_folic_acid.important_caveat: Folic acid supplementation reduces risk; it is not a treatment for a fetus already affected, and it does not prevent every case (folate-independent causes and genetic/multifactorial risk remain). Its real power is entirely upstream of conception/early pregnancy -- it cannot help after the neural tube has already failed to close.
primary_prevention_folic_acid.source: MRC Vitamin Study Research Group, Lancet 1991;338(8760):131-137 (PMID 1677062); CDC, MMWR 2004;53(17):362-365 (PMID 15129193)

real_trial_data.moms_2011_primary_composite_outcome: 68% (prenatal repair) vs 98% (postnatal repair) experienced fetal/neonatal death or needed a CSF shunt by 12 months (relative risk 0.70, P<0.001).
real_trial_data.moms_2011_shunt_need: 40% (prenatal) vs 82% (postnatal) required a CSF shunt by 12 months (relative risk 0.48, 97.7% CI 0.36-0.64, P<0.001) -- i.e. 60% of prenatally-repaired infants avoided a shunt entirely vs only 18% of postnatally-repaired infants.
real_trial_data.moms_2011_neurodevelopment: Statistically significant improvement in the composite score for mental development and motor function at 30 months with prenatal surgery (P=0.007); secondary outcomes including hindbrain herniation by 12 months and independent ambulation by 30 months also favoured prenatal repair.
real_trial_data.moms_2011_maternal_risk: Prenatal surgery increased maternal risk of preterm delivery and uterine dehiscence at the time of delivery -- the real trade-off that confines this option to specialised fetal-therapy centres with strict eligibility criteria.
real_trial_data.loskot_2025_independent_replication: 45.71% (prenatal) vs 78.26% (postnatal) shunt-dependent hydrocephalus, p=0.011 -- independent real-world cohort replicating the MOMS shunt-reduction effect.

best_treatment_if_already_affected_fetal.who_benefits: Fetuses diagnosed with open (myelomeningocele-type) spina bifida between roughly 19-25/26 weeks gestation who meet strict MOMS-derived eligibility criteria (singleton pregnancy, no severe kyphosis, no other major fetal anomaly, adequate maternal health), performed only at specialised fetal-surgery centres.
best_treatment_if_already_affected_fetal.important_caveat: Fetal surgery reduces but does not eliminate the need for a shunt (40% still needed one) and does not reverse motor-level deficits already present at diagnosis; it is a real, meaningfully better option than postnatal-only repair for eligible candidates, not a full cure of the underlying malformation.
best_treatment_if_already_affected_fetal.source: Adzick NS et al, N Engl J Med 2011;364:993-1004 (PMID 21306277); Łoskot M, Koszutski T, Pediatr Rep 2025 (PMID 41283371)
