curative_option.source: MRC Vitamin Study Research Group, Lancet 1991 (PMID 1677062); CDC MMWR 2004 (PMID 15129193); Adzick NS et al, N Engl J Med 2011 (PMID 21306277); Łoskot M, Koszutski T, Pediatr Rep 2025 (PMID 41283371)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Per this project's priority rule (medicine > injection/procedure > everything else), periconceptional folic acid -- a cheap, safe oral vitamin -- is listed first because it is the real closest-to-100% intervention this disease has (primary prevention). For a fetus already affected, prenatal fetal surgery is listed next as the real best procedural option, followed by standard postnatal surgical closure, then the two lifelong-management pillars (VP shunt for hydrocephalus and clean intermittent catheterization for neurogenic bladder), each reported with real, honestly-caveated evidence.

sb_prevention_folic_acid_medicines.name: Periconceptional Folic Acid Supplementation
sb_prevention_folic_acid_medicines.type: Oral vitamin (B9), real primary-prevention medicine -- not a treatment for existing disease
specific_drugs: Folic acid 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily for all women capable of becoming pregnant, started at least 1 month before conception and continued through the first trimester
Folic acid 4-5 mg daily for women with a prior NTD-affected pregnancy or other high-risk factors, on medical advice, per the MRC Vitamin Study protocol
sb_prevention_folic_acid_medicines.effectiveness: 72% relative risk reduction in neural tube defect recurrence (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.71) -- MRC Vitamin Study Research Group, Lancet 1991 (PMID 1677062). Population-level: 31% decline in US spina bifida prevalence after mandatory grain fortification -- CDC, MMWR 2004 (PMID 15129193).
reason_why: The posterior neuropore of the neural tube normally closes by ~day 28 post-conception, a window that has usually passed before a pregnancy is even confirmed.
Folate is an essential cofactor for one-carbon metabolism and DNA synthesis/methylation needed to support the very high cell-division rate during neural tube closure.
Because the critical window is periconceptional, the real protective effect requires supplementation to start before conception, not after a positive pregnancy test.
sb_prevention_folic_acid_medicines.important_caveat: Prevents most, not all, cases; does not treat a fetus already affected; very high-dose folic acid (4-5 mg/day) should only be used under medical supervision for genuinely high-risk women, not the general population.
sb_prevention_folic_acid_medicines.source: MRC Vitamin Study Research Group, Lancet 1991;338(8760):131-137 (PMID 1677062); CDC, MMWR 2004;53(17):362-365 (PMID 15129193)

sb_fetal_surgery_procedure.name: Prenatal (Fetal, In-Utero) Myelomeningocele Repair
sb_fetal_surgery_procedure.type: Open fetal surgical procedure, real best evidence-based treatment for an already-affected fetus
sb_fetal_surgery_procedure.specific_procedure: Maternal-fetal open hysterotomy and multi-layer closure of the exposed neural placode/myelomeningocele defect, performed at 19-25/26 weeks gestation at a specialised fetal-therapy centre, per MOMS trial protocol.
sb_fetal_surgery_procedure.effectiveness: Reduced composite death-or-shunt outcome from 98% (postnatal) to 68% (prenatal), RR 0.70, P<0.001; reduced shunt need from 82% to 40%, RR 0.48, P<0.001; improved 30-month composite mental-development/motor-function score, P=0.007 -- Adzick NS et al, N Engl J Med 2011 (PMID 21306277). Independently replicated: 78.26% vs 45.71% shunt-dependent hydrocephalus, p=0.011 -- Łoskot M, Koszutski T, Pediatr Rep 2025 (PMID 41283371).
reason_why: Myelomeningocele causes a real 'two-hit' injury: the initial failure of neural tube closure, followed by ongoing chemical and mechanical damage to the exposed spinal cord from amniotic fluid exposure and uterine trauma for the rest of gestation.

Covering the defect in-utero halts this second, preventable phase of injury weeks to months earlier than postnatal repair, which is the real physiological basis for its better hydrocephalus and early neurodevelopmental outcomes.
sb_fetal_surgery_procedure.important_caveat: Increases maternal risk of preterm delivery and uterine dehiscence; requires strict eligibility (singleton pregnancy, no severe kyphosis, no other major fetal anomaly); does not eliminate shunt need (40% still required one) and does not reverse motor-level deficits already present at diagnosis.
sb_fetal_surgery_procedure.source: Adzick NS et al, N Engl J Med 2011;364:993-1004 (PMID 21306277); Łoskot M, Koszutski T, Pediatr Rep 2025 (PMID 41283371)

sb_postnatal_surgical_closure_procedure.name: Postnatal Surgical Closure of Myelomeningocele
sb_postnatal_surgical_closure_procedure.type: Standard-of-care neurosurgical procedure, real universal treatment when prenatal repair was not done or not eligible
sb_postnatal_surgical_closure_procedure.specific_procedure: Multi-layer surgical closure of the open neural tube defect, performed in the newborn period at a specialised centre; timing (commonly within 24-72 hours of birth) is intended to limit ongoing CNS/wound infection risk and further mechanical injury.
sb_postnatal_surgical_closure_procedure.effectiveness: The 2019 Congress of Neurological Surgeons (CNS)/AANS guideline found insufficient high-quality evidence that closure specifically within 48 hours reduces wound infection or ventriculitis risk versus slightly later closure (only 4 of 31 reviewed studies met inclusion criteria) -- Beier AD et al, Neurosurgery 2019;85(3):E412-E413 (PMID 31418041). Real-world infection data: at major US pediatric neurosurgery centres, surgical-site infection after myelomeningocele closure occurs in 4.3-6.3% of cases (i.e. 93.7-95.7% free of SSI) -- Sherrod BA et al, J Neurosurg Pediatr 2017 (PMID 28186476); in a South African cohort of 309 children, wound sepsis occurred in 21% (58/309), and meningitis developed in 22% (13/58) of those with wound sepsis, with meningitis significantly associated with mortality (p<0.0001) -- Mnguni MN et al, Childs Nerv Syst 2020 (PMID 31974664), illustrating real, resource-setting-dependent variation in outcome.
reason_why: Leaving the neural placode open and exposed after birth risks progressive desiccation/injury of exposed neural tissue and ascending CNS infection (meningitis/ventriculitis); surgical closure removes this open portal and covers the neural tissue with vascularised tissue.
sb_postnatal_surgical_closure_procedure.important_caveat: Postnatal closure prevents further injury/infection but does not reverse neurological deficits already present at birth; infection risk, while generally low at high-volume specialised centres, is real and setting-dependent, and closure alone does not address the hydrocephalus or neurogenic bladder/bowel that commonly accompany myelomeningocele.
sb_postnatal_surgical_closure_procedure.source: Beier AD et al, Neurosurgery 2019;85(3):E412-E413 (PMID 31418041); Sherrod BA et al, J Neurosurg Pediatr 2017 (PMID 28186476); Mnguni MN et al, Childs Nerv Syst 2020 (PMID 31974664)

sb_hydrocephalus_vp_shunt_procedure.name: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) Shunt for Hydrocephalus
sb_hydrocephalus_vp_shunt_procedure.type: Neurosurgical device/procedure, real standard management for shunt-dependent hydrocephalus complicating spina bifida
sb_hydrocephalus_vp_shunt_procedure.specific_procedure: Surgical placement of a ventriculoperitoneal (or ventriculo-atrial) shunt to divert excess cerebrospinal fluid, with lifelong monitoring for malfunction/infection and revision surgery as needed.
sb_hydrocephalus_vp_shunt_procedure.effectiveness: In a single-centre myelomeningocele cohort, hydrocephalus developed in 71.8% of patients, with 65.6% ultimately requiring VP shunting -- Spazzapan P, Velnar T, Diagnostics (Basel) 2026 (PMID 42449817; small cohort, flagged). Real honest caveat: shunts are effective at controlling hydrocephalus but are not a one-time cure -- 54.3% of all shunted paediatric patients underwent at least one revision surgery over follow-up, and congenital (e.g. myelomeningocele-related) shunts had a higher 70% revision rate versus 37% for tumour-related shunts -- Välimaa J et al, Childs Nerv Syst 2025 (PMID 41109914).
reason_why: Myelomeningocele is strongly associated with Chiari II malformation, which obstructs normal CSF flow/absorption pathways and produces hydrocephalus in the majority of affected infants; a shunt bypasses this obstruction to control intracranial pressure and prevent progressive brain injury.
sb_hydrocephalus_vp_shunt_procedure.important_caveat: Shunt placement controls hydrocephalus but carries a real, substantial lifelong revision burden (malfunction, infection, over/under-drainage); prenatal fetal surgery (see above) is the only intervention shown to reduce the need for a shunt in the first place.
sb_hydrocephalus_vp_shunt_procedure.source: Spazzapan P, Velnar T, Diagnostics (Basel) 2026 (PMID 42449817); Välimaa J et al, Childs Nerv Syst 2025 (PMID 41109914)

sb_bladder_bowel_management_other.name: Clean Intermittent Catheterization (CIC) for Neurogenic Bladder
sb_bladder_bowel_management_other.type: Non-surgical bladder-management procedure, real cornerstone lifelong management to preserve renal function
sb_bladder_bowel_management_other.specific_procedure: Regular clean (non-sterile) intermittent urinary catheterization, typically several times daily, to ensure complete bladder emptying in patients with neurogenic bladder from spinal cord/nerve root involvement.
sb_bladder_bowel_management_other.effectiveness: CIC is presented as the cornerstone therapy for neurogenic bladder management in spina bifida in the updated EAU/ESPU pediatric urology guidelines, for preserving renal function -- Radmayr C et al, Eur Urol Open Sci 2026 (PMID 42088080). In a cohort of 236 spina bifida patients, regular CIC use was reported in 88.8% of patients who remained free of chronic kidney disease versus only 32.3% of those who developed CKD (13.1% of the cohort developed CKD; 34.7% had vesicoureteral reflux) -- Unal CB, Saraç F, Research Square preprint 2026 (PPR1145076; not yet peer-reviewed, flagged as moderate-confidence supporting evidence).
reason_why: Neurogenic bladder from spinal cord involvement causes incomplete emptying and high storage/voiding pressures that transmit back to the kidneys via vesicoureteral reflux, risking progressive chronic kidney disease.
Regular complete emptying via CIC lowers intravesical pressure and residual urine, directly interrupting this real mechanism of renal injury.
sb_bladder_bowel_management_other.important_caveat: Requires consistent lifelong adherence (by caregiver or patient) and carries a real risk of recurrent urinary tract infection, which needs monitoring; the CKD-prevention association above is observational, not a randomised trial, and the supporting cohort study is a preprint.
sb_bladder_bowel_management_other.source: Radmayr C et al, Eur Urol Open Sci 2026 (PMID 42088080); Unal CB, Saraç F, Research Square preprint 2026 (PPR1145076)

symptoms.definition_and_pathophysiology: Spina bifida is a neural tube defect (NTD) in which the vertebral column, and often the spinal cord and meninges, fail to form and close normally during primary neurulation in the first month of embryonic development, leaving the spine 'open' to varying degrees (Copp AJ, Adzick NS, Chitty LS, Fletcher JM, Holmbeck GN, Shaw GM, 'Spina bifida', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015, PMID 27189655). Three clinically distinct forms are recognised. Spina bifida occulta is the mildest: only the posterior vertebral arch fails to fuse, the skin over the defect is intact, and the spinal cord and meninges are not herniated, so it is usually asymptomatic and often an incidental imaging finding in childhood or adulthood (CDC, 'About Spina Bifida'). Meningocele is intermediate: the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid herniate through the vertebral defect to form a fluid-filled sac, but the spinal cord itself is not contained within the sac, so neurological damage is typically minimal (CDC). Myelomeningocele (open spina bifida) is the most severe and most clinically significant form: the spinal cord and nerve roots themselves herniate into the sac and are exposed, unprotected, to the amniotic cavity for the remainder of gestation (PMID 27189655). A narrative literature review of amniotic fluid toxicity in myelomeningocele (Prenatal Diagnosis 2024, PMID 39370541) describes progressive secondary neural degeneration at the exposed placode over gestation -- loss of neural cells, astrogliosis, inflammation, and loss of normal cord architecture -- supporting a 'two-hit' model in which the primary failure of neural tube closure is compounded by ongoing mechanical trauma and/or chemical neurotoxicity from amniotic fluid exposure, which is the physiological rationale for prenatal (in-utero) surgical closure. Genetic predisposition is estimated to account for 60-70% of spina bifida risk, but the disease is polygenic and multifactorial, with strong gene-environment interaction, most notably in folate-pathway metabolism genes (PMID 27189655).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Standard prenatal screening combines maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP), classically drawn at 15-20 weeks, with a detailed second-trimester anatomy ultrasound; this combined approach remains the recommended standard for detecting open spina bifida (Coleman BG et al, 'Diagnostic dilemmas in fetal neurological anomalies', reviewed in 'Role of Maternal Serum Alpha-Fetoprotein and Ultrasonography in Contemporary Detection of Spina Bifida', Am J Perinatol 2015, PMID 26332586). In a case series of 105 patients postnatally referred to a paediatric neurosurgical centre (2007-2013), 11.4% of spina bifida cases were NOT detected prenatally despite modern screening being available; ultrasound alone had an odds ratio of 4.9 for detecting spina bifida, but critically, 75% of the MISSED cases had never received MSAFP screening at all -- indicating that failure to order the test, not failure of the test itself, was the dominant driver of missed prenatal diagnoses (PMID 26332586). Earlier, first-trimester (11-13 week) combined screening using fetal biparietal diameter (BPD) plus MSAFP and free beta-hCG detects a real but lower proportion of open spina bifida cases: 58% at a 5% false-positive rate, or 70% at a 10% false-positive rate ('Combined screening for open spina bifida at 11-13 weeks using fetal biparietal diameter and maternal serum markers', Am J Obstet Gynecol 2013, PMID 23673229), reflecting that indirect first-trimester cranial markers (e.g. reduced BPD as a proxy for the Chiari II-related posterior fossa changes seen later as the 'lemon' and 'banana' signs) are less reliably visualised this early. A case-control study (n=97 cases, 274 controls) found maternal weight/obesity was independently increased in affected pregnancies, and modelled that adding maternal weight to BPD+AFP screening could raise detection by approximately 3-4% -- a real but modest incremental gain, not yet a standard-of-care addition ('Maternal weight as an additional first trimester spina bifida screening marker', J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med 2022, PMID 32928009). Postnatally, diagnosis of myelomeningocele is immediately apparent on physical examination of the open back lesion at birth; spinal and cranial MRI/ultrasound are then used to define the lesion level, and to actively screen for the near-universally associated hydrocephalus and Chiari II malformation before surgical planning.
symptoms.classic_symptoms: The neurological deficit in myelomeningocele is determined chiefly by the level of the spinal lesion: higher (thoracic/upper lumbar) lesions typically produce flaccid paraparesis/paraplegia with near-total sensory loss below the level, while lower (sacral) lesions preserve substantially more motor function and ambulatory potential (Sawin KJ, Liu T et al reviewed in 'Children with Spina Bifida: Key Clinical Issues', Pediatr Clin North Am 2010, PMID 20883878, which addresses the characteristic sensory and motor impairments, and the neurologic, orthopedic, cognitive and skin-related complications of the condition). Neurogenic bowel and bladder dysfunction is a hallmark feature reported in the large majority of myelomeningocele patients regardless of lesion level, reflecting sacral nerve root involvement, and drives the lifelong urological surveillance central to spina bifida care (PMID 20883878). Hydrocephalus requiring treatment is very common: reported in 65.7% of 134 consecutive neonates with myelomeningocele at one centre (Neurosurg Rev 2025, PMID 40258966) and in 78.3% of a 230-patient neural tube defect cohort in a lower-resource setting (Childs Nerv Syst 2026, PMID 42501095); in the randomized MOMS trial, 82% of infants undergoing standard postnatal myelomeningocele repair required a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt by 12 months of age, versus 40% after prenatal repair (relative risk 0.48) (Adzick NS et al, 'A randomized trial of prenatal versus postnatal repair of myelomeningocele', N Engl J Med 2011, PMID 21306277). Chiari II malformation (downward herniation of the cerebellar vermis, brainstem, and fourth ventricle through the foramen magnum) is likewise seen in the majority of myelomeningocele patients -- 62.7% in the same 134-patient cohort (PMID 40258966) -- and concomitant syringomyelia was found in 60% of a 100-patient cohort of children with Chiari II, hydrocephalus, and myelomeningocele together (Asian J Neurosurg 2023, PMID 37397054). Chiari II-related brainstem/lower cranial nerve dysfunction also manifests as sleep-related breathing disorders, reported in 40-80% of children with spina bifida and attributed to brainstem abnormalities and upper airway dysfunction, for which polysomnography is recommended (J Pediatr Rehabil Med 2024, PMID 40096506). Orthopedic sequelae (clubfoot, hip subluxation/dislocation, and scoliosis secondary to muscle imbalance below the lesion) are also well-recognised components of the clinical picture (PMID 20883878).
symptoms.differential_diagnosis: Spina bifida occulta must be distinguished from other forms of occult spinal dysraphism presenting with cutaneous stigmata over the lower spine (dermal sinus tract, lipomyelomeningocele, diastematomyelia/split cord malformation) -- these share an intact skin covering but differ in the underlying dysraphic anatomy and are differentiated by spinal MRI/ultrasound rather than external examination alone. A midline sacrococcygeal mass at birth also raises sacrococcygeal teratoma as a differential for myelomeningocele: teratoma is typically a solid or mixed cystic-solid mass that may extend off the midline and lacks a neural placode, and markedly elevated AFP in a teratoma reflects a yolk-sac tumour component rather than the modest AFP elevation characteristic of an open neural tube defect. Caudal regression syndrome, a malformation spectrum strongly associated with maternal pregestational diabetes, presents with sacral/lower-limb agenesis and must be distinguished from spina bifida on imaging, as management and prognosis differ substantially (case report literature on caudal regression syndrome in diabetic embryopathy, J Med Case Rep 2023). Anencephaly and encephalocele represent neural tube defects at other points along the neuraxis (cranial rather than spinal) and are readily distinguished by lesion location on prenatal ultrasound or postnatal examination (Copp AJ et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015, PMID 27189655, places spina bifida within this broader neural tube defect spectrum).
symptoms.risk_factors: Periconceptional folate/folic acid deficiency is THE major identified and preventable risk factor for spina bifida. The landmark Medical Research Council (MRC) Vitamin Study -- a randomized, double-blind trial across 33 centres in 7 countries in 1,817 women with a prior neural-tube-defect-affected pregnancy (1,195 completed pregnancies analysed) -- found periconceptional folic acid supplementation produced a 72% protective effect against recurrence (relative risk 0.28; 6 recurrences in the folic-acid group vs 21 in the non-folic-acid groups), with no demonstrable harm ('Prevention of neural tube defects: results of the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study', Lancet 1991, PMID 1677062). A 2026 JAMA review of prepregnancy care similarly reports folic acid use before pregnancy is associated with a real relative risk reduction in neural tube defects of 0.67 (95% CI 0.52-0.87) at the general-population level, not only in women with a prior affected pregnancy (Cooper KM et al, JAMA 2026, PMID 42008245). Genetic predisposition contributes an estimated 60-70% of overall spina bifida risk, acting as a polygenic, multifactorial trait with strong interaction with folate-pathway genes and environmental folate status (Copp AJ et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015, PMID 27189655). Maternal antiepileptic drug exposure, specifically valproic acid, is a well-documented teratogenic risk: in a reviewed cohort of 69 cases of fetal valproate syndrome from prenatal valproic acid monotherapy exposure, neural tube defects were seen in 3% of the sample (Kozma C, 'Valproic acid embryopathy', Am J Med Genet 2001, PMID 11223853) -- a risk substantially above general-population baseline. Maternal pregestational diabetes and maternal obesity are both established, independent risk factors for spina bifida (Copp AJ et al, PMID 27189655; StatPearls, 'Diabetic Embryopathy', 2025, which lists neural tube defects including spina bifida and anencephaly among the characteristic anomalies of diabetic embryopathy); a precise numeric relative-risk multiplier for maternal diabetes could not be independently verified against a primary source in this research session and is therefore not quantified here. Maternal hyperthermia/fever in early pregnancy is also listed as a risk factor by the CDC (CDC, 'About Spina Bifida').
symptoms.epidemiology: Globally, spina bifida occurs in approximately 1 per 1,000 births, making it one of the most common congenital malformations (Copp AJ et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015, PMID 27189655). In the United States, approximately 1,251-1,278 babies are born with spina bifida each year, or about 1 in every 2,857 births, and at least 92,551 people were living with spina bifida in the US in 2019 (3.20 per 10,000 insured individuals) (CDC, 'Spina Bifida Data and Statistics'). Racial/ethnic prevalence per 10,000 live births differs: Hispanic 3.80, non-Hispanic White 3.09, non-Hispanic Black 2.73 (CDC). Mandatory folic acid fortification of enriched cereal grain products in the US, begun in 1998, produced a real, documented 28% decrease in neural tube defect prevalence, and a 70% reduction in spina bifida lesion severity when comparing pre- and post-fortification cohorts (most of the improvement attributable to fewer higher/upper-spine, more severe lesions); fortification is estimated to prevent approximately 1,300 neural tube defects annually in the US (CDC, 'Spina Bifida Data and Statistics'). This fortification-driven decline illustrates the direct, population-level payoff of the folic acid risk factor described above. Outcomes and case-mix differ sharply where prenatal screening and folate fortification infrastructure are limited: a two-year single-centre retrospective review in Ethiopia of 230 confirmed neural tube defect cases found myelomeningocele in 77.8% of cases, a lumbosacral lesion level in 39.4% (most common), hydrocephalus in 78.3%, postoperative complications in 33.8%, and an in-hospital mortality rate of 4.6%, alongside markedly limited access to physical rehabilitation (only 45.4% of patients received it) (Childs Nerv Syst 2026, PMID 42501095) -- underscoring that the epidemiological burden of spina bifida is substantially shaped by preventive and health-system factors, not biology alone.
symptoms.natural_history: Fetal (prenatal) surgical closure of myelomeningocele before 26 weeks' gestation, established by the randomized Management of Myelomeningocele Study (MOMS trial, n=183 enrolled, 158 evaluated at 12 months), measurably alters the disease's natural history compared with standard postnatal repair: the composite outcome of fetal/neonatal death or need for a VP shunt by 12 months occurred in 68% of the prenatal-surgery group versus 98% of the postnatal-repair group, shunt placement itself was needed in 40% versus 82% (relative risk 0.48), and the prenatal-surgery group showed improved mental development and motor function composite scores at 30 months along with better ambulation -- at the cost of a real increase in preterm delivery and uterine dehiscence risk (Adzick NS et al, N Engl J Med 2011, PMID 21306277). The timing of postnatal surgical closure of an open myelomeningocele materially affects infection risk: in a study of 3,775 neonates in a national database, overall infection occurred in 18% of patients, and closure delayed 2 or more days after birth was associated with a 65-88% relative increase in infection rate compared with same-day closure ('Infection rate correlated with time to repair of open neural tube defects (myelomeningoceles): an institutional and national study', Childs Nerv Syst 2016, PMID 27444296) -- direct evidence that prompt postnatal closure is not merely traditional practice but measurably reduces a real, quantified complication. After initial closure, a substantial minority of children go on to develop secondary (acquired) tethered cord syndrome -- affecting, on average, 30% of children after myelomeningocele repair -- which produces delayed neurological, orthopedic, and urological deterioration in a previously stable patient, driven by ongoing traction/ischemic injury at a low-lying, scarred conus medullaris (Cureus 2020 literature update, PMID 33072445). Longitudinal cross-sectional data in adults with spina bifida (n=196) found that younger adults (under 46 years) carried a higher burden of secondary conditions -- hydrocephalus, Chiari II malformation, tethered cord symptoms, and latex allergy -- than older cohorts, reflecting how changing multidisciplinary care practices over successive birth cohorts continue to reshape the disease's long-term course (Brain Behav 2020, PMID 32633090). A 2026 review on orthopedic surgical trends in adults with spina bifida explicitly notes that 'advances in multidisciplinary care have increased life expectancy' for people born with the condition, though a precise quantified survival-to-adulthood percentage could not be independently verified against a primary source in this research session and is therefore not stated as a number here (Disability and Health Journal 2026).
symptoms.clinical_takeaway: Spina bifida spans a real clinical spectrum from asymptomatic occulta to severe, multisystem myelomeningocele, but the single most impactful and genuinely preventable lever is periconceptional folic acid: randomized-trial evidence shows a 72% reduction in recurrence with supplementation in high-risk women (PMID 1677062), and population-level mandatory fortification produced a real, measured 28% decline in neural tube defect prevalence and 70% reduction in lesion severity (CDC data) -- this is a genuine, already-proven public-health cure-by-prevention story, not a theoretical one. For pregnancies already affected, combined MSAFP-plus-ultrasound prenatal screening is the real diagnostic backbone, but a meaningful fraction of missed cases (11.4% in one referral cohort, PMID 26332586) reflects screening never having been ordered rather than a limitation of the test itself, and correcting that access gap is itself an actionable improvement. Once diagnosed, real trial evidence supports fetal surgical closure before 26 weeks to reduce shunt dependency and improve motor outcomes (MOMS trial, PMID 21306277), and same-day-to-24-hour postnatal closure when prenatal repair is not performed, since delay of 2 or more days measurably increases infection risk by 65-88% (PMID 27444296). Lifelong follow-up must proactively and repeatedly screen for the near-universal comorbidities of hydrocephalus/shunt status and Chiari II-related brainstem dysfunction (including sleep-disordered breathing, present in up to 80% of children, PMID 40096506), and must treat any new neurological, urological, or orthopedic decline in a previously stable patient as a possible secondary tethered cord syndrome (affecting about 30% of patients, PMID 33072445) rather than as baseline disease progression, since detethering surgery is time-sensitive.

spina_bifida.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Three real red-flag scenarios in a spina bifida/myelomeningocele patient must bypass routine follow-up and trigger urgent/emergent action. (1) A newly born infant with an OPEN myelomeningocele (exposed neural placode, visible CSF leak) is a neurosurgical emergency: surgical closure should occur the same day or within 24 hours whenever feasible, because in a national database study of 3,775 neonates, closure delayed by 2 or more days after birth was associated with a 65-88% relative INCREASE in infection rate (meningitis/ventriculitis) compared with same-day closure, against a baseline overall infection rate of 18% ('Infection rate correlated with time to repair of open neural tube defects (myelomeningoceles): an institutional and national study', Childs Nerv Syst 2016, PMID 27444296). (2) Signs of shunt malfunction / acute hydrocephalus decompensation -- headache, vomiting, lethargy or altered consciousness, irritability, a bulging fontanelle in infants, new strabismus or upward-gaze palsy ('sunsetting' eyes), or seizures -- in any spina bifida patient with a VP shunt require emergent neurosurgical evaluation and imaging; shunt failure is a common and dangerous real event, occurring within 2 years in 7.7% of a 4,192-patient spina bifida cohort (J Pediatr Rehabil Med 2017, PMID 29125513), and in a 42-patient cohort undergoing surgery for symptomatic Chiari II malformation, 55% required shunt-malfunction surgery, with a 4.7% early neonatal mortality rate from decompensation in that same cohort (Childs Nerv Syst 2020, PMID 32474814). (3) New or progressively worsening neurological, urological, or orthopedic decline in a previously neurologically stable spina bifida patient -- worsening gait, new or progressing scoliosis, increasing spasticity, new back pain, or a change in bladder/bowel pattern -- must be treated as a possible secondary tethered cord syndrome, which affects on average 30% of children after myelomeningocele repair (Cureus 2020, PMID 33072445), and warrants urgent MRI and neurosurgical referral rather than being dismissed as expected baseline disease, since detethering surgery is time-sensitive to prevent permanent additional neurological deficit.

narcolepsy.name: Narcolepsy

definition.finding: Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological sleep disorder of hypersomnolence. Narcolepsy type 1 (NT1, narcolepsy with cataplexy) is caused by loss of hypothalamic hypocretin (orexin) neurons; narcolepsy type 2 (NT2, narcolepsy without cataplexy) has normal or only mildly reduced CSF hypocretin-1 and its cause is less well defined. Narcolepsy with cataplexy affects an estimated 0.02% of adults worldwide, has onset usually in the teenage/young-adult years, and persists throughout life.
definition.source: Dauvilliers Y, Arnulf I, Mignot E, 'Narcolepsy with cataplexy', Lancet 2007;369:499-511 (PMID 17292770)

orexin_hypocretin_neuron_loss.finding: Nishino et al showed that hypocretin (orexin) was undetectable in the CSF of 7 of 9 people with narcolepsy studied, establishing hypocretin transmission failure as the core biochemical abnormality of human narcolepsy. Thannickal et al then directly quantified the neuropathology in post-mortem hypothalami and found human narcoleptics have an 85%-95% reduction in the number of hypocretin (Hcrt) neurons, while neighbouring melanin-concentrating-hormone (MCH) neurons (intermixed with Hcrt cells in the normal brain) were not reduced, showing the cell loss is relatively specific to hypocretin neurons; gliosis in the hypocretin cell region was consistent with a degenerative process.
orexin_hypocretin_neuron_loss.source: Nishino S, Ripley B, Overeem S, Lammers GJ, Mignot E, 'Hypocretin (orexin) deficiency in human narcolepsy', Lancet 2000;355:39-40 (PMID 10615891); Thannickal TC et al., 'Reduced Number of Hypocretin Neurons in Human Narcolepsy', Neuron 2000;27:469-474 (PMID 11055430)

autoimmune_mechanism_and_hla.finding: The cause of hypocretin neuron loss is believed to be autoimmune since most patients with narcolepsy-cataplexy carry the HLA DQB1*06:02 allele, which predisposes to the disorder. In a case-control study of Brazilian patients, DQB1*06:02 was carried by 61.9% of narcolepsy type 1 patients versus 18.0% of controls (and versus 18.8% of narcolepsy type 2 patients without cataplexy), and DRB1*15:01 was carried by 47.6% of NT1 patients versus 8.0% of controls - both markedly enriched in NT1 relative to controls and to NT2. The magnitude of this enrichment (HLA class II association) is the principal evidence cited for an autoimmune mechanism targeting hypocretin neurons, though the exact autoantigen/effector mechanism is not settled.
autoimmune_mechanism_and_hla.source: Dauvilliers Y, Arnulf I, Mignot E, Lancet 2007;369:499-511 (PMID 17292770); Case-control HLA class II study, J Clin Sleep Med 2024 (PMID 39150697) - note: this specific 61.9%/18.0% figure is from a single Brazilian cohort (21 NT1 patients, 100 controls); broader international literature reports HLA-DQB1*06:02 frequencies that vary by ethnicity, but a single universally-cited pooled percentage could not be independently verified this session and is therefore omitted
autoimmune_mechanism_and_hla.confidence: high for the qualitative HLA association; moderate for the exact quantitative frequency, which is cohort-specific

post_infectious_trigger.finding: An environmental trigger is implicated alongside the genetic (HLA) susceptibility: the incidence of narcolepsy type 1 has been observed to rise following pandemic influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 infection itself, and separately following administration of the AS03-adjuvanted pandemic H1N1 vaccine (Pandemrix) used in the 2009-2010 pandemic, supporting a post-infectious/immune-triggered model of onset in genetically susceptible individuals.
post_infectious_trigger.source: Narrative review, Int J Mol Sci 2024 (PMID 39595997)
post_infectious_trigger.confidence: high for the qualitative association; see risk_factors below for the quantitative Pandemrix data

icsd3_classification.finding: Per ICSD-3, narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) is diagnosed when cataplexy is present (with supportive MSLT/CSF findings); narcolepsy type 2 (NT2) is diagnosed when the same objective sleep-test criteria are met but cataplexy is absent. A 2026 cohort study of narcolepsy diagnosed by ICSD-3 criteria explicitly classified patients as NT1 'when cataplexy was present' and NT2 'when MSLT criteria were met without cataplexy'.

mslt_psg_numeric_criteria.finding: The objective sleep-test (MSLT, preceded by overnight PSG to exclude other causes of sleepiness) criterion used for narcolepsy diagnosis is a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less across the naps, together with 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) (a SOREMP on the preceding night PSG may substitute for one of the two daytime SOREMPs). A 2026 study on negative-MSLT narcolepsy cases explicitly frames the negative/non-diagnostic result as 'mean sleep latency > 8 min or sleep onset REM periods (SOREMPs) < 2', confirming these are the positive-criterion cut-points in current use. An illustrative severe case (adolescent NT2) showed a mean sleep latency of 1.25 minutes with SOREMPs in 3 of 4 naps, well past the diagnostic threshold.
mslt_psg_numeric_criteria.source: Biscarini F et al., 'To diagnose narcolepsy type 1 after a negative multiple sleep latency test...', Sleep 2026 (PMID 42189945); case report, Cureus 2026 (PMID 42181370)

csf_hypocretin_criterion.finding: A CSF hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) level of 110 pg/mL or below (roughly one-third of mean normal/control values on standard radioimmunoassay) is used as an alternative, direct biochemical diagnostic criterion for narcolepsy type 1, and is especially useful when MSLT results are negative or equivocal: in one series, CSF-HCRT1 <110 pg/mL was found in 34 cases with a negative MSLT, increasing NT1 diagnoses by 9.9% in that cohort. Cross-platform validation (LC-MS versus radioimmunoassay) showed 88% concordance for classifying hypocretin-deficient (NT1) status using the <=110 pg/mL threshold.
csf_hypocretin_criterion.source: Biscarini F et al., Sleep 2026 (PMID 42189945); assay comparison, Sleep Med 2026 (PMID 42127723)
csf_hypocretin_criterion.confidence: high for the threshold and its use; the exact concordance/uplift percentages are from single cohorts

diagnostic_delay.finding: Diagnosis is frequently delayed: a multicentre analysis found a median diagnostic delay of 4 years for narcolepsy type 1, 5 years for narcolepsy type 2, and 8 years for idiopathic hypersomnia, although the delay has been shortening over recent decades. A separate study found women had significantly longer diagnostic delays than men and a significantly higher rate of misdiagnosis before the correct diagnosis of narcolepsy was made.

excessive_daytime_sleepiness.finding: Narcolepsy (with or without cataplexy) is characterised by severe, irresistible daytime sleepiness with disabling, often sudden 'sleep attacks', and disturbed, fragmented nocturnal sleep with frequent movement and awakening; weight gain is also described. EDS is typically the first and most universal symptom.
excessive_daytime_sleepiness.source: Dauvilliers Y, Arnulf I, Mignot E, Lancet 2007;369:499-511 (PMID 17292770)

cataplexy.finding: Cataplexy - sudden, usually brief loss of muscle tone typically triggered by strong emotion (laughter, surprise) - is the defining feature that separates narcolepsy type 1 from type 2; per ICSD-3 classification used in current cohorts, NT1 is diagnosed specifically 'when cataplexy was present' while NT2 requires the same MSLT criteria 'without cataplexy'.
cataplexy.source: Sleep Med X 2026 (PMID 42756839); Dauvilliers Y et al., Lancet 2007 (PMID 17292770)

sleep_paralysis_and_hallucinations.finding: Narcolepsy can be associated with sleep-onset or sleep-offset paralysis (the inability to move for a period at sleep onset/waking despite being conscious) and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations (vivid, often frightening dream-like perceptual experiences occurring at sleep onset or waking) - both reflect intrusion of REM-sleep phenomena (atonia, dreaming) into wakefulness.
sleep_paralysis_and_hallucinations.source: Dauvilliers Y, Arnulf I, Mignot E, Lancet 2007;369:499-511 (PMID 17292770)

idiopathic_hypersomnia.finding: Idiopathic hypersomnia (IH) is the closest mimic of narcolepsy type 2 and remains difficult to distinguish because of overlapping excessive daytime sleepiness and long sleep duration; diagnostic delay for IH (median 8 years) is longer than for NT1 (4 years) or NT2 (5 years). One distinguishing feature under study is sleep-inertia duration, which is longer in IH than in narcolepsy; an optimal sleep-inertia-duration cutpoint of 25 minutes has been reported to separate IH from narcolepsy type 1 in one cohort.
idiopathic_hypersomnia.source: Sleep Advances 2024 (PMID 39211350); Sleep Med 2024 (PMID 39067151); J Sleep Res 2026 (PMID 40817031)
idiopathic_hypersomnia.confidence: moderate - sleep-inertia cutoff is from a single study and not yet a formal diagnostic criterion

obstructive_sleep_apnea_and_other_hypers.finding: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and other causes of disrupted nocturnal sleep must be excluded because they produce daytime sleepiness that can mimic narcolepsy; overnight polysomnography preceding the MSLT is required in the diagnostic pathway specifically to rule out OSA and other sleep-disrupting conditions before attributing a short mean sleep latency to narcolepsy itself. OSA and narcolepsy can also co-exist, which complicates diagnosis and management.
obstructive_sleep_apnea_and_other_hypers.source: Sleep Med X 2024 (PMID 39386319, comorbidity of OSA and narcolepsy)

depression_and_psychiatric_misdiagnosis.finding: Excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy is frequently misattributed to a mental/psychiatric disorder (e.g. depression) before the correct diagnosis is reached, which is a documented cause of diagnostic delay; women in particular show a significantly higher rate of pre-diagnosis misdiagnosis than men.
depression_and_psychiatric_misdiagnosis.source: Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 2026 (PMID 42388395); Sleep Med 2025 (PMID 40157243)

genetic_hla_association.finding: The principal known genetic risk factor is the HLA class II allele DQB1*06:02 (often co-inherited with DRB1*15:01), which is markedly over-represented in narcolepsy type 1 patients compared with controls (61.9% vs 18.0% for DQB1*06:02, and 47.6% vs 8.0% for DRB1*15:01, in one case-control cohort). This HLA association is the strongest known genetic risk factor and is consistent with an autoimmune mechanism of hypocretin-neuron loss.
genetic_hla_association.source: J Clin Sleep Med 2024 (PMID 39150697); Dauvilliers Y et al., Lancet 2007 (PMID 17292770)
genetic_hla_association.confidence: high for the association; the exact percentage is cohort-specific (see note in pathophysiology section)

post_h1n1_infection_and_pandemrix_vaccin.finding: Both natural pandemic influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 infection and, independently, the AS03-adjuvanted Pandemrix H1N1 vaccine used during the 2009-2010 pandemic were followed by a real, measured rise in narcolepsy type 1 incidence in some populations. In a Finnish national cohort study of 4-19 year-olds, the incidence of narcolepsy was 9.0 per 100,000 person-years in vaccinated individuals versus 0.7 per 100,000 person-years in the unvaccinated, a rate ratio of 12.7 (95% CI 6.1-30.8); the vaccine-attributable risk was estimated at 1 in 16,000 vaccinated 4-19 year-olds (95% CI 1:13,000-1:21,000). This is understood as a post-infectious/immune-triggered onset of narcolepsy type 1 in genetically (HLA-DQB1*06:02) susceptible individuals, and the specific Pandemrix-associated risk was geographically and formulation-restricted (most clearly documented in Finland and Sweden with this particular AS03-adjuvanted vaccine, not H1N1 vaccination in general).
post_h1n1_infection_and_pandemrix_vaccin.source: Nohynek H et al., 'AS03 adjuvanted AH1N1 vaccine associated with an abrupt increase in the incidence of childhood narcolepsy in Finland', PLoS One 2012;7:e33536 (PMID 22470453); Int J Mol Sci 2024 review (PMID 39595997)
post_h1n1_infection_and_pandemrix_vaccin.confidence: high - real, previously investigated national-cohort finding; scope limited to the specific vaccine/population studied, not a general anti-vaccination claim

prevalence.finding: Narcolepsy with cataplexy has been estimated to affect about 0.02% of adults worldwide (i.e. roughly 20 per 100,000). More recent national-registry data give somewhat different figures depending on case ascertainment and population: a Taiwanese national health-insurance analysis found a diagnosed narcolepsy prevalence of 9.98 per 100,000 (concluding this is likely an underestimate/under-diagnosis relative to other countries), while multiple other national studies (UK, New Zealand, Japan) have separately quantified incidence/prevalence in their own populations. Onset is usually in the teenage/young-adult years.
prevalence.source: Dauvilliers Y, Arnulf I, Mignot E, Lancet 2007;369:499-511 (PMID 17292770); Huang YS et al., Sleep 2025 (PMID 40390183)
prevalence.confidence: moderate - prevalence estimates vary substantially by country/ascertainment method; a single universal figure could not be verified this session

chronic_lifelong_course.finding: Narcolepsy with cataplexy typically begins in the teenage/young-adult years and persists throughout the patient's lifetime; it is described as an under-recognised disease, underscoring the importance of general practitioners and other primary-care workers identifying abnormal daytime sleepiness early to shorten the diagnostic delay (median several years, see diagnostic_framework).
chronic_lifelong_course.source: Dauvilliers Y, Arnulf I, Mignot E, Lancet 2007;369:499-511 (PMID 17292770); J Sleep Res 2026 (PMID 40817031)

summary.finding: Narcolepsy type 1 is a specific, biologically defined disease (autoimmune-mediated loss of 85-95% of hypothalamic hypocretin neurons in a genetically HLA-DQB1*06:02-susceptible individual, often following an immune trigger) that presents with excessive daytime sleepiness plus cataplexy, and is confirmed objectively by MSLT (mean sleep latency <=8 min with >=2 SOREMPs) or CSF hypocretin-1 <=110 pg/mL; narcolepsy type 2 shares the sleepiness and objective sleep-test findings without cataplexy and without hypocretin deficiency. Because the sleepiness and REM-intrusion symptoms overlap with idiopathic hypersomnia, OSA and depression, diagnostic delay of several years is common and the single most useful step to shorten it is early, deliberate objective sleep testing (PSG + MSLT +/- CSF hypocretin) whenever a patient reports irresistible daytime sleep attacks, especially if cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hypnagogic hallucinations are also present.
summary.source: Synthesis of Dauvilliers Y et al. Lancet 2007 (PMID 17292770), Thannickal TC et al. Neuron 2000 (PMID 11055430), Nishino S et al. Lancet 2000 (PMID 10615891), Biscarini F et al. Sleep 2026 (PMID 42189945), J Sleep Res 2026 (PMID 40817031)

narcolepsy.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Sudden, irresistible 'sleep attacks' and cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone) in narcolepsy are a real, measured cause of motor-vehicle and occupational accidents and MUST trigger an explicit safety warning (do not drive or operate machinery while sleepy; seek urgent medical review of treatment) rather than being treated as a routine symptom. In a French case-control study of drivers with central disorders of hypersomnolence (narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia), untreated patients had significantly increased odds of a recent car crash versus healthy controls (OR 2.21, 95% CI 1.30-3.76), and patients treated for under 5 years still had increased odds (OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.26-3.30); only patients treated for 5 or more years no longer showed a significant excess risk (OR 1.23, 95% CI 0.56-2.69), showing the excess accident risk is real but can be reduced with sustained treatment. A separate driving-behaviour study of drivers with narcolepsy or idiopathic hypersomnia found 61% had experienced at least one lifetime accident or near-miss, with crash-involved drivers showing significantly higher sleepiness scores than those without crashes (14+/-4 vs 11+/-5, p<0.04). Clinically: any patient with narcolepsy who drives, operates machinery, or works at height/around hazards should be explicitly counselled on this real accident risk, screened for treatment adequacy, and advised on local rules for reporting the condition to driving-licence authorities where applicable; new or worsening sleep attacks or cataplexy in a driver is a safety-critical finding, not a routine follow-up item. [Sources: Pizza F et al., 'Car crashes and central disorders of hypersomnolence: a French study', PLoS One 2015;10:e0129386 (PMID 26052938); driving-behaviour study, Sleep 2024 (PMID 39208413)]
narcolepsy.icd11_hint: ICD-11 code 7A20 Narcolepsy (with subcodes 7A20.0 Narcolepsy type 1, 7A20.1 Narcolepsy type 2, 7A20.Z Narcolepsy unspecified) is the code widely cited in current sleep-medicine literature; the ICD-10-CM legacy equivalents are G47.41 Narcolepsy without cataplexy and G47.42 Narcolepsy with cataplexy. The exact ICD-11 code could NOT be independently confirmed against a live WHO ICD-11 browser/API query in this research session (the WHO ICD API requires OAuth authentication not available here, and the public browser page is JavaScript-rendered, returning no code text to any fetch attempted in this session). FLAGGED for independent verification against icd.who.int before clinical/coding use.
narcolepsy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by irreversible, autoimmune-mediated destruction of the small population of hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus; a 2022 review states plainly that 'the irreversible loss of hypocretin neurons is responsible for the main symptoms' and that the destruction mechanism is 'highly suspected to be autoimmune, or dysimmune' (J Sleep Res 2022, PMID 35624073; see also Front Immunol 2026, PMID 42416062, on the immune/neural-circuit basis). No currently approved therapy regenerates these neurons or reverses this loss, so narcolepsy remains a chronic, lifelong condition with NO cure. However, real modern pharmacotherapy achieves real, substantial control of both major symptom domains: pitolisant reduces weekly cataplexy rate by a median 75% versus 38% with placebo (rate ratio 0.512, p<0.0001, HARMONY CTP trial, PMID 28129985); sodium oxybate suppresses cataplexy attacks to a median of 0 per 2 weeks while continued on treatment versus a median of 21 per 2 weeks after blinded withdrawal to placebo (p<0.001, PMID 15033130); and solriamfetol normalises the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS <=10) in up to 49.2% of patients versus 15.5% on placebo (PMID 33226332). The real closest-to-disease-modifying approach now emerging is the class of selective orexin receptor-2 (OX2R) agonists, which pharmacologically replace the missing orexin signal at its own receptor rather than just boosting downstream wake-promoting monoamine tone: oveporexton (TAK-861), in two 2026 phase 3 trials (First Light and Radiant Light), reduced ESS by 9.7-11.8 points (versus 1.5-1.7 with placebo) and cut median weekly cataplexy rate by 79.0%-88.8% (N Engl J Med 2026, PMID 42714024) -- the largest symptom-control effect size reported to date in narcolepsy type 1, and it has been described as the first-in-class OX2R agonist reaching approval for this indication (Drug Discov Ther 2026, PMID 42618292). An earlier OX2R agonist, TAK-994, showed comparable efficacy but was discontinued in 2022 for dose-dependent liver toxicity, illustrating that this drug class is real and effective but still maturing (Ann Med Surg (Lond) 2026, PMID 41497057). None of this regenerates the destroyed neurons or constitutes a cure -- it is real, evidence-based, near-normalisation-level symptom control, which is the honest, current ceiling of narcolepsy therapy.

curative_option.name: No Cure Exists -- Combination Pharmacotherapy Is the Real Closest-to-Best-Control Approach, With the Selective Orexin-Receptor-2 Agonist Oveporexton as the Emerging Closest-to-Disease-Modifying Option
curative_option.note: Narcolepsy type 1 results from irreversible autoimmune destruction of hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons (PMID 35624073); no approved therapy regenerates these neurons, so there is honestly no cure. The realistic best real-world outcome today is combination pharmacotherapy (a wake-promoting agent or pitolisant for EDS, plus sodium oxybate/low-sodium oxybate or pitolisant for cataplexy), and the newest, largest-effect real trial data belongs to the orexin receptor-2 agonist oveporexton, which most directly targets the disease's root neurochemical deficit.

real_trial_data.oveporexton_first_light_and_radiant_ligh: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in narcolepsy type 1 (First Light n=168, Radiant Light n=105, ages 16-70): 12 weeks of oveporexton improved Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency by 14.3-19.8 minutes (vs -0.4 to -0.8 minutes with placebo), reduced Epworth Sleepiness Scale by 9.7-11.8 points (vs 1.5-1.7 points with placebo), and cut median weekly cataplexy rate by 79.0%-88.8% -- the largest reported effect size of any narcolepsy therapy to date (N Engl J Med 2026, PMID 42714024).
real_trial_data.pitolisant_harmony_ctp_2017: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: pitolisant reduced weekly cataplexy rate by a median 75% from baseline vs 38% with placebo (rate ratio 0.512, 95% CI 0.43-0.60, p<0.0001) (Lancet Neurol 2017, PMID 28129985).
real_trial_data.sodium_oxybate_withdrawal_trial_2004: Blinded withdrawal to placebo caused cataplexy attacks to rebound to a median of 21 per 2 weeks, vs a median of 0 per 2 weeks in patients continued on sodium oxybate (p<0.001) (Sleep Med 2004, PMID 15033130).
real_trial_data.tak994_discontinuation: An earlier oral OX2R agonist, TAK-994, showed comparable early efficacy but was discontinued in 2022 due to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, before oveporexton's improved-safety next-generation molecule succeeded it (Ann Med Surg (Lond) 2026, PMID 41497057).

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Nothing here is curative in the sense of reversing hypocretin-neuron loss or achieving permanent drug-free remission. What is real: combination pharmacotherapy, and now oveporexton specifically, can bring ESS and cataplexy frequency close to normal population levels for many patients for as long as the medicine is continued -- a real, substantial, near-normalisation of daily function, but not a cure, and it reverts if treatment stops.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Oveporexton and other OX2R agonists require an at least partially intact orexin receptor-2 signalling pathway downstream of the lost neurons to work; patients with primary orexin receptor gene mutations (a very rare cause of narcolepsy) have not been specifically studied in the 2026 phase 3 program and may not respond the same way.
curative_option.important_caveat: Adverse events were more common with oveporexton than placebo (86-89% vs 43-54% of patients), chiefly increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia; this is a new drug class with a shorter real-world safety track record than the decades-established sodium oxybate/modafinil/pitolisant options, and the prior TAK-994 hepatotoxicity signal in the same drug class means liver-function monitoring and long-term surveillance remain warranted.
curative_option.source: N Engl J Med 2026 (PMID 42714024); Lancet Neurol 2017 (PMID 28129985); Sleep Med 2004 (PMID 15033130); Ann Med Surg (Lond) 2026 (PMID 41497057); J Sleep Res 2022 (PMID 35624073)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for narcolepsy (types 1 and 2): first-line and second-line wake-promoting medicines for excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), the dual-indication histamine H3-antagonist pitolisant, anticataplectic medicines (oxybates and off-label antidepressants), and the emerging orexin receptor-2 (OX2R) agonist drug class that most closely approaches disease-modifying therapy. Diagnostic criteria and clinical features are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial, guideline, or cohort. Narcolepsy has NO cure (see CURABILITY_NOTE / curative_option above); this survey ranks real symptom-control medicines only -- there is no real, guideline-endorsed injection or surgical procedure for narcolepsy, so priority order here runs first-line medicine to second-line/off-label medicine to emerging medicine, per BalanceAI convention of medicine before injection/procedure before everything else.

narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.name: Modafinil -- Real First-Line, AASM Strong-Recommendation Wake-Promoting Medicine for Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS)
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.type: Wake-promoting agent (atypical stimulant, weak dopamine reuptake inhibitor), oral, first-line medicine for EDS
specific_drugs: Modafinil 200-400 mg once daily each morning (brand: Provigil, Modalert)
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.effectiveness: In the pivotal 18-center, 9-week, placebo-controlled, double-blind RCT (n=283), modafinil significantly reduced all measures of sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Multiple Sleep Latency Test, and Maintenance of Wakefulness Test, with sustained efficacy over 40 weeks of open-label follow-up ('Randomized trial of modafinil for the treatment of pathological somnolence in narcolepsy', US Modafinil in Narcolepsy Multicenter Study Group, Ann Neurol 1998, PMID 9450772). In a separate dosing-regimen RCT, 82% of patients on modafinil 400 mg once daily were rated 'much improved' or 'very much improved' on Clinical Global Impression, versus only 27% on 200 mg once daily (Clin Neuropharmacol 2003, PMID 14520165). A 2024 comparative trial reported a mean Epworth Sleepiness Scale improvement of 5.0 (SD 2.7) points with modafinil over 12 weeks (CNS Drugs 2024, PMID 39306601). Modafinil carries the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's strongest ('We recommend') evidence grade for adult narcolepsy (J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 34743789).
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.reason_why: Modafinil promotes wakefulness primarily by weakly inhibiting the dopamine transporter (DAT) and increasing extracellular dopamine in wake-promoting circuits, with additional activating effects on hypothalamic histaminergic arousal pathways; unlike traditional amphetamine stimulants it produces more selective cortical activation with a lower abuse/dependence liability.
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.important_caveat: Modafinil treats EDS only and has no meaningful effect on cataplexy, hallucinations, or sleep paralysis, so most patients with cataplexy need a second, cataplexy-directed medicine added; common side effects are headache, nausea, and anxiety, and modafinil reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives via CYP3A4 induction.
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.real_working_solution: Modafinil 200 mg on waking (titrated to 400 mg/day in one or two doses) is the standard real-world first medicine tried in newly diagnosed narcolepsy with EDS, per AASM strong recommendation.
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.source: US Modafinil in Narcolepsy Multicenter Study Group, Ann Neurol 1998 (PMID 9450772); Clin Neuropharmacol 2003 (PMID 14520165); CNS Drugs 2024 (PMID 39306601); AASM guideline, J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 34743789)

narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.name: Armodafinil -- Real AASM Conditional-Recommendation Long-Acting Wake-Promoting Alternative
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.type: Wake-promoting agent (R-enantiomer of modafinil), oral, conditional-recommendation medicine for EDS
specific_drugs: Armodafinil 150-250 mg once daily each morning (brand: Nuvigil, Waklert)
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.effectiveness: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2021 clinical practice guideline gives armodafinil a conditional recommendation for adult narcolepsy (J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 34743789), reflecting its shared active R-enantiomer pharmacology with modafinil, whose EDS efficacy is separately established at the strong-recommendation level in the same guideline.
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.reason_why: Armodafinil is the single, longer-half-life R-enantiomer of racemic modafinil, giving more sustained plasma levels through the afternoon via the same weak dopamine-transporter-inhibition wake-promoting mechanism.
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.important_caveat: Evidence base is smaller and more indirect than for modafinil itself (conditional vs strong AASM grade); the same drug-interaction (CYP3A4 induction reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy) and cataplexy-non-coverage caveats as modafinil apply.
narc_eds_first_line_wakefulness_medicine.source: AASM guideline, J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 34743789)

narc_eds_second_line_medicines.name: Solriamfetol -- Real AASM Strong-Recommendation Dopamine-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor for EDS (TONES Trial Program)
narc_eds_second_line_medicines.type: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (DNRI), oral, second-line-to-first-line medicine for EDS
specific_drugs: Solriamfetol 75-150 mg once daily on waking (brand: Sunosi)
narc_eds_second_line_medicines.effectiveness: In a post-hoc pooled analysis of the phase 3 TONES trials in narcolepsy (n=231), a normal Epworth Sleepiness Scale score (<=10) was achieved in 30.5%-49.2% of solriamfetol-treated patients (dose-dependent) versus 15.5% on placebo, and a clinically meaningful >=25% ESS reduction occurred in 44.1%-62.7% versus 27.6% on placebo (J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 33226332). Solriamfetol carries an AASM strong recommendation for adult narcolepsy (J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 34743789).
narc_eds_second_line_medicines.reason_why: Solriamfetol selectively inhibits reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine (DNRI) with much lower affinity for serotonin transport than typical antidepressants, increasing extracellular catecholamine tone in wake-promoting cortical and subcortical circuits without the broader monoamine-releasing action of amphetamines.
narc_eds_second_line_medicines.important_caveat: Like modafinil, solriamfetol treats EDS only, not cataplexy; it requires washout from MAO inhibitors, and can raise blood pressure and heart rate, requiring monitoring in patients with cardiovascular disease.
narc_eds_second_line_medicines.real_working_solution: Solriamfetol 75 mg on waking, titrated to 150 mg/day, is a real evidence-based option for patients with inadequate EDS control on modafinil/armodafinil, or as an alternative first-line choice per AASM guidance.
narc_eds_second_line_medicines.source: J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 33226332); AASM guideline, J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 34743789)

narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.name: Pitolisant -- Real AASM Strong-Recommendation Histamine H3-Receptor Antagonist/Inverse Agonist, Dual Efficacy for EDS AND Cataplexy
narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.type: Selective histamine H3-receptor antagonist/inverse agonist, oral, first-line dual-indication medicine (non-scheduled, non-controlled)
specific_drugs: Pitolisant 4.5-35.6 mg once daily on waking, up-titrated over 1-3 weeks (brand: Wakix)
narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.effectiveness: In the pivotal HARMONY CTP randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with narcolepsy and cataplexy, pitolisant reduced the weekly cataplexy rate by a median 75% from baseline versus 38% with placebo (rate ratio 0.512, 95% CI 0.43-0.60, p<0.0001) (Lancet Neurol 2017, PMID 28129985). A pooled analysis of the HARMONY 1 and HARMONY CTP placebo-controlled trials reported Cohen's d effect sizes of 0.61-0.86 for EDS and up to 0.86 for cataplexy, with a number-needed-to-treat (NNT) of 3-5 for EDS and 3-4 for cataplexy (CNS Drugs 2022, PMID 34935103). In a dedicated paediatric RCT (children >=6 years, n=110), pitolisant produced a significantly greater improvement in combined EDS/cataplexy symptom score than placebo (Ullanlinna Narcolepsy Scale mean change -6.3 vs -2.6, least-squares mean difference -3.7, p=0.007) (Lancet Neurol 2023, PMID 36931805). Pitolisant carries an AASM strong recommendation for adult narcolepsy (J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 34743789).
narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.reason_why: Pitolisant blocks and inverse-agonises presynaptic histamine H3 autoreceptors, increasing synthesis and release of histamine from tuberomammillary-nucleus wake-promoting neurons; because histaminergic tone is itself normally driven by orexin/hypocretin neurons, boosting histamine release partially substitutes for the missing orexin signal, which is the proposed mechanism for pitolisant's unusual dual efficacy against both EDS and cataplexy in a single non-scheduled medicine.
narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.important_caveat: Full clinical effect takes 1-3 weeks of up-titration to build; it is contraindicated in patients with QT prolongation, requires dose reduction in hepatic/renal impairment, and should not be combined with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors.
narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.real_working_solution: Pitolisant is a real evidence-based first-line choice, especially attractive for patients wanting one non-controlled medicine covering both EDS and cataplexy instead of separate agents.
narc_dual_eds_and_cataplexy_medicines.source: Lancet Neurol 2017 (PMID 28129985); CNS Drugs 2022 (PMID 34935103); Lancet Neurol 2023 (PMID 36931805); AASM guideline, J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 34743789)

narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.name: Sodium Oxybate -- Real AASM Strong-Recommendation Nightly Anticataplectic and EDS Medicine (Also Improves Nocturnal Sleep Architecture)
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.type: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) sodium salt, oral solution taken at bedtime and again 2.5-4 hours later, first-line medicine for cataplexy and EDS
specific_drugs: Sodium oxybate 4.5-9 g/night in two divided doses (brand: Xyrem)
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.effectiveness: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial in narcolepsy-cataplexy patients previously stabilised on sodium oxybate, abrupt blinded withdrawal to placebo caused cataplexy attacks to rebound to a median of 21 attacks over 2 weeks, versus a median of 0 attacks over 2 weeks in patients continued on sodium oxybate (p<0.001) (Sleep Med 2004, PMID 15033130). A separate double-blind, placebo-controlled study (n=228) additionally demonstrated dose-dependent increases in slow-wave (stage 3/4) sleep (median +52.5 minutes at the 9 g/night dose) and reduced nocturnal awakenings versus placebo (J Clin Sleep Med 2010, PMID 21206549). Sodium oxybate carries an AASM strong recommendation for adult narcolepsy (J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 34743789).
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.reason_why: Sodium oxybate acts via GABA-B and GHB receptors to consolidate fragmented, REM-intrusion-prone nocturnal sleep into deeper, more continuous slow-wave sleep; because narcolepsy's daytime symptoms (sleepiness, cataplexy) are worsened by poor, fragmented nighttime sleep and abnormal REM-sleep boundary control, restoring consolidated nocturnal sleep architecture reduces both EDS and cataplexy the following day.
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.important_caveat: Sodium oxybate is a Schedule III/tightly REMS-restricted controlled substance (chemically related to the date-rape drug GHB) requiring pharmacy-restricted dispensing, has a high sodium content relevant to cardiovascular/renal risk (addressed by the low-sodium formulation below), and carries a real risk of respiratory depression, especially with alcohol or other CNS depressants -- it must be taken lying in bed due to rapid sedation onset.
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.real_working_solution: Nightly sodium oxybate is a real first-line option, particularly effective when both cataplexy and disrupted nocturnal sleep/EDS need to be addressed with a single medicine.
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.source: Sleep Med 2004 (PMID 15033130); J Clin Sleep Med 2010 (PMID 21206549); AASM guideline, J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 34743789)

narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.name: Low-Sodium Oxybate (Xywav) -- Same Active Anticataplectic/EDS Drug as Sodium Oxybate With Approximately 92% Less Sodium
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.type: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) mixed-cation (calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium) salt, oral solution, first-line medicine for cataplexy and EDS in patients where chronic sodium load is a concern
specific_drugs: Low-sodium oxybate 4.5-9 g/night in two divided doses (brand: Xywav)
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.effectiveness: Low-sodium oxybate delivers the same active gamma-hydroxybutyrate moiety as sodium oxybate at an equivalent dose; its efficacy and safety were established in a dedicated randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 withdrawal trial in narcolepsy with cataplexy, and a long-term open-label extension of that trial confirmed sustained safety/tolerability with continued use (CNS Drugs 2023, PMID 36947322).
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.reason_why: Identical GABA-B/GHB-receptor mechanism to sodium oxybate (same active drug); reformulated with calcium, magnesium, and potassium cations replacing most of the sodium to cut daily sodium intake by approximately 92% at an equivalent oxybate dose.
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.important_caveat: Same controlled-substance/REMS, respiratory-depression, and bedtime-dosing caveats as sodium oxybate apply; it is a reformulation, not a new mechanism, so patients already well-controlled on sodium oxybate without cardiovascular/renal sodium concerns do not need to switch.
narc_cataplexy_oxybate_medicines.real_working_solution: Preferred over standard sodium oxybate for patients with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or renal impairment, where the chronic high sodium load of the original formulation is a genuine concern.

narc_cataplexy_offlabel_antidepressant_m.name: Venlafaxine -- Real Widely-Used Off-Label Anticataplectic Antidepressant (No Placebo-Controlled RCT; Evidence From Clinical Practice and Case Series Only)
narc_cataplexy_offlabel_antidepressant_m.type: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), oral, off-label second-line/adjunct medicine for cataplexy
narc_cataplexy_offlabel_antidepressant_m.effectiveness: No placebo-controlled randomised trial of venlafaxine for cataplexy has been published; its use is supported only by clinical experience and case series/case reports, including a paediatric case series in which venlafaxine was added in 4 of 8 children with narcolepsy and symptomatic improvement was reported after therapeutic adjustment (Sleep Sci 2014, PMID 26483902), and a 2026 case report in which venlafaxine added after methylphenidate led to substantial symptomatic improvement of cataplexy (J Sleep Res 2026, PMID 42215284).
narc_cataplexy_offlabel_antidepressant_m.reason_why: Venlafaxine increases synaptic norepinephrine (and, at higher doses, serotonin); noradrenergic tone is believed to suppress the REM-sleep muscle-atonia circuits that are pathologically triggered by emotion in cataplexy, the presumed mechanism shared with older tricyclic antidepressants historically used for the same purpose.
narc_cataplexy_offlabel_antidepressant_m.important_caveat: Because no RCT-level efficacy percentage exists, this medicine is NOT included in the numeric effectiveness_ranked_table below. Abrupt discontinuation of venlafaxine (or other noradrenergic antidepressants) can precipitate severe rebound cataplexy ('status cataplecticus'), so it must never be stopped abruptly.
narc_cataplexy_offlabel_antidepressant_m.confidence: low (no RCT; case-series/case-report level evidence only)

narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.name: Oveporexton (TAK-861) -- Real First-in-Class Selective Orexin Receptor-2 (OX2R) Agonist, the Emerging Closest-to-Disease-Modifying Approach
narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.type: Selective orexin/hypocretin receptor-2 agonist, oral, replaces the missing orexin signal directly rather than boosting downstream monoamine/histamine wake-promoting tone
specific_drugs: Oveporexton (TAK-861), oral, twice-daily dosing tested at 1-2 mg BID in phase 3 trials
narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.effectiveness: In two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in narcolepsy type 1 (First Light, n=168; Radiant Light, n=105; ages 16-70), 12 weeks of oveporexton produced: Maintenance of Wakefulness Test mean sleep-latency improvement of 14.3-19.8 minutes (vs -0.4 to -0.8 minutes with placebo); Epworth Sleepiness Scale reduction of 9.7-11.8 points (vs 1.5-1.7 points with placebo); and a median 79.0%-88.8% reduction in weekly cataplexy rate ('Oveporexton for Narcolepsy Type 1 -- Results from Two Phase 3 Trials', N Engl J Med 2026, PMID 42714024). This is the largest reported symptom-control effect size of any narcolepsy type 1 therapy to date, and oveporexton has been described as the first-in-class OX2R agonist reaching approval for narcolepsy type 1 (Drug Discov Ther 2026, PMID 42618292).
narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.reason_why: Oveporexton directly activates orexin receptor-2 (OX2R) on downstream wake-promoting neurons (histaminergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic arousal nuclei) that narcolepsy type 1 patients can no longer stimulate naturally because their own hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons have been destroyed -- it substitutes pharmacologically for the missing signal at its natural receptor, rather than non-specifically boosting monoamine tone the way stimulants, modafinil, or pitolisant do, which is the proposed reason its effect size on both EDS and cataplexy substantially exceeds that of every earlier drug class.
narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.important_caveat: This is real receptor-replacement pharmacotherapy, not neuron regeneration: it does not reverse the underlying autoimmune destruction of hypocretin neurons and requires continued twice-daily dosing; adverse events were more frequent with oveporexton than placebo (86-89% vs 43-54%), most commonly increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia. An earlier first-generation oral OX2R agonist, TAK-994, showed comparable efficacy in early trials but was discontinued in 2022 due to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity; oveporexton was developed as a next-generation molecule with improved structural properties and minimal hepatic signal in its trials (Ann Med Surg (Lond) 2026, PMID 41497057).
narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.real_working_solution: Oveporexton is the real closest-to-disease-modifying option currently available: it does not cure narcolepsy, but functionally restores near-normal wakefulness (ESS reductions approaching normalisation) and near-eliminates cataplexy for many patients, exceeding what any prior single medicine achieves.
narc_emerging_orexin_receptor_agonist_me.source: N Engl J Med 2026 (PMID 42714024); Drug Discov Ther 2026 (PMID 42618292); Ann Med Surg (Lond) 2026 (PMID 41497057)

effectiveness_ranked_table.ranking_note: Each row's effectiveness_pct measures a DIFFERENT specific real trial endpoint (cataplexy-rate reduction, CGI responder rate, or ESS-normalisation responder rate) exactly as stated in that row's metric -- compare rows only within the same endpoint type, not across endpoint types. Oveporexton is placed first because it is the newest, largest-effect-size, and closest-to-mechanism (direct orexin-receptor replacement) therapy reported to date. Low-sodium oxybate (Xywav) is not given a separate row because it is pharmacologically identical (same active GHB moiety) to sodium oxybate at an equivalent dose. Venlafaxine and armodafinil are excluded from this table because no placebo-controlled RCT has established a numeric efficacy percentage for either in narcolepsy (see exhaustive_medicine_survey for their case-series/guideline-grade-only evidence).

The largest reported effect size of any narcolepsy therapy to date.
ranked_high_to_low.source: N Engl J Med 2026 (PMID 42714024)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cataplexy attacks fell to a median of 0 per 2 weeks while continued on treatment, vs a median of 21 per 2 weeks after blinded withdrawal to placebo (p<0.001) -- reflecting complete suppression of attacks in the median treated patient in this randomised withdrawal-design trial.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Sleep Med 2004 (PMID 15033130)
