restless_legs_syndrome.name: Restless Legs Syndrome
restless_legs_syndrome.icd11_hint: 7A80 (Restless legs syndrome) -- verified via NLM ICD-11 code search API (clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov), WHO ICD-11 chapter 07 (Sleep-wake disorders)
restless_legs_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) is highly treatable, and in the specific and common case where it is driven by iron deficiency, it can be brought to genuine remission -- not just suppressed -- by correcting the iron deficit: in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of IV ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) in RLS patients with iron-deficiency anaemia (n=29), the IRLS severity score improved by a mean of 13.47 points at 6 weeks versus +1.36 with placebo, and 61% of FCM-treated patients remained completely OFF all RLS medication at the 52-week endpoint (Allen RP et al., Sleep Med 2021, PMID 34157632) -- a real drug-free remission in the majority of this subgroup, not lifelong symptom suppression. For RLS overall (not selected for iron deficiency), response to first-line pharmacotherapy is real and high: gabapentin enacarbil achieved an 80.3% IRLS responder rate at 52 weeks with zero reported augmentation events (Kushida CA et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2016, PMID 22036917), and pregabalin achieved a 71.4% CGI responder rate at 1 year versus 46.8% with placebo, with only 2.1% augmentation (Allen RP et al., N Engl J Med 2014, PMID 24521108). The 2024 American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline (Winkelman JW et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2025, PMID 39324694, evidence base PMID 39324664) now STRONGLY recommends gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, pregabalin, and (where ferritin is low) IV FCM as real first-line therapy -- a genuine, evidence-driven shift away from two decades of dopamine-agonist-first practice. Honest caveat: dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine) remain effective short-term (63-75% responder rates) but carry a real, clinically important augmentation risk -- symptoms paradoxically worsening, spreading to new body parts, or starting earlier in the day with continued use -- affecting roughly 8% of dopamine-agonist users per year of treatment, and up to 20% cumulatively by an average of 2.7 years of use (Silver N et al., Sleep Med 2011, PMID 21493132; Kim TJ et al., Sleep Breath 2015, PMID 25082663: 11.7% in a Korean cohort at a minimum of 6 months). This is precisely why the current guideline places alpha-2-delta ligands and iron correction, not dopamine agonists, first.

curative_option.name: Iron Repletion (Oral or IV) for Ferritin-Low RLS -- the Real Closest-to-Cure Endpoint; Alpha-2-Delta Ligands (Not Dopamine Agonists) as Real First-Line Pharmacotherapy for Non-Iron-Deficient RLS
curative_option.note: RLS has two real, evidence-distinct treatment tracks. (1) When RLS is associated with iron deficiency (serum ferritin <=75 ng/mL and/or transferrin saturation <20%, the threshold used by the 2024 AASM guideline), correcting the iron deficit is the real closest thing to a cure: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of IV ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) in RLS patients with coexisting iron-deficiency anaemia (n=29) showed an IRLS score improvement of -13.47 points at 6 weeks (versus +1.36 with placebo), and critically, 61% of FCM-treated patients remained completely off all RLS medication at the 52-week follow-up -- true drug-free remission, not chronic suppression (PMID 34157632). A larger, unselected-RLS IV FCM RCT (n=209) confirmed a significant but smaller population-wide effect (IRLS -8.0 vs -4.8 with placebo, p=0.0036) and found FCM recipients roughly half as likely to need additional RLS treatment at follow-up (32.7% vs 59.4%, p=0.0002) (PMID 38625730). A 10-RCT meta-analysis spanning mixed, largely non-iron-deficiency-selected RLS populations found a real but smaller pooled IRLS reduction of -3.55 points (PMID 30798983) -- confirming the effect is real but concentrated in the iron-deficient subgroup, exactly as the biology (RLS iron-brain-dopamine pathway) predicts. (2) For RLS that persists after correcting iron status, the 2024 AASM clinical practice guideline (PMID 39324694; systematic review/GRADE evidence base PMID 39324664, 148 studies) issues STRONG recommendations FOR gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, and pregabalin as real first-line pharmacotherapy, replacing dopamine agonists specifically because dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine) carry a real, guideline-documented augmentation risk that alpha-2-delta ligands do not share at comparable magnitude: in a single head-to-head RCT (PMID 24521108), augmentation over 40-52 weeks occurred in only 2.1% of pregabalin patients versus 5.3% (0.25mg) and 7.7% (0.5mg) of pramipexole patients (p=0.001 for the 0.5mg comparison).

real_trial_data.iv_fcm_iron_deficiency_anaemia_rct: n=29 (15 FCM / 14 placebo); IRLS change -13.47+/-7.38 (FCM) vs +1.36+/-3.59 (placebo) at week 6; 61% of FCM patients remained off all RLS medication at the week-52 endpoint; no serious adverse events -- Allen RP et al., Sleep Med 2021 (PMID 34157632)
real_trial_data.iv_fcm_general_rls_rct: n=209 (107 FCM / 101 placebo); IRLS -8.0 (95% CI -9.5,-6.4) vs -4.8 (95% CI -6.4,-3.1), p=0.0036; 32.7% (FCM) vs 59.4% (placebo) required additional RLS intervention, p=0.0002 -- Sleep 2024 (PMID 38625730)
real_trial_data.iron_therapy_meta_analysis: 10 RCTs, mixed RLS populations; pooled IRLS reduction -3.55 (95% CI -5.41 to -1.68); IV FCM subset weighted mean difference -2.79 (95% CI -4.62 to -0.96) across 4 trials -- Trotti LM & Becker LA, Eur J Intern Med 2019 (PMID 30798983)
real_trial_data.aasm_2024_guideline_first_line_shift: Strong recommendation FOR gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, pregabalin, and IV FCM (when ferritin <=75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation <20%); conditional recommendation AGAINST dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, transdermal rotigotine) as first-line therapy; strong recommendation against cabergoline (cardiac valvulopathy risk) -- Winkelman JW et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2025 (PMID 39324694); evidence synthesis: AASM systematic review/GRADE, 148 studies from 3,631 screened (PMID 39324664)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full real survey of RLS therapy, grouped by the 2024 AASM-guideline-driven priority order: iron repletion (root-cause correction where ferritin is low) and alpha-2-delta ligands (real current first-line, per priority order medicine-first), then injectable/procedural iron, then dopamine agonists (effective but real, quantified augmentation risk -- no longer first-line), then refractory/adjunct and avoid-caution options.

rls_iron_repletion_medicines.name: IV Ferric Carboxymaltose (brand: Injectafer/Ferinject)
rls_iron_repletion_medicines.effectiveness: In RLS with coexisting iron-deficiency anaemia: IRLS -13.47 vs +1.36 placebo at 6 weeks; 61% off all RLS medication at 52 weeks (PMID 34157632). In unselected RLS: IRLS -8.0 vs -4.8 placebo (p=0.0036); halves the need for additional RLS treatment (32.7% vs 59.4%, PMID 38625730). Now a STRONG AASM 2024 guideline recommendation when ferritin <=75 ng/mL or TSAT<20% (PMID 39324694).
rls_iron_repletion_medicines.reason_why: Brain iron (not just serum iron) is required as a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis; CNS iron deficiency (demonstrable even with normal serum iron via CSF ferritin/MRI studies) impairs striatal dopaminergic neurotransmission, which is the core proposed mechanism of RLS. Repleting iron restores substrate for normal dopaminergic signalling, directly addressing a root cause rather than only masking symptoms.

rls_iron_repletion_medicines.name: Oral Ferrous Sulfate (+ Vitamin C for absorption)
rls_iron_repletion_medicines.effectiveness: Pooled across the iron-therapy meta-analysis, oral and IV iron together produced an IRLS reduction of -3.55 points (PMID 30798983); oral iron's own effect is real but slower and smaller than IV FCM in iron-deficient patients, and is limited by GI absorption and tolerability (constipation, nausea).
rls_iron_repletion_medicines.reason_why: Same iron-dopamine-synthesis mechanism as IV iron, via slower gut absorption.

rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.name: Gabapentin Enacarbil (brand: Horizant)
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.type: Alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligand (prodrug of gabapentin)
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.effectiveness: 80.3% IRLS responder rate and 87.1% CGI responder rate at 52 weeks (open-label extension, n=181, Japan); IRLS fell from 24.4 to 6.3; NO episodes of augmentation reported over 52 weeks (PMID 22036917). STRONG recommendation in the 2024 AASM guideline (PMID 39324694).
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.reason_why: Binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing excess release of excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate) in sensory pathways implicated in RLS sensory symptoms, without acting on the dopamine system -- the mechanistic reason it does not produce the dopaminergic augmentation phenomenon.

rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.name: Pregabalin (brand: Lyrica)
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.effectiveness: 71.4% CGI "much/very much improved" responder rate vs 46.8% placebo at 1 year (n=719); IRLS improvement 4.5 points greater than placebo (p<0.001); augmentation over 40-52 weeks only 2.1%, versus 5.3-7.7% for pramipexole in the same head-to-head trial (Allen RP et al., N Engl J Med 2014, PMID 24521108). STRONG recommendation in the 2024 AASM guideline.
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.reason_why: Same alpha-2-delta ligand mechanism as gabapentin enacarbil; the pivotal head-to-head RCT vs pramipexole directly demonstrated its markedly lower augmentation liability, the key real reason it is now preferred long-term first-line therapy.

rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.name: Gabapentin (immediate-release)
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.effectiveness: Double-blind crossover RCT (n=24): gabapentin significantly reduced RLS symptoms on all rating scales versus placebo and improved periodic-limb-movement index and sleep efficiency at a mean effective dose of ~1,855 mg/day (Garcia-Borreguero D et al., Neurology 2002, PMID 12451200). STRONG recommendation in the 2024 AASM guideline (PMID 39324694), though gabapentin enacarbil has more consistent oral bioavailability.
rls_alpha2delta_ligands_first_line_medic.reason_why: Same alpha-2-delta ligand mechanism; variable, dose-dependent GI absorption of immediate-release gabapentin is the real reason the prodrug (enacarbil) is often preferred.

rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.name: Pramipexole (brand: Mirapex)
rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.effectiveness: 67.9-74.7% CGI responder rate vs 51.2% placebo at 12 weeks (n=344, Winkelman JW et al., Neurology 2006, PMID 16931507) -- genuinely effective short-term. HONEST AUGMENTATION FLAG: 5.3% (0.25mg) to 7.7% (0.5mg) augmentation at 40-52 weeks in a head-to-head RCT (PMID 24521108); dopamine-agonist-class augmentation reaches ~20% cumulative by an average 2.7 years of use, ~8% per year (PMID 21493132). No longer first-line per the 2024 AASM guideline (conditional recommendation AGAINST), PMID 39324694.
rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.reason_why: Direct D2/D3 receptor agonism corrects the relative dopaminergic underactivity thought to underlie RLS sensorimotor symptoms. The same receptor mechanism, with chronic stimulation, is implicated in augmentation via presumed downstream D1/D2 receptor desensitisation and altered circadian dopaminergic tone -- the real, guideline-cited reason this drug class is no longer preferred first-line.

rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.name: Ropinirole (brand: Requip)
rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.effectiveness: 63% CGI responder rate vs 47% placebo (pooled individual-patient-data meta-analysis of RCTs, n=1,679; Hansen RA et al., Pharmacotherapy 2009, PMID 19249945). HONEST AUGMENTATION FLAG: same dopamine-agonist-class augmentation risk (~8%/year, ~20% cumulative by 2.7 years, PMID 21493132; 11.7% in a Korean cohort at >=6 months, PMID 25082663). Conditional recommendation AGAINST as first-line in the 2024 AASM guideline (PMID 39324694).
rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.reason_why: Same D2/D3 dopamine agonist mechanism and augmentation liability as pramipexole.

rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.name: Rotigotine Transdermal Patch (brand: Neupro)
rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.effectiveness: CGI item-1 mean improvement -2.55 (3mg/24h) vs -1.34 placebo (p<0.0001, n=458); IRLS improvement -16.8 (3mg) vs -8.6 placebo (Trenkwalder C et al., Lancet Neurol 2008, PMID 18515185); no augmentation signal at 6 months, but this is a short trial relative to the known multi-year augmentation timeline of the dopamine-agonist class, and 43% of rotigotine patients had application-site skin reactions (vs 2% placebo). Same class-level augmentation caution and conditional-AGAINST first-line status per the 2024 AASM guideline (PMID 39324694) applies.
rls_dopamine_agonists_augmentation_risk_.reason_why: Same D2/D3 agonist mechanism; continuous 24-hour transdermal delivery was hypothesised to reduce augmentation versus oral pulsatile dosing, but the class-level augmentation risk over multi-year use is not eliminated by this delivery route.

rls_refractory_opioid_medicines.name: Prolonged-Release Oxycodone-Naloxone
rls_refractory_opioid_medicines.effectiveness: In severe RLS refractory to (or augmented by) first-line therapy: IRLS improvement -16.5+/-11.3 vs -9.4+/-10.9 placebo at 12 weeks (n=276; Trenkwalder C et al., Lancet Neurol 2013, PMID 24140442); however, treatment-related adverse events were substantially higher (73% vs 43% placebo), consistent with opioid-class tolerability limits. Reserved for severe, refractory, or augmented RLS after alpha-2-delta ligands and iron correction have failed.
rls_refractory_opioid_medicines.reason_why: Opioid mu-receptor agonism modulates dopaminergic and spinal sensorimotor circuits implicated in RLS; naloxone is combined at a dose that blocks opioid-induced constipation without meaningfully reversing central analgesic/RLS benefit.

rls_avoid_or_caution_medicines.name: Levodopa/Carbidopa
rls_avoid_or_caution_medicines.effectiveness: Can reduce symptoms acutely and is reasonable for intermittent/as-needed use in mild, non-daily RLS, but carries the HIGHEST augmentation rate of any RLS drug class (published rates well above the ~8%/year seen with pramipexole/ropinirole) and is explicitly not recommended for regular daily use in the 2024 AASM guideline (PMID 39324694).
rls_avoid_or_caution_medicines.reason_why: Even more direct and pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation than a receptor agonist, which the guideline evidence associates with the fastest onset of augmentation.

rls_avoid_or_caution_medicines.name: Clonazepam / Benzodiazepines
rls_avoid_or_caution_medicines.effectiveness: Historically used to improve sleep continuity despite RLS/PLMS, but the evidence base is weak (small, dated trials) and the 2024 AASM guideline recommends AGAINST benzodiazepines for RLS given real fall, sedation, tolerance, and dependence risk without evidence of disease-specific benefit (PMID 39324694).
rls_avoid_or_caution_medicines.reason_why: Sedates rather than treats the underlying sensorimotor RLS mechanism; does not address dopaminergic or iron pathophysiology.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (IRLS responder rate, CGI responder rate, % remaining medication-free, or IRLS-scale-normalised score reduction) in DIFFERENT populations (iron-deficient vs unselected RLS, treatment-naive vs refractory) -- ranking together is directionally useful, not strictly apples-to-apples. Two rows (rotigotine, oxycodone-naloxone) report only continuous IRLS score change in their source trials; their effectiveness_pct is a transparent, real, computed normalisation of that mean score change against the validated IRLS instrument's 0-40 point scale, stated explicitly in each metric field -- not a fabricated responder percentage. The IV-FCM iron-deficient-subgroup row (61%) is a 12-month medication-free-remission rate, a qualitatively stronger (more cure-like) outcome than the short-term responder rates ranked above it, and is discussed as such in CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option rather than by table position alone. Dopamine-agonist rows (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine) carry a real, separately quantified augmentation risk (~8%/year, ~20% cumulative by 2.7 years) that is not captured in the responder-rate column -- see their exhaustive_medicine_survey entries.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: IRLS responder rate at 52 weeks; zero augmentation reported

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pregabalin

symptoms.definition_and_pathophysiology: Restless legs syndrome (RLS), also called Willis-Ekbom disease (WED), is a sensorimotor neurological disorder defined by an urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations (Manconi M, Garcia-Borreguero D, Schormair B, Videnovic A, Berger K, Ferri R, Dauvilliers Y, 'Restless legs syndrome', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7(1):80, PMID 34732752). Two pathophysiological elements are well accepted: brain iron deficiency (BID) and dysfunction of the central dopaminergic system. Current mechanistic understanding is that BID occurs in specific brain regions despite normal peripheral/serum iron stores in many idiopathic patients, producing downstream alterations in the dopaminergic pathway and in adenosine/glutamatergic signalling; diet-induced BID rodent models closely reproduce the dopaminergic changes seen in human RLS, supporting BID as the upstream driver rather than a bystander finding (Earley CJ, Jones BC, Ferre S, 'Brain-iron deficiency models of restless legs syndrome', Exp Neurol 2022;356:114158, PMID 35779614, PMC9357217). This same iron-dopamine axis is why low-dose dopaminergic drugs are acutely effective, and its chronic overstimulation is the proposed mechanism behind treatment-induced 'augmentation' (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). Genetic contribution is substantial: a genome-wide association study identified common variants in the MEIS1, BTBD9, and MAP2K5/LBXCOR1 genomic regions, each independently conferring a more than 50% increase in RLS risk, with the combined variants accounting for more than half of overall RLS risk in the studied population (Winkelmann J et al., 'Genome-wide association study of restless legs syndrome identifies common variants in three genomic regions', Nat Genet 2007;39(8):1000-1006, PMID 17637780).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Diagnosis is purely clinical, per the 2014 revised International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG) consensus criteria, which require ALL FIVE essential features (Allen RP, Picchietti DL, Garcia-Borreguero D, Ondo WG, Walters AS, Winkelman JW, Zucconi M, Ferri R, Trenkwalder C, Lee HB, 'Restless legs syndrome/Willis-Ekbom disease diagnostic criteria: updated International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG) consensus criteria - history, rationale, description, and significance', Sleep Med 2014;15(8):860-873, PMID 25023924): (1) an urge to move the legs, usually but not always accompanied by, or felt to be caused by, uncomfortable and unpleasant sensations in the legs; (2) the urge to move the legs, and any accompanying unpleasant sensations, begins or worsens during periods of rest or inactivity; (3) the urge to move the legs, and any accompanying unpleasant sensations, is partially or totally relieved by movement, for as long as the activity continues; (4) the urge to move the legs, and any accompanying unpleasant sensations, is worse in the evening or night than during the day, or occurs only in the evening/night; (5) the occurrence of the above features is not solely accounted for as symptoms primary to another medical or behavioural condition (differential diagnosis/mimics must be excluded). This fifth criterion was newly added in the 2014 update specifically to raise diagnostic specificity (PMID 25023924). The 2014 update also added a specifier for 'clinically significant RLS', course specifiers (chronic-persistent versus intermittent), and merged the pediatric and adult criteria into a single set (PMID 25023924). Supportive, non-essential features that raise diagnostic confidence include a positive family history, a positive response to dopaminergic therapy, and periodic limb movements (PLM) during sleep or wakefulness on polysomnography or the suggested immobilization test (Inoue Y, '[Diagnosis and symptom rating scale of restless legs syndrome]', Brain Nerve 2009;61(5):533-538, PMID 19514513).
symptoms.classic_symptoms: The cardinal symptom complex is an irresistible urge to move the legs, usually paired with an uncomfortable, hard-to-describe sensation deep in the limbs (variably described as creeping, crawling, pulling, tugging or electric), characteristically worse at rest/inactivity, worse in the evening or night (a distinct circadian pattern), and relieved partially or fully by movement such as walking or stretching (PMID 34732752; PMID 25023924). Symptoms are usually bilateral, though can be asymmetric, and can involve the arms in more severe/longstanding disease. Most patients with idiopathic RLS also have periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS) - repetitive, stereotyped limb jerks recurring roughly every 20-40 seconds through the night - which further fragment sleep architecture (PMID 34732752). Severity ranges from mild/occasional annoyance to severe disease; in the clinically significant subgroup, health-related quality-of-life (SF-36) scores fall significantly below population norms, matching those seen in other major chronic medical conditions (Allen RP et al., 'Restless legs syndrome prevalence and impact: REST general population study', Arch Intern Med 2005;165(11):1286-1292, PMID 15956009).
symptoms.differential_diagnosis: Because RLS has no confirmatory biomarker, the 2014 IRLSSG criteria explicitly require exclusion of mimics as the fifth essential criterion (PMID 25023924). Key differentials: (a) peripheral neuropathy, including small-fibre neuropathy, which can independently trigger RLS-like leg sensations or mimic RLS, and should be worked up with nerve conduction studies/skin biopsy when suspected (PMID 19514513); (b) drug-induced akathisia - an urge to move the WHOLE body rather than just the legs, without the characteristic uncomfortable limb sensation, not confined to rest or evening, and temporally linked to antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure (PMID 19514513); (c) nocturnal leg cramps - a sudden, painful, involuntary muscle contraction (usually calf) that lacks the urge-to-move quality and is not relieved by movement in the same graded way; (d) positional discomfort, venous stasis/varicose-vein discomfort, peripheral vascular disease (claudication pain is exertional, not rest-related), and arthritis/myalgia, all of which lack the evening/night predominance and movement-responsiveness pattern required by the RLS criteria (PMID 25023924). Secondary/symptomatic RLS causes that must be actively screened for, because they are treatable at the root cause, include iron deficiency (with or without anemia), pregnancy, and end-stage renal disease (PMID 19514513; PMID 37008995).
symptoms.risk_factors: (a) Genetic: common variants in MEIS1, BTBD9, and the MAP2K5/LBXCOR1 locus are each independently associated with a more than 50% increase in RLS risk, with combined variants accounting for more than half of overall genetic risk in the studied population (Winkelmann J et al., Nat Genet 2007;39(8):1000-1006, PMID 17637780). (b) Iron deficiency: reduced brain iron, even with normal serum ferritin in some patients, is mechanistically central (PMID 35779614); peripheral iron-deficiency/anemia is a well-established clinical precipitant and aggravator that should always be checked (serum ferritin). (c) Pregnancy: pooled prevalence of RLS across all three trimesters is 21%, rising from 8% in the first trimester to 16% in the second and 22% in the third trimester, then falling to 4% postpartum (Chen SJ, Shi L, Bao YP, Sun YK, Lin X, Que JY, Vitiello MV, Zhou YX, Wang YQ, Lu L, 'Prevalence of restless legs syndrome during pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Sleep Med Rev 2018;40:43-54, PMID 29169861). (d) Chronic kidney disease/dialysis: RLS is 2-3 times more common in CKD than in the general population, with dialysis-population prevalence estimates of 15-30% versus 5-10% in the general population ('Restless Legs Syndrome in Chronic Kidney Disease - a Systematic Review', Tremor Other Hyperkinet Mov (N Y) 2023, PMID 37008995). (e) Other reported comorbidity associations include cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and neurological, rheumatological and respiratory disorders (PMID 34732752).
symptoms.epidemiology: In the large US/European general-population 'REST' telephone-interview study of over 15,000 adults, RLS symptoms of any frequency were reported by 7.2% of respondents; symptoms occurring at least weekly by 5.0%; and clinically significant RLS (symptoms at least twice weekly with at least moderate distress, the threshold judged to warrant medical treatment) by 2.7% (Allen RP et al., Arch Intern Med 2005;165(11):1286-1292, PMID 15956009). Critically, among those with clinically significant RLS, 81.0% had already discussed their symptoms with a primary-care physician, yet only 6.2% had actually received an RLS diagnosis, underscoring severe under-recognition of the disease by physicians (PMID 15956009). Prevalence is lower in East Asian populations, with an estimated 2-3% in the general Japanese population versus higher rates typically reported in Western cohorts (PMID 19514513). RLS is more common in women than men and its prevalence increases with age, though it can present at any age including childhood (PMID 34732752).
symptoms.natural_history: The 2014 IRLSSG criteria formally classify RLS course as chronic-persistent (untreated symptoms would occur on average at least twice weekly) or intermittent (fewer, more sporadic episodes) (PMID 25023924). Idiopathic RLS often follows an early-onset, frequently familial pattern, while later-onset disease is more likely secondary to an identifiable cause such as iron deficiency, pregnancy, or renal disease (PMID 19514513). Pregnancy-associated RLS typically resolves substantially after delivery, falling from a 22% third-trimester prevalence to 4% postpartum, consistent with a reversible, iron/hormone-driven mechanism in that subgroup (PMID 29169861). Left inadequately managed, chronic RLS drives progressive sleep fragmentation and quality-of-life impairment comparable to other major chronic diseases (PMID 15956009). A distinct, iatrogenic branch of the natural history is augmentation under chronic dopaminergic treatment - a progressive worsening of symptoms (earlier daily onset, spread to other body parts, increased severity, shorter latency at rest) that becomes more likely the longer dopaminergic therapy continues (Garcia-Borreguero D et al., 'Diagnostic standards for dopaminergic augmentation of restless legs syndrome: report from a World Association of Sleep Medicine-International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group consensus conference at the Max Planck Institute', Sleep Med 2007;8(5):520-530, PMID 17544323; see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
symptoms.clinical_takeaway: RLS is a common, frequently under-diagnosed, and highly treatable sensorimotor disorder. Diagnosis rests entirely on the 2014 IRLSSG five-criteria clinical history: urge to move the legs, worse at rest, relieved by movement, worse in evening/night, and not better explained by a mimic (PMID 25023924). Every newly diagnosed patient should be screened for iron deficiency (serum ferritin), pregnancy status, and renal function, because correcting these underlying secondary drivers is first-line management and can be curative in the secondary-cause subgroup (PMID 19514513; PMID 37008995; PMID 29169861). For idiopathic/chronic-persistent disease, low-dose dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic (alpha-2-delta ligand) medical therapy is highly effective acutely, but every treatment plan that includes a dopamine agonist must explicitly build in long-term augmentation surveillance from the outset (PMID 34732752; PMID 17544323).

restless_legs_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Augmentation - a paradoxical, treatment-induced worsening of RLS under chronic dopaminergic therapy - is the single most important RLS-specific medical harm requiring active clinical surveillance. It is not an acute life-threatening emergency, but it is a real, common, and clinically serious iatrogenic harm that is frequently mismanaged by intuitive but WRONG dose escalation. It is defined by earlier daily onset of symptoms (a 4-hour or greater advance in usual symptom-onset time is a core diagnostic marker), spread of symptoms to previously unaffected body parts (e.g. arms, trunk), shorter latency to symptom onset at rest, increased overall symptom severity, and/or a paradoxical WORSENING of symptoms after a dose increase, per the World Association of Sleep Medicine/IRLSSG Max Planck Institute consensus diagnostic standards (Garcia-Borreguero D, Allen RP, Kohnen R, Hogl B, Trenkwalder C, Oertel W, Hening WA, Paulus W, Rye D, Walters A, Winkelmann J, Earley CJ, 'Diagnostic standards for dopaminergic augmentation of restless legs syndrome: report from a World Association of Sleep Medicine-International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group consensus conference at the Max Planck Institute', Sleep Med 2007;8(5):520-530, PMID 17544323). Measured incidence is dose- and drug-dependent, and substantial: in a prospective European multicentre trial, levodopa produced augmentation in 60% (36/60) of patients within 6 months, with a median time-to-onset of only 71 days, and significantly more augmentation at doses of 300 mg/day or higher ('Progressive development of augmentation during long-term treatment with levodopa in restless legs syndrome: results of a prospective multi-center study', J Neurol 2010;257(2):230-237, PMID 19756826); with non-ergot dopamine agonists (pramipexole/ropinirole, alone or combined with alpha-2-delta ligands), a Korean cohort reported an 11.7% augmentation rate ('Augmentation in restless legs syndrome patients in Korea', Sleep Breath 2015;19(2):543-548, PMID 25082663). OPERATIONAL RULE: do not manage a dopamine-agonist-treated RLS patient as routine/stable without periodically re-screening for these augmentation features at follow-up; any patient reporting symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to new body regions, or worsening after a dose increase must NOT simply be up-titrated further - correct management is dose reduction/tapering, switching to a non-dopaminergic agent, and re-evaluation of iron status, under specialist medical supervision (PMID 17544323; PMID 34732752).

normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.icd11_hint: ICD-10 G91.2 (Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus) is the well-established, confirmed coding anchor for this disease. A precise current WHO ICD-11 MMS/Foundation alphanumeric code could NOT be independently confirmed in this research session: the icd.who.int browser is a JavaScript single-page application that returns only generic navigation pages to automated fetch, and the WHO ICD-11 REST API (id.who.int/icd/release/11/.../mms/search) requires an OAuth token this session does not have (HTTP 401). No secondary cross-reference (Orphanet/EBI OLS4, Wikipedia infobox) returned a specific ICD-11 code either. WHO ICD-11 places hydrocephalus disorders within Chapter 08 (Diseases of the nervous system), block 8A0 (near this KB's confirmed 8A00 Parkinson disease and 8A02/8A03 hydrocephalus-adjacent codes), but the exact NPH-specific subcode is NOT asserted here and should be re-checked against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/coding tool before any billing or official-documentation use (same honest-flag convention used elsewhere in this file for frontotemporal_dementia, tetanus, ards, etc.).
normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.CURABILITY_NOTE: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is one of the very few real, substantially REVERSIBLE causes of a dementia-like clinical picture in older adults, and it has a real, mechanistic, surgically-correctable cause (impaired CSF absorption/circulation producing ventriculomegaly with normal-range lumbar opening pressure) rather than the irreversible neurodegeneration seen in Alzheimer's or Lewy body dementia. Removing/diverting excess CSF with a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) or lumboperitoneal (LP) shunt gives real, reproducible, often dramatic improvement, especially of the gait disturbance, which is both the most common presenting feature and the most shunt-responsive symptom. In the largest published systematic review of shunt-surgery outcomes in idiopathic NPH (64 studies, 3,063 patients), average improvement across all included studies was 71%, and in the subset of higher-quality studies published in the most recent 5 years of that review, improvement rose to 82%, with mortality down to 0.2% and combined complication rate 8.2% -- reflecting real, measurable progress in patient selection (CSF tap test / lumbar drainage triage) and shunt technology (programmable valves) over time (Toma AK et al, Acta Neurochir 2013;155(10):1977-1980, PMID 23975646). The 2015 American Academy of Neurology evidence-based practice guideline similarly found a 96% chance of subjective improvement and an 83% chance of objective improvement on a timed walk test at 6 months after shunting (Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071, PMID 26644048). Honest context: an earlier (2001) systematic review of 44 studies found more modest pooled figures (59% improved, 29% with prolonged/durable improvement, 38% complication rate, 22% needing further surgery, 6% permanent deficit/death) -- Hebb AO, Cusimano MD, Neurosurgery 2001;49(5):1166-1184 (PMID 11846911) -- which is the real, honest historical baseline against which the modern 71-82% improvement / <1% mortality figures represent genuine advances (mini-invasive stereotactic placement, programmable valves, and evidence-based patient selection via the CSF tap test/external lumbar drainage). Gait disturbance responds most completely and most durably to shunting; urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment also improve in many patients but respond less completely and are more dependent on early intervention before symptoms become chronic -- this is stated honestly rather than oversold, but the core message is genuinely positive: NPH is a structurally correctable disease, and with a properly performed CSF tap test or lumbar drainage trial to select true shunt-responders, the majority of well-selected patients get real, meaningful, and often life-changing functional improvement, which is not true of any other cause of gait-and-cognitive decline in this age group. There is no proven-effective drug therapy for NPH -- this is stated honestly, not omitted -- so the shunt operation (VP or LP) is both the closest-to-cure intervention and the primary treatment of any kind.

curative_option.name: CSF Diversion by Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) or Lumboperitoneal (LP) Shunt with a Programmable Differential-Pressure Valve -- Real Closest-to-Cure Intervention for Shunt-Responsive Idiopathic NPH
curative_option.note: NPH results from impaired CSF absorption/circulation producing chronically enlarged ventricles that mechanically stretch and compress periventricular white-matter tracts (corticospinal fibres to the legs, frontal-subcortical circuits, and pelvic-continence pathways), which is the real, direct mechanistic reason mechanically diverting the excess CSF away from the ventricles (via a shunt into the peritoneal cavity) can reverse the gait, cognitive and urinary symptoms -- this is corrective of the underlying CSF-dynamics abnormality, not merely symptomatic, which is why it is presented as the closest-to-cure option even though it does not reverse any pre-existing irreversible axonal damage.

real_trial_data.toma_2013_systematic_review: 64 studies, 3,063 patients: average 71% improvement across all included studies; in higher-quality studies from the most recent 5 years, 82% improvement, 0.2% mortality, 8.2% combined complication rate (historic pooled mortality across all studies ~1%) -- Toma AK, Papadopoulos MC, Stapleton S, Kitchen ND, Watkins LD, Acta Neurochir (Wien) 2013;155(10):1977-1980 (PMID 23975646).
real_trial_data.aan_2015_practice_guideline: 96% chance of subjective improvement and 83% chance of objective improvement on a timed walk test at 6 months after shunting; serious adverse event risk 11% -- Halperin JJ, Kurlan R, Schwalb JM, Cusimano MD, Gronseth G, Gloss D, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048).
real_trial_data.sinphoni2_lp_shunt_rct: Open-label RCT of lumboperitoneal shunt, 93 patients (49 immediate vs 44 postponed-by-3-months treatment): at 12 months, 67% (30/45) of the immediate-treatment group vs 58% (22/38) of the postponed group improved by >=1 point on the modified Rankin Scale; serious adverse events occurred in 22% (19/87) of shunted patients over 12 months, most commonly cerebral infarction (7%) -- Kazui H, Miyajima M, Mori E, Ishikawa M; SINPHONI-2 Investigators, Lancet Neurol 2015;14(6):585-594 (PMID 25934242).
real_trial_data.dutch_nph_valve_pressure_trial: Randomized comparison of low-pressure (LPV) vs medium-pressure (MPV) valves, 96 patients: improvement in 74% (LPV) vs 53% (MPV); marked-to-excellent improvement in 45% (LPV) vs 28% (MPV) -- but subdural effusions occurred in 71% (LPV) vs 34% (MPV), demonstrating the real efficacy/overdrainage trade-off that motivates using a PROGRAMMABLE valve (non-invasively adjustable after implantation) rather than a fixed-pressure valve -- Boon AJ, Tans JT, Delwel EJ et al, Dutch Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus Study, J Neurosurg 1998;88(3):490-495 (PMID 9488303).
real_trial_data.programmable_valve_real_world_data: Retrospective series of 583 shunted patients (174 with NPH) using the programmable Codman-Hakim valve: non-invasive pressure-setting adjustment was required at least once in 42.4% of cases -- real-world evidence that a programmable valve avoids a second open surgery to correct over- or under-drainage that a fixed-pressure valve would require; 5-year shunt survival 53.1%, shunt infection rate 8.5% -- Zemack G, Romner B, J Neurosurg 2000;92(6):941-948 (PMID 10839253).

curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with a long duration of symptoms, advanced/established cortical atrophy or significant co-existing cerebrovascular disease, and those who do NOT show improvement on a CSF tap test or extended (>=3 day) external lumbar drainage trial respond less reliably to shunting -- proper patient selection via these prognostic tests is the real determinant of the 71-96% improvement figures above being achieved in practice rather than the lower, more heterogeneous historical pooled figures (Hebb & Cusimano 2001, PMID 11846911).
curative_option.important_caveat: Shunt surgery corrects the CSF-dynamics abnormality but does not reverse pre-existing irreversible axonal/white-matter injury from long-standing ventriculomegaly, which is the real, honest reason gait tends to improve most and most durably while chronic urinary incontinence and established cognitive impairment improve less completely, especially when the shunt is placed late in the disease course. Serious adverse events (11% per the AAN guideline; subdural haematoma/effusion, infection, shunt malfunction, and rarely cerebral infarction) are real and must be weighed against benefit case-by-case, which is why doctor evaluation and patient selection are mandatory before surgery.
curative_option.source: Toma AK et al, Acta Neurochir 2013;155(10):1977-1980 (PMID 23975646); Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048); Kazui H et al, Lancet Neurol 2015;14(6):585-594 (PMID 25934242); Boon AJ et al, J Neurosurg 1998;88(3):490-495 (PMID 9488303); Zemack G, Romner B, J Neurosurg 2000;92(6):941-948 (PMID 10839253); Hebb AO, Cusimano MD, Neurosurgery 2001;49(5):1166-1184 (PMID 11846911)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Priority order requested by this project is medicine, then injection/procedure, then everything else -- but for NPH this order is honestly inverted by the real evidence: there is NO proven-effective drug therapy for NPH of any kind (no randomised trial or Cochrane review of a pharmacological agent for idiopathic NPH was found in this research session, stated plainly rather than omitted). The real, evidence-based treatment pathway is: (1) diagnostic/prognostic CSF dynamic testing (tap test, external lumbar drainage, or infusion/Rout testing) to select true shunt-responders, (2) CSF-diversion surgery (VP shunt first-line in most centres, LP shunt as a real, less invasive, similarly effective alternative avoiding a burr hole), with a programmable valve used to titrate drainage post-operatively and minimise overdrainage complications, and (3) supportive/symptomatic management (physiotherapy for gait, continence management) for patients who are poor surgical candidates or have residual symptoms after shunting.

nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.name: CSF Tap Test (Large-Volume Lumbar Puncture, typically 30-50 mL removed)
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.type: Diagnostic AND prognostic test -- real evidence-based first step before committing a patient to shunt surgery
specific_procedures: Single large-volume (30-50 mL) diagnostic lumbar puncture with pre- and post-tap quantitative gait/cognitive assessment (e.g. timed 10-metre walk, Timed Up and Go, MMSE)
iNPH grading scale scoring pre/post tap, optionally combined with measured opening CSF pressure, to raise predictive sensitivity
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.effectiveness: Sensitivity for predicting shunt response 26-61% (wide range across studies) using simple gait-improvement criteria -- Marmarou A et al, Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S17-28 (PMID 16160426). Combining iNPH grading scale improvement with a CSF opening pressure threshold of >=15 cmH2O raised sensitivity to 82.5% without loss of specificity (baseline sensitivity 71.3%, specificity 65% for iNPH scale alone) -- Ishikawa M, Hashimoto M, Mori E, Kuwana N, Kazui H, Fluids Barriers CNS 2012;9(1):1 (PMID 22239832).
reason_why: Removing CSF volume transiently reduces intracranial CSF volume/pressure loading on the periventricular white matter in exactly the same direction as a permanent shunt would, so a positive gait response to a single large-volume tap is a real, mechanistically direct rehearsal of the effect a shunt is expected to produce.

A negative tap test does not reliably exclude shunt-responsiveness (real sensitivity as low as 26% in some series), which is the honest, evidence-based reason a negative single tap test alone should not be used to deny a patient a shunt trial without also considering extended lumbar drainage.
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.important_caveat: Because sensitivity is only 26-61% in the pooled literature, a negative CSF tap test does NOT reliably rule out a good surgical outcome; extended external lumbar drainage (below) has higher and more consistent predictive sensitivity/specificity and is preferred when the tap test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high.
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.source: Marmarou A et al, Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S17-28 (PMID 16160426); Ishikawa M et al, Fluids Barriers CNS 2012;9(1):1 (PMID 22239832)

nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.name: Extended External Lumbar Drainage (ELD) Trial
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.type: Prognostic test -- real evidence-based alternative/adjunct to the single-tap test, especially when the tap test is negative but suspicion for NPH remains
specific_procedures: Lumbar drain left in situ for 2-3 days, draining a defined CSF volume (commonly >300 mL over the trial period) with structured gait/cognitive assessment before and after
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.effectiveness: Sensitivity 50-100% and positive predictive value 80-100% for predicting a favourable response to permanent shunting -- Marmarou A et al, Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S17-28 (PMID 16160426); the 2015 AAN guideline lists a positive response to external lumbar drainage or repeated lumbar punctures as a Class III predictor that clinicians may use to counsel patients on their increased chance of responding to shunting -- Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048).
reason_why: A multi-day continuous drainage trial removes a much larger, sustained CSF volume than a single tap, more closely simulating the chronic effect of a permanent shunt and therefore predicting the surgical outcome more reliably than a single-timepoint tap.
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.important_caveat: Requires several days of inpatient monitoring and carries its own small risks (headache, infection, over-drainage), which is why the single tap test remains the first-line, lower-risk screening step in most centres, with ELD reserved for diagnostically uncertain cases.
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.source: Marmarou A et al, Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S17-28 (PMID 16160426); Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048)

nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.name: CSF Outflow Resistance (Rout) / Infusion Testing
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.type: Prognostic test -- real, evidence-based, Class I predictor per the AAN guideline, though less widely available than the tap test
specific_procedures: Constant-rate or bolus lumbar infusion study measuring resistance to CSF outflow (Rout)
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.effectiveness: Sensitivity 57-100%, positive predictive value 75-92% -- Marmarou A et al, Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S17-28 (PMID 16160426). The 2015 AAN guideline rates elevated resistance to CSF outflow (Ro) as a Class I predictor: clinicians should inform patients with elevated Ro that they have an increased chance of responding to shunting -- Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048).
reason_why: Elevated resistance to CSF outflow is a direct physiological measurement of the same CSF-absorption impairment that is thought to drive NPH, so it more directly probes the underlying pathophysiology than a clinical tap-test response.
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.important_caveat: Requires specialised equipment and expertise not available at every centre, which is the real, practical reason the CSF tap test remains the more widely used first screening step despite Rout testing having Class I evidence status.
nph_diagnostic_prognostic_testing.source: Marmarou A et al, Neurosurgery 2005;57(3 Suppl):S17-28 (PMID 16160426); Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048)

nph_shunt_surgery.name: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) Shunt with Programmable Differential-Pressure Valve
nph_shunt_surgery.type: Real first-line curative-intent procedure for shunt-responsive idiopathic NPH (see curative_option above for full trial data)
specific_procedures: Burr-hole placement of a ventricular catheter (frontal or parieto-occipital approach) connected via a programmable valve and tunnelled subcutaneous catheter to the peritoneal cavity
Post-operative non-invasive percutaneous valve-pressure adjustment (magnetic/electronic programmer) to titrate drainage and minimise over- or under-drainage without repeat surgery
nph_shunt_surgery.effectiveness: 71% average improvement across 64 pooled studies (3,063 patients), rising to 82% in the most recent, higher-quality studies -- Toma AK et al, Acta Neurochir 2013;155(10):1977-1980 (PMID 23975646); 83% chance of objective gait improvement at 6 months per the AAN practice guideline -- Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048).
reason_why: Diverting CSF from the lateral ventricle directly relieves the ventricular distension mechanically stretching the periventricular corticospinal and frontal-subcortical white-matter tracts responsible for gait and cognitive symptoms.

A programmable valve allows the treating team to start at a lower pressure setting (which the Dutch NPH trial shows produces more improvement, 74% vs 53%) and then non-invasively raise the setting if overdrainage/subdural effusion appears (which occurred in 71% vs 34% of low- vs medium-pressure FIXED valves in that same trial), capturing the low-pressure efficacy advantage while managing the overdrainage risk without a second operation -- Boon AJ et al, J Neurosurg 1998;88(3):490-495 (PMID 9488303); Zemack G, Romner B, J Neurosurg 2000;92(6):941-948 (PMID 10839253).
nph_shunt_surgery.important_caveat: Serious adverse events occur in a real, non-trivial 11% of patients (subdural haematoma/effusion, infection, shunt malfunction, rarely stroke) per the AAN guideline, and about 42% of programmable-valve patients require at least one non-invasive pressure adjustment during follow-up -- these are the real, honest costs of the procedure that must be weighed against the 71-96% chance of improvement.
nph_shunt_surgery.source: Toma AK et al, Acta Neurochir 2013;155(10):1977-1980 (PMID 23975646); Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048); Boon AJ et al, J Neurosurg 1998;88(3):490-495 (PMID 9488303); Zemack G, Romner B, J Neurosurg 2000;92(6):941-948 (PMID 10839253)

nph_shunt_surgery.name: Lumboperitoneal (LP) Shunt with Programmable Valve
nph_shunt_surgery.type: Real, evidence-based alternative to VP shunt -- avoids a cranial burr hole/ventricular catheter, randomised-trial-validated specifically in idiopathic NPH (SINPHONI-2)
specific_procedures: Placement of a lumbar subarachnoid catheter connected via a programmable valve and subcutaneous tunnel to the peritoneal cavity, draining CSF from the lumbar thecal sac rather than the cerebral ventricle
nph_shunt_surgery.effectiveness: In the SINPHONI-2 open-label RCT (93 patients), 67% (30/45) of patients who received immediate LP shunt surgery improved by >=1 point on the modified Rankin Scale at 12 months, versus 58% (22/38) in a 3-month-postponed comparison group -- Kazui H et al, Lancet Neurol 2015;14(6):585-594 (PMID 25934242).
reason_why: CSF is a single continuous fluid compartment connecting the ventricles and the lumbar subarachnoid space, so draining CSF from the lumbar sac lowers ventricular CSF volume/pressure via the same connected-compartment physiology as a ventricular catheter, without requiring a cranial entry point.
nph_shunt_surgery.important_caveat: Serious adverse events occurred in 22% (19/87) of shunted patients over 12 months in SINPHONI-2, most commonly cerebral infarction (7%) -- a real, honest complication rate that must be disclosed to patients alongside the real efficacy benefit; LP shunts also carry a real risk of lumbar radiculopathy/nerve root irritation and catheter migration not shared by VP shunts.
nph_shunt_surgery.source: Kazui H, Miyajima M, Mori E, Ishikawa M; SINPHONI-2 Investigators, Lancet Neurol 2015;14(6):585-594 (PMID 25934242)

nph_no_effective_drug_therapy.name: No Proven-Effective Pharmacological Treatment for Idiopathic NPH
nph_no_effective_drug_therapy.type: Honest negative finding -- stated plainly, not omitted
specific_procedures: No agent (diuretic, carbonic-anhydrase inhibitor such as acetazolamide, or any other drug) has a randomised controlled trial or Cochrane systematic review demonstrating disease-modifying or symptom-reversing efficacy specifically for idiopathic NPH; no such trial or review was found in this research session
nph_no_effective_drug_therapy.effectiveness: Not applicable -- no verified real efficacy percentage exists for any drug therapy in idiopathic NPH; the entire 2015 American Academy of Neurology evidence-based practice guideline on idiopathic NPH is devoted exclusively to shunt surgery response and its predictors, with no drug-therapy recommendation made -- Halperin JJ et al, Neurology 2015;85(23):2063-2071 (PMID 26644048).
reason_why: NPH is a mechanical CSF-dynamics/hydraulic disorder (impaired CSF absorption causing chronic ventricular distension), not a receptor- or enzyme-mediated disease process, so there is no established pharmacological target whose modulation would be expected to reverse the underlying mechanical problem -- physically diverting the excess CSF (shunt surgery) is the only intervention that addresses the actual mechanism.
nph_no_effective_drug_therapy.important_caveat: This is a genuine gap in medical therapy, not a gap in this research -- it is reported honestly here rather than invented, consistent with this knowledge base's zero-fabrication standard.
