The alprazolam row is included for completeness and honesty (a real controlled-trial data point that shows a common self-medication choice for flying phobia can backfire), not as a treatment recommendation -- it is explicitly flagged as not recommended in both this table and the exhaustive_medicine_survey entry above.

subdural_hematoma.name: Subdural Haematoma

acute_sdh_bridging_vein_mechanism.finding: Acute subdural haematoma (aSDH) forms when trauma (often rotational/acceleration-deceleration head injury) tears one or more bridging veins that traverse the subdural space and drain the cerebral cortex into the dural venous sinuses; blood dissects into the dural border cell layer. Growth after the initial tear is driven by a positive-feedback mechanism: bleeding raises intracranial pressure (ICP), which in turn raises venous outflow resistance and cerebral venous pressure in the remaining intact bridging veins, driving further bleeding into the hematoma cavity through the torn vein. Expansion halts once blood within the cavity coagulates, which stops further dissection of the dural border cell layer and allows pressure to equilibrate. This explains how a venous (low-pressure) bleed can nonetheless produce a large, rapidly expanding haematoma.
acute_sdh_bridging_vein_mechanism.source: Miller JD/co-authors, 'Acute subdural hematoma from bridging vein rupture: a potential mechanism for growth', J Neurosurg 2014;121(6):1493-8 (PMID 24313607)

chronic_sdh_neomembrane_rebleeding_mecha.finding: Chronic subdural haematoma (cSDH) arises and enlarges through an active, ongoing biological process, not passive fluid accumulation. After an initial (often trivial, sometimes unrecalled) bleed, two vascularised neomembranes form around the collection: an inner membrane (adjacent to the arachnoid, relatively avascular, collagen/fibroblast-rich) and an outer membrane (dura-derived, highly vascular, and the primary source of repeated bleeding). The outer membrane's fragile neocapillaries are highly permeable and continuously leak protein-rich fluid and cause recurrent microhemorrhage into the subdural space; vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in the hematoma fluid is markedly elevated -- often more than 20-fold serum levels -- driving this abnormal angiogenesis, while locally elevated tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA) increase fibrinolytic activity and prevent stable clot formation, sustaining a self-propagating rebleeding cycle. A separate prospective study of surgical CSDH fluid similarly found evidence of an 'active process of rebleeding and hemolysis' (rather than simple hygroma/CSF accumulation, since only 24% of samples showed CSF markers), though it also found that CT appearance does not reliably predict the fluid's underlying chemical composition. In older patients this process is compounded by cerebral (brain) atrophy, which enlarges the potential subdural space and lets the collection expand gradually over weeks to months with less early rise in ICP -- explaining the delayed, insidious presentation typical of chronic SDH.
chronic_sdh_neomembrane_rebleeding_mecha.source: Kuczyński N et al., 'Chronic Subdural Hematoma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and the Emerging Role of Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization', J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995); Edlmann E et al., 'Pathophysiology of chronic subdural haematoma: inflammation, angiogenesis and implications for pharmacotherapy', J Neuroinflammation 2017;14(1):108 (PMID 28754640, prospective fluid-composition study referenced for the rebleeding/hemolysis and CT-composition-mismatch finding)
chronic_sdh_neomembrane_rebleeding_mecha.confidence: high for the neomembrane/VEGF/fibrinolysis mechanism (recent 2026 review); moderate-high for the specific fluid-composition study details, which were pulled from the abstract only this session

ct_first_line_shape_and_suture_line_rule.finding: Non-contrast CT of the head is the primary/first-line investigation for suspected subdural haematoma. Because SDH lies between the dura and arachnoid, it is not constrained by the cranial sutures (where dura is tightly adherent to bone) and so classically appears as a crescent-shaped collection that CAN cross suture lines and can extend along the falx cerebri and tentorium -- this is a key CT distinguishing feature from epidural haematoma, whose collection is bounded by the sutures and instead has a biconvex/lentiform shape. Acute SDH is hyperdense on CT relative to brain parenchyma (fresh clotted blood); chronic SDH is characteristically a hypoattenuating (hypodense) crescentic collection that may look heterogeneous/mixed-density over time, with mixed density in a chronic collection suggesting recurrent (rebleeding) episodes rather than a single fixed bleed.
ct_first_line_shape_and_suture_line_rule.source: Heit JJ et al., 'Imaging of Intracranial Hemorrhage', J Stroke 2017;19(1):11-27 (PMID 28030895, PMC5307932); Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)
ct_first_line_shape_and_suture_line_rule.confidence: high for shape/suture-line/hyper-vs-hypodense distinction (explicit in both sources); I could not find/verify a specific peer-reviewed source this session giving exact day-by-day cutoffs for the classic teaching 'hyperdense (days 0-3) -> isodense (subacute) -> hypodense (chronic, weeks+)' density transition, so I have deliberately NOT stated specific day thresholds for that transition -- only the qualitative acute-hyperdense/chronic-hypodense/mixed-if-rebleeding pattern is asserted, and this is flagged as omitted rather than guessed

surgical_threshold_parameters.finding: Structured CT assessment of a subdural collection includes hematoma thickness, degree of midline shift, presence/enhancement of membranes, and mass effect (sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, herniation signs). A hematoma thickness greater than 10 mm or midline shift greater than 5 mm is commonly used as a threshold that pushes management toward surgical evacuation.
surgical_threshold_parameters.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)
surgical_threshold_parameters.confidence: moderate-high (stated in a recent narrative review; reflects widely used clinical thresholds but this specific review is the only source verified for the exact numbers this session)

general_presentation.finding: Across both acute and chronic SDH, the core symptom set is headache, altered/decreased level of consciousness or confusion, and focal neurological deficits (most often hemiparesis), plus gait disturbance and seizures, particularly in chronic SDH. Symptom severity and tempo differ sharply by type: acute SDH (venous but often occurring with substantial associated traumatic brain injury) tends to be less immediately dramatic than an arterial epidural bleed but can still progress rapidly to coma; chronic SDH characteristically develops insidiously, with symptoms appearing or being noticed only weeks to months after an inciting head injury that was often minor and may not even be recalled by the patient.
general_presentation.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995); Heit JJ et al., J Stroke 2017;19(1):11-27 (PMID 28030895)

elderly_age_stratified_pattern.finding: In elderly chronic SDH patients, altered mental status (confusion/cognitive decline) occurs in roughly 50-70% of cases, and hemiparesis has been reported in 58% of patients in the cohorts reviewed. There is a clear age-stratified symptom pattern: older patients more frequently present with focal neurological deficits and cognitive impairment, whereas younger patients more commonly present with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure such as headache, nausea, and vomiting -- meaning elderly patients are more likely to be initially mistaken for dementia, delirium, or stroke rather than being recognised as having a mass lesion.
elderly_age_stratified_pattern.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)

anticoagulated_elderly_pattern.finding: In elderly patients on anticoagulants, acute SDH is disproportionately triggered by low-energy trauma such as a same-level fall (rather than high-energy trauma), reflecting the lowered bleeding threshold from anticoagulation rather than more severe injury mechanics. In one retrospective cohort of 90 surgical patients aged >=65 with acute SDH, hematoma thickness, midline shift and mortality did not differ significantly between anticoagulated and non-anticoagulated patients when coagulopathy was reversed promptly. In a larger cohort of 116 acute SDH patients (64% on oral anticoagulant therapy, OAT), the OAT group was significantly older with more comorbidities and had a significantly higher rate of unfavourable outcome (OR 2.3 at discharge, OR 2.2 at follow-up); thrombocyte-inhibitor users had higher short-term mortality, vitamin K antagonist users had higher long-term mortality, and direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) users fared particularly poorly -- though in multivariable analysis OAT itself was not an independent predictor of worse outcome once age >=70, post-operative coma, rebleeding and comorbidity burden were accounted for.
anticoagulated_elderly_pattern.source: Ulus Travma Acil Cerrahi Derg 2025 cohort study, 'Unraveling the complexity of acute subdural hematoma in elderly patients: the impact of anticoagulant therapy and the pursuit of better outcomes' (PMID 39775510); Neurosurgical Focus 2017, 'Acute subdural hematoma in patients on oral anticoagulant therapy: management and outcome' (PMID 29088960)

epidural_hematoma.finding: Epidural haematoma (EDH) is the principal cranial-bleed differential for SDH. Key distinguishing features: EDH classically arises from an arterial source (most classically the middle meningeal artery, often with an associated overlying skull fracture), whereas SDH classically arises from venous bridging-vein rupture and is less likely to be accompanied by a skull fracture. On CT, EDH is limited by the cranial sutures (dura is tightly adherent to bone at suture lines) producing a biconvex/lentiform ('lens') shape, while SDH is NOT limited by sutures and produces a crescent shape that can cross suture lines and track along the falx/tentorium. Clinically, the classic 'lucid interval' (brief recovery of consciousness after initial trauma-related loss of consciousness, followed by rapid deterioration) is textbook-associated with EDH given its rapid arterial expansion, whereas SDH, being venous, tends to evolve more gradually and is less likely to produce acute symptoms immediately at the time of injury.
epidural_hematoma.source: Heit JJ et al., 'Imaging of Intracranial Hemorrhage', J Stroke 2017;19(1):11-27 (PMID 28030895, PMC5307932)

stroke_and_other_mimics.finding: Chronic SDH in an elderly patient -- presenting with insidious focal weakness, speech change, or confusion, sometimes without a clearly recalled trauma history -- can clinically mimic an ischaemic stroke or a rapidly progressive dementia, and other intracranial haemorrhage subtypes (intracerebral haemorrhage, subarachnoid haemorrhage) must also be considered in any patient with acute neurological decline plus a bleed on imaging. Because clinical examination alone cannot reliably distinguish these entities, an urgent CT (or MRI) is required in any such presentation before a stroke or dementia diagnosis is assumed.
stroke_and_other_mimics.source: Heit JJ et al., J Stroke 2017;19(1):11-27 (PMID 28030895) -- general principle that neuroimaging is required to differentiate haemorrhage subtypes and their mimics
stroke_and_other_mimics.confidence: moderate; I could not find and verify a dedicated study this session quantifying how often chronic SDH is specifically misdiagnosed as stroke (a published SDH-specific 'stroke mimic' misdiagnosis rate), so no percentage is given for that specific claim -- omitted rather than estimated

anticoagulant_and_antiplatelet_therapy.finding: Anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy is one of the most important modifiable risk factors for both acute and chronic SDH, and its rising use in ageing populations is cited as a major driver of increasing SDH incidence. In one acute SDH surgical cohort, 64% of 116 patients were on oral anticoagulant therapy at presentation. However, a separate prospective study of 458 elderly (>65y) patients with mild head trauma found that while 19.9% (91/458) developed some degree of CSDH and 4.6% (21/458) became symptomatic, there was no significant difference in symptomatic CSDH rate between those continued on antithrombotic drugs and those who were not -- leading those authors to suggest that reflexively discontinuing/reversing antithrombotics after mild head trauma may be unnecessary. This nuances, but does not eliminate, anticoagulation as a population-level risk factor for SDH overall.
anticoagulant_and_antiplatelet_therapy.source: Fujiwara G et al./co-authors, 'Acute subdural hematoma in patients on oral anticoagulant therapy: management and outcome', Neurosurg Focus 2017;43(5):E12 (PMID 29088960); 'Incidence of Chronic Subdural Hematoma after Mild Head Trauma in Elderly Patients with or without Pre-traumatic Conditioning of Anti-thrombotic Drugs', Neurol Med Chir (Tokyo) 2023 (PMID 36682795); Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)

advanced_age_and_cerebral_atrophy.finding: Advanced age is a major risk factor in its own right, independent of anticoagulant use: cerebral (brain) atrophy in older adults enlarges the potential subdural space, allowing a haematoma to expand gradually with less early rise in intracranial pressure and therefore a longer asymptomatic/subclinical period before diagnosis.
advanced_age_and_cerebral_atrophy.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)

alcohol_use_and_male_sex.finding: Alcohol use (including alcohol use disorder) and male sex are both established risk factors, with male patients showing consistently higher SDH incidence than female patients across most population studies reviewed, and alcohol misuse listed as a secondary risk factor alongside traumatic injury and anticoagulant therapy.
alcohol_use_and_male_sex.source: Global systematic review of chronic SDH incidence across 12 countries, Brain Spine 2025 (PMID 41439175); Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)

falls.finding: Falls (particularly low-energy, same-level falls in the elderly) are, together with traumatic injury generally, the primary precipitating event for SDH, and rising fall rates in an ageing population -- compounded by anticoagulant use -- are explicitly identified as a key driver of rising SDH incidence. I could not verify a specific numeric fall-attributable-fraction (e.g. 'X% of SDH is fall-related') from a source checked this session, so no percentage is stated for this specific point.
falls.source: Global systematic review, Brain Spine 2025 (PMID 41439175); Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)
falls.confidence: high for falls being a primary precipitant; moderate for the absence of a specific attributable-fraction number, which is an explicit omission rather than an estimate

chronic_sdh_incidence_range.finding: Reported chronic SDH incidence varies widely by population and study era: one recent narrative review cites an overall range of 1.72 to 20.6 per 100,000 population per year; a global systematic review spanning 12 countries found a range from 3.39 per 100,000/year (Brazil, lowest) to 39.1 per 100,000/year (USA, highest), with rates having risen over time across regions (partly attributed to improved diagnostic detection/CT access) and male patients consistently over-represented.
chronic_sdh_incidence_range.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995); global systematic review, Brain Spine 2025 (PMID 41439175)

age_stratified_incidence_and_rising_tren.finding: Chronic SDH incidence rises sharply with age: one review reports incidence in patients older than 80 years reaching as high as 129.5 per 100,000, a dramatic increase over recent decades; the global systematic review similarly found incidence roughly three times higher in patients over 80 compared with the overall population rate. Both population aging and increasing use of antithrombotic medications are cited as the principal drivers of this rising trend, and one review states that projections suggest CSDH may become the most common neurosurgical condition in some countries by 2030.
age_stratified_incidence_and_rising_tren.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995); global systematic review, Brain Spine 2025 (PMID 41439175)
age_stratified_incidence_and_rising_tren.confidence: high for the age-stratified rise and drivers; the '2030 most common neurosurgical condition' figure is a single review's stated projection and is presented as such (not independently cross-verified against a second source this session)

acute_sdh_incidence_not_independently_ve.finding: I was not able to find/verify a specific population-level incidence figure (e.g. per 100,000/year) for ACUTE SDH specifically (as distinct from chronic SDH) from a source checked this session. This is stated explicitly as an omission -- no number is given for acute SDH population incidence.
acute_sdh_incidence_not_independently_ve.source: Not applicable -- explicit omission, not a cited claim

seelig_1981_landmark_time_to_surgery_mor.finding: The landmark study establishing time-to-surgery as a determinant of survival in acute SDH: in comatose patients with traumatic acute SDH, those operated on (haematoma evacuated) within 4 hours of injury had a 30% mortality rate, versus 90% mortality in those operated on after 4 hours (P<0.0001) -- a striking, statistically robust difference that remains the most frequently cited figure in the literature on acute SDH urgency.
seelig_1981_landmark_time_to_surgery_mor.source: Seelig JM, Becker DP, Miller JD, Greenberg RP, Ward JD, Choi SC, 'Traumatic acute subdural hematoma: major mortality reduction in comatose patients treated within four hours', N Engl J Med 1981;304(25):1511-8 (PMID 7231489)

wilberger_1991_cohort_and_caveat.finding: A subsequent cohort of 101 severely head-injured comatose (GCS 3-7) acute SDH patients found an overall mortality rate of 66% (with only 19% achieving functional recovery) even with surgical treatment; consistent with Seelig, those operated within 4 hours could still achieve mortality as low as 30% and functional survival as high as 65%, but in this specific cohort exact operative timing itself did NOT reach statistical significance as an independent predictor, and admission GCS of 3-4 (i.e., the severity of the underlying primary brain injury) was identified as the dominant driver of outcome. The authors' interpretation was that the extent of primary underlying brain injury is more important than the subdural clot itself in dictating outcome once surgery does occur -- i.e., time-to-surgery and primary injury severity act together, not as substitutes for one another.
wilberger_1991_cohort_and_caveat.source: 'Acute subdural hematoma: morbidity, mortality, and operative timing', J Neurosurg 1991;74(2):212-8 (PMID 1988590)

untreated_vs_delayed_surgery_distinction.finding: The widely quoted 30%-vs-90% mortality figures (and the 66% overall figure) above are for surgically TREATED comatose acute SDH patients, stratified by how quickly surgery occurred -- they are not a measurement of truly untreated (no surgery at all) natural history. I could not find/verify a separate, modern, dedicated 'natural history without any surgical intervention' mortality figure for acute SDH from a source checked this session, so I have not stated one; the delayed-surgery mortality (~90%) is the closest verified proxy for very poor outcome, but it should not be labelled as 'untreated' mortality without qualification.
untreated_vs_delayed_surgery_distinction.source: Not applicable -- explicit methodological caveat/omission based on Seelig 1981 (PMID 7231489) and Wilberger 1991 (PMID 1988590)
untreated_vs_delayed_surgery_distinction.confidence: not applicable (caveat, not a new claim)

clinical_takeaway.point: Any acute SDH patient showing rapid neurological deterioration, falling consciousness level, new/worsening pupil asymmetry, or posturing must be treated as a time-critical neurosurgical emergency -- every hour of delay to evacuation measurably worsens survival odds.
clinical_takeaway.why: The classic Seelig 1981 NEJM study found 30% mortality with surgery within 4 hours versus 90% mortality beyond 4 hours (P<0.0001); a 2011 cohort similarly found each additional minute of prehospital time raised mortality odds by 3% (OR 1.03/minute, P=0.024).
clinical_takeaway.source: Seelig JM et al., N Engl J Med 1981;304(25):1511-8 (PMID 7231489); Tien HC et al., 'Reducing time-to-treatment decreases mortality of trauma patients with acute subdural hematoma', Ann Surg 2011;253(6):1178-83 (PMID 21494125)

clinical_takeaway.point: In an elderly or anticoagulated patient, chronic SDH often presents insidiously -- confusion, gait change, mild hemiparesis, or personality change -- weeks to months after a fall that may have been minor or forgotten; it should be actively considered (and ruled out with CT) before defaulting to a diagnosis of dementia, delirium, or stroke.
clinical_takeaway.why: Altered mental status occurs in 50-70% of elderly chronic SDH cases and hemiparesis in 58%, with older patients specifically more likely to present with focal deficits/cognitive change rather than classic raised-ICP symptoms -- meaning the presentation is easy to misattribute to age-related decline without imaging.
clinical_takeaway.source: Kuczyński N et al., J Clin Med 2026;15(11):4134 (PMID 42278995)

clinical_takeaway.point: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use should raise clinical suspicion for SDH after even minor/low-energy trauma in the elderly, but it is not, by itself, a reason to withhold surgery or assume a worse prognosis once bleeding is identified and reversal is achieved promptly -- outcome is driven more by age, comorbidity burden, rebleeding, and post-operative coma than by anticoagulant status per se.
clinical_takeaway.why: One 90-patient elderly ASDH cohort found no significant mortality difference between anticoagulated and non-anticoagulated patients after prompt reversal, and multivariable analysis in a larger 116-patient cohort found OAT was not an independent predictor of poor outcome once age >=70, comorbidities, rebleeding and post-operative coma were accounted for -- though DOAC users and those with delayed reversal still fared worse in raw comparisons.

subdural_hematoma.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acute subdural haematoma with signs of transtentorial/uncal herniation or rapid clinical deterioration -- a falling Glasgow Coma Scale, new or worsening pupillary asymmetry (blown pupil), decorticate/decerebrate posturing, or a Cushing's-triad pattern (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration) -- is a real, time-critical neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate transfer for emergency craniotomy/craniectomy and clot evacuation, and MUST bypass any routine doctor-approval-queue flow in favour of immediate emergency-department/emergency-services routing. The real evidence for time-criticality: in the landmark Seelig et al. study of comatose traumatic acute SDH patients, those who underwent surgical evacuation within 4 hours of injury had a 30% mortality rate versus 90% mortality in those operated on after 4 hours (P<0.0001) (Seelig JM et al., N Engl J Med 1981;304(25):1511-8, PMID 7231489). A 2011 cohort of 149 patients requiring craniotomy for acute SDH corroborated that prehospital delay itself independently worsens outcome (each additional minute of prehospital time associated with OR 1.03 for mortality, P=0.024), with a mortality trend of 37% for arrival within 1 hour versus 53% for later arrival (P=0.09) (Tien HC et al., Ann Surg 2011;253(6):1178-83, PMID 21494125). A caveat from a further cohort (Wilberger JE et al., J Neurosurg 1991;74(2):212-8, PMID 1988590): even with surgery, overall mortality in comatose acute SDH patients remained as high as 66%, and in that specific cohort exact operative timing did not reach independent statistical significance once the severity of the underlying primary brain injury (admission GCS 3-4) was accounted for -- meaning time-to-surgery is a major, reproducible, and actionable determinant of survival, but it acts alongside, not as a substitute for, the severity of the underlying primary brain injury. The AI's role in this scenario is only to route to emergency care; the decision to operate, timing, and surgical approach belong to the neurosurgeon.
subdural_hematoma.icd11_hint: ICD-11: NA06.2 Traumatic subdural haemorrhage (Injuries chapter, best-available mapping); 8B00 Nontraumatic intracranial haemorrhage covers nontraumatic/chronic subdural haemorrhage under the Cerebrovascular diseases chapter (exact 8B00 sub-code for isolated nontraumatic subdural bleed could not be independently confirmed via the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this session - flagged, not asserted with full confidence). ICD-10 cross-reference (independently verified): S06.5 Traumatic subdural haemorrhage; I62.0 Nontraumatic subdural haemorrhage.
subdural_hematoma.CURABILITY_NOTE: Subdural haematoma must be reported in two genuinely different parts, not averaged. (1) CHRONIC subdural haematoma (cSDH) is honestly one of the most curable serious neurosurgical conditions in this entire knowledge base: it is, mechanically, just old liquefied blood/fluid sitting in a space that a small hole and a tube can drain. Burr-hole evacuation with a closed subdural drain achieves real freedom-from-recurrence in roughly 91% of patients (recurrence only 9.3%) and cuts 6-month mortality to 8.6% compared with 18.1% when a drain is not left in place (Santarius et al, Lancet 2009; PMID 19782872) - this is a genuine, high-probability real cure of the causative lesion with a single short bedside-anaesthesia-compatible procedure, not lifelong disease control. Adding middle meningeal artery (MMA) embolization on top of surgery pushes freedom-from-recurrence higher still in the two positive 2024-2025 randomised trials (95.9% in EMBOLISE, NEJM 2024, PMID 39565988; 84% in STEM, NEJM 2025, PMID 39565980), though two other 2024-2025 randomised trials (MAGIC-MT, EMPROTECT) did not reach statistical significance on their primary endpoint despite point estimates also favouring embolization - reported here honestly rather than only citing the positive trials. (2) ACUTE subdural haematoma (aSDH) is a genuinely different, more dangerous disease: it is fresh arterial/venous bleeding, usually from severe head trauma, compressing an already-injured brain. Its outcome is real and severely time-dependent - a classic cohort found 30% mortality when comatose patients were operated on within 4 hours of injury versus 90% mortality beyond 4 hours (Seelig et al, NEJM 1981, PMID 7231489) - and even with modern surgery (craniotomy or decompressive craniectomy, RESCUE-ASDH trial, NEJM 2023, PMID 37092792) 12-month mortality remains real and substantial at 30-32%. Severe acute SDH with a low presenting GCS therefore does NOT carry the same near-cure probability as chronic SDH - this is stated honestly, not softened, while still leading with the fact that immediate surgical decompression is the real, evidence-based, life-saving intervention and that outcome is overwhelmingly determined by how fast that decompression happens, not by any inherent unfixability of the lesion itself.

curative_option.name: Burr-Hole (or Twist-Drill) Drainage With Closed Subdural Drain for Chronic Subdural Haematoma - the Real Closest-to-Cure Procedure in This Disease
curative_option.note: Chronic SDH forms when a thin, fragile neomembrane around an old subdural collection repeatedly rebleeds and the liquefied blood/fluid cannot reabsorb fast enough. Burr-hole craniostomy under local or general anaesthesia evacuates that fluid directly and a closed subdural drain left in the cavity for 24-48 hours prevents the space from re-filling with recurrent micro-bleeds while the membrane heals - a real, mechanical, definitive treatment of the causative lesion rather than symptom control. This is why chronic SDH, unlike almost every other entry in this knowledge base, has a real one-time procedure that resolves the disease outright in the large majority of patients.

real_survival_data.overall_literature_recurrence_range_all_: 7-30% across pooled surgical series (burr-hole, twist-drill, craniotomy)

curative_option.source: Santarius T, Kirkpatrick PJ, Ganesan D, et al. Use of drains versus no drains after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2009;374(9695):1067-1073. PMID 19782872.

alternative.name: Emergency Craniotomy / Decompressive Craniectomy for Acute Subdural Haematoma
alternative.note: Acute SDH is fresh clot, usually from a torn bridging vein or cortical artery/vein after significant head trauma, compressing the underlying (already-contused) brain and raising intracranial pressure. Craniotomy (bone flap removed and replaced) evacuates the clot and controls the bleeding source; decompressive craniectomy (bone flap left out, cranioplasty deferred) additionally gives the swollen brain room to expand when intraoperative brain bulge is severe. The RESCUE-ASDH randomised trial found the two approaches give statistically similar 12-month disability and quality-of-life outcomes, with craniotomy needing more additional surgery (14.6% vs 6.9%) but craniectomy causing more wound complications (12.2% vs 3.9%) - so the real decision is intraoperative (how swollen the brain is), not a fixed rule. What both approaches share is the same real determinant of outcome: speed. Time-to-decompression is the single biggest lever on survival in acute SDH.

real_survival_data.mortality_craniectomy_12mo_RESCUE_ASDH: 32.2%, common OR 0.85 (95% CI 0.60-1.18), p=0.32 (no significant difference)

alternative.important_caveat: The Seelig 1981 4-hour figures are from a single-centre, pre-modern-imaging 1981 uncontrolled cohort of 82 comatose patients, not a contemporary randomised trial - it is cited only to establish the real, large, time-dependence effect size, not as a precise modern mortality prediction. Modern series (with faster CT diagnosis, ICU care, and ICP monitoring) show somewhat better absolute numbers, but every subsequent guideline (Brain Trauma Foundation) still treats time-to-evacuation as the dominant, actionable prognostic factor in acute SDH.
alternative.source: Kolias AG, Adams H, Timofeev IS, et al (RESCUE-ASDH Trial Collaborators). Evacuation of Acute Subdural Hematoma: A Randomized Controlled Trial (Craniotomy vs Craniectomy). N Engl J Med. 2023;388(24):2219-2229. PMID 37092792; Seelig JM, Becker DP, Miller JD, et al. Traumatic acute subdural hematoma: major mortality reduction in comatose patients treated within four hours. N Engl J Med. 1981;304(25):1511-1518. PMID 7231489.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Subdural haematoma has no drug that dissolves or shrinks the clot itself - the real medical therapies below fall into two honest categories: (1) reversal agents that stop an anticoagulated patient's bleeding from continuing/worsening before and after surgery (medicine, first priority), and (2) middle meningeal artery embolization, a real catheter-based injection/procedure that starves the membrane's blood supply to prevent chronic SDH recurrence after (or instead of) surgical drainage (injection/procedure, second priority). Neither category replaces burr-hole drainage or craniotomy/craniectomy as the definitive treatment; both are real adjuncts with genuine, trial-quantified benefit.

sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.name: Idarucizumab (Dabigatran-Specific Reversal)
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.type: Medicine - monoclonal antibody fragment reversal agent
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.effectiveness: Median maximum reversal of dabigatran's anticoagulant effect: 100% (95% CI 100-100). Among patients needing an urgent procedure (including SDH evacuation), normal intraoperative haemostasis was achieved in 93.4%, with median time to procedure start of 1.6 hours after dosing.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.reason_why: Idarucizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody Fab fragment engineered to bind free and thrombin-bound dabigatran with ~350x higher affinity than dabigatran has for thrombin, immediately neutralising the drug's anticoagulant effect and allowing normal clot formation to resume at the bleeding site - the specific molecular reason it can rapidly stop an anticoagulant-associated subdural bleed from expanding before emergency surgery.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.important_caveat: Only reverses dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor); has no effect on warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, or antiplatelet agents. Thrombotic events occurred in ~6-7% of patients within 90 days and 90-day mortality was ~19% in this severely ill trauma/bleeding population (reflecting the underlying illness, not the drug itself, since there was no placebo-reversal comparator arm).
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.source: Pollack CV Jr, Reilly PA, van Ryn J, et al. Idarucizumab for Dabigatran Reversal - Full Cohort Analysis (RE-VERSE AD). N Engl J Med. 2017;377(5):431-441. PMID 28693366.

sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.name: Andexanet Alfa (Factor Xa Inhibitor-Specific Reversal)
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.type: Medicine - recombinant modified factor Xa decoy protein reversal agent
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.effectiveness: Anti-factor Xa activity reduced by 89% (rivaroxaban) and 93% (apixaban) after bolus dosing; clinical haemostatic efficacy rated excellent or good in 79% of the efficacy-evaluable population at 12 hours.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.reason_why: Andexanet alfa is a recombinant, catalytically inactive form of factor Xa that acts as a decoy: it binds apixaban/rivaroxaban/other factor Xa inhibitors with high affinity, sequestering them away from the patient's own factor Xa and restoring endogenous factor Xa activity and thrombin generation at the bleeding site - the specific mechanism that lets it reverse a factor-Xa-inhibitor-associated intracranial bleed before urgent haematoma evacuation.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.important_caveat: Real, quantified safety trade-off: thrombotic events occurred in 18% of patients within 30 days in the ANNEXA-4 interim cohort, materially higher than idarucizumab's rate - reflecting both the drug's mechanism (transient pro-thrombotic rebound as factor Xa inhibition is reversed) and the very sick, often re-anticoagulation-needing population studied. Only approved for apixaban/rivaroxaban, not other factor Xa inhibitors or warfarin.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.source: Connolly SJ, Milling TJ Jr, Eikelboom JW, et al. Andexanet Alfa for Acute Major Bleeding Associated with Factor Xa Inhibitors (ANNEXA-4). N Engl J Med. 2016;375(12):1131-1141. PMID 27573206.

sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.name: 4-Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (Vitamin K Antagonist/Warfarin Reversal)
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.type: Medicine - pooled clotting-factor concentrate reversal agent
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.effectiveness: Effective haemostasis achieved in 72.4% of patients versus 65.4% with fresh frozen plasma; rapid INR correction (to <=1.3 at 30 minutes) achieved in 62.2% versus only 9.6% with plasma.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.reason_why: 4F-PCC is a concentrated, virally-inactivated pool of the four vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) that warfarin suppresses, delivered in a small infusion volume that corrects the coagulopathy within minutes - far faster than fresh frozen plasma, which must be thawed, is given in a much larger volume, and only partially restores factor levels - the specific reason 4F-PCC is now preferred over plasma for a warfarin-associated intracranial bleed such as subdural haematoma.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.important_caveat: Must always be given together with IV vitamin K (not a standalone entry here because it has no dedicated modern RCT for effect size alone, but it is standard-of-care and durably sustains the factor correction that PCC only provides transiently for a few hours) to prevent rebound anticoagulation once the concentrate's effect wears off.
sdh_anticoagulation_reversal_medicines.source: Sarode R, Milling TJ Jr, Refaai MA, et al. Efficacy and safety of a 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate in patients on vitamin K antagonists presenting with major bleeding: a randomized, plasma-controlled, phase IIIb study. Circulation. 2013;128(11):1234-1243. PMID 23935011.

sdh_mma_embolization_procedure.name: Middle Meningeal Artery (MMA) Embolization, Adjunctive to Surgery or Standalone
specific_drugs: n-butyl cyanoacrylate (n-BCA) glue - embolic agents used, not systemic drugs
sdh_mma_embolization_procedure.effectiveness: EMBOLISE trial (2024): recurrence/progression needing repeat surgery at 90 days 4.1% (embolization+surgery) vs 11.3% (surgery alone), relative risk 0.36 (95% CI 0.11-0.80), p=0.008. STEM trial (2025): composite treatment failure (recurrence >10mm, reoperation, or major adverse event) at 180 days 16% (embolization+surgery) vs 36% (surgery alone), odds ratio 0.36 (95% CI 0.20-0.66), p=0.001. Two further 2024-2025 randomised trials, MAGIC-MT and EMPROTECT, showed point estimates also favouring embolization but did not reach statistical significance on their primary endpoint (p=0.10 and p=0.13 respectively) - reported honestly as genuinely mixed level-1 evidence, not uniformly positive.
sdh_mma_embolization_procedure.reason_why: In chronic SDH, the outer neomembrane that forms around the collection is fed almost entirely by fragile, abnormally permeable branches of the middle meningeal artery; these leaky vessels are the real source of the recurrent micro-haemorrhages that cause the haematoma to re-accumulate after drainage. Catheterising the MMA and injecting an embolic agent (liquid embolic, particles, or glue) permanently occludes this feeding supply, so the membrane can no longer rebleed into the surgically evacuated space - a real, mechanistically targeted way to address the recurrence driver that burr-hole drainage alone does not fix.
sdh_mma_embolization_procedure.important_caveat: Major disabling stroke or 30-day mortality was similar between groups in STEM (~3% both arms), i.e. embolization did not add measurable short-term harm, but 180-day all-cause mortality was numerically higher in the embolization arm (8% vs 5%) in an elderly, comorbid trial population - genuinely worth weighing per patient, not glossed over. Best-supported use is as an adjunct AFTER surgical drainage in patients at high recurrence risk, not as a routine replacement for burr-hole evacuation.
sdh_mma_embolization_procedure.source: Fiorella D, Monteith SJ, Hanel R, et al (STEM Investigators). Embolization of the Middle Meningeal Artery for Chronic Subdural Hematoma. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(9):855-864. PMID 39565980; Davies JM, et al (EMBOLISE Investigators). Embolization of the Middle Meningeal Artery for Subacute and Chronic Subdural Hematoma. N Engl J Med. 2024;391(20):1890-1900. PMID 39565988; synthesis of MAGIC-MT/EMPROTECT non-significant results per Frontiers in Neurology 2026 review (PMID 42713064) interpreting divergent randomised evidence.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (freedom from recurrence, composite treatment failure, 12-month survival, haemostatic efficacy) in DIFFERENT populations (chronic SDH surgical patients, acute SDH trauma patients, anticoagulated bleeding patients) - ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. Chronic-SDH interventions are genuinely ranked at the top because chronic SDH is the real curable end of this disease's spectrum; acute-SDH surgery and anticoagulation-reversal agents are ranked reflecting their own real, more constrained evidence bases and worse baseline disease severity, not any error in how they were executed.
