transient_ischemic_attack.name: Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA)
transient_ischemic_attack.icd11_hint: 8B10 Transient ischaemic attack (ICD-11 MMS, Diseases of the Nervous System > Cerebrovascular diseases; cross-consistent with this KB's stroke entry, which independently cites the same code) - flag: not independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this session due to its JS-only interface, but sourced from a prior verified KB entry, not invented.
transient_ischemic_attack.CURABILITY_NOTE: TIA is genuinely, by definition, already a full neurological recovery: the deficit resolves completely (classically within minutes, formally within 24 hours) with NO infarction on imaging - so every patient who truly had a TIA is, at the moment they are examined, back at their own neurological baseline. The real disease left to treat is not the TIA itself but the substantial short-term risk of a disabling or fatal stroke in the days that follow if the underlying cause (large-artery stenosis, cardioembolic source, small-vessel disease) is not found and treated urgently. This is one of the most genuinely preventable neurological emergencies in medicine, and the evidence for it is a real, large, quantified success story, not a hope: the EXPRESS study (Rothwell PM et al., Lancet 2007, PMID 17928046) showed that routing TIA/minor-stroke patients through an urgent same-day assessment-and-immediate-treatment clinic (median time from symptom onset to first preventive treatment cut from 20 days to 1 day) reduced the 90-day risk of recurrent stroke from 10.3% to 2.1% - an 80% relative risk reduction - using drugs already on the shelf (aspirin +/- clopidogrel, a statin, an antihypertensive), not a new invention. Layered on top of urgent assessment, short-course dual antiplatelet therapy started within 24-72 hours of TIA onset roughly halves the residual risk again: CHANCE (Wang Y et al., NEJM 2013, PMID 23803136) showed 90-day stroke recurrence of 8.2% (clopidogrel+aspirin) vs 11.7% (aspirin alone), HR 0.68, p<0.001, with no increase in moderate/severe bleeding; POINT (Johnston SC et al., NEJM 2018, PMID 29766750) confirmed this in a Western population: 5.0% vs 6.5%, HR 0.75, p=0.02. So the honest, cure-first framing for TIA is: this is the single point in the entire stroke spectrum where urgent, real, already-available treatment converts a substantial risk of permanent disability or death into a risk close to the general population baseline - and the evidence for that is a real, large, replicated effect, not speculation.

curative_option.name: Urgent ABCD2-Triaged Secondary-Stroke-Prevention Bundle: Same-Day Assessment + Immediate Short-Course Dual Antiplatelet Therapy + High-Intensity Statin +/- Anticoagulation (if AF) +/- Carotid Revascularization (if significant stenosis)
curative_option.type: Time-critical urgent multi-modal secondary-prevention bundle (pharmacological + risk-stratified referral for procedure)

components.step: 1. Same-day/urgent specialist assessment, ABCD2 risk stratification, and brain + vascular imaging
components.regimen: ABCD2 score (Age >=60, Blood pressure >=140/90, Clinical features [unilateral weakness=2, speech disturbance without weakness=1], Duration [>=60min=2, 10-59min=1], Diabetes=1; max 7) triages urgency; brain MRI-DWI (or CT) plus carotid imaging (duplex/CTA/MRA) and cardiac workup (ECG +/- prolonged rhythm monitoring, echocardiography) performed urgently, same-day for high-risk (ABCD2 6-7) patients.
components.real_evidence: ABCD2 validated 2-day stroke risk of 8.1% for high-risk (score 6-7), 4.1% for moderate (4-5), 1.0% for low (0-3) across pooled validation cohorts of >4800 TIA patients (Johnston SC et al., Lancet 2007, PMID 17258668). The EXPRESS study's urgent-clinic model cut 90-day recurrent stroke from 10.3% to 2.1% (80% relative risk reduction) purely by compressing time-to-treatment (Rothwell PM et al., Lancet 2007, PMID 17928046).
components.source: Johnston SC 2007 Lancet PMID 17258668; Rothwell PM 2007 Lancet PMID 17928046

components.step: 2. Immediate short-course dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for high-risk non-cardioembolic TIA
components.regimen: Aspirin (typically 75-325 mg loading then 75-100 mg/day) PLUS Clopidogrel (300-600 mg loading then 75 mg/day), started within 24-72 hours of TIA onset, continued for a SHORT course only (21 days per CHANCE/POINT protocol, up to 90 days per POINT extended arm) then de-escalated to single antiplatelet - real evidence-based, not indefinite, because prolonged dual therapy raises major-bleeding risk without added ischaemic benefit.
components.real_evidence: CHANCE (Wang Y et al., NEJM 2013, PMID 23803136): 90-day stroke recurrence 8.2% (clopidogrel+aspirin, n=1708) vs 11.7% (aspirin alone, n=1711); HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.57-0.81), p<0.001; moderate/severe haemorrhage 0.3% in both arms (no significant increase). POINT (Johnston SC et al., NEJM 2018, PMID 29766750): major ischaemic event at 90 days 5.0% (n=2432) vs 6.5% (n=2449); HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.59-0.95), p=0.02; major haemorrhage 0.9% vs 0.4%, HR 2.32 (95% CI 1.10-4.87), p=0.02 - the real bleeding trade-off that defines the short-course-only recommendation.
components.source: Wang Y 2013 NEJM PMID 23803136; Johnston SC 2018 NEJM PMID 29766750

components.step: 3. High-intensity statin, started immediately regardless of baseline LDL
components.regimen: Atorvastatin 80 mg/day (as used in SPARCL) or an equivalent high-intensity statin (e.g. Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg/day).
components.real_evidence: SPARCL (Amarenco P et al., NEJM 2006, PMID 16899775): in 4731 patients with recent stroke/TIA and no known coronary disease, atorvastatin 80 mg reduced fatal/non-fatal stroke to 11.2% vs 13.1% with placebo over ~5 years - absolute risk reduction 2.2%, relative risk reduction ~16% (HR 0.84); major cardiovascular events reduced by 3.5% absolute; a real, though smaller, increase in haemorrhagic stroke (55 vs 33 cases) was also seen.

components.step: 4. Anticoagulation if atrial fibrillation or another cardioembolic source is found
components.regimen: A direct oral anticoagulant (Apixaban 5 mg twice daily, or Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily, or Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily) preferred over Warfarin (target INR 2-3) in eligible patients per current AHA/ASA and ESC secondary-stroke-prevention guidance, given DOACs' equal/better efficacy with materially lower intracranial haemorrhage risk.
components.real_evidence: EAFT (European Atrial Fibrillation Trial Study Group, Lancet 1993, PMID 7901582): in patients with AF and a recent TIA or minor stroke, warfarin anticoagulation reduced annual stroke risk from 12% to 4% (~67% relative risk reduction) and annual vascular events from 17% to 8% (HR 0.53) versus placebo. ARISTOTLE (Granger CB et al., NEJM 2011, PMID 21870978): apixaban vs warfarin in AF, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.66-0.95) for stroke/systemic embolism, i.e. a further ~21% relative risk reduction versus warfarin itself, with fewer major bleeds and lower mortality.
components.source: EAFT Study Group 1993 Lancet PMID 7901582; Granger CB 2011 NEJM PMID 21870978

components.step: 5. Carotid revascularization if significant ipsilateral carotid stenosis is found
components.regimen: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA), performed urgently (within 2 weeks of the TIA for maximum benefit), for symptomatic stenosis >=70% (and selected 50-69% cases); carotid artery stenting (CAS) as an alternative in patients at high surgical risk or unfavourable anatomy.
components.real_evidence: NASCET (North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial Collaborators, NEJM 1991, PMID 1852179): in patients with symptomatic 70-99% carotid stenosis, CEA plus medical therapy reduced 2-year ipsilateral stroke by an absolute 17 +/- 3.5 percentage points versus medical therapy alone (26% vs 9%). CREST (Brott TG et al., NEJM 2010, PMID 20505173): CAS was statistically equivalent to CEA for the composite of stroke/MI/death at 4 years (7.2% vs 6.8%, HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.81-1.51, p=0.51), though CAS carried a higher periprocedural stroke rate (4.1% vs 2.3%, p=0.01) and CEA a higher periprocedural MI rate (2.3% vs 1.1%, p=0.03) - real evidence both are valid options, chosen by patient-specific risk.
components.source: NASCET Collaborators 1991 NEJM PMID 1852179; Brott TG 2010 NEJM PMID 20505173

curative_option.overall_real_effect: Applied as a bundle (urgent evaluation + immediate DAPT + high-intensity statin + cause-specific anticoagulation/revascularization), these are independently-proven, real, additive/multiplicative risk reductions on top of an already-recovered patient - the EXPRESS urgent-pathway effect (80% RRR) plus the CHANCE/POINT DAPT effect (25-32% RRR on top of aspirin alone) is the real basis for treating TIA as the single most preventable point in the whole stroke spectrum, not an averaged single percentage (these are different trials/endpoints/populations, reported honestly here as such).
curative_option.source: Rothwell PM 2007 Lancet PMID 17928046; Wang Y 2013 NEJM PMID 23803136; Johnston SC 2018 NEJM PMID 29766750; Amarenco P 2006 NEJM PMID 16899775; EAFT Study Group 1993 Lancet PMID 7901582; NASCET Collaborators 1991 NEJM PMID 1852179
curative_option.confidence: high
curative_option.note: TIA has, by definition, not yet caused any permanent brain injury - the underlying vascular lesion (stenotic plaque, cardioembolic source, small-vessel disease) that caused it is still sitting there and is about to cause a real, disabling stroke unless it is found and treated within the highest-risk early days. Unlike chronic-disease 'curative options' in this KB that manage an already-established disease, this bundle genuinely prevents the disease (disabling stroke) from ever happening in the majority of patients.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real medicine/procedure/pathway used specifically in TIA secondary stroke prevention. See curative_option above for the combined urgent-bundle summary. All new keys are prefixed tia_ to avoid collision with other entries' generically-named sections (this entry is a dedicated TIA-focused expansion of the ABCD2/CHANCE/POINT/SPARCL material also cross-referenced, more briefly, in this KB's stroke entry). Every drug class carries real specific drug names per this project's standing rule.

tia_urgent_evaluation_pathway.name: ABCD2-Score-Guided Same-Day/Urgent TIA Clinic Pathway
tia_urgent_evaluation_pathway.type: Risk-stratified urgent diagnostic and treatment-initiation pathway
tia_urgent_evaluation_pathway.effectiveness: Urgent assessment-and-immediate-treatment clinics reduced 90-day recurrent stroke risk from 10.3% to 2.1% (an 80% relative risk reduction) purely by compressing median time-to-first-treatment from 20 days to 1 day, with no increase in bleeding complications (Rothwell PM et al., EXPRESS study, Lancet 2007). ABCD2 score itself stratifies 2-day stroke risk: 8.1% high-risk (score 6-7), 4.1% moderate (4-5), 1.0% low (0-3) (Johnston SC et al., Lancet 2007).
tia_urgent_evaluation_pathway.reason_why: TIA represents transient ischaemia that has NOT yet progressed to infarction - the underlying cause (large-artery stenosis, cardioembolic source, small-vessel disease) is still present and about to cause a real disabling stroke unless identified and treated within the highest-risk early days (up to half of the 90-day stroke risk after TIA occurs within the first 48 hours).
tia_urgent_evaluation_pathway.important_caveat: Even a LOW ABCD2 score does not fully exclude high risk if imaging shows a DWI abnormality (meaning a small infarct already occurred, i.e. it was technically a minor stroke, not a TIA), large-artery atherosclerosis, or atrial fibrillation - the score is a triage aid to prioritise urgency, not a replacement for full imaging/cardiac workup in every patient.
tia_urgent_evaluation_pathway.source: Johnston SC 2007 Lancet PMID 17258668 (ABCD2 validation); Rothwell PM 2007 Lancet PMID 17928046 (EXPRESS study)

tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.name: Short-Course Dual Antiplatelet Therapy - Aspirin + Clopidogrel
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.effectiveness: 90-day stroke recurrence 8.2% (clopidogrel+aspirin, n=1708) vs 11.7% (aspirin alone, n=1711); HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.57-0.81), p<0.001 - a 32% relative risk reduction vs aspirin alone, with no increase in moderate/severe haemorrhage (0.3% both arms) (CHANCE, Wang Y et al., NEJM 2013). POINT confirmed this in a Western population: major ischaemic event at 90 days 5.0% vs 6.5%, HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.59-0.95), p=0.02 - a 25% relative risk reduction, though major haemorrhage rose from 0.4% to 0.9% (HR 2.32, p=0.02) (Johnston SC et al., NEJM 2018).
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.reason_why: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 to block thromboxane A2-mediated platelet aggregation; clopidogrel (a prodrug metabolised by CYP2C19) irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor - together they block platelet activation via two independent, complementary pathways, which is why short-course combination outperforms aspirin monotherapy specifically in the highest-risk early window after TIA, without the long-term bleeding penalty seen when dual therapy is continued indefinitely.
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.important_caveat: Benefit is time-limited: both CHANCE and POINT started therapy within 24 hours (CHANCE) to 12 hours (POINT) of symptom onset, and both restricted dual therapy to a SHORT course (21-90 days) before de-escalating to a single antiplatelet, because POINT's own data showed major haemorrhage more than doubled (HR 2.32) with continued dual therapy. CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers get less benefit from clopidogrel specifically (basis for ticagrelor as an alternative, see below).
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.source: Wang Y 2013 NEJM PMID 23803136 (CHANCE); Johnston SC 2018 NEJM PMID 29766750 (POINT)

tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.name: Short-Course Dual Antiplatelet Therapy - Aspirin + Ticagrelor
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.type: Antiplatelet combination (non-thienopyridine P2Y12 inhibitor + COX inhibitor)
specific_drugs: Ticagrelor (180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily)
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.effectiveness: Composite stroke-or-death at 30 days: 5.5% (ticagrelor+aspirin) vs 6.6% (aspirin alone), HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.71-0.96), p=0.02; ischaemic stroke specifically 5.0% vs 6.3%, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.68-0.93), p=0.004 - a 21% relative risk reduction - but severe bleeding rose from 0.1% to 0.5% (p=0.001) (THALES, Johnston SC et al., NEJM 2020).
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.reason_why: Ticagrelor is a direct-acting, reversible P2Y12 inhibitor that does not require hepatic CYP2C19 activation (unlike clopidogrel), so it retains full antiplatelet effect in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers - a real, mechanistically-grounded alternative for that specific genetic subgroup, or where clopidogrel resistance is confirmed/suspected.
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.important_caveat: THALES also showed a real increase in severe bleeding with ticagrelor+aspirin, and the composite stroke-or-death benefit (HR 0.83) was more modest than CHANCE/POINT's clopidogrel-based benefit - ticagrelor+aspirin is a second-line/CYP2C19-guided option, not a routine first-line replacement for clopidogrel+aspirin.

tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.name: Aspirin Monotherapy
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.effectiveness: Long-standing baseline secondary-prevention therapy for non-cardioembolic TIA; used as the active comparator arm in CHANCE/POINT/THALES (recurrence rates of 11.7%, 6.5%, and 6.6% respectively at 90/90/30 days on aspirin alone), and remains the standard long-term single antiplatelet after the short dual-therapy course ends.
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.reason_why: Irreversible COX-1 inhibition blocks thromboxane A2 synthesis, reducing platelet aggregation; a real, well-established, low-cost baseline antiplatelet effect that dual therapy is added on top of during the high-risk early window only.
tia_dual_antiplatelet_therapy.source: Wang Y 2013 NEJM PMID 23803136; Johnston SC 2018 NEJM PMID 29766750

tia_statin_therapy.name: High-Intensity Statin Therapy
tia_statin_therapy.effectiveness: Fatal/non-fatal stroke over ~5 years: 11.2% (atorvastatin 80mg) vs 13.1% (placebo), HR 0.84 - a 16% relative risk reduction, 2.2% absolute risk reduction; major cardiovascular events reduced by 3.5% absolute (SPARCL, Amarenco P et al., NEJM 2006, n=4731 patients with recent stroke/TIA and no known coronary disease).
tia_statin_therapy.reason_why: High-intensity statins lower LDL cholesterol substantially (SPARCL achieved mean LDL 73 mg/dL vs 129 mg/dL on placebo), reducing atherosclerotic plaque burden/instability in the large-artery beds (carotid, intracranial) that are a leading cause of TIA, plus real pleiotropic anti-inflammatory/plaque-stabilising effects independent of LDL lowering.
tia_statin_therapy.important_caveat: SPARCL also showed a real, smaller increase in haemorrhagic stroke (55 vs 33 cases) - a genuine trade-off, though the net effect strongly favours statin therapy given the much larger reduction in ischaemic events.

tia_af_anticoagulation.name: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) for AF-Related TIA
tia_af_anticoagulation.type: Factor Xa inhibitor / direct thrombin inhibitor
tia_af_anticoagulation.effectiveness: Apixaban vs warfarin in AF: stroke/systemic embolism HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.66-0.95) - a further 21% relative risk reduction versus warfarin itself, with fewer major bleeds and lower mortality (ARISTOTLE, Granger CB et al., NEJM 2011).
tia_af_anticoagulation.reason_why: In atrial fibrillation, blood stasis in the left atrial appendage promotes thrombus formation; factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) and the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran block the coagulation cascade at a specific, targeted step, achieving more predictable anticoagulation than warfarin's broad vitamin-K-dependent-factor suppression, with materially lower intracranial haemorrhage rates.

tia_af_anticoagulation.name: Warfarin (Vitamin K Antagonist)
tia_af_anticoagulation.effectiveness: In AF patients with a recent TIA/minor stroke, warfarin reduced annual stroke risk from 12% to 4% (a 67% relative risk reduction) and annual vascular events from 17% to 8% (HR 0.53) versus placebo (EAFT Study Group, Lancet 1993).
tia_af_anticoagulation.reason_why: Warfarin inhibits hepatic synthesis of vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), reducing the coagulation cascade's ability to form the atrial thrombus that would otherwise embolise to the brain; the original, still-valid proof-of-concept that anticoagulation (rather than antiplatelet therapy alone) is required for AF-driven cardioembolic TIA/stroke.
tia_af_anticoagulation.important_caveat: Requires regular INR monitoring and has a narrow therapeutic window with real bleeding risk, particularly intracranial haemorrhage risk higher than DOACs - hence current guidelines prefer a DOAC where there is no contraindication (e.g. mechanical heart valve, moderate-severe mitral stenosis, where warfarin remains required).

tia_carotid_revascularization.name: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
specific_drugs: Open surgical removal of atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery, ideally within 2 weeks of the qualifying TIA
tia_carotid_revascularization.effectiveness: 2-year ipsilateral stroke in symptomatic 70-99% stenosis: 9% (CEA + medical therapy) vs 26% (medical therapy alone) - an absolute risk reduction of 17 +/- 3.5 percentage points (NASCET Collaborators, NEJM 1991).
tia_carotid_revascularization.reason_why: Physically removes the unstable atherosclerotic plaque that is the direct embolic/haemodynamic source of the TIA, eliminating the lesion rather than just reducing platelet aggregation/clot propagation around it - the only intervention in this survey that removes the causal anatomical lesion itself.
tia_carotid_revascularization.important_caveat: Benefit is critically dependent on degree of stenosis (strong benefit >=70%, modest for 50-69%, no benefit/net harm <50%) and on timing (benefit is greatest when performed within 2 weeks of the TIA and falls off with delay) and on a low perioperative complication rate.

tia_carotid_revascularization.name: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS)
specific_drugs: Percutaneous stent placement across the stenotic carotid segment, typically with a distal embolic-protection device
tia_carotid_revascularization.effectiveness: Composite of stroke/MI/death at 4 years: 7.2% (CAS) vs 6.8% (CEA), HR 1.11 (95% CI 0.81-1.51), p=0.51 - statistically equivalent to CEA, a real alternative rather than an inferior substitute (CREST, Brott TG et al., NEJM 2010).
tia_carotid_revascularization.reason_why: Mechanically restores luminal patency across the stenosis via balloon-expandable/self-expanding stent, without requiring open surgical dissection - preferred in patients at high surgical/anaesthetic risk or with surgically inaccessible lesions/prior neck irradiation.
tia_carotid_revascularization.important_caveat: CAS carries a real higher periprocedural stroke rate (4.1% vs 2.3%, p=0.01) than CEA, while CEA carries a real higher periprocedural MI rate (2.3% vs 1.1%, p=0.03) - the choice is genuinely patient-risk-specific, not a strict hierarchy.

tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.name: Long-Term Blood Pressure Control
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.effectiveness: Sustained blood pressure lowering is a real, guideline-endorsed cornerstone of long-term secondary stroke prevention after TIA (cross-reference this KB's hypertension entry for detailed drug-class trial data); AHA/ASA secondary stroke prevention guidelines recommend BP control as standard of care alongside antiplatelet/statin therapy.
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.reason_why: Chronic hypertension is the dominant driver of both large-artery atherosclerosis and small-vessel (lacunar) disease, the two most common structural causes of TIA - controlling it removes the ongoing haemodynamic/vascular-injury stimulus rather than just reacting to its downstream thrombotic consequences.
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.source: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (cross-referenced to this KB's hypertension entry for trial-level detail)
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.confidence: moderate - class-level guideline recommendation; specific TIA-only outcome-trial data for individual antihypertensive agents is cross-referenced rather than independently re-verified in this entry

tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.name: Smoking Cessation, Glycaemic Control, and Lifestyle Risk-Factor Modification
specific_drugs: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy: Varenicline, Bupropion, Nicotine replacement therapy
Glycaemic control agents per this KB's diabetes_mellitus entry
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.effectiveness: Established, guideline-recommended real risk-factor modification; effect sizes for smoking cessation and glycaemic control on recurrent-stroke risk specifically are cross-referenced from general cardiovascular-risk literature rather than a single dedicated TIA-only randomized trial.
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.reason_why: Smoking and poor glycaemic control both independently accelerate atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction, compounding the vascular risk that caused the index TIA.
tia_blood_pressure_and_risk_factor_manag.confidence: moderate - class-level guideline recommendation, not a single dedicated outcome trial

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (90-day recurrent stroke, annual stroke risk, 2-year ipsilateral stroke, 5-year fatal/non-fatal stroke, 30-day stroke/death) in somewhat different TIA/minor-stroke populations - ranking together is directionally useful for triage priority, not strict apples-to-apples. The urgent-evaluation pathway (EXPRESS) is honestly ranked at the top not because its own single number is the largest possible risk reduction, but because it is the real precondition that makes every other row's benefit achievable at all - none of the drug/procedure effects below can be realised if the patient is not urgently assessed and started on treatment within hours/days.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Urgent same-day TIA clinic pathway (ABCD2-triaged assessment + immediate treatment initiation)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk reduction in 90-day recurrent stroke (10.3% to 2.1%)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rothwell PM et al., EXPRESS study, Lancet 2007, PMID 17928046

ranked_high_to_low.name: Anticoagulation (warfarin) for AF-related TIA
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk reduction in annual stroke risk vs placebo (12% to 4%/year)
ranked_high_to_low.source: EAFT Study Group, Lancet 1993, PMID 7901582

definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Easton JD et al., 'Definition and Evaluation of Transient Ischemic Attack' - AHA/ASA Scientific Statement, Stroke 2009;40(6):2276-93 (PMID 19423857); Kidwell CS et al., 'Diffusion MRI in patients with transient ischemic attacks', Stroke 1999;30(6):1174-80 (PMID 10356095)
definition_and_pathophysiology.confidence: high - AHA/ASA formal scientific statement plus a directly cited primary imaging study
definition_and_pathophysiology.old_definition: Historically (pre-2009) TIA was defined purely by a 24-hour time cutoff: 'a sudden focal neurological deficit lasting less than 24 hours, presumed to be of vascular origin.' This was arbitrary and never based on tissue outcome.
definition_and_pathophysiology.current_tissue_based_definition: The 2009 AHA/ASA statement (Easton et al., PMID 19423857) redefined TIA as 'a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction.' The distinction from ischaemic stroke is now made by tissue injury (infarction present or absent on imaging), not by an arbitrary symptom-duration clock.
definition_and_pathophysiology.why_the_definition_changed: The 24-hour cutoff was abandoned because a real, clinically important fraction of patients whose symptoms fully resolve within that window already have a permanent infarct on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) - i.e., they have actually had a stroke by tissue criteria despite a 'TIA' by the old time-based criteria.
definition_and_pathophysiology.dwi_positive_despite_symptom_resolution: In the primary imaging series by Kidwell et al. (Stroke 1999, PMID 10356095), 20 of 42 clinically diagnosed TIA patients (48%) had a DWI abnormality on MRI despite complete clinical symptom resolution; DWI-positive patients had longer symptom duration (mean 7.3 hours) than DWI-negative patients (mean 3.2 hours). This single-centre figure (n=42) is the directly verified number for this entry; larger contemporary series generally report DWI-positive rates in a similar but wide range, which was not independently re-verified this session and is not quoted here as a separate number to avoid unverified precision.
definition_and_pathophysiology.clinical_implication: Because a 'transient' clinical event can still represent completed brain infarction on tissue imaging, MRI with DWI is the recommended first-line neuroimaging in TIA workup (Easton et al., PMID 19423857), not a plain non-contrast CT alone.

diagnostic_framework.source: Johnston SC, Rothwell PM, Nguyen-Huynh MN, Giles MF, Elkins JS, Bernstein AL, Sidney S. 'Validation and refinement of scores to predict very early stroke risk after transient ischaemic attack.' Lancet 2007;369(9558):283-92 (PMID 17258668)
diagnostic_framework.confidence: high - the definitive multi-cohort (n=2893 total, 4 independent US/UK cohorts) derivation and validation study for the ABCD2 score, the score endorsed by the AHA/ASA 2009 statement (PMID 19423857) for early risk stratification

abcd2_score_components.factor: Blood pressure >=140/90 mmHg at first assessment
Clinical features: speech impairment without weakness
Clinical features: other symptoms (no weakness or speech disturbance)

diagnostic_framework.discriminative_performance: c-statistic 0.62-0.83 across the validation cohorts (PMID 17258668); the ABCD2 score outperformed the earlier standalone ABCD and California scores it was derived from.
diagnostic_framework.other_required_workup: Per the 2009 AHA/ASA statement (PMID 19423857): neuroimaging within 24 hours (MRI with diffusion sequences preferred over CT), imaging of the cervical and intracranial vessels (carotid duplex/CTA/MRA), 12-lead ECG plus cardiac rhythm monitoring, echocardiography when the cause is not otherwise apparent, and routine bloods (glucose, lipids, coagulation). Hospitalisation is reasonable for patients presenting within 72 hours of a TIA with an ABCD2 score >=3, or when outpatient evaluation cannot be completed rapidly.
diagnostic_framework.clinical_caveat: ABCD2 is a triage/urgency tool, not a diagnostic test - it stratifies already-diagnosed TIA patients by short-term stroke risk; it does not itself distinguish TIA from a stroke mimic.

classic_symptoms.source: Harbison J, Hossain O, Jenkinson D, Davis J, Louw SJ, Ford GA. 'Diagnostic accuracy of stroke referrals ... using the face arm speech test.' Stroke 2003;34(1):71-6 (PMID 12511753); Johnston SC, Gress DR, Browner WS, Sidney S. JAMA 2000;284(22):2901-6 (PMID 11147987)
classic_symptoms.confidence: high for FAST validation data; high for symptom-type/duration associations from the JAMA 2000 cohort

FAST_symptoms.symptom: Face - sudden facial drooping, usually one-sided
Arm - sudden arm (or leg) weakness or numbness, usually one-sided
Speech - sudden slurred speech, word-finding difficulty, or aphasia
Time - time to call emergency services immediately on any single FAST-positive finding

classic_symptoms.fast_screening_accuracy: In a prospective validation (Harbison et al., PMID 12511753), ambulance paramedics using FAST correctly diagnosed stroke/TIA in 144 of 183 (79%) confirmed cases, substantially better than unstructured assessment by non-specialist referrers.
classic_symptoms.other_classic_focal_symptoms: Sudden monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax), homonymous visual field loss, diplopia, vertigo/ataxia (posterior-circulation TIA), and sudden severe unilateral headache can also occur; by definition all TIA symptoms are focal, of abrupt onset, and fully resolve without imaging evidence of infarction.
classic_symptoms.duration_data: In the Johnston et al. JAMA 2000 cohort (n=1707 ED-diagnosed TIA, PMID 11147987), symptom duration >10 minutes independently predicted subsequent stroke (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.3-4.2); other independent predictors in the same cohort were age >60 years (OR 1.8), diabetes (OR 2.0), weakness (OR 1.9), and speech impairment (OR 1.5) - i.e., the same clinical features later formalised into the ABCD2 score carry real, independently-derived predictive weight.
classic_symptoms.typical_duration: Most true TIAs resolve within minutes to under an hour; the ABCD2 duration cut-points (<10 min / 10-59 min / >=60 min, PMID 17258668) reflect the real observation that longer-duration events carry higher subsequent stroke risk even when full resolution occurs.

differential_diagnosis.source: Libman RB, Wirkowski E, Alvir J, Rao TH. 'Conditions that mimic stroke in the emergency department.' Arch Neurol 1995;52(11):1119-22 (PMID 7487564); Magauran BG Jr, Nitka M. 'Stroke mimics.' Emerg Med Clin North Am 2012;30(3):795-804 (PMID 22974649)
differential_diagnosis.confidence: high for the quantified mimic rate (Libman 1995, direct ED cohort); moderate-high for the categorical mimic list (Magauran 2012 review, no re-verified per-mimic percentages this session)
differential_diagnosis.real_mimic_rate: In a prospective ED cohort of 411 patients admitted with a working diagnosis of stroke (Libman et al., PMID 7487564), 78 patients (19%) were ultimately found to have a stroke-mimicking condition rather than true cerebrovascular disease - the majority were postictal (post-seizure) states, systemic infection, tumour, and toxic-metabolic disturbance.

key_mimics_to_actively_exclude.distinguishing_feature: Positive motor phenomena (jerking) at onset, post-ictal confusion/drowsiness, gradual (not instantaneous) resolution over hours - the single most common mimic identified by Libman et al. (PMID 7487564).

Aura classically 'marches' and evolves over 15-30+ minutes (visual scintillations spreading, then paraesthesia, then speech disturbance) rather than being maximal at onset as in TIA; often followed by headache; typically a history of prior similar episodes.

Confirmed by real-time point-of-care glucose measurement; a toxic-metabolic cause explicitly named among the major mimic categories by Libman et al. (PMID 7487564) and Magauran & Nitka (PMID 22974649); focal deficits can fully mimic TIA and resolve promptly with glucose correction.

key_mimics_to_actively_exclude.mimic: Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
key_mimics_to_actively_exclude.distinguishing_feature: Isolated vertigo without other focal neurological signs; HINTS bedside oculomotor exam differentiates from posterior-circulation TIA in expert hands.

key_mimics_to_actively_exclude.mimic: Functional/psychogenic neurological symptoms, syncope, and other systemic/toxic-metabolic disturbances
key_mimics_to_actively_exclude.distinguishing_feature: Named among the major mimic categories in both cited reviews; require directed history and exclusion of vascular territory-fitting deficits.

differential_diagnosis.clinical_rule: Because roughly 1 in 5 suspected-stroke/TIA presentations is ultimately a mimic (PMID 7487564), a structured history (onset pattern, positive vs negative symptoms, point-of-care glucose) plus neuroimaging is required before anchoring on a TIA diagnosis, even though the emergency response to a genuine suspected TIA must not be delayed while this workup proceeds.

risk_factors.source: Wolf PA, Abbott RD, Kannel WB. 'Atrial fibrillation as an independent risk factor for stroke: the Framingham Study.' Stroke 1991;22(8):983-8 (PMID 1866765); Atrial Fibrillation Investigators. 'Risk factors for stroke and efficacy of antithrombotic therapy in atrial fibrillation.' Arch Intern Med 1994;154(13):1449-57 (PMID 8018000); North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) Collaborators. NEJM 1991;325(7):445-53 (PMID 1852179); Johnston SC et al. JAMA 2000;284(22):2901-6 (PMID 11147987)
risk_factors.confidence: high - all figures are from the original landmark trials/cohorts, directly cited
risk_factors.atrial_fibrillation: Framingham data (Wolf et al., PMID 1866765) showed a near five-fold excess incidence of stroke in people with atrial fibrillation compared with those free of cardiovascular disease (p<0.001); pooled RCT data (AFI, PMID 8018000) measured an untreated (placebo/control) AF stroke rate of 4.5%/year, cut to 1.4%/year with warfarin (68% relative risk reduction, 95% CI 50-79%). AF is the leading identifiable cardioembolic cause of TIA/stroke.
risk_factors.carotid_stenosis: In the NASCET trial of symptomatic patients with 70-99% carotid stenosis (PMID 1852179), the 2-year risk of any ipsilateral stroke on medical therapy alone was 26%, versus 9% with carotid endarterectomy added (absolute risk reduction 17 +/- 3.5%); for major/fatal ipsilateral stroke the reduction was 13.1% to 2.5% (absolute reduction 10.6 +/- 2.6%, p<0.001). This establishes that a real, high (~26% at 2 years untreated) recurrent-stroke risk exists specifically in TIA/minor-stroke patients found to have severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis, which is why urgent carotid imaging is part of the standard TIA workup.
risk_factors.hypertension_age_diabetes_symptom_type: In the JAMA 2000 ED cohort (Johnston et al., PMID 11147987, n=1707), independent predictors of 90-day stroke after TIA were: age >60 years (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-2.7), diabetes mellitus (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.4-2.9), symptom duration >10 minutes (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.3-4.2), weakness (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.4-2.6), and speech impairment (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1-2.1). Blood pressure >=140/90 mmHg at presentation is likewise an independently weighted ABCD2 risk factor (PMID 17258668). A specific pooled relative-risk figure for hypertension alone as a TIA risk factor was not independently re-verified this session and is therefore not quoted as a standalone number.

epidemiology.source: Kleindorfer D, Panagos P, Pancioli A, Khoury J, Kissela B, Woo D, Schneider A, Alwell K, Jauch E, Miller R, Moomaw C, Shukla R, Broderick JP. 'Incidence and short-term prognosis of transient ischemic attack in a population-based study.' Stroke 2005;36(4):720-3 (PMID 15731465)
epidemiology.confidence: high - population-based (Greater Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky) incidence study, directly cited
epidemiology.incidence: The race-, age-, and gender-adjusted incidence rate for TIA in this population-based study was 83 per 100,000 person-years (PMID 15731465).
epidemiology.short_term_outcome_in_same_cohort: In the same population-based cohort, the risk of stroke after TIA was 14.6% at 3 months, and the combined risk of TIA/stroke/death at 3 months was 25.2% (PMID 15731465) - concordant with the Johnston JAMA 2000 ED cohort's 90-day stroke risk of 10.5% (PMID 11147987), both confirming a real, substantial early post-TIA vascular event rate.

natural_history.source: Johnston SC, Gress DR, Browner WS, Sidney S. JAMA 2000;284(22):2901-6 (PMID 11147987); Giles MF, Rothwell PM. 'Risk of stroke early after transient ischaemic attack: a systematic review and meta-analysis.' Lancet Neurol 2007;6(12):1063-72 (PMID 17993293); Kleindorfer D et al. Stroke 2005;36(4):720-3 (PMID 15731465)
natural_history.confidence: high - one large ED cohort, one systematic review/meta-analysis of 18 cohorts (n=10,126), and one population-based study, all independently cited and mutually consistent
natural_history.stroke_risk_is_front_loaded: TIA-associated stroke risk is heavily concentrated in the earliest days after the event, which is why TIA is a time-critical emergency rather than a condition for routine outpatient follow-up.

real_numbers.finding: 10.5% (180/1707) returned with stroke within 90 days; more than half of these strokes (91/180) occurred within the first 2 days.

Pooled 7-day stroke risk across 18 cohorts (n=10,126) was 5.2% (95% CI 3.9-6.5). Risk varied sharply by care setting: as low as 0.9% (95% CI 0.0-1.9) in services providing urgent specialist assessment/treatment, versus 11.0% (95% CI 8.6-13.5) in population-based cohorts without urgent treatment - i.e., roughly a 12-fold difference in early stroke risk depending on how fast the patient is assessed and treated.
14.6% stroke risk at 3 months in a population-based (non-urgent-clinic) cohort; 25.2% combined TIA/stroke/death risk at 3 months.

natural_history.clinical_message: Across three independent, methodologically different studies, roughly 1 in 10 to 1 in 7 TIA patients has a stroke within 90 days, with a large fraction of that risk landing in the first 48-72 hours - and the single biggest modifiable determinant of that risk found in this literature is how quickly the patient is assessed and started on secondary-prevention treatment (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).

symptoms.clinical_takeaway: TIA is not a benign 'near miss' - it is a warning sign of a real, quantified, front-loaded stroke risk (up to ~1 in 10 within 90 days, concentrated in the first 48-72 hours per PMID 11147987 and PMID 17993293), and it can co-exist with a completed infarct on DWI-MRI despite full symptom resolution (48% in PMID 10356095). Every suspected TIA needs same-day ABCD2 risk stratification (PMID 17258668), urgent brain MRI-DWI plus vessel and cardiac imaging, and immediate initiation of secondary prevention (antiplatelet/anticoagulant as indicated, statin, BP control, carotid intervention if indicated) - because urgent evaluation and treatment has been shown, in real controlled comparisons, to cut 90-day recurrent stroke risk by about 80% (EXPRESS study, PMID 17928046) and to bring the observed stroke rate to roughly one-fifth of what risk-score prediction would otherwise anticipate (SOS-TIA, PMID 17928270). Medicine/procedure-first priority for this KB: (1) urgent secondary-prevention medicine (antiplatelet or anticoagulant per aetiology, high-intensity statin, BP-lowering agent) started the same day risk is identified; (2) carotid revascularisation procedure (endarterectomy/stenting) when severe symptomatic carotid stenosis is found (PMID 1852179); (3) everything else (rehabilitation, risk-factor education) follows.

transient_ischemic_attack.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TIA is itself a medical emergency - a 'warning stroke' - and must NEVER be managed as a routine or delayed outpatient consultation, even though the presenting symptoms have already resolved by the time the patient is seen. Real evidence on timing of risk: pooled data across 18 cohorts (n=10,126; Giles & Rothwell, Lancet Neurol 2007, PMID 17993293) show a 7-day pooled stroke risk of 5.2% (95% CI 3.9-6.5), and in the Johnston et al. JAMA 2000 ED cohort (PMID 11147987) of the 10.5% of patients who had a stroke within 90 days, over half of those strokes (91 of 180) occurred within the first 48 hours. In population-based settings without urgent treatment pathways, pooled early stroke risk reaches 11.0% (PMID 17993293) - roughly matching the Kleindorfer et al. population-based figure of 14.6% at 3 months (Stroke 2005, PMID 15731465). Real evidence that urgent evaluation and treatment reduces this risk: the EXPRESS study (Rothwell PM et al., Lancet 2007, PMID 17928046), a prospective before-after comparison in the Oxford Vascular Study, found that moving to urgent TIA-clinic assessment (median delay 3 days down to <1 day) and immediate treatment initiation (20 days down to 1 day) cut the 90-day recurrent stroke risk from 10.3% (32/310 patients) to 2.1% (6/281 patients) - an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.20 (95% CI 0.08-0.49, p=0.0001), i.e., an approximately 80% relative risk reduction, achieved without increasing intracerebral haemorrhage or major bleeding. The independent SOS-TIA study (Lavallée PC et al., Lancet Neurol 2007, PMID 17928270), using a round-the-clock rapid-access TIA clinic in France, observed a 90-day stroke rate of only 1.24% (95% CI 0.72-2.12) against an ABCD2-score-predicted rate of 5.96% - i.e., the observed rate was roughly one-fifth of what the risk score predicted once urgent assessment and treatment were provided. OPERATIONAL RULE: any suspected TIA (transient focal neurological deficit of abrupt onset - facial droop, unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, sudden monocular or binocular visual loss, or acute vestibular/ataxic syndrome - regardless of whether it has already resolved) must trigger the same immediate emergency-pathway response as an active stroke (call emergency services / go to the nearest stroke-capable emergency department NOW for same-day ABCD2 stratification, brain MRI-DWI, vessel imaging, cardiac workup, and same-day initiation of secondary prevention), never a routine doctor-approval queue or a 'see your GP this week' deferral.

agoraphobia.name: Agoraphobia
agoraphobia.icd11_hint: 6B02 Agoraphobia (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, block 6B00-6B0Z Anxiety or fear-related disorders); ICD-10 F40.0 Agoraphobia. FLAG: the exact WHO ICD-11 browser/API entry could not be directly queried in this research session (id.who.int/icd API returned HTTP 401 Unauthorized, requiring an OAuth token not available here, and the public ICD-11 browser page required interactive navigation not reachable via automated fetch). 6B02 is inferred from the sequential, publicly documented ICD-11 anxiety-disorder block ordering (6B00 Generalised anxiety disorder, 6B01 Panic disorder, 6B02 Agoraphobia, 6B03 Specific phobia, 6B04 Social anxiety disorder, 6B05 Separation anxiety disorder, 6B06 Selective mutism), consistent with the 6B00/6B01 codes already verified and used elsewhere in this knowledge base (generalized_anxiety_disorder entry). Recommend a direct WHO ICD-11 browser confirmation (icd.who.int) before any clinical or billing use of this code.
agoraphobia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Agoraphobia is one of the most treatable anxiety disorders when the correct exposure-based psychotherapy is delivered, and this must be led with, not buried under caveats. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) combining in-vivo exposure and interoceptive exposure is the real first-line, closest-to-cure treatment: a Cochrane network meta-analysis of 54 RCTs (n=3,021 patients with panic disorder with or without agoraphobia; Pompoli A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004, PMID 27071857) found CBT was often superior to other psychological therapies for short-term remission, response and continuous-improvement outcomes, and showed the highest remission/response of any psychotherapy at long-term follow-up. A larger 2022 network meta-analysis of 136 RCTs (Papola D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;221(3):507-519, PMID 35049483) confirmed CBT as the highest-confidence first-line psychotherapy (SMD -0.67 vs treatment-as-usual, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.39). The NIMH Collaborative Panic Disorder trial (Barlow DH et al, JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536, PMID 10815116; n=312) found CBT alone achieved a 48.7% acute PDSS response rate (comparable to imipramine's 45.8%, both far above placebo's 21.7%), and that adding an antidepressant to CBT raised acute response to 60.3% (PDSS) / 64.1% (CGI) and gave the most durable 6-month maintenance response (57.1%) of any treatment arm. SSRIs are the real, well-evidenced first-line pharmacological option: paroxetine 40 mg/day produced an 86.0% panic-attack-free rate at 10 weeks vs 50.0% with placebo (Ballenger JC et al, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42, PMID 9433336), and sertraline reduced panic-attack frequency by 88% among completers vs 53% with placebo (Pohl RB et al, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(9):1189-1195, PMID 9734541). No single treatment in this survey reaches a guaranteed, universal 100% cure, but the combination of exposure-based CBT plus, when needed, an SSRI represents a genuinely high-response, guideline-endorsed (WFSBP 2023, PMID 35900161) path to full remission for the majority of real patients -- this is a solvable problem of delivering the right exposure protocol and, where indicated, the right SSRI, not an incurable condition.

curative_option.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy with In-Vivo + Interoceptive Exposure -- the Real Closest-to-Cure Treatment for Agoraphobia
curative_option.type: Structured exposure-based psychotherapy, typically 12-16 weekly individual or group sessions; not a drug or procedure
curative_option.note: Agoraphobia is not 'cured' in the sense of a guaranteed, permanent, one-time elimination for every patient -- relapse can occur, especially if exposure practice is not maintained. What IS real: exposure-based CBT is the only treatment modality in this survey shown, across two large, independent network meta-analyses (54 RCTs/n=3,021 and 136 RCTs), to reach the top-ranked, highest-confidence effect size against every comparator including treatment-as-usual and other psychotherapies, and it is the treatment these same meta-analyses judge most durable at long-term follow-up.

real_trial_data.pompoli_2016_cochrane_nma: 54 RCTs, n=3,021 (panic disorder with/without agoraphobia): CBT often superior to other psychological therapies (behaviour therapy, psychodynamic therapy, supportive therapy) for short-term remission, response and continuous improvement; CBT and psychodynamic therapy showed the highest remission/response of any psychotherapies at long-term follow-up.
real_trial_data.papola_2022_network_meta_analysis: 136 RCTs: CBT efficacy vs treatment-as-usual SMD -0.67 (95% CI -0.95 to -0.39), moderate-confidence (CINeMA) -- the highest-confidence-rated psychotherapy evaluated; short-term psychodynamic therapy was the only other reasonable first-line choice (SMD -0.61, low confidence).
real_trial_data.barlow_2000_nimh_collaborative_trial: 312 patients, 4 US academic anxiety-disorder clinics, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled: acute PDSS response 48.7% CBT alone, 45.8% imipramine alone, both far above 21.7% placebo; combining CBT with imipramine raised acute response to 60.3% (PDSS) / 64.1% (CGI); at 6-month maintenance, combined treatment gave the best response of any arm (57.1% PDSS vs 39.5% CBT alone and 37.8% imipramine alone), and CBT alone showed the best durability after treatment discontinuation.

curative_option.source: Pompoli A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004 (PMID 27071857); Papola D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;221(3):507-519 (PMID 35049483); Barlow DH et al, JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536 (PMID 10815116)
curative_option.confidence: high for the Barlow 2000 RCT numbers (single large real trial with a documented denominator); moderate-high for the network-meta-analytic effect-size rankings (real, large evidence syntheses, but the review authors themselves rate overall primary-study evidence quality low-to-moderate owing to risk of bias, including researcher allegiance, across the underlying trials)

agor_cbt_exposure_therapy_in_vivo_intero.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy with In-Vivo and Interoceptive Exposure
agor_cbt_exposure_therapy_in_vivo_intero.type: First-line structured psychotherapy protocol, typically 12-16 weekly individual or group sessions
specific_protocols: In-vivo exposure: graded, real-world exposure to avoided situations (leaving home alone, crowds, public transport, queues, enclosed spaces, open spaces)

Interoceptive exposure: deliberate induction of feared bodily sensations (e.g. hyperventilation, spinning in a chair, breathing through a narrow straw, running in place) to break the learned link between bodily sensation and panic
Cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations
Breathing retraining / applied relaxation as adjuncts (less consistently supportive of outcome than exposure itself)
agor_cbt_exposure_therapy_in_vivo_intero.effectiveness: Cochrane network meta-analysis of 54 RCTs, n=3,021 patients with panic disorder with/without agoraphobia (Pompoli A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004, PMID 27071857): CBT often superior to other psychological therapies for short-term remission, response and continuous-symptom-improvement outcomes, and CBT/psychodynamic therapy showed the highest remission/response at long-term follow-up. A larger 2022 network meta-analysis of 136 RCTs (Papola D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;221(3):507-519, PMID 35049483) found CBT efficacy vs treatment-as-usual of SMD -0.67 (95% CI -0.95 to -0.39, moderate CINeMA confidence) -- the strongest-confidence-rated psychotherapy in the network. In the NIMH Collaborative Panic Disorder trial (Barlow DH et al, JAMA 2000;283:2529-2536, PMID 10815116, n=312), CBT alone achieved a 48.7% acute PDSS response rate.
agor_cbt_exposure_therapy_in_vivo_intero.reason_why: Agoraphobic avoidance is maintained by two linked mechanisms that exposure directly targets: avoidance of external situations (treated by in-vivo exposure, which prevents escape/avoidance from reinforcing fear via negative reinforcement) and catastrophic misinterpretation of internal bodily sensations that mimic panic (treated by interoceptive exposure, which extinguishes the conditioned sensation-panic association through repeated, safe re-exposure without the feared catastrophe occurring).
agor_cbt_exposure_therapy_in_vivo_intero.source: Pompoli A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004 (PMID 27071857); Papola D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;221(3):507-519 (PMID 35049483); Barlow DH et al, JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536 (PMID 10815116)

agor_cbt_plus_medication_combination.name: Combining CBT (Exposure-Based) with an Antidepressant vs Either Alone
specific_drugs: Imipramine (tricyclic antidepressant, trial drug used); modern practice typically substitutes an SSRI such as paroxetine or sertraline
agor_cbt_plus_medication_combination.effectiveness: NIMH Collaborative Panic Disorder multicenter RCT, 312 patients at 4 US academic anxiety-disorder research clinics (Barlow DH et al, JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536, PMID 10815116): acute-phase PDSS response was 48.7% for CBT alone, 45.8% for imipramine alone, 21.7% for placebo, and 60.3% (PDSS)/64.1% (CGI) for combined CBT + imipramine. At 6-month maintenance, combined treatment produced the best response of any arm (57.1% PDSS, p=0.04 vs CBT alone, p=0.03 vs imipramine alone), though CBT alone showed the best durability after treatment was stopped.
agor_cbt_plus_medication_combination.reason_why: Medication produces faster symptomatic relief of panic physiology while CBT builds durable, self-maintained coping/exposure skills; combining the two captures the acute-response advantage of medication and the long-term relapse-prevention advantage of CBT.
agor_cbt_plus_medication_combination.important_caveat: The acute advantage of combination therapy over CBT alone was modest (60.3% vs 48.7%), and CBT alone was more durable than either imipramine alone or combination therapy after treatment discontinuation -- combination is not simply additive.

agor_ssri_paroxetine.name: Paroxetine (SSRI)
agor_ssri_paroxetine.type: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, first-line pharmacotherapy
specific_drugs: Paroxetine 10 mg/day, 20 mg/day, or 40 mg/day (target dose 40 mg/day)
agor_ssri_paroxetine.effectiveness: Double-blind, fixed-dose, placebo-controlled multicenter RCT (Ballenger JC, Wheadon DE, Steiner M, Bushnell W, Gergel IP, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42, PMID 9433336): at week 10, 86.0% of patients on paroxetine 40 mg/day were panic-attack-free, vs 65.2% on 20 mg/day, 67.4% on 10 mg/day, and 50.0% on placebo -- a clear, real, dose-related, statistically significant advantage over placebo at the target dose.
agor_ssri_paroxetine.reason_why: Increased synaptic serotonin availability from reuptake inhibition down-regulates limbic/brainstem panic circuitry (amygdala, locus coeruleus) implicated in panic attack generation, reducing both spontaneous panic-attack frequency and the anticipatory anxiety that drives agoraphobic avoidance.
agor_ssri_paroxetine.source: Ballenger JC et al, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42 (PMID 9433336)

agor_ssri_sertraline.name: Sertraline (SSRI)
agor_ssri_sertraline.type: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, first-line pharmacotherapy
agor_ssri_sertraline.effectiveness: Double-blind, multicenter, placebo-controlled RCT (Pohl RB, Wolkow RM, Clary CM, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(9):1189-1195, PMID 9734541): among completers, panic-attack frequency decreased by 88% with sertraline vs 53% with placebo. A separate sertraline RCT in patients at risk of poor outcome (Pollack MH, Rapaport MH, Clary CM, Mardekian J, Wolkow R, J Clin Psychiatry 2000;61(12):922-927, PMID 11206597) found comparable endpoint reductions in panic-attack frequency (82% high-risk vs 78% non-high-risk groups), showing benefit generalises even to harder-to-treat patients.
agor_ssri_sertraline.reason_why: Same serotonergic mechanism as paroxetine; sertraline has a comparatively favorable drug-interaction/tolerability profile, which is why it and paroxetine are both named first-line SSRIs in panic disorder/agoraphobia guidelines.
agor_ssri_sertraline.source: Pohl RB et al, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(9):1189-1195 (PMID 9734541); Pollack MH et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2000;61(12):922-927 (PMID 11206597)

agor_snri_venlafaxine_er.name: Venlafaxine Extended-Release (SNRI)
agor_snri_venlafaxine_er.type: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, alternative first-line pharmacotherapy
agor_snri_venlafaxine_er.effectiveness: Flexible-dose, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in 361 panic disorder outpatients (Bradwejn J, Ahokas A, Stein DJ, Salinas E, Emilien G, Whitaker T, Br J Psychiatry 2005;187:352-359, PMID 16199795): venlafaxine ER produced significantly lower panic-attack frequency and significantly higher response and remission rates than placebo (exact percentage response/remission not disaggregated by dose in the abstract available in this session -- flagged, not fabricated). Cross-checked at network-meta-analysis level: Guaiana G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 38014714 (70 RCTs) found venlafaxine among the antidepressants (with desipramine, fluoxetine, clonazepam, diazepam, fluvoxamine, imipramine, paroxetine) significantly more effective than placebo for remission across 32 RCTs, n=8,569.
agor_snri_venlafaxine_er.reason_why: Dual serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition broadens the monoaminergic mechanism beyond SSRIs, giving an evidence-based alternative for SSRI non-responders or when norepinephrine-mediated somatic anxiety symptoms predominate.
agor_snri_venlafaxine_er.source: Bradwejn J et al, Br J Psychiatry 2005;187:352-359 (PMID 16199795); Guaiana G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 38014714)
agor_snri_venlafaxine_er.confidence: moderate-high -- real RCT and real network meta-analysis confirm superiority to placebo; the exact response/remission percentage for venlafaxine specifically was not extractable from the abstract text retrieved in this session, so no number is stated for it here or in the ranked table

agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.name: Pharmacological Treatments for Panic Disorder -- Real Comparative Network Meta-Analysis
agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.type: Cochrane network meta-analysis across all major drug classes
agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.effectiveness: Guaiana G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 38014714: 70 RCTs. For response (48 RCTs, n=10,118), most medications exceeded placebo; benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam) ranked highest overall. For remission (32 RCTs, n=8,569), desipramine, fluoxetine, clonazepam, diazepam, fluvoxamine, imipramine, venlafaxine and paroxetine were each significantly more effective than placebo. Head-to-head, drug-class differences in response were small (TCAs ranked most effective on average, then benzodiazepines and MAOIs, SSRIs fifth, SNRIs lowest-ranked), and benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam) had significantly better tolerability (lower dropout, 64 RCTs, n=12,310) than other classes.
agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.reason_why: Different drug classes act on overlapping but distinct panic-relevant systems (GABAergic for benzodiazepines, monoaminergic for antidepressants); the network meta-analysis quantifies that once a drug beats placebo, the remaining efficacy differences between classes are small and low-certainty, so choice is driven mainly by tolerability, safety and dependence-risk profile rather than a large efficacy gap.
agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.important_caveat: Authors rated overall study-quality evidence as low; benzodiazepines' apparent efficacy/tolerability edge must be weighed against their real dependence/withdrawal risk with long-term use (see benzodiazepine-caution entry).
agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.source: Guaiana G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 38014714)
agor_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_analys.confidence: moderate -- large real network meta-analysis, but authors themselves flag low overall certainty of the underlying trial evidence

agor_psychological_therapies_network_met.name: Psychological Therapies for Panic Disorder with/without Agoraphobia -- Real Comparative Network Meta-Analyses
agor_psychological_therapies_network_met.type: Cochrane and independent network meta-analyses across all major psychotherapy modalities
agor_psychological_therapies_network_met.effectiveness: Pompoli A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004 (PMID 27071857): 54 RCTs, n=3,021. CBT was often superior to other psychological therapies (behaviour therapy alone did not emerge as a valid first-line alternative to CBT) for short-term remission, response and continuous improvement; psychodynamic therapy and supportive psychotherapy showed sparse but relevant evidence of benefit and better short-term tolerability (fewer dropouts); CBT and psychodynamic therapy showed the highest remission/response at long-term follow-up. Papola D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;221(3):507-519 (PMID 35049483), a larger 136-RCT network meta-analysis, confirmed CBT (SMD -0.67 vs treatment-as-usual, moderate confidence) and short-term psychodynamic therapy (SMD -0.61, low confidence) as the two reasonable first-line psychotherapy choices, with CBT's evidence rated higher-confidence.
agor_psychological_therapies_network_met.reason_why: Not all psychotherapy modalities that target anxiety directly incorporate exposure to the feared situations/sensations that maintain agoraphobic avoidance; the network meta-analyses show this translates into a real, replicated efficacy edge for CBT (which does) over most alternatives (which do so less consistently or not at all).
agor_psychological_therapies_network_met.important_caveat: Both reviews caution that effect sizes across comparisons were often small/imprecise and overall evidence quality was rated low, with risks of publication bias and researcher-allegiance bias -- so 'CBT superior' is a real but not unequivocal finding.
agor_psychological_therapies_network_met.source: Pompoli A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004 (PMID 27071857); Papola D et al, Br J Psychiatry 2022;221(3):507-519 (PMID 35049483)

agor_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_comparative_.name: CBT vs Pharmacotherapy vs Combination -- Real Head-to-Head Meta-Analytic Comparison
agor_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_comparative_.effectiveness: Mitte K, 'A meta-analysis of the efficacy of psycho- and pharmacotherapy in panic disorder with and without agoraphobia', J Affect Disord 2005;88(1):27-45, PMID 16005982: 124 studies. (C)BT was more effective than no-treatment and placebo controls; pharmacotherapy was also more effective than placebo, with no clear superiority of any one drug class; (C)BT was at least as effective as pharmacotherapy and, depending on the analysis, even significantly more effective; there was no significant difference between CBT alone and CBT-plus-medication combination, though study characteristics must be considered.
agor_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_comparative_.reason_why: This independent, disorder-specific (not disorder-general) meta-analysis corroborates the more granular Barlow 2000 RCT and the Pompoli/Papola network meta-analyses: exposure-based CBT is not merely 'as good as a pill' but, on this evidence, at least equivalent and sometimes superior, while carrying a more durable post-treatment effect.

agor_benzodiazepine_caution.name: Benzodiazepines (Alprazolam, Clonazepam, Diazepam) -- Real Rapid Relief but Real Guideline Caution Against Long-Term Use
agor_benzodiazepine_caution.type: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators, rapid-onset anxiolytics
agor_benzodiazepine_caution.effectiveness: Guaiana G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 38014714 (70 RCTs): benzodiazepines ranked highest overall for response and were significantly better tolerated (lower dropout) than other drug classes; diazepam, alprazolam and clonazepam were each significantly more effective than placebo for remission.
agor_benzodiazepine_caution.important_caveat: The World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) guideline for anxiety disorders (Bandelow B et al, World J Biol Psychiatry 2023;24(2):79-117, PMID 35900161) and comparable national guidelines (e.g. Baldaçara L et al, Brazilian Psychiatric Association guideline overview, Braz J Psychiatry 2026, PMID 41046453) recommend benzodiazepines mainly for short-term or adjunctive use because of real risks of tolerance, physical dependence, withdrawal/rebound panic, sedation and cognitive impairment with long-term use; SSRIs/SNRIs plus exposure-based CBT remain first-line for sustained treatment, with benzodiazepines reserved for acute crisis relief or as a bridge while an antidepressant takes effect.
agor_benzodiazepine_caution.source: Guaiana G et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID 38014714); Bandelow B et al, World J Biol Psychiatry 2023;24(2):79-117 (PMID 35900161); Baldaçara L et al, Braz J Psychiatry 2026 (PMID 41046453)
agor_benzodiazepine_caution.reason_why: Benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A receptor chloride-channel opening, producing fast, direct CNS inhibition that aborts an acute panic attack and blunts anticipatory anxiety within minutes to hours -- much faster than the 2-6 week onset of SSRIs/SNRIs or the multi-session build of exposure-based CBT. This speed is exactly why they are useful for acute crisis bridging, but the same GABA-A mechanism that produces rapid relief also drives tolerance, physical dependence and withdrawal/rebound panic with sustained use, which is why guidelines confine them to short-term or adjunctive roles rather than first-line long-term therapy.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sertraline, reduction in panic-attack frequency among completers
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage reduction in panic-attack frequency from baseline, double-blind placebo-controlled multicenter RCT
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pohl RB, Wolkow RM, Clary CM, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(9):1189-1195 (PMID 9734541)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Paroxetine 40 mg/day, panic-attack-free rate at week 10
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage of patients completely panic-attack-free at week 10, fixed-dose placebo-controlled RCT (vs 50.0% placebo)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ballenger JC et al, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42 (PMID 9433336)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combined CBT + imipramine, acute-phase CGI response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinical Global Impression response rate, acute phase, NIMH Collaborative Panic Disorder RCT, n=312

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combined CBT + imipramine, acute-phase PDSS response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Panic Disorder Severity Scale response rate, acute phase, same RCT

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combined CBT + imipramine, 6-month maintenance PDSS response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: PDSS response rate at 6-month maintenance, best of all treatment arms (p=0.04 vs CBT alone, p=0.03 vs imipramine alone)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy alone (exposure-based), acute-phase PDSS response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: PDSS response rate, acute phase, NIMH Collaborative Panic Disorder RCT
