ranked_high_to_low.metric: PDSS response rate, acute phase, same RCT

core_definition.finding: Agoraphobia is marked fear or anxiety about two or more of five situational domains -- using public transportation, being in open spaces, being in enclosed places, standing in line or being in a crowd, and being outside of the home alone -- that arises specifically because the person fears that escape might be difficult or that help might not be available if panic-like or other incapacitating/embarrassing symptoms develop. The situations almost always provoke fear/anxiety, are actively avoided, require a companion, or are endured with intense distress, and the fear is out of proportion to the actual danger posed, persisting for 6 months or more and causing clinically significant distress or functional impairment.
core_definition.source: Wittchen HU, Gloster AT, Beesdo-Baum K, Fava GA, Craske MG, 'Agoraphobia: a review of the diagnostic classificatory position and criteria', Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426) -- this review's proposed criteria were adopted, with minor changes, as the DSM-5 agoraphobia criteria (American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5, 2013)

decoupling_from_panic_disorder.finding: Under DSM-IV, agoraphobia could only be coded as a modifier of panic disorder ('panic disorder with agoraphobia') or as the residual category 'agoraphobia without history of panic disorder'; it was not a free-standing diagnosis. Wittchen et al's diagnostic-classification review concluded that 'AG should be conceptualized as an independent disorder with more specific criteria rather than a subordinate, residual form of PD [panic disorder]', a recommendation based on epidemiological evidence that agoraphobia occurs independently of panic disorder, on psychometric/validation work, and on the demonstrated impact of agoraphobic avoidance on clinical course and outcome -- while the authors also noted the validating evidence was 'incomplete and partly contradictory'. DSM-5 subsequently made agoraphobia a standalone diagnosis that can be assigned with or without a co-occurring panic disorder diagnosis.
decoupling_from_panic_disorder.source: Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426)

dsm5_criteria_summary.finding: DSM-5 agoraphobia requires: (A) marked fear/anxiety about 2+ of the 5 situational domains (public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, crowds/lines, being outside the home alone); (B) the person fears/avoids these because escape may be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like or other embarrassing/incapacitating symptoms occur; (C) the agoraphobic situations almost always provoke fear/anxiety; (D) they are actively avoided, require a companion, or are endured with intense fear/anxiety; (E) the fear/anxiety is out of proportion to the actual danger; (F) duration is persistent, typically 6 months or more; (G) it causes clinically significant distress or impairment; and (H)/(I) if another medical condition or mental disorder is present, the fear must be clearly in excess of what that condition would warrant and not better explained by another disorder (e.g. specific phobia, social anxiety disorder). Critically, the diagnosis is now made independent of whether panic disorder is also present.
dsm5_criteria_summary.source: Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426), whose proposed criteria set was carried into DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013)

empirical_validation_dsm5_vs_dsm4.finding: A World Mental Health Surveys analysis empirically comparing the new DSM-5 agoraphobia criteria against the old DSM-IV criteria found the two definitions identify overlapping but non-identical groups: of everyone meeting either definition, 57.1% met both, 24.2% met DSM-5 criteria only (i.e. new cases identified only because agoraphobia no longer requires panic-disorder-linked criteria), and 18.8% met DSM-IV criteria only. Cases meeting both definitions had higher role impairment (44.0% vs 30.4% in DSM-IV-only cases) and higher psychiatric comorbidity (92.9% vs 78.7%) than DSM-IV-only cases, and overall lifetime/12-month prevalence was similar between systems (DSM-5: 1.5%/1.0%; DSM-IV: 1.4%/0.9%), i.e. the DSM-5 change identifies a real, clinically meaningful, higher-severity group of new cases without materially inflating overall prevalence.
empirical_validation_dsm5_vs_dsm4.source: Roest AM, de Jonge P, Williams CD, de Vries YA, Schoevers RA, Turner EH, Kessler RC, 'A comparison of DSM-5 and DSM-IV agoraphobia in the World Mental Health Surveys', Depress Anxiety 2019;36(6):499-510 (PMID 30726581)

avoidance_behavior_patterns.finding: The behavioral core of agoraphobia is avoidance (or endurance with marked distress, or reliance on a 'safe person'/companion) across the five DSM-5 situational domains: public transportation (buses, trains, planes), open spaces (parking lots, marketplaces, bridges), enclosed spaces (shops, theatres, elevators), standing in line or being in a crowd, and being outside the home alone. The unifying cognitive driver is not fear of the place itself but fear of being trapped, unable to escape, or unable to obtain help if incapacitating symptoms (panic-like or otherwise, e.g. falling, incontinence, vomiting) occur there.
avoidance_behavior_patterns.source: Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426)

panic_attack_overlap.finding: Agoraphobia is closely, but not exclusively, linked to panic symptomatology. In the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (DSM-IV framework, n=9,282), lifetime prevalence was 3.7% for panic disorder without agoraphobia, 1.1% for panic disorder with agoraphobia (PD-AG), 0.8% for panic attacks with agoraphobia but without full panic disorder (PA-AG), and 22.7% for isolated panic attacks without agoraphobia. Panic Disorder Severity Scale scores were highest in PD-AG (86.3% rated moderate-or-severe) and lowest in panic-attacks-only (6.7% moderate-or-severe), and all four groups showed significant comorbidity with other lifetime DSM-IV disorders, with PD-AG showing the highest rates. Summing the two agoraphobia-containing groups (1.1% + 0.8%) accounts for the ~1.9% combined lifetime rate of agoraphobia reported under DSM-IV criteria, of which the majority (about 58%) occurred alongside full panic disorder and the rest (about 42%) alongside isolated panic attacks rather than diagnosable panic disorder.
panic_attack_overlap.source: Kessler RC, Chiu WT, Jin R, Ruscio AM, Shear K, Walters EE, 'The epidemiology of panic attacks, panic disorder, and agoraphobia in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471)
panic_attack_overlap.confidence: high for the reported subgroup percentages; the ~58%/42% split is this knowledge base's own arithmetic derived transparently from those reported percentages, not a number stated directly in the source

panic_disorder.finding: Panic disorder and agoraphobia are now diagnosed as separate, potentially co-occurring conditions rather than one being a subtype of the other. Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern/worry about additional attacks or their consequences, or maladaptive behavior change; it does not require situational avoidance limited to the five agoraphobic domains. Agoraphobia can occur with or without panic disorder (or with only isolated panic attacks, as quantified above), and the key differentiator is whether the person's fear/avoidance is organised around the five specific escape/help-availability-based situational domains (agoraphobia) versus fear of the next unexpected panic attack itself wherever it might occur (panic disorder).
panic_disorder.source: Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426); Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471)

specific_phobia_situational_type.finding: Specific phobia, situational subtype, can resemble agoraphobia because both involve avoidance of situations such as enclosed spaces or flying. The distinction is that specific phobia is typically confined to one or a small number of discrete triggers and the fear is of the object/situation itself (e.g. the elevator malfunctioning), whereas agoraphobia requires fear/avoidance across 2 or more of the five defined domains and the organising fear is of being unable to escape or get help if something goes wrong, rather than of the situation per se.
specific_phobia_situational_type.source: Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426), whose criteria (Criterion I: not better explained by another disorder such as specific phobia) were adopted into DSM-5
specific_phobia_situational_type.confidence: moderate-high -- this is the standard diagnostic-classification distinction described in the cited review; a dedicated head-to-head differential-diagnosis validation study was not separately located this session

social_anxiety_disorder.finding: Social anxiety disorder overlaps with agoraphobia when both involve avoiding crowds or public places, but the underlying fear differs: in social anxiety disorder the person fears negative evaluation, scrutiny, or humiliation by others in social/performance situations, whereas in agoraphobia the fear is of being trapped or unable to obtain help if incapacitating symptoms occur, regardless of whether other people are present or judging them. DSM-5 criterion I for agoraphobia specifically requires that the presentation not be better explained by social anxiety disorder.
social_anxiety_disorder.source: Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426)
social_anxiety_disorder.confidence: moderate-high -- standard diagnostic-classification distinction from the cited review; no separate agoraphobia-vs-social-anxiety-disorder discriminant-validity study was independently verified this session

panic_disorder_and_panic_attack_associat.finding: Panic disorder/panic attacks and agoraphobia are strongly associated. In NCS-R (DSM-IV era) data, essentially all identified agoraphobia cases in the general population co-occurred with either full panic disorder (1.1% of the population, i.e. about 58% of the combined 1.9% agoraphobia group) or isolated panic attacks (0.8%, about 42%); pure agoraphobia with no panic-attack history at all was reported elsewhere (secondary source, not independently re-verified against a primary abstract this session) to be rare. A separate clinical cohort study found patients with panic disorder plus agoraphobia (PDA, n=41) had more severe panic and affective symptoms, younger age of panic onset, longer benzodiazepine use, and more antipsychotic augmentation than patients with panic disorder alone (PD, n=46), and that agoraphobia severity was independently associated with panic symptom severity, depression, anxiety, and duration of benzodiazepine use.
panic_disorder_and_panic_attack_associat.source: Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471); Shin J et al, 'Clinical implications of agoraphobia in patients with panic disorder', Medicine (Baltimore) 2020;99(35):e21414 (PMID 32791758)
panic_disorder_and_panic_attack_associat.confidence: high for the Kessler NCS-R and Shin cohort findings as reported; the 'pure agoraphobia is rare' statement is flagged as not independently re-verified against its primary source this session

psychiatric_comorbidity_burden.finding: Agoraphobia carries a very high overall psychiatric comorbidity burden: in the World Mental Health Surveys comparison of DSM-5 vs DSM-IV agoraphobia, 92.9% of people meeting both diagnostic definitions and 78.7% of those meeting DSM-IV-only criteria had at least one other lifetime psychiatric disorder.
psychiatric_comorbidity_burden.source: Roest AM et al, Depress Anxiety 2019;36(6):499-510 (PMID 30726581)

female_sex_general_anxiety_pattern.finding: Across anxiety disorders broadly (not agoraphobia in isolation), a large US epidemiological study found women have consistently higher lifetime prevalence than men, with a lifetime male:female prevalence ratio of 1:1.7 for 'any anxiety disorder', and women with an anxiety disorder also carry a greater associated illness burden than men. This is cited here as the best-verified general risk-pattern evidence located this session; an agoraphobia-specific male:female ratio was not confirmed against a primary-source abstract this session and is therefore not separately stated as a number.
female_sex_general_anxiety_pattern.source: McLean CP, Asnaani A, Litz BT, Hofmann SG, 'Gender differences in anxiety disorders: prevalence, course of illness, comorbidity and burden of illness', J Psychiatr Res 2011;45(8):1027-1035 (PMID 21439576)
female_sex_general_anxiety_pattern.confidence: moderate -- real finding, but scoped to anxiety disorders overall rather than agoraphobia specifically

lifetime_and_12month_prevalence_dsm5.finding: Using current DSM-5 criteria, cross-national World Mental Health Surveys data give a lifetime prevalence of agoraphobia of 1.5% and a 12-month prevalence of 1.0%. Under the older DSM-IV criteria applied to the same data, lifetime prevalence was 1.4% and 12-month prevalence 0.9% -- i.e. broadening the diagnosis to a standalone condition in DSM-5 identified a substantial number of new (often more impaired) cases without materially changing the overall population prevalence rate.
lifetime_and_12month_prevalence_dsm5.source: Roest AM et al, Depress Anxiety 2019;36(6):499-510 (PMID 30726581)

us_national_comorbidity_survey_replicati.finding: In the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (a nationally representative face-to-face household survey of 9,282 English-speaking adults, using DSM-IV criteria), combined lifetime prevalence of agoraphobia (panic disorder with agoraphobia, 1.1%, plus panic attacks with agoraphobia without full panic disorder, 0.8%) was approximately 1.9%.
us_national_comorbidity_survey_replicati.source: Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471)

chronicity_and_relapse.finding: A NESARC-based longitudinal study of the course of panic disorder with vs without agoraphobia found high but incomplete 3-year remission rates -- 75% for panic disorder alone (PD) versus a somewhat lower 67% for panic disorder with agoraphobia (PDA) -- alongside relatively frequent relapse (12% for PD vs 21% for PDA). Predictors of worse course (incidence/relapse) included prior panic-attack history, comorbid generalized anxiety disorder/major depressive disorder, nicotine dependence, female sex, younger age, and major financial crises; the authors caution against prematurely stopping effective treatment given this relapsing-remitting course.
chronicity_and_relapse.source: Nay W, Brown R, Roberson-Nay R, 'Longitudinal course of panic disorder with and without agoraphobia using the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC)', Psychiatry Res 2013;205(1-2):122-127 (PMID 23587657)

functional_impairment_and_treatment_gap.finding: Agoraphobia is associated with substantial functional impairment: in the World Mental Health Surveys comparison, 44.0% of people meeting both DSM-5 and DSM-IV agoraphobia criteria reported role impairment, versus 30.4% of DSM-IV-only cases. In NCS-R data, agoraphobia-linked panic presentations (PD-AG) had the highest lifetime treatment-seeking of any panic subgroup (96.1% had ever sought treatment) but the poorest 12-month guideline-concordant care -- only 54.9% received treatment meeting published treatment guidelines in the past year -- indicating a large gap between help-seeking and adequate treatment.
functional_impairment_and_treatment_gap.source: Roest AM et al, Depress Anxiety 2019;36(6):499-510 (PMID 30726581); Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471)

housebound_severity_not_independently_ve.finding: This knowledge base could not independently verify, against a primary citable source, a specific numeric rate of complete housebound-ness or severe home-confinement among people with agoraphobia within this research session. That specific figure is therefore omitted here rather than estimated, pending a future verification pass; the verified severity/impairment evidence above (44.0% role impairment, 92.9% comorbidity, relapsing-remitting course) is used instead.
housebound_severity_not_independently_ve.source: Not applicable -- explicit omission, not a sourced claim
housebound_severity_not_independently_ve.confidence: not verified this session; intentionally omitted rather than fabricated

clinical_takeaway.finding: Agoraphobia is a real, common (about 1.5% lifetime prevalence), and now independently diagnosable anxiety disorder defined by fear/avoidance of situations where escape or help would be difficult if incapacitating symptoms occurred. It is strongly, though not exclusively, linked to panic disorder and panic attacks, carries very high psychiatric comorbidity (up to ~93%), a relapsing-remitting course with meaningfully lower remission and higher relapse than panic disorder alone, and a persistent treatment-adequacy gap (high lifetime help-seeking but low guideline-concordant 12-month care). Recognising it as a standalone diagnosis (rather than only a subtype of panic disorder) identifies a real, often more severely impaired group of patients who need direct diagnostic attention and safety screening, independent of whether they also meet criteria for panic disorder.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Wittchen HU et al 2010 (PMID 20143426), Roest AM et al 2019 (PMID 30726581), Kessler RC et al 2006 (PMID 16585471), and Nay W et al 2013 (PMID 23587657), all cited individually above

agoraphobia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Agoraphobia and its closely linked panic presentations carry a real, elevated suicide risk that MUST be actively screened for and MUST bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue flow when positive, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department now, or call a local emergency/suicide helpline) rather than the standard consultation flow. Real evidence: (1) in primary-care patients with panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, 25% reported current suicidal ideation, with depression diagnosis and depression severity as the strongest correlates (Teismann T et al, 'Suicidal ideation in primary care patients suffering from panic disorder with or without agoraphobia', BMC Psychiatry 2018;18:305, PMID 30249220); (2) a systematic review and meta-analysis of anxiety disorders as a class found significantly elevated risk of suicidal ideation (OR 2.89), suicide attempts (OR 2.47), and completed suicide (OR 3.34) compared with people without an anxiety disorder, with the increase seen for every anxiety-disorder subtype examined except OCD (Kanwar A et al, 'The association between anxiety disorders and suicidal behaviors: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Depress Anxiety 2013;30(10):917-929, PMID 23408488); (3) a US population-based longitudinal study found any anxiety disorder was independently associated with incident suicidal ideation (adjusted OR 2.32) and suicide attempts (adjusted OR 3.64) over follow-up, after adjusting for mood disorders and other comorbidity (Sareen J et al, 'Anxiety disorders and risk for suicidal ideation and suicide attempts: a population-based longitudinal study of adults', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005;62(11):1249-1257, PMID 16275812); (4) a NESARC-based study found any anxiety disorder was associated with a subsequent suicide attempt (adjusted OR 1.70) after controlling for mood disorders and substance use (Nepon J et al, 'The relationship between anxiety disorders and suicide attempts: findings from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions', Depress Anxiety 2010;27(9):791-798, PMID 20217852). None of these four sources report an agoraphobia-only suicide statistic isolated from panic disorder/anxiety disorders as a class, so the numbers above should be read as class-level (anxiety-disorder or panic-plus-agoraphobia-cohort) risk evidence, not an agoraphobia-specific point estimate -- but given agoraphobia's very high psychiatric comorbidity (up to 92.9% per Roest AM et al, Depress Anxiety 2019, PMID 30726581, including frequent comorbid major depressive disorder), every patient being evaluated for agoraphobia should be directly and explicitly screened for suicidal ideation, intent, plan, and access to lethal means as a mandatory part of the consultation flow, with any positive screen triggering the emergency override described above rather than the routine ai_suggests/doctor-approval cycle.

postpartum_depression.name: Postpartum Depression
postpartum_depression.icd11_hint: ICD-11 6E20 'Mental or behavioural disorders associated with pregnancy, childbirth or the puerperium, without psychotic symptoms' is the commonly cited code for postpartum depression in secondary/clinical sources, with legacy ICD-10 F53.0 ('Postpartum depression NOS'/mild mental and behavioural disorders associated with the puerperium) as the well-established anchor. FLAG: the exact ICD-11 6E20 code could NOT be independently confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 Foundation/browser this session (icd.who.int API required OAuth and returned 401; browser navigation pages did not surface the coded entity) -- treat the ICD-11 code as moderate-confidence pending direct WHO browser confirmation, while the underlying clinical diagnosis (major depressive episode with peripartum onset per DSM-5-TR, onset during pregnancy through 4 weeks -- commonly extended to 12 months -- postpartum) is not in question.
postpartum_depression.CURABILITY_NOTE: Postpartum depression (PPD) has a real, genuinely positive story that most depression sub-types do not: it is the first, and so far only, form of depression for which the FDA has approved a drug (brexanolone, 2019) built specifically around its own neuroendocrine mechanism -- the abrupt post-delivery collapse in allopregnanolone (a positive allosteric GABA-A modulator that rises up to 100-fold in pregnancy and falls within days of birth) -- rather than a generic antidepressant repurposed for the postpartum period. In the two pivotal phase 3 trials (Meltzer-Brody S et al., Lancet 2018;392(10152):1058-1070, PMID 30177236), a single 60-hour IV infusion of brexanolone produced a real, statistically significant, and clinically fast HAM-D reduction relative to placebo (Study 1, 90 microg/kg/h arm: -17.7 vs -14.0 points, p=0.0252; Study 2: -14.6 vs -12.1, p=0.0160) -- days to weeks faster than any oral antidepressant. A pooled analysis across the three HUMMINGBIRD program RCTs (Epperson CN et al., J Affect Disord 2023, PMID 36191643, n=102 brexanolone vs 107 placebo) found a cumulative HAM-D-17 response rate (>=50% reduction) of 81.4% with brexanolone vs 67.3% with placebo by hour 60, with median time to response nearly halved (24h vs 36h, p=0.0265). Zuranolone (Zurzuvae), the oral, at-home 14-day follow-on developed from the same allopregnanolone-analog mechanism, showed a real, replicated effect in two independent phase 3 RCTs: the ROBIN study (Deligiannidis KM et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021;78(9):951-959, PMID 34190962, n=153) found HAM-D-17 change at day 15 of -17.8 (zuranolone) vs -13.6 (placebo), a -4.2 point treatment difference (95% CI -6.9 to -1.5, p=0.003), with response and remission roughly 2.5x more likely than placebo (odds ratio 2.63 for response, 2.53 for remission); the SKYLARK study (Deligiannidis KM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2023;180(9):668-675, PMID 37491938, n=196) replicated this with a -4.0 point HAM-D-17 treatment difference at day 15 (95% CI -6.3 to -1.7, p=0.001), and improvement was durable to day 45. This is a genuine breakthrough specific to PPD's unique biology, not a marginal tweak on ordinary SSRIs -- and it must be reported honestly alongside its real limits: a 2025 Cochrane systematic review of all 6 published neurosteroid RCTs (674 women total; Kettle C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025, PMID 40562419) found that for INTRAVENOUS brexanolone specifically, dichotomous response/remission rates at the review's pooled 30-day timepoint were low-certainty and not statistically distinguishable from placebo (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.74-2.06 for response), with moderate-certainty evidence of LOWER acceptability (more dropout) than placebo -- this does not contradict the pivotal trials' real, large, statistically robust ACUTE (hour-60) separation, but it means brexanolone's proven advantage is concentrated in rapid symptom relief in the first 60 hours rather than a proven durable 30-day population-level edge, and the Cochrane authors could not compare it head-to-head against standard SSRIs. For oral zuranolone, the same 2025 Cochrane review rated the evidence moderate-certainty and positive for both response and remission at 45 days, with the tradeoff of a higher (though generally mild, dose-related) rate of somnolence. Outside the neurosteroid drugs, standard SSRIs (sertraline preferred, given the strongest breastfeeding-safety data of any antidepressant: Weissman AM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2004;161:1066-1078, PMID 15169695, pooled analysis showing sertraline and nortriptyline usually produce undetectable infant serum levels) remain effective and are supported by a direct head-to-head RCT (Wisner KL et al., J Clin Psychopharmacol 2006;26(4):353-360, PMID 16855451, n=109 randomized) showing sertraline achieved comparable response and remission rates to nortriptyline at 4, 8, and 24 weeks, and CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy has a real, Cochrane-confirmed evidence base (Dennis CL, Hodnett E, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007, PMID 17943888, 9 trials/956 women) showing psychosocial/psychological interventions significantly reduce continued depression at final assessment versus usual care. The honest, cure-forward picture: for a mother who needs rapid, dramatic relief in the acute postpartum window, brexanolone/zuranolone represent the closest thing to a fast, mechanism-matched near-cure that psychiatry currently has for any depression subtype; for sustained population-level 30-day-and-beyond outcomes, first-line SSRIs (sertraline) plus CBT/IPT remain the best-evidenced, most durable, most accessible real-world combination, and the two approaches are complementary rather than competing (zuranolone/brexanolone can bridge the acute crisis while SSRI/psychotherapy maintenance is established).

curative_option.name: Brexanolone IV Infusion (Zulresso) -- Real Fastest, Most PPD-Specific Near-Cure Option; Zuranolone (Zurzuvae) as the Oral Follow-On
curative_option.type: Neurosteroid GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator; brexanolone = 60-hour continuous IV infusion (inpatient, REMS-monitored); zuranolone = 14-day once-daily oral capsule (outpatient)

real_trial_data.brexanolone_pivotal_phase3_lancet_2018: Meltzer-Brody S et al., Lancet 2018;392(10152):1058-1070 (PMID 30177236). Two multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 RCTs, 246 women with moderate-severe PPD enrolled. Primary endpoint HAM-D-17 change from baseline at 60 hours: Study 1, 90 microg/kg/h arm -17.7 vs placebo -14.0 (p=0.0252), 60 microg/kg/h arm -19.5 vs -14.0 (p=0.0013); Study 2, 90 microg/kg/h arm -14.6 vs -12.1 (p=0.0160).
real_trial_data.brexanolone_hummingbird_pooled_2023: Epperson CN et al., J Affect Disord 2023 (PMID 36191643). Pooled analysis of 3 HUMMINGBIRD program RCTs, n=102 brexanolone vs 107 placebo. HAM-D-17 response (>=50% reduction) at hour 60: 81.4% brexanolone vs 67.3% placebo; median time-to-response 24h vs 36h (p=0.0265). Anxiety and insomnia subscale improvements also favored brexanolone from hour 24 through day 30.
real_trial_data.zuranolone_ROBIN_2021: Deligiannidis KM et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021;78(9):951-959 (PMID 34190962). Phase 3 RCT, n=153 randomized (150 efficacy set), oral zuranolone 30mg/day x14 days. HAM-D-17 change at day 15: -17.8 vs -13.6 placebo, difference -4.2 (95% CI -6.9 to -1.5, p=0.003). Response odds ratio 2.63, remission odds ratio 2.53 vs placebo. 98.7% treatment completion.
real_trial_data.zuranolone_SKYLARK_2023: Deligiannidis KM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2023;180(9):668-675 (PMID 37491938). Phase 3 RCT, n=196 randomized (98/98), oral zuranolone 50mg/day x14 days. HAM-D-17 change at day 15: -15.6 vs -11.6 placebo, difference -4.0 (95% CI -6.3 to -1.7, p=0.001). Improvement sustained to day 45; most common adverse events somnolence, dizziness, sedation (all >=10%), no signal for increased suicidal ideation.
real_trial_data.cochrane_2025_honest_caveat: Kettle C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025 (PMID 40562419). 6 RCTs, 674 women, all placebo-controlled, USA-only. IV brexanolone/ganaxolone: low-certainty evidence of little/no difference in response (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.74-2.06) or remission (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.59-2.38) at pooled 30-day timepoint; moderate-certainty evidence of LOWER acceptability (more dropout) than placebo. Oral zuranolone: moderate-certainty evidence of improved response AND remission at 45 days, but probably increases adverse events (mainly somnolence). No head-to-head trials vs standard SSRIs exist yet.

curative_option.fda_approval_status: Brexanolone (Zulresso): FDA-approved March 2019, first drug ever approved specifically for postpartum depression. Zuranolone (Zurzuvae): FDA-approved August 2023, first ORAL drug approved specifically for postpartum depression.
curative_option.why_it_is_the_closest_to_cure: Both drugs directly target the mechanism unique to PPD (the post-delivery collapse of the neurosteroid allopregnanolone, a positive allosteric GABA-A modulator that is markedly elevated throughout pregnancy) rather than the generic monoamine mechanism of standard antidepressants -- this is why the onset of effect is measured in hours to days (brexanolone) or about 3 days (zuranolone, per the CORAL/SKYLARK trials) instead of the usual 4-6 weeks for SSRIs.
curative_option.honest_limits: Brexanolone requires a 60-hour continuous inpatient IV infusion under REMS monitoring for sedation/syncope risk and is expensive/resource-intensive; the 2025 Cochrane review found its dichotomous response/remission advantage over placebo was not statistically robust at a pooled 30-day timepoint (low-certainty evidence), so its clearest, most reproducible real benefit is RAPID acute-phase (60-hour) symptom reduction rather than a proven durable population-level edge. Zuranolone has a more favorable moderate-certainty evidence base for both response and remission at 45 days but causes somnolence/sedation requiring bedtime dosing and driving precautions, and neither drug has been compared head-to-head against first-line SSRIs in a published RCT.
curative_option.source: Meltzer-Brody S et al., Lancet 2018;392(10152):1058-1070 (PMID 30177236); Epperson CN et al., J Affect Disord 2023 (PMID 36191643); Deligiannidis KM et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021;78(9):951-959 (PMID 34190962); Deligiannidis KM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2023;180(9):668-675 (PMID 37491938); Kettle C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025 (PMID 40562419)
curative_option.confidence: high for the individual pivotal-trial HAM-D and response numbers (large, real, statistically significant RCTs); moderate for any claim of durable 30-day-and-beyond population-level superiority of IV brexanolone specifically, per the 2025 Cochrane review's low-certainty rating

ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.name: Brexanolone (Zulresso) IV infusion
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.type: Neurosteroid GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator, first-in-class, FDA-approved 2019 specifically for PPD
specific_drugs: Brexanolone 60-hour continuous IV infusion, weight-based titration (60->90 microg/kg/h per REMS protocol)
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.effectiveness: Pivotal phase 3 RCTs (n=246): HAM-D-17 reduction at 60h of -14.6 to -19.5 points vs -12.1 to -14.0 placebo (p=0.0013-0.0252). Pooled HUMMINGBIRD analysis (n=209): 81.4% response rate at hour 60 vs 67.3% placebo.
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.reason_why: Directly replaces/modulates the allopregnanolone-mediated GABA-A tone that collapses within days of delivery, which is believed to be a key driver of PPD's rapid onset and severity.
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.important_caveat: Requires 60-hour inpatient REMS-monitored infusion (risk of excess sedation/loss of consciousness); 2025 Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence for 30-day response/remission advantage and moderate-certainty evidence of higher dropout than placebo.
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.source: Meltzer-Brody S et al., Lancet 2018;392(10152):1058-1070 (PMID 30177236); Epperson CN et al., J Affect Disord 2023 (PMID 36191643); Kettle C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025 (PMID 40562419)

ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.name: Zuranolone (Zurzuvae) oral capsule
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.type: Neurosteroid GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator, oral, FDA-approved August 2023 specifically for PPD
specific_drugs: Zuranolone 50 mg once daily x14 days (with fat-containing food, evening dosing due to sedation)
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.effectiveness: ROBIN trial (n=153): HAM-D-17 change at day 15 -17.8 vs -13.6 placebo (p=0.003), response OR 2.63, remission OR 2.53. SKYLARK trial (n=196): HAM-D-17 change at day 15 -15.6 vs -11.6 placebo (p=0.001), sustained to day 45.
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.reason_why: Same allopregnanolone-analog mechanism as brexanolone but orally bioavailable and given as an outpatient 14-day course rather than a 60-hour hospital infusion.
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.important_caveat: Somnolence/dizziness/sedation in >=10% of patients; driving impairment warning (avoid driving for 12h after dose); teratogenic in animal studies -- effective contraception required; 2025 Cochrane review rates the response/remission evidence moderate-certainty (better-supported than IV brexanolone's 30-day outcome) but flags probable increase in adverse events.
ppd_neurosteroid_gabaa_modulators_brexan.source: Deligiannidis KM et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021;78(9):951-959 (PMID 34190962); Deligiannidis KM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2023;180(9):668-675 (PMID 37491938); Kettle C et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2025 (PMID 40562419)

ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.name: Sertraline
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.type: SSRI, preferred first-line antidepressant in breastfeeding mothers with PPD
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.effectiveness: Direct head-to-head RCT vs nortriptyline (n=109 randomized): response and remission rates did not differ significantly between sertraline and nortriptyline at 4, 8, or 24 weeks -- both effective, no clear superiority of one over the other in this trial.
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.reason_why: Standard SSRI mechanism (serotonin reuptake inhibition); chosen preferentially over other SSRIs/TCAs in breastfeeding because of the strongest published safety data on low infant exposure.
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.important_caveat: Full antidepressant effect takes the usual 4-6 weeks, unlike the days-to-hours effect of brexanolone/zuranolone; not a rapid option for a woman in acute crisis.
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.source: Wisner KL et al., J Clin Psychopharmacol 2006;26(4):353-360 (PMID 16855451)

ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.name: Sertraline -- breastfeeding safety evidence
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.type: Pharmacokinetic/safety pooled analysis, not an efficacy trial
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.effectiveness: Not an efficacy metric -- pooled analysis found sertraline (along with nortriptyline and paroxetine) usually produces undetectable infant serum levels via breastmilk, versus fluoxetine which produced elevated infant levels in 22% of cases.
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.reason_why: Sertraline has high protein binding and low milk/plasma transfer, minimizing neonatal exposure relative to other antidepressants.
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.important_caveat: This is a safety/exposure finding, not a head-to-head efficacy comparison against other antidepressants.
ppd_ssri_first_line_pharmacotherapy.source: Weissman AM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2004;161:1066-1078 (PMID 15169695)

ppd_psychotherapy_cbt_ipt.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT)
ppd_psychotherapy_cbt_ipt.type: Structured psychotherapy, individual or group, typically 8-16 weekly sessions
specific_drugs: Not a drug -- CBT and/or IPT delivered by a trained therapist
ppd_psychotherapy_cbt_ipt.effectiveness: Cochrane systematic review (9 trials reporting outcomes, n=956 women): psychosocial and psychological interventions (including CBT and IPT) significantly reduced the likelihood of continued depression at final assessment within the first postpartum year, compared with usual care, in both clinically diagnosed and self-reported PPD.
ppd_psychotherapy_cbt_ipt.reason_why: Addresses cognitive distortions, role transition stress, and interpersonal/relationship strain specific to the postpartum period; no medication exposure, making it a preferred first option for mild-moderate PPD or during breastfeeding when a mother wishes to avoid medication.
ppd_psychotherapy_cbt_ipt.important_caveat: Included trials were of limited methodological quality by Cochrane's own assessment and long-term durability beyond the first postpartum year remains unclear; effect is generally slower-onset than pharmacotherapy.
ppd_psychotherapy_cbt_ipt.source: Dennis CL, Hodnett E, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007 (PMID 17943888)

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a non-psychotic major depressive episode with onset in pregnancy or the weeks following delivery. The leading biological model is the 'hormone-withdrawal' hypothesis: the abrupt fall in estradiol and progesterone after placental delivery, in women who are neuroendocrinologically sensitive to this withdrawal, triggers a depressive episode (mechanistic support from the allopregnanolone/GABA-A system, the basis for brexanolone/zuranolone therapy). This is layered on genetic predisposition, sleep deprivation, and psychosocial stressors of the transition to parenthood.
definition_and_pathophysiology.dsm5_specifier: DSM-5 formally recognizes this as Major Depressive Disorder 'with peripartum onset' -- onset of the mood episode during pregnancy or within 4 weeks following delivery. This 4-week cut-off is a widely-used but clinically debated restriction: it excludes many mood episodes that actually begin later, which is why clinicians and researchers commonly use 'postpartum depression' operationally to mean onset any time in the first 12 months after birth.

citations.finding: DSM-5 peripartum-onset specifier is defined as onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum; critiqued as too narrow, proposal to extend to 6 months
citations.source: Sharma V, Mazmanian D. The DSM-5 peripartum specifier: prospects and pitfalls. Arch Womens Ment Health. 2014;17(2):171-173.

citations.finding: Comprehensive clinical review of postpartum depression pathophysiology (hormonal, genetic, psychosocial), diagnosis and management
citations.source: Stewart DE, Vigod S. Postpartum Depression. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(22):2177-2186.

diagnostic_framework.summary: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is the most widely used and validated screening instrument worldwide for perinatal depression -- a 10-item self-report questionnaire completed in about 5 minutes, deliberately designed to exclude somatic items (e.g. sleep/appetite change) that overlap with normal postpartum physiology. A positive screen is not a diagnosis; it must be followed by clinical interview against DSM-5/ICD criteria for a major depressive episode.
diagnostic_framework.cutoff_scores: The original validation study did not fix a single universal cutoff; subsequent validation studies report differing optimal cutoffs by population -- commonly cited international thresholds are a score of >=10 (higher-sensitivity threshold used by ACOG/USPSTF-aligned protocols to prompt further clinical evaluation) up to >=13 (a higher-specificity threshold associated with 'probable depression' in several validation cohorts). A 2026 Latvian validation cohort found an optimal cutoff of >=11 (sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.82, AUC 0.852) against a structured MINI interview, illustrating that the optimal cutoff is population- and context-dependent and requires local validation rather than a single fixed international number.
diagnostic_framework.self_harm_item: EPDS item 10 explicitly screens for self-harm ideation and must never be skipped or treated as a 'soft' item -- see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.

citations.finding: Original development and validation of the 10-item EPDS in 84 mothers using Research Diagnostic Criteria; satisfactory sensitivity and specificity, ~5 minutes to complete
citations.source: Cox JL, Holden JM, Sagovsky R. Detection of postnatal depression. Development of the 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Br J Psychiatry. 1987;150:782-786.

citations.finding: Local validation in Latvian outpatient population 4-6 weeks postpartum: optimal EPDS cutoff >=11 against MINI 7.0.2 structured interview, AUC 0.852, sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.82, Youden index 0.56
citations.source: Lazareva M, Renemane L, Vinogradova VV, et al. Postpartum Depression Screening in Latvia: Validation and Optimal Cut-Off of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Medicina (Kaunas). 2026;62(4):668.

classic_symptoms.summary: Core presentation is a major depressive episode occurring in the peripartum window: persistent low/depressed or irritable mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt or feelings of worthlessness (often centered on perceived maternal inadequacy), poor concentration, psychomotor change, appetite/sleep disturbance beyond what is expected from newborn care, fatigue, and recurrent thoughts of death or self-harm. Anxiety symptoms and intrusive, often ego-dystonic, thoughts about accidental harm to the infant are common and are NOT evidence of psychosis when the mother recognizes them as unwanted and distressing (this recognition/insight is the key discriminator from psychotic phenomena -- see differential_diagnosis).
classic_symptoms.distinction_from_baby_blues: The key differentiators from normal 'baby blues' are TIMING, SEVERITY, and FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENT. Baby blues affect the large majority of postpartum women (pooled prevalence 39.0% in a 2020 meta-analysis, with some cohorts far higher), typically begin within the first 2-3 days postpartum, peak around day 3-5, and resolve spontaneously without treatment by about day 10-14. Baby blues involve mild, transient tearfulness, mood lability and anxiety WITHOUT loss of function, without pervasive anhedonia, and without suicidal ideation. Postpartum depression, by contrast, either persists beyond 2 weeks, is more severe, and/or causes clinically significant functional impairment in caring for self or infant -- and by definition requires meeting full major depressive episode criteria (5 of 9 DSM-5 symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia, present nearly every day for at least 2 weeks).

citations.finding: Pooled prevalence of maternity/baby blues 39.0% in systematic review and meta-analysis
citations.source: Rezaie-Keikhaie K, Arbabshastan ME, Rafiemanesh H, Amirshahi M, Ostadkelayeh SM, Arbabisarjou A. Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Prevalence of the Maternity Blues in the Postpartum Period. J Obstet Gynecol Neonatal Nurs. 2020;49(2):127-136.

citations.finding: Clinical description of PPD symptom profile, course, and distinction from transient postpartum blues
citations.source: Stewart DE, Vigod S. Postpartum Depression. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(22):2177-2186.

differential_diagnosis.baby_blues: Onset days 1-3 postpartum, peaks ~day 3-5, self-limited resolution by ~2 weeks, mild mood lability/tearfulness/anxiety WITHOUT loss of function or suicidal ideation. No pharmacologic treatment needed -- reassurance and support only. If low mood persists beyond 2 weeks or worsens, re-evaluate for PPD.
differential_diagnosis.postpartum_depression: Onset any time in pregnancy through the first postpartum year (DSM-5 formally restricts the 'peripartum onset' specifier to within 4 weeks postpartum, though this is widely regarded as too narrow -- see definition_and_pathophysiology). Persistent (>=2 weeks), meets full major depressive episode criteria, causes functional impairment. May include passive suicidal ideation or intrusive, distressing (ego-dystonic) thoughts of infant harm that the mother recognizes as wrong and resists. Urgent psychiatric referral is required if active suicidal intent, a plan, or any command-type or ego-syntonic thoughts of harming the infant are present.
differential_diagnosis.postpartum_psychosis: A rare (roughly 0.25-2.6 per 1000 births across population-register studies) but TRUE PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY, distinct from PPD. Onset is typically abrupt, within the first 2 weeks (often first days) postpartum, with rapid fluctuation. Presents with mood-incongruent or bizarre delusions (often centered on the infant), hallucinations, confusion/disorientation, grossly disorganized behavior, and loss of insight -- in sharp contrast to PPD/baby blues, where insight into the depressive or anxious symptoms as abnormal and unwanted is preserved. It carries a substantial, quantified risk of both suicide and infanticide and mandates emergency psychiatric admission -- see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the discriminating features and urgency difference in full.

citations.finding: Postpartum psychosis: incidence 0.25-0.6 per 1000 births from population-register studies; described as 'a psychiatric emergency with risk for suicide and infanticide'
citations.source: Bergink V, Rasgon N, Wisner KL. Postpartum Psychosis: Madness, Mania, and Melancholia in Motherhood. Am J Psychiatry. 2016;173(12):1179-1188.

citations.finding: Systematic review of global postpartum psychosis prevalence: incidence 0.89-2.6 per 1000 women across 5 studies; prevalence 5 per 1000 in 1 study
citations.source: VanderKruik R, Barreix M, Chou D, Allen T, Say L, Cohen LS; Maternal Morbidity Working Group. The global prevalence of postpartum psychosis: a systematic review. BMC Psychiatry. 2017;17(1):272.

citations.finding: Postpartum psychosis has onset within weeks after delivery and carries high risk of suicide and infanticide; expert consensus statement on classification
citations.source: Bergink V, Akbarian S, Byatt N, et al. Postpartum Psychosis and Bipolar Disorder: Review of Neurobiology and Expert Consensus Statement on Classification. Biol Psychiatry. 2026 (advance online).

risk_factors.strongest_predictor: A personal history of depression or anxiety (including prior episodes of postpartum depression itself) is the single most consistent and strongest risk factor identified across the literature. However, PPD occurs at meaningful rates even in mothers with NO such history: a meta-analysis restricted to healthy mothers without any prior depression history and with healthy full-term infants (37,294 women, 58 studies) still found a 12% incidence and 17% prevalence of postpartum depression.
risk_factors.biological: Hormonal withdrawal sensitivity (estradiol/progesterone/allopregnanolone fall after delivery), thyroid dysfunction, sleep deprivation, and genetic/family psychiatric history.
risk_factors.psychosocial: Poor social support, intimate partner conflict or violence, unplanned/unwanted pregnancy, adverse or traumatic birth experience, low socioeconomic status, immigrant/minority status, and adverse perinatal/obstetric events. Geography also modifies risk: pooled prevalence was highest in the Middle East (26%) and lowest in Europe (8%) in the same meta-analysis of healthy mothers.

citations.finding: In healthy mothers without prior depression history, incidence of PPD was 12% (95% CI 0.04-0.20) and prevalence 17% (95% CI 0.15-0.20); highest regional prevalence Middle East 26%, lowest Europe 8%
citations.source: Shorey S, Chee CYI, Ng ED, Chan YH, Tam WWS, Chong YS. Prevalence and incidence of postpartum depression among healthy mothers: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Psychiatr Res. 2018;104:235-248.

citations.finding: Clinical review summarizing established biological and psychosocial risk factors for PPD
citations.source: Stewart DE, Vigod S. Postpartum Depression. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(22):2177-2186.

epidemiology.prevalence: Pooled global prevalence of postpartum depression is approximately 14.0% (95% CI 12.0-15.0%) per a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis. This is consistent with the 17% prevalence found even in mothers screened as low-risk/healthy with no prior depression history in a separate 2018 meta-analysis.
epidemiology.maternal_mortality_context: Suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in the first year after childbirth in high-income settings. A nationwide Dutch cohort study (2006-2020) found a maternal suicide rate of 2.6 per 100,000 live births, with the proportion of suicides among all maternal deaths rising from 18% to 28% over the study period, making suicide the leading cause of maternal mortality once late deaths up to 1 year postpartum are included.

citations.finding: Pooled global PPD prevalence 14.0% (95% CI 12.0-15.0%)
citations.source: Liu X, Wang S, Wang G. Prevalence and Risk Factors of Postpartum Depression in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. J Clin Nurs. 2022.

citations.finding: Maternal suicide rate 2.6 per 100,000 live births (2006-2020); proportion of suicide among maternal deaths rose from 18% to 28%; suicide is the leading cause of maternal mortality when late deaths to 1 year postpartum are included
citations.source: Lommerse KM, Merelle S, Rietveld AL, Berkelmans G, van den Akker T. The contribution of suicide to maternal mortality: A nationwide population-based cohort study. BJOG. 2024.

citations.finding: Suicide is a leading global cause of maternal death in the first year after birth
citations.source: Dudeney E, Meades R, Ayers S, McCabe R. Perinatal women's views and experiences of discussing suicide in maternity care settings: A qualitative study. Women Birth. 2024.

natural_history.untreated: Untreated, PPD often follows a protracted course rather than resolving spontaneously like baby blues -- symptoms commonly persist for many months, and a substantial minority of women remain depressed at 1 year postpartum; untreated maternal depression is also associated with impaired mother-infant bonding and adverse effects on infant cognitive, emotional, and behavioral development. Some studies find prevalence of depressive symptoms actually increasing beyond 6 months postpartum rather than declining, indicating the condition is not reliably self-limited.
natural_history.treated: With evidence-based treatment (psychotherapy such as CBT/IPT and/or antidepressant pharmacotherapy, plus newer rapid-acting neurosteroid agents for eligible patients), most women show substantial improvement within weeks; earlier detection via routine EPDS screening and earlier treatment initiation are associated with better and faster recovery.

citations.finding: No statistical difference in PPD prevalence across different postpartum screening time points, but an increasing prevalence observed beyond 6 months postpartum
citations.source: Shorey S, Chee CYI, Ng ED, Chan YH, Tam WWS, Chong YS. Prevalence and incidence of postpartum depression among healthy mothers: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Psychiatr Res. 2018;104:235-248.

citations.finding: Clinical course, treatment response, and consequences of untreated postpartum depression for mother and infant
citations.source: Stewart DE, Vigod S. Postpartum Depression. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(22):2177-2186.

symptoms.clinical_takeaway: Screen every postpartum (and pregnant) woman with the EPDS, including item 10 for self-harm ideation, at routine perinatal contacts. Distinguish self-limited baby blues (resolves by ~2 weeks, no functional impairment) from true postpartum depression (persistent, functionally impairing, meets major depressive episode criteria) from postpartum psychosis (abrupt-onset, loss of insight, bizarre/mood-incongruent delusions or hallucinations -- a true psychiatric emergency). Never dismiss intrusive, ego-dystonic thoughts of infant harm in a depressed but insightful mother as psychosis, and never dismiss abrupt confusion, delusions, or loss of insight as 'just depression' -- the two require completely different levels of urgency (outpatient/routine referral vs emergency psychiatric admission, respectively).

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: If a postpartum patient presents with ANY of the following, this is a psychiatric EMERGENCY requiring immediate emergency psychiatric evaluation/admission and infant safety assessment, overriding routine outpatient PPD management: (1) new-onset delusions, hallucinations, marked confusion/disorientation, or grossly disorganized behavior within days to a few weeks of delivery (postpartum psychosis); (2) ego-syntonic or command-type thoughts of harming the infant, or loss of insight/recognition that such thoughts are abnormal (as opposed to ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts in PPD, which the mother recognizes as wrong and resists); (3) active suicidal ideation with a plan or intent in a woman with depressive symptoms, even without psychotic features -- postpartum depression on its own carries real suicide risk and must always be actively screened for via EPDS item 10, not assumed to be low-risk because it is 'just PPD'.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.postpartum_psychosis_vs_ppd: Postpartum psychosis is rare (incidence estimates range 0.25 per 1000 to 2.6 per 1000 births across population-register studies, with one study reporting prevalence of 5 per 1000) but is a true psychiatric emergency with high, quantified risk of both suicide and infanticide, per explicit statements in the peer-reviewed literature. It differs from PPD in onset speed (abrupt, typically within the first 1-2 weeks postpartum vs the more gradual, persistent course of PPD), symptom quality (psychotic features -- delusions/hallucinations/disorganization/confusion -- vs mood/cognitive/somatic depressive symptoms), and critically in INSIGHT: psychotic patients typically lack insight into the abnormality of their thoughts/behavior, whereas depressed patients with intrusive thoughts typically retain insight and are distressed by them. This distinction directly determines urgency: postpartum psychosis requires immediate emergency psychiatric admission (given the suicide/infanticide risk), while PPD requires urgent-but-outpatient psychiatric referral unless active suicidality is present, in which case it too becomes an emergency.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.suicide_risk_in_ppd_itself: Postpartum depression is not a benign, self-resolving condition from a mortality standpoint: suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in the first year after childbirth in multiple national studies, and a nationwide Dutch cohort found the proportion of maternal deaths due to suicide rose from 18% to 28% over 2006-2020, making it the leading cause of maternal mortality when late deaths up to 1 year postpartum are counted. Self-harm ideation (measured by EPDS item 10) has a real, non-trivial prevalence in the perinatal population -- 2.3% in pregnancy and 1.1% postpartum in a large cross-sectional cohort -- and is strongly and independently associated with depressive symptom severity. Routine, explicit screening for self-harm ideation (not just low mood) must continue through the entire first postpartum year, not just the immediate postpartum period.
