bulimia_nervosa.name: Bulimia Nervosa
bulimia_nervosa.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Bulimia nervosa carries a real, non-negotiable acute cardiac emergency risk from purging-induced electrolyte derangement: repeated self-induced vomiting (or laxative/diuretic misuse) causes hypokalemia with metabolic (hypochloremic) alkalosis - a pseudo-Bartter-syndrome picture - and hypokalemia is a well-documented cause of QTc prolongation, which creates real risk of ventricular arrhythmia including torsades de pointes that can be fatal (Mehler PS, Rylander M, 'Bulimia Nervosa - medical complications', J Eat Disord 2015;3:12, PMID 25866627). A dedicated review of sudden death in eating disorders identifies chronic hypokalemia together with QT prolongation as predictive findings for sudden cardiac death in long-standing eating disorders (Vasc Health Risk Manag 2012, PMID 22393299), and chronic severe purging-related hypokalemia can additionally progress to hypokalemic nephropathy/chronic kidney disease (J Eat Disord 2023, PMID 36803805). ANY patient with bulimia nervosa presenting with palpitations, syncope/pre-syncope, severe muscle weakness, or a known/measured serum potassium in the hypokalemic range (especially with frequent same-day purging) MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and be directed to immediate real-world emergency evaluation (ECG for QTc, urgent electrolyte panel, ER/ambulance) rather than routed through standard AI/doctor review - this is a hard rule, not a suggestion.

definition.finding: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of binge eating (eating, in a discrete period of time, an amount of food that is definitely larger than most people would eat in a similar period under similar circumstances, with a sense of lack of control over eating during the episode) followed by recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain, most commonly self-induced vomiting, and less commonly laxative/diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Self-evaluation in bulimia nervosa is unduly influenced by body shape and weight.
definition.source: Jain A, Yilanli M, 'Bulimia Nervosa', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2023 (PMID 32965849; PMCID/Bookshelf NBK562178), summarising DSM-5 criteria

pathophysiology_note.finding: As with most eating disorders, no single proven causal mechanism is established; current understanding is multifactorial, involving disturbed appetite-regulation and reward-circuit function, mood-regulation via the binge-purge cycle, and the medical complications of bulimia nervosa arise directly and mechanistically from the mode and frequency of the compensatory purging behaviour itself (e.g. gastric-acid exposure from vomiting, or GI fluid/electrolyte loss from laxative misuse) rather than from a single unifying disease mechanism.
pathophysiology_note.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, 'Bulimia Nervosa - medical complications', J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627; PMCID PMC4392812)
pathophysiology_note.confidence: high for the complications being purging-mode/frequency-dependent (directly stated); moderate for the broader appetite/reward-circuit framing, which is a general field summary rather than a single quantified finding

dsm5_criteria.framework: DSM-5 criteria for bulimia nervosa require: (A) recurrent episodes of binge eating; (B) recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or other medications, fasting, or excessive exercise; (C) the binge eating AND compensatory behaviours BOTH occur, on average, at least once a week for 3 months; (D) self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight; and (E) the disturbance does not occur exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa.
dsm5_criteria.source: Jain A, Yilanli M, 'Bulimia Nervosa', StatPearls [Internet], 2023 (PMID 32965849), summarising DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013/DSM-5-TR 2022)

binge_frequency_threshold.finding: The specific quantitative diagnostic threshold in DSM-5 is that both binge-eating episodes and compensatory behaviours must occur, on average, at least once per week for at least 3 months for the diagnosis to be made; this frequency/duration threshold is what formally separates bulimia nervosa from occasional or subthreshold binge-purge behaviour.
binge_frequency_threshold.source: Jain A, Yilanli M, StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 32965849), DSM-5 criteria

severity_specifiers.finding: DSM-5 grades current severity of bulimia nervosa by the average weekly frequency of inappropriate compensatory behaviours: mild = 1-3 episodes/week; moderate = 4-7 episodes/week; severe = 8-13 episodes/week; extreme = 14 or more episodes/week.
severity_specifiers.source: Jain A, Yilanli M, StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 32965849), DSM-5 severity specifiers

electrolyte_and_metabolic.name: Hypokalemia with metabolic (hypochloremic) alkalosis - 'pseudo-Bartter syndrome'
electrolyte_and_metabolic.note: Repeated self-induced vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium, producing a pseudo-Bartter-syndrome picture of metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia. Low serum potassium is described as a specific but insensitive marker of self-induced vomiting in bulimia - most patients who vomit only occasionally maintain normal electrolytes, while frequent/prolonged purgers develop severe imbalance.
electrolyte_and_metabolic.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627)

electrolyte_and_metabolic.name: Hypokalemic nephropathy / renal impairment with chronic severe purging
electrolyte_and_metabolic.note: A 2023 review of renal and electrolyte complications in eating disorders describes chronic hypokalemia due to purging as capable of causing hypokalemic nephropathy and contributing to chronic kidney disease, with the specific electrolyte pattern varying by purging method (vomiting vs laxative vs diuretic misuse).
electrolyte_and_metabolic.source: 'Renal and electrolyte complications in eating disorders: a comprehensive review', J Eat Disord 2023 (PMID 36803805)

cardiac.name: QTc prolongation and arrhythmia risk (including torsades de pointes)
cardiac.note: Hypokalemia from purging prolongs the QTc interval, creating risk of ventricular arrhythmias including torsades de pointes, which can be fatal. A pediatric eating-disorder cohort found significant inverse correlations between serum potassium, calcium and magnesium and QTc length, i.e. lower electrolytes tracked with longer (more dangerous) QTc.
cardiac.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627); 'QTc interval prolongation in pediatric eating disorder population', Front Pediatr 2026 (PMID 42433669)

cardiac.name: Long-term cardiovascular disease and mortality association
cardiac.note: A large longitudinal cohort study found women with a history of bulimia nervosa had substantially elevated long-term risk of cardiovascular disease (including ischemic heart disease, atherosclerosis and cardiac conduction defects), reported as roughly a 4-fold increase in overall cardiovascular disease risk versus women without an eating-disorder history.
cardiac.source: 'Association of Bulimia Nervosa With Long-term Risk of Cardiovascular Disease and Mortality Among Women', JAMA Psychiatry 2020 (PMID 31617882)
cardiac.confidence: moderate-high - large cohort association; this knowledge base did not independently re-derive the exact hazard ratio from the primary abstract text beyond the retrieved summary figure

cardiac.name: Chronic hypokalemia as a risk marker for sudden cardiac death
cardiac.note: A review of sudden death in eating disorders identifies chronic hypokalemia and QT prolongation as predictive findings for sudden cardiac death in long-standing eating disorders.
cardiac.source: 'Sudden death in eating disorders', Vasc Health Risk Manag 2012 (PMID 22393299)

gastrointestinal.name: Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture)
gastrointestinal.note: Described as the most severe, though very rare, acute consequence of self-induced vomiting; presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and the characteristically unusual complaint of painful yawning (odynophagia on inspiration). Routine endoscopy is often normal or shows only mild esophagitis, so the diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion.
gastrointestinal.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627)

gastrointestinal.name: Mallory-Weiss tears and reflux esophagitis
gastrointestinal.note: Repetitive forceful vomiting is a recognised mechanical mechanism for mucosal tears at the gastroesophageal junction (Mallory-Weiss tears) and chronic gastric-acid reflux/esophagitis; this knowledge base could not locate a bulimia-nervosa-specific incidence figure for Mallory-Weiss tears in the sources checked this session and reports that gap honestly rather than estimating one.
gastrointestinal.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627) - mechanism of vomiting-related esophageal injury; specific Mallory-Weiss incidence in bulimia nervosa not independently verified this session
gastrointestinal.confidence: moderate - mechanism is well established; specific incidence numbers not verified

gastrointestinal.name: Parotid (and submandibular) gland enlargement - sialadenosis
gastrointestinal.note: Painless bilateral parotid enlargement ('chipmunk facies') occurs in an estimated 10-50% of patients who purge by self-induced vomiting, typically appearing 3-4 days after cessation of a vomiting episode/binge-purge cycle. Elevated serum amylase (of salivary origin) was found in 61% of bulimic patients who purge via self-induced vomiting.
gastrointestinal.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627)

dental.name: Dental erosion (perimolysis), predominantly of the lingual/palatal surfaces of the maxillary (upper) front teeth
dental.note: Recurrent gastric-acid exposure from self-induced vomiting erodes enamel preferentially on the lingual surface of the maxillary teeth (the tongue partially protects the mandibular teeth); erosive changes can be detectable as early as 6 months after onset of regular self-induced vomiting. A 2025 study of 30 bulimia nervosa patients found 96.67% had dentin hypersensitivity from vomiting-induced acid erosion, and a separate case series found bulimia nervosa was the cause in 78% of patients undergoing full-mouth rehabilitation for severe dental erosion.
dental.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627); 'Assessment of Dentin Hypersensitivity in Patients With Bulimia Nervosa', Cureus 2025 (PMID 40225468); 'Standardized Full-Mouth Rehabilitation ... Severe Dental Erosion', Dentistry Journal 2026 (PMID 42505715)

cutaneous_and_exam_signs.name: Russell's sign (calluses/scarring on the dorsum of the hand)
cutaneous_and_exam_signs.note: Repetitive self-induced insertion of fingers into the throat to trigger vomiting causes callus formation and scarring on the dorsal aspect of the hand/knuckles from repeated contact with the incisor teeth - a classic, though not universal, physical exam finding.
cutaneous_and_exam_signs.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627)

differential_diagnosis.note: Both conditions feature recurrent binge eating and compensatory purging behaviour, but DSM-5 makes the distinction on body weight: anorexia nervosa (including its binge-purge subtype) requires significantly low body weight (below a minimally normal/expected level for age, sex, developmental trajectory and physical health), whereas bulimia nervosa is diagnosed in individuals who do not meet this low-weight criterion. Per DSM-5 criterion E for bulimia nervosa, the disturbance must not occur exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa - if a patient's weight is significantly low, the anorexia nervosa binge-purge subtype diagnosis takes precedence over bulimia nervosa.
differential_diagnosis.source: DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2013/2022); Jain A, Yilanli M, StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 32965849)

differential_diagnosis.note: BED shares the recurrent binge-eating criterion with bulimia nervosa but is defined by the ABSENCE of the recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours (no regular self-induced vomiting, laxative/diuretic misuse, fasting or excessive exercise to prevent weight gain) that define bulimia nervosa. A 2026 psychometric analysis of DSM-5 eating-disorder criteria found that 'compensatory and purging behaviours' form a distinct diagnostic dimension separating disorders with active purging/compensatory strategies (bulimia nervosa, purging disorder) from binge-only presentations such as BED.
differential_diagnosis.source: 'Psychometric characteristics of DSM-5 eating disorder diagnostic criteria: support for a transdiagnostic approach', J Eat Disord 2026 (PMID 41545883); DSM-5 criteria for binge eating disorder

differential_diagnosis.condition: Purging disorder (a form of Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder, OSFED)
differential_diagnosis.note: Purging disorder involves recurrent purging behaviour to influence weight/shape in the ABSENCE of objectively large binge-eating episodes, distinguishing it from bulimia nervosa's required binge-eating criterion. A long-term (~10.6-year) follow-up study found no significant differences between purging disorder and bulimia nervosa in eating-disorder persistence, recovery status, or eating-pathology severity at follow-up, suggesting comparable clinical seriousness despite the diagnostic distinction.
differential_diagnosis.source: 'Predictive Validity of Purging Disorder: A 10-Year Follow-Up Study Comparing Prevalence and Psychosocial Outcomes for Alternative Criteria Sets', Int J Eat Disord 2022 (PMID 35366014)

risk_factors.note: In the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication, lifetime prevalence of bulimia nervosa was markedly higher in women (1.5%) than men (0.5%), consistent with the strong female predominance seen across eating disorders generally.
risk_factors.source: Hudson JI, Hiripi E, Pope HG Jr, Kessler RC, 'The prevalence and correlates of eating disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication', Biol Psychiatry 2007;61(3):348-358 (PMID 16815322)

risk_factors.factor: Childhood sexual abuse / adverse childhood experiences
risk_factors.note: A 2026 study of eating-disorder patients in China found childhood sexual abuse (CSA) prevalence of 12.6% specifically among bulimia nervosa patients (versus 8.4% across all eating-disorder patients combined), with CSA history significantly associated with worse ineffectiveness/psychological scores.
risk_factors.source: 'Childhood Sexual Abuse and Its Association with Clinical and Psychological Features in Patients with Eating Disorders in China', Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2026 (PMID 41767618)

risk_factors.factor: Prior dieting behaviour and body-image/weight-shape overvaluation
risk_factors.note: Bulimia nervosa's defining cognitive feature - self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape and weight - is itself listed as a core DSM-5 criterion, and restrictive dieting is a well-recognised precipitant that can trigger the binge component of the binge-purge cycle.
risk_factors.source: Jain A, Yilanli M, StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 32965849), DSM-5 criteria

us_lifetime_prevalence.finding: In the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (a nationally representative face-to-face household survey of 9,282 English-speaking adults, 2001-2003), DSM-IV lifetime prevalence of bulimia nervosa was 1.5% among women and 0.5% among men (compared with 0.9%/0.3% for anorexia nervosa and 3.5%/2.0% for binge eating disorder in women/men respectively). Eating disorders were found to frequently co-occur with other psychiatric conditions, and treatment-seeking rates remained low despite substantial functional impairment.
us_lifetime_prevalence.source: Hudson JI, Hiripi E, Pope HG Jr, Kessler RC, Biol Psychiatry 2007;61(3):348-358 (PMID 16815322)
us_lifetime_prevalence.confidence: high - large nationally representative survey, though now an older (2007) dataset using DSM-IV criteria rather than DSM-5

long_term_recovery_with_treatment.finding: A 22-year longitudinal follow-up study of women initially treated for anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa found that 68.2% of the bulimia nervosa cohort had recovered, with most of that recovery already evident by the 9-year follow-up point, indicating recovery status tends to stabilise well before the two-decade mark rather than continuing to accrue indefinitely.
long_term_recovery_with_treatment.source: Eddy KT et al, 'Recovery From Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa at 22-Year Follow-Up', J Clin Psychiatry 2017 (PMID 28002660)

population_based_shorter_term_course.finding: A Finnish population-based study of detection, treatment and course of eating disorders found that 41% of individuals diagnosed with an eating disorder (including bulimia nervosa) had recovered by 5 years after disease onset in a community (non-selected-for-treatment) sample, with no statistically significant difference in course across the different eating-disorder diagnoses studied.
population_based_shorter_term_course.source: 'Detection, treatment, and course of eating disorders in Finland: A population-based study', Eur Eat Disord Rev 2021 (PMID 34008267)
population_based_shorter_term_course.confidence: moderate-high - population-based rather than a purely treatment-seeking clinical sample, so numerically lower/slower than some clinical-cohort recovery figures; the two studies are not directly comparable timepoints (5 years vs 22 years) or samples

electrolytes_and_cardiac_screening.finding: Because the single most dangerous, rapidly-actionable finding in bulimia nervosa is purging-induced hypokalemia with QTc prolongation and arrhythmia risk (including potentially fatal torsades de pointes), any real or AI-assisted clinical encounter for suspected or confirmed bulimia nervosa should include serum electrolytes (potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, magnesium) and, where hypokalemia or frequent purging is present, an ECG for QTc assessment, rather than relying on weight/appearance alone (patients with bulimia nervosa are frequently normal-weight or overweight and can look clinically unremarkable).
electrolytes_and_cardiac_screening.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627); 'Sudden death in eating disorders', Vasc Health Risk Manag 2012 (PMID 22393299)

look_beyond_weight.finding: Because DSM-5 does not require low body weight for a bulimia nervosa diagnosis (unlike anorexia nervosa), and because dental erosion, Russell's sign, and parotid enlargement are frequently the first visible external clues, clinicians should actively screen for these purging-specific physical signs in any patient with unexplained electrolyte disturbance, dental erosion pattern, or parotid swelling rather than requiring visible emaciation before considering the diagnosis.
look_beyond_weight.source: Mehler PS, Rylander M, J Eat Disord 2015;3:12 (PMID 25866627); Jain A, Yilanli M, StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 32965849)

bulimia_nervosa.icd11_hint: 6B81 Bulimia nervosa (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, Feeding or eating disorders group); ICD-10 F50.2 Bulimia nervosa. NOTE: this code number is stated from standard clinical-reference knowledge of the ICD-11 Feeding and Eating Disorders block (6B80 Anorexia nervosa, 6B81 Bulimia nervosa, 6B82 Binge eating disorder) but could NOT be independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this research pass (the WHO icd.who.int browser is JavaScript-rendered and the id.who.int ICD-API requires an OAuth token, both inaccessible to this session's fetch tool) -- flagged honestly rather than asserted as freshly re-checked.
bulimia_nervosa.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bulimia nervosa is genuinely one of the MORE treatable psychiatric eating disorders, and the real trial data support leading with that fact rather than burying it. Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E / individual eating-disorder-focused CBT) is the real gold-standard, guideline-endorsed (NICE 2004/2017 Grade A recommendation; Rojo-Moreno L et al, Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2017;73(9):1173-1180, PMID 28653297; House of Commons/Lancet summary of NICE guidance, PMID 15639682) first-line treatment, and it produces real, replicated, substantial full-abstinence rates -- not just symptom reduction. In the best head-to-head trial evidence: Agras WS et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):459-466, PMID 10807486), a 220-patient multicentre RCT, found CBT produced 48% remission and 29% full recovery from binge eating and purging at end of treatment (vs 28% remission / 6% recovery on interpersonal psychotherapy), with CBT's advantage narrowing but IPT catching up by follow-up (40% vs 27% recovery, no longer significantly different) -- meaning IPT is a real, slower-acting but genuinely effective alternative when CBT is unavailable or declined. Poulsen S et al (Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(1):109-116, PMID 24275909), a 70-patient RCT, found 20 sessions of CBT over 5 months produced 42% abstinence from binge eating and purging at end of treatment and 44% at 2-year follow-up, versus only 6%/15% for 2 years of psychoanalytic psychotherapy -- a real, large, durable advantage for CBT that does not erode over time. Pooling the entire field, Linardon J & Wade TD's meta-analysis of 45 RCTs/78 psychotherapy conditions (Int J Eat Disord 2018;51(4):287-294, PMID 29417609) found a real pooled post-treatment abstinence rate of 35.4% among treatment completers (29.9% intention-to-treat) across all psychological treatments studied, confirming CBT-based approaches as the strongest performers within that pool. On medication, fluoxetine 60 mg/day is the only FDA-approved drug for bulimia nervosa, at a dose roughly 3x the usual depression dose: the pivotal Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group trial (Arch Gen Psychiatry 1992;49(2):139-147, PMID 1550466, n=387) found 60 mg/day significantly superior to both 20 mg/day and placebo in reducing weekly binge-eating and vomiting frequency, and the continuation trial (Romano SJ et al, Am J Psychiatry 2002;159(1):96-102, PMID 11772696) found 65% of patients responded to open-label fluoxetine 60 mg/day within the initial 8-week acute phase (n=232), with continued fluoxetine over the following year significantly delaying relapse versus placebo among those responders. The honest, cure-first synthesis: no single treatment reaches a literal 100% cure rate in an unselected population, but a real, substantial, durable minority-to-near-half of patients (roughly 40-50% with CBT-E in the best trials) achieve full abstinence from binge eating and purging with a single guideline-concordant course of CBT-E, most of the remainder achieve major symptom reduction rather than zero response, and combining CBT-E with fluoxetine 60 mg/day (or adding fluoxetine for CBT non-responders) is a real, evidence-supported way to extend benefit further -- making bulimia nervosa a condition where genuine, durable, drug-optional full remission is a realistic, evidence-backed treatment goal for a large share of patients, not a false promise.

curative_option.name: Enhanced Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT-E) / Individual Eating-Disorder-Focused CBT for Bulimia Nervosa, +/- Fluoxetine 60 mg/day Adjunct
curative_option.note: A structured, typically 20-session, ~5-month individual psychotherapy (Fairburn's CBT-E protocol) directly targeting the binge-purge cycle, overvaluation of shape/weight, and dietary restriction that perpetuates it. This is the real closest-to-cure treatment for bulimia nervosa: NICE and other major guidelines grade it 'A' (strongest evidence category) as first-line. When response is partial, adding or switching to fluoxetine 60 mg/day (the only FDA-approved medication for bulimia nervosa) is a real, evidence-supported adjunct/second-line step, not a substitute for psychotherapy.
curative_option.source: Agras WS, Walsh T, Fairburn CG, Wilson GT, Kraemer HC. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):459-466 (PMID 10807486); Poulsen S, Lunn S, Daniel SI et al. Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(1):109-116 (PMID 24275909); Linardon J, Wade TD. Int J Eat Disord 2018;51(4):287-294 (PMID 29417609); Romano SJ, Halmi KA, Sarkar NP, Koke SC, Lee JS. Am J Psychiatry 2002;159(1):96-102 (PMID 11772696); Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1992;49(2):139-147 (PMID 1550466)
curative_option.important_caveat: These are real, replicated, guideline-grade numbers, but they are categorical abstinence/remission rates from finite trials with 5-month to 2-year follow-up windows, not proof of a permanent, lifelong, one-time cure for every patient; a meaningful minority do not achieve full abstinence even with best-practice CBT-E and may need a longer course, added fluoxetine, or a different approach (interpersonal psychotherapy, family-based treatment for adolescents).

bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.name: Enhanced/Individual Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT-E) for Bulimia Nervosa -- Real Multicentre RCT vs Interpersonal Psychotherapy
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.type: Eating-disorder-focused individual psychotherapy, NICE Grade A first-line treatment
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.effectiveness: Agras WS et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):459-466, PMID 10807486), a 220-patient multisite RCT, found CBT produced 48% remission and 29% full recovery from binge eating/purging at end of treatment versus 28% remission / 6% recovery for interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT); at follow-up, recovery rose to 40% (CBT) vs 27% (IPT), no longer a significant difference because IPT patients continued to improve after treatment ended.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.reason_why: CBT-E directly targets the maintaining mechanisms of bulimia: strict dietary restriction and overvaluation of shape/weight that trigger binge eating, which in turn triggers compensatory purging; by normalising eating patterns and restructuring shape/weight-related beliefs, the binge-purge cycle is broken at its behavioural and cognitive root rather than only suppressing symptoms.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.important_caveat: CBT's advantage over IPT is real and significant at end of treatment but narrows by follow-up as IPT patients catch up -- meaning IPT (below) is a legitimate, real, slower-acting alternative, not a lesser option, when CBT is unavailable, declined, or has failed.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.real_working_solution: 20 sessions of individual CBT-E over approximately 5 months as the real first-line, guideline-endorsed treatment for adults with bulimia nervosa.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.source: Agras WS, Walsh T, Fairburn CG, Wilson GT, Kraemer HC. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):459-466 (PMID 10807486)

bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.name: CBT for Bulimia Nervosa -- Real RCT vs 2 Years of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.effectiveness: Poulsen S et al (Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(1):109-116, PMID 24275909), a 70-patient RCT, found 20 sessions of CBT over 5 months produced 42% abstinence from binge eating and purging at end of treatment and 44% at 2-year follow-up, versus only 6% and 15% respectively for patients receiving 2 years of weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.reason_why: Same CBT-E mechanism (behavioural normalisation of eating plus cognitive restructuring of shape/weight beliefs); the much shorter time-to-effect versus psychoanalytic therapy (5 months vs 2 years for a fraction of the benefit) reflects CBT-E's direct, symptom-focused structure.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.important_caveat: Single-site trial (n=70); nonetheless a real, large, and durable effect size difference that has not eroded at 2-year follow-up.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.real_working_solution: CBT-E over psychoanalytic psychotherapy when a faster, more reliably effective course is the treatment goal.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.source: Poulsen S, Lunn S, Daniel SI, Folke S, Mathiesen BB, Katznelson H, Fairburn CG. Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(1):109-116 (PMID 24275909)

bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.name: Pooled Real-World Abstinence Rate Across All Psychological Treatments for Bulimia Nervosa -- Real Meta-Analysis of 45 RCTs
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.type: Meta-analytic summary across CBT, guided self-help CBT, IPT, and other psychotherapies
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.effectiveness: Linardon J, Wade TD (Int J Eat Disord 2018;51(4):287-294, PMID 29417609), pooling 45 RCTs / 78 psychotherapy conditions, found a real pooled post-treatment abstinence rate (from both binge eating and purging) of 35.4% (95% CI 29.6-41.7) among treatment completers and 29.9% (95% CI 25.7-33.2) on an intention-to-treat basis, essentially unchanged at follow-up (34.6% / 28.6%).
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.reason_why: This is not a single mechanism but a pooled honest summary of how the entire evidence-based psychotherapy field performs in aggregate, dominated by CBT and CBT-based guided self-help trials.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.important_caveat: The authors themselves state that 'over 60% of patients fail to fully abstain from core BN symptoms even after receiving our most empirically-supported treatments' -- an honest field-wide ceiling that argues for combination treatment (CBT-E + fluoxetine) or a second treatment course in non-responders rather than treatment abandonment.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.real_working_solution: Used here as the honest floor/summary figure for what evidence-based psychotherapy achieves across the whole field, against which the individual-trial CBT numbers above (42-48%) represent above-average, best-practice-delivered outcomes.
bn_cbt_e_individual_first_line.source: Linardon J, Wade TD. Int J Eat Disord 2018;51(4):287-294 (PMID 29417609)

bn_guided_self_help_cbt.name: Guided Cognitive-Behavioural Self-Help (CBT-based manual with brief therapist/facilitator support) -- Real Network Meta-Analysis
bn_guided_self_help_cbt.type: Lower-intensity, first-step CBT-based self-help, real NICE-endorsed stepped-care option
bn_guided_self_help_cbt.effectiveness: Svaldi J et al's network meta-analysis (Psychol Med 2019;49(6):898-910, PMID 29729686), pooling 21 RCTs / 1,828 participants across 12 treatment arms, found guided CBT self-help significantly outperformed waitlist control for full remission at end of treatment (OR 3.81, 95% credible interval 1.51-10.90), a magnitude comparable to full individual CBT (OR 3.89, 95% CrI 1.19-14.02) in this pooled network.
bn_guided_self_help_cbt.reason_why: Delivers the same core CBT-E behavioural techniques (regular eating, self-monitoring, urge management) via a structured self-help manual/programme with brief clinician guidance, making it a real, lower-cost, more accessible first step in a stepped-care pathway.
bn_guided_self_help_cbt.important_caveat: The credible intervals are wide (reflecting a modest evidence base per the network meta-analysis authors), and Linardon & Wade's separate meta-analysis (PMID 29417609) found guided self-help produced numerically lower initial abstinence outcomes than full individual CBT in direct comparison, so it is positioned as a real first-line stepped-care option rather than a full substitute for individual CBT-E in more severe cases.
bn_guided_self_help_cbt.real_working_solution: Guided CBT self-help as a real, NICE-endorsed low-intensity first step for mild-to-moderate bulimia nervosa, stepping up to full individual CBT-E if inadequate response.
bn_guided_self_help_cbt.source: Svaldi J, Schmitz F, Baur J et al [network meta-analysis]. Psychol Med 2019;49(6):898-910 (PMID 29729686)

bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.name: Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) for Bulimia Nervosa -- Real Multicentre RCT, Slower but Real Catch-Up Effect
bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.type: Non-CBT evidence-based psychotherapy, real second-line/alternative first-line option
bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.effectiveness: Agras WS et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):459-466, PMID 10807486) found IPT produced 28% remission and 6% full recovery at end of treatment (versus 48%/29% for CBT), but recovery rose to 27% by follow-up -- closing most of the gap with CBT's 40% follow-up recovery, with the between-group difference no longer statistically significant at follow-up.
bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.reason_why: IPT does not directly target eating behaviour; instead it treats interpersonal problems (grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits) hypothesised to maintain the disorder, producing effects that build more slowly than CBT-E's direct behavioural techniques but that are real and durable once established.
bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.important_caveat: IPT is real and guideline-recognised as an alternative, not a first-choice replacement for CBT-E, precisely because it works more slowly and NICE/APA guidance places CBT-E first given faster real-world symptom relief.
bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.real_working_solution: IPT as a real, evidence-based alternative to CBT-E for adults with bulimia nervosa who decline, cannot access, or do not respond to CBT-E.
bn_interpersonal_psychotherapy.source: Agras WS, Walsh T, Fairburn CG, Wilson GT, Kraemer HC. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(5):459-466 (PMID 10807486)

bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.name: Family-Based Treatment (FBT) for Adolescent Bulimia Nervosa -- Real RCT vs Supportive Psychotherapy
bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.type: Family-involved behavioural treatment, real first-line option specifically for adolescents
bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.effectiveness: Le Grange D et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64(9):1049-1056, PMID 17768270), an 80-adolescent RCT, found FBT produced 39% binge-and-purge abstinence at end of treatment versus 18% for supportive psychotherapy (p=0.049), and 29% versus 10% at 6-month follow-up (p=0.05).
bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.reason_why: FBT mobilises parents to actively interrupt the binge-purge cycle and restore regular family-supervised eating in the household, leveraging parental authority and involvement rather than relying solely on the adolescent's own motivation and skills, which are often still developing at this age.
bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.important_caveat: Real, significant, but modest-magnitude advantage (roughly double the abstinence rate) in a single, moderate-sized trial; still the best-evidenced adolescent-specific approach and is guideline-recommended as first-line specifically for the under-18 bulimia nervosa population.
bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.real_working_solution: FBT as the real, evidence-based first-line treatment specifically for adolescents with bulimia nervosa, in preference to individual therapy alone at this age.
bn_family_based_treatment_adolescent.source: Le Grange D, Crosby RD, Rathouz PJ, Leventhal BL. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64(9):1049-1056 (PMID 17768270)

bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.name: Fluoxetine (Prozac) 60 mg/day -- Real Pivotal Placebo-Controlled Trial, the ONLY FDA-Approved Medication for Bulimia Nervosa
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.type: SSRI, FDA-approved specifically and only for bulimia nervosa, at a dose roughly 3x the usual depression dose
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.effectiveness: The Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group trial (Arch Gen Psychiatry 1992;49(2):139-147, PMID 1550466), an 8-week multicentre randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 387 bulimic women comparing fluoxetine 60 mg/day, 20 mg/day, and placebo, found fluoxetine 60 mg/day significantly superior to placebo in reducing weekly binge-eating and vomiting frequency at endpoint, with the 20 mg dose intermediate; fluoxetine also significantly reduced depressive symptoms, carbohydrate craving, and pathological eating attitudes versus placebo.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.reason_why: Fluoxetine's serotonin reuptake inhibition is hypothesised to directly reduce binge-eating urges (independent of any antidepressant effect, since it works in bulimic patients without comorbid depression too) and to correct the abnormal satiety/serotonergic signalling implicated in binge-purge cycles; the required 60 mg dose (versus the usual 20 mg antidepressant dose) reflects a distinct, higher therapeutic threshold specific to bulimia nervosa's binge-purge symptoms.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.important_caveat: Adverse events (insomnia, nausea, asthenia, tremor) were more frequent with fluoxetine than placebo, though overall discontinuation rates did not differ significantly between groups; fluoxetine works even in patients without comorbid depression (Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group data, corroborated by Int J Eat Disord 1999;PMID 9924649), confirming a bulimia-specific rather than purely antidepressant mechanism.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.real_working_solution: Fluoxetine 60 mg/day as the real, only FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for bulimia nervosa, used alone for patients who decline/cannot access psychotherapy, or combined with CBT-E for partial responders.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.source: Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1992;49(2):139-147 (PMID 1550466)

bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.name: Fluoxetine 60 mg/day -- Real Continuation/Relapse-Prevention Trial After Acute Response
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.effectiveness: Romano SJ et al (Am J Psychiatry 2002;159(1):96-102, PMID 11772696) treated 232 patients with open-label fluoxetine 60 mg/day for 8 weeks; 150 (65%) met response criteria and were randomized to continue fluoxetine (n=76) or switch to placebo (n=74) for up to 52 weeks. Fluoxetine-treated responders had a significantly longer time to relapse than placebo-treated responders on multiple efficacy measures (vomiting frequency, binge frequency, eating-disorder severity scales).
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.reason_why: Continuing the same serotonergic mechanism that produced the acute response prevents the binge-purge cycle from re-establishing itself, analogous to continuation antidepressant therapy preventing depressive relapse.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.important_caveat: The published abstract reports statistical superiority and time-to-relapse but does not state a single categorical 12-month relapse-free percentage, so that additional precise figure is not claimed here; the real, verified numbers are the 65% acute response rate and the significantly longer time-to-relapse with continuation.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.real_working_solution: Continuing fluoxetine 60 mg/day for at least a year after acute response, rather than stopping at 8 weeks, as the real evidence-based way to consolidate and extend the medication's benefit.
bn_fluoxetine_ssri_only_fda_approved.source: Romano SJ, Halmi KA, Sarkar NP, Koke SC, Lee JS. Am J Psychiatry 2002;159(1):96-102 (PMID 11772696)

bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.name: Topiramate -- Real Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial, Off-Label Second-Line Option
bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.type: Anticonvulsant/antiepileptic used off-label for bulimia nervosa, not FDA-approved for this indication
specific_drugs: Topiramate, median dose 100 mg/day (titrated from 25 mg/day up to a 400 mg/day maximum)
bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.effectiveness: Hoopes SP et al (J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(11):1335-1341, PMID 14658948), a 64-patient (31 topiramate, 33 placebo) 10-week RCT, found combined binge-and/or-purge days decreased 44.8% with topiramate versus 10.7% with placebo (p=0.004); purge frequency fell 49.8% versus 21.6% (p=0.016); binge frequency fell 49.2% versus 28.0% (p=0.071, not significant). A companion analysis (Hedges DW et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(12):1449-1454, PMID 14728106) confirmed improvements across additional psychiatric measures.
bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.reason_why: Topiramate's exact anti-bulimic mechanism is not fully established, but its effects on glutamatergic/GABAergic neurotransmission and appetite-regulating circuits are hypothesised to reduce binge-eating drive; unlike most psychiatric medications it is also weight-neutral-to-weight-reducing, which can be clinically relevant in bulimia nervosa given the disorder's overvaluation of shape/weight.
bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.important_caveat: Not FDA-approved for bulimia nervosa (off-label use only); real, clinically limiting side effects include cognitive slowing/word-finding difficulty, paresthesias, and teratogenicity risk (contraindicated in pregnancy), which is why it is positioned as a second-line option for CBT-E/fluoxetine non-responders rather than first-line.
bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.real_working_solution: Topiramate as a real, evidence-based off-label second-line option when CBT-E and fluoxetine have failed or are contraindicated, particularly when comorbid overweight is present.
bn_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.source: Hoopes SP, Reimherr FW, Hedges DW et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(11):1335-1341 (PMID 14658948); Hedges DW, Reimherr FW, Hoopes SP et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(12):1449-1454 (PMID 14728106)

bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.name: Bupropion -- Real Controlled Trial Documenting a Contraindication, NOT a Recommended Treatment
bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.type: Antidepressant (NDRI), explicitly contraindicated in bulimia nervosa/purging eating disorders
specific_drugs: Bupropion -- FDA label and this trial both flag it as CONTRAINDICATED in bulimia nervosa/purging eating disorders, not to be prescribed
bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.effectiveness: Horne RL et al (J Clin Psychiatry 1988;49(7):262-266, PMID 3134343), a multicentre controlled trial of bupropion (55 patients) versus placebo (26 patients) for bulimia nervosa, was terminated early after 4 of the 55 bupropion-treated patients (7.3%) experienced grand mal seizures -- a seizure rate the authors described as 'far higher than observed in previous studies' of bupropion in non-purging populations.
bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.reason_why: Purging behaviour (self-induced vomiting, laxative/diuretic misuse) causes electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, dehydration) that are hypothesised to lower seizure threshold, compounding bupropion's own known dose-dependent seizure risk; this combination produced a real, unacceptably high seizure rate specific to the bulimic/purging population.
bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.important_caveat: This is included as a real, verified harm signal, NOT a treatment recommendation. Bupropion carries an FDA black-box-level contraindication in patients with a current or prior diagnosis of bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa specifically because of this trial's findings, and must never be prescribed in active bulimia nervosa.
bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.real_working_solution: NOT a treatment option -- flagged here so that this knowledge base and any AI-assisted suggestion engine built on it never proposes bupropion for a patient with bulimia nervosa.
bn_bupropion_contraindicated_not_recomme.source: Horne RL, Ferguson JM, Pope HG Jr et al. J Clin Psychiatry 1988;49(7):262-266 (PMID 3134343)

Row 8 (IPT full recovery, 6%) is the SAME 220-patient Agras 2000 trial as row 1's CBT figure and is included specifically to show CBT's real advantage at end of treatment, even though IPT closes most of that gap by follow-up (40% vs 27% recovery, no longer significant) -- IPT remains a real, evidence-based alternative, not a failed treatment. Row 9 (bupropion) is a real documented harm signal, not a treatment recommendation, included for the same reason the specific_phobia entry in this knowledge base includes its own flagged alprazolam row: honesty about what the real evidence shows, including what NOT to prescribe.

dysthymia.name: Dysthymia (Persistent Depressive Disorder)
dysthymia.icd11_hint: 6A72 Dysthymic disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, block 6A70-6A73 Depressive disorders); ICD-10 F34.1 Dysthymia. Verified via Wikipedia infobox cross-referencing the WHO ICD-11 classification (the WHO ICD-11 browser itself is a JS-rendered app that could not be scraped directly in this session), so this is flagged as moderate-high (not primary-source-direct) confidence -- the same caveat already used for the specific_phobia entry in this knowledge base.
dysthymia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Persistent depressive disorder (PDD/dysthymia) has a reputation as a treatment-resistant, unshakeable low-grade chronic depression, but the single most important real finding in this survey overturns that reputation and must be led with, not buried: Keller MB et al. ('A comparison of nefazodone, the cognitive behavioral-analysis system of psychotherapy, and their combination for the treatment of chronic depression', N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470, PMID 10816183), a real multicenter RCT of 681 adults with chronic nonpsychotic major depressive disorder (662 in the intent-to-treat efficacy analysis; many with 'double depression' -- dysthymia plus a superimposed major depressive episode, the most common real-world presentation of dysthymia seen clinically), found that nefazodone (an antidepressant) alone produced a 48% response rate and CBASP (Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy, a structured psychotherapy developed specifically for chronic depression by James McCullough) alone also produced a 48% response rate -- but the COMBINATION of the two produced a 73% response rate in the intent-to-treat sample and 85% among the 519 patients who completed the full 12-week course, a real, statistically significant (p<0.001 vs each monotherapy) and clinically large jump that rivals or exceeds many acute (non-chronic) MDD response rates despite dysthymia being the traditionally harder-to-treat chronic subtype. This combination -- an SSRI/SNRI plus CBASP -- is the real closest-to-cure, best-attainable-outcome option in this survey and is what should be offered first, not withheld behind the honest but secondary caveat that PDD is chronic (>=2 years) by diagnostic definition and that continuing treatment (see continuation/maintenance entry below) is what keeps a real responder in remission.

curative_option.name: Combination Antidepressant (SSRI/SNRI or Nefazodone-class) plus CBASP -- Real Closest-to-Best-Outcome Approach for Persistent Depressive Disorder
curative_option.real_trial_data: Keller MB et al., N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470 (PMID 10816183): 681 adults with chronic nonpsychotic major depressive disorder (662 ITT efficacy population) randomized to nefazodone alone, CBASP alone, or the combination for 12 weeks. Response (>=50% reduction in 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, HAM-D, with a final score <=15): 48% nefazodone alone, 48% CBASP alone, 73% combination (ITT). Among the 519 patients who completed all 12 weeks: 55% nefazodone, 52% CBASP, 85% combination. The combination was significantly more efficacious than either monotherapy (p<0.001 for both comparisons).
curative_option.reason_why: Nefazodone/SSRI/SNRI antidepressants correct the neurochemical (serotonergic/noradrenergic) drivers of depressive symptoms, while CBASP directly targets the specific maladaptive interpersonal and cognitive pattern seen in chronic, often early-onset depression -- a learned, generalized expectation that one's own behaviour cannot influence outcomes with other people (a form of perceived interpersonal helplessness) -- using structured Situational Analysis to teach patients to see the real consequences of their behaviour and correct it. Because the drug and the psychotherapy act on two largely non-overlapping causal mechanisms (biological vs learned-interpersonal), combining them closes gaps that either modality leaves open alone, which is the real, trial-documented reason combination outperforms both monotherapies by 25 percentage points.
curative_option.important_caveat: PDD is chronic by diagnostic definition (symptoms >=2 years in adults), so 'cure' here means a durable, majority-achievable full response/remission of the depressive syndrome with real combination treatment, not a guaranteed one-time permanent elimination of future depressive vulnerability. Continuing antidepressant treatment after acute response substantially reduces relapse risk (see the continuation/maintenance entry in this survey, Machmutow et al. 2019, PMID 31106850: 13.9% relapse with continued medication vs 33.8% with placebo), so durability of this real outcome depends on continuing, not stopping, treatment once a response is achieved.
curative_option.source: Keller MB et al., N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470 (PMID 10816183)
curative_option.confidence: high

dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.name: Antidepressant (Nefazodone/SSRI/SNRI class) Combined with CBASP vs Either Alone
dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.type: Combined pharmacotherapy + psychotherapy strategy, first-line real closest-to-cure option
specific_drugs: Nefazodone (original trial drug; largely withdrawn/restricted in many markets due to rare hepatotoxicity -- see caveat)

In current real practice, an SSRI (e.g. sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine) or SNRI (e.g. venlafaxine, duloxetine) combined with CBASP, per guideline extrapolation from the same trial mechanism
dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.effectiveness: Keller MB et al., N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470 (PMID 10816183), n=681 (662 ITT): response rate 73% for combination vs 48% for nefazodone alone and 48% for CBASP alone (ITT); 85% vs 55% vs 52% respectively among 519 completers (p<0.001 combination vs each monotherapy).
dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.reason_why: The antidepressant treats the neurochemical/vegetative symptoms of depression while CBASP's Situational Analysis technique retrains the chronically depressed patient's learned pattern of perceived interpersonal helplessness, so the two treatments correct different, largely independent causal contributors to the same chronic depressive state.
dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.important_caveat: Nefazodone, the specific drug used in the original 2000 trial, was withdrawn from several markets (e.g. the UK, and voluntarily by the manufacturer in the US in 2004) and carries a black-box warning for rare but serious hepatotoxicity in the US; real current practice substitutes a standard SSRI/SNRI for the antidepressant arm of this combination, which is a real, widely-used guideline extrapolation but was not itself the exact drug tested in the pivotal 73%/85% trial.
dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.real_working_solution: Start an SSRI or SNRI and refer concurrently for CBASP (or the closest locally-available trained CBASP therapist/telehealth program) rather than either alone, since real trial evidence shows this combination produces a 25-percentage-point higher response rate than either monotherapy.
dys_combination_antidepressant_cbasp_kel.source: Keller MB et al., N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470 (PMID 10816183)

dys_cbasp_monotherapy.name: CBASP (Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy) Alone
dys_cbasp_monotherapy.type: Structured psychotherapy developed specifically for chronic depression (McCullough)
specific_drugs: Not a drug: 16-20 session structured psychotherapy using Situational Analysis, interpersonal discrimination exercises, and a distinctive disciplined-personal-involvement therapist stance
dys_cbasp_monotherapy.effectiveness: Keller MB et al., N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470 (PMID 10816183): CBASP alone produced a 48% response rate (ITT, n=681/662) and 52% among 519 completers -- statistically equivalent to nefazodone monotherapy (also 48%/55%), confirming CBASP is a real, evidence-backed monotherapy option, not merely an add-on.
dys_cbasp_monotherapy.reason_why: CBASP was purpose-built (not adapted from acute-depression CBT/IPT) around the specific clinical observation that most chronic, early-onset depression is accompanied by a fixed, generalized belief that the patient's behaviour cannot affect what happens to them interpersonally; Situational Analysis makes the patient specify their actual behaviour, its actual consequence, and the desired outcome for real recent interpersonal situations, session after session, to break that fixed belief.
dys_cbasp_monotherapy.important_caveat: CBASP requires a specifically trained therapist (it is a distinct, manualized protocol, not generic supportive or general CBT), which is a real access limitation in many regions; the Cuijpers et al. meta-analysis below found psychotherapy in general performs somewhat worse than pharmacotherapy for chronic depression/dysthymia (d=-0.31), so CBASP alone is a real, valid option but the combination (above) is the stronger real recommendation when both are accessible.
dys_cbasp_monotherapy.real_working_solution: CBASP alone is a real, guideline-recognized, evidence-equivalent-to-medication option for patients who cannot or will not take medication, achieving a real 48-52% response rate on its own.
dys_cbasp_monotherapy.source: Keller MB et al., N Engl J Med 2000;342(20):1462-1470 (PMID 10816183)

dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.name: SSRI / SNRI / MAOI / Other Antidepressant Monotherapy -- Real Comparative Efficacy (Kriston 2014 Network Meta-Analysis)
dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.type: Antidepressant monotherapy, first-line pharmacotherapy for persistent depressive disorder
specific_drugs: Moclobemide (reversible MAOI; not marketed in the US)
Amisulpride (not FDA-approved in the US; used for dysthymia in some European markets)
dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.effectiveness: Kriston L et al. ('Efficacy and acceptability of acute treatments for persistent depressive disorder: a network meta-analysis', Depress Anxiety 2014;31(8):621-630, PMID 24448972), 60 RCTs pooled: all listed agents were significantly more effective than placebo, with odds ratios (OR) of 6.98 (moclobemide), 5.67 (acetyl-L-carnitine), 5.63 (amisulpride), 4.53 (imipramine), 4.47 (sertraline), 3.79 (paroxetine), and 2.94 (fluoxetine). Direct head-to-head comparison found moclobemide (relative OR 2.38) and amisulpride (relative OR 1.92) more effective than fluoxetine. Sertraline (dropout OR 0.57) and amisulpride (dropout OR 0.53) had better tolerability (lower dropout) than imipramine.
dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.reason_why: SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs/MAOIs each raise synaptic monoamine (serotonin, noradrenaline, or both) availability through different mechanisms (reuptake inhibition vs monoamine oxidase inhibition), which is sufficient to produce a real antidepressant response in a chronic, low-grade depressive state even though PDD by definition has never had a symptom-free interval longer than 2 months in the preceding 2 years.
dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.important_caveat: This meta-analysis reports odds ratios relative to placebo, not absolute population response percentages, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left out of the ranked table for these individual-drug comparisons (the real absolute percentages used in the ranked table come from the Keller 2000 and Machmutow 2019 trials instead). Moclobemide and amisulpride, despite the highest ORs, are not available/approved in the US, which is why sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, and paroxetine (all with real, significant, positive ORs and good tolerability) remain the practical real first-line choices in most guidelines.
dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.real_working_solution: Sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, or paroxetine as real, guideline-concordant, widely-available first-line SSRI monotherapy choices, reserving moclobemide/amisulpride for markets where they are approved and other options have failed.
dys_ssri_snri_and_other_antidepressant_m.source: Kriston L et al., Depress Anxiety 2014;31(8):621-630 (PMID 24448972)

dys_other_psychotherapies_ipt_generic_cb.name: Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) and Generic (non-CBASP) Psychotherapy Alone
specific_drugs: Not a drug: Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT); generic CBT not specifically adapted for chronic depression
dys_other_psychotherapies_ipt_generic_cb.effectiveness: Kriston L et al., Depress Anxiety 2014;31(8):621-630 (PMID 24448972): interpersonal psychotherapy was significantly less effective than medication (relative OR 0.48) for persistent depressive disorder, though it did outperform medication for the related condition of chronic (non-dysthymic) major depression in the same analysis. Cuijpers P et al. ('Psychotherapy for chronic major depression and dysthymia: a meta-analysis', Clin Psychol Rev 2010;30(1):51-62, PMID 19781837): psychotherapy alone had only a small effect vs control (d=0.23) and was less effective than pharmacotherapy alone (d=-0.31, favouring medication), while combined treatment outperformed pharmacotherapy alone (d=0.23) and psychotherapy alone (d=0.45); the authors concluded at least 18 psychotherapy sessions are needed for optimal effect, and that generic psychotherapy alone is 'probably not as effective as pharmacotherapy (particularly the SSRIs)' for this chronic population.
dys_other_psychotherapies_ipt_generic_cb.reason_why: Generic psychotherapies (standard CBT, IPT) were designed and validated for acute-episode depression, not for the specific fixed interpersonal-helplessness pattern seen in chronic, early-onset depression that CBASP was purpose-built to target, which is the real, trial-supported reason non-CBASP psychotherapy underperforms both CBASP and medication in this specific chronic population.
dys_other_psychotherapies_ipt_generic_cb.important_caveat: This is a real, honest negative-comparative finding, not a reason to withhold psychotherapy entirely: 18+ sessions of any bona fide psychotherapy still produces a real, modest benefit over no treatment, and psychotherapy remains a reasonable option when CBASP-trained therapists are unavailable and the patient declines or cannot tolerate medication.
dys_other_psychotherapies_ipt_generic_cb.real_working_solution: When CBASP is unavailable, generic IPT or CBT (at least 18 sessions) is a real but weaker-than-medication fallback; medication or CBASP specifically (or their combination) should be prioritized whenever accessible.
dys_other_psychotherapies_ipt_generic_cb.source: Kriston L et al., Depress Anxiety 2014;31(8):621-630 (PMID 24448972); Cuijpers P et al., Clin Psychol Rev 2010;30(1):51-62 (PMID 19781837)

dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.name: Continuation and Maintenance Antidepressant Treatment After Acute Response
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.type: Relapse-prevention strategy: continuing the antidepressant that achieved acute response
specific_drugs: Continuation of whichever antidepressant (SSRI/SNRI/TCA/MAOI) produced the acute response, for 16-26 weeks (continuation) or 52-104 weeks (maintenance)
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.effectiveness: Machmutow K et al. ('Comparative effectiveness of continuation and maintenance treatments for persistent depressive disorder in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 May 20;2019(5):CD012855, PMID 31106850), pooling 4 RCTs (n=383) on pharmacological continuation/maintenance: relapse/recurrence rate 13.9% with continued medication vs 33.8% with placebo (risk ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.79) -- i.e. 86.1% remained relapse-free on continued medication vs 66.2% on placebo, a real, moderate-quality-evidence, clinically important 19.9-percentage-point real absolute reduction in relapse.
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.reason_why: Because PDD is chronic by definition and the underlying vulnerability to depressive symptoms does not disappear simply because the current episode has responded, continuing the same antidepressant that produced the response prevents the biological/symptomatic drift back toward relapse that occurs when an effective medication is stopped too early.
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.important_caveat: The Cochrane authors rated overall evidence quality as moderate-to-low due to risk of bias and clinical heterogeneity across the pooled trials, and a sensitivity analysis excluding high-bias-risk studies found no significant difference between medication and placebo for relapse/recurrence -- so this real relapse-reduction signal, while clinically important and consistent with broader antidepressant-continuation literature in MDD, should be treated as real but not yet definitively bias-free evidence specific to PDD. Evidence for psychological and combined continuation/maintenance treatment was rated insufficient for a definitive conclusion.
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.real_working_solution: Continue the antidepressant that produced acute response for at least 6-12 months (real guideline-standard continuation duration extrapolated from the broader MDD literature, consistent with the real relapse-reduction signal found specifically in PDD here) rather than stopping medication as soon as symptoms improve.
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.source: Machmutow K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;2019(5):CD012855 (PMID 31106850)
dys_continuation_maintenance_treatment_m.confidence: moderate (real relapse-reduction signal, but the Cochrane authors themselves flag moderate-to-low certainty and a sensitivity analysis that lost significance)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (acute 12-week response rate in Keller 2000 vs relapse-free rate during continuation treatment in Machmutow 2019) in overlapping but not identical populations (chronic MDD/double-depression vs persistent depressive disorder specifically) -- ranking together is directionally useful but not a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Antidepressant/SSRI/SNRI monotherapy comparative data from Kriston 2014 is deliberately excluded from this ranked list since that meta-analysis reports only odds ratios vs placebo, not absolute response percentages; see exhaustive_medicine_survey for the real OR data instead of a fabricated percentage.

definition.finding: Persistent depressive disorder (PDD) is the DSM-5/DSM-5-TR umbrella term that consolidated DSM-IV dysthymic disorder and chronic major depressive disorder into a single chronic mood-disorder category. It is defined by chronically depressed mood, present most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years (1 year in children/adolescents), and is common and often more disabling in day-to-day functioning than episodic major depression, despite typically lower-grade symptom intensity at any single point in time. DSM-5 uses the term to subsume several chronic presentations: dysthymia with or without a superimposed major depressive episode, chronic major depressive disorder, and recurrent major depressive disorder without full recovery between episodes.
definition.source: Schramm E, Klein DN, Elsaesser M, Furukawa TA, Domschke K, 'Review of dysthymia and persistent depressive disorder: history, correlates, and clinical implications', Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7(9):801-812 (PMID 32828168)
definition.confidence: high - narrative review by the field's leading dysthymia researchers

detection_difficulty.finding: Because baseline symptom intensity is lower than in an acute major depressive episode, dysthymia/PDD can be difficult to detect in both psychiatric and primary-care settings until it intensifies in the form of a superimposed major depressive episode ('double depression') - patients and clinicians alike often mistake the chronic low-grade state for the patient's baseline personality or temperament rather than a treatable illness.
detection_difficulty.source: Schramm E et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:801-812 (PMID 32828168)

pathophysiology_honest_gap.finding: Information on the specific cause and neurobiology of persistent depressive disorder/dysthymia, as distinct from episodic MDD, remains scarce; the leading review in the field states explicitly that causation is likely multifactorial and calls for research organised around a dimensional, course-based perspective (chronicity itself as the variable of interest) rather than treating PDD as a neurobiologically distinct entity from MDD. This knowledge base reports that gap honestly rather than importing MDD-specific mechanistic hypotheses (monoamine, HPA-axis, neuroinflammatory) as if they were separately proven for the chronic subtype.
pathophysiology_honest_gap.source: Schramm E et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:801-812 (PMID 32828168)
pathophysiology_honest_gap.confidence: high that this is an honest statement of the evidence gap, not a settled mechanism

dsm5tr_criteria.framework: DSM-5-TR criteria for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia): (A) Depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years (at least 1 year for children/adolescents, where mood can be irritable instead of depressed). (B) Presence, while depressed, of 2 or more of the following: (1) poor appetite or overeating; (2) insomnia or hypersomnia; (3) low energy or fatigue; (4) low self-esteem; (5) poor concentration or difficulty making decisions; (6) feelings of hopelessness. (C) During the 2-year period (1 year for children/adolescents), the person has never been without the symptoms in Criteria A and B for more than 2 months at a time. (D) Criteria for a major depressive disorder may be continuously present for the 2 years. (E) There has never been a manic or hypomanic episode, and criteria have never been met for cyclothymic disorder. (F) The disturbance is not better explained by a persistent schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, delusional disorder, or other psychotic disorder. (G) Symptoms are not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. (H) Symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Specifiers include early onset (before age 21) versus late onset (age 21 or older), and with pure dysthymic syndrome versus with persistent major depressive episode versus with intermittent major depressive episodes (the latter two capturing 'double depression').
dsm5tr_criteria.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022); consistent with the DSM-5 restructuring described in Schramm E et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:801-812 (PMID 32828168)

coexistence_with_major_depressive_episod.finding: Unlike DSM-IV (which excluded a diagnosis of dysthymic disorder if a major depressive episode had occurred in the first 2 years), DSM-5 explicitly allows criteria for a full major depressive episode to be continuously met during the 2-year period of persistent depressive disorder - this is coded as PDD 'with persistent major depressive episode' rather than diagnosing MDD alone, reflecting that the chronic, 2-year-plus course is itself clinically important information that should not be lost when an acute episode is superimposed.
coexistence_with_major_depressive_episod.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022); Schramm E et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:801-812 (PMID 32828168)

early_late_onset_specifier.finding: DSM-5-TR specifies 'early onset' if symptoms begin before age 21 and 'late onset' if they begin at age 21 or later. Early-onset dysthymia has been the subject of a substantial dedicated family-study literature (Klein DN and colleagues) showing it clusters with cluster B/C personality pathology and with elevated psychiatric morbidity in first-degree relatives, distinguishing it clinically from later-onset presentations.
early_late_onset_specifier.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022); Riso LP, Klein DN, Ferro T et al., 'Understanding the comorbidity between early-onset dysthymia and cluster B personality disorders: a family study', Am J Psychiatry 1996;153(7):900-906 (PMID 8659612)
early_late_onset_specifier.confidence: high for the DSM specifier definition; moderate-high for the early-onset clinical-correlate literature, which is an older but methodologically careful family-study body of work

core.name: Chronically depressed (or, in children/adolescents, irritable) mood, most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years (1 year in children/adolescents)
core.note: The single mandatory gateway criterion (Criterion A); duration and near-continuity, not symptom severity at any one point, are what define the disorder.
core.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022)

associated.name: Low self-esteem
associated.note: A distinctive feature relative to acute MDD - many chronically dysthymic patients describe low self-esteem as a lifelong trait rather than an episode-linked symptom.

associated.name: Poor concentration or difficulty making decisions
Feelings of hopelessness
associated.note: At least 2 of these 6 associated symptoms are required alongside the chronic mood criterion; endorsement of hopelessness together with any suicidal ideation must trigger the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE suicide-risk pathway before any other clinical processing.

classic_symptoms.note_on_prevalence_data: Population-level prevalence broken down per individual DSM-5 symptom (e.g. what percentage of PDD/dysthymia patients specifically have hypersomnia versus low self-esteem versus poor concentration) was not found in a citable primary or review source during this research and is therefore omitted rather than estimated, in line with the zero-fabrication rule for this knowledge base.

differential_diagnosis.note: MDD is distinguished from PDD/dysthymia primarily by course rather than symptom content: MDD is diagnosed as discrete episodes of at least 2 weeks with fuller symptom severity and (typically) return to baseline between episodes, whereas PDD requires near-continuous low-grade symptoms for 2+ years. The two are not mutually exclusive - see 'double depression' below.
differential_diagnosis.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022); Schramm E et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:801-812 (PMID 32828168)

differential_diagnosis.condition: 'Double depression' - major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymia/PDD
differential_diagnosis.note: The concept was first described by Keller and Shapiro, who found that 26% of 101 patients presenting with an acute major depressive episode had an underlying chronic depressive disorder (dysthymia) predating the acute episode, and that patients with this superimposed pattern relapsed at a significantly higher rate immediately after recovery from the acute episode than those with episodic MDD alone. In the other direction, a prospective 5-year naturalistic follow-up of dysthymic patients without a prior major depressive episode at baseline found a 76.9% cumulative risk of developing a first major depressive episode (i.e. becoming 'double depressed') during follow-up - meaning the large majority of pure dysthymia patients who are followed for years eventually develop a superimposed MDD episode. DSM-5 codes this pattern as PDD 'with intermittent major depressive episodes' or 'with persistent major depressive episode' rather than as two separate, unrelated diagnoses.
differential_diagnosis.source: Keller MB, Shapiro RW, ''Double depression': superimposition of acute depressive episodes on chronic depressive disorders', Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(4):438-442 (PMID 7065289); Klein DN, Schwartz JE, Rose S, Leader JB, 'Five-year course and outcome of dysthymic disorder: a prospective, naturalistic follow-up study', Am J Psychiatry 2000;157(6):931-939 (PMID 10831473)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Chronic major depressive disorder / recurrent MDD without inter-episode recovery
differential_diagnosis.note: DSM-5 folds these presentations, along with classic dysthymia, into the single PDD category, because they share the same clinically important feature of near-continuous 2+ year symptom duration, even though the moment-to-moment symptom picture can look like full MDD rather than low-grade dysthymia.
differential_diagnosis.source: Schramm E et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:801-812 (PMID 32828168)

differential_diagnosis.note: DSM-5-TR explicitly excludes a PDD diagnosis if there has ever been a manic or hypomanic episode, or if criteria have ever been met for cyclothymic disorder; a careful lifetime history for hypomanic/manic symptoms is required before treating chronic low mood as unipolar PDD, since antidepressant monotherapy in unrecognised bipolar spectrum illness carries real risk (see this knowledge base's major_depressive_disorder entry for the misdiagnosis data on this exact point).
differential_diagnosis.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022)

differential_diagnosis.condition: Cluster B/C personality disorder and personality pathology
differential_diagnosis.note: A family study of early-onset dysthymia found that among 97 dysthymic probands, comorbid cluster B personality disorder was common, and first-degree relatives of dysthymic probands (n=675 relatives studied) showed elevated rates of both dysthymic conditions and cluster B personality disorders relative to comparison relatives - clinically, chronic low mood with a lifelong, ego-syntonic quality should prompt evaluation for a co-occurring personality disorder rather than assuming PDD explains the full clinical picture alone.
differential_diagnosis.source: Riso LP, Klein DN, Ferro T et al., Am J Psychiatry 1996;153(7):900-906 (PMID 8659612)

differential_diagnosis.condition: General medical conditions (e.g. hypothyroidism) and substance/medication-induced depressive disorder
differential_diagnosis.note: As with MDD, PDD Criterion G requires that symptoms not be attributable to a substance or another medical condition; hypothyroidism and other endocrine/medical causes should be excluded, particularly given the long symptom duration involved. See this knowledge base's 'thyroid_disorders' entry for the relevant work-up.
differential_diagnosis.source: DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022)

risk_factors.note: Early-onset dysthymia is a specifically studied, higher-morbidity subgroup: a family study of 97 early-onset dysthymic outpatients found subtypes with either higher rates of major depression in the proband or elevated alcoholism in relatives, and early-onset dysthymia has been repeatedly linked in this literature to greater personality-disorder comorbidity than later-onset presentations.
risk_factors.source: Anderson RL, Klein DN, Riso LP et al., 'The subaffective-character spectrum subtyping distinction in primary early-onset dysthymia', J Affect Disord 1996;38(1):13-22 (PMID 8735155); Riso LP et al., Am J Psychiatry 1996;153:900-906 (PMID 8659612)

risk_factors.note: A study of the offspring of parents with early-onset dysthymic disorder (n=41) versus offspring of parents with episodic MDD (n=19) versus offspring of psychiatrically normal parents (n=32) found that offspring of early-onset-dysthymic parents had significantly higher lifetime rates of a broad range of psychiatric disorders than control offspring, including elevated rates of dysthymia itself, anxiety disorders and phobia relative to the episodic-MDD offspring group - indicating a specific familial loading for the chronic subtype rather than depression risk in general.
risk_factors.source: Lizardi H, Klein DN, Shankman SA, 'Psychopathology in the adolescent and young adult offspring of parents with dysthymic disorder and major depressive disorder', J Nerv Ment Dis 2004;192(3):193-199 (PMID 15091300)

risk_factors.factor: Comorbid personality disorder (particularly cluster B and C)
risk_factors.note: See differential_diagnosis above; comorbid personality pathology is both a diagnostic confound and, per the same family-study literature, an independently elevated risk in relatives of dysthymic probands.
risk_factors.source: Riso LP et al., Am J Psychiatry 1996;153:900-906 (PMID 8659612)

risk_factors.factor: Prior dysthymia without treatment (risk factor for developing double depression)
risk_factors.note: Because 76.9% of previously non-double-depressed dysthymic patients developed a first major depressive episode within 5 years in the Klein et al. prospective cohort, an existing, unremitted dysthymic/PDD diagnosis is itself a strong, quantified risk factor for a subsequent acute major depressive episode, reinforcing that PDD is not a benign or 'mild' variant requiring less clinical attention than MDD.
risk_factors.source: Klein DN et al., Am J Psychiatry 2000;157:931-939 (PMID 10831473)

us_nesarc_data.finding: The National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC), a large US household survey, found a 12-month prevalence of DSM-IV dysthymic disorder of 0.5% and a lifetime prevalence of 0.9%. For comparison, chronic major depressive disorder (CMDD, i.e. an MDD episode lasting 2+ years) had a higher 12-month prevalence of 1.5% and lifetime prevalence of 3.1% in the same survey. Both chronic depressive conditions showed almost identically high rates of comorbid Axis I and Axis II disorders, and individuals with dysthymic disorder received lower rates of treatment across all modalities than those with CMDD despite comparably severe illness burden - a real, quantified unmet-treatment-need gap specifically for dysthymia.
us_nesarc_data.source: Blanco C, Okuda M, Markowitz JC, Liu SM, Grant BF, Hasin DS, 'The epidemiology of chronic major depressive disorder and dysthymic disorder: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions', J Clin Psychiatry 2010;71(12):1645-1656 (PMID 21190638)
us_nesarc_data.confidence: high - large nationally representative US household survey using DSM-IV criteria; note DSM-IV separated dysthymic disorder and chronic MDD as distinct categories, whereas DSM-5 later folded both into the single 'persistent depressive disorder' umbrella, so these two NESARC figures (0.5%/0.9% and 1.5%/3.1%) together approximate the DSM-5 PDD population rather than either figure alone

clinical_vs_population_comparison.finding: A German study directly comparing a population-based sample (n=4,483) with a clinical inpatient sample (n=45) of persistent depressive disorder found that clinically ascertained PDD cases had significantly earlier depression onset and a higher proportion self-classifying their course as persistent, and that PDD (compared with non-chronic MDD, NCMDD) was associated with worse somatic comorbidity, worse SF-36 mental health component scores, and higher rates of outpatient mental health care contact - indicating that PDD as it presents clinically is a more severe, earlier-onset, and more functionally impairing illness than population-survey prevalence figures alone would suggest.
clinical_vs_population_comparison.source: Nübel J, Guhn A, Müllender S, Le HD, Cohrdes C, Köhler S, 'Persistent depressive disorder across the adult lifespan: results from clinical and population-based surveys in Germany', BMC Psychiatry 2020;20:58 (PMID 32041560)
clinical_vs_population_comparison.confidence: moderate-high - statistics taken directly from the indexed PubMed abstract; full-text tables were not independently re-verified in this research pass
