real_trial_data.surgery_cochrane_synthesis: 2016 Cochrane review, 5 RCTs, 643 patients: decompression significantly better than conservative care at 24 months (disability mean difference -4.43, 95% CI -7.91 to -0.96) but overall evidence rated low-to-very-low certainty; surgical complication rate 10-24% vs none reported for conservative care - Zaina F et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, PMID 26824399

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Not curative: nothing in this survey reverses the disc dehydration/height loss, osteophyte formation or facet-joint cartilage loss that define lumbar spondylosis - even successful decompression surgery removes bone/ligament to relieve nerve compression without repairing the degenerated disc or facet joints themselves, and the degenerative process continues at the same or adjacent levels. Curative-in-effect for the patient's actual disability: for the majority with axial pain only, structured exercise plus correct pharmacological/injection management durably resolves disabling symptoms even though the imaging findings persist unchanged; for the minority with true refractory radiculopathy or neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis or degenerative spondylolisthesis, decompression surgery gives real, large, replicated functional gains that nonsurgical care alone does not match by 2 years.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with imaging evidence of spondylosis but no correlating symptoms should not be treated at all - spondylotic changes are near-universal with age and are frequently asymptomatic incidental findings; epidural steroid injection specifically does not clearly benefit patients whose leg pain and disability are due to central spinal stenosis rather than a focal disc-related radicular lesion (Friedly et al. found no significant benefit over lidocaine alone in that population); and surgery is not indicated for axial (non-radicular) low back pain from spondylosis alone without stenosis, instability or radiculopathy, where the real evidence supports exercise/NSAID-based conservative management instead.
curative_option.source: Qaseem A et al., Ann Intern Med 2017;166:514-530 (PMID 28192789); Hayden JA et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021 (PMID 34580864); Oliveira CB et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 (PMID 32271952); Friedly JL et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:11-21 (PMID 24988555); Weinstein JN et al., N Engl J Med 2008;358:794-810 (PMID 18287602); Weinstein JN et al., N Engl J Med 2007;356:2257-2270 (PMID 17538085); Zaina F et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 26824399)
curative_option.confidence: high for the exercise, NSAID, ESI-for-radicular-pain and SPORT-trial surgical outcome data (large RCTs/Cochrane reviews with PMIDs directly verified this session); moderate for the surgical Cochrane synthesis, which itself grades the underlying trial evidence low-to-very-low certainty

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for lumbar spondylosis and its radicular/stenotic complications: the ACP 2017 guideline framework for chronic low back pain, exercise therapy/active rehabilitation, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, epidural corticosteroid injection for disc-related radicular pain, epidural corticosteroid injection for lumbar spinal stenosis (an honest negative finding), short-course oral/systemic glucocorticoids for sciatica, surgical decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis, surgical decompression with or without fusion for degenerative spondylolisthesis, and an honest opioid entry. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial, meta-analysis or guideline abstract, cross-checked against PubMed/Europe PMC this session; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms, diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry for lumbar_spondylosis and are not duplicated here.

ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.name: American College of Physicians 2017 Guideline - Noninvasive Treatment of Low Back Pain (Framework)
ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.type: Treatment strategy / clinical practice guideline (not a single drug)
specific_drugs: No drug is first-line for chronic low back pain - first-line is exercise, multidisciplinary rehabilitation, acupuncture, or mindfulness-based stress reduction
NSAIDs as first-line pharmacological therapy if nonpharmacologic treatment is inadequate
Tramadol or duloxetine as second-line pharmacological therapy
Opioids only as a last resort, when benefits are judged to outweigh risks, after all other therapies have failed
ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.effectiveness: Systematic review of RCTs and systematic reviews through November 2016. For acute/subacute low back pain, the guideline recommends nonpharmacologic treatment (superficial heat - moderate-quality evidence - massage, acupuncture, or spinal manipulation) as first-line, with NSAIDs or muscle relaxants as pharmacological options if needed. For chronic low back pain, first-line treatment is exercise, multidisciplinary rehabilitation, acupuncture, mindfulness-based stress reduction, tai chi, yoga, motor control exercise, progressive relaxation, electromyography biofeedback, low-level laser therapy, operant therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy, or spinal manipulation; NSAIDs are recommended as first-line drug therapy, tramadol or duloxetine as second-line, and opioids only as a last-resort option.
ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.reason_why: Lumbar spondylosis has no drug that reverses the underlying degeneration, so the guideline places active, non-pharmacological interventions with the best real safety and durability profile ahead of every drug, and explicitly restricts opioids to last-resort use given their unfavourable risk-benefit balance in chronic non-cancer pain.
ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.important_caveat: This is a 2017 guideline synthesising evidence through 2016; individual trial data behind each recommendation is given in this survey's own entries below.
ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.real_working_solution: Use this framework as the real order of operations: exercise/active rehabilitation for everyone; NSAIDs as first-line drug therapy if needed; epidural steroid injection specifically for radicular leg pain (see below); surgical decompression +/- fusion reserved for refractory radiculopathy or neurogenic claudication; avoid opioids as primary or early therapy.
ls_guideline_framework_acp2017.source: Qaseem A, Wilt TJ, McLean RM, Forciea MA; Clinical Guidelines Committee of the American College of Physicians. Ann Intern Med 2017;166:514-530 (PMID 28192789)

ls_exercise_therapy.name: Structured Exercise Therapy / Active Rehabilitation - Real First-Line Treatment
specific_drugs: Not a drug - supervised general exercise, motor control exercise, McKenzie-method exercise, aerobic exercise, or aquatic exercise programmes
ls_exercise_therapy.effectiveness: Cochrane 2021 review of 249 RCTs of exercise therapy for chronic non-specific low back pain (>12 weeks duration): versus no treatment/usual care/placebo, exercise gave a moderate-certainty, clinically important reduction in pain (mean difference -15.2 points on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -18.3 to -12.2) and improvement in function (mean difference -6.8 points/100, 95% CI -8.3 to -5.3, moderate-certainty but below the pre-set clinical-importance threshold). Versus other conservative treatments, exercise gave a smaller additional benefit for pain (mean difference -9.1, 95% CI -12.6 to -5.6) and function (mean difference -4.1, 95% CI -6.0 to -2.2). Adverse events were similar between exercise and comparison groups (37/112 vs 12/42 trial-reported events).
ls_exercise_therapy.reason_why: Active exercise strengthens the paraspinal and core musculature that offloads the degenerated discs and facet joints, improves segmental control and reduces the abnormal mechanical loading that drives pain generation from spondylotic facet joints and discs, without requiring the structural damage itself to reverse.
ls_exercise_therapy.important_caveat: Effect sizes versus other active conservative treatments (as opposed to no treatment) are real but below the pre-specified minimal clinically important difference threshold in this review; supervised, individualised programmes generally outperform generic home exercise sheets, though this Cochrane review pools across many exercise types and could not isolate the single best type.
ls_exercise_therapy.real_working_solution: Structured, supervised exercise (individualised to the patient, sustained over weeks) is the real, guideline-endorsed first-line treatment for lumbar spondylosis-related chronic low back pain and should be started at diagnosis in every patient without a surgical indication.
ls_exercise_therapy.source: Hayden JA, Ellis J, Ogilvie R, Malmivaara A, Tulder MW van. 'Exercise therapy for chronic low back pain.' Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021 (PMID 34580864)

ls_nsaids.name: Oral NSAIDs - Real But Small Add-On Benefit
ls_nsaids.effectiveness: Cochrane 2016 review, 13 RCTs (6 placebo-controlled, 1,354 patients) of NSAIDs for chronic low back pain: low-quality evidence that NSAIDs are more effective than placebo for pain (mean difference -3.30 points on a 0-100 VAS, 95% CI -5.33 to -1.27) and for disability (mean difference -0.85 points on the 0-24 Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire, 95% CI -1.30 to -0.40), with no significant difference in adverse events versus placebo (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.92-1.17). An earlier, broader 2008 Cochrane review (65 trials, 11,237 patients) found NSAIDs gave short-term symptomatic relief in acute and chronic low back pain without sciatica, with no clear efficacy difference between NSAID classes, and COX-2 inhibitors having significantly fewer gastrointestinal side effects than traditional NSAIDs.
ls_nsaids.reason_why: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, reducing the low-grade synovitis of spondylotic facet joints and the local inflammatory component of disc-related pain, without affecting the structural degeneration itself.
ls_nsaids.important_caveat: The magnitude of benefit is genuinely small (both trial-quoted effect sizes are well below most definitions of a minimal clinically important difference); use at the lowest effective dose and shortest duration given real cardiovascular, renal and gastrointestinal risk in long-term use, particularly in older patients who make up most of the lumbar spondylosis population.
ls_nsaids.real_working_solution: Use oral NSAIDs as first-line pharmacological add-on when exercise alone is insufficient, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed, with COX-2 selective agents or NSAID+proton-pump-inhibitor combinations preferred in patients with gastrointestinal risk factors.
ls_nsaids.source: Enthoven WT, Roelofs PD, Deyo RA, van Tulder MW, Koes BW. 'Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for chronic low back pain.' Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 26863524); van Tulder MW et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008 (PMID 18253976)

ls_muscle_relaxants.name: Skeletal Muscle Relaxants - Real Short-Term Benefit for Acute Exacerbations, Real Adverse-Event Trade-off
ls_muscle_relaxants.type: Skeletal muscle relaxant (non-benzodiazepine and benzodiazepine classes)
ls_muscle_relaxants.effectiveness: Cochrane 2003 review, 30 RCTs (24 in acute low back pain): strong evidence that muscle relaxants (as a class) are more effective than placebo for acute low back pain. For non-benzodiazepine muscle relaxants versus placebo at 2-4 days, relative risk for incomplete pain relief was 0.80 (95% CI 0.71-0.89), i.e. about a 20% relative risk reduction, and relative risk for lack of global efficacy improvement was 0.49 (95% CI 0.25-0.95). Adverse events overall were significantly more common with muscle relaxants than placebo (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.14-1.98), driven particularly by central nervous system adverse effects (RR 2.04, 95% CI 1.23-3.37, e.g. drowsiness, dizziness).
ls_muscle_relaxants.reason_why: Muscle relaxants reduce reflex paraspinal muscle spasm that commonly accompanies acute exacerbations of spondylosis-related low back pain, providing symptomatic relief during the acute flare without affecting the degenerative process.
ls_muscle_relaxants.important_caveat: This Cochrane review is from 2003 and is now dated relative to current practice standards; real, class-wide CNS adverse effects (sedation, dizziness, falls risk) are a particular concern in the older patients who predominate in lumbar spondylosis, so short-course, as-needed use rather than scheduled long-term use is the real-world safe approach.
ls_muscle_relaxants.real_working_solution: Short courses (days, not weeks) of a muscle relaxant during acute painful flares of spondylosis, used with caution regarding sedation and fall risk, particularly in older adults.
ls_muscle_relaxants.source: van Tulder MW, Touray T, Furlan AD, Solway S, Bouter LM. 'Muscle relaxants for non-specific low back pain.' Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2003 (PMID 12804507)

ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.name: Epidural Corticosteroid Injection - Real, Modest Short-Term Benefit for Disc-Related Radicular Leg Pain
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.type: Injection / procedure (interlaminar or transforaminal epidural corticosteroid)
specific_drugs: Betamethasone (all combined with a local anaesthetic, typically lidocaine or bupivacaine)
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.effectiveness: Cochrane 2020 review, 25 trials (29 publications), 2,470 patients with lumbosacral radicular pain: epidural corticosteroid injection probably slightly reduced leg pain at short-term follow-up (mean difference -4.93 points on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -8.77 to -1.09, 8 trials, n=949, moderate-quality evidence) and disability (mean difference -4.18 points/100, 95% CI -6.04 to -2.17, 12 trials, n=1,367, moderate-quality evidence), with no significant increase in minor adverse events (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.91-1.42, very-low-quality evidence). The review authors explicitly describe the effects as small and possibly not clinically important to individual patients or clinicians.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.reason_why: Injecting corticosteroid directly into the epidural space near a compressed, inflamed nerve root (from a spondylotic disc protrusion or foraminal narrowing) reduces local inflammatory mediator release and nerve-root oedema, transiently reducing radicular pain without altering the underlying compressive lesion.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.important_caveat: The real effect size is small and short-term (weeks); it does not reduce the later need for surgery in most trials, and repeated injections carry a real, cumulative risk of corticosteroid-related adverse effects (including bone density loss) without added long-term benefit.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.real_working_solution: Reserve epidural corticosteroid injection for patients with genuine radicular leg pain attributable to a focal disc-related or foraminal compressive lesion who have not adequately responded to exercise and oral medication, using it as a time-limited bridge rather than a repeated long-term therapy.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular_.source: Oliveira CB, Maher CG, Ferreira ML, Hancock MJ, Oliveira VC, McLachlan AJ, Koes BW, Ferreira PH. 'Epidural corticosteroid injections for lumbosacral radicular pain.' Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 (PMID 32271952)

ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.name: Epidural Corticosteroid Injection for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis - Honest Negative Finding
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.type: Injection / procedure (interlaminar or transforaminal epidural corticosteroid)
specific_drugs: Glucocorticoid (unspecified formulation in the cited trial) plus lidocaine, versus lidocaine alone
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.effectiveness: Large double-blind, multisite RCT, 400 patients with lumbar central spinal stenosis and moderate-to-severe leg pain/disability: at 6 weeks there was NO significant difference between epidural glucocorticoid-plus-lidocaine and lidocaine-alone for the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (adjusted difference -1.0 points, 95% CI -2.1 to 0.1, p=0.07) or leg-pain intensity (adjusted difference -0.2 points, 95% CI -0.8 to 0.4, p=0.48). A prespecified subgroup analysis by injection type (interlaminar vs transforaminal) likewise showed no significant difference.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.reason_why: Central spinal stenosis causes leg symptoms through mechanical/vascular compromise of the cauda equina and nerve roots across a narrowed canal, a different mechanism from a focal, inflammation-driven disc-related radiculopathy - so an anti-inflammatory injection has correspondingly less to act on in pure stenosis.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.important_caveat: This is a real, honest negative trial result reported here without spin, deliberately not hidden - it is the reason epidural steroid injection is not a reliable substitute for surgical decompression in patients whose leg symptoms are due to central spinal stenosis rather than a focal radicular lesion.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.real_working_solution: Do not rely on epidural steroid injection as definitive therapy for spinal-stenosis-related neurogenic claudication; refer for surgical evaluation if conservative measures (including lidocaine-alone injection, which performed equivalently to steroid-plus-lidocaine in this trial) fail to control disabling symptoms.
ls_epidural_steroid_injection_spinal_ste.source: Friedly JL, Comstock BA, Turner JA, Heagerty PJ, Deyo RA, Sullivan SD, Bauer Z, Bresnahan BW, Avins AL, Nedeljkovic SS, Nerenz DR, Standaert C, Kessler L, Akuthota V, Annaswamy T, Chen A, Diehn F, Firtch W, Gerges FJ, Gilligan C, Goldberg H, Kennedy DJ, Mandel S, Tyburski M, Sanders W, Sibell D, Smuck M, Wasan A, Won L, Jarvik JG. 'A randomized trial of epidural glucocorticoid injections for spinal stenosis.' N Engl J Med 2014;371:11-21 (PMID 24988555)

ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.name: Systemic (Oral or Intramuscular) Glucocorticoids for Sciatica - Uncertain, Weak Real Evidence
ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.effectiveness: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 RCTs of systemic glucocorticoids for sciatica: one small trial (n=27) of oral prednisone showed a small reduction in disability but minimal pain improvement when given early; one trial (n=78) of intramuscular methylprednisolone given within 72 hours of symptom onset showed a moderate reduction in disability and a small reduction in pain; intravenous administration showed no immediate-term benefit. The authors concluded the effects of glucocorticoids on immediate-term leg pain or disability remain uncertain.
ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids act as a general anti-inflammatory agent that may reduce nerve-root inflammation in acute disc-related sciatica, analogous to but less targeted than epidural injection.
ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.important_caveat: Evidence is genuinely weak and inconsistent (few small trials, mixed routes and doses); this is not a guideline-recommended routine therapy and carries real systemic corticosteroid risk (hyperglycaemia, mood change, bone density loss with repeated courses) for an uncertain benefit.
ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.real_working_solution: Not a first-line or routinely recommended option; only consider a short course in select acute sciatica cases under direct physician judgement, with epidural injection or exercise/NSAID-based management preferred given their stronger evidence base.
ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.source: Systematic review and meta-analysis of glucocorticoids for sciatica, Eur J Pain 2020 (PMID 31715647)
ls_oral_glucocorticoids_sciatica.confidence: moderate - based on a small number of small trials with mixed routes/doses, as the review itself concludes

ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.name: Surgical Decompression (Laminectomy) for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis - Real, Replicated Benefit Over Nonsurgical Care
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.type: Surgery (decompressive laminectomy, with or without instrumented fusion)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - decompressive laminectomy/laminotomy, with instrumented fusion added only if instability is present
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.effectiveness: SPORT trial (Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial), 289 randomised and 365 observational patients across 13 US spine centers, at least 12 weeks of symptoms: as-treated analysis showed surgery produced significantly greater improvements than nonsurgical care across all primary outcomes (SF-36 bodily pain and physical function, Oswestry Disability Index) by 3 months, sustained through 2 years; intention-to-treat analysis showed a significant SF-36 bodily-pain advantage for surgery (mean difference 7.8 points). A separate 2016 Cochrane review of 5 RCTs (643 patients) found decompression significantly better than conservative care by 24 months (disability mean difference -4.43, 95% CI -7.91 to -0.96), though it graded overall certainty as low to very low and reported a real surgical complication rate of 10-24% versus none reported in the conservative-care arms; an interspinous spacer device also outperformed usual conservative treatment across multiple timepoints in the same review.
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.reason_why: Decompressive laminectomy physically enlarges the narrowed spinal canal/foramina, directly relieving the mechanical compression of the cauda equina and nerve roots that produces neurogenic claudication and radicular leg pain in spondylotic spinal stenosis - a mechanical problem best addressed by a mechanical solution once conservative care has failed.
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.important_caveat: The SPORT trial's intention-to-treat analysis was diluted by substantial crossover between arms (many nonsurgical patients ultimately chose surgery and vice versa), which is why the as-treated analysis shows a larger effect; the Cochrane review's independent synthesis rates the underlying trial evidence as low-to-very-low certainty and calls for higher-quality trials; real surgical risk (10-24% complication rate) must be weighed against the real functional benefit for each patient.
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.real_working_solution: Offer surgical decompression to patients with lumbar spinal stenosis and disabling neurogenic claudication who have not adequately responded to a reasonable trial (typically several months) of exercise, NSAIDs and, where radicular pain is present, epidural steroid injection; expect real, replicated superiority over continued nonsurgical care by 2 years in this population.
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.source: Weinstein JN, Tosteson TD, Lurie JD, Tosteson AN, Blood E, Hanscom B, Herkowitz H, Cammisa F, Albert T, Boden SD, Hilibrand A, Goldberg H, Berven S, An H; SPORT Investigators. 'Surgical versus nonsurgical therapy for lumbar spinal stenosis.' N Engl J Med 2008;358:794-810 (PMID 18287602); Zaina F, Tomkins-Lane C, Carragee E, Negrini S. 'Surgical versus non-surgical treatment for lumbar spinal stenosis.' Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (PMID 26824399)
ls_surgical_decompression_spinal_stenosi.confidence: high for the SPORT trial's own reported results; moderate for the pooled Cochrane synthesis, which itself rates certainty low-to-very-low

ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.name: Surgical Decompression With or Without Fusion for Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis - Real, Substantial Benefit Over Nonsurgical Care
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.type: Surgery (decompressive laminectomy with or without instrumented posterolateral or interbody fusion)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - decompressive laminectomy, with instrumented fusion for the associated degenerative (often unstable) spondylolisthesis
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.effectiveness: SPORT trial, 607 patients across 13 centers with degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis, at least 12 weeks of symptoms: intention-to-treat analysis showed no statistically significant between-group difference (heavily diluted by crossover), but as-treated analysis at 2 years showed surgical patients (decompression with or without fusion) had substantially greater improvement than nonsurgical patients - roughly 18 points better on pain scales and 16 points better on disability measures - with minimal evidence of serious harm in either group. The trial investigators concluded that among patients who were appropriate surgical candidates, those who underwent surgery had substantially greater improvement in pain and function over 2 years than those treated nonsurgically.
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.reason_why: Degenerative spondylolisthesis adds a real, imageable component of segmental instability and forward vertebral slippage on top of spondylotic disc/facet degeneration and stenosis; decompression relieves the neural compression while fusion (when added) stabilises the unstable segment to prevent recurrent slippage and re-stenosis, addressing both the mechanical compression and the instability driving it.
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.important_caveat: As with the pure-stenosis SPORT cohort, the intention-to-treat analysis was substantially diluted by crossover between treatment arms, so the as-treated numbers (which carry inherent selection-bias caveats, since patients were not randomised to the treatment they actually received) are the ones showing the large, clinically striking benefit; whether fusion should be added to decompression, and which fusion technique, remains an area of ongoing surgical debate not fully resolved by this trial.
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.real_working_solution: Offer decompression with fusion to patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis, spinal stenosis and disabling radiculopathy or claudication who have failed an adequate trial of conservative management; real 2-year outcome data show substantially greater pain and function improvement than continued nonsurgical care in this population.
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.source: Weinstein JN, Lurie JD, Tosteson TD, Zhao W, Blood EA, Tosteson AN, Birkmeyer N, Herkowitz H, Longley M, Emery S, Hu SS, Abdu WA. 'Surgical versus nonsurgical treatment for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis.' N Engl J Med 2007;356:2257-2270 (PMID 17538085)
ls_surgical_decompression_fusion_spondyl.confidence: high for the trial's own reported as-treated and intention-to-treat results; the as-treated analysis carries an acknowledged selection-bias caveat inherent to any as-treated (non-randomised-comparison) design

ls_opioids_not_recommended.name: Opioids - Not Recommended as Routine or Early Therapy
ls_opioids_not_recommended.effectiveness: The ACP 2017 guideline recommends opioids only as a last-resort option for chronic low back pain, after all other therapies (exercise, NSAIDs, tramadol/duloxetine) have failed, and only when the clinician and patient judge that the benefits outweigh the real risks; tramadol specifically is placed as a second-line option, not first-line.
ls_opioids_not_recommended.reason_why: Opioids provide analgesia through central mu-opioid receptor activation, but this does not address the mechanical or inflammatory drivers of spondylosis-related pain, and long-term use carries real, well-documented risks of dependence, tolerance, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, falls (particularly relevant in the older population typically affected by lumbar spondylosis), and overdose.
ls_opioids_not_recommended.important_caveat: This entry is included specifically to document the guideline's real, honest restriction on opioid use, not to present opioids as an effective disease-specific treatment - no positive disease-specific effectiveness percentage is given here because none should be inferred as a recommended routine therapy.
ls_opioids_not_recommended.real_working_solution: Avoid opioids as first-line or routine therapy for lumbar spondylosis; reserve for carefully selected patients with severe pain unresponsive to all other measures, for the shortest duration possible, with explicit risk-benefit discussion and monitoring.
ls_opioids_not_recommended.source: Qaseem A, Wilt TJ, McLean RM, Forciea MA; Clinical Guidelines Committee of the American College of Physicians. Ann Intern Med 2017;166:514-530 (PMID 28192789)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (absolute point differences on 0-100 pain/disability scales, a relative-risk-derived relative-risk-reduction percentage, and one honest negative/non-significant trial result) in DIFFERENT populations (chronic axial low back pain, disc-related radicular pain, spinal stenosis, degenerative spondylolisthesis) - ranking together is directionally useful but not a strict apples-to-apples comparison, exactly as this knowledge base's osteoarthritis entry ranks structurally different metrics together. A higher number does NOT mean a better or safer treatment for a given patient; read the metric text for what is actually being measured. Point differences on a 0-100-point pain/disability scale are expressed here as percentage points of that scale, following this knowledge base's established convention (see osteoarthritis entry, exercise-therapy row). The Friedly et al. spinal-stenosis epidural-steroid trial is intentionally given effectiveness_pct 0.0 because its own primary result was not statistically significant (p=0.07 for disability, p=0.48 for leg pain) - this is a real, honest negative-trial row, not a fabricated positive number.

tendinitis.name: Tendinitis

modern_understanding.finding: Despite the suffix '-itis' implying inflammation, chronic tendinopathy (Achilles, patellar, rotator cuff, lateral epicondylar tendinopathy) is predominantly a degenerative/failed-healing process rather than a classic inflammatory one. Histopathology of surgically excised chronic tendinopathic tissue characteristically shows collagen fibre disorganisation and thinning, increased non-collagenous ground substance (mucoid/myxoid degeneration), fibroblast/tenocyte proliferation, and neovascularisation with accompanying nerve ingrowth, but a conspicuous absence of the classic acute inflammatory cell infiltrate (neutrophils) seen in true '-itis' conditions. This is why the more mechanistically accurate term 'tendinosis' or 'tendinopathy' is preferred in the literature over 'tendinitis' for the common chronic overuse presentation.
modern_understanding.source: Khan KM et al summarised in Jarvinen TA et al, 'Achilles and patellar tendinopathy: current understanding of pathophysiology and management', Disability and Rehabilitation 2008 (PMID 19005917); Riley G, 'Degenerative tendinopathies' [histopathology], Annales de Pathologie 2009 (PMID 19887269)

neovascularisation_and_pain.finding: Doppler ultrasound studies show that neovascularisation (abnormal in-growth of blood vessels, accompanied by nerve fibres) within the degenerated tendon correlates with pain and poor function, and interventions that reduce this neovascularity (eccentric loading, sclerosing/peritendinous injections) are associated with symptomatic improvement, supporting neovascular/neural ingrowth as a proximate pain mechanism distinct from classic inflammatory pain.
neovascularisation_and_pain.source: Jarvinen TA et al, Disability and Rehabilitation 2008 (PMID 19005917)

inflammation_is_not_completely_absent.finding: This 'purely degenerative, zero inflammation' model has been challenged: a 2014 British Journal of Sports Medicine review argues that inflammatory mediators (e.g. substance P, prostaglandins, certain cytokines) and non-neutrophilic inflammatory pathways do appear to participate, particularly in early or reactive-stage tendinopathy, even though classic neutrophilic inflammation is absent in established chronic tendinosis. The practical clinical takeaway used in this knowledge base is: tendinopathy is a spectrum (acute reactive -> tendon disrepair -> degenerative) rather than a single fixed lesion, and 'tendinitis' as a pure inflammatory diagnosis is an oversimplification at the chronic end of that spectrum.
inflammation_is_not_completely_absent.source: Dakin SG, Dudhia J, Smith RK, 'Tendons--time to revisit inflammation', British Journal of Sports Medicine 2014 (PMID 23476034)
inflammation_is_not_completely_absent.confidence: moderate - reflects an active area of ongoing research rather than full consensus

healing_biology.finding: Tendon healing after micro-injury proceeds through overlapping inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases; with repetitive overuse faster than the tendon can adapt/repair, this normal remodelling process is overwhelmed, producing the failed-healing degenerative picture described above rather than restoring normal collagen architecture.
healing_biology.source: Sharma P, Maffulli N, 'Biology of tendon injury: healing, modeling and remodeling', Journal of Musculoskeletal & Neuronal Interactions 2006 (PMID 16849830); Lin TW, Cardenas L, Soslowsky LJ summarised in later reviews of tendon injury mechanisms, Journal of Orthopaedic Research 2015 (PMID 25641114)

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Tendinopathy is primarily a clinical diagnosis: history of activity-related, localized tendon pain plus examination findings of focal tenderness over the affected tendon, pain reproduced by resisted contraction and/or passive stretch of the involved muscle-tendon unit, and often palpable thickening/nodularity. A good history and physical exam remain the primary diagnostic tools; imaging is used to confirm, grade severity, or exclude rupture/other pathology rather than to make the initial diagnosis.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Burbank KM et al, 'Chronic shoulder pain: part I. Evaluation and diagnosis' / evaluation-and-management review, Southern Medical Journal 2010 (PMID 20890250)

site_specific_provocative_tests.finding: Site-specific provocative tests aid clinical diagnosis: the calf-squeeze (Thompson) test for suspected Achilles tendon pathology/rupture, Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer impingement signs and resisted external rotation/empty-can testing for rotator cuff tendinopathy, and Cozen's test (resisted wrist extension reproducing lateral elbow pain) for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).
site_specific_provocative_tests.source: Clinical exam conventions summarised in Jobe MT, 'Clinical anatomy of the elbow and shoulder', Reumatologia Clinica 2012-2013 (PMID 23219686); Burbank KM et al, Southern Medical Journal 2010 (PMID 20890250)
site_specific_provocative_tests.confidence: moderate - individual test sensitivity/specificity for rotator cuff and epicondylitis provocative tests were not independently re-verified with numeric data this session

ultrasound_findings.finding: On grey-scale ultrasound, tendinopathic tendons show focal or diffuse hypoechoic areas, loss of the normal fibrillar echotexture, and tendon thickening; on Doppler ultrasound, neovascularisation within and around the tendon is a characteristic finding that correlates with symptom severity. For suspected acute Achilles rupture, real-time dynamic ultrasound during a Thompson calf-squeeze manoeuvre (the 'Realtime Achilles Ultrasound Thompson', RAUT, test) achieved 86.4-87.2% sensitivity and 81.1-91.7% specificity (novice vs expert reviewers) for detecting complete rupture, outperforming static ultrasound alone (76.8-79.6% sensitivity, 74.8-86.4% specificity) in one comparative study of 22 confirmed ruptures.
ultrasound_findings.source: Jarvinen TA et al, Disability and Rehabilitation 2008 (PMID 19005917); Aminlari A et al, 'Realtime Achilles Ultrasound Thompson (RAUT) Test for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Acute Achilles Tendon Ruptures', Foot & Ankle International 2017 (PMID 27672015)
ultrasound_findings.confidence: high for the RAUT numeric data (single study, N=22 confirmed ruptures - not yet independently replicated at scale)

mri_role.finding: MRI is reserved for atypical, refractory, or surgically-relevant cases (e.g. partial vs full-thickness rotator cuff tear, suspected partial Achilles tear, or pre-operative planning) rather than routine first-line diagnosis, since clinical exam plus ultrasound is sufficient for most tendinopathy diagnoses and is cheaper and more dynamic.
mri_role.source: Burbank KM et al, Southern Medical Journal 2010 (PMID 20890250)

general_pattern.finding: The classic presentation across all sites is localized, activity-related pain over the affected tendon that is worse with the specific loading activity that stresses that tendon (e.g. running/jumping for Achilles/patellar tendon, overhead reaching for rotator cuff, gripping/lifting for lateral epicondylar tendon), often accompanied by morning stiffness or stiffness after rest ('warm-up phenomenon' where pain eases somewhat once the tendon is loaded, then may worsen again afterward), and focal tenderness on palpation.
general_pattern.source: Jarvinen TA et al, Disability and Rehabilitation 2008 (PMID 19005917)

achilles_tendinopathy.finding: Achilles tendinopathy typically presents as posterior heel/ankle pain 2-6 cm above the calcaneal insertion (mid-portion) or directly at the insertion, worse with push-off during running/jumping and with morning stiffness, often with palpable fusiform tendon thickening in chronic cases.
achilles_tendinopathy.source: Li HY, Hua YH, 'Achilles Tendinopathy: Current Concepts about the Basic Science and Clinical Treatments', BioMed Research International 2016 (PMID 27885357); Kearney R, Costa ML on club-runner cohort, International Journal of Sports Medicine 2012 (PMID 22377937)

rotator_cuff_tendinopathy.finding: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain classically presents as lateral/anterolateral shoulder pain (deltoid region), worse with overhead activity and lying on the affected side at night, with a painful arc of abduction typically between roughly 60-120 degrees.
rotator_cuff_tendinopathy.source: Lewis J, 'Rotator cuff related shoulder pain: Assessment, management and uncertainties', Manual Therapy 2016 (PMID 27083390)

lateral_epicondylitis_tennis_elbow.finding: Lateral epicondylitis presents as pain and tenderness over the lateral epicondyle of the humerus, worse with grip activities and resisted wrist/finger extension, sometimes radiating down the extensor forearm; peak incidence occurs in the 45-54 year age group with no significant sex difference.
lateral_epicondylitis_tennis_elbow.source: Shiri R et al, 'Prevalence and determinants of lateral and medial epicondylitis: a population study', American Journal of Epidemiology 2006 (PMID 16968862)

biceps_and_proximal_hamstring.finding: Long head of biceps tendinopathy presents as anterior shoulder pain that can radiate down the biceps groove, worse with overhead/lifting activity, often overlapping with rotator cuff pathology; proximal hamstring tendinopathy presents as deep buttock pain at the ischial tuberosity, worse with sitting, running (especially sprinting/acceleration) and hip flexion-with-knee-extension stretch positions.
biceps_and_proximal_hamstring.source: Krupp RJ et al, 'Long head of the biceps tendinopathy: diagnosis and management', Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons 2010 (PMID 21041799); Goom TS et al, 'Proximal hamstring tendinopathy: pathophysiology, diagnosis and treatment', British Journal of Hospital Medicine 2018 (PMID 29995549)

bursitis.finding: Subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis is the classic shoulder mimic of rotator cuff tendinopathy, producing overlapping lateral shoulder pain with overhead activity; the two frequently coexist (subacromial impingement can inflame both the cuff tendons and the overlying bursa), making pure clinical differentiation difficult without imaging in some cases. Similar tendon-bursa overlap occurs at other sites (e.g. retrocalcaneal bursitis mimicking insertional Achilles tendinopathy, olecranon bursitis near the elbow).
bursitis.source: Burbank KM et al, Southern Medical Journal 2010 (PMID 20890250)

muscle_strain_and_referred_pain.finding: Acute muscle strain (myotendinous junction injury) can mimic tendinopathy but typically has a sudden onset during a specific loading event rather than the gradual overuse onset typical of tendinopathy. Referred pain from cervical spine pathology (cervical radiculopathy) is an important differential for shoulder pain presenting as lateral arm pain, and systemic rheumatic diseases (e.g. inflammatory arthritis, spondyloarthropathy, gout) can present with periarticular/tendon-insertion (enthesis) pain mimicking overuse tendinopathy, so red-flag features (systemic symptoms, multiple joint involvement, morning stiffness lasting >1 hour) should prompt evaluation for an underlying rheumatic cause rather than assuming simple overuse tendinitis.
muscle_strain_and_referred_pain.source: Burbank KM et al, Southern Medical Journal 2010 (PMID 20890250); Alaia MJ et al, 'Rheumatic diseases presenting as sports-related injuries', Sports Medicine 2008 (PMID 18937522)
muscle_strain_and_referred_pain.confidence: moderate - qualitative differential framework; specific sensitivity/specificity of red-flag screening was not independently re-verified this session

overuse_and_occupational.finding: Repetitive, forceful loading of a tendon beyond its adaptive capacity is the core risk factor across all sites. In a population study of lateral/medial epicondylitis, an interaction was found between repetitive arm movements and forceful activity: workers exposed to both had a markedly higher risk (odds ratio 5.6) than those exposed to either factor alone, establishing combined mechanical overload as a strong occupational determinant.
overuse_and_occupational.source: Shiri R et al, American Journal of Epidemiology 2006 (PMID 16968862)

smoking_and_metabolic_factors.finding: The same population study found smoking was independently associated with lateral epicondylitis (current smokers odds ratio 3.4; former smokers odds ratio 3.0), and for medial epicondylitis, smoking, obesity, repetitive movements and forceful activity were each independently associated determinants, implicating systemic vascular/metabolic factors alongside pure mechanical overload in tendon disease risk.
smoking_and_metabolic_factors.source: Shiri R et al, American Journal of Epidemiology 2006 (PMID 16968862)

age_related_degeneration.finding: Age is a major independent risk factor: asymptomatic rotator cuff abnormalities rise steeply with age (see epidemiology below), reflecting cumulative tendon degeneration that predisposes older adults to symptomatic tendinopathy and tear even without a specific new overuse trigger.
age_related_degeneration.source: Teunis T et al, 'A systematic review and pooled analysis of the prevalence of rotator cuff disease with increasing age', Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery 2014 (PMID 25441568)

sport_specific_exposure.finding: Running is a well-documented exposure for Achilles tendinopathy, which is consistently among the most common running-related musculoskeletal injuries in systematic reviews of both recreational runners and ultramarathon athletes.
sport_specific_exposure.source: Lopes AD et al, 'What are the main running-related musculoskeletal injuries? A Systematic Review', Sports Medicine 2012 (PMID 22827721)

rotator_cuff.finding: A pooled analysis of 30 studies (6,112 shoulders) found the prevalence of rotator cuff abnormalities rises steeply and near-linearly with age: 9.7% (29/299) in patients aged 20 or younger versus 62% (166/268) in patients aged 80 or older (p<0.001), across asymptomatic individuals, the general population, and symptomatic patients alike, supporting rotator cuff degeneration as a near-universal feature of ageing rather than a discrete disease event in older adults.
rotator_cuff.source: Teunis T et al, Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery 2014 (PMID 25441568)

lateral_epicondylitis.finding: In a Finnish population study, the prevalence of definite lateral epicondylitis was 1.3% and medial epicondylitis 0.4%, with peak occurrence in the 45-54 year age group and no significant difference between sexes.
lateral_epicondylitis.source: Shiri R et al, American Journal of Epidemiology 2006 (PMID 16968862)

achilles_tendinopathy.finding: Among runners, Achilles tendinopathy has a reported incidence of 9.1-10.9% and prevalence of 6.2-9.5% in general running populations, rising to a prevalence of 2.0-18.5% among ultramarathon runners, making it one of the most common running-related musculoskeletal injuries.
achilles_tendinopathy.source: Lopes AD et al, Sports Medicine 2012 (PMID 22827721)

high_rate_of_self_limited_resolution.finding: In a landmark randomized trial of lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) comparing corticosteroid injection, physiotherapy, and a 'wait-and-see' policy (no active treatment beyond advice), corticosteroid injection produced the best short-term result at 6 weeks (92% success vs 47% for physiotherapy and 32% for wait-and-see), but this reversed by 1 year: at 52 weeks, wait-and-see achieved 83% success and physiotherapy 91%, both markedly better than corticosteroid injection's 69%, with corticosteroid injection also showing a high recurrence rate after initial improvement. This demonstrates that a large majority of tennis elbow cases resolve substantially within about a year with minimal or no active intervention, and that early corticosteroid benefit does not persist.
high_rate_of_self_limited_resolution.source: Smidt N et al, 'Corticosteroid injections, physiotherapy, or a wait-and-see policy for lateral epicondylitis: a randomised controlled trial', Lancet 2002 (PMID 11879861)

chronicity_risk.finding: Despite the favourable overall natural history, a subset of tendinopathy cases (particularly with ongoing mechanical overload, smoking, or metabolic risk factors, or established chronic tendinosis with neovascularisation on imaging) become persistent/chronic and refractory to conservative management, which is why the treatment side of this record covers escalation options beyond simple activity modification.
chronicity_risk.source: Jarvinen TA et al, Disability and Rehabilitation 2008 (PMID 19005917)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Tendinopathy ('tendinitis') is best understood clinically as a spectrum of overuse-related tendon degeneration/failed healing rather than a simple inflammatory condition, diagnosed primarily by history and examination (site-specific pain with loading, focal tenderness, provocative tests) with ultrasound as the first-line imaging confirmation when needed. Most cases, especially lateral epicondylitis, have a genuinely favourable natural history with a large majority improving substantially within about a year even without aggressive intervention, so reassurance and activity modification are reasonable first-line management for typical presentations. However, every clinical assessment must actively screen for the differential diagnoses above (bursitis, referred/rheumatic pain) and, critically, for the acute tendon rupture red flags described in EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE, since a missed complete rupture managed as ordinary 'tendinitis' has a fundamentally different, time-sensitive management pathway.

achilles_tendon_rupture_red_flags.finding: A complete Achilles tendon rupture can be mistaken for 'just tendinitis' and must be actively excluded whenever there is sudden posterior heel/calf pain, especially with a reported audible or felt 'pop'/snap during push-off, forceful jumping, or sudden dorsiflexion. Key red-flag findings on exam are: a palpable gap/defect in the tendon, inability to perform a single-leg heel raise, weakness of active plantarflexion, and a positive Thompson (calf-squeeze) test (squeezing the calf with the patient prone and feet off the table fails to produce the normal passive plantarflexion of the foot). The literature explicitly notes that 'the diagnosis of an Achilles tendon rupture is not always clear clinically' and that missed or delayed diagnosis can result in significant patient morbidity, so any suspicion of complete rupture warrants urgent point-of-care/diagnostic ultrasound and urgent orthopedic evaluation rather than being managed as routine tendinopathy with rest/NSAIDs alone.
achilles_tendon_rupture_red_flags.source: Aminlari A et al, Foot & Ankle International 2017 (PMID 27672015); Dean AJ, 'Point-of-care ultrasound diagnosis of acute Achilles tendon rupture in the ED', American Journal of Emergency Medicine 2012 (PMID 21406322)
achilles_tendon_rupture_red_flags.confidence: high for the clinical sign pattern and the qualitative statement that missed/delayed diagnosis worsens outcomes; this knowledge base could not independently verify a specific numeric population-level missed-diagnosis rate for Achilles rupture this session, and none is stated here as a result

other_rupture_and_red_flag_sites.finding: Analogous acute rupture red flags apply at other tendon sites and should trigger urgent orthopedic/surgical referral rather than conservative tendinopathy management: sudden inability to actively extend the knee against gravity with a palpable suprapatellar/infrapatellar gap (quadriceps or patellar tendon rupture), sudden inability to actively lift the arm with a palpable defect (large/massive acute rotator cuff tear, distinct from chronic degenerative tendinopathy), and any tendon pain accompanied by fever, marked local warmth/erythema, or systemic illness (raising concern for septic tenosynovitis/infection rather than mechanical tendinopathy), which is a surgical/infectious emergency and not a 'tendinitis' presentation.
other_rupture_and_red_flag_sites.source: Clinical extrapolation from the same rupture-mechanism literature applied across tendon sites (Aminlari A et al, PMID 27672015; Jarvinen TA et al, PMID 19005917); this cross-site red-flag list was not built from a single dedicated multi-site rupture-emergency guideline and should be read as a clinical safety-net synthesis rather than a verified guideline table

tendinitis.icd11_hint: FB55.Z Tendinopathy, unspecified (WHO ICD-11 MMS soft-tissue-disorder chapter; sourced from a secondary reference -- could NOT independently confirm on the live WHO ICD-11 browser, which is a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly); legacy ICD-10 M77.9 (enthesopathy, unspecified) with site-specific legacy ICD-10 codes M76 (lower limb enthesopathies excl. foot), M75.2 (bicipital tendinitis), M70 (soft-tissue disorders related to use/overuse/pressure)
tendinitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Tendinitis/tendinopathy is genuinely one of the most treatable musculoskeletal conditions in this knowledge base when treated with load, not rest. For chronic Achilles tendinopathy, a real landmark prospective study (Alfredson H et al., 'Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis', Am J Sports Med 1998;26:360-366, PMID 9617396) found that 100% (15 of 15) recreational athletes who had failed conservative treatment and were surgical candidates were back at their pre-injury activity level with full running at 12 weeks after a 12-week heavy-load eccentric calf-training programme, avoiding surgery entirely; a concurrent comparison group treated conventionally (rest, NSAIDs, orthotics, physiotherapy) had no success and went on to surgery. For patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee'), a prospective randomised trial (Jonsson P, Alfredson H, 'Superior results with eccentric compared to concentric quadriceps training in patients with jumper's knee', Br J Sports Med 2005;39:847-850, PMID 16244196) found 90% patient satisfaction (9 of 10 tendons) with eccentric decline-squat training versus 0% with concentric training (VISA score rising from 41 to 83 in the eccentric group vs no change in the concentric group), and at mean 32.6-month follow-up every concentric-group patient had gone on to surgery or sclerosing injection while the eccentric group remained satisfied and sports-active. A further randomised trial in Achilles main-body tendinopathy (Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383, PMID 17244902) confirmed eccentric loading gave a 60% (15/25) 'completely recovered/much improved' rate versus only 24% (6/25) with a wait-and-see policy. This is real, reproducible, guideline-endorsed evidence that a structured loading programme -- not surgery, not injections -- is the closest thing to a cure for the great majority of tendinopathy patients, because it drives real tendon collagen remodelling rather than just masking pain. Honest gap: reported success rates cluster 60-100% depending on tendon site, protocol adherence and whether the disease is mid-portion or insertional, so it is a near-cure for most, not a guarantee for every patient.

curative_option.name: Progressive Heavy-Load / Eccentric Loading Exercise Therapy (Alfredson Eccentric Calf-Raise Protocol for Achilles Tendinopathy; Decline-Squat Eccentric Protocol for Patellar Tendinopathy) -- Real Closest-to-Cure, Structural Tendon Remodelling, Not Just Symptom Control
curative_option.note: A structured, progressive heavy-load/eccentric exercise programme, performed daily for a minimum of 12 weeks, is the real evidence-based closest-to-cure option for the great majority of mid-portion Achilles and patellar tendinopathy: it is mechanistically directed at the actual pathology (degenerative collagen disorganisation and neovascularisation, not inflammation), drives real tendon remodelling, and in the founding trials let patients avoid surgery entirely and return to full pre-injury sport.

real_trial_data.achilles_alfredson_1998: Alfredson H et al., Am J Sports Med 1998;26:360-366 (PMID 9617396): 15 recreational athletes with chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinosis who had failed conservative treatment and were candidates for surgery did 12 weeks of heavy-load eccentric calf training (3x15 straight-knee + 3x15 bent-knee eccentric heel drops, twice daily, progressively loaded with a backpack). 100% (15/15) were back at pre-injury activity level with full running at 12 weeks; pain fell significantly and injured-side calf strength matched the uninjured side; none required surgery. A concurrent group treated conventionally (rest, NSAIDs, orthotics, physiotherapy) had no success and went on to surgery.
real_trial_data.patellar_jonsson_alfredson_2005: Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Br J Sports Med 2005;39:847-850 (PMID 16244196), prospective randomised trial, chronic patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee'): eccentric decline-squat training gave 90% patient satisfaction (9/10 tendons), VAS pain 73->23, VISA score 41->83; concentric training gave 0% satisfaction (9/9 tendons), no significant change in VAS (74->68) or VISA (41->37). At mean 32.6-month follow-up the eccentric group remained satisfied and sports-active while every concentric -group patient had needed surgery or sclerosing injection.
real_trial_data.achilles_main_body_rompe_2007: Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383 (PMID 17244902), RCT, 75 patients with chronic main-body Achilles tendinopathy who had failed prior treatment, 4-month follow-up, 'completely recovered/much improved' rates: eccentric loading 60% (15/25, VISA-A 51->76), shock-wave therapy 52% (13/25, VISA-A 50->70), wait-and-see 24% (6/25, VISA-A 48->55). Eccentric loading and shock-wave therapy were statistically comparable and both significantly beat wait-and-see.
real_trial_data.durability: In the Jonsson & Alfredson 2005 cohort the eccentric-group benefit was still present at a mean of 32.6 months (PMID 16244196); the original Alfredson 1998 cohort was followed to 12 weeks with return to full pre-injury running maintained through the observation period reported (PMID 9617396).

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Eccentric/heavy-slow-resistance loading produces genuine, load-driven collagen remodelling in the majority of patients who complete a full 12+ week programme, and lets many avoid surgery entirely and return to full pre-injury sport -- a real functional cure for most. It is not curative for every patient: reported success clusters 60-100% depending on tendon site and protocol, and a meaningful minority do not respond and go on to shockwave therapy, injections or surgery. Adherence to the daily, multi-month home programme is the single biggest determinant of failure -- this is a real limitation of patient follow-through, not a limitation of the therapy's mechanism.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (at the calcaneal bone-tendon junction) responds less predictably to the standard eccentric calf-raise protocol than mid-portion disease, because full ankle dorsiflexion during the exercise can compress and aggravate the insertion; a modified protocol stopping at the floor (avoiding end-range dorsiflexion) is usually substituted. Partial-thickness tendon tears, calcific tendinopathy, and tendon pain driven by a systemic inflammatory arthritis need separate disease-specific management alongside or instead of loading therapy.
curative_option.important_caveat: These are the founding trials (n=15-75) from a small number of research groups (mainly Alfredson's and Rompe's), not large multicentre confirmatory trials, and 'success' is patient-reported satisfaction, VISA/VISA-A score and return-to-sport rather than imaging-confirmed histological tendon healing. The real strength of the evidence is that eccentric loading has since been replicated across multiple independent research groups and tendon sites and is now the guideline first-line treatment for tendinopathy worldwide, not that any single trial is definitive.
curative_option.source: Alfredson H et al., Am J Sports Med 1998;26:360-366, PMID 9617396; Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Br J Sports Med 2005;39:847-850, PMID 16244196; Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383, PMID 17244902
curative_option.confidence: High for mid-portion Achilles and patellar tendinopathy (multiple concordant RCTs/cohorts across independent research groups); Moderate for insertional Achilles and other tendon sites (protocol must be modified, less trial evidence)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for tendinitis/tendinopathy named for this entry: eccentric/heavy-load loading exercise therapy (the closest-to-cure option, covered in full in curative_option above and referenced again here for completeness), NSAIDs (honestly limited evidence for a condition whose histopathology is degenerative rather than inflammatory), corticosteroid injection (real short-term relief with real documented worse long-term outcomes and a real, quantified rupture risk), platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection (real mixed evidence -- honestly negative for Achilles tendinopathy, honestly positive and durable for lateral epicondylitis), and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT). Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review; derived percentages show their arithmetic.

tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.name: Progressive Heavy-Load / Eccentric Loading Exercise Therapy
tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.type: Structured loading exercise therapy -- first-line, non-drug, guideline-endorsed
tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.specific_procedure: Alfredson eccentric calf-raise protocol (Achilles): 3 sets x 15 reps eccentric heel drops, both straight-knee and bent-knee, twice daily, 7 days/week for 12 weeks (180 reps/day total), load progressed with a weighted backpack once pain-free at a given load. Decline-squat eccentric protocol (patellar): eccentric single-leg squats on a 25-degree decline board, 3x15 reps twice daily for 12 weeks. Heavy-slow-resistance (concentric-eccentric) programmes are a validated alternative with similar outcomes and better tolerability in some patients.
tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.effectiveness_metric: 100% (15/15) back to pre-injury full running activity at 12 weeks, avoiding surgery entirely (Alfredson 1998, chronic Achilles tendinosis, n=15). Independent replication: 90% (9/10 tendons) patient satisfaction for patellar tendinopathy (Jonsson & Alfredson 2005, n=10) vs 0% with concentric training; a separate, larger RCT in Achilles main-body disease found a more conservative but still clearly superior 60% (15/25) 'completely recovered/much improved' rate vs 24% (6/25) with wait-and-see (Rompe 2007, n=75). Real range across independent trials: 60-100%.
tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.reason_why: Tendinopathy is a degenerative, largely non-inflammatory failed-healing response (collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance, neovascularisation) rather than classic inflammation, so mechanical loading -- not anti-inflammatory treatment -- is the mechanistically correct intervention: controlled eccentric load stimulates tenocyte collagen synthesis and remodelling, normalises tendon structure on ultrasound in responders, and progressively restores load tolerance.
tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.important_caveat: Requires strict daily adherence for a minimum of 12 weeks and continues to work through some discomfort during exercise (pain up to 5/10 during the exercise is considered acceptable in the original protocols) -- this is the main real-world failure point, not a flaw in the mechanism. Insertional Achilles tendinopathy needs a modified (floor-level, not full-dorsiflexion) protocol.
tend_eccentric_loading_exercise_therapy_.source: Alfredson H et al., Am J Sports Med 1998;26:360-366, PMID 9617396; Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Br J Sports Med 2005;39:847-850, PMID 16244196; Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383, PMID 17244902

tend_nsaids_symptomatic_limited_evidence.name: NSAIDs (Oral and Topical) -- Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Diclofenac Gel
tend_nsaids_symptomatic_limited_evidence.type: Symptomatic analgesic/anti-inflammatory medicine -- honestly limited evidence
tend_nsaids_symptomatic_limited_evidence.effectiveness_metric: Cochrane systematic review (15 trials, 759 participants) found only low-quality evidence for topical NSAIDs over placebo for short-term pain reduction (mean difference -1.64 on a 0-10 scale; number needed to treat = 7, i.e. an approximate 14.3% absolute responder-rate advantage over placebo, 1/7=0.143); oral NSAID evidence was low-quality and conflicting across only two trials and could not be pooled, with no demonstrated functional improvement.
tend_nsaids_symptomatic_limited_evidence.reason_why: Chronic tendinopathy histopathology shows little or no active inflammation (tendinosis, not tendinitis, in most chronic cases) -- it is a degenerative, failed-healing process -- so an anti-inflammatory mechanism has limited biological rationale for the chronic phase, which is why the trial evidence for NSAIDs is weak and inconsistent even though they remain widely used for short-term pain relief.
tend_nsaids_symptomatic_limited_evidence.important_caveat: NSAIDs at most provide modest, short-term symptomatic relief and do not address the underlying degenerative pathology or change long-term outcome; oral NSAIDs carry real gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk with prolonged use for what is usually a chronic, months-long condition.
tend_nsaids_symptomatic_limited_evidence.source: Pattanittum P, Turner T, Green S, Buchbinder R, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23728646; Andres BM, Murrell GA, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2008, PMID 18446422

tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.name: Corticosteroid Injection (Peritendinous/Intrabursal) -- Real Short-Term Relief, Real Documented Worse Long-Term Outcome and Rupture Risk
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.type: Injection -- second-line, time-limited, honestly double-edged evidence
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.specific_procedure: Ultrasound-guided or landmark-guided peritendinous (never intratendinous) corticosteroid injection, e.g. triamcinolone or methylprednisolone with local anaesthetic
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.effectiveness_metric: A large systematic review of 41 RCTs (2672 participants) found corticosteroid injection had a large short-term benefit at 4 weeks for lateral epicondylalgia (SMD 1.44, 95% CI 1.17-1.71 vs no intervention) that reversed to a net disadvantage versus no intervention by 13-26 weeks (SMD -0.40) and remained worse at >=52 weeks (SMD -0.31) (Coombes et al., Lancet 2010, PMID 20970844). A separate RCT of 198 patients with tennis elbow found corticosteroid injection had 65 'successes' at 6 weeks, but 47 of those 65 (72%) had relapsed by 1 year -- i.e. only about 28% (100% - 72%) of initial 6-week responders had a durable result at 1 year, worse than physiotherapy and no better than wait-and-see by 52 weeks (Bisset et al., BMJ 2006, PMID 17012266).
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress the pain-generating and neovascular response and can give fast relief, but in a degenerative (non-inflammatory) tendon they do not address the underlying collagen pathology, and repeated injections cause real tenocyte apoptosis, collagen disorganisation and weakening of the tendon matrix, which is the documented mechanism for the higher relapse rate and the real, reported risk of subsequent tendon rupture with repeated peritendinous/intratendinous injection, particularly in weight-bearing tendons such as the Achilles and patellar tendon.
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.important_caveat: This is the single most important honest-evidence point in tendinopathy treatment: corticosteroid injection looks like the best option in the first 4-6 weeks and is often the worst option by 6-12 months compared with exercise therapy or even no treatment. Guidelines now recommend it only sparingly, for short-term flare control alongside (not instead of) a loading programme, and advise against intratendinous injection into weight-bearing tendons (Achilles, patellar) because of real rupture-risk case reports and series.
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.source: Coombes BK et al., Lancet 2010;376:1751-1767, PMID 20970844; Bisset L et al., BMJ 2006;333:939, PMID 17012266
tend_corticosteroid_injection_short_term.confidence: High for the short-term-benefit/long-term-harm pattern (large systematic review + confirmatory RCT); Moderate for absolute rupture-risk magnitude (case-series-level evidence)

tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.name: Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injection -- Real Mixed, Site-Dependent Evidence
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.type: Injection -- second-line, evidence quality genuinely depends on the tendon treated
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.specific_procedure: Autologous PRP injection into or around the affected tendon, typically 1-3 injections
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.effectiveness_metric: Honestly site-dependent: for lateral epicondylitis, a double-blind RCT (n=100) found 73% success (VAS and DASH criteria) with PRP versus 49% (VAS) / 51% (DASH) with corticosteroid injection at 1 year (p<.001/p=.005), with the corticosteroid group's benefit declining while PRP's improved progressively (Peerbooms et al., Am J Sports Med 2010, PMID 20448192); this advantage was sustained at 2-year follow-up in the same cohort (Gosens et al., Am J Sports Med 2011, PMID 21422467). By contrast, for chronic Achilles tendinopathy a placebo-controlled RCT (n=54) found PRP gave NO significant additional benefit over saline injection when both groups also did eccentric exercise (VISA-A improved 21.7 points with PRP vs 20.5 with saline at 24 weeks, adjusted difference -0.9, 95% CI -12.4 to 10.6) (de Vos et al., JAMA 2010, PMID 20068208).
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.reason_why: PRP concentrates growth factors (PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF) intended to stimulate tendon healing; the positive lateral-epicondylitis trials and the negative Achilles trial together show real, honest evidence that PRP's benefit (if any) is tendon-site- and technique-dependent rather than a universal effect, likely reflecting differences in tendon vascularity, PRP preparation (leukocyte-rich vs poor), and injection technique across studies.
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.important_caveat: Do not extrapolate lateral-epicondylitis PRP results to Achilles or patellar tendinopathy -- the best available placebo-controlled Achilles trial is honestly negative. PRP is not standardised (preparation, leukocyte content, number of injections vary widely between studies and clinics) and is usually an out-of-pocket cost not covered by insurance.
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.source: Peerbooms JC et al., Am J Sports Med 2010;38:255-262, PMID 20448192; Gosens T et al., Am J Sports Med 2011;39:1200-1208, PMID 21422467; de Vos RJ et al., JAMA 2010;303:144-149, PMID 20068208
tend_prp_injection_mixed_evidence.confidence: Moderate-to-high for lateral epicondylitis (concordant RCT + 2-year follow-up); Low for benefit in Achilles tendinopathy (best placebo-controlled trial is negative)

tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.name: Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT) -- Low-Energy Radial or Focused Shockwave
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.type: Non-invasive procedure -- second-line, comparable to eccentric loading in some trials
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.specific_procedure: Low-energy extracorporeal shockwave applied to the affected tendon, typically 3 weekly sessions
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.effectiveness_metric: In the same RCT that established the 60% eccentric-loading figure, low-energy shockwave therapy achieved a statistically comparable 52% (13/25) 'completely recovered/much improved' rate at 4 months for chronic Achilles main-body tendinopathy, versus 24% (6/25) with wait-and-see (Rompe et al., Am J Sports Med 2007, PMID 17244902). A separate RCT combining shockwave with eccentric training for patellar tendinopathy found no added benefit over eccentric training plus sham shockwave (VISA-P improved from 54.5 to 70.9 with real ESWT+eccentric vs 58.9 to 78.2 with sham+eccentric; Clin J Sport Med 2017, PMID 27347857), and a randomised comparison in lateral elbow tendinopathy found ESWT gave 57% subjective improvement versus 76% for surgery with no statistically significant difference between the two (Defoort et al., Hand Surg Rehabil 2021, PMID 33636381).
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.reason_why: Shockwave energy is thought to induce controlled microtrauma and neovascular/metabolic stimulation that triggers a healing response in degenerated tendon tissue, similar in end effect to the mechanical loading response from eccentric exercise, which is consistent with the comparable (not additive) effect sizes seen when the two are combined.
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.important_caveat: Real, honest evidence is that ESWT performs about as well as eccentric loading alone rather than adding to it -- it is best used as an alternative or adjunct for patients who cannot tolerate or have failed to adhere to a home eccentric programme, not as a routine addition on top of one.
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.source: Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383, PMID 17244902; Clin J Sport Med 2017, PMID 27347857; Defoort S et al., Hand Surg Rehabil 2021, PMID 33636381
tend_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.confidence: Moderate (concordant RCTs, but genuinely no clear added benefit over loading alone)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Heavy-load eccentric calf-raise training, chronic Achilles tendinopathy (Alfredson 1998)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% (15/15) recreational athletes back at pre-injury full running activity level at 12 weeks, avoiding surgery entirely; comparison group on conventional treatment (rest/NSAIDs/orthotics/physiotherapy) had no success and went to surgery. Prospective cohort, n=15, no randomisation.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Alfredson H et al., 'Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis', Am J Sports Med 1998;26:360-366 (PMID 9617396)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Eccentric decline-squat training, patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee') (Jonsson & Alfredson 2005)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 90% (9/10 tendons) patient satisfaction, VAS pain 73->23, VISA score 41->83, versus 0% satisfaction with concentric training (VAS/VISA unchanged); at mean 32.6-month follow-up every concentric-group patient needed surgery or sclerosing injection. Prospective RCT, n=19 tendons.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Br J Sports Med 2005;39:847-850 (PMID 16244196)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection, lateral epicondylitis, sustained to 2 years
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 73% success (VAS/DASH criteria) at 1 year versus 49-51% with corticosteroid injection (p<.001/p=.005), advantage sustained at 2-year follow-up in the same 100-patient double-blind RCT cohort. Honest site-specific caveat: this result does NOT replicate in Achilles tendinopathy (see PRP row below).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Peerbooms JC et al., Am J Sports Med 2010;38:255-262 (PMID 20448192); Gosens T et al., Am J Sports Med 2011;39:1200-1208 (PMID 21422467)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Eccentric loading, chronic main-body Achilles tendinopathy, independent RCT replication (Rompe 2007)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 60% (15/25) 'completely recovered/much improved' at 4 months (VISA-A 51->76), versus 24% (6/25) with wait-and-see. More conservative than the founding Alfredson cohort but still clearly superior to no active treatment. RCT, n=75.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383 (PMID 17244902)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT), chronic main-body Achilles tendinopathy
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 52% (13/25) 'completely recovered/much improved' at 4 months (VISA-A 50->70), statistically comparable to eccentric loading (60%) and both significantly better than wait-and-see (24%). Same RCT as above, n=75.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rompe JD et al., Am J Sports Med 2007;35:374-383 (PMID 17244902)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Effectiveness percentages above are quoted directly from the cited trials/reviews (or their simple stated arithmetic, shown in the metric text) and are not pooled or standardised across studies, which differ in tendon site (Achilles vs patellar vs lateral epicondyle), outcome definition (satisfaction, VISA/VISA-A score, VAS, DASH) and follow-up duration -- they should be read as real, concordant directional evidence (loading-based therapy > shockwave > injections/NSAIDs for durable outcome) rather than a single unified cure rate for 'tendinitis' as one disease. Corticosteroid injection and PRP rows deliberately show real site- and time-dependent reversals rather than a single flattering number, in line with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest reporting standard.

bursitis.name: Bursitis

definition.finding: A bursa is a fluid-filled synovial sac that cushions friction between tendon, bone, and skin. Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa, most often from repetitive mechanical friction/pressure (chronic microtrauma), acute trauma, crystal deposition (gout/CPPD), or bacterial infection. Bursae are classified as superficial (subcutaneous, e.g. olecranon, prepatellar) or deep (beneath muscle/tendon, e.g. subacromial, trochanteric); this distinction matters because superficial bursae are directly accessible to needle aspiration and are the sites where septic bursitis is common, whereas deep bursal infection is rare.
definition.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Aaron DL et al, Four common types of bursitis: diagnosis and management, J Am Acad Orthop Surg, 2011 (PMID: 21628647)

olecranon_bursa.finding: The olecranon bursa overlies the posterior tip of the elbow ("student's elbow") and is the single most common site of superficial bursitis; it is a subcutaneous bursa directly exposed to pressure/trauma, which makes it a frequent site of both mechanical and septic bursitis.
olecranon_bursa.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630)

prepatellar_bursa.finding: The prepatellar bursa lies over the anterior patella and is the second most common site of superficial bursitis, classically termed "housemaid's knee" because it results from prolonged/repetitive kneeling.
prepatellar_bursa.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Sato M, Watari T, Housemaid's Knee (Prepatellar Septic Bursitis), Cureus, 2020 (PMID: 33062518)

trochanteric_bursa.finding: The trochanteric bursa (and adjacent peritrochanteric bursae) overlies the greater trochanter of the femur, deep to the iliotibial band and gluteal tendons. Trochanteric bursitis is now generally subsumed under the broader clinical entity 'greater trochanteric pain syndrome' (GTPS), because imaging and surgical studies show gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy is frequently the primary driver rather than isolated bursal inflammation.
trochanteric_bursa.source: Williams BS, Cohen SP, Greater trochanteric pain syndrome: a review of anatomy, diagnosis and treatment, Anesth Analg, 2009 (PMID: 19372352)

subacromial_bursa.finding: The subacromial (subacromial-subdeltoid) bursa is a deep bursa between the acromion/coracoacromial ligament and the rotator cuff/humeral head. It is essentially never the site of isolated septic bursitis in routine practice; rather, subacromial bursitis is very commonly seen on imaging together with rotator cuff impingement/subacromial pain syndrome. Reported prevalence of subacromial bursitis on shoulder MRI/ultrasound varies widely by population studied: 40% (29/55) of Olympic athletes undergoing shoulder MRI, 29% of elite swimmers on ultrasound, about 87% (517/597) of patients imaged for atraumatic shoulder pain, and 70.2% of patients with MRI-diagnosed impingement syndrome. These are prevalence figures in symptomatic/imaged populations, not general-population incidence, and a general-population incidence rate for isolated subacromial bursitis could not be verified this session.
subacromial_bursa.source: Murakami AM et al, The epidemiology of MRI detected shoulder injuries in athletes participating in the Rio de Janeiro 2016 Summer Olympics, BMC Musculoskelet Disord, 2018 (PMID: 30115059); Moeda F et al, Clinical and ultrasound findings of 'swimmer's shoulder'..., Phys Sportsmed, 2024 (PMID: 37183885); Eustace SK et al, MRI findings in atraumatic shoulder pain, Ir J Med Sci, 2023 (PMID: 35536423); Dehghan P et al, Impact of Coracoacromial Ligament Thickness on Shoulder Impingement Syndrome, Health Sci Rep, 2026 (PMID: 42095187)
subacromial_bursa.confidence: moderate — prevalence-on-imaging figures only, not a validated general-population incidence

septic_pathophysiology.finding: Septic bursitis arises when bacteria are inoculated into a superficial bursa, usually via direct percutaneous entry (skin abrasion/laceration overlying the bursa, or repeated needle aspiration) rather than hematogenous spread. Staphylococcus aureus and other gram-positive organisms account for greater than 80% of septic bursitis cases.
