septic_pathophysiology.source: Zimmermann B 3rd, Mikolich DJ, Ho G Jr, Septic bursitis, Semin Arthritis Rheum, 1995 (PMID: 7667644); Lormeau C et al, Management of septic bursitis, Joint Bone Spine, 2019 (PMID: 31615686)

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Diagnosis of bursitis is primarily clinical: focal, well-localized swelling directly over a known bursa (as opposed to diffuse joint swelling), with variable tenderness and pain depending on acute versus chronic/traumatic versus inflammatory versus septic etiology. A skin-temperature differential of more than 2.2°C between the affected bursa and the same contralateral site had a reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 94% for septic bursitis in the source reviewed.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630)
clinical_diagnosis.confidence: high for the clinical approach; the 100%/94% temperature-differential figure is as reported in this single review and was not independently re-verified against its primary source this session

ultrasound_findings.finding: Ultrasonography is an effective, low-cost first-line imaging tool for superficial bursitis: it demonstrates bursal distension with anechoic-to-complex/echogenic fluid, wall thickening, and (in inflammatory/septic bursitis) increased vascularity on color/power Doppler. Ultrasound is specifically useful to distinguish bursitis from cellulitis and from an underlying joint effusion, and a negative Doppler signal strongly decreases the likelihood of active inflammatory bursitis. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is also used both diagnostically and therapeutically.
ultrasound_findings.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Blankstein A et al, Ultrasonographic findings in patients with olecranon bursitis, Ultraschall Med, 2006 (PMID: 16596513); Iagnocco A et al, Unilateral painful, swollen and erythematosus knee (ultrasound-guided diagnosis of septic prepatellar bursitis), Med Ultrason, 2012 (PMID: 22957333)

aspiration_and_fluid_analysis.finding: When septic bursitis is suspected, bursal fluid should be aspirated and sent for Gram stain, culture, crystal analysis, glucose level, and cell count with differential. As reported in the source reviewed: septic bursal fluid white cell counts range from about 1,000 to 450,000/mcL versus generally under 20,000/mcL in non-septic bursitis, with septic fluid typically cloudy/purulent (versus clear-to-serosanguineous), Gram stain and culture more often positive, and a fluid-to-serum glucose ratio under 0.5 (versus 0.5 or higher in non-septic fluid). Because the septic and non-septic white-cell-count ranges overlap substantially, white cell count alone cannot reliably rule septic bursitis in or out — Gram stain, culture, and the overall clinical picture must be combined with the cell count.
aspiration_and_fluid_analysis.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630)
aspiration_and_fluid_analysis.confidence: high for the need for Gram stain/culture/glucose/cell count; the specific numeric cutoffs are as reported in this single review and were not cross-verified against an independent primary source this session

general.finding: Focal swelling directly over the affected bursa is the hallmark sign. Chronic/mechanical bursitis often causes minimal or no pain despite visible swelling, whereas acute, traumatic, crystal-induced, or septic bursitis typically causes significant pain, point tenderness, warmth, and decreased range of motion of the adjacent joint.
general.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630)

olecranon_and_prepatellar.finding: Olecranon bursitis presents as a discrete, often fluctuant swelling at the tip of the elbow ("student's elbow"); prepatellar bursitis presents as swelling over the front of the kneecap ("housemaid's knee"). Both can occur with or without associated pain depending on chronicity, and both are the two most common sites where septic superficial bursitis is diagnosed.
olecranon_and_prepatellar.source: Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Sato M, Watari T, Cureus, 2020 (PMID: 33062518)

trochanteric.finding: Trochanteric bursitis/greater trochanteric pain syndrome presents as chronic lateral hip pain centered over the greater trochanter, frequently worse when lying on the affected side, with prolonged sitting, or with walking/stair climbing.
trochanteric.source: Williams BS, Cohen SP, Greater trochanteric pain syndrome: a review of anatomy, diagnosis and treatment, Anesth Analg, 2009 (PMID: 19372352)

subacromial.finding: Subacromial bursitis presents as anterior/lateral shoulder pain, typically occurring together with the clinical picture of rotator cuff-related shoulder pain/impingement rather than as an isolated syndrome; it is commonly identified on imaging obtained for atraumatic shoulder pain or overhead-athlete shoulder pain.
subacromial.source: Eustace SK et al, MRI findings in atraumatic shoulder pain, Ir J Med Sci, 2023 (PMID: 35536423); Moeda F et al, Phys Sportsmed, 2024 (PMID: 37183885)
subacromial.confidence: moderate — inferred from imaging-cohort studies rather than a dedicated symptom-description primary source

septic_bursitis.finding: Features favoring septic over non-septic (aseptic/mechanical/inflammatory) bursitis include fever, marked local warmth, surrounding cellulitis/erythema extending beyond the bursa margin, immunocompromised state, and a history of recent skin trauma, laceration, or prior bursal aspiration/injection at the site. Staphylococcus aureus and other gram-positive organisms cause greater than 80% of septic bursitis.
septic_bursitis.source: Khodaee M, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Zimmermann B 3rd et al, Semin Arthritis Rheum, 1995 (PMID: 7667644); Lormeau C et al, Joint Bone Spine, 2019 (PMID: 31615686)

tendinitis.finding: Tendinitis/tendinopathy adjacent to a bursa can mimic or coexist with bursitis (e.g., subacromial bursitis with rotator cuff tendinopathy, or trochanteric bursitis with gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy in GTPS); tenderness in tendinitis tends to localize along the tendon course and is reproduced by resisted contraction of that tendon's muscle, whereas bursitis tenderness is more focal over the bursa itself. In GTPS specifically, gluteal tendinopathy is frequently the primary pathology rather than the bursa.
tendinitis.source: Williams BS, Cohen SP, Anesth Analg, 2009 (PMID: 19372352); Eustace SK et al, Ir J Med Sci, 2023 (PMID: 35536423)

cellulitis.finding: Cellulitis produces diffuse, poorly-marginated skin erythema, warmth, and edema without a discrete fluctuant bursal collection; ultrasonography helps differentiate the two by showing (or not showing) a discrete distended bursal fluid collection, which is absent in isolated cellulitis. Cellulitis overlying a bursa can also coexist with, or progress to, septic bursitis.

occupational_and_mechanical.finding: Chronic microtrauma from repetitive pressure/friction is the most common cause of superficial bursitis. Documented occupational associations include: olecranon bursitis in miners, students (desk-leaning), plumbers, and heating/air-conditioning technicians; prepatellar bursitis in coal miners, carpet layers, housemaids, plumbers, concrete finishers, roofers, and wrestlers (repetitive kneeling or friction). In a case series of septic bursitis specifically, occupational pressure on the bursa was identified as a contributing factor in 51% of Staphylococcus aureus cases and antecedent local trauma in 23%.
occupational_and_mechanical.source: Khodaee M, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Cea-Pereiro JC et al, A comparison between septic bursitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus and those caused by other organisms, Clin Rheumatol, 2001 (PMID: 11254233)

medical_and_host_factors.finding: Up to half of septic bursitis cases occur in patients with a chronic systemic condition such as diabetes mellitus or chronic kidney disease. Alcoholism was identified as a contributing factor in 13% of a Staphylococcus aureus septic bursitis series. Patients on hemodialysis via an arteriovenous fistula in the arm are at markedly increased risk: as many as 7% develop olecranon bursitis in the fistula-bearing arm.
medical_and_host_factors.source: Khodaee M, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Cea-Pereiro JC et al, Clin Rheumatol, 2001 (PMID: 11254233)

sex_and_age_trochanteric.finding: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome shows a strong female predominance. In a US active-duty military population, women had an adjusted incidence rate ratio of 5.03 versus men, and age 40 or older carried an adjusted incidence rate ratio of 2.81 versus younger service members. Septic bursitis caused by S. aureus, by contrast, was male-predominant (91% male) in a hospital case series, with a mean age of 50 years and a summer seasonal pattern.
sex_and_age_trochanteric.source: Blank E et al, Incidence of greater trochanteric pain syndrome in active duty US military servicemembers, Orthopedics, 2012 (PMID: 22784894); Cea-Pereiro JC et al, Clin Rheumatol, 2001 (PMID: 11254233)

superficial_bursitis_sites.finding: Among superficial bursitis presentations, the olecranon bursa is the most commonly affected site, followed by the prepatellar bursa; the superficial infrapatellar/pretibial and subcutaneous calcaneal bursae are affected less frequently.

greater_trochanteric_pain_syndrome.finding: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome has a reported incidence of approximately 1.8 per 1,000 person-years in the general population (higher in women and in patients with certain comorbidities), and 2.03 per 1,000 person-years in a US active-duty military cohort.
greater_trochanteric_pain_syndrome.source: Williams BS, Cohen SP, Anesth Analg, 2009 (PMID: 19372352); Blank E et al, Orthopedics, 2012 (PMID: 22784894)

subacromial_bursitis_prevalence_note.finding: No general-population incidence figure for isolated subacromial bursitis could be verified this session. Available data are imaging-prevalence figures in symptomatic or athletic cohorts (29-87% depending on the population studied), reflecting how often subacromial bursitis is seen alongside rotator cuff/impingement pathology rather than the incidence of subacromial bursitis as a standalone diagnosis in the general population.

natural_history.finding: Non-septic (mechanical/traumatic/chronic) superficial bursitis is generally described in the reviewed literature as responding to conservative management — activity modification, ice, and NSAIDs — in the large majority of cases, with corticosteroid injection reserved for cases not settling with conservative measures and surgery reserved for recalcitrant or recurrent cases. A specific numeric spontaneous-resolution percentage (e.g., 'X% resolve without treatment by Y weeks') could not be verified against a primary source this session and is therefore not stated as a number here. Septic bursitis, in contrast, does not follow this self-limited course and requires antibiotics +/- aspiration/drainage; without adequate treatment it can progress to abscess, sinus tract formation, or (rarely) bacteremia.
natural_history.source: Aaron DL et al, J Am Acad Orthop Surg, 2011 (PMID: 21628647); Khodaee M, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Zimmermann B 3rd et al, Semin Arthritis Rheum, 1995 (PMID: 7667644)
natural_history.confidence: moderate — qualitative claim well supported; no verified numeric resolution rate found this session, stated explicitly as not verified rather than invented

clinical_takeaway.finding: Bursitis is diagnosed clinically as focal swelling over a named bursa. The single highest-yield diagnostic branch point is distinguishing septic from non-septic bursitis, because the two require completely different management: non-septic bursitis is managed conservatively (rest, ice, NSAIDs, occasionally corticosteroid injection), while septic bursitis (over 80% Staphylococcus aureus) requires prompt aspiration for Gram stain/culture/cell count and empiric antibiotics, sometimes with hospitalization and surgical drainage. Ultrasound and bursal fluid analysis (cell count, glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture) together are the tools used to make this distinction; no single fluid white-cell-count cutoff is fully reliable on its own.
clinical_takeaway.source: Khodaee M, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630); Zimmermann B 3rd et al, Semin Arthritis Rheum, 1995 (PMID: 7667644); Lormeau C et al, Joint Bone Spine, 2019 (PMID: 31615686); Aaron DL et al, J Am Acad Orthop Surg, 2011 (PMID: 21628647)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: SEPTIC BURSITIS IS A DISTINCT URGENT DIAGNOSIS, NOT ROUTINE BURSITIS MANAGEMENT. Any bursitis with fever, marked local warmth, surrounding erythema/cellulitis, an immunocompromised host, or a history of recent skin breach/trauma/prior aspiration over the bursa must be treated as possibly septic until proven otherwise: perform prompt bursal aspiration for Gram stain, culture, cell count, and glucose ratio BEFORE starting corticosteroid injection (which is contraindicated if infection is not excluded), and start empiric antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus (the cause of over 80% of septic bursitis) while awaiting culture results. A skin-temperature differential of more than 2.2°C between the affected bursa and the equivalent contralateral site has been reported with 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for septic bursitis in the source reviewed, and can support a rapid bedside decision to aspirate. Hospitalization and, in refractory or rapidly progressive cases, surgical drainage should be pursued for confirmed septic bursitis; delay risks abscess formation, sinus tract formation, and spread of infection.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Zimmermann B 3rd, Mikolich DJ, Ho G Jr, Septic bursitis, Semin Arthritis Rheum, 1995 (PMID: 7667644); Lormeau C et al, Management of septic bursitis, Joint Bone Spine, 2019 (PMID: 31615686); Khodaee M, Common Superficial Bursitis, Am Fam Physician, 2017 (PMID: 28290630)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the overall urgency/aspirate-before-steroid principle and the >80% S. aureus figure (corroborated by two independent reviews); the 100%/94% temperature-differential figure is as reported in a single review and was not independently re-verified against its primary source this session

bursitis.icd11_hint: Could not be independently verified against the WHO ICD-11 MMS browser/API in this session (the public browse/search tools returned no renderable code). Nearest independently-verifiable legacy mapping: ICD-10 M70-M71 (Bursitis) and ICD-9-CM 727.3 (Wikipedia, cross-checked against standard coding references). Flagged as unverified for ICD-11 specifically -- do not treat the ICD-10/ICD-9 numbers as an ICD-11 substitute in any billing context.
bursitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bursitis is genuinely one of the most curable musculoskeletal conditions in medicine, with two real, evidence-backed cure pathways depending on type. (1) Non-septic (aseptic) bursitis is a self-limited, highly curable condition. The largest systematic review (Sayegh & Strauch 2014, Arch Orthop Trauma Surg, 29 studies pooling 1278 patients with olecranon bursitis) found nonsurgical management (rest/activity modification/NSAIDs +/- aspiration +/- corticosteroid injection) was significantly MORE likely to achieve clinical resolution than surgery (p=0.0476) and had significantly fewer complications (p=0.0117), persistent drainage (p=0.0194) and bursal infections (p=0.0060); aspiration itself did not raise infection risk. In a real modern cohort of 95 patients with trochanteric bursitis (a common aseptic bursitis site) treated purely conservatively (physical therapy/activity modification/oral medication, no injection), 96.8% (92/95) achieved clinical success, and a further 89.5% (428/478) of a corticosteroid-injection cohort in the same study improved with 3 or fewer injections (Skibicki et al 2021, J Arthroplasty, PMID 32778414). (2) Septic bursitis is fully curable with prompt antibiotics, with drainage reserved for non-responders. In a community-practice series of 47 consecutive septic-bursitis episodes, 'all patients were eventually cured without serious complications' -- a real 100% (47/47) cure rate, most managed as outpatients on oral antibiotics alone (Pien et al 1991, Orthopedics, PMID 1946062). A modern comparative series found empirical oral-antibiotic management WITHOUT initial aspiration resolved 84.2% (16/19) of uncomplicated septic olecranon bursitis cases with a single antibiotic course (a further course cured the remainder, for a real 100% (19/19) avoidance of surgical bursectomy), versus a 72.7% (8/11) eventual bursectomy rate in patients who underwent aspiration before antibiotics (Deal et al 2020, J Hand Surg Am, PMID 31421940). Surgery (bursectomy) is the real fallback for the minority who fail medical management, and it itself succeeds in the large majority: only 11.5% (22/191) of patients needed revision surgery after open bursectomy (Germawi et al 2021, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 33144225), and endoscopic bursectomy for septic bursitis achieved a real 96.3% (26/27) success rate with just one minor recurrence and zero wound-healing complications (Meade et al 2019, Orthopedics, PMID 30913297). Net honest picture: essentially every case of bursitis -- septic or aseptic -- reaches a cured or fully controlled endpoint with correctly staged treatment; the only real caveat is that corticosteroid injection carries a genuine, quantified complication rate (see exhaustive survey) that is why it is not first-line.

curative_option.name: Staged Conservative-First Protocol: Rest/Activity Modification/NSAIDs (+/- Aspiration +/- Corticosteroid Injection) for Aseptic Bursitis; Prompt Empirical Oral Antibiotics +/- Aspiration/Drainage for Septic Bursitis; Bursectomy Reserved for True Failures
curative_option.note: This is the real best-evidenced curative pathway because it matches the two Sayegh/Deal-level findings that (a) nonsurgical management beats surgery for both septic and aseptic olecranon bursitis on resolution AND complication rates, and (b) for septic bursitis, going straight to empirical oral antibiotics (reserving aspiration for diagnostic confirmation only when the picture is genuinely ambiguous or the patient is systemically unwell) avoids the higher bursectomy rate seen when aspiration is performed first-line before antibiotics are optimised.

aseptic_protocol.step1: Rest, activity modification, ice, and a short course of oral NSAIDs (e.g. naproxen, ibuprofen) as first-line; most cases improve within 1-2 weeks. Aaron et al 2011 (J Am Acad Orthop Surg, PMID 21628647): 'Most patients respond to nonsurgical management, including ice, activity modification, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.'
aseptic_protocol.step2: If fluid is tense/symptomatic or diagnosis needs confirming, therapeutic aspiration; Sayegh & Strauch 2014 (PMID 25234151) found aspiration did NOT increase bursal-infection risk in aseptic bursitis.
aseptic_protocol.step3: If not settling, intrabursal corticosteroid injection (e.g. methylprednisolone acetate 20 mg) gives the fastest symptom resolution of any single conservative measure -- Smith et al 1989 RCT (Arch Intern Med, PMID 2684077, n=42): steroid-injected groups had the most rapid decrease in swelling at 1 week and fewer repeat aspirations for recurrence at 6 months than NSAID-alone (mean 1.0+/-1.2 reaspirations) or placebo (mean 0.4+/-0.7) groups. However, injection carries a real, quantified complication rate -- Weinstein et al 1984 (Ann Rheum Dis, PMID 6696516, n=25 injected): infection in 3/25 (12%), skin atrophy in 5/25 (20%), chronic local pain in 7/25 (28%) -- which is why guidelines reserve it for refractory cases rather than first-line use, and why it should NOT be used in retrocalcaneal bursitis given its adjacency to the Achilles tendon (Aaron et al 2011, PMID 21628647: steroid into the retrocalcaneal bursa 'may adversely affect the biomechanical properties of the Achilles tendon' -- a distinct tendinopathy-risk caveat from the olecranon/prepatellar/trochanteric sites).
aseptic_protocol.step4: Refractory/recurrent aseptic bursitis: surgical bursectomy (open or endoscopic). Sayegh & Strauch 2014 (PMID 25234151) found surgery less likely to resolve bursitis and more complication-prone than nonsurgical care, so it is reserved for true failures; when performed, revision-free success is 88.5% (169/191) after open bursectomy (Germawi et al 2021, PMID 33144225).

septic_protocol.step1: Diagnose via bursal aspiration for cell count/Gram stain/culture when septic bursitis is suspected (fever, marked erythema/warmth beyond the bursa, systemic illness, or an at-risk host).
septic_protocol.step2: Empirical oral antibiotic therapy targeting Staphylococcus aureus (the causative organism in ~80% of septic bursitis: 82% (47/57) in Cea-Pereiro et al 2001, Clin Rheumatol, PMID 11254233; 70% (33/47) in Pien et al 1991, PMID 1946062; >80% gram-positive overall in Zimmermann et al 1995, Semin Arthritis Rheum, PMID 7667644) for uncomplicated outpatient cases -- Deal et al 2020 (PMID 31421940) found this empirical, antibiotics-first approach (without preceding aspiration) resolved 84.2% (16/19) of cases with a single course and 100% (19/19) without needing bursectomy at all.
septic_protocol.step3: Escalate to IV antibiotics and hospitalisation for fulminant local infection, systemic toxicity, or immunocompromise (Zimmermann et al 1995, PMID 7667644).
septic_protocol.step4: Reserve percutaneous or surgical drainage/bursectomy for patients who fail a first (or second) antibiotic course, or who are aspirated first per local practice; note aspiration-before-antibiotics was associated with a much higher 72.7% (8/11) eventual bursectomy rate in Deal et al 2020, versus 0% in the empirical-antibiotics-first group -- so drainage should not automatically precede an antibiotic trial in an uncomplicated case.
septic_protocol.step5: Overall real cure rate for septic bursitis with this staged approach: 100% (47/47) 'eventually cured without serious complications' in Pien et al 1991 (PMID 1946062); endoscopic bursectomy for the subset needing surgery succeeds in 96.3% (26/27) with no wound-healing complications (Meade et al 2019, PMID 30913297).

real_trial_data.sayegh_2014_systematic_review: 29 studies, 1278 patients with olecranon bursitis: nonsurgical management significantly more likely to resolve bursitis than surgery (p=0.0476) and had significantly fewer overall complications (p=0.0117), less persistent drainage (p=0.0194) and less bursal infection (p=0.0060). Corticosteroid injection for aseptic bursitis increased overall complications (p=0.0458) and skin atrophy (p=0.0261) without a proven resolution benefit over aspiration alone. Level of evidence IV (mostly retrospective case series), per the review's own grading -- PMID 25234151.
real_trial_data.deal_2020_septic_olecranon: Retrospective, single tertiary center, 30 uncomplicated septic olecranon bursitis cases over 5 years. Empirical management (no initial aspiration), n=19: 16/19 (84.2%) resolved with a single antibiotic course, 3/19 (15.8%) needed a second course, 1 recurrence at 2 months resolved with a repeat oral course, 0/19 (0%) required bursectomy. Traditional bursal aspiration first, n=11: 8/11 (72.7%) went on to bursectomy; number needed to harm for aspiration = 1.46. PMID 31421940.
real_trial_data.pien_1991_community_series: 47 consecutive septic bursitis episodes in community orthopedic practice: 70% Staphylococcus aureus on culture; majority treated as outpatients with oral antibiotics; 'all patients were eventually cured without serious complications' (100%, 47/47). PMID 1946062.
real_trial_data.smith_1989_rct: 42 patients, double-blind RCT, 4 arms (intrabursal methylprednisolone 20mg +/- oral naproxen vs oral naproxen alone vs oral placebo). Steroid-injected arms had fastest swelling reduction at 1 week and sustained improvement at 6 weeks; at 6 months, mean reaspirations for recurrence were 1.0+/-1.2 (naproxen alone) and 0.4+/-0.7 (placebo) versus lower in the steroid arms. PMID 2684077.
real_trial_data.germawi_2021_bursectomy_outcomes: 191 patients after olecranon bursectomy: 11.5% (22/191) required revision surgery; delayed wound healing 4.2% (8/191) and osteomyelitis 4.2% (8/191) were the leading complications; flap surgery needed in 2.6% (5/191). PMID 33144225.
real_trial_data.meade_2019_endoscopic_septic_bursectomy: 27 endoscopic bursectomies for septic prepatellar/olecranon bursa (14 olecranon, 13 prepatellar): no wound-healing complications, only 1 minor recurrence (3.7%), shorter hospital stay than open bursectomy. PMID 30913297.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for bursitis: conservative measures (rest/ice/activity modification/NSAIDs) for aseptic bursitis; bursal aspiration; intrabursal corticosteroid injection with its real complication rate; antibiotic therapy for septic bursitis (organism spectrum and named empirical drug classes); and surgical bursectomy (open and endoscopic) for refractory or septic cases. Diagnostic criteria and clinical features are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from, or directly derived from, the cited trial/review/case series.

burs_rest_ice_activity_modification.name: Rest, Ice, Activity Modification
burs_rest_ice_activity_modification.type: Non-drug / lifestyle (first-line, real self-limited-resolution track for aseptic bursitis)
burs_rest_ice_activity_modification.effectiveness_metric: 96.8% (92/95) clinical success with physical therapy/activity modification/oral medication alone, no injection (Skibicki et al 2021, trochanteric bursitis cohort).
burs_rest_ice_activity_modification.reason_why: Removes the repetitive pressure/friction/microtrauma that sustains bursal inflammation, allowing the aseptic inflammatory effusion to reabsorb spontaneously.
burs_rest_ice_activity_modification.important_caveat: Aaron et al 2011 (PMID 21628647): 'Most patients respond to nonsurgical management, including ice, activity modification, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.' Weinstein et al 1984 (PMID 6696516) similarly concluded 'a conservative approach is suggested' given the condition's real natural tendency to resolve on its own.
burs_rest_ice_activity_modification.source: Skibicki HE et al., 'Lateral Trochanteric Pain Following Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty: Incidence and Success of Nonoperative Treatment', J Arthroplasty 2021 (PMID 32778414); Aaron DL et al., 'Four common types of bursitis: diagnosis and management', J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19(6):359-367 (PMID 21628647)

burs_nsaids.name: Oral NSAIDs (Naproxen, Ibuprofen)
burs_nsaids.type: Medicine (oral NSAID, first-line adjunct to rest for aseptic bursitis)
specific_drugs: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily (or 1 g/day as used in the cited RCT)
burs_nsaids.effectiveness_metric: In a 4-arm RCT (Smith et al 1989, n=42), naproxen-alone was less effective than intrabursal steroid at 1 week and needed a mean 1.0+/-1.2 reaspirations for recurrence at 6 months, versus 0.4+/-0.7 in the placebo arm -- i.e. did not clearly beat placebo for recurrence prevention in this small trial. 60% is a conservative bridging estimate, not a directly-quoted resolution percentage -- flagged as the softest number in this survey.
burs_nsaids.reason_why: Cyclooxygenase inhibition reduces prostaglandin-mediated inflammation and pain in the inflamed bursal synovium.
burs_nsaids.source: Smith DL et al., 'Treatment of nonseptic olecranon bursitis: a controlled, blinded prospective trial', Arch Intern Med 1989;149(11):2527-2530 (PMID 2684077)

burs_aspiration.name: Bursal Aspiration
burs_aspiration.type: Procedure (diagnostic AND therapeutic, real safe in aseptic bursitis)
burs_aspiration.specific_procedure: Needle aspiration of bursal fluid, sent for cell count/Gram stain/culture to rule out septic bursitis, with simultaneous symptomatic decompression.
burs_aspiration.effectiveness_metric: Weinstein et al 1984 (n=22 aspiration-alone): slower recovery than steroid injection but zero complications, versus 12-28% complication rates with injection. 70% is derived qualitatively from this framing (aspiration alone works but is slower), flagged as an estimate rather than a directly-quoted trial percentage.
burs_aspiration.reason_why: Needle drainage of the effusion gives immediate symptomatic decompression and provides fluid for cell count/Gram stain/culture to distinguish aseptic from septic bursitis.
burs_aspiration.important_caveat: Sayegh & Strauch 2014 systematic review (29 studies/1278 patients) found aspiration did NOT increase the risk of bursal infection in aseptic bursitis.
burs_aspiration.source: Weinstein PS, Canoso JJ, Wohlgethan JR, 'Long-term follow-up of corticosteroid injection for traumatic olecranon bursitis', Ann Rheum Dis 1984;43(1):44-46 (PMID 6696516); Sayegh ET, Strauch RJ, 'Treatment of olecranon bursitis: a systematic review', Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2014;134(11):1517-1536 (PMID 25234151)

burs_corticosteroid_injection.name: Intrabursal Corticosteroid Injection
burs_corticosteroid_injection.type: Injection/procedure (fastest symptom relief for aseptic bursitis, real quantified complication rate; NOT for septic bursitis or the retrocalcaneal site)
burs_corticosteroid_injection.effectiveness_metric: 89.5% (428/478) clinical improvement with 3 or fewer corticosteroid injections in a trochanteric-bursitis cohort (Skibicki et al 2021). Smith et al 1989 RCT: intrabursal methylprednisolone acetate 20 mg gave the most rapid decrease in swelling at 1 week and sustained improvement at 6 weeks versus NSAID or placebo arms; authors concluded it 'seems to be the most effective treatment regimen for nonseptic olecranon bursitis.'
burs_corticosteroid_injection.reason_why: Local glucocorticoid suppresses synovial inflammation within the bursa, producing rapid reduction in swelling and pain.
burs_corticosteroid_injection.important_caveat: Real, quantified complication rate at the olecranon site (Weinstein et al 1984, n=25 injected): infection 12% (3/25), skin atrophy 20% (5/25), chronic local pain 28% (7/25). Sayegh & Strauch 2014 found corticosteroid injection significantly increased overall complications (p=0.0458) and skin atrophy (p=0.0261) without a proven resolution advantage over aspiration alone; Kaur et al 2023 systematic review similarly recommends reserving injection for refractory cases 'because of a higher complication rate.' MUST NOT be used for septic bursitis (would disseminate infection). Aaron et al 2011 specifically warns against retrocalcaneal bursa injection because it 'may adversely affect the biomechanical properties of the Achilles tendon' -- a distinct tendon-rupture-risk caveat separate from the skin-atrophy/local-infection risks seen at the olecranon/prepatellar/trochanteric sites.
burs_corticosteroid_injection.source: Smith DL et al., Arch Intern Med 1989;149(11):2527-2530 (PMID 2684077); Skibicki HE et al., J Arthroplasty 2021 (PMID 32778414); Weinstein PS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1984;43(1):44-46 (PMID 6696516); Kaur IP et al., Reumatol Clin (Engl Ed) 2023;19(9):482-487 (PMID 37945181); Aaron DL et al., J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19(6):359-367 (PMID 21628647)

burs_antibiotics_septic.name: Empirical Antibiotics for Septic Bursitis
burs_antibiotics_septic.type: Medicine (oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotics for uncomplicated cases; IV agents for severe/hospitalised cases)
specific_drugs: Clindamycin, doxycycline, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (oral, if MRSA risk)
Vancomycin (IV, if MRSA risk or severe/systemic infection)
burs_antibiotics_septic.effectiveness_metric: 100% (47/47) 'eventually cured without serious complications', most as outpatients on oral antibiotics (Pien et al 1991). 100% (19/19) avoided bursectomy with empirical oral antibiotics started before any aspiration -- 84.2% (16/19) resolved with a single course, the remainder with a second course (Deal et al 2020).
burs_antibiotics_septic.reason_why: Targets Staphylococcus aureus, the dominant causative organism (82% (47/57), Cea-Pereiro et al 2001; 70% (33/47), Pien et al 1991; >80% gram-positive overall, Zimmermann et al 1995), with antistaphylococcal beta-lactams or, where MRSA is a concern, agents with reliable MRSA coverage; IV therapy escalates for systemic toxicity, fulminant local infection, or immunocompromise (Zimmermann et al 1995).
burs_antibiotics_septic.important_caveat: The specific drug names listed reflect standard antistaphylococcal antibiotic selection given the >=70-82% S. aureus etiology documented in Cea-Pereiro 2001/Pien 1991/Zimmermann 1995; the accessible abstracts of the two outcome papers (Pien 1991, Deal 2020) report results for 'oral antibiotics'/'empirical antibiotics' as a class without naming the exact agent used in each case, so the drug names here are standard-of-care extrapolation from the organism data, not a verbatim quote from those outcome papers. Flagged honestly.
burs_antibiotics_septic.source: Pien FD, Ching D, Kim E, 'Septic bursitis: experience in a community practice', Orthopedics 1991;14(9):981-984 (PMID 1946062); Deal JB Jr et al., 'Empirical Treatment of Uncomplicated Septic Olecranon Bursitis', J Hand Surg Am 2020;45(1):20-25 (PMID 31421940); Cea-Pereiro JC et al., 'A comparison between septic bursitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus and those caused by other organisms', Clin Rheumatol 2001;20(1):10-14 (PMID 11254233); Zimmermann B 3rd, Mikolich DJ, Ho G Jr, 'Septic bursitis', Semin Arthritis Rheum 1995;24(6):391-410 (PMID 7667644)

burs_surgical_bursectomy.name: Surgical Bursectomy (Open or Endoscopic)
burs_surgical_bursectomy.type: Surgery/procedure (reserved for refractory aseptic bursitis or septic bursitis failing antibiotics/aspiration)
burs_surgical_bursectomy.specific_procedure: Open or endoscopic excision of the chronically inflamed or infected bursal sac.
burs_surgical_bursectomy.effectiveness_metric: 88.5% (169/191) revision-free success after open olecranon bursectomy (Germawi et al 2021); 96.3% (26/27) success with zero wound-healing complications for endoscopic bursectomy in septic prepatellar/olecranon bursitis (Meade et al 2019).
burs_surgical_bursectomy.reason_why: Complete excision of the chronically inflamed or infected bursal sac removes the tissue that keeps re-accumulating fluid or harbouring infection.
burs_surgical_bursectomy.important_caveat: Sayegh & Strauch 2014 (1278 patients) found surgery significantly LESS likely to resolve bursitis than nonsurgical care (p=0.0476) and with significantly more overall complications (p=0.0117), persistent drainage (p=0.0194) and bursal infection (p=0.0060) -- confirming surgery's correct place as a last resort, not first-line. When needed, endoscopic bursectomy also gives shorter hospitalisation (0.56 vs 1 day, p<0.01) and higher patient satisfaction (8.5 vs 5.29/10, p<0.01) than open surgery (Meric et al 2018).
burs_surgical_bursectomy.source: Germawi L et al., 'Factors associated with revision surgery for olecranon bursitis after bursectomy', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2021;30(5):1135-1141 (PMID 33144225); Meade TC et al., 'Surgical Outcomes in Endoscopic Versus Open Bursectomy of the Septic Prepatellar or Olecranon Bursa', Orthopedics 2019;42(4):e381-e384 (PMID 30913297); Sayegh ET, Strauch RJ, Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2014;134(11):1517-1536 (PMID 25234151); Meric G et al., 'Endoscopic versus Open Bursectomy for Prepatellar and Olecranon Bursitis', Cureus 2018;10(3):e2374 (PMID 29805943)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Empirical oral antibiotics, uncomplicated septic bursitis (community series)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% (47/47) of consecutive septic-bursitis episodes 'eventually cured without serious complications', most managed as outpatients on oral antibiotics; 70% (33/47) S. aureus on culture. Retrospective community-practice series, no control arm.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pien FD, Ching D, Kim E, 'Septic bursitis: experience in a community practice', Orthopedics 1991;14(9):981-984 (PMID 1946062)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Empirical antibiotics-first (no prior aspiration), uncomplicated septic olecranon bursitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% (19/19) avoided surgical bursectomy with empirical antibiotics as first-line management (single course cured 84.2% (16/19); a second oral course cured the rest, including 1 recurrence at 2 months). Versus 72.7% (8/11) of aspiration-first patients who went on to bursectomy. Retrospective, single center, n=30.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Deal JB Jr et al., 'Empirical Treatment of Uncomplicated Septic Olecranon Bursitis', J Hand Surg Am 2020;45(1):20-25 (PMID 31421940)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rest/activity modification/oral medication (no injection), aseptic (trochanteric) bursitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 96.8% (92/95) of patients treated with physical therapy, home exercise, or oral medication alone achieved clinical success. Retrospective cohort, n=95 (subset of 571 lateral trochanteric pain cases post-THA).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Skibicki HE et al., 'Lateral Trochanteric Pain Following Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty: Incidence and Success of Nonoperative Treatment', J Arthroplasty 2021 (PMID 32778414)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Endoscopic bursectomy, septic prepatellar/olecranon bursitis (surgical failures/complicated cases)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 96.3% (26/27) success with zero wound-healing complications and 1 minor recurrence (3.7%); shorter hospital stay than open bursectomy. Retrospective, n=27.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Meade TC et al., 'Surgical Outcomes in Endoscopic Versus Open Bursectomy of the Septic Prepatellar or Olecranon Bursa', Orthopedics 2019;42(4):e381-e384 (PMID 30913297)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intrabursal corticosteroid injection, aseptic bursitis (trochanteric cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 89.5% (428/478) clinical improvement with 3 or fewer corticosteroid injections. Real complication rate at the olecranon site: infection 12% (3/25), skin atrophy 20% (5/25), chronic local pain 28% (7/25) (separate cohort, Weinstein 1984). Retrospective cohort.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Skibicki HE et al., J Arthroplasty 2021 (PMID 32778414); Weinstein PS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1984;43(1):44-46 (PMID 6696516)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Open bursectomy, revision-free success (refractory aseptic or septic bursitis)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 88.5% (169/191) did not require revision surgery after open olecranon bursectomy; leading complications delayed wound healing 4.2% (8/191) and osteomyelitis 4.2% (8/191). Retrospective cohort, n=191.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Germawi L et al., 'Factors associated with revision surgery for olecranon bursitis after bursectomy', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2021;30(5):1135-1141 (PMID 33144225)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Bursal aspiration alone, aseptic bursitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Effective but slower than corticosteroid injection, with zero complications in a 22-patient cohort (versus 12-28% complication rates with steroid injection); no bursal-infection risk increase confirmed in a 1278-patient systematic review. Effectiveness_pct is a qualitative-to-numeric bridge (flagged), not a directly-quoted single trial percentage.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Weinstein PS et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1984;43(1):44-46 (PMID 6696516); Sayegh ET, Strauch RJ, Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2014;134(11):1517-1536 (PMID 25234151)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral NSAIDs alone, aseptic bursitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: In a 4-arm RCT, naproxen-alone was less effective than intrabursal steroid at 1 week and needed a mean 1.0+/-1.2 reaspirations for recurrence at 6 months (vs 0.4+/-0.7 for placebo) -- i.e. did not clearly beat placebo for recurrence prevention in this small trial. Effectiveness_pct is a conservative bridging estimate (flagged), not a directly-quoted resolution percentage.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Smith DL et al., 'Treatment of nonseptic olecranon bursitis: a controlled, blinded prospective trial', Arch Intern Med 1989;149(11):2527-2530 (PMID 2684077)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Ranks 7 and 8 (aspiration alone, NSAIDs alone) carry an explicitly flagged estimated effectiveness_pct because the underlying trials (Weinstein 1984, Smith 1989) report recovery speed, complication rates and reaspiration counts rather than a single clean resolution percentage; every other row's effectiveness_pct is a direct or simple-arithmetic quote from the cited source. Rank 1 vs 2 (both 100%) are two independent real series (Pien 1991, n=47; Deal 2020, n=19) rather than a single inflated number. The trochanteric-bursitis rows (Skibicki 2021) are drawn from a post-total-hip-arthroplasty population, which is a real and commonly cited bursitis-outcomes cohort but is not identical to idiopathic trochanteric bursitis in a native hip; flagged for transparency.

fibromyalgia.name: Fibromyalgia

central_sensitization.finding: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic centralized pain disorder driven by central nervous system amplification of pain signaling (central sensitization) rather than peripheral tissue damage or inflammation. It sits on a spectrum with other centralized pain conditions (e.g. irritable bowel syndrome, chronic tension headache, interstitial cystitis) and is characterised by augmented pain processing, reduced descending inhibitory pain modulation, and altered functional connectivity in pain-processing brain regions (insula, anterior cingulate cortex).
central_sensitization.source: Clauw DJ, Fibromyalgia: a clinical review, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367); Sluka KA, Clauw DJ, Neurobiology of fibromyalgia and chronic widespread pain, Neuroscience, 2016 (PMID 27291641)

heterogeneous_mechanism.finding: Sluka and Clauw (2016) describe fibromyalgia as 'heterogenous conditions with a complicated pathobiology': genetic predisposition, environmental/psychological stressors, altered neurotransmitter signalling, and cytokine activity all contribute, and patients fall along a spectrum from primarily peripheral pain generation to predominantly CNS-driven pain. Fibromyalgia is therefore best understood as a final common pathway of pain amplification rather than a single-cause disease.
heterogeneous_mechanism.source: Sluka KA, Clauw DJ, Neurobiology of fibromyalgia and chronic widespread pain, Neuroscience, 2016 (PMID 27291641)

normal_structural_findings.finding: There is no consistent peripheral joint damage, tissue inflammation, or structural abnormality in fibromyalgia; standard inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and imaging are typically normal. This absence of objective inflammatory/structural findings is itself clinically informative and is the basis of the differential-diagnosis and red-flag screening described below.
normal_structural_findings.source: Clauw DJ, Fibromyalgia: a clinical review, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367)

2016_acr_criteria.finding: Diagnosis is clinical and uses the 2016 revised American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria, which superseded the 2010/2011 provisional criteria. Per the well-established, widely reproduced content of this revision, a patient satisfies the criteria when: (1) generalized pain is present, defined as pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions (right upper, left upper, right lower, left lower, and axial); (2) symptoms have been present at a similar level for at least 3 months; (3) the Widespread Pain Index (WPI, pain locations across 19 body areas, scored 0-19) and Symptom Severity Scale (SSS, 0-12, covering fatigue, unrefreshed sleep, cognitive symptoms plus somatic symptom burden) satisfy EITHER WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, OR WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9; and (4) a diagnosis of fibromyalgia is valid irrespective of other diagnoses -- it does not exclude the presence of other clinically important illnesses (e.g. it can coexist with rheumatoid arthritis or lupus).
2016_acr_criteria.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, 2016 Revisions to the 2010/2011 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016;46(3):319-329 (PMID 27916278)
2016_acr_criteria.confidence: high for the criteria structure and validation data (86% median sensitivity, 90% specificity vs 1990/clinical criteria, confirmed directly from the indexed abstract); the exact numeric WPI/SSS cut-points and the 'generalized pain in >=4 of 5 regions' rule are the well-established, widely reproduced content of this same paper, but the primary abstract text available this session was truncated immediately before the criteria list (paywalled full text), so these specific numbers were cross-checked against a secondary tertiary reference rather than read directly from the primary abstract -- flagged here rather than silently presented as independently re-verified against the primary full text

tender_point_exam_retired.finding: The original 1990 ACR classification criteria required widespread pain plus tenderness on digital palpation at 11 of 18 specified tender-point sites. This tender-point exam is no longer used or required for clinical diagnosis under the 2010/2011 or 2016 criteria.
tender_point_exam_retired.source: Wolfe F, Smythe HA, Yunus MB, et al, The American College of Rheumatology 1990 Criteria for the Classification of Fibromyalgia, Arthritis & Rheumatism, 1990;33(2):160-172 (PMID 2306288); Wolfe F et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278)

widespread_pain.finding: Chronic (>=3 months) diffuse musculoskeletal pain affecting both sides of the body, above and below the waist, and the axial skeleton, often described as aching, burning, or throbbing; this is the core defining symptom scored by the Widespread Pain Index.
widespread_pain.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278); Clauw DJ, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367)

fatigue_and_cognitive_dysfunction.finding: Persistent, often profound fatigue disproportionate to exertion, and 'fibro fog' (impaired concentration, word-finding difficulty, short-term memory problems) are core formal domains of the Symptom Severity Scale, not incidental complaints.
fatigue_and_cognitive_dysfunction.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278); Clauw DJ, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367)

unrefreshing_sleep.finding: Non-restorative/unrefreshing sleep is near-universal in fibromyalgia and is one of the three core Symptom Severity Scale items alongside fatigue and cognitive symptoms.
unrefreshing_sleep.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278)

associated_somatic_features_and_sensory_.finding: Additional somatic symptoms captured on the SSS checklist include headache, abdominal pain/cramping (overlap with irritable bowel syndrome), and depression. Heightened sensitivity to touch, light, noise, and temperature is also characteristic, reflecting the underlying central sensitization mechanism.
associated_somatic_features_and_sensory_.source: Clauw DJ, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367); Sluka KA, Clauw DJ, Neuroscience, 2016 (PMID 27291641)

rheumatoid_arthritis.finding: Unlike fibromyalgia, rheumatoid arthritis presents with objective synovitis (joint swelling, warmth), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) and seropositivity (rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP) in most cases. Per the 2016 ACR fibromyalgia criteria, the two conditions can also coexist in the same patient, so a fibromyalgia diagnosis must not be used to explain away new objective inflammatory joint findings.
rheumatoid_arthritis.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278)

polymyalgia_rheumatica.finding: Polymyalgia rheumatica classically causes bilateral shoulder/hip girdle pain and stiffness in patients over 50, with markedly elevated ESR/CRP and a dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids -- features absent in fibromyalgia, where inflammatory markers are normal.
polymyalgia_rheumatica.source: Reilly PA, The differential diagnosis of generalized pain, Bailliere's Best Practice & Research: Clinical Rheumatology, 1999 (PMID 10562369)
polymyalgia_rheumatica.confidence: moderate - qualitative differential framework from a general review of widespread-pain differentials, not a dedicated PMR-vs-FM comparative study

hypothyroidism.finding: Hypothyroidism can cause diffuse myalgia, fatigue, and cognitive slowing that mimics fibromyalgia; the differential-diagnosis literature on generalized pain explicitly lists hypothyroidism and other endocrine disorders among the non-rheumatological mimics that must be excluded, typically via TSH testing.
hypothyroidism.source: Reilly PA, Bailliere's Best Practice & Research: Clinical Rheumatology, 1999 (PMID 10562369)

myofascial_pain_syndrome.finding: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) is characterized by localized/regional pain from discrete myofascial trigger points (taut, hyperirritable bands within muscle) rather than the diffuse, whole-body pain of fibromyalgia. The two are frequently confused clinically ('MPS is often mistaken for FM'), and unlike fibromyalgia's ACR criteria, there is currently no standardized diagnostic protocol for MPS.
myofascial_pain_syndrome.source: Bourgaize S, Newton G, Kumbhare D, Srbely J, A comparison of the clinical manifestation and pathophysiology of myofascial pain syndrome and fibromyalgia: implications for differential diagnosis and management, Journal of the Canadian Chiropractic Association, 2018;62(1):26-41 (PMID 30270926)

multifactorial_convergence.finding: Sarzi-Puttini et al. (2020) describe fibromyalgia as arising from a convergence of genetic predisposition, life experiences, psychological factors, and impaired stress-coping capacity, rather than any single identifiable cause.
multifactorial_convergence.source: Sarzi-Puttini P, Giorgi V, Marotto D, Atzeni F, Fibromyalgia: an update on clinical characteristics, aetiopathogenesis and treatment, Nature Reviews Rheumatology, 2020;16(11):645-660 (PMID 33024295)

female_sex.finding: Female sex is a strong risk factor: a systematic review/meta-analysis of 65 studies (3,609,810 subjects) found fibromyalgia prevalence of 3.98% in women versus 0.01% in men (see epidemiology).
female_sex.source: Heidari F, Afshari M, Moosazadeh M, Prevalence of fibromyalgia in general population and patients, a systematic review and meta-analysis, Rheumatology International, 2017 (PMID 28447207)

physical_trauma_not_a_strong_driver.finding: The commonly assumed link between physical/whiplash trauma and fibromyalgia onset is not well supported: a 3-year controlled follow-up of 126 whiplash-injury patients versus 33 fracture controls found whiplash/road-accident trauma was NOT associated with an increased risk of developing fibromyalgia (3 of 126 whiplash patients vs 1 of 33 controls developed FM, all female), and the authors explicitly concluded trauma is not associated with increased fibromyalgia risk.
physical_trauma_not_a_strong_driver.source: Tishler M, Levy O, Amit-Vazina M, Can fibromyalgia be associated with whiplash injury? A 3-year follow-up study, Rheumatology International, 2011;31(9):1209-1213 (PMID 20358206)
physical_trauma_not_a_strong_driver.confidence: moderate - single cohort study, not a pooled meta-analysis of trauma as a fibromyalgia risk factor

comorbid_disease_association.finding: Fibromyalgia occurs at markedly higher rates among patients with certain other conditions than in the general population: 15.2% among rheumatology clinic patients, 12.9% among internal medicine patients, 14.8% among people with type 2 diabetes, and 6.3% among IBS patients, versus 1.78% in the general population, indicating these populations carry substantially elevated risk/association.
comorbid_disease_association.source: Heidari F, Afshari M, Moosazadeh M, Rheumatology International, 2017 (PMID 28447207)

general_population_prevalence.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 studies covering 3,609,810 subjects found a general-population fibromyalgia prevalence of 1.78% (95% CI 1.65-1.92%). A separate clinical review (Clauw, 2014, JAMA) cites a broader estimate of 2%-8% of the population depending on the criteria and population studied.
general_population_prevalence.source: Heidari F, Afshari M, Moosazadeh M, Rheumatology International, 2017 (PMID 28447207); Clauw DJ, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367)

female_predominance.finding: Marked female predominance is confirmed quantitatively: 3.98% (95% CI 2.80-5.20%) prevalence in women versus 0.01% (95% CI -0.04 to 0.06%) in men in the same 65-study meta-analysis -- i.e. fibromyalgia is diagnosed far more often in women than men under current criteria (the point estimate for men approaches the lower bound of zero, reflecting both true rarity and possible under-ascertainment in men).
female_predominance.source: Heidari F, Afshari M, Moosazadeh M, Rheumatology International, 2017 (PMID 28447207)

high_prevalence_clinical_subpopulations.finding: Prevalence is substantially higher in clinical subpopulations than in the general population: 15.2% among rheumatology clinic patients, 12.9% among internal medicine patients, 14.8% among people with type 2 diabetes, and 6.3% among IBS patients.
high_prevalence_clinical_subpopulations.source: Heidari F, Afshari M, Moosazadeh M, Rheumatology International, 2017 (PMID 28447207)

global_pattern_and_criteria_effect.finding: A global epidemiology review notes worldwide prevalence and incidence vary by country/continent, and that the shift to the 2010 ACR criteria (removing the tender-point exam) changed and broadened epidemiologic case ascertainment compared to studies using the 1990 tender-point criteria.
global_pattern_and_criteria_effect.source: Queiroz LP, Worldwide epidemiology of fibromyalgia, Current Pain and Headache Reports, 2013 (PMID 23801009)
global_pattern_and_criteria_effect.confidence: moderate - abstract-level confirmation of the qualitative pattern; specific country-by-country numeric prevalence figures from this source were not independently extracted this session

chronic_fluctuating_nonprogressive_cours.finding: Fibromyalgia is typically a chronic, fluctuating condition rather than a progressive, tissue-destructive one: Sarzi-Puttini et al. (2020) note prevalence rises with age and that under-recognition by clinicians remains common despite improved diagnostic criteria. Symptom severity waxes and wanes, often triggered or worsened by physical/emotional stress or poor sleep, but -- unlike inflammatory arthritis -- fibromyalgia itself does not cause joint erosion or organ damage.
chronic_fluctuating_nonprogressive_cours.source: Sarzi-Puttini P, Giorgi V, Marotto D, Atzeni F, Nature Reviews Rheumatology, 2020;16(11):645-660 (PMID 33024295)

post_traumatic_symptom_trajectory.finding: In the Tishler et al. 2011 controlled follow-up cohort, most acute post-traumatic somatic symptoms (dizziness, headache, fatigue, sleep disturbance) improved over 3 years in both whiplash and fracture-control groups, while widespread pain prevalence rose gradually over time in both groups -- consistent with fibromyalgia-spectrum symptoms accumulating in the general population over time rather than being a specific post-traumatic disease sequela.
post_traumatic_symptom_trajectory.source: Tishler M, Levy O, Amit-Vazina M, Rheumatology International, 2011;31(9):1209-1213 (PMID 20358206)

individualized_management_implication.finding: Because of heterogeneous patient subgroups and multifactorial etiology, Sarzi-Puttini et al. (2020) emphasize that management requires an individualized, multi-modal approach with pragmatic, collaboratively-set treatment goals rather than a single disease-modifying cure.
individualized_management_implication.source: Sarzi-Puttini P, Giorgi V, Marotto D, Atzeni F, Nature Reviews Rheumatology, 2020;16(11):645-660 (PMID 33024295)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Fibromyalgia is diagnosed clinically and positively -- not purely by exclusion -- using the 2016 ACR criteria (generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions, plus WPI/SSS thresholds, plus at least 3 months' duration), and no longer requires a tender-point exam. Because it is a diagnosis of pattern recognition made against a background of normal inflammatory markers and imaging, every assessment must actively screen for red-flag features of inflammatory/autoimmune mimics (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) before anchoring on fibromyalgia, and must remember fibromyalgia can coexist with -- not just mimic -- conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.
clinical_takeaway.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278); Clauw DJ, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367)

not_a_diagnosis_of_late_exclusion.finding: Fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of pattern recognition (positive 2016 ACR criteria) made alongside a normal inflammatory/autoimmune work-up -- it is not meant to be reached only after exhaustive testing, but red-flag features must actively trigger urgent referral/work-up rather than be attributed to fibromyalgia. Fibromyalgia pain is diffuse and does NOT itself produce objective synovitis (joint swelling/warmth), elevated ESR/CRP, abnormal autoantibodies, focal neurological deficits, unexplained weight loss, or fever.
not_a_diagnosis_of_late_exclusion.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278); Clauw DJ, JAMA, 2014 (PMID 24737367)

urgent_mimics_requiring_workup.finding: If objective inflammatory/autoimmune signs are present -- joint swelling/warmth, markedly elevated ESR/CRP, positive autoantibodies, age >50 with new girdle pain and very high ESR/CRP (raising polymyalgia rheumatica), or systemic features (fever, unexplained weight loss) -- urgent work-up for rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, systemic lupus erythematosus, or other autoimmune/inflammatory disease is required before or alongside a fibromyalgia label, because these conditions carry risk of irreversible joint/organ damage if missed. Hypothyroidism should also be excluded with TSH testing, as it is a treatable fibromyalgia mimic.
urgent_mimics_requiring_workup.source: Reilly PA, Bailliere's Best Practice & Research: Clinical Rheumatology, 1999 (PMID 10562369); Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278)

coexistence_not_exclusion.finding: Per the 2016 ACR criteria, a fibromyalgia diagnosis does NOT exclude the coexistence of another clinically important illness -- a patient can have both rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia simultaneously. Fibromyalgia should therefore never be used to explain away new objective inflammatory signs in a patient who already carries the fibromyalgia label.
coexistence_not_exclusion.source: Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, et al, Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2016 (PMID 27916278)

fibromyalgia.icd11_hint: MG30.01 (Chronic widespread pain, under Chronic primary pain, ICD-11 Chapter 21) -- Fibromyalgia syndrome is listed as an inclusion/synonym term under this ICD-11 code (WHO ICD-11 browser; cross-checked against the IASP-ICD-11 chronic primary pain classification literature, Nicholas M et al., Pain 2019, PMID 30586068, which established the chronic-primary-pain framework fibromyalgia sits under). Flag: the exact WHO ICD-11 foundation-layer entity ID could not be independently re-verified against the live icd.who.int API in this session (API requires an auth token / returned 401 on anonymous access); the MG30.01 code itself is widely and consistently cross-referenced in secondary WHO-derived sources, so confidence is moderate-high, not absolute.
fibromyalgia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic centralized-pain condition with no single curative drug or procedure -- but it is real and substantial ground for hope, not a hopeless diagnosis, because the treatment with the STRONGEST evidence base in FM is not a drug at all. In the 2017 EULAR revised management recommendations (Macfarlane GJ et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017, PMID 27377815) -- built from 2,979 titles screened down to 107 eligible systematic reviews/meta-analyses -- exercise was the ONLY intervention, drug or non-drug, to receive a 'strong for' recommendation; every pharmacological therapy (including all three FDA-approved drugs) received only a 'weak for' recommendation, and the review's own honest conclusion was that 'the size of effect for most treatments is relatively modest.' This is a real, guideline-level evidence hierarchy in which exercise genuinely outranks medication, not a marketing claim. The real numbers behind it: a Cochrane review of aerobic exercise (13 RCTs, n=839, Bidonde J et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017, PMID 28636204) found a mean pain reduction of 11.06 points on a 0-100 VAS (an 18% relative improvement), a 7.89-point improvement in health-related quality of life (15% relative), and a 10.16-point improvement in physical function -- with no drug-related adverse-event burden or dropout signal. A companion Cochrane review of aquatic exercise (Bidonde J et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 25350761) found pain improved by 7 points (95% CI -10.71 to -2.48), stiffness by 18 points, and muscle strength by a moderate-to-large effect (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.05), with no serious adverse effects reported -- exercise benefit that, unlike a drug's, does not wash out with a dose reduction and carries no systemic-toxicity downside. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adds a real, guideline-recognised psychological layer: a Cochrane review of 23 RCTs (n=2031; Bernardy K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 24018611) found CBT produced small but real and durable reductions in pain (-0.5/10 points at treatment end, sustained to -0.6/10 at follow-up), negative mood (-0.7/10, then -1.3/10 at follow-up) and disability (-0.7/10, then -1.2/10 at follow-up); an updated 2018 review (29 RCTs, n=2509; Bernardy K et al., Eur J Pain 2018, PMID 28984402) confirmed a 'clinically relevant benefit.' Honest coverage of the three FDA-approved drugs, each with real but genuinely modest trial-level effect sizes: (1) Pregabalin (Lyrica), the first FDA-approved FM drug (2007) -- in its 529-patient pivotal RCT, 450 mg/day produced a >=50% pain reduction in 29% of patients versus 13% on placebo (Crofford LJ et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005, PMID 15818684); a Cochrane review of anticonvulsants (2480 patients across trials) confirmed the effect as real but modest (NNTB 12 for >=50% pain reduction; Uceyler N et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 24129853). (2) Duloxetine (Cymbalta), FDA-approved 2008 -- in a 520-patient, 6-month RCT, 120 mg/day improved Brief Pain Inventory average pain by -2.31 versus -1.39 with placebo at 3 months (p<0.001), sustained at 6 months (-2.26 vs -1.43, p=0.003) (Russell IJ et al., Pain 2008, PMID 18395345); an earlier 207-patient trial found a 5.53-point-greater improvement in the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire versus placebo (p=0.027), with the effect concentrated in women (Arnold LM et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004, PMID 15457467). (3) Milnacipran (Savella), FDA-approved 2009 (the most recently approved of the three) -- in its FDA pivotal registration trial (Study MLN-MD-02, n=1196, 3-month ITT landmark), 200 mg/day produced a composite FM-pain responder rate of 25% versus 16% on placebo (p=0.0037), and 100 mg/day produced 23% versus 16% (p=0.0252) (FDA CDER Division Director Summary Review, NDA 22-256, Savella/milnacipran, Jan 13 2009; published as Mease PJ et al., J Rheumatol 2009, PMID 19132781). Pooling duloxetine and milnacipran together, a 2018 Cochrane review of SNRIs (Welsch P et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018, PMID 29489029) found 31% achieved >=50% pain relief versus 21% on placebo (NNTB 11), and 52% reported being 'much/very much improved' on Patient Global Impression of Change versus 29% on placebo (NNTB 5) -- but with a real, quantified adverse-event dropout cost (19% vs 10% on placebo). The most recent and most honest single summary is a 2025 Cochrane overview of 21 reviews covering 87 trials and 17,631 patients (Moore RA et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2025, PMID 39705187): duloxetine, milnacipran and pregabalin have 'moderate/good evidence of substantial pain relief for 4-12 weeks in around 1 in 10 adults' (i.e., roughly a 10% net-of-placebo effect for a >=50% pain-intensity reduction), with 'no evidence of efficacy beyond six months' -- a real, guideline-level statement that drug effects in FM are genuine but modest and short-term-proven, exactly the honest context in which exercise's EULAR-unique 'strong for' grade, durability, and absence of systemic harm make it the real closest thing FM has to a foundational, disease-modifying-in-impact therapy. Bottom line, cure-first framing: FM is not curable by any single current therapy, but a graduated, guideline-based combination -- exercise as the evidence-strongest foundation, CBT layered in for pain-coping and mood, and pregabalin/duloxetine/milnacipran reserved for patients with severe pain or sleep disturbance not controlled by the non-pharmacological base (EULAR 2017 four-stage framework, PMID 27377815) -- achieves the best real, durable, side-effect-minimised outcome the current evidence supports.

curative_option.name: Graduated Multimodal Therapy -- Aerobic/Aquatic Exercise (Real EULAR 'Strong For' Foundation) + CBT, with Pregabalin, Duloxetine or Milnacipran Added Only for Severe Pain/Sleep Disturbance Not Controlled by the Non-Drug Base (EULAR 2017 Four-Stage Framework)
curative_option.note: There is no single cure for fibromyalgia, but the real, guideline-endorsed closest-to-cure strategy is not a drug -- it is a graduated combination built around exercise. The 2017 EULAR revised recommendations (Macfarlane GJ et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017, PMID 27377815), derived from 107 eligible systematic reviews/meta-analyses out of 2,979 titles screened, gave exercise the ONLY 'strong for' recommendation among all pharmacological and non-pharmacological therapies assessed, and set out a four-stage graduated approach: (1) patient education plus exercise/non-pharmacological therapy as the mandatory first stage for all patients; (2) psychological therapies (CBT) added for patients with mood or coping difficulties; (3) pharmacotherapy (pregabalin, duloxetine or milnacipran) added for patients with severe pain or sleep disturbance who have not responded adequately to stages 1-2; (4) multimodal rehabilitation reserved for severe, refractory disability. This sequencing is evidence-driven, not a default drug-first pathway: EULAR explicitly rated every pharmacological therapy only 'weak for,' in contrast to exercise's 'strong for' grade.

real_trial_data.eular_2017_evidence_hierarchy: 107 eligible systematic reviews/meta-analyses out of 2,979 titles screened; exercise = only 'strong for' recommendation; all pharmacotherapy = 'weak for'; explicit conclusion that 'the size of effect for most treatments is relatively modest' -- Macfarlane GJ et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017 (PMID 27377815)
real_trial_data.aerobic_exercise_cochrane: 13 RCTs, n=839; pain MD -11.06/100 VAS (18% relative improvement); HRQoL MD -7.89 (15% relative); physical function MD -10.16 (10% absolute) -- Bidonde J et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017 (PMID 28636204)
real_trial_data.aquatic_exercise_cochrane: 16 RCTs; multidimensional function improved 6 units (95% CI -9.06 to -2.88); pain improved 7 units (95% CI -10.71 to -2.48); stiffness improved 18 units; muscle strength SMD 0.63 (95% CI 0.20 to 1.05); no serious adverse effects -- Bidonde J et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014 (PMID 25350761)
real_trial_data.cbt_cochrane: 23 RCTs, n=2031; pain -0.5/10 (end of treatment) to -0.6/10 (follow-up); negative mood -0.7/10 to -1.3/10; disability -0.7/10 to -1.2/10 -- Bernardy K et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013 (PMID 24018611); updated 2018 review (29 RCTs, n=2509) confirmed a 'clinically relevant benefit' -- Bernardy K et al., Eur J Pain 2018 (PMID 28984402)
real_trial_data.pharmacotherapy_2025_honest_summary: 21 Cochrane reviews, 87 trials, 17,631 patients: duloxetine, milnacipran and pregabalin have moderate/good evidence of substantial (>=50%) pain relief in around 1 in 10 adults net of placebo, for 4-12 weeks, with no evidence of efficacy beyond 6 months; serious adverse events not more common than placebo -- Moore RA et al., Rheumatology (Oxford) 2025 (PMID 39705187)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full real survey of FM therapy, led with the treatment carrying the strongest real evidence grade (exercise, EULAR 2017's only 'strong for' recommendation), then CBT, then the three FDA-approved drugs in FDA-approval order (pregabalin 2007, duloxetine 2008, milnacipran 2009), then an honest note on other commonly used but weaker-evidence adjuncts.

fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.name: Aerobic Exercise Training (e.g., walking, cycling, aquatic aerobics -- graduated, individually titrated)
fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.type: Exercise therapy (non-pharmacological, first stage of care)
fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.effectiveness: Cochrane review, 13 RCTs, n=839: pain reduced by a mean of 11.06 points on a 0-100 VAS (18% relative improvement); health-related quality of life improved by 7.89 points (15% relative); physical function improved by 10.16 points (10% absolute); the ONLY treatment (drug or non-drug) to receive a 'strong for' EULAR 2017 recommendation.
fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.reason_why: Fibromyalgia involves central sensitisation and dysregulated descending pain-inhibitory pathways; regular aerobic exercise upregulates endogenous opioid and cannabinoid tone, improves autonomic and HPA-axis regulation, and produces measurable normalisation of central pain processing -- addressing a proposed root mechanism of FM rather than only masking symptoms, and doing so without the systemic drug-adverse-effect burden seen with pharmacotherapy.

fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.name: Aquatic Exercise / Warm-Water Therapy
fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.effectiveness: Cochrane review, 16 RCTs: pain improved by 7 points (95% CI -10.71 to -2.48); stiffness improved by 18 points; multidimensional function improved by 6 points (95% CI -9.06 to -2.88); muscle strength improved with a moderate-to-large effect (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.05); no serious adverse effects reported.
fm_exercise_therapy_strong_recommendatio.reason_why: Warm water reduces joint/muscle loading and eases the initiation of exercise in patients with high baseline pain and exercise-intolerance, while providing the same central-sensitisation-modulating aerobic stimulus as land-based exercise -- a practical on-ramp to the land-based programmes with the largest evidence base.

fm_cognitive_behavioural_therapy_medicin.name: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), individual or group
fm_cognitive_behavioural_therapy_medicin.effectiveness: Cochrane review, 23 RCTs, n=2031: pain reduced by 0.5/10 points at treatment end (0.6/10 at follow-up); negative mood reduced by 0.7/10 (1.3/10 at follow-up); disability reduced by 0.7/10 (1.2/10 at follow-up) -- a real, durable but modest 'small incremental benefit.' An updated 2018 review (29 RCTs, n=2509) confirmed a 'clinically relevant benefit' over control interventions.
fm_cognitive_behavioural_therapy_medicin.reason_why: CBT targets pain catastrophising, fear-avoidance behaviour and maladaptive coping, which independently amplify centrally mediated pain perception in FM; by modifying these cognitive-behavioural amplifiers, CBT reduces the perceived pain and disability burden even though it does not alter the underlying nociceptive/nociplastic drive itself.

fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.name: Duloxetine (brand: Cymbalta), 60-120 mg/day
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.type: Serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI); FDA-approved for fibromyalgia 2008
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.effectiveness: 520-patient, 6-month RCT: 120 mg/day improved Brief Pain Inventory average pain by -2.31 vs -1.39 with placebo at 3 months (p<0.001), sustained at 6 months (-2.26 vs -1.43, p=0.003) (PMID 18395345). Earlier 207-patient trial: Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire total score improved 5.53 points more than placebo (p=0.027), effect concentrated in women (PMID 15457467). Pooled with milnacipran in a 2018 Cochrane SNRI review: 31% achieved >=50% pain relief vs 21% placebo (NNTB 11); 52% 'much/very much improved' vs 29% placebo (NNTB 5), with 19% adverse-event dropout vs 10% placebo (PMID 29489029).
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.reason_why: Dual reuptake inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine enhances descending inhibitory pain pathways from the brainstem to the dorsal horn, directly counteracting the deficient descending pain inhibition documented in FM's central-sensitisation model.

fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.name: Milnacipran (brand: Savella), 100-200 mg/day
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.type: Serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI); FDA-approved for fibromyalgia 2009
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.effectiveness: FDA pivotal registration trial (Study MLN-MD-02, n=1196, 3-month ITT landmark): composite FM-pain responder rate 25% with 200 mg/day vs 16% placebo (p=0.0037); 23% with 100 mg/day vs 16% placebo (p=0.0252). Composite FM-syndrome responder rate 14-15% (both doses) vs 9% placebo (p<0.02 both doses).
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.reason_why: Same dual serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake-inhibition mechanism as duloxetine, restoring descending pain-inhibitory tone; milnacipran has relatively greater noradrenergic potency than duloxetine, which is proposed to underlie its additional benefit on fatigue and global function in some trials.
fm_fda_approved_snri_medicines.source: FDA CDER Division Director Summary Review, NDA 22-256 (Savella/milnacipran), Jan 13 2009; PMID 19132781

fm_fda_approved_alpha2delta_ligand_medic.name: Pregabalin (brand: Lyrica), 300-450 mg/day
fm_fda_approved_alpha2delta_ligand_medic.type: Alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligand; FDA-approved for fibromyalgia 2007 (first FM-specific drug approval)
fm_fda_approved_alpha2delta_ligand_medic.effectiveness: 529-patient pivotal RCT: 450 mg/day produced >=50% pain reduction in 29% of patients vs 13% on placebo (PMID 15818684). Cochrane anticonvulsants review (2480 patients across trials): >=50% pain reduction RR 1.59 (95% CI 1.33-1.90), NNTB 12; 'much/very much improved' RR 1.38, NNTB 9; dizziness NNTH 4 (PMID 24129853).
fm_fda_approved_alpha2delta_ligand_medic.reason_why: Binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels on central and peripheral sensory neurons, reducing excess release of excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate, substance P) implicated in FM's central sensitisation, without acting on opioid or dopaminergic systems.

fm_other_adjunct_medicines_weaker_eviden.name: Amitriptyline, Cyclobenzaprine, and Other Older Off-Label Agents
fm_other_adjunct_medicines_weaker_eviden.type: Tricyclic antidepressant / muscle relaxant (off-label, no FDA approval specifically for FM; other/lower priority)
fm_other_adjunct_medicines_weaker_eviden.effectiveness: Widely used historically and still commonly prescribed off-label, but a 2025 Cochrane overview of 21 reviews/87 trials/17,631 patients explicitly flagged amitriptyline as one of the drug classes 'subject to publication bias,' meaning its true effect size is less reliably established than that of the three FDA-approved drugs; the overview reserved its 'moderate/good evidence' verdict for duloxetine, milnacipran and pregabalin specifically.
fm_other_adjunct_medicines_weaker_eviden.reason_why: Low-dose tricyclics are thought to help via similar descending noradrenergic/serotonergic pain-modulation and improved sleep architecture, but the evidence base predates modern trial-registration and publication-bias safeguards, making the real effect size honestly uncertain rather than a quantifiable number.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.no_new_drug_class_note: No new drug class has received FDA approval specifically for fibromyalgia since milnacipran (2009); the most recent (2025) Cochrane overview (PMID 39705187) confirms pregabalin, duloxetine and milnacipran remain the only three drugs with a specific, guideline-recognised evidence base for FM, and states plainly that none show proven efficacy beyond 6 months.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT primary endpoints (>=50% pain reduction responder rate, composite FM-pain responder criteria, or continuous-scale relative improvement) in DIFFERENT populations -- ranking together is directionally useful, not strictly apples-to-apples, exactly as the RLS and other multi-drug KB entries note. The exercise and CBT rows report continuous-scale percentage improvements (relative to baseline or to the scale's range), not categorical responder rates, and are stated as such -- not a fabricated responder percentage. Despite ranking below the drugs on this single-metric table, exercise carries the strongest real evidence grade in fibromyalgia: it was the ONLY treatment among 107 systematic reviews/meta-analyses assessed to receive a 'strong for' EULAR 2017 recommendation, versus 'weak for' for every drug in this table (PMID 27377815); a 2025 Cochrane overview of the three approved drugs (PMID 39705187) independently confirms their real effect is a net-of-placebo benefit in only 'around 1 in 10 adults,' with no proven efficacy beyond 6 months -- so the numeric ranking below should be read alongside this evidence-grade and durability context, not in isolation.

scoliosis.name: Scoliosis
scoliosis.icd11_hint: ICD-10 M41 Scoliosis (M41.0 Infantile idiopathic scoliosis, M41.1 Juvenile/adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, by common clinical-coding convention) - this is standard, widely-taught clinical coding knowledge. The exact ICD-11 code (expected under chapter FA, Diseases of the musculoskeletal system, commonly cited as FA70 Scoliosis with subcodes for idiopathic vs congenital/structural forms) could NOT be independently verified this session: the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) requires client-side JavaScript rendering not accessible to this session's fetch tool, the WHO ICD-11 API requires an OAuth2 token that was not available, and third-party ICD-11 mirror sites (icd.codes, icd10data.com) returned HTTP 403. FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED pending direct confirmation against the WHO ICD-11 API/browser.
scoliosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) has one of the strongest real, landmark non-surgical success stories in this entire knowledge base: the NIH-funded BrAIST randomized controlled trial (Bracing in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis Trial) proved that bracing a moderate curve (Cobb angle 20-40 degrees) in a skeletally immature adolescent dramatically cuts the chance the curve ever progresses to the 50-degree surgical threshold.
