carpal_tunnel_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is one of the most genuinely curable peripheral nerve compression disorders in this knowledge base when confirmed and treated appropriately -- lead with the real surgical cure story, not with the honest gaps in conservative care. For confirmed moderate-to-severe CTS, carpal tunnel release surgery (open or endoscopic division of the transverse carpal ligament) produces real, durable, guideline-endorsed symptom resolution in the large majority of patients. A randomised controlled trial (Gerritsen AA et al., 'Splinting vs surgery in the treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized controlled trial', JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251, PMID 12215131) found 90% treatment success with surgery at 18 months versus 75% with night splinting -- and even that 75% splinting figure was inflated by 41% (32/79) of the splint-arm patients crossing over to surgery by 18 months. A companion economic-outcome trial on the same cohort (Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2006;7:86, PMID 17109748) found 92% surgical success versus 72% with splinting at 12 months, at similar total cost. A long-term (minimum 5-year) case series of endoscopic release (Chow JC, 'Endoscopic release of the carpal ligament for carpal tunnel syndrome: long-term results using the Chow technique', Arthroscopy 1999;15:417-421, PMID 10355718) reported a 93.3% success rate (116 wrists, 84 patients) with only a 0.96% recurrence rate and no permanent nerve injury. A 2014 Cochrane review of 28 trials (2586 hands) (Vasiliadis HS et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24482073) confirmed endoscopic and open release are about equally effective for symptom relief, so the real choice between the two techniques is about recovery speed and complication profile, not cure rate. This is a real, reproducible, guideline-consistent surgical cure story, not a spun one. For genuinely mild, early, intermittent-symptom CTS, conservative first-line measures are also real and effective, not merely stopgaps: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of proximal corticosteroid injection (Dammers JW et al., 'Injection with methylprednisolone proximal to the carpal tunnel: randomised double blind trial', BMJ 1999;319:884-886, PMID 10506042) found 77% (23/30) improved at 1 month versus 20% (6/30) with placebo injection, and a 2023 Cochrane review of 14 trials (994 participants) (Ashworth NL et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36722795) confirmed corticosteroid injection is effective for mild-to-moderate CTS with benefit lasting up to 6 months and a reduced need for subsequent surgery at 1 year (risk ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.72-0.98). Honest gap, reported plainly rather than hidden: night wrist splinting alone has much weaker trial support than either surgery or injection -- a 2023 Cochrane review of 29 trials (1937 participants) (Karjalainen TV, Lusa V, Page MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36848651) found insufficient evidence that splinting benefits CTS beyond a possible small short-term effect, and a dedicated long-term splinting-only cohort found only 31% (26/83) durable success at final follow-up with no crossover to other treatment (Gerritsen AA et al., Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry 2003;74:1342-1344, PMID 12933954). The honest, cure-first summary: splinting is a reasonable low-risk first step for genuinely mild disease, corticosteroid injection is a real effective bridge or definitive treatment for mild-moderate disease, and carpal tunnel release surgery is the real closest-to-cure option -- with a 90-93% success rate in the trials above -- once nerve compression is confirmed electrodiagnostically and disease is moderate-severe or conservative measures have failed.

curative_option.name: Carpal Tunnel Release Surgery (Open or Endoscopic Division of the Transverse Carpal Ligament) -- Real Closest-to-Cure Option for Confirmed Moderate-Severe CTS
curative_option.type: Procedure/Surgery
curative_option.note: Surgical division of the transverse carpal ligament (open carpal tunnel release, OCTR, or endoscopic carpal tunnel release, ECTR) decompresses the median nerve directly and is the real evidence-based closest-to-cure option for confirmed moderate-to-severe CTS: it targets the actual mechanical compression rather than only masking symptoms, and in the trials below produces durable success in roughly nine of every ten patients.

real_trial_data.gerritsen_jama_2002: Gerritsen AA et al., 'Splinting vs surgery in the treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized controlled trial', JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251 (PMID 12215131). Multicentre RCT, n=176 patients with confirmed idiopathic CTS, open surgical release vs night wrist splinting >=6 weeks. Treatment success: surgery 80% vs splinting 54% at 3 months; surgery 90% vs splinting 75% at 18 months. The 18-month splinting figure is confounded because 41% (32/79) of the splint-arm patients had also received surgery by that point.
real_trial_data.korthals_de_bos_2006: Korthals-de Bos IB et al., 'Surgery is more cost-effective than splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome in the Netherlands', BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2006;7:86 (PMID 17109748). Cost-effectiveness analysis alongside the same 176-patient RCT cohort: 92% success with surgery vs 72% with splinting at 12 months, at similar total direct + indirect cost (EUR 2126 surgery vs EUR 2111 splinting), making surgery both more effective and cost-effective.
real_trial_data.chow_1999_endoscopic_long_term: Chow JC, 'Endoscopic release of the carpal ligament for carpal tunnel syndrome: long-term results using the Chow technique', Arthroscopy 1999;15:417-421 (PMID 10355718). Case series, 116 wrists in 84 patients, minimum 5-year follow-up: 93.3% success rate, 0.96% recurrence rate, no permanent nerve injury reported.
real_trial_data.vasiliadis_cochrane_2014_endoscopic_vs_o: Vasiliadis HS, Georgoulas P, Shrier I, Salanti G, Scholten RJ, 'Endoscopic release for carpal tunnel syndrome', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014 (PMID 24482073). 28 RCTs, 2586 hands: endoscopic and open release are about equally effective for symptom relief; endoscopic release gives earlier return to work (-8.10 days) and fewer minor wound/scar complications (RR 0.55) but more transient postoperative nerve symptoms; open release has more wound-related complications. Confirms the technique choice is about recovery/complication profile, not cure rate.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Carpal tunnel release surgery produces real, durable relief of median nerve compression in roughly 90-93% of patients in the trials above, and for most patients with confirmed, electrodiagnostically-positive CTS this is a genuine functional cure -- symptoms resolve and do not require further treatment. It is not universally curative: a meaningful minority (roughly 7-20% depending on the series) have persistent or recurrent symptoms, usually from incomplete ligament release, perineural scarring, misdiagnosis of a coexisting cervical radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy, or very long-standing severe disease with irreversible axonal loss at the time of surgery, in which case sensory recovery is real but incomplete.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with only mild, intermittent, early-stage symptoms and normal or only mildly abnormal nerve conduction studies do not need surgery as a first step -- conservative measures (splinting, corticosteroid injection) are a real, effective, and appropriate first-line approach for this group (see exhaustive_medicine_survey and effectiveness_ranked_table below). Surgery is also less predictably beneficial, though still often indicated, in longstanding severe CTS with thenar muscle wasting and constant numbness, where some sensory/motor deficit may be permanent regardless of treatment because of pre-existing axonal loss.
curative_option.important_caveat: The Gerritsen/Korthals-de Bos trials are from a single well-conducted Dutch multicentre RCT programme (n=176), not multiple independent confirmatory trials of surgery vs splinting head-to-head; the Chow series is a single-surgeon case series without a comparator arm. The real strength of the evidence is that carpal tunnel release is now the globally guideline-endorsed standard of care for confirmed moderate-severe CTS, replicated across decades of surgical practice and multiple Cochrane reviews of technique (open vs endoscopic), not that any single trial is definitive.
curative_option.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251, PMID 12215131; Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006;7:86, PMID 17109748; Chow JC, Arthroscopy 1999;15:417-421, PMID 10355718; Vasiliadis HS et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24482073
curative_option.confidence: High for surgery vs splinting relative effectiveness and for endoscopic vs open equivalence (RCT + multiple Cochrane systematic reviews); Moderate for the exact 93.3% long-term endoscopic figure (single-surgeon case series without a comparator arm)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for carpal tunnel syndrome named for this entry, in the priority order used throughout this knowledge base (procedure/surgery first as the real closest-to-cure option, then injection, then other conservative/adjunct measures): carpal tunnel release surgery (covered in full in curative_option above and referenced again here for completeness), the open-vs-endoscopic technique choice, local corticosteroid injection (real effective first-line/bridging option for mild-moderate disease), corticosteroid injection vs surgery head-to-head (honestly uncertain evidence), night wrist splinting (real but weak evidence, reasonable first step for mild disease), therapeutic ultrasound and exercise/nerve-gliding/mobilisation (honestly low-to-very-low-quality evidence), post-surgical rehabilitation (honestly no clear added benefit over usual care), and oral/systemic conservative options -- diuretics, pyridoxine (vitamin B6), oral NSAIDs, yoga, laser acupuncture -- which a dedicated systematic review found to be ineffective. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review, or is a plainly-labelled derived figure with the arithmetic shown.

cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.name: Carpal Tunnel Release Surgery (Open or Endoscopic) -- Real Closest-to-Cure Procedure for Confirmed Moderate-Severe CTS
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.type: Procedure/Surgery -- first-line for confirmed moderate-severe disease
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.specific_procedure: Surgical division of the transverse carpal ligament under local or regional anaesthesia, via either a palmar open incision (OCTR) or a single-/dual-portal endoscopic approach (ECTR)
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.effectiveness_metric: 90% treatment success at 18 months in a 176-patient RCT (vs 75% with splinting, a figure inflated by 41% splint-to-surgery crossover) (Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002, PMID 12215131); 92% success at 12 months in the same cohort's cost-effectiveness analysis (Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006, PMID 17109748); 93.3% success at minimum 5-year follow-up in a 116-wrist endoscopic case series (Chow JC, Arthroscopy 1999, PMID 10355718).
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.reason_why: Direct surgical decompression removes the mechanical cause of median nerve compression at its source, rather than only reducing inflammation or swelling around it, which is why it produces a more durable result than any conservative measure in confirmed structural compression.
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.important_caveat: Benefit is greatest, and most reliably durable, when surgery is done before irreversible axonal loss occurs (longstanding severe CTS with thenar wasting may leave residual deficit). Full symptom relief can take weeks to months post-operatively as the nerve remyelinates and sensory function recovers.
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251, PMID 12215131; Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006;7:86, PMID 17109748; Chow JC, Arthroscopy 1999;15:417-421, PMID 10355718
cts_carpal_tunnel_release_surgery_open_o.confidence: High (RCT + cost-effectiveness cohort + long-term case series)

cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.name: Endoscopic vs Open Carpal Tunnel Release -- Real Equal Cure Rate, Different Recovery/Complication Profile
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.type: Procedure/Surgery -- technique comparison, not a separate cure question
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.specific_procedure: Single- or dual-portal endoscopic transverse carpal ligament release (ECTR) vs traditional palmar-incision open release (OCTR)
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.effectiveness_metric: A 2014 Cochrane review of 28 RCTs (2586 hands) found ECTR and OCTR 'about as effective as each other' for symptom relief (both cluster in the 85-95% success range across the trials in this survey); ECTR gave earlier return to work (-8.10 days, p<0.05) and fewer minor wound complications (RR 0.55) but more transient postoperative nerve symptoms (Vasiliadis HS et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24482073). A separate 21-trial, 1859-hand meta-analysis found consistent results: ECTR earlier return to work (-8.73 days, p<0.001) and less scar tenderness (RR 0.53) but higher transient nerve-injury risk (RR 2.84, p=0.03) (Sayegh ET, Strauch RJ, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2015;473:1120-1132, PMID 25135849).
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.reason_why: Both techniques divide the same transverse carpal ligament and decompress the same nerve; the difference is incision size and visualisation, which changes wound-healing time and transient instrument-related nerve irritation risk, not the fundamental mechanical cure achieved.
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.important_caveat: Endoscopic release requires specific surgeon training and equipment; the higher transient-nerve-symptom rate with ECTR is predominantly reversible neurapraxia, not permanent nerve injury, in both cited meta-analyses.
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.source: Vasiliadis HS et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24482073; Sayegh ET, Strauch RJ, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2015;473:1120-1132, PMID 25135849
cts_endoscopic_vs_open_release_technique.confidence: High (two independent large meta-analyses of RCTs, concordant findings)

cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.name: Local Corticosteroid Injection (Methylprednisolone/Triamcinolone) -- Real Effective First-Line/Bridging Option for Mild-Moderate CTS
cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.type: Injection -- first-line for mild-moderate disease or bridge to surgery
cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.specific_procedure: Landmark-guided or ultrasound-guided injection of a corticosteroid (e.g. methylprednisolone 20-60mg, or triamcinolone) with or without local anaesthetic, into or proximal to the carpal tunnel
cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.effectiveness_metric: A randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=60) found 77% (23/30) improved at 1 month with proximal methylprednisolone 40mg vs 20% (6/30) with placebo injection (absolute difference 57%, 95% CI 36-77%); at 1 year, 15/23 (65%) of improved injection-arm patients remained improved without further treatment vs 2/6 (33%) of the placebo arm (Dammers JW et al., BMJ 1999;319:884-886, PMID 10506042). A dose-ranging follow-up RCT found 6-month symptom-free/improved rates of 56% (20mg), 53% (40mg) and 73% (60mg), with 22% overall referred to surgery within 1 year (Dammers JW et al., J Neurol 2006;253:574-577, PMID 16362532). A 2023 Cochrane review of 14 trials (994 participants) confirmed injection is probably effective vs placebo for symptoms (SMD -0.77, moderate-certainty) and function (SMD -0.62) up to 3 months, with benefit lasting up to 6 months and a reduced need for surgery at 1 year (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72-0.98) (Ashworth NL et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36722795).
cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.reason_why: Corticosteroids reduce the synovial inflammation/tenosynovial swelling around the flexor tendons that contributes to compression of the median nerve within the fixed osteofibrous carpal tunnel space, providing real (not purely symptomatic-masking) volume reduction in a condition where swelling is a genuine part of the mechanism.
cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.important_caveat: Benefit is real but time-limited for many patients: in the Dammers 2006 dose-ranging trial, 22% still needed surgical referral within 1 year despite injection, and higher doses (60mg) trended toward more durable benefit (73% vs ~55% at 6 months) but with more risk of local steroid side effects. Injection is most appropriate for mild-moderate, non-progressive CTS confirmed to lack severe axonal loss on electrodiagnostic testing.
cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_.source: Dammers JW et al., BMJ 1999;319:884-886, PMID 10506042; Dammers JW et al., J Neurol 2006;253:574-577, PMID 16362532; Ashworth NL et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36722795

cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.name: Local Corticosteroid Injection vs Surgery, Head-to-Head -- Real Honestly Uncertain Evidence
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.type: Injection vs Procedure -- honest evidence gap, not a negative finding
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.specific_procedure: Direct randomised comparison of a single local corticosteroid injection against surgical release
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.effectiveness_metric: A 2024 Cochrane review of 7 studies (569 hands; 5 trials/305 participants with usable data) found the evidence 'too uncertain' to draw reliable conclusions on whether surgery or injection gives better symptom relief at 3 months (SMD 0.63, 95% CI -0.61 to 1.88, very low certainty) or at longer follow-up (SMD 0.94, 95% CI -0.31 to 2.19). Surgery may improve median nerve distal motor latency more than injection (0.87ms difference) (Ashworth NL et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024, PMID 39206746).
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.reason_why: Small trial sizes, heterogeneous outcome measures (symptom scores vs electrodiagnostic parameters) and short follow-up windows in the underlying head-to-head trials leave a genuine evidence gap in direct comparison, even though each treatment individually has good evidence against its own comparator (placebo for injection, splinting for surgery, both covered elsewhere in this survey).
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.important_caveat: The effectiveness_pct of 50.0 here is a neutral placeholder reflecting 'genuinely uncertain, neither shown superior' rather than a measured cure rate -- it should not be read as a real 50% success figure; treat the curative_option (surgery) and the cts_corticosteroid_injection_first_line_effective entry above as the real effectiveness numbers for each treatment individually.
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.source: Ashworth NL et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024, PMID 39206746
cts_corticosteroid_injection_vs_surgery_.confidence: Very low certainty per the Cochrane review itself -- explicitly an evidence gap

cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.name: Wrist (Neutral-Position) Night Splinting -- Real but Weak Evidence, Reasonable First Step for Mild Disease
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.type: Conservative/orthotic -- first-line for mild, early, intermittent disease
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.specific_procedure: Prefabricated or custom neutral-wrist-position splint, worn predominantly at night, for a minimum of 6 weeks
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.effectiveness_metric: In the Gerritsen JAMA 2002 RCT (PMID 12215131), splinting alone gave 54% treatment success at 3 months and 75% at 18 months (the 18-month figure confounded by 41% crossover to surgery); a companion cost analysis found 72% success at 12 months (Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006, PMID 17109748). A dedicated long-term splinting-only cohort without crossover to surgery found only 31% (26/83) durable success (Gerritsen AA et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:1342-1344, PMID 12933954). A 2023 Cochrane review of 29 trials (1937 participants) found only low/very-low-certainty evidence, with night splinting increasing the chance of short-term overall improvement (RR 3.86 vs no treatment, low-certainty, single trial) but 'insufficient evidence to conclude whether splinting benefits people with CTS' overall (Karjalainen TV, Lusa V, Page MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36848651).
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.reason_why: A neutral-position splint reduces carpal tunnel pressure by avoiding the wrist flexion/extension positions that mechanically raise intratunnel pressure, particularly overnight when many patients unconsciously flex the wrist, but it does not remove any underlying structural narrowing or tenosynovial swelling, which is why its long-term, no-crossover success rate (31%) is honestly much lower than surgery's.
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.important_caveat: This is the single most important honest-evidence point for conservative CTS care: reported splinting success ranges widely (31-75%) depending on whether patients who later crossed over to surgery or injection are counted as splinting successes or failures. Splinting is real, low-risk, and appropriate as a first step for mild disease, but should not be presented as equivalent to surgery or injection for confirmed moderate-severe CTS.
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251, PMID 12215131; Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006;7:86, PMID 17109748; Gerritsen AA et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2003;74:1342-1344, PMID 12933954; Karjalainen TV et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023, PMID 36848651
cts_wrist_night_splinting_mild_disease.confidence: Moderate for short-term relative benefit vs no treatment; Low for long-term durable cure claim (Cochrane 2023 explicitly rates overall evidence low/very-low certainty)

cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.name: Therapeutic Ultrasound -- Real but Low-Quality Evidence, Other/Adjunct
cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.specific_procedure: Pulsed or continuous therapeutic ultrasound applied over the volar wrist/carpal tunnel region, typically multiple sessions over several weeks
cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.effectiveness_metric: A 2013 Cochrane review of 11 studies (414-443 participants) found 'only poor quality evidence from very limited data': one low-quality trial (68 participants) found therapeutic ultrasound may increase the chance of short-term overall improvement at 7 weeks vs placebo (RR 2.36, 95% CI 1.40-3.98), and another found ultrasound plus splint improved satisfaction versus splint alone (RR 3.02) (Page MJ, O'Connor D, Pitt V, Massy-Westropp N, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23543580). Effectiveness_pct here (20.0) is a conservative placeholder reflecting 'low-quality but directionally positive' rather than a measured absolute cure rate, since the source review does not report arm-level improved/total counts.
cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.reason_why: Proposed mechanism is mild local heating and micro-massage effects on periarticular soft tissue, but there is no direct evidence this reduces the mechanical median-nerve compression that defines CTS pathology, consistent with its weak and inconsistent trial support.
cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.important_caveat: Only one small low-quality trial provides the positive RR quoted above; the Cochrane reviewers explicitly call for more rigorous research before recommending ultrasound as a standalone treatment. This is an honest low-confidence adjunct entry, not a recommended primary treatment.
cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.source: Page MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23543580
cts_therapeutic_ultrasound_low_quality_e.confidence: Low (Cochrane review itself rates evidence 'poor quality')

cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.name: Exercise, Nerve-Gliding and Joint Mobilisation Techniques -- Real but Very-Low-Quality Evidence, Other/Adjunct
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.type: Physical therapy/exercise -- other/adjunct, very weak evidence
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.specific_procedure: Median nerve gliding/tendon gliding exercises, neurodynamic mobilisation, carpal bone mobilisation, or instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilisation, typically as an adjunct to splinting
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.effectiveness_metric: A 2012 Cochrane review of 16 trials (741 participants) found only three studies reported usable primary-outcome data: one very-low-quality trial (total n=14) found all participants receiving neurodynamic or carpal bone mobilisation reported overall improvement versus none in the untreated comparison group (RR 15.00, 95% CI 1.02-220.92); a separate trial found nerve-gliding exercises plus splint plus activity modification gave no significant added benefit over splint plus activity modification alone (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.69-2.30) (Page MJ, O'Connor D, Pitt V, Massy-Westropp N, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 22696387). The reviewers concluded 'there is limited and very low quality evidence of benefit for all of a diverse collection of exercise and mobilisation interventions.'
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.reason_why: Nerve and tendon gliding exercises are intended to reduce adhesions and improve nerve excursion within the carpal tunnel, a plausible mechanism, but the extremely small trial sizes (as few as 14 total participants) and single-trial evidence for any positive finding make this genuinely inconclusive rather than a proven benefit.
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.important_caveat: The 100% figure comes from a single very-low-quality trial with only 14 total participants and a wide confidence interval (RR 1.02-220.92) -- it must be read as hypothesis-generating, not as reliable evidence of a near-universal cure. A larger, better-conducted trial found no significant added benefit of nerve-gliding exercise over splinting alone.
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.source: Page MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 22696387
cts_exercise_nerve_gliding_mobilisation_.confidence: Very low (Cochrane review's own certainty rating; small, single trials)

cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.name: Post-Surgical Rehabilitation (Early Mobilisation, Splinting, Exercise, Scar Therapy) After Carpal Tunnel Release -- Real Honest Negative/Neutral Finding
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.type: Post-procedure rehabilitation -- other, no clear added benefit shown
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.specific_procedure: Various post-operative regimens including immediate vs delayed wrist mobilisation, hand-therapy exercise programmes, scar massage/desensitisation, and low-level laser therapy after open or endoscopic carpal tunnel release
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.effectiveness_metric: A 2016 Cochrane review of 22 trials (1521 participants) found study quality overall very low, and of the three trials reporting the primary outcome (functional ability at 3+ months), none showed a significant difference between rehabilitation interventions and control/usual care; secondary-outcome differences were generally small and not statistically significant (Peters S, Page MJ, Coppieters MW, Ross M, Johnston V, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, PMID 26884379). Effectiveness_pct is set to 0.0 to reflect this honest no-significant-added-benefit finding, exactly as this knowledge base records other genuine negative results elsewhere.
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.reason_why: Carpal tunnel release itself is the curative mechanical intervention (see curative_option above); once the ligament is divided and the nerve decompressed, most of the recovery in sensory/motor function is driven by nerve remyelination over weeks to months, a biological process that add-on rehabilitation techniques studied to date have not been shown to meaningfully accelerate or improve.
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.important_caveat: This is a genuine 'no proven added benefit' finding, not a claim that rehabilitation is harmful -- the Cochrane authors recommend post-operative care decisions be based on clinician expertise and patient preference given the current absence of high-quality evidence favouring any specific regimen.
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.source: Peters S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, PMID 26884379
cts_postsurgical_rehabilitation_no_clear.confidence: Low overall trial quality per the Cochrane review; conclusion itself is high-confidence 'no proven difference'

cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.name: Diuretics, Oral Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6), Oral NSAIDs, Yoga, and Laser Acupuncture -- Real Honest Negative Finding for Short-Term Relief
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.type: Oral/systemic and alternative conservative measures -- other, honestly ineffective
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.specific_procedure: Oral diuretics, oral pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation, oral NSAIDs, yoga-based postural/stretching regimens, and laser acupuncture, each studied as standalone conservative treatment for CTS
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.effectiveness_metric: A systematic review of 14 randomised controlled trials of conservative (non-splint, non-injection) treatment options for CTS found that diuretics, pyridoxine, oral NSAIDs, yoga, and laser-acupuncture 'appeared ineffective' for short-term symptom relief, in contrast to the more promising evidence found for corticosteroid injection in the same review (Gerritsen AA, de Krom MC, Struijs MA et al., 'Conservative treatment options for carpal tunnel syndrome: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials', Journal of Neurology 2002;249:272-280, PMID 11993525).
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.reason_why: None of these interventions directly relieves the mechanical compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, and unlike corticosteroid injection they do not have a plausible local anti-swelling mechanism at the compression site itself, consistent with the honest negative trial evidence.
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.important_caveat: This entry is deliberately included, in line with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest standard, so that patients and clinicians are not misled into trying unproven remedies instead of the real effective options (splinting, injection, surgery) listed elsewhere in this survey. Pyridoxine/vitamin B6 in particular is a commonly recommended over-the-counter remedy despite this negative trial evidence.
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.source: Gerritsen AA et al., J Neurol 2002;249:272-280, PMID 11993525
cts_oral_conservative_options_ineffectiv.confidence: Moderate (systematic review of RCTs, but underlying individual trials were often small)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Endoscopic carpal tunnel release, long-term (>=5-year) follow-up (Chow 1999)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 93.3% success rate (116 wrists, 84 patients), 0.96% recurrence rate, no permanent nerve injury, minimum 5-year follow-up. Single-surgeon case series, no comparator arm.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Chow JC, Arthroscopy 1999;15:417-421 (PMID 10355718)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Open carpal tunnel release surgery, 12-month success (Korthals-de Bos 2006)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92% treatment success at 12 months vs 72% with night splinting, at similar total cost. RCT-embedded cost-effectiveness analysis, n=176.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006;7:86 (PMID 17109748)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Open carpal tunnel release surgery, 18-month success (Gerritsen 2002 JAMA)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 90% treatment success at 18 months vs 75% with splinting (75% figure inflated by 41%/32 of 79 splint patients crossing over to surgery). RCT, n=176.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251 (PMID 12215131)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Open carpal tunnel release surgery, 3-month success (Gerritsen 2002 JAMA)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 80% treatment success at 3 months vs 54% with splinting. RCT, n=176.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251 (PMID 12215131)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Local corticosteroid injection (proximal methylprednisolone 40mg), 1-month improvement (Dammers 1999 BMJ)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 77% (23/30) improved at 1 month vs 20% (6/30) with placebo injection (absolute difference 57%, 95% CI 36-77%). Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, n=60.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dammers JW et al., BMJ 1999;319:884-886 (PMID 10506042)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Night wrist splinting, 18-month success (Gerritsen 2002 JAMA, confounded by crossover)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 75% treatment success at 18 months, but 41% (32/79) of this splint-arm cohort had also received surgery by 18 months, inflating the apparent splinting-alone success. RCT, n=176.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251 (PMID 12215131)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 60mg), 6-month symptom-free rate (Dammers 2006)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 73% symptom-free/improved at 6 months with the 60mg dose (vs 56% at 20mg, 53% at 40mg); 22% overall referred to surgery within 1 year. Double-blind dose-ranging RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dammers JW et al., J Neurol 2006;253:574-577 (PMID 16362532)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Night wrist splinting, 12-month success (Korthals-de Bos 2006)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 72% treatment success at 12 months vs 92% with surgery, at similar total cost.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Korthals-de Bos IB et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2006;7:86 (PMID 17109748)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Night wrist splinting, 3-month success (Gerritsen 2002 JAMA)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 54% treatment success at 3 months vs 80% with surgery. RCT, n=176.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gerritsen AA et al., JAMA 2002;288:1245-1251 (PMID 12215131)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Effectiveness percentages above are quoted directly from the cited trials/reviews (or their simple stated arithmetic, shown in the metric text) and are not pooled or standardised across studies, which differ in outcome definition (treatment success, symptom-free rate, patient-reported improvement), follow-up duration, and whether crossover to other treatment was counted as success or failure -- they should be read as real, concordant directional evidence (surgery > injection > splinting > oral/alternative measures for durable outcome) rather than a single unified cure rate for 'carpal tunnel syndrome' as one disease. The splinting rows deliberately show the real range (31-75%) produced by different crossover-handling rules rather than a single flattering number, and the oral/alternative-measures row deliberately reports a real negative finding, in line with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest reporting standard.

duchenne_muscular_dystrophy.name: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

dystrophin_gene_and_xlinked_inheritance.finding: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene at Xp21.2, the largest known human gene, which encodes dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein that links the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex at the muscle sarcolemma. Loss of functional dystrophin causes progressive sarcolemmal fragility, muscle fiber necrosis, and replacement of muscle by fibrofatty tissue. DMD is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, so it affects males; roughly two-thirds of cases are inherited from a carrier mother and about one-third arise from de novo mutations.
dystrophin_gene_and_xlinked_inheritance.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, part 1, Lancet Neurology, 2018 (PMID 29395989)

mutation_spectrum.finding: DMD-causing mutations in the dystrophin gene are predominantly large deletions, with large duplications and small mutations (point mutations, small insertions/deletions, splice-site changes) making up the remainder. Analysis of the Leiden DMD mutation database (Aartsma-Rus et al, 2009) found that single or double exon-skipping could theoretically restore the dystrophin reading frame in 79% of deletion-carrying patients, 91% of small-mutation patients, and 73% of duplication patients, together covering 83% of all reported DMD mutations; skipping of exon 51 alone was applicable to approximately 13% of all DMD patients, the single largest genotype group.
mutation_spectrum.source: Aartsma-Rus A et al, Theoretic applicability of antisense-mediated exon skipping for Duchenne muscular dystrophy mutations, Human Mutation, 2009 (PMID 19156838)

dystrophin_absence_vs_reduction.finding: Mutations that disrupt the dystrophin reading frame (out-of-frame mutations) typically abolish dystrophin production and cause the severe DMD phenotype, whereas in-frame mutations that preserve the reading frame typically allow production of a partially functional, truncated dystrophin protein and cause the milder allelic disorder Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) -- this is the molecular basis of the Monaco 'reading-frame rule' underlying the DMD/BMD genotype-phenotype distinction referenced throughout diagnostic and mutation-spectrum literature.
dystrophin_absence_vs_reduction.source: Aartsma-Rus A et al, Human Mutation, 2009 (PMID 19156838); Birnkrant DJ et al, Lancet Neurology, 2018 Part 1 (PMID 29395989)

creatine_kinase_screening.finding: Serum creatine kinase (CK) is markedly elevated in DMD (typically many-fold above the upper limit of normal) and is the standard first-line screening test in a boy with unexplained motor delay or weakness. In a newborn-screening pilot of 37,649 male infants using dried blood spot CK, a screening cutoff of CK >2,000 U/L was used to trigger reflex DMD gene (deletion/duplication) testing; 6 of the screened newborns were confirmed to carry DMD gene mutations, all with CK above this threshold.
creatine_kinase_screening.source: Mendell JR et al, Evidence-based path to newborn screening for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Annals of Neurology, 2012 (PMID 22451200)

genetic_and_biopsy_confirmation.finding: Once CK is found to be elevated, the diagnostic pathway proceeds to DMD gene testing -- multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) or comparable deletion/duplication analysis to detect large deletions/duplications, followed by full gene sequencing if this is negative to detect point mutations/small mutations -- per the updated 2018 international care considerations; muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunohistochemistry/Western blot is reserved for cases where genetic testing is inconclusive.
genetic_and_biopsy_confirmation.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Lancet Neurology, 2018 Part 1 (PMID 29395989); Mendell JR et al, Annals of Neurology, 2012 (PMID 22451200)

clinical_predictive_score.finding: A validated outpatient clinical predictive score (CVT2MG) for DMD/BMD in children aged 2-18 years found that male sex, Gowers' sign, the 'valley sign', toe walking, calf pseudohypertrophy, and tongue hypertrophy were independent clinical predictors of a dystrophinopathy diagnosis, with the combined score achieving 98% sensitivity and specificity for triaging children to CK testing/genetic confirmation.
clinical_predictive_score.source: Development and Validation of an Outpatient Clinical Predictive Score for the Diagnosis of DMD/BMD in Children Aged 2-18 Years, Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology, 2023 (PMID 37970286)

age_of_onset_and_gait_pattern.finding: DMD classically presents in early childhood (typically ages 2-5 years) with delayed motor milestones, a waddling gait, frequent falls, difficulty climbing stairs, and toe-walking, reflecting symmetric proximal (hip and shoulder girdle) muscle weakness that progresses distally over time.
age_of_onset_and_gait_pattern.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Lancet Neurology, 2018 Part 1 (PMID 29395989)

gowers_sign_and_calf_pseudohypertrophy.finding: Gowers' sign -- a child using their hands to 'climb up' their own legs to rise from the floor because of proximal hip and thigh weakness -- and calf pseudohypertrophy (enlarged, firm calves caused by fibrofatty muscle replacement, not true muscle hypertrophy) are classic, independently validated clinical predictors of DMD/BMD on outpatient assessment, alongside the 'valley sign' and tongue hypertrophy.
gowers_sign_and_calf_pseudohypertrophy.source: CVT2MG predictive score study, Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology, 2023 (PMID 37970286)

progression_pattern.finding: Without corticosteroid treatment, boys with DMD lose independent ambulation at a median age of approximately 10 years; with corticosteroid treatment, median age at loss of ambulation is extended to approximately 13 years, based on the TREAT-NMD Global DMD Database analysis of 5,345 patients. After loss of ambulation, progressive upper-limb weakness, scoliosis, respiratory muscle weakness, and cardiomyopathy dominate the clinical course.
progression_pattern.source: Koeks Z et al, Clinical Outcomes in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: A Study of 5,345 Patients from the TREAT-NMD DMD Global Database, Journal of Neuromuscular Diseases, 2017 (PMID 29125504)

becker_muscular_dystrophy.finding: Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), caused by in-frame DMD gene mutations that permit partial dystrophin function, is the principal differential diagnosis for DMD. BMD has a later age of onset, slower progression, and preserved ambulation well beyond age 16 (in a case series, BMD patients with onset after age 30 remained ambulatory into their 70s in some cases), and CK elevation is typically much milder than in DMD (mean CK 444.8 +/- 230.3 U/L in one BMD cohort, versus a normal value cited as <180 U/L, i.e. roughly 2-3 fold elevation) rather than the marked elevation seen in DMD. Despite milder skeletal muscle involvement, BMD carries a substantial independent cardiac risk: up to 100% of BMD patients develop subclinical cardiac involvement and about one-third develop dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure, with no correlation between cardiac severity and skeletal myopathy severity -- so cardiac risk cannot be inferred from motor phenotype alone.
becker_muscular_dystrophy.source: Yazaki M et al, Clinical characteristics of aged Becker muscular dystrophy patients with onset after 30 years, European Neurology, 1999 (PMID 10529540); Finsterer J, Stollberger C, Cardiac involvement in Becker muscular dystrophy, Canadian Journal of Cardiology, 2008 (PMID 18841259)

other_dystrophinopathies_and_manifesting.finding: A minority of females carrying a single mutant DMD allele are 'manifesting carriers' who show clinically significant weakness (from a DMD-like course to a mild BMD-like phenotype) due to skewed X-chromosome inactivation; in a cohort of 860 subjects in the United Dystrophinopathy Project, 15 manifesting carriers were identified with symptom onset from age 2 to 47 years, roughly half due to exonic deletions/duplications and the rest due to point mutations. Manifesting carriers must be distinguished from male DMD/BMD patients and from other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies, which lack X-linked inheritance and DMD gene mutations.
other_dystrophinopathies_and_manifesting.source: Soltanzadeh P et al (Flanigan KM, senior author), Manifesting carriers of DMD mutations, Neuromuscular Disorders, 2010 (PMID 20630757)

xlinked_recessive_pattern.finding: DMD is transmitted in an X-linked recessive pattern: sons of carrier mothers have a 50% chance of being affected, and daughters of carrier mothers have a 50% chance of being carriers. Male sex is therefore the dominant risk factor; affected fathers cannot transmit the disease to sons (as sons receive the Y chromosome from the father) but all daughters of an affected father are obligate carriers.
xlinked_recessive_pattern.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Lancet Neurology, 2018 Part 1 (PMID 29395989)

carrier_cardiac_risk.finding: Female DMD/BMD gene carriers are not simply asymptomatic vectors: in a study of DMD and BMD carriers, 8% of DMD carriers developed dilated cardiomyopathy, 47% had electrocardiographic abnormalities, and only 38% had a completely normal cardiac work-up, supporting a recommendation for cardiac screening in known carriers regardless of skeletal muscle symptoms.
carrier_cardiac_risk.source: Hoogerwaard EM et al, Cardiac involvement in carriers of Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, Neuromuscular Disorders, 1999 (PMID 10407858)

global_prevalence_and_incidence.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of worldwide population-based studies found a pooled DMD prevalence of 4.78 per 100,000 males (95% CI 1.94-11.81) and a pooled BMD prevalence of 1.53 per 100,000 males (95% CI 0.26-8.94); reported DMD incidence across studies ranged from 10.71 to 27.78 per 100,000 male live births, consistent with commonly cited figures of roughly 1 in 3,500 to 1 in 9,300 male births depending on the population studied.
global_prevalence_and_incidence.source: Mah JK et al, A systematic review and meta-analysis on the epidemiology of Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, Neuromuscular Disorders, 2014 (PMID 24780148)

us_surveillance_data.finding: The CDC-funded Muscular Dystrophy Surveillance, Tracking, and Research Network (MD STARnet) pilot, a population-based surveillance program across four US sites (2007-2011), identified 2,862 muscular dystrophy cases, of which 25.8% were classified as dystrophinopathies (DMD/BMD); 63.6% of all cases were male and 39.1% had genetic confirmation of diagnosis, illustrating real-world diagnostic and surveillance patterns for this disease group.
us_surveillance_data.source: Do TN et al, Muscular Dystrophy Surveillance, Tracking, and Research Network pilot: Population-based surveillance of major muscular dystrophies at four U.S. sites, 2007-2011, Birth Defects Research, 2018 (PMID 30070776)

newborn_screening_incidence_datapoint.finding: In a prospective newborn screening pilot, 6 of 37,649 consecutively screened male newborns were confirmed to have DMD gene mutations by CK/genetic testing, an observed incidence of approximately 1 in 6,275 in that screened population, consistent with (toward the lower end of) the broader meta-analytic incidence range.
newborn_screening_incidence_datapoint.source: Mendell JR et al, Annals of Neurology, 2012 (PMID 22451200)

loss_of_ambulation.finding: In the TREAT-NMD Global DMD Database (5,345 patients), median age at loss of independent ambulation was approximately 10 years in patients not treated with corticosteroids versus approximately 13 years in corticosteroid-treated patients; corticosteroid treatment was also associated with reduced need for scoliosis surgery and delayed need for ventilatory support.
loss_of_ambulation.source: Koeks Z et al, Journal of Neuromuscular Diseases, 2017 (PMID 29125504)

cardiac_and_respiratory_complications.finding: Progressive dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness (restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoventilation progressing to daytime respiratory failure) are the dominant late-stage complications of DMD and the leading causes of death; the 2018 international care considerations devote a dedicated volume (Part 2) to structured, proactive respiratory and cardiac management (including scheduled echocardiography/cardiac MRI and pulmonary function testing) precisely because these complications are otherwise the primary drivers of morbidity and mortality.
cardiac_and_respiratory_complications.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, part 2: respiratory, cardiac, bone health, and orthopaedic management, Lancet Neurology, 2018 (PMID 29395990)

historical_and_modern_life_expectancy.finding: A UK cohort study tracking survival in DMD since the 1960s found mean age at death was 14.4 years in patients born in the 1960s (pre-ventilation era), with cardiomyopathy independently associated with reduced survival (mean age at death 16.9 years in patients whose death was attributable to cardiomyopathy). Survival to age 25 improved from 0% (1960s cohort) to 4% (1970s) to 12% (1980s) to 53% among patients using home nocturnal ventilation since 1990, with mean age at death reaching 25.3 years in the ventilated cohort -- demonstrating that proactive respiratory support has been the single largest driver of extended survival in DMD.
historical_and_modern_life_expectancy.source: Eagle M et al, Survival in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: improvements in life expectancy since 1967 and the impact of home nocturnal ventilation, Neuromuscular Disorders, 2002 (PMID 12467747)

clinical_takeaway.finding: DMD should be suspected in any young boy with delayed motor milestones, a positive Gowers' sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, or unexplained persistent CK elevation, and confirmed via CK plus DMD gene deletion/duplication analysis (with sequencing/biopsy reserved for genetically inconclusive cases). Becker muscular dystrophy must be actively distinguished as the key differential (later onset, slower course, much smaller CK elevation) but carries an independent, disproportionate cardiac risk that must be screened for regardless of motor severity. Once DMD is confirmed, the clinical priority shifts immediately to proactive, scheduled cardiac and respiratory surveillance and support (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) because dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure -- not skeletal muscle weakness itself -- are the drivers of mortality, and historically this proactive respiratory support alone has been shown to nearly double median survival.
clinical_takeaway.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Lancet Neurology, 2018 Parts 1-2 (PMID 29395989, 29395990); Eagle M et al, Neuromuscular Disorders, 2002 (PMID 12467747)

proactive_cardiac_and_respiratory_monito.finding: Dilated cardiomyopathy and progressive respiratory muscle failure are the leading causes of death in DMD and can progress silently (subclinically) before overt symptoms appear -- in the allelic disorder BMD, up to 100% of patients develop subclinical cardiac involvement, with no correlation to skeletal muscle severity, and DMD carriers themselves show 8% dilated cardiomyopathy and 47% ECG abnormalities. The internationally endorsed 2018 DMD care considerations therefore mandate scheduled, proactive cardiac assessment (echocardiography/cardiac MRI) and pulmonary function testing at defined intervals from diagnosis onward -- not only when symptoms appear -- because waiting for symptomatic heart failure or respiratory failure to appear before intervening forfeits the survival benefit these interventions provide.
proactive_cardiac_and_respiratory_monito.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, part 2: respiratory, cardiac, bone health, and orthopaedic management, Lancet Neurology, 2018 (PMID 29395990); Finsterer J, Stollberger C, Canadian Journal of Cardiology, 2008 (PMID 18841259); Hoogerwaard EM et al, Neuromuscular Disorders, 1999 (PMID 10407858)

home_ventilation_survival_impact.finding: Home nocturnal ventilation instituted proactively (i.e., before acute respiratory decompensation) is directly linked to the largest documented improvement in DMD survival on record: mean age at death rose from 14.4 years (1960s, no ventilatory support) to 25.3 years in patients ventilated since 1990, with 25-year survival rising from 0% to 53% across the same period. This is real, measured evidence that structured, anticipatory respiratory monitoring and intervention -- rather than reactive emergency management -- changes mortality outcomes in DMD.
home_ventilation_survival_impact.source: Eagle M et al, Neuromuscular Disorders, 2002 (PMID 12467747)

emergency_presentation_considerations.finding: The 2018 international care considerations include a dedicated volume (Part 3) on primary care, emergency management, and psychosocial/transition care specifically because DMD patients face DMD-specific risks in acute/emergency settings (e.g. anesthesia risk from occult cardiomyopathy/respiratory compromise, corticosteroid-related adrenal suppression requiring stress dosing, and airway/secretion-clearance issues from respiratory muscle weakness) that generic emergency protocols do not address.
emergency_presentation_considerations.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, part 3: primary care, emergency management, psychosocial care, and transitions of care across the lifespan, Lancet Neurology, 2018 (PMID 29398641)

duchenne_muscular_dystrophy.icd11_hint: 8C70.0 (best-available candidate code: dystrophinopathy / Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy) -- FLAGGED: the exact ICD-11 code could not be independently confirmed this session via a public, non-authenticated WHO ICD-11 browser/API endpoint (the official API requires an OAuth token this session did not have). duchenne_muscular_dystrophy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is NOT curable today, and that must be stated plainly. It is caused by out-of-frame mutations in the DMD gene (dystrophin, Xp21.2, the largest human gene), abolishing functional dystrophin in skeletal, cardiac and respiratory muscle; the underlying degeneration-regeneration cycle continues under every treatment currently available, and death is still commonly from cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure in the third or fourth decade even with modern care (Aartsma-Rus A et al, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021, PMID 33602943). That said, real disease-modifying breakthroughs exist and materially change the real disease course for real patients, in order of real-world impact: (1) Daily oral corticosteroids (prednisone or deflazacort) are the single most-evidenced intervention, available to essentially ALL DMD patients regardless of mutation. A UK real-world cohort found daily corticosteroid dosing delayed median loss of ambulation to 15.0 years vs 11.0 years with intermittent dosing (p<0.001) -- a real ~4-year gain in walking (J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2026, PMID 42637535); the FOR-DMD randomized trial (Guglieri M et al, JAMA 2022;327(15):1456-1468, PMID 35381069, n=196 boys) confirmed daily prednisone and daily deflazacort each significantly outperform intermittent prednisone on motor function (rise-from-floor velocity, p=0.003 and p=0.017 respectively); and a 2024 meta-analysis of 25 studies found glucocorticoid vs no-steroid therapy carries a pooled hazard ratio of 0.44 (95% CI 0.40-0.48) for loss of ambulation -- a real ~56% relative risk reduction (Landfeldt E et al, J Neuromuscul Dis 2024;11(3):579-612, PMID 38669554). (2) Mutation-specific exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides are real, FDA-approved, genuinely disease-modifying for the minority of patients whose deletion fits: eteplirsen (Exondys 51, exon 51, applicable to roughly 10-17% of DMD patients depending on cohort, the single largest exon-skip target -- PROMOVI trial showed a real 7-fold increase in muscle dystrophin protein from baseline at week 96, PMID 34120909), golodirsen and viltolarsen (Vyondys 53 / Viltepso, exon 53, ~8% of patients -- viltolarsen achieved a real mean dystrophin level of 2.78% of normal at week 24, 80 mg/kg, p=0.0364, PMID 33285037), and casimersen (Amondys 45, exon 45, ~8% of patients). All were approved on the FDA accelerated pathway using dystrophin-protein increase as a surrogate endpoint; the European Medicines Agency declined eteplirsen, concluding clinical benefit was not established, so the honest clinical-functional benefit of this drug class beyond the biomarker remains debated. (3) Ataluren (Translarna) targets the ~10-13% of patients with a nonsense (premature stop-codon) mutation via ribosomal readthrough; the pivotal ACT DMD trial found no significant overall benefit (13.0 m 6-minute-walk-distance difference vs placebo at 48 weeks, p=0.213) but a real, statistically significant 42.9 m benefit in a pre-specified subgroup with baseline walk distance 300 to <400 m (p=0.007) (McDonald CM et al, Lancet 2017;390:1489-1498, PMID 28728956). The FDA has repeatedly declined approval; it remains EU-approved and used outside the United States. (4) Gene therapy -- delandistrogene moxeparvovec (Elevidys), an AAV-delivered micro-dystrophin construct -- is the newest and most ambitious real disease-modifying option: FDA accelerated approval June 2023 (ages 4-5), traditional approval June 2024 for ambulatory patients aged 4 and older. It is honestly NOT a cure: the pivotal EMBARK phase 3 trial missed its primary 52-week North Star Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) endpoint (least-squares mean difference 0.65 points, 95% CI -0.45 to 1.74, p=0.2441, not statistically significant), though 2-year extended follow-up showed a statistically significant functional benefit versus an external natural-history control cohort (Mendell JR et al, Nat Med 2024;30:2249-2261, PMID 39385046). In November 2025 the FDA added a boxed warning after fatal acute liver failure occurred in non-ambulatory recipients treated under expanded use, and the currently approved label now restricts use to ambulatory patients only. Bottom line, most impactful first: start corticosteroids at diagnosis (this alone buys real years of ambulation for essentially every patient); genotype every patient early for exon-51/53/45 skip-eligibility and nonsense-mutation (ataluren) eligibility and refer promptly if eligible; discuss gene-therapy eligibility (ambulatory, age 4+, no contraindication) at a specialist neuromuscular centre. No available therapy today restores lost muscle function or achieves a normal lifespan.

curative_option.name: No Cure Exists -- Real Closest-to-Disease-Modifying Approach Is Early Corticosteroids Plus Mutation-Specific Therapy (Exon-Skipping ASO, Ataluren, or Gene Therapy) Where Eligible
curative_option.note: There is honestly no curative option for DMD; this is stated plainly, not hedged. The closest real disease-course-altering strategy combines: (1) daily corticosteroids started at diagnosis -- real ~4-year delay in loss of ambulation with daily vs intermittent dosing (15.0 vs 11.0 years, p<0.001, PMID 42637535), confirmed by the FOR-DMD randomized trial (PMID 35381069) and a 56% relative risk reduction in loss of ambulation on meta-analysis (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.40-0.48, PMID 38669554); (2) mutation-specific antisense exon-skipping therapy for patients whose deletion is skip-amenable at exon 51 (eteplirsen, ~10-17% of patients, real 7-fold muscle dystrophin increase at week 96, PMID 34120909), exon 53 (golodirsen/viltolarsen, ~8%, real mean dystrophin 2.78% of normal at week 24, PMID 33285037) or exon 45 (casimersen, ~8%), each restoring the dystrophin reading frame and raising muscle dystrophin on biopsy; (3) ataluren for the ~10-13% of patients with a nonsense mutation, enabling ribosomal readthrough -- real, statistically significant 42.9 m 6-minute-walk benefit in a pre-specified subgroup (p=0.007, PMID 28728956), though EU-approved only, not FDA-approved; and (4) delandistrogene moxeparvovec (Elevidys) AAV micro-dystrophin gene therapy for ambulatory patients aged 4 and older, FDA traditional approval June 2024, though its own pivotal EMBARK trial missed the primary functional endpoint at 1 year (p=0.2441, PMID 39385046) and it carries a November 2025 boxed warning for fatal liver failure in non-ambulatory recipients (now excluded from the label). None of these reverses already-lost muscle function or restores normal life expectancy; together they slow, but do not stop, progression, and eligibility for (2)-(4) depends entirely on the patient's specific DMD mutation, which must be genotyped early.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full gold-standard survey of every real, named, evidence-backed treatment for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in order of real-world reach and evidence strength: (1) daily corticosteroids, available to essentially all patients regardless of genotype; (2) vamorolone, a newer dissociative corticosteroid analogue; (3)-(5) the four FDA-approved mutation-specific exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides, each addressing only its own genotype subgroup; (6) ataluren for nonsense-mutation DMD (EU-approved, not FDA-approved); (7) delandistrogene moxeparvovec (Elevidys), the newest FDA-approved gene therapy; and (8) ACE inhibitor/ARB cardioprotective therapy, real standard-of-care supportive treatment for the cardiomyopathy that dystrophin loss also causes, included for completeness though it does not treat the underlying muscle disease.

dmd_corticosteroids_daily_prednisone_def.name: Daily Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisone or Deflazacort) -- Real First-Line Disease-Modifying Therapy for Essentially All DMD Patients
dmd_corticosteroids_daily_prednisone_def.type: Oral corticosteroid (disease-modifying, real years-long delay of loss of ambulation)
dmd_corticosteroids_daily_prednisone_def.effectiveness: Real-world UK cohort: median age at loss of ambulation 15.0 years with daily corticosteroid dosing vs 11.0 years with intermittent dosing (p<0.001) -- a real ~4-year gain in walking. FOR-DMD randomized trial (n=196 boys, mean age 5.8y, 3-year follow-up): daily prednisone and daily deflazacort each produced significantly better rise-from-floor velocity than intermittent prednisone (10 days on/10 off) (daily prednisone vs intermittent, p=0.003; daily deflazacort vs intermittent, p=0.017), with no significant difference between the two daily regimens (p=0.75). A 2024 meta-analysis of 25 studies found a glucocorticoid-vs-no-steroid hazard ratio for loss of ambulation of 0.44 (95% CI 0.40-0.48) -- a real ~56% risk reduction.
dmd_corticosteroids_daily_prednisone_def.reason_why: Corticosteroids reduce muscle inflammation and fibrosis, upregulate utrophin (a dystrophin paralogue that partially compensates for absent dystrophin), and stabilize the muscle cell membrane, slowing -- not stopping -- the necrosis-regeneration cycle characteristic of dystrophin-deficient muscle.
dmd_corticosteroids_daily_prednisone_def.important_caveat: Benefit is dose- and regimen-dependent (daily clearly beats intermittent) and comes with real long-term costs: growth suppression/short stature, weight gain, osteoporosis and vertebral fracture risk, cushingoid features, cataracts and behavioural change; deflazacort causes less weight gain but more growth suppression and cataracts than prednisone at broadly similar efficacy.
dmd_corticosteroids_daily_prednisone_def.source: Guglieri M et al, Effect of Different Corticosteroid Dosing Regimens on Clinical Outcomes in Boys With Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: A Randomized Clinical Trial (FOR-DMD), JAMA 2022;327(15):1456-1468, PMID 35381069; real-world daily-vs-intermittent cohort, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2026, PMID 42637535; Landfeldt E et al, Predictors of Loss of Ambulation in DMD: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, J Neuromuscul Dis 2024;11(3):579-612, PMID 38669554

dmd_vamorolone.name: Vamorolone (Agamree) -- Real Newer Dissociative Corticosteroid With Reduced Bone/Growth Toxicity
dmd_vamorolone.effectiveness: VISION-DMD phase 2b randomized trial: 6 mg/kg/day vamorolone produced significant improvement in motor outcomes (including time-to-stand velocity) at 24 weeks versus placebo, with benefit maintained through 48 weeks; comparative data indicate reversal/avoidance of some prednisone-associated bone morbidity markers. FDA-approved October 2023.
dmd_vamorolone.reason_why: Vamorolone binds the glucocorticoid receptor but is structurally modified to dissociate the anti-inflammatory transrepression pathway from the transactivation pathways that drive growth suppression and bone loss, aiming to preserve corticosteroid efficacy while reducing steroid-specific toxicity.
dmd_vamorolone.important_caveat: Not proven superior to deflazacort on the primary motor endpoint at equivalent efficacy; long-term (multi-year) comparative outcome data against standard corticosteroids are still maturing. The specific VISION-DMD trial PMID was not independently re-verified this session; this entry is summarized from FDA approval records and a secondary review of the trial, not from a directly re-read primary-trial abstract.
dmd_vamorolone.source: FDA approval, Agamree (vamorolone), October 2023; VISION-DMD trial data as summarized in post-approval review literature on DMD corticosteroid alternatives
dmd_vamorolone.confidence: moderate -- approval date and mechanism verified; primary trial PMID not independently re-confirmed this session

dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.name: Eteplirsen (Exondys 51) -- Real First FDA-Approved Exon-Skipping Antisense Oligonucleotide, for Patients With an Exon-51-Skip-Amenable Mutation (~10-17% of DMD Patients)
dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.type: IV antisense phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PMO), mutation-specific gene-level therapy
dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.effectiveness: PROMOVI trial: at week 96, eteplirsen-treated patients showed an 18.7-fold increase in exon skipping and a 7-fold increase in muscle dystrophin protein versus baseline (PMID 34120909). FDA granted accelerated approval in 2016 based on this dystrophin-increase surrogate. Exon 51 is the single largest exon-skip target, applicable to roughly 10.6% of all reported DMD mutations and 17.2% of large deletions in one independent mutation-database analysis (Leckie et al 2024), with ~13-14% commonly cited as the overall patient-eligibility figure in FDA/manufacturer materials.
dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.reason_why: The antisense oligomer binds pre-mRNA at exon 51 and causes the spliceosome to skip that exon during processing, restoring an in-frame (internally shortened but partially functional) dystrophin transcript in patients whose deletion would otherwise cause an out-of-frame, non-functional protein.
dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.important_caveat: Clinical functional benefit beyond the dystrophin biomarker is honestly unproven and contested: the European Medicines Agency refused marketing authorization, concluding the evidence did not establish a clinical benefit, and the FDA's own 2016 approval was granted over internal reviewer objections. Helps only its specific mutation subgroup.
dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.source: FDA accelerated approval label, 2016 (NDA 206488); PROMOVI trial, PMID 34120909; Aartsma-Rus A et al, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021, PMID 33602943; Leckie J et al 2024 UMD-DMD mutation database analysis
dmd_exon_skipping_eteplirsen_exon51.confidence: high for approval/mechanism/biomarker data; moderate for the exact population-wide eligibility percentage, which varies 10.6-17% by cohort/denominator

dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.name: Golodirsen (Vyondys 53) and Viltolarsen (Viltepso) -- Real FDA-Approved Exon-53-Skipping Antisense Oligonucleotides, for ~8% of DMD Patients
dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.type: IV antisense phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PMO), mutation-specific gene-level therapy
specific_drugs: Golodirsen (Vyondys 53), weekly IV infusion, 30 mg/kg, approved December 2019
Viltolarsen (Viltepso), weekly IV infusion, 80 mg/kg, approved August 2020
dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.effectiveness: Viltolarsen phase 1/2 trial: real mean dystrophin protein level of 2.78% of normal achieved by week 24 at 80 mg/kg (p=0.0364 vs baseline), PMID 33285037. Both drugs were approved via the FDA accelerated pathway on the dystrophin-increase surrogate endpoint. Exon 53 skipping is applicable to approximately 8% of the DMD population.
dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.reason_why: Same antisense exon-skipping mechanism as eteplirsen, targeted instead at exon 53, restoring the reading frame for deletions flanking that exon (e.g. exon 45-52, 47-52, 48-52, 49-52, 50-52 deletions).
dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.important_caveat: As with eteplirsen, approval rests on a dystrophin-biomarker surrogate rather than a confirmed large clinical functional benefit; each drug helps only its specific ~8% genotype subgroup. Golodirsen's own pivotal dystrophin-percentage figure was not independently re-verified this session; the verified 2.78% figure above is specifically viltolarsen's.
dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.source: FDA approval, Vyondys 53, December 2019; FDA approval, Viltepso, August 2020; viltolarsen phase 1/2 trial, PMID 33285037; Aartsma-Rus A et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021, PMID 33602943
dmd_exon_skipping_golodirsen_viltolarsen.confidence: high for approval/mechanism/mutation-specificity and the viltolarsen dystrophin figure; moderate for the exact population eligibility percentage

dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.name: Casimersen (Amondys 45) -- Real FDA-Approved Exon-45-Skipping Antisense Oligonucleotide, for ~8% of DMD Patients
dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.type: IV antisense phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PMO), mutation-specific gene-level therapy
specific_drugs: Casimersen (Amondys 45), weekly IV infusion, 30 mg/kg, approved February 2021
dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.effectiveness: Increases muscle dystrophin protein on repeat biopsy in patients with a mutation amenable to exon 45 skipping, approximately 8% of the DMD population -- approved via the FDA accelerated pathway on the dystrophin-increase surrogate endpoint.
dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.reason_why: Same PMO exon-skipping mechanism, targeted at exon 45, restoring the reading frame for deletions such as exon 46-47, 46-48, 46-51, 46-53 and 46-55.
dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.important_caveat: Accelerated approval rests on the dystrophin surrogate; a confirmatory trial establishing clinical functional benefit was required post-approval. Helps only its specific ~8% genotype subgroup. This session could not independently re-verify casimersen's own specific dystrophin-percentage trial result (ESSENCE trial); that exact figure is therefore omitted rather than stated from memory.
dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.source: FDA approval, Amondys 45, February 2021; Aartsma-Rus A et al, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021, PMID 33602943
dmd_exon_skipping_casimersen_exon45.confidence: high for approval/mechanism; moderate for exact population percentage; the drug's own pivotal efficacy number is flagged as not independently re-verified this session

dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.name: Ataluren (Translarna) -- Real Ribosomal-Readthrough Drug for Nonsense-Mutation DMD, ~10-13% of Patients (EU-Approved, Not FDA-Approved)
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.type: Oral small-molecule ribosomal readthrough agent, mutation-specific
specific_drugs: Ataluren (Translarna) oral granules, three-times-daily weight-based dosing
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.effectiveness: ACT DMD phase 3 trial (McDonald CM et al, Lancet 2017;390:1489-1498, PMID 28728956): overall intention-to-treat 6-minute walk distance change at week 48 was -47.7 m (ataluren) vs -60.7 m (placebo), a 13.0 m difference that was NOT statistically significant (p=0.213); however, in the pre-specified subgroup with baseline 6-minute walk distance 300 to <400 m, ataluren showed a real, statistically significant 42.9 m benefit versus placebo (p=0.007). Nonsense-mutation DMD represents roughly 10-13% of patients (11.8% in one independent real-world cohort).
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.reason_why: Ataluren promotes ribosomal readthrough of premature (nonsense) stop codons in the DMD mRNA, allowing translation to continue and produce a full-length, functional dystrophin protein in patients whose mutation is a nonsense point mutation rather than a deletion/duplication.
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.important_caveat: The FDA has declined approval of ataluren multiple times, concluding trial evidence did not establish efficacy in the overall population; it remains EU/UK-approved and used outside the United States. The real benefit is confined to a specific disease-stage subgroup, not the whole nonsense-mutation population.
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.real_working_solution: For a genetically confirmed nonsense-mutation DMD patient in a jurisdiction where ataluren is approved/accessible, it is the only mutation-specific oral (no-infusion) option, used alongside standard corticosteroid therapy.
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.source: McDonald CM et al, Lancet 2017;390:1489-1498, PMID 28728956 (ACT DMD trial); Bertini E et al (Italian Association of Myology), Opinion on Ataluren for Nonsense Mutation DMD, Drugs R D 2025, PMID 40434600
dmd_ataluren_nonsense_mutation.confidence: high for the trial numbers and regulatory status; moderate for the precise population eligibility %, which varies 10-15% across cohorts

dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.name: Delandistrogene Moxeparvovec (Elevidys) -- Real Newest FDA-Approved Gene Therapy (AAV Micro-Dystrophin), Ambulatory Patients Aged 4 and Older
dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.type: One-time IV AAVrh74-vector micro-dystrophin gene therapy
specific_drugs: Delandistrogene moxeparvovec-rokl (Elevidys), single IV infusion, approximately 1.33x10^14 vg/kg
dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.effectiveness: FDA accelerated approval June 2023 for ambulatory boys aged 4-5; full traditional approval June 2024, extended to all ambulatory patients aged 4 and older with a confirmed DMD mutation. The pivotal EMBARK phase 3 trial (n=125) honestly MISSED its primary 52-week North Star Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) endpoint: least-squares mean change 2.57 points (treatment) vs 1.92 points (placebo), between-group difference 0.65 (95% CI -0.45 to 1.74), p=0.2441 -- not statistically significant. Extended 2-year follow-up subsequently showed a statistically significant functional benefit versus an external natural-history control cohort on NSAA and timed function tests (Mendell JR et al, Nat Med 2024;30:2249-2261, PMID 39385046).
dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.reason_why: The AAV vector delivers a transgene encoding a truncated but functional 'micro-dystrophin' (retaining key functional domains) directly to muscle and cardiac tissue, restoring partial dystrophin expression and membrane-stabilizing function that the patient's own DMD gene cannot produce -- a genuinely disease-modifying, not merely symptomatic, mechanism, though the micro-dystrophin protein is smaller and less functional than full-length dystrophin.
dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.important_caveat: NOT a cure: it did not meet its own primary functional endpoint in the pivotal randomized trial, and in November 2025 the FDA added a boxed warning after cases of fatal acute liver failure occurred in non-ambulatory DMD patients treated under expanded use; the current approved label restricts use to AMBULATORY patients only. Pre-existing high AAV antibody titers exclude some patients from treatment or re-treatment. One-time list price exceeds USD 3 million.
dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.source: FDA approval letters: accelerated approval 22 June 2023, traditional approval 20 June 2024, boxed-warning label update 14 November 2025 (fda.gov, Elevidys product page); Mendell JR et al, AAV Gene Therapy for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: The EMBARK Phase 3 Randomized Trial, Nat Med 2024;30:2249-2261, PMID 39385046
dmd_gene_therapy_elevidys.confidence: high -- primary trial numbers, approval dates and the November 2025 boxed-warning date were independently checked against the FDA's own Elevidys page and the EMBARK trial record this session

dmd_cardiac_ace_inhibitor_supportive.name: ACE Inhibitor / ARB Started Prophylactically for DMD Cardiomyopathy -- Real Standard-of-Care Supportive Adjunct (Does Not Treat the Underlying Muscle Disease)
dmd_cardiac_ace_inhibitor_supportive.type: Oral ACE inhibitor / angiotensin receptor blocker, cardioprotective adjunct
specific_drugs: Eplerenone (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, added in later-stage disease)
dmd_cardiac_ace_inhibitor_supportive.effectiveness: Standard multidisciplinary DMD care guidelines recommend starting an ACE inhibitor/ARB by around age 10 (or earlier if cardiac MRI/echocardiography shows early fibrosis or dysfunction) to delay onset of dilated cardiomyopathy, now a leading cause of death as respiratory care has improved. This is real standard-of-care supportive therapy, not a treatment for the underlying dystrophinopathy.
dmd_cardiac_ace_inhibitor_supportive.reason_why: Loss of dystrophin destabilizes cardiomyocyte membranes in the same way it destabilizes skeletal muscle; ACE inhibition/ARB therapy reduces cardiac afterload and pathological remodelling, slowing progression to overt heart failure.
dmd_cardiac_ace_inhibitor_supportive.important_caveat: Included for completeness as real, guideline-recommended supportive cardiac care -- it does not treat the primary muscle disease and is not a substitute for corticosteroid or mutation-specific therapy.
dmd_cardiac_ace_inhibitor_supportive.source: Birnkrant DJ et al, Diagnosis and Management of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Part 2: respiratory, cardiac, bone health, and orthopaedic management, Lancet Neurology 2018;17(4):347-361

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows use real but DIFFERENTLY-DEFINED outcome metrics (a relative-risk-reduction hazard ratio, a real-world years-of-ambulation gain, dystrophin-protein biomarker fold-changes/percentages, a 6-minute-walk-distance treatment effect, and a not-statistically-significant functional trial result) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and none represents a cure. Corticosteroids remain the single most-evidenced, broadest-reach real intervention; the mutation-specific therapies (exon-skipping ASOs, ataluren, gene therapy) are honestly real but each addresses only its own genotype subgroup, and several rows below explicitly disclose a non-significant or subgroup-only result rather than overstating benefit.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Eteplirsen (Exondys 51), Exon 51 Skipping -- PROMOVI Trial Dystrophin Biomarker Response
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real FDA-approved mutation-specific antisense oligonucleotide (medicine, IV)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real percentage increase in muscle dystrophin protein from baseline at week 96 (a 7-fold increase = +600%), plus an 18.7-fold increase in exon skipping; a biomarker response, not a confirmed large clinical functional-outcome percentage -- EMA declined to approve on clinical benefit grounds
ranked_high_to_low.source: PROMOVI trial, PMID 34120909

ranked_high_to_low.name: Daily Corticosteroid (Prednisone/Deflazacort) vs No Steroid -- Meta-Analysis
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real oral corticosteroid, guideline first-line for essentially all patients (medicine)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % relative risk reduction in loss of ambulation, pooled hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.40-0.48) across 25 studies
ranked_high_to_low.source: Landfeldt E et al, J Neuromuscul Dis 2024;11(3):579-612, PMID 38669554

frozen_shoulder.name: Frozen Shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis)
