frozen_shoulder.icd11_hint: Could not be independently verified against the WHO ICD-11 MMS browser/API in this session (the WHO ICD-11 REST API requires an authenticated OAuth bearer token, and the public browse UI is JavaScript-rendered and returned no renderable code via fetch). Nearest independently-verifiable legacy mapping: ICD-10 M75.0 (Adhesive capsulitis of shoulder) / ICD-9-CM 726.0 (Wikipedia, cross-checked against standard coding references). Flagged as unverified for ICD-11 specifically -- do not treat the ICD-10/ICD-9 numbers as an ICD-11 substitute in any billing context.
frozen_shoulder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Frozen shoulder is a genuinely favourable-prognosis condition: the overwhelming majority of patients recover good, near-normal shoulder function even on the natural course alone, and real active treatment meaningfully speeds up and improves that recovery. The classic natural-history study (Reeves 1975, Scand J Rheumatol, PMID 1198072) followed 41 untreated/minimally-treated patients for 5-10 years through the three classic stages (pain, stiffness, recovery; average total duration 30.1 months) and found only 3 of 41 (7.3%) were left with a handicapping restriction at final recovery -- a real 92.7% (38/41) good functional outcome without any procedural intervention. A modern RCT (Diercks & Stevens 2004, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 15383804, n=77) found 'supervised neglect' (supportive therapy plus gentle exercise within pain limits) achieved a normal/near-normal painless shoulder (Constant score >=80) in 89% of patients by 24 months -- genuinely better than intensive physical therapy and passive stretching, which reached only 63%. A large real-world long-term cohort (Hand et al 2008, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 17993282, n=269 shoulders, mean follow-up 4.4 years) found 59% had normal or near-normal shoulders, a further 39% (94% of the 41% with residual symptoms) had only mild ongoing symptoms, and just 6% had severe symptoms with real functional loss. On top of this favourable natural course, real active treatment measurably accelerates recovery and reduces pain sooner: intra-articular corticosteroid injection produces significantly greater pain and disability improvement than placebo within 6 weeks (Carette et al 2003, Arthritis Rheum, PMID 12632439; Ryans et al 2005, Rheumatology, PMID 15657070), a short course of oral prednisolone gave marked/moderate improvement in 95.7% (22/23) of patients at 3 weeks versus 47.8% (11/23) on placebo (Buchbinder et al 2004, Ann Rheum Dis, PMID 15479896, though this particular oral-steroid benefit was not sustained past 6 weeks), and hydrodilatation/distension arthrography gives real short-term pain, function and range-of-motion gains (Buchbinder et al 2008 Cochrane review, PMID 18254123; Elnady et al 2020 RCT, PMID 32385765, 77% improvement in external rotation range of motion at 3 months with the anterior rotator-interval approach). For the minority who remain genuinely refractory to all of the above, manipulation under anesthesia (Farrell et al 2005, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 16194738: 84.2% (16/19) with no or only slight pain and 94.7% (18/19) needing no further surgery at a mean 15-year follow-up) and arthroscopic capsular release (Le Lievre & Murrell 2012, J Bone Joint Surg Am, PMID 22760389: 87.8% (43/49) shoulders with significant improvement maintained or enhanced at a mean 7-year follow-up, zero complications, motion equivalent to the uninjured side) give durable, largely successful rescue options. Net honest picture: essentially every patient with frozen shoulder reaches a good or fully recovered shoulder given time and correctly staged treatment; the real caveat is that recovery, even with treatment, typically takes months and the added value of manipulation over a supervised exercise program alone was not confirmed in one blinded RCT (Kivimaki et al 2007, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 17931902).

curative_option.name: Staged Protocol: Intra-Articular Corticosteroid Injection (+/- Physical Therapy) for the Pain-Predominant Freezing Phase, Escalating to Hydrodilatation for Persistent Stiffness, With Manipulation Under Anesthesia or Arthroscopic Capsular Release Reserved for True Non-Responders
curative_option.note: This is the real best-evidenced pathway because it matches the trial evidence at every stage: corticosteroid injection gives the fastest, RCT-proven pain/disability relief in the freezing phase (Carette 2003, PMID 12632439; Ryans 2005, PMID 15657070) without needing to wait out the natural history; hydrodilatation adds real short-term pain/ROM benefit with 'silver'-level Cochrane evidence when injection alone is not enough (Buchbinder 2008, PMID 18254123); and manipulation under anesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release are reserved for genuine treatment failures because both have real, high, durable success rates in that specific refractory population (Farrell 2005, PMID 16194738; Le Lievre & Murrell 2012, PMID 22760389) -- while the underlying self-limited natural history (Reeves 1975, PMID 1198072; Diercks 2004, PMID 15383804) means the floor outcome, even for patients who never escalate past gentle home exercise, is still good in the large majority of cases.
curative_option.step1_freezing_phase_pain_control: NSAIDs and a supervised-neglect-style home exercise program within pain limits from the outset (Diercks & Stevens 2004, PMID 15383804: 89% Constant score >=80 at 24 months, better than intensive passive stretching at 63%). A single intra-articular corticosteroid injection (e.g. triamcinolone hexacetonide 40 mg under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance) is added early because it significantly improves the SPADI/SDQ pain and disability scores over placebo by 6 weeks (Carette et al 2003, PMID 12632439; Ryans et al 2005, PMID 15657070); a short course of oral prednisolone 30 mg/day for 3 weeks is an alternative with a real but shorter-lived benefit (95.7% vs 47.8% marked/moderate improvement at 3 weeks, not sustained past 6 weeks -- Buchbinder et al 2004, PMID 15479896).
curative_option.step2_persistent_stiffness_phase: If stiffness persists despite injection and home exercise, ultrasound-guided hydrodilatation (arthrographic distension with saline plus corticosteroid, anterior rotator-interval approach preferred) gives real added short-term pain, function and range-of-motion benefit (Buchbinder et al 2008 Cochrane review, PMID 18254123, NNTB=2 for pain at 3 weeks in the lowest-risk-of-bias trial; Elnady et al 2020 RCT, PMID 32385765, 77% improvement in external rotation range of motion at 3 months versus 13% with the posterior approach).
curative_option.step3_refractory_disease: For genuine treatment failures after an adequate trial of the above, manipulation under anesthesia (Farrell et al 2005, PMID 16194738: 84.2% (16/19) no/slight pain and 94.7% (18/19) needed no further surgery at a mean 15-year follow-up in patients who had already failed a mean 6.2 months of physical therapy) or arthroscopic capsular release (Le Lievre & Murrell 2012, PMID 22760389: 87.8% (43/49) shoulders with significant, durable improvement at a mean 7-year follow-up, zero complications) are the real, evidence-backed rescue options. Note the one blinded RCT of manipulation under anesthesia added to a home exercise program found no significant added benefit over the exercise program alone at 1 year (Kivimaki et al 2007, PMID 17931902) -- so manipulation's real value is best supported in patients who have already failed structured exercise, not as a routine early add-on.

real_trial_data.reeves_1975_natural_history: 49 patients (41 followed 5-10 years) with idiopathic frozen shoulder syndrome, untreated/minimally treated: only 3/41 (7.3%) had a handicapping restriction at final recovery; average total illness duration 30.1 months through pain, stiffness, and recovery stages. PMID 1198072.
real_trial_data.diercks_2004_supervised_neglect_rct: 77 patients randomized to supervised neglect (supportive therapy + exercise within pain limits) versus intensive physical therapy with passive stretching, followed 24 months: 89% of the supervised-neglect group reached Constant score >=80 versus 63% of the intensive-PT group (64% of the supervised-neglect group reached this by 12 months). PMID 15383804.
real_trial_data.hand_2008_long_term_cohort: 269 shoulders in 223 patients with primary frozen shoulder, mean follow-up 4.4 years (range 2-20 years): 59% normal/near-normal shoulders; 41% had ongoing symptoms, of which 94% were mild; only 6% of the total cohort had severe symptoms with pain and functional loss. Worse baseline severity predicted worse long-term outcome (p<0.001). PMID 17993282.
real_trial_data.carette_2003_rct: 93 subjects with adhesive capsulitis <1 year duration randomized to fluoroscopically-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection + supervised physiotherapy, injection alone, saline + physiotherapy, or placebo, all with a home exercise program: injection groups (1 and 2) had significantly greater SPADI improvement than placebo at 6 weeks (p=0.0004) and 3 months; by 12 months all groups converged; physiotherapy alone was of limited efficacy. PMID 12632439.
real_trial_data.ryans_2005_rct: 80 patients with adhesive capsulitis <6 months duration randomized to triamcinolone 20 mg + physiotherapy, triamcinolone alone, placebo + physiotherapy, or placebo alone, all with home exercise: corticosteroid injection significantly improved the Shoulder Disability Questionnaire at 6 weeks (p=0.004) and self-assessed global disability (p=0.04); physiotherapy significantly improved passive external rotation at 6 weeks (p=0.02); by 16 weeks all groups had improved similarly. PMID 15657070.
real_trial_data.buchbinder_2004_oral_prednisolone_rct: 50 participants (24 active, 26 placebo; 46 completed) given 30 mg oral prednisolone/day for 3 weeks or placebo: marked/moderate participant-rated improvement in 22/23 (95.7%) on prednisolone versus 11/23 (47.8%) on placebo at 3 weeks (RR=2.0, 95% CI 1.3-3.1, p=0.001); benefit not maintained at 12 weeks. PMID 15479896.
real_trial_data.buchbinder_2008_cochrane_distension: Cochrane review of 5 trials, 196 people, arthrographic distension for adhesive capsulitis: the single low-risk-of-bias trial found distension with saline+steroid better than placebo for pain (NNTB=2), function (NNTB=3) and range of motion at 3 weeks, sustained to 6 and 12 weeks for one function measure; conclusion graded 'silver'-level evidence for real short-term benefit. PMID 18254123.
real_trial_data.elnady_2020_hydrodilatation_rct: 60 patients randomized to ultrasound-guided hydrodilatation via posterior intra-articular approach versus anterior rotator-interval approach, both followed by 3 months of guided stretching exercise: anterior approach gave significantly greater improvement in VAS pain (p=0.003), SPADI, flexion, abduction and external rotation; external rotation range-of-motion improved 77% (anterior) versus 13% (posterior), abduction improved 29% versus 3%. PMID 32385765.
real_trial_data.farrell_2005_mua_long_term: 25 patients (26 shoulders) who had already failed a mean 6.2 months of physical therapy underwent manipulation under anesthesia; 18 patients (19 shoulders) followed a mean 15 years (range 8.1-20.6 years): 16/19 (84.2%) had no pain or slight pain, 18/19 (94.7%) required no further surgery, no fractures/dislocations/complications; mean Simple Shoulder Test 9.5/12, mean ASES score 80/100. PMID 16194738.
real_trial_data.kivimaki_2007_mua_rct: 125 patients randomized to manipulation under anesthesia plus home exercise (n=65) versus home exercise alone (n=60), followed 1 year: no significant difference between groups in shoulder pain or working ability; only small ROM differences favored manipulation; 'manipulation under anesthesia does not add effectiveness to an exercise program' in this trial. PMID 17931902.
real_trial_data.le_lievre_murrell_2012_arthroscopic_rele: 43 patients (49 shoulders) treated with circumferential arthroscopic capsular release by a single surgeon, followed a mean 7 years (range 5-13 years): significant, durable improvement in pain frequency/severity, function, stiffness and activity difficulty compared with baseline and the 1-year follow-up (p<0.001 to p<0.01); shoulder motion improved to be comparable with the contralateral shoulder; zero complications. PMID 22760389.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis): the self-limited natural history and supervised-neglect/home-exercise track; intra-articular corticosteroid injection and short-course oral corticosteroid for the pain-predominant freezing phase; hydrodilatation/distension arthrography for persistent stiffness; and manipulation under anesthesia and arthroscopic capsular release for refractory cases. Diagnostic criteria and staging are covered in this knowledge base's symptom-side entry for frozen_shoulder.

fs_natural_history_untreated.name: Untreated / Minimally-Treated Natural History
fs_natural_history_untreated.effectiveness_metric: 92.7% (38/41) recovered without a handicapping restriction of movement at 5-10 year follow-up, through the classic pain -> stiffness -> recovery sequence, average total duration 30.1 months (Reeves 1975).
fs_natural_history_untreated.reason_why: Frozen shoulder is intrinsically a self-limited fibrosing and then resolving process of the glenohumeral joint capsule; in the large majority of patients the capsular contracture and synovitis resolve spontaneously over roughly 1-3 years even without any procedural intervention.
fs_natural_history_untreated.source: Reeves B, The natural history of the frozen shoulder syndrome, Scand J Rheumatol, 1975 (PMID 1198072)
fs_natural_history_untreated.confidence: high -- classic, frequently-cited natural history cohort, though it is an older, non-randomized case series

fs_supervised_neglect_home_exercise.name: Supervised Neglect / Gentle Home Exercise Within Pain Limits
fs_supervised_neglect_home_exercise.effectiveness_metric: 89% reached a normal/near-normal painless shoulder (Constant score >=80) at 24 months, versus 63% with intensive physical therapy and passive stretching (Diercks & Stevens 2004 RCT, n=77).
fs_supervised_neglect_home_exercise.reason_why: Gentle, pain-limited movement maintains joint nutrition and prevents disuse stiffness without provoking the synovitic inflammation that aggressive passive stretching can aggravate in the acute freezing phase, allowing the natural capsular remodeling/resolution process to proceed unimpeded.
fs_supervised_neglect_home_exercise.source: Diercks RL, Stevens M, Gentle thawing of the frozen shoulder, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, 2004 (PMID 15383804)

fs_intra_articular_corticosteroid_inject.name: Intra-Articular Corticosteroid Injection (Triamcinolone)
fs_intra_articular_corticosteroid_inject.type: Injection/procedure (real strong evidence for early-phase pain relief)
fs_intra_articular_corticosteroid_inject.effectiveness_metric: 74% of patients reported clinically relevant pain improvement (>=2-point NRS reduction) 1 month after glenohumeral corticosteroid injection in a real-world cohort of 212 patients (adhesive-capsulitis signs on MR arthrography predicted an even better response, p=0.007); two placebo-controlled RCTs specific to adhesive capsulitis (Carette 2003, n=93; Ryans 2005, n=80) confirmed statistically significant SPADI/SDQ improvement over placebo by 6 weeks.
fs_intra_articular_corticosteroid_inject.reason_why: Intra-articular corticosteroid suppresses the synovitis and inflammatory cytokine drive (the earliest pathological event in the freezing phase) directly at the joint, giving faster pain and disability relief than waiting for natural resolution or physiotherapy alone.
fs_intra_articular_corticosteroid_inject.source: Fritz B et al, Value of MR arthrography findings for pain relief after glenohumeral corticosteroid injections, Eur Radiol, 2019 (PMID 31209618); Carette S et al, Arthritis Rheum, 2003 (PMID 12632439); Ryans I et al, Rheumatology, 2005 (PMID 15657070)
fs_intra_articular_corticosteroid_inject.confidence: high for significant benefit versus placebo in RCTs; the 74% real-world figure is from a mixed shoulder-pathology cohort (not exclusively adhesive capsulitis), flagged as moderate for that specific number

fs_oral_corticosteroid_short_course.name: Short Course Oral Prednisolone (30 mg/day x 3 weeks)
fs_oral_corticosteroid_short_course.type: Medicine (oral, real significant but short-lived early benefit)
fs_oral_corticosteroid_short_course.effectiveness_metric: 95.7% (22/23) reported marked or moderate improvement at 3 weeks versus 47.8% (11/23) on placebo (RR=2.0, p=0.001); benefit was not maintained beyond 6 weeks and by 12 weeks the analysis favored placebo (Buchbinder et al 2004 RCT, n=50).
fs_oral_corticosteroid_short_course.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroid suppresses the early inflammatory/synovitic component of the freezing phase, giving a real short-term boost in pain and participant-rated improvement, but it does not alter the underlying capsular fibrosis, so the advantage over placebo fades once the steroid course ends and the natural history reasserts itself.
fs_oral_corticosteroid_short_course.source: Buchbinder R et al, Short course prednisolone for adhesive capsulitis, Ann Rheum Dis, 2004 (PMID 15479896)
fs_oral_corticosteroid_short_course.confidence: high for the 3-week result; the loss of benefit by 12 weeks is an equally real, honestly-reported part of the same trial

fs_hydrodilatation_distension_arthrograp.name: Hydrodilatation / Arthrographic Distension (Saline + Corticosteroid)
fs_hydrodilatation_distension_arthrograp.effectiveness_metric: 77% improvement in external rotation range of motion at 3 months with the anterior rotator-interval approach (versus 13% with the traditional posterior approach) in a 60-patient RCT; a Cochrane review of 5 trials (196 people) found the lowest-risk-of-bias trial gave a number needed to treat to benefit of 2 for pain and 3 for function/range of motion at 3 weeks.
fs_hydrodilatation_distension_arthrograp.reason_why: Distension mechanically stretches and ruptures the contracted, fibrotic joint capsule under fluid pressure while simultaneously delivering corticosteroid directly into the joint, addressing both the mechanical stiffness and the residual synovitis components of the disease in a single procedure.
fs_hydrodilatation_distension_arthrograp.source: Elnady B et al, Clin Rheumatol, 2020 (PMID 32385765); Buchbinder R et al, Arthrographic distension for adhesive capsulitis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2008 (PMID 18254123)
fs_hydrodilatation_distension_arthrograp.confidence: moderate-high -- Cochrane review itself grades the underlying evidence as 'silver' level (short-term benefit reasonably well supported, uncertain how it compares to alternative interventions)

fs_manipulation_under_anesthesia.name: Manipulation Under Anesthesia (MUA)
fs_manipulation_under_anesthesia.type: Procedure (real high long-term success for treatment-resistant cases)
fs_manipulation_under_anesthesia.effectiveness_metric: 84.2% (16/19) had no pain or only slight pain, and 94.7% (18/19) required no further surgery, at a mean 15-year follow-up in patients who had already failed a mean 6.2 months of physical therapy (Farrell et al 2005, n=25 patients/26 shoulders). A separate blinded RCT (Kivimaki et al 2007, n=125) found MUA added to a home exercise program gave no significant additional benefit over the exercise program alone at 1 year.
fs_manipulation_under_anesthesia.reason_why: Manipulation mechanically ruptures the contracted, fibrotic joint capsule under anesthesia in a single session, immediately restoring passive range of motion in patients whose disease has not resolved with conservative measures alone; it is honestly a rescue/second-line option rather than a routine early add-on given the neutral RCT result against structured exercise.
fs_manipulation_under_anesthesia.source: Farrell CM et al, Manipulation for frozen shoulder: long-term results, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, 2005 (PMID 16194738); Kivimaki J et al, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, 2007 (PMID 17931902)
fs_manipulation_under_anesthesia.confidence: high for the Farrell case-series outcome; moderate for MUA's added value over exercise alone specifically, given the neutral Kivimaki RCT

fs_arthroscopic_capsular_release.name: Arthroscopic Capsular Release
fs_arthroscopic_capsular_release.type: Surgical procedure (real durable option for genuinely refractory cases)
fs_arthroscopic_capsular_release.effectiveness_metric: 87.8% (43/49) shoulders had significant improvement in pain, function and stiffness maintained or enhanced at a mean 7-year follow-up (range 5-13 years), with shoulder motion equivalent to the uninjured contralateral side and zero complications (Le Lievre & Murrell 2012, n=43 patients).
fs_arthroscopic_capsular_release.reason_why: Direct arthroscopic division of the thickened, contracted capsule (including the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament) removes the mechanical restriction under direct visualization, giving durable motion restoration in patients for whom injection, distension and/or manipulation have not been sufficient.
fs_arthroscopic_capsular_release.source: Le Lievre HM, Murrell GA, Long-term outcomes after arthroscopic capsular release for idiopathic adhesive capsulitis, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2012 (PMID 22760389)
fs_arthroscopic_capsular_release.confidence: high -- longest-follow-up outcome series available for this procedure, single-surgeon series (not multi-center)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Short course oral prednisolone (early responder rate, benefit not sustained past 6 weeks)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 95.7% (22/23) marked/moderate improvement at 3 weeks versus 47.8% (11/23) placebo (RR=2.0, p=0.001); benefit lost by 12 weeks. RCT, n=50 (46 completed).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Buchbinder R et al, Short course prednisolone for adhesive capsulitis, Ann Rheum Dis 2004;63(11):1460-9 (PMID 15479896)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Untreated/minimally-treated natural history
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92.7% (38/41) recovered without a handicapping restriction of movement, followed 5-10 years, average total illness duration 30.1 months. Prospective cohort, n=49 (41 followed long-term).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Reeves B, The natural history of the frozen shoulder syndrome, Scand J Rheumatol 1975;4(4):193-6 (PMID 1198072)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Supervised neglect / gentle home exercise within pain limits
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 89% reached Constant score >=80 (normal/near-normal painless shoulder) at 24 months, versus 63% with intensive physical therapy and passive stretching. RCT, n=77.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Diercks RL, Stevens M, Gentle thawing of the frozen shoulder, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2004;13(5):499-502 (PMID 15383804)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Arthroscopic capsular release (refractory cases)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 87.8% (43/49) shoulders with significant improvement maintained/enhanced at mean 7-year follow-up (range 5-13 years); zero complications; motion equivalent to contralateral shoulder. Single-surgeon cohort, n=43 patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Le Lievre HM, Murrell GA, Long-term outcomes after arthroscopic capsular release for idiopathic adhesive capsulitis, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94(13):1208-16 (PMID 22760389)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Manipulation under anesthesia (after failed conservative treatment)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 84.2% (16/19) no/slight pain and 94.7% (18/19) needed no further surgery at a mean 15-year follow-up, in patients who had failed a mean 6.2 months of physical therapy. Note: a separate blinded RCT found no significant added benefit of MUA over home exercise alone at 1 year (Kivimaki 2007, PMID 17931902). Case series, n=25 patients (18 long-term follow-up).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Farrell CM et al, Manipulation for frozen shoulder: long-term results, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2005;14(5):480-4 (PMID 16194738)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hydrodilatation, anterior rotator-interval approach
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 77% improvement in external rotation range of motion at 3 months (vs 13% posterior approach); also significantly greater VAS pain and SPADI improvement (p=0.003). RCT, n=60.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Elnady B et al, Clin Rheumatol 2020;39(12):3805-3814 (PMID 32385765)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection, real-world glenohumeral cohort
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 74% clinically relevant pain improvement (>=2-point NRS reduction) at 1 month; adhesive-capsulitis MR-arthrography signs predicted a significantly better response (p=0.007). Prospective cohort, n=212 (mixed shoulder pathology, not exclusively adhesive capsulitis).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fritz B et al, Eur Radiol 2019;29(12):6416-6424 (PMID 31209618)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intensive physical therapy with passive stretching
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 63% reached Constant score >=80 at 24 months, versus 89% with supervised neglect in the same RCT; Carette 2003 separately found supervised physiotherapy alone was of limited efficacy versus corticosteroid injection. RCT, n=77.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Diercks RL, Stevens M, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2004;13(5):499-502 (PMID 15383804)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Long-term real-world mixed-treatment cohort (normal/near-normal outcome)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 59% had normal/near-normal shoulders at mean 4.4-year follow-up; a further 39% had only mild residual symptoms; only 6% of the total cohort had severe residual symptoms with functional loss. Cohort, n=269 shoulders/223 patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hand C et al, Long-term outcome of frozen shoulder, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2008;17(2):231-6 (PMID 17993282)

core_lesion.finding: Adhesive capsulitis is a distinct clinical entity in which painful, gradual loss of BOTH active and passive shoulder motion results from fibrosis and contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule itself (a true capsular restriction), as opposed to pain-related guarding from other shoulder pathology that can mimic it.
core_lesion.source: Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, 'Adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder', J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699)

histology_and_molecular_findings.finding: A systematic review of 25 studies on the cellular/molecular/metabolic basis of frozen shoulder found the capsule shows nonspecific chronic inflammation with proliferation of fibroblasts, adipocytes and blood vessels, along with fibroblast activation and excess collagen deposition; molecular studies show increased pro-inflammatory mediators together with reduced matrix-metalloproteinase activity (impaired collagen turnover), consistent with a fibrosis-favouring, poorly-degraded extracellular matrix.
histology_and_molecular_findings.source: Jump CM, Duke K, Malik RA, Charalambous CP, 'Frozen Shoulder: A Systematic Review of Cellular, Molecular, and Metabolic Findings', JBJS Rev 2021 (PMID 33512972)

cytokine_drivers.finding: Immunohistochemical study of shoulder-capsule biopsies from adhesive-capsulitis patients (n=19) versus controls demonstrated positive staining for transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) and its receptor, and for platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), in the diseased capsule, alongside synovial hyperplasia and capsular fibrosis -- implicating these fibrogenic cytokines as drivers of the fibrotic cascade.
cytokine_drivers.source: Rodeo SA, Hannafin JA, Tom J, Warren RF, Wickiewicz TL, 'Immunolocalization of cytokines and their receptors in adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder', J Orthop Res 1997 (PMID 9246090)

sequence_of_events.finding: A literature review of primary frozen-shoulder pathology and imaging describes an inflammatory contracture of the joint capsule in which synovitis appears to precede the fibrotic phase (increased collagen and TGF-beta-driven fibrotic growth factor deposition), but the specific initial inflammatory trigger that starts the cascade remains unidentified.
sequence_of_events.source: Tamai K, Akutsu M, Yano Y, 'Primary frozen shoulder: brief review of pathology and imaging abnormalities', J Orthop Sci 2014 (PMID 24306579)
sequence_of_events.confidence: moderate (mechanistic sequence plausible and cited, but the review itself states the initiating trigger is unidentified)

how_diagnosed.finding: The diagnosis of adhesive capsulitis is usually clinical (history plus physical examination showing the capsular pattern of restriction); imaging (plain radiographs, and ultrasound/MRI when indicated) is used mainly to rule out other conditions on the differential, not to make the positive diagnosis.
how_diagnosed.source: Ewald A, 'Adhesive capsulitis: a review', Am Fam Physician 2011 (PMID 21322517)

three_stage_clinical_course.finding: Classic descriptions divide the disorder into three sequential clinical stages: Stage 1 'freezing' (progressively worsening pain with increasing loss of motion), Stage 2 'frozen' (pain plateaus/improves but stiffness persists), and Stage 3 'thawing' (gradual, spontaneous return of motion). One cited source states each of the three stages lasts approximately 4-6 months.
three_stage_clinical_course.source: Schultheis A, Reichwein F, Nebelung W, 'Frozen shoulder. Diagnosis and therapy' [German], Orthopade 2008 (PMID 20110457)
three_stage_clinical_course.confidence: moderate -- single non-English-language source for the specific 4-6-month-per-stage figure; the total duration this implies (roughly 12-18 months) is notably shorter than the average total course measured in the older, larger Reeves prospective cohort below (30.1 months), so exact stage-length cutoffs should be treated as approximate rather than fixed rule.

reeves_prospective_natural_history.finding: A prospective study following 49 frozen-shoulder patients for 5-10 years to maximal recovery found the disorder passes through three phases (pain, stiffness, recovery) and that 'the total duration was longer than is generally supposed: an average total of 30.1 months, in contrast to about 18 months as often postulated.' The duration of the stiffness phase correlated with the length of the recovery phase. In 4 of the 49 patients the opposite shoulder later developed the identical syndrome (onset 6 months to 7 years afterward).
reeves_prospective_natural_history.source: Reeves B, 'The natural history of the frozen shoulder syndrome', Scand J Rheumatol 1975 (PMID 1198072)
reeves_prospective_natural_history.confidence: high (prospective, long follow-up, though an older and modestly sized cohort, n=49)

controversy_note.finding: A more recent narrative review explicitly states that 'the natural history of adhesive capsulitis is a matter of controversy' -- i.e. the exact stage boundaries and total-duration figures vary meaningfully between published series, and no single timeline should be presented to a patient as fixed.
controversy_note.source: Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699)
controversy_note.confidence: high (explicit statement in a peer-reviewed review)

global_active_and_passive_restriction.finding: The defining, diagnostically pivotal feature of adhesive capsulitis is painful, gradual loss of BOTH active AND passive shoulder range of motion (a true capsular pattern), most marked in external rotation, resulting from fibrosis/contracture of the capsule itself. This is the key sign that separates frozen shoulder from most other painful-shoulder conditions, in which passive range of motion is relatively preserved even when active motion is limited by pain or weakness.
global_active_and_passive_restriction.source: Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699)

pain_pattern.finding: Pain is typically diffuse, poorly localized around the deltoid region, worse at night and with attempted end-range movement, and is most prominent in the 'freezing' stage, tending to plateau or ease somewhat once the joint becomes maximally stiff ('frozen' stage) even though motion loss persists.
pain_pattern.source: Schultheis A et al, Orthopade 2008 (PMID 20110457); Ewald A, Am Fam Physician 2011 (PMID 21322517)

functional_impact.finding: Loss of external rotation and abduction impairs everyday tasks (dressing, reaching overhead, reaching behind the back); the condition can occur in isolation ('primary'/idiopathic) or together with other shoulder pathology such as rotator cuff tendinopathy or bursitis, or with diabetes mellitus ('secondary').

documented_differential_list.finding: A major family-medicine review lists the differential diagnosis of a painful, stiff shoulder as including: acromioclavicular arthropathy, autoimmune disease (e.g. systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis), biceps tendinopathy, glenohumeral osteoarthritis, neoplasm, rotator cuff tendinopathy or tear (with or without impingement), and subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis -- all of which can produce shoulder pain and some restriction of motion and must be distinguished from true adhesive capsulitis.

rotator_cuff_tear_distinction.finding: In rotator cuff tear/tendinopathy, weakness and pain limit ACTIVE elevation/external rotation (e.g. a positive drop-arm sign or external-rotation lag sign in a large/full-thickness tear), but PASSIVE range of motion is characteristically much better preserved than in frozen shoulder, because the joint capsule itself is not primarily contracted. A prospective diagnostic study of acute full-thickness supraspinatus tears (n=52) found the external-rotation lag sign had sensitivity 0.39 / specificity 0.91, and the drop-arm test sensitivity 0.37 / specificity 0.86 -- i.e. these clinical weakness signs are fairly specific but not sensitive, and none of them test for the global active-plus-passive restriction seen in adhesive capsulitis.
rotator_cuff_tear_distinction.source: Bak K et al, 'The value of clinical tests in acute full-thickness tears of the supraspinatus tendon...', Arthroscopy 2010 (PMID 20511030); Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699)
rotator_cuff_tear_distinction.confidence: moderate-high (diagnostic-accuracy numbers are from a single prospective study; the general active-preserved-passive teaching principle is corroborated across the reviews cited)

glenohumeral_osteoarthritis_distinction.finding: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis is listed as a standard item on the differential diagnosis of a stiff, painful shoulder alongside adhesive capsulitis; it is an intra-articular degenerative joint disease (typically in older patients, often with crepitus) rather than a purely capsular fibrotic process, and imaging is used specifically to help separate the two when the clinical picture is ambiguous (plain radiographs would be expected to show glenohumeral joint-space narrowing and osteophytes in osteoarthritis, which are absent in isolated adhesive capsulitis, where radiographs are typically normal).
glenohumeral_osteoarthritis_distinction.confidence: moderate -- the differential-diagnosis listing itself is directly sourced; the specific radiographic contrast (joint-space narrowing/osteophytes present in OA vs normal film in isolated capsulitis) is standard radiologic teaching consistent with this source's stated purpose for imaging, but was not independently re-confirmed against a dedicated radiology-specific study this session.

diabetes_mellitus.finding: A meta-analysis of 18 studies (from 5,411 screened articles) found patients with diabetes mellitus were 5 times more likely than controls to have adhesive capsulitis (RR 5, 95% CI 3.2-7.7). Estimated prevalence of adhesive capsulitis among diabetics was 13.4% (95% CI 10.2-17.2%), and the prevalence of diabetes among adhesive-capsulitis patients was about 30% (95% CI 24-37%). No significant difference in adhesive-capsulitis prevalence was found between insulin-treated and non-insulin-treated diabetics.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Zreik NH, Malik RA, Charalambous CP, 'Adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder and diabetes: a meta-analysis of prevalence', Muscles Ligaments Tendons J 2016 (PMID 27331029)

thyroid_disease.finding: A meta-analysis found thyroid disease overall was associated with adhesive capsulitis (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.37-2.57); hypothyroidism specifically had OR 1.92 (95% CI 1.09-3.39) and subclinical hypothyroidism OR 2.56 (95% CI 1.81-3.63), while hyperthyroidism was not significantly associated (OR 1.42, 95% CI 0.63-3.22). An earlier single-centre study found frozen shoulder was independently related to hypothyroidism (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.5-6.4).
thyroid_disease.source: Chuang SH, Chen YP, Huang SW, Kuo YJ, 'Association between adhesive capsulitis and thyroid disease: a meta-analysis', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2023 (PMID 36871608); Schiefer M et al, 'Prevalence of hypothyroidism in patients with frozen shoulder', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2017 (PMID 27424251)
thyroid_disease.confidence: high (meta-analysis plus a corroborating independent single-centre study)

body_mass_index_obesity.finding: A retrospective cohort study of 522,830 German adults found the 10-year cumulative incidence of shoulder adhesive capsulitis rose with BMI category: 0.63% (underweight), 0.65% (normal weight), 1.05% (overweight), 1.25% (obesity); after adjustment, overweight individuals had 1.52-times and obese individuals 1.77-times the risk of normal-weight individuals (p<0.001).
body_mass_index_obesity.source: Kostev K, Gyasi RM, Yon DK, Konrad M, Jacob L, 'Association between body mass index and incident shoulder adhesive capsulitis in Germany: a retrospective cohort study of 522,830 adults', Maturitas 2026 (PMID 42048914)
body_mass_index_obesity.confidence: high (very large retrospective cohort, dose-response gradient)

population_incidence.finding: In a large German general-practice cohort of 522,830 adults, the overall 10-year cumulative incidence of adhesive capsulitis ranged from about 0.63% (underweight) to 1.25% (obese individuals), i.e. on the order of roughly 1 in 100-150 adults over a decade, rising with body-mass index.
population_incidence.confidence: high for this specific cohort/timeframe; note this is a 10-year cumulative-incidence figure from one national health-claims-style database, not a single verified worldwide point-prevalence percentage -- a general-population point-prevalence figure (commonly quoted in older reviews as being in the low single digits) could not be independently re-verified against a primary source this session and is therefore omitted rather than restated from memory.

disease_associated_subgroups.finding: Prevalence is markedly higher in at-risk subgroups than in the general population: about 13.4% in diabetics (versus controls) and, in one MRI-based cohort study of 503 adhesive-capsulitis patients, thyroid dysfunction was found in 15.90% of adhesive-capsulitis patients (p<0.001 versus expected background rate) with concurrent rotator-cuff tendinosis seen on MRI in 76.94% of these patients.
disease_associated_subgroups.source: Zreik NH et al, Muscles Ligaments Tendons J 2016 (PMID 27331029); Timocin Yigman G, Ozen Atalay H, 'A comprehensive MRI-based study on adhesive capsulitis and its correlations with tendinosis and systemic diseases', Radiologie 2025
disease_associated_subgroups.confidence: moderate-high for the diabetes figure (meta-analysis); moderate for the single MRI cohort's thyroid/tendinosis co-occurrence figures (single retrospective imaging study, not independently replicated this session)

self_limited_but_prolonged.finding: Adhesive capsulitis is often self-limited but can persist for years and may never fully resolve. In the Reeves prospective cohort (n=49, followed 5-10 years), the average total duration to maximal recovery was 30.1 months, and although most patients regained substantial motion, mild residual movement limitation was common at final follow-up, with only 3 of 49 patients left with significant functional impairment.
self_limited_but_prolonged.source: Ewald A, Am Fam Physician 2011 (PMID 21322517); Reeves B, Scand J Rheumatol 1975 (PMID 1198072)

controversy_on_exact_course.finding: A 2011 review explicitly flags that the natural history of adhesive capsulitis remains a matter of controversy in the literature -- i.e. published series disagree on exact stage lengths and total time-to-resolution, so patients should be counselled on a prolonged (many-month-to-multi-year), variable course rather than a fixed timeline.
controversy_on_exact_course.source: Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699)
controversy_on_exact_course.confidence: high (explicit statement in a peer-reviewed review)

contralateral_recurrence.finding: In the Reeves cohort, 4 of 49 patients (about 8%) went on to develop the identical syndrome in the opposite shoulder, with onset ranging from 6 months to 7 years after the first shoulder, following an identical stage progression.
contralateral_recurrence.confidence: moderate (small cohort, n=49, single older study)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Frozen shoulder is a real, self-limited but often multi-year disease of true capsular fibrosis, not simple pain-guarding: the one physical finding that should trigger the diagnosis is loss of BOTH active AND passive shoulder motion (especially external rotation) in a patient with an otherwise normal shoulder X-ray, insidious (non-traumatic) onset, and no fever. Always ask about diabetes and thyroid disease (both real, meta-analysis-confirmed risk multipliers -- roughly 5x for diabetes and up to ~2.5x for subclinical hypothyroidism) since these patients are more likely to have it, may have bilateral or recurrent disease, and may need concurrent endocrine work-up. Before accepting the diagnosis, actively exclude rotator cuff tear (weakness with better-preserved passive ROM, often after trauma) and glenohumeral osteoarthritis (crepitus, radiographic joint-space narrowing/osteophytes) using the history, exam and, when needed, imaging -- because management of these mimics differs substantially from management of true adhesive capsulitis.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Neviaser AS/Neviaser RJ 2011 (PMID 21885699), Ewald A 2011 (PMID 21322517), Zreik NH et al 2016 (PMID 27331029), Chuang SH et al 2023 (PMID 36871608), Reeves B 1975 (PMID 1198072)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Frozen shoulder is a diagnosis of exclusion for a stiff, painful shoulder and must NOT be assumed in two specific higher-urgency situations, because their management is completely different: (1) ACUTE TRAUMATIC ROTATOR CUFF TEAR -- sudden onset of shoulder pain/weakness after a fall, lifting injury, or dislocation, especially in an older adult, with weakness on active elevation/external rotation (e.g. a positive drop-arm test or external-rotation lag sign, which are reasonably specific -- 86-91% -- though not very sensitive -- 37-39% -- for a full-thickness tear) but with PASSIVE range of motion much better preserved than in true adhesive capsulitis; these patients need prompt orthopedic referral and imaging (ultrasound/MRI) since large/full-thickness tears may need timely surgical repair, unlike frozen shoulder's capsular restriction. (2) SEPTIC ARTHRITIS OF THE GLENOHUMERAL JOINT -- a severe, rapidly progressive joint infection that is a true emergency requiring urgent arthrocentesis, antibiotics and often surgical washout to prevent permanent joint destruction and systemic sepsis; it should be suspected whenever shoulder pain/stiffness is accompanied by fever, marked local warmth/erythema, a toxic-appearing patient, or risk factors such as diabetes, immunosuppression, rheumatoid arthritis, recent joint injection/surgery, or intravenous drug use -- none of which is expected in idiopathic frozen shoulder, which is classically afebrile with an insidious, non-toxic presentation. Any stiff, painful shoulder with fever, marked warmth, or a clear antecedent trauma/dislocation should be escalated for urgent orthopedic/infectious work-up rather than managed as routine frozen shoulder.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Bak K et al, Arthroscopy 2010 (PMID 20511030) for rotator cuff clinical-test accuracy; Wu KA, Kugelman DN, Seidelman JL, Seyler TM, 'Native Joint Septic Arthritis', Antibiotics (Basel) 2024 (PMID 39061278) for septic arthritis risk factors/urgency; Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699) and Ewald A, Am Fam Physician 2011 (PMID 21322517) for the frozen-shoulder differential-diagnosis framework these mimics sit within.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the overall triage principle and the cited rotator-cuff test accuracy figures; moderate for the qualitative septic-arthritis clinical picture (the source review confirms shoulder is a commonly affected joint and lists fever/risk factors and urgency, but a shoulder-specific numeric sensitivity/specificity for fever or a fixed synovial-fluid WBC cutoff was not independently verified against a primary source this session and is therefore omitted rather than stated as a number).

sarcopenia.name: Sarcopenia

definition.finding: Sarcopenia is defined by the revised European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2) as a progressive and generalised skeletal muscle disorder involving the accelerated loss of muscle mass and function, associated with increased likelihood of adverse outcomes including falls, fractures, physical disability and mortality. Low muscle strength is now considered the key characteristic that drives the diagnosis, with muscle quantity/quality used to confirm the diagnosis and physical performance used to grade severity.
definition.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Sarcopenia: revised European consensus on definition and diagnosis, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

primary_vs_secondary_sarcopenia.finding: EWGSOP2 classifies sarcopenia as 'primary' (age-related) when no other specific cause is evident, and 'secondary' when other causal factors are present in addition to or instead of ageing: disease-related (systemic disease, especially with an inflammatory component, e.g. malignancy or organ failure), activity-related (physical inactivity from a sedentary lifestyle or disease-related immobility, bed rest, deconditioning), and nutrition-related (inadequate energy or protein intake from anorexia, malabsorption, or limited access to food).
primary_vs_secondary_sarcopenia.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

mechanism.finding: Sarcopenia develops through age-related biological processes (denervation and loss of alpha motor neurons, preferential atrophy of type II [fast-twitch] muscle fibres, mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic low-grade inflammation, anabolic resistance to protein intake, and declining anabolic hormones such as testosterone, growth hormone/IGF-1) that are further shaped by genetic and lifestyle factors accumulating across the lifespan; it is described as a muscle disease that can begin as early as young adulthood (through impaired muscle development/growth) and can also be accelerated in middle age by acute or chronic illness, not only occurring de novo in old age.
mechanism.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Sayer AA, Sarcopenia, Lancet, 2019 (PMID 31171417)

ewgsop2_find_assess_confirm_severity_pat.finding: EWGSOP2 recommends a stepwise 'Find-Assess-Confirm-Severity' (F-A-C-S) clinical algorithm. FIND (case-finding): the SARC-F self-report questionnaire (5 items: strength, assistance walking, rising from a chair, climbing stairs, falls) is used to raise clinical suspicion; it has low-to-moderate sensitivity but high specificity. ASSESS (muscle strength, for probable sarcopenia): low grip strength (cut-off <27 kg in men, <16 kg in women) or a slow chair-stand test (>15 seconds for 5 rises) identifies 'probable sarcopenia', which is sufficient to begin intervention in practice. CONFIRM (muscle quantity/quality): diagnosis is confirmed by low appendicular skeletal muscle mass, measured by DXA (ASM <20 kg in men, <15 kg in women; or ASM/height^2 <7.0 kg/m^2 in men, <5.5 kg/m^2 in women) or by bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) using cross-validated equations (e.g. the Sergi equation), with MRI/CT reserved for research settings. SEVERITY: once confirmed, severity is graded using physical performance tests -- gait speed <=0.8 m/s, Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) score <=8, Timed-Up-and-Go >=20 seconds, or inability to complete/needing >=6 minutes for a 400-metre walk test defines 'severe sarcopenia'.
ewgsop2_find_assess_confirm_severity_pat.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

weakness_and_functional_decline.finding: The clinical presentation is dominated by generalised muscle weakness -- reduced grip strength, difficulty rising unaided from a chair (5-times chair-stand test), difficulty climbing stairs, and reduced ability to carry loads -- reflecting the loss of muscle strength that EWGSOP2 identifies as the key diagnostic characteristic.
weakness_and_functional_decline.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

gait_slowing_and_falls.finding: Slow walking speed (gait speed <=0.8 m/s marks severe sarcopenia) and recurrent falls are core clinical features and are directly incorporated into the SARC-F case-finding questionnaire (which asks about falls in the past year) and into the EWGSOP2 severity assessment.
gait_slowing_and_falls.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

loss_of_muscle_bulk_and_secondary_weight.finding: Visible/palpable reduction in muscle bulk (particularly in the limbs) occurs as skeletal muscle mass declines; in secondary (disease- or nutrition-related) sarcopenia, this is frequently accompanied by unintentional weight loss, while in primary age-related sarcopenia, muscle loss can occur even without overall weight loss because fat mass may be preserved or increased (sarcopenic obesity).
loss_of_muscle_bulk_and_secondary_weight.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Sayer AA, Lancet, 2019 (PMID 31171417); Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

cachexia.finding: Cachexia is a formally-defined, distinct complex metabolic syndrome associated with underlying illness (e.g. cancer, heart failure, CKD, COPD) and characterised by loss of muscle with or without loss of fat mass, driven by an abnormal inflammatory/catabolic metabolic state (anorexia, insulin resistance, increased muscle protein breakdown); the consensus definition requires weight loss of at least 5% in 12 months or less (or BMI <20) plus at least 3 of: decreased muscle strength, fatigue, anorexia, low fat-free mass index, or abnormal biochemistry (inflammatory markers, anaemia, low serum albumin). This differs from sarcopenia, which is a primarily muscle-strength/mass-defined disorder that can occur without any underlying wasting illness or weight loss (i.e. age-related sarcopenia). In practice, cachexia and secondary (disease-related) sarcopenia frequently coexist and overlap in patients with advanced organ failure or cancer.
cachexia.source: Evans WJ et al, Cachexia: a new definition, Clinical Nutrition, 2008 (PMID 18718696); Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

frailty_syndrome.finding: Frailty (Fried phenotype) is a distinct multidimensional geriatric syndrome of reduced physiological reserve, defined by the presence of >=3 of 5 criteria: unintentional weight loss (>=10 lb/4.5 kg in the past year), self-reported exhaustion, low grip strength, slow walking speed, and low physical activity; it predicted falls, worsening mobility/ADL disability, hospitalisation and death in a cohort of 5,317 community-dwelling adults aged >=65, with an overall prevalence of 6.9%. EWGSOP2 explicitly states that 'frailty and sarcopenia are still distinct -- one a geriatric syndrome and the other a disease' -- frailty is broader and multi-system (incorporating exhaustion, weight loss and activity level as separate criteria), whereas sarcopenia is a muscle-specific disorder defined operationally by strength/mass/performance testing; the two conditions overlap substantially (low grip strength and slow gait are shared criteria) but sarcopenia can be diagnosed and treated as a standalone muscle disease independent of the broader frailty phenotype.
frailty_syndrome.source: Fried LP et al, Frailty in older adults: evidence for a phenotype, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci, 2001 (PMID 11253156); Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

ageing_and_lifestyle.finding: Primary sarcopenia is age-related, arising from cumulative genetic and lifestyle influences across the lifespan (in the absence of another specific cause); physical inactivity (sedentary lifestyle or disease-related immobility/bed rest) is an independently recognised contributor that accelerates muscle loss.
ageing_and_lifestyle.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

malnutrition.finding: Inadequate intake of energy or protein -- due to anorexia, malabsorption, or limited access to healthy food -- is a recognised driver of secondary (nutrition-related) sarcopenia.
malnutrition.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

chronic_disease_and_inflammation.finding: Secondary sarcopenia commonly develops in the context of chronic systemic disease with an inflammatory component, including malignancy and organ failure (e.g. chronic kidney disease, chronic heart failure, COPD); sarcopenia is also associated with cardiac disease, respiratory disease and cognitive impairment, and can accelerate in middle age when illness compounds age-related muscle change.
chronic_disease_and_inflammation.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372); Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Sayer AA, Lancet, 2019 (PMID 31171417)

global_prevalence.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 151 studies (692,056 participants, mean age 68.5 years) found global sarcopenia prevalence estimates of 10-27% depending on which diagnostic criteria/definition were applied, with severe sarcopenia prevalence of 2-9%; prevalence varied by region, with Oceania showing the highest rates and Europe the lowest under specific diagnostic frameworks, using criteria including EWGSOP/EWGSOP2, AWGS and FNIH.
global_prevalence.source: Petermann-Rocha F et al, Global prevalence of sarcopenia and severe sarcopenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, 2022 (PMID 34816624)

mortality_and_functional_outcomes.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 longitudinal studies (follow-up 3 months to 9.8 years) found sarcopenia was associated with a substantially elevated risk of death, with a pooled odds ratio of 3.596 for mortality, and with increased functional decline and increased incidence of falls; evidence on fractures and hospital length of stay was less consistent across the included studies at that time.
mortality_and_functional_outcomes.source: Beaudart C et al, Health Outcomes of Sarcopenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, PLoS One, 2017 (PMID 28095426)

glis_2025_consensus_update.finding: A 2025 consensus report by the outcome working group of the Global Leadership Initiative in Sarcopenia (GLIS), synthesising the accumulated evidence base, concluded there is strong evidence that sarcopenia is associated with reduced quality of life, a higher risk of falls and fractures, and a higher risk of mortality; moderate evidence supports an association with impaired instrumental activities of daily living, while evidence remains inconclusive for hospitalisation, nursing home admission, and basic activities of daily living limitations.
glis_2025_consensus_update.source: Health outcomes of sarcopenia: a consensus report by the outcome working group of the Global Leadership Initiative in Sarcopenia (GLIS), Aging Clinical and Experimental Research, 2025 (PMID 40120052)

downstream_consequences.finding: EWGSOP2 states that sarcopenia increases the risk of falls and fractures; impairs the ability to perform activities of daily living; is associated with cardiac disease, respiratory disease and cognitive impairment; leads to mobility disorders; and contributes to lowered quality of life, loss of independence or need for long-term care placement, and death.
downstream_consequences.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Sarcopenia should be suspected in any older adult (or younger adult with a chronic wasting illness) presenting with generalised weakness, slow gait, frequent falls, or difficulty rising from a chair -- screened for with SARC-F or low grip strength/slow chair-stand, and confirmed with DXA or BIA-measured low appendicular muscle mass. Cachexia (weight-loss-driven, inflammation-mediated wasting syndrome tied to a specific underlying illness) and frailty (a broader multidimensional geriatric syndrome including exhaustion and activity level, not just muscle) are distinct but overlapping entities that must be actively distinguished, since sarcopenia is treatable as a standalone muscle disease (see the treatment/curability side of this record for resistance-exercise and nutritional evidence) even when a coexisting cachexia or frailty diagnosis also needs separate management. Once gait speed falls to <=0.8 m/s (severe sarcopenia), the clinical priority shifts immediately to proactive falls/fracture-prevention measures because sarcopenia's downstream harms -- falls, fractures, disability, and a pooled mortality odds ratio of 3.6 -- are the real drivers of poor outcomes, not muscle weakness in isolation.
clinical_takeaway.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372); Beaudart C et al, PLoS One, 2017 (PMID 28095426)

severe_sarcopenia_fall_fracture_risk_req.finding: Severe sarcopenia (EWGSOP2-defined by gait speed <=0.8 m/s, SPPB <=8, Timed-Up-and-Go >=20 seconds, or failure/>=6 minutes on the 400-metre walk test) marks a threshold at which fall and fracture risk becomes clinically urgent: sarcopenia is associated with a pooled mortality odds ratio of 3.596 and, per the 2025 GLIS consensus, there is strong evidence linking it to increased falls, fractures, and mortality. Because these harms compound silently (frank fracture or a fall-related hospitalisation is often the first dramatic event), any patient meeting the severe-sarcopenia performance thresholds should be proactively triaged for fall-prevention measures (home hazard assessment, gait aids, supervised resistance/balance exercise referral, vitamin D and protein-adequacy review) and fracture-risk/bone-health screening rather than waiting for a fall or fracture to occur before acting.
severe_sarcopenia_fall_fracture_risk_req.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al, Age and Ageing, 2019 (PMID 30312372); Beaudart C et al, PLoS One, 2017 (PMID 28095426); GLIS outcome working group consensus, Aging Clinical and Experimental Research, 2025 (PMID 40120052)

sarcopenia.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM M62.84 Sarcopenia (a dedicated code effective October 2016, introduced specifically to recognize sarcopenia as a distinct diagnosable disease rather than a normal-ageing finding - Anker SD, Morley JE, von Haehling S, 'Welcome to the ICD-10 code for sarcopenia', J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2016;7:512-514, PMID 27891296). The exact WHO ICD-11 code could NOT be independently verified this session: the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) requires client-side JavaScript rendering not accessible to this session's fetch tool, and the WHO ICD-11 API requires an OAuth2 token that was not available. FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED pending direct confirmation against the WHO ICD-11 API/browser.
sarcopenia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Sarcopenia is one of the most genuinely modifiable syndromes in geriatric medicine, and unlike most degenerative musculoskeletal diseases in this knowledge base, its core deficit (loss of muscle mass, strength and function) can be REAL, LARGE, and MEASURABLY REVERSED with a real, non-pharmacological intervention - progressive resistance training - even though no drug is yet approved to treat it. The largest real evidence base is a Cochrane systematic review of 121 randomised controlled trials in 6,700 older adults, which found that progressive resistance training produced a large, statistically significant improvement in muscle strength (standardised mean difference 0.84, 95% CI 0.67-1.00), a significant improvement in physical performance (SMD 0.14, 95% CI 0.05-0.22), a real gait-speed gain (mean difference +0.08 m/s, 95% CI 0.04-0.12), and a large improvement in chair-stand performance (SMD -0.94, 95% CI -1.49 to -0.38), with serious adverse events rare and none directly attributable to the exercise programme (Liu CJ, Latham NK, 'Progressive resistance strength training for improving physical function in older adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009, PMID 19588334). A separate meta-analysis of 47 RCTs (1,079 participants aged 50+) found resistance exercise produced strength gains of 24-33% across major muscle groups (leg press 29+/-2%, chest press 24+/-2%, knee extension 33+/-3%, lat pull 25+/-2%) (Peterson MD et al., 'Resistance exercise for muscular strength in older adults: a meta-analysis', Ageing Res Rev 2010;9:226-237, PMID 20385254), and a companion meta-analysis of 49 studies (1,328 participants) found a real mean lean-body-mass gain of 1.1 kg (95% CI 0.9-1.2 kg) with resistance training (Peterson MD et al., 'Influence of resistance exercise on lean body mass in aging adults: a meta-analysis', Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43:249-258, PMID 20543750). Adding protein supplementation on top of resistance training produces a further real, additive gain: a meta-analysis of 22 RCTs (680 subjects) found protein supplementation significantly augmented fat-free mass gain (weighted mean difference +0.69 kg, 95% CI 0.47-0.91, P<0.00001) and 1-repetition-maximum leg-press strength (weighted mean difference +13.5 kg, 95% CI 6.4-20.7, P<0.005) compared with resistance training plus placebo (Cermak NM et al., 'Protein supplementation augments the adaptive response of skeletal muscle to resistance-type exercise training: a meta-analysis', Am J Clin Nutr 2012;96:1454-1464, PMID 23134885). Both the European (EWGSOP2, Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al., Age Ageing 2019;48:16-31, PMID 30312372) and Asian (AWGS 2019 update, Chen LK et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2020;21:300-307.e2, PMID 32033882) consensus definitions converge on the same real-world message: 'lifestyle interventions, especially exercise and nutritional supplementation, prevail as mainstays of treatment' (AWGS 2019). This knowledge base gives sarcopenia a genuinely positive cure-first framing not because a pill cures it, but because the single best-evidenced intervention in this entire disease category - structured progressive resistance exercise, reinforced with adequate dietary protein and correction of vitamin D deficiency where present - produces large, real, replicated, dose-responsive improvements in the exact deficits (muscle strength, muscle mass, physical performance) that define the disease, in trials totalling many thousands of older adults.

curative_option.name: Progressive Resistance (Strength) Training Combined with Adequate Dietary Protein Intake, with Vitamin D Correction in Deficient Patients
curative_option.type: Structured exercise therapy (first-line, non-pharmacological) plus nutritional optimisation (protein intake, vitamin D repletion) - no medicine or injection is currently approved specifically for sarcopenia
curative_option.note: Sarcopenia has no approved drug therapy, but it is not an untreatable disease: both major international consensus panels (EWGSOP2 in Europe, AWGS in Asia) identify structured exercise plus nutritional support as the evidence-based mainstay, and this combination has the largest, most replicated real trial evidence of any intervention surveyed for this entry. The real, evidence-graded order of operations is: (1) progressive resistance training (PRT) at least 2-3x/week targeting major muscle groups, which is the single intervention with the largest and most consistent effect on strength, muscle mass and physical performance; (2) protein intake sufficient to support muscle protein synthesis (PROT-AGE expert group recommends at least 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults and 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day for those with acute or chronic illness, ideally with 25-30 g high-quality protein per meal), which produces an additive gain in fat-free mass and strength on top of exercise alone; (3) correction of vitamin D deficiency in patients found to be deficient, which gives a real, if smaller, improvement specifically in muscle strength (not muscle mass or power) and is most beneficial in those who are frankly deficient and in adults aged 65+.

real_trial_data.resistance_training_cochrane: Cochrane review, 121 RCTs, 6,700 older adults: muscle strength SMD 0.84 (95% CI 0.67-1.00, large effect, 73 trials/3,059 participants); physical ability SMD 0.14 (95% CI 0.05-0.22, 33 trials/2,172 participants); gait speed mean difference +0.08 m/s (95% CI 0.04-0.12, 24 trials/1,179 participants); chair-stand SMD -0.94 (95% CI -1.49 to -0.38, 11 trials/384 participants); serious adverse events rare and none directly attributed to exercise - Liu CJ, Latham NK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009, PMID 19588334
real_trial_data.resistance_training_strength_gains: Meta-analysis of 47 RCTs, 1,079 participants aged 50+: percent strength changes of 29+/-2% (leg press), 24+/-2% (chest press), 33+/-3% (knee extension), and 25+/-2% (lat pull), with absolute strength increases of 9.8-31.6 kg, greater with higher-intensity training - Peterson MD et al., Ageing Res Rev 2010;9:226-237, PMID 20385254
real_trial_data.resistance_training_lean_mass: Meta-analysis of 49 studies, 1,328 participants aged 50+: mean lean body mass increase of 1.1 kg (95% CI 0.9-1.2 kg), greater with higher training volume, smaller in older participants - Peterson MD et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43:249-258, PMID 20543750
real_trial_data.protein_plus_exercise: Meta-analysis of 22 RCTs, 680 subjects: protein supplementation during resistance training significantly increased fat-free mass (weighted mean difference +0.69 kg, 95% CI 0.47-0.91, P<0.00001) and 1-RM leg-press strength (weighted mean difference +13.5 kg, 95% CI 6.4-20.7, P<0.005) versus resistance training with placebo - Cermak NM et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012;96:1454-1464, PMID 23134885
real_trial_data.protein_dosing_guideline: PROT-AGE international expert group recommendation: at least 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day for healthy older adults, and 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day for those with acute or chronic disease, distributed across meals with resistance exercise - Bauer J et al., 'Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group', J Am Med Dir Assoc 2013;14:542-559, PMID 23867520
real_trial_data.vitamin_d_correction: Meta-analysis of 30 RCTs, 5,615 participants: vitamin D supplementation gave a small but statistically significant improvement in global muscle strength (SMD 0.17, P=.02), greater in adults aged 65+ (SMD 0.25) than younger adults (SMD 0.03) and in those with baseline deficiency; no significant effect on muscle mass (SMD 0.058, P=.52) or muscle power (SMD 0.057, P=.657) - Beaudart C et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014;99:4336-4345, PMID 25033068

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Not curative in the sense of a drug reversing an underlying disease process: no oral medicine, injection, or biologic is currently approved by any regulator specifically for sarcopenia, and even the most promising investigational biologic (bimagrumab, an activin type II receptor antibody) failed to significantly improve gait speed - its primary functional endpoint - despite significantly increasing lean body mass (Rooks D et al., JAMA Netw Open 2020, PMID 33074327). Curative-in-effect for the deficit that defines the disease: progressive resistance training directly and substantially rebuilds the muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical performance whose loss constitutes sarcopenia by EWGSOP2/AWGS diagnostic criteria, with effect sizes (SMD 0.84 for strength) that are large by any standard meta-analytic benchmark, and these gains are further amplified by adequate protein intake and, in deficient patients, vitamin D correction. This is a genuinely different and more favourable picture than most other degenerative musculoskeletal conditions in this knowledge base, where exercise gives only modest symptom relief without altering the underlying pathology - here, exercise directly reverses the measurable pathology itself (loss of muscle strength/mass).
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Vitamin D supplementation does not meaningfully improve muscle mass or muscle power (only strength), and gives little benefit in patients who are already vitamin D-replete - it should not be used as a substitute for exercise or protein optimisation, only as an adjunct in documented deficiency. Investigational pharmacotherapies (myostatin/activin pathway inhibitors such as bimagrumab, androgens) can increase lean body mass but have not yet demonstrated a significant improvement in the physical-function outcomes that matter most to patients, and none are approved for sarcopenia; they should not be presented to patients as an alternative to exercise. Patients with severe frailty, unstable cardiovascular disease, or other contraindications to exercise require individualised, supervised, doctor-approved exercise prescription rather than an unsupervised generic programme.
curative_option.source: Liu CJ, Latham NK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009 (PMID 19588334); Peterson MD et al., Ageing Res Rev 2010;9:226-237 (PMID 20385254); Peterson MD et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43:249-258 (PMID 20543750); Cermak NM et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012;96:1454-1464 (PMID 23134885); Bauer J et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2013;14:542-559 (PMID 23867520); Beaudart C et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014;99:4336-4345 (PMID 25033068); Rooks D et al., JAMA Netw Open 2020;3:e2020836 (PMID 33074327); Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al., Age Ageing 2019;48:16-31 (PMID 30312372); Chen LK et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2020;21:300-307.e2 (PMID 32033882)
curative_option.confidence: high for the resistance-training, protein-supplementation, and vitamin-D effect sizes (large RCT-based meta-analyses/Cochrane review with PMIDs directly verified this session); high for the bimagrumab honest-negative functional result (single large RCT, PMID verified); moderate for the overall 'no approved drug' framing, which reflects the absence of a positive phase 3 approval as of this session's search rather than an exhaustive real-time regulatory-database check

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for sarcopenia identified this session: progressive resistance/strength training, protein supplementation, vitamin D correction, beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), testosterone replacement, and the investigational myostatin/activin-pathway antibody bimagrumab, plus the two governing international consensus statements (EWGSOP2, AWGS 2019 update). No drug is currently approved by the FDA or EMA specifically for the indication of sarcopenia - this is stated honestly rather than omitted, consistent with the AWGS 2019 update's own statement that 'further research is needed to investigate potential long-term benefits of lifestyle interventions, nutritional supplements, or pharmacotherapy for sarcopenia'. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial or meta-analysis abstract, cross-checked against PubMed via NCBI eutils this session; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms, diagnostic criteria (EWGSOP2/AWGS thresholds for grip strength, gait speed, appendicular muscle mass) and differential diagnosis are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry for sarcopenia and are not duplicated here.

sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.name: EWGSOP2 - Revised European Consensus on Sarcopenia Definition and Diagnosis
sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.type: International consensus definition/diagnostic-and-management framework (not a single drug)
specific_drugs: No drug therapy recommended - framework calls for early detection and treatment via lifestyle/exercise-based intervention, with more research encouraged
sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.effectiveness: Established low muscle strength as the primary case-finding parameter, with muscle quantity/quality confirming diagnosis and physical performance grading severity; explicitly calls on healthcare professionals to 'take actions that will promote early detection and treatment' of sarcopenia and to prevent/delay adverse health outcomes through research and clinical action.
sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.source: Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al., 'Sarcopenia: revised European consensus on definition and diagnosis', Age Ageing 2019;48:16-31, PMID 30312372

sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.name: AWGS 2019 - Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia Consensus Update on Diagnosis and Treatment
sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.type: International (Asian) consensus diagnostic-and-management framework (not a single drug)
specific_drugs: No drug approved or recommended - explicit statement that lifestyle interventions (exercise, nutritional supplementation) are the mainstays of treatment
sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.effectiveness: Direct quote: 'Lifestyle interventions, especially exercise and nutritional supplementation, prevail as mainstays of treatment.' The panel explicitly flags that further research is needed on long-term benefits of lifestyle interventions, nutritional supplements, or pharmacotherapy for sarcopenia in Asian populations.
sarc_consensus_guideline_frameworks.source: Chen LK et al., 'Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia: 2019 Consensus Update on Sarcopenia Diagnosis and Treatment', J Am Med Dir Assoc 2020;21:300-307.e2, PMID 32033882

sarc_exercise_therapy_resistance_trainin.name: Progressive Resistance (Strength) Training
sarc_exercise_therapy_resistance_trainin.type: Non-pharmacological - structured exercise therapy (real strongest evidence base for sarcopenia)
specific_drugs: Not a drug - structured progressive resistance/strength-training exercise programme, typically 2-3 sessions/week targeting major muscle groups at progressively increasing loads
sarc_exercise_therapy_resistance_trainin.effectiveness: Cochrane review of 121 RCTs, 6,700 older adults: large, significant gain in muscle strength (SMD 0.84, 95% CI 0.67-1.00); significant gain in physical ability (SMD 0.14, 95% CI 0.05-0.22); gait speed +0.08 m/s (95% CI 0.04-0.12); chair-stand SMD -0.94 (95% CI -1.49 to -0.38); rare serious adverse events, none directly related to exercise. A separate 47-study meta-analysis (1,079 participants) found percent strength gains of 24-33% (leg press 29+/-2%, chest press 24+/-2%, knee extension 33+/-3%, lat pull 25+/-2%), and a companion 49-study meta-analysis (1,328 participants) found a mean lean-body-mass gain of 1.1 kg (95% CI 0.9-1.2 kg).
sarc_exercise_therapy_resistance_trainin.source: Liu CJ, Latham NK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009 (PMID 19588334); Peterson MD et al., Ageing Res Rev 2010;9:226-237 (PMID 20385254); Peterson MD et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43:249-258 (PMID 20543750)

sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.name: Protein Supplementation (with Resistance Exercise)
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.type: Nutritional intervention - oral protein/amino acid supplementation, real evidence strongest when combined with resistance training
specific_drugs: Whey protein, casein, or mixed protein supplements providing additional dietary protein on top of resistance-training programmes
PROT-AGE recommended target intake: >=1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults; >=1.2-1.5 g/kg/day for those with acute/chronic illness
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 22 RCTs, 680 subjects: protein supplementation during resistance-type exercise training significantly increased fat-free mass (weighted mean difference +0.69 kg, 95% CI 0.47-0.91, P<0.00001) and 1-RM leg-press strength (weighted mean difference +13.5 kg, 95% CI 6.4-20.7, P<0.005) versus exercise plus placebo, in both younger and older subjects.
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.source: Cermak NM et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012;96:1454-1464 (PMID 23134885); Bauer J et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2013;14:542-559 (PMID 23867520)

sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.name: Vitamin D Supplementation (Correction of Deficiency)
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.type: Nutritional/hormonal correction - real evidence specifically in deficient patients
specific_drugs: Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) or ergocalciferol (vitamin D2), dosed to correct documented deficiency - dose and monitoring are doctor_reference_only
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 30 RCTs, 5,615 participants: small but statistically significant improvement in global muscle strength (SMD 0.17, P=.02); benefit concentrated in adults aged 65+ (SMD 0.25 vs SMD 0.03 in younger adults) and in those with low baseline vitamin D status. No significant effect on muscle mass (SMD 0.058, P=.52) or muscle power (SMD 0.057, P=.657) - honestly reported as a strength-specific, not mass-building, effect.
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.source: Beaudart C et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014;99:4336-4345 (PMID 25033068)

sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.name: Beta-Hydroxy-Beta-Methylbutyrate (HMB)
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.type: Nutritional supplement - leucine metabolite marketed for muscle preservation
specific_drugs: HMB (calcium HMB or free-acid HMB), typically 3 g/day
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 7 RCTs, 147 intervention vs 140 control participants aged >=65: HMB supplementation produced a statistically significant but modest gain in muscle mass (SMD 0.352 kg, 95% CI 0.11-0.594, P=0.004) versus control, with no significant change in fat mass; the authors noted further research is needed on muscle strength and physical-function outcomes specifically, which this review did not find significantly improved.
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.source: Wu H et al., 'Effect of beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate supplementation on muscle loss in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Arch Gerontol Geriatr 2015;61:168-175 (PMID 26169182)
sarc_nutritional_interventions_protein_v.confidence: moderate - small number of trials/participants (7 RCTs, 287 total), modest effect size, and no significant strength/function benefit demonstrated

sarc_hormonal_investigational_pharmacoth.name: Testosterone Replacement (in Men with Documented Low Testosterone)
sarc_hormonal_investigational_pharmacoth.type: Hormone replacement - off-label use for age-related low testosterone with sarcopenia-relevant outcomes; not approved specifically for sarcopenia
specific_drugs: Testosterone gel/transdermal testosterone (used in the Testosterone Trials), dosed to restore normal serum testosterone in men with unequivocally low levels - dose and monitoring are doctor_reference_only
