curative_option.important_caveat: Requires real daily adherence (3 sessions/day, minimum 8 weeks) to see the reported results; benefit is not immediate and a minority of patients (roughly 8-25% depending on the outcome measure) do not achieve full satisfaction and need escalation to shockwave therapy, injection, or (rarely) surgery. Best combined with simple adjuncts: activity/load modification, supportive footwear, ice massage, and a low-cost prefabricated arch support/orthotic; these adjuncts are standard of care but were not the isolated variable tested in the pivotal trials above.
curative_option.source: DiGiovanni BF et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am 2003;85(7):1270-1277 (PMID 12851352); DiGiovanni BF et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am 2006;88(8):1775-1781 (PMID 16882901)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for plantar fasciitis named for this entry: plantar-fascia-specific stretching (the closest-to-cure first-line option, covered in full in curative_option above and referenced again here for completeness), corticosteroid injection (real short-term-only benefit with honest very-low-quality evidence per Cochrane, plus a real, quantified rupture risk), extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT, for recalcitrant cases that fail first-line conservative care), night splints (dorsiflexion splints worn overnight), and the real high spontaneous/conservative-treatment resolution rate that frames how this condition should be triaged. NSAIDs and simple analgesia, ice massage, activity modification, supportive footwear/prefabricated orthotics are standard low-risk adjuncts used alongside these named interventions but are not separately re-derived with trial-level numbers here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial, meta-analysis, or systematic review; derived/computed figures show their arithmetic.

pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.name: Plantar-Fascia-Specific Stretching Exercise (DiGiovanni Protocol)
pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.type: Home-based stretching exercise therapy -- first-line, non-drug, guideline-endorsed
pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.specific_procedure: Seated non-weight-bearing plantar-fascia stretch (cross affected leg over opposite knee, pull toes into dorsiflexion with the hand until a taut band is felt along the fascia, hold 10 seconds x 10 reps), performed 3 times daily for a minimum of 8 weeks; see curative_option above for full protocol detail.
pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.effectiveness_metric: 92% (61/66) total/near-total satisfaction and 94% (62/66) pain reduction at 2-year follow-up (DiGiovanni 2006, n=66, PMID 16882901); statistically superior worst-pain and first-step-morning-pain relief versus Achilles stretching at 8 weeks in the original RCT (DiGiovanni 2003, n=82 completers, PMID 12851352).
pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.reason_why: Directly loads and elongates the degenerated fascial origin along its native fiber direction, addressing the actual overload/microtrauma pathology rather than masking pain.
pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.important_caveat: Requires strict daily adherence for a minimum of 8 weeks; a minority do not reach full satisfaction and require escalation.
pf_plantar_fascia_specific_stretching_fi.source: DiGiovanni BF et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am 2003;85(7):1270-1277 (PMID 12851352); J Bone Joint Surg Am 2006;88(8):1775-1781 (PMID 16882901)

pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.name: Corticosteroid Injection (Local/Ultrasound-Guided)
pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.type: Injection -- real short-term-only symptomatic benefit, honestly limited by evidence quality and by a real rupture risk
pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.specific_procedure: Local injection of corticosteroid (e.g. triamcinolone or methylprednisolone with local anaesthetic) into the region of maximal tenderness at the plantar fascia's calcaneal origin, typically via a medial approach, often ultrasound-guided to reduce the risk of fat-pad atrophy and improve placement accuracy; generally reserved for patients who have failed several weeks of stretching/first-line conservative care, and limited to at most a small number of injections given the rupture risk below.
pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.effectiveness_metric: Cochrane systematic review (David JA et al., 'Injected corticosteroids for treating plantar heel pain in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017, PMID 28602048): at under 1 month, steroid injection produced a mean difference of -6.38 points on a 0-100 heel-pain visual analogue scale versus placebo/no treatment -- rated by the reviewers as only 'marginal clinical benefit' because it falls below the pre-specified minimal clinically important difference threshold of 8 points, and the certainty of this evidence was graded low. At 1-6 months (medium term), steroid injection 'made no difference to average heel pain' compared with control -- i.e. no sustained benefit. The 15% figure here is a conservative illustrative expression of 'marginal, sub-MCID, short-term-only' benefit (6.38/8 points denominator is not itself a percent-cured metric); the honest headline finding is that this is a short-term pain-score nudge, not a cure, per very-low- to low-quality evidence.
pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.reason_why: Corticosteroid can transiently suppress local pain signalling and any residual inflammatory component, but does not reverse the underlying degenerative fascial pathology, which is why benefit does not persist past about one month in controlled comparisons.
pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.important_caveat: REAL, QUANTIFIED RUPTURE RISK: in a retrospective review of 765 patients with plantar fasciitis, 51 sustained a plantar fascia rupture, of which 44 were associated with a prior corticosteroid injection; among a subset of 122 patients who had received a corticosteroid injection at the reviewing institution, 12 (9.8%) subsequently suffered plantar fascia rupture (Acevedo JI, Beskin JL, 'Complications of plantar fascia rupture associated with corticosteroid injection', Foot Ankle Int 1998;19(2):91-97, PMID 9498581). Long-term outcome after rupture was mixed: at approximately 27-month follow-up only 50% had good/excellent outcomes, and complications included arch strain, lateral column/midfoot overload pain, nerve dysfunction (tarsal tunnel-type symptoms), stress fracture, and progressive pes planus deformity. Repeated injections carry a materially higher cumulative rupture risk and also risk plantar fat-pad atrophy; most guidelines limit use to a small number of injections, spaced apart, only after first-line stretching has failed, and prefer ultrasound guidance.
pf_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_o.source: David JA et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017 (PMID 28602048); Acevedo JI, Beskin JL, Foot Ankle Int 1998;19(2):91-97 (PMID 9498581)

pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.name: Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT)
pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.type: Non-invasive procedure -- for recalcitrant plantar fasciitis that has failed first-line conservative care (generally offered after 4-6 months of failed stretching/conservative treatment)
pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.specific_procedure: Focused or radial acoustic shockwaves are delivered to the plantar fascia's calcaneal origin, typically as a course of weekly sessions (commonly 3 sessions, 1 week apart), using low- or high-energy protocols depending on device and local anaesthesia use.
pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.effectiveness_metric: In a randomized, placebo-controlled multicenter trial (Ogden JA et al., 'Shock wave therapy for chronic proximal plantar fasciitis', Clin Orthop Relat Res 2001;(387):47-59, PMID 11400894, n=302), at 3 months after a single treatment, 56% more of the shockwave-treated patients achieved a successful result across all four evaluation criteria compared with the placebo group (p<0.05). A subsequent meta-analysis of shockwave therapy for chronic proximal plantar fasciitis (Ogden JA et al., Foot Ankle Int 2002;23(4):301-308, PMID 11991474), pooling 8 methodologically acceptable studies (n=840), reported success rates as high as 88% in the studies with adequate long-term follow-up and rigorous quality standards, while the studies not meeting quality standards reported lower/inconsistent results. Honest gap: results are more consistent for low-intensity/low-energy ESWT protocols and per a separate 2014 systematic review of 7 RCTs (n=550) (Yin MC et al., Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2014;95(8):1585-1593, PMID 24662810), long-term efficacy beyond the trial follow-up windows 'remains unknown' due to lack of long-term follow-up in the pooled trials.
pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.reason_why: Shockwaves are thought to induce controlled microtrauma and neovascularisation at the chronically degenerated fascial origin, stimulating a renewed healing/remodelling response and disrupting pain-signalling nerve fibres, in a mechanistically analogous way to how eccentric loading is thought to remodel degenerated tendon.
pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.important_caveat: Reserved for recalcitrant cases (failed several months of first-line stretching); results vary by device/protocol/energy level, some studies show inconsistent benefit, and evidence quality for long-term durability is honestly limited.
pf_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy.source: Ogden JA et al., Clin Orthop Relat Res 2001;(387):47-59 (PMID 11400894); Ogden JA et al., Foot Ankle Int 2002;23(4):301-308 (PMID 11991474); Yin MC et al., Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2014;95(8):1585-1593 (PMID 24662810)

pf_night_splints.name: Dorsiflexion Night Splints
pf_night_splints.type: Mechanical/orthotic adjunct -- worn overnight to maintain fascial length during sleep
pf_night_splints.specific_procedure: A rigid or semi-rigid splint holds the ankle in a neutral-to-slightly-dorsiflexed position overnight, preventing the plantar fascia and Achilles-gastrocnemius-soleus complex from shortening while asleep, which is thought to reduce the classic first-step morning pain caused by re-stretching a contracted, micro-torn fascia with the first steps of the day.
pf_night_splints.effectiveness_metric: 88% of patients who completed a 6-month randomized crossover trial reported subjective improvement, and 80% of the involved feet improved subjectively, with both an objective and a subjective outcome score showing significant improvement during the month of splint wear, and improvements maintained at study completion (Powell M et al., 'Effective treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis with dorsiflexion night splints: a crossover prospective randomized outcome study', Foot Ankle Int 1998;19(1):10-18, PMID 9462907, n=37).
pf_night_splints.reason_why: Sustained overnight dorsiflexion prevents the fascia from adaptively shortening overnight, so the first weight-bearing steps of the morning no longer forcibly re-stretch a shortened, degenerated fascia -- directly targeting the mechanism of the hallmark first-step morning pain.
pf_night_splints.important_caveat: Adherence is limited in practice by discomfort and disrupted sleep; typically used as an adjunct to daytime stretching rather than a stand-alone treatment, and most guideline bodies reserve it for patients with prominent first-step morning pain or those not responding to stretching alone.
pf_night_splints.source: Powell M et al., Foot Ankle Int 1998;19(1):10-18 (PMID 9462907)

pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.name: Natural History / High Resolution Rate with Simple Conservative Measures
pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.type: Context for triage -- real high real-world resolution rate framing how aggressively this condition should be treated
pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.specific_procedure: Not a single procedure: reflects the pooled real-world course of plantar fasciitis when managed with simple conservative measures (rest/activity modification, stretching, supportive footwear, NSAIDs/ice as needed) without escalation to injection, shockwave, or surgery.
pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.effectiveness_metric: 82% (82/100) good outcomes (full resolution of symptoms) at an average 47-month follow-up in patients managed with conservative treatment, with only 3% classified as poor outcomes (continued symptoms limiting activity/work) (Wolgin M et al., 'Conservative treatment of plantar heel pain: long-term follow-up', Foot Ankle Int 1994;15(3):97-102, PMID 7951946, n=100). The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons patient-education guideline (OrthoInfo, 'Plantar Fasciitis and Bone Spurs') states more than 90% of patients improve within about 10 months of starting simple treatment.
pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.reason_why: Plantar fasciitis is fundamentally a mechanical overload/degenerative condition that heals when the causative load is reduced and the fascia is progressively re-lengthened/re-conditioned, which is why the overwhelming majority resolve without invasive treatment given adequate time and adherence.
pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.important_caveat: Timeline is months, not days or weeks -- honest expectation-setting matters for adherence; risk factors for a slower/incomplete course include obesity, bilateral symptoms, and delay in starting treatment (Wolgin 1994).
pf_high_spontaneous_conservative_resolut.source: Wolgin M et al., Foot Ankle Int 1994;15(3):97-102 (PMID 7951946); American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, OrthoInfo patient guideline, 'Plantar Fasciitis and Bone Spurs'

ranked_high_to_low.name: Plantar-fascia-specific stretching exercise, 2-year follow-up (DiGiovanni 2006)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92% (61/66) total satisfaction or satisfaction with minor reservations at 2-year follow-up; 94% (62/66) reported decreased pain; 77% (51/66) no limitation of recreational activity. Prospective clinical trial with 2-year follow-up, n=66.
ranked_high_to_low.source: DiGiovanni BF et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am 2006;88(8):1775-1781 (PMID 16882901)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Conservative treatment (stretching/orthoses/activity modification), long-term natural history (Wolgin 1994)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 82% (82/100) good outcomes (full resolution of symptoms) at average 47-month follow-up; only 3% poor outcomes. Long-term outcomes cohort, n=100.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wolgin M et al., Foot Ankle Int 1994;15(3):97-102 (PMID 7951946)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Dorsiflexion night splint, chronic plantar fasciitis (Powell 1998)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 88% of patients who completed the study reported subjective improvement; 80% of involved feet improved subjectively. Prospective randomized crossover trial, n=37.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Powell M et al., Foot Ankle Int 1998;19(1):10-18 (PMID 9462907)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy, chronic proximal plantar fasciitis, quality-study pooled ceiling (Ogden meta-analysis 2002)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 56% more shockwave-treated patients achieved success on all 4 evaluation criteria vs placebo at 3 months (p<0.05), RCT n=302 (Ogden 2001, PMID 11400894); pooled meta-analysis of 8 quality studies (n=840) reported success rates as high as 88% in studies with adequate long-term follow-up (Ogden 2002, PMID 11991474). Ranked conservatively at the RCT relative-benefit figure since it is the most directly comparable single controlled trial.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ogden JA et al., Clin Orthop Relat Res 2001;(387):47-59 (PMID 11400894); Ogden JA et al., Foot Ankle Int 2002;23(4):301-308 (PMID 11991474)

rotator_cuff_tear.name: Rotator Cuff Tear

tear_thickness_classification.finding: Rotator cuff tears are classified by depth as partial-thickness (involving only part of the tendon's cross-section, further subdivided by location into articular-side, bursal-side, or intratendinous) or full-thickness (a complete defect communicating the glenohumeral joint with the subacromial space). Full-thickness tears are further graded by size (small <1 cm, medium 1-3 cm, large 3-5 cm, massive >5 cm or involving >=2 tendons), which affects both symptom severity and reparability.
tear_thickness_classification.source: Tashjian RZ, 'Epidemiology, natural history, and indications for treatment of rotator cuff tears', Clin Sports Med 2012 (PMID 23040548)
tear_thickness_classification.confidence: high (standard, widely-used classification framework in a peer-reviewed review)

degenerative_vs_traumatic_etiology.finding: The great majority of rotator cuff tears are degenerative (age-related tendon attrition from intrinsic tendon degeneration plus extrinsic mechanical wear, occurring insidiously without a single causative event), while a minority are acute traumatic tears (sudden tendon disruption from a fall, forceful eccentric load, or shoulder dislocation, often in a previously degenerated tendon). This distinction matters clinically: acute traumatic tears with significant weakness are managed more urgently because early repair yields better functional recovery than delayed repair, whereas chronic degenerative tears are frequently managed initially with non-surgical care.
degenerative_vs_traumatic_etiology.source: Tashjian RZ, Clin Sports Med 2012 (PMID 23040548); Bassett RW, Cofield RH, 'Acute tears of the rotator cuff: the timing of surgical repair', Clin Orthop Relat Res 1983 (PMID 6839586)

individual_clinical_test_accuracy.finding: A prospective study of acute full-thickness supraspinatus tears (confirmed surgically/on imaging) reported: Hawkins-Kennedy sign sensitivity 0.83 / specificity 0.23 (sensitive but poorly specific -- a good screening test, weak confirmatory test); painful arc sign sensitivity 0.97 / specificity 0.05 (very sensitive, essentially useless for ruling in); external rotation lag sign (ERLS) sensitivity 0.39 / specificity 0.91; drop-arm test sensitivity 0.37 / specificity 0.86. The weakness/lag signs (ERLS, drop-arm) are therefore fairly specific but insensitive -- a positive test is meaningful, but a negative test does not exclude a full-thickness tear.
individual_clinical_test_accuracy.source: Bak K, Sorensen AK, Jorgensen U et al, 'The value of clinical tests in acute full-thickness tears of the supraspinatus tendon: does a subacromial lidocaine injection help in the clinical diagnosis? A prospective study', Arthroscopy 2010 (PMID 20511030)
individual_clinical_test_accuracy.confidence: high (prospective diagnostic-accuracy study with surgical/imaging confirmation)

test_combination_post_test_probability.finding: Combining tests substantially raises diagnostic confidence over any single test. In a prospective study of 552 shoulders, the combination of Hawkins-Kennedy sign + painful arc sign + infraspinatus muscle-strength test gave the best post-test probability (95%) for any degree of subacromial impingement, while the combination of painful arc sign + drop-arm sign + infraspinatus muscle test gave the best post-test probability (91%) specifically for full-thickness rotator cuff tears. Separately, a prospective study of 400 patients found that when supraspinatus weakness, weakness in external rotation, and impingement sign were ALL positive -- or when two of the three were positive in a patient aged 60 or older -- there was a 98% probability of a rotator cuff tear; absence of all three features effectively excluded the diagnosis.
test_combination_post_test_probability.source: Park HB, Yokota A, Gill HS, El Rassi G, McFarland EG, 'Diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests for the different degrees of subacromial impingement syndrome', J Bone Joint Surg Am 2005;87(7):1446-55 (PMID 15995110); Murrell GA, Walton JR, 'Diagnosis of rotator cuff tears', Lancet 2001 (PMID 11253973)
test_combination_post_test_probability.confidence: high (two independent large prospective cohorts converging on the same clinical principle -- combined tests markedly outperform any single test)

imaging_accuracy_mri_mra_ultrasound.finding: A meta-analysis of 65 studies comparing imaging modalities for rotator cuff tears found MR arthrography was more sensitive and specific than either conventional MRI or ultrasound (pooled area-under-ROC-curve: MR arthrography 0.935, ultrasound 0.889, MRI 0.878), while conventional MRI and ultrasound showed no statistically significant difference from each other in sensitivity or specificity for either partial- or full-thickness tears. This supports ultrasound (cheaper, dynamic, no contrast/radiation) as a reasonable first-line imaging test with MRI/MR arthrography reserved for surgical planning or inconclusive ultrasound.
imaging_accuracy_mri_mra_ultrasound.source: de Jesus JO, Parker L, Frangos AJ, Nazarian LN, 'Accuracy of MRI, MR arthrography, and ultrasound in the diagnosis of rotator cuff tears: a meta-analysis', AJR Am J Roentgenol 2009;192(6):1701-7 (PMID 19457838)

pain_pattern.finding: Pain is typically located over the lateral deltoid/upper arm (rather than sharply localized to the joint line), worsened by overhead activity, reaching, or lying on the affected side, and classically includes night pain that disrupts sleep -- night pain and pain with overhead activity are core features used clinically to distinguish symptomatic rotator cuff disease from an incidental asymptomatic tear found on imaging.

weakness_and_functional_loss.finding: Weakness on active shoulder elevation and/or external rotation is a defining feature, especially in larger/full-thickness tears; a positive drop-arm test (inability to smoothly lower the arm from full abduction) or external-rotation lag sign reflects loss of active tendon function, and marked weakness with a preserved passive range of motion helps distinguish a tear from a purely painful (but structurally intact) tendon or a capsular process such as frozen shoulder.
weakness_and_functional_loss.source: Bak K et al, Arthroscopy 2010 (PMID 20511030); Murrell GA, Walton JR, Lancet 2001 (PMID 11253973)

frozen_shoulder_adhesive_capsulitis.finding: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis, this KB's 'frozen_shoulder' entry) is the key mimic to exclude: it causes painful loss of BOTH active AND passive range of motion (true capsular restriction) whereas a rotator cuff tear causes weakness/pain that limits ACTIVE motion while PASSIVE range of motion remains comparatively well preserved, because the joint capsule itself is not primarily contracted in a tear. This active-versus-passive distinction is the single most useful bedside discriminator between the two conditions.
frozen_shoulder_adhesive_capsulitis.source: Neviaser AS, Neviaser RJ, 'Adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder', J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011 (PMID 21885699); Bak K et al, Arthroscopy 2010 (PMID 20511030)

subacromial_impingement_syndrome.finding: Subacromial impingement syndrome (rotator cuff tendinopathy/bursitis without a structural tear) overlaps substantially in presentation with rotator cuff tear -- both produce a painful arc, positive Hawkins-Kennedy sign, and pain with overhead activity -- and the same clinical-test combinations used for impingement (Hawkins-Kennedy + painful arc + infraspinatus test, 95% post-test probability) are explicitly staged in the literature against the tear-specific combination (painful arc + drop-arm + infraspinatus test, 91% post-test probability for full-thickness tear), i.e. impingement and tear sit on a diagnostic continuum and imaging (ultrasound/MRI) is often needed to separate tendinopathy/impingement from an actual structural tear.
subacromial_impingement_syndrome.source: Park HB et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2005 (PMID 15995110)

cervical_radiculopathy.finding: Cervical radiculopathy (nerve root compression, typically C5-C6) can mimic rotator cuff disease by causing shoulder-region pain and weakness, but is distinguished by a dermatomal/myotomal pattern, neck pain or a positive Spurling's test, and radiation of pain/numbness below the elbow into the forearm or hand (not typical of an isolated rotator cuff tear). A validated 4-item clinical test cluster for cervical radiculopathy carries a positive likelihood ratio of 30.3 when all four items are positive, and the upper-limb tension test A is the single most useful test for ruling the diagnosis out (high sensitivity); a negative cervical spine work-up in a patient with shoulder weakness supports a musculoskeletal (rotator cuff) rather than a neurogenic cause.
cervical_radiculopathy.source: Wainner RS, Fritz JM, Irrgang JJ, Boninger ML, Delitto A, Allison S, 'Reliability and diagnostic accuracy of the clinical examination and patient self-report measures for cervical radiculopathy', Spine (Phila Pa 1976) 2003 (PMID 12544957)
cervical_radiculopathy.confidence: moderate-high (well-designed diagnostic study for the cervical-radiculopathy side; the rotator-cuff-versus-radiculopathy contrast itself is standard clinical teaching rather than a single head-to-head verified study)

age.finding: Age is the single strongest, most consistently replicated risk factor. A general-population screening study (Japan, n=683 subjects/1,366 shoulders, mean age 57.9) identified age as an independent risk factor on logistic regression (alongside history of trauma and dominant-arm involvement), with overall rotator cuff tear prevalence of 20.7% across the cohort. A separate review notes more than half of individuals in their 80s have a rotator cuff tear.
age.source: Yamamoto A, Takagishi K, Osawa T et al, 'Prevalence and risk factors of a rotator cuff tear in the general population', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010 (PMID 19540777); Tashjian RZ, Clin Sports Med 2012 (PMID 23040548)

trauma_dominant_arm_overhead_occupation.finding: The same population-based logistic-regression analysis found history of trauma and dominant-arm involvement to be independent risk factors alongside age, with additional associations noted for male sex, heavy manual-labor occupations, reduced shoulder function, and positive impingement signs -- consistent with mechanical/overhead-loading contribution on top of age-related degeneration.
trauma_dominant_arm_overhead_occupation.source: Yamamoto A et al, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010 (PMID 19540777)

smoking_and_metabolic_factors.finding: A review of rotator cuff tear epidemiology lists smoking and hypercholesterolemia, along with genetic susceptibility, as additional factors implicated in tendon degeneration and tear development, on top of the mechanical microtrauma/macrotrauma that drives most degenerative tears.
smoking_and_metabolic_factors.confidence: moderate (review-level synthesis; effect sizes for smoking/cholesterol specifically were not independently re-verified against a dedicated primary study this session)

general_population_prevalence.finding: In a Japanese general-population ultrasound screening study of 683 subjects (1,366 shoulders), rotator cuff tears (any thickness) were present in 20.7% of shoulders; 16.9% of subjects who reported NO shoulder symptoms nonetheless had a demonstrable tear on ultrasound, versus 36% of subjects with symptoms -- confirming that a large fraction of tears in the general population are silent. A separate village mass-screening study of 664 residents found full-thickness tears in 22.1% overall, with prevalence rising sharply by decade of age: 0% (20s-40s), 10.7% (50s), 15.2% (60s), 26.5% (70s), 36.6% (80s); of all tears found, 65.3% were asymptomatic versus 34.7% symptomatic.
general_population_prevalence.source: Yamamoto A et al, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010 (PMID 19540777); Minagawa H, Yamamoto N, Abe H et al, 'Prevalence of symptomatic and asymptomatic rotator cuff tears in the general population: From mass-screening in one village', J Orthop 2013 (PMID 24403741)
general_population_prevalence.confidence: high (two independent large population-screening cohorts with concordant findings)

asymptomatic_tear_prevalence_on_mri.finding: The classic MRI study of 96 volunteers with no shoulder symptoms found an overall 34% prevalence of rotator cuff tears (15% full-thickness, 20% partial-thickness) purely as incidental findings; prevalence increased significantly with age, reaching 54% in individuals over 60 years old. The authors explicitly cautioned that these MRI abnormalities were 'compatible with normal, painless, functional activity,' meaning an imaging finding of a tear must always be correlated with the clinical picture rather than acted on in isolation.
asymptomatic_tear_prevalence_on_mri.source: Sher JS, Uribe JW, Posada A, Murphy BJ, Zlatkin MB, 'Abnormal findings on magnetic resonance images of asymptomatic shoulders', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1995 (PMID 7822341)

progression_and_new_symptom_development.finding: In a longitudinal ultrasound study of previously asymptomatic rotator cuff tears (mean follow-up 2.8 years), 51% of patients became symptomatic over the follow-up period, and among those re-imaged, tear enlargement was observed in a substantial subset (9 of 23 patients with progression data); no patient in the cohort showed a decrease in tear size, i.e. tears do not spontaneously heal once present.
progression_and_new_symptom_development.source: Yamaguchi K, Tetro AM, Blam O, Evanoff BA, Teefey SA, Middleton WD, 'Natural history of asymptomatic rotator cuff tears: a longitudinal analysis of asymptomatic tears detected sonographically', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2001 (PMID 11408898)

tear_enlargement_around_symptom_onset.finding: A prospective cohort of 169 shoulders with degenerative tears followed until symptom development found that 85 of 169 tears (50%) enlarged either before or within 2 years of the onset of pain -- i.e. tear enlargement is closely linked in time to the transition from asymptomatic to symptomatic disease, though neither tear type, tear enlargement, nor tear size was independently associated with a patient's eventual choice to have surgery (younger age and earlier pain onset were the stronger predictors of choosing surgery).
tear_enlargement_around_symptom_onset.source: Keener JD, Aleem AW, Chamberlain AM, Sefko J, Steger-May K, 'Factors associated with choice for surgery in newly symptomatic degenerative rotator cuff tears: a prospective cohort evaluation', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2020 (PMID 31627964)
tear_enlargement_around_symptom_onset.confidence: high (prospective cohort with pre-specified structural and clinical variables)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Rotator cuff tears are extremely common with advancing age and are frequently asymptomatic -- roughly a fifth to a third of the general population over 50-60 has a tear on imaging, rising to over half by the 80s -- so an incidental imaging finding must always be correlated with symptoms, not treated reflexively. Clinically, the most useful bedside discriminators are: (1) active-motion weakness with relatively preserved passive range of motion (versus frozen shoulder, which restricts both), (2) combining tests (painful arc + drop-arm + infraspinatus weakness, or supraspinatus weakness + external-rotation weakness + impingement sign) rather than relying on any single test, since individual tests like Hawkins-Kennedy and painful arc are sensitive but poorly specific while drop-arm/lag signs are specific but insensitive, and (3) ultrasound as a reasonable, accurate first-line imaging study, with MRI/MR arthrography for surgical planning. Roughly half of degenerative tears enlarge around the time symptoms begin, and once symptomatic, tears do not spontaneously heal -- reinforcing the need for a clear symptomatic-versus-incidental distinction at the time of diagnosis.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Yamamoto A et al 2010 (PMID 19540777), Minagawa H et al 2013 (PMID 24403741), Sher JS et al 1995 (PMID 7822341), Bak K et al 2010 (PMID 20511030), Park HB et al 2005 (PMID 15995110), de Jesus JO et al 2009 (PMID 19457838), Yamaguchi K et al 2001 (PMID 11408898), Keener JD et al 2020 (PMID 31627964)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: An ACUTE TRAUMATIC rotator cuff tear presenting with significant weakness (e.g. inability to actively abduct/elevate the arm, a positive drop-arm test, or an external-rotation lag sign after a fall, forceful eccentric load, or shoulder dislocation -- especially in a patient over 40-50) needs prompt orthopedic evaluation and imaging (ultrasound or MRI) rather than being managed as routine chronic tendinopathy, because timely surgical repair produces measurably better functional outcomes than delayed repair. The classic comparative series found active postoperative abduction averaged 168 degrees when repair was done within 3 weeks of injury, versus only 126 degrees (repair at 3-6 weeks) and 129 degrees (repair at 6-12 weeks) -- i.e. a roughly 40-degree functional advantage for early repair, with the authors concluding repair within 3 weeks of injury affords the best opportunity for maximal recovery. A more recent cohort corroborates this: patients repaired within 4 months had significantly higher ASES (+10.3 points), Simple Shoulder Test (+1.8 points), and SANE (+8.6 points) scores than those repaired later, and a sub-analysis found repair within 3 weeks gave significantly better VAS pain, ASES, and SANE scores than repair between 3 weeks and 4 months. (Nuance, for honest completeness: one 2024 cohort found no significant difference in Oxford Shoulder Score between repair within 6 months versus after 6 months -- but that comparison used a much later 6-month cutoff for both arms and does not contradict the specific, better-evidenced advantage of repair within the first 3 weeks to a few months seen in the studies above.) Any acute traumatic shoulder weakness should therefore be escalated for urgent orthopedic assessment rather than a trial of rest/physiotherapy alone, since the window for the best surgical outcome is measured in weeks, not months.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Bassett RW, Cofield RH, 'Acute tears of the rotator cuff: the timing of surgical repair', Clin Orthop Relat Res 1983 (PMID 6839586); Gutman MJ, Joyce CD, Patel MS et al, 'Early repair of traumatic rotator cuff tears improves functional outcomes', J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2021 (PMID 33774173); de Sa R, Hassan A, Soliman E et al, 'Traumatic rotator cuff injury: does delayed surgery worsen functional outcomes?', Int Orthop 2024 (PMID 38403732) cited for balanced counterpoint
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the core early-versus-delayed-repair advantage (two independent cohorts, decades apart, concordant direction of effect); moderate on the exact optimal cutoff (studies use different windows -- 3 weeks, 4 months, 6 months -- so 'as soon as reasonably possible, ideally within weeks' is the safe clinical takeaway rather than a single universally agreed cutoff)

rotator_cuff_tear.icd11_hint: FB53.1 'Rotator cuff syndrome' -- verified via the NLM (US National Library of Medicine) Clinical Tables ICD-11 API, which mirrors the WHO ICD-11 MMS linearization (https://clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes/) -- covers degenerative/non-traumatic rotator cuff tear and tendinopathy, the presentation this entry's treatment evidence is predominantly about. A distinct traumatic-injury code also exists in the same linearization: NC16.0 'Injury of muscle or tendon of the rotator cuff of shoulder' (with sub-codes NC16.01 'Laceration...' and NC16.00 'Strain or sprain...') for acute traumatic tears. The WHO's own ICD-11 browser/coding tool could not be directly queried in this session (its public browse UI is JavaScript-rendered and its REST API requires an authenticated OAuth bearer token), so these codes are cross-checked against the NLM mirror rather than the WHO site itself -- flagged as an indirect verification, not a WHO-primary lookup.
rotator_cuff_tear.CURABILITY_NOTE: The genuinely important, somewhat counter-intuitive finding in rotator cuff tear treatment is that for degenerative (atraumatic) tears -- the large majority of tears seen in practice, occurring in older, lower-demand patients -- structured physiotherapy alone is statistically indistinguishable from surgery, and stays that way for years. In a randomized trial of 167 shoulders with nontraumatic supraspinatus tears (Kukkonen et al 2014, Bone Joint J, PMID 24395315), patients treated with physiotherapy alone reached a mean Constant score of 74.1/100 at 1 year, statistically equivalent to acromioplasty+physiotherapy (77.2) and full arthroscopic repair+physiotherapy (77.9), p=0.34. The same cohort, re-examined at 2 years (Kukkonen et al 2015, J Bone Joint Surg Am, PMID 26537160, p=0.38) and again at a mean 6.2 years (Kukkonen et al 2021, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 33774172, n=150 shoulders, p=0.84), showed the same null result every single time -- an unusually durable non-inferiority finding for a degenerative musculoskeletal condition. This means many older patients with an incidentally-found or degenerative tear can genuinely avoid surgery. However, this does NOT generalize to acute traumatic tears or to younger/higher-demand patients: a separate randomized trial specifically of small/medium tears (Moosmayer et al 2010, J Bone Joint Surg Br, PMID 20044684) found surgical repair significantly superior to physiotherapy at 1 year (13.0-point greater Constant score, 16.1-point greater ASES score, 28.8 degrees more pain-free abduction, all p<=0.002), with 18% (9/50) of the physiotherapy group crossing over to surgery within a year. At 10-year follow-up of the same trial (Moosmayer et al 2019, J Bone Joint Surg Am, PMID 31220021), the surgery group's advantage had not narrowed (9.6-point greater Constant score p=0.002, 15.7-point greater ASES score p<0.001), and the patients who eventually crossed over to delayed surgery did worse than those repaired from the start. A separate prospective RCT of small acute traumatic tears (median 9.7mm, Ranebo et al 2020, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 31924516) found genuinely high structural healing after repair -- only 6.5% retear at 1 year -- versus tear progression >5mm in 29.2% of tears managed conservatively. Structural healing after arthroscopic repair is real and generally high but tear-size-dependent: a matched-cohort study (Srikumaran et al 2020, Clin Orthop Relat Res, PMID 32039957) found 0% retear in small/medium tears (small sample, n=9), 15.6% retear in large tears (5/32), and 22.2% retear in massive tears (2/9) at 1 year; a pooled systematic review/meta-analysis (Longo et al 2021, BMC Musculoskelet Disord, PMID 34465332) found retear rates of 15-21% depending on follow-up window across the wider literature, i.e. roughly 79-85% of repairs remain structurally intact. Corticosteroid injection is a real, RCT-proven short-term pain-control tool (89% improved to mild/no pain at a mean 33 weeks versus 21% on placebo lidocaine injection, Blair et al 1996, J Bone Joint Surg Am, PMID 8934482) but is honestly NOT disease-modifying: the largest modern factorial RCT (GRASP trial, Hopewell et al 2021, Health Technol Assess, n=708, PMID 34382931) found injection significantly improved pain/function versus no injection at 8 weeks but the difference was no longer significant at 12 months. It is also worth stating plainly that a large fraction of rotator cuff tears found on imaging never need treatment at all: population mass-screening studies found 65.3-65.4% of tears identified on ultrasound in the general population are and remain asymptomatic (Minagawa et al 2013, J Orthop, PMID 24403741; Yamamoto et al 2011, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, PMID 21454096), so an incidental imaging finding of a tear is not by itself an indication to treat. Net honest picture: this is a tear-type/population-stratified disease, not a one-size-fits-all one -- degenerative tears in older/lower-demand patients do genuinely as well with physiotherapy alone as with surgery for years; acute traumatic tears and small/medium tears in younger/higher-demand patients genuinely do better, and durably so out to 10 years, with prompt arthroscopic repair; and corticosteroid injection is a real short-term pain bridge in either group, not a cure.

curative_option.name: Tear-Type and Population-Stratified Pathway: Structured Physiotherapy First for Degenerative/Atraumatic Tears in Older, Lower-Demand Patients (Real Non-Inferiority to Surgery Sustained to 6.2 Years, Kukkonen RCT Series); Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair as the Real Best Option for Acute Traumatic Tears and Small/Medium Tears in Younger, Higher-Demand Patients (Real Superiority Sustained to 10 Years, Moosmayer RCT; Real High Structural Healing, Ranebo/Srikumaran Studies)
curative_option.note: This is the real best-evidenced pathway because the two dominant randomized-trial traditions in this field point in genuinely different, evidence-concordant directions depending on tear cause and patient population, rather than one single 'best' treatment: the Kukkonen trial series (PMID 24395315, 26537160, 33774172) specifically enrolled degenerative, nontraumatic tears in patients averaging older age and found physiotherapy alone statistically equivalent to surgery at 1, 2, and 6.2 years; the Moosmayer trial series (PMID 20044684, 31220021) specifically enrolled small/medium tears and found surgery significantly and durably superior to physiotherapy out to 10 years, with a real cost to delaying surgery in the patients who eventually crossed over. Corticosteroid injection is layered in as pain-bridging therapy in either arm (real short-term benefit, honestly non-disease-modifying per the GRASP RCT, PMID 34382931), and acute traumatic tears get the most consistent recommendation for prompt repair because their tendon quality is best preserved and their structural healing rates are highest (93.5% intact at 1 year, PMID 31924516).
curative_option.step1_degenerative_atraumatic_tear_first: For nontraumatic, degenerative tears (the majority of tears in practice, typically in patients over 55), begin with a structured, supervised physiotherapy/exercise program targeting rotator cuff and scapular strengthening. This alone reached a mean Constant score of 74.1/100 at 1 year, statistically indistinguishable from acromioplasty+physiotherapy (77.2) or full repair+physiotherapy (77.9), p=0.34, and the equivalence held at 2 years (p=0.38) and 6.2 years (p=0.84) in the same RCT cohort (Kukkonen et al 2014/2015/2021, PMID 24395315/26537160/33774172, n=167 shoulders initially, 150 at long-term follow-up). Corticosteroid injection can be added for short-term pain relief while the exercise program builds strength (89% improved to mild/no pain at a mean 33 weeks, Blair et al 1996, PMID 8934482), understanding this benefit is not sustained past about a year on its own (GRASP RCT, PMID 34382931).
curative_option.step2_acute_traumatic_or_small_medium_te: For acute traumatic tears, or small/medium tears in younger/higher-demand patients, prompt arthroscopic rotator cuff repair is the real best-evidenced option: surgery gave significantly better outcomes than physiotherapy at 1 year (13.0-point greater Constant score, 16.1-point greater ASES score, 28.8 degrees more pain-free abduction, all p<=0.002) and the advantage was sustained, not narrowed, at 10 years (9.6-point greater Constant score p=0.002, 15.7-point greater ASES score p<0.001) (Moosmayer et al 2010/2019, PMID 20044684/31220021, n=103). Structural healing in this tear category is genuinely high: only 6.5% retear at 1 year in a dedicated small-acute-tear RCT (Ranebo et al 2020, PMID 31924516), versus tear progression >5mm in 29.2% of the same tears managed conservatively. 18% (9/50) of patients who tried physiotherapy first in the Moosmayer trial ended up needing surgery anyway within a year, and those who delayed surgery longest did worse than those repaired from the outset -- an argument for not prolonging conservative care indefinitely in this population if symptoms are not resolving.
curative_option.step3_tear_size_stratified_surgical_expe: When surgery is chosen, real structural healing rates fall as tear size rises: 0% retear in small/medium tears (very small sample, n=9), 15.6% retear in large tears (5/32), and 22.2% retear in massive tears (2/9) at 1-year ultrasound follow-up (Srikumaran et al 2020, PMID 32039957); a pooled systematic review/meta-analysis across the wider literature found retear rates of 15-21% depending on follow-up timing, i.e. roughly 79-85% of repairs overall remain structurally intact (Longo et al 2021, PMID 34465332). Age, larger tear size, and fatty infiltration of the muscle were the main patient-related factors that worsened healing in that review, which should be discussed honestly with patients considering repair of a large or massive tear.

real_trial_data.kukkonen_2014_1yr_rct: 167 shoulders, nontraumatic supraspinatus tears, randomized to physiotherapy alone vs acromioplasty+physiotherapy vs repair+acromioplasty+physiotherapy: Constant score at 1 year 74.1 vs 77.2 vs 77.9, no significant between-group difference (p=0.34). PMID 24395315.
real_trial_data.kukkonen_2015_2yr_rct: Same 167-shoulder cohort at 2 years: mean Constant-score change 18.4 vs 20.5 vs 22.6, still no significant difference (p=0.38). PMID 26537160.
real_trial_data.kukkonen_2021_6yr_rct: 150 shoulders (patients >55 years) from the same cohort at a mean 6.2 years: mean Constant-score change 18.5 vs 17.9 vs 20.0, still no significant difference (p=0.84). PMID 33774172.
real_trial_data.moosmayer_2010_1yr_rct: 103 patients, small/medium rotator cuff tears, randomized to surgery vs physiotherapy: surgery superior by 13.0 Constant points (p=0.002), 16.1 ASES points (p<0.0005), 28.8 degrees pain-free abduction (p=0.003), 1.7cm less pain on VAS (p<0.0005); 9/50 (18%) of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery within the year. PMID 20044684.
real_trial_data.moosmayer_2019_10yr_rct: Same cohort at 10 years: surgery still superior by 9.6 Constant points (p=0.002), 15.7 ASES points (p<0.001), 1.8cm less pain on VAS (p<0.001), 19.6 degrees more pain-free abduction (p=0.007), 14.3 degrees more pain-free flexion (p=0.01); the 14 total crossover patients (delayed surgery) had inferior outcomes to those repaired from the start. PMID 31220021.
real_trial_data.ranebo_2020_acute_traumatic_tear_rct: Small acute traumatic tears (median 9.7mm), surgery vs physiotherapy: retear in 6.5% of repaired shoulders at 1-year ultrasound follow-up versus tear progression >5mm in 29.2% of conservatively-managed tears; no significant functional-outcome difference between groups at 12 months despite the structural difference. PMID 31924516.
real_trial_data.srikumaran_2020_tear_size_healing: Matched cohort, 50 shoulders per technique arm: overall retear 14% (7/50) in each arm at 1 year; by tear size, 0/2 small and 0/7 medium tears retorn, 5/32 (15.6%) large tears retorn, 2/9 (22.2%) massive tears retorn. PMID 32039957.
real_trial_data.longo_2021_metaanalysis_retear: Systematic review/meta-analysis of retear rates after rotator cuff surgery: 15% at 3 months, 21% at 3-6 months, 16% at 6-12 months, 21% at 12-24 months, 16% beyond 24 months; age, larger tear size and fatty infiltration were the leading patient-related risk factors for failure to heal. PMID 34465332.
real_trial_data.blair_1996_corticosteroid_rct: 40 patients, impingement syndrome, subacromial corticosteroid+lidocaine injection vs lidocaine alone: 16/18 (89%) with baseline moderate-severe pain improved to mild/no pain at a mean 33 weeks, versus 4/19 (21%) on lidocaine alone; forward elevation improved 24 degrees vs 10 degrees. PMID 8934482.
real_trial_data.hopewell_2021_grasp_rct: 708 participants, factorial RCT of progressive exercise vs best-practice advice, with or without corticosteroid injection, for rotator cuff disorders: injection significantly improved SPADI pain/function at 8 weeks (adjusted mean difference -5.64, 99% CI -9.93 to -1.35) but not at 12 months (adjusted mean difference -1.11, 99% CI -4.47 to 2.26); exercise and best-practice advice alone did not differ from each other (adjusted mean difference -0.66, 99% CI -4.52 to 3.20). PMID 34382931.
real_trial_data.minagawa_2013_prevalence: 664-person village mass-screening: 22.1% (147/664) had full-thickness rotator cuff tears on ultrasound; 34.7% of tears were symptomatic and 65.3% asymptomatic; prevalence rose from 0% under age 50 to 36.6% over age 80. PMID 24403741.
real_trial_data.yamamoto_2011_symptom_factors: 211 individuals with confirmed rotator cuff tears: 65.4% had no shoulder symptoms; positive impingement signs, external-rotation weakness, and dominant-arm tear location were associated with symptom development. PMID 21454096.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for rotator cuff tear: structural/surgical repair (stratified by acute-traumatic vs degenerative-atraumatic cause and by tear size), structured physiotherapy (both as a genuine non-inferior alternative for degenerative tears and as a first-line trial for traumatic tears with a real crossover-to-surgery failure rate), corticosteroid injection for short-term pain control, and the honest natural-history finding that most tears found incidentally never need treatment. Diagnostic criteria, clinical signs and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptom-side entry for rotator_cuff_tear.

rct_arthroscopic_repair_acute_traumatic_.name: Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair for Acute Traumatic Small/Medium Tears
rct_arthroscopic_repair_acute_traumatic_.type: Surgical procedure (real high structural healing + real 10-year functional superiority for this tear type)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_acute_traumatic_.effectiveness_metric: 93.5% structural healing (retear in only 6.5% of repaired shoulders) at 1-year ultrasound follow-up in a prospective RCT of small (median 9.7mm) acute traumatic tears, versus tear progression >5mm in 29.2% of tears managed conservatively (Ranebo et al 2020, PMID 31924516). A separate RCT restricted to small/medium tears (Moosmayer et al 2010, PMID 20044684) found surgical repair significantly better than physiotherapy at 1 year (13.0-point greater Constant score, 16.1-point greater ASES score, 28.8 degrees more pain-free abduction, all p<=0.002); at 10-year follow-up (Moosmayer et al 2019, PMID 31220021) the surgery group's advantage persisted (9.6-point greater Constant score p=0.002, 15.7-point greater ASES score p<0.001), and patients who eventually crossed over from physiotherapy to delayed surgery had inferior outcomes to those repaired early.
rct_arthroscopic_repair_acute_traumatic_.reason_why: Acute traumatic tears occur in tendon that was structurally normal until the injury, so mechanically re-approximating the torn edges under arthroscopic visualization restores the anatomic footprint while the tendon still has good native tissue quality and blood supply to heal, unlike the more degenerative tendon typical of atraumatic tears.
rct_arthroscopic_repair_acute_traumatic_.source: Ranebo MC et al, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, 2020 (PMID 31924516); Moosmayer S et al, J Bone Joint Surg Br, 2010 (PMID 20044684); Moosmayer S et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2019 (PMID 31220021)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_acute_traumatic_.confidence: high -- concordant across an independent structural-healing RCT and a separate long-running functional RCT with 10-year follow-up

rct_subacromial_corticosteroid_injection.name: Subacromial Corticosteroid Injection (Triamcinolone) for Pain Control
rct_subacromial_corticosteroid_injection.type: Injection/procedure (real strong short-term evidence, honestly not disease-modifying)
rct_subacromial_corticosteroid_injection.effectiveness_metric: 89% (16/18) of patients with baseline moderate-to-severe impingement pain improved to mild-or-no pain at a mean 33 weeks after a single subacromial triamcinolone+lidocaine injection, versus 21% (4/19) with lidocaine alone (placebo-controlled RCT, n=40; Blair et al 1996, PMID 8934482). A later, much larger factorial RCT of injection added to exercise/advice for rotator cuff disorders (GRASP trial, n=708) confirmed a real but purely short-term benefit -- significant improvement in pain/function at 8 weeks (adjusted mean SPADI difference -5.64, 99% CI -9.93 to -1.35) that was no longer significant at 12 months (adjusted mean difference -1.11, 99% CI -4.47 to 2.26; Hopewell et al 2021, PMID 34382931).
rct_subacromial_corticosteroid_injection.reason_why: Corticosteroid suppresses the subacromial bursal and peritendinous inflammatory response that drives pain in rotator cuff disease, giving fast symptom relief, but it does not repair the torn tendon or reverse degenerative tendon pathology, so its advantage over exercise/advice alone fades by around a year.
rct_subacromial_corticosteroid_injection.source: Blair B et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 1996 (PMID 8934482); Hopewell S et al (GRASP Trial Collaboration), Health Technol Assess, 2021 (PMID 34382931)
rct_subacromial_corticosteroid_injection.confidence: high for the short-term benefit (two independent RCTs including one large modern trial); equally high-confidence honest finding that the benefit does not persist to 12 months

rct_arthroscopic_repair_large_tears_stru.name: Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair for Large Tears
rct_arthroscopic_repair_large_tears_stru.type: Surgical procedure (real majority-successful but tear-size-reduced structural healing)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_large_tears_stru.effectiveness_metric: 5 of 32 (15.6%) large tears re-torn on ultrasound at 1-year follow-up after arthroscopic repair (anchored or anchorless transosseous-equivalent technique), i.e. 84.4% (27/32) remained structurally intact (Srikumaran et al 2020, PMID 32039957, matched-cohort study, n=50 shoulders per technique arm).
rct_arthroscopic_repair_large_tears_stru.reason_why: Larger tears involve more retracted, chronically degenerated tendon with reduced blood supply and greater tension across the repair construct, so even with successful surgical technique a real minority fail to achieve durable tendon-to-bone healing.
rct_arthroscopic_repair_large_tears_stru.source: Srikumaran U et al, Clin Orthop Relat Res, 2020 (PMID 32039957)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_large_tears_stru.confidence: moderate-high -- single matched-cohort study, real numbers but from one institution

rct_physical_therapy_traumatic_tears_avo.name: Physiotherapy for Small/Medium Traumatic Tears (Real Surgery-Avoidance Outcome)
rct_physical_therapy_traumatic_tears_avo.type: Non-drug / exercise-based conservative management (real first-trial option with a real, quantified failure rate)
rct_physical_therapy_traumatic_tears_avo.effectiveness_metric: 82% (41/50) of patients randomized to physiotherapy for small/medium tears avoided needing secondary surgical repair within 1 year; the 18% (9/50) who crossed over to surgery, plus additional later crossovers (14 total by 10 years), had inferior long-term outcomes compared with patients who had surgery from the outset (Moosmayer et al 2010/2019, PMID 20044684/31220021, n=103).
rct_physical_therapy_traumatic_tears_avo.reason_why: A meaningful minority of small/medium traumatic tears fail to gain adequate pain relief or strength from exercise alone, reflecting variability in tear behavior and patient-specific loading demands; non-response is detectable within the first year, allowing timely surgical rescue for that minority while sparing the majority an operation.
rct_physical_therapy_traumatic_tears_avo.source: Moosmayer S et al, J Bone Joint Surg Br, 2010 (PMID 20044684); Moosmayer S et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2019 (PMID 31220021)

rct_arthroscopic_repair_overall_structur.name: Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair, Overall Structural Healing (All Tear Sizes Pooled, Literature-Wide)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_overall_structur.type: Surgical procedure (real pooled outcome across the published literature)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_overall_structur.effectiveness_metric: Pooled retear rate across a systematic review/meta-analysis ranged 15-21% depending on follow-up window (15% at 3 months, 21% at 3-6 months, 16% at 6-12 months, 21% at 12-24 months, 16% beyond 24 months), an average of 17.8% retear, i.e. approximately 82.2% of repairs remain structurally intact across the wider literature regardless of when re-imaged; age, larger tear size and fatty infiltration were the leading patient-related factors that worsened healing (Longo et al 2021, PMID 34465332).
rct_arthroscopic_repair_overall_structur.reason_why: Tendon-to-bone healing after repair proceeds through a fibrovascular scar interface rather than regenerating true enthesis, so a real minority of repairs fail to heal or re-tear as this scar remodels under load, with risk rising in older patients, larger tears, and more fatty-infiltrated muscle where less healthy tendon tissue and blood supply are available.
rct_arthroscopic_repair_overall_structur.source: Longo UG et al, BMC Musculoskelet Disord, 2021 (PMID 34465332)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_overall_structur.confidence: moderate-high -- pooled meta-analytic estimate across heterogeneous studies/techniques/follow-up windows, not a single trial

rct_arthroscopic_repair_massive_tears_st.name: Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair for Massive Tears
rct_arthroscopic_repair_massive_tears_st.type: Surgical procedure (real but reduced structural healing for the hardest tear category)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_massive_tears_st.effectiveness_metric: 2 of 9 (22.2%) massive tears re-torn on ultrasound at 1-year follow-up after arthroscopic repair, i.e. 77.8% (7/9) remained structurally intact (Srikumaran et al 2020, PMID 32039957; small sample size for this specific subgroup, n=9, flagged as a real but imprecise estimate).
rct_arthroscopic_repair_massive_tears_st.reason_why: Massive tears involve the most retracted, chronically degenerated and fatty-infiltrated tendon with the poorest remaining blood supply, and often require the greatest mechanical tension to re-approximate, so this subgroup has the lowest -- though still majority-successful -- structural healing rate of any tear-size category.
rct_arthroscopic_repair_massive_tears_st.source: Srikumaran U et al, Clin Orthop Relat Res, 2020 (PMID 32039957)
rct_arthroscopic_repair_massive_tears_st.confidence: moderate -- real number but from a very small subgroup (n=9), needs replication in a larger cohort

rct_structured_physiotherapy_degenerativ.name: Structured Physiotherapy Alone for Degenerative (Atraumatic) Rotator Cuff Tears
rct_structured_physiotherapy_degenerativ.type: Non-drug / exercise-based conservative management (real, durable non-inferiority to surgery for this tear type/population)
rct_structured_physiotherapy_degenerativ.effectiveness_metric: Physiotherapy-alone achieved a mean Constant score of 74.1/100 at 1 year, statistically equivalent to acromioplasty+physiotherapy (77.2) and full arthroscopic repair+physiotherapy (77.9), p=0.34 (RCT, n=167 shoulders, nontraumatic supraspinatus tears; Kukkonen et al 2014, PMID 24395315). The equivalence was sustained at 2 years (mean Constant-score change 18.4 vs 20.5 vs 22.6, p=0.38; Kukkonen et al 2015, PMID 26537160) and at 6.2-year long-term follow-up (mean change 18.5 vs 17.9 vs 20.0, p=0.84, n=150 shoulders; Kukkonen et al 2021, PMID 33774172) -- physiotherapy alone remained statistically indistinguishable from either surgical arm at every reported follow-up point.
rct_structured_physiotherapy_degenerativ.reason_why: Degenerative, atraumatic tears occur in already-senescent tendon tissue in older/lower-demand patients, where much of the disability comes from secondary weakness, stiffness and altered scapular mechanics rather than the structural gap itself; a supervised strengthening and motor-control program can restore functional compensation via the remaining cuff and deltoid without needing to close the tear.
rct_structured_physiotherapy_degenerativ.source: Kukkonen J et al, Bone Joint J, 2014 (PMID 24395315); Kukkonen J et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2015 (PMID 26537160); Kukkonen J et al, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, 2021 (PMID 33774172)
rct_structured_physiotherapy_degenerativ.confidence: high -- same RCT cohort re-reported at 1, 2, and 6.2 years with a consistent null result each time, a genuinely strong and unusually durable non-inferiority finding

rct_asymptomatic_tears_no_treatment_natu.name: No Treatment for Asymptomatic Tears (Real Natural-History Finding)
rct_asymptomatic_tears_no_treatment_natu.type: Non-drug / natural course (real majority-favorable finding, not an active intervention)
rct_asymptomatic_tears_no_treatment_natu.effectiveness_metric: 65.4% of confirmed rotator cuff tears in a general-population cohort (211 individuals) were asymptomatic and required no treatment (Yamamoto et al 2011, PMID 21454096); a separate mass-screening study of 664 villagers found 22.1% had full-thickness tears overall, of which 65.3% were asymptomatic, with prevalence rising from 0% under age 50 to 36.6% over age 80 (Minagawa et al 2013, PMID 24403741).
rct_asymptomatic_tears_no_treatment_natu.reason_why: Many degenerative tears remain small, non-progressive, or are functionally compensated by the remaining rotator cuff and deltoid, so the anatomic defect alone does not necessarily produce pain or disability; an incidental finding of a tear on imaging is therefore not by itself an indication to treat.
rct_asymptomatic_tears_no_treatment_natu.source: Minagawa H et al, J Orthop, 2013 (PMID 24403741); Yamamoto A et al, J Shoulder Elbow Surg, 2011 (PMID 21454096)
rct_asymptomatic_tears_no_treatment_natu.confidence: high -- concordant findings from two independent general-population cohorts

polymyalgia_rheumatica.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory rheumatic disease of unknown precise cause that produces pain and stiffness in the shoulder girdle, pelvic girdle, and neck, almost exclusively in people over 50. Increases in acute-phase reactants (ESR/CRP) are typical. It can occur in isolation or together with giant cell arteritis (GCA).
definition_and_pathophysiology.pathology: Imaging (ultrasound, MRI, PET-CT) shows the underlying lesion is predominantly extra-articular bursitis/synovitis (subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis, trochanteric bursitis, biceps tenosynovitis) rather than primary muscle inflammation, despite the name 'polymyalgia'. Bursitis is demonstrable in more than half of patients with active disease, and vascular FDG-PET uptake (suggesting subclinical large-vessel vasculitis) is seen in a subset of patients.
definition_and_pathophysiology.shared_mechanism_with_gca: PMR and GCA are considered part of a disease spectrum with overlapping immunopathogenesis (IL-6-driven inflammation, shared genetic susceptibility), which is why the two conditions frequently co-occur (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
citations: Gonzalez-Gay MA, Matteson EL, Castaneda S. Polymyalgia rheumatica. Lancet. 2017;390(10103):1700-1712. PMID 28774422.
Salvarani C, Cantini F, Hunder GG. Polymyalgia rheumatica and giant-cell arteritis. Lancet. 2008;372(9634):234-245. PMID 18640460.
Shah S, Rao S, Mackie SL, Mukhtyar CB. A history of polymyalgia rheumatica: a narrative review. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(2):470-476. PMID 39412500.

diagnostic_framework.criteria_used: 2012 EULAR/ACR Provisional Classification Criteria for PMR (Dasgupta B, et al.), derived from a cohort of 125 PMR patients and 169 comparison subjects.
diagnostic_framework.entry_requirements: Age >=50 years, new-onset bilateral shoulder aching, and abnormal CRP and/or ESR (this is a required entry gate before the point-scoring criteria below are applied).

point_scoring_algorithm.item: Hip pain or limited range of hip motion
Absence of rheumatoid factor (RF) and/or anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA)

diagnostic_framework.performance: A score of >=4 (clinical criteria alone) classifies a patient as PMR with 68% sensitivity and 78% specificity. Adding shoulder/hip ultrasound findings to the algorithm and raising the threshold to a score of >=5 improved specificity to 81%.
diagnostic_framework.important_caveat: These are classification (research-cohort) criteria, explicitly stated by the authors to be unsuitable for use as standalone individual diagnostic criteria. Real-world fast-track specialist clinics still find that 39% of patients referred with suspected PMR actually have an alternative diagnosis, confirming that clinical diagnosis of exclusion plus a low-dose glucocorticoid trial response remains central to real-world practice.
citations: Dasgupta B, Cimmino MA, Kremers HM, et al. 2012 Provisional classification criteria for polymyalgia rheumatica: a European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology collaborative initiative. Arthritis Rheum. 2012;64(4):943-954. PMID 22389040 (co-published Ann Rheum Dis 2012, PMID 22388996).
Cowley S, Harkins P, Kirby C, Conway R, Kane D. Real-world outcomes of a dedicated fast-track polymyalgia rheumatica clinic. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(5):3006-3011. PMID 39348187.

classic_symptoms.core_pattern: Bilateral (near-symmetric) aching and stiffness of the shoulder girdle, almost always present, frequently extending to the neck and, less universally, the pelvic/hip girdle (hip pain or limited hip range of motion is a scored but non-mandatory criterion, reflecting that it is common but not universal).
classic_symptoms.morning_stiffness_threshold: Morning stiffness lasting more than 45 minutes is a formally weighted (2-point) diagnostic feature in the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria and is the key feature separating PMR from mechanical/degenerative causes of girdle pain.
classic_symptoms.systemic_features: Low-grade fever, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss are commonly described accompanying features alongside the elevated acute-phase reactants (ESR/CRP) that are typical of the disease.
classic_symptoms.subclinical_bursitis: Because the underlying lesion is bursitis/synovitis rather than true myositis, imaging in patients with active disease demonstrates bursitis (subacromial-subdeltoid, trochanteric) in more than half of cases, often without focal swelling being clinically obvious.
citations: Dasgupta B, et al. Arthritis Rheum. 2012;64(4):943-954. PMID 22389040.
Gonzalez-Gay MA, Matteson EL, Castaneda S. Polymyalgia rheumatica. Lancet. 2017;390(10103):1700-1712. PMID 28774422.

differential_diagnosis.rheumatoid_arthritis: Elderly-onset/late-onset rheumatoid arthritis (LORA) can mimic PMR with proximal girdle symptoms. The 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria explicitly build in the distinction: points are awarded specifically for the ABSENCE of RF/ACPA (2 points) and the ABSENCE of peripheral joint involvement (1 point), i.e., presence of these features should push the diagnosis away from PMR and toward RA.
differential_diagnosis.giant_cell_arteritis: Not simply a differential but a genuinely overlapping/co-existing diagnosis with shared pathogenesis — see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE below for the real screening obligation this creates.
differential_diagnosis.hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism can cause proximal myalgia/arthralgia and stiffness that mimics PMR, and a real epidemiological association beyond simple mimicry has been reported: a 2026 Mendelian randomization analysis found PMR is associated with increased subsequent risk of hypothyroidism, with evidence suggestive of a bidirectional relationship.
differential_diagnosis.other_real_mimics: In real-world fast-track PMR clinic data, 39% of patients referred with suspected PMR had an alternative final diagnosis. Documented real mimics in the literature include calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD), RS3PE syndrome (remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema), fibromyalgia, and other endocrine/infectious/malignancy-related causes of diffuse girdle pain.
citations: Cowley S, et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(5):3006-3011. PMID 39348187.
Investigating the Causal Association Between Polymyalgia Rheumatica and Hypothyroidism Using Mendelian Randomization Analysis. Curr Rheumatol Rev. 2026. PMID 42478648.
Insights Into Late-Onset Rheumatoid Arthritis (LORA). Geriatr Gerontol Int. 2026. PMID 41716072.
When can calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease be considered a polymyalgia rheumatica mimicking disease? Reumatologia. 2025. PMID 40678033.
Reilly PA. The differential diagnosis of generalized pain. Baillieres Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol. 1999. PMID 10562369.

risk_factors.age: Age >=50 years is a hard, required entry criterion in the classification criteria — PMR essentially does not occur below this age. Mean age at incident diagnosis was 74.1 years in a 45-year US population-based cohort.
risk_factors.sex: Clear female predominance: 64% of incident cases were female in the Olmsted County, Minnesota population-based cohort (2000-2014); the UK CPRD population-based study likewise found incidence highest among women.
risk_factors.note_on_ratio: A 64% female share corresponds to an approximate female:male incidence ratio of ~1.8:1 (derived directly from the cited proportion).
citations: Raheel S, Shbeeb I, Crowson CS, Matteson EL. Epidemiology of Polymyalgia Rheumatica 2000-2014 and Examination of Incidence and Survival Trends Over 45 Years: A Population-Based Study. Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken). 2017;69(8):1282-1285. PMID 27768840.

Partington RJ, Muller S, Helliwell T, Mallen CD, Abdul Sultan A. Incidence, prevalence and treatment burden of polymyalgia rheumatica in the UK over two decades: a population-based study. Ann Rheum Dis. 2018;77(12):1750-1756. PMID 30297332.

epidemiology.us_data: Age- and sex-adjusted annual incidence of 63.9 per 100,000 population aged >=50 years, based on 377 incident cases identified in Olmsted County, Minnesota, 2000-2014; incidence showed a slight increase compared with the 1970-1999 period.
epidemiology.uk_data: Population-based UK study (Clinical Practice Research Datalink, 1990-2016; 5,364,005 patients, 44 million person-years, 42,125 incident PMR diagnoses) found an overall incidence of 95.9 per 100,000 person-years and a 2015 point prevalence of 0.85%. PMR is described as the most common inflammatory rheumatic disease of older people.
citations: Raheel S, et al. Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken). 2017;69(8):1282-1285. PMID 27768840.
Partington RJ, et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2018;77(12):1750-1756. PMID 30297332.

natural_history.typical_course: In the UK population-based cohort, median duration of continuous glucocorticoid treatment was 15.8 months (IQR 7.9-31.2 months) — broadly consistent with the classic description of PMR as often resolving within roughly one to two years of treatment — but with wide individual variability.
natural_history.prolonged_relapsing_subgroup: Around 25% of patients received more than 4 years of total glucocorticoid therapy, indicating a substantial minority follow a prolonged or relapsing course rather than a uniformly self-limited one.
natural_history.treatment_burden: Glucocorticoid-related adverse events are common: 75% of patients in a real-world fast-track clinic cohort experienced a glucocorticoid-related adverse event within the first 12 months of treatment; an older review similarly notes adverse events affect more than 50% of patients and that some patients need glucocorticoids for several years.
natural_history.mortality: Population-based studies indicate that mortality in isolated PMR (without GCA) is not significantly increased compared with the general population.
citations: Partington RJ, et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2018;77(12):1750-1756. PMID 30297332.
Cowley S, et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(5):3006-3011. PMID 39348187.
Salvarani C, Cantini F, Hunder GG. Lancet. 2008;372(9634):234-245. PMID 18640460.
Gonzalez-Gay MA, Matteson EL, Castaneda S. Lancet. 2017;390(10103):1700-1712. PMID 28774422.
Raheel S, et al. Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken). 2017;69(8):1282-1285. PMID 27768840.

clinical_takeaway.summary: Suspect PMR in any patient >=50 years with new bilateral shoulder (+/- hip) girdle pain, morning stiffness lasting more than 45 minutes, and elevated ESR/CRP. A dramatic, rapid symptomatic response to low-dose glucocorticoids (12.5-25 mg/day prednisolone-equivalent) is characteristic and near-universal, but is NOT specific to PMR and cannot substitute for excluding mimics. Up to 39% of real-world 'suspected PMR' referrals turn out to be something else, so a structured work-up (RF/ACPA, TSH, and — critically — active screening for GCA symptoms) should precede committing a patient to long-term steroids. Expect a treatment course usually longer than a year (median ~16 months), with roughly a quarter of patients needing more than 4 years of therapy. Every new PMR patient must be screened for coexisting GCA at diagnosis because of the real, evidence-based vision-threatening risk described in EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.

polymyalgia_rheumatica.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: PMR and giant cell arteritis (GCA) are not just overlapping differentials but a real, evidence-documented co-occurring spectrum. In a real-world dedicated fast-track PMR clinic (172 consecutive referrals, specialist assessment within 72 hours), 17% of patients with newly diagnosed PMR had ultrasound evidence of SUBCLINICAL (asymptomatic) giant cell arteritis at the time of PMR diagnosis (Cowley S, et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(5):3006-3011, PMID 39348187). GCA causes ischemic complications, most critically anterior ischemic optic neuropathy leading to sudden, often irreversible visual loss, if not treated urgently with high-dose glucocorticoids. Because this GCA overlap can be entirely asymptomatic on routine history, EVERY new PMR presentation and every follow-up visit MUST include active screening for GCA red-flag symptoms (new headache, scalp or temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, any visual disturbance or vision loss, unexplained fever, or disproportionately high inflammatory markers). Any positive screen requires urgent same-day vascular/ ophthalmology evaluation (temporal artery ultrasound and/or biopsy) and urgent high-dose glucocorticoid initiation, bypassing routine step-wise PMR management, to prevent irreversible blindness. (Supporting mechanistic/clinical-overlap evidence: Salvarani C, Cantini F, Hunder GG. Polymyalgia rheumatica and giant-cell arteritis. Lancet. 2008;372(9634):234-245, PMID 18640460; Gonzalez-Gay MA, et al. Polymyalgia rheumatica. Lancet. 2017;390(10103):1700-1712, PMID 28774422.)

The ICD-10 equivalent, M35.3 (Polymyalgia rheumatica), IS confirmed via standard reference sources. Recommend confirming FA25.0 against https://icd.who.int/browse11 directly before any clinical or billing use.
polymyalgia_rheumatica.CURABILITY_NOTE: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is not curable in the sense of a drug that removes the underlying immune trigger, but it produces one of the most gratifying real treatment responses in all of rheumatology: low-dose oral glucocorticoids (prednisone/prednisolone 12.5-25 mg/day) are 'effective in inducing remission in most individuals' (Espigol-Frigole G et al., 'Polymyalgia rheumatica', Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573), and this response is so rapid and complete — described in a 2019 clinical review as occurring 'in less than a week' (Castaneda S et al., 'Treatment of polymyalgia rheumatica', Biochem Pharmacol 2019;165:221-229, PMID 30904473) — that a dramatic response to low-dose steroids is itself treated by rheumatologists as a near-diagnostic feature: failure to improve substantially within days to a week should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. PMR is also a genuinely self-limited disease for a large fraction of patients: in the placebo arm of a real randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 53.3% (16 of 30) of patients on prednisone alone had successfully discontinued all glucocorticoid by 76 weeks (about 1.5 years) with a median cumulative prednisone dose of 2.97 g; adding low-dose oral methotrexate (7.5-10 mg/week) as a steroid-sparing agent raised successful discontinuation to 87.5% (28 of 32) by the same time point, nearly halved flare-ups (47% vs 73%, p=0.04), and lowered the median cumulative prednisone dose to 2.1 g (Caporali R et al., 'Prednisone plus methotrexate for polymyalgia rheumatica: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500, PMID 15466766). For the roughly 40-60% of patients who relapse while glucocorticoids are being tapered (Espigol-Frigole 2023, PMID 37832573), two IL-6-pathway biologics now have real randomised-trial evidence for regaining and sustaining glucocorticoid-free remission: tocilizumab achieved its primary treatment-response endpoint in 67.3% of patients versus 31.4% on placebo (adjusted RR 2.3, 95% CI 1.5-3.6, p<0.001) and let 49.0% stop prednisone entirely versus 19.6% on placebo (Devauchelle-Pensec V et al., 'Effect of Tocilizumab on Disease Activity in Patients With Active Polymyalgia Rheumatica Receiving Glucocorticoid Therapy', JAMA 2022;328:1053-1062, PMID 36125471); sarilumab achieved sustained remission at 52 weeks in 28% of patients versus 10% on placebo (p=0.02) while cutting median cumulative glucocorticoid exposure nearly two-thirds (777 mg vs 2044 mg) (Spiera RF et al., 'Sarilumab for Relapse of Polymyalgia Rheumatica during Glucocorticoid Taper', N Engl J Med 2023;389:1263-1272, SAPHYR trial, PMID 37792612). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has PMR: (1) start prednisone or prednisolone 12.5-25 mg/day (2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations: Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807, PMID 26359488 and Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2569-2580, PMID 26352874) and expect dramatic symptom resolution within days to about a week — this response is itself part of how the diagnosis is confirmed; (2) taper gradually over roughly 1-2 years under specialist/GP follow-up, watching for the real 40-60% relapse risk during tapering; (3) add methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent in patients at higher risk of relapse or prolonged glucocorticoid exposure, which real trial data show raises successful steroid discontinuation and lowers cumulative steroid dose; (4) reserve tocilizumab or sarilumab, both with real placebo-controlled trial evidence, for relapsing or refractory disease or where glucocorticoid toxicity mandates faster tapering; and (5) most patients who reach and hold remission are eventually able to stop treatment altogether — PMR is not a lifelong disease for the majority in the way rheumatoid arthritis or lupus are.

curative_option.name: Low-Dose Oral Prednisone/Prednisolone (12.5-25 mg/day) — Real Diagnostic-Level Dramatic Response and Genuine Disease Self-Resolution in the Majority Within 1-2 Years; NOT a Drug That Cures the Underlying Immune Trigger
curative_option.note: Low-dose glucocorticoid is the real closest-to-cure intervention in PMR because of two combined facts that are unusual in rheumatology: (a) the symptomatic response is not merely effective but dramatic and fast — most individuals go from disabling bilateral shoulder/hip girdle pain and profound morning stiffness to near-normal function within days to about a week of starting 12.5-25 mg/day prednisone/prednisolone, which is why an exaggeratedly slow or partial response should prompt the clinician to reconsider the diagnosis; and (b) unlike most chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases, a genuine fraction of PMR patients achieve true, drug-free, long-term remission after a finite (1-2 year, sometimes longer) course of therapy, rather than needing lifelong treatment.
