real_trial_data.speed_and_completeness_of_initial_respon: '12.5-25.0 mg prednisone per day are effective in inducing remission in most individuals' (Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573); a 2019 clinical review describes the initial glucocorticoid response as occurring 'in less than a week' (Castaneda S et al., Biochem Pharmacol 2019;165:221-229, PMID 30904473).
real_trial_data.real_rct_prednisone_alone_discontinuatio: In the placebo arm of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=30 on prednisone alone, no methotrexate), 53.3% (16 of 30) had successfully discontinued all glucocorticoid by 76 weeks; median cumulative prednisone dose was 2.97 g; 73% (22 of 30) had at least one flare-up during the study (Caporali R et al., Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500, PMID 15466766).
real_trial_data.real_rct_methotrexate_added_discontinuat: Adding oral methotrexate to prednisone in the same trial raised successful glucocorticoid discontinuation to 87.5% (28 of 32) by 76 weeks (risk difference 34 percentage points, p=0.003), reduced flare-ups to 47% (15 of 32, p=0.04), and lowered median cumulative prednisone dose to 2.1 g (Caporali R et al., Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500, PMID 15466766).
real_trial_data.relapse_risk_during_tapering: Relapses occur in 40-60% of patients when glucocorticoids are tapered (Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573).
real_trial_data.guideline_dosing_and_taper_framework: The 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations for the management of PMR (GRADE methodology) set out eight overarching principles and nine specific recommendations covering initial glucocorticoid dose and subsequent tapering regimens, the option of intramuscular glucocorticoid, and the role of methotrexate as a steroid-sparing DMARD (Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807, PMID 26359488; Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2569-2580, PMID 26352874). The exact week-by-week milligram taper steps in these recommendations were not independently re-extracted from open full text in this research session (both journals are paywalled to the automated tools used) and are therefore not quoted here as specific numbers to avoid any risk of misquoting the guideline — the abstract-level scope above (PMID 26359488/26352874) is what was directly verified.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect for a genuine fraction of patients: symptoms resolve rapidly and, after a finite (typically 1-2 year) course of tapering glucocorticoid, a majority of patients (53.3% on prednisone alone, 87.5% with added methotrexate, by 76 weeks in the Caporali RCT, PMID 15466766) are able to stop all treatment and remain well without further drug therapy. Not curative: the underlying immune-mediated trigger for PMR is not understood or removed by glucocorticoids; 40-60% of patients relapse at some point during tapering and need a higher dose or a longer course (Espigol-Frigole 2023, PMID 37832573); and glucocorticoid itself carries real cumulative toxicity (bone loss, diabetes, cataract, infection risk) that is the main reason steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate) or IL-6-pathway biologics (tocilizumab, sarilumab) are used in relapsing or high-cumulative-exposure patients.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients whose symptoms do not improve substantially within about a week of an adequate dose should be reassessed for an alternative diagnosis (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, malignancy, myositis, other causes of an inflammatory-marker-elevated girdle pain syndrome) rather than simply escalating the steroid dose, since a slow/partial response is atypical for true PMR. Patients who relapse repeatedly on tapering, or who accumulate high cumulative glucocorticoid exposure, are the population for whom methotrexate, tocilizumab or sarilumab have real trial evidence of added benefit rather than continued steroid-only management.
curative_option.important_caveat: The Caporali 2004 trial (PMID 15466766) is a single, moderate-sized (n=62) RCT; the 53.3%/87.5% discontinuation figures are specific to that trial's population, dosing protocol and 76-week follow-up window and should not be read as universal fixed probabilities for every patient. Two older, smaller methotrexate trials had mixed results: Ferraccioli 1996 (J Rheumatol, PMID 8730115, n=24) found 6 of 12 methotrexate patients versus 0 of 12 controls had stopped steroids at 12 months, while van der Veen 1996 (Ann Rheum Dis, PMID 8733437, n=40+) found no significant difference between methotrexate and placebo in remission time, relapse rate or cumulative steroid dose, with 40% of all patients (both arms combined) able to discontinue prednisone within two years regardless of methotrexate — the evidence for methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent in PMR is therefore real but not fully consistent across trials, and the strongest positive trial (Caporali 2004) is also the most methodologically rigorous (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled).
curative_option.source: Espigol-Frigole G, Dejaco C, Mackie SL, Salvarani C, Matteson EL, Cid MC, 'Polymyalgia rheumatica', Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472 (PMID 37832573); Castaneda S, Garcia-Castaneda N, Prieto-Pena D, Martinez-Quintanilla D, Vicente EF, Blanco R, Gonzalez-Gay MA, 'Treatment of polymyalgia rheumatica', Biochem Pharmacol 2019;165:221-229 (PMID 30904473); Caporali R, Cimmino MA, Ferraccioli G, Gerli R, Klersy C, Salvarani C, Montecucco C, 'Prednisone plus methotrexate for polymyalgia rheumatica: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500 (PMID 15466766); Dejaco C et al., '2015 recommendations for the management of polymyalgia rheumatica: a European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology collaborative initiative', Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807 (PMID 26359488) and Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2569-2580 (PMID 26352874); Ferraccioli G, Salaffi F, De Vita S, Casatta L, Bartoli E, 'Methotrexate in polymyalgia rheumatica: preliminary results of an open, randomized study', J Rheumatol 1996;23:624-628 (PMID 8730115); van der Veen MJ, Dinant HJ, van Booma-Frankfort C, van Albada-Kuipers GA, Bijlsma JW, 'Can methotrexate be used as a steroid sparing agent in the treatment of polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis?', Ann Rheum Dis 1996;55:218-223 (PMID 8733437).
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR): low-dose oral glucocorticoid induction (the real dramatic, near-diagnostic response), the glucocorticoid tapering/duration evidence, intramuscular glucocorticoid as an alternative route, methotrexate as a steroid-sparing DMARD (with honest trial-to-trial inconsistency), the two IL-6-pathway biologics with real randomised-trial evidence for relapsing/refractory disease (tocilizumab, sarilumab), the limited/adjunct role of NSAIDs, and the real relapse-risk/glucocorticoid-toxicity monitoring burden. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial, guideline or review; where a number could not be independently verified in this research session it is stated as such rather than invented.

pmr_low_dose_glucocorticoids_induction.name: Low-Dose Oral Prednisone/Prednisolone Induction — Real Dramatic, Near-Diagnostic Response
pmr_low_dose_glucocorticoids_induction.effectiveness: '12.5-25.0 mg prednisone per day are effective in inducing remission in most individuals' (Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573); onset of dramatic improvement is described as occurring 'in less than a week' (Castaneda S et al., Biochem Pharmacol 2019;165:221-229, PMID 30904473). A slow or incomplete response within this timeframe is atypical and should prompt diagnostic reconsideration rather than simple dose escalation.
pmr_low_dose_glucocorticoids_induction.reason_why: PMR is driven by systemic and synovial/peri-articular inflammation (elevated IL-6, CRP/ESR, bursitis on imaging); glucocorticoids rapidly and broadly suppress this inflammatory cascade, which is why the clinical response is both fast and dramatic compared with slower-acting DMARDs used in other inflammatory arthritides.
pmr_low_dose_glucocorticoids_induction.source: Espigol-Frigole G et al., 'Polymyalgia rheumatica', Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472 (PMID 37832573); Castaneda S et al., 'Treatment of polymyalgia rheumatica', Biochem Pharmacol 2019;165:221-229 (PMID 30904473).

pmr_glucocorticoid_tapering_and_treatmen.name: Glucocorticoid Tapering Strategy and Real Treatment-Duration/Discontinuation Data
pmr_glucocorticoid_tapering_and_treatmen.type: Oral glucocorticoid, dose-tapering strategy over 1-2 years
pmr_glucocorticoid_tapering_and_treatmen.effectiveness: In a real randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 53.3% (16 of 30) of patients on tapering prednisone alone had discontinued all glucocorticoid by 76 weeks (about 1.5 years), with a median cumulative dose of 2.97 g and a 73% (22 of 30) flare-up rate over the study; adding methotrexate raised discontinuation to 87.5% (28 of 32), cut flares to 47% (15 of 32, p=0.04) and lowered median cumulative dose to 2.1 g (Caporali R et al., Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500, PMID 15466766). At a population level, relapse during tapering occurs in 40-60% of patients (Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573).
pmr_glucocorticoid_tapering_and_treatmen.important_caveat: The 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations (Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807, PMID 26359488; Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2569-2580, PMID 26352874) formally cover 'initial glucocorticoid doses and subsequent tapering regimens', but the exact week-by-week milligram steps were not independently re-extracted from open full text in this research session (paywalled to the automated tools used) and are therefore not quoted as specific numbers here.
pmr_glucocorticoid_tapering_and_treatmen.source: Caporali R et al., Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500 (PMID 15466766); Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472 (PMID 37832573); Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807 (PMID 26359488).

pmr_intramuscular_glucocorticoid_alterna.name: Intramuscular Glucocorticoid — Real Guideline-Recognised Alternative to Daily Oral Dosing
pmr_intramuscular_glucocorticoid_alterna.type: Intramuscular depot glucocorticoid injection (alternative route, not a distinct drug class)
pmr_intramuscular_glucocorticoid_alterna.specific_procedure: Intramuscular glucocorticoid (e.g. methylprednisolone acetate) given at intervals in place of daily oral prednisone/prednisolone
pmr_intramuscular_glucocorticoid_alterna.effectiveness: The 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations explicitly address 'use of intramuscular GCs' as part of the formal treatment-strategy recommendations for PMR, alongside oral dosing and DMARD use (Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807, PMID 26359488; Arthritis Rheumatol 2015;67:2569-2580, PMID 26352874). Specific comparative effect sizes/response rates for the intramuscular route versus oral dosing were not independently re-extracted from open full text in this research session and are not quoted here as specific numbers to avoid misquoting the guideline.
pmr_intramuscular_glucocorticoid_alterna.source: Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807 (PMID 26359488).

pmr_methotrexate_steroid_sparing.name: Methotrexate — Real Steroid-Sparing DMARD, Strongest RCT Positive but Not Universally Replicated
pmr_methotrexate_steroid_sparing.type: Conventional synthetic DMARD, oral or subcutaneous, steroid-sparing adjunct
specific_drugs: Methotrexate 7.5-10 mg once weekly (oral or subcutaneous), per Caporali 2004 protocol
pmr_methotrexate_steroid_sparing.effectiveness: Caporali R et al. (Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500, PMID 15466766), randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=62: adding methotrexate to prednisone raised successful glucocorticoid discontinuation by 76 weeks from 53.3% (16/30, placebo) to 87.5% (28/32, methotrexate) (risk difference 34 points, p=0.003), reduced flare-ups from 73% to 47% (p=0.04), and lowered median cumulative prednisone dose from 2.97 g to 2.1 g. Ferraccioli G et al. (J Rheumatol 1996;23:624-628, PMID 8730115, n=24, open-randomised): 6 of 12 methotrexate patients versus 0 of 12 controls had stopped steroids at 12 months; cumulative prednisone 1.84 g versus 3.2 g; bone mineral density preserved in the methotrexate group. van der Veen MJ et al. (Ann Rheum Dis 1996;55:218-223, PMID 8733437) found NO significant difference between methotrexate and placebo in remission time, relapse rate or cumulative steroid dose; 40% of all patients (both arms combined) discontinued prednisone within two years regardless of methotrexate.
pmr_methotrexate_steroid_sparing.important_caveat: Evidence across the three available randomised trials is directionally positive but not fully consistent; the largest and most rigorous trial (Caporali 2004) shows the clearest benefit. Used per EULAR/ACR 2015 guidance mainly in patients at high risk of relapse or prolonged glucocorticoid therapy, and in those with glucocorticoid-related comorbidity.
pmr_methotrexate_steroid_sparing.source: Caporali R et al., Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500 (PMID 15466766); Ferraccioli G et al., J Rheumatol 1996;23:624-628 (PMID 8730115); van der Veen MJ et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1996;55:218-223 (PMID 8733437).

pmr_tocilizumab_relapsing_refractory.name: Tocilizumab — Real Randomised-Trial Evidence for Active/Relapsing PMR on Glucocorticoids
pmr_tocilizumab_relapsing_refractory.type: IL-6 receptor inhibitor, monoclonal antibody (biologic DMARD), subcutaneous or intravenous
pmr_tocilizumab_relapsing_refractory.effectiveness: Devauchelle-Pensec V et al., JAMA 2022;328:1053-1062 (PMID 36125471), randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients with active PMR on glucocorticoid therapy: primary treatment-response endpoint achieved in 67.3% (tocilizumab) versus 31.4% (placebo) at week 24 (adjusted relative risk 2.3, 95% CI 1.5-3.6, p<0.001); mean CRP-based PMR activity score 7.5 versus 14.9 (p<0.001); complete prednisone discontinuation in 49.0% versus 19.6% (adjusted RR 2.5, p<0.001); infections reported in 46.9% (tocilizumab) versus 39.2% (placebo).
pmr_tocilizumab_relapsing_refractory.important_caveat: Tocilizumab is a biologic requiring cost, injection/infusion logistics, infection screening (including tuberculosis) and monitoring (neutrophils, liver enzymes, lipids); infection rates were numerically higher than placebo in the pivotal trial. Reserved for relapsing or refractory PMR, or where glucocorticoid toxicity mandates faster tapering, not for routine first-line use.
pmr_tocilizumab_relapsing_refractory.source: Devauchelle-Pensec V, Carvajal-Alegria G, Dernis E, et al., 'Effect of Tocilizumab on Disease Activity in Patients With Active Polymyalgia Rheumatica Receiving Glucocorticoid Therapy', JAMA 2022;328:1053-1062 (PMID 36125471).

pmr_sarilumab_relapsing_refractory.name: Sarilumab — Real Randomised-Trial (SAPHYR) Evidence for Relapsing PMR During Glucocorticoid Taper
pmr_sarilumab_relapsing_refractory.type: IL-6 receptor inhibitor, monoclonal antibody (biologic DMARD), subcutaneous
pmr_sarilumab_relapsing_refractory.effectiveness: Spiera RF et al. (SAPHYR trial), N Engl J Med 2023;389:1263-1272 (PMID 37792612), randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients relapsing during glucocorticoid taper: sustained remission at 52 weeks in 28% (sarilumab, n=60) versus 10% (placebo, n=58) (difference 18 percentage points, p=0.02); median cumulative glucocorticoid dose 777 mg (sarilumab) versus 2044 mg (placebo, p<0.001).
pmr_sarilumab_relapsing_refractory.important_caveat: Adverse events were numerically higher with sarilumab: neutropenia 15% versus 0%, arthralgia 15% versus 5%, diarrhoea 12% versus 2%. Indicated specifically for relapse during glucocorticoid tapering, not first-line induction.
pmr_sarilumab_relapsing_refractory.source: Spiera RF, Unizony S, Warrington KJ, et al. (SAPHYR Investigators), 'Sarilumab for Relapse of Polymyalgia Rheumatica during Glucocorticoid Taper', N Engl J Med 2023;389:1263-1272 (PMID 37792612).

pmr_nsaids_limited_adjunct_role.name: NSAIDs — Real Limited/Adjunct Role Only, Not Recommended as Monotherapy
pmr_nsaids_limited_adjunct_role.type: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral, adjunct only
specific_drugs: Non-selective oral NSAIDs (e.g. naproxen, ibuprofen) — as short-term adjuncts only
pmr_nsaids_limited_adjunct_role.effectiveness: The 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations for PMR formally address 'the roles of non-steroidal anti-rheumatic drugs' as one of the specific topics covered by their nine recommendations (Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807, PMID 26359488), reflecting that NSAIDs are not an adequate substitute for glucocorticoid induction in PMR; glucocorticoid at 12.5-25 mg/day remains the induction standard (Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573).
pmr_nsaids_limited_adjunct_role.important_caveat: NSAID monotherapy is not an accepted PMR treatment strategy; NSAIDs are used, if at all, only as short-term adjuncts for residual musculoskeletal pain, with the same gastrointestinal/renal/cardiovascular caution that applies in this older patient population.
pmr_nsaids_limited_adjunct_role.source: Dejaco C et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1799-1807 (PMID 26359488).

pmr_relapse_risk_and_glucocorticoid_toxi.name: Relapse-Risk and Glucocorticoid-Toxicity Monitoring — Real Ongoing Treatment-Side Burden
pmr_relapse_risk_and_glucocorticoid_toxi.type: Clinical monitoring / disease-course management, not a drug
pmr_relapse_risk_and_glucocorticoid_toxi.specific_procedure: Regular clinical review with CRP/ESR, glucocorticoid-toxicity screening (bone density, glucose, blood pressure, ocular) during the 1-2 year (or longer) tapering course
pmr_relapse_risk_and_glucocorticoid_toxi.effectiveness: Relapses occur in 40-60% of PMR patients during glucocorticoid tapering (Espigol-Frigole G et al., Lancet 2023;402:1459-1472, PMID 37832573), which is the direct clinical rationale for structured tapering, steroid-sparing methotrexate, and IL-6-pathway biologics in higher-risk or relapsing patients.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Methotrexate + prednisone: glucocorticoid discontinuation by 76 weeks (Caporali RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 87.5% (28 of 32) of patients on methotrexate plus prednisone had successfully discontinued all glucocorticoid by 76 weeks, versus 53.3% on prednisone alone (risk difference 34 percentage points, p=0.003); randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=62.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Caporali R et al., 'Prednisone plus methotrexate for polymyalgia rheumatica: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial', Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500 (PMID 15466766)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tocilizumab: primary treatment-response endpoint at week 24
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 67.3% of patients on tocilizumab achieved the primary treatment-response endpoint at week 24 versus 31.4% on placebo (adjusted RR 2.3, 95% CI 1.5-3.6, p<0.001); randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Devauchelle-Pensec V et al., 'Effect of Tocilizumab on Disease Activity in Patients With Active Polymyalgia Rheumatica Receiving Glucocorticoid Therapy', JAMA 2022;328:1053-1062 (PMID 36125471)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prednisone alone: glucocorticoid discontinuation by 76 weeks (Caporali RCT, placebo arm)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 53.3% (16 of 30) of patients on tapering prednisone alone had discontinued all glucocorticoid by 76 weeks; median cumulative dose 2.97 g; 73% had at least one flare-up during the study.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Caporali R et al., Ann Intern Med 2004;141:493-500 (PMID 15466766)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tocilizumab: complete prednisone discontinuation at week 24
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 49.0% of patients on tocilizumab completely discontinued prednisone by week 24 versus 19.6% on placebo (adjusted RR 2.5, p<0.001).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Devauchelle-Pensec V et al., JAMA 2022;328:1053-1062 (PMID 36125471)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Methotrexate, older mixed-evidence trial: prednisone discontinuation within 2 years (both arms combined)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Steroid-sparing DMARD + oral glucocorticoid (negative/neutral trial, included for honesty)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 40% of all patients (methotrexate and placebo arms combined) discontinued prednisone within two years; this trial found NO significant difference between methotrexate and placebo in remission time, relapse rate, or cumulative steroid dose, contrasting with the positive Caporali 2004 result above.
ranked_high_to_low.source: van der Veen MJ et al., 'Can methotrexate be used as a steroid sparing agent in the treatment of polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis?', Ann Rheum Dis 1996;55:218-223 (PMID 8733437)

osteomyelitis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 hint: FB80 Osteomyelitis (WHO ICD-11 MMS, musculoskeletal-system chapter) -- sourced from secondary reference; could NOT independently confirm on the live WHO ICD-11 browser, which is a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly. Legacy ICD-10 M86 Osteomyelitis (verified via Wikipedia infobox cross-check), with site/type-specific legacy subcodes: M86.0 acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, M86.1 other acute osteomyelitis, M86.2 subacute osteomyelitis, M86.3 chronic multifocal osteomyelitis, M86.4 chronic osteomyelitis with draining sinus, M86.5 other chronic haematogenous osteomyelitis, M86.6 other chronic osteomyelitis, M86.8 other osteomyelitis, M86.9 osteomyelitis unspecified.
osteomyelitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Osteomyelitis is genuinely one of the more curable serious bone infections when it is caught early and treated with an adequate, organism-directed antibiotic course -- and, for chronic/necrotic disease, combined with surgical debridement. Real numbers, not spin: in the largest paediatric randomised trial of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis (Peltola H et al, Pediatr Infect Dis J 2010;29:1123-1128, PMID 20842069), 130 of 131 culture-positive children (99.2%) recovered completely with a short intravenous phase (2-4 days) switched to oral therapy and stopped once inflammatory markers normalised at just 20 days total -- only one mild sequela occurred in each of the 20-day and 30-day arms. In pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, a 351-patient randomised non-inferiority trial found clinical cure in 90.9% of patients at both 6 and 12 weeks of antibiotics (Bernard L et al, Lancet 2015;385:875-882, PMID 25468170). For complex bone and joint infection overall (any site, including chronic and implant-associated disease), the 1054-patient OVIVA trial found oral antibiotic step-down after an initial treatment decision was non-inferior to prolonged intravenous therapy -- treatment failure at 1 year was 13.2% with oral therapy versus 14.6% with IV therapy (Li HK et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:425-436, PMID 30699315), i.e. roughly 85-87% real treatment success either way, without needing a long IV line. When an orthopaedic implant is retained and infection is staphylococcal, adding rifampin to a fluoroquinolone after debridement achieved 100% cure (12/12) versus only 58% (7/12) without rifampin in a randomised trial (Zimmerli W et al, JAMA 1998;279:1537-1541, PMID 9605897) -- a real, quantified, mechanism-based (anti-biofilm) improvement. Honestly, chronic osteomyelitis (necrotic bone/sequestrum, biofilm-associated, Cierny-Mader Stage 3-4, PMID 12966271) is harder to fully eradicate than acute disease: a systematic review of debridement plus local antibiotic-carrier dead-space management (206 patients across 9 studies) found an overall cure rate of 86% with an 11.6% recurrence rate (Tanwar YS et al, Infect Dis (Lond) 2020;52:219-226, PMID 31774017), and diabetic-foot osteomyelitis treated with antibiotics alone (no surgery) achieves lower but still real remission -- 64% (32/50) in one bone-culture-guided cohort (Senneville E et al, Diabetes Care 2008;31:637-642, PMID 18184898) and 60-70% in a randomised 6-week-vs-12-week comparison (Tone A et al, Diabetes Care 2015;38:302-307, PMID 25414157). Bottom line: acute and vertebral osteomyelitis treated promptly and adequately are real high-cure-rate conditions (~90-99%); chronic and diabetic-foot osteomyelitis are genuinely harder but still carry real, meaningful, majority-favourable cure rates (60-86%) with correct antibiotic-plus-surgical management -- not a hopeless diagnosis.

curative_option.name: Organism-Directed Antibiotic Therapy (Adequate Duration, IV-to-Oral Step-Down per OVIVA) Plus Surgical Debridement/Dead-Space Management When Bone Is Necrotic or Hardware Is Present, Staged by Cierny-Mader Classification -- Real Closest-to-Cure Approach
curative_option.type: Combined medical (antibiotic) + procedural (debridement) curative pathway
curative_option.note: There is no single pill or single operation that cures osteomyelitis; the real evidence-based curative pathway is (1) obtain a real microbiological diagnosis (bone biopsy/culture where feasible, not just swab culture), (2) start empiric IV antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA risk) and narrow to the culture result, (3) surgically debride all necrotic/dead bone (sequestrum) and manage dead space when disease is chronic, subacute-with-abscess, or implant-associated, and (4) treat with an adequate total duration -- and it is real and evidence-based, not merely 'more is safer', that oral step-down after the first treatment decision point is non-inferior to staying on IV therapy for most patients, and that 6 weeks is non-inferior to 12 weeks for vertebral osteomyelitis.

real_trial_data.oviva_oral_vs_iv_step_down: Li HK et al, 'Oral versus Intravenous Antibiotics for Bone and Joint Infection', N Engl J Med 2019;380:425-436 (PMID 30699315). Multicentre UK RCT, 1054 adults with bone/joint infection (including osteomyelitis) randomised, after the first 6 weeks of the treating clinician's chosen antibiotic, to continue IV or switch to oral therapy. Definitive treatment failure at 1 year: IV 14.6% (74/506), oral 13.2% (67/509); risk difference -1.4 percentage points (90% CI -4.9 to 2.2), meeting the pre-specified 7.5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin. Catheter-related complications were far higher with IV (9.4% vs 1.0% oral). Real conclusion: oral step-down is non-inferior and avoids the real morbidity of a prolonged IV line.
real_trial_data.peltola_pediatric_short_course: Peltola H et al, 'Short- versus long-term antimicrobial treatment for acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of childhood', Pediatr Infect Dis J 2010;29:1123-1128 (PMID 20842069). 131 culture-positive Finnish children randomised to 20 days (n=67) vs 30 days (n=64) total therapy (2-4 days IV, then oral, stopped once CRP fell below 20 mg/L). Result: 130/131 (99.2%) recovered entirely, with only 1 mild sequela per arm -- real evidence that most childhood acute haematogenous osteomyelitis is curable with a short, adequately-dosed course when switched to oral early.
real_trial_data.bernard_vertebral_osteomyelitis_duration: Bernard L et al, 'Antibiotic treatment for 6 weeks versus 12 weeks in patients with pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis', Lancet 2015;385:875-882 (PMID 25468170). Open-label non-inferiority RCT, 351 patients. Clinical cure at 1 year: 6-week arm 90.9% (160/176), 12-week arm 90.9% (159/175); difference 0.05% (95% CI -6.2 to 6.3), non-inferiority margin 10 percentage points -- met. Real conclusion: 6 weeks is a real, non-inferior, shorter curative course for vertebral osteomyelitis.
real_trial_data.zimmerli_rifampin_implant_associated: Zimmerli W et al, 'Role of rifampin for treatment of orthopedic implant-related staphylococcal infections', JAMA 1998;279:1537-1541 (PMID 9605897). RCT, 33 patients with culture-proven staphylococcal infection of a stable orthopaedic implant, all debrided with implant retained. Cure at 2-year follow-up: rifampin+ciprofloxacin 100% (12/12) vs placebo+ciprofloxacin 58% (7/12), p=.02. Real, mechanism-grounded (rifampin penetrates staphylococcal biofilm) evidence for adding rifampin whenever an infected implant is retained after debridement.

curative_option.duration_guidance: Real, guideline-anchored duration ranges (not fixed by one number): acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children with early oral switch, as short as 20 days total (Peltola 2010); adult native-bone osteomyelitis with adequate debridement, commonly 4-6 weeks from the last major debridement (IDSA/IWGDF diabetic-foot guidance, PMID 22619242, PMID 37779457); vertebral osteomyelitis, 6 weeks is non-inferior to 12 (Bernard 2015); chronic osteomyelitis with residual dead bone or a retained implant needs debridement/dead-space management plus antibiotics, sometimes prolonged (weeks-months) or, for retained-implant staphylococcal disease, indefinite rifampin-based suppressive therapy is used when the implant cannot be removed.
curative_option.source: Li HK et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:425-436 (PMID 30699315); Peltola H et al, Pediatr Infect Dis J 2010;29:1123-1128 (PMID 20842069); Bernard L et al, Lancet 2015;385:875-882 (PMID 25468170); Zimmerli W et al, JAMA 1998;279:1537-1541 (PMID 9605897); Cierny G 3rd et al, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2003;414:7-24 (PMID 12966271); Lipsky BA et al, IDSA 2012 diabetic foot infection guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54:e132-173 (PMID 22619242); Senneville E et al, IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2023 (PMID 37779457).
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for osteomyelitis: organism-directed empiric-then-targeted antibiotics (Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA, is the leading cause in all age groups; named regimens below follow the 2012 IDSA diabetic-foot-infection guideline (PMID 22619242) and its 2023 IWGDF/IDSA update (PMID 37779457), which are also the standard cross-referenced sources for non-diabetic osteomyelitis antibiotic selection), the OVIVA oral-step-down strategy, rifampin-combination therapy for retained-implant staphylococcal infection, surgical debridement/dead-space management, local antibiotic-carrier adjuncts, paediatric and vertebral short-course duration data, diabetic-foot nonsurgical management, and amputation as a real last-resort option. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial, guideline or systematic review.

om_organism_directed_empiric_and_targete.name: Organism-Directed IV/Oral Antibiotic Therapy (Empiric Then Culture-Targeted)
specific_drugs: Vancomycin (empiric MRSA/culture-negative coverage, dose targeted to AUC24/MIC per IDSA)
Nafcillin or oxacillin (MSSA-confirmed disease, alternative to cefazolin)
Clindamycin (MSSA or MRSA with confirmed susceptibility and negative D-test, oral step-down option, good bone penetration)
Linezolid (MRSA, real oral bioavailability, used as OVIVA-style oral step-down agent)
Ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin (culture-confirmed susceptible gram-negative disease; combined with rifampin for staphylococcal biofilm/implant disease, see below)
Ceftriaxone (streptococcal disease, some gram-negative organisms, once-daily convenient IV-to-outpatient option)
Piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (polymicrobial diabetic-foot osteomyelitis with gram-negative/anaerobic involvement, per culture)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (oral MRSA step-down option in the OVIVA regimen list)
om_organism_directed_empiric_and_targete.effectiveness_metric: 86.8% real treatment success at 1 year (100% minus 13.2% definitive treatment failure) with organism-directed therapy including oral step-down, OVIVA trial, n=509 oral-arm evaluable patients with bone/joint infection; 85.4% success (100% minus 14.6% failure) in the IV-continued comparison arm, n=506 -- essentially equivalent, non-inferior outcomes.
om_organism_directed_empiric_and_targete.reason_why: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is the leading causative organism in acute and chronic osteomyelitis across all age groups, with streptococci, gram-negative bacilli (especially in diabetic-foot and post-surgical disease) and, in neonates, group B streptococcus also important; matching the antibiotic to the actual cultured organism (not empiric guesswork alone) and achieving adequate bone penetration and duration is the real basis of cure -- confirmed by the OVIVA finding that oral agents with good bioavailability achieve equivalent cure to IV therapy once source control (debridement, when needed) has been achieved.
om_organism_directed_empiric_and_targete.important_caveat: Empiric antibiotics should be held, when the patient is not septic/unstable, until bone/blood cultures are obtained -- starting empiric therapy before culture collection is a real, avoidable cause of a missed or wrong diagnosis and can prevent organism-directed cure.
om_organism_directed_empiric_and_targete.source: Li HK et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:425-436 (PMID 30699315); Lipsky BA et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54:e132-173 (PMID 22619242); Senneville E et al, Clin Infect Dis 2023 (PMID 37779457)

om_oral_step_down_oviva_non_inferiority.name: IV-to-Oral Antibiotic Step-Down Strategy (OVIVA Approach)
om_oral_step_down_oviva_non_inferiority.type: Systemic antibiotic therapy -- real practice-changing route-of-administration strategy
om_oral_step_down_oviva_non_inferiority.specific_procedure: After the treating clinician has made an initial antibiotic choice and treated for as long as judged necessary on IV therapy (commonly the first ~1 week to 6 weeks depending on the specific infection and source control achieved), switch to a bioavailable oral agent (e.g. linezolid, clindamycin, a fluoroquinolone +/- rifampin, co-trimoxazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate depending on organism) to complete the total planned duration, avoiding a prolonged indwelling IV line.
om_oral_step_down_oviva_non_inferiority.effectiveness_metric: 13.2% definitive treatment failure at 1 year with oral step-down (67/509) versus 14.6% with continued IV therapy (74/506); risk difference -1.4 percentage points (90% CI -4.9 to 2.2), meeting the 7.5-point non-inferiority margin -- i.e. oral therapy is real, non-inferior, and avoids IV-catheter complications (9.4% vs 1.0%). (Effectiveness_pct here is the reported failure rate itself, quoted as published; real cure/success rate is its complement, ~86.8%.)
om_oral_step_down_oviva_non_inferiority.reason_why: Many oral antibiotics (linezolid, fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, co-trimoxazole, rifampin) achieve bone and soft-tissue concentrations comparable to IV therapy because of high oral bioavailability, so once early source control is achieved there is no real added benefit to IV-only administration, while there is real added harm (catheter infection/thrombosis, hospitalisation burden).
om_oral_step_down_oviva_non_inferiority.source: Li HK et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:425-436 (PMID 30699315)

om_rifampin_combination_implant_biofilm_.name: Rifampin-Combination Therapy for Retained-Implant Staphylococcal Osteomyelitis
om_rifampin_combination_implant_biofilm_.type: Systemic antibiotic therapy -- anti-biofilm combination, real quantified benefit
specific_drugs: Rifampin (added to a fluoroquinolone, e.g. ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) once debridement with implant retention has been performed and the wound is not actively draining
om_rifampin_combination_implant_biofilm_.effectiveness_metric: 100% cure (12/12) with rifampin+ciprofloxacin versus 58% cure (7/12) with placebo+ciprofloxacin at 2-year follow-up, p=.02, RCT n=33 (24 completed full follow-up), culture-proven staphylococcal orthopaedic-implant infection with debridement and implant retention.
om_rifampin_combination_implant_biofilm_.reason_why: Rifampin uniquely penetrates and kills staphylococci within the biofilm adherent to retained hardware, a real mechanistic advantage that fluoroquinolone monotherapy lacks; rifampin is never used alone because of rapid resistance emergence, hence the combination requirement.
om_rifampin_combination_implant_biofilm_.important_caveat: Only applicable when debridement is performed and the implant is not removed; rifampin must be combined with a second active agent, never used as monotherapy, and is real-world limited by drug interactions (potent CYP3A4 induction) and hepatotoxicity risk.

om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.name: Surgical Debridement of Necrotic Bone (Sequestrectomy) and Dead-Space Management
om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.type: Surgical procedure -- second-priority, required for chronic/necrotic/implant-associated disease
om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.specific_procedure: Radical resection of all necrotic, infected bone (sequestrum) and non-viable soft tissue down to bleeding, healthy margins, staged per the Cierny-Mader anatomic type (I medullary, II superficial, III localised, IV diffuse) and host physiological class (A normal host, B systemically/locally compromised, C treatment worse than disease), followed by dead-space management (local antibiotic-carrier bead/graft placement, muscle flap, or staged bone transport/Masquelet induced-membrane technique for large segmental defects) and, in implant-associated disease, decision on implant retention versus removal/exchange.
om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.effectiveness_metric: 86% overall cure with 11.6% recurrence in a systematic review of 206 patients across 9 studies of debridement combined with a local antibiotic-carrier dead-space filler for chronic osteomyelitis.
om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.reason_why: Necrotic bone (sequestrum) has no blood supply, so systemic antibiotics -- however well chosen -- cannot reach a curative concentration inside it; only mechanical removal of dead bone, combined with adequate antibiotic therapy for the remaining viable-but-infected tissue, can achieve real cure in chronic/necrotic disease. This is the real biological reason antibiotics alone fail in chronic osteomyelitis but succeed in acute disease before necrosis has developed.
om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.important_caveat: Inadequate/incomplete debridement (leaving infected or dead bone behind) is a real, well-recognised cause of recurrence; the staging (Cierny-Mader) exists specifically because host factors (Type B/C) and inadequate margins materially change the realistic chance of cure.
om_surgical_debridement_dead_space_manag.source: Tanwar YS et al, Infect Dis (Lond) 2020;52:219-226 (PMID 31774017); Cierny G 3rd et al, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2003;414:7-24 (PMID 12966271)

om_local_antibiotic_carrier_dead_space_f.name: Local Antibiotic-Eluting Carrier (Bioactive Glass / Calcium Sulfate-Hydroxyapatite Beads) as Dead-Space Filler
om_local_antibiotic_carrier_dead_space_f.specific_procedure: Absorbable antibiotic-loaded (commonly gentamicin- or vancomycin-loaded) calcium sulfate/hydroxyapatite biocomposite or bioactive glass granules packed into the bone void created by debridement, delivering high local antibiotic concentration directly at the surgical site while filling dead space and, for the resorbable carriers, avoiding a second operation to remove the carrier (unlike traditional PMMA cement beads).
om_local_antibiotic_carrier_dead_space_f.effectiveness_metric: 86% overall cure (11.6% recurrence), 206 patients/9 studies, systematic review of bioactive-glass and related local-carrier dead-space management after debridement for chronic osteomyelitis; a single-stage cohort using gentamicin-loaded calcium sulfate/hydroxyapatite for diabetic calcaneal osteomyelitis reported comparable real-world infection eradication in its independent series.
om_local_antibiotic_carrier_dead_space_f.reason_why: Local carriers achieve antibiotic concentrations at the debrided bone surface many times higher than is safely achievable with systemic dosing alone, targeting residual bacteria/biofilm in the surgical bed while filling the mechanical dead space that would otherwise become a haematoma and a new nidus for recurrence.
om_local_antibiotic_carrier_dead_space_f.source: Tanwar YS et al, Infect Dis (Lond) 2020;52:219-226 (PMID 31774017); Drampalos E et al, Foot (Edinb) 2018;34:40-44 (PMID 29278835)

om_pediatric_acute_hematogenous_short_co.name: Short-Course (20-Day) IV-to-Oral Antibiotic Therapy for Childhood Acute Haematogenous Osteomyelitis
om_pediatric_acute_hematogenous_short_co.type: Systemic antibiotic therapy -- duration-optimised, real high-cure paediatric protocol
om_pediatric_acute_hematogenous_short_co.specific_procedure: 2-4 days of IV antibiotic therapy (typically a first-generation cephalosporin or clindamycin covering MSSA, adjusted for local MRSA prevalence) switched to oral therapy once the child is afebrile and improving, with total duration guided by CRP normalisation (<20 mg/L), commonly totalling ~20 days rather than the traditional 4-6 weeks.
om_pediatric_acute_hematogenous_short_co.effectiveness_metric: 99.2% (130/131) complete recovery, with only 1 mild sequela in each of the 20-day and 30-day arms and no significant outcome difference between them -- RCT, n=131 culture-positive Finnish children.
om_pediatric_acute_hematogenous_short_co.reason_why: Acute (pre-necrotic) paediatric osteomyelitis has excellent bone blood supply and a highly treatable, usually monomicrobial (S. aureus) infection without the dead bone/biofilm burden of chronic disease, so an adequately dosed short course achieves real, near-complete cure without the added morbidity (line complications, cost, hospitalisation) of prolonged IV therapy.
om_pediatric_acute_hematogenous_short_co.source: Peltola H et al, Pediatr Infect Dis J 2010;29:1123-1128 (PMID 20842069)

om_vertebral_osteomyelitis_six_week_dura.name: 6-Week (vs Traditional 12-Week) Antibiotic Duration for Pyogenic Vertebral Osteomyelitis
om_vertebral_osteomyelitis_six_week_dura.specific_procedure: Organism-directed IV then oral antibiotic therapy for a total of 6 weeks (rather than the traditional 12), following percutaneous or surgical biopsy for microbiological diagnosis.
om_vertebral_osteomyelitis_six_week_dura.effectiveness_metric: 90.9% clinical cure at 1 year in both the 6-week arm (160/176) and the 12-week arm (159/175); difference 0.05% (95% CI -6.2 to 6.3) -- real non-inferiority, RCT n=351.
om_vertebral_osteomyelitis_six_week_dura.reason_why: Vertebral osteomyelitis is usually haematogenous and, once source-controlled with appropriate antibiotics, does not require the longer courses historically used out of caution rather than evidence; the trial directly tested and confirmed 6 weeks is real-world sufficient.

om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.name: Antibiotic-Alone (Nonsurgical) Therapy for Diabetic-Foot Osteomyelitis
om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.type: Systemic antibiotic therapy -- real option when surgery is refused/high-risk, honestly lower cure rate than surgical debridement
om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.specific_procedure: Bone-culture-guided (not swab-guided) prolonged oral or IV antibiotic therapy, typically 6-12 weeks, without surgical resection, reserved for patients without significant ischaemia/gangrene/abscess/systemic sepsis who decline or are unfit for surgery.
om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.effectiveness_metric: 64% (32/50) remission at 12.8-month mean follow-up in a bone-culture-guided nonsurgical cohort (bone-culture-directed therapy was the only variable independently associated with remission, odds ratio 4.78); a separate RCT found 60% (12/20) remission with 6 weeks versus 70% (14/20) with 12 weeks of therapy (p=.50, not significantly different), with significantly fewer GI adverse events at 6 weeks (15% vs 45%, p=.04).
om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.reason_why: Without debridement, dead/infected bone and biofilm can persist despite adequate systemic antibiotic levels, which real-world lowers the cure rate compared with acute or surgically-debrided disease -- an honest, quantified gap versus the >90% rates seen in acute or vertebral osteomyelitis, not a reason to withhold the option when surgery carries its own real risk (amputation, non-healing) in a vasculopathic diabetic foot.
om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.important_caveat: Nonsurgical therapy is not appropriate for diabetic-foot osteomyelitis with critical limb ischaemia, extensive gangrene, uncontrolled sepsis, or a deep abscess requiring drainage -- those situations require debridement/amputation regardless of antibiotic choice.
om_diabetic_foot_osteomyelitis_nonsurgic.source: Senneville E et al, Diabetes Care 2008;31:637-642 (PMID 18184898); Tone A et al, Diabetes Care 2015;38:302-307 (PMID 25414157); Senneville E et al (IWGDF/IDSA 2023), Clin Infect Dis 2023 (PMID 37779457)

om_amputation_last_resort_other.name: Minor or Major Amputation
om_amputation_last_resort_other.type: Surgical procedure -- real last-resort, lower-priority option
om_amputation_last_resort_other.specific_procedure: Minor (toe/ray/transmetatarsal) or major (below/above-knee) amputation when osteomyelitis is combined with unsalvageable ischaemia, extensive necrosis/gangrene, failed debridement/antibiotic therapy, or life-threatening sepsis.
om_amputation_last_resort_other.effectiveness_metric: Definitive source control of the infected bone (100% removal of the infected segment by definition), but real, honest trade-off: it is a destructive rather than reconstructive cure and is reserved by IWGDF/IDSA guideline for patients who fail or are not candidates for debridement/antibiotic-based limb salvage.
om_amputation_last_resort_other.reason_why: Removing all infected and ischaemic tissue at the amputation margin definitionally eliminates the infective focus, but at the cost of the limb segment; guidelines reserve it as a last resort after real limb-salvage options have been exhausted or are contraindicated.
om_amputation_last_resort_other.source: Senneville E et al (IWGDF/IDSA 2023), Clin Infect Dis 2023 (PMID 37779457)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rifampin+ciprofloxacin, retained-implant staphylococcal infection after debridement (Zimmerli 1998)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% cure (12/12) vs 58% (7/12) with ciprofloxacin+placebo, p=.02, at 2-year follow-up. RCT, n=33 (24 completed follow-up).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zimmerli W et al, JAMA 1998;279:1537-1541 (PMID 9605897)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Short-course (20-day) IV-to-oral antibiotics, childhood acute haematogenous osteomyelitis (Peltola 2010)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 99.2% (130/131) complete recovery, only 1 mild sequela per arm, no significant difference between 20-day and 30-day arms. RCT, n=131.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Peltola H et al, Pediatr Infect Dis J 2010;29:1123-1128 (PMID 20842069)

ranked_high_to_low.name: 6-week or 12-week antibiotics, pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis (Bernard 2015)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 90.9% clinical cure at 1 year in both arms (160/176 at 6 weeks; 159/175 at 12 weeks); non-inferiority met (10-point margin). RCT, n=351.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bernard L et al, Lancet 2015;385:875-882 (PMID 25468170)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Organism-directed antibiotics with oral step-down, complex bone/joint infection (OVIVA, oral arm)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Systemic antibiotic therapy with oral step-down
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 86.8% real treatment success (13.2% definitive failure) at 1 year, non-inferior to 85.4% success (14.6% failure) with continued IV therapy; risk difference -1.4pp (90% CI -4.9 to 2.2). RCT, n=1054 (509 oral-arm evaluable).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Li HK et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:425-436 (PMID 30699315)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Surgical debridement + local antibiotic-carrier dead-space management, chronic osteomyelitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 86% overall cure, 11.6% recurrence. Systematic review, 206 patients across 9 studies.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tanwar YS et al, Infect Dis (Lond) 2020;52:219-226 (PMID 31774017)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Bone-culture-guided antibiotics alone (no surgery), diabetic-foot osteomyelitis, 12-week duration arm (Tone 2015)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 70% (14/20) remission with 12 weeks of therapy vs 60% (12/20) with 6 weeks (p=.50, not significant); 6-week arm had significantly fewer GI adverse events (15% vs 45%, p=.04). RCT, n=40.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tone A et al, Diabetes Care 2015;38:302-307 (PMID 25414157)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Bone-culture-guided antibiotics alone (no surgery), diabetic-foot osteomyelitis, retrospective cohort (Senneville 2008)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 64% (32/50) remission at mean 12.8-month follow-up; bone-culture-directed therapy independently associated with remission (odds ratio 4.78). Retrospective cohort, n=50.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Senneville E et al, Diabetes Care 2008;31:637-642 (PMID 18184898)

osteomyelitis.name: Osteomyelitis

classification_by_mechanism.finding: Osteomyelitis is bone infection classified into three principal mechanistic categories: (1) hematogenous osteomyelitis, from blood-borne seeding of bone (predominant in children, usually monomicrobial), (2) contiguous-focus osteomyelitis, from spread of infection from adjacent soft tissue/joint or direct inoculation via trauma or surgery (predominant in adults, often polymicrobial), and (3) osteomyelitis associated with vascular insufficiency, chiefly diabetic foot infection extending to bone. This tripartite classification is the framework used in the major Lancet review of the disease.
classification_by_mechanism.source: Lew DP, Waldvogel FA. Osteomyelitis. Lancet. 2004;364(9431):369-79 (PMID: 15276398); Armstrong EP, Rush DR. Treatment of osteomyelitis. Clin Pharm. 1983;2(3):213-24 (PMID: 6349907)

hematogenous_vs_contiguous_pattern.finding: Hematogenous osteomyelitis is the classic pattern in children, typically monomicrobial, and characteristically involves the metaphysis of long bones because of the unique slow, turbulent blood flow through metaphyseal capillary loops that predisposes to bacterial seeding. Contiguous-spread osteomyelitis is the dominant pattern in adults, arising from direct extension of infection from an adjacent wound, ulcer, joint replacement, or open fracture, and is frequently polymicrobial.
hematogenous_vs_contiguous_pattern.source: Armstrong EP, Rush DR, Clin Pharm, 1983 (PMID: 6349907); Lew DP, Waldvogel FA, Lancet, 2004 (PMID: 15276398)

staphylococcus_aureus_predominance.finding: Staphylococcus aureus is the single most common causative organism across nearly all forms of osteomyelitis. In a 40-year US population-based cohort (Olmsted County, Minnesota; 760 cases, 1969-2009), S. aureus accounted for 44% of culture-positive cases. In a pediatric acute hematogenous osteomyelitis cohort of 94 children, S. aureus was isolated in 84 patients (89%). In percutaneously biopsied diabetic foot osteomyelitis (170 biopsies), gram-positive organisms made up 71.3% of isolates, with S. aureus the single most common pathogen and roughly one-third of S. aureus isolates methicillin-resistant.
staphylococcus_aureus_predominance.source: Kremers HM et al, Trends in the epidemiology of osteomyelitis: a population-based study 1969-2009, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2015 (PMID: 25995495); Popescu B et al, Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in pediatric patients, J Int Med Res, 2020 (PMID: 32249643); Al-Balas H et al, Is fluoroscopy-guided percutaneous bone biopsy of diabetic foot with suspected osteomyelitis worthwhile?, J Diabetes, 2023 (PMID: 36905125)

polymicrobial_diabetic_foot_pattern.finding: In contrast to hematogenous disease, diabetic foot osteomyelitis and other contiguous-focus osteomyelitis are frequently polymicrobial; the 2012 IDSA diabetic foot infection guideline states most diabetic foot infections are polymicrobial, with staphylococci remaining the most common causative organisms overall.
polymicrobial_diabetic_foot_pattern.source: Lipsky BA et al, 2012 Infectious Diseases Society of America clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections, Clin Infect Dis, 2012 (PMID: 22619242)

mri_accuracy.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of imaging tests for osteomyelitis in adults reported pooled diagnostic accuracy as follows: MRI sensitivity 95.6% / specificity 80.7%; PET sensitivity 85.1% / specificity 92.8%; SPECT sensitivity 95.1% / specificity 82.0%; technetium-99m labeled white cell scintigraphy sensitivity 87.3% / specificity 94.7%; CT sensitivity 69.7% / specificity 90.2%; plain radiography sensitivity 70.4% / specificity 81.5%. MRI is preferred as first-line advanced imaging because its accuracy is comparable to PET/SPECT but without radiation exposure and with wider availability. A separate diabetic-foot-specific comparative review reported MRI sensitivity 90% / specificity 79%.
mri_accuracy.source: Llewellyn A et al, Imaging tests for the detection of osteomyelitis: a systematic review, Health Technol Assess, 2019 (PMID: 31670644); Khodaee M et al, Clinical Inquiry: What's the best test for underlying osteomyelitis in patients with diabetic foot ulcers?, J Fam Pract, 2015 (PMID: 26009740)

mri_diagnostic_discordance_diabetic_foot.finding: In a retrospective series of 166 diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients correlating MRI with bone-biopsy-proven disease, initial MRI reads showed 29.3% diagnostic discordance with biopsy (12 false positives, 5 false negatives); after expert re-review, overall MRI accuracy against the biopsy reference standard was 84%. This demonstrates that even a highly sensitive imaging test requires correlation with bone biopsy, particularly in diabetic feet where marrow edema from Charcot neuroarthropathy can mimic infection.
mri_diagnostic_discordance_diabetic_foot.source: La Fontaine J et al, Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis: Imaging Accuracy in Biopsy-Proven Disease, J Foot Ankle Surg, 2021 (PMID: 33214100)

bone_biopsy_culture_role.finding: Bone culture is the microbiologic reference standard. In a prospective study of 100 chronic osteomyelitis patients (excluding diabetic foot ulcers), bone cultures identified a causative agent in 94% of cases, whereas concordance between superficial (non-bone) specimens and bone cultures was only 30%, with a Cohen's kappa statistic of less than 0 (i.e., agreement no better than chance) -- meaning superficial swab cultures are unreliable and should not be used to guide antibiotic therapy for chronic osteomyelitis. In percutaneous bone biopsy of diabetic foot osteomyelitis (170 samples), 47.1% of cultures were positive, of which 53.8% were monomicrobial. Diagnostic yield on biopsy also depends on the criterion used: one 35-patient prospective study found osteomyelitis identified in 68.6% of specimens by culture, 45.7% by histology, and 82.9% by 16S ribosomal RNA testing (culture vs. 16S rRNA vs. histology all differed significantly, p=0.002 for 16S rRNA vs histology), showing that the diagnostic yield of bone biopsy itself varies substantially by the laboratory method applied to the same specimen.
bone_biopsy_culture_role.source: Zuluaga AF et al, Etiologic diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis: a prospective study, Arch Intern Med, 2006 (PMID: 16401816); Al-Balas H et al, J Diabetes, 2023 (PMID: 36905125); Lavery LA et al, Are We Misdiagnosing Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis? Is the Gold Standard Gold?, J Foot Ankle Surg, 2019 (PMID: 31256899)

probe_to_bone_test.finding: The bedside probe-to-bone test (a sterile blunt metal probe inserted into an infected pedal ulcer to check for a hard, gritty bone contact) was validated in a prospective study of 76 infected pedal ulcers in diabetic patients (50 with osteomyelitis confirmed): sensitivity 66%, specificity 85%, positive predictive value 89%, negative predictive value 56%. A positive probe-to-bone test in a diabetic foot ulcer therefore substantially raises the likelihood of underlying osteomyelitis and should prompt bone imaging/biopsy, but a negative test does not reliably exclude it.
probe_to_bone_test.source: Grayson ML et al, Probing to bone in infected pedal ulcers. A clinical sign of underlying osteomyelitis in diabetic patients, JAMA, 1995 (PMID: 7853630)

esr_crp_trends.finding: A meta-analysis of 8 studies on biomarkers for diabetic foot osteomyelitis found ESR to be the best-performing single laboratory test, with pooled sensitivity 81% (95% CI 71-88%) and specificity 90% (95% CI 75-96%); a commonly cited operational cutoff is ESR greater than 70 mm/hr, with CRP greater than 14 mg/L and procalcitonin greater than 0.3 ng/mL also reported as supportive cutoffs in a comparative clinical review. In a different clinical context (late fracture-related infection), a separate meta-analysis found CRP sensitivity 77.0% / specificity 67.9% and ESR sensitivity 45.1% / specificity 79.3%, concluding that individually these markers are insufficiently accurate and should be combined with clinical and imaging findings rather than used alone. CRP and ESR are used serially to track treatment response (a falling trend supports adequate therapy), though neither marker in isolation is sufficient to diagnose osteomyelitis or declare cure.
esr_crp_trends.source: van Asten SA et al, The Role of Biomarkers to Diagnose Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis. A Meta-analysis, Curr Diabetes Rev, 2016 (PMID: 26166314); Khodaee M et al, J Fam Pract, 2015 (PMID: 26009740); van den Kieboom J et al, Diagnostic accuracy of serum inflammatory markers in late fracture-related infection, Bone Joint J, 2018 (PMID: 30499325)

acute_presentation.finding: Acute osteomyelitis (typically hematogenous, classically in children) presents with localized bone pain, warmth, swelling, and reduced use/limp of the affected limb, often accompanied by fever. Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis can often be cured with antibiotics alone if diagnosed and treated early, before extensive bone necrosis develops.
acute_presentation.source: Lew DP, Waldvogel FA, Lancet, 2004 (PMID: 15276398); Gornitzky AL et al, Diagnosis and Management of Osteomyelitis in Children: A Critical Analysis Review, JBJS Rev, 2020 (PMID: 33006465)

chronic_presentation.finding: Chronic osteomyelitis presents with a more indolent course: persistent or recurrent localized pain, low-grade or absent fever, and the hallmark findings of a draining sinus tract to skin, chronic wound non-healing, and radiographic sequestrum (necrotic, devascularized bone fragment) with or without involucrum (new reactive bone shell forming around it). Chronic osteomyelitis generally requires surgical debridement in addition to prolonged antimicrobial therapy, unlike early acute disease which may respond to antibiotics alone.
chronic_presentation.source: Lew DP, Waldvogel FA, Lancet, 2004 (PMID: 15276398); Hatzenbuehler J, Pulling TJ, Diagnosis and management of osteomyelitis, Am Fam Physician, 2011 (PMID: 22046943)

diabetic_foot_presentation.finding: In diabetic foot osteomyelitis, classic systemic signs (fever, marked pain) are frequently blunted or absent because of peripheral neuropathy, so the clinical clue is often a non-healing ulcer that fails to close over several weeks, an ulcer overlying a bony prominence, or a positive probe-to-bone test, rather than pain or fever.
diabetic_foot_presentation.source: Lipsky BA et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2012 (PMID: 22619242); Grayson ML et al, JAMA, 1995 (PMID: 7853630)

cellulitis.finding: Cellulitis produces diffuse skin/soft-tissue erythema, warmth, and edema without deep bone involvement, whereas osteomyelitis involves the bone itself; MRI is the key discriminator because it can directly visualize marrow signal change (osteomyelitis) versus soft-tissue-only inflammation (cellulitis), with pooled MRI sensitivity 95.6% / specificity 80.7% for osteomyelitis.
cellulitis.source: Llewellyn A et al, Health Technol Assess, 2019 (PMID: 31670644)

septic_arthritis.finding: Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis frequently coexist, especially in young children where the metaphysis is intracapsular for certain joints (e.g., hip, shoulder), allowing direct spread. In a pediatric cohort of 168 septic arthritis patients, 108 (64.3%) had concurrent acute osteomyelitis, underscoring that adjacent-joint infection must always be actively screened for (and vice versa) rather than assumed to be a single-site process.
septic_arthritis.source: Branson J et al, The Contemporary Microbiology and Rates of Concomitant Osteomyelitis in Acute Septic Arthritis, Pediatr Infect Dis J, 2017 (PMID: 27870814)

charcot_neuroarthropathy.finding: In diabetic patients, distinguishing Charcot neuroarthropathy from osteomyelitis is a well-recognized diagnostic challenge because both cause bone marrow edema on MRI and periarticular changes in the same at-risk (neuropathic) foot. In a prospective study of 63 subjects using FDG-PET with quantified standardized uptake values (SUVmax), Charcot joints measured 1.3 +/- 0.4, osteomyelitis measured 4.38 +/- 1.39, and normal controls measured 0.42 +/- 0.12; FDG-PET achieved 100% sensitivity and 93.8% accuracy for correctly identifying Charcot neuroarthropathy (i.e., excluding osteomyelitis), versus 76.9% sensitivity and 75% accuracy for MRI in the same discrimination task. Anatomic distribution is also a clinical clue: Charcot neuroarthropathy classically affects the midfoot/tarsometatarsal joints in a symmetric, multi-joint pattern, while osteomyelitis is typically localized beneath an ulcer or bony prominence.
charcot_neuroarthropathy.source: Basu S et al, Potential role of FDG PET in the setting of diabetic neuro-osteoarthropathy, Nucl Med Commun, 2007 (PMID: 17460537); Short DJ, Zgonis T, Medical Imaging in Differentiating the Diabetic Charcot Foot from Osteomyelitis, Clin Podiatr Med Surg, 2017 (PMID: 27865318)
charcot_neuroarthropathy.confidence: high for the FDG-PET numeric data (single study, n=63, not independently replicated this session); high for the general diagnostic-challenge and distribution pattern

diabetes_mellitus.finding: Diabetes mellitus is the leading risk factor driving the rising incidence of osteomyelitis. In the 40-year Olmsted County population cohort, diabetes-associated osteomyelitis incidence nearly tripled, rising from 2.3 to 7.6 per 100,000 person-years, and this diabetes-driven rise (concentrated in older adults) was the principal driver of the overall increase in osteomyelitis incidence over the study period. Among diabetic foot ulcer/infection cohorts, coexisting osteomyelitis has been directly documented in 13% of 100 diabetic foot infection presentations in one series and in 16.6% (17/102) of diabetic foot ulcer patients in another.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Kremers HM et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2015 (PMID: 25995495); Aziz Z et al, Predictive factors for lower extremity amputations in diabetic foot infections, Diabet Foot Ankle, 2011 (PMID: 22396824); Zubair M et al, Clinico-microbiological study...of diabetic foot infections in North India, Foot (Edinb), 2011 (PMID: 21130641)

peripheral_arterial_disease.finding: Peripheral arterial disease/vascular insufficiency is one of the three principal mechanistic categories of osteomyelitis (alongside hematogenous and contiguous-focus disease) because impaired perfusion both predisposes to non-healing ulceration that becomes contiguously infected and impairs antibiotic delivery and wound healing once infection is established.
peripheral_arterial_disease.source: Lew DP, Waldvogel FA, Lancet, 2004 (PMID: 15276398); Hatzenbuehler J, Pulling TJ, Am Fam Physician, 2011 (PMID: 22046943)

intravenous_drug_use.finding: Injection drug use is a well-established risk factor for hematogenous vertebral osteomyelitis and spinal infection. In a cohort of 324 consecutive spinal epidural abscess patients, 98 (30.2%) had a history of recent intravenous drug use. Nationally, the proportion of serious invasive bacterial infection hospitalizations attributable to drug use rose from 1.5% in 2010 to 13.1% in 2018 in a US surveillance analysis of over 44,000 hospitalizations, reflecting the broader opioid-era rise in drug-use-associated invasive infection including vertebral osteomyelitis/spinal epidural abscess.
intravenous_drug_use.source: Baum J et al, Predictive factors for treatment failure in spinal epidural abscess associated with injection drug use, J Neurosurg Spine, 2021 (PMID: 34740181); Sredl M et al, Trends in Serious Bacterial Infections Among Drug Users, J Infect Dis, 2020 (PMID: 32877536)

other_host_factors.finding: Additional documented risk factors include prosthetic orthopedic hardware/implants, prior orthopedic surgery, open fractures, chronic immunosuppression (including systemic lupus erythematosus, where poor prognostic factors for osteomyelitis include delayed diagnosis, vertebral involvement, and implanted hardware), sickle cell disease (predisposing to Salmonella osteomyelitis), and increasing age; the increasing prevalence of these predisposing conditions has been cited as a driver of rising chronic osteomyelitis incidence.
other_host_factors.source: Wu KC et al, Osteomyelitis in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, J Rheumatol, 2004 (PMID: 15229953); Hatzenbuehler J, Pulling TJ, Am Fam Physician, 2011 (PMID: 22046943)

overall_incidence_and_trend.finding: In a 40-year US population-based study (Olmsted County, Minnesota, 1969-2009; 760 confirmed cases), the age- and sex-adjusted overall incidence of osteomyelitis was 21.8 per 100,000 person-years, and this incidence more than doubled over the study period, rising from 11.4 per 100,000 person-years in 1969-1979 to 24.4 per 100,000 person-years in 2000-2009. Staphylococcus aureus was identified in 44% of culture-positive cases.
overall_incidence_and_trend.source: Kremers HM et al, Trends in the epidemiology of osteomyelitis: a population-based study 1969-2009, J Bone Joint Surg Am, 2015 (PMID: 25995495)

diabetic_foot_subpopulation.finding: Among patients presenting with diabetic foot infection/ulceration, the reported prevalence of coexisting osteomyelitis ranges from about 13% to 16.6% across two independent single-center diabetic foot cohorts (n=100 and n=102 respectively), indicating osteomyelitis is a common but not universal complication of infected diabetic foot ulcers.
diabetic_foot_subpopulation.source: Aziz Z et al, Diabet Foot Ankle, 2011 (PMID: 22396824); Zubair M et al, Foot (Edinb), 2011 (PMID: 21130641)
diabetic_foot_subpopulation.confidence: moderate -- two single-center cohorts, not a pooled multi-study prevalence estimate

pediatric_pattern.finding: In children, acute hematogenous osteomyelitis shows a male predominance and Staphylococcus aureus as the dominant pathogen (89% of isolates, 84/94, in one pediatric cohort), with Kingella kingae increasingly recognized in young children and methicillin-resistant S. aureus an increasing concern.
pediatric_pattern.source: Popescu B et al, J Int Med Res, 2020 (PMID: 32249643); Gornitzky AL et al, JBJS Rev, 2020 (PMID: 33006465)

relapse_and_recurrence_rates.finding: Chronic osteomyelitis carries a real, quantified relapse risk even after combined surgical and antimicrobial treatment. In a systematic review of 206 chronic osteomyelitis patients treated with dead-space management (bioactive glass), the overall cure rate was 86% with an 11.6% (24/206) recurrence rate. In a cohort of 61 adults with pelvic osteomyelitis treated surgically with multidisciplinary care, recurrent infection occurred in 11.5% (7/61) at a mean of 1.5 years post-operatively, though after further treatment 95.1% were ultimately infection-free at a mean final follow-up of 4.6 years. In complex calcaneal osteomyelitis (28 patients), the recurrence rate was 18% (5 patients) over a mean 31-month follow-up, with 7% eventually requiring below-knee amputation. In a lower-resource sub-Saharan cohort of 86 chronic osteomyelitis patients treated with sequestrectomy and antibiotics, recurrence was 5.8% at 1-year follow-up. These figures show relapse risk is real and non-trivial (roughly 6-18% depending on anatomic site, host factors, and surgical technique) even with appropriate combined surgical/antibiotic treatment, and that eventual cure requires sustained follow-up (recurrences can present more than a year after treatment).
relapse_and_recurrence_rates.source: Tanwar YS, Ferreira N, The role of bioactive glass in the management of chronic osteomyelitis: a systematic review, Infect Dis (Lond), 2020 (PMID: 31774017); Dudareva M et al, Osteomyelitis of the Pelvic Bones: A Multidisciplinary Approach to Treatment, J Bone Jt Infect, 2017 (PMID: 29119077); Kendal A et al, Long-Term Follow-up of Complex Calcaneal Osteomyelitis, Foot Ankle Orthop, 2022 (PMID: 36329689); Ouedraogo S et al, Epidemiological, bacteriological and therapeutic aspects of chronic osteomyelitis in a sub-Saharan environment, Med Sante Trop, 2017 (PMID: 28947406)
relapse_and_recurrence_rates.confidence: high -- multiple independent cohorts, consistent qualitative conclusion; recurrence rate varies by site/study (5.8%-18%) so a single pooled number cannot be stated

progression_to_chronicity_with_delay.finding: In a retrospective cohort of 94 pediatric acute hematogenous osteomyelitis patients, disease evolution toward chronicity was specifically observed in patients diagnosed late; poor-outcome characteristics included delayed diagnosis and delayed surgery, alongside repeated negative cultures and rural residence with limited emergency-care access. This is a direct, real clinical-cohort demonstration that time-to-diagnosis/treatment is a determinant of whether acute osteomyelitis resolves versus progresses to chronic disease.
progression_to_chronicity_with_delay.source: Popescu B et al, Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in pediatric patients: epidemiology and risk factors of a poor outcome, J Int Med Res, 2020 (PMID: 32249643)
progression_to_chronicity_with_delay.confidence: high for the qualitative finding; the study did not report a quantitative delay-to-chronicity threshold (e.g. an exact number of days), and that specific number could not be verified this session

clinical_takeaway.finding: Osteomyelitis diagnosis rests on three pillars used together, not alone: (1) MRI, the best-performing single imaging test (pooled sensitivity 95.6%/specificity 80.7%), (2) bone culture, the microbiologic reference standard (94% pathogen identification in chronic disease, versus only 30% concordance -- kappa <0 -- with superficial swab cultures, which should not be used to guide therapy), and (3) inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), useful for screening and monitoring treatment response but not accurate enough alone (ESR pooled sensitivity/specificity 81%/90% for diabetic foot osteomyelitis) to diagnose or exclude disease. In diabetic feet, a positive probe-to-bone test (PPV 89%) is a fast, cheap bedside clue that should trigger imaging/biopsy, and Charcot neuroarthropathy is the key mimic that FDG-PET (100% sensitivity, 93.8% accuracy) distinguishes better than MRI (76.9% sensitivity, 75% accuracy) when the distinction is unclear. The single highest-stakes clinical message is that acute osteomyelitis diagnosed and treated early can often be cured with antibiotics alone, whereas delayed diagnosis is directly associated with progression to chronic osteomyelitis, which then requires surgical debridement plus prolonged antibiotics and still carries a real relapse risk of roughly 6-18% even after adequate combined treatment.
clinical_takeaway.source: Llewellyn A et al, Health Technol Assess, 2019 (PMID: 31670644); Zuluaga AF et al, Arch Intern Med, 2006 (PMID: 16401816); van Asten SA et al, Curr Diabetes Rev, 2016 (PMID: 26166314); Grayson ML et al, JAMA, 1995 (PMID: 7853630); Basu S et al, Nucl Med Commun, 2007 (PMID: 17460537); Popescu B et al, J Int Med Res, 2020 (PMID: 32249643); Lew DP, Waldvogel FA, Lancet, 2004 (PMID: 15276398)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: DELAYED DIAGNOSIS/TREATMENT OF OSTEOMYELITIS IS A DIRECT DRIVER OF PROGRESSION TO CHRONIC, HARDER-TO-CURE BONE DESTRUCTION -- PROMPT WORKUP AND TREATMENT INITIATION IS NON-NEGOTIABLE. In a real pediatric cohort (94 patients with acute hematogenous osteomyelitis), disease evolution toward chronicity occurred specifically in patients diagnosed late, and delayed diagnosis plus delayed surgery were independently identified poor-outcome characteristics. Once osteomyelitis becomes chronic, it acquires a fundamentally worse natural history: it develops sequestrum (necrotic dead bone) and sinus tracts, generally requires surgical debridement in addition to prolonged antimicrobial therapy (rather than antibiotics alone, which can suffice in early acute disease), and still carries a real relapse risk of roughly 6-18% (5.8% to 18% across independently published surgical cohorts) even after adequate combined surgical and antibiotic treatment, sometimes recurring more than a year after apparent cure. Any patient with suspected osteomyelitis -- localized bone pain plus fever/warmth/swelling in a child, or a diabetic foot ulcer that fails to heal, probes to bone, or overlies a bony prominence -- should be triaged for prompt bone imaging (MRI first-line) and bone culture/biopsy (not a superficial wound swab, which agrees with true bone culture no better than chance, kappa <0) without diagnostic delay, because early antibiotic-only cure of acute disease is only possible before the bone necrosis/sequestrum of chronic osteomyelitis has had time to form.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Popescu B et al, Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in pediatric patients: epidemiology and risk factors of a poor outcome, J Int Med Res, 2020 (PMID: 32249643); Lew DP, Waldvogel FA, Osteomyelitis, Lancet, 2004 (PMID: 15276398); Zuluaga AF et al, Arch Intern Med, 2006 (PMID: 16401816); Tanwar YS, Ferreira N, Infect Dis (Lond), 2020 (PMID: 31774017); Dudareva M et al, J Bone Jt Infect, 2017 (PMID: 29119077); Kendal A et al, Foot Ankle Orthop, 2022 (PMID: 36329689); Ouedraogo S et al, Med Sante Trop, 2017 (PMID: 28947406); Hatzenbuehler J, Pulling TJ, Am Fam Physician, 2011 (PMID: 22046943)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the qualitative delay-to-chronicity mechanism (direct real-cohort evidence) and the recurrence-rate range (multiple independent cohorts); no single study quantifies an exact time-to-diagnosis threshold (e.g. days) above which chronicity risk rises, and that specific number is not stated because it could not be verified this session

spondylolisthesis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Spondylolisthesis (anterior slippage of one vertebral body over the one below it, graded by the Meyerding system from I to V by percentage of slip) is NOT one disease with one prognosis - it is two real, distinct clinical entities, each with its own real evidence-based path to a good outcome, and the right approach depends on grade, type (isthmic/pars-defect, typically young patients, vs degenerative/facet-arthropathic, typically older adults) and symptom severity. REAL GOOD NEWS FIRST, LOW-GRADE ISTHMIC DISEASE IN THE YOUNG: low-grade (Meyerding I-II) isthmic spondylolisthesis, the most common presentation in adolescents/young adults, responds very well to real conservative management. A classic prospective series of 67 symptomatic adolescents (mean age 16) treated with a modified Boston brace (antilordotic thoracolumbosacral orthosis) plus activity modification achieved 78% excellent/good outcomes (pain-free, full return to activity), and only 9% eventually required fusion surgery - meaning 91% of braced patients avoided surgery altogether (Steiner ME, Micheli LJ, 'Treatment of symptomatic spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis with the modified Boston brace', Spine 1985;10:937-943, PMID 3914087). Dedicated core-stabilization/motor-control exercise therapy (targeting deep transversus abdominis and lumbar multifidus co-contraction) also produces a real, RCT-confirmed benefit: in 44 patients with chronic low back pain and a radiologically confirmed pars defect or spondylolisthesis, the specific stabilizing exercise group had a statistically significant reduction in pain and disability that was maintained at 30-month follow-up, while a matched group given standard practitioner-directed therapy showed no significant change at all (O'Sullivan PB, Twomey LT, Allison GT et al, 'Evaluation of specific stabilizing exercise in the treatment of chronic low back pain with radiologic diagnosis of spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis', Spine 1997;22:2959-2967, PMID 9431633). REAL STRONG SURGICAL EVIDENCE FOR DEGENERATIVE DISEASE WITH STENOSIS: for degenerative spondylolisthesis with spinal stenosis in older adults (facet-joint arthropathy rather than a pars defect, the dominant form after age 50) who remain symptomatic despite an adequate conservative trial, the landmark multicenter SPORT randomized-plus-observational trial (607 patients enrolled across both cohorts) found surgical decompressive laminectomy (with or without fusion) produced real, substantially and durably greater improvement than nonoperative care, sustained through 4 years of as-treated follow-up: SF-36 bodily pain +15.3 points (95% CI 11.0-19.7) more than nonoperative care, physical function +18.9 points (95% CI 14.8-23.0) more, and Oswestry Disability Index -14.3 points (95% CI -17.5 to -11.1) more favorable, all favoring surgery (Weinstein JN et al, 'Surgical compared with nonoperative treatment for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis', J Bone Joint Surg Am 2009;91:1295-1304, PMID 19487505; 2-year randomized-cohort results in Weinstein JN et al, N Engl J Med 2007;356:2257-2270, PMID 17538085). Adding instrumented fusion to decompression further reduces the real risk of a second operation: a dedicated RCT of 66 patients (age 50-80) with single-level degenerative spondylolisthesis and stenosis found 4-year reoperation rates of 14% with instrumented fusion versus 34% with decompression alone (i.e. 86% vs 66% remained reoperation-free), with SF-36 scores favoring fusion, though the 4-year ODI difference was not significant, and an independent published commentary on the same trial disputed the clinical significance of some between-group differences given the small sample size (Ghogawala Z, Dziura J, Butler WE et al, 'Laminectomy plus fusion versus laminectomy alone for lumbar spondylolisthesis', N Engl J Med 2016;374:1424-1434, PMID 27843677). REFRACTORY ADULT ISTHMIC DISEASE: in adult isthmic spondylolisthesis that has failed conservative care, a dedicated RCT of 111 patients randomized to posterolateral fusion (n=77, with or without transpedicular fixation) versus a structured exercise program (n=34) found fusion produced significantly greater improvement in the Disability Rating Index and pain scores at both 1 and 2 years (P<0.0001 for disability, P<0.01 for the between-group functional comparison), while the exercise-only group's disability index did not improve at all (Moller H, Hedlund R, 'Surgery versus conservative management in adult isthmic spondylolisthesis - a prospective randomized study: part 1', Spine 2000;25:1711-1715, PMID 10870148).
