BOTTOM LINE - lead with the real strongest evidence: most low-grade adolescent isthmic spondylolisthesis is a genuine conservative-management success story (78% excellent/good with bracing, 91% avoid surgery entirely), and for older patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis and stenosis who need surgery, decompression with or without instrumented fusion gives a real, large, durable improvement over continued nonoperative care per the SPORT trial, with instrumented fusion cutting the real reoperation risk roughly in half versus decompression alone.

curative_option.name: Grade- and Type-Stratified Management: Bracing + Activity Modification/Core-Stabilization Exercise for Low-Grade Adolescent Isthmic Spondylolisthesis (Real First-Line, High Success), Escalating to Decompression +/- Instrumented Fusion for Degenerative Spondylolisthesis With Stenosis, or Posterolateral Fusion for Refractory Adult Isthmic Disease
curative_option.type: Conservative bracing (modified Boston brace) and core-stabilization exercise therapy, real first-line for low-grade isthmic disease in adolescents/young adults; surgical decompressive laminectomy with or without instrumented posterolateral/interbody fusion, for degenerative spondylolisthesis with spinal stenosis or refractory adult isthmic spondylolisthesis
curative_option.note: There is no medicine that cures the structural vertebral slip itself - spondylolisthesis is a mechanical/anatomic diagnosis, not a drug-responsive disease process, so oral analgesics/NSAIDs are symptomatic-only (see exhaustive_medicine_survey) and are NOT the real first-line intervention here. The real first-line, highest-evidence intervention for the most common presentation (low-grade isthmic disease in the young) is a non-drug, non-surgical physical intervention - bracing and/or specific stabilizing exercise - which genuinely resolves symptoms and prevents progression to surgery in the large majority of patients. For older patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis and stenosis, or for adults with isthmic disease refractory to conservative care, surgery (decompression +/- fusion) is the real, trial-proven definitive step, analogous in evidentiary strength to the SPORT-trial data used for herniated disc and lumbar stenosis in this knowledge base.

real_trial_data.steiner_micheli_1985_bracing: Prospective series, 67 symptomatic adolescents (mean age 16.0 years) with spondylolysis or grade I spondylolisthesis treated with a modified Boston brace (antilordotic TLSO) for a mean follow-up of 2.5 years: 78% (52/67) achieved excellent/good results (pain-free, full return to activity), 13% (9/67) had residual mild symptoms, and only 9% (6/67) subsequently required fusion surgery - i.e. 91% avoided surgery; 12 patients showed radiographic evidence of pars-defect healing - Steiner ME, Micheli LJ, Spine 1985;10:937-943, PMID 3914087
real_trial_data.osullivan_1997_specific_stabilizing_exer: RCT, 44 patients with chronic low back pain and a radiologically confirmed pars defect or spondylolisthesis, randomized to a 10-week specific stabilizing exercise program (deep transversus abdominis/lumbar multifidus co-contraction training integrated into functional tasks) vs standard practitioner-directed therapy: the specific-exercise group had a statistically significant reduction in pain intensity and functional disability that was maintained at 3, 6 and 30-month follow-up, while the control group showed no significant change at any time point - O'Sullivan PB, Twomey LT, Allison GT, Spine 1997;22:2959-2967, PMID 9431633
real_trial_data.moller_hedlund_2000_fusion_vs_exercise_a: RCT, 111 adult patients with isthmic spondylolisthesis, randomized to posterolateral fusion with or without transpedicular fixation (n=77) vs a structured exercise program (n=34), 93% follow-up at 2 years: the surgical group had significant improvement in the Disability Rating Index and pain (VAS) at both 1 and 2 years (P<0.0001), while in the exercise group the Disability Rating Index did not change at all and pain decreased only slightly (P<0.02); overall functional outcome was significantly better with surgery at both 1- and 2-year assessments (P<0.01) - Moller H, Hedlund R, Spine 2000;25:1711-1715, PMID 10870148
real_trial_data.sport_2yr_randomized_2007: SPORT randomized cohort, 304 patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis: as-treated analysis combining randomized and observational cohorts (607 patients) at 2 years showed surgery (decompressive laminectomy +/- fusion) improved SF-36 bodily pain by 18.1 points more (95% CI 14.5-21.7), physical function by 18.3 points more (95% CI 14.6-21.9), and Oswestry Disability Index by -16.7 points more (95% CI -19.5 to -13.9) than nonoperative care; the strict intention-to-treat analysis of the randomized cohort alone was not significant due to substantial (~40% each way) treatment crossover - Weinstein JN et al, N Engl J Med 2007;356:2257-2270, PMID 17538085
real_trial_data.sport_4yr_astreated_2009: SPORT as-treated analysis extended to 4 years (randomized cohort 304 + observational cohort 303; 66% of randomized-to-surgery patients and 54% of randomized-to-nonoperative patients had received surgery by 4 years): the clinically relevant advantages of surgery reported at 2 years were maintained at 4 years - bodily pain +15.3 points (95% CI 11.0-19.7), physical function +18.9 points (95% CI 14.8-23.0), Oswestry Disability Index -14.3 points (95% CI -17.5 to -11.1), all favoring surgery - Weinstein JN et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2009;91:1295-1304, PMID 19487505
real_trial_data.ghogawala_2016_fusion_plus_decompression: RCT, 66 patients (age 50-80) with single-level degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis, randomized to instrumented posterolateral fusion plus decompression vs decompression alone: at 4 years, reoperation occurred in 14% of the fusion group vs 34% of the decompression-alone group (i.e. 86% vs 66% remained reoperation-free); SF-36 physical-component scores favored fusion at 2 and 4 years, but the 4-year Oswestry Disability Index difference was not statistically significant; a published commentary on this trial noted the small sample size and disputed the clinical significance of some between-group differences - Ghogawala Z, Dziura J, Butler WE et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:1424-1434, PMID 27843677

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Genuinely curative-in-effect (full symptom resolution, return to normal activity, surgery avoided) for the real majority of the most common presentation: low-grade isthmic spondylolisthesis in adolescents/young adults treated with bracing and/or specific stabilizing exercise resolves symptoms without surgery in the large majority (Steiner & Micheli 1985: 91% avoided surgery; O'Sullivan 1997: durable benefit to 30 months). For degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis and for adult isthmic disease refractory to conservative care, surgery does not reverse the underlying vertebral slip or facet arthropathy, but decompression (+/- instrumented fusion) removes the compressive/mechanical cause of pain and produces real, large, durable functional gains that are sustained for at least 4 years per the SPORT and Ghogawala trials - this is the real closest-to-cure option once conservative management has failed in this population, analogous to fusion/decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis elsewhere in this knowledge base.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic low-grade spondylolisthesis found incidentally on imaging generally does not need bracing, exercise, or surgery - these trials enrolled symptomatic patients. Patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis and stenosis who have not yet had an adequate trial of nonoperative care (activity modification, physical therapy, epidural steroid injection where indicated) should not be rushed to surgery, since SPORT's own nonoperative arm also improved over time, just to a real, smaller and less durable degree than the surgical arm.
curative_option.source: Steiner ME, Micheli LJ, Spine 1985 (PMID 3914087); O'Sullivan PB et al, Spine 1997 (PMID 9431633); Moller H, Hedlund R, Spine 2000 (PMID 10870148); Weinstein JN et al, N Engl J Med 2007 (PMID 17538085); Weinstein JN et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2009 (PMID 19487505); Ghogawala Z et al, N Engl J Med 2016 (PMID 27843677)
curative_option.confidence: high - all PMIDs directly verified via PubMed/NCBI eutils this session, including abstract-quoted numeric results; ICD-11 code not independently verified (WHO API requires OAuth2 not available this session)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for spondylolisthesis: bracing and core-stabilization exercise for low-grade isthmic disease, symptomatic NSAID/analgesic use, epidural corticosteroid injection for radicular pain, and surgical fusion/decompression for adult isthmic and degenerative disease. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review, cross-checked against PubMed/NCBI eutils and Europe PMC this session; where a clean responder/success percentage was not reported in the abstract, the real point-estimate or significance data is given instead and the entry is excluded from the ranked percentage table below rather than assigning a fabricated number. Symptoms and diagnostic criteria are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry for spondylolisthesis and are not duplicated here.

spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.name: Modified Boston Brace (Antilordotic TLSO) for Symptomatic Low-Grade Isthmic Spondylolisthesis - Real First-Line, High-Success Non-Surgical Option
specific_drugs: Not a drug - custom-molded modified Boston brace, antilordotic thoracolumbosacral orthosis worn full-time then weaned over weeks to months
spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.effectiveness: 78% excellent/good outcome (pain-free, full return to activity) and 91% avoided fusion surgery altogether, at a mean 2.5-year follow-up in 67 symptomatic adolescents (mean age 16) with spondylolysis or grade I spondylolisthesis
spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.reason_why: The antilordotic brace reduces lumbar lordosis and restricts flexion-extension motion across the pars interarticularis defect and slipped segment, reducing the repetitive mechanical stress that drives pain and, in a subset of patients, allows radiographic healing of the pars defect itself (seen in 12 of the 67 patients in the founding series).
spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.important_caveat: Evidence base is a single-arm prospective series without a randomized no-brace control group; brace effectiveness for higher-grade (III-V) slips or for degenerative (as opposed to isthmic) spondylolisthesis has not been separately established by this study.
spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.real_working_solution: For a symptomatic adolescent/young adult with a low-grade isthmic spondylolisthesis, a real, high-success first step is a period of antilordotic bracing plus activity modification before any consideration of surgery.
spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.source: Steiner ME, Micheli LJ, Spine 1985;10:937-943, PMID 3914087
spl_adolescent_bracing_boston_brace.confidence: high - PMID verified via PubMed eutils this session

spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.name: Specific Stabilizing (Core/Motor-Control) Exercise Therapy - Real RCT-Confirmed Durable Benefit for Spondylolysis/Spondylolisthesis-Related Low Back Pain
specific_drugs: Not a drug - supervised deep transversus abdominis and lumbar multifidus co-contraction ('specific stabilizing exercise') training integrated into functional movements, 10-week program
spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.effectiveness: Statistically significant reduction in pain intensity and functional disability, maintained at 30-month follow-up, versus no significant change in a matched group given standard practitioner-directed therapy (n=44 total, chronic low back pain with radiologically confirmed pars defect or spondylolisthesis); exact VAS/disability percentage values were not given in the abstract, only significance data, so this entry is not placed in the ranked percentage table below.
spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.reason_why: Deep segmental stabilizer training (transversus abdominis, lumbar multifidus) improves dynamic control of the unstable/deficient segment at the pars defect or slipped level, reducing the abnormal shear loading that provokes pain, independent of correcting the anatomic slip itself.
spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.important_caveat: Small trial (n=44); the specific-exercise protocol requires supervised, individualized coaching rather than generic back-strengthening exercises, and the trial did not report a slip-progression or surgery-avoidance rate.
spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.real_working_solution: A supervised, specific (not generic) core-stabilization exercise program is a real, evidence-backed non-drug option, complementary to bracing, for chronic pain in confirmed spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis.
spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.source: O'Sullivan PB, Twomey LT, Allison GT, Spine 1997;22:2959-2967, PMID 9431633
spl_core_stabilization_exercise_therapy.confidence: high - PMID verified via PubMed eutils this session

spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.name: Oral NSAIDs for Symptomatic Pain Relief - Real But Non-Disease-Modifying
spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.effectiveness: Cochrane systematic review of 65 RCTs (11,237 patients) with nonspecific low back pain (not spondylolisthesis-specific): statistically significant benefit for NSAIDs versus placebo, but effect sizes were described by the review authors as small, and NSAIDs were no more effective than paracetamol for acute pain while causing more side effects
spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.reason_why: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory pain sensitization around the affected facet joints, pars defect, or associated soft tissue, providing symptomatic relief without altering the underlying vertebral slip, instability, or nerve-root compression.
spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.important_caveat: This evidence is for nonspecific low back pain generally, not a spondylolisthesis-specific trial; NSAIDs do NOT prevent slip progression, do not heal a pars defect, and do not substitute for bracing/exercise in the young or for decompression in stenotic degenerative disease - they are an adjunct for symptom control only.
spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.real_working_solution: Short-course NSAIDs are a reasonable real adjunct for pain flares alongside bracing, exercise therapy, or peri-operative care, but should not be relied upon as the primary treatment.
spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.source: Roelofs PA et al, Spine 2008;33:1766-1774, PMID 18580547
spl_nsaids_symptomatic_analgesia.confidence: moderate - PMID verified this session, but evidence is for nonspecific low back pain, not spondylolisthesis-specific

spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.name: Epidural Corticosteroid Injection for Radicular Leg Pain - Real Modest Short-Term Benefit
specific_drugs: Epidural injection of a corticosteroid (e.g. triamcinolone, methylprednisolone, or dexamethasone) with or without local anesthetic
spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.effectiveness: Cochrane review, 25 trials, 2,470 patients with lumbosacral radicular pain (spinal stenosis/spondylolisthesis-related nerve-root compression being among the causes covered): epidural corticosteroid injection reduced short-term leg pain by a mean difference of -4.93 points/100 (95% CI -8.77 to -1.09) and disability by -4.18 points/100 (95% CI -6.04 to -2.17) versus placebo, described by the review authors as a real but small effect
spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.reason_why: Injected corticosteroid locally suppresses inflammation and neurogenic sensitization around a compressed or irritated nerve root at the level of the slip/stenosis, giving temporary pain relief without changing the underlying vertebral alignment or canal dimensions.
spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.important_caveat: This review pools multiple causes of lumbosacral radicular pain, not spondylolisthesis alone; benefit is short-term and modest, and injections do not reduce the eventual need for decompressive surgery in patients who are genuinely failing conservative care.
spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.real_working_solution: A real, reasonable bridging option for radicular leg pain from spondylolisthesis-related nerve-root compression while pursuing bracing/exercise (young, isthmic) or as a trial before committing to surgery (older, degenerative with stenosis).
spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.source: Oliveira CB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020, PMID 32271952
spl_epidural_steroid_injection_radicular.confidence: moderate - PMID verified this session in the herniated-disc entry of this same knowledge base; not spondylolisthesis-specific

spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.name: Posterolateral Spinal Fusion for Adult Isthmic Spondylolisthesis - Real Superior Outcome vs Exercise Alone
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.specific_procedure: Posterolateral lumbar fusion, with or without transpedicular (pedicle screw) instrumentation, at the level of the isthmic slip
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.effectiveness: RCT, 111 adult patients with isthmic spondylolisthesis, fusion (n=77) vs structured exercise program (n=34): fusion produced significantly greater improvement in the Disability Rating Index and pain (VAS) at both 1 and 2 years (P<0.0001), while the exercise group's disability index did not improve at all; overall functional outcome significantly favored surgery at both time points (P<0.01); 93% follow-up at 2 years. Exact responder/success percentage not reported in the abstract, so this entry is described here rather than assigned a table percentage.
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.reason_why: Fusion eliminates motion and abnormal shear loading across the unstable/slipped isthmic segment, removing the mechanical driver of pain that an exercise program alone cannot correct once conservative treatment has already failed to control symptoms.
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.important_caveat: This trial enrolled adults who had already failed an initial period of conservative care; it does not show fusion is superior to a first trial of bracing/exercise, only that fusion outperforms ongoing exercise therapy in patients selected for randomization to surgery.
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.real_working_solution: For adult isthmic spondylolisthesis with persistent symptoms despite an adequate conservative trial, fusion is a real, significantly more effective option than continued exercise therapy alone.
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.source: Moller H, Hedlund R, Spine 2000;25:1711-1715, PMID 10870148
spl_posterolateral_fusion_adult_isthmic.confidence: high - PMID verified via PubMed eutils this session

spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.name: Decompressive Laminectomy (+/- Fusion) for Degenerative Spondylolisthesis With Spinal Stenosis - Real SPORT-Trial Superiority to Nonoperative Care
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.specific_procedure: Standard decompressive laminectomy, with or without instrumented fusion, for degenerative spondylolisthesis with associated spinal stenosis
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.effectiveness: SPORT trial as-treated analysis (607 patients across randomized + observational cohorts) at 4 years: surgery improved SF-36 bodily pain by 15.3 points more (95% CI 11.0-19.7), physical function by 18.9 points more (95% CI 14.8-23.0), and Oswestry Disability Index by 14.3 points more (95% CI 11.1-17.5) than nonoperative care, all statistically significant and sustained from the 2-year results
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.reason_why: Laminectomy directly enlarges the stenotic spinal canal/neural foramina narrowed by the degenerative slip and facet hypertrophy, relieving mechanical nerve-root and cauda equina compression that nonoperative care cannot reverse.
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.important_caveat: Substantial treatment crossover in the randomized cohort (~40-54% each way by 4 years) means the intention-to-treat analysis alone was not statistically significant; the as-treated numbers above better reflect real per-protocol effect but carry some confounding-by-indication risk.
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.real_working_solution: For degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis that remains symptomatic despite an adequate nonoperative trial, decompressive surgery gives a real, large, durable functional improvement, comparable in strength of evidence to SPORT-trial data used elsewhere in this knowledge base for disc herniation and spinal stenosis.
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.source: Weinstein JN et al, N Engl J Med 2007;356:2257-2270, PMID 17538085; Weinstein JN et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2009;91:1295-1304, PMID 19487505
spl_decompression_nonoperative_degenerat.confidence: high - both PMIDs verified via PubMed/Europe PMC this session

spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.name: Instrumented Fusion Added to Decompression vs Decompression Alone - Real Reoperation-Rate Reduction
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.specific_procedure: Instrumented posterolateral fusion plus decompressive laminectomy, compared head-to-head with decompression (laminectomy) alone
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.effectiveness: RCT, 66 patients (age 50-80) with single-level degenerative spondylolisthesis and stenosis: 4-year reoperation rate 14% with fusion vs 34% with decompression alone (86% vs 66% remained reoperation-free); SF-36 scores favored fusion at 2 and 4 years, though the 4-year ODI difference was not statistically significant
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.reason_why: Instrumented fusion stabilizes the operated segment against further slippage or adjacent instability created by removing bone during decompression, reducing the mechanical driver of recurrent symptoms that leads to reoperation after decompression alone.
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.important_caveat: Small trial (n=66); a published commentary on this same study disputed the clinical significance of some between-group differences given the sample size, and fusion carries real added surgical time, blood loss and cost versus decompression alone - this is a genuinely debated tradeoff in spine surgery, not a settled unanimous verdict.
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.real_working_solution: Adding instrumented fusion to decompression is a real, evidence-supported way to reduce the reoperation risk in degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis, though the magnitude of overall functional benefit beyond decompression alone remains genuinely debated in the literature.
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.source: Ghogawala Z et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:1424-1434, PMID 27843677
spl_decompression_plus_fusion_vs_decompr.confidence: high - PMID verified via PubMed/Europe PMC this session

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT study designs, populations and endpoints (adolescent bracing symptom/surgery-avoidance outcomes vs adult reoperation-free rates after fusion vs decompression) - ranking them together is directionally useful (conservative bracing for low-grade isthmic disease and surgical fusion for degenerative disease with stenosis both achieve real high success on their own respective endpoints) but is NOT a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Specific stabilizing exercise (O'Sullivan 1997), posterolateral fusion vs exercise (Moller & Hedlund 2000), NSAIDs, epidural steroid injection, and the SPORT-trial decompression-vs-nonoperative point-difference results are excluded from the ranked list below because their source abstracts report significance levels or point-estimate differences rather than responder/success percentages, not because they lack real evidence (see exhaustive_medicine_survey and curative_option for their real numbers).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Adolescent Bracing - Surgery Avoidance
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of braced symptomatic adolescents who avoided fusion surgery (only 9% required later fusion), mean 2.5-year follow-up, n=67
ranked_high_to_low.source: Steiner ME, Micheli LJ, Spine 1985, PMID 3914087

ranked_high_to_low.name: Instrumented Fusion + Decompression - Reoperation-Free Rate
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion reoperation-free at 4 years (14% required reoperation)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ghogawala Z et al, N Engl J Med 2016, PMID 27843677

ranked_high_to_low.name: Adolescent Bracing - Excellent/Good Symptom Outcome
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Excellent/good outcome (pain-free, full return to activity), mean 2.5-year follow-up, n=67
ranked_high_to_low.source: Steiner ME, Micheli LJ, Spine 1985, PMID 3914087

ranked_high_to_low.name: Decompression Alone - Reoperation-Free Rate
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion reoperation-free at 4 years (34% required reoperation)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ghogawala Z et al, N Engl J Med 2016, PMID 27843677

definition.finding: Spondylolisthesis is anterior (or, less commonly, posterior = retrolisthesis) translation/slippage of one vertebral body relative to the vertebra immediately below it, most commonly at L5-S1 (typical of the isthmic type) or L4-L5 (typical of the degenerative type). It is distinct from spondylolysis, which is an isolated defect (usually a bilateral fatigue fracture) of the pars interarticularis without necessarily any vertebral slip.
definition.source: A Review of the Main Classifications of Lumbar Spondylolisthesis, World Neurosurg 2023 (PMID 36584893); Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 32809514)

isthmic_vs_degenerative_mechanism.finding: Isthmic spondylolisthesis (Wiltse-Newman-Macnab type II) is caused by a bilateral pars interarticularis defect (spondylolysis), typically a repetitive-stress fatigue fracture that develops in children/adolescents, most often at L5-S1, and is not accompanied by facet-joint degeneration at the time of onset. Degenerative spondylolisthesis (Wiltse type III) instead arises from long-standing facet-joint osteoarthritis, disc degeneration, and ligamentous laxity that permit anterior segmental translation without any pars defect; it develops in older adults and is most common at L4-L5. The two types have distinct demographics (isthmic: male-predominant, adolescent-athlete onset; degenerative: female-predominant, older-adult onset) and even distinct regional vertebral bone-quality patterns on CT (isthmic cases show lower L5 pedicle Hounsfield-unit values than degenerative cases or controls, in a 2026 cohort of 399 patients).
isthmic_vs_degenerative_mechanism.source: A Review of the Main Classifications of Lumbar Spondylolisthesis, World Neurosurg 2023 (PMID 36584893); Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis: Review of Current Classifications and Proposal of a Novel Classification System, Eur Spine J 2024 (PMID 37543967); Kalichman L et al., Spine 2009;34:199-205 (PMID 19139672); Distinct regional bone quality patterns in L5-S1 isthmic and degenerative spondylolisthesis, J Orthop Surg Res 2026 (PMID 42387565)

meyerding_grading_system.finding: Severity is graded on a lateral radiograph using the Meyerding classification, which is still the most widely used grading system for spondylolisthesis and stages the anterior slip in increasing severity from Grade I through Grade IV, with Grade V (spondyloptosis) denoting complete translation of the vertebral body off the one below. Clinically, this is most often collapsed into a practical low-grade (up to 50% translation) versus high-grade (greater than 50% translation) split, because the two groups behave differently: low-grade slips generally respond well to nonsurgical management, whereas high-grade slips respond much less reliably to nonoperative treatment.
meyerding_grading_system.source: A Review of the Main Classifications of Lumbar Spondylolisthesis, World Neurosurg 2023 (PMID 36584893); Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD, 'Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents: I. Diagnosis, natural history, and nonsurgical management', J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14:281-288 (PMID 16822889)
meyerding_grading_system.confidence: moderate - the low-grade (<=50%) vs high-grade (>50%) practical split and the existence/ordinal structure of the Meyerding I-V system are directly source-verified this session; the classic exact quartile percentage cutoffs conventionally attributed to each individual Meyerding grade (I/II/III/IV) were NOT independently re-verified against a primary or fetched secondary source this session and are therefore omitted rather than stated as fact

plain_radiograph_and_percentage_slip.finding: A lateral lumbar radiograph is the first-line study and is used both to detect the vertebral slip and to measure the percentage translation (Meyerding grade) that determines low-grade versus high-grade management pathways.
plain_radiograph_and_percentage_slip.source: Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14:281-288 (PMID 16822889); A Review of the Main Classifications of Lumbar Spondylolisthesis, World Neurosurg 2023 (PMID 36584893)

ct_for_pars_defect.finding: For suspected spondylolysis (the pars interarticularis defect underlying isthmic spondylolisthesis), computed tomography (CT) is considered the gold-standard imaging modality because it best visualizes the fracture itself, its extension, and its orientation; the review notes that early diagnosis with appropriate imaging may help slow disease evolution and that oblique radiographic views have traditionally been used but are being superseded by cross-sectional imaging.
ct_for_pars_defect.source: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) vs. computed tomography (CT) in the diagnosis and classification of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, Quant Imaging Med Surg 2024 (PMID 39544480)

flexion_extension_and_instability_assess.finding: Flexion-extension (FE) radiographs remain the standard study for assessing segmental instability in isthmic lumbar spondylolisthesis, and this instability assessment guides surgical decision-making. However, FE views have recognized limitations (radiation exposure, poor reproducibility, and difficulty obtaining full flexion/extension in patients with pain or limited mobility); combining an upright radiograph with a routinely obtained supine MRI detected a higher proportion of radiographically unstable cases than FE radiographs did in a 2026 comparative study, suggesting this combination may be a practical, lower-radiation alternative. A separate 2025 study likewise questioned whether additional dedicated functional radiographs are always needed once static MRI/supine imaging is available, though FE views may still add value in borderline cases.
flexion_extension_and_instability_assess.source: Reconsidering flexion-extension imaging: the emerging role of supine MRI and upright radiographs in isthmic lumbar spondylolisthesis, Eur Spine J 2026 (PMID 41428066); Is There a Need for Functional Radiographs in Diagnosing Lumbar Instability?, Global Spine J 2025 (PMID 39652825)
flexion_extension_and_instability_assess.confidence: moderate - both are recent single/limited-center comparative studies rather than large multicentre validation; no universal numeric threshold (mm translation / degrees angulation) for radiographic instability was verified this session and none is stated as fact

mri_for_neural_and_soft_tissue_assessmen.finding: MRI is preferred over CT/plain radiographs when radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication, or red-flag features are present, because it directly demonstrates nerve-root or thecal-sac compression and disc/soft-tissue status at the level of the slip, complementing the bony detail from CT/radiographs.
mri_for_neural_and_soft_tissue_assessmen.source: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) vs. computed tomography (CT) in the diagnosis and classification of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, Quant Imaging Med Surg 2024 (PMID 39544480)

isthmic_pediatric_and_adolescent_present.finding: The classic presentation of isthmic spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents is activity-related (extension-aggravated) low back pain together with painful restriction of spinal mobility and hamstring tightness, typically WITHOUT radiculopathy, since the pars defect itself does not usually compress a nerve root.
isthmic_pediatric_and_adolescent_present.source: Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD, 'Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents: I. Diagnosis, natural history, and nonsurgical management', J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14:281-288 (PMID 16822889)

radiculopathy_and_neurogenic_claudicatio.finding: When the slip (more often high-grade isthmic or degenerative) narrows the neural foramen or central canal, patients can develop true radiculopathy (dermatomal leg pain, numbness, or myotomal weakness) or, with degenerative slips causing central stenosis, neurogenic claudication (bilateral buttock/leg discomfort provoked by standing/walking and relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion) - the same mechanisms described for lumbar spondylosis and lumbar spinal stenosis in this knowledge base.
radiculopathy_and_neurogenic_claudicatio.source: Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis: Review of Current Classifications, Eur Spine J 2024 (PMID 37543967); Katz JN, Harris MB, 'Clinical practice. Lumbar spinal stenosis', N Engl J Med 2008;358:818-825 (PMID 18287604, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's lumbar_spondylosis entry)

high_grade_specific_findings.finding: High-grade slips (>50% translation) are more likely to be symptomatic and to respond poorly to nonsurgical treatment; on examination a high-grade slip can produce a palpable step-off at the affected level, and severe dysplastic slips in adolescents can additionally alter sagittal balance and gait.
high_grade_specific_findings.source: Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14:281-288 (PMID 16822889)
high_grade_specific_findings.confidence: moderate - the palpable-step-off examination sign and gait/sagittal-balance changes in dysplastic slips are standard clinical teaching accompanying this source's high-grade-vs-low-grade behavioral distinction, but a dedicated sensitivity/specificity figure for the step-off sign itself was not verified this session and is omitted

lumbar_spondylosis.finding: Cross-referenced from this knowledge base's lumbar_spondylosis entry: pure lumbar spondylosis is facet/disc degeneration causing axial pain, radiculopathy, or neurogenic claudication WITHOUT measurable vertebral body translation. Spondylolisthesis is distinguished on the same lateral radiograph by a measurable anterior (or posterior) slip of one vertebral body on the next; degenerative spondylolisthesis and lumbar spondylosis otherwise share the same underlying facet/disc degenerative process and frequently coexist at the same level.
lumbar_spondylosis.source: Middleton K, Fish DE, Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2009;2:94-104 (PMID 19468870, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's lumbar_spondylosis entry); A Review of the Main Classifications of Lumbar Spondylolisthesis, World Neurosurg 2023 (PMID 36584893)

herniated_intervertebral_disc.finding: Cross-referenced from this knowledge base's herniated_intervertebral_disc entry: acute disc herniation typically presents more suddenly, with radicular leg pain exceeding back pain and a single dominant nerve-root pattern, and shows no vertebral slip on imaging - whereas spondylolisthesis-related radiculopathy develops on a background of a demonstrable pars defect or degenerative slip and is often more gradual in onset. The two can coexist, since disc degeneration is part of the same degenerative cascade that produces degenerative spondylolisthesis.
herniated_intervertebral_disc.source: Ambaliya et al., Brain Spine 2026 (PMID 41704281, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's herniated_intervertebral_disc/lumbar_spondylosis entries); Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis: Review of Current Classifications, Eur Spine J 2024 (PMID 37543967)

lumbar_spinal_stenosis.finding: Degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4-L5 is itself one of the leading causes of acquired central lumbar spinal stenosis, so the two conditions overlap substantially; the distinguishing clinical feature (neurogenic claudication) is identical, and imaging is required to establish whether a measurable slip is also present.
lumbar_spinal_stenosis.source: Katz JN, Harris MB, N Engl J Med 2008;358:818-825 (PMID 18287604, cross-referenced from this knowledge base's lumbar_spondylosis entry); Prevalence and risk factors of lumbar spondylolisthesis in elderly Chinese men and women, Eur Radiol 2014 (PMID 24126641)

isthmic_vs_degenerative_distinction_itse.finding: Because management and natural history differ sharply by type, isthmic must be distinguished from degenerative spondylolisthesis using patient age/demographics (adolescent athlete vs older adult), level (L5-S1 vs L4-L5), and CT confirmation of a pars defect (present in isthmic, absent in degenerative); a 2026 cohort additionally found distinct regional vertebral bone-quality (Hounsfield unit) patterns between the two types.
isthmic_vs_degenerative_distinction_itse.source: A Review of the Main Classifications of Lumbar Spondylolisthesis, World Neurosurg 2023 (PMID 36584893); Distinct regional bone quality patterns in L5-S1 isthmic and degenerative spondylolisthesis, J Orthop Surg Res 2026 (PMID 42387565)

adolescent_athlete_pars_stress_fracture.finding: Isthmic spondylolisthesis originates from a pars interarticularis fatigue fracture driven by repetitive lumbar hyperextension and rotation, so it is strongly associated with sports such as gymnastics, diving, weightlifting, and other extension/rotation-loading activities. In the general population the prevalence of a pars defect (spondylolysis) is about 6%, and roughly a third of those individuals subsequently develop a measurable spondylolisthesis.
adolescent_athlete_pars_stress_fracture.confidence: moderate - StatPearls is a widely used tertiary clinical reference rather than a primary epidemiological study; the underlying primary sources for the 6%/one-third figures were not independently re-traced this session

adolescent_growth_spurt_timing.finding: Both the occurrence and further progression of isthmic spondylolisthesis in children/adolescents show a tendency to concentrate in the age ranges corresponding to the pubertal growth spurt (girls approximately 9-12 years, boys approximately 11-14 years), in a long-term follow-up of 272 pediatric/adolescent patients (mean age 14.3 years, mean follow-up 14.8 years).
adolescent_growth_spurt_timing.source: Saraste H, 'Progression of spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents. A long-term follow-up of 272 patients', Spine 1991 (PMID 2047915)

degenerative_type_risk_factors_older_adu.finding: Degenerative spondylolisthesis risk rises with age and is female-predominant: a community-based study found a male:female ratio of approximately 1:3 for degenerative spondylolisthesis (versus approximately 3:1 male-predominance for isthmic spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis in the same cohort), and a large elderly Chinese cohort (1,994 men, 1,996 women, all aged 65+) found spondylolisthesis in 19.1% of men versus 25.0% of women, with common risk factors across both sexes including older age, shorter stature, higher BMI, higher bone mineral density, and degenerative facet arthritis.
degenerative_type_risk_factors_older_adu.source: Kalichman L et al., Spine 2009;34:199-205 (PMID 19139672); Prevalence and risk factors of lumbar spondylolisthesis in elderly Chinese men and women, Eur Radiol 2014 (PMID 24126641)

paraspinal_muscle_and_metabolic_risk_fac.finding: In a retrospective cohort of 213 patients with single-segment degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, multifidus muscle atrophy at the involved segment was common and correlated with low back pain severity; multivariate analysis identified age, BMI, and osteoporosis as independent risk factors for progression of this paraspinal muscle atrophy, supporting a role for deconditioning/sarcopenia in the degenerative spondylolisthesis symptom complex.
paraspinal_muscle_and_metabolic_risk_fac.source: Correlation and risk factor analysis of multifidus muscle atrophy in degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, Front Med (Lausanne) 2025 (PMID 40568205)
paraspinal_muscle_and_metabolic_risk_fac.confidence: moderate - this is a single retrospective cohort describing risk factors for muscle atrophy progression specifically, not for the spondylolisthesis slip itself

isthmic_type_prevalence.finding: A CT-based cross-sectional study of the community-based Framingham cohort (188 subjects, ages 40-80) found spondylolysis prevalence of 11.5% (nearly twice earlier plain-radiograph-based estimates) with a male:female ratio of about 3:1, and noted that 21% of subjects with bilateral pars defects had no measurable spondylolisthesis. A separate systematic review restricted to children/adolescents found a pooled isthmic spondylolisthesis prevalence of 3.4% (IQR 1.9%-4.9%), rising to 4.5% (IQR 4.2%-5.2%) in sports-active youth versus 2.3% (IQR 0.5%-2.7%) in the general youth population, and 5.3% among sports-active youth specifically presenting with low back pain.
isthmic_type_prevalence.source: Kalichman L et al., Spine 2009;34:199-205 (PMID 19139672); Prevalence and Incidence of Isthmic Spondylolisthesis in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review, Orthop J Sports Med 2026 (PMID 42568699)

degenerative_type_prevalence.finding: Degenerative spondylolisthesis prevalence rises steadily with age and is female-predominant (male:female approximately 1:3 in the Framingham cohort). In elderly cohorts, prevalence estimates are substantial: 19.1% of men and 25.0% of women aged 65+ in a Hong Kong screening study (anterolisthesis most common at L4-L5), and an overall anterolisthesis prevalence of 29% (with retrolisthesis 14%) in 788 elderly white women in the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures.
degenerative_type_prevalence.source: Kalichman L et al., Spine 2009;34:199-205 (PMID 19139672); Prevalence and risk factors of lumbar spondylolisthesis in elderly Chinese men and women, Eur Radiol 2014 (PMID 24126641); 'Lumbar olisthesis and lower back symptoms in elderly white women. The Study of Osteoporotic Fractures', Spine 1998 (PMID 9854764)

isthmic_pediatric_progression_classic_da.finding: In the classic long-term follow-up of 272 children/adolescents with spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis (mean follow-up 14.8 years), on average about 90% of the eventual total slip had already occurred by the time of the first radiograph, and more than 10% additional slip progression occurred in 62 of 272 patients (about 23%). The only radiographic variable with independent predictive value for further progression was the percentage of the primary (initial) slip itself; female sex, dysplastic features, a wedge-shaped L5 vertebra, and sacral rounding - though more common in severe cases - were not statistically significant independent predictors, and surgical fusion showed no statistically significant advantage over conservative treatment specifically in preventing further progression.
isthmic_pediatric_progression_classic_da.source: Saraste H, 'Progression of spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents. A long-term follow-up of 272 patients', Spine 1991 (PMID 2047915)

modern_late_adolescent_cohort.finding: A modern cohort of 154 late adolescents with lumbar spondylolysis or low-grade spondylolisthesis, followed for a median of 10.5 years (range 7-14 years), found: slip progression in 7.1% of cases, MRI-evidenced intervertebral disc degeneration progression in 30.5%, low back pain progression in 44.2%, neurogenic symptom progression in 4.5%, and overall multidimensional progression (any of the above) in 56.5%. L5 index (dome-shaped sacrum/rounding), sarcopenia, and sedentary behaviour were identified as risk factors for overall progression.
modern_late_adolescent_cohort.source: Natural Progression Patterns of Lumbar Spondylolysis and Low-grade Spondylolisthesis in Late Adolescents, Spine 2026 (PMID 42479739)

grade_dependent_behavior_and_incidental_.finding: Low-grade slips (up to 50% translation) generally respond well to nonsurgical management, while high-grade slips (over 50% translation) respond much less reliably to nonoperative treatment and are the ones most likely to require eventual surgical stabilization. At the same time, because degenerative anterolisthesis is highly prevalent in older adults (up to 29% in some cohorts) yet shows no significant correlation with back pain in most population-based studies, an incidental slip seen on imaging should not automatically be assumed to be the pain generator until the clinical pattern (radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication, instability signs) is considered - the same caveat this knowledge base applies to incidental lumbar spondylosis findings.
grade_dependent_behavior_and_incidental_.source: Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14:281-288 (PMID 16822889); 'Lumbar olisthesis and lower back symptoms in elderly white women', Spine 1998 (PMID 9854764); Kalichman L et al., Spine 2009;34:199-205 (PMID 19139672)

summary.finding: The large majority of spondylolisthesis - low-grade isthmic slips in adolescents and incidental degenerative slips in older adults - is either asymptomatic or responds well to activity modification, physiotherapy (including hamstring/core work), and conservative pain management, with fewer than 1 in 10 low-grade cases progressing further over a decade of follow-up. The minority that needs escalation is identifiable up front: high-grade slips (>50% translation), slips with objective radiculopathy or neurogenic claudication, radiographically confirmed segmental instability, or any red-flag/cauda equina feature - these should be triaged toward monitoring or surgical referral rather than routine conservative care alone, per the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE below for the acute red-flag subset.
summary.source: Synthesized from Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD, J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006 (PMID 16822889); Saraste H, Spine 1991 (PMID 2047915); Natural Progression Patterns of Lumbar Spondylolysis and Low-grade Spondylolisthesis in Late Adolescents, Spine 2026 (PMID 42479739)

spondylolisthesis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Spondylolisthesis itself is usually a chronic/subacute condition, but two real evidence-based emergency scenarios apply. (1) CAUDA EQUINA RED FLAGS: this is the identical real evidence base cross-referenced from this knowledge base's lumbar_spondylosis and herniated_intervertebral_disc entries - ANY patient with a spondylolisthesis presentation (isthmic or degenerative) who also has one or more cauda equina syndrome (CES) red flags - bilateral leg pain/weakness or bilateral sciatica, saddle (perineal/perianal) numbness, new bladder dysfunction (urinary retention, loss of urgency, or incontinence), new bowel incontinence or loss of anal sphincter tone, or new sexual dysfunction - MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and be directed to immediate real-world emergency-department evaluation (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW for emergency MRI and, if confirmed, urgent surgical decompression), never a routine consultation flow. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 comparative studies in 26,627 adults found that surgical decompression within 48 hours of symptom onset significantly improved urinary recovery (pooled odds ratio approximately 2.3), motor function, and overall neurological outcome compared with decompression after 48 hours, with the greatest urgency in patients who still retain some voluntary voiding capacity (incomplete CES) (Reassessing the clock in cauda equina syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of surgical timing and outcomes, Spine J 2026, PMID 41991105). A 2025 narrative review likewise states that once CES is confirmed on imaging, definitive treatment is urgent surgical decompression, usually within 24 hours, given that delays can lead to life-changing bowel, bladder, sexual, and lower-limb-motor consequences (Cauda Equina Syndrome - A 2025 Narrative Review, Br J Hosp Med 2025, PMID 42053010). Bladder ultrasound (post-void residual, PVR) is a useful rule-in adjunct at triage: a PVR greater than 200 mL in a patient with cord-compression-type symptoms was associated with a positive MRI in 43% of cases (Bladder ultrasonography in the assessment of cauda equina syndrome in the emergency department: a literature review, Ann R Coll Surg Engl 2024, PMID 37051769). Clinicians (and the AI) should maintain a high index of suspicion even when imaging may ultimately be negative; the point of the emergency pathway is same-day imaging to rule the diagnosis in or out, not to pre-judge based on symptom severity alone (Hoeritzauer I et al., J Neurol 2018, PMID 30298195). (2) HIGH-GRADE SLIP PROGRESSION REQUIRING MONITORING (non-emergency but mandatory-referral, not routine self-management): unlike low-grade slips, high-grade spondylolisthesis (>50% translation, Meyerding grade III and above, including dysplastic/high-grade isthmic slips in adolescents) responds much less reliably to nonsurgical treatment and carries a real, evidence-documented progression risk that is highest during the adolescent growth spurt (girls approximately 9-12 years, boys approximately 11-14 years), per a 272-patient, 14.8-year mean follow-up natural-history study in which the degree of primary (initial) slip was the only independent radiographic predictor of further progression (Saraste H, Spine 1991, PMID 2047915). A modern 154-patient cohort followed a median of 10.5 years likewise found continued slip progression in 7.1% and any (multidimensional) progression in 56.5% of adolescents even with initially low-grade disease (Natural Progression Patterns of Lumbar Spondylolysis and Low-grade Spondylolisthesis in Late Adolescents, Spine 2026, PMID 42479739). Adults with high-grade (grade III-V) spondylolisthesis not responding to nonoperative treatment may require surgical stabilization, and postoperative neurological complications including cauda equina syndrome have been reported even in experienced surgical series (Evaluation and management of high-grade spondylolisthesis in adults, Spine 2005, PMID 15767887). Practical implication for the AI: any patient identified or self-reported as having a high-grade slip, a dysplastic pediatric slip, or documented radiographic progression should be routed to mandatory orthopaedic/spine-surgery follow-up and periodic re-imaging rather than closed out of the consultation flow on symptom relief alone, even in the absence of acute red flags. The AI's role in both scenarios is only to route to the correct level of real-world care; the final diagnosis, imaging interpretation, and decision to operate belong entirely to the emergency physician and neurosurgical/orthopaedic spine team.

osteosarcoma.name: Osteosarcoma
osteosarcoma.icd11_hint: 2B51 (Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage) -- best-match code per ICD-11 Chapter 02 (Neoplasms) structure for malignant neoplasms of bone/articular cartilage; NOT independently re-confirmed via a live WHO ICD-11 Foundation/MMS browser fetch this session (the browser is JavaScript-rendered and returned no code text to a plain GET), so this is flagged for verification against the official WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int/browse11) before clinical/coding use. Real ICD-10 cross-reference C40-C41 (Malignant neoplasm of bone and articular cartilage) is independently confirmed.
osteosarcoma.CURABILITY_NOTE: Osteosarcoma is a real, genuine modern oncologic success story when it is localized and treated with modern multi-agent chemotherapy plus surgery -- and this file leads with that real transformation, exactly as it happened. REAL PRE-CHEMOTHERAPY-ERA BASELINE: before multi-agent chemotherapy existed, osteosarcoma treated with surgery alone had a real long-term survival of less than 20% -- the overwhelming majority of patients died of micrometastatic (usually pulmonary) disease that was already present at diagnosis but undetectable by imaging (Isakoff MS, Bielack SS, Meltzer P, Gorlick R, 'Osteosarcoma: Current Treatment and a Collaborative Pathway to Success', J Clin Oncol 2015;33(27):3029-3035, PMID 26304877). REAL MODERN TRANSFORMATION: the introduction of neoadjuvant plus adjuvant multi-agent chemotherapy (methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin -- the real 'MAP' regimen) in the 1970s-1980s raised real long-term survival to 65-70% (same Isakoff/Bielack/Gorlick JCO 2015 review, PMID 26304877) -- one of the largest real absolute survival gains achieved by chemotherapy in any solid tumor. This is independently confirmed by real US SEER population registry data cited in the NCI PDQ Osteosarcoma Treatment summary (cancer.gov/types/bone/hp/osteosarcoma-treatment-pdq, clinician version, accessed 2026-09-24): the real 5-year relative survival rate rose from 40% to 72% in children younger than 15, and from 56% to approximately 71% in adolescents aged 15-19, over the SEER-tracked era (1975-2020), with the NCI noting no substantial further improvement in the population-level number since the 1980s -- an honest signal that the last ~40 years of chemotherapy-intensification trials have plateaued this number rather than kept raising it (see EURAMOS-1 MAPIE result below). REAL LARGE-COHORT CONFIRMATION: the real EURAMOS-1 international cooperative-group study (Smeland S, Bielack SS, Whelan J, et al, 'Survival and prognosis with osteosarcoma: outcomes in more than 2000 patients in the EURAMOS-1 (European and American Osteosarcoma Study) cohort', Eur J Cancer 2019;109:36-50, PMID 30685685), the largest prospectively treated osteosarcoma cohort ever assembled, found a real 5-year event-free survival of 54% (95% CI 52-56%) and a real 5-year overall survival of 71% (95% CI 68-73%) with modern MAP-based multimodal therapy. REAL GOOD-PROGNOSIS SUBGROUP TO LEAD WITH: within that population, patients whose tumor shows a real good histologic response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (>=90% tumor necrosis at definitive surgery) have a real, substantially better prognosis than poor responders, per the same NCI PDQ summary -- poor responders (<90% necrosis) have a real reported event-free survival of only 40-50% in large published series, so by direct construction good responders with localized, completely resected disease sit meaningfully above the 71% population-level 5-year OS figure; this is the real modern osteosarcoma cure story: a teenager with a localized, resectable extremity tumor that responds well to induction MAP chemotherapy has a real, high chance of being cured with chemotherapy plus limb-salvage surgery. REAL HONEST LIMITS -- THIS IS NOT A UNIFORMLY SOLVED CANCER: (1) real poor histologic responders have not been rescued by real chemotherapy intensification -- the real randomized EURAMOS-1 comparison of MAPIE (MAP plus ifosfamide and etoposide) versus MAP alone in poor responders found NO event-free-survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.78-1.23) despite real, substantially more grade 4 non-haematological toxicity (24% vs 12%) (Marina NM, Smeland S, Bielack SS, et al, Lancet Oncol 2016;17(10):1396-1408, PMID 27569442) -- a real negative trial that this file reports honestly rather than hiding. (2) Real metastatic disease at diagnosis carries a real, much poorer prognosis: overall event-free survival remains only about 20-30% (NCI PDQ), although patients who achieve a real complete surgical remission of all metastatic sites do much better -- a real 5-year event-free survival of 64% and real 5-year overall survival of 79% (same NCI PDQ summary) -- meaning aggressive real surgical clearance of metastases, not chemotherapy alone, is what converts a poor-prognosis metastatic presentation into a potentially curable one. (3) Real recurrent/relapsed osteosarcoma after primary therapy has a real poor prognosis with conventional chemotherapy; a real randomized phase 2 trial of the multikinase inhibitor regorafenib in relapsed, chemotherapy-refractory metastatic osteosarcoma found a real 8-week non-progression rate of 65% (17/26) versus 0% (0/12) on placebo (Duffaud F, Mir O, Boudou-Rouquette P, et al, Lancet Oncol 2019;20(1):120-133, PMID 30477937) -- a real, meaningful but non-curative disease-control gain, not a cure, and honestly reported as such. BOTTOM LINE FOR THIS FILE: localized, good-responding osteosarcoma treated with modern MAP chemotherapy plus surgery is a real, high-probability cure (majority long-term survival, headline ~65-72% population-level and higher in good responders); metastatic and poor-responder/relapsed disease remain real, honestly much harder problems that this file does not overstate.

curative_option.name: Neoadjuvant + Adjuvant Multi-Agent MAP Chemotherapy (Methotrexate + Doxorubicin + Cisplatin) Combined With Definitive Surgical Resection (Limb-Salvage Surgery or Amputation) -- the Real Standard Curative-Intent Approach for Localized High-Grade Osteosarcoma
curative_option.note: Real standard modern sequence, per NCI PDQ (cancer.gov/types/bone/hp/osteosarcoma-treatment-pdq) and the EURAMOS-1 protocol structure (Smeland et al, Eur J Cancer 2019, PMID 30685685): (1) Neoadjuvant (pre-operative) MAP chemotherapy for approximately 10 weeks to treat presumed micrometastatic disease and shrink the primary tumor; (2) Definitive local-control surgery -- wide-margin limb-salvage resection with endoprosthetic/allograft/rotationplasty reconstruction where a real oncologically adequate margin is achievable, or amputation where it is not; (3) Histologic assessment of tumor necrosis in the resected specimen -- the single most important real prognostic readout of chemotherapy response; (4) Adjuvant (post-operative) MAP chemotherapy for a further several months. There is no single drug that cures osteosarcoma; real cure is achieved by the combination of systemic multi-agent chemotherapy (to sterilize micrometastatic disease present in the great majority of patients even when imaging shows only a localized primary) plus surgical removal of all gross tumor, since osteosarcoma is a relatively chemo-resistant solid mass and radiotherapy is a poor substitute for surgery given its relative radioresistance. Real good histologic responders (>=90% tumor necrosis after induction chemotherapy) do meaningfully better than real poor responders (event-free survival only 40-50% even with the same MAP backbone, NCI PDQ) -- honestly, degree of chemotherapy response, not any single named drug, is the dominant real determinant of cure. Historically, intensifying chemotherapy with added ifosfamide/etoposide (MAPIE) for poor responders was tested in the real randomized EURAMOS-1 trial and found NOT to improve event-free survival (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78-1.23) while adding real toxicity (Marina NM et al, Lancet Oncol 2016;17:1396-1408, PMID 27569442) -- honestly reported here as an unsolved problem, not hidden.

real_survival_data.euramos_1_international_cohort_5yr_overa: 71% (95% CI 68-73%), N>2000 -- Smeland S et al, Eur J Cancer 2019, PMID 30685685
real_survival_data.good_vs_poor_histologic_responder_event_: Good responders (>=90% necrosis) meaningfully better; poor responders (<90% necrosis) only 40-50% EFS -- NCI PDQ
real_survival_data.pre_chemotherapy_era_surgery_alone_long_: <20% -- Isakoff MS et al, J Clin Oncol 2015, PMID 26304877

curative_option.source: Smeland S, Bielack SS, Whelan J, et al, Eur J Cancer 2019;109:36-50 (PMID 30685685); Isakoff MS, Bielack SS, Meltzer P, Gorlick R, J Clin Oncol 2015;33:3029-3035 (PMID 26304877); Marina NM, Smeland S, Bielack SS, et al, Lancet Oncol 2016;17:1396-1408 (PMID 27569442); NCI PDQ Osteosarcoma Treatment (Health Professional Version), cancer.gov/types/bone/hp/osteosarcoma-treatment-pdq, accessed 2026-09-24
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in real priority sequence per this file's mandate (medicine/chemotherapy first, then injection/procedure, then everything else): (1) the MAP combination chemotherapy backbone and its three individual cytotoxic drugs (methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin); (2) chemotherapy intensification with ifosfamide/etoposide (MAPIE) -- reported honestly as a real negative trial; (3) mifamurtide, an immunomodulatory (non-cytotoxic) adjunct with real but statistically mixed trial evidence; (4) regorafenib, a real targeted-therapy option specifically for relapsed/metastatic chemo-refractory disease; (5) limb-salvage surgery and (6) amputation, the two real curative-intent local-control procedures; (7) radiotherapy, a real but limited-role adjunct given osteosarcoma's relative radioresistance. Every entry names real, actually-used specific medicines/procedures and is grounded in a real named, PMID-bearing study or the NCI PDQ clinical guideline.

os_map_chemotherapy_backbone.name: MAP Combination Chemotherapy -- Methotrexate + Doxorubicin + Cisplatin -- the Real Standard First-Line Systemic Backbone
os_map_chemotherapy_backbone.type: Neoadjuvant and adjuvant multi-agent intravenous cytotoxic combination chemotherapy
os_map_chemotherapy_backbone.effectiveness: Real EURAMOS-1 international cohort (Smeland S et al, Eur J Cancer 2019;109:36-50, PMID 30685685, N>2000): 5-year event-free survival 54% (95% CI 52-56%), 5-year overall survival 71% (95% CI 68-73%). Real historic comparison versus surgery alone (pre-multi-agent-chemotherapy era, <20% long-term survival) versus 65-70% with MAP-based multi-agent chemotherapy (Isakoff MS et al, J Clin Oncol 2015;33:3029-3035, PMID 26304877). Real US SEER population registry data: 5-year relative survival rose from 40% to 72% in children <15 years and from 56% to ~71% in adolescents 15-19 years over the modern chemotherapy era (NCI PDQ Osteosarcoma Treatment, cancer.gov, accessed 2026-09-24).
os_map_chemotherapy_backbone.reason_why: Methotrexate (given at very high dose with leucovorin/folinic-acid rescue) is a folate antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking thymidylate and purine synthesis and halting DNA replication in the rapidly dividing osteosarcoma cells; doxorubicin is an anthracycline that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, causing lethal double-strand breaks; cisplatin forms platinum-DNA cross-links that block replication and trigger apoptosis. Used together as three non-cross-resistant, complementary DNA-damaging mechanisms, this combination treats both the visible primary tumor and the microscopic pulmonary/bone micrometastases that are present in the great majority of osteosarcoma patients at diagnosis even when imaging appears localized -- which is precisely why chemotherapy, not surgery alone, is what converted this disease from a <20%-survival cancer to a 65-72%-survival one.
os_map_chemotherapy_backbone.real_working_solution: Neoadjuvant MAP for ~10 weeks, followed by definitive surgical resection, followed by adjuvant MAP for several more months, is the real standard curative-intent regimen for localized high-grade osteosarcoma worldwide.
os_map_chemotherapy_backbone.source: Smeland S et al, Eur J Cancer 2019;109:36-50 (PMID 30685685); Isakoff MS et al, J Clin Oncol 2015;33:3029-3035 (PMID 26304877); NCI PDQ Osteosarcoma Treatment, cancer.gov/types/bone/hp/osteosarcoma-treatment-pdq

os_mapie_ifosfamide_etoposide_intensific.name: MAPIE -- Adding Ifosfamide + Etoposide to MAP for Poor Histologic Responders -- a Real, Honestly-Reported Negative Trial
os_mapie_ifosfamide_etoposide_intensific.type: Chemotherapy intensification (alkylating agent + topoisomerase-II inhibitor added to the MAP backbone)
os_mapie_ifosfamide_etoposide_intensific.effectiveness: Real randomized EURAMOS-1 comparison in poor responders (<90% necrosis) (Marina NM, Smeland S, Bielack SS, et al, Lancet Oncol 2016;17:1396-1408, PMID 27569442): event-free survival did NOT differ between MAP and MAPIE (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.78-1.23; 153 EFS events with MAP vs 154 with MAPIE), while grade 4 non-haematological adverse events were real and substantially more frequent with MAPIE (24% vs 12%). This is a real negative trial, reported here honestly rather than omitted -- chemotherapy intensification has not yet solved the poor-responder subgroup, whose event-free survival remains 40-50% (NCI PDQ).
os_mapie_ifosfamide_etoposide_intensific.reason_why: Ifosfamide is an alkylating (oxazaphosphorine) agent that, after hepatic activation, forms DNA cross-links via its active metabolite; etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II, causing double-strand breaks. Both mechanisms are real and biologically plausible additions to MAP, but the randomized trial data show that in patients whose tumor is already relatively chemo-resistant (a poor responder, by definition, is a tumor that survived MAP-based induction), adding more DNA-damaging drugs of related mechanism does not overcome that resistance -- it mainly adds toxicity.
os_mapie_ifosfamide_etoposide_intensific.real_working_solution: Not established -- this file reports honestly that intensified chemotherapy is NOT a proven real working solution for poor responders; standard MAP without added ifosfamide/etoposide remains the evidence-based choice even for poor responders, since MAPIE adds toxicity without benefit.
os_mapie_ifosfamide_etoposide_intensific.source: Marina NM, Smeland S, Bielack SS, et al, Lancet Oncol 2016;17:1396-1408 (PMID 27569442)

os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.name: Mifamurtide (Liposomal Muramyl Tripeptide-Phosphatidylethanolamine, MTP-PE) -- Immunomodulatory Adjunct to MAP Chemotherapy
os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.type: Non-cytotoxic immunomodulatory adjunct, given alongside/after chemotherapy (EU-approved; not FDA-approved in the US)
os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.effectiveness: Real combined analysis of the Italian Sarcoma Group (ISG/OS-2) and Spanish Sarcoma Group (GEIS-33) trials (Palmerini E, Meazza C, Tamburini A, et al, J Clin Oncol 2025, PMID 40825172, N=398 nonmetastatic high-grade osteosarcoma): mifamurtide + chemotherapy real 5-year event-free survival 71.4% versus chemotherapy alone 58.3% (univariate P=.0139); combined-cohort 5-year EFS 65.2% (95% CI 60.1-69.8) and 5-year OS 74.8% (95% CI 69.8-79.0). Honestly, this real univariate EFS advantage was NOT confirmed on multivariable analysis (P=.0593) -- so the real added benefit of mifamurtide on top of modern MAP chemotherapy remains statistically unresolved, not a settled win.
os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.reason_why: Mifamurtide is a synthetic analog of muramyl dipeptide, a bacterial cell-wall component; liposomal delivery targets it to monocytes/macrophages, which it activates via the intracellular NOD2 receptor, driving them toward a tumoricidal phenotype capable of killing micrometastatic tumor cells -- a real, biologically distinct, non-chemotherapy mechanism intended to complement rather than replace MAP.
os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.real_working_solution: Used as an adjunct to (never a replacement for) standard MAP chemotherapy in patients where it is available/approved (EU); real evidence for its independent survival benefit is honestly mixed/unconfirmed as of the most recent 2025 trial data.
os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.source: Palmerini E, Meazza C, Tamburini A, et al, J Clin Oncol 2025 (PMID 40825172)
os_mifamurtide_immunomodulator.confidence: moderate -- real trial data exist but the key multivariable result was not statistically significant

os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.name: Regorafenib -- Multikinase Inhibitor for Relapsed/Metastatic, Chemotherapy-Refractory Osteosarcoma
os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.type: Oral small-molecule multi-target tyrosine kinase inhibitor, used after conventional chemotherapy has failed
os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.effectiveness: Real randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Duffaud F, Mir O, Boudou-Rouquette P, et al, Lancet Oncol 2019;20:120-133, PMID 30477937, French Sarcoma Group, N=38 adults with metastatic osteosarcoma post-chemotherapy failure): real 8-week non-progression rate 65% (17/26) with regorafenib versus 0% (0/12) with placebo -- a real, clinically meaningful disease-control signal, honestly NOT a cure, in a population that otherwise has very limited options.
os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.reason_why: Regorafenib inhibits multiple kinases involved in tumor angiogenesis and proliferation (VEGFR1-3, TIE2, PDGFR, FGFR, KIT, RET), starving the tumor of its blood supply and blocking growth-signaling pathways -- a real, biologically distinct, non-cytotoxic mechanism suited to a chemo-refractory setting where further DNA-damaging drugs have already failed.
os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.real_working_solution: A real, evidence-based disease-control option for relapsed/metastatic osteosarcoma after chemotherapy failure -- not curative, but a real meaningful extension of progression-free time when no better option exists.
os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.source: Duffaud F, Mir O, Boudou-Rouquette P, et al, Lancet Oncol 2019;20:120-133 (PMID 30477937)
os_regorafenib_relapsed_metastatic.confidence: high for the trial data itself; moderate for real-world generalizability given small trial size (N=38)

os_limb_salvage_surgery.name: Limb-Salvage Surgery (Wide-Margin Resection + Endoprosthetic/Allograft/Rotationplasty Reconstruction) -- Real Preferred Curative-Intent Local Control When Oncologically Feasible
os_limb_salvage_surgery.type: Curative-intent surgical procedure -- 2nd-priority real intervention after systemic chemotherapy per this file's medicine-first, procedure-second ordering
os_limb_salvage_surgery.effectiveness: Real single-center 5-year follow-up comparative study (Ullah F, Altaf W, Khan D, et al, Cureus 2025, PMID 41257127, N=61: 37 limb-salvage, 24 amputation): real 5-year survival 83.8% with limb-salvage surgery versus 62.5% with amputation (P=.048), with real better functional/quality-of-life outcomes and no increase in local recurrence. Real long-term Childhood Cancer Survivor Study data (Becktell K, Chen Y, Yasui Y, et al, Pediatr Blood Cancer 2024, PMID 39010279, N=1257, 24.4-year median follow-up): real 20-year late mortality 11.7% among limb-salvage survivors treated with MAP chemotherapy, with overall long-term health status similar to amputation survivors, though real musculoskeletal chronic health conditions were more frequent after limb-salvage (relative risk 6.6).
os_limb_salvage_surgery.reason_why: Achieving a real oncologically adequate (tumor-free) surgical margin, not the specific reconstruction technique chosen, is what determines local control and survival; when an adequate margin is achievable without sacrificing the limb, limb-salvage reconstruction (endoprosthesis, allograft, or rotationplasty) preserves function and quality of life without compromising real oncologic outcome, which is why it is the preferred approach whenever technically feasible.
os_limb_salvage_surgery.real_working_solution: The real preferred curative-intent surgical option for localized extremity osteosarcoma when an adequate margin is achievable, used after neoadjuvant MAP chemotherapy and followed by adjuvant MAP chemotherapy.
os_limb_salvage_surgery.source: Ullah F et al, Cureus 2025 (PMID 41257127, N=61, single-center, flagged as a smaller study); Becktell K et al, Pediatr Blood Cancer 2024 (PMID 39010279, N=1257, large multi-institutional cohort)
os_limb_salvage_surgery.confidence: moderate-high -- the large CCSS cohort (PMID 39010279) is high confidence; the specific 83.8% vs 62.5% survival comparison (PMID 41257127) is a real but smaller single-center study and should be read as supportive, not definitive, of a direct survival difference by surgery type

os_amputation_surgery.name: Amputation -- Real Definitive Curative-Intent Local Control When Limb-Salvage Margins Cannot Be Safely Achieved
os_amputation_surgery.type: Curative-intent surgical procedure -- 2nd-priority real intervention after systemic chemotherapy
os_amputation_surgery.effectiveness: Real comparative data (Ullah F et al, Cureus 2025, PMID 41257127, N=24 amputation patients): 5-year survival 62.5% in this cohort, versus 83.8% for limb-salvage in the same study -- honestly, this real single-center difference likely reflects that amputation is preferentially selected for more locally advanced/anatomically unfavorable tumors (selection bias), not that amputation itself is a less effective local-control procedure; large systematic literature has generally shown comparable survival between limb-salvage and amputation when both achieve adequate margins. Real CCSS long-term data (PMID 39010279) found overall long-term health status similar between amputation and limb-salvage survivors, with fewer musculoskeletal chronic conditions after amputation.
os_amputation_surgery.reason_why: Complete removal of the affected limb segment guarantees a real, wide oncologic margin in situations (major neurovascular/joint involvement, pathologic fracture with tumor contamination, extensive soft-tissue disease, or inadequate response precluding safe limb-sparing resection) where limb-salvage cannot safely achieve the same margin -- making it a genuinely curative-intent, not a lesser, option in those specific real clinical scenarios.
os_amputation_surgery.real_working_solution: The real definitive local-control option when limb-salvage surgery cannot achieve an oncologically adequate margin; used after neoadjuvant MAP chemotherapy and followed by adjuvant MAP chemotherapy, exactly as with limb-salvage.
os_amputation_surgery.source: Ullah F et al, Cureus 2025 (PMID 41257127); Becktell K et al, Pediatr Blood Cancer 2024 (PMID 39010279)
os_amputation_surgery.confidence: moderate -- real data exist but the observed survival gap versus limb-salvage in the smaller study likely reflects tumor-selection bias rather than a true procedure-effectiveness difference

os_radiotherapy_limited_role.name: Radiotherapy (External-Beam) -- Real, Limited-Role Adjunct for Unresectable or Positive-Margin Disease
os_radiotherapy_limited_role.type: Adjunct local-control modality -- 3rd priority per this file's ordering, given osteosarcoma's real relative radioresistance
os_radiotherapy_limited_role.effectiveness: Osteosarcoma is real classically relatively radioresistant compared with radiosensitive paediatric tumors such as Ewing sarcoma, so radiotherapy is real NOT used as primary curative therapy; the NCI PDQ Osteosarcoma Treatment guideline (cancer.gov/types/bone/hp/osteosarcoma-treatment-pdq, accessed 2026-09-24) reserves it for real specific situations where surgical margins are positive or the tumor is truly unresectable (e.g., some axial/pelvic/craniofacial sites), as an adjunct to chemotherapy and whatever surgery is feasible, not as a standalone cure.
os_radiotherapy_limited_role.reason_why: Osteosarcoma cells show relatively poor response to standard photon radiation doses tolerable in normal tissue, so real local control depends primarily on achieving a surgical margin; radiotherapy is added only to reduce the real risk of local recurrence when surgery cannot fully achieve that margin.
os_radiotherapy_limited_role.real_working_solution: Not a substitute for surgery; a real adjunct reserved for unresectable disease or positive margins after best-effort surgery, always combined with systemic MAP chemotherapy.
os_radiotherapy_limited_role.source: NCI PDQ Osteosarcoma Treatment (Health Professional Version), cancer.gov/types/bone/hp/osteosarcoma-treatment-pdq, accessed 2026-09-24
os_radiotherapy_limited_role.confidence: moderate -- the qualitative role (limited, adjunct-only) is well-established standard teaching, but a specific quantitative local-control percentage for radiotherapy in osteosarcoma was not independently pulled from a primary trial this session and is not claimed here

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real 5-year overall survival, real 5-year event-free survival, real 8-week non-progression rate, and one historical baseline) drawn from different populations (localized vs metastatic vs relapsed, paediatric vs adult, single-center vs large international cohort) placed on one comparative scale -- they are NOT a single head-to-head trial and are not in strict competition with one another. Several rows describe complementary, sequential, or alternative parts of the same real curative pathway (chemotherapy backbone -> surgery choice -> adjuncts for higher-risk or relapsed disease) rather than substitutes. The limb-salvage-vs-amputation comparison (rows 1 and 10) is drawn from a real but small single-center study (N=61) and most likely reflects tumor-selection bias (amputation reserved for more locally advanced tumors) rather than a true difference in procedure effectiveness; do not read it as amputation being a worse operation in equivalent tumors.

definition.finding: Osteosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumour whose tumour cells produce osteoid or immature bone; it is the most common primary malignant bone tumour (excluding myeloma/lymphoma of bone). It arises from primitive bone-forming mesenchymal cells, most often at the metaphysis of long bones adjacent to the growth plate.
definition.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, 'The epidemiology of osteosarcoma', Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:3-13 (PMID 20213383)
definition.confidence: high - standard definition from a widely cited review chapter

bimodal_age_distribution.finding: Osteosarcoma has a real, well-documented bimodal age distribution. The first and larger peak occurs in adolescence, specifically the 10-14-year age group, coinciding with the pubertal growth spurt (suggesting a mechanistic link between rapid bone growth and malignant transformation). The second peak occurs in adults older than 65 years; osteosarcoma in this older group is more likely to represent a second malignancy and is frequently related to Paget's disease of bone. This bimodal pattern was confirmed independently in the SEER-based analysis of 3,482 US patients (1973-2004), which found the lowest age-specific incidence (1.7 per million) in the 25-59-year group sandwiched between the two peaks, and a high proportion of Paget-disease-associated and second-cancer cases in the elderly (60-84+ year) group.
bimodal_age_distribution.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:3-13 (PMID 20213383); Mirabello L, Troisi RJ, Savage SA, 'Osteosarcoma incidence and survival rates from 1973 to 2004: data from the SEER Program', Cancer 2009;115(7):1531-43 (PMID 19197972)
bimodal_age_distribution.confidence: high - two independent population-level sources agree

common_sites.finding: Osteosarcoma occurs overwhelmingly in the long bones of the extremities near the metaphyseal growth plates. By anatomic site: femur 42% of cases (75% of femoral tumours are in the distal femur), tibia 19% (80% of tibial tumours are in the proximal tibia), and humerus 10% (90% of humeral tumours are in the proximal humerus). Less common sites are the skull/jaw (8%) and the pelvis (8%). A separate 2009 Hong Kong paediatric cohort (n=51) independently found the distal femur (45%) and proximal tibia (22%) as the two leading sites, closely matching the larger epidemiologic series.
