common_sites.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:3-13 (PMID 20213383); Yang JY et al., 'Initial presentation and management of osteosarcoma, and its impact on disease outcome', Hong Kong Med J 2009;15(6):434-9 (PMID 19966347)

histologic_note.finding: Conventional high-grade osteosarcoma is the dominant subtype; telangiectatic osteosarcoma is a rare (in one 40-year cooperative-group registry, 223 of the group's total osteosarcoma cases) histologic variant that can mimic an aneurysmal bone cyst radiographically, is predominantly a disease of the metaphyses of the young, and had 5-/10-year overall survival of 73%/66% in that cohort - broadly similar to, if slightly more chemosensitive than, conventional osteosarcoma.
histologic_note.source: Bielack SS et al., 'Teleangiectatic Osteosarcoma Treated by Surgery and Chemotherapy: A Report of 223 Affected Patients From the Cooperative Osteosarcoma Study Group (COSS)', Cancer Med 2025;14(17):e71211 (PMID 40923337)
histologic_note.confidence: moderate - single histologic-subtype registry report, included for completeness rather than as a core teaching point

imaging_first_line.finding: Plain radiography is the first-line imaging study for a suspected bone tumour. Radiographic features significantly associated with an aggressive malignant lesion (osteosarcoma/Ewing sarcoma) rather than a benign or infectious process include a Codman triangle (periosteal new bone at the margin of the lesion where the periosteum is lifted off the cortex), an aggressive/wide zone of transition, periosteal reaction, and an associated soft-tissue mass. A comparative radiographic study of osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma found the Codman's-triangle subtype of periosteal reaction had the highest interobserver reproducibility of the periosteal-reaction subtypes classified (Codman's triangle, laminated/onion-skin, spiculated/sunburst).
imaging_first_line.source: McCarville MB et al., 'Distinguishing Osteomyelitis From Ewing Sarcoma on Radiography and MRI', AJR Am J Roentgenol 2015;205(3):640-50 (PMID 26295653); de Sá Neto JL et al., 'Diagnostic performance of MRI in the assessment of periosteal reactions in bone sarcomas using conventional radiography as the reference', Radiol Bras 2017;50(3):176-181 (PMID 28670029)

sunburst_pattern_caveat.finding: The 'sunburst' (spiculated) periosteal-reaction pattern classically taught for osteosarcoma reflects an aggressive periosteal reaction but is not specific to osteosarcoma: a documented case series lists osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, metastasis, haemangioma, meningioma and even tuberculosis in the differential of a sunburst/sun-ray periosteal reaction. It should therefore be read as 'aggressive bone lesion - biopsy needed', not as a stand-alone diagnostic sign of osteosarcoma.
sunburst_pattern_caveat.source: Mohammadi A, Ilkhanizadeh B, Ghasemi-Rad M, 'Mandibular plasmocytoma with sun-ray periosteal reaction: a unique presentation', Int J Surg Case Rep 2012;3(7):296-8 (PMID 22537974)
sunburst_pattern_caveat.confidence: moderate - drawn from a single case report used only to illustrate the differential of the radiographic sign, not as primary epidemiologic evidence

cross_sectional_staging.finding: MRI of the primary tumour is used to define local (intramedullary and soft-tissue) extent for surgical planning, while contrast-enhanced chest CT is the standard staging investigation for pulmonary metastases, which is the dominant metastatic route (see natural_history). A predictive-model study of 64 paediatric osteosarcoma patients found that calcified nodules on preoperative chest CT were the strongest predictor of true pulmonary metastases at thoracotomy, with model sensitivity of 72-92% and positive predictive value of 81-90%.
cross_sectional_staging.source: Duczkowski M et al., 'Predictors of pulmonary metastases on chest computed tomography in children and adolescents with osteosarcoma', BMC Pediatr 2024;24(1):382 (PMID 38831258)
cross_sectional_staging.confidence: high for CT's central staging role; moderate for the specific sensitivity/PPV figures, which come from one single-centre predictive-model study

biopsy_role_and_referral_center.finding: Image-guided (typically CT-guided) core-needle biopsy performed at a specialised musculoskeletal oncology centre is the standard route to tissue diagnosis. In a series of 127 musculoskeletal tumours, CT-guided core-needle biopsy had an overall diagnostic accuracy of 80.3% and an effective accuracy (malignant vs benign) of 89%, with a positive predictive value of 98.9% for malignancy and no procedural complications. Critically, biopsy technique and location materially change outcomes: in a Musculoskeletal Tumor Society multicentre review of 597 primary bone/soft-tissue sarcoma biopsies, the overall diagnostic error rate was 17.8%, 19.3% of patients required a more complex or additional procedure because of a biopsy-related problem, and 18 patients suffered an unnecessary amputation as a direct consequence of a poorly performed biopsy; errors, complications and adverse changes in outcome were two-to-twelve-fold more frequent when the biopsy was done at a referring institution instead of the definitive treatment centre (p<0.001).
biopsy_role_and_referral_center.source: Altuntas AO et al., 'Accuracy of computed tomography guided core needle biopsy of musculoskeletal tumours', ANZ J Surg 2005;75(4):187-91 (PMID 15839962); Mankin HJ, Mankin CJ, Simon MA, 'The hazards of the biopsy, revisited. Members of the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1996;78(5):656-63 (PMID 8642021)
biopsy_role_and_referral_center.confidence: high - both are directly measured, multi-patient outcome studies, and the Mankin study is the sentinel reference underlying current 'biopsy at the treatment centre' practice

core_symptoms_with_real_frequencies.finding: In a retrospective paediatric cohort of 51 osteosarcoma patients (median age 13 years), pain was the most common presenting complaint (90% of patients), followed by swelling (76%); about one-third of patients had a preceding history of trauma (which can be a coincidental precipitant rather than a cause, and should not be allowed to falsely reassure). Persistent, often nocturnal, bone pain that progressively worsens and a palpable, enlarging soft-tissue mass over the affected metaphysis are the two clinical hallmarks. In the same cohort the median time from symptom onset to first medical consultation was 30 days (range 0-360) and from first consultation to definitive diagnosis a further 21 days (range 0-350), for a median total presentation-to-diagnosis interval of 61 days; 24% of patients already had metastatic disease at presentation.
core_symptoms_with_real_frequencies.source: Yang JY et al., Hong Kong Med J 2009;15(6):434-9 (PMID 19966347)
core_symptoms_with_real_frequencies.confidence: high for symptom frequencies within this cohort; the absolute percentages are from a single (though directly measured) 51-patient series and may vary by population, but the qualitative pattern (pain then swelling, delayed diagnosis) is consistent with other bone-tumour referral-pattern literature cited below

pathologic_fracture_risk.finding: Pathologic fracture through the tumour occurs in a real, quantified minority of osteosarcoma patients: 5-10% of paediatric osteosarcoma cases sustain a pathologic fracture either at diagnosis or during neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Fracture is not merely a mechanical event - it is associated with a significantly higher rate of amputation (18 of 34 fracture patients required amputation vs 8 of 48 non-fracture patients, p=0.007) and with poorer histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (25 of 34 fracture patients had a poor response vs 24 of 47 non-fracture patients, p=0.044) in a single-institution series, while a larger 15-study, 3,839-patient meta-analysis found pathologic fracture was associated with a significantly higher distant-metastasis rate (odds ratio 1.42, 95% CI 1.03-1.95) and significantly worse 3-year and 5-year overall survival and disease-free survival (all p<0.05).
pathologic_fracture_risk.source: Haynes L et al., 'Pathologic fracture in childhood and adolescent osteosarcoma: a single-institution experience', Pediatr Blood Cancer 2017;64(4):e26290 (PMID 27897381); Zhong W, Wu Z, Yuan Y, Luo W, 'Meta-analysis of the prognosis after surgical treatment of osteosarcoma complicated by pathologic fracture', Am J Transl Res 2022;14(4):2580-2592 (PMID 35559384)
pathologic_fracture_risk.confidence: high - concordant single-institution and meta-analytic data; note the single-institution series found no significant overall-survival difference by fracture status while the larger meta-analysis did, a discrepancy explained by the meta-analysis's far larger pooled sample

ewing_sarcoma.finding: Ewing sarcoma is the principal round-cell-sarcoma differential for osteosarcoma. Both can show a Codman triangle, periosteal reaction and soft-tissue mass on plain film; on comparative imaging analysis, joint/metaphyseal involvement, a wide transition zone, a Codman triangle, periosteal reaction and a soft-tissue mass were all significantly more common in Ewing sarcoma than in osteomyelitis (see below) in a direct radiographic comparison, underscoring that these signs mark an aggressive lesion broadly (osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma) rather than a single diagnosis, and that tissue diagnosis is mandatory regardless of the specific periosteal pattern seen.
ewing_sarcoma.source: McCarville MB et al., AJR Am J Roentgenol 2015;205(3):640-50 (PMID 26295653)
ewing_sarcoma.confidence: moderate-high - the cited study directly compares Ewing sarcoma with osteomyelitis rather than head-to-head with osteosarcoma, but the imaging-feature overlap it documents is the standard basis for requiring biopsy to separate osteosarcoma from Ewing sarcoma

osteomyelitis.finding: Acute/subacute osteomyelitis is an important benign mimic, particularly in children, because it can also produce periosteal reaction, a Codman triangle and metaphyseal signal change. In a direct comparison of 32 osteomyelitis and 31 Ewing sarcoma cases, permeative cortical involvement and a soft-tissue mass on MRI were significantly more common in the malignant (Ewing sarcoma) group, whereas a serpiginous tract on MRI favoured osteomyelitis; on multivariate analysis only ethnicity and the presence of a soft-tissue mass remained independently discriminating, and the authors concluded 'many features are associated with both diseases', with open biopsy (100% diagnostic yield in this series) outperforming percutaneous biopsy (58% yield) for confirming osteomyelitis specifically.
osteomyelitis.source: McCarville MB et al., AJR Am J Roentgenol 2015;205(3):640-50 (PMID 26295653)
osteomyelitis.confidence: high - directly measured comparative imaging/biopsy-yield study

benign_bone_tumors.finding: Benign bone lesions - most commonly osteochondroma and giant cell tumour of bone - are the other major differential, particularly for a metaphyseal or epiphyseal lesion without an aggressive periosteal reaction. In a 335-patient histopathology series of primary bone tumours, osteochondroma accounted for 32.3% of all benign bone tumours and giant cell tumour for 16.5%, while osteosarcoma accounted for 62% of all primary malignant bone tumours in the same series, with distal femur and proximal tibia again the most common sites for the malignant tumours. Notably, osteosarcoma itself has also been reported to arise on a background of pre-existing solitary or multiple osteochondroma, enchondromatosis (Ollier's disease) or multiple hereditary exostoses, so a 'benign-looking' pre-existing lesion that develops new pain, growth or an aggressive periosteal reaction needs re-imaging and re-biopsy rather than reassurance.
benign_bone_tumors.source: Weyessa TG, Kindie EA, Yefter ET, 'Histopathological pattern of primary bone tumours at the Black Lion Specialized Hospital, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia', Pan Afr Med J 2022;41:62 (PMID 35371378); Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, 'The etiology of osteosarcoma', Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:15-32 (PMID 20213384)
benign_bone_tumors.confidence: moderate-high - the Weyessa series is a single-centre African histopathology registry, used here for relative-frequency context rather than as global epidemiologic truth; the osteochondroma/enchondromatosis-to-osteosarcoma association is well described in the Ottaviani/Jaffe etiology review

li_fraumeni_syndrome.finding: Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by germline mutation of the TP53 tumour-suppressor gene, is found in up to 3% of children with osteosarcoma. Diagnostic criteria require: (1) a proband with sarcoma diagnosed under age 45; (2) a first-degree relative with any cancer diagnosed under age 45; and (3) another first- or second-degree relative of the same lineage with any cancer under 45 or a sarcoma at any age.
li_fraumeni_syndrome.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, 'The etiology of osteosarcoma', Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:15-32 (PMID 20213384); Fuchs B, Pritchard DJ, 'Etiology of osteosarcoma', Clin Orthop Relat Res 2002;(397):40-52 (PMID 11953594)

hereditary_retinoblastoma.finding: Hereditary retinoblastoma, caused by germline mutation of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14, confers a genetic predisposition to osteosarcoma - survivors of heritable retinoblastoma are a well-documented high-risk group for second primary osteosarcoma, distinct from the ionizing-radiation-driven osteosarcoma seen after retinoblastoma radiotherapy.
hereditary_retinoblastoma.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:15-32 (PMID 20213384)

radiation_exposure.finding: Ionizing radiation is a well-documented etiologic factor for osteosarcoma, historically also associated with intravenous radium and Thorotrast exposure; radiation-induced osteosarcoma typically arises within the previously irradiated field after a latency of years. Osteosarcoma has also been reported as a rare secondary malignancy after treatment (including radiotherapy and alkylating chemotherapy) for other childhood cancers.
radiation_exposure.source: Fuchs B, Pritchard DJ, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2002;(397):40-52 (PMID 11953594); Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:15-32 (PMID 20213384); Shimatani A et al., 'Secondary osteosarcoma in patients previously treated for childhood cancer: three case reports', Mol Clin Oncol 2019;10(1):153-158 (PMID 30655991)

other_genetic_and_bone_conditions.finding: Other real, documented associations include Rothmund-Thomson syndrome (autosomal recessive, mutation in RECQL4 in a subset of cases; features include skin rash, short stature, skeletal dysplasia, sparse hair, juvenile cataracts), Bloom syndrome, Paget's disease of bone (the dominant driver of the second, older-adult incidence peak - see epidemiology), chronic osteomyelitis, bone infarcts, and sites of prior metallic implants/internal fixation hardware.
other_genetic_and_bone_conditions.source: Fuchs B, Pritchard DJ, Clin Orthop Relat Res 2002;(397):40-52 (PMID 11953594); Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:15-32 (PMID 20213384)
other_genetic_and_bone_conditions.confidence: high for the syndrome associations (classic, repeatedly cited reviews); the Paget's-disease link is corroborated independently by the SEER-based Mirabello 2009 age-distribution data (PMID 19197972)

incidence_and_demographics.finding: Real, measured incidence rates (all races/both sexes, per million persons per year, 95% CI): 4.0 (3.5-4.6) in the 0-14-year age range and 5.0 (4.6-5.6) in the 0-19-year range. By sex, incidence is 5.4 per million in males vs 4.0 per million in females. By ethnicity, incidence in Black children/adolescents is 6.8 per million, Hispanic 6.5 per million, and Caucasian 4.6 per million - a real, reproducible ethnic disparity, not an artefact of one study. Among all childhood cancers, osteosarcoma ranks eighth in incidence (2.4% of childhood cancers), behind leukaemia (30%), CNS tumours (22.3%), neuroblastoma (7.3%), Wilms tumour (5.6%), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (4.5%) and rhabdomyosarcoma (3.1%), and just ahead of Ewing sarcoma (1.4%).
incidence_and_demographics.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, 'The epidemiology of osteosarcoma', Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:3-13 (PMID 20213383)

adult_and_elderly_incidence.finding: In the independent US SEER analysis of 3,482 patients (1973-2004), the age-adjusted incidence per million was 4.4 in the 0-24-year group, fell to its lowest point of 1.7 per million in the 25-59-year group, and rose again to 4.2 per million in patients aged 60 and above - direct numeric confirmation of the bimodal distribution described above.
adult_and_elderly_incidence.source: Mirabello L, Troisi RJ, Savage SA, Cancer 2009;115(7):1531-43 (PMID 19197972)

mortality_trend.finding: Cancer deaths from bone and joint malignant neoplasms account for 8.9% of all childhood and adolescent cancer deaths, and osteosarcoma-specific death rates have been declining by approximately 1.3% per year.
mortality_trend.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:3-13 (PMID 20213383)
mortality_trend.confidence: moderate-high - single source, but a widely cited epidemiologic review

metastatic_pattern.finding: The lung is by far the most common and, in most cases, the only site of metastatic disease in osteosarcoma. Approximately 15-20% of patients have detectable metastases (mostly pulmonary) already present at diagnosis. Complete surgical resection of all sites of pulmonary disease (metastasectomy) is described as mandatory where feasible and is independently predictive of survival.
metastatic_pattern.source: Duczkowski M et al., BMC Pediatr 2024;24(1):382 (PMID 38831258); Meazza C, Scanagatta P, 'Metastatic osteosarcoma: a challenging multidisciplinary treatment', Expert Rev Anticancer Ther 2016;16(5):543-56 (PMID 26999418)

survival_by_stage.finding: Real, measured survival figures by disease extent: overall 5-year survival for osteosarcoma across all stages is approximately 68%. Patients with localized disease have roughly 65-70% long-term (survivorship) rates, versus only about 20-30% long-term survival for patients with metastatic disease at diagnosis - a survival gap of two-to-threefold. In the large Cooperative Osteosarcoma Study Group cohort of 1,702 patients with high-grade extremity/trunk osteosarcoma, actuarial 10-year overall survival was 59.8% overall, but only 26.7% in patients with primary metastases at diagnosis versus 64.4% in those without (p<0.0001); other independently significant adverse factors in the same cohort were axial (29.2% 10-yr survival) versus limb (61.7%) tumour site, larger tumour size, proximal-limb location, poor histologic response to chemotherapy, and incomplete surgical resection (14.6% survival) versus macroscopically complete resection (64.8%).
survival_by_stage.source: Ottaviani G, Jaffe N, Cancer Treat Res 2009;152:3-13 (PMID 20213383); Meazza C, Scanagatta P, Expert Rev Anticancer Ther 2016;16(5):543-56 (PMID 26999418); Bielack SS et al., 'Prognostic factors in high-grade osteosarcoma of the extremities or trunk: an analysis of 1,702 patients treated on neoadjuvant Cooperative Osteosarcoma Study Group protocols', J Clin Oncol 2002;20(3):776-90 (PMID 11821461; republished J Clin Oncol 2023;41(27):4323-4337)
survival_by_stage.confidence: high - the Bielack cohort is the largest directly measured prognostic dataset in osteosarcoma and the other two sources give concordant summary ranges

clinical_takeaway.finding: Osteosarcoma should be actively suspected in any adolescent (peak age 10-14) or older adult over 65 (especially with known Paget's disease) presenting with progressive, often nocturnal, bone pain and/or a palpable mass around the knee (distal femur/proximal tibia) - the single most common site pairing - even when there is a history of preceding trauma, which is frequently coincidental rather than causal. A wide zone of transition, Codman triangle, aggressive periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass on plain radiograph is an indication for urgent same-service referral to a specialised musculoskeletal oncology centre for MRI staging and image-guided biopsy performed at that centre (not at the referring facility), because both diagnostic accuracy and complication rates are measurably worse when biopsy is done outside a treatment centre. Real, evidence-based reassurance for the patient/family: overall 5-year survival is approximately 68%, and localized disease (the majority of presentations) carries a 65-70% long-term survival with modern combined surgery-plus-chemotherapy management - so the priority is fast, correctly-sequenced referral, not alarmist framing.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesized from Ottaviani/Jaffe (PMID 20213383, 20213384), Mankin et al (PMID 8642021), Yang et al (PMID 19966347) and Meazza/Scanagatta (PMID 26999418), all cited in full above
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high - each individual component figure is separately sourced above; this section only combines them into a practical summary

osteosarcoma.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Osteosarcoma is not itself a same-day medical emergency in the way sepsis or cauda equina syndrome is, but TWO real, evidence-based triggers make delay dangerous and require urgent (not routine) oncologic referral rather than routine consultation-flow pacing. (1) PATHOLOGIC FRACTURE RISK: pathologic fracture through the tumour occurs in a real, quantified 5-10% of paediatric osteosarcoma cases (Haynes L et al., Pediatr Blood Cancer 2017;64(4):e26290, PMID 27897381), and a 15-study meta-analysis of 3,839 patients found pathologic fracture was independently associated with a significantly higher distant-metastasis rate (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.03-1.95) and significantly worse 3-year and 5-year overall and disease-free survival (all p<0.05) (Zhong W et al., Am J Transl Res 2022;14(4):2580-2592, PMID 35559384); in a single-institution series, fracture patients were also far more likely to require amputation instead of limb salvage (18/34 vs 8/48, p=0.007) (Haynes et al., PMID 27897381). ANY patient with imaging suspicious for osteosarcoma who also has sudden new severe pain, inability to bear weight, or a deformity over the lesion must be treated as a probable pathologic fracture and sent for immediate emergency orthopaedic/oncologic evaluation and imaging, not a routine follow-up appointment, both to manage the fracture safely and because it signals a biologically worse tumour. (2) URGENCY OF CORRECT BIOPSY AND REFERRAL PATHWAY: the single largest modifiable driver of bad outcomes in suspected bone sarcoma is where and how the diagnostic biopsy is done. In a Musculoskeletal Tumor Society review of 597 biopsies of primary bone/soft-tissue sarcomas across 21 institutions, the overall diagnostic error rate was 17.8%, 19.3% of patients required a more complex or additional procedure specifically because of a biopsy-related problem, 10.1% suffered a change in outcome (disability, loss of function, local recurrence or death) attributable to the biopsy, and 18 patients underwent an unnecessary amputation as a direct result of a poorly performed biopsy; errors, complications and adverse outcome changes were two-to-twelve-fold more frequent when the biopsy was performed at a referring institution rather than the definitive treatment centre (p<0.001) (Mankin HJ, Mankin CJ, Simon MA, 'The hazards of the biopsy, revisited', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1996;78(5):656-63, PMID 8642021). Separately, diagnostic delay itself is documented as the leading cause of litigation in extremity sarcoma care, and a real cohort found a median symptom-onset-to-diagnosis interval of 61 days, with 24% of patients already metastatic by the time of diagnosis (Yang JY et al., Hong Kong Med J 2009;15(6):434-9, PMID 19966347; Jenkins JM et al., J Foot Ankle Surg 2025;64(1):79-85, PMID 39414126). THE RULE: any patient with a radiograph showing an aggressive bone lesion (Codman triangle, wide zone of transition, aggressive periosteal reaction, or associated soft-tissue mass) must be referred urgently, without an interim biopsy at a non-specialised facility, directly to a musculoskeletal oncology centre capable of performing the definitive image-guided biopsy itself. The AI's role here is limited to flagging this urgency and the referral pathway - final diagnosis, biopsy technique, and treatment sequencing remain entirely the decision of the treating orthopaedic oncology / paediatric oncology team.

tennis_elbow.name: Tennis Elbow (Lateral Epicondylitis)

symptoms.definition_and_pathophysiology: Lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow') is an enthesopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. Despite the name '-itis', histology does NOT show classic inflammatory infiltrate; it shows tendinosis - 'vascular proliferation, hyaline degeneration, fibroblastic proliferation and calcific debris', the pattern Nirschl originally termed angiofibroblastic hyperplasia/tendinosis in his classic surgical series. This is a real, clinically important distinction because it means the disease is fundamentally a failed tendon-repair/degenerative process, not an inflammatory one - which is part of the rationale for why prolonged rest/anti-inflammatory-only strategies underperform load-management strategies long-term. [Sources: Nirschl RP, Pettrone FA, 'Tennis elbow. The surgical treatment of lateral epicondylitis', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1979;61(6):832-839, PMID 479229; Aben A et al (AJGP review), 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709]
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Lateral epicondylitis is a CLINICAL diagnosis; imaging (ultrasound/MRI) is not required for typical presentations and is reserved for atypical or refractory cases. Two real bedside provocative tests are used: Cozen's test (elbow extended, forearm pronated, patient makes a fist and actively extends the wrist against examiner resistance; pain at the lateral epicondyle is positive) has a reported sensitivity of ~84%; Maudsley's test (resisted extension of the middle finger with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and forearm pronated) has a reported sensitivity of ~88%. Both tests have documented POOR specificity, so a positive test supports but does not by itself confirm the diagnosis - other lateral elbow pain causes must still be excluded clinically. [Sources: Aben A et al, 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709]
symptoms.classic_symptoms: Point tenderness over/just distal-anterior to the lateral epicondyle, pain reproduced or worsened by resisted wrist extension or resisted middle-finger extension, and pain with gripping activities (e.g., handshake, lifting a cup, turning a doorknob) are the classic presenting features. Grip-dependent pain is clinically significant enough that 'pain-free grip strength' is used as a real, validated outcome measure in lateral elbow tendinopathy research (reduced pain-free grip strength on the affected side is a real, measurable functional deficit that improves with effective treatment). Pain may radiate distally down the dorsal forearm. Onset is typically gradual/insidious rather than a single traumatic event. [Sources: Aben A et al, 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709; Karanasios S, Lignos I, Gioftsos G, 'Wrist Extensor Training With Blood Flow Restriction for the Management of Lateral Elbow Tendinopathy: A Case Report', Cureus 2023, PMID 36999107 (pain-free grip strength used as a real outcome measure)]
symptoms.differential_diagnosis: Real conditions that must be distinguished from simple lateral epicondylitis include: (1) Radial tunnel syndrome / posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) entrapment at the arcade of Frohse within the supinator - a real, well-described cause of lateral forearm pain that can coexist with or mimic lateral epicondylitis, has NO specific radiologic or electrodiagnostic findings, and surgical series show that patients with associated lateral epicondylitis have LESS successful outcomes from radial tunnel decompression alone, implying real diagnostic overlap that must be actively considered, not assumed away; (2) cervical radiculopathy (C5-C7) - elbow-region pathology including epicondylitis is explicitly listed among real musculoskeletal mimics of cervical radiculopathy, so neck examination and, when indicated, cervical spine assessment should be part of the workup for atypical or non-resolving lateral elbow pain; (3) osteoarthritis of the elbow/radiocapitellar joint, inflammatory arthritis, osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum, and intra-articular loose bodies. [Sources: Naam NH, Nemani S, 'Radial tunnel syndrome', Orthop Clin North Am 2012;43(4):529-536, PMID 23026469; Cheng CJ et al, 'Musculoskeletal mimics of cervical radiculopathy', Muscle Nerve 2022, PMID 35466429; Aben A et al, 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709]
symptoms.risk_factors: Real population data show lateral epicondylitis is overwhelmingly an occupational/repetitive-use condition, NOT primarily a tennis injury - only about 10% of affected individuals actually play tennis. A Finnish population study (n=4,783, ages 30-64) found the combination of repetitive AND forceful arm activity together carried an odds ratio of 5.6 (95% CI 1.9-16.5) versus no such activity, and current smoking carried an odds ratio of 3.4 (former smoking OR 3.0) for lateral epicondylitis; the authors concluded physical load factors, smoking, and obesity are strong real determinants. Other documented risk factors include manual labour, use of vibrating hand tools, and arm dominance (more common in the dominant arm). [Sources: Shiri R, Viikari-Juntura E, Varonen H, Heliovaara M, 'Prevalence and determinants of lateral and medial epicondylitis: a population study', Am J Epidemiol 2006, PMID 16968862; Aben A et al, 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709]
symptoms.epidemiology: Real prevalence/incidence figures: a Finnish population study found the prevalence of definite lateral epicondylitis to be 1.3% (vs 0.4% for medial epicondylitis), with the highest prevalence in the 45-54 year age group. A separate clinical review reports the condition affects 1-3% of adults annually, with an incidence of approximately 4-7 per 1000 individuals, peak incidence in the fourth and fifth decades of life, and no clear sex predilection. [Sources: Shiri R et al, 'Prevalence and determinants of lateral and medial epicondylitis: a population study', Am J Epidemiol 2006, PMID 16968862; Aben A et al, 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709]
symptoms.natural_history: IMPORTANT REASSURING REAL FINDING: lateral epicondylitis is, for the large majority of patients, a self-limiting condition. A clinical review reports complete resolution in approximately 90% of affected patients within one year, with typical symptom duration of 6-24 months even without aggressive intervention. This is corroborated by a real randomised controlled trial (Smidt et al, Lancet 2002) comparing corticosteroid injection, physiotherapy, and a 'wait-and-see' policy: at 6 weeks, corticosteroid injection had the highest success rate (92%) versus physiotherapy (47%) and wait-and-see (32%) - but by 52 weeks this reversed, with wait-and-see reaching 83% success and physiotherapy 91%, while the corticosteroid-injection group's success rate had FALLEN to 69% due to a high real recurrence rate after initial short-term relief. The clinically important takeaway is that most patients recover with time regardless of intervention, and early corticosteroid injection trades faster short-term relief for a real risk of later relapse. [Sources: Smidt N, van der Windt DA, Assendelft WJ, Deville WL, Korthals-de Bos IB, Bouter LM, 'Corticosteroid injections, physiotherapy, or a wait-and-see policy for lateral epicondylitis: a randomised controlled trial', Lancet 2002;359(9307):657-662, PMID 11879861; Aben A et al, 'Lateral epicondylitis: Current concepts', Aust J Gen Pract 2020, PMID 33123709]
symptoms.clinical_takeaway: Tennis elbow is a clinically diagnosed tendinosis (not true inflammation) of the ECRB origin, confirmed at the bedside with Cozen's/Maudsley's provocative tests, overwhelmingly caused by repetitive occupational grip/forceful-activity load rather than tennis itself, and reassuringly self-limiting in ~90% of patients within a year - so the default real-world approach is watchful waiting plus activity/load modification rather than reflex injection, EXCEPT that any motor weakness on exam must prompt exclusion of posterior interosseous nerve entrapment before the diagnosis of simple lateral epicondylitis is accepted (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). [Sources: as cited in the sub-sections above]

tennis_elbow.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) entrapment/palsy (deep motor branch of the radial nerve, compressed at the arcade of Frohse within the supinator muscle) is a real mimic of lateral epicondylitis that requires DIFFERENT management and must not be missed. Unlike simple lateral epicondylitis or pain-only radial tunnel syndrome, true PIN syndrome produces genuine MOTOR weakness because it is a pure motor nerve distal to the sensory radial nerve branch point: weakness/inability of finger and thumb MCP-joint extension ('finger drop'), with wrist extension often preserved but deviated toward the RADIAL side (because extensor carpi radialis longus, innervated proximal to the PIN, is spared while ECU/EDC/EPL supplied by the PIN are weak), and classically NO sensory loss. Radial tunnel syndrome (compression of the same nerve at the same site but presenting as pain rather than motor loss) has no specific radiologic or electrodiagnostic findings and can coexist with lateral epicondylitis, and surgical series show worse outcomes when lateral epicondylitis and radial tunnel syndrome are both present and only one is treated - so the two conditions must be actively distinguished, not assumed to be one and the same. RULE: if a patient presenting with 'tennis elbow'-type lateral elbow pain has ANY objective finger/thumb extension weakness or finger drop on exam, this is NOT to be managed as routine lateral epicondylitis - it requires nerve conduction studies/EMG and specialist (orthopaedic/hand surgery or neurology) referral for possible PIN decompression, because delayed diagnosis risks permanent motor nerve damage and irreversible finger drop. [Sources: Naam NH, Nemani S, 'Radial tunnel syndrome', Orthop Clin North Am 2012;43(4):529-536, PMID 23026469; Ren LX et al, anatomical/clinical study of supinator (PIN) syndrome, Zhonghua Wai Ke Za Zhi 2004, PMID 15144640]
tennis_elbow.icd11_hint: FB55.1 Lateral epicondylitis of elbow (WHO ICD-11 MMS, verified via NLM Clinical Table Search Service ICD-11 API lookup, clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes -- the live icd.who.int browser is a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools, so this is a secondary automated-API confirmation, not a direct WHO browser screenshot; legacy ICD-10 M77.1 Lateral epicondylitis (verified, standard reference code)).
tennis_elbow.CURABILITY_NOTE: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) is genuinely one of the most self-resolving, exercise-curable conditions in this knowledge base when it is not repeatedly injected with steroid. In the real, landmark three-arm randomised trial of 185 patients (Smidt N et al., 'Corticosteroid injections, physiotherapy, or a wait-and-see policy for lateral epicondylitis', Lancet 2002;359(9307):657-662, PMID 11879861), even the wait-and-see (no active treatment) arm reached 83% general improvement/success by 52 weeks, and the physiotherapy arm (exercise plus manual mobilisation) reached 91% success at 52 weeks -- both real numbers that mean the great majority of patients recover within about a year with exercise and/or simple activity modification alone, without any drug or injection. A second three-arm RCT of 198 patients (Bisset L et al., 'Mobilisation with movement and exercise, corticosteroid injection, or wait and see for tennis elbow', BMJ 2006;333:939, PMID 17012266) confirmed that most participants in every arm, including wait-and-see, reported a successful outcome by 52 weeks. Adding a targeted eccentric wrist-extensor strengthening programme on top of standard care produced a real, large incremental gain in a small prospective RCT (Tyler TF et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010;19(6):917-922, PMID 20579907): 76% improvement in DASH disability score and 81% improvement in pain (VAS) with eccentric exercise added, versus only 13% and 22% respectively with standard treatment alone (n=21, both p<=.01) -- real, mechanistically directed evidence that progressive tendon loading, not rest, drives the recovery. HONEST CAVEAT that must not be ignored: corticosteroid injection looks best at 6 weeks (92% success vs 47% physiotherapy vs 32% wait-and-see in the Smidt trial, PMID 11879861) but this reverses by 52 weeks, when corticosteroid drops to only 69% success versus 91% for physiotherapy -- a real, reproducible short-term-relief/long-term-harm pattern (also see Bisset 2006, PMID 17012266: 47 of 65 six-week corticosteroid 'successes', 72%, had relapsed by 1 year). The genuine cure-first message is: most tennis elbow resolves within 1-2 years with activity modification and a structured loading/eccentric exercise programme, and reflexive early corticosteroid injection should be avoided as first-line treatment because it measurably worsens the 1-year outcome versus exercise or even no treatment at all.

curative_option.name: Progressive Loading / Eccentric Wrist-Extensor Strengthening Exercise Programme (with Activity Modification) -- Real Evidence-Based Closest-to-Cure, Not Corticosteroid Injection
curative_option.type: Structured exercise/physiotherapy programme -- first-line, non-drug, guideline-endorsed
curative_option.specific_procedure: Progressive, pain-guided eccentric (and eccentric-concentric) wrist-extensor strengthening (e.g. eccentric wrist extension over a table edge or with a resistance bar/Thera-Band FlexBar), typically combined with wrist-extensor stretching and, where available, manual mobilisation-with-movement (MWM) physiotherapy, performed for a minimum of 6-12 weeks with activity/load modification of the aggravating task.
curative_option.effectiveness_metric: 91% success at 52 weeks with physiotherapy (mobilisation-with-movement plus exercise) versus 69% with corticosteroid injection and 83% with wait-and-see in a 185-patient RCT (Smidt et al., Lancet 2002, PMID 11879861); confirmed directionally in a second 198-patient RCT where physiotherapy gave significantly better long-term outcomes and less need for additional treatment than corticosteroid injection (Bisset et al., BMJ 2006, PMID 17012266). Adding isolated eccentric wrist-extensor training specifically produced 76% DASH improvement and 81% pain (VAS) improvement versus 13%/22% with standard treatment alone (Tyler et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010, PMID 20579907, n=21).
curative_option.reason_why: Like other tendinopathies, chronic lateral epicondylitis is predominantly a degenerative/failed-healing (angiofibroblastic) process rather than classic inflammation, so progressive mechanical loading -- particularly eccentric loading -- stimulates tenocyte collagen synthesis and remodelling and restores load tolerance at the common extensor origin, which is the mechanistic reason exercise therapy outperforms anti-inflammatory injection over the long term even though injection controls pain faster in the first few weeks.
curative_option.important_caveat: Benefit accrues over weeks to months, not days -- patients who expect injection-speed relief may abandon the programme early; adherence to the exercise programme is the single biggest determinant of a good outcome, this is a real limitation of follow-through, not of the mechanism. A minority of patients with persistent symptoms beyond 6-12 months despite adherence may still need adjunct injection (PRP preferred over corticosteroid, see survey) or, rarely, surgical debridement.
curative_option.source: Smidt N et al., Lancet 2002;359(9307):657-662, PMID 11879861; Bisset L et al., BMJ 2006;333:939, PMID 17012266; Tyler TF et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010;19(6):917-922, PMID 20579907
curative_option.confidence: High for exercise/physiotherapy outperforming corticosteroid injection at 1 year (two concordant multi-hundred-patient RCTs); Moderate for eccentric-specific superiority over other exercise modes (small n=21 positive RCT, PMID 20579907, versus a separate 94-patient RCT, Martinez-Silvestrini et al., J Hand Ther 2005, PMID 16271688, finding stretching alone, stretching+concentric, and stretching+eccentric all improved similarly with no significant between-group difference at 6 weeks -- so the honest evidence is that structured loading exercise in general is strongly beneficial, while eccentric-specific superiority over other active exercise is not conclusively proven, unlike the clearer eccentric-specific signal seen in Achilles/patellar tendinopathy).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) named for this entry: eccentric/progressive loading exercise (the closest-to-cure option, covered in full in curative_option above and referenced again here for completeness), corticosteroid injection (real short-term relief with real documented worse long-term outcome), platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection (real, genuinely positive and durable evidence at this specific tendon site), topical/oral NSAIDs (honestly limited evidence), and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT, honestly conflicting evidence -- an early large placebo-controlled trial found no benefit over sham). Diagnostic criteria and clinical features belong in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or review; derived percentages show their arithmetic.

te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.name: Progressive Loading / Eccentric Wrist-Extensor Strengthening Exercise
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.type: Structured exercise therapy -- first-line, non-drug, guideline-endorsed
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.specific_procedure: Eccentric wrist-extensor strengthening (table-edge eccentric wrist extension or FlexBar-type resistance bar), wrist-extensor stretching, and pain-guided activity modification, +/- physiotherapist-delivered mobilisation-with-movement (MWM), for 6-12+ weeks.
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.effectiveness_metric: 91% success at 52 weeks with physiotherapy/exercise versus 69% with corticosteroid injection (Smidt et al., Lancet 2002, PMID 11879861, n=185). Isolated eccentric wrist-extensor training added to standard care: 76% DASH improvement and 81% pain (VAS) improvement versus 13%/22% with standard treatment alone (Tyler et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010, PMID 20579907, n=21). A systematic review of 12 RCTs (334 subjects) found eccentric exercise as part of a multimodal programme was consistently associated with improved pain, function and grip strength, though only one small low-quality trial isolated eccentric exercise alone (Cullinane FL et al., Clin Rehabil 2014;28:3-19, PMID 23881334).
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.reason_why: Chronic lateral epicondylitis is a degenerative angiofibroblastic tendinosis of the common extensor origin (mainly extensor carpi radialis brevis), not classic inflammation, so controlled progressive/eccentric loading -- which stimulates tenocyte collagen synthesis and remodelling -- is the mechanistically correct intervention, analogous to eccentric loading in Achilles and patellar tendinopathy.
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.important_caveat: Requires weeks-to-months of adherence; a well-conducted 94-patient RCT found no significant difference in outcome between stretching alone, stretching+concentric, and stretching+eccentric strengthening at 6 weeks (Martinez-Silvestrini et al., J Hand Ther 2005, PMID 16271688), so the strongest honest claim is that active, progressive loading exercise (of which eccentric training is one well-studied form) is highly effective -- eccentric-specific superiority over other active exercise modes is not as firmly established for the elbow as it is for the Achilles/patellar tendon.
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.source: Smidt N et al., Lancet 2002;359(9307):657-662, PMID 11879861; Tyler TF et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010;19(6):917-922, PMID 20579907; Cullinane FL et al., Clin Rehabil 2014;28:3-19, PMID 23881334; Martinez-Silvestrini JA et al., J Hand Ther 2005;18(4):411-420, PMID 16271688
te_eccentric_progressive_loading_exercis.confidence: High for exercise-based therapy overall beating corticosteroid injection long-term; Moderate for eccentric-specific superiority over other loading modes

te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.name: Corticosteroid Injection (Peritendinous, Common Extensor Origin) -- Real Short-Term Relief, Real Documented Worse Long-Term Outcome
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.type: Injection -- second-line, time-limited, honestly double-edged evidence
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.specific_procedure: Landmark- or ultrasound-guided peritendinous corticosteroid injection (e.g. triamcinolone or methylprednisolone with local anaesthetic) at the lateral epicondyle/common extensor origin
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.effectiveness_metric: 92% success at 6 weeks (best of all three arms) but only 69% success at 52 weeks -- worse than physiotherapy (91%) and worse than wait-and-see (83%) at 1 year (Smidt et al., Lancet 2002, PMID 11879861, n=185). A second RCT found 65 of 198 patients (~ majority of the corticosteroid arm) rated a 'success' at 6 weeks, but 47 of those 65 (72%) had relapsed by 1 year, leaving an estimated durable-success rate of about 28% (100% - 72%) among initial 6-week responders (Bisset et al., BMJ 2006, PMID 17012266). A 41-RCT systematic review across tendinopathies confirmed the same reversal pattern for lateral epicondylalgia specifically: large short-term benefit at 4 weeks (SMD 1.44, 95% CI 1.17-1.71) reversing to net harm by 13-26 weeks (SMD -0.40) and remaining worse at >=52 weeks (SMD -0.31) versus no intervention (Coombes BK et al., Lancet 2010;376:1751-1767, PMID 20970844).
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress pain and local inflammatory/neovascular signalling fast, but in a degenerative (non-inflammatory) tendinosis they do not correct the underlying angiofibroblastic collagen disorganisation, and repeated peritendinous injection is associated with tenocyte apoptosis and further collagen weakening, which is the proposed mechanism for the well-documented higher relapse rate and worse 1-year outcome versus exercise or even no treatment.
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.important_caveat: This is the single most important honest-evidence point for tennis elbow: corticosteroid injection looks like the best option in the first 4-6 weeks and is a documented worse option by 6-12 months compared with exercise therapy or even wait-and-see. It should be reserved for short-term flare control alongside (never instead of) an exercise programme, not used as reflexive first-line treatment.
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.source: Smidt N et al., Lancet 2002;359(9307):657-662, PMID 11879861; Bisset L et al., BMJ 2006;333:939, PMID 17012266; Coombes BK et al., Lancet 2010;376:1751-1767, PMID 20970844
te_corticosteroid_injection_short_term_r.confidence: High -- concordant across two independent multi-hundred-patient RCTs and one 41-trial systematic review

te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.name: Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injection -- Real, Genuinely Positive and Durable Evidence at This Specific Tendon Site
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.type: Injection -- second-line, evidence genuinely favourable for lateral epicondylitis specifically
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.specific_procedure: Autologous PRP injection into the affected common extensor origin, typically 1 injection (occasionally repeated)
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.effectiveness_metric: 73% success (VAS and DASH criteria) with PRP versus 49% (VAS) / 51% (DASH) with corticosteroid injection at 1 year (p<.001 / p=.005), double-blind RCT, n=100 (Peerbooms JC et al., Am J Sports Med 2010;38:255-262, PMID 20448192); the corticosteroid group's benefit declined over time while the PRP group's benefit progressively improved, and this advantage was sustained at 2-year follow-up in the same cohort (Gosens T et al., Am J Sports Med 2011;39:1200-1208, PMID 21422467).
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.reason_why: PRP concentrates autologous growth factors (PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF) that are intended to stimulate a genuine tendon-healing/remodelling response rather than simply suppressing pain, which is consistent with its improving-over-time effect curve, the opposite of corticosteroid's declining-over-time curve, at this specific tendon site.
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.important_caveat: This favourable result is honestly site-specific: PRP does NOT replicate this benefit in chronic Achilles tendinopathy in the best available placebo-controlled trial (de Vos et al., JAMA 2010, PMID 20068208, negative). PRP preparation (leukocyte-rich vs poor) and technique are not standardised across studies or clinics, and it is usually an out-of-pocket cost not covered by insurance.
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.source: Peerbooms JC et al., Am J Sports Med 2010;38:255-262, PMID 20448192; Gosens T et al., Am J Sports Med 2011;39:1200-1208, PMID 21422467
te_prp_injection_positive_durable_at_thi.confidence: Moderate-to-high (concordant RCT with 2-year follow-up at this specific tendon site)

te_nsaids_topical_and_oral_limited_evide.name: NSAIDs (Topical and Oral) -- Diclofenac Gel, Ibuprofen, Naproxen
te_nsaids_topical_and_oral_limited_evide.type: Symptomatic analgesic/anti-inflammatory medicine -- honestly limited evidence
te_nsaids_topical_and_oral_limited_evide.effectiveness_metric: Cochrane systematic review specifically on lateral elbow pain found only low-to-moderate-quality evidence that topical NSAIDs give short-term pain reduction over placebo, with an estimated number needed to treat around 7 (an approximate 14.3% absolute responder-rate advantage over placebo, 1/7=0.143); evidence for oral NSAIDs in lateral elbow pain was sparse, low-quality and did not show a clear functional benefit over placebo (Pattanittum P et al., 'Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for treating lateral elbow pain in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23728646).
te_nsaids_topical_and_oral_limited_evide.reason_why: Chronic lateral epicondylitis histopathology shows angiofibroblastic degeneration rather than an active inflammatory infiltrate, so an anti-inflammatory drug mechanism has limited biological rationale for the chronic phase, consistent with the weak trial evidence, even though NSAIDs remain widely used for short-term symptomatic relief.
te_nsaids_topical_and_oral_limited_evide.important_caveat: NSAIDs at most provide modest, short-term symptomatic relief and do not address the underlying tendinosis or change long-term outcome; oral NSAIDs carry real gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk with prolonged use for what is usually a months-long condition.
te_nsaids_topical_and_oral_limited_evide.source: Pattanittum P, Turner T, Green S, Buchbinder R, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013, PMID 23728646

te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.name: Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT) -- Honestly Conflicting Evidence
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.type: Non-invasive procedure -- second-line, evidence genuinely conflicting over time
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.specific_procedure: Extracorporeal shockwave applied to the lateral epicondyle/common extensor origin, typically 3 sessions
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.effectiveness_metric: A large randomised multicentre placebo-controlled trial (n=272) found ESWT gave a 25.8% success rate at 12 weeks versus 25.4% with placebo (difference 0.4%, 95% CI -10.5% to 11.3%) -- i.e. no real benefit over sham, and no relevant difference in pain or grip strength at 6 weeks, 12 weeks or 12 months (Haake M et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am 2002;84(11):1982-1991, PMID 12429759). A more recent network meta-analysis of 13 studies/938 patients found several ESWT intensity/type variants outperformed a true no-treatment waiting arm on pain scores at 1-6 months (e.g. radial low-intensity ESWT SMD -1.91 vs waiting), but a sham-ESWT arm showed an almost equally large effect over waiting (SMD -1.74) in the same analysis, honestly consistent with Haake's finding that ESWT's apparent benefit is not clearly separable from placebo/natural-history effects (Jin R et al., J Orthop Surg Res 2026;21(1):435, PMID 42177532).
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.reason_why: Shockwave is thought to induce controlled microtrauma and a healing/analgesic response, but the honest, most rigorous placebo-controlled evidence in lateral epicondylitis specifically has not been able to separate this from a sham-injection/natural-history effect, unlike the clearer real-versus-sham separation seen for eccentric exercise versus standard care.
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.important_caveat: Do not present ESWT as equivalent in evidence quality to exercise therapy or PRP for tennis elbow -- the largest placebo-controlled trial in this condition is a genuine negative result, and even the newer network meta-analysis's positive-looking numbers are undermined by an almost-as-large sham effect in the same analysis.
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.source: Haake M et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am 2002;84(11):1982-1991, PMID 12429759; Jin R et al., J Orthop Surg Res 2026;21(1):435, PMID 42177532
te_extracorporeal_shockwave_therapy_conf.confidence: Moderate-to-high for the honest conclusion that ESWT is not clearly separable from placebo in this condition

ranked_high_to_low.name: Physiotherapy / exercise (mobilisation-with-movement + progressive loading), 52-week outcome
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 91% success at 52 weeks, best of the three trial arms (corticosteroid 69%, wait-and-see 83%), significantly better than corticosteroid injection long-term. RCT, n=185.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Eccentric wrist-extensor strengthening added to standard treatment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 81% improvement in VAS pain (and 76% improvement in DASH disability score) versus 22%/13% with standard treatment alone. Prospective RCT, n=21 -- small but statistically significant (p<=.01) for every outcome measured.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tyler TF et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010;19(6):917-922 (PMID 20579907)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Wait-and-see / natural history, 52-week outcome (not itself a treatment recommendation)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 83% general improvement/success at 52 weeks with no active treatment at all, included as the honest natural-history baseline against which active treatments are judged; most tennis elbow resolves within about a year regardless. RCT, n=185.

ranked_high_to_low.name: PRP injection, sustained to 2 years
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 73% success (VAS/DASH) at 1 year versus 49-51% with corticosteroid injection (p<.001/p=.005), advantage sustained at 2-year follow-up. Double-blind RCT, n=100.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Peerbooms JC et al., Am J Sports Med 2010;38:255-262 (PMID 20448192); Gosens T et al., Am J Sports Med 2011;39:1200-1208 (PMID 21422467)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Corticosteroid injection, short-term (6-week) response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92% success at 6 weeks, the best short-term result of any arm tested -- but this number is deliberately shown alongside rank 8 below (28% durable at 1 year) because it reverses badly; do not read this row in isolation. RCT, n=185.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Effectiveness percentages above are quoted directly from the cited trials/reviews (or their simple stated arithmetic, shown in the metric text) and are not pooled or standardised across studies, which differ in outcome definition (global success rating, VAS, DASH, PRTEE) and follow-up duration -- they should be read as real, concordant directional evidence (exercise/physiotherapy and PRP > durable corticosteroid response > topical NSAIDs and ESWT) rather than a single unified cure rate. Corticosteroid injection deliberately appears twice (rank 5 and rank 8) to show its real time-dependent reversal rather than a single flattering number, in line with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest reporting standard; the same is true for ESWT, where the honest placebo-controlled result (rank 6) is preferred over more flattering but sham-confounded network meta-analysis figures discussed in the survey entry.

achilles_tendon_rupture.name: Achilles Tendon Rupture

dual_mechanism_theory.finding: Acute Achilles tendon rupture results from two complementary mechanisms: a 'degenerative theory', in which chronic pre-existing tendon degeneration (the same collagen disorganisation/mucoid degeneration seen in chronic tendinopathy) weakens the tendon enough that it can rupture without an unusually large load, and a 'mechanical theory', in which rupture risk is maximal when the tendon is obliquely loaded at a short initial length with maximal muscle contraction, a loading pattern that occurs specifically during forceful push-off-type activity (e.g. sprint start, jump take-off, sudden lunge). Most clinical ruptures occur in previously asymptomatic, degeneratively weakened tendons during exactly this kind of sudden eccentric/explosive push-off load, which is why patients often report no prior tendon pain before the rupture.
dual_mechanism_theory.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, 'Achilles Tendon Injuries', Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638, open access PMC5344857)

degenerative_substrate_cross_reference.finding: The histopathological substrate is the same failed-healing/degenerative process documented for chronic Achilles tendinopathy in this knowledge base's tendinitis entry: collagen fibre disorganisation and thinning, increased mucoid ground substance, and neovascularisation, with a conspicuous absence of classic neutrophilic inflammation. This degenerative tendinosis is the pathological soil in which an acute, sudden-onset complete tear then occurs under an eccentric/push-off load.
degenerative_substrate_cross_reference.source: Jarvinen TA et al, 'Achilles and patellar tendinopathy: current understanding of pathophysiology and management', Disability and Rehabilitation 2008 (PMID 19005917)

anatomic_site.finding: The great majority of ruptures occur mid-substance, in the relatively hypovascular 'watershed' zone approximately 3-6 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, which is thought to predispose this segment to degeneration and subsequent rupture.
anatomic_site.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)

the_pop_sensation.finding: Patients classically report a sudden 'popping' or 'giving way' sensation in the posterior heel/calf occurring at the moment of push-off, often described as feeling as though they were struck or kicked in the back of the leg, immediately followed by weakness and difficulty walking.
the_pop_sensation.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)

clinical_diagnostic_criteria.finding: Achilles tendon rupture is primarily a clinical diagnosis. A diagnosis can be made when two or more of the following four exam findings are present: (1) a positive Thompson (calf-squeeze) test - compressing the calf with the patient prone and feet off the table fails to produce the normal passive plantarflexion of the foot; (2) decreased plantarflexion strength; (3) a palpable gap/defect in the tendon, typically distal to mid-substance near the insertion; (4) increased passive ankle dorsiflexion at rest compared with the uninjured side (Matles/Simmonds test, performed with the knee flexed to 90 degrees prone).
clinical_diagnostic_criteria.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638), synthesising Maffulli N, American Journal of Sports Medicine 1998 (PMID 9548122)

thompson_and_matles_test_accuracy.finding: In a prospective study of 174 patients with surgically confirmed complete Achilles tendon rupture plus 28 controls, the calf-squeeze (Thompson) test was the single most sensitive clinical sign at 96% sensitivity, and the Matles test (resting-dorsiflexion) was second at 88% sensitivity; gap palpation was the least sensitive test when performed in an awake patient (though it improved under anaesthesia). All four tests had a high positive predictive value, and at least two of the four tests were positive in every one of the 174 confirmed-rupture patients, supporting the '2-or-more-positive' clinical diagnostic rule above. This is the same numeric dataset this knowledge base's tendinitis entry references for the calf-squeeze manoeuvre.
thompson_and_matles_test_accuracy.source: Maffulli N, 'The clinical diagnosis of subcutaneous tear of the Achilles tendon. A prospective study in 174 patients', American Journal of Sports Medicine 1998 (PMID 9548122); cross-verified in Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)
thompson_and_matles_test_accuracy.confidence: high (single prospective study, N=174 confirmed cases + 28 controls, not independently re-run at scale since, but consistently cited/replicated across the specialty literature)

dynamic_ultrasound_and_raut.finding: Dynamic ultrasound is a useful confirmatory/adjunct tool: a gap of more than 5 mm between tendon edges on dynamic imaging is used as a threshold indicating that surgical intervention is warranted. Real-time dynamic ultrasound performed during a Thompson calf-squeeze manoeuvre (the 'Realtime Achilles Ultrasound Thompson', RAUT, test) achieved 86.4-87.2% sensitivity and 81.1-91.7% specificity (novice vs expert reviewers) for detecting complete rupture, outperforming static ultrasound alone (76.8-79.6% sensitivity, 74.8-86.4% specificity) in a comparative study of 22 confirmed ruptures - the same RAUT dataset used in this knowledge base's tendinitis entry.
dynamic_ultrasound_and_raut.source: Aminlari A et al, 'Realtime Achilles Ultrasound Thompson (RAUT) Test for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Acute Achilles Tendon Ruptures', Foot & Ankle International 2017 (PMID 27672015)
dynamic_ultrasound_and_raut.confidence: high for the RAUT numeric data (single study, N=22 confirmed ruptures - not yet independently replicated at scale)

mri_role.finding: MRI is not routinely used for acute diagnosis; it is reserved for patients with inconclusive clinical exam findings and for subacute or chronic tears, since clinical exam plus dynamic ultrasound is sufficient, cheaper, and faster for the typical acute presentation.
mri_role.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)

acute_presentation.finding: Sudden, severe posterior heel/calf pain at the moment of push-off, jump take-off, or sudden forced dorsiflexion, frequently accompanied by an audible/felt 'pop' or snap and a sensation of being struck in the back of the leg, followed immediately by weakness, an inability to rise onto the toes (single-leg heel raise), and an antalgic/flat-footed limp.
acute_presentation.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)

palpable_gap.finding: A palpable gap or defect is typically found in the mid-substance to distal tendon (commonly within the 3-6 cm hypovascular watershed zone proximal to the calcaneal insertion) and is one of the four core clinical diagnostic signs, though it is a less sensitive sign than the Thompson or Matles tests when examined in an awake, guarding patient, since swelling/haematoma can mask the defect.
palpable_gap.source: Maffulli N, American Journal of Sports Medicine 1998 (PMID 9548122); Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)

deceptive_residual_plantarflexion.finding: A clinically important trap: patients with a complete Achilles rupture can often still weakly plantarflex the foot against gravity (not against resistance) using the secondary plantarflexors (tibialis posterior, peroneus longus/brevis, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus), and some can even walk with a limp. This preserved-but-weakened active plantarflexion can mislead an examiner who does not specifically test the Thompson sign and resisted plantarflexion strength, which is one reason this injury has a reputation for being under-recognised on casual exam.
deceptive_residual_plantarflexion.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)
deceptive_residual_plantarflexion.confidence: high for the anatomical/mechanistic explanation; qualitative reputation statement, not tied to a specific numeric miss-rate in this citation

achilles_tendinopathy_partial_tear.finding: Chronic Achilles tendinopathy (this knowledge base's separate 'tendinitis' entry) and partial Achilles tears present with posterior heel/ankle pain and tenderness but, unlike complete rupture, preserve a normal (negative) Thompson test and largely preserved resisted plantarflexion strength, with pain that is typically gradual-onset and activity-related rather than a single sudden traumatic 'pop'. Partial tears can blur this distinction and may require dynamic ultrasound or MRI to differentiate definitively from a chronic tendinopathic thickening.
achilles_tendinopathy_partial_tear.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638); cross-referenced against this knowledge base's tendinitis entry (Li HY, Hua YH, BioMed Research International 2016, PMID 27885357)
achilles_tendinopathy_partial_tear.confidence: high for the complete-rupture-vs-tendinopathy Thompson-test distinction; moderate for partial-tear differentiation specifics, which were not independently re-verified with dedicated numeric data this session

gastrocnemius_tear_tennis_leg.finding: Acute gastrocnemius muscle tear at the myotendinous junction ('tennis leg') is the classic mimic of Achilles rupture: it also presents with sudden posterior calf pain during push-off/sprinting, but the tear is typically more proximal (mid-calf, at the medial gastrocnemius myotendinous junction) rather than in the distal watershed zone, the Thompson test remains negative (intact passive plantarflexion) because the Achilles tendon itself is intact, and resisted plantarflexion, while painful, is not lost outright the way it is with complete rupture.
gastrocnemius_tear_tennis_leg.source: Clinical distinction extrapolated from the Achilles-rupture diagnostic-criteria literature (Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, PMID 28194638) applied to the well-described anatomic mimic; a dedicated head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy study directly comparing gastrocnemius tear versus Achilles rupture was not identified/independently verified this session
gastrocnemius_tear_tennis_leg.confidence: moderate - anatomically and mechanistically sound but not backed by a dedicated comparative-accuracy study found this session

plantaris_tendon_rupture.finding: Isolated plantaris tendon rupture can mimic acute Achilles injury with sudden posteromedial calf pain, but it is a far more benign, self-limited injury: the Achilles tendon itself is intact, the Thompson test is negative, and plantarflexion strength is preserved, since the plantaris is a vestigial muscle absent in a minority of people and contributes negligibly to plantarflexion power.
plantaris_tendon_rupture.source: Spina AA, 'The plantaris muscle: anatomy, injury, imaging, and treatment', Journal of the Canadian Chiropractic Association 2007 (PMID 17885678)
plantaris_tendon_rupture.confidence: moderate - anatomy/mimic description well supported, but this source is a narrative anatomy review rather than a diagnostic-accuracy study

deep_vein_thrombosis.finding: Acute calf pain and swelling from deep vein thrombosis is an important differential/red-flag mimic to exclude in patients presenting with posterior calf pain without a clear traumatic push-off mechanism or audible pop, since the management and urgency differ completely from a tendon rupture.
deep_vein_thrombosis.source: General clinical differential-diagnosis convention for acute calf pain; not tied to a specific rupture-focused comparative study verified this session
deep_vein_thrombosis.confidence: moderate - standard clinical safety-net differential, qualitative only

age_and_sex.finding: Achilles tendon rupture most commonly affects relatively active, middle-aged adults rather than elite young athletes, with a mean patient age in the literature ranging from 37 to 43.5 years (the classic 'weekend warrior' demographic), and a strong male predominance, with a male:female ratio reported in the literature ranging from 5.5:1 up to 30:1 depending on the population studied.
age_and_sex.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)

medication_associated_risk.finding: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics and corticosteroids have each been shown to weaken the Achilles tendon, producing associated tendinitis and an increased risk of rupture, and this risk is even higher in patients over 60 years old. The foundational case-control study establishing the fluoroquinolone-Achilles tendon disorder association was a large Dutch case-control study using the PHARMO record-linkage database.
medication_associated_risk.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638), citing van der Linden PD et al, 'Fluoroquinolones and risk of Achilles tendon disorders: case-control study', BMJ 2002 (PMID 12039823)
medication_associated_risk.confidence: high for the qualitative drug-class association and the age>60 amplification; the specific numeric relative-risk/odds-ratio value from the original van der Linden case-control study could not be independently re-extracted and verified this session, so no specific RR/OR number is stated here

activity_and_mechanism.finding: The dominant activity risk is participation in sports involving abrupt, repetitive jumping, sprinting, and forceful push-off (e.g. badminton, basketball, tennis, football), which reproduce the short-muscle-length maximal-contraction loading pattern that mechanically predisposes to rupture; a substantial and apparently growing share of ruptures also now occur in non-sports/non-athletic contexts.
activity_and_mechanism.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638); Lantto I et al, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2015 (PMID 24862178)

seasonal_pattern.finding: A retrospective single-center US study found a statistically significant seasonal pattern, with Achilles tendon rupture incidence peaking in spring (P = 0.015) and reaching its lowest point in fall (P < 0.001); sports-related ruptures specifically were also most frequent in spring and least frequent in fall.
seasonal_pattern.source: Caldwell JE, Lightsey HM, Trofa DP et al, seasonal-variation study, Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Global Research & Reviews 2018 (PMID 30631830)
seasonal_pattern.confidence: moderate - single-center US retrospective study (level IV evidence), not yet independently replicated in other populations to this knowledge base's verification this session

finland_33_year_trend.finding: In a 33-year population-based study from Oulu, Finland (hospital records 1979-2011), the overall incidence of Achilles tendon rupture rose dramatically, from 2.1 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 0.3-7.7) in 1979 to 21.5 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 14.6-30.6) in 2011, with the mean annual increase in incidence being 2.4% higher (95% CI 1.3-4.7) for non-sports-related ruptures than for sports-related ruptures. Increased incidence was attributable mainly to sports-related injuries during the middle study decade and to non-sports-related injuries in the final period.
finland_33_year_trend.source: Lantto I, Heikkinen J, Flinkkilä T, Ohtonen P, Leppilahti J, 'Epidemiology of Achilles tendon ruptures: increasing incidence over a 33-year period', Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2015 (PMID 24862178)

sweden_trend.finding: A Swedish population dataset (as cited in a comprehensive 2017 review) similarly showed rising incidence, from 47 per 100,000 in men and 12 per 100,000 in women in an earlier period, up to 55.2 per 100,000 in men and 14.7 per 100,000 in women by 2012, confirming the same rising-incidence pattern and consistent male predominance seen in the Finnish data.
sweden_trend.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638), citing Swedish national registry data
sweden_trend.confidence: moderate - figure taken from a secondary citation within a peer-reviewed review; the original Swedish primary-source study was not independently re-verified with its own PMID this session

outcome_if_treated_promptly.finding: When treated promptly, re-rupture rates for acute Achilles tendon rupture are low: in historical (largely pre-2002) studies comparing treatment strategies without modern early-functional-rehabilitation protocols, the pooled re-rupture rate was 12.6% in conservatively (non-operatively) treated patients versus 3.5% in operatively treated patients - i.e. surgery reduced re-rupture risk by roughly 8.8 percentage points versus non-operative treatment without functional rehab. However, once an early-functional-rehabilitation protocol (early controlled range-of-motion) is used for non-operative management, re-rupture rates become statistically equivalent to surgical repair, while operative treatment carries a roughly four-fold higher infection rate than non-operative treatment.
outcome_if_treated_promptly.source: Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638); Lantto I et al, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2015 (PMID 24862178)

consequence_of_missed_or_delayed_diagnos.finding: If a rupture is missed or its treatment is delayed, it can progress to a chronic Achilles tendon rupture, which in a recent Swedish population study accounted for 11% of all Achilles tendon ruptures. In that same study, the outcome gap between prompt and delayed/chronic management was large: patients who underwent surgical reconstruction for an established chronic rupture had a median Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score (ATRS) of 77 versus only 34 for those managed non-surgically once chronic, with a functional recovery rate of 85% versus 40% respectively - i.e. once a rupture has become chronic, outcomes are substantially worse than for an acute rupture treated promptly by either surgical or modern non-operative functional-rehab pathways, and even surgical salvage of a chronic tear does not fully close that outcome gap.
consequence_of_missed_or_delayed_diagnos.source: Nilsson N, Larsson E, Dyrehag E, Carmont M, Brorsson A, Nilsson Helander K, 'Incidence, reason for treatment delay and patient-reported outcome of patients affected by a chronic Achilles tendon rupture', BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2026 (PMID 42067876)
consequence_of_missed_or_delayed_diagnos.confidence: high (single population-based study, most recent and most directly on-point data identified this session for delayed/missed-rupture natural history)

cause_of_delay.finding: In the same chronic-rupture cohort, the dominant driver of delayed diagnosis/treatment was patient-side delay in seeking care rather than clinician misdiagnosis: 84% of chronic-rupture patients had delayed seeking medical attention themselves, while only a small minority of cases involved an incorrect diagnosis by a clinician - 1% misdiagnosed at the initial trauma-related visit and 3% misdiagnosed at a later medical visit (roughly 4% combined clinician-attributable misdiagnosis rate). The authors explicitly conclude that chronic Achilles tendon rupture is primarily due to patient's delay rather than the relatively rare event of clinician misdiagnosis.
cause_of_delay.source: Nilsson N, Larsson E, Dyrehag E, Carmont M, Brorsson A, Nilsson Helander K, BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2026 (PMID 42067876)
cause_of_delay.confidence: high - this is the specific, verified, population-level missed/delayed-diagnosis rate this knowledge base was previously unable to source for this injury (see the tendinitis entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE note on this gap)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Suspect complete Achilles tendon rupture in anyone with sudden posterior calf/heel pain and a felt or heard 'pop' during push-off, jumping, or forced dorsiflexion - especially a middle-aged (mean age ~37-43.5 years), male, recreationally active patient, or anyone recently on a fluoroquinolone antibiotic or corticosteroid (particularly if over 60). Do not be reassured by preserved-but-weak active plantarflexion: specifically perform and document the Thompson (calf-squeeze) test (96% sensitive) and the Matles resting-dorsiflexion test (88% sensitive) - two or more of the four core clinical signs (positive Thompson, weak plantarflexion, palpable gap, increased resting dorsiflexion) make the diagnosis. Dynamic ultrasound (with a >5 mm gap indicating surgical candidacy) can confirm equivocal cases; MRI is reserved for inconclusive or chronic presentations. The real, verified risk of delay is not primarily clinician error (only ~4% of chronic cases trace to clinician misdiagnosis) but patient delay in seeking care (84% of chronic cases) - so patient education to present immediately, combined with a low threshold for the Thompson test in any acute calf-pain presentation, is what prevents progression to chronic rupture (11% of all cases) and its markedly worse functional outcome (ATRS 34 vs 77, recovery 40% vs 85%).
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Maffulli N (PMID 9548122), Egger AC & Berkowitz MJ (PMID 28194638), Lantto I et al (PMID 24862178), Nilsson N et al (PMID 42067876), Aminlari A et al (PMID 27672015)

prompt_diagnosis_prevents_chronic_ruptur.finding: Achilles tendon rupture is a commonly discussed 'easily missed' diagnosis in emergency/first-contact settings because compensatory plantarflexion from secondary muscles (tibialis posterior, peroneals, flexor hallucis/digitorum longus) can mask the loss of the primary plantarflexor, so an exam that stops at 'can the patient move the foot' rather than specifically performing the Thompson (calf-squeeze) test can be falsely reassuring. The best real, population-level, verified data identified this session (a 2026 Swedish cohort study) shows that only about 11% of all Achilles tendon ruptures progress to a chronic (missed/delayed) rupture, and of those, only roughly 4% are attributable to an actual clinician misdiagnosis (1% at the initial trauma visit, 3% at a later visit) - the remaining 84% of chronic-rupture cases are due to the patient themselves delaying presentation, not clinician error.
