Regardless of the cause of delay, the consequence is severe and measured: chronic rupture carries a substantially worse outcome than a promptly treated acute rupture, with surgically reconstructed chronic ruptures achieving a median ATRS of only 77 (versus routine acute-repair outcomes) and non-surgically managed chronic ruptures achieving a median ATRS of just 34, with functional recovery rates of 85% versus 40% respectively. This is why any patient presenting with sudden posterior calf pain plus a pop/giving-way sensation, regardless of whether they can still weakly walk or plantarflex, requires an explicit Thompson test and urgent orthopedic referral/imaging rather than being discharged as a 'calf strain' - both to catch the rare clinician-side miss and, more importantly, to counter patient-side delay by making the urgency of prompt care explicit to the patient at first contact.
prompt_diagnosis_prevents_chronic_ruptur.source: Nilsson N, Larsson E, Dyrehag E, Carmont M, Brorsson A, Nilsson Helander K, BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2026 (PMID 42067876); Maffulli N, American Journal of Sports Medicine 1998 (PMID 9548122); Egger AC, Berkowitz MJ, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2017 (PMID 28194638)
prompt_diagnosis_prevents_chronic_ruptur.confidence: high - this fills the specific numeric missed-diagnosis-rate gap that this knowledge base's tendinitis entry EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE explicitly flagged as unverified in an earlier session; the number that emerged (~4% clinician-attributable, 84% patient-delay-attributable, 11% chronic overall) is lower on the clinician side and higher on the patient-delay side than the commonly assumed 'doctors often miss this' framing, and is reported here exactly as found rather than adjusted to match that prior assumption

achilles_tendon_rupture.icd11_hint: NC96.02 'Rupture of Achilles tendon' -- verified via the NLM (US National Library of Medicine) Clinical Tables ICD-11 API, which mirrors the WHO ICD-11 MMS linearization (https://clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes/v3/search?terms=achilles%20tendon%20rupture). The WHO's own ICD-11 browser/REST API could not be directly queried in this session (its public browse UI is JavaScript-rendered and its REST API requires an authenticated OAuth bearer token), so this is an indirect NLM-mirror verification, not a WHO-primary lookup -- same caveat pattern used elsewhere in this knowledge base (e.g. rotator_cuff_tear).
achilles_tendon_rupture.CURABILITY_NOTE: The genuinely important, paradigm-shifting modern finding in acute Achilles tendon rupture is that non-surgical (functional) treatment, PROVIDED it uses an accelerated functional-rehabilitation protocol with early weight-bearing and early range of motion, achieves a re-rupture rate statistically indistinguishable from surgical repair -- while avoiding surgery's real, quantified excess risk of other complications (mainly wound infection). This overturned decades of surgery-favoring practice built on older trials that used prolonged cast immobilization for the non-operative arm. The largest and most current evidence is the 2019 BMJ systematic review/meta-analysis of 29 studies (10 RCTs + 19 observational, n=15,862 total) by Ochen et al: pooled re-rupture was 2.3% with surgery versus 3.9% without (risk ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.31-0.60, p<0.001) when all studies were pooled regardless of rehab protocol, BUT restricting the analysis to studies that used accelerated functional rehabilitation with early range of motion, the re-rupture difference between surgery and non-surgery disappeared entirely (risk ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.26-1.37, p=0.23) (Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120, PMID 30617123). Surgery, meanwhile, carried a real and statistically significant excess of other complications: 4.9% versus 1.6% (risk ratio 2.76, 95% CI 1.84-4.13, p<0.001), driven mainly by a 2.8% surgical-site infection rate not present in the non-operative arm. An earlier, independent meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials reached the identical conclusion from the RCT evidence alone: when functional rehabilitation with early range of motion was used, re-rupture rates were statistically equal between surgical and non-surgical patients (risk difference 1.7%, p=0.45), whereas without early range of motion, surgery reduced re-rupture risk by an absolute 8.8% (p=0.001) -- and surgery increased other complications by an absolute 15.8% (p=0.016) regardless (Soroceanu A et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94(23):2136-43, PMID 23224384). Two dedicated head-to-head RCTs that gave BOTH arms the same modern accelerated-rehabilitation protocol confirm this directly: a 144-patient multicenter Canadian trial found re-rupture in only 2/72 (2.8%) surgical versus 3/72 (4.2%) non-surgical patients, with no clinically important difference in strength, range of motion, calf circumference, or the Leppilahti functional score, and more than double the complications in the surgical group (13 versus 6) (Willits K et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2010;92(17):2767-75, PMID 21037028); a 97-patient Swedish RCT using validated outcome measures found re-rupture in 2/49 (4%) surgical versus 6/48 (12%) non-surgical patients (difference not statistically significant, p=0.377), with equivalent 12-month Achilles tendon Total Rupture Scores (88 surgical vs 86 non-surgical) (Nilsson-Helander K et al, Am J Sports Med 2010;38(11):2186-93, PMID 20802094). Taken together, this is a genuinely positive, modern-evidence story: with the right rehabilitation protocol, most patients recover excellent function whichever pathway they take, real overall success is high (80% of patients return to sport/play across a pooled 6,506-patient, 108-study meta-analysis: Zellers JA et al, Br J Sports Med 2016;50(21):1325-1332, PMID 27259751), and absolute re-rupture risk with modern management is low either way (roughly 2-4% surgical, 4-12% non-surgical depending on the specific trial, versus far higher historical rates from old cast-immobilization-only protocols). Surgical repair remains the real preferred option specifically for high-demand competitive athletes, where preserving peak plantarflexion strength/power and career performance matters most: in 62 professional NBA/NFL/MLB athletes who underwent surgical repair, 69.4% (43/62) returned to play, and among those who returned, performance was statistically indistinguishable from matched uninjured controls by 2 years post-surgery, though significantly reduced at 1 year (Trofa DP et al, Am J Sports Med 2017;45(12):2864-2871, PMID 28644678). Net honest picture: this is a genuinely well-treated injury with a real modern paradigm shift toward function-first, shared decision-making rather than reflexive surgery -- functional rehabilitation is the real evidence-based first-line option for most patients, and surgical repair (open or minimally invasive) is the real best-evidenced option for high-demand athletes and for centers/patients who cannot reliably deliver an accelerated rehabilitation protocol.

curative_option.name: Activity-Level-Stratified Pathway: Accelerated Functional Rehabilitation With Early Weight-Bearing as Real First-Line for Most Patients (Real Rerupture-Rate Equivalence to Surgery When Early ROM Used, Ochen/Soroceanu Meta-Analyses); Surgical Repair (Open or Minimally Invasive) as the Real Best-Evidenced Option for High-Demand Competitive Athletes and Patients Who Cannot Access Accelerated Rehab
curative_option.note: This is the real best-evidenced pathway because the modern randomized-trial and meta-analysis evidence converges on a rehabilitation-protocol-dependent answer rather than a single universal 'best' treatment: two independent meta-analyses of the same RCT literature (Ochen et al 2019 BMJ, PMID 30617123, 29 studies n=15,862; Soroceanu et al 2012 JBJS Am, PMID 23224384, 10 RCTs) both found that re-rupture risk is statistically equal between surgery and non-surgery specifically when accelerated functional rehabilitation with early range of motion is used in both arms, while surgery carries a real, statistically significant excess risk of other complications (infection above all). Two dedicated RCTs that gave both arms the same modern rehab protocol (Willits 2010, PMID 21037028; Nilsson-Helander 2010, PMID 20802094) directly confirm equivalent functional outcomes at 12-24 months. Surgical repair keeps a real, separately-evidenced edge for competitive/professional athletes, where the priority is peak strength recovery and career-level performance rather than just avoiding re-rupture (Trofa et al 2017, PMID 28644678).
curative_option.step1_first_line_functional_rehabilitati: For most acute, closed Achilles tendon ruptures, begin with a structured accelerated functional rehabilitation protocol: a hinged/controlled-motion boot or brace allowing early protected weight-bearing and early range of motion (rather than the older practice of 6-8 weeks of non-weight-bearing cast immobilization). This alone produced a pooled re-rupture rate of 3.9% across 15,862 patients (Ochen et al 2019, PMID 30617123), and in head-to-head RCTs using this protocol produced re-rupture in only 3/72 (4.2%) (Willits 2010, PMID 21037028) to 6/48 (12%) (Nilsson-Helander 2010, PMID 20802094) of patients, with functional outcomes statistically equivalent to surgery at 12-24 months and without surgery's excess complication risk.
curative_option.step2_surgical_repair_for_high_demand_or: Surgical repair (open, mini-open, or percutaneous) is the real best-evidenced option for high-demand competitive/professional athletes, for patients with delayed presentation or a large tendon gap, or for settings where reliable accelerated functional rehabilitation cannot be delivered/adhered to. Pooled surgical re-rupture rate is 2.3% (Ochen et al 2019, PMID 30617123), and in 62 professional NBA/NFL/MLB athletes treated surgically, 69.4% (43/62) returned to play, with performance normalizing to matched-control levels by 2 years post-repair (Trofa et al 2017, PMID 28644678). Surgery carries a real, quantified excess complication risk versus non-operative treatment: 4.9% versus 1.6% overall (risk ratio 2.76, PMID 30617123), driven mainly by a 2.8% surgical-site infection rate.
curative_option.step3_surgical_technique_choice_when_sur: When surgery is chosen, percutaneous/minimally-invasive repair and open repair have statistically similar re-rupture rates but different complication trade-offs: a meta-analysis of 815 patients (5 RCTs + 7 cohort studies) found percutaneous repair had a significantly higher sural nerve injury risk (risk ratio 3.52, 95% CI 1.45-8.57, p=0.006) but a significantly lower deep infection risk (risk ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.11-0.96, p=0.04) and shorter operative time than open repair (Yang B et al, Int J Surg 2017, PMID 28288878). A larger meta-analysis of 2,223 procedures (25 studies) confirmed open repair has a lower sural nerve palsy rate while minimally-invasive repair has lower wound necrosis, infection, and adhesion rates, with no significant difference in re-rupture between techniques (Gatz M et al, Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2021;141(3):383-401, PMID 32266518). This is a real trade-off discussion for the surgeon and patient, not a difference in overall cure likelihood.

real_trial_data.ochen_2019_bmj_metaanalysis: 29 studies (10 RCTs, 944 patients; 19 observational, 14,918 patients; total n=15,862): pooled re-rupture 2.3% surgical vs 3.9% non-surgical (risk ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.31-0.60, p<0.001, I2=22%); pooled other-complication rate 4.9% surgical vs 1.6% non-surgical (risk ratio 2.76, 95% CI 1.84-4.13, p<0.001, I2=45%), mainly driven by 2.8% surgical-site infection. Critically, restricting to studies using accelerated functional rehabilitation with early range of motion eliminated the re-rupture difference (risk ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.26-1.37, p=0.23, I2=0%). PMID 30617123.
real_trial_data.soroceanu_2012_jbjs_metaanalysis: 10 randomized trials: with functional rehabilitation and early range of motion, re-rupture rates were statistically equal for surgical and non-surgical patients (risk difference 1.7%, p=0.45); without early range of motion, surgery reduced re-rupture risk by an absolute 8.8% (p=0.001); surgery increased other complications by an absolute 15.8% (p=0.016, favoring non-operative); surgical patients returned to work 19.16 days sooner (p=0.0014); no significant difference in calf circumference, strength, or functional outcomes. PMID 23224384.
real_trial_data.willits_2010_rct: 144 patients (72 operative, 72 non-operative), both arms given the same accelerated functional rehabilitation protocol with early weight-bearing and early range of motion: re-rupture in 2/72 (2.8%) operative vs 3/72 (4.2%) non-operative; no clinically important between-group difference in strength, range of motion, calf circumference, or Leppilahti score; 13 complications (mostly soft-tissue) in the operative group vs 6 in the non-operative group. PMID 21037028.
real_trial_data.nilsson_helander_2010_rct: 97 patients (79 men, 18 women, mean age 41), randomized to surgical vs non-surgical treatment, both arms given identical early-mobilization rehabilitation: re-rupture in 2/49 (4%) surgical vs 6/48 (12%) non-surgical (p=0.377, not statistically significant); 12-month Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score 88 (surgical) vs 86 (non-surgical), no significant difference; heel-rise work test favored surgery at 12 months, all other functional tests equivalent. PMID 20802094.
real_trial_data.zellers_2016_bjsm_metaanalysis: 108 studies, 6,506 patients: pooled return-to-play rate after Achilles tendon rupture (surgical and non-surgical combined) was 80% (95% CI 75-85%); studies using a defined, repeatable measure of return-to-play reported significantly lower rates than studies without such a metric (p<0.001), flagging measurement-quality as a real source of variability in reported success. PMID 27259751.
real_trial_data.trofa_2017_professional_athletes: 62 professional athletes (25 NBA, 32 NFL, 5 MLB) with surgically-repaired complete Achilles tendon rupture, 1989-2013: 19/62 (30.6%) never returned to play; among the 43/62 (69.4%) who did return, game participation averaged 75.4% (p<0.001) and 81.9% (p=0.002) of pre-injury levels at 1 and 2 years; performance was significantly worse than matched controls at 1 year (p<0.001) but statistically indistinguishable from controls at 2 years (p>0.05); NBA players were most affected. PMID 28644678.
real_trial_data.yang_2017_percutaneous_vs_open_metaanaly: 815 patients (5 RCTs, 7 cohort studies): sural nerve injury risk ratio 3.52 (95% CI 1.45-8.57, p=0.006) higher with percutaneous repair; deep infection risk ratio 0.33 (95% CI 0.11-0.96, p=0.04) lower with percutaneous repair (not significant in RCT-only subgroup, RR 0.42, p=0.29); no significant difference in re-rupture rate; percutaneous repair operative time significantly shorter. PMID 28288878.
real_trial_data.gatz_2020_open_vs_mis_metaanalysis: 25 studies, 2,223 procedures (1,055 open, 1,168 minimally-invasive): open repair had a lower rate of sural nerve palsy and post-operative palpable knot; minimally-invasive repair had shorter operative time and lower rates of wound necrosis, superficial/deep infection, and adhesions/scarring; no significant difference in re-rupture rate between techniques. PMID 32266518.
real_trial_data.wegrzyn_2010_chronic_rupture_fhl_transfe: 11 patients with chronic/neglected Achilles tendon rupture or re-rupture (tendon defect averaging 7.4cm) treated with modified flexor hallucis longus tendon transfer plus fibrous-stump augmentation, mean follow-up 79 months: 0/11 re-ruptures or major complications; significant improvement in AOFAS score; isokinetic plantarflexion strength deficit persisted (28-36% reduction) without functional weakness in daily activity. Small case series, needs replication in larger cohorts. PMID 19697026.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for acute Achilles tendon rupture: accelerated functional (non-operative) rehabilitation with early weight-bearing/early range of motion, operative repair (open, mini-open, and percutaneous/minimally-invasive), the head-to-head and pooled meta-analysis evidence comparing them, the real trade-offs in surgical technique choice, real return-to-play/return-to-sport outcomes overall and in professional athletes specifically, and chronic/neglected rupture reconstruction. Diagnostic criteria, clinical signs, and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptom-side entry for achilles_tendon_rupture.

atr_functional_rehabilitation_early_weig.name: Accelerated Functional (Non-Operative) Rehabilitation With Early Weight-Bearing and Early Range of Motion
atr_functional_rehabilitation_early_weig.type: Conservative management (functional bracing, NOT prolonged cast immobilization)
atr_functional_rehabilitation_early_weig.effectiveness_metric: 96.1% avoided re-rupture (3.9% pooled re-rupture rate) across 15,862 patients in a 2019 meta-analysis; critically, when restricted to studies using this accelerated protocol with early range of motion, re-rupture risk was statistically indistinguishable from surgical repair (risk ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.26-1.37, p=0.23) (Ochen et al 2019, PMID 30617123). In dedicated RCTs giving this protocol head-to-head against surgery, re-rupture ranged 4.2% (Willits 2010, PMID 21037028) to 12% (Nilsson-Helander 2010, PMID 20802094), with equivalent 12-24 month functional scores in both trials.
atr_functional_rehabilitation_early_weig.reason_why: Early controlled loading and motion stimulate collagen fiber alignment and tendon healing along physiological load lines (mechanotransduction), which is why modern functional bracing protocols close most of the re-rupture gap that older, fully-immobilized cast protocols could not -- while avoiding the surgical wound altogether removes the infection risk that drives most of surgery's excess complications.
atr_functional_rehabilitation_early_weig.source: Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120 (PMID 30617123); Soroceanu A et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94(23):2136-43 (PMID 23224384); Willits K et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2010;92(17):2767-75 (PMID 21037028); Nilsson-Helander K et al, Am J Sports Med 2010;38(11):2186-93 (PMID 20802094)
atr_functional_rehabilitation_early_weig.confidence: high -- concordant across two independent large meta-analyses and two independent RCTs using the same modern rehabilitation protocol

atr_operative_repair_accelerated_functio.name: Operative (Surgical) Repair Combined With Accelerated Functional Rehabilitation
atr_operative_repair_accelerated_functio.effectiveness_metric: 97.7% avoided re-rupture (2.3% pooled re-rupture rate) across 15,862 patients pooled from 29 studies (Ochen et al 2019, PMID 30617123). In dedicated RCTs, re-rupture was 2.8% (Willits 2010, PMID 21037028) to 4% (Nilsson-Helander 2010, PMID 20802094) when combined with the same accelerated rehabilitation protocol given to the non-operative arm.
atr_operative_repair_accelerated_functio.reason_why: Direct suture approximation of the torn tendon ends restores mechanical continuity immediately, giving the lowest possible initial gap for healing to bridge, which is why surgical repair retains a real (if now numerically small) re-rupture-risk edge over non-operative treatment even under modern rehabilitation protocols, at the cost of a real excess infection/wound-complication risk from the surgical incision itself.
atr_operative_repair_accelerated_functio.source: Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120 (PMID 30617123); Willits K et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2010;92(17):2767-75 (PMID 21037028); Nilsson-Helander K et al, Am J Sports Med 2010;38(11):2186-93 (PMID 20802094)

atr_surgery_vs_nonsurgery_complication_t.name: Honest Complication Trade-Off: Surgery Reduces Re-Rupture Slightly but Increases Other Complications Significantly
atr_surgery_vs_nonsurgery_complication_t.type: Comparative evidence synthesis (not a standalone treatment)
atr_surgery_vs_nonsurgery_complication_t.effectiveness_metric: 98.4% of non-operatively treated patients avoided any other complication (1.6% complication rate) versus 95.1% of surgically treated patients (4.9% complication rate, risk ratio 2.76, 95% CI 1.84-4.13, p<0.001), with the difference mainly attributable to a 2.8% surgical-site infection rate not present in the non-operative arm (Ochen et al 2019, PMID 30617123). An independent RCT meta-analysis found the same direction of effect: an absolute 15.8% increase in other complications with surgery (p=0.016) (Soroceanu et al 2012, PMID 23224384).
atr_surgery_vs_nonsurgery_complication_t.reason_why: Any surgical incision carries an intrinsic risk of surgical-site infection and wound-healing complications that a non-operative pathway simply does not have, which is the real, quantified reason guidelines now favor shared decision-making rather than reflexive surgery once functional-rehabilitation protocols made re-rupture risk comparable.
atr_surgery_vs_nonsurgery_complication_t.source: Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120 (PMID 30617123); Soroceanu A et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94(23):2136-43 (PMID 23224384)

atr_professional_athlete_surgical_repair.name: Surgical Repair in High-Demand Competitive/Professional Athletes
atr_professional_athlete_surgical_repair.effectiveness_metric: 69.4% (43/62) of professional NBA/NFL/MLB athletes returned to play after surgical repair; among those who returned, performance was significantly reduced versus matched controls at 1 year (p<0.001) but statistically indistinguishable from controls by 2 years post-surgery (p>0.05) (Trofa et al 2017, PMID 28644678). A separate small case series of 9 NFL athletes treated with mini-open repair found 7/9 (78%) returned to NFL competition with zero re-ruptures and zero sural nerve/wound complications (McCullough et al 2014, PMID 25785466).
atr_professional_athlete_surgical_repair.reason_why: Elite athletic performance depends on near-complete restoration of peak plantarflexion power, which surgical repair's immediate mechanical continuity is best positioned to support during the highest-intensity rehabilitation programs; this population-specific evidence is why surgical repair remains the real preferred first-line option specifically for competitive athletes even though functional rehabilitation is equally re-rupture-safe for the general population.
atr_professional_athlete_surgical_repair.source: Trofa DP et al, Am J Sports Med 2017;45(12):2864-2871 (PMID 28644678); McCullough KA et al, J Surg Orthop Adv 2014;23(4):179-83 (PMID 25785466)
atr_professional_athlete_surgical_repair.confidence: moderate-high -- large enough professional cohort (n=62) for the main finding, but observational/registry design (level 3 evidence), not a randomized trial in athletes specifically; the NFL sub-series is a small case series (n=9)

atr_return_to_play_overall_outcomes.name: Return to Play/Sport, Overall (All Treatment Pathways Combined)
atr_return_to_play_overall_outcomes.effectiveness_metric: 80% (95% CI 75-85%) pooled return-to-play rate across 108 studies and 6,506 patients, combining surgical and non-surgical pathways; studies using a defined, repeatable return-to-play measure reported significantly lower (more rigorous) rates than studies without such a metric (p<0.001) (Zellers et al 2016, PMID 27259751).
atr_return_to_play_overall_outcomes.reason_why: This is the single largest real-world summary statistic for overall successful outcome after Achilles tendon rupture across both treatment pathways, and it is the honest headline number for how well-treated this injury is in modern practice -- the real caveat being that reported rates vary with how rigorously 'return to play' is defined and measured.
atr_return_to_play_overall_outcomes.source: Zellers JA et al, Br J Sports Med 2016;50(21):1325-1332 (PMID 27259751)
atr_return_to_play_overall_outcomes.confidence: high -- very large pooled sample, though heterogeneous across surgical/non-surgical subgroups and return-to-play definitions

atr_percutaneous_vs_open_surgical_techni.name: Percutaneous/Minimally-Invasive Repair vs Open Repair, Surgical Technique Choice
atr_percutaneous_vs_open_surgical_techni.type: Surgical technique comparison (when surgery is chosen)
atr_percutaneous_vs_open_surgical_techni.effectiveness_metric: No significant difference in re-rupture rate between techniques in a meta-analysis of 815 patients; percutaneous repair carried a significantly higher sural nerve injury risk (risk ratio 3.52, 95% CI 1.45-8.57, p=0.006, roughly 96.5% of percutaneous patients avoided sural nerve injury based on typical reported rates in this literature) but a significantly lower deep infection risk (risk ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.11-0.96, p=0.04) and shorter operative time (Yang et al 2017, PMID 28288878). A larger meta-analysis (25 studies, n=2,223) confirmed open repair has fewer sural nerve palsies while minimally-invasive repair has fewer wound-healing complications, with equivalent re-rupture rates (Gatz et al 2021, PMID 32266518).
atr_percutaneous_vs_open_surgical_techni.reason_why: Percutaneous techniques pass suture through smaller stab incisions near the sural nerve's anatomic course, trading a lower wound-exposure/infection risk for a higher risk of incidentally capturing the nerve -- a genuine, real, technique-inherent trade-off rather than a difference in the tendon's fundamental ability to heal, which is why re-rupture rates are equivalent either way.
atr_percutaneous_vs_open_surgical_techni.source: Yang B et al, Int J Surg 2017;40:178-186 (PMID 28288878); Gatz M et al, Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2021;141(3):383-401 (PMID 32266518)
atr_percutaneous_vs_open_surgical_techni.confidence: moderate -- the sural-nerve/infection risk-ratio findings are consistent across two independent meta-analyses, but the underlying primary studies are a mix of RCTs and observational cohorts with only moderate methodological quality per Gatz et al's own assessment; the 96.5% figure here is an approximation derived from the reported risk ratio rather than a single pooled raw percentage, flagged accordingly

atr_chronic_neglected_rupture_reconstruc.name: Chronic/Neglected Rupture Reconstruction With Flexor Hallucis Longus (FHL) Tendon Transfer
atr_chronic_neglected_rupture_reconstruc.type: Reconstructive surgical procedure (other/lower-priority, specific to delayed-presentation or re-rupture cases with a large tendon gap)
atr_chronic_neglected_rupture_reconstruc.effectiveness_metric: 0/11 (100% avoided) re-rupture or major complication at a mean 79-month follow-up in a case series of chronic/neglected ruptures or re-ruptures with an average 7.4cm tendon defect, treated with modified FHL transfer plus fibrous-stump augmentation; AOFAS score significantly improved, though isokinetic plantarflexion strength deficit of 28-36% persisted without functional weakness in daily activity (Wegrzyn et al 2010, PMID 19697026).
atr_chronic_neglected_rupture_reconstruc.reason_why: When the native tendon gap is too large (chronic retraction, re-rupture, or delayed presentation beyond several weeks) for direct end-to-end repair, transferring the flexor hallucis longus tendon provides a vascularized, functionally-analogous plantarflexor to bridge the defect, restoring push-off function even though it cannot restore 100% of native tendon strength.
atr_chronic_neglected_rupture_reconstruc.source: Wegrzyn J et al, Int Orthop 2010;34(8):1187-92 (PMID 19697026)
atr_chronic_neglected_rupture_reconstruc.confidence: moderate -- real outcome data but a very small case series (n=11) from a single center; needs replication in larger cohorts before the 100% figure can be generalized

ranked_high_to_low.name: Chronic/neglected rupture reconstruction, FHL tendon transfer (small series)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 0/11 re-rupture or major complication at mean 79-month follow-up; small case series (n=11), needs replication.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wegrzyn J et al, Int Orthop 2010;34(8):1187-92 (PMID 19697026)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Operative repair + accelerated functional rehabilitation (pooled re-rupture avoidance)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 97.7% avoided re-rupture (2.3% pooled re-rupture rate). Meta-analysis, 29 studies, n=15,862.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120 (PMID 30617123)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Operative repair, direct RCT (Willits 2010, both arms same accelerated rehab)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 70/72 (97.2%) avoided re-rupture. RCT, n=144.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Willits K et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2010;92(17):2767-75 (PMID 21037028)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-surgical repair, direct RCT (Nilsson-Helander 2010, early mobilization)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 47/49 (96%) avoided re-rupture; 12-month ATRS 88, no significant difference vs non-surgical arm (86). RCT, n=97.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Nilsson-Helander K et al, Am J Sports Med 2010;38(11):2186-93 (PMID 20802094)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-operative accelerated functional rehabilitation (pooled re-rupture avoidance)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 96.1% avoided re-rupture (3.9% pooled rate); statistically equal to surgery when early-ROM protocol used (risk ratio 0.60, p=0.23). Meta-analysis, 29 studies, n=15,862.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120 (PMID 30617123)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-operative accelerated rehabilitation, direct RCT (Willits 2010)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 69/72 (95.8%) avoided re-rupture; no clinically important functional difference vs surgery. RCT, n=144.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Willits K et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2010;92(17):2767-75 (PMID 21037028)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Non-operative treatment, overall-complication avoidance
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 98.4% avoided any other complication (1.6% rate) vs 95.1% surgical (4.9% rate, RR 2.76, p<0.001), mainly driven by surgical-site infection. Meta-analysis, n=15,862.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ochen Y et al, BMJ 2019;364:k5120 (PMID 30617123)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Return to play/sport, overall (all pathways combined)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 80% (95% CI 75-85%) pooled return-to-play rate. Meta-analysis, 108 studies, n=6,506.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zellers JA et al, Br J Sports Med 2016;50(21):1325-1332 (PMID 27259751)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Surgical repair, professional/high-demand athletes, return to play
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 69.4% (43/62) returned to play; those who returned matched control-level performance by 2 years. Cohort study (level 3), n=62.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Trofa DP et al, Am J Sports Med 2017;45(12):2864-2871 (PMID 28644678)

dupuytrens_contracture.name: Dupuytren's Contracture
dupuytrens_contracture.icd11_hint: Not independently confirmed this session - the official WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) is a JavaScript single-page app that automated fetch tools cannot render, so no live lookup was possible. Secondary coding references commonly list Dupuytren disease / palmar fascial fibromatosis under ICD-11 chapter FB (musculoskeletal), code FB81.2 'Palmar fascial fibromatosis [Dupuytren]', with ICD-10-CM equivalent M72.0 - flagging FB81.2 as UNVERIFIED against the primary WHO source and recommending manual confirmation before clinical/billing use.
dupuytrens_contracture.CURABILITY_NOTE: Dupuytren's contracture is a progressive fibroproliferative disease of the palmar fascia that is NOT curable in the sense of stopping the underlying fibrotic diathesis for life, but real, high, immediate anatomical correction of an existing contracture is very achievable and should be led with, not buried under recurrence caveats. For an established MCP-joint contracture, the least invasive real effective option is collagenase clostridium histolyticum (CCH, brand Xiaflex) injection: in the pivotal randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled CORD I trial (Hurst LC et al., N Engl J Med 2009;361:968-79, PMID 19726771; n=308), 64.0% of collagenase-treated joints reached the primary endpoint of contracture reduced to 0-5 degrees versus 6.8% with placebo (P<0.001), with joint range of motion improving from 43.9 to 80.7 degrees versus 45.3 to 49.5 degrees with placebo. The confirmatory CORD II trial (Gilpin D et al., J Hand Surg Am 2010;35(12):2027-38, PMID 21134613) found 44.4% of cords reached 0-5 degrees versus 4.8% placebo (P<0.001), with a mean 70.5% reduction in degree of joint contracture from baseline to 30 days after the last injection - real, large, immediate correction from a single office-based injection under local anaesthesia, no incision required. Percutaneous needle aponeurotomy (needle fasciotomy) is a comparably minimally invasive real alternative: in a randomised trial (van Rijssen AL et al., J Hand Surg Am 2006;31(5):717-25, PMID 16713831) it achieved 63% correction of total passive extension deficit at 6 weeks with 0% major complications, versus 79% correction with 5% major complications for limited fasciectomy. For severe, PIP-joint, multi-cord, or recurrent disease, limited (segmental) fasciectomy remains the most durable real option: the same cohort's 5-year follow-up (van Rijssen AL, Ter Linden H, Werker PM, Plast Reconstr Surg 2012;129(2):469-77, PMID 21987045) found 5-year recurrence of only 20.9% after limited fasciectomy versus 84.9% after needle aponeurotomy (P<0.001), and recurrence occurred significantly sooner in the needle group. Recurrence rates are real and significant with every treatment modality long-term and must be stated honestly: the CORDLESS long-term follow-up of collagenase-treated joints that initially achieved clinical success (Peimer CA et al., J Hand Surg Am 2015;40(7):1597-605, PMID 26096221) found 47% of successfully treated joints had recurred (>=20 degrees worsening) by 5 years (MCP 39%, PIP 66% - i.e. more than half of MCP-joint injections remained recurrence-free at 5 years); needle aponeurotomy recurs even faster and more often (84.9% at 5 years, above); limited fasciectomy is the most durable at 20.9% recurrence at 5 years, and even 'firebreak' dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin grafting - traditionally believed to lower recurrence further by replacing the diseased skin - showed no statistically significant recurrence benefit over standard fasciectomy in a prospective randomised trial (Ullah AS, Dias JJ, Bhowal B, J Bone Joint Surg Br 2009;91(3):374-8, PMID 19258615; pooled recurrence 12.2% at 3 years across both arms). Bottom line, honestly stated: the correction of an existing contracture is real, large, and well above placebo/no-treatment with all three main modalities; none of them is a permanent cure of the underlying palmar fibromatosis diathesis, and repeat treatment should be expected over a patient's lifetime, especially with the less invasive options.

curative_option.name: Severity- and joint-stratified treatment ladder: collagenase injection or needle aponeurotomy first-line for MCP-joint disease, limited fasciectomy for PIP-joint/severe/recurrent disease, radiotherapy only for pre-contracture early (nodule-only) disease
curative_option.note: There is no drug or procedure that cures the underlying Dupuytren diathesis (a fibroblast-driven fascial fibromatosis with a strong genetic/Northern-European predisposition); treatment targets the mechanical contracture once it interferes with hand function, chosen by joint involved and severity.

by_severity.stage: Early / pre-contracture (Tubiana stage N: nodule or pretendinous cord only, no joint contracture)
by_severity.recommended: Radiotherapy (external beam, e.g. 30 Gy in fractions) to arrest progression - NOT a treatment for existing contracture, and NOT indicated once a fixed contracture exists
by_severity.effectiveness: 13-year results: stage N disease remained stable or regressed in 87% of hands after radiotherapy; stage N/I in 70%; but once contracture reached stage I, 62% progressed despite radiotherapy, and stage II, 86% progressed - i.e. radiotherapy only reliably halts disease BEFORE a fixed contracture forms. 66% of patients reported long-term symptom relief. Mild late skin toxicity (atrophy/dry desquamation) in 32%, no radiotherapy-induced malignancy observed.
by_severity.source: Betz N, Ott OJ, Adamietz B, Sauer R, Fietkau R, Keilholz L. 'Radiotherapy in early-stage Dupuytren's contracture. Long-term results after 13 years.' Strahlenther Onkol. 2010;186(2):82-90. PMID 20127225

by_severity.stage: Established MCP-joint contracture (single cord, mild-moderate deformity)
by_severity.recommended: Collagenase clostridium histolyticum (CCH) injection as first-line least-invasive option, OR percutaneous needle aponeurotomy as an equally minimally-invasive alternative
by_severity.effectiveness: Collagenase CORD I: 64.0% of joints reached 0-5 degrees residual contracture vs 6.8% placebo (P<0.001). Collagenase CORD II: 44.4% reached 0-5 degrees vs 4.8% placebo; mean 70.5% contracture reduction. Needle aponeurotomy: 63% correction of total passive extension deficit at 6 weeks, 0% major complication rate.
by_severity.source: Hurst LC et al. NEJM 2009;361:968-79 (PMID 19726771); Gilpin D et al. J Hand Surg Am 2010;35(12):2027-38 (PMID 21134613); van Rijssen AL et al. J Hand Surg Am 2006;31(5):717-25 (PMID 16713831)

by_severity.stage: PIP-joint contracture, severe/multi-cord disease, or recurrence after minimally-invasive treatment
by_severity.recommended: Limited (segmental) fasciectomy; dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin graft considered for aggressive diathesis/recurrent disease although RCT evidence does not show it reduces recurrence versus fasciectomy alone
by_severity.effectiveness: Limited fasciectomy: 79% correction of total passive extension deficit at 6 weeks (vs 63% for needle aponeurotomy), 5-year recurrence only 20.9% (most durable of all options studied). Firebreak dermofasciectomy vs standard fasciectomy RCT: pooled recurrence 12.2% at 3 years, no significant difference between the two techniques.
by_severity.source: van Rijssen AL et al. J Hand Surg Am 2006;31(5):717-25 (PMID 16713831); van Rijssen AL, Ter Linden H, Werker PM. Plast Reconstr Surg 2012;129(2):469-77 (PMID 21987045); Ullah AS, Dias JJ, Bhowal B. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2009;91(3):374-8 (PMID 19258615)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full survey of every real, evidence-based non-surgical medicine, injection, and surgical intervention used for Dupuytren's contracture, each with real trial effectiveness data, mechanism, source, and honesty confidence flag. Priority order per protocol: medicine/injection first, then procedure, then adjuncts.

medicines.name: Collagenase clostridium histolyticum (CCH) injection (brand: Xiaflex/Xiapex)
medicines.type: Injectable enzymatic medicine (FDA-approved 2010; first and only FDA-approved non-surgical pharmacologic treatment)
medicines.effectiveness: CORD I (n=308, RCT, double-blind, placebo-controlled): 64.0% of collagenase-treated joints vs 6.8% placebo reached contracture reduced to 0-5 degrees (P<0.001); ROM improved 43.9 deg to 80.7 deg vs 45.3 deg to 49.5 deg with placebo; all secondary endpoints met (P<=0.002). CORD II (n=66 cords): 44.4% vs 4.8% reached 0-5 degrees (P<0.001); mean 70.5% reduction in contracture at 30 days post-injection. CORDLESS 5-year durability: of joints that achieved initial clinical success, 47% recurred (>=20 degrees worsening) by 5 years (MCP 39%, PIP 66%) - meaning 61% of MCP joints remained recurrence-free at 5 years.
medicines.reason_why: Mixture of two collagenase enzymes (AUX-I and AUX-II, from Clostridium histolyticum) injected directly into the palpable collagen cord; enzymatically lyses the collagen (types I and III) that makes up the pathological Dupuytren cord, allowing the surgeon/hand therapist to manually rupture the weakened cord and extend the finger the next day - a targeted biochemical fasciotomy without a surgical incision.
medicines.source: Hurst LC, Badalamente MA, Hentz VR, et al. 'Injectable collagenase clostridium histolyticum for Dupuytren's contracture.' N Engl J Med. 2009;361(10):968-79. PMID 19726771. | Gilpin D, Coleman S, Hall S, et al. J Hand Surg Am. 2010;35(12):2027-38. PMID 21134613. | Peimer CA, Blazar P, Coleman S, et al. J Hand Surg Am. 2015;40(7):1597-605. PMID 26096221.
medicines.confidence: high - multiple large RCTs plus long-term open-label extension

medicines.name: Percutaneous needle aponeurotomy (needle fasciotomy, PNF)
medicines.type: Minimally invasive percutaneous procedure (needle used to mechanically divide the cord through the skin, local anaesthesia, no incision)
medicines.effectiveness: 63% correction of total passive extension deficit at 6 weeks, 0% major complication rate (vs 79% correction / 5% major complications for limited fasciectomy in the same RCT). Same cohort at 5 years: 84.9% recurrence vs 20.9% for limited fasciectomy (P<0.001); recurrence occurred significantly sooner with PNF. 53% of patients still preferred PNF given the option of easy repeat treatment.
medicines.reason_why: A hypodermic needle is used percutaneously to perforate and mechanically weaken/transect the pathological cord at multiple levels along its length, then the finger is manually extended to rupture the remaining fibrous tissue - lowest morbidity and fastest recovery of any active treatment, but the cord is left in place (not excised), which is the mechanistic reason for its markedly higher recurrence rate versus excisional surgery.
medicines.source: van Rijssen AL, Gerbrandy FS, Ter Linden H, Klip H, Werker PM. J Hand Surg Am. 2006;31(5):717-25. PMID 16713831. | van Rijssen AL, Ter Linden H, Werker PM. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012;129(2):469-77. PMID 21987045.
medicines.confidence: high - randomised trial with 5-year follow-up

medicines.name: Limited (segmental/selective) fasciectomy
medicines.type: Surgical excision of the diseased fascial cord
medicines.effectiveness: 79% correction of total passive extension deficit at 6 weeks; 5% major complication rate. Most durable option studied: only 20.9% recurrence at 5 years (vs 84.9% for needle aponeurotomy, P<0.001).
medicines.reason_why: Open surgical excision physically removes the pathological palmar fascia cord rather than merely dividing or enzymatically weakening it, which removes more of the diathesis-affected tissue and mechanically explains its superior durability versus needle aponeurotomy or collagenase, at the cost of a formal incision, longer recovery, and higher (though still modest, ~5%) major-complication rate (digital nerve/artery injury, infection, hematoma, complex regional pain syndrome, flare reaction).
medicines.source: van Rijssen AL, Gerbrandy FS, Ter Linden H, Klip H, Werker PM. J Hand Surg Am. 2006;31(5):717-25. PMID 16713831. | van Rijssen AL, Ter Linden H, Werker PM. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012;129(2):469-77. PMID 21987045.
medicines.confidence: high - randomised trial with 5-year follow-up; long-standing surgical gold standard

medicines.name: Dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin graft ('firebreak' graft)
medicines.type: Surgical excision plus skin replacement, reserved for severe/recurrent/aggressive diathesis disease
medicines.effectiveness: Prospective RCT comparing firebreak dermofasciectomy vs standard fasciectomy: pooled recurrence 12.2% at 3 years, with NO statistically significant difference in correction or recurrence between the skin-graft and non-graft groups - i.e. the graft did not prove superior in this trial despite long-standing clinical belief that replacing the overlying diseased dermis interrupts the fibrotic field.
medicines.reason_why: Excises the cord together with the overlying skin (believed by many surgeons to harbour early myofibroblastic disease activity) and replaces it with a full-thickness skin graft, intended to act as a biological 'firebreak' against local recurrence; reserved in practice for recurrent disease, aggressive Dupuytren diathesis (young age of onset, bilateral, ectopic disease e.g. Ledderhose/Peyronie, strong family history), or when overlying skin is directly involved/tethered.
medicines.source: Ullah AS, Dias JJ, Bhowal B. 'Does a firebreak full-thickness skin graft prevent recurrence after surgery for Dupuytren's contracture?: a prospective, randomised trial.' J Bone Joint Surg Br. 2009;91(3):374-8. PMID 19258615.
medicines.confidence: moderate - single RCT; result (no added benefit) contradicts long-standing surgical dogma and is honestly reported as such rather than assuming superiority

medicines.name: External beam radiotherapy (early/nodular stage only)
medicines.type: Non-invasive radiation therapy, disease-modifying only BEFORE a fixed contracture forms
medicines.effectiveness: 13-year long-term results: stage N (nodule/cord, no contracture) remained stable or regressed in 87% of hands; stage N/I in 70%. Once a fixed contracture was already present, radiotherapy was far less useful - stage I: 62% progressed anyway; stage II: 86% progressed anyway. 66% long-term symptom relief overall. Mild late skin toxicity in 32%; no radiation-induced malignancy observed.
medicines.reason_why: Low-dose fractionated radiotherapy is theorised to reduce fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis in the early proliferative phase of the disease, before irreversible collagen cross-linking and cord contracture set in - explaining why it works well in stage N/N-I disease but not once a mechanical contracture already exists.
medicines.source: Betz N, Ott OJ, Adamietz B, Sauer R, Fietkau R, Keilholz L. Strahlenther Onkol. 2010;186(2):82-90. PMID 20127225.
medicines.confidence: moderate-high - large single-centre long-term cohort, not an RCT, but the only long-term (13-year) dataset for this indication

medicines.name: Intralesional corticosteroid injection into an early nodule
medicines.type: Off-label anti-inflammatory injection, used for painful/tender early nodules only
medicines.effectiveness: Not supported by any adequately powered RCT for altering contracture progression; used empirically in some hand-surgery practice guidelines for symptomatic relief of a tender early nodule, not for correcting or preventing established contracture.
medicines.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress local fibroblast proliferation and inflammatory mediator release, which may transiently soften and reduce tenderness of an early inflamed nodule, but there is no real trial evidence it prevents cord formation or contracture.
medicines.source: No adequately powered RCT identified in this search; included for completeness per exhaustive-survey requirement and explicitly flagged as weak/unverified evidence rather than assigned a fabricated effectiveness percentage.
medicines.confidence: low - included transparently as an unproven, non-recommended-as-primary option, not a real cure or correction modality

medicines.name: Topical/injectable verapamil (investigational)
medicines.effectiveness: Limited small-scale/preclinical and case-series evidence for anti-fibrotic effect (via reduced fibroblast collagen and extracellular matrix production, extrapolated from its use in other fibroproliferative conditions such as keloid and Peyronie's disease); no adequately powered RCT in Dupuytren's contracture identified in this search establishing a real effectiveness percentage.
medicines.reason_why: Verapamil inhibits fibroblast collagen synthesis and increases collagenase activity in vitro, the same rationale used for its off-label use in other fibromatoses (keloid, Peyronie's disease), but this has not been confirmed in an adequately powered Dupuytren's contracture trial.
medicines.source: No adequately powered Dupuytren-specific RCT identified in this search; included for completeness and explicitly flagged as investigational/unproven rather than assigned a fabricated effectiveness percentage.
medicines.confidence: low - investigational, not a recommended real-world treatment for this disease based on the evidence located this session

medicines.name: Hand therapy: post-procedure splinting and stretching
medicines.effectiveness: Used after collagenase injection, needle aponeurotomy, or fasciectomy to maintain the achieved extension and reduce (not eliminate) recurrence; evidence for splinting as a stand-alone or added intervention is mixed and it does not correct an existing contracture on its own.
medicines.reason_why: Night extension splinting is intended to counteract the fibroblast/myofibroblast contractile tendency that drives recurrence during wound remodelling after a procedure, but does not itself lyse or excise diseased tissue.
medicines.source: Standard hand-surgery post-procedure adjunct per major hand-surgery guidelines (e.g. British Society for Surgery of the Hand); no single definitive RCT quantifying splinting's independent effectiveness percentage was identified in this search, so no fabricated number is given.
medicines.confidence: moderate - accepted adjunct in clinical practice, effect size not independently quantified this session

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (proportion reaching 0-5 degrees residual contracture vs percent correction of total passive extension deficit vs percent stable/regressed at long-term follow-up vs recurrence-free rate) in DIFFERENT populations and joints (MCP vs PIP) - ranking together is directionally useful for treatment selection, not a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Radiotherapy is included as a disease-modifying option for pre-contracture (stage N) disease only, not as a treatment for an existing contracture, and is ranked/labelled accordingly. Intralesional steroid and topical verapamil are deliberately excluded from the ranked list (rather than assigned a fabricated percentage) since no adequately powered RCT establishing a real effectiveness number for either was identified in this search - see exhaustive_medicine_survey for their honest low-confidence entries.
