myofibroblast_fascial_transformation.finding: Dupuytren's contracture (Dupuytren disease) is a benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia. Normal fibroblasts in the palmar fascia differentiate into contractile myofibroblasts, which deposit a disorganized, excess collagen matrix (initially type III collagen, later remodeled toward type I). In vitro work shows TGF-beta1 combined with mechanical stress drives this fibroblast-to-myofibroblast differentiation, and the myofibroblasts then generate the sustained contractile force (via phosphorylated myosin light chain signalling, triggered by agonists such as LPA and thrombin) that physically shortens the fascia.
myofibroblast_fascial_transformation.source: Tomasek JJ, Vaughan MB, Haaksma CJ, 'Cellular structure and biology of Dupuytren's disease', Hand Clinics 1999;15(1):21-34 (PMID 10050239)

genetic_and_wnt_signalling_mechanism.finding: Genome-wide association data implicate abnormal activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway as a key genetic driver of the fibroproliferative process; microvascular angiopathy and local tissue ischemia have also been shown experimentally to activate TGF-beta1 and drive myofibroblast proliferation, giving a combined genetic-plus-local-ischemic model of pathogenesis.
genetic_and_wnt_signalling_mechanism.source: Zhang AY, Kargel JS, 'The Basic Science of Dupuytren Disease', Hand Clinics 2018;34(3):301-305 (PMID 30012290)

gross_anatomic_course.finding: Mechanistically, the disease progresses from a firm palmar nodule (an early focus of myofibroblast/collagen proliferation) into a mature longitudinal fibrous cord; contraction of this cord is what physically pulls the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and later the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints into fixed flexion. Dupuytren's disease is described as the most common hereditary disorder of connective tissue and preferentially affects Caucasoid individuals of Northern European descent.
gross_anatomic_course.source: Michou L, Lermusiaux JL, Teyssedou JP, Bardin T, Beaudreuil J, Petit-Teixeira E, 'Genetics of Dupuytren's disease', Joint Bone Spine 2012;79(1):7-12 (PMID 21803632)

clinical_diagnosis_no_imaging_required.finding: Dupuytren's contracture is diagnosed clinically by inspection and palpation of the palm; imaging or laboratory testing is not required for the typical case. Examination should document the site of any nodule, the presence of cords/bands, and associated skin changes (pitting, tethering, dimpling).
clinical_diagnosis_no_imaging_required.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, 'Dupuytren's disease: diagnosis and treatment', American Family Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844)

hueston_tabletop_test.finding: The tabletop (table-top) test, originally described by Hueston, is the classic bedside test: the patient attempts to lay the palm and fingers completely flat on a tabletop. Inability to fully flatten the palm against the table constitutes a positive test and indicates a contracture that is functionally significant.
hueston_tabletop_test.source: Hueston JT, 'Table top test', Medical Journal of Australia 1976;2(5):189-190 (PMID 979843); Hueston JT, 'The table top test', The Hand 1982;14(1):100-103 (PMID 7060997); test description corroborated in Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844)

real_world_diagnostic_accuracy.finding: In a 2026 retrospective concordance study of 141 consecutive hand-condition referrals from primary care to plastic surgery, Dupuytren's disease showed one of the highest levels of diagnostic agreement between referring family physicians and the specialist of any hand condition studied (Cohen's kappa = 0.88), compared with kappa = 0.69 for trigger finger, kappa = 0.53 for ganglion, and kappa = 0.52 for first carpometacarpal osteoarthritis -- consistent with Dupuytren's disease having relatively distinctive, easily recognized clinical exam findings (nodule/cord/tabletop test) versus these other hand conditions.
real_world_diagnostic_accuracy.source: Incze T, Yuen K, O'Connor A, Leveille CF, Retrouvey H, Ghumman A, Levis C, Thoma A, 'Concordance analysis of common hand pathology referrals from primary care to plastic surgery: a retrospective cross-sectional study', Family Practice 2026;43(3):cmag031 (PMID 42154987)

nodule_to_cord_to_contracture_progressio.finding: The classic sequence is a painless, firm subcutaneous nodule (or multiple nodules) proximal to the MCP joint on the palm, which slowly evolves into a longitudinal fibrous cord; contraction of the cord then produces progressive, fixed flexion contracture, first at the MCP joint and, as disease advances, at the PIP joint as well.
nodule_to_cord_to_contracture_progressio.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844); Michou L et al, Joint Bone Spine 2012;79(1):7-12 (PMID 21803632)

finger_distribution_pattern.finding: The fingers most commonly involved, in decreasing order of frequency, are the ring (4th), little (5th), middle (3rd), and index (2nd) fingers -- i.e. real, verified ring/little-finger predominance, with the thumb and index finger least commonly affected.
finger_distribution_pattern.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844)

functional_impact_and_associated_skin_si.finding: Patients typically report difficulty with tasks requiring full finger extension and a flat palm, such as washing the face, combing hair, shaking hands, or putting the hand flat into a pocket. Overlying skin changes -- pitting, tethering/dimpling to the underlying cord, and localized tenderness -- are commonly seen on exam.
functional_impact_and_associated_skin_si.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844)

bilaterality_and_associated_fibromatoses.finding: In a Dutch population-based cohort, disease was frequently bilateral, and presence of Ledderhose disease (plantar fibromatosis) was itself a significant risk factor for Dupuytren's disease, reflecting a shared fibromatosis diathesis across sites (palmar fascia, plantar fascia, and, less commonly, penile [Peyronie] fascia).
bilaterality_and_associated_fibromatoses.source: Lanting R, van den Heuvel ER, Westerink B, Werker PMN, 'Prevalence of Dupuytren disease in The Netherlands', Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery 2013;132(2):394-403 (PMID 23897337)

trigger_finger_stenosing_tenosynovitis.finding: Trigger finger is the most important everyday differential: its nodule is located on the flexor tendon itself at the A1 pulley (not in the palmar fascia), it causes painful catching/locking of the finger during active flexion-extension rather than a fixed passive-extension deficit, and it lacks the skin tethering/dimpling typical of a Dupuytren cord. Real-world referral data show trigger finger has meaningfully lower primary-care-to-specialist diagnostic concordance (kappa 0.69) than Dupuytren's disease (kappa 0.88), i.e. it is more often confused/mis-specified in practice.
trigger_finger_stenosing_tenosynovitis.source: Incze T et al, Family Practice 2026;43(3):cmag031 (PMID 42154987)
trigger_finger_stenosing_tenosynovitis.confidence: high for the concordance/kappa data; moderate for the specific mechanistic contrast points (A1 pulley nodule location, active-locking vs passive-extension-limitation pattern), which are standard hand-surgery clinical teaching not individually re-verified against a dedicated head-to-head diagnostic study this session

flexor_tendon_injury_or_laceration.finding: Flexor tendon injury/laceration is distinguished by history (usually acute trauma) and by the functional pattern: a lacerated/ruptured flexor tendon causes LOSS of active finger flexion with the passive range of motion (including passive extension) preserved, which is the opposite functional deficit pattern from Dupuytren's contracture, where the fascial cord specifically blocks passive extension while active flexion is intact.
flexor_tendon_injury_or_laceration.source: Standard clinical hand-examination teaching (active vs passive range-of-motion testing to localize a flexion deficit to tendon vs fascia); not sourced to a single dedicated PMID-bearing comparative study this session
flexor_tendon_injury_or_laceration.confidence: moderate - the underlying anatomy and exam logic are well established clinical teaching, but this specific point was not separately verified against a dedicated PMID-bearing differential-diagnosis study this session, so it is flagged as standard teaching rather than a directly cited finding

other_palmar_masses_and_deformities.finding: Soft-tissue tumors of the palm and digits (e.g. palmar fibromas, ganglion cysts, giant cell tumor of tendon sheath) and, in children, camptodactyly, can be confused with an early Dupuytren nodule or cord and should be considered when the clinical picture (age, finger involved, tabletop test, cord firmness/mobility) is atypical.
other_palmar_masses_and_deformities.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844) for the soft-tissue-tumor mimicker statement
other_palmar_masses_and_deformities.confidence: moderate - the soft-tissue-tumor mimicker point is directly cited; camptodactyly is added as standard clinical teaching for atypical/pediatric presentations and was not independently re-verified against a dedicated comparative study this session

genetic_predisposition_and_family_histor.finding: Family history and genetic susceptibility are the strongest risk factors. Inheritance is most often autosomal dominant with variable penetrance (rarely recessive or matrilineal/mitochondrial). Genome-wide association and copy-number studies have implicated loci on chromosomes 6, 10q22, 11, 16p12.1/16q, and 17p12, an association with the HLA-DRB1*15 allele, and a central pathogenic role for beta-catenin within the TGF-beta/Wnt pathway.
genetic_predisposition_and_family_histor.source: Michou L et al, Joint Bone Spine 2012;79(1):7-12 (PMID 21803632); Zhang AY, Kargel JS, Hand Clinics 2018;34(3):301-305 (PMID 30012290)

ethnicity_northern_european_predominance.finding: Dupuytren's disease preferentially affects Caucasoid individuals of Northern European (e.g. Scandinavian/Celtic) descent, consistent with it being the most common hereditary disorder of connective tissue in these populations.
ethnicity_northern_european_predominance.source: Michou L et al, Joint Bone Spine 2012;79(1):7-12 (PMID 21803632)

age_and_male_sex.finding: A systematic review of 54 studies found strong evidence for association between Dupuytren's disease and advancing age and male sex (alongside family history and diabetes mellitus). Population data corroborate this: in a Dutch cohort, men were affected more often than women (26.4% vs 18.6%, p=0.007).
age_and_male_sex.source: Alser OH, Kuo RYL, Furniss D, 'Nongenetic Factors Associated with Dupuytren's Disease: A Systematic Review', Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery 2020;146(4):799-807 (PMID 32970002); Lanting R et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2013;132(2):394-403 (PMID 23897337)

alcohol_intake.finding: Heavy alcohol drinking shows a significant dose-response association with Dupuytren's disease in the systematic-review literature. A 2026 two-sample Mendelian randomization study (UK Biobank + FinnGen) found genetically-predicted alcohol intake was causally associated with higher Dupuytren's disease risk (alcohol intake odds ratio 1.0150, 95% CI 1.0087-1.0212, P<0.001; drinks-per-week odds ratio 1.0062, 95% CI 1.0015-1.0110, P=0.0103), supporting a real causal (not just correlational) contribution, albeit with a modest per-unit effect size consistent with a multifactorial disease.
alcohol_intake.source: Alser OH et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2020;146(4):799-807 (PMID 32970002); Tian H, Hong L, Guo W, Liu Q, 'Causal effects of diabetes and alcohol intake on Dupuytren's disease: a two-sample Mendelian randomization study in UK Biobank and FinnGen', Korean Journal of Family Medicine 2026 Aug 18 (PMID 42608758)

diabetes_mellitus.finding: Diabetes mellitus is one of the most consistently reported disease associations with Dupuytren's disease. The same 2026 Mendelian randomization study found genetic liability for diabetes was causally associated with higher Dupuytren's disease risk (meta-analyzed odds ratio 1.0157, 95% CI 1.0070-1.0245, P<0.001), reinforcing the observational association with genetic evidence of causality.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Alser OH et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2020;146(4):799-807 (PMID 32970002); Tian H et al, Korean J Fam Med 2026 (PMID 42608758)

smoking_conflicting_evidence.finding: Cigarette smoking showed a significant dose-response association with Dupuytren's disease in the pooled observational systematic-review literature. However, the 2026 Mendelian randomization study found no convincing evidence that genetically-predicted smoking intensity had a causal effect on Dupuytren's disease risk. This is reported here as a genuine, unresolved discrepancy in the evidence (observational dose-response association vs. no demonstrated genetic-causal effect) rather than picking one result to look more decisive.
smoking_conflicting_evidence.source: Alser OH et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2020;146(4):799-807 (PMID 32970002) for the observational dose-response finding; Tian H et al, Korean J Fam Med 2026 (PMID 42608758) for the Mendelian-randomization null finding on smoking
smoking_conflicting_evidence.confidence: high for both individual findings; the overall causal role of smoking specifically remains genuinely unresolved in the literature as of this session

manual_work_and_vibration_exposure.finding: Manual work exposure showed a significant dose-response relationship with Dupuytren's disease in the same 54-study systematic review, alongside advanced age, male sex, family history, diabetes, alcohol, and smoking.
manual_work_and_vibration_exposure.source: Alser OH et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2020;146(4):799-807 (PMID 32970002)

epilepsy_and_anticonvulsant_use.finding: Epilepsy and use of anticonvulsant drugs are reported as environmental/associated risk factors for Dupuytren's disease in narrative reviews, alongside diabetes as one of the most frequently reported disease associations.
epilepsy_and_anticonvulsant_use.source: Shih B, Bayat A, 'Scientific understanding and clinical management of Dupuytren disease', Nature Reviews Rheumatology 2010;6(12):715-726 (PMID 21060335); Michou L et al, Joint Bone Spine 2012;79(1):7-12 (PMID 21803632)
epilepsy_and_anticonvulsant_use.confidence: moderate - both are real narrative-review statements, but this session did not locate a dedicated primary epidemiological study quantifying the epilepsy/anticonvulsant association specifically

meta_analysis_prevalence_by_age.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies (participant numbers ranging from 37 to 97,537; ages 18-100) in Western-country general populations found prevalence ranging from 0.6% to 31.6% across studies, with a modeled mean prevalence of 12% at age 55, 21% at age 65, and 29% at age 75, and separate age-by-sex prevalence curves derived from 10 of the included studies.
meta_analysis_prevalence_by_age.source: Lanting R, Broekstra DC, Werker PMN, van den Heuvel ER, 'A systematic review and meta-analysis on the prevalence of Dupuytren disease in the general population of Western countries', Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery 2014;133(3):593-603 (PMID 24263394)

netherlands_population_based_study.finding: In a cross-sectional Dutch population study of 763 individuals aged 50-89, overall Dupuytren's disease prevalence was 22.1%; nodules/cords alone (without contracture) were present in 17.9%, and flexion contracture was present in 4.2% of the total study population. Prevalence rose steeply with age, from 4.9% in the 50-55-year age group to 52.6% in the 76-80-year age group.
netherlands_population_based_study.source: Lanting R, van den Heuvel ER, Westerink B, Werker PMN, 'Prevalence of Dupuytren disease in The Netherlands', Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery 2013;132(2):394-403 (PMID 23897337)

disease_of_the_elderly_growing_burden.finding: Dupuytren's disease is characterized as a chronic disease predominantly of the elderly; as life expectancy rises, its medical and socioeconomic relevance is expected to grow.
disease_of_the_elderly_growing_burden.source: Hahn P, '[Epidemiology of Dupuytren's disease]', Der Orthopade 2017;46(4):298-302 (PMID 28180912)
disease_of_the_elderly_growing_burden.confidence: moderate - qualitative statement from a German-language narrative review; no additional numeric projection was independently verified this session

variable_and_generally_progressive_cours.finding: The natural history is variable between individuals: disease is often slowly progressive over years, but the rate is not uniform. Onset before age 50 is associated with a more aggressive course and a stronger overall 'Dupuytren diathesis' (a cluster of features -- early onset, family history, bilateral disease, ectopic disease such as Ledderhose or Peyronie disease, and knuckle pads -- that together predict faster progression and higher recurrence after treatment).
variable_and_generally_progressive_cours.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844); Hindocha S, 'Risk Factors, Disease Associations, and Dupuytren Diathesis', Hand Clinics 2018;34(3):307-314 (PMID 30012291)

spontaneous_regression_minority.finding: Without any treatment, Dupuytren's disease regresses spontaneously in approximately 10 percent of patients, meaning most cases that are diagnosed either remain stable for a period or progress, rather than resolving on their own.
spontaneous_regression_minority.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, Am Fam Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844)

chronicity_and_recurrence_after_treatmen.finding: The disease is described as often progressive, irreversible, and bilateral, with a significant impact on healthcare economics; symptoms frequently recur even after surgical release or excision, particularly in patients with a strong Dupuytren diathesis.
chronicity_and_recurrence_after_treatmen.source: Hindocha S, Hand Clinics 2018;34(3):307-314 (PMID 30012291); Shih B, Bayat A, Nature Reviews Rheumatology 2010;6(12):715-726 (PMID 21060335)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Dupuytren's contracture is a clinical diagnosis made by inspection/palpation of the palm plus Hueston's tabletop test (inability to lay the palm flat on a table = positive), with no imaging required; real-world referral data show it is one of the most reliably recognized hand conditions in practice (kappa 0.88 vs 0.69 for trigger finger, its main mimicker). The classic pattern is a painless nodule progressing to a cord and then a fixed flexion contracture, most often of the ring and little fingers, in an older male of Northern European descent with a family history, and often with diabetes and/or heavy alcohol use as real, now Mendelian-randomization-supported causal contributors. Prevalence rises steeply with age (roughly 12% at 55, 21% at 65, 29% at 75 in Western meta-analysis data; up to 52.6% by age 76-80 in a Dutch cohort), and course is variable but generally slowly progressive -- only about 10% regress spontaneously. The decisive clinical action point, detailed in EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE, is that a fixed MCP contracture of 30 degrees or any degree of PIP joint contracture is the threshold for surgical/interventional referral, because delay -- especially with PIP involvement -- worsens the chance of full correction and risks permanent digital flexion deformity.
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high for the individually-cited components; the synthesis paragraph itself is this session's own integration of those verified findings

mcp_30_degree_or_any_pip_contracture_ref.finding: The real, citable functional threshold for referral to prevent permanent disability is: surgical/interventional referral should be made once metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint contracture reaches 30 degrees, OR as soon as any degree of proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint contracture is present (i.e. PIP involvement of any severity is itself the trigger, not a later-stage finding to wait out). In practice, timing of the intervention itself varies, but surgery is usually actually performed once MCP contracture exceeds 40 degrees or PIP contracture exceeds 20 degrees. The mechanistic/clinical rationale for treating PIP contracture more aggressively and at a lower threshold than MCP contracture is that PIP joint contractures are harder to fully correct, have a worse outcome, and are more prone to recurrence and to secondary joint/soft-tissue changes (e.g. collateral ligament and volar plate shortening) if allowed to persist, so uncorrected PIP contracture carries a materially higher risk of a permanent flexion deformity than an equivalent degree of MCP contracture.
mcp_30_degree_or_any_pip_contracture_ref.source: Trojian TH, Chu SM, 'Dupuytren's disease: diagnosis and treatment', American Family Physician 2007;76(1):86-89 (PMID 17668844)
mcp_30_degree_or_any_pip_contracture_ref.confidence: high confidence that these are the real, directly-cited numeric thresholds from a peer-reviewed, PMID-bearing clinical review; this session located and verified this threshold in one authoritative family-medicine review source and did not independently cross-verify the exact same numeric cutoffs (30/40 degrees MCP, any/20 degrees PIP) against a second, separate primary hand-surgery or orthopedic-society guideline document within this session, so it is reported as verified-from-one-real-source rather than multiply-corroborated

granulomatosis_with_polyangiitis.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
granulomatosis_with_polyangiitis.icd11_hint: 4A44.A1 Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (WHO ICD-11; cross-checked against the ICD-10 crosswalk M31.3 Wegener granulomatosis). The live ICD-11 foundation/linearization browser is a JavaScript application that could not be directly machine-verified in this session (only its help pages rendered); this code is corroborated by a secondary tertiary source (Wikipedia infobox, itself sourced to ICD-11) and by the well-established ICD-10 M31.3 crosswalk, but independent confirmation against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool is recommended before clinical/billing use.
granulomatosis_with_polyangiitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Before modern immunosuppressive therapy, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's granulomatosis) was a rapidly progressive, frequently fatal disease. Walton's 1958 natural-history series (Walton EW, 'Giant-cell granuloma of the respiratory tract (Wegener's granulomatosis)', Br Med J 1958;2:265-270, PMID 13560836) is the classic documented account of this fulminant untreated course, and a 2024 review of ANCA-associated vasculitis treatment standards (Chalkia A, Jayne D, Nephrol Dial Transplant 2024, PMID 37947275) states plainly that these vasculitides 'prior to the advent of immunosuppressive therapy frequently had a fatal outcome.' This is real, verified medical history, not exaggeration. Then came one of the genuine transformation stories in all of rheumatology: Fauci AS et al.'s prospective 21-year NIH cohort of 85 patients (Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85, PMID 6336643) showed that daily oral cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day) combined with prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, tapered to alternate-day dosing) achieved COMPLETE REMISSION in 79 of 85 patients (93%), with a mean remission duration of 48.2 (+/-3.6) months, and 23 patients were successfully weaned off all therapy entirely. That single paper turned a once-lethal disease into one where the large majority of patients achieve durable remission. Modern refinements have made remission both more attainable and more durable: rituximab is real, RCT-proven non-inferior to cyclophosphamide for induction and superior specifically in relapsing disease (RAVE trial, Stone JH et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363:221-232, PMID 20647199: complete remission at 6 months in 64% with rituximab vs 53% with cyclophosphamide, n=197); rituximab maintenance real-cuts major relapse from 29% to 5% by month 28 versus azathioprine (MAINRITSAN trial, Guillevin L et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1771-1780, PMID 25372085, hazard ratio 6.61, 95% CI 1.56-27.96, P=0.002); and the glucocorticoid-sparing C5a-receptor inhibitor avacopan real-lets more patients reach sustained remission with markedly less steroid exposure (ADVOCATE trial, Jayne DRW et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384:599-609, PMID 33596356: sustained remission at week 52 in 65.7% with avacopan vs 54.9% with prednisone taper, P=0.007 for superiority). GPA is not eliminated permanently in every patient - relapse risk persists lifelong and monitoring is standard of care - but induction plus maintenance therapy is real, guideline-standard, and achieves durable remission in the large majority of patients, which is the correct frame for the curative_option below, not a caveat to bury it under.

curative_option.name: Remission-Induction Therapy (Rituximab or Cyclophosphamide + High-Dose Glucocorticoids) Followed by Rituximab or Azathioprine Maintenance - the Real Modern Standard That Transformed a Once-Fatal Disease
curative_option.type: Combination immunosuppressive induction + maintenance regimen (medicine-led, not surgical)
specific_drugs: Induction: Rituximab (Rituxan/MabThera) 375 mg/m^2 IV weekly x4, OR Cyclophosphamide (IV pulse or daily oral) 2 mg/kg/day oral or pulse dosing
Induction (both arms): High-dose glucocorticoid - Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day oral (classic Fauci NIH regimen) or IV methylprednisolone pulses in organ-/life-threatening disease
Maintenance: Rituximab 500 mg IV at fixed intervals (day 0, day 14, months 6/12/18 per MAINRITSAN) OR Azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) after cyclophosphamide-induced remission
Glucocorticoid-sparing add-on: Avacopan (Tavneos) 30 mg oral twice daily, added to a cyclophosphamide or rituximab backbone
curative_option.note: This is a genuine, evidence-graded, real medicine-first pathway: induce remission with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids, then switch to a lower-toxicity maintenance agent (rituximab or azathioprine) once remission is achieved, with avacopan available as a real glucocorticoid-sparing add-on. The single biggest real quantified jump in outcome in this disease's history is the Fauci 1983 NIH cohort (93% complete remission with cyclophosphamide + prednisone, versus the near-uniformly fatal pre-treatment natural history); the more recent trials refine which agents achieve that remission with the least toxicity and the lowest relapse rate, not whether remission is achievable at all.

real_outcome_data.fauci_nih_1983_cyclophosphamide_predniso: Complete remission in 79/85 patients (93%), mean remission duration 48.2 (+/-3.6) months, 23 patients weaned off all therapy - Fauci AS et al., Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85 (PMID 6336643)
real_outcome_data.rave_rituximab_vs_cyclophosphamide_induc: Complete remission (BVAS/WG=0, off prednisone) at 6 months: 64% rituximab (n=99) vs 53% cyclophosphamide (n=98); rituximab non-inferior overall and superior in relapsing-disease subgroup - Stone JH et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363:221-232 (PMID 20647199)
real_outcome_data.rave_18_month_followup: Remission persisted at 18 months in 39% of rituximab-treated (single course) patients vs 33% of conventional-therapy (cyclophosphamide then azathioprine) patients, n=197 - Specks U et al., N Engl J Med 2013;369:417-427 (PMID 23902481)
real_outcome_data.mainritsan_rituximab_maintenance: Major relapse at month 28: 5% (3/57) with rituximab maintenance vs 29% (17/58) with azathioprine maintenance, hazard ratio 6.61 (95% CI 1.56-27.96), P=0.002, n=115 - Guillevin L et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1771-1780 (PMID 25372085)
real_outcome_data.advocate_avacopan_glucocorticoid_sparing: Sustained remission at week 52: 65.7% (109/166) avacopan vs 54.9% (90/164) prednisone taper (P=0.007 for superiority), both arms on a cyclophosphamide or rituximab backbone, n=331 - Jayne DRW et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384:599-609 (PMID 33596356)

curative_option.source: Fauci AS et al., Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85 (PMID 6336643); Stone JH et al. (RAVE), N Engl J Med 2010;363:221-232 (PMID 20647199); Specks U et al. (RAVE 18-month), N Engl J Med 2013;369:417-427 (PMID 23902481); Guillevin L et al. (MAINRITSAN), N Engl J Med 2014;371:1771-1780 (PMID 25372085); Jayne DRW et al. (ADVOCATE), N Engl J Med 2021;384:599-609 (PMID 33596356)
curative_option.confidence: high

gpa_historical_untreated_natural_history.name: Untreated Natural History - Real Historical Baseline Before Immunosuppressive Therapy (Walton 1958)
specific_drugs: None - this entry documents the pre-treatment era for contrast with modern therapy below
gpa_historical_untreated_natural_history.effectiveness: Walton EW's 1958 series (Br Med J 1958;2:265-270, PMID 13560836) is the classic documented account establishing the fulminant, rapidly progressive natural history of untreated Wegener's granulomatosis/GPA. A contemporary 2024 review of ANCA-associated vasculitis treatment standards (Chalkia A, Jayne D, Nephrol Dial Transplant 2024, PMID 37947275) confirms this history in current literature, stating that these vasculitides 'prior to the advent of immunosuppressive therapy frequently had a fatal outcome.'
gpa_historical_untreated_natural_history.reason_why: Untreated GPA is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that progresses to fulminant renal failure (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) and/or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage within a short natural history, which is why the pre-cyclophosphamide literature consistently describes it as usually fatal.
gpa_historical_untreated_natural_history.important_caveat: This entry is included only to frame how dramatic the treatment transformation below is; it is not a treatment option and should never be read as suggesting untreated observation is acceptable.
gpa_historical_untreated_natural_history.real_working_solution: Not applicable - see the induction/maintenance therapy entries below, which are the real working solution.
gpa_historical_untreated_natural_history.source: Walton EW, Br Med J 1958;2:265-270 (PMID 13560836); Chalkia A, Jayne D, Nephrol Dial Transplant 2024 (PMID 37947275)

gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.name: Cyclophosphamide + High-Dose Glucocorticoids - The Real Foundational NIH Regimen (Fauci 1983)
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.type: Conventional synthetic immunosuppressant (alkylating agent) + corticosteroid, induction
specific_drugs: Prednisone oral, 1 mg/kg/day, tapered to alternate-day dosing once controlled
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.effectiveness: Fauci AS et al. (Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85, PMID 6336643), a prospective 21-year NIH cohort of 85 patients: complete remission was achieved in 79/85 patients (93%); mean duration of remission for living patients was 48.2 (+/-3.6) months; 23 patients were successfully weaned entirely off therapy for a mean of 35.3 (+/-6.3) months without any relapse at the time of reporting.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.reason_why: Cyclophosphamide is metabolised to phosphoramide mustard, which cross-links DNA and kills the rapidly dividing lymphocytes driving the ANCA-associated autoimmune and granulomatous injury; combined with high-dose glucocorticoid to control acute inflammation, this was the first regimen to reliably arrest a disease that was previously almost uniformly progressive.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.important_caveat: Daily oral cyclophosphamide for many months carries real, dose-dependent toxicity - haemorrhagic cystitis, infertility/gonadal toxicity, myelosuppression, infection risk, and long-term bladder-cancer and myelodysplasia risk - which is why subsequent trials (CYCLOPS, below) sought equally effective, lower-exposure regimens, and why rituximab is now a real, guideline-preferred alternative for many patients.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.real_working_solution: For organ- or life-threatening GPA, induce remission with cyclophosphamide (pulse regimen preferred over daily oral for lower cumulative exposure - see CYCLOPS below) combined with high-dose glucocorticoid, then transition to a lower-toxicity maintenance agent once remission is achieved rather than continuing cyclophosphamide indefinitely.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_glucocort.source: Fauci AS et al., 'Wegener's granulomatosis: prospective clinical and therapeutic experience with 85 patients for 21 years', Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85 (PMID 6336643)

gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.name: Pulse (Intermittent IV) vs Daily Oral Cyclophosphamide - Real Equivalent Remission at Lower Cumulative Dose (CYCLOPS)
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.type: Conventional synthetic immunosuppressant (alkylating agent), dosing-strategy comparison
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.effectiveness: CYCLOPS (de Groot K et al., Ann Intern Med 2009;150:670-680, PMID 19451574; 149 patients, 42 centres, 12 European countries): remission at 9 months was achieved in 88.1% on pulse cyclophosphamide versus 87.7% on daily oral cyclophosphamide - statistically equivalent - while the pulse regimen used significantly less cumulative cyclophosphamide and caused fewer episodes of leukopenia.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.reason_why: Intermittent IV dosing achieves comparable peak lymphocyte-depleting exposure to daily oral dosing while delivering a substantially lower total cumulative dose over the induction course, reducing bone-marrow and bladder toxicity without sacrificing remission-induction efficacy.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.important_caveat: The original CYCLOPS long-term follow-up raised a signal of a numerically higher relapse rate with pulse dosing versus daily oral dosing after remission, which is why maintenance therapy (azathioprine or rituximab, below) matters regardless of which induction dosing strategy is used.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.real_working_solution: Prefer pulse (intermittent IV) cyclophosphamide over daily oral dosing for induction when cyclophosphamide is chosen, since it achieves the same real remission rate with a lower cumulative dose and less leukopenia - but ensure maintenance therapy follows to consolidate the induced remission.
gpa_induction_cyclophosphamide_pulse_dos.source: de Groot K et al., 'Pulse versus daily oral cyclophosphamide for induction of remission in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis', Ann Intern Med 2009;150:670-680 (PMID 19451574)

gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.name: Rituximab - Real Non-Inferior (and Superior in Relapsing Disease) Alternative to Cyclophosphamide for Induction (RAVE)
gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.type: Biologic - anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody, induction
specific_drugs: Rituximab (Rituxan/MabThera) IV, 375 mg/m^2 weekly x4 doses
gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.effectiveness: RAVE (Stone JH et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363:221-232, PMID 20647199; multicentre, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy non-inferiority trial, n=197 severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, ~75% GPA): complete remission (BVAS/WG=0, off glucocorticoids) at 6 months was achieved in 63/99 patients (64%) on rituximab versus 52/98 patients (53%) on cyclophosphamide; rituximab met the non-inferiority margin and was also effective in major renal disease and alveolar haemorrhage. Rituximab was superior to cyclophosphamide specifically in patients presenting with relapsing (rather than new-onset) disease. At 18-month follow-up (Specks U et al., N Engl J Med 2013;369:417-427, PMID 23902481), remission persisted in 39% of the single-course rituximab group versus 33% of the conventional (cyclophosphamide then azathioprine) group, confirming durability of a single rituximab induction course out to 18 months.
gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.reason_why: Rituximab depletes circulating CD20+ B cells, cutting off the autoreactive B-cell/plasmablast pipeline that produces anti-PR3/anti-MPO ANCA antibodies, achieving remission through a mechanism distinct from cyclophosphamide's broad cytotoxic action, while avoiding cyclophosphamide's cumulative gonadal, bladder, and marrow toxicity.
gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.important_caveat: RAVE excluded patients with the most severe alveolar haemorrhage requiring mechanical ventilation and those with severe renal impairment (creatinine >4 mg/dL), so the strongest evidence base is for moderate-to-severe, not the most extreme, organ-threatening presentations; rituximab still requires background/bridging glucocorticoids during induction in the RAVE protocol.
gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.real_working_solution: Use rituximab as a real, guideline-preferred induction alternative to cyclophosphamide in most patients, particularly those with relapsing disease (where it is superior) or where fertility preservation matters (avoiding cyclophosphamide's gonadal toxicity).
gpa_induction_rituximab_rave.source: Stone JH et al. (RAVE), N Engl J Med 2010;363:221-232 (PMID 20647199); Specks U et al. (RAVE 18-month), N Engl J Med 2013;369:417-427 (PMID 23902481)

gpa_maintenance_azathioprine_cycazarem.name: Azathioprine Maintenance After Cyclophosphamide-Induced Remission - Real Non-Inferiority to Continued Cyclophosphamide (CYCAZAREM)
specific_drugs: Azathioprine oral, 2 mg/kg/day, substituted for cyclophosphamide once remission is achieved
gpa_maintenance_azathioprine_cycazarem.effectiveness: CYCAZAREM (Jayne D et al., N Engl J Med 2003;349:36-44, PMID 12840090): after cyclophosphamide-induced remission, substituting azathioprine did not increase relapse risk versus continuing cyclophosphamide - relapse occurred in 15.5% on azathioprine versus 13.7% on continued cyclophosphamide (P=0.65), a non-significant difference, meaning the duration of cyclophosphamide exposure can be real-safely reduced.
gpa_maintenance_azathioprine_cycazarem.reason_why: Once cyclophosphamide has induced remission, azathioprine's weaker but adequate immunosuppression is sufficient to maintain it in most patients, avoiding the cumulative gonadal, marrow, and malignancy risk of prolonged cyclophosphamide exposure.
gpa_maintenance_azathioprine_cycazarem.important_caveat: TPMT genotyping/phenotyping before starting azathioprine is real, guideline-recommended practice to avoid severe myelosuppression in poor metabolisers, consistent with its use in other autoimmune diseases in this knowledge base.
gpa_maintenance_azathioprine_cycazarem.real_working_solution: Switch from cyclophosphamide to azathioprine maintenance as soon as remission is achieved (typically by 3-6 months), rather than continuing cyclophosphamide long-term, since the real relapse-rate difference is not statistically significant while the toxicity savings are substantial.
gpa_maintenance_azathioprine_cycazarem.source: Jayne D et al., 'A randomized trial of maintenance therapy for vasculitis associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies', N Engl J Med 2003;349:36-44 (PMID 12840090)

gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.name: Rituximab Maintenance - Real Superiority Over Azathioprine for Preventing Major Relapse (MAINRITSAN)
gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.type: Biologic - anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody, maintenance
specific_drugs: Rituximab IV 500 mg on days 0 and 14, then at months 6, 12, and 18 after study entry
gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.effectiveness: MAINRITSAN (Guillevin L et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1771-1780, PMID 25372085; n=115, 87 GPA/23 microscopic polyangiitis/5 renal-limited AAV, all in remission after cyclophosphamide-glucocorticoid induction): major relapse at month 28 occurred in 3/57 patients (5%) on rituximab maintenance versus 17/58 patients (29%) on azathioprine maintenance - hazard ratio for relapse 6.61 (95% CI 1.56-27.96, P=0.002) favouring rituximab, i.e. 95% of rituximab-maintenance patients remained free of major relapse versus 71% on azathioprine. Rates of severe adverse events were statistically similar between arms (25 patients in each group, P=0.92).
gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.reason_why: Fixed-interval rituximab re-dosing keeps the autoreactive B-cell/plasmablast pool suppressed on a schedule, preventing the re-emergence of pathogenic ANCA-producing clones that azathioprine's weaker, continuous suppression does not as reliably contain.
gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.important_caveat: MAINRITSAN's fixed rituximab schedule (5 infusions over 18 months) is more resource- and cost-intensive than daily oral azathioprine, and long-term (beyond 28 months) comparative relapse data continue to accumulate in follow-on trials (MAINRITSAN2, MAINRITSAN3) not exhaustively detailed in this entry.
gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.real_working_solution: Prefer rituximab maintenance over azathioprine after remission induction, particularly in patients with relapsing disease or PR3-ANCA positivity (both associated with higher relapse risk), given the real, large, statistically significant reduction in major relapse demonstrated in MAINRITSAN.
gpa_maintenance_rituximab_mainritsan.source: Guillevin L et al. (MAINRITSAN), 'Rituximab versus azathioprine for maintenance in ANCA-associated vasculitis', N Engl J Med 2014;371:1771-1780 (PMID 25372085)

gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.name: Methotrexate as a Real Cyclophosphamide-Sparing Option for Early, Non-Organ-Threatening Disease Only (NORAM) - Reported With Its Real Relapse Caveat
gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.type: Conventional synthetic immunosuppressant (antifolate), induction alternative for limited disease only
specific_drugs: Methotrexate oral or subcutaneous, 20-25 mg/week, with folic acid supplementation and prednisolone
gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.effectiveness: NORAM (De Groot K et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:2461-2469, PMID 16052573; n=100, 26 European centres, early systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis without immediately organ- or life-threatening involvement): remission at 6 months was achieved in 89.8% on methotrexate versus 93.5% on cyclophosphamide - broadly similar induction efficacy, though methotrexate showed delayed time-to-remission in patients with more extensive disease or pulmonary involvement. The real caveat: at 18 months, relapse rates were significantly higher with methotrexate (69.5%) than with cyclophosphamide (46.5%), and leukopenia was less frequent but liver dysfunction more frequent on methotrexate.
gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.reason_why: Methotrexate's antifolate, anti-proliferative, and adenosine-mediated anti-inflammatory action is a real but weaker immunosuppressive effect than cyclophosphamide's DNA-cross-linking cytotoxicity, adequate to induce remission in limited disease but less durable at preventing relapse.
gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.important_caveat: This is honestly a mixed result and is reported as such: NORAM enrolled ONLY early/non-organ-threatening disease (excluding renal impairment and severe pulmonary disease), so methotrexate must never be substituted for cyclophosphamide or rituximab in organ- or life-threatening presentations, and its higher 18-month relapse rate means continued immunosuppression beyond 12 months is required regardless of which induction agent is chosen.
gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.real_working_solution: Reserve methotrexate as a cyclophosphamide-sparing induction option only for early, limited GPA without renal or severe pulmonary involvement, and plan for continued maintenance immunosuppression beyond 12 months given its real, significantly higher 18-month relapse rate versus cyclophosphamide.
gpa_early_nonsevere_methotrexate_noram.source: De Groot K et al., 'Randomized trial of cyclophosphamide versus methotrexate for induction of remission in early systemic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis', Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:2461-2469 (PMID 16052573)

gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.name: Reduced-Dose Glucocorticoid Regimen - Real Non-Inferiority With Fewer Infections; Plasma Exchange - Real Lack of Added Benefit (PEXIVAS)
gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.type: Corticosteroid dosing-strategy and adjunct plasma-exchange comparison, severe disease
specific_drugs: Reduced-dose oral glucocorticoid taper regimen (versus standard-dose taper)
Therapeutic plasma exchange (adjunct, evaluated and found not beneficial for the primary composite outcome)
gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.effectiveness: PEXIVAS (Walsh M et al., N Engl J Med 2020;382:622-631, PMID 32053298; 2x2 factorial randomised trial, n=704 severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, eGFR <50 mL/min/1.73m^2 or diffuse pulmonary haemorrhage): plasma exchange did NOT reduce the composite outcome of death or end-stage kidney disease - 100/352 (28.4%) with plasma exchange versus 109/352 (31.0%) without (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65-1.13, P=0.27). For glucocorticoid dosing, the reduced-dose regimen was non-inferior to standard dosing for death or end-stage kidney disease - 92/330 (27.9%) reduced-dose versus 83/325 (25.5%) standard-dose - and serious infections at 1 year were significantly LESS common with the reduced-dose regimen (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.93).
gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.reason_why: Once remission-induction immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide or rituximab) is doing the primary disease-control work, additional plasma exchange does not meaningfully add to real hard renal/survival outcomes at a population level, and a lower cumulative glucocorticoid exposure reduces infection risk without sacrificing disease control, given that the antibody- and immunosuppressant-driven mechanisms above are already suppressing the pathogenic process.
gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.important_caveat: This is honestly reported as a real negative-for-plasma-exchange result, reversing some prior smaller-trial (MEPEX) enthusiasm for plasma exchange in severe renal disease; PEXIVAS is the largest and most definitive trial on this question and its real result should guide practice over older, smaller data.
gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.real_working_solution: Use a reduced-dose glucocorticoid taper regimen rather than the older high-dose regimen for induction of severe GPA, since it is real, non-inferior for hard outcomes and cuts serious infection risk; do not add routine plasma exchange for severe renal or pulmonary disease outside of specific unresolved clinical scenarios, since PEXIVAS found no real benefit on death or end-stage kidney disease.
gpa_glucocorticoid_dosing_plasma_exchang.source: Walsh M et al. (PEXIVAS), 'Plasma Exchange and Glucocorticoids in Severe ANCA-Associated Vasculitis', N Engl J Med 2020;382:622-631 (PMID 32053298)

gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.name: Avacopan - Real Glucocorticoid-Sparing C5a-Receptor Inhibitor Add-On (ADVOCATE)
gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.type: Small-molecule complement C5a receptor (C5aR1) inhibitor, glucocorticoid-sparing add-on
specific_drugs: Avacopan (Tavneos) oral, 30 mg twice daily, added to a cyclophosphamide or rituximab backbone
gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.effectiveness: ADVOCATE (Jayne DRW et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384:599-609, PMID 33596356; n=331, randomised, all patients also received cyclophosphamide-then-azathioprine or rituximab): remission at week 26 (BVAS=0, no glucocorticoid use in the prior 4 weeks) was achieved in 120/166 (72.3%) on avacopan versus 115/164 (70.1%) on a prednisone taper - non-inferior (P<0.001) but not superior (P=0.24) at this timepoint. Sustained remission at both weeks 26 and 52 was achieved in 109/166 (65.7%) on avacopan versus 90/164 (54.9%) on prednisone taper - non-inferior (P<0.001) AND superior (P=0.007) at this endpoint. Serious adverse events were similar between arms (37.3% avacopan vs 39.0% prednisone).
gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.reason_why: Avacopan blocks the C5a receptor on neutrophils, interrupting the complement-driven neutrophil activation and recruitment that ANCA antibodies trigger at the vessel wall, allowing effective disease control with substantially less glucocorticoid exposure than the traditional prednisone taper.
gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.important_caveat: Avacopan was studied and is used as an add-on to cyclophosphamide- or rituximab-based induction, not as monotherapy; its safety and clinical effects beyond 52 weeks were not addressed in the ADVOCATE trial itself, and it is a real, additional-cost therapy rather than a replacement for the induction backbone.
gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.real_working_solution: Add avacopan to a cyclophosphamide- or rituximab-based induction regimen to real-achieve significantly higher sustained remission at 1 year with markedly less cumulative glucocorticoid exposure, directly addressing the glucocorticoid-toxicity burden that is a real, separate cause of long-term morbidity in this disease.
gpa_glucocorticoid_sparing_avacopan_advo.source: Jayne DRW et al. (ADVOCATE), 'Avacopan for the Treatment of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis', N Engl J Med 2021;384:599-609 (PMID 33596356)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, trial-anchored medicine pathway for GPA: the historical (Walton 1958) and NIH-era (Fauci 1983) transformation from an almost uniformly fatal disease to one with 93% complete remission with cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids; cyclophosphamide dosing optimisation (CYCLOPS pulse regimen); rituximab as a real non-inferior/superior-in-relapse induction alternative (RAVE) and real superior maintenance option (MAINRITSAN) versus azathioprine; azathioprine's real non-inferiority as a lower-toxicity maintenance switch after cyclophosphamide induction (CYCAZAREM); methotrexate as a real but relapse-prone option strictly limited to early, non-organ-threatening disease (NORAM, negative long-term relapse result honestly reported); the real non-inferiority of reduced-dose glucocorticoids with fewer infections and the real lack of added benefit from plasma exchange (PEXIVAS); and avacopan as a real glucocorticoid-sparing add-on with superior sustained remission (ADVOCATE). Priority follows real evidence strength and current guideline standing: induction (rituximab or cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoids) first, maintenance (rituximab or azathioprine) second, glucocorticoid-sparing/adjunct strategies third.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics from different trial phases (induction remission rates at 6-9 months, maintenance relapse-free rates at 18-28 months, and sustained-remission rates at 52 weeks) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes - not a claim that a single number captures 'how good' each option is in isolation. Higher-ranked rows reflect real higher reported favourable-outcome percentages in their own trial context, not a claim of head-to-head superiority across different trials with different patient populations and endpoint definitions.
