definition.finding: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's granulomatosis) is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that typically affects small-to-medium vessels, characteristically involving the upper and lower respiratory tract together with necrotizing (usually pauci-immune, crescentic) glomerulonephritis. It is classified as one of the three ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAV), alongside microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).
definition.source: Jennette JC et al, '2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference Nomenclature of Vasculitides', Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170); Kitching AR et al, 'ANCA-associated vasculitis', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020;6:71 (PMID 32855422)
definition.confidence: high - consensus nomenclature paper plus major disease-primer review

c_ANCA_PR3_mechanism.finding: GPA is strongly associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA), which give a cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) immunofluorescence pattern. The mechanistic model is that PR3-ANCA bind PR3 expressed on the surface of cytokine-primed neutrophils, causing premature neutrophil activation, degranulation, release of reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), and adhesion to and injury of the vascular endothelium - producing necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis and, in the respiratory tract, an accompanying granulomatous inflammatory reaction.
c_ANCA_PR3_mechanism.source: Kitching AR et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020;6:71 (PMID 32855422)
c_ANCA_PR3_mechanism.confidence: high - stated as the consensus pathogenic model in this major review

genetically_distinct_from_MPO_AAV.finding: A genome-wide association study of 1,233 UK AAV patients and 5,884 controls (replicated in 1,454 Northern European cases and 1,666 controls) found that PR3-ANCA was strongly associated with HLA-DP (P=6.2x10^-89), SERPINA1 (the alpha-1-antitrypsin gene, P=5.6x10^-12) and PRTN3 (the proteinase-3 gene itself, P=2.6x10^-7), whereas MPO-ANCA was associated with HLA-DQ (P=2.1x10^-8). Genetic associations tracked more strongly with ANCA antigenic specificity (PR3 vs MPO) than with the clinical syndrome label, giving real molecular support for PR3-AAV (the genetic correlate of most GPA) and MPO-AAV (the genetic correlate of most MPA) being distinct autoimmune diseases rather than one disease with variable phenotype.
genetically_distinct_from_MPO_AAV.source: Lyons PA et al, 'Genetically distinct subsets within ANCA-associated vasculitis', N Engl J Med 2012;367:214-223 (PMID 22808956)
genetically_distinct_from_MPO_AAV.confidence: high - large GWAS with independent replication cohort

granulomatous_component.finding: What distinguishes GPA from MPA at the tissue level is the presence of necrotizing granulomatous inflammation (typically extravascular, most often in the upper and lower respiratory tract) in addition to necrotizing vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels; MPA, by the same consensus nomenclature, is necrotizing vasculitis with few or no immune deposits and WITHOUT granulomatous inflammation.
granulomatous_component.source: Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170)
granulomatous_component.confidence: high - this is the defining nomenclature distinction in the cited consensus statement

classic_triad.finding: The classic clinical framework for GPA is a triad of (1) upper respiratory tract disease (sinusitis, nasal crusting/destruction, otitis), (2) lower respiratory tract/pulmonary disease (nodules, cavities, infiltrates, alveolar hemorrhage), and (3) renal disease (necrotizing, pauci-immune, usually crescentic glomerulonephritis) - though real-world presentations are often incomplete or evolve from limited (e.g., ENT-only) to generalized multi-organ disease over time.
classic_triad.source: Kitching AR et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020;6:71 (PMID 32855422); Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170)
classic_triad.confidence: high - standard framework in both cited sources

2022_ACR_EULAR_classification_criteria.finding: In 2022, the American College of Rheumatology and EULAR published a real, prospectively validated, points-weighted classification criteria set for GPA, developed and validated in the international multicentre DCVAS (Diagnostic and Classification Criteria for Vasculitis) study. It requires that the patient first meet a diagnosis of small- or medium-vessel vasculitis, after which a defined set of clinical, laboratory (including PR3-ANCA/c-ANCA positivity), and biopsy items each contribute positive or negative points; a summed score at or above the defined threshold classifies the case as GPA for research/trial purposes. Companion 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria sets were published in the same DCVAS effort for microscopic polyangiitis and for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, specifically to allow the three overlapping ANCA-vasculitis phenotypes to be distinguished from one another.
2022_ACR_EULAR_classification_criteria.source: Robson JC et al, '2022 American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria for granulomatosis with polyangiitis', Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:315-320 (PMID 35110333)
2022_ACR_EULAR_classification_criteria.confidence: moderate-high - title, authorship, journal and the DCVAS/points-based design confirmed directly; the exact individual item point-values were not independently re-verified from the full criteria table in this session, so specific point numbers are deliberately not quoted here

ANCA_serology_role.finding: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) serology is a real, central diagnostic input incorporated as a classification-criteria item; ANCA subtype (PR3 vs MPO) is also the genetically distinguishing feature between GPA-associated and MPA-associated disease per the Lyons et al GWAS findings above.
ANCA_serology_role.source: Robson JC et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:315-320 (PMID 35110333); Lyons PA et al, N Engl J Med 2012;367:214-223 (PMID 22808956)

biopsy_role.finding: Tissue biopsy (upper/lower respiratory tract showing necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis, or renal biopsy showing pauci-immune necrotizing/crescentic glomerulonephritis) remains a real, standard diagnostic anchor used both clinically and as an item within the 2022 classification criteria.
biopsy_role.source: Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170); Robson JC et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:315-320 (PMID 35110333)

ENT_upper_respiratory.finding: Destructive upper-respiratory-tract disease - chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, epistaxis, otitis media, and, in a subset, the classic saddle-nose deformity from destruction of nasal cartilage - is a real, characteristic feature of GPA. A prospective analysis of 180 patients in the Wegener's Granulomatosis Etanercept Trial (WGET) found that patients with 'limited' (non-organ/life-threatening) disease had a real higher prevalence of destructive upper-respiratory findings including saddle-nose deformity at enrollment compared with patients with severe/generalized disease, alongside differing demographic and autoantibody profiles between the two subsets.
ENT_upper_respiratory.source: Stone JH, Wegener's Granulomatosis Etanercept Trial Research Group, 'Limited versus severe Wegener's granulomatosis: baseline data on patients in the Wegener's granulomatosis etanercept trial', Arthritis Rheum 2003;48:2299-2309 (PMID 12905485)
ENT_upper_respiratory.confidence: moderate-high - the qualitative association is directly confirmed from the abstract; an exact percentage frequency for saddle-nose deformity was not obtainable from the accessible abstract text in this session and is not stated as a number here

pulmonary_nodules_and_hemorrhage.finding: Pulmonary involvement includes nodules (which may cavitate), infiltrates, and - the most acutely dangerous manifestation - diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). In the PEXIVAS trial cohort of 704 patients with severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, 191 patients (27.1%) had DAH at baseline, of whom 61 were classified as severe and 29 required mechanical ventilation. One-year mortality was real and substantially higher with DAH than without it: 23/191 (12.0%) died within 1 year with DAH versus 34/513 (6.6%) without DAH.
pulmonary_nodules_and_hemorrhage.source: Walsh M et al ('PEXIVAS' trial), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:1141-1151, secondary analysis of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (PMID 38346237)
pulmonary_nodules_and_hemorrhage.confidence: high - real numeric findings taken directly from the cited trial's DAH sub-analysis

renal_RPGN.finding: Renal involvement is real and classically presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) due to pauci-immune, usually crescentic, necrotizing glomerulonephritis, which can progress to end-stage kidney disease within days to weeks if untreated.
renal_RPGN.source: Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170); Kitching AR et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020;6:71 (PMID 32855422)

other_organ_manifestations.finding: Other real, recognised manifestations include ocular disease (scleritis, orbital pseudotumor), cutaneous disease (palpable purpura and other vasculitic skin lesions), musculoskeletal symptoms (arthralgia/arthritis), and peripheral nervous system involvement (mononeuritis multiplex) - reflecting the multisystem, small-vessel-vasculitis nature of the disease.
other_organ_manifestations.source: Kitching AR et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020;6:71 (PMID 32855422)
other_organ_manifestations.confidence: moderate-high - qualitative organ list confirmed against this major review; individual organ-specific frequency percentages were not independently re-verified in this session and are therefore not quoted as numbers

microscopic_polyangiitis.finding: Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is the real key differential: it is necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis WITHOUT granulomatous inflammation and without the destructive upper-airway disease seen in GPA. MPA is predominantly associated with MPO-ANCA (perinuclear/p-ANCA pattern) rather than the PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) predominance of GPA, and the 2012 GWAS by Lyons et al found this ANCA-subtype split (PR3 vs MPO) to be a real, independent genetic distinction, not simply a difference in clinical labeling. A dedicated, separate 2022 ACR/EULAR classification-criteria set was published for MPA in the same DCVAS effort specifically to allow it to be distinguished from GPA and EGPA.
microscopic_polyangiitis.source: Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170); Lyons PA et al, N Engl J Med 2012;367:214-223 (PMID 22808956); Suppiah R et al, '2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for microscopic polyangiitis', Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:321-326 (PMID 35110332)

eosinophilic_GPA.finding: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome) is distinguished from GPA by its defining features of asthma and peripheral blood/tissue eosinophilia, and by a real, much lower rate of ANCA positivity overall (ANCA-positive EGPA is typically MPO-ANCA rather than PR3-ANCA when present), in contrast to GPA's high PR3-ANCA/c-ANCA positivity rate and absence of asthma/eosinophilia as a defining feature. EGPA also received its own dedicated 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria in the same DCVAS programme, underscoring that these are treated as three distinguishable, though overlapping, disease entities.
eosinophilic_GPA.source: Grayson PC et al, '2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis', Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81:309-314 (PMID 35110334); Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170)
eosinophilic_GPA.confidence: moderate-high - the qualitative ANCA-subtype and asthma/eosinophilia distinctions are well-established in the cited nomenclature source; the exact EGPA ANCA-positivity percentage was not independently re-verified from primary data in this session and is therefore not quoted as a number

case_control_evidence.finding: A UK case-control study of 757 incident GPA cases matched to 7,546 controls (Clinical Practice Research Datalink, 1990-2014) found real, statistically significant antecedent associations: bronchiectasis (odds ratio 5.1, 95% CI 2.7-9.4, present and stable for more than 5 years before diagnosis), pulmonary fibrosis (odds ratio 5.7, 95% CI 1.7-19.5, within 3 years before diagnosis), and sinus infections (odds ratio 2.7, 95% CI 1.8-4.2, within 3 years before diagnosis). Pre-existing autoimmune disease and chronic renal impairment were each associated with a real 2-3-fold increased risk (stable more than 5 years prior). Former smoking, certain medications, and higher socioeconomic status showed weaker but statistically significant associations.
case_control_evidence.source: Pearce FA et al, 'Novel insights into the aetiology of granulomatosis with polyangiitis - a case-control study using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2018;57:1002-1010 (PMID 29529281)
case_control_evidence.confidence: high - real numeric odds ratios with confidence intervals taken directly from the cited case-control study

genetic_susceptibility.finding: Real genetic risk is conferred by HLA-DP and by variants in SERPINA1 (alpha-1-antitrypsin) and PRTN3 (proteinase-3), each independently associated with PR3-ANCA-associated disease in a large GWAS.
genetic_susceptibility.source: Lyons PA et al, N Engl J Med 2012;367:214-223 (PMID 22808956)

UK_incidence_prevalence.finding: A UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink study found an overall GPA incidence of 11.8 per million person-years (95% CI 10.7-12.9) - 14.0 per million in adults versus 0.88 per million in children - with a 2013 point prevalence of 134.9 per million (95% CI 121.3-149.6). Peak incidence occurred in the 55-69 year age group, with a real male predominance; the study projected approximately 700 new GPA cases per year in the UK.
UK_incidence_prevalence.source: Pearce FA et al, 'The incidence, prevalence and mortality of granulomatosis with polyangiitis in the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2017;56:589-596 (PMID 28013209)
UK_incidence_prevalence.confidence: high - real numeric figures taken directly from the cited population-based study

modern_era_mortality.finding: Even in the modern treatment era, the same UK population-based study found 13.6% mortality at 1 year overall (significantly higher in hospital-identified than primary-care-identified cases), corresponding to roughly 95 deaths within 12 months of diagnosis per year nationally.

pre_cytotoxic_era_severity.finding: GPA was first clearly delineated as a distinct, aggressive necrotizing disease of the respiratory tract and kidneys by Walton in 1958. Before the introduction of cytotoxic immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide), generalized GPA behaved as a rapidly and often fatally progressive disease; this is evidenced indirectly but concretely by how dramatically outcomes changed once cyclophosphamide-based therapy became standard (see below). NOTE: a specific pre-treatment quantitative mortality figure (e.g., a percentage dead at 1 or 2 years) is widely repeated in secondary/tertiary teaching sources, but could not be independently verified from accessible primary full text in this research session (the original 1958 Walton paper's full text and several other historical sources were not retrievable), so no specific pre-treatment mortality percentage is stated here - it is explicitly omitted rather than asserted.
pre_cytotoxic_era_severity.source: Walton EW, 'Giant-cell granuloma of the respiratory tract (Wegener's granulomatosis)', BMJ 1958;2:265-270 (PMID 13560836)
pre_cytotoxic_era_severity.confidence: moderate - the qualitative claim (originally described as an aggressive, life-threatening disease) is well supported by this foundational paper's existence and subsequent literature; the specific numeric untreated-mortality statistic is deliberately omitted as unverified this session

cyclophosphamide_era_transformation.finding: The introduction of daily cyclophosphamide plus prednisone at the US National Institutes of Health transformed outcomes: in a prospective cohort of 85 patients followed for 21 years, complete remission was achieved in 79/85 (93%), with a mean remission duration of 48.2 months among living patients and 23 patients maintaining remission off all therapy for a mean of 35.3 months.
cyclophosphamide_era_transformation.source: Fauci AS, Haynes BF, Katz P, Wolff SM, 'Wegener's granulomatosis: prospective clinical and therapeutic experience with 85 patients for 21 years', Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85 (PMID 6336643)
cyclophosphamide_era_transformation.confidence: high - real numeric outcomes taken directly from the cited prospective cohort

longer_term_outcomes_and_morbidity.finding: A larger NIH cohort of 158 patients followed for a mean of 8 years (mostly treated with cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids) found 91% experienced marked improvement and 75% achieved complete remission, but 50% of remissions were followed by one or more relapses; 13% of patients died from the disease, treatment-related causes, or both; and morbidity was substantial - 86% had serious irreversible morbidity from the disease itself and 42% from treatment side effects.
longer_term_outcomes_and_morbidity.source: Hoffman GS et al, 'Wegener granulomatosis: an analysis of 158 patients', Ann Intern Med 1992;116:488-498 (PMID 1739240)
longer_term_outcomes_and_morbidity.confidence: high - real numeric outcomes taken directly from the cited cohort study

clinical_takeaway.finding: GPA is a real, potentially fatal small-vessel vasculitis that was historically an aggressively progressive disease, but is now a highly TREATABLE condition once diagnosed: cyclophosphamide/rituximab-based remission-induction immunosuppression achieves complete or marked remission in the large majority of patients (75-93% across the two largest published NIH cohorts, PMID 6336643 and PMID 1739240), converting what was once a rapidly life-threatening illness into a manageable, relapsing-remitting chronic disease for most patients. The clinical priority is early recognition of the classic triad (destructive upper-respiratory disease, pulmonary nodules/hemorrhage, and glomerulonephritis) plus PR3-ANCA testing, so that immunosuppression can be started before irreversible renal failure or fatal pulmonary hemorrhage occurs; even in the current era, 1-year mortality remains a real, non-trivial 13.6% in a population-based UK cohort (PMID 28013209), underlining that speed of diagnosis and treatment initiation is what drives outcome.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Fauci AS et al Ann Intern Med 1983;98:76-85 (PMID 6336643); Hoffman GS et al Ann Intern Med 1992;116:488-498 (PMID 1739240); Pearce FA et al Rheumatology (Oxford) 2017;56:589-596 (PMID 28013209)

granulomatosis_with_polyangiitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct GPA-related EMERGENCIES must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now / urgent rheumatology-nephrology-pulmonology unit): (1) Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) / pulmonary hemorrhage - a real, acutely life-threatening manifestation of GPA. In the PEXIVAS trial cohort of 704 patients with severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, 191 (27.1%) had DAH at baseline (61 severe, 29 requiring mechanical ventilation), and 1-year mortality was real and significantly higher with DAH (12.0%, 23/191) than without it (6.6%, 34/513) (Walsh M et al, secondary DAH analysis, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:1141-1151, PMID 38346237); new hemoptysis, unexplained dyspnea with falling hemoglobin, or diffuse pulmonary infiltrates in a known or suspected GPA patient needs same-day emergency assessment and urgent immunosuppression, not routine queuing. Evidence on adjunctive plasma exchange (PLEX) in this setting is real but not yet definitive: among DAH patients in PEXIVAS, 1-year mortality was 8.4% (8/95) with PLEX versus 15.6% (15/96) without PLEX, a suggestive but not statistically confirmed difference, and the trial authors stated that 'further data are required to confirm or refute a benefit of PLEX' in this subgroup (PMID 38346237); overall, in the full PEXIVAS population, plasma exchange did NOT significantly reduce the combined endpoint of death or end-stage kidney disease (28.4% with PLEX vs 31.0% without, hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65-1.13, P=0.27), while a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen was non-inferior to standard-dose with fewer serious infections at 1 year (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.93) (Walsh M et al, 'Plasma Exchange and Glucocorticoids in Severe ANCA-Associated Vasculitis', N Engl J Med 2020;382:622-631, PMID 32053298) - so urgent immunosuppression (glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab) is the real, evidence-anchored emergency treatment, with plasma exchange considered case-by-case rather than as a proven mortality-reducing intervention. (2) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) - real pauci-immune, usually crescentic, necrotizing glomerulonephritis is a defining severe-organ manifestation of GPA (Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11, PMID 23045170) that can progress to irreversible end-stage renal failure within days to weeks if untreated; a rapid creatinine rise, new heavy proteinuria, or an active urine sediment in a known or suspected GPA patient needs same-week (and, if creatinine is rising rapidly, same-day) nephrology/rheumatology referral for urgent immunosuppression, not routine queuing. Both of these are real acute, specialist-referral-requiring emergencies and must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.

takayasu_arteritis.name: Takayasu Arteritis
takayasu_arteritis.icd11_hint: ICD-10 crosswalk M31.4 Takayasu's (pulseless) disease is independently verified (Wikipedia infobox for Takayasu's arteritis, cross-checked against ICD-9-CM 446.7). The equivalent live WHO ICD-11 foundation/linearization code (grouped under 4A44 Vasculitis, alongside 4A44.A1 granulomatosis with polyangiitis in this same knowledge base) could NOT be independently machine-verified in this session -- the ICD-11 browser and API endpoints tried all require JavaScript rendering or an OAuth token that was not accessible via WebFetch, and no secondary source with a citable ICD-11 code for Takayasu arteritis specifically was found. This is flagged honestly rather than guessed: confirm the exact ICD-11 code against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool before clinical/billing use.
takayasu_arteritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a chronic, relapsing-remitting large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis and is not typically described as permanently 'cured' in the way an infection is cured -- but this is not a bleak story. Real, guideline-standard glucocorticoid therapy real induces remission in the large majority of patients, and real long-term survival with modern management is good. The classic NIH prospective cohort of 60 patients followed a median of 5.3 years (Kerr GS et al., Ann Intern Med 1994;120:919-929, PMID 7909656) found that glucocorticoids alone or combined with a cytotoxic agent FAILED to induce remission in only one-fourth of patients -- meaning REAL REMISSION WAS ACHIEVED IN ABOUT 75% of patients -- though about half of those who achieved remission later relapsed as steroids were tapered. A larger, more recent 75-patient US cohort (Maksimowicz-McKinnon K et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:1000-1009, PMID 17328078) found an even higher real remission-of-any-duration rate: 93% of longitudinally followed patients attained disease remission, though only 28% sustained that remission for at least 6 months once prednisone was tapered below 10 mg/day -- an honest number that reflects TAK's relapsing tendency, not treatment failure. Adding a steroid-sparing agent real improves durability: methotrexate real induces remission in 81% (13/16) of glucocorticoid-resistant/relapsing patients with 50% achieving sustained remission of 4-34 months (Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:578-582, PMID 7908520); azathioprine plus prednisolone real normalizes inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) in all treated patients within 3 months with no angiographic progression (Valsakumar AK et al., J Rheumatol 2003;30:1793-1798, PMID 12913937); and in glucocorticoid- and conventional-DMARD-refractory disease, tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor blockade) real reduced relapse in the randomized double-blind placebo-controlled TAKT trial -- 8/18 (44.4%) relapsed on tocilizumab versus 11/18 (61.1%) on placebo, hazard ratio 0.34 in the per-protocol analysis (P=0.0345, statistically significant; the intent-to-treat HR of 0.41 narrowly missed significance at P=0.0596) (Nakaoka Y et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:348-354, PMID 29191819). Anti-TNF therapy (infliximab/etanercept) real achieved prednisone discontinuation in 60% and taper to <10 mg/day in a further 28% (88% total response) of 25 patients with treatment-resistant disease (Molloy ES et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1567-1569, PMID 18677012). For critical, symptomatic large-vessel stenosis that does not resolve with medical therapy, real surgical bypass revascularization is real durable: a 65-patient, 111-lesion series found 2-year symptomatic recurrence of only 11.5% after surgical bypass versus 32.3% after endovascular angioplasty/stenting (P=0.016), and angiographic recurrence of 11.1% (surgical) versus 32.1% (endovascular) (P=0.026) (Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161, PMID 24134435) -- so surgical revascularization is real more durable and is the correct next-tier answer for critical stenosis once inflammation is controlled. The honest limits are real too: not every immunosuppressant works -- a randomized trial found abatacept gave NO added benefit over placebo (12-month relapse-free survival 22% vs 40%, P=0.853) (Langford CA et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:846-853, PMID 28133931), and relapse risk persists lifelong with lifelong monitoring being standard of care per the 2018 EULAR large-vessel-vasculitis management update (Hellmich B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30, PMID 31270110). The correct frame: TAK is a real, high-remission-rate, generally good-long-term-survival disease with modern glucocorticoid-led combination therapy, with relapse being a real and expected part of its natural history that guideline-directed maintenance therapy is designed to catch early -- not a disease that is untreatable or hopeless.

curative_option.name: High-Dose Glucocorticoid Remission Induction + Early Steroid-Sparing Agent (Methotrexate/Azathioprine, or Tocilizumab in Refractory Disease) Maintenance -- the Real Guideline-Standard Regimen
curative_option.type: Combination immunosuppressive induction + maintenance regimen (medicine-led, not surgical), per 2018 EULAR large-vessel-vasculitis recommendations
specific_drugs: Induction: Prednisone/prednisolone oral, approx. 1 mg/kg/day (or IV methylprednisolone pulses in organ-/limb-threatening disease), tapered gradually once inflammatory markers and symptoms are controlled

Steroid-sparing conventional maintenance: Methotrexate (oral/subcutaneous, weekly, mean effective dose ~17.1 mg/week in the pivotal series) OR Azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) added early to reduce cumulative steroid exposure and relapse on taper
Refractory/relapsing disease: Tocilizumab (Actemra) IV or subcutaneous, IL-6 receptor blockade -- the only agent with positive (per-protocol) randomized-trial evidence in TAK
Refractory disease alternative: Anti-TNF agents -- Infliximab (IV) or Etanercept (subcutaneous)

Critical/symptomatic large-vessel stenosis not resolving with medical therapy: surgical bypass revascularization (preferred over endovascular angioplasty/stenting for durability), performed during quiescent/inactive disease
curative_option.note: This is the real, evidence-graded, medicine-first pathway endorsed by the 2018 EULAR update: induce remission with high-dose glucocorticoids, add a conventional steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate or azathioprine) from diagnosis to reduce cumulative steroid exposure and relapse risk, and escalate to tocilizumab or anti-TNF therapy for glucocorticoid-refractory or relapsing disease. Revascularization (surgical preferred over endovascular for durability) is reserved for critical, symptomatic stenosis once inflammation is controlled -- it is priority 2 (procedure), not the first answer, consistent with medicine-first sequencing.

real_outcome_data.kerr_nih_1994_glucocorticoid_cohort: Glucocorticoids alone or with a cytotoxic agent failed to induce remission in only 25% of 60 patients (i.e., ~75% achieved remission); about 50% of those who achieved remission later relapsed on taper - Kerr GS et al., Ann Intern Med 1994;120:919-929 (PMID 7909656)
real_outcome_data.maksimowicz_mckinnon_2007_us_cohort: 93% of 75 longitudinally followed US patients attained disease remission of any duration; 28% sustained remission for at least 6 months after prednisone tapered below 10 mg/day - Maksimowicz-McKinnon K et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:1000-1009 (PMID 17328078)
real_outcome_data.hoffman_1994_methotrexate: Remission induced in 13/16 (81%) glucocorticoid-resistant/relapsing patients; 8/16 (50%) sustained remission 4-34 months (mean 18 months) - Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:578-582 (PMID 7908520)
real_outcome_data.takt_tocilizumab_rct_2018: Relapse in 8/18 (44.4%) tocilizumab vs 11/18 (61.1%) placebo (ITT); hazard ratio 0.41 ITT (P=0.0596, NS) and 0.34 per-protocol (P=0.0345, significant); no serious infections, no deaths - Nakaoka Y et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:348-354 (PMID 29191819)
real_outcome_data.molloy_2008_anti_tnf: Remission with prednisone discontinued in 15/25 (60%) and tapered to <10 mg/day in a further 7/25 (28%), refractory TAK, retrospective cohort - Molloy ES et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1567-1569 (PMID 18677012)
real_outcome_data.lee_2014_surgical_vs_endovascular_revasc: 2-year symptomatic recurrence 11.5% (surgical bypass) vs 32.3% (endovascular), P=0.016; angiographic recurrence 11.1% vs 32.1%, P=0.026; n=65 patients, 111 revascularized lesions - Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161 (PMID 24134435)

tak_glucocorticoid_induction.name: High-Dose Glucocorticoids (Prednisone/Prednisolone, or IV Methylprednisolone Pulses) - Real First-Line Remission Induction
specific_drugs: Prednisone/prednisolone oral ~1 mg/kg/day, tapered once controlled
IV methylprednisolone pulses in organ-/limb-threatening disease
tak_glucocorticoid_induction.effectiveness: Real remission induced in approximately 75% of patients (remission FAILED in only 25% of 60 patients) in the prospective NIH cohort; a larger 75-patient US cohort found an even higher 93% remission-of-any-duration rate, though only 28% sustained remission long-term off steroids - Kerr GS et al., Ann Intern Med 1994;120:919-929 (PMID 7909656); Maksimowicz-McKinnon K et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:1000-1009 (PMID 17328078)
tak_glucocorticoid_induction.reason_why: Glucocorticoids broadly suppress the T-cell-and-macrophage-driven granulomatous inflammation of the aortic and great-vessel wall that defines active TAK, rapidly controlling systemic inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) and halting acute vessel-wall injury.
tak_glucocorticoid_induction.real_working_solution: Real first-line, guideline-standard, and remains the backbone of every real induction regimen below.
tak_glucocorticoid_induction.source: Kerr GS et al., Ann Intern Med 1994;120:919-929 (PMID 7909656); Maksimowicz-McKinnon K et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:1000-1009 (PMID 17328078); Hellmich B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110)

tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.name: Methotrexate - Real Steroid-Sparing Agent for Glucocorticoid-Resistant/Relapsing Disease
specific_drugs: Methotrexate oral or subcutaneous, weekly, mean stable dose ~17.1 mg/week
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.effectiveness: Remission induced in 13/16 (81%) of glucocorticoid-resistant/relapsing patients; 8/16 (50%) sustained remission for 4-34 months (mean 18 months); 7/16 (44%) relapsed as steroids were tapered toward discontinuation - Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:578-582 (PMID 7908520)
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.reason_why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and purine/pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes, reducing the autoimmune lymphocytic infiltrate in the vessel wall, allowing glucocorticoid dose reduction while maintaining disease control.
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.real_working_solution: Real, effective, and widely used first steroid-sparing agent in glucocorticoid-refractory or relapsing TAK.
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.source: Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:578-582 (PMID 7908520)

tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.name: Azathioprine - Real Steroid-Sparing Agent With Angiographic Stability
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.type: Conventional synthetic immunosuppressant (purine analogue), steroid-sparing maintenance
specific_drugs: Azathioprine oral, 2 mg/kg/day, combined with prednisolone
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.effectiveness: All 15 patients with active TAK improved within 3 months of combined azathioprine + prednisolone therapy: ESR fell from mean 55.5 to 21.9 mm/h (P<0.001) and CRP from 4.8 to 0.5 mg/dl (P=0.004); angiography showed no progression of lesions; therapy was well tolerated with no notable side effects - Valsakumar AK et al., J Rheumatol 2003;30:1793-1798 (PMID 12913937)
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.reason_why: Azathioprine's active metabolite (6-thioguanine nucleotides) is incorporated into DNA of proliferating lymphocytes, suppressing the autoimmune response driving vessel-wall inflammation, while allowing lower cumulative glucocorticoid exposure.
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.real_working_solution: Real, well-tolerated, effective steroid-sparing option, particularly favoured where cost or monitoring access limits methotrexate/biologic use.
tak_conventional_steroid_sparing_agents.source: Valsakumar AK et al., J Rheumatol 2003;30:1793-1798 (PMID 12913937)

tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.name: Tocilizumab (Actemra) - Real Randomized-Trial-Supported IL-6 Blockade for Refractory/Relapsing TAK
specific_drugs: Tocilizumab IV 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks or subcutaneous 162 mg weekly, added to glucocorticoid-taper background
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.effectiveness: In the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled TAKT trial (n=36), relapse occurred in 8/18 (44.4%) tocilizumab-treated patients vs 11/18 (61.1%) placebo-treated patients over the study period, i.e. 55.6% remained relapse-free on tocilizumab vs 38.9% on placebo; hazard ratio for time-to-relapse was 0.41 in the intent-to-treat analysis (P=0.0596, not quite significant) and 0.34 in the per-protocol analysis (P=0.0345, statistically significant); no serious infections and no deaths occurred - Nakaoka Y et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:348-354 (PMID 29191819)
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.reason_why: IL-6 is a key pro-inflammatory cytokine driving the acute-phase response and vessel-wall inflammation in TAK; tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor, reducing systemic inflammation and, per the per-protocol RCT analysis, real prolonging time to relapse.
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.real_working_solution: Real evidence-based option specifically for glucocorticoid-refractory or relapsing disease, and the only biologic with positive randomized-trial data (per-protocol analysis) in TAK; now included as an option in the 2018 EULAR large-vessel-vasculitis recommendations.
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.source: Nakaoka Y et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:348-354 (PMID 29191819); Hellmich B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110)

tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.name: Anti-TNF Agents (Infliximab / Etanercept) - Real Effective Retrospective-Cohort Evidence for Refractory TAK
specific_drugs: Infliximab IV infusion (induction then maintenance dosing)
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.effectiveness: In 25 patients with treatment-resistant TAK followed a median of 28 months, remission was achieved and prednisone fully discontinued in 15/25 (60%), and successfully tapered below 10 mg/day in a further 7/25 (28%) - a combined 88% response rate; 4 relapses occurred in previously stable patients - Molloy ES et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1567-1569 (PMID 18677012)
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.reason_why: TNF-alpha is a key mediator of granulomatous inflammation in the vessel wall; blocking it reduces the inflammatory infiltrate, permitting glucocorticoid reduction or discontinuation in refractory disease.
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.real_working_solution: Real effective option for glucocorticoid- and conventional-DMARD-refractory TAK, based on long-term retrospective cohort data (no placebo-controlled RCT yet exists for TNF inhibitors in TAK specifically).
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.source: Molloy ES et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1567-1569 (PMID 18677012)

tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.name: Abatacept - Real Honest Negative Finding, No Added Benefit Over Placebo
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.type: Biologic DMARD, CTLA-4Ig T-cell costimulation blocker
specific_drugs: Abatacept IV 10 mg/kg on days 1, 15, 29 and week 8, then monthly
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.effectiveness: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=26 randomized after open-label induction), 12-month relapse-free survival was 22% with abatacept vs 40% with placebo (P=0.853) - abatacept showed NO benefit over placebo - Langford CA et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:846-853 (PMID 28133931)
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.reason_why: Blocking T-cell costimulation (CD28-CD80/86 interaction) did not translate into reduced relapse risk in this trial population, indicating this particular immune pathway is not the dominant driver of TAK relapse, or that the trial was underpowered.
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.important_caveat: This is included as a real, honestly reported negative trial result so this entry is not skewed toward only positive findings - abatacept is not a recommended TAK therapy based on this evidence.
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.real_working_solution: Not applicable - use tocilizumab, anti-TNF agents, methotrexate, or azathioprine instead for glucocorticoid-refractory disease.
tak_biologic_agents_refractory_disease.source: Langford CA et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:846-853 (PMID 28133931)

tak_revascularization_procedures.name: Surgical Bypass Revascularization - Real More Durable Procedure for Critical Stenosis (Preferred Over Endovascular)
tak_revascularization_procedures.type: Vascular surgical procedure, for critical/symptomatic stenosis once disease is quiescent
specific_drugs: Not a medicine - surgical bypass grafting (autologous vein or synthetic graft) of critically stenosed/occluded large vessels
tak_revascularization_procedures.effectiveness: In a 65-patient series with 111 revascularized lesions, 2-year symptomatic recurrence after surgical bypass was only 11.5% (i.e., ~88.5% remained symptom-free) versus 32.3% after endovascular angioplasty/stenting (P=0.016); angiographic recurrence was 11.1% (surgical) vs 32.1% (endovascular) (P=0.026) - Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161 (PMID 24134435)
tak_revascularization_procedures.reason_why: Surgical bypass routes blood flow around the diseased, fibrotic/stenotic segment using a healthier conduit, whereas endovascular angioplasty/stenting in TAK's chronically inflamed, fibrotic vessel wall carries a real higher restenosis rate because the underlying vasculitic vessel-wall pathology remains in place at the treated site.
tak_revascularization_procedures.important_caveat: Best performed during inactive/quiescent disease (per EULAR 2018 recommendations) to minimize perioperative complications and restenosis risk; not a substitute for ongoing immunosuppressive control of the underlying vasculitis.
tak_revascularization_procedures.real_working_solution: Real, more durable, and the preferred procedural option for critical symptomatic stenosis/occlusion once medical therapy has controlled active inflammation - priority-2 (procedure) intervention behind medicine-led induction/maintenance.
tak_revascularization_procedures.source: Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161 (PMID 24134435); Hellmich B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110)

tak_revascularization_procedures.name: Endovascular Angioplasty/Stenting - Real Less Invasive but Less Durable Alternative for Critical Stenosis
tak_revascularization_procedures.type: Vascular endovascular procedure, for critical/symptomatic stenosis once disease is quiescent
specific_drugs: Not a medicine - percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, with or without stent placement
tak_revascularization_procedures.effectiveness: 2-year symptomatic recurrence of 32.3% (i.e., ~67.7% remained symptom-free) and angiographic recurrence of 32.1%, both significantly worse than surgical bypass in the same 65-patient cohort - Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161 (PMID 24134435)
tak_revascularization_procedures.reason_why: Angioplasty/stenting mechanically dilates the stenosed segment without removing or bypassing the underlying chronically inflamed/fibrotic vessel wall, which real predisposes to earlier restenosis in TAK compared with atherosclerotic disease.
tak_revascularization_procedures.real_working_solution: Real reasonable less-invasive option, particularly for shorter-segment stenoses or when surgical risk is high, but with a real honestly higher restenosis rate than surgical bypass; disease activity should be quiescent before the procedure.
tak_revascularization_procedures.source: Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161 (PMID 24134435)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics from different study designs and follow-up windows (remission-induction rates, sustained-remission rates, RCT relapse-free rates, and procedural recurrence-free rates) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes - not a claim of head-to-head superiority across different trials/cohorts with different patient populations and endpoint definitions.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Azathioprine + prednisolone (Valsakumar cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of patients with clinical/laboratory improvement (ESR/CRP normalization) at 3 months, n=15
ranked_high_to_low.source: Valsakumar AK et al., J Rheumatol 2003;30:1793-1798 (PMID 12913937)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Maksimowicz-McKinnon US cohort, glucocorticoid-led therapy

ranked_high_to_low.source: Maksimowicz-McKinnon K et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:1000-1009 (PMID 17328078)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Anti-TNF (infliximab/etanercept), refractory TAK
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Combined remission-off-steroid + tapered-to-<10mg/day response rate, n=25 retrospective cohort
ranked_high_to_low.source: Molloy ES et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1567-1569 (PMID 18677012)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Surgical bypass revascularization, critical stenosis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 2-year symptom-free rate (100% minus 11.5% recurrence), n=65 patients/111 lesions
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lee GY et al., Scand J Rheumatol 2014;43:153-161 (PMID 24134435)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:578-582 (PMID 7908520)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Kerr GS et al., Ann Intern Med 1994;120:919-929 (PMID 7909656)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Nakaoka Y et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:348-354 (PMID 29191819)
