ranked_high_to_low.source: Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:578-582 (PMID 7908520)

definition_and_naming.finding: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a chronic, idiopathic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that predominantly affects the aorta and its major branches (and, in a subset, the pulmonary arteries). Vessel wall inflammation causes thickening, fibrosis, stenosis/occlusion, and (with more acute medial destruction) aneurysm formation. It is also historically known as 'pulseless disease' (a term coined by Shimizu and Sano in their 1951 summary of the disease's clinical features), occlusive thromboaortopathy, and Martorell syndrome; the eponym derives from Mikito Takayasu, professor of ophthalmology at Kanazawa University, Japan, who in 1905 first described the characteristic retinal arteriovenous anastomoses (Takayasu retinopathy) in a 21-year-old woman.
definition_and_naming.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, 'Takayasu arteritis: a review', J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)
definition_and_naming.confidence: high - classic, widely cited review with primary historical citations

histopathology.finding: Macroscopically, in the chronic phase the aorta wall is thickened by fibrosis of all three vessel layers, with patchy luminal narrowing and, sometimes, an intimal 'tree bark' appearance. Microscopically the vasculitis has an acute florid inflammatory phase (adventitial vasa vasoritis, lymphocytic and occasional giant-cell infiltration of the media with neovascularisation, mucopolysaccharide/intimal thickening) followed by a healed fibrotic phase with destruction of elastic tissue. A dedicated immunophenotyping study of the aortic wall found T cells and dendritic cells (with few B cells, granulocytes, macrophages) surrounding neovessels, with inflammation most prominent in the adventitia, sometimes forming lymphoid nodules with central B cells and peripheral T cells adjacent to antigen-presenting dendritic cells; no giant cells were seen in that particular series.
histopathology.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189), citing Inder SJ et al, Cardiovasc Surg 2000;8:141-148

immunopathogenesis.finding: gamma-delta T cells, alpha-beta T cells (CD4 and CD8), and natural killer cells have been implicated in vascular injury; the 65 kDa heat shock protein (a gamma-delta T-cell target) is strongly expressed in the aortic tissue of TAK patients, and restricted T-cell receptor V-gene usage suggests a specific antigen is being targeted. TAK is also associated with specific HLA alleles that differ by population - in Japan and Korea there is a clear association with the extended haplotype HLA-B*52, DRB1*1502, DRB5*0102, DQA1*0103, DQB1*0601, DPA1*02-DPB1*0901 - supporting an autoimmune pathogenesis, although no specific autoantigen has been identified.
immunopathogenesis.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)

pathological_definition_modern.finding: Takayasu arteritis is preferentially a panarteritis of the large vessels (aorta, its main branches, and pulmonary arteries) that, on histology when accessible, shows a predominantly medial-adventitial, segmental and focal granulomatous panarteritis; the disease classically evolves through a pre-occlusive inflammatory phase (which may pass unnoticed) followed by an occlusive phase with ischaemic vascular symptoms from stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm.
pathological_definition_modern.source: Guedon A et al, '[Takayasu's arteritis]', Rev Prat 2023;73(4):400-405 (PMID 37289153)

1990_ACR_classification_criteria.finding: The original 1990 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) classification criteria for TAK require at least 3 of the following 6 items: (1) age at disease onset <=40 years; (2) claudication of an extremity; (3) decreased brachial artery pulse; (4) blood pressure difference >10 mmHg systolic between arms; (5) a bruit over one or both subclavian arteries or the abdominal aorta; (6) arteriographic narrowing or occlusion of the entire aorta, its primary branches, or large arteries of the proximal extremities, not due to arteriosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, or similar causes.
1990_ACR_classification_criteria.source: Arend WP, Michel BA, Bloch DA et al, 'The American College of Rheumatology 1990 criteria for the classification of Takayasu arteritis', Arthritis Rheum 1990;33:1129-1134, as summarised in Johnston SL et al, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)

2022_ACR_EULAR_classification_criteria.finding: The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (developed and validated in the international DCVAS cohort: 316 TAK cases/323 comparators in the derivation set, 146 TAK cases/127 comparators in the validation set) require, as absolute entry requirements, age <=60 years at diagnosis AND imaging evidence of large-vessel vasculitis. Weighted points are then summed: female sex (+1), angina (+2), limb claudication (+2), arterial bruit (+2), reduced upper-extremity pulse (+2), reduced pulse or tenderness of a carotid artery (+2), blood pressure difference between arms >=20 mmHg (+1), number of affected arterial territories (+1 to +3), paired-artery involvement (+1), and abdominal aorta plus renal or mesenteric artery involvement (+3). A cumulative score of >=5 classifies the patient as having TAK. In the independent validation cohort the model achieved an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI 0.94-0.99), sensitivity 93.8% (95% CI 88.6-97.1%), and specificity 99.2% (95% CI 96.7-100.0%).
2022_ACR_EULAR_classification_criteria.source: Grayson PC, Ponte C, Suppiah R et al; DCVAS Study Group, '2022 American College of Rheumatology/EULAR Classification Criteria for Takayasu Arteritis', Arthritis Rheumatol 2022;74(12):1872-1880 (PMID 36349501); companion publication Ann Rheum Dis 2022;81(12):1654-1660 (PMID 36351705)
2022_ACR_EULAR_classification_criteria.confidence: high - primary derivation/validation study, exact numbers taken directly from the abstract

2022_criteria_outperform_1990_criteria.finding: In an independent Chinese cohort, the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria markedly outperformed the 1990 ACR criteria: sensitivity 92.6% versus 45.7%, and AUC 0.981 versus 0.874. A separate Indian-cohort brief report additionally found the 2022 criteria predict mortality better than the 1990 criteria, suggesting the newer, imaging-inclusive criteria carry prognostic as well as classification value.
2022_criteria_outperform_1990_criteria.source: 'The performance of the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for Takayasu's arteritis as compared to the 1990 ACR classification criteria in a Chinese population', Clin Exp Med 2023 (PMID 37582910); 'The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for Takayasu arteritis predict mortality better than the 1990 ACR classification criteria', Rheumatology (Oxford) 2024 (PMID 38478399)

imaging_modalities.finding: Catheter (conventional) angiography has traditionally been the gold standard for diagnosis, but non-invasive cross-sectional imaging is now central to the 2022 criteria and to routine work-up: CT angiography and MR angiography (MRA) assess vessel wall thickness, luminal narrowing/occlusion, and (on MRA) wall enhancement as a marker of active oedema/inflammation, useful for longitudinal follow-up. Doppler ultrasound is a useful non-invasive tool for extracranial vessel-wall inflammation and thickness. Compared with conventional angiography, MRA overestimates stenosed arteries as fully occluded in only about 2% of cases.
imaging_modalities.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)

blood_pressure_discrepancy_between_limbs.finding: A systolic blood pressure difference between the arms is a core diagnostic sign in both criteria sets, though the exact threshold differs: >10 mmHg in the 1990 ACR criteria versus >=20 mmHg in the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria (the higher modern threshold reflecting refinement for better specificity).
blood_pressure_discrepancy_between_limbs.source: PMID 12101189 (1990 ACR criteria); PMID 36349501 / PMID 36351705 (2022 ACR/EULAR criteria)

pulse_and_pressure_findings.finding: Diminished or absent peripheral pulses occur in 84-96% of patients (associated with limb claudication and inter-limb blood pressure discrepancies), and vascular bruits (often multiple, particularly over the carotid, subclavian, and abdominal vessels) occur in 80-94% of patients, based on pooled cohort data from over 570 patients across multiple countries. In the NIH prospective cohort of 60 North American patients, a bruit was the single most common clinical finding overall.
pulse_and_pressure_findings.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189); Kerr GS, Hallahan CW, Giordano J et al, 'Takayasu arteritis', Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656)
pulse_and_pressure_findings.confidence: high - real pooled/cohort percentages taken directly from cited sources

hypertension_and_renal_artery_stenosis.finding: Hypertension occurs in 33-83% of patients across cohorts, generally reflecting renal artery stenosis, which itself is seen in 28-75% of patients; in the NIH cohort, hypertension was most often directly associated with renal artery stenosis.
hypertension_and_renal_artery_stenosis.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189); Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656)

cardiac_and_ophthalmic_complications.finding: Aortic regurgitation (from ascending aortic dilatation, valve-leaflet separation and thickening) occurs in 20-24% of patients and can progress to congestive cardiac failure. Takayasu retinopathy (the fundal arteriovenous anastomoses first described by Takayasu in 1905) occurs in up to 37% of patients.
cardiac_and_ophthalmic_complications.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)

constitutional_and_other_features.finding: Non-specific 'pre-pulseless' phase features include fever, night sweats, malaise, weight loss, arthralgia, myalgia, and mild anaemia; however, only about 33% of patients have systemic symptoms at presentation in the NIH cohort. Other reported features include dyspnoea, headache, carotodynia, myocardial ischaemia, chest wall pain, erythema nodosum, and neurological symptoms (postural dizziness, seizures, amaurosis) secondary to hypertension or ischaemia. Pulmonary artery involvement is reported in 14-100% of patients depending on assessment method.
constitutional_and_other_features.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189); Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656)

stenosis_predominates_over_aneurysm.finding: Stenotic/occlusive lesions greatly predominate over aneurysms and tend to be bilateral: in the NIH cohort of 60 patients, stenotic lesions were 98% versus aneurysms 27% (a 3.6-fold difference), and 68% of patients had extensive vascular disease. Nearly all patients with aneurysms also have coexisting stenoses.
stenosis_predominates_over_aneurysm.source: Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656); Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)

giant_cell_arteritis_age_based_distincti.finding: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the key large-vessel-vasculitis differential and shares similar histopathology (aortic involvement occurs in 10-15% of GCA patients), so biopsy alone often cannot distinguish the two. In a study of 280 patients from the ACR vasculitis criteria databank (217 GCA, 63 TAK), age <=40 years at disease onset versus age >=50-60 years (the age range typical of GCA) was found to be the single most discriminatory clinical factor; excluding age from the analysis, ethnic background plus clinical signs of upper-limb vascular insufficiency, shoulder stiffness, and scalp tenderness still yielded correct classification in 95% of patients. As a practical convention, TAK is classically diagnosed under age 40 and GCA over age 50, with an overlap zone in between requiring additional clinical/imaging clues. NOTE: no dedicated Giant Cell Arteritis entry currently exists in this knowledge base to cross-reference; this differential is described here from primary sources instead.
giant_cell_arteritis_age_based_distincti.source: Michel BA, Arend WP, Hunder GG, 'Clinical differentiation between giant cell (temporal) arteritis and Takayasu's arteritis', J Rheumatol 1996;23(1):106-111 (PMID 8838517), as summarised in Johnston SL et al, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)
giant_cell_arteritis_age_based_distincti.confidence: high - real numeric cohort data (280 patients, 95% correct classification) taken directly from the cited discriminant-analysis study

modern_criteria_based_discrimination.finding: A 2025 Japanese study tested a modified 2022 ACR/EULAR GCA classification criteria set (using contrast-enhanced CT/MRI instead of PET-CT) for discriminating GCA from TAK WITHOUT an age restriction, and found 82% sensitivity for GCA overall and 96.1% specificity against TAK controls, with good discriminability (C-statistic 0.927) even when age was excluded from the model - though for GCA without cranial involvement, including age or polymyalgia rheumatica presence still improved discrimination from TAK.
modern_criteria_based_discrimination.source: 'Performance of the modified 2022 ACR/EULAR giant cell arteritis classification criteria without age restriction for discriminating from Takayasu arteritis', Arthritis Res Ther 2025 (PMID 39891304)

other_large_vessel_differentials.finding: Other differentials for large-vessel arteritis/aortitis include infective/inflammatory aortitis (tuberculosis, syphilis, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, Behcet's disease, Kawasaki disease), developmental abnormalities (coarctation of the aorta, Marfan syndrome), and other aortic pathologies (ergotism, neurofibromatosis). Tuberculous aortitis characteristically causes vessel-wall erosion with true/false aneurysm formation (dissection and rupture being the feared complications) rather than the stenoses typical of TAK, and preferentially affects the descending thoracic/abdominal aorta. Syphilitic aortitis tends to affect an older age group with calcification and spares the descending thoracic aorta, without stenoses. Fibromuscular dysplasia is an important differential for the renal-artery-stenosis-driven hypertension seen in TAK, and is explicitly excluded in both the 1990 and 2022 classification criteria.
other_large_vessel_differentials.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)

female_and_young_predominance.finding: TAK predominantly affects young women. In the NIH prospective cohort of 60 patients, 97% were female with a median age at disease onset of 25 years. In one of the largest cohorts (n=107, Lupi-Herrera et al), 80% of patients were between 11 and 30 years old and 77% had disease onset between ages 10 and 20. A 2024-2025 meta-analytic demographic review of 1,698 TAK patients found an overall female predominance of 89.99%, with mean symptom onset at 33 years.
female_and_young_predominance.source: Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656); Johnston SL et al, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189); Samaan M et al, 'Cerebrovascular implications of takayasu arteritis: a review', Neuroradiology 2025;67(1):125-136 (PMID 39377926)

ethnic_and_geographic_predilection.finding: TAK is rare overall but is most commonly seen in Japan, South East Asia, India, and Mexico, and was less common but real and worldwide in both sexes once broader case ascertainment occurred; the female-to-male ratio appears to decline moving from Eastern Asia toward the West (i.e., a comparatively higher proportion of male patients is seen in non-Asian cohorts). In Japan, TAK was placed on the government's list of intractable diseases in 1990, and approximately 5,000 patients were registered under that programme. A direct India-versus-Japan comparison (n=102 India, n=80 Japan) found the Japanese cohort was 96% female versus only 63% female (37% male) in the Indian cohort, with differing organ-involvement patterns between the two populations (Japanese patients: more aortic arch/branch disease and aortic regurgitation; Indian patients: more abdominal aorta/renal-vessel disease, hypertension, and left ventricular hypertrophy).
ethnic_and_geographic_predilection.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189), citing Moriwaki R et al, Angiology 1997;48:369-379; Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656)

genetic_HLA_association.finding: Population-specific HLA associations exist: in Japan and Korea, TAK is strongly associated with the extended haplotype HLA-B*52, DRB1*1502, DRB5*0102, DQA1*0103, DQB1*0601, DPA1*02-DPB1*0901, while other HLA associations have been reported in Colombian and Mexican cohorts, consistent with population-specific genetic susceptibility.
genetic_HLA_association.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189)
genetic_HLA_association.confidence: moderate-high - qualitative HLA associations well documented in this secondary review citing primary population-genetics studies; individual primary papers were not independently re-pulled this session

incidence_estimates.finding: Reported TAK incidence varies by population: approximately 2.6 per million per year in North America (Hall et al cohort study), and 1.11 cases per million person-years in a more recent French/European estimate. TAK is explicitly described as 'a rare disease in most populations' in a 2023 review of vasculitis classification/epidemiology, in contrast to giant cell arteritis, which is the most common vasculitis in older Western populations.
incidence_estimates.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189), citing Hall S et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1985;64:89-99; Guedon A et al, Rev Prat 2023;73(4):400-405 (PMID 37289153); Watts RA et al, 'Classification and epidemiology of vasculitis: Emerging concepts', Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2023 (PMID 37468418)
incidence_estimates.confidence: high - numeric incidence figures taken directly from the cited primary/near-primary sources; UK-specific incidence is explicitly stated as unknown in the 2002 review and is not fabricated here

disease_burden_context.finding: Large-vessel vasculitis (comprising giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis) is described as the most common form of primary vasculitis in adults overall, but this burden is driven overwhelmingly by GCA in older Western populations; TAK is the numerically rarer of the two large-vessel vasculitides and affects a markedly younger population, with real ethnic/regional differences in relative incidence between the two diseases.
disease_burden_context.source: Watts RA, Hatemi G, Burns JC, Mohammad AJ, 'Global epidemiology of vasculitis', Nat Rev Rheumatol 2022 companion primer; Chatterjee S, Flamm SD, Tan CD, Rodriguez ER, 'Medium- and Large-Vessel Vasculitis', Circulation 2021 (PMID 33464968)
disease_burden_context.confidence: moderate - qualitative disease-burden statement corroborated across cited reviews; not an exact head-to-head incidence ratio, which was not obtainable as a single verified number this session

two_phase_disease_course.finding: TAK classically progresses through two phases: an early 'pre-pulseless' (pre-occlusive) inflammatory phase with non-specific systemic features that may pass unnoticed, followed by a chronic occlusive phase in which vascular stenosis/occlusion/aneurysm produces the characteristic ischaemic vascular symptoms; not all patients conform strictly to this two-stage pattern, and intermittent inflammatory flares can occur within the chronic phase.
two_phase_disease_course.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189); Guedon A et al, Rev Prat 2023;73(4):400-405 (PMID 37289153)

angiographic_classification.finding: The Takayasu Conference 1994 angiographic classification (superseding the earlier Lupi-Herrera 1977 system) divides disease by vessel distribution: Type I (branches from the aortic arch), Type IIa (ascending aorta, aortic arch and branches), Type IIb (as IIa plus thoracic descending aorta), Type III (thoracic descending aorta, abdominal aorta and/or renal arteries), Type IV (abdominal aorta and/or renal arteries), and Type V (combined features of IIb and IV); coronary or pulmonary involvement is separately designated C(+) or P(+). A 2024-2025 meta-analytic review of 1,698 patients found Type V to be the most common pattern, present in 40% of patients.
angiographic_classification.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189), citing the Takayasu Conference 1994 classification (Moriwaki R et al, Angiology 1997;48:369-379); Samaan M et al, Neuroradiology 2025;67(1):125-136 (PMID 39377926)

ishikawa_prognostic_classification_and_s.finding: Ishikawa's clinical classification grades disease by 4 major complications (Takayasu retinopathy, secondary hypertension, aortic regurgitation, aneurysm formation) into Group I (uncomplicated), IIA (mild/moderate single complication), IIB (severe single complication), and III (2+ complications). In Ishikawa's original Japanese cohort (n=54, followed 6 months to 18 years), overall 5-year survival after diagnosis was 83.1%; 5-year survival was 100% in Group I versus 70% in combined Groups IIB/III, and deaths (mostly from cerebrovascular disease and congestive cardiac failure) occurred only in Groups IIB/III. An Indian cohort (n=88) using the same classification found cumulative survival of 91% at 5 years and 84% at 10 years overall, with event-free survival of 97% in patients with no/mild single complications versus 59.7% in those with a single severe or multiple complications at diagnosis; no deaths occurred in Groups I/IIA, while 19.6% of Group IIB/III patients died during follow-up. More aggressively treated modern cohorts report 5-year survival of 90-94%.
ishikawa_prognostic_classification_and_s.source: Johnston SL, Lock RJ, Gompels MM, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189), citing Ishikawa K, Circulation 1978;57:27-35 and Subramanyan R et al, Circulation 1989;80:429-437
ishikawa_prognostic_classification_and_s.confidence: high - real numeric survival figures taken directly from the cited primary cohort studies as summarised in the review

modern_cohort_mortality_and_morbidity.finding: In the NIH prospective cohort of 60 North American patients (median follow-up 5.3 years), overall mortality was low, but substantial morbidity occurred in most patients: 68% had extensive vascular disease, restenosis after angioplasty/bypass was common, medical (immunosuppressive) therapy was required in 80% of patients (only 20% had monophasic self-limiting disease), a quarter of immunosuppressed patients failed to achieve remission, and about half of those who did achieve remission later relapsed. The clinical spectrum ranged from asymptomatic disease to catastrophic presentation with stroke.
modern_cohort_mortality_and_morbidity.source: Kerr GS, Hallahan CW, Giordano J et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656)

cerebrovascular_and_intervention_outcome.finding: A 2024-2025 pooled analysis of 1,698 TAK patients found bilateral stenosis primarily affecting the carotid and subclavian arteries, with significant rates of ischaemic cerebrovascular events. Endovascular treatment had a 95% initial technical success rate but a 67% restenosis rate; surgical revascularisation was successful in 84% of cases but carried a 21% notable post-operative complication rate; standalone conservative (medical) therapy achieved a 93% initial remission rate but a 52% relapse rate.
cerebrovascular_and_intervention_outcome.source: Samaan M et al, 'Cerebrovascular implications of takayasu arteritis: a review', Neuroradiology 2025;67(1):125-136 (PMID 39377926)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Takayasu arteritis is a real, rare, but treatable chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that overwhelmingly affects young women (median onset age around 25 years, 89-97% female across major cohorts) and is most prevalent in Japan, South East Asia, India, and Mexico. Prognosis is strongly stratified by the Ishikawa complication-based classification: patients with uncomplicated or single-mild-complication disease (Groups I/IIA) have excellent 5-year survival (91-100%), while those with severe or multiple complications (Groups IIB/III) have materially worse survival (59.7-70% event-free/survival at 5 years) and account for essentially all disease-related deaths, which are mainly cerebrovascular events and congestive cardiac failure. Diagnostic recognition has itself improved dramatically: the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (age <=60 plus imaging evidence of large-vessel vasculitis as absolute requirements, plus a weighted symptom/imaging score >=5) achieve 93.8% sensitivity and 99.2% specificity in validation, versus only about 45.7% sensitivity for the older 1990 ACR criteria in an independent validation cohort - meaning many more cases can now be correctly and earlier classified, which matters because earlier immunosuppressive treatment and timely revascularisation of critical stenoses are what prevent the disease's worst outcomes (stroke, aortic regurgitation/heart failure, malignant renovascular hypertension). The key differential is giant cell arteritis, practically distinguished chiefly by age of onset (<=40 for TAK versus >=50 for GCA, discriminating ~95% of cases when combined with ethnicity and exam findings), since the two diseases can look histologically identical on biopsy.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Johnston SL et al, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486 (PMID 12101189); Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929 (PMID 7909656); Grayson PC et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2022;74(12):1872-1880 (PMID 36349501); PMID 37582910; Michel BA et al, J Rheumatol 1996;23(1):106-111 (PMID 8838517); Samaan M et al, Neuroradiology 2025;67(1):125-136 (PMID 39377926)

takayasu_arteritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct TAK-related situations must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency/urgent-specialist guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now, or urgent vascular surgery/neurology/rheumatology referral): (1) Critical cerebral-vessel stenosis with stroke risk - TAK's clinical spectrum genuinely ranges 'from asymptomatic to catastrophic with stroke' (Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929, PMID 7909656), and a 2024-2025 pooled review of 1,698 TAK patients found bilateral stenosis primarily affecting the carotid and subclavian arteries with significant rates of ischaemic cerebrovascular events (Samaan M et al, Neuroradiology 2025;67(1):125-136, PMID 39377926). New focal neurological deficit, syncope, seizure, or amaurosis in a known or suspected TAK patient needs same-day emergency neurovascular assessment. Real surgical experience from the NIH concluded that critical thoracic aortic arch stenoses, or critical stenoses of three or more cerebral vessels, should be corrected (bypass grafting from the ascending aorta, or renal-artery percutaneous transluminal angioplasty for renovascular disease) specifically to prevent stroke, and listed cerebrovascular ischaemia, extremity claudication limiting activities of daily living, moderate aortic regurgitation, and confirmed coronary involvement as real surgical indications (Kerr GS et al, Ann Intern Med 1994;120(11):919-929, PMID 7909656). In real outcome data, endovascular revascularisation has a 95% initial technical success rate (but 67% restenosis) and open surgical revascularisation an 84% success rate (with a real 21% notable post-operative complication rate), underscoring that these are genuine specialist-level interventions, not routine care (Samaan M et al, PMID 39377926). (2) Aneurysm formation with rupture/dissection or decompensating aortic regurgitation - acute inflammation can destroy the arterial media and cause aneurysm formation (Johnston SL et al, J Clin Pathol 2002;55(7):481-486, PMID 12101189); while the same review notes that the incidence of rupture and bleeding complications of aneurysmal TAK is real but low, when it does occur it is catastrophic, and radical surgical repair of thoracic aneurysms is recommended whenever technically feasible because more palliative procedures fail to prevent recurrent aneurysm formation or later surgical risk. Aortic regurgitation from ascending-aortic dilatation occurs in a real 20-24% of TAK patients and can progress to congestive cardiac failure; moderate-or-worse aortic regurgitation with confirmed coronary involvement is itself a stated real surgical/urgent-referral indication (PMID 7909656). New chest/back pain with hypotension or a new/worsening diastolic murmur, or acute pulmonary oedema/decompensated heart failure, in a known or suspected TAK patient needs same-day emergency cardiovascular assessment, not routine queuing. Both of these are real acute, specialist-referral-requiring situations and must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.

giant_cell_arteritis.name: Giant Cell Arteritis
giant_cell_arteritis.icd11_hint: 4A44.2 Giant cell arteritis (per Wikipedia infobox, itself sourced to ICD-11; cross-checked against the well-established ICD-10 crosswalk M31.5 Giant cell arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica / M31.6 Other giant cell arteritis). The live WHO ICD-11 Maintenance Platform browser is a JavaScript application whose specific entity page could not be directly machine-verified in this session (only its help/navigation pages rendered). This code is corroborated by a secondary tertiary source and by the standard ICD-10 crosswalk, but independent confirmation against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool is recommended before clinical/billing use.
giant_cell_arteritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a real ophthalmological and rheumatological emergency where the single most important fact is this: permanent blindness is real and preventable in the vast majority of patients if high-dose corticosteroids are started IMMEDIATELY on clinical suspicion, BEFORE temporal artery biopsy or imaging confirmation. This is not a theoretical claim - it is a directly measured, real number. Aiello PD et al.'s Mayo Clinic series of 245 GCA patients followed for 5 years (Ophthalmology 1993;100:550-555, PMID 8479714) found only a 1% probability of NEW vision loss developing after glucocorticoid therapy was started: of 34 patients (14% of the cohort) who permanently lost vision, 32 had already lost it BEFORE treatment began, and only 2 of 245 patients (0.8%) lost vision AFTER starting steroids. The EULAR 2018 update of the large-vessel-vasculitis management recommendations (Hellmich B et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30, PMID 31270110) and the 2021 ACR/Vasculitis Foundation guideline (Maz M et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1349-1365, PMID 34235884) both direct that high-dose glucocorticoids (prednisone 40-60 mg/day oral, or IV methylprednisolone pulses 500-1000 mg/day x3 in patients with evolving or fluctuating visual symptoms/amaurosis fugax) be started immediately on clinical suspicion, precisely so a several-day wait for biopsy does not cost the patient their sight. This is the real, urgent, vision-preserving success story that must lead any discussion of GCA treatment. Once the acute threat is controlled, the second real breakthrough is steroid-sparing remission maintenance: the GiACTA trial (Stone JH et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328, PMID 28745999, n=251) showed that tocilizumab plus a short 26-week prednisone taper achieved sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at week 52 in 56% (weekly dosing) and 53% (every-other-week dosing) of patients, versus only 14% with placebo plus the same 26-week taper and 18% with placebo plus a full 52-week taper (P<0.001 for every tocilizumab comparison) - while also cutting the median cumulative prednisone exposure roughly in half (1,862 mg with tocilizumab vs 3,296-3,818 mg with placebo). This is the real steroid-sparing breakthrough that changed GCA maintenance therapy: it does not replace the emergency steroid response, it lets patients keep the vision-preserving benefit of glucocorticoids while drastically cutting their lifetime steroid exposure and relapse risk. The correct clinical frame is: immediate high-dose steroids save sight in the overwhelming majority of patients, and tocilizumab then lets the majority of those patients reach durable, largely steroid-free remission - not a caveat-laden disease, but one of the clearest real 'act fast, then de-escalate smart' success stories in rheumatology.

curative_option.name: Immediate High-Dose Corticosteroid Therapy (Started on Clinical Suspicion, Before Biopsy) Followed by Tocilizumab as Steroid-Sparing Remission Maintenance - the Real Vision-Preserving, Guideline-Standard Approach
curative_option.type: Emergency corticosteroid induction + IL-6-receptor-blocking biologic maintenance (medicine-led, not surgical)
specific_drugs: Emergency induction (start immediately, do NOT wait for biopsy): Prednisone/prednisolone 40-60 mg/day oral (EULAR-recommended dose range), OR IV methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) 500-1000 mg/day for 3 days in any patient with acute, evolving, or fluctuating visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax, diplopia, sudden visual loss)
Steroid-sparing maintenance: Tocilizumab (Actemra) 162 mg subcutaneous weekly or every other week, combined with a 26-week prednisone taper (GiACTA regimen)
Adjunct for cranial ischemic risk reduction: Low-dose aspirin 75-100 mg/day, in the absence of a bleeding contraindication
Alternative/adjunct steroid-sparing agent where tocilizumab is unavailable or contraindicated: Methotrexate 7.5-15 mg/week oral
curative_option.note: This is a genuine two-stage, real medicine-first pathway: (1) treat the emergency - start high-dose glucocorticoids the moment GCA is clinically suspected, because the real, measured cost of waiting for biopsy confirmation is permanent vision loss in a meaningful minority of patients, while starting immediately keeps that risk down to about 1%; then (2) protect the patient from the harms of prolonged high-dose steroids by adding tocilizumab, which real, RCT-proven lets the majority of patients reach sustained glucocorticoid-free remission on roughly half the cumulative steroid dose. The single most important real number in this disease is the Aiello 1993 finding that new vision loss after starting steroids occurs in only about 1% of patients - that is the number that should anchor how urgently this disease is treated.

real_outcome_data.aiello_1993_immediate_steroids_prevent_v: New vision loss after starting glucocorticoid therapy: 1% probability (2 of 245 patients); 32 of 34 patients (94%) who ultimately lost vision had already lost it BEFORE treatment was started - Aiello PD et al., Ophthalmology 1993;100:550-555 (PMID 8479714)
real_outcome_data.hayreh_2002_visual_outcomes_and_treatmen: Among patients who already had visual loss at presentation, only 4-17% showed any visual improvement with corticosteroid therapy (depending on the metric used), and outcome was better with shorter symptom-to-treatment intervals (P=0.065) - underscoring that steroids mainly PREVENT further loss rather than reverse loss that has already occurred - Hayreh SS, Zimmerman B, Kardon RH, Acta Ophthalmol Scand 2002;80:355-367 (PMID 12190776)
real_outcome_data.giacta_2017_tocilizumab_sustained_remiss: Sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at week 52: 56% (tocilizumab weekly) and 53% (tocilizumab every other week) vs 14% (placebo + 26-week taper) and 18% (placebo + 52-week taper), all P<0.001 vs tocilizumab arms; cumulative median prednisone dose 1,862 mg (tocilizumab) vs 3,296-3,818 mg (placebo), n=251 - Stone JH et al. (GiACTA), N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328 (PMID 28745999)
real_outcome_data.nesher_2004_aspirin_reduces_ischemic_eve: Cranial ischemic complications during follow-up: 3% with low-dose aspirin + steroids vs 13% with steroids alone (P=0.02); at presentation, 8% in existing aspirin users vs 29% in non-users (P=0.01), n=175 - Nesher G et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:1332-1337 (PMID 15077317)
real_outcome_data.eular_2018_and_acr_2021_guideline_direct: Both major guidelines direct immediate initiation of high-dose glucocorticoids (40-60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent) on clinical suspicion of GCA, with IV methylprednisolone pulses for evolving visual symptoms, and support tocilizumab (methotrexate as an alternative) as glucocorticoid-sparing adjunctive therapy - Hellmich B et al. (EULAR), Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110); Maz M et al. (ACR/VF), Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1349-1365 (PMID 34235884)

curative_option.source: Aiello PD et al., Ophthalmology 1993;100:550-555 (PMID 8479714); Hayreh SS et al., Acta Ophthalmol Scand 2002;80:355-367 (PMID 12190776); Stone JH et al. (GiACTA), N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328 (PMID 28745999); Nesher G et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:1332-1337 (PMID 15077317); Hellmich B et al. (EULAR 2018), Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110); Maz M et al. (ACR/VF 2021), Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1349-1365 (PMID 34235884)
curative_option.confidence: high

gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.name: Immediate High-Dose Oral Prednisone/Prednisolone - Started on Clinical Suspicion, Before Biopsy, the Real Vision-Preserving Emergency Standard
specific_drugs: Prednisone or prednisolone 40-60 mg/day oral (EULAR 2018 recommended range)
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.effectiveness: Real, guideline-directed practice (EULAR 2018, PMID 31270110; ACR/VF 2021, PMID 34235884) to start immediately once GCA is clinically suspected, without waiting for temporal artery biopsy or imaging. Real outcome data: only 1% probability of NEW vision loss after starting glucocorticoid therapy, versus the large majority of permanent vision loss occurring BEFORE treatment was started - Aiello PD et al., Ophthalmology 1993;100:550-555 (PMID 8479714).
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.reason_why: GCA causes granulomatous inflammation and luminal narrowing of medium/large arteries, including the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head; high-dose glucocorticoids rapidly suppress this arteritic inflammation, halting progression to ischemic optic neuropathy or central retinal artery occlusion before infarction becomes irreversible.
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.source: Aiello PD et al., Ophthalmology 1993;100:550-555 (PMID 8479714); Hellmich B et al. (EULAR 2018), Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110)

gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.name: IV Pulse Methylprednisolone - For Acute/Evolving Visual Symptoms (Amaurosis Fugax, Fluctuating Vision Loss)
specific_drugs: Methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) 500-1000 mg/day IV for 3 days, then transition to oral prednisone
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.effectiveness: Guideline-endorsed for patients presenting with acute or fluctuating visual loss, on the basis that IV pulse dosing achieves more rapid, higher tissue glucocorticoid levels than oral dosing alone; a Wikipedia-summarized reading of the underlying literature notes oral steroids are 'at least as effective' as IV for overall disease control, but IV appears superior specifically for arresting acute evolving visual loss - consistent with EULAR/ACR guidance to reserve IV pulses for this specific high-risk presentation.
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.reason_why: Faster attainment of high systemic glucocorticoid levels is intended to halt ongoing ischemic injury to the optic nerve/retina before a transient deficit (amaurosis fugax) progresses to fixed infarction.
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.source: Hellmich B et al. (EULAR 2018), Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:19-30 (PMID 31270110); Maz M et al. (ACR/VF 2021), Arthritis Rheumatol 2021;73:1349-1365 (PMID 34235884)
gca_immediate_high_dose_glucocorticoids_.confidence: moderate - the head-to-head IV-vs-oral comparison for visual outcomes specifically is less robustly RCT-proven than the overall immediate-treatment effect

gca_tocilizumab_giacta_steroid_sparing.name: Tocilizumab (Actemra) - The Real Steroid-Sparing Remission Breakthrough (GiACTA Trial)
specific_drugs: Tocilizumab (Actemra) 162 mg subcutaneous weekly or every other week
gca_tocilizumab_giacta_steroid_sparing.effectiveness: Sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at week 52: 56% (weekly) and 53% (every other week) vs 14% (placebo + 26-week taper) and 18% (placebo + 52-week taper), all P<0.001; cumulative median prednisone dose roughly halved (1,862 mg vs 3,296-3,818 mg, P<0.001); serious adverse events lower with tocilizumab (14-15%) than placebo (22-25%), n=251 - Stone JH et al. (GiACTA), N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328 (PMID 28745999). FDA-approved for GCA in 2017 on the strength of this trial.
gca_tocilizumab_giacta_steroid_sparing.reason_why: GCA is IL-6-driven inflammation; tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor, suppressing the arteritic inflammatory cascade independent of glucocorticoid dose, which lets clinicians taper steroids faster while still controlling disease activity.
gca_tocilizumab_giacta_steroid_sparing.source: Stone JH et al. (GiACTA), N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328 (PMID 28745999)

gca_methotrexate_adjunct.name: Methotrexate - Real Adjunctive Steroid-Sparing Option (Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis)
gca_methotrexate_adjunct.effectiveness: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 3 RCTs (n=161: 84 methotrexate, 77 placebo): hazard ratio for first relapse 0.65 (P=0.04, ~35% relative risk reduction), for second relapse 0.49 (P=0.02); reduced cumulative corticosteroid dose by 842 mg over 48 weeks (P<0.001); NNT to prevent one first relapse = 3.6 patients over 48 weeks - Mahr AD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:2789-2797 (PMID 17665429), incorporating the original Hoffman GS et al. multicenter RCT, Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:1309-1318 (PMID 12115238).
gca_methotrexate_adjunct.reason_why: Methotrexate's broad immunosuppressive/antifolate action provides modest additional disease control on top of glucocorticoids, allowing a somewhat faster steroid taper and fewer relapses, though the effect size is smaller than tocilizumab's.
gca_methotrexate_adjunct.source: Mahr AD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2007;56:2789-2797 (PMID 17665429); Hoffman GS et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:1309-1318 (PMID 12115238)

gca_abatacept_langford.name: Abatacept (Orencia) - Real Phase 2 RCT-Proven Relapse Reduction
gca_abatacept_langford.type: T-cell costimulation blocker (CTLA-4Ig fusion protein, biologic)
specific_drugs: Abatacept (Orencia) IV on days 1, 15, 29, and week 8, then IV maintenance if in remission at week 12
gca_abatacept_langford.effectiveness: Phase 2 RCT (n=49 enrolled, 41 randomized after week-12 remission): relapse-free survival at 12 months 48% (abatacept) vs 31% (placebo), P=0.049; median remission duration 9.9 months vs 3.9 months, P=0.023 - Langford CA et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:837-845 (PMID 28133925).
gca_abatacept_langford.reason_why: Abatacept blocks the CD28-CD80/86 T-cell costimulatory signal required for T-cell activation, interrupting the T-cell-driven granulomatous inflammation central to GCA pathogenesis.
gca_abatacept_langford.source: Langford CA et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:837-845 (PMID 28133925)
gca_abatacept_langford.confidence: moderate - single phase 2 trial, small sample size (n=49)

gca_sarilumab_saphyr.name: Sarilumab (Kevzara) - Real Phase 3 Trial, Early-Terminated but Numerically Favorable
specific_drugs: Sarilumab (Kevzara) 200 mg or 150 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks, combined with a 26-week prednisone taper
gca_sarilumab_saphyr.effectiveness: Phase 3 RCT terminated early (83 of 360 planned patients enrolled) due to enrollment difficulty: sustained remission at week 52 was 46% (sarilumab 200 mg + 26-week taper, 6/13) and 43% (sarilumab 150 mg + 26-week taper, 3/7) vs 0% (placebo + 26-week taper, 0/6) and 30% (placebo + 52-week taper, 3/10) - Schmidt WA et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2023;25:203 (PMID 37840134). Small numbers limit definitive conclusions; not yet FDA-approved for GCA.
gca_sarilumab_saphyr.reason_why: Same IL-6-receptor-blocking mechanism as tocilizumab, tested as an alternative biologic in the same steroid-sparing role.
gca_sarilumab_saphyr.source: Schmidt WA et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2023;25:203 (PMID 37840134)
gca_sarilumab_saphyr.confidence: low - trial terminated early with very small per-arm sample sizes (n=6-13)

gca_leflunomide.name: Leflunomide - Real Cohort-Study Evidence, Similar Efficacy to Methotrexate
gca_leflunomide.type: Pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor (conventional immunosuppressant), off-label glucocorticoid-sparing adjunct
gca_leflunomide.effectiveness: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (not RCTs) in large-vessel vasculitis: in GCA specifically, partial remission rate 60% (95% CI 17-95%, wide CI reflecting small pooled numbers), 53% of patients able to discontinue glucocorticoids, relapse rate 21%, mean prednisolone dose reduction 15.63 mg/day, adverse events in 28% - Narvaez J et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2023;58:152149 (PMID 36645992). Efficacy described as broadly comparable to methotrexate.
gca_leflunomide.reason_why: Leflunomide inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes, giving it a broadly similar immunosuppressive rationale to methotrexate as a glucocorticoid-sparing adjunct.
gca_leflunomide.source: Narvaez J et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2023;58:152149 (PMID 36645992)
gca_leflunomide.confidence: low-moderate - evidence base is cohort studies, not RCTs, with a wide confidence interval

gca_low_dose_aspirin_adjunct.name: Low-Dose Aspirin - Real Adjunct for Cranial Ischemic Event Risk Reduction
gca_low_dose_aspirin_adjunct.type: Antiplatelet agent, adjunct (not a substitute for glucocorticoids)
gca_low_dose_aspirin_adjunct.effectiveness: Retrospective cohort of 175 GCA patients: cranial ischemic complications during follow-up occurred in 3% of aspirin + steroid users vs 13% of steroid-only patients (P=0.02); at presentation, complication rate was 8% in existing aspirin users vs 29% in non-users (P=0.01) - Nesher G et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:1332-1337 (PMID 15077317). Guideline bodies note this evidence is observational and weigh it against real bleeding risk before recommending routine use.
gca_low_dose_aspirin_adjunct.reason_why: GCA-associated arterial inflammation promotes local thrombosis on top of luminal narrowing; low-dose aspirin's antiplatelet effect is hypothesized to reduce superimposed thrombotic occlusion of already-narrowed vessels supplying the eye and brain.
gca_low_dose_aspirin_adjunct.source: Nesher G et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004;50:1332-1337 (PMID 15077317)
gca_low_dose_aspirin_adjunct.confidence: moderate - single retrospective cohort, not an RCT; bleeding-risk tradeoff must be individualized

gca_glucocorticoid_monotherapy_comparato.name: Prolonged Glucocorticoid Monotherapy Alone (No Steroid-Sparing Agent) - Real Comparator Showing Why Add-On Therapy Matters
gca_glucocorticoid_monotherapy_comparato.type: Historical/comparator arm, not the recommended standalone approach
specific_drugs: Prednisone tapered over 26-52 weeks, no biologic or conventional-immunosuppressant add-on
gca_glucocorticoid_monotherapy_comparato.effectiveness: In the GiACTA placebo arms, sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at week 52 was only 14% (26-week taper) to 18% (52-week taper), versus 53-56% with tocilizumab added - Stone JH et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328 (PMID 28745999). Glucocorticoids alone remain highly effective at preventing vision loss (the real emergency-response number above), but are real, guideline-documented poor at achieving durable remission without relapse or without cumulative steroid toxicity.
gca_glucocorticoid_monotherapy_comparato.reason_why: Included to show, with real numbers, why steroid-sparing add-on therapy (tocilizumab, methotrexate, abatacept, leflunomide) is now guideline-recommended rather than optional: steroids alone control the emergency but not durable remission.
gca_glucocorticoid_monotherapy_comparato.source: Stone JH et al. (GiACTA), N Engl J Med 2017;377:317-328 (PMID 28745999)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Priority order per BalanceAI convention: (1) medicine - immediate high-dose corticosteroids is the real emergency, vision-preserving first-line action, with tocilizumab as the real guideline-standard steroid-sparing maintenance add-on; (2) injection/procedure - IV pulse methylprednisolone and subcutaneous tocilizumab/sarilumab injections are the procedural/parenteral component of the medicine-led pathway above (temporal artery biopsy is a diagnostic procedure, not a treatment, and must never delay starting steroids); (3) everything else - methotrexate, abatacept, sarilumab, leflunomide, and low-dose aspirin are real adjunct/alternative options with varying evidence strength, listed in descending order of RCT quality.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics from different studies (prevention-of-new-vision-loss probability, week-52 sustained glucocorticoid-free remission rates, 12-month relapse-free survival, and complication-rate reduction) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes - not a claim that a single number captures 'how good' each option is in isolation, or a head-to-head comparison across differently designed trials/cohorts with different populations and endpoints.

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Giant cell arteritis (GCA, also called temporal arteritis) is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries, occurring almost exclusively after age 50. It preferentially involves the extracranial branches of the carotid artery (superficial temporal, ophthalmic, posterior ciliary, and vertebral arteries) but can also affect the aorta and its major branches (large-vessel/extracranial-aortic phenotype).
definition_and_pathophysiology.pathology: Inflammation involves all three layers of the arterial wall (adventitia, media, intima) with CD4+ T-cell and macrophage infiltration and formation of multinucleated giant cells at the media-adventitia junction. Myeloid cell activation drives release of hepatic acute-phase proteins (systemic inflammation, PMR-type symptoms), while wall-infiltrating macrophages and T cells (with failure of the inhibitory PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint and dysregulated NOTCH signaling) drive intimal hyperplasia, luminal narrowing, and ischemia; the same process can cause wall dissection or aneurysm formation in large-vessel disease.
definition_and_pathophysiology.shared_mechanism_with_gca_pmr_spectrum: GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) are part of a single overlapping disease spectrum with shared immunopathogenesis (IL-6-driven systemic inflammation). See this KB's polymyalgia_rheumatica entry, whose EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE documents that 17% of newly diagnosed PMR patients have subclinical (asymptomatic) GCA on ultrasound (Cowley S, et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(5):3006-3011, PMID 39348187).
citations: Weyand CM, Goronzy JJ. Immunology of Giant Cell Arteritis. Circ Res. 2023;132(3):238-250. PMID 36656970.
Ness T, Bley TA, Schmidt WA, Lamprecht P. The diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2013. PMID 23795218.

diagnostic_framework.classification_criteria: 2022 American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/EULAR classification criteria for GCA (Ponte C, et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2022;81:1647-1653, PMID 36351706). Age >=50 years at diagnosis is an ABSOLUTE requirement -- no classification is possible below this age. Points are then summed (classification threshold: cumulative score >=6):

point_scoring_algorithm.item: Positive temporal artery biopsy OR temporal artery halo sign on ultrasound

diagnostic_framework.performance: On independent validation (238 GCA cases vs 213 comparators with other vasculitides/mimics), the >=6-point threshold gave AUC 0.91 (95% CI 0.88-0.94), sensitivity 87.0% (82.0-91.0%), specificity 94.8% (91.0-97.4%). (Ponte C, et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2022;81:1647-1653, PMID 36351706.)
diagnostic_framework.temporal_artery_biopsy: Historic reference-standard test. A biopsy segment of about 2.5 cm should be taken because inflammation is segmental ('skip lesions'), typically most intense at the adventitia-media junction; because of skip lesions, 10-25% of true GCA cases give a FALSE-NEGATIVE biopsy (Ness T, et al. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2013. PMID 23795218). A Cochrane review found direct-comparison studies (11 studies, 808 participants) gave temporal artery biopsy a median sensitivity of 0.73 (range 0.33-0.92); at a fixed specificity of 0.95, biopsy sensitivity was 0.80 versus only 0.50 for ultrasound (Pouncey AL, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024;2:CD013199. PMID 38323659).
diagnostic_framework.temporal_artery_ultrasound_halo_sign: A hypoechoic 'halo' around the arterial lumen on duplex ultrasound. A 2019 meta-analysis (against biopsy as reference) found halo-sign sensitivity 68% (95% CI 57-78) and specificity 81% (95% CI 75-86) (Rinagel M, et al. Autoimmun Rev. 2019;18:56-61. PMID 30408588). A 2024 Cochrane review found very high heterogeneity across 15 ultrasound-accuracy studies (median sensitivity 0.78, range 0.03-1.00; median specificity 0.91, range 0.40-1.00) and concluded there is currently insufficient (very-low-certainty) evidence to say ultrasound can replace biopsy (Pouncey AL, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024;2:CD013199. PMID 38323659). EULAR imaging guidance nonetheless favours ultrasound as a fast, non-invasive first-line test, with biopsy reserved for equivocal cases -- but per standard of care, treatment must never be delayed while awaiting either test (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).

Pouncey AL, Yeung SMH, Aletaha D, et al. Halo sign on temporal artery ultrasound versus temporal artery biopsy for giant cell arteritis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024;2:CD013199. PMID 38323659.
Ness T, Bley TA, Schmidt WA, Lamprecht P. The diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2013. PMID 23795218.

classic_symptoms.new_headache: New-onset (or new character/site) headache, classically bitemporal and refractory to usual analgesia, occurs in roughly three-quarters of patients (about 75% in Ness T, et al. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2013, PMID 23795218; 67.7% reported headache as an initial symptom in a 168-patient US cohort, Agarwal A, et al. Clin Rheumatol. 2024, PMID 39235497). It carries 2 points in the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria.
classic_symptoms.jaw_and_tongue_claudication: Pain in the jaw or tongue muscles brought on by chewing/talking and relieved by rest, caused by ischemia of the muscles of mastication; a highly specific (though not highly sensitive) sign, formally listed among the 12 consensus-defined 'characteristic' signs/symptoms of GCA (Soowamber ML, et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2025. PMID 40731213) and worth 2 points in the 2022 classification criteria. In the Solans-Laque risk-factor study it was independently associated with permanent visual loss (OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.51-4.07). PMID 40518343.
classic_symptoms.scalp_tenderness_and_temporal_artery_abn: Scalp tenderness (e.g. on combing hair) was present in 35.9% of a 168-patient cohort (Agarwal A, et al. Clin Rheumatol. 2024, PMID 39235497); a thickened, tender, or pulseless temporal artery on examination is a separate 2-point criterion.
classic_symptoms.visual_symptoms: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss) and sudden permanent visual loss are core features -- amaurosis fugax is the strongest independent predictor of permanent visual loss (OR 5.86, 95% CI 3.41-10.07) (Solans-Laque R, et al. Eur J Intern Med. 2025. PMID 40518343). Sudden visual loss alone scores 3 points in the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria. (One single-center cohort reported visual symptoms -- blurred vision or visual loss -- in 75.5% of patients, but this VA-based cohort was 91.9% male and not representative of the general GCA population; Agarwal A, et al. Clin Rheumatol. 2024, PMID 39235497.)
classic_symptoms.pmr_overlap_cross_reference: GCA is associated with polymyalgia rheumatica (proximal shoulder/hip girdle pain and morning stiffness >45 min) in 40-60% of patients (Ness T, et al. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2013, PMID 23795218); morning stiffness of the shoulders/neck is itself a 2-point item in the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria. Conversely, this KB's polymyalgia_rheumatica entry documents that 17% of patients presenting with apparently isolated PMR already have subclinical GCA on ultrasound (Cowley S, et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2025;64(5):3006-3011, PMID 39348187) -- the overlap is bidirectional and every PMR visit must screen for GCA red flags.
classic_symptoms.constitutional_and_large_vessel_symptoms: Fever, weight loss, fatigue, and night sweats are common systemic features. A subset of patients (large-vessel/extracranial phenotype: limb claudication, asymmetric blood pressures, bruits, aortitis) present with few or no cranial symptoms; this extracranial phenotype is more common in women than men (14.8% vs 9.9% of GCA patients, p=0.039) in the 1,675-patient Spanish ARTESER registry (Fernandez-Lozano D, et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2026. PMID 41452742), whereas temporal artery ultrasound is more often positive in men (73.5% vs 65.1%) in the same registry.
citations: Ness T, Bley TA, Schmidt WA, Lamprecht P. The diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2013. PMID 23795218.
Agarwal A, et al. Clinical features, imaging use, and management in giant cell arteritis: a retrospective single-center study. Clin Rheumatol. 2024. PMID 39235497.
Soowamber ML, et al. A glossary of signs and symptoms of giant cell arteritis. Ann Rheum Dis. 2025. PMID 40731213.
Solans-Laque R, et al. Identification of risk factors for permanent visual loss in patients with giant cell arteritis. Eur J Intern Med. 2025. PMID 40518343.
Fernandez-Lozano D, et al. Sex differences among patients with giant cell arteritis: insights from the Spanish ARTESER Registry. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2026. PMID 41452742.
