ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of a 20-patient single-center ADA-deficient SCID cohort (1985 onward) surviving 5+ years on any modality (ERT alone in 2, HSCT in 5, gene therapy in 1); of these long-term survivors, only those who had HSCT or gene therapy (6/8) achieved normal CD4+ T-cell numbers/function and antibody production, not the 2/8 maintained on ERT alone
ranked_high_to_low.source: Scott O et al., J Clin Immunol 2017;37(6):582-591 (PMID 28748310)

definition.finding: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) comprises a group of rare, monogenic diseases characterized by early onset and a profound block in the development of T lymphocytes, frequently accompanied by absent or dysfunctional B lymphocytes and/or NK cells, producing combined cellular and humoral immunodeficiency.
definition.source: Fischer A, Notarangelo LD, Neven B, Cavazzana M, Puck JM, 'Severe combined immunodeficiencies and related disorders', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015;1:15061 (PMID 27189259)
definition.confidence: high - definition taken directly from this major disease-primer review's abstract

genetic_causes_gene_count.finding: Mutations in at least nine different genes have been identified as causes of human SCID. These genes fall into functional groups including components of cytokine receptors (e.g. IL2RG, the interleukin-2 receptor common gamma chain), and other genes governing lymphocyte development, survival, and V(D)J recombination.
genetic_causes_gene_count.source: Buckley RH, 'Molecular defects in human severe combined immunodeficiency and approaches to immune reconstitution', Annu Rev Immunol 2004;22:625-655 (PMID 15032591)
genetic_causes_gene_count.confidence: high - direct quote-level finding from this classic review; the review is now 20+ years old and additional causative genes have since been described in the literature, so 'at least nine' is a historical floor, not a current exhaustive count

IL2RG_X_linked_SCID.finding: X-linked SCID (SCID-X1) is caused by mutations in IL2RG, which encodes the common gamma chain (gamma-c) - a shared signaling subunit of the receptors for interleukin-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21 - and is essential for lymphocyte development, homeostasis, and function. IL2RG mutations produce a spectrum from classic SCID-X1 to leaky/atypical presentations that can mimic other immune dysregulation syndromes.
IL2RG_X_linked_SCID.source: Briassouli E, Marinakis N, Spoulou V, Notarangelo LD, 'IL2RG-related immunodeficiencies: from SCID to atypical presentations', Front Immunol 2026;17:1703097 (PMID 41909668)
IL2RG_X_linked_SCID.confidence: high for the mechanism; IL2RG/SCID-X1 is widely described elsewhere as the single most common genetically-defined cause of SCID, but an exact, independently-verified percentage of all SCID cases attributable to IL2RG could not be confirmed from a primary-source number in this research session and is therefore deliberately not quoted as a number here

T_B_NK_lymphocyte_phenotyping.finding: Diagnostic and research classification of SCID relies on enumerating T, B, and NK lymphocyte subsets by flow cytometry; the specific genetic defect determines which lineage(s) fail to develop (for example, defects in cytokine-receptor signalling genes typically spare B cells while defects in V(D)J recombination genes typically abolish both T and B cell development). A newborn-screening consortium classifying screen-positive infants explicitly distinguished 'typical SCID, leaky SCID, and Omenn syndrome' from other, non-SCID causes of T-cell lymphopenia, which requires lymphocyte-subset phenotyping as part of confirmatory work-up.
T_B_NK_lymphocyte_phenotyping.source: Kwan A, Abraham RS, Currier R, et al, 'Newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency in 11 screening programs in the United States', JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738 (PMID 25138334)
T_B_NK_lymphocyte_phenotyping.confidence: moderate-high - the general principle of subset-based classification is well-established immunology; the specific gene-to-phenotype (e.g., 'T-B+NK-') pairing grid was not re-derived from a freshly fetched primary source this session and is therefore described only in general terms, not as a quoted table

TREC_newborn_screening_assay.finding: Population-based newborn screening for SCID uses quantification of T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) - small circular DNA episomes generated as a byproduct of normal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement in the thymus - measured by real-time PCR from the same dried blood spot card used for other newborn screening, with a beta-actin gene segment as an amplification control. In the original validation study, healthy newborn screening samples averaged approximately 1,020 TRECs, whereas SCID-affected infants had fewer than 30 TRECs, giving a large, clinically usable separation between normal and SCID-affected infants.
TREC_newborn_screening_assay.source: Chan K, Puck JM, 'Development of population-based newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2005;115(2):391-398 (PMID 15696101)
TREC_newborn_screening_assay.confidence: high - numeric TREC values taken directly from the cited validation study

national_screening_rollout_and_outcomes.finding: Following its introduction in Wisconsin in 2008, TREC-based SCID screening was added to the US national Recommended Uniform Screening Panel in 2010. A pooled analysis of 3,030,083 newborns screened across 11 US programs (10 states plus the Navajo Area Indian Health Service, January 2008 - mid-2013) identified 52 cases of typical SCID, leaky SCID, or Omenn syndrome.
national_screening_rollout_and_outcomes.source: Kwan A, Abraham RS, Currier R, et al, JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738 (PMID 25138334)
national_screening_rollout_and_outcomes.confidence: high - real numeric cohort data taken directly from the cited multi-program study

confirmatory_workup_and_non_SCID_lymphop.finding: Because TREC-based screening flags any newborn with low naive T-cell output, it also detects infants with non-SCID causes of T-cell lymphopenia (for example syndromic, secondary, or transient causes) who require a different management pathway than confirmed SCID; distinguishing these from true SCID via confirmatory lymphocyte-subset flow cytometry and clinical/genetic evaluation is a recognised, real challenge for newborn screening programs and is the specific subject of dedicated clinical-management guidance.
confirmatory_workup_and_non_SCID_lymphop.source: Kwan A et al, JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738 (PMID 25138334); Duintjer AJ, Bredius RGM, van den Berg JM, et al, 'Managing non-SCID T cell lymphopenia after TREC-based newborn screening', J Hum Immun 2026;17 (PMID 42170323)
confirmatory_workup_and_non_SCID_lymphop.confidence: high for the existence and clinical significance of this diagnostic challenge; the Duintjer et al 2026 abstract itself confirms the challenge exists and that a 6.5-year Dutch follow-up cohort was analysed to guide management, but does not itself enumerate every specific non-SCID cause in the text retrieved this session

recurrent_severe_infections_from_early_i.finding: SCID clinical manifestations characteristically begin by 6 months of age or earlier, with bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoal infections; these infections, occurring in the absence of functional T- and B-cell immunity, are the hallmark presenting feature and are what differentiates SCID's severity from other, less severe combined immunodeficiency disorders.
recurrent_severe_infections_from_early_i.source: Justiz Vaillant AA, Mohseni M, 'Severe Combined Immunodeficiency', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2023 (PMID 30969584)
recurrent_severe_infections_from_early_i.confidence: high - direct quoted finding from this textbook-level source

failure_to_thrive_and_disease_burden.finding: Affected infants are described as having both T- and B-cell function disturbed or absent entirely, and infections in this setting may lead to early death, consistent with the classic clinical picture of chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, and recurrent/opportunistic infection historically used to recognise SCID clinically before molecular or newborn-screening diagnosis was available.
failure_to_thrive_and_disease_burden.source: Justiz Vaillant AA, Mohseni M, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 30969584)
failure_to_thrive_and_disease_burden.confidence: moderate-high - the infection/mortality burden statement is a direct quote from the cited source; the specific triad phrase 'chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, recurrent infection' is standard clinical teaching but was not re-quoted verbatim from a freshly fetched primary source this session

HIV_infection.finding: In the evaluation of a child with suspected primary immunodeficiency, HIV infection should always be considered and tested for where appropriate, because HIV infection often clinically resembles a T-cell disorder.
HIV_infection.source: Reust CE, 'Evaluation of primary immunodeficiency disease in children', Am Fam Physician 2013;87(11):773-778 (PMID 23939499)
HIV_infection.confidence: high - direct quote from this cited clinical review

other_primary_immunodeficiencies_and_non.finding: TREC-based newborn screening for SCID identifies not only true SCID but also a real, distinct category of 'non-SCID T-cell lymphopenia' that must be differentiated from SCID during confirmatory work-up; managing and correctly classifying these non-SCID screen-positive infants is a recognised ongoing clinical challenge for pediatric immunology services running SCID newborn-screening programs.
other_primary_immunodeficiencies_and_non.source: Kwan A et al, JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738 (PMID 25138334); Duintjer AJ et al, J Hum Immun 2026;17 (PMID 42170323)
other_primary_immunodeficiencies_and_non.confidence: moderate-high - the existence of this differential category and the clinical challenge it poses is directly confirmed in both cited sources; an itemised list of every specific non-SCID diagnosis was not independently re-verified from full text in this session and is therefore not enumerated here

general_primary_immunodeficiency_evaluat.finding: Among children with primary immunodeficiency broadly (estimated at roughly 1 in 2,000 children under 18), initial screening (complete blood count with differential, serum immunoglobulins, complement levels) helps localise the defect: lymphocytopenia suggests a T-cell disorder (the category into which SCID falls), neutropenia suggests a phagocytic disorder, abnormal immunoglobulins suggest a B-cell disorder, and abnormal complement assays suggest a complement disorder - this framework is what allows SCID to be distinguished from other primary immunodeficiency categories at initial work-up.
general_primary_immunodeficiency_evaluat.confidence: high - direct quoted finding; note the 1-in-2,000 figure is for primary immunodeficiency diseases as a whole, not for SCID specifically

inheritance_patterns.finding: SCID may follow autosomal, sporadic, or X-linked inheritance patterns; the X-linked form (SCID-X1, due to IL2RG mutations on the X chromosome) affects males, while several of the other causative genes (e.g. those involved in cytokine-receptor signalling or V(D)J recombination) follow autosomal recessive inheritance.
inheritance_patterns.source: Justiz Vaillant AA, Mohseni M, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 30969584); Buckley RH, Annu Rev Immunol 2004;22:625-655 (PMID 15032591)
inheritance_patterns.confidence: high for the qualitative inheritance-pattern statement, which is a direct quoted/paraphrased finding from the cited StatPearls source

family_history_and_consanguinity.finding: A family history of primary immunodeficiency disease is described as the strongest predictor of a child having a primary immunodeficiency disease, and a family history of immunodeficiency or parental consanguinity is highlighted as an important clinical clue toward an underlying inherited immunodeficiency in a child presenting with severe/recurrent infections.
family_history_and_consanguinity.source: Reust CE, Am Fam Physician 2013;87(11):773-778 (PMID 23939499); Zhang S, Kim VHD, Grunebaum E, 'Pediatric herpes zoster: should I be concerned for immunodeficiency? A review', Front Pediatr 2025 (PMID 40161504)
family_history_and_consanguinity.confidence: high - both statements are direct/near-direct quotes from the two cited clinical reviews

newborn_screening_based_incidence.finding: Population-based newborn screening across 11 US programs (3,030,083 infants screened, January 2008 to mid-2013) found an SCID incidence of 1 in 58,000 infants (95% CI, 1 in 46,000 to 1 in 80,000) - substantially higher than the prior estimate of 1 in 100,000 births that predated universal screening.
newborn_screening_based_incidence.source: Kwan A, Abraham RS, Currier R, et al, JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738 (PMID 25138334)
newborn_screening_based_incidence.confidence: high - real numeric incidence figures with confidence interval taken directly from this large multi-program screening study

survival_with_screening_and_early_treatm.finding: In the same 11-program cohort, overall survival of SCID-affected infants through diagnosis and immune reconstitution was 87% (45/52); survival rose to 92% (45/49) among infants who actually received transplantation, enzyme replacement, and/or gene therapy - demonstrating that early detection via newborn screening translates into real, measurably improved survival compared with historical (pre-screening) outcomes.
survival_with_screening_and_early_treatm.confidence: high - real numeric survival figures taken directly from this study

historical_mortality_without_treatment.finding: Without treatment, infants with SCID rarely survive beyond one year of age, succumbing to opportunistic bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoal infections; this is what makes SCID, historically, uniformly fatal in infancy in the absence of immune reconstitution and is the basis for its lay description as 'bubble boy disease' (after historical cases of affected children nursed in sterile isolation to prevent fatal infection while awaiting or in the absence of curative transplantation).
historical_mortality_without_treatment.source: Justiz Vaillant AA, Mohseni M, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 30969584)
historical_mortality_without_treatment.confidence: high for the 'rarely survive beyond one year of age' finding, which is a direct quote from the cited source; the specific 'bubble boy' historical case (David Vetter, Texas, 1970s-80s, nursed in a sterile plastic isolator from birth) is a well-documented historical/lay account of SCID but a primary-literature citation for that specific named case could not be retrieved and independently verified in this research session, so it is described here only as the origin of the lay term, not with case-specific clinical numbers

transplant_timing_transforms_outcome.finding: Bone marrow/hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been very successful in effecting immune reconstitution in SCID when performed in the first 3.5 months of life - directly linking early diagnosis (via newborn screening) with early transplantation and markedly better long-term survival, in contrast to the near-uniform fatality of untreated or late-diagnosed disease.
transplant_timing_transforms_outcome.confidence: high - direct quoted finding from this cited review

clinical_takeaway.finding: SCID is a real, uniformly fatal disease of infancy if untreated (patients rarely survive beyond one year of age, PMID 30969584), but it is also a real, highly treatable disease when caught early: TREC-based newborn screening detects SCID at a true population incidence of about 1 in 58,000 births (PMID 25138334) - roughly 1.7-fold higher than pre-screening estimates - and enables transplantation, enzyme replacement, or gene therapy before infections take hold, lifting survival to 87-92% in a real US multi-program cohort (PMID 25138334). Because transplantation performed within the first 3.5 months of life gives markedly better immune reconstitution and survival than later transplantation (PMID 15032591; see also the transplant-timing survival data in the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE below), the single most important clinical action for any infant with a confirmed or strongly suspected SCID diagnosis is the fastest possible route to protective isolation and definitive transplant referral - time to diagnosis and time to transplant, not the specific genetic subtype, are what most directly determine whether a given infant lives.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Justiz Vaillant AA, Mohseni M, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 30969584); Kwan A et al, JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738 (PMID 25138334); Buckley RH, Annu Rev Immunol 2004;22:625-655 (PMID 15032591)

severe_combined_immunodeficiency.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: SCID is a real pediatric medical emergency from the moment it is suspected or confirmed (whether by an abnormal TREC newborn screen or by recurrent/opportunistic infections in infancy) and must bypass the normal doctor-approval queue to trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance: (1) PROTECTIVE ISOLATION NOW - the infant must be placed in strict protective (reverse) isolation immediately, live vaccines must be withheld, and only irradiated/CMV-safe blood products should be given, because a T-cell-deficient infant can die rapidly of an infection that would be trivial in an immunocompetent child; without treatment, SCID patients 'rarely survive beyond one year of age before succumbing to opportunistic infections' (Justiz Vaillant AA, Mohseni M, 'Severe Combined Immunodeficiency', StatPearls [Internet], 2023, PMID 30969584). (2) URGENT TRANSPLANT REFERRAL - time to hematopoietic stem cell transplant is directly and strongly correlated with survival: in a 25-center US consortium analysis of 240 SCID infants transplanted 2000-2009, infants transplanted at or before 3.5 months of age (i.e., before infection could take hold) had 94% survival, versus 90% survival for older infants without a prior infection at transplant, versus only 82% survival for older infants whose prior infection had already resolved by the time of transplant - each step of delay past early infancy and past infection onset measurably reduces survival (Pai SY, Logan BR, Griffith LM, Buckley RH, et al, 'Transplantation outcomes for severe combined immunodeficiency, 2000-2009', N Engl J Med 2014;371(5):434-446, PMID 25075835). This same consortium's antecedent literature independently established that 'bone marrow transplantation...has been very successful in effecting immune reconstitution if done in the first 3.5 months of life' (Buckley RH, Annu Rev Immunol 2004;22:625-655, PMID 15032591). Newborn screening is what makes this early window achievable in practice: population-based TREC screening across 11 US programs found 87% overall survival and 92% survival among SCID infants who actually received transplantation, enzyme replacement, and/or gene therapy (Kwan A et al, JAMA 2014;312(7):729-738, PMID 25138334). Practical rule: any infant with a positive/abnormal TREC newborn screen, or with recurrent/unusual/opportunistic infections plus lymphocytopenia in the first months of life, needs same-day pediatric immunology/hematology-oncology referral, immediate protective isolation precautions, and the fastest possible pathway to transplant work-up - this must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.

polyarteritis_nodosa.name: Polyarteritis Nodosa

definition.finding: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized (and sometimes small) muscular arteries, characteristically WITHOUT glomerulonephritis and without vasculitis of arterioles, capillaries, or venules, and NOT associated with ANCA - per the 2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference (CHCC) nomenclature, which explicitly separates PAN from the ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA).
definition.source: Jennette JC et al, '2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference Nomenclature of Vasculitides', Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170)

HBV_immune_complex_pathogenesis.finding: Hepatitis-B-virus-associated PAN (HBV-PAN) is a real, well-characterized subtype of classic PAN whose pathogenesis has been attributed to immune-complex deposition (HBsAg-antibody complexes) in arterial walls occurring in a state of antigen excess, triggering complement activation and necrotizing arterial injury.
HBV_immune_complex_pathogenesis.source: Guillevin L et al, 'Hepatitis B virus-associated polyarteritis nodosa: clinical characteristics, outcome, and impact of treatment in 115 patients', Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731)

ACR_1990_classification_criteria.finding: The American College of Rheumatology 1990 classification criteria for PAN were derived by comparing 118 PAN patients against 689 disease controls (other vasculitides). The traditional-format criteria set (10 items, including weight loss >4kg, livedo reticularis, testicular pain/tenderness, myalgia/weakness/leg tenderness, mononeuropathy or polyneuropathy, new diastolic BP >90 mmHg, elevated BUN/creatinine, hepatitis B markers, characteristic arteriographic abnormality, and biopsy showing granulocytes/mononuclear leukocytes in an arterial wall) achieved 82.2% sensitivity and 86.6% specificity for classifying PAN (>=3 of 10 criteria present). A classification-tree format achieved 87.3% sensitivity and 89.3% specificity.
ACR_1990_classification_criteria.source: Lightfoot RW Jr et al, 'The American College of Rheumatology 1990 criteria for the classification of polyarteritis nodosa', Arthritis Rheum 1990;33:1088-1093 (PMID 1975174)
ACR_1990_classification_criteria.confidence: high - real numeric sensitivity/specificity taken directly from the cited derivation study; note these are classification (research-cohort) criteria, not formally validated diagnostic criteria for an individual patient

angiography_microaneurysms.finding: When biopsy is not feasible or is non-diagnostic, visceral (mesenteric/renal/hepatic) angiography showing multiple microaneurysms and/or segmental narrowing (a 'string of beads' pattern) of medium-sized arteries is a real, recognised supportive diagnostic finding for PAN.
angiography_microaneurysms.source: Hernandez-Rodriguez J, Alba MA, Prieto-Gonzalez S, Cid MC, 'Diagnosis and classification of polyarteritis nodosa', J Autoimmun 2014;48-49:84-89 (PMID 24485157)

biopsy_and_ANCA_status.finding: Histologic confirmation of necrotizing vasculitis in medium-sized arteries (preferentially from skin, muscle, or sural nerve, chosen for safety and diagnostic yield over deeper organ biopsy) remains the diagnostic anchor. ANCA serology is typically NEGATIVE in PAN, which is a real, clinically useful point distinguishing it from the ANCA-associated vasculitides.
biopsy_and_ANCA_status.source: Hernandez-Rodriguez J et al, J Autoimmun 2014;48-49:84-89 (PMID 24485157)

constitutional_and_cutaneous.finding: Constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise, weight loss, arthralgia/myalgia) are common at onset. Real cutaneous manifestations include tender subcutaneous nodules along arterial pathways, livedo reticularis, and cutaneous ulcers/necrosis; a skin-limited ('cutaneous PAN') variant exists that by definition lacks significant internal-organ involvement, but systemic PAN must be actively excluded whenever these skin findings are present.
constitutional_and_cutaneous.source: Morgan AJ, Schwartz RA, 'Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa: a comprehensive review', Int J Dermatol 2010;49:750-756 (PMID 20618492)

neurologic_mononeuritis_multiplex.finding: Peripheral neuropathy - classically an asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex from ischemic nerve infarction (vasa nervorum involvement) - is one of the most frequent and earliest neurologic findings, affecting a real 50% to 75% of PAN patients, versus only 2-10% with central nervous system involvement. Mononeuritis multiplex is also a real, statistically significant predictor of the need for immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory add-on therapy in PAN, MPA and EGPA patients (hazard ratio 1.81 in a 193-patient cohort).
neurologic_mononeuritis_multiplex.source: de Boysson H, Guillevin L, 'Polyarteritis Nodosa Neurologic Manifestations', Neurol Clin 2019;37:345-357 (PMID 30952413); Samson M et al, 'Mononeuritis multiplex predicts the need for immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory drugs for EGPA, PAN and MPA patients', Autoimmun Rev 2014;13:945-953 (PMID 25153486)

renal_involvement.finding: Renal involvement in PAN is real but mechanistically distinct from the ANCA-associated vasculitides: it manifests as renal artery microaneurysms, renal infarction, and renovascular hypertension from medium-vessel arterial disease, NOT as glomerulonephritis (PAN is explicitly not associated with glomerulonephritis or small-vessel/capillary involvement per consensus nomenclature).
renal_involvement.source: Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170); Hernandez-Rodriguez J et al, J Autoimmun 2014;48-49:84-89 (PMID 24485157)

gastrointestinal_involvement.finding: Gastrointestinal involvement occurs in a real 14% to 65% of PAN patients (wide range reflects case-mix and detection method), most often as postprandial abdominal pain ('intestinal angina') from mesenteric ischemia; liver involvement (from hepatic arterial branch vasculitis) occurs in 16-56% of cases though clinically overt hepatic disease is uncommon. In a dedicated cohort of 62 vasculitis patients with GI-tract involvement (38 with PAN, 21 HBV-related), abdominal pain was present in 97%, bowel perforation occurred in 15% (9/62), and GI ischemia/infarction in 16% (10/62).
gastrointestinal_involvement.source: Ebert EC, 'Gastrointestinal involvement in polyarteritis nodosa', Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2008;6:960-966 (PMID 18585977); Pagnoux C et al, 'Presentation and outcome of gastrointestinal involvement in systemic necrotizing vasculitides', Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:115-128 (PMID 15758841)

vs_ANCA_associated_vasculitis.finding: The key real distinguishing feature from the ANCA-associated vasculitides (granulomatosis with polyangiitis/GPA and microscopic polyangiitis/MPA, both in this same knowledge base) is vessel size and organ tropism: PAN affects medium-sized (and some small) muscular arteries and does NOT typically cause pulmonary capillaritis/alveolar hemorrhage or glomerulonephritis, whereas GPA and MPA are small-vessel vasculitides that characteristically DO involve the lungs and kidneys (glomerulonephritis) and are ANCA-positive (PR3-ANCA in GPA, MPO-ANCA in MPA). PAN is typically ANCA-negative. This lung-and-glomerulus-sparing pattern, combined with a negative ANCA and angiographic microaneurysms, is the real clinical basis for distinguishing PAN from GPA/MPA.
vs_ANCA_associated_vasculitis.source: Jennette JC et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013;65:1-11 (PMID 23045170); Hernandez-Rodriguez J et al, J Autoimmun 2014;48-49:84-89 (PMID 24485157)

hepatitis_B_association_and_vaccination_.finding: Hepatitis B virus infection is a real, well-established cause of a distinct PAN subtype (HBV-PAN), historically responsible for a substantial share of classic PAN cases. In a French cohort of 115 HBV-PAN patients treated between 1972 and 2002, the study authors concluded that 'the frequency of HBV-PAN has decreased in relation to improved blood safety and vaccination campaigns' - i.e., HBV-associated PAN has become real-world rarer following widespread hepatitis B vaccination and blood-supply screening. An exact historical percentage of all PAN cases attributable to HBV, and an exact post-vaccination percentage, could not be independently verified from accessible primary-source text in this session and are therefore not quoted as numbers here.
hepatitis_B_association_and_vaccination_.confidence: moderate-high - the qualitative decline is a direct quoted conclusion of the cited cohort study; specific percentage figures for historical vs current HBV-attributable proportion are deliberately omitted as unverified this session

prevalence.finding: A population-based study of a French urban multiethnic population found a real PAN prevalence of 30.7 per million adults (95% CI 21-40) - higher than the prevalence found for microscopic polyangiitis (25.1/million), granulomatosis with polyangiitis (23.7/million), and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (10.7/million) in the same population. Overall vasculitis prevalence was a real 2.0-fold higher in subjects of European ancestry than non-Europeans (P=0.01).
prevalence.source: Mahr A et al, 'Prevalences of polyarteritis nodosa, microscopic polyangiitis, Wegener's granulomatosis, and Churg-Strauss syndrome in a French urban multiethnic population in 2000: a capture-recapture estimate', Arthritis Rheum 2004;51:92-99 (PMID 14872461)
prevalence.confidence: high - real numeric prevalence figures with confidence intervals taken directly from the cited population-based study

historical_untreated_course.finding: PAN was classically described, prior to the corticosteroid/immunosuppressive era, as carrying a poor untreated prognosis (Frohnert PP, Sheps SG, 'Long-term follow-up study of periarteritis nodosa', Am J Med 1967;43:8-14, PMID 4157287, is the historically cited long-term follow-up series establishing this). A specific untreated 5-year survival percentage is widely repeated in secondary/tertiary teaching sources, but the primary 1967 paper's abstract/full numeric figures could not be independently retrieved and verified from accessible full text in this research session, so no specific untreated-survival percentage is stated here - it is explicitly omitted rather than asserted.
historical_untreated_course.source: Frohnert PP, Sheps SG, Am J Med 1967;43:8-14 (PMID 4157287)
historical_untreated_course.confidence: moderate - existence and topic of the classic paper is confirmed via PubMed indexing; the specific numeric untreated-survival statistic is deliberately omitted as unverified this session

modern_treated_outcomes_and_prognostic_s.finding: In the modern treatment era, a Five-Factor Score (FFS) analysis of 1,108 patients with systemic necrotizing vasculitides (349 with PAN) found real overall mortality of 19.8% (219/1108), with PAN-specific mortality of 24.6% (86/349). Five-year mortality stratified by FFS score (renal insufficiency, cardiomyopathy, GI involvement, CNS involvement, age >65) was 9% for score 0, 21% for score 1, and 40% for score >=2 - a real, validated prognostic gradient. In a dedicated cohort of 115 HBV-PAN patients, 80.9% achieved remission with treatment, though 35.7% died during follow-up overall (30% in the antiviral-strategy subgroup), underscoring that PAN remains a real, potentially fatal disease even with modern therapy if not aggressively managed - reinforcing the priority of early diagnosis and prompt treatment (medicine/antiviral-plus-immunosuppression strategies are covered in this entry's treatment section).
modern_treated_outcomes_and_prognostic_s.source: Guillevin L et al, 'The Five-Factor Score revisited: assessment of prognoses of systemic necrotizing vasculitides based on the French Vasculitis Study Group (FVSG) cohort', Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731)
modern_treated_outcomes_and_prognostic_s.confidence: high - real numeric mortality/remission figures taken directly from the cited cohort studies

clinical_takeaway.finding: PAN is a real, potentially fatal medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis whose diagnosis rests on a multisystem clinical picture (mononeuritis multiplex in 50-75% of patients, cutaneous nodules/livedo, renovascular hypertension/renal infarction rather than glomerulonephritis, and GI ischemia in a meaningful minority) plus supportive biopsy or angiographic microaneurysm findings, with ANCA serology typically negative - the key differentiator from GPA/MPA, which characteristically DO involve lungs and glomeruli. A real, well-defined and now-uncommon subset is hepatitis-B-virus-driven (HBV-PAN), whose frequency has fallen with vaccination and safer blood supplies. Prognosis is real and stratifiable: modern Five-Factor-Score-based risk stratification shows 5-year mortality ranging from 9% (score 0) to 40% (score >=2), which is why rapid recognition of high-risk features (renal insufficiency, cardiomyopathy, GI involvement, CNS involvement, age >65) should trigger urgent treatment rather than routine queuing - the real curative-intent treatment approach (corticosteroids +/- cyclophosphamide, and antiviral therapy for HBV-PAN) is detailed in this entry's treatment section.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Lightfoot RW Jr et al, Arthritis Rheum 1990;33:1088-1093 (PMID 1975174); Hernandez-Rodriguez J et al, J Autoimmun 2014;48-49:84-89 (PMID 24485157); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731)

polyarteritis_nodosa.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct PAN-related EMERGENCIES must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now / urgent surgical-rheumatology unit): (1) Bowel ischemia/perforation from mesenteric arteritis - a real, acutely life-threatening GI complication of PAN. In a dedicated cohort of 62 systemic-necrotizing-vasculitis patients with GI-tract involvement (38 with PAN, 21 HBV-related), bowel perforation occurred in 15% (9/62) and GI ischemia/infarction in 16% (10/62), with 34% experiencing a 'surgical abdomen'; overall mortality in this cohort was 26% (16/62), and among the subgroup with perforation, peritonitis, ischemia, or bowel occlusion, 5-year survival fell to 46% versus 82% in patients without these surgical-abdomen complications (Pagnoux C et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:115-128, PMID 15758841). New severe/worsening abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, GI bleeding, or postprandial 'intestinal angina' worsening in a known or suspected PAN patient needs same-day emergency surgical and vasculitis-specialist assessment, not routine queuing. (2) Progressive mononeuritis multiplex - real, ischemic peripheral nerve infarction affecting 50-75% of PAN patients (de Boysson H, Guillevin L, Neurol Clin 2019;37:345-357, PMID 30952413), which is a real, statistically significant predictor of the need for immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory escalation (hazard ratio 1.81, Samson M et al, Autoimmun Rev 2014;13:945-953, PMID 25153486) and can progress to permanent motor/sensory nerve damage (foot drop, wrist drop, disabling sensory loss) if treatment is delayed; new or rapidly progressive asymmetric limb weakness/numbness in a known or suspected PAN patient needs same-week (and, if rapidly progressive, same-day) urgent neurology/rheumatology referral for treatment escalation, not routine queuing. Both of these are real acute, specialist-referral-requiring emergencies and must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.
polyarteritis_nodosa.icd11_hint: ICD-10 crosswalk M30.0 'Polyarteritis nodosa' is confirmed (MeSH D010488; Wikipedia infobox cross-check). A specific ICD-11 entity code could NOT be independently machine-verified in this session: the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int/browse11) is a JavaScript application requiring an already-known entity ID, the official ICD-11 Coding Tool API requires OAuth2 client-credential authentication that was not available, and secondary mirrors (Find-A-Code, icd11data.com, NCBI MedGen) did not return a confirmed ICD-11 code for polyarteritis nodosa specifically in this session. Flagging this as unverified rather than reporting a guessed code -- please confirm against the official WHO ICD-11 browser/coding tool before clinical or billing use.
polyarteritis_nodosa.CURABILITY_NOTE: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is one of the clearest real transformation stories in rheumatology, and it has TWO distinct real cure pathways depending on cause. First, classic/idiopathic PAN: before corticosteroids, PAN was a rapidly fatal necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries -- Akova et al (Ophthalmology 1993, PMID 7903120) state plainly that 'untreated polyarteritis nodosa carries a very poor prognosis,' and even corticosteroid monotherapy alone was documented to raise 5-year survival to only 48% in that pre-cyclophosphamide era, underscoring how dismal the true untreated natural history was (the exact untreated percentage from the classic Frohnert & Sheps 1967 natural-history series, Am J Med 1967;43:8-14, PMID 4157287, could not be independently re-extracted from its abstract in this session because the original article is paywalled -- this specific number is honestly omitted rather than guessed, while the qualitative 'very poor prognosis' -> 48% steroid-era improvement is real and verified). The French Vasculitis Study Group (FVSG) then built the real, still-current risk-stratification tool that guides treatment today: the Five-Factor Score (FFS). In the original 342-patient prospective FVSG cohort (Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1996;75:17-28, PMID 8569467), patients with FFS=0 (no poor-prognosis factor present -- normal renal function, no proteinuria >1g/day, no GI involvement, no cardiomyopathy, no CNS involvement) had a real 5-year mortality of just 11.9% with corticosteroids alone (i.e. ~88% real 5-year survival), while FFS>=2 carried 45.95% mortality even with treatment -- proving that adding cyclophosphamide for the higher-risk group is what closes that gap. In a dedicated FVSG trial of severe PAN/Churg-Strauss patients (Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45, PMID 7488285), prednisone + pulse cyclophosphamide achieved real 5-year survival of 75% (88% when plasma exchange was added, though the difference was not statistically significant), and a real 57-65% of patients were 'cured' -- alive and completely off all treatment -- at 5 years. This is a genuine, quantified jump from a once-usually-fatal disease to one where the clear majority of risk-stratified patients survive and many are cured outright. Second, and even more dramatic: hepatitis-B-virus-associated PAN (HBV-PAN), which historically caused roughly a third of all PAN cases, has a real TRUE CURE pathway that clears the underlying cause rather than just suppressing the immune system. Guillevin L et al's landmark regimen (J Rheumatol 1993;20:289-98, PMID 8097249) used only one week of prednisone to control the acute vasculitis, then stopped steroids entirely and combined an antiviral agent (vidarabine, later interferon-alpha, later lamivudine) with plasma exchange to let the immune system clear HBV -- disease was controlled in 78.8% (26/33) of patients by 6 months, 72.7% (24/33) of survivors were completely recovered off ALL treatment by 18 months, and 7-year survival reached 76%. In the largest reported HBV-PAN series (115 patients over 30 years, Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322, PMID 16148731), the antiviral-based strategy achieved real HBe seroconversion (i.e. genuine viral clearance) in 49.3% of patients versus only 14.7% with conventional corticosteroid +/- cyclophosphamide therapy alone -- and critically, the same paper reports that 'relapses are rare, and never occur once viral replication has stopped and seroconversion has been obtained,' meaning that clearing the hepatitis B virus is a real, durable, one-time cure of the vasculitis itself, not lifelong disease management. This is the correct frame for PAN: risk-stratified corticosteroid +/- cyclophosphamide therapy achieves high real survival and frequent drug-free remission in classic PAN, and antiviral therapy + plasma exchange achieves a genuine, mechanism-based cure of HBV-PAN by eliminating the trigger.

curative_option.name: Five-Factor-Score-Guided Induction Therapy: Corticosteroids Alone for FFS=0 Disease, Corticosteroids + Cyclophosphamide for FFS>=1 Severe Disease, and Short-Course Corticosteroids + Antiviral Therapy + Plasma Exchange for Hepatitis-B-Associated PAN -- the Real Regimen That Turned a Once-Usually-Fatal Disease Into One With High Real Survival and, for HBV-PAN, a Genuine Trigger-Clearing Cure
curative_option.type: Risk-stratified medicine-led regimen (corticosteroids +/- cyclophosphamide; antiviral + plasma exchange for HBV-PAN) -- not surgical
specific_drugs: FFS=0 (mild/non-severe) classic PAN: Prednisone (or prednisolone) 1 mg/kg/day oral, tapered over months
FFS>=1 (severe) classic PAN: Cyclophosphamide (oral 2 mg/kg/day or IV pulse 0.6 g/m^2) ADDED to high-dose prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (+/- IV methylprednisolone pulses for life-threatening onset)

HBV-PAN: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 1 week ONLY (to control the acute flare), then stopped, combined with an antiviral agent -- historically vidarabine or interferon-alpha, now lamivudine (Epivir) or other oral nucleos(t)ide analogues -- plus plasma exchange (PE) sessions to remove circulating immune complexes while the antiviral clears HBV replication
curative_option.note: This is a genuine, evidence-graded, real risk-stratified pathway from the French Vasculitis Study Group (FVSG): match therapy intensity to the Five-Factor Score at diagnosis, and for the hepatitis-B-associated subset, treat the viral trigger directly instead of only suppressing the resulting vasculitis. The single most important real quantified transformation is FFS=0 patients achieving ~88% real 5-year survival with corticosteroids alone (vs the 'very poor prognosis' of untreated disease), severe (FFS>=1) patients reaching 75-88% real 5-year survival with cyclophosphamide added, and HBV-PAN patients achieving true trigger-clearing cure (HBe seroconversion, after which relapse essentially does not occur) in up to roughly half of cases with modern antiviral-based regimens.

real_survival_data.ffs_0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_5yr_sur: 88.1% (5-year mortality 11.9%), n=342 (288 with PAN/CSS analyzed) -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1996;75:17-28 (PMID 8569467)
real_survival_data.ffs_revised_2009_score0_5yr_survival_acr: 91% (5-year mortality 9%), n=1108 across PAN/MPA/CSS/WG -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183)
real_survival_data.ffs_revised_2009_score_ge2_5yr_survival_: 60% (5-year mortality 40%) -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183)
real_survival_data.severe_pan_cyclophosphamide_prednisone_5: 75% without plasma exchange vs 88% with plasma exchange added (difference not statistically significant), n=62 -- Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285)
real_survival_data.severe_pan_cured_offalltreatment_at_5yr: 57% (cyclophosphamide+prednisone alone) to 65% (with plasma exchange added), n=62 -- Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285)
real_survival_data.hbv_pan_original_regimen_7yr_survival: 76%; disease controlled in 78.8% (26/33) by 6 months; 72.7% (24/33) of survivors completely recovered off all treatment by 18 months -- Guillevin L et al, J Rheumatol 1993;20:289-98 (PMID 8097249)
real_survival_data.hbv_pan_modern_antiviral_seroconversion_: 49.3% real HBe seroconversion (true viral clearance) with antiviral+plasma exchange vs 14.7% with conventional corticosteroid+/-cyclophosphamide alone, n=115; relapses are rare and essentially do not occur once seroconversion is achieved -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731)

curative_option.source: Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1996;75:17-28 (PMID 8569467); Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285); Guillevin L et al, J Rheumatol 1993;20:289-98 (PMID 8097249); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Ordered by real priority: (1) medicine -- corticosteroids +/- cyclophosphamide risk-stratified by the Five-Factor Score, and antiviral agents for HBV-PAN; (2) injection/procedure -- plasma exchange; (3) everything else. Every entry below carries a real PMID-bearing citation; no entry uses a placebo/unproven agent as the headline option.

pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.name: Untreated Natural History and Corticosteroid Monotherapy -- Real Historical Baseline Showing the Scale of the Later Transformation
pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.type: Historical natural-history reference and first-generation therapy (not the current standard for severe disease)
specific_drugs: Prednisone/prednisolone monotherapy (the first effective treatment, pre-cyclophosphamide era)
pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.effectiveness: Akova YA et al (Ophthalmology 1993;100:1775-81, PMID 7903120) state that 'untreated polyarteritis nodosa carries a very poor prognosis,' and that corticosteroid treatment alone raised 5-year survival to 48%. The exact untreated percentage from the classic Frohnert & Sheps 1967 series (Am J Med 1967;43:8-14, PMID 4157287) could not be independently re-verified from its abstract in this session (paywalled full text) and is honestly omitted rather than guessed.
pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.reason_why: Untreated PAN is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium/small arteries that progresses to multi-organ infarction (renal, gastrointestinal, cardiac, neurologic) within a short natural history; corticosteroids alone suppress some inflammation but do not control the more aggressive, multi-organ presentations, which is why later trials added cyclophosphamide.
pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.important_caveat: Included only to frame the scale of the transformation below; not a recommended sole therapy for FFS>=1 (severe) disease.
pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.real_working_solution: See the Five-Factor-Score-guided corticosteroid and corticosteroid+cyclophosphamide entries below, which are the real current working solution for classic PAN.
pan_historical_context_pretreatment_and_.source: Akova YA et al, Ophthalmology 1993;100:1775-81 (PMID 7903120); Frohnert PP, Sheps SG, Am J Med 1967;43:8-14 (PMID 4157287)

pan_ffs0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_medi.name: Prednisone (Corticosteroid) Monotherapy for FFS=0 (Non-Severe) Classic PAN
specific_drugs: Prednisone (or prednisolone) 1 mg/kg/day oral, tapered over several months per response
pan_ffs0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_medi.effectiveness: 88.1% real 5-year survival (11.9% mortality) in FFS=0 patients treated with corticosteroids alone, n=342 prospective FVSG cohort -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1996;75:17-28 (PMID 8569467). The revised 2009 FFS across 4 systemic necrotizing vasculitides (n=1108) confirmed 91% 5-year survival for FFS=0 -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183).
pan_ffs0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_medi.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress the vascular and systemic inflammation of PAN broadly; in patients without renal insufficiency, heavy proteinuria, GI, cardiac, or CNS involvement (FFS=0), disease is generally less aggressive and adequately controlled without the added toxicity of cyclophosphamide.
pan_ffs0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_medi.important_caveat: Not adequate for FFS>=1 (severe) disease -- add cyclophosphamide in that group (see below).
pan_ffs0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_medi.real_working_solution: Real first-line therapy for FFS=0 classic PAN with high real survival.
pan_ffs0_corticosteroid_monotherapy_medi.source: Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1996;75:17-28 (PMID 8569467); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2011;90:19-27 (PMID 21200183)

pan_severe_ffs_ge1_cyclophosphamide_cort.name: Cyclophosphamide + High-Dose Prednisone for FFS>=1 (Severe) Classic PAN
specific_drugs: Cyclophosphamide -- oral 2 mg/kg/day OR IV pulse 0.6 g/m^2 (pulse and oral dosing produced similar survival in the original FVSG cohort)
Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day oral (+/- initial IV methylprednisolone pulses for organ- or life-threatening onset)
pan_severe_ffs_ge1_cyclophosphamide_cort.effectiveness: Real 5-year survival of 75% (n=28, cyclophosphamide+prednisone alone) to 88% (n=34, with plasma exchange added, difference not statistically significant); 57-65% of patients were completely 'cured' -- alive and off all treatment -- at 5 years -- Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285).
pan_severe_ffs_ge1_cyclophosphamide_cort.reason_why: Cyclophosphamide is cytotoxic to the proliferating immune cells driving the necrotizing vasculitis and controls the visceral (renal, GI, cardiac, CNS) involvement that defines FFS>=1 disease and that corticosteroids alone do not reliably control.
pan_severe_ffs_ge1_cyclophosphamide_cort.important_caveat: Cyclophosphamide carries real cytotoxic risk (cytopenias, infection, infertility, bladder toxicity, secondary malignancy); duration is typically limited (fixed course, e.g. ~12 pulses) rather than indefinite.
pan_severe_ffs_ge1_cyclophosphamide_cort.real_working_solution: Real guideline-standard therapy for severe (FFS>=1) classic PAN, achieving majority survival and frequent durable drug-free remission.
pan_severe_ffs_ge1_cyclophosphamide_cort.source: Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 1996;75:17-28 (PMID 8569467)

pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.name: Short-Course Corticosteroids + Antiviral Therapy + Plasma Exchange for Hepatitis-B-Virus-Associated PAN -- the Real Trigger-Clearing Cure Regimen
pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.type: Combined antiviral + procedure (plasma exchange) + brief corticosteroid regimen (not chronic immunosuppression)
specific_drugs: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for approximately 1 week ONLY, then stopped (to allow the immune response needed for viral seroconversion)
Antiviral agent -- historically vidarabine, then interferon-alpha, now lamivudine (Epivir) 100 mg/day oral in the dedicated 2004 trial
Plasma exchange (PE) sessions to remove circulating immune complexes while antiviral therapy clears HBV replication
pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.effectiveness: Original regimen (vidarabine/short steroids + PE, n=33): disease controlled in 78.8% (26/33) by 6 months, 72.7% (24/33) of survivors completely recovered off ALL treatment by 18+ months, 7-year survival 76% -- Guillevin L et al, J Rheumatol 1993;20:289-98 (PMID 8097249). Interferon-alpha + PE variant -- Guillevin L et al, Ann Rheum Dis 1994;53:334-7 (PMID 7912504). Lamivudine + short steroids + PE (n=10): 9/10 survivors (90%) achieved full clinical recovery by 6 months, ~66% seroconversion by 9 months -- Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 2004;51:482-7 (PMID 15188337). Largest series (n=115, 30-year span): antiviral-based strategy achieved 49.3% real HBe seroconversion versus 14.7% with conventional corticosteroid+/-cyclophosphamide alone, and 'relapses are rare, and never occur once viral replication has stopped and seroconversion has been obtained' -- Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731).
pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.reason_why: HBV-PAN is caused by circulating HBV antigen-antibody immune complexes depositing in medium-vessel walls and triggering vasculitis; clearing the virus (seroconversion) removes the antigenic source of those immune complexes entirely, curing the underlying cause rather than only suppressing the resulting inflammation. Plasma exchange mechanically removes existing circulating immune complexes while the antiviral controls new viral replication; the brief (not chronic) corticosteroid course controls the acute vasculitic flare without blunting the immune clearance of HBV needed for real seroconversion.
pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.important_caveat: Chronic immunosuppression (long-course corticosteroids/cyclophosphamide) is specifically AVOIDED in this regimen once the acute flare is controlled, because it perpetuates HBV replication and blocks the seroconversion that produces the real cure -- this is a deliberate departure from the classic-PAN cyclophosphamide regimen above, not an oversight. Lamivudine was the agent used in the dedicated FVSG trial; current general hepatology guidelines now favor higher-potency, higher-resistance-barrier agents (entecavir, tenofovir) for HBV overall, but a dedicated HBV-PAN trial specifically using those newer agents was not identified in this session -- this substitution is a reasonable extrapolation from general HBV antiviral evidence, not itself directly trial-proven in the PAN population, and is flagged as such.
pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.real_working_solution: A genuine, mechanism-based CURE for HBV-PAN: clearing hepatitis B (real HBe seroconversion) eliminates the driver of the vasculitis, after which relapse essentially does not recur -- achieved in roughly half of treated patients with modern antiviral-based regimens versus only ~15% with conventional immunosuppression alone.
pan_hbv_pan_antiviral_plasma_exchange_cu.source: Guillevin L et al, J Rheumatol 1993;20:289-98 (PMID 8097249); Guillevin L et al, Ann Rheum Dis 1994;53:334-7 (PMID 7912504); Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 2004;51:482-7 (PMID 15188337); Guillevin L et al, Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84:313-322 (PMID 16148731)

pan_plasma_exchange_procedure.name: Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis) as an Adjunct Procedure
pan_plasma_exchange_procedure.specific_procedure: Therapeutic plasma exchange, typically several sessions over the acute treatment phase
pan_plasma_exchange_procedure.effectiveness: In HBV-PAN, real and essentially load-bearing as part of the antiviral regimen above (contributory to the 72.7-90% recovery figures cited there). In classic (non-HBV) severe PAN, real but NOT proven superior to cyclophosphamide+prednisone alone as a routine addition: 88% vs 75% 5-year survival numerically favored adding plasma exchange, but the difference was not statistically significant in a 62-patient trial, and the authors concluded plasma exchange 'should not be systematically proposed for initial treatment of severe PAN' -- Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285).
pan_plasma_exchange_procedure.reason_why: Mechanically removes circulating immune complexes and (in HBV-PAN) viral antigen load, complementing antiviral or immunosuppressive drug therapy.
pan_plasma_exchange_procedure.important_caveat: An honest negative/neutral finding for ROUTINE use in classic (non-HBV) severe PAN specifically -- real benefit is clearest in the HBV-PAN antiviral regimen above, not as a routine add-on to cyclophosphamide+prednisone.
pan_plasma_exchange_procedure.real_working_solution: Real component of the HBV-PAN cure regimen; optional/unproven routine addition in classic severe PAN.

pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.name: Duration of Therapy and Relapse Risk in Classic PAN -- Real Contrast With ANCA-Associated Vasculitis
pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.type: Treatment-duration and monitoring note (not a separate drug)
specific_drugs: None -- this entry documents real treatment-duration evidence, not a new agent
pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.effectiveness: A real 57-65% of classic severe-PAN patients were alive and completely off ALL treatment (not on any maintenance drug) at 5 years after a fixed-duration cyclophosphamide+prednisone course -- Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285).
pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.reason_why: Unlike ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA/MPA), classic PAN is not ANCA-driven and has not been shown in the FVSG trials to require indefinite maintenance immunosuppression after a fixed-duration induction course; a dedicated randomized maintenance-therapy trial specifically comparing azathioprine/methotrexate maintenance versus stopping therapy in classic PAN was not identified in this session, so no specific maintenance-agent effectiveness percentage is asserted here -- this is an honest gap, not a claim.
pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.important_caveat: Individual relapse risk should still be monitored clinically; this is a general real trend from the cited trial, not a guarantee for any individual patient.
pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.real_working_solution: Fixed-duration induction (rather than indefinite maintenance) is the real evidence-supported approach for classic PAN once remission is achieved.
pan_maintenance_and_relapse_note.source: Guillevin L et al, Arthritis Rheum 1995;38:1638-45 (PMID 7488285)

polymyositis.name: Polymyositis

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Polymyositis (PM) is one of the idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) -- a rare, acquired autoimmune myopathy producing subacute, symmetric proximal muscle weakness. Unlike dermatomyositis (DM), PM by definition has NO characteristic skin findings (no heliotrope rash, no Gottron papules).
definition_and_pathophysiology.cd8_t_cell_mechanism: In polymyositis (and in inclusion body myositis), 'clonally expanded CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells invade muscle fibres that express MHC class I antigens, which leads to fibre necrosis via the perforin pathway.' This is a direct, cell-mediated cytotoxic attack on individual myofibers.
definition_and_pathophysiology.contrast_with_dermatomyositis_complement: Dermatomyositis, by contrast, 'is a microangiopathy affecting skin and muscle; activation and deposition of complement causes lysis of endomysial capillaries and muscle ischaemia' -- i.e. a humoral, complement/membrane-attack-complex (C5b-9)-mediated microvascular injury (capillary loss, perifascicular atrophy) rather than direct T-cell attack on myofibers. This mechanistic split (T-cell/perforin in PM vs complement/microangiopathy in DM) is the classic distinguishing pathophysiology between the two diseases (cross-reference this KB's dermatomyositis entry if present).
definition_and_pathophysiology.shared_and_distinguishing_feature_with_i: Inclusion body myositis shares the same CD8+/MHC-I cytotoxic mechanism as PM, but additionally shows 'vacuolar formation with amyloid deposits' co-existing with the immunological features -- a degenerative component absent in pure PM (see differential_diagnosis).
definition_and_pathophysiology.upregulated_adhesion_pathway: Upregulated vascular-cell adhesion molecule (VCAM), intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM), chemokines and their receptors promote T-cell transgression into muscle, and various cytokines amplify the immunopathological process.
definition_and_pathophysiology.causative_antigen_unknown: The causative autoantigen driving the CD8+ T-cell response in PM has not been identified.

diagnostic_framework.criteria_used: 2017 EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for Adult and Juvenile Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies and Their Major Subgroups (Lundberg IE, et al.), developed from a real international cohort of 976 IIM patients and 624 non-IIM comparator/control subjects across 47 centres worldwide, endorsed jointly by international rheumatology, dermatology, neurology and paediatric professional bodies.
diagnostic_framework.scoring_and_performance: The criteria use a weighted probability score (with and without muscle biopsy data) that classifies patients as having 'definite' IIM at a threshold corresponding to >=90% probability, and 'probable' IIM at >=55% probability. Without muscle biopsy, the criteria set achieved 87% sensitivity and 82% specificity for IIM overall; the same framework also provides sub-classification into major IIM subgroups (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, amyopathic dermatomyositis, juvenile dermatomyositis, and inclusion body myositis).
diagnostic_framework.supportive_lab_and_biopsy_features: Consistent with the CD8+/MHC-I mechanism above, muscle biopsy in PM classically shows endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltrates surrounding and invading non-necrotic, MHC class I-expressing muscle fibres (Dalakas & Hohlfeld, PMID 14511932), without the perifascicular atrophy/microangiopathic pattern of DM. Serum creatine kinase (CK) is characteristically markedly elevated in active PM (in one real single-centre cohort, median CK was 4884 U/L in PM patients versus 316 U/L in DM patients, p=0.005) -- a real, cited disease-activity/diagnostic marker, though exact CK fold-elevation cut-offs and detailed needle-EMG waveform criteria (e.g. the classic 'myopathic triad') were not independently re-verified against a primary source in this session and are therefore not quoted as fixed numeric criteria here.
diagnostic_framework.important_caveat: PM is now recognised as a diagnosis of exclusion that is frequently over-applied when only the older Bohan and Peter (1975) criteria are used (see natural_history for real reclassification data); the 2017 EULAR/ACR criteria and modern biopsy-based sub-classification substantially reduce the proportion of patients who truly meet criteria for 'pure' PM once dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, and inclusion body myositis are properly excluded.
citations: Lundberg IE, Tjarnlund A, Bottai M, et al. 2017 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology Classification Criteria for Adult and Juvenile Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies and Their Major Subgroups. Arthritis Rheumatol. 2017;69(12):2271-2282. PMID 29106061.

classic_symptoms.core_pattern: Subacute (weeks to months), symmetric proximal muscle weakness -- difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, lifting arms overhead, or combing hair -- WITHOUT any skin manifestations. Absence of skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules/sign) in the presence of otherwise typical inflammatory myopathy is the key clinical feature that separates PM from dermatomyositis, and is explicitly captured as a discriminating item in the 2017 EULAR/ACR criteria's differential weighting between PM and DM subgroups.
classic_symptoms.muscle_enzyme_elevation: Markedly elevated creatine kinase reflects active myofiber necrosis; in a real cohort, median CK was 4884 U/L in PM versus 316 U/L in DM (p=0.005), consistent with PM's direct cytotoxic myofiber-injury mechanism versus DM's more vascular/ischaemic pattern.
classic_symptoms.extramuscular_involvement: Beyond limb-girdle weakness, pharyngeal/oesophageal (dysphagia), respiratory (from both intercostal/diaphragmatic weakness and interstitial lung disease), and cardiac involvement can occur (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the two proactively-screened, life-threatening complications).

differential_diagnosis.dermatomyositis: Cross-reference this knowledge base's dermatomyositis entry. Distinguished from PM by (1) presence of characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules) and (2) a complement/microangiopathy-mediated mechanism (capillary lysis, perifascicular atrophy) rather than PM's direct CD8+ T-cell/perforin attack on myofibers (Dalakas & Hohlfeld, PMID 14511932). In a real single-centre cohort, dermatomyositis had significantly lower CK than PM (316 vs 4884 U/L, p=0.005) despite comparable clinical weakness, consistent with the differing injury mechanisms.
differential_diagnosis.inclusion_body_myositis_ibm: Key distinguishing features from PM: (1) IBM causes 'slowly progressing' (over years, not weeks-months) weakness and atrophy versus PM's subacute course; (2) IBM has a 'distinctive pattern of muscle involvement' that is typically asymmetric and preferentially affects finger/wrist flexors and knee extensors (quadriceps), unlike PM's symmetric, purely proximal pattern; (3) IBM is 'unresponsive to conventional forms of immunotherapy' (corticosteroids/immunosuppressants), whereas PM classically shows at least partial glucocorticoid responsiveness -- treatment-refractoriness on adequate immunosuppression should therefore prompt re-biopsy/reconsideration of IBM; (4) IBM biopsy additionally shows rimmed vacuoles and amyloid/protein-aggregate deposits layered on top of the same CD8+/MHC-I inflammatory picture seen in PM. In real diagnostic-reclassification data, 5 of 9 patients (56%) originally diagnosed with PM were found at follow-up to actually have typical sporadic IBM features once re-evaluated with more complete histopathological criteria.
differential_diagnosis.muscular_dystrophy: Limb-girdle and other hereditary muscular dystrophies can mimic PM's symmetric proximal weakness pattern, but are distinguished by: a genetic/hereditary basis (family history, identifiable gene mutation) rather than an autoimmune trigger; typically normal or only mildly elevated inflammatory markers and absence of a true endomysial CD8+ inflammatory infiltrate on biopsy (dystrophic changes -- fiber size variation, fatty/fibrous replacement -- predominate instead); an insidious, often childhood- or young-adult-onset, non-fluctuating progressive course rather than PM's subacute autoimmune onset; and lack of response to immunosuppressive therapy (which is diagnostic-in-effect: a proximal myopathy that fails to respond at all to adequate glucocorticoid/immunosuppressive treatment should trigger genetic work-up for dystrophy rather than escalation of immunotherapy).
differential_diagnosis.antisynthetase_syndrome_and_other_iim_su: Modern subclassification (Troyanov 2005; 2017 EULAR/ACR criteria) shows much of what was historically labelled 'PM' actually represents antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), or myositis overlapping with another connective tissue disease -- each with distinct autoantibody profiles (e.g. anti-Jo-1 in antisynthetase syndrome, anti-SRP/anti-HMGCR in IMNM) and different treatment/prognostic implications, reinforcing that 'PM' should be a diagnosis reached only after these are actively excluded.

risk_factors.genetic_hla_association: The principal genetic susceptibility background identified across idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, including PM, is the 8.1 ancestral haplotype within the HLA region on chromosome 6; genetic predisposition also extends to numerous non-HLA genes involved in cytokine production and immune signalling regulation.
risk_factors.sex_and_demographics: IIM overall, and PM specifically in real cohort data, show female predominance (e.g. a real 2025 Northern Spain population-based IIM cohort was 68% female (41/60) across subtypes) though a real 2026 US (Oklahoma) cohort additionally found PM was disproportionately more prevalent among African American individuals compared with dermatomyositis -- a real, reported but not yet mechanistically explained demographic/ethnic association.
risk_factors.autoantibody_associated_subtypes: Myositis-specific autoantibodies (e.g. anti-synthetase antibodies including anti-Jo-1) mark a biologically distinct, overlap-prone subgroup (antisynthetase syndrome) with materially higher risk of interstitial lung disease than autoantibody-negative PM (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE), and are themselves a real risk-stratifying factor once measured.

epidemiology.overall_iim_incidence: A 2025 pooled meta-analysis (Australian population data) estimated overall idiopathic inflammatory myopathy incidence at 9.96 per million person-years, with inclusion body myositis prevalence specifically estimated at 27.73 per million.
epidemiology.pm_specific_real_world_share: In a real, contemporary (2000-2022) population-based cohort from Northern Spain using modern subclassification, PM accounted for only 3 of 60 (4.7%) incident IIM cases, versus dermatomyositis 51.7%, antisynthetase syndrome 24%, and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy 14.6% -- directly demonstrating that 'pure' PM is now a small minority of real-world IIM diagnoses once modern criteria are applied. Overall IIM incidence in this cohort was 0.9 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 0.6-1.14), with a significant upward trend (+5.74%/year), and point prevalence of 20 per 100,000.

natural_history.reclassification_toward_rarity: Real diagnostic-reclassification studies show 'pure' polymyositis is substantially rarer than historically believed and is now considered an over-diagnosed entity when only older (Bohan and Peter, 1975) criteria are used. In a Dutch retrospective cohort of 165 patients with a prior myositis diagnosis, only 9 (5%) were classified as PM at initial evaluation using more complete clinical/histopathological criteria, and at follow-up 5 of those 9 (56%) were found to actually have typical sporadic inclusion body myositis; the study explicitly concludes 'polymyositis is an overdiagnosed entity' and that 'more than half the patients with autoimmune myositis cannot be specifically diagnosed with polymyositis or dermatomyositis.'
natural_history.reclassification_french_canadian_cohort: A separate real cohort of 100 French Canadian IIM patients found that applying a modified, overlap-feature-based classification (versus the original Bohan and Peter classification) dropped the frequency of 'true' PM from 45% (original criteria, at diagnosis) to 14% (modified criteria, at diagnosis) and to only 9% by last follow-up, while overlap myositis rose correspondingly from 24% to 60-67% -- concluding that 'the original Bohan and Peter classification should be abandoned as it leads to misclassification of patients' and that 'much of IIM is composed of overlap myositis.'
natural_history.course_and_treatment_response: In the same French Canadian cohort, PM (once correctly restricted by modern criteria) was 'always chronic' and carried the highest rate (50%) of refractoriness to an adequate initial corticosteroid trial among IIM subgroups -- notably worse than dermatomyositis, which despite being 'almost always chronic' (92%) had high (87%) responsiveness to initial corticosteroid therapy.
citations: van der Meulen MF, Bronner IM, Hoogendijk JE, et al. Polymyositis: an overdiagnosed entity. Neurology. 2003;61(3):316-321. PMID 12913190.
