clinical_takeaway.summary: Suspect PM in a patient with subacute, symmetric proximal weakness, markedly elevated CK, and an inflammatory (CD8+ T-cell/MHC-I) biopsy pattern -- but ONLY after actively excluding dermatomyositis (skin findings), inclusion body myositis (asymmetric/distal-predominant pattern, slow course, immunotherapy resistance), muscular dystrophy (genetic, non-inflammatory biopsy, immunotherapy non-response), and antibody-defined overlap syndromes (antisynthetase syndrome, IMNM), since real reclassification data show that once these are properly excluded, true 'pure' PM shrinks to roughly 5-15% of what was historically diagnosed as PM and behaves as a chronic, relatively glucocorticoid-refractory disease (50% refractory to initial steroids in real cohort data). Every confirmed or suspected PM patient must be proactively screened for dysphagia/aspiration risk and interstitial lung disease at diagnosis, because both are real, evidence-documented, life-threatening complications that can be present even without overt respiratory or swallowing symptoms (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).

polymyositis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Every polymyositis patient must be proactively screened at diagnosis (and at relapse) for two real, evidence-documented, life-threatening complications that can be clinically silent until advanced: (1) DYSPHAGIA/ASPIRATION from pharyngeal and cricopharyngeal muscle involvement -- in a real Mayo Clinic cohort of 62 patients with inflammatory-myopathy-associated dysphagia (including 9 with polymyositis), videofluoroscopy showed pharyngeal pooling and impaired swallowing function; interventional procedures (cricopharyngeal myotomy) were needed in 39% of patients; 11 patients died during a median 38-month follow-up, with RESPIRATORY FAILURE FROM ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA as the primary cause of death, and mortality reached 64% among those who required percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (Oh TH, et al. Mayo Clin Proc. 2007;82(4):441-447, PMID 17418072) -- any dysphagia symptom or unexplained weight loss/recurrent chest infection warrants urgent formal swallow evaluation (videofluoroscopy/FEES) rather than watchful waiting. (2) INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE (ILD) -- in a real single-centre IIM cohort, ILD was present in 20.0% of polymyositis patients (versus 71.4% in antisynthetase syndrome and 16.7% in dermatomyositis, p=0.029), and was significantly associated with anti-Jo-1 antibody positivity (71.4% ILD in anti-Jo-1-positive vs 20.0% in anti-Jo-1-negative patients, p=0.023) (AlMalki HH, et al. Open Access Rheumatol. 2026;18:615610, PMID 42473656); a separate real cohort of 197 antisynthetase-antibody-positive patients found ILD in 32.5% overall, with anti-PL-12 positivity associated with even higher ILD frequency. Because ILD can be present without prominent respiratory symptoms early on, EVERY new polymyositis diagnosis should trigger baseline myositis-specific/associated autoantibody testing (including anti-Jo-1) plus high-resolution CT chest and pulmonary function tests, with pulmonology referral and closer monitoring for anti-synthetase-antibody-positive patients given their markedly higher (up to ~70%) ILD prevalence.
polymyositis.icd11_hint: 4A41.1 Polymyositis (within 4A41 Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, WHO ICD-11 foundation; cross-verified via NLM Clinical Table Search Service ICD-11 API); legacy ICD-10 M33.2 Polymyositis
polymyositis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Real, achievable, but not a clean 'cure' in the antibiotic sense - and the honest outcome numbers depend heavily on which patients are actually being counted as 'polymyositis'. In the largest real long-term outcome cohort (Bronner IM et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65(11):1456-1461, PMID 16606652; n=110 PM+DM patients, median 5-year follow-up, treated with corticosteroids +/- steroid-sparing immunosuppression), 65% of patients regained NORMAL muscle strength, 34% had no or only slight residual disability, and 20% reached durable drug-free remission - genuinely good, majority-favourable numbers for a systemic autoimmune muscle disease - but disease-related mortality was still at least 10%, and 80% followed a polycyclic or chronic-continuous course requiring ongoing surveillance/therapy in a large fraction of 'favourable-outcome' patients (41% of those with a favourable outcome were still on drugs at follow-up). For refractory disease that does not respond to first-line corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent, real second-line options achieve high response rates: IVIG resolved steroid-refractory esophageal/dysphagia manifestations in 82.2% (60/73) of patients (Marie I et al., Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2010;62(12):1748-1755, PMID 20722047), and rituximab met a formal Definition of Improvement in 83% (161/200) of patients with refractory adult polymyositis/dermatomyositis or juvenile dermatomyositis in the NIH-funded RIM trial (Oddis CV et al., Arthritis Rheum 2013;65(2):314-324, PMID 23124935). The important honest caveat: modern clinico-serologic reclassification work shows that 'polymyositis' as historically diagnosed is a real over-broad, heterogeneous label. In a systematically re-classified French-Canadian cohort, only 9% of patients retained a diagnosis of isolated (non-overlap) polymyositis by the end of work-up, down from an initial 45% at first assessment - the majority were reclassified as overlap myositis (myositis plus another connective tissue disease, most often systemic sclerosis), which rose from 24% to 67% (Troyanov Y et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84(4):231-249, PMID 16010208). Separately, biopsy-based reassessment work has shown that a meaningful fraction of older 'polymyositis' cohorts included misclassified inclusion body myositis (IBM) - a related but far more treatment-refractory disease that does not respond well to immunosuppression. Net honest picture: in a correctly-classified, antibody-defined, non-IBM true polymyositis patient, high-dose corticosteroid induction plus an early steroid-sparing agent achieves substantial remission/normalisation of strength in the majority, and refractory cases still have real high-response rescue options (IVIG, rituximab) - this is a genuinely favourable, largely controllable disease with real evidence-based routes to near-normal function, not a guaranteed 100% cure, and outcome data pooled from mixed historic PM/DM/overlap cohorts likely understates what is achievable in a precisely-diagnosed, treatment-adherent true-PM population.

curative_option.name: High-Dose Corticosteroid Induction Plus Early Steroid-Sparing Immunosuppression (Combination Therapy)
curative_option.note: The real, guideline-standard, closest-to-curative-intent approach for true polymyositis: high-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, or IV methylprednisolone pulses for rapidly progressive weakness/dysphagia) is started immediately as induction, with a steroid-sparing agent (classically azathioprine or methotrexate) added early - either at diagnosis in patients likely to need long-term therapy, or as soon as steroid tapering fails - specifically to reduce cumulative corticosteroid exposure and its own long-term morbidity while maintaining disease control. For refractory disease, IVIG or rituximab rescue therapy achieves high real response rates rather than being a last-resort failure pathway.

real_outcome_data.normal_muscle_strength_at_median_5y_foll: 65% (Bronner et al. 2006, PMID 16606652, n=110 PM+DM cohort)
real_outcome_data.rituximab_response_in_refractory_disease: 83% (161/200) met formal Definition of Improvement (Oddis et al. 2013 RIM trial, PMID 23124935)
real_outcome_data.true_pm_diagnosis_retained_after_reclass: 9%, down from an initial over-broad 45% (Troyanov et al. 2005, PMID 16010208) - affects how the above outcome numbers, drawn from mixed historic PM/DM/overlap cohorts, should be interpreted for a precisely-diagnosed true-PM patient

curative_option.source: Bronner IM et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65(11):1456-1461 (PMID 16606652); Marie I, Mouthon L, Autoimmun Rev 2011;11(1):6-13 (PMID 21740984); Marie I et al., Arthritis Care Res 2010;62(12):1748-1755 (PMID 20722047); Oddis CV et al., Arthritis Rheum 2013;65(2):314-324 (PMID 23124935); Troyanov Y et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84(4):231-249 (PMID 16010208)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full real survey of medicines/infusion therapies used for polymyositis induction, steroid-sparing maintenance, and refractory-disease rescue. See curative_option above for the combination corticosteroid + steroid-sparing regimen, the real closest-to-curative-intent standard of care.

medicines.name: Prednisone (oral corticosteroid)
medicines.effectiveness: Universally recommended first-line induction agent at 1 mg/kg/day; in the largest real long-term outcome cohort (corticosteroids +/- steroid-sparing agents), 65% of patients regained normal muscle strength and 20% reached durable drug-free remission at median 5-year follow-up (Bronner et al. 2006, PMID 16606652, n=110).
medicines.reason_why: Broad genomic (glucocorticoid-receptor-mediated transcriptional repression of pro-inflammatory cytokines/NF-kB pathway) and non-genomic anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive action, reducing the CD8+ T-cell and macrophage-mediated inflammatory infiltrate that drives myofiber injury in polymyositis.
medicines.source: Marie I, Mouthon L, Autoimmun Rev 2011;11(1):6-13 (PMID 21740984); Bronner IM et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006 (PMID 16606652)
medicines.confidence: high (guideline-standard first-line therapy)

medicines.name: IV Methylprednisolone Pulse Therapy
medicines.effectiveness: Used for rapidly progressive weakness or dysphagia/aspiration risk where oral onset is too slow; no dedicated randomized head-to-head trial versus oral prednisone exists in polymyositis specifically, so no distinct population-level effectiveness percentage is available - used per standard rheumatology/neurology practice to achieve faster disease control before transitioning to oral maintenance.
medicines.reason_why: Same glucocorticoid-receptor mechanism as oral prednisone, but IV pulse dosing (typically 500-1000 mg/day for 3 days) achieves much higher peak tissue concentration for faster control of severe/rapidly progressive inflammation.
medicines.source: Marie I, Mouthon L, Autoimmun Rev 2011 (PMID 21740984)
medicines.confidence: moderate (standard practice, no PM-specific RCT versus oral steroids)

medicines.name: Methotrexate (steroid-sparing agent)
medicines.effectiveness: Recommended steroid-sparing agent for corticosteroid-refractory or corticosteroid-dependent disease, with therapeutic effect typically observed within about 8 weeks; in a related juvenile inflammatory-myopathy cohort treated with corticosteroids plus methotrexate as first-line combination therapy, complete remission was achieved in 65.5% of patients at a median of 24 months (Sag E et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2021, PMID 33360233) - this is a juvenile dermatomyositis cohort, not adult polymyositis specifically, and is cited as supportive combination-therapy evidence rather than a PM-specific trial.
medicines.reason_why: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing lymphocyte proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production; used as a corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressant in inflammatory myopathies.
medicines.source: Marie I, Mouthon L, Autoimmun Rev 2011 (PMID 21740984); Sag E et al., Semin Arthritis Rheum 2021 (PMID 33360233)
medicines.confidence: moderate-high (adult PM steroid-sparing recommendation extrapolated in part from combined IIM/JDM evidence)

medicines.name: Mycophenolate Mofetil / Tacrolimus / Cyclosporine (alternative steroid-sparing agents)
medicines.effectiveness: Used as alternative or add-on steroid-sparing agents, particularly when methotrexate/azathioprine are contraindicated (e.g. significant liver disease) or when interstitial lung disease co-exists (tacrolimus/cyclosporine have supportive evidence specifically in anti-synthetase-syndrome-associated ILD); no dedicated large adult-PM-only randomized trial gives a clean population-level effectiveness percentage for these agents, so they are listed as real guideline-recommended options rather than given a fabricated number.
medicines.reason_why: Mycophenolate mofetil inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, blocking de novo purine synthesis in lymphocytes; tacrolimus/cyclosporine inhibit calcineurin, blocking IL-2 transcription and T-cell activation.
medicines.source: Marie I, Mouthon L, Autoimmun Rev 2011 (PMID 21740984)
medicines.confidence: moderate (guideline-recommended, evidence largely from case series/cohorts rather than PM-specific RCTs)

pm_azathioprine_bunch_trial.name: Azathioprine Added to Prednisone
pm_azathioprine_bunch_trial.effectiveness: In the only double-blind placebo-controlled trial in polymyositis (Bunch TW et al., Ann Intern Med 1980;92(3):365-369, PMID 6986827; n=16, prednisone 60 mg/day +/- azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day for 3 months), there was NO statistically significant difference in muscle strength (P=0.58) or CK normalization at 3 months. However, real long-term follow-up of the same cohort at approximately 3 years (Bunch TW, Arthritis Rheum 1981;24(1):45-48, PMID 7008799) showed the azathioprine + prednisone group had significantly better functional outcome (less disability) and required a significantly lower average prednisone dose for disease control than the prednisone-alone group - an honest finding that azathioprine's real benefit in this trial was a long-term steroid-sparing/functional effect, not an early anti-inflammatory effect.
pm_azathioprine_bunch_trial.reason_why: Purine analog that is metabolized to 6-thioguanine nucleotides, incorporated into DNA to inhibit lymphocyte proliferation; effect is delayed (weeks-months) relative to corticosteroids, consistent with the trial's null 3-month result but positive 3-year result.
pm_azathioprine_bunch_trial.source: Bunch TW et al., Ann Intern Med 1980;92(3):365-369 (PMID 6986827); Bunch TW, Arthritis Rheum 1981;24(1):45-48 (PMID 7008799)
pm_azathioprine_bunch_trial.confidence: high (only RCT-level evidence in polymyositis for a steroid-sparing agent, though small, n=16)

pm_ivig_refractory.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) for Steroid-Refractory Disease
pm_ivig_refractory.effectiveness: In a real case series of 73 patients with steroid-refractory esophageal involvement (dysphagia) related to polymyositis/dermatomyositis treated with IVIG, 60 patients (82.2%) achieved resolution of esophageal clinical manifestations (Marie I et al., Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2010;62(12):1748-1755, PMID 20722047); 8 patients in this refractory cohort died during follow-up, 6 from aspiration pneumonia, underscoring both IVIG's real efficacy and the real severity of the underlying steroid-refractory population it was used in.
pm_ivig_refractory.reason_why: Proposed mechanisms include Fc-receptor blockade on macrophages, neutralization of pathogenic autoantibodies/complement components (particularly relevant to the complement-mediated microangiopathy of dermatomyositis, and by extension overlapping IIM pathology), and modulation of cytokine networks.
pm_ivig_refractory.source: Marie I et al., Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2010;62(12):1748-1755 (PMID 20722047)
pm_ivig_refractory.confidence: high for the specific steroid-refractory esophageal/dysphagia indication reported (n=73); general IVIG efficacy data for limb-girdle weakness in PM specifically (as opposed to dermatomyositis, where IVIG has stronger RCT evidence) is less robust and extrapolated in part from the closely related DM/IIM literature

pm_rituximab_rim_trial.name: Rituximab for Refractory Disease
pm_rituximab_rim_trial.effectiveness: In the NIH-funded RIM (Rituximab in Myositis) randomized placebo-phase trial of 200 patients with refractory adult polymyositis, adult dermatomyositis, or juvenile dermatomyositis (Oddis CV et al., Arthritis Rheum 2013;65(2):314-324, PMID 23124935), 161 patients (83%) met a formal Definition of Improvement over the 44-week trial period, with no significant difference between early versus delayed rituximab timing - meaning nearly all patients ultimately improved on rituximab regardless of when it was started, a genuinely strong real response rate in a population that had already failed corticosteroids plus at least one other immunosuppressant.
pm_rituximab_rim_trial.reason_why: Depletes CD20+ B lymphocytes, reducing autoantibody production (e.g. anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, anti-Mi-2) and B-cell antigen-presentation-driven T-cell activation implicated in myositis pathogenesis.
pm_rituximab_rim_trial.source: Oddis CV et al., Arthritis Rheum 2013;65(2):314-324 (PMID 23124935)
pm_rituximab_rim_trial.confidence: high (large NIH-funded multicentre RCT, though the 83% figure pools adult PM with adult and juvenile DM rather than being PM-isolated)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.pm_diagnostic_reclassification_note: Real diagnostic caveat that materially affects how to read every outcome number above: 'polymyositis' has historically been an over-diagnosed, heterogeneous label. In a systematic clinico-serologic re-classification of 100 French-Canadian patients originally labelled with an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, only 9% retained a diagnosis of isolated (non-overlap) polymyositis by the end of work-up, down from an initial 45% at first assessment - most were reclassified as overlap myositis (myositis with another connective tissue disease, most commonly systemic sclerosis, present in about 43% of overlap cases), which rose from 24% to 67% of the cohort (Troyanov Y et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 2005;84(4):231-249, PMID 16010208). Antisynthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1 and related antibodies, often with interstitial lung disease, mechanic's hands, and arthritis) and inclusion body myositis (a mimicking but far more treatment-refractory disease, especially in patients over 50 with distal/asymmetric weakness and poor immunosuppressant response) are the two most clinically important real reclassification categories to exclude before treating a patient as 'true' polymyositis, since neither antisynthetase-syndrome-associated myositis nor IBM shares the same favourable corticosteroid-responsiveness profile implied by mixed historic PM outcome cohorts.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials/cohorts measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (formal Definition-of-Improvement in a mixed refractory PM+DM population, resolution of steroid-refractory dysphagia specifically, and long-term muscle-strength/disability/remission outcomes in a general treated PM+DM cohort) in DIFFERENT populations - ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. Also see the diagnostic reclassification caveat above (Troyanov 2005, PMID 16010208): only about 9% of historically-labelled 'polymyositis' patients meet strict criteria for isolated PM once overlap myositis and antisynthetase syndrome are separated out, and inclusion body myositis is a further real misdiagnosis risk - so the numbers below, drawn from mixed/legacy PM+DM cohorts, likely understate what is achievable in a correctly-classified, antibody-defined, non-IBM true-PM population.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab (refractory adult PM + adult/juvenile DM, RIM trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Patients meeting formal Definition of Improvement after failing corticosteroids + >=1 immunosuppressant, 44-week trial, n=200
ranked_high_to_low.source: Oddis CV et al., Arthritis Rheum 2013 (PMID 23124935)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG (steroid-refractory esophageal/dysphagia involvement in PM+DM)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinical resolution of esophageal manifestations, n=73
ranked_high_to_low.source: Marie I et al., Arthritis Care Res 2010 (PMID 20722047)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Corticosteroid +/- steroid-sparing combination therapy (real-world long-term cohort)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Patients with normal muscle strength at median 5-year follow-up, n=110 PM+DM cohort
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bronner IM et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006 (PMID 16606652)

dermatomyositis.name: Dermatomyositis

complement_mediated_microangiopathy.finding: Dermatomyositis (DM) is fundamentally a complement-mediated microangiopathy of skin and muscle, distinct in mechanism from polymyositis (PM) and inclusion body myositis (IBM). Activation of the classical/lectin complement pathway leads to deposition of the C5b-9 membrane attack complex (MAC) on endomysial capillary endothelium. This was directly demonstrated by immunofluorescence/immunoperoxidase staining of muscle biopsies: MAC deposits were found on intramuscular capillaries in every DM biopsy studied, appearing before any inflammatory-cell infiltrate or muscle-fiber necrosis was visible on light microscopy, indicating the vascular injury is the primary, initiating event rather than a bystander effect of inflammation.
complement_mediated_microangiopathy.source: Kissel JT, Mendell JR, Rammohan KW, 'Microvascular deposition of complement membrane attack complex in dermatomyositis', N Engl J Med 1986;314:329-334 (PMID 3945256)
complement_mediated_microangiopathy.confidence: high - original seminal immunopathology study, mechanism reaffirmed in later reviews

perifascicular_atrophy_and_ischemia.finding: MAC-mediated capillary lysis causes muscle ischemia that is most severe at the periphery of the muscle fascicle (a vascular watershed zone), producing the pathognomonic biopsy finding of perifascicular atrophy - atrophic, often basophilic fibers concentrated at the fascicle edge while central fibers are relatively spared. This contrasts mechanistically with PM/IBM, in which clonally expanded CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly invade MHC-class-I-expressing, non-necrotic muscle fibers and cause fiber necrosis via the perforin/granzyme pathway - an endomysial, cell-mediated process rather than a microvascular/complement-mediated one.
perifascicular_atrophy_and_ischemia.confidence: high - classic authoritative review, mechanism widely reproduced

myositis_specific_antibody_subtypes.finding: Distinct myositis-specific autoantibodies (MSAs) correlate with distinct DM clinical subtypes in terms of cutaneous manifestations, systemic organ involvement, and malignancy risk. Real, characterized subtypes include: anti-Mi-2 (classic DM skin/muscle disease, generally good prognosis, low malignancy risk), anti-MDA5/anti-CADM-140 (frequently amyopathic or hypomyopathic skin disease with a strong association to rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease), anti-NXP2 (associated with calcinosis and, in adults, elevated malignancy risk), anti-TIF1-gamma (the antibody most strongly linked to malignancy-associated DM), and anti-SAE (often initial cutaneous-only disease with later muscle/systemic involvement, and dysphagia).
myositis_specific_antibody_subtypes.source: DeWane ME, Waldman R, Lu J, 'Dermatomyositis: Clinical features and pathogenesis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82:267-281 (PMID 31279808)
myositis_specific_antibody_subtypes.confidence: high - modern peer-reviewed dermatology/rheumatology reference review

EULAR_ACR_2017_classification_criteria.finding: The 2017 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for adult and juvenile idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) were derived from 976 IIM patients and 624 non-IIM comparators (mostly other myopathies/muscular dystrophies) across 47 centers, using a probability-based scoring algorithm (with and without muscle biopsy features) that weights: age at onset, pattern/symmetry of muscle weakness (proximal > distal, symmetric), dysphagia, characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, Gottron's sign), serum creatine kinase (CK)/muscle-enzyme elevation, anti-Jo-1 (antisynthetase) antibody positivity, and, when biopsy is available, specific histopathologic features (e.g., perifascicular atrophy for DM). A calculated probability score of >=55% (without biopsy) classifies a patient as having IIM, with separate sub-scoring that further classifies the patient into DM, amyopathic DM, juvenile DM, PM, or IBM subgroups.
EULAR_ACR_2017_classification_criteria.source: Lundberg IE, Tjarnlund A, Bottai M et al, '2017 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for adult and juvenile idiopathic inflammatory myopathies and their major subgroups', Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:2271-2282 (PMID 29106061); simultaneously published in Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:1955-1964 (PMID 29079590); methodology detailed in Bottai M et al, RMD Open 2017;3:e000507 (PMID 29177080)
EULAR_ACR_2017_classification_criteria.confidence: high - jointly endorsed international classification criteria, primary derivation study

creatine_kinase_and_muscle_enzymes.finding: Serum creatine kinase (CK) is typically elevated in DM (often several-fold above normal, though it can be normal in amyopathic or anti-MDA5-predominant disease), and is included as a weighted diagnostic item in the EULAR/ACR 2017 criteria along with other muscle enzymes (aldolase, LDH, AST/ALT of muscle origin). CK elevation correlates with active myositis and is used to monitor disease activity and treatment response, but a normal CK does NOT exclude DM, particularly in amyopathic or anti-MDA5-antibody-associated phenotypes where skin and lung disease can dominate with minimal or absent muscle enzyme elevation.
creatine_kinase_and_muscle_enzymes.source: Lundberg IE et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:2271-2282 (PMID 29106061); DeWane ME et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82:267-281 (PMID 31279808)

muscle_biopsy_and_MRI.finding: Muscle biopsy showing perifascicular atrophy with MAC deposition on endomysial capillaries remains a key confirmatory diagnostic feature when the clinical picture is ambiguous or biopsy is otherwise indicated; MAC immunostaining on biopsy has been proposed specifically as a diagnostic adjunct in cases with atypical or overlapping features. Short-tau inversion recovery (STIR) MRI of proximal muscles is a real, clinically useful adjunct that identifies muscle edema (active myositis) and can guide biopsy site selection, distinguishing active inflammation from chronic fibro-fatty change, though it is not part of the formal EULAR/ACR classification score.
muscle_biopsy_and_MRI.source: Jain A, Sharma MC, Sarkar C et al, 'Detection of the membrane attack complex as a diagnostic tool in dermatomyositis', Acta Neurol Scand 2011;123:122-129 (PMID 20497129); Dalakas MC, Lancet 2003;362:971-982 (PMID 14511932)
muscle_biopsy_and_MRI.confidence: high for biopsy/MAC finding; moderate for MRI-STIR role (well-established in clinical practice but not independently re-verified via a dedicated primary study this session)

cutaneous_hallmarks.finding: The two pathognomonic cutaneous findings of DM are: (1) heliotrope rash - a violaceous-to-erythematous rash with periorbital edema on the upper eyelids, and (2) Gottron's papules - violaceous, often scaly papules/plaques over the extensor surfaces of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (a flat, non-papular variant over the same distribution is termed Gottron's sign). Other real cutaneous findings include the 'shawl sign' (erythema over the posterior neck/shoulders/upper back), 'V-sign' (erythema over the anterior neck/chest), periungual telangiectasia with cuticular overgrowth, and 'mechanic's hands' (hyperkeratotic, fissured skin on the lateral fingers, seen especially with antisynthetase-syndrome overlap).
cutaneous_hallmarks.source: DeWane ME, Waldman R, Lu J, J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82:267-281 (PMID 31279808); Waldman R, DeWane ME, Lu J, 'Dermatomyositis: Diagnosis and treatment', J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82:283-296 (PMID 31279813)

proximal_muscle_weakness.finding: Symmetric, proximal muscle weakness (shoulder girdle, hip girdle - difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or raising the arms overhead) is the classic muscular manifestation, typically developing subacutely over weeks; neck flexor weakness and dysphagia (from pharyngeal/esophageal striated-muscle involvement) are also real and clinically important findings. Cutaneous disease can precede, follow, or occur without any detectable muscle weakness (amyopathic/hypomyopathic DM), and its severity does not reliably track with muscle disease severity or systemic involvement.
proximal_muscle_weakness.source: DeWane ME, Waldman R, Lu J, J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82:267-281 (PMID 31279808); Dalakas MC, Lancet 2003;362:971-982 (PMID 14511932)

polymyositis.finding: Polymyositis (PM) is mechanistically and clinically distinguished from DM by the ABSENCE of the characteristic cutaneous findings (no heliotrope rash, no Gottron's papules/sign) - PM is a 'diagnosis of exclusion' among the IIMs requiring that skin disease and other identifiable causes (drug-induced myopathy, muscular dystrophy, IBM) be ruled out. Pathologically, PM shows endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltration of non-necrotic, MHC-class-I-expressing fibers rather than the perifascicular, complement/microangiopathy pattern of DM.

inclusion_body_myositis.finding: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is distinguished from both DM and PM by: (1) typically asymmetric weakness with a distinctive distal-and-proximal distribution (classically early involvement of finger flexors and knee extensors/quadriceps), (2) onset generally after age 50 and a slowly progressive (over years) rather than subacute course, (3) muscle biopsy showing rimmed vacuoles with amyloid deposits (in addition to the endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltrate shared with PM) - a distinctive combined degenerative-and-inflammatory histopathology not seen in DM or PM, and (4) characteristic resistance/poor response to immunosuppressive therapy, which is a real clinically useful distinguishing feature since DM and PM are generally immunosuppression-responsive.

malignancy_association.finding: DM carries a real, clinically critical association with occult malignancy that mandates age-appropriate cancer screening at diagnosis. A meta-analysis of 10 cohort studies found a pooled standardized incidence ratio (SIR) for cancer in DM of 4.79 (95% CI 3.71-5.87) versus the general population. A separate meta-analysis of 20 studies found dermatomyositis carried a pooled relative risk (RR) of malignancy of 5.50 (95% CI 4.31-6.70), compared with only 1.62 (95% CI 1.19-2.04) for polymyositis alone - malignancy risk in DM is substantially higher than in PM. Anti-TIF1-gamma antibody positivity is the myositis-specific antibody most strongly associated with malignancy-associated DM (anti-NXP2 also carries elevated adult malignancy risk), and should prompt intensified age- and risk-appropriate cancer screening (and consideration of PET-CT) beyond routine age-based screening.
malignancy_association.source: Olazagasti JM, Baez PJ, Wetter DA, Ernste FC, 'Cancer risk in dermatomyositis: a meta-analysis of cohort studies', Am J Clin Dermatol 2015;16:89-98 (PMID 25721032); Yang Z, Lin F, Qin B et al, 'Polymyositis/dermatomyositis and malignancy risk: a meta-analysis study', J Rheumatol 2015;42:282-291 (PMID 25448790); DeWane ME et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82:267-281 (PMID 31279808)
malignancy_association.confidence: high - concordant, adequately powered independent meta-analyses

incidence_and_prevalence.finding: In a population-based cohort study (Olmsted County, Minnesota, USA), the age- and sex-adjusted incidence of dermatomyositis (all subtypes) was 9.63 per 1,000,000 person-years (95% CI 6.09-13.17), of which clinically amyopathic DM accounted for 2.08 per 1,000,000 person-years; the age- and sex-adjusted prevalence was 21.42 per 100,000 persons (95% CI 13.07-29.77). 76% of identified patients were female, and 28% had a malignant condition diagnosed during the study period.
incidence_and_prevalence.source: Bendewald MJ, Wetter DA, Li X, Davis MD, 'Incidence of dermatomyositis and clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis: a population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota', Arch Dermatol 2010;146:26-30 (PMID 20083689)
incidence_and_prevalence.confidence: high - well-conducted population-based epidemiologic cohort, though numbers are specific to one US county population and may not generalize precisely to other populations

malignancy_timing.finding: Malignancy risk in DM is not uniformly distributed over time: the meta-analysis by Yang et al found the increased malignancy risk was 'more significant in patients within the first year of myositis diagnosis' (as well as in male patients), meaning cancer screening intensity should be highest in the first 1-3 years after DM diagnosis, with continued vigilance for at least 3-5 years given some cases present at latency.
malignancy_timing.source: Yang Z, Lin F, Qin B et al, J Rheumatol 2015;42:282-291 (PMID 25448790)

anti_MDA5_ILD_course.finding: Anti-MDA5 antibody (originally described as anti-CADM-140) marks a distinct, high-risk DM natural-history subtype: it is strongly associated with clinically amyopathic or hypomyopathic disease and with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) that can lead to respiratory failure within weeks of onset. An ELISA assay for anti-MDA5 showed 85% sensitivity and 100% specificity for identifying patients with clinically amyopathic DM and/or rapidly progressive ILD in the original characterizing cohort. A subsequent systematic review/meta-analysis of predictors of mortality in myositis-associated ILD found the odds ratio for death associated with anti-MDA5 antibody positivity was 6.20 (95% CI 3.58-10.71) - roughly a six-fold increase in mortality odds.
anti_MDA5_ILD_course.source: Sato S, Hirakata M, Kuwana M et al, 'RNA helicase encoded by melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 is a major autoantigen in patients with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis: association with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease', Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:2193-2200 (PMID 19565506); Hannah JR et al, 'A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Predictors of Mortality in Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathy-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease', J Rheumatol 2023;50:373-383 (PMID 36379584)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Dermatomyositis is a real, complement-mediated microangiopathy of skin and muscle (Kissel 1986, PMID 3945256), clinically anchored by heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules plus symmetric proximal weakness, diagnosed using the 2017 EULAR/ACR probability-based classification criteria (PMID 29106061/29079590) combining clinical features, CK elevation, myositis-specific antibodies, and (when available) biopsy showing perifascicular atrophy. It is differentiated from polymyositis (no skin disease) and inclusion body myositis (asymmetric distal-plus-proximal weakness, rimmed vacuoles, immunosuppression-refractory course) (Dalakas 2003, PMID 14511932). Two real findings must never be missed at diagnosis: (1) DM carries a pooled cancer SIR of 4.79-5.50x the general population, concentrated in the first year after diagnosis and highest with anti-TIF1-gamma antibody, mandating age-appropriate malignancy screening in every new DM patient (PMID 25721032, 25448790); and (2) anti-MDA5-antibody-positive DM identifies a distinct rapidly-progressive-ILD phenotype with a six-fold increase in mortality odds (OR 6.20, PMID 36379584), requiring urgent pulmonary evaluation and antibody testing at presentation rather than routine work-up timelines.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Kissel JT et al, N Engl J Med 1986;314:329-334 (PMID 3945256); Dalakas MC, Lancet 2003;362:971-982 (PMID 14511932); Lundberg IE et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:2271-2282 (PMID 29106061); Olazagasti JM et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2015;16:89-98 (PMID 25721032); Yang Z et al, J Rheumatol 2015;42:282-291 (PMID 25448790); Hannah JR et al, J Rheumatol 2023;50:373-383 (PMID 36379584)

dermatomyositis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct dermatomyositis-related situations must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency/urgent-specialist guidance: (1) Anti-MDA5-antibody-positive rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) - a real, acutely life-threatening pulmonary complication seen especially with clinically amyopathic or hypomyopathic DM. Anti-MDA5 (originally CADM-140) antibody was characterized with 85% sensitivity and 100% specificity for identifying patients with amyopathic DM and/or RP-ILD (Sato S et al, Arthritis Rheum 2009;60:2193-2200, PMID 19565506), and a systematic review/meta-analysis of predictors of mortality in myositis-associated ILD found the odds ratio for death with anti-MDA5 positivity was 6.20 (95% CI 3.58-10.71) (Hannah JR et al, J Rheumatol 2023;50:373-383, PMID 36379584) - a roughly six-fold increase in mortality odds. New or rapidly worsening dyspnea, hypoxia, dry cough, or fever in a known or suspected DM patient (especially with absent/mild muscle weakness) needs same-day emergency pulmonology/rheumatology assessment and anti-MDA5 antibody testing, not routine queuing. (2) Occult-malignancy screening imperative at diagnosis - DM carries a pooled cancer standardized incidence ratio of 4.79 (95% CI 3.71-5.87) versus the general population (Olazagasti JM et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2015;16:89-98, PMID 25721032), with a separate meta-analysis finding a pooled relative risk of 5.50 (95% CI 4.31-6.70) for DM versus only 1.62 for polymyositis, and this elevated risk was 'more significant in patients within the first year of myositis diagnosis' (Yang Z et al, J Rheumatol 2015;42:282-291, PMID 25448790). Every newly diagnosed DM patient - especially anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 antibody-positive patients - requires prompt, age-appropriate malignancy screening (and consideration of PET-CT) at diagnosis and close follow-up through at least the first 1-3 years; this must not be deferred or treated as optional. Both of these are real, evidence-based, specialist-referral-requiring situations and must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.
dermatomyositis.icd11_hint: 4A41 Dermatomyositis (WHO ICD-11 MMS, Chapter 4 -- Diseases of the immune system, block 4A40-4A4Z 'Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies': 4A40 Polymyositis, 4A41 Dermatomyositis, 4A42 Inclusion body myositis, 4A43 Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy); legacy ICD-10 M33.1 Other dermatomyositis / M33.0 Juvenile dermatomyositis -- FLAG: the live WHO ICD-11 API (id.who.int) requires an OAuth token and returned 401/404 to unauthenticated fetches in this research session, so the exact code could not be re-verified against the live WHO browser in this session; the 4A41 stem code and ICD-10 M33.1 crosswalk are from standard medical-coding reference structure and should be spot-checked against a live WHO ICD-11 login before clinical/billing use.
dermatomyositis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Dermatomyositis (DM) does not have a single pill that reverses the underlying autoimmune process in every patient in every case, and that must be stated plainly. But real modern combination therapy achieves real, substantial, often durable remission in a genuine majority of patients, and one intervention -- intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) -- represents a real, FDA-recognized breakthrough with real randomized-trial numbers behind it, not marketing language. LEAD STORY -- IVIG IS A REAL, PROVEN, TRIAL-VALIDATED TREATMENT: the ProDERM trial (Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022, PMID 36198179), a 95-patient, placebo-controlled, 16-week randomized trial of IVIG (Octagam 10%, 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks), found that 79% of IVIG-treated patients (37 of 47) achieved a Total Improvement Score (TIS) of at least 20 versus 44% of placebo patients (21 of 48) -- an absolute difference of 35 percentage points (95% CI 17-53, P<0.001). A post-hoc analysis of the same trial (PMID 40616720) showed IVIG also resolved extra-muscular disease activity in the majority of affected patients: arthralgia fell from 68.1% to 0% of affected patients (P<0.001) and fatigue from 68.1% to 3.3% (P=0.008). This RCT-level evidence is the real basis on which Octagam 10% carries an FDA-recognized indication specifically for dermatomyositis in adults -- to the researcher's knowledge this makes it the first and only IVIG product with a dermatomyositis-specific U.S. approval, though the exact FDA approval letter/date could not be independently re-verified against a live FDA.gov page in this research session (WebFetch returned 401/403/404 on FDA.gov, DailyMed and manufacturer pages) and should be confirmed against the current Octagam 10% prescribing information before that specific regulatory claim is repeated as fact. CORTICOSTEROIDS REMAIN THE REAL FIRST-LINE INDUCTION AGENT: high-dose oral or IV-pulse corticosteroids (e.g. prednisone/prednisolone ~0.75-1 mg/kg/day, or IV methylprednisolone pulses for severe/organ-threatening disease) are the real, universally-used first-line induction therapy in every major trial and cohort reviewed here -- every arm of the randomized PRINTO trial in juvenile DM (Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016, PMID 26645190) and the adult skin-remission cohort (Wolstencroft PW et al, JAMA Dermatol 2018, PMID 29114741) used background corticosteroids, and 38% of a 74-patient adult DM cohort achieved real clinical skin remission over 3 years of combination management. STEROID-SPARING COMBINATION THERAPY REAL SUBSTANTIALLY IMPROVES OUTCOMES OVER STEROIDS ALONE: in the randomized PRINTO trial (juvenile DM, n=139), adding methotrexate to prednisone achieved a real PRINTO-20 improvement in 72% of patients at 6 months versus 51% with prednisone alone (P=0.0228), with a real, significantly longer time to treatment failure; a separate 58-patient juvenile DM cohort treated with corticosteroids (100%) plus methotrexate (93%) achieved real complete remission in 65.5% of patients at a median of 24 months (PMID 33360233). Mycophenolate mofetil has real, if smaller-scale, supporting evidence: it was independently associated with adult skin clinical remission (odds ratio 6.00, 95% CI 1.66-21.78, P=.01) in the JAMA Dermatol cohort, and achieved successful steroid taper without relapse in 6 of 10 patients (60%) in an early case series (Rowin J et al, Neurology 2006, PMID 16636243) -- though that same small series documented a real, serious opportunistic-infection signal (3 of 10 patients, 1 death), underscoring that this is real immunosuppression with real risk, not a benign add-on. Azathioprine's real evidence is more nuanced and must be stated honestly: the classic randomized Bunch trial (Ann Intern Med 1980, PMID 6986827) found NO significant additional strength benefit from adding azathioprine to prednisone at 3 months, but its own long-term follow-up (Arthritis Rheum 1981, PMID 7008799) found the combination arm had real, better functional outcomes and required significantly less prednisone at 3 years -- i.e. azathioprine's real benefit in this trial was a slow steroid-sparing effect, not a fast one. RITUXIMAB IS A REAL OPTION FOR REFRACTORY DISEASE: in the RIM trial (Oddis CV et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013, PMID 23124935, n=200 across PM/DM/juvenile DM), 83% of patients (161 of 195) achieved a pre-defined Definition of Improvement by 44 weeks, although the trial's specific primary comparison (early vs delayed rituximab timing) was honestly negative (P=0.74) -- the real, useful reading is that rituximab produced substantial improvement in the large majority of refractory patients, just not faster when given earlier. THE ONE HONEST, SEVERE EXCEPTION -- ANTI-MDA5-ASSOCIATED RAPIDLY PROGRESSIVE INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE (RP-ILD): this specific DM subset carries a real, much worse prognosis and needs stated separately, not folded into the good-news numbers above. A 2023 meta-analysis of 29 cohorts/2645 anti-MDA5-positive DM patients found RP-ILD was by far the single strongest mortality predictor (hazard ratio 9.34, 95% CI 6.39-13.6, P<0.01), well ahead of older age (HR 1.54) or male sex (HR 2.07) (PMID 37348186). The real, honest, and encouraging answer to that danger is that early, aggressive, triple-agent immunosuppression changes the outcome dramatically: a prospective Japanese study of combined high-dose glucocorticoids + tacrolimus + IV cyclophosphamide in 29 new-onset anti-MDA5-RP-ILD patients achieved 89% 6-month survival versus 33% in a historical step-up-therapy control group (P<0.0001) (Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020, PMID 31524333) -- i.e. the correct response to this high-risk subgroup is real, faster, more aggressive multi-drug therapy from the outset, not a step-up approach, and doing so converts a mostly-fatal 6-month course into a mostly-survived one. BOTTOM LINE: dermatomyositis is genuinely one of the more treatable major autoimmune diseases in this knowledge base when corticosteroid induction is combined early with a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate having the strongest randomized evidence) and, in IVIG-eligible or refractory patients, IVIG itself -- a combination that real trial and cohort data show puts the large majority of patients into good functional control and a meaningful fraction into durable remission -- while anti-MDA5 RP-ILD is the real exception that requires immediate, more aggressive combination immunosuppression rather than the standard step-up approach.

curative_option.name: High-Dose Corticosteroid Induction Plus Early Steroid-Sparing Combination Therapy (Methotrexate or Azathioprine), With IVIG Added for IVIG-Eligible or Refractory/Extra-Muscular Disease, and Immediate Triple-Agent Escalation for Anti-MDA5 RP-ILD -- Precise Honesty: Real, Trial-Proven, Substantial Remission in the Majority, Not a Guaranteed Universal Drug-Free Cure
curative_option.note: There is no single randomized trial proving one fixed regimen 'cures' adult dermatomyositis, and that must be stated plainly. What real trial and cohort evidence does support is a layered, sequenced strategy: (1) induce with high-dose corticosteroids; (2) add a steroid-sparing agent early rather than waiting for steroid failure -- the randomized PRINTO trial showed this real, statistically significant benefit for methotrexate (and ciclosporin) over prednisone alone; (3) add IVIG in patients who are IVIG-eligible, have prominent extra-muscular (arthritis/fatigue) disease, or fail step (2) -- the ProDERM RCT is the strongest single piece of level-1 evidence in this entire disease; (4) for the anti-MDA5-RP-ILD subset specifically, skip the slow step-up approach and start high-dose glucocorticoid + tacrolimus + IV cyclophosphamide (+/- plasmapheresis) immediately, because the Tsuji trial shows this converts a mostly-fatal course into a mostly-survived one within 6 months.

real_trial_data.proderm_ivig_rct: Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID 36198179): 95 patients randomized to IVIG (Octagam 10%, 2.0 g/kg q4 weeks) or placebo for 16 weeks. TIS>=20 achieved by 79% (37/47) IVIG vs 44% (21/48) placebo, difference 35 percentage points (95% CI 17-53, P<0.001). Post-hoc extra-muscular analysis (PMID 40616720): arthralgia 68.1%->0% (P<0.001), fatigue 68.1%->3.3% (P=0.008), arthritis 36.2%->17.8% (P=0.01). Safety: 9 IVIG-related serious adverse events over 40 weeks including 6 thromboembolic events; common AEs headache 42%, pyrexia 19%, nausea 16%.
real_trial_data.printo_methotrexate_rct: Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016 (PMID 26645190): 139 new-onset juvenile DM patients randomized to prednisone alone (n=47), prednisone+ciclosporin (n=46), or prednisone+methotrexate (n=46). PRINTO-20 response at 6 months: 51% vs 70% vs 72% respectively (P=0.0228); time to treatment failure 16.7 months (prednisone alone) vs 53.3 months (prednisone+ciclosporin, P=0.009); prednisone+methotrexate had the best safety profile and steroid-sparing effect, median time to clinical remission 41.9 months.
real_trial_data.anti_mda5_rpild_triple_therapy: Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 31524333): 29 new-onset anti-MDA5-positive DM-ILD patients treated with high-dose glucocorticoids + tacrolimus + IV cyclophosphamide (+plasmapheresis if worsening) vs 15 historical step-up-therapy controls. 6-month survival 89% vs 33% (P<0.0001).

curative_option.effectiveness_pct_note: 79.0 reflects the single strongest level-1 RCT number available (ProDERM IVIG TIS>=20 response rate at 16 weeks, PMID 36198179); real combination-therapy remission rates vary by regimen and are given per-agent in effectiveness_ranked_table below -- no single 'cure percentage' for the whole disease is supported by the literature and none is asserted here.
curative_option.source: Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID 36198179); Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016 (PMID 26645190); Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 31524333)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for dermatomyositis found in this research pass: first-line corticosteroid induction; steroid-sparing conventional immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, calcineurin inhibitors); IVIG (the only agent with a dermatomyositis-specific RCT-backed FDA-recognized indication); rituximab for refractory disease; and the anti-MDA5-associated rapidly-progressive-ILD aggressive combination protocol, which is a distinct, higher-urgency treatment pathway. Diagnostic criteria, autoantibody subtypes and symptom-side epidemiology are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Priority order follows this knowledge base's convention: medicines first, then injection/infusion-based procedures (IVIG, rituximab, cyclophosphamide), then everything else.

dm_first_line_corticosteroids.name: Prednisone / Prednisolone (+/- IV Methylprednisolone Pulse) -- First-Line Induction Immunosuppression
dm_first_line_corticosteroids.type: Oral corticosteroid (+ IV pulse corticosteroid for severe disease)
specific_drugs: Prednisone (generic; India brands include Wysolone, Omnacortil as prednisolone)
Methylprednisolone (brand Solu-Medrol) -- IV pulse dosing (e.g. 500-1000mg/day x3 days) for severe muscle weakness, dysphagia, or organ-threatening disease
dm_first_line_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Used as background induction therapy in every arm of the randomized PRINTO juvenile-DM trial and the adult skin-remission cohort reviewed here; in the PRINTO trial, prednisone alone still achieved a real PRINTO-20 response in 51% of patients at 6 months (24/47) (PMID 26645190); in a 74-patient adult DM cohort managed with corticosteroid-based regimens, 38% achieved clinical skin remission over 3 years of follow-up (PMID 29114741).
dm_first_line_corticosteroids.reason_why: Broad, rapid genomic and non-genomic suppression of T-cell and B-cell-mediated autoimmune activity and of the type-I-interferon-driven inflammatory pathway that drives muscle fiber and perifascicular capillary injury in dermatomyositis.
dm_first_line_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Corticosteroid monotherapy alone is real but sub-optimal -- the randomized PRINTO data show it is significantly outperformed by early combination with methotrexate or ciclosporin (51% vs 72%/70% response, P=0.0228), and long-term high-dose steroid use carries the standard real toxicity burden (osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, myopathy, cataracts, avascular necrosis), which is itself a reason to add a steroid-sparing agent early rather than escalating steroid dose alone.
dm_first_line_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Universal first-line induction agent, typically prednisone/prednisolone ~0.75-1mg/kg/day (or IV methylprednisolone pulses for severe/organ-threatening disease) with an early steroid-sparing agent added rather than waiting for steroid failure, per the real PRINTO trial result below.
dm_first_line_corticosteroids.source: Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016 (PMID 26645190); Wolstencroft PW et al, JAMA Dermatol 2018 (PMID 29114741)

dm_steroid_sparing_methotrexate.name: Methotrexate (Added Early to Prednisone) -- Strongest Randomized Evidence Among Steroid-Sparing Agents
specific_drugs: Methotrexate (oral or subcutaneous, typically 15-25mg/week) with folic/folinic acid supplementation
dm_steroid_sparing_methotrexate.effectiveness: In the randomized PRINTO trial (n=139, juvenile DM), prednisone+methotrexate achieved a PRINTO-20 response in 72% of patients (33/46) at 6 months versus 51% (24/47) with prednisone alone (P=0.0228), the best steroid-sparing effect and safety profile of the three arms, and a real, significantly longer time to treatment failure than prednisone alone (PMID 26645190). A separate 58-patient juvenile DM cohort treated with corticosteroids (100%) plus methotrexate (93%) achieved complete remission in 65.5% of patients at a median of 24 months, with a 26.3% relapse rate (PMID 33360233).
dm_steroid_sparing_methotrexate.reason_why: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, suppressing rapidly-dividing autoreactive lymphocyte proliferation and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production, allowing real reduction of corticosteroid dose while maintaining disease control.
dm_steroid_sparing_methotrexate.important_caveat: Real hepatotoxicity, cytopenia, and pneumonitis risk requires regular monitoring (LFTs, CBC); contraindicated in pregnancy; the PRINTO trial was conducted in juvenile DM, and while methotrexate is real standard-of-care in adult DM by extrapolation and extensive real-world use, this specific randomized efficacy number is a pediatric-population result, not an adult RCT result.
dm_steroid_sparing_methotrexate.real_working_solution: Real first-choice steroid-sparing agent to add early (not after steroid failure) in both adult and juvenile dermatomyositis, per the PRINTO trial's real head-to-head randomized result.
dm_steroid_sparing_methotrexate.source: Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016 (PMID 26645190); juvenile DM long-term remission cohort (PMID 33360233)

dm_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.name: Azathioprine (Added to Prednisone) -- Real Slow Steroid-Sparing Benefit, Honestly No Fast Benefit
dm_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.effectiveness: The classic randomized, double-blind Bunch trial (n=16, Ann Intern Med 1980, PMID 6986827) found NO statistically significant additional strength benefit from adding azathioprine to prednisone at 3 months (P=0.58). However, the same cohort's long-term follow-up (Arthritis Rheum 1981, PMID 7008799) found the azathioprine+prednisone arm had real, statistically better functional outcomes and required significantly less prednisone for disease control at 3 years than prednisone alone -- i.e. a real but slow (multi-year, not multi-month) steroid-sparing effect.
dm_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.reason_why: Purine synthesis inhibition suppresses lymphocyte proliferation; onset of clinically meaningful immunosuppressive effect is slower than methotrexate, consistent with the trial's null 3-month result but positive 3-year result.
dm_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.important_caveat: This is one of the more honestly-mixed evidence bases in this entry -- do not present azathioprine as producing fast improvement; its real, trial-demonstrated value is long-term steroid-sparing and functional benefit, and it requires TPMT/NUDT15 status consideration and CBC/LFT monitoring for myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity risk.
dm_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.real_working_solution: Real alternative steroid-sparing agent, particularly where methotrexate is contraindicated (e.g. significant liver disease) or not tolerated; expect benefit over a multi-year, not multi-month, timeframe based on the only randomized trial with long-term follow-up.
dm_steroid_sparing_azathioprine.source: Bunch TW et al, Ann Intern Med 1980 (PMID 6986827); Bunch TW, Arthritis Rheum 1981 (PMID 7008799)

dm_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.name: Mycophenolate Mofetil -- Real Cohort-Level Association With Skin Remission, Real But Small Prospective Evidence
dm_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.effectiveness: In a 74-patient adult DM cohort (JAMA Dermatol 2018, PMID 29114741), mycophenolate mofetil use was independently and significantly associated with achieving clinical skin remission (odds ratio 6.00, 95% CI 1.66-21.78, P=.01) among the 38% of the cohort who reached remission over 3 years. In an earlier small case series (Rowin J et al, Neurology 2006, PMID 16636243, n=10), successful corticosteroid taper without disease relapse was achieved in 60% (6/10) of patients. A separate 19-patient Japanese cohort found CK improved significantly when mycophenolate was combined with a calcineurin inhibitor (P=0.04) but not with mycophenolate alone (P=0.39) (Hanaoka H et al, Clin Rheumatol 2019, PMID 30218287).
dm_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.reason_why: Selectively inhibits de novo purine synthesis in proliferating T and B lymphocytes, suppressing the autoantibody- and cytotoxic-T-cell-driven components of dermatomyositis with a more lymphocyte-selective mechanism than azathioprine.
dm_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.important_caveat: The Rowin 2006 case series, while showing a real 60% steroid-taper success rate, also documented a real, serious safety signal: opportunistic infections occurred in 3 of 10 patients, with 1 death -- a disproportionately high rate for a series this size, and a genuine reason for careful infection monitoring, not a reason to avoid the drug outright given its real remission-association benefit in the larger 2018 cohort.
dm_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.real_working_solution: Real alternative or add-on steroid-sparing agent, particularly favored for cutaneous disease given its independent association with real skin-remission in the largest cohort reviewed, and often combined with a calcineurin inhibitor for resistant myositis/CK elevation.
dm_steroid_sparing_mycophenolate.source: Wolstencroft PW et al, JAMA Dermatol 2018 (PMID 29114741); Rowin J et al, Neurology 2006 (PMID 16636243); Hanaoka H et al, Clin Rheumatol 2019 (PMID 30218287)

dm_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.name: Ciclosporin / Tacrolimus -- Real Randomized Evidence (Ciclosporin) and Real Combination Evidence (Tacrolimus)
dm_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.effectiveness: In the randomized PRINTO trial, prednisone+ciclosporin achieved a PRINTO-20 response in 70% of patients (32/46) at 6 months versus 51% with prednisone alone, and a real, significantly longer time to treatment failure (53.3 vs 16.7 months, P=0.009) (PMID 26645190). Tacrolimus is a core component of the real 89%-vs-33%-6-month-survival triple-therapy regimen for anti-MDA5 rapidly-progressive ILD (see dm_anti_mda5_rpild group below, PMID 31524333), and combined with mycophenolate produced significant CK improvement (P=0.04) versus mycophenolate alone (P=0.39) (PMID 30218287).
dm_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.reason_why: Inhibits calcineurin-dependent IL-2 transcription in activated T-cells, producing rapid, potent T-cell-mediated immunosuppression -- mechanistically complementary to the antiproliferative agents above and to corticosteroids.
dm_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.important_caveat: Real nephrotoxicity and hypertension risk requires renal function and blood-pressure monitoring; the PRINTO ciclosporin arm had a less favorable safety profile than the methotrexate arm in that same trial, which is why methotrexate is generally preferred first among steroid-sparing agents where both are options.
dm_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.real_working_solution: Real steroid-sparing option, particularly tacrolimus as part of aggressive combination therapy for anti-MDA5-associated ILD, and ciclosporin as a real randomized-trial-proven alternative to methotrexate in juvenile DM.
dm_steroid_sparing_calcineurin_inhibitor.source: Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016 (PMID 26645190); Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 31524333); Hanaoka H et al, Clin Rheumatol 2019 (PMID 30218287)

dm_ivig.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG, Octagam 10%) -- Real Randomized-Trial-Proven, FDA-Recognized Dermatomyositis-Specific Treatment
specific_drugs: Octagam 10% (the specific product studied in the ProDERM RCT, 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks)
dm_ivig.effectiveness: ProDERM trial (Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022, PMID 36198179): randomized, placebo-controlled, 95 patients. At week 16, TIS>=20 achieved by 79% of IVIG patients (37/47) versus 44% of placebo patients (21/48) -- absolute difference 35 percentage points (95% CI 17-53, P<0.001); higher improvement thresholds (TIS>=40, TIS>=60) also favored IVIG. Post-hoc analysis (PMID 40616720) showed real resolution of extra-muscular disease activity: arthralgia 68.1%->0% (P<0.001), fatigue 68.1%->3.3% (P=0.008), arthritis 36.2%->17.8% (P=0.01).
dm_ivig.reason_why: Polyclonal IgG modulates Fc-receptor-mediated inflammation, neutralizes pathogenic autoantibodies and complement components, and inhibits complement-mediated perifascicular capillary destruction, the specific microvascular injury mechanism believed central to dermatomyositis pathology.
dm_ivig.important_caveat: Real, serious thromboembolic risk: 9 IVIG-related serious adverse events occurred over the 40-week ProDERM observation period, including 6 thromboembolic events -- meaningful in patients with vascular risk factors, and requiring real clinical risk-benefit assessment before use. Creatine kinase levels did not differ meaningfully between IVIG and placebo groups in the trial despite the real clinical improvement, meaning CK is not a reliable marker of IVIG response in this disease.
dm_ivig.real_working_solution: The single strongest randomized-controlled-trial-proven pharmacologic intervention for dermatomyositis identified in this survey; used for IVIG-eligible patients, those with prominent extra-muscular disease activity, or those refractory to corticosteroid+steroid-sparing-agent combination therapy. To the researcher's knowledge Octagam 10% carries an FDA-recognized dermatomyositis-specific indication built on this trial, though the precise FDA approval letter/date was not independently re-verifiable via live FDA.gov/DailyMed access in this research session and should be confirmed against current prescribing information before being repeated as a standalone regulatory claim.
dm_ivig.source: Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID 36198179); post-hoc extra-muscular analysis (PMID 40616720)

dm_biologics_rituximab.name: Rituximab -- Real Substantial Improvement in Refractory Disease, Honestly Negative on Its Specific Primary Timing Endpoint
dm_biologics_rituximab.effectiveness: RIM trial (Oddis CV et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013, PMID 23124935): 200 patients randomized (76 polymyositis, 76 adult DM, 48 juvenile DM) to early versus delayed (week-8) rituximab; 195 completed analysis. 83% of all randomized patients (161/195) achieved a pre-defined Definition of Improvement by 44 weeks, with median time to improvement ~20 weeks in both arms. The trial's specific primary comparison (does earlier rituximab work faster than delayed rituximab) was honestly negative (P=0.74 by log-rank test), and secondary endpoints also did not significantly differ by timing.
dm_biologics_rituximab.reason_why: Depletes CD20-positive B-cells, reducing autoantibody production (including anti-MDA5, anti-Jo-1 and other myositis-specific antibodies) and antigen presentation to autoreactive T-cells.
dm_biologics_rituximab.important_caveat: The real, honest reading of RIM is nuanced: it does NOT prove rituximab is superior to placebo in a classic sense (there was no placebo-only arm beyond the timing comparison), but the real 83% improvement rate across both arms, in a population that was by definition refractory enough to be enrolled in a rituximab trial, is a genuinely useful real-world data point supporting its use in treatment-refractory dermatomyositis, particularly anti-MDA5-associated and anti-synthetase-associated disease in current clinical practice, even though the timing question it was designed to answer came back negative.
dm_biologics_rituximab.real_working_solution: Real option for corticosteroid- and conventional-steroid-sparing-agent-refractory dermatomyositis, and used in combination with mycophenolate mofetil in some real reported anti-MDA5-RP-ILD salvage cases.
dm_biologics_rituximab.source: Oddis CV et al, Arthritis Rheum 2013 (PMID 23124935)

dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.name: Immediate Triple-Agent Combination (High-Dose Glucocorticoid + Tacrolimus + IV Cyclophosphamide, +/- Plasmapheresis) for Anti-MDA5-Associated Rapidly Progressive ILD -- Real, Dramatic, Trial-Proven Survival Benefit Over Step-Up Therapy
dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.type: Combined IV/oral immunosuppression protocol, procedure-adjacent (plasmapheresis when escalated)
dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.effectiveness: Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 31524333): 29 new-onset anti-MDA5-positive DM-ILD patients treated with this combined protocol from diagnosis versus 15 historical controls treated with conventional step-up therapy. 6-month survival: 89% vs 33% (P<0.0001). This is the real, specific, quantified answer to the much-worse anti-MDA5-RP-ILD prognosis described in a 2023 meta-analysis of 29 cohorts/2645 patients, where RP-ILD carried the strongest mortality hazard ratio of any factor studied (HR 9.34, 95% CI 6.39-13.6, P<0.01) (PMID 37348186).
dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.reason_why: Anti-MDA5-positive RP-ILD is driven by an intense type-I-interferon/macrophage-activation-like inflammatory storm in the lung that a slow step-up approach cannot outpace; simultaneous T-cell (tacrolimus), B-cell/broad cytotoxic (cyclophosphamide), and non-specific (high-dose glucocorticoid) suppression from day one, escalated to plasmapheresis if worsening, matches the required speed of immunosuppression to the speed of the real disease process.
dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.important_caveat: Real, meaningful infection risk from triple immunosuppression -- cytomegalovirus reactivation was frequently observed over the 52-week Tsuji protocol, requiring real, proactive opportunistic-infection monitoring and prophylaxis; this is an intensive, hospital-based protocol appropriate specifically for the anti-MDA5-RP-ILD subgroup, not a substitute for standard step-wise therapy in patients without this specific high-risk antibody/lung phenotype.
dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.real_working_solution: Real, specific, trial-quantified answer for the one genuinely much-worse-prognosis subset of dermatomyositis (anti-MDA5-positive RP-ILD): start all three agents immediately at diagnosis rather than waiting for step-up failure, escalating to plasmapheresis for clinical deterioration.
dm_anti_mda5_rpild_aggressive_therapy.source: Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 31524333); anti-MDA5 mortality meta-analysis (PMID 37348186)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Corticosteroid induction + early steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate preferred) +/- IVIG -- combined real standard-of-care package
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real practical top-line answer: this layered combination, not any single drug, is what produces good real functional control and, in a meaningful fraction, durable remission in the large majority of dermatomyositis patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ruperto N et al, Lancet 2016 (PMID 26645190); Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID 36198179)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Anti-MDA5-RP-ILD immediate triple therapy (glucocorticoid + tacrolimus + IV cyclophosphamide)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 6-month survival 89% (triple therapy) vs 33% (historical step-up controls), P<0.0001
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tsuji H et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2020 (PMID 31524333)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab (refractory dermatomyositis/polymyositis/juvenile DM, RIM trial)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG (Octagam 10%, ProDERM trial)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Aggarwal R et al, N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID 36198179)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: 72% PRINTO-20 response at 6 months (33/46) vs 51% (24/47) prednisone alone, P=0.0228; longest time to remission but best safety profile of the 3 trial arms

allergic_rhinitis.name: Allergic Rhinitis
allergic_rhinitis.icd11_hint: CA08.0 Allergic rhinitis (WHO ICD-11 MMS, verified via NLM ICD-11 API mirror; CA08.00 allergic rhinitis due to pollen, CA08.03 other allergic rhinitis, CA08.0Z unspecified; parent CA08 Vasomotor or allergic rhinitis); legacy ICD-10 J30.1-J30.4
allergic_rhinitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Allergic rhinitis is NOT curable in the sense of erasing the underlying atopic (IgE-mediated) predisposition, but it is one of the few common chronic conditions where a real disease-modifying treatment exists and has been proven in randomised trials to change the natural course of the disease, not just mask symptoms. Almost every other drug class for allergic rhinitis - intranasal corticosteroids, oral or intranasal antihistamines, leukotriene receptor antagonists, decongestants, mast cell stabilisers - is purely symptomatic: it works only while it is being taken and symptoms return within days of stopping. Allergen immunotherapy (AIT) is different. In a randomised, placebo-controlled trial, patients who received 3-4 years of subcutaneous grass-pollen immunotherapy (SCIT) and then STOPPED had symptom scores that remained markedly lower than never-treated controls even 3 years after the last injection (median symptom score 504 in the group that stopped therapy vs 2863 in untreated controls - 82.4% lower, computed (2863-504)/2863 - with no significant difference from the group that continued injections, P=0.60; Durham SR et al., N Engl J Med 1999;341:468-475, PMID 10441602). The same disease-modifying persistence has been shown for the sublingual route: a 5-year double-blind trial of a grass SLIT-tablet found the rhinoconjunctivitis symptom score was still 25-36% lower than placebo 2 full years after the 3-year course of tablets had ended (Durham SR et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2012;129:717-725, PMID 22285278), and a companion trial found a 26% lower symptom score and 29% lower medication score 1 year after stopping (Durham SR et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:131-138, PMID 20109743). In children, a 3-year course of subcutaneous immunotherapy for grass/birch pollen allergy also cut the long-term risk of going on to develop asthma: at 10-year follow-up (7 years after stopping treatment) only 25% (16/64) of treated children had developed asthma versus 45.3% (24/53) of untreated controls - a 44.8% relative risk reduction (computed 1-(25/45.3); adjusted odds ratio for remaining asthma-free 4.6, 95% CI 1.5-13.7; Jacobsen L et al., Allergy 2007;62:943-948, PMID 17620073, the PAT study). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has allergic rhinitis: (1) confirm the trigger allergen(s) by history plus skin-prick or specific IgE testing; (2) start first-line pharmacotherapy immediately for symptom control - an intranasal corticosteroid (fluticasone furoate or propionate, mometasone furoate) is the single most effective drug class (Weiner JM et al., BMJ 1998;317:1624-1629, PMID 9848901: intranasal corticosteroids beat oral antihistamines on nasal blockage, discharge, sneezing and itch across 16 RCTs/2267 patients, with 74% lower odds of symptom deterioration, computed 1-0.26 from the pooled odds ratio) - combined with a second-generation oral antihistamine (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) if symptoms are not fully controlled, or a combination intranasal azelastine-fluticasone spray for moderate-to-severe disease; (3) for the patient whose symptoms persist despite adequate pharmacotherapy, who wants to reduce long-term medication need, or who has a documented single dominant allergen (grass, ragweed, birch, house dust mite), allergen immunotherapy - subcutaneous injections or a sublingual tablet, taken for 3 years - is the real option that can produce lasting, medication-free remission and reduce the risk of the allergic march progressing to asthma; and (4) reserve omalizumab (anti-IgE) and other add-on measures for refractory disease or when allergic rhinitis coexists with allergic asthma. Pharmacotherapy alone controls the great majority of patients adequately and is appropriate first-line care; immunotherapy is the treatment to reach for when a lasting, disease-modifying result rather than day-to-day suppression is the goal.

curative_option.name: Allergen Immunotherapy (Subcutaneous SCIT or Sublingual SLIT-Tablet) - Real Disease-Modifying Treatment With Persistent Remission Documented Years After Stopping; Not a Cure of the Underlying Atopic Predisposition but the Only Intervention That Changes the Natural Course of Allergic Rhinitis
curative_option.note: This is the real special case among allergic rhinitis treatments. Every other therapy in this survey (intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines, leukotriene antagonists, decongestants) works only while the patient keeps taking it. Allergen immunotherapy retrains the immune response to the causal allergen(s) and, in randomised placebo-controlled trials, keeps working for years after the course of injections or tablets stops. It is described here as disease-modifying / potentially curative in effect, and NOT as an absolute cure, because: benefit is allergen-specific (it does not treat allergies the patient was not desensitised to), a meaningful minority of trial participants do not reach a fully symptom-free state, and the underlying atopic tendency to make IgE against new allergens is not eliminated.

real_trial_data.scit_long_term_remission_after_stopping: Durham SR et al., 'Long-term clinical efficacy of grass-pollen immunotherapy', N Engl J Med 1999;341:468-475 (PMID 10441602): randomised, placebo-controlled/observational comparison. Median seasonal symptom scores: continued immunotherapy 921, discontinued after 3-4 years 504, never-treated controls 2863. Symptom scores in the group that STOPPED treatment were 82.4% lower than untreated controls (computed (2863-504)/2863) and were not significantly different from the group still on injections (P=0.60), showing the benefit persists after stopping. Authors' conclusion: 'three to four years of immunotherapy induces prolonged clinical remission... accompanied by persistent alteration in immunologic reactivity.'
real_trial_data.slit_tablet_disease_modification_2yr_pos: Durham SR et al. (5-year GT-08 extension trial), 'SQ-standardized sublingual grass immunotherapy: confirmation of disease modification 2 years after 3 years of treatment in a randomized trial', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2012;129:717-725 (PMID 22285278): 238 participants; 2 years after stopping a 3-year course of the Timothy-grass SLIT-tablet, the active group's rhinoconjunctivitis daily symptom score was 25-36% lower than placebo (P<=.004) and combined symptom+medication score was 27-41% lower (P<=.003); days with severe symptoms were 49-63% fewer (P<.0001).
real_trial_data.slit_tablet_sustained_1yr_post_treatment: Durham SR et al. (GT-08 trial), J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:131-138 (PMID 20109743): 257 subjects, randomised placebo-controlled phase III trial; 1 year after completing 3 years of grass SLIT-tablet treatment, mean rhinoconjunctivitis symptom score was 26% lower (P<.001) and medication score was 29% lower (P=.022) than placebo, with immunologic changes (allergen-specific IgG4, blunted seasonal IgE rise) sustained in parallel.
real_trial_data.pediatric_asthma_prevention_10yr_pat_stu: Jacobsen L et al. (PAT study, 10-year follow-up), Allergy 2007;62:943-948 (PMID 17620073): 147 subjects aged 16-25 assessed 10 years after starting a 3-year course of subcutaneous grass/birch immunotherapy (7 years after stopping). Asthma had developed in 16 of 64 (25%) actively treated subjects versus 24 of 53 (45.3%) untreated controls - a 44.8% relative risk reduction (computed 1-(25/45.3)); odds ratio for remaining asthma-free 4.6 (95% CI 1.5-13.7, adjusted for baseline bronchial hyper-responsiveness and asthma status, longitudinal model across 3/5/10-year visits, P=0.0075). Rhinoconjunctivitis symptom improvement and reduced conjunctival allergen sensitivity also persisted at 10 years.
real_trial_data.pediatric_asthma_prevention_3yr_pat_stud: Möller C et al. (PAT study), J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;109:251-256 (PMID 11842293): 205 children aged 6-14 randomised to 3 years of subcutaneous immunotherapy or open control; among children without asthma at baseline, actively treated children had significantly fewer asthma symptoms after 3 years (odds ratio 2.52, P<.05) and significantly improved methacholine bronchial provocation results (P<.05).
real_trial_data.scit_cochrane_meta_analysis: Calderon MA et al., 'Allergen injection immunotherapy for seasonal allergic rhinitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;(1):CD001936 (PMID 17253469): 51 trials, 2871 participants (1645 active, 1226 placebo). Pooled standardised mean difference (SMD) for symptom score reduction -0.73 (95% CI -0.97 to -0.50, P<0.00001) and for medication score -0.57 (95% CI -0.82 to -0.33, P<0.00001). Systemic adrenaline-requiring reactions in 0.13% of active injections vs 0.01% of placebo injections; no fatalities across the pooled trials.
real_trial_data.slit_cochrane_meta_analysis: Radulovic S et al., 'Sublingual immunotherapy for allergic rhinitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010;(12):CD002893 (PMID 21154351): 60 trials, 49 pooled (2333 SLIT, 2256 placebo). Pooled SMD for symptoms -0.49 (95% CI -0.64 to -0.34, P<0.00001) and medication use -0.32 (95% CI -0.43 to -0.21, P<0.00001). No trial reported severe systemic reactions, anaphylaxis, or need for adrenaline.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect: for the specific allergen(s) included in the vaccine/tablet, 3-4 years of immunotherapy produces symptom and medication reductions that are still measurable, and in the PAT study reduce the risk of progressing to asthma, years after the course has finished - a real disease-modifying, potentially near-curative outcome unmatched by any purely symptomatic drug. Not curative: immunotherapy does not treat sensitisation to allergens outside the treatment extract, atopic patients can still develop new sensitisations, benefit is not universal (Cochrane pooled effect sizes are moderate, not a 100% responder rate), and guidelines still describe a typical 3-5 year course as needed for durable effect rather than a single intervention.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with polysensitisation to many unrelated allergens where a single extract will not cover their triggers, patients who cannot commit to the 3-5 year course needed for durable benefit, and patients with severe/uncontrolled asthma or contraindications to SCIT (in whom the systemic reaction risk, while low at 0.13% per injection, is least acceptable). SLIT has a better safety profile (no reported anaphylaxis in the Cochrane pooled trials) and is preferred when unsupervised, at-home dosing is needed.
curative_option.important_caveat: The strongest disease-modification evidence (Durham 1999, Durham 2010/2012, PAT study) comes from trials of a small number of specific allergen extracts (grass and birch pollen) using specific standardised products; results should not be assumed to generalise identically to every allergen extract or every commercial SLIT-tablet without its own trial data. The PAT study's 10-year cohort had substantial attrition (from 205 enrolled to 147 assessed, and only 117 of those free of asthma at baseline), so the 44.8% relative-risk-reduction figure is a completer analysis. Immunotherapy requires correct allergen identification (skin-prick or specific IgE testing) and is administered/prescribed under medical supervision (SCIT always in a clinical setting because of anaphylaxis risk; SLIT typically initiated under medical supervision).
