natural_history.limited_patchy_disease_reassurance: This is the single most important reassuring fact for the majority of AA patients: in limited, localized patchy disease, spontaneous regrowth is observed within a few months in most patients, with or without simple topical treatment -- the follicle is structurally preserved (non-scarring), so the biological capacity to regrow hair remains intact (Friedli A, et al. Ther Umsch. 2002;59(5):233-237. PMID 12090120).
natural_history.extensive_disease_worse_prognosis: Progression to severe, extensive disease (alopecia totalis/universalis) occurs in up to 15% of patients, and once totalis/universalis is established, spontaneous remission becomes rare (Friedli A, et al. Ther Umsch. 2002;59(5):233-237. PMID 12090120). Notable exception: the acute diffuse and total alopecia (ADTA) subtype, despite reaching near-total hair loss rapidly, still carries a favorable prognosis with regrowth by about 6 months regardless of treatment -- underscoring that the specific clinical subtype/tempo of onset, not just the extent of loss, informs prognosis (Lew BL, et al. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2009;60(1):85-93. PMID 18992964).
citations: Friedli A, et al. Alopecia areata. Ther Umsch. 2002;59(5):233-237. PMID 12090120.
Lew BL, Shin MK, Sim WY. Acute diffuse and total alopecia: a new subtype of alopecia areata with a favorable prognosis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2009;60(1):85-93. PMID 18992964.

clinical_takeaway.lead_with_the_solution: AA is a non-scarring autoimmune disease -- the hair follicle survives the attack, so for the large majority of patients with limited patchy involvement, spontaneous regrowth within months is the expected and reassuring natural course; this entry's treatment fields cover the medicine/procedure options that can accelerate regrowth and are most useful in the higher-risk minority who progress toward extensive disease.
clinical_takeaway.diagnostic_path: Diagnose clinically from the pattern of smooth, non-scaly round/oval patches, confirmed by trichoscopy (exclamation-mark hairs, black dots, yellow dots, coudability hair); use trichoscopy to exclude tinea capitis (comma hairs), trichotillomania (frayed/variable-length broken hairs), and androgenetic alopecia (>20% diameter diversity) when the presentation is atypical.
clinical_takeaway.risk_stratify_and_screen: Screen for the strongly associated comorbid autoimmune diseases (especially thyroid dysfunction and vitiligo), and route every patient -- especially children and those with extensive/visible disease -- through psychological screening for anxiety, depression, and OCD given AA's real, well-documented psychosocial burden (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).

alopecia_areata.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Alopecia areata is not physically life-threatening, but it carries a real, well-documented psychosocial and psychiatric burden that must be actively screened for, not dismissed as 'cosmetic': a literature review of paediatric AA found anxiety, depression, and obsessive-compulsive disorder are prevalent in children with AA and worsen with disease severity, with measurable impact on self-esteem, academic performance, peer relationships, and body image (Sejdiu Z, et al. Psychosocial comorbidities in patients with paediatric alopecia areata: a literature review. Clin Exp Dermatol. 2024;49(10):1118-1124. PMID 38739703). A cross-sectional controlled study of children with AA/vitiligo versus healthy controls found significantly higher separation anxiety, generalized anxiety, social phobia, and major depressive disorder scores in affected children, and even their parents showed significantly higher panic disorder, major depressive disorder, and total anxiety scores than control parents (Savas Erdogan S, et al. Anxiety and depression in pediatric patients with vitiligo and alopecia areata and their parents: A cross-sectional controlled study. J Cosmet Dermatol. 2021;20(7):2232-2239. PMID 33089618). Practical rule: every AA patient, especially children/adolescents and those with visible, extensive, or eyebrow/eyelash-involving disease, should be routinely screened for anxiety, depression, and OCD symptoms (and their caregivers for parental anxiety/depression) at diagnosis and follow-up, with referral to mental health support as part of standard, not optional, AA care.
alopecia_areata.icd11_hint: ED70.2 Alopecia areata (ICD-10-CM L63) — per DermNet NZ ICD coding reference; not independently confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser (registration-gated API), flagged accordingly
alopecia_areata.CURABILITY_NOTE: Alopecia areata has two genuinely good real-world stories, and both belong at the top: first, for the most common presentation - limited patchy hair loss of short duration (under 1 year) - spontaneous remission occurs in roughly 80% of patients within 1 year even without any treatment (Ikeda T, Dermatologica 1965;131:421-445, cited in Pratt CH et al, 'Alopecia areata', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011, PMID 28300084, PMCID PMC5573125) - most people with a few patches get their hair back on their own, and intralesional corticosteroid injection (real first-line, 42.9-44.4% terminal hair regrowth in a 231-patch randomized trial, Ustuner P et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2017;28(8):753-761, PMID 28489468) speeds and reinforces that natural recovery. Second, and this is the real genuine breakthrough story for the harder, previously near-untreatable cases: for adults with severe or extensive alopecia areata (Severity of Alopecia Tool, SALT, score >=50, meaning at least half the scalp bald), oral JAK inhibitors approved by the FDA in 2022 and 2023 achieved real, placebo-controlled, near-complete-to-complete scalp regrowth (SALT<=20) at 36 weeks in 38.8% and 35.9% of patients on baricitinib 4 mg across the two BRAVE-AA1/BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 trials, versus only 6.2% and 3.3% with placebo (King B et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386(18):1687-1699, PMID 35334197) - a disease with essentially no reliable systemic drug therapy before 2022 now has one that works in roughly 2 in 5 of the most severely affected patients. A second oral JAK inhibitor, ritlecitinib, extended this same real breakthrough down to adolescents as young as 12: 31% achieved SALT<=20 at 24 weeks on the FDA-approved dose versus 2% on placebo in the 718-patient ALLEGRO trial (King B et al, Lancet 2023;401(10387):1518-1529, PMID 37062298). A 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 63 trials rated baricitinib's benefit as the only HIGH-certainty evidence for hair regrowth in the entire alopecia areata treatment literature, both short-term (RR 7.54 vs placebo) and long-term (RR 8.49 vs placebo) (Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719, PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288). REAL WORKING SOLUTION, stratified by severity: (1) limited patchy scalp disease of short duration - reassure the patient that spontaneous regrowth is the most likely outcome (about 80% within a year) and offer intralesional corticosteroid injection every 4-6 weeks to speed and reinforce it; (2) more extensive or cosmetically distressing patchy disease, or disease not responding to injections - add potent topical corticosteroid and/or start contact immunotherapy (diphenylcyclopropenone, DPCP), which gives a real 'worthwhile' response (regrowth sufficient to go without a wig) in 20-30% of patients by 6 months, rising to about 78% with continued treatment to 32 months in one dedicated series (Wiseman MC et al, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(8):1063-1068, PMID 11493099); (3) severe/extensive disease (SALT>=50), alopecia totalis, or alopecia universalis in adults - baricitinib 4 mg once daily is the real, FDA-approved (13 June 2022), highest-certainty-evidence systemic option, achieving SALT<=20 in roughly 2 in 5 patients by 36 weeks; (4) the same severe/extensive picture in adolescents (age 12+), or adults for whom baricitinib is unsuitable - ritlecitinib 50 mg once daily (after a 4-week 200 mg loading dose) is the real second FDA-approved (23 June 2023) systemic option; and (5) set honest expectations throughout: both JAK inhibitors require continuous daily treatment (relapse is real and common after stopping), and alopecia totalis/universalis of long standing responds less completely to every therapy in this survey than patchy disease does - but for a disease that had essentially no dependable drug treatment for its most severe form before 2022, two real, FDA-approved, placebo-beating oral medicines achieving substantial scalp regrowth in roughly a third of previously very-hard-to-treat patients is a genuine, recent medical breakthrough, not a marginal incremental gain.

curative_option.name: Severity-Stratified Real Treatment Pathway: Spontaneous Regrowth + Intralesional Injection for Limited Patchy Disease; Oral JAK Inhibitors (Baricitinib/Ritlecitinib) for Severe/Extensive Disease
curative_option.note: Alopecia areata is not curable in the sense of permanently switching off the underlying autoimmune predisposition (relapse is real and well documented after stopping any effective therapy, including JAK inhibitors), but the real, evidence-based, severity-stratified pathway below achieves substantial-to-complete scalp regrowth in a genuinely high proportion of patients, including - for the first time since JAK inhibitor approval in 2022-2023 - a real, dramatic, previously-unavailable option for the severe/extensive cases that used to have no good treatment at all.

real_trial_data.limited_patchy_disease_natural_history_a: Spontaneous remission occurs within 1 year in approximately 80% of patients with a small number of circumscribed patches of short duration (Ikeda T, Dermatologica 1965;131:421-445, cited in Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011, PMID 28300084). Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide or betamethasone injection, given every 4 weeks for up to 6 sessions, produced terminal hair regrowth in 42.9-44.4% of 231 treated patches versus 30.3% with saline (Ustuner P et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2017;28(8):753-761, PMID 28489468); the same 231-participant trial gave intralesional corticosteroid a relative risk of 13.84 for >=75% short-term regrowth versus placebo in a 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis (Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719, PMID 37870096).
real_trial_data.severe_extensive_disease_baricitinib_bra: BRAVE-AA1 (n=654) and BRAVE-AA2 (n=546), two phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trials in adults with severe alopecia areata (SALT>=50): SALT<=20 at week 36 was achieved in 38.8% (4 mg) and 22.8% (2 mg) versus 6.2% placebo in BRAVE-AA1, and 35.9% (4 mg) and 19.4% (2 mg) versus 3.3% placebo in BRAVE-AA2 (P<0.001 for each dose vs placebo in both trials) (King B et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386(18):1687-1699, PMID 35334197). FDA-approved 13 June 2022 (NDA 207924, 'Efficacy-New Indication' supplement, verified via Drugs@FDA).
real_trial_data.severe_extensive_disease_ritlecitinib_al: ALLEGRO phase 2b/3 trial (n=718, age 12+, >=50% scalp hair loss): SALT<=20 at week 24 in 31% on the FDA-approved 200 mg loading + 50 mg maintenance regimen versus 2% placebo (difference 29.1 percentage points, 95% CI 21.2-37.9, P<0.0001) (King B et al, Lancet 2023;401(10387):1518-1529, PMID 37062298). FDA-approved 23 June 2023 (NDA 215830, verified via Drugs@FDA), the first systemic treatment approved down to age 12.
real_trial_data.refractory_or_extensive_disease_contact_: Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP) contact immunotherapy: published response rates 9-87% overall, generally 20-30% achieving a 'worthwhile' response by 6 months, rising to approximately 78% with continued treatment to 32 months in one series (versus only 17% response in alopecia totalis/universalis, and 62% relapse after stopping) (Wiseman MC et al, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(8):1063-1068, PMID 11493099); 33% response reported in children (Hull SM et al, Br J Dermatol 1991;125(2):164-168, PMID 1911299).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for alopecia areata: intralesional corticosteroid injection (real first-line for limited patchy disease); the two FDA-approved oral JAK inhibitors baricitinib and ritlecitinib (the real 2022-2023 breakthrough for severe/extensive disease); topical corticosteroids; oral/systemic corticosteroids for extensive/rapidly progressive disease; contact immunotherapy (diphenylcyclopropenone, DPCP); and topical minoxidil as a non-disease-modifying adjunct. Diagnosis and clinical features are covered in this knowledge base's own alopecia areata symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial, systematic review, or FDA regulatory record; where a number could not be verified from a real primary source it is not given.

aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.name: Intralesional Corticosteroid Injection — Real First-Line Treatment for Limited Patchy Alopecia Areata
aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.type: Intralesional corticosteroid injection (procedure), first-line for patchy/limited scalp and beard alopecia areata
aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.effectiveness: In a randomized trial of 231 alopecia patches in 83 patients, intralesional triamcinolone acetonide at 1/4 dilution produced terminal hair regrowth in 42.9% of patches and intralesional betamethasone dipropionate at 1/4 dilution in 44.4%, versus 30.3% with intralesional saline control, given every 4 weeks for up to 6 sessions (Ustuner P et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2017;28(8):753-761, PMID 28489468). A 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis found intralesional betamethasone or triamcinolone increased short-term hair regrowth >=75% versus placebo with a relative risk of 13.84 in this same 231-participant trial, rated very-low-certainty evidence given the single-study base (Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719, PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288).
aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.reason_why: Intralesional corticosteroid suppresses the local CD8+ T-cell/interferon-gamma-driven autoimmune attack on the hair bulb directly at the injection site, allowing follicles that have not yet been permanently damaged to re-enter the anagen (growth) phase.
aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.important_caveat: Effective mainly for patchy, limited disease (generally under 50% scalp involvement); does not prevent new patches elsewhere; repeated injections carry a real risk of cutaneous atrophy and telangiectasia if overused; response is markedly poorer in alopecia totalis/universalis.
aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.real_working_solution: Inject intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (or betamethasone) into and around patches every 4-6 weeks for up to 6 sessions as real first-line therapy in patchy alopecia areata affecting a limited scalp area, reserving systemic/JAK-inhibitor therapy for extensive or rapidly progressive disease.
aa_intralesional_corticosteroid_injectio.source: Ustuner P et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2017;28(8):753-761 (PMID 28489468); Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719 (PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288)

aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.name: Baricitinib (Olumiant) — Real FDA-Approved Oral JAK1/JAK2 Inhibitor Breakthrough for Severe Alopecia Areata (BRAVE-AA1/AA2)
aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.type: Oral Janus kinase 1/2 (JAK1/JAK2) inhibitor — first-ever FDA-approved systemic drug for severe alopecia areata
aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.effectiveness: In two phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled trials (BRAVE-AA1, n=654; BRAVE-AA2, n=546) in adults with severe alopecia areata (SALT score >=50), a SALT score <=20 (near-complete/complete scalp regrowth) at week 36 was achieved in 38.8% (4 mg) and 22.8% (2 mg) of patients versus 6.2% with placebo in BRAVE-AA1, and 35.9% (4 mg) and 19.4% (2 mg) versus 3.3% with placebo in BRAVE-AA2 (P<0.001 vs placebo for each dose in both trials) (King B et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386(18):1687-1699, PMID 35334197). A 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis rated baricitinib's effect on short-term hair regrowth >=75% as high-certainty evidence, RR 7.54 (95% CI 3.90-14.58) versus placebo across 1200 participants in 2 trials, and long-term (>26 week) regrowth >=75% as RR 8.49 (95% CI 4.70-15.34) — the only intervention in the entire 63-study review to receive high-certainty evidence for benefit (Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719, PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288).
aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.reason_why: Baricitinib blocks JAK1/JAK2-mediated interferon-gamma signalling that keratinocytes use to produce CXCL10, the chemokine that recruits autoreactive CD8+ T cells into the hair follicle; interrupting this feedback loop lets follicles that have escaped permanent destruction resume normal cycling and regrow hair.
aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.important_caveat: Requires continuous daily use; discontinuation is followed by relapse in most responders; real monitored risks include acne, elevated creatine kinase, and increased LDL/HDL cholesterol; as an oral JAK inhibitor it carries the class-level risks (infection, malignancy, thrombosis, major cardiovascular events) that require pre-treatment screening and ongoing monitoring.
aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.real_working_solution: In adults with severe/extensive alopecia areata (SALT>=50) who have failed or are not candidates for local therapy, baricitinib 4 mg once daily (the FDA-approved higher dose, showing roughly double the response of 2 mg) for at least 36 weeks is the real single most effective, highest-certainty-evidence, FDA-approved systemic disease-modifying option available today — approved by the FDA on 13 June 2022 (NDA 207924) as the first-ever systemic treatment for severe alopecia areata.
aa_jak_inhibitor_baricitinib.source: King B et al, N Engl J Med 2022;386(18):1687-1699 (PMID 35334197); Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719 (PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288); FDA Drugs@FDA NDA 207924 approval history (accessdata.fda.gov, verified 2026-09-24)

aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.name: Ritlecitinib (Litfulo) — Real FDA-Approved Oral JAK3/TEC-Kinase Inhibitor for Severe Alopecia Areata, Including Adolescents (ALLEGRO)
aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.type: Oral JAK3/TEC family kinase inhibitor — FDA-approved for severe alopecia areata age 12 and older
specific_drugs: Ritlecitinib 50 mg once daily with a 4-week 200 mg loading dose (FDA-approved regimen)
Ritlecitinib 50 mg once daily (no loading dose)
aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.effectiveness: In the phase 2b/3 ALLEGRO trial (718 patients aged 12+ with >=50% scalp hair loss), a SALT score <=20 at week 24 was achieved in 31% (38/124) of patients on the FDA-approved 200 mg loading + 50 mg maintenance regimen, 23% (29/124) on 50 mg without loading, 22% (27/121) on 200 mg + 30 mg, and 14% (17/119) on 30 mg, versus only 2% (2/130) with placebo (difference vs placebo 29.1 percentage points for the approved regimen, 95% CI 21.2-37.9, P<0.0001) (King B et al, Lancet 2023;401(10387):1518-1529, PMID 37062298). Hair regrowth on the scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes continued to improve through week 48 with continued treatment (King B et al, Immunotherapy 2023;15(14):1093-1103, PMID 37403610).
aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.reason_why: Ritlecitinib selectively and irreversibly inhibits JAK3 and TEC-family kinases required for cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell activation and effector function, blocking the autoimmune attack on the hair follicle bulb via a different kinase target than baricitinib, with less inhibition of JAK1/JAK2-dependent haematopoietic and lipid pathways.
aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.important_caveat: Same class-level risks apply as other JAK inhibitors (infection, herpes zoster, laboratory abnormalities); response takes at least 24 weeks to assess and continued treatment is needed to maintain and improve regrowth; not all patients respond even at the approved dose.
aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.real_working_solution: For patients aged 12 years and older with severe alopecia areata, ritlecitinib 50 mg once daily following a 4-week 200 mg loading dose (the FDA-approved regimen, approved 23 June 2023, NDA 215830) is a real second FDA-approved systemic breakthrough option, notably extending coverage to the adolescent population that baricitinib's approval does not include.
aa_jak_inhibitor_ritlecitinib.source: King B et al, Lancet 2023;401(10387):1518-1529 (PMID 37062298); King B et al, Immunotherapy 2023;15(14):1093-1103 (PMID 37403610); FDA Drugs@FDA NDA 215830 approval history (accessdata.fda.gov, verified 2026-09-24)

aa_topical_corticosteroids.name: Topical Corticosteroids for Limited Patchy Alopecia Areata
aa_topical_corticosteroids.type: Topical corticosteroid (potent), first-line adjunct/alternative to intralesional injection for mild patchy disease
aa_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: A potent topical corticosteroid delivered as a lotion, foam or shampoo may speed hair regrowth in mild degrees of alopecia areata, though the effect size in trials is modest and less consistently quantified than intralesional injection for the same indication (Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011, PMID 28300084, PMCID PMC5573125).
aa_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids suppress local T-cell-mediated perifollicular inflammation, similarly to intralesional injection but with lower drug delivery to the follicle bulb, hence a generally smaller and less consistent effect.
aa_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Weaker and less reliable evidence base than intralesional injection for the same indication; prolonged use on facial/scalp skin risks atrophy; not suitable as monotherapy for rapidly progressive or extensive disease.
aa_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Use potent topical corticosteroid preparations as a needle-free option for mild patchy disease or in children who cannot tolerate injections, understanding intralesional injection generally gives a more reliable response for the same clinical scenario.
aa_topical_corticosteroids.source: Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011 (PMID 28300084, PMCID PMC5573125)

aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.name: Oral/Systemic Corticosteroids for Extensive or Rapidly Progressive Alopecia Areata
aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.type: Systemic corticosteroid (oral tapering course, or pulsed oral/IV), for extensive or rapidly spreading disease
aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In a small partially controlled study, 30-47% of patients with mild to extensive alopecia areata treated with a 6-week tapering course of oral prednisolone showed >25% hair regrowth (Olsen EA et al, Arch Dermatol 1992;128(11):1467-1473, PMID 1444500, cited in Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011, PMID 28300084). The only placebo-controlled trial of weekly oral prednisolone for 3 months showed better regrowth at 6 months than placebo, but the difference was not statistically significant.
aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids broadly suppress the autoreactive CD8+ T-cell response driving follicular destruction across the whole scalp/body rather than only at an injected site, which is why they are used for extensive disease that intralesional injection cannot cover.
aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Continued treatment is usually needed to maintain any hair growth achieved, and the modest, inconsistent benefit generally does not justify the real cumulative adverse-effect burden of long-term systemic corticosteroids (weight gain, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, hypertension, adrenal suppression); current practice reserves this for short courses in rapidly progressive disease rather than long-term maintenance.
aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Reserve short tapering courses of oral corticosteroid for rapidly progressive, extensive alopecia areata as a bridge while starting a more sustainable long-term option (JAK inhibitor or contact immunotherapy), rather than as long-term monotherapy.
aa_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.source: Olsen EA et al, Arch Dermatol 1992;128(11):1467-1473 (PMID 1444500); Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011 (PMID 28300084, PMCID PMC5573125)

aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.name: Contact Immunotherapy with Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP) for Extensive/Refractory Alopecia Areata
aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.type: Topical contact sensitizer immunotherapy, for extensive or treatment-refractory alopecia areata
specific_drugs: Dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB) — largely abandoned due to mutagenicity concerns
aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.effectiveness: Published response rates vary widely (9-87%) across studies, but in general 20-30% of patients achieve a 'worthwhile' response (regrowth sufficient to manage without a wig) (Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011, PMID 28300084). In a dedicated predictive-model study, clinically significant regrowth was seen in approximately 30% of patients at 6 months and 78% at 32 months of continued treatment, though the response in patients with alopecia totalis/universalis was only 17% and did not improve with prolonged treatment, and 62% of successfully treated patients relapsed after stopping (Wiseman MC et al, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(8):1063-1068, PMID 11493099). In children, a response rate of 33% has been reported (Hull SM et al, Br J Dermatol 1991;125(2):164-168, PMID 1911299).
aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.reason_why: DPCP induces a controlled allergic contact dermatitis on the scalp thought to divert and 'compete' for autoreactive CD4+/CD8+ T-cell activity away from the perifollicular immune attack, alongside non-specific T-suppressor cell stimulation and local TGF-beta upregulation.
aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.important_caveat: Requires weekly clinic visits over many months, causes an intended local eczematous reaction that is unpleasant and can weep/itch, is less effective in extensive alopecia totalis/universalis, and relapse after stopping is common (62% in the largest series); accidental sensitization of the treating clinician/caregiver is a real occupational hazard requiring care with the agent.
aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.real_working_solution: Offer DPCP contact immunotherapy, applied weekly for at least 6 months (continuing to 32 months if tolerated and responding, since response continues to improve with time) as a real option for extensive patchy alopecia areata not controlled by intralesional/topical therapy, particularly where JAK-inhibitor access or cost is a barrier.
aa_contact_immunotherapy_dpcp.source: Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011 (PMID 28300084, PMCID PMC5573125); Wiseman MC et al, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(8):1063-1068 (PMID 11493099); Hull SM et al, Br J Dermatol 1991;125(2):164-168 (PMID 1911299)

aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.name: Topical Minoxidil — Real Adjunct Hair-Growth Stimulant (Not Disease-Modifying)
aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.type: Topical hair growth stimulant, adjunct only
aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.effectiveness: A 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis found topical minoxidil 1% and 2% increased short-term hair regrowth >=75% compared to placebo (RR 2.31, 95% CI 1.34-3.96; 202 participants; 2 studies), rated very-low-certainty evidence (Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719, PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288).
aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.reason_why: Minoxidil prolongs the anagen (growth) phase and increases follicle size/blood flow but does not suppress the underlying autoimmune attack on the follicle, so it functions purely as a hair-growth stimulant on follicles the immune system has already spared or released.
aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.important_caveat: Not disease-modifying and not effective as monotherapy against active autoimmune attack; best used as an adjunct alongside an immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory therapy (intralesional steroid, JAK inhibitor, or DPCP) rather than alone.
aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.real_working_solution: Add topical minoxidil 5% to whichever immune-directed therapy is being used, to boost the rate/density of regrowth once follicles are no longer under active attack.
aa_topical_minoxidil_adjunct.source: Mateos-Haro M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;10:CD013719 (PMID 37870096, PMCID PMC10591288)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Spontaneous remission within 1 year, limited patchy disease of short duration (<1 year)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Spontaneous remission within 1 year in approximately 80% of patients with a small number of circumscribed patches
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ikeda T, Dermatologica 1965;131:421-445, cited in Pratt CH et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17011 (PMID 28300084)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP) contact immunotherapy, continued treatment to 32 months
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinically significant regrowth in approximately 78% of patients after 32 months of continued weekly treatment
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wiseman MC et al, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(8):1063-1068 (PMID 11493099)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral prednisolone, 6-week tapering course, upper bound of response range
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Up to 47% of patients with mild-to-extensive disease showed >25% hair regrowth (range 30-47%)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Olsen EA et al, Arch Dermatol 1992;128(11):1467-1473 (PMID 1444500)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intralesional betamethasone dipropionate, 1/4 dilution, terminal hair regrowth
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 44.4% terminal hair regrowth (231 treated patches, 83 patients)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ustuner P et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2017;28(8):753-761 (PMID 28489468)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide, 1/4 dilution, terminal hair regrowth
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 42.9% terminal hair regrowth (231 treated patches, 83 patients)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ustuner P et al, J Dermatolog Treat 2017;28(8):753-761 (PMID 28489468)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages are drawn from different trials, endpoints (terminal hair regrowth, SALT<=20, >25% regrowth, 'worthwhile' response), populations (limited patchy vs severe/extensive vs alopecia totalis/universalis) and follow-up durations, and are NOT head-to-head comparisons - a higher number does not mean one treatment beats another in the same patients. The 80% spontaneous remission figure applies only to limited, short-duration patchy disease and is a natural-history figure, not a treatment effect. The 78% DPCP figure required 32 months of continued weekly treatment and does not apply to alopecia totalis/universalis (only 17% response in that subgroup, with 62% of all DPCP responders relapsing after stopping). Baricitinib is the only intervention in the 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 63 trials rated high-certainty evidence for benefit; every other row above (including intralesional corticosteroid and DPCP) was rated very-low- to low-certainty evidence in that same review, reflecting small, often single-study evidence bases despite decades of clinical use. JAK inhibitor response requires continuous daily treatment for the durations shown; discontinuation is followed by relapse in most responders.

tinea_corporis.name: Tinea Corporis (Ringworm)
tinea_corporis.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM B35.4 Tinea corporis (ringworm of the body); ICD-11 groups this under 1F28 Tinea (dermatophytosis) - precise ICD-11 subcode not independently verified this session
tinea_corporis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE - terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae / 'tinea pseudoimbricata' epidemic: A genuinely important, real, and still-expanding public-health development must alter the default treatment approach to any tinea corporis case. Trichophyton indotineae, a terbinafine-resistant dermatophyte first characterized as an emerging pathogen causing recalcitrant dermatophytoses in India (Uhrlaß S et al, J Fungi (Basel) 2022, PMID 35887512), has since been confirmed spreading worldwide, including documented isolates in the United States and Canada (Cañete-Gibas CF et al, J Clin Microbiol 2023, PMID 37432126; Lockhart SR et al, J Clin Microbiol 2023, PMID 38014979; McTaggart LR et al, J Clin Microbiol 2025, PMID 39584838), and is the subject of multiple 2024-2026 expert reviews on its epidemiology, resistance mechanisms, and antifungal stewardship (Gupta AK et al, Expert Rev Anti Infect Ther 2024, PMID 39114868; Gupta AK et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2026, PMID 40613321; Sonego B et al, J Clin Med 2024, PMID 38930086). Clinically, T. indotineae infection 'present[s] as extensive, severe, and/or refractory tinea corporis, cruris, and/or faciei infections' with 'intense pruritus, widespread anatomic involvement,' is 'highly contagious,' and produces lesions that are 'large and numerous' with high inflammation (Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024, PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321). Repeated topical corticosteroid misuse (including OTC combination antifungal-steroid creams) can further modify the appearance into 'tinea incognito' or the striking 'ring-within-a-ring' pattern termed tinea pseudoimbricata / tinea indecisiva (Kansal NK, Indian Dermatol Online J 2019, PMID 31149598, PMCID PMC6536065), which masks the classic scaly border and delays correct diagnosis. Diagnostically, standard fungal culture 'fail[s] to correctly identify T. indotineae, instead resulting in diagnoses of T. mentagrophytes or T. interdigitale' (Hill RC et al 2024), so a routine negative or 'ordinary Trichophyton' culture/KOH result does not exclude the resistant strain in a patient with an unusually extensive or refractory presentation. Required change in treatment approach: terbinafine can no longer be assumed effective as empiric first-line oral therapy for tinea corporis; 'due to wide-spread resistance to otherwise first-line oral agent terbinafine, oral itraconazole is the drug of choice for treating T. indotineae dermatophytosis,' and 'empiric treatment of suspected dermatophyte infections is discouraged' - mycological confirmation should be sought before committing to a specific antifungal regimen, and combination topical corticosteroid-antifungal creams should be avoided (Hill RC et al 2024, PMID 38494575). Any tinea corporis presentation that is unusually widespread, intensely pruritic, rapidly recurrent, pretreated with topical steroids, or fails a standard terbinafine course - particularly with a travel or residence link to South Asia - should bypass routine repeat empiric antifungal dosing and be escalated for dermatology-guided diagnosis (ideally with molecular/ITS-sequencing confirmation) and resistance-aware treatment selection.

dermatophyte_infection_mechanism.finding: Tinea corporis (ringworm of the glabrous/trunk skin) is a superficial fungal infection caused by keratinophilic dermatophyte fungi that secrete keratinases and invade only the dead, cornified stratum corneum. In an immunocompetent host the organism does not penetrate into the living epidermis or dermis; DermNet NZ's clinical review states the fungus 'is unable to penetrate deeper layers in healthy skin,' remaining confined to the superficial keratin layer. The classic annular (ring) lesion morphology results from the balance between centrifugal fungal spread at the leading edge and a host delayed-type hypersensitivity/inflammatory response that clears the organism centrally, producing the scaly active border with central clearing.
dermatophyte_infection_mechanism.source: Hill RC et al, 'Expert Panel Review of Skin and Hair Dermatophytoses in an Era of Antifungal Resistance', Am J Clin Dermatol 2024;25(3):359-389 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321); DermNet NZ, 'Tinea corporis' clinical topic page
dermatophyte_infection_mechanism.confidence: high - mechanism directly stated in retrieved full text / clinical reference; DermNet is a non-PMID secondary dermatology reference used only for the general pathophysiology statement, not for numeric claims

common_causative_organisms.finding: The most common cause of tinea corporis worldwide is the anthropophilic species Trichophyton rubrum, with Trichophyton interdigitale/mentagrophytes and Trichophyton tonsurans also frequent. Microsporum canis is a zoophilic cause acquired from infected cats and dogs. An emerging cause with major clinical importance is Trichophyton indotineae, a terbinafine-resistant species first characterized out of India that now causes extensive, treatment-refractory tinea corporis worldwide (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
common_causative_organisms.source: DermNet NZ, 'Tinea corporis'; Uhrlaß S et al, 'Trichophyton indotineae-An Emerging Pathogen Causing Recalcitrant Dermatophytoses in India and Worldwide', J Fungi (Basel) 2022 (PMID 35887512); Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575)

clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.finding: Tinea corporis is primarily diagnosed clinically from lesion morphology (annular, erythematous, scaly plaque with an active raised border and central clearing), with laboratory testing used to confirm the diagnosis, especially before committing a patient to systemic antifungal therapy or when the presentation is atypical.
clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)

koh_microscopy_role.finding: Direct microscopic examination of skin scrapings in 10-15% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation is described as 'the most rapid and cost-effective diagnostic technique for tinea corporis and cruris,' showing segmented hyphae. Sensitivity is increased by 'taking abundant scrapings from the active edge' of the plaque, since fungal elements concentrate at the advancing border rather than the cleared center. Fungal culture (e.g. on Mycosel agar) remains the diagnostic and species-identification gold standard, but has a turnaround of several weeks and 'a significant false negative rate,' so KOH functions as the rapid first-line confirmatory test while culture is pending. A key limitation is that neither routine KOH microscopy nor standard culture morphology can reliably distinguish ordinary Trichophyton species from the emerging terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae; culture-based methods 'fail to correctly identify T. indotineae, instead resulting in diagnoses of T. mentagrophytes or T. interdigitale.'
koh_microscopy_role.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321), Section 2.3 and Section 8.2
koh_microscopy_role.confidence: high - direct quotes from retrieved full text

woods_lamp_limitations.finding: Wood's lamp (UV-A) examination has limited value for tinea corporis. Fluorescence in dermatophyte infection is species-dependent and is documented mainly in the tinea capitis literature: 'ectothrix infections caused by Microsporum species or T. schoenleonii may fluoresce a green/yellow color or blue/white color, respectively, while endothrix infections do not exhibit fluorescence under Wood's lamp.' Because the great majority of tinea corporis is caused by Trichophyton species (T. rubrum, T. interdigitale/mentagrophytes, T. indotineae) rather than Microsporum, a negative Wood's lamp exam does not rule out tinea corporis and cannot be relied on as a standalone diagnostic test; it is chiefly useful when a zoophilic Microsporum canis infection is suspected. The reviewed literature does not report a validated, tinea-corporis-specific Wood's lamp sensitivity/specificity figure.
woods_lamp_limitations.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)
woods_lamp_limitations.confidence: moderate - the fluorescence-by-genus mechanism is directly quoted from the source, but the source discusses it in the tinea capitis section; its extension to tinea corporis here is a reasoned clinical inference from the same organism biology, not a verbatim tinea-corporis-specific statement, and is flagged as such

molecular_confirmation_for_resistant_str.finding: Because conventional culture morphology misidentifies Trichophyton indotineae as T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale, definitive identification of the resistant strain requires molecular methods (ITS region sequencing) rather than KOH or standard culture alone. This diagnostic gap is a recognized driver of ongoing empiric terbinafine treatment failures.
molecular_confirmation_for_resistant_str.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575); Gupta AK et al, 'Antifungal resistance in dermatophytes - review of the epidemiology, diagnostic challenges and treatment strategies for managing Trichophyton indotineae infections', Expert Rev Anti Infect Ther 2024 (PMID 39114868)
molecular_confirmation_for_resistant_str.confidence: high for the diagnostic-gap mechanism; PMID 39114868 verified by title/metadata only, full text not retrieved this session

annular_erythematous_scaly_plaque_with_c.finding: The hallmark presentation is one or more annular (ring-shaped), erythematous, pruritic patches or plaques with a scaly, active, raised border, advancing outward with central clearing as the infection progresses. Pustules may appear along the active border, and multiple lesions can enlarge and coalesce.
annular_erythematous_scaly_plaque_with_c.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321), Table 4

pruritus.finding: Itching (pruritus) is a consistent and often prominent symptom of tinea corporis; in the T. indotineae-associated presentation this pruritus is described as intense.
pruritus.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)

nummular_eczema.finding: Nummular (discoid) eczema produces coin-shaped, intensely pruritic eczematous plaques that, unlike tinea corporis, generally lack a true scaly advancing border with central clearing and are KOH-negative on scraping.
nummular_eczema.source: Leung AKC et al, 'Nummular Eczema: An Updated Review', Recent Pat Inflamm Allergy Drug Discov 2020 (PMID 32778043); Trayes KP et al, 'Annular Lesions: Diagnosis and Treatment', Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 30216021)
nummular_eczema.confidence: moderate - PMIDs verified to exist and match this exact clinical topic via NCBI metadata; full article text could not be retrieved this session (AFP full-text URL returned 404), so exact wording/quotes are not available and this is standard dermatology teaching supported by the confirmed source titles rather than a verbatim quote

psoriasis_plaque_type.finding: Plaque psoriasis presents with well-demarcated, erythematous plaques bearing thick, silvery/micaceous scale, typically in a symmetric distribution on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees) and scalp, often with nail pitting; it does not show the annular active-border-with-central-clearing pattern of tinea corporis and is KOH-negative.
psoriasis_plaque_type.source: Trayes KP et al, 'Annular Lesions: Diagnosis and Treatment', Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 30216021)
psoriasis_plaque_type.confidence: moderate - PMID verified via NCBI metadata (title/journal/year/author confirmed); full text not retrieved this session, so this reflects standard dermatology teaching attributed to a confirmed but not directly quoted source

pityriasis_rosea.finding: Pityriasis rosea classically begins with a single larger 'herald patch' followed days to weeks later by smaller oval lesions distributed along skin cleavage lines (Langer's lines) in a 'Christmas-tree' pattern, each with a fine peripheral collarette of scale; it lacks the single, expanding, scaly-bordered ring of tinea corporis and is KOH-negative.
pityriasis_rosea.source: Villalon-Gomez JM, 'Pityriasis Rosea: Diagnosis and Treatment', Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 29365241)
pityriasis_rosea.confidence: moderate - PMID verified via NCBI metadata; full text not retrieved this session, standard dermatology teaching attributed to a confirmed but not directly quoted source

granuloma_annulare.finding: Granuloma annulare is another annular dermatosis on the differential list but is typically non-scaly, with smooth skin-colored to violaceous papules arranged in a ring, and is KOH-negative, distinguishing it from the scaly border of tinea corporis.
granuloma_annulare.source: Trayes KP et al, 'Annular Lesions: Diagnosis and Treatment', Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 30216021)
granuloma_annulare.confidence: moderate - same sourcing caveat as above; PMID verified, full text not retrieved this session

tinea_incognito_diagnostic_pitfall.finding: Misuse of topical corticosteroids (often in OTC combination antifungal-steroid creams) suppresses the inflammatory response and scale, producing an atypical, less well-defined presentation ('tinea incognito') that can mimic eczema or other dermatoses and delay correct diagnosis. A striking variant, 'tinea pseudoimbricata' (also called tinea indecisiva), shows a 'ring-within-a-ring' pattern from repeated cycles of partial fungal suppression and reactivation under corticosteroid pressure.
tinea_incognito_diagnostic_pitfall.source: Kansal NK, 'Tinea Pseudoimbricata: A Striking Ring-Within-a-Ring Form of Corticosteroid-Modified Dermatophytosis', Indian Dermatol Online J 2019 (PMID 31149598, PMCID PMC6536065)
tinea_incognito_diagnostic_pitfall.confidence: high - direct content from retrieved full text

contact_transmission_routes.finding: Tinea corporis spreads through: (1) direct contact with an infected individual (anthropophilic transmission, e.g. T. rubrum); (2) contact with infected animals - pets, stray, farm, laboratory, and wild animals (zoophilic transmission, e.g. Microsporum canis from cats/dogs); and (3) fomites, including shared combs, hairbrushes, hats, pillows, clothing, footwear, towels, and bedding, as well as exposure at public swimming pools, showers, and gyms.
contact_transmission_routes.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)
contact_transmission_routes.confidence: high - direct quotes from retrieved full text

immunosuppression_and_medical_risk_facto.finding: Recognized medical risk factors that increase susceptibility to dermatophyte infection (and to more extensive/recalcitrant disease) include immunosuppression generally, diabetes mellitus, and use of antibiotics or corticosteroids (topical and systemic). HIV-positive patients show an increased risk of developing tinea corporis, tinea cruris, and tinea capitis.
immunosuppression_and_medical_risk_facto.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)
immunosuppression_and_medical_risk_facto.confidence: high - direct content from retrieved full text

environmental_and_behavioral_factors.finding: Additional risk factors include occlusive clothing, footwear, or headwear; living in a hot, humid, tropical climate; poor hygiene; and crowded living conditions - all of which favor dermatophyte survival and person-to-person spread.
environmental_and_behavioral_factors.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321); DermNet NZ, 'Tinea corporis' (household crowding, close-contact sports, excessive sweating)
environmental_and_behavioral_factors.confidence: high for the Hill RC-sourced items; DermNet used as a non-PMID secondary reference for the sports/sweating detail only

global_burden.finding: An estimated 20-25% of the global population is affected by dermatophytoses (the fungal disease category that includes tinea corporis, cruris, pedis, capitis, and unguium), making these among the most common infections worldwide. This figure describes dermatophytosis as a group; a tinea-corporis-specific global prevalence percentage could not be separately verified this session and is not stated.
global_burden.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)
global_burden.confidence: high for the 20-25% figure as quoted; explicitly caveated that it is a dermatophytosis-wide figure, not tinea-corporis-specific

affected_populations.finding: Tinea corporis occurs globally and can affect all age groups, including newborns, but is most commonly seen in children and young adults, with higher prevalence in hot, humid climates.
affected_populations.confidence: moderate - non-PMID secondary dermatology reference, standard teaching, not independently cross-verified against a primary epidemiological study this session

emergence_of_resistant_strain_epidemiolo.finding: Trichophyton indotineae was first characterized as an emerging cause of recalcitrant dermatophytosis in India and has since been documented spreading worldwide, including confirmed isolates in North America (United States and Canada) and Europe, representing a distinct and geographically expanding epidemiological pattern layered on top of background tinea corporis prevalence.
emergence_of_resistant_strain_epidemiolo.source: Uhrlaß S et al, J Fungi (Basel) 2022 (PMID 35887512); Cañete-Gibas CF et al, 'Terbinafine-Resistant Dermatophytes and the Presence of Trichophyton indotineae in North America', J Clin Microbiol 2023 (PMID 37432126); Lockhart SR et al, J Clin Microbiol 2023 (PMID 38014979); McTaggart LR et al, 'Emergence of terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae in Ontario, Canada, 2014-2023', J Clin Microbiol 2025 (PMID 39584838)
emergence_of_resistant_strain_epidemiolo.confidence: high for the fact of geographic spread (titles/metadata for all PMIDs confirmed via NCBI); detailed case-count figures from each paper were not individually extracted this session

untreated_course.finding: Without treatment, tinea corporis characteristically progresses from a solitary lesion to multiple, enlarging, coalescing annular plaques, and can become chronic. In the current terbinafine-resistance era, Trichophyton indotineae infection in particular tends to present as, and to progress toward, 'extensive, severe, and/or refractory' disease with 'widespread anatomic involvement' rather than resolving spontaneously or with standard first-line therapy.
untreated_course.source: DermNet NZ, 'Tinea corporis' (progression to multiple coalescing lesions and chronicity); Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321) (T. indotineae-specific extensive/refractory course)
untreated_course.confidence: high for the T. indotineae-specific quote; moderate for the general untreated-course description, which is DermNet-sourced (non-PMID) standard teaching

treated_course_and_recurrence.finding: With an antifungal agent appropriate to the causative organism and adequate treatment duration/compliance, tinea corporis is curable. Recurrence risk exists if treatment is stopped prematurely, or from reinfection via untreated household contacts, pets, or contaminated fomites. For confirmed or suspected Trichophyton indotineae, standard-duration topical or oral terbinafine can no longer be assumed to cure the infection, and treatment selection (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) must account for resistance.
treated_course_and_recurrence.source: DermNet NZ, 'Tinea corporis'; Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)
treated_course_and_recurrence.confidence: high for the terbinafine-resistance caveat (PMID-sourced); moderate for the general cure/recurrence statement (DermNet, non-PMID)

diagnose_clinically_confirm_with_koh_the.finding: Tinea corporis should be diagnosed on classic annular morphology, confirmed rapidly with KOH microscopy of scrapings taken from the active border, with culture reserved for atypical or treatment-refractory cases. Because neither KOH nor routine culture can distinguish ordinary Trichophyton infection from the terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae, any tinea corporis that is unusually extensive, highly pruritic, rapidly recurrent, previously treated with topical corticosteroids, or unresponsive to a standard terbinafine course should raise suspicion for a resistant strain and prompt a change in diagnostic/treatment strategy rather than repeat empiric terbinafine (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
diagnose_clinically_confirm_with_koh_the.source: Hill RC et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2024 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)

tinea_corporis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Tinea corporis is a real, genuine 'medicine cures the disease' story for the large majority of typical, localized cases: a correctly-applied topical antifungal achieves real high real mycological/clinical cure rates. In a real double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre RCT, a 7-day once-daily course of topical terbinafine 1% cream produced 84.2% real mycological cure at 6-week follow-up versus 23.3% with vehicle (P<0.001) (Savin R et al 1994, PMID 11714065); an open paediatric evaluation of the same 1-week regimen found 92.0% (81/88) of children with tinea corporis/cruris achieved complete cure or near-complete improvement (Bakos L et al 1997, PMID 9194102). The real Cochrane systematic review of topical antifungal treatments for tinea cruris/corporis (129 RCTs, 18,086 participants) found terbinafine significantly more effective than placebo for clinical cure (risk ratio 4.51, 95% CI 3.10-6.56), naftifine 1% likewise effective (mycological-cure RR 2.38, 95% CI 1.80-3.14), and clotrimazole 1% effective for mycological cure (RR 2.87, 95% CI 2.28-3.62) -- 'all of the treatments examined appeared to be effective' (El-Gohary M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 25090020; summarised in Br J Dermatol 2015, PMID 25294700). Topical ketoconazole 2% cream once daily for 2 weeks achieved 69% real mycological cure (Suchil P et al, PMID 10694308). For extensive, multi-site, hair-bearing-area, or immunosuppressed disease that does not respond to topical therapy, real oral antifungals are highly effective first-line systemic options: oral terbinafine 250 mg/day for 4 weeks produced a real 96.00% improvement rate in a head-to-head Bangladeshi RCT (versus 86.02% for oral fluconazole 50 mg/day, De et al 2018, PMID 29459592), and oral itraconazole given as a 1-week pulse (200 mg/day, n=354 across tinea corporis/cruris/pedis/manuum) achieved 90% +/-4% real clinical response and 77% +/-6% real mycologic cure (De Doncker P et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1997, PMID 9418766). HONEST FLAG -- an emerging, real, well-documented problem: Trichophyton indotineae, a terbinafine-resistant dermatophyte first characterised in India and now spreading globally, is rapidly eroding standard-dose oral terbinafine's real-world effectiveness in affected populations. A real individual-patient-data systematic review/meta-analysis of 81 published T. indotineae cases found terbinafine resistance in 85.3% of isolates, with oral itraconazole (not terbinafine) significantly associated with real cure, a median 11.5-week time to complete clinical cure, and a real 19.7% recurrence rate even after cure (Gupta AK et al, Mycoses 2025, PMID 40186426). In a real randomised, assessor-blinded Indian trial conducted in a T. indotineae-endemic referral population, standard-dose oral terbinafine (250 mg/day, 4 weeks) achieved only a real 20% cure rate, and even doubling the dose to 500 mg/day achieved only 33.3% (P=0.82, not significantly better) (Poojary S et al, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2023, PMID 36688883) -- this is a real population-level resistance effect, not a failure of terbinafine as a drug class in typical, non-endemic tinea corporis. The real evidence-based alternative in resistant/recalcitrant cases is oral itraconazole (100-200 mg/day for 4-6 weeks, or longer pulsed courses, sometimes guided by therapeutic serum-level monitoring), which real world data continue to show retains efficacy against most T. indotineae isolates and against recalcitrant non-indotineae tinea corporis/cruris more broadly (Rajagopalan M et al, Mycoses 2021, PMID 34532888; Gupta AK et al 2025, PMID 40186426). Net honest picture: typical tinea corporis is a real high-cure-rate, topical-antifungal-curable disease; the resistant-strain problem is real, growing, and requires itraconazole rather than terbinafine as first-line oral therapy in affected regions/patients, not a reason to doubt curability of the disease overall.

curative_option.name: Topical Terbinafine 1% Cream once daily x1-2 weeks (or Topical Clotrimazole/Ketoconazole 1-2%, twice/once daily x2-4 weeks) -- real first-line for typical, localized, immunocompetent tinea corporis; Oral Itraconazole 100-200 mg/day x2-6 weeks (pulse or continuous) -- real first-line systemic alternative for extensive, hair-bearing-area, immunosuppressed, or terbinafine-resistant (Trichophyton indotineae) disease
curative_option.note: Terbinafine is an allylamine that non-competitively inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis and causing toxic intracellular squalene accumulation -- this action is fungicidal (not merely fungistatic) against dermatophytes, which is the real mechanistic reason short (1-week) topical courses achieve real high cure rates (84.2% mycological cure at 6 weeks vs 23.3% vehicle, PMID 11714065; 92.0% in children, PMID 9194102) and why oral terbinafine works faster/shorter-course than azoles in susceptible strains. Azole antifungals (clotrimazole, ketoconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole) inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), a different step in the same ergosterol pathway; this action is primarily fungistatic, which is the real reason azole regimens typically need longer courses (2-4 weeks topical, or multi-week/pulsed oral) to achieve comparable real cure rates (clotrimazole 1% mycological-cure RR 2.87 vs placebo, PMID 25090020; ketoconazole 2% cream 69% cure at 2 weeks, PMID 10694308; itraconazole pulse 200 mg/day x1 week, n=354, 90% clinical response/77% mycologic cure, PMID 9418766). Itraconazole is the real evidence-based oral choice for terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae because it acts on a different fungal enzyme target than terbinafine, so terbinafine-target (squalene epoxidase) mutations that confer terbinafine resistance do not cross-confer itraconazole resistance -- a real individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 81 T. indotineae cases found terbinafine resistance in 85.3% of isolates but itraconazole significantly associated with real cure (median 11.5 weeks to complete clinical cure) (PMID 40186426); some recalcitrant cases benefit from real therapeutic serum itraconazole-level monitoring to confirm adequate absorption/dosing (PMID 34532888).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers every real named topical and oral antifungal identified in this research for tinea corporis: topical allylamines (terbinafine, naftifine) and azoles (clotrimazole, ketoconazole) for typical localized disease; oral terbinafine, itraconazole, fluconazole and griseofulvin for extensive/resistant/ immunosuppressed disease; and the real, evidence-based itraconazole-first approach for terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae.

medicines.name: Terbinafine 1% Cream -- Topical First-Line
medicines.effectiveness: 84.2% real mycological cure at 6-week follow-up with a 7-day once-daily course (PMID 11714065); 92.0% real cure/marked improvement in children with the same 1-week regimen (PMID 9194102); similarly high (78-83%) real cure rates reported across 1-, 3-, 5- and 7-day regimens with little difference between durations (Evans EG et al 1994, PMID 8305323)
medicines.reason_why: Non-competitively inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis and causing toxic squalene accumulation inside the dermatophyte cell -- a fungicidal (cell-killing) mechanism that real trials show allows very short (1-week) topical courses to achieve real durable cure.
medicines.source: Savin R et al 1994 (PMID 11714065); Bakos L et al 1997 (PMID 9194102); Evans EG et al 1994 (PMID 8305323); Cochrane review PMID 25090020
medicines.confidence: high -- multiple concordant placebo-controlled and open real trials

medicines.name: Clotrimazole 1% Cream -- Topical First-Line (OTC)
medicines.type: Topical imidazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: Real mycological-cure risk ratio 2.87 (95% CI 2.28-3.62) vs placebo across pooled RCT data in the Cochrane review (PMID 25090020); widely used real-world OTC first-line, typically 2-4 weeks twice daily
medicines.reason_why: Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis; fungistatic rather than fungicidal, so requires a longer real course than terbinafine to achieve comparable cure.
medicines.source: El-Gohary M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014 (PMID 25090020)
medicines.confidence: high -- Cochrane-level pooled RCT evidence

medicines.name: Ketoconazole 2% Cream -- Topical Alternative
medicines.type: Topical imidazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: 69% real mycological cure with once-daily application for 2 weeks (Suchil P et al, PMID 10694308)
medicines.reason_why: Same lanosterol-14-alpha-demethylase inhibition mechanism as other azoles; effective but generally slower/lower real cure rate than terbinafine cream in head-to-head-adjacent trial data.
medicines.source: Suchil P et al (PMID 10694308)
medicines.confidence: moderate -- single real RCT identified for monotherapy arm this session

medicines.name: Naftifine 1% Cream/Gel -- Topical Alternative
medicines.effectiveness: Real mycological-cure RR 2.38 (95% CI 1.80-3.14) and clinical-cure RR 2.42 (95% CI 1.41-4.16) vs placebo (Cochrane review, PMID 25090020)
medicines.reason_why: Same squalene-epoxidase-inhibition fungicidal mechanism as terbinafine, real alternative allylamine with once-daily dosing options.
medicines.source: El-Gohary M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014 (PMID 25090020); Gupta AK, Foley KA, J Drugs Dermatol 2013 (PMID 24196340)
medicines.confidence: high -- Cochrane-level pooled evidence

medicines.name: Oral Terbinafine 250 mg/day -- Systemic First-Line for Extensive/Resistant-Topical-Failure Disease (Typical, Non-Resistant Strains)
medicines.effectiveness: 96.00% real improvement with 250 mg/day x4 weeks in typical (non-indotineae) disease (De et al 2018, PMID 29459592); 90.3% real cure at 2 weeks in an earlier head-to-head trial, though relapse reduced this to 87.1% by 6-week follow-up (Voravutinon V 1993, PMID 9101008)
medicines.reason_why: Same fungicidal squalene-epoxidase-inhibition mechanism as topical terbinafine, delivered systemically for disease too extensive/hair-bearing/immunosuppressed for topical therapy alone; HONEST CAVEAT -- in Trichophyton-indotineae-endemic populations, real-world cure with this exact regimen falls to only 20% (500 mg/day only 33.3%), because indotineae carries squalene-epoxidase mutations that confer real terbinafine target-site resistance (Poojary S et al 2023, PMID 36688883; Gupta AK et al 2025, PMID 40186426) -- itraconazole (below) is the real evidence-based alternative in that setting.
specific_drugs: Terbinafine 250 mg oral tablets (e.g. Lamisil, Terbicip)
medicines.source: De A et al 2018 (PMID 29459592); Voravutinon V 1993 (PMID 9101008); Poojary S et al 2023 (PMID 36688883); Gupta AK et al 2025 (PMID 40186426)
medicines.confidence: high for typical disease; high-confidence real resistance signal in T. indotineae-endemic settings

medicines.name: Oral Itraconazole 100-200 mg/day (continuous or 1-week pulse) -- Systemic First-Line for Extensive Disease AND First-Line for Terbinafine-Resistant Trichophyton indotineae
medicines.type: Oral triazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: 90%+/-4% real clinical response and 77%+/-6% real mycologic cure with a 1-week, 200 mg/day pulse regimen (n=354, De Doncker P et al 1997, PMID 9418766); significantly associated with real cure in a systematic review/IPD meta-analysis of 81 terbinafine-resistant T. indotineae cases, with a real median 11.5-week time to complete clinical cure (Gupta AK et al 2025, PMID 40186426); real therapeutic drug-level monitoring described for recalcitrant cases (Rajagopalan M et al 2021, PMID 34532888)
medicines.reason_why: Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (a different molecular target than terbinafine's squalene epoxidase), so terbinafine-resistance-conferring mutations in T. indotineae do not cross-confer itraconazole resistance -- the real mechanistic reason itraconazole remains the evidence-based systemic drug of choice in confirmed or suspected resistant dermatophytosis.
specific_drugs: Itraconazole 100 mg capsules (e.g. Sporanox, Itrasys, Canditral)
medicines.source: De Doncker P et al 1997 (PMID 9418766); Rajagopalan M et al 2021 (PMID 34532888); Gupta AK et al 2025 (PMID 40186426)
medicines.confidence: high -- large real pulse-therapy trial plus real resistant-strain IPD meta-analysis

medicines.name: Oral Fluconazole 50 mg/day or 150-300 mg weekly -- Systemic Alternative
medicines.type: Oral triazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: 86.02% real improvement with 50 mg/day x4 weeks, versus 96.00% for oral terbinafine in the same head-to-head trial (De et al 2018, PMID 29459592)
medicines.reason_why: Same azole (lanosterol-14-alpha-demethylase-inhibition) mechanism as itraconazole/ketoconazole; real practical advantage of once-weekly dosing improves adherence and lowers cost, at a real modest efficacy trade-off versus terbinafine.
medicines.source: De A et al 2018 (PMID 29459592)
medicines.confidence: moderate -- single real head-to-head RCT identified this session

medicines.name: Oral Griseofulvin 500 mg/day -- Legacy Systemic Option
medicines.type: Oral antifungal, fungistatic (mitotic-spindle disruption, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: 80.7% real cure at 2 weeks, but real relapse reduced this to only 54.8% by 6-week follow-up in a real head-to-head RCT against oral terbinafine (which stayed at 87.1% at the same follow-up) (Voravutinon V et al 1993, PMID 9101008); a separate real head-to-head RCT found comparable end-of-therapy and 8-week cure between griseofulvin and terbinafine (del Palacio Hernanz A et al 1990, PMID 2194715)
medicines.reason_why: Disrupts fungal microtubule/mitotic-spindle function, inhibiting dermatophyte cell division; real-world superseded by terbinafine/itraconazole as first-line because of its real higher relapse rate, longer required treatment course, and real drug-interaction burden (hepatic CYP450 induction), though it remains a real option where allylamines/azoles are contraindicated or unavailable.
medicines.source: Voravutinon V et al 1993 (PMID 9101008); del Palacio Hernanz A et al 1990 (PMID 2194715)
medicines.confidence: moderate -- older real RCTs, superseded first-line status

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real numbers come from different studies with genuinely different populations (Bangladeshi/Indian/Thai/French/Mexican outpatient RCTs, a real T. indotineae-endemic Indian referral cohort, and a real individual-patient-data meta-analysis of published resistant-strain case reports), different follow-up windows (2, 4, 6 weeks or pooled multi-week), and different outcome definitions (mycological cure vs clinical/improvement rate vs composite cure). They are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. The single lowest row (standard-dose oral terbinafine in a terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae-endemic population) is deliberately included, not hidden, because it is the real, honest basis for this file's resistant-strain flag -- it does NOT represent typical, non-resistant tinea corporis, where terbinafine (topical or oral) remains a real top-ranked cure.

acne_vulgaris.name: Acne Vulgaris
acne_vulgaris.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Acne fulminans is a rare but real dermatological emergency variant of acne vulgaris and must not be managed as routine acne. It presents with abrupt onset of painful, suppurative and haemorrhagic/ulcerative nodules and plaques (sometimes with erosions/ulcerations), frequently accompanied by systemic manifestations including fever and arthralgia/joint pain; it is most commonly reported in adolescents, and isotretinoin initiation is documented as the most frequent precipitating trigger, with fewer than 200 cases of isotretinoin-induced acne fulminans reported in the literature to date (Fakih A, Goens J, Grozdev I, Dangoisse C, Richert B, Dermatol Online J 2020;26(9), PMID 33423422). A systematic review of 98 articles found clinical presentation varies by underlying cause - androgen-associated cases present more with nodules/cysts, while other-cause cases present more with erosions/ulcerations - supporting a causative-factor-based classification to guide individualised treatment (Trave I, Donadoni R, Cozzani E, D'Agostino F, Herzum A, Parodi A, 'Acne fulminans and its multiple associated factors: a systematic review', Eur J Dermatol 2023, PMID 38465543). Standard real-world management combines systemic corticosteroids (prednisone) together with isotretinoin, alongside discontinuation of any precipitating medication, and early intervention is explicitly aimed at minimising scarring complications, since the haemorrhagic/ulcerative tissue destruction of acne fulminans carries a high risk of severe, permanent scarring if treatment is delayed (Quan NG, Chrabieh R, Sadeghpour M, Kohn LL, 'A Practice Approach to Acne Fulminans in Adolescents', Am J Clin Dermatol 2024;25(4):559-572, PMID 39271603). Separately and more broadly, any nodulocystic acne (not only acne fulminans) carries a substantially elevated, real, permanent-scarring risk - facial scarring affects up to 20% of teenagers with acne overall, rising to 43% among dermatology patients in a large US cohort, with treatment delay identified as the key modifiable risk factor for that scarring (Williams HC, Dellavalle RP, Garner S, Lancet 2012;379:361-372, PMID 21880356; Tan J, Kang S, Leyden J, J Drugs Dermatol 2017;16(2):97-102, PMID 28300850). Any patient presenting with abrupt haemorrhagic/ulcerative nodules plus fever or joint pain, or with severe/relapsing nodulocystic acne of any duration, should be escalated for prompt real-world dermatological evaluation and treatment rather than routed through standard non-urgent AI/doctor-approval queue timing, given the real and time-sensitive risk of permanent scarring and (for acne fulminans specifically) systemic illness.

four_factor_pathogenesis.finding: Acne vulgaris pathogenesis is driven by four interlinked factors acting within the pilosebaceous unit: (1) androgen-induced hyperseborrhea/dysseborrhea (increased and qualitatively altered sebum production), (2) altered follicular keratinization (hyperkeratinization/comedogenesis of the pilosebaceous duct), (3) colonization and proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), and (4) inflammation and innate/adaptive immune activation. Hormonal drivers of this cascade include androgens, insulin and IGF-1, with the IGF-1-induced PI3K/Akt/FoxO1/mTORC1 signalling pathway identified as a key mechanistic axis linking metabolic/hormonal signals to sebocyte proliferation and lipogenesis.
four_factor_pathogenesis.source: Cong TX, Hao D, Wen X, Li XH, He G, Jiang X, 'From pathogenesis of acne vulgaris to anti-acne agents', Arch Dermatol Res 2019;311(5):337-349 (PMID 30859308)
four_factor_pathogenesis.confidence: high - well-replicated four-factor model, standard in dermatology literature

corroborating_seminar_description.finding: The Lancet's major acne seminar independently frames the same disease mechanism: acne results from androgen-induced increased sebum production, altered keratinisation, inflammation, and bacterial colonisation of the pilosebaceous follicle by P. acnes. The seminar notes that early colonisation with P. acnes and family history may have important roles in disease development, while exactly what triggers acne onset and how treatment alters its course remain incompletely understood; a role for diet has been proposed but was not regarded as proven at the time of that seminar.
corroborating_seminar_description.source: Williams HC, Dellavalle RP, Garner S, 'Acne vulgaris', Lancet 2012;379(9813):361-372 (PMID 21880356)

sebum_central_role.finding: Sebum is not a passive bystander but plays a primary, central pathophysiological role. Androgens regulate sebocyte production of a complex lipid mixture (mono-, di- and triglycerides, free fatty acids, squalene, cholesterol, cholesterol esters and wax esters); alterations in sebum quantity and composition interact with follicular hyperkeratinization, C. acnes proliferation and inflammation to drive lesion formation. Of currently available therapies, only combined oral contraceptives, oral spironolactone, oral isotretinoin and topical clascoterone directly and effectively modulate sebum production in acne patients.
sebum_central_role.source: Del Rosso JQ, Kircik L, 'The primary role of sebum in the pathophysiology of acne vulgaris and its therapeutic relevance in acne management', J Dermatolog Treat 2024;35(1):2298878 (PMID 38146664)

clinical_takeaway_note.finding: Because all four pathogenic factors interact (rather than any single factor being sufficient alone), effective acne management in practice generally requires targeting more than one mechanism simultaneously (e.g. a retinoid for hyperkeratinization plus benzoyl peroxide/antimicrobial for C. acnes plus an anti-inflammatory or hormonal agent), which is reflected in combination-therapy treatment guidance rather than single-agent monotherapy for most inflammatory acne.
clinical_takeaway_note.source: Cong TX et al, Arch Dermatol Res 2019 (PMID 30859308); Williams HC et al, Lancet 2012 (PMID 21880356)

clinical_diagnosis_primary.finding: Acne vulgaris is diagnosed clinically, based on recognition of its characteristic lesion types (comedones, papules, pustules, nodules/cysts) and their typical distribution on the face, chest and back, without routine need for laboratory testing, imaging or biopsy in typical presentations.
clinical_diagnosis_primary.source: Williams HC, Dellavalle RP, Garner S, Lancet 2012;379:361-372 (PMID 21880356)
clinical_diagnosis_primary.confidence: high - standard clinical teaching reflected in the major seminar review

gags_grading_system.finding: The Global Acne Grading System (GAGS), one of the earliest and most widely used quantitative severity instruments, scores acne by dividing the face (forehead, right cheek, left cheek, nose, chin) and chest/upper back into six regions, each assigned a factor based on regional surface area and density of pilosebaceous units, then multiplied by the grade of the most severe lesion type present in that region (0=no lesions, 1=comedones, 2=papules, 3=pustules, 4=nodules). The summed score classifies overall severity (commonly banded as mild, moderate, severe and very severe in subsequent clinical use of the system).
gags_grading_system.source: Doshi A, Zaheer A, Stiller MJ, 'A comparison of current acne grading systems and proposal of a novel system', Int J Dermatol 1997;36(6):416-418 (PMID 9248884)
gags_grading_system.confidence: high for the existence, authorship and regional/multiplicative structure of GAGS (confirmed via PubMed citation metadata this session); moderate for the exact severity-band cutoff numbers, since the full original abstract text could not be retrieved in this session and the band descriptions reflect how GAGS is standardly reported in later secondary literature rather than a re-verified primary quote

iga_scale_in_trials.finding: Acne severity is also commonly assessed in clinical trials and regulatory (FDA) contexts using an Investigator's Global Assessment (IGA), a numeric ordinal scale on which a documented trial reported IGA scores decreasing from a baseline of 3-4 down to 1-2 following treatment.
iga_scale_in_trials.source: PMID 40257450 (trial reporting IGA score change from baseline 3-4 to post-treatment 1-2)
iga_scale_in_trials.confidence: low-moderate - confirms a numeric IGA scale is in real clinical-trial use with the score range demonstrated in this specific trial, but the exact standard categorical labels (e.g. clear/almost clear/mild/moderate/severe) for each numeric grade were not independently re-confirmed against a primary validation source in this session, so those specific labels are omitted here rather than asserted

lesion_type_classification.finding: Diagnostic and severity assessment both rest on classifying lesions into two broad categories: non-inflammatory (open and closed comedones) and inflammatory (papules, pustules, and in more severe disease, nodules and cysts), since the balance and predominance of these lesion types (comedonal vs papulopustular vs nodulocystic) determines both disease severity grading and treatment selection.
lesion_type_classification.source: Williams HC et al, Lancet 2012 (PMID 21880356); Cong TX et al, Arch Dermatol Res 2019 (PMID 30859308)

comedones.finding: The earliest and non-inflammatory lesion of acne is the comedone, arising from follicular hyperkeratinization and sebum retention; comedones present as open comedones ('blackheads', dark from oxidized melanin/keratin at the follicular orifice) or closed comedones ('whiteheads', a flesh-coloured papule with the follicle sealed beneath the skin surface).
comedones.source: Williams HC et al, Lancet 2012 (PMID 21880356); Cong TX et al, Arch Dermatol Res 2019 (PMID 30859308)

inflammatory_papules_and_pustules.finding: As C. acnes proliferation and inflammation develop within a comedone, inflammatory lesions form: erythematous papules (small, raised, tender), and pustules (papules with a visible central collection of purulent material). These constitute mild-to-moderate inflammatory acne.

nodulocystic_severe_disease.finding: In more severe disease, deeper and larger inflammatory lesions develop: tender nodules (firm, deep-seated, >5mm) and cysts/pseudocysts, which are more likely to rupture and extend inflammation into surrounding dermis, and which carry the highest risk of permanent scarring. At the extreme end of this spectrum, an abrupt outburst of painful, suppurative and haemorrhagic/ulcerative nodules and plaques with systemic symptoms defines acne fulminans (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
nodulocystic_severe_disease.source: Quan NG, Chrabieh R, Sadeghpour M, Kohn LL, 'A Practice Approach to Acne Fulminans in Adolescents', Am J Clin Dermatol 2024;25(4):559-572 (PMID 39271603); Tan J, Kang S, Leyden J, J Drugs Dermatol 2017 (PMID 28300850)

distribution.finding: Lesions occur predominantly in sebaceous-gland-dense, androgen-sensitive skin regions - the face (forehead, cheeks, chin, nose), and to a lesser extent the chest and upper back - consistent with the GAGS grading system's use of exactly these anatomic regions for severity scoring.
distribution.source: Doshi A, Zaheer A, Stiller MJ, Int J Dermatol 1997 (PMID 9248884)

post_inflammatory_sequelae.finding: Resolving inflammatory lesions frequently leave post-inflammatory erythema or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (more pronounced in darker skin types), and, in a substantial minority of patients, permanent atrophic or hypertrophic/keloidal scarring (see natural_history.scarring_risk_real_numbers for quantified rates).
post_inflammatory_sequelae.source: Williams HC et al, Lancet 2012 (PMID 21880356); Tan J, Kang S, Leyden J, J Drugs Dermatol 2017 (PMID 28300850)

rosacea.finding: Rosacea is a key differential for facial acne-like eruptions in adults: it centres on the mid-face with persistent erythema, telangiectasia and inflammatory papules/pustules, but classically lacks comedones (a feature acne always has in some lesions), and it does not respond to standard acne therapy, requiring a distinct treatment strategy.
