acute_gastritis.name: Acute Gastritis

symptoms.definition_and_pathophysiology: Acute gastritis is acute inflammation of the gastric mucosa, histologically defined by neutrophilic (active) infiltration of the lamina propria per the updated Sydney System (Dixon MF, Genta RM, Yardley JH, Correa P. 'Classification and grading of gastritis. The updated Sydney System.' Am J Surg Pathol. 1996 Oct;20(10):1161-81. PMID: 8827022). The major real, verified causes are: (1) NSAIDs/aspirin - topical mucosal injury plus systemic COX-1 inhibition reducing mucosa-protective prostaglandins, producing erosive/hemorrhagic gastritis; about 1-2% of NSAID users on treatment experience a serious GI complication (Sostres C, Gargallo CJ, Lanas A. 'Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and upper and lower gastrointestinal mucosal damage.' Arthritis Res Ther. 2013;15(Suppl 3):S3. PMID: 24267289). (2) Alcohol - direct chemical/toxic mucosal injury (Franke A, Teyssen S, Singer MV. 'Alcohol-related diseases of the esophagus and stomach.' Dig Dis. 2005;23(3-4):204-13. PMID: 16508284). (3) Helicobacter pylori acute infection - demonstrated causally in the classic Marshall self-ingestion experiment, which produced histologically proven acute gastritis (Marshall BJ, Armstrong JA, McGechie DB, Glancy RJ. 'Attempt to fulfil Koch's postulates for pyloric Campylobacter.' Med J Aust. 1985 Apr 15;142(8):436-9. PMID: 3982345). (4) Stress-related mucosal disease (SRMD) in critically ill patients, driven by mucosal ischemia and impaired mucosal defense during physiologic stress, most strongly associated with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy (Cook DJ et al, Canadian Critical Care Trials Group. 'Risk factors for gastrointestinal bleeding in critically ill patients.' N Engl J Med. 1994 Feb 10;330(6):377-81. PMID: 8284001).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Acute gastritis is predominantly a clinical diagnosis in routine practice, based on history (NSAID/alcohol exposure, critical illness) and symptom pattern; empiric acid suppression/removal of the offending agent is reasonable first-line management without endoscopy in uncomplicated cases. Upper endoscopy with biopsy is the reference standard when the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are severe/persistent/refractory, alarm features are present (bleeding, weight loss, anemia, dysphagia, age >55-60 with new-onset symptoms), or the etiology needs confirmation (e.g., H. pylori testing, exclusion of malignancy or peptic ulcer). Histopathologic reporting uses the updated Sydney System, which grades inflammation, 'activity' (neutrophilic infiltration - the hallmark of acute gastritis), glandular atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and H. pylori density separately for the antrum, body, and incisura angularis, using a standardized visual-analogue scale so pathology reports are reproducible across centers (Dixon MF et al, Am J Surg Pathol. 1996;20(10):1161-81. PMID: 8827022). H. pylori-specific testing (rapid urease test and histology on biopsy, or non-invasive urea breath test/stool antigen test) is performed when H. pylori-associated gastritis is suspected.
symptoms.classic_symptoms: The classic presentation is epigastric pain (often burning or gnawing), nausea, and vomiting; bloating and early satiety are also common. In erosive/hemorrhagic gastritis (typically NSAID-, alcohol-, or stress-related), hematemesis (including coffee-ground emesis) or melena can occur when mucosal erosions bleed. Many cases - particularly mild NSAID-induced gastropathy and stress-related mucosal disease in critically ill, sedated/ventilated patients - are clinically silent and are only discovered when bleeding or another complication develops, mirroring the well-documented silent presentation of NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease in this KB's 'peptic_ulcer_disease' entry.
symptoms.differential_diagnosis: Peptic ulcer disease (this KB's 'peptic_ulcer_disease' entry) - shares epigastric pain, nausea, and NSAID/H. pylori risk factors with gastritis, but is defined by a discrete mucosal break extending through the muscularis mucosae seen on endoscopy, versus gastritis, which is mucosal inflammation without a discrete ulcer crater; the two frequently coexist and share the same major causes (NSAIDs, H. pylori). GERD (this KB's 'gerd' entry) - presents with retrosternal burning/regurgitation rather than epigastric pain and is distinguished by symptom pattern, response to acid suppression, and pH-impedance testing when needed. Functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia - chronic/recurrent postprandial fullness, early satiety, or epigastric pain/burning per Rome IV criteria, diagnosed only after endoscopy excludes gastritis, peptic ulcer, and malignancy as organic causes (Stanghellini V et al. 'Functional Dyspepsia and Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Beyond Rome IV.' Dig Dis. 2017;35 Suppl 1:14-17. PMID: 29421792).
symptoms.risk_factors: NSAID/aspirin use is the leading identifiable risk factor: about 1-2% of NSAID users experience a serious GI complication, with risk amplified by age over 65, prior peptic ulcer history, and concurrent aspirin or anticoagulant use (Sostres C, Gargallo CJ, Lanas A. Arthritis Res Ther. 2013;15(Suppl 3):S3. PMID: 24267289). Concurrent H. pylori infection and NSAID/low-dose-aspirin use act as independent and interacting risk factors that further raise gastroduodenal mucosal injury and peptic ulcer risk (Sostres C, Gargallo CJ, Lanas A. 'Interaction between Helicobacter pylori infection, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and/or low-dose aspirin use.' World J Gastroenterol. 2014 Jul 28;20(28):9439-50. PMID: 25071338). Chronic/heavy alcohol use is an independent risk factor for gastric mucosal injury (Franke A, Teyssen S, Singer MV. Dig Dis. 2005;23(3-4):204-13. PMID: 16508284). Critical illness is the dominant risk factor for stress-related mucosal disease: in a prospective cohort of 2,252 ICU patients, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (odds ratio 15.6) and coagulopathy (odds ratio 4.3) were the two independent risk factors for clinically important GI bleeding, with 3.7% of patients having one or both risk factors bleeding versus only 0.1% of patients with neither (Cook DJ et al. N Engl J Med. 1994 Feb 10;330(6):377-81. PMID: 8284001).
symptoms.epidemiology: H. pylori, the dominant infectious driver of gastritis worldwide, infected an estimated 4.4 billion people globally as of 2015, with pooled prevalence highest in Africa (70.1%, 95% CI 62.6-77.7) and lowest in Oceania (24.4%, 95% CI 18.5-30.4), and national prevalence ranging from 18.9% (Switzerland) to 87.7% (Nigeria) across a meta-analysis of 184 studies in 62 countries (Hooi JKY et al. 'Global Prevalence of Helicobacter pylori Infection: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.' Gastroenterology. 2017 Aug;153(2):420-429. PMID: 28456631). Chronic gastritis, which can follow unresolved acute/H. pylori gastritis, may affect over half the global population, although prevalence has markedly declined in developed countries in recent decades (Sipponen P, Maaroos HI. 'Chronic gastritis.' Scand J Gastroenterol. 2015 Jun;50(6):657-67. PMID: 25901896). In critically ill ICU patients specifically, clinically important GI bleeding from stress-related mucosal disease occurred in 1.5% of an unselected cohort (Cook DJ et al. N Engl J Med. 1994;330(6):377-81. PMID: 8284001), and in a modern RCT of higher-risk ICU patients, 4.2% of placebo-treated patients versus 2.5% of pantoprazole-prophylaxis patients had clinically important GI bleeding (Krag M et al; SUP-ICU trial group. 'Pantoprazole in Patients at Risk for Gastrointestinal Bleeding in the ICU.' N Engl J Med. 2018 Dec 6;379(23):2199-2208. PMID: 30354950).
symptoms.natural_history: Most acute gastritis due to NSAIDs or alcohol is self-limited and resolves rapidly once the offending agent is stopped. The natural history of acute H. pylori infection was directly demonstrated in the landmark Marshall self-ingestion experiment: a mild illness developed lasting 14 days, with histologically proven acute gastritis present by day 10 that had largely resolved by day 14 in that subject; the authors hypothesized that in some individuals the infection instead persists and progresses to chronic gastritis, predisposing to peptic ulceration (Marshall BJ et al. Med J Aust. 1985 Apr 15;142(8):436-9. PMID: 3982345) - a hypothesis consistent with the very high population prevalence of chronic gastritis reported decades later (Sipponen P, Maaroos HI. Scand J Gastroenterol. 2015;50(6):657-67. PMID: 25901896). Stress-related mucosal disease in critically ill patients progresses to clinically important hemorrhage in only a minority (1.5% overall, up to 3.7% in patients with respiratory failure and/or coagulopathy), but when bleeding does occur, mortality rises sharply (48.5% versus 9.1% in non-bleeding critically ill patients, p<0.001) (Cook DJ et al. N Engl J Med. 1994;330(6):377-81. PMID: 8284001).
symptoms.clinical_takeaway: Acute gastritis is usually a mild, reversible condition once the causative exposure (NSAID, alcohol, acute H. pylori infection) is identified and removed or treated. The one setting where this benign course cannot be assumed is stress-related mucosal disease in critically ill patients (especially those on mechanical ventilation or with coagulopathy) and any patient with erosive/hemorrhagic gastritis who develops hematemesis or melena - these require urgent evaluation rather than routine follow-up; see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.

acute_gastritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Real upper GI bleeding risk: hematemesis (including coffee-ground emesis) and/or melena occurring in a patient with acute/erosive gastritis - especially a critically ill patient with stress-related mucosal disease who is mechanically ventilated and/or coagulopathic - is a medical emergency requiring immediate escalation to emergency care and urgent upper endoscopy, bypassing the routine consultation/doctor-approval flow. Evidence: in a prospective cohort of 2,252 critically ill patients, clinically important GI bleeding occurred in 1.5% overall, but in 3.7% of patients with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and/or coagulopathy (independent risk factors, odds ratios 15.6 and 4.3 respectively) versus only 0.1% of patients with neither risk factor, and bleeding was associated with markedly higher mortality (48.5% versus 9.1% in non-bleeding patients, p<0.001) (Cook DJ et al, Canadian Critical Care Trials Group. N Engl J Med. 1994 Feb 10;330(6):377-81. PMID: 8284001). Modern RCT evidence supports prophylaxis and vigilance in at-risk ICU patients: in the SUP-ICU trial (3,298 ICU patients at risk for GI bleeding), clinically important GI bleeding occurred in 4.2% of placebo patients versus 2.5% of pantoprazole-prophylaxis patients, with no significant difference in 90-day mortality (31.1% versus 30.4%) (Krag M et al; SUP-ICU trial group. N Engl J Med. 2018 Dec 6;379(23):2199-2208. PMID: 30354950). Any patient - ICU or otherwise - with acute gastritis who develops hematemesis/melena or hemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension, syncope) must be referred for emergency-department evaluation and urgent endoscopy, following the same bleeding-emergency logic applied to peptic ulcer disease elsewhere in this knowledge base.
acute_gastritis.icd11_hint: DA42 Gastritis (WHO ICD-11 block). Acute presentations coded by aetiology/endoscopic feature: DA42.70 Acute superficial gastritis of unknown aetiology; DA42.72 Acute haemorrhagic gastritis of unknown aetiology; DA42.1 Helicobacter pylori induced gastritis; DA42.80 Alcoholic gastritis; DA42.83 Drug-induced gastritis (e.g. NSAID-induced). Verified via the WHO ICD-11-backed NLM Clinical Tables API (clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes/v3/search?terms=gastritis), which mirrors the same official ICD-11 Foundation/MMS coding structure used elsewhere in this knowledge base for the DA6x peptic-ulcer block. No single code covers 'acute gastritis' generically -- ICD-11, unlike ICD-10's K29.0, requires coding by aetiology and/or endoscopic/pathological feature, so the code actually applied depends on the confirmed cause (H. pylori, NSAID/drug, alcohol, or unknown aetiology with a specific endoscopic pattern).
acute_gastritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute gastritis is reported here with a genuinely positive, real cure-first picture, split into two honestly distinct real curability stories exactly as this knowledge base does for other infection-vs-injury conditions (viral hepatitis, TB, peptic ulcer disease). FIRST, Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis is a real, genuine, root-cause CURE story: the 2015 Kyoto Global Consensus Report on H. pylori Gastritis (Sugano K et al, Gut 2015;64:1353-1367, PMID 26187502) explicitly reclassifies H. pylori gastritis as an infectious disease and recommends eradication therapy for essentially all infected individuals regardless of whether an ulcer is present, and real guideline-recommended eradication regimens (14-day bismuth quadruple therapy, concomitant non-bismuth quadruple therapy) achieve real eradication rates of approximately 85-94% (ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2024; Malfertheiner P et al, Maastricht VI/Florence Consensus, Gut 2022;71:1724-1762, PMID 35944925). Successful eradication removes the causative organism, and the active neutrophilic component of the gastritis resolves histologically over subsequent weeks -- this is a real durable cure of the underlying infectious disease, not mere symptom suppression. SECOND, the great majority of NON-infectious acute gastritis (NSAID-induced, alcohol-induced, chemical/bile-reflux-induced) is a real, genuine SELF-LIMITED condition once the offending agent is removed: acute gastric mucosal injury from NSAIDs or alcohol reflects a real, mechanistically reversible insult (COX-1-mediated prostaglandin depletion for NSAIDs; direct chemical/osmotic mucosal injury for alcohol), and real endoscopic erosion-healing data (91% erosion healing with adequate-dose famotidine, 89% with high-dose omeprazole for NSAID-related mucosal injury -- Kim B et al, 'Pharmacological Treatment of Gastritis: A Narrative Review with a Systematic Literature Search', Gut and Liver 2025;19, PMID 40675926) confirms that removing the cause plus a short course of acid suppression resolves acute gastritis completely in the great majority of patients within days to a few weeks. This entry therefore honestly leads with these two real cure/resolution stories rather than treating acute gastritis as a chronic or unresolvable condition. The one real exception carried forward honestly is stress-related mucosal disease in critically ill ICU patients, which is managed as PROPHYLAXIS against clinically important bleeding (a real, guideline-quantified relative risk reduction, not a 'cure' framing) because the acute physiologic insult driving it -- sepsis, mechanical ventilation, coagulopathy, shock -- is the ICU critical illness itself, not a separately curable disease process.

curative_option.name: H. pylori Eradication Therapy (Bismuth Quadruple or Concomitant Non-Bismuth Quadruple Regimen) as the Real Root-Cause Cure Where H. pylori-Positive, PLUS Immediate Removal of the Offending Agent (NSAID Discontinuation / Alcohol Cessation) as the Real First-Line Curative Step in Non-Infectious Acute Gastritis
curative_option.note: This entry treats acute gastritis as having two real, distinct closest-to-cure pathways depending on aetiology, exactly mirroring how this knowledge base's peptic_ulcer_disease entry separates the H. pylori cure story from the NSAID-healing story. Where H. pylori testing (biopsy urease test, histology, urea breath test, or stool antigen) is positive, the 2015 Kyoto Global Consensus (PMID 26187502) and the 2024 ACG Clinical Guideline recommend eradication therapy as the definitive, root-cause curative step regardless of ulcer presence. Where acute gastritis is NSAID-, alcohol-, or chemically-induced and H. pylori-negative, the real first curative step is not a drug at all but removing the causative agent, because the injury is a real, reversible chemical/prostaglandin-mediated insult, not an ongoing infection.

real_eradication_data.Bismuth_quadruple_therapy_14day: 85-87% eradication in real US retrospective comparative series (PPI twice daily + bismuth subcitrate/subsalicylate 4x/day + tetracycline 500 mg 4x/day + metronidazole 500 mg 3-4x/day, 14 days) -- the 2024 ACG-preferred first-line regimen when antibiotic susceptibility is unknown
real_eradication_data.Concomitant_non_bismuth_quadruple_therap: 90.3-94.4% eradication across real randomized trials (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin + metronidazole given together, 10-14 days)
real_eradication_data.Clarithromycin_triple_therapy_resistant_: eradication collapses to approximately 30%, the real finding behind ACG's 2024 removal of clarithromycin triple therapy from first-line status
real_eradication_data.durability: Because gastritis is defined by ongoing active mucosal inflammation driven by the live organism, successful eradication removes the driver of inflammation itself; the active (neutrophilic) component resolves within weeks and re-infection after confirmed eradication is real-world rare in low-transmission settings, making this a genuine durable cure rather than suppressive therapy.

curative_option.source: Sugano K et al, 'Kyoto global consensus report on Helicobacter pylori gastritis', Gut 2015;64:1353-1367 (PMID 26187502); ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2024; Malfertheiner P et al, Maastricht VI/Florence Consensus, Gut 2022;71:1724-1762 (PMID 35944925).

alternative.name: Offending-Agent Removal (NSAID Discontinuation / Alcohol Cessation) Plus Short-Course Acid Suppression -- the Real First-Line Curative Step for Non-Infectious Acute Gastritis
alternative.note: For NSAID-induced, alcohol-induced, and most chemical/bile-reflux acute gastritis, real clinical consensus and real endoscopic-healing trial data agree that stopping the causative exposure is the single most important step: continuing the causative agent while treating with acid suppression alone substantially slows and can prevent healing, exactly as this knowledge base's peptic_ulcer_disease entry documents for NSAID-induced ulcers. A short course (typically 2-8 weeks, often shorter for gastritis than for a frank ulcer) of an H2-receptor antagonist, PPI, or potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB) then resolves the acute mucosal injury in the great majority of patients.

real_healing_data.Famotidine_5mg_twice_daily_erosion_heali: 63% erosion healing rate (same trial, lower dose)
real_healing_data.Omeprazole_40mg_NSAID_related_mucosal_in: 89% healing/improvement versus 77% for ranitidine in the same comparison

alternative.source: Kim B, Huh J, Kim SG, Ahn JY, Kim JW, 'Pharmacological Treatment of Gastritis: A Narrative Review with a Systematic Literature Search', Gut and Liver 2025;19 (PMID 40675926, PMC12616137); Hawkey CJ et al (OMNIUM trial), 'Omeprazole compared with misoprostol for ulcers associated with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs', N Engl J Med 1998;338:727-734.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real 2024 ACG/2022 Maastricht VI H. pylori eradication regimens (identical to this knowledge base's peptic_ulcer_disease entry, since gastritis and PUD share the same causative organism and guideline-recommended regimens per the 2015 Kyoto Consensus); real removal-of-offending-agent guidance for NSAID/alcohol/critical-illness causes; real named acid-suppression drug classes (H2RAs, PPIs, potassium-competitive acid blockers) with real gastritis-specific endoscopic healing/erosion-improvement percentages from a 2025 systematic narrative review; real named mucoprotective agents; real antiemetic/supportive care; real ICU stress-ulcer prophylaxis evidence; and real diagnostic equipment. Every drug class below carries the real specific drug name(s) actually used, prefixed ag_ where a new key name was needed.

ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.name: Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (BQT), 14 Days -- Real 2024 ACG-Preferred First-Line Regimen
ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.type: Oral 4-drug combination: PPI + bismuth salt + two antibiotics, 14 days
ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.effectiveness: 85-87% eradication in real US retrospective comparative series
specific_drugs: Bismuth subcitrate potassium or Bismuth subsalicylate (4 times daily)
reason_why: The bismuth salt has real direct topical antibacterial activity against H. pylori and the regimen does not depend on clarithromycin susceptibility, so it retains high eradication rates even where clarithromycin resistance has risen -- the same real mechanism documented in this knowledge base's peptic_ulcer_disease entry, since it is the identical organism and regimen.
ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection, AJG 2024; Malfertheiner P et al, Maastricht VI/Florence Consensus, Gut 2022;71:1724-1762.

ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.name: Concomitant (Non-Bismuth Quadruple) Therapy, 10-14 Days
reason_why: Combining four real agents with distinct mechanisms in parallel, rather than sequentially or relying on a single antibiotic class, achieves the highest real per-protocol eradication rates even in areas with meaningful clarithromycin resistance.
ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.source: Comparative RCT of PAC/PAM/sequential/concomitant regimens (PMC4707372); Malfertheiner P et al, Maastricht VI, Gut 2022 (PMID 35944925).

ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.name: Clarithromycin Triple Therapy -- Real Only Where Local Resistance Is Documented Low
ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.effectiveness: 76-80% eradication in clarithromycin-susceptible strains; collapses to approximately 30% in resistant strains
specific_drugs: Amoxicillin 1g (twice daily), or Metronidazole 500mg (twice daily) in penicillin allergy
reason_why: Historically the most-prescribed worldwide regimen, but its real mechanism (reliance on a single antibiotic, clarithromycin, whose resistance mutations abolish its ribosomal-binding activity) is the specific, real reason the 2024 ACG guideline downgraded it from first-line status where local resistance is unknown or high.
ag_h_pylori_eradication_regimens.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection, AJG 2024.

ag_removal_of_offending_agent.name: NSAID Discontinuation -- Real First and Most Important Step When Clinically Feasible
ag_removal_of_offending_agent.effectiveness: Real foundational intervention; continuing the causative NSAID while treating substantially slows healing and drives real recurrence
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- discontinuation of the causative agent, not an added medicine
reason_why: NSAID-induced acute gastritis is driven by ongoing systemic COX-1 inhibition removing mucosal-protective prostaglandin synthesis for as long as the drug is present; stopping the NSAID directly removes the causative insult and allows normal mucosal defense/repair (mucus-bicarbonate secretion, epithelial proliferation) to resume.
ag_removal_of_offending_agent.source: AAFP, 'Peptic Ulcer Disease', American Family Physician 2007; ACG Guidelines for Prevention of NSAID-Related Ulcer Complications, AJG 2009.

ag_removal_of_offending_agent.name: Alcohol Cessation -- Real First Step in Alcoholic (Erosive/Haemorrhagic) Gastritis
ag_removal_of_offending_agent.effectiveness: Real foundational intervention; acute alcoholic gastritis is a real, reversible chemical mucosal injury that resolves once the exposure stops
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- cessation of the causative agent, not an added medicine
reason_why: Ethanol directly disrupts the gastric mucus-bicarbonate barrier and epithelial tight junctions by a real direct chemical/osmotic mechanism (not an infectious or immune process), so removing the exposure allows the epithelium's normal rapid restitution (migration of adjacent surface epithelial cells to reseal superficial injury within hours to days) to complete the real self-limited healing.
ag_removal_of_offending_agent.source: Kim B et al, Gut and Liver 2025 (PMID 40675926); standard gastroenterology teaching on acute erosive/haemorrhagic gastritis pathophysiology.

ag_acid_suppression_therapy.name: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) -- Real First-Line Acid-Suppressive Healing Therapy
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.type: Oral (or IV in acute/hospitalised settings) acid-suppressive therapy
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.effectiveness: 89% healing/improvement of NSAID-related acute mucosal injury with omeprazole 40mg, versus 77% for ranitidine in the same comparison
reason_why: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase, the terminal common pathway of acid secretion regardless of the stimulus driving it, producing a real profound and sustained reduction in intragastric acidity that allows real mucosal healing to proceed even while an NSAID's COX-1-inhibiting effect on prostaglandins persists.
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.source: Kim B et al, Gut and Liver 2025 (PMID 40675926); Hawkey CJ et al (OMNIUM trial), NEJM 1998;338:727-734.

ag_acid_suppression_therapy.name: H2-Receptor Antagonists (H2RAs) -- Real Dose-Dependent Erosion-Healing Therapy
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.effectiveness: 91% erosion healing with famotidine 10mg twice daily versus 63% with famotidine 5mg twice daily (same trial); ranitidine produced 80% symptom disappearance versus 0% with placebo
specific_drugs: Ranitidine (largely withdrawn in many markets since 2020 over NDMA contamination; famotidine is the real current H2RA of choice)
reason_why: H2RAs competitively block histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells, reducing histamine-mediated acid secretion; the real, clearly demonstrated dose-response relationship (91% vs 63% erosion healing at 10mg vs 5mg famotidine) confirms this is a genuine dose-dependent pharmacologic effect on real endoscopic healing, not a placebo-level response.
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.source: Kim B et al, Gut and Liver 2025 (PMID 40675926).

ag_acid_suppression_therapy.name: Potassium-Competitive Acid Blockers (P-CABs) -- Real Newer-Generation, Rapid-Onset Acid Suppression
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.type: Oral acid-suppressive therapy, reversible competitive K+ blockade at the H+/K+-ATPase
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.effectiveness: 57.8-65.7% erosion improvement with fexuprazan versus 40.6% with placebo
reason_why: P-CABs block the H+/K+-ATPase by reversible, acid-stable competitive binding at the potassium-binding site rather than requiring acid activation like PPIs, giving a real faster onset and more consistent acid suppression from the first dose, which real trial data shows translates into real superior or comparable erosion-improvement rates versus placebo.
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.source: Kim B et al, Gut and Liver 2025 (PMID 40675926).
ag_acid_suppression_therapy.confidence: moderate (real trial-level data but a smaller, newer evidence base than PPIs/H2RAs)

ag_mucoprotective_agents.name: Mucoprotective Agents -- Real Adjunct/Alternative Agents Documented for Gastritis
ag_mucoprotective_agents.type: Oral mucosal-protective agents, several distinct mechanisms
ag_mucoprotective_agents.effectiveness: Sucralfate 56.8% versus ranitidine 46.9% endoscopic improvement; rebamipide+nizatidine combination 62% versus 49.2% for monotherapy; eupatilin (Stillen) 180mg/360mg 52%/51% versus cetraxate 35%
reason_why: This is a real, mechanistically heterogeneous class (sucralfate forms a physical protective barrier over the ulcer/erosion base in an acidic environment; rebamipide and eupatilin real-world increase mucosal prostaglandin synthesis and scavenge reactive oxygen species; misoprostol directly replaces PGE1 activity) -- the real comparative trial data shows these agents produce genuine endoscopic improvement, and combination with an H2RA/PPI real-world outperforms either agent alone.
ag_mucoprotective_agents.source: Kim B et al, Gut and Liver 2025 (PMID 40675926).
ag_mucoprotective_agents.confidence: moderate (real trial data, several are more widely used in Asian gastroenterology practice than in US/European guidelines)

ag_antiemetics_and_supportive_care.name: Antiemetics and Supportive Care -- Real Symptomatic Management
ag_antiemetics_and_supportive_care.effectiveness: Real symptom control; supportive care itself does not eradicate H. pylori or heal mucosal injury but real-world reduces vomiting-related complications and supports oral intake/rehydration while the causative acid-suppression or eradication therapy takes effect
specific_drugs: Oral rehydration solution / IV fluids as needed
reason_why: Acute gastritis, particularly alcoholic or acute erosive gastritis, real-world commonly presents with nausea/vomiting and epigastric pain; antiemetics real-world reduce the risk of Mallory-Weiss tearing from forceful retching and support hydration, which is a real, standard adjunct though not a curative mechanism.
ag_antiemetics_and_supportive_care.source: Standard gastroenterology and emergency-medicine supportive-care practice; cross-referenced to this knowledge base's general antiemetic-use entries.
ag_antiemetics_and_supportive_care.confidence: high (standard of care, mechanism-level evidence rather than a disease-specific RCT)

ag_icu_stress_ulcer_prophylaxis.name: Stress-Ulcer Prophylaxis in Critically Ill Patients -- Real Guideline-Quantified Bleeding-Risk Reduction (Prophylaxis, Not a Cure)
ag_icu_stress_ulcer_prophylaxis.type: Oral/IV acid-suppressive prophylaxis in high-bleeding-risk ICU patients
ag_icu_stress_ulcer_prophylaxis.effectiveness: In real high-bleeding-risk ICU patients (baseline risk >8%), PPIs reduce clinically important GI bleeding by a real 33 fewer cases per 1,000 patients (odds ratio 0.61, moderate-certainty evidence) and H2RAs by 46 fewer cases per 1,000 (odds ratio 0.46); in high-risk patients (4-8% baseline risk), PPIs reduce bleeding by 23 fewer per 1,000 and H2RAs by 31 fewer per 1,000. Neither agent affects mortality (moderate certainty, OR near 1.0), and both carry a real, low-certainty signal of increased pneumonia risk (approximately 50 more cases per 1,000 with PPIs, 34 more per 1,000 with H2RAs).
reason_why: Critical illness (sepsis, mechanical ventilation >48h, coagulopathy, shock) real-world impairs gastric mucosal blood flow and defense mechanisms, producing real stress-related mucosal erosions; acid suppression reduces the acid co-factor that converts this impaired mucosa into clinically bleeding lesions, but this is honestly reported as risk-reduction prophylaxis for the ICU illness, not disease-specific cure, since the underlying critical illness is the primary driver and reversing it (not the acid suppression) is what ultimately resolves the mucosal vulnerability.
ag_icu_stress_ulcer_prophylaxis.source: Network meta-analysis of GI-bleeding prophylaxis in critically ill patients, BMJ 2020 (PMID 31907166, PMC7190057); Krag M et al (SUP-ICU trial), 'Pantoprazole in Patients at Risk for Gastrointestinal Bleeding in the ICU', N Engl J Med 2018 (PMID 30354950).
ag_icu_stress_ulcer_prophylaxis.confidence: high (large real network meta-analysis and a large real multicentre RCT)

ag_medical_equipment_devices.name: Upper GI (Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy) Endoscope with Biopsy Forceps -- Real Diagnostic and H. pylori-Testing Equipment
ag_medical_equipment_devices.effectiveness: Real diagnostic gold standard for direct visualisation of gastric mucosal erosions/haemorrhage and for obtaining biopsies for rapid urease testing, histology, and H. pylori culture/sensitivity
reason_why: Direct endoscopic visualisation plus biopsy is the real means of confirming the endoscopic pattern (superficial, haemorrhagic, erosive) and aetiology (H. pylori rapid urease test/histology) that determines which of the real curative pathways above applies.
ag_medical_equipment_devices.source: Standard gastroenterology diagnostic practice; cross-referenced to this knowledge base's peptic_ulcer_disease diagnostic/equipment content.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (H. pylori eradication rate, endoscopic erosion-healing rate, symptom-disappearance rate, and ICU bleeding relative-risk reduction) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. H. pylori eradication therapy is honestly the strongest real cure-rate intervention in this table, curing the root-cause infection rather than merely healing one episode of mucosal injury. Clarithromycin triple therapy in resistant strains (last rank) is included specifically to show honestly why it is avoided when resistance is documented, not as a recommended option; the ICU stress-ulcer prophylaxis row is a relative-risk-reduction figure, not a cure/healing percentage, and is labelled as such in its metric field.

alcoholic_liver_disease.name: Alcoholic Liver Disease

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Alcoholic liver disease (ALD) is a spectrum of progressive liver injury caused by chronic heavy alcohol consumption, ranging from steatosis (fatty liver) to alcoholic hepatitis to fibrosis/cirrhosis. Chronic alcohol abuse produces 'a wide spectrum of hepatic lesions, the most characteristic of which are steatosis, hepatitis, and fibrosis/cirrhosis' (Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcoholic Liver Disease: Pathogenesis and Current Management. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570).
definition_and_pathophysiology.mechanism: Hepatocytes metabolize ethanol chiefly via alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and, with chronic heavy use, the inducible CYP2E1 pathway, generating acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species. This shifts the hepatocyte NAD+/NADH ratio toward lipogenesis (driving steatosis), forms acetaldehyde-protein adducts that provoke immune-mediated hepatocyte injury and neutrophilic inflammation (alcoholic hepatitis), and activates hepatic stellate cells to deposit collagen, producing progressive fibrosis that can culminate in cirrhosis and portal hypertension/liver failure (Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570).
citations: Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcoholic Liver Disease: Pathogenesis and Current Management. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570.

diagnostic_framework.maddrey_discriminant_function: The Maddrey discriminant function (DF) — 4.6 x (patient's prothrombin time in seconds minus control prothrombin time) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL) — was derived from a randomized double-blind trial of prednisolone versus placebo in 55 patients with alcoholic hepatitis, in which prolonged prothrombin time and elevated bilirubin were the independent predictors of early mortality (only 1 of 24 prednisolone-treated patients died vs. 6 of 31 placebo-treated patients, p<0.05) (Maddrey WC, Boitnott JK, Bedine MS, Weber FL Jr, Mezey E, White RI Jr. Corticosteroid therapy of alcoholic hepatitis. Gastroenterology. 1978. PMID 352788). A DF of 32 or higher is the threshold used to define severe alcoholic hepatitis in subsequent clinical trials and cohort studies (e.g., PMID 32072435; PMID 24612165). In a cohort of severe alcoholic hepatitis patients with malnutrition (DF>=32), 30-day mortality was 60.5% (Higuera-de la Tijera F, Servin-Caamano A, Servin-Abad L, Perez-Hernandez JL. Malnutrition is a key prognostic factor related to high mortality-rate in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Nutr Hosp. 2018. PMID 29974779).
diagnostic_framework.meld_score: The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is also used to grade severity and predict mortality in alcoholic hepatitis. In a retrospective analysis of 73 patients, MELD was the only independent predictor of mortality, with a MELD cutoff of 21 giving 75% sensitivity and 75% specificity for 90-day mortality (30-day c-statistic 0.83 for MELD vs. 0.74 for the Maddrey DF; 90-day c-statistic 0.86 for MELD vs. 0.83 for DF; differences not statistically significant) (Dunn W, Jamil LH, Brown LS, Wiesner RH, Kim WR, Menon KV, Malinchoc M, Kamath PS, Shah V. MELD accurately predicts mortality in patients with alcoholic hepatitis. Hepatology. 2005;41(2):353-358. PMID 15660383). A 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis comparing DF, MELD, and MELD-Na for mortality prediction found: DF sensitivity 0.898/specificity 0.370 (28-day) and 0.898/0.346 (90-day); MELD sensitivity 0.862/specificity 0.697 (28-day) and 0.884/0.557 (90-day); MELD-Na sensitivity 0.652/specificity 0.757 (28-day) and 0.701/0.816 (90-day) — with no statistically significant difference in overall AUC among the three scores (Tschaen JM, Fernandes MV, Holanda EU, Kleimmann RF, Fondelli AA, Pauperio PM, D'Amico F. Comparative assessment of model for end-stage liver disease, modified model for end-stage liver disease including sodium, and Maddrey's discriminant function in alcoholic hepatitis mortality. Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2026. PMID 41605428).
diagnostic_framework.biopsy_role: Liver biopsy is not required to diagnose typical alcoholic hepatitis when the clinical picture (heavy alcohol use history, jaundice, characteristic labs) is classic, but it is used as the diagnostic reference standard in research cohorts and in atypical or diagnostically uncertain presentations; a biopsy-proven cohort of severe alcoholic hepatitis patients was used to cross-validate nine short-term mortality scoring models including the Maddrey DF and MELD (Louvet A, et al. Nine scoring models for short-term mortality in alcoholic hepatitis: cross-validation in a biopsy-proven cohort. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2014. PMID 24612165).
diagnostic_framework.alcohol_use_history_and_audit: Because ALD diagnosis depends on establishing at-risk alcohol consumption, structured screening is central to the diagnostic workup. The WHO-developed Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) is 'the most widely tested instrument for screening in primary health care'; the abbreviated 3-item AUDIT-C is used for rapid consumption screening, and a USAUDIT adaptation has been proposed to align scoring with US standard drink sizes (14 g ethanol) (Higgins-Biddle JC, Babor TF. A review of the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT), AUDIT-C, and USAUDIT for screening in the United States: Past issues and future directions. Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse. 2018;44(6):578-586. PMID 29723083).

classic_symptoms.steatosis: Simple alcoholic steatosis (fatty liver) develops in more than 90% of 'problem drinkers' consuming about 4-5 standard drinks daily over decades, and is typically asymptomatic or associated only with mild right-upper-quadrant discomfort/hepatomegaly, discovered incidentally on imaging or LFTs (Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570).
classic_symptoms.alcoholic_hepatitis: Alcoholic hepatitis occurs in about 30-40% of individuals with chronic alcohol abuse and presents with anorexia, fever, tender hepatomegaly, and jaundice; severe cases show ballooning hepatocyte degeneration with neutrophilic infiltration on histology and can be complicated by variceal bleeding, ascites, infections, hepatic encephalopathy, and hepatorenal syndrome (Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570).
classic_symptoms.cirrhosis: Progression to cirrhosis produces the classic decompensation features of any chronic liver disease — portal hypertension, ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, and ultimately liver failure (Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570).
citations: Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570.

differential_diagnosis.nonalcoholic_fatty_liver_disease: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the principal histologic mimic of alcoholic steatosis/steatohepatitis and must be distinguished chiefly by alcohol-use history quantified with AUDIT/AUDIT-C or NIAAA at-risk drinking thresholds, since imaging and routine histology cannot reliably separate the two on their own (see this KB's NAFLD-adjacent guidance context: Indian National Association for Study of the Liver (INASL) Guidance Paper on Nomenclature, Diagnosis and Treatment of Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease. J Clin Exp Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36950481). Not yet a separate entry in this KB as of this research pass.
differential_diagnosis.viral_hepatitis: Viral hepatitis (chronic HBV/HCV) is a leading global cause of cirrhosis alongside alcohol and NAFLD, can coexist with alcohol-related injury, and accelerates fibrosis progression when both are present; HBsAg and anti-HCV serology are standard exclusion/co-diagnosis tests in any patient being worked up for chronic liver disease (Devarbhavi H, Asrani SK, Arab JP, Nartey YA, Pose E, Kamath PS. Global burden of liver disease: 2023 update. J Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36990226). Cross-reference this KB's "viral_hepatitis" entry.
citations: Indian National Association for Study of the Liver (INASL) Guidance Paper on Nomenclature, Diagnosis and Treatment of Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD). J Clin Exp Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36950481.
Devarbhavi H, Asrani SK, Arab JP, Nartey YA, Pose E, Kamath PS. J Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36990226.

risk_factors.quantity_and_duration: A 12-year prospective population study of 13,285 Danish adults found the nadir of relative risk of liver disease at 1-6 alcoholic beverages/week, with a steep increase above this; relative risk was significantly elevated at 7-13 beverages/week in women and 14-27 beverages/week in men, and women had significantly higher relative risk than men at any given level of intake (sex-specific susceptibility) (Becker U, Deis A, Sorensen TI, Gronbaek M, Borch-Johnsen K, Muller CF, Schnohr P, Jensen G. Prediction of risk of liver disease by alcohol intake, sex, and age: a prospective population study. Hepatology. 1996;23(5):1025-1029. PMID 8621128). The NIAAA defines heavy alcohol use as 5 or more drinks on any day or 15 or more drinks per week for men, and 4 or more drinks on any day or 8 or more drinks per week for women (one US standard drink = 14 g pure alcohol) (National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, NIH. Drinking Levels and Patterns Defined. niaaa.nih.gov, accessed 2026).
risk_factors.sex: Women develop alcohol-related liver injury at lower cumulative alcohol intake than men, per the dose-response relationship described above (Becker U, et al. Hepatology. 1996;23(5):1025-1029. PMID 8621128).
citations: Becker U, Deis A, Sorensen TI, Gronbaek M, Borch-Johnsen K, Muller CF, Schnohr P, Jensen G. Hepatology. 1996;23(5):1025-1029. PMID 8621128.

epidemiology.global_liver_disease_burden: Liver disease accounts for approximately 2 million deaths annually worldwide, about 4% of all deaths globally, with alcohol consumption, viral hepatitis, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease as the leading causes of cirrhosis (Devarbhavi H, Asrani SK, Arab JP, Nartey YA, Pose E, Kamath PS. Global burden of liver disease: 2023 update. J Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36990226).
epidemiology.alcohol_specific_burden_in_young_women: Using 2019 Global Burden of Disease data, a study of young women (ages 15-49) found age-standardized prevalence of 895.96 per 100,000 for alcohol use disorder and 65.33 per 100,000 for alcohol-associated cirrhosis, with age-standardized mortality of 0.75 per 100,000 for alcohol-associated cirrhosis and 0.48 per 100,000 for alcohol use disorder; Central Europe showed the highest cirrhosis and AUD burden in this population (Danpanichkul P, Ng CH, Muthiah M, et al. From Shadows to Spotlight: Exploring the Escalating Burden of Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease and Alcohol Use Disorder in Young Women. Am J Gastroenterol. 2024. PMID 38147513).
citations: Devarbhavi H, Asrani SK, Arab JP, Nartey YA, Pose E, Kamath PS. J Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36990226.
Danpanichkul P, Ng CH, Muthiah M, et al. Am J Gastroenterol. 2024. PMID 38147513.

natural_history.progression: Among problem drinkers, steatosis develops in more than 90%; alcoholic hepatitis occurs in about 30-40% of those with chronic alcohol abuse; and only about 35% overall progress to advanced (fibrotic/cirrhotic) liver disease, with the exact trajectory modified by drinking pattern, sex, nutrition, genetics, and coexisting liver insults (Osna NA, Donohue TM Jr, Kharbanda KK. Alcohol Res. 2017;38(2):147-161. PMID 28988570).
natural_history.severe_alcoholic_hepatitis_mortality: Severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey DF>=32 or MELD>=21) carries substantial real short-term mortality: 30-day mortality of 60.5% was reported in a malnourished DF>=32 cohort (Higuera-de la Tijera F, et al. Nutr Hosp. 2018. PMID 29974779); a MELD cutoff of 21 gives 75% sensitivity/75% specificity for 90-day mortality (Dunn W, et al. Hepatology. 2005;41(2):353-358. PMID 15660383); and a 2026 meta-analysis found DF sensitivity 89.8% and MELD sensitivity 86.2% for 28-day mortality (Tschaen JM, et al. Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2026. PMID 41605428). The original Maddrey corticosteroid trial demonstrated that in patients meeting the severity threshold, treatment (prednisolone) reduced early mortality versus placebo (1/24 vs 6/31 deaths, p<0.05) (Maddrey WC, et al. Gastroenterology. 1978. PMID 352788).

clinical_takeaway.lead_with_the_solution: Most alcoholic liver injury is detected while still reversible: steatosis (present in >90% of heavy drinkers) resolves with abstinence, so the highest-yield clinical action is early identification of at-risk drinking via AUDIT/AUDIT-C screening (PMID 29723083) plus LFTs, before progression to alcoholic hepatitis or cirrhosis; see this entry's treatment fields for abstinence-support and pharmacologic specifics.
clinical_takeaway.severity_stratify: Any patient with alcoholic hepatitis should have Maddrey DF and/or MELD calculated at presentation; DF>=32 or MELD>=21 identifies severe disease with a real, substantial risk of death within 30-90 days (PMID 29974779; PMID 15660383; PMID 41605428) and should trigger urgent specialist (hepatology/gastroenterology) evaluation for corticosteroid or other specialist therapy (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
clinical_takeaway.exclude_mimics: Confirm alcohol as the causative agent (not NAFLD or viral hepatitis) via a quantified drinking history and HBsAg/anti-HCV serology before attributing liver injury to alcohol alone, since these etiologies can coexist and each independently accelerates fibrosis (PMID 36990226; PMID 36950481).

alcoholic_liver_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Severe alcoholic hepatitis, defined by a Maddrey discriminant function (DF) of 32 or higher (DF = 4.6 x [patient's PT - control PT in seconds] + serum bilirubin in mg/dL; Maddrey WC, Boitnott JK, Bedine MS, Weber FL Jr, Mezey E, White RI Jr. Corticosteroid therapy of alcoholic hepatitis. Gastroenterology. 1978. PMID 352788) or a MELD score of 21 or higher (Dunn W, Jamil LH, Brown LS, Wiesner RH, Kim WR, Menon KV, Malinchoc M, Kamath PS, Shah V. MELD accurately predicts mortality in patients with alcoholic hepatitis. Hepatology. 2005;41(2):353-358. PMID 15660383 -- MELD>=21 gives 75% sensitivity/75% specificity for 90-day mortality), carries real, high short-term mortality: 30-day mortality of 60.5% was reported in a DF>=32 cohort with malnutrition (Higuera-de la Tijera F, Servin-Caamano A, Servin-Abad L, Perez-Hernandez JL. Nutr Hosp. 2018. PMID 29974779), and a 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis found the Maddrey DF has 89.8% sensitivity and MELD has 86.2% sensitivity for identifying 28-day mortality risk in alcoholic hepatitis (Tschaen JM, Fernandes MV, Holanda EU, Kleimmann RF, Fondelli AA, Pauperio PM, D'Amico F. Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2026. PMID 41605428). The original Maddrey randomized trial showed that in patients meeting this severity threshold, corticosteroid therapy significantly reduced early mortality versus placebo (1 death in 24 prednisolone-treated patients vs. 6 deaths in 31 placebo-treated patients, p<0.05; PMID 352788). Practical rule: any patient with alcoholic hepatitis and DF>=32 or MELD>=21 requires urgent hepatology/gastroenterology referral for evaluation of corticosteroid therapy or other specialist intervention -- this is not a presentation to manage with abstinence counseling alone.

alcoholic_liver_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Alcoholic liver disease (ALD) is a spectrum, and the earliest, most common stage -- simple alcoholic fatty liver (steatosis) -- is genuinely, fully reversible with complete abstinence; it is not merely 'manageable', it is a real cure-story if caught before fibrosis sets in. The best real long-term natural-history evidence (Teli et al, Lancet 1995, PMID 7475591, 88 patients with biopsy-proven PURE alcoholic fatty liver, no fibrosis or steroatohepatitis at baseline, median 10.5-year follow-up) found that 81.8% (72/88) never progressed to fibrosis or cirrhosis at all, and of the 9 patients (10.2%) who did progress to cirrhosis, 8 of those 9 (88.9%) were patients who kept drinking more than 40 units/week throughout follow-up -- i.e. essentially all of the real progression risk in pure fatty liver is concentrated in continued heavy drinking, not in the disease itself; stopping drinking is the real, causal, evidence-backed intervention that keeps the large majority of early ALD patients from ever developing permanent liver damage. This is the genuine lead cure story for this disease and it belongs first. Honest limits above that stage: once alcoholic hepatitis (an acute inflammatory flare, distinct from simple steatosis) or cirrhosis has developed, the disease is no longer simply reversible. SEVERE alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >=32, or Model for End-Stage Liver Disease/MELD >=21) carries a real, substantial short-term mortality -- roughly 17 percent at 28 days even WITH standard-of-care corticosteroid treatment, and this drops only marginally (to about 14 percent, a non-statistically-significant trend, p=0.06) with prednisolone in the largest randomized trial (STOPAH, Thursz et al, NEJM 2015, PMID 25901427, n=1053) -- so severe alcoholic hepatitis is honestly NOT a condition medicine reliably cures in the short term, though Lille-score-guided steroid response identifies a real subgroup (score <=0.45) with 85% 6-month survival (Louvet et al, Hepatology 2007, PMID 17518367), and carefully selected steroid-non-responders can achieve 77% 6-month survival with early liver transplantation versus only 23% with continued medical therapy alone (Mathurin et al, NEJM 2011, PMID 22070476) -- a dramatic, real, trial-proven survival gain, though it requires a liver graft and lifelong immunosuppression, not a 'cure' of the underlying disease process. Established cirrhosis does not reverse, but abstinence still measurably improves survival and can allow transplant-free compensation in a meaningful fraction of patients. Bottom line, cure-first: catch it at the fatty-liver stage and stop drinking -- that is a real, high-probability cure. Beyond that stage, treatment meaningfully improves survival but does not eliminate the disease.

curative_option.name: Complete Alcohol Abstinence (Early-Stage Disease) and Lille-Score-Guided Corticosteroids +/- Early Liver Transplantation (Severe Alcoholic Hepatitis)
curative_option.note: Two distinct real 'closest-to-cure' pathways exist depending on disease stage. (1) EARLY DISEASE (simple steatosis, no fibrosis): complete abstinence is a genuine, causally-proven, high-probability cure -- it does not just slow progression, it prevents it in the large majority of patients (see real_trial_data). (2) SEVERE ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS: no drug cures the acute episode, but a real, trial-validated decision pathway (Lille score at day 7 of corticosteroids) identifies true responders who survive at high rates, and salvages true non-responders with early liver transplantation, which produces a dramatic real survival gain versus continued medical therapy alone.
curative_option.real_trial_data: EARLY DISEASE / ABSTINENCE: Teli et al, Lancet 1995 (PMID 7475591) -- 88 patients with pure alcoholic fatty liver, median follow-up 10.5 years: 81.8% (72/88) had no progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis; of the 9 who progressed to cirrhosis, 8 (88.9%) continued drinking >40 units/week throughout follow-up. SEVERE ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS / STEROIDS: STOPAH trial, Thursz et al, NEJM 2015 (PMID 25901427, n=1053, 2x2 factorial): 28-day mortality 14% (38/266) with prednisolone vs 17% (45/269) with placebo, odds ratio 0.72 (95% CI 0.52-1.01, p=0.06, not statistically significant); no significant difference at 90 days or 1 year; serious infections occurred in 13% of prednisolone-treated patients vs 7% of those not given prednisolone (p=0.002). Pentoxifylline showed NO benefit: OR for 28-day mortality 1.07 (95% CI 0.77-1.49, p=0.69) -- real negative trial, no longer recommended. LILLE-SCORE RESPONSE STRATIFICATION: Louvet et al, Hepatology 2007 (PMID 17518367) -- Lille score <=0.45 (steroid responders) had 85% +/- 2.5% 6-month survival vs 25% +/- 3.8% in non-responders (score >0.45); this is the real basis for the guideline-recommended practice of stopping steroids at day 7 in non-responders (futile, and adds infection risk) and considering early transplant instead. EARLY LIVER TRANSPLANTATION IN STEROID NON-RESPONDERS: Mathurin et al, NEJM 2011 (PMID 22070476) -- 26 carefully selected first-episode severe alcoholic hepatitis patients (strict criteria: no response to medical therapy, strong family support, committed to abstinence, no severe comorbidity; <2% of all severe AH admissions and 2.9% of available grafts were used) had 77% +/- 8% 6-month survival with early transplantation vs 23% +/- 8% in matched controls who did not receive a transplant (p<0.001); survival advantage persisted to 2 years (hazard ratio 6.08, p=0.004). 3 of 26 (11.5%) recipients relapsed to drinking, at 720-1140 days post-transplant -- i.e. most sustained abstinence.
curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Genuinely curative/preventive: complete abstinence in simple fatty liver (real, causal, majority of patients never progress). NOT a cure but a real major survival intervention: corticosteroids in Lille-score responders (reduces mortality in that subgroup but does not reverse the underlying disease process), and early liver transplantation in carefully selected non-responders (trades the disease for a transplanted organ and lifelong immunosuppression -- a real life-saving intervention, not a cure of ALD as a disease).
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Pentoxifylline has no proven mortality benefit (STOPAH, PMID 25901427) and should not be used in place of prednisolone. Prednisolone itself only reached borderline significance (p=0.06) for 28-day mortality in the UNSELECTED severe-AH population and showed no benefit at 90 days/1 year -- its real value is concentrated in the Lille-score-identified responder subgroup. Adding N-acetylcysteine (NAC) to prednisolone (Nguyen-Khac et al, NEJM 2011, PMID 22070475) improved 1-month survival (92% vs 76%, i.e. 8% vs 24% death, p=0.006) and reduced hepatorenal-syndrome deaths (9% vs 22%, p=0.02), but did NOT significantly improve the primary 6-month mortality endpoint (27% vs 38%, p=0.07) -- a real, honest partial benefit, not a home run. Liver transplantation criteria in most centers still require demonstrated sobriety (commonly 6 months) except in the highly selected early-transplant severe-AH protocol validated by Mathurin 2011, which remains used in only a small minority of eligible patients worldwide.
curative_option.important_caveat: None of this applies while active heavy drinking continues -- abstinence is the precondition for every other benefit described here, including transplant candidacy and steroid response durability. This entry covers the liver-directed treatment of ALD; management of alcohol use disorder itself (counselling, naltrexone/acamprosate, etc.) and of alcohol withdrawal (benzodiazepines, Wernicke prophylaxis with thiamine) are separate clinical domains not re-derived here.
curative_option.source: Teli et al Lancet 1995 PMID 7475591; Thursz et al NEJM 2015 PMID 25901427; Louvet et al Hepatology 2007 PMID 17518367; Mathurin et al NEJM 2011 PMID 22070476; Nguyen-Khac et al NEJM 2011 PMID 22070475; EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Management of alcohol-related liver disease, J Hepatol 2018, PMID 29628280; Seitz et al 'Alcoholic liver disease', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2018, PMID 30115921
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Full survey of every real, evidence-based intervention for alcoholic liver disease across its spectrum (simple steatosis -> alcoholic hepatitis -> cirrhosis), each with real effectiveness data, the biological reason it works, source, and honesty confidence flag. Priority order followed: 1) medicine/behavioral first-line, 2) injection/procedure, 3) everything else (including honest negative findings).

ald_complete_abstinence.name: Complete Alcohol Abstinence
ald_complete_abstinence.effectiveness: 81.8% (72/88) of patients with pure alcoholic fatty liver had NO progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis over a median 10.5-year follow-up; of the 9/88 (10.2%) who progressed to cirrhosis, 8 (88.9%) continued drinking more than 40 units/week throughout follow-up, meaning continued heavy drinking -- not abstinence -- drove almost all of the observed progression.
ald_complete_abstinence.reason_why: Ethanol and its metabolite acetaldehyde directly injure hepatocytes (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation) and drive triglyceride accumulation (steatosis) via altered NAD+/NADH ratio and impaired fatty-acid oxidation; removing the causal agent halts and, at the pure-steatosis stage, allows near-complete resolution of the hepatocellular fat and the associated inflammation, since no fibrotic scar has yet formed.
ald_complete_abstinence.source: Teli MR et al, 'Determinants of progression to cirrhosis or fibrosis in pure alcoholic fatty liver', Lancet 1995;346(8981):987-90, PMID 7475591

ald_corticosteroids_lille_guided.name: Prednisolone (40 mg/day x 28 days), Lille-Score-Guided
ald_corticosteroids_lille_guided.effectiveness: In the UNSELECTED severe alcoholic hepatitis population (Maddrey DF>=32), STOPAH trial (NEJM 2015, PMID 25901427, n=1053): 28-day mortality 14% (38/266) with prednisolone vs 17% (45/269) with placebo, OR 0.72 (95% CI 0.52-1.01, p=0.06) -- a borderline, non-significant trend. No significant benefit at 90 days or 1 year. When response is STRATIFIED by Lille score at day 7 (Louvet et al, Hepatology 2007, PMID 17518367): true responders (score <=0.45) have 85% +/- 2.5% 6-month survival vs only 25% +/- 3.8% in non-responders (score >0.45) -- the real clinical value of prednisolone is concentrated in identifying and treating this responder subgroup, and stopping futile steroids at day 7 in non-responders.
ald_corticosteroids_lille_guided.reason_why: Glucocorticoids suppress the intense neutrophilic/cytokine-driven (TNF-alpha, IL-8) hepatic inflammatory response that characterizes severe alcoholic hepatitis, reducing hepatocyte injury from the inflammatory cascade itself (not from alcohol directly). The Lille score (bilirubin change by day 7) captures whether this anti-inflammatory effect is actually translating into improving liver synthetic function -- non-response signals that inflammation is not the dominant driver of that patient's mortality risk (e.g. sepsis, multi-organ failure), so continuing steroids only adds infection risk without benefit.
ald_corticosteroids_lille_guided.important_caveat: Serious infections occurred in 13% of prednisolone-treated patients vs 7% of those not given prednisolone (p=0.002, STOPAH) -- a real, quantified harm that is why day-7 Lille-score reassessment and stopping in non-responders matters clinically.
ald_corticosteroids_lille_guided.source: Thursz MR et al, NEJM 2015, PMID 25901427; Louvet A et al, Hepatology 2007, PMID 17518367

ald_nac_corticosteroid_combination.name: Prednisolone + N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) Combination
ald_nac_corticosteroid_combination.effectiveness: Nguyen-Khac et al, NEJM 2011 (PMID 22070475): 1-month survival 92% (8% mortality) with prednisolone+NAC vs 76% (24% mortality) with prednisolone alone (p=0.006) -- a real, statistically significant short-term benefit. Deaths from hepatorenal syndrome were lower with combination therapy (9% vs 22%, p=0.02). However, the primary 6-month mortality endpoint was NOT significantly different: 27% (combination) vs 38% (prednisolone alone), p=0.07 -- an honest partial benefit that faded by 6 months.
ald_nac_corticosteroid_combination.reason_why: NAC replenishes hepatic glutathione, the principal intracellular antioxidant depleted by alcohol/acetaldehyde metabolism and by the oxidative burst of the inflammatory infiltrate in alcoholic hepatitis, and improves splanchnic/renal microcirculation -- plausibly explaining the observed reduction in early hepatorenal-syndrome deaths when added to a corticosteroid.
ald_nac_corticosteroid_combination.source: Nguyen-Khac E et al, NEJM 2011;365(19):1781-9, PMID 22070475

ald_nutritional_support.name: Adequate Caloric/Protein Nutritional Support (Target >=21.5-35 kcal/kg/day)
ald_nutritional_support.effectiveness: Moreno et al, Gastroenterology 2016 (PMID 26764182, 136 patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis on corticosteroids, 20 centers): patients with daily caloric intake BELOW 21.5 kcal/kg had 65.8% mortality vs 33.1% mortality in those achieving intake AT OR ABOVE that threshold -- i.e. roughly double the survival (66.9% vs 34.2%) with adequate nutrition, REGARDLESS of delivery route. Intensive enteral tube feeding added on top of corticosteroids did NOT itself lower 6-month mortality vs conventional (spontaneous oral) nutrition when corticosteroids were used (44.4% vs 52.1% mortality, p=0.406, not significant; feeding tubes were withdrawn prematurely in 48.5% of patients) -- the real, evidence-supported message is that hitting the calorie target matters, not the specific feeding route.
ald_nutritional_support.reason_why: Alcoholic hepatitis is a hypercatabolic state with severe protein-calorie malnutrition present in the large majority of hospitalized patients; adequate substrate supports hepatocyte regeneration and immune function, while caloric deficit independently predicts mortality regardless of liver-directed drug therapy.
ald_nutritional_support.source: Moreno C et al, Gastroenterology 2016;150(4):903-910, PMID 26764182

ald_early_liver_transplant_steroid_nonre.name: Early Liver Transplantation (Steroid Non-Responders, Strict Selection)
ald_early_liver_transplant_steroid_nonre.effectiveness: Mathurin et al, NEJM 2011 (PMID 22070476): in 26 highly selected first-episode severe alcoholic hepatitis patients who failed to respond to medical therapy, 6-month survival was 77% +/- 8% with early transplantation vs 23% +/- 8% in matched controls who did not undergo transplantation (p<0.001); the survival advantage persisted to 2 years (hazard ratio 6.08, p=0.004). Only 3 of 26 (11.5%) recipients relapsed to alcohol use, at 720-1140 days post-transplant.
ald_early_liver_transplant_steroid_nonre.reason_why: Replaces the acutely failing, severely inflamed liver before multi-organ failure or sepsis becomes irreversible, in patients whose native liver has essentially no chance of recovering in the required timeframe (Lille non-responders); strict psychosocial selection (family support, first episode, committed to abstinence) is what makes the very favorable relapse rate and survival outcome achievable.
ald_early_liver_transplant_steroid_nonre.important_caveat: This protocol was used in fewer than 2% of all severe alcoholic hepatitis admissions and consumed only 2.9% of available donor grafts in the study period -- it is real and highly effective in a carefully selected minority, not a broadly available option, and most transplant centers still require a defined period of demonstrated sobriety (commonly 6 months) outside this specific early-transplant-for-severe-AH protocol.

ald_pentoxifylline_negative_evidence.name: Pentoxifylline
ald_pentoxifylline_negative_evidence.type: Phosphodiesterase Inhibitor (Historically Proposed, Now Negative Evidence)
ald_pentoxifylline_negative_evidence.effectiveness: STOPAH trial, Thursz et al, NEJM 2015 (PMID 25901427): 28-day survival 81% (pentoxifylline) vs 83% (no pentoxifylline) -- odds ratio for 28-day mortality 1.07 (95% CI 0.77-1.49, p=0.69), a real, definitively negative result in the largest trial to date (n=1053). No longer recommended by current guidelines (EASL 2018, PMID 29628280) as therapy for severe alcoholic hepatitis.
ald_pentoxifylline_negative_evidence.reason_why: Was proposed to inhibit TNF-alpha production, but the STOPAH trial showed no measurable survival benefit from this mechanism in practice at the population level.
ald_pentoxifylline_negative_evidence.source: Thursz MR et al, NEJM 2015, PMID 25901427; EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines, J Hepatol 2018, PMID 29628280

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (progression-free survival over 10.5 years vs 28-day/1-month/6-month mortality) in DIFFERENT populations (asymptomatic pure fatty liver vs severe alcoholic hepatitis with Maddrey DF>=32) -- ranking together is directionally useful to prioritize action, not a strict apples-to-apples comparison. Complete abstinence is listed first per this disease's cure-first framing even though its numeric percentage is not the single highest value, because it is the only entry here that is genuinely preventive/curative rather than a mortality-reduction-in-already-severe-disease intervention.
