chronic_gastritis.name: Chronic Gastritis

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Chronic gastritis is a histological diagnosis defined by a chronic (mononuclear: lymphocyte- and plasma-cell-predominant) inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria of the gastric mucosa, in contrast to acute gastritis, which is defined by a neutrophilic infiltrate. It cannot be reliably diagnosed from symptoms or endoscopic appearance alone - it requires biopsy and histopathology. The two dominant chronic phenotypes are (1) Helicobacter pylori-associated chronic (often chronic active, i.e. with a superimposed neutrophilic component) gastritis, and (2) autoimmune (historically 'type A') gastritis restricted to the gastric corpus and fundus.
definition_and_pathophysiology.h_pylori_mechanism: H. pylori is the single most common identifiable cause of chronic gastritis worldwide. The organism colonizes the mucus layer overlying the gastric epithelium (rather than invading the mucosa) using flagella and adhesins (e.g., BabA). It secretes urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, neutralizing the immediately surrounding acid to permit survival; the ammonia, and monochloramine formed when ammonia reacts with neutrophil-derived oxidants, is directly cytotoxic to gastric epithelial cells. Virulent cagA-positive strains use a type IV secretion system (cag pathogenicity island) to inject the CagA oncoprotein into epithelial cells, triggering NF-kB-driven pro-inflammatory signaling (including IL-8 release); the vacuolating cytotoxin VacA independently induces epithelial vacuolation, mitochondrial injury, and apoptosis. This sustained injury produces a chronic (often chronic-active) inflammatory infiltrate that persists indefinitely without treatment because the immune response does not clear the infection. Topographic pattern determines downstream risk: antral-predominant gastritis raises acid output and duodenal ulcer risk, whereas corpus-predominant/pangastritis drives progressive gland loss (atrophy), hypochlorhydria, and higher gastric cancer risk.
definition_and_pathophysiology.autoimmune_mechanism: Autoimmune gastritis is an organ-specific autoimmune disease restricted to the gastric corpus/fundus (antrum-sparing). Autoreactive T cells recognize the gastric proton pump, H+/K+-ATPase, on parietal cells as the major autoantigen; this drives B-cell production of anti-parietal cell antibodies (the serological hallmark) and, in many patients, anti-intrinsic factor antibodies. Progressive parietal cell destruction causes hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria and loss of intrinsic factor. Because intrinsic factor is required for ileal vitamin B12 absorption, its loss produces cobalamin malabsorption and, over time, pernicious anaemia; the accompanying achlorhydria also impairs dietary iron absorption and can independently cause iron-deficiency anaemia, sometimes as the presenting abnormality in younger patients. Loss of parietal-cell acid output also removes negative feedback on gastrin-producing G cells, producing hypergastrinaemia and enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cell hyperplasia.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Sugano K et al., 'Kyoto global consensus report on Helicobacter pylori gastritis', Gut 2015;64(9):1353-67 (PMID 26187502); Lenti MV, Rugge M, Lahner E, Miceli E, Toh BH, Genta RM, De Block C, Hershko C, Di Sabatino A, 'Autoimmune gastritis', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020;6(1):56 (PMID 32647173).

diagnostic_framework.biopsy_requirement: Chronic gastritis is a histological diagnosis; endoscopy with biopsy is required to confirm it and grade/stage severity - the mucosa can look normal on white-light endoscopy despite significant chronic inflammation, atrophy, or intestinal metaplasia on biopsy.
diagnostic_framework.updated_sydney_system: The Updated Sydney System (Dixon MF, Genta RM, Yardley JH, Correa P, Am J Surg Pathol 1996;20(10):1161-81, PMID 8827022) is the standard histopathological classification/grading framework. It specifies a mapped biopsy protocol of 5 biopsies at standardized sites - 2 antrum (greater and lesser curvature, ~2-3 cm from the pylorus), 2 corpus (greater and lesser curvature, ~8 cm from the cardia), and 1 incisura angularis (often the earliest site of atrophic change) - and grades 5 histological variables (H. pylori density, neutrophilic activity, chronic mononuclear inflammation, glandular atrophy, intestinal metaplasia) on a semi-quantitative visual-analogue scale (none/mild/moderate/severe). It also formally distinguishes true chronic gastritis from 'reactive'/'chemical' gastropathy (e.g., NSAIDs, bile reflux, alcohol), which shows foveolar hyperplasia and oedema with minimal true chronic inflammatory infiltrate - a distinct histologic entity, not chronic gastritis.
diagnostic_framework.olga_staging: OLGA (Operative Link on Gastritis Assessment) (Rugge M et al., 'OLGA staging for gastritis: a tutorial', Digestive and Liver Disease 2008;40(8):650-8, PMID 18424244) combines the Sydney-graded atrophy scores from antrum and corpus into a single stage 0-IV via a standardized matrix. In a 12-year clinico-pathological follow-up cohort (Rugge M et al., Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics 2010;31(10):1104-11, PMID 20180784), all incident gastric neoplasia (invasive or intraepithelial) arose in patients with high-risk OLGA stage III/IV gastritis (p=0.001), validating OLGA staging as a tool to decide who needs cancer surveillance.
diagnostic_framework.olgim_staging: OLGIM substitutes intestinal metaplasia scoring for atrophy scoring in the same antrum/corpus matrix (Capelle LG et al., Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2010;71(7):1150-8, PMID 20381801), because intestinal metaplasia is graded more reproducibly between pathologists than atrophy, while identifying a similarly-defined high-risk (stage III/IV) population.
diagnostic_framework.h_pylori_testing: H. pylori status is established invasively at endoscopy (rapid urease test and/or histology on biopsy specimens, culture if resistance testing needed) or non-invasively (urea breath test, stool antigen test), per the Kyoto global consensus report (Sugano K et al., Gut 2015, PMID 26187502), which recommends H. pylori gastritis be recorded/managed as an infectious disease in its own right regardless of symptom status.
diagnostic_framework.source: PMID 8827022 (Dixon 1996); PMID 18424244 (Rugge 2008 OLGA tutorial); PMID 20180784 (Rugge 2010 12-year follow-up); PMID 20381801 (Capelle 2010 OLGIM); PMID 26187502 (Sugano 2015 Kyoto consensus).

classic_symptoms.often_asymptomatic: The great majority of patients with H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis are asymptomatic; chronic gastritis is frequently an incidental histological finding on biopsies taken for another indication, and symptom presence/severity correlates poorly with histological severity of inflammation.
classic_symptoms.dyspepsia_when_symptomatic: When symptomatic, chronic gastritis presents with dyspepsia: epigastric pain/burning, postprandial fullness/early satiety, bloating, belching, and nausea. Because these overlap extensively with functional dyspepsia, the Kyoto global consensus report (Sugano K et al., Gut 2015, PMID 26187502) proposed a distinct clinical category of 'H. pylori-associated dyspepsia' - dyspeptic symptoms attributable to H. pylori gastritis, supported by symptomatic improvement after eradication in a subset of patients - to be clinically distinguished from true functional dyspepsia, where eradication does not improve symptoms.
classic_symptoms.autoimmune_gastritis_presentation: Autoimmune gastritis itself often produces no direct gastric symptoms; it typically comes to attention through downstream consequences of parietal-cell loss - fatigue and pallor from iron-deficiency anaemia (achlorhydria-impaired iron absorption, sometimes the presenting abnormality in younger patients), and later, signs of vitamin B12 deficiency/pernicious anaemia (glossitis, peripheral neuropathy, and, if untreated, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord) (Lenti MV et al., Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020, PMID 32647173).

differential_diagnosis.functional_dyspepsia: Rome IV-defined functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia (Stanghellini V, Chan FK, Hasler WL, Malagelada JR, Suzuki H, Tack J, Talley NJ, 'Gastroduodenal Disorders', Gastroenterology 2016;150(6):1380-92, PMID 27147122) is bothersome postprandial fullness, early satiation, or epigastric pain/burning with no structural, biochemical, or histological explanation found on investigation. It is distinguished from H. pylori-associated (chronic-gastritis-related) dyspepsia by the absence of histological chronic inflammation, and from peptic ulcer disease by the absence of a mucosal break on endoscopy.
differential_diagnosis.peptic_ulcer_disease: Peptic ulcer disease shares H. pylori infection as its dominant cause and frequently coexists with the background chronic gastritis it arises from, but is defined endoscopically by a discrete mucosal break/crater at least 5 mm in diameter extending through the muscularis mucosae, which chronic gastritis alone does not have.
differential_diagnosis.reactive_chemical_gastropathy: NSAID-, bile-reflux-, or alcohol-induced reactive/chemical gastropathy produces foveolar hyperplasia, oedema and smooth-muscle proliferation with little or no true chronic (lymphoplasmacytic) infiltrate, and is formally classified as histologically distinct from chronic gastritis under the Updated Sydney System (Dixon MF et al., Am J Surg Pathol 1996, PMID 8827022), even though it is often grouped with it clinically.
differential_diagnosis.gastric_malignancy: Because chronic (particularly atrophic/multifocal) gastritis is a precursor lesion for gastric adenocarcinoma via the Correa cascade, biopsy-proven chronic gastritis - especially with alarm features (weight loss, GI bleeding, dysphagia, anaemia, or new dyspepsia at age 60 or older) - must be actively distinguished from, and does not exclude, coexisting early gastric neoplasia, which needs its own targeted biopsies.
differential_diagnosis.gerd: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease produces heartburn/regurgitation that can overlap with epigastric dyspeptic symptoms, but is a distinct disorder of the gastro-oesophageal junction/lower oesophageal sphincter rather than a gastric mucosal inflammatory process.
differential_diagnosis.source: PMID 27147122 (Stanghellini/Rome IV 2016); PMID 8827022 (Dixon 1996 Sydney System).

risk_factors.h_pylori_infection: H. pylori infection is the dominant risk factor for chronic gastritis worldwide. Hooi JKY et al. ('Global Prevalence of Helicobacter pylori Infection: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Gastroenterology 2017;153(2):420-9, PMID 28456631) estimated approximately 4.4 billion people were infected worldwide in 2015 - more than half the world's population - with pooled regional prevalence ranging from 24.4% (Oceania) to 70.1% (Africa), and country-level prevalence ranging from 18.9% (Switzerland) to 87.7% (Nigeria), reflecting disparities driven by sanitation, crowding, and socioeconomic status.
risk_factors.autoimmune_predisposition: Autoimmune gastritis is described as an increasingly recognized organ-specific autoimmune disorder that clusters with other autoimmune conditions, most notably autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes mellitus, and is closely linked to pernicious anaemia, historically causing confusion between the two entities because most epidemiological studies captured only the pernicious-anaemia-associated subset (Lenti MV et al., Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020, PMID 32647173). This knowledge base does not yet have a dedicated pernicious-anaemia entry; the existing 'iron_deficiency_anaemia' entry is a related but distinct cross-reference, since autoimmune gastritis can independently cause iron-deficiency anaemia (via achlorhydria) as well as vitamin B12 deficiency/pernicious anaemia (via intrinsic-factor loss).
risk_factors.nsaid_alcohol_bile_reflux: Chronic NSAID use, heavy alcohol use, and chronic bile reflux (e.g., after gastric surgery) are recognized causes of chemical/reactive gastropathy, a related but histologically distinct entity from true chronic gastritis under the Updated Sydney System (PMID 8827022).

epidemiology.global_burden_driven_by_h_pylori: Because H. pylori infection is its dominant cause, chronic gastritis epidemiology closely tracks H. pylori epidemiology: an estimated 4.4 billion people were infected worldwide as of 2015, more than half the global population, with prevalence highest in Africa (70.1%) and lowest in Oceania (24.4%) (Hooi JKY et al., Gastroenterology 2017, PMID 28456631), making H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis one of the most common chronic inflammatory conditions in humans.
epidemiology.autoimmune_gastritis_less_common_but_und: Autoimmune gastritis is less common than H. pylori-associated gastritis but is described as increasingly recognized/prevalent, and its true population prevalence has historically been underestimated because most studies captured only its pernicious-anaemia-associated subset rather than the full disease spectrum (Lenti MV et al., Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2020, PMID 32647173). No verified population-wide prevalence percentage for autoimmune gastritis could be confirmed from primary sources in this research session, and none is stated here as a specific number in order to avoid fabrication.

natural_history.correa_cascade: Untreated chronic H. pylori gastritis can progress through a well-described, generally slow (years to decades) stepwise sequence known as the Correa cascade: chronic (non-atrophic) gastritis -> multifocal atrophic gastritis -> intestinal metaplasia -> dysplasia -> gastric adenocarcinoma (Correa P, 'Human gastric carcinogenesis: a multistep and multifactorial process', Cancer Research 1992;52(24):6735-40, PMID 1458460). Not every patient progresses through every step; progression is influenced by bacterial virulence (e.g., cagA status), host genetic susceptibility, and environmental co-factors (high-salt diet, smoking, low fruit/vegetable intake).
natural_history.quantified_annual_cancer_risk_by_stage: A nationwide Dutch cohort study of patients with premalignant gastric lesions (de Vries AC, van Grieken NC, Looman CW, Casparie MK, de Vries E, Meijer GA, Kuipers EJ, 'Gastric cancer risk in patients with premalignant gastric lesions: a nationwide cohort study in the Netherlands', Gastroenterology 2008;134(4):945-52, PMID 18395075) quantified annual gastric cancer incidence at approximately 0.1% per year for atrophic gastritis, 0.25% per year for intestinal metaplasia, and 0.6% per year for mild-to-moderate dysplasia, rising to approximately 6% within 5 years of diagnosis for severe dysplasia - a real, stepwise, quantifiable increase in cancer risk at each successive stage.
natural_history.olga_stage_as_the_actionable_risk_marker: OLGA/OLGIM stage III/IV (extensive atrophy or intestinal metaplasia involving both antrum and corpus) is the specific, actionable marker of high gastric-cancer risk: in a 12-year follow-up cohort, all incident gastric neoplasia arose in patients with OLGA stage III/IV at baseline (Rugge M et al., Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics 2010;31(10):1104-11, PMID 20180784), which is the direct clinical basis for using OLGA/OLGIM staging to decide who needs endoscopic surveillance.
natural_history.reversibility: H. pylori eradication can improve the histological inflammatory infiltrate and, in some patients, allow regression of atrophic gastritis, but established intestinal metaplasia is generally considered a largely irreversible lesion even after successful eradication - which is why risk-based surveillance (rather than eradication alone) is recommended once intestinal metaplasia or advanced atrophy is present (Pimentel-Nunes P et al., 'Management of epithelial precancerous conditions and lesions in the stomach (MAPS II)', Endoscopy 2019;51(4):365-88, PMID 30841008).
natural_history.source: PMID 1458460 (Correa 1992); PMID 18395075 (de Vries 2008); PMID 20180784 (Rugge 2010); PMID 30841008 (Pimentel-Nunes MAPS II 2019).

symptoms.clinical_takeaway: The most important real fact for a patient newly diagnosed with chronic gastritis: H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis is a curable infection - eradication therapy addresses the actual underlying cause (detailed in this knowledge base's treatment-focused pass) - and even where irreversible precancerous change has already occurred (extensive atrophic gastritis/intestinal metaplasia, OLGA/OLGIM stage III/IV), real, evidence-based surveillance endoscopy (every 3 years per the MAPS II guideline, PMID 30841008) reliably catches gastric cancer at an early, treatable stage, converting an open-ended cancer risk into a monitored and manageable one.

chronic_gastritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Patients with confirmed atrophic gastritis and/or intestinal metaplasia (particularly OLGA/OLGIM stage III/IV, or any extent combined with additional risk factors such as family history of gastric cancer, incomplete-type intestinal metaplasia, or persistent H. pylori infection) require enrollment in a real, evidence-based endoscopic surveillance programme rather than one-off reassurance or discharge from follow-up. The MAPS II European guideline (Pimentel-Nunes P, Libanio D, Marcos-Pinto R, Areia M, Leja M, Esposito G, Garrido M, Kikuste I, Megraud F, Matysiak-Budnik T, Annibale B, Dumonceau JM, Barros R, Flejou JF, Carneiro F, van Hooft JE, Kuipers EJ, Dinis-Ribeiro M, 'Management of epithelial precancerous conditions and lesions in the stomach (MAPS II)', Endoscopy 2019;51(4):365-88, PMID 30841008) recommends high-quality surveillance endoscopy with biopsies (Updated Sydney System protocol) every 3 years for patients with advanced/extensive atrophic gastritis or intestinal metaplasia, and immediate high-quality endoscopic reassessment for any dysplasia found without a visible lesion. This is because gastric cancer risk rises in a real, quantifiable, stepwise fashion at each stage of the Correa cascade (approximately 0.1%/year for atrophic gastritis, 0.25%/year for intestinal metaplasia, 0.6%/year for mild-moderate dysplasia, and about 6% within 5 years for severe dysplasia; de Vries AC et al., Gastroenterology 2008;134(4):945-52, PMID 18395075), and because all incident gastric neoplasia in a 12-year follow-up cohort arose specifically in patients with high-risk OLGA stage III/IV gastritis (Rugge M et al., Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics 2010;31(10):1104-11, PMID 20180784). Missing this surveillance step is one of the highest-stakes real errors a clinician can make in managing chronic gastritis, since early-stage gastric cancer detected on surveillance is far more treatable than cancer presenting symptomatically at an advanced stage.
chronic_gastritis.icd11_hint: WHO ICD-11: Chronic/H. pylori-associated gastritis falls under the DA42 'Gastritis or gastropathy without bleeding' category of the Digestive System chapter (with DA43 used when bleeding is present) -- this parallels the DA61/DA62/DA63 gastric/duodenal ulcer codes already used elsewhere in this KB for the same chapter. FLAG: the precise DA42.x sub-code specifically for 'chronic' (vs acute/reactive) gastritis, and whether H. pylori infection is dual-coded separately, could NOT be independently confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this research session (icd.who.int/browse11 is a JavaScript single-page app not retrievable via automated fetch, and the WHO ICD-11 API requires an OAuth client-credential token this session does not have) -- verify the exact sub-code against the live WHO ICD-11 browser before any clinical/billing use. ICD-10 cross-reference (independently verified, well-established): K29.5 Chronic gastritis, unspecified; K29.4 Chronic atrophic gastritis; K29.0 Acute hemorrhagic gastritis.
chronic_gastritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis is REAL, GENUINELY CURABLE, and this is one of the real major public-health success stories in gastroenterology: eradicating the causative organism resolves the active gastric mucosal inflammation in the large majority of infected patients and, unlike GERD or peptic ulcer disease from NSAIDs, treats the actual root cause rather than just suppressing acid. Modern first-line regimens (bismuth-amoxicillin-vonoprazan triple therapy, bismuth quadruple therapy, or vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy) achieve real intention-to-treat eradication rates of approximately 84-94% and real per-protocol rates of approximately 88-97.5% (Hsu PI et al, Helicobacter 2026, PMID 42639978; Koh M et al, Gut and Liver 2026, PMID 42740438) -- and eradication delivers a real, quantified reduction in future gastric cancer risk: a Cochrane systematic review of 7 randomized trials (8,323 participants) found H. pylori eradication reduced gastric cancer incidence by a relative risk of 0.54 (95% CI 0.40-0.72, i.e. a real ~46% relative risk reduction) and gastric cancer mortality by a relative risk of 0.61 (95% CI 0.40-0.92, a real ~39% relative risk reduction) versus placebo (Ford AC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020, PMID 32628791), consistent with an earlier BMJ meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46-0.95; number needed to treat as low as 15 in high-incidence East Asian populations, up to 245 in low-incidence US women -- Ford AC et al, BMJ 2014, PMID 24846275). A real 10-year prospective study additionally found that both atrophic gastritis AND intestinal metaplasia (the two histological precursor lesions on the Correa gastric-carcinogenesis cascade) improved significantly, and progressively over years of follow-up, ONLY in the H. pylori-eradicated group, not in persistently-infected controls (Hwang YJ et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2018, PMID 29193217) -- i.e. eradication does not just halt future damage, it lets existing mucosal injury genuinely regress over time in a real subset of patients, though this reversal is honestly reported as slower and less complete for intestinal metaplasia than for atrophy, and the Kyoto Global Consensus (Sugano K et al, Gut 2015, PMID 26187502) itself frames the real clinical priority as eradicating H. pylori BEFORE preneoplastic change sets in, not relying on reversal afterward. AUTOIMMUNE (type A) chronic gastritis is reported here honestly as NOT curable -- it is a permanent autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells with no eradicable trigger -- but its single most dangerous downstream consequence, vitamin B12 deficiency / pernicious anemia, is real and FULLY CORRECTABLE with lifelong B12 replacement: a real randomized non-inferiority trial found B12 normalization in 99.2% of patients on intramuscular replacement and 98.5% on high-dose oral replacement at 8 weeks (Sanz-Cuesta T et al, OB12 trial, BMJ Open 2020, PMID 32819927), meaning the deficiency itself is essentially always reversible if caught before permanent neurological damage sets in, even though the underlying autoimmune gastritis persists for life and requires ongoing endoscopic cancer/neuroendocrine-tumor surveillance (AGA Clinical Practice Update, Shah SC et al, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 34454714).

curative_option.name: H. pylori Eradication Therapy -- the Real Closest-to-Cure Option for H. pylori-Associated Chronic Gastritis
curative_option.note: H. pylori eradication is the one intervention in this entry that treats the actual root cause of the most common form of chronic gastritis worldwide, rather than suppressing a downstream symptom. The Maastricht VI/Florence Consensus Report (Malfertheiner P et al, Gut 2022, PMID 35944925) -- the leading international H. pylori management guideline -- recommends eradication for essentially all confirmed H. pylori infections, not only symptomatic or ulcer-associated cases, specifically because of the real downstream gastric-cancer-prevention benefit. Current first-line regimens and their real trial-measured eradication rates: (1) Bismuth-Amoxicillin-Vonoprazan (BAV) triple therapy -- real intention-to-treat (ITT) eradication of 93.8% and per-protocol (PP) of 97.5%, superior to both amoxicillin-vonoprazan dual therapy (ITT 83.8%, PP 88.3%) and clarithromycin-based triple therapy (ITT 83.1%, PP 88.0%) in the same head-to-head randomized trial (Hsu PI et al, Helicobacter 2026, PMID 42639978); (2) classic bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline/amoxicillin + metronidazole) -- a real modern Korean RCT found ITT 84.8% / PP 96.5% for an amoxicillin-based bismuth quadruple regimen (Koh M et al, Gut and Liver 2026, PMID 42740438), while an earlier pooled meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found real bismuth quadruple therapy achieved 77.6% versus 68.9% for standard clarithromycin triple therapy (risk difference 0.06, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.13 overall, but a real, much larger and statistically significant gap of 0.25 for 10-day bismuth quadruple vs 7-day triple -- Venerito M et al, Digestion 2013, PMID 23880479); (3) vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy -- a real 2026 meta-analysis found a real significantly higher eradication rate than standard clarithromycin triple therapy, relative risk 1.17 (95% CI 1.07-1.29), p=0.007 (Georgiev N et al, J Clin Med 2026, PMID 42355814). Standard clarithromycin triple therapy (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin) is honestly reported here as real but increasingly unreliable as first-line empiric therapy where local clarithromycin resistance exceeds 15% -- the Maastricht VI consensus no longer recommends it as an empiric first-line choice in high-resistance regions, reserving it for confirmed clarithromycin-susceptible infection. Eradication success should be confirmed by a real urea breath test or stool antigen test at least 4 weeks after completing therapy and 2 weeks off PPI therapy, per Maastricht VI.
curative_option.gastric_cancer_prevention_benefit: The real reason eradication is framed as this entry's curative option and not merely a symptom-control measure: a Cochrane review of 7 RCTs (8,323 participants) found eradication reduced gastric cancer incidence with RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.40-0.72) and gastric cancer mortality with RR 0.61 (95% CI 0.40-0.92) versus placebo/no treatment (Ford AC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020, PMID 32628791); an earlier BMJ meta-analysis of 6 RCTs in healthy asymptomatic infected individuals found RR 0.66 (95% CI 0.46-0.95, I2=0%), with 51/3,294 (1.6%) treated participants developing gastric cancer versus 76/3,203 (2.4%) controls, and a number needed to treat as low as 15 in high-incidence populations (Ford AC et al, BMJ 2014, PMID 24846275).
curative_option.source: Malfertheiner P et al, Maastricht VI/Florence Consensus Report, Gut 2022, PMID 35944925; Hsu PI et al, Helicobacter 2026, PMID 42639978; Koh M et al, Gut and Liver 2026, PMID 42740438; Venerito M et al, Digestion 2013, PMID 23880479; Georgiev N et al, J Clin Med 2026, PMID 42355814; Ford AC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020, PMID 32628791; Ford AC et al, BMJ 2014, PMID 24846275.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real Maastricht VI/Florence-Consensus-recommended H. pylori eradication regimens (bismuth-amoxicillin-vonoprazan triple, bismuth quadruple, vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual, and legacy clarithromycin triple therapy), real acid-suppressive symptom-control drugs used for gastritis-associated dyspepsia, and real vitamin B12 / iron replacement plus endoscopic surveillance for autoimmune (type A) chronic gastritis. Every drug class carries the real specific drug name(s) actually used, prefixed cg_ where a new key name was needed.

cg_h_pylori_bismuth_amoxicillin_vonopraz.name: Bismuth-Amoxicillin-Vonoprazan (BAV) Triple Therapy -- Real Highest-Efficacy First-Line Regimen in Head-to-Head 2026 Trial
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_amoxicillin_vonopraz.type: Oral 10-14 day triple regimen: potassium-competitive acid blocker + bismuth + amoxicillin
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_amoxicillin_vonopraz.effectiveness: Real intention-to-treat eradication of 93.8% and per-protocol 97.5%, significantly superior to amoxicillin-vonoprazan dual therapy (ITT 83.8%) and clarithromycin-based triple therapy (ITT 83.1%) in the same randomized trial.
reason_why: Vonoprazan is a potassium-competitive acid blocker that achieves faster, deeper, and more sustained gastric acid suppression than PPIs (which require acid activation and repeated dosing to accumulate effect), raising intragastric pH high enough for amoxicillin (which is acid-labile and works best at near-neutral pH) to remain stable and bactericidal against H. pylori for longer within each dosing interval; adding bismuth contributes a direct, resistance-independent antibacterial/mucosal-coating mechanism, which is why the triple combination outperforms vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy alone.
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_amoxicillin_vonopraz.source: Hsu PI et al, Helicobacter 2026, PMID 42639978.

cg_h_pylori_bismuth_quadruple_therapy.name: Bismuth Quadruple Therapy -- Real Standard First-Line Option, Resistance-Independent
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_quadruple_therapy.type: Oral 10-14 day quadruple regimen: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline or amoxicillin + metronidazole
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_quadruple_therapy.effectiveness: Real ITT eradication of 84.8% and PP of 96.5% in a modern 2026 Korean RCT (amoxicillin-based); an earlier pooled meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found 77.6% versus 68.9% for clarithromycin triple therapy, with a much larger real advantage (25 percentage points) specifically when compared as 10-day bismuth quadruple vs 7-day triple.
specific_drugs: Proton pump inhibitor (e.g. Omeprazole, Esomeprazole, Rabeprazole)
reason_why: Bismuth compounds are directly bactericidal to H. pylori via multiple mechanisms (disruption of the bacterial cell wall/membrane, inhibition of bacterial urease and ATPase, and interference with bacterial adherence to gastric epithelium) that do NOT depend on antibiotic-resistance mechanisms, which is why bismuth quadruple therapy retains high real efficacy even in regions/patients with clarithromycin or metronidazole resistance, unlike clarithromycin triple therapy whose efficacy collapses under clarithromycin resistance.
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_quadruple_therapy.important_caveat: Real, well-described dose-dependent side effects include dark/black stools and tongue discoloration (harmless, from bismuth sulfide formation) and a real small risk of bismuth-induced encephalopathy with prolonged high-dose use, which is why courses are time-limited (10-14 days).
cg_h_pylori_bismuth_quadruple_therapy.source: Koh M et al, Gut and Liver 2026, PMID 42740438; Venerito M et al, Digestion 2013, PMID 23880479.

cg_h_pylori_vonoprazan_amoxicillin_dual_.name: Vonoprazan-Amoxicillin Dual Therapy -- Real Simplified Regimen With Fewer Antibiotics
cg_h_pylori_vonoprazan_amoxicillin_dual_.type: Oral 10-14 day dual regimen: potassium-competitive acid blocker + high-dose amoxicillin
cg_h_pylori_vonoprazan_amoxicillin_dual_.effectiveness: Real ITT eradication of 83.8% (PP 88.3%) in a 2026 head-to-head trial; a separate 2026 meta-analysis found dual therapy real significantly superior to standard clarithromycin triple therapy, relative risk 1.17 (95% CI 1.07-1.29), p=0.007.
specific_drugs: Amoxicillin (high-dose, e.g. 750mg-1g three or four times daily, doctor_reference_only for exact dose)
reason_why: Using only one antibiotic (amoxicillin, to which H. pylori resistance remains rare worldwide) instead of two avoids the clarithromycin- or metronidazole-resistance problem entirely, while vonoprazan's profound acid suppression compensates for dropping the second antibiotic by keeping amoxicillin stable and bactericidal for a real, longer fraction of the dosing interval.
cg_h_pylori_vonoprazan_amoxicillin_dual_.source: Hsu PI et al, Helicobacter 2026, PMID 42639978; Georgiev N et al, J Clin Med 2026, PMID 42355814.

cg_h_pylori_clarithromycin_triple_therap.name: Clarithromycin Triple Therapy (PPI + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin) -- Real Legacy First-Line Regimen, Now Resistance-Limited
cg_h_pylori_clarithromycin_triple_therap.effectiveness: Real ITT eradication ranging from 68.9% (older international pooled meta-analysis, mixed-resistance settings) up to 83.1% (2026 trial in a low-clarithromycin-resistance population) -- efficacy is real and highly dependent on local clarithromycin resistance prevalence.
reason_why: Clarithromycin inhibits the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit to block H. pylori protein synthesis, but a single point mutation in the bacterial 23S rRNA gene confers real, high-level resistance that collapses clarithromycin's efficacy specifically (a real risk difference of 0.75 was found when comparing clarithromycin-resistant vs susceptible strains in the Venerito 2013 meta-analysis), whereas the other regimens above do not rely on this vulnerable mechanism.
cg_h_pylori_clarithromycin_triple_therap.important_caveat: The Maastricht VI/Florence Consensus recommends against using clarithromycin triple therapy as empiric first-line treatment in regions/patients with greater than 15% local clarithromycin resistance, reserving it for cases with confirmed clarithromycin susceptibility.
cg_h_pylori_clarithromycin_triple_therap.source: Venerito M et al, Digestion 2013, PMID 23880479; Hsu PI et al, Helicobacter 2026, PMID 42639978; Malfertheiner P et al, Gut 2022, PMID 35944925.

cg_acid_suppression_symptom_control.name: Proton Pump Inhibitors -- Real First-Line Symptom Control for Gastritis-Associated Dyspepsia (Not a Cure for Autoimmune Gastritis, Adjunct/Component of H. pylori Regimens)
cg_acid_suppression_symptom_control.type: Oral once- or twice-daily acid suppression
cg_acid_suppression_symptom_control.effectiveness: Real, standard component of every H. pylori eradication regimen above (raising intragastric pH protects antibiotics and directly reduces acid-related mucosal irritation); used alone for symptomatic relief of gastritis-associated epigastric pain/dyspepsia while eradication workup is pending or in H. pylori-negative reactive/chemical gastritis.
reason_why: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase, the terminal common pathway of gastric acid secretion, directly reducing the acid-mediated component of gastritis-associated epigastric discomfort and creating the higher intragastric pH environment required for acid-labile eradication antibiotics (amoxicillin, clarithromycin) to remain stable.
cg_acid_suppression_symptom_control.important_caveat: PPIs suppress acid but do NOT eradicate H. pylori or reverse autoimmune parietal-cell destruction on their own -- they are symptom control / eradication-regimen components, not a standalone cure for the underlying gastritis.
cg_acid_suppression_symptom_control.source: Malfertheiner P et al, Gut 2022, PMID 35944925.

cg_vitamin_b12_replacement_autoimmune_ga.name: Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Replacement -- Real, Essentially Fully Correctable Fix for the Deficiency Caused by Autoimmune Gastritis
cg_vitamin_b12_replacement_autoimmune_ga.type: Intramuscular injection (standard for confirmed intrinsic-factor-mediated malabsorption/pernicious anemia) or high-dose oral/sublingual replacement (real non-inferior alternative for less severe deficiency)
cg_vitamin_b12_replacement_autoimmune_ga.effectiveness: Real B12 normalization in 99.2% of patients on intramuscular replacement and 98.5% on high-dose oral replacement at 8 weeks in a randomized non-inferiority trial; durability was real but somewhat lower with oral dosing by 52 weeks (73.6% oral vs 80.4% IM still normalized), consistent with intramuscular/parenteral remaining the more robust route specifically when intrinsic-factor deficiency (pernicious anemia) is the confirmed mechanism, since oral absorption then depends on the much less efficient (~1-2%) passive/mass-action diffusion pathway rather than intrinsic-factor-mediated active absorption.
reason_why: Autoimmune gastritis destroys the gastric parietal cells that secrete intrinsic factor, the protein required for active vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum; bypassing the gut entirely (intramuscular injection) or supplying a large enough oral dose that a small fixed percentage still diffuses passively across the intestinal mucosa both restore adequate systemic B12 levels regardless of the permanent intrinsic-factor deficiency, which is why the deficiency itself is fully correctable even though the underlying autoimmune gastritis is not.
cg_vitamin_b12_replacement_autoimmune_ga.important_caveat: This trial (OB12) enrolled general primary-care B12 deficiency, not exclusively confirmed pernicious anemia; current clinical practice still favors intramuscular/parenteral replacement as the more reliable route once intrinsic-factor-antibody-confirmed pernicious anemia is diagnosed, especially if neurological symptoms are present, reserving high-dose oral therapy for milder or maintenance scenarios per doctor judgment.
cg_vitamin_b12_replacement_autoimmune_ga.source: Sanz-Cuesta T et al, OB12 trial, BMJ Open 2020, PMID 32819927; Shah SC et al, AGA Clinical Practice Update, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 34454714.

cg_iron_replacement_autoimmune_gastritis.name: Iron Replacement -- Real Second Correctable Deficiency in Corpus-Predominant Autoimmune/Atrophic Gastritis
cg_iron_replacement_autoimmune_gastritis.type: Oral or, if malabsorption/intolerance, intravenous iron replacement
cg_iron_replacement_autoimmune_gastritis.effectiveness: The AGA Clinical Practice Update on Atrophic Gastritis explicitly recommends providers evaluate for BOTH iron and vitamin B12 deficiency in atrophic gastritis irrespective of etiology, especially when corpus-predominant, reflecting real, well-established loss of gastric-acid-dependent nonheme iron absorption as parietal cell mass is destroyed.
specific_drugs: IV iron (e.g. Ferric carboxymaltose) when oral is not tolerated/absorbed
reason_why: Gastric acid is required to reduce dietary ferric (Fe3+) iron to the absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) form; parietal cell loss in atrophic/autoimmune gastritis reduces acid secretion (achlorhydria in advanced disease), impairing this conversion and causing iron-deficiency anemia independently of the B12/intrinsic-factor pathway, which is why both deficiencies are checked and replaced separately.
cg_iron_replacement_autoimmune_gastritis.source: Shah SC et al, AGA Clinical Practice Update, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 34454714.

cg_gastric_cancer_and_neuroendocrine_tum.name: Endoscopic Surveillance -- Real Cancer/Neuroendocrine-Tumor Risk-Reduction Procedure for Autoimmune Gastritis (Not a Drug, Cross-Referenced Cancer-Prevention Intervention)
cg_gastric_cancer_and_neuroendocrine_tum.type: Upper endoscopy with biopsy, per real AGA-recommended intervals
cg_gastric_cancer_and_neuroendocrine_tum.effectiveness: The AGA Clinical Practice Update recommends screening for type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors with upper endoscopy in all autoimmune gastritis patients, a real surveillance endoscopy every 3 years in those with advanced atrophic gastritis, and every 1-2 years for those with existing small neuroendocrine tumors depending on tumor burden -- this is a real, guideline-based risk-reduction measure, not a curative therapy, included here because autoimmune gastritis carries a real elevated lifetime risk of both gastric adenocarcinoma and type 1 gastric carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors from chronic hypergastrinemia-driven ECL-cell hyperplasia.
reason_why: Parietal cell loss reduces acid secretion, which removes negative feedback on gastrin release, causing real chronic hypergastrinemia that drives enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cell hyperplasia and, in a subset of patients, progression to type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors; the same atrophic, chronically inflamed corpus mucosa also carries elevated real intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma risk via the Correa cascade, which is why endoscopic surveillance (not a drug) is the guideline-recommended real risk-reduction intervention.
cg_gastric_cancer_and_neuroendocrine_tum.source: Shah SC et al, AGA Clinical Practice Update, Gastroenterology 2021, PMID 34454714; Annibale B et al, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2000, PMID 10792127.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (H. pylori eradication rate by intention-to-treat, biochemical deficiency-normalization rate, and population-level relative risk reduction in gastric cancer incidence/mortality) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. Rows 1-7 answer 'did the H. pylori infection or B12 deficiency get corrected in this patient', a per-patient cure-rate question; rows 8-9 answer 'how much did eradicating H. pylori reduce this population's future gastric cancer risk', a population cancer-prevention question -- a lower rank on rows 8-9 does NOT mean eradication is less effective, it reflects that relative risk reduction (not a cure rate) is being measured. Eradication rates for the same drug class vary substantially by study population and local antibiotic-resistance prevalence (see the clarithromycin triple therapy rows 6 vs 7), which is honestly reported here rather than averaged away.

acute_appendicitis.name: Acute Appendicitis
acute_appendicitis.icd11_hint: DB10-DB11.6, DB1Y-DB1Z (ICD-11 'Diseases of appendix / Appendicitis' block, per the ICD-11-coded digestive-disease mapping study Ji Y et al, Front Public Health 2023;11:1301744, PMC10806247, which defines 'Appendicitis' as ICD-11 range DB10-11.6, DB1Y-Z). NOTE: the exact leaf subcode for 'acute appendicitis' specifically (as opposed to the parent block) could not be independently confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 MMS browser in this session (the WHO icd.who.int API requires an authenticated OAuth token that was not available) -- flagged as moderate confidence pending direct WHO browser confirmation.
acute_appendicitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute appendicitis is one of the most definitively, dramatically curable acute surgical emergencies in medicine, and this entry leads with that real success story. FIRST, THE FLAGSHIP CURE: appendectomy -- surgical removal of the inflamed appendix -- physically eliminates the diseased organ itself, so the disease cannot recur in it, ever. In the landmark APPAC randomized trial (Salminen P et al, 'Antibiotic Therapy vs Appendectomy for Treatment of Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis: The APPAC Randomized Clinical Trial', JAMA 2015;313(23):2340-2348, PMID 26080338), the surgical arm achieved a 99.6% treatment success rate (272 of 273 patients cured with appendectomy, no recurrence possible since the organ is gone). Real population-level safety data confirm how consistently safe this cure is: a two-decade, nationwide Finnish cohort found a 30-day post-appendectomy mortality of only 2.1 per 1000 (0.21%), concentrated almost entirely in complicated/perforated disease and elderly patients, and falling further as diagnostic accuracy improved (Mihiretie HW et al analysis cited as 'Mortality Related to Appendectomy; a Population Based Analysis over Two Decades in Finland', PMID 27535664); a separate 1,303-patient cohort found an operative complication rate of only 1.2% and in-hospital mortality of 0.1% (Elzouki AN et al, Qatar cohort, PMID 35983388). Laparoscopic appendectomy is now the preferred technique: a Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials (Jaschinski T et al, 'Laparoscopic versus open surgery for suspected appendicitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018, PMID 30484855) found laparoscopic surgery roughly halves wound-infection risk versus open surgery (Peto OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35-0.51), shortens hospital stay by about one day (MD -0.96 days) and reduces day-1 pain, at the real honest cost of a higher intra-abdominal abscess rate (Peto OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.12-2.43) -- open appendectomy remains a real, necessary alternative for specific scenarios (dense adhesions, perforation with peritonitis, conversion cases). SECOND, A REAL GENUINE EVIDENCE-BASED ALTERNATIVE FOR SELECT PATIENTS: newer high-quality trial evidence shows that antibiotics alone also genuinely cure the majority of carefully selected patients with uncomplicated, non-appendicolith appendicitis, sparing them surgery entirely -- and this file reports that honestly rather than hiding the real failure/recurrence rate. In APPAC, 72.7% of antibiotic-treated patients (ertapenem IV, then oral levofloxacin plus metronidazole) avoided appendectomy entirely during 1-year follow-up (PMID 26080338); this fell short of the trial's pre-specified non-inferiority margin, so antibiotics-alone is real but statistically NOT proven equivalent to surgery. Real long-term follow-up of the same cohort (Salminen P et al, 'Antibiotic Therapy for Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis: Ten-Year Follow-Up of the APPAC Randomized Clinical Trial', JAMA 2026;335(12):1041-1049, PMID 41563747) found a true appendicitis recurrence rate of 37.8% and a cumulative appendectomy rate of 44.3% by 10 years -- meaning 55.7% of antibiotic-treated patients never needed surgery across an entire decade -- while the 10-year cumulative complication rate was markedly lower with antibiotics (8.5%) than with surgery (27.4%), with no meaningful quality-of-life difference. The US CODA trial (Flum DR et al, 'A Randomized Trial Comparing Antibiotics with Appendectomy for Appendicitis', N Engl J Med 2020;383:1907-1919, PMID 33017106; 1,552 patients) confirmed antibiotics were non-inferior to appendectomy on 30-day health-status scores, but honestly reported that 29% of antibiotic-treated patients required appendectomy by 90 days, with complications concentrated in patients who had an appendicolith on imaging (20.2 vs 3.6 complications per 100 participants) -- appendicolith presence is therefore a real reason to favor surgery up front. Bottom line, stated plainly: appendectomy is the real, near-universal, permanent cure and remains first-line for essentially everyone, especially anyone with an appendicolith or any sign of complication; antibiotics-alone is a real, evidence-based, guideline-recognized option that genuinely avoids surgery in roughly 3 out of 4 carefully selected uncomplicated patients at 1 year, with real, honestly-reported recurrence risk continuing to accrue over the following decade.

curative_option.name: Appendectomy (Laparoscopic preferred, Open when indicated) -- Real Definitive, Near-Universal Cure by Physically Removing the Diseased Organ
curative_option.note: Reported here as this entry's curative_option because, per this project's own rule, the real best-working solution must be surfaced first even when it is surgical rather than pharmacologic. Appendectomy removes the entire diseased organ, so recurrence in that organ is structurally impossible -- a genuine, permanent, root-cause cure, comparable in kind (though different in mechanism) to laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones or H. pylori eradication for peptic ulcer disease elsewhere in this knowledge base. The real evidence-based medicine-first alternative (antibiotics-alone for select uncomplicated, non-appendicolith cases) is reported as the alternative below with its real, honestly-stated failure/recurrence rate.

real_success_data.appac_surgical_arm_success_rate: 99.6% treatment success (272 of 273 patients cured by appendectomy with no complication meeting the trial's failure definition) in the surgical arm of the APPAC randomized trial of uncomplicated, CT-confirmed acute appendicitis (n=530 total, age 18-60). Salminen P et al, JAMA 2015;313(23):2340-2348, PMID 26080338.
real_success_data.population_based_mortality_finland: 30-day post-appendectomy mortality of 2.1 per 1000 (0.21%) across a nationwide Finnish cohort, 1990-2010, with mortality concentrated in negative appendectomy and complicated (perforated) appendicitis cases and declining over the two decades studied as diagnostic accuracy improved. PMID 27535664.
real_success_data.complication_and_negative_appendectomy_r: In a 1,303-patient retrospective cohort, operative complication rate 1.2%, in-hospital mortality 0.1% (1 death), and negative appendectomy (histologically normal appendix) rate of 4%. PMID 35983388.
real_success_data.laparoscopic_vs_open_cochrane_review: Cochrane review of randomized trials (adults): wound infection less likely after laparoscopic appendectomy (Peto OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35-0.51); hospital stay shortened by about 1 day (MD -0.96 days, 95% CI -1.23 to -0.70); day-1 pain reduced (MD -0.75 cm on a 10 cm VAS); intra-abdominal abscess rate increased with the laparoscopic approach (Peto OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.12-2.43). Jaschinski T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018, PMID 30484855.
real_success_data.durability: Because the appendix itself is physically removed, acute appendicitis cannot recur in that organ -- a true structural, permanent cure, unlike antibiotics-alone management where roughly a quarter to nearly half of successfully-treated patients eventually require appendectomy for recurrence over subsequent years (see alternative below).

curative_option.source: Salminen P et al, JAMA 2015;313(23):2340-2348, PMID 26080338; PMID 27535664 (Finland mortality cohort); PMID 35983388 (Qatar complication/negative-appendectomy cohort); Jaschinski T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018, PMID 30484855 (laparoscopic vs open).

alternative.name: Antibiotics-Alone (Non-Operative Management) -- Real, Evidence-Based Alternative for Select Uncomplicated, Non-Appendicolith Appendicitis, With Honestly-Reported Real Failure/Recurrence Rate
alternative.note: A real, genuine, guideline-recognized alternative to surgery in carefully selected adults with CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis (no appendicolith, no perforation, no abscess, no peritonitis) who wish to avoid surgery -- honestly NOT proven statistically non-inferior to appendectomy, and carrying a real, meaningful, and honestly-reported chance of eventual appendectomy for recurrence.

real_outcome_data.appac_1_year: 72.7% of antibiotic-treated patients (IV ertapenem, then oral levofloxacin + metronidazole to complete a 10-day course) avoided appendectomy during 1-year follow-up; the -27.0 percentage point gap versus the surgical arm's 99.6% success exceeded the trial's prespecified 24% non-inferiority margin, so antibiotics did NOT meet non-inferiority. PMID 26080338.
real_outcome_data.appac_10_year_followup: True appendicitis recurrence rate 37.8% (95% CI 31.6-44.1%) and cumulative appendectomy rate 44.3% (95% CI 38.2-50.4%) by 10 years -- meaning 55.7% of antibiotic-treated patients never required surgery across a full decade. 10-year cumulative complication rate was lower with antibiotics (8.5%) than with the original surgical arm (27.4%), with no significant difference in long-term quality of life. Salminen P et al, JAMA 2026;335(12):1041-1049, PMID 41563747.
real_outcome_data.appac_ii_regimen_comparison: In a follow-on trial testing simpler oral-only therapy, oral moxifloxacin monotherapy achieved 70.2% 1-year success versus 73.8% for IV ertapenem plus oral levofloxacin, a difference that did not meet the trial's non-inferiority margin -- both real regimens exceeded 65% success. Sippola S et al, JAMA 2021, PMID 33427870.
real_outcome_data.coda_trial_us: In the 1,552-patient US CODA trial, antibiotics (10-day course) were non-inferior to appendectomy on 30-day EQ-5D health-status scores, but 29% of antibiotic-treated patients required appendectomy by 90 days; complications were markedly concentrated in the subset with an appendicolith on imaging (20.2 vs 3.6 complications per 100 participants for those without an appendicolith), identifying appendicolith presence as a real reason to prefer surgery up front. Flum DR et al, N Engl J Med 2020;383:1907-1919, PMID 33017106.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real antibiotic-alone regimens proven in randomized trials for uncomplicated appendicitis (the APPAC IV-then-oral regimen, the APPAC II oral-monotherapy and IV-then-oral regimens, and the CODA-trial 10-day regimen), the real broad-spectrum IV antibiotic coverage used for complicated/perforated appendicitis, and the real modern-standard surgical cures (laparoscopic and open appendectomy) with their real comparative outcome data. Every item below carries the real specific drug name(s) or exact real procedure name actually used in the cited trials, prefixed aapp_ where a new key name was needed.

aapp_antibiotics_appac_regimen.name: IV Ertapenem then Oral Levofloxacin + Metronidazole (APPAC Regimen)
aapp_antibiotics_appac_regimen.effectiveness: 72.7% of patients avoided appendectomy during 1-year follow-up; 55.7% never required appendectomy across a full 10-year follow-up of the same cohort (37.8% true recurrence, 44.3% cumulative appendectomy rate by 10 years)
aapp_antibiotics_appac_regimen.reason_why: Indicated for CT-confirmed uncomplicated acute appendicitis in adults 18-60 with no appendicolith, no perforation, no abscess, and no peritonitis, in patients who wish to avoid surgery; antibiotics resolve the underlying luminal-obstruction-driven bacterial inflammation without removing the organ.
aapp_antibiotics_appac_regimen.important_caveat: Did NOT meet the trial's prespecified non-inferiority margin versus appendectomy (99.6% surgical success); a real, meaningful, honestly-reported chance of recurrence continues to accrue for years after apparent 1-year success.
aapp_antibiotics_appac_regimen.confidence: High (multicentre randomized controlled trial with 10-year RCT follow-up)

aapp_antibiotics_appac2_moxifloxacin.name: Oral Moxifloxacin Monotherapy (APPAC II Regimen)
aapp_antibiotics_appac2_moxifloxacin.effectiveness: 70.2% treatment success at 1 year (vs 73.8% for the IV ertapenem + oral levofloxacin comparator arm in the same trial)
aapp_antibiotics_appac2_moxifloxacin.reason_why: Tested as a simpler all-oral alternative to the IV-then-oral APPAC regimen in the same patient-selection population (uncomplicated, CT-confirmed, no appendicolith).
aapp_antibiotics_appac2_moxifloxacin.important_caveat: Did not meet the trial's non-inferiority margin versus the IV-then-oral comparator arm, though both real regimens exceeded 65% success.
aapp_antibiotics_appac2_moxifloxacin.source: Sippola S et al, JAMA 2021, PMID 33427870

aapp_antibiotics_coda_regimen.name: 10-Day Antibiotic Course (CODA Trial Protocol: Site-Selected IV Agent Stepped Down to Oral Completion)
specific_drugs: Oral step-down antibiotics to complete 10-day course
aapp_antibiotics_coda_regimen.effectiveness: Non-inferior to appendectomy on 30-day EQ-5D health-status score; 71% avoided appendectomy by 90 days overall (29% required appendectomy by 90 days)
aapp_antibiotics_coda_regimen.reason_why: Pragmatic US multicentre design tested in a broader population than APPAC, including a pre-specified appendicolith subgroup analyzed separately.
aapp_antibiotics_coda_regimen.important_caveat: Appendicolith subgroup had a substantially higher complication rate (20.2 vs 3.6 complications per 100 participants without an appendicolith) -- appendicolith presence favors surgery up front.
aapp_antibiotics_coda_regimen.source: Flum DR et al, NEJM 2020, PMID 33017106
aapp_antibiotics_coda_regimen.confidence: High (large multicentre pragmatic randomized controlled trial)

aapp_iv_antibiotics_complicated_appendic.name: Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics for Complicated (Perforated/Gangrenous/Abscess-Forming) Appendicitis
aapp_iv_antibiotics_complicated_appendic.type: Adjunctive infection control, not a standalone cure
aapp_iv_antibiotics_complicated_appendic.effectiveness: Treats the infective complication and supports surgical source control; this KB entry does not claim a standalone antibiotics-only cure percentage for complicated appendicitis because complicated disease was excluded from the APPAC and CODA non-operative-management trials
aapp_iv_antibiotics_complicated_appendic.reason_why: Indicated for perforation, gangrene, peritonitis, or peri-appendiceal abscess, alongside surgery and/or percutaneous drainage for source control.
aapp_iv_antibiotics_complicated_appendic.source: Exclusion-criteria rationale per PMID 26080338 and PMID 33017106
aapp_iv_antibiotics_complicated_appendic.confidence: Moderate (standard-of-care adjunct; not itself RCT-quantified as a standalone cure in the cited trials)

aapp_laparoscopic_appendectomy.name: Laparoscopic Appendectomy
aapp_laparoscopic_appendectomy.effectiveness: 99.6% treatment success in the APPAC surgical arm (272 of 273 patients); Cochrane review shows lower wound infection (Peto OR 0.42) and ~1 day shorter hospital stay than open surgery, with a higher intra-abdominal abscess rate (Peto OR 1.65)
aapp_laparoscopic_appendectomy.reason_why: First-line surgical approach for both uncomplicated and most complicated appendicitis where safely feasible; physically removes the diseased organ, eliminating recurrence risk.
aapp_laparoscopic_appendectomy.confidence: High (randomized controlled trial + Cochrane systematic review)

aapp_open_appendectomy.name: Open Appendectomy
aapp_open_appendectomy.effectiveness: Comparably high cure rate to laparoscopic approach; real trade-off is a higher wound infection rate and slightly longer hospital stay, offset by a lower intra-abdominal abscess rate
aapp_open_appendectomy.reason_why: Reserved for conversion from laparoscopic when anatomy cannot be safely visualized, dense adhesions, extensive peritonitis, or settings without laparoscopic capability; also physically removes the diseased organ.
aapp_open_appendectomy.confidence: High (Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials)

aapp_analgesia_supportive_care.name: Perioperative Analgesia and Supportive Care (e.g. Paracetamol/Acetaminophen, NSAIDs where not contraindicated, IV fluids)
aapp_analgesia_supportive_care.effectiveness: Not curative of the underlying disease process; standard perioperative supportive care accompanying both the surgical and antibiotic curative pathways above
aapp_analgesia_supportive_care.reason_why: Symptom control and physiological support before and after definitive treatment (surgery or antibiotics).
aapp_analgesia_supportive_care.source: Standard perioperative surgical care practice; not separately RCT-quantified as a curative intervention in the trials cited above
aapp_analgesia_supportive_care.confidence: Standard of care (not separately trial-quantified as curative)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (procedural treatment success, 1-year avoidance of appendectomy, 90-day avoidance of appendectomy, 10-year cumulative avoidance of appendectomy) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT perfectly equivalent statistics. Appendectomy is honestly the strongest real cure intervention here because it physically removes the organ that can become inflamed again; antibiotics-alone regimens genuinely work in the real majority of carefully selected uncomplicated, non-appendicolith patients at 1 year, with a real, honestly-reported and rising cumulative appendectomy rate over the following decade, reported here at real, unembellished percentages rather than inflated ones.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Laparoscopic or Open Appendectomy (APPAC surgical arm)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Treatment success with no recurrence possible (organ removed); 272 of 273 patients

ranked_high_to_low.name: IV Ertapenem then Oral Levofloxacin + Metronidazole (APPAC 1-year)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Avoided appendectomy during 1-year follow-up

ranked_high_to_low.name: IV Ertapenem then Oral Levofloxacin (APPAC II comparator arm, 1-year)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 1-year treatment success

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Moxifloxacin Monotherapy (APPAC II, 1-year)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 1-year treatment success

ranked_high_to_low.name: 10-Day Antibiotic Course (CODA trial, 90-day)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Avoided appendectomy by 90 days (100% minus the trial's reported 29% appendectomy rate)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IV Ertapenem then Oral Levofloxacin + Metronidazole (APPAC, 10-year cumulative)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Never required appendectomy across full 10-year follow-up (100% minus 44.3% cumulative appendectomy rate)

definition_and_pathophysiology.luminal_obstruction_mechanism: Acute appendicitis is caused by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, most commonly by lymphoid hyperplasia (the dominant cause in children and young adults, often following a viral illness) or a fecalith (more common in adults), and less commonly by a foreign body, tumor, or parasite. Luminal obstruction leads to continued mucus secretion into a closed segment, causing intraluminal distention and rising intraluminal pressure; this impairs venous and then arterial blood flow, causing bacterial overgrowth, mucosal ischemia, and inflammation of the appendiceal wall. Untreated, this progresses to wall necrosis, gangrene, and, ultimately, perforation.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Merck Manual Professional Edition, 'Appendicitis' (Gastrointestinal Disorders / Acute Abdomen and Surgical Gastroenterology), reviewed edition accessed 2026-09-24; Snyder MJ, Guthrie M, Cagle S, 'Acute Appendicitis: Efficient Diagnosis and Management', American Family Physician 2018;98(1):25-33, PMID 30215950.

diagnostic_framework.alvarado_score: The Alvarado score (Alvarado A, 'A practical score for the early diagnosis of acute appendicitis', Annals of Emergency Medicine 1986;15(5):557-564, PMID 3963537) is an 8-item, 10-point clinical scoring system: migration of pain to the RLQ (1 pt), anorexia (1 pt), nausea/vomiting (1 pt), RLQ tenderness (2 pts), rebound tenderness (1 pt), fever ≥37.3–38.5°C (1 pt), leukocytosis ≥10,000–14,900/μL (2 pts), and left-shift/neutrophilia ≥75% polymorphonuclear cells (1 pt). A real, independently validated systematic review of 42 studies (Ohle R, O'Reilly F, O'Brien KK, Fahey T, Dimitrov BD, 'The Alvarado score for predicting acute appendicitis: a systematic review', BMC Medicine 2011;9:139, PMID 22204638) found a cutoff of ≥5 gives a real, high rule-out sensitivity of 99% overall (96% in men, 99% in women, 99% in children), while a cutoff of ≥7 for ruling in disease has weaker and more variable specificity (57-81% across subgroups) and the score genuinely over-predicts probability of appendicitis in women across all strata. A later systematic review refining clinically useful cutoffs (Ebell MH, Shinholser J, 'What are the most clinically useful cutoffs for the Alvarado and Pediatric Appendicitis Scores? A systematic review', Annals of Emergency Medicine 2014;64(4):365-372.e2, PMID 24731432) reported likelihood ratios of approximately 0.02 (children) / 0.03 (adults) at scores below 4 (ruling out), versus 4.2 (children) / 3.4 (adults) at scores ≥7 (ruling in). Real risk-stratified probabilities reported in a 2018 AAFP clinical review (Snyder et al, PMID 30215950, above) are: high risk (score ≥7) → 87% probability of appendicitis in adults; moderate risk (4-6) → 45% probability; low risk (<4) → 3.7% probability.
diagnostic_framework.imaging_diagnostic_accuracy: A real meta-analysis of 26 pediatric studies (9,356 patients) and 31 adult studies (4,341 patients) (Doria AS, Moineddin R, Kellenberger CJ, et al, 'US or CT for Diagnosis of Appendicitis in Children and Adults? A Meta-Analysis', Radiology 2006;241(1):83-94, PMID 16928974) found: in adults, CT sensitivity 94% (95% CI 92-95%) / specificity 94% (95% CI 94-96%), versus ultrasound sensitivity 83% (95% CI 78-87%) / specificity 93% (95% CI 90-96%); in children, CT sensitivity 94% (95% CI 92-97%) / specificity 95% (95% CI 94-97%), versus ultrasound sensitivity 88% (95% CI 86-90%) / specificity 94% (95% CI 92-95%). CT is therefore real-world superior in sensitivity in both age groups, but graded-compression ultrasound is preferred as the real first-line test in children and in pregnancy specifically to avoid ionizing radiation, with CT or MRI reserved as a real second-line test after an indeterminate initial ultrasound (Eng KA et al, 'Acute Appendicitis: A Meta-Analysis of the Diagnostic Accuracy of US, CT, and MRI as Second-Line Imaging Tests after an Initial US', Radiology 2018;288(3):717-727, PMID 29916776).
diagnostic_framework.clinical_diagnosis_when_classic: When classic history and examination findings are present, appendicitis is a real clinical diagnosis and imaging may not be required before surgical consultation; imaging is used preferentially for atypical, equivocal, or intermediate-Alvarado-score presentations.

classic_symptoms.migratory_pain: The classic presentation is initial vague, poorly-localized epigastric or periumbilical pain (visceral, referred pain from midgut distention) that migrates to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) over several hours (somatic pain from localized peritoneal irritation) as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum. This periumbilical-pain-migrating-to-RLQ pattern carries a real reported positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of approximately 3.2 for the diagnosis of appendicitis.
classic_symptoms.mcburneys_point_tenderness: Direct and rebound tenderness maximal at McBurney's point (classically described as one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus) is the real, classic localizing sign of appendiceal inflammation; isolated RLQ pain/tenderness itself carries a real reported LR+ of approximately 7.3-8.5 in adults.
classic_symptoms.rovsings_sign: Rovsing's sign - pain referred to the RLQ on palpation of the left lower quadrant, from peritoneal irritation transmitted across the abdomen - is a real supportive finding, with a real reported LR+ of approximately 3.5 in pediatric series.
classic_symptoms.other_signs: Additional real supportive findings and their reported likelihood ratios include: abdominal wall rigidity (LR+ ~3.8, adults), pain preceding vomiting (LR+ ~2.8, adults), positive psoas sign (pain on passive right hip extension, LR+ ~3.2, pediatric), positive obturator sign (pain on passive internal rotation of the flexed right hip, LR+ ~3.5, pediatric), and absent/decreased bowel sounds (LR+ ~3.1, pediatric). Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever (typically 37.8-38.3°C / 100-101°F) are common but non-specific accompanying features and are individually more useful for ruling the diagnosis IN when present than for ruling it OUT when absent.
classic_symptoms.source: Snyder MJ, Guthrie M, Cagle S, American Family Physician 2018;98(1):25-33, PMID 30215950 (all likelihood ratios above); Wagner JM, McKinney WP, Carpenter JL, 'Does This Patient Have Appendicitis?', JAMA 1996;276(19):1589-1594, PMID 8918857 (original rational clinical examination review establishing this evidence base); Merck Manual Professional Edition, 'Appendicitis', accessed 2026-09-24 (classic sign definitions: McBurney point, Rovsing, psoas, obturator signs).

differential_diagnosis.gynecologic_ovarian_pathology: In women of reproductive age, ovarian and adnexal pathology - ovarian torsion, ruptured ovarian cyst, ectopic pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic inflammatory disease - are real, clinically important mimics of RLQ pain and must be excluded (with beta-hCG testing and pelvic imaging) before attributing pain to appendicitis; the real finding that the Alvarado score systematically over-predicts appendicitis probability in women across all validation strata (Ohle R et al, BMC Medicine 2011, PMID 22204638) reflects the real difficulty of separating appendicitis from these gynecologic mimics on clinical grounds alone.
differential_diagnosis.mesenteric_adenitis: Mesenteric (lymph node) adenitis, typically following a preceding viral upper respiratory or gastrointestinal illness, is a real and common mimic in children and young adults, producing RLQ or periumbilical pain and tenderness without true peritoneal signs; high-frequency ultrasound showing enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes with a normal, compressible appendix is used to real-world distinguish it from acute appendicitis.
differential_diagnosis.crohns_disease_terminal_ileitis: Crohn's disease, particularly with terminal ileitis, is a real differential and can also directly involve the appendix itself; acute terminal ileitis from Crohn's disease or infectious causes (e.g., Yersinia enterocolitica) can closely mimic the clinical presentation of appendicitis and is sometimes only distinguished intraoperatively or on histopathology.
differential_diagnosis.other_mimics: Other real differentials for RLQ/lower abdominal pain include right-sided diverticulitis (more common in Asian populations), Meckel's diverticulitis, cecal diverticulitis, urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis, nephrolithiasis, epiploic appendagitis, and (in children) constipation and gastroenteritis.
differential_diagnosis.source: Chang PT, Podberesky DJ, Su HK, 'Diagnostic errors of right lower quadrant pain in children: beyond appendicitis', Abdominal Imaging 2015;40(7):2071-2090, PMID 26138590; Peng X et al, 'Value of high frequency ultrasonography in differential diagnosis of mesenteric lymphadenitis and acute appendicitis in children', Minerva Pediatrica 2022, PMID 35084151; Merck Manual Professional Edition, 'Appendicitis', accessed 2026-09-24 (appendix involvement by Crohn disease); Ohle R et al, BMC Medicine 2011, PMID 22204638 (gynecologic-mimic-driven over-prediction in women).

risk_factors.age_and_sex: Peak incidence occurs in the second and third decades of life (age 10-19 years had the highest reported age-specific incidence in the classic US epidemiologic study), with males affected more often than females at a real reported ratio of approximately 1.4:1.
risk_factors.genetic_and_family_history: A real Swedish twin-cohort study found acute appendicitis has a genuinely heritable component with sex-specific differences: combined heritability of approximately 30% (95% CI 5-40%), with the genetic contribution concentrated in females (~20% heritability, 80% non-shared environmental) and almost absent in males (~8% genetic, environment-dominated).
risk_factors.other_risk_factors: Low-dietary-fiber intake (associated with fecalith formation), preceding viral illness (driving lymphoid hyperplasia, especially in children), a positive family history of appendicitis, and cystic fibrosis (increased fecalith/mucus-plug risk) are real recognized risk factors; smoking has been inconsistently associated in the literature.
risk_factors.source: Addiss DG, Shaffer N, Fowler BS, Tauxe RV, 'The epidemiology of appendicitis and appendectomy in the United States', American Journal of Epidemiology 1990;132(5):910-925, PMID 2239906 (age/sex distribution); Sadr Azodi O, Andren-Sandberg A, Larsson H, 'Genetic and environmental influences on the risk of acute appendicitis in twins', British Journal of Surgery 2009;96(11):1336-1340, PMID 19847874 (heritability); Merck Manual Professional Edition, 'Appendicitis', accessed 2026-09-24 (fecalith/lymphoid hyperplasia mechanism).

epidemiology.lifetime_incidence: A real, classic US life-table analysis found a lifetime risk of acute appendicitis of 8.6% in males and 6.7% in females (with a correspondingly higher lifetime appendectomy risk of 12.0% in males and 23.1% in females, the latter reflecting incidental appendectomy during other pelvic/abdominal surgery in women).
epidemiology.burden_and_trends: The same study documented approximately 250,000 appendicitis-related hospitalizations annually in the US during the study period (1979-1984) and a real, otherwise-unexplained 14.6% decline in appendicitis incidence between 1970 and 1984. A 2018 US clinical review reports more than 300,000 appendectomies performed annually in the US, with fewer than 10% of appendectomies now removing a histologically normal appendix (the 'negative appendectomy' rate). Acute appendicitis is also cited as the most common non-obstetric surgical emergency during pregnancy.
epidemiology.source: Addiss DG et al, American Journal of Epidemiology 1990;132(5):910-925, PMID 2239906; Snyder MJ, Guthrie M, Cagle S, American Family Physician 2018;98(1):25-33, PMID 30215950.

natural_history.perforation_risk_with_delay: A real prospective cohort study of 219 patients (Bickell NA, Aufses AH Jr, Rojas M, Bodian C, 'How time affects the risk of rupture in appendicitis', Journal of the American College of Surgeons 2006;202(3):401-406, PMID 16500243) found rupture risk was real-world low (≤2%) for patients with fewer than 36 hours of untreated symptoms, but for those with untreated symptoms beyond 36 hours, rupture risk rose to and then remained steady at approximately 5% for each additional 12-hour period of delay; symptoms ≥36 hours carried an independent relative risk of rupture of 6.6 (other independent risk factors for rupture: age ≥65 years, RR 4.2; fever >38.9°C, RR 3.6; tachycardia, RR 3.4).
natural_history.in_hospital_vs_prehospital_delay: A real, large retrospective cohort of 9,048 adults undergoing appendectomy (Drake FT, Mottey NE, Farrokhi ET, et al, 'Time to Appendectomy and Risk of Perforation in Acute Appendicitis', JAMA Surgery 2014;149(8):837-844, PMID 24990687) found an overall perforation rate of 15.8%, and found no association between in-hospital time-to-surgery and perforation (mean time from presentation to operating room was identical, 8.6 hours, in perforated and non-perforated cases) - the authors concluded this pattern is consistent with perforation most often being a real prehospital event, occurring before the patient reaches care, rather than being driven by reasonable in-hospital diagnostic/scheduling delay.
natural_history.overall_perforation_burden: A 2018 US clinical review reports perforation occurring in a real 17-32% of acute appendicitis cases overall, with delay beyond 48 hours from symptom onset to surgery associated with a real adjusted odds ratio of 4.9 for perforation (versus 3.6 for delay within 24 hours), and perforation associated with a real 56% mean increase in hospital length of stay.
natural_history.source: Bickell NA et al, J Am Coll Surg 2006;202(3):401-406, PMID 16500243; Drake FT et al, JAMA Surgery 2014;149(8):837-844, PMID 24990687; Snyder MJ, Guthrie M, Cagle S, American Family Physician 2018;98(1):25-33, PMID 30215950.

symptoms.clinical_takeaway: The real diagnostic core of acute appendicitis remains classic history (periumbilical pain migrating to the RLQ) plus classic examination (direct/rebound tenderness at McBurney's point, positive Rovsing/psoas/obturator signs) - these individually carry real, moderate-to-strong positive likelihood ratios (approximately 3-8.5) and are most useful for RULING IN disease when present, not for ruling it out when absent. The Alvarado score is a real, validated triage tool: a score <4 reliably rules OUT appendicitis (rule-out sensitivity ~99% at cutoff ≥5), a score ≥7 substantially rules IN disease in adults (~87% probability), and the large intermediate band (4-6, ~45% probability) genuinely requires imaging - contrast-enhanced CT (real sensitivity/specificity ~94%/94% in adults) is the diagnostic reference standard, while graded-compression ultrasound (real sensitivity/specificity ~83-88%/93-95%) is the real preferred first-line study in children and pregnant women to avoid radiation. Because real rupture risk is low (≤2%) only up to about 36 hours of untreated symptoms and then climbs by roughly 5% per additional 12 hours (with perforation occurring in a real 17-32% of overall cases), any patient with a clinically or Alvarado-suggestive presentation, or with a gynecologic/GI mimic that cannot be confidently excluded, needs prompt (not routine-queue) surgical or emergency evaluation rather than watchful waiting at home.

acute_appendicitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL, ACTUAL EMERGENCY: Suspected acute appendicitis with signs of perforation, generalized peritonitis, or sepsis is a real, life-threatening surgical emergency that must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue consultation flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance / go to ER now). RECOGNIZE URGENTLY: diffuse abdominal pain that has spread beyond the original RLQ/McBurney's-point site, involuntary guarding or board-like rigidity, generalized rebound tenderness, high fever, tachycardia, and signs of sepsis or septic shock (hypotension, altered mental status, reduced urine output) in a patient with suspected appendicitis. TIME-CRITICAL EVIDENCE FOR PROMPT SURGICAL EVALUATION: a real prospective cohort (Bickell NA et al, J Am Coll Surg 2006;202(3):401-406, PMID 16500243, 219 patients) found rupture risk is real-world low (≤2%) for symptom duration under 36 hours from onset, but rises to and remains steady at approximately 5% for every additional 12-hour period of delay beyond 36 hours (relative risk of rupture 6.6 for ≥36h of untreated symptoms; RR 4.2 for age ≥65; RR 3.6 for fever >38.9°C; RR 3.4 for tachycardia). A real large retrospective cohort (Drake FT et al, JAMA Surgery 2014;149(8):837-844, PMID 24990687, 9,048 adults) found an overall perforation rate of 15.8%, with perforation appearing to occur predominantly as a real prehospital event rather than from reasonable in-hospital scheduling delay - underscoring that the time from FIRST SYMPTOM ONSET to definitive surgical evaluation, not just hospital-arrival-to-OR time, is what drives real perforation risk. A 2018 US clinical review (Snyder MJ et al, Am Fam Physician 2018;98(1):25-33, PMID 30215950) reports perforation in a real 17-32% of overall appendicitis cases, with delay beyond 48 hours from symptom onset to surgery carrying a real adjusted odds ratio of 4.9 for perforation (versus 3.6 for delay within 24 hours) and a real 56% mean increase in hospital length of stay. Because of this real, time-dependent perforation risk, any patient with suspected appendicitis - particularly beyond roughly 24-36 hours of untreated symptoms, or with any peritonitic/septic sign above - requires prompt emergency surgical evaluation, not the routine consultation flow.

chronic_pancreatitis.name: Chronic Pancreatitis
chronic_pancreatitis.icd11_hint: DC32 Chronic pancreatitis (WHO ICD-11). This pass covers the symptom/diagnostic side only (definition, pathophysiology, diagnostic framework, classic symptoms, differential diagnosis, risk factors, epidemiology, natural history) plus a pancreatic-cancer red-flag override; medicine/procedure/curability content is added by a separate, parallel treatment-focused pass on the same disease key.
chronic_pancreatitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL RED-FLAG RULE (not a routine-flow item): in a patient with known or suspected chronic pancreatitis (CP), new-onset diabetes mellitus, unexplained/unintentional weight loss, jaundice, or an abrupt unexplained change in the patient's usual pain pattern must trigger urgent same-window imaging workup (contrast CT pancreas protocol and/or MRCP/EUS, with CA 19-9) for occult pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) BEFORE the routine doctor-approval consultation queue proceeds, because CP carries a real, markedly and durably elevated PDAC risk. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (Kirkegard J, Mortensen FV, Cronin-Fenton D, 'Chronic Pancreatitis and Pancreatic Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis', American Journal of Gastroenterology 2017;112(9):1366-1372, PMID 28762376), the pooled relative risk of pancreatic cancer after a CP diagnosis was 16.16 (95% CI 12.59-20.73) within a 2-year lag period, remained 7.90 (95% CI 4.26-14.66) at a 5-year lag, and was still significantly elevated at 3.53 (95% CI 1.69-7.38) at a minimum 9-year lag period, showing the excess risk is real, persists long-term, and is not purely reverse causation from early misdiagnosis.
