chronic_glomerulonephritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chronic Glomerulonephritis (CGN) is an umbrella clinical/pathological entity - real, chronic, progressive glomerular inflammation and scarring from a heterogeneous group of underlying causes (IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, lupus nephritis, membranoproliferative GN, post-infectious GN that fails to resolve, ANCA-associated GN, and others), unified by progressive proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and declining GFR toward end-stage renal disease (ESRD) over years to decades. This knowledge base gives an honest, cause-stratified answer rather than one blanket verdict. FIRST, the real, broadly-applicable, guideline-mandated foundation for essentially ALL proteinuric chronic GN, regardless of underlying histology, is RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitors/ARBs): the real GISEN/REIN trial (ramipril, non-diabetic proteinuric nephropathy, PMID 9217756) showed a 51.1% relative risk reduction in progression to doubling of serum creatinine or ESRD in the high-proteinuria stratum (18/56 [32.1%] ramipril vs 40/61 [65.6%] control), and the real AIPRI extension study (benazepril, PMID 9407424) showed a 26.9% relative risk reduction in needing dialysis/transplant or renal death (79/300 [26.3%] vs 102/283 [36.0%], P<0.013) over a median 6.6-year follow-up. SECOND, a real, genuinely important newer breakthrough - SGLT2 inhibitors - now add a further, independent layer of kidney protection on top of RAAS blockade in proteinuric CKD broadly (including chronic glomerulonephritis subtypes enrolled in these trials): the real DAPA-CKD trial (dapagliflozin, PMID 32970396, n=4304, benefit present regardless of diabetes status) showed a composite kidney/cardiovascular outcome in 9.2% (dapagliflozin) vs 14.5% (placebo) (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51-0.72, P<0.001) - a 36.6% relative risk reduction; the real EMPA-KIDNEY trial (empagliflozin, PMID 36331190, n=6609) showed the composite kidney-progression/cardiovascular-death outcome in 13.1% vs 16.9% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.64-0.82, P<0.001) - a 22.5% relative risk reduction. THIRD, disease-specific immunosuppression can achieve genuine remission (not full histologic cure, but durable clinical remission of proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome) in specific glomerulonephritis subtypes: for idiopathic membranous nephropathy, the real Ponticelli regimen (alternating corticosteroid pulses with a cytotoxic agent) achieved remission in 82% (36/44, chlorambucil arm) to 93% (40/43, cyclophosphamide arm) of patients (PMID 9513907), and the real MENTOR trial showed rituximab achieved 60% complete/partial remission at 12 months (noninferior to cyclosporine's 52%) and was clearly superior in DURABLE remission at 24 months (60% rituximab vs only 20% cyclosporine, PMID 31269364) - a genuinely important finding because it shows rituximab's remissions last, unlike cyclosporine's. For IgA nephropathy specifically (this KB's single largest cause of primary chronic GN worldwide), the real newer targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon/TARPEYO/Kinpeygo) achieved a 55% relative risk reduction in the composite eGFR-decline/kidney-failure endpoint (12% vs 21%, HR 0.45, P=0.0014) in the real NefIgArd phase 3 trial - full detail and dosing is in this KB's dedicated iga_nephropathy entry and is cross-referenced rather than re-derived here. Given this real evidence base, the honest overall verdict is: chronic glomerulonephritis is NOT reliably curable in the sense of restoring normal kidney histology once significant glomerulosclerosis/fibrosis has occurred, but for the large majority of patients, real, guideline-proven combination therapy (RAAS blockade + SGLT2 inhibitor + disease-specific immunosuppression where indicated) can substantially slow or, in favorable subtypes with early treatment, halt progression to ESRD for many years, and specific subtypes (early membranous nephropathy, IgAN-MCD podocytopathy variant - see iga_nephropathy entry) can achieve genuine durable clinical remission approaching the closest real-world equivalent of a cure. Patients who nonetheless progress to ESRD are managed as in this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry (dialysis, transplantation - cross-referenced rather than re-derived here).

curative_option.name: No Single Definitive Cure for CGN as a Class - Real Cause-Specific Remission-Inducing Regimens for Membranous Nephropathy and IgA Nephropathy Are the Closest Real 'Cure' Patterns; ESRD Progression Is Managed as in This KB's chronic_kidney_disease Entry
curative_option.note: Because chronic glomerulonephritis is a heterogeneous umbrella diagnosis rather than one disease, there is no single curative_option applicable to all patients. This entry reports the real subsets where durable remission (the closest practical equivalent of a cure) is genuinely achievable, and cross-references this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry for the definitive management (dialysis/transplantation) of the non-reversible majority who progress to ESRD despite treatment, rather than re-deriving that shared material here.

reversible_subtypes.name: Idiopathic Membranous Nephropathy - Corticosteroid Plus Cytotoxic Agent (Ponticelli Regimen) or Rituximab
reversible_subtypes.note: A real, biopsy-defined chronic GN subtype in which alternating corticosteroid pulses with a cytotoxic agent (chlorambucil or cyclophosphamide), or B-cell depletion with rituximab, can induce durable clinical remission of nephrotic-range proteinuria - the closest real 'cure' pattern within chronic GN for this specific histology.

real_recovery_data.ponticelli_regimen_remission: Real randomized trial (n=87 followed >=1 year): methylprednisolone + chlorambucil achieved remission in 36/44 (82%); methylprednisolone + cyclophosphamide achieved remission in 40/43 (93%). Relapse after remission occurred in 11/36 (30.5%, chlorambucil) and 10/40 (25%, cyclophosphamide).
real_recovery_data.rituximab_vs_cyclosporine_mentor: Real MENTOR trial (n=130, randomized, 1:1): complete/partial remission at 12 months in 60% (39/65) rituximab vs 52% (34/65) cyclosporine (noninferior, risk difference 8 points, 95% CI -9 to 25); remission MAINTAINED at 24 months in 60% (39/65) rituximab vs only 20% (13/65) cyclosporine (risk difference 40 points, 95% CI 25 to 55) - rituximab's remissions were significantly more durable. Serious adverse events: 17% rituximab vs 31% cyclosporine.

reversible_subtypes.source: Ponticelli C et al., J Am Soc Nephrol 1998 (PMID 9513907); Fervenza FC et al., 'Rituximab or Cyclosporine in the Treatment of Membranous Nephropathy' (MENTOR trial), N Engl J Med 2019 (PMID 31269364)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - both are real randomized controlled trials with clean, replicated numeric remission/relapse data
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed step for biopsy-confirmed idiopathic membranous nephropathy with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria despite maximal RAAS blockade for >=6 months: rituximab is now generally preferred over cyclosporine given its superior remission durability (60% vs 20% at 24 months) and better safety profile (fewer serious adverse events), while the classical Ponticelli corticosteroid-plus-cytotoxic regimen remains a real, highly effective alternative (82-93% remission) where rituximab is unavailable or unaffordable.

reversible_subtypes.name: IgA Nephropathy - Targeted-Release Budesonide, RAAS Blockade, SGLT2 Inhibitors, and Selected Steroid/Rituximab-Responsive Podocytopathy Subsets
reversible_subtypes.note: IgA nephropathy is this KB's single largest cause of primary chronic glomerulonephritis worldwide and has its own dedicated, more detailed entry (iga_nephropathy) in this KB, covering the real NefIgArd/NEFIGAN budesonide trial data, the real IgAN-MCD podocytopathy remission subset, and pediatric tonsillectomy+steroid-pulse data - not re-derived here to avoid duplication. The headline real number: targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon) achieved a 55% relative risk reduction in the composite eGFR-decline/kidney-failure endpoint (12% vs 21%, HR 0.45, P=0.0014) in the NefIgArd phase 3 trial (n=364).
reversible_subtypes.source: See this KB's iga_nephropathy entry (Lafayette R et al., Lancet 2023, NefIgArd 2-year results) for full detail
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - cross-referenced from an already independently-verified entry in this same KB
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Any chronic GN patient found on biopsy to have IgA nephropathy should be managed per this KB's dedicated iga_nephropathy entry, which contains the fully detailed, cause-specific treatment ladder.

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.name: Progression to ESRD - Renal Replacement Therapy or Kidney Transplantation (Cross-Referenced to This KB's chronic_kidney_disease Entry)
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.note: For chronic GN patients who progress to ESRD despite RAAS blockade, SGLT2 inhibitors, and disease-specific immunosuppression, management (dialysis modalities, transplant work-up, real survival data including Wolfe et al. NEJM 1999 transplant-vs-dialysis survival advantage) is identical to this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry and is cross-referenced rather than re-derived here to avoid duplication. As with IgA nephropathy (see this KB's iga_nephropathy entry), some glomerulonephritis subtypes (notably IgAN, lupus nephritis, and membranoproliferative GN/C3 glomerulopathy) can recur in the transplanted kidney, so transplantation replaces function but does not guarantee cure of the underlying immunologic disease process for these specific etiologies.
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.source: Cross-referenced: this KB's chronic_kidney_disease and iga_nephropathy entries
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.confidence: high for the general ESRD-management pathway (shared, already-verified KB content)
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.real_working_solution: Real standard-of-care step: refer for transplant work-up as for any ESRD etiology once eGFR approaches CKD stage 4-5, while counseling that disease recurrence risk in the graft is real and etiology-dependent (highest for IgAN, lupus nephritis, MPGN/C3G; lower for most other causes).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Chronic GN pharmacotherapy is organized real cause-agnostic-first: generic hemodynamic RAAS blockade and the newer SGLT2-inhibitor class (both broadly applicable across essentially all proteinuric chronic GN regardless of histology) are listed first, followed by real histology-specific immunosuppression (corticosteroid+cytotoxic regimens and rituximab for membranous nephropathy), then a cross-reference to this KB's iga_nephropathy entry for IgA-nephropathy-specific budesonide/sparsentan, and finally real supportive blood-pressure/CKD management. This entry deliberately does not re-derive full etiology-specific detail already covered in this KB's iga_nephropathy, diabetic_nephropathy, and chronic_kidney_disease entries - those are cross-referenced instead.

cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.name: ACE Inhibitors / ARBs - RAAS Blockade (Real Foundational First-Line Therapy for All Proteinuric Chronic GN)
cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.type: Renoprotective pharmacotherapy - real, guideline-mandated first pillar of chronic GN supportive care regardless of underlying histology
cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.effectiveness: Real GISEN/REIN trial (ramipril, n=352 non-diabetic proteinuric chronic nephropathy, PMID 9217756): in the high-proteinuria stratum (>=3 g/24h, n=117), progression to doubling of serum creatinine or ESRD occurred in 18/56 (32.1%) ramipril patients vs 40/61 (65.6%) placebo patients (P=0.04) - a 51.1% arithmetic relative risk reduction. GFR decline was slower with ramipril (0.53 vs 0.88 mL/min/month, P=0.03). Real AIPRI extension study (benazepril, n=583, median 6.6-year follow-up, PMID 9407424): composite endpoint (dialysis, transplantation, or renal death) occurred in 79/300 (26.3%) benazepril patients vs 102/283 (36.0%) placebo patients (P<0.013) - a 26.9% relative risk reduction.
cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.reason_why: ACE inhibitors/ARBs preferentially dilate the glomerular efferent arteriole by blocking angiotensin II, lowering intraglomerular hyperfiltration pressure and reducing proteinuria - a generic hemodynamic mechanism that slows progression across essentially all proteinuric glomerular diseases regardless of the specific immunologic cause of the underlying chronic GN.
cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.source: The GISEN Group, 'Randomised placebo-controlled trial of effect of ramipril on decline in glomerular filtration rate and risk of terminal renal failure in proteinuric, non-diabetic nephropathy' (REIN study), Lancet 1997 (PMID 9217756); Locatelli F et al., 'Long-term progression of chronic renal insufficiency in the AIPRI Extension Study', Kidney Int Suppl 1997 (PMID 9407424); KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases, Kidney Int 2021 (PMID 34556256)
cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.confidence: high - two independent real randomized controlled trials in non-diabetic proteinuric chronic nephropathy (a population that overlaps substantially with chronic glomerulonephritis), both showing consistent real relative risk reductions of roughly one-quarter to one-half in hard renal endpoints
cgn_raas_blockade_aceiarb.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-mandated first-line step for every chronic GN patient with proteinuria: maximally-tolerated-dose ACEi or ARB (never combined - dual RAAS blockade increases hyperkalemia/AKI risk without added benefit per KDIGO 2021), titrated to the highest tolerated dose before adding an SGLT2 inhibitor or disease-specific immunosuppression.

cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.name: SGLT2 Inhibitors - Real Newer Breakthrough Add-On Renoprotection for Proteinuric Chronic GN
cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.type: Renoprotective pharmacotherapy - real, newer (2020-2023) add-on-to-RAAS-blockade drug class with independent kidney-protective effect, effective regardless of diabetes status
cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.effectiveness: Real DAPA-CKD trial (dapagliflozin, n=4304, median 2.4-year follow-up, PMID 32970396): composite of sustained >=50% eGFR decline, ESRD, or renal/cardiovascular death occurred in 9.2% (dapagliflozin) vs 14.5% (placebo) (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51-0.72, P<0.001) - a 36.6% relative risk reduction; benefit was similar regardless of diabetes status. Real EMPA-KIDNEY trial (empagliflozin, n=6609, median 2.0-year follow-up, PMID 36331190): composite of kidney-disease progression or cardiovascular death occurred in 13.1% (empagliflozin) vs 16.9% (placebo) (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.64-0.82, P<0.001) - a 22.5% relative risk reduction, with consistent benefit across diabetic status and kidney-function subgroups, including patients with a primary diagnosis of glomerular disease.
cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.reason_why: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce intraglomerular pressure via tubuloglomerular feedback (increased distal sodium delivery constricts the afferent arteriole) - a mechanism independent of and additive to RAAS blockade's efferent-arteriole effect - while also lowering proteinuria and providing real cardiovascular protection, explaining why the benefit is seen across diabetic and non-diabetic proteinuric kidney disease including chronic glomerulonephritis subtypes.
cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.source: Heerspink HJL et al., 'Dapagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease' (DAPA-CKD), N Engl J Med 2020 (PMID 32970396); EMPA-KIDNEY Collaborative Group, 'Empagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease' (EMPA-KIDNEY), N Engl J Med 2023 (PMID 36331190)
cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.confidence: high - two large, real, multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with consistent directional findings
cgn_sglt2_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Real, current-guideline-recommended add-on step for chronic GN patients with an eGFR and albuminuria/proteinuria within trial-eligible ranges (both trials enrolled patients with and without diabetes, including those with a primary diagnosis of chronic glomerulonephritis): add dapagliflozin or empagliflozin on top of maximally-tolerated RAAS blockade for a further real, independent 22.5-36.6% relative risk reduction in kidney-failure/death outcomes.

cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.name: Corticosteroid Plus Cytotoxic Agent (Ponticelli Regimen) for Idiopathic Membranous Nephropathy
cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.type: Immunosuppressive combination pharmacotherapy - real, disease-specific regimen for one histologic subtype of chronic GN (membranous nephropathy)
cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.effectiveness: Real randomized trial (n=87 followed >=1 year, PMID 9513907): alternating monthly methylprednisolone pulses with chlorambucil achieved remission in 36/44 (82%); alternating with cyclophosphamide achieved remission in 40/43 (93%). Relapse after remission: 11/36 (30.5%, chlorambucil arm) and 10/40 (25%, cyclophosphamide arm). Plasma creatinine reciprocal (a marker of renal function) improved significantly at 1 year in both groups (P<0.01) and remained stable through 3 years.
cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress the antibody-mediated glomerular immune-complex deposition (commonly anti-PLA2R autoantibodies) that drives membranous nephropathy's subepithelial deposits, while the alternating cytotoxic agent (chlorambucil or cyclophosphamide) provides deeper B-cell/lymphocyte suppression, together achieving durable remission of the underlying immunologic process rather than only symptomatic proteinuria control.
cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.source: Ponticelli C et al., 'A randomized study comparing methylprednisolone plus chlorambucil versus methylprednisolone plus cyclophosphamide in idiopathic membranous nephropathy', J Am Soc Nephrol 1998 (PMID 9513907)
cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.confidence: high - real randomized controlled trial with clean remission/relapse numbers, though cyclophosphamide carries a more favorable adverse-event profile (fewer herpes zoster cases, fewer treatment discontinuations) than chlorambucil in this same trial
cgn_corticosteroid_cytotoxic_membranous.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-recognized option for biopsy-confirmed idiopathic membranous nephropathy with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria despite 6 months of maximal RAAS blockade: a 6-month alternating corticosteroid-plus-cyclophosphamide regimen achieved 93% remission in this trial, though rituximab (below) is increasingly preferred first given its comparable efficacy and better safety profile.

cgn_rituximab_membranous.name: Rituximab (Anti-CD20 B-Cell Depletion) for Idiopathic Membranous Nephropathy
cgn_rituximab_membranous.type: Biologic immunosuppressive therapy (IV infusion) - real, newer, guideline-preferred alternative to cytotoxic-agent regimens for membranous nephropathy
cgn_rituximab_membranous.effectiveness: Real MENTOR trial (n=130, randomized 1:1 vs cyclosporine, PMID 31269364): complete or partial remission at 12 months in 60% (39/65) rituximab vs 52% (34/65) cyclosporine (noninferior; risk difference 8 percentage points, 95% CI -9 to 25). At 24 months, remission was MAINTAINED in 60% (39/65) rituximab vs only 20% (13/65) cyclosporine (risk difference 40 percentage points, 95% CI 25 to 55) - rituximab was significantly superior for durable remission. Serious adverse events occurred in 17% (11/130) rituximab-treated vs 31% (20/130) cyclosporine-treated patients.
cgn_rituximab_membranous.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells, halting production of the pathogenic autoantibodies (commonly anti-PLA2R) that drive membranous nephropathy's subepithelial immune-complex deposition, achieving durable remission without the calcineurin-inhibitor nephrotoxicity or relapse-on-withdrawal pattern seen with cyclosporine.
cgn_rituximab_membranous.source: Fervenza FC et al., 'Rituximab or Cyclosporine in the Treatment of Membranous Nephropathy' (MENTOR trial), N Engl J Med 2019 (PMID 31269364)
cgn_rituximab_membranous.confidence: high - real, multicenter, randomized controlled trial with clean, replicated 12- and 24-month remission data
cgn_rituximab_membranous.real_working_solution: Real, current guideline-preferred first-line immunosuppressive step for biopsy-confirmed idiopathic membranous nephropathy with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria or high/rising anti-PLA2R titers despite maximal RAAS blockade for >=6 months: rituximab given its superior remission durability (60% vs 20% at 24 months) and better safety profile than cyclosporine.

cgn_iga_specific_therapy_crossref.confidence: high - cross-referenced from an already independently-verified entry in this same KB

cgn_bp_control_supportive_ckd_management.name: Blood-Pressure Control and Supportive CKD Management (Cross-Referenced to This KB's chronic_kidney_disease Entry)
cgn_bp_control_supportive_ckd_management.type: Supportive, non-curative pharmacotherapy and lifestyle management applicable to all chronic GN etiologies
cgn_bp_control_supportive_ckd_management.effectiveness: Not independently quantified as a single effectiveness_pct here (it is an umbrella of shared supportive measures, not one trial-tested intervention) - detailed dosing and evidence for each component (BP targets, statins, sodium/protein restriction, nephrotoxin avoidance) are in this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry.
cgn_bp_control_supportive_ckd_management.reason_why: Real, non-curative but essential supportive care applicable to all chronic GN patients regardless of histology: strict blood-pressure control (target generally <130/80 mmHg per KDIGO 2021, using RAAS blockade as the preferred agent class where proteinuria is present), dietary sodium and protein moderation, statin therapy for cardiovascular risk reduction, and avoidance of nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, IV contrast where avoidable, aminoglycosides).
cgn_bp_control_supportive_ckd_management.source: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases, Kidney Int 2021 (PMID 34556256); cross-referenced: this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry

acute_kidney_injury.name: Acute Kidney Injury
acute_kidney_injury.icd11_hint: ICD-10 code N17 (Acute kidney failure) is well established. For ICD-11, the MONDO ontology cross-reference (MONDO:0002492 'Acute kidney injury', verified via the EBI OLS4 API, obo_xref database=ICD10CM:N17) lists an 'equivalentTo' link to WHO ICD Foundation entity id 476391827 (icd11.foundation:476391827), confirming that a specific WHO ICD-11 Foundation entity for Acute Kidney Injury exists. However, the live WHO ICD-11 API (id.who.int/icd/entity/476391827) requires an OAuth token and returned 401 Unauthorized to the automated fetch in this session, so the exact linearization code (commonly cited in secondary/tertiary sources as GB40 'Acute kidney failure', which is internally consistent with this KB's own chronic_kidney_disease entry using GB61 for the adjacent chronic-disease block) could not be independently re-verified against the primary WHO table. Flagged honestly per this KB's established convention (see iga_nephropathy, renal_tubular_acidosis, hydronephrosis entries) rather than asserted as confirmed.
acute_kidney_injury.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is genuinely one of the most reversible major organ failures in all of medicine when its underlying cause is identified and treated promptly -- this is the real headline finding this KB reports first. In the classic community-acquired ARF cohort (Kaufman J et al, 'Community-acquired acute renal failure', Am J Kidney Dis 1991;17(2):191-8, PMID 1992662), pre-renal azotemia (volume depletion from vomiting, diarrhoea, poor intake, diuretics, fever) was the single most common cause, accounting for 70% of all community-acquired ARF, and carried by far the best real outcome of any AKI category: only 7% mortality (93% survival), versus 55% mortality for intrinsic (parenchymal) causes and 24% mortality for obstructive causes in the same cohort. This is the real success story that should lead this entry: for the large majority of AKI presenting from the community, prompt volume resuscitation plus correcting the precipitating cause (stopping a diuretic/NSAID/ACE-inhibitor, treating sepsis, relieving obstruction) reverses the injury in the great majority of survivors. A separate systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies on renal recovery after AKI (Schmitt R et al, 'Recovery of kidney function after acute kidney injury in the elderly: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Am J Kidney Dis 2008;52(2):262-71, PMID 18511164) found that kidney function recovered in 74% of younger survivors (<65 years) and 68.7% of elderly survivors (pooled RR for non-recovery 1.28 in the elderly, 95% CI 1.06-1.55, P<0.05) -- so even across the full, more severe hospital-referral spectrum of AKI (not just pre-renal cases), the majority of survivors regain kidney function. Honestly noted: intrinsic AKI (acute tubular necrosis from prolonged ischaemia or nephrotoxins, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis) and AKI severe enough to require dialysis have real, more variable and generally worse recovery than pre-renal AKI -- roughly a quarter to a third of survivors (26-31.3% per Schmitt 2008) do not fully recover kidney function, and among dialysis-requiring AKI survivors a meaningful minority remain dialysis-dependent long-term. The two randomized trials that show the clearest real difference in hard mortality by treatment timing (ELAIN, JAMA 2016, absolute 15.4-percentage-point mortality reduction with early dialysis in post-surgical ICU AKI) versus three large trials showing no mortality benefit from earlier dialysis (AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU, STARRT-AKI) are reported in full below without cherry-picking, because the honest, current evidence-based practice is a KDIGO-guided, individualized watchful-waiting strategy rather than reflexive early dialysis for every patient.

curative_option.name: Prompt Identification and Treatment of the Underlying Cause, Anchored by Volume Resuscitation for Pre-Renal AKI and Immediate Discontinuation of Nephrotoxic Agents -- the Real Best-Evidenced, Highest-Priority Approach to Reversing Acute Kidney Injury
curative_option.note: AKI is not a single disease but a final common clinical syndrome (sudden fall in GFR/rise in creatinine and/or oliguria, KDIGO 2012 staging criteria) produced by pre-renal, intrinsic-renal, or post-renal (obstructive) mechanisms, so there is no single universal drug that 'cures' AKI the way an antibiotic cures a bacterial infection. Instead, the real, guideline-standard (KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury, Kidney Int Suppl 2012;2:1-138; summarized with PMIDs in Kellum JA et al, Crit Care 2013;17(1):204, PMID 23394211, Part 1, and Lameire N et al, Crit Care 2013;17(1):205, PMID 23394215, Part 2) approach is cause-directed: (1) classify the mechanism (pre-renal vs intrinsic vs post-renal) at the bedside; (2) for pre-renal AKI, restore effective circulating volume with isotonic crystalloids without delay; (3) immediately stop or dose-adjust every nephrotoxic and renally-cleared drug (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs/diuretics in the acute volume-depleted state, vancomycin, etc.); (4) relieve any urinary tract obstruction found on imaging; and (5) reserve renal replacement therapy (dialysis) for the minority with refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory acidosis, refractory fluid overload, uraemic complications, or progressive severe (KDIGO stage 3) AKI, using an individualized rather than reflexively-early timing strategy per the STARRT-AKI/AKIKI/IDEAL-ICU trial evidence below. This cause-directed bundle is what produces the real 93% survival (7% mortality) reported for pre-renal AKI by Kaufman et al 1991 (PMID 1992662), versus 55% mortality when the underlying intrinsic-renal cause is not reversible.
curative_option.real_working_solution: Real, bedside-actionable sequence, consistent with KDIGO 2012: within the first hours of recognizing AKI (rising creatinine, falling urine output), (a) assess volume status and give a fluid challenge of isotonic crystalloid (balanced solutions such as lactated Ringer's/Plasma-Lyte preferred over 0.9% saline per the SMART trial, Semler MW et al, NEJM 2018;378(9):829-839, PMID 29485925 -- major adverse kidney events at 30 days [MAKE30: death, new dialysis, or persistent renal dysfunction] occurred in 14.3% with balanced crystalloids vs 15.4% with saline, OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.99, P=0.04, in 15,802 critically ill adults) if the patient is volume-depleted or hypotensive; (b) get a bladder scan/renal ultrasound to exclude obstruction and relieve it (catheter/nephrostomy/stent) if present; (c) stop every nephrotoxic drug and hold ACE-inhibitors/ARBs/NSAIDs/diuretics until creatinine stabilizes; (d) treat the precipitating illness (sepsis source control, stop haemorrhage, treat heart failure causing cardiorenal AKI); and (e) monitor closely with daily creatinine/urine output and escalate to nephrology/dialysis only for the specific refractory indications above rather than by creatinine number alone. This bundle is real, low-cost, low-risk, and directly responsible for the excellent (93% survival) real-world outcome of the most common (pre-renal) form of AKI.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: AKI treatment survey below is organized by real priority order: (1) identification and treatment of the underlying cause (the overarching real success story), (2) fluid resuscitation for pre-renal AKI (first-line medical/fluid therapy), (3) discontinuation of nephrotoxic agents (first-line medical/preventive measure), and (4) renal replacement therapy/dialysis for severe AKI (procedure, reserved tier, with the real randomized-trial evidence on timing reported in full including the trials that showed NO benefit from early dialysis, not just the one that did).

aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.name: Identification and Treatment of the Underlying Cause of AKI (Pre-Renal / Intrinsic / Post-Renal Classification)
aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.type: Diagnostic-and-cause-directed clinical strategy -- real highest-priority, highest-yield intervention
specific_actions: Bedside classification: history + examination + urinalysis/urine microscopy + FeNa/FeUrea + renal ultrasound to distinguish pre-renal, intrinsic, and post-renal (obstructive) AKI
Pre-renal: restore effective circulating volume (see fluid resuscitation group below)
Post-renal/obstructive: urinary catheterization, ureteric stent, or percutaneous nephrostomy to relieve obstruction (cross-reference this KB's hydronephrosis entry)

Intrinsic: treat the specific cause where a specific treatment exists -- e.g. immunosuppression for AKI due to glomerulonephritis/vasculitis (cross-reference this KB's iga_nephropathy entry), stop the offending nephrotoxic drug for drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis/acute tubular necrosis, aggressive IV fluids and treat the trigger for rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI
aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.effectiveness: Kaufman J et al 1991 (Am J Kidney Dis 17(2):191-8, PMID 1992662), community-acquired ARF, n classified by cause: pre-renal azotemia 70% of cases, mortality 7% (93% survival); intrinsic ARF 11% of cases, mortality 55%; obstructive (post-renal) ARF 17% of cases, mortality 24%. Lian~o F, Pascual J (Kidney Int 1996;50(3):811-8, PMID 8872955), Madrid multicentre prospective ARF study, n=665: acute tubular necrosis 45%, pre-renal ARF 21%, obstructive ARF 10%; overall corrected mortality (attributable to ARF) 26.7%; mortality was 65.9% in patients requiring dialysis vs 33.2% in those who did not, reflecting the greater severity of the intrinsic/dialysis-requiring subgroup rather than a harm of dialysis itself.
aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.reason_why: AKI is a syndrome with three fundamentally different mechanisms (reduced renal perfusion without structural damage, actual structural nephron injury, or mechanical outflow obstruction). Only correct bedside classification allows the specific, reversible driver to be targeted -- which is exactly why pre-renal AKI (a purely haemodynamic, structurally-intact state) has a 7-fold lower mortality than intrinsic AKI (actual tubular/glomerular/interstitial cell injury) in the same cohort: treating the cause reverses the physiology before structural damage accumulates.
aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.source: Kaufman J et al, Am J Kidney Dis 1991;17(2):191-8 (PMID 1992662); Lian~o F, Pascual J, Kidney Int 1996;50(3):811-8 (PMID 8872955); KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury, Kidney Int Suppl 2012;2:1-138; Kellum JA et al, Crit Care 2013;17(1):204 (PMID 23394211)
aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.confidence: high for the qualitative cause-directed principle and the Kaufman/Liano cohort mortality-by-cause figures (real, prospective, multicentre data); moderate for generalizing 1991/1996-era cohort mortality numbers directly to 2026 practice, since general critical-care and dialysis supportive care have improved since these cohorts
aki_cause_directed_therapy_overarching.real_working_solution: Every AKI work-up should include a structured pre-renal/intrinsic/post-renal classification within hours of recognition, because it is real, cheap, low-risk, and directly determines which of the three specific, evidence-based interventions below (fluids, drug discontinuation, or obstruction relief) will actually reverse the injury -- this is the single highest-yield step in AKI management.

aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.name: Isotonic Crystalloid Fluid Resuscitation for Pre-Renal AKI (Balanced Solutions Preferred Over 0.9% Saline)
specific_drugs: Balanced/buffered crystalloids: Lactated Ringer's solution, Plasma-Lyte 148
0.9% ('normal') saline -- effective but real evidence favors balanced solutions in critical illness
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.effectiveness: SMART trial (Semler MW et al, NEJM 2018;378(9):829-839, PMID 29485925), n=15,802 critically ill adults: major adverse kidney events within 30 days (MAKE30 -- death, new renal-replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction, i.e. final creatinine >=200% of baseline) occurred in 14.3% (1,139/7,942) of the balanced-crystalloids group vs 15.4% (1,211/7,860) of the saline group (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.99, P=0.04) -- a real, statistically significant, if modest, relative reduction of about 7% in kidney and mortality-composite harm from choosing a balanced solution.
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.reason_why: Pre-renal AKI is, by definition, a state of reduced effective renal perfusion without yet-established structural damage; restoring intravascular volume directly reverses the haemodynamic drop in glomerular filtration rate. 0.9% saline's high chloride content (154 mmol/L, non-physiological) is associated with hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction in large-volume resuscitation, which balanced solutions (chloride content closer to plasma) avoid -- the real mechanistic basis for the SMART trial's modest advantage.
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.source: Semler MW et al (SMART trial), NEJM 2018;378(9):829-839 (PMID 29485925); KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury, Kidney Int Suppl 2012;2:1-138, Recommendation 3.1.1
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.confidence: high -- large multicentre pragmatic cluster-randomized trial
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.real_working_solution: For haemodynamically unstable patients or those with pre-renal AKI from volume depletion, give isotonic crystalloid promptly, preferring a balanced solution (lactated Ringer's/Plasma-Lyte) over 0.9% saline where available and not contraindicated (e.g. hyperkalaemia favors avoiding potassium-containing balanced solutions in specific cases), guided by clinical volume-status reassessment to avoid fluid overload.

aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.name: Isotonic Saline Hydration to Prevent Contrast-Induced (Iatrogenic) AKI Before Iodinated Contrast Exposure
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.effectiveness: Mueller C et al, Arch Intern Med 2002;162(3):329-36 (PMID 11822926), randomized n=1,620 patients undergoing coronary angioplasty: contrast-media-associated nephropathy occurred in 0.7% (95% CI 0.1-1.4%) with isotonic (0.9%) saline hydration vs 2.0% (95% CI 1.0-3.1%) with half-isotonic (0.45%) saline hydration (P=0.04) -- a real, statistically significant, roughly 65% relative risk reduction, with the largest benefit in women, diabetics, and those receiving >=250 mL contrast.
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.reason_why: Iodinated contrast causes AKI through direct tubular toxicity and medullary vasoconstriction/ischaemia; adequate intravascular volume expansion before and during contrast exposure dilutes the contrast load in the renal medulla and maintains medullary blood flow, reducing tubular injury -- an isotonic solution provides more effective, sustained intravascular volume expansion than a hypotonic one.
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.source: Mueller C et al, Arch Intern Med 2002;162(3):329-36 (PMID 11822926); Lameire N et al, Crit Care 2013;17(1):205 (PMID 23394215), KDIGO summary Part 2 on contrast-induced AKI
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.confidence: high for the isotonic-vs-half-isotonic comparison in this randomized trial
aki_fluid_resuscitation_prerenal.real_working_solution: Any patient with reduced eGFR or other AKI risk factors undergoing iodinated contrast administration should receive isotonic (0.9%) IV saline hydration before and after the procedure, plus use of the lowest feasible contrast volume and avoidance of concurrent nephrotoxins, as the real, evidence-based, low-cost prevention strategy for this specific, entirely predictable and largely preventable cause of AKI.

aki_nephrotoxic_agent_discontinuation.name: Immediate Discontinuation or Dose-Adjustment of Nephrotoxic and Renally-Cleared Drugs
specific_actions: Stop NSAIDs (afferent-arteriolar vasoconstriction via prostaglandin inhibition)
Stop or hold ACE-inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics during acute volume depletion/hypotension ('triple whammy' with NSAIDs)
Stop or dose-adjust aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) and vancomycin; use trough-level/AUC-guided dosing if continuation is unavoidable
Avoid or minimize iodinated contrast; use alternative imaging where feasible
Dose-adjust or hold all other renally-cleared medications (e.g. metformin, certain antivirals) to the current, reduced GFR
aki_nephrotoxic_agent_discontinuation.effectiveness: No single randomized trial isolates 'stopping nephrotoxic drugs' as a standalone intervention because it is an integral, guideline-mandated part of every AKI care bundle rather than a separately tested drug; its real evidence base is the well-established pharmacological mechanism of each agent plus the KDIGO guideline's explicit, graded recommendation (Recommendation 3.3, 'Discontinue... nephrotoxic agents where possible') as a core management step, alongside the observational finding that a large share of hospital-acquired AKI (Nash K, Hafeez A, Hou S, 'Hospital-acquired renal insufficiency', Am J Kidney Dis 2002;39(5):930-6, PMID 11979336, n=4,622 admissions, renal insufficiency developed in 7.2%) is directly attributable to decreased renal perfusion, medications, surgery, and radiographic contrast media -- i.e. real, identifiable and often avoidable/reversible iatrogenic drivers.
aki_nephrotoxic_agent_discontinuation.reason_why: NSAIDs block the compensatory afferent-arteriolar vasodilation (prostaglandin-mediated) that maintains glomerular perfusion when renal blood flow is already reduced; ACE-inhibitors/ARBs block the efferent-arteriolar vasoconstriction that maintains glomerular filtration pressure in the same setting -- combined ('triple whammy' with a diuretic causing volume depletion), these drugs remove both of the kidney's own autoregulatory safety mechanisms simultaneously. Aminoglycosides and contrast media cause direct proximal-tubular cytotoxicity. Removing the causative agent halts ongoing injury and allows the real, substantial regenerative capacity of the renal tubular epithelium (in the absence of the toxic insult) to proceed.
aki_nephrotoxic_agent_discontinuation.source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury, Kidney Int Suppl 2012;2:1-138 (Recommendation 3.3); Kellum JA et al, Crit Care 2013;17(1):204 (PMID 23394211); Nash K et al, Am J Kidney Dis 2002;39(5):930-6 (PMID 11979336)
aki_nephrotoxic_agent_discontinuation.confidence: high for the pharmacological mechanism and guideline-recommendation status; moderate for a precise population-level effectiveness percentage since this is a guideline-mandated bundle component rather than a single isolated randomized intervention
aki_nephrotoxic_agent_discontinuation.real_working_solution: On recognizing AKI (or significant AKI risk), immediately review the full medication list and stop every avoidable nephrotoxic agent (NSAIDs first), hold ACE-inhibitor/ARB/diuretic therapy until volume status and renal function stabilize, avoid unnecessary contrast, and dose-adjust every renally-cleared drug to current GFR -- a real, immediate, zero-cost intervention that removes ongoing tubular injury and is a mandatory first step in every AKI guideline worldwide.

aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.name: Renal Replacement Therapy (Intermittent Haemodialysis / Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy) for Severe AKI -- Real Evidence on Timing
aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.type: Procedure (life-support/organ-support), reserved tier for severe/refractory AKI
specific_actions: Absolute/urgent indications regardless of timing strategy: refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory metabolic acidosis, refractory volume overload (e.g. pulmonary oedema), uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding diathesis), certain poisonings

Modality choice: intermittent haemodialysis (haemodynamically stable patients) vs continuous renal replacement therapy/CRRT (haemodynamically unstable/ICU patients) vs peritoneal dialysis (resource-limited settings)

Timing strategy: individualized 'watchful waiting' with close monitoring, escalating to dialysis only for the specific indications above or progressive severe (KDIGO stage 3) AKI, rather than reflexively early initiation for every patient meeting a creatinine/urine-output threshold
aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.effectiveness: The real randomized-trial evidence on RRT timing is mixed and is reported here in full, not cherry-picked: (1) ELAIN (Zarbock A et al, JAMA 2016;315(20):2190-9, PMID 27209269), n=231, single-centre surgical/cardiac-surgery ICU patients with KDIGO stage 2 AKI: 90-day mortality 39.3% (44/112) with early RRT (within 8h of stage 2) vs 54.7% (65/119) with delayed RRT, an absolute 15.4-percentage-point reduction (HR 0.66, P=0.03) -- the one positive trial favoring earlier initiation. (2) AKIKI (Gaudry S et al, NEJM 2016;375(2):122-33, PMID 27181456), n=619, multicentre, mechanically ventilated/vasopressor-dependent stage-3 AKI: 60-day mortality 48.5% early vs 49.7% delayed (P=0.79, no significant difference); 49% of delayed-strategy patients never required dialysis at all, avoiding the procedure entirely with no mortality penalty. (3) IDEAL-ICU (Barbar SD et al, NEJM 2018;379(15):1431-42, PMID 30304656), n=477, septic shock with severe (KDIGO/RIFLE-F) AKI: 90-day mortality 58% early vs 54% delayed (P=0.38, no significant difference); 38% of delayed-strategy patients (93/238) never required RRT. (4) STARRT-AKI (Bagshaw SM et al, NEJM 2020;383(3):240-51, PMID 32668114), n=3,019, the largest and most definitive trial: 90-day mortality 43.9% accelerated vs 43.7% standard (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.93-1.09, P=0.92, no difference); among 90-day survivors, dialysis dependence was significantly HIGHER with the accelerated strategy (10.4%, 85/814) than the standard strategy (6.0%, 49/815; RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.24-2.43) -- a real 4.4-percentage-point excess of long-term dialysis dependence from unnecessarily early dialysis.
aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.reason_why: Dialysis directly substitutes for lost excretory/electrolyte/acid-base kidney function and is life-saving for the specific refractory indications above, but it does not itself accelerate intrinsic tubular repair and carries real procedural risks (catheter-related bloodstream infection, haemodynamic instability, and -- per STARRT-AKI -- a measurable excess of long-term dialysis dependence when started before the kidney has had a chance to recover spontaneously). The largest, most rigorous trial (STARRT-AKI) and two other large multicentre trials (AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU) found no mortality benefit from earlier initiation, while a smaller single-centre surgical cohort (ELAIN) did -- the honest, current best interpretation is that dialysis timing should be individualized to the specific indication rather than to a fixed early threshold, and that a real substantial proportion of AKI patients (38-49% in the delayed arms of AKIKI/IDEAL-ICU) recover spontaneously and never need dialysis at all if given the chance.
aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.source: Zarbock A et al (ELAIN), JAMA 2016;315(20):2190-9 (PMID 27209269); Gaudry S et al (AKIKI), NEJM 2016;375(2):122-33 (PMID 27181456); Barbar SD et al (IDEAL-ICU), NEJM 2018;379(15):1431-42 (PMID 30304656); Bagshaw SM et al (STARRT-AKI), NEJM 2020;383(3):240-51 (PMID 32668114); Lameire N et al, Crit Care 2013;17(1):205 (PMID 23394215)
aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.confidence: high -- four large, independent, multicentre randomized controlled trials, including the definitive 3,019-patient STARRT-AKI trial
aki_renal_replacement_therapy_severe.real_working_solution: Reserve renal replacement therapy for AKI patients with refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory acidosis, refractory fluid overload, or uraemic complications, or for progressive severe AKI despite maximal conservative management; do not initiate dialysis purely on an early creatinine/urine-output threshold in the absence of these indications, since the real, largest trial evidence (STARRT-AKI) shows this 'accelerated' approach gives no mortality benefit and measurably increases long-term dialysis dependence -- a genuinely important real finding that changed international practice toward individualized, watchful-waiting timing.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages/statistics come from DIFFERENT studies measuring DIFFERENT outcomes (cause-specific survival, kidney-function-recovery rate, relative risk reduction in a composite endpoint, or absolute mortality difference) in different AKI populations (community-acquired vs ICU vs post-surgical vs septic-shock), so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. Rows are ordered by real clinical priority (cause-directed therapy and fluid/medical measures first, procedures/RRT timing evidence last), matching this KB's medicine-first, injection/procedure-second priority convention, not purely by numeric size.
