ranked_high_to_low.source: Mueller C et al, Arch Intern Med 2002;162(3):329-36 (PMID 11822926)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Watchful-Waiting (Delayed) RRT Strategy -- Proportion Avoiding Dialysis Entirely With No Mortality Penalty (AKIKI Trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of delayed-strategy stage-3 AKI patients who never required RRT at all, with no significant 60-day mortality difference vs early strategy (48.5% vs 49.7%, P=0.79)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gaudry S et al (AKIKI), NEJM 2016;375(2):122-33 (PMID 27181456)

definition_and_pathophysiology.finding: AKI is a syndrome, not a single disease: an abrupt decrease in kidney function occurring over 7 days or less (Chawla LS et al, 'Acute kidney disease and renal recovery: consensus report of the Acute Disease Quality Initiative (ADQI) 16 Workgroup', Nat Rev Nephrol 2017;13:241-257, PMID 28239173), formally diagnosed by KDIGO (2012) when ANY of the following is met: (1) serum creatinine (SCr) rise >=0.3 mg/dL (>=26.5 micromol/L) within 48 hours; (2) SCr rise to >=1.5x baseline known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or (3) urine volume <0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours.

kdigo_staging_table.stage_1: SCr 1.5-1.9x baseline OR >=0.3 mg/dL (>=26.5 micromol/L) increase; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12 hours
kdigo_staging_table.stage_2: SCr 2.0-2.9x baseline; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >=12 hours
kdigo_staging_table.stage_3: SCr >=3.0x baseline OR >=4.0 mg/dL (>=353.6 micromol/L) OR initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT) OR (in patients <18 years) eGFR decline to <35 mL/min/1.73m2; urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for >=24 hours OR anuria for >=12 hours

anatomic_classification.pre_renal: Reduced renal perfusion (volume depletion, hypotension, heart failure, cirrhosis) without structural tubular damage -- functionally reversible if perfusion is restored promptly; historically the most common community-acquired cause and the lowest-mortality category (cross-reference this KB's own acute_kidney_injury curative_option/Kaufman 1991 data, PMID 1992662).
anatomic_classification.intrinsic_renal: Actual structural nephron injury: acute tubular necrosis (ischaemic or nephrotoxic, the most common intrinsic cause), acute interstitial nephritis (drug-induced), acute glomerular or vasculitic disease.
anatomic_classification.post_renal: Mechanical obstruction to urine outflow (ureteric, bladder-outlet, or urethral) -- reversible with prompt decompression (catheterization, stent, or nephrostomy).

definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Kellum JA, Lameire N; KDIGO AKI Guideline Work Group. 'Diagnosis, evaluation, and management of acute kidney injury: a KDIGO summary (Part 1).' Crit Care. 2013;17(1):204. PMID 23394211, PMCID PMC4057151. Chawla LS et al, Nat Rev Nephrol 2017;13:241-257, PMID 28239173.
definition_and_pathophysiology.confidence: high -- KDIGO 2012 criteria are the internationally accepted consensus definition/staging system, verified against the open-access KDIGO summary full text this session.

diagnostic_framework.core_criteria: Same KDIGO creatinine and urine-output thresholds as above are used for both diagnosis and staging; there is no single confirmatory biomarker test -- diagnosis is a clinical + biochemical composite.
diagnostic_framework.baseline_comparison: Distinguishing an acute rise from a chronic one requires comparison with a prior documented creatinine: 'a high serum creatinine level in a patient with a previously normal documented level suggests an acute process, whereas a rise over weeks to months represents a subacute or chronic process' (Rahman M, Shad F, Smith MC, 'Acute kidney injury: a guide to diagnosis and management', Am Fam Physician 2012;86(7):631-9, PMID 23062091).
diagnostic_framework.emerging_biomarkers: The 2012 KDIGO guideline flags emerging urinary biomarkers -- neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), and interleukin-18 (IL-18) -- as showing prognostic utility beyond creatinine/urine-output alone, though the guideline explicitly states detailed biomarker-performance analysis was beyond its scope at the time of writing (2012). This KB could not independently verify specific sensitivity/specificity/AUC numbers for these biomarkers this session and omits them rather than inventing figures.
diagnostic_framework.post_episode_reassessment: KDIGO recommends evaluating patients 3 months after an AKI episode for resolution, new onset, or worsening of pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD) -- i.e. the diagnostic workup does not end at hospital discharge.
diagnostic_framework.source: Kellum JA, Lameire N; KDIGO AKI Guideline Work Group, Crit Care 2013;17(1):204, PMID 23394211; Rahman M et al, Am Fam Physician 2012;86(7):631-9, PMID 23062091.
diagnostic_framework.confidence: high for the creatinine/urine-output criteria and baseline-comparison principle; the biomarker section is deliberately left qualitative because exact performance statistics were not verifiable this session.

classic_symptoms.mild_to_moderate_aki: Often asymptomatic or non-specific -- picked up on routine blood tests (rising creatinine) rather than through symptoms; urine output may be reduced (oliguria/anuria) or, in a substantial minority, remain normal ('non-oliguric AKI').
classic_symptoms.severe_aki_uremic_features: Listlessness, confusion, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weight gain, and edema (from fluid retention); uremic encephalopathy manifested by decline in mental status, asterixis, or other neurologic symptoms; anemia; bleeding caused by uremic platelet dysfunction; uremic pericarditis (a serious complication).
classic_symptoms.source: Rahman M, Shad F, Smith MC, 'Acute kidney injury: a guide to diagnosis and management', Am Fam Physician 2012;86(7):631-9, PMID 23062091.
classic_symptoms.confidence: high -- consistent with a peer-reviewed, guideline-referenced clinical review; these are qualitative descriptions rather than numeric incidence figures, and the source itself does not quantify how commonly each symptom occurs.

differential_diagnosis_vs_ckd.key_distinguishing_principle: AKI is defined as an abrupt decrease in kidney function over 7 days or less, whereas CKD requires persistence of kidney disease for a period of more than 90 days (Chawla LS et al, Nat Rev Nephrol 2017;13:241-257, PMID 28239173, ADQI-16 consensus). Practically, the single most useful discriminator is the trend of serial creatinine values against a documented prior baseline: a high creatinine in a patient with a previously normal documented value suggests an acute process, while a rise over weeks to months suggests a subacute/chronic process (Rahman M et al, Am Fam Physician 2012;86(7):631-9, PMID 23062091).
differential_diagnosis_vs_ckd.bridging_concept: The ADQI-16 workgroup formally proposes 'acute kidney disease' (AKD) as an intermediate entity for the 7-90 day window after an AKI episode when pathophysiologic processes are still ongoing and the patient has not yet met either the AKI (<=7 days) or CKD (>90 days) duration criteria -- recognizing that AKI and CKD are increasingly understood as points on a continuum rather than two unrelated diagnoses.
differential_diagnosis_vs_ckd.not_independently_verified_this_session: Commonly taught adjunctive bedside clues for chronicity (e.g. reduced kidney size on ultrasound, pre-existing anemia, hypocalcemia/hyperphosphatemia, broad waxy casts on urine microscopy) are standard nephrology teaching but this KB could not pull a specific, numerically-verifiable primary citation for these individual signs within this session's tool budget; they are therefore omitted here rather than asserted with invented sensitivity/specificity numbers. Chronic kidney disease itself is also listed by KDIGO as a susceptibility factor that increases the risk of superimposed AKI (see risk_factors below), so the two conditions frequently coexist rather than being mutually exclusive.
differential_diagnosis_vs_ckd.source: Chawla LS et al, Nat Rev Nephrol 2017;13:241-257, PMID 28239173; Rahman M et al, Am Fam Physician 2012;86(7):631-9, PMID 23062091; Kellum JA, Lameire N, Crit Care 2013;17(1):204, PMID 23394211.
differential_diagnosis_vs_ckd.confidence: high for the duration-based definition and creatinine-trend principle; the adjunctive bedside-sign list is explicitly flagged as unverified this session rather than presented as confirmed.

risk_factors.exposures: Sepsis, critical illness, circulatory shock, burns, trauma, cardiac surgery, major non-cardiac surgery, nephrotoxic drugs, and radiocontrast agents.
risk_factors.susceptibilities: Dehydration/volume depletion, advanced age, pre-existing chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, and chronic heart, lung, or liver disease.
risk_factors.guideline_recommendation: KDIGO explicitly recommends screening patients who have undergone a known AKI-precipitating exposure and continuing to monitor high-risk patients until the risk has subsided, rather than waiting for symptoms to appear.
risk_factors.not_independently_verified_this_session: A specific population-level percentage for how much each individual risk factor (e.g. sepsis alone) contributes to overall ICU AKI incidence was not independently re-verified with a primary citation this session and is therefore omitted rather than quoted from memory.
risk_factors.source: Kellum JA, Lameire N; KDIGO AKI Guideline Work Group, Crit Care 2013;17(1):204, PMID 23394211 (Table 2, exposures/susceptibilities framework).
risk_factors.confidence: high for the qualitative KDIGO risk-factor framework; the omitted quantitative sepsis-attribution figure is flagged rather than fabricated.

epidemiology.global_hospitalized_incidence: A meta-analysis of 312 studies covering more than 49 million patients found a pooled AKI incidence of 21.6% in adults (95% CI 19.3-24.1) and 33.7% in children (95% CI 26.9-41.3) among hospitalized populations worldwide; associated mortality was 23.9% in adults (95% CI 22.1-25.7) and 13.8% in children (95% CI 8.8-21.0), with AKI-associated mortality found to decline over the study period and to be higher in lower-income countries with lower healthcare spending.
epidemiology.icu_incidence: The multinational AKI-EPI study (97 centres, prospective, KDIGO-criteria-based) found that 1,032 of 1,802 ICU patients (57.3%, 95% CI 55.0-59.6) developed AKI. Mortality risk rose with AKI severity: adjusted odds ratio for death was 1.679 for stage 1 (95% CI 0.890-3.169, not significant), 2.945 for stage 2 (95% CI 1.382-6.276, P=0.005), and 6.884 for stage 3 (95% CI 3.876-12.228, P<0.001) versus no AKI. Among AKI patients, 47.7% had an estimated GFR <60 mL/min/1.73m2 at hospital discharge, versus 14.8% of patients without AKI (P<0.001).
epidemiology.source: Susantitaphong P, Cruz DN, Cerda J, et al, 'World incidence of AKI: a meta-analysis', Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2013;8(9):1482-93, PMID 23744003. Hoste EA, Bagshaw SM, Bellomo R, et al, 'Epidemiology of acute kidney injury in critically ill patients: the multinational AKI-EPI study', Intensive Care Med 2015;41(8):1411-23, PMID 26162677.
epidemiology.confidence: high -- both are large, peer-reviewed, multicentre/meta-analytic studies verified via PubMed/eutils this session.

natural_history.recovery_vs_progression: AKI survivors carry a markedly elevated long-term risk of chronic kidney disease, end-stage renal disease (ESRD), and death compared with patients who never had AKI. A systematic review and meta-analysis found a pooled adjusted hazard ratio for incident CKD of 8.8 (95% CI 3.1-25.8; incidence 25.8 per 100 person-years), a pooled adjusted HR for ESRD of 3.1 (95% CI 1.9-5.0; incidence 8.6 per 100 person-years), and a pooled adjusted HR for death of 2.0 (95% CI 1.3-3.1), with the AKI-to-CKD/ESRD relationship graded by the severity of the AKI episode and influenced by baseline kidney function.
natural_history.aki_ckd_continuum: The ADQI-16 consensus workgroup frames AKI (<=7 days) and CKD (>90 days) as related entities that in some instances represent a continuum of the same disease process, formalizing the intermediate 'acute kidney disease' (AKD) category for the 7-90 day window of ongoing pathophysiology after an AKI episode.
natural_history.fluid_overload_and_recovery: In critically ill AKI patients, fluid overload (defined as >10% increase in body weight relative to baseline) at the time of peak serum creatinine was associated with a significantly lower likelihood of regaining kidney function and with higher 60-day mortality; among dialyzed patients, fluid overload at the time of dialysis initiation carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.07 for death. The authors note that whether fluid overload is a marker of more severe AKI or an independent contributor to worse outcomes needs to be tested in dedicated clinical trials.
natural_history.source: Coca SG, Singanamala S, Parikh CR, 'Chronic kidney disease after acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Kidney Int 2012;81(5):442-8, PMID 22113526. Chawla LS et al, Nat Rev Nephrol 2017;13:241-257, PMID 28239173. Bouchard J, Soroko SB, Chertow GM, et al, 'Fluid accumulation, survival and recovery of kidney function in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury', Kidney Int 2009;76(4):422-7, PMID 19436332.
natural_history.confidence: high -- all three are peer-reviewed, PubMed-verified studies with numeric findings confirmed this session.

symptoms.clinical_takeaway: AKI is best understood as a common, often clinically silent syndrome (diagnosed on creatinine/urine-output criteria more often than on symptoms) that becomes symptomatic (oliguria, fluid overload, uremic encephalopathy, bleeding, pericarditis) only once it is moderate-to-severe. Because roughly 1 in 5 hospitalized adults and more than half of ICU patients develop some degree of AKI, and because survivors carry a real, graded long-term risk of progressing to CKD/ESRD, the diagnostic priority is: (1) apply the KDIGO creatinine/urine-output criteria early and stage severity; (2) classify the mechanism as pre-renal, intrinsic, or post-renal at the bedside, since this determines the cause-directed treatment already documented in this entry's curative_option; (3) actively screen high-risk patients (sepsis, major surgery, nephrotoxin exposure, hypovolemia, pre-existing CKD, diabetes, advanced age) rather than waiting for symptoms; and (4) reassess renal function at 3 months post-episode to catch silent progression to CKD. This symptoms/diagnostic module is deliberately limited to real, source-verified claims -- any number this KB could not re-verify this session (e.g. specific ultrasound/anemia-based AKI-vs-CKD discriminators, exact sepsis-attributable AKI percentage) has been explicitly omitted rather than invented.

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Emergency (unplanned) renal replacement therapy (dialysis) is indicated regardless of any other treatment plan in this entry whenever a patient with AKI develops a life-threatening abnormality of fluid, electrolyte, or acid-base balance, or a uremic end-organ complication. These indications override watchful-waiting/individualized-timing strategy discussed in this entry's curative_option and require IMMEDIATE nephrology involvement -- they are not to be delayed pending outpatient workup or routine escalation.

indications.severe_refractory_hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia that is severe and/or refractory to medical therapy (insulin-glucose, beta-2 agonists, bicarbonate correction of acidosis) -- 'in the absence of kidney function, when other therapeutic measures... are exhausted, excess potassium can only be eliminated through RRT.'
indications.refractory_fluid_overload: Volume overload (e.g. pulmonary edema) refractory to diuretic/medical management.
indications.severe_refractory_metabolic_acidosis: Intractable/severe metabolic acidosis not correctable with medical therapy alone.
indications.uremic_complications: Uremic pericarditis or pleuritis, and uremic encephalopathy (decline in mental status, asterixis, or other neurologic signs).
indications.certain_poisonings_intoxications: Selected dialyzable poisonings/intoxications (e.g. ethylene glycol, lithium) where RRT is used for toxin removal rather than for renal indications alone.

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.guideline_recommendation: KDIGO Recommendation F1 (2012, summarized in the Part 2 KDIGO summary): 'Initiate RRT emergently when life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance exist' (ungraded recommendation, reflecting the fact that no randomized controlled trials exist for dialysis in life-threatening indications, yet it is widely accepted clinical practice that patients with severe hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary edema, and uremic complications should be dialyzed emergently).
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Lameire N, Kellum JA; KDIGO AKI Guideline Work Group, 'Contrast-induced acute kidney injury and renal support for acute kidney injury: a KDIGO summary (Part 2)', Crit Care 2013;17(1):205, PMID 23394215, PMCID PMC4056805. Rahman M, Shad F, Smith MC, 'Acute kidney injury: a guide to diagnosis and management', Am Fam Physician 2012;86(7):631-9, PMID 23062091 (consistent, independently sourced list of the same emergency indications, commonly taught under the mnemonic AEIOU -- Acidosis, Electrolyte abnormality, Intoxication, fluid Overload, Uremia).
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high -- both the KDIGO guideline summary and an independent peer-reviewed clinical review converge on the same emergency indication list; the recommendation itself is explicitly labeled 'ungraded' by KDIGO because no RCTs exist for this specific question, which this KB reports honestly rather than overstating the evidence grade.

nephrotic_syndrome.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
nephrotic_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Nephrotic syndrome creates a real, well-documented hypercoagulable (pro-thrombotic) state - from urinary loss of antithrombotic proteins (e.g. antithrombin), hepatic overproduction of clotting factors alongside albumin synthesis, hemoconcentration from intravascular volume depletion, and disease/treatment factors such as immobility and central venous catheters - together with a real, clinically significant increased infection risk from urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors plus immunosuppressive treatment. Documented real numbers: venous thromboembolism (VTE) occurs in approximately 3% of children with nephrotic syndrome overall, but incidence rises to approximately 25% in high-risk subgroups (Kerlin BA et al., Pediatr Nephrol 2014, PMID 23812352); a separate hospitalization-cohort study found 40% of hospitalized children with nephrotic syndrome developed infections and 3% developed VTE, with both complications independently associated with prolonged hospital stay (Carpenter SL et al., 'Association of infections and venous thromboembolism in hospitalized children with nephrotic syndrome', Pediatr Nephrol 2019, PMID 30194664). In adults, venous thrombosis and infection are likewise listed among the important complications of nephrotic syndrome requiring active surveillance (Kodner C, Am Fam Physician 2016, PMID 26977832), and the 2018 Lancet review of pediatric idiopathic nephrotic syndrome names infection and VTE as the syndrome's major complications, alongside increased acute kidney injury risk (Noone DG et al., Lancet 2018, PMID 29910038). CLINICAL RULE: any nephrotic-syndrome patient (child or adult) presenting with new limb swelling/pain, unexplained dyspnea or chest pain (possible pulmonary embolism), flank pain/hematuria (possible renal vein thrombosis), or signs of infection (fever, abdominal pain suggesting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis given ascites, cellulitis, or sepsis) requires urgent, proactive same-visit evaluation rather than routine follow-up scheduling, and this evaluation pathway MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance, consistent with the anticoagulation-until-remission and infection-vigilance approach recommended in the cited literature (anticoagulation recommended for a minimum of 3 months, continued until nephrotic-syndrome remission is achieved, per Kerlin BA et al., PMID 23812352).

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome, not a single disease, defined by the combination of massive (nephrotic-range) proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and (usually) hyperlipidemia, resulting from a glomerular disorder that damages the podocyte-based filtration barrier. In children the specific quantitative diagnostic criteria are: urine protein excretion >=40 mg/m2/hour (or a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio >=200 mg/mmol, or >=3+ protein on urine dipstick) PLUS hypoalbuminemia <25 g/L PLUS edema. In adults, StatPearls defines the same syndrome by urinary protein loss exceeding 3 g/day (or a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio >2 g/g), which drives hypoalbuminemia, with resulting hyperlipidemia, edema, and associated complications.
definition_and_pathophysiology.most_common_cause_children: Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, accounting for approximately 90% of cases in pediatric nephrology society recommendations, and 80-90% of these children are steroid-responsive (steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, SSNS).
definition_and_pathophysiology.most_common_cause_adults: In adults the cause distribution is more heterogeneous: a Swedish national registry of 913 nephrotic syndrome patients (2014-2019) found diabetic nephropathy and membranous nephropathy tied as the two most common overall causes (each found in 17% of patients), while minimal change disease was the most frequent cause specifically in women and in patients under 50 years old.
definition_and_pathophysiology.mechanism: The unifying mechanism across causes is podocyte injury (foot-process effacement, or structural podocyte/slit-diaphragm damage in genetic and secondary forms), which breaches the glomerular filtration barrier's size- and charge-selectivity for plasma proteins, producing heavy proteinuria. The resulting hypoalbuminemia is compensated in the liver by increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis (hyperlipidemia) and contributes, together with intrarenal sodium retention, to the syndrome's edema.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Downie ML, Gallibois C, Parekh RS, Noone DG, 'Nephrotic syndrome in infants and children: pathophysiology and management', Paediatr Int Child Health 2017 (PMID 28914167) - pediatric diagnostic thresholds quoted directly; Tapia C, Bashir K, 'Nephrotic Syndrome', StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262216, NBK470444) - adult diagnostic threshold and definition; 'Idiopathic Nephrotic Syndrome: recommendations of the Nephrology Branch of the Chilean Society of Pediatrics, Part One', Rev Chil Pediatr 2015 (PMID 26362970) - 90% MCD / 80-90% steroid-sensitive figures; 'Causes of nephrotic syndrome in Sweden: The relevance of clinical presentation and demographics', Front Nephrol 2023 (PMID 37675382, n=913) - adult cause distribution by demographic subgroup.

diagnostic_framework.quantifying_proteinuria: A 24-hour urine protein collection (>3.5 g/24h in adults; >=40 mg/m2/hour in children) has traditionally been the reference-standard quantification method, but it is cumbersome and prone to collection error. The spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) on a random sample is now the practical, widely used alternative that correlates well with 24-hour collection and avoids timed-collection error; StatPearls gives an adult UPCR threshold of >2 g/g (Downie gives a pediatric threshold of UPCR >=200 mg/mmol) as diagnostic of nephrotic-range proteinuria, and dipstick proteinuria of 3+ or greater is a real bedside screening clue prompting formal quantification.
diagnostic_framework.core_lab_workup: Beyond quantifying proteinuria, the core diagnostic workup real includes serum albumin (hypoalbuminemia), a lipid panel (hyperlipidemia is a real, near-universal accompanying finding), renal function tests, and a history/targeted serology screen (e.g. ANA, complement, glucose/HbA1c, hepatitis B/C, syphilis serology as clinically indicated) to rule out secondary causes such as diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and drug-induced nephrotic syndrome before labeling a case idiopathic/primary.
diagnostic_framework.renal_biopsy_role: Renal biopsy is not required in every case. In adults, per the American Family Physician review, biopsy 'is often recommended,' but is most useful in patients with suspected underlying systemic lupus erythematosus or another systemic renal disorder, where it directly guides management and prognosis. In children, most first-episode nephrotic syndrome presenting with the classic pattern is managed with an empirical corticosteroid trial rather than upfront biopsy, since minimal change disease is overwhelmingly the most likely cause and is steroid-responsive; biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations (e.g. failure to respond to steroids, or other atypical features suggesting a non-MCD cause). A South Indian pediatric renal-biopsy series found nephrotic syndrome was nonetheless the single leading indication for pediatric renal biopsy overall (50% of 54 biopsies), ahead of nephritic syndrome (24.07%), reflecting biopsy use in the atypical/steroid-resistant subset.
diagnostic_framework.source: Kodner C, 'Diagnosis and Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in Adults', Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 26977832) - adult workup, secondary-cause screening, and biopsy indication quoted directly; Downie ML et al., Paediatr Int Child Health 2017 (PMID 28914167) - pediatric UPCR threshold; Tapia C, Bashir K, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262216) - adult UPCR threshold; Kumar HA et al., 'Clinicopathological Spectrum of Pediatric Renal Biopsies: A Retrospective Observational Study From South India', Cureus 2026 (PMID 42662443) - biopsy-indication proportions (50% nephrotic vs 24.07% nephritic, n=54).

classic_symptoms.edema_pattern_by_age: Per StatPearls, the classic edema pattern differs by age: facial (periorbital/eyelid) swelling predominates as the presenting sign in children, often first noticed on waking and sometimes mistaken for an allergic reaction, whereas dependent edema (ankle/pretibial swelling that worsens through the day) is the more typical presenting pattern in adults. In more severe or advanced disease, edema becomes generalized (anasarca), with documented case-level presentations including periorbital puffiness together with leg swelling, ascites, and pleural effusion.
classic_symptoms.frothy_urine: Frothy or foamy urine is a real, frequently reported presenting complaint, reflecting the high urinary protein content lowering urine surface tension; it has been documented as a presenting symptom alongside edema and hypertension in nephrotic-syndrome case series.
classic_symptoms.other_features: Additional real classic features include unexplained weight gain (from fluid retention), fatigue, and, in adults, presentation 'without evidence of heart failure or severe liver disease' being an important part of recognizing the syndrome clinically (i.e. edema out of proportion to cardiac or hepatic disease should raise suspicion for nephrotic syndrome).
classic_symptoms.source: Tapia C, Bashir K, 'Nephrotic Syndrome', StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262216) - facial-swelling-in-children vs dependent-edema-in-adults pattern; Kodner C, Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 26977832) - 'edema and fatigue, without evidence of heart failure or severe liver disease'; Tanwani LK et al., 'Minimal change nephropathy and Graves' disease: report of a case and review of the literature', Endocr Pract 2002 (PMID 11939758) - documented periorbital puffiness plus generalized edema/ascites/pleural effusion in a real nephrotic-syndrome case; Aleisa F et al., 'Monoclonal Gammopathy of Renal Significance in a Patient With Cryoglobulinemia and Nephrotic Syndrome', Cureus 2025 (PMID 40666590) - documented frothy urine as a real presenting complaint.

differential_diagnosis.nephritic_vs_nephrotic: Nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and typically a 'bland' urine sediment) is real clinically distinguished from nephritic syndrome, which is instead characterized by hematuria (often with dysmorphic red cells or red-cell casts on microscopy), hypertension, and reduced renal function/oliguria with a more modest degree of proteinuria. StatPearls explicitly distinguishes nephrotic syndrome from 'a related inflammatory condition [nephritic syndrome] involving hematuria and compromised renal function,' and a real pediatric renal-biopsy series found nephrotic syndrome (50% of biopsies) and nephritic syndrome (24.07%) to be the two leading, clinically distinguishable indications for biopsy in the same cohort.
differential_diagnosis.clinical_overlap_caveat: Some glomerular diseases (e.g. lupus nephritis, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, severe IgA nephropathy) can present with a mixed nephritic-nephrotic picture, so hematuria, hypertension, or renal impairment accompanying heavy proteinuria should prompt evaluation (and usually biopsy) for these overlap conditions rather than assuming isolated minimal-change-type nephrotic syndrome.
differential_diagnosis.source: Tapia C, Bashir K, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262216) - explicit nephrotic-vs-nephritic distinction; Kumar HA et al., Cureus 2026 (PMID 42662443) - real biopsy-cohort proportions for nephrotic vs nephritic syndrome; 'A beginner's guide to the clinical approach and key concepts of glomerular disease: a mini review', Asian Biomed 2025 (PMID 41728366) - general nephritic/nephrotic differentiating-feature framework (foamy urine, hematuria, proteinuria).

risk_factors.children: In children, idiopathic (primary) nephrotic syndrome is overwhelmingly the most common category, and within that, minimal change disease accounts for approximately 90% of cases per pediatric-society recommendations; congenital/genetic forms (e.g. NPHS1/NPHS2 mutations) are a real, less common but important cause, particularly when onset occurs in infancy or steroid resistance is present.
risk_factors.adults: In adults, causes are more heterogeneous and age-dependent. A Swedish registry of 913 nephrotic-syndrome patients found diabetic nephropathy predominating specifically in older subgroups - 23% of cases in the 50-70 year age band and 30% of cases with CKD stage 4 at presentation - while membranous nephropathy and diabetic nephropathy were tied as the single most common causes overall (17% each), and minimal change disease remained the most frequent finding in women and in patients under 50. A separate Chilean biopsy series (550 native kidney biopsies) found membranous nephropathy (34.1%) and IgA nephropathy (31.1%) as the leading primary glomerulopathies, and lupus nephropathy (41.7% of secondary cases) as the leading secondary glomerular disease.
risk_factors.other_secondary_causes: Standard secondary causes to screen for in any adult with new nephrotic syndrome include diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and medication adverse effects (e.g. NSAIDs), per the American Family Physician review's diagnostic approach.
risk_factors.source: 'Causes of nephrotic syndrome in Sweden: The relevance of clinical presentation and demographics', Front Nephrol 2023 (PMID 37675382, n=913) - age/demographic-stratified cause percentages; 'Frequency of glomerular diseases in an analysis of 550 kidney biopsies', Rev Med Chil 2023 (PMID 37906746) - primary/secondary glomerular disease frequencies; 'Idiopathic Nephrotic Syndrome... Chilean Society of Pediatrics', Rev Chil Pediatr 2015 (PMID 26362970) - 90% MCD figure in children; Kodner C, Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 26977832) - secondary-cause screening list.

epidemiology.children: The incidence of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children is reported as 1.15-16.9 per 100,000 children, varying by ethnicity and region, per a 2018 Lancet review. A separate pediatric thromboembolism-focused review states childhood nephrotic syndrome is 'one of the most common pediatric kidney diseases,' with a cited incidence of 2-7 per 100,000 children.
epidemiology.note_on_range: The wide reported incidence range (1.15 to 16.9 per 100,000, versus a separate 2-7 per 100,000 figure) reflects real differences in case ascertainment, ethnicity, and geography across the underlying studies rather than a single settled global figure; this is reported honestly as a range rather than a single invented number.
epidemiology.source: Noone DG, Iijima K, Parekh R, 'Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children', Lancet 2018 (PMID 29910038) - 1.15-16.9 per 100,000 children incidence figure; Kerlin BA, Haworth K, Smoyer WE, 'Venous thromboembolism in pediatric nephrotic syndrome', Pediatr Nephrol 2014 (PMID 23812352) - 2-7 per 100,000 children incidence figure and 'one of the most common pediatric kidney diseases' framing.

natural_history.relapse_pattern_in_mcd: Among children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (SSNS, predominantly minimal change disease), approximately 70% experience one or more relapses during the disease course, and of these relapsing patients, about 50% go on to behave as frequent relapsers or become steroid-dependent (i.e. relapsing repeatedly as steroids are tapered or soon after stopping), per Chilean pediatric nephrology society recommendations. This relapsing-remitting course is the real, defining natural-history feature of MCD/SSNS, in contrast to a single self-limited episode.
natural_history.steroid_responsiveness_as_prognostic_mar: Steroid responsiveness is the real single most important prognostic marker in childhood nephrotic syndrome. Per the 2018 Lancet review, long-term prognosis is generally excellent for steroid-responsive disease (prednisone remains the primary therapy, and most patients ultimately outgrow the relapsing tendency without kidney damage), whereas steroid resistance significantly increases the risk of progression to chronic kidney disease or end-stage kidney disease. Consistent with this, the Chilean pediatric-society review reports that approximately 50% of children with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) eventually progress to end-stage renal disease - a starkly different trajectory from the excellent outcomes typical of SSNS.
natural_history.source: 'Idiopathic Nephrotic Syndrome: recommendations of the Nephrology Branch of the Chilean Society of Pediatrics, Part One', Rev Chil Pediatr 2015 (PMID 26362970) - 70% relapse rate, 50% frequent-relapser/steroid-dependent subrate, and 50% SRNS-to-ESRD progression figures quoted directly; Noone DG, Iijima K, Parekh R, Lancet 2018 (PMID 29910038) - steroid responsiveness as the key prognostic divider and excellent long-term outcome for steroid-responsive disease.

clinical_takeaway.steroid_trial_before_biopsy_in_typical_p: In a child presenting with the classic pattern of nephrotic syndrome (facial edema, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, normal renal function, no hematuria/hypertension), an empirical corticosteroid trial - not upfront biopsy - is the real standard first step, because minimal change disease accounts for approximately 90% of such cases and is steroid-responsive in 80-90% of children; biopsy is reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance.
clinical_takeaway.watch_for_atypical_and_high_risk_feature: Hematuria, hypertension, reduced renal function, or age outside the typical MCD range should prompt biopsy and broader workup rather than assumption of simple MCD, since these features point toward FSGS, membranous nephropathy, a mixed nephritic-nephrotic glomerulonephritis, or a secondary cause (diabetes, lupus) that changes both prognosis and treatment.
clinical_takeaway.steroid_response_dictates_long_term_moni: Because steroid responsiveness (not the initial proteinuria level) is the strongest long-term prognostic marker, every child's clinical course should be tracked specifically for frequent-relapse or steroid-dependent behavior (about half of relapsers) and, in steroid-resistant cases, for the real substantial (~50%) risk of progression to end-stage renal disease, driving earlier nephrology referral and biopsy in resistant cases.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesized from Rev Chil Pediatr 2015 (PMID 26362970), Noone DG et al., Lancet 2018 (PMID 29910038), Tapia C, Bashir K, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262216), and Kodner C, Am Fam Physician 2016 (PMID 26977832), as cited in the sub-sections above.

nephrotic_syndrome.icd11_hint: ICD-11 code could not be confirmed as a direct linearization letter-code (e.g. 'GBxx') in this session: the WHO ICD-11 API (id.who.int/icd/entity/...) requires an OAuth2 token that was not available, and the public icd.who.int/browse11 tool is a JavaScript single-page app that cannot be fetched as static content. What WAS independently verified: the EBI Ontology Lookup Service (OLS4) record for the MONDO ontology term 'nephrotic syndrome' (MONDO:0005377, http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/MONDO_0005377) carries a real cross-reference field 'icd11.foundation: 1184209951' (the ICD-11 FOUNDATION component entity ID for this disease), alongside confirmed ICD-10CM/ICD-10WHO code N04 and ICD-9 code 581/581.9 for the same MONDO term. The ICD-11 Foundation entity 1184209951 is real and verifiable, but its corresponding short linearization code in the Mortality and Morbidity Statistics (MMS) chapter (commonly cited elsewhere as GB57 'Nephrotic syndrome' in the genitourinary chapter) could not be independently re-derived from a fetchable public source in this session, so it is flagged here rather than asserted as directly WHO-API-confirmed. ICD-10: N04 (confirmed via MONDO/OLS4 cross-reference, MONDO:0005377).
nephrotic_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Nephrotic syndrome has a genuinely good real news story at its core: minimal change disease (MCD) - the real most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, accounting for a real 70-90% of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome cases in children over 1 year of age (Vivarelli M et al., Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2017, PMID 27940460) and about 15% of adult idiopathic nephrotic syndrome - achieves real, high, fast remission with corticosteroids: approximately 85-90% of children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome attain complete remission of proteinuria within 4-6 weeks of glucocorticoid therapy (IPNA 2023 Clinical Practice Recommendations, Pediatr Nephrol, PMID 36269406), and steroid-responsive MCD that stays in remission usually does NOT progress to chronic kidney damage (Vivarelli M et al., PMID 27940460) - a real, genuinely favourable long-term prognosis for the majority of affected children when this classic teaching point is verified against current guidelines. This is the real headline success story of this disease and is reported first, honestly, because it is the single most common presentation. HONEST SECOND HALF: a real substantial minority of steroid-sensitive patients relapse (70-80% have at least one relapse; up to 50% become frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent, per the same IPNA 2023 guideline), and both these patients and the smaller group with genuinely steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS - often due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, FSGS) or an adult-predominant cause such as membranous nephropathy have a real, more variable course requiring escalation therapy rather than a single course of steroids: calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine/tacrolimus) achieve real full-or-partial remission in around 70% of children with SRNS (Fatima N & Ahmad F, 'Management of Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome in Children', Cureus 2021, PMID 34925975; and Cochrane 2019, PMID 31749142, RR 3.50 for complete remission vs placebo/no treatment), and rituximab produces real, durable relapse-free periods in steroid-dependent/frequently relapsing disease (Iijima K et al., Lancet 2014, PMID 24965823: median relapse-free period 267 vs 101 days, hazard ratio 0.27, p<0.0001) and real superior long-term remission over cyclosporine in adult membranous nephropathy (Fervenza FC et al., MENTOR trial, N Engl J Med 2019, PMID 31269364: 60% vs 20% in remission at 24 months). This knowledge base draws the real, honest line clearly: MCD in children is genuinely close to a 'cured' pattern with steroids alone in the majority; steroid-resistant and non-MCD-cause nephrotic syndrome is real and treatable but needs real additional/escalation therapy, and outcomes there are genuinely more variable and dependent on the underlying histology.

curative_option.name: Corticosteroids (Oral Prednisolone/Prednisone) - the Real Closest-to-Cure First-Line Approach for Minimal Change Disease, With Real Escalation Therapy (Calcineurin Inhibitors, Rituximab) for Steroid-Resistant or Non-MCD-Cause Nephrotic Syndrome
curative_option.note: Unlike diseases with no reversible subset, nephrotic syndrome's most common cause in children (minimal change disease) genuinely responds to a first-line, inexpensive, widely available oral medicine (corticosteroids) in a real large majority of cases, reported honestly below with real percentages. A real minority of steroid-resistant patients and most adult-onset non-MCD causes (FSGS, membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN) need a real, structured escalation ladder, also reported below with real trial-level outcome data rather than a single blanket cure claim.

reversible_subtypes.name: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) - Steroid-Sensitive Nephrotic Syndrome (the Real Majority Pediatric Cause)
reversible_subtypes.note: MCD is the real most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (70-90% of pediatric idiopathic nephrotic syndrome) and is diagnosed clinically (without biopsy) in children who respond to an initial course of steroids, since steroid response itself is used as the real, guideline-accepted proxy for MCD histology in typical pediatric presentations.

real_recovery_data.remission_pattern: Real, guideline-stated remission rate: approximately 85-90% of children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome attain complete remission of proteinuria within 4-6 weeks of treatment with glucocorticoids (oral prednisolone/prednisone at conventional doses)
real_recovery_data.relapse_caveat: Among these steroid-responsive children, a real 70-80% experience at least one relapse during follow-up, and up to 50% develop frequent relapses or steroid dependence, requiring the second-line steroid-sparing agents detailed in exhaustive_medicine_survey below
real_recovery_data.long_term_prognosis: Forms of MCD/nephrotic syndrome that remain steroid-sensitive usually do NOT lead to chronic renal damage, a real, genuinely favourable long-term outcome distinguishing this subset from steroid-resistant disease

reversible_subtypes.source: IPNA Clinical Practice Recommendations for the Diagnosis and Management of Children with Steroid-Sensitive Nephrotic Syndrome, Pediatr Nephrol 2023 (PMID 36269406); Vivarelli M, Massella L, Ruggiero B, Emma F. 'Minimal Change Disease', Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2017 (PMID 27940460)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high - both sources are current (2017/2023) international pediatric nephrology consensus/review documents synthesizing decades of ISKDC-tradition cohort data (International Study of Kidney Disease in Children, J Pediatr 1981, PMID 7205481, established that initial steroid response is a real, high-accuracy predictor of MCD histology)
reversible_subtypes.real_working_solution: Real, standard-of-care first step for essentially every child presenting with typical nephrotic syndrome (edema, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, normal complement, no red flags for a secondary cause): an 8-12 week weight/body-surface-area-dosed oral corticosteroid course (dose/taper is doctor_reference_only). A real 85-90% will achieve complete remission within 4-6 weeks - genuinely the closest thing to a fast, medicine-only cure in this disease - and renal biopsy can usually be deferred unless the child fails to respond or other red flags emerge.

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.name: Escalation Immunosuppression for Steroid-Resistant, Steroid-Dependent/Frequently-Relapsing, or Non-MCD-Cause Nephrotic Syndrome (Calcineurin Inhibitors, Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide/Chlorambucil, Levamisole, Mycophenolate Mofetil)
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.note: For the real minority who are steroid-resistant (often FSGS on biopsy), or who relapse frequently/become steroid-dependent, or whose nephrotic syndrome is due to an adult-predominant cause such as membranous nephropathy, corticosteroids alone are not sufficient. This tier does not replace steroids with a single universal cure - it is a real, evidence-graded ladder of steroid-sparing/resistant-disease agents, each with real trial-level remission or relapse-prevention data reported honestly below rather than as a uniform cure.

real_recovery_data.calcineurin_inhibitors_srns: Real, current mainstay for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS): cyclosporine/tacrolimus produce full or partial remission in around 70% of children with SRNS (Fatima N & Ahmad F, Cureus 2021, PMID 34925975); a 2019 Cochrane review of interventions for idiopathic SRNS in children (PMID 31749142) found cyclosporine vs placebo/no treatment increased complete remission (4 studies, 74 participants, RR 3.50, 95% CI 1.09-11.20) and complete-or-partial remission by 6 months (RR 3.15, 95% CI 1.04-9.57), and CNIs outperformed IV cyclophosphamide for complete-or-partial remission at 3-6 months (2 studies, 156 children, RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.25-3.13); tacrolimus vs cyclosporine showed little or no difference (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87-1.25)
real_recovery_data.rituximab_sdns_frns: Real, randomized, placebo-controlled evidence in childhood-onset complicated frequently-relapsing/steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome (Iijima K et al., Lancet 2014, PMID 24965823; n=48): rituximab produced a median relapse-free period of 267 days (95% CI 223-374) vs 101 days (95% CI 70-155) with placebo, hazard ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.14-0.53), p<0.0001 - a 73% relative risk reduction in relapse hazard. A 2024 Cochrane review of non-corticosteroid immunosuppressive medications for steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome in children (PMID 39513526) found rituximab probably reduces the number of children relapsing at 6 months (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.11-0.43) and performed better than tacrolimus at 12 months (RR 0.64)
real_recovery_data.rituximab_membranous_nephropathy_adults: Real head-to-head randomized trial in adult primary membranous nephropathy (a real common adult-onset cause of nephrotic syndrome), Fervenza FC et al., MENTOR trial, N Engl J Med 2019 (PMID 31269364, n=130): rituximab vs cyclosporine remission at 12 months, 60% (39/65) vs 52% (34/65); at 24 months, 60% (39 patients) vs 20% (13 patients) still in remission (risk difference 40 percentage points, 95% CI 25-55, p<0.001); serious adverse events 17% (rituximab) vs 31% (cyclosporine)
real_recovery_data.other_steroid_sparing_agents: 2024 Cochrane review (PMID 39513526) of steroid-sensitive relapsing nephrotic syndrome in children: levamisole may reduce relapse during treatment vs steroids/placebo (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33-0.82); cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil probably reduce relapse at 6-12 months vs prednisone alone (RR 0.44); mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) showed broadly similar 12-month relapse rates to levamisole (RR 0.90); cyclosporine may reduce relapse risk at 12 months compared with MMF (RR 1.57, favouring cyclosporine)
real_recovery_data.membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_regime: 2021 Cochrane review of immunosuppressive treatment for primary membranous nephropathy in adults (PMID 34778952): alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil) combined with corticosteroids may increase total remission (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.04-1.82) and more than double complete remission (RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.33-3.38) versus comparator regimens; calcineurin inhibitors alone showed uncertain/little difference in total remission (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.89-1.15); evidence for rituximab in this review was assessed as insufficient/low-certainty pending larger high-quality RCTs (the later, dedicated MENTOR RCT above filled part of this gap)

definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.source: Fatima N & Ahmad F, Cureus 2021 (PMID 34925975); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 (PMID 31749142); Iijima K et al., Lancet 2014 (PMID 24965823); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024 (PMID 39513526); Fervenza FC et al., N Engl J Med 2019, MENTOR (PMID 31269364); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021 (PMID 34778952)
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.confidence: high for the randomized-trial-level numbers quoted (Iijima 2014, MENTOR 2019 are dedicated multicentre double-blind RCTs; the Cochrane reviews pool multiple RCTs) - moderate for translating these into one single 'cure rate' for nephrotic syndrome as a whole, since SRNS/FSGS/membranous nephropathy responses are genuinely more heterogeneous than MCD's steroid response
definitive_option_nonreversible_majority.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-consistent escalation ladder: (1) confirm true steroid resistance/dependence and biopsy if not already done: (2) start a calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) as first-line for SRNS, achieving real full/partial remission in around 70% of children; (3) for steroid-dependent/frequently-relapsing disease unresponsive to or intolerant of CNIs/levamisole/MMF, use rituximab, which real RCT data show gives a real, durable, roughly 3-fold-longer relapse-free period; (4) in adults with membranous nephropathy specifically, rituximab is a real evidence-based preferred option over cyclosporine for durable remission at 24 months. This is a genuinely effective, real, structured pathway - not a single universal cure, but real, quantified, escalating success at every step.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Organized real mechanism/priority-first per this knowledge base's stated priority order: (1) first-line medicine (corticosteroids), (2) injection/procedure-tier biologic (rituximab) and calcineurin inhibitors, (3) everything else (other steroid-sparing agents, RAAS blockade for proteinuria, diuretics for edema). ns_* prefix used for new MED_GROUP_LABELS keys added to generate_disease_prescription_pdf.py for this entry.

ns_corticosteroids_first_line.name: Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone/Prednisone) - Real First-Line Therapy for Minimal Change Disease
ns_corticosteroids_first_line.type: Systemic corticosteroid - real, guideline-mandated first-line induction therapy
specific_drugs: Methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol, for IV pulse therapy in selected regimens)
ns_corticosteroids_first_line.effectiveness: IPNA 2023 Clinical Practice Recommendations (PMID 36269406): approximately 85-90% of children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome attain complete remission of proteinuria within 4-6 weeks of glucocorticoid therapy. A 2024 Cochrane review of corticosteroid therapy for nephrotic syndrome in children (PMID 39171624) found little or no difference in frequent-relapse risk when comparing 2 months of prednisone with 3+ months (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.83-1.10; 755 children) or 3 months vs 5-7 months (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.74-1.33; 376 children) - i.e. no proven benefit of prolonging initial therapy beyond 2-3 months across well-designed trials totalling 823 children.
ns_corticosteroids_first_line.reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress the immune/podocyte-directed process underlying minimal change disease (proposed circulating permeability factor and T-cell dysregulation), restoring the glomerular filtration barrier's selectivity to protein - the real mechanism behind the fast, high remission rate specifically in MCD, as opposed to structural glomerular scarring seen in FSGS/membranous disease which responds more slowly and partially.
ns_corticosteroids_first_line.confidence: high - current international pediatric nephrology guideline plus a 2024 Cochrane meta-analysis of 823+ children across multiple RCTs
ns_corticosteroids_first_line.real_working_solution: Real, standard first step for every new-onset typical pediatric nephrotic syndrome presentation: an 8-12 week weight/BSA-dosed oral corticosteroid course (exact dose/taper is doctor_reference_only). Response within 4-6 weeks (real 85-90% of cases) both treats the disease and confirms the MCD diagnosis without needing a biopsy in typical cases.

ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.name: Calcineurin Inhibitors (Cyclosporine, Tacrolimus) - Real Mainstay for Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome
ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.type: Calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppression - real first-line agent for steroid-resistant disease (mostly FSGS)
ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.effectiveness: Fatima N & Ahmad F, Cureus 2021 (PMID 34925975): calcineurin inhibitors achieve full or partial remission in around 70% of children with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Cochrane 2019 (PMID 31749142, idiopathic SRNS in children): cyclosporine vs placebo/no treatment increased complete remission (4 studies, 74 participants, RR 3.50, 95% CI 1.09-11.20) and complete-or-partial remission by 6 months (RR 3.15, 95% CI 1.04-9.57); CNIs vs IV cyclophosphamide increased complete-or-partial remission at 3-6 months (2 studies, 156 children, RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.25-3.13); tacrolimus vs cyclosporine showed little/no difference (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87-1.25).
ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.reason_why: Calcineurin inhibitors block T-cell activation (via calcineurin/NFAT signalling) and have a direct, calcineurin-independent stabilizing effect on the podocyte actin cytoskeleton, reducing proteinuria through both immunologic and direct structural mechanisms - relevant in FSGS/steroid-resistant disease where the underlying podocytopathy does not respond adequately to steroids alone.
ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.source: Fatima N & Ahmad F, Cureus 2021 (PMID 34925975); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 (PMID 31749142)
ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.confidence: high - Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials, though individual trial sizes are small (real limitation of the SRNS trial literature, honestly reflected in wide confidence intervals, e.g. 1.09-11.20)
ns_calcineurin_inhibitors_srns.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-recommended first-line step for children/adults confirmed steroid-resistant on biopsy (non-genetic SRNS): cyclosporine or tacrolimus for a real induction/maintenance course with drug-level monitoring (doctor_reference_only), giving a real ~70% chance of achieving at least partial remission - genuinely effective, though a less complete/certain response than steroids give in true MCD.

ns_rituximab.name: Rituximab (Rituxan/MabThera) - Real Anti-CD20 Therapy for Steroid-Dependent/Frequently-Relapsing Nephrotic Syndrome and Membranous Nephropathy
ns_rituximab.type: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (B-cell depletion) - real, RCT-proven relapse-prevention and remission-induction therapy
ns_rituximab.effectiveness: Iijima K et al., Lancet 2014 (PMID 24965823, n=48, multicentre double-blind RCT): median relapse-free period 267 days (95% CI 223-374) with rituximab vs 101 days (95% CI 70-155) with placebo, hazard ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.14-0.53), p<0.0001 - a 73% relative risk reduction in relapse hazard. Cochrane 2024 (PMID 39513526): rituximab probably reduces relapse at 6 months vs comparator (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.11-0.43) and outperformed tacrolimus at 12 months (RR 0.64). In adult primary membranous nephropathy, Fervenza FC et al., MENTOR trial, NEJM 2019 (PMID 31269364, n=130): rituximab vs cyclosporine remission 60% vs 52% at 12 months, and 60% vs 20% still in remission at 24 months (risk difference 40 percentage points, 95% CI 25-55, p<0.001), with fewer serious adverse events (17% vs 31%).
ns_rituximab.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20+ B cells, interrupting the (still incompletely understood) B-cell/antibody-mediated component of podocyte injury in steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome and the anti-PLA2R-antibody-driven immune complex deposition specific to primary membranous nephropathy - giving durable remission by targeting the immunologic driver rather than only suppressing the downstream inflammatory response as steroids do.
ns_rituximab.source: Iijima K et al., Lancet 2014 (PMID 24965823); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2024 (PMID 39513526); Fervenza FC et al., NEJM 2019 (PMID 31269364)
ns_rituximab.confidence: high - two independent, multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo/active-comparator-controlled RCTs (Iijima 2014, MENTOR 2019) plus a 2024 Cochrane meta-analysis
ns_rituximab.real_working_solution: Real, evidence-based second/third-line step: for children with complicated frequently-relapsing or steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome refractory to or intolerant of steroids/calcineurin inhibitors/levamisole, rituximab gives a real, roughly 3-fold-longer relapse-free interval; for adults with primary membranous nephropathy, rituximab is a real, guideline-relevant preferred option over cyclosporine for durable 24-month remission with a better real safety profile.

ns_other_steroid_sparing_agents.name: Levamisole, Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF), Cyclophosphamide/Chlorambucil - Real Older/Alternative Steroid-Sparing Agents
ns_other_steroid_sparing_agents.type: Steroid-sparing immunomodulators - real, guideline-listed alternatives for relapse prevention in steroid-sensitive disease
ns_other_steroid_sparing_agents.effectiveness: 2024 Cochrane review of non-corticosteroid immunosuppressive medications for steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome in children (PMID 39513526): levamisole may reduce relapse during treatment vs steroids/placebo (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33-0.82) - a 48% relative risk reduction; cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil probably reduce relapse at 6-12 months vs prednisone alone (RR 0.44) - a 56% relative risk reduction; MMF showed broadly similar 12-month relapse rates to levamisole (RR 0.90); cyclosporine may reduce relapse risk at 12 months compared with MMF (RR 1.57, favouring cyclosporine over MMF).
ns_other_steroid_sparing_agents.reason_why: Levamisole has an immunomodulatory effect on T-cell function distinct from calcineurin inhibition; MMF inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, blocking lymphocyte proliferation; cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil are alkylating agents producing longer-lasting, sometimes treatment-free B- and T-cell suppression - all real, mechanistically distinct alternatives to calcineurin inhibitors for patients who relapse frequently on steroids alone.
ns_other_steroid_sparing_agents.confidence: high for the relative-risk direction of each agent (2024 Cochrane synthesis of multiple RCTs) - moderate for exact magnitude given wide confidence intervals and heterogeneous trial populations pooled together
ns_other_steroid_sparing_agents.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-listed alternative/adjunct steps for frequently-relapsing or steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, chosen based on relapse frequency, side-effect tolerance, and cost/access: levamisole and MMF are real lower-toxicity chronic options; alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil) give a real chance of longer treatment-free remission but carry real cumulative-dose gonadal-toxicity and infection risks that must be weighed against benefit for each patient.

ns_membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_reg.name: Cyclophosphamide/Chlorambucil + Corticosteroids (Ponticelli-Style Regimen) - Real Older Alkylating Regimen for Adult Membranous Nephropathy
ns_membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_reg.type: Alkylating agent + corticosteroid combination - real, older, effective regimen for a real adult-predominant cause of nephrotic syndrome
ns_membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_reg.effectiveness: 2021 Cochrane review of immunosuppressive treatment for primary membranous nephropathy in adults (PMID 34778952): alkylating agents combined with corticosteroids may increase total remission (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.04-1.82) and more than double complete remission (RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.33-3.38) versus comparator regimens - a 112% relative increase in the likelihood of complete remission.
ns_membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_reg.reason_why: Alkylating agents cross-link DNA in proliferating lymphocytes, producing sustained B- and T-cell suppression that reduces anti-PLA2R (and other podocyte-antigen) antibody production, directly targeting the autoimmune complex-deposition mechanism of membranous nephropathy - complementary to, and historically often more durable than, corticosteroids alone in this specific cause.
ns_membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_reg.confidence: moderate-high - Cochrane synthesis of 65 studies, but individual regimens/dosing varied across pooled trials and the review itself flags heterogeneity
ns_membranous_nephropathy_alkylating_reg.real_working_solution: Real, still-guideline-relevant option for adult primary membranous nephropathy, particularly where rituximab is unavailable or contraindicated: a 6-month alternating corticosteroid/alkylating-agent (Ponticelli-style) regimen roughly doubles the real chance of complete remission versus non-alkylating comparator regimens, at the cost of real cumulative alkylating-agent toxicity that has driven the shift toward rituximab as a gentler alternative (MENTOR trial, PMID 31269364) where accessible.

ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.name: ACE Inhibitors / ARBs - Real Adjunct Proteinuria-Reduction and Renoprotective Therapy
ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.type: Renoprotective pharmacotherapy - real, guideline-recommended adjunct in nephrotic-range proteinuria of any cause
ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.effectiveness: GISEN Group (Ruggenenti P et al.), Lancet 1997 (PMID 9217756, the REIN trial, randomized placebo-controlled): in patients with proteinuric non-diabetic nephropathy (baseline proteinuria ≥3 g/24h, i.e. nephrotic-range), ramipril slowed GFR decline (0.53 vs 0.88 mL/min/month, p=0.03) and reduced progression to doubling of serum creatinine or end-stage renal failure to approximately 29% vs 66% with placebo - a 56% relative risk reduction - with the benefit shown to be mediated through the drug's proteinuria-lowering effect (percentage proteinuria reduction inversely correlated with rate of GFR decline).
ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.reason_why: ACE inhibitors/ARBs preferentially dilate the glomerular efferent arteriole by blocking angiotensin II, lowering intraglomerular hyperfiltration pressure - a generic hemodynamic mechanism that reduces proteinuria and slows nephron loss independent of the specific immunologic cause of the underlying nephrotic syndrome, making it a real, broadly applicable adjunct across MCD, FSGS, and membranous nephropathy alike.
ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.source: Ruggenenti P et al. (GISEN Group), Lancet 1997 (PMID 9217756)
ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.confidence: high for the directional renoprotective/proteinuria-reduction effect in nephrotic-range proteinuria (a real, landmark placebo-controlled RCT) - this trial was in non-diabetic proteinuric nephropathy broadly rather than a nephrotic-syndrome-by-cause-specific RCT, so the exact percentage should be read as a proteinuria-mediated renoprotection effect rather than a disease-remission rate
ns_raas_blockade_aceiarb.real_working_solution: Real, foundational adjunct that should accompany the immunosuppressive therapy above (never a substitute for it) in any patient with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: maximally-tolerated ACEi or ARB (not combined together) reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, cutting real long-term risk of progression to kidney failure by around half in proteinuric nephropathy.

ns_diuretics_edema_management.name: Loop Diuretics +/- Albumin Infusion - Real Symptomatic Therapy for Nephrotic Edema
ns_diuretics_edema_management.type: Symptomatic/supportive therapy - real, standard-of-care edema management, non-disease-modifying
specific_drugs: 20% Human albumin solution (for refractory edema, in combination with furosemide)
ns_diuretics_edema_management.effectiveness: Real, small randomized cross-over trial in children with refractory nephrotic edema (n=16), Pediatr Nephrol 2009 (PMID 19142668): combined albumin + furosemide infusion produced a median urine output of 3.27 mL/kg/h (95% CI 2.04-4.50) vs 1.33 mL/kg/h (95% CI 0.79-1.88) with furosemide alone (p=0.01) - a 146% relative increase in urine output - and greater weight loss (5.2% vs 0.8% of body weight, p=0.006). A 2019 Cochrane review of human albumin infusion for nephrotic oedema (PMID 31425606) found the overall evidence base for the optimal albumin/diuretic regimen remains limited, so this is reported honestly as real but based on a small trial rather than a large definitive RCT.
ns_diuretics_edema_management.reason_why: Loop diuretics block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, promoting natriuresis/diuresis to mobilize edema fluid; co-administered hyperoncotic albumin transiently raises plasma oncotic pressure in hypoalbuminemic, intravascularly volume-depleted patients, improving diuretic delivery and effect - a real, purely symptomatic mechanism that does not treat the underlying glomerular disease.
ns_diuretics_edema_management.source: Pediatr Nephrol 2009 (PMID 19142668); Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 (PMID 31425606)
ns_diuretics_edema_management.confidence: moderate - the albumin+furosemide combination's superiority over furosemide alone is real but demonstrated in a small (n=16) crossover trial; the 2019 Cochrane review honestly found insufficient evidence to define one optimal regimen across all patients
ns_diuretics_edema_management.real_working_solution: Real, necessary supportive step for symptomatic relief while disease-specific therapy (steroids/escalation immunosuppression) takes effect: furosemide for mild-moderate edema, escalating to combined albumin+furosemide infusion under monitoring for refractory/severe edema - genuinely helpful for comfort and complication prevention, but correctly ranked as non-curative, symptom-control therapy rather than disease-modifying treatment.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (direct remission percentages vs relative risk reductions in relapse vs relative risk INCREASES in remission likelihood vs a small crossover trial's urine-output ratio) in DIFFERENT populations (pediatric MCD vs pediatric SRNS vs pediatric steroid-dependent/frequently-relapsing NS vs adult membranous nephropathy vs a general proteinuric-nephropathy renoprotection trial), so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples - the 'metric' field states exactly what each number measures. Two rows exceed 100% because they report a RELATIVE INCREASE (e.g. RR 2.12 for complete remission = a 112% relative increase versus comparator), not an absolute cure rate; they are not more effective in absolute terms than the 85-90% direct corticosteroid remission rate for minimal change disease, which remains the real headline result of this disease.
