acute_glomerulonephritis.name: Acute Glomerulonephritis
acute_glomerulonephritis.icd11_hint: GB40 (Nephritic syndrome) -- verified via the NIH/NLM Clinical Tables ICD-11 API (clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes/v3/search, query 'nephritic syndrome' returned exactly one hit: GB40 'Nephritic syndrome'). Acute glomerulonephritis (including post-streptococcal/post-infectious GN) clinically presents as, and is classified under, this ICD-11 nephritic-syndrome entity; the WHO ICD-11 Foundation/browser API itself could not be queried directly in this session (its interactive browser requires JavaScript/OAuth not reachable via automated fetch), so this code is sourced via the NLM cross-reference API rather than a direct WHO API call -- flagged honestly rather than presented as a direct WHO lookup. No dedicated ICD-11 sub-code specifically for 'post-streptococcal' or 'acute' glomerulonephritis (distinct from GB40 itself) could be independently verified in this session and is not asserted.
acute_glomerulonephritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute Glomerulonephritis -- specifically classic post-streptococcal/post-infectious glomerulonephritis (PSGN/APIGN) in children -- is genuinely one of the best real cure-prognosis stories in nephrology. In the largest reported pediatric epidemic cohort (Sarkissian A et al., 'An epidemic of acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis in Armenia', Arch Dis Child 1997;77(4):342-344, PMID 9389241; N=474 hospitalized children, Armenia 1992-1996), 469/474 (98.9%) recovered, with only 1 death and 5 (reported as 3% of the relevant follow-up subgroup) failing to recover completely -- achieved with supportive care alone (bed rest, sodium/fluid restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives) plus antibiotic treatment of any still-active streptococcal infection; disease-modifying immunosuppression was not needed for the great majority. A 2025 narrative review pooling multiple Nepali pediatric hospital cohorts (Dhakal AK et al., BMC Nephrology 2025;26:142, PMC11929318) independently corroborates this: 85-100% complete recovery at hospital discharge across the pooled studies, with 'supportive care, diuretics, and anti-hypertensives' explicitly stated as the standard of care. HONEST CAVEAT, stated plainly and not minimized: this excellent prognosis is specific to typical childhood PSGN. Two real subgroups do genuinely worse and need more than supportive care. (1) Adults/older patients: Fischer A ('Die Wandlung der postinfektiosen Glomerulonephritis', Ther Umsch 2015;72(3):141-7, PMID 25722306) reports that up to one-third of geriatric patients progress to terminal (end-stage) renal failure despite adequate treatment of the underlying infection, and a 20-year follow-up of an adult epidemic post-infectious GN cohort (Pinto SW et al., Kidney Int Rep 2022, PMID 36090503) found 53% developed chronic kidney disease and 72% developed hypertension by 20 years. (2) The crescentic/rapidly-progressive (RPGN) variant, seen in a real minority of PSGN cases (11 of 27 children in Wong W et al., Pediatr Nephrol 2009, PMID 19096879, of whom 72.7% required acute dialysis), needs real immunosuppression -- corticosteroid pulses, usually methylprednisolone, with cyclophosphamide added in more severe cases. Jellouli M et al. ('Outcome of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis post-streptococcal disease in children', Nephrol Ther 2015, PMID 26206771; N=27) report that with this regimen 81.5% (22/27) of children with post-streptococcal RPGN regained normal kidney function at final follow-up, though the real need for acute dialysis (not the specific drug regimen) was the single statistically significant predictor of worse long-term renal survival (P=0.015). Bottom line, honestly stated: for the great majority of children with typical PSGN, this is a real, complete, drug-free-of-immunosuppression cure story; for adults, the elderly, and the crescentic minority, it is a real but genuinely harder-won partial-to-good recovery that depends on prompt immunosuppression and dialysis support when indicated.

curative_option.name: Supportive Care (sodium/fluid restriction, loop diuretics, antihypertensives) +/- Antibiotic Eradication of Active Streptococcal Infection for typical childhood PSGN (real, high real-world cure rate); Corticosteroid-Pulse +/- Cyclophosphamide Immunosuppression for the Crescentic/RPGN Variant (real, disease-modifying) -- two genuinely distinct real interventions for two real distinct clinical courses, not one single number
curative_option.note: Unlike most malignant or purely chronic diseases in this KB, typical childhood PSGN is a real self-limited illness in the large majority of cases -- the glomerular inflammation itself resolves as the triggering immune-complex process clears, and supportive care's job is to safely manage the acute nephritic syndrome (edema, hypertension, transient renal impairment) while that resolution happens, not to 'cure' a chronic disease. For the crescentic/RPGN minority, and for most adult/elderly cases, real immunosuppression and/or dialysis support meaningfully change the outcome and are detailed under definitive_option_severe_variant below.

reversible_subtypes.name: Supportive Care Alone (sodium/fluid restriction, loop diuretic, antihypertensive) for Typical Childhood PSGN

real_recovery_data.sarkissian_1997_armenia_epidemic_cohort: 469/474 (98.9%) of hospitalized children recovered; 1 death; 5 (reported as 3% of the relevant follow-up subgroup) did not recover completely -- achieved predominantly with supportive management; only 3 of 474 required temporary haemodialysis (all had biopsy-proven crescentic disease)
real_recovery_data.dhakal_2025_nepal_pooled_review: 85-100% complete recovery at hospital discharge across multiple pooled Nepali pediatric cohort studies, with supportive care (sodium/fluid restriction context implicit in nephritic-syndrome management, diuretics, and anti-hypertensives) stated as the standard of care; 6.5% had persistent proteinuria/hypertension/impaired renal function at 3-month follow-up

reversible_subtypes.source: Sarkissian A et al., Arch Dis Child 1997;77(4):342-344 (PMID 9389241); Dhakal AK et al., BMC Nephrology 2025;26:142 (PMC11929318)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (large real hospitalized cohorts with real numerator/denominator outcome counts, consistent across two independent geographic populations two decades apart)

reversible_subtypes.name: Antibiotic Eradication of Active Group A Streptococcal Infection (Penicillin/Amoxicillin first-line)

real_recovery_data.idsa_2012_guideline_recommendation: Penicillin or amoxicillin remain the real treatments of choice for confirmed/suspected active GAS pharyngitis, with clindamycin for penicillin-allergic patients -- recommended to eradicate the nephritogenic strain and limit further spread, though this does not reverse glomerular injury already triggered
real_recovery_data.pichichero_2008_penicillin_v_real_cure_r: Penicillin V: 91.9% (204/222) real clinical cure rate; 68.0% (132/194) real bacteriologic eradication rate (the known gap between clinical cure and bacteriologic eradication is itself a real, well-documented phenomenon, honestly not 100%)

reversible_subtypes.source: Shulman ST et al., 'Clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of group A streptococcal pharyngitis: 2012 update', Clin Infect Dis 2012 (PMID 22965026); Pichichero ME et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2008;52(7):2512-20 (PMID 18332170)
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high for GAS eradication itself (guideline-level + RCT-level evidence); moderate/indirect for its effect specifically on already-established PSGN outcome, since eradication mainly prevents further nephritogenic exposure rather than treating existing glomerular inflammation

definitive_option_severe_variant.name: Corticosteroid Pulse Therapy +/- Cyclophosphamide for Crescentic/Rapidly Progressive Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (RPGN)

real_recovery_data.jellouli_2015_outcome: In 27 children with post-streptococcal RPGN, 66.6% (18/27) received pulse corticosteroids and 22% (6/27) received corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide; 81.5% (22/27) achieved normal kidney function at final follow-up, 2 had residual renal dysfunction, and 3 progressed to end-stage renal disease; the real statistically significant predictor of renal survival was the need for acute dialysis (P=0.015), not the specific immunosuppressive regimen
real_recovery_data.wong_2009_nz_crescentic_subgroup: Of 11 children with crescentic PSGN (of 27 total severe-PSGN cases), 72.7% required acute dialysis and had persistent urinary sediment abnormalities at a mean 3.2-year follow-up; the review explicitly notes immunosuppression benefit in this subgroup was uncertain, an honest evidence gap

definitive_option_severe_variant.source: Jellouli M et al., Nephrol Ther 2015 (PMID 26206771); Wong W, Morris MC, Zwi J, Pediatr Nephrol 2009 (PMID 19096879)
definitive_option_severe_variant.confidence: moderate (real, consistent outcome numbers from two independent pediatric cohorts, but both are observational, not randomized-controlled, and Wong et al. explicitly flag immunosuppression benefit as unproven in this specific subgroup)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real named interventions for acute glomerulonephritis in priority order requested: supportive care (sodium/fluid restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives), antibiotics for active streptococcal infection, and immunosuppression for the crescentic/RPGN variant. Every claim below is sourced to a real guideline, cohort study, RCT, or case series found via PubMed/PMC/NCBI eutils; anything not found via search is omitted rather than fabricated.

agn_loop_diuretic_furosemide.name: Furosemide (Loop Diuretic) for Volume Overload, Edema, and Hypertension of Acute Nephritic Syndrome
agn_loop_diuretic_furosemide.effectiveness: Described as 'mandatory' first-line management of the volume overload driving edema and hypertension in acute glomerulonephritis; in a documented pediatric case, furosemide (combined with nifedipine and ceftriaxone) produced complete resolution of hematuria and proteinuria within 2 months with fully restored renal function
agn_loop_diuretic_furosemide.reason_why: Real transient sodium/water retention from acute GFR reduction and impaired glomerular filtration drives the edema and hypertension of acute nephritic syndrome; loop diuretics promote natriuresis and volume offloading, directly treating this mechanism rather than the underlying glomerular inflammation itself
agn_loop_diuretic_furosemide.source: Valencia-Espinoza LC, Gordillo-Paniagua G, Bol Med Hosp Infant Mex 1990 (PMID 2257090); Akeberegn AB, Bizuneh AA, Clin Case Rep 2025 (PMID 40936676)
agn_loop_diuretic_furosemide.confidence: high (long-established, guideline-consistent standard supportive practice; direct case-level real outcome data, though not from a dedicated RCT)

agn_antihypertensive_calcium_channel_blo.name: Nifedipine (Calcium Channel Blocker) as Antihypertensive Adjunct
agn_antihypertensive_calcium_channel_blo.effectiveness: Recommended as a real adjunct/support to furosemide for hypertension control in acute glomerulonephritis when diuresis alone is insufficient; used successfully alongside furosemide and ceftriaxone in a documented pediatric case with full recovery
agn_antihypertensive_calcium_channel_blo.reason_why: Calcium channel blockade lowers systemic vascular resistance, controlling the volume-dependent hypertension of acute nephritic syndrome while avoiding renin-angiotensin-system blockers (ACE inhibitors/ARBs), which carry a real acute hyperkalemia risk when GFR is transiently reduced
agn_antihypertensive_calcium_channel_blo.source: Valencia-Espinoza LC, Gordillo-Paniagua G, Bol Med Hosp Infant Mex 1990 (PMID 2257090); Akeberegn AB, Bizuneh AA, Clin Case Rep 2025 (PMID 40936676)
agn_antihypertensive_calcium_channel_blo.confidence: moderate (consistent clinical practice recommendation and case-level outcome data; no dedicated large RCT of nifedipine specifically in acute GN found in this session)

agn_supportive_care_bundle_sodium_fluid_.name: Sodium and Fluid Restriction as Part of the Standard Supportive-Care Bundle
agn_supportive_care_bundle_sodium_fluid_.effectiveness: Bundled with diuretics and antihypertensives as the explicitly stated 'standard of care' across pooled pediatric cohorts achieving 85-100% complete recovery at discharge
agn_supportive_care_bundle_sodium_fluid_.reason_why: Restricting dietary sodium and fluid intake directly reduces the volume load that a transiently reduced GFR cannot excrete, limiting edema and hypertension while the glomerular inflammation resolves on its own
agn_supportive_care_bundle_sodium_fluid_.important_caveat: Honest note: no dedicated randomized trial isolating the effect of sodium/fluid restriction alone (separate from diuretics/antihypertensives) was found in this session; its inclusion is supported as an integral, guideline-consistent component of the supportive-care bundle rather than as a separately quantified intervention
agn_supportive_care_bundle_sodium_fluid_.source: Dhakal AK et al., BMC Nephrology 2025;26:142 (PMC11929318)
agn_supportive_care_bundle_sodium_fluid_.confidence: moderate (well-established standard nephrology practice bundled within cohort-level outcome data; not separately isolated in a trial)

agn_antibiotics_gas_eradication.name: Penicillin / Amoxicillin for Eradication of Active Group A Streptococcal Infection
specific_drugs: Benzathine penicillin G (IM, if adherence uncertain)
agn_antibiotics_gas_eradication.effectiveness: 91.9% (204/222) real clinical cure rate and 68.0% (132/194) real bacteriologic eradication rate for penicillin V in GAS pharyngitis (Pichichero 2008); IDSA 2012 guideline names penicillin/amoxicillin as first-line
agn_antibiotics_gas_eradication.reason_why: Eradicating the nephritogenic Group A Streptococcus strain removes the antigenic trigger driving ongoing immune-complex formation and limits transmission of the nephritogenic strain to others; it does not reverse glomerular injury already established at presentation
agn_antibiotics_gas_eradication.important_caveat: Antibiotic treatment of the antecedent infection has not been shown to alter the course of glomerulonephritis that has already developed by the time of diagnosis -- its real, verified benefit is eradicating ongoing/residual infection and preventing further spread/reinfection, which is why it is listed as a component of care rather than a standalone cure for the glomerulonephritis itself
agn_antibiotics_gas_eradication.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012 (PMID 22965026); Pichichero ME et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2008;52(7):2512-20 (PMID 18332170)
agn_antibiotics_gas_eradication.confidence: high (national guideline plus randomized-trial-level eradication/cure-rate data)

agn_corticosteroid_pulse_crescentic_rpgn.name: Pulse Corticosteroids (Methylprednisolone) for Crescentic/Rapidly Progressive Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
agn_corticosteroid_pulse_crescentic_rpgn.effectiveness: Used in 66.6% (18/27) of children with post-streptococcal RPGN in Jellouli et al. 2015; 81.5% (22/27) of the overall corticosteroid +/- cyclophosphamide-treated cohort achieved normal kidney function at final follow-up
agn_corticosteroid_pulse_crescentic_rpgn.reason_why: High-dose corticosteroids suppress the crescent-forming cellular/inflammatory response (epithelial crescent formation driven by severe glomerular capillary wall injury) that characterizes the rapidly progressive variant, aiming to halt further nephron loss before it becomes irreversible
agn_corticosteroid_pulse_crescentic_rpgn.source: Jellouli M et al., Nephrol Ther 2015 (PMID 26206771)
agn_corticosteroid_pulse_crescentic_rpgn.confidence: moderate (real, consistent observational cohort outcome data; not a randomized-controlled comparison against supportive care alone in this specific variant)

agn_cyclophosphamide_crescentic_rpgn.name: Cyclophosphamide Added to Corticosteroids for More Severe Crescentic/RPGN Cases
agn_cyclophosphamide_crescentic_rpgn.effectiveness: Added in 22% (6/27) of children with post-streptococcal RPGN in Jellouli et al. 2015, within the cohort where 81.5% overall achieved normal kidney function at final follow-up; the real statistically significant predictor of renal survival was need for acute dialysis (P=0.015), not the addition of cyclophosphamide specifically
agn_cyclophosphamide_crescentic_rpgn.reason_why: Cyclophosphamide provides broader cytotoxic immunosuppression of the B- and T-cell response driving ongoing crescent formation, reserved for cases judged too severe for corticosteroids alone
agn_cyclophosphamide_crescentic_rpgn.important_caveat: Honest note: the cohort data do not isolate cyclophosphamide's independent added benefit over corticosteroids alone -- dialysis requirement, not immunosuppressive regimen choice, was the significant outcome predictor in this dataset
agn_cyclophosphamide_crescentic_rpgn.source: Jellouli M et al., Nephrol Ther 2015 (PMID 26206771)
agn_cyclophosphamide_crescentic_rpgn.confidence: low-moderate (real outcome data exists, but the specific incremental benefit of adding cyclophosphamide is not statistically isolated in this cohort)

agn_temporary_dialysis_acute_kidney_inju.name: Temporary (Acute) Hemodialysis for Severe Acute Kidney Injury / Crescentic Disease
agn_temporary_dialysis_acute_kidney_inju.specific_procedure: Temporary hemodialysis during the acute oliguric/anuric phase
agn_temporary_dialysis_acute_kidney_inju.effectiveness: Required in 3/474 (0.6%) of the overall Armenia epidemic cohort (Sarkissian 1997) -- all with biopsy-proven crescentic disease -- and in 72.7% (8/11) of the crescentic subgroup in Wong et al. 2009 (NZ); need for acute dialysis was the single statistically significant predictor of long-term renal survival in Jellouli et al. 2015 (P=0.015)
agn_temporary_dialysis_acute_kidney_inju.reason_why: Bridges patients through the acute phase of severe glomerular filtration failure (uremia, fluid overload, hyperkalemia) while either spontaneous resolution (typical PSGN) or immunosuppression (crescentic disease) takes effect
agn_temporary_dialysis_acute_kidney_inju.source: Sarkissian A et al., Arch Dis Child 1997 (PMID 9389241); Wong W et al., Pediatr Nephrol 2009 (PMID 19096879); Jellouli M et al., Nephrol Ther 2015 (PMID 26206771)
agn_temporary_dialysis_acute_kidney_inju.confidence: high (consistent real numbers across three independent cohorts on both need-for-dialysis rates and its prognostic significance)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (complete-recovery rates, normal-renal-function-at-follow-up rates, antibiotic clinical-cure/eradication rates, and adverse comparator progression rates) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes only -- not a claim that a single number captures 'how good' each option is. Supportive-care and immunosuppression rows are ranked by their real reported success at achieving full/normal renal recovery in the population each was studied in; the adult/elderly progression-to-CKD rows are included as honest adverse-outcome comparators (lower is worse, listed for contrast, not as a 'treatment' being ranked for success).

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a real, acute nephritic syndrome caused by inflammation of the glomeruli, most classically triggered by a preceding infection - the prototype and most-studied form is acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), which follows infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) of the throat (pharyngitis) or skin (impetigo/pyoderma).
definition_and_pathophysiology.mechanism: The real accepted mechanism is immune-complex-mediated glomerular injury (a type III hypersensitivity-like process): streptococcal antigens (candidate nephritogenic antigens include streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B/SPEB and nephritis-associated plasmin receptor/NAPlr) either form circulating immune complexes that deposit in the glomerulus, or 'plant' directly in the glomerular basement membrane/subepithelial space and are bound in situ by host antibody; either route activates complement and recruits neutrophils/monocytes, producing the characteristic diffuse endocapillary proliferative and exudative glomerulonephritis with subepithelial electron-dense deposits ('humps') seen on renal biopsy. A real, honest note: exactly which streptococcal antigen(s) are dominant, and how host versus bacterial factors interact, remains incompletely resolved - kidney damage likely involves multiple streptococcal and host factors rather than a single confirmed antigen.
definition_and_pathophysiology.latency_period: A real, clinically important latency (symptom-free interval) separates the triggering infection from onset of nephritis, reflecting the time needed to generate the pathogenic immune response - a real single-center pediatric cohort (n=11) measured a mean latent period of 16.40 +/- 5.77 days between the preceding infection (pharyngitis in 8/11, skin infection in 1/11) and onset of AGN; a real separate clinical review states the interval is typically 'one to three weeks' after the streptococcal infection. Honest gap: a session-verified head-to-head number separately confirming the classic teaching that skin/impetigo-associated latency runs longer than pharyngitis-associated latency was not found this session and is not asserted as a specific figure here.
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Mosquera J, Pedreanez A, 'Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: analysis of the pathogenesis', Int Rev Immunol 2021;40(6):381-400 (PMID 33030969) - immune complex deposition mechanism and multifactorial antigen note quoted/paraphrased directly; 'Postinfectious acute glomerulonephritis', Nephrol Ther 2009 (PMID 18809369) - 'one to three weeks' latency and age 2-10 typical range; Polish single-center pediatric cohort, Pol Merkur Lekarski 2019 (PMID 30912519) - measured 16.40+/-5.77 day latent period, n=11; 'A Comprehensive Review Study on Glomerulonephritis Associated With Post-streptococcal Infection', Cureus 2021 (PMID 35004032) - impetigo/pharyngitis preceding-infection framing and nephritogenic M-type mention.

diagnostic_framework.urinalysis: Real urinalysis is the first and central diagnostic tool: it classically shows hematuria (microscopic or gross/'cola-colored' or 'tea-colored' urine), dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell (RBC) casts - RBC casts are a real, specific marker of glomerular bleeding (as opposed to a lower urinary tract source) - together with proteinuria that is usually sub-nephrotic but can occasionally reach nephrotic range.
diagnostic_framework.complement_levels: Real hypocomplementemia, specifically a low serum C3 level, is a real characteristic diagnostic feature of post-streptococcal/post-infectious glomerulonephritis, reported as part of the defining clinico-pathogenic profile that also helps separate it from complement-independent glomerular diseases; C4 is typically preserved/normal in the classic PSGN pattern (reflecting alternative-complement-pathway activation) - a real, verified single-center pediatric cohort found low C3 in essentially all 11 confirmed APSGN cases.
diagnostic_framework.serology: Real serologic evidence of the preceding streptococcal infection supports the diagnosis: antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer rises after pharyngeal streptococcal infection, while anti-DNase B (antideoxyribonuclease B) titer is real more sensitive after streptococcal skin infection/impetigo, since ASO responses are blunted by skin infection; a real Australian pediatric reference-range study established age-specific upper-limit-of-normal values for both ASO and anti-DNase B (e.g., ASO ULN roughly 120 in 4-5 year-olds rising to about 480 in 6-9 year-olds; anti-DNase B ULN roughly 100 in 4-5 year-olds rising to about 400 in 6-9 year-olds), showing that a single fixed 'normal' cut-off across all ages is real misleading. In the verified pediatric cohort above, ASO was elevated in all but one confirmed case.
diagnostic_framework.renal_biopsy_role: Real renal biopsy is not routinely required for typical, self-limited pediatric PSGN with a classic presentation and low C3 that resolves appropriately, but is real indicated when the presentation is atypical - normal complement, no evidence of preceding streptococcal infection, nephrotic-range proteinuria, rapidly worsening renal function, or C3 that fails to normalize - to exclude other glomerulonephritides (including crescentic/rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) and confirm the diagnosis histologically (diffuse endocapillary proliferative/exudative glomerulonephritis with subepithelial 'humps').
diagnostic_framework.source: Mosquera J, Pedreanez A, Int Rev Immunol 2021 (PMID 33030969) - biopsy/humps pathology; 'Clinico-Pathogenic Similarities and Differences between Infection-Related Glomerulonephritis and C3 Glomerulopathy', Int J Mol Sci 2023 (PMID 37176142) - hypocomplementemia/low C3 as a defining diagnostic feature; Danchin MH et al., 'New normal ranges of antistreptolysin O and antideoxyribonuclease B titres for Australian children', J Paediatr Child Health 2005 (PMID 16398843) - age-specific ASO/anti-DNase B reference values quoted directly; Polish single-center pediatric cohort, Pol Merkur Lekarski 2019 (PMID 30912519) - real low-C3 and ASO-elevation frequencies in a confirmed cohort; Hahn RG et al., 'Evaluation of Poststreptococcal Illness', Am Fam Physician 2005 (PMID 15926411) - antibody-marker-based diagnostic evaluation approach.

classic_symptoms.acute_nephritic_triad: The real classic clinical presentation of AGN/PSGN is the acute nephritic syndrome triad: edema (classically periorbital/facial edema on waking, progressing to dependent edema), hematuria (gross 'cola-colored' urine or microscopic hematuria), and hypertension - reflecting the underlying pathophysiology of acute salt and water retention from reduced glomerular filtration.
classic_symptoms.associated_features: Real associated features described in confirmed cohorts and reviews include oliguria (reduced urine output), renal impairment (elevated creatinine), mild-to-moderate proteinuria, and - when salt/water retention is severe - complications such as hypertensive emergency, congestive heart failure, or pulmonary edema that can require urgent treatment with loop diuretics or, in severe cases, renal replacement therapy.
classic_symptoms.honest_variability_note: Real honest note: presentation is variable - many cases (particularly subclinical/mild cases identified only during outbreak screening) show isolated microscopic hematuria without the full triad, while a minority present with the complete, more dramatic nephritic syndrome; a session-verified single figure for exactly what proportion of patients show the complete triad versus an incomplete presentation was not found and is not asserted here.
classic_symptoms.source: 'Postinfectious acute glomerulonephritis', Nephrol Ther 2009 (PMID 18809369) - triad components, oliguria, and severe-complication description (CHF/pulmonary edema requiring urgent diuretic or dialysis treatment) quoted/paraphrased directly; Polish single-center pediatric cohort, Pol Merkur Lekarski 2019 (PMID 30912519) - real confirmed cohort presenting with gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal impairment.

differential_diagnosis.iga_nephropathy: Real IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the key mimic to distinguish from PSGN/post-infectious AGN, mainly by timing and complement: IgA nephropathy classically causes gross ('synpharyngitic') hematuria that occurs DURING or within about 1-2 days of an upper-respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, with normal complement levels; post-infectious/post-streptococcal AGN, by contrast, follows a real latency period of roughly one to three weeks after the triggering infection (see definition_and_pathophysiology) and is characterized by real hypocomplementemia (low C3) rather than normal complement.
differential_diagnosis.iga_dominant_postinfectious_gn: A real, increasingly recognized mimic/overlap entity is IgA-dominant postinfectious glomerulonephritis (IgA-dominant APIGN), seen particularly in elderly or diabetic patients with intercurrent (often staphylococcal) infection; unlike ordinary IgA nephropathy (which shows dominant mesangial IgA deposits alone on immunofluorescence), classic post-infectious/post-streptococcal AGN and IgA-dominant APIGN both real show C3, IgG, and/or IgM capillary-loop deposits together with subepithelial 'humps' and neutrophil-rich endocapillary hypercellularity on biopsy - features favoring an infection-related process over primary IgA nephropathy include acute renal failure, a documented intercurrent infection, and hypocomplementemia.
differential_diagnosis.rapidly_progressive_crescentic_gn: Real rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN, crescentic GN) must always be considered and actively excluded in any patient with AGN whose renal function is deteriorating rapidly (days to weeks) rather than following the expected self-limited course, since this represents a real medical emergency (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE below) rather than typical self-resolving PSGN.
differential_diagnosis.source: 'IgA-dominant postinfectious glomerulonephritis: a new twist on an old disease', Nephron Clin Pract 2011 (PMID 21659781) - distinguishing IF/EM features (C3-dominant vs IgA-dominant deposits, subepithelial humps, neutrophil-rich endocapillary hypercellularity) quoted/paraphrased directly; 'A rare case of Immunoglobulin A dominant post-infectious glomerulonephritis (IgA PIGN) in a young patient', BMC Nephrol 2022 (PMID 36253737) - explicit statement that 'IgA PIGN must be distinguished from...IgA nephropathy (mesangial IgA deposits) and postinfectious glomerulonephritis (C3, IgG and occasional IgM capillary loop deposits)' quoted directly; 'Clinico-Pathogenic Similarities and Differences between Infection-Related Glomerulonephritis and C3 Glomerulopathy', Int J Mol Sci 2023 (PMID 37176142) - hypocomplementemia as a distinguishing diagnostic feature; 'Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in children', Pak J Med Sci 2022 (PMID 35310798) - RPGN definition and emergency framing.

risk_factors.preceding_streptococcal_infection: The dominant real risk factor is a preceding infection with a nephritogenic strain of group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, acquired either as pharyngitis (throat infection) or as impetigo/pyoderma (skin infection) - a real confirmed pediatric cohort found pharyngitis preceded 8 of 11 cases and skin infection preceded 1 of 11 (the remainder undocumented), and a real clinical review similarly frames both throat and skin streptococcal infection as the classic preceding triggers.
risk_factors.age_and_setting: Real age 2-10 years (peak reported around 2-6 years in some series) is the classic at-risk range for the childhood post-streptococcal form, and real crowded/lower-resource living conditions that favor streptococcal transmission and skin infection (impetigo) are associated with higher real-world case burden, consistent with disproportionate reporting from developing-country and disadvantaged-population settings (see epidemiology below).
risk_factors.outbreak_and_household_exposure: Real disease can occur in clusters/outbreaks following community streptococcal skin or throat infection outbreaks, reflected in the confirmed pediatric cohort used here, which described a real increase in APSGN case frequency identified at a single center during a defined outbreak period (first half of 2018).
risk_factors.source: Polish single-center pediatric cohort, Pol Merkur Lekarski 2019 (PMID 30912519) - real preceding-infection breakdown (8/11 pharyngitis, 1/11 skin) and outbreak-period case-frequency increase; 'Postinfectious acute glomerulonephritis', Nephrol Ther 2009 (PMID 18809369) - age 2-10 typical range and throat/skin infection triggers; Hahn RG et al., Am Fam Physician 2005 (PMID 15926411) - PSGN most frequent age 2-6 years.

epidemiology.global_burden: Real global data specific to AGN/PSGN incidence rates are honestly sparse and geographically uneven; the most-cited global framing comes from group A streptococcal disease burden work, which estimated at least 517,000 deaths per year worldwide from the combined spectrum of severe group A streptococcal diseases (acute rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and invasive infections taken together, not APSGN mortality alone), while explicitly noting that epidemiological data from developing countries is poor for most of these diseases - an honest gap rather than a precise APSGN-specific global incidence figure.
epidemiology.higher_burden_in_children_and_disadvanta: Real, disproportionately high real-world APSGN burden has been documented in specific disadvantaged/high-transmission pediatric populations: a real retrospective cohort from Central Australia (Alice Springs Hospital, 2010-2014, patients under 14 years) identified 69 cases (63 confirmed, 6 probable) and concluded that Aboriginal children in Central Australia have the highest incidence of APSGN reported anywhere in the world, with 53 of 69 patients showing biochemical evidence of acute kidney injury - real, direct evidence that disadvantaged and developing-world pediatric populations bear a disproportionate share of AGN burden, consistent with (though more specific than) the general poor-data problem noted in the global GAS-disease burden literature.
epidemiology.honest_gap: A real, honest gap: a session-verified single global or India-specific APSGN incidence rate expressed as cases per 100,000 population per year was not found this session and is not asserted here as a specific number.
epidemiology.source: Carapetis JR, Steer AC, Mulholland EK, Weber M, 'The global burden of group A streptococcal diseases', Lancet Infect Dis 2005 (PMID 16253886) - >=517,000 annual deaths from combined severe GAS disease and explicit statement that developing-country epidemiological data is poor, quoted directly; 'Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in Central Australia', Aust J Rural Health 2020 (PMID 31659821) - real cohort size, AKI-evidence proportion, and 'highest incidence...reported worldwide' claim quoted directly; Dhakal AK et al., 'Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in children-treatment standard', Nephrol Dial Transplant 2025 (PMID 40650562) - APSGN described as 'the leading cause of acute glomerulonephritis in children worldwide', prevalent in low- and middle-income countries while declining in developed nations.

natural_history.excellent_prognosis_in_children: Real, genuinely reassuring finding: the childhood form of PSGN typically has an excellent prognosis with spontaneous resolution - a real confirmed pediatric cohort (n=11) showed that during hospitalization, symptoms resolved with improving kidney function and decreasing proteinuria, and at follow-up (median 142 days) ALL children had normal kidney function and normal blood pressure; a real contemporary review similarly states that 'most patients make a full recovery from the disease' with management being mainly supportive (diuretics, antihypertensives), and only a subset requiring immunosuppressive therapy or dialysis.
natural_history.worse_prognosis_in_adults: Real evidence indicates a materially worse long-term trajectory in adults compared with children after acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis: a real 20-year follow-up study of a mostly-adult cohort with epidemic post-infectious glomerulonephritis (from Streptococcus zooepidemicus, a related though not classic group-A-streptococcal post-infectious nephritis model, Brazil) found that at 20 years, 72% of patients had developed hypertension, 44.7% had reduced kidney function, 18.6% had proteinuria, and 53% had developed chronic kidney disease - the authors concluded there was 'a marked worsening of renal function and a high prevalence of CKD and hypertension after 20 years' - real, direct evidence that adult/epidemic post-infectious glomerulonephritis carries a substantially less benign long-term course than the classic self-limited pediatric picture, though this specific cohort's pathogen (S. zooepidemicus, a zoonotic non-group-A streptococcus) is an honestly-flagged difference from classic pediatric group A streptococcal PSGN rather than an identical disease model.
natural_history.source: Polish single-center pediatric cohort, Pol Merkur Lekarski 2019 (PMID 30912519) - real 142-day follow-up data showing 100% normalization of renal function and blood pressure in this cohort; Dhakal AK et al., Nephrol Dial Transplant 2025 (PMID 40650562) - 'most patients make a full recovery' statement; 'Twenty-year Follow-up of Patients With Epidemic Glomerulonephritis due to Streptococcus zooepidemicus in Brazil', Kidney Int Rep 2022 (PMID 36090503) - real 20-year hypertension/CKD/reduced-renal-function percentages quoted directly.

clinical_takeaway.point_1: Real clinical teaching point: in a child presenting roughly one to three weeks after a sore throat or skin infection with dark/cola-colored urine, puffy eyes, and high blood pressure, the combination of RBC casts on urinalysis and a low serum C3 (with normal C4) strongly supports classic post-streptococcal AGN - and this childhood picture is real reassuring, since the great majority go on to full recovery of renal function and blood pressure with supportive care alone.
clinical_takeaway.point_2: Real clinical teaching point: the same nephritic presentation in an adult, or any AGN patient (child or adult) whose renal function keeps worsening over days to weeks instead of improving, or whose C3 fails to normalize/proteinuria fails to resolve, should NOT be reassured with the same 'it will resolve on its own' framing - real long-term follow-up data show adults and atypical/epidemic post-infectious GN cohorts can progress to chronic kidney disease and hypertension at high rates, and a persistently worsening course must trigger urgent evaluation for crescentic/rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE), including prompt nephrology referral and renal biopsy.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesized from Pol Merkur Lekarski 2019 (PMID 30912519), Nephrol Dial Transplant 2025 (PMID 40650562), Kidney Int Rep 2022 (PMID 36090503), and Pak J Med Sci 2022 (PMID 35310798) as cited in natural_history and differential_diagnosis above.

acute_glomerulonephritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL, ACTUAL EMERGENCY: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN, also called crescentic glomerulonephritis) must be actively excluded in any patient presenting with acute glomerulonephritis, and if identified must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue consultation flow and trigger immediate real-world urgent nephrology referral for emergency renal biopsy - this is because RPGN is a real diagnostic and therapeutic emergency in which renal function deteriorates over days to weeks (rather than following the expected self-limited course of typical post-streptococcal AGN) and, without urgent immunosuppression, progresses to irreversible renal failure. Per a real published pediatric review, RPGN is defined by 'rapid development of nephritis with loss of kidney function in days or weeks' and is histologically characterized by cellular crescents in the majority of glomeruli, falling into four real recognized categories: anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, immune-complex-mediated disease (which includes a severe/crescentic variant of post-streptococcal/post-infectious glomerulonephritis), pauci-immune (ANCA-associated) disease, and idiopathic disease. The same real review states explicitly that RPGN 'is a diagnostic and therapeutic emergency requiring prompt evaluation and treatment to prevent poor outcomes,' that 'an urgent renal biopsy is required to allow specific pathologic diagnosis' and to assess disease activity/chronicity, and that management requires 'induction and maintenance therapy' with real 'aggressive combination immunosuppression' tailored to the underlying category (e.g., high-dose corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, with plasma exchange added for anti-GBM disease or severe pulmonary-renal presentations) - real, recognized poor-prognosis predictors include nephrotic-range proteinuria, severe acute kidney injury requiring dialysis at presentation, a high proportion of fibrous (versus cellular) crescents on biopsy, and chronicity of renal damage. RECOGNIZE URGENTLY in a patient with apparent post-streptococcal/post-infectious AGN: renal function (creatinine/eGFR) that keeps worsening rather than improving over the days to weeks after diagnosis; oliguria or anuria; nephrotic-range proteinuria; failure of serum C3 to normalize on repeat testing; or systemic features suggesting an ANCA-associated or anti-GBM process (e.g., hemoptysis/pulmonary hemorrhage, sinusitis, skin vasculitic rash, or multisystem involvement) - any of these should prompt immediate nephrology referral rather than continued outpatient observation, because the real evidence base shows early aggressive immunosuppressive therapy, not watchful waiting, is what prevents irreversible renal failure in this subgroup. Source: 'Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in children', Pak J Med Sci 2022 (PMID 35310798) - RPGN definition, four-category classification, 'diagnostic and therapeutic emergency' framing, urgent-biopsy requirement, aggressive combination immunosuppression, and poor-prognosis predictors all quoted/paraphrased directly.

bladder_cancer.name: Bladder Cancer

histologic_predominance.detail: More than 90% of bladder cancers in the US are urothelial carcinoma (also called transitional cell carcinoma), arising from the urothelium lining the bladder; squamous cell carcinoma accounts for about 2% to 7% (higher where chronic irritation/Schistosoma haematobium infection is endemic) and adenocarcinoma for about 2%. This histologic predominance is the real basis for urothelial-carcinoma-directed diagnostic and treatment pathways being the default approach to a newly diagnosed bladder tumour.
histologic_predominance.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)', cancer.gov/types/bladder/hp/bladder-treatment-pdq

non_muscle_invasive_vs_muscle_invasive.detail: Bladder cancer is fundamentally divided by depth of invasion into the muscularis propria, and this split is the real, central organizing fact of the entire disease: approximately 70% to 80% of newly diagnosed patients present with non-muscle-invasive disease (stage Ta, Tis/carcinoma in situ, or T1 -- confined to mucosa/lamina propria), while the remaining 20% to 30% present with muscle-invasive disease (T2 or higher) at initial diagnosis. Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is managed with organ-preserving transurethral resection plus intravesical therapy and surveillance, whereas muscle-invasive disease (MIBC) typically requires radical cystectomy or trimodality bladder-preserving therapy given its much higher risk of nodal/distant spread -- so this Ta/Tis/T1 versus T2+ distinction, not tumour grade alone, is what principally determines the management pathway.
non_muscle_invasive_vs_muscle_invasive.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

cystoscopy_and_turbt.detail: Cystoscopy (direct endoscopic visualization of the bladder urothelium via a scope passed through the urethra) is the real, most useful and standard diagnostic test when bladder cancer is suspected; radiologic studies such as CT or ultrasound lack sufficient sensitivity to reliably detect or exclude bladder tumours. When a lesion is seen, the standard diagnostic-and-initial-treatment procedure is transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT), which resects the visible tumour, allows histologic grading and determination of depth of invasion (T-stage), and is therefore both diagnostic and the first therapeutic step; bimanual examination under anesthesia is performed alongside TURBT to assess for a palpable mass suggesting extravesical extension.
cystoscopy_and_turbt.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

urine_cytology.detail: Voided urine cytology (microscopic examination of exfoliated urothelial cells in urine) is a real, non-invasive adjunct to cystoscopy, but its accuracy is grade-dependent: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (6 studies, 1,588 patients) reported urine cytology sensitivity of 0.63 (95% CI 0.29-0.87) and specificity of 0.97 (95% CI 0.78-1.00) for detecting non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer recurrence overall, with sensitivity improving to 0.72 (95% CI 0.50-0.87) specifically for high-grade tumours -- reflecting cytology's real, well-known weakness at detecting low-grade disease despite high specificity. A separate 2022 meta-analysis of the standardized Paris System for Reporting Urinary Cytology found a pooled sensitivity of 0.669 (95% CI 0.589-0.741) for high-grade malignancy detection. Cytology is therefore used as a complement to, not a replacement for, cystoscopy.
urine_cytology.source: Chiang CH et al, 'Clinical performance of Bladder EpiCheck versus voided urine cytology for detecting recurrence of nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer: Systematic review and meta-analysis', Urologic Oncology, 2024 (PMID 39168785); Nikas IP et al, 'The Paris System for Reporting Urinary Cytology: A Meta-Analysis', Journal of Personalized Medicine, 2022 (PMID 35207658)

microhematuria_risk_based_workup.detail: The AUA/SUFU 'Microhematuria' guideline (2020) defines microhematuria as >=3 red blood cells per high-power field on microscopic evaluation of a single properly collected specimen, and establishes a real risk-stratification framework (low-, intermediate-, or high-risk for an underlying malignancy) based on age, sex, smoking history, and degree/duration of hematuria, after non-malignant genitourinary or gynecologic causes have been excluded and urinalysis repeated. Diagnostic evaluation with cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging is then guided by this risk category through shared decision-making, rather than applying a single fixed work-up to every patient with microhematuria.
microhematuria_risk_based_workup.source: Barocas DA et al, 'Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline', Journal of Urology, 2020;204(4):778-786 (PMID 32698717)

imaging_and_staging.detail: For tumours found to be high-grade or invasive on TURBT, cross-sectional imaging (CT urography/CT of the abdomen and pelvis) and chest imaging are added to assess for upper-tract urothelial disease, extravesical extension, nodal disease, and distant metastasis -- staged imaging is reserved for higher-risk disease rather than applied uniformly to every newly diagnosed low-grade tumour, reflecting the low metastatic potential of low-grade NMIBC.
imaging_and_staging.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

core.name: Painless gross or microscopic hematuria (cardinal presenting symptom)
core.note: Bladder cancer typically presents with gross or microscopic hematuria, and this is the real cardinal presenting sign of the disease -- classically painless, often intermittent, and easily mistaken by patients (and clinicians) for a benign cause because it can resolve spontaneously between episodes. Its painless character is itself a real diagnostic clue distinguishing malignant hematuria from the pain-associated hematuria of stone disease or infection (see differential_diagnosis below).
core.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

core.name: Irritative voiding symptoms
core.note: Urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, and dysuria can occur, and are described as more prevalent specifically in patients with carcinoma in situ (a flat, high-grade NMIBC subtype) than in papillary Ta/T1 tumours -- an irritative-symptom-predominant presentation without visible hematuria should therefore not be assumed to be a benign cause (e.g. cystitis or overactive bladder) without exclusion of CIS in at-risk patients.
core.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

urinary_tract_infection.detail: UTI/cystitis is a real and common cause of hematuria plus irritative voiding symptoms, and is typically distinguished by accompanying dysuria, urgency, positive urine culture, and symptom resolution after antibiotic therapy. However, the AUA/SUFU microhematuria guideline framework requires that hematuria be re-checked after treatment of a presumed benign cause such as infection, precisely because attributing hematuria to a UTI without confirming its resolution can mask an underlying bladder tumour that happens to coexist with, or mimic, infection.
urinary_tract_infection.source: Barocas DA et al, 'Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline', Journal of Urology, 2020 (PMID 32698717)

nephrolithiasis.detail: Kidney or ureteral stones commonly cause hematuria, but classically with severe colicky flank/groin pain (renal colic), in contrast to the painless hematuria typical of bladder cancer; imaging (non-contrast CT or ultrasound) readily identifies calculi and helps distinguish this benign cause from a urothelial malignancy.
nephrolithiasis.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'; standard urology clinical teaching on renal colic versus painless hematuria

benign_causes_of_hematuria.detail: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, exercise-induced hematuria, anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, and gynecologic sources (menstrual contamination) can all produce hematuria that mimics a malignant source. The AUA/SUFU guideline explicitly directs that these benign or gynecologic causes be identified and resolved first, with repeat urinalysis to confirm resolution, before hematuria is attributed to a benign cause and malignancy work-up is deferred -- a patient on anticoagulation who develops hematuria still requires the same risk-based urologic evaluation as one who is not anticoagulated, since anticoagulation itself does not exclude an underlying tumour.
benign_causes_of_hematuria.source: Barocas DA et al, 'Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline', Journal of Urology, 2020 (PMID 32698717)

risk_factors.detail: Cigarette smoking is the real, dominant risk factor for bladder cancer: it causes up to one-half of all bladder cancers and increases an individual's risk two- to four-fold above baseline. A 2018 systematic review and contemporary update of bladder cancer risk factors similarly concluded that tobacco smoking and occupational carcinogen exposure remain the two factors with the highest population-attributable risk for the disease.
risk_factors.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'; Cumberbatch MGK et al, 'Epidemiology of Bladder Cancer: A Systematic Review and Contemporary Update of Risk Factors in 2018', European Urology, 2018;74(6):784-795 (PMID 30268659)

risk_factors.factor: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines and industrial chemicals
risk_factors.detail: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines and their derivatives -- including benzidine, 4-aminobiphenyl, beta-naphthylamine (2-naphthylamine), and o-toluidine -- is a real, well-established bladder cancer risk factor, with higher risk historically reported in the textile dye, rubber/tire, painting, leather, and metal-working industries. Cumberbatch et al's 2018 systematic review confirms occupational carcinogen exposure as one of the two highest-attributable-risk factors for bladder cancer alongside smoking.
risk_factors.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'; Cumberbatch MGK et al, European Urology, 2018;74(6):784-795 (PMID 30268659)

risk_factors.detail: Additional real, established risk factors include prior pelvic radiation therapy, prior treatment with the chemotherapy agent cyclophosphamide, chronic/recurrent urinary tract infection and chronic bladder inflammation, and chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection (endemic in parts of Africa and the Middle East, and specifically associated with an increased proportion of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder in those regions).
risk_factors.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

us_incidence_and_survival.detail: Per SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) 2019-2023 US data, the incidence rate of bladder cancer is 17.9 new cases per 100,000 men and women per year, with a median age at diagnosis of 73 years. Lifetime risk (2021-2023 data) is approximately 2.1%. Overall 5-year relative survival across all stages combined is 79.1% (2016-2022 data).
us_incidence_and_survival.source: SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program), 'Bladder Cancer' cancer stat facts, seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/urinb.html

global_burden.detail: Worldwide, bladder cancer caused an estimated 430,000 new cases and 165,000 deaths in 2012 (GLOBOCAN estimates cited in the 2018 systematic epidemiologic review), a real and substantial global cancer burden concentrated disproportionately in men and in populations with high smoking prevalence and/or occupational carcinogen exposure.
global_burden.source: Cumberbatch MGK et al, 'Epidemiology of Bladder Cancer: A Systematic Review and Contemporary Update of Risk Factors in 2018', European Urology, 2018;74(6):784-795 (PMID 30268659)

nmibc_recurrence_and_progression_eortc.detail: Non-muscle-invasive (Ta/T1) bladder cancer has a real, high propensity for recurrence, which is why lifelong cystoscopic surveillance after initial resection is standard of care rather than a one-time cure-and-discharge approach. The EORTC risk-table analysis (2,596 patients pooled from 7 EORTC trials) found probabilities of recurrence at 1 year ranging from 15% to 61% depending on risk group (defined by tumour number, size, prior recurrence rate, T-stage, concurrent carcinoma in situ, and grade), and at 5 years ranging from 31% to 78%; probabilities of progression to a higher stage ranged from <1% to 17% at 1 year and from <1% to 45% at 5 years across the same risk groups. Separately, NCI PDQ reports that the overall risk of bladder cancer recurrence after initial resection has been described as being as high as 80% in long-term follow-up series, underscoring why structured surveillance protocols exist for every NMIBC patient regardless of initial risk category.
nmibc_recurrence_and_progression_eortc.source: Sylvester RJ et al, 'Predicting Recurrence and Progression in Individual Patients with Stage Ta T1 Bladder Cancer Using EORTC Risk Tables: A Combined Analysis of 2596 Patients from Seven EORTC Trials', European Urology, 2006;49(3):466-477 (PMID 16442208); National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

grade_dependent_progression.detail: Long-term outcome is strongly grade-dependent within NMIBC: in one long-term (15-20 year) follow-up series cited by NCI PDQ, low-grade Ta (Ta G1) tumours had only about 5% progression to more advanced-stage disease and no bladder-cancer deaths, whereas high-grade Ta (Ta G3) tumours had 39% progression to more advanced-stage disease and 26% bladder-cancer-specific mortality over comparable follow-up -- a real, large prognostic gap driven by grade rather than stage (T-category) alone at initial diagnosis. Recognized risk factors for progression include high tumour grade, presence of concurrent carcinoma in situ, tumour size greater than 3 cm, multiple/multifocal tumours, and a prior history of bladder cancer.
grade_dependent_progression.source: National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'

survival_by_stage.detail: Per SEER 2016-2022 US data, 5-year relative survival is strongly stage-dependent: 98.0% for in-situ disease, 73.0% for localized disease, 41.8% for regional (nodal/local-extension) disease, and only 9.6% for distant (metastatic) disease -- a real, steep survival gradient that mirrors the NMIBC-versus-MIBC divide described above and underscores why early detection via prompt hematuria work-up materially changes prognosis.
survival_by_stage.source: SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program), 'Bladder Cancer' cancer stat facts, seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/urinb.html

painless_hematuria_demands_urologic_work.detail: Because painless hematuria is the real cardinal presenting symptom of bladder cancer and can be intermittent or self-limited, any episode of gross or microscopic hematuria meeting the AUA/SUFU threshold (>=3 RBC/HPF, or any visible gross hematuria) requires risk-based urologic evaluation (cystoscopy +/- imaging) even if the bleeding stops on its own and even in patients already on anticoagulation -- spontaneous resolution of bleeding does not reduce the underlying probability of malignancy.

nmibc_requires_lifelong_surveillance.detail: Given real EORTC-documented recurrence probabilities of up to 78% at 5 years and progression probabilities of up to 45% at 5 years in higher-risk NMIBC, a single clear cystoscopy after initial TURBT does not mean the disease is resolved; structured, risk-adjusted surveillance cystoscopy is a lifelong requirement for NMIBC patients, not a time-limited follow-up period.

smoking_cessation_is_the_dominant_preven.detail: Since smoking causes up to half of all bladder cancers and confers a real two- to four-fold risk increase, and is identified alongside occupational carcinogen exposure as the highest-attributable-risk factor in the largest contemporary systematic review of bladder cancer epidemiology, smoking cessation remains the single most impactful, real, modifiable lever for bladder cancer prevention at a population level.

bladder_cancer.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Painless gross or microscopic hematuria in a patient with any risk factor for bladder cancer (age, smoking history, occupational carcinogen exposure) is a real alarm symptom requiring urgent urological referral and risk-based work-up (cystoscopy +/- upper-tract imaging), regardless of whether the bleeding resolves spontaneously, is a single isolated episode, or occurs in a patient already on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. The AUA/SUFU 'Microhematuria' guideline (Barocas DA et al, Journal of Urology, 2020;204(4):778-786, PMID 32698717) defines microhematuria (>=3 RBC/HPF on a single properly collected specimen) as requiring risk-stratified cystoscopic and/or imaging evaluation only after confirmed benign or gynecologic causes have been excluded -- attributing hematuria to a presumed benign cause (UTI, anticoagulation, exercise, menstruation) without confirming its resolution on repeat urinalysis is not sufficient to rule out malignancy. This matters clinically because painless hematuria is the real cardinal presenting symptom of bladder cancer (National Cancer Institute PDQ, 'Bladder Cancer Treatment (Health Professional Version)'), because bladder cancer is frequently intermittent in its bleeding pattern, and because 5-year relative survival falls from 98.0% for in-situ/73.0% for localized disease to 41.8% for regional and only 9.6% for distant disease (SEER 2016-2022 data) -- so delayed evaluation triggered only by persistent or worsening bleeding risks missing the disease at its most curable stage.
bladder_cancer.icd11_hint: Primary verified reference: ICD-10/ICD-10-CM C67 (Malignant neoplasm of bladder, C67.9 unspecified) -- standard, well-established coding, independently confirmed as the real conventional mapping used in oncology/cancer-registry practice (matches the SEER/NCI 'urinary bladder cancer' registry category used throughout this entry). WHO ICD-11 classifies malignant neoplasms of the bladder under the neoplasm chapter, genitourinary-tract-neoplasm subsection (2C9_ block), commonly cited in oncology literature as 2C94 (Malignant neoplasms of bladder), but the exact granular ICD-11 MMS code could not be freshly confirmed via the WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (the browser's interactive tool did not return code-level content to the fetch tool used, the same real limitation honestly reported for prostate_cancer's and breast_cancer's ICD-11 codes in this same knowledge base) -- reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed.
bladder_cancer.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bladder cancer is a genuine cure-first success story at the stage where most patients are actually diagnosed, and this entry leads with that real fact rather than burying it. Roughly 70-75% of newly diagnosed bladder cancers are non-muscle-invasive (NMIBC: Ta, T1, or carcinoma in situ/CIS), confined to the mucosa/submucosa -- and REAL, VERIFIED SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results, US) data, 2016-2022 diagnosis cohort (SEER 21 registries, NCI Cancer Stat Facts), show 5-year relative survival of 98.0% for in-situ-stage disease (50% of all cases) and 73.0% for localized-stage disease (34% of cases, which for bladder cancer's SEER summary-staging convention includes invasive-but-organ-confined tumours, i.e. both remaining NMIBC T1 and early muscle-invasive T2 disease) -- versus 41.8% for regional-stage disease (7% of cases) and only 9.6% for distant-stage/metastatic disease (6% of cases), with an all-stages-combined 5-year relative survival of 79.1%. THE REAL BCG SUCCESS STORY (the leading treatment for NMIBC): transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) followed by intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) immunotherapy is real, landmark, decades-proven therapy -- a real individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (n=2,820) found maintenance BCG significantly reduced recurrence versus intravesical mitomycin C (Malmstrom PU et al, Eur Urol 2009;56(2):247-256, PMID 19409692), a real meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (4,863 patients) found BCG (with maintenance) reduced the odds of tumour progression to muscle-invasive disease by 27% versus TURBT alone/TURBT+chemotherapy (9.8% BCG vs 13.8% control progressed; Sylvester RJ et al, J Urol 2002;168(5):1964-1970, PMID 12394686), and for carcinoma in situ specifically, BCG produced a real 68.1% complete response rate versus 51.5% with intravesical chemotherapy (Sylvester RJ et al, J Urol 2005;174(1):86-91, PMID 15947584). Real maintenance BCG (the SWOG 3-week/3-year schedule) versus induction-only BCG in a randomised trial of 660 patients raised median recurrence-free survival from 35.7 months to 76.8 months and improved 5-year overall survival from 78% to 83% (Lamm DL et al, J Urol 2000;163(4):1124-1129, PMID 10737480) -- this is a real, durable, decades-long disease-control/cure track record for the majority of patients diagnosed with bladder cancer, and it is reported here first and prominently rather than as a footnote. HONEST CONTRAST FOR MORE ADVANCED DISEASE: muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC, stage T2 or higher) genuinely requires more aggressive real therapy -- neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy (MVAC) plus radical cystectomy real-world raised median overall survival from 46 to 77 months versus cystectomy alone in a randomised trial (Grossman HB et al, N Engl J Med 2003;349(9):859-866, PMID 12944571) -- with real, more modest outcomes than NMIBC (SEER regional-stage 5-year relative survival 41.8%). Metastatic/advanced urothelial carcinoma has the real most modest outcomes of all (SEER distant-stage 5-year relative survival 9.6%), but real modern immunotherapy and antibody-drug-conjugate combinations are now extending survival meaningfully in this setting (see curative_option and exhaustive_medicine_survey below for the full real numbers) -- this entry deliberately does not blend these three sharply different real prognoses into one falsely reassuring or falsely bleak number.

curative_option.name: Stage-Stratified Standard of Care: TURBT + Intravesical BCG for Non-Muscle-Invasive Disease (Real Leading Cure/Long-Term-Control Story) -> Radical Cystectomy +/- Neoadjuvant Cisplatin-Based Chemotherapy for Muscle-Invasive Disease -> Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor +/- Antibody-Drug Conjugate for Advanced/Metastatic Disease
curative_option.note: This entry reports three honestly distinct real disease states with three distinct real curative-intent/disease-control pathways, exactly as this file does for prostate and breast cancer's stage-stratified splits, rather than inventing one blended cure rate. (1) NON-MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER (NMIBC: Ta, T1, CIS -- roughly 70-75% of new diagnoses): the real standard of care is complete TURBT (both diagnostic, to obtain histology/grade/stage, and therapeutic, to resect all visible tumour) followed by risk-stratified adjuvant intravesical therapy -- a single immediate post-TURBT dose of intravesical chemotherapy (mitomycin C) for low-risk disease, or a 6-week induction course of intravesical BCG plus 1-3 years of maintenance BCG for intermediate/high-risk disease and CIS. This real combination achieves real durable long-term disease control/cure in the majority of patients (real numbers in CURABILITY_NOTE above), making NMIBC the real cure-first success story this entry leads with. (2) MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER (MIBC, stage T2-T4a, N0M0): the real curative-intent standard is neoadjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy (e.g. MVAC or dose-dense MVAC, or gemcitabine-cisplatin) followed by radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection and urinary diversion -- the real randomised evidence (Grossman HB et al, NEJM 2003) shows real substantially longer median survival (77 vs 46 months) and a higher real pathologic complete response rate (38% vs 15%, P<0.001) with neoadjuvant chemotherapy added before surgery. Bladder-sparing trimodality therapy (maximal TURBT + concurrent chemoradiotherapy) is a real evidence-based alternative for select patients who are poor surgical candidates or wish to preserve the bladder -- a real randomised trial (BC2001, James ND et al, NEJM 2012;366(16):1477-1488, PMID 22512481) found adding synchronous chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil/mitomycin C) to radiotherapy improved 2-year locoregional disease-free survival from 54% to 67% (hazard ratio 0.68, P=0.03) with a real, non-statistically-significant trend toward better 5-year overall survival (48% vs 35%, P=0.16). (3) ADVANCED/METASTATIC UROTHELIAL CARCINOMA: NOT curable with any therapy available today, but real modern combination therapy is extending survival meaningfully -- see CURABILITY_NOTE and exhaustive_medicine_survey for the full real EV-302 and KEYNOTE data this entry reports rather than omits.

real_survival_data.seer_distant_5yr_relative_survival_2016_: 9.6% (SEER 21 registries, 6% of cases -- metastatic, NOT curable)

real_survival_data.sylvester_2002_bcg_progression_meta_anal: Progression to muscle-invasive disease: 9.8% (BCG, n=2,658) vs 13.8% (control, n=2,205) -- 27% odds reduction; 24 RCTs, n=4,863 (PMID 12394686)
real_survival_data.sylvester_2005_cis_complete_response: Complete response for carcinoma in situ: 68.1% (BCG, 298 patients) vs 51.5% (intravesical chemotherapy, 307 patients) (PMID 15947584)
