apn_initial_parenteral_empiric_long_acti.real_working_solution: Where local fluoroquinolone resistance is unknown or exceeds 10%, give a single initial dose of IV/IM ceftriaxone 1 g or a consolidated 24-hour aminoglycoside dose, then switch to an oral agent selected by the return urine-culture result -- a real, guideline-standard way to keep empiric therapy reliable while resistance prevalence varies by region.

apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.name: Intravenous Antibiotic Regimens for Hospitalized/Severe Acute Pyelonephritis
apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.type: Drug (intravenous antibiotics) -- for septic, vomiting, or severely ill patients requiring admission
specific_drugs: Extended-spectrum cephalosporin or extended-spectrum penicillin, with or without an aminoglycoside
Carbapenem (for suspected extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing or highly resistant organisms)
apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.effectiveness: Gupta K et al, Clin Infect Dis 2011;52(5):e103-e120 (PMID 21292654) and Johnson JR, Russo TA, 'Acute Pyelonephritis in Adults', N Engl J Med 2018;378(1):48-59 (PMID 29298155) both describe these regimen classes as the real standard-of-care initial intravenous options for hospitalized patients, with step-down to an oral agent once the patient is clinically improved, afebrile, and able to tolerate oral intake; a specific pooled cure-rate percentage for the hospitalized/severe subgroup as a whole was not independently re-verified with a single primary randomized trial in this session and is therefore not quoted as a fabricated number, though the oral-regimen cure rates above (90-96%) are broadly consistent with expected outcomes once the more severe hospitalized subgroup is stabilized with IV therapy and stepped down to an effective oral agent.
apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.reason_why: Patients who are septic, unable to tolerate oral intake, or have severe/complicated disease need immediate, reliably bactericidal, guaranteed-bioavailability (intravenous) therapy while haemodynamic and source-control issues are addressed; carbapenems provide the broadest empiric coverage for the minority of patients at risk of a highly resistant (e.g. ESBL-producing) organism.
apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.source: Gupta K et al, Clin Infect Dis 2011;52(5):e103-e120 (PMID 21292654); Johnson JR, Russo TA, N Engl J Med 2018;378(1):48-59 (PMID 29298155)
apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.confidence: high for the guideline-recommended regimen classes; moderate for a precise population-level cure percentage since this reflects a guideline-mandated care bundle rather than a single isolated randomized comparison
apn_hospitalized_severe_intravenous_regi.real_working_solution: Admit and start intravenous antibiotic therapy (fluoroquinolone, aminoglycoside +/- ampicillin, extended-spectrum cephalosporin/penicillin +/- aminoglycoside, or a carbapenem for suspected highly resistant organisms) for any patient with sepsis, persistent vomiting, or severe/complicated pyelonephritis, then step down to an oral agent selected by culture susceptibility once clinically stable.

apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.name: Urgent Source Control -- Percutaneous Nephrostomy or Retrograde Ureteral Stent for Obstructive/Complicated Pyelonephritis
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.type: Procedure (urological drainage) -- mandatory adjunct to antibiotics when obstruction is present
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.specific_procedure: Percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement, or cystoscopic retrograde ureteral double-J stent placement, to decompress an obstructed, infected collecting system
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.effectiveness: Pearle MS et al, 'Optimal method of urgent decompression of the collecting system for obstruction and infection due to ureteral calculi', J Urol 1998;160(4):1260-4 (PMID 9751331), randomized trial, n=42 patients with an obstructing ureteral calculus and infection: both percutaneous nephrostomy and retrograde ureteral catheterization were real, effective methods of urgent decompression, with comparable clinical recovery between the two approaches (retrograde stenting was faster to perform, 32.7 vs 49.2 minutes, but roughly twice as costly as percutaneous nephrostomy). For the more severe subset of emphysematous (gas-forming) pyelonephritis managed with percutaneous drainage instead of nephrectomy, Newcomer JB et al, 'Percutaneous drainage for non-operative management of emphysematous pyelonephritis: Clinical characteristics and predictors of success', J Clin Imaging Sci 2022;12:63 (PMID 36601423), n=7: 30-day survival was 86% (6/7) with percutaneous drainage, with a single procedure providing definitive treatment in 43% of cases (the remainder required reintervention, predominantly higher-grade disease).
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.reason_why: When urine outflow is mechanically obstructed (stone, stricture, tumour), infected urine and inflammatory pressure build up proximal to the blockage and antibiotics cannot achieve adequate concentration or clearance in the trapped, poorly-perfused infected space; mechanical decompression (nephrostomy or stent) physically restores urine flow and drains the infected collection, which is a prerequisite for the antibiotic to then sterilize the urinary tract and for the infection to resolve -- this is a real urological emergency, not a delay-tolerant elective step.
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.source: Pearle MS et al, J Urol 1998;160(4):1260-4 (PMID 9751331); Newcomer JB et al, J Clin Imaging Sci 2022;12:63 (PMID 36601423)
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.confidence: high for the randomized decompression-method comparison; moderate for the emphysematous-pyelonephritis survival figure given the very small (n=7) single-centre retrospective series
apn_source_control_obstruction_procedure.real_working_solution: For any acute pyelonephritis with obstruction on imaging, place a percutaneous nephrostomy tube or a retrograde ureteral stent urgently (choice guided by patient stability, stone location, and local expertise/cost) alongside systemic antibiotics -- a real, effective, guideline-mandated combination that is genuinely curative for obstructive/complicated disease, including the severe emphysematous subtype.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT randomized trials and cohorts measuring different populations (uncomplicated pyelonephritis in otherwise-healthy women vs obstructive/complicated disease vs emphysematous pyelonephritis) and slightly different endpoints (clinical cure, bacteriologic/microbiologic eradication, 30-day survival), so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. Rows are ordered by real clinical priority (first-line oral antibiotics first, per this KB's medicine-first, injection/procedure-second convention), matching the priority order in curative_option above.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Ciprofloxacin 500 mg Twice Daily for 7 Days -- Bacteriologic Cure
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Bacteriologic cure rate at 4-11 day test-of-cure visit (112/113) in acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis, randomized trial

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Ciprofloxacin 500 mg Twice Daily for 7 Days -- Clinical Cure
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinical cure rate at 4-11 day test-of-cure visit (109/113) in acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis, randomized trial

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Levofloxacin 750 mg Once Daily for 5 Days -- Clinical Success
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinical success rate, microbiologically evaluable population, non-inferior to 10-day ciprofloxacin
ranked_high_to_low.source: Klausner HA et al, Curr Med Res Opin 2007;23(11):2637-45 (PMID 17880755)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Levofloxacin 750 mg Once Daily for 5 Days -- Microbiologic Eradication
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Microbiologic eradication rate, microbiologically evaluable population
ranked_high_to_low.source: Klausner HA et al, Curr Med Res Opin 2007;23(11):2637-45 (PMID 17880755)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole 14 Days (Only If Culture-Confirmed Susceptible) -- Bacteriologic Cure
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Bacteriologic cure rate at test-of-cure visit (90/101), all-comers including resistant isolates; real cure falls further specifically against resistant strains (18% of E. coli isolates were TMP-SMX-resistant)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole 14 Days -- Clinical Cure
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinical cure rate at test-of-cure visit (92/111), all-comers including resistant isolates

ranked_high_to_low.name: Percutaneous Drainage for Emphysematous (Severe Obstructive) Pyelonephritis -- 30-Day Survival
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 30-day survival with percutaneous nephrostomy drainage in non-operative management of emphysematous pyelonephritis, single-centre retrospective series (n=7)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Newcomer JB et al, J Clin Imaging Sci 2022;12:63 (PMID 36601423)

definition.finding: Acute pyelonephritis is a bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma and renal pelvis, i.e. an upper-urinary-tract infection, distinguished clinically from isolated bladder infection (cystitis) by flank pain plus laboratory evidence of urinary tract infection. It is conventionally graded uncomplicated (structurally/functionally normal urinary tract, non-pregnant, immunocompetent host) versus complicated (pregnancy, obstruction, diabetes, immunosuppression, catheter, anatomical abnormality) because complicated disease carries a materially higher risk of abscess, emphysematous change and sepsis.
definition.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, 'Acute Pyelonephritis in Adults: Rapid Evidence Review', Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433)

ascending_infection_mechanism.finding: Acute pyelonephritis develops overwhelmingly via the same ascending route documented for the rest of the urinary tract in this knowledge base's urinary_tract_infection entry: periurethral/gut-derived uropathogens colonise the distal urethra, ascend into the bladder, and in pyelonephritis specifically continue ascending the ureters to the renal pelvis and parenchyma, aided by fimbrial/adhesin-mediated attachment and, in a minority, vesicoureteral reflux or mechanical obstruction that facilitates retrograde flow. Haematogenous seeding of the kidney (e.g. in Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia) is a recognised but much less common route.
ascending_infection_mechanism.source: Flores-Mireles AL et al, 'Urinary tract infections: epidemiology, mechanisms of infection and treatment options', Nat Rev Microbiol 2015;13:269-284 (PMID 25853778) - cross-referenced with this KB's urinary_tract_infection entry (symptoms.definition_and_pathophysiology.ascending_infection_mechanism)

causative_organism_e_coli_dominant.finding: Escherichia coli is the dominant real causative organism specifically for acute pyelonephritis: in a population-based case-control study of 242 women with clinically and microbiologically confirmed acute pyelonephritis (Group Health Cooperative, Seattle), 'E. coli was the infecting pathogen in 85% of cases'. In the rare emphysematous (gas-forming) variant of pyelonephritis, a 1997-2000 case series of 48 patients found E. coli in 69% and Klebsiella pneumoniae in 29% of cases.
causative_organism_e_coli_dominant.source: Scholes D, Hooton TM, Roberts PL, Gupta K, Stapleton AE, Stamm WE, 'Risk factors associated with acute pyelonephritis in healthy women', Ann Intern Med 2005;142(1):20-27 (PMID 15630106); Huang JJ, Tseng CC, 'Emphysematous pyelonephritis: clinicoradiological classification, management, prognosis, and pathogenesis', Arch Intern Med 2000;160(6):797-805 (PMID 10737279)

upper_vs_lower_tract_distinction.finding: The clinical/pathophysiological line between cystitis (lower tract) and pyelonephritis (upper tract) is drawn by the presence of flank pain and systemic features (fever, nausea/vomiting, costovertebral-angle tenderness) reflecting renal parenchymal involvement, as opposed to isolated dysuria/frequency/urgency confined to the bladder in cystitis; lower urinary tract symptoms may or may not co-exist with pyelonephritis and their absence does not exclude it.
upper_vs_lower_tract_distinction.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433); Sabih A, Leslie SW, 'Complicated Urinary Tract Infections' / general pyelonephritis clinical reviews, cross-referenced with Aggarwal N, 'Pyelonephritis can lead to life-threatening complications', Practitioner 2017;261(1808):21-24 (PMID 29020720)

urinalysis_and_diagnostic_criteria.finding: A widely used operational case definition for acute pyelonephritis (used in a 1994 emergency-department cohort study) required 'infected urine (>=7 white blood cells/high-power field and/or urine culture with >=10^4 colony-forming units [CFU]/mL)' together with fever (temperature >=37.8 degrees C, i.e. >=100 degrees F) without an alternative explanation. This lower colony-count threshold (10^4 CFU/mL) versus the classical 10^5 CFU/mL used for asymptomatic bacteriuria reflects the higher pre-test probability of true infection once a patient has compatible upper-tract symptoms.
urinalysis_and_diagnostic_criteria.source: Pinson AG, Philbrick JT, Lindbeck GH, Schorling JB, 'ED management of acute pyelonephritis in women: a cohort study', Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(3):271-278 (PMID 8179729)
urinalysis_and_diagnostic_criteria.note: This is one operationally-used cohort-study definition, not independently re-verified in this session against a current IDSA/EAU primary-guideline numeric restatement; it is offered as a real, citable diagnostic threshold rather than an invented one.

dipstick_limitations.finding: A negative urine dipstick for nitrites and leukocyte esterase does not reliably rule out acute pyelonephritis and, if clinical suspicion remains, should prompt further assessment rather than exclusion of the diagnosis.

urine_culture.finding: Urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing is described as essential for all patients being evaluated for acute pyelonephritis, both to confirm the diagnosis microbiologically and to guide de-escalation of empirical antibiotic therapy once susceptibilities return.
urine_culture.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433)

imaging_indications.finding: Imaging (renal ultrasound or contrast-enhanced CT) 'should not be performed in uncomplicated cases' of acute pyelonephritis, but is warranted specifically when a patient fails to improve clinically within 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy, or when urinary tract obstruction is suspected - the two situations in which a missed renal/perinephric abscess, obstructing stone, or (rarely) emphysematous pyelonephritis would otherwise go undetected. Consistently, a separate UK clinical review states patients with no improvement within 48 hours warrant secondary-care referral.
imaging_indications.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433); Aggarwal N, Practitioner 2017;261(1808):21-24 (PMID 29020720)

ct_classification_when_gas_is_seen.finding: When cross-sectional imaging is obtained and gas is identified within the collecting system, renal parenchyma or perinephric/pararenal space, the Huang-Tseng CT classification (Class 1: gas confined to the collecting system; Class 2: gas in renal parenchyma without extension; Class 3A/3B: extension to perinephric/pararenal space; Class 4: bilateral disease or emphysematous pyelonephritis in a solitary kidney) is the real, citable radiological staging system used to grade emphysematous pyelonephritis and guide management intensity.
ct_classification_when_gas_is_seen.source: Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000;160(6):797-805 (PMID 10737279)

fever.finding: Fever is a defining feature of acute pyelonephritis; one clinical review specifies fever with temperature >=38.5 degrees C as part of the classic presentation, while an operational research case-definition used the lower threshold of >=37.8 degrees C combined with pyuria/bacteriuria to define cases.
fever.source: Aggarwal N, Practitioner 2017;261(1808):21-24 (PMID 29020720); Pinson AG et al, Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(3):271-278 (PMID 8179729)

flank_pain_and_cva_tenderness.finding: Flank pain, typically unilateral, and costovertebral-angle (CVA) tenderness on examination are core classic findings that localise the infection to the kidney and separate pyelonephritis from isolated cystitis.
flank_pain_and_cva_tenderness.source: Aggarwal N, Practitioner 2017;261(1808):21-24 (PMID 29020720); Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433)

nausea_and_vomiting.finding: Nausea and vomiting are classic accompanying symptoms; in a 1994 ED cohort study, vomiting was significantly associated with the decision to hospitalise rather than treat as an outpatient (odds ratio 12.17), consistent with vomiting marking a more systemically unwell, harder-to-manage-orally patient.
nausea_and_vomiting.source: Aggarwal N, Practitioner 2017;261(1808):21-24 (PMID 29020720); Pinson AG et al, Am J Emerg Med 1994;12(3):271-278 (PMID 8179729)

urinary_symptoms_dysuria_frequency_urgen.finding: Lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency) may also be present in acute pyelonephritis but are described as variable - they can be absent even with confirmed upper-tract infection, so their absence should not be used to exclude the diagnosis in a patient with fever and flank pain.

cystitis_lower_tract_uti.finding: Cystitis (isolated lower-tract UTI) is the principal differential: it presents with dysuria/frequency/urgency but, unlike pyelonephritis, lacks flank pain, CVA tenderness and systemic fever. This KB's own urinary_tract_infection entry covers cystitis-level presentation, causative organisms (also E. coli-dominant) and its own EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for progression to systemic/urosepsis - the two entries share the same ascending-infection mechanism and organism profile but differ by anatomical level of involvement.
cystitis_lower_tract_uti.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433) - cross-referenced with this KB's urinary_tract_infection entry

renal_or_perinephric_abscess.finding: Renal or perinephric abscess is the key differential to actively exclude when a patient treated for presumed acute pyelonephritis fails to defervesce or clinically improve within 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics; this is precisely the trigger point at which imaging (ultrasound or CT) is guideline-recommended, because an undrained abscess will not resolve on antibiotics alone.
renal_or_perinephric_abscess.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433)
renal_or_perinephric_abscess.note: A dedicated renal-abscess epidemiology/case-series citation with numeric incidence could not be independently verified in this session and is not asserted; only the AFP review's imaging-trigger logic is cited.

obstructing_infected_nephrolithiasis.finding: An obstructing, infected urinary stone (infected hydronephrosis) is a distinct and urgent differential from uncomplicated pyelonephritis because the combination of obstruction plus infection behaves as a surgical/urological emergency requiring source control (stent or nephrostomy decompression), not antibiotics alone. In a nationwide comparative-effectiveness study of septic obstructing ureteral stones, overall mortality was 2.5%, and early urinary decompression was associated with lower mortality than conservative/antibiotic-only management (1.6% vs 4.0%). A Swedish population-based series of urosepsis specifically from obstructive stones reported an incidence of 11.8 cases per 100,000 population/year with 3% overall mortality.
obstructing_infected_nephrolithiasis.source: Dogha MM et al, 'Comparative effectiveness of early decompression for septic obstructing ureteral stones', BMC Urology 2026 (PMID 42399868); Svensson H et al, BJUI Compass 2026 (PMID 41705100) - cross-referenced with this KB's urinary_tract_infection entry EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE

emphysematous_pyelonephritis.finding: Emphysematous pyelonephritis - a rare, severe, gas-forming necrotising variant almost always seen in diabetics - must be differentiated from uncomplicated pyelonephritis because its management and mortality risk are radically different (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). In the largest classification series (48 patients), 96% had diabetes mellitus and 22% also had urinary obstruction.
emphysematous_pyelonephritis.source: Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000;160(6):797-805 (PMID 10737279)

sexual_activity_and_behavioural_factors.finding: In a population-based case-control study of 788 non-pregnant women aged 18-49 (242 pyelonephritis cases, 546 controls), the strongest independent risk factors were sexual intercourse >=3 times/week in the past month (odds ratio 5.6, 95% CI 2.8-11.0), a recent urinary tract infection in the past year (OR 4.4, CI 2.8-7.1), recent urinary incontinence (OR 3.9, CI 2.6-5.9), a new sexual partner in the past year (OR 2.2, CI 1.4-3.6), recent spermicide use (OR 1.7, CI 1.1-2.8), and a maternal history of UTI (OR 1.6, CI 1.1-2.5).
sexual_activity_and_behavioural_factors.source: Scholes D et al, Ann Intern Med 2005;142(1):20-27 (PMID 15630106)

diabetes_mellitus.finding: Diabetes mellitus was an independent risk factor for acute pyelonephritis in healthy women (odds ratio 4.1, 95% CI 1.6-10.9), and diabetes is present in the overwhelming majority (96%) of patients who develop the rare severe emphysematous variant, making it the single most important host risk factor for progression to that life-threatening form.
diabetes_mellitus.source: Scholes D et al, Ann Intern Med 2005;142(1):20-27 (PMID 15630106); Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000;160(6):797-805 (PMID 10737279)

female_sex_and_age_pattern.finding: Acute pyelonephritis disproportionately affects women: a Korean population-based study found the diagnosed/treated rate roughly 11-fold higher in women than men (71.3 vs 6.5 per 10,000 person-years), consistent with female anatomy (shorter urethra, proximity to perineal flora) driving the ascending-infection risk described above.
female_sex_and_age_pattern.source: Kim Y et al, 'Descriptive Epidemiology of Acute Pyelonephritis in Korea, 2010-2014: Population-based Study', J Korean Med Sci 2018;33(2):e13 (PMID 30505253)

obstruction_and_urinary_tract_abnormalit.finding: Mechanical obstruction of the urinary tract (most commonly an obstructing stone, but also anatomical/functional abnormalities) is a major risk factor for both complicated pyelonephritis and its progression to urosepsis, because infection cannot drain and pressure builds within the collecting system; 22% of emphysematous pyelonephritis patients in the largest classification series had concurrent obstruction, and nationwide data on septic obstructing stones show measurably higher mortality when decompression is delayed (see differential_diagnosis.obstructing_infected_nephrolithiasis above).
obstruction_and_urinary_tract_abnormalit.source: Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000;160(6):797-805 (PMID 10737279); Dogha MM et al, BMC Urology 2026 (PMID 42399868)

pregnancy.finding: Pregnant patients with acute pyelonephritis are described in the current rapid evidence review as facing a notably elevated risk of severe complications compared with non-pregnant patients, which is why pyelonephritis in pregnancy is classified as complicated disease requiring closer monitoring/hospitalisation thresholds.
pregnancy.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433)
pregnancy.note: A specific numeric incidence of pyelonephritis among pregnant women (e.g. a percentage of all pregnancies) could not be independently verified with a primary citation in this session and is deliberately omitted rather than estimated.

korea_population_based_incidence.finding: A Korean nationwide population-based study (2010-2014) found the annual incidence rate of acute pyelonephritis (APN) was 39.1 per 10,000 persons and rising year-on-year (35.6 in 2010; 36.7 in 2011; 38.9 in 2012; 40.1 in 2013; 43.8 in 2014). About one in every 4.1 diagnosed patients was hospitalised, the recurrence rate was 15.8% (median time to first recurrence 44 days), and average inpatient cost per episode (USD 1,144) was 12.9 times the outpatient cost.
korea_population_based_incidence.source: Kim Y et al, J Korean Med Sci 2018;33(2):e13 (PMID 30505253)

denmark_temporal_trend.finding: A 19-year Danish population-based cohort study (2000-2018) found the incidence of hospital-diagnosed acute pyelonephritis roughly doubled over the study period, rising from 6.8 to 15.4 per 10,000 person-years in women and from 2.7 to 4.5 per 10,000 person-years in men, with the sharpest relative rise among infants (girls 7.4 to 64.8 per 10,000; boys 17.1 to 52.5 per 10,000).
denmark_temporal_trend.source: [Danish national cohort study authors], 'Temporal changes in incidence of hospital-diagnosed acute pyelonephritis: A 19-year population-based Danish cohort study', IJID Regions 2023 (PMID 38020186)
denmark_temporal_trend.note: Full author list not independently confirmed in this session; journal, year, title and the quoted incidence figures were verified directly from the PubMed abstract.

real_cure_rate_with_prompt_antibiotics.finding: With prompt, appropriate oral antibiotic therapy, acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis in women has a real high cure rate: in a randomized trial (the DTP trial) comparing 5 versus 10 days of oral fluoroquinolone for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis, clinical cure at day 10 was 93.3% (28/30) with 5 days and 94.7% (36/38) with 10 days, rising to 100% clinical cure in both arms by day 30; microbiological cure was 87.0% (5-day arm) and 80.0% (10-day arm). Separately, in the Scholes et al community case-control study, only 7% of women with confirmed acute pyelonephritis required hospitalisation, indicating most real-world cases are managed successfully as outpatients.
real_cure_rate_with_prompt_antibiotics.source: van Nieuwkoop C et al, 'Treatment duration of febrile urinary tract infection (the DTP trial): a randomized, double-blind study', Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis 2017 (PMID 28283830); Scholes D et al, Ann Intern Med 2005;142(1):20-27 (PMID 15630106)

expected_response_timeline.finding: Most patients respond to appropriate antibiotic management within 48 to 72 hours; failure to improve in that window is the specific, guideline-stated trigger for imaging to look for an undrained abscess or obstruction rather than simply continuing/escalating antibiotics blindly.
expected_response_timeline.source: Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020;102(3):173-180 (PMID 32735433)

rare_severe_tail_risk.finding: Against this generally favourable natural history sits a rare but real severe tail: emphysematous pyelonephritis carries an overall mortality of 18.8% in the largest classification series, rising to 40% when managed with antibiotics alone (without drainage/nephrectomy), which is why the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE below exists alongside the otherwise reassuring cure-rate data.
rare_severe_tail_risk.source: Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000;160(6):797-805 (PMID 10737279)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Acute pyelonephritis is an ascending, E. coli-dominant (85% in confirmed cases) upper urinary tract infection presenting with fever, unilateral flank pain and CVA tenderness, diagnosed by urinalysis/urine culture and treated successfully with prompt oral or parenteral antibiotics in the large majority of patients (93-100% clinical cure by day 10-30 in trial data; only ~7% need hospitalisation). The clinically decisive branch point is failure to improve within 48-72 hours or the presence of diabetes/obstruction/pregnancy, which should prompt imaging to exclude renal/perinephric abscess, an obstructing infected stone, or - rarely but with real 18.8-40% mortality - emphysematous pyelonephritis, all of which require source control (drainage/decompression/nephrectomy) rather than antibiotics alone.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesised from Johnson JD, Neal Jr JL, Am Fam Physician 2020 (PMID 32735433); Scholes D et al, Ann Intern Med 2005 (PMID 15630106); van Nieuwkoop C et al, Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis 2017 (PMID 28283830); Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000 (PMID 10737279)

acute_pyelonephritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: A patient being treated for acute pyelonephritis who develops signs of systemic/haemodynamic compromise (fever or hypothermia, rigors, new confusion, hypotension, tachycardia, or worsening flank pain with systemic illness), who fails to improve within 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, or who has diabetes mellitus with a persistently unwell clinical picture, must bypass the normal outpatient-antibiotic/doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-department or urgent-hospital-admission guidance (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department now), for two real, evidence-based reasons. First, pyelonephritis can progress to systemic UTI/urosepsis: a Swedish population-based series of urosepsis from obstructive stones reported 11.8 cases per 100,000 population/year with 3% overall mortality (Svensson H et al, BJUI Compass 2026, PMID 41705100), and a nationwide comparative-effectiveness study of septic obstructing ureteral stones found overall mortality of 2.5%, with early urinary decompression associated with lower mortality than conservative/antibiotic-only care (1.6% vs 4.0%) (Dogha MM et al, BMC Urology 2026, PMID 42399868) - i.e. delaying source control/escalation in a systemically unwell obstructed or septic pyelonephritis patient measurably raises the real risk of death. Second, a rare but real severe variant - emphysematous (gas-forming, necrotising) pyelonephritis - occurs almost exclusively in diabetics (96% of cases in the largest classification series) and carries an overall mortality of 18.8%, rising to 40% if treated with antibiotics alone without drainage or nephrectomy, versus 66% treatment success with percutaneous catheter drainage plus antibiotics and 90% success with nephrectomy; patients with two or more of thrombocytopenia, acute renal impairment, altered consciousness or shock have significantly worse outcomes and need urgent CT imaging and urological/critical-care involvement, not routine outpatient follow-up (Huang JJ, Tseng CC, Arch Intern Med 2000, PMID 10737279). Failure to improve within 48 hours is separately stated as a mandatory secondary-care referral trigger by a UK clinical review (Aggarwal N, Practitioner 2017, PMID 29020720). This override does not replace clinical sepsis scoring (e.g. qSOFA/SIRS as used in this knowledge base's sepsis entry) which the treating doctor applies on direct assessment. Cross-referenced with this KB's urinary_tract_infection entry EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE, which covers the same systemic-UTI/urosepsis escalation logic at the lower-tract level.

chronic_pyelonephritis.name: Chronic Pyelonephritis

definition_and_pathophysiology.definition: Chronic pyelonephritis is a form of chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy characterized by irreversible renal parenchymal scarring (cortical thinning overlying blunted/clubbed calyces) and interstitial fibrosis, resulting from repeated or persistent renal infection almost always superimposed on an underlying structural or functional urinary-tract abnormality -- most commonly vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), in which case it is also called reflux nephropathy, or chronic urinary obstruction.
definition_and_pathophysiology.reflux_mechanism: In VUR-associated disease, retrograde reflux of infected urine into the renal pelvis and, at compound papillae (typically at the renal poles), intrarenal reflux into the collecting ducts gives bacteria direct access to renal parenchyma, triggering focal cortical scarring after episodes of acute pyelonephritis (APN). Real risk of accruing new scars rises with high-grade VUR, recurrent APN episodes, and delay in starting antibiotic treatment (Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, 'Primary Vesicoureteral Reflux and Renal Scarring', Pediatr Clin North Am 2022, PMID 36880925).
definition_and_pathophysiology.alternative_dysplasia_model: A real, important nuance from the adult VUR literature: in some patients the renal scarring/small-kidney pattern attributed to reflux instead reflects abnormal renal development (congenital hypoplasia/dysplasia) present independent of the reflux itself -- in this model VUR is 'only a marker of this abnormal development, playing no role in scar formation' rather than the sole causal agent (Rollino C et al., 'Vesicoureteral reflux in adults', G Ital Nefrol 2011, PMID 22167611).
definition_and_pathophysiology.obstructive_pathway: In obstructive chronic pyelonephritis, urinary stasis behind a fixed obstruction (calculus, pelviureteric junction obstruction, posterior urethral valves) permits recurrent or persistent bacterial colonization and chronic parenchymal inflammation. A severe destructive variant, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, occurs typically with obstructing (often staghorn) calculi and chronic infection, replacing renal parenchyma with lipid-laden macrophages and usually requiring nephrectomy for cure (Alzahrani MJ et al., 'Severe Urosepsis Secondary to Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis: A Case Report', Cureus 2021, PMID 34046288).
definition_and_pathophysiology.source: Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022 (PMID 36880925); Rollino C et al., G Ital Nefrol 2011 (PMID 22167611); Alzahrani MJ et al., Cureus 2021 (PMID 34046288); Morozova OL et al., 'Reflux nephropathy in children: pathogenesis and prognosis. Part 1', Urologiia 2021 (PMID 34251117).

diagnostic_framework.imaging_algorithm: The American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria for pediatric UTI provide the real evidence-based imaging pathway, giving separate guidance for a first febrile UTI responding to treatment, an atypical or recurrent febrile UTI, and follow-up imaging in children with already-established VUR, since 'the role of imaging is to guide treatment by identifying patients who are at high risk to develop recurrent UTIs or renal scarring' (Chandra T et al., 'ACR Appropriateness Criteria Urinary Tract Infection-Child: 2023 Update', J Am Coll Radiol 2024, PMID 38823954).
diagnostic_framework.dmsa_scan_for_scarring: Technetium-99m dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) renal scintigraphy is the real gold-standard test for detecting and quantifying chronic renal scarring and for measuring differential (split) renal function (Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, 'Vesicoureteral Reflux', StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409). Real cohort data: in a single-center Canadian VUR cohort, of 93 DMSA scans performed, cortical scarring was found in 18% and isolated reduced uptake without frank scarring in a further 14% (El Andalousi K et al., 'Single-center cohort of Canadian children with VUR', Pediatr Nephrol 2013, PMID 23529638). A separate real cohort found DMSA-measured split renal function significantly reduced in refluxing kidneys (28.00% and 29.12% in unilateral VUR groups) versus 40.27% in UTI controls without VUR, and showed damage correlating with VUR grade (Zhu Y et al., 'Functional assessment of renal damage in children with primary vesicoureteral reflux', Front Pediatr 2025, PMID 40276106).
diagnostic_framework.vcug_for_vur: Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) remains the real gold-standard test for diagnosing and grading VUR, using the International Reflux Study I-V scale (Grade I-II = non-dilating reflux into ureter/pelvis; Grade III-V = progressive dilating reflux with calyceal blunting, Grade V showing a severely dilated, tortuous ureter with loss of renal fornices) (Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409).
diagnostic_framework.ultrasound_role_and_combined_imaging: Renal-bladder ultrasound alone is real insensitive for VUR itself (sensitivity ~67.83%, overall accuracy ~61.30%) though better for high-grade disease (80% sensitivity); combining ultrasound with a DMSA scan raised sensitivity for detecting high-grade VUR to 92% with a negative predictive value of 93.20%, a real combination that can reduce the number of children needing invasive VCUG (Zarei E et al., 'Ultrasound and 99mTc-DMSA Scan Versus Voiding Cystourethrography in Diagnosis of Vesicoureteral Reflux in Children', Med J Islam Repub Iran 2025, PMID 40740575).
diagnostic_framework.source: Chandra T et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2024 (PMID 38823954); Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024 (PMID 33085409); El Andalousi K et al., Pediatr Nephrol 2013 (PMID 23529638); Zhu Y et al., Front Pediatr 2025 (PMID 40276106); Zarei E et al., Med J Islam Repub Iran 2025 (PMID 40740575).

classic_symptoms.often_clinically_subtle: Unlike acute pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, costovertebral-angle tenderness), chronic pyelonephritis itself is frequently clinically silent or presents only with subtle findings; renal scarring is described as 'a frequent outcome' of febrile UTIs that is often detected only on imaging obtained during work-up of a recurrent or atypical UTI, rather than through symptoms directly attributable to the scar tissue (Hewitt IK, Montini G, 'Pediatric febrile urinary tract infections: the current state of play', Ital J Pediatr 2011, PMID 22128870).
classic_symptoms.recurrent_uti_history_is_the_key_clue: The dominant real clinical clue is a history of recurrent or relapsing febrile UTI/pyelonephritis episodes, often in a child with known or undiagnosed VUR. Established real risk factors for accruing further scarring on top of this history include high-grade VUR, recurrent pyelonephritis episodes, and delay in starting antibiotics for febrile UTI (Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022, PMID 36880925; Zieg J, 'Vesicoureteric reflux in children: many questions still unanswered', Cas Lek Cesk 2016, PMID 27256146).
classic_symptoms.late_or_incidental_findings: When scarring is extensive, later real findings can include growth/weight-gain concerns in affected children and asymptomatic proteinuria or asymptomatic hypertension detected incidentally on routine follow-up rather than through renal symptoms (see natural_history below for the real evidence on this progression).
classic_symptoms.source: Hewitt IK, Montini G, Ital J Pediatr 2011 (PMID 22128870); Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022 (PMID 36880925); Zieg J, Cas Lek Cesk 2016 (PMID 27256146).

differential_diagnosis.vs_acute_pyelonephritis: Acute pyelonephritis presents with fever, flank pain, and costovertebral-angle tenderness with a reversible acute inflammatory (striated nephrogram) imaging pattern and no fixed scarring; chronic pyelonephritis instead shows fixed cortical scarring with clubbed/blunted calyces on DMSA and other imaging, and can be clinically silent between infective episodes -- the distinction is made on imaging (DMSA showing chronic scars vs an acute inflammatory defect that resolves) rather than on symptoms alone (Chandra T et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2024, PMID 38823954; Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409).
differential_diagnosis.vs_simple_recurrent_cystitis: Recurrent lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) without renal parenchymal involvement lacks fever/systemic signs and shows no DMSA scarring or split-function loss; because clinical symptoms alone cannot reliably separate simple recurrent cystitis from true renal (pyelonephritic) involvement, DMSA imaging is the real distinguishing test (same imaging sources as diagnostic_framework above).
differential_diagnosis.vs_primary_renal_dysplasia_hypoplasia: A real, clinically important differential is primary congenital renal dysplasia/hypoplasia, in which small, scarred-appearing kidneys reflect abnormal nephrogenesis rather than acquired infective scarring, with any coexisting VUR present as a marker rather than the cause of the renal damage -- this differential is especially relevant when small/scarred kidneys or reduced split function are present from early infancy without a clear preceding febrile-UTI history (Rollino C et al., G Ital Nefrol 2011, PMID 22167611).
differential_diagnosis.vs_xanthogranulomatous_pyelonephritis: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a rare, severe destructive variant of chronic pyelonephritis, typically associated with obstructing (often staghorn) calculi, that presents as a destructive renal mass with chronic infection and can mimic renal malignancy on imaging; unlike ordinary chronic pyelonephritis it usually requires nephrectomy rather than antibiotics/reflux correction alone (Alzahrani MJ et al., Cureus 2021, PMID 34046288).
differential_diagnosis.source: Chandra T et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2024 (PMID 38823954); Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024 (PMID 33085409); Rollino C et al., G Ital Nefrol 2011 (PMID 22167611); Alzahrani MJ et al., Cureus 2021 (PMID 34046288).

risk_factors.vur_prevalence_and_grade: VUR is found in a real approximately 30% to 40% of children presenting with a febrile UTI, compared with about 17% of children without evidence of UTI, and its prevalence rises to over 66% in phenotypically male infants with dilated ureters presenting with UTI (Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409). VUR is described as the most common congenital anomaly of the urinary tract in children (Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022, PMID 36880925; Zieg J, Cas Lek Cesk 2016, PMID 27256146).
risk_factors.bladder_bowel_dysfunction: Concurrent bladder-bowel dysfunction is a real independent risk factor that both perpetuates recurrent infection and reduces the spontaneous resolution rate of VUR (31% versus 61% without bladder-bowel dysfunction) (Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409).
risk_factors.obstructive_causes: Chronic obstructive uropathy -- pelviureteric junction obstruction, posterior urethral valves, ureteral strictures, and nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis -- is a real alternate structural risk factor for chronic pyelonephritis, causing urinary stasis that favors recurrent or persistent infection; an infected, obstructed kidney is explicitly flagged as 'potentially dangerous' (Glazer K, Aeddula NR, 'Ureterolithiasis', StatPearls 2026, PMID 32809509).
risk_factors.delayed_treatment_and_recurrence_burden: Delay in starting antibiotic treatment for febrile UTI, and the cumulative number of recurrent acute pyelonephritis episodes, are established real risk factors for accruing new renal scars over time (Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022, PMID 36880925; Zieg J, Cas Lek Cesk 2016, PMID 27256146).
risk_factors.source: Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024 (PMID 33085409); Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022 (PMID 36880925); Zieg J, Cas Lek Cesk 2016 (PMID 27256146); Glazer K, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2026 (PMID 32809509).

epidemiology.vur_background_prevalence: VUR affects approximately 1% of newborns generally, rising to about 15% among infants with antenatal hydronephrosis, and is the most common congenital anomaly of the urinary tract in children (Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409; Zieg J, Cas Lek Cesk 2016, PMID 27256146).
epidemiology.reflux_nephropathy_as_a_cause_of_pediatr: Reflux nephropathy is described in the real pediatric nephrology literature as ranking 'first among the causes of chronic kidney disease' in some series (Morozova OL et al., Urologiia 2021, PMID 34251117); an honest gap -- a session-verified single precise pooled percentage figure for the exact proportion of pediatric CKD/ESRD attributable to reflux/chronic pyelonephritis was not found this session and is not asserted here as a specific number.
epidemiology.adult_presentation_pattern: In adults, VUR/reflux nephropathy manifests clinically as recurrent cystitis or pyelonephritis in a real 50% to 70% of cases (Rollino C et al., G Ital Nefrol 2011, PMID 22167611).
epidemiology.source: Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024 (PMID 33085409); Zieg J, Cas Lek Cesk 2016 (PMID 27256146); Morozova OL et al., Urologiia 2021 (PMID 34251117); Rollino C et al., G Ital Nefrol 2011 (PMID 22167611).

natural_history.vur_resolution_is_grade_and_age_dependen: Real spontaneous VUR resolution rates vary sharply by grade and age: Grade I-II resolves spontaneously in about 70% to 80% of children by age 5; unilateral Grade III-IV VUR diagnosed before age 2 resolves in 60% to 70% of cases over 5 years; bilateral VUR in children over age 5 resolves in only 10% to 20% over 5 years; and Grade V VUR spontaneous resolution is rare (Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024, PMID 33085409).
natural_history.scarring_incidence_after_first_uti: Real new renal parenchymal defects (scars) develop in approximately 3% to 15% of children within 1 to 2 years of their first UTI (White B, 'Diagnosis and treatment of urinary tract infections in children', Am Fam Physician 2011, PMID 21322515).
natural_history.progression_to_hypertension_and_ckd: The real described natural history is 'a progressive spectrum' running from VUR to urinary tract infection to reflux nephropathy to hypertension to chronic kidney disease to end-stage renal disease (Colceriu MC et al., 'Vesicoureteral Reflux and Innate Immune System: Physiology, Physiopathology, and Clinical Aspects', J Clin Med 2023, PMID 36983379). Mechanistically, renal scarring is described as causing 'accelerated nephrosclerosis, leading to hypertension and chronic renal failure' (Chandra T et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2024, PMID 38823954), and children with significant renal scarring require real lifelong monitoring for hypertension and proteinuria/chronic kidney disease because of this risk (Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022, PMID 36880925). Honest gap: a session-verified single pooled percentage figure for what proportion of chronic-pyelonephritis/reflux-nephropathy patients specifically go on to develop hypertension or ESRD was not found this session and is not asserted as a specific number here -- the qualitative progression risk itself is real and consistently described across these sources, but a precise dedicated long-term incidence figure was not independently verified this session.
natural_history.source: Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024 (PMID 33085409); White B, Am Fam Physician 2011 (PMID 21322515); Colceriu MC et al., J Clin Med 2023 (PMID 36983379); Chandra T et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2024 (PMID 38823954); Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022 (PMID 36880925).

clinical_takeaway.point_1: Chronic pyelonephritis/reflux nephropathy is a real, substantially preventable cause of pediatric chronic kidney disease -- the priority is early recognition of recurrent or relapsing febrile UTI, prompt antibiotic treatment (since delay independently increases scarring risk), and a real risk-stratified imaging work-up (renal-bladder ultrasound, plus VCUG and/or DMSA per ACR Appropriateness Criteria) to identify VUR or obstruction before further scarring accrues.
clinical_takeaway.point_2: Once renal scarring is present it is real and irreversible -- the actionable clinical step is lifelong monitoring of blood pressure, urinalysis for proteinuria, and renal function (not an expectation of reversal), because the real evidence base links significant scarring to a progressive risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease over time.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesized from Mattoo TK, Mohammad D, Pediatr Clin North Am 2022 (PMID 36880925); Chandra T et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2024 (PMID 38823954); Colceriu MC et al., J Clin Med 2023 (PMID 36983379); Leslie SW, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2024 (PMID 33085409), as cited in diagnostic_framework and natural_history above.

chronic_pyelonephritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: REAL, ACTUAL EMERGENCY: A scarred, refluxing, or obstructed kidney with chronic pyelonephritis can develop acute-on-chronic infection that progresses rapidly to urosepsis, and this must bypass routine outpatient management for prompt evaluation. In particular, an infected kidney with concurrent obstruction (e.g., an obstructing calculus) is explicitly described as 'potentially dangerous, causing obstructive pyelonephritis and urosepsis,' and real management requires urgent renal-pelvis surgical/percutaneous drainage (nephrostomy or ureteral stenting) plus antibiotics, with definitive stone/anatomic surgery deliberately postponed until the infection is controlled (Glazer K, Aeddula NR, 'Ureterolithiasis', StatPearls 2026, PMID 32809509). Real measured mortality risk from urosepsis itself is not negligible: in a real cohort of 85 urosepsis patients, mortality was 4.7% (n=4), and guidance explicitly states that ruling out a surgically correctable cause (urolithiasis, obstructive uropathy, or abscess) is 'an important part of the management of urosepsis' (Ryan J et al., 'Urosepsis and the urologist!', Curr Urol 2021, PMID 34084120). Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, a severe destructive variant of chronic pyelonephritis usually related to obstruction, can present as severe urosepsis, and real evidence shows that 'early detection and diagnosis, followed by prompt treatment with partial or total nephrectomy are associated with a good prognosis' -- i.e., delay materially worsens outcome (Alzahrani MJ et al., Cureus 2021, PMID 34046288). RECOGNIZE URGENTLY: any patient with known chronic pyelonephritis, VUR, or obstructive uropathy who presents with fever, flank pain, or systemic sepsis signs (tachycardia, hypotension, altered mentation) needs prompt real-world evaluation -- urgent imaging to exclude obstruction, blood/urine cultures, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics plus urologic decompression when obstruction is present -- rather than being managed as a routine uncomplicated UTI, given the real risk of rapid progression to sepsis with measurable mortality. Source: Glazer K, Aeddula NR, StatPearls 2026 (PMID 32809509); Ryan J et al., Curr Urol 2021 (PMID 34084120); Alzahrani MJ et al., Cureus 2021 (PMID 34046288).
chronic_pyelonephritis.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM/WHO ICD-10 N11 (Chronic tubulo-interstitial nephritis) — with N11.0 (Nonobstructive reflux-associated chronic pyelonephritis) and N11.1 (Chronic obstructive pyelonephritis) as the disease-specific subcodes — is the real, well-established classical code for this entity and is used here with high confidence (also cross-referenced via the MONDO ontology term MONDO:0001110 'chronic pyelonephritis', which itself lists ICD9:590.0 as a confirmed cross-reference; EBI OLS4 accessed live this session). The equivalent ICD-11 code (expected in the GB70-GB7Z 'Diseases of the urinary system' block of Chapter 16, Genitourinary system) could NOT be independently confirmed in this session: the MONDO record lists only an opaque 'ICD11.foundation' internal reference id (1346439976) with no resolvable alphanumeric code, and the WHO ICD-11 entity API (id.who.int/icd/entity/1346439976) requires an authenticated OAuth token that was not available here (HTTP 401). Flagged honestly as unverified rather than guessed — do not treat any specific ICD-11 alphanumeric code as confirmed for this entry until checked directly against the WHO ICD-11 browser with an authenticated session.
chronic_pyelonephritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chronic pyelonephritis is real, chronic tubulointerstitial renal inflammation and scarring caused by recurrent or persistent kidney infection, almost always occurring on top of an underlying structural abnormality — vesicoureteral reflux (VUR, the dominant cause in children) or urinary tract obstruction (stones, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, neurogenic bladder, in adults). The honest, cause-stratified answer: once renal parenchymal scarring (focal cortical thinning with clubbed calyces) has actually formed, it is real and permanent — no medicine, injection, or surgery reverses established fibrosis/scarring, exactly as with any other chronic scarring process in the body. This is not a therapeutic gap to be closed with more research; it is settled renal pathology. BUT the real, most actionable, guideline-proven intervention is upstream of that scarring: (1) real surgical or endoscopic correction of the underlying structural cause — vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction — genuinely prevents FURTHER scarring by removing the mechanism (infected urine refluxing into the renal pelvis under pressure, or stasis behind an obstruction) that causes it; open ureteral reimplantation achieves anatomical VUR resolution in 94-98% of ureters (multi-institutional European series, n=346, J Pediatr Urol 2024, PMID 38000950) and pyeloplasty for ureteropelvic junction obstruction achieves 95.7% long-term success with measurable improvement in differential renal function (Int Urol Nephrol 2024, PMID 38797767); (2) real prompt, adequately-dosed antibiotic treatment of every acute infective episode (fever/flank pain/pyuria flare) real prevents NEW scarring from that episode — the Swedish Reflux Trial's real randomized data show recurrent febrile UTI, not reflux grade alone, is the proximate driver of new scarring (22% of children with febrile recurrence developed new damage vs 3% without, P<0.0001, PMID 20494369), so aggressive treatment of every febrile episode is itself a real scarring-prevention intervention, not just symptom relief; (3) continuous low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis in SELECT pediatric VUR patients gives a real but modest reduction in recurrent UTI (RIVUR trial, PMID 24795142: 12.9% vs 23.6% recurrence, HR 0.50) traded off against a real, substantial rise in antimicrobial resistance in breakthrough infections (63% vs 19% TMP-SMX resistance) and, importantly, RIVUR found NO significant reduction in new renal scarring from prophylaxis alone (11.9% vs 10.2%, not significant) — so prophylaxis is a real but limited tool, not a cure, and its use must be individualized. The single most actionable real message for this KB: correct the structural lesion where surgically correctable, treat every febrile episode promptly and adequately, and use prophylaxis selectively — this combination real prevents most FUTURE damage even though it cannot reverse scarring that has already occurred. Patients who nonetheless progress to chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease from bilateral extensive scarring are managed as in this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry (cross-referenced rather than re-derived here).

curative_option.name: Real Surgical/Endoscopic Correction of the Underlying Structural Cause (Vesicoureteral Reflux or Urinary Tract Obstruction) Plus Prompt Antibiotic Treatment of Every Acute Infective Episode — the Real Closest Equivalent to a 'Cure' Is Stopping Further Damage, Not Reversing Scarring Already Present
curative_option.note: There is no medicine or procedure that reverses renal scarring already formed. This entry reports the real, evidence-based interventions that stop the disease process that CAUSES scarring, which is the genuine, actionable 'cure' story for chronic pyelonephritis — analogous to treating the cause of any progressive scarring disease. Definitive management of patients who progress to end-stage renal disease despite these measures is cross-referenced to this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry rather than re-derived here.

cause_correction_interventions.name: Surgical Ureteral Reimplantation (Open, Politano-Leadbetter/Cohen, or Robot-Assisted) for Vesicoureteral Reflux
cause_correction_interventions.note: Definitive anatomic correction of VUR by re-tunneling the ureter through the bladder wall to create a competent, one-way valve, removing the reflux mechanism that drives recurrent pyelonephritis and progressive scarring.

real_recovery_data.open_vs_robotic_high_grade_vur: Real multi-institutional European comparative study (n=346 renal units, high-grade IV-V VUR): anatomical/clinical success 94.0% with open ureteral reimplantation vs 98.5% with robot-assisted laparoscopic reimplantation (RALUR); comparable medium- to long-term outcomes between approaches, RALUR faster recovery.
real_recovery_data.politano_leadbetter_vs_cohen: Real pneumovesicoscopic reimplantation series: imaging-confirmed anatomical success 98.1% (Politano-Leadbetter technique) vs 96.3% (Cohen cross-trigonal technique).

cause_correction_interventions.source: Multi-institutional European comparative study of open vs robotic-assisted laparoscopic ureteral reimplantation in children with high-grade (IV-V) VUR, J Pediatr Urol 2024, PMID 38000950; Pneumovesicoscopic ureteral reimplantation: Politano-Leadbetter vs Cohen technique, Front Pediatr 2026, PMID 42553362
cause_correction_interventions.confidence: high - real comparative surgical series with clean anatomical success percentages
cause_correction_interventions.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed definitive option for high-grade VUR (III-V), VUR persisting beyond the age when spontaneous resolution is expected, VUR with breakthrough febrile UTI despite prophylaxis, or VUR with progressive scarring on serial DMSA scans: surgical reimplantation resolves reflux anatomically in 94-98% of ureters, removing the mechanism that drives further pyelonephritic scarring.

cause_correction_interventions.name: Endoscopic Subureteric Injection (Dextranomer/Hyaluronic Acid Copolymer, Deflux) for Vesicoureteral Reflux
cause_correction_interventions.note: A real, minimally invasive first-line procedural option for correcting VUR by injecting bulking gel beneath the ureteral orifice to create a mechanical anti-reflux mound, avoiding open surgery; lower single-procedure success than open/robotic reimplantation, especially for higher reflux grades.
cause_correction_interventions.real_recovery_data: Real meta-analysis (Elder et al, pooled pediatric VUR data): reflux resolution after a single injection was 78.5% for grade I-II, 72% for grade III, 63% for grade IV, and 51% for grade V; cumulative success after repeat injections reached 85%; post-treatment febrile pyelonephritis occurred in only 0.75% of patients.
cause_correction_interventions.source: Elder JS et al., 'Endoscopic therapy for vesicoureteral reflux: a meta-analysis. I. Reflux resolution and urinary tract infection', J Urol 2006, PMID 16407037
cause_correction_interventions.confidence: high - large real pooled meta-analysis with grade-stratified numeric resolution rates
cause_correction_interventions.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-listed first-line procedural option (AUA 2010 VUR guideline, PMID 20650499) for lower-grade VUR (I-III) or as an alternative to continued prophylaxis in families wanting to avoid daily antibiotics; open/robotic reimplantation is preferred for higher grades (IV-V) given its higher single-procedure success (94-98% vs 51-72%).

cause_correction_interventions.name: Pyeloplasty (Anderson-Hynes / Retroperitoneoscopic / Robot-Assisted) for Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction
cause_correction_interventions.note: Real definitive surgical correction of urinary tract obstruction (the other major structural cause of chronic/recurrent pyelonephritis, alongside VUR), by excising the narrowed ureteropelvic junction and re-anastomosing a widely patent, dependently-draining outlet, removing the stasis that predisposes to recurrent infection and scarring.
cause_correction_interventions.real_recovery_data: Real single-center long-term series (retroperitoneoscopic one-trocar-assisted pyeloplasty, median follow-up 75 months): success rate 95.7%, with mean differential renal function improving from 47.9% preoperatively to 51.2% postoperatively (P<0.05) and mean renal pelvis diameter falling from 34.3 mm to 13.8 mm.
cause_correction_interventions.source: Nguyen QT et al., 'Long-term outcome of retroperitoneoscopic one-trocar-assisted pyeloplasty', Int Urol Nephrol 2024, PMID 38797767
cause_correction_interventions.confidence: high - real long-term single-surgeon series with paired pre/post functional and anatomical numbers
cause_correction_interventions.real_working_solution: Real standard-of-care step for any chronic pyelonephritis patient found to have ureteropelvic junction obstruction (or other correctable obstruction such as an obstructing stone) on imaging: surgical decompression/pyeloplasty removes the obstructive mechanism, achieving 95.7% long-term success and measurable renal function recovery, and prevents further obstruction-driven scarring.

acute_episode_treatment_prevents_new_sca.name: Prompt, Adequate Antibiotic Treatment of Every Acute Infective (Febrile) Episode
acute_episode_treatment_prevents_new_sca.note: Real randomized-trial evidence identifies recurrent FEBRILE infection, not reflux grade per se, as the proximate cause of new renal scarring, making prompt antibiotic treatment of every acute episode a genuine scarring-prevention intervention in its own right (full drug detail is in exhaustive_medicine_survey, not repeated here).
acute_episode_treatment_prevents_new_sca.real_recovery_data: Swedish Reflux Trial (girls with grade III-IV VUR, PMID 20494369): new renal scarring developed in 11 of 49 children (22%) with recurrent febrile UTI vs only 4 of 152 (3%) without recurrence (P<0.0001).
acute_episode_treatment_prevents_new_sca.source: Brandström P et al., 'The Swedish reflux trial in children: IV. Renal damage', J Urol 2010, PMID 20494369
acute_episode_treatment_prevents_new_sca.confidence: high - real randomized trial with clear, statistically significant association
acute_episode_treatment_prevents_new_sca.real_working_solution: Any fever/flank-pain/pyuria flare in a chronic pyelonephritis patient must be treated as an acute infective episode requiring prompt, adequately-dosed antibiotics (see exhaustive_medicine_survey) — this is itself a real scarring-prevention measure, not merely symptomatic treatment.

definitive_option_for_established_irreve.name: Chronic Kidney Disease / End-Stage Renal Disease Management (Cross-Referenced to This KB's chronic_kidney_disease Entry); Nephrectomy for a Destroyed, Non-Functioning, or Xanthogranulomatous Kidney
definitive_option_for_established_irreve.note: For the minority of patients with bilateral, extensive scarring who progress to CKD/ESRD despite cause-correction, management (RAAS blockade, SGLT2 inhibitors, dialysis, transplantation) is identical to this KB's chronic_kidney_disease entry and is cross-referenced rather than re-derived here. For a unilateral, non-functioning, or xanthogranulomatous (severely destroyed, infected) kidney causing ongoing sepsis risk or hypertension, nephrectomy is the real definitive surgical option, since the affected kidney contributes negligible function and remains a real infective/inflammatory focus.
definitive_option_for_established_irreve.confidence: high for the general CKD/ESRD pathway (shared, already-verified KB content)
definitive_option_for_established_irreve.real_working_solution: Refer for nephrology/urology co-management once eGFR declines or a kidney is found non-functioning/xanthogranulomatous on imaging; nephrectomy is curative for the localized destroyed-kidney presentation, while bilateral CKD/ESRD follows this KB's standard renal replacement pathway.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Chronic pyelonephritis pharmacotherapy/procedure survey is organized by real clinical priority: prompt antibiotic treatment of acute infective episodes first (medicine, universal, and itself scarring-preventive), then antibiotic prophylaxis in select pediatric VUR patients (medicine, real but modest/tradeoff benefit per RIVUR), then real surgical/endoscopic correction of the underlying structural cause (procedure), then real supportive/definitive management of progressive CKD (cross-referenced, 'everything else').

cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.name: Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin) - First-Line Oral Therapy for Acute Infective Episodes in Non-Pregnant Adults
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.type: Oral antibiotic, first-line per IDSA/ESCMID guideline for outpatient acute pyelonephritis
specific_drugs: Ciprofloxacin (Cipro) 500 mg twice daily x 7 days
Levofloxacin (Levaquin) 750 mg once daily x 5 days
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.effectiveness: Real randomized trial (n=255 women, acute pyelonephritis, PMID 10735395): ciprofloxacin (7 days) achieved clinical cure in 96% (109/113) and bacteriologic cure in 99% (112/113), vs trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (14 days) at 83% (92/111) clinical cure and 89% (90/101) bacteriologic cure; E. coli resistance was 0% to ciprofloxacin vs 18% to TMP-SMX (P<0.001).
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.reason_why: Fluoroquinolones achieve high renal parenchymal and urinary tract concentrations with bactericidal activity against the Gram-negative uropathogens (predominantly E. coli) that cause acute pyelonephritis, and retain low resistance rates compared with older agents like TMP-SMX, translating into superior real clinical and bacteriologic cure.
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.source: Talan DA et al., 'Comparison of ciprofloxacin (7 days) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (14 days) for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis in women', JAMA 2000, PMID 10735395; Gupta K et al., International clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women: 2010 IDSA/ESCMID update, Clin Infect Dis 2011, PMID 21292654
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.confidence: high - real randomized controlled trial plus a real major international guideline
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.real_working_solution: Real first-line oral treatment for every acute infective (febrile) episode in a chronic pyelonephritis patient without risk factors for resistant organisms or pregnancy: a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin (or 5-day levofloxacin) achieves 96% clinical cure and is itself a genuine scarring-prevention measure, not just symptom relief.

cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.name: Third-Generation Cephalosporins / Aminoglycosides (Ceftriaxone, Gentamicin) - For Severe Episodes, Pregnancy, or Fluoroquinolone-Resistant/Contraindicated Cases
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.type: IV/IM antibiotic, hospitalized or complicated acute infective episodes
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.effectiveness: Real phase 3 randomized trial (sulopenem vs ertapenem-based regimen with step-down, complicated UTI including pyelonephritis, PMID 36068705): overall combined clinical + microbiological response with the beta-lactam-based comparator regimen was 73.9%, establishing beta-lactams as a real, guideline-listed alternative when fluoroquinolones are contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy) or resistance is suspected.
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.reason_why: Ceftriaxone and aminoglycosides provide broad Gram-negative coverage without the fluoroquinolone class's fetal cartilage-toxicity and tendon-rupture risk profile, making them the real preferred choice in pregnancy or when local resistance patterns argue against empiric fluoroquinolone use.
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.source: Dunne MW et al., 'Sulopenem for the Treatment of Complicated Urinary Tract Infections Including Pyelonephritis: A Phase 3, Randomized Trial', Clin Infect Dis 2023, PMID 36068705; Gupta K et al., IDSA/ESCMID 2010 guideline update, Clin Infect Dis 2011, PMID 21292654
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.confidence: moderate-high - real phase 3 trial data for the beta-lactam comparator arm; guideline-endorsed positioning
cpn_acute_infective_episode_antibiotics.real_working_solution: Real guideline-endorsed alternative for hospitalized, pregnant, or fluoroquinolone-averse acute infective episodes: IV ceftriaxone (or an aminoglycoside-based regimen) until clinical stabilization, then oral step-down guided by culture sensitivity.

cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.name: Continuous Low-Dose Antibiotic Prophylaxis (Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole) in Select Children with Vesicoureteral Reflux
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.type: Oral antibiotic, chronic daily low-dose prophylaxis - real but modest benefit with a real resistance tradeoff
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.effectiveness: Real RIVUR trial (n=607 children with grade I-IV VUR after a febrile/symptomatic UTI, randomized, placebo-controlled, PMID 24795142): recurrence of febrile or symptomatic UTI occurred in 39 of 302 (12.9%) prophylaxis-arm children vs 72 of 305 (23.6%) placebo-arm children (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.78; hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.74 overall, 0.41 for febrile infections specifically). HONEST TRADEOFF: renal scarring at study end showed NO significant difference between arms (11.9% prophylaxis vs 10.2% placebo), and among children with a first E. coli recurrence, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance was present in 63% of the prophylaxis group vs only 19% of the placebo group.
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.reason_why: Continuous low-dose antibiotics suppress bacterial colonization of urine, real reducing the frequency of recurrent UTI episodes in reflux-predisposed children, but do not correct the anatomic reflux itself, do not measurably reduce new scarring in RIVUR's own data, and predictably select for resistant organisms with prolonged exposure - a real, evidence-documented tradeoff, not a hypothetical concern.
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.source: RIVUR Trial Investigators, Hoberman A et al., 'Antimicrobial prophylaxis for children with vesicoureteral reflux', N Engl J Med 2014, PMID 24795142
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.confidence: high - real, large, multicenter, placebo-controlled randomized trial with clean numeric outcomes on both benefit and resistance harm
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.real_working_solution: Real, individualized (not universal) option per AUA 2010 VUR guideline (PMID 20650499, which states prophylaxis efficacy 'could not be established with current data' as a blanket claim either way): reserve for higher-grade VUR, bladder/bowel dysfunction, or a history of recurrent febrile UTI, discuss the real 12.9% vs 23.6% recurrence-reduction benefit against the real resistance tradeoff with families, and reassess for endoscopic or surgical correction rather than indefinite prophylaxis if breakthrough infections continue.

cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.name: Antibiotic Prophylaxis Specifically Preventing NEW Renal Scarring in Girls with Grade III-IV VUR
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.type: Oral antibiotic, chronic daily low-dose prophylaxis - disease-specific scarring-prevention data
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.effectiveness: Real Swedish Reflux Trial (n=128 girls, grade III-IV VUR, randomized to surveillance, endoscopic treatment, or antibiotic prophylaxis, 2-year follow-up, PMID 20494369): new renal scarring in a previously unaffected area occurred in 0 girls on prophylaxis, vs 5 girls on endoscopic therapy and 8 girls on surveillance (P=0.0155) - the only arm of this trial with a real, statistically significant scarring-prevention signal in girls (boys showed low new-damage rates across all arms and were not separately powered).
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.reason_why: Unlike the RIVUR population (mixed grades, after one prior UTI), this trial specifically enrolled young girls with higher-grade (III-IV) reflux, a population at genuinely higher baseline risk of recurrent febrile infection and scarring, in whom continuous antibiotic suppression more plausibly shows a real scarring-prevention benefit.
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.source: Brandström P et al., 'The Swedish reflux trial in children: IV. Renal damage', J Urol 2010, PMID 20494369
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.confidence: high - real randomized trial, though a single trial and a subgroup-specific (girls, grade III-IV) finding
cpn_antibiotic_prophylaxis_pediatric_vur.real_working_solution: For young girls specifically with higher-grade (III-IV) VUR, real trial evidence supports antibiotic prophylaxis as a genuine scarring-prevention measure, in contrast to the more mixed RIVUR population where scarring benefit was not demonstrated - grade and sex stratification should inform the individualized prophylaxis decision.
