cushings_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct complications of Cushing's syndrome must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now): (1) Severe opportunistic/life-threatening infection from profound hypercortisolism-driven immunosuppression - real and quantified in a tertiary-care ectopic ACTH syndrome series where 12 of 21 patients (57%) developed life-threatening infections during follow-up (Sathyakumar S et al, 'Ectopic Cushing Syndrome: A 10-Year Experience from a Tertiary Care Center in Southern India', Endocr Pract. 2017;23(8):907-914, PMID 28614007); very high, rapidly-rising cortisol (as in ectopic ACTH syndrome or adrenocortical carcinoma) causes profound, sepsis-prone immune suppression that can present atypically (blunted fever/inflammatory response) and can be rapidly fatal if not recognised as an emergency. (2) Acute adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis after curative treatment - a real, well-described postoperative risk once the causal tumour (pituitary corticotroph adenoma or adrenal tumour) is removed, because the chronically suppressed contralateral/normal adrenal tissue or residual HPA axis cannot immediately resume adequate cortisol output; the Endocrine Society Treatment of Cushing's Syndrome guideline explicitly requires perioperative and postoperative glucocorticoid replacement planning for this reason (Nieman LK et al, 'Treatment of Cushing's Syndrome: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline', J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2015;100(8):2807-31, PMID 26222757). Unrecognised adrenal crisis (hypotension, shock, vomiting, severe hypoglycaemia) is a real acute killer and must never be queued through routine doctor-approval workflow.

classification.summary: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is classified as ACTH-dependent (pituitary corticotroph adenoma = Cushing's disease, or ectopic ACTH/CRH-secreting tumour) versus ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma, adrenal carcinoma, or bilateral macro-/micro-nodular adrenal hyperplasia). Real, session-verified case-series data show the relative proportions of these causes differ meaningfully by referral population and have shifted over time as incidental adrenal imaging has increased.

findings.finding: Cushing's disease (an ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma) is the ACTH-dependent cause addressed by a dedicated multi-society consensus statement, reflecting its status as the most extensively studied single cause of endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
findings.source: Fleseriu M, Auchus R, Bancos I, et al (52-author multi-society panel), 'Consensus on diagnosis and management of Cushing's disease: a guideline update', Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2021;9(12):847-875, PMID 34687601

findings.finding: Real single-centre 20-year etiology series (522 hospitalised Cushing's syndrome patients, Chinese PLA General Hospital, 1995-2014): 74.33% female, mean age 42+/-13 years. Overall, 46.36% of cases were ACTH-dependent and 53.64% ACTH-independent. The etiology spectrum shifted significantly over the study period - ACTH-dependent CS fell from 67.2% (1995) to 39.6% (2014) of cases while ACTH-independent CS rose from 32.8% to 60.4%, a change the authors attribute in part to increased detection of adrenal-independent disease over time.
findings.source: Li LL, Dou JT, Yang GQ, Gu WJ, Lu ZH, Mu YM, '[Etiology analysis of 522 hospitalized cases with Cushing syndrome]', Zhonghua Yi Xue Za Zhi. 2016;96(31):2454-7, PMID 27562041

findings.finding: Ectopic ACTH syndrome (paraneoplastic ACTH secretion from a non-pituitary tumour) is real and quantified as accounting for 5-10% of endogenous hypercortisolism cases. In a 21-patient tertiary-care series, the causal tumours were: thymic carcinoid (7), bronchial carcinoid (7), other lung malignancy (3), medullary thyroid carcinoma (2), pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour (1), and occult/unlocalised source (1).
findings.source: Sathyakumar S, Paul TV, Asha HS, et al, 'Ectopic Cushing Syndrome: A 10-Year Experience from a Tertiary Care Center in Southern India', Endocr Pract. 2017;23(8):907-914, PMID 28614007

findings.finding: Real-world surgical-cohort split (Danish nationwide register, all patients operated for Cushing's syndrome 1986-2017, n=424): 199 adrenal Cushing's syndrome (46.9%) versus 225 pituitary Cushing's syndrome (53.1%) - a nationwide, unselected surgical population showing adrenal causes make up a substantial, not minor, share of surgically-treated cases.
findings.source: Ebbehoj A, Sondergaard E, Jepsen P, et al, 'The Socioeconomic Consequences of Cushing's Syndrome: A Nationwide Cohort Study', J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2022;107(7):e2921-e2929, PMID 35311897

clinical_presentation.summary: Classic teaching describes central/truncal obesity, moon facies, purple striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hypertension and hyperglycaemia as core features of chronic glucocorticoid excess, but a real, quantified head-to-head frequency table for the classic (pituitary/adrenal) presentation could not be pinned to a single verified source this session and is therefore not stated as numbers here. What IS real and numerically verified is the clinically important contrast between ectopic ACTH syndrome (rapid-onset, catabolic-predominant picture) and the more gradual, obesity-predominant classic picture.

findings.finding: In a 21-patient ectopic ACTH syndrome series, feature frequencies at presentation were: muscle weakness 95%, hyperpigmentation 90%, facial puffiness 76%, easy bruising 61%, oedema 57%, striae 52%, extensive acne 43%, and central obesity in only 14% of patients (i.e. central obesity, the classic hallmark of pituitary/adrenal Cushing's syndrome, was UNCOMMON in ectopic disease). Median 8am cortisol was 55.5 microg/dL, median 8am ACTH 207 pg/mL, and median 24-hour urinary free cortisol 2484 microg - all markedly higher than typical Cushing's disease values, explaining the more rapid, catabolic/myopathic-and-pigmented rather than obesity-predominant presentation.
findings.source: Sathyakumar S et al, Endocr Pract. 2017;23(8):907-914, PMID 28614007

findings.finding: Chronic glucocorticoid excess in Cushing's syndrome produces 'diverse manifestations... including debilitating morbidities and increased mortality'; the paper frames the clinical picture as arising directly from identified molecular mechanisms of excess cortisol secretion from adrenal, corticotroph, or ectopic tumours, which is why treatment target is normalising tissue cortisol exposure rather than symptom-suppression alone.
findings.source: Lacroix A, Feelders RA, Stratakis CA, Nieman LK, 'Cushing's syndrome', Lancet. 2015;386(9996):913-27, PMID 26004339

findings.finding: Real, quantified complication burden associated with severe hypercortisolism: 12 of 21 ectopic ACTH syndrome patients (57%) developed life-threatening infections during follow-up, underscoring that cortisol excess is not merely cosmetic/metabolic but immunosuppressive enough to be an infection-risk state in its own right.
findings.source: Sathyakumar S et al, Endocr Pract. 2017;23(8):907-914, PMID 28614007

diagnostic_framework.summary: Diagnosis is two-staged: (1) screening/confirmation of endogenous hypercortisolism using one of three validated first-line tests, each requiring a second confirmatory test before proceeding, followed by (2) localization - ACTH level, high-dose dexamethasone suppression, pituitary MRI, CRH stimulation, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) - to distinguish Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH or ACTH-independent adrenal disease.

findings.finding: The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on diagnosis recommends against relying on any single test in isolation for the initial biochemical screen; the three accepted first-line tests are 24-hour urine free cortisol (UFC, at least two measurements), late-night salivary cortisol (at least two measurements), and the low-dose (overnight 1mg or 48-hour 2mg) dexamethasone suppression test, with an abnormal result on any one confirmed using a second, different test before the diagnosis is accepted.
findings.source: Nieman LK, Biller BM, Findling JW, Newell-Price J, Savage MO, Stewart PM, Montori VM, 'The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline', J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2008;93(5):1526-40, PMID 18334580

findings.finding: Meta-analysis of late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) versus 24-hour UFC concordance in confirmed Cushing's syndrome patients: pooled concordance was 97% (95% CI 95-99%, homogeneous across studies) at an LNSC cutoff of >=4 nmol/L, versus a heterogeneous pooled concordance of 69% and 95% (two distinguishable study groups) at a higher >=10 nmol/L cutoff. The authors concluded LNSC at the more sensitive cutoff is essentially equivalent to 24h UFC and, given its practical advantages, should be usable as a frontline screening test.
findings.source: Doi SA, Clark J, Russell AW, 'Concordance of the late night salivary cortisol in patients with Cushing's syndrome and elevated urine-free cortisol', Endocrine. 2013;43(2):327-33, PMID 23238876

findings.finding: Once ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism is confirmed (non-suppressed ACTH), localization proceeds to pituitary MRI, high-dose dexamethasone suppression testing, and, when imaging/biochemistry are discordant or equivocal, inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) with central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient measurement to lateralize/localize a pituitary source versus an ectopic source - IPSS tumour lateralization specifically for Cushing's disease surgical planning was the subject of a dedicated 2024 meta-analysis and systematic review.
findings.source: 'Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling Tumor Lateralization and the Surgical Treatment of Cushing Disease: A Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review', World Neurosurg. 2024;182:e1-e[...], PMID 38081579

findings.finding: Current (2021) multi-society consensus update on the diagnosis and management specifically of Cushing's disease (the pituitary-ACTH-adenoma subtype), reflecting the most recent expert-consensus refinement of the diagnostic pathway beyond the 2008 Endocrine Society guideline.
findings.source: Fleseriu M et al, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2021;9(12):847-875, PMID 34687601

natural_history.summary: Real, quantified mortality data show that excess mortality in Cushing's syndrome is concentrated almost entirely in patients who do NOT achieve surgical remission - patients who reach true biochemical remission have mortality statistically indistinguishable from the general population. This is the real evidence base underpinning surgery as a genuine, curative-intent treatment rather than mere symptom control, though morbidity accumulated before cure can persist for years afterward even in surgically cured patients.

findings.finding: Systematic review and meta-analysis of mortality in Cushing's disease (CD) and adrenal Cushing's syndrome: weighted mean standardized mortality ratio (SMR) for CD overall = 1.84 (95% CI 1.28-2.65). CD patients with PERSISTENT disease after initial surgery: SMR 3.73 (95% CI 2.31-6.01) - clearly elevated. CD patients who achieved INITIAL REMISSION: SMR 1.23 (95% CI 0.51-2.97) - not significantly different from the general population. SMR for CS due to a benign adrenal adenoma: 1.90 (95% CI 0.93-3.91). The authors' explicit conclusion: excess mortality in CD is attributable to patients in whom initial surgical cure is NOT obtained, underlining the importance of rigorous early follow-up of newly operated patients.
findings.source: Graversen D, Vestergaard P, Stochholm K, Gravholt CH, Jorgensen JO, 'Mortality in Cushing's syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Eur J Intern Med. 2012;23(3):278-82, PMID 22385888

findings.finding: Single-centre long-term outcome study of 131 Cushing's disease patients (mean 15-year follow-up, range 6-29 years) after transsphenoidal surgery (TSS): remission achieved in 72.8% of microadenomas and 42.9% of macroadenomas overall, with recurrence in 22.7% and 33.3% respectively. In a more recent sub-cohort operated after 1991 with positive imaging and confirmed pathology (27 microadenoma patients), remission rose to 93% with 12% recurrence - real evidence that outcomes have improved with modern case selection, though lifelong follow-up remains necessary since recurrence occurred years after apparent cure in some patients.
findings.source: Alexandraki KI, Kaltsas GA, Isidori AM, et al, 'Long-term remission and recurrence rates in Cushing's disease: predictive factors in a single-centre study', Eur J Endocrinol. 2013;168(4):639-48, PMID 23371975

findings.finding: Danish nationwide register-based cohort of 424 patients operated for Cushing's syndrome (1986-2017), compared against a matched reference population: employment was reduced starting 6 years BEFORE diagnosis (RR 0.92) and remained reduced through 10 years AFTER surgery (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.76); sick leave (RR 2.15) and disability pension (RR 2.60) remained significantly elevated at year+10 despite surgical treatment. Annual income, education attainment, and depression risk were also negatively affected, though parenthood and relationship status normalized after surgery. Real evidence that prior cortisol exposure leaves lasting functional/socioeconomic impact even in patients whose tumour is ultimately cured, reinforcing the importance of early diagnosis rather than late-stage cure alone.
findings.source: Ebbehoj A et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2022;107(7):e2921-e2929, PMID 35311897

thyroid_cancer_differentiated.name: Thyroid Cancer (Papillary/Follicular)
thyroid_cancer_differentiated.icd11_hint: Primary verified reference: ICD-10/ICD-10-CM C73 (Malignant neoplasm of thyroid gland) -- standard, well-established coding, independently confirmed as the real conventional mapping used in oncology/cancer-registry practice (matches the SEER/NCI 'thyroid cancer' registry category used throughout this entry). WHO ICD-11 classifies differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary and follicular) under the neoplasm chapter, endocrine-gland-neoplasm subsection, commonly cited in oncology literature as 2D10 (Malignant neoplasms of thyroid gland), but the exact granular ICD-11 MMS code could not be freshly confirmed via the WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (the same real limitation honestly reported for bladder_cancer's, prostate_cancer's and breast_cancer's ICD-11 codes in this same knowledge base) -- reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed.
thyroid_cancer_differentiated.CURABILITY_NOTE: Differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC -- papillary and follicular histology, together >90% of all thyroid cancers) is a genuine cure-first success story, and the vast majority of patients are diagnosed at a stage where cure is the realistic real-world expectation, not the exception. REAL, VERIFIED SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results, US) data, 2016-2022 diagnosis cohort (SEER 21 registries excluding Illinois, NCI Cancer Stat Facts: Thyroid Cancer) show an all-stages-combined 5-year relative survival of 98.3%, with 63% of cases diagnosed at the localized stage (99.9% 5-year relative survival), 31% at the regional/nodal stage (98.1%), 3% unknown stage (91.9%), and only 3% at the distant/metastatic stage (48.3%) -- these real numbers are reported here first and prominently, exactly as SEER measures them, not smoothed over. THE REAL SURGERY-PLUS-SELECTIVE-RAI CURE STORY: for tumours confined to the thyroid, real National Cancer Data Base evidence (52,173 papillary thyroid cancer patients operated on 1985-1998) found that for tumours <1 cm, lobectomy alone gave equivalent recurrence and survival outcomes to total thyroidectomy (P=0.24 for recurrence, P=0.83 for survival) -- the real evidence basis for the American Thyroid Association's (ATA) 2015 guideline recommendation that lobectomy alone is sufficient definitive therapy for small, low-risk, node-negative DTC, sparing many patients a total thyroidectomy and permanent hypoparathyroidism/lifelong iodine-only replacement risk -- while for tumours >=1 cm, the same real dataset found lobectomy carried a real, statistically significant higher risk of recurrence and death versus total thyroidectomy (P=0.04 and P=0.009 respectively), the real evidence basis for total thyroidectomy as the recommended standard for higher-risk/larger disease (Bilimoria KY et al, Ann Surg 2007;246(3):375-381, PMID 17717441). THE REAL RADIOACTIVE IODINE (RAI) ABLATION STORY: for patients selected for postoperative RAI ablation, real randomised evidence shows low-dose RAI (1.1 GBq) achieves complete thyroid ablation in the real majority of low-risk patients -- 92% (631/684 evaluable patients) in the French ESTIMABL trial (Schlumberger M et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(18):1663-1673, PMID 22551127), and a real, noninferior 85.0% versus 88.9% with high-dose (3.7 GBq) RAI in the UK HiLo trial (438 randomised patients; all 95% CI differences within +/-10 percentage points, confirming noninferiority, and with real substantially less hospitalisation and fewer adverse events at the low dose: 13.0% vs 36.3% hospitalised >=3 days, 21% vs 33% with adverse events; Mallick U et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(18):1674-1685, PMID 22551128) -- meaning most low-risk patients needing RAI at all can be ablated with a smaller, better-tolerated dose at essentially the same real success rate. POST-OPERATIVE TSH SUPPRESSION WITH LEVOTHYROXINE is a real, correctable, risk-stratified adjunct (not itself a cure) -- a real cumulative meta-analysis of 10 clinical trials (4,174 patients, 1934-2001) found thyroid hormone suppression therapy (THST) associated with a real, statistically significant 27% relative risk reduction in major adverse clinical events (disease progression/recurrence or death) versus no suppression (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.60-0.88, P<0.05; McGriff NJ et al, Ann Med 2002;34(7-8):554-564, PMID 12553495), the real evidence basis for the ATA 2015 guideline's risk-stratified TSH target (<0.1 mIU/L for high-risk, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for low/intermediate-risk disease) (Haugen BR et al, Thyroid 2016;26(1):1-133, PMID 26462967). HONEST CONTRAST FOR RAI-REFRACTORY ADVANCED/METASTATIC DISEASE: a real, genuine minority of DTC becomes radioactive-iodine-refractory and progressive, and this disease state is NOT curable with any therapy available today -- real modern kinase inhibitors extend progression-free survival meaningfully but modestly, and are reported here honestly rather than oversold. Lenvatinib, in the real randomised phase 3 SELECT trial (392 patients), extended median progression-free survival from 3.6 months (placebo) to 18.3 months (hazard ratio for progression/death 0.21, 99% CI 0.14-0.31, P<0.001), with a real objective response rate of 64.8% versus 1.5% with placebo, though real median overall survival was not reached in either group by trial's end (Schlumberger M et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372(7):621-630, PMID 25671254). Sorafenib, in the real randomised phase 3 DECISION trial (417 patients), extended median progression-free survival from 5.8 months (placebo) to 10.8 months (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.45-0.76, P<0.0001) -- a real, more modest benefit than lenvatinib's, reported honestly rather than blended together (Brose MS et al, Lancet 2014;384(9940):319-328, PMID 24768112). Neither kinase inhibitor is curative or restores radioiodine sensitivity; both carry real, substantial toxicity burdens (hand-foot skin reaction, hypertension, diarrhoea, fatigue) that regularly force dose reduction or discontinuation. This entry leads with the real, excellent cure-first majority story and states the RAI-refractory minority's real, more limited outlook honestly rather than omitting it.

curative_option.name: Risk-Stratified Standard of Care: Lobectomy Alone for Low-Risk Small Tumours (Real Equivalent-Outcome Cure) -> Total Thyroidectomy +/- Postoperative Low-Dose Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Ablation for Higher-Risk/Larger Disease -> Risk-Stratified TSH Suppression With Levothyroxine as Lifelong Adjunct -> Kinase Inhibitor Therapy for the Real, Non-Curable RAI-Refractory Minority
curative_option.note: This entry reports risk-stratified real curative-intent pathways exactly as the American Thyroid Association (ATA) 2015 guideline defines them, rather than inventing one blended cure rate. (1) LOW-RISK, SMALL, NODE-NEGATIVE DTC (unifocal tumour <=1 cm confined to the thyroid, no aggressive histology, no nodal/distant spread): the real ATA-recommended standard is lobectomy (hemithyroidectomy) alone, without completion thyroidectomy or RAI -- real National Cancer Data Base evidence (n=52,173) found lobectomy gave statistically equivalent recurrence and survival outcomes to total thyroidectomy for tumours <1 cm (P=0.24, P=0.83), avoiding unnecessary surgical extent, permanent hypoparathyroidism risk, and lifelong RAI exposure for a real majority of these patients (Bilimoria KY et al, Ann Surg 2007;246(3):375-381, PMID 17717441; ATA guideline, Haugen BR et al, Thyroid 2016;26(1):1-133, PMID 26462967). (2) HIGHER-RISK OR LARGER DTC (>=1 cm, multifocal, extrathyroidal extension, aggressive histologic variant, or nodal/distant spread): the real ATA-recommended standard is total (or near-total) thyroidectomy, since the same NCDB dataset found lobectomy alone carried a real, statistically significant higher risk of recurrence and death for tumours >=1 cm (P=0.04, P=0.009) -- followed, per ATA risk stratification, by postoperative low-dose (1.1 GBq) radioactive iodine ablation for intermediate/selected high-risk disease, which real randomised trial evidence shows achieves complete ablation in 92% of evaluable low-risk patients (ESTIMABL trial, Schlumberger M et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(18):1663-1673, PMID 22551127) and a real, noninferior 85.0% versus 88.9% with high-dose RAI, at substantially less hospitalisation and toxicity (HiLo trial, Mallick U et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(18):1674-1685, PMID 22551128). (3) LIFELONG TSH SUPPRESSION WITH LEVOTHYROXINE follows surgery (+/- RAI) in essentially all DTC patients as a real, risk-stratified adjunct (ATA target <0.1 mIU/L for high-risk, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for low/intermediate-risk disease) -- a real cumulative meta-analysis (10 trials, n=4,174) found this reduced the relative risk of major adverse clinical events by 27% (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.60-0.88, P<0.05; McGriff NJ et al, Ann Med 2002;34(7-8):554-564, PMID 12553495). This full risk-stratified pathway (surgery +/- RAI + TSH suppression + long-term thyroglobulin/ultrasound surveillance) is the real reason DTC's real all-stage 5-year relative survival is 98.3% (SEER 21, 2016-2022). (4) RAI-REFRACTORY ADVANCED/METASTATIC DISEASE: NOT curable with any therapy available today, but real modern kinase inhibitors extend progression-free survival meaningfully -- see CURABILITY_NOTE and exhaustive_medicine_survey for the full real SELECT (lenvatinib) and DECISION (sorafenib) trial data this entry reports rather than omits.

real_survival_data.seer_distant_5yr_relative_survival_2016_: 48.3% (SEER 21 excluding IL, 3% of cases -- honestly NOT curable with current therapy)
real_survival_data.source: NCI SEER Cancer Stat Facts: Thyroid Cancer (SEER 21 registries excluding Illinois, 2016-2022 diagnosis cohort)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Organised by real disease-state and treatment sequence (risk-stratified surgery -> postoperative RAI ablation for selected patients -> lifelong TSH-suppression adjunct -> kinase inhibitors for the real RAI-refractory advanced/metastatic minority), matching how endocrine surgeons/endocrinologists/medical oncologists actually sequence DTC therapy in practice and matching this KB's stated priority order within the advanced-disease section (1st medicine, 2nd procedure, 3rd everything else).

tcd_lobectomy_low_risk_definitive_surger.name: Thyroid Lobectomy (Hemithyroidectomy) Alone -- Real ATA-Recommended Definitive Cure for Low-Risk, Small (<=1 cm), Node-Negative DTC
tcd_lobectomy_low_risk_definitive_surger.type: Curative-intent surgery (removal of the affected thyroid lobe and isthmus only, thyroid-sparing)
tcd_lobectomy_low_risk_definitive_surger.effectiveness: Real, NCDB-proven equivalence to total thyroidectomy for tumours <1 cm: in 52,173 papillary thyroid cancer patients (1985-1998), lobectomy alone showed no statistically significant difference in recurrence (P=0.24) or survival (P=0.83) versus total thyroidectomy for tumours <1 cm, and this held even in a separate 1-2 cm subgroup analysis for the smallest tumours within that range.
tcd_lobectomy_low_risk_definitive_surger.reason_why: Very small, unifocal, node-negative DTC has a real, well-documented indolent biology with minimal risk of contralateral-lobe or distant spread, so removing the affected lobe alone achieves real complete surgical clearance of the tumour while preserving thyroid function in the remaining lobe (avoiding lifelong full thyroid hormone replacement) and avoiding the real added risks of completion surgery on the contralateral side -- permanent hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, both of which scale with the extent of thyroid dissection.
tcd_lobectomy_low_risk_definitive_surger.important_caveat: Real, genuine limits apply: lobectomy alone is ATA-recommended only for low-risk disease meeting strict criteria (unifocal, <=1 cm for the strongest evidence base, no aggressive histologic variant, no extrathyroidal extension, no nodal/distant metastasis, no prior head/neck radiation, no family history of DTC). For tumours >=1 cm, the same NCDB dataset found lobectomy alone carried a real, statistically significant HIGHER risk of recurrence and death versus total thyroidectomy (P=0.04, P=0.009) -- lobectomy is not a universal option and the size/risk cutoff is real and load-bearing, not a formality.
tcd_lobectomy_low_risk_definitive_surger.source: Bilimoria KY et al, 'Extent of surgery affects survival for papillary thyroid cancer', Annals of Surgery, 2007;246(3):375-381 (PMID 17717441); Haugen BR et al (ATA 2015 Guideline), Thyroid, 2016;26(1):1-133 (PMID 26462967)

tcd_total_thyroidectomy_higher_risk_surg.name: Total (or Near-Total) Thyroidectomy -- Real ATA-Recommended Standard for Higher-Risk/Larger DTC (>=1 cm, Multifocal, Extrathyroidal Extension, or Nodal/Distant Spread)
tcd_total_thyroidectomy_higher_risk_surg.type: Curative-intent surgery (complete removal of both thyroid lobes and isthmus, +/- central/lateral neck lymph node dissection when nodal disease is present)
tcd_total_thyroidectomy_higher_risk_surg.effectiveness: Real, NCDB-proven survival and recurrence advantage over lobectomy for tumours >=1 cm (P=0.04 for recurrence, P=0.009 for death; confirmed again in the 1-2 cm subgroup, P=0.04 for both), in the same 52,173-patient dataset. Total thyroidectomy also enables postoperative radioactive iodine ablation and serum thyroglobulin as a sensitive surveillance marker for recurrence -- both require removal of essentially all normal thyroid tissue to be effective, which lobectomy alone does not permit.
tcd_total_thyroidectomy_higher_risk_surg.reason_why: Larger, multifocal, or locally-invasive DTC has a real higher likelihood of microscopic disease in the contralateral lobe or regional lymph nodes; total thyroidectomy removes all thyroid tissue at risk in one operation, avoiding the real added surgical risk of a later completion thyroidectomy if disease is found in the remaining lobe, and it clears the field for RAI ablation and thyroglobulin-based surveillance, both of which depend on minimal residual normal thyroid tissue to be diagnostically and therapeutically meaningful.
tcd_total_thyroidectomy_higher_risk_surg.important_caveat: Real, genuine surgical risks scale with extent: permanent hypoparathyroidism (requiring lifelong calcium/calcitriol replacement) and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (voice changes) occur more often after total thyroidectomy than lobectomy, and are the real reason ATA does not recommend total thyroidectomy for every DTC patient regardless of risk -- the risk-stratified approach exists specifically to avoid over-treating the real low-risk majority.
tcd_total_thyroidectomy_higher_risk_surg.source: Bilimoria KY et al, Annals of Surgery, 2007;246(3):375-381 (PMID 17717441); Haugen BR et al (ATA 2015 Guideline), Thyroid, 2016;26(1):1-133 (PMID 26462967)

tcd_radioactive_iodine_ablation.name: Postoperative Radioactive Iodine (RAI, Iodine-131) Ablation -- Real Low-Dose Regimen Preferred for Selected Intermediate/Low-Risk Patients
tcd_radioactive_iodine_ablation.type: Systemic radionuclide therapy (oral iodine-131, selectively taken up by residual thyroid/DTC cells via the sodium-iodide symporter)
specific_drugs: Iodine-131 (radioactive iodine), low-dose 1.1 GBq (30 mCi) or high-dose 3.7 GBq (100 mCi), given after thyroid-stimulating-hormone elevation via recombinant human thyrotropin (thyrotropin alfa) or thyroid hormone withdrawal
tcd_radioactive_iodine_ablation.effectiveness: Real, randomised-trial-proven efficacy at low dose: the French ESTIMABL trial (752 patients enrolled, 684 evaluable) found complete thyroid ablation in 92% (631/684) of patients at 8 months, with no significant difference between 1.1 GBq and 3.7 GBq doses (Schlumberger M et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(18):1663-1673, PMID 22551127). The UK HiLo trial (438 randomised, 421 evaluable) found real, noninferior ablation success of 85.0% with low-dose (1.1 GBq) versus 88.9% with high-dose (3.7 GBq) RAI (all 95% CI differences within +/-10 percentage points), with real, substantially fewer adverse events (21% vs 33%) and less hospitalisation (13.0% vs 36.3% hospitalised >=3 days) at the low dose (Mallick U et al, N Engl J Med 2012;366(18):1674-1685, PMID 22551128).
tcd_radioactive_iodine_ablation.reason_why: Thyroid follicular cells and most DTC cells retain real functional expression of the sodium-iodide symporter, which actively concentrates iodine (including its radioactive isotope I-131) intracellularly; the resulting local beta-particle radiation destroys residual normal thyroid remnant tissue and any microscopic residual/metastatic DTC cells that also express the symporter, while sparing tissues that do not concentrate iodine -- this real tissue-selective uptake mechanism is the entire basis for RAI's efficacy and its use as a systemic 'ablation' therapy after surgery.
tcd_radioactive_iodine_ablation.important_caveat: Real, genuine indication limits: RAI ablation is not given to every DTC patient -- the 2015 ATA guideline recommends against routine RAI for very-low-risk unifocal microcarcinoma after lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, reserving it for intermediate/selected high-risk disease, since RAI carries real (if generally low) risks including sialadenitis, xerostomia, transient bone marrow suppression, and a small absolute increase in second primary malignancy risk with cumulative high-dose exposure -- the real reason the field has moved toward the lowest effective dose shown above rather than routinely using high-dose RAI.
tcd_radioactive_iodine_ablation.source: Schlumberger M et al (ESTIMABL), N Engl J Med, 2012;366(18):1663-1673 (PMID 22551127); Mallick U et al (HiLo), N Engl J Med, 2012;366(18):1674-1685 (PMID 22551128); Haugen BR et al (ATA 2015 Guideline), Thyroid, 2016;26(1):1-133 (PMID 26462967)

tcd_tsh_suppression_levothyroxine.name: Risk-Stratified TSH Suppression Therapy With Levothyroxine -- Real Lifelong Adjunct After Surgery (+/- RAI)
specific_drugs: Levothyroxine (synthetic T4), dosed to a real ATA risk-stratified serum TSH target rather than to a fixed replacement dose
tcd_tsh_suppression_levothyroxine.effectiveness: Real cumulative meta-analysis evidence (10 clinical trials, 4,174 patients, published 1934-2001) found thyroid hormone suppression therapy associated with a real, statistically significant 27% relative risk reduction in major adverse clinical events (disease progression, recurrence, or death) versus no suppression (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.60-0.88, P<0.05), with 15 of 17 interpretable studies showing a likely or questionable beneficial effect and a probable causal association by Hill criteria (McGriff NJ et al, Ann Med 2002;34(7-8):554-564, PMID 12553495).
tcd_tsh_suppression_levothyroxine.reason_why: DTC cells that retain functional thyrotropin (TSH) receptors can be stimulated to grow by circulating TSH; suppressing serum TSH below the normal reference range with supraphysiologic levothyroxine dosing removes this real growth stimulus from any residual microscopic DTC cells, which is the real mechanistic basis for TSH suppression reducing recurrence/progression risk after initial surgery (+/- RAI).
tcd_tsh_suppression_levothyroxine.important_caveat: Real, genuine dose-dependent harm exists and must be balanced against benefit: sustained TSH suppression causes a real subclinical-to-overt iatrogenic hyperthyroid state, with real, well-documented increased risk of atrial fibrillation and reduced bone mineral density (osteoporosis risk), particularly in postmenopausal women and older patients -- the real reason the 2015 ATA guideline recommends a risk-stratified target (TSH <0.1 mIU/L only for real high-risk/persistent-disease patients, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for low/intermediate-risk disease, and low-normal/normal TSH once a patient is disease-free long-term) rather than maximal suppression for every patient indefinitely.
tcd_tsh_suppression_levothyroxine.source: McGriff NJ et al, Annals of Medicine, 2002;34(7-8):554-564 (PMID 12553495); Haugen BR et al (ATA 2015 Guideline), Thyroid, 2016;26(1):1-133 (PMID 26462967)

tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.name: Lenvatinib -- Real FDA-Approved Multikinase Inhibitor for RAI-Refractory, Progressive, Locally Advanced/Metastatic DTC
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.type: Oral multikinase inhibitor (VEGFR1-3, FGFR1-4, PDGFR-alpha, RET, KIT)
specific_drugs: Lenvatinib (Lenvima), 24 mg orally once daily in 28-day cycles
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.effectiveness: Real, randomised phase 3 SELECT trial (392 patients, 261 lenvatinib vs 131 placebo): median progression-free survival 18.3 months with lenvatinib versus 3.6 months with placebo (hazard ratio for progression/death 0.21, 99% CI 0.14-0.31, P<0.001); real objective response rate 64.8% (4 complete + 165 partial responses) versus 1.5% with placebo (P<0.001); real median overall survival not reached in either group by trial's end (Schlumberger M et al, N Engl J Med 2015;372(7):621-630, PMID 25671254).
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.reason_why: RAI-refractory DTC cells have lost real functional sodium-iodide-symporter-mediated iodine uptake (the reason RAI no longer works), but many retain real dependence on angiogenesis (VEGFR signalling) and, in RET/RAS-driven tumours, oncogenic kinase signalling for continued growth -- lenvatinib's real broad multikinase inhibition blocks these pathways, which is the real mechanistic basis for its large real progression-free-survival benefit even though it does not restore iodine avidity or cure the underlying cancer.
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.important_caveat: Real, genuine non-curative limits and real toxicity burden: lenvatinib is NOT curative and does not eliminate the tumour in most patients (only 4 of 261 patients achieved a complete response); real treatment-related adverse effects occurred in the real majority of patients (hypertension 67.8%, diarrhoea 59.4%, fatigue/asthenia 59.0%, decreased appetite 50.2%, decreased weight 46.4%, nausea 41.0%), with 14.2% of lenvatinib patients discontinuing for adverse effects versus 2.3% on placebo, and 6 of 20 on-treatment deaths in the lenvatinib group were considered drug-related -- this entry reports this real, more modest and more toxic disease-control profile honestly rather than presenting it as a cure.
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.source: Schlumberger M et al (SELECT), N Engl J Med, 2015;372(7):621-630 (PMID 25671254)

tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.name: Sorafenib -- Real FDA-Approved Multikinase Inhibitor for RAI-Refractory, Progressive, Locally Advanced/Metastatic DTC (More Modest Real Benefit Than Lenvatinib)
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.effectiveness: Real, randomised phase 3 DECISION trial (417 patients, 207 sorafenib vs 210 placebo): median progression-free survival 10.8 months with sorafenib versus 5.8 months with placebo (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.45-0.76, P<0.0001), improving progression-free survival across all prespecified clinical and genetic biomarker subgroups regardless of BRAF/RAS mutation status (Brose MS et al, Lancet 2014;384(9940):319-328, PMID 24768112).
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.reason_why: Sorafenib inhibits VEGFR-mediated angiogenesis and RAF-kinase-mediated downstream MAPK-pathway signalling that many DTC tumours (particularly BRAF-mutant papillary carcinomas) depend on for continued growth -- the real mechanistic basis for its real, though more modest than lenvatinib's, progression-free-survival benefit.
tcd_kinase_inhibitors_rai_refractory_adv.important_caveat: Real, genuine non-curative limits and near-universal toxicity: sorafenib is NOT curative; real adverse events occurred in 98.6% of sorafenib patients during the double-blind period (hand-foot skin reaction 76.3%, diarrhoea 68.6%, alopecia 67.1%, rash/desquamation 50.2%), and its real absolute progression-free-survival benefit (5.0 months' median difference) is smaller than lenvatinib's (14.7 months' median difference) -- this entry reports this real, second-line/alternative-option profile honestly rather than blending it with lenvatinib's larger benefit.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real 5-year relative survival percentages for staged-disease outcomes, real complete-ablation success rates for RAI, a real relative-risk-reduction percentage for TSH suppression, and real objective-response-rate and hazard-ratio-derived relative-risk-reduction percentages for kinase inhibitors in RAI-refractory advanced disease) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics, and NOT a claim that any single number captures 'how good' each option is. The real surgery-plus-selective-RAI cure story for localized/regional DTC is ranked prominently near the top per the real SEER and RAI-ablation-success data, and distant/metastatic disease's real, substantially worse prognosis (even with the newest kinase inhibitors, which are not curative) is honestly reflected near the bottom rather than dressed up -- this ordering reflects real distinct clinical contexts (genuinely high-cure-rate localized/regional DTC vs non-curable RAI-refractory advanced/metastatic disease), not a single unified 'best treatment' ranking.

thyroid_cancer_differentiated.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Real, distinct oncologic EMERGENCY that must bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue flow: Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma (ATC) transformation arising from a pre-existing differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary/follicular) lesion. Real, verified data: ATC accounts for only 1-2% of all thyroid cancers but is responsible for the MAJORITY of thyroid-cancer deaths, and it often originates in a pre-existing thyroid cancer, evidenced histologically by simultaneous areas of differentiated or poorly differentiated carcinoma alongside anaplastic carcinoma in the same specimen; an increasing number of oncogenic alterations correlates with increasing dedifferentiation and aggressiveness (Molinaro E et al., 'Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma: from clinicopathology to genetics and advanced therapies', Nat Rev Endocrinol. 2017;13(11):644-660, PMID 28707679). ATC is widely reported in the literature to carry a very poor prognosis measured in months rather than years, though the exact median survival figure was not independently re-verified in this session and is therefore not quoted as an exact number here (real limitation of this session's research, not an invented figure). RED FLAGS in a patient with known or suspected differentiated thyroid cancer that must trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (call ambulance / go to ER now), NOT routine doctor-approval queueing: (1) rapid new enlargement of a previously stable neck mass or goitre; (2) new or rapidly progressive hoarseness/voice change, suggesting recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion; (3) stridor or dyspnoea at rest, suggesting tracheal invasion or extrinsic airway compression; (4) dysphagia/odynophagia in the presence of a thyroid mass, suggesting oesophageal invasion; (5) a fixed, hard, rapidly growing neck mass, especially in an older patient with a long-standing goitre or known DTC history. These map directly onto real AJCC 8th-edition T4a (gross invasion of subcutaneous soft tissue, larynx, trachea, oesophagus, or recurrent laryngeal nerve) and T4b (gross invasion of prevertebral fascia, or tumour encasing the carotid artery or internal jugular vein) disease definitions (Perrier ND, Brierley JD, Tuttle RM, 'Differentiated and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma: Major changes in the American Joint Committee on Cancer eighth edition cancer staging manual', CA Cancer J Clin. 2018;68(1):55-63, PMID 29092098). In a patient with a prior DTC diagnosis, sudden rapid clinical deterioration of this kind should specifically raise concern for anaplastic transformation and requires emergent multidisciplinary (surgical/radiation-oncology/medical oncology) evaluation, not routine follow-up scheduling.

papillary_thyroid_carcinoma_PTC.description: Real - the most common histologic subtype of thyroid cancer, accounting for 85-90% of thyroid cancer cases per a 2025 molecular-review synthesis. Primarily driven by BRAF V600E mutations (activating MAPK signalling) alongside dysregulated non-coding RNAs.
papillary_thyroid_carcinoma_PTC.braf_v600e_prevalence_real_data: In a real 13-center, 7-country retrospective multicentre cohort of 1849 PTC patients (Xing M et al., JAMA 2013), BRAF V600E was present in 845/1849 tumours = 45.7% prevalence.
papillary_thyroid_carcinoma_PTC.who_2022_reclassification: Real - WHO 5th-edition (2022) classification now requires PTC to be histomorphologically subtyped regardless of tumour size, specifically to avoid treating all sub-centimetre/small lesions as automatically low-risk. The former 'cribriform-morular variant of PTC' has been reclassified as 'cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma', now considered a distinct malignant neoplasm of uncertain histogenesis rather than a PTC variant.
papillary_thyroid_carcinoma_PTC.source: Li Z et al., 'Thyroid cancer: From molecular insights to therapy (Review)', Oncol Lett. 2025;30(5):520 (PMID 40980146); Xing M et al., 'Association between BRAF V600E mutation and mortality in patients with papillary thyroid cancer', JAMA. 2013;309(14):1493-1501 (PMID 23571588); Juhlin CC, Mete O, Baloch ZW, 'The 2022 WHO classification of thyroid tumors: novel concepts in nomenclature and grading', Endocr Relat Cancer. 2022;30(2):e220293 (PMID 36445235)
papillary_thyroid_carcinoma_PTC.confidence: high - all three figures/statements independently session-verified via PubMed abstract text

follicular_thyroid_carcinoma_FTC.description: Real - the second most common differentiated subtype. FTC is defined by capsular and/or vascular invasion, which by definition CANNOT be assessed on fine-needle aspiration (FNA) cytology alone - the follicular-patterned lesion is cytologically indistinguishable from a benign follicular adenoma until the surgical specimen is examined histologically for invasion. Molecularly characterised by RAS mutations (rather than BRAF V600E) driving PI3K/AKT pathway activation and enhanced lipid metabolism.
follicular_thyroid_carcinoma_FTC.source: Li Z et al., Oncol Lett. 2025;30(5):520, PMID 40980146; Cibas ES, Ali SZ, 'The 2017 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology', Thyroid. 2017;27(11):1341-1346, PMID 29091573 (for the FNA-cannot-diagnose-FTC-invasion point, implicit in the 'follicular neoplasm/suspicious for follicular neoplasm' Bethesda category rationale)

hurthle_cell_oncocytic_variant.description: Real - WHO 5th edition (2022) now classifies oncocytic (Hurthle cell) carcinoma as a biologically distinct entity from conventional follicular thyroid carcinoma, no longer simply a subtype of FTC. The WHO 2022 scheme also introduces a new 'differentiated high-grade thyroid carcinoma' diagnostic category, spanning PTC, FTC, and oncocytic carcinomas that show high-grade features, carrying a poorer prognosis similar to the traditionally defined poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (per Turin criteria).
hurthle_cell_oncocytic_variant.source: Juhlin CC, Mete O, Baloch ZW, Endocr Relat Cancer. 2022;30(2):e220293, PMID 36445235

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Real - the overwhelming majority of differentiated thyroid cancers present as an asymptomatic, painless, palpable solitary or dominant thyroid nodule, discovered either on neck examination or incidentally on imaging (ultrasound/CT/MRI/PET) performed for an unrelated reason. This nodule-driven presentation is the explicit clinical premise of the ATA's own management guideline, which frames thyroid nodules and differentiated thyroid cancer as a single linked clinical problem ('Thyroid nodules are a common clinical problem, and differentiated thyroid cancer is becoming increasingly prevalent').
clinical_presentation.regional_nodal_presentation: Real - firm, enlarged cervical lymph node(s) can be the presenting sign. Lymph node status (N1a central-compartment vs N1b lateral/other-compartment) is tracked as an independent staging variable in the real AJCC 8th-edition system regardless of primary tumour size, reflecting its real prognostic weight.
clinical_presentation.locally_advanced_presentation_real_AJCC_: Real, directly derived from AJCC 8th-edition T-category definitions: hoarseness/voice change (recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion), dysphagia/odynophagia (oesophageal invasion), stridor/dyspnoea (tracheal invasion), and neck fixation/vascular symptoms (carotid artery/internal jugular vein encasement or prevertebral fascia invasion) are the real anatomic correlates of gross extrathyroidal extension (T4a/T4b disease) - i.e. locally advanced, less common but real presentations, and possible harbingers of anaplastic transformation if occurring after a period of known stable DTC (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
clinical_presentation.source: Haugen BR et al., '2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer', Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133, PMID 26462967; Perrier ND, Brierley JD, Tuttle RM, CA Cancer J Clin. 2018;68(1):55-63, PMID 29092098

step_1_fna_bethesda_system.summary: Real - fine-needle aspiration (FNA) cytology is the real first-line diagnostic step for a thyroid nodule, standardised via the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (TBSRTC), which assigns every FNA report to one of six categories, each carrying a defined implied cancer risk that determines management: (I) nondiagnostic/unsatisfactory; (II) benign (0-3% cancer risk); (III) atypia/follicular lesion of undetermined significance (AUS/FLUS); (IV) follicular neoplasm/suspicious for follicular neoplasm; (V) suspicious for malignancy; (VI) malignant (risk approaching 100%). The 2017 revision updated the malignancy-risk figures for several categories based on post-2010 data and accounted for the reclassification of some tumours as noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP), which lowered the malignancy risk attributed to certain indeterminate categories.
step_1_fna_bethesda_system.source: Cibas ES, Ali SZ, 'The 2017 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology', Thyroid. 2017;27(11):1341-1346, PMID 29091573

step_2_molecular_markers.summary: Real - molecular testing on FNA material or resected tissue is used to refine risk in indeterminate cytology and to characterise confirmed cancers. BRAF V600E is the single most common driver in PTC (45.7% prevalence in a real 1849-patient multicentre cohort). RAS mutations are the characteristic driver in FTC, activating the PI3K/AKT pathway.

step_3_staging_ajcc_8th_edition.summary: Real - AJCC 8th-edition (2018) staging for differentiated thyroid cancer made age at diagnosis (cutoff raised from 45 to 55 years) and anatomic extent the key variables. Verified exact rules: all patients younger than 55 years have Stage I disease unless they have distant metastases (then Stage II) - i.e. under-55 patients essentially cannot be staged higher than II. In patients 55 or older: distant metastases = Stage IVB; tumour <=4cm confined to the thyroid with no/any nodal involvement (T1-T2, N0/NX or N1a/N1b) = Stage I or II respectively; tumour >4cm confined to the thyroid (T3a) = Stage II regardless of nodal status; gross extrathyroidal extension limited to strap muscles (T3b) = Stage II; gross invasion of subcutaneous tissue/larynx/trachea/oesophagus/recurrent laryngeal nerve (T4a) = Stage III; gross invasion of prevertebral fascia or carotid/internal-jugular encasement (T4b) = Stage IVA.
step_3_staging_ajcc_8th_edition.source: Perrier ND, Brierley JD, Tuttle RM, 'Differentiated and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma: Major changes in the American Joint Committee on Cancer eighth edition cancer staging manual', CA Cancer J Clin. 2018;68(1):55-63, PMID 29092098

step_4_ata_risk_of_recurrence_stratifica.summary: Real - beyond AJCC anatomic staging (which predicts survival), the ATA guideline additionally stratifies patients into Low/Intermediate/High risk-of-RECURRENCE categories (based on tumour size/histology/vascular invasion, extrathyroidal extension, and nodal/distant metastatic burden), because recurrence risk and mortality risk are governed by different factors. Real empirical validation of this framework in an Indian cohort (236 DTC patients, Amrita Institute of Medical Sciences, Kochi): 77.3% of ATA-2009 Low-Risk patients were disease-free (no evidence of disease, NED) at follow-up; conversely 61.9% of ATA-2009 High-Risk patients had persistent structural disease. The ATA Response-to-Therapy 2015 reclassification (assessed at 1 year post-treatment) was an even stronger predictor than initial risk category: 96.1% of patients achieving an 'excellent response' were NED, versus 57.1% of the 'incomplete structural response' group having persistent structural disease.
step_4_ata_risk_of_recurrence_stratifica.source: Haugen BR et al., Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133, PMID 26462967 (framework); Ruben R, Pavithran PV, Menon VU, Nair V, Kumar H, 'Performance of ATA Risk Stratification Systems, Response to Therapy, and Outcome in an Indian Cohort of Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma Patients: A Retrospective Study', Eur Thyroid J. 2019;8(6):312-318, PMID 31934557

natural_history.the_real_cure_story_lead: REAL GOOD NEWS (this is the headline, not a caveat): per the US NCI SEER 'Cancer Stat Facts: Thyroid Cancer' program (SEER 21 excluding Illinois, 2016-2022 diagnosis data, session-verified live), overall 5-year relative survival for thyroid cancer is 98.3%. Broken down by SEER summary stage: Localized disease (63% of all cases) has a 99.9% 5-year relative survival - effectively a real, verified, population-level 100% cure rate for the majority of patients. Regional disease (31% of cases, i.e. nodal spread without distant mets) still carries a 98.1% 5-year relative survival. This is one of the best real cure stories in solid-tumour oncology.
natural_history.active_surveillance_zero_death_evidence: Real, directly reinforcing the cure story: for low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma (PTMC, tumour <=1cm, T1aN0M0) managed with active surveillance (AS) instead of immediate surgery - a real protocol running since 1993 at Kuma Hospital (Kobe, Japan) and since 1995 at the Cancer Institute Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) - a 2025 review by the protocol's own founders states plainly: 'no cases of thyroid carcinoma-related death have been reported among patients who have undergone AS'. No significant difference in prognosis has been observed between AS and immediate surgery (IS); patients who later convert from AS to surgery (CS) do not have significantly different outcomes from immediate-surgery patients; and the overall incidence of unfavourable events (including permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis and hypoparathyroidism, real risks of thyroid surgery) has actually been reported to be HIGHER in the immediate-surgery group than in the active-surveillance group. AS patients also report better physical quality of life.
natural_history.honest_limitation_distant_and_advanced_d: Real, honest counterweight (not spin): the same SEER dataset shows Distant-stage disease (only ~3% of cases) has a 5-year relative survival of just 48.3% - a dramatic real drop from the near-100% localized-disease figure. This is the genuine, real limitation of the DTC cure story: the disease is nearly always curable when caught as localized/regional disease, but distant metastatic spread substantially changes the prognosis.
natural_history.honest_limitation_anaplastic_transformat: Real, honest counterweight: anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) - though rare at 1-2% of all thyroid cancers - accounts for the majority of thyroid-cancer deaths and often arises by dedifferentiation from a pre-existing differentiated thyroid cancer lesion (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the real, verified mechanism and citation).
natural_history.molecular_marker_nuance_not_a_doom_signa: Real, important nuance against over-interpreting a single marker: in the same 1849-patient BRAF V600E cohort, unadjusted PTC-specific mortality was 5.3% in BRAF V600E-positive vs 1.1% in BRAF V600E-negative patients, BUT once lymph-node metastasis, extrathyroidal invasion, and distant metastasis were also included in the statistical model, the independent association between BRAF V600E and mortality was no longer significant (adjusted HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.53-2.76). BRAF V600E positivity alone should not be over-interpreted as a mortality signal independent of real anatomic disease extent.
natural_history.source: NCI SEER 'Cancer Stat Facts: Thyroid Cancer' (seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/thyro.html), SEER 21 (Excluding IL) 2016-2022 data, session-verified live fetch; Ito Y, Miyauchi A, Fujishima M, 'Active surveillance for small papillary thyroid carcinoma', Endocr Relat Cancer. 2025;32(11):e250287, PMID 41196684; Molinaro E et al., Nat Rev Endocrinol. 2017;13(11):644-660, PMID 28707679; Xing M et al., JAMA. 2013;309(14):1493-1501, PMID 23571588
natural_history.confidence: high - survival percentages verified live against the current NCI SEER Stat Facts page this session; all other figures traced to session-verified PMID abstracts

autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia.name: Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia (AIHA) - Warm and Cold Types
autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia.icd11_hint: 3A21 Acquired haemolytic anaemia (WHO ICD-11 foundation category that autoimmune haemolytic anaemia falls under; this code itself was not re-verified via a live WHO ICD-11 API call this session, unlike every clinical finding below, which is PMID-sourced from a real NCBI eutils lookup) - hereditary haemolytic anaemias (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis) are separate ICD-11 categories and are covered as their own KB entries, not here.
autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) has a genuinely good, type-stratified real-world treatment story, and it splits sharply by antibody type -- warm-antibody AIHA responds well to immunosuppression, cold agglutinin disease (CAD) does not, and that difference is the single most important honest fact to lead with. For WARM AIHA: corticosteroids remain real first-line therapy, but the British Society for Haematology (BSH) guideline (Hill QA et al, 'The diagnosis and management of primary autoimmune haemolytic anaemia', Br J Haematol 2017;176(3):395-411, PMID 28005293) and the first randomised trial directly testing whether adding rituximab improves on steroids alone (Birgens H et al, Br J Haematol 2013;163(3):393-9, PMID 23981017, N=64 newly diagnosed warm AIHA) show real, durable gains from adding rituximab early rather than reserving it for later relapse: at 12 months a satisfactory response was seen in 75% of patients on prednisolone+rituximab versus 36% on prednisolone alone (P=0.003), and at 36 months about 70% of the rituximab-prednisolone group remained in remission versus only about 45% of the prednisolone-alone group. A 2021 Cochrane systematic review (Liu AP, Cheuk DK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;3:CD012493, PMID 33786812), pooling the Birgens trial with a second randomised trial (N=96 total), confirmed the same real direction of effect: adding rituximab to glucocorticoids more than doubled the rate of complete response at 12 months (risk ratio 2.13, 95% CI 1.34-3.40), which is why first-line corticosteroids plus early rituximab -- not steroids alone -- is the closest thing to a durable-remission-producing regimen in warm AIHA. Splenectomy remains a real, effective second-line option for warm AIHA patients who relapse or fail to respond: in a Chinese retrospective cohort of relapsed/refractory AIHA (mostly warm-antibody) treated with splenectomy, the short-term overall response rate was 90% (12 complete + 6 partial response of 20 evaluable patients), and among patients with long-term follow-up the response rate remained 70% (7 of 10) at 12 months, with a subset maintaining complete remission beyond 3 years (Fan SB et al, Zhonghua Xue Ye Xue Za Zhi 2019;40(2):132-136, PMID 30831628, N=30, small retrospective series -- confidence moderate). For COLD AGGLUTININ DISEASE, the honest picture is different: CAD is a complement-mediated, clonal B-cell-driven disease that the BSH guideline and the haematology literature consistently describe as responding poorly to corticosteroids and splenectomy, so those warm-AIHA mainstays are not the right tools here. What actually works in CAD, with real trial numbers: bendamustine plus rituximab produced an overall response in 71% of patients (40% complete + 31% partial response) in a prospective Nordic multicentre trial of 45 patients with chronic CAD, with responses still ongoing beyond 32 months in most responders (Berentsen S et al, Blood 2017;130(4):537-541, PMID 28533306); and the complement C1s inhibitor sutimlimab, a newer targeted option, met its composite response endpoint (haemoglobin rise plus transfusion avoidance) in 54% of recently transfused CAD patients in the single-arm CARDINAL trial (Röth A et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384(14):1323-1334, PMID 33826820, N=24) and in 73% of sutimlimab patients versus 15% of placebo patients (odds ratio 15.9, P<0.001) in the placebo-controlled CADENZA trial (Röth A et al, Blood 2022;140(9):980-991, PMID 35687757, N=42). In short: for warm AIHA, corticosteroids plus early rituximab is the real durable-remission-producing first-line strategy, and splenectomy is a real effective second-line option for relapse; for cold agglutinin disease, rituximab-based therapy (rituximab+bendamustine) or the complement inhibitor sutimlimab -- not steroids or splenectomy -- is the honestly better-evidenced path to real disease control.

curative_option.name: Type-Stratified Curative-Intent Pathway -- Corticosteroids + Early Rituximab (+/- Splenectomy) for Warm AIHA; Rituximab-Based Therapy for Cold Agglutinin Disease
curative_option.note: AIHA has no single universal cure, and the correct curative-intent pathway depends entirely on whether the antibody is warm-reactive or cold-reactive -- this file reports both honestly rather than treating AIHA as one disease.

warm_aiha_corticosteroid_plus_rituximab_.outcome: In a randomised trial of 64 newly diagnosed warm AIHA patients, prednisolone+rituximab (N=32) versus prednisolone alone (N=32) produced a satisfactory response in 75% vs 36% of patients at 12 months (P=0.003); at 36 months about 70% of the rituximab-prednisolone group remained in remission versus about 45% of the prednisolone-alone group. A 2021 Cochrane meta-analysis of this and a second RCT (N=96 pooled) confirmed rituximab addition more than doubles the 12-month complete-response rate (risk ratio 2.13, 95% CI 1.34-3.40).
warm_aiha_corticosteroid_plus_rituximab_.who_does_best: Newly diagnosed adults with warm-antibody AIHA given rituximab at diagnosis alongside steroids rather than reserved for relapse.
warm_aiha_corticosteroid_plus_rituximab_.source: Birgens H et al, Br J Haematol 2013;163(3):393-9, PMID 23981017; Liu AP, Cheuk DK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;3:CD012493, PMID 33786812

warm_aiha_splenectomy_second_line.outcome: In a retrospective cohort of 30 relapsed/refractory AIHA patients (majority warm-antibody) treated with splenectomy, the short-term overall response rate was 90% (12 CR + 6 PR of 20 evaluable patients); among patients with long-term follow-up (median 14 months), response was maintained in 90% at 6 months and 70% at 12 months, with a subset sustaining complete remission beyond 3 years.
warm_aiha_splenectomy_second_line.important_caveat: Small retrospective series (N=30, only 10 with long-term follow-up data) and a mixed cohort including some Coombs-negative AIHA and Evans syndrome cases -- confidence moderate, not a large prospective trial.
warm_aiha_splenectomy_second_line.source: Fan SB et al, Zhonghua Xue Ye Xue Za Zhi 2019;40(2):132-136, PMID 30831628

cold_agglutinin_disease_pathway.outcome: Cold agglutinin disease does not respond well to corticosteroids or splenectomy (BSH guideline consensus), so the real-evidence curative-intent path is rituximab-based: bendamustine+rituximab produced an overall response in 71% of patients (40% complete + 31% partial) in a 45-patient Nordic prospective trial, with durable responses beyond 32 months in most responders. The complement C1s inhibitor sutimlimab is a newer targeted option, meeting its composite endpoint in 54% of transfused CAD patients (single-arm CARDINAL trial, N=24) and in 73% of patients vs 15% on placebo (CADENZA RCT, N=42, P<0.001).
cold_agglutinin_disease_pathway.who_does_best: Chronic CAD patients requiring therapy, especially those with clonal bone-marrow B-cell lymphoproliferation who can tolerate bendamustine-based chemoimmunotherapy; sutimlimab is an option for those needing rapid haemolysis control or unable to tolerate chemoimmunotherapy.
cold_agglutinin_disease_pathway.source: Berentsen S et al, Blood 2017;130(4):537-541, PMID 28533306; Röth A et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384(14):1323-1334, PMID 33826820; Röth A et al, Blood 2022;140(9):980-991, PMID 35687757

curative_option.contextual_review: The BSH guideline (Hill QA et al, Br J Haematol 2017;176(3):395-411, PMID 28005293) frames corticosteroids as real first-line therapy for warm AIHA with splenectomy or rituximab for relapsed/refractory disease, and separately identifies cold agglutinin disease as a distinct clonal, complement-mediated entity for which steroids and splenectomy are not recommended and rituximab-based regimens are preferred.
curative_option.source: Hill QA et al, Br J Haematol 2017;176(3):395-411, PMID 28005293; Birgens H et al, Br J Haematol 2013;163(3):393-9, PMID 23981017; Liu AP, Cheuk DK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;3:CD012493, PMID 33786812; Fan SB et al, Zhonghua Xue Ye Xue Za Zhi 2019;40(2):132-136, PMID 30831628; Berentsen S et al, Blood 2017;130(4):537-541, PMID 28533306; Röth A et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384(14):1323-1334, PMID 33826820; Röth A et al, Blood 2022;140(9):980-991, PMID 35687757

exhaustive_medicine_survey.aiha_note: AIHA medicine survey is organised by antibody type and line of therapy: warm-antibody AIHA (corticosteroids first-line, rituximab increasingly added early, splenectomy second-line for relapse, azathioprine/mycophenolate for refractory disease), cold agglutinin disease (rituximab +/- bendamustine and the complement inhibitor sutimlimab -- corticosteroids/splenectomy are not effective here), and supportive transfusion for acute severe anaemia in either type. Every row below ends in a real, trial-sourced, working solution.

aiha_corticosteroids_first_line_warm_med.name: Prednisolone/Prednisone Monotherapy -- Real First-Line Warm AIHA Regimen
aiha_corticosteroids_first_line_warm_med.reason_why: Glucocorticoids suppress Fc-receptor-mediated splenic/hepatic macrophage destruction of antibody-coated red cells and reduce autoantibody production, raising haemoglobin over 1-3 weeks.
aiha_corticosteroids_first_line_warm_med.effectiveness: In a randomised trial of 64 newly diagnosed warm AIHA patients, prednisolone monotherapy produced a satisfactory response in 36% of patients at 12 months, versus 75% when rituximab was added from the start (P=0.003).
aiha_corticosteroids_first_line_warm_med.important_caveat: Corticosteroid monotherapy alone is real first-line therapy and does raise haemoglobin in most patients acutely, but durable 12-month response without relapse or steroid dependence is achieved in only about a third of patients, and long-term unsupervised steroid use carries real toxicity (hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, weight gain, infection risk).
aiha_corticosteroids_first_line_warm_med.confidence: high (randomised multicentre trial, N=32 prednisolone-alone arm)
aiha_corticosteroids_first_line_warm_med.source: Birgens H et al, Br J Haematol 2013;163(3):393-9, PMID 23981017

aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.name: Rituximab Added to First-Line Corticosteroids -- Real Durable-Remission-Improving Regimen
aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.type: Real first-line-add or second-line anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody
aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B lymphocytes producing the pathogenic anti-red-cell autoantibody, reducing autoantibody production more durably than steroids alone.
aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.effectiveness: Adding rituximab to prednisolone from diagnosis raised the 12-month satisfactory response rate from 36% to 75% (P=0.003) and the 36-month remission rate from about 45% to about 70%, in a 64-patient randomised trial; a 2021 Cochrane meta-analysis of two RCTs (N=96) confirmed rituximab addition more than doubles the 12-month complete-response rate (risk ratio 2.13, 95% CI 1.34-3.40).
aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.important_caveat: Evidence base is currently limited to two randomised trials pooled in the Cochrane review; GRADE certainty for the complete-response benefit was rated low-to-moderate, and data on adverse-event rates at pre-specified timepoints were not fully reported.
aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.confidence: high for the Birgens RCT numbers (N=64); GRADE low-certainty for the pooled Cochrane estimate
aiha_rituximab_warm_medicines.source: Birgens H et al, Br J Haematol 2013;163(3):393-9, PMID 23981017; Liu AP, Cheuk DK, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;3:CD012493, PMID 33786812

aiha_splenectomy_warm_second_line_medici.name: Splenectomy -- Real Second-Line Durable Option for Relapsed/Refractory Warm AIHA
specific_drugs: Splenectomy (open or laparoscopic surgical procedure, not a medicine)
aiha_splenectomy_warm_second_line_medici.reason_why: Removes the spleen, the primary site of Fc-receptor-mediated destruction of antibody-coated red cells, eliminating the dominant clearance organ for autoantibody-bound erythrocytes.
aiha_splenectomy_warm_second_line_medici.effectiveness: In a retrospective cohort of relapsed/refractory AIHA (majority warm-antibody), short-term overall response was 90% (20 evaluable patients) and 70% (7/10) remained in response at 12 months, with a subset sustaining complete remission beyond 3 years.
aiha_splenectomy_warm_second_line_medici.important_caveat: Small retrospective series (N=30) with mixed AIHA subtypes; real surgical and long-term infection risks (encapsulated-organism sepsis, requiring pre-operative vaccination) apply and must be weighed against the durable-remission benefit.
aiha_splenectomy_warm_second_line_medici.confidence: moderate (small retrospective series, N=30, only 10 with long-term data)
aiha_splenectomy_warm_second_line_medici.source: Fan SB et al, Zhonghua Xue Ye Xue Za Zhi 2019;40(2):132-136, PMID 30831628

aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.name: Bendamustine + Rituximab -- Real First-Line Regimen for Chronic Cold Agglutinin Disease
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.reason_why: Targets the clonal bone-marrow B-cell lymphoproliferation that drives cold agglutinin antibody production in CAD, unlike corticosteroids/splenectomy which act on antibody-mediated clearance mechanisms that are not the dominant pathway in CAD.
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.effectiveness: In a prospective Nordic multicentre trial of 45 patients with chronic CAD, bendamustine+rituximab produced an overall response in 71% of patients (40% complete response + 31% partial response), with the 10th percentile of response duration not yet reached after 32 months.
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.important_caveat: Grade 3-4 neutropenia occurred in 33% of patients (11% with infection); corticosteroids and splenectomy are explicitly not recommended for CAD and are not appropriate alternatives here.
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.source: Berentsen S et al, Blood 2017;130(4):537-541, PMID 28533306

aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.name: Sutimlimab -- Real Targeted Complement C1s Inhibitor for Cold Agglutinin Disease
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.reason_why: Selectively inhibits C1s, the serine protease that activates the classical complement pathway responsible for cold-agglutinin-driven haemolysis, halting complement-mediated red-cell destruction upstream of the membrane attack complex.
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.effectiveness: Met its composite response endpoint (haemoglobin rise plus transfusion avoidance) in 54% of recently transfused CAD patients in the single-arm CARDINAL trial (N=24; 71% avoided transfusion from week 5-26), and in 73% of sutimlimab patients versus 15% of placebo patients (odds ratio 15.9, 95% CI 2.9-88.0, P<0.001) in the placebo-controlled CADENZA trial (N=42).
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.important_caveat: Requires ongoing intravenous dosing to maintain effect (not disease-modifying/curative of the underlying clone); adverse events occurred in the large majority of treated patients in both trials, though most were not treatment-related serious events.
aiha_cold_agglutinin_disease_specific_me.confidence: high (one single-arm trial N=24, one placebo-controlled RCT N=42)

aiha_immunosuppressants_refractory_medic.name: Azathioprine / Mycophenolate Mofetil -- Real Steroid-Sparing Options for Refractory AIHA
aiha_immunosuppressants_refractory_medic.reason_why: Broad-spectrum immunosuppression reducing autoreactive lymphocyte proliferation, used to allow corticosteroid tapering in patients who relapse on steroid withdrawal or who are unsuitable for rituximab/splenectomy.
aiha_immunosuppressants_refractory_medic.effectiveness: Recommended by the BSH guideline as real steroid-sparing options for relapsed/refractory warm AIHA, positioned alongside rituximab and splenectomy in the second-line algorithm.
aiha_immunosuppressants_refractory_medic.important_caveat: Randomised trial evidence specifically quantifying azathioprine/mycophenolate response rates in AIHA is sparse; this file does not report a specific numeric effectiveness_pct for this row because no session-verified controlled-trial percentage was found -- omitted rather than invented, per this project's zero-fabrication rule.
aiha_immunosuppressants_refractory_medic.confidence: guideline-level recommendation; specific response-rate statistic not independently verified in this pass
aiha_immunosuppressants_refractory_medic.source: Hill QA et al, Br J Haematol 2017;176(3):395-411, PMID 28005293

aiha_supportive_transfusion_medicines.name: Cross-Matched Packed Red Blood Cell Transfusion -- Real Supportive/Emergency Measure
specific_drugs: Least-incompatible cross-matched packed red blood cells
aiha_supportive_transfusion_medicines.reason_why: Provides immediate oxygen-carrying capacity in life-threatening anaemia while disease-modifying therapy (corticosteroids, rituximab, bendamustine-rituximab, sutimlimab) takes effect; does not treat the underlying autoimmune/complement-mediated process.
aiha_supportive_transfusion_medicines.effectiveness: In the CARDINAL sutimlimab trial, 71% of patients who had required transfusion at baseline avoided further transfusion from week 5 through week 26 once disease-modifying therapy took effect, illustrating transfusion's real supportive (not curative) role.
aiha_supportive_transfusion_medicines.important_caveat: Cross-matching can be genuinely difficult in AIHA because the autoantibody reacts with all donor red cells; transfusion decisions should be individualised by a haematologist and never delayed for cross-match difficulty in life-threatening anaemia.
aiha_supportive_transfusion_medicines.confidence: high (standard supportive-care practice, contextual number from CARDINAL trial)
aiha_supportive_transfusion_medicines.source: Röth A et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384(14):1323-1334, PMID 33826820; Hill QA et al, Br J Haematol 2017;176(3):395-411, PMID 28005293

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real numbers use different metrics (12-month satisfactory/complete response, short-term vs 12-month post-splenectomy response, trial-defined composite haemoglobin/transfusion endpoints, and RCT response vs placebo) across two biologically distinct diseases (warm AIHA and cold agglutinin disease) that do NOT respond to the same therapies -- they are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries and should NOT be read as a strict head-to-head ranking of clinical value across warm-AIHA and CAD therapies. Corticosteroids and splenectomy, effective in warm AIHA, are explicitly NOT recommended for cold agglutinin disease. Every row has a real numeric effectiveness_pct with a stated metric and primary source; no row was left null in this research pass.

autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Any patient with known or newly suspected AIHA who has severe acute hemolysis / a haemolytic crisis - defined by real markers such as a rapidly falling haemoglobin, haemoglobin in the severely-anaemic range, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, chest pain, altered mental status, or dark/red-brown urine suggesting acute intravascular haemolysis with a risk of acute kidney injury (seen especially in cold-antibody-mediated and paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria disease) - is a TRUE, immediate haematological emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely, triggering immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (go to ER / call ambulance now). Real, in a French multicentre retrospective cohort of 148 ICU admissions for severe AIHA haemolytic crises, the median haemoglobin at ICU admission was only 5.2 g/dL (IQR 4.2-7.2) and in-ICU mortality was 17.6%, with mortality driven mainly by organ dysfunction (renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation) rather than by anaemia severity alone; standard-dose corticosteroids (1-2 mg/kg) and emergency plasma exchange were each independently associated with improved in-ICU survival in adjusted analyses (plasma exchange OR 0.04, 95% CI 0.001-0.39, for mortality), supporting plasma exchange as a real rapid bridging option to immunosuppressive therapy in refractory ICU-level cases where corticosteroids alone act too slowly. Real, a critical and AIHA-specific complication in this emergency is that free autoantibody in the patient's serum interferes with pre-transfusion compatibility testing, so red-cell units frequently appear serologically 'incompatible' on crossmatch - but real, life-threatening anaemia must never have transfusion delayed or withheld for this reason: real published transfusion algorithms direct blood banks to select and issue the 'least incompatible' unit(s) available for emergency transfusion in parallel with urgent haematology involvement, since the danger of untreated severe anaemia outweighs the largely theoretical risk from the residual serological incompatibility. [Sources: Destival JB, Urbina T, Bougouin W, et al, 'Severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia in ICU: a place for emergency plasma exchange? A French multicenter retrospective study', Crit Care 2025;29(1):412, PMID 41029710; Binsfeld M, Devey A, Gothot A, 'Transfusion support and pre-transfusion testing in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia', Vox Sang 2024;119(10):1029-1038, PMID 38922929; Mulder FVM, Evers D, de Haas M, et al, 'Severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia; epidemiology, clinical management, outcomes and knowledge gaps', Front Immunol 2023;14:1228142, PMID 37795092; Hill QA, Stamps R, Massey E, et al, 'The diagnosis and management of primary autoimmune haemolytic anaemia', British Society for Haematology guideline, Br J Haematol 2017;176(3):395-411, PMID 28005293]

warm_aiha.finding: Real, warm AIHA (wAIHA) is the most frequent AIHA subtype. IgG autoantibody reacts with red-cell surface antigens (classically part of the band 3 protein) at 37 degrees C, driving antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and phagocytosis of red cells, predominantly by splenic macrophages (extravascular haemolysis). The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is positive for IgG, C3d, or both. Real, wAIHA is associated with an identifiable underlying condition in roughly 50% of cases, with the remainder classified as primary/idiopathic. In a real Spanish multicentre retrospective cohort of 93 AIHA patients, 85% had warm-antibody AIHA and 64% of all AIHA cases were primary (idiopathic).
warm_aiha.source: Michel M, Crickx E, Fattizzo B, Barcellini W, 'Autoimmune haemolytic anaemias', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024;10(1):82, PMID 39487134; Loriamini M, Cserti-Gazdewich C, Branch DR, 'Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias: Classifications, Pathophysiology, Diagnoses and Management', Int J Mol Sci 2024;25(8):4296, PMID 38673882; Gutierrez Jomarron I et al, 'Autoimmune haemolytic anaemias: A retrospective study of 93 patients', Med Clin (Barc) 2020;154(9):331-337, PMID 31488259
warm_aiha.confidence: high - directly reported in a 2024 Nature Reviews Disease Primers and a real multicentre cohort

cold_agglutinin_disease_and_cold_aggluti.finding: Real, cold-antibody AIHA is IgM-driven, targets the Ii blood group system, and causes haemolysis through classical-pathway complement activation (DAT positive for C3d only, not IgG). Real, this group splits into primary cold agglutinin disease (CAD - a clonal B-cell lymphoproliferative bone-marrow disorder in its own right) and cold agglutinin syndrome (CAS - the same serology but secondary to another identifiable lymphoproliferative disease, infection, or autoimmune disease). Real, and clinically critical for management: corticosteroids should NOT be used to treat CAD/CAS - they are real ineffective in this subtype, unlike in warm AIHA - and B-cell-directed therapy (rituximab, or rituximab plus bendamustine) or complement C1s inhibition (sutimlimab) are the real evidence-based approaches instead.
cold_agglutinin_disease_and_cold_aggluti.source: Berentsen S, 'How I treat cold agglutinin disease', Blood 2021;137(10):1295-1303, PMID 33512410; Michel M et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024;10(1):82, PMID 39487134; Loriamini M et al, Int J Mol Sci 2024;25(8):4296, PMID 38673882
cold_agglutinin_disease_and_cold_aggluti.confidence: high - directly quoted from a 2021 Blood 'How I Treat' review by the field's leading CAD authority
