aplas_allogeneic_hsct_sibling_vs_mud.reason_why: The conditioning regimen (ATG plus cyclophosphamide, sometimes with fludarabine or low-dose total body irradiation) ablates the autoreactive T-cell-mediated immune attack that is destroying the patient's own hematopoietic stem cells, then the infused donor graft fully repopulates the marrow with a new, non-autoimmune-targeted hematopoietic system -- addressing the root autoimmune destruction rather than only suppressing it, which is why transplant is the real closest option to a durable, treatment-free cure.
aplas_allogeneic_hsct_sibling_vs_mud.real_working_solution: HLA-matched sibling donor HSCT is the real preferred curative-intent option in younger, fit patients with an available sibling donor; matched unrelated donor HSCT is the real next-best alternative in patients lacking a matched sibling donor.
aplas_allogeneic_hsct_sibling_vs_mud.source: Chen X et al, Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2018;24:86-90 (PMID 29032265); Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204:784-804 (PMID 38247114); Bacigalupo A, Blood 2017;129:1428-1436 (PMID 28096088)

aplas_atg_cyclosporine_immunosuppression.name: Antithymocyte Globulin (ATG) Plus Cyclosporine Immunosuppressive Therapy -- Horse ATG Preferred Over Rabbit ATG
aplas_atg_cyclosporine_immunosuppression.type: Combination immunosuppressive therapy targeting the autoreactive T-cells destroying hematopoietic stem cells
aplas_atg_cyclosporine_immunosuppression.effectiveness: Real hematologic response at 6 months: horse ATG 68% (95% CI 56-80) vs rabbit ATG 37% (95% CI 24-49), P<0.001. Real 3-year overall survival: horse ATG 96% (censored at HSCT)/94% (uncensored) vs rabbit ATG 76%/70% (P=0.04/0.008), N=120 randomized.
aplas_atg_cyclosporine_immunosuppression.reason_why: ATG depletes and modulates the autoreactive T-lymphocytes attacking hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells; cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor, further suppresses T-cell activation by blocking IL-2 gene transcription -- together relieving the immune attack enough for surviving stem cells to recover hematopoiesis without requiring a full transplant.
aplas_atg_cyclosporine_immunosuppression.real_working_solution: Horse (equine) ATG plus cyclosporine is the real standard first-line IST backbone for patients without a matched sibling donor or unsuitable for upfront transplant, per the BSH 2024 guideline; rabbit ATG is real but statistically inferior as first-line therapy and is reserved for settings where horse ATG is unavailable, or for retreatment.
aplas_atg_cyclosporine_immunosuppression.source: Scheinberg P et al, N Engl J Med 2011;365:430-438 (PMID 21812672); Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204:784-804 (PMID 38247114)
specific_drugs: Rabbit Antithymocyte Globulin (Thymoglobulin) -- real but inferior first-line alternative

aplas_eltrombopag_added_to_ist.name: Eltrombopag Added to Standard ATG + Cyclosporine Immunosuppression
aplas_eltrombopag_added_to_ist.type: Oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonist added to first-line immunosuppressive therapy from treatment start
aplas_eltrombopag_added_to_ist.effectiveness: Real complete response 58% and overall response 94% at 6 months in the cohort receiving eltrombopag from day 1 to 6 months, versus a historical IST-alone cohort's complete response 10% and overall response 66%; real 2-year survival 97%, N=92 -- Townsley DM et al, N Engl J Med 2017;376:1540-1550 (PMID 28423296).
aplas_eltrombopag_added_to_ist.reason_why: Eltrombopag stimulates the thrombopoietin receptor (MPL) on residual hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, promoting their proliferation and multilineage differentiation, which augments marrow recovery when combined with the T-cell-suppressing action of ATG plus cyclosporine -- directly addressing the reduced stem-cell reserve that can limit the efficacy of immunosuppression given alone.
aplas_eltrombopag_added_to_ist.real_working_solution: Adding eltrombopag to standard horse-ATG plus cyclosporine from the start of treatment is real, BSH-2024-guideline-endorsed first-line practice that produces substantially higher hematologic response rates than IST alone.
aplas_eltrombopag_added_to_ist.source: Townsley DM et al, N Engl J Med 2017;376:1540-1550 (PMID 28423296); Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204:784-804 (PMID 38247114)

aplas_supportive_care.name: Supportive Care -- Blood/Platelet Transfusion Support, Growth Factors, and Infection Prophylaxis
aplas_supportive_care.effectiveness: Not curative on its own; real, guideline-mandated throughout the disease course to prevent bleeding- and infection-related mortality while definitive therapy (HSCT or IST) takes effect -- Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204:784-804 (PMID 38247114).
aplas_supportive_care.reason_why: Severe pancytopenia from marrow failure causes real bleeding and infection risk before, and while, definitive therapy restores hematopoiesis; transfusion support and antimicrobial prophylaxis bridge this vulnerable window and prevent mortality from cytopenia-related complications rather than treating the underlying marrow failure itself.
aplas_supportive_care.real_working_solution: Leukoreduced and irradiated red-cell and platelet transfusion support, antimicrobial/antifungal prophylaxis, and growth factor support in specific settings, alongside HSCT or IST, per the BSH 2024 guideline.
aplas_supportive_care.source: Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204:784-804 (PMID 38247114)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real 3-year overall survival from single/multi-center transplant and IST cohorts, and real 6-month hematologic response rates from a prospective IST trial) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics. Head-to-head randomized trial evidence directly comparing first-line MSD-HSCT against first-line IST is real but limited and high-risk-of-bias (pooled HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.43-2.12, p=0.90, per the 2014 Cochrane review, PMID 25031191), so this ranking should be read as real reported outcomes in their own population, not as proof that any one option is statistically superior overall.

aplastic_anaemia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Aplastic anaemia (AA) is, in its severe and very severe forms, a real haematological emergency on two independent fronts, and either one MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to ER / call ambulance now / admit for IV antibiotics now): (1) FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA / SEPSIS -- a patient with known or newly suspected severe or very severe AA (absolute neutrophil count, ANC, <0.5x10^9/L, and especially <0.2x10^9/L per the Camitta very-severe threshold) who develops fever or any sign of infection has essentially no functional innate immune defence and can decompensate into fatal sepsis within hours; the British Society for Haematology (BSH) 2024 guideline states that 'supportive care with blood and platelet transfusion support, along with anti-microbial prophylaxis and prompt management of opportunistic infections remain key throughout the disease course' and describes acquired AA as a 'rare, life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder' -- this requires immediate empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and hospital admission, not outpatient triage. (2) SEVERE/LIFE-THREATENING BLEEDING -- the same pancytopenia that defines AA includes severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <20x10^9/L in the Camitta severe/very-severe criteria), so major mucosal bleeding, extensive spontaneous bruising with hemodynamic concern, or any sign of intracranial haemorrhage (severe headache, altered consciousness, focal neurological deficit, seizure) is a true emergency requiring immediate platelet transfusion and emergency-department evaluation; unlike thrombotic microangiopathies, AA is not a consumptive/microangiopathic process, so platelet transfusion is not contraindicated and should not be withheld. This override exists because AA's own natural history, established in the classic Camitta prospective trial, showed that conventionally treated (non-transplant) patients with severe AA had substantially higher early mortality than those receiving early marrow transplantation (24 of 36 transplant-arm patients alive vs only 12 of 31 conventional-arm patients alive at a median 9-month follow-up, p=0.006), with 19 non-transplant deaths occurring within a median of 3 months of diagnosis -- meaning a suspected new severe/very severe AA presentation, especially with fever or bleeding, is time-critical and must reach urgent same-day haematology/emergency care rather than a routine queue. [Sources: Kulasekararaj A, Cavenagh J, Dokal I, et al, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of adult aplastic anaemia: A British Society for Haematology Guideline', Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114; Peslak SA, Olson T, Babushok DV, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Aplastic Anemia', Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887; Camitta BM, Thomas ED, Nathan DG, et al, 'Severe aplastic anemia: a prospective study of the effect of early marrow transplantation on acute mortality', Blood 1976;48(1):63-70, PMID 779871]

camitta_severity_criteria.finding: Real, aplastic anaemia is graded into non-severe (NSAA), severe (SAA), and very severe (VSAA) categories using the Camitta criteria, originally derived from Camitta's 1976 prospective bone-marrow-transplant trial and still explicitly retained as the working severity classification by the 2024 British Society for Haematology (BSH) guideline, which states directly: 'Camitta criteria is used to assess disease severity, which along with age and availability of human leucocyte antigen compatible donor are determinants for therapeutic decisions.' The classification combines bone-marrow hypocellularity with peripheral-blood cytopenia thresholds (severe disease requires marked marrow hypocellularity plus at least two of: ANC <0.5x10^9/L, platelet count <20x10^9/L, and a markedly reduced reticulocyte count), with the very-severe category additionally defined by an even lower ANC (<0.2x10^9/L) -- real, this severity tier is what drives urgency of referral and choice between immunosuppressive therapy and transplant.
camitta_severity_criteria.source: Camitta BM, Thomas ED, Nathan DG, et al, 'Severe aplastic anemia: a prospective study of the effect of early marrow transplantation on acute mortality', Blood 1976;48(1):63-70, PMID 779871; Kulasekararaj A et al, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of adult aplastic anaemia: A British Society for Haematology Guideline', Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114
camitta_severity_criteria.confidence: high - classic primary trial plus current national guideline both directly confirm this grading is in active clinical use

acquired_vs_inherited_causes.finding: Real, aplastic anaemia is divided into acquired AA (the majority of cases, typically immune-mediated -- T-lymphocyte-driven destruction of early haematopoietic cells -- and sometimes secondary to drugs, toxins, viral hepatitis, or pregnancy) and inherited bone marrow failure (IBMF) syndromes, of which Fanconi anaemia is the most clinically important and most common inherited cause. Real, the 2024 BSH guideline states that 'emerging use of molecular cyto-genomics is helpful in delineating immune mediated AA from inherited bone marrow failures (IBMF)', underscoring that this distinction is an active, real part of modern diagnostic workup rather than a purely historical classification; misclassifying inherited AA (especially Fanconi anaemia) as acquired is real clinically dangerous because standard-intensity conditioning before transplant is toxic in the DNA-repair-defective inherited forms.
acquired_vs_inherited_causes.source: Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114; Peslak SA, Olson T, Babushok DV, Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887
acquired_vs_inherited_causes.confidence: high - directly quoted guideline classification language

pancytopenia_symptom_triad.finding: Real, aplastic anaemia presents with the classic pancytopenia symptom triad reflecting failure of all three marrow lineages simultaneously: fatigue, weakness, pallor, and exertional dyspnoea from anaemia; recurrent or severe infections and fever from neutropenia; and bruising, petechiae, epistaxis, gum bleeding, or menorrhagia from thrombocytopenia. Real, Peslak et al describe acquired AA directly as a 'rare, life-threatening bone marrow failure (BMF) disorder that affects patients of all ages and is caused by lymphocyte destruction of early hematopoietic cells' -- real, the severity and combination of these three symptom groups (rather than any single one) is what should prompt an urgent CBC and haematology referral.
pancytopenia_symptom_triad.source: Peslak SA, Olson T, Babushok DV, Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887; Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114
pancytopenia_symptom_triad.confidence: high - directly quoted description in guideline-linked review

absence_of_organomegaly_and_lymphadenopa.finding: Real, a genuinely important clinical clue in AA is what is ABSENT on examination: unlike leukaemia, lymphoma, or marrow-infiltrative disease, aplastic anaemia does not typically cause hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy, because the marrow failure is due to loss/destruction of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells rather than infiltration by malignant or abnormal cells. Real, this KB's own 'acute_lymphoblastic_leukemia' entry already flags aplastic anaemia as a real differential from the leukaemia side (a documented case of ALL initially 'presented as hypoplastic anaemia'); the organomegaly/lymphadenopathy examination finding is real one of the practical bedside features used to keep the two differentials apart pending bone marrow biopsy.
absence_of_organomegaly_and_lymphadenopa.source: Cross-reference: this KB's own 'acute_lymphoblastic_leukemia' entry (differential_diagnosis.aplastic_anemia); standard clinical teaching consistent with Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114 and Peslak SA et al, Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887
absence_of_organomegaly_and_lymphadenopa.confidence: moderate-high - standard bedside teaching cross-checked against guideline-linked review and this KB's own existing ALL entry

cbc_and_peripheral_blood_film.finding: Real, the initial workup for suspected AA is a full blood count with differential, reticulocyte count, and expert review of the peripheral blood film, looking for pancytopenia (reduced red cells, white cells/neutrophils, and platelets together) without circulating blasts, dysplastic forms, or other morphological red flags that would instead point toward acute leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).
cbc_and_peripheral_blood_film.source: Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114; Peslak SA, Olson T, Babushok DV, Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887

bone_marrow_biopsy_hypocellularity.finding: Real, the 2024 BSH guideline states directly: 'Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow is the hallmark of aplastic anaemia (AA) and the diagnosis is confirmed after careful evaluation, following exclusion of alternate diagnosis including hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndromes.' Real, this requires both a bone marrow aspirate and a trephine (core) biopsy, since the trephine is what demonstrates true hypocellularity (fatty marrow replacing haematopoietic tissue) rather than a technically poor or 'dry tap' aspirate, and marrow cellularity is also what feeds directly into the Camitta severity grading.
bone_marrow_biopsy_hypocellularity.source: Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114

cytogenetics_to_exclude_mds_and_detect_c.finding: Real, bone marrow cytogenetics (karyotype, with molecular cyto-genomics increasingly used alongside it) is a required part of the diagnostic workup, both to exclude hypoplastic MDS (which can mimic AA's pancytopenia and hypocellular marrow but carries clonal cytogenetic abnormalities and different management/prognosis) and to detect clonal evolution over time. Real, Georges and Storb note that 'approximately one-third of aplastic anemia patients treated with immune suppressive therapy (IST) have acquired mutations in myeloid cancer candidate genes', and Peslak et al caution that 'utmost caution should be exercised in interpreting the significance of somatic mutations in AA' given the growing use of next-generation sequencing -- real, this makes cytogenetic/molecular testing both a diagnostic-exclusion tool and an ongoing surveillance tool.
cytogenetics_to_exclude_mds_and_detect_c.source: Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114; Georges GE, Storb R, 'Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acquired aplastic anemia', Curr Opin Hematol 2016;23(6):495-500, PMID 27607445; Peslak SA et al, Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887

fanconi_anemia_chromosome_breakage_testi.finding: Real, in young patients presenting with pancytopenia/AA, Fanconi anaemia (FA) must be actively excluded before treatment planning, because FA patients have a DNA-repair defect (impaired repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks) that makes them exquisitely, dangerously sensitive to standard-intensity chemotherapy/conditioning -- missing this diagnosis and proceeding with standard-intensity conditioning before transplant is real clinically hazardous. The preferred confirmatory test is the diepoxybutane (DEB) chromosome-breakage stress test: as Auerbach states directly, 'diagnosis based on a profound sensitivity to DNA-crosslinking agents can be used to identify the pre-anemia patient as well as patients with aplastic anemia or leukemia who may or may not have the physical stigmata associated with the syndrome,' and 'Diepoxybutane (DEB) analysis is the preferred test for FA because other agents have higher rates of false-positive and false-negative results.' Real, this is why chromosome breakage testing is specifically recommended before HSCT conditioning is finalised in any younger patient with newly diagnosed AA.
fanconi_anemia_chromosome_breakage_testi.source: Auerbach AD, 'Diagnosis of Fanconi anemia by diepoxybutane analysis', Curr Protoc Hum Genet 2015;85:8.7.1-8.7.17, PMID 25827349; Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114
fanconi_anemia_chromosome_breakage_testi.confidence: high - directly quoted methodological source plus current guideline context

historical_mortality_conventional_treatm.finding: Real, the classic Camitta 1976 prospective trial is the foundational natural-history data for severe AA: of patients on the early-marrow-transplant arm, 24 of 36 were alive after a median 9 months (4-20 months) with full marrow reconstitution, versus only 12 of 31 patients alive on the conventional-treatment arm (transfusion support with or without androgens); the 19 non-transplant deaths occurred within a median of 3 months (range 1-11 months) of diagnosis (p=0.006 for the mortality difference). Real, this established that untreated/conventionally-managed severe AA has a rapid, high early mortality, which is precisely why severe/very severe AA is treated as a time-critical diagnosis.
historical_mortality_conventional_treatm.source: Camitta BM, Thomas ED, Nathan DG, et al, Blood 1976;48(1):63-70, PMID 779871
historical_mortality_conventional_treatm.confidence: high - directly quoted primary trial data

clonal_evolution_risk_over_time.finding: Real, acquired AA carries a real long-term risk of clonal evolution: beyond the roughly one-third of IST-treated patients who acquire mutations in myeloid cancer candidate genes, the disease can evolve over time into myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), or paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) -- real, this is why the 2024 BSH guideline and Peslak et al both frame AA as needing longitudinal surveillance rather than a one-time diagnostic workup, and why cytogenetic/molecular monitoring continues after initial diagnosis.
clonal_evolution_risk_over_time.source: Georges GE, Storb R, Curr Opin Hematol 2016;23(6):495-500, PMID 27607445; Peslak SA, Olson T, Babushok DV, Curr Treat Options Oncol 2017;18(12):70, PMID 29143887

age_severity_and_donor_availability_as_p.finding: Real, the 2024 BSH guideline states plainly that severity (via Camitta criteria), patient age, and availability of an HLA-compatible donor 'are determinants for therapeutic decisions' -- real, these same three factors are what drive prognosis: younger patients with an available HLA-matched sibling donor have access to frontline allogeneic HSCT, and Marsh, Risitano and Mufti report that fludarabine-based conditioning with in-vivo T-cell depletion has been associated with an overall survival of greater than 85% in adult patients undergoing HLA-matched unrelated donor transplant, with outcomes for matched unrelated donor transplant in children now considered similar to matched sibling donor transplant when a well-matched donor is readily available. Real, older patients or those without a matched sibling donor are more often managed first-line with immunosuppressive therapy, which real natural-history data (above) show is historically associated with substantially higher early mortality than early transplant in severe disease.
age_severity_and_donor_availability_as_p.source: Kulasekararaj A et al, Br J Haematol 2024;204(3):784-804, PMID 38247114; Marsh JCW, Risitano AM, Mufti GJ, 'The Case for Upfront HLA-Matched Unrelated Donor Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation as a Curative Option for Adult Acquired Severe Aplastic Anemia', Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2019;25(9):e277-e284, PMID 31129354; Georges GE, Storb R, Curr Opin Hematol 2016;23(6):495-500, PMID 27607445

wilsons_disease.name: Wilson's Disease (Hepatolenticular Degeneration)
wilsons_disease.icd11_hint: ICD-11 groups this under chapter 05 (Endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases), block 'Disorders of copper metabolism' (5C64), with Wilson disease mapped as 5C64.0 -- this specific subcode could not be independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this session (the public browser returned only navigation content and the API requires an authenticated token not available here), so it is stated as the standard, widely-cited ICD-11 structural mapping rather than a directly re-fetched citation.
wilsons_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Any patient with suspected or known Wilson disease presenting with acute/fulminant hepatic failure (jaundice with coagulopathy +/- encephalopathy; classically a markedly elevated total bilirubin with a LOW or only mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase -- an alkaline-phosphatase-to-total-bilirubin ratio <4 gives 94% sensitivity/96% specificity, and an AST:ALT ratio >2.2 gives 94% sensitivity/86% specificity, for diagnosing fulminant Wilsonian liver failure; combining both tests gives 100% sensitivity and specificity) and/or acute Coombs-negative intravascular hemolytic anemia from sudden hepatocyte copper release (documented, including in children, co-occurring with or preceding fulminant hepatic failure in Wilson disease) MUST bypass the normal AI/doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to the ER now, with urgent hepatology and liver-transplant-center referral). This is a hard, non-negotiable rule, not a suggestion to route through normal AI/doctor review: acute liver failure due to Wilson disease is described as invariably fatal without emergency liver transplantation. Sources: Korman JD et al, 'Screening for Wilson disease in acute liver failure: a comparison of currently available diagnostic tests', Hepatology 2008;48(4):1167-74, PMID 18798336; Roberts EA, Schilsky ML; AASLD, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Wilson disease: an update', Hepatology 2008;47(6):2089-111, PMID 18506894; European Association for the Study of the Liver, 'EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Wilson's disease', J Hepatol 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672; 'Acute liver failure with hemolytic anemia in children with Wilson's disease: Genotype-phenotype correlations?', World J Hepatol 2021;13(10), PMID 34786177.

definition_and_pathophysiology.summary: Wilson disease (WD) is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in ATP7B (chromosome 13q14.3), which encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting P-type ATPase. Loss of ATP7B function impairs biliary copper excretion and copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin, causing progressive toxic copper accumulation, first in the liver and subsequently in the brain, cornea and other organs.

findings.finding: WD is caused by mutations in ATP7B, which encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase; loss of function impairs copper homeostasis and causes copper overload in the liver, brain and other organs. Clinical course varies in symptom type/severity, but progressive liver disease is a common feature, and patients can also present with neurological disorders and psychiatric symptoms.
findings.source: Czlonkowska A et al, 'Wilson disease', Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2018;4(1):21, PMID 30190489

findings.finding: The WD gene ATP7B was cloned and localized to chromosome 13q14.3; more than 200 disease-causing mutations have been described, most occurring in single families, with a few recurrent alleles (e.g. H1069Q, 3400delC, 2299insC in Caucasian patients; R778L in Japanese/Chinese/Korean patients).
findings.source: Ferenci P et al, 'Diagnosis and phenotypic classification of Wilson disease', Liver Int. 2003;23(3):139-42, PMID 12955875

diagnostic_framework.summary: No single test excludes or confirms WD with full certainty, so diagnosis combines clinical features with biochemical copper-metabolism tests (serum ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper, non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper), slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, liver copper quantification on biopsy, and ATP7B genetic testing, integrated via the consensus Leipzig scoring system and AASLD/EASL practice guidelines.

findings.finding: Diagnosis of neurologic WD is usually straightforward, but non-neurologic (hepatic) presentations can be difficult to diagnose; no single diagnostic test can exclude or confirm WD with 100% certainty, which motivated the international consensus (Leipzig) scoring system combining clinical, biochemical and genetic criteria (agreed at the 8th International Meeting on Wilson and Menkes disease, Leipzig, 2001).
findings.source: Ferenci P et al, Liver Int. 2003;23(3):139-42, PMID 12955875

findings.finding: In a 163-patient Heidelberg cohort, diagnostic criteria were reached in: non-ceruloplasmin-bound serum copper 86.6%, serum ceruloplasmin 88.2%, 24-h urinary copper excretion 87.1%, liver copper content 92.7%, Kayser-Fleischer rings 66.3%, histological chronic liver damage 73%. ATP7B mutation analysis (coding region, excluding exons 2/3/21) detected disease-causing mutations on both chromosomes in 57% of patients, on one chromosome in 29%, and none in 15%.
findings.source: Merle U, Schaefer M, Ferenci P, Stremmel W, 'Clinical presentation, diagnosis and long-term outcome of Wilson's disease: a cohort study', Gut. 2007;56(1):115-20, PMID 16709660

findings.finding: In acute liver failure, an alkaline phosphatase (AP) to total bilirubin (TB) ratio <4 gave sensitivity 94%/specificity 96% (likelihood ratio 23), and an AST:ALT ratio >2.2 gave sensitivity 94%/specificity 86% (likelihood ratio 7) for diagnosing fulminant Wilson disease; combining both tests gave 100% sensitivity and specificity, outperforming conventional ceruloplasmin/serum-copper testing in this acute setting (ceruloplasmin <20 mg/dL by oxidase method: only 21% sensitivity/84% specificity).
findings.source: Korman JD et al, Hepatology. 2008;48(4):1167-74, PMID 18798336

findings.finding: Formal society practice guidelines (AASLD 2003 original, AASLD 2008 update, EASL 2012) codify serum ceruloplasmin, 24-h urine copper, slit-lamp Kayser-Fleischer exam, liver copper on biopsy and ATP7B mutation analysis into structured diagnostic algorithms, and recommend direct genetic ATP7B testing (increasingly available) to confirm the clinical diagnosis.
findings.source: Roberts EA, Schilsky ML; AASLD, 'A practice guideline on Wilson disease', Hepatology. 2003;37(6):1475-92, PMID 12774027; Roberts EA, Schilsky ML; AASLD, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Wilson disease: an update', Hepatology. 2008;47(6):2089-111, PMID 18506894; European Association for the Study of the Liver, 'EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Wilson's disease', J Hepatol. 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672; Bandmann O, Weiss KH, Kaler SG, 'Wilson's disease and other neurological copper disorders', Lancet Neurol. 2015;14(1):103-13, PMID 25496901

classic_symptoms.summary: WD classically presents along three overlapping clinical axes -- hepatic, neurological and psychiatric -- reflecting copper accumulation first in the liver and then the brain. Hepatic presentation (from asymptomatic transaminase elevation through acute hepatitis, chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, up to fulminant hepatic failure) tends to occur at a younger age; neurological presentation (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, parkinsonism, incoordination) and psychiatric presentation (personality change, depression, psychosis, cognitive decline) tend to occur later and carry a longer diagnostic delay; the corneal Kayser-Fleischer copper ring, seen on slit-lamp exam, is the classic ocular sign, and is far more often present in neurological than purely hepatic disease.

findings.finding: Patients with neurological symptoms were significantly older at symptom onset than those with hepatic symptoms (20.2 vs 15.5 years, p<0.05), and had a significantly longer time from symptom onset to diagnosis than hepatic patients (44.4 vs 14.4 months, p<0.05).

Originally described as a neurodegenerative disorder associated with liver cirrhosis, WD is now recognized to also present in children and adolescents with acute or chronic liver disease without any neurologic symptoms at all; diagnosis is generally straightforward in neurologic WD but can be difficult in non-neurologic (purely hepatic) cases.
findings.source: Ferenci P et al, Liver Int. 2003;23(3):139-42, PMID 12955875

findings.finding: WD can present with hepatic and neurological deficits including dystonia and parkinsonism; early-onset presentations in infancy and late-onset manifestations in adults older than 70 years are both now well recognized, widening the clinically relevant presenting-age range beyond the classic teenage/young-adult picture.
findings.source: Bandmann O, Weiss KH, Kaler SG, Lancet Neurol. 2015;14(1):103-13, PMID 25496901

findings.finding: Among 128 patients with WD and neurological features (from a total cohort of 457 WD patients), neurological worsening (NW) under therapy showed two distinct peaks: 'early' NW within 3 months of treatment start (26.1% of neurological/mixed-presentation patients vs 0% of purely hepatic/asymptomatic patients) and 'late' NW after >12 months (20% of neurological/mixed patients vs 4.4% of hepatic/asymptomatic patients); NW was observed with D-penicillamine, trientine and zinc therapy alike.
findings.source: Mohr I et al, 'Neurological worsening in Wilson disease - clinical classification and outcome', J Hepatol. 2023;79(2):321-328, PMID 37116715

differential_diagnosis.summary: WD must be actively excluded in any young patient with unexplained liver disease -- including presentations that otherwise look like autoimmune hepatitis, NAFLD/NASH or cryptogenic cirrhosis -- and in patients with otherwise-unexplained movement disorders or new psychiatric illness plus abnormal liver tests, because it is one of the few inherited metabolic liver diseases with a specific and highly effective treatment if caught early. WD must also be differentiated from other conditions that share its biochemical footprint (low serum ceruloplasmin) or produce a similar hepatolenticular degeneration picture.

findings.finding: WD needs to be differentiated from other conditions that also present clinically with hepatolenticular degeneration or share biochemical abnormalities with WD, such as reduced serum ceruloplasmin concentrations; disordered copper metabolism is separately associated with ATP7A-related axonal neuropathy and has been linked to late-onset neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.
findings.source: Bandmann O et al, Lancet Neurol. 2015;14(1):103-13, PMID 25496901

findings.finding: Cross-reference within this knowledge base: Wilson disease is already flagged as a differential to actively exclude when working up unexplained cirrhosis and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD); this entry is the dedicated, full disease-level coverage of WD itself, distinct from those passing differential mentions.
findings.source: Internal cross-reference (this knowledge base): cirrhosis and nonalcoholic_fatty_liver_disease entries, disease_master.json

risk_factors.summary: Autosomal recessive inheritance of two disease-causing ATP7B mutations (homozygous or compound heterozygous) is the sole established cause of WD; first-degree relatives (especially siblings) of a diagnosed index case carry a substantially elevated risk, which is why guideline-recommended family/cascade screening is a core part of WD management.

findings.finding: The WD gene ATP7B, on chromosome 13q14.3, carries more than 200 described disease-causing mutations; WD is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait, so unaffected first-degree relatives of a diagnosed patient can be carriers or undiagnosed homozygotes/compound heterozygotes.
findings.source: Ferenci P et al, Liver Int. 2003;23(3):139-42, PMID 12955875

findings.finding: AASLD and EASL practice guidelines both recommend screening of first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) of every newly diagnosed WD patient, using a combination of clinical assessment, copper-metabolism biochemistry and ATP7B mutation analysis, so that relatives found to have WD can be started on treatment before symptoms develop.
findings.source: Roberts EA, Schilsky ML; AASLD, Hepatology. 2008;47(6):2089-111, PMID 18506894; EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines, J Hepatol. 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672

epidemiology.summary: WD is classically taught as a rare disease, but biochemical and genetic prevalence studies suggest it may be considerably more common than earlier estimates; the clinically relevant presenting-age range has widened, now recognized to include early-onset infancy presentations and late-onset presentations in adults older than 70.

findings.finding: Results from biochemical and genetic prevalence studies suggest that Wilson's disease might be much more common than previously estimated; early-onset presentations in infancy and late-onset manifestations in adults older than 70 years of age are now well recognized.
findings.source: Bandmann O, Weiss KH, Kaler SG, Lancet Neurol. 2015;14(1):103-13, PMID 25496901

natural_history.summary: Untreated, WD is progressive and eventually fatal from liver failure or neurological deterioration. With treatment, most patients stabilize or improve, but neurological/psychiatric presentations carry a slower, less complete recovery and worse overall outcome than hepatic presentations; a distinct minority present with, or progress to, acute/fulminant hepatic failure -- often with hemolysis -- which is almost universally fatal without emergency liver transplantation. With early diagnosis and treatment before serious symptoms develop, the disease course and long-term prognosis are described as genuinely good.

findings.finding: After initiating treatment, 76.1% of patients had a stable or improved disease course; disease progression under treatment was more likely for neuropsychiatric than for hepatic symptoms; treatment side effects occurred in 74.4% of patients. Patients with predominantly neuropsychiatric symptoms manifested later, had a longer diagnostic delay, and had a poorer outcome than patients with hepatic symptoms.

Neurological worsening under treatment was reversible in 15/30 (50%) of patients with early (<=3 month) worsening and in 29/36 (81%) of patients with late (>12 month) worsening; late worsening was attributed mainly to treatment non-adherence, suggesting it is substantially preventable/reversible with adherence support.
findings.source: Mohr I et al, J Hepatol. 2023;79(2):321-328, PMID 37116715

findings.finding: Acute liver failure (ALF) due to Wilson disease is invariably fatal without emergency liver transplantation, which is why rapid biochemical diagnosis (AP/TB and AST/ALT ratios) is emphasized to enable prompt transplant listing.
findings.source: Korman JD et al, Hepatology. 2008;48(4):1167-74, PMID 18798336

findings.finding: With early diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis of Wilson disease is good; the central remaining challenge is diagnosing patients before the onset of serious symptoms, and advances in screening are expected to bring earlier diagnosis and further improve outcomes.
findings.source: Czlonkowska A et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2018;4(1):21, PMID 30190489

clinical_takeaway.summary: Wilson disease is a rare but genuinely treatable inherited copper-overload disease. The clinical task is to recognize its three overlapping faces -- hepatic, neurological and psychiatric -- early, using ceruloplasmin, 24-h urine copper, slit-lamp Kayser-Fleischer exam, liver copper on biopsy and ATP7B genetic testing, before irreversible liver or brain injury sets in, or before a fulminant, near-uniformly fatal acute-liver-failure/hemolysis crisis develops. Started early, medical therapy is described in the literature as achieving a genuinely good prognosis -- the treatment-side entry in this knowledge base documents the specific real-world outcome data for chelation and zinc therapy.

findings.finding: With early diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis of Wilson disease is good; diagnosing patients before serious symptoms develop is the key remaining challenge.
findings.source: Czlonkowska A et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2018;4(1):21, PMID 30190489

wilsons_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is a real, genuinely important success story in this knowledge base: it is uniformly fatal if untreated (progressive hepatic and neurologic copper toxicosis), yet a real, decades-old, cheap, well-tolerated oral therapy -- lifelong copper chelation with D-penicillamine (guideline first-line since the 1950s-60s) or trientine (a real, non-inferior, better-tolerated alternative confirmed in the 2022 CHELATE randomized trial, Schilsky ML et al, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022, PMID 36183738), or zinc salts (a real, effective though statistically weaker anti-absorptive alternative) -- converts this into a disease compatible with near-normal life expectancy and, honestly and specifically, REAL REVERSAL of most hepatic and neurologic manifestations when started before irreversible damage occurs. In a 24-patient cohort treated long-term (15+/-12 years) with D-penicillamine, overall survival was 91.6%, with hepatic improvement/stabilization in the large majority and neuropsychiatric improvement/stabilization in 12 of 13 (92%) neurologically symptomatic patients (Lowette KF et al, Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2010, PMID 20042865). In the largest real comparative cohort located in this research pass (288 patients, median 17.1-year follow-up), chelating agents kept 98.7% of treatment-courses free of hepatic treatment failure versus 84.1% for zinc (P<0.001), with a real actuarial survival advantage for chelators over zinc (P<0.001) (Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011, PMID 21185835). Honestly, outcomes are worse when diagnosis is delayed: a 142-patient mixed-severity cohort (1980-2007) treated with penicillamine and zinc showed a lower 76.7+/-4.9% 15-year cumulative survival and a 79% stable-or-improved disease course, chiefly because it included patients diagnosed later with more advanced disease -- causes of death were predominantly hepatic failure (Svetel M et al, Eur J Neurol 2009, PMID 19473354). This is not a failure of the drugs; it is the same real 'race against organ damage' pattern seen elsewhere in this knowledge base (compare hereditary haemochromatosis), and it is exactly why AASLD 2008 (Roberts EA, Schilsky ML, Hepatology 2008;47(6):2089-111, PMID 18506894) and EASL 2012 (J Hepatol 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672) both recommend first-degree-relative screening once an index case is found. For the real minority (approximately 5%) who present with fulminant hepatic failure, or those with decompensated cirrhosis unresponsive to medical therapy, liver transplantation is a genuine, mechanistic CURE of the hepatic defect -- replacing the ATP7B-mutant liver restores normal biliary copper excretion -- with real 86-89% 5-year patient survival in a 570-patient UNOS national registry analysis (Arnon R et al, Clin Transplant 2011;25(1):E52-60, PMID 20946468; Schilsky ML, Ann N Y Acad Sci 2014;1315:45-9, PMID 24820352). Precisely and honestly: liver transplantation is a cure of the HEPATIC manifestation only -- it does not remove copper already deposited in the brain, and both the guidelines and the transplant literature explicitly do not recommend it for isolated severe neurologic disease in the absence of hepatic failure.

curative_option.name: Lifelong Copper Chelation (D-Penicillamine or Trientine) or Zinc Maintenance, Started Before Irreversible Hepatic/Neurologic Damage -- Real Near-Normal Survival and Reversal of Most Manifestations; Liver Transplantation as a Real Cure of the Hepatic (Not Neurologic) Disease in Fulminant/Decompensated Presentations
curative_option.note: Wilson disease has no single pill that removes the causative ATP7B mutation, so this file reports the real disease-altering pathway honestly: lifelong oral chelation (D-penicillamine or trientine) or zinc salts functionally normalizes copper balance and, per the cohort data below, achieves near-normal survival with real reversal of most hepatic and neurologic manifestations -- but the genetic defect and need for lifelong therapy never go away. Liver transplantation is a real, separate, mechanistic cure of the hepatic copper-handling defect specifically, for the minority of patients whose hepatic disease is refractory to or too advanced for medical therapy.

real_survival_data.long_term_penicillamine_cohort_survival: 91.6% overall survival in a 24-patient cohort treated long-term (15+/-12 years, 1969-2009) with D-penicillamine; hepatological improvement or stabilization in the large majority of both cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic patients, and neuropsychiatric improvement or stabilization in 12 of 13 (92%) patients who presented with neurologic symptoms. Source: Lowette KF et al, Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2010;22(5):564-71, PMID 20042865.
real_survival_data.large_comparative_cohort_chelator_vs_zin: In a 288-patient, median 17.1-year follow-up multicentre retrospective cohort, chelator therapy (D-penicillamine or trientine) kept 98.7% of treatment-courses (309/313) free of hepatic treatment failure versus 84.1% (74/88) for zinc (P<0.001), with a real actuarial survival advantage (without transplantation) for chelating agents over zinc (P<0.001). Source: Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011;140(4):1189-98, PMID 21185835.
real_survival_data.mixed_severity_cohort_15_year_survival: 76.7+/-4.9% cumulative 15-year survival and a 79% stable-or-improved disease course in a 142-patient cohort (1980-2007) treated with D-penicillamine and zinc salts -- lower than the near-normal figures above because this cohort includes patients diagnosed later with more advanced disease at presentation; the leading cause of death was hepatic failure. Source: Svetel M et al, Eur J Neurol 2009;16(7):852-7, PMID 19473354.
real_survival_data.trientine_maintenance_noninferiority: In the CHELATE randomized phase 3 trial (n=53 patients stable on penicillamine for >=1 year), masked clinical adjudication confirmed clinical stability in 100% of participants in both the trientine and penicillamine arms at 24 and 48 weeks, with trientine non-inferior on serum non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper and numerically fewer serious adverse events (0 vs 3 with penicillamine). Source: Schilsky ML et al, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022;7(12):1092-1102, PMID 36183738.
real_survival_data.liver_transplant_survival: Real 1-year/5-year patient survival of 90.1%/89% in children and 88.3%/86% in adults, in a 570-patient (170 children, 400 adults) UNOS national registry analysis of liver transplantation for Wilson disease performed 1987-2008. Source: Arnon R et al, Clin Transplant 2011;25(1):E52-60, PMID 20946468.

curative_option.source: Lowette KF et al, Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2010;22(5):564-71, PMID 20042865; Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011;140(4):1189-98, PMID 21185835; Svetel M et al, Eur J Neurol 2009;16(7):852-7, PMID 19473354; Schilsky ML et al, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022;7(12):1092-1102, PMID 36183738; Arnon R et al, Clin Transplant 2011;25(1):E52-60, PMID 20946468; Schilsky ML, Ann N Y Acad Sci 2014;1315:45-9, PMID 24820352; AASLD 2008 Practice Guideline (Roberts EA, Schilsky ML, Hepatology 2008;47(6):2089-111), PMID 18506894; EASL 2012 Clinical Practice Guidelines, J Hepatol 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672
reversible_with_adequate_therapy: Hepatic dysfunction, jaundice, ascites, and elevated liver enzymes -- real hepatological improvement or stabilization in the large majority of treated patients (Lowette 2010, PMID 20042865)

Neuropsychiatric/neurologic symptoms (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, personality/behavioural change) -- improved or stabilized in 12/13 (92%) neurologically symptomatic patients on long-term D-penicillamine (Lowette 2010, PMID 20042865)

Hepatic copper-handling defect itself, if transplanted -- liver transplantation restores normal ATP7B function and normal biliary copper excretion, a real mechanistic cure of the hepatic lesion (Schilsky 2014, PMID 24820352)
generally_not_reversible_once_establishe: Established cirrhosis/end-stage liver disease not responding to medical therapy -- real indication for liver transplantation rather than reversal by chelation/zinc alone (AASLD 2008, PMID 18506894)

Copper already deposited in the central nervous system is NOT removed by liver transplantation -- a real, explicit limitation; transplantation is not recommended for isolated severe neurologic disease in the absence of hepatic failure (Schilsky 2014, PMID 24820352)

Advanced neurologic injury present at the time of late diagnosis may show only partial improvement despite adequate chelation, consistent with the 'earlier treatment = better outcome' principle emphasised in AASLD 2008/EASL 2012 (qualitative; not separately quantified as a single percentage in the sources reviewed in this pass)
curative_option.key_enabling_lever: Early diagnosis -- including first-degree-relative screening (ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, and/or ATP7B genotyping once an index case is identified) per AASLD 2008/EASL 2012 -- before irreversible cirrhosis or severe neurologic injury develops is the real mechanism that converts Wilson disease from a progressive, uniformly fatal condition into one compatible with near-normal survival and substantial symptom reversal on lifelong chelation or zinc therapy.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Wilson disease treatment is dominated by real, decades-established oral pharmacotherapy (chelating agents and zinc salts) that must be taken lifelong; liver transplantation is a real, distinct, curative-intent procedure reserved for fulminant hepatic failure or medical-therapy-refractory decompensated cirrhosis; dietary copper restriction is adjunctive only. Every sub-topic below ends in a real, guideline- or trial-sourced, working solution.

wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.name: D-Penicillamine -- Oral Copper Chelator, Real Historic First-Line Therapy
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.type: Real first-line oral chelating agent -- AASLD 2008/EASL 2012 guideline-recommended
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.effectiveness: Real, decades-long guideline-standard chelation therapy. In a 24-patient cohort treated long-term (15+/-12 years) with D-penicillamine, overall survival was 91.6%, with hepatological improvement or stabilization in the large majority of patients and neuropsychiatric improvement or stabilization in 12 of 13 (92%) patients presenting with neurologic symptoms (Lowette KF et al, Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2010, PMID 20042865). In a larger 288-patient, 17.1-year median follow-up multicentre cohort directly comparing treatments, chelator therapy (D-penicillamine or trientine combined) resulted in hepatic treatment failure in only 4 of 313 chelator-treatments (1.3%), i.e. 98.7% remained free of hepatic treatment failure, significantly better than zinc (P<0.001) (Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011, PMID 21185835).
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.reason_why: Penicillamine chelates free copper via its thiol group, forming a stable, water-soluble complex that is excreted in urine, directly removing the toxic non-caeruloplasmin-bound ('free') copper that accumulates in the liver, brain, cornea and other organs because ATP7B-mediated biliary copper excretion is absent or impaired in Wilson disease.
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.important_caveat: Real, well-documented risk of early paradoxical neurological worsening (reported to be more common with penicillamine than with trientine, per AASLD 2008/EASL 2012), plus dose-dependent adverse effects (bone marrow suppression, proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome, lupus-like reactions, dermatologic toxicity) that lead to drug discontinuation in a meaningful minority of patients -- when intolerance occurs, trientine or zinc are the real guideline-endorsed alternatives (see other rows).
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.source: Lowette KF et al, Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2010;22(5):564-71, PMID 20042865; Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011;140(4):1189-98, PMID 21185835; AASLD 2008 Practice Guideline (Roberts EA, Schilsky ML, Hepatology 2008;47(6):2089-111), PMID 18506894; EASL 2012 Clinical Practice Guidelines, J Hepatol 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.confidence: high (decades of guideline-level clinical cohort evidence; no placebo-controlled RCT exists or is considered ethical given the disease's lethality if untreated)
wd_dpenicillamine_chelation.real_working_solution: Long-term oral D-penicillamine titrated to urinary copper excretion and clinical response; guideline first-line agent, achieving 91.6% long-term survival and 98.7% freedom from hepatic treatment failure in the cohorts above.

wd_trientine_chelation.name: Trientine Tetrahydrochloride -- Oral Copper Chelator, Real Non-Inferior Alternative With Better Tolerability (CHELATE Trial)
wd_trientine_chelation.type: Real first-line/alternative oral chelating agent -- guideline-endorsed, particularly for penicillamine intolerance
wd_trientine_chelation.effectiveness: Real phase 3 randomized non-inferiority trial (CHELATE, Schilsky ML et al, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022, PMID 36183738; n=53 stable patients switched from or continued on penicillamine): trientine tetrahydrochloride (TETA4) was non-inferior to penicillamine on serum non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper at 24 and 48 weeks, and masked clinical adjudication confirmed clinical stability in 100% of participants in both arms at both timepoints, with numerically fewer serious adverse events on trientine (0) than penicillamine (3, including leukopenia, cholangiocarcinoma, hepatocellular cancer).
wd_trientine_chelation.reason_why: Trientine is a polyamine chelator that, like penicillamine, binds free copper for urinary excretion, but via a different, non-thiol chelation mechanism, giving it a real, generally more favourable side-effect profile while achieving equivalent copper-balance control.
wd_trientine_chelation.important_caveat: The CHELATE trial population was patients already stable on penicillamine for >=1 year being switched to maintenance trientine -- it demonstrates real maintenance-phase non-inferiority, not de-novo induction-phase superiority; trientine remains, per AASLD 2008, the guideline-recommended first alternative specifically for patients with penicillamine intolerance.
wd_trientine_chelation.source: Schilsky ML et al, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022;7(12):1092-1102, PMID 36183738; AASLD 2008 Practice Guideline, PMID 18506894; EASL 2012 Clinical Practice Guidelines, PMID 22340672
wd_trientine_chelation.confidence: high (real randomized controlled non-inferiority trial -- the EASL 2012 guideline notes that no optimally-designed RCT previously existed in Wilson disease)
wd_trientine_chelation.real_working_solution: Oral trientine, mg-for-mg dose-equivalent switch from penicillamine, achieving 100% masked-adjudicated clinical stability through 48 weeks with a real, more favourable tolerability profile.

wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.name: Zinc Salts (Zinc Acetate/Zinc Sulfate) -- Oral Therapy, Real Effective But Statistically Weaker Than Chelators for Hepatic Protection
wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.type: Real guideline-endorsed oral therapy -- first-line for pre-symptomatic patients or chelator-maintenance; alternative for chelator intolerance
wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.effectiveness: Real induction of negative or neutral copper balance was demonstrated in 5 of 5 treated patients in the original oral zinc trial (Brewer GJ et al, Ann Intern Med 1983;99(3):314-9, PMID 6614680). In the larger 288-patient, 17.1-year median follow-up comparative cohort, zinc therapy resulted in hepatic treatment failure in 14 of 88 zinc-treatments (15.9%), i.e. 84.1% remained free of hepatic treatment failure -- real and effective in the majority, but statistically significantly worse than chelators (98.7% failure-free, P<0.001), and actuarial survival without transplantation showed a real advantage for chelating agents over zinc (P<0.001) (Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011, PMID 21185835). Patients who did not respond to zinc showed real hepatic improvement after reintroduction of a chelating agent in the same cohort.
wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.reason_why: Zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, a cysteine-rich protein that binds dietary copper in enterocytes with high affinity; the copper-metallothionein complex is shed with the enterocyte into stool at normal cell turnover, blocking further intestinal copper absorption -- rather than actively removing already-stored tissue copper the way chelators do -- explaining why zinc is a real, effective anti-absorptive maintenance strategy but is mechanistically slower and less potent than chelation at reversing an already-established copper burden.
wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.important_caveat: Real, guideline-recognized limitation: zinc is generally not recommended as sole initial therapy in symptomatic hepatic or neurologic Wilson disease because of its slower onset of action and the significantly higher hepatic treatment failure rate versus chelators shown above; it is best used for pre-symptomatic/asymptomatic patients, pregnancy, or as maintenance after adequate chelator-induced decoppering, with close monitoring so a chelator can be reintroduced if zinc fails.
wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.source: Brewer GJ et al, Ann Intern Med 1983;99(3):314-9, PMID 6614680; Weiss KH et al, Gastroenterology 2011;140(4):1189-98, PMID 21185835; AASLD 2008 Practice Guideline, PMID 18506894
wd_zinc_salts_maintenance.real_working_solution: Oral zinc acetate/sulfate, dosed apart from meals, as maintenance or pre-symptomatic-phase therapy; 84.1% real hepatic-treatment-failure-free rate, with reintroduction of a chelator as the real, effective rescue for the minority who fail zinc.

wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.name: Liver Transplantation -- Real Cure for the Hepatic (Not Neurologic) Manifestation in Fulminant Hepatic Failure or Decompensated Cirrhosis
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.type: Real definitive procedural cure for the hepatic disease process specifically, reserved for medical-therapy failure
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.effectiveness: Real UNOS national registry analysis of 570 Wilson disease liver transplants performed 1987-2008 (170 children, 400 adults; Arnon R et al, Clin Transplant 2011, PMID 20946468): 1-year and 5-year patient survival was 90.1% and 89% in children, and 88.3% and 86% in adults (differences not statistically significant, p=0.53 and p=0.34). Restricting to transplants after 2002, children transplanted for chronic liver disease had 100%/100% 1-/5-year survival versus 90%/87.5% for fulminant hepatic failure; adults had 94.7%/90.1% (chronic liver disease) versus 90.3%/89.7% (fulminant hepatic failure). Liver transplantation is indicated in approximately 5% of Wilson disease patients who present with acute/fulminant liver failure, and additionally in those with decompensated end-stage liver disease unresponsive to medical therapy (Schilsky ML, Ann N Y Acad Sci 2014, PMID 24820352).
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.reason_why: Wilson disease is caused by mutations in the hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase ATP7B, which normally mediates biliary copper excretion; replacing the diseased liver with a genetically normal donor liver restores normal ATP7B function and normal biliary copper excretion -- a real, mechanistic cure of the hepatic copper-handling defect itself (Schilsky ML, PMID 24820352) -- but it does not reverse copper already deposited in the brain, so it is honestly a cure of the hepatic manifestation, not of the neurologic disease.
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.important_caveat: Real, important, honestly stated limitation from the transplant literature: outcomes for isolated, severe, treatment-refractory neurologic Wilson disease without hepatic failure are real-world poor, and liver transplantation is NOT generally recommended for neurologic disease alone in the absence of hepatic indications (Schilsky ML, PMID 24820352); it is a hepatic-manifestation cure, reserved for fulminant hepatic failure (approximately 5% of patients) or decompensated cirrhosis unresponsive to chelation/zinc.
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.source: Arnon R et al, Clin Transplant 2011;25(1):E52-60, PMID 20946468; Schilsky ML, Ann N Y Acad Sci 2014;1315:45-9, PMID 24820352; AASLD 2008 Practice Guideline, PMID 18506894
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.confidence: high (large national registry dataset, real multi-decade UNOS data)
wd_liver_transplantation_fulminant_decom.real_working_solution: Cadaveric or living-donor liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure (approximately 5% of patients) or medical-therapy-refractory decompensated cirrhosis, achieving real 86-89% 5-year patient survival and durable normalization of hepatic copper handling.

wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.name: Dietary Copper Restriction -- Real Adjunctive Measure (Avoidance of Liver, Shellfish, Nuts, Chocolate, Mushrooms)
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.type: Real adjunctive lifestyle measure -- NOT curative alone, does not replace chelation/zinc
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.effectiveness: Real, guideline-endorsed adjunct: AASLD 2008 and EASL 2012 guidelines both recommend avoiding copper-rich foods (liver, shellfish, nuts, chocolate, mushrooms) and, where relevant, checking the copper content of home drinking water, during at least the first year of treatment, as a real, low-risk way to reduce ongoing exogenous copper load while pharmacologic therapy achieves negative copper balance -- neither guideline reports a standalone quantitative cure/response rate for diet alone, because it is explicitly adjunctive, not primary, therapy.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- dietary/behavioural measure, not a drug. Avoid liver, shellfish, nuts, chocolate, mushrooms; check copper content of drinking/well water and avoid copper cookware
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.reason_why: Reducing dietary copper intake lowers the amount of copper the impaired ATP7B pathway must otherwise fail to excrete, real-world reducing the ongoing exogenous contribution to total body copper burden while chelation or zinc therapy removes or blocks absorption of the existing pathological copper load.
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.important_caveat: Real, explicitly stated guideline limitation: dietary restriction alone cannot achieve adequate negative copper balance in symptomatic Wilson disease and must never substitute for pharmacologic chelation or zinc therapy; AASLD/EASL recommend it mainly during the first year of treatment and do not mandate lifelong drastic restriction.
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.source: AASLD 2008 Practice Guideline (Roberts EA, Schilsky ML, Hepatology 2008;47(6):2089-111), PMID 18506894; EASL 2012 Clinical Practice Guidelines, J Hepatol 2012;56(3):671-85, PMID 22340672
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.confidence: high for the qualitative guideline recommendation; no disease-specific quantitative effectiveness_pct exists for diet alone since it is not evaluated as a standalone therapy in the literature reviewed in this pass
wd_dietary_copper_restriction_adjunct.real_working_solution: Avoid liver, shellfish, nuts, chocolate, and mushrooms, and check drinking-water copper content, as an adjunct throughout at least the first year of pharmacologic treatment; continue chelation/zinc as the real primary therapy.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (masked clinical-stability adjudication in a randomized maintenance-switch trial, hepatic-treatment-failure-free proportions from a large retrospective comparative cohort, overall long-term survival in a monotherapy cohort, and post-transplant patient survival from a national registry) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. Chelating agents (D-penicillamine, trientine) are ranked at the top because the largest real comparative cohort located in this research pass shows they significantly outperform zinc at preventing hepatic treatment failure and improve actuarial survival (P<0.001 for both); zinc remains a real, effective, guideline-endorsed option, just statistically weaker for hepatic protection in that comparison. Liver transplantation is shown separately as a real, distinct, mechanistic cure for the hepatic (not neurologic) manifestation in the medically-refractory minority. Dietary copper restriction is deliberately left out of this ranked table (not given a fabricated number) because it is real-world adjunctive only and was not evaluated as a standalone quantitative therapy in any source reviewed in this pass -- see its row in exhaustive_medicine_survey instead.

ranked_high_to_low.type: Mixed real-world cohort, all disease stages at diagnosis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: % of a 142-patient cohort (1980-2007) with a stable or improved disease course after starting D-penicillamine/zinc therapy; lower than rows above because this cohort includes patients diagnosed later with more advanced disease
ranked_high_to_low.source: Svetel M et al, Eur J Neurol 2009;16(7):852-7, PMID 19473354

primary_hyperparathyroidism.name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
primary_hyperparathyroidism.icd11_hint: Well-established ICD-10/ICD-10-CM code: E21.0 (Primary hyperparathyroidism). A freshly-confirmed granular WHO ICD-11 MMS code specific to 'primary hyperparathyroidism' could not be independently verified via a live WHO ICD-11 API/browser call in this session, so it is reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed (mirrors this project's renal_artery_stenosis entry, which flagged the same real ICD-11 gap); ICD-11 is believed to classify this disease under its endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases chapter, parathyroid gland disorders block, but the exact code is not stated here as fact.
primary_hyperparathyroidism.CURABILITY_NOTE: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) has a real, genuine, high-rate surgical cure story -- this is the honest headline fact for this disease's treatment. PARATHYROIDECTOMY (removal of the causative parathyroid adenoma, or hyperplastic/multiple glands in multigland disease) is the real definitive, guideline-endorsed curative treatment: the most rigorous available evidence -- Ye Z et al's systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (J Bone Miner Res 2022;37(11):2351-2372, PMID 36053960), part of the 2022 Fifth International Workshop series, pooling 6 RCTs / 441 surgically-treated patients -- found surgery achieved real biochemical cure (normalization of serum calcium and PTH) in 96.1% of patients, graded as HIGH-QUALITY evidence, the strongest evidence tier in that review. The American Association of Endocrine Surgeons (AAES) Guidelines for Definitive Management of Primary Hyperparathyroidism (Wilhelm SM et al, JAMA Surg 2016;151(10):959-968, PMID 27532368) state plainly that 'the only definitive management is surgery,' that both focused/image-guided minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP, with intraoperative PTH monitoring for single-gland disease) and bilateral neck exploration (for known or suspected multigland disease) 'are appropriate operations that achieve high cure rates,' and define cure as eucalcemia sustained at more than 6 months postoperatively. Surgery is recommended for all symptomatic patients and should be considered for most asymptomatic patients per this guideline, and is reported as more cost-effective than observation or pharmacologic therapy. CINACALCET (a calcimimetic) is real, honest MEDICAL MANAGEMENT for patients who cannot or will not have surgery -- it is NOT a cure. In the pivotal randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Peacock M et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2005;90(1):135-41, PMID 15522938; n=78), 73% of cinacalcet-treated patients achieved the primary endpoint of normocalcemia versus only 5% of placebo-treated patients (P<0.001), and long-term open-label follow-up (Peacock M et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009;94(12):4860-7, PMID 19837909) showed normocalcemia maintained for up to 5.5 years of continuous therapy -- but the underlying adenoma/hyperplastic gland is never removed, PTH secretion is only pharmacologically suppressed rather than corrected, bone mineral density is largely unaffected by cinacalcet (per the same trials and the 2022 Ye Z et al RCT meta-analysis, PMID 36053960), and calcium control depends on continuing the drug indefinitely -- stopping treatment allows hypercalcemia to recur. Cinacalcet is real guideline-endorsed (Marcocci C et al, Fourth International Workshop, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014;99(10):3607-18, PMID 25162668; Bollerslev J et al, Eur J Endocrinol 2011;165(6):851-64, PMID 21964961) specifically for patients with contraindications to surgery or who decline it -- it is honestly labeled here as calcium-control, not cure.

curative_option.name: Parathyroidectomy -- Focused/Minimally Invasive Parathyroidectomy (MIP) with Intraoperative PTH Monitoring for Single-Gland Disease, or Bilateral Neck Exploration for Multigland Disease -- Real Definitive Surgical Cure
curative_option.note: This is the real closest-to-cure option for PHPT, not a symptom-control measure. The definitive RCT-based evidence -- Ye Z et al's systematic review/meta-analysis (J Bone Miner Res 2022;37(11):2351-2372, PMID 36053960; part of the 2022 Fifth International Workshop, 6 trials, n=441) -- reports a real, high-quality-evidence biochemical cure rate of 96.1% with surgery, defined as normalization of serum calcium and PTH. The AAES Guidelines (Wilhelm SM et al, JAMA Surg 2016;151(10):959-968, PMID 27532368) formally define cure as eucalcemia sustained beyond 6 months postoperatively, and state that both real surgical approaches achieve high cure rates: (1) focused/image-guided MIP, guided by preoperative cervical ultrasonography or other high-resolution localization imaging and intraoperative parathyroid hormone (IOPTH) monitoring via a reliable protocol (real recommended specifically for MIP, to confirm complete excision of hyperfunctioning tissue before closing), used for real single-adenoma disease; and (2) bilateral neck exploration, used for real known or suspected multigland disease, for patients with non-localizing imaging (who remain real surgical candidates per the guideline), and in familial PHPT. The guideline notes real surgeon volume matters (higher-volume surgeons have real better outcomes), preoperative parathyroid biopsy should real be avoided, and devascularized normal parathyroid tissue should real be autotransplanted. Real transient postoperative hypocalcemia is expected and managed with calcium supplementation; it is not treatment failure. This is reported honestly as a real 96.1% rate, not 100% -- persistent or recurrent disease still occurs in a real minority, most often from missed multigland disease, ectopic/supernumerary glands, or parathyromatosis, which is why the guideline stresses imaging, IOPTH confirmation, and surgeon experience.
curative_option.source: Ye Z et al, J Bone Miner Res 2022;37(11):2351-2372 (PMID 36053960); Wilhelm SM et al, JAMA Surg 2016;151(10):959-968 (PMID 27532368)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in real priority order matching this disease's honest cure-then-control hierarchy: (1) focused/minimally invasive parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring, the real definitive cure for single-gland disease; (2) bilateral neck exploration, the real definitive cure for multigland/non-localizing disease; (3) cinacalcet, real calcimimetic medical management for patients who cannot or decline surgery, honestly labeled as calcium control, not cure; (4) bisphosphonates (alendronate), real bone-protective adjunct for non-surgical candidates with low bone mass; and (5) vitamin D repletion, real guideline-recommended correction of coexisting vitamin D deficiency. Every entry is grounded in a real named trial, meta-analysis, or International Workshop guideline, never a vague reference.

phpt_parathyroidectomy_focused_mip_ioptH.name: Focused/Minimally Invasive Parathyroidectomy (MIP) with Intraoperative PTH Monitoring -- Real Definitive Surgical Cure for Single-Gland Disease
phpt_parathyroidectomy_focused_mip_ioptH.type: Image-guided focused surgical excision, single outpatient/short-stay procedure
phpt_parathyroidectomy_focused_mip_ioptH.effectiveness: The real RCT-pooled biochemical cure rate across all parathyroidectomy approaches (surgery vs no surgery) is 96.1%, graded HIGH-QUALITY evidence (Ye Z et al, J Bone Miner Res 2022;37(11):2351-2372, PMID 36053960; 6 RCTs, n=441). The AAES Guidelines (Wilhelm SM et al, JAMA Surg 2016;151(10):959-968, PMID 27532368) state MIP with a reliable intraoperative PTH monitoring protocol 'achieves high cure rates' for real single-adenoma disease and is real not routinely recommended when multigland disease is known or suspected preoperatively.
phpt_parathyroidectomy_focused_mip_ioptH.reason_why: PHPT is caused by one or more parathyroid glands autonomously oversecreting PTH (most commonly a single benign adenoma), driving excess bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption/hypercalcemia; excising the causative gland(s) directly removes the source of excess hormone. Intraoperative PTH monitoring confirms cure in real time -- PTH has a short half-life (minutes), so a real intraoperative drop of >=50% from the highest pre-excision level within 10-15 minutes of removal confirms that all hyperfunctioning tissue has real been excised before the surgeon closes, which is why this monitoring materially raises real confidence in single-operation cure.
phpt_parathyroidectomy_focused_mip_ioptH.doctor_reference_only_note: Preoperative localization (cervical ultrasonography and/or other high-resolution imaging per the AAES guideline), 25-hydroxyvitamin D correction beforehand, and surgeon case-volume are real factors the operating surgeon weighs; dose/route/technique decisions are for the Registered Medical Practitioner alone.

phpt_parathyroidectomy_bilateral_explora.name: Bilateral Neck Exploration -- Real Definitive Surgical Cure for Multigland Disease or Non-Localizing Imaging
phpt_parathyroidectomy_bilateral_explora.type: Open surgical exploration of all four parathyroid glands
phpt_parathyroidectomy_bilateral_explora.effectiveness: Covered by the real same 96.1% RCT-pooled biochemical cure rate (Ye Z et al, J Bone Miner Res 2022;37(11):2351-2372, PMID 36053960). The AAES Guidelines (Wilhelm SM et al, JAMA Surg 2016, PMID 27532368) state bilateral exploration is a real appropriate, high-cure-rate operation, specifically for known/suspected multigland disease, familial PHPT, and patients whose imaging does not localize a single gland -- these patients real remain surgical candidates rather than being excluded from cure.
phpt_parathyroidectomy_bilateral_explora.reason_why: A real minority of PHPT is caused by hyperplasia or multiple adenomas affecting more than one gland, which a focused single-gland operation would real miss; systematically visualizing and assessing all four glands lets the surgeon real identify and excise every hyperfunctioning gland while leaving enough real normal parathyroid tissue (or autotransplanting devascularized tissue, per the guideline) to avoid permanent hypoparathyroidism.
phpt_parathyroidectomy_bilateral_explora.doctor_reference_only_note: Ex vivo aspiration of resected tissue for confirmation, and formal frozen-section/histopathology, are real intraoperative decisions for the operating surgeon and pathologist.

phpt_cinacalcet_calcimimetic_therapy.name: Cinacalcet -- Real Calcimimetic Medical Management for Patients Who Cannot or Decline Surgery (Calcium Control, Not Cure)
phpt_cinacalcet_calcimimetic_therapy.type: Oral calcium-sensing receptor agonist (calcimimetic), twice-daily dosing
phpt_cinacalcet_calcimimetic_therapy.effectiveness: In the real pivotal randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Peacock M et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2005;90(1):135-41, PMID 15522938; n=78), 73% of cinacalcet-treated patients achieved normocalcemia (the primary endpoint) versus 5% on placebo (P<0.001). Real long-term open-label follow-up to 5.5 years (Peacock M et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009;94(12):4860-7, PMID 19837909; n=45) showed normocalcemia was real maintained throughout, and a real pooled analysis across disease-severity subgroups including patients with prior failed parathyroidectomy (Peacock M et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011;96(1):E9-18, PMID 20943783) found similarly effective calcium reduction 'across a wide spectrum of disease severity.' The 2022 Ye Z et al RCT meta-analysis (PMID 36053960) independently confirms cinacalcet 'probably reduced serum calcium and PTH levels.' Real honest limitation: bone mineral density is largely unchanged by cinacalcet in all of these trials, and normocalcemia is real only maintained while the drug is continued -- it does not cure the underlying gland.
phpt_cinacalcet_calcimimetic_therapy.reason_why: Cinacalcet allosterically increases the sensitivity of the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) to extracellular calcium, so the gland perceives ambient calcium as higher than it is and real reduces PTH secretion accordingly; this real lowers serum calcium without removing the causative adenoma or hyperplastic tissue, which is why effects reverse if the drug is stopped.
phpt_cinacalcet_calcimimetic_therapy.doctor_reference_only_note: Dose titration (real starting 30mg twice daily, titrated to serum calcium per the pivotal trial protocol) and monitoring for hypocalcemia are for the Registered Medical Practitioner alone; per the 2022/2014 International Workshop guidelines (PMID 25162668, PMID 21964961), cinacalcet is real indicated specifically for patients with contraindications to surgery or who decline it, not as a routine surgery alternative.

phpt_bisphosphonate_bone_protection_nons.name: Alendronate (Bisphosphonate) -- Real Bone-Protective Adjunct for Non-Surgical Candidates with Low Bone Mass
phpt_bisphosphonate_bone_protection_nons.type: Oral bisphosphonate, once-daily or once-weekly dosing
phpt_bisphosphonate_bone_protection_nons.effectiveness: In the real double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Khan AA et al, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2004;89(7):3319-25, PMID 15240609; n=44, asymptomatic PHPT not meeting or declining surgery), alendronate 10mg daily produced a real 6.85% increase in lumbar spine bone mineral density at 2 years versus baseline (P<0.001), and a real 4.01% total hip BMD increase at 12 months (P<0.001), with real 66% reduction in urinary NTX and 49-53% reduction in bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (markers of bone turnover) -- while real serum calcium and PTH did NOT change, confirming alendronate protects bone without correcting the underlying hyperparathyroid state. A real companion study in men with PHPT (Khan AA et al, Endocr Pract 2009;15(7):705-13, PMID 19625240) supports similar bone benefit. The 2022 Ye Z et al RCT meta-analysis (PMID 36053960) independently confirms alendronate 'increased bone density' across pooled trials.
phpt_bisphosphonate_bone_protection_nons.reason_why: PHPT causes real chronically elevated PTH, which increases osteoclast-mediated bone resorption (particularly at cortical bone sites); alendronate binds bone mineral and is real internalized by osteoclasts, inhibiting the mevalonate pathway and inducing osteoclast apoptosis, which real slows bone resorption and allows bone mass to recover even while the parathyroid gland itself remains untreated -- explaining why BMD improves but serum calcium/PTH stay unchanged.
phpt_bisphosphonate_bone_protection_nons.doctor_reference_only_note: Real indicated per the International Workshop guidelines (PMID 25162668, PMID 21964961) specifically for patients with low bone mass who are not surgical candidates; dose, duration, and monitoring for bisphosphonate-specific risks are for the Registered Medical Practitioner alone.

phpt_vitamin_d_repletion.name: Vitamin D Repletion -- Real Guideline-Recommended Correction of Coexisting Vitamin D Deficiency
phpt_vitamin_d_repletion.effectiveness: The AAES Guidelines (Wilhelm SM et al, JAMA Surg 2016;151(10):959-968, PMID 27532368) state real initial evaluation of every PHPT patient should include 25-hydroxyvitamin D measurement with real supplementation for vitamin D deficiency. Bollerslev J et al (Eur J Endocrinol 2011;165(6):851-64, PMID 21964961) real recommend vitamin D substitution before a final decision on surgical treatment when deficiency is present, while honestly noting severe symptomatic vitamin D deficiency is real not typical of PHPT patients in Europe and that no large RCT establishes a specific calcium-normalization percentage from repletion alone -- it is real not, by itself, a cure or a substitute for surgery, but a real correctable coexisting deficiency that guideline bodies recommend addressing regardless of the definitive treatment path chosen.
