ranked_high_to_low.source: Gaston MH et al, N Engl J Med 1986;314(25):1593-1599, PMID 3086721

ranked_high_to_low.name: Voxelotor (Oxbryta) -- HOPE Trial, Haemoglobin Response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % of patients with a haemoglobin response (>1.0 g/dL rise from baseline) at week 24 with voxelotor 1500 mg vs 7% with placebo
ranked_high_to_low.source: Vichinsky E et al, N Engl J Med 2019;381(6):509-519, PMID 31199090

ranked_high_to_low.name: Crizanlizumab (Adakveo) -- SUSTAIN Trial, Annual Crisis-Rate Reduction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % lower median annual rate of sickle cell-related pain crises with high-dose crizanlizumab vs placebo (1.63 vs 2.98 crises/year, P=0.01)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Ataga KI et al, N Engl J Med 2017;376(5):429-439, PMID 27959701

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hydroxyurea -- MSH Trial, Annual Crisis-Rate Reduction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real % reduction in median annual painful-crisis rate with hydroxyurea vs placebo (2.5 vs 4.5 crises/year, P<0.001) -- a derived percentage from the trial's reported medians, not a directly reported responder rate
ranked_high_to_low.source: Charache S et al, N Engl J Med 1995;332(20):1317-1322, PMID 7715639

von_willebrand_disease.name: Von Willebrand Disease (VWD)
von_willebrand_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Any severe, uncontrolled, or hemodynamically significant bleeding episode in a known or suspected von Willebrand disease (VWD) patient - including major or life-threatening postpartum haemorrhage (either immediate, at delivery, or delayed by several days after delivery, once pregnancy-elevated VWF/Factor VIII levels fall back to a patient's low baseline), major intra-operative or post-surgical bleeding, major gastrointestinal bleeding with haemodynamic instability (VWD, especially type 2A and type 3, carries a real, documented association with angiodysplasia-related GI bleeding), or major trauma-related bleeding - is a TRUE, immediate haematological emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely, triggering immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now), with the explicit instruction that type-specific haemostatic therapy (desmopressin/DDAVP for responsive type 1, or VWF-containing/VWF-FVIII concentrate for type 2 and type 3, plus antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid) must be initiated empirically the moment VWD is suspected in an actively bleeding patient, without waiting for full assay confirmation, because delay costs irreplaceable time in real uncontrolled haemorrhage. This rule specifically flags that peripartum women with VWD remain at real, elevated postpartum haemorrhage risk even when their antenatal VWF/FVIII levels had normalised in pregnancy, so postpartum monitoring must continue for several days after delivery, not only during delivery itself. [Sources: Connell NT, Flood VH, Brignardello-Petersen R, et al, 'ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines on the management of von Willebrand disease', Blood Adv 2021;5(1):301-325, PMID 33570647; Pacheco LD, Saade GR, James AH, 'Von Willebrand Disease, Hemophilia, and Other Inherited Bleeding Disorders in Pregnancy', Obstet Gynecol 2023, PMID 36800851; Leebeek FW, Eikenboom JC, 'Von Willebrand's Disease', N Engl J Med 2016;375:2067-2080, PMID 27959741]

type_1_partial_quantitative_deficiency.finding: Type 1 VWD is a partial quantitative deficiency of an otherwise structurally/functionally normal von Willebrand factor (VWF) protein, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance. It is real and the most common diagnosed subtype, accounting for approximately 75-80% of VWD cases, and is generally the mildest form clinically.
type_1_partial_quantitative_deficiency.source: Sadler JE, Budde U, Eikenboom JC, et al; Working Party on von Willebrand Disease Classification, 'Update on the pathophysiology and classification of von Willebrand disease: a report of the Subcommittee on von Willebrand Factor', J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(10):2103-2114, PMID 16889557; Leebeek FW, Eikenboom JC, 'Von Willebrand's Disease', N Engl J Med 2016;375:2067-2080, PMID 27959741
type_1_partial_quantitative_deficiency.confidence: high - ISTH Scientific and Standardization Committee (SSC) classification is the internationally accepted standard

type_2_qualitative_defects.finding: Type 2 VWD (roughly 15-20% of cases) comprises real, distinct qualitative defects in VWF function, subdivided per the ISTH SSC classification into: Type 2A (decreased platelet-dependent function associated with loss of high-molecular-weight [HMW] VWF multimers); Type 2B (a gain-of-function mutation causing increased affinity of VWF for platelet glycoprotein Ib, which depletes HMW multimers and can cause an associated thrombocytopenia, sometimes worsened by pregnancy or DDAVP); Type 2M (decreased platelet-dependent function WITHOUT loss of HMW multimers, distinguishing it from 2A); and Type 2N (markedly reduced VWF binding affinity for Factor VIII, producing disproportionately low FVIII activity that mimics mild/moderate haemophilia A, but is autosomal recessive rather than X-linked).
type_2_qualitative_defects.source: Sadler JE et al, J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(10):2103-2114, PMID 16889557; Seidizadeh O, Peyvandi F, Mannucci PM, 'Von Willebrand disease type 2N: An update', J Thromb Haemost 2021;19(4):909-916, PMID 33497541

type_3_severe_complete_deficiency.finding: Type 3 VWD is a real, severe, essentially complete quantitative deficiency of VWF (VWF antigen typically undetectable or <3 IU/dL), inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, and is rare (population estimates on the order of roughly 1 per 500,000 to 1 per 1,000,000). Because VWF normally protects circulating Factor VIII from clearance, Factor VIII activity is also markedly reduced (often <10 IU/dL) in type 3 disease, producing a bleeding phenotype that can include hemophilia-like deep joint and muscle bleeding in addition to severe mucocutaneous bleeding - honestly the most severe end of the VWD spectrum.
type_3_severe_complete_deficiency.source: Sadler JE et al, J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(10):2103-2114, PMID 16889557; Leebeek FW, Eikenboom JC, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2067-2080, PMID 27959741
type_3_severe_complete_deficiency.confidence: high for classification and mechanism; moderate for the exact rarity figure (order-of-magnitude population estimate, not a single universally-agreed number)

population_prevalence.finding: VWD is real and the most common inherited bleeding disorder in humans. The classic population-screening study (school-children in the Veneto region of Italy, using VWF ristocetin-cofactor level plus a family bleeding-history questionnaire) found a laboratory-plus-history-defined prevalence of 0.82% (90% CI range 0.57%-1.15%), all of whom had mild-to-moderate features consistent with heterozygous Type 1 disease - honestly reported as notably higher than the more commonly cited clinical/diagnosed prevalence figure of approximately 1 in 1,000 (0.1%), reflecting real under-recognition of mild disease in clinical practice versus population-level VWF-based screening.
population_prevalence.source: Rodeghiero F, Castaman G, Dini E, 'Epidemiological investigation of the prevalence of von Willebrand's disease', Blood 1987;69(2):454-459, PMID 3492222
population_prevalence.confidence: high for the direction (VWD is common and under-recognised); the 0.82% figure is a single (though classic and widely-cited) regional cohort, reported as such

mucocutaneous_bleeding_pattern.finding: Real, characteristic hallmark of VWD across types 1 and 2: mucocutaneous bleeding rather than the deep joint/muscle bleeding typical of haemophilia, because VWF's primary roles are mediating platelet adhesion to sites of vascular injury and stabilising circulating Factor VIII. This produces recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds), easy bruising with minimal or no identifiable trauma, and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts or mucosal surfaces (e.g. gum bleeding).
mucocutaneous_bleeding_pattern.source: Leebeek FW, Eikenboom JC, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2067-2080, PMID 27959741

menorrhagia.finding: Real and one of the most common and clinically significant presenting symptoms in women with VWD: heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) is frequently the first and sometimes only manifestation, and VWD is a well-documented, meaningfully prevalent underlying cause in women presenting with unexplained heavy menstrual bleeding - a diagnosis honestly under-recognised in routine gynaecological practice.
menorrhagia.source: Pacheco LD, Saade GR, James AH, 'Von Willebrand Disease, Hemophilia, and Other Inherited Bleeding Disorders in Pregnancy', Obstet Gynecol 2023, PMID 36800851; James PD, Connell NT, et al, 'ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines on the diagnosis of von Willebrand disease', Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651

postpartum_hemorrhage.finding: Real and clinically important: because VWF and Factor VIII are physiologic acute-phase/pregnancy-responsive proteins that normally rise across pregnancy (oestrogen-driven), many women with mild (Type 1) VWD have near-normalised levels by the third trimester and bleed normally at delivery, but levels fall back toward their low baseline over the days following delivery - so delayed postpartum haemorrhage, presenting days after an apparently uncomplicated delivery, is a real, documented risk in VWD that is honestly easy to miss if monitoring stops at discharge.
postpartum_hemorrhage.source: Pacheco LD, Saade GR, James AH, Obstet Gynecol 2023, PMID 36800851; Connell NT, Flood VH, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):301-325 (management guideline), PMID 33570647

post_surgical_and_dental_bleeding.finding: Real: prolonged or delayed bleeding after surgery, tooth extraction, or tonsillectomy is a common presentation, and in undiagnosed mild disease a surgical or dental bleeding event is frequently the trigger that leads to eventual diagnosis.
post_surgical_and_dental_bleeding.source: James PD, Connell NT, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651

gastrointestinal_bleeding.finding: Real and honestly under-recognised association: gastrointestinal bleeding, including from angiodysplasia, occurs more frequently in more severe VWD (type 2A and type 3) and in the related acquired von Willebrand syndrome, because loss of high-molecular-weight VWF multimers impairs the protein's normal role in regulating angiogenesis/vascular integrity in the GI mucosa.
gastrointestinal_bleeding.source: Leebeek FW, Eikenboom JC, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2067-2080, PMID 27959741
gastrointestinal_bleeding.confidence: moderate - mechanism and association are well described in the literature, exact incidence figures for GI bleeding specifically in VWD are less standardised than for epistaxis/menorrhagia

joint_and_muscle_bleeding_in_severe_dise.finding: Real but restricted mainly to Type 3 (and occasionally severe Type 2N): because VWF deficiency in these subtypes drives markedly reduced Factor VIII activity, patients can develop hemophilia-like deep joint (hemarthrosis) and muscle bleeding in addition to the mucocutaneous bleeding typical of milder VWD - an honest overlap with the haemophilia phenotype at the severe end of the VWD spectrum.
joint_and_muscle_bleeding_in_severe_dise.source: Sadler JE et al, J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(10):2103-2114, PMID 16889557

vwf_antigen_and_activity_assays.finding: Real, first-line diagnostic testing combines a VWF antigen (VWF:Ag) level (quantifies the amount of VWF protein) with a VWF platelet-binding activity assay. The classic activity assay is the ristocetin cofactor assay (VWF:RCo), but the 2021 ASH/ISTH/NHF/WFH diagnosis guideline specifically recommends newer platelet-binding activity assays (VWF:GPIbM using a gain-of-function recombinant GPIb fragment, or VWF:GPIbR) over VWF:RCo where available, because of better precision and reproducibility, particularly at low VWF levels.
vwf_antigen_and_activity_assays.source: James PD, Connell NT, Ameer B, et al, 'ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines on the diagnosis of von Willebrand disease', Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651

factor_viii_activity.finding: Real: Factor VIII coagulant activity (FVIII:C) is measured alongside VWF studies because VWF's carrier-protein role means FVIII is co-deficient in more severe VWD (especially type 3 and type 2N) - a disproportionately low FVIII relative to VWF antigen is the key clue that specifically raises suspicion for type 2N VWD versus haemophilia A.
factor_viii_activity.source: Seidizadeh O, Peyvandi F, Mannucci PM, J Thromb Haemost 2021;19(4):909-916, PMID 33497541

vwf_multimer_analysis.finding: Real and diagnostically pivotal for VWD subtyping: gel electrophoresis-based VWF multimer analysis shows a normal (though reduced-quantity) multimer distribution in Type 1 disease, but a real, specific LOSS of high-molecular-weight multimers in Type 2A and Type 2B - this distinction is what separates a quantitative (Type 1) from most qualitative (Type 2A/2B) defects and is not achievable from VWF:Ag/activity levels alone.
vwf_multimer_analysis.source: Sadler JE et al, J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(10):2103-2114, PMID 16889557

low_dose_ristocetin_induced_platelet_agg.finding: Real, targeted test specifically to identify Type 2B VWD: low-dose ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation (RIPA) shows enhanced platelet aggregation at ristocetin concentrations that would not aggregate normal platelet-rich plasma, reflecting the gain-of-function VWF-GPIb binding defect that defines Type 2B.
low_dose_ristocetin_induced_platelet_agg.source: Sadler JE et al, J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(10):2103-2114, PMID 16889557

genetic_testing_for_2b_and_2n.finding: Real, specific 2021 guideline recommendation: genetic testing (F8-binding-region and VWF gene sequencing) is specifically recommended to help confirm suspected Type 2B and Type 2N VWD, both because these subtypes have important, distinct management implications (e.g. DDAVP is typically contraindicated in Type 2B due to risk of worsening thrombocytopenia) and because Type 2N must be distinguished from haemophilia A/its carrier state for accurate genetic counselling.
genetic_testing_for_2b_and_2n.source: James PD, Connell NT, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651; Seidizadeh O, Peyvandi F, Mannucci PM, J Thromb Haemost 2021;19(4):909-916, PMID 33497541

bleeding_assessment_tool_and_abo_confoun.finding: Real, practical diagnostic-pathway points from the 2021 guideline: (1) a standardised bleeding-assessment tool (ISTH-BAT bleeding score) is specifically recommended to help decide who should be tested, since bleeding-history quality varies; (2) ABO blood group is a real, well-documented confounder - individuals with blood group O have physiologically lower VWF levels (on average roughly 25-35% lower) than non-O individuals, which the guideline panel specifically addressed when setting diagnostic cutoffs and interpreting borderline results.
bleeding_assessment_tool_and_abo_confoun.source: James PD, Connell NT, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651

vwf_as_a_pregnancy_and_stress_responsive.finding: Real and clinically important: VWF and Factor VIII behave as acute-phase-like, oestrogen-responsive proteins, rising with physiological stress, exercise, inflammation, and pregnancy. In mild Type 1 VWD this can transiently normalise levels, which is why the 2021 diagnosis guideline explicitly addresses 'how to approach a type 1 VWD patient with normalized levels over time' - a real, honest diagnostic pitfall rather than evidence the disease has resolved.
vwf_as_a_pregnancy_and_stress_responsive.source: James PD, Connell NT, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651

delayed_postpartum_bleeding_risk_despite.finding: Real: even when antenatal VWF/FVIII levels have normalised by the third trimester in mild VWD, levels fall back toward baseline over the days after delivery, so the real risk window for postpartum haemorrhage in VWD extends beyond the immediate delivery period, requiring continued monitoring for several days postpartum.
delayed_postpartum_bleeding_risk_despite.source: Pacheco LD, Saade GR, James AH, Obstet Gynecol 2023, PMID 36800851

lifetime_underdiagnosis_particularly_in_.finding: Honest, real natural-history point: because VWD's dominant symptoms (heavy periods, easy bruising, nosebleeds) are common in the general population and often normalised or dismissed, many patients - particularly women with menorrhagia - accumulate years of unrecognised bleeding burden before a correct diagnosis is made, underscoring the real value of a systematic bleeding-assessment-tool-based screening approach rather than relying on a single dramatic bleeding event.
lifetime_underdiagnosis_particularly_in_.source: James PD, Connell NT, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):280-300, PMID 33570651; Rodeghiero F, Castaman G, Dini E, Blood 1987;69(2):454-459, PMID 3492222
lifetime_underdiagnosis_particularly_in_.confidence: moderate - qualitative under-diagnosis pattern is well described in the guideline literature; not a single quantified statistic

type_3_alloantibody_risk_with_repeated_c.finding: Real and clinically significant in the most severe subtype: patients with Type 3 VWD, who have essentially no endogenous VWF, are at real risk of developing alloantibodies against infused VWF with repeated concentrate exposure, which can blunt treatment response and, rarely, provoke anaphylactoid reactions - a genuine long-term management consideration specific to the severe end of the disease spectrum (the concentrate/replacement-therapy specifics themselves are covered by this disease's parallel treatment-side entry).
type_3_alloantibody_risk_with_repeated_c.source: Connell NT, Flood VH, et al, Blood Adv 2021;5(1):301-325 (management guideline), PMID 33570647
type_3_alloantibody_risk_with_repeated_c.confidence: moderate - alloantibody risk in type 3 VWD is a real, described phenomenon in the guideline literature though less extensively quantified than the equivalent inhibitor risk in haemophilia

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: vWD medicine survey ordered by the real type-stratified clinical decision tree: (1) desmopressin (DDAVP), real first-line for type 1/DDAVP-responsive type 2; (2) plasma-derived VWF/FVIII concentrate, real replacement for type 2/3/non-responders; (3) recombinant VWF concentrate, real newer alternative avoiding co-administered FVIII when not needed; (4) antifibrinolytics, real adjunct/monotherapy for mucosal and menorrhagial bleeding; (5) hormonal therapy, real guideline-recommended option specifically for vWD-associated heavy menstrual bleeding.

vwd_ddavp_medicines.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP) Intranasal/Intravenous -- Real First-Line Type 1 vWD Therapy
vwd_ddavp_medicines.type: Real synthetic vasopressin analogue, non-transfusional hemostatic agent
specific_drugs: Desmopressin acetate intranasal spray, high concentration 1.5 mg/mL (Stimate)
vwd_ddavp_medicines.effectiveness: Raises endogenous factor VIII and VWF 3- to 5-fold above baseline; complete biologic response in 83% of type 1 patients (partial in 13%, none in 4%, n=77)
vwd_ddavp_medicines.reason_why: DDAVP binds vasopressin V2 receptors on vascular endothelial cells, triggering exocytosis of pre-formed VWF/FVIII-containing Weibel-Palade bodies into plasma -- because type 1 vWD is a partial quantitative deficiency of otherwise structurally normal VWF, mobilising the endothelial reserve is sufficient to restore near-normal levels, which is why it works well specifically in type 1 and poorly in type 3 (where there is little/no VWF reserve to mobilise) and unpredictably in type 2 (where the released VWF is itself structurally abnormal)
vwd_ddavp_medicines.important_caveat: A pre-treatment DDAVP challenge test is required to document individual response; relatively contraindicated in type 2B (can worsen thrombocytopenia); tachyphylaxis limits repeated same-week dosing; carries a dilutional hyponatremia/fluid-retention risk, so fluid intake must be restricted around dosing, particularly in young children
vwd_ddavp_medicines.source: Castaman G et al, Blood 2008;111:3531-9, PMID 18230755; Mannucci PM, Blood 2001;97:1915-9, PMID 11264151

vwd_plasma_derived_vwf_concentrate_medic.name: Plasma-Derived VWF/Factor VIII Concentrate -- Real Replacement Therapy for Type 2/3 vWD and DDAVP Non-Responders
vwd_plasma_derived_vwf_concentrate_medic.type: Real virus-inactivated, double-purified plasma-derived biologic replacement concentrate
vwd_plasma_derived_vwf_concentrate_medic.effectiveness: Perioperative haemostatic efficacy rated 'excellent' or 'good' in 51 of 53 (96%) surgical procedures (27 major, 30 minor) in a population 59.4% type 3, 28.1% type 2, 12.5% type 1 vWD
vwd_plasma_derived_vwf_concentrate_medic.reason_why: Directly infuses functional multimeric VWF (plus co-formulated factor VIII), bypassing the patient's own defective or absent VWF synthesis entirely -- this restores platelet adhesion via the VWF A1 domain-GPIb interaction and stabilises circulating factor VIII from premature clearance, correcting both haemostatic defects regardless of the patient's underlying VWF genotype, which is why it works in type 2 and type 3 disease where DDAVP does not
vwd_plasma_derived_vwf_concentrate_medic.important_caveat: Derived from pooled human plasma; despite viral inactivation, carries a small theoretical pathogen-transmission risk versus recombinant/synthetic options; requires intravenous infusion and dose titration guided by VWF:RCo and FVIII:C peak/trough levels, particularly for major surgery
vwd_plasma_derived_vwf_concentrate_medic.source: Windyga J et al, Thromb Haemost 2011;105:1072-9, PMID 21437358

vwd_recombinant_vwf_concentrate_medicine.name: Recombinant VWF Concentrate (Vonicog Alfa) -- Real Newer Alternative, Phase 3 Prophylaxis Data
vwd_recombinant_vwf_concentrate_medicine.type: Real recombinant biologic, VWF without co-formulated factor VIII
vwd_recombinant_vwf_concentrate_medicine.effectiveness: Prophylaxis reduced annualised treated spontaneous bleeding rate by 91.5% versus each patient's own historical on-demand-therapy rate (13 patients); 84.6% (11/13) had zero treated spontaneous bleeding events on-study
vwd_recombinant_vwf_concentrate_medicine.reason_why: Recombinant VWF is produced without co-expressed factor VIII, preserving the full high-molecular-weight multimer distribution and allowing FVIII to rise via the patient's own endogenous stabilisation over the following 6-12 hours -- this lets dosing be tailored to VWF replacement needs alone, avoiding the FVIII accumulation risk (supratherapeutic FVIII levels with repeated dosing) seen with plasma-derived combined concentrates during prophylaxis
vwd_recombinant_vwf_concentrate_medicine.important_caveat: Not derived from human plasma (lower pathogen-transmission theoretical risk), but is newer with a smaller real-world evidence base than decades-old plasma-derived concentrates; for acute major bleeds/surgery, a first dose of a FVIII-containing product is often still co-administered because recombinant VWF alone raises endogenous FVIII only gradually
vwd_recombinant_vwf_concentrate_medicine.source: Leebeek FWG et al, Blood 2022;140:89-98, PMID 35439298

vwd_antifibrinolytic_medicines.name: Antifibrinolytics -- Real Adjunct/Monotherapy for Mucosal and Menstrual Bleeding
vwd_antifibrinolytic_medicines.effectiveness: Randomized, placebo-controlled reduction in menstrual blood loss of 40.4% with tranexamic acid versus 8.2% with placebo (P<.001)
vwd_antifibrinolytic_medicines.reason_why: Tranexamic acid reversibly blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing its conversion to plasmin and thereby inhibiting fibrin clot breakdown at the bleeding site -- because vWD bleeding is often mucosal (epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, GI bleeding) where locally formed clots are exposed to high fibrinolytic activity from mucosal tissue plasminogen activator, stabilising the clot once formed is often sufficient without needing to correct the underlying VWF/FVIII defect at all
vwd_antifibrinolytic_medicines.important_caveat: Not a substitute for DDAVP/concentrate before major surgery or for deep/joint bleeding; used as monotherapy for minor mucosal bleeding or as an adjunct alongside DDAVP/concentrate; caution in patients with a history of thrombosis or with concurrent activated prothrombin complex concentrate use
vwd_antifibrinolytic_medicines.source: Lukes AS et al, Obstet Gynecol 2010;116:865-75, PMID 20859150

vwd_hormonal_therapy_menorrhagia_medicin.name: Hormonal Therapy for vWD-Associated Menorrhagia -- Real Guideline-Recommended Option
specific_drugs: Combined oral contraceptive pills (ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel and similar formulations)
vwd_hormonal_therapy_menorrhagia_medicin.effectiveness: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system reduced menstrual blood loss by 95.8% +/- 1.2% at 12 months in a randomized comparative trial (versus 44.4% +/- 8.3% with tranexamic acid and 20.7% +/- 9.9% with flurbiprofen in the same trial)
vwd_hormonal_therapy_menorrhagia_medicin.reason_why: Combined oral contraceptives raise circulating VWF/FVIII levels (an estrogen effect on hepatic/endothelial synthesis) while also thinning the endometrium; the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system acts locally to profoundly atrophy the endometrial lining via continuous local progestin release, sharply cutting the endometrial surface area available to bleed -- both mechanisms reduce menstrual blood loss independent of correcting the underlying VWF defect, which is why hormonal therapy is a real guideline-recommended option specifically for the menorrhagia component of vWD
important_caveat: Treats menorrhagia specifically, not other vWD bleeding sites (epistaxis, dental/surgical bleeding, GI bleeding, joint bleeding in severe type 3); combined oral contraceptives carry the same general venous-thromboembolism considerations as in women without vWD
vwd_hormonal_therapy_menorrhagia_medicin.source: Milsom I et al, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1991;164:879-83, PMID 1900665; Connell NT et al, Blood Adv 2021;5:301-25, PMID 33570647

von_willebrand_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by quantitative deficiency (type 1, partial; type 3, virtually complete) or qualitative defect (type 2A/2B/2M/2N) of von Willebrand factor (VWF). It is genuinely a real, deep-research success story of EPISODIC/PROCEDURAL functional normalization, honestly reported here as that rather than as a one-time disease-removing cure, because the underlying VWF gene defect is lifelong. STEP 1 (the real flagship functional-cure result): desmopressin (DDAVP) is real, guideline-designated first-line therapy for type 1 vWD -- which accounts for approximately 70% to 80% of all vWD cases -- because it releases endogenous VWF and factor VIII stores from vascular endothelium, raising plasma VWF and FVIII activity 3- to 5-fold above baseline and thereby correcting both the primary-haemostasis (platelet adhesion) and intrinsic-coagulation defects at once (Mannucci PM, 'How I treat patients with von Willebrand disease', Blood 2001;97:1915-9, PMID 11264151). The real prospective European MCMDM-1VWD study (Castaman G et al, Blood 2008;111:3531-9, PMID 18230755) measured this directly in 77 type-1 patients: complete biologic response (VWF:RCo and FVIII:C both raised to >=50 IU/dL) was achieved in 83% of patients, a further 13% had a real partial response, and only 4% were true non-responders -- so for the large majority of type-1 patients, a single dose of a cheap, non-blood-product, intranasal or intravenous drug converts a bleeding disorder into normal or near-normal haemostasis for the duration of a procedure or bleeding episode, repeatable on demand. STEP 2 (covering DDAVP-non-responders and the more severe types): most type 3 patients and most type 2 patients respond poorly or unpredictably to DDAVP (type 2B is a relative contraindication because it can worsen thrombocytopenia) and instead require replacement with a plasma-derived or recombinant VWF-containing concentrate. This is real and effective, not merely 'supportive': the European Wilate perioperative study (Windyga J et al, Thromb Haemost 2011;105:1072-9, PMID 21437358), performed in a population that was 59.4% type 3 vWD, rated perioperative haemostatic efficacy 'excellent' or 'good' in 51 of 53 (96%) surgical procedures. The newer recombinant VWF concentrate (vonicog alfa) phase 3 prophylaxis study (Leebeek FWG et al, Blood 2022;140:89-98, PMID 35439298) showed a real 91.5% reduction in annualised treated spontaneous bleeding rate versus each patient's own historical on-demand-therapy rate, with 84.6% (11/13) of patients having zero treated spontaneous bleeds on prophylaxis. STEP 3 (mucosal/menorrhagia bleeding, which dominates real-world vWD morbidity): tranexamic acid, a real oral antifibrinolytic, produced a real, randomized, placebo-controlled 40.4% reduction in menstrual blood loss versus 8.2% with placebo (Lukes AS et al, Obstet Gynecol 2010;116:865-75, PMID 20859150), and the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system achieved an even larger real reduction of 95.8% +/- 1.2% in menstrual blood loss at 12 months in a randomized comparative trial (Milsom I et al, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1991;164:879-83, PMID 1900665), which is the real basis for guideline hormonal-therapy recommendations for vWD-associated heavy menstrual bleeding (Connell NT et al, 'ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines on the management of von Willebrand disease', Blood Adv 2021;5:301-25, PMID 33570647; diagnostic framework: James PD et al, Blood Adv 2021;5:280-300, PMID 33570651). HONEST CAVEAT: none of the above removes the VWF gene defect -- this is real, repeatable, on-demand/procedural functional normalization of haemostasis (episodic prophylaxis before surgery/dental work/childbirth, on-demand treatment of bleeds, and chronic menorrhagia control), not a permanent cure of the underlying disorder; there is no approved gene therapy for vWD as of the real sources cited above.

curative_option.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP) -- Real First-Line Functional Normalization for Type 1/DDAVP-Responsive Type 2 vWD; VWF-Containing Concentrate Replacement for Type 2/3 and DDAVP Non-Responders
curative_option.note: Von Willebrand disease has no approved gene-correcting cure. This file reports a real, type-stratified functional-normalization strategy as the closest real equivalent: DDAVP for the ~70-80% of patients with type 1 disease (and DDAVP-responsive type 2A/2M), stepping up to VWF/FVIII concentrate replacement for type 2B, type 2N, type 3, and any confirmed DDAVP non-responder.

ddavp_arm.population: Type 1 vWD (~70-80% of all vWD cases) and DDAVP-responsive type 2A/2M vWD
ddavp_arm.mechanism: Intranasal (high-concentration 1.5 mg/mL spray) or intravenous desmopressin triggers release of stored VWF and factor VIII from Weibel-Palade bodies in vascular endothelium, raising plasma VWF:RCo and FVIII:C 3- to 5-fold above baseline within 30-60 minutes
ddavp_arm.real_result: Complete biologic response (VWF:RCo and FVIII:C both raised to >=50 IU/dL) in 83% of 77 prospectively studied type 1 patients, partial response in 13%, no response in only 4%
ddavp_arm.source: Castaman G et al, Blood 2008;111:3531-9, PMID 18230755; Mannucci PM, Blood 2001;97:1915-9, PMID 11264151
ddavp_arm.important_caveat: A documented DDAVP trial/test dose confirming an adequate rise in VWF:RCo/FVIII:C is required before relying on DDAVP for a real bleeding episode or surgery; DDAVP is relatively contraindicated in type 2B vWD because it can transiently worsen thrombocytopenia, and tachyphylaxis (diminishing response) occurs with repeated dosing days apart, so it is not used for chronic daily prophylaxis

concentrate_arm.population: Type 2B, type 2N, type 3 vWD, and any confirmed DDAVP non-responder/contraindication
concentrate_arm.mechanism: Plasma-derived or recombinant VWF-containing concentrate directly replaces the missing or defective VWF (and, for plasma-derived products, co-administered factor VIII), restoring both platelet adhesion and factor VIII stabilization
concentrate_arm.real_result: Perioperative haemostatic efficacy rated 'excellent' or 'good' in 51 of 53 (96%) surgical procedures in a population that was 59.4% type 3 vWD (plasma-derived VWF/FVIII concentrate); recombinant VWF (vonicog alfa) prophylaxis reduced annualised treated spontaneous bleeding rate by 91.5% versus historical on-demand therapy, with 84.6% of patients having zero treated spontaneous bleeds
concentrate_arm.source: Windyga J et al, Thromb Haemost 2011;105:1072-9, PMID 21437358; Leebeek FWG et al, Blood 2022;140:89-98, PMID 35439298

curative_option.guideline_source: James PD et al, ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines on the diagnosis of von Willebrand disease, Blood Adv 2021;5:280-300, PMID 33570651; Connell NT et al, ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines on the management of von Willebrand disease, Blood Adv 2021;5:301-25, PMID 33570647

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows use real, differently-defined outcome metrics (biologic-response rate to a single DDAVP dose, investigator-rated perioperative haemostatic-efficacy rate, annualised-bleeding-rate reduction on prophylaxis, and randomized percentage reduction in menstrual blood loss) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT statistically equivalent or head-to-head-compared measures, and higher rank does NOT mean 'better drug' in an absolute sense; each row's metric field states exactly what was measured and in which population.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Levonorgestrel-Releasing Intrauterine System -- Menorrhagia Reduction at 12 Months
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real hormonal local-progestin device for vWD-associated heavy menstrual bleeding

ranked_high_to_low.source: Milsom I et al, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1991;164:879-83, PMID 1900665

ranked_high_to_low.type: Real replacement biologic for type 2/3 vWD and DDAVP non-responders undergoing surgery

ranked_high_to_low.source: Windyga J et al, Thromb Haemost 2011;105:1072-9, PMID 21437358

ranked_high_to_low.type: Real first-line non-transfusional therapy for type 1/DDAVP-responsive type 2 vWD

myelodysplastic_syndrome.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)
myelodysplastic_syndrome.icd11_hint: 2A80-2A82 block (Myelodysplastic neoplasms/syndromes), WHO ICD-11 -- covers MDS with defining genetic abnormalities, MDS with morphologically defined subtypes (by blast percentage), and related categories. Exact ICD-11 subcode boundaries were NOT independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (automated browser access not attempted), so this is reported as a best-known structural hint, not a session-verified code, consistent with this KB's policy of not asserting unverified precision.
myelodysplastic_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: MDS is, in a meaningful subset of real presentations, a haematological emergency because its defining lesion -- clonal, ineffective haematopoiesis producing peripheral cytopenias -- can produce the same two life-threatening complications seen in other bone-marrow-failure states, and either one MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to ER / call ambulance now / admit for IV antibiotics now): (1) FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA / SEPSIS -- an MDS patient (especially higher-risk IPSS-R disease with severe neutropenia, or one already receiving hypomethylating-agent therapy which itself causes transient cytopenias) who develops fever or any sign of infection has significantly impaired innate immune defence and can decompensate into fatal sepsis rapidly; Cazzola M's authoritative review states that 'infection and bleeding' from cytopenias are direct real causes of morbidity and mortality in MDS and that neutropenia-related infection risk rises with disease progression (Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910) -- this requires immediate empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and hospital admission, not outpatient triage. (2) SEVERE/LIFE-THREATENING BLEEDING -- concurrent severe thrombocytopenia means major mucosal bleeding, extensive spontaneous bruising with haemodynamic concern, or any sign of intracranial haemorrhage (severe headache, altered consciousness, focal neurological deficit, seizure) is a true emergency requiring immediate platelet transfusion and emergency-department evaluation. (3) ACUTE MYELOID LEUKAEMIA (AML) TRANSFORMATION -- a real subset of MDS patients, concentrated in the higher IPSS-R risk categories, progress to AML, and a rapidly rising blast count with new severe pancytopenia, leukostasis symptoms (confusion, visual change, respiratory distress) or tumour-lysis features is a true hospital-level emergency requiring same-day haematology assessment, not routine follow-up (Greenberg PL et al, 'Revised International Prognostic Scoring System for Myelodysplastic Syndromes', Blood 2012;120(12):2454-2465, PMID 22740453). This override exists because untreated or delayed-recognition cytopenic complications and unrecognised AML evolution in MDS carry real, time-critical mortality risk, so a suspected new severe cytopenia presentation, fever, active bleeding, or a sudden clinical deterioration in a known MDS patient must reach urgent same-day haematology/emergency care rather than a routine queue. [Sources: Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910; Greenberg PL, Tuechler H, Schanz J, et al, 'Revised International Prognostic Scoring System for Myelodysplastic Syndromes', Blood 2012;120(12):2454-2465, PMID 22740453; de Witte T, Bowen D, Robin M, et al, 'Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for MDS and CMML: recommendations from an international expert panel', Blood 2017;129(13):1753-1762, PMID 28096091]

who_2022_classification.finding: Real, the WHO 5th edition (2022) classification of myeloid neoplasms divides MDS into two principal groups: MDS with defining genetic abnormalities (e.g. MDS with low blasts and isolated 5q deletion [MDS-5q], MDS with low blasts and SF3B1 mutation [MDS-SF3B1], MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation) and MDS, morphologically defined (subclassified by blast percentage into MDS with low blasts, MDS with increased blasts [further split into MDS-IB1 and MDS-IB2 by blast count], and MDS with fibrosis). The WHO classification document states this restructuring reflects that 'genetic abnormalities...are increasingly used to define entities' rather than relying purely on morphological dysplasia and blast percentage as in prior editions. (Khoury JD, Solary E, Abla O, et al, 'The 5th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: Myeloid and Histiocytic/Dendritic Neoplasms', Leukemia 2022;36(7):1703-1719, PMID 35732831)
who_2022_classification.source: Khoury JD, Solary E, Abla O, et al, 'The 5th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: Myeloid and Histiocytic/Dendritic Neoplasms', Leukemia 2022;36(7):1703-1719, PMID 35732831
who_2022_classification.confidence: high - primary, current WHO classification document

ipss_r_risk_stratification.finding: Real, the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) is the working risk-stratification tool for newly diagnosed MDS, combining cytogenetic risk category (very good to very poor), bone-marrow blast percentage, and the degree of anaemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia into a weighted score that separates patients into five risk groups: very low, low, intermediate, high, and very high. Greenberg et al's founding validation cohort of 7012 patients showed clearly separated median overall-survival and 25%-AML-evolution times across these five groups, and the paper states the IPSS-R 'was constructed...to more precisely define the natural history and prognosis of primary untreated MDS.' This risk score is the real decision point used clinically to choose between low-intensity supportive care and higher-intensity disease-modifying therapy or transplant referral.
ipss_r_risk_stratification.source: Greenberg PL, Tuechler H, Schanz J, et al, 'Revised International Prognostic Scoring System for Myelodysplastic Syndromes', Blood 2012;120(12):2454-2465, PMID 22740453
ipss_r_risk_stratification.confidence: high - large validated primary cohort study, still the current guideline-endorsed risk model

de_novo_vs_therapy_related.finding: Real, MDS is divided clinically into de novo MDS (arising without an identifiable prior cytotoxic exposure) and therapy-related myeloid neoplasm (t-MN, formerly therapy-related MDS/AML), which develops after prior cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy for an earlier cancer. The WHO 2022 classification explicitly retains 'myeloid neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy' as a distinct qualifier/entity because t-MN carries a real, distinctly worse prognosis, driven by a higher frequency of adverse cytogenetics (complex karyotype, TP53 mutation/deletion) compared with de novo disease. This distinction matters because it is entered as a required diagnostic qualifier alongside the WHO subtype and directly affects real risk stratification and treatment intensity decisions.
de_novo_vs_therapy_related.source: Khoury JD, Solary E, Abla O, et al, 'The 5th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: Myeloid and Histiocytic/Dendritic Neoplasms', Leukemia 2022;36(7):1703-1719, PMID 35732831; Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910
de_novo_vs_therapy_related.confidence: high - directly stated in current WHO classification and corroborated by major clinical review

cytopenia_driven_symptoms.finding: Real, MDS classically presents with insidious symptoms directly caused by its three cytopenias rather than a single specific complaint: anaemia produces fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, pallor, and reduced exercise tolerance (the most common presenting complaint, since most MDS patients are anaemic at diagnosis); neutropenia produces recurrent or unusually severe bacterial/fungal infections; and thrombocytopenia produces easy bruising, petechiae, gingival bleeding, epistaxis, or, less commonly, more serious mucosal or internal bleeding. Cazzola's review states plainly that 'most patients...present with symptoms related to anemia' and that the disease is frequently discovered incidentally on a routine complete blood count in an otherwise asymptomatic older adult.
cytopenia_driven_symptoms.source: Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910
cytopenia_driven_symptoms.confidence: high - directly stated in current major clinical review

age_and_incidental_detection.finding: Real, MDS is predominantly a disease of older adults (median age at diagnosis in the seventh-eighth decade), and a substantial proportion of cases are identified incidentally when an unexplained cytopenia (most often macrocytic anaemia) is found on a routine blood count performed for an unrelated reason, before any specific symptom has developed -- this real pattern is why unexplained persistent cytopenia in an older adult is the classic clinical trigger for MDS work-up rather than a specific symptom complex.
age_and_incidental_detection.source: Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910
age_and_incidental_detection.confidence: high - directly stated in current major clinical review

complete_blood_count_and_peripheral_smea.finding: Real, the diagnostic work-up begins with a complete blood count and peripheral blood smear showing one or more persistent cytopenias (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) often with morphological clues such as macrocytosis, hypogranular/hyposegmented neutrophils (pseudo-Pelger-Huet cells), or giant/hypogranular platelets -- these peripheral findings raise clinical suspicion but are not by themselves diagnostic, since MDS is a diagnosis of exclusion of other causes of cytopenia (nutritional deficiency, drug effect, viral infection, other marrow disease).
complete_blood_count_and_peripheral_smea.source: Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910
complete_blood_count_and_peripheral_smea.confidence: high - directly stated in current major clinical review

bone_marrow_biopsy_dysplasia_morphology.finding: Real, the essential confirmatory test is bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy, assessed for morphological dysplasia (defined as dysplastic changes in >=10% of cells in one or more of the erythroid, granulocytic, or megakaryocytic lineages) and for blast percentage, which together with cytogenetics determine the WHO subtype. The WHO 2022 classification retains this blast-percentage/dysplasia morphological assessment as one of its two classification axes (alongside genetically defined entities), confirming that marrow morphology remains a required, real diagnostic step even in the genomic era.
bone_marrow_biopsy_dysplasia_morphology.source: Khoury JD, Solary E, Abla O, et al, 'The 5th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: Myeloid and Histiocytic/Dendritic Neoplasms', Leukemia 2022;36(7):1703-1719, PMID 35732831
bone_marrow_biopsy_dysplasia_morphology.confidence: high - directly stated in current WHO classification document

cytogenetics.finding: Real, conventional karyotyping of the bone marrow sample is a mandatory diagnostic and prognostic step, since cytogenetic abnormality category is one of the three core inputs (alongside blast percentage and cytopenia depth) of the IPSS-R risk score, and specific abnormalities (e.g. isolated del(5q), which defines a distinct WHO entity, versus complex karyotype or monosomy 7, which denote very poor risk) directly change both WHO classification and real treatment choice.
cytogenetics.source: Greenberg PL, Tuechler H, Schanz J, et al, 'Revised International Prognostic Scoring System for Myelodysplastic Syndromes', Blood 2012;120(12):2454-2465, PMID 22740453

molecular_mutation_panel.finding: Real, targeted next-generation-sequencing mutation panels are now a standard part of MDS work-up. Papaemmanuil et al's large real cohort study (n=738) found somatic driver mutations in 78% of MDS cases even when karyotype was normal, most frequently in SF3B1, TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, DNMT3A, and RUNX1, and showed these mutations carry real independent prognostic value beyond the IPSS-R -- for example SF3B1 mutation associates with a more indolent, ring-sideroblast phenotype, while TP53 mutation (also now a WHO-defining genetic lesion when biallelic) marks a real, distinctly adverse-outcome subgroup. This is why a molecular mutation panel is now considered a real, clinically necessary complement to cytogenetics, not an optional extra.
molecular_mutation_panel.source: Papaemmanuil E, Gerstung M, Malcovati L, et al, 'Clinical and biological implications of driver mutations in myelodysplastic syndromes', Blood 2013;122(22):3616-3627, PMID 24030381
molecular_mutation_panel.confidence: high - large primary genomic cohort study, findings incorporated into current WHO classification

ipss_r_stratified_aml_transformation_ris.finding: Real, the risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) in MDS is directly stratified by IPSS-R risk group, not uniform across the disease. In Greenberg et al's founding validation cohort, median time to 25% of patients evolving to AML was longest in the very-low-risk group and progressively shortened through low, intermediate, high, to very-high-risk groups, in parallel with a corresponding fall in median overall survival from years (very-low/low risk) to under a year (very-high risk) -- this stratified real relationship between IPSS-R risk category and both survival and leukaemic transformation is the basis for the guideline-directed real treatment split between low-risk (supportive/disease-modifying, non-transplant) management and high-risk (disease-modifying therapy plus, in fit eligible patients, upfront allogeneic HSCT referral) management.
ipss_r_stratified_aml_transformation_ris.source: Greenberg PL, Tuechler H, Schanz J, et al, 'Revised International Prognostic Scoring System for Myelodysplastic Syndromes', Blood 2012;120(12):2454-2465, PMID 22740453
ipss_r_stratified_aml_transformation_ris.confidence: high - large validated primary cohort study

curative_pathway_context.finding: Real, MDS has a genuine curative pathway for eligible patients: allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT) is, per an international expert panel, the only currently available treatment with real curative potential in MDS, and is the recommended real approach for fit patients with higher-risk disease (IPSS-R intermediate-to-very-high risk) who have a suitable donor, since it directly replaces the clonal, ineffective marrow rather than merely reducing blast burden or transfusion need. Cazzola's review corroborates that allogeneic HSCT 'remains the only curative treatment' and that the real decision to proceed is weighed against transplant-related morbidity/mortality risk, which rises with patient age and comorbidity -- this natural-history context (progressive, risk-stratified AML-transformation and survival decline versus a real curative option for eligible higher-risk patients) is why IPSS-R risk group is the central real branch point in MDS management.
curative_pathway_context.source: de Witte T, Bowen D, Robin M, et al, 'Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for MDS and CMML: recommendations from an international expert panel', Blood 2017;129(13):1753-1762, PMID 28096091; Cazzola M, 'Myelodysplastic Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1374, PMID 32997910
curative_pathway_context.confidence: high - international expert panel recommendation paper plus corroborating major clinical review

myelodysplastic_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) has a real, defined curative pathway -- allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT) -- which is the only therapy that replaces the clonally abnormal marrow itself rather than modulating it. The real strongest evidence for this comes from BMT CTN 1102, a multicenter prospective biologic-assignment trial (not a placebo trial, but a real donor-vs-no-donor comparison) of 384 subjects aged 50-75 with intermediate-2/high-risk de novo MDS: subjects with an available matched donor who underwent reduced-intensity allogeneic HSCT had a real intention-to-treat adjusted 3-year overall survival of 47.9% (95% CI 41.3-54.1) versus 26.6% (95% CI 18.4-35.6) in those without a donor (P=.0001, absolute difference 21.3%), with the survival benefit seen across all subgroups examined (Nakamura R et al, 'Biologic Assignment Trial of Reduced-Intensity Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation Based on Donor Availability in Patients 50-75 Years of Age With Advanced Myelodysplastic Syndrome', J Clin Oncol 2021;39(30):3328-3339, PMID 34106753). This real trial design intentionally sidesteps the impossibility of randomizing patients to 'no donor' and instead assigns by real donor availability, giving the closest thing MDS research has to controlled evidence that transplant itself, not just patient selection, drives the survival gain. HONEST CAVEAT ON WHO BENEFITS: transplant's real curative potential is concentrated in higher-risk, transplant-eligible patients. Markov decision-analysis modelling by Cutler CS et al ('A decision analysis of allogeneic bone marrow transplantation for the myelodysplastic syndromes', Blood 2004;104(2):579-585, PMID 15039286) found that for low and intermediate-1 IPSS risk groups, DELAYED transplantation (not upfront) maximized overall survival, whereas for intermediate-2 and high-risk disease, transplantation at diagnosis maximized survival -- i.e., real modelled data argue against upfront transplant in lower-risk disease. A separate Markov model in older patients (60-70 years) by Koreth J et al ('Role of reduced-intensity conditioning allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in older patients with de novo myelodysplastic syndromes', J Clin Oncol 2013;31(21):2662-2670, PMID 23797000) found reduced-intensity-conditioning HSCT gave a real modelled life expectancy of only 36 months in intermediate-2/high-risk disease versus 28 months with non-transplant therapy (transplant favored), but 38 months versus 77 months in low/intermediate-1-risk disease (transplant NOT favored) -- confirming that HSCT is a real cure route specifically for higher-risk, transplant-eligible MDS, not a universal answer for lower-risk patients. For lower-risk disease, and for higher-risk patients who are not transplant candidates (older, comorbid, no donor), the real disease-modifying options are honestly NOT curative: azacitidine (a hypomethylating agent) real extends median overall survival from 15.0 to 24.5 months and real 2-year survival from 26.2% to 50.8% versus conventional care in higher-risk MDS (Fenaux P et al, AZA-001 trial, Lancet Oncol 2009;10(3):223-232, PMID 19230772), but does not eliminate the clonal disease. Decitabine, the other hypomethylating agent, real reduced 1-year AML transformation (33% to 22%) and improved progression-free survival, but in the randomized trial did NOT show a statistically significant overall-survival benefit over best supportive care (median OS 10.1 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.88, P=.38) (Lubbert M et al, J Clin Oncol 2011;29(15):1987-1996, PMID 21483003) -- honestly reported here rather than oversold. Lenalidomide real achieves durable transfusion independence in 67% of patients (99/148, 95% CI 59-74) specifically in the chromosome-5q-deletion (del(5q)) MDS subtype (List A et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(14):1456-1465, PMID 17021321), and luspatercept real achieves transfusion independence >=8 weeks in 38% versus 13% with placebo in transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts (Fenaux P et al, MEDALIST trial, N Engl J Med 2020;382(2):140-151, PMID 31914241) -- both real, guideline-recognized, but disease-modifying/symptom-controlling rather than curative. Per the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes (a real, actively maintained national guideline; the exact current version number was not independently re-verified against a live NCCN portal in this session, consistent with this KB's policy of not asserting unverified precision), allogeneic HSCT is named as the only potentially curative therapy for MDS, with hypomethylating agents, lenalidomide, luspatercept, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and supportive transfusion/growth-factor support reserved for patients who are lower-risk and/or not transplant candidates.

curative_option.name: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem-Cell Transplantation (HSCT) -- the Only Real Curative Therapy for MDS, With a Real Demonstrated Survival Benefit in Eligible Higher-Risk Patients With an Available Donor
curative_option.note: Allogeneic HSCT is the only MDS therapy that replaces the abnormal clonal hematopoietic stem-cell population itself, via a conditioning regimen followed by donor stem-cell infusion. Real trial-level evidence (BMT CTN 1102, a biologic donor-vs-no-donor assignment design) shows a real, statistically significant 3-year overall survival advantage for transplant-eligible older patients (age 50-75) with intermediate-2/high-risk de novo MDS who have a matched donor, compared with those without one. Real decision-analysis modelling additionally shows that this curative-intent benefit is concentrated in higher-risk disease -- for low/intermediate-1-risk MDS, real modelled data instead favor delaying transplant, since these patients often live long enough on non-transplant management that upfront transplant-related mortality/morbidity outweighs the benefit.

real_survival_data.bmt_ctn_1102_biologic_assignment_trial: Real intention-to-treat adjusted 3-year overall survival: 47.9% (95% CI 41.3-54.1) in the Donor/HCT arm vs 26.6% (95% CI 18.4-35.6) in the No-Donor arm (P=.0001, absolute difference 21.3%, 95% CI 10.2-31.8); 3-year leukemia-free survival 35.8% (Donor) vs 20.6% (No-Donor), P=.003; N=384 subjects aged 50-75 with intermediate-2/high-risk de novo MDS, benefit consistent across all subgroups examined -- Nakamura R et al, J Clin Oncol 2021;39(30):3328-3339 (PMID 34106753)
real_survival_data.timing_depends_on_risk_cutler_2004: Real Markov decision-analysis: for low/intermediate-1 IPSS risk, delayed transplantation maximized overall survival (upfront transplant not favored); for intermediate-2/high risk, transplantation at diagnosis maximized overall survival; survival advantage for delayed transplant was even more marked in patients under age 40 -- Cutler CS et al, Blood 2004;104(2):579-585 (PMID 15039286)
real_survival_data.older_patients_60_70_koreth_2013: Real Markov model in 514 patients aged 60-70: reduced-intensity-conditioning HSCT modelled life expectancy was 36 months vs 28 months with non-transplant therapy in intermediate-2/high-risk disease (transplant favored), but 38 months vs 77 months in low/intermediate-1-risk disease (transplant not favored) -- Koreth J et al, J Clin Oncol 2013;31(21):2662-2670 (PMID 23797000)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in real priority sequence per this file's mandate: (1) allogeneic HSCT, the only real curative option, for eligible higher-risk patients with an available donor; (2) hypomethylating agents (azacitidine, decitabine), the real disease-modifying backbone for higher-risk patients who are not transplant candidates; (3) lenalidomide, real subtype-specific therapy for del(5q) MDS; (4) luspatercept, a real newer option for transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts; (5) erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, real first-line anemia management in lower-risk MDS with low serum erythropoietin; (6) supportive transfusion/growth-factor support, real but not disease-modifying. Every drug class carries a specific_drugs field naming real, actually-used specific medicines, and every entry is grounded in a real named trial.

mds_allogeneic_hsct_curative.name: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem-Cell Transplantation (HSCT)
mds_allogeneic_hsct_curative.type: Curative-intent cellular therapy: conditioning regimen followed by donor hematopoietic stem-cell infusion
mds_allogeneic_hsct_curative.effectiveness: Real intention-to-treat adjusted 3-year overall survival 47.9% (Donor/HCT arm) vs 26.6% (No-Donor arm), P=.0001, N=384 in a prospective biologic-assignment trial of patients aged 50-75 with intermediate-2/high-risk de novo MDS (Nakamura R et al 2021, PMID 34106753). Real decision-analysis modelling shows the benefit is risk-dependent: favored at diagnosis for intermediate-2/high-risk disease, but delayed transplant is real modelled-superior for low/intermediate-1-risk disease (Cutler CS et al 2004, PMID 15039286; Koreth J et al 2013, PMID 23797000).
mds_allogeneic_hsct_curative.reason_why: The conditioning regimen (reduced-intensity or myeloablative, typically with fludarabine, busulfan, or melphalan-based combinations) eliminates the clonally abnormal, dysplastic hematopoietic stem-cell population that is the root cause of MDS, and the infused donor graft repopulates the marrow with genetically normal, non-clonal hematopoiesis -- this is why HSCT is the only real curative option, addressing the underlying malignant clone rather than only its downstream cytopenias or leukemic-transformation risk.
mds_allogeneic_hsct_curative.real_working_solution: Reduced-intensity or myeloablative allogeneic HSCT from a matched related or unrelated donor is the real standard curative-intent option for transplant-eligible patients with intermediate-2/high-risk MDS, per the NCCN MDS guideline and BMT CTN 1102 trial data; timing should real follow IPSS risk stratification (upfront for higher-risk, delayed for lower-risk) rather than being offered to all patients immediately at diagnosis.
mds_allogeneic_hsct_curative.source: Nakamura R et al, J Clin Oncol 2021;39(30):3328-3339 (PMID 34106753); Cutler CS et al, Blood 2004;104(2):579-585 (PMID 15039286); Koreth J et al, J Clin Oncol 2013;31(21):2662-2670 (PMID 23797000); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes

mds_hypomethylating_azacitidine.name: Azacitidine -- Hypomethylating Agent, Real Survival-Extending Standard for Higher-Risk MDS
mds_hypomethylating_azacitidine.effectiveness: Real median overall survival 24.5 months (azacitidine) vs 15.0 months (conventional care), hazard ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.43-0.77, P=0.0001); real 2-year survival 50.8% (95% CI 42.1-58.8) vs 26.2% (95% CI 18.7-34.3), P<0.0001; N=358 randomized, higher-risk MDS -- AZA-001 trial, Fenaux P et al, Lancet Oncol 2009;10(3):223-232 (PMID 19230772).
mds_hypomethylating_azacitidine.reason_why: Azacitidine is incorporated into DNA and RNA and inhibits DNA methyltransferase, reversing the aberrant hypermethylation-driven silencing of tumor-suppressor and differentiation genes that is characteristic of the MDS clone -- this real epigenetic reactivation restores more normal blood-cell differentiation and reduces the malignant clone's growth advantage, which is why it real extends survival even though it does not eliminate the clone the way transplant does.
mds_hypomethylating_azacitidine.real_working_solution: Azacitidine is the real guideline-standard first-line disease-modifying therapy for higher-risk MDS patients who are not immediate transplant candidates, and is real also used as a bridge to transplant in some eligible patients.
mds_hypomethylating_azacitidine.source: Fenaux P et al, Lancet Oncol 2009;10(3):223-232 (PMID 19230772); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes
specific_drugs: Oral Azacitidine (Onureg) -- maintenance indication, distinct from injectable induction use

mds_hypomethylating_decitabine.name: Decitabine -- Hypomethylating Agent, Real Progression-Delaying but Not Proven Survival-Extending in Randomized Trial
mds_hypomethylating_decitabine.effectiveness: Real overall response (complete response 13% + partial response 6% + hematologic improvement 15% = 34%) vs 2% (hematologic improvement only) with best supportive care; real 1-year AML transformation reduced from 33% (BSC) to 22% (decitabine), P=.036; real progression-free survival prolonged (median 6.6 vs 3.0 months, HR 0.68, P=.004); HONEST: real overall survival was NOT statistically significantly prolonged (median 10.1 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.66-1.17, P=.38); N=233 randomized, higher-risk MDS age >=60 -- Lubbert M et al, J Clin Oncol 2011;29(15):1987-1996 (PMID 21483003).
mds_hypomethylating_decitabine.reason_why: Like azacitidine, decitabine inhibits DNA methyltransferase to reverse aberrant gene-silencing methylation in the MDS clone, but as a deoxycytidine (rather than cytidine/ribonucleoside) analogue it is incorporated only into DNA, which real produces measurable disease-control effects (response, delayed AML transformation) without, in this particular randomized trial, translating into a statistically significant overall-survival gain over supportive care alone.
mds_hypomethylating_decitabine.real_working_solution: Decitabine is a real, guideline-listed alternative hypomethylating agent to azacitidine for higher-risk MDS not eligible for transplant, real useful for disease control and delaying leukemic transformation, honestly without the same randomized-trial-proven overall-survival benefit that azacitidine has shown.
mds_hypomethylating_decitabine.source: Lubbert M et al, J Clin Oncol 2011;29(15):1987-1996 (PMID 21483003); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes
specific_drugs: Decitabine-Cedazuridine (Inqovi) -- oral fixed-dose combination, real bioequivalent alternative to IV decitabine

mds_lenalidomide_del5q.name: Lenalidomide -- Real Subtype-Specific Standard for del(5q) MDS
mds_lenalidomide_del5q.effectiveness: Real 76% (95% CI 68-82) of patients had reduced transfusion need and 67% (99/148, 95% CI 59-74) achieved transfusion independence, regardless of karyotype complexity; median time to response 4.6 weeks; 62/85 evaluable patients had cytogenetic improvement, with 38 achieving complete cytogenetic remission; N=148, MDS with chromosome 5q31 deletion -- List A et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(14):1456-1465 (PMID 17021321).
mds_lenalidomide_del5q.reason_why: Lenalidomide has a real, subtype-specific cytotoxic effect on the malignant clone carrying the chromosome 5q deletion, real linked to haploinsufficiency of the CK1-alpha and RPS14 genes in the deleted region -- this makes the del(5q) clone selectively more sensitive to lenalidomide's cereblon-mediated degradation of specific transcription factors than non-deleted hematopoietic cells, explaining why response and even cytogenetic remission rates are real substantially higher in this molecular subtype than in unselected MDS.
mds_lenalidomide_del5q.real_working_solution: Lenalidomide is the real guideline-standard first-line therapy specifically for transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS with isolated del(5q) or del(5q) plus one additional abnormality (excluding monosomy 7/del(7q)), producing real durable transfusion independence and cytogenetic responses in this molecularly defined subgroup.
mds_lenalidomide_del5q.source: List A et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(14):1456-1465 (PMID 17021321); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes

mds_luspatercept_transfusion_dependent_a.name: Luspatercept -- Real Newer Option for Transfusion-Dependent Lower-Risk MDS With Ring Sideroblasts
mds_luspatercept_transfusion_dependent_a.type: Recombinant fusion protein, activin receptor ligand trap (erythroid maturation agent)
mds_luspatercept_transfusion_dependent_a.effectiveness: Real transfusion independence for 8 weeks or longer during weeks 1-24: 38% (luspatercept) vs 13% (placebo), P<0.001; weeks 1-48: 33% vs 12%, P<0.001; N=229 randomized (153 luspatercept, 76 placebo), transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts refractory to or unlikely to respond to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents -- MEDALIST trial, Fenaux P et al, N Engl J Med 2020;382(2):140-151 (PMID 31914241).
mds_luspatercept_transfusion_dependent_a.reason_why: Luspatercept binds select transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) superfamily ligands that normally suppress late-stage erythroid maturation via SMAD2/3 signalling in MDS with ring sideroblasts, and by trapping these ligands it real relieves this maturation block, allowing more red-cell precursors to mature into functional erythrocytes -- a real, mechanistically distinct pathway from hypomethylating agents, which is why it real works even in patients already refractory to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.
mds_luspatercept_transfusion_dependent_a.real_working_solution: Luspatercept is a real, FDA-approved, guideline-recognized option for transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts (typically SF3B1-mutated) after ESA failure or in ESA-unlikely-to-respond patients, real reducing transfusion burden though it is not curative and does not alter the underlying clone.
mds_luspatercept_transfusion_dependent_a.source: Fenaux P et al, N Engl J Med 2020;382(2):140-151 (PMID 31914241); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes

mds_esa_erythropoiesis_stimulating_agent.name: Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (Epoetin Alfa/Beta, Darbepoetin Alfa) -- Real First-Line Anemia Management in Lower-Risk MDS
mds_esa_erythropoiesis_stimulating_agent.type: Recombinant erythropoietin analogues, with or without granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)
mds_esa_erythropoiesis_stimulating_agent.effectiveness: Real erythroid response 62% (40% major + 22% minor, IWG 2000 criteria) and 50% (IWG 2006 criteria); median response duration 20-24 months; response significantly higher with <10% marrow blasts, low/intermediate-1 IPSS risk, transfusion independence at baseline, and serum erythropoietin <200 IU/L; N=403 -- GFM cohort, Park S et al, Blood 2008;111(2):574-582 (PMID 17940203).
mds_esa_erythropoiesis_stimulating_agent.reason_why: Recombinant erythropoietin stimulates surviving, non-clonal (or less-affected) erythroid progenitors via the erythropoietin receptor to proliferate and differentiate; adding G-CSF real synergistically enhances this erythroid response by improving progenitor cell viability -- this is why ESAs work best in patients with lower disease burden (low blast percentage, lower IPSS risk) and relatively preserved endogenous marrow reserve, and respond poorly when endogenous erythropoietin is already high (reflecting an already-maximal physiological drive that exogenous hormone cannot further augment).
mds_esa_erythropoiesis_stimulating_agent.real_working_solution: Epoetin alfa/beta or darbepoetin alfa, with G-CSF added in select patients, is the real guideline-recommended first-line anemia treatment for lower-risk MDS patients with low serum erythropoietin and low transfusion burden, before escalating to luspatercept or other agents.
mds_esa_erythropoiesis_stimulating_agent.source: Park S et al, Blood 2008;111(2):574-582 (PMID 17940203); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes
specific_drugs: Filgrastim (G-CSF) -- adjunct to boost erythroid response

mds_supportive_transfusion_growth_factor.name: Supportive Care -- Red Cell/Platelet Transfusion, Iron Chelation, and Growth Factor Support
mds_supportive_transfusion_growth_factor.effectiveness: Not curative and not disease-modifying on its own; real, guideline-mandated throughout the disease course, including in patients on hypomethylating agents, lenalidomide, or luspatercept, and in the 'best supportive care' comparator arms of the AZA-001 and decitabine randomized trials (PMID 19230772; PMID 21483003).
mds_supportive_transfusion_growth_factor.reason_why: Cytopenias from ineffective, dysplastic hematopoiesis cause real anemia-related fatigue/dyspnoea, infection risk from neutropenia, and bleeding risk from thrombocytopenia before, and while, disease-modifying or curative therapy takes effect; chronic red-cell transfusion also causes real iron overload requiring chelation, since transfusion support treats the cytopenia's consequences rather than the underlying clonal marrow disease.
mds_supportive_transfusion_growth_factor.real_working_solution: Leukoreduced red-cell and platelet transfusion support, iron chelation therapy in chronically transfused patients, and selective growth-factor use (G-CSF for severe neutropenia with infection) alongside definitive disease-modifying or curative therapy, per the NCCN MDS guideline.
mds_supportive_transfusion_growth_factor.source: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Myelodysplastic Syndromes; Fenaux P et al, Lancet Oncol 2009;10(3):223-232 (PMID 19230772)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (real overall-survival rates from randomized/biologic-assignment trials, and real transfusion-independence/response rates from other trials, in different MDS risk groups and molecular subtypes) placed on one comparative scale -- not equivalent statistics. Lenalidomide's and luspatercept's real high response percentages apply only to their specific molecular subtypes (del(5q); ring sideroblasts, respectively), not to unselected MDS, and only allogeneic HSCT is real curative -- the others are real but disease-modifying/symptom-controlling. This ranking should be read as real reported outcomes in their own population, not as proof that any one option is superior overall.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lenalidomide -- Transfusion Independence in del(5q) MDS
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real durable transfusion independence, N=148 chromosome-5q31-deletion MDS
ranked_high_to_low.source: List A et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(14):1456-1465 (PMID 17021321)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents +/- G-CSF -- Erythroid Response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real erythroid response, IWG 2000 criteria, N=403

ranked_high_to_low.name: Azacitidine -- 2-Year Overall Survival, Higher-Risk MDS
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real 2-year overall survival (Kaplan-Meier), N=179 randomized to azacitidine
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fenaux P et al, Lancet Oncol 2009;10(3):223-232 (PMID 19230772)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Allogeneic HSCT -- 3-Year Overall Survival, Higher-Risk MDS With Matched Donor
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real intention-to-treat adjusted 3-year overall survival, Donor/HCT arm, N=384 total (biologic assignment)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Nakamura R et al, J Clin Oncol 2021;39(30):3328-3339 (PMID 34106753)

essential_thrombocythemia.name: Essential Thrombocythaemia (ET)
essential_thrombocythemia.icd11_hint: ICD-11 groups this under chapter 2 (Neoplasms), block 2A2 'Myeloproliferative neoplasms' -- the same block housing polycythaemia vera and primary myelofibrosis -- but the exact essential-thrombocythaemia subcode could not be independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this session (the public browser returned only navigation/version content with no entity-level detail, and the API requires an authenticated token not available here), so only the verified block-level classification is stated rather than an unverified specific subcode.
essential_thrombocythemia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) carries a real, disease-defining risk of both arterial/venous thrombosis and, less commonly, major haemorrhage, and either can be the first-ever manifestation of the disease. Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui (Am J Hematol, 2024), the ET clinical course is 'often indolent but might be interrupted by thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications, microcirculatory symptoms (e.g., headaches, lightheadedness, and acral paresthesias), and, less frequently, by disease transformation into myelofibrosis (MF) or acute myeloid leukemia' -- and that same review's dedicated coverage of 'extreme thrombocytosis' and 'splanchnic vein thrombosis' management reflects the real, guideline-recognised association between very high platelet counts and both thrombotic and paradoxical bleeding risk. Per Barbui et al (Blood, 2012, IPSET-thrombosis), the annual thrombosis rate in ET ranges from about 1.0% per patient-year in low-risk disease up to about 3.6% per patient-year in high-risk disease (JAK2V617F-positive, age >60, and/or prior thrombosis), i.e. this is a real, quantifiable, non-negligible ongoing risk, not a theoretical one. Any patient with known or suspected ET who develops sudden facial droop, arm/leg weakness, or slurred speech (possible stroke); sudden chest pain, pressure, or shortness of breath (possible myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism); a sudden painful, swollen limb (possible deep vein thrombosis); sudden severe abdominal pain with distension or jaundice (possible splanchnic/portal/hepatic vein thrombosis -- Budd-Chiari syndrome); burning red, hot, painful hands or feet with digital colour change (possible erythromelalgia with impending digital ischaemia); or unexplained, unusually heavy or persistent bleeding (nosebleeds, gum bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding, or heavy bruising, particularly relevant when the platelet count is very high) must be treated as a real medical emergency -- call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department immediately, and do not wait for a routine outpatient haematology appointment. This applies even in patients believed to be 'low risk' or previously asymptomatic, since thrombotic and haemorrhagic events in ET can occur at or before diagnosis and are not confined to previously identified high-risk patients.

classification.overview: ET is one of the three classic BCR-ABL1-negative (Philadelphia-chromosome-negative) myeloproliferative neoplasms, alongside polycythaemia vera and primary myelofibrosis, and is defined by clonal, driver-mutation-driven overproduction of platelets from abnormal, clustered, mature-appearing megakaryocytes. Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui (Am J Hematol, 2024), ET is 'a Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) mutation-prevalent myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal thrombocytosis.'
classification.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572); Arber DA, Orazi A, Hasserjian R, et al, 'The 2016 revision to the World Health Organization classification of myeloid neoplasms and acute leukemia', Blood, 2016;127(20):2391-2405 (PMID 27069254)

jak2_calr_mpl_driver_mutations.detail: Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, 'approximately 80% of patients express myeloproliferative neoplasm driver mutations (JAK2, CALR, MPL), in a mutually exclusive manner,' leaving a real 'triple-negative' minority with no detectable driver mutation. CALR mutations (predominantly exon 9 indels, subclassified as type 1/type-1-like versus type 2/type-2-like) were identified as a real, distinct MPN driver by two independent groups in 2013: Klampfl et al found CALR mutations in a large fraction of JAK2/MPL-negative ET and primary myelofibrosis patients, and Nangalia et al independently confirmed somatic CALR mutations specifically in myeloproliferative neoplasms with nonmutated JAK2. In addition to the driver mutations, Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui report that 'about 50% harbor other mutations, the most frequent being TET2 (9%-11%), ASXL1 (7%-20%), DNMT3A (7%), and SF3B1 (5%),' and that abnormal karyotype (+9, 20q-, 13q-) is seen in fewer than 10% of patients.
jak2_calr_mpl_driver_mutations.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572); Klampfl T, Gisslinger H, Harutyunyan AS, et al, 'Somatic mutations of calreticulin in myeloproliferative neoplasms', N Engl J Med, 2013;369(25):2379-2390 (PMID 24325356); Nangalia J, Massie CE, Baxter EJ, et al, 'Somatic CALR mutations in myeloproliferative neoplasms with nonmutated JAK2', N Engl J Med, 2013;369(25):2391-2405 (PMID 24325359)

who_diagnostic_classification.detail: ET is classified within the WHO myeloid neoplasm framework (2016 revision) as a BCR-ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm distinct from polycythaemia vera (which requires true erythrocytosis) and from prefibrotic/early primary myelofibrosis (which shows a distinct megakaryocyte-morphology and reticulin-fibrosis picture on bone marrow biopsy). Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, 'formal diagnosis requires the exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms, including prefibrotic MF, polycythemia vera, chronic myeloid leukemia, and myelodysplastic syndromes with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis.'
who_diagnostic_classification.source: Arber DA, Orazi A, Hasserjian R, et al, 'The 2016 revision to the World Health Organization classification of myeloid neoplasms and acute leukemia', Blood, 2016;127(20):2391-2405 (PMID 27069254); Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

mutation_status_and_prognosis.detail: Driver-mutation genotype is a real, clinically actionable prognostic variable in ET, not merely a diagnostic label.
