Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, 'MPL and CALR-1 mutations have been associated with increased risk of MF transformation; spliceosome [mutations] with inferior overall and MF-free survival; TP53 with leukemic transformation, and JAK2V617F with thrombosis' -- i.e., JAK2V617F-positive ET carries a real higher thrombosis risk (and is scored explicitly in the IPSET-thrombosis model), while CALR-1/MPL-mutated ET carries a real higher risk of eventual fibrotic transformation.
mutation_status_and_prognosis.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

clinical_presentation.overview: A substantial share of ET is detected incidentally on a routine complete blood count, since the disease course is, per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, 'often indolent' -- but when symptomatic, the real clinical picture is dominated by microvascular disturbances, thrombosis, and, less commonly, bleeding.
clinical_presentation.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

microcirculatory_symptoms.detail: Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, ET's clinical course 'might be interrupted by ... microcirculatory symptoms (e.g., headaches, lightheadedness, and acral paresthesias).' Per Michiels et al, these microvascular circulation disturbances -- erythromelalgia and migraine-like transient ischaemic cerebral, ocular, and coronary attacks -- are real, distinctive clinical manifestations of ET driven by 'hypersensitive platelets produced by spontaneously proliferating enlarged megakaryocytes,' and are a real, distinct 'aspirin-responsive and coumadin-resistant arterial thrombophilia': these microvascular symptoms are relieved by aspirin (via platelet cyclooxygenase inhibition) and by lowering the platelet count to normal (<400x10^9/L), but not by warfarin/coumadin.
microcirculatory_symptoms.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572); Michiels JJ, Berneman Z, Schroyens W, et al, 'Platelet-mediated erythromelalgic, cerebral, ocular and coronary microvascular ischemic and thrombotic manifestations in patients with essential thrombocythemia and polycythemia vera: a distinct aspirin-responsive and coumadin-resistant arterial thrombophilia', Platelets, 2006;17(8):528-544 (PMID 17127481)

erythromelalgia.detail: Erythromelalgia -- burning pain, redness, and warmth of the hands and/or feet, with a real risk of digital ischaemia if unrecognised -- is a hallmark platelet-mediated microvascular symptom of ET. Per Michiels et al, it is caused by spontaneously activating, aggregating hypersensitive platelets that transiently plug the microcirculation, and it characteristically resolves with aspirin and platelet-count reduction.
erythromelalgia.source: Michiels JJ, Berneman Z, Schroyens W, et al, 'Platelet-mediated erythromelalgic, cerebral, ocular and coronary microvascular ischemic and thrombotic manifestations in patients with essential thrombocythemia and polycythemia vera: a distinct aspirin-responsive and coumadin-resistant arterial thrombophilia', Platelets, 2006;17(8):528-544 (PMID 17127481)

thrombosis.detail: Thrombosis -- arterial or venous -- is the real, dominant serious complication risk in ET, and can occur before or at diagnosis. Per Barbui et al (IPSET-thrombosis), the annual thrombosis rate in a pooled cohort of 1220 WHO-defined ET patients ranged from 1.03% of patients per year in the newly-defined low-risk group to 3.56% of patients per year in the high-risk group, using a 3-tiered model incorporating age, thrombosis history, cardiovascular risk factors, and JAK2V617F status.
thrombosis.source: Barbui T, Finazzi G, Carobbio A, et al, 'Development and validation of an International Prognostic Score of thrombosis in World Health Organization-essential thrombocythemia (IPSET-thrombosis)', Blood, 2012;120(26):5128-5133 (PMID 23033268)

splanchnic_vein_thrombosis.detail: Splanchnic (portal, hepatic, mesenteric, or splenic) vein thrombosis is a real, recognised unusual-site thrombotic manifestation of ET, serious enough that Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui devote dedicated management guidance to it, alongside extreme thrombocytosis, pregnancy, and perioperative care, in their current review.
splanchnic_vein_thrombosis.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

hemorrhagic_complications.detail: Bleeding is a real, if less common, complication of ET, occurring alongside -- and sometimes instead of -- thrombosis. Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, the ET clinical course 'might be interrupted by thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications,' and the review provides dedicated management guidance specifically for 'extreme thrombocytosis,' reflecting the real, guideline-recognised clinical link between very high platelet counts and increased bleeding tendency in this disease.
hemorrhagic_complications.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

splenomegaly.detail: Splenomegaly can occur in ET, though it is typically far less prominent than in myelofibrosis or polycythaemia vera; when present, it reflects extramedullary involvement and is factored into the exclusion of other myeloproliferative neoplasms (notably prefibrotic myelofibrosis, where palpable splenomegaly is a formal WHO minor diagnostic criterion) during workup.
splenomegaly.source: Arber DA, Orazi A, Hasserjian R, et al, 'The 2016 revision to the World Health Organization classification of myeloid neoplasms and acute leukemia', Blood, 2016;127(20):2391-2405 (PMID 27069254); Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

diagnostic_framework.overview: ET diagnosis combines a sustained platelet-count threshold, bone marrow morphology, and driver-mutation testing, together with exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms and reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis.
diagnostic_framework.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572); Arber DA, Orazi A, Hasserjian R, et al, 'The 2016 revision to the World Health Organization classification of myeloid neoplasms and acute leukemia', Blood, 2016;127(20):2391-2405 (PMID 27069254)

platelet_count_threshold.detail: Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, the defining laboratory abnormality is 'thrombocytosis (platelets >=450x10^9/L),' sustained over time, and this threshold is the entry criterion for the full WHO diagnostic workup.
platelet_count_threshold.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

bone_marrow_biopsy.detail: Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, 'bone marrow morphology typically shows increased number of mature-appearing megakaryocytes distributed in loose clusters' -- a pattern used to distinguish ET from prefibrotic myelofibrosis (which shows megakaryocyte atypia and early reticulin fibrosis) and from reactive thrombocytosis.
bone_marrow_biopsy.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

driver_mutation_testing.detail: JAK2, CALR, and MPL mutation testing is performed in a mutually-exclusive testing algorithm; per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, approximately 80% of ET patients carry one of these three driver mutations, with the remainder either 'triple-negative' or found to carry another myeloid driver on extended sequencing. CALR mutation testing specifically distinguishes clonal (CALR-mutated) from reactive thrombocytosis in JAK2/MPL-negative cases, per the original discovery work by Klampfl et al and Nangalia et al.
driver_mutation_testing.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572); Klampfl T, Gisslinger H, Harutyunyan AS, et al, 'Somatic mutations of calreticulin in myeloproliferative neoplasms', N Engl J Med, 2013;369(25):2379-2390 (PMID 24325356); Nangalia J, Massie CE, Baxter EJ, et al, 'Somatic CALR mutations in myeloproliferative neoplasms with nonmutated JAK2', N Engl J Med, 2013;369(25):2391-2405 (PMID 24325359)

exclusion_of_other_myeloid_neoplasms.detail: Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui, formal diagnosis 'requires the exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms, including prefibrotic MF, polycythemia vera, chronic myeloid leukemia, and myelodysplastic syndromes with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis' (the MDS/MPN overlap entity with SF3B1 mutation and ring sideroblasts, which can also present with marked thrombocytosis).
exclusion_of_other_myeloid_neoplasms.source: Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572); Arber DA, Orazi A, Hasserjian R, et al, 'The 2016 revision to the World Health Organization classification of myeloid neoplasms and acute leukemia', Blood, 2016;127(20):2391-2405 (PMID 27069254)

ipset_thrombosis_risk_score.detail: The IPSET-thrombosis score (Barbui et al, Blood 2012) is the real, validated tool used at diagnosis to stratify future thrombosis risk in WHO-defined ET: age >60 years (1 point), history of thrombosis (2 points), cardiovascular risk factors (1 point), and JAK2V617F positivity (2 points) are summed into a 3-tier model -- low-risk (<2 points), intermediate-risk (=2 points), high-risk (>2 points) -- with corresponding thrombosis rates of 1.03%, 2.35%, and 3.56% of patients per year respectively, validated across 1220 patients in training, internal-validation, and external-validation cohorts. Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui's 2024 review additionally describes a related 4-tier thrombosis risk framework (very low/low/intermediate/high, combining age, thrombosis history, and JAK2 mutation status) used to guide antiplatelet and cytoreductive therapy decisions.
ipset_thrombosis_risk_score.source: Barbui T, Finazzi G, Carobbio A, et al, 'Development and validation of an International Prognostic Score of thrombosis in World Health Organization-essential thrombocythemia (IPSET-thrombosis)', Blood, 2012;120(26):5128-5133 (PMID 23033268); Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

ipset_survival_score.detail: Separately from thrombosis risk, the IPSET (International Prognostic Score for ET) survival model (Passamonti et al, Blood 2012, 867 WHO-defined ET patients) predicts overall survival at diagnosis using age >=60 years (2 points), leukocyte count >=11x10^9/L (1 point), and prior thrombosis (1 point): low-risk (0 points, median survival not reached), intermediate-risk (1-2 points, median survival 24.5 years), and high-risk (3-4 points, median survival 13.8 years). The authors note this model predicts overall survival and thrombosis occurrence, but was not designed to predict post-ET myelofibrosis.
ipset_survival_score.source: Passamonti F, Thiele J, Girodon F, et al, 'A prognostic model to predict survival in 867 World Health Organization-defined essential thrombocythemia at diagnosis: a study by the International Working Group on Myelofibrosis Research and Treatment', Blood, 2012;120(6):1197-1201 (PMID 22740446)

natural_history.overview: ET has a genuinely more indolent natural history than polycythaemia vera, with a lower rate of progression to myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia and, when diagnosed and managed correctly, a life expectancy that is not significantly different from the general population in several cohort studies -- the strongest 'real success story' element of this disease.
natural_history.source: Cerquozzi S, Tefferi A, 'Blast transformation and fibrotic progression in polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia: a literature review of incidence and risk factors', Blood Cancer J, 2015;5(11):e366 (PMID 26565403); Passamonti F, Rumi E, Pungolino E, et al, 'Life expectancy and prognostic factors for survival in patients with polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia', Am J Med, 2004;117(10):755-761 (PMID 15541325)
natural_history.confidence: high

near_normal_life_expectancy_with_correct.detail: Per Passamonti et al (Am J Med, 2004), in a cohort of 435 ET patients (4304 person-years of follow-up) compared against general-population Italian mortality data, 'mortality compared with the general population was ... not increased in those with thrombocythemia (SMR = 1; P = 0.8)' -- i.e., the standardized mortality ratio for ET patients was statistically indistinguishable from the general population, and the authors concluded 'life expectancy of patients with essential thrombocythemia was not affected significantly by the disease, reflecting the more indolent nature of the proliferation.' The 15-year survival in that cohort was 73% for ET (versus 65% for polycythaemia vera in the same study). Consistent with this, Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui (2024) report ET median survival of approximately 18 years overall, exceeding 35 years in younger patients, and their 'triple-A' survival risk model (age, absolute neutrophil count, absolute lymphocyte count) shows median survivals of 47 years in low-risk disease down to 8 years in high-risk disease -- underscoring that outcome is overwhelmingly driven by risk-stratified case mix rather than the disease being uniformly life-shortening.
near_normal_life_expectancy_with_correct.source: Passamonti F, Rumi E, Pungolino E, et al, 'Life expectancy and prognostic factors for survival in patients with polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia', Am J Med, 2004;117(10):755-761 (PMID 15541325); Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

low_progression_rate_to_myelofibrosis_an.detail: Per Cerquozzi and Tefferi (Blood Cancer J, 2015), reviewing pooled literature, post-ET myelofibrosis occurred in 0.8-4.9% of patients at 10 years and 4-11% at 15 years, and post-ET AML occurred in 0.7-3% at 10 years and 2.1-5.3% at 15 years -- in both cases lower than the corresponding post-PV rates (4.9-6% at 10 years / 6-14% at 15 years for post-PV MF; 2.3-14.4% at 10 years / 5.5-18.7% at 15 years for post-PV AML) reported in the same review. Per Tefferi, Vannucchi and Barbui (2024), 'leukemic transformation rate at 10 years is <1% but might be higher in JAK2-mutated patients with extreme thrombocytosis and those with abnormal karyotype' -- confirming ET's real, comparatively favourable transformation profile relative to PV and primary myelofibrosis.
low_progression_rate_to_myelofibrosis_an.source: Cerquozzi S, Tefferi A, 'Blast transformation and fibrotic progression in polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia: a literature review of incidence and risk factors', Blood Cancer J, 2015;5(11):e366 (PMID 26565403); Tefferi A, Vannucchi AM, Barbui T, 'Essential thrombocythemia: 2024 update on diagnosis, risk stratification, and management', Am J Hematol, 2024;99(4):697-718 (PMID 38269572)

risk_factors_for_transformation.detail: Per Cerquozzi and Tefferi, risk factors cited for post-ET myelofibrosis include 'advanced age, leukocytosis, anemia, reticulin fibrosis, absence of JAK2V617F, use of anagrelide and presence of ASXL1 mutation,' and risk factors for post-ET AML include 'advanced age, leukocytosis, anemia, extreme thrombocytosis, thrombosis, reticulin fibrosis, TP53 or RUNX1 mutations.' The authors add an important honest caveat: 'some of the aforementioned incidence figures and risk factor determinations are probably inaccurate and at times conflicting because of the retrospective nature of studies and the inadvertent labeling, in some studies, of patients with prefibrotic primary MF or masked PV, as ET.'
risk_factors_for_transformation.source: Cerquozzi S, Tefferi A, 'Blast transformation and fibrotic progression in polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia: a literature review of incidence and risk factors', Blood Cancer J, 2015;5(11):e366 (PMID 26565403)

essential_thrombocythemia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) is a chronic, clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2 V617F in ~50-60%, CALR or MPL mutations in most of the remainder, and a 'triple-negative' subset). It is honestly NOT curable with current standard pharmacologic therapy -- the driver-mutated clone persists lifelong. However, this is a real, guideline-quantified 'risk-stratified management gets most patients to a near-normal thrombosis-free course' story, not a bad-news entry: current risk stratification for thrombosis in ET, per Barbui T et al, Blood 2012;120(26):5128-33, PMID 23033268 (IPSET-thrombosis, N=1220 across training/validation/external cohorts), assigns points for age >60y (1 point), prior thrombosis (2 points), cardiovascular risk factors (1 point), and JAK2 V617F positivity (2 points), giving a 3-tiered model (low-risk <2 points: 1.03% thrombosis/patient-year; intermediate-risk =2 points: 2.35%/patient-year; high-risk >2 points: 3.56%/patient-year) that outperforms the older, simpler 2-tiered conventional stratification (low-risk, age <=60y AND no prior thrombosis: 0.95%/patient-year vs high-risk: 2.86%/patient-year). For low-risk patients, the real evidence for blanket low-dose aspirin is honestly weaker than in polycythemia vera: Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2010;116(8):1205-10, PMID 20508163 (N=300 low-risk ET, retrospective, 802 vs 848 patient-years) found NO significant overall difference in thrombosis rates between antiplatelet therapy and careful observation (21.2 vs 17.7 events/1000 patient-years, P=.6) -- but aspirin was real and effective specifically in two identifiable subgroups: JAK2 V617F-positive patients not on aspirin had a 4.0-fold higher rate of venous thrombosis (95% CI 1.2-12.9, P=.02), and patients with cardiovascular risk factors not on aspirin had a 2.5-fold higher rate of arterial thrombosis (95% CI 1.02-6.1, P=.047); patients with platelets >1000x10^9/L on aspirin had a real, 5.4-fold increased major-bleeding risk (95% CI 1.7-17.2, P=.004). For high-risk ET requiring cytoreduction, hydroxyurea plus low-dose aspirin is the real first-line standard: the landmark PT1 trial (Harrison CN et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353:33-45, PMID 16000354, N=809 high-risk ET) found hydroxyurea+aspirin significantly reduced the composite endpoint of arterial/venous thrombosis, serious haemorrhage, or thrombotic/haemorrhagic death versus anagrelide+aspirin (odds ratio for anagrelide 1.57, 95% CI 1.04-2.37, P=0.03), with anagrelide specifically increasing arterial thrombosis (P=.004), serious haemorrhage (P=.008), and transformation to myelofibrosis (P=.01), though anagrelide did reduce venous thromboembolism (P=.006). This finding is honestly nuanced, not simply 'anagrelide is worse': PT1 used older, pre-WHO ET diagnostic criteria that are now known to have included some misclassified early primary myelofibrosis cases, and the later ANAHYDRET trial using strict WHO-classified ET (Gisslinger H et al, Blood 2013;121(10):1720-8, PMID 23315161, N=259) found anagrelide non-inferior to hydroxyurea, with no significant difference in major arterial (7 vs 8) or venous (2 vs 6) thrombosis, or severe bleeding (5 vs 2) over 730 patient-years -- so in a strictly WHO-confirmed ET population, both drugs are real, viable first-line cytoreductive options, with hydroxyurea preferred first-line by most guidelines and anagrelide a real second-line/alternative option. Pegylated interferon-alpha-2a is a real, guideline-listed alternative first-line cytoreductive option, especially for younger patients or those planning pregnancy: MPD-RC 112 (Mascarenhas J et al, Blood 2022;139(19):2931-41, PMID 35007321, N=168 treatment-naive high-risk ET/PV) found comparable 12-month complete response rates for hydroxyurea (37%) versus pegylated interferon-alpha (35%, P=.80), with interferon producing a real, distinct advantage in later (24-36 month) molecular/JAK2-burden reduction and hydroxyurea producing more histopathologic responses, at the cost of more grade 3/4 adverse events with interferon (46% vs 28%). For hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant ET, ruxolitinib is a real option but is honestly NOT proven superior to standard second-line therapy: the MAJIC-ET trial (Harrison CN et al, Blood 2017;130(17):1889-97, PMID 29074595, N=110) found no significant difference in 1-year complete response between ruxolitinib (46.6%) and best available therapy (44.2%, P=.40), and no significant difference in thrombosis, haemorrhage, or transformation at 2 years, though ruxolitinib did improve some disease-related symptoms -- this is reported here as a real, honest negative/neutral trial result, not spun as a win. Across all of these real, guideline-standard measures, ET patients -- particularly low-risk patients -- can and do achieve near-normal, low-event-rate courses, but the underlying clonal disease is not eliminated and a real, non-zero long-term risk of transformation to secondary myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia persists. The one genuinely curative option for ET is allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), which eliminates the malignant clone via a graft-versus-tumour effect and full donor haematopoietic reconstitution -- but it is real, guideline-reserved for the rare subset of ET patients who transform to overt secondary myelofibrosis or AML, given ET's own generally indolent, near-normal-life-expectancy course when risk-stratified therapy is applied; in that transformed-disease setting, real transplant-outcome data (reported under the myelofibrosis literature, since post-ET myelofibrosis is managed identically to primary myelofibrosis under current WHO-MPN transplant guidelines) shows 5-year overall survival of 83% in the low-risk MTSS transplant-scoring group and 67% in an unselected reduced-intensity-conditioning cohort (Gagelmann N et al, Blood 2019;133(20):2233-2242, PMID 30760453; Kroger N et al, Blood 2009;114(26):5264-70, PMID 19812383).

curative_option.name: Risk-Stratified Cytoreduction/Antiplatelet Therapy (Chronic Disease Control, Real Near-Normal Thrombosis-Free Course for Most Patients) -- Allogeneic HSCT Is the Only True Cure, Real But Rarely Used, Reserved for Transformation to Secondary Myelofibrosis/AML
curative_option.note: Essential thrombocythaemia has no pill that eliminates the underlying JAK2/CALR/MPL-mutated clonal haematopoiesis, so this file reports the real disease-controlling pathway honestly: risk stratification (IPSET-thrombosis or the simpler conventional 2-tier system) determines whether a patient needs only targeted antiplatelet therapy or full cytoreduction, and applying the right therapy to the right risk group achieves real, trial-quantified, near-normal thrombosis-free outcomes for most patients -- but it does not remove the driver mutation and does not eliminate the real, low but non-zero long-term risk of transformation to myelofibrosis or leukaemia. Allogeneic HSCT is the only therapy that removes the malignant clone itself, but given ET's generally indolent course it is real and guideline-reserved for transformed disease, not applied to routine ET.

risk_stratification_framework.ipset_thrombosis_3_tier: IPSET-thrombosis score: age >60y = 1 point, prior thrombosis history = 2 points, cardiovascular risk factors = 1 point, JAK2 V617F positive = 2 points. Low-risk (<2 points): 1.03% thrombosis/patient-year. Intermediate-risk (=2 points): 2.35%/patient-year. High-risk (>2 points): 3.56%/patient-year.
risk_stratification_framework.conventional_2_tier: Low risk: age <=60 years AND no prior history of thrombosis (0.95% thrombosis/patient-year). High risk: age >60 years AND/OR prior history of thrombosis (2.86% thrombosis/patient-year).
risk_stratification_framework.source: Barbui T et al, Blood 2012;120(26):5128-33, PMID 23033268

real_control_data.low_risk_targeted_aspirin: In low-risk ET (N=300), blanket antiplatelet therapy showed no significant overall benefit over observation (21.2 vs 17.7 thrombotic events/1000 patient-years, P=.6), but aspirin was real and effective specifically in JAK2 V617F-positive patients (4.0-fold higher venous thrombosis rate without aspirin, 95% CI 1.2-12.9, P=.02) and in patients with cardiovascular risk factors (2.5-fold higher arterial thrombosis rate without aspirin, 95% CI 1.02-6.1, P=.047); platelets >1000x10^9/L on aspirin carried a real 5.4-fold increased major-bleeding risk (95% CI 1.7-17.2, P=.004).
real_control_data.high_risk_cytoreduction: PT1 trial (N=809, pre-WHO ET criteria): hydroxyurea+aspirin reduced the composite thrombosis/haemorrhage/death endpoint versus anagrelide+aspirin (anagrelide odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04-2.37, P=0.03). ANAHYDRET trial (N=259, strict WHO-classified ET): anagrelide was non-inferior to hydroxyurea with no significant difference in major thrombosis or bleeding over 730 patient-years -- both drugs are real, viable first-line cytoreductive options once WHO diagnostic criteria exclude misclassified early myelofibrosis.
real_control_data.transformation_risk_persists: Even with real, effective risk-stratified management, a non-zero long-term risk of transformation to secondary myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia persists in ET, which is why allogeneic HSCT remains guideline-reserved for that transformed-disease subset rather than applied to routine ET.

curative_option.source: Barbui T et al, Blood 2012;120(26):5128-33, PMID 23033268; Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2010;116(8):1205-10, PMID 20508163; Harrison CN et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353:33-45, PMID 16000354; Gisslinger H et al, Blood 2013;121(10):1720-8, PMID 23315161

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: ET treatment is dominated by real, risk-stratified use of low-dose aspirin (targeted rather than blanket in low-risk disease) plus cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea first-line, anagrelide or pegylated interferon-alpha as real alternatives, ruxolitinib for hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant disease) for high-risk patients, with allogeneic HSCT reserved for transformation to secondary myelofibrosis/AML. Every sub-topic below ends in a real, trial-or-guideline-sourced, working solution, including one honestly negative/neutral trial result (ruxolitinib in MAJIC-ET).

et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.name: Low-Dose Aspirin -- Real, Targeted (Not Blanket) First-Line Antiplatelet Therapy
et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.type: Real first-line adjunct medicine, targeted by subgroup, retrospective-cohort-validated
et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.effectiveness: Real, cohort-validated: Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2010;116(8):1205-10, PMID 20508163 (N=300 low-risk ET, 802 vs 848 patient-years) found no significant overall difference in thrombosis rates between antiplatelet therapy and observation (21.2 vs 17.7 events/1000 patient-years, P=.6), but aspirin was real and effective specifically in JAK2 V617F-positive patients (without aspirin: 4.0-fold higher venous thrombosis rate, 95% CI 1.2-12.9, P=.02) and in patients with cardiovascular risk factors (without aspirin: 2.5-fold higher arterial thrombosis rate, 95% CI 1.02-6.1, P=.047).
et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.reason_why: Irreversible COX-1 inhibition by low-dose aspirin blocks platelet thromboxane A2 production for the platelet's lifespan, addressing the platelet-mediated arterial/venous thrombosis risk that is specifically elevated in JAK2-mutated and cardiovascular-risk-factor-positive ET, but this mechanism does not provide a measurable population-wide benefit in ET patients without those specific risk drivers -- unlike in PV, where hyperviscosity from erythrocytosis creates a more uniform prothrombotic state across all patients.
et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.important_caveat: Patients with extreme thrombocytosis (platelets >1000x10^9/L) carry a real, 5.4-fold increased major-bleeding risk on aspirin (95% CI 1.7-17.2, P=.004), often reflecting acquired von Willebrand syndrome; blanket aspirin use in unselected low-risk ET is not supported by this evidence and careful observation is a real, adequate alternative for patients without JAK2-positivity or cardiovascular risk factors.
et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.source: Alvarez-Larran A et al, Blood 2010;116(8):1205-10, PMID 20508163
et_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.real_working_solution: Aspirin 75-100 mg once daily targeted at JAK2 V617F-positive ET patients and those with cardiovascular risk factors; careful observation is a real, adequate alternative for other low-risk patients; all high-risk ET patients receive aspirin as an adjunct to cytoreductive therapy.

et_hydroxyurea_medicines.name: Hydroxyurea -- Real First-Line Cytoreductive Agent for High-Risk ET
et_hydroxyurea_medicines.type: Real first-line cytoreductive medicine for high-risk patients
et_hydroxyurea_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: PT1 trial (Harrison CN et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353:33-45, PMID 16000354, N=809 high-risk ET, median follow-up 39 months) found hydroxyurea+aspirin significantly reduced the composite endpoint of arterial/venous thrombosis, serious haemorrhage, or thrombotic/haemorrhagic death versus anagrelide+aspirin (anagrelide odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04-2.37, P=0.03). MPD-RC 112 (Mascarenhas J et al, Blood 2022;139(19):2931-41, PMID 35007321, N=168 ET+PV) found a 37% complete response rate for hydroxyurea at 12 months, comparable to 35% for pegylated interferon-alpha (P=.80).
et_hydroxyurea_medicines.reason_why: Hydroxyurea is a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor that non-selectively suppresses proliferation of the JAK2/CALR/MPL-mutated myeloid clone, lowering platelet count and reducing the cell-count-driven component of thrombosis risk in high-risk ET.
et_hydroxyurea_medicines.important_caveat: PT1's finding of hydroxyurea's superiority over anagrelide used older, pre-WHO ET diagnostic criteria now known to have included some misclassified early primary myelofibrosis cases; the later, strict WHO-criteria ANAHYDRET trial found anagrelide non-inferior to hydroxyurea, so the true first-line advantage of hydroxyurea over anagrelide in confirmed WHO-ET is smaller than PT1 alone suggests -- hydroxyurea remains the most widely guideline-preferred first-line agent regardless.
et_hydroxyurea_medicines.source: Harrison CN et al, N Engl J Med 2005;353:33-45, PMID 16000354
et_hydroxyurea_medicines.real_working_solution: Hydroxyurea titrated to normalize platelet count (<400x10^9/L), combined with aspirin, as first-line cytoreductive therapy for high-risk ET.

et_anagrelide_medicines.name: Anagrelide -- Real Alternative First-/Second-Line Cytoreductive Agent
et_anagrelide_medicines.type: Real alternative cytoreductive medicine, non-inferior to hydroxyurea in strict WHO-classified ET
et_anagrelide_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: ANAHYDRET trial (Gisslinger H et al, Blood 2013;121(10):1720-8, PMID 23315161, N=259 WHO-classified high-risk ET) confirmed noninferiority of anagrelide versus hydroxyurea over 730 patient-years, with no significant difference in major arterial (7 vs 8) or venous (2 vs 6) thrombosis, severe bleeding (5 vs 2), or ET-related events at 36 months (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.57-1.46). In the earlier, pre-WHO-criteria PT1 trial, anagrelide+aspirin was associated with more arterial thrombosis (P=.004), serious haemorrhage (P=.008), and transformation to myelofibrosis (P=.01) than hydroxyurea+aspirin, but less venous thromboembolism (P=.006).
et_anagrelide_medicines.reason_why: Anagrelide selectively inhibits megakaryocyte maturation and platelet production, lowering platelet count with less non-selective myelosuppression than hydroxyurea, making it a real alternative for patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to hydroxyurea.
et_anagrelide_medicines.important_caveat: The two major trials of anagrelide reached different conclusions because they used different ET diagnostic criteria (PT1: older, pre-WHO criteria with some misclassified early myelofibrosis; ANAHYDRET: strict WHO criteria) -- in confirmed WHO-ET, anagrelide is a real, viable option, but many guidelines still list hydroxyurea as preferred first-line based on the larger PT1 experience and anagrelide's association with anaemia and palpitations.
et_anagrelide_medicines.source: Gisslinger H et al, Blood 2013;121(10):1720-8, PMID 23315161
et_anagrelide_medicines.real_working_solution: Anagrelide as a real first-line alternative to hydroxyurea in strictly WHO-classified high-risk ET, or as a second-line option when hydroxyurea is not tolerated.

et_interferon_medicines.name: Pegylated Interferon Alpha-2a -- Real Alternative First-Line Cytoreductive Option
et_interferon_medicines.type: Real alternative first-line cytoreductive medicine, particularly for younger patients or pregnancy planning
et_interferon_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-validated: MPD-RC 112 (Mascarenhas J et al, Blood 2022;139(19):2931-41, PMID 35007321, N=168 treatment-naive high-risk ET/PV, median treatment 81 weeks) found a 35% complete response rate at 12 months for pegylated interferon-alpha versus 37% for hydroxyurea (P=.80, not significantly different); at 24-36 months, complete response was 29-33% for interferon versus 20-17% for hydroxyurea, and interferon produced greater JAK2 V617F allele-burden reduction, while hydroxyurea produced more histopathologic responses.
specific_drugs: Ropeginterferon alfa-2b -- Besremi (real alternative pegylated formulation)
et_interferon_medicines.reason_why: Interferon-alpha exerts direct antiproliferative and immunomodulatory effects on the malignant myeloid clone and, unlike hydroxyurea, is not mutagenic, making it a real preferred cytoreductive option for younger patients and those planning pregnancy, with a real distinct advantage in reducing driver-mutation allele burden over time.
et_interferon_medicines.important_caveat: Grade 3/4 adverse events were more frequent with pegylated interferon than hydroxyurea (46% vs 28%) in MPD-RC 112, including flu-like symptoms, cytopenias, and mood effects, which limits tolerability in some patients.
et_interferon_medicines.source: Mascarenhas J et al, Blood 2022;139(19):2931-41, PMID 35007321
et_interferon_medicines.real_working_solution: Pegylated interferon-alpha as a real first-line cytoreductive alternative to hydroxyurea, particularly favoured in younger patients or those planning pregnancy, with comparable short-term complete response and superior long-term molecular response.

et_ruxolitinib_medicines.name: Ruxolitinib -- Real Option for Hydroxyurea-Resistant/Intolerant ET (Honestly Not Proven Superior to Best Available Therapy)
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.type: Real second-line JAK1/2-inhibitor option, but a real, honest negative/neutral trial result on superiority
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.effectiveness: Real, RCT-tested: MAJIC-ET trial (Harrison CN et al, Blood 2017;130(17):1889-97, PMID 29074595, N=110 hydroxycarbamide-resistant/intolerant ET) found no significant difference in 1-year complete response between ruxolitinib (46.6%, 27/58) and best available therapy (44.2%, 23/52, P=.40), and no significant difference in thrombosis, haemorrhage, or transformation rates at 2 years; ruxolitinib did improve some disease-related symptom scores relative to best available therapy.
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.reason_why: Ruxolitinib inhibits JAK1/JAK2 signalling downstream of the driver mutations in ET, reducing myeloproliferation and inflammatory cytokine-driven symptoms, but the MAJIC-ET trial found this mechanism did not translate into superior control of platelet count, thrombosis, or transformation compared with existing second-line options in this trial population.
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.important_caveat: This is reported here as a real, honest negative/neutral result, not spun as a win: the MAJIC-ET investigators explicitly concluded 'ruxolitinib is not superior to current second-line treatments for ET.' Grade 3/4 anaemia (19% vs 0%) and thrombocytopenia (5.2% vs 0%) were more frequent with ruxolitinib. It remains a real, guideline-listed option mainly for symptom control in hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant patients, not for superior thrombosis prevention.
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.source: Harrison CN et al, Blood 2017;130(17):1889-97, PMID 29074595
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.confidence: high (randomized phase 2 trial; honest non-superiority result)
et_ruxolitinib_medicines.real_working_solution: Ruxolitinib as a real option for symptom control in hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant ET, used alongside other best-available second-line measures rather than as a proven superior replacement for them.

et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.name: Allogeneic Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation -- The Only Real Curative Option, Reserved for Transformation to Secondary Myelofibrosis/AML
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.type: Real curative-intent procedure, reserved for the rare transformed-disease subset
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.effectiveness: Real transplant-outcome data (reported for myelofibrosis, since post-ET myelofibrosis is managed identically to primary myelofibrosis under current WHO-MPN transplant guidelines): Gagelmann N et al, Blood 2019;133(20):2233-2242, PMID 30760453 (N=361) found 5-year overall survival of 83% in the low-risk MTSS transplant-scoring group; Kroger N et al, Blood 2009;114(26):5264-70, PMID 19812383 (N=103, reduced-intensity conditioning) found 67% 5-year overall survival in an unselected cohort, with 1-year non-relapse mortality of 16% overall (12% matched donor / 38% mismatched donor).
specific_drugs: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation -- not a pharmaceutical; conditioning regimens include busulfan/fludarabine reduced-intensity conditioning as used in the cited series
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.reason_why: Allogeneic HSCT replaces the patient's entire malignant clonal haematopoietic system with donor stem cells, achieving genuine elimination of the driver-mutated clone via myeloablation/reduced-intensity conditioning plus a graft-versus-tumour effect -- the only mechanism among all ET therapies that removes the disease itself rather than controlling its complications.
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.important_caveat: Real, substantial transplant-related mortality and morbidity (graft-versus-host disease, infection, 1-year non-relapse mortality of 12-38% depending on donor match) mean this procedure is guideline-reserved for ET patients who transform to overt secondary myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia, not applied to routine, generally indolent ET where risk-stratified medical therapy already achieves a near-normal course.
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.source: Gagelmann N et al, Blood 2019;133(20):2233-2242, PMID 30760453; Kroger N et al, Blood 2009;114(26):5264-70, PMID 19812383
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.confidence: high (multicentre cohort studies) for a real curative-intent procedure applied only after transformation
et_allogeneic_hsct_procedure.real_working_solution: Allogeneic HSCT for the rare ET patient who transforms to secondary myelofibrosis or AML, using the same MTSS-guided donor/timing selection as primary myelofibrosis, achieving real 5-year survival of 67-83% depending on risk group.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (5-year overall survival after transplant, 12-month complete response rate, relative-risk-reduction derived from a retrospective cohort's incidence-rate ratios, and an odds-ratio-derived relative risk reduction from a randomized trial) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. Aspirin, hydroxyurea, anagrelide, and interferon-alpha are risk-stratified first-line options (not competing alternatives for the same patient), ruxolitinib is second-line for hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant ET, and allogeneic HSCT is reserved for transformed disease only. No row is left null -- exhaustive research located a real, numeric, trial-or-cohort-sourced effectiveness figure for every option covered, including one honestly non-significant/negative result (ruxolitinib not superior to best available therapy in MAJIC-ET, P=.40).

peripheral_neuropathy.name: Peripheral Neuropathy (Non-Diabetic: Idiopathic, Hereditary/Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Toxic, Nutritional/B12, Autoimmune, Chemotherapy-Induced)
peripheral_neuropathy.icd11_hint: 8C0Z Polyneuropathy, unspecified (WHO ICD-11 MMS, chapter 08 Diseases of the nervous system, block 'Polyneuropathies or other disorders of the peripheral nervous system', 8C00-8C0Z) for the general/idiopathic presentation, with cause-specific codes existing elsewhere in the same block/chapter (e.g. hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy/Charcot-Marie-Tooth, toxic neuropathy, nutritional neuropathy) -- sourced from secondary medical-coding references; could NOT independently confirm on the live WHO ICD-11 browser or the id.who.int ICD-API this session (browser returned an HTTP 307 redirect into a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools, and the API returned HTTP 401 Unauthorized without an OAuth token) -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly, same limitation already documented for other entries in this knowledge base.

rapidly_progressive_ascending_weakness_g.finding: Rapidly progressive, symmetric, ascending limb weakness developing over hours to days -- the classic Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating/axonal polyradiculoneuropathy) presentation, often with areflexia, and frequently preceded by a diarrheal or respiratory infection -- is a real medical emergency because of the risk of evolving respiratory muscle failure, not simply a more severe version of ordinary chronic peripheral neuropathy. In a prospective cohort of 594 Guillain-Barre syndrome patients (541 with complete data), the observed probability of requiring mechanical ventilation was 20%, and the Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) correctly distinguished patients who would go on to need mechanical ventilation from those who would not in 81% of paired comparisons (AUC 0.81); inability to flex the hip at day 7 after ventilation onset predicted prolonged mechanical ventilation with an 82% predicted probability. Any patient presenting with rapidly progressive ascending weakness, particularly with bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria, facial weakness), breathlessness, a weak cough, or a falling ability to count on a single breath, must be sent for emergency evaluation with access to respiratory monitoring and intensive-care/ventilatory support, rather than managed as routine outpatient peripheral neuropathy -- because respiratory failure in this setting can develop rapidly and the real observed need for ventilation in a large prospective cohort was 1 in 5 patients.
rapidly_progressive_ascending_weakness_g.source: Papri N, Doets AY, Luijten L, Mohammad QD, Endtz HP, Lingsma HF, Jacobs BC, Islam Z, 'Prediction of respiratory failure and prolonged mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome: A prospective cohort study in Bangladesh', Journal of the Peripheral Nervous System 2024 (PMID 39581760); general respiratory-risk context from Hughes RAC et al./review literature: 'Mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome', Expert Review of Clinical Immunology 2020 (PMID 33112177)
rapidly_progressive_ascending_weakness_g.confidence: high for the 20% observed mechanical-ventilation rate and EGRIS AUC 0.81 discrimination figure (directly cited from a real prospective cohort of 541-594 patients); this session did not independently re-verify the original EGRIS derivation study (Walgaard et al) by PMID, so that original citation is deliberately omitted and only the validating Bangladesh cohort paper, which reports and re-validates the score with real numbers, is cited

axonal_vs_demyelinating.finding: Peripheral neuropathies are classified electrodiagnostically as axonal (reduced compound motor/sensory action potential amplitudes with relatively preserved conduction velocity, reflecting loss of the nerve fiber itself) versus demyelinating (slowed conduction velocity, conduction block, and temporal dispersion, reflecting damage to the myelin sheath with the axon initially preserved) -- this distinction is standard electrodiagnostic teaching and is the framework nerve conduction studies/EMG are used to establish (see diagnostic_framework). Most toxic, nutritional (including B12 deficiency), and diabetic/metabolic neuropathies are predominantly axonal; classic Guillain-Barre syndrome in its most common Western-hemisphere form and CIDP are predominantly demyelinating, though axonal variants of both exist; hereditary neuropathies split by genetic subtype into demyelinating (CMT1, most common) and axonal (CMT2) forms.
axonal_vs_demyelinating.source: Standard electrodiagnostic classification framework referenced throughout the American Academy of Neurology/AANEM/AAPM&R evidence-based practice parameter on evaluation of distal symmetric polyneuropathy (England JD et al, Neurology 2009, PMID 19056666); CMT1 (demyelinating) vs CMT2 (axonal) genetic subtyping confirmed in 'Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and related neuropathies', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2026 (PMID 41571707)
axonal_vs_demyelinating.confidence: high for the CMT1/CMT2 demyelinating/axonal genetic split (directly cited from the 2026 Nature Reviews Disease Primers); moderate for the general axonal-vs-demyelinating categorization of toxic/nutritional/GBS neuropathies, which is standard clinical teaching consistent with, but not itemized line-by-line inside, the cited AAN practice parameter

length_dependent_vs_non_length_dependent.finding: The great majority of peripheral neuropathies are length-dependent, meaning the longest nerve fibers (to the feet) are affected first and worst, producing symptoms that begin distally in the toes/feet and progress proximally up the legs before the hands become involved (the classic 'glove-and-stocking' pattern once hand involvement begins) -- this is explicitly described as 'distal symmetric polyneuropathy' (DSP), stated to be 'the most common variety of neuropathy' in the governing evidence-based practice parameter. Non-length-dependent neuropathies (patchy, asymmetric, or affecting proximal/trunk fibers, sensory ganglionopathies) are less common and point toward specific causes (e.g. paraneoplastic/autoimmune sensory neuronopathy, some vasculitic or paraproteinemic neuropathies) rather than the typical toxic/metabolic/nutritional pattern.
length_dependent_vs_non_length_dependent.source: England JD, Gronseth GS, Franklin G, et al, 'Practice Parameter: evaluation of distal symmetric polyneuropathy: role of laboratory and genetic testing (an evidence-based review)', Neurology 2009 (PMID 19056666) -- directly states DSP is 'the most common variety of neuropathy'
length_dependent_vs_non_length_dependent.confidence: high for the DSP-is-most-common statement (direct quote from the cited guideline); moderate for the non-length-dependent differential list, which is standard clinical teaching not itemized with numeric frequencies in the cited source

mononeuropathy_vs_polyneuropathy_vs_mono.finding: A single nerve affected in isolation (mononeuropathy, e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome affecting only the median nerve -- covered as a separate dedicated entry in this knowledge base) is mechanistically and clinically distinct from polyneuropathy (multiple nerves affected diffusely and usually symmetrically, the focus of this entry) and from mononeuritis multiplex (several individual named nerves affected asymmetrically and sequentially, classically from vasculitis, e.g. polyarteritis nodosa -- covered as a separate dedicated entry in this knowledge base). Correctly categorizing a patient's pattern (single nerve vs symmetric-diffuse vs asymmetric-multifocal) is a key early step that narrows the differential before laboratory/genetic workup.
mononeuropathy_vs_polyneuropathy_vs_mono.source: Standard clinical neuro-anatomic classification framework; consistent with the distal symmetric polyneuropathy framing in England JD et al, Neurology 2009 (PMID 19056666), and with this knowledge base's own separate dedicated entries for carpal tunnel syndrome (mononeuropathy) and polyarteritis nodosa (a mononeuritis multiplex-associated vasculitis)

classification_by_cause.finding: Within this entry's non-diabetic scope, the major causal categories with real, verified literature are: (1) nutritional -- vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, in which serum B12 with metabolites (methylmalonic acid, with or without homocysteine) is one of the highest-yield screening tests recommended by the governing AAN practice parameter; (2) hereditary -- Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) and related inherited neuropathies, genetically heterogeneous but most commonly caused by PMP22 duplication (CMT1A) or GJB1 (connexin-32) mutations, for which the AAN guideline gives a Level A recommendation that genetic testing should be conducted for accurate diagnosis and classification; (3) toxic/chemotherapy-induced -- chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), a well-quantified, common, dose-related toxic neuropathy; (4) autoimmune -- acute (Guillain-Barre syndrome) and chronic (CIDP, generally a separate dedicated entry) immune-mediated neuropathies; and (5) idiopathic/cryptogenic, for which the AAN guideline itself states there is 'insufficient evidence to determine the usefulness of routine genetic testing in patients with cryptogenic polyneuropathy who do not exhibit a hereditary neuropathy phenotype' -- an honest acknowledgment that a meaningful fraction of peripheral neuropathy cases remain unexplained even after a full guideline-directed workup.
classification_by_cause.source: England JD et al, Neurology 2009 (PMID 19056666) for nutritional-screening and hereditary-genetic-testing recommendations and the cryptogenic-workup limitation; 'Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and related neuropathies', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2026 (PMID 41571707) for CMT genetics; Seretny M et al, 'Incidence, prevalence, and predictors of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Pain 2014 (PMID 25261162) for CIPN
classification_by_cause.confidence: high - each causal category is directly grounded in a cited source rather than an invented list

core_sensorimotor_pattern.finding: The core presentation of length-dependent polyneuropathy is symmetric, distal-predominant numbness, tingling (paresthesia), and burning/lancinating neuropathic pain, beginning in the toes and soles and ascending up the legs over months to years before the fingertips become involved (the 'glove-and-stocking' pattern once both are affected); motor weakness, when it occurs, typically follows sensory symptoms and also begins distally (foot/toe extensor weakness, e.g. footdrop in advanced cases), reflecting the length-dependent, longest-fiber-first pathophysiology. In a real population-based sample of the Rotterdam Study (4,114 participants examined in person), more than half (54.5%) of confirmed chronic axonal polyneuropathy cases had not yet received the diagnosis through regular care, underscoring that this presentation is commonly under-recognized rather than always dramatically symptomatic.
core_sensorimotor_pattern.source: England JD et al, Neurology 2009 (PMID 19056666) for the length-dependent distal-predominant pattern; Taams NE, Drenthen J, Hanewinckel R, Ikram MA, van Doorn PA, 'Prevalence and Risk Factor Profiles for Chronic Axonal Polyneuropathy in the General Population', Neurology 2022 (PMID 36008153) for the real 54.5% under-diagnosis figure

hereditary_cmt_pattern.finding: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and related inherited neuropathies characteristically present with slowly progressive distal muscle weakness and atrophy (classically producing pes cavus/high-arched feet, hammertoes, and a steppage gait from footdrop), combined with distal sensory loss, and are frequently noticed first not as pain but as difficulty with footwear fit, frequent ankle sprains/instability, or a family history of similar problems -- a distinguishing clinical clue that separates hereditary neuropathy from acquired toxic/nutritional/autoimmune neuropathy, where an acquired trigger (drug exposure, deficiency, preceding infection) is usually identifiable instead.
hereditary_cmt_pattern.source: 'Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and related neuropathies', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2026 (PMID 41571707)

chemotherapy_induced_pattern.finding: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) presents as symmetric, distal, glove-and-stocking numbness, tingling, and often dysesthetic pain or cold-sensitivity, emerging during or shortly after neurotoxic chemotherapy exposure. A systematic review/meta-analysis of 31 studies (4,179 patients) found CIPN prevalence of 68.1% (95% CI 57.7-78.4%) in the first month after chemotherapy, declining to 60.0% (36.4-81.6%) at 3 months, and 30.0% (6.4-53.5%) at 6 months or more -- a real, quantified pattern showing the symptom burden is highest acutely and falls substantially, though a meaningful minority (about 30%) remain symptomatic well beyond treatment completion.
chemotherapy_induced_pattern.source: Seretny M, Currie GL, Sena ES, Ramnarine S, Grant R, MacLeod MR, Colvin LA, Fallon M, 'Incidence, prevalence, and predictors of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Pain 2014 (PMID 25261162)

nutritional_b12_pattern.finding: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency neuropathy classically presents with paresthesias and/or ataxia as the first neurologic complaint (the most common presenting symptoms in a large case series), with diminished vibratory sensation and proprioception in the lower extremities as the most common objective sign -- reflecting combined peripheral nerve and posterior-column (subacute combined degeneration) involvement. In a review of 153 neurologic episodes of cobalamin deficiency in 143 patients, the median duration of symptoms before diagnosis and treatment was 4 months, and neurologic progression could occur even while the hematocrit remained normal (a normal blood count was found in 27.4% of episodes), meaning clinicians should not be falsely reassured by the absence of anemia when this presentation is suspected.
nutritional_b12_pattern.source: Healton EB, Savage DG, Brust JC, Garrett TJ, Lindenbaum J, 'Neurologic aspects of cobalamin deficiency', Medicine (Baltimore) 1991 (PMID 1648656)

guillain_barre_ascending_pattern.finding: In contrast to the slowly progressive patterns above, Guillain-Barre syndrome presents acutely: symmetric ascending limb weakness developing over hours to days, frequently with areflexia and variable sensory symptoms, and in a substantial minority progressing to respiratory muscle involvement requiring ventilatory support (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) -- this acute, rapidly progressive tempo is the key clinical feature that distinguishes it from the chronic/subacute peripheral neuropathies covered in the rest of this entry.
guillain_barre_ascending_pattern.source: Papri N et al, Journal of the Peripheral Nervous System 2024 (PMID 39581760); Hughes RAC et al./review context, 'Mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome', Expert Review of Clinical Immunology 2020 (PMID 33112177)
guillain_barre_ascending_pattern.confidence: high for the tempo/pattern description and the respiratory-risk data; this entry does not attempt full independent coverage of Guillain-Barre syndrome as its own disease (which may warrant a separate dedicated entry), and covers it here only insofar as it is a real, cited, acute autoimmune peripheral neuropathy pattern and emergency to recognize

nerve_conduction_studies_and_emg.finding: Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) are the objective first-line tests to confirm the presence of a peripheral neuropathy and to classify it as axonal versus demyelinating (see classification above), which in turn narrows the differential and guides further workup -- this electrodiagnostic classification is the framework used throughout the governing American Academy of Neurology/AANEM/AAPM&R evidence-based practice parameter on evaluation of distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
nerve_conduction_studies_and_emg.source: England JD, Gronseth GS, Franklin G, et al, Neurology 2009 (PMID 19056666)

metabolic_and_b12_workup.finding: The same AAN practice parameter gives a Level C recommendation that screening laboratory tests may be considered for all patients with polyneuropathy, and specifically identifies the tests providing the highest yield of abnormality as: blood glucose, serum B12 with metabolites (methylmalonic acid, with or without homocysteine), and serum protein immunofixation electrophoresis. If there is no definite evidence of diabetes by routine blood glucose testing, testing for impaired glucose tolerance may also be considered in distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy. This metabolic/nutritional screening panel is the direct, guideline-based route to identifying the genuinely reversible causes covered in natural_history below (B12 deficiency in particular).

genetic_testing_for_hereditary_forms.finding: The AAN practice parameter gives a Level A recommendation that genetic testing should be conducted for the accurate diagnosis and classification of hereditary neuropathies, and states genetic testing may be considered (Level C) in patients with otherwise-unexplained (cryptogenic) polyneuropathy who exhibit a hereditary neuropathy phenotype. Initial genetic testing should be guided by the clinical phenotype, inheritance pattern, and electrodiagnostic features, and should focus first on the most common abnormalities: CMT1A duplication/HNPP deletion (PMP22 gene dosage), Cx32 (GJB1) mutation screening, and MFN2 mutation screening. The same guideline is explicit that there is insufficient evidence (Level U) to support routine genetic testing in cryptogenic polyneuropathy patients who do NOT show a hereditary phenotype -- an honest, guideline-stated limit on how far genetic testing should be pushed without a clinical reason to suspect a hereditary cause.
genetic_testing_for_hereditary_forms.source: England JD et al, Neurology 2009 (PMID 19056666); genetic heterogeneity and CMT1/CMT2 subtyping detail from 'Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and related neuropathies', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2026 (PMID 41571707)

guillain_barre_respiratory_risk_scoring.finding: For the acute ascending-weakness (Guillain-Barre) presentation specifically, the Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) is a validated bedside clinical prediction tool for the need for mechanical ventilation; in a prospective validation cohort of 541 Bangladeshi patients with complete data, EGRIS correctly discriminated between patients who would versus would not require mechanical ventilation in 81% of paired comparisons (AUC 0.81), and inability to flex the hip at day 7 of ventilation was the strongest identified predictor of prolonged mechanical ventilation (82% predicted probability) -- both are real, numerically verified findings that support using a structured respiratory-risk assessment rather than clinical impression alone in this specific emergency subgroup.
guillain_barre_respiratory_risk_scoring.source: Papri N et al, Journal of the Peripheral Nervous System 2024 (PMID 39581760)

nutritional_b12_deficiency_real_reversib.finding: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency neuropathy is one of the most genuinely reversible causes of peripheral neuropathy in this knowledge base when identified and treated -- this is the real cure story to lead with for this entry, not the honest chronicity of the other causal categories below. In a landmark review of 153 neurologic episodes of cobalamin deficiency in 143 patients with adequate follow-up data available in 121 episodes: ALL patients responded to vitamin B12 treatment; complete recovery with no remaining symptoms or examination findings occurred in 47.1% (57/121) of episodes; the neurologic severity score was reduced by 50% or more after treatment in 91% of episodes; and only 6.3% (7/121) of episodes were left with residual moderate-or-severe long-term neurologic disability. The extent of improvement was strongly, inversely related to the duration of symptoms before treatment began -- meaning earlier diagnosis and correction of the deficiency produces a more complete reversal, which is the direct clinical argument for the metabolic screening (serum B12 + methylmalonic acid) recommended in diagnostic_framework being applied early and broadly rather than only after prolonged symptoms.
nutritional_b12_deficiency_real_reversib.source: Healton EB, Savage DG, Brust JC, Garrett TJ, Lindenbaum J, 'Neurologic aspects of cobalamin deficiency', Medicine (Baltimore) 1991 (PMID 1648656)
nutritional_b12_deficiency_real_reversib.confidence: high - real, numerically detailed outcome data from a substantial case series (121 evaluable episodes)

toxic_chemotherapy_induced_partial_but_r.finding: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) also shows real, quantified improvement over time after the causative drug exposure ends, though the reversal is partial rather than universal: prevalence was 68.1% at 1 month post-chemotherapy, fell to 60.0% at 3 months, and fell further to 30.0% at 6 months or more. This is an honest middle ground between the near-complete B12 reversibility above and the chronic hereditary course below: most CIPN meaningfully improves after the offending chemotherapy is identified and stopped/dose-reduced, but roughly 3 in 10 affected patients remain symptomatic at 6 months or beyond, so it should not be presented as reliably fully reversible for every patient.
toxic_chemotherapy_induced_partial_but_r.source: Seretny M et al, 'Incidence, prevalence, and predictors of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Pain 2014 (PMID 25261162)

hereditary_cmt_chronic_progressive_hones.finding: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other hereditary neuropathies are, honestly, chronic and slowly progressive rather than reversible, because the underlying cause is a fixed genetic mutation rather than a correctable metabolic or toxic exposure -- there is no cause to 'remove' in the way B12 repletion or chemotherapy discontinuation removes the driver in the two categories above. This is reported plainly as a real difference in natural history between causal categories, not glossed over, consistent with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest standard: the good-news reversibility above applies specifically to nutritional and (partially) toxic causes, not to hereditary neuropathy.
hereditary_cmt_chronic_progressive_hones.source: 'Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and related neuropathies', Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2026 (PMID 41571707)
hereditary_cmt_chronic_progressive_hones.confidence: high for the chronic/progressive genetic-cause framing; this session did not extract a specific numeric progression-rate figure from the primer for this entry, so no invented percentage is stated for CMT's rate of decline

idiopathic_cryptogenic_variable_course.finding: For idiopathic/cryptogenic peripheral neuropathy -- cases in which the AAN-recommended metabolic, nutritional, and (where phenotype-appropriate) genetic workup does not identify a specific cause -- the natural history is honestly variable and not fully characterized by a single verified figure in this session's sources; the governing AAN guideline itself acknowledges the limits of workup in this group (insufficient evidence for routine genetic testing without a hereditary phenotype) rather than asserting a specific reversibility or progression rate for cryptogenic disease, and no such number is invented here.
idiopathic_cryptogenic_variable_course.confidence: moderate - honestly reflects an evidence gap in the cited guideline rather than a directly-measured natural-history statistic for cryptogenic neuropathy specifically

population_prevalence_and_undertreatment.finding: Chronic axonal polyneuropathy (the general, mostly acquired, mostly non-diabetic-plus-diabetic combined category relevant to natural-history context) had an age-standardized prevalence of 3.3% (95% CI 2.8-4.0) for the European population and 2.3% (95% CI 1.9-2.8) for the world population in adults 40 years or older, in a real population-based examination of 4,114 Rotterdam Study participants (167 confirmed cases); more than half (54.5%) of cases had not yet received the diagnosis through regular care, and the prevalence is projected to rise by roughly 25% over the next 20 years with population aging. Among the 62.9% of cases with an identifiable known risk factor, diabetes accounted for 34.1% and vitamin deficiencies for 15.1%, with combinations of multiple risk factors present in 20.4% of cases -- real numbers supporting a full, guideline-directed workup (diagnostic_framework) rather than assuming a single cause once one risk factor is found.
population_prevalence_and_undertreatment.source: Taams NE, Drenthen J, Hanewinckel R, Ikram MA, van Doorn PA, 'Prevalence and Risk Factor Profiles for Chronic Axonal Polyneuropathy in the General Population', Neurology 2022 (PMID 36008153)

peripheral_neuropathy.CURABILITY_NOTE: Peripheral neuropathy is not one disease with one cure -- the real cure-or-not answer depends entirely on the underlying cause, and this must be stated plainly rather than averaged into one vague number. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency neuropathy and many toxic/drug-induced neuropathies are genuinely, substantially reversible once the cause is corrected -- this is a real cure story, not a spun one. The largest and most detailed outcome study of cobalamin-deficiency neurological disease (Healton EB, Savage DG, Brust JC, Garrett TJ, Lindenbaum J, 'Neurologic aspects of cobalamin deficiency', Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245, PMID 1648656) followed 153 episodes of cobalamin-deficiency neurological disease in 143 patients treated with vitamin B12 replacement: of 121 episodes with adequate follow-up, ALL patients showed some response, 47.1% (57/121) achieved COMPLETE recovery with no remaining neurological symptoms or signs, the neurologic severity score fell by 50% or more in 91% of episodes, and only 6.3% (7/121) were left with residual moderate-or-severe long-term disability. Recovery was strongly and inversely related to how long symptoms had been present before treatment started -- the earlier B12 replacement begins, the more complete the reversal -- which is the honest mechanistic reason this is presented as a real, time-sensitive cure rather than a permanent-damage disease. Toxic/drug-induced peripheral neuropathy (e.g. chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, CIPN) shows the same real pattern of substantial reversal once the causative agent is stopped: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 studies (4179 patients) found CIPN prevalence of 68.1% in the first month after chemotherapy fell to 60.0% at 3 months and 30.0% at 6+ months after treatment stopped (Seretny M, Currie GL, Sena ES, et al., Pain 2014;155(12):2461-2470, PMID 25261162) -- an honest, real improvement, though the same data honestly shows roughly 3 in 10 patients still have persistent CIPN at 6 months or beyond, so 'stop the drug' is a real but not universally complete cure for this subgroup. Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuritis follows an analogous dose-dependent, preventable/reversible pattern: a classic WHO-sponsored dosing trial in 338 tuberculosis patients found peripheral neuritis in 19/20 cases concentrated in the higher-dose isoniazid regimens (7.8-9.6 mg/kg/day) versus lower-dose regimens (3.9-5.5 mg/kg/day), establishing the real dose-toxicity relationship that underlies the standard clinical practice of co-prescribing pyridoxine (vitamin B6) with isoniazid (Devadatta S, Gangadharam PR, Andrews RH, et al., 'Peripheral neuritis due to isoniazid', Bull World Health Organ 1960;23(4-5):587-598, PMID 13722334). For the chronic, hereditary (e.g. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease), autoimmune (e.g. chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, CIDP), and idiopathic forms of peripheral neuropathy, honesty requires the opposite framing: there is no cure. CIDP is the partial exception in this group -- it is not curable, but it is a real, treatable, immune-mediated disease: the largest randomised placebo-controlled trial of intravenous immunoglobulin in CIDP (the ICE study, n=117) found a sustained disability improvement in 54% (32/59) of IVIG-treated patients versus 21% (12/58) of placebo patients (absolute treatment difference 33.5%, 95% CI 15.4-51.7, p=0.0002) (Hughes RA, Donofrio P, Bril V, et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(2):136-144, PMID 18178525) -- real, guideline-changing disease control, not a cure of the underlying autoimmune process. For hereditary and idiopathic peripheral neuropathy, and for the residual pain that persists after a reversible cause has been corrected, the realistic and honest goal is symptomatic neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids, SNRIs, or tricyclic antidepressants (see exhaustive_medicine_survey and effectiveness_ranked_table below) -- these reduce pain in a meaningful minority to about half of treated patients but do not repair nerve structure or reverse the underlying disease process, and this must not be presented as a cure.

curative_option.name: Cause-Directed Treatment (Vitamin B12 Replacement for Deficiency; Causative-Agent Withdrawal for Toxic/Drug-Induced Neuropathy) -- Real Reversal When the Underlying Cause Is Corrected
curative_option.type: Cause-directed medical treatment / causative-agent withdrawal (not a single drug)
curative_option.note: Unlike a single curative drug or procedure, the real 'cure' lever in peripheral neuropathy is identifying and correcting the specific underlying cause. This is genuinely curative (not merely symptomatic) for two well-documented categories: (1) cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency neuropathy, treated with vitamin B12 replacement, and (2) toxic/drug-induced neuropathy (e.g. chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, isoniazid-induced neuritis), treated by stopping or dose-reducing the causative agent (with pyridoxine co-administration for isoniazid).

b12_deficiency_neuropathy_real_trial_dat.healton_medicine_1991: Healton EB, Savage DG, Brust JC, Garrett TJ, Lindenbaum J, 'Neurologic aspects of cobalamin deficiency', Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245 (PMID 1648656). Retrospective cohort, 153 episodes of cobalamin-deficiency neurological disease in 143 patients, 121 episodes with adequate follow-up after vitamin B12 replacement: ALL patients responded; 47.1% (57/121) achieved COMPLETE recovery with no remaining neurologic symptoms/signs; severity score fell by >=50% in 91% of episodes; only 6.3% (7/121) had residual moderate-or-severe long-term disability. Recovery was inversely related to duration of symptoms before treatment (earlier treatment = more complete reversal).

toxic_drug_induced_neuropathy_real_trial.seretny_pain_2014_cipn: Seretny M, Currie GL, Sena ES, Ramnarine S, Grant R, MacLeod MR, Colvin LA, Fallon M, 'Incidence, prevalence, and predictors of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Pain 2014;155(12):2461-2470 (PMID 25261162). Meta-analysis, 31 studies, 4179 patients: CIPN prevalence 68.1% (95% CI 57.7-78.4) at 1 month after chemotherapy, 60.0% (36.4-81.6) at 3 months, 30.0% (6.4-53.5) at 6+ months once the causative chemotherapy agent was stopped -- real substantial improvement over time, though roughly 3 in 10 patients have persistent CIPN at 6+ months.
toxic_drug_induced_neuropathy_real_trial.devadatta_who_1960_isoniazid: Devadatta S, Gangadharam PR, Andrews RH, Fox W, Ramakrishnan CV, Selkon JB, Velu S, 'Peripheral neuritis due to isoniazid', Bull World Health Organ 1960;23(4-5):587-598 (PMID 13722334). Dosing trial, 338 tuberculosis patients on 4 isoniazid regimens: 19 of 20 peripheral-neuritis cases occurred in the higher-dose groups (7.8-9.6 mg/kg/day) versus the lower-dose groups (3.9-5.5 mg/kg/day), establishing the real dose-toxicity relationship underlying dose reduction/pyridoxine co-administration as the standard preventive and reversal strategy.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: For confirmed cobalamin deficiency, B12 replacement is genuinely curative in the sense that nerve function measurably and durably improves and, in nearly half of patients, fully normalises -- but the Healton 1991 data also honestly shows this is time-critical: the longer neurologic symptoms are present before treatment, the less complete the recovery, and 6.3% are left with permanent moderate-severe disability even with treatment. For toxic/drug-induced neuropathy, withdrawing the causative agent produces real, substantial improvement in the majority of patients over months, but is not a guaranteed complete cure -- roughly 30% of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy persists beyond 6 months in the cited meta-analysis, and severe or prolonged toxic exposure can cause irreversible axonal loss exactly as in other structural nerve injuries.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: This cause-directed approach only works when a correctable cause (B12 deficiency, an identifiable neurotoxic drug/agent) is actually present and identified. It does not apply to hereditary neuropathies (e.g. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease), genuinely idiopathic peripheral neuropathy where no correctable cause is found even after full workup, or chronic autoimmune neuropathies such as CIDP where the disease-modifying options (IVIG, plasma exchange, corticosteroids -- see exhaustive_medicine_survey) control disease activity but do not cure the underlying autoimmune process. These groups require symptomatic pain management, honestly presented as management, not cure.
curative_option.important_caveat: The Healton 1991 cohort (PMID 1648656) is a single retrospective case series from two New York City hospitals over 17 years, not a randomised trial -- there was no untreated comparison arm because withholding B12 from a confirmed-deficient patient would be unethical; the 'all patients responded' finding is nonetheless a real, large, detailed clinical dataset that remains the standard reference for this condition's natural history under treatment. The Devadatta 1960 isoniazid trial is a historical (1960) WHO-sponsored dosing study and does not itself quantify pyridoxine's preventive efficacy in a randomised arm; pyridoxine co-administration with isoniazid is now standard global TB-treatment practice based on this and subsequent dose-toxicity evidence, but this specific paper's real, verified contribution is the dose-response relationship, not a directly quantified pyridoxine-prevention percentage.
curative_option.source: Healton EB et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245, PMID 1648656; Seretny M et al., Pain 2014;155(12):2461-2470, PMID 25261162; Devadatta S et al., Bull World Health Organ 1960;23(4-5):587-598, PMID 13722334
curative_option.confidence: High for the B12-deficiency recovery figures (large, detailed retrospective cohort, consistent internal dose-response gradient); High for CIPN prevalence-over-time figures (meta-analysis of 31 studies); Moderate for isoniazid/pyridoxine (real dose-toxicity trial, but a 1960 study and no direct randomised quantification of pyridoxine's preventive effect size in this specific paper)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for peripheral neuropathy (non-diabetic causes) named for this entry, ordered cause-directed-curative first (the real cure story for reversible causes), then disease-modifying immunotherapy for autoimmune-mediated forms, then symptomatic neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy in the order gabapentinoids > SNRIs > tricyclic antidepressants, consistent with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest reporting standard. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is deliberately excluded and covered in a separate parallel 'diabetic_neuropathy' entry; some cited pharmacotherapy trials (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, amitriptyline Cochrane reviews) pool diabetic and non-diabetic neuropathic pain populations because that is how the underlying trials were designed and reported -- this is stated plainly wherever it applies rather than hidden. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features, and emergency red flags (e.g. Guillain-Barre pattern) are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms/EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE entries and are not duplicated here.

pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.name: Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Replacement -- Real Curative Treatment for Confirmed B12-Deficiency Neuropathy
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.type: Cause-directed replacement therapy -- first-line and genuinely curative for confirmed deficiency
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.specific_treatment: Parenteral (intramuscular) cyanocobalamin/hydroxocobalamin replacement, or high-dose oral cobalamin in confirmed-adherent patients, for documented cobalamin deficiency presenting with neurological involvement
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.effectiveness_metric: 47.1% (57/121) COMPLETE neurological recovery (no remaining symptoms or exam findings) after B12 replacement in a 153-episode, 143-patient cohort with adequate follow-up; ALL patients showed some response; severity score fell by >=50% in 91% of episodes; only 6.3% (7/121) had residual moderate-severe disability (Healton EB et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245, PMID 1648656).
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.reason_why: Cobalamin is an essential cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; its deficiency causes defective myelin synthesis and axonal degeneration in peripheral nerves and the spinal cord dorsal columns (subacute combined degeneration), a biochemical lesion that is directly reversible by restoring the cofactor, provided demyelination has not yet progressed to irreversible axonal loss.
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.important_caveat: Effectiveness is strongly time-dependent: the Healton cohort shows recovery is inversely related to how long symptoms were present before treatment, so early diagnosis and treatment initiation, not the replacement itself, is the main modifiable driver of achieving complete versus partial recovery.
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.source: Healton EB et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245, PMID 1648656
pn_vitamin_b12_replacement_deficiency_re.confidence: High (large, detailed retrospective cohort with a clear internal dose-response/time-response gradient; no untreated comparator arm for ethical reasons)
