pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.name: Withdrawal or Dose Reduction of the Causative Toxic Agent/Drug -- Real Substantial Reversal for Toxic/Drug-Induced Neuropathy
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.type: Cause-directed management -- first-line for confirmed toxic/drug-induced neuropathy
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.specific_treatment: Discontinuation or dose reduction of the identified neurotoxic agent (e.g. chemotherapy agent such as paclitaxel, oxaliplatin, or vincristine; isoniazid; amiodarone; or other implicated drug/toxin), with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) co-administration specifically for isoniazid
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.effectiveness_metric: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy prevalence fell from 68.1% at 1 month to 30.0% at 6+ months after the causative chemotherapy was stopped -- a real 56% relative reduction, i.e. roughly 70% of patients with early CIPN no longer have it by 6+ months (Seretny M et al., Pain 2014;155(12):2461-2470, PMID 25261162). For isoniazid, a WHO-sponsored 338-patient dosing trial found peripheral neuritis was concentrated in higher-dose regimens (19/20 cases in the 7.8-9.6 mg/kg/day groups), establishing the real dose-toxicity relationship that underlies dose reduction and pyridoxine co-administration as standard practice (Devadatta S et al., Bull World Health Organ 1960;23(4-5):587-598, PMID 13722334).
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.reason_why: Toxic/drug-induced neuropathy results from ongoing direct neurotoxic injury (mitochondrial dysfunction, microtubule disruption, or metabolic interference with pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent pathways for isoniazid); removing the toxic exposure allows the peripheral nervous system's real regenerative capacity to restore function, up to the point of irreversible axonal loss from prolonged/severe exposure.
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.important_caveat: This is a real but incomplete cure at the population level: about 30% of patients with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy in the cited meta-analysis still have persistent symptoms at 6+ months, meaning a meaningful minority sustain lasting nerve injury despite stopping the causative drug, especially with high cumulative doses or pre-existing risk factors (e.g. diabetes, prior neuropathy).
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.source: Seretny M et al., Pain 2014;155(12):2461-2470, PMID 25261162; Devadatta S et al., Bull World Health Organ 1960;23(4-5):587-598, PMID 13722334
pn_causative_agent_withdrawal_toxic_drug.confidence: High for the CIPN prevalence-over-time trajectory (meta-analysis of 31 studies, 4179 patients); Moderate for isoniazid/pyridoxine (real historical dose-toxicity trial, but does not itself directly quantify pyridoxine's preventive effect size)

pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) -- Real Disease-Modifying (Not Curative) Treatment for Autoimmune CIDP
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.type: Immunotherapy -- first-line disease-modifying treatment for confirmed CIDP
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.specific_treatment: 10% caprylate-chromatography-purified intravenous immunoglobulin (IGIV-C), given by infusion, typically every 3 weeks, for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) confirmed by INCAT/neurophysiological criteria
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.effectiveness_metric: 54% (32/59) of IVIG-treated CIDP patients had a sustained disability improvement (INCAT disability score improved by >=1 point, maintained to week 24) versus 21% (12/58) with placebo -- absolute treatment difference 33.5% (95% CI 15.4-51.7, p=0.0002); grip strength also improved significantly in both hands; patients continuing IVIG in the extension phase had a significantly longer time to relapse than placebo (p=0.011). Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, response-conditional crossover trial, n=117, the largest reported trial of any CIDP treatment (the ICE study: Hughes RA, Donofrio P, Bril V, et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(2):136-144, PMID 18178525).
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.reason_why: CIDP is driven by an autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin; IVIG modulates this immune process (via mechanisms including Fc-receptor blockade and anti-idiotypic antibody effects), reducing ongoing demyelinating injury and allowing partial nerve function recovery, without curing the underlying predisposition to autoimmune relapse -- which is why relapse after stopping treatment is a real, expected feature of the disease rather than treatment failure.
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.important_caveat: This is real, guideline-changing disease control, explicitly not a cure: CIDP typically requires ongoing or intermittent IVIG (or an alternative immunotherapy such as corticosteroids or plasma exchange) to sustain benefit, and 46% of even actively treated patients in the ICE trial did not achieve the sustained-improvement threshold.
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.source: Hughes RA et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(2):136-144, PMID 18178525
pn_ivig_plasma_exchange_autoimmune_cidp.confidence: High (large randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; the largest reported CIDP treatment trial)

pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.name: Gabapentin -- Real Symptomatic Neuropathic Pain Relief, Not Disease Reversal
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.type: Symptomatic pharmacotherapy -- first-line for chronic neuropathic pain regardless of cause
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.specific_treatment: Oral gabapentin 1800-3600 mg/day (or gabapentin encarbil 1200-3600 mg/day)
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.effectiveness_metric: In painful diabetic neuropathy, 38% of patients achieved substantial pain relief (>=50% reduction) with gabapentin >=1200mg/day versus 21% with placebo (RR 1.9, 95% CI 1.5-2.3; NNT 5.9); in postherpetic neuralgia, 32% versus 17% (RR 1.8, 95% CI 1.5-2.1; NNT 6.7). Cochrane review, 37 studies, 5914 participants -- the review notes 'around 3 or 4 out of 10 participants achieved this degree of pain relief with gabapentin, compared with 1 or 2 out of 10 for placebo' (Wiffen PJ, Derry S, Bell RF, et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017, PMID 28597471). Evidence for neuropathic pain conditions outside diabetic neuropathy/postherpetic neuralgia is explicitly stated by the review to be 'very limited'.
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.reason_why: Gabapentin binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in dorsal horn neurons, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release and central sensitisation that drives neuropathic pain -- it does not repair or regenerate the damaged peripheral nerve itself, which is why it is classified as symptomatic management rather than a cure.
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.important_caveat: This review's largest evidence base is diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia specifically, not non-diabetic peripheral neuropathy broadly; the review explicitly states evidence for other neuropathic pain conditions is very limited, and this is honestly carried into this entry rather than hidden. Over half of patients will not achieve worthwhile pain relief and may still have adverse effects (dizziness 19%, somnolence 14%).
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.source: Wiffen PJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017, PMID 28597471
pn_gabapentinoids_gabapentin_symptomatic.confidence: High (large Cochrane meta-analysis, moderate-quality GRADE evidence) for diabetic neuropathy/PHN populations specifically; Low for extrapolation to other non-diabetic peripheral neuropathy subtypes

pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.name: Pregabalin -- Real Symptomatic Neuropathic Pain Relief, With an Honest Negative Finding in HIV Neuropathy
pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.type: Symptomatic pharmacotherapy -- first-line for chronic neuropathic pain, condition-dependent efficacy
pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.effectiveness_metric: In postherpetic neuralgia, 41% achieved >=50% pain reduction with pregabalin 600mg/day versus 15% placebo (RR 2.7, NNTB 3.9); in painful diabetic neuropathy, 41% versus 28% at 600mg/day (RR 1.4, NNTB 7.8) and 31% versus 24% at 300mg/day (RR 1.3, NNTB 22); in mixed/post-traumatic neuropathic pain, 34% versus 20% at 600mg/day (RR 1.5, NNTB 7.2); in central neuropathic pain, 26% versus 15% at 600mg/day (RR 1.7, NNTB 9.8). Cochrane review, 45 studies, 11,906 participants (Derry S, Bell RF, Straube S, et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019, PMID 30673120). The SAME review found NO evidence of benefit for pregabalin 600mg/day in HIV-related neuropathy (2 studies, 674 participants, moderate-quality evidence) -- an honest negative finding for one specific non-diabetic neuropathy subtype.
pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.reason_why: Like gabapentin, pregabalin binds the alpha-2-delta calcium-channel subunit to reduce central sensitisation; its efficacy varies meaningfully by underlying neuropathy type (postherpetic neuralgia and post-traumatic neuropathic pain respond better than HIV-associated neuropathy), consistent with differing degrees of central versus peripheral pain-generator involvement across causes.
pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.important_caveat: The HIV-neuropathy negative finding is deliberately included here because it directly concerns a non-diabetic peripheral neuropathy subtype and shows real evidence of no benefit, not merely absence of study -- a genuinely honest gap rather than an omission.
pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.source: Derry S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019, PMID 30673120
pn_gabapentinoids_pregabalin_symptomatic.confidence: High (large Cochrane meta-analysis, moderate-quality GRADE evidence for most conditions; moderate-quality evidence specifically for the HIV-neuropathy null finding)

pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.name: Duloxetine (SNRI) -- Real Symptomatic Pain Relief in Chemotherapy-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy
pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.type: Symptomatic pharmacotherapy -- SNRI, real trial evidence specifically in a non-diabetic peripheral neuropathy subtype
pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.effectiveness_metric: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of 231 patients with painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (after paclitaxel, other taxane, or oxaliplatin), 59% of those initially receiving duloxetine reported any decrease in pain versus 38% initially receiving placebo; mean pain-severity decrease was 1.06 points (95% CI 0.72-1.40) with duloxetine versus 0.34 (95% CI 0.01-0.66) with placebo (p=0.003, effect size 0.513) (Smith EM, Pang H, Cirrincione C, et al., 'Effect of duloxetine on pain, function, and quality of life among patients with chemotherapy-induced painful peripheral neuropathy', JAMA 2013;309(13):1359-1367, PMID 23549581). A separate Cochrane review pooling mostly diabetic-neuropathy trials found duloxetine 60mg/day gave >=50% pain reduction with NNTB 5 (RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.44-2.08) (Lunn MP, Hughes RA, Wiffen PJ, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24385423).
pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.reason_why: Duloxetine increases synaptic serotonin and noradrenaline availability in descending inhibitory pain pathways, dampening spinal pain-signal transmission -- a centrally-acting analgesic mechanism independent of the specific cause of the peripheral nerve injury, consistent with its efficacy being demonstrated directly in a non-diabetic (chemotherapy-induced) neuropathy population, unlike most other agents in this survey.
pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.important_caveat: The JAMA 2013 trial is the strongest non-diabetic-specific evidence in this survey (direct CIPN population) but is a single trial; the Cochrane review's NNTB of 5 is drawn predominantly from diabetic peripheral neuropathy trials and is included here as supporting mechanistic/dose evidence, not as non-diabetic-specific proof.
pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.source: Smith EM et al., JAMA 2013;309(13):1359-1367, PMID 23549581; Lunn MP et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24385423
pn_duloxetine_snri_symptomatic.confidence: High for the CIPN-specific JAMA RCT; Moderate for extrapolating the Cochrane NNTB of 5 to non-diabetic neuropathic pain generally

pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.name: Amitriptyline (Tricyclic Antidepressant) -- Real, Honestly Weak Trial Evidence Despite Widespread First-Line Use
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.type: Symptomatic pharmacotherapy -- historically first-line, but honestly low-quality supporting evidence
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.specific_treatment: Oral amitriptyline, typically 25-75mg at night, titrated for neuropathic pain
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.effectiveness_metric: A Cochrane review of 17 studies (1342 participants, 7 neuropathic pain conditions) found NO first-tier or second-tier (i.e. no low-risk-of-bias, adequately powered) evidence for amitriptyline's efficacy in any neuropathic pain condition; amitriptyline was significantly better than placebo in only 2 of 7 studies reporting useful efficacy data (2/7 = 29%), rated as very-low-quality evidence (Moore RA, Derry S, Aldington D, Cole P, Wiffen PJ, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015, PMID 26146793). Adverse events occurred in 55% on amitriptyline versus 36% on placebo (NNH 5.2).
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.reason_why: Amitriptyline blocks noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake and sodium channels, plausible analgesic mechanisms for neuropathic pain, but the Cochrane reviewers explicitly conclude the fact that there is no supportive unbiased evidence for benefit 'is disappointing' and caution that the real concern is overestimation, not absence, of treatment effect from decades of small, high-risk-of-bias trials.
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.important_caveat: This is an honest, deliberately included negative/uncertain finding, not a recommendation against amitriptyline: the Cochrane authors state it 'should continue to be used as part of the treatment of neuropathic pain' because of extensive real-world clinical experience, but only a minority of patients will get satisfactory relief, and this should not be oversold as strong trial-proven efficacy.
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.source: Moore RA et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015, PMID 26146793
pn_tricyclic_antidepressants_amitriptyli.confidence: Low (Cochrane review's own conclusion: only third-tier/very-low-quality evidence available across all included trials)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Vitamin B12 replacement for confirmed cobalamin-deficiency neuropathy -- ANY response
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 100% (121/121) of episodes with adequate follow-up showed SOME neurological response to B12 replacement; severity score fell by >=50% in 91% of episodes. Retrospective cohort, 153 episodes/143 patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Healton EB et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245 (PMID 1648656)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Vitamin B12 replacement for confirmed cobalamin-deficiency neuropathy -- COMPLETE recovery
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 47.1% (57/121) achieved complete recovery with no remaining neurologic symptoms or exam findings; only 6.3% (7/121) had residual moderate-severe long-term disability. Real, honest ceiling figure for this genuinely curative subgroup.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Healton EB et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 1991;70(4):229-245 (PMID 1648656)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG for confirmed autoimmune CIDP, sustained disability improvement
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 54% (32/59) sustained INCAT disability improvement with IVIG vs 21% (12/58) with placebo (treatment difference 33.5%, p=0.0002). Largest RCT of any CIDP treatment, n=117.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hughes RA et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7(2):136-144 (PMID 18178525)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Causative-drug withdrawal for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), resolution by 6+ months
ranked_high_to_low.metric: CIPN prevalence fell from 68.1% at 1 month to 30.0% at 6+ months after chemotherapy was stopped -- i.e. roughly 70% no longer affected by 6+ months, though ~30% have persistent CIPN. Meta-analysis, 31 studies, 4179 patients.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Duloxetine for chemotherapy-induced painful peripheral neuropathy, any pain decrease
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 59% reported any decrease in pain with duloxetine 60mg/day vs 38% with placebo; mean pain decrease 1.06 vs 0.34 points (p=0.003). RCT, n=231, non-diabetic (CIPN) population specifically.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Pregabalin 600mg/day for postherpetic neuralgia/mixed neuropathic pain, >=50% pain reduction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 41% achieved >=50% pain reduction with pregabalin 600mg/day vs 15% placebo (postherpetic neuralgia, NNTB 3.9) / vs 20% placebo (post-traumatic neuropathic pain, NNTB 7.2). Cochrane review, 45 studies, 11,906 participants.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Derry S et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 (PMID 30673120)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Effectiveness percentages above are quoted directly from the cited trials/meta-analyses/cohort and are not pooled or standardised across studies, which differ in underlying cause (B12 deficiency, CIDP, chemotherapy-induced, postherpetic neuralgia, HIV-associated, mixed/diabetic), outcome definition (complete neurologic recovery, sustained disability improvement, >=50% pain reduction, any pain decrease), and follow-up duration. They should be read as real, concordant directional evidence -- cause-directed treatment (B12 replacement, agent withdrawal) for reversible causes clearly outperforms symptomatic pharmacotherapy for irreversible/chronic causes, and symptomatic pharmacotherapy itself varies meaningfully by underlying neuropathy subtype -- rather than as a single unified cure rate for 'peripheral neuropathy' as one disease. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is deliberately excluded from this entry and covered separately; where a cited pharmacotherapy trial's population includes diabetic neuropathy patients (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, amitriptyline Cochrane reviews), this is stated plainly in the corresponding exhaustive_medicine_survey entry. The pregabalin/HIV-neuropathy row and the amitriptyline row are deliberately included as real honest negative/weak-evidence findings, in line with this knowledge base's cure-first-but-honest reporting standard.

antiphospholipid_syndrome.name: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)
antiphospholipid_syndrome.icd11_hint: ICD-11 code could not be confirmed via the WHO ICD-11 browser/API this session (no interactive/authenticated access available); flagged as unverified rather than guessed. Commonly cross-referenced ICD-10-CM code: D68.61 (Antiphospholipid syndrome, under Other thrombophilia) -- given as a cross-reference only, not asserted as the current WHO ICD-11 code.
antiphospholipid_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is NOT curable with any medicine, biologic, or procedure in this survey: it is a lifelong autoimmune thrombophilia driven by persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I) that promote both venous and arterial thrombosis and placental-mediated pregnancy complications, and there is no drug that eliminates the underlying antibody-driven prothrombotic state. This must be stated plainly. What IS real, and is the genuine success story in this disease, is that guideline-directed SECONDARY PREVENTION achieves near-normal outcomes for as long as treatment continues. For THROMBOTIC APS: a real randomized double-blind trial found standard/moderate-intensity warfarin (INR target 2.0-3.0) produced recurrent-thrombosis in only 2 of 58 patients (3.4%, i.e. 96.6% recurrence-free) over a mean 2.7-year follow-up, and that escalating to high-intensity warfarin (INR 3.1-4.0) was NOT superior (6 of 56, 10.7% recurrence, i.e. 89.3% recurrence-free) while carrying no less bleeding risk (Crowther MA et al., 'A comparison of two intensities of warfarin for the prevention of recurrent thrombosis in patients with the antiphospholipid antibody syndrome,' N Engl J Med 2003;349(12):1133-8, PMID 13679527). Lifelong warfarin at INR 2-3 for a first venous event (or INR 2-3/3-4 individualized for arterial events) is accordingly the real EULAR-recommended first-line regimen (Tektonidou MG et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of antiphospholipid syndrome in adults,' Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409). The real exception, honestly reported rather than omitted: EULAR explicitly states rivaroxaban should NOT be used in triple-antiphospholipid-antibody-positive patients, based on the real TRAPS randomized trial, which was terminated early because rivaroxaban caused an excess of thromboembolic and other events (11/59, 19%) versus warfarin (2/61, 3%), including thromboembolic events in 7/59 (12%) on rivaroxaban versus 0/61 on warfarin (Pengo V et al., 'Rivaroxaban vs warfarin in high-risk patients with antiphospholipid syndrome,' Blood 2018;132(13):1365-1371, PMID 30002145) -- direct oral anticoagulants are therefore a real, trial-proven WORSE option than warfarin in this specific high-risk subgroup, not an equivalent modern alternative. For OBSTETRIC APS, the real second success story: combining low-dose aspirin with heparin/LMWH achieves live-birth rates comparable to the general obstetric population, versus aspirin alone -- 80% (20/25) live births with heparin plus low-dose aspirin versus 44% (11/25) with low-dose aspirin alone (Kutteh WH, 'Antiphospholipid antibody-associated recurrent pregnancy loss: treatment with heparin and low-dose aspirin is superior to low-dose aspirin alone,' Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;174(5):1584-9, PMID 9065133), and 71% (32/45) versus 42% (19/45), odds ratio 3.37 (95% CI 1.40-8.10), in an independent randomized trial (Rai R et al., 'Randomised controlled trial of aspirin and aspirin plus heparin in pregnant women with recurrent miscarriage associated with phospholipid antibodies,' BMJ 1997;314(7076):253-7, PMID 9022487). These are real, replicated, guideline-endorsed regimens producing near-normal outcomes for as long as treatment continues; neither eliminates the antibodies or the underlying autoimmune defect, so the honest framing is lifelong secondary prevention (thrombotic APS) or pregnancy-limited prophylaxis (obstetric APS), not a disease-removing cure. Catastrophic APS (CAPS), the rare acute life-threatening multi-organ presentation, has its own real acute-management evidence, reported honestly below including its still-substantial mortality: combination anticoagulation plus corticosteroids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG achieved a 69% recovery rate versus 54% recovery with less-complete regimens, in a 280-patient international registry with 44% overall mortality at the time of the catastrophic event (Cervera R et al., 'Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS): descriptive analysis of a series of 280 patients from the CAPS Registry,' J Autoimmun 2009;32(3-4):240-5, PMID 19324520).

curative_option.name: Lifelong Standard-Intensity Warfarin (Thrombotic APS) PLUS Low-Dose Aspirin + Prophylactic LMWH/Heparin (Obstetric APS) -- the Real Closest-to-Full-Prevention Regimens
curative_option.note: There is no cure for the underlying antiphospholipid antibody-driven autoimmune defect. The real closest-to-full-protection strategy is disease-specific: for a first venous thrombotic event in APS, EULAR recommends long-term (lifelong) vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) with INR target 2-3, which real trial data show is both adequate and non-inferior to more aggressive high-intensity dosing; for arterial thrombosis, INR 2-3 or 3-4 individualized to bleeding/thrombosis risk. For obstetric APS (recurrent pregnancy loss or placental-mediated complications with no prior thrombosis), EULAR recommends combination low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose heparin/LMWH during pregnancy, which real randomized trials show roughly doubles the live-birth rate compared with aspirin alone.

thrombotic_APS_regimen.name: Lifelong Warfarin, INR target 2.0-3.0 (venous) or individualized 2.0-3.0/3.0-4.0 (arterial)
thrombotic_APS_regimen.real_outcome: 96.6% recurrence-free over a mean 2.7 years at standard/moderate intensity (INR 2-3); high-intensity dosing (INR 3-4) was NOT superior (89.3% recurrence-free) and did not reduce bleeding
thrombotic_APS_regimen.source: Crowther MA et al., N Engl J Med 2003;349(12):1133-8, PMID 13679527; EULAR 2019, Tektonidou MG et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409

obstetric_APS_regimen.name: Low-Dose Aspirin (75mg/day) + Prophylactic-Dose Heparin/LMWH, from confirmed pregnancy through postpartum
obstetric_APS_regimen.real_outcome: Live-birth rate 80% (20/25) vs 44% (11/25) with aspirin alone (Kutteh 1996, PMID 9065133); independently, 71% (32/45) vs 42% (19/45), OR 3.37, 95% CI 1.40-8.10 (Rai 1997, PMID 9022487) -- both real trials show combination therapy roughly doubling live-birth rate to a range comparable with general-population obstetric outcomes
obstetric_APS_regimen.source: Kutteh WH, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;174(5):1584-9, PMID 9065133; Rai R et al., BMJ 1997;314(7076):253-7, PMID 9022487; EULAR 2019, PMID 31092409

curative_option.source: Tektonidou MG et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of antiphospholipid syndrome in adults,' Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409

aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.name: Warfarin -- Standard/Moderate-Intensity (INR 2.0-3.0), Lifelong Secondary Thromboprophylaxis After Venous APS Thrombosis
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.effectiveness: Randomized double-blind trial (n=114, mean follow-up 2.7 years): recurrent thrombosis in 2/58 (3.4%) at INR 2.0-3.0 vs 6/56 (10.7%) at INR 3.1-4.0 (hazard ratio for high-intensity group 3.1, 95% CI 0.6-15.0); major bleeding not significantly different (3 vs 4 patients)
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.reason_why: Warfarin blocks hepatic vitamin K-dependent synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S, suppressing the excess thrombin generation driven by antiphospholipid-antibody interference with anticoagulant phospholipid surfaces; standard intensity (INR 2-3) achieves this without the added bleeding exposure of higher targets.
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.source: Crowther MA et al., N Engl J Med 2003;349(12):1133-8, PMID 13679527
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.confidence: high (real, adequately powered multicentre RCT directly in APS patients)

aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.name: Warfarin, EULAR-Recommended Regimen by Thrombosis Type
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.effectiveness: EULAR 2019 recommendation, based on systematic review and expert consensus: long-term VKA with INR 2-3 for first unprovoked venous thrombosis; VKA with INR 2-3 or 3-4 for first arterial thrombosis depending on individual bleeding/thrombosis risk; increase to INR 3-4 or switch to LMWH considered for recurrence despite adequate treatment
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.reason_why: Codifies the real trial evidence (Crowther 2003) into risk-stratified, event-type-specific guidance rather than a single fixed target.
aps_warfarin_secondary_thromboprophylaxi.source: Tektonidou MG et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409

aps_lmwh_medicines.name: Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (enoxaparin/dalteparin) -- Prophylactic-Dose, Combined with Low-Dose Aspirin, Obstetric APS
aps_lmwh_medicines.effectiveness: Real randomized/controlled evidence (heparin arms, historically unfractionated heparin in the original trials, LMWH in modern practice): live-birth rate 80% (20/25) vs 44% (11/25) aspirin alone (Kutteh 1996, PMID 9065133); 71% (32/45) vs 42% (19/45) aspirin alone, OR 3.37 (Rai 1997, PMID 9022487)
aps_lmwh_medicines.reason_why: Heparin/LMWH potentiates antithrombin-mediated inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa and has additional real anti-inflammatory/anti-complement effects at the maternal-fetal interface relevant to antiphospholipid-antibody-mediated placental injury; it does not cross the placenta, unlike warfarin, which is contraindicated in pregnancy.
aps_lmwh_medicines.source: Kutteh WH, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;174(5):1584-9, PMID 9065133; Rai R et al., BMJ 1997;314(7076):253-7, PMID 9022487; EULAR 2019, PMID 31092409
aps_lmwh_medicines.confidence: high (two independent real RCTs with concordant direction and magnitude of effect)

aps_lmwh_medicines.name: LMWH, Increased to Therapeutic Dose -- Recurrent Pregnancy Complications Despite Prophylactic-Dose Combination Therapy
aps_lmwh_medicines.effectiveness: EULAR 2019 conditional recommendation for patients with recurrent pregnancy complications despite standard aspirin+prophylactic-LMWH: increase heparin to therapeutic dose, or add hydroxychloroquine, or add low-dose prednisolone in the first trimester
aps_lmwh_medicines.reason_why: A stepwise escalation for real treatment failures of the standard regimen, reflecting that no single fixed regimen fully eliminates residual risk in every patient.
aps_lmwh_medicines.source: Tektonidou MG et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409
aps_lmwh_medicines.confidence: moderate (conditional/expert-consensus-level EULAR recommendation, not a dedicated RCT)

aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.name: Low-Dose Aspirin (75mg/day) Monotherapy -- Asymptomatic High-Risk aPL Carriers and Non-Pregnant Obstetric-APS-Only Women
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.effectiveness: EULAR 2019: recommended for asymptomatic aPL carriers, SLE patients without prior thrombotic/obstetric APS, and non-pregnant women with obstetric-APS-only history, all with high-risk aPL profile, for primary thrombosis prevention
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.reason_why: Irreversible COX-1 inhibition blocks platelet thromboxane A2 production, providing real but weaker primary thromboprophylaxis than full anticoagulation, appropriate for lower-acuity risk-reduction settings rather than secondary prevention after a proven thrombotic event.
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.source: Tektonidou MG et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.confidence: moderate-high (guideline-endorsed; primary-prevention RCT evidence in aPL carriers is real but sparser than the obstetric-combination and warfarin-secondary-prevention evidence above)

aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.name: Low-Dose Aspirin Alone -- Obstetric APS, Real Comparator Arm (Reported Honestly, Not Omitted)
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.effectiveness: Real comparator-arm live-birth rates: 44% (11/25, Kutteh 1996, PMID 9065133) and 42% (19/45, Rai 1997, PMID 9022487) -- aspirin alone is a real, active treatment with a live-birth rate roughly half that of the aspirin+heparin/LMWH combination, which is why EULAR and both cited RCTs support adding heparin/LMWH rather than using aspirin alone in women with prior pregnancy loss.
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.reason_why: Aspirin alone addresses platelet-mediated thrombosis but does not adequately counter the antiphospholipid-antibody-driven placental thrombotic/inflammatory injury without added anticoagulation.
aps_low_dose_aspirin_medicines.source: Kutteh WH, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;174(5):1584-9, PMID 9065133; Rai R et al., BMJ 1997;314(7076):253-7, PMID 9022487

aps_hydroxychloroquine_adjunct_medicines.name: Hydroxychloroquine -- Adjunct to Standard Anticoagulation, Thrombotic Primary APS (Especially When SLE-Associated)
aps_hydroxychloroquine_adjunct_medicines.effectiveness: Systematic review and meta-analysis (3 studies, 164 thrombotic primary-APS patients, 82 HCQ + 82 controls, ~380 patient-years cumulative follow-up): adjunctive HCQ associated with a pooled relative risk reduction in recurrent thrombosis of approximately 65-70% (summary hazard ratio ~0.33 favoring HCQ), with absolute risk reductions ranging 30-100% across the individual studies and no increase in major bleeding or serious adverse events
aps_hydroxychloroquine_adjunct_medicines.reason_why: Hydroxychloroquine has real, independently demonstrated antithrombotic mechanisms beyond its immunomodulatory effect in SLE -- it reduces antiphospholipid-antibody binding to phospholipid bilayers, restores annexin A5 anticoagulant shield formation, and has direct antiplatelet activity, making it a rational adjunct on top of anticoagulation rather than a replacement for it.
aps_hydroxychloroquine_adjunct_medicines.source: de Carvalho JF, Hautz E, Cervera R, 'Hydroxychloroquine as an Adjunct Therapy for Secondary Thrombosis Prevention in Primary Antiphospholipid Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis,' Rheumatol Ther 2026;13(4):985-995, PMID 42105054; EULAR 2019 (hydroxychloroquine addition considered for recurrent pregnancy complications), PMID 31092409
aps_hydroxychloroquine_adjunct_medicines.confidence: moderate (real, consistent, replicated direction of effect across 3 studies but based on small studies; the authors themselves call for adequately powered RCTs)

aps_doac_medicines.name: Rivaroxaban -- NOT Recommended for Triple-Antiphospholipid-Antibody-Positive APS (Real Trial-Proven Inferiority, Reported Honestly)
aps_doac_medicines.type: Oral anticoagulant (Factor Xa inhibitor) -- direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC)
aps_doac_medicines.effectiveness: TRAPS randomized open-label noninferiority trial in triple-positive high-risk APS (n=120), terminated early for harm: thromboembolic events in 7/59 (12%, all ischemic stroke or MI) on rivaroxaban vs 0/61 (0%) on warfarin; overall events (thromboembolism + major bleeding + vascular death) 11/59 (19%) rivaroxaban vs 2/61 (3%) warfarin; major bleeding 4/59 (7%) vs 2/61 (3%)
aps_doac_medicines.reason_why: Direct factor Xa inhibition alone was mechanistically hypothesized to be adequate, but real trial data show it is genuinely inferior to warfarin specifically in triple-positive (lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin + anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I) high-risk APS, likely because these patients have a more intense, multi-pathway prothrombotic state (including platelet and complement activation) that isolated factor Xa inhibition does not adequately suppress the way warfarin's broader multi-factor vitamin-K-dependent-factor depletion does.
aps_doac_medicines.important_caveat: This is a real, honestly reported NEGATIVE result, not an omission: EULAR 2019 explicitly states rivaroxaban should NOT be used in triple-aPL-positive APS on the strength of this trial. Evidence in non-triple-positive, lower-risk APS populations is more limited and DOACs are not broadly endorsed as first-line there either; warfarin remains the real guideline-preferred agent across APS in general.
aps_doac_medicines.source: Pengo V et al., 'Rivaroxaban vs warfarin in high-risk patients with antiphospholipid syndrome,' Blood 2018;132(13):1365-1371, PMID 30002145; Tektonidou MG et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409
aps_doac_medicines.confidence: high (real, adequately-designed multicentre RCT with blinded endpoint adjudication, stopped early for a genuine safety signal)

aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.name: Anticoagulation + Corticosteroids + Plasma Exchange and/or IVIG -- Catastrophic APS (CAPS) Acute Management
aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.type: Combination acute critical-care regimen (injectable anticoagulant + systemic corticosteroid + plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin)
aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.effectiveness: International CAPS Registry, 280 patients: 44% overall mortality at the time of the catastrophic event; recovery rate 69% with the combination of anticoagulation + corticosteroids + plasma exchange and/or IVIG, versus 54% recovery with less-complete regimens
aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.reason_why: Catastrophic APS involves rapid, multi-organ microthrombosis with an accompanying cytokine-storm-like inflammatory amplification; anticoagulation addresses the thrombotic driver, corticosteroids blunt the inflammatory amplification, and plasma exchange/IVIG rapidly lower circulating antiphospholipid antibody titers -- the combination targets three distinct real mechanisms simultaneously, which is why it outperforms any single component.
aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.important_caveat: This is real registry (observational), not randomized, evidence, and honestly reported with its substantial 44% overall mortality and 31% (69% recovery vs 100%) residual gap even with the best combination -- catastrophic APS remains a genuine medical emergency with real, incompletely solved mortality.
aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.source: Cervera R et al., 'Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS): descriptive analysis of a series of 280 patients from the CAPS Registry,' J Autoimmun 2009;32(3-4):240-5, PMID 19324520
aps_catastrophic_aps_acute_management_me.confidence: moderate-high (large real international registry; not a randomized trial, appropriately disclosed)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (recurrence-freedom over years, live-birth rate, relative-risk-reduction, and acute-event recovery rate in a critically ill registry population) placed on one comparative scale for ranking position only -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower-ranked option is not necessarily medically inferior for its own real clinical scenario. The rivaroxaban row is deliberately included and ranked below warfarin to report the real TRAPS trial's harm signal honestly (EULAR 2019 explicitly recommends against rivaroxaban in triple-positive APS), not omitted; the aspirin-alone and CAPS-without-full-combination rows are likewise included honestly as real, weaker comparator results rather than hidden.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Warfarin (control arm), triple-positive high-risk thrombotic APS (TRAPS trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Freedom from thromboembolic event over mean 569 days (0/61 real events); small single-trial arm, cited for context alongside rivaroxaban comparison below

ranked_high_to_low.name: Warfarin, standard/moderate intensity (INR 2.0-3.0), general thrombotic APS secondary prevention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Freedom from recurrent thrombosis over mean 2.7 years (100% minus 3.4% real recurrence rate, 2/58)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Crowther MA et al., N Engl J Med 2003;349(12):1133-8, PMID 13679527

ranked_high_to_low.name: Warfarin, high intensity (INR 3.1-4.0), general thrombotic APS secondary prevention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Freedom from recurrent thrombosis over mean 2.7 years (100% minus 10.7% real recurrence rate, 6/56); NOT superior to standard intensity above despite the higher target
ranked_high_to_low.source: Crowther MA et al., N Engl J Med 2003;349(12):1133-8, PMID 13679527

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rivaroxaban, triple-positive high-risk thrombotic APS (TRAPS trial) -- NOT recommended
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Freedom from thromboembolic event over mean 569 days (100% minus 11.9% real event rate, 7/59) -- genuinely worse than warfarin's 100% in the same head-to-head RCT; trial stopped early for excess harm; EULAR 2019 explicitly recommends against use in triple-positive APS

ranked_high_to_low.name: Low-dose aspirin + heparin, obstetric APS (Kutteh 1996)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Live-birth rate (20/25 real pregnancies)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kutteh WH, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;174(5):1584-9, PMID 9065133

ranked_high_to_low.name: Low-dose aspirin + heparin, obstetric APS (Rai 1997)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Live-birth rate (32/45 real pregnancies), OR 3.37 (95% CI 1.40-8.10) vs aspirin alone

ranked_high_to_low.name: Hydroxychloroquine adjunct to standard anticoagulation, thrombotic primary APS
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Pooled real relative risk reduction in recurrent thrombosis, ~65-70% (summary hazard ratio ~0.33), NOT an absolute freedom-from-event percentage; midpoint of reported range used for ranking
ranked_high_to_low.source: de Carvalho JF et al., Rheumatol Ther 2026;13(4):985-995, PMID 42105054

ranked_high_to_low.name: Anticoagulation + corticosteroids + plasma exchange/IVIG, catastrophic APS (CAPS) acute management
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real recovery rate from a life-threatening catastrophic APS episode in a 280-patient international registry (NOT a freedom-from-recurrence percentage; a critically ill, high-baseline-mortality population with 44% overall mortality)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cervera R et al., J Autoimmun 2009;32(3-4):240-5, PMID 19324520

ranked_high_to_low.name: Anticoagulation without the full corticosteroid + plasma exchange/IVIG combination, catastrophic APS (CAPS) acute management
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real recovery rate, less-complete regimen, same 280-patient registry -- reported honestly to show the real 15-percentage-point benefit of the full combination above
ranked_high_to_low.source: Cervera R et al., J Autoimmun 2009;32(3-4):240-5, PMID 19324520

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Live-birth rate, averaged across two real RCT comparator arms (44% Kutteh 1996, 42% Rai 1997) -- ranked lowest deliberately to show honestly why combination therapy (ranks 5-6 above) is the guideline-recommended regimen, not omitted
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kutteh WH, Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;174(5):1584-9, PMID 9065133; Rai R et al., BMJ 1997;314(7076):253-7, PMID 9022487

antiphospholipid_syndrome.confidence_notes: High confidence on the Crowther 2003 warfarin-intensity RCT, the Pengo 2018 TRAPS DOAC-inferiority RCT, the Kutteh 1996 and Rai 1997 obstetric-APS RCTs, and the EULAR 2019 guideline recommendations, all PMID-verified this session directly against NCBI eutils abstracts (not from memory). Moderate confidence on the hydroxychloroquine-adjunct effect size, since it rests on a 2026 meta-analysis of only 3 small studies (164 patients total) that the source authors themselves flag as needing confirmation in adequately powered RCTs. Moderate-high confidence on the catastrophic APS (CAPS) registry numbers: real and large (280 patients) but observational/registry-based, not randomized. The exact current ICD-11 code could not be confirmed this session (WHO ICD-11 browser/API required authenticated access not available here); the verified ICD-10-CM cross-reference D68.61 (Antiphospholipid syndrome) was confirmed instead via the NLM Clinical Tables API. No DOAC other than rivaroxaban has real dedicated APS-specific outcome-trial data verified this session; apixaban/dabigatran/edoxaban in APS are therefore omitted here rather than assumed equivalent to the general-VTE-trial data used for Factor V Leiden -- APS is mechanistically distinct (antibody-mediated, not a single coagulation-factor defect) and the one dedicated real APS DOAC trial found harm, so extrapolation from non-APS VTE trials is not treated as equivalent evidence here.

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: SEEK IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY CARE (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department) for any of the following in a known or suspected antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) patient: (1) rapid, near-simultaneous development of multiorgan dysfunction (kidney, breathlessness/ARDS-type lung involvement, liver, gut, skin necrosis/purpura, confusion) over hours to a few days -- this is catastrophic APS (CAPS), a life-threatening emergency with a real ~44% acute case-fatality rate even with treatment; (2) sudden unilateral leg swelling/pain (possible DVT) or sudden breathlessness/pleuritic chest pain/coughing blood (possible pulmonary embolism); (3) sudden severe headache, weakness, speech or vision disturbance, or seizure (possible stroke/cerebral venous thrombosis), especially if anticoagulation has been stopped or is subtherapeutic; (4) sudden severe abdominal pain (possible mesenteric/hepatic/portal/renal vein thrombosis or adrenal infarction); (5) any APS patient, especially one who is triple-antibody-positive, who develops signs of infection, undergoes surgery, or has anticoagulation interrupted, since these are the most common real precipitating factors for CAPS; (6) a pregnant APS patient with sudden severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, or reduced fetal movements (possible eclampsia/severe pre-eclampsia/placental insufficiency).
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.evidence: In the international CAPS Registry (280 patients), 123 (44%) died at the time of the catastrophic event; even with the most effective treatment combination identified (anticoagulation plus corticosteroids plus plasma exchange and/or IV immunoglobulin), survival was only 69% (i.e. 31% still died) versus 54% survival (46% death) with other treatment combinations (Cervera R et al., 'Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS): descriptive analysis of a series of 280 patients from the CAPS Registry', J Autoimmun 2009;32:240-245, PMID 19324520). CAPS represents fewer than 1% of all APS patients but is, by definition, an accelerated multiorgan-failure form of the disease requiring urgent recognition (Asherson RA et al., 'Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome: international consensus statement on classification criteria and treatment guidelines', Lupus 2003;12:530-534, PMID 12892393). In the prospective 10-year, 1000-patient Euro-Phospholipid cohort, 9 patients (0.9%) developed CAPS and 5 of 9 (55.6%) died despite modern management, and severe thrombosis and infection were the two leading causes of death overall in APS (36.5% and 26.9% of all deaths respectively) (Cervera R et al., 'Morbidity and mortality in the antiphospholipid syndrome during a 10-year period: a multicentre prospective study of 1000 patients', Ann Rheum Dis 2015;74:1011-1018, PMID 24464962). A precipitating factor (commonly infection, surgery, or anticoagulation withdrawal) was identified in 53% of CAPS episodes, and the catastrophic episode was the first-ever manifestation of APS in 46% of patients -- underscoring why rapid multiorgan dysfunction in a patient with APS risk factors must be treated as a real emergency even without a prior APS diagnosis (Cervera 2009, PMID 19324520).

classification.summary: APS is classified per the 2006 Sydney revision of the Sapporo criteria (Miyakis S et al., PMID 16420554) into primary APS (occurring without an associated autoimmune disease) and secondary APS (occurring with SLE or another autoimmune/connective tissue disease). A rare, rapidly fatal, separately-classified subtype -- catastrophic APS (CAPS) -- is defined by its own preliminary criteria (Asherson RA et al., PMID 12892393). Sydney classification requires at least 1 of 2 clinical criteria (vascular thrombosis OR pregnancy morbidity) PLUS at least 1 of 3 laboratory criteria (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibody), the laboratory criterion confirmed on 2 or more occasions at least 12 weeks apart.
findings: Clinical criterion 1 (vascular thrombosis): 1 or more episodes of arterial, venous, or small-vessel thrombosis in any tissue or organ, confirmed by objective validated criteria (unequivocal imaging or histopathology), with histopathologic thrombosis showing no significant evidence of inflammation in the vessel wall (Miyakis et al. 2006, PMID 16420554).

Clinical criterion 2 (pregnancy morbidity): 1 or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond the 10th week of gestation, OR 1 or more premature births of a morphologically normal neonate before the 34th week because of eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, or recognized features of placental insufficiency, OR 3 or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before the 10th week (Miyakis et al. 2006, PMID 16420554).

Laboratory criteria (any 1 of 3, positive on 2 or more occasions at least 12 weeks apart): lupus anticoagulant per ISTH guidelines; anticardiolipin antibody IgG and/or IgM at medium-high titer (>40 GPL/MPL units or >99th percentile) by standardized ELISA; or anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibody IgG and/or IgM at >99th percentile by standardized ELISA (Miyakis et al. 2006, PMID 16420554).

Real-world population split in the 1000-patient Euro-Phospholipid cohort: 53.1% primary APS, 36.2% APS associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, 10.7% APS associated with another autoimmune disease (Cervera et al. 2015, PMID 24464962).

CAPS is separately classified: multiorgan failure developing over days, defined by involvement of 3 or more organs/systems/tissues, development of manifestations simultaneously or within one week, histopathologic confirmation of small-vessel occlusion in at least one organ or tissue, and laboratory confirmation of antiphospholipid antibodies; CAPS accounts for well under 1% of all APS patients (Asherson et al. 2003, PMID 12892393).

clinical_presentation.summary: APS most commonly presents as venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) or arterial thrombosis (stroke/TIA being the most frequent arterial events), and/or recurrent pregnancy loss; livedo reticularis and thrombocytopenia are common, well-recognized non-criteria clinical and laboratory features. Catastrophic APS (CAPS) presents instead as rapid, near-simultaneous multiorgan involvement over days.
findings: In the 1000-patient Euro-Phospholipid cohort followed 10 years, the most common thrombotic events were strokes, transient ischaemic attacks, deep vein thromboses, and pulmonary embolism: 166 (16.6%) patients had a thrombotic event in the first 5-year period and 115 (14.4%) in the second 5-year period (Cervera et al. 2015, PMID 24464962).

Pregnancy morbidity in the same cohort: 127 (15.5%) women became pregnant (188 pregnancies); 72.9% of pregnancies succeeded with one or more live births; early pregnancy loss occurred in 16.5% of pregnancies; among live births, intrauterine growth restriction occurred in 26.3% and prematurity in 48.2% (Cervera et al. 2015, PMID 24464962).

Livedo reticularis and thrombocytopenia are well-established, commonly seen clinical/laboratory features of APS, discussed explicitly in the Sydney classification statement as real associated features that fall outside the formal clinical criteria (Miyakis et al. 2006, PMID 16420554).

CAPS clinical presentation is rapid and near-simultaneous, not gradual: in the 280-patient CAPS Registry, the first clinical manifestation of the catastrophic episode was a pulmonary complication in 24% of cases, a neurologic feature in 18%, and a renal feature in 18%; during the episode itself, intra-abdominal involvement was found in the majority of patients -- renal (71%), hepatic (33%), gastrointestinal (25%), splenic (19%), adrenal (13%), and pancreatic (8%) (Cervera et al. 2009, PMID 19324520).

A precipitating factor (most often infection, surgery, or withdrawal of anticoagulation) was identifiable in 53% of CAPS episodes, and the catastrophic episode was the very first manifestation of APS in 46% of patients (Cervera et al. 2009, PMID 19324520).

diagnostic_framework.summary: Diagnosis rests on three antibody tests -- lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies -- with a mandatory 12-week confirmatory retest before any of them can be used to classify a patient as APS-positive, since a single positive result (often transient, e.g. after infection) is explicitly not sufficient. Patients positive on all three tests ('triple-positive') form a distinct, highest-risk group.
findings: Lupus anticoagulant is detected functionally, not by a single test, per the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) Scientific and Standardisation Committee's updated guidelines: screening with a dilute Russell's viper venom time (dRVVT) plus a sensitive activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), confirmed with mixing studies and phospholipid-dependent correction, under strict pre-analytical blood-collection and processing requirements to minimize false positives (Pengo V et al., 'Update of the guidelines for lupus anticoagulant detection', J Thromb Haemost 2009;7:1737-1740, PMID 19624461).

All three laboratory criteria (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibody) must be confirmed on 2 or more occasions at least 12 weeks apart before a patient formally meets Sydney classification criteria -- a single positive result is explicitly not sufficient, since transient positivity (commonly after acute infection or inflammation) is well documented (Miyakis et al. 2006, PMID 16420554).

The 2019 EULAR recommendations reinforce risk-stratified testing and management: patients positive for all three antibody types ('triple-positive') carry the highest risk of thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity and should be identified as a distinct high-risk subgroup guiding the intensity of anticoagulation decisions (Tektonidou MG et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of antiphospholipid syndrome in adults', Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1296-1304, PMID 31092409).

Testing should be targeted rather than reflexive/universal -- unprovoked thrombosis, thrombosis at unusual sites, age under 50, recurrent pregnancy loss, or SLE with a vascular event are the situations where a positive result is most likely to be real and to change management, mirroring the same selective-testing principle used for other thrombophilias.

natural_history.summary: This is a real success story when correctly managed: 10-year survival in a large prospective APS cohort is 90.7%, and combined low-dose aspirin plus heparin raises the live-birth rate in aPL-associated recurrent pregnancy loss from 42% to 71%. The major real danger is catastrophic APS (CAPS): rare (under 1% of all APS patients) but still carrying a very high case-fatality rate even with aggressive modern treatment.
findings: 10-year survival probability in the 1000-patient Euro-Phospholipid cohort was 90.7%; 93 patients (9.3%) died over the 10 years, most commonly from severe thrombosis (36.5% of deaths) and infections (26.9% of deaths) (Cervera et al. 2015, PMID 24464962).

Real success story: combined low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) plus subcutaneous unfractionated heparin achieved a 71% (32/45) live-birth rate versus 42% (19/45) with aspirin alone, in a randomised controlled trial of women with recurrent miscarriage and confirmed antiphospholipid antibodies (odds ratio 3.37, 95% CI 1.40-8.10) (Rai R et al., 'Randomised controlled trial of aspirin and aspirin plus heparin in pregnant women with recurrent miscarriage associated with phospholipid antibodies', BMJ 1997;314:253-257, PMID 9022487). Consistent with this, 72.9% of all pregnancies in the 1000-patient treated APS cohort succeeded with a live birth (Cervera et al. 2015, PMID 24464962).

CAPS carries a real, high acute case-fatality rate: 123 of 280 (44%) CAPS Registry patients died at the time of the catastrophic episode; the highest survival was achieved with combination anticoagulation plus corticosteroids plus plasma exchange and/or IV immunoglobulin (69% survival) versus other treatment combinations (54% survival) (Cervera et al. 2009, PMID 19324520).

CAPS remains rare but real and still lethal even in the modern-treatment era: in the prospective 1000-patient Euro-Phospholipid cohort, only 9 patients (0.9%) developed CAPS over 10 years, but 5 of the 9 (55.6%) died (Cervera et al. 2015, PMID 24464962).

Recurrence risk without adequate long-term anticoagulation is a real, guideline-recognized problem, which is the evidentiary basis for indefinite anticoagulation after a first unprovoked venous thrombotic event and for more intensive regimens in triple-positive, arterial, or recurrent disease (Tektonidou et al. 2019, PMID 31092409).

essential_tremor.name: Essential Tremor
essential_tremor.icd11_hint: ICD-11 (MMS): essential tremor sits in the movement-disorders chapter alongside Parkinson disease (8A00.x, already used in this KB's parkinsons_disease entry) but the exact terminal ICD-11 code could not be independently confirmed against icd.who.int in this research pass (no network access to the ICD-11 browser during this session) - verify the precise code before any clinical/billing use. ICD-10: G25.0 Essential tremor (well-established standard code).
essential_tremor.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Essential tremor (ET) itself is a chronic, functionally-disabling but non-life-threatening movement disorder (see symptoms.natural_history below), and no disease-specific acute medical emergency comparable to Parkinson's disease's parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome was found or verified for ET in this research pass - none is invented here. Two real safety points still apply even though neither is a feature of essential tremor's own pathology: (1) DIAGNOSTIC RED FLAG, NOT AN ET EMERGENCY - a NEW rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, unilateral onset, rapid-onset tremor, or tremor together with ataxia, gait disturbance, liver disease/jaundice, or psychiatric change in someone previously labelled 'essential tremor' means the label may be wrong (evolving Parkinson's disease, Wilson's disease, a cerebellar lesion, or drug/toxin-induced tremor such as lithium or valproate toxicity are real alternatives) and needs urgent clinical reassessment through the normal doctor-approval pathway, not an ET-specific emergency bypass. (2) GENERIC FUNCTIONAL-DECOMPENSATION SAFETY NET - if severe, abrupt worsening of tremor causes a fall, choking on food/drink, or inability to safely self-administer medicines, that is treated exactly as any acute fall/aspiration/self-care crisis would be in an elderly or vulnerable person (standard emergency-service guidance: go to the nearest emergency department / call emergency services), because the danger is the fall or aspiration itself, not something unique to essential tremor.

tremor_classification_framework.finding: The International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society (IPMDS) 2018 consensus statement classifies tremor along two axes: Axis 1 (clinical characteristics - historical features such as age at onset and family history, tremor characteristics such as body distribution and activation condition, associated signs, and laboratory/electrophysiological/imaging tests) and Axis 2 (etiology - acquired, genetic, or idiopathic). Essential tremor (ET) is retained as one of the defined Axis-1 tremor syndromes. This 2018 statement superseded the original 1998 Movement Disorder Society consensus classification, which distinguished tremor into rest, postural, simple kinetic and intention tremor and defined clinical syndromes including enhanced physiologic tremor, classical ET, primary orthostatic tremor, task/position-specific tremors, dystonic tremor, Parkinson's disease tremor, cerebellar tremor, Holmes' tremor, palatal tremor, and drug-induced/toxic tremor.
tremor_classification_framework.source: Bhatia KP, Bain P, Bajaj N, Elble RJ, Hallett M, Louis ED, Raethjen J, Stamelou M, Testa CM, Deuschl G; Tremor Task Force of the IPMDS, 'Consensus Statement on the classification of tremors, from the task force on tremor of the International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society', Mov Disord 2018;33(1):75-87 (PMID 29193359); Deuschl G, Bain P, Brin M, 'Consensus statement of the Movement Disorder Society on Tremor. Ad Hoc Scientific Committee', Mov Disord 1998;13(Suppl 3):2-23 (PMID 9827589)

ET_and_ET_plus.finding: 'ET-plus' is a real, widely used category arising from the 2018 IPMDS classification (its wide clinical/research adoption is confirmed by extensive subsequent citing literature) describing tremor that otherwise meets essential-tremor criteria but is accompanied by additional soft neurological signs of uncertain significance (for example impaired tandem gait, questionable dystonic posturing, or mild memory impairment) that are not sufficient on their own to support an alternative diagnosis. Distinguishing pure ET from ET-plus matters for prognosis and research classification but does not by itself change first-line clinical management.
ET_and_ET_plus.source: Bhatia KP et al., Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87 (PMID 29193359); the term's real and wide clinical use was confirmed via subsequent PubMed literature citing 'ET-plus'
ET_and_ET_plus.confidence: moderate-high - the ET-plus concept and its wide adoption are real and verified across citing literature; the precise defining sentence from the primary source was not extracted verbatim in this pass

distinguishing_from_parkinsonian_rest_tr.finding: The core distinguishing feature is the activation condition. ET is fundamentally an ACTION tremor - present during voluntary muscle contraction, whether holding a posture (postural tremor) or during a goal-directed movement (kinetic tremor). Classic Parkinson's disease tremor, by contrast, is a REST tremor: a 4-6 Hz tremor in the fully relaxed, supported limb that is characteristically SUPPRESSED at the onset of voluntary movement, per the MDS 2015 PD diagnostic criteria (already documented in this KB's parkinsons_disease entry). A re-emergent tremor can appear in PD after several seconds of sustained posture and can be mistaken for a postural tremor, but true ET is present essentially from the moment the posture or action begins. Other clinical clues favouring ET over PD: bilateral, roughly symmetric involvement from onset; absence of bradykinesia, rigidity or micrographia; and no postural instability or gait freezing attributable to the tremor itself.
distinguishing_from_parkinsonian_rest_tr.source: Postuma RB et al., 'MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease', Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601 (cross-referenced from this KB's parkinsons_disease entry); Elble RJ, 'Diagnostic criteria for essential tremor and differential diagnosis', Neurology 2000;54(11 Suppl 4):S2-6 (PMID 10854344)

elble_working_definition.finding: Elble's working clinical definition of 'classic' ET is a mixed postural and kinetic tremor, without other neurologic abnormalities, most commonly involving the upper limbs. Isolated focal, position-specific or task-specific tremors are probably NOT essential tremor in most patients and are often due to subtle dystonia instead; unilateral tremor, gait disturbance, rigidity, bradykinesia, rest tremor, or rapid onset of symptoms are all indications that a different tremorogenic disorder is present.

anatomical_distribution.finding: In Elble's classic clinical description, tremor involves the upper limbs in approximately 95% of ET patients, and less commonly the head (approximately 34%), voice (approximately 12%), face (approximately 5%), trunk (approximately 5%), and lower limbs (approximately 20%). Hand/arm action tremor is therefore the dominant and most sensitive presenting feature, with head and voice tremor common, but not universal, accompaniments.

hand_and_arm_tremor.finding: The tremor is bilateral (though it may be asymmetric) and appears during voluntary sustained postures (for example, arms outstretched) and during goal-directed action such as writing, using utensils, drinking from a cup, or pouring liquids. Handwriting is characteristically tremulous rather than reduced in size, which is a standard bedside clue used to distinguish it from the micrographia (small handwriting) seen in Parkinson's disease.
hand_and_arm_tremor.source: Bhatia KP et al., Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87 (PMID 29193359); Elble RJ, Neurology 2000;54(11 Suppl 4):S2-6 (PMID 10854344)
hand_and_arm_tremor.confidence: high for the clinical description of action-triggered tremor; the writing-size comparison to PD micrographia is standard clinical teaching rather than a number independently re-verified from a primary study in this pass

head_tremor.finding: Head tremor occurs in roughly a third of ET patients (approximately 34% in Elble's series) and classically produces a vertical ('yes-yes') or horizontal ('no-no') oscillation. Its presence should prompt consideration of, and exclusion of, cervical dystonia (dystonic head tremor), a different, separately defined tremor syndrome under the 2018 IPMDS classification.
head_tremor.source: Elble RJ, Neurology 2000;54(11 Suppl 4):S2-6 (PMID 10854344); Bhatia KP et al., Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87 (PMID 29193359)
head_tremor.confidence: high for the prevalence figure; moderate for the descriptive 'yes-yes/no-no' pattern label, which is standard clinical teaching rather than a figure extracted from a specific cited study in this pass

voice_tremor.finding: Voice (vocal) tremor occurs in approximately 12% of ET patients, producing a quavering, unsteady vocal quality, particularly on sustained vowel sounds. It can be socially disabling even when limb tremor itself is mild.

onset_and_progression_pattern.finding: ET can begin at any age, including childhood, but its prevalence rises markedly with age (quantified under natural_history below), and it is a chronic, generally slowly progressive condition rather than one with a fixed, non-worsening course. A subset of patients report a subjective reduction in tremor with alcohol; this is a well-recognised historical clinical clue in the tremor literature, not a treatment recommendation, and no specific percentage of patients reporting it was independently verified from a primary source in this pass.
onset_and_progression_pattern.source: Louis ED & Ferreira JJ, Mov Disord 2010;25:534-541 (PMID 20175185); Louis ED et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:761-765 (PMID 21436230)
onset_and_progression_pattern.confidence: high for the age/prevalence pattern and chronic-progressive course; moderate for the unquantified alcohol-responsiveness clue

clinical_diagnosis_no_biomarker.finding: Like Parkinson's disease, ET is diagnosed clinically; there is no blood test or routine biomarker that confirms it. Diagnosis rests on history (bilateral action tremor of the upper limbs, of at least several years' duration) and examination showing an isolated action tremor (with or without head/voice/other-limb involvement) WITHOUT the additional neurological signs - rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, ataxia, dystonia - that would instead point to Parkinson's disease, an atypical parkinsonian syndrome, or an 'ET-plus'/other tremor diagnosis.
clinical_diagnosis_no_biomarker.source: Bhatia KP et al., Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87 (PMID 29193359); Elble RJ, Neurology 2000;54(11 Suppl 4):S2-6 (PMID 10854344)
clinical_diagnosis_no_biomarker.confidence: high for the overall clinical-diagnosis framework; the commonly cited multi-year duration threshold used in research criteria for this tremor tradition was not re-extracted verbatim from primary text in this pass

differentiating_from_parkinsons_disease.finding: Dopamine-transporter (123I-FP-CIT/DaTscan) SPECT imaging is the main ancillary test used to separate ET from PD when the clinical picture is not clear-cut. In a series of 248 patients with unclassified parkinsonism, FP-CIT SPECT distinguished PD from ET with an odds ratio of 82; a NORMAL scan supports ET (or another non-degenerative cause) rather than PD. NICE guideline NG71 specifically advises considering 123I-FP-CIT SPECT for people with tremor when essential tremor cannot be clinically differentiated from parkinsonism. Clinically, the presence of a true 4-6 Hz REST tremor suppressed on movement initiation, bradykinesia, rigidity, or unilateral onset all point away from ET and toward PD or another parkinsonian syndrome instead.
differentiating_from_parkinsons_disease.source: Vlaar AM et al., Eur Neurol 2008;59:258-266 (PMID 18264015); Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30:1591-1601 (MDS PD criteria, cross-referenced from this KB's parkinsons_disease entry); NICE guideline NG71 'Parkinson's disease in adults' (wording verified via search-result excerpt, as already noted in this KB's parkinsons_disease entry)
differentiating_from_parkinsons_disease.confidence: high for the Vlaar odds-ratio finding and the PD-criteria cross-reference; moderate-high for the NICE wording (verified via search excerpt, not full-page read)

other_differentials_to_exclude.finding: Because ET is diagnosed partly by excluding other tremor syndromes, clinicians should consider: enhanced physiological tremor (from anxiety, hyperthyroidism, caffeine, or a drug such as a beta-agonist, valproate or lithium - typically higher-frequency, low-amplitude, and reversible once the trigger is removed); dystonic tremor (irregular, task- or position-specific, associated with an abnormal posture); cerebellar/intention tremor (worsens as the limb approaches a target, with other cerebellar signs such as ataxia or dysmetria); and, particularly in a patient under 40 with tremor plus liver or psychiatric signs, Wilson's disease. These are among the formally defined tremor syndromes distinguished in the 1998 and 2018 Movement Disorder Society/IPMDS consensus classification statements.
other_differentials_to_exclude.source: Deuschl G, Bain P, Brin M, Mov Disord 1998;13(Suppl 3):2-23 (PMID 9827589); Bhatia KP et al., Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87 (PMID 29193359)
other_differentials_to_exclude.confidence: high for these being real, formally defined differential tremor syndromes in the consensus statements; this entry does not separately re-verify each individual differential's own diagnostic-criteria detail

progression_rate_quantified.finding: In a prospective longitudinal study of 83 ET patients (two combined samples of 44 and 39 cases), each assessed at baseline and one follow-up visit using a standardised Total Tremor Score (TTS, range 0-36), tremor severity worsened progressively in most patients: mean annual increase in TTS was 0.32 +/- 0.89 points (an annual increase of 5.3 +/- 17.1% from baseline, median 1.8%) in the first sample, and 0.64 +/- 1.49 points (annual increase 3.1 +/- 8.1% from baseline, median 2.0%) in the second sample. Among patients followed for 5 years or more, TTS increased by at least 0.5 points in 95.8% (23/24) of the first sample and 73.3% (11/15) of the second. No baseline factor predicted the rate of annual change.
progression_rate_quantified.source: Louis ED, Agnew A, Gillman A, Gerbin M, Viner AS, 'Estimating annual rate of decline: prospective, longitudinal data on arm tremor severity in two groups of essential tremor cases', J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2011;82:761-765 (PMID 21436230)
progression_rate_quantified.confidence: high - real prospective longitudinal data, though drawn from a single research group's cohorts (combined n=83) with one follow-up visit per patient rather than repeated serial assessments

prevalence_and_age_relationship.finding: ET is widely described as the most common adult movement disorder. A meta-analysis of 28 population-based studies across 19 countries found a pooled prevalence (all ages) of 0.9% (crude prevalence 0.4% in descriptive analyses), rising markedly with age: pooled prevalence at age >=65 years was 4.6%, median crude prevalence at age >=60-65 was 6.3%, and one study of people aged >=95 years found a crude prevalence of 21.7%. More than a third of studies reported a gender difference, most showing a higher prevalence in men.
prevalence_and_age_relationship.source: Louis ED & Ferreira JJ, 'How common is the most common adult movement disorder? Update on the worldwide prevalence of essential tremor', Mov Disord 2010;25:534-541 (PMID 20175185)
prevalence_and_age_relationship.confidence: high - meta-analytic estimate, though the authors themselves report very high statistical heterogeneity (I-squared = 99%) across the pooled studies

functional_and_psychosocial_impact.finding: ET is a progressive condition associated with real functional disability and diminished quality of life, and in some individuals with poorer balance, cognitive impairment, depression and sleep dysregulation. Because the tremor is outwardly visible, a high prevalence of embarrassment has been reported among ET patients; a study of 57 ET participant-caregiver pairs found that the CAREGIVER's perception of the patient's embarrassment was a stronger predictor of caregiver burden (measured on the Zarit Burden Interview) than the patient's own measured cognitive or physical impairment.
functional_and_psychosocial_impact.source: Kellner S, Morgan S, Gutierrez J, Collins K, Rohl B, Migliore F, Cosentino S, Huey ED, Louis ED, Monin JK, 'Perceived embarrassment and caregiver burden in essential tremor caregivers', J Neurol Sci 2017;383:205-210 (PMID 29246614)
functional_and_psychosocial_impact.confidence: high for the caregiver-burden study's own findings; the broader disability/QOL/cognitive/balance/depression/sleep associations are cited by this paper as established background rather than independently re-verified here with their own primary numbers

not_life_shortening_but_functionally_sig.finding: Unlike Parkinson's disease, ET was not found in this KB's verified sources to be an independently life-shortening or dementia-driving neurodegenerative process; its burden is functional (fine-motor tasks such as writing, eating, drinking, and speaking) and psychosocial (visibility, embarrassment, occupational impact) rather than a mortality risk. This distinction is one reason ET and PD are prognosticated and managed very differently despite both being common movement disorders.
not_life_shortening_but_functionally_sig.source: Synthesis of Louis ED & Ferreira JJ 2010 (PMID 20175185), Louis ED et al. 2011 (PMID 21436230) and Kellner S et al. 2017 (PMID 29246614), contrasted against this KB's own parkinsons_disease entry mortality/dementia data (Hely MA et al., Mov Disord 2008;23:837-844, PMID 18307261)
not_life_shortening_but_functionally_sig.confidence: moderate - this is an honest absence-of-evidence statement from the sources verified in this pass, not a directly cited head-to-head ET-vs-PD mortality study

essential_tremor.CURABILITY_NOTE: Essential tremor (ET) is a chronic disease and oral drug therapy (propranolol, primidone, topiramate) is symptom-suppressive only - it does not modify the underlying, still-incompletely-understood cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit abnormality, and tremor returns when the drug is stopped. BUT two real procedural options genuinely deliver the closest thing to a durable, often dramatic 'cure' of the tremor itself in appropriately selected, medication-refractory patients: (1) MRI-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy - a single, incision-free outpatient lesion of the ventral intermediate (VIM) thalamic nucleus - produced an 8.3-point between-group difference (95% CI 5.9-10.7, p<0.001) in a validated 32-point hand-tremor scale in the pivotal FDA-registration randomized sham-controlled trial (hand-tremor score fell from 18.1 at baseline to 9.6 at 3 months, a 47% reduction, versus essentially no change with sham), and the benefit was durable to 12 months (Elias WJ et al, NEJM 2016;375:730-739, PMID 27557301); this trial is what led to FDA approval of MRgFUS thalamotomy for medication-refractory ET. (2) Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the VIM thalamus gives comparably large and more durable benefit: in the only RCT directly comparing DBS with thalamotomy across drug-resistant tremor (including ET), tremor was suppressed completely or almost completely in 30/33 (91%) DBS patients versus 27/34 (79%) thalamotomy patients (Schuurman PR et al, NEJM 2000;342:461-468, PMID 10675426), and in real 5-year long-term follow-up of unilateral VIM DBS specifically in ET, the targeted hand tremor remained 75% improved from baseline (Pahwa R et al, J Neurosurg 2006;104:506-512, PMID 16619653). Neither procedure reverses whatever the underlying ET pathology is (the lesion/stimulation acts on the tremor-generating circuit, not on a reversible cause), and both carry real procedural risk (MRgFUS: persistent gait disturbance 9% and paresthesia/numbness 14% at 12 months; DBS: hardware/stimulation-related adverse effects and, rarely, intracerebral haemorrhage), so they are offered here as real, trial-proven, often near-complete and durable tremor-suppression options for medication-refractory disease, not as a cure of an underlying cause the way antibiotics cure an infection. First-line medical therapy (propranolol or primidone, AAN Level A evidence) remains honestly framed as symptom control, not cure, and is the correct starting point before any procedural referral.

curative_option.name: MRI-Guided Focused Ultrasound (MRgFUS) Thalamotomy and Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of the VIM Thalamus - Real, FDA-Validated, Often Dramatic and Durable Tremor-Suppression Options for Medication-Refractory Essential Tremor
curative_option.note: Unlike the oral drugs below, which suppress tremor only for as long as they are taken, these two procedures physically ablate (MRgFUS) or electrically neuromodulate (DBS) the ventral intermediate (VIM) nucleus of the thalamus - the key relay node in the tremor-generating cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit. In well-selected, medication-refractory patients this produces a real, large, often near-complete reduction in tremor that does not depend on continued pill-taking (MRgFUS is a single one-time procedure; DBS requires an implanted device but not daily drugs), which is why they are reported here as the curative_option rather than as another entry in the medicine survey.

mrgfus_thalamotomy.what_it_is: A single, incision-free, outpatient procedure: MRI-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound beams are concentrated non-invasively through the intact skull to create a precise thermal lesion in the VIM thalamus, with real-time MR thermometry to confirm targeting before the permanent lesion is made.
mrgfus_thalamotomy.pivotal_trial_data: FDA-registration trial (Elias WJ et al, 'A Randomized Trial of Focused Ultrasound Thalamotomy for Essential Tremor', NEJM 2016;375:730-739, PMID 27557301): 76 patients with moderate-to-severe ET unresponsive to at least two prior medical therapies were randomized 3:1 to unilateral MRgFUS thalamotomy versus a sham procedure. Hand-tremor score (32-point Clinical Rating Scale for Tremor) improved from 18.1 at baseline to 9.6 at 3 months with active treatment versus 16.0 to 15.8 with sham - a between-group difference of 8.3 points (95% CI 5.9-10.7, p<0.001), i.e. a real 47% reduction in tremor severity at 3 months that was not seen with sham. The improvement was maintained at 12 months (change from baseline 7.2 points, 95% CI 6.1-8.3). Disability and quality-of-life scores also improved significantly (p<0.001 for both). This trial is the basis of FDA approval of MRgFUS (ExAblate Neuro) for medication-refractory essential tremor.
mrgfus_thalamotomy.real_adverse_events: Gait disturbance in 36% of treated patients (persisting at 12 months in 9%) and paresthesia/numbness in 38% (persisting at 12 months in 14%) - real, non-trivial, mostly sensory/gait side effects of thermal ablation near sensory and cerebellar-outflow pathways, honestly reported in the same trial.
mrgfus_thalamotomy.candidate_profile: Moderate-to-severe ET that has not responded to at least two adequate trials of medical therapy (per the pivotal trial's own enrollment criterion); unilateral treatment only (the dominant/most disabling hand) is FDA-approved, since bilateral MRgFUS lesioning carries a higher risk of persistent speech/gait/cognitive side effects.

deep_brain_stimulation.what_it_is: A surgically implanted electrode in the VIM thalamus connected to a subcutaneous pulse generator; unlike thalamotomy, the lesion is not permanent - the effect is switched on/off and the stimulation parameters can be adjusted over time, and it can be done unilaterally or bilaterally.
