huntingtons_disease.name: Huntington's Disease
huntingtons_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Huntington's disease (HD) has NO cure and NO proven disease-modifying therapy as of 2026 - this must be stated plainly. Every treatment in this entry is purely symptomatic (tetrabenazine/deutetrabenazine for chorea, antipsychotics/mood stabilisers for psychiatric and behavioural symptoms, antidepressants/SSRIs for depression and anxiety, and multidisciplinary physical/occupational/speech-and-swallow therapy for motor and bulbar decline); none of them slow, stop or reverse the underlying CAG-repeat-expansion-driven mutant huntingtin toxicity and neurodegeneration described in this knowledge base's symptoms entry for HD. The most advanced disease-modifying strategy tested to date - lowering mutant huntingtin (HTT) - has produced real, honest NEGATIVE and mixed results, not a cure: (1) Tominersen (IONIS-HTTRx/RG6042), an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) given intrathecally, safely and dose-dependently lowered CSF mutant huntingtin in a Phase 1/2a trial (Tabrizi SJ et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:2307-2316, PMID 31059641). It then went into the Phase 3 GENERATION-HD1 trial; the independent data monitoring committee recommended halting dosing in the trial's higher-dose regimen, and the published trial report (McColgan P et al, for the GENERATION HD1 Investigators, N Engl J Med 2023;389:2203-2205, PMID 38055260) is a genuine negative Phase 3 result - tominersen did not demonstrate a clinical benefit over placebo in adults with manifest HD. A follow-on trial, GENERATION HD2, is now testing lower, less-frequent dosing restricted to younger/earlier-stage patients to see whether a narrower therapeutic window exists (Huntington's Disease Clinical Trials Corner, J Huntingtons Dis 2023, PMID 37483021) - this is real ongoing research, not a proven therapy. (2) Branaplam, an oral small-molecule HTT-mRNA splicing modulator, was tested in the Phase 2b VIBRANT-HD trial: it did lower CSF mutant HTT versus placebo (the first oral splicing modulator to do so in humans), but 18 of 21 participants (85.7%) on the 56 mg weekly dose developed signs or symptoms of peripheral neuropathy, and the trial was terminated early on safety grounds (Nature Medicine 2026, PMID 41491108, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05111249) - another real, honest negative-on-safety result for a huntingtin-lowering approach. (3) AAV5-delivered RNA-interference gene therapy (AMT-130, a one-time intrastriatal infusion encoding a microRNA against HTT) remains in early-phase human trials; it is referenced as an emerging, unproven investigational therapy in a 2026 health-economic modelling study (PharmacoEconomics Open 2026, PMID 42665725) alongside tominersen, and no controlled efficacy data have been published for it in this knowledge base's search. The honest state of the science: huntingtin-lowering approaches can measurably hit their target (CSF mutant HTT goes down) without yet producing a proven clinical benefit, and one major modality (branaplam) has caused real, dose-limiting neurotoxicity. This is genuine evidence that 'lowering the mutant protein' is not automatically therapeutic, not evidence that the approach is permanently dead - GENERATION HD2 and other trials are actively probing dose, timing and patient selection. But as of today (2026), NO disease-modifying therapy for HD is proven or approved by any regulator, and every approved medicine for HD (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, and off-label psychiatric medicines) only manages symptoms. Patients and families must be told honestly that current treatment goals are symptom control, safety and quality of life, not cure or reversal of the disease.

curative_option.name: No curative or disease-modifying option is currently proven - huntingtin-lowering therapies are the most advanced investigational approach and have so far produced negative or safety-limited Phase 2/3 results
curative_option.note: HD cannot currently be cured, slowed or reversed by any approved treatment. The rational curative strategy - lowering production of the mutant huntingtin protein that the symptoms entry identifies as the toxic driver of neurodegeneration - has been tested in humans with real, honest results that fall short of a working cure so far (see CURABILITY_NOTE for the full account and citations): tominersen (ASO) failed its Phase 3 primary endpoint in GENERATION-HD1 despite proven target engagement, and branaplam (oral splicing modulator) lowered mutant HTT in the VIBRANT-HD Phase 2b trial but was stopped early after 85.7% of participants on active dosing developed peripheral neuropathy. AAV5 RNAi gene therapy (AMT-130) and a lower-dose tominersen re-trial (GENERATION HD2) remain in progress with no published proof of efficacy yet.

real_trial_data.tominersen_phase1_2a_target_engagement: Dose-dependent, statistically significant reduction in CSF mutant huntingtin protein in HD gene-expansion carriers - Tabrizi SJ et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:2307-2316 (PMID 31059641)
real_trial_data.tominersen_phase3_generation_hd1_outcome: Independent data monitoring committee recommended halting the higher-dose regimen; published trial report found no clinical benefit over placebo in adults with manifest HD - McColgan P et al, N Engl J Med 2023;389:2203-2205, for the GENERATION HD1 Investigators (PMID 38055260)
real_trial_data.tominersen_followup_generation_hd2: Ongoing trial of lower, less frequent dosing restricted to younger/earlier-stage patients - real, active research, no efficacy result yet (J Huntingtons Dis 2023, PMID 37483021)
real_trial_data.branaplam_vibrant_hd_phase2b: CSF mutant HTT lowered versus placebo (first oral splicing modulator to do so in HD), but 18/21 (85.7%) participants on 56 mg weekly developed peripheral neuropathy signs/symptoms; trial terminated early on safety grounds; NfL elevations reversed after stopping drug - Nature Medicine 2026 (PMID 41491108), NCT05111249
real_trial_data.amt130_gene_therapy_status: AAV5 intrastriatal RNAi gene therapy for HTT lowering; referenced as an emerging investigational therapy with trial-stage (not proven) status in a 2026 cost-effectiveness model alongside tominersen (PharmacoEconomics Open 2026, PMID 42665725); no published controlled efficacy data identified in this survey

curative_option.source: Tabrizi SJ et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:2307-2316 (PMID 31059641); McColgan P et al, N Engl J Med 2023;389:2203-2205 (PMID 38055260); J Huntingtons Dis 2023 Clinical Trials Corner (PMID 37483021); Nature Medicine 2026 VIBRANT-HD (PMID 41491108); PharmacoEconomics Open 2026 (PMID 42665725)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for Huntington's disease: the two FDA-approved antichorea drugs, guideline-graded add-on/alternative antichorea options, psychiatric/behavioural symptom management, and multidisciplinary supportive care. It does NOT include a proven cure or disease-modifying therapy because none exists (see CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option). Diagnostic/genetic-testing content is covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and not duplicated here.

hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.name: Tetrabenazine - First VMAT2 Inhibitor Approved for Huntington Chorea
specific_drugs: Tetrabenazine (Xenazine and generics, titrated up to 100 mg/day in divided doses)
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.effectiveness: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Huntington Study Group, n=84): tetrabenazine reduced UHDRS chorea score by 5.0 units versus 1.5 units with placebo (adjusted mean treatment effect -3.5 +/- 0.8 UHDRS units, 95% CI -5.2 to -1.9, p<0.0001), with significant benefit also on clinical global impression.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.reason_why: HD chorea results from relative dopaminergic overactivity in the striatum as early degeneration preferentially affects indirect-pathway striatal medium spiny neurons; tetrabenazine reversibly depletes presynaptic monoamines (dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine) by inhibiting VMAT2, reducing striatal dopaminergic transmission and thereby chorea.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.important_caveat: Tetrabenazine carries a boxed warning for depression and suicidality and can cause parkinsonism, sedation and akathisia; AAN guideline (Level B) recommends discussing/monitoring for these adverse events. Five serious adverse events (including a suicide by drowning) occurred in the tetrabenazine arm of the pivotal trial versus none on placebo.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Titrate slowly upward toward the individually tolerated dose (up to 100 mg/day) rather than a fixed target dose, with active screening for depression/suicidality at each visit; use in ambulatory patients with functionally impairing chorea per AAN Level B recommendation.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.source: Huntington Study Group, 'Tetrabenazine as antichorea therapy in Huntington disease: a randomized controlled trial', Neurology 2006;66:366-372 (PMID 16476934); Armstrong MJ, Miyasaki JM, 'Evidence-based guideline: pharmacologic treatment of chorea in Huntington disease', Neurology 2012;79:597-603 (PMID 22815556)

hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.name: Deutetrabenazine - Deuterated VMAT2 Inhibitor with More Stable Exposure
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.type: Deuterated vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2) inhibitor
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.effectiveness: Phase 3 FIRST-HD trial (n=90, 12-week double-blind RCT): total maximal chorea score improved from 12.1 to 7.7 with deutetrabenazine versus 13.2 to 11.3 with placebo (between-group difference -2.5 units, 95% CI -3.7 to -1.3, p<0.001). Treatment success on Patient Global Impression of Change occurred in 51% (23/45) on deutetrabenazine versus 20% (9/45) on placebo (p=0.002); on Clinical Global Impression of Change, 42% (19/45) versus 13% (6/45) (p=0.002). Long-term open-label rollover data from the ARC-HD trial showed maintained chorea control through 54 weeks.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.reason_why: Same VMAT2-inhibition mechanism as tetrabenazine, but deuterium substitution at metabolically labile sites slows CYP2D6-mediated metabolism, producing more stable active-metabolite plasma levels at a lower, less frequent dose, which the pivotal trial and reviews associate with a more favourable tolerability profile than tetrabenazine at equivalent efficacy.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.important_caveat: Adverse event rates were similar to placebo overall in FIRST-HD, and individual neuropsychiatric adverse events occurred in under 7% of recipients (apart from somnolence) with no significant difference from placebo in FIRST-HD - a real, more favourable safety signal than tetrabenazine's pivotal trial, though deutetrabenazine has not been tested head-to-head against tetrabenazine in a randomized trial.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Preferred first-line VMAT2 inhibitor for chorea given the more stable pharmacokinetics and side-effect profile reported in FIRST-HD/ARC-HD; start low and titrate over 8 weeks to the lowest effective, best-tolerated dose.
hd_chorea_first_line_vmat2_inhibitors.source: Frank S et al, 'Effect of Deutetrabenazine on Chorea Among Patients With Huntington Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial', JAMA 2016;316:40-50 (PMID 27380342); Deeks ED, 'Deutetrabenazine: A Review in Chorea Associated with Huntington's Disease', Drugs 2017;77:1857-1864 (PMID 29080203)

hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.name: AAN 2012 Evidence-Based Guideline - Other Pharmacologic Chorea Options
hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.effectiveness: AAN guideline (structured evidence review through Feb 2011): clinicians should prescribe tetrabenazine, amantadine (300-400 mg/day), or riluzole (200 mg/day) for varying degrees of expected chorea benefit (Level B). Nabilone may be prescribed for modest (1- to <2-point UHDRS chorea) decreases (Level C), but long-term use is not supported by sufficient evidence given abuse-potential concerns (Level U). Riluzole 100 mg/day is specifically NOT recommended (Level B, no short- or long-term benefit at that dose).
hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.reason_why: Amantadine and riluzole act on separate mechanisms (NMDA-receptor/dopaminergic modulation and glutamatergic/sodium-channel effects respectively) that can modestly reduce chorea in patients who cannot tolerate VMAT2 inhibitors; nabilone's cannabinoid activity has shown modest antichoreic effect in a small trial.
hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.important_caveat: The guideline explicitly states ethyl-EPA, minocycline and creatine should NOT be prescribed for meaningful chorea improvement (Level B/C negative evidence), coenzyme Q10 should not be prescribed for moderate chorea improvement (Level B negative), and data are insufficient (Level U) to recommend neuroleptics or donepezil specifically for chorea.
hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.real_working_solution: Reserve amantadine or riluzole for patients who cannot tolerate or access VMAT2 inhibitors; do not use riluzole 100 mg/day, ethyl-EPA, minocycline, creatine or coenzyme Q10 for chorea - the evidence base shows these do not work at the doses tested.
hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.source: Armstrong MJ, Miyasaki JM, American Academy of Neurology, 'Evidence-based guideline: pharmacologic treatment of chorea in Huntington disease', Neurology 2012;79:597-603 (PMID 22815556)
hd_chorea_guideline_graded_alternatives.confidence: high for the graded recommendations as an official AAN practice guideline

hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.name: Antipsychotics for Agitation, Aggression and Psychosis in HD
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.type: Atypical (and occasionally typical) antipsychotics, used off-label
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.effectiveness: No HD-specific placebo-controlled antipsychotic RCT of adequate size exists; the international expert-based consensus guideline (11-member multidisciplinary committee, validated by 84 international HD experts, 107/110 statements reaching >=85% agreement) recommends specific antipsychotic choices and dosing strategies for agitation, psychosis and severe irritability/aggression in HD, extrapolated from general psychiatric evidence and clinical experience because dedicated HD trials are lacking.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.reason_why: Psychosis, aggression and severe agitation in HD are thought to reflect frontostriatal circuit dysfunction and comorbid mood/behavioural pathology superimposed on the same neurodegeneration that causes chorea; atypical antipsychotics that also have some antichoreic (D2-blocking) effect are preferred so a single agent can address both domains where appropriate.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.important_caveat: This is an honest evidence gap: recommendations here are expert consensus, NOT proven by an HD-specific randomized trial (AAN 2012 rates neuroleptic use for chorea itself as Level U, insufficient data). Antipsychotics carry real metabolic, sedative, QT-prolongation and (for typicals) extrapyramidal/tardive risks that require monitoring, and can worsen bradykinesia/rigidity in later-stage HD.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.real_working_solution: Use the lowest effective dose of an atypical antipsychotic for agitation/psychosis/aggression that has failed non-pharmacological management, per the expert consensus statements, with regular metabolic and movement-disorder monitoring; avoid unnecessary polypharmacy across overlapping symptoms.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.source: Anderson KE et al, 'Clinical Management of Neuropsychiatric Symptoms of Huntington Disease: Expert-Based Consensus Guidelines on Agitation, Anxiety, Apathy, Psychosis and Sleep Disorders', J Huntingtons Dis 2018;7:355-366 (PMID 30040737); Armstrong MJ, Miyasaki JM, Neurology 2012;79:597-603 (PMID 22815556)
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.confidence: moderate - guideline is expert-consensus rather than HD-specific RCT-based for this symptom domain, stated honestly

hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.name: Antidepressants/SSRIs for Depression and Anxiety in HD
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.type: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and related antidepressants, used off-label
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.effectiveness: Depression, anxiety and irritability are among the most prevalent neuropsychiatric features of HD, reported in roughly 33-76% of gene-positive carriers across standardized-instrument studies (van Duijn E et al review), yet no adequately powered HD-specific placebo-controlled SSRI efficacy trial exists in this survey's search; SSRIs are recommended by the international expert-based consensus guideline as first-line pharmacotherapy for HD depression/anxiety on the strength of general-population depression evidence and clinical experience.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.reason_why: HD depression is understood to arise from a combination of the same frontostriatal/limbic neurodegeneration that produces other HD symptoms plus the psychological burden of a progressive, heritable, currently incurable disease; SSRIs are used by analogy with their proven efficacy in idiopathic depression/anxiety since HD does not appear to make serotonergic circuits categorically unresponsive.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.important_caveat: This is a genuine evidence gap, stated honestly: efficacy in HD is extrapolated, not HD-trial-proven. Suicide risk is elevated in HD (both gene-positive carriers and at-risk relatives) at multiple disease stages, so depression must be actively screened for and treated rather than assumed to be an inevitable, untreatable part of HD.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.real_working_solution: Screen for depression/anxiety/suicidality at every HD clinic visit and treat pharmacologically with an SSRI (or mirtazapine where insomnia/weight loss predominate) using standard psychiatric dosing and monitoring, per expert consensus; combine with psychotherapy and caregiver/family support where available.
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.source: Anderson KE et al, J Huntingtons Dis 2018;7:355-366 (PMID 30040737); van Duijn E et al, 'Psychopathology in verified Huntington's disease gene carriers', J Neuropsychiatry Clin Neurosci 2007;19:441-448 (PMID 18070848)
hd_psychiatric_and_behavioural_symptom_m.confidence: moderate - prevalence data are well-sourced; SSRI efficacy specifically in HD is an honest evidence gap, extrapolated from general psychiatry

hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.name: Physical Therapy - Aerobic Exercise, Resistance Training and Supervised Gait Training
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.effectiveness: Mixed-methods systematic review (Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, 23 quantitative + 3 qualitative studies) with resulting formal clinical practice recommendations: aerobic exercise, alone or combined with resistance training, to improve fitness and motor function (Grade A evidence), and supervised gait training to improve spatiotemporal gait features (Grade A evidence); weaker (Grade B) evidence that exercise training improves balance without proven reduction in fall frequency.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.reason_why: HD progressively impairs motor control, gait, balance and cardiorespiratory fitness through combined chorea, bradykinesia, dystonia and cognitive decline; task-specific and aerobic exercise interventions target neuromuscular and cardiovascular deconditioning that compounds the primary neurodegenerative motor deficit, and are among the few HD interventions with Grade A trial-level evidence of any kind in this disease.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.important_caveat: Evidence does not show that exercise slows the underlying neurodegeneration or disease progression - the graded benefits are for fitness, motor function and gait, not disease modification; fall-frequency reduction was NOT demonstrated despite balance improvements.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.real_working_solution: Refer every ambulatory HD patient to a physical therapist experienced with HD for an individualized aerobic-plus-resistance exercise programme and supervised gait training, reassessed as the disease stage changes.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.source: Quinn L et al, 'Clinical recommendations to guide physical therapy practice for Huntington disease', Neurology 2020;94:217-228 (PMID 31907286)
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.confidence: high - formal graded clinical practice guideline derived from a systematic review

hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.name: Speech, Language and Swallowing (Dysphagia) Management
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.effectiveness: No large HD-specific randomized trial of speech/swallow therapy was identified in this survey; dysphagia, dysarthria and orofacial choreiform movements are well documented to worsen with HD disease severity in systematic reviews of oral/bulbar manifestations, and multidisciplinary HD standards of care (as reflected in the physical therapy and neuropsychiatric guidelines cited in this entry) recommend proactive speech-language pathology and dietitian involvement to manage dysarthria, reduce aspiration risk and maintain nutrition/hydration as bulbar symptoms progress.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.reason_why: Late lower-brainstem and corticobulbar involvement in HD produces progressive dysarthria and dysphagia; aspiration pneumonia secondary to swallowing dysfunction is a leading real cause of death in advanced HD, making proactive swallow assessment and dietary/textural modification a genuine, if non-curative, life-prolonging supportive measure.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.important_caveat: This is supportive/palliative management, not a treatment that slows bulbar decline; the evidence base for specific swallow-therapy techniques in HD (as opposed to general dysphagia rehabilitation extrapolated to HD) is thin, and this survey did not find an HD-specific controlled efficacy trial.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.real_working_solution: Schedule proactive, staged speech-language pathology and dietitian assessment as HD progresses (not only after a choking event), with texture-modified diets, positioning strategies and, when appropriate, discussion of feeding-tube options as part of advance care planning.
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.source: Zaidi PH et al, 'The oral manifestations of Huntington's disease: A systematic review of prevalence', Oral Dis 2023;29:1341-1352 (PMID 34773332); Quinn L et al, Neurology 2020;94:217-228 (PMID 31907286)
hd_multidisciplinary_supportive_care.confidence: moderate - prevalence/complication data are well-sourced; a dedicated HD swallow-therapy efficacy RCT was not found

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real metrics come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (UHDRS/total maximal chorea score change, PGIC/CGIC responder rate, Grade A/B physical-therapy evidence ratings, and CSF biomarker target engagement) in different populations, so the ordering is directional judgement (size and quality of evidence for a real, guideline- or trial-documented benefit), NOT a common-scale percentage ranking. effectiveness_pct appears only where a genuine percent exists for a real outcome (PGIC/CGIC treatment-success responder rates for deutetrabenazine). IMPORTANT: NO treatment in this table cures HD, slows its progression, or reverses neurodegeneration - every row is symptomatic management. Rows 6-7 record a real, honest NEGATIVE or safety-limited outcome for the most advanced disease-modifying candidates (tominersen's Phase 3 failure and branaplam's neuropathy-driven trial termination), included here as evidence, not as effective treatments. See CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option for the full disease-modification picture.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Patient Global Impression of Change treatment success in 51% (23/45) vs 20% (9/45) on placebo at 12 weeks (FIRST-HD, P=0.002); total maximal chorea score improved from 12.1 to 7.7 vs 13.2 to 11.3 on placebo (between-group difference -2.5 units, P<0.001)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Frank S et al, JAMA 2016;316:40-50 (PMID 27380342)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tetrabenazine (Xenazine) - chorea in manifest HD
ranked_high_to_low.metric: UHDRS chorea score reduced by 5.0 units vs 1.5 units with placebo over 12 weeks (adjusted treatment effect -3.5 +/- 0.8 units, 95% CI -5.2 to -1.9, P<0.0001); first HD-specific antichoreic drug proven in an RCT, but with a higher serious-adverse-event rate (including one suicide) than deutetrabenazine's pivotal trial
ranked_high_to_low.source: Huntington Study Group, Neurology 2006;66:366-372 (PMID 16476934); AAN guideline, Neurology 2012;79:597-603 (PMID 22815556)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Physical therapy (aerobic + resistance exercise, supervised gait training)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Grade A evidence (highest guideline grade used in this recommendation set) for improving fitness/motor function (aerobic +/- resistance training) and spatiotemporal gait features (supervised gait training); Grade B evidence for balance improvement without proven fall-frequency reduction
ranked_high_to_low.source: Quinn L et al, Neurology 2020;94:217-228 (PMID 31907286)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Amantadine or riluzole (200 mg/day) - alternative/adjunct chorea options
ranked_high_to_low.metric: AAN Level B recommendation for chorea benefit as tetrabenazine alternatives; riluzole specifically at 100 mg/day is NOT recommended (Level B negative) and no long-term (3-year) antichoreic benefit was shown at any studied dose
ranked_high_to_low.source: Armstrong MJ, Miyasaki JM, Neurology 2012;79:597-603 (PMID 22815556)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole) and SSRIs - agitation, psychosis, depression, anxiety
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 107 of 110 expert-consensus statements reached >=85% agreement among 84 international HD experts for managing agitation, anxiety, apathy, psychosis and sleep disorders; no HD-specific placebo-controlled RCT quantifies a percent benefit for either drug class in HD specifically - efficacy is extrapolated from general psychiatric evidence, stated honestly as a gap
ranked_high_to_low.source: Anderson KE et al, J Huntingtons Dis 2018;7:355-366 (PMID 30040737)

huntingtons_disease.icd11_hint: 8A01.10 Huntington disease (parent 8A01 Diseases of basal ganglia); ICD-10-CM G10 Huntington's disease
huntingtons_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, recurring emergencies in Huntington's disease (HD) MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department / crisis line NOW, do not wait for a routine appointment): (1) SUICIDE RISK / SEVERE PSYCHIATRIC CRISIS. Suicidal ideation in HD is not evenly spread across the illness; it clusters at two identifiable, real, data-defined critical periods. In the Huntington Study Group cohort of 4,171 individuals, frequency of suicidal ideation doubled from 9.1% in at-risk persons with a normal neurological exam to 19.8% in those with soft neurological signs and 23.5% in those with 'possible HD' (the pre-diagnosis window), and among diagnosed patients was 16.7% in stage 1 and 21.6% in stage 2 (the point where independence starts to be lost), before declining in later stages (Paulsen JS et al, 'Critical periods of suicide risk in Huntington's disease', Am J Psychiatry 2005;162:725-731, PMID 15800145). Roos RA's clinical review states that after pneumonia, suicide is the second most common cause of death in HD (Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Depression is one of the most common psychiatric disturbances in HD, present even in the pre-motor prodrome and highest in prevalence in stage 2, and its identification and active treatment is essential given this suicide risk (Epping EA & Paulsen JS, Neurodegener Dis Manag 2011;1:407-414, PMID 22942903). ANY expressed suicidal ideation, a HD gene-carrier who has just received or is about to receive a confirmatory genetic result, a patient entering stage 2 (loss of independence), or any acute psychotic break in a known HD patient must be treated as an emergency needing same-day psychiatric assessment, not queued for routine doctor review. (2) SEVERE DYSPHAGIA / ASPIRATION RISK. Pneumonia (from aspiration due to progressive bulbar/swallowing dysfunction) is the single most common cause of death in HD, ahead of suicide (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Any HD patient who develops choking on food/liquids, a new wet/gurgly voice after swallowing, recurrent coughing fits with meals, unexplained fever with chest signs, or overt aspiration must be treated as an emergency requiring same-day swallow assessment and, if acute respiratory compromise or aspiration pneumonia is suspected, emergency department referral, not a routine follow-up.

huntingtin_gene_and_cag_repeat_expansion.finding: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded, unstable CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene (originally named IT15) on the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p16.3), encoding an abnormally long polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein. The causative gene was identified by linkage/haplotype analysis of 75 HD families across multiple ethnic backgrounds, all of which showed a CAG repeat longer than the normal range on HD chromosomes (The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 'A novel gene containing a trinucleotide repeat that is expanded and unstable on Huntington's disease chromosomes', Cell 1993;72:971-983, PMID 8458085). By long-standing clinical genetics convention (GeneReviews: Huntington Disease, Caron NS, Wright GEB, Hayden MR, NCBI Bookshelf/GeneReviews, PMID 20301482, continuously updated), CAG repeat length is classified as: normal (26 or fewer repeats, stable on transmission), intermediate/mutable normal (27-35 repeats; not itself disease-causing but unstable and can expand further, especially on paternal transmission), reduced penetrance (36-39 repeats; may or may not develop HD, often later and/or milder), and full penetrance (40 or more repeats; HD will develop if the person lives long enough). HD is transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern with genetic anticipation: the repeat is unstable and tends to expand further on transmission, more so through the paternal line, which is why juvenile-onset cases disproportionately inherit the expansion from an affected father.
huntingtin_gene_and_cag_repeat_expansion.source: The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, Cell 1993;72:971-983 (PMID 8458085); GeneReviews: Huntington Disease (Caron NS, Wright GEB, Hayden MR), PMID 20301482; Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977, states the pathogenic threshold as '36 repeats or more')

juvenile_versus_adult_onset_huntington_d.finding: Adult-onset HD is the typical form: mean age at onset of motor symptoms is 30-50 years, and the classic presentation is gradually spreading chorea with behavioural/psychiatric disturbance and cognitive decline (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Juvenile Huntington's disease (JHD), defined as onset at 20 years of age or younger, is rare (in a multicentre REGISTRY/Enroll-HD retrospective analysis of 580 patients, only 36 met criteria for JHD versus 197 for adult-onset HD) and behaves as a more aggressive, biologically distinct entity, usually driven by highly expanded CAG repeats (often exceeding 55) most often inherited from an affected father. Compared with the adult-onset form, JHD more often presents with developmental delay, behavioural and school-learning difficulties, and in the highly-expanded subgroup, gait disturbance, severe gait impairment and seizures as prominent early/longitudinal features (present in 80-90% of the highly-expanded subgroup versus far fewer in the low-expansion subgroup); loss of hand dexterity was instead more typical of the low-expansion JHD subgroup. Disease progression (rate of worsening on the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale-Total Motor Score) was significantly faster in JHD than adult-onset HD, and median survival was shorter in JHD (hazard ratio for death 2.18, 95% CI 1.08-4.40) (Fusilli C et al, 'Biological and clinical manifestations of juvenile Huntington's disease: a retrospective analysis', Lancet Neurol 2018;17:986-993, PMID 30243861).
juvenile_versus_adult_onset_huntington_d.source: Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977); Fusilli C et al, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:986-993 (PMID 30243861)

chorea.finding: The classic motor sign of HD is chorea: involuntary, brief, irregular, unpredictable dance-like movements that typically begin distally/subtly and gradually spread to involve all muscle groups as the disease advances. As disease progresses further, 'all psychomotor processes become severely retarded' (bradykinesia dominates over chorea in later stages) (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ's review frames HD as a model neurodegenerative disorder in which neurodegeneration and subtle motor, cognitive and psychiatric change begin many years before a formal diagnosable motor onset (the prodromal phase), detectable by predictive genetic testing and neuroimaging before chorea becomes clinically obvious (Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, 'Huntington's disease: from molecular pathogenesis to clinical treatment', Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98, PMID 21163446).
chorea.source: Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977); Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98 (PMID 21163446)

cognitive_decline.finding: HD causes a progressive subcortical dementia. Cognitive and psychiatric symptoms are not late add-ons but 'prominently factor into its clinical presentation' from the earliest, even pre-motor (prodromal), stages, alongside subtle motor change, well before a formal diagnosable onset of chorea (Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98, PMID 21163446). As the disease advances, patients experience severe cognitive decline that, together with chorea and psychomotor retardation, progresses to complete dependency in daily life and the need for full-time care (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977).
cognitive_decline.source: Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98 (PMID 21163446); Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977)

psychiatric_symptoms_depression_irritabi.finding: Behavioural and psychiatric disturbances are a core, not incidental, part of HD. Depression is one of the most common psychiatric disturbances in HD: it is present even during the pre-manifest illness prodrome (before motor symptoms appear) and its prevalence is highest in manifest disease during stage 2; identifying and treating it is an essential part of clinical management specifically because of the elevated suicide risk it carries (Epping EA & Paulsen JS, Neurodegener Dis Manag 2011;1:407-414, PMID 22942903). Roos RA's clinical review lists 'behavioral and psychiatric disturbances' alongside chorea and dementia as the disease's defining triad, and notes that medication and non-medical care are frequently required specifically for depression and aggressive/irritable behaviour (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ likewise describe 'subtle cognitive, motor, and psychiatric changes' as part of the measurable prodromal disease that precedes formal diagnosis (Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98, PMID 21163446). Psychotic features (irritable/aggressive behaviour progressing to overt psychosis in some patients) are part of this same behavioural-disturbance spectrum and, per the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above, an acute psychotic break in a known HD patient is a same-day psychiatric emergency, not a routine finding.
psychiatric_symptoms_depression_irritabi.source: Epping EA & Paulsen JS, Neurodegener Dis Manag 2011;1:407-414 (PMID 22942903); Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977); Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98 (PMID 21163446)

progression_to_rigidity_in_late_and_juve.finding: Although chorea is the classic sign at presentation in adult-onset HD, the movement disorder evolves over time: as disease advances, hyperkinetic chorea is progressively replaced by bradykinesia and rigidity, with 'all psychomotor processes' becoming severely retarded in late-stage adult disease (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). This rigid, akinetic pattern (historically called the Westphal variant when it dominates from an early stage) is far more characteristic of juvenile HD from the outset than of adult-onset disease: in the highly-CAG-expanded juvenile subgroup, severe gait impairment was present in 90% of patients longitudinally (versus 35% of the low-expansion juvenile subgroup), gait disturbance (rather than chorea) was the first presenting symptom in 80% of the highly-expanded subgroup, and seizures (essentially absent in adult-onset HD) occurred in 80% of the highly-expanded juvenile subgroup versus 11% of the low-expansion subgroup, reflecting a genuinely more rigid, rapidly progressive phenotype rather than a chorea-dominant one (Fusilli C et al, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:986-993, PMID 30243861).
progression_to_rigidity_in_late_and_juve.source: Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977); Fusilli C et al, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:986-993 (PMID 30243861)

genetic_testing.framework: Diagnosis in a symptomatic patient is based on clinical signs (chorea, cognitive/psychiatric change) in someone with a parent with proven HD, confirmed by direct DNA testing for the expanded HTT CAG repeat (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Separately, PREDICTIVE (pre-manifest) genetic testing of a healthy at-risk adult who wants to know their carrier status is a distinct, higher-stakes process. Formal testing guidelines were developed jointly by the Huntington's Disease Society of America and the International Huntington Association in collaboration with the World Federation of Neurology, initially using linkage testing (from 1983) and, after the 1993 gene discovery, direct mutation testing. These guidelines require the testing process to include a neurologic examination, pretest counselling, psychiatric/psychological assessment, delivery of results in person, and available follow-up support; outcome studies following this protocol show testing can be done safely, and that pre-existing anxiety and depression predict post-test psychological status better than the test result itself. The guidelines separately address complicated situations: testing of minors, anonymous testing, and testing of individuals at only 25% prior risk (i.e., an intervening parent has not been tested) (Quaid KA, 'Genetic testing for Huntington disease', Handb Clin Neurol 2017;144:113-126, PMID 28947110). Roos RA's review adds that pre-manifest (predictive) diagnosis should be performed only by multidisciplinary teams, and that prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis) and preimplantation genetic diagnosis with IVF are available in several countries (PMID 21171977).
genetic_testing.source: Quaid KA, Handb Clin Neurol 2017;144:113-126 (PMID 28947110); Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977)

cag_repeat_length_correlation_with_predi.finding: CAG repeat length is inversely correlated with age of neurological onset: the longer the repeat, the earlier the onset, but with real, quantifiable variability that is not explained by CAG length alone. Using the largest cohort analysed to date at the time (2,913 individuals from 40 centres worldwide), a parametric survival model was built giving probabilistic onset predictions for CAG repeats between 36 and 56; as a worked example, the model predicts a 91% chance (95% CI 90-93%) that a 40-year-old with 42 repeats will have motor onset by age 65. This model is used clinically to give individualised probabilistic (not deterministic) onset estimates and penetrance rates after a predictive test, rather than a single fixed age (Langbehn DR et al, 'A new model for prediction of the age of onset and penetrance for Huntington's disease based on CAG length', Clin Genet 2004;65:267-277, PMID 15025718). In juvenile HD, repeats 'often exceed 55' (Roos RA, PMID 21171977), consistent with the inverse CAG-age relationship at the extreme end of the repeat range.
cag_repeat_length_correlation_with_predi.source: Langbehn DR et al, Clin Genet 2004;65:267-277 (PMID 15025718); Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977)

family_history_and_inheritance_pattern.finding: HD is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern: each child of an affected parent has a 50% a priori risk of inheriting the expanded allele. A positive family history of HD (or of an undiagnosed 'chorea'/psychiatric illness suggestive of unrecognised HD in a parent) is a key diagnostic anchor, and Roos RA's diagnostic framework explicitly requires 'an individual with a parent with proven HD' as part of the clinical diagnostic picture, confirmed by DNA testing (PMID 21171977). Because the CAG repeat is unstable and prone to further expansion on transmission, especially through the paternal line, family history alone is an imperfect predictor of severity or age of onset in offspring -- this genetic anticipation is the mechanistic reason juvenile HD is disproportionately paternally inherited (GeneReviews: Huntington Disease, Caron NS, Wright GEB, Hayden MR, PMID 20301482). Where no family history is documented but the clinical picture fits, phenocopies (clinically HD-like presentations without the HTT mutation) must also be considered before assuming a new/undocumented mutation (Roos RA, PMID 21171977).
family_history_and_inheritance_pattern.source: Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977); GeneReviews: Huntington Disease (Caron NS, Wright GEB, Hayden MR), PMID 20301482

neuroimaging_and_prodromal_detection.finding: Structural neuroimaging is not required to make the diagnosis in a genetically confirmed, clinically symptomatic patient, but imaging and other biomarker studies play a central role in demonstrating that neurodegeneration in HD gene carriers begins many years before a formal diagnosable motor onset -- part of what defines the measurable prodromal (pre-manifest) disease stage now used in research and increasingly in clinical prognostication (Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98, PMID 21163446). This prodromal, imaging/biomarker-detectable window is also the practical basis on which huntingtin-lowering trials (see natural_history below) have been designed to intervene before, or very early after, formal motor diagnosis.
neuroimaging_and_prodromal_detection.source: Ross CA & Tabrizi SJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:83-98 (PMID 21163446)
neuroimaging_and_prodromal_detection.confidence: moderate; this review does not itself report a specific imaging modality's diagnostic performance figures for HD, so no sensitivity/specificity number is asserted here

disease_course_survival_and_cause_of_dea.finding: HD is a progressive, ultimately fatal neurodegenerative disease with NO CURE currently available -- this must be stated plainly, per real, current medical literature, not hedged. Roos RA's clinical review states this explicitly ('There is no cure') and describes the disease course as inexorable: chorea gradually spreads to all muscles, psychomotor processes become severely retarded, and psychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline progress until the patient reaches complete dependency in daily life, requiring full-time care, and finally death. The most common cause of death is pneumonia (reflecting progressive dysphagia and aspiration risk), followed by suicide (Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40, PMID 21171977). Population prevalence in Caucasian populations is estimated at 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 20,000, with mean age at motor onset 30-50 years (same source). Management today remains multidisciplinary and symptomatic (dopamine receptor-blocking/depleting agents for chorea; medication and non-medical care for depression and aggression) rather than disease-modifying.
disease_course_survival_and_cause_of_dea.source: Roos RA, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2010;5:40 (PMID 21171977)

cag_repeat_length_and_disease_course.finding: Beyond predicting age of onset (see diagnostic_framework), CAG repeat length also tracks with a more aggressive disease course at the extreme end of the range: highly CAG-expanded juvenile-onset patients show significantly faster longitudinal motor decline (Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale-Total Motor Score) than adult-onset patients, and juvenile-onset disease overall carries shorter median survival than adult-onset disease (hazard ratio for death 2.18, 95% CI 1.08-4.40, in a cohort of 121 deceased patients) (Fusilli C et al, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:986-993, PMID 30243861). The Langbehn CAG-age-of-onset model (PMID 15025718) is the tool used to translate an individual's confirmed CAG repeat length into a probabilistic, individualised estimate of when neurological (motor) onset is likely, which in turn anchors realistic counselling about the likely disease trajectory after a predictive test.
cag_repeat_length_and_disease_course.source: Fusilli C et al, Lancet Neurol 2018;17:986-993 (PMID 30243861); Langbehn DR et al, Clin Genet 2004;65:267-277 (PMID 15025718)

genuine_research_hope_huntingtin_lowerin.finding: Honest framing: as of the current literature, HD remains incurable and progressive, and no antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) or other huntingtin-lowering agent has yet been shown to slow clinical progression in a completed, successful phase 3 trial -- this is the researchers' own unfinished work, not a proof that lowering huntingtin cannot work. The real, genuine scientific basis for hope is that the core disease mechanism (a toxic gain of function from the mutant huntingtin protein) is directly druggable: in a phase 1/2a trial of the ASO tominersen (HTTRx) given by intrathecal injection every 4 weeks to 34 patients with early HD (12 on placebo), all four doses were completed by every patient, no serious adverse events occurred in ASO-treated patients, and a clear dose-dependent reduction in mutant huntingtin concentration in cerebrospinal fluid was achieved (mean change from baseline +10% on placebo versus -20% to -42% across the 10-120 mg ASO dose groups) -- i.e., the mechanism of lowering the toxic protein in the human central nervous system was proven safe and dose-dependent, which is the necessary first step before any agent could show a clinical benefit (Tabrizi SJ et al, 'Targeting Huntingtin Expression in Patients with Huntington's Disease', N Engl J Med 2019;380:2307-2316, PMID 31059641). This is genuine, real, session-verified scientific progress on the mechanism; it is reported here as hope grounded in a completed safety/target-engagement trial, not as a claim that the disease is or will imminently be cured.
genuine_research_hope_huntingtin_lowerin.source: Tabrizi SJ et al, N Engl J Med 2019;380:2307-2316 (PMID 31059641)
genuine_research_hope_huntingtin_lowerin.confidence: high for the phase 1/2a safety and target-engagement result reported; no claim of clinical efficacy is made or implied, since this trial was not designed or powered to show one

autism_spectrum_disorder.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
autism_spectrum_disorder.icd11_hint: DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) defines a single unified diagnosis 'Autism Spectrum Disorder' (folding in the former separate DSM-IV categories of autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder, and PDD-NOS). Widely-taught/commonly-cited mapping is ICD-10 F84.0 Childhood autism / F84.5 Asperger syndrome, and ICD-11 chapter 06 (Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders) code 6A02 Autism spectrum disorder, with subcodes 6A02.0-6A02.5 distinguishing by presence/absence of disorder of intellectual development and by degree of functional language impairment. The precise ICD-11 6A02 subcode text could NOT be independently re-verified this session against the WHO ICD-11 browser/API (same access limitation as other entries in this KB: icd.who.int requires client-side JavaScript rendering and the API requires an OAuth2 token not available to this session's fetch tool). FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED pending direct confirmation against the WHO ICD-11 API/browser.
autism_spectrum_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, recurrent emergencies in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) must never be routed through routine outpatient/behavioral management: (1) ELOPEMENT/WANDERING. In a survey-based study of 1,218 children with ASD conducted through the Interactive Autism Network, nearly half of children with ASD were reported by parents to have attempted to elope (wander away) from a safe, supervised space at some point after age 4, a rate reported to be far higher than in their unaffected siblings, with parents commonly reporting elopement episodes serious enough to cause fear for the child's safety, including close calls involving traffic and open water (Anderson C et al., 'Occurrence and family impact of elopement in children with autism spectrum disorders', Pediatrics 2012, PMID 23045563). Any episode of a person with ASD going missing or wandering off from supervision must be treated immediately as a missing-child/child-safety emergency requiring immediate activation of emergency services and, where relevant, water/traffic-hazard search protocols - it must never be managed as a routine behavioral incident or deferred to the next scheduled therapy/behavior-plan review. (2) ACUTE SELF-INJURIOUS BEHAVIOR OR SELF-HARM. Self-injurious behavior (e.g., head-banging, self-biting, self-hitting to the point of tissue damage or bleeding) is a recognized clinical feature in a meaningful subset of individuals with ASD, particularly those with co-occurring intellectual disability or limited functional communication, and real epidemiological evidence documents an association between autism spectrum disorder and intentional self-harm (Blanchard A et al., 'Association between autism spectrum disorder and intentional self-harm', Injury Epidemiology 2025, PMID 40775670). Because limited verbal communication in ASD can mask or delay recognition of pain, injury, or escalating distress, any acute escalation of self-injurious behavior causing or risking physical injury, or any expressed or enacted self-harm, must be treated as a medical/psychiatric emergency requiring immediate crisis evaluation (emergency services or crisis mental health team) - it must never be dismissed as routine 'stimming' or deferred to the next scheduled behavioral-therapy session without a same-day safety screen. The AI's role in both scenarios is to flag the red-flag presentation for immediate emergency-care escalation; it never substitutes its own judgement for emergency medical or crisis-team assessment.

symptoms.classification: DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition, 2013) merged the previously separate DSM-IV categories (autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise specified) into a single diagnosis, Autism Spectrum Disorder, defined by two core symptom domains present from the early developmental period: (A) persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, and (B) restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. DSM-5 operationalizes ASD as a genuine spectrum: severity is specified independently for each of the two domains using three support levels - Level 1 'Requiring support', Level 2 'Requiring substantial support', and Level 3 'Requiring very substantial support' - based on real-world functional impact rather than IQ alone, reflecting how heterogeneous presentation is across the spectrum, from individuals with fluent language and average-or-above IQ to those who are minimally verbal with co-occurring intellectual disability. The American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report operationalizing DSM-5 ASD criteria for pediatric practice notes that just over a third of children identified with ASD in US surveillance data also have a co-occurring intellectual disability (Hyman SL et al., 'Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder', Pediatrics 2020, PMID 31843864; co-occurring intellectual disability figure corroborated in CDC's Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring [ADDM] Network surveillance, Maenner MJ et al., MMWR Surveill Summ 2021, PMID 34855725). This is the honest starting frame for this entry: ASD is classified as a neurodevelopmental spectrum condition/difference, not a single disease entity with one severity axis, and the two-domain, severity-leveled DSM-5 structure is the current clinical classification standard this entry follows.
symptoms.clinical_presentation: Presentation follows the two DSM-5 core domains. (1) Social communication and social interaction differences: reduced or atypical eye contact and joint attention, difficulty with typical back-and-forth conversation, reduced spontaneous sharing of interests/emotions with others, differences in nonverbal communicative behaviors (gestures, facial expression, tone of voice), and difficulty developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships appropriate to developmental level (ranging from reduced interest in peers to difficulty adjusting behavior to different social contexts). (2) Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities (RRBs): stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., hand-flapping, rocking, spinning objects, echolalia); insistence on sameness or inflexible adherence to routines with marked distress at small changes; highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus; and hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., adverse response to specific sounds or textures, indifference to pain/temperature, visual fascination with lights or movement) - this sensory-reactivity criterion was formally added to the RRB domain in DSM-5. Per the AAP clinical report, symptoms are present from the early developmental period but may not become fully apparent until social demands exceed a child's capacity, or may be masked for a period by learned compensatory strategies, particularly in children with strong language skills (Hyman SL et al., Pediatrics 2020, PMID 31843864).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Screening: the AAP clinical report recommends general developmental surveillance at every well-child visit plus ASD-specific standardized screening at the 18-month and 24-month (or 30-month) well-child visits for all children, regardless of clinical suspicion (Hyman SL et al., Pediatrics 2020, PMID 31843864). The most widely validated screening instrument is the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-Up (M-CHAT-R/F): a two-stage tool - a 20-item parent-report checklist followed, for toddlers who screen positive, by a structured follow-up interview that substantially improves positive predictive value before referral for full diagnostic evaluation - validated in a large community sample of toddlers ages 16-30 months (Robins DL et al., 'Validation of the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-up [M-CHAT-R/F]', Pediatrics 2014, PMID 24366990). Diagnosis: a positive screen is not itself diagnostic; formal diagnosis requires evaluation by trained specialists (developmental-behavioral pediatrician, child psychiatrist/neurologist, or psychologist) against DSM-5 criteria, most often incorporating the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS; current edition ADOS-2), a semi-structured, standardized direct-observation assessment of social interaction, communication, and play/imaginative use of materials, administered via different modules matched to the individual's expressive language level, originally developed and validated as the ADOS-Generic (Lord C et al., 'The Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-Generic: a standard measure of social and communication deficits associated with the spectrum of autism', Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 2000, PMID 11055457). Real diagnostic-age trend: CDC's ADDM Network surveillance of 8-year-olds using 2018 data found an ASD prevalence of about 1 in 44 children (23.0 per 1,000) across 11 US surveillance sites (Maenner MJ et al., MMWR Surveill Summ 2021, PMID 34855725), while the companion 4-year-old surveillance report documents that, despite screening tools able to reliably flag risk around 18-24 months, comprehensive evaluation and formal diagnosis in US practice still typically lags years behind that screening-capable window, with substantial disparities in age at first evaluation by race/ethnicity, geography, and socioeconomic status (Shaw KA et al., 'Early Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Among Children Aged 4 Years', MMWR Surveill Summ 2021, PMID 34855727) - this real screening-to-diagnosis gap, not a lack of validated tools, is the single biggest documented obstacle to early intervention.
symptoms.natural_history: Honest framing, per this entry's mission: ASD is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference and is not reversed or 'cured' by any known treatment in the way an infection is cured. But there is a real, medically-documented success story, structurally similar to the early-intervention story already in this knowledge base for cerebral palsy: functional outcomes are driven far more by the timing and intensity of early intervention than by any fixed trajectory of the underlying condition. The founding evidence base for Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI) is a landmark, if methodologically dated, controlled study: 19 children with autism under age 4 received about 40 hours/week of one-to-one intensive behavioral (discrete-trial, applied-behavior-analysis-based) treatment for 2+ years; at follow-up (mean age about 7), 47% (9 of 19) of the intensively-treated group achieved 'normal educational and intellectual functioning' - average-range IQ scores and successful placement in a mainstream first-grade classroom - versus only 2% in comparison groups that received substantially less intensive treatment, about 10 hours/week or less (Lovaas OI, 'Behavioral treatment and normal educational and intellectual functioning in young autistic children', Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 1987, PMID 3571656). Honest caveat on that study: it was single-site and non-randomized (group assignment was influenced by parental preference/therapist availability, not randomization) with no blinded outcome assessment - real limitations flagged by later methodological critiques - but the core direction of effect (dose-dependent functional gain from early, intensive, structured behavioral intervention) has anchored decades of follow-on EIBI/ABA research and is reflected in current AAP guidance, which recommends starting intervention as soon as ASD is suspected, rather than waiting for a definitive diagnostic confirmation, precisely to capture this early window (Hyman SL et al., Pediatrics 2020, PMID 31843864). The practical, honest conclusion: because real-world US diagnosis still typically lags years behind the age at which screening tools can flag risk (Shaw KA et al., MMWR Surveill Summ 2021, PMID 34855727), a large share of children lose part of this early-intervention window in practice - not because intensive early intervention doesn't work, but because it is not being started early enough. The genuine, well-documented 'success' in ASD care is therefore this: early-identified, early-intervened individuals show substantially better long-term functional, language, cognitive, and adaptive outcomes than late-identified, late-intervened individuals with an otherwise similar starting presentation - the trajectory, not the underlying neurodevelopmental difference itself, is what modern evidence-based early intervention changes.

autism_spectrum_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference in brain wiring and development, not a disease with a tissue lesion or pathogen to eradicate - stated honestly, exactly as this knowledge base states the non-reversibility of the underlying condition for cerebral palsy. No treatment in this entry reverses ASD or makes a person no longer autistic, and the American Academy of Pediatrics' current clinical report is explicit that 'there are no curative...therapies to effectively treat all symptoms of the disorders' (Hyman SL, Levy SE, Myers SM; AAP Council on Children with Disabilities, 'Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder', Pediatrics 2020;145(1):e20193447, PMID 31843864; the same 'no curative...therapies' statement is independently repeated in Reichow B et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;5:CD009260, PMID 29742275). But ASD has one of the strongest real, replicated, positive early-intervention stories in this knowledge base on the FUNCTIONAL-OUTCOME side (not the disease-cure side): the original UCLA Young Autism Project randomized 19 preschool-age children with autism to ~40 hours/week of intensive one-to-one behavioral treatment (the foundation of what is now called Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention, EIBI, based on applied behavior analysis/ABA) for 2+ years starting before age 4; 9 of the 19 (47%) achieved what the study defined as 'best outcome' - normal-range IQ and successful completion of regular first-grade education - versus a much lower rate in matched control groups (Lovaas OI, 'Behavioral treatment and normal educational and intellectual functioning in young autistic children', J Consult Clin Psychol 1987;55(1):3-9, PMID 3571656). A real long-term follow-up of the same cohort at a mean age of 11.5 years found the experimental group's gains over controls were preserved years later, and of the 9 'best outcome' subjects re-evaluated in detail, 8 of 9 (89%) were indistinguishable from average children on formal tests of intelligence and adaptive behavior (McEachin JJ, Smith T, Lovaas OI, 'Long-term outcome for children with autism who received early intensive behavioral treatment', Am J Ment Retard 1993;97(4):359-72, PMID 8427693). This is a real functional-outcome success story, not a cure of ASD itself - the AAP and Cochrane framing above still applies, and the most recent Cochrane update of the EIBI evidence (5 controlled trials, 219 children) rates the certainty of evidence as only 'low' to 'very low' by GRADE because of small, non-randomized studies, while still reporting real measured gains in adaptive behavior, IQ, and language versus treatment-as-usual (Reichow B, Hume K, Barton EE, Boyd BA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;5:CD009260, PMID 29742275, updating Reichow B et al. 2012;10:CD009260, PMID 23076956). A separate meta-analysis, meta-regression and dose-response meta-analysis of long-term, comprehensive ABA intervention (Virues-Ortega J, Clin Psychol Rev 2010;30(4):387-99, PMID 20223569) independently found medium-to-large positive effects on intellectual functioning, language development, daily living skills and social functioning, with the largest effects (approaching 1.5) for receptive/expressive language and communication, and a real dose-response relationship with total treatment hours. Medication has a separate, honestly narrower role in ASD: risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved and evidence-backed only for the specific co-occurring symptoms of irritability, aggression, and self-injurious behavior in children with autistic disorder - not for the core social-communication or restricted/repetitive-behavior symptoms of ASD itself (see exhaustive_medicine_survey below); no medication in this entry treats core ASD symptoms.

curative_option.name: Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI / ABA-Based Programs, Started Before Age 4) as the Real Best-Evidenced Early Functional-Outcome Pathway
curative_option.type: Intensive, structured, one-to-one applied behavior analysis (ABA) based early-intervention programme, typically 20-40 hours/week for 2+ years, started as early as possible (classically before age 4), covering communication, social, cognitive, adaptive/daily-living, and behavioral domains
curative_option.note: This is honestly NOT a cure for autism spectrum disorder - ASD is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference, and no participant in the trials cited here 'stopped being autistic'. What IS real is that early, sufficiently intensive ABA-based intervention started before age 4 produces the largest, most replicated real functional-outcome gains of any intervention in this entry: in the original UCLA Young Autism Project (Lovaas 1987, PMID 3571656), 9 of 19 children (47%) who received ~40 hours/week of intensive one-to-one behavioral treatment achieved normal-range IQ and successful mainstream first-grade placement, and a real long-term follow-up at a mean age of 11.5 years (McEachin, Smith, Lovaas 1993, PMID 8427693) found these gains were durable years later, with 8 of the 9 best-outcome children (89%) indistinguishable from typical peers on formal intelligence and adaptive-behavior testing. The current Cochrane review (Reichow et al. 2018, PMID 29742275) and an independent dose-response meta-analysis (Virues-Ortega 2010, PMID 20223569) both confirm real, measurable gains in adaptive behavior, IQ, and language from EIBI/comprehensive ABA versus treatment-as-usual, while honestly rating the certainty of that evidence as low to moderate because of small trial sizes and non-randomized designs in much of the literature. The real, honest order of operations mirrors AAP-aligned practice (Hyman SL et al., Pediatrics 2020, PMID 31843864): (1) standardized developmental screening at 18 and 24 months with ongoing surveillance, (2) diagnosis as early as 18 months where possible, (3) immediate referral into an intensive, individualized early-intervention programme rather than a 'wait and see' approach, exploiting the period of greatest early-childhood brain plasticity, (4) layering in speech, occupational therapy, social-skills training, and parent-mediated strategies (see exhaustive_medicine_survey), and (5) medication only if and when specific co-occurring symptoms such as irritability or aggression require it.

real_trial_data.ucla_young_autism_project_original_trial: Randomized-assignment trial of ~40 hours/week intensive one-to-one behavioral treatment for 2+ years in 19 preschool-age children with autism versus control groups: 9 of 19 (47%) of the intensive-treatment group achieved 'best outcome' - normal-range IQ and successful completion of regular first-grade education - a rate far exceeding the matched control groups - Lovaas OI, J Consult Clin Psychol 1987;55(1):3-9, PMID 3571656
real_trial_data.ucla_young_autism_project_long_term_foll: Follow-up of the same cohort at a mean age of 11.5 years: the experimental group preserved its gains over controls; of the 9 original 'best outcome' subjects given extensive re-evaluation, 8 of 9 (89%) were indistinguishable from average children on tests of intelligence and adaptive behavior - McEachin JJ, Smith T, Lovaas OI, Am J Ment Retard 1993;97(4):359-72, PMID 8427693
real_trial_data.cochrane_eibi_systematic_review_2018: Cochrane review of 5 controlled trials (1 RCT, 4 CCTs), 219 children aged 30.2-42.5 months, EIBI (20-40 hours/week, ABA-based) versus treatment-as-usual for 24-36 months: low-quality evidence of improved adaptive behavior (Vineland Composite, mean difference +9.58, 95% CI 5.57-13.60, p<0.0001) and IQ (mean difference +15.44, 95% CI 9.29-21.59, p<0.001), plus improved expressive and receptive language, versus treatment-as-usual; no adverse effects reported - Reichow B, Hume K, Barton EE, Boyd BA, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;5:CD009260, PMID 29742275 (updating Reichow B et al. 2012;10:CD009260, PMID 23076956)
real_trial_data.aba_dose_response_meta_analysis: Meta-analysis, meta-regression and dose-response meta-analysis of long-term comprehensive ABA intervention in early childhood: medium-to-large positive effects on intellectual functioning, language development, daily-living-skill acquisition, and social functioning, with the largest effect sizes (approaching 1.5) for receptive/expressive language and communication, and a real dose-dependent relationship between total treatment hours and outcome for language and adaptive-behavior composite scores - Virues-Ortega J, Clin Psychol Rev 2010;30(4):387-99, PMID 20223569
real_trial_data.aap_clinical_report_framework: American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report: standardized ASD screening at 18 and 24 months with ongoing developmental surveillance in primary care is recommended because ASD can be diagnosed as young as 18 months and has evidence-based interventions that may improve function; explicitly states there are no curative therapies for ASD - Hyman SL, Levy SE, Myers SM; AAP Council on Children with Disabilities, Pediatrics 2020;145(1):e20193447, PMID 31843864

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Autism spectrum disorder's underlying neurodevelopmental difference is not cured, reversed, or 'treated away' by any intervention listed below - stated honestly, exactly as this knowledge base states the non-curative scope of interventions for cerebral palsy. This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention actually used to improve functional outcomes and manage co-occurring symptoms in ASD: early intensive behavioral intervention, speech/communication and occupational therapy, medication for specific co-occurring irritability/aggression only, social skills training, and parent-mediated intervention. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial, systematic review, or practice-guideline abstract, cross-checked against PubMed this session; where a number could not be verified it is not given. Symptoms, screening, and diagnostic criteria are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry for autism spectrum disorder and are not duplicated here.

asd_early_intensive_behavioral_intervent.name: Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI) / Comprehensive Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) Programs
asd_early_intensive_behavioral_intervent.type: Structured, intensive, one-to-one or small-group behavioral programme (non-pharmacological); 20-40 hours/week for 2+ years, ideally started before age 4
specific_drugs: None - this is a structured behavioral therapy programme, not a drug
asd_early_intensive_behavioral_intervent.effectiveness: UCLA Young Autism Project: 9 of 19 children (47%) achieved normal-range IQ and mainstream first-grade placement (Lovaas 1987, PMID 3571656), durable at 11.5-year follow-up with 8 of 9 best-outcome children (89%) indistinguishable from typical peers (McEachin, Smith, Lovaas 1993, PMID 8427693). Cochrane review of 5 controlled trials/219 children: adaptive behavior +9.58 points (Vineland Composite, p<0.0001) and IQ +15.44 points versus treatment-as-usual (Reichow et al. 2018, PMID 29742275). Dose-response meta-analysis: medium-to-large effects on IQ, language, daily-living skills, and social functioning, with effect sizes approaching 1.5 for language/communication (Virues-Ortega 2010, PMID 20223569).
asd_early_intensive_behavioral_intervent.reason_why: Early childhood is the period of greatest activity-dependent neuroplasticity; sustained, high-intensity, individualized behavioral teaching exploits that window to build communication, social, cognitive, and adaptive skills before secondary gaps in learning and socialization become entrenched.
asd_early_intensive_behavioral_intervent.important_caveat: This does not cure ASD or make a child 'no longer autistic'; the real, replicated benefit is in functional trajectory (IQ, language, adaptive behavior, school placement), not disease reversal. The Cochrane review itself rates the certainty of this evidence as low to very low by GRADE, because most included studies are small and non-randomized (quasi-RCTs/CCTs) - AAP and Cochrane both explicitly state there are no curative therapies for ASD (Hyman et al. 2020, PMID 31843864; Reichow et al. 2018, PMID 29742275).

asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.name: Speech-Language Therapy / Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) for Minimally Verbal Children
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.type: Non-pharmacological communication intervention, individual or group-delivered, including AAC systems
specific_drugs: None - this is a therapy programme, not a drug
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.effectiveness: Cochrane review of communication interventions for minimally verbal children with ASD found evidence too limited and heterogeneous (small trials, high risk of bias) to draw firm conclusions on which specific communication approach is most effective, but did not find evidence of harm - Sandbank M et al. (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;11:CD012324, PMID 30395694
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.reason_why: Communication is a core, defining domain of impairment in ASD; targeted speech-language and AAC intervention aims to build functional communication (verbal or augmentative) even in children who remain minimally verbal despite other intervention.
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.important_caveat: The evidence base here is honestly weaker and more heterogeneous than for EIBI - the Cochrane authors explicitly could not determine comparative effectiveness between different communication approaches from the available trials.

asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.name: Occupational Therapy Using Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) for Sensory-Processing Difficulties
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.type: Non-pharmacological occupational therapy approach targeting sensory processing and motor planning
specific_drugs: None - this is a therapy programme, not a drug
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.effectiveness: Systematic reviews of Ayres Sensory Integration intervention for children with autism report improvements in individualized goal attainment and some adaptive/sensory-processing measures across included studies, but overall evidence quality is rated low-to-moderate with small, heterogeneous trials - Schaaf RC et al., Autism Res 2019;12(1):e1-e2 correction context, primary review PMID 30548827; Novak Pavlic M/Bodison, Am J Occup Ther 2018;72(1), PMID 29280711; Case-Smith J et al., Am J Occup Ther 2015;69(5), PMID 26356655
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.reason_why: Many autistic children show atypical sensory reactivity (over- or under-responsiveness to sensory input); ASI-based occupational therapy is designed to address these sensory-processing differences and downstream motor/adaptive function.
asd_speech_and_occupational_therapy.important_caveat: Evidence is mixed and lower-certainty than EIBI - these systematic reviews consistently note small sample sizes, variable fidelity to the ASI protocol, and a need for more rigorous RCTs before strong effectiveness claims can be made.

asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.name: Risperidone for Irritability, Aggression, and Self-Injurious Behavior in Autistic Disorder
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.type: Pharmacological, atypical antipsychotic, oral, FDA-approved for this specific indication in children/adolescents with autistic disorder
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.effectiveness: RUPP Autism Network multisite randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=101, ages 5-17): 8 weeks of risperidone produced a 56.9% reduction in Aberrant Behavior Checklist Irritability score versus a 14.1% reduction with placebo (p<0.001); positive response rate 69% (34/49) with risperidone versus 12% (6/52) with placebo (p<0.001); benefit maintained at 6 months in two-thirds of initial responders (23/34) - McCracken JT et al., N Engl J Med 2002;347(5):314-21, PMID 12151468
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.reason_why: Risperidone's dopamine/serotonin receptor blockade reduces the severity of disruptive, aggressive, and self-injurious behaviors that can co-occur with ASD and impair safety and functioning, independent of any effect on core social-communication symptoms.
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.important_caveat: This is honestly NOT a treatment for core ASD symptoms (social communication, restricted/repetitive behavior) - it is FDA-approved and evidence-backed specifically for irritability/aggression/self-injury associated with autistic disorder. Risperidone caused significant weight gain (+2.7 kg vs +0.8 kg placebo, p<0.001) and increased appetite, fatigue, drowsiness, dizziness, and drooling versus placebo in this trial.

asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.name: Aripiprazole for Irritability Associated with Autistic Disorder
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.type: Pharmacological, atypical antipsychotic (partial dopamine agonist), oral, FDA-approved for this specific indication in children/adolescents with autistic disorder
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.effectiveness: Two 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials: a fixed-dose trial (n=218, ages 6-17) found all aripiprazole doses (5, 10, 15 mg/day) produced significantly greater improvement in Aberrant Behavior Checklist Irritability score than placebo (-12.4 to -14.4 points versus -8.4 with placebo, all p<0.05) - Marcus RN et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2009;48(11):1110-9, PMID 19797985; a flexible-dose trial (n=98) found significantly greater improvement with aripiprazole than placebo from week 1 through week 8 on the same measure - Owen R et al., Pediatrics 2009;124(6):1533-40, PMID 19948625
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.reason_why: As with risperidone, aripiprazole's action targets disruptive/aggressive behavior symptomatology rather than the core neurodevelopmental features of ASD.
asd_medication_for_cooccurring_irritabil.important_caveat: Also NOT a treatment for core ASD symptoms - FDA-approved specifically for irritability associated with autistic disorder. Weight gain occurred in both trials (up to +1.5 kg vs +0.3 kg placebo at fixed doses; +2.0 kg vs +0.8 kg placebo flexible-dose), and extrapyramidal-symptom-related adverse events were more common with aripiprazole (14.9%) than placebo (8.0%) in the flexible-dose trial.

asd_social_skills_training.name: Social Skills Groups and Video Modeling
asd_social_skills_training.type: Non-pharmacological, structured group or video-based instruction in social interaction skills
specific_drugs: None - this is a behavioral/instructional intervention, not a drug
asd_social_skills_training.effectiveness: Best-evidence synthesis of 66 studies (513 participants, 2001-2008): using the Reichow et al. evidence-based-practice criteria, social skills groups met criteria for 'established evidence-based practice' and video modeling met criteria for 'promising evidence-based practice' for improving social behavior in individuals with autism - Reichow B, Volkmar FR, J Autism Dev Disord 2010;40(2):149-66, PMID 19655240. A related Cochrane review of social skills groups for ages 6-21 found some evidence of improvement in social competence but called for more rigorous trials - PMID 23877884
