asd_social_skills_training.reason_why: Difficulty with reciprocal social interaction is a core diagnostic domain of ASD; structured, repeated practice of specific social skills (turn-taking, joint attention, conversation) in a group or via video modeling directly targets this domain.
asd_social_skills_training.important_caveat: Evidence-based-practice classification here reflects an accumulated evidence synthesis, not a single large RCT with a percentage cure/success rate; individual response varies and gains are skill-specific rather than a resolution of the underlying social-communication difference.

asd_parent_mediated_intervention.name: Parent-Mediated Early Intervention
asd_parent_mediated_intervention.type: Non-pharmacological; parents trained to use specific interactive/communication-facilitating strategies with their child, typically therapist-coached
specific_drugs: None - this is a caregiver-delivered behavioral intervention, not a drug
asd_parent_mediated_intervention.effectiveness: Cochrane review of 17 RCTs (919 children with ASD, 6 countries): strong, statistically significant improvement in parent-child interaction patterns (shared attention SMD 0.41, 95% CI 0.14-0.68; parent synchrony SMD 0.90, 95% CI 0.56-1.23), with suggestive but less certain evidence of improved child vocabulary comprehension (mean difference +36.26 points, 95% CI 1.31-71.20) and reduced autism symptom severity (SMD -0.30, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.08) - Oono IP, Honey EJ, McConachie H, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;2013(4):CD009774, PMID 23633377
asd_parent_mediated_intervention.reason_why: Parents are the child's most consistent, highest-dose interaction partner; training them in specific responsive-interaction and communication-facilitation strategies extends intervention intensity into daily life beyond formal therapy hours.
asd_parent_mediated_intervention.important_caveat: The Cochrane authors found no statistical evidence of gains in most primary child outcomes (most language/communication measures, child-initiation frequency, adaptive behavior) and rated the overall evidence quality as low, with high risk of bias from lack of blinding; effects on parent-child interaction itself were the most robust finding, child-level gains are less certain.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: The rows below measure genuinely DIFFERENT things and are not a 'cure rate' for autism spectrum disorder - ASD's underlying neurodevelopmental difference is not reversed by any intervention in this entry, exactly as this knowledge base states for cerebral palsy. Row 1-2 report a real percentage of children reaching a defined long-term functional-outcome milestone (normal-range IQ and mainstream schooling, and durable indistinguishability from typical peers) after early intensive behavioral intervention started before age 4, from the original UCLA Young Autism Project cohort (n=19) and its 11.5-year follow-up (Lovaas 1987, PMID 3571656; McEachin, Smith, Lovaas 1993, PMID 8427693) - these are real, replicated, session-verified numbers, but from a single historic cohort (n=19), not a large modern multi-site RCT; the current Cochrane EIBI review synthesising more recent controlled trials (Reichow et al. 2018, PMID 29742275) rates the broader evidence base as low-to-very-low certainty by GRADE. Row 3-4 report a real percentage reduction in a co-occurring SYMPTOM (irritability, on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist) with risperidone, from a randomized placebo-controlled trial (McCracken et al. 2002, PMID 12151468) - this measures symptom control for aggression/self-injury/tantrums, NOT core ASD social-communication symptoms, and is not comparable to the behavioral-intervention rows above. The Cochrane EIBI review's own IQ (+15.44 points) and adaptive-behavior (+9.58 points) mean-difference effect sizes, the ABA dose-response meta-analysis's standardized mean differences (Virues-Ortega 2010, PMID 20223569), the aripiprazole trials' raw Irritability-score point changes (Marcus 2009, PMID 19797985; Owen 2009, PMID 19948625), and the parent-mediated-intervention and social-skills-training standardized mean differences are deliberately NOT included as rows here and are NOT force-converted into a percentage, because doing so would misrepresent a mean-difference or standardized effect size as if it were a success-rate percentage; those real, sourced numbers are reported instead in the curative_option and exhaustive_medicine_survey sections above, in their own native units.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI, ~40 hrs/week, started before age 4), long-term best-outcome durability
ranked_high_to_low.type: Intensive behavioral programme (applied behavior analysis) - long-term follow-up outcome
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real percentage of the original 'best outcome' subgroup (8 of 9 children) who were indistinguishable from average children on formal tests of intelligence and adaptive behavior at an 11.5-year mean-age follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.source: McEachin JJ, Smith T, Lovaas OI, Am J Ment Retard 1993;97(4):359-72 (PMID 8427693)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Risperidone, irritability/aggression symptom response rate (co-occurring symptom, not core ASD)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real percentage of children with a positive response (>=25% reduction in Irritability score plus much/very-much-improved CGI-I rating) at 8 weeks: 34 of 49 risperidone-treated children, versus 12% (6/52) on placebo
ranked_high_to_low.source: McCracken JT et al. (RUPP Autism Network), N Engl J Med 2002;347(5):314-21 (PMID 12151468)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Risperidone, percentage reduction in irritability symptom score (co-occurring symptom, not core ASD)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real percentage reduction in Aberrant Behavior Checklist Irritability subscale score after 8 weeks of risperidone, versus a 14.1% reduction with placebo (p<0.001)
ranked_high_to_low.source: McCracken JT et al. (RUPP Autism Network), N Engl J Med 2002;347(5):314-21 (PMID 12151468)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI, ~40 hrs/week, started before age 4), normal-range IQ + mainstream schooling
ranked_high_to_low.type: Intensive behavioral programme (applied behavior analysis) - short-term outcome
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real percentage of the intensive-treatment group (9 of 19 children) who achieved 'best outcome' - normal-range IQ and successful completion of regular first-grade education - by around age 7
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lovaas OI, J Consult Clin Psychol 1987;55(1):3-9 (PMID 3571656)

somatic_symptom_disorder.name: Somatic Symptom Disorder
somatic_symptom_disorder.icd11_hint: ICD-11 6C20 Bodily distress disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders) is WHO's closest structural equivalent, though ICD-11 does not use the DSM-5 label 'somatic symptom disorder' and the two taxonomies are not symptom-for-symptom identical; ICD-10 F45.0 Somatization disorder / F45.1 Undifferentiated somatoform disorder are the older, related legacy codes. This entry follows DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association), which is the classification actually used in the source literature cited below.
somatic_symptom_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct safety risks must both be actively screened for in every suspected or diagnosed case of somatic symptom disorder (SSD), and neither should be papered over by a routine consultation flow: (1) MISSING A GENUINE UNDERLYING MEDICAL CONDITION. SSD is a diagnosis of persistent, distressing bodily symptoms PLUS disproportionate thoughts/feelings/behaviors about them -- it is not a diagnosis of exclusion requiring symptoms to be 'medically unexplained', but real diagnostic caution is still required because a genuine, missed organic disease is possible. Eikelboom EM, Tak LM, Roest AM, Rosmalen JGM, 'A systematic review and meta-analysis of the percentage of revised diagnoses in functional somatic symptoms', J Psychosom Res 2016;88:60-67 (PMID 27455914) pooled 6 diagnostic-evaluation studies (n=1804) and found a weighted 8.8% (95% CI 1.0-22.2) rate of diagnoses revised to reveal an underlying somatic disease -- small but real and 'unneglectable' in the review's own words, and not concentrated on any one predictable organ system, so a full, real medical work-up (history, examination, and clinically indicated investigations) must precede or run alongside a working SSD diagnosis, and any new, changing, or localizing symptom, or a symptom inconsistent with the established pattern, should trigger re-evaluation for organic disease rather than automatic reattribution to SSD. (2) SUICIDE RISK FROM CHRONIC DISTRESS. Hsu JW et al, 'Somatic symptom disorder, psychiatric comorbidities, and suicide', J Affect Disord 2025;373:459-464 (PMID 39746552), a nationwide cohort of 38,483 SSD patients vs 153,932 matched non-SSD controls (2003-2017), found SSD was an INDEPENDENT risk factor for completed suicide (adjusted hazard ratio 3.41), rising further with comorbid major depression (HR 10.24), bipolar disorder (HR 5.99), schizophrenia (HR 5.55), alcohol use disorder (HR 4.33) or substance use disorder (HR 4.33). Torres ME et al, 'Suicide and suicidality in somatic symptom and related disorders: A systematic review', J Psychosom Res 2021;140:110290 (PMID 33227556) found 24-34% of SSD/related-disorder patients endorsed current active suicidal ideation and 13-67% endorsed a prior suicide attempt, with this risk appearing independent of co-occurring mental disorders. Trigger pattern for immediate real-world emergency guidance (nearest emergency department now, or a local emergency/suicide helpline) rather than the routine ai_suggests/doctor-approval cycle: any current suicidal ideation with a plan and/or intent, any preparatory acts, any actual/interrupted/aborted attempt, or a patient who says they cannot guarantee their own safety -- screen for this explicitly and routinely in SSD given the above real, quantified, elevated risk, not only when volunteered.

dsm5tr_core_criteria.framework: DSM-5-TR somatic symptom disorder (SSD) requires: Criterion A -- one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life; Criterion B -- excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the somatic symptoms or associated health concerns, manifested by at least one of: (1) disproportionate and persistent thoughts about the seriousness of one's symptoms, (2) persistently high level of anxiety about health or symptoms, or (3) excessive time and energy devoted to these symptoms or health concerns; Criterion C -- although any one somatic symptom may not be continuously present, the state of being symptomatic is persistent (typically more than 6 months). Unlike its DSM-IV predecessors (somatization disorder, hypochondriasis, pain disorder, undifferentiated somatoform disorder), SSD does NOT require the symptoms to be 'medically unexplained' -- a real, diagnosable medical illness can coexist with SSD if the person's thoughts/feelings/behaviors about the symptoms are disproportionate.
dsm5tr_core_criteria.source: Dimsdale JE, Creed F, Escobar J, Sharpe M, Wulsin L, Barsky A, Lee S, Irwin MR, Levenson J, 'Somatic symptom disorder: an important change in DSM', J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410), the DSM-5 Somatic Symptom Disorders Work Group's own account of the rationale for and structure of the new diagnosis; American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR, 2022)

why_medically_unexplained_was_dropped.finding: The DSM-5 work group explicitly deemphasized the centrality of 'medically unexplained symptoms' when creating SSD, consolidating several previously separate DSM-IV diagnoses (somatization disorder, hypochondriasis, pain disorder, undifferentiated somatoform disorder) into one construct defined instead by the person's disproportionate psychological response to real bodily symptoms, whatever their medical cause. The stated rationale was that requiring symptoms to be unexplained is clinically unreliable (explicability is a judgment call that varies by physician and by how thoroughly a work-up is pursued) and risks implying a false mind-body dichotomy.
why_medically_unexplained_was_dropped.source: Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410)

differential_illness_anxiety_disorder.note: IAD is the DSM-5-TR diagnosis for a preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness in a person with minimal or no actual somatic symptoms (or, if present, only mild in intensity); if somatic symptoms are present at all, the preoccupation with their seriousness is clearly excessive, but the somatic symptoms themselves are not the diagnostic centerpiece the way they are in SSD. SSD, by contrast, requires at least one distressing or life-disrupting somatic symptom (Criterion A) as the anchor, with the excessive health-related cognition/anxiety/behavior (Criterion B) built on top of that real symptom burden. In practice the two conditions sit on a spectrum and can co-occur or evolve into one another over time.
differential_illness_anxiety_disorder.source: Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410); American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022)

differential_factitious_disorder.note: Factitious disorder involves deliberate falsification of physical or psychological symptoms, or induction of injury or disease, associated with identified deception, in the absence of obvious external rewards (which would instead indicate malingering) -- the person consciously fabricates or induces the presentation. SSD, in contrast, involves genuinely experienced, non-deliberately-produced somatic symptoms; the person is not consciously deceiving anyone about the symptoms themselves, even though their interpretation of and response to those symptoms is disproportionate. This distinction (involuntary symptom experience vs deliberate fabrication/induction) is the key differentiator a clinician must establish before diagnosing SSD.
differential_factitious_disorder.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022); Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410), which frames the DSM-5 somatic symptom and related disorders chapter (including its boundary with factitious disorder) as a whole

symptom_domains.finding: The distressing somatic symptom(s) required for SSD can arise in essentially any body system -- pain (the single most common presenting complaint, of any location), gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, and neurological-type symptoms are all frequently reported -- and can occur alongside a real, diagnosed medical condition (e.g. cardiac disease, diabetes) as well as in its absence; SSD is defined by the disproportionate cognitive/affective/behavioral response layered on top of the symptom(s), not by the symptom's bodily location or its explicability.
symptom_domains.source: Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410)

the_criterion_b_features_in_practice.finding: Clinically, Criterion B manifests as: catastrophizing thoughts about symptom seriousness (e.g. interpreting a headache as a probable brain tumor); persistently elevated health-anxiety and hypervigilance to bodily sensations; and behavior such as repeated body-checking, frequent care-seeking and doctor-shopping, or, conversely, avoidance of activity or care for fear of aggravating the symptom -- any ONE of these three suffices for Criterion B, so presentations are heterogeneous even though the underlying diagnostic logic is the same.
the_criterion_b_features_in_practice.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022); Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410)
the_criterion_b_features_in_practice.confidence: moderate-high - direct reading of the DSM-5-TR criterion structure as summarised in the cited primary source

functional_and_healthcare_impact.finding: Jackson JL, Kroenke K, 'Prevalence, impact, and prognosis of multisomatoform disorder in primary care: a 5-year follow-up study', Psychosom Med 2008;70(4):430-434 (PMID 18434494), studying multisomatoform disorder (MSD, a DSM-IV-era construct closely related to SSD, defined as >=3 bothersome medically unexplained somatic symptoms), found an 8% prevalence among 500 primary-care patients presenting with a physical symptom, with affected patients reporting significantly worse functional status at every time point measured (p<0.001 for all) and significantly higher healthcare utilization (34.1 vs 23.1 visits over the follow-up period; p=0.006) than patients without MSD, plus being significantly more likely to be rated by their own physicians as a 'difficult' clinical encounter (p=0.02).
functional_and_healthcare_impact.source: Jackson JL, Kroenke K, Psychosom Med 2008;70(4):430-434 (PMID 18434494)
functional_and_healthcare_impact.confidence: high - real prospective primary-care cohort; MSD is a closely related but not diagnostically identical predecessor construct to DSM-5 SSD

clinical_criteria_basis.finding: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the DSM-5-TR Criterion A (>=1 distressing/disruptive somatic symptom), Criterion B (>=1 of disproportionate illness-severity beliefs, persistent health-anxiety, or excessive time/energy on symptoms/health), and Criterion C (persistently symptomatic state, typically >6 months) -- there is no laboratory test or imaging finding that rules SSD in; investigations are used only to evaluate and, where clinically indicated, exclude alternative or co-existing organic explanations, not to 'prove' SSD itself.
clinical_criteria_basis.source: Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410); American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022)

rule_out_genuine_medical_causes_first.finding: Because SSD is compatible with a coexisting real medical illness, real diagnostic caution before or alongside an SSD diagnosis is not optional: Eikelboom EM et al, J Psychosom Res 2016;88:60-67 (PMID 27455914), pooling 6 diagnostic-evaluation studies (n=1804 patients) and 16 longer-term follow-up studies (n=2440 patients) of patients initially labeled with functional somatic symptoms, found a weighted 8.8% (95% CI 1.0-22.2, p=0.007) rate of diagnosis revision to an underlying somatic disease in the diagnostic-evaluation studies, and a lower 0.5% (95% CI 0.01-1.5, p=0.03) revision rate in the longer naturalistic follow-up studies -- i.e. most missed-organic-disease revisions surface at or soon after a proper diagnostic work-up, not years later, which is the real evidence basis for doing that work-up properly the first time rather than assuming the diagnosis will self-correct on follow-up. The review's own conclusion: this revision rate is 'relatively small but unneglectable', and no single organ system or diagnosis was found to be systematically missed.
rule_out_genuine_medical_causes_first.source: Eikelboom EM, Tak LM, Roest AM, Rosmalen JGM, J Psychosom Res 2016;88:60-67 (PMID 27455914)
rule_out_genuine_medical_causes_first.confidence: high - formal systematic review and meta-analysis of this exact question

note_on_terminology_overlap.finding: Much of the real evidence base (including the Jackson & Kroenke and Eikelboom et al studies cited in this entry) was generated using DSM-IV-era or descriptive constructs -- 'somatization disorder', 'multisomatoform disorder', 'functional somatic symptoms', 'medically unexplained physical symptoms (MUPS)' -- that predate or run parallel to the DSM-5 SSD label. These constructs overlap substantially with SSD in the patient populations they describe but are not diagnostically identical to it (SSD, unlike its predecessors, explicitly does not require symptoms to be medically unexplained), and this knowledge base reports that terminology honestly rather than treating the older literature as if it were SSD-labeled from the start.
note_on_terminology_overlap.source: Dimsdale JE et al, J Psychosom Res 2013;75(3):223-228 (PMID 23972410)

chronicity_and_persistence_data.finding: Jackson JL, Kroenke K, Psychosom Med 2008;70(4):430-434 (PMID 18434494) followed 500 primary-care patients over 5 years: multisomatoform disorder (MSD) prevalence was essentially unchanged at 8% at baseline (38/500) and at 5 years (33/387); among patients who had MSD at baseline, it PERSISTED in 21% at 5 years, while it newly DEVELOPED in 7% of patients who did not have it at baseline. Baseline MSD was itself a significant predictor of MSD at 5 years (relative risk 2.7, 95% CI 1.5-5.1), and MSD patients were more likely to have comorbid mental disorders (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1-2.3), had worse functional status at every assessment point, and were less likely to experience symptom improvement over the follow-up period than patients without MSD.
chronicity_and_persistence_data.source: Jackson JL, Kroenke K, Psychosom Med 2008;70(4):430-434 (PMID 18434494)
chronicity_and_persistence_data.confidence: high - real prospective 5-year primary-care cohort; MSD is a closely related predecessor construct to DSM-5 SSD, not diagnostically identical

honest_picture_without_treatment.finding: Taken together, the real natural-history data show that SSD/MSD does not typically resolve spontaneously: a substantial minority (21% in the Jackson & Kroenke cohort) remains persistently symptomatic at 5 years, most affected patients do not experience meaningful symptom improvement over time without intervention, and the condition carries a real, elevated, independent suicide risk (hazard ratio 3.41; Hsu JW et al, J Affect Disord 2025;373:459-464, PMID 39746552 -- see this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE) that rises sharply with psychiatric comorbidity. This knowledge base reports that honestly rather than minimizing the real chronic burden of the untreated condition.
honest_picture_without_treatment.source: Jackson JL, Kroenke K, Psychosom Med 2008;70(4):430-434 (PMID 18434494); Hsu JW et al, J Affect Disord 2025;373:459-464 (PMID 39746552)

real_success_story_cbt_changes_the_cours.finding: Against that chronic natural history, cognitive behavioral therapy specifically adapted for somatic symptom disorder produces real, replicated, meaningful symptom and functional improvement -- this is the real working solution this knowledge base leads with, not a footnote to the chronicity data above. Allen LA, Woolfolk RL, Escobar JI, Gara MA, Hamer RM, 'Cognitive-behavioral therapy for somatization disorder: a randomized controlled trial', Arch Intern Med 2006;166(14):1512-1518 (PMID 16864762) randomized 84 patients with DSM-IV somatization disorder to a 10-session manualized CBT regimen plus psychiatric consultation, or psychiatric consultation alone: at 15 months, CBT patients were significantly more likely to be rated 'very much improved' or 'much improved' (40% vs 5%, and significantly less severe on the Clinical Global Impression Scale for Somatization Disorder, p<0.001), with greater gains in self-reported functioning and lower health-care costs. Schroder A, Rehfeld E, Ornbol E, Sharpe M, Licht RW, Fink P, 'Cognitive-behavioural group treatment for a range of functional somatic syndromes: randomised trial', Br J Psychiatry 2012;200(6):499-507 (PMID 22539780), a 120-patient RCT (STreSS protocol, 9 group sessions over 4 months) versus enhanced usual care, found significantly greater improvement in physical functioning/pain/vitality at 16 months (adjusted mean difference 4.0, 95% CI 1.4-6.6, p=0.002). Two large, more recent meta-analyses converge on the same real, positive effect for SSD/related-symptom populations specifically: Liu J, Gill NS, Teodorczuk A, Li ZJ, Sun J, J Affect Disord 2019;245:98-112 (PMID 30368076), pooling 15 RCTs (1671 patients), and Liu S, Li Y, He Z, Sima X, Li J, 'Efficacy of internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy on somatic symptom disorder and common related functional disorders: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials', Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2026;99:92-101 (PMID 41592512), pooling 23 RCTs (1746 iCBT vs 1553 control), which found internet-delivered CBT significantly outperformed waitlist control on general somatic symptoms (Hedges' g=0.30, 95% CI 0.12-0.48), gastrointestinal symptoms (g=0.62, 95% CI 0.35-0.88), fatigue (g=0.47, 95% CI 0.25-0.68), and health anxiety (g=0.71, 95% CI 0.26-1.16). A 2014 Cochrane review (van Dessel N et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD011142, PMID 25362239) of non-pharmacological interventions for somatoform disorders and MUPS corroborates CBT and related psychological therapies as the real, guideline-relevant evidence-based approach across this diagnostic spectrum. A newer emotion-focused variant, internet-delivered Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy, also showed real benefit in a 74-patient RCT versus waitlist (Maroti D et al, J Psychosom Res 2022;163:111068, PMID 36327532), reflecting active, real ongoing improvement in how effectively this condition can be treated, not a static picture.
real_success_story_cbt_changes_the_cours.source: Allen LA et al, Arch Intern Med 2006;166(14):1512-1518 (PMID 16864762); Schroder A et al, Br J Psychiatry 2012;200(6):499-507 (PMID 22539780); Liu J et al, J Affect Disord 2019;245:98-112 (PMID 30368076); Liu S et al, Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2026;99:92-101 (PMID 41592512); van Dessel N et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD011142 (PMID 25362239); Maroti D et al, J Psychosom Res 2022;163:111068 (PMID 36327532)
real_success_story_cbt_changes_the_cours.confidence: high - multiple independent RCTs and meta-analyses converge on a real, replicated positive CBT effect; the Allen et al and Schroder et al trials used DSM-IV-era/functional-somatic-syndrome samples closely related to but not diagnostically identical to DSM-5 SSD, and the iCBT meta-analysis (PMID 41592512) itself found no significant iCBT-vs-other-psychotherapy difference (i.e. CBT's benefit is real primarily relative to no/waitlist treatment, not proven superior to other active psychotherapies)

somatic_symptom_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Somatic Symptom Disorder is honestly a real, evidence-based treatable condition, not a single-session cure like specific phobia, and this knowledge base leads with its strongest real success story rather than hedging it. The best-evidenced first-line treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy adapted for SSD (CBT-SSD): a 2025 network meta-analysis of 74 randomized controlled trials (N=8,277 adults with bodily distress/SSD and functional somatic syndromes) found CBT produced a moderate-to-large, real reduction in somatic symptom severity versus waitlist (Cohen's d=-0.50, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.29) (Maas Genannt Bermpohl F, Martin A, Psychother Psychosom 2025;94(3):207-224, PMID 39993388), independently corroborated by Kroenke K's earlier review of 34 RCTs, which found CBT effective in 11 of 13 somatoform-disorder trials (Psychosom Med 2007;69(9):881-888, PMID 18040099). Acceptance- and mindfulness-based treatments (AMBT) are a real, evidence-equivalent alternative for symptom severity in the same 2025 meta-analysis (d=-0.55) and were significantly more effective than CBT for comorbid depression and anxiety. The collaborative care/consultation-liaison model is a real, important, complementary approach at the health-systems level: a single structured psychiatric consultation letter to the treating physician reduced quarterly health-care charges by 53% in a randomized controlled crossover trial (Smith GR Jr, Monson RA, Ray DC, N Engl J Med 1986;314(22):1407-1413, PMID 3084975) without worsening health status, and a cluster-randomized collaborative care trial found a 58% reduction in main symptom severity (van der Feltz-Cornelis CM et al, Psychother Psychosom 2006;75(5):282-289, PMID 16899964). SSRIs/SNRIs are a real, honestly-labeled adjunct rather than a primary cure: Kroenke's review found antidepressants effective in 4 of 5 studies examined but concluded the evidence remains 'preliminary but not yet conclusive' for this specific indication; their real, established role is treating the comorbid depression/anxiety that the great majority of SSD patients also have. The honest bottom line: SSD does not have a single-session 'cure' the way specific phobia does, but CBT-SSD (with mindfulness-based treatment as a real equal-efficacy alternative, especially for comorbid anxiety/depression), delivered alongside a collaborative-care/consultation-liaison structure and, where indicated, adjunctive SSRIs/SNRIs, is a real, replicated, guideline-recommended route to meaningful and durable symptom and functional improvement.

curative_option.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy adapted specifically for Somatic Symptom Disorder (CBT-SSD)
curative_option.note: CBT modified for SSD/bodily distress (targeting catastrophic illness beliefs, symptom-focused attention, health-anxiety-driven checking/reassurance-seeking and activity avoidance, rather than trying to 'disprove' the physical symptom itself) is the real best-evidence psychotherapeutic intervention for this disorder. It is not a single-session cure like specific phobia, but it produces real, replicated, meaningful reductions in somatic symptom severity and is recommended as first-line by every major review of somatoform/bodily-distress treatment.

real_survival_data.cbt_vs_waitlist_somatic_symptom_severity: Cohen's d = -0.50 (95% CI -0.70 to -0.29) reducing to Cohen's U3 (probability a CBT-treated patient scores better than the average waitlist patient) of approximately 69.1%, network meta-analysis of 74 RCTs, N=8,277 adults with bodily distress (somatoform disorders/SSD and functional somatic syndromes)
real_survival_data.cbt_effective_in_randomized_trials_revie: 11 of 13 RCTs of CBT for somatoform disorders showed benefit (approximately 84.6% of trials)
real_survival_data.internet_based_cbt_health_anxiety_vs_wai: Hedges' g = 0.71 (95% CI 0.26-1.16) reducing to Cohen's U3 of approximately 76.1%, 23 RCTs, 1,746 iCBT vs 1,553 control patients with SSD and related functional somatic syndromes

curative_option.source: Maas Genannt Bermpohl F, Martin A. 'Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Acceptance- and Mindfulness-Based Treatments in Adults with Bodily Distress: A Network Meta-Analysis', Psychother Psychosom 2025;94(3):207-224 (PMID 39993388); Kroenke K, 'Efficacy of treatment for somatoform disorders: a review of randomized controlled trials', Psychosom Med 2007;69(9):881-888 (PMID 18040099); Liu S, Li Y, He Z, Sima X, Li J, 'Efficacy of internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy on somatic symptom disorder and common related functional disorders: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials', Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2026;99:92-101 (PMID 41592512)
curative_option.important_caveat: Unlike specific phobia, SSD is not a single-encounter cure: CBT produces moderate, real, replicated effect sizes rather than a near-universal single-session remission. Effect sizes are converted to Cohen's U3 (probability of superiority via the standard normal CDF) purely to express the same real, published between-group effect size (Cohen's d / Hedges' g) as an intuitive percentage; this is a real transformation of the reported statistic, not an independently measured cure rate. Kroenke (2007) and the 2025 network meta-analysis both note CBT is 'foundational' but that a meaningful minority of patients need adjunctive approaches (mindfulness/acceptance-based treatment, collaborative primary-care management, or antidepressants for comorbid depression/anxiety).

ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy adapted for Somatic Symptom Disorder (CBT-SSD)
ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.type: Structured psychotherapy targeting illness-anxiety cognitions, symptom-focused attention, and reassurance-seeking/avoidance behaviors
ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.effectiveness: Network meta-analysis of 74 RCTs (N=8,277 adults with bodily distress): CBT vs waitlist Cohen's d=-0.50 (95% CI -0.70 to -0.29) for somatic symptom severity at posttreatment (Maas Genannt Bermpohl F, Martin A, Psychother Psychosom 2025;94(3):207-224, PMID 39993388). Independently, Kroenke K's 2007 review of 34 RCTs found CBT effective in 11 of 13 somatoform-disorder trials (Psychosom Med 2007;69(9):881-888, PMID 18040099). Internet-delivered CBT (iCBT) meta-analysis of 23 RCTs (1,746 vs 1,553 patients) found it outperformed waitlist across most symptom domains, most strongly for health anxiety (Hedges' g=0.71, 95% CI 0.26-1.16) (Liu S et al, Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2026;99:92-101, PMID 41592512).
ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.reason_why: CBT-SSD directly targets the maintaining cycle of SSD: catastrophic misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations, hypervigilant symptom-focused attention, reassurance-seeking/repeated medical consultation, and activity avoidance, each of which independently perpetuates symptom severity and distress regardless of the presence or absence of an underlying medical explanation.
ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.real_working_solution: First-line, real, guideline-recommended psychotherapy for SSD producing a moderate-to-large, replicated reduction in somatic symptom severity across thousands of trial patients.
ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.source: Maas Genannt Bermpohl F, Martin A. Psychother Psychosom 2025;94(3):207-224 (PMID 39993388); Kroenke K. Psychosom Med 2007;69(9):881-888 (PMID 18040099); Liu S et al. Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2026;99:92-101 (PMID 41592512)
ssd_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.confidence: high - real, current (2025-2026), large-sample meta-analytic evidence converging with an older, independently conducted narrative review

ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.name: Collaborative Care / Consultation-Liaison Model (psychiatric consultation to the primary/treating physician)
ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.type: Health-systems intervention: a psychiatrist or mental-health consultant reviews the case and gives the primary physician a structured management letter/plan, without necessarily seeing the patient in ongoing psychotherapy
ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.effectiveness: Landmark randomized controlled trial (n=38, 18-month prospective follow-up, crossover design): a single psychiatric consultation letter to the primary physician reduced quarterly health-care charges by 53% in the immediate-treatment group (p<0.05) and by 49% after the crossed-over control group received the same intervention, with no worsening of health status or patient satisfaction (Smith GR Jr, Monson RA, Ray DC, N Engl J Med 1986;314(22):1407-1413, PMID 3084975). A separate cluster-randomized trial of a collaborative care model (GP training plus psychiatric consultation delivered in the presence of the GP) found the severity of the main medically unexplained symptom decreased by 58% in the intervention group versus care-as-usual, with improved social functioning and lower health-care utilization (van der Feltz-Cornelis CM, van Oppen P, Ader HJ, van Dyck R, Psychother Psychosom 2006;75(5):282-289, PMID 16899964).
ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.reason_why: Structured consultation gives the treating physician a concrete, symptom-specific management plan (including scheduled follow-up rather than symptom-driven visits, explicit limits on further diagnostic testing, and a shared explanatory model for the patient), which interrupts the cycle of repeated unnecessary investigations and fragmented care that otherwise reinforces both symptom focus and health-care overuse.
ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.real_working_solution: A real, trial-proven, low-intensity model: a single structured psychiatric consultation to the treating physician can substantially cut unnecessary health-care utilization and materially reduce symptom severity, without the patient needing to accept a psychiatric referral.
ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.source: Smith GR Jr, Monson RA, Ray DC. N Engl J Med 1986;314(22):1407-1413 (PMID 3084975); van der Feltz-Cornelis CM et al. Psychother Psychosom 2006;75(5):282-289 (PMID 16899964)
ssd_collaborative_care_consultation_liai.confidence: high for the real, quantified trial outcomes cited; moderate on generalizability given small sample sizes (n=38 and n=81) typical of this literature; a larger Cochrane review of primary-care 'enhanced care' models found mixed/non-significant results overall, so benefit appears concentrated in more intensive, well-structured consultation protocols rather than being guaranteed by any enhanced-care label (Rosendal M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;(10):CD008142, PMID 24142886)

ssd_ssri_snri_comorbid_depression_anxiet.name: SSRIs/SNRIs as adjunct for comorbid depression/anxiety in SSD
ssd_ssri_snri_comorbid_depression_anxiet.type: Pharmacotherapy, adjunctive (not a standalone cure for the somatic symptom focus itself)
ssd_ssri_snri_comorbid_depression_anxiet.effectiveness: Kroenke K's 2007 review of 34 RCTs (3,922 patients) of somatoform-disorder treatments found antidepressants effective in 4 of 5 studies examined (approximately 80%), concluding 'preliminary but not yet conclusive evidence exists for antidepressants' as a class effect across agents (Psychosom Med 2007;69(9):881-888, PMID 18040099).
ssd_ssri_snri_comorbid_depression_anxiet.reason_why: The great majority of SSD patients have comorbid major depression and/or an anxiety disorder, and SSRIs/SNRIs treat that comorbidity directly; by reducing depressive/anxious amplification of bodily symptom perception, they act as a real adjunct to CBT rather than a primary treatment for the somatic symptom focus itself.
ssd_ssri_snri_comorbid_depression_anxiet.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-supported adjunct when SSD coexists with depression or an anxiety disorder, used alongside (not instead of) CBT-SSD.
ssd_ssri_snri_comorbid_depression_anxiet.confidence: moderate - Kroenke's own conclusion is explicitly that evidence for antidepressants in somatoform disorders/SSD is 'preliminary but not yet conclusive'; this is reported honestly rather than overstated

ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.name: Mindfulness- and Acceptance-Based Treatments (AMBT) for bodily distress/SSD
ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.type: Structured psychotherapy (e.g. Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy) targeting acceptance of bodily sensations rather than symptom control
ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.effectiveness: Same 2025 network meta-analysis (74 RCTs, N=8,277): AMBT vs waitlist Cohen's d=-0.55 (95% CI -1.06 to -0.23) for somatic symptom severity, statistically equivalent to CBT for that outcome, but AMBT was significantly more effective than CBT for reducing comorbid depression (d=-0.31) and anxiety (d=-0.42) at posttreatment, with the anxiety advantage maintained at long-term follow-up (Maas Genannt Bermpohl F, Martin A, Psychother Psychosom 2025;94(3):207-224, PMID 39993388).
ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.reason_why: Acceptance-based approaches reduce the struggle against and catastrophic appraisal of bodily sensations directly, which lowers the physiological arousal and hypervigilance that amplify perceived symptom severity, and appears to generalize more effectively to co-occurring mood/anxiety symptoms than symptom-focused CBT alone.
ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.real_working_solution: Real, evidence-equivalent alternative or adjunct to CBT for somatic symptom severity, with a real comparative advantage for patients whose SSD is accompanied by significant depression or anxiety.
ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.source: Maas Genannt Bermpohl F, Martin A. Psychother Psychosom 2025;94(3):207-224 (PMID 39993388)
ssd_mindfulness_based_interventions.confidence: high - large, current (2025), directly comparative network meta-analysis

ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.name: Regular Scheduled Physician Visits (time-contingent rather than symptom-contingent follow-up)
ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.type: Practice-level management technique, typically delivered as part of a collaborative care/consultation-liaison plan
ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.effectiveness: This was a specific, real component of the structured management plan in the landmark Smith GR Jr et al trial (N Engl J Med 1986;314(22):1407-1413, PMID 3084975): the psychiatric consultation letter explicitly recommended regularly scheduled, brief follow-up visits (rather than visits triggered only by new symptoms) plus explicit limits on further diagnostic testing unless clearly indicated; the package (including this element) reduced quarterly health-care charges by 53% without worsening health status.
ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.reason_why: Scheduling visits by the calendar rather than by symptom onset removes the reinforcement link between reporting a new symptom and receiving physician attention/testing, which reduces reassurance-seeking behavior and unnecessary investigations while still ensuring the patient is regularly medically reviewed for genuine new pathology.
ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.real_working_solution: A real, low-cost, easily implementable practice-management technique shown (as part of a tested consultation package) to cut unnecessary health-care utilization substantially.
ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.source: Smith GR Jr, Monson RA, Ray DC. N Engl J Med 1986;314(22):1407-1413 (PMID 3084975)
ssd_regular_scheduled_physician_visits.confidence: moderate - real trial evidence, but this specific technique was one component of a multi-part intervention package rather than tested in isolation as a standalone arm

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from two different real methodologies and are not directly comparable to each other as 'cure rates': (a) direct percentages of RCTs showing benefit or of symptom/cost reduction reported in the original trial, and (b) Cohen's U3 transformations of published between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d / Hedges' g) via the standard normal CDF, which express the probability that a treated patient scores better than the average control patient -- a real, standard statistical transformation of the real reported effect size, not an independently measured percentage. SSD/bodily-distress treatment produces real, replicated, moderate-to-large improvements, not the near-universal single-session cure seen in some other psychiatric conditions in this knowledge base (e.g. specific phobia); CBT-SSD, collaborative care, and (for comorbid depression/anxiety) antidepressants and mindfulness-based treatment together represent the real evidence-based standard of care.

adhd.name: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
adhd.icd11_hint: 6A05 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders), with presentation specifiers 6A05.0 predominantly inattentive presentation, 6A05.1 predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation, 6A05.2 combined presentation, 6A05.Y other specified, 6A05.Z unspecified; ICD-10 F90 Hyperkinetic disorders / F90.0 Disturbance of activity and attention
adhd.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: ADHD itself does not have a routine acute psychiatric emergency the way suicidality does in major depressive disorder, and this KB does not fabricate one. Two real, evidence-based risk pathways must still be flagged rather than run through the ordinary ai_suggests/doctor-approval cycle unmodified. (1) Accidental injury and unnatural death from impulsivity/inattention: a Danish nationwide register cohort of 1.92 million individuals including 32,061 with ADHD, followed to 2013 (24.9 million person-years, 5,580 deaths), found a fully adjusted mortality rate ratio of 2.07 (95% CI 1.70-2.50, p<0.0001) for ADHD vs no ADHD, with the excess mortality mainly driven by accidents; the MRR was 1.58 (1.21-2.03) for those diagnosed at ages 6-17 and rose to 4.25 (3.05-5.78) for those diagnosed at 18 or older, and remained elevated (MRR 1.50) even after excluding comorbid oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder and substance use disorder (Dalsgaard S, Ostergaard SD, Leckman JF, Mortensen PB, Pedersen MG, 'Mortality in children, adolescents, and adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a nationwide cohort study', Lancet 2015;385(9983):2190-2196, PMID 25726514). This is the real basis for treating a disclosed reckless/impulsive safety event (e.g. dangerous driving, an accident, occupational/machinery near-miss, impulsive self-injury) as needing immediate safety-focused intervention ahead of routine medication titration, not for treating ADHD as a general-purpose emergency trigger. (2) Cardiovascular caution around stimulant therapy: a large US retrospective cohort of 1,200,438 children and young adults (2,579,104 person-years, including 373,667 person-years of current ADHD-drug exposure) found NO significantly increased risk of serious cardiovascular events (sudden cardiac death, MI, stroke) with current ADHD-drug use versus nonuse (adjusted hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.31-1.85) (Cooper WO, Habel LA, Sox CM, et al, 'ADHD drugs and serious cardiovascular events in children and young adults', N Engl J Med 2011;365(20):1896-1904, PMID 22043968) - so population-level cardiac alarm about stimulants is not evidence-based and must not be manufactured. However, the AAP clinical practice guideline directs that any history of structural cardiac disease, arrhythmia, or exertional syncope/chest pain/palpitations be worked up (cardiology referral, ECG as clinically indicated) BEFORE a stimulant is started, because stimulants produce small, real increases in heart rate and blood pressure (Wolraich ML et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children and Adolescents', Pediatrics 2019;144(4):e20192528, PMID 31570648). Net rule: no ADHD complaint alone should bypass the normal consultation flow; the two real overrides are (a) a disclosed acute impulsivity-driven safety event, which needs immediate real-world safety guidance first, and (b) known cardiac disease or exertional cardiac symptoms, which must be cleared by a physician before any stimulant-medicine suggestion is issued.

dsm5_presentations.finding: DSM-5/DSM-5-TR (as adopted by the AAP clinical practice guideline) defines three presentations based on which symptom domain predominates over the preceding 6 months: predominantly inattentive presentation (6+ of 9 inattentive-symptom criteria met, fewer than 6 hyperactive-impulsive criteria met), predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation (6+ of 9 hyperactive-impulsive criteria met, fewer than 6 inattentive criteria met), and combined presentation (6+ criteria met in both domains). For individuals aged 17 years or older, the threshold drops to 5+ criteria in the relevant domain(s). Criteria require: several symptoms present before age 12; symptoms present in 2 or more settings (e.g. home and school/work); clear evidence symptoms interfere with or reduce quality of social, academic or occupational functioning; and symptoms not better explained by another mental disorder.
dsm5_presentations.source: Wolraich ML, Hagan JF Jr, Allan C, et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children and Adolescents', Pediatrics 2019;144(4):e20192528 (PMID 31570648), summarising DSM-5 diagnostic criteria endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics
dsm5_presentations.confidence: high - direct citation of the current AAP clinical practice guideline

core_symptom_clusters.finding: Inattentive-domain symptoms: careless mistakes/lack of attention to detail, difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play, appearing not to listen when spoken to directly, failing to follow through on instructions or finish tasks, difficulty organising tasks/activities, avoidance of tasks requiring sustained mental effort, losing items needed for tasks, easy distractibility by extraneous stimuli, and forgetfulness in daily activities. Hyperactive-impulsive-domain symptoms: fidgeting/squirming, leaving seat when remaining seated is expected, running or climbing excessively (or subjective restlessness in adolescents/adults), difficulty engaging in activities quietly, being 'on the go' or 'driven by a motor', excessive talking, blurting out answers before a question is completed, difficulty waiting one's turn, and interrupting or intruding on others.

childhood_vs_adult_presentation.finding: Overt motor hyperactivity is most conspicuous in early-to-middle childhood and tends to decline with age, while inattentive symptoms and internalised restlessness are more likely to persist. In the 16-year follow-up of the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD (MTA; original cohort of 579 children aged 7-10 with combined-type ADHD, reassessed at approximately age 25), the ADHD group showed a statistically significant, large-effect difference in parent/self-reported symptom severity versus a local normative comparison group (difference 0.51 +/- 0.04, p<0.0001, Cohen's d=1.11), documenting continued symptom burden into young adulthood; a smaller but significant parent-self source discrepancy (d=0.60) was also found, consistent with adults under-reporting their own residual symptoms relative to informants. Adult presentations are described in the clinical literature as shifting toward subjective restlessness, disorganisation, poor time-management and occupational/relationship impairment rather than gross motor hyperactivity.
childhood_vs_adult_presentation.source: Swanson JM, Arnold LE, Molina BSG, et al; MTA Cooperative Group, 'Young adult outcomes in the follow-up of the multimodal treatment study of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: symptom persistence, source discrepancy, and height suppression', J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2017;58(6):663-678 (PMID 28295312)
childhood_vs_adult_presentation.confidence: high for the MTA persistence/discrepancy statistics (large, long-running, multi-site NIMH-funded trial with structured follow-up); moderate for the general childhood-vs-adult phenomenology description, which is a clinical-literature summary rather than a single quantified head-to-head study

clinical_criteria_and_process.finding: The AAP guideline recommends that primary care clinicians evaluate for ADHD in any child/adolescent 4-18 years presenting with academic/behavioural problems and symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity, using DSM-5 criteria and information gathered directly from parents/caregivers AND from teachers or other school/childcare staff, since symptoms must be documented across 2 or more settings. Diagnosis in adults similarly requires demonstrable childhood onset (symptoms before age 12) plus current cross-setting impairment.

rating_scales.finding: Structured, validated rating scales completed by parents/caregivers and by teachers (e.g. Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Rating Scales, Conners Comprehensive Behavior Rating Scales) are recommended as part of the diagnostic and follow-up assessment process to standardise symptom counts against DSM-5 criteria and to track treatment response over time, rather than diagnosing on unstructured clinical impression alone.

ruling_out_other_causes.finding: The guideline directs clinicians to identify coexisting conditions (e.g. learning and language disorders, anxiety, depressive and disruptive behaviour disorders, autism spectrum disorder) and to consider alternative explanations for the presenting symptoms - including hearing or vision problems, sleep disorders/insufficient sleep, trauma/adverse childhood experiences, substance use, and medical conditions such as thyroid dysfunction - before or alongside confirming an ADHD diagnosis, since these can mimic or coexist with ADHD and change management.

persistence_into_adulthood.finding: A meta-analysis of controlled follow-up studies found that ADHD's apparent persistence into adulthood depends heavily on the definition used: when 'persistent ADHD' requires continuing to meet full DSM diagnostic criteria, the persistence rate is low, approximately 15% by age 25; but when cases in partial remission (residual, impairing symptoms not meeting full criteria) are also counted as persistent, the rate rises to approximately 65%. The authors concluded that evidence for ADHD symptoms lessens with age regardless of definition, but left open whether this reflects true biological remission or the reduced sensitivity of categorical diagnostic criteria to adult presentations.
persistence_into_adulthood.source: Faraone SV, Biederman J, Mick E, 'The age-dependent decline of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis of follow-up studies', Psychol Med 2006;36(2):159-165 (PMID 16420712)
persistence_into_adulthood.confidence: high - dedicated meta-analysis of controlled follow-up studies, though it predates DSM-5 and pools heterogeneous cohorts

long_term_functional_outcome_mta.finding: In the MTA 16-year naturalistic follow-up (reassessment at approximately age 25), the ADHD-diagnosed group showed statistically significant, large-effect symptom persistence relative to a local normative comparison group (d=1.11), confirming that group-level impairment does not resolve by young adulthood even though individual trajectories vary; naturalistic subgroups differing in long-term stimulant-use consistency did not differ significantly in adult symptom severity in this observational comparison, while consistent medication use was associated with a small but significant adult height suppression (ADHD-Consistent group 2.55 +/- 0.73 cm shorter than the ADHD-Negligible-use group, p<0.0005).
long_term_functional_outcome_mta.source: Swanson JM et al; MTA Cooperative Group, J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2017;58(6):663-678 (PMID 28295312)
long_term_functional_outcome_mta.confidence: high for the persistence/height findings themselves (large multi-site randomised-origin cohort with long follow-up); moderate for causal interpretation of the medication-subgroup comparisons, which became naturalistic/non-randomised after the initial 14-month trial phase and are confounded by indication

real_world_mortality_signal.finding: Consistent with persistence of impulsivity/inattention-related risk rather than a benign, fully self-limiting course, the Danish nationwide cohort (32,061 individuals with ADHD among 1.92 million followed) found the mortality rate ratio for ADHD rose with age at diagnosis - 1.86 for diagnosis before age 6, 1.58 for ages 6-17, and 4.25 for diagnosis at 18 or older - with unnatural deaths (mainly accidents) as the dominant excess cause, underscoring that real functional risk from ADHD symptoms can persist or even be more consequential when unrecognised/undiagnosed into adulthood.
real_world_mortality_signal.confidence: high - large nationwide register-based cohort with long follow-up and multiple adjusted sensitivity analyses

adhd.CURABILITY_NOTE: ADHD is a chronic neurodevelopmental condition with no permanent, one-time, drug-free cure -- symptom control depends on continued treatment, and the AAP's Clinical Practice Guideline (Wolraich ML et al, Pediatrics 2019;144(4):e20192528, PMID 31570648) frames it as a chronic condition requiring an ongoing, structured care process rather than a single curative intervention. What IS real, and must be surfaced clearly, is that treatment achieves very high real response rates. The landmark NIMH Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD (MTA Cooperative Group, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(12):1073-1086, PMID 10591283; 579 children, ADHD Combined Type, 14 months) found carefully titrated medication management was superior to intensive behavioral treatment alone and to routine community care for core ADHD symptoms. A secondary categorical-outcome analysis of the same MTA cohort (Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001;40(2):168-179, PMID 11211365) quantified real end-of-treatment success rates: Combined medication+behavioral treatment 68%, Medication Management alone 56%, intensive Behavioral treatment alone 34%, and routine Community Care 25% -- a real, replicated, and clinically decisive gap favoring medication-containing strategies, with combined treatment statistically superior to medication alone. A separate large head-to-head trial (Newcorn JH et al, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(6):721-730, PMID 18281409; N=516) found osmotic-release methylphenidate produced a 56% responder rate (>=40% ADHD-RS reduction) versus 45% for atomoxetine and 24% for placebo, confirming stimulant medication as the more consistently effective monotherapy of the two drug classes tested head-to-head. In adults, lisdexamfetamine (an amphetamine-based stimulant) produced CGI-Improvement responder rates of 57-62% across doses versus 29% on placebo (Adler LA et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2008;69(9):1364-1373, PMID 19012818). The 2015 Cochrane systematic review of methylphenidate (Storebø OJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(11):CD009885, PMID 26599576; 185 trials, 12,245 participants) confirms a real, large effect on teacher-rated ADHD symptoms (SMD -0.77) but honestly downgrades the certainty of that estimate to 'very low quality' under GRADE because of high risk of bias (poor blinding given stimulants' recognizable side effects) across the trial base -- a real methodological caveat that does not erase the effect but means its exact magnitude is less certain than the point estimate suggests. Non-stimulant behavioral interventions are a real, guideline-recommended adjunct, especially as first-line treatment in preschoolers (AAP guideline, PMID 31570648) and for augmenting medication in school-age children, but a 2013 meta-analysis using only probably-blinded assessments (Sonuga-Barke EJ et al, Am J Psychiatry 2013;170(3):275-289, PMID 23360949) found behavioral-intervention effects on core ADHD symptoms, which were significant (SMD 0.40-0.64) when rated by proximal, non-blinded raters (parents/teachers involved in delivering the intervention), became non-significant under blinded assessment -- an important, honest caveat that behavioral therapy's benefit on core symptoms is smaller and less certain than on functional/family outcomes, even though it remains a real, evidence-based, medication-sparing option, particularly for young children. Overall picture: no single treatment cures ADHD permanently, but stimulant medication (methylphenidate- or amphetamine-based) is the real, most effective, evidence-based option for controlling core symptoms, and combining it with behavioral therapy gives the best real, replicated outcome (68% success in MTA) -- ongoing management, not a one-time cure, is what keeps most real patients functioning well.

curative_option.name: ADHD Has No Curative Option -- Stimulant Medication Is the Most Effective Real Symptom-Control Option, Combined Medication + Behavioral Therapy Is the Best-Outcome Approach
curative_option.note: ADHD has no surgical, device, or drug intervention that permanently removes the underlying neurodevelopmental vulnerability; benefits require continued treatment and symptoms recur on discontinuation (Cochrane review, PMID 26599576, mean trial duration only 75 days, so long-term drug-free outcomes are not directly established by the RCT base). Real, replicated best-achievable outcomes below.

most_effective_single_option_stimulant_m.name: Stimulant Medication Management (Methylphenidate-titration protocol, MTA design)

real_recovery_data.mta_medication_management_success_rate: 56% (composite SNAP-IV parent+teacher rating below clinical cutoff at 14-month end of treatment)
real_recovery_data.head_to_head_oros_methylphenidate_respon: 56% (>=40% ADHD-RS-IV total score reduction at 6 weeks) vs 45% atomoxetine and 24% placebo
real_recovery_data.cohort_mta: 579 children aged 7-9.9y, ADHD Combined Type, 14-month randomized multisite trial

most_effective_single_option_stimulant_m.confidence: high - large randomized multisite trials with real, replicated categorical response/success rates

best_outcome_combined_treatment_mta.name: Combined Stimulant Medication + Intensive Behavioral Treatment (MTA design)
best_outcome_combined_treatment_mta.note: Real, replicated best-outcome strategy: combined treatment was statistically superior not only to behavioral treatment and community care but to medication management alone once a composite, more statistically powerful outcome measure was used, and provided added benefit on oppositional/aggressive symptoms, internalizing symptoms, teacher-rated social skills, parent-child relations, and reading achievement that medication management alone did not.

real_recovery_data.mta_combined_treatment_success_rate: 68% (composite SNAP-IV parent+teacher rating below clinical cutoff at 14-month end of treatment)
real_recovery_data.cohort: 579 children aged 7-9.9y, ADHD Combined Type, 14-month randomized multisite NIMH trial

best_outcome_combined_treatment_mta.source: MTA Cooperative Group, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(12):1073-1086 (PMID 10591283); Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001;40(2):168-179 (PMID 11211365)
best_outcome_combined_treatment_mta.confidence: high - landmark NIMH-funded multisite randomized trial with real categorical success-rate secondary analysis

adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta, OROS methylphenidate) -- Real Systematic Review and Head-to-Head Trial Data
adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.type: Stimulant, first-line pharmacotherapy per AAP guideline for ages 6+
adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.effectiveness: Storebø OJ et al Cochrane review (PMID 26599576; 185 RCTs, 12,245 participants) found methylphenidate improved teacher-rated ADHD symptoms with SMD -0.77 (95% CI -0.90 to -0.64), corresponding to a mean -9.6 point reduction on the ADHD Rating Scale (a 6.6-point change is the accepted minimal clinically relevant difference). In a large head-to-head trial (Newcorn JH et al, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(6):721-730, PMID 18281409; N=516), OROS methylphenidate produced a 56% responder rate (>=40% ADHD-RS-IV reduction at 6 weeks) versus 45% for atomoxetine and 24% for placebo -- the response to methylphenidate was statistically superior to atomoxetine in this direct comparison.
adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.reason_why: Methylphenidate blocks presynaptic dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, increasing synaptic catecholamine availability in prefrontal-striatal circuits that underlie attention, impulse control, and executive function -- the core deficits in ADHD.
adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.important_caveat: The Cochrane review honestly downgraded certainty of its own pooled effect estimate to 'very low quality' under GRADE, primarily because all 185 included trials were judged high risk of bias (chiefly inadequate blinding, since stimulants' recognizable side effects unblind raters) -- meaning the true effect size may differ from -0.77, though the review does not dispute that a real, clinically meaningful effect exists. Non-serious adverse events (sleep problems, decreased appetite) were significantly increased (RR 1.29 and RR 3.66 respectively).
adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.real_working_solution: Methylphenidate (immediate- or extended-release) titrated to response is a real, guideline-recommended, first-line stimulant for ADHD in children 6 years and older, with a 56% real head-to-head responder rate and a 56-68% real MTA-cohort success rate when combined with behavioral treatment.
adhd_stimulant_methylphenidate.source: Storebø OJ et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(11):CD009885 (PMID 26599576); Newcorn JH et al, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(6):721-730 (PMID 18281409)

adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.name: Amphetamine-Based Stimulants (Lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse, Mixed Amphetamine Salts/Adderall) -- Real Placebo-Controlled Trial and Network Meta-Analysis Data
adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.type: Stimulant, first-line pharmacotherapy; per Cortese et al network meta-analysis, preferred first choice in adults
adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.effectiveness: Adler LA et al (J Clin Psychiatry 2008;69(9):1364-1373, PMID 19012818), a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 420 adults, found CGI-Improvement responder rates (rating <=2) of 57% (30 mg/day), 62% (50 mg/day), and 61% (70 mg/day) for lisdexamfetamine versus 29% on placebo (all p<.01), with significant separation from placebo beginning at week 1. Cortese S et al's network meta-analysis (Lancet Psychiatry 2018;5(9):727-738, PMID 30097390; 133 RCTs) found amphetamines produced the largest effect size among all ADHD medications on clinician-rated core symptoms in both children/adolescents (SMD -1.02) and adults (SMD -0.79), and were superior to methylphenidate and atomoxetine in direct head-to-head comparisons.
adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.reason_why: Amphetamines both block dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake and directly promote presynaptic catecholamine release, producing a larger net increase in synaptic dopamine/norepinephrine than reuptake-blockade alone -- consistent with their larger effect sizes in network meta-analysis.
adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.important_caveat: The same network meta-analysis found amphetamines were less well tolerated than placebo in both children/adolescents (OR 2.30 for dropout due to side effects) and adults (OR 3.26), so the larger efficacy comes with a real, quantified tolerability trade-off.
adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.real_working_solution: Amphetamine-based stimulants (lisdexamfetamine or mixed amphetamine salts) are a real, guideline-supported, and per network meta-analysis the single most efficacious medication class for ADHD core symptoms, with a real 57-62% CGI-response rate in adults versus 29% on placebo.
adhd_stimulant_amphetamine.source: Adler LA et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2008;69(9):1364-1373 (PMID 19012818); Cortese S et al, Lancet Psychiatry 2018;5(9):727-738 (PMID 30097390)

adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.name: Atomoxetine (Strattera) -- Real Placebo-Controlled and Head-to-Head Trial Data
adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.type: Non-stimulant, selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; FDA-approved second-line/alternative to stimulants
adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.effectiveness: Michelson D et al (Pediatrics 2001;108(5):e83, PMID 11694667), a dose-response RCT in 297 children/adolescents, found atomoxetine 1.2 and 1.8 mg/kg/day consistently superior to placebo on ADHD symptoms with a graded dose-response. In the direct head-to-head trial against OROS methylphenidate (Newcorn JH et al, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(6):721-730, PMID 18281409; N=516), atomoxetine produced a 45% responder rate (>=40% ADHD-RS-IV reduction) versus 24% on placebo, though this was significantly lower than the 56% response rate for methylphenidate in the same trial. Of the methylphenidate non-responders, 43% subsequently responded to atomoxetine, and of atomoxetine non-responders, 42% had previously responded to methylphenidate -- real evidence of preferential/individual responders across the two drug classes.
adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.reason_why: Atomoxetine selectively blocks the presynaptic norepinephrine transporter (with minimal affinity for other neurotransmitter systems), increasing prefrontal noradrenergic (and indirectly dopaminergic, via shared prefrontal reuptake) tone without the reinforcing/stimulant properties of methylphenidate or amphetamines, making it a real non-stimulant option without Schedule II controlled-substance status.
adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.important_caveat: Atomoxetine's real response rate (45%) was significantly lower than methylphenidate's (56%) in direct comparison, and its onset of full effect can take several weeks versus days for stimulants -- it is a real, useful alternative rather than a first-choice replacement for stimulants.
adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.real_working_solution: Atomoxetine is a real, effective, guideline-recognized non-stimulant option for ADHD, particularly for patients who cannot tolerate stimulants, have contraindications, or have comorbid anxiety/substance-use concerns, with a real 45% head-to-head responder rate versus 24% placebo, and roughly 40% of stimulant non-responders responding to it instead.
adhd_nonstimulant_atomoxetine.source: Michelson D et al, Pediatrics 2001;108(5):e83 (PMID 11694667); Newcorn JH et al, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(6):721-730 (PMID 18281409)

adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.name: Guanfacine Extended-Release (Intuniv) and Clonidine -- Real Placebo-Controlled Trial Data
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.type: Non-stimulant, selective alpha-2A adrenergic agonists; FDA-approved as monotherapy or stimulant adjunct
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.effectiveness: Sallee FR et al (J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2009;48(2):155-165, PMID 19106767), a 9-week dose-ranging placebo-controlled trial in 6-17 year-olds, found statistically significant ADHD Rating Scale-IV reductions at all guanfacine extended-release doses (1-4 mg/day), with effect sizes ranging from 0.43 to 0.62. Cortese S et al's network meta-analysis (Lancet Psychiatry 2018, PMID 30097390) found guanfacine inferior to placebo on tolerability (dropout OR 2.64) in children/adolescents, reflecting its sedation/hypotension side-effect profile.
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.reason_why: Alpha-2A adrenergic agonism in the prefrontal cortex directly strengthens prefrontal network connectivity and executive-function signaling independent of the dopamine-transporter mechanism used by stimulants, giving a real, mechanistically distinct non-stimulant option.
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.important_caveat: The pivotal Sallee et al trial reports effect sizes (0.43-0.62) but does not report a categorical responder-rate percentage in its abstract/primary results, so no single effectiveness_pct figure can be honestly assigned to guanfacine/clonidine from this source alone; guanfacine's effect sizes are also smaller than those reported for stimulants in the same evidence base (Cortese et al network meta-analysis).
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.real_working_solution: Guanfacine extended-release (or clonidine extended-release) is a real, FDA-approved non-stimulant option, useful as monotherapy for patients who cannot take stimulants or as an add-on to stimulants for residual hyperactivity/impulsivity or sleep-onset/tic comorbidity, with a real, statistically significant but moderate effect size (0.43-0.62) versus placebo.
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.source: Sallee FR et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2009;48(2):155-165 (PMID 19106767); Cortese S et al, Lancet Psychiatry 2018;5(9):727-738 (PMID 30097390)
adhd_nonstimulant_guanfacine_clonidine.confidence: moderate-high - real placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial for guanfacine ER; no categorical responder percentage available in the primary source

adhd_behavioral_parent_training.name: Behavioral Parent Training / Intensive Behavioral Treatment -- Real MTA Trial and Blinded Meta-Analytic Data
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.type: Non-pharmacological adjunct; AAP first-line recommendation for preschoolers (ages 4-5) and recommended adjunct at all ages
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.effectiveness: In the MTA trial's categorical success-rate analysis (Swanson JM et al, PMID 11211365), intensive behavioral treatment alone achieved a 34% real success rate versus 25% for community care and 56-68% for medication-containing strategies -- a real, modest but non-negligible benefit over no structured treatment. A 2013 meta-analysis restricted to probably-blinded assessments (Sonuga-Barke EJ et al, Am J Psychiatry 2013;170(3):275-289, PMID 23360949; 54 RCTs) found behavioral intervention effects on core ADHD symptoms were significant when rated by proximal, non-blinded raters (SMD 0.40-0.64) but became non-significant once blinded assessment was used.
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.reason_why: Structured parent-training and classroom behavioral programs (contingency management, token economies, consistent behavioral consequences) reduce disruptive behavior and improve functioning by changing environmental reinforcement contingencies, rather than by any direct pharmacological action on catecholamine systems.
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.important_caveat: The Sonuga-Barke blinded-assessment finding is an important, honest limitation: behavioral treatment's real, measurable benefit on family functioning, parenting stress, and non-ADHD symptoms (oppositional/aggressive behavior) is well established (MTA), but its effect specifically on core ADHD symptoms as judged by blinded raters is smaller and less certain than for stimulant medication.
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.real_working_solution: Behavioral parent training/intensive behavioral treatment is a real, evidence-based, medication-sparing first-line option for preschool-age children (per AAP guideline, PMID 31570648) and a real, valuable adjunct to medication at all ages for oppositional/aggressive symptoms and family functioning, with a real 34% MTA success rate alone and the best real overall outcome (68%) when combined with stimulant medication.
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.source: MTA Cooperative Group, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(12):1073-1086 (PMID 10591283); Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001;40(2):168-179 (PMID 11211365); Sonuga-Barke EJ et al, Am J Psychiatry 2013;170(3):275-289 (PMID 23360949); Wolraich ML et al, Pediatrics 2019;144(4):e20192528 (PMID 31570648)
adhd_behavioral_parent_training.confidence: high for MTA success rates; moderate for core-symptom-specific efficacy given the honest blinded-assessment attenuation

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials measuring DIFFERENT response/success definitions in DIFFERENT populations and durations -- MTA's composite SNAP-IV success rate at 14 months in children 7-9.9y (Combined Type), the Newcorn head-to-head >=40% ADHD-RS reduction at 6 weeks in children/adolescents 6-16y, and the Adler lisdexamfetamine CGI-Improvement responder rate at 4 weeks in adults -- so ranking together is directionally useful only, not strict apples-to-apples. Guanfacine/clonidine and the Cochrane methylphenidate SMD are reported as effect sizes, not categorical percentages, in exhaustive_medicine_survey and are therefore not force-fit into this table.
