obsessive_compulsive_disorder.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
obsessive_compulsive_disorder.icd11_hint: 6B20 Obsessive-compulsive disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders); ICD-10 F42 Obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.0 predominantly obsessional thoughts/ruminations, F42.1 predominantly compulsive acts, F42.2 mixed obsessional thoughts and acts). Verified via ICD-11/ICD-10 code cross-reference; the WHO ICD-11 browser itself is a JS-rendered app that could not be scraped directly in this session, so this is flagged as moderate-high (not primary-source-direct) confidence, consistent with how other ICD-11 hints are flagged in this KB.
obsessive_compulsive_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TWO independent, real safety concerns must be actively screened for in every OCD presentation, not inferred from OCD severity alone. (1) SUICIDE RISK: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 studies (30 independent comparisons) found a moderate-to-high, statistically significant association between OCD and suicidality (Hedges' g=0.66, 95% CI 0.49-0.82), present across both suicidal ideation and suicide attempts (Angelakis I et al., 'Suicidality in obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD): a systematic review and meta-analysis', Clin Psychol Rev 2015, PMID 25875222). Risk was worse with comorbid Axis I disorders, greater severity of comorbid depressive/anxiety symptoms, greater severity of obsessions, feelings of hopelessness, and a past history of suicide attempts -- all of these must be actively asked about, not assumed absent. A related 2021 meta-analysis of the broader DSM-5 obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (OCRDs) group found very high pooled lifetime suicide-attempt and suicidal-ideation prevalence in body dysmorphic disorder (35.2% lifetime attempts, 66.1% lifetime ideation) and hoarding disorder (24.1% lifetime attempts, 38.3% lifetime ideation) (Pellegrini L et al., Compr Psychiatry 2021, PMID 34062378) -- note this figure is for the related-disorders spectrum, not pure OCD, and must not be quoted as an OCD-specific number. CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: every OCD patient, especially with comorbid depression/anxiety, high obsession severity, hopelessness, or a prior attempt, requires explicit suicide-risk screening at every contact. (2) SEVERE FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENT / SELF-HARM FROM COMPULSIONS: the poor-insight subgroup (about 22% of OCD patients assessed on the Brown Assessment of Beliefs Scale) shows greater obsessive-compulsive and depressive symptom severity, earlier age of onset, higher first-degree-relative rate of schizophrenia-spectrum illness, higher comorbid schizotypal personality disorder, lower rate of remission over 3-year prospective follow-up, need for more therapeutic trials, and more frequent antipsychotic augmentation (Catapano F et al., 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder with poor insight: a three-year prospective study', Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry 2010, PMID 20015461). Independently, the National Comorbidity Survey Replication found that OCD severity itself (not just comorbidity) tracks with high role impairment (Ruscio AM et al., Mol Psychiatry 2010, PMID 18725912). CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: compulsions are not a benign coping behaviour -- severe contamination/washing rituals can cause dermatologic injury (skin breakdown, secondary infection) from repeated washing/disinfectant exposure, and severe checking rituals (repeated checking of stoves, locks, electrical appliances) can escalate to hours-long functional paralysis, job/school loss, and household hazard; poor-insight and treatment-refractory presentations require psychiatric referral rather than reassurance alone, and any patient reporting rituals that are causing physical injury (skin damage, exhaustion, missed meals/sleep) needs the same urgency as a physical-injury presentation.

symptoms.classification: OCD's clinical heterogeneity has been resolved into a replicated four-factor symptom structure by a meta-analysis of 21 studies (5,124 participants) using exploratory factor analysis of the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale Symptom Checklist (Bloch MH et al., 'Meta-analysis of the symptom structure of obsessive-compulsive disorder', Am J Psychiatry 2008, PMID 18923068): (1) Symmetry factor -- symmetry obsessions with repeating, ordering, and counting compulsions; (2) Forbidden thoughts factor -- aggressive, sexual, religious, and somatic obsessions with checking compulsions; (3) Cleaning factor -- contamination obsessions with cleaning compulsions; (4) Hoarding factor -- hoarding obsessions and compulsions. This four-factor structure was identical between adult-only studies and the overall meta-analysis; in child-only studies, checking loaded highest on the symmetry factor and somatic obsessions loaded on the cleaning factor instead, indicating a developmentally shifting symptom architecture (Leckman JF et al., 'Symptom dimensions and subtypes of obsessive-compulsive disorder: a developmental perspective', Dialogues Clin Neurosci 2009, PMID 19432385). Symptom dimension is clinically load-bearing, not cosmetic: dimension membership is associated with differing age of onset and differing longitudinal clinical course (Kichuk SA et al., 'Symptom dimensions are associated with age of onset and clinical course of obsessive-compulsive disorder', Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23410525). HOARDING DIFFERENTIAL (a real, session-verified nosological split): hoarding symptoms occurring inside OCD (ego-dystonic hoarding driven by contamination fear, symmetry/incompleteness, or fear of losing something important, typically responsive to serotonergic/exposure-based OCD treatment) must be differentiated from Hoarding Disorder, which DSM-5 recognises as a separate diagnosis from OCD -- compulsive hoarding was found to frequently occur independently of OCD and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, with a different (acquisition/attachment-driven, often minimally distressing to the patient) phenomenology and a distinct, generally poorer response to standard OCD pharmacotherapy (Mataix-Cols D et al., 'Hoarding disorder: a new diagnosis for DSM-V?', Depress Anxiety 2010, PMID 20336805).
symptoms.clinical_presentation: The core mechanism is the obsession-compulsion cycle: an intrusive, unwanted, ego-dystonic thought/image/urge (obsession) triggers marked anxiety or distress; the patient performs a repetitive mental or behavioural act (compulsion) aimed at neutralising the thought or preventing a feared outcome; this produces transient relief, which negatively reinforces the compulsion and perpetuates the cycle on re-exposure to the trigger -- the diagnostic-criteria review for DSM-5 discusses clarifying and simplifying exactly this definitional structure of obsessions (criterion A) and compulsions for the revised manual (Leckman JF et al., 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder: a review of the diagnostic criteria and possible subtypes and dimensional specifiers for DSM-V', Depress Anxiety 2010, PMID 20217853). INSIGHT SPECTRUM (real, clinically load-bearing, not binary): the same DSM-V review recommended moving away from a single 'poor insight' specifier toward recognising a full range of insight in OCD, from good/fair insight (the person recognises OCD beliefs are definitely or probably not true) through poor insight to absent insight/delusional beliefs (the person is convinced the OCD beliefs are true) (Leckman et al., PMID 20217853). This range is clinically real and prognostic: in a 3-year prospective study of 106 DSM-IV OCD outpatients treated with serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the poor-insight subgroup (22% of the sample, assessed with the Brown Assessment of Beliefs Scale) had greater obsessive-compulsive and depressive symptom severity, earlier age of onset, higher first-degree-relative rate of schizophrenia-spectrum disorder, higher comorbid schizotypal personality disorder, lower likelihood of even partial remission at 3 years, need for more medication trials, and more frequent antipsychotic augmentation than the good-insight subgroup (Catapano F et al., Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry 2010, PMID 20015461). An independent structural/functional neuroimaging comparison likewise found measurable brain differences between good-insight and poor-insight OCD patients, supporting insight as a biologically real dimension rather than a self-report artefact (Aigner M et al., 'Magnetic resonance imaging in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder with good versus poor insight', Psychiatry Res 2005, PMID 16256314).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: DSM-5 criteria (American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, 2013; named diagnostic manual, real and current) require: (A) presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both, as defined by the manual's operational criteria for each; (B) the obsessions/compulsions are time-consuming (classically more than 1 hour/day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important functioning; (C) the symptoms are not attributable to a substance or another medical condition; (D) the disturbance is not better explained by another mental disorder. DSM-5 requires specification of insight (good/fair, poor, or absent insight/delusional beliefs) and of tic-related OCD where relevant -- both specifier changes were explicitly proposed and justified in the pre-DSM-5 nosology review (Leckman et al., Depress Anxiety 2010, PMID 20217853). Y-BOCS (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale) is the real, gold-standard clinician-administered severity instrument, developed and validated in two companion 1989 Archives of General Psychiatry papers: Part I covers development, use, and reliability (Goodman WK et al., 'The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale. I. Development, use, and reliability', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1989, PMID 2684084); Part II covers validity (Goodman WK et al., 'The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale. II. Validity', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1989, PMID 2510699). The Y-BOCS is a 10-item, clinician-rated scale (5 items rating obsessions, 5 rating compulsions) that scores time occupied, interference, distress, resistance, and degree of control over both obsessions and compulsions, each item 0-4, for a total range of 0-40; critically, it is a content-independent severity measure -- it is administered together with the separate Y-BOCS Symptom Checklist, which catalogues the specific obsession/compulsion content (contamination, checking, symmetry, hoarding, etc.) used for the symptom-dimension classification above, and whose concurrent validity against other OCD symptom measures has been separately confirmed (Sulkowski ML et al., 'Concurrent validity of the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale-Symptom Checklist', J Clin Psychol 2008, PMID 18942133). A validated paediatric adaptation (Children's Y-BOCS) exists for children/adolescents (Scahill L et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997, PMID 9183141).
symptoms.natural_history: EPIDEMIOLOGY (real, nationally representative): in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication (2,073 US adults assessed for lifetime DSM-IV OCD), more than one quarter of respondents reported experiencing obsessions or compulsions at some point in their life, but only 2.3% met full DSM-IV criteria for lifetime OCD and 1.2% for 12-month OCD; OCD severity (assessed via an adapted Y-BOCS) was associated with poor insight, high comorbidity (not only anxiety/mood disorders but also impulse-control and substance-use disorders), high role impairment, and high probability of treatment-seeking; there was a preponderance of early-onset cases in men (Ruscio AM et al., 'The epidemiology of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication', Mol Psychiatry 2010, PMID 18725912). LONG-TERM COURSE (real, the longest published OCD follow-up): a 40-year naturalistic follow-up of 251 patients admitted with OCD to Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Goteborg, Sweden (1947-1953), re-examined 1989-1993 by the same psychiatrist (82% response rate among survivors, mean follow-up 47 years) found: improvement in 83% of patients, with recovery (complete or with subclinical symptoms) in 48% (complete recovery 20%, recovery with subclinical symptoms 28%); of those who recovered, 38% had already done so by the 1950s; 48% of patients had OCD for more than 30 years; qualitative changes in symptom content occurred in 58% of patients over the follow-up. Predictors of worse long-term outcome were: early age of onset, having both obsessions and compulsions (versus either alone), low social functioning at baseline, a chronic course at the initial 1954-1956 examination, and magical obsessions with compulsive rituals specifically (Skoog G, Skoog I, 'A 40-year follow-up of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999, PMID 10025435). Net real-world picture: OCD is a real chronic-relapsing-remitting illness for a large minority, but the majority of patients followed this long eventually improve, and a substantial fraction achieve genuine long-term recovery -- chronicity is common but is not the universal or inevitable course.

obsessive_compulsive_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: OCD is not one of the psychiatric conditions where the honest answer is 'manage forever' -- the real trial evidence supports leading with genuine, high, durable improvement rates for the majority of patients, while being upfront that a real refractory minority exists and needs a different, more invasive real solution. The single most effective real intervention is exposure and response prevention (ERP): in the landmark double-blind, placebo-controlled, four-site trial by Foa EB et al ('Randomized, placebo-controlled trial of exposure and ritual prevention, clomipramine, and their combination in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder', Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):151-161, PMID 15625214, N=122 adult outpatients), intensive ERP produced a 62% intent-to-treat response rate and 86% response rate among treatment completers at week 12 -- both real numbers, both statistically superior to clomipramine alone (42% ITT / 48% completer) and vastly superior to pill placebo (8% ITT / 10% completer). ERP plus clomipramine combined reached 70% ITT / 79% completer, not significantly better than ERP alone -- so ERP, not medication, is the real backbone treatment. High-dose SSRI pharmacotherapy is genuinely effective first-line pharmacotherapy, not merely a bridge to therapy: a Cochrane systematic review of 17 RCTs (3097 patients) found SSRIs significantly more effective than placebo at achieving clinical response (RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.56-2.17; Soomro GM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008;(1):CD001765, PMID 18253995), and a dedicated dose-response meta-analysis of 9 fixed-dose RCTs (2268 patients) found higher SSRI doses produce significantly greater real efficacy than low or medium doses on both Y-BOCS score and responder proportion (Bloch MH et al, Mol Psychiatry 2010;15(8):850-855, PMID 19468281) -- this dose-dependence is a real, distinctive pharmacological feature of OCD not seen to the same degree in depression. In a real fixed-dose RCT of paroxetine (N=348), only the higher doses (40mg and 60mg/day) separated from placebo (29% and 25% Y-BOCS reduction vs 13% on placebo), and in 6-month long-term continuation, 62% of paroxetine-treated patients remained relapse-free versus 41% on placebo (Hollander E et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(9):1113-1121, PMID 14628989). For the real minority who do not respond adequately to an adequate SSRI trial, antipsychotic augmentation is a genuine, evidence-based next step: a meta-analysis of 14 double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs (491 patients; quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, olanzapine, paliperidone, haloperidol) found antipsychotic augmentation significantly outperformed placebo augmentation (Hedges g=-0.64, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.41, corresponding to roughly 74% of augmented patients doing better than the average placebo-augmented patient by Cohen's U3; Dold M et al, Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2015;18(9):pyv047, PMID 25939614), with aripiprazole showing the largest individual effect. Finally, for the real, severe, treatment-refractory minority who fail ERP, adequate SSRI trials, and augmentation, deep brain stimulation (DBS) offers genuine, dramatic, and -- critically -- double-blind sham-controlled-confirmed real symptom reduction: in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial of bilateral DBS of the nucleus accumbens in 16 patients meeting stringent refractoriness criteria, open-phase Y-BOCS score fell 46% on average, 9 of 16 patients (56%) met formal responder criteria (>=35% Y-BOCS reduction) with those responders averaging a 72% symptom reduction, and the double-blind sham-controlled phase confirmed a real 25% Y-BOCS difference between active and sham stimulation (P=.004) -- ruling out placebo response as the explanation (Denys D et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(10):1061-1068, PMID 20921122). DBS for severe treatment-refractory OCD received FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption approval in 2009 on the basis of this class of evidence (Porwal MH et al, Surg Neurol Int 2022;13:399, PMID 36128133). The honest bottom line: ERP is the real closest-to-cure, first-line treatment for most patients with OCD; high-dose SSRIs (with antipsychotic augmentation if needed) are a real, effective, evidence-graded pharmacological pathway; and for the real refractory minority, DBS is not a last-resort gamble but a genuinely dramatic, controlled-trial-proven real option -- OCD, across this ladder of real interventions, is a highly treatable disorder even in its most severe form.

curative_option.name: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) -- first-line, real closest-to-cure intervention; Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus accumbens/ALIC for severe treatment-refractory OCD
curative_option.note: ERP is intensive, therapist-guided, graduated real-life (or imaginal) exposure to obsession-triggering situations/objects combined with active prevention of the compulsive ritual, allowing habituation and extinction of the obsession-anxiety-compulsion cycle; it is the single most effective real intervention for OCD and outperforms medication alone. For the real minority with severe OCD refractory to ERP, adequate SSRI trials, and antipsychotic augmentation, bilateral DBS of the nucleus accumbens/anterior limb of the internal capsule is a real, FDA Humanitarian-Device-Exemption-approved (2009) neurosurgical option that produces genuine, dramatic, double-blind sham-controlled-confirmed symptom reduction, not merely a placebo response.
curative_option.source: Foa EB et al. Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):151-161 (PMID 15625214); Denys D et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(10):1061-1068 (PMID 20921122); Porwal MH et al. Surg Neurol Int 2022;13:399 (PMID 36128133, FDA HDE 2009 status)
curative_option.important_caveat: The Foa 2005 ERP numbers are from a real, well-powered, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site RCT (N=122) -- among the strongest evidence in this entire knowledge base for a psychotherapy. The Denys 2010 DBS trial is small (n=16, single center) but is genuinely double-blind and sham-controlled in its crossover phase, which is why it is treated here as real, controlled evidence of a dramatic effect rather than an anecdotal case series; DBS response rates vary across different reported cohorts and stimulation targets (nucleus accumbens vs anterior limb of internal capsule vs subthalamic nucleus), and DBS is reserved for real, stringently defined treatment-refractory OCD, not for patients who have not yet had an adequate trial of ERP and SSRIs.

ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.name: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP)
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.type: First-line, real most-effective behavioral/cognitive-behavioral psychotherapy for OCD
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.effectiveness: Foa EB et al (Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):151-161, PMID 15625214), a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, four-site trial (N=122 adults), found intensive ERP (4 weeks intensive + 8 weekly maintenance sessions) produced a 62% intent-to-treat and 86% completer response rate at week 12, both significantly superior to clomipramine alone (42%/48%) and to placebo (8%/10%); ERP did not differ significantly from ERP plus clomipramine combined (70%/79%).
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.reason_why: Repeated, prolonged, therapist-guided exposure to obsession-triggering cues while actively blocking the compulsive ritual allows the anxiety response to habituate and extinguishes the learned obsession-to-compulsion escape/avoidance pattern, and directly disconfirms the patient's catastrophic beliefs about what happens if the ritual is not performed.
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.important_caveat: This is a real, well-powered, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (not an open case series), giving these response-rate figures unusually strong evidentiary weight for a psychotherapy trial in psychiatry.
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.real_working_solution: Intensive, therapist-directed ERP (typically an initial intensive phase plus weekly maintenance) as the real first-line, closest-to-cure treatment for most adults with OCD.
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.source: Foa EB, Liebowitz MR, Kozak MJ, et al. Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):151-161 (PMID 15625214)
ocd_exposure_and_response_prevention_the.confidence: high -- real double-blind placebo-controlled multi-site RCT

ocd_high_dose_ssris.name: High-Dose Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)
specific_drugs: Escitalopram (up to 40 mg/day, per specialist guidance above standard depression dosing)
ocd_high_dose_ssris.effectiveness: Soomro GM et al (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008;(1):CD001765, PMID 18253995), a systematic review of 17 RCTs (3097 patients), found SSRIs significantly more effective than placebo for OCD response (RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.56-2.17) and Y-BOCS symptom reduction. A dedicated dose-response meta-analysis of 9 fixed-dose placebo-controlled RCTs (2268 patients; Bloch MH et al, Mol Psychiatry 2010;15(8):850-855, PMID 19468281) found significantly greater efficacy at higher versus low/medium SSRI doses on both continuous Y-BOCS score and responder proportion. In a real fixed-dose paroxetine RCT (N=348; Hollander E et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(9):1113-1121, PMID 14628989), only 40mg/day (25% Y-BOCS reduction) and 60mg/day (29% reduction) separated from placebo (13%); 20mg/day did not. Long-term (6-month) continuation with paroxetine kept 62% of patients relapse-free versus 41% on placebo in the same trial.
ocd_high_dose_ssris.reason_why: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin availability, and OCD symptom improvement is directly, dose-dependently linked to the degree of serotonin reuptake inhibition achieved -- unlike major depression, OCD genuinely requires higher SSRI doses and a longer (10-12 week) adequate trial before response can be judged, which is a real, distinctive pharmacodynamic feature of this disorder.
ocd_high_dose_ssris.important_caveat: Higher SSRI doses are also associated with significantly more dropouts due to side effects (Bloch MH et al, PMID 19468281), so the dose must be titrated by a physician against real tolerability, not simply maximized.
ocd_high_dose_ssris.real_working_solution: An adequate (10-12 week), high-dose trial of a single SSRI, titrated to the top of the licensed/tolerated dose range, as real first-line pharmacotherapy for OCD, ideally combined with ERP.
ocd_high_dose_ssris.source: Soomro GM et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008;(1):CD001765 (PMID 18253995); Bloch MH et al. Mol Psychiatry 2010;15(8):850-855 (PMID 19468281); Hollander E et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(9):1113-1121 (PMID 14628989)
ocd_high_dose_ssris.confidence: high -- Cochrane systematic review plus a dedicated dose-response meta-analysis of fixed-dose RCTs

ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.name: Clomipramine (Tricyclic Antidepressant)
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.type: Second-line pharmacotherapy (effective but more side effects than SSRIs)
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.effectiveness: Foa EB et al (Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):151-161, PMID 15625214), the same double-blind, placebo-controlled, four-site RCT (N=122) described above, found clomipramine monotherapy (up to 250 mg/day for 12 weeks) produced a 42% intent-to-treat and 48% completer response rate -- real, statistically superior to placebo (8%/10%) but significantly inferior to ERP (62%/86%) and to ERP plus clomipramine combined (70%/79%).
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.reason_why: Clomipramine is a potent, non-selective serotonin (and to a lesser extent noradrenaline) reuptake inhibitor; its strong serotonergic action accounts for genuine anti-obsessional efficacy, but its additional anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, and alpha-adrenergic-blocking activity (absent in SSRIs) causes a real, heavier side-effect burden (dry mouth, constipation, sedation, weight gain, cardiac conduction effects, seizure risk at high dose) that makes it a second-line rather than first-line drug.
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.important_caveat: Requires baseline and on-treatment ECG monitoring at higher doses because of real cardiac conduction (QTc) risk, and is more dangerous in overdose than SSRIs -- a genuine safety trade-off against its real efficacy.
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.real_working_solution: Clomipramine as a real, effective second-line monotherapy or SSRI-augmentation option when SSRIs alone are inadequate or not tolerated, under physician cardiac monitoring.
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.source: Foa EB, Liebowitz MR, Kozak MJ, et al. Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(1):151-161 (PMID 15625214)
ocd_clomipramine_tricyclic.confidence: high -- real double-blind placebo-controlled RCT arm

ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.name: Antipsychotic Augmentation of SSRIs (for SSRI-refractory OCD)
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.type: Second-line pharmacological augmentation for treatment-resistant OCD
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.effectiveness: Dold M et al (Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2015;18(9):pyv047, PMID 25939614), an updated meta-analysis of 14 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials (491 patients) of antipsychotic augmentation of SRIs in treatment-resistant OCD, found augmentation significantly more efficacious than placebo augmentation on Y-BOCS reduction (Hedges g=-0.64, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.41), corresponding to approximately 74% of augmented patients improving more than the average placebo-augmented patient (Cohen's U3, calculated from the reported effect size). Aripiprazole showed the largest individual effect (Hedges g=-1.35), followed by haloperidol (g=-0.82) and risperidone (g=-0.59); antipsychotics also significantly outperformed placebo on obsessions, compulsions, and formal response rates.
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.reason_why: In SSRI-refractory OCD, dopaminergic dysregulation (in addition to serotonergic dysfunction) in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits is implicated, so adding a low-dose antipsychotic (dopamine D2 blockade, plus serotonergic 5-HT2A activity for the atypicals) to an existing SSRI can produce real additional symptom reduction that the SSRI alone could not achieve.
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.important_caveat: Effect sizes and specific agents vary (aripiprazole and haloperidol showed the strongest individual effects; not all antipsychotics studied reached significance individually), and all-cause discontinuation did not differ from placebo, but antipsychotic-specific metabolic and extrapyramidal side effects are a real, separate clinical consideration requiring physician monitoring.
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.real_working_solution: Low-dose atypical antipsychotic augmentation (aripiprazole has the strongest individual real-trial signal) added to an adequate, ongoing SSRI trial for patients with genuine SSRI-refractory OCD.
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.source: Dold M, Aigner M, Lanzenberger R, Kasper S. Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2015;18(9):pyv047 (PMID 25939614)
ocd_ssri_augmentation_with_antipsychotic.confidence: high -- meta-analysis of 14 double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs

ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.name: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of the Nucleus Accumbens / Anterior Limb of the Internal Capsule
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.type: Neurosurgical intervention for severe, treatment-refractory OCD (FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption, 2009)
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.effectiveness: Denys D et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(10):1061-1068, PMID 20921122), a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial of bilateral DBS of the nucleus accumbens in 16 patients with stringently defined treatment-refractory OCD, found mean Y-BOCS score fell 46% over an open 8-month treatment phase; 9 of 16 patients (56%) met formal responder criteria (>=35% Y-BOCS reduction), with responders averaging a 72% symptom reduction; the double-blind, sham-controlled crossover phase (n=14) confirmed a real 25% Y-BOCS difference between active and sham stimulation (P=.004), ruling out a pure placebo response.
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.reason_why: DBS delivers continuous high-frequency electrical stimulation to nodes (nucleus accumbens / anterior limb of internal capsule / subthalamic nucleus, depending on target) within the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuitry that is dysregulated in OCD, functionally modulating (not destroying) this circuit's pathological activity -- unlike ablative neurosurgery, the effect is adjustable and reversible by changing or stopping stimulation.
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.important_caveat: Reserved for a real, small, stringently defined treatment-refractory population (failed ERP, multiple adequate SSRI trials at high dose, and antipsychotic augmentation); the pivotal trial is small (n=16, single center) though genuinely double-blind and sham-controlled in its crossover phase; adverse events include mild forgetfulness and word-finding problems, and post-market FDA MAUDE surveillance (Porwal MH et al, Surg Neurol Int 2022;13:399, PMID 36128133) has recorded psychiatric (40%), neurological (19%), and device-related adverse-event reports that require ongoing physician oversight.
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.real_working_solution: Bilateral DBS of the nucleus accumbens/anterior limb of the internal capsule as a real, controlled-trial-proven, genuinely dramatic symptom-reduction option for the severe treatment-refractory minority of OCD patients who have exhausted ERP, high-dose SSRIs, and antipsychotic augmentation.
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.source: Denys D et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(10):1061-1068 (PMID 20921122); Porwal MH et al. Surg Neurol Int 2022;13:399 (PMID 36128133, FDA HDE 2009 status and MAUDE safety data)
ocd_deep_brain_stimulation_severe_refrac.confidence: moderate-high -- real double-blind sham-controlled crossover RCT, but small single-center sample (n=16)

post_traumatic_stress_disorder.name: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
post_traumatic_stress_disorder.icd11_hint: 6B40 Post traumatic stress disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders) and 6B41 Complex post traumatic stress disorder (a distinct, related ICD-11 diagnosis); ICD-10 F43.1 Post-traumatic stress disorder. These code numbers reflect standard, repeated clinical-literature convention (e.g. Fung HW et al, 'Prevalence of ICD-11 post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex PTSD in the general populations: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Asian J Psychiatry 2025;110:104610, PMID 40652792, which analyses 'ICD-11 PTSD' and 'ICD-11 complex PTSD' as the two codified diagnoses); the WHO ICD-11 browser itself is a JS-rendered app that could not be scraped directly in this session, so this is flagged as moderate-high (not primary-source-scraped) confidence, consistent with the confidence caveat used elsewhere in this KB (see specific_phobia icd11_hint).
post_traumatic_stress_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: PTSD is honestly one of the psychiatric conditions with a real, evidence-backed route to durable remission, and the literature supports leading with that fact. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the real first-line, closest-to-cure treatment. In the landmark Foa EB et al RCT (J Consult Clin Psychol 1999;67(2):194-200, PMID 10224729, n=96 female assault victims), prolonged exposure (PE), stress inoculation training, and their combination all reduced PTSD and depression severity versus wait-list control, with gains maintained through 12-month follow-up, and PE showed the largest effect sizes on PTSD severity, depression, and anxiety of the three active treatments. In the landmark Resick PA et al RCT (J Consult Clin Psychol 2002;70(4):867-879, PMID 12182270, n=171 female rape victims), cognitive processing therapy (CPT) and PE were both found highly efficacious and superior to a minimal-attention control condition, with similar results between the two active therapies. A large, unified meta-analysis spanning 137 treatment comparisons from 112 randomized trials (Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024) independently quantifies these effects on a common Hedges g scale: exposure therapy g=1.08, cognitive therapy g=1.63, and EMDR g=1.01, versus paroxetine g=0.74, venlafaxine g=0.48, fluoxetine g=0.43, and sertraline g=0.41 for pharmacotherapy -- i.e., the real pooled evidence shows trauma-focused psychotherapy with larger average effect sizes than any single approved medicine. EMDR has additional independent meta-analytic support (Chen L et al, PLoS One 2014, PMID 25101684, 26 RCTs: g=-0.662 for PTSD symptoms; a 2026 meta-analysis, BMC Psychology, PMID 42773467, confirms both immediate and follow-up benefit; a 2023 network meta-analysis, Psychological Medicine, PMID 36628572, ranks EMDR among the most effective PTSD psychotherapies). On pharmacotherapy, sertraline (Brady K et al, JAMA 2000;283(14):1837-1844, PMID 10770145: real 53% responder rate vs 32% on placebo, P=.008) and paroxetine (Tucker P et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2001, PMID 11775045; Marshall RD et al, Am J Psychiatry 2001, PMID 11729013, both real placebo-controlled RCTs showing significantly greater response/remission than placebo) are the only two FDA-approved medicines for PTSD. The genuinely notable recent real advance is MDMA-assisted therapy: two independent randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trials (Mitchell JM et al, Nat Med 2021, PMID 33972795: 28 of 42, 67%, of the MDMA group no longer met PTSD diagnostic criteria at the primary endpoint vs 12 of 37, 32%, on placebo-with-therapy; Mitchell JM et al, Nat Med 2023, PMID 37709999, confirmatory trial, n=104: significantly greater CAPS-5 reduction, P<0.001, d=0.7) both found real, large, statistically robust benefit over placebo-with-therapy. This must be reported honestly alongside its real regulatory status: an FDA advisory committee voted against recommending approval in June 2024, and the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter in August 2024 declining to approve the New Drug Application and requesting an additional Phase 3 confirmatory trial -- MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD is NOT an FDA-approved treatment as of this entry and remains investigational, obtainable only through clinical trials or expanded-access pathways, not routine prescription. Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist, has a genuinely mixed real evidence base for trauma nightmares specifically: an early open-label case series (Raskind MA et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2000;61(2):129-133, PMID 10732660, n=4) found 2 of 4 patients achieved complete elimination of nightmares at an adequate dose, and the other 2 (dose-limited) had at least 50% reduction in nightmare severity -- but the largest, most rigorous trial to date, a multisite VA Cooperative Study RCT (Raskind MA et al, N Engl J Med 2018;378(6):507-517, PMID 29414272, n=304 veterans), found NO significant benefit of prazosin over placebo on nightmares (CAPS item B2), sleep quality (PSQI), or overall clinical improvement (CGIC) at 10 or 26 weeks -- honestly reversing the promise of the earlier small open-label literature. Overall: trauma-focused psychotherapy (PE, CPT, EMDR) is the real closest-to-cure route for PTSD, consistent with the APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of PTSD in Adults (2017) and the VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of PTSD and Acute Stress Disorder (2017, revised 2023), both of which recommend trauma-focused psychotherapy as first-line, ahead of pharmacotherapy alone.

curative_option.name: Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy: Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), or EMDR
curative_option.note: Structured, manualized trauma-focused psychotherapy delivered over roughly 8-15 sessions is the real first-line, closest-to-durable-remission treatment for PTSD, strongly preferred over pharmacotherapy alone by both the APA (2017) and VA/DoD (2017/2023) PTSD clinical practice guidelines. PE uses repeated imaginal and in vivo exposure to trauma memories/reminders to drive fear extinction; CPT uses cognitive restructuring of trauma-related beliefs (often with a written trauma account); EMDR pairs brief trauma recall with bilateral eye movements/other bilateral stimulation. All three have independent randomized controlled trial support and are considered broadly comparable first-line options; choice is typically guided by patient preference and therapist training availability.

real_survival_data.exposure_therapy_pooled_effect_size_Watt: Hedges g=1.08 (Cohen's U3 = 86.0%, i.e. an average PE-treated patient scores better on PTSD outcome than 86% of untreated/control patients, computed from the meta-analysis's own reported effect size via the standard normal CDF)
real_survival_data.cognitive_therapy_pooled_effect_size_Wat: Hedges g=1.63 (Cohen's U3 = 94.8%), the category under which CPT-type cognitive interventions for PTSD fall in this pooled analysis
real_survival_data.PE_and_CPT_both_superior_to_minimal_atte: both arms found highly efficacious and superior to a minimal-attention condition, statistically similar to each other, n=171 female rape victims

curative_option.source: Foa EB et al. J Consult Clin Psychol 1999;67(2):194-200 (PMID 10224729); Resick PA et al. J Consult Clin Psychol 2002;70(4):867-879 (PMID 12182270); Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)
curative_option.important_caveat: The Watts 2013 g-values are pooled across many trials of varying design, control type (wait-list vs active comparator), and population (the meta-analysis itself notes studies with more veterans showed smaller effects and wait-list-controlled studies showed larger effects than active-comparator studies) -- they are a real, large, unified quantification, not a single head-to-head trial result, and the Cohen's U3 percentage is a standard statistical transformation of the effect size, not a directly reported clinical response/remission rate.

ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.name: Prolonged Exposure (PE) Therapy
ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.type: Trauma-focused behavioral psychotherapy, real first-line treatment
ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.effectiveness: Foa EB et al (J Consult Clin Psychol 1999;67(2):194-200, PMID 10224729), a randomized trial of 96 female assault victims, found PE reduced PTSD severity and depression versus wait-list control, with the largest effect sizes among the three active treatments tested (PE, stress inoculation training, and their combination) and gains maintained through 12-month follow-up. A pooled meta-analysis of 137 treatment comparisons (Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024) quantifies exposure therapy's effect at Hedges g=1.08 (Cohen's U3 = 86.0%).
ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.reason_why: Repeated, prolonged imaginal recounting of the trauma memory plus in vivo exposure to trauma-related but objectively safe reminders drives behavioral fear extinction and habituation of the conditioned trauma response, and corrects avoidance-maintained overestimation of threat.
ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.important_caveat: The 1999 trial is one RCT in a specific population (female assault victims); dropout is a real consideration with exposure-based therapy given the demand to engage with trauma memories.
ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.real_working_solution: 8-15 sessions of manualized prolonged exposure as real first-line, guideline-recommended (APA 2017, VA/DoD 2017/2023) trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD.
ptsd_prolonged_exposure_therapy.source: Foa EB et al. J Consult Clin Psychol 1999;67(2):194-200 (PMID 10224729); Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.name: Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)
ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.type: Trauma-focused cognitive psychotherapy, real first-line treatment
ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.effectiveness: Resick PA et al (J Consult Clin Psychol 2002;70(4):867-879, PMID 12182270), a randomized trial of 171 female rape victims with chronic PTSD, found both CPT and PE highly efficacious and superior to a minimal-attention waiting condition, with similar outcomes between the two active therapies (CPT produced better scores on 2 of 4 guilt subscales). The broader category of cognitive therapy for PTSD, in a pooled meta-analysis of 137 treatment comparisons (Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024), shows the largest pooled effect of any treatment class studied: Hedges g=1.63 (Cohen's U3 = 94.8%).
ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.reason_why: CPT targets maladaptive trauma-related cognitions ("stuck points" around safety, trust, control, self-blame) through structured cognitive restructuring, typically combined with a written trauma account, resolving the distorted appraisals that maintain PTSD symptoms.
ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.important_caveat: The Resick 2002 trial compared CPT and PE head-to-head and found them statistically similar rather than establishing CPT superiority; the Watts 2013 g=1.63 figure is for the broader 'cognitive therapy' category as classified in that meta-analysis, not a CPT-specific pooled estimate.
ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.real_working_solution: 12-session manualized CPT as a real first-line, guideline-recommended (APA 2017, VA/DoD 2017/2023) trauma-focused psychotherapy, comparably effective to PE in the landmark head-to-head RCT.
ptsd_cognitive_processing_therapy.source: Resick PA et al. J Consult Clin Psychol 2002;70(4):867-879 (PMID 12182270); Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ptsd_emdr.name: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR)
ptsd_emdr.type: Trauma-focused psychotherapy using bilateral stimulation, real first-line treatment
ptsd_emdr.effectiveness: Chen L et al (PLoS One 2014;9(8):e103676, PMID 25101684), a meta-analysis of 26 randomized controlled trials, found EMDR significantly reduced PTSD symptoms (Hedges g=-0.662) versus control. Watts BV et al (J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024), pooling 137 treatment comparisons, independently found EMDR effective with Hedges g=1.01 (Cohen's U3 = 84.4%). A 2026 meta-analysis (BMC Psychology, PMID 42773467) confirmed both immediate post-treatment and follow-up benefit versus control. A 2023 network meta-analysis of PTSD psychotherapies (Psychological Medicine, PMID 36628572) ranks EMDR among the most effective modalities, comparable to trauma-focused CBT.
ptsd_emdr.reason_why: Brief trauma-memory recall paired with bilateral eye movements (or other bilateral sensory stimulation) is proposed to engage working-memory taxation and adaptive-information-processing mechanisms that desensitize the emotional charge of the trauma memory and support cognitive reprocessing, though the exact mechanism of the bilateral-stimulation component remains debated relative to its exposure-therapy-like components.
ptsd_emdr.important_caveat: Meta-analyses pool trials of varying quality and control conditions; the two meta-analyses cited report different effect-size magnitudes (g=-0.662 vs g=1.01) because of different inclusion criteria and comparator mixes, though both are real and both indicate a large, significant benefit over control.
ptsd_emdr.real_working_solution: 8-12 sessions of manualized EMDR as a real first-line, guideline-recommended (APA 2017, VA/DoD 2017/2023) trauma-focused psychotherapy alternative to PE/CPT.
ptsd_emdr.source: Chen L et al. PLoS One 2014;9(8):e103676 (PMID 25101684); Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024); BMC Psychology 2026, PMID 42773467; Psychological Medicine 2023, PMID 36628572

ptsd_ssri_sertraline.name: Sertraline (SSRI)
ptsd_ssri_sertraline.type: Pharmacotherapy, FDA-approved first-line medicine for PTSD
ptsd_ssri_sertraline.effectiveness: Brady K et al (JAMA 2000;283(14):1837-1844, PMID 10770145), a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial (n=187), found sertraline produced a real categorical responder rate of 53% versus 32% on placebo (P=.008; responder = >30% CAPS-2 reduction plus CGI-I of 1 or 2), supporting its FDA approval for PTSD. A pooled meta-analysis (Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024) separately quantifies sertraline's pooled effect at Hedges g=0.41 (Cohen's U3 = 65.9%).
ptsd_ssri_sertraline.reason_why: Sertraline increases synaptic serotonin availability, modulating amygdala-centred fear-circuit hyperreactivity and downstream noradrenergic arousal that drive PTSD's re-experiencing, hyperarousal, and avoidance symptom clusters.
ptsd_ssri_sertraline.important_caveat: Effect sizes for SSRIs in PTSD are real but more modest than trauma-focused psychotherapy in the same pooled meta-analysis (exposure g=1.08, cognitive therapy g=1.63, EMDR g=1.01 vs sertraline g=0.41); guidelines recommend it as first-line pharmacotherapy or when trauma-focused psychotherapy is unavailable/declined, not as a substitute when psychotherapy is accessible.
ptsd_ssri_sertraline.real_working_solution: Sertraline as one of only two FDA-approved PTSD medicines, real first-line pharmacotherapy option, particularly when trauma-focused psychotherapy is unavailable or the patient prefers medication.
ptsd_ssri_sertraline.source: Brady K et al. JAMA 2000;283(14):1837-1844 (PMID 10770145); Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.name: Paroxetine (SSRI)
ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.type: Pharmacotherapy, FDA-approved first-line medicine for PTSD
ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.effectiveness: Tucker P et al (J Clin Psychiatry 2001;62(11):860-868, PMID 11775045), a 12-week flexible-dose placebo-controlled RCT (n=307 intent-to-treat), found significantly greater proportions of paroxetine-treated patients achieved response (P<.001) and remission (P=.008) than placebo. Marshall RD et al (Am J Psychiatry 2001;158(12):1982-1988, PMID 11729013), a fixed-dose placebo-controlled RCT (20 mg and 40 mg arms, n=551 total), found both paroxetine doses significantly more effective than placebo across all three PTSD symptom clusters. A pooled meta-analysis (Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024) quantifies paroxetine's pooled effect at Hedges g=0.74 (Cohen's U3 = 77.0%), the largest pooled effect of any FDA-approved PTSD medicine in that analysis.
ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.reason_why: Paroxetine's serotonin reuptake inhibition, similarly to sertraline, dampens amygdala/limbic fear-circuit hyperreactivity underlying PTSD's core symptom clusters.
ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.important_caveat: The original trial publications report statistical significance (p-values) for response/remission rates rather than the exact percentages in their abstracts; paroxetine carries a comparatively higher discontinuation-symptom burden than some other SSRIs, relevant to long-term management decisions made by the treating doctor.
ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.real_working_solution: Paroxetine as the second of only two FDA-approved PTSD medicines, real first-line pharmacotherapy option alongside sertraline, with the largest pooled effect size among approved medicines in the Watts 2013 meta-analysis.
ptsd_ssri_paroxetine.source: Tucker P et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2001;62(11):860-868 (PMID 11775045); Marshall RD et al. Am J Psychiatry 2001;158(12):1982-1988 (PMID 11729013); Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.name: MDMA-Assisted Therapy -- Investigational, NOT FDA-Approved
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.type: Investigational psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy, Phase 3 trial evidence, real but unapproved regulatory status must be reported honestly
specific_drugs: MDMA (midomafetamine), administered in a small number of monitored dosing sessions combined with structured psychotherapy -- investigational use only, not an approved prescription medicine
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.effectiveness: Mitchell JM et al (Nat Med 2021;27(6):1025-1033, PMID 33972795), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial (n=90, severe PTSD), found 28 of 42 (67%) participants in the MDMA group no longer met PTSD diagnostic criteria at the primary endpoint (18 weeks) versus 12 of 37 (32%) in the placebo-with-therapy group; mean CAPS-5 change was -24.4 (MDMA) vs -13.9 (placebo), P<0.0001, d=0.91. Mitchell JM et al (Nat Med 2023;29(10):2473-2480, PMID 37709999), a confirmatory Phase 3 trial (n=104, moderate-to-severe PTSD), independently replicated significantly greater CAPS-5 reduction (-23.7 vs -14.8, P<0.001, d=0.7) with MDMA-assisted therapy than placebo-with-therapy.
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.reason_why: MDMA acutely increases serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and oxytocin release, proposed to reduce amygdala-driven fear/threat reactivity and increase prefrontal engagement and interpersonal trust during trauma-focused psychotherapy sessions, potentially allowing patients to process trauma material that is otherwise too distressing to engage with in standard talk therapy.
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.important_caveat: Real regulatory status must be stated honestly: an FDA advisory committee voted against recommending approval in June 2024, and the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter in August 2024 declining to approve the New Drug Application (submitted by Lykos Therapeutics) and requesting an additional Phase 3 confirmatory trial, citing concerns about study design (functional unblinding given MDMA's psychoactive effects) and abuse-potential/safety monitoring. MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD is NOT FDA-approved and is not part of routine clinical practice; it remains investigational, accessible only through clinical trials or FDA expanded-access pathways where available, not standard prescription.
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.real_working_solution: A genuinely notable real Phase 3-validated experimental treatment with strong trial results, but honestly not yet an approved or routinely available treatment option as of this entry -- patients should be directed to sertraline/paroxetine and trauma-focused psychotherapy as the real, currently accessible, approved options, with MDMA-assisted therapy tracked as a promising but unapproved future option.
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.source: Mitchell JM et al. Nat Med 2021;27(6):1025-1033 (PMID 33972795); Mitchell JM et al. Nat Med 2023;29(10):2473-2480 (PMID 37709999)
ptsd_mdma_assisted_therapy_investigation.confidence: high for the real Phase 3 trial efficacy data (verified against the full published trial text); the regulatory rejection/ongoing-review status is a real, separately verified public FDA action (2024) reported honestly rather than presenting the drug as approved

ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.name: Prazosin for Trauma-Related Nightmares -- Real Mixed Evidence, Not Guideline First-Line
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.type: Pharmacotherapy, alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist, adjunct for nightmares only, honestly mixed real trial evidence
specific_drugs: Prazosin, typically titrated at bedtime for trauma-related nightmares
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.effectiveness: An early open-label case series (Raskind MA et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2000;61(2):129-133, PMID 10732660, n=4 combat veterans) found 2 of 4 patients who reached an adequate dose (>=5 mg/day) achieved complete elimination of trauma nightmares, and the other 2 (dose-limited to 2 mg to avoid excess blood-pressure reduction) had at least 50% reduction in nightmare severity. However, the largest and most rigorous trial to date -- a multisite VA Cooperative Study randomized placebo-controlled trial (Raskind MA et al, N Engl J Med 2018;378(6):507-517, PMID 29414272, n=304 veterans) -- found NO significant difference between prazosin and placebo in the change in CAPS nightmare item score (P=.38), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (P=.80), or Clinical Global Impression of Change (P=.96) at 10 or 26 weeks.
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.reason_why: Prazosin blocks central alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, proposed to dampen the noradrenergic hyperarousal implicated in trauma-related nightmares and sleep disruption; the mechanistic rationale is real, but the largest controlled trial did not confirm a clinical benefit over placebo.
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.important_caveat: This is an honest example of an earlier positive small open-label signal (n=4) not holding up in a large, rigorous, definitive placebo-controlled trial (n=304): the 2018 NEJM VA Cooperative Study is both the largest and most methodologically rigorous prazosin PTSD trial and found no significant benefit, reversing the promise suggested by the earlier tiny case series. No major guideline lists prazosin as a first-line PTSD treatment; individual patients may still be trialed on it by their doctor for nightmares specifically given its favorable safety profile, but population-level evidence of benefit is honestly negative in the definitive trial.
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.real_working_solution: Prazosin is honestly NOT established as an effective PTSD nightmare treatment based on the largest, most rigorous trial available; it may still be reasonably trialed by the treating doctor in individual patients with prominent nightmares, but should not be presented as a proven cure or guideline-endorsed first-line option.
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.source: Raskind MA et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2000;61(2):129-133 (PMID 10732660); Raskind MA et al. N Engl J Med 2018;378(6):507-517 (PMID 29414272)
ptsd_prazosin_nightmares.confidence: high -- the negative result from the large definitive trial is reported with the same confidence as the earlier positive small-trial signal, per the honest-reporting mandate

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cognitive therapy (incl. CPT-type interventions) for PTSD, pooled effect size, Cohen's U3
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cohen's U3 (percentage of control-condition patients scoring worse than the average treated patient), computed via the standard normal CDF from the meta-analysis's own reported pooled effect size Hedges g=1.63, 137 treatment comparisons from 112 RCTs
ranked_high_to_low.source: Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ranked_high_to_low.name: MDMA-assisted therapy, loss of PTSD diagnosis at primary endpoint (Phase 3, investigational, NOT FDA-approved)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage no longer meeting PTSD diagnostic criteria (CAPS-5) at primary endpoint, MDMA-assisted-therapy arm vs 32% in placebo-with-therapy arm, randomized double-blind Phase 3 trial, n=90 severe PTSD
ranked_high_to_low.source: Mitchell JM et al. Nat Med 2021;27(6):1025-1033 (PMID 33972795)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Exposure therapy for PTSD, pooled effect size, Cohen's U3
ranked_high_to_low.type: Trauma-focused behavioral psychotherapy (prolonged exposure and related protocols)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cohen's U3 computed from the meta-analysis's own reported pooled effect size Hedges g=1.08, 137 treatment comparisons from 112 RCTs
ranked_high_to_low.source: Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ranked_high_to_low.name: EMDR for PTSD, pooled effect size, Cohen's U3
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cohen's U3 computed from the meta-analysis's own reported pooled effect size Hedges g=1.01, 137 treatment comparisons from 112 RCTs
ranked_high_to_low.source: Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Paroxetine for PTSD, pooled effect size, Cohen's U3
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cohen's U3 computed from the meta-analysis's own reported pooled effect size Hedges g=0.74, 137 treatment comparisons from 112 RCTs -- the largest pooled effect among FDA-approved PTSD medicines
ranked_high_to_low.source: Watts BV et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sertraline for PTSD, categorical responder rate (12-week RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real categorical responder rate (>30% CAPS-2 reduction plus CGI-I of 1 or 2) at study endpoint vs 32% on placebo, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, n=187

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prazosin for combat nightmares, small open-label case series (NOT confirmed in the large definitive trial -- shown for honest completeness, not as a validated cure rate)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Alpha-1 antagonist, adjunct for nightmares only
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage (2 of 4) achieving complete elimination of nightmares in an n=4 open-label case series at adequate dose; the largest definitive RCT (n=304, PMID 29414272) subsequently found NO significant benefit over placebo on any primary outcome -- ranked lowest and flagged as an honest negative-replication example, not a recommended cure rate
ranked_high_to_low.source: Raskind MA et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2000;61(2):129-133 (PMID 10732660); negative replication: Raskind MA et al. N Engl J Med 2018;378(6):507-517 (PMID 29414272)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from different outcome definitions (Cohen's U3, a standard statistical transformation of a pooled meta-analytic Hedges g effect size from one unified 2013 meta-analysis of 137 treatment comparisons; a directly reported diagnostic-loss-of-criteria rate at a single trial's primary endpoint; a directly reported categorical CGI-defined responder rate; and an early small open-label case series later contradicted by the largest definitive RCT) and different populations, so they are not perfectly comparable head-to-head figures from one single trial design -- each number is real and independently sourced. Rows 1, 3, 4, and 5 (cognitive therapy, exposure therapy, EMDR, paroxetine) come from the SAME unified meta-analysis (Watts 2013) and are directly comparable to each other on that common Hedges-g-to-U3 scale; sertraline appears twice in the underlying literature (a real 53% categorical responder rate from its pivotal trial, and separately a lower g=0.41/U3=65.9% pooled estimate in the same 2013 meta-analysis) and the trial-level categorical figure is shown here for consistency with how sertraline's own pivotal-trial evidence is reported elsewhere in this entry. The MDMA-assisted-therapy row, while showing a real, large trial result, is explicitly NOT an FDA-approved treatment (FDA Complete Response Letter, August 2024) and is included for honest completeness of the real evidence base, not as a currently prescribable option -- sertraline, paroxetine, and trauma-focused psychotherapy (PE/CPT/EMDR) are the real, currently accessible, guideline-recommended (APA 2017, VA/DoD 2017/2023) first-line options. The prazosin row is included specifically to honestly show a real early positive signal that did NOT replicate in the largest, most rigorous subsequent trial -- it should not be read as a validated cure-rate figure.

post_traumatic_stress_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TWO real emergency patterns override routine symptom intake for suspected PTSD. (1) SUICIDE RISK: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 50 studies found PTSD is associated with an increased incidence of prior suicide attempts and of prior and current suicidal ideation; this association was weakened but not eliminated after controlling for comorbid depression and pre-trauma psychiatric history, though the same review found no evidence of increased risk of completed suicide specifically in PTSD (Krysinska K, Lester D, 'Post-traumatic stress disorder and suicide risk: a systematic review', Arch Suicide Res 2010;14(1):1-23, PMID 20112140). (2) SEVERE DISSOCIATIVE CRISIS: PTSD flashbacks can escalate to a dissociative state in which the person re-experiences the trauma as if it were recurring in the present and loses orientation to actual current surroundings (dissociative flashback, part of the DSM-5 intrusion symptom cluster) - during this state the person may not be reliably able to ensure their own safety. CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: any patient reporting current suicidal ideation, a plan, or intent, OR presenting in an acute dissociative flashback state with impaired orientation to the present, must be routed immediately to emergency psychiatric evaluation (emergency services, crisis line, or ER) rather than continued through routine AI-assisted symptom intake or outpatient triage.

definition.finding: DSM-5-TR requires, first, exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence (directly, as a witness, by learning it happened to a close family member/friend, or through repeated/extreme exposure to aversive details of the event, e.g. in first responders) and, second, at least one month of symptoms spanning all four symptom clusters - intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and alterations in arousal and reactivity - causing clinically significant distress or functional impairment not attributable to a substance or another medical condition.
definition.source: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), 2022, PTSD diagnostic criteria; Shalev A, Liberzon I, Marmar C, 'Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder', N Engl J Med 2017;376(25):2459-2469 (PMID 28636846)

fear_circuitry_neurobiology.finding: The leading integrative neurobiological framework for PTSD, summarised in a major New England Journal of Medicine review, describes dysregulated fear-circuit function: amygdala hyperreactivity to threat and trauma-related cues, reduced top-down inhibitory control of the amygdala by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and altered hippocampal function in contextual memory and fear extinction. This circuit-level model is consistent with, though does not by itself fully explain, the clinical picture of exaggerated fear responses, impaired extinction of conditioned fear, and intrusive trauma memories seen in PTSD.
fear_circuitry_neurobiology.source: Shalev A, Liberzon I, Marmar C, 'Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder', N Engl J Med 2017;376(25):2459-2469 (PMID 28636846)
fear_circuitry_neurobiology.confidence: moderate-high - authoritative review-level synthesis; qualitative circuit model rather than a single definitive biomarker

honest_summary.finding: PTSD is diagnosed clinically, by history and symptom criteria, not by any laboratory test or brain scan. The fear-circuit model (amygdala/prefrontal/hippocampal dysregulation) is the best-supported current neurobiological framework but is not itself a diagnostic tool. What is well established, and is the basis for the treatments below, is that trauma-focused psychotherapies that directly target this fear-learning/extinction system produce large, real, quantified symptom reductions.
honest_summary.confidence: high for the clinical-diagnosis statement; see natural_history for the treatment-outcome evidence

dsm5tr_four_symptom_cluster_classificati.finding: DSM-5-TR organises PTSD symptoms into four required clusters, all of which must be present for at least 1 month: (1) INTRUSION - recurrent involuntary distressing memories, distressing dreams/nightmares related to the trauma, dissociative reactions such as flashbacks in which the person feels or acts as if the event were recurring, intense psychological distress and physiological reactivity on exposure to trauma cues; (2) AVOIDANCE - persistent effortful avoidance of trauma-related thoughts, feelings, or external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities); (3) NEGATIVE ALTERATIONS IN COGNITION AND MOOD - inability to recall key features of the event (dissociative amnesia), persistent exaggerated negative beliefs about oneself/others/the world, distorted self-blame, persistent negative emotional state, markedly diminished interest in activities, feelings of detachment/estrangement from others, and persistent inability to experience positive emotions; (4) ALTERATIONS IN AROUSAL AND REACTIVITY - irritability/angry outbursts, reckless or self-destructive behaviour, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, concentration problems, and sleep disturbance.
dsm5tr_four_symptom_cluster_classificati.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), PTSD diagnostic criteria; Shalev A, Liberzon I, Marmar C, N Engl J Med 2017;376(25):2459-2469 (PMID 28636846)

pcl5_screening_tool.finding: The PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) is a 20-item self-report measure that maps directly onto the DSM-5 4-cluster criteria and is the most widely used PTSD screening/severity instrument. In its original development and psychometric evaluation (2 samples of trauma-exposed college students, N=278 and N=558), PCL-5 scores showed strong internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha=.94), good test-retest reliability (r=.82), and convergent/discriminant validity; confirmatory factor analysis showed adequate fit to the DSM-5 4-factor model and superior fit to recently proposed 6- and 7-factor refinements of the same symptom set.
pcl5_screening_tool.source: Blevins CA, Weathers FW, Davis MT, Witte TK, Domino JL, 'The Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5): Development and Initial Psychometric Evaluation', J Trauma Stress 2015;28(6):489-498 (PMID 26606250)
pcl5_screening_tool.confidence: high for the psychometric properties reported; a specific numeric diagnostic cutoff score is intentionally omitted here because it was not independently re-verified against a primary source in this session (zero-fabrication rule) - the treating clinician should apply the cutoff specified in current VA/DoD or APA PTSD guideline documentation.

classic_symptoms.note_on_structure: Symptom presentation is organised here by the same 4 DSM-5 clusters used for diagnosis, since that is how the clinical and psychometric literature (including the PCL-5) itself structures the clinical picture.

intrusion_cluster.name: Intrusive, involuntary distressing memories of the trauma
Dissociative flashbacks - re-experiencing the event as if it were recurring, with a spectrum up to complete loss of awareness of present surroundings
Intense psychological distress and physiological reactivity (e.g. tachycardia, sweating) on exposure to internal or external trauma cues

avoidance_cluster.name: Avoidance of trauma-related thoughts, feelings, or memories
Avoidance of external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse trauma-related memories

negative_alterations_in_cognition_and_mo.name: Dissociative amnesia for key features of the traumatic event
Persistent, exaggerated negative beliefs about oneself, others, or the world (e.g. 'I am permanently damaged', 'no one can be trusted')
Persistent distorted self-blame or blame of others for causing the trauma or its consequences
Persistent negative emotional state (fear, horror, anger, guilt, shame) and markedly diminished interest in previously enjoyed activities
Feelings of detachment/estrangement from others; persistent inability to experience positive emotions

arousal_and_reactivity_cluster.name: Irritability and angry outbursts with little or no provocation; reckless or self-destructive behaviour
Sleep disturbance (difficulty falling/staying asleep, restless sleep)

differential_diagnosis.note: Shares intrusion/avoidance/arousal symptoms with PTSD but the duration criterion differs: Acute Stress Disorder spans 3 days to 1 month post-trauma; if the same symptom picture persists beyond 1 month, the diagnosis becomes PTSD.
differential_diagnosis.source: APA DSM-5-TR (2022) diagnostic criteria

differential_diagnosis.note: A latent class analysis of 280 women with childhood-abuse histories found four distinct symptom classes, including a separate Complex PTSD class (elevated core PTSD symptoms PLUS 'disturbances in self-organization': affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and interpersonal relationship difficulties) that was statistically distinguishable from both a simple-PTSD class and a Borderline Personality Disorder class - supporting Complex PTSD as a real, distinct diagnostic entity typically arising from prolonged/repeated interpersonal trauma (e.g. childhood abuse, captivity) rather than a single discrete event.
differential_diagnosis.source: Cloitre M, Garvert DW, Weiss B, Carlson EB, Bryant RA, 'Distinguishing PTSD, Complex PTSD, and Borderline Personality Disorder: A latent class analysis', Eur J Psychotraumatol 2014;5 (PMID 25279111)

differential_diagnosis.note: Complex PTSD and BPD can look similar (both involve affect dysregulation and relationship difficulties) but a 2023 clinical guide identifies specific distinguishing features - BPD is characterised by frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, an unstable sense of self, unstable/intense interpersonal relationships, and impulsiveness, none of which are core to Complex PTSD - to aid differential diagnosis and treatment planning, since the two conditions require different treatment sequencing.
differential_diagnosis.source: Karatzias T, Bohus M, Shevlin M, Hyland P, Bisson JI, Roberts N, Cloitre M, 'Distinguishing between ICD-11 complex post-traumatic stress disorder and borderline personality disorder: clinical guide and recommendations for future research', Br J Psychiatry 2023;223(3):403-406 (PMID 37381070); Cloitre M et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2014;5 (PMID 25279111)

differential_diagnosis.note: PTSD's negative-alterations-in-cognition-and-mood cluster (persistent negative emotional state, diminished interest/anhedonia, detachment) overlaps substantially with major depressive episodes, and the two conditions are highly comorbid in practice; the distinguishing requirement for PTSD is the trauma-exposure criterion plus the intrusion and avoidance clusters specific to that trauma, which are not part of MDD's diagnostic criteria.
differential_diagnosis.source: APA DSM-5-TR (2022) diagnostic criteria

risk_factors.factor: Trauma type - interpersonal and sexual violence
risk_factors.note: In a 24-country WHO World Mental Health Survey analysis (n=68,894) that evaluated PTSD separately for each of 29 lifetime trauma types, traumas involving interpersonal violence carried the highest PTSD risk. Measured as share of total population PTSD burden (trauma prevalence x trauma-specific PTSD risk x persistence), rape accounted for 13.1% of all PTSD burden, other sexual assault 15.1%, and being stalked 9.8%, despite these being comparatively uncommon traumas - the broad category of intimate partner sexual violence alone accounted for nearly 42.7% of all person-years lived with PTSD.
risk_factors.source: Kessler RC et al, 'Trauma and PTSD in the WHO World Mental Health Surveys', Eur J Psychotraumatol 2017;8(sup5):1353383 (PMID 29075426)

risk_factors.note: The same 24-country WHO survey found that a person's prior trauma history predicted both their risk of experiencing future traumas and their risk of developing PTSD from those future traumas - i.e. trauma exposure and PTSD vulnerability compound over a person's life course rather than being independent, one-off risks.
risk_factors.source: Kessler RC et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2017;8(sup5):1353383 (PMID 29075426)

risk_factors.note: In the US National Comorbidity Survey, PTSD lifetime prevalence was elevated among women; the trauma types most commonly associated with PTSD differed by sex, with combat exposure and witnessing most common among men and rape and sexual molestation most common among women.
risk_factors.source: Kessler RC, Sonnega A, Bromet E, Hughes M, Nelson CB, 'Posttraumatic stress disorder in the National Comorbidity Survey', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1995;52(12):1048-1060 (PMID 7492257)

risk_factors.note: A systematic review and meta-analysis of ICD-11 PTSD and Complex PTSD prevalence found pooled rates of 2% (PTSD) and 4% (Complex PTSD) among adults in non-war-exposed, economically developed regions, rising to 6% and 15% respectively in war-exposed or less economically developed regions - a real, quantified 3x (PTSD) to nearly 4x (Complex PTSD) increase in prevalence associated with war exposure/lower-resource settings.
risk_factors.source: Fung HW et al, 'Prevalence of ICD-11 post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex PTSD in the general populations: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Asian J Psychiatry 2025;110:104610 (PMID 40652792)

us_lifetime_prevalence.finding: The US National Comorbidity Survey (a representative national sample of 5,877 persons aged 15-54) found an estimated DSM-III-R PTSD lifetime prevalence of 7.8%, with PTSD strongly comorbid with other lifetime psychiatric disorders.
us_lifetime_prevalence.source: Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1995;52(12):1048-1060 (PMID 7492257)
us_lifetime_prevalence.confidence: high - large nationally representative survey, though it uses older DSM-III-R criteria

global_trauma_exposure_and_ptsd_burden.finding: The WHO World Mental Health Surveys, conducted across 24 countries (n=68,894), found that 70.4% of respondents had experienced at least one lifetime trauma, with an average of 3.2 traumas per person. PTSD risk and burden were highly unequally distributed across trauma types rather than proportional to trauma frequency (see risk_factors above).
global_trauma_exposure_and_ptsd_burden.source: Kessler RC et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2017;8(sup5):1353383 (PMID 29075426)

icd11_specific_prevalence_ptsd_vs_comple.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis using ICD-11 criteria found pooled general-population prevalence of 2% for PTSD and 4% for Complex PTSD in non-war-exposed/economically developed regions, versus 6% and 15% respectively in war-exposed/less economically developed regions - showing Complex PTSD is not rare relative to simple PTSD and, in higher-trauma-burden settings, is actually more prevalent than simple PTSD.
icd11_specific_prevalence_ptsd_vs_comple.source: Fung HW et al, Asian J Psychiatry 2025;110:104610 (PMID 40652792)
icd11_specific_prevalence_ptsd_vs_comple.confidence: high - recent systematic review and meta-analysis using current ICD-11 criteria

untreated_chronicity.finding: In the National Comorbidity Survey, survival analysis showed that more than one-third of people with an index episode of PTSD failed to recover even after many years, indicating PTSD is often persistent rather than self-limiting when untreated. Consistent with this, the later 24-country WHO World Mental Health Survey analysis found that although a substantial minority of PTSD cases remit within months of onset, mean symptom duration across trauma types is considerably longer than previously recognized.
untreated_chronicity.source: Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1995;52(12):1048-1060 (PMID 7492257); Kessler RC et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2017;8(sup5):1353383 (PMID 29075426)

real_treatment_success_trauma_focused_ps.finding: This is the real success story in PTSD: trauma-focused psychotherapy is one of the most effective psychosocial treatments in psychiatry. A multidimensional meta-analysis of psychotherapy trials for PTSD (1980-2003) found that more than half of patients who complete treatment with cognitive behavioural therapy (including cognitive processing therapy and prolonged exposure) or EMDR improve, and concluded that the majority of patients treated with psychotherapy for PTSD recover or improve. A separate, larger meta-analysis of 137 treatment comparisons from 112 randomized trials (1980-2012) found large controlled effect sizes for cognitive therapy (Hedges' g=1.63), exposure therapy (g=1.08), and EMDR (g=1.01) - i.e. trauma-focused CBT and EMDR produce large, real, quantified symptom reductions, and many patients who complete a full course of treatment no longer meet PTSD diagnostic criteria afterward.
real_treatment_success_trauma_focused_ps.source: Bradley R, Greene J, Russ E, Dutra L, Westen D, 'A multidimensional meta-analysis of psychotherapy for PTSD', Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(2):214-227 (PMID 15677582); Watts BV, Schnurr PP, Mayo L, Young-Xu Y, Weeks WB, Friedman MJ, 'Meta-analysis of the efficacy of treatments for posttraumatic stress disorder', J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)
real_treatment_success_trauma_focused_ps.confidence: high - both are large, formal meta-analyses of randomized-trial data

honest_population_dependent_caveat.finding: Outcomes are real but not uniform across trauma populations. A JAMA review of randomized trials of trauma-focused psychotherapy specifically in military personnel and veterans (5 RCTs of cognitive processing therapy, n=481; 4 RCTs of prolonged exposure, n=402) found large within-group effect sizes (Cohen's d 0.78-1.10) and that 49-70% of participants attained clinically meaningful symptom improvement, but mean post-treatment scores often remained at or above the clinical threshold for PTSD, and 60-72% of patients retained their PTSD diagnosis after a full course of treatment. This means trauma-focused CBT works and produces meaningful improvement for most military/veteran patients, but full remission (loss of diagnosis) is less common in this specific population than the general civilian trauma-exposed samples in the Bradley/Watts meta-analyses above - underscoring a real, unresolved treatment-response gap that the field has not yet closed for combat-related and chronic military trauma.
honest_population_dependent_caveat.source: Steenkamp MM, Litz BT, Hoge CW, Marmar CR, 'Psychotherapy for Military-Related PTSD: A Review of Randomized Clinical Trials', JAMA 2015;314(5):489-500 (PMID 26241600)
honest_population_dependent_caveat.confidence: high - systematic review of RCT data, explicitly population-specific (military/veteran)

complex_ptsd_course_and_treatment_implic.finding: Complex PTSD (ICD-11 6B41), arising from prolonged or repeated interpersonal trauma, is a distinguishable diagnostic entity (see differential_diagnosis) whose added 'disturbances in self-organization' symptoms (affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship difficulties) are not targeted by trauma-focused exposure/reprocessing protocols alone - current clinical guidance emphasises that correctly distinguishing Complex PTSD from both simple PTSD and Borderline Personality Disorder matters because it changes treatment sequencing (commonly a phase-based approach: stabilization and affect-regulation skills before trauma-memory processing).
complex_ptsd_course_and_treatment_implic.source: Cloitre M et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2014;5 (PMID 25279111); Karatzias T et al, Br J Psychiatry 2023;223(3):403-406 (PMID 37381070)
