complex_ptsd_course_and_treatment_implic.confidence: moderate-high - construct validity and differential-diagnosis guidance are well supported; this KB's symptom-side scope does not extend to specific phase-based treatment-protocol efficacy data, which belongs to a separate treatment-focused pass

lead_with_the_real_success_story.finding: PTSD is a highly and genuinely treatable condition. Trauma-focused psychotherapies - cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, and EMDR - produce large, real, meta-analytically quantified effect sizes (g approximately 1.0-1.6) and the majority of patients who complete treatment recover or substantially improve, with many no longer meeting PTSD diagnostic criteria afterward (Bradley et al 2005, PMID 15677582; Watts et al 2013, PMID 23842024). This success is real and should be the leading message for any patient newly diagnosed with PTSD.
lead_with_the_real_success_story.source: Bradley R et al, Am J Psychiatry 2005;162(2):214-227 (PMID 15677582); Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013;74(6):e541-550 (PMID 23842024)

screen_with_pcl5_and_apply_the_emergency.finding: The PCL-5 should anchor structured screening and severity tracking rather than unstructured clinical impression alone (Blevins et al 2015, PMID 26606250). However, the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE (suicide risk, severe dissociative crisis) takes priority over routine screening or symptom intake whenever either is present, and must be checked first, not after a full symptom history is taken.
screen_with_pcl5_and_apply_the_emergency.source: Blevins CA et al, J Trauma Stress 2015;28(6):489-498 (PMID 26606250); Krysinska K, Lester D, Arch Suicide Res 2010;14(1):1-23 (PMID 20112140)

panic_disorder.name: Panic Disorder
panic_disorder.icd11_hint: 6B01 Panic disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, block 6B00-6B0Z Anxiety or fear-related disorders); ICD-10 F41.0 Panic disorder [episodic paroxysmal anxiety]. This code is consistent with, and cross-referenced from, the already-verified generalized_anxiety_disorder entry (which cites 6B01 as its panic-disorder differential) and the agoraphobia entry (6B02, inferred from the same sequential ICD-11 anxiety-disorder block ordering: 6B00 GAD, 6B01 Panic disorder, 6B02 Agoraphobia, 6B03 Specific phobia, 6B04 Social anxiety disorder). FLAG: the exact WHO ICD-11 browser/API entry could not be directly queried in this research session (id.who.int/icd API requires an OAuth token not available here); recommend direct WHO ICD-11 browser confirmation (icd.who.int) before any clinical or billing use of this code.
panic_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Panic disorder carries a real, elevated, directly-documented suicide risk that MUST be actively screened for and MUST bypass the routine doctor-approval-queue flow when positive, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department now, or call a local emergency/suicide helpline) rather than the standard consultation flow. Real evidence, specific to panic disorder: (1) Teismann T et al, 'Suicidal ideation in primary care patients suffering from panic disorder with or without agoraphobia', BMC Psychiatry 2018;18:305 (PMID 30249220) found 25% of primary-care panic disorder patients reported current suicidal ideation, with depression diagnosis and depression severity as the strongest correlates; (2) Kanwar A et al, 'The association between anxiety disorders and suicidal behaviors: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Depress Anxiety 2013;30(10):917-929 (PMID 23408488) found anxiety disorders as a class (including panic disorder) carry significantly elevated risk of suicidal ideation (OR 2.89), suicide attempts (OR 2.47), and completed suicide (OR 3.34) versus people without an anxiety disorder; (3) Sareen J et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005;62(11):1249-1257 (PMID 16275812) found any anxiety disorder independently associated with incident suicidal ideation (adjusted OR 2.32) and suicide attempts (adjusted OR 3.64) after adjusting for mood disorders and other comorbidity. Every patient being evaluated for panic disorder should be directly and explicitly screened for suicidal ideation, intent, plan, and access to lethal means as a mandatory part of the consultation flow, with any positive screen triggering the emergency override described above rather than the routine ai_suggests/doctor-approval cycle.

dsm5_panic_attack_definition.finding: A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes, accompanied by 4 or more of 13 physical/cognitive symptoms: palpitations/pounding heart or accelerated heart rate; sweating; trembling or shaking; sensations of shortness of breath or smothering; feelings of choking; chest pain or discomfort; nausea or abdominal distress; feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed, or faint; chills or heat sensations; paraesthesias (numbness or tingling sensations); derealization or depersonalization; fear of losing control or 'going crazy'; and fear of dying. DSM-5 retains the distinction between 'expected' panic attacks (with an obvious cue/trigger) and 'unexpected' panic attacks (no obvious cue), which is central to diagnosing panic disorder.
dsm5_panic_attack_definition.source: Craske MG, Kircanski K, Epstein A, Wittchen HU, Pine DS, Lewis-Fernandez R, Hinton D, 'Panic disorder: a review of DSM-IV panic disorder and proposals for DSM-V', Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270) -- the direct panic-disorder analogue of the Wittchen et al agoraphobia review already used in this knowledge base's agoraphobia entry, and whose recommendations were carried into DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013)

dsm5_panic_disorder_criteria.finding: DSM-5 panic disorder requires: (A) recurrent UNEXPECTED panic attacks; (B) at least one attack followed by 1 month or more of persistent concern or worry about additional panic attacks or their consequences (e.g. losing control, having a heart attack, 'going crazy'), or a significant maladaptive change in behavior related to the attacks (e.g. avoiding exercise or unfamiliar situations); and (C) the disturbance is not attributable to a substance or another medical condition, and not better explained by another mental disorder. Panic disorder and agoraphobia are independently codable DSM-5 diagnoses -- a patient can be diagnosed with panic disorder with or without a co-occurring agoraphobia diagnosis (see this knowledge base's agoraphobia entry for the decoupling history).
dsm5_panic_disorder_criteria.source: Craske MG et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270); cross-referenced against Wittchen HU, Gloster AT, Beesdo-Baum K, Fava GA, Craske MG, 'Agoraphobia: a review of the diagnostic classificatory position and criteria', Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426), already used in this knowledge base's agoraphobia entry

with_without_agoraphobia_prevalence_spli.finding: In the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (DSM-IV framework, n=9,282), lifetime prevalence was 3.7% for panic disorder without agoraphobia and 1.1% for panic disorder with agoraphobia (PD-AG) -- i.e. most panic disorder in the general population occurs without agoraphobia, but the subgroup with agoraphobia had the most severe illness of any panic-spectrum group studied (86.3% rated moderate-or-severe on the Panic Disorder Severity Scale, versus far lower rates in the other subgroups) and the highest comorbidity with other lifetime DSM-IV disorders.
with_without_agoraphobia_prevalence_spli.source: Kessler RC, Chiu WT, Jin R, Ruscio AM, Shear K, Walters EE, 'The epidemiology of panic attacks, panic disorder, and agoraphobia in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471) -- already used in this knowledge base's agoraphobia entry

panic_attack_symptom_cluster.finding: The core presenting event is the panic attack itself: a discrete episode of intense fear/discomfort peaking within minutes, drawing on the 13-symptom DSM-5 list (palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea/abdominal distress, dizziness/light-headedness, chills or hot flushes, paraesthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying), of which 4 or more must be present. Because the somatic symptoms (chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea, dizziness) so closely resemble cardiac and other acute medical emergencies, patients with panic disorder use medical (not only psychiatric) services frequently and repeatedly.
panic_attack_symptom_cluster.source: Craske MG et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270); Weissman MM, Klerman GL, Markowitz JS, Ouellette R, N Engl J Med 1989;321(18):1209-1214 (PMID 2797086), which explicitly notes 'panic symptoms can mimic those of other medical disorders' driving frequent medical-service use

anticipatory_anxiety.finding: DSM-5 Criterion B requires persistent (1+ month) concern or worry about having additional panic attacks or about their feared consequences (e.g. having a heart attack, losing control, 'going crazy') -- this anticipatory anxiety, sometimes described clinically as 'fear of fear', is a defining cognitive feature of panic disorder distinct from the panic attacks themselves, and can persist and drive impairment even between attacks.
anticipatory_anxiety.source: Craske MG et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270)

avoidance_behavior.finding: DSM-5 Criterion B is satisfied either by anticipatory anxiety or by a significant maladaptive change in behavior related to the attacks -- e.g. avoiding exercise, caffeine, unfamiliar places, or situations previously associated with an attack. When this avoidance organises specifically around fear of being unable to escape or get help across the five agoraphobic situational domains (public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds/lines, being outside the home alone), it meets criteria for a separate, co-occurring agoraphobia diagnosis rather than being folded into panic disorder itself; in NCS-R data roughly 1.1% of the population had panic disorder with agoraphobia versus 3.7% without it.
avoidance_behavior.source: Craske MG et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270); Kessler RC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(4):415-424 (PMID 16585471); Wittchen HU et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):113-133 (PMID 20143426) as already used in this knowledge base's agoraphobia entry

somatic_symptom_burden_and_healthcare_us.finding: Because panic symptoms mimic other medical disorders, people with panic disorder are disproportionately represented among patients presenting acutely with chest pain. An Australian ED cohort study of 338 consecutive chest-pain patients found a clinical diagnosis of panic disorder in 5.6% (95% CI 3.4-8.6%), while a separate US ED series found panic-like anxiety in 44% of patients with unexplained chest pain (physicians recognised only 7.4% of those cases); an earlier Montreal Heart Institute ED cohort found panic disorder in 25% of consecutive chest-pain presentations, and at 2-year follow-up this group (versus non-panic-disorder chest-pain patients) reported significantly more repeat ED visits for chest pain (40% vs 14%), more hospitalizations (31% vs 11%), and worse self-rated general health (22% vs 9% rating it 'poor').
somatic_symptom_burden_and_healthcare_us.source: Greenslade JH et al, 'Panic Disorder in Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Chest Pain: Prevalence and Presenting Symptoms', Heart Lung Circ 2017;26(12):1310-1316 (PMID 28256404) -- already used in this knowledge base's ischaemic_heart_disease entry; Fleet RP et al, CJEM 2003;5(4):247-254 (PMID 17472767)

clinical_diagnosis_no_biomarker.finding: Panic disorder is diagnosed clinically against the DSM-5 criteria described above (recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus 1+ month of anticipatory anxiety or maladaptive avoidance) -- there is no laboratory test or imaging biomarker that establishes the diagnosis. The diagnosis is explicitly one of exclusion: DSM-5 Criterion C requires that the disturbance not be attributable to a substance or another medical condition, and not be better explained by another mental disorder.
clinical_diagnosis_no_biomarker.source: Craske MG et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270)

ruling_out_cardiac_causes_first.finding: Because the panic-attack symptom cluster (chest pain/tightness, palpitations, dyspnoea, dizziness, sweating, sense of impending doom) so closely mirrors acute coronary syndrome, a real and adequately negative cardiac work-up (ECG plus vital signs and troponin/risk stratification as clinically indicated) must precede a panic-disorder diagnosis in any patient presenting with these symptoms, particularly on a first episode or in a patient with cardiac risk factors. This is not a theoretical concern: real ED cohorts have found panic disorder in 5.6% to 25% of consecutive chest-pain presentations depending on setting and case-finding method, and recognition by treating physicians is poor (only 7.4% of probable cases recognised in one US series, over 92% undiagnosed at ED discharge).
ruling_out_cardiac_causes_first.source: Greenslade JH et al, Heart Lung Circ 2017;26(12):1310-1316 (PMID 28256404); Fleet RP et al, CJEM 2003;5(4):247-254 (PMID 17472767)

ruling_out_other_medical_causes.finding: DSM-5 Criterion C for panic disorder (disturbance not attributable to a substance or another medical condition) reflects standard clinical practice of excluding other conditions that can present with panic-like paroxysmal symptoms before finalising a psychiatric diagnosis -- including hyperthyroidism, cardiac arrhythmias, pulmonary embolism, hypoglycemia, vestibular disorders, and substance intoxication or withdrawal (e.g. caffeine, stimulants, alcohol withdrawal). This knowledge base did not independently locate a single dedicated panic-disorder-specific study quantifying the yield of each of these individual medical rule-outs within this research session; the exclusion requirement itself is directly sourced to the DSM-5 criteria review below, and its component differentials are the standard medical teaching for paroxysmal-symptom presentations rather than a separately verified statistic.
ruling_out_other_medical_causes.source: Craske MG et al, Depress Anxiety 2010;27(2):93-112 (PMID 20099270), Criterion C discussion
ruling_out_other_medical_causes.confidence: moderate -- the exclusion criterion itself is high-confidence and directly sourced; the specific list of alternative medical causes is standard clinical teaching not independently re-verified against a dedicated primary study this session

cbt_and_pharmacotherapy_real_success_sto.finding: Panic disorder is one of the most treatment-responsive psychiatric conditions: in a 312-patient randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial across 4 US anxiety research clinics, both cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) alone and imipramine alone were significantly superior to placebo, with acute intent-to-treat response rates (Panic Disorder Severity Scale) of 48.7% for CBT and 45.8% for imipramine versus 21.7% for placebo; after 6 months of maintenance treatment, response rates were 39.5% (CBT) and 37.8% (imipramine) versus 13.0% (placebo), and combined CBT-plus-imipramine reached a 57.1% maintenance response rate. CBT's benefit proved the most durable: 6 months after treatment discontinuation, 31.9% of the CBT-alone group and 41.0% of the CBT-plus-placebo group remained responders by Clinical Global Impression rating, versus only 19.7% for imipramine alone. A 2016 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 60 studies (3,021 patients in the quantitative synthesis) confirmed CBT as the most extensively studied and generally best-performing psychological therapy for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, including the highest long-term remission/response among therapies compared, though the review cautioned that individual effect sizes were often small and evidence quality low-to-moderate.
cbt_and_pharmacotherapy_real_success_sto.source: Barlow DH, Gorman JM, Shear MK, Woods SW, 'Cognitive-behavioral therapy, imipramine, or their combination for panic disorder: A randomized controlled trial', JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536 (PMID 10815116); Pompoli A, Furukawa TA, Imai H, Tajika A, Efthimiou O, Salanti G, 'Psychological therapies for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia in adults: a network meta-analysis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011004 (PMID 27071857)

long_term_remission_and_relapse.finding: A NESARC-based longitudinal study of the real-world course of panic disorder with vs without agoraphobia found high 3-year remission rates -- 75% for panic disorder alone (PD) versus a somewhat lower 67% for panic disorder with agoraphobia (PDA) -- with relatively infrequent relapse (12% for PD vs 21% for PDA). Predictors of a worse course included prior panic-attack history, comorbid generalized anxiety disorder or major depressive disorder, nicotine dependence, female sex, younger age, and major financial crises.
long_term_remission_and_relapse.source: Nay W, Brown R, Roberson-Nay R, 'Longitudinal course of panic disorder with and without agoraphobia using the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC)', Psychiatry Res 2013;205(1-2):122-127 (PMID 23587657) -- already used in this knowledge base's agoraphobia entry

untreated_course_and_the_real_treatment_.finding: The tragedy in panic disorder is under-treatment, not a lack of an effective treatment: a 2-year follow-up of emergency-department chest-pain patients found that those with confirmed panic disorder (versus those without) showed significant worsening of panic symptoms, agoraphobic avoidance, depression, and trait anxiety, plus significantly greater suicidal ideation (32% vs 9%) and far higher repeat ED use and hospitalization -- yet only 22% of these confirmed panic-disorder patients had received any form of mental health treatment for their symptoms. This contrasts sharply with the real, high response and remission rates achievable with CBT and/or pharmacotherapy above, underscoring that the chronic, disabling course seen in practice is a real and largely preventable consequence of under-recognition and under-treatment, not a ceiling on how well panic disorder can respond to treatment when it is actually given.
untreated_course_and_the_real_treatment_.source: Fleet RP, Lavoie KL, Martel JP, Dupuis G, Marchand A, Beitman BD, CJEM 2003;5(4):247-254 (PMID 17472767)

apa_practice_guideline_context.finding: The American Psychiatric Association's Work Group on Panic Disorder published a formal Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients with Panic Disorder (Am J Psychiatry 1998), establishing CBT and/or pharmacotherapy (SSRIs, other antidepressants, or benzodiazepines) as evidence-based first-line treatments. This 1998 guideline was subsequently updated by the APA as a second edition in 2009; this knowledge base independently verified the original 1998 guideline's PubMed record this session but did not independently re-verify the 2009 second edition against its own primary bibliographic record, so that update is noted here for context rather than cited as independently confirmed.
apa_practice_guideline_context.source: American Psychiatric Association, Work Group on Panic Disorder, 'Practice guideline for the treatment of patients with panic disorder', Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(5 Suppl):1-34 (PMID 9585731)
apa_practice_guideline_context.confidence: high for the 1998 guideline's existence/content; the 2009 second-edition update is named but not independently re-verified this session

panic_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Panic disorder is not eliminated in the sense of a guaranteed, permanent, one-time, drug-free cure for every patient, but the real, session-verified evidence shows that a genuine majority of patients reach a durable, panic-free or near-panic-free state with correctly delivered treatment, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) built around interoceptive exposure (deliberate, repeated exposure to the feared bodily sensations of panic -- racing heart, dizziness, breathlessness -- until the catastrophic misinterpretation of them extinguishes) is the real treatment most consistently shown to be both highly effective and durable after treatment ends. Arntz A (Behav Res Ther 2002;40(3):325-341, PMID 11863242), a randomized trial of cognitive therapy versus interoceptive exposure in patients with panic disorder without agoraphobia (n=69), found that in BOTH treatment arms a high percentage of patients were panic-free at post-treatment and remained so at both 4-week and 6-month follow-up, with panic-free rates ranging 75-92% across conditions and timepoints -- a real, replicated, durable outcome, not a short-lived response. Craske MG et al (Br J Clin Psychol 1997;36(1):85-99, PMID 9051281), a component RCT in panic disorder with agoraphobia (n=38), found that the arm that specifically included interoceptive exposure (versus an arm substituting breathing retraining) was more effective at post-treatment and, importantly, more effective still at 6-month follow-up on panic frequency, phobic fears, and general anxiety -- direct evidence that the interoceptive-exposure component specifically drives the durable gain, not just CBT in general. Barlow DH et al (JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536, PMID 10815116), a 312-patient, 4-site NIMH collaborative RCT in panic disorder with/without mild-to-moderate agoraphobia, found acute Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS) response rates of 48.7% for CBT alone and 45.8% for imipramine alone, both far above 21.7% for placebo; combining CBT with imipramine raised acute response to 60.3% (PDSS)/64.1% (CGI); critically, at 6-month maintenance, combined treatment gave the best response of any arm (57.1%), but after treatment was later discontinued, CBT-alone patients showed the best durability of any arm, holding gains better than imipramine-alone or combined-treatment patients once the drug was withdrawn. On pharmacotherapy: SSRIs and SNRIs are real, effective, guideline-recommended first-line options, comparable to CBT in acute efficacy per two independent meta-analyses (Mitte K, Psychol Bull 2005;131(5):785-795 covering panic disorder, PMID 16005982, finding (C)BT at least as effective as pharmacotherapy and sometimes more so; Bakker A et al, Acta Psychiatr Scand 2002;106(3):163-167, PMID 12197851, a 43-study meta-analysis finding SSRIs and TCAs equally effective for panic-free rate but SSRIs far better tolerated, 18% vs 31% drop-out). Paroxetine 40mg/day produced an 86.0% panic-free rate at 10 weeks versus 50.0% on placebo in a 278-patient double-blind fixed-dose RCT (Ballenger JC et al, Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42, PMID 9433336); venlafaxine ER (an SNRI) significantly improved response and remission rates versus placebo in a 361-patient RCT (Bradwejn J et al, Br J Psychiatry 2005;187:352-359, PMID 16199795), consistent with the 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 70 RCTs (Guaiana G et al, PMID 38014714) which found SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs and benzodiazepines were ALL more effective than placebo for response, with little difference between classes, though paroxetine and fluoxetine show stronger evidence than sertraline within the SSRI class. Alprazolam produced rapid, real relief (82% moderately-improved-or-better versus 43% on placebo, and 50% panic-free versus 28% on placebo, both at week 4, in a 526-patient trial: Ballenger JC et al, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(5):413-422, PMID 3282478; confirmed at 1,168-patient scale by the Cross-National Collaborative Panic Study, Br J Psychiatry 1992;160:191-202, PMID 1540759), but benzodiazepines carry the same real tolerance/dependence/withdrawal liability documented across the anxiety disorders, which is why current guidelines reserve them for short-term/bridge use. CBT is itself a proven, real solution to that specific problem: in a controlled trial of patients trying to stop long-term high-potency benzodiazepines, adding a 10-week group CBT program to a slow taper produced successful discontinuation in 76% of patients (13/17) versus 25% (4/16) with taper alone, and 77% of the CBT group remained benzodiazepine-free at 3-month follow-up (Otto MW et al, Am J Psychiatry 1993;150(10):1485-1490, PMID 8379551). No single treatment surveyed here reaches a documented, replicated 100% cure rate in an unselected panic-disorder population, but the honest, evidence-grounded picture is that CBT with interoceptive exposure gets a genuine majority of patients to a durable panic-free state that holds at 6-month follow-up, SSRI/SNRI pharmacotherapy is a comparably effective real first-line alternative or adjunct, and CBT additionally provides a proven route off long-term benzodiazepine use for patients who need to discontinue it.

curative_option.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy with Interoceptive Exposure -- the Real Closest-to-Cure Treatment for Panic Disorder
curative_option.type: Structured exposure-based psychotherapy, typically 10-16 individual or group sessions combining cognitive restructuring, interoceptive exposure (deliberate exposure to feared bodily sensations), and (where agoraphobic avoidance is present) in-vivo exposure; not a drug or procedure
curative_option.note: Panic disorder is not guaranteed to be permanently and completely eliminated for every patient by any single treatment course, and relapse can occur, especially without maintenance practice. What IS real: two independent randomized trials that isolated interoceptive exposure specifically (rather than CBT as an undifferentiated package) found it produces high, durable panic-free rates and out-performs a comparator missing that component at follow-up, and a landmark large multi-site RCT found CBT alone was the most durable treatment of any arm once active treatment was discontinued.

real_trial_data.arntz_2002_ct_vs_interoceptive_exposure: Randomized trial, panic disorder without agoraphobia, n=69: cognitive therapy and interoceptive exposure were both highly effective, with panic-free rates ranging 75-92% across conditions at post-treatment, 4-week follow-up, and 6-month follow-up -- i.e. the gain was durable, not just an acute-phase effect.
real_trial_data.craske_1997_interoceptive_exposure_compo: Randomized component trial, panic disorder with agoraphobia, n=38: the treatment arm that included interoceptive exposure (vs an arm substituting breathing retraining, both alongside cognitive restructuring and in-vivo exposure) was more effective at post-treatment on panic frequency, overall severity and functioning, and MORE effective still at 6-month follow-up on panic frequency, phobic fears, general anxiety and functioning -- direct evidence the interoceptive-exposure component itself drives durable improvement.
real_trial_data.barlow_2000_nimh_collaborative_trial: 312 patients, 4 US academic anxiety-disorder clinics, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled: acute PDSS response 48.7% CBT alone, 45.8% imipramine alone, both far above 21.7% placebo; combining CBT with imipramine raised acute response to 60.3% (PDSS)/64.1% (CGI); at 6-month maintenance (while still on treatment), combined treatment gave the best response of any arm (57.1% PDSS vs 39.5% CBT alone and 37.8% imipramine alone), but CBT alone showed the best durability of any arm after treatment was later discontinued.
real_trial_data.deacon_2013_optimizing_interoceptive_exp: Randomized trial, n=120 with elevated anxiety sensitivity: an intensive delivery of interoceptive exposure (optimizing inhibitory learning) produced significantly greater reductions in anxiety sensitivity and fearful responding than the standard low-dose interoceptive-exposure protocol from Barlow and Craske's Panic Control Treatment manual, suggesting real, actionable room to further improve on already-effective interoceptive exposure delivery.

curative_option.source: Arntz A. Behav Res Ther 2002;40(3):325-341 (PMID 11863242); Craske MG, Rowe M, Lewin M, Noriega-Dimitri R. Br J Clin Psychol 1997;36(1):85-99 (PMID 9051281); Barlow DH et al. JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536 (PMID 10815116); Deacon B, Kemp JJ, Dixon LJ, Sy JT, Farrell NR, Zhang AR. Behav Res Ther 2013;51(9):588-596 (PMID 23872701)
curative_option.confidence: high for the Arntz 2002, Craske 1997 and Barlow 2000 randomized-trial numbers (real, documented denominators); moderate-high for generalizing the Deacon 2013 anxiety-sensitivity-analogue finding to full panic-disorder populations, since that trial recruited on elevated anxiety sensitivity rather than a formal panic-disorder diagnosis

pand_cbt_interoceptive_exposure_arntz200.name: Cognitive Therapy vs Interoceptive Exposure -- Real Randomized Trial, Panic Disorder Without Agoraphobia
pand_cbt_interoceptive_exposure_arntz200.type: Structured exposure-based/cognitive psychotherapy, first-line non-drug treatment
pand_cbt_interoceptive_exposure_arntz200.effectiveness: Arntz A (Behav Res Ther 2002;40(3):325-341, PMID 11863242), n=69 randomized: no significant differences between CT and IE on panic frequency, daily anxiety or a composite symptom score at post-test, 4-week or 6-month follow-up; in BOTH conditions a high percentage of patients were panic-free at post-test and follow-up, ranging 75-92%.
pand_cbt_interoceptive_exposure_arntz200.reason_why: Both approaches directly target the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations that drives panic -- CT by verbally challenging the misinterpretation, IE by repeatedly and safely producing the feared sensations until the misinterpretation extinguishes through direct experience -- and both produced comparably high, durable remission.
pand_cbt_interoceptive_exposure_arntz200.important_caveat: The trial reports a 75-92% panic-free RANGE across the two conditions and three assessment points rather than one single pooled figure; the conservative low end of that real range is used in the ranked table rather than an averaged or high-end estimate.
pand_cbt_interoceptive_exposure_arntz200.real_working_solution: A structured 12-session course of cognitive therapy OR interoceptive exposure (both real, comparably effective options) as first-line treatment for panic disorder without agoraphobia.

pand_cbt_component_craske1997.name: Interoceptive Exposure vs Breathing Retraining Within CBT -- Real Component RCT, Panic Disorder With Agoraphobia
specific_drugs: Interoceptive exposure + cognitive restructuring + in-vivo exposure
Breathing retraining + cognitive restructuring + in-vivo exposure
pand_cbt_component_craske1997.effectiveness: Craske MG, Rowe M, Lewin M, Noriega-Dimitri R (Br J Clin Psychol 1997;36(1):85-99, PMID 9051281), n=38 randomized: the interoceptive-exposure arm was more effective at post-treatment (panic frequency, overall severity, functioning) and more effective still at 6-month follow-up (panic frequency, phobic fears, general anxiety, functioning) than the breathing-retraining arm.
pand_cbt_component_craske1997.reason_why: Interoceptive exposure directly extinguishes fear of the bodily sensations themselves, whereas breathing retraining primarily manages symptoms rather than eliminating the underlying catastrophic-misinterpretation mechanism, which is the likely reason its relative advantage widened, not narrowed, by 6-month follow-up.
pand_cbt_component_craske1997.important_caveat: Small trial (n=38) with attrition limiting follow-up analyses; no categorical panic-free percentage reported in the abstract, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to this entry.
pand_cbt_component_craske1997.real_working_solution: Include interoceptive exposure specifically (not just breathing retraining) as a core CBT component for panic disorder, since it produces a real, durable advantage that grows over follow-up.
pand_cbt_component_craske1997.source: Craske MG, Rowe M, Lewin M, Noriega-Dimitri R. Br J Clin Psychol 1997;36(1):85-99 (PMID 9051281)

pand_cbt_plus_medication_barlow2000.name: CBT, Imipramine, or Their Combination -- Real NIMH Multi-Site RCT
pand_cbt_plus_medication_barlow2000.effectiveness: Barlow DH et al (JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536, PMID 10815116), n=312, 4 US academic anxiety clinics, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled: acute PDSS response 48.7% CBT alone, 45.8% imipramine alone, 21.7% placebo; combined 60.3% (PDSS)/64.1% (CGI). At 6-month maintenance: combined 57.1%, CBT alone 39.5%, imipramine alone 37.8%. CBT alone showed the best durability of any arm after treatment discontinuation.
pand_cbt_plus_medication_barlow2000.reason_why: CBT and imipramine act via different mechanisms (learned cognitive-behavioral change vs monoamine reuptake inhibition) and their acute benefits combine additively; CBT's durability advantage reflects that it teaches a skill that persists once the drug's pharmacological support is withdrawn.
pand_cbt_plus_medication_barlow2000.important_caveat: Combined treatment produced the single highest acute and 6-month response rate, but CBT alone -- despite a lower peak response -- held up best once treatment stopped, so the 'best' option depends on whether the goal is peak short-term response or durability after discontinuation.
pand_cbt_plus_medication_barlow2000.real_working_solution: Combined CBT + an SSRI/SNRI (or imipramine) for the strongest acute and maintenance response; CBT alone (with or without a taper of medication) when long-term drug-free durability is the priority.
pand_cbt_plus_medication_barlow2000.source: Barlow DH, Gorman JM, Shear MK, Woods SW. JAMA 2000;283(19):2529-2536 (PMID 10815116)

pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.name: Paroxetine -- Real Double-Blind, Fixed-Dose, Placebo-Controlled Trial
pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.type: SSRI, first-line pharmacotherapy, FDA-approved for panic disorder
pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.effectiveness: Ballenger JC et al (Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42, PMID 9433336), n=278 randomized: despite a mean of 9.5-11.6 full panic attacks during screening, 86.0% of patients on paroxetine 40mg/day, 65.2% on 20mg, and 67.4% on 10mg were free of full panic attacks by week 10, versus 50.0% on placebo; the 40mg group showed significantly greater global improvement than placebo, evident by week 4.
pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.reason_why: Paroxetine's selective serotonin reuptake inhibition reduces amygdala-driven fear responding over several weeks; the dose-response signal (40mg outperforming 20mg) supports up-titrating non-remitters.
pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.important_caveat: 40mg/day was the minimum dose statistically superior to placebo across the majority of outcome measures in this trial; some individual patients responded at lower doses, but the labeled effective dose from this pivotal trial is 40mg/day.
pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.real_working_solution: Paroxetine 40mg/day (up-titrated from a lower starting dose) as a real, FDA-approved first-line SSRI for panic disorder.
pand_ssri_paroxetine_ballenger1998.source: Ballenger JC, Wheadon DE, Steiner M, Bushnell W, Gergel IP. Am J Psychiatry 1998;155(1):36-42 (PMID 9433336)

pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.name: Sertraline -- Real Flexible-Dose, Placebo-Controlled Multicenter Trial
pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.type: SSRI, first-line pharmacotherapy, FDA-approved for panic disorder
pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.effectiveness: Pollack MH et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 1998;55(11):1010-1016, PMID 9819070), n=176 randomized, 10-site: sertraline produced significantly greater improvement than placebo on panic-attack frequency (p=.01), CGI Improvement (p=.01) and Severity (p=.009), PDSS ratings (p=.03), and quality-of-life scores (p=.003), with adverse-event rates similar to placebo.
pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.reason_why: Same serotonin-reuptake-inhibition mechanism as paroxetine; sertraline's real advantage in general practice is a favorable drug-interaction profile.
pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.important_caveat: This trial's abstract reports statistical significance (p-values) rather than a categorical response/remission percentage, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to this entry rather than estimating one.
pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.real_working_solution: Sertraline 50-200 mg/day as a real, guideline-endorsed first-line SSRI alternative to paroxetine for panic disorder.
pand_ssri_sertraline_pollack1998.source: Pollack MH, Otto MW, Worthington JJ, Manfro GG, Wolkow R. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1998;55(11):1010-1016 (PMID 9819070)

pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.name: Venlafaxine Extended-Release -- Real Flexible-Dose, Placebo-Controlled Trial
pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.type: SNRI, first-line pharmacotherapy, FDA-approved for panic disorder
pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.effectiveness: Bradwejn J et al (Br J Psychiatry 2005;187:352-359, PMID 16199795), n=361 randomized: venlafaxine ER produced lower mean panic-attack frequency, a higher proportion free from limited-symptom panic attacks, and higher response and remission rates than placebo, with improvements also in anticipatory anxiety, fear and avoidance.
pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.reason_why: Dual serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition broadens the monoaminergic mechanism beyond SSRIs, giving an evidence-based alternative when norepinephrine-mediated somatic anxiety symptoms predominate or SSRIs are not tolerated.
pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.important_caveat: The trial did not find venlafaxine ER superior to placebo specifically on freedom from FULL-symptom panic attacks at final evaluation (only on frequency, limited-symptom freedom, response and remission), and the exact response/remission percentage was not disaggregated by dose in the available abstract, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned here.
pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.real_working_solution: Venlafaxine ER 75-225 mg/day as a real first-line SNRI option for panic disorder, particularly for SSRI non-responders.
pand_snri_venlafaxine_bradwejn2005.source: Bradwejn J, Ahokas A, Stein DJ, Salinas E, Emilien G, Whitaker T. Br J Psychiatry 2005;187:352-359 (PMID 16199795)

pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.name: Alprazolam -- Real Large Placebo-Controlled Multicenter Trial, Rapid Relief
pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.type: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator, short-term anxiolytic
pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.effectiveness: Ballenger JC et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(5):413-422, PMID 3282478), n=526: by week 4, 82% of alprazolam recipients were rated moderately improved or better versus 43% on placebo, and 50% of alprazolam recipients were free of panic attacks versus 28% on placebo; significant drug-placebo differences were evident from week 1. Confirmed at larger scale (n=1,168) by the Cross-National Collaborative Panic Study (Br J Psychiatry 1992;160:191-202, PMID 1540759): alprazolam and imipramine were similarly effective and both superior to placebo by week 8, though alprazolam improved faster (weeks 1-2 vs week 4 for imipramine).
pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.reason_why: Alprazolam potentiates GABA-A receptor chloride currents, producing fast, real anxiolysis and blockade of panic attacks within days, faster than any antidepressant.
pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.important_caveat: Real, significantly more placebo patients (102/234) than alprazolam patients (21/247) dropped out of the Ballenger 1988 trial citing ineffectiveness -- a real efficacy signal, not a safety one -- but benzodiazepines carry a separate, serious dependence/withdrawal liability that limits their long-term use (see pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_otto1993).
pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.real_working_solution: Alprazolam as real, rapid short-term/bridge relief for acute panic disorder while an SSRI/SNRI or CBT takes effect, not as a standalone long-term monotherapy.
pand_benzodiazepine_alprazolam_ballenger.source: Ballenger JC, Burrows GD, DuPont RL Jr, Lesser IM, Noyes R Jr, Pecknold JC, Rifkin A, Swinson RP. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(5):413-422 (PMID 3282478); Cross-National Collaborative Panic Study, Second Phase Investigators. Br J Psychiatry 1992;160:191-202 (PMID 1540759)

pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.name: CBT for Benzodiazepine Discontinuation -- Real Controlled Randomized Trial
pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.type: Structured group CBT program combined with slow benzodiazepine taper
pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.effectiveness: Otto MW et al (Am J Psychiatry 1993;150(10):1485-1490, PMID 8379551), n=33 randomized, patients on alprazolam or clonazepam for at least 6 months wanting to stop: successful discontinuation was achieved in 76% (13/17) of patients receiving CBT plus taper versus 25% (4/16) with taper alone; at 3-month follow-up, 77% of the CBT group who had successfully discontinued remained benzodiazepine-free.
pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.reason_why: CBT teaches cognitive reappraisal of withdrawal-related sensations and behavioral coping strategies that directly counter the rebound anxiety and catastrophic misinterpretation that otherwise derail benzodiazepine tapers.
pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.important_caveat: Small trial (n=33), but a real, controlled, randomized design with a large, clinically important effect size and directly relevant real-world applicability for the many panic-disorder patients already on long-term benzodiazepines.
pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.real_working_solution: Add a structured CBT program to any slow benzodiazepine taper in a panic-disorder patient who needs to discontinue long-term benzodiazepine use -- a real, evidence-based way to more than triple discontinuation success.
pand_benzodiazepine_discontinuation_cbt_.source: Otto MW, Pollack MH, Sachs GS, Reiter SR, Meltzer-Brody S, Rosenbaum JF. Am J Psychiatry 1993;150(10):1485-1490 (PMID 8379551)

pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.name: Pharmacological Treatments for Panic Disorder -- Real Cochrane Network Meta-Analysis
pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.type: Network meta-analysis, all major antidepressant classes and benzodiazepines vs placebo
pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.effectiveness: Guaiana G et al (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD012729, PMID 38014714), 70 RCTs: for the response outcome (48 RCTs, n=10,118), all drug classes were more effective than placebo, with little difference between classes overall; for remission (32 RCTs, n=8,569), desipramine, fluoxetine, clonazepam, diazepam, fluvoxamine, imipramine, venlafaxine and paroxetine were all more effective than placebo with clinically meaningful effects; within SSRIs, paroxetine and fluoxetine showed stronger evidence than sertraline; benzodiazepines had the lowest dropout (best tolerability) but overall study quality for benzodiazepine-vs-placebo comparisons was rated low.
pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.reason_why: This synthesis of 70 real RCTs confirms that the pharmacological mechanism (serotonergic, noradrenergic, or GABAergic) matters less than adequate dosing and duration -- most classes converge on real, clinically meaningful efficacy for panic disorder, supporting flexible first-line drug choice based on tolerability and comorbidity rather than assumed differences in raw efficacy.
pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.important_caveat: The review's own authors flag that overall study quality was moderate (antidepressants vs placebo) to low (benzodiazepines vs placebo) with unclear/high risk of bias across multiple domains in the underlying trials, and no single pooled response/remission percentage is given per drug class in the abstract, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to this entry.
pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.real_working_solution: Choose among SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs or (short-term) benzodiazepines based on individual tolerability and comorbidity profile, since the 2023 Cochrane evidence finds no strong overall efficacy difference between classes for panic disorder response.
pand_pharmacotherapy_network_meta_cochra.source: Guaiana G, Meader N, Barbui C, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD012729 (PMID 38014714)

pand_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_mitte2005.name: CBT vs Pharmacotherapy -- Real Comparative Meta-Analysis, Panic Disorder With and Without Agoraphobia
pand_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_mitte2005.effectiveness: Mitte K (Psychol Bull 2005;131(5):785-795, PMID 16005982), 124 studies: (C)BT was more effective than no-treatment and placebo controls; pharmacotherapy was more effective than placebo with no superiority of any one drug class; (C)BT was at least as effective as pharmacotherapy and, depending on the analysis, significantly MORE effective; no significant difference was found between (C)BT alone and combination treatment.
pand_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_mitte2005.reason_why: CBT and pharmacotherapy act on different mechanistic levels but converge on comparable, and by some analyses superior, real symptom reduction for panic disorder, supporting CBT as a genuine first-line standalone option, not merely an adjunct to medication.
pand_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_mitte2005.important_caveat: This is a broad meta-analytic synthesis across 124 heterogeneous studies rather than a single head-to-head percentage figure, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to this entry.
pand_cbt_vs_pharmacotherapy_mitte2005.real_working_solution: (C)BT as a real, evidence-based standalone first-line option for panic disorder, at least equivalent to pharmacotherapy in efficacy.

pand_cognitive_therapy_vs_relaxation_cla.name: Cognitive Therapy vs Applied Relaxation vs Imipramine -- Real Comparative RCT
pand_cognitive_therapy_vs_relaxation_cla.effectiveness: Clark DM et al (Br J Psychiatry 1994;164(6):759-769, PMID 7952982), n=64: all three treatments were superior to a 3-month waiting-list control; cognitive therapy was superior to both applied relaxation and imipramine on most measures at 3 months; at 6 months cognitive therapy did not differ from imipramine and both were superior to applied relaxation; a number of imipramine patients relapsed between 6 and 15 months, and at 15 months cognitive therapy was again superior to both comparators, though on fewer measures than at 3 months.
pand_cognitive_therapy_vs_relaxation_cla.reason_why: Cognitive therapy directly targets the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations that drives panic, producing a faster and, on this evidence, more durable effect than either general relaxation training or imipramine, whose benefit partially eroded with relapse after 6 months.
pand_cognitive_therapy_vs_relaxation_cla.important_caveat: No categorical response/remission percentage is reported in the abstract, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to this entry; the real, clinically important finding here is imipramine's relapse pattern between 6 and 15 months versus cognitive therapy's more sustained advantage.
pand_cognitive_therapy_vs_relaxation_cla.real_working_solution: Cognitive therapy as a real first-line option with a demonstrated durability advantage over both applied relaxation and imipramine out to 15 months.
pand_cognitive_therapy_vs_relaxation_cla.source: Clark DM, Salkovskis PM, Hackmann A, Middleton H, Anastasiades P, Gelder M. Br J Psychiatry 1994;164(6):759-769 (PMID 7952982)

pand_combined_therapy_cochrane_furukawa2.name: Combined Psychotherapy Plus Antidepressants -- Real Cochrane Systematic Review
pand_combined_therapy_cochrane_furukawa2.effectiveness: Furukawa TA, Watanabe N, Churchill R (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;(1):CD004364, PMID 17253502), 23 randomized comparisons (21 trials, 1,709 patients): in acute-phase treatment, combined therapy was superior to antidepressant pharmacotherapy alone (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.02-1.52) and to psychotherapy alone (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.05-1.31); after the acute phase, as long as the drug was continued, combination superiority persisted; after treatment termination, combined therapy remained more effective than pharmacotherapy alone (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23-2.11) and as effective as psychotherapy alone (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.79-1.16).
pand_combined_therapy_cochrane_furukawa2.reason_why: Combining CBT's durable, skill-based mechanism with an antidepressant's faster acute pharmacological effect captures real, additive short-term benefit, while CBT's component of the combination is what sustains the advantage over medication alone after treatment ends.
pand_combined_therapy_cochrane_furukawa2.important_caveat: Results are reported as relative risks (RR) of response rather than absolute percentages, so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to this entry; combined therapy also produced more dropouts due to side effects than psychotherapy alone (NNH around 26).
pand_combined_therapy_cochrane_furukawa2.real_working_solution: Combine CBT with an antidepressant for the strongest acute response, with the expectation that CBT's contribution is what preserves the advantage over medication alone after the combined course ends.
pand_combined_therapy_cochrane_furukawa2.source: Furukawa TA, Watanabe N, Churchill R. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;(1):CD004364 (PMID 17253502)

pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.name: SSRIs vs TCAs -- Real Meta-Analysis
pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.type: Comparative-efficacy and tolerability evidence, antidepressant classes
pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.effectiveness: Bakker A, van Balkom AJ, Spinhoven P (Acta Psychiatr Scand 2002;106(3):163-167, PMID 12197851), 43 studies (2,367 patients pretest, 1,804 post-test): no difference between SSRIs and TCAs on panic, agoraphobia, depression or general-anxiety effect sizes, nor in the percentage of patients free of panic attacks at post-test; however, drop-out was significantly lower with SSRIs (18%) than TCAs (31%).
pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.reason_why: Both drug classes ultimately raise synaptic monoamine availability and produce comparable real anxiolytic/antipanic effects, but SSRIs' more favorable side-effect profile (versus TCAs' anticholinergic and cardiac effects) is the real mechanistic reason for their better tolerability and lower drop-out.
pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.important_caveat: The specific panic-free percentage from this meta-analysis is not stated as a single pooled number in the abstract (only that it 'did not differ' between classes), so no effectiveness_pct is assigned to the efficacy claim; the 18%/31% figures are drop-out (tolerability) rates, not efficacy rates, so they are also not used as an effectiveness_pct.
pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.real_working_solution: Prefer an SSRI over a TCA as first-line pharmacotherapy for panic disorder given equal efficacy and substantially better tolerability (lower drop-out).
pand_ssri_vs_tca_meta_bakker2002.source: Bakker A, van Balkom AJ, Spinhoven P. Acta Psychiatr Scand 2002;106(3):163-167 (PMID 12197851)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Rows are not directly comparable: they mix categorical panic-free rates, 'moderately improved or better' response rates, PDSS/CGI responder rates, and a benzodiazepine-discontinuation success rate, each with a different real denominator and definition drawn directly from its source trial. Several real, high-quality sources (Craske 1997, sertraline/Pollack 1998, venlafaxine/Bradwejn 2005, the 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis, Mitte 2005, Clark 1994, Furukawa 2007 Cochrane, Bakker 2002) are deliberately EXCLUDED from this ranked table because their abstracts report p-values, relative risks, or qualitative superiority rather than a stated percentage, and no percentage has been estimated or invented for them; see exhaustive_medicine_survey for their full real findings. See CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option for the durability context (interoceptive-exposure CBT's advantage growing, not shrinking, by 6-month follow-up; CBT alone's superior durability after treatment discontinuation) that a single ranked percentage cannot convey.

borderline_personality_disorder.name: Borderline Personality Disorder
borderline_personality_disorder.icd11_hint: ICD-11 6D10 Personality disorder (dimensional, severity-graded model) with the 'Borderline pattern' qualifier specifier (6D11.5); ICD-10 F60.31 Emotionally unstable personality disorder, borderline type
borderline_personality_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Active suicidality, self-harm and parasuicidal behaviour in a person with suspected or diagnosed borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a real, life-threatening emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department NOW, or call a local emergency/suicide helpline) rather than the routine consultation flow. Recurrent suicidal behaviour, gestures/threats, and self-mutilating behaviour are themselves a core DSM-5-TR diagnostic criterion of BPD (not an incidental complication), so every BPD presentation must include explicit, careful documentation of current suicidal ideation/intent/plan AND of any recent self-harm or parasuicidal acts, assessed and recorded separately - clinicians must not assume that a history of repeated attempts or gestures signals a low desire to die; each episode requires its own independent risk assessment. Real-world scale of the risk: suicide risk in BPD is approximately 40 times higher than in the general population (MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)', msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-24). In a dedicated review, at least three-quarters of BPD patients attempt suicide at least once and approximately 10% eventually die by suicide; the highest-risk patients are those with prior attempts, comorbid major depressive disorder or substance use disorder, high hopelessness, high impulsivity, a turbulent early life, or antisocial traits (Black DW, Blum N, Pfohl B, Hale N, 'Suicidal behavior in borderline personality disorder: prevalence, risk factors, prediction, and prevention', J Pers Disord 2004;18(3):226-239, PMID 15237043). Red-flag features requiring urgent psychiatric/emergency evaluation rather than the normal ai_suggests/doctor-approval cycle: any current suicidal ideation with a plan and/or intent; any actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempt; escalating frequency/severity of self-mutilation; comorbid major depression or substance use; and any recent major interpersonal loss or perceived abandonment (a specific, well-documented trigger for acute crisis in BPD, per DSM-5-TR criterion 1). A candidate-medicine-plus-efficacy% suggestion must never be the first or only output when any of these red flags are present; safety triage and real-world emergency-service guidance comes first, medicine selection second.
borderline_personality_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) has a genuinely strong, real, evidence-backed success story that must lead this note, and it is psychotherapy, not medication. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT, Marsha Linehan's landmark treatment) has real randomized-trial evidence of reducing suicidal and self-harm behaviour: in the original 1-year RCT (n=44 chronically parasuicidal women), DBT produced fewer and less medically severe parasuicide episodes, fewer inpatient psychiatric days, and better treatment retention than treatment-as-usual (Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 1991;48(12):1060-1064, PMID 1845222). In the pivotal 2-year RCT/follow-up (n=101 women with recent suicidal/self-injurious behaviour), DBT patients were half as likely to make a suicide attempt than those given expert non-behavioural community therapy (hazard ratio 2.66, p=.005), had fewer psychiatric hospitalizations (p=.007) and emergency department visits (p=.04), and were far less likely to drop out of treatment (hazard ratio 3.2, p<.001) (Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(7):757-766, PMID 16818865). The honest complication that must not be buried: a separately well-conducted RCT (McMain SF et al., Am J Psychiatry 2009;166(12):1365-1374, PMID 19755574, n=180) found DBT produced equal, not superior, improvement compared with General Psychiatric Management (a well-specified combination of psychodynamically-informed therapy plus symptom-targeted medication following APA guideline recommendations) -- meaning DBT's real advantage is proven most clearly against unstructured treatment-as-usual, and other well-structured, guideline-concordant approaches (including Mentalization-Based Treatment, MBT, and Transference-Focused Psychotherapy, TFP) also achieve real, substantial improvement. On the question the mission asks first -- can BPD actually be cured, long-term, in real patients -- the strongest real answer comes from Mary Zanarini's McLean Study of Adult Development, a real prospective cohort followed for 16 years (n=290 inpatients with BPD): by 16-year follow-up, borderline patients achieved sustained symptomatic remission rates of 78%-99% across follow-up waves, similar in the end to comparison personality-disorder patients, though sustained full recovery (remission plus good social/vocational functioning) was lower, at 40%-60% (Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2012;169(5):476-483, PMID 22737693). The earlier 10-year report from the same real cohort found 93% attained at least a 2-year symptomatic remission, 86% attained a sustained remission lasting at least 4 years, and 50% achieved full recovery (symptomatic remission plus good functioning) at some point, with recovery, once attained, relatively stable (only 34% later lost it) (Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2010;167(6):663-667, PMID 20395399). Mentalization-Based Treatment (MBT) has its own real long-term controlled data: at 8-year follow-up (5 years after MBT ended), the MBT-by-partial-hospitalization group had far lower suicidality (23% vs 74% in treatment-as-usual) and far fewer patients still meeting full diagnostic criteria for BPD (13% vs 87% in treatment-as-usual) (Bateman A, Fonagy P, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(5):631-638, PMID 18347003). The 2020 Cochrane review of 75 RCTs (n=4507) confirms BPD-tailored psychotherapy (mainly DBT and MBT) produces a clinically meaningful reduction in BPD symptom severity versus treatment-as-usual (standardised mean difference -0.52, moderate-quality evidence), with MBT specifically associated with large relative reductions in suicidality (relative risk 0.10) and self-harm (relative risk 0.62) versus treatment-as-usual, though this MBT-specific evidence is rated low-quality and comes from only 3 small trials (Storebo OJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5:CD012955, PMID 32368793). The honest other side that must not be softened: unlike many medical illnesses in this knowledge base, NO medication has an FDA-approved indication for treating borderline personality disorder itself, in the United States or elsewhere. The 2010 Cochrane pharmacotherapy review (27 RCTs) found mood stabilisers (topiramate, lamotrigine, valproate semisodium) and second-generation antipsychotics (aripiprazole, olanzapine) showed the most benefit for specific symptom clusters (e.g. affective instability, impulsivity, anger), but the evidence does not support any drug improving overall BPD severity, is based mostly on small single studies with low robustness, and SSRIs specifically lack high-level evidence of effectiveness (Lieb K et al., Br J Psychiatry 2010;196(1):4-12, PMID 20044651). The 2024 updated American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Borderline Personality Disorder confirms psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, TFP, and other structured approaches) as the primary, guideline-recommended treatment, with medication positioned only as a targeted adjunct for specific symptoms, never as a stand-alone or curative treatment (American Psychiatric Association, Am J Psychiatry 2024 Nov 1, PMID 39482953). The real, honest overall picture: BPD is a genuinely, majority-treatable-to-remission illness with the right structured, evidence-based psychotherapy (DBT is the most extensively RCT-validated, but MBT and TFP have real comparable controlled evidence) sustained over years, and most real patients followed long enough (10-16 years) do achieve durable symptomatic remission -- but full functional recovery is harder and slower to reach than remission of core symptoms, and no pill cures the disorder itself.

curative_option.name: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) -- the Real Best-Evidenced Structured Psychotherapy for BPD
curative_option.note: DBT is the most extensively randomized-trial-validated treatment in this entry: it is the treatment with the largest number of independent RCTs (one-third of all trials in the 2020 Cochrane review), the longest track record (since 1991), and the clearest evidence of a real, replicated reduction in the outcome that matters most in BPD -- death and near-death from suicidal/self-injurious behaviour. Its real value is not a single miracle number but a body of trials, each individually real, that converge on the same finding.

real_survival_data.original_1991_rct_parasuicide_reduction: Fewer and less medically severe parasuicide episodes, fewer inpatient psychiatric days, better treatment retention vs treatment-as-usual over 1 year (n=44 chronically parasuicidal women with BPD)
real_survival_data.2006_two_year_rct_suicide_attempt: DBT patients half as likely to make a suicide attempt vs expert non-behavioural community therapy (hazard ratio 2.66, p=.005); fewer psychiatric hospitalizations (p=.007) and ED visits (p=.04); 3.2x lower dropout (p<.001), n=101 women with recent suicidal/self-injurious behaviour
real_survival_data.2020_cochrane_review_self_harm_and_sever: DBT vs treatment-as-usual: standardised mean difference -0.60 for BPD severity, -0.28 for self-harm, -0.36 for psychosocial functioning (based on a subset of 3-7 trials each, ~150-380 participants)
real_survival_data.honest_equivalence_finding: In one rigorous head-to-head RCT (McMain 2009, n=180), DBT was NOT superior to General Psychiatric Management (a well-specified guideline-based alternative combining psychodynamic therapy and symptom-targeted medication) -- both arms improved equally on suicidal/self-harm frequency and severity over 1 year

curative_option.source: Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 1991;48(12):1060-1064 (PMID 1845222); Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(7):757-766 (PMID 16818865); Storebo OJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5:CD012955 (PMID 32368793); McMain SF et al., Am J Psychiatry 2009;166(12):1365-1374 (PMID 19755574)
curative_option.important_caveat: DBT's real superiority is most clearly proven against unstructured treatment-as-usual or non-specialist community care, not against other well-structured, guideline-based specialist treatments (General Psychiatric Management, MBT, TFP), which achieve broadly comparable real improvement in rigorous head-to-head RCTs. DBT is a long, resource-intensive treatment (typically 1 year of weekly individual therapy plus group skills training plus therapist consultation team) and requires trained DBT-specific therapists, which limits real-world access.
curative_option.confidence: high for the suicide-attempt/self-harm reduction and retention data across multiple independent RCTs; high also for the honest equivalence-with-GPM finding, which is itself real and load-bearing evidence, not a limitation of DBT specifically

bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.name: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT)
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.type: Structured outpatient cognitive-behavioural psychotherapy combining individual therapy, group skills training (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness), telephone coaching, and a therapist consultation team
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.specific_procedure: Typically 1 year of weekly individual DBT therapy plus weekly group skills-training sessions, structured around a hierarchy that prioritises reducing life-threatening behaviour first, then therapy-interfering behaviour, then quality-of-life-interfering behaviour
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.effectiveness: Half the rate of suicide attempts vs expert community therapy (hazard ratio 2.66, p=.005), n=101 2-year RCT; fewer/less severe parasuicide episodes vs treatment-as-usual, n=44 original 1-year RCT; standardised mean difference -0.60 for BPD severity vs treatment-as-usual across pooled trials
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.reason_why: DBT was purpose-built for chronically suicidal BPD patients by directly targeting the emotion-dysregulation and impulsive-crisis-behaviour cycle with structured skills training, a hierarchical treatment target order that puts staying alive first, and a therapist consultation team designed to prevent burnout and treatment dropout in this specific, hard-to-treat population -- explaining why its strongest, most consistent real advantage is retention and reduction of suicidal/self-harm behaviour rather than a single overall-severity metric.
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.important_caveat: Not proven superior to other well-specified, guideline-based specialist treatments (General Psychiatric Management, MBT, TFP) in head-to-head RCTs; requires extensive therapist training and is resource-intensive, limiting real-world availability.
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.real_working_solution: First-line, most extensively RCT-validated psychotherapy for BPD, especially where chronic suicidality/self-harm is the presenting problem; recommended in the APA 2024 practice guideline alongside MBT and TFP as evidence-based structured treatments.
bpd_dialectical_behavior_therapy.source: Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 1991;48(12):1060-1064 (PMID 1845222); Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(7):757-766 (PMID 16818865); McMain SF et al., Am J Psychiatry 2009;166(12):1365-1374 (PMID 19755574); Storebo OJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5:CD012955 (PMID 32368793)

bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.name: Mentalization-Based Treatment (MBT)
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.type: Structured psychodynamically-informed psychotherapy (originally partial-hospitalization-based, later adapted to outpatient), individual plus group format
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.specific_procedure: 18 months of mentalization-based treatment (originally delivered via partial hospitalization) focused on improving the patient's capacity to understand their own and others' mental states (thoughts, feelings, intentions) underlying interpersonal behaviour, followed by maintenance mentalizing group therapy
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.effectiveness: At 8-year follow-up (5 years after MBT ended): suicidality 23% (MBT) vs 74% (treatment-as-usual); only 13% of MBT patients still met full diagnostic criteria for BPD vs 87% of treatment-as-usual patients (i.e. 87% of MBT patients no longer met full diagnostic criteria, vs only 13% of TAU patients), n=41 original RCT cohort. In the 2020 Cochrane review, MBT vs TAU showed relative risk 0.10 for suicidality and 0.62 for self-harm (3 small trials, n=218-252, low-quality evidence)
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.reason_why: By directly training the capacity to mentalize (to reflect on one's own and others' mental states rather than reacting to them), MBT targets a mechanism specifically implicated in BPD's interpersonal instability and affect dysregulation, and its real advantage over treatment-as-usual widened rather than shrank over the 5 years after treatment ended, suggesting a genuinely durable change in underlying functioning rather than a treatment-dependent effect.
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.important_caveat: The core 8-year follow-up trial is small (n=41) and originates from a single specialist UK unit; the larger relative-risk figures for suicidality/self-harm from the 2020 Cochrane review are explicitly rated low-quality evidence from only 3 small trials, so the very large relative-risk reductions (RR 0.10) should be read as promising but not yet as robust as the DBT evidence base.
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.real_working_solution: Guideline-recognised (APA 2024) evidence-based alternative to DBT, with the strongest available long-term (8-year) controlled follow-up data of any BPD psychotherapy in this survey.
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.source: Bateman A, Fonagy P, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(5):631-638 (PMID 18347003); Storebo OJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5:CD012955 (PMID 32368793)
bpd_mentalization_based_therapy.confidence: high for the 8-year follow-up data; moderate-low for the pooled relative-risk figures, which the Cochrane authors themselves rate low-quality

bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.name: Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP)
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.type: Structured, twice-weekly psychodynamic psychotherapy based on object-relations theory
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.specific_procedure: 1 year of twice-weekly individual TFP sessions focused on exploring and working through the patient's distorted representations of self and others as they emerge in the relationship (transference) with the therapist
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.effectiveness: In a 3-arm RCT (n=90) comparing TFP, DBT, and dynamic supportive treatment over 1 year: TFP and DBT were both significantly associated with improvement in suicidality; TFP alone was significantly associated with improvement in anger, irritability, and verbal/direct assault, and (with supportive treatment) improvement in impulsivity; TFP showed change across the most domains (six) of any of the three treatments
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.reason_why: By working directly, in real time, with the intense and often distorted patient-therapist relationship patterns that mirror the patient's real-world interpersonal instability, TFP gives clinicians a direct, observable target for the core relational disturbance of BPD, which the trial's authors argue may explain why it showed change across more outcome domains (anger, impulsivity/aggression specifically) than DBT or supportive treatment in this particular head-to-head comparison.
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.important_caveat: This is a single, moderate-sized (n=90) RCT from one research group with a strong theoretical/institutional investment in TFP (Kernberg's own centre); it has not been as extensively independently replicated as the DBT evidence base, and the trial was not designed or powered as a definitive superiority comparison.
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.real_working_solution: Guideline-recognised (APA 2024) evidence-based structured psychodynamic alternative to DBT and MBT, with particular RCT-documented benefit for anger and aggression/irritability symptoms.
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.source: Clarkin JF, Levy KN, Lenzenweger MF, Kernberg OF, Am J Psychiatry 2007;164(6):922-928 (PMID 17541052)
bpd_transference_focused_psychotherapy.confidence: moderate -- real RCT data, but from a single trial by the therapy's originating group

bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.name: Symptom-Targeted Pharmacotherapy (Mood Stabilisers and Second-Generation Antipsychotics) -- No FDA-Approved Indication for BPD Itself
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.type: Adjunctive drug treatment (mood stabilisers: topiramate, lamotrigine, valproate semisodium; second-generation antipsychotics: aripiprazole, olanzapine)
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.specific_procedure: Off-label prescribing targeted at specific symptom clusters (affective instability, impulsivity, anger, transient psychotic-like symptoms) as an adjunct to psychotherapy, following APA/GPM-style symptom-targeted prescribing rather than treating BPD as a single unified target
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.effectiveness: 2010 Cochrane review of 27 RCTs: most beneficial effects for specific symptom clusters were found for topiramate, lamotrigine, valproate semisodium (mood stabilisers) and aripiprazole, olanzapine (second-generation antipsychotics), but evidence does not support any drug improving overall BPD severity; findings rated as low robustness, based mostly on single small studies; SSRIs specifically lack high-level evidence of effectiveness
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.reason_why: Because BPD's core pathology is understood as a disorder of emotion regulation, interpersonal functioning, and identity rather than a single neurochemical deficit, no drug class targets its full syndrome the way, for example, antidepressants target major depressive episodes -- so rational prescribing in BPD targets specific, drug-responsive symptom clusters (e.g. anticonvulsant mood stabilisers for affective/impulsive instability, low-dose antipsychotics for transient cognitive-perceptual symptoms) rather than aiming to cure the disorder itself with medication.
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.important_caveat: NO medication has an FDA-approved indication for treating borderline personality disorder itself, anywhere. The 2024 APA guideline and General Psychiatric Management model both frame medication strictly as a time-limited, symptom-targeted adjunct to psychotherapy, not a primary or stand-alone treatment; polypharmacy without symptom-specific justification is explicitly discouraged in the literature.
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.real_working_solution: Rational, symptom-targeted (not diagnosis-targeted) adjunctive prescribing under the same guideline-based framework used in McMain's real General Psychiatric Management arm, which performed equally well to DBT in a rigorous RCT -- medication has a real, if limited and non-curative, adjunctive role alongside evidence-based psychotherapy, never as a replacement for it.
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.source: Lieb K, Vollm B, Rucker G, Timmer A, Stoffers JM, Br J Psychiatry 2010;196(1):4-12 (PMID 20044651); American Psychiatric Association, Am J Psychiatry 2024 Nov 1 (PMID 39482953); McMain SF et al., Am J Psychiatry 2009;166(12):1365-1374 (PMID 19755574)
bpd_symptom_targeted_pharmacotherapy.confidence: high for the honest absence of FDA approval and lack of overall-severity benefit; moderate for the specific-symptom-cluster benefits, which the Cochrane authors themselves rate as low-robustness, mostly single small studies

ranked_high_to_low.name: McLean Study of Adult Development, 16-year follow-up -- sustained symptomatic remission (upper bound)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Real-world prospective cohort (natural course + real-world treatment, not a single manualised therapy)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Sustained symptomatic remission ranged 78%-99% across eight successive 2-year follow-up waves over 16 years, n=290 inpatients with BPD
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2012;169(5):476-483 (PMID 22737693)

ranked_high_to_low.name: McLean Study of Adult Development, 10-year follow-up -- attained at least 2-year symptomatic remission
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 93% of patients attained a remission of symptoms lasting at least 2 years over the 10-year study, n=290 inpatients with BPD
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2010;167(6):663-667 (PMID 20395399)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mentalization-Based Treatment vs treatment-as-usual -- suicidality relative risk reduction
ranked_high_to_low.type: Psychodynamically-informed structured psychotherapy, pooled RCT evidence
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative risk 0.10 for suicidality vs treatment-as-usual (~90% relative risk reduction), 3 trials, n=218 -- Cochrane-rated low-quality evidence from small trials
ranked_high_to_low.source: Storebo OJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5:CD012955 (PMID 32368793)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mentalization-Based Treatment, 8-year follow-up -- no longer meeting full BPD diagnostic criteria
ranked_high_to_low.type: Structured psychodynamic partial-hospitalization psychotherapy, RCT with long-term follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 87% of MBT patients no longer met full diagnostic criteria for BPD at 8-year follow-up, vs only 13% of treatment-as-usual patients, n=41
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bateman A, Fonagy P, Am J Psychiatry 2008;165(5):631-638 (PMID 18347003)

ranked_high_to_low.name: McLean Study of Adult Development, 10-year follow-up -- sustained remission lasting at least 4 years
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 86% of patients attained a sustained remission lasting at least 4 years over the 10-year study, n=290
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2010;167(6):663-667 (PMID 20395399)

ranked_high_to_low.name: McLean Study of Adult Development, 16-year follow-up -- sustained full recovery (upper bound)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Sustained recovery (remission plus good social/vocational functioning) ranged 40%-60% across follow-up waves over 16 years, n=290
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2012;169(5):476-483 (PMID 22737693)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Dialectical Behavior Therapy vs expert community therapy -- suicide attempt reduction
ranked_high_to_low.metric: DBT patients half as likely to make a suicide attempt vs expert non-behavioural community therapy (hazard ratio 2.66, p=.005), n=101
ranked_high_to_low.source: Linehan MM et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(7):757-766 (PMID 16818865)

ranked_high_to_low.name: McLean Study of Adult Development, 10-year follow-up -- full recovery attained
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 50% of patients achieved full recovery (symptomatic remission plus good social/vocational functioning) at some point over the 10-year study, n=290; of those who recovered, only 34% later lost it
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zanarini MC et al., Am J Psychiatry 2010;167(6):663-667 (PMID 20395399)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows are not directly comparable head-to-head (different designs: naturalistic prospective cohort of real-world-treated patients [Zanarini/McLean] vs randomized controlled trials of specific manualised therapies [DBT, MBT]; different outcome definitions: symptomatic remission vs full recovery vs suicidality/self-harm relative risk; and, for the two MBT relative-risk rows, low-quality evidence from only 3 small trials each per the Cochrane authors' own GRADE rating). They are ranked together only to give an honest, single, real-numbers view of the strongest available evidence for each named outcome. Symptom-targeted pharmacotherapy (mood stabilisers, second-generation antipsychotics) is deliberately omitted from this ranked table: the 2010 Cochrane pharmacotherapy review (PMID 20044651) reports benefit only on specific symptom-rating-scale scores, not a comparable remission/recovery/relative-risk percentage, and inventing one to force a ranking would violate this knowledge base's no-fabrication rule; its real, symptom-specific evidence is described narratively in exhaustive_medicine_survey above.
