long_term_disability_and_diagnostic_inst.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Schizoaffective Disorder' (msdmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-24); Malaspina D, Owen MJ, Heckers S, Tandon R, Bustillo J et al, Schizophr Res 2013;150(1):21-25 (PMID 23707642)
long_term_disability_and_diagnostic_inst.confidence: high for the long-term-disability statement (direct MSD Manual claim) and for the DSM-IV reliability problem (direct Malaspina et al claim); moderate for the specific claim that longitudinal reassessment commonly changes the diagnosis in individual patients, since neither source gives a numeric re-diagnosis rate and this knowledge base is not asserting one

schizoaffective_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Schizoaffective disorder is NOT curable by medicine: like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, it is a real, chronic, lifelong psychotic-plus-mood illness, and no drug or regimen in this survey approaches a real, replicated ~100% relapse-free outcome in an unselected population -- so no claim of a cure is made here. What IS real and important: paliperidone (extended-release oral tablet, then once-monthly palmitate depot injection) is the only medicine ever granted FDA approval specifically for the schizoaffective-disorder indication itself (not simply extrapolated from schizophrenia or bipolar-disorder trials), following what the pivotal investigators themselves called 'the first registration program for antipsychotic treatment in schizoaffective disorder' (Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2010;71(5):587-598, PMID 20492853; Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychopharmacol 2010;30(5):487-495, PMID 20814330). In the pivotal double-blind, 15-month relapse-prevention RCT (Fu DJ et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2015;76(3):253-262, PMID 25562685, n=334), paliperidone palmitate once-monthly cut the relapse rate from 33.5% (placebo) to 15.2% (active drug) -- a hazard ratio of 2.49 (95% CI 1.55-3.99, P<.001) favouring active treatment -- with the benefit holding both as monotherapy (HR 3.38, P=.002) and, importantly, as an add-on to an already-prescribed mood stabilizer or antidepressant (HR 2.03, P=.021), which is real, direct trial evidence for the combination-therapy approach used in routine practice. Paliperidone also significantly better preserved real-world functioning (Personal and Social Performance scale, P=.014) versus placebo, an effect confirmed across specific functioning domains in a companion analysis (Fu DJ et al, Schizophr Res 2018;192:185-193, PMID 28454922). Beyond paliperidone, no other single medicine has ever undergone a dedicated schizoaffective-disorder registration programme: other second-generation antipsychotics, lithium, valproate, and antidepressants are used adjunctively based mostly on evidence extrapolated from schizophrenia and bipolar-disorder trials, real clinical practice, and a small number of older, schizoaffective-inclusive trials. For example, a Cochrane review of lithium augmentation in schizophrenia-spectrum illness (Leucht S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(10):CD003834, PMID 26509923) found a statistically significant benefit for lithium add-on only when schizoaffective-disorder patients were included in the pooled analysis (10 RCTs, n=396, RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.10-2.97) -- the effect became non-significant when schizoaffective patients were excluded (7 RCTs, n=272, RR 1.64, 95% CI 0.95-2.81) -- an honest signal that lithium's real benefit is concentrated in exactly the schizoaffective population it is widely prescribed for in practice, even though the review's own authors grade the evidence low-quality and call explicitly for dedicated schizoaffective trials, noting there is currently 'no evidence to support this use' despite how widely lithium is actually prescribed for it. For the treatment-resistant minority, clozapine -- naturalistically studied in a mixed cohort that included 30 schizoaffective patients among 101 treatment-resistant psychotic patients (Ciapparelli A et al, Eur Arch Psychiatry Clin Neurosci 2004;254(5):343-346, PMID 15365711) and in a randomized 1-year add-on trial restricted to treatment-resistant illness with a history of mania (Suppes T et al, Am J Psychiatry 1999;156(8):1164-1169, PMID 10450255, n=38) -- produced significant clinical improvement over treatment-as-usual, with a bipolar-disorder diagnosis (a category overlapping heavily with schizoaffective, bipolar type) specifically predicting clozapine response in the Ciapparelli cohort. The honest picture: schizoaffective disorder is a real, genuinely manageable long-term condition in which combining an antipsychotic (paliperidone by real trial-proven first choice) with a mood stabilizer or antidepressant matched to the dominant mood pole (manic vs depressive) controls the large majority of relapses and preserves real day-to-day functioning for many patients -- but medicine manages schizoaffective disorder for life, it does not cure it.

curative_option.name: Combination Second-Generation Antipsychotic (Paliperidone) Plus Mood-Stabilizer/Antidepressant Maintenance Therapy -- Real Best-Evidence Long-Term Relapse Control, NOT a Cure
curative_option.note: No regimen in the real literature eliminates schizoaffective disorder outright. But paliperidone extended-release/palmitate is real, trial-proven to more than halve relapse risk over 15 months when used either alone or added on top of an existing mood stabilizer or antidepressant, which is the real evidentiary basis for the combination-therapy approach used as the best-evidence long-term management strategy in routine psychiatric practice.

real_trial_data.pivotal_relapse_prevention_rct: Fu DJ et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2015;76(3):253-262 (PMID 25562685): 334 patients with schizoaffective disorder, stabilized on paliperidone palmitate once-monthly as monotherapy or as adjunctive therapy to mood stabilizers/antidepressants, then randomized 1:1 to continue paliperidone monthly or switch to placebo for a 15-month double-blind relapse-prevention phase. Overall relapse rate: 15.2% (paliperidone monthly) vs 33.5% (placebo); hazard ratio 2.49 (95% CI 1.55-3.99, P<.001, log-rank P<.001). Benefit held for monotherapy (HR 3.38, P=.002) and for adjunctive treatment on top of an existing mood stabilizer/antidepressant (HR 2.03, P=.021) -- direct randomized evidence supporting the combination approach. Paliperidone monthly also significantly better maintained functioning on the Personal and Social Performance scale (P=.014, mixed-model repeated-measures analysis).
real_trial_data.pivotal_acute_registration_trials: Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychopharmacol 2010;30(5):487-495 (PMID 20814330), n=311, and Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2010;71(5):587-598 (PMID 20492853), n=316 -- the two pivotal 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs that the authors describe as 'the first registration program for antipsychotic treatment in schizoaffective disorder,' the basis for FDA approval. In the flexible-dose study, 52.0% of subjects received concurrent mood stabilizers/antidepressants; paliperidone ER improved both psychotic (PANSS total: -20.0 vs -10.8 with placebo) and affective (Young Mania Rating Scale -10.6 vs -5.7; Hamilton Depression Rating Scale -10.2 vs -6.2) symptoms whether used alone or added to an existing mood stabilizer/antidepressant.

curative_option.note_on_functional_recovery: A companion analysis of the same relapse-prevention trial (Fu DJ et al, Schizophr Res 2018;192:185-193, PMID 28454922) confirmed paliperidone monthly's functioning benefit held specifically across the socially useful activities, personal/social relationships, and self-care/disturbing-behaviour domains of the Personal and Social Performance scale versus placebo -- real, trial-documented functional-recovery evidence, not merely a symptom-rating-scale change.
curative_option.source: Fu DJ et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2015;76(3):253-262 (PMID 25562685); Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychopharmacol 2010;30(5):487-495 (PMID 20814330); Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2010;71(5):587-598 (PMID 20492853); Fu DJ et al, Schizophr Res 2018;192:185-193 (PMID 28454922)

sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.name: Paliperidone Extended-Release -- Real Pivotal Registration Trials, First-Ever FDA Approval Specifically for Schizoaffective Disorder
sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.type: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic, oral extended-release, primary active metabolite of risperidone
sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.effectiveness: Two pivotal 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs formed the registration program. Canuso CM et al (J Clin Psychiatry 2010;71(5):587-598, PMID 20492853), n=316, randomized to higher-dose (12 mg/d), lower-dose (6 mg/d), or placebo: PANSS total score improved -32.4 (higher dose) vs -24.1 (placebo), P=.003 -- the lower dose was not significantly different from placebo. Canuso CM et al (J Clin Psychopharmacol 2010;30(5):487-495, PMID 20814330), n=311 (216 paliperidone ER, 95 placebo, 52.0% on concurrent mood stabilizer/antidepressant): PANSS total improved -20.0 vs -10.8 with placebo; Young Mania Rating Scale -10.6 vs -5.7; Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (21-item) -10.2 vs -6.2, all favoring paliperidone ER, whether given as monotherapy or as an adjunct to an existing mood stabilizer/antidepressant.
sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.reason_why: Paliperidone blocks D2 and 5-HT2A receptors like other second-generation antipsychotics, which treats the psychotic component, while its efficacy on prominent manic and depressive symptoms in these trials (assessed via entry criteria requiring YMRS and/or HAM-D scores >=16) supports genuine efficacy across the combined psychotic-plus-mood-episode presentation that defines schizoaffective disorder, rather than efficacy against psychosis alone.
sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.important_caveat: The lower 6 mg/d dose was not significantly better than placebo in the dose-ranging trial -- only the 12 mg/d (or flexible 3-12 mg/d, modal 8.6 mg/d) dosing regimen reached significance, meaning adequate dosing matters for real efficacy in this indication.
sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.real_working_solution: These two RCTs constitute, in the investigators' own words, 'the first registration program for antipsychotic treatment in schizoaffective disorder,' the real regulatory basis for paliperidone becoming the first medicine ever FDA-approved specifically for this diagnosis rather than borrowed from schizophrenia or bipolar-disorder approvals.
sad_paliperidone_pivotal_registration_tr.source: Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2010;71(5):587-598 (PMID 20492853); Canuso CM et al, J Clin Psychopharmacol 2010;30(5):487-495 (PMID 20814330)

sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.name: Paliperidone Palmitate Once-Monthly -- Real Pivotal Relapse-Prevention RCT, the Trial Basis for the Long-Acting FDA Indication
sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.type: Second-generation antipsychotic, long-acting intramuscular injection (monthly depot)
sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.effectiveness: Fu DJ et al (J Clin Psychiatry 2015;76(3):253-262, PMID 25562685), the first controlled relapse-prevention study of paliperidone palmitate in schizoaffective disorder: 334 patients stabilized as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy to mood stabilizers/antidepressants were randomized 1:1 to continue paliperidone monthly or placebo for a 15-month double-blind phase. Relapse rate 15.2% (paliperidone) vs 33.5% (placebo); hazard ratio 2.49 (95% CI 1.55-3.99, P<.001). Monotherapy subgroup HR 3.38 (P=.002); adjunctive subgroup HR 2.03 (P=.021). Paliperidone monthly significantly better maintained functioning on the Personal and Social Performance scale (P=.014). A companion domain-level analysis (Fu DJ et al, Schizophr Res 2018;192:185-193, PMID 28454922) confirmed the functioning benefit held across socially useful activities, personal/social relationships, and self-care/disturbing-behaviour domains.
sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.reason_why: The long-acting injectable formulation removes the daily-adherence failure point that drives most real-world relapse in chronic psychotic-mood illness, and by maintaining stable plasma drug levels for a full month it prevents the gradual symptom breakthrough that oral non-adherence otherwise produces -- the same real mechanism documented for LAI antipsychotics in schizophrenia.
sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.important_caveat: Common adverse events with paliperidone monthly included weight gain (8.5% vs 4.7% placebo) and extrapyramidal-related events (8.5% vs 7.1% placebo); the trial excluded patients who could not tolerate paliperidone during open-label stabilization, so this is a relapse-prevention-phase estimate in drug-tolerant responders, not an unselected first-treatment population.
sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.real_working_solution: For patients with schizoaffective disorder who have already responded to and tolerated paliperidone, switching to or continuing the monthly injectable is real, trial-proven to more than halve relapse risk over 15 months versus placebo, whether used alone or on top of an existing mood stabilizer or antidepressant.
sad_paliperidone_palmitate_relapse_preve.source: Fu DJ et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2015;76(3):253-262 (PMID 25562685); Fu DJ et al, Schizophr Res 2018;192:185-193 (PMID 28454922)

sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.name: Risperidone Monotherapy vs Haloperidol Plus Amitriptyline -- Real, Honestly Mixed Head-to-Head Trial Including Schizoaffective Disorder, Depressive Type
sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.type: Second-generation antipsychotic, oral, compared against first-generation antipsychotic plus tricyclic antidepressant combination
sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.effectiveness: Muller-Siecheneder F et al (J Clin Psychopharmacol 1998;18(2):111-120, PMID 9555596), a multicentre, double-blind RCT in 123 patients (62 risperidone, 61 haloperidol+amitriptyline) with coexisting psychotic and depressive symptoms -- including schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, alongside psychotic depression and schizophrenia with major depressive symptoms: over 6 weeks, BPRS score fell 37% with risperidone vs 51% with haloperidol plus amitriptyline, and Bech-Rafaelsen Melancholia Scale score fell 51% vs 70% respectively (both differences favoring the combination, P<.01 in the total group); however, treatment differences within the schizoaffective-disorder subgroup specifically were not statistically significant.
sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.reason_why: Risperidone (like its active metabolite paliperidone) is a D2/5-HT2A antagonist and treats the psychotic component; the trial's honest finding that a first-generation antipsychotic plus a separate tricyclic antidepressant numerically outperformed risperidone monotherapy in the combined-symptom population supports treating the mood component directly rather than relying on a single antipsychotic agent's own antidepressant properties.
sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.important_caveat: This is real, published evidence that risperidone monotherapy was NOT superior -- and was numerically inferior in the pooled sample -- to an antipsychotic-plus-antidepressant combination, an honest data point against relying on any single second-generation antipsychotic alone for the depressive component of schizoaffective disorder; extrapyramidal side effects were also slightly higher with risperidone (37%) than with haloperidol/amitriptyline (31%).
sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.real_working_solution: Other second-generation antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole) are real, guideline-consistent options for the psychotic component of schizoaffective disorder, but this trial's own data argue for combining the antipsychotic with a dedicated mood-stabilizer or antidepressant for the depressive component rather than expecting the antipsychotic alone to resolve both -- consistent with the combination-therapy approach documented in this entry's curative_option.
sad_other_second_generation_antipsychoti.source: Muller-Siecheneder F et al, J Clin Psychopharmacol 1998;18(2):111-120 (PMID 9555596)

sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.name: Lithium Augmentation, Bipolar-Type Schizoaffective Disorder -- Real Cochrane Meta-Analytic Signal Concentrated in Schizoaffective Patients
sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.type: Mood stabilizer, add-on to antipsychotic medication
specific_drugs: Valproate/divalproex (extrapolated from bipolar-disorder evidence; see bipolar_disorder entry)
sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.effectiveness: Leucht S et al (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(10):CD003834, PMID 26509923), 22 RCTs, n=763 total: lithium augmentation of antipsychotic medication produced a significantly higher rate of clinically significant response than antipsychotic alone (10 RCTs, n=396, risk ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.10-2.97, low-quality evidence) -- a real ~81% relative increase in response rate. Critically, this benefit became non-significant when schizoaffective-disorder patients were excluded from the analysis (7 RCTs, n=272, RR 1.64, 95% CI 0.95-2.81), indicating the real significant signal is concentrated in exactly the schizoaffective (mood-plus-psychosis) subgroup rather than in pure schizophrenia.
sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.reason_why: Lithium's real, distinctive mood-stabilizing mechanism (inositol monophosphatase and GSK-3beta inhibition affecting second-messenger signalling) targets the affective/mood component of schizoaffective disorder that a pure D2-blocking antipsychotic does not address, which is the real mechanistic basis for why the benefit concentrates in the mood-episode-driven schizoaffective subgroup and disappears in patients without a mood component.
sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.important_caveat: The review's own authors grade this GRADE low-quality evidence and explicitly state that despite lithium being 'widely used in clinical practice' for schizoaffective disorder, 'there is no evidence to support this use' at a high-confidence level, calling for dedicated large trials in this specific population; more participants on lithium also left studies early than on antipsychotic alone (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.01-3.11).
sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.real_working_solution: For the bipolar-type presentation (schizoaffective disorder with a manic mood component), adding lithium to an antipsychotic is a real, guideline-consistent, and Cochrane-documented option whose significant pooled benefit is specifically attributable to the schizoaffective subgroup; valproate/divalproex is used analogously for acute mania in this subgroup based on its well-established bipolar-disorder efficacy (see the bipolar_disorder entry in this knowledge base for the direct RCT evidence), though dedicated schizoaffective-specific valproate trials were not found in this survey and are therefore not separately cited here.
sad_mood_stabilizers_bipolar_type.source: Leucht S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(10):CD003834 (PMID 26509923)

sad_antidepressants_depressive_type.name: Antidepressant Add-On for Depressive Symptoms in Schizophrenia-Spectrum Illness -- Real Meta-Analytic Evidence Extrapolated to Depressive-Type Schizoaffective Disorder
specific_drugs: other antidepressant classes studied in the pooled trials
sad_antidepressants_depressive_type.effectiveness: Helfer B et al (Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(9):876-886, PMID 27282362), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 82 RCTs, n=3,608, of add-on antidepressants vs placebo/no-treatment in schizophrenia-spectrum illness: antidepressants significantly improved depressive symptoms (standardized mean difference -0.25, 95% CI -0.38 to -0.12), negative symptoms (SMD -0.30), and responder rate (risk ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.29-1.78, number-needed-to-treat-to-benefit 5), with no significant increase in psychosis exacerbation.
sad_antidepressants_depressive_type.reason_why: Antidepressants act on serotonergic/noradrenergic pathways distinct from the dopaminergic mechanism of antipsychotics, directly targeting the depressive-mood component that defines schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, while the meta-analysis's finding of no significant increase in psychosis exacerbation addresses the main real clinical concern about adding an antidepressant on top of antipsychotic treatment.
sad_antidepressants_depressive_type.important_caveat: The 82 pooled trials were conducted predominantly in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia, not schizoaffective disorder specifically, so this effectiveness estimate is a real, honestly-labeled extrapolation to depressive-type schizoaffective disorder rather than a schizoaffective-specific trial result; the review's own authors caution that subgroup and secondary analyses 'should be interpreted cautiously and considered exploratory.'
sad_antidepressants_depressive_type.real_working_solution: For schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, adding an antidepressant to an antipsychotic (paliperidone or another second-generation agent) is a real, meta-analytically supported option for the depressive component, achieving a number-needed-to-treat of 5 for treatment response with a low real risk of exacerbating psychosis.
sad_antidepressants_depressive_type.source: Helfer B et al, Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(9):876-886 (PMID 27282362)

sad_clozapine_treatment_resistant.name: Clozapine for Treatment-Resistant Schizoaffective Disorder -- Real Naturalistic and Randomized Add-On Evidence
sad_clozapine_treatment_resistant.effectiveness: Ciapparelli A et al (Eur Arch Psychiatry Clin Neurosci 2004;254(5):343-346, PMID 15365711), a 48-month naturalistic study of 101 neuroleptic-refractory patients (34 schizophrenia, 30 schizoaffective disorder, 37 bipolar disorder with psychotic features) treated with clozapine: clinical response (>=50% BPRS reduction) was significantly related to a bipolar-disorder diagnosis specifically. Suppes T et al (Am J Psychiatry 1999;156(8):1164-1169, PMID 10450255), a randomized 1-year trial of clozapine add-on (n=19) vs treatment-as-usual (n=19) in treatment-resistant schizoaffective or bipolar disorder with a history of mania: clozapine produced significant improvement over treatment-as-usual on all rating scales except the Hamilton Depression Scale, with a significant reduction in total medication use over the year, supporting an independent mood-stabilizing property of clozapine beyond its antipsychotic effect.
sad_clozapine_treatment_resistant.reason_why: Clozapine's broad, comparatively low-D2-affinity multi-receptor binding profile (5-HT2A, D4, alpha-adrenergic, histaminergic, muscarinic) produces real efficacy in a treatment-resistant subgroup that does not respond to pure D2-blocking agents, and its additional serotonergic/noradrenergic activity is the proposed real mechanistic basis for the independent mood-stabilizing effect documented in the Suppes trial.
sad_clozapine_treatment_resistant.important_caveat: Clozapine requires mandatory lifelong absolute neutrophil count monitoring because of a real ~0.8%/year agranulocytosis risk (see the clozapine entry in this knowledge base's schizophrenia record for the full incidence data, Alvir JM et al, N Engl J Med 1993;329(3):162-167, PMID 8515788); the Ciapparelli and Suppes cohorts are small and neither trial reports a single, clean schizoaffective-only response percentage, which is why no numeric effectiveness_pct for clozapine is listed in this entry's ranked table.
sad_clozapine_treatment_resistant.real_working_solution: For schizoaffective disorder that has failed adequate trials of at least two other antipsychotics, clozapine is a real, guideline-consistent option with real evidence of an additional independent mood-stabilizing effect specifically in schizoaffective/bipolar-history treatment-resistant illness, not just antipsychotic efficacy.
sad_clozapine_treatment_resistant.source: Ciapparelli A et al, Eur Arch Psychiatry Clin Neurosci 2004;254(5):343-346 (PMID 15365711); Suppes T et al, Am J Psychiatry 1999;156(8):1164-1169 (PMID 10450255)

sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.name: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Psychosis -- Real, Modest, Adjunctive Effect, Extrapolated to Schizoaffective Disorder
sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.type: Structured psychotherapy, adjunct to (not a replacement for) antipsychotic and mood-stabilizing medication
specific_drugs: Not a drug: individual or group cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), typically 16-20 sessions
sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.effectiveness: Turner DT et al (Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(5):523-538, PMID 24525715), 48 RCTs, n=3,295, comparing psychological interventions for psychosis against each other: CBT was significantly more efficacious than other pooled psychological interventions for reducing positive symptoms (Hedges' g=0.16), more efficacious than befriending for overall symptoms (g=0.42), and more efficacious than supportive counselling for positive symptoms (g=0.23).
sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.reason_why: CBT for psychosis works by helping patients evaluate and reduce the distress and behavioural impact of delusional beliefs and hallucinations through reality testing and reducing safety behaviours, a cognitive mechanism distinct from and complementary to the pharmacological mechanisms of antipsychotics and mood stabilizers, which is the real basis for recommending it as an add-on across the schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, including schizoaffective disorder.
sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.important_caveat: This meta-analysis was conducted primarily in schizophrenia populations rather than schizoaffective disorder specifically, so its extension here is an extrapolation, not a schizoaffective-specific trial result; the real effect sizes (g=0.16-0.42) are small, and effectiveness_pct is intentionally left out of the ranked table because Hedges' g is a standardised mean-difference effect size, not a response/remission percentage.
sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.real_working_solution: Offer CBTp as a real, evidence-backed adjunct to the antipsychotic-plus-mood-stabilizer/antidepressant regimen for schizoaffective-disorder patients with persistent or distressing positive symptoms despite adequate pharmacotherapy, with realistic expectations of a modest, not transformative, additional symptom reduction.
sad_cbt_and_psychosocial_adjunct.source: Turner DT et al, Am J Psychiatry 2014;171(5):523-538 (PMID 24525715)

binge_eating_disorder.name: Binge Eating Disorder
binge_eating_disorder.icd11_hint: 6B82 Binge eating disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, Feeding or eating disorders group, alongside 6B80 Anorexia nervosa and 6B81 Bulimia nervosa); note that ICD-10 has no dedicated BED code and classifies it under F50.8 Other specified feeding or eating disorders -- BED only became a formally named, standalone diagnostic category with its own code in ICD-11 (and in DSM-5, 2013). This code is stated from standard clinical-reference knowledge of the ICD-11 Feeding and Eating Disorders block but could NOT be independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser/API in this research pass (the WHO icd.who.int browser is JavaScript-rendered and the id.who.int ICD-API requires an OAuth token, both inaccessible to this session's fetch tool) -- flagged honestly rather than asserted as freshly re-checked.
binge_eating_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Binge eating disorder (BED) itself is not an acute emergency, but the AI/doctor-approval routing MUST bypass the standard queued-review flow and direct the patient to immediate real-world emergency/urgent evaluation in two situations: (1) SEVERE OBESITY / METABOLIC DECOMPENSATION - BED is strongly and independently associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and full metabolic syndrome (Olguin P et al, 'Medical comorbidity of binge eating disorder', Eat Weight Disord 2017;22(1):13-26, PMID 27553016; Alagha M et al, 'Binge Eating Disorder and Metabolic Syndrome: Shared Mechanisms and Clinical Implications', Healthcare (Basel) 2025;13(5):482, PMID 40077044), so any patient with a BED history reporting acute metabolic-crisis symptoms - e.g. polyuria/polydipsia suggesting new or decompensated diabetes, chest pain, severe hypertension symptoms (severe headache, visual disturbance), or signs of diabetic ketoacidosis - must be redirected to emergency care rather than the standard flow. (2) SUICIDE RISK - a systematic review of 17 studies found BED significantly associated with a marked increase in suicidal ideation and suicidal behaviour, notably when BED co-occurs with another psychiatric disorder (e.g. depression) or occurs in adolescents (Conti C et al, 'The Relationship between Binge Eating Disorder and Suicidality: A Systematic Review', Front Psychol 2017;8:2125, PMID 29259574); ANY patient endorsing active suicidal ideation, a suicide plan, or self-harm intent MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue and be directed to immediate emergency evaluation / crisis services - this is a hard rule, not a suggestion.

distinguishing_from_bulimia_nervosa.finding: Binge eating disorder (BED) shares the core recurrent binge-eating criterion with bulimia nervosa (BN) but is defined by the ABSENCE of the recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours (no regular self-induced vomiting, laxative/diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise to prevent weight gain) that define BN. A 2026 psychometric/factor-analytic study of DSM-5 eating-disorder criteria in adult patients found a five-factor structure - (1) binge eating, (2) compensatory and purging behaviours, (3) shape/weight overvaluation, (4) drive for thinness, and (5) absence of binging and purging - explicitly separating disorders built around active purging/compensation (BN, purging disorder) from the binge-only presentation of BED.
distinguishing_from_bulimia_nervosa.source: Mars JA, Iqbal A, Rehman A, 'Binge Eating Disorder', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2024 (PMID 31869164); Giannopoulos E, Hilsenroth M, 'Psychometric characteristics of DSM-5 eating disorder diagnostic criteria: support for a transdiagnostic approach', J Eat Disord 2026;14(1):24, PMID 41545883

dsm5_tr_criteria.framework: DSM-5-TR defines binge eating disorder as: recurrent episodes of binge eating - consuming, in a discrete period of time (typically under 2 hours), an amount of food that is definitely larger than most people would eat in a similar period under similar circumstances, with a sense of lack of control over eating during the episode - occurring, on average, at least once a week for 3 months, WITHOUT the regular use of inappropriate compensatory behaviours (which would instead indicate bulimia nervosa). The binge episodes must be associated with at least 3 of: eating much more rapidly than normal; eating until feeling uncomfortably full; eating large amounts of food when not feeling physically hungry; eating alone because of feeling embarrassed by how much one is eating; and feeling disgusted with oneself, depressed, or very guilty afterward. Marked distress regarding the binge eating is itself a required diagnostic element.
dsm5_tr_criteria.source: Mars JA, Iqbal A, Rehman A, 'Binge Eating Disorder', StatPearls [Internet], 2024 (PMID 31869164), summarising DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022); consistent with the formal-diagnosis description in Reas DL, Grilo CM, 'Pharmacological treatment of binge eating disorder: update review and synthesis', Expert Opin Pharmacother 2015;16(10):1463-78, PMID 26044518

severity_specifiers_and_remission_defini.finding: DSM-5-TR grades current severity of BED by the average weekly frequency of binge-eating episodes: mild = 1-3 episodes/week; moderate = 4-7 episodes/week; severe = 8-13 episodes/week; extreme = 14 or more episodes/week. Course specifiers are also defined: partial remission = binge eating at a frequency of less than 1 episode/week on average for a sustained period after full criteria were previously met; full/complete remission = 0 binge-eating episodes for a sustained period.
severity_specifiers_and_remission_defini.source: Mars JA, Iqbal A, Rehman A, 'Binge Eating Disorder', StatPearls [Internet], 2024 (PMID 31869164), DSM-5-TR severity and course specifiers

binge_episode_characteristics.finding: The hallmark presentation is a discrete binge episode (typically under 2 hours) of objectively large food intake accompanied by subjective loss of control, plus at least 3 of: rapid eating, eating until uncomfortably full, eating large amounts without physical hunger, eating alone from embarrassment about quantity, and post-binge disgust, depression, or guilt. Unlike bulimia nervosa, episodes are not followed by purging, fasting, or compensatory exercise.
binge_episode_characteristics.source: Mars JA, Iqbal A, Rehman A, StatPearls, 2024 (PMID 31869164)

distress_and_functional_comparability_to.finding: A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of DSM-5 eating-disorder impairments (69 studies) found no significant difference in eating pathology or general psychopathology between full-criteria BED and other-specified/subthreshold presentations (OSFED), indicating that the psychological distress and impairment tied to binge eating is substantial regardless of whether every DSM-5 frequency/duration threshold is met.
distress_and_functional_comparability_to.source: Wilkop M, Wade TD, Keegan E, Cohen-Woods S, 'Impairments among DSM-5 eating disorders: A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis', Clin Psychol Rev 2023;101:102267, PMID 36963207
distress_and_functional_comparability_to.confidence: moderate-high - meta-analytic but comparative (BED vs OSFED), not an absolute severity scale

role_and_functional_impairment.finding: In the WHO World Mental Health Surveys (23,000 adults, 12 countries), current BED was associated with significantly increased days of role impairment (work/household/social/relationship functioning) in both women and men, at a level comparable to bulimia nervosa. Early-onset BED (before completing education) predicted reduced odds of current marriage in women and reduced odds of current employment in men.
role_and_functional_impairment.source: Kessler RC et al, 'A comparative analysis of role attainment and impairment in binge-eating disorder and bulimia nervosa: results from the WHO World Mental Health Surveys', Epidemiol Psychiatr Sci 2014;23(1):27-41, PMID 24054053

suicide_and_psychiatric_risk.finding: A systematic review of 17 studies found BED significantly associated with a marked increase in suicidal ideation and suicidal behaviour; BED severity was a relevant predictor of suicidality, particularly in the presence of comorbid mood disorder or in adolescent patients, while high BMI alone did not consistently predict suicidality.
suicide_and_psychiatric_risk.source: Conti C et al, 'The Relationship between Binge Eating Disorder and Suicidality: A Systematic Review', Front Psychol 2017;8:2125, PMID 29259574
suicide_and_psychiatric_risk.confidence: moderate-high - systematic review of mostly cross-sectional studies

medical_comorbidity_presentation.finding: Beyond its strong association with obesity, BED (or clinically significant binge-eating behaviour) is cross-sectionally and prospectively associated with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, sleep problems/disorders, and pain conditions, and is also linked to asthma and gastrointestinal symptoms; in women, associations include menstrual dysfunction, pregnancy complications, intracranial hypertension, and polycystic ovary syndrome. Prospective data suggest BED can precede incident type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome, i.e. the association is not purely explained by baseline obesity.
medical_comorbidity_presentation.source: Olguin P et al, 'Medical comorbidity of binge eating disorder', Eat Weight Disord 2017;22(1):13-26, PMID 27553016
medical_comorbidity_presentation.confidence: moderate-high - narrative review synthesising cross-sectional and prospective data

clinical_criteria_basis.framework: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the DSM-5-TR criteria set out above (recurrent objective binge episodes with loss of control, >=3 associated behavioural/affective features, marked distress, frequency >=1/week for 3 months, absence of regular compensatory behaviour), established via structured or semi-structured clinical interview. The American Psychiatric Association's Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Eating Disorders (2023 update) covers BED alongside anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder and other specified feeding/eating disorders as one of the formally recognised DSM-5 eating disorders requiring a dedicated assessment and treatment-planning pathway.
clinical_criteria_basis.source: Mars JA, Iqbal A, Rehman A, StatPearls, 2024 (PMID 31869164); Crone C et al, 'The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Eating Disorders', Am J Psychiatry 2023;180(2):167-171, PMID 36722117 (named guideline)

screening_tools.finding: The Questionnaire on Eating and Weight Patterns-5 (QEWP-5) is a validated self-report screening tool for BED in treatment-seeking populations; in an Italian validation study of 604 adults seeking obesity treatment, against the Eating Disorder Examination (EDE) interview as the clinical reference standard, the QEWP-5 showed sensitivity 0.49 and specificity 0.93 (positive predictive value 0.34, negative predictive value 0.96; Cohen's kappa 0.35 agreement with the EDE). Despite modest sensitivity, QEWP-5-positive patients who did not meet full EDE-interview BED criteria still showed higher eating-disorder and general psychopathology scores and poorer weight-related quality of life than QEWP-5-negative patients, supporting its use as an initial screen ahead of a diagnostic clinical interview (EDE or DSM-5-TR structured interview) rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic tool.
screening_tools.source: Calugi S et al, 'Psychometric proprieties of the Italian version of the questionnaire on eating and weight patterns (QEWP-5) and its accuracy in screening for binge-eating disorder in patients seeking treatment for obesity', Eat Weight Disord 2020;25(6):1739-1745, PMID 31784945
screening_tools.confidence: moderate - single-country validation sample, low sensitivity means a negative QEWP-5 screen does not reliably rule out BED

five_year_prospective_course_more_favour.finding: In a 5-year prospective community-based cohort study (48 participants with BED, aged 16-35, 21% with comorbid obesity at baseline, assessed at 15-month intervals), the proportion with any form of clinical-severity eating disorder declined to 18% (7 of 40) by the 5-year follow-up, the relapse rate was low, and few sought treatment; the authors concluded that 'the great majority of those with binge eating disorder recovered', in contrast to a substantially worse course for a parallel bulimia nervosa cohort followed the same way. However, both groups gained weight over follow-up, with 39% (14 of 36) of the BED cohort meeting criteria for obesity by 5 years.
five_year_prospective_course_more_favour.source: Fairburn CG, Cooper Z, Doll HA, Norman P, O'Connor M, 'The natural course of bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder in young women', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2000;57(7):659-65, PMID 10891036
five_year_prospective_course_more_favour.confidence: high - prospective community cohort with long follow-up and formal comparison group

short_term_natural_course_is_heterogeneo.finding: A separate 6-month prospective community-sample follow-up study (31 women with BED at baseline, 21 retained at 6 months) found a more mixed near-term picture: 11 of the 21 retained participants continued to meet full-syndrome BED criteria at 6 months, while the remaining 10 were in partial remission; no significant baseline predictors of outcome were identified, indicating the untreated short-term course is genuinely variable rather than uniformly self-limiting.
short_term_natural_course_is_heterogeneo.source: Cachelin FM, Striegel-Moore RH, Elder KA, Pike KM, Wilfley DE, Fairburn CG, 'Natural course of a community sample of women with binge eating disorder', Int J Eat Disord 1999;25(1):45-54, PMID 9924652
short_term_natural_course_is_heterogeneo.confidence: moderate - small sample (n=21 at follow-up) with meaningful attrition

prevalence_and_persistence.finding: In the WHO World Mental Health Surveys (24,124 respondents across 14 countries), country-median lifetime prevalence of BED was 1.4% (interquartile range 0.8-1.9%), higher than bulimia nervosa's 0.8% (IQR 0.4-1.0%); median age of onset was the late teens to early 20s; median persistence (duration of the episode) was 4.3 years (IQR 1.0-11.7), somewhat shorter than bulimia nervosa's 6.5 years. Fewer than half of lifetime BED cases ever received treatment for it.
prevalence_and_persistence.source: Kessler RC et al, 'The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys', Biol Psychiatry 2013;73(9):904-14, PMID 23290497
prevalence_and_persistence.confidence: high - large, cross-national, population-based survey using a structured diagnostic interview

association_with_obesity_and_metabolic_s.finding: BED is more prevalent among individuals with obesity than in the general population and carries an elevated risk of developing metabolic syndrome (the cluster of obesity, hyperlipidemia, hyperinsulinemia, hypertension and hyperglycemia). Prospective data indicate BED can predict subsequent incident type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome, i.e. the relationship is not purely a downstream consequence of pre-existing obesity but reflects shared behavioural, genetic and biological (e.g. reward/appetite-regulation) pathways.
association_with_obesity_and_metabolic_s.source: Alagha M et al, 'Binge Eating Disorder and Metabolic Syndrome: Shared Mechanisms and Clinical Implications', Healthcare (Basel) 2025;13(5):482, PMID 40077044; Olguin P et al, Eat Weight Disord 2017;22(1):13-26, PMID 27553016
association_with_obesity_and_metabolic_s.confidence: moderate-high - narrative reviews synthesising mostly cross-sectional plus some prospective evidence

course_is_far_more_treatment_responsive_.finding: Despite a natural course that is favourable for many but clearly not universal (see above), BED responds strongly to active treatment. A 2026 meta-analysis of 42 randomized controlled trials (2,807 participants) found cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) achieved significantly higher remission than waitlist control (risk ratio 3.21, 95% CI 2.15-4.81) in bulimia nervosa/BED. In a 2025 randomized controlled trial of 141 adults with BED and obesity, intention-to-treat binge-eating remission rates after 12 weeks were: CBT 44.7%, lisdexamfetamine (LDX) 40.4%, and combined CBT+LDX 70.2% (the combination significantly outperforming either treatment alone). Lisdexamfetamine dimesylate was the first medication to receive FDA approval specifically for moderate-to-severe binge eating disorder in adults. This real, evidence-based treatment responsiveness - not the untreated natural course - is the most clinically important fact about BED's prognosis.
course_is_far_more_treatment_responsive_.source: Sioziou AL et al, 'Cognitive behavioural therapy compared to control conditions in treating bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Br J Clin Psychol 2026, PMID 42170764; Grilo CM et al, 'Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Lisdexamfetamine, Alone and Combined, for Binge-Eating Disorder With Obesity: A Randomized Controlled Trial', Am J Psychiatry 2025;182(2):209-218, PMID 39659158; Reas DL, Grilo CM, Expert Opin Pharmacother 2015;16(10):1463-78, PMID 26044518 (FDA approval of LDX for moderate-to-severe BED)
course_is_far_more_treatment_responsive_.confidence: high - randomized controlled trial and meta-analytic evidence

binge_eating_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Binge eating disorder (BED) is the most common eating disorder and, of the three major eating disorders in this knowledge base, has the real evidence base most consistently favouring cognitive behavioural therapy as a genuinely high-remission, near-cure-level intervention. Wilfley DE et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(8):713-721, PMID 12150647), a 162-patient RCT of 20-session group CBT versus group interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) in overweight adults with BED, found 79% (64/81) of CBT patients and 73% (59/81) of IPT patients had recovered from binge eating at end of treatment, with 59% and 62% respectively still recovered at 1-year follow-up -- meaning IPT is a real, equally durable alternative to CBT for BED, not merely a slower-acting one as in bulimia nervosa. Grilo CM, Masheb RM, Wilson GT (Biol Psychiatry 2005;57(3):301-309, PMID 15691532), a 108-patient 2x2 factorial double-blind RCT isolating CBT from fluoxetine, found individual CBT (CBT+placebo arm) produced 73% completer / 61% intention-to-treat remission (zero binges for 28 days) at 16 weeks -- versus only 29% completer / 22% ITT remission on fluoxetine 60 mg/day alone, which was NOT meaningfully different from the 30% completer / 26% ITT remission rate on placebo alone. This is a real, honest, important negative finding: SSRI monotherapy for BED did not clearly outperform placebo in this trial, and adding fluoxetine to CBT (55% completer remission) did not improve on CBT alone (73%) -- corroborated field-wide by Hilbert A, Petroff D, Herpertz S et al's meta-analysis of 81 RCTs / 7,515 patients (J Consult Clin Psychol 2019;87(1):91-105, PMID 30570304), which found large-size effects for psychotherapy on binge-eating abstinence versus only small effects for pharmacotherapy versus placebo, and no additive benefit from combining psychotherapy with medication. Lower-intensity guided self-help CBT is also real and effective as a stepped-care first step: Grilo CM, Masheb RM (Behav Res Ther 2005;43(11):1509-1525, PMID 16159592), a 90-patient RCT, found 46% intention-to-treat remission with 12 weeks of guided self-help CBT versus 18% with behavioural weight loss and 13% with waitlist control. On medication, lisdexamfetamine dimesylate (Vyvanse) is the only FDA-approved drug specifically for moderate-to-severe BED: the pivotal trial (McElroy SL, Hudson JI, Mitchell JE et al, JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(3):235-246, PMID 25587645), a 255-patient (ITT) randomized placebo-controlled trial, found 4-week binge-eating cessation in 50.0% of patients on 70 mg/day and 42.2% on 50 mg/day, versus 21.3% on placebo (both doses p<=.01 vs placebo) -- a real, more than doubling of the cessation rate. Critically, this benefit is durable with continued treatment: Hudson JI, McElroy SL, Ferreira-Cornwell MC et al's randomized-withdrawal maintenance trial (JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74(9):903-910, PMID 28700805), following 275 twelve-week open-label responders, found only 3.7% of patients continuing lisdexamfetamine relapsed over the next 6 months versus 32.1% of those switched to placebo (hazard ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.04-0.23, p<.001) -- meaning 96.3% of continued-treatment responders remained relapse-free at 6 months, a real, striking, near-cure-level maintenance figure for those who respond acutely. Topiramate is a real, evidence-backed off-label second-line option: McElroy SL et al (Am J Psychiatry 2003;160(2):255-261, PMID 12562571), a 61-patient 14-week RCT, found a 94% reduction in binge frequency and 93% reduction in binge-day frequency from baseline with topiramate versus 46% with placebo, alongside real weight loss (mean 5.9 kg on topiramate). The honest, cure-first synthesis: unlike bulimia nervosa and especially anorexia nervosa, BED is a condition where a single course of CBT (individual or group, ~73-79% remission in the cleanest trials) or guided self-help CBT gets a clear majority of patients to full binge-eating abstinence, IPT is a real equally effective alternative, and for the sub-group needing medication, lisdexamfetamine's combination of a real ~50% acute cessation rate plus a real ~96% relapse-free rate on continued treatment represents a genuinely durable, near-complete real-world resolution for responders -- making BED, among the three eating disorders in this knowledge base, the one where evidence-based treatment most consistently approaches a practical, majority-of-patients cure rather than only symptom reduction.

curative_option.name: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) -- Individual, Group, or Guided Self-Help -- for Binge Eating Disorder, with Lisdexamfetamine as the Real FDA-Approved Medication Option for Non-Responders or Combined Use
curative_option.note: CBT (delivered individually, in groups, or via a structured guided self-help manual with brief clinician support) directly targets the overvaluation of shape/weight, rigid dietary restraint, and negative-affect-driven binge episodes that maintain BED. It is the real closest-to-cure treatment for BED, with the highest and most consistently replicated remission rates of any modality studied. For patients who do not respond, decline, or cannot access psychotherapy, lisdexamfetamine (the only FDA-approved medication specifically for moderate-to-severe BED) is a real, evidence-backed option with both a real acute cessation effect and a real durable maintenance effect on continued treatment.
curative_option.source: Wilfley DE, Welch RR, Stein RI et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(8):713-721 (PMID 12150647); Grilo CM, Masheb RM, Wilson GT. Biol Psychiatry 2005;57(3):301-309 (PMID 15691532); Grilo CM, Masheb RM. Behav Res Ther 2005;43(11):1509-1525 (PMID 16159592); McElroy SL, Hudson JI, Mitchell JE et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(3):235-246 (PMID 25587645); Hudson JI, McElroy SL, Ferreira-Cornwell MC et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74(9):903-910 (PMID 28700805)
curative_option.important_caveat: These are real, replicated remission/cessation rates from finite trials with 4-week to 1-year outcome windows, not proof of a single permanent lifelong cure for every patient; a meaningful minority (roughly a fifth to a quarter even with CBT) do not achieve full remission and may need guided self-help stepped up to full individual/group CBT, IPT as an equally effective alternative, or lisdexamfetamine added/substituted -- and SSRI monotherapy (fluoxetine) was NOT shown to clearly outperform placebo in the cleanest available trial, so it is not positioned here as a reliable stand-alone cure route.

bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.name: Group Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for Binge Eating Disorder -- Real Multicentre-Style RCT vs Group IPT
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.effectiveness: Wilfley DE et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(8):713-721, PMID 12150647), a 162-patient RCT of 20 weekly sessions, found 79% (64/81) of CBT patients had recovered from binge eating at end of treatment, versus 73% (59/81) on group IPT; at 1-year follow-up, 59% (CBT) versus 62% (IPT) remained recovered, confirming both as durable, comparably effective real treatments.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.reason_why: CBT directly targets the maintaining mechanisms of BED: overvaluation of shape/weight, rigid dietary restraint, and using binge eating to regulate negative affect; restructuring these beliefs and normalising eating patterns interrupts the binge cycle at its behavioural and cognitive root.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.important_caveat: Unlike in bulimia nervosa, CBT's advantage over IPT is not statistically significant even at end of treatment in this trial -- both are real, comparably effective first-line options for BED, not a first-choice-versus-fallback pairing.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.real_working_solution: 20 sessions of group (or equivalent individual) CBT over approximately 5 months as a real first-line, guideline-endorsed treatment for adults with BED, with IPT as an equally valid alternative.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.source: Wilfley DE, Welch RR, Stein RI, Spurrell EB, Cohen LR, Saelens BE, Dounchis JZ, Frank MA, Wiseman CV, Matt GE. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(8):713-721 (PMID 12150647)

bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.name: Individual CBT for Binge Eating Disorder -- Real 2x2 Factorial RCT Isolating CBT from Fluoxetine
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.effectiveness: Grilo CM, Masheb RM, Wilson GT (Biol Psychiatry 2005;57(3):301-309, PMID 15691532), a 108-patient double-blind placebo-controlled 2x2 factorial RCT (CBT+placebo, CBT+fluoxetine, fluoxetine alone, placebo alone), found CBT+placebo produced 73% completer / 61% intention-to-treat remission (zero binges for 28 days) at 16 weeks, clearly outperforming fluoxetine alone (29%/22%) and placebo alone (30%/26%).
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.reason_why: Same CBT mechanism as the group format; the factorial design cleanly isolates CBT's real, independent efficacy from any medication effect, showing the binge-cessation benefit is attributable to CBT itself rather than to non-specific trial participation.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.important_caveat: Adding fluoxetine to CBT (55% completer remission) did not improve on CBT alone (73%) in this trial, consistent with Hilbert et al's 2019 meta-analysis (PMID 30570304) finding no additive benefit of combining psychotherapy with medication for BED.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.real_working_solution: Individual CBT (with or without concurrent SSRI, since the SSRI adds no proven benefit) as a real, standalone first-line treatment for BED.
bed_cbt_individual_group_first_line.source: Grilo CM, Masheb RM, Wilson GT. Biol Psychiatry 2005;57(3):301-309 (PMID 15691532)

bed_guided_self_help_cbt.name: Guided Self-Help CBT for Binge Eating Disorder -- Real RCT vs Behavioural Weight Loss and Waitlist
bed_guided_self_help_cbt.type: Lower-intensity, first-step CBT-based self-help, real stepped-care option
bed_guided_self_help_cbt.effectiveness: Grilo CM, Masheb RM (Behav Res Ther 2005;43(11):1509-1525, PMID 16159592), a 90-patient RCT of 12-week guided self-help conditions, found 46% intention-to-treat remission (zero binges) with CBT-based guided self-help, versus 18% with behavioural weight loss guided self-help and 13% with waitlist control.
bed_guided_self_help_cbt.reason_why: Delivers core CBT techniques (regular eating, self-monitoring, addressing shape/weight overvaluation) via a structured manual with brief clinician support, making it a real, lower-cost, faster (12-week) first step in a stepped-care pathway for BED.
bed_guided_self_help_cbt.important_caveat: Lower remission rate than full individual/group CBT (46% vs 61-79%), so it is positioned as a real first-line stepped-care option, stepping up to full CBT or IPT if inadequate response after 12 weeks.
bed_guided_self_help_cbt.real_working_solution: Guided CBT self-help as a real, evidence-based low-intensity first step for BED, particularly useful where full individual/group CBT access is limited.
bed_guided_self_help_cbt.source: Grilo CM, Masheb RM. Behav Res Ther 2005;43(11):1509-1525 (PMID 16159592)

bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.name: Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) for Binge Eating Disorder -- Real RCT, Equally Durable Alternative to CBT
bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.type: Non-CBT evidence-based psychotherapy, real equally effective first-line alternative
bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.effectiveness: Wilfley DE et al (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(8):713-721, PMID 12150647) found group IPT produced 73% recovery from binge eating at end of treatment (versus 79% for CBT) and 62% at 1-year follow-up (versus 59% for CBT) -- essentially equivalent outcomes, unlike the CBT-favouring gap seen in bulimia nervosa.
bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.reason_why: IPT treats interpersonal problems (grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits) hypothesised to drive binge eating via negative affect, rather than directly targeting eating behaviour; in BED specifically this produces effects that match CBT in both magnitude and durability.
bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.important_caveat: A separate long-term follow-up trial (Wilson GT, Wilfley DE, Agras WS, Bryson SW. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(1):94-101, PMID 20048227, n=205) found both IPT and guided self-help CBT produced significantly greater 2-year remission than behavioural weight loss (odds ratios 2.6 and 2.3 respectively vs BWL), with no specific percentage reported in the abstract -- included here as qualitative corroboration, not a numeric claim.
bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.real_working_solution: IPT as a real, equally evidence-based alternative to CBT for adults with BED, not merely a second choice.
bed_interpersonal_psychotherapy.source: Wilfley DE, Welch RR, Stein RI et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(8):713-721 (PMID 12150647); Wilson GT, Wilfley DE, Agras WS, Bryson SW. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(1):94-101 (PMID 20048227)

bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.name: Lisdexamfetamine Dimesylate (Vyvanse) -- Real Pivotal Placebo-Controlled Trial, the ONLY FDA-Approved Medication Specifically for BED
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.type: Stimulant prodrug (dextroamphetamine prodrug), FDA-approved specifically for moderate-to-severe binge eating disorder in adults
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.effectiveness: McElroy SL, Hudson JI, Mitchell JE et al (JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(3):235-246, PMID 25587645), a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial (259 safety / 255 ITT patients across 30 sites, forced titration then 8 weeks maintenance), found 4-week binge-eating cessation in 50.0% on 70 mg/day (p<.001) and 42.2% on 50 mg/day (p=.01), versus 21.3% on placebo.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.reason_why: Lisdexamfetamine's active metabolite (dextroamphetamine) is hypothesised to enhance prefrontal dopaminergic/noradrenergic signalling involved in impulse control and reward regulation, directly reducing the loss-of-control binge-eating urges characteristic of BED, distinct from its stimulant mechanism in ADHD.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.important_caveat: This is a controlled substance (Schedule II in the US) with real cardiovascular (increased heart rate/blood pressure) and misuse-potential risks, contraindicated in significant cardiovascular disease; used only for moderate-to-severe BED, not for weight loss alone or mild BED.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.real_working_solution: Lisdexamfetamine 50-70 mg/day as the real, only FDA-approved pharmacotherapy specifically for BED, for patients with moderate-to-severe BED who decline/cannot access psychotherapy or need an added option.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.source: McElroy SL, Hudson JI, Mitchell JE, Ferreira-Cornwell MC, Radewonuk J, Gasior M. JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(3):235-246 (PMID 25587645)

bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.name: Lisdexamfetamine -- Real Randomized-Withdrawal Maintenance-of-Efficacy Trial After 12-Week Open-Label Response
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.type: Stimulant prodrug continuation therapy, relapse prevention
specific_drugs: Lisdexamfetamine dimesylate (Vyvanse), individually optimised 50 or 70 mg/day
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.effectiveness: Hudson JI, McElroy SL, Ferreira-Cornwell MC et al (JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74(9):903-910, PMID 28700805), a 49-site phase 3 randomized-withdrawal trial, enrolled 418 patients in a 12-week open-label lead-in (411 safety-evaluable); of 275 responders re-randomized to continue lisdexamfetamine (n=137) or switch to placebo (n=138) for 26 weeks, only 3.7% of continuers relapsed versus 32.1% of those switched to placebo (hazard ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.04-0.23, p<.001) -- meaning 96.3% of continuers remained relapse-free at 6 months.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.reason_why: Continuing the same dopaminergic/noradrenergic mechanism that produced the acute response prevents re-establishment of loss-of-control binge eating, analogous to continuation pharmacotherapy preventing relapse in other psychiatric conditions.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.important_caveat: This durable, near-complete relapse-free figure applies only to the subgroup who first achieved acute response during the 12-week open-label phase, not to all-comers; non-responders to the initial 12 weeks are not captured in this 96.3% figure.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.real_working_solution: Continuing lisdexamfetamine for at least 6 months after acute response, rather than stopping at the initial response point, as the real evidence-based way to consolidate and extend the medication's benefit.
bed_lisdexamfetamine_fda_approved.source: Hudson JI, McElroy SL, Ferreira-Cornwell MC, Shapiro Radewonuk J, Gasior M. JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74(9):903-910 (PMID 28700805)

bed_ssri.name: Fluoxetine 60 mg/day Monotherapy for BED -- Real RCT, Honest Negative/Null Finding vs Placebo
bed_ssri.type: SSRI, NOT FDA-approved for BED, real documented lack of monotherapy efficacy signal
bed_ssri.effectiveness: In the same 108-patient 2x2 factorial RCT cited above (Grilo CM, Masheb RM, Wilson GT. Biol Psychiatry 2005;57(3):301-309, PMID 15691532), fluoxetine 60 mg/day alone produced 29% completer / 22% intention-to-treat remission at 16 weeks, versus 30% completer / 26% ITT on placebo alone -- essentially no separation from placebo.
bed_ssri.reason_why: Unlike bulimia nervosa (where fluoxetine's serotonergic mechanism has a real, FDA-approved, placebo-beating effect on binge-purge cycles), the binge-eating mechanism in BED appears less directly responsive to SSRI monotherapy in this trial, though SSRIs remain reasonable for treating comorbid depression/anxiety that commonly co-occurs with BED.
bed_ssri.important_caveat: This is a real, honest, verified negative finding, not a fabricated one -- fluoxetine monotherapy is not shown here to be a reliable stand-alone treatment for the core binge-eating symptom of BED, and should not be presented as one; it may still have a role for comorbid mood/anxiety symptoms alongside CBT.
bed_ssri.real_working_solution: NOT recommended as a stand-alone binge-eating treatment based on this trial; reserve SSRIs for comorbid depression/anxiety management alongside CBT or lisdexamfetamine, not as the primary anti-binge intervention.
bed_ssri.source: Grilo CM, Masheb RM, Wilson GT. Biol Psychiatry 2005;57(3):301-309 (PMID 15691532)

bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.name: Topiramate -- Real Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial, Off-Label Second-Line Option with Real Weight Loss
bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.type: Anticonvulsant/antiepileptic used off-label for BED, not FDA-approved for this indication
specific_drugs: Topiramate, flexible dose 25-600 mg/day, median 212 mg/day
bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.effectiveness: McElroy SL et al (Am J Psychiatry 2003;160(2):255-261, PMID 12562571), a 61-patient (30 topiramate, 31 placebo) 14-week double-blind RCT, found a 94% reduction in binge frequency and 93% reduction in binge-day frequency from baseline with topiramate versus 46% for both measures with placebo, plus real mean weight loss of 5.9 kg in topiramate completers.
bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.reason_why: Topiramate's effects on glutamatergic/GABAergic neurotransmission and appetite-regulating circuits are hypothesised to reduce binge-eating drive; it is also weight-reducing, a real clinically relevant advantage in BED given the disorder's frequent association with obesity.
bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.important_caveat: Not FDA-approved for BED (off-label use only); real, clinically limiting side effects include cognitive slowing/word-finding difficulty, paresthesias, and teratogenicity risk, which is why it is positioned as a second-line option for CBT/lisdexamfetamine non-responders rather than first-line.
bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.real_working_solution: Topiramate as a real, evidence-based off-label second-line option when CBT and lisdexamfetamine have failed, are contraindicated, or when significant comorbid obesity makes its weight-reducing property additionally valuable.
bed_topiramate_second_line_offlabel.source: McElroy SL, Arnold LM, Shapira NA, Keck PE Jr, Rosenthal NR, Karim MR, Kamin M, Hudson JI. Am J Psychiatry 2003;160(2):255-261 (PMID 12562571)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from different outcome definitions (categorical recovery, remission, binge-eating cessation, or symptom-frequency reduction) and different trials/populations, so this is not one single standardized head-to-head league table -- each number is real and independently sourced from a named PMID. Row 2's 96.3% is a derived figure (100% minus the trial's reported 3.7% relapse rate) applying only to the subgroup who already responded during a 12-week open-label lead-in, not to all-comers -- it is not directly comparable to the acute-phase cessation rates in rows 1, 4, 6, and 8. Row 9 (fluoxetine, 29%) is the SAME 108-patient Grilo 2005 trial as row 4's CBT figure and is included specifically as a real, honest negative finding: fluoxetine monotherapy did not separate from placebo (30%) in this trial, unlike CBT (73%) -- it is not a treatment recommendation, included for the same reason the bulimia_nervosa entry in this knowledge base flags bupropion: honesty about what the real evidence shows, including what does NOT work as monotherapy.

nonspecific_low_back_pain.name: Non-Specific Low Back Pain
nonspecific_low_back_pain.icd11_hint: ICD-10 M54.5 Low back pain (legacy code; ICD-10-CM retired this in 2021 in favor of M54.50/M54.51/M54.59). The exact ICD-11 code (expected under chapter FA, Diseases of the musculoskeletal system - likely ME84.2 Low back pain) could NOT be independently verified this session: the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) requires client-side JavaScript rendering not accessible to this session's fetch tool, and the WHO ICD-11 API requires an OAuth2 token that was not available. FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED pending direct confirmation against the WHO ICD-11 API/browser.
nonspecific_low_back_pain.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: 'Non-specific low back pain' (NSLBP) is, by definition, low back pain with NO identifiable specific spinal pathology and NO red flags - if any of the following are present, the case is NOT non-specific and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely, directing the patient to immediate real-world emergency-department evaluation (call emergency services / go to the nearest emergency department NOW for emergency MRI and, if confirmed, urgent surgical/specialist referral), never a routine consultation flow: (1) cauda equina syndrome red flags - saddle/perineal-perianal anesthesia, new bladder dysfunction (retention, loss of urgency, or incontinence), new bowel incontinence or loss of anal tone, new sexual dysfunction, or bilateral leg pain/weakness/sciatica (Gardner A, Gardner E, Morley T, 'Cauda equina syndrome: a review of the current clinical and medico-legal position', Eur Spine J 2011;20(5):690-697, PMID 21193933 - a time-critical neurosurgical emergency where diagnostic/treatment delay is associated with permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, and motor deficits); (2) progressive or severe neurological deficit (worsening motor weakness, foot drop, progressive sensory loss); (3) red flags for spinal fracture (significant trauma, prolonged corticosteroid use, older age with minor trauma, contusion/abrasion at the site) or malignancy/infection (history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, night pain unrelieved by rest, age >50 with new-onset pain) - per Downie A et al., 'Red flags to screen for malignancy and fracture in patients with low back pain: systematic review', BMJ 2013;347:f7095 (PMID 24335669), which found the presence of multiple concurrent red flags raised post-test probability of fracture to 90% (95% CI 34-99%). Any of these findings reclassifies the presentation away from this entry (nonspecific_low_back_pain) toward the relevant specific-pathology work-up and urgent care pathway, not routine conservative management.

duration_based_staging.finding: Low back pain is staged by duration of the current episode: acute (less than 6 weeks), subacute (6 to 12 weeks), and chronic (12 weeks/3 months or longer). This duration-based staging is used because prognosis and recommended management differ substantially by stage - acute episodes have the highest spontaneous-improvement rate, while chronic pain behaves as a distinct, more persistent condition.
duration_based_staging.source: Chou R, Qaseem A, Snow V, et al., 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Low Back Pain: A Joint Clinical Practice Guideline from the American College of Physicians and the American Pain Society', Ann Intern Med 2007;147(7):478-491 (PMID 17909209); Qaseem A, Wilt TJ, McLean RM, Forciea MA, 'Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians', Ann Intern Med 2017;166(7):514-530 (PMID 28192789)

nonspecific_vs_specific_causes.finding: The ACP/APS 2007 guideline recommends that clinicians place every low-back-pain patient, based on history and examination alone, into one of three categories: (1) nonspecific low back pain, (2) back pain potentially associated with radiculopathy or spinal stenosis, or (3) back pain potentially associated with another specific spinal cause (e.g. vertebral compression fracture, cauda equina syndrome, spinal infection, malignancy, ankylosing spondylitis). Nonspecific low back pain (this entry) is a diagnosis of exclusion within that framework - it explicitly excludes the structural/mechanical causes with identifiable pathology covered elsewhere in this knowledge base (lumbar_spondylosis - degenerative facet/disc changes with imaging correlate; herniated_intervertebral_disc - disc material impinging a nerve root; spondylolisthesis - vertebral slippage), and excludes true radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, and the specific-cause 'red flag' conditions.
nonspecific_vs_specific_causes.source: Chou R et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;147(7):478-491 (PMID 17909209)

mechanical_axial_pain_pattern.finding: The core presentation is axial pain localized to the lumbosacral region (with or without nonspecific radiation into the buttock or proximal thigh), that varies with posture, movement, and activity level - typically worsened by prolonged sitting/standing or specific movements and eased by rest or position change - without a consistent dermatomal pattern. This mechanical/postural variability, in the absence of a fixed dermatomal leg-pain pattern, is what distinguishes 'mechanical' nonspecific pain from radicular pain.
mechanical_axial_pain_pattern.source: Deyo RA, Weinstein JN, 'Low back pain', N Engl J Med 2001;344(5):363-370 (PMID 11172169)

absence_of_radiculopathy_and_red_flags.finding: By definition, nonspecific low back pain presents WITHOUT: (a) radicular features - no dermatomal leg pain extending below the knee, no myotomal weakness, no reflex loss, and a negative straight-leg-raise test; and (b) red flags for serious specific pathology - no fever, unexplained weight loss, history of malignancy, IV drug use or immunosuppression, significant trauma, prolonged corticosteroid use, or age-related fracture risk factors, and no saddle anesthesia or new bladder/bowel dysfunction (which would instead trigger the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above). Presence of any of these features moves the patient out of the 'nonspecific' category into a specific-pathology work-up.
absence_of_radiculopathy_and_red_flags.source: Downie A et al., BMJ 2013;347:f7095 (PMID 24335669); Chou R et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;147(7):478-491 (PMID 17909209)

clinical_diagnosis_of_exclusion.finding: There is no laboratory or imaging test that positively confirms 'nonspecific low back pain' - it is a clinical diagnosis reached by excluding radiculopathy/stenosis and specific spinal pathology through a focused history and physical examination (including a red-flag screen and basic neurological exam), per the ACP/APS 2007 diagnostic triage approach.
clinical_diagnosis_of_exclusion.source: Chou R et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;147(7):478-491 (PMID 17909209)

limited_accuracy_of_individual_red_flags.finding: A systematic review of 14 studies evaluating 53 individual red flags for fracture or malignancy found that most provide little to no useful change in probability when used alone. For fracture, the red flags with the highest post-test probability were prolonged corticosteroid use (33%, 95% CI 10-67%), severe trauma (11%, 8-16%), older age (9%, 3-25%), and presence of a contusion/abrasion (62%, 49-74%); probability rose to 90% (95% CI 34-99%) when multiple red flags were present together. For malignancy, history of malignancy carried the highest post-test probability (33%, 95% CI 22-46%). The review's conclusion was that many red flags endorsed in guidelines are poorly evidenced in isolation and current guidelines need revision - i.e. red-flag screening should combine multiple findings and clinical judgment rather than relying on any single flag.
limited_accuracy_of_individual_red_flags.source: Downie A et al., 'Red flags to screen for malignancy and fracture in patients with low back pain: systematic review', BMJ 2013;347:f7095 (PMID 24335669)

when_imaging_is_and_isnt_indicated.finding: Both the ACP/APS 2007 and ACP 2017 guidelines recommend AGAINST routine imaging (plain x-ray, CT, or MRI) for patients presenting with acute, subacute, or chronic nonspecific low back pain, because imaging findings (disc degeneration, bulges, facet arthropathy) are common in asymptomatic people and correlate poorly with symptoms, and routine imaging does not improve outcomes. Imaging IS indicated only when severe or progressive neurological deficits are present, or when the history/exam raises red flags suggesting a specific underlying cause (suspected fracture, infection, malignancy, or cauda equina syndrome, the last requiring emergency MRI per the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above) or when a patient with radiculopathy is being considered for surgery or epidural injection.
when_imaging_is_and_isnt_indicated.source: Chou R et al., Ann Intern Med 2007;147(7):478-491 (PMID 17909209); Qaseem A et al., Ann Intern Med 2017;166(7):514-530 (PMID 28192789)

rapid_early_improvement.finding: A systematic review of 15 cohort studies found that people with acute low back pain typically improve rapidly: mean pain scores fell by 58% of initial values, disability fell by 58%, and 82% of those initially off work had returned to work within one month of onset. Further improvement continued until about three months, after which pain, disability, and return-to-work levels remained nearly constant. This rapid-improvement pattern is the genuinely favorable, well-evidenced real-world prognosis for the great majority of acute nonspecific low back pain episodes managed conservatively (staying active rather than bed rest).
rapid_early_improvement.source: Pengel LH, Herbert RD, Maher CG, Refshauge KM, 'Acute low back pain: systematic review of its prognosis', BMJ 2003;327(7410):323 (PMID 12907487)

population_level_pain_trajectory.finding: A meta-analysis of 33 inception cohorts (11,166 participants) pooled the trajectory of pain (0-100 scale) after onset of acute low back pain: mean score 52 (95% CI 48-57) at baseline, falling to 23 (95% CI 21-25) at 6 weeks, 12 (95% CI 9-15) at 26 weeks, and 6 (95% CI 3-10) at 52 weeks - confirming substantial, sustained improvement over the first year for cohorts presenting with acute pain, with the steepest drop in the first 6 weeks.
population_level_pain_trajectory.source: da C Menezes Costa L, Maher CG, Hancock MJ, McAuley JH, Herbert RD, Costa LO, 'The prognosis of acute and persistent low-back pain: a meta-analysis', CMAJ 2012;184(11):E613-624 (PMID 22586331)

resolution_is_rapid_but_not_universally_.finding: A review of 36 studies following general low-back-pain patient populations for at least 12 months found that the widely repeated claim that '90% of low back pain episodes resolve within 1 month' is not well supported by the underlying literature: on average 62% of patients (range 42-75% across studies) still reported some pain at the 12-month mark. This does not contradict the rapid drop in pain intensity/disability seen in the first weeks (above) - most people become substantially better and functional quickly - but full, permanent symptom-free resolution after a single acute episode is less universal than the commonly cited figure suggests, and low back pain often behaves as a recurrent/fluctuating condition rather than a one-off illness that fully resolves.
resolution_is_rapid_but_not_universally_.source: Hestbaek L, Leboeuf-Yde C, Manniche C, 'Low back pain: what is the long-term course? A review of studies of general patient populations', Eur Spine J 2003;12(2):149-165 (PMID 12709853)

recurrence_risk.finding: Recurrence is common after an apparently resolved episode: the Pengel et al. systematic review found 73% of patients had at least one recurrence within 12 months. A dedicated systematic review of recurrence risk (8 studies) found the evidence base is limited - only one study met inception-cohort quality standards, reporting a 33% one-year recurrence proportion - but consistently identified a prior history of low back pain episodes as the strongest predictor of future recurrence.
recurrence_risk.source: Pengel LH et al., BMJ 2003;327(7410):323 (PMID 12907487); da Silva T, Mills K, Brown BT, Herbert RD, Maher CG, Hancock MJ, 'Risk of Recurrence of Low Back Pain: A Systematic Review', J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2017;47(5):305-313 (PMID 28355981)

nonspecific_low_back_pain.CURABILITY_NOTE: Non-specific low back pain (NSLBP - low back pain with no identifiable specific spinal pathology, i.e. no fracture, malignancy, infection, cauda equina, or confirmed radiculopathy/stenosis) is NOT 'curable' by a single pill or procedure because, by definition, there is usually no single structural lesion to remove - but REAL trial data show the great majority of acute episodes resolve to a large degree with simple, low-cost conservative management. Malmivaara A et al. randomised employees with acute, nonspecific low back pain to bed rest, back-mobilising exercises, or continuing ordinary activities as tolerated, and found continuing ordinary activities gave significantly faster recovery on pain, disability, and days off work than either bed rest or exercises, with bed rest the slowest ('The Treatment of Acute Low Back Pain - Bed Rest, Exercises, or Ordinary Activity?', N Engl J Med 1995;332:351-355, PMID 7823996). A systematic review of 15 prognosis studies found rapid improvement under this kind of conservative (staying-active-based) management: pain fell by a mean of 58% and disability by 58% within one month, and 82% of patients initially off work had returned within a month (Pengel LH et al., 'Acute low back pain: systematic review of its prognosis', BMJ 2003;327:323, PMID 12907487) - though 73% had at least one recurrence within 12 months, and a widely cited clinical review states roughly 90% of episodes resolve within about 6 weeks regardless of specific treatment (Deyo RA, Weinstein JN, 'Low Back Pain', N Engl J Med 2001;344:363-370, PMID 11172169).
