Long-term durability is real and documented: in a 3-to-6-year follow-up of PCIT completers originally treated for ODD (Hood KK, Eyberg SM, J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 2003;32(3):419-429, PMID 12881030; 23 of 50 original completers located and reassessed), mothers reported the significant post-treatment behavioral and parenting gains were maintained years later, with disruptive behavior continuing to decrease over time since treatment. Quantitatively, the largest and most recent meta-analysis of psychosocial treatment for early disruptive behavior (Comer JS, Chow C, Chan PT, Cooper-Vince C, Wilson LA, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2013;52(1):26-36, PMID 23265631; 36 controlled trials, 3,042 children, mean age 4.7y) found a large overall effect (Hedges' g=0.82), with behavioral treatments specifically producing the largest effects (g=0.88), and problems of oppositionality/noncompliance -- the core ODD symptom domain -- showing a large effect of g=0.76 versus a smaller g=0.61 for impulsivity/hyperactivity, i.e. ODD's own core symptoms respond especially well to these treatments relative to comorbid ADHD-type symptoms. A Cochrane systematic review (Furlong M, McGilloway S, Bywater T, Hutchings J, Smith SM, Donnelly M, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008225, PMID 22336837; 13 trials, 1,078 participants) confirmed statistically significant, real reductions in child conduct problems for behavioral/CBT group-based parenting programs both by parent report (SMD -0.53, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.34) and independent assessment (SMD -0.44, 95% CI -0.77 to -0.11), plus significant improvements in parental mental health and positive parenting and significant reductions in harsh/negative parenting -- and found the intervention cost-effective at approximately $2,500/family (GBP 1,712/EUR 2,217) to bring an average child with clinical-level conduct problems into the non-clinical range. A head-to-head meta-analysis of PCIT versus Triple P (Thomas R, Zimmer-Gembeck MJ, J Abnorm Child Psychol 2007;35(3):475-495, PMID 17333363; 24 studies) found PCIT's effect sizes were large for parent-reported child and parent behavior (moderate only for the abbreviated variant), and PCIT was one of only two programs shown to improve independently OBSERVED child behavior, not just parent-reported behavior -- an important real methodological strength since parent-report alone can be biased by the same parents who delivered/rated the intervention. Real, honest feature of this evidence base: none of these verified primary trials report a single clean categorical 'percent achieved full diagnostic remission of ODD' figure in their published abstracts/results summaries (unlike, e.g., the MTA's SNAP-IV-based success-rate percentages used for ADHD) -- the field's standard outcome metric for PMT/PCIT trials is a continuous standardized mean difference/effect size on validated behavior rating scales (ECBI, CBCL, SNAP) or a categorical 'moved into normal range' comparison, not a diagnostic-cutoff responder percentage -- so this KB reports the real, large, replicated effect sizes above rather than inventing a percentage figure that does not exist in the verified primary sources. Medication has NO FDA-approved indication for ODD itself; it is only real and evidence-based when targeting a specific comorbid condition -- most commonly comorbid ADHD, where stimulant medication (methylphenidate/amphetamine) combined with behavioral treatment achieved a real, replicated 68% success rate in the NIMH MTA trial (Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001;40(2):168-179, PMID 11211365) and importantly also produced added benefit specifically on oppositional/aggressive symptoms beyond what medication management alone achieved (MTA Cooperative Group, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(12):1073-1086, PMID 10591283). Overall real picture: ODD is a genuinely high-treatability childhood disorder when PMT or PCIT is delivered -- large, replicated, guideline-endorsed effects on the exact core symptom domain, durable to 3-6 years, real even in abbreviated/resource-lean formats -- making early psychosocial treatment (not medication) the correct, real, first-line answer for ODD itself.

curative_option.name: Parent Management Training (PMT) and Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) -- Real Best-Evidence Psychosocial Treatments, Large and Durable Effects on Core ODD Symptoms
curative_option.note: No drug or procedure cures ODD; PMT/PCIT are the real, AACAP-guideline-endorsed, first-line treatments with the largest and most consistent evidence base specifically for the defiance/noncompliance/oppositionality symptom domain, with documented durability to 3-6 years.

real_recovery_data.meta_analytic_effect_oppositionality_non: Hedges' g = 0.76 (large effect) specifically for problems of oppositionality and noncompliance, pooled across 36 controlled trials, N=3,042 children, mean age 4.7y
real_recovery_data.meta_analytic_effect_behavioral_treatmen: Hedges' g = 0.88 for behavioral treatments specifically (largest of all psychosocial treatment types studied), g = 1.17 vs treatment-as-usual comparisons
real_recovery_data.cochrane_parent_rated_conduct_problems: SMD -0.53 (95% CI -0.72 to -0.34), 13 trials, N=1,078 participants
real_recovery_data.pcit_long_term_maintenance: Gains maintained 3-6 years post-treatment in mothers' reports (23 of 50 original ODD-diagnosed PCIT completers located and reassessed)
real_recovery_data.kazdin_combined_pmt_psst_rct: Combined PMT+PSST placed a significantly greater proportion of children (N=97, ages 7-13) within the normal/nonclinic range of functioning than either single treatment, at posttreatment and 1-year follow-up
real_recovery_data.cohorts: Comer 2013 meta-analysis: 36 RCTs, 3,042 children; Furlong 2012 Cochrane review: 13 trials, 1,078 participants; Kazdin 1992 RCT: 97 children ages 7-13; Nixon 2003 RCT: 54 ODD preschoolers + 21 nonclinical comparison; Hood & Eyberg 2003 follow-up: 23 of 50 original PCIT completers

curative_option.source: Comer JS et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2013;52(1):26-36 (PMID 23265631); Furlong M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008225 (PMID 22336837); Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747 (PMID 1401389); Nixon RD et al, J Consult Clin Psychol 2003;71(2):251-260 (PMID 12699020); Hood KK, Eyberg SM, J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 2003;32(3):419-429 (PMID 12881030); Steiner H, Remsing L, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2007;46(1):126-141 (PMID 17195736)
curative_option.confidence: high for the pooled effect sizes (large multi-trial meta-analyses and a Cochrane systematic review, plus ODD-specific RCTs); no single categorical diagnostic-remission percentage exists in the verified primary literature for PMT/PCIT specifically -- see CURABILITY_NOTE for why.

odd_parent_management_training.name: Parent Management Training (PMT) -- Real RCT and Meta-Analytic Data
odd_parent_management_training.type: First-line psychosocial treatment; behavioral parent-training in individual or group family sessions, guideline-recommended per AACAP practice parameter
specific_interventions: Behavioral parent management training (contingency management, differential attention, effective commands, token/point systems)
odd_parent_management_training.effectiveness: Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D (J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747, PMID 1401389), a randomized trial in 97 children aged 7-13 referred for severe antisocial/oppositional behavior, found PMT (alone and combined with problem-solving skills training) produced significant improvement in child functioning at posttreatment and 1-year follow-up, with PMT+PSST combined placing a significantly greater proportion of children within the normal (nonclinic) range than PMT alone. A Cochrane systematic review of behavioral/CBT group-based parenting programs (Furlong M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008225, PMID 22336837; 13 trials, N=1,078) found statistically significant reductions in child conduct problems by parent report (SMD -0.53, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.34) and independent assessment (SMD -0.44, 95% CI -0.77 to -0.11).
odd_parent_management_training.reason_why: PMT retrains the parent-child interaction contingencies that reinforce defiant/noncompliant behavior -- teaching parents to consistently reward compliance and prosocial behavior and to apply calm, predictable, non-coercive consequences for defiance -- directly targeting the coercive parent-child cycle that maintains ODD symptoms.
odd_parent_management_training.important_caveat: Primary PMT trials report outcomes as standardized mean differences/effect sizes on validated rating scales (CBCL, ECBI) or categorical 'moved into normal range' comparisons, not a single diagnostic-remission percentage, so no effectiveness_pct figure can be honestly assigned from the verified primary sources (see CURABILITY_NOTE).
odd_parent_management_training.real_working_solution: PMT is a real, AACAP-guideline-endorsed, first-line, medication-free treatment for ODD with a large, replicated randomized-trial and Cochrane-review evidence base showing significant, durable reductions in the core defiant/noncompliant behaviors that define the disorder.
odd_parent_management_training.source: Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747 (PMID 1401389); Kazdin AE, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997;36(10):1349-1356 (PMID 9334547); Furlong M et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008225 (PMID 22336837); Steiner H, Remsing L, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2007;46(1):126-141 (PMID 17195736)

odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.name: Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) -- Real RCT and Long-Term Maintenance Data, ODD-Specific
odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.type: First-line, live-coached dyadic behavioral therapy for preschool/young-school-age children, developed and validated specifically in ODD/conduct-problem populations
specific_interventions: Child-Directed Interaction (CDI) phase -- differential attention/positive reinforcement skills coaching
Parent-Directed Interaction (PDI) phase -- effective, consistent command-and-consequence skills coaching, delivered live in-session via earpiece
odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.effectiveness: Eyberg SM, Boggs SR, Algina J (Psychopharmacol Bull 1995;31(1):83-91, PMID 7675994) established the original PCIT treatment model and outcome measures for preschool conduct-problem behavior. In a randomized trial of 64 families of preschoolers specifically diagnosed with ODD (Schuhmann EM et al, J Clin Child Psychol 1998;27(1):34-45, PMID 9561935), the immediate-treatment group showed statistically and clinically significant improvement in child behavior and parenting versus waitlist, with gains maintained at 4-month follow-up. A second randomized trial in ODD preschoolers (Nixon RD et al, J Consult Clin Psychol 2003;71(2):251-260, PMID 12699020; N=54 clinical, 21 nonclinical comparison) found standard 12-session PCIT produced a superior clinically significant effect immediately post-treatment, with an abbreviated format converging to comparable gains by 6-month follow-up. Long-term durability was confirmed 3 to 6 years after treatment (Hood KK, Eyberg SM, J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 2003;32(3):419-429, PMID 12881030): mothers of originally ODD-diagnosed children reported the post-treatment gains were maintained years later. A meta-analysis comparing parenting programs (Thomas R, Zimmer-Gembeck MJ, J Abnorm Child Psychol 2007;35(3):475-495, PMID 17333363; 24 studies) found PCIT had large effect sizes on parent-reported outcomes and was one of only two programs shown to improve independently observed (not just parent-reported) child behavior.
odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.reason_why: PCIT directly restructures the real-time parent-child interaction via live coaching (therapist observing through a one-way mirror/earpiece), first strengthening the parent-child relationship and attention/reward contingencies (CDI), then teaching consistent, calm, predictable limit-setting for noncompliance (PDI) -- addressing both the relational and behavioral-contingency mechanisms that maintain oppositional/defiant behavior in vivo, not just in a therapist's office.
odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.important_caveat: As with PMT, the verified PCIT RCTs report continuous clinical-significance/effect-size outcomes (ECBI Intensity/Problem scores, CBCL) rather than a single categorical diagnostic-remission percentage in their published abstracts, so no effectiveness_pct is force-fit here; PCIT also requires an intensive, live-coached format (typically 12-20 weekly sessions) that is real but resource-intensive, though the abbreviated/telehealth-assisted format (Nixon et al, PMID 12699020) converges to comparable 6-month outcomes in the real trial.
odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.real_working_solution: PCIT is a real, evidence-based, first-line treatment developed and validated specifically for ODD in young children, with real randomized-trial evidence of statistically and clinically significant improvement, durability to 3-6 years, and effectiveness even in an abbreviated delivery format.
odd_parent_child_interaction_therapy.source: Eyberg SM, Boggs SR, Algina J, Psychopharmacol Bull 1995;31(1):83-91 (PMID 7675994); Schuhmann EM et al, J Clin Child Psychol 1998;27(1):34-45 (PMID 9561935); Nixon RD et al, J Consult Clin Psychol 2003;71(2):251-260 (PMID 12699020); Hood KK, Eyberg SM, J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 2003;32(3):419-429 (PMID 12881030); Thomas R, Zimmer-Gembeck MJ, J Abnorm Child Psychol 2007;35(3):475-495 (PMID 17333363)

odd_problem_solving_skills_training.name: Problem-Solving Skills Training (PSST) -- Real RCT Data, Alone and Combined with PMT
odd_problem_solving_skills_training.type: Child-directed cognitive-behavioral treatment targeting social-cognitive problem-solving deficits; typically combined with PMT for older children/adolescents with more severe oppositional-aggressive behavior
specific_interventions: Structured, in-vivo social-cognitive problem-solving skills training sessions with the child (identifying problems, generating alternative solutions, considering consequences, self-evaluation)
odd_problem_solving_skills_training.effectiveness: Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D (J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747, PMID 1401389; N=97, ages 7-13, randomized to PSST alone, PMT alone, or PSST+PMT combined) found each treatment improved child functioning at posttreatment and 1-year follow-up, with PSST+PMT combined producing the most marked, pervasive, and durable changes in both child and parent functioning and placing a significantly greater proportion of children within the normal range than either single treatment.
odd_problem_solving_skills_training.reason_why: PSST targets the child's own social-cognitive processing deficits (hostile attribution bias, impulsive/aggressive response selection) that drive defiant and aggressive reactions to perceived provocation, complementing PMT's parent-side contingency-management approach rather than duplicating it -- the real, mechanistic reason the combination outperforms either treatment alone.
odd_problem_solving_skills_training.important_caveat: PSST is real and evidence-based mainly as an adjunct to PMT rather than a freestanding first-line ODD treatment, and (as above) the pivotal trial reports categorical 'proportion within normal range' comparisons rather than a single extractable diagnostic-remission percentage in its published abstract.
odd_problem_solving_skills_training.real_working_solution: PSST, combined with PMT, is a real, randomized-trial-validated approach producing the most marked and durable improvement of the combinations tested, particularly relevant for older children/adolescents with ODD and comorbid aggressive/antisocial features.
odd_problem_solving_skills_training.source: Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747 (PMID 1401389)

odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.name: Medication for Comorbid ADHD/Aggression -- Real, Symptom-Targeted Only, No FDA-Approved Drug for ODD Itself
odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.type: Pharmacotherapy, adjunctive/symptom-targeted only -- never a standalone or first-line ODD treatment
specific_drugs: Stimulant medication for comorbid ADHD: Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta/OROS methylphenidate); Amphetamine-based stimulants (Lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse, mixed amphetamine salts/Adderall)
Atomoxetine (Strattera) as non-stimulant alternative for comorbid ADHD
Alpha-2 agonists (Guanfacine extended-release/Intuniv, Clonidine extended-release/Kapvay) sometimes used off-label/adjunctively for severe irritability/aggression
odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.effectiveness: No medication has an FDA-approved indication for ODD itself. The AACAP ODD Practice Parameter (Steiner H, Remsing L, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2007;46(1):126-141, PMID 17195736) places medication within a multimodal plan mainly for comorbid conditions. Where ODD coexists with ADHD (a very common comorbidity), treating the ADHD directly and reliably improves oppositional/aggressive symptoms as a real secondary benefit: the NIMH MTA trial found combined stimulant medication + intensive behavioral treatment achieved a 68% real composite success rate (SNAP-IV) at 14 months versus 56% for medication alone, 34% for behavioral treatment alone, and 25% for community care (Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001;40(2):168-179, PMID 11211365), and the original MTA trial specifically reported added benefit of combined treatment on oppositional/aggressive symptoms beyond medication management alone (MTA Cooperative Group, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(12):1073-1086, PMID 10591283).
odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.reason_why: Stimulants and atomoxetine improve dopaminergic/noradrenergic prefrontal-striatal function underlying the inattention/impulsivity of comorbid ADHD; reducing impulsivity secondarily reduces the frequency of impulsive oppositional/defiant reactions -- a real, indirect (not ODD-specific) mechanism, since the medication is treating the comorbid ADHD, not the oppositional-defiant symptom pattern itself.
odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.important_caveat: This is real, symptom-targeted, comorbidity-driven pharmacotherapy only -- it must never be presented or used as a standalone or first-line treatment for ODD itself, since no RCT establishes a medication effect on core ODD symptoms in the absence of a treatable comorbidity, and the AACAP guideline places psychosocial treatment (PMT/PCIT) ahead of medication in the real, guideline-recommended treatment sequence for ODD.
odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.real_working_solution: When ODD coexists with ADHD, treating the ADHD with guideline-recommended medication (alone, and best combined with behavioral treatment) produces a real 56-68% MTA success rate and a real, documented secondary reduction in oppositional/aggressive symptoms -- but this treats the comorbidity, not ODD itself, and is never a substitute for PMT/PCIT.
odd_medication_comorbid_adhd_aggression.source: Steiner H, Remsing L, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2007;46(1):126-141 (PMID 17195736); Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001;40(2):168-179 (PMID 11211365); MTA Cooperative Group, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(12):1073-1086 (PMID 10591283)

odd_school_based_intervention.name: School-Based / Teacher-Partnered Behavioral Intervention -- Real RCT Data
odd_school_based_intervention.type: Real, evidence-based adjunct/generalization-focused intervention delivered via teacher training and classroom behavioral programs, often paired with parent training
specific_interventions: Teacher classroom-management training (praise/attention contingencies, consistent limit-setting)
Combined parent + teacher training partnership programs (e.g. Incredible Years Parent-Teacher partnership, Head Start-based delivery)
odd_school_based_intervention.effectiveness: Webster-Stratton C, Reid J, Hammond M (J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2001;42(7):943-952, PMID 11693589; N=99 children aged 4-8 with early-onset conduct problems) found children receiving the Incredible Years Dinosaur Social Skills and Problem-Solving child-training curriculum showed significantly more clinically significant improvement in aggressive/noncompliant behavior (parent report, teacher report, and independent observation) versus waitlist control, maintained at 1-year follow-up. In a real prevention-level trial (Webster-Stratton C, Reid MJ, Hammond M, J Clin Child Psychol 2001;30(3):283-302, PMID 11501247; 272 Head Start mothers/children, 61 teachers), a combined parent-and-teacher training program produced significantly fewer conduct problems at school, with the highest-risk children showing the largest clinically significant reductions, maintained at 1-year follow-up.
odd_school_based_intervention.reason_why: Since ODD symptoms are defined partly by cross-setting impairment (home and school), extending consistent behavioral contingency management into the classroom (via teacher training) and into peer/social-skill domains (via child-directed curricula) generalizes the same contingency-management/problem-solving mechanisms used in PMT/PCIT to the second real-world setting where defiant behavior occurs, rather than leaving school behavior unaddressed.
odd_school_based_intervention.important_caveat: School-based intervention is real and evidence-based as an adjunct/generalization strategy, not a substitute for individual PMT/PCIT when a child already meets full ODD diagnostic criteria; again, the primary trials report clinically-significant-change and observational outcome comparisons rather than an extractable single diagnostic-remission percentage.
odd_school_based_intervention.real_working_solution: Teacher-partnered and classroom-based behavioral/social-skills programs are a real, RCT-validated way to generalize ODD treatment gains to school, with documented clinically significant, durable improvement in the cross-setting defiant/aggressive behavior that the ODD diagnosis specifically requires.
odd_school_based_intervention.source: Webster-Stratton C, Reid J, Hammond M, J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2001;42(7):943-952 (PMID 11693589); Webster-Stratton C, Reid MJ, Hammond M, J Clin Child Psychol 2001;30(3):283-302 (PMID 11501247)
odd_school_based_intervention.confidence: moderate-high -- real RCT/prevention-trial data, but for early-onset conduct problems broadly rather than formally-diagnosed-ODD samples specifically

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Unlike ADHD's MTA/Newcorn trials, the core ODD-specific randomized trials of PMT and PCIT (Kazdin 1992, PMID 1401389; Schuhmann 1998, PMID 9561935; Nixon 2003, PMID 12699020) and the pooled meta-analyses/Cochrane review (Comer 2013, PMID 23265631; Furlong 2012, PMID 22336837) report outcomes as standardized mean differences/Hedges' effect sizes and categorical 'moved into normal range' comparisons, not as a single diagnostic-remission percentage extractable from their published abstracts/results -- so no fabricated effectiveness_pct is assigned to PMT, PCIT, PSST, or school-based intervention here. The only rows below with a real, verified effectiveness_pct are medication for comorbid ADHD (reusing this KB's own verified adhd entry data), which is symptom-targeted for the comorbidity only and never a substitute for PMT/PCIT as ODD's real first-line treatment. The real, verified effect sizes for the psychosocial treatments are: oppositionality/noncompliance meta-analytic effect Hedges' g=0.76 (Comer 2013, PMID 23265631, 36 RCTs, N=3,042); Cochrane parent-rated conduct-problem SMD -0.53, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.34 (Furlong 2012, PMID 22336837, 13 trials, N=1,078); PMT+PSST combined qualitatively superior to either alone at 1-year follow-up (Kazdin 1992, PMID 1401389, N=97) -- see exhaustive_medicine_survey and CURABILITY_NOTE for full real data and sources.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combined Stimulant Medication + Behavioral Treatment for comorbid ADHD (MTA) -- symptom-targeted only, not an ODD-specific treatment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Composite SNAP-IV parent+teacher success rate at 14-month end of treatment, in children with ADHD (with or without comorbid ODD)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001 (PMID 11211365)

ranked_high_to_low.name: MTA Medication Management alone for comorbid ADHD -- symptom-targeted only
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Composite SNAP-IV parent+teacher success rate at 14-month end of treatment
ranked_high_to_low.source: Swanson JM et al, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2001 (PMID 11211365)

dissociative_identity_disorder.name: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID)
dissociative_identity_disorder.icd11_hint: ICD-11 (WHO) lists dissociative identity disorder as the diagnosis that replaces the older 'multiple personality disorder' category, per Roepke S, Priebe K, Schmahl C, Kleim B, Rosner R, Ehring T, 'Dissociative Identity Disorder and Partial Dissociative Identity Disorder', Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225 (PMID 41711447): 'The diagnosis dissociative identity disorder (DID) replaces multiple personality disorder in the ICD-11.' The exact WHO ICD-11 alphanumeric code could not be independently verified against a citing peer-reviewed source within this session (the WHO ICD-11 browser is a JS-rendered app that could not be directly scraped, the same limitation flagged for other entries in this KB, e.g. specific_phobia/PTSD icd11_hint) -- this hint is limited to the verified naming/replacement fact rather than a guessed code number.
dissociative_identity_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TWO real emergency patterns override routine symptom intake for suspected dissociative identity disorder (DID). (1) SUICIDE AND SELF-HARM RISK: in a series of 236 clinician-reported cases of multiple personality disorder (the prior name for DID) collected from 203 clinicians across North America, 72% of patients had attempted suicide at least once (Ross CA, Norton GR, 'Suicide and parasuicide in multiple personality disorder', Psychiatry 1989;52(3):365-71, PMID 2772094). In a separate naturalistic study of 221 dissociative disorder patients (including DID), dissociation severity and depression severity each independently and accurately classified patients into nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) and suicide-attempt groups, meaning that current dissociative symptom intensity itself is a real, measurable marker of near-term self-harm and suicide risk, not just a background feature (Webermann AR, Myrick AC, Taylor CL, Chasson GS, Brand BL, 'Dissociative, depressive, and PTSD symptom severity as correlates of nonsuicidal self-injury and suicidality in dissociative disorder patients', J Trauma Dissociation 2016;17(1):67-80, PMID 26211678). (2) DISSOCIATIVE CRISIS / FUGUE-LIKE STATE: DID is characterized by two or more distinct personality states, typically accompanied by amnesia from one state to another, with marked discontinuities in the experience of self and in the ability to take charge of one's own actions (Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026, PMID 41711447); the disorder's dissociative phenomenology also includes depersonalization and trance-like phenomena (Dell PF, 'Dissociative phenomenology of dissociative identity disorder', J Nerv Ment Dis 2002;190(1):10-5, PMID 11838024). CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: a patient found in an unfamiliar location or time period unable to account for a period of time (amnesic/fugue-like gap), or presenting mid-switch with loss of orientation and impaired control over their own actions, cannot reliably ensure their own safety during that episode and, combined with the high background rate of suicidality and self-harm in this population, must be routed immediately to emergency psychiatric evaluation (emergency services, crisis line, or ER) rather than continued through routine AI-assisted symptom intake or outpatient triage. Any patient reporting current suicidal ideation, a plan, or intent must likewise be routed immediately to emergency care.

dsm5_icd11_core_definition.finding: DID is defined by the presence of two or more distinct personality states (dissociative identities), typically accompanied by amnesia from one state to another; the personality states are associated with marked discontinuities in the experience of self and in the ability to take charge of one's own actions. In 'partial DID', these discontinuities are less marked (i.e. subjective identity fragmentation without full behavioural takeover by alternate states in all cases). ICD-11 uses this DID diagnosis in place of the older 'multiple personality disorder' label.
dsm5_icd11_core_definition.source: Roepke S, Priebe K, Schmahl C, Kleim B, Rosner R, Ehring T, 'Dissociative Identity Disorder and Partial Dissociative Identity Disorder', Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225 (narrative review), PMID 41711447

dissociation_as_a_unifactorial_taxon.finding: Administering the Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation (MID) to 34 DID patients, 23 dissociative-disorder-not-otherwise-specified (DDNOS) patients, 52 mixed-psychiatric-disorder patients and 58 normal controls, DID patients scored significantly higher than all three comparison groups on 27 distinct dissociation-related variables. Factor analysis of the MID's 11 dissociation dimensions extracted a single factor accounting for 85% of the variance, supporting the classification of dissociation (amnesia, depersonalization, 'hearing voices'/identity-alteration phenomena, trance, etc.) as one unified underlying clinical construct with multiple surface presentations, rather than several unrelated symptom clusters.
dissociation_as_a_unifactorial_taxon.source: Dell PF, 'Dissociative phenomenology of dissociative identity disorder', J Nerv Ment Dis 2002;190(1):10-5, PMID 11838024

diagnostic_validity_is_actively_conteste.finding: DID's classification is not settled science: a 2026 narrative review found a marked overlap between DID and other trauma-associated disorders, especially complex PTSD (cPTSD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD), and concluded that the available data 'tend not to support central constructs of DID', including the postulated amnesia between personality states, and that there is 'no robust evidence for the efficacy of any specific treatment'. This stands in contrast to an earlier etiological review that argued DID is an empirically robust, biopsychosocially grounded chronic disorder that cannot be explained away as iatrogenic, suggestible, malingered, or role-played. Both positions are from peer-reviewed sources and are recorded here rather than resolved, since presenting DID as either fully settled or fully debunked would misrepresent the real state of the evidence.
diagnostic_validity_is_actively_conteste.source: Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447; contrasted with Şar V, Dorahy MJ, Krüger C, 'Revisiting the etiological aspects of dissociative identity disorder: a biopsychosocial perspective', Psychol Res Behav Manag 2017;10:137-146, PMID 28496375
diagnostic_validity_is_actively_conteste.confidence: moderate (genuine, cited scientific controversy, not a KB gap)

identity_disruption_and_switching.finding: The hallmark clinical feature is disruption of identity: the presence of two or more distinct personality states, each associated with its own relatively enduring pattern of perceiving, relating to, and thinking about the environment and self, and marked discontinuities in the sense of self and personal agency (the felt experience of being in control of one's own actions, thoughts and body) when the person is in a given state or 'switches' between states.
identity_disruption_and_switching.source: Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447

interidentity_amnesia.finding: Amnesia from one personality state to another is typically part of the clinical picture, and has been theorised as arising from an enduring decoupling of psychological modes that creates separate senses of self, with metamemory processes implicated in interidentity amnesia. However, a 2026 review of the empirical literature found the available data 'tend not to support' this postulated amnesia between personality states as robustly as the classic clinical model assumes - so amnesia should be actively assessed in each case rather than simply presumed present.
interidentity_amnesia.source: Şar V, Dorahy MJ, Krüger C, Psychol Res Behav Manag 2017;10:137-146, PMID 28496375; controversy noted in Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026, PMID 41711447

real_trauma_history_association.finding: DID is described as a chronic post-traumatic disorder in which developmentally stressful events in childhood - including abuse, emotional neglect, disturbed attachment, and boundary violations - are central and typical etiological factors, with familial, societal and cultural factors able to shape the trauma and/or its expression. Neurobiological differences have also been demonstrated between dissociative identity states within DID patients and between DID patients and controls.
real_trauma_history_association.source: Şar V, Dorahy MJ, Krüger C, Psychol Res Behav Manag 2017;10:137-146, PMID 28496375
real_trauma_history_association.confidence: high (real, well-replicated association; exact causal mechanism still under study per the same source)

self_harm_and_suicidality_as_a_presentin.finding: Suicidal ideation and suicide attempts are among the most common presenting features of DID: in a 236-case North American clinician-reported series, 72% of patients had attempted suicide. In a separate 221-patient sample of dissociative disorder patients, higher current dissociation severity (and, separately, higher depression severity) accurately distinguished patients with recent nonsuicidal self-injury or suicide attempts from those without, i.e. dissociative symptom intensity itself tracks real-time self-harm risk.
self_harm_and_suicidality_as_a_presentin.source: Ross CA, Norton GR, Psychiatry 1989;52(3):365-71, PMID 2772094; Webermann AR et al, J Trauma Dissociation 2016;17(1):67-80, PMID 26211678

overlap_with_cptsd_and_borderline_person.finding: There is marked symptomatic overlap between DID and other trauma-associated disorders, in particular complex PTSD (cPTSD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) - both of which can independently produce dissociative symptoms, affective instability and identity disturbance - making careful differential assessment essential before assigning a DID diagnosis.
overlap_with_cptsd_and_borderline_person.source: Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447

structured_clinical_interview_scid_d_r.finding: The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Dissociative Disorders-Revised (SCID-D-R) is a validated structured interview with reported good-to-excellent reliability and validity across multiple countries; its documented clinical applications include psychological and forensic evaluation, treatment planning, differential diagnosis, and specifically the evaluation of possible malingering.
structured_clinical_interview_scid_d_r.source: Steinberg M, 'Advances in the clinical assessment of dissociation: the SCID-D-R', Bull Menninger Clin 2000;64(2):146-63, PMID 10842445

multidimensional_inventory_of_dissociati.finding: The Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation (MID) is a validated 218-item self-report instrument measuring 14 major facets of pathological dissociation via 23 diagnostic scales, designed for patients presenting with a mixture of dissociative, posttraumatic and borderline symptoms; it showed internal reliability, temporal stability, convergent, discriminant and construct validity, and predicted an additional 18% of variance in weighted childhood-abuse scores beyond the older Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES).
multidimensional_inventory_of_dissociati.source: Dell PF, 'The multidimensional inventory of dissociation (MID): A comprehensive measure of pathological dissociation', J Trauma Dissociation 2006;7(2):77-106, PMID 16769667

differentiating_from_other_conditions.finding: Because of the real overlap with cPTSD and BPD (both of which have validated, evidence-based treatments of their own), a 2026 review concluded that DID and partial DID 'should only be assigned if alternative explanations of the patient's clinical manifestations have been excluded' - i.e. DID is a diagnosis of careful exclusion, not a first-pass label for any patient with dissociative or identity-related complaints. Structured interviews (SCID-D-R) are explicitly validated for evaluating malingering as part of this differential process.
differentiating_from_other_conditions.source: Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447; Steinberg M, Bull Menninger Clin 2000;64(2):146-63, PMID 10842445

cross_disorder_discrimination_evidence.finding: An empirical overview concluded DID 'can be accurately discriminated from other disorders, especially when structured diagnostic interviews assess identity alterations and amnesia', reporting a general population prevalence of approximately 1%, with the highest prevalence found in emergency psychiatric settings - directly conflicting with the 2026 review's more skeptical conclusion on diagnostic validity above, and recorded here as the other side of the same genuine, unresolved debate.
cross_disorder_discrimination_evidence.source: Dorahy MJ, Brand BL, Sar V, Krüger C, Stavropoulos P, Martínez-Taboas A, Lewis-Fernández R, Middleton W, 'Dissociative identity disorder: An empirical overview', Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2014;48(5):402-17, PMID 24788904
cross_disorder_discrimination_evidence.confidence: moderate (conflicts with PMID 41711447 above; both retained rather than picking a side)

chronic_course.finding: DID is characterised in the etiological literature as a chronic post-traumatic disorder rooted in childhood developmental trauma, implying a persistent, typically long-standing course rather than an acute, self-limiting presentation.
chronic_course.source: Şar V, Dorahy MJ, Krüger C, Psychol Res Behav Manag 2017;10:137-146, PMID 28496375

research_base_is_small_and_concentrated.finding: A review of DID research published from 2011-2021 found 104 empirical studies and 56 case studies, yielding only about 1354 new DID cases in total (average sample size approximately 20 per study), with only 40% of reported cases being genuinely new (the rest were re-analyses of prior samples) and 74% of all new cases contributed by just six research groups worldwide, mostly in Western countries and especially the United States. The reviewer concluded research on DID is 'steady but methodologically limited in ways that make generalization, especially about etiology, difficult' - a real constraint on how confidently any natural-history or prevalence claim about DID can be generalised.
research_base_is_small_and_concentrated.source: Boysen GA, 'Dissociative Identity Disorder: A Review of Research From 2011 to 2021', J Nerv Ment Dis 2024;212(3):174-186, PMID 38412243
research_base_is_small_and_concentrated.confidence: high (about the state of the evidence itself)

high_background_suicide_and_self_harm_bu.finding: Untreated/real-world course data show a high real burden of self-directed harm: 72% lifetime suicide-attempt rate in a 236-case series, with dissociation and depression severity tracking who goes on to self-harm or attempt suicide within a given period - indicating the natural course of unmanaged DID carries substantial ongoing mortality/morbidity risk rather than being benign.
high_background_suicide_and_self_harm_bu.source: Ross CA, Norton GR, Psychiatry 1989;52(3):365-71, PMID 2772094; Webermann AR et al, J Trauma Dissociation 2016;17(1):67-80, PMID 26211678

prevalence_and_setting.finding: DID prevalence is estimated at approximately 1% of the general population, with the highest concentration found in emergency psychiatric settings, consistent with a disorder that frequently presents acutely (e.g. via self-harm, suicidality, or dissociative crisis) rather than being picked up incidentally in routine, non-psychiatric care.
prevalence_and_setting.source: Dorahy MJ et al, Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2014;48(5):402-17, PMID 24788904
prevalence_and_setting.confidence: moderate-high (prevalence estimates in DID are disputed given the methodological limitations noted above, PMID 38412243)

dissociative_identity_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a disorder where the real 2026 evidence base is genuinely split, and honest reporting requires stating both sides. On the positive side, the prospective, international, naturalistic Treatment of Patients with Dissociative Disorders (TOP DD) study, following DID/dissociative-disorder-not-otherwise-specified patients and their community clinicians over 30 months of ongoing outpatient treatment, found that reductions in dissociative symptoms over the study period were significantly associated with reductions in PTSD and general-distress severity (Brand BL, Stadnik R, J Trauma Dissociation 2013;14(3):328-341, PMID 23627481); that patients who improved over the 30 months had significantly fewer revictimization events and life stressors than those who worsened (Myrick AC, Brand BL, Putnam FW, J Trauma Dissociation 2013;14(4):375-389, PMID 23796170); that a stronger patient-rated therapeutic alliance predicted better outcome, with effect sizes stronger than typically seen in other patient groups (Cronin E, Brand BL, Mattanah JF, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2014;5:22676, PMID 24616755); and that longer engagement in specialized treatment was associated with real reductions in inpatient hospitalization days and outpatient service cost estimates over time (Myrick AC et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2017;8(1):1375829, PMID 29038681). A related randomized-design-informing TOP DD Network study of a structured web-based psychoeducational adjunct (skills for emotion regulation, safety planning, and symptom management, layered onto patients' ongoing individual therapy) found real reductions in dissociation and PTSD symptoms, improved emotion regulation, and reduced non-suicidal self-injury at 1- and 2-year follow-up in 111 DID/complex-DD patients, with overall-sample effect sizes Cohen's |d| = 0.44-0.90 (Cohen's U3 = 67.0%-81.6%, computed via the standard normal CDF from the paper's own reported effect sizes), and larger, faster gains in the subgroup with higher baseline dissociation, |d| = 0.54-1.04 (U3 = 70.5%-85.1%), versus |d| = 0.24-0.75 (U3 = 59.5%-77.3%) in the lower-baseline-dissociation subgroup (Brand BL et al, J Trauma Stress 2019;32(1):156-166, PMID 30698858). The field's consensus clinical guideline, the ISSTD 'Guidelines for Treating Dissociative Identity Disorder in Adults, Third Revision' (J Trauma Dissociation 2011;12(2):115-187, PMID 21391103; summary version PMID 21391104), sets out a phase-oriented model of care -- Phase 1 safety/stabilization/symptom reduction, Phase 2 working through and processing traumatic memory, Phase 3 identity integration and rehabilitation -- as the standard structure of treatment, explicitly not on a fixed timeline; many patients require years of Phase 1 stabilization work, and the guideline recognizes partial resolution or increased inter-identity cooperation/co-consciousness (short of full identity fusion) as legitimate, real treatment outcomes alongside full integration. This must be reported honestly alongside a serious, recent methodological counterweight: a 2026 narrative review in a major peer-reviewed medical journal (Roepke S, Priebe K, Schmahl C, Kleim B, Rosner R, Ehring T, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447) found that only a small number of empirical DID studies exist, most with major methodological limitations, that none are randomized controlled trials of a DID-specific intervention, that the available data show marked diagnostic overlap between DID and complex PTSD/borderline personality disorder and do not support core proposed DID constructs including inter-identity amnesia, and concluded 'there is no robust evidence for the efficacy of any specific treatment' for DID as its own diagnostic entity -- recommending that validated complex-PTSD/BPD treatments be considered before assigning a DID diagnosis. A 2024 systematic review of individual psychodynamically informed psychotherapy for DID similarly found the evidence base to consist of small case series and observational reports rather than randomized trials (J Trauma Dissociation 2024;25(2), PMID 38146918). No medication is FDA-approved for DID itself; pharmacotherapy is real adjunct-only management of comorbid depressive, anxiety, or PTSD symptoms, never a treatment for the dissociative process itself (Gentile JP, Dillon KS, Gillig PM, Innov Clin Neurosci 2013;10(2):22-29, PMID 23556139). Honest synthesis: phase-oriented trauma-focused psychotherapy under the ISSTD three-phase model is the real, guideline-recommended, best-evidence pathway toward genuine symptom reduction and, for a meaningful subset of patients over a period of years, greater identity integration -- the TOP DD naturalistic outcome data are real and directionally positive -- but this evidence is naturalistic/observational rather than placebo- or waitlist-controlled RCT evidence of the kind available for PTSD, and a serious, recent methodological critique of the field means the controlled-trial cure rate for DID specifically is not established and should not be overstated.

curative_option.name: Phase-Oriented Trauma Therapy: ISSTD Three-Phase Model (Stabilization -> Trauma Processing -> Integration)
curative_option.note: The ISSTD 'Guidelines for Treating Dissociative Identity Disorder in Adults, Third Revision' (J Trauma Dissociation 2011;12(2):115-187, PMID 21391103; summary PMID 21391104) is the field's consensus clinical guideline and structures real-world treatment into three phases, typically spanning years rather than the 8-15 sessions seen in PTSD-focused protocols: Phase 1 establishes safety, affect-regulation and coping skills, and reduces high-risk symptoms (self-injury, suicidality, severe dissociative crises) before trauma-focused work begins; Phase 2 works through traumatic memories at a paced, tolerable rate once the patient is sufficiently stabilized; Phase 3 works toward greater cooperation, co-consciousness, and communication between dissociated identity states, consolidating a more unified sense of self and daily functioning -- full fusion/integration is a real, achievable goal for some patients, while increased inter-identity cooperation and symptom resolution short of full fusion is recognized by the guideline as a legitimate outcome for others. The naturalistic, international TOP DD study and its TOP DD Network web-adjunct arm provide the real outcome data behind this model's use.

real_survival_data.top_dd_30_month_naturalistic_followup_di: Reductions in dissociative symptoms (amnesia, depersonalization/derealization, absorption) over 30 months of ongoing phase-oriented outpatient treatment were significantly associated with reductions in PTSD and general-distress severity, in a prospective international sample of DID/DDNOS patient-therapist pairs (PMID 23627481)
real_survival_data.top_dd_improvers_vs_worseners_revictimiz: Among 49 TOP DD patients who showed sudden marked improvement or worsening over 30 months, improvers had significantly fewer revictimization events and life stressors than those who worsened (PMID 23796170)
real_survival_data.top_dd_network_web_adjunct_effect_sizes_: 1- and 2-year follow-up of a structured web-based psychoeducational adjunct layered on ongoing phase-oriented individual therapy (n=111 DID/complex-DD patients) found real reductions in dissociation and PTSD symptoms, improved emotion regulation, and reduced non-suicidal self-injury, overall sample Cohen's |d| = 0.44-0.90 (Cohen's U3 = 67.0%-81.6%, computed via the standard normal CDF from the paper's own reported effect sizes), with larger/faster gains in higher-baseline-dissociation patients, |d| = 0.54-1.04 (U3 = 70.5%-85.1%) (PMID 30698858)
real_survival_data.top_dd_hospitalization_cost_reduction_My: Patients further along in phase-oriented treatment had significantly lower inpatient-hospitalization and outpatient-service cost estimates than patients still in early safety/stabilization stages, and utilization/cost estimates decreased longitudinally over the 30-month study (PMID 29038681)

curative_option.source: ISSTD. Guidelines for treating dissociative identity disorder in adults, third revision. J Trauma Dissociation. 2011;12(2):115-187 (PMID 21391103); summary version (PMID 21391104); Brand BL, Stadnik R. J Trauma Dissociation. 2013;14(3):328-341 (PMID 23627481); Myrick AC, Brand BL, Putnam FW. J Trauma Dissociation. 2013;14(4):375-389 (PMID 23796170); Cronin E, Brand BL, Mattanah JF. Eur J Psychotraumatol. 2014;5:22676 (PMID 24616755); Myrick AC et al. Eur J Psychotraumatol. 2017;8(1):1375829 (PMID 29038681); Brand BL et al. J Trauma Stress. 2019;32(1):156-166 (PMID 30698858)
curative_option.important_caveat: All of the outcome data above come from a single naturalistic, non-randomized, non-placebo-controlled international cohort (TOP DD and its TOP DD Network adjunct arm), with a substantial attrition rate (>50% by 30 months in the cost-estimate paper, PMID 29038681) -- it is real, directionally positive, prospective outcome data, but it is not RCT evidence of the kind available for PTSD (PE/CPT/EMDR) in this KB. A 2026 narrative review (Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447) independently concluded that 'there is no robust evidence for the efficacy of any specific treatment' for DID as its own diagnostic entity, that available DID studies mostly have major methodological limitations, and that DID shows marked overlap with complex PTSD and borderline personality disorder, for which validated treatments already exist -- this is a real, serious counterweight that must be reported alongside the TOP DD findings, not omitted.

did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.name: Phase-Oriented Trauma Therapy (ISSTD Three-Phase Model: Stabilization, Trauma Processing, Integration)
did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.type: Structured, guideline-based trauma-focused psychotherapy framework, real first-line approach
did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.effectiveness: The ISSTD Third Revision guideline (PMID 21391103, summary PMID 21391104) is the consensus real-world treatment framework. Outcome support comes from the naturalistic TOP DD study: dissociative-symptom reduction over 30 months of phase-oriented outpatient treatment was significantly linked to reduced PTSD/distress severity (PMID 23627481); improvers had fewer revictimizations than those who worsened (PMID 23796170); a stronger patient-rated alliance predicted better outcome (PMID 24616755); and the TOP DD Network web-adjunct arm found real symptom-reduction effect sizes of Cohen's |d| = 0.44-1.04 (Cohen's U3 = 67.0%-85.1%) at 1-2 year follow-up (PMID 30698858). A 2026 methodological review (PMID 41711447) found no RCT-level efficacy evidence exists for any specific DID treatment and questions core diagnostic constructs -- reported here for honesty, not to erase the real naturalistic outcome data above.
did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.reason_why: Phase 1 builds safety, affect-regulation, and coping skills and reduces high-risk symptoms (self-injury, suicidality, dissociative crises) before trauma-focused work begins, since unstabilized trauma processing carries a real risk of destabilization in DID; Phase 2 processes traumatic memory at a paced, tolerable rate once stabilized; Phase 3 works toward greater cooperation, co-consciousness, and communication between dissociated identity states, consolidating a more unified sense of self and improved daily functioning.
did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.important_caveat: Evidence is naturalistic/observational (TOP DD), not RCT-controlled; treatment duration is typically measured in years, not weeks; a 2026 review (PMID 41711447) found no robust RCT-level efficacy evidence for any specific DID treatment and disputes core DID diagnostic constructs (e.g., inter-identity amnesia), recommending validated complex-PTSD/BPD treatments be considered first.
did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.real_working_solution: Multi-year, phase-oriented individual psychotherapy (Phase 1 stabilization -> Phase 2 trauma processing -> Phase 3 integration/rehabilitation) per the ISSTD guideline, the real best-evidence, guideline-recommended pathway toward genuine symptom reduction and, for a meaningful subset of patients, identity integration.
did_phase_oriented_trauma_therapy.source: ISSTD. J Trauma Dissociation. 2011;12(2):115-187 (PMID 21391103); summary (PMID 21391104); Brand BL, Stadnik R. J Trauma Dissociation. 2013;14(3):328-341 (PMID 23627481); Myrick AC et al. J Trauma Dissociation. 2013;14(4):375-389 (PMID 23796170); Cronin E et al. Eur J Psychotraumatol. 2014;5:22676 (PMID 24616755); Brand BL et al. J Trauma Stress. 2019;32(1):156-166 (PMID 30698858); Roepke S et al. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2026;123(8):220-225 (PMID 41711447)

did_emdr_adapted.name: EMDR Adapted for DID (used within Phase 2 of the phase-oriented model)
did_emdr_adapted.type: Bilateral-stimulation trauma-reprocessing therapy, technique-modified/paced for dissociative patients
did_emdr_adapted.effectiveness: No dedicated randomized controlled trial or naturalistic outcome study of EMDR specifically for DID could be located via NCBI PubMed search in this session. The ISSTD guideline (PMID 21391103) discusses EMDR as one of several usable Phase 2 trauma-processing techniques, with modifications (slower pacing, fractionated/titrated processing of trauma fragments rather than whole-memory exposure, integration with ego-state/parts work) recommended for dissociative patients because unmodified standard EMDR protocols carry a real risk of destabilization or abreaction if used before adequate Phase 1 stabilization. This is far less robust than the EMDR evidence base for PTSD itself, where a pooled meta-analysis gives Hedges g=1.01 (Cohen's U3=84.4%) across 26 RCTs (Watts BV et al, J Clin Psychiatry 2013, PMID 23842024, cited in this KB's post_traumatic_stress_disorder entry) -- no comparable DID-specific pooled effect size exists in the verified literature.
did_emdr_adapted.reason_why: As adapted for dissociative patients, bilateral stimulation is applied to carefully selected, titrated trauma fragments (rather than full memory exposure) with the aim of desensitizing traumatic material while reducing the real risk of dissociative destabilization during reprocessing.
did_emdr_adapted.important_caveat: No DID-specific randomized or naturalistic outcome trial could be verified; ISSTD guideline explicitly warns against using EMDR (or other trauma-processing techniques) before adequate Phase 1 safety/stabilization in DID patients, given real destabilization/abreaction risk. No effectiveness_pct is reported for this option because none genuinely exists in the verified literature.
did_emdr_adapted.real_working_solution: Used, per therapist EMDR training and patient stabilization readiness, as one of several Phase 2 trauma-processing techniques (alongside imaginal exposure, cognitive processing, and ego-state work) within the ISSTD three-phase model -- not independently validated for DID by any located RCT.

did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.name: Pharmacotherapy for Comorbid Depression/Anxiety/PTSD Symptoms (Adjunct Only -- No FDA-Approved Medication for DID Itself)
did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.type: Adjunct pharmacotherapy targeting comorbid symptoms, not the dissociative process
specific_drugs: prazosin (alpha-1 antagonist, adjunct for trauma nightmares)
quetiapine (atypical antipsychotic, off-label adjunct for severe intrusive symptoms/agitation)
did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.effectiveness: No medication has FDA approval for dissociative identity disorder itself, and no medication is curative for the dissociative process. A 2013 clinical review (Gentile JP, Dillon KS, Gillig PM, Innov Clin Neurosci 2013;10(2):22-29, PMID 23556139) summarizes psychopharmacology recommendations for DID as adjunctive management of comorbid depressive, anxiety, and PTSD symptoms alongside phase-oriented psychotherapy, not as a treatment for the dissociative identity structure itself. SSRI/SNRI and prazosin efficacy figures for the comorbid target symptoms themselves come from the general depression/PTSD literature (e.g., sertraline/paroxetine PTSD RCTs already cited in this KB's post_traumatic_stress_disorder entry), not from DID-specific trials.
did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.reason_why: SSRIs/SNRIs treat comorbid depressive and anxiety/PTSD symptoms via the same serotonergic/noradrenergic mechanisms established in the general depression/PTSD/anxiety literature; prazosin is used adjunctively for trauma-related nightmares via alpha-1 adrenergic blockade; atypical antipsychotics are sometimes used off-label for severe intrusive symptoms or agitation. None of these target the dissociative identity structure itself.
did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.important_caveat: Adjunct only, never a substitute for phase-oriented psychotherapy in DID; no controlled DID-specific pharmacotherapy trial exists; no effectiveness_pct is reported for DID itself because none genuinely exists.
did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.real_working_solution: Adjunct psychopharmacology targeted at specific comorbid symptoms (depression, anxiety, PTSD intrusion/hyperarousal, nightmares), prescribed alongside -- never instead of -- phase-oriented trauma psychotherapy.
did_medication_comorbid_symptoms.source: Gentile JP, Dillon KS, Gillig PM. Innov Clin Neurosci. 2013;10(2):22-29 (PMID 23556139)

did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.name: Hospitalization / Crisis Stabilization for Severe Cases
did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.type: Acute inpatient psychiatric stabilization, real safety-net adjunct for high-risk presentations
did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.effectiveness: The TOP DD naturalistic cohort found that patients further along in phase-oriented treatment had significantly lower inpatient-hospitalization and outpatient-service cost estimates than patients still struggling with early safety/stabilization-stage issues, and that these utilization/cost estimates decreased longitudinally over the 30-month study (Myrick AC et al, Eur J Psychotraumatol 2017;8(1):1375829, PMID 29038681). The ISSTD guideline (PMID 21391103) identifies safety planning and crisis management for self-injury/suicidality as a foundational Phase 1 task, reflecting the real, elevated rates of non-suicidal self-injury and suicide attempts documented in DID patients (PMID 30698858).
did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.reason_why: Acute inpatient stabilization provides real, time-limited external containment during suicidality, severe self-injury, or acute dissociative crises, while Phase 1 outpatient stabilization skills (safety planning, affect regulation, grounding) are built up; it functions as a safety-net adjunct, not a treatment for the dissociative process.
did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.important_caveat: Hospitalization itself does not treat or resolve dissociative identity structure; the TOP DD cost/utilization finding is naturalistic and correlational (the paper's own conclusion states it is not clear whether treatment itself caused the observed reduction in utilization); no effectiveness_pct is reported for DID cure/integration because none genuinely exists for hospitalization as such.
did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.real_working_solution: Time-limited acute inpatient stabilization for suicidality, severe self-injury, or acute dissociative crisis, used alongside -- and to enable continuation of -- outpatient phase-oriented psychotherapy.
did_hospitalization_crisis_stabilization.source: Myrick AC et al. Eur J Psychotraumatol. 2017;8(1):1375829 (PMID 29038681); ISSTD. J Trauma Dissociation. 2011;12(2):115-187 (PMID 21391103)
