effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: All five rows are Cohen's U3 conversions (via the standard normal CDF) of real effect sizes reported in a single study, the TOP DD Network web-based psychoeducational adjunct trial (PMID 30698858) -- a naturalistic, non-placebo-controlled, single-arm pre/post design layered on top of patients' ongoing individual phase-oriented psychotherapy, not an independent RCT of phase-oriented therapy itself. They are shown across the reported low-to-high effect-size range and dissociation-severity subgroups because that full range is what the paper itself reports, not because these are five independently validated treatments. No DID-specific RCT-controlled effectiveness percentage exists in the verified literature for phase-oriented therapy, EMDR-for-DID, or comorbid-symptom pharmacotherapy as compared to a control condition -- this is a real, honest limit of the current evidence base, independently confirmed by a 2026 methodological review (Roepke S et al, Dtsch Arztebl Int 2026;123(8):220-225, PMID 41711447) which found 'no robust evidence for the efficacy of any specific treatment' for DID as its own diagnostic entity. EMDR-adapted-for-DID and comorbid-symptom pharmacotherapy are omitted from this ranked table because no genuine DID-specific numeric effectiveness percentage exists for either in the verified literature; both are still real, guideline-referenced options and are described in exhaustive_medicine_survey.

body_dysmorphic_disorder.name: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD)
body_dysmorphic_disorder.icd11_hint: 6B21 Body dysmorphic disorder (ICD-11, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, grouping 6B2 Obsessive-compulsive or related disorders, alongside 6B20 OCD, 6B22 Olfactory reference disorder, 6B23 Hypochondriasis, 6B24 Hoarding disorder, 6B25 Body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders); DSM-5/ICD-10-CM F45.22 Body dysmorphic disorder. Flagged moderate-high (not primary-source-direct) confidence: the WHO ICD-11 browser is a JS-rendered app that could not be scraped directly in this session (page returned only navigation chrome, no entity content) -- same limitation and same confidence flag already used elsewhere in this KB (e.g. the obsessive_compulsive_disorder entry) for this exact reason.
body_dysmorphic_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: BDD is genuinely, substantially treatable with the right two interventions -- but the real evidence is equally clear that the treatment patients most often seek first (cosmetic/dermatologic correction of the perceived defect) is not one of them and typically fails to resolve the disorder. On the medication side, BDD is a serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor-responsive disorder, but -- as it is for its OCD-spectrum relative -- higher-than-standard-depression doses and a longer trial are usually required, not merely 'depression dosing': Grant JE, Phillips KA ('Recognizing and treating body dysmorphic disorder', Ann Clin Psychiatry 2005;17(4):205-210, PMID 16402752) state explicitly that higher doses of serotonin reuptake inhibitors and longer treatment trials than those used for many other psychiatric disorders, including depression, are often needed to effectively treat BDD. This is real, trial-confirmed, not theoretical: in the only published randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pharmacotherapy trial in BDD (Phillips KA, Albertini RS, Rasmussen SA, 'A randomized placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine in body dysmorphic disorder', Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(4):381-388, PMID 11926939, N=67), fluoxetine produced a 53% (18/34) response rate on the BDD-YBOCS versus 18% (6/33) on placebo (chi-square=8.8, P=.003), with delusional BDD patients responding just as well as nondelusional patients and zero delusional patients responding to placebo -- real evidence that even the most severe, poor-insight presentations are pharmacologically treatable, not a reason to withhold medication. A second real double-blind trial (Hollander E et al., 'Clomipramine vs desipramine crossover trial in body dysmorphic disorder', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(11):1033-1039, PMID 10565503, N=29) found the serotonergic tricyclic clomipramine significantly superior to the noradrenergic comparator desipramine on BDD severity, delusionality, and functional disability, independent of comorbidity or insight level -- confirming this is a specifically serotonergic-mechanism disorder, not a general antidepressant-responsive one. On the psychotherapy side, cognitive-behavioral therapy specifically adapted for BDD (CBT-BDD, using exposure, response prevention, and perceptual retraining rather than generic CBT) is the real evidence-based psychotherapy of choice (Grant & Phillips 2005, PMID 16402752): in the first manualized randomized trial (Wilhelm S et al., 'Modular cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder: a randomized controlled trial', Behav Ther 2014;45(3):314-327, PMID 24680228, N=36 adults), 81% of all participants (immediate-treatment plus waitlisted patients subsequently treated) met responder criteria (>=30% BDD-YBOCS reduction) by posttreatment, with 50% of the immediate-CBT group already responding by week 12 versus 12% of the waitlist group (P=.026) -- and gains were maintained at 3- and 6-month follow-up. A pilot randomized trial extended this to adolescents (Mataix-Cols D, Krebs G et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2015;54(11):895-904, PMID 26506580, N=30), finding 40% (6/15) of CBT-treated adolescents were sustained responders versus 6.7% (1/15) on psychoeducation-plus-monitoring control (P=.031). The honest, important counter-finding: the treatment BDD patients most often actually seek -- cosmetic surgery, dermatologic, or other appearance-altering procedures -- does not resolve BDD and often perpetuates or worsens it. Crerand CE, Franklin ME, Sarwer DB ('Body dysmorphic disorder and cosmetic surgery', Plast Reconstr Surg 2006;118(7):167e-180e, PMID 17102719), reviewing this literature, state plainly that retrospective outcome studies suggest persons with BDD typically do not benefit from cosmetic procedures, while pharmacotherapy and CBT do. This was confirmed prospectively, not just retrospectively: Tignol J et al. ('Body dysmorphic disorder and cosmetic surgery: evolution of 24 subjects with a minimal defect in appearance 5 years after their request for cosmetic surgery', Eur Psychiatry 2007;22(8):520-524, PMID 17900876, N=24 at 5-year follow-up) found that of 7 BDD patients who actually underwent the cosmetic surgery they sought, 6 (85.7%) still met full BDD diagnostic criteria 5 years later and showed higher handicap and psychiatric comorbidity than non-BDD surgical patients -- despite high patient-reported satisfaction with the surgical outcome itself, i.e., the surgery 'worked' cosmetically but did not treat the underlying disorder, and in some initially non-BDD patients, BDD emerged after their procedure. The honest bottom line: BDD is a real, substantially treatable disorder via high-dose serotonergic pharmacotherapy and BDD-adapted CBT (majority-response evidence from real double-blind and randomized-controlled trials), but the appearance-focused fix patients instinctively pursue first is a real documented treatment failure mode that must be actively redirected toward psychiatric care, not indulged.

curative_option.name: High-dose SSRI pharmacotherapy combined with CBT specifically adapted for BDD (CBT-BDD) -- real best-evidence combination
curative_option.note: Neither medication nor psychotherapy alone has been tested against their combination in a head-to-head BDD RCT, but each independently produces majority-level real response rates in double-blind/randomized trials, and both are recommended together as first-line by the review literature (Grant JE, Phillips KA, Ann Clin Psychiatry 2005, PMID 16402752). High-dose SSRIs (dosed similarly to OCD, higher than standard depression dosing, with a longer 10-16 week adequate trial) treat the serotonergic component; CBT-BDD adds exposure, response prevention, and perceptual retraining aimed specifically at the appearance-preoccupation and mirror-checking/camouflaging rituals that generic CBT does not target. Clomipramine is a real, effective second-line/SSRI-alternative option when SSRIs are inadequate or not tolerated.
curative_option.source: Phillips KA et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(4):381-388 (PMID 11926939); Wilhelm S et al. Behav Ther 2014;45(3):314-327 (PMID 24680228); Mataix-Cols D, Krebs G et al. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2015;54(11):895-904 (PMID 26506580); Grant JE, Phillips KA. Ann Clin Psychiatry 2005;17(4):205-210 (PMID 16402752)
curative_option.important_caveat: The Phillips 2002 fluoxetine trial and the Wilhelm 2014 CBT-BDD trial are both real, methodologically strong studies (double-blind placebo-controlled RCT for medication; randomized controlled trial with blinded independent raters for CBT), but BDD pharmacotherapy evidence is limited to a small number of controlled trials (this KB found only two published double-blind BDD medication RCTs: Phillips 2002 fluoxetine and Hollander 1999 clomipramine-vs-desipramine) -- smaller than the evidence base for OCD or depression. The Wilhelm 2014 CBT trial (N=36) and the Mataix-Cols/Krebs 2015 adolescent pilot (N=30) are both real RCTs but modestly sized; a larger head-to-head trial of CBT-BDD versus supportive psychotherapy (Wilhelm S et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2019;76(4):363-373, PMID 30785624, N=120) found CBT-BDD's superiority over supportive psychotherapy was site-specific (significant at one site, not the other), so CBT-BDD's advantage over a good, BDD-informed supportive therapist is real but not universally replicated across settings.

bdd_high_dose_ssris.name: High-Dose Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)
bdd_high_dose_ssris.effectiveness: Phillips KA, Albertini RS, Rasmussen SA (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(4):381-388, PMID 11926939), the only published double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled BDD pharmacotherapy RCT (N=67), found fluoxetine significantly more effective than placebo on the BDD-YBOCS beginning at week 8 and continuing through week 12 (F(1,64)=16.5, P<.001); response rate was 53% (18/34) with fluoxetine versus 18% (6/33) with placebo (chi-square=8.8, P=.003). Response was independent of BDD duration/severity and of comorbid major depression, OCD, or personality disorder, and delusional BDD patients responded to fluoxetine as well as nondelusional patients did (with zero delusional responders on placebo) -- real evidence that SSRIs work across the full BDD insight spectrum, including the delusional variant.
bdd_high_dose_ssris.reason_why: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin availability; as in OCD, BDD symptom improvement is linked to the degree of serotonin reuptake inhibition achieved, but requires both a higher dose ceiling and a longer adequate trial (Grant JE, Phillips KA, Ann Clin Psychiatry 2005, PMID 16402752) than standard depression dosing before response can be fairly judged.
bdd_high_dose_ssris.important_caveat: Only one double-blind placebo-controlled fixed-population BDD SSRI RCT has been published (Phillips 2002); dose-response has not been separately isolated in a dedicated fixed-dose BDD trial the way it has for OCD (Bloch et al. 2010), so the specific high-dose recommendation here is extrapolated from the OCD-spectrum dosing principle articulated in the Grant & Phillips 2005 review rather than from a BDD-specific fixed-dose RCT.
bdd_high_dose_ssris.real_working_solution: An adequate (typically 12-16 week), high-dose trial of a single SSRI, titrated toward the top of the licensed/tolerated range under physician supervision, as real first-line pharmacotherapy for BDD, ideally combined with CBT-BDD.
bdd_high_dose_ssris.source: Phillips KA, Albertini RS, Rasmussen SA. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(4):381-388 (PMID 11926939); Grant JE, Phillips KA. Ann Clin Psychiatry 2005;17(4):205-210 (PMID 16402752)
bdd_high_dose_ssris.confidence: high for SSRI efficacy over placebo (real double-blind RCT); moderate for the specific high-dose figures, which are extrapolated from the OCD-spectrum dosing principle rather than a BDD-specific fixed-dose RCT

bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.name: Clomipramine (Tricyclic Antidepressant, serotonin reuptake inhibitor)
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.type: Second-line pharmacotherapy for SSRI-inadequate or SSRI-intolerant BDD
specific_drugs: Clomipramine (dose titrated under physician cardiac monitoring)
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.effectiveness: Hollander E et al ('Clomipramine vs desipramine crossover trial in body dysmorphic disorder', Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(11):1033-1039, PMID 10565503), a 16-week double-blind crossover RCT (N=29), found clomipramine significantly superior to the active noradrenergic comparator desipramine on obsessive preoccupation with the perceived defect, repetitive checking/camouflaging behaviors, global symptom severity, and functional disability. Superiority held independent of comorbid OCD, depression, or social phobia, and regardless of whether the patient's belief was held with insight or delusional intensity.
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.reason_why: Clomipramine is a potent, non-selective serotonin (and, to a lesser extent, noradrenaline) reuptake inhibitor; the crossover design directly isolated its serotonergic action as the active mechanism by showing superiority over desipramine, an equally potent but purely noradrenergic reuptake inhibitor -- real evidence that BDD's pharmacological responsiveness is serotonin-specific, not a generic antidepressant/anxiolytic effect.
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.important_caveat: The Hollander 1999 abstract reports statistically significant superiority on multiple continuous severity measures but does not report a discrete categorical responder-rate percentage, so no numeric effectiveness_pct for clomipramine is included in the ranked table below (a percentage figure was not verifiable from the primary source in this session and has not been invented). Clomipramine requires baseline and on-treatment ECG monitoring at higher doses for real cardiac conduction (QTc) risk and is more dangerous in overdose than SSRIs.
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.real_working_solution: Clomipramine as a real, RCT-confirmed effective second-line option (monotherapy or SSRI-augmentation) when an adequate high-dose SSRI trial is inadequate or not tolerated, under physician cardiac monitoring.
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.source: Hollander E, Allen A, Kwon J, et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1999;56(11):1033-1039 (PMID 10565503)
bdd_clomipramine_ssri_refractory.confidence: high for real superiority over an active comparator (double-blind crossover RCT); no verified numeric responder-rate figure available

bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.name: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy specifically adapted for Body Dysmorphic Disorder (CBT-BDD)
bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.effectiveness: Wilhelm S et al ('Modular cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder: a randomized controlled trial', Behav Ther 2014;45(3):314-327, PMID 24680228), a randomized trial (N=36 adults; 22-session manualized CBT-BDD vs 12-week waitlist), found 50% of immediate-CBT participants met responder criteria (>=30% BDD-YBOCS reduction) by week 12 versus 12% of waitlisted participants (P=.026); by posttreatment, 81% of all participants (immediate CBT-BDD plus waitlisted patients subsequently treated) met responder criteria, with large effect size on BDD-YBOCS reduction (d=2.1, P<.0001) and gains maintained at 3- and 6-month follow-up; mean patient-satisfaction score was 87.3%. A pilot RCT extended this to adolescents (Mataix-Cols D, Krebs G et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2015;54(11):895-904, PMID 26506580, N=30, ages 12-18), finding 40% (6/15) of CBT-treated adolescents were sustained responders at posttreatment and 2-month follow-up versus 6.7% (1/15) on a psychoeducation-plus-monitoring control (P=.031). The original proof-of-concept came from Veale D et al ('Body dysmorphic disorder: a cognitive behavioural model and pilot randomised controlled trial', Behav Res Ther 1996;34(9):717-729, PMID 8936754, N=19), the first BDD RCT, which found significant pre-post improvement on BDD-specific measures and depressed mood in the CBT arm versus no change in the waiting-list arm (no discrete responder percentage reported). A larger trial (Wilhelm S et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2019;76(4):363-373, PMID 30785624, N=120) comparing CBT-BDD against therapist-delivered supportive psychotherapy found CBT-BDD's advantage was site-specific -- significant at one site, not detected at the other -- indicating real but not universally replicated superiority over a good BDD-informed supportive therapist.
bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.reason_why: CBT-BDD adds BDD-specific modules (perceptual retraining to correct selective attention to disliked body parts, exposure to feared social/appearance-related situations, and response prevention for mirror-checking, camouflaging, reassurance-seeking, and skin-picking rituals) on top of standard cognitive restructuring, directly targeting the appearance-preoccupation-to-ritual cycle that generic, unmodified CBT protocols do not specifically address.
bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.important_caveat: The Wilhelm 2014 and Mataix-Cols/Krebs 2015 trials are both real randomized trials but are modestly sized (N=36 and N=30); the Wilhelm 2019 replication (N=120) found site-specific rather than universal superiority over supportive psychotherapy, so CBT-BDD's real advantage should be read as substantial-but-not-yet-uniformly-replicated across treatment settings.
bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.real_working_solution: A course of manualized CBT-BDD (exposure, response prevention, perceptual retraining, cognitive restructuring), typically 18-22 weekly sessions, as real first-line evidence-based psychotherapy for BDD across both adult and adolescent age groups.
bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.source: Wilhelm S et al. Behav Ther 2014;45(3):314-327 (PMID 24680228); Mataix-Cols D, Krebs G et al. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2015;54(11):895-904 (PMID 26506580); Veale D et al. Behav Res Ther 1996;34(9):717-729 (PMID 8936754); Wilhelm S et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2019;76(4):363-373 (PMID 30785624)
bdd_cbt_adapted_for_bdd.confidence: high for real efficacy over waitlist/psychoeducation control (randomized trials with blinded independent raters); moderate for magnitude of superiority over an active, BDD-informed supportive-therapy comparator (site-specific replication)

bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.name: Cosmetic Surgery, Dermatologic, and Other Appearance-Altering Medical Procedures
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.type: NOT a real treatment for BDD -- documented to fail to resolve BDD symptoms and to often worsen the disorder; included here as an honest, evidence-based contraindication, not a recommended option
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.effectiveness: Crerand CE, Franklin ME, Sarwer DB ('Body dysmorphic disorder and cosmetic surgery', Plast Reconstr Surg 2006;118(7):167e-180e, PMID 17102719), reviewing this literature, report that 7-15% of patients presenting for cosmetic procedures meet criteria for BDD, and that retrospective outcome studies suggest persons with BDD typically do not benefit from cosmetic procedures, in direct contrast to their real response to pharmacotherapy and CBT. This was confirmed prospectively by Tignol J et al ('Body dysmorphic disorder and cosmetic surgery: evolution of 24 subjects with a minimal defect in appearance 5 years after their request for cosmetic surgery', Eur Psychiatry 2007;22(8):520-524, PMID 17900876): of 30 patients with a minimal appearance defect who requested cosmetic surgery (12 with BDD, 18 without), 24 were re-evaluated 5 years later; of the 7 BDD patients who actually underwent surgery, 6 (85.7%) still met full BDD diagnostic criteria at 5-year follow-up and showed higher handicap and psychiatric comorbidity than non-BDD surgical patients -- despite patients in both groups reporting high satisfaction with the surgical outcome itself. The study additionally found that 3 initially non-BDD patients had developed BDD by follow-up, i.e., the procedure did not merely fail to help in existing BDD but was temporally associated with new BDD onset in some patients.
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.reason_why: BDD's core pathology is a distorted, ego-syntonic perception of and preoccupation with the body part, not an objective defect that surgical or dermatologic correction can address; correcting or altering the physical feature does not correct the underlying perceptual/cognitive distortion, so preoccupation, checking, and camouflaging behaviors typically persist, relocate to a new body area, or intensify after the procedure, and the trust and finality that surgery implies can also reinforce, rather than interrupt, appearance-focused rumination.
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.important_caveat: Patient-reported satisfaction with the cosmetic outcome itself does not equal resolution of BDD -- the Tignol 2007 data show both can be true simultaneously (high surgical satisfaction, persistent BDD diagnosis), which is precisely why surgeons and dermatologists relying on patient satisfaction as an outcome measure can be misled into believing the procedure 'worked' for a BDD patient when the disorder itself is unchanged or worse. This is a real, documented reason major cosmetic/dermatologic and plastic-surgery professional guidance regards a positive BDD screen as a contraindication to elective appearance-altering procedures pending psychiatric evaluation.
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.real_working_solution: Not a working solution -- the real working solutions for BDD are high-dose SSRI pharmacotherapy and CBT-BDD (above). Patients presenting to cosmetic/dermatologic providers who screen positive for BDD should be referred for psychiatric evaluation and treatment before any elective appearance-altering procedure is considered.
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.source: Crerand CE, Franklin ME, Sarwer DB. Plast Reconstr Surg 2006;118(7):167e-180e (PMID 17102719); Tignol J, Biraben-Gotzamanis L, Martin-Guehl C, et al. Eur Psychiatry 2007;22(8):520-524 (PMID 17900876)
bdd_cosmetic_dermatologic_procedures_not.confidence: high -- a real prospective 5-year follow-up study (Tignol 2007) plus a peer-reviewed review of the retrospective outcome literature (Crerand 2006) concur

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage meeting BDD-YBOCS responder criteria, N=67 double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (18/34 fluoxetine)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Phillips KA et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002;59(4):381-388 (PMID 11926939)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage meeting >=30% BDD-YBOCS reduction responder criteria at week 12, immediate-CBT arm, same RCT

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Figures are drawn from different trial designs, outcome definitions (BDD-YBOCS categorical response, sustained responder classification, 5-year diagnostic persistence), and age groups (adult vs adolescent), and are not directly interchangeable head-to-head effect sizes; they are presented together only to rank the real, verified magnitude of benefit (or, for cosmetic surgery, real documented lack of benefit) each intervention has demonstrated in its own controlled/prospective study. The Phillips 2002 fluoxetine RCT and Wilhelm 2014 CBT-BDD RCT are this KB's two strongest, most directly comparable BDD intervention trials (both real, controlled, with a discrete categorical responder outcome). The cosmetic-surgery row is deliberately included, ranked lowest, and phrased as a resolution-rate percentage (rather than omitted) specifically because clinical and patient decision-making in BDD is otherwise skewed toward believing appearance correction is the treatment; the real prospective evidence (Tignol 2007, N=7 operated BDD patients at 5-year follow-up) says the opposite.

body_dysmorphic_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TWO independent, real safety concerns must be actively screened for in every Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) presentation. (1) SUICIDE RISK -- among the highest of any psychiatric disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies found a significant positive association between BDD and suicidality overall (OR=3.63, 95% CI 2.62-4.63), with significantly increased odds for both suicide attempts (OR=3.30, 95% CI 2.18-4.43) and suicidal ideation (OR=2.57, 95% CI 1.44-3.69) (Angelakis I, Gooding PA, Panagioti M, 'Suicidality in body dysmorphic disorder (BDD): A systematic review with meta-analysis', Clin Psychol Rev 2016, PMID 27607741). A representative German nationwide population-based survey of 2,510 adults found that, compared with people without BDD, people with current BDD (1.8% population prevalence) reported far higher rates of suicidal ideation (31.0% vs 3.5%) and suicide attempts specifically due to appearance concerns (22.2% vs 2.1%) (Buhlmann U et al., 'Updates on the prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder: a population-based survey', Psychiatry Res 2010, PMID 20452057). A 2021 meta-analysis of the broader DSM-5 Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders (OCRD) group found very high pooled lifetime suicide-attempt (35.2%) and suicidal-ideation (66.1%) prevalence specifically in BDD (Pellegrini L et al., 'Suicidality in patients with obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (OCRDs): A meta-analysis', Compr Psychiatry 2021, PMID 34062378). In an early but detailed 30-case clinical series, 17% of BDD patients had made suicide attempts, and functional collapse was severe: 97% avoided normal social/occupational activities and 30% had been housebound because of their symptoms (Phillips KA et al., 'Body dysmorphic disorder: 30 cases of imagined ugliness', Am J Psychiatry 1993, PMID 8422082). CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: every BDD patient requires explicit, repeated suicide-risk screening regardless of apparent symptom severity, because population-level data (not just treatment-seeking clinical samples) show this risk elevation is real and large. (2) UNNECESSARY / HARMFUL COSMETIC-SURGERY-SEEKING: persons with BDD frequently seek surgical and minimally invasive cosmetic treatments for their perceived defect, but a cross-sectional study of 200 BDD patients found overall BDD severity improved with only 2.3% of the surgical/minimally-invasive treatments received, and that physicians were more likely to provide the requested surgical/MI treatment than other requested cosmetic treatments despite this poor longer-term outcome (Crerand CE, Menard W, Phillips KA, 'Surgical and minimally invasive cosmetic procedures among persons with body dysmorphic disorder', Ann Plast Surg 2010, PMID 20467296). The population-based survey above similarly found a markedly higher rate of prior cosmetic surgery in people with BDD than without (15.6% vs 3.0%) (Buhlmann et al., PMID 20452057), and a clinical review of cosmetic-surgery psychosocial outcomes concluded that some patients are never satisfied with cosmetic interventions despite good procedural outcomes, specifically because of an underlying, unaddressed body dysmorphic disorder (Castle DJ, Honigman RJ, Phillips KA, 'Does cosmetic surgery improve psychosocial wellbeing?', Med J Aust 2002, PMID 12064961); the 1993 case series above likewise found patients responded poorly to surgical, dermatologic, and dental treatments (PMID 8422082). CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: a patient requesting or repeatedly pursuing cosmetic surgical/dermatologic procedures for a perceived defect that appears absent or slight to an outside observer needs BDD screening before referral to a cosmetic procedure, not reassurance or facilitation of the requested procedure alone; unnecessary surgery in BDD does not resolve, and can worsen, the underlying preoccupation and distress.

symptoms.classification: DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, 2013; named diagnostic manual, real and current) classifies Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) under the Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders chapter, requiring: (A) preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear only slight to others; (B) at some point during the course of the disorder, the person has performed repetitive behaviors (e.g., mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (e.g., comparing their appearance with that of others) in response to the appearance concerns; (C) the preoccupation causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning; (D) the appearance preoccupation is not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight in an individual whose symptoms meet diagnostic criteria for an eating disorder. These criteria, and the rationale for the wording changes from DSM-IV (including the addition of criterion B to explicitly capture compulsive BDD behaviors, and refinement of criteria C/D to sharpen the eating-disorder boundary), were reviewed and recommended by the pre-DSM-5 nosology working group (Phillips KA, Wilhelm S, Koran LM, Didie ER, Fallon BA, Feusner J, Stein DJ, 'Body dysmorphic disorder: some key issues for DSM-V', Depress Anxiety 2010, PMID 20533368). MUSCLE DYSMORPHIA SPECIFIER (real, but with an honest evidentiary caveat): DSM-5 added a 'with muscle dysmorphia' specifier for BDD patients preoccupied with the idea that their body build is too small or insufficiently muscular, tracing to the original case-series description and proposed diagnostic criteria (Pope HG Jr, Gruber AJ, Choi P, Olivardia R, Phillips KA, 'Muscle dysmorphia. An underrecognized form of body dysmorphic disorder', Psychosomatics 1997, PMID 9427852); its inclusion as a specifier (rather than a standalone diagnosis) was explicitly recommended for clinical utility despite limited data (Phillips et al., PMID 20533368, point 7). However, a systematic review of 34 eligible studies published 1997-2014 found the existing evidence -- mostly small, cross-sectional, non-clinical-sample studies at the lowest methodological-quality tier -- does not fulfil established (Blashfield et al.) criteria for the validity, clinical utility, or nosological classification of muscle dysmorphia as its own diagnostic entity; 41% of the publications reviewed considered the evidence insufficient to support inclusion of muscle dysmorphia in any existing psychiatric category (Santos Filho CA, Tirico PP, Stefano SC, Touyz SW, Claudino AM, 'Systematic review of the diagnostic category muscle dysmorphia', Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2016, PMID 26553217) -- i.e., DSM-5 correctly places it as a specifier of BDD, not (yet) a separately validated disorder, and this evidentiary gap should not be minimised. INSIGHT SPECIFIERS (real, unified nosology since DSM-5): DSM-III-R and DSM-IV split BDD's delusional form (the patient has complete conviction the perceived defect is real) into the psychosis section as a type of delusional disorder, somatic type, separate from nondelusional BDD in the somatoform section, despite little empirical evidence supporting that split at the time. A systematic evidence review found BDD's delusional and nondelusional variants share far more similarities than differences across validators, including similar response to serotonergic pharmacotherapy, and recommended -- and DSM-5 adopted -- classifying both forms as the SAME disorder with a single insight specifier spanning good/fair insight, poor insight, to absent insight/delusional beliefs (Phillips KA, Hart AS, Simpson HB, Stein DJ, 'Delusional versus nondelusional body dysmorphic disorder: recommendations for DSM-5', CNS Spectr 2014, PMID 23659348). This is clinically load-bearing: a delusional-intensity BDD presentation is not automatically a primary psychotic disorder requiring antipsychotic-first management -- SSRIs remain an appropriate first-line treatment across the insight spectrum, mirroring how OCD's own insight specifier was established (see this KB's obsessive_compulsive_disorder entry; Leckman JF et al., PMID 20217853).
symptoms.clinical_presentation: The core mechanism mirrors OCD's obsession-compulsion cycle but is appearance-focused: a preoccupying belief that a specific body part (most commonly hair, nose, or skin) has a defect that is objectively absent or slight triggers marked distress, which drives repetitive behaviors or mental acts aimed at checking, hiding, fixing, or gaining reassurance about the perceived flaw; these behaviors provide only transient relief, reinforcing the cycle on re-exposure. In one of the earliest detailed clinical case series (30 DSM-III-R BDD patients, 17 men/13 women), the most common perceived defects involved the hair, nose, and skin, with a lifetime average of four separate bodily preoccupations per patient; 73% of patients reported excessive mirror checking, 63% reported attempts to camouflage their perceived defect (e.g., with makeup, hairstyle, clothing, posture, or body positioning), and 73% reported associated ideas or delusions of reference (the belief that other people specifically notice or mock the perceived defect) (Phillips KA, McElroy SL, Keck PE Jr, Pope HG Jr, Hudson JI, 'Body dysmorphic disorder: 30 cases of imagined ugliness', Am J Psychiatry 1993, PMID 8422082). A more recent clinical review confirms the same core repetitive-behavior repertoire -- mirror checking, camouflaging, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance-seeking about appearance from others, and repeatedly comparing one's appearance with that of other people -- matching DSM-5's own criterion B examples, and notes insight into the irrationality of these beliefs and behaviors is often poor (Singh AR, Veale D, 'Understanding and treating body dysmorphic disorder', Indian J Psychiatry 2019, PMID 30745686). The functional consequence is severe and typically hidden from clinicians because of shame: in the same 1993 case series, 97% of patients avoided normal social or occupational activities because of their symptoms, and 30% had been housebound at some point (PMID 8422082). A validated, clinician-administered severity instrument exists specifically for BDD -- the 12-item Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale Modified for Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD-YBOCS), developed and validated in a sample of 125 BDD subjects with good interrater and test-retest reliability and demonstrated sensitivity to treatment-related change (Phillips KA, Hollander E, Rasmussen SA, Aronowitz BR, DeCaria C, Goodman WK, 'A severity rating scale for body dysmorphic disorder: development, reliability, and validity of a modified version of the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale', Psychopharmacol Bull 1997, PMID 9133747), with its factor structure and construct validity still being actively refined in current research (Wilhelm S et al., J Obsessive Compuls Relat Disord 2024, PMID 39866242).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Diagnosis rests on the DSM-5 four-criterion structure above (Phillips KA et al., PMID 20533368), and two differentials are clinically load-bearing rather than academic. DIFFERENTIATING FROM NORMAL APPEARANCE CONCERNS: mild dissatisfaction with one's appearance is near-universal and not pathological; the pre-DSM-5 nosology review explicitly concluded that 'a clinical significance criterion seems necessary for BDD to differentiate it from normal appearance concerns' (Phillips et al., PMID 20533368) -- i.e., the diagnostic threshold is not the presence of appearance concern itself but (a) the concern being about a defect that is objectively absent or slight to an outside observer, combined with (b) clinically significant distress or functional impairment, and (c) the presence of associated repetitive behaviors/mental acts (criterion B), not merely occasional grooming or checking. DIFFERENTIATING FROM EATING DISORDERS: BDD and eating disorders share overlapping features (both are appearance/body-image-focused and both involve repetitive body-checking or avoidance behaviors); DSM-5 criterion D resolves this by excluding a BDD diagnosis when the appearance preoccupation is better explained by concerns about body fat or weight in a person who meets criteria for an eating disorder -- concern exclusively about being fat/overweight in the context of disordered eating is coded as an eating disorder, whereas concern about other body regions (skin, hair, nose, muscularity, etc.), with or without co-occurring weight concerns, supports a BDD diagnosis (Phillips et al., PMID 20533368, point 4). A further historical misclassification is instructive: ICD-10 classified BDD as a form of hypochondriacal disorder (illness-anxiety-focused), but the same nosology review found 'no empirical evidence that BDD and hypochondriasis are the same disorder' and judged ICD-10's hypochondriacal-disorder criteria unsuitable for BDD (Phillips et al., PMID 20533368, point 8) -- ICD-11 has since corrected this by giving BDD its own place in the Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders grouping rather than under illness-anxiety disorders (Stein DJ et al., PMID 26590514).
symptoms.natural_history: EPIDEMIOLOGY (real, population-representative): a nationwide German survey of 2,510 adults found current DSM-IV BDD prevalence of 1.8% by self-report criteria (Buhlmann U, Glaesmer H, Mewes R, Fama JM, Wilhelm S, Brahler E, Rief W, 'Updates on the prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder: a population-based survey', Psychiatry Res 2010, PMID 20452057). Prevalence is markedly higher, and markedly underdetected, in clinical settings: a US Veterans Affairs primary-care behavioral-health clinic found 11% current and 12% lifetime BDD among 100 patients, of whom only 8.3% had ever actually been diagnosed with BDD -- i.e., the disorder is substantially underdiagnosed even inside mental-health settings -- and BDD was significantly associated with elevated rates of suicide attempts, major depression, and OCD (Kelly MM, Zhang J, Phillips KA, Psychiatry Res 2015, PMID 25935375). CHRONICITY: in the earliest detailed case series, mean age of BDD onset was 15 years and mean illness duration was 18 years at the time of assessment, indicating a typically adolescent-onset, long-chronicity course (Phillips KA et al., Am J Psychiatry 1993, PMID 8422082). LONGITUDINAL COURSE (real, naturalistic, up to 8-year follow-up): in the Harvard/Brown Anxiety Research Project, a prospective naturalistic study of 514 participants ascertained for anxiety disorders, BDD prevalence was 3.3% current/4.3% lifetime at baseline, and BDD was associated with significantly poorer global functioning than not having BDD; over up to 8 years of follow-up, the probability of full recovery from BDD was 0.76 and the probability of recurrence once remitted was 0.14 (Bjornsson AS, Dyck I, Moitra E, Stout RL, Weisberg RB, Keller MB, Phillips KA, 'The clinical course of body dysmorphic disorder in the Harvard/Brown Anxiety Research Project (HARP)', J Nerv Ment Dis 2011, PMID 21206248) -- note this cohort was ascertained for anxiety disorders generally, not specifically for treatment-seeking BDD, so this relatively favourable recovery figure should not be over-generalised to severe, treatment-refractory BDD clinical samples, where the 1993 case series above (mean 18-year duration at presentation, PMID 8422082) suggests a much more chronic picture. COMORBIDITY (real, high across studies): in the 1993 case series, lifetime comorbidity was 93% for a major mood disorder, 73% for an anxiety disorder, and 33% for a psychotic disorder (PMID 8422082). In a large OCD cohort (N=605), the subgroup with comorbid presumed BDD had significantly higher rates of lifetime traumatic-event exposure and presumed PTSD than OCD patients without BDD, and among those with comorbid PTSD, significantly higher rates of major depressive disorder and panic disorder (Valderrama J, Hansen SK, Pato C, Phillips K, Knowles J, Pato MT, Psychiatry Res 2020, PMID 32446006). Net real-world picture: BDD is a common, frequently adolescent-onset, often-chronic, and substantially underdiagnosed disorder with very high psychiatric comorbidity, but naturalistic follow-up data show meaningful recovery is achievable in a general (non-severely-refractory) population -- chronicity is common but is not the universal or inevitable course, and this supports the treatment-response data covered elsewhere in this KB rather than a fatalistic natural-history picture.

adjustment_disorder.name: Adjustment Disorder
adjustment_disorder.icd11_hint: ICD-11: Adjustment disorder, Chapter 06 Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, 'Disorders specifically associated with stress' grouping (widely cited in the literature as code 6B43, but the exact alphanumeric code was not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-11 browser source in this research session and is therefore stated with moderate confidence only); ICD-10 F43.2 Adjustment disorders (the diagnostic code used by Casey P et al., J Affect Disord 2015;174:441-446, PMID 25553405, to diagnose their real adjustment-disorder patient cohort).
adjustment_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Active suicidality / suicide risk in a person with suspected or diagnosed adjustment disorder is a real, life-threatening emergency and MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow, triggering immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the nearest emergency department NOW, or call a local emergency/suicide helpline) rather than the routine consultation flow. This override is especially critical in adjustment disorder because clinicians and patients commonly under-rate its risk: the MSD Manual Professional Version explicitly notes that adjustment disorder carries an increased suicide risk despite sometimes being viewed as a 'mild' diagnosis (MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders', merckmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-24). Two real studies quantify exactly why the 'mild diagnosis' assumption is dangerous here. First, in 370 psychiatric/liaison-psychiatry patients diagnosed with either adjustment disorder or a depressive episode across three Dublin hospitals, those with adjustment disorder became suicidal at LOWER depressive-symptom severity scores than those with a full depressive episode -- i.e. a patient can turn suicidal in adjustment disorder before their mood symptoms look 'severe enough' to worry about by depressive-episode standards (Casey P, Jabbar F, O'Leary E, Doherty AM, 'Suicidal behaviours in adjustment disorder and depressive episode', J Affect Disord 2015;174:441-446, PMID 25553405). Second, a psychological autopsy study of 19 adolescent suicide victims found that the suicidal process in those diagnosed with adjustment disorder was significantly SHORTER and more rapidly evolving than in suicide victims with other psychiatric diagnoses, with no prior history of emotional or behavioural problems in adolescence -- meaning the acute-stressor context of adjustment disorder can produce a fast, low-warning escalation to suicide risk rather than the longer prodrome a clinician might expect to be able to catch (Portzky G, Audenaert K, van Heeringen K, 'Adjustment disorder and the course of the suicidal process in adolescents', J Affect Disord 2005;87(2-3):265-270, PMID 16005078). Trigger pattern for override: any current suicidal ideation with a plan and/or intent, any preparatory acts (e.g. acquiring means, writing a note, giving away possessions), any actual, interrupted or aborted suicide attempt, or a patient/carer who says they cannot guarantee their own safety -- applied with a LOWER threshold of clinical suspicion in adjustment disorder than the apparent mood-symptom severity alone would suggest, precisely because of the two findings above. A candidate-medicine-plus-efficacy% suggestion must never be the first or only output when any of these red flags are present; safety triage and real-world emergency-service guidance comes first, medicine selection second.

dsm5tr_subtypes.finding: DSM-5-TR classifies adjustment disorder into six subtypes based on the predominant symptom presentation: (1) with depressed mood, (2) with anxiety, (3) with mixed anxiety and depressed mood, (4) with disturbance of conduct, (5) with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct, and (6) unspecified (for maladaptive reactions not otherwise classifiable in the above). DSM-5-TR does not specify these symptom criteria in further operationalised detail beyond the subtype label itself, and most real patients present with a mixed rather than an isolated symptom pattern.
dsm5tr_subtypes.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (merckmanuals.com, accessed 2026-09-24), summarising DSM-5-TR criteria

icd11_alternative_symptom_model.finding: ICD-11 breaks from DSM-5-TR's mood/conduct-subtype model and instead defines adjustment disorder by two core symptom domains: (1) preoccupation with the stressor or its consequences (excessive worry, rumination, or intrusive thoughts about it) and (2) failure to adapt (impaired ability to manage day-to-day functioning because of the stressor). This is a genuinely different diagnostic concept from DSM-5-TR's subtype system, not merely a relabeling, and the two frameworks are not guaranteed to identify the same patients.
icd11_alternative_symptom_model.source: Zelviene P, Kazlauskas E, 'Adjustment disorder: current perspectives', Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2018;14:375-381 (PMID 29416339); Bachem R, Casey P, 'Adjustment disorder: A diagnosis whose time has come', J Affect Disord 2018;227:243-253 (PMID 29107817)

core_presentation.finding: Adjustment disorder presents as emotional or behavioural symptoms that develop in direct response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor (e.g. job loss, relationship breakdown, a new medical diagnosis, financial crisis), with onset within 3 months of the stressor per DSM-5-TR (or within 1 month per ICD-11 -- see diagnostic_framework). Symptoms must cause clinically significant distress that is out of proportion to the severity of the stressor, and/or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, without meeting full criteria for another mental disorder.
core_presentation.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (accessed 2026-09-24), DSM-5-TR criteria; Zelviene P, Kazlauskas E, Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2018;14:375-381 (PMID 29416339), ICD-11 timing criteria

real_world_prevalence_context.finding: Adjustment disorder is common but its measured prevalence varies enormously with population and diagnostic algorithm: an estimated 1-2% in the general population, but far higher in stressor-exposed or clinical samples -- up to 18.9% among injury survivors at 3-month follow-up, and 9.2% among Swedish primary-care patients. In a dedicated high-risk cohort of 330 people who had involuntarily lost their job (the Zurich Adjustment Disorder Study), 27.3% reported the ICD-11 AjD core symptom pattern, and 13.8% of men and 17.2% of women met the full ICD-11 diagnostic criteria including the exclusion algorithm.
real_world_prevalence_context.source: Zelviene P, Kazlauskas E, Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2018;14:375-381 (PMID 29416339); Perkonigg A, Lorenz L, Maercker A, 'Prevalence and correlates of ICD-11 adjustment disorder: Findings from the Zurich Adjustment Disorder Study', Int J Clin Health Psychol 2018;18(3):209-217 (PMID 30487926)
real_world_prevalence_context.confidence: high for the Zurich cohort figures (a real, direct-measurement study); moderate for the general-population 1-2% estimate, which the source review itself flags as unreliable because no single established diagnostic algorithm is used consistently across studies

dsm5_vs_icd11_divergence.finding: DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 use materially different diagnostic concepts for the same disorder name. DSM-5-TR requires onset within 3 months of the stressor and classifies by symptom subtype (depressed mood/anxiety/conduct, see classification); ICD-11 requires onset within 1 month of the stressor and instead requires two specific core symptoms -- preoccupation with the stressor and failure to adapt. Both frameworks require that symptoms resolve within 6 months after the stressor and its consequences have ended, and both require that the presentation does not meet full criteria for another mental or behavioural disorder -- i.e. adjustment disorder is, in practice, a diagnosis of exclusion in both systems.
dsm5_vs_icd11_divergence.source: Zelviene P, Kazlauskas E, Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2018;14:375-381 (PMID 29416339); Bachem R, Casey P, J Affect Disord 2018;227:243-253 (PMID 29107817); MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (accessed 2026-09-24)

differentiating_from_normal_stress_respo.finding: Because almost everyone reacts emotionally to a significant stressor, the diagnostic line between adjustment disorder and a normal, non-pathological stress reaction rests on two criteria rather than the presence of distress alone: the distress must be clearly out of proportion to the severity or nature of the stressor, and/or it must cause clinically significant impairment in functioning. A stress reaction that is proportionate and does not impair functioning does not meet criteria, however unpleasant it feels to the patient.
differentiating_from_normal_stress_respo.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (accessed 2026-09-24), DSM-5-TR criteria

differentiating_from_ptsd_and_acute_stre.finding: Adjustment disorder is differentiated from PTSD and acute stress disorder primarily by the nature of the stressor and the symptom cluster required: PTSD and acute stress disorder require exposure to a specifically traumatic/life-threatening stressor and a defined cluster of intrusion, avoidance, negative-mood, and hyperarousal symptoms, whereas adjustment disorder can follow any identifiable stressor (traumatic or not, e.g. divorce, job loss, illness) and does not require that specific symptom cluster. If full PTSD/acute stress disorder criteria are met, that diagnosis takes precedence over adjustment disorder.
differentiating_from_ptsd_and_acute_stre.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (accessed 2026-09-24), DSM-5-TR differential diagnosis

differentiating_from_mdd_and_anxiety_dis.finding: If a patient's symptoms meet full criteria for major depressive disorder, an anxiety disorder, or another specific mental disorder, that diagnosis is used instead of adjustment disorder, even if a clear stressor triggered it -- adjustment disorder is reserved for clinically significant stress reactions that fall short of another disorder's full criteria. This exclusionary rule has a real safety implication that must not be misread as reassuring: in a study of 370 psychiatric/liaison-psychiatry patients, those diagnosed with adjustment disorder became suicidal at LOWER depressive-symptom severity scores than those diagnosed with a full depressive episode, so the 'lesser' diagnostic label does not track a lower level of real suicide risk (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
differentiating_from_mdd_and_anxiety_dis.source: MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (accessed 2026-09-24); Casey P, Jabbar F, O'Leary E, Doherty AM, J Affect Disord 2015;174:441-446 (PMID 25553405)

real_excellent_prognosis_lead_finding.finding: The best real long-term outcome data on adjustment disorder comes from a 5-year prospective follow-up of 100 patients originally diagnosed with the disorder: 79% of the adults were completely well at follow-up (with a further 8% having had only an intervening problem before recovering), and most of the small minority who did go on to a further diagnosis developed major depression or alcoholism, not a severe or psychotic illness. Chronicity of the original presentation and behavioural (conduct) symptoms were the strongest predictors of the minority who did poorly -- i.e. the disorder itself has a genuinely good real-world prognosis for most patients, and the identifiable risk markers for the worse-course minority are already known rather than unpredictable.
real_excellent_prognosis_lead_finding.source: Andreasen NC, Hoenk PR, 'The predictive value of adjustment disorders: a follow-up study', Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(5):584-590 (PMID 7072842)
real_excellent_prognosis_lead_finding.confidence: high - real prospective 5-year follow-up, the original validating outcome study for this diagnosis

adolescent_outcome_caveat.finding: The same 1982 follow-up study found a less favourable picture in adolescents: 57% were well at 5-year follow-up (13% with only an intervening problem), and those who did become ill went on to a broader range of diagnoses including schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, antisocial personality, alcoholism and drug use disorder -- meaning the excellent-prognosis story is strongest in adults, and adolescent adjustment disorder should be followed more closely rather than assumed to resolve as reliably.
adolescent_outcome_caveat.source: Andreasen NC, Hoenk PR, Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(5):584-590 (PMID 7072842)

resolution_once_stressor_resolves.finding: Both major diagnostic systems build the expectation of resolution directly into the definition: ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR both require that symptoms resolve within 6 months after the stressor and its consequences have ended. Consistent with this, many individuals with adjustment disorder recover without any formal treatment at all, drawing on their own inner resources and existing social support -- the disorder is fundamentally a time-limited, stressor-driven reaction rather than a fixed trait or chronic illness.
resolution_once_stressor_resolves.source: Zelviene P, Kazlauskas E, Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2018;14:375-381 (PMID 29416339); MSD Manual Professional Version, 'Adjustment Disorders' (accessed 2026-09-24)

suicide_risk_despite_good_average_progno.finding: The good average prognosis does not eliminate real acute risk in a subset of patients. Adjustment disorder patients have been shown to become suicidal at lower depressive-symptom severity than those with a full depressive episode, and a psychological autopsy study of adolescent suicide victims found the suicidal process in those with adjustment disorder was significantly shorter and more rapidly evolving, with no prior history of emotional/behavioural problems -- so the excellent long-run prognosis coexists with a real, fast-onset minority risk pathway that requires active screening rather than reassurance alone (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
suicide_risk_despite_good_average_progno.source: Casey P, Jabbar F, O'Leary E, Doherty AM, J Affect Disord 2015;174:441-446 (PMID 25553405); Portzky G, Audenaert K, van Heeringen K, J Affect Disord 2005;87(2-3):265-270 (PMID 16005078)

adjustment_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Adjustment disorder (AjD) is real-world one of the most favourable-prognosis diagnoses in all of psychiatry, and this must be stated plainly rather than hedged. The single most-cited hard number for its natural course is Andreasen NC & Hoenk PR's 5-year prospective follow-up of 100 patients originally diagnosed with adjustment disorder (Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(5):584-590, PMID 7072842): 79% of the adults were completely well at 5-year follow-up (with a further 8% having had only one intervening problem), versus 57% of the adolescents (13% with one intervening problem) -- adults with this diagnosis overwhelmingly do not go on to develop another psychiatric illness. On top of that already-favourable natural course, real active treatment measurably shortens the illness and speeds functional recovery: van der Klink JJ et al's cluster-randomised controlled trial of 192 employees on first sick leave for adjustment disorder (Occup Environ Med 2003;60(6):429-437, PMID 12771395) found that by 12 months essentially ALL patients (192/192, both the structured activating/problem-solving intervention arm and the guideline-based care-as-usual arm) had returned to work, with the active intervention arm getting there faster and with a lower sick-leave recurrence rate. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised controlled trials (3,027 participants total) concluded that both in-person and internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are effective for reducing adjustment-disorder symptoms (Cowansage KP et al, Psychiatry Res 2025;353:116739, PMID 41005147), and an earlier systematic review found that more than half of all tested psychological therapies for adult AjD contained CBT components (O'Donnell ML et al, J Trauma Stress 2018;31(3):321-331, PMID 29958336). The honest caveat, stated directly rather than buried: O'Donnell et al's GRADE appraisal rated the overall quality of the evidence for every psychological and pharmacological treatment as low to very low (small trials, heterogeneous outcome measures, few placebo-controlled designs), and a separate prognosis review of 31 studies covering 1,385,358 participants found that AjD, while generally milder and faster-resolving than other mental disorders, 'not uncommonly' transitions to a more severe mental-health diagnosis over time (Morgan MA et al, J Psychiatr Res 2022;156:498-510, PMID 36347110). None of this changes the bottom line: brief, structured, problem-focused psychotherapy (supportive counselling, CBT, problem-solving/activating therapy) delivered promptly after the stressor is the real, evidence-backed way to convert AjD's already-excellent natural prognosis into a fast, high-probability full functional recovery, and pharmacotherapy has a real but strictly secondary, symptom-limited role (short-course anxiolytic/hypnotic for anxiety or insomnia only) because there is no robust randomised evidence for antidepressants as a primary AjD treatment (Casey P, CNS Drugs 2009;23(11):927-938, PMID 19845414).

curative_option.name: Brief, Structured Psychotherapy (Supportive Counselling / CBT / Problem-Solving-Activating Therapy) Delivered Promptly After the Stressor -- Real Very-High Population-Level Recovery, Riding on Adjustment Disorder's Own Excellent Natural Course
curative_option.note: Adjustment disorder is, by definition, a time-limited stress-response condition (DSM-5/ICD-11 both require onset within 3 months of an identifiable stressor and resolution within 6 months of the stressor or its consequences ending). Real evidence shows two things stack in the patient's favour: (1) the untreated/naturalistic course is already one of the best in psychiatry, and (2) brief, active, problem-focused psychological treatment (supportive psychotherapy, CBT, or a structured problem-solving/activating intervention) measurably shortens the illness and accelerates return to normal functioning on top of that. This combination -- not a single drug or a single dramatic procedure -- is the real closest-to-a-cure pathway for AjD.

real_survival_data.adults_completely_well_at_5_year_natural: 79% (n=100 adult+adolescent cohort at diagnosis; adult subgroup fully well, 8% further had only one intervening problem) -- Andreasen NC, Hoenk PR, Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(5):584-590, PMID 7072842
real_survival_data.adolescents_completely_well_at_5_year_na: 57% (13% further had only one intervening problem) -- same study, PMID 7072842 -- real, lower-prognosis subgroup, driven mainly by chronicity and behavioural symptoms as predictors of poor outcome
real_survival_data.return_to_work_by_12_months_with_active_: 100% (192 of 192 patients on first sick leave for adjustment disorder, intention-to-treat, both the structured activating/problem-solving intervention arm and the guideline-based care-as-usual arm) -- van der Klink JJ et al, Occup Environ Med 2003;60(6):429-437, PMID 12771395; the active intervention arm reached return-to-work significantly faster at 3 months and had a lower sick-leave recurrence rate than care-as-usual
real_survival_data.good_outcome_rate_short_term_dynamic_psy: 50% (16 of 32 consecutive adjustment-disorder patients met reliable-clinical-change criteria for good outcome by the end of up to 40 sessions of short-term dynamic psychotherapy) -- Kramer U, Pascual-Leone A, Despland JN, de Roten Y, J Consult Clin Psychol 2015;83(1):187-198, PMID 25244391

curative_option.source: Andreasen NC, Hoenk PR, 'The predictive value of adjustment disorders: a follow-up study', Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(5):584-590 (PMID 7072842); van der Klink JJ, Blonk RW, Schene AH, van Dijk FJ, 'Reducing long term sickness absence by an activating intervention in adjustment disorders: a cluster randomised controlled design', Occup Environ Med 2003;60(6):429-437 (PMID 12771395); Kramer U, Pascual-Leone A, Despland JN, de Roten Y, 'One minute of grief: emotional processing in short-term dynamic psychotherapy for adjustment disorder', J Consult Clin Psychol 2015;83(1):187-198 (PMID 25244391); Cowansage KP et al, 'Treatments for adjustment disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials', Psychiatry Res 2025;353:116739 (PMID 41005147)
curative_option.important_caveat: The 79%/57% figures are naturalistic follow-up outcomes (not a treatment trial), and the 100% return-to-work figure was reached by BOTH study arms at 12 months (the active intervention's real, verified advantage was speed and recurrence, not a higher final ceiling, since guideline-based Dutch occupational care-as-usual is itself an active, structured brief intervention rather than no treatment). The 50% STDP good-outcome figure is from a single uncontrolled cohort (n=32) rated by reliable-change statistics, not a placebo-controlled percentage. O'Donnell ML et al's 2018 systematic review (PMID 29958336) rated the overall quality of evidence for AjD psychological treatments as low to very low using GRADE, so these real numbers should be read as strong, consistent, real-world signals of a highly favourable, treatment-responsive condition -- not as a single precise, universally-guaranteed cure rate.
curative_option.confidence: high for the real favourable natural-course statistics and the real 12-month return-to-work outcome; moderate for the precise STDP good-outcome percentage given the small uncontrolled cohort

adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.name: Brief Supportive Psychotherapy
adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.type: First-line, real, low-intensity structured counselling psychotherapy (typically 4-8 sessions) focused on the identified stressor
adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.effectiveness: O'Donnell ML et al (J Trauma Stress 2018;31(3):321-331, PMID 29958336), a systematic review of 29 studies on AjD treatment, found supportive/counselling-based approaches among the diverse real psychological therapies tested for AjD, with the majority (59%) of all identified AjD studies testing a psychological rather than pharmacological therapy.
adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.reason_why: AjD is defined by a real, identifiable external stressor rather than an endogenous biological process, so structured emotional support, normalisation of the stress response, and active problem-focused listening directly target the maintaining factor (unresolved distress about the stressor) rather than a neurochemical target, which is why brief supportive work is disproportionately effective here compared with more biologically-driven psychiatric conditions.
adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.real_working_solution: Prompt (within days to a few weeks of the stressor), brief, structured supportive counselling as the real first-line treatment for uncomplicated adjustment disorder, deliverable by a GP, counsellor, or occupational physician without requiring specialist psychiatric referral in most cases.
adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.source: O'Donnell ML, Metcalf O, Watson L, Phelps A, Varker T, J Trauma Stress 2018;31(3):321-331 (PMID 29958336); Casey P, CNS Drugs 2009;23(11):927-938 (PMID 19845414)
adj_brief_supportive_psychotherapy.confidence: high for brief supportive intervention being the real first-line default; moderate for a single population-wide effectiveness percentage given GRADE-rated low-to-very-low evidence quality

adj_cbt_structured.name: Structured Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), In-Person or Internet-Delivered
adj_cbt_structured.type: Real, evidence-supported structured psychotherapy: cognitive restructuring plus behavioural coping/anxiety-control techniques, typically 4-8 sessions
adj_cbt_structured.effectiveness: Cowansage KP et al (Psychiatry Res 2025;353:116739, PMID 41005147), a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised controlled trials totalling 3,027 participants, found that both internet-based and in-person CBT may be effective for reducing adjustment-disorder symptoms -- the most robust, most recent, and largest real evidence base of any AjD treatment reviewed here. Separately, Sanz Cruces JM et al (Span J Psychol 2018;21:E50, PMID 30442217), a randomised primary-care trial of 8 weekly group CBT sessions (n=31 treatment vs n=20 waitlist), found statistically significant post-treatment reductions in anxiety (F=4.11, p=.048, eta-squared=.08) and depressive symptoms (F=2.41, p=.029, eta-squared=.10) and improved physical (eta-squared=.13) and emotional (eta-squared=.18) quality of life versus waitlist.
adj_cbt_structured.reason_why: Cognitive restructuring directly targets the catastrophic or overwhelmed appraisal of the stressor that drives AjD's anxious/depressive symptoms, while behavioural coping-skills training (problem-solving, activity scheduling, relaxation) rebuilds the functional coping capacity that the acute stressor disrupted -- mechanistically matched to a condition defined by a real external precipitant rather than an endogenous mood/anxiety disorder.
adj_cbt_structured.important_caveat: The 2025 meta-analysis (PMID 41005147) itself calls for more RCTs to confirm which specific treatment strategies work best; it did not report a single pooled population-wide remission percentage in its abstract. The Sanz Cruces 2018 primary-care RCT (PMID 30442217) reports statistically significant effect sizes, not a remission/response percentage.
adj_cbt_structured.real_working_solution: 4-8 sessions of structured CBT (in-person or internet-delivered) as the best-evidenced, most-studied real psychotherapy for adjustment disorder as of the most recent (2025) meta-analysis of randomised trials.
adj_cbt_structured.source: Cowansage KP, Milligan T, Morgan MA, et al, Psychiatry Res 2025;353:116739 (PMID 41005147); Sanz Cruces JM et al, Span J Psychol 2018;21:E50 (PMID 30442217); Fernández-Buendía S et al, J Affect Disord 2024;347:29-38 (PMID 37992766, technology-supported treatments meta-analysis of 9 studies also showing superior efficacy of intervention groups over control)
adj_cbt_structured.confidence: high that structured CBT is real, evidence-supported, and the most-studied AjD psychotherapy; moderate for any single precise population-wide effectiveness percentage, since the primary meta-analyses report pooled statistical significance/effect sizes rather than a single agreed remission rate

adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.name: Structured Problem-Solving / Activating Therapy (Occupational-Medicine Model)
adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.type: Real, manualised brief intervention combining problem-solving therapy with graded activity/return-to-function coaching, originally developed and RCT-tested for work-related adjustment disorder
adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.effectiveness: van der Klink JJ et al (Occup Environ Med 2003;60(6):429-437, PMID 12771395), a cluster-randomised controlled trial of 192 employees on first sick leave for adjustment disorder, found the structured activating/problem-solving intervention produced significantly faster return to work at 3 months and a lower sickness-leave recurrence rate than guideline-based care as usual; by 12 months, 100% of patients in both arms had returned to work.
adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.reason_why: The intervention reframes the patient's role from a passive 'sick' role to an active problem-solver working through the specific real-world obstacles (workplace conflict, role overload, bereavement-related disruption, etc) that the stressor created, which directly targets AjD's defining feature -- impaired coping with an identifiable stressor -- rather than treating it as a generic mood or anxiety syndrome.
adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.real_working_solution: A structured, few-session problem-solving/activating intervention as the real best-evidenced treatment specifically for work/functional-impairment-predominant adjustment disorder, with a real, verified 100% 12-month return-to-work outcome in a 192-patient cluster-RCT.
adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.source: van der Klink JJ, Blonk RW, Schene AH, van Dijk FJ, Occup Environ Med 2003;60(6):429-437 (PMID 12771395)
adj_problem_solving_activating_therapy.confidence: high -- real cluster-randomised controlled trial with intention-to-treat analysis and a clear, verified outcome

adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.name: Short-Term Symptomatic Medication for Specific Anxiety or Sleep Symptoms (Adjunct Only, Not a Substitute for Psychotherapy)
adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.type: Real, time-limited pharmacological symptom control -- non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic (etifoxine) or, where used, a short benzodiazepine/hypnotic course -- reserved for distressing anxiety or insomnia that impairs the patient's ability to engage with psychotherapy
adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.effectiveness: Stein DJ (Adv Ther 2015;32(1):57-68, PMID 25620535), a double-blind RCT of 202 outpatients with adjustment disorder with anxiety across 17 primary-care sites, found etifoxine (150 mg/day) non-inferior to alprazolam (1.5 mg/day) on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale at day 28, with etifoxine showing continued improvement after treatment discontinuation (versus symptom rebound with alprazolam) and fewer treatment-related adverse events. An earlier double-blind trial (Servant D et al, Encephale 1998;24(6):569-574, PMID 9949940, n=170) found etifoxine's global improvement and efficacy index significantly better than buspirone.
adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.important_caveat: Casey P (CNS Drugs 2009;23(11):927-938, PMID 19845414) states plainly that there are no robust studies demonstrating benefit from antidepressants in adjustment disorder, and that pharmacotherapy here is limited to symptomatic management of anxiety or insomnia, not a primary or curative treatment. Neither the Stein 2015 nor the Servant 1998 trial reports a specific population responder/remission percentage in the abstract; both report scale-score and comparative-efficacy outcomes.
adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.real_working_solution: A short, time-limited course of a non-dependence-forming anxiolytic (etifoxine) or, second-line and with caution, a brief benzodiazepine course, used only as a bridge to control acute anxiety/insomnia symptoms while brief psychotherapy (the real primary treatment) takes effect -- not as a stand-alone treatment for adjustment disorder.
adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.source: Stein DJ, Adv Ther 2015;32(1):57-68 (PMID 25620535); Servant D, Graziani PL, Moyse D, Parquet PJ, Encephale 1998;24(6):569-574 (PMID 9949940); Casey P, CNS Drugs 2009;23(11):927-938 (PMID 19845414)
adj_short_term_symptomatic_medication.confidence: high for the real adjunct-only, symptom-limited role of pharmacotherapy; moderate for etifoxine's comparative-efficacy numbers given industry sponsorship of the 2015 trial

adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.name: Psychoeducation and Stress-Management / Relaxation Training
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.type: Real, low-intensity adjunct intervention: explaining the real, time-limited nature of AjD, normalising the stress response, and teaching structured relaxation/stress-management skills
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.effectiveness: O'Donnell ML et al (J Trauma Stress 2018;31(3):321-331, PMID 29958336) identified relaxation-technique-based interventions among the real psychological therapies tested for AjD (2 of 29 included studies); Hsiao FH et al (Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2014;36(2):214-219, PMID 24342115), a randomised trial of an 8-week body-mind-spirit group psychotherapy (n=34) versus one-session psychoeducation control (n=37) in AjD with depressed mood, found no significant differential change in self-reported depression/anxiety between groups, but did find a significant reduction in suicidal ideation and a favourable shift in diurnal cortisol patterns in the active psychotherapy group.
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.reason_why: Psychoeducation reduces the real, common fear that AjD symptoms mean a permanent or severe mental illness (directly leveraging the real 79% five-year full-recovery statistic above), while structured relaxation/stress-management skills give the patient an active, practicable tool for the acute physiological arousal the stressor produced.
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.important_caveat: The Hsiao 2014 RCT (PMID 24342115) is an important honest negative-adjacent finding: on its primary depression/anxiety outcome, one-session psychoeducation alone performed no differently from 8 weeks of active group psychotherapy, which argues psychoeducation has real value but should not be treated as a full substitute for structured CBT/problem-solving therapy when depressive symptoms or suicidal ideation are prominent.
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.real_working_solution: Structured psychoeducation (explaining AjD's real, time-limited, highly favourable natural course) combined with basic stress-management/relaxation skills as a real, low-cost adjunct suitable for every patient, alongside -- not instead of -- brief supportive psychotherapy or CBT when symptoms are more than mild.
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.source: O'Donnell ML, Metcalf O, Watson L, Phelps A, Varker T, J Trauma Stress 2018;31(3):321-331 (PMID 29958336); Hsiao FH et al, Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2014;36(2):214-219 (PMID 24342115)
adj_psychoeducation_stress_management.confidence: moderate -- real trial data exists but is mixed/limited on primary symptom outcomes

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from methodologically different sources (a naturalistic 5-year follow-up cohort, a 12-month cluster-randomised intention-to-treat outcome, and a small uncontrolled reliable-change cohort) and are not a single head-to-head comparison of treatments on one shared outcome measure. O'Donnell ML et al (J Trauma Stress 2018;31(3):321-331, PMID 29958336) rated the overall quality of evidence for AjD treatments as low to very low using GRADE; these numbers should be read as real, consistent, replicated-in-direction signals that adjustment disorder is a highly favourable-prognosis, highly treatment-responsive condition, not as precisely comparable head-to-head effectiveness figures.

ranked_high_to_low.type: Real-world functional-recovery outcome, structured brief psychosocial intervention
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Percentage of patients (n=192) who had returned to work by 12-month follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.source: van der Klink JJ, Blonk RW, Schene AH, van Dijk FJ, Occup Environ Med 2003;60(6):429-437 (PMID 12771395)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Andreasen NC, Hoenk PR, Am J Psychiatry 1982;139(5):584-590 (PMID 7072842)

conduct_disorder.name: Conduct Disorder
conduct_disorder.icd11_hint: ICD-11 6C91 Conduct-dissocial disorder (WHO ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics, grouped under 'Disruptive behaviour or dissocial disorders'), the successor to ICD-10 F91 Conduct disorders; DSM-5-TR retains a discrete category, 312.81/312.82/312.89 Conduct Disorder (childhood-onset type/adolescent-onset type/unspecified onset), with an optional 'with limited prosocial emotions' specifier. This KB verified the ICD-11 top-level code (6C91) directly against the WHO ICD-11 reference this session; the exact numeric onset sub-codes under 6C91 could not be independently confirmed this session (the WHO browser is JavaScript-rendered and not machine-readable via fetch) and are therefore not stated as fact here - only the DSM-5-TR onset-type wording, which is independently verified, is used for the onset classification below.
conduct_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Unlike adult antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), where two 2020 Cochrane reviews found the treatment evidence base essentially insufficient to draw any conclusion, Conduct Disorder in children and adolescents is the one point in the antisocial spectrum with real, randomised, replicated trial evidence that structured family- and community-based intervention can genuinely reduce -- not merely describe -- antisocial behaviour, arrests, incarceration time and later psychopathology. The original Multisystemic Therapy (MST) randomised trial found MST youths had fewer arrests, fewer self-reported offenses and 10 fewer weeks incarcerated than youths receiving usual state youth services (Henggeler SW, Melton GB, Smith LA, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(6):953-961, PMID 1460157, n=84), and a randomised trial of Parent Management Training combined with child-directed Problem-Solving Skills Training in children referred for severe antisocial behaviour found combined treatment placed a greater proportion of children within the normal, nonclinic range of functioning than either treatment alone, with durable gains at 1-year follow-up (Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747, PMID 1401389, n=97). An early pooled meta-analysis of MST (Curtis NM et al., J Fam Psychol 2004;18(3):411-419, PMID 15382965, 7 studies/708 participants) reported treated youths/families functioning better than roughly 70% of comparison youths/families post-treatment (d=0.55), though this fell to d=0.26 in real-world community-therapist studies versus d=0.81 in tightly supervised efficacy trials. Honestly, the newest and most methodologically rigorous synthesis -- a 2025 correlated-hierarchical-effects meta-analysis judged against a minimum clinically important difference rather than statistical significance alone -- found only limited evidence that MST or Functional Family Therapy (FFT) are superior to usual care in reducing delinquent/antisocial behaviour in adolescence specifically (Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446, PMID 39428056, 16 RCTs/4,095 participants for MST, 7 RCTs/1,471 for FFT), directly correcting the more favourable earlier evidence-clearinghouse ratings these programs had received. Reading both bodies of evidence honestly together: real, replicated benefit exists, it is real-world modest rather than curative in the sense of eliminating the disorder, and the most rigorous synthesis available finds it most reliable the earlier in childhood the intervention starts (this knowledge base's antisocial_personality_disorder entry documents the strongest single body of evidence, the 25-year Fast Track kindergarten prevention trial, for exactly this reason).
