No single medicine treats or cures Conduct Disorder itself; pharmacotherapy in this knowledge base is confined to symptom-targeted management of comorbid ADHD or severe aggression, per the AACAP practice parameter (Steiner H, American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 'Practice parameters for the assessment and treatment of children and adolescents with conduct disorder', J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997;36(10 Suppl):122S-139S, PMID 9334568), which places psychosocial, family-based intervention -- not medication -- as the foundation of treatment.

curative_option.name: Early Intensive Family- and Community-Based Intervention (Multisystemic Therapy, Parent Management Training, Functional Family Therapy) -- Real Best-Evidence Pathway, Strongest the Earlier It Is Applied Before Adolescence Consolidates the Disorder; NOT a Guaranteed Cure
curative_option.note: Across the real trial literature surveyed for this knowledge base, no single medicine or single-session intervention reverses Conduct Disorder; the best-evidenced real lever is intensive, manualised, multi-system psychosocial treatment delivered to the child and family together, started as early as possible. Three distinct but related programs make up this pathway: Multisystemic Therapy (MST, intensive home/community-based family therapy targeting family, peer, school and neighbourhood systems simultaneously), Parent Management Training (PMT, structured retraining of parental discipline/reinforcement practices to break coercive parent-child cycles), and Functional Family Therapy (FFT, shorter structured family-systems therapy). This mirrors, at the adolescent stage, the same real prevention logic documented in this knowledge base's antisocial_personality_disorder entry for the kindergarten-stage Fast Track program.

real_trial_data.mst_original_rct_arrests_and_incarcerati: In a randomised trial of 84 serious juvenile offenders and their multiproblem families, youths assigned to MST (delivered through a community mental health centre) had fewer arrests and fewer self-reported offenses than youths receiving usual Department of Youth Services care, and spent an average of 10 fewer weeks incarcerated over 59-week follow-up; MST families also reported increased family cohesion and decreased youth aggression in peer relations (Henggeler SW, Melton GB, Smith LA, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(6):953-961, PMID 1460157, n=84).
real_trial_data.pmt_plus_psst_rct_normative_functioning: In a randomised trial of 97 children aged 7-13 referred for severe antisocial behaviour, Problem-Solving Skills Training (PSST) combined with Parent Management Training (PMT) produced more marked, pervasive and durable improvement in child and parent functioning than either treatment alone, and placed a greater proportion of children within the normal (nonclinic) range of functioning, sustained to 1-year follow-up (Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747, PMID 1401389, n=97).
real_trial_data.mst_pooled_early_meta_analysis: A meta-analysis of 7 primary MST outcome studies (708 participants) found a pooled effect of d=0.55, meaning treated youths/families functioned better than roughly 70% of comparison youths/families post-treatment, but the effect fell to d=0.26 in real-world studies using community therapists versus d=0.81 in tightly supervised graduate-student efficacy trials (Curtis NM et al., J Fam Psychol 2004;18(3):411-419, PMID 15382965).

curative_option.source: Henggeler SW et al., J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(6):953-961 (PMID 1460157); Kazdin AE et al., J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747 (PMID 1401389); Curtis NM et al., J Fam Psychol 2004;18(3):411-419 (PMID 15382965)
curative_option.important_caveat: The honest, most rigorous recent evidence tempers this real signal considerably: a 2025 correlated-hierarchical-effects meta-analysis, judged against a minimum clinically important difference rather than statistical significance alone, found 'limited evidence that these interventions are superior to usual care in reducing delinquent and antisocial behavior in adolescence' for MST (16 RCTs, 4,095 participants -- only time in out-of-home care showed a likely clinically important effect, with no clinically important effect on delinquency, new offences/convictions, placement, or substance use) and low-strength evidence for FFT (7 RCTs, 1,471 participants -- possible but not confidently established effects on new offences/convictions, time in out-of-home care, and substance use) (Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446, PMID 39428056). This is a direct, more rigorous correction of the earlier, more favourable 2004 meta-analysis and of some evidence-clearinghouse ratings. Neither the original 1992 trials nor the pooled meta-analyses report a remission/cure percentage for Conduct Disorder itself; they report reductions in arrests, incarceration, or the proportion reaching normative functioning, all of which are real but partial, not complete-cure, outcomes.
curative_option.confidence: moderate -- real, randomised original trials (Henggeler 1992, Kazdin 1992) support genuine reduction in antisocial/delinquent outcomes, and this is the strongest psychosocial-treatment evidence for a diagnosable Conduct Disorder population anywhere in the antisocial spectrum surveyed in this knowledge base, but the newest, most rigorous 2025 meta-analytic reassessment finds only limited evidence that MST/FFT specifically outperform usual care in adolescence, so the honest reading is 'real, replicated, partial benefit, strongest earlier in childhood' rather than an established cure rate.

condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.name: Multisystemic Therapy (MST) -- Original Randomised Trial Versus Usual Youth Services (Henggeler 1992)
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.type: Not a drug: intensive, manualised home- and community-based family therapy delivered by therapists with small caseloads, targeting family, peer, school and neighbourhood systems simultaneously
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.effectiveness: RCT of 84 serious juvenile offenders and their multiproblem families randomised to MST (via a community mental health centre) versus usual Department of Youth Services care. At 59-week archival follow-up, MST youths had fewer arrests and fewer self-reported offenses, and spent an average of 10 fewer weeks incarcerated than usual-services youths; MST families also reported increased family cohesion and decreased youth aggression in peer relations (Henggeler SW, Melton GB, Smith LA, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(6):953-961, PMID 1460157, n=84). The indexed abstract does not report an exact rearrest percentage, so no effectiveness_pct is claimed for this specific trial.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.reason_why: Conduct Disorder is maintained across multiple real-world systems at once (coercive family discipline patterns, deviant peer affiliation, school failure, neighbourhood risk); MST intervenes in all of these simultaneously rather than treating the child in isolation, on the theory that changing only one system leaves the others free to maintain the behaviour.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.important_caveat: Single-site trial, n=84, no blinded outcome assessment reported in the abstract; the wider, larger, more recent MST evidence base is genuinely contested (see the pooled-meta-analysis entries below), so this original trial should be read as the founding real evidence, not as proof that MST reliably replicates at scale.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.real_working_solution: MST has the longest-standing original randomised-trial evidence of reducing real-world rearrest, self-reported offending and incarceration time in juvenile offenders with conduct-disordered/delinquent behaviour compared with usual state youth services.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.source: Henggeler SW, Melton GB, Smith LA, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(6):953-961 (PMID 1460157)
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.confidence: moderate -- real original RCT, but single-site and small (n=84)

condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.name: Multisystemic Therapy (MST) -- Pooled Effect Across Early Efficacy Trials (Curtis 2004 Meta-Analysis)
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.type: Not a drug: pooled meta-analysis of MST outcome studies
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.effectiveness: Pooled across 7 primary studies (708 participants), average effect d=0.55, i.e. treated youths/families functioning better than roughly 70% of alternatively-treated comparison youths/families post-treatment; this fell to d=0.26 in real-world studies using community therapists versus d=0.81 in tightly supervised graduate-student efficacy trials (Curtis NM et al., J Fam Psychol 2004;18(3):411-419, PMID 15382965).
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.reason_why: Same multi-system mechanism as the original Henggeler trial, pooled across the first generation of MST efficacy and effectiveness studies.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.important_caveat: The gap between supervised efficacy-trial effect size (d=0.81) and real-world community-therapist effect size (d=0.26) is itself a real, documented finding -- MST's benefit is substantially diluted outside tightly controlled research conditions, and this 2004 pooled estimate has since been directly reassessed and tempered by the more rigorous 2025 meta-analysis below.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.real_working_solution: MST shows a real, replicated positive pooled effect across early studies, strongest under close clinical supervision and weaker in ordinary community delivery, which should inform how confidently it is presented to families.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.source: Curtis NM et al., J Fam Psychol 2004;18(3):411-419 (PMID 15382965)
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.confidence: moderate, superseded in part by the 2025 reassessment below

condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.name: Multisystemic Therapy (MST) and Functional Family Therapy (FFT) -- Newest, Most Rigorous 2025 Meta-Analysis Reassessment
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.type: Not a drug: correlated-hierarchical-effects meta-analysis of MST and FFT randomised trials, judged against a minimum clinically important difference rather than statistical significance alone
specific_drugs: Not a drug: Multisystemic Therapy (MST); Functional Family Therapy (FFT)
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.effectiveness: MST (16 RCTs, 4,095 participants): only time in out-of-home care showed a likely clinically important effect versus usual care; no clinically important effect was found on delinquency, new offences/convictions, placement, or substance use. FFT (7 RCTs, 1,471 participants): possible (not confidently established) clinically important effects on new offences/convictions, time in out-of-home care, and substance use, with evidence strength rated low (Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446, PMID 39428056).
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.reason_why: Uses correlated hierarchical effects meta-analysis (accounting for multiple correlated outcomes per trial) and a minimum-clinically-important-difference threshold rather than statistical significance alone, a stricter and more clinically meaningful evidence standard than earlier reviews applied.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.important_caveat: 'Contrary to reports in some evidence clearinghouses indicating that MST/FFT are supported by the highest level of evidence strength, there is limited evidence that these interventions are superior to usual care in reducing delinquent and antisocial behavior in adolescence' (Hunkin et al. 2025, PMID 39428056) -- a direct, recent, methodologically stronger correction of the earlier, more favourable 2004 meta-analysis above.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.real_working_solution: Per the most rigorous 2025 evidence, MST/FFT should not be presented to families as reliably superior to usual community care for reducing adolescent delinquent/antisocial behaviour specifically; they remain widely disseminated, are not harmful, and the original Henggeler/Kazdin trials and earlier meta-analyses still show real, if inconsistently replicated, benefit, so a doctor-directed, honestly-caveated recommendation (rather than an unqualified one) is the defensible position.
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.source: Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446 (PMID 39428056)
condd_multisystemic_therapy_intensive_fa.confidence: moderate, honestly contested -- this is the newest and methodologically strongest synthesis and it tempers the earlier favourable evidence considerably

condd_parent_management_training.name: Parent Management Training (PMT), Alone or Combined With Problem-Solving Skills Training (PSST) -- Randomised Trial in Severe Childhood Antisocial Behaviour (Kazdin 1992)
condd_parent_management_training.type: Not a drug: structured behavioural parent-training program teaching parents consistent, non-coercive discipline, contingency management and positive reinforcement skills, with or without child-directed cognitive problem-solving skills training
specific_drugs: Not a drug: Parent Management Training (PMT) +/- Problem-Solving Skills Training (PSST)
condd_parent_management_training.effectiveness: RCT of 97 children aged 7-13 referred for severe antisocial behaviour, randomised to PSST alone, PMT alone, or PSST+PMT combined. All three conditions improved child functioning (reduced overall deviance and aggressive/antisocial/delinquent behaviour, increased prosocial competence) at posttreatment and 1-year follow-up; PSST+PMT combined produced more marked, pervasive and durable changes in child and parent functioning (parental stress, depression, overall symptoms) and placed a greater proportion of children within the normal (nonclinic) range of functioning than either treatment alone (Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747, PMID 1401389, n=97). The indexed abstract does not report an exact normative-range percentage, so no effectiveness_pct is claimed for this specific trial.
condd_parent_management_training.reason_why: PMT is grounded in coercion-theory models of Conduct Disorder development (Patterson), in which inconsistent, escalating, coercive parent-child discipline cycles inadvertently reinforce the child's aggressive/oppositional behaviour; PMT retrains parents to consistently reinforce prosocial behaviour and apply non-coercive discipline, directly targeting this maintaining mechanism.
condd_parent_management_training.important_caveat: The published abstract does not separately quantify the exact percentage of children reaching normative functioning, nor does it isolate PMT-alone effect size from the combined PSST+PMT condition with a specific number; the honest summary is 'combined treatment worked significantly better than either component alone,' not a precise cure percentage.
condd_parent_management_training.real_working_solution: PMT, especially combined with child-directed problem-solving skills training, is real, randomised-trial-supported, and endorsed as an evidence-based first-line psychosocial treatment for childhood Conduct Disorder/severe antisocial behaviour by the AACAP practice parameter.
condd_parent_management_training.source: Kazdin AE, Siegel TC, Bass D, J Consult Clin Psychol 1992;60(5):733-747 (PMID 1401389); American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 'Practice parameters for the assessment and treatment of children and adolescents with conduct disorder', J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997;36(10 Suppl):122S-139S (PMID 9334568)
condd_parent_management_training.confidence: moderate -- real RCT evidence, cross-referenced against a named professional-society practice parameter

condd_functional_family_therapy.name: Functional Family Therapy (FFT) for Adolescent Conduct-Disordered/Delinquent Behaviour
condd_functional_family_therapy.type: Not a drug: shorter, structured family-systems therapy targeting family communication and problem-solving patterns that maintain adolescent antisocial behaviour
specific_drugs: Not a drug: Functional Family Therapy (FFT)
condd_functional_family_therapy.effectiveness: In the newest, most rigorous 2025 meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 1,471 participants), FFT showed possible, but not confidently established, clinically important effects versus usual care on new offences/convictions, time in out-of-home care, and substance use; evidence strength was rated low (Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446, PMID 39428056).
condd_functional_family_therapy.reason_why: FFT targets dysfunctional family communication, problem-solving and relational patterns hypothesised to maintain the adolescent's antisocial behaviour, using a shorter, more structured protocol than MST.
condd_functional_family_therapy.important_caveat: Low evidence strength per the 2025 review's own rating; effects are described as 'possible' rather than established, and this is a smaller evidence base (7 RCTs) than MST's (16 RCTs).
condd_functional_family_therapy.real_working_solution: FFT has a real but currently low-certainty signal of benefit on offence/re-offence and placement outcomes in adolescents with conduct problems; it is a reasonable doctor-and-family-directed option but should not be presented as definitively superior to usual community care.
condd_functional_family_therapy.source: Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446 (PMID 39428056)
condd_functional_family_therapy.confidence: low-moderate -- low evidence strength per the review's own GRADE-style rating

condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.name: Stimulant Medication (Methylphenidate, Amphetamines) for Aggression in Children With Comorbid ADHD -- 2002 Meta-Analysis, NOT a Treatment for Conduct Disorder Itself
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.type: Central nervous system stimulant, symptom-targeted for aggression-related behaviour in comorbid ADHD, explicitly NOT curative of Conduct Disorder
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.effectiveness: Meta-analysis of 28 studies (1970-2001; 28 independent effects for overt aggression, 7 for covert aggression) in children with ADHD found an overall weighted mean effect size of d=0.84 for overt aggression-related behaviours and d=0.69 for covert aggression-related behaviours, similar in magnitude to stimulant effects on core ADHD symptoms. Critically, the same meta-analysis found that comorbid Conduct Disorder is associated with a diminished stimulant effect size for overt aggression (Connor DF, Glatt SJ, Lopez ID, Jackson D, Melloni RH Jr, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2002;41(3):253-261, PMID 11886019).
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.reason_why: Stimulants improve dopaminergic/noradrenergic prefrontal regulation of impulse control and attention in ADHD, which secondarily reduces reactive, impulsivity-driven aggressive outbursts; this is a symptom-level effect on the comorbid ADHD, not a mechanism that treats the conduct-disordered behaviour pattern itself.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.important_caveat: The same meta-analysis explicitly found that comorbid Conduct Disorder diminishes the stimulant effect size for overt aggression -- meaning stimulants work least well for aggression exactly in the population that also has full Conduct Disorder, not just ADHD. This is symptom management of comorbid ADHD, never a treatment for Conduct Disorder itself.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.real_working_solution: In children with ADHD plus aggression, stimulants have real, meta-analytically supported, moderate-to-large effect sizes on aggression-related behaviour, but this benefit is reduced when full Conduct Disorder is also present, and stimulants should be understood as comorbid-ADHD symptom management, with the family/psychosocial interventions above remaining the primary lever against Conduct Disorder itself.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.source: Connor DF, Glatt SJ, Lopez ID, Jackson D, Melloni RH Jr, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2002;41(3):253-261 (PMID 11886019)
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.confidence: moderate -- real meta-analysis, but effect specifically attenuated in the comorbid-Conduct-Disorder subgroup that is this entry's actual population

condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.name: Alpha-2 Adrenergic Agonist (Clonidine), Alone or Combined With Methylphenidate, for Comorbid ADHD With Aggressive Oppositional/Conduct Disorder -- Small Pilot RCT, No Placebo Arm
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.type: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, symptom-targeted for aggression/impulsivity in comorbid ADHD, NOT curative of Conduct Disorder
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.effectiveness: Small pilot randomised, blinded, 3-month comparison (8 children per group, ages 6-16, no placebo arm) of methylphenidate (MPH) monotherapy, clonidine monotherapy, or MPH+clonidine combination in children with ADHD comorbid with aggressive Oppositional Defiant Disorder or Conduct Disorder. All three groups showed significant improvement in attention, impulsivity, oppositional and conduct-disordered symptoms on parent/teacher rating scales and laboratory measures, with few significant differences between groups (only the clonidine-monotherapy group showed significantly decreased fine motor speed) (Connor DF, Barkley RA, Davis HT, Clin Pediatr (Phila) 2000;39(1):15-25, PMID 10660814, n=24).
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.reason_why: Alpha-2 agonists reduce noradrenergic outflow from the locus coeruleus, hypothesised to dampen hyperarousal-driven impulsivity and reactive aggression, complementing stimulants' effect on attentional/inhibitory control.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.important_caveat: This is a small (n=24), unreplicated pilot study with no placebo comparison, so improvement cannot be fully separated from natural course, non-specific attention, or expectancy effects; it should be read as preliminary safety/feasibility evidence for symptom-targeted combination pharmacotherapy in comorbid ADHD+Conduct Disorder, not as disorder-curing evidence.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.real_working_solution: Clonidine, alone or added to a stimulant, has preliminary pilot-trial evidence of safety and symptom improvement in aggressive comorbid ADHD/Conduct Disorder, but given the lack of a placebo arm and small sample, it should be considered a doctor-directed adjunct for comorbid-symptom control, not a Conduct-Disorder treatment in its own right.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.source: Connor DF, Barkley RA, Davis HT, Clin Pediatr (Phila) 2000;39(1):15-25 (PMID 10660814)
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.confidence: low -- small unreplicated pilot study, no placebo arm

condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.name: Risperidone (Atypical Antipsychotic) for Aggression and Conduct Problems in Disruptive Behaviour Disorders -- 2017 Cochrane Review
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.type: Atypical antipsychotic, symptom-targeted for aggression/conduct-problem behaviour, NOT curative of Conduct Disorder and carrying real metabolic risk
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.effectiveness: Cochrane review of 10 RCTs (896 children/youths aged 5-18, 8 trials assessed risperidone). Pooling 3 risperidone studies (238 participants), aggression on the Aberrant Behaviour Checklist-Irritability subscale improved by a mean difference of 6.49 points versus placebo (95% CI 4.19-8.79, low-quality evidence, scale range 0-45). Pooling 2 risperidone studies (225 participants), conduct problems on the Nisonger Child Behaviour Rating Form-Conduct Problem subscale improved by a mean difference of 8.61 points versus placebo (95% CI 5.74-11.49, moderate-quality evidence, scale range 0-48), judged by the review authors as likely clinically significant. Risperidone also caused significant weight gain (2.37 kg more than placebo over the trial period, 95% CI 0.26-4.49 kg, moderate-quality evidence) (Loy JH, Merry SN, Hetrick SE, Stasiak K, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;8:CD008559, PMID 28791693). No exact remission/response percentage is reported, so no effectiveness_pct is claimed for this scale-based outcome.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.reason_why: Risperidone's dopamine D2/serotonin 5-HT2A antagonism is hypothesised to dampen limbic-driven reactive aggression and irritability, independent of any effect on the underlying conduct-disordered behaviour pattern or its psychosocial causes.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.important_caveat: The Cochrane authors' own conclusion: 'Given the effectiveness of parent-training interventions in the management of these disorders, and the somewhat equivocal evidence on the efficacy of medication, it is important not to use medication alone' -- explicitly ranking psychosocial/family-based treatment above medication and warning against monotherapy. Weight gain is a real, clinically significant adverse effect, and evidence for other atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, ziprasidone) was inadequate to support their use.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.real_working_solution: Risperidone has real, replicated (though low-to-moderate certainty), short-term RCT evidence of reducing aggression and conduct-problem symptom scores in disruptive behaviour disorders, but per the review authors' own conclusion it should be used, if at all, as a doctor-directed adjunct to family/parent-training intervention -- never as medication alone -- and its real metabolic cost (weight gain) must be weighed against its symptom benefit.
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.source: Loy JH, Merry SN, Hetrick SE, Stasiak K, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;8:CD008559 (PMID 28791693)
condd_medication_for_comorbid_adhd_aggre.confidence: low-to-moderate -- Cochrane's own GRADE ratings range low to moderate across outcomes

condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.name: Fast Track -- 10-Year Multi-Component School/Family Prevention Program for High-Risk Kindergarteners, Real Randomised Reduction in Lifetime Conduct Disorder in the Highest-Risk Subgroup
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.type: Not a drug: manualised multi-component prevention program (parent behaviour-management training + home visiting, child social-cognitive-skills training, reading tutoring, peer coaching, classroom social-emotional curricula), delivered kindergarten through grade 10 to school-cluster-randomised high-risk children, before Conduct Disorder is diagnosed
specific_drugs: Not a drug: school- and family-based multi-component prevention program
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.effectiveness: In 891 early-starting high-risk kindergarteners randomised by school cluster to Fast Track versus control, a significant intervention-by-initial-risk interaction showed the program prevented the lifetime prevalence of Conduct Disorder, Oppositional Defiant Disorder, ADHD, and any externalizing diagnosis assessed after grades 3, 6, 9 and 12, concentrated among children at highest initial risk (Conduct Problems Prevention Research Group, Child Dev 2011;82(1):331-345, PMID 21291445, n=891). At age 25 (n=702 psychiatrically interviewed), 59% of the intervention group versus 69% of controls had at least one externalizing, internalizing or substance-abuse psychiatric problem on blinded interview (odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.43-0.81, number needed to treat = 8) -- a relative risk reduction of (69-59)/69 x 100 = 14.5% in any such diagnosis; intervention participants also had lower violent (-0.37) and drug (-0.43) crime-conviction scores and higher well-being scores (+0.19) (Dodge KA et al., Am J Psychiatry 2015;172(1):59-70, PMID 25219348).
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.reason_why: Fast Track targets the developmental precursors of Conduct Disorder (coercive parent-child discipline cycles, deficient social-cognitive skills, school failure, deviant peer affiliation) during the sensitive kindergarten-through-adolescence window, before the disorder consolidates, making it a real prevention pathway rather than a treatment applied after diagnosis.
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.important_caveat: The benefit was real but concentrated in the highest-risk subgroup, and even there it was a reduction (69% to 59% for any psychiatric problem at 25), not elimination, of risk; this is a 10-year, whole-family/whole-school resource-intensive program, not something deliverable as a brief clinical intervention to a child already diagnosed with Conduct Disorder.
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.real_working_solution: Fast Track is the best-evidenced, longest-followed (25-year, blinded-outcome) real prevention program shown in a randomised trial to reduce the lifetime rate of diagnosed Conduct Disorder and later adult psychopathology/crime in high-risk children; combined with MST/PMT/FFT for children already showing conduct-disordered behaviour, it represents this knowledge base's most evidence-grounded real answer to Conduct Disorder across the whole developmental window.
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.source: Conduct Problems Prevention Research Group, Child Dev 2011;82(1):331-345 (PMID 21291445); Dodge KA et al., Am J Psychiatry 2015;172(1):59-70 (PMID 25219348)
condd_school_based_multicomponent_preven.confidence: moderate-high -- randomised, blinded-outcome, 25-year follow-up trial data, effect concentrated in the highest-risk subgroup

ranked_high_to_low.name: Multisystemic Therapy (MST) -- pooled effect vs comparison treatment (earlier, more favourable meta-analysis)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Treated youths/families functioning better than an estimated 70% of alternatively-treated comparison youths/families post-treatment (Cohen's d=0.55 pooled across 7 primary studies), n=708
ranked_high_to_low.source: Curtis NM et al., J Fam Psychol 2004;18(3):411-419 (PMID 15382965)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Risperidone -- conduct-problem symptom-score reduction vs placebo (short-term, symptom-targeted only)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Mean difference of 8.61 points lower (improved) on the Nisonger Child Behaviour Rating Form-Conduct Problem subscale (scale range 0-48) versus placebo (95% CI 5.74-11.49), judged likely clinically significant by review authors; 2 pooled RCTs, 225 participants. This is a raw scale-score mean difference, not a response/remission percentage, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null rather than converting an untested scale fraction into a fabricated percentage.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Loy JH et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;8:CD008559 (PMID 28791693)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Multisystemic Therapy (MST) and Functional Family Therapy (FFT) -- newest, most rigorous 2025 meta-analysis re-assessment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: MST: no clinically important effect found vs usual care on delinquency, new offences/convictions, placement in out-of-home care, or substance use (only time in out-of-home care showed a likely clinically important effect); 16 RCTs, n=4,095. FFT: possible but low-strength-evidence effects on new offences/convictions, time in out-of-home care, and substance use; 7 RCTs, n=1,471. No comparable percentage is reported for a null/low-strength clinically-important-difference finding, so effectiveness_pct is intentionally left null.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hunkin H et al., J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2025;64(4):427-446 (PMID 39428056)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows are not directly comparable head-to-head: rank 1 and rank 4 are two meta-analyses of the same MST program that directly disagree with each other -- the field's own newest, most rigorous synthesis (rank 4, 2025) corrects the more favourable earlier meta-analysis (rank 1, 2004) using stricter, minimum-clinically-important-difference evidence standards and a much larger pooled sample. Rank 2 (Fast Track) is a blinded, 25-year, single-cohort RCT of an intensive whole-childhood prevention program measured against control on adult psychiatric outcomes, applied before Conduct Disorder is diagnosed rather than as treatment after diagnosis. Rank 3 (risperidone) is short-term, symptom-targeted pharmacotherapy with real but scale-score (not percentage-remission) evidence, and per the reviewing Cochrane authors' own conclusion should not be used as medication alone given the stronger evidence base for parent-training/family interventions. No row in this table, and no medicine or psychotherapy trial found anywhere in this survey, reports a real, replicated remission/cure percentage for Conduct Disorder itself; the honest picture is real, replicated, partial reduction in antisocial/delinquent outcomes, strongest when psychosocial family-based intervention starts earliest in childhood.

conduct_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Conduct Disorder (CD) has two real, distinct safety dimensions that must bypass the routine consultation-and-medicine-suggestion flow and trigger immediate risk-assessment/escalation rather than a candidate-medicine-plus-efficacy% answer as the first response. (1) RISK OF HARM TO OTHERS: DSM-5-TR's own CD criteria are organised into four categories of severity-graded, real safety-relevant behaviour - aggression to people and animals (including bullying, physical fights, weapon use, physical cruelty to people, physical cruelty to animals, forcing sexual activity on someone), and destruction of property (including fire-setting) - and the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry's own Practice Parameters for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents with Conduct Disorder direct that safety and risk (to self, to others, including weapon use, fire-setting, and cruelty to people or animals) be assessed as a priority alongside diagnosis, not deferred to routine treatment planning (Steiner H, American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 'Practice parameters for the assessment and treatment of children and adolescents with conduct disorder', J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997;36(10 Suppl):122S-139S, PMID 9334568; summarised in Steiner H, Dunne JE, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997;36(10):1482-1485, PMID 9334562). Real longitudinal outcome data show this risk is not theoretical: in the Dunedin birth-cohort study, individuals on the life-course-persistent antisocial trajectory (the pathway most closely tied to childhood-onset CD) were, at age 32, 'engaging in serious violence' (Odgers CL, Moffitt TE, Broadbent JM, et al, 'Female and male antisocial trajectories: from childhood origins to adult outcomes', Dev Psychopathol 2008;20(2):673-716, PMID 18423100). Any disclosure of weapon use, fire-setting, cruelty to animals or people, forced sexual activity, or a specific target of threatened harm must trigger an immediate structured safety/risk-assessment referral (child and adolescent psychiatry or forensic mental health services), not a medicine suggestion. This is compounded when the 'with limited prosocial emotions' (callous-unemotional, CU) specifier is present, since CU traits mark a developmentally and etiologically distinct subgroup associated with more severe, more instrumental, and more stable aggression (Frick PJ, Ray JV, Thornton LC, Kahn RE, 'Annual research review: A developmental psychopathology approach to understanding callous-unemotional traits in children and adolescents with serious conduct problems', J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2014;55(6):532-548, PMID 24117854). (2) RISK OF HARM TO SELF: CD is real-world, frequently comorbid with major depressive disorder and other psychiatric conditions (Mohan L, Yilanli M, Deniz I, Ray S, 'Conduct Disorder', StatPearls, StatPearls Publishing, 2023, PMID 29261891), and depression is this KB's own established trigger for routine suicide-risk screening; a child or adolescent presenting with CD symptoms plus any disclosed low mood, hopelessness, self-harm, or suicidal ideation must be routed to the same immediate real-world safety pathway (nearest emergency department / local crisis line, urgent child-and-adolescent-psychiatry referral) used elsewhere in this KB for acute suicide risk, rather than the routine consultation flow. Net rule: no CD complaint alone should bypass the normal consultation flow, but a disclosed act or plan of serious harm to a person or animal, fire-setting, weapon use, or any self-harm/suicidal content must be treated as a real safety emergency ahead of, and instead of, an ai_suggests medicine-and-efficacy answer.

dsm5_onset_types_and_severity.finding: DSM-5-TR classifies Conduct Disorder into three onset-based types based on age at first symptom: childhood-onset type (at least one criterion characteristic of CD prior to age 10 years), adolescent-onset type (no criterion characteristic of CD prior to age 10 years), and unspecified onset (CD criteria met but insufficient information available to determine whether onset was before or after age 10). Severity is rated mild (few conduct problems beyond the diagnostic threshold, and problems cause relatively minor harm to others), moderate (intermediate number of conduct problems and effect on others), or severe (many conduct problems beyond the diagnostic threshold, or conduct problems causing considerable harm to others). The diagnosis requires 3 or more of 15 specific criteria (grouped into four categories) present in the past 12 months, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months, causing clinically significant impairment in social, academic or occupational functioning.
dsm5_onset_types_and_severity.source: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR, 2022), diagnostic criteria for Conduct Disorder (312.81/312.82/312.89); cross-referenced against Mohan L, Yilanli M, Deniz I, Ray S, 'Conduct Disorder', StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf/PubMed, PMID 29261891) and the AACAP Practice Parameters for Conduct Disorder (Steiner H, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 1997;36(10 Suppl):122S-139S, PMID 9334568)
dsm5_onset_types_and_severity.confidence: high - direct citation of current DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria, cross-checked against a session-verified StatPearls review and the named AACAP practice parameter

limited_prosocial_emotions_specifier.finding: DSM-5 added 'with limited prosocial emotions' as a formal specifier for Conduct Disorder, requiring 2 or more of the following displayed persistently over at least 12 months and in multiple relationships/settings: lack of remorse or guilt (does not feel bad or guilty when doing wrong, except when caught and/or facing punishment); callous-lack of empathy (disregards and is unconcerned about the feelings of others); unconcerned about performance (does not show concern about poor/problematic performance at school, work or other important activities); and shallow or deficient affect (does not express feelings or show emotions to others, except in ways that seem shallow, insincere, or superficial, or when emotional expressions are used for gain). This specifier operationalises callous-unemotional (CU) traits, which research had already identified as marking a clinically and etiologically distinct subgroup of children/adolescents with serious conduct problems before the specifier was formally added to DSM-5.
limited_prosocial_emotions_specifier.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Conduct Disorder specifiers; Frick PJ, Ray JV, Thornton LC, Kahn RE, 'Annual research review: A developmental psychopathology approach to understanding callous-unemotional traits in children and adolescents with serious conduct problems', J Child Psychol Psychiatry 2014;55(6):532-548 (PMID 24117854), which states CU traits were incorporated into DSM-5 as a CD specifier based on this research

aggression_to_people_and_animals.finding: Bullies, threatens, or intimidates others; initiates physical fights; has used a weapon that can cause serious physical harm to others (e.g. a bat, brick, broken bottle, knife, gun); has been physically cruel to people; has been physically cruel to animals; has stolen while confronting a victim (e.g. mugging, purse snatching, extortion, armed robbery); has forced someone into sexual activity.
aggression_to_people_and_animals.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Conduct Disorder criterion category A1-A7; cross-referenced against StatPearls, 'Conduct Disorder' (PMID 29261891), which describes CD as 'characterized by a pattern of behaviors that demonstrates aggression and violation of the rights of others'

destruction_of_property.finding: Has deliberately engaged in fire-setting with the intention of causing serious damage; has deliberately destroyed others' property (other than by fire-setting).
destruction_of_property.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Conduct Disorder criterion category B1-B2

deceitfulness_or_theft.finding: Has broken into someone else's house, building, or car; often lies to obtain goods or favours or to avoid obligations (i.e. 'cons' others); has stolen items of nontrivial value without confronting a victim (e.g. shoplifting, forgery, but without breaking and entering).
deceitfulness_or_theft.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Conduct Disorder criterion category C1-C3

serious_violations_of_rules.finding: Often stays out at night despite parental prohibitions, beginning before age 13; has run away from home overnight at least twice while living in the parental/parental-surrogate home (or once without returning for a lengthy period); is often truant from school, beginning before age 13.
serious_violations_of_rules.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Conduct Disorder criterion category D1-D3

clinical_diagnostic_criteria.finding: Diagnosis requires a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms/rules are violated, manifested by at least 3 of the 15 criteria across the four categories above in the past 12 months, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months, and clinically significant impairment in social, academic or occupational functioning. If the individual is 18 or older, criteria for Antisocial Personality Disorder must not be met (i.e. the diagnosis is CD in a minor, or CD-with-later-ASPD-onset if the person is over 18 but does not yet meet full ASPD criteria). Diagnosis rests on a thorough psychiatric evaluation, including history from multiple informants (parents/caregivers, school), because CD is frequently comorbid with ADHD, learning disorders and depression, all of which must be assessed before attributing the full symptom picture to CD alone.
clinical_diagnostic_criteria.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Conduct Disorder diagnostic criteria; Mohan L, Yilanli M, Deniz I, Ray S, 'Conduct Disorder', StatPearls (PMID 29261891): 'Conduct disorder is comorbid with many other psychiatric conditions, including depression, ADHD, learning disorders, and thus a thorough psychiatric evaluation is required'; AACAP Practice Parameters (Steiner H, PMID 9334568)

differentiating_from_oppositional_defian.finding: StatPearls explicitly frames Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) as a precursor that 'can be seen as' preceding CD within the same disruptive-behaviour-disorder spectrum. The clinical distinction is one of severity and rights-violation: ODD (per the AACAP's own separate practice parameter for ODD) is characterised by a pattern of negativistic, hostile, and defiant behaviour (angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, vindictiveness) without the serious aggression, property destruction, deceit/theft, or rule violations that define CD; CD is diagnosed instead of, and takes precedence over, ODD when a person's behaviour meets criteria for both, since CD represents violation of the basic rights of others and major societal norms, which ODD by definition does not include. In DSM-5-TR, ODD is not diagnosed if criteria are met for CD.
differentiating_from_oppositional_defian.source: Mohan L, Yilanli M, Deniz I, Ray S, 'Conduct Disorder', StatPearls (PMID 29261891): 'ODD can be seen as a precursor to CD'; Steiner H, Remsing L, Work Group on Quality Issues, 'Practice parameter for the assessment and treatment of children and adolescents with oppositional defiant disorder', J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2007;46(1):126-141 (PMID 17195736); American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), ODD diagnostic notes on the CD-precedence rule

developmental_taxonomy_two_real_pathways.finding: Moffitt's dual developmental taxonomy, built to reconcile the fact that antisocial behaviour shows strong continuity over age while its prevalence rises roughly 10-fold during adolescence, identifies two distinct groups with different natural histories: a small life-course-persistent (LCP) group whose neuropsychological problems interact cumulatively with a criminogenic environment across development, culminating in a stable antisocial/pathological personality that persists into adulthood; and a much larger adolescence-limited (AL) group whose antisocial behaviour is confined to the teenage years, driven by a 'maturity gap' that makes antisocial behaviour temporarily normative/adjustive, and who typically desist as adults.
developmental_taxonomy_two_real_pathways.source: Moffitt TE, 'Adolescence-limited and life-course-persistent antisocial behavior: a developmental taxonomy', Psychol Rev 1993;100(4):674-701 (PMID 8255953)

childhood_onset_vs_adolescent_onset_prog.finding: Using the Dunedin longitudinal cohort, childhood-onset delinquents (matching DSM's childhood-onset CD type) had documented backgrounds of inadequate parenting, neurocognitive problems, and early temperament/behaviour problems, whereas adolescent-onset delinquents did not carry these pathological childhood backgrounds - this pattern held for both sexes. The male-to-female ratio was 10:1 for childhood-onset delinquency but only 1.5:1 for adolescence-onset delinquency, showing childhood-onset CD is both more sex-skewed and more biologically/environmentally 'loaded' than adolescent-onset CD. This is the real evidentiary basis for DSM-5-TR's separate childhood-onset vs adolescent-onset CD types carrying different prognostic weight: childhood-onset CD is the higher-risk trajectory for persistence into adult antisocial personality disorder.
childhood_onset_vs_adolescent_onset_prog.source: Moffitt TE, Caspi A, 'Childhood predictors differentiate life-course persistent and adolescence-limited antisocial pathways among males and females', Dev Psychopathol 2001;13(2):355-375 (PMID 11393651)

real_trajectory_outcomes_to_age_32.finding: In the Dunedin birth-cohort study (general growth mixture modelling identifying life-course-persistent, adolescent-onset, childhood-limited, and low trajectory groups in both sexes), individuals on the life-course-persistent pathway - male and female alike - were, by age 32, engaging in serious violence and experiencing significant mental-health, physical-health, and economic problems; those on the adolescent-onset pathway were also experiencing difficulties at age 32, though to a lesser extent than the LCP group. More males than females followed the LCP trajectory, but the childhood origins and adult consequences of the trajectories were otherwise similar across sexes - i.e. this is not a male-only phenomenon.
real_trajectory_outcomes_to_age_32.source: Odgers CL, Moffitt TE, Broadbent JM, Dickson N, Hancox RJ, Harrington H, Poulton R, Sears MR, Thomson WM, Caspi A, 'Female and male antisocial trajectories: from childhood origins to adult outcomes', Dev Psychopathol 2008;20(2):673-716 (PMID 18423100)

relationship_to_later_antisocial_persona.finding: DSM-5-TR formally defines Antisocial Personality Disorder as requiring evidence of Conduct Disorder with onset before age 15, making childhood/adolescent CD a diagnostic prerequisite for adult ASPD, not merely a correlate; ASPD cannot be diagnosed in someone without a CD history before age 15. However, continuity is not universal or automatic - it is the childhood-onset, and especially the childhood-onset-with-limited-prosocial-emotions, subgroup that carries the highest risk of continuing into adult ASPD (per the LCP-trajectory data above), while most adolescent-onset CD resolves by adulthood. This KB's own Antisocial Personality Disorder entry documents that ASPD itself remains a chronic, real, and difficult-to-treat condition once it consolidates in adulthood (Black DW, 'The Natural History of Antisocial Personality Disorder', Can J Psychiatry 2015;60(7):309-314, PMID 26175389) - which is precisely why this KB's real prevention evidence (see Fast Track / Multisystemic Therapy documented under antisocial_personality_disorder) targets the childhood/adolescent CD window rather than waiting for adult ASPD to develop.
relationship_to_later_antisocial_persona.source: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022), Antisocial Personality Disorder criterion C; Odgers CL et al, Dev Psychopathol 2008;20(2):673-716 (PMID 18423100); Black DW, Can J Psychiatry 2015;60(7):309-314 (PMID 26175389)

insomnia_disorder.name: Insomnia Disorder
insomnia_disorder.icd11_hint: 7A00 Chronic insomnia (ICD-11, Chapter 07 Sleep-wake disorders); ICD-10 G47.00 Insomnia, unspecified / F51.0 Insomnia not due to a substance or known physiological condition (nonorganic insomnia, Chapter V Mental and behavioural disorders). Verified via ICD-11/ICD-10 chapter and code cross-reference; the WHO ICD-11 browser itself is a JS-rendered app that could not be scraped directly in this session, so this is flagged as moderate-high (not primary-source-direct) confidence, consistent with how other ICD-11 hints are flagged in this KB.
insomnia_disorder.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TWO independent, real safety concerns must be actively screened for in every chronic insomnia presentation, not inferred from insomnia severity alone. (1) SUICIDE RISK: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 comparative observational studies in psychiatric patients found that co-morbid sleep disturbance was significantly associated with increased suicidal behaviour overall (pooled OR=1.99, 95% CI 1.72-2.30, P<0.001), and in subgroup analysis by sleep-disorder type, insomnia specifically (along with parasomnias and sleep-related breathing disorders, but not hypersomnias) was significantly associated with suicidal behaviour (Malik S et al, 'The association between sleep disturbances and suicidal behaviors in patients with psychiatric diagnoses: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Syst Rev 2014, PMID 24568642). The association held across multiple psychiatric conditions independently (depression OR=3.05, PTSD OR=2.56, panic disorder OR=3.22, schizophrenia OR=12.66), meaning insomnia is not a passive marker of the underlying disorder but an independently actionable risk signal. CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: every chronic insomnia patient, especially with comorbid depression, anxiety, PTSD, or psychotic-spectrum illness, requires explicit suicide-risk screening at every contact, not reassurance that 'it's just poor sleep'. (2) DRIVING / ACCIDENT RISK FROM SEVERE SLEEP DEPRIVATION: the EQUINOX international cross-sectional survey of 5,293 subjects with insomnia across 10 countries (ICSD-10 criteria) found 20.9% reported at least one home accident in the past 12 months, 10.1% at least one work accident, 9% reported having fallen asleep while driving at least once, and 4.1% reported at least one car accident attributed to their sleepiness, independent of any hypnotic medication effect (Leger D et al, 'Insomnia and accidents: cross-sectional study (EQUINOX) on sleep-related home, work and car accidents in 5293 subjects with insomnia from 10 countries', J Sleep Res 2014, PMID 24237855). CLINICAL SAFETY IMPLICATION: any patient reporting severe sleep restriction, microsleeps, or having fallen asleep at the wheel needs explicit, direct counselling on not driving or operating heavy machinery until sleep is restored, with the same urgency as any other acute safety risk -- this is not a lifestyle inconvenience, it is a real and quantified accident-risk exposure.

symptoms.classification: DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, 2013; named diagnostic manual, real and current) defines Insomnia Disorder as a predominant complaint of dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, associated with one (or more) of: difficulty initiating sleep, difficulty maintaining sleep (characterised by frequent awakenings or problems returning to sleep after awakenings), or early-morning awakening with inability to return to sleep. To meet full diagnostic threshold the sleep difficulty must occur at least 3 nights per week, be present for at least 3 months, occur despite adequate opportunity for sleep, and not be better explained by another sleep-wake disorder, the physiological effects of a substance, or a coexisting mental/medical condition. DSM-5 specifies course subtypes: episodic (symptoms present 1-3 months), persistent/chronic (symptoms present 3 months or longer), and recurrent (2 or more episodes within 1 year). ACUTE vs CHRONIC: insomnia symptoms lasting under 3 months (often adjustment/acute insomnia tied to a clear stressor) are distinguished from chronic insomnia disorder, which meets the full duration and frequency threshold above. COMORBID vs PRIMARY: DSM-5 and the International Classification of Sleep Disorders, Third Edition (ICSD-3, American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2014) both moved away from labelling insomnia as 'primary' versus 'secondary to' another condition, collapsing prior ICSD-2 subtypes (psychophysiological, idiopathic, paradoxical insomnia, etc.) into a single 'Insomnia Disorder' category and explicitly allowing it to be diagnosed alongside another mental disorder, medical condition, or other sleep disorder when the insomnia is a clinically significant focus of treatment in its own right, rather than assuming it will resolve passively once the comorbid condition is treated (Sateia MJ, 'International classification of sleep disorders-third edition: highlights and modifications', Chest 2014, PMID 25367475).
symptoms.clinical_presentation: Insomnia disorder presents along three overlapping symptom axes, each independently diagnostic under DSM-5/ICSD-3: (1) DIFFICULTY FALLING ASLEEP (sleep-onset insomnia) -- prolonged sleep onset latency, typically clinically defined as more than 20-30 minutes to fall asleep; (2) DIFFICULTY STAYING ASLEEP (sleep-maintenance insomnia) -- frequent nocturnal awakenings with difficulty returning to sleep, or early-morning awakening earlier than desired with inability to resume sleep; (3) NON-RESTORATIVE / POOR-QUALITY SLEEP -- the patient may obtain a conventionally adequate number of hours yet report the sleep as unrefreshing, light, or poor-quality; this is a real and distinct complaint axis in the diagnostic criteria, not merely a subjective add-on. DAYTIME IMPAIRMENT is a required diagnostic feature (the sleep complaint must cause clinically significant distress or impairment), and is measurably real: a meta-analysis of studies comparing objectively/subjectively defined insomnia patients against good sleepers on validated neuropsychological tests found insomnia patients performed reliably worse on tasks of working memory, episodic memory, and problem-solving, with primarily small-to-moderate effect sizes, while simple attention and most aspects of executive function beyond problem-solving showed smaller, less consistent deficits -- meaning daytime cognitive impairment in insomnia is real but selective, not a uniform global deficit, so screening should probe memory and complex-task performance specifically rather than relying on a vague 'feels foggy' complaint alone (Fortier-Brochu E et al, 'Insomnia and daytime cognitive performance: a meta-analysis', Sleep Med Rev 2012, PMID 21636297). Patients also commonly report daytime fatigue, low mood/irritability, reduced concentration, and preoccupation/worry about sleep itself, which can become a self-perpetuating driver of the disorder (sleep-related performance anxiety).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: CLINICAL CRITERIA: diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 or ICSD-3 criteria applied through a structured sleep history (onset, duration, frequency, 24-hour sleep-wake pattern, pre-sleep behaviours, medical/psychiatric/medication/substance review) -- this is graded a strong (A) recommendation in the 2023 European Insomnia Guideline update, which specifies the diagnostic procedure as clinical interview covering sleep and medical history, plus the use of sleep questionnaires and diaries, with physical examination and additional measures added where indicated (Riemann D et al, 'The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023', J Sleep Res 2023, PMID 38016484). SLEEP DIARIES are the standard objective-adjacent tool: patient-completed daily logs of bed time, estimated sleep-onset latency, awakenings, final wake time, and out-of-bed time, typically kept for at least 1-2 weeks, used both to confirm the diagnostic pattern and to track treatment response. ACTIGRAPHY: the two major guideline bodies genuinely differ here and this KB records both rather than forcing false consensus -- the 2018 American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) clinical practice guideline gives a conditional recommendation FOR using actigraphy to estimate sleep parameters in adult patients with insomnia disorder (Smith MT et al, 'Use of Actigraphy for the Evaluation of Sleep Disorders and Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline', J Clin Sleep Med 2018, PMID 29991437), whereas the 2023 European Insomnia Guideline update grades actigraphy as NOT recommended for the routine evaluation of insomnia (grade C), reserving it for differential-diagnostic purposes (grade A) (Riemann et al, PMID 38016484). WHEN TO REFER FOR POLYSOMNOGRAPHY (PSG): PSG is not indicated for routine, uncomplicated insomnia. The European guideline (grade A/B) specifies PSG should be used to evaluate suspicion of another sleep disorder (periodic limb movement disorder, sleep-related breathing disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea, etc.), treatment-resistant insomnia that has not responded to first-line management, and other specific clinical indications (Riemann et al, PMID 38016484) -- i.e., PSG is a differential-diagnosis and treatment-failure escalation tool, not a first-line insomnia test.
symptoms.natural_history: CHRONICITY IS THE NORM, NOT THE EXCEPTION: the only published population-based 3-year longitudinal natural-history study of insomnia (388 adults with insomnia at baseline, mean age 44.8 years, 61% women, followed annually for 3 years using standardised diagnostic algorithms) found that 74% reported insomnia for at least 1 year (2 consecutive annual assessments) and 46% reported insomnia persisting across the entire 3-year study; the course was more likely to be persistent in those with more severe insomnia at baseline (full insomnia syndrome vs subsyndromal symptoms), in women, and in older adults. The 3-year remission rate was 54%, but of those who did remit, 27% eventually relapsed -- so even 'recovered' insomnia carries a real, substantial relapse risk that must be tracked, not treated as a closed case (Morin CM et al, 'The natural history of insomnia: a population-based 3-year longitudinal study', Arch Intern Med 2009, PMID 19273774). This untreated/naturalistic course is materially worse than the treated course: cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the guideline first-line treatment (strong recommendation, AASM 2021 clinical practice guideline for multicomponent CBT-I in chronic insomnia disorder, Edinger JD et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2021, PMID 33164742; also graded A/first-line in the European Insomnia Guideline, Riemann et al, PMID 38016484), and in a randomized controlled trial of 160 adults with persistent insomnia, patients who received extended maintenance CBT after initial combined therapy achieved a 68% remission rate at 6-month follow-up (vs 42% for those who continued medication during the extended phase), showing that structured, guideline-directed treatment can durably reverse a course that is otherwise prone to persistence and relapse (Morin CM et al, 'Cognitive behavioral therapy, singly and combined with medication, for persistent insomnia: a randomized controlled trial', JAMA 2009, PMID 19454639).

insomnia_disorder.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chronic insomnia disorder is NOT reversed by any single drug, but real, well-powered, guideline-endorsed treatment achieves durable, drug-free remission in a genuine share of patients when delivered correctly, and both major guideline bodies converge on the same first-line answer. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2021 clinical practice guideline (Edinger JD et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(2):255-262, PMID 33164742) gives a STRONG recommendation for multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) for chronic insomnia disorder in adults, and the American College of Physicians' 2016 guideline (Qaseem A et al, Ann Intern Med 2016;165(2):125-133, PMID 27136449) gives a strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence that ALL adult patients receive CBT-I as the INITIAL treatment, reserving medication for a weak, shared-decision-making add-on only if CBT-I alone fails. The real remission numbers back this up: in Morin CM et al's randomized controlled trial (JAMA 2009;301(19):2005-2015, PMID 19454639, N=160), CBT-I alone produced a 60% treatment-response rate and 39% remission rate (Insomnia Severity Index-defined) after 6 weeks of acute therapy -- statistically indistinguishable from CBT plus zolpidem (61%/44%) -- and among patients who received combined therapy up front and were then switched to CBT-I alone for 6-month extended maintenance therapy, remission reached a real 68% at 6-month follow-up, versus only 42% among patients who continued taking zolpidem during maintenance (P=.04) -- the best real long-term outcome in this trial came from patients who ended up on CBT-I without ongoing medication. A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 RCTs / 1,162 patients (Trauer JM et al, Ann Intern Med 2015;163(3):191-204, PMID 26054060) found CBT-I produced clinically meaningful, sustained improvements versus inactive comparators at post-treatment -- sleep efficiency improved by a real 9.91 percentage points (95% CI 8.09-11.73), wake-after-sleep-onset by 26.0 minutes, and sleep-onset latency by 19.0 minutes -- with no adverse outcomes reported, unlike hypnotic medication. This is the closest thing to a real, guideline-certified, drug-free route to lasting remission in this knowledge base for a chronic disorder: a structured, typically 4-8 session behavioral therapy that a genuine majority of patients can be weaned onto without medication and stay well on for at least 6-12 months. Pharmacotherapy is real and effective for symptom control but is honestly a second-line, largely short-term tool: an FDA-submitted-data meta-analysis of the non-benzodiazepine Z-drugs (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone; Huedo-Medina TB et al, BMJ 2012;345:e8343, PMID 23248080, 13 studies / 4,378 patients) found a real but small effect versus placebo on polysomnographic sleep latency (between-group standardised mean difference -0.36, 95% CI -0.57 to -0.16) and explicitly concluded the effect was 'of questionable clinical importance' despite statistical significance, on top of real, well-documented tolerance, dependence, and rebound-insomnia risk with continued nightly use that CBT-I does not carry. Newer dual orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant) and low-dose doxepin show real, guideline-acknowledged efficacy for sleep onset/maintenance with a more favourable dependence profile than benzodiazepine-type hypnotics, but none of these medications is curative -- they treat the night's sleep, not the disorder, and symptoms generally return on discontinuation, whereas CBT-I's gains are the one real, replicated, guideline-endorsed treatment shown to persist after treatment stops.

curative_option.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) -- first-line, real guideline-endorsed closest-to-durable-remission treatment
curative_option.note: CBT-I is a structured, typically 4-8 session, multicomponent behavioral/cognitive therapy combining sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring of dysfunctional sleep beliefs, and (optionally) relaxation training. It is the only insomnia treatment shown in real, controlled, guideline-cited trials to produce gains that persist after treatment stops, and is now the STRONG, first-line recommendation of both the AASM (2021) and ACP (2016), ahead of any medication.

real_survival_data.CBT_plus_zolpidem_response_rate_6_weeks_: 61% (45/74) -- not significantly different from CBT alone, P=.84
real_survival_data.combined_therapy_then_CBT_alone_maintena: 68% (20/30) -- best real long-term outcome in the trial, P=.04 vs continued-zolpidem arm
real_survival_data.CBT_i_meta_analysis_sleep_efficiency_abs: 9.91 percentage points (95% CI 8.09-11.73), N=1162 across 20 RCTs

curative_option.source: Morin CM et al. JAMA 2009;301(19):2005-2015 (PMID 19454639); Trauer JM et al. Ann Intern Med 2015;163(3):191-204 (PMID 26054060); Edinger JD et al. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(2):255-262 (PMID 33164742, AASM guideline, STRONG recommendation); Qaseem A et al. Ann Intern Med 2016;165(2):125-133 (PMID 27136449, ACP guideline, strong recommendation / moderate-quality evidence)
curative_option.important_caveat: Morin 2009 is a real, well-conducted RCT but modestly sized (N=160, single Canadian academic sleep centre); response/remission percentages are Insomnia Severity Index clinical thresholds, not an objective polysomnographic cure, and even the best long-term arm (68%) leaves a real minority not in remission at 6 months. Trauer 2015's pooled effects are on continuous diary measures (sleep-onset latency / wake-after-sleep-onset / sleep efficiency), not categorical remission, and its included trials excluded insomnia comorbid with other medical/sleep/psychiatric disease, limiting generalisability to many real-world comorbid-insomnia patients. No trial in this survey shows CBT-I curing insomnia in 100% of patients -- durable majority remission with a strong, first-line guideline recommendation is the real, honest ceiling here, not a permanent one-time cure for every patient.

ins_cbt_i.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I)
ins_cbt_i.type: First-line, real guideline-endorsed multicomponent behavioral/cognitive psychotherapy
ins_cbt_i.effectiveness: Morin CM et al (JAMA 2009;301(19):2005-2015, PMID 19454639, N=160 RCT) found CBT-I alone produced a 60% response and 39% remission rate (Insomnia Severity Index) after 6 weeks, statistically equivalent to CBT plus zolpidem (61%/44%); during 6-month extended/maintenance therapy and follow-up, patients maintained on CBT-I alone after combined acute therapy reached 68% remission, versus only 42% among those who continued zolpidem during maintenance (P=.04). A 2015 systematic review/meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (1,162 patients; Trauer JM et al, Ann Intern Med 2015;163(3):191-204, PMID 26054060) found CBT-I improved sleep-onset latency by 19.03 min, wake-after-sleep-onset by 26.00 min, and sleep efficiency by 9.91 percentage points versus inactive comparators at post-treatment, with effects sustained at later follow-up and no adverse outcomes reported.
ins_cbt_i.reason_why: CBT-I directly targets the behavioral and cognitive mechanisms that perpetuate chronic insomnia after an acute precipitant has resolved -- conditioned arousal to the bed/bedroom (addressed by stimulus control), excessive time-in-bed relative to actual sleep (addressed by sleep restriction, which increases homeostatic sleep drive), and catastrophic or dysfunctional beliefs about sleep (addressed by cognitive restructuring) -- per the predisposing-precipitating-perpetuating (3P) model, so gains persist without ongoing nightly drug exposure.
ins_cbt_i.important_caveat: Real gains are not universal: even the best-performing arm in Morin 2009 left 32% of patients not in remission at 6 months, and Trauer 2015's included trials excluded insomnia comorbid with other medical/sleep/psychiatric disorders, so pooled effects may not generalise to many real-world comorbid-insomnia patients. Access to trained CBT-I therapists is limited in practice, though digital/self-guided CBT-I programs are a real, guideline-acknowledged access-expanding option not separately re-verified with a dedicated PMID here.
ins_cbt_i.real_working_solution: Structured, typically 4-8 session, therapist-delivered multicomponent CBT-I (sleep restriction + stimulus control + cognitive restructuring +/- relaxation) as the real first-line, guideline-mandated treatment, with medication reserved as an add-on only if CBT-I alone is insufficient.
ins_cbt_i.source: Morin CM et al. JAMA 2009;301(19):2005-2015 (PMID 19454639); Trauer JM et al. Ann Intern Med 2015;163(3):191-204 (PMID 26054060); Edinger JD et al. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(2):255-262 (PMID 33164742); Qaseem A et al. Ann Intern Med 2016;165(2):125-133 (PMID 27136449)
ins_cbt_i.confidence: high -- two real guideline bodies (AASM strong recommendation, ACP strong recommendation / moderate-quality evidence) plus a real placebo/medication-controlled RCT and a real 20-RCT meta-analysis

ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.name: Zolpidem and Non-Benzodiazepine 'Z-Drug' Hypnotics
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.type: Second-line, short-term pharmacotherapy (GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators)
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.effectiveness: Huedo-Medina TB et al (BMJ 2012;345:e8343, PMID 23248080), a meta-analysis of 13 FDA-submitted RCTs (4,378 patients) covering all 3 approved Z-drugs, found a real but small between-group effect versus placebo on polysomnographic sleep latency (standardised mean difference -0.36, 95% CI -0.57 to -0.16) and decreased polysomnographic sleep latency by a mean 22 minutes (95% CI -33 to -11) versus placebo; effects were larger with higher doses and with zolpidem specifically.
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.reason_why: Z-drugs potentiate GABA-A receptor chloride-channel activity at the alpha-1 subunit, producing rapid sedative-hypnotic effects that shorten sleep latency and increase sleep continuity for the night the drug is taken, without treating the underlying conditioned/behavioral perpetuating factors.
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.important_caveat: The same meta-analysis explicitly concluded the drug effect, while statistically significant, was 'of questionable clinical importance', and Z-drugs carry real, well-documented risks of tolerance, physiological/psychological dependence, rebound insomnia on discontinuation, and (per FDA boxed warnings) complex sleep behaviors -- risks CBT-I does not carry. The ACP and AASM guidelines position medication as a second-line, shared-decision-making, generally short-term add-on, not a first-line or curative treatment.
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.real_working_solution: Short-term (days-to-weeks) zolpidem or another Z-drug at the lowest effective dose for acute symptom relief or as an add-on when CBT-I alone is insufficient, with a plan to taper rather than continue indefinitely.
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.source: Huedo-Medina TB et al. BMJ 2012;345:e8343 (PMID 23248080); Qaseem A et al. Ann Intern Med 2016;165(2):125-133 (PMID 27136449)
ins_zolpidem_z_drugs.confidence: high for the effect-size numbers (real FDA-submitted-data meta-analysis); the dependence/rebound risk framing is well-established clinical knowledge cited via the ACP guideline rather than a single dedicated PMID

ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.name: Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists (DORAs)
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.type: Second-line pharmacotherapy, newer mechanism, more favourable dependence profile
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.effectiveness: Herring WJ et al (Biol Psychiatry 2016;79(2):136-148, PMID 25526970), two pivotal phase 3 RCTs (N=1021 and N=1019), found suvorexant 40/30 mg superior to placebo on subjective and polysomnographic sleep onset/maintenance measures at week 1, month 1, and month 3. Michelson D et al (Lancet Neurol 2014;13(5):461-471, PMID 24680372), a 1-year RCT (N=781), found suvorexant improved subjective total sleep time by 38.7 min versus 16.0 min on placebo at month 1 (difference 22.7 min, 95% CI 16.4-29.0, P<0.0001), sustained safely over 1 year. Rosenberg R et al (JAMA Netw Open 2019;2(12):e1918254, PMID 31880796), a phase 3 RCT in adults >=55 years (N=1006), found lemborexant 10 mg improved polysomnographic sleep efficiency by an absolute 8.0 percentage points versus placebo (95% CI 6.6-9.5, P<.001) and reduced wake-after-sleep-onset by 25.4 min versus placebo, also outperforming zolpidem extended-release on second-half-of-night wake time.
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.reason_why: Orexin (hypocretin) neuropeptides from the lateral hypothalamus promote wakefulness by activating OX1/OX2 receptors on arousal-system nuclei; suvorexant and lemborexant block both receptors, suppressing the wake-promoting signal to allow sleep onset and maintenance, a mechanistically distinct approach from GABA-A potentiation.
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.important_caveat: Both are real, FDA-approved, guideline-acknowledged options with a lower reported abuse-liability/dependence signal than benzodiazepine-type hypnotics in their pivotal trials, but neither trial shows a cure -- efficacy was assessed only during active nightly treatment, and DORAs are positioned as second-line pharmacotherapy, not as a first-line or guideline-preferred alternative to CBT-I.
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.real_working_solution: Suvorexant or lemborexant as a real, second-line pharmacological option for sleep onset and maintenance difficulty, particularly when a lower dependence-risk profile than traditional hypnotics is desired.
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.source: Herring WJ et al. Biol Psychiatry 2016;79(2):136-148 (PMID 25526970); Michelson D et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13(5):461-471 (PMID 24680372); Rosenberg R et al. JAMA Netw Open 2019;2(12):e1918254 (PMID 31880796)
ins_dual_orexin_receptor_antagonists.confidence: high -- real, large, multi-site, double-blind, placebo/active-comparator-controlled phase 3 RCTs

ins_low_dose_doxepin.name: Low-Dose Doxepin
ins_low_dose_doxepin.type: Second-line pharmacotherapy, sleep-maintenance-targeted (selective H1-histamine antagonism at low dose)
ins_low_dose_doxepin.effectiveness: Krystal AD et al (Sleep 2010;33(11):1553-1561, PMID 21102997), a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in elderly chronic-primary-insomnia patients (n=240), found doxepin 3 mg produced statistically significant improvement versus placebo on wake-time-after-sleep-onset, total sleep time, and overall sleep efficiency from night 1 (all P<0.0001), sustained through night 85 (12 weeks) with significance maintained for wake-after-sleep-onset, total sleep time, overall sleep efficiency, and sleep efficiency in the last quarter of the night; doxepin 1 mg produced significant improvement on several of the same measures.
ins_low_dose_doxepin.reason_why: At low (1-6 mg) doses, doxepin acts as a highly selective histamine H1-receptor antagonist without meaningful anticholinergic or antidepressant-range activity, promoting sleep maintenance (particularly in the second half of the night and early-morning awakening, the elderly's dominant complaint) without the next-day sedation or anticholinergic burden of higher tricyclic antidepressant doses.
ins_low_dose_doxepin.important_caveat: This is, per the authors, the longest placebo-controlled, double-blind, polysomnographic insomnia-medication trial in the elderly to date, a real strength, but the trial reports statistical significance (P-values) on continuous sleep measures rather than a categorical responder/remission percentage, so no fabricated effectiveness_pct is assigned to this option; it is a real, second-line, sleep-maintenance-targeted option, not a cure.
ins_low_dose_doxepin.real_working_solution: Low-dose doxepin (1-6 mg nightly) as a real second-line option specifically for sleep-maintenance insomnia and early-morning awakening, especially in older adults, given its favourable next-day and anticholinergic safety profile at these doses.
ins_low_dose_doxepin.confidence: high for the trial's own reported outcomes; no independent large meta-analysis cross-checked here

ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.name: Ramelteon (Melatonin Receptor Agonist)
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.type: Second-line pharmacotherapy, sleep-onset-targeted (MT1/MT2 receptor agonism, non-scheduled, no dependence signal)
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.effectiveness: Erman M et al (Sleep Med 2006;7(1):17-24, PMID 16309958), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 5-period crossover trial (n=107), found all tested ramelteon doses (4, 8, 16, 32 mg) produced statistically significant reductions in latency to persistent sleep and increases in total sleep time versus placebo, with no next-day residual effects on mood, psychomotor performance, or memory at any dose.
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.reason_why: Ramelteon is a highly selective agonist at MT1/MT2 melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, reinforcing the endogenous circadian sleep-onset signal rather than directly sedating via GABA-A, which explains its real sleep-onset benefit with no observed next-day impairment or documented dependence/abuse signal.
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.important_caveat: The trial reports statistically significant directional effects (reduced latency, increased total sleep time) but not a magnitude expressed as a percentage or responder rate, so no fabricated effectiveness_pct is assigned to this option here; ramelteon's real-world effect size is generally considered modest and it targets sleep-onset difficulty specifically, not sleep-maintenance insomnia.
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.real_working_solution: Ramelteon 8 mg nightly as a real, non-scheduled, dependence-signal-free second-line option specifically for sleep-onset difficulty.
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.source: Erman M et al. Sleep Med 2006;7(1):17-24 (PMID 16309958)
ins_ramelteon_melatonin_agonist.confidence: moderate -- real double-blind placebo-controlled crossover RCT, but modest sample size (n=107) and no large independent meta-analysis cross-checked here

ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.name: Stimulus Control and Sleep Restriction Therapy (Single-Component Behavioral Techniques); Sleep Hygiene Education
ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.type: Adjunct/component behavioral techniques, real guideline-graded (not equivalent to full multicomponent CBT-I)
