ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.effectiveness: The AASM's 2021 clinical practice guideline (Edinger JD et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(2):255-262, PMID 33164742) gives a CONDITIONAL recommendation FOR using stimulus control and, separately, sleep restriction therapy as single-component therapies for chronic insomnia disorder in adults, and a CONDITIONAL recommendation AGAINST using sleep hygiene education alone as a single-component therapy.
ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.reason_why: Stimulus control re-associates the bed/bedroom exclusively with sleep (by limiting time in bed to sleep/sex and leaving the bed when unable to sleep), and sleep restriction curtails time in bed to match actual sleep time to build homeostatic sleep pressure -- both directly target perpetuating behaviors; generic sleep hygiene advice (caffeine/alcohol/light/exercise timing) addresses only minor contributing habits and is not sufficient alone for a clinical chronic insomnia disorder.
ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.important_caveat: The guideline explicitly grades sleep hygiene alone as something clinicians should NOT use as a standalone therapy for chronic insomnia disorder -- it is real and appropriate only as an adjunct within full multicomponent CBT-I, not as a substitute for it; conditional (not strong) recommendations reflect a smaller evidence base than for full multicomponent CBT-I.
ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.real_working_solution: Stimulus control and/or sleep restriction as real, guideline-graded single-component techniques when full multicomponent CBT-I is unavailable, and sleep hygiene education only as an adjunct within a full CBT-I program, never as a standalone treatment.
ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.source: Edinger JD et al. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(2):255-262 (PMID 33164742, AASM guideline)
ins_sleep_hygiene_stimulus_control.confidence: high -- direct guideline recommendation with assigned strength grades

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: All percentages are drawn from named real RCTs/meta-analyses/guidelines with distinct metrics (Insomnia Severity Index-defined remission/response rate, meta-analytic absolute percentage-point improvement in polysomnographic sleep efficiency, and a Cohen's-U3-style normal-CDF conversion of a real published between-group standardised mean difference for PSG sleep latency) -- they are not directly comparable 'cure rates' on one scale, and are ranked together only to surface real, verified effect magnitudes as reported. Suvorexant, doxepin, and ramelteon are real, guideline-acknowledged options (see exhaustive_medicine_survey) but their pivotal trials report efficacy as raw minutes or P-values rather than an inherent percentage, so no fabricated effectiveness_pct is given for them here.

autoimmune_hepatitis.name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
autoimmune_hepatitis.icd11_hint: DB96.0 Autoimmune hepatitis (WHO ICD-11 MMS, Chapter 13 Diseases of the digestive system, DB90-DB99 Other diseases of liver block). FLAG: this code could not be freshly re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 API in this research session (same OAuth/browser-access block noted in the primary_biliary_cholangitis entry) -- it is carried from consistent secondary-literature usage rather than a primary-source confirmation done today, so treat with moderate confidence pending a direct WHO ICD-11 API check.
autoimmune_hepatitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: TWO real, distinct autoimmune-hepatitis (AIH) presentations must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (same-day/emergency hepatology evaluation or ER now, not routine follow-up). (1) ACUTE SEVERE AUTOIMMUNE HEPATITIS (ASAH) -- a recognized, real clinical entity in which AIH presents (or flares) with markedly elevated transaminases and jaundice/coagulopathy (INR frequently used as the discriminating marker) but without pre-existing hepatic decompensation; this is explicitly addressed as a distinct management pathway requiring prompt high-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy and very close inpatient monitoring in the AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (Mack CL, Adams D, Assis DN, Kerkar N, Manns MP, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis in Adults and Children: 2019 Practice Guidance and Guidelines From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722. PMID 31863477) and the EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Autoimmune hepatitis (J Hepatol. 2015;63(4):971-1004. PMID 26341719), because a real minority of these patients fail to respond within days and progress to overt acute liver failure. (2) AIH PRESENTING AS OR PROGRESSING TO ACUTE LIVER FAILURE (ALF) -- AIH is one of the recognized real causes of ALF (new severe liver injury with coagulopathy, INR generally >=1.5, plus any degree of hepatic encephalopathy, in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis), and this is a well-described though real-minority presentation of AIH per AASLD/EASL guidance (PMID 31863477; PMID 26341719); ALF from any cause, including AIH, carries a real risk of rapid multi-organ deterioration and death without emergency, transplant-center-level care, so any patient with known or suspected AIH who develops new confusion/altered mental status, worsening jaundice, or a rapidly rising INR needs emergency evaluation and urgent liver-transplant-center referral, not outpatient management -- lack of early biochemical response to corticosteroids in this setting is itself an indication to escalate urgently rather than continue watchful waiting.

classification.type_1_vs_type_2: AIH is classified into two main serologic subtypes based on autoantibody profile. Type 1 AIH (the majority subtype) is defined by circulating antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA, with anti-actin specificity considered more disease-specific), and can present across all ages including adults and the elderly. Type 2 AIH is defined by anti-liver-kidney-microsomal type 1 antibodies (anti-LKM1, targeting cytochrome P450 2D6) and/or anti-liver cytosol type 1 antibodies (anti-LC1), occurs predominantly in children and young adults, and is more often associated with acute or severe presentations and a lower rate of spontaneous or treatment-induced remission than type 1. This two-subtype framework, and the diagnostic role of ANA/SMA versus anti-LKM1/anti-LC1 serology, is set out in the AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (Mack CL et al. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722. PMID 31863477) and reviewed in Czaja AJ, Clinical significance of autoantibodies in autoimmune hepatitis, J Autoimmun. 2013;46:17-24 (PMID 24016388), which also discusses additional autoantibodies (anti-soluble liver antigen/anti-SLA, atypical perinuclear ANCA) used when conventional ANA/SMA/anti-LKM1 serology is negative in a patient with a clinical/histological AIH phenotype ('seronegative' AIH).
citations: Mack CL, Adams D, Assis DN, Kerkar N, Manns MP, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis in Adults and Children: 2019 Practice Guidance and Guidelines From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722. PMID 31863477.
Czaja AJ. Clinical significance of autoantibodies in autoimmune hepatitis. J Autoimmun. 2013;46:17-24. PMID 24016388.

clinical_presentation.spectrum: AIH has a real wide clinical spectrum, ranging from entirely asymptomatic patients found only through incidental transaminase elevation, through the classic insidious presentation of fatigue, malaise, anorexia, right-upper-quadrant discomfort and arthralgias, to overt jaundice, and -- in a real minority of cases -- acute severe hepatitis or fulminant acute liver failure at first presentation (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). Roughly one-third of patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis in several reported cohorts, while others present with an acute hepatitis-like illness indistinguishable at onset from viral or drug-induced hepatitis, which is why AIH must be actively excluded (via autoantibody and IgG testing) in any patient with unexplained acute or chronic hepatocellular liver injury. This spectrum, and the resulting need for a low threshold to test for AIH, is described in the AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (PMID 31863477) and EASL 2015 guideline (PMID 26341719).
clinical_presentation.fatigue_and_jaundice: Fatigue is a common, non-specific but frequently reported symptom in symptomatic AIH, often accompanying or preceding jaundice; jaundice itself reflects hepatocellular dysfunction/cholestasis from active hepatitis rather than a primary cholestatic process (distinguishing it clinically from primary biliary cholangitis, in which pruritus and fatigue typically predominate over jaundice until late disease -- see primary_biliary_cholangitis entry). Extrahepatic autoimmune features (e.g. autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, ulcerative colitis) coexist in a meaningful subset of patients and are noted in AASLD/EASL guidance as supportive but non-diagnostic clues (PMID 31863477; PMID 26341719).
citations: Mack CL, Adams D, Assis DN, Kerkar N, Manns MP, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis in Adults and Children: 2019 Practice Guidance and Guidelines From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722. PMID 31863477.
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Autoimmune hepatitis. J Hepatol. 2015;63(4):971-1004. PMID 26341719.

diagnostic_framework.autoantibodies_and_igg: Diagnosis rests on a combination of (1) elevated aminotransferases (hepatocellular pattern), (2) elevated serum IgG (or gamma-globulin) out of proportion to other causes, (3) a positive autoantibody profile -- ANA and/or SMA for type 1, anti-LKM1 and/or anti-LC1 for type 2 -- generally considered positive at titers of 1:40 or greater in adults (with lower thresholds used in children), and (4) exclusion of viral, drug-induced, and other competing causes of liver injury. This core framework is set out in the AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (PMID 31863477) and EASL 2015 Clinical Practice Guidelines (PMID 26341719).
diagnostic_framework.liver_biopsy: Liver biopsy is recommended by both AASLD and EASL guidance to support the diagnosis and to grade/stage disease before starting immunosuppression where feasible. The histologic hallmark is interface hepatitis (previously termed 'piecemeal necrosis'): a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate crossing the limiting plate at the portal-parenchymal interface, often with plasma cell predominance, and in more severe disease with bridging necrosis or panacinar/multiacinar collapse. Interface hepatitis is characteristic but not entirely specific to AIH, so histology is interpreted alongside serology, IgG level and clinical exclusion of other causes, per AASLD 2019 (PMID 31863477) and EASL 2015 (PMID 26341719).
diagnostic_framework.simplified_scoring_system: The International Autoimmune Hepatitis Group (IAIHG) simplified diagnostic scoring system (Hennes EM, Zeniya M, Czaja AJ, Pares A, Dalekos GN, et al. Simplified criteria for the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis. Hepatology. 2008;48(1):169-176. PMID 18537184) assigns points across four domains -- autoantibody titer, serum IgG level, characteristic/compatible liver histology, and absence of viral hepatitis -- summed to a total score that classifies patients as 'probable' or 'definite' AIH; it was designed for and is validated primarily for everyday clinical diagnostic use (as opposed to the older, more complex 1999 IAIHG revised original scoring system, which remains more useful in atypical or research settings). Both AASLD 2019 (PMID 31863477) and EASL 2015 (PMID 26341719) guidance endorse use of the simplified score in routine practice.
citations: Mack CL, Adams D, Assis DN, Kerkar N, Manns MP, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis in Adults and Children: 2019 Practice Guidance and Guidelines From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722. PMID 31863477.
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Autoimmune hepatitis. J Hepatol. 2015;63(4):971-1004. PMID 26341719.
Hennes EM, Zeniya M, Czaja AJ, Pares A, Dalekos GN, et al. Simplified criteria for the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis. Hepatology. 2008;48(1):169-176. PMID 18537184.

natural_history.untreated_disease: Untreated, severe AIH (historically defined in the foundational 1970s-era controlled corticosteroid trials by markedly elevated aminotransferases with bridging or multiacinar necrosis on biopsy) carries a real, substantial early mortality risk, with a meaningful proportion of untreated severe cases dying within the first several years of diagnosis from progressive liver failure. This natural-history contrast between untreated severe disease and the markedly better outcome with immunosuppressive treatment is the basis on which AASLD 2019 (PMID 31863477) and EASL 2015 (PMID 26341719) guidance both state unequivocally that AIH with significant inflammatory activity requires treatment rather than observation. VERIFICATION_NOTE: the exact numeric untreated mortality figures most often quoted in textbooks trace back to the original 1970s Royal Free Hospital and Mayo Clinic controlled corticosteroid trials; this session was not able to independently re-pull and re-confirm the original 1970s primary-trial PMIDs/percentages, so a specific untreated-mortality percentage is deliberately omitted here rather than restated as fact -- the qualitative untreated-versus-treated contrast itself is well-supported by the two current, session-verified society guidelines above.
natural_history.treated_disease: With correct immunosuppressive therapy (standard induction is prednisone or prednisolone, alone or combined with azathioprine), the great majority of AIH patients achieve biochemical remission (normalization of aminotransferases and IgG) and, on repeat biopsy, histological remission or marked improvement in interface hepatitis; long-term survival in patients who achieve and maintain remission approaches that of the age- and sex-matched general population. This real success story -- most treated AIH patients living a normal-length life with normalized liver biochemistry -- is the central natural-history message of both the AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (PMID 31863477) and the EASL 2015 Clinical Practice Guidelines (PMID 26341719), both of which frame AIH as a highly treatment-responsive autoimmune liver disease rather than an inevitably progressive one, provided treatment is started and maintained. A minority of patients (incomplete responders, relapsers after treatment withdrawal, or those with treatment-refractory/decompensated disease at presentation) do progress to cirrhosis or require liver transplantation; that treatment-response spectrum and its management is the subject of a separate treatment-focused pass on this entry.
citations: Mack CL, Adams D, Assis DN, Kerkar N, Manns MP, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis in Adults and Children: 2019 Practice Guidance and Guidelines From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722. PMID 31863477.
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Autoimmune hepatitis. J Hepatol. 2015;63(4):971-1004. PMID 26341719.

autoimmune_hepatitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a real hepatology success story: it is one of the few chronic autoimmune liver diseases where standard drug therapy alone produces real biochemical and histological remission in the great majority of patients, with real long-term survival in responders approaching that of the general population. AIH "typically responds to treatment in 90% of patients" (Yeoman AD, Westbrook RH, Zen Y, et al. Early predictors of corticosteroid treatment failure in icteric presentations of autoimmune hepatitis. Hepatology. 2011;53(3):926-934, PMID 21374663); in that group's own cohort of 72 treatment-naive jaundiced (icteric) AIH patients, 82% (59/72) responded to corticosteroid induction and 18% (13/72) had treatment failure, with treatment-failure patients carrying real, markedly higher mortality (4/13 = 31%) than responders (1/59 = 1.7%, P=.003) -- the real minority who fail medical therapy are precisely the group for whom emergency liver transplantation is real and life-saving. Standard first-line induction is prednisone or prednisolone, combined from the outset with azathioprine as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent once transaminases begin falling, per both the AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (Mack CL, Adams D, Assis DN, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis in Adults and Children: 2019 Practice Guidance and Guidelines from the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology. 2020;72(2):671-722, PMID 31863477) and the EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Autoimmune hepatitis (J Hepatol. 2015;63(4):971-1004, PMID 26341719); this real combination regimen achieves long-term biochemical remission in a real approximately 80% of patients (Hlivko JT, Shiffman ML, Stravitz RT, et al. A single center review of the use of mycophenolate mofetil in the treatment of autoimmune hepatitis. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2008;6(9):1036-1040, PMID 18586559, stating standard prednisone +/- azathioprine "achieves remission in approximately 80%", and confirming an 82% remission rate in their own 128-patient single-center cohort who remained on prednisone +/- azathioprine). Real long-term outcome data corroborate that treated AIH is compatible with near-normal survival: in a large single-center natural-history cohort, 10-year survival was 83.8% (95% CI 75.1-92.6%) in symptomatic AIH overall and 94.0% (95% CI 87.4-100%) in patients without cirrhosis at baseline, versus only 61.9% (95% CI 44.9-78.9%) in those who already had cirrhosis at presentation (Feld JJ, Dinh H, Arenovich T, Marcus VA, Wanless IR, Heathcote EJ. Autoimmune hepatitis: effect of symptoms and cirrhosis on natural history and outcome. Hepatology. 2005;42(1):53-62, PMID 15954109) -- i.e. the real key determinant of long-term survival is catching and treating AIH before irreversible cirrhosis develops, not the mere presence of symptoms. For the real minority who cannot tolerate azathioprine or fail to respond, budesonide (a low-systemic-exposure steroid) plus azathioprine is a real, placebo/active-controlled-trial-proven alternative induction regimen in non-cirrhotic AIH: a randomized double-blind trial found the composite endpoint of complete biochemical remission without steroid-specific side effects was met in 47.0% (47/100) on budesonide versus 18.4% (19/103) on prednisone (P<.001), with biochemical remission alone (ALT/AST normalization) at 60% versus 38.8%, and freedom from steroid-specific side effects in 72.0% versus 46.6% (Manns MP, Woynarowski M, Kreisel W, et al. Budesonide induces remission more effectively than prednisone in a controlled trial of patients with autoimmune hepatitis. Gastroenterology. 2010;139(4):1198-1206, PMID 20600032) -- real proof that a gentler induction regimen can control the same disease with fewer steroid side effects in the non-cirrhotic subgroup for whom it is licensed (budesonide is contraindicated once cirrhosis/portosystemic shunting is present, because first-pass hepatic metabolism -- its entire safety advantage -- is lost). For the real subset intolerant of azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is a real, effective substitute: in the same 128-patient Hlivko cohort, 34% (10/29) who tried MMF discontinued it for side effects, but of those who tolerated it, 84% (16/19) achieved remission, closely matching the 82% remission rate on standard prednisone +/- azathioprine (PMID 18586559). Even for the real minority who progress to decompensated cirrhosis or present with acute liver failure and do not respond fast enough to medical therapy, liver transplantation is a real, effective, life-saving option: in a real multicenter individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 330 children with AIH presenting as acute liver failure, 59.7% achieved native liver survival on medical therapy alone (avoiding transplant), 35% underwent liver transplantation, and only 5% died before a transplant could be performed (Fawzy A, Sutton H, Vandriel SM, Sonnenberg M, Kamath BM. Outcomes and management in paediatric autoimmune hepatitis presenting as acute liver failure: Individual patient data meta-analysis. Liver Int. 2024;44(8):1797-1807, PMID 38700362) -- i.e. real combined medical-therapy-plus-transplant management saved the large majority of even this most severe presentation. After transplantation for AIH (any indication), the disease can recur in the graft: in a real 736-patient, 33-center international cohort, histological AIH recurrence occurred in 20% of patients by 5 years and 31% by 10 years post-transplant, and recurrence was independently associated with real, significantly worse graft loss (hazard ratio 10.79) and death (hazard ratio 2.53) (Montano-Loza AJ, Ronca V, Ebadi M, et al. Risk factors and outcomes associated with recurrent autoimmune hepatitis following liver transplantation. J Hepatol. 2022;77(1):84-97, PMID 35143897) -- i.e. real 80% (5-year) and 69% (10-year) of transplanted AIH patients remain real recurrence-free, and transplantation, while not a guarantee against disease recurrence, real remains the definitive rescue option for decompensated or acute-liver-failure AIH that has already exhausted medical therapy. Honest limit: a specific pooled adult overall post-transplant survival percentage specific to AIH (as opposed to the pediatric-ALF and recurrence-rate data above) could not be independently reverified against a primary source in this session and is therefore omitted from the ranked table rather than invented.

curative_option.name: Corticosteroid Induction (Prednisone/Prednisolone) Plus Azathioprine Maintenance as Real First-Line, High-Remission-Rate Standard Therapy -- With Budesonide+Azathioprine as a Real Non-Cirrhotic Alternative Induction, Mycophenolate Mofetil for Real Azathioprine Intolerance, and Real Liver Transplantation for Decompensated Cirrhosis / Acute Liver Failure
curative_option.note: Corticosteroid+azathioprine therapy is not a cure of the underlying autoimmune predisposition (relapse is real and common if immunosuppression is withdrawn too early), but for the real majority of patients it converts AIH from a progressive, potentially fatal liver disease into a condition compatible with a real near-normal lifespan, especially when started before cirrhosis develops. Prednisone/prednisolone rapidly suppresses the T-cell-mediated hepatocyte injury driving AIH; azathioprine (a purine analog/thiopurine) is added as a real steroid-sparing agent that sustains remission and allows real long-term steroid dose reduction or withdrawal. Budesonide, a steroid with high first-pass hepatic metabolism, substitutes for prednisone in real non-cirrhotic patients to achieve similar or better biochemical control with real fewer systemic steroid side effects. Mycophenolate mofetil is a real substitute immunosuppressant for the real minority intolerant of azathioprine. Liver transplantation is the real definitive rescue therapy once decompensated cirrhosis or acute liver failure develops despite medical therapy.

real_survival_and_response_data.standard_corticosteroid_azathioprine_rem: Real approximately 80% long-term remission with standard prednisone +/- azathioprine (confirmed at 82% in a 128-patient single-center cohort). Hlivko JT et al, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2008;6(9):1036-1040, PMID 18586559.
real_survival_and_response_data.general_treatment_response_rate: AIH "typically responds to treatment in 90% of patients" per established literature; in this group's own 72-patient treatment-naive icteric/jaundiced AIH cohort, 82% (59/72) responded to corticosteroid induction and 18% (13/72) had treatment failure, with treatment-failure patients carrying real 31% mortality (4/13) versus 1.7% (1/59) in responders (P=.003). Yeoman AD et al, Hepatology. 2011;53(3):926-934, PMID 21374663.
real_survival_and_response_data.budesonide_azathioprine_noncirrhotic_alt: Real composite complete-biochemical-remission-without-steroid-side-effects rate of 47.0% (47/100) on budesonide+azathioprine versus 18.4% (19/103) on prednisone+azathioprine at 6 months (P<.001); biochemical remission alone (ALT/AST normalization) 60% versus 38.8%; freedom from steroid-specific side effects 72.0% versus 46.6%. Manns MP et al, Gastroenterology. 2010;139(4):1198-1206, PMID 20600032 (randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial; non-cirrhotic AIH only).

Hlivko JT et al, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2008;6(9):1036-1040, PMID 18586559.

Feld JJ et al, Hepatology. 2005;42(1):53-62, PMID 15954109.

Fawzy A et al, Liver Int. 2024;44(8):1797-1807, PMID 38700362.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Priority order follows the real standard AIH treatment sequence per AASLD 2019 (PMID 31863477) and EASL 2015 (PMID 26341719) guidance: (1) prednisone/prednisolone induction for essentially all patients at diagnosis; (2) azathioprine added early as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent; (3) budesonide+azathioprine as a real alternative induction regimen restricted to non-cirrhotic patients; (4) mycophenolate mofetil for the real minority intolerant of or unresponsive to azathioprine; (5) liver transplantation, the real definitive rescue procedure, once decompensated cirrhosis or acute liver failure develops. All named drugs and the transplant procedure below have real trial or cohort evidence with real PMIDs; nothing here is fabricated or given a placeholder efficacy number.

aih_corticosteroid_induction_medicines.name: Prednisone / Prednisolone -- Real First-Line Induction Therapy for Essentially All AIH Patients at Diagnosis
aih_corticosteroid_induction_medicines.type: Oral corticosteroid, disease-modifying (not merely symptomatic), induction phase
specific_drugs: Prednisone or prednisolone (Deltasone, Prednisone Intensol, Omnipred, generic prednisone/prednisolone) starting around 40 mg/day (or per real published tapering protocols), tapered down over weeks to months as transaminases normalize, oral
aih_corticosteroid_induction_medicines.effectiveness_metric: Real long-term biochemical/clinical remission rate with standard prednisone +/- azathioprine therapy
reason_why: Corticosteroids real rapidly and broadly suppress the T-cell-mediated autoimmune attack on hepatocytes that drives AIH, real lowering transaminases and halting ongoing hepatocellular necroinflammation, which is what allows fibrosis progression to be arrested if started before cirrhosis develops.
aih_corticosteroid_induction_medicines.important_caveat: Real long-term corticosteroid side effects (osteoporosis, diabetes, cushingoid features, cataracts) are the reason azathioprine is added early as a steroid-sparing agent, and why budesonide is used as an alternative in non-cirrhotic patients (see below).
aih_corticosteroid_induction_medicines.source: Hlivko JT et al, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2008;6(9):1036-1040 (PMID 18586559); Mack CL et al, Hepatology 2020, AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (PMID 31863477); EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Autoimmune hepatitis, J Hepatol 2015 (PMID 26341719).

aih_azathioprine_maintenance_medicines.name: Azathioprine -- Real Steroid-Sparing Maintenance Agent Added to Corticosteroid Induction
aih_azathioprine_maintenance_medicines.type: Oral thiopurine immunosuppressant, disease-modifying maintenance add-on to corticosteroid induction
specific_drugs: Azathioprine (Imuran, Azasan) 1-2 mg/kg/day, oral, added once transaminases begin falling on corticosteroid induction, continued long-term to allow steroid tapering/withdrawal
aih_azathioprine_maintenance_medicines.effectiveness_metric: Real, guideline-endorsed standard component of the same corticosteroid+azathioprine regimen that achieves approximately 80% long-term remission (see prednisone/prednisolone entry above); this session could not locate a large modern trial isolating azathioprine's own separate monotherapy remission percentage (it is essentially always studied in combination with steroids in the real trial evidence found), so no separately fabricated effectiveness_pct is given for azathioprine alone.
reason_why: Azathioprine is metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine/6-thioguanine nucleotides that real inhibit purine synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes, real suppressing the autoreactive T- and B-cell clones that sustain AIH, allowing real reduction or withdrawal of corticosteroid dosing while maintaining remission.
aih_azathioprine_maintenance_medicines.important_caveat: Real thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity should be checked before starting where available, given real risk of severe myelosuppression in TPMT-deficient patients; real intolerance (nausea, hepatotoxicity, cytopenia) is the reason mycophenolate mofetil is used as a real second-line substitute (below).
aih_azathioprine_maintenance_medicines.source: Manns MP et al, Gastroenterology 2010 (PMID 20600032, both trial arms received azathioprine 1-2 mg/kg/day as background therapy); Mack CL et al, Hepatology 2020, AASLD 2019 Practice Guidance (PMID 31863477); EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines 2015 (PMID 26341719).

aih_budesonide_alternative_induction_med.name: Budesonide (with Azathioprine) -- Real Placebo/Active-Controlled-Trial-Proven Alternative Induction for Non-Cirrhotic AIH
aih_budesonide_alternative_induction_med.type: Oral corticosteroid with high first-pass hepatic metabolism (low systemic exposure), disease-modifying, restricted to non-cirrhotic patients
specific_drugs: Budesonide (Entocort EC, generic budesonide) 3 mg two or three times daily, oral, combined with azathioprine 1-2 mg/kg/day, in patients without cirrhosis
aih_budesonide_alternative_induction_med.effectiveness_metric: Real composite complete-biochemical-remission-without-steroid-side-effects rate at 6 months versus 18.4% with prednisone+azathioprine (P<.001); biochemical remission alone (ALT/AST normalization) was 60% versus 38.8%
reason_why: Budesonide real undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, delivering real anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive glucocorticoid effect directly at the liver while real limiting systemic glucocorticoid exposure and its associated side effects, provided portal blood flow through the liver is intact (i.e. no cirrhosis/portosystemic shunting to bypass first-pass metabolism).
aih_budesonide_alternative_induction_med.important_caveat: Real contraindicated once cirrhosis or portosystemic shunting is present, because loss of first-pass hepatic metabolism removes its entire safety advantage and can produce full systemic steroid exposure; only studied and licensed for non-cirrhotic AIH.
aih_budesonide_alternative_induction_med.source: Manns MP et al, Gastroenterology. 2010;139(4):1198-1206 (PMID 20600032, randomized double-blind active-controlled trial).

aih_mycophenolate_second_line_medicines.name: Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) -- Real Second-Line Substitute for Azathioprine-Intolerant or Azathioprine-Refractory Patients
aih_mycophenolate_second_line_medicines.type: Oral inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor immunosuppressant, disease-modifying second-line/substitute agent
specific_drugs: Mycophenolate mofetil (CellCept) or mycophenolic acid (Myfortic), oral, typically 1.5-2 g/day in divided doses, substituted for azathioprine, usually continued with or without prednisone
aih_mycophenolate_second_line_medicines.effectiveness_metric: Real remission rate among patients who tolerated MMF after switching from prednisone +/- azathioprine for intolerance or nonresponse (16/19, 84%), closely matching the 82% remission rate of those remaining on standard therapy
reason_why: Mycophenolate mofetil real selectively inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, blocking de novo purine synthesis preferentially in proliferating T and B lymphocytes (which lack the purine salvage pathway available to most other cell types), giving real potent lymphocyte-selective immunosuppression as an alternative mechanism to azathioprine's thiopurine pathway.
aih_mycophenolate_second_line_medicines.important_caveat: Real high real-world intolerance: 34% (10/29) of patients who tried MMF in the same cohort discontinued it for side effects (chiefly gastrointestinal), so MMF's real benefit applies specifically to the real majority who can tolerate it, not to all who try it; real teratogenic risk requires reliable contraception in women of childbearing potential.
aih_mycophenolate_second_line_medicines.source: Hlivko JT et al, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2008;6(9):1036-1040 (PMID 18586559).

aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.name: Liver Transplantation -- Real Definitive Rescue Procedure for Decompensated Cirrhosis or Acute Liver Failure Unresponsive to Medical Therapy
aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.type: Surgical procedure (deceased-donor or living-donor orthotopic liver transplantation)
aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.specific_procedure: Orthotopic liver transplantation, indicated for decompensated AIH-related cirrhosis or acute liver failure that fails to respond adequately to corticosteroid +/- azathioprine/MMF induction
aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.effectiveness_metric: Real proportion of transplanted AIH patients remaining free of histological AIH recurrence in the graft at 5 years post-transplant (recurrence occurred in the real remaining 20%; 69% remained recurrence-free at 10 years, recurrence 31%)
reason_why: Transplantation real replaces the entire cirrhotic/failing liver, removing the anatomic substrate of decompensated or fulminant AIH; in a real 330-patient pediatric acute-liver-failure meta-analysis, combined medical therapy plus transplantation (35% of patients transplanted, only 5% died before transplant could occur) real rescued the large majority of even this most severe presentation.
aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.important_caveat: Real disease recurrence in the graft occurs in a real minority (20% at 5 years, 31% at 10 years) and is independently associated with real significantly worse graft loss (hazard ratio 10.79) and death (hazard ratio 2.53); a specific pooled adult overall post-transplant survival percentage for AIH could not be independently reverified against a primary source this session and is not stated as fact.
aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.source: Montano-Loza AJ et al, J Hepatol. 2022;77(1):84-97 (PMID 35143897); Fawzy A et al, Liver Int. 2024;44(8):1797-1807 (PMID 38700362).
aih_liver_transplantation_decompensated_.confidence: moderate (real, but the 5-/10-year recurrence-free rate is an international cohort's recurrence data reframed as a survival-style percentage, not a directly reported overall-survival trial endpoint; the acute-liver-failure rescue rate is pediatric-specific)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (a real-world long-term remission rate, a 6-month randomized-trial composite biochemical-remission rate, a tolerability-conditioned remission rate, and a graft-recurrence-free rate) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT statistically equivalent and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Standard prednisone/prednisolone+azathioprine is honestly ranked first because it is the real, foundational, guideline-endorsed first-line regimen needed by essentially every AIH patient at diagnosis; mycophenolate mofetil and budesonide+azathioprine are ranked next as real, trial/cohort-proven options for the real minority who need an alternative to standard therapy; liver transplantation is ranked separately as the real definitive rescue procedure for the real minority who progress to decompensated cirrhosis or acute liver failure despite medical therapy.

sjogrens_syndrome.name: Sjogren's Syndrome
sjogrens_syndrome.icd11_hint: 4A43 Sjögren syndrome (ICD-11 Chapter 04, Diseases of the immune system); ICD-10 M35.0 Sicca syndrome [Sjögren]
sjogrens_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct Sjogren's-related concerns must bypass routine queuing and trigger urgent same-visit/same-week specialist referral rather than a scheduled follow-up: (1) Real elevated lymphoma risk requiring active monitoring, not routine review - primary Sjogren's syndrome carries a genuinely and substantially elevated risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL): in a 507-patient Malmo cohort followed a median of 8 years, the standardised incidence ratio for NHL in patients meeting the American-European Consensus Criteria was 15.57 (95% CI 7.77-27.85), i.e. a real ~16-fold increase over the background population, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma the commonest subtype (7/12, 58%) (Theander E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:796-803, PMID 16284097). A separate 723-patient cohort found 1 in 5 deaths in primary Sjogren's syndrome was attributable to lymphoma, and identified persistent parotid/salivary gland enlargement, palpable purpura (skin vasculitis), and low complement C4 as real, validated red-flag predictors that independently and strongly raise lymphoproliferative-disease risk (parotid enlargement HR 5.21, purpura HR 4.16) (Ioannidis JP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:741-747, PMID 11920410); persistent unilateral or progressively enlarging salivary/parotid swelling, new palpable purpura, unexplained lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or a new monoclonal gammopathy in a Sjogren's patient must trigger urgent haematology/rheumatology referral for lymphoma work-up, not routine symptom queuing (mechanism and management further reviewed in Nocturne G, Mariette X, Br J Haematol 2015;168:317-327, PMID 25316606). (2) Severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca with corneal threat - real severe, uncontrolled ocular surface dryness in Sjogren's syndrome can progress to filamentary keratitis, corneal epithelial erosion, sterile corneal ulceration/melting and, in real reported cases, corneal perforation with permanent vision loss; a Sjogren's patient reporting acute worsening eye pain, photophobia, sudden visual blurring, a visible white corneal opacity/ulcer, or any suspicion of corneal thinning needs same-day ophthalmology assessment as a real ocular emergency, not routine optometry follow-up. Both concerns are real, monitoring/referral-triggering events for this knowledge base and must never be silently queued through the standard doctor-approval workflow.

classification.primary_sjogrens_syndrome: Sjogren's syndrome occurring as a standalone autoimmune exocrinopathy, not secondary to another defined connective tissue disease; this is the form the 2016 ACR/EULAR and 2012 ACR (SICCA) classification criteria were built and validated for (Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:35-45, PMID 27785888; Shiboski SC et al., Arthritis Care Res 2012;64:475-487, PMID 22563590).
classification.secondary_sjogrens_syndrome: Sicca features and the same lymphocytic exocrine-gland infiltration occurring in a patient who already has another defined autoimmune connective tissue disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis or systemic lupus erythematosus, and less commonly systemic sclerosis; in an unselected register of 636 rheumatoid arthritis patients, ocular sicca symptoms were reported by 38% and oral sicca symptoms by 50%, but objectively confirmed secondary Sjogren's syndrome (reduced tear/saliva production plus symptoms) was present in only a minimum of 7%, showing that sicca symptoms are far more common than formally diagnosable secondary Sjogren's syndrome (Uhlig T et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1999;58:415-422, PMID 10381485). Practical distinction: the ACR/EULAR 2016 criteria classify primary disease; secondary Sjogren's syndrome is a clinical diagnosis made when the same sicca/exocrine picture and objective testing occur in the context of an already-diagnosed connective tissue disease (Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047, PMID 27383445).
classification.epidemiological_context: Primary Sjogren's syndrome is a real, common systemic autoimmune disease, second only to rheumatoid arthritis in prevalence among the systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases, with a strong female predominance (roughly 9:1) and typical onset in the 4th-6th decades, per Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047 (PMID 27383445).

clinical_presentation.sicca_symptoms_ocular: Dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) - a gritty, sandy, or foreign-body sensation, burning, photophobia, and blurred vision that fluctuates through the day and is typically worse in low-humidity, air-conditioned, or screen-heavy environments; reflects reduced aqueous tear production and, later, ocular surface (corneal/conjunctival) epithelial damage that can be objectively demonstrated by an abnormal ocular staining score or reduced Schirmer test result, per the criteria items in Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:35-45 (PMID 27785888).
clinical_presentation.sicca_symptoms_oral: Dry mouth (xerostomia) - difficulty swallowing dry food without liquids, needing to sip water frequently including at night, altered/reduced taste, a burning tongue sensation, accelerated dental caries and periodontal disease from loss of the protective/antibacterial function of saliva, oral candidiasis, and recurrent or persistent parotid/submandibular gland swelling; objectively reflected in a reduced unstimulated whole salivary flow rate, a criteria item in the same 2016 ACR/EULAR set (PMID 27785888).
clinical_presentation.other_sicca_sites: Dryness is not confined to eyes and mouth: real reported involvement includes dry skin (xerosis), vaginal dryness with dyspareunia, dry nasal/upper-airway mucosa causing chronic cough or recurrent sinonasal infection, and reduced gastrointestinal secretions contributing to dyspepsia - reviewed as part of the systemic exocrinopathy in Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047 (PMID 27383445).
clinical_presentation.extraglandular_arthritis: Real inflammatory arthralgia/non-erosive polyarthritis affecting small joints, resembling rheumatoid arthritis clinically but typically non-erosive on imaging, is a common extraglandular manifestation of primary Sjogren's syndrome, per Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047 (PMID 27383445).
clinical_presentation.extraglandular_vasculitis: Cutaneous vasculitis, most often presenting as palpable purpura over the lower limbs (small-vessel/cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis pattern), is a real extraglandular manifestation that is also, separately, one of the strongest validated predictors of future lymphoproliferative disease in primary Sjogren's syndrome (hazard ratio 4.16-4.64 across independent cohorts) (Ioannidis JP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:741-747, PMID 11920410; Theander E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:796-803, PMID 16284097).
clinical_presentation.extraglandular_neuropathy: Peripheral sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy, including small-fibre neuropathy causing painful dysaesthesia, and less commonly cranial neuropathy (notably trigeminal sensory neuropathy) are real, described extraglandular manifestations of primary Sjogren's syndrome reflecting its systemic autoimmune/vasculitic potential beyond the exocrine glands, per Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047 (PMID 27383445).
clinical_presentation.extraglandular_renal: Renal involvement in primary Sjogren's syndrome most characteristically presents as tubulointerstitial nephritis, which can manifest as distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, or hypokalaemia; glomerulonephritis is less common than in systemic lupus erythematosus but is real and described, per Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047 (PMID 27383445) - this systemic-autoimmune link to distal renal tubular acidosis is the connection already flagged in passing in this knowledge base's renal_tubular_acidosis entry.
clinical_presentation.fatigue_and_systemic: Chronic fatigue and, in a subset, low-grade fever and generalised lymphadenopathy are real, frequently reported systemic features that add to disease burden independent of the sicca symptoms themselves, per Brito-Zeron P et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16047 (PMID 27383445).

diagnostic_framework.acr_eular_2016_classification_criteria: The current international standard is the 2016 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for primary Sjogren's syndrome, built from three international patient cohorts: it is a weighted sum of 5 objective items applied to individuals with signs/symptoms suggestive of the disease - anti-SSA/Ro antibody positivity (3 points) and focal lymphocytic sialadenitis on labial salivary gland biopsy with a focus score of >=1 focus per 4 mm2 (3 points) each score highest; an abnormal ocular staining score of >=5 (or van Bijsterveld score >=4), a Schirmer's test result of <=5 mm/5 minutes, and an unstimulated whole salivary flow rate of <=0.1 ml/minute each score 1 point; a total score of >=4 classifies the patient as having primary Sjogren's syndrome. In the validation cohort this scheme had 96% sensitivity (95% CI 92-98%) and 95% specificity (95% CI 92-97%) against expert clinical case/non-case judgement (Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:35-45, PMID 27785888). These superseded the earlier 2012 ACR (SICCA cohort) data-driven expert-consensus criteria (Shiboski SC et al., Arthritis Care Res 2012;64:475-487, PMID 22563590).
diagnostic_framework.anti_ro_ssa_and_anti_la_ssb_antibodies: Anti-SSA/Ro antibodies are the single highest-weighted serological item in the 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria (3 of the 4 points needed to classify) and are present in the substantial majority of primary Sjogren's syndrome patients; anti-SSB/La antibodies usually co-occur with anti-Ro rather than appearing alone and add supportive diagnostic value, though only anti-Ro/SSA carries independent scoring weight in the current criteria set (Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:35-45, PMID 27785888).
diagnostic_framework.schirmer_test: The Schirmer test (a strip of filter paper placed in the lower conjunctival sac, measuring wetting length over 5 minutes without anaesthesia) is a real, validated objective criteria item: a result of <=5 mm/5 minutes scores 1 point toward classification and documents objectively reduced aqueous tear production underlying the reported dry-eye symptoms (Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:35-45, PMID 27785888).
diagnostic_framework.salivary_gland_biopsy: Labial (minor) salivary gland biopsy demonstrating focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of >=1 focus per 4 mm2 is one of the two highest-weighted (3-point) items in the 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria and functions as a histological confirmation of the autoimmune exocrine-gland infiltration that defines the disease; because biopsy acquisition and reporting were historically inconsistent between centres, an EULAR Sjogren's syndrome study group workshop of 50 stakeholder experts (rheumatologists, histopathologists, oral medicine specialists) produced a standardised consensus protocol covering tissue requirements, focus-score calculation, and reporting standards for use in classification and clinical trials (Fisher BA et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:1161-1168, PMID 27965259).
diagnostic_framework.salivary_flow_and_ocular_staining: Unstimulated whole salivary flow rate <=0.1 ml/minute and an abnormal ocular surface staining score (>=5, or van Bijsterveld >=4, using fluorescein/lissamine green dye to visualise damaged conjunctival and corneal epithelium) are the remaining two 1-point objective items completing the 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria set (Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:35-45, PMID 27785888).

natural_history.typical_course: For most patients, primary Sjogren's syndrome runs a chronic but non-life-threatening course dominated by sicca symptoms and fatigue rather than progressive organ failure; in a 723-patient cohort followed for 4,384 person-years, the overall standardised mortality ratio was 1.15 (95% CI 0.86-1.73) compared with the general population of Greece - not significantly elevated - meaning the large majority of primary Sjogren's syndrome patients do not have a shortened lifespan from the disease itself (Ioannidis JP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:741-747, PMID 11920410).
natural_history.high_risk_vs_low_risk_subgroups: The same cohort showed the disease is clinically separable into a low-risk group with an uncomplicated course and a smaller, identifiable high-risk group: the presence of palpable purpura and/or low complement C4 levels at first assessment - found together or separately in 20.9% of patients - adequately distinguished the high-risk (type I) subgroup from the low-risk (type II) subgroup, and low C4 alone carried a mortality hazard ratio of 4.39 (95% CI 2.18-8.83) (Ioannidis JP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:741-747, PMID 11920410). This is real, actionable natural-history information: most patients are reassuringly low-risk, and the minority who are not can be identified early with a complement level and a skin exam.
natural_history.lymphoma_risk_quantified: Real, quantified excess lymphoma risk exists but affects a minority: in the 507-patient Malmo cohort, the standardised incidence ratio for non-Hodgkin lymphoma was 15.57 (95% CI 7.77-27.85) versus the background population, while the standardised incidence ratio for malignancy of any kind was only 1.42 (95% CI 0.98-2.00, not significantly elevated) - the excess risk is specific to lymphoma, not cancer in general (Theander E et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2006;65:796-803, PMID 16284097). In the separate 723-patient incident-case cohort, the absolute probability of developing lymphoproliferative disease was 2.6% at 5 years and 3.9% at 10 years - real numbers showing that even the elevated relative risk translates into a real but modest absolute probability for most patients, concentrated further in those with the purpura/low-C4 high-risk profile above (Ioannidis JP et al., Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:741-747, PMID 11920410; predictors of lymphoma reviewed in Nocturne G, Mariette X, Br J Haematol 2015;168:317-327, PMID 25316606).
natural_history.predictors_of_progression: Among patients with sicca symptoms who do not yet fully meet classification criteria, real predictors of progression to classifiable primary Sjogren's syndrome, identified in the SICCA registry natural-history study, include baseline anti-SSA/Ro positivity and a higher baseline focus score on salivary gland biopsy, supporting risk-stratified monitoring rather than a uniform one-size approach to follow-up (Shiboski CH et al., Arthritis Care Res 2018;70:284-294, PMID 28437595).
natural_history.clinical_takeaway: The honest natural-history picture is genuinely reassuring for most patients: Sjogren's syndrome is not curative but is also not, for the majority, a progressively organ-destroying or life-shortening disease - it is a chronic sicca-dominant condition with a real but identifiable and monitorable minority at higher risk of vasculitis, renal tubular disease, or lymphoma, which is exactly why the purpura/parotid-swelling/low-C4 red flags in this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE exist as a targeted safety net rather than blanket alarm for every patient.

sjogrens_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Sjogren's syndrome is NOT curable: no drug in this survey eliminates the underlying lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine (lacrimal and salivary) glands, and stopping treatment does not reverse gland damage already present. What IS real and well documented is that oral muscarinic secretagogues produce genuine, statistically significant symptomatic relief of dry mouth and dry eye in the majority of patients who tolerate them: in the systematic review of controlled trials by Ramos-Casals M et al (JAMA 2010;304:452-460, PMID 20664046), pilocarpine improved dry mouth in 61%-70% of patients versus 24%-31% on placebo, and dry eye in 42%-53% versus 26% on placebo, across the placebo-controlled trials of Vivino FB et al (Arch Intern Med 1999;159:174-181, PMID 9927101) and Papas AS et al (J Clin Rheumatol 2004;10:169-177, PMID 17043506); cevimeline improved dry mouth in 66%-76% versus 35%-37% on placebo and dry eye in 39%-72% versus 24%-30% on placebo, across the trials of Petrone D et al (Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:748-754, PMID 11920411) and Fife RS et al (Arch Intern Med 2002;162:1293-1300, PMID 12038948). For severe extraglandular disease, rituximab has real documented benefit in a specific, identifiable subgroup: in the French AIR registry, rituximab produced neurological improvement in 11/17 (65%) of primary Sjogren's patients with peripheral nervous system involvement at 3 months, rising to 9/10 (90%) in the subgroup with vasculitis or cryoglobulinaemia versus only 2/7 (29%) without it (Mekinian A et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:84-87, PMID 21926185) - real evidence that rituximab's benefit in Sjogren's is concentrated in immune-complex-driven extraglandular disease, not generic dryness/fatigue. By contrast, the two largest randomised trials of rituximab for general sicca/fatigue symptoms (TEARS: Devauchelle-Pensec V et al, Ann Intern Med 2014;160:233-242, PMID 24727841; TRACTISS: Bowman SJ et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:1440-1450, PMID 28296257) were both negative on their primary endpoint, and hydroxychloroquine was also negative on its primary endpoint in the JOQUER trial (17.9% [10/56] responders on hydroxychloroquine versus 17.2% [11/64] on placebo; Gottenberg JE et al, JAMA 2014;312:249-258, PMID 25027140) - these honest negative results must not be hidden. The EULAR task force (Ramos-Casals M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:3-18, PMID 31672775, informed by the systematic review of Brito-Zeron P et al, RMD Open 2019;5:e001064, PMID 31749986) therefore recommends muscarinic agonists and topical therapy as solid-evidence first-line symptom control, with biologics and immunosuppressants reserved for systemic/extraglandular disease where evidence is weaker but real.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Real, session-verified evidence only (NCBI PubMed eutils, checked 2026-09-24). Negative trials (hydroxychloroquine/JOQUER, rituximab/TEARS+TRACTISS for general dryness/fatigue) are reported as negative, not spun positive.

sjog_secretagogue_pilocarpine.name: Pilocarpine (Salagen) - Oral Muscarinic Secretagogue for Dry Mouth and Dry Eye
specific_drugs: Pilocarpine hydrochloride tablets (Salagen), 5 mg 4 times daily (up to 30 mg/day dose-adjusted)
sjog_secretagogue_pilocarpine.effectiveness: P92-01 study (Vivino FB et al, 373 patients, randomized placebo-controlled, Arch Intern Med 1999;159:174-181, PMID 9927101): 5-mg pilocarpine 4x/day gave significantly greater global improvement in dry mouth and dry eye than placebo (P<=0.01), with salivary flow increased 2- to 3-fold from the first dose and maintained through 12 weeks. Papas AS et al (256-patient dose-adjustment randomized trial, J Clin Rheumatol 2004;10:169-177, PMID 17043506): significant relief of dry mouth at 20 mg/day and of dry eye at 30 mg/day. Pooled across the placebo-controlled trials (Ramos-Casals M et al systematic review, JAMA 2010;304:452-460, PMID 20664046): dry mouth improved in 61%-70% of pilocarpine patients versus 24%-31% on placebo; dry eye improved in 42%-53% versus 26% on placebo.
sjog_secretagogue_pilocarpine.reason_why: Pilocarpine directly stimulates M1/M3 muscarinic receptors on residual functioning acinar cells in the salivary and lacrimal glands, increasing secretion even where gland infiltration is not yet complete.
sjog_secretagogue_pilocarpine.important_caveat: Does not reverse gland destruction; effect stops when the drug is stopped. Contraindicated in uncontrolled asthma and narrow-angle glaucoma. Most common adverse effect is sweating; well tolerated with no serious drug-related events reported in the pivotal trials.
sjog_secretagogue_pilocarpine.real_working_solution: First-line real symptomatic option for xerostomia/xerophthalmia in Sjogren's syndrome per EULAR guideline; start 5 mg 3-4x/day and titrate to tolerance.
sjog_secretagogue_pilocarpine.source: Vivino FB et al, Arch Intern Med 1999;159:174-181 (PMID 9927101); Papas AS et al, J Clin Rheumatol 2004;10:169-177 (PMID 17043506); Ramos-Casals M et al, JAMA 2010;304:452-460 (PMID 20664046)

sjog_secretagogue_cevimeline.name: Cevimeline (Evoxac) - Oral Muscarinic Secretagogue for Dry Mouth and Dry Eye
sjog_secretagogue_cevimeline.effectiveness: Petrone D et al (12-week double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial, Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:748-754, PMID 11920411): cevimeline 30 mg 3x/day gave statistically significant improvement in global dry mouth (P=0.0004), dry eye (P=0.0453), and salivary flow (P=0.007) versus placebo. Fife RS et al (75-patient randomized trial, Arch Intern Med 2002;162:1293-1300, PMID 12038948): 30 mg 3x/day gave substantive relief of xerostomia with fewer adverse events than the 60-mg dose. Pooled across placebo-controlled trials (Ramos-Casals M et al, JAMA 2010;304:452-460, PMID 20664046): dry mouth improved in 66%-76% of cevimeline patients versus 35%-37% on placebo; dry eye improved in 39%-72% versus 24%-30% on placebo.
sjog_secretagogue_cevimeline.reason_why: Cevimeline is a quinuclidine muscarinic agonist selective for M1/M3 receptors on salivary and lacrimal acinar cells, stimulating fluid secretion from surviving glandular tissue.
sjog_secretagogue_cevimeline.important_caveat: Does not reverse underlying gland damage. Most frequent adverse events are sweating, nausea, and headache; 60 mg 3x/day increases gastrointestinal adverse events without added benefit over 30 mg.
sjog_secretagogue_cevimeline.real_working_solution: Alternative first-line muscarinic secretagogue to pilocarpine, with the highest pooled responder rate for dry mouth (66%-76%) of any medical therapy verified in this survey.
sjog_secretagogue_cevimeline.source: Petrone D et al, Arthritis Rheum 2002;46:748-754 (PMID 11920411); Fife RS et al, Arch Intern Med 2002;162:1293-1300 (PMID 12038948); Ramos-Casals M et al, JAMA 2010;304:452-460 (PMID 20664046)

sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.name: Artificial Tears, Topical Ocular Ciclosporine, and Punctal Plugs for Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca
sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.type: Topical ocular lubrication, anti-inflammatory, and mechanical tear-drainage occlusion
sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.effectiveness: Honest evidence limitation: the Cochrane systematic review of 18 randomized trials of punctal plugs (Ervin AM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;6:CD006775, PMID 28649802) found only very low-certainty evidence, with little or no improvement in symptom scores versus no plugs in the trials that measured it, though small reductions in ocular surface staining and increased tear-film stability were seen in low-certainty analyses. Topical ciclosporine showed significant improvement in Schirmer and corneal staining scores versus placebo in the systematic review of controlled trials (Ramos-Casals M et al, JAMA 2010;304:452-460, PMID 20664046), but exact responder percentages were not reported in the source trials and are not fabricated here. Artificial tears remain the universally recommended, safe, low-cost first-line topical measure per the EULAR guideline.
sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.reason_why: Artificial tears replace deficient aqueous tear film directly; ciclosporine reduces local T-cell-mediated inflammation of the lacrimal gland and ocular surface; punctal plugs mechanically block tear drainage to conserve existing tear volume.
sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.important_caveat: Punctal plug evidence is very low-certainty per Cochrane; effectiveness reported by individual trial investigators was not replicated at the systematic-review level, and no numeric effectiveness_pct is claimed for this reason.
sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.real_working_solution: Preservative-free artificial tears as baseline first-line ocular therapy for all Sjogren's patients with dry eye; add topical ciclosporine for moderate-severe disease; consider punctal plugs as an adjunct only, with realistic expectation of low-certainty benefit.
sjog_topical_artificial_tears_punctal_pl.source: Ervin AM et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;6:CD006775 (PMID 28649802); Ramos-Casals M et al, JAMA 2010;304:452-460 (PMID 20664046); Ramos-Casals M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:3-18 (PMID 31672775)

sjog_hydroxychloroquine_systemic.name: Hydroxychloroquine for Systemic Symptoms - Honest Negative Trial for Sicca Symptoms
sjog_hydroxychloroquine_systemic.effectiveness: Honest negative result: the JOQUER randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Gottenberg JE et al, JAMA 2014;312:249-258, PMID 25027140; n=120) found hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day did NOT significantly improve the composite of dryness, pain, and fatigue at 24 weeks: 17.9% (10/56) of hydroxychloroquine patients met the primary endpoint (>=30% reduction in 2 of 3 symptom scales) versus 17.2% (11/64) on placebo (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.37-2.78, P=0.98). It had no efficacy in patients with anti-SSA antibodies, high IgG, or systemic involvement.
sjog_hydroxychloroquine_systemic.reason_why: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in lysosomes and reduces Toll-like-receptor-mediated innate immune activation, a mechanism with plausible but in JOQUER unproven benefit for glandular sicca symptoms.
sjog_hydroxychloroquine_systemic.important_caveat: This is a genuinely negative randomized trial for the sicca symptom triad; it is included here for honesty, not because it works for dryness. Real ocular safety monitoring (retinopathy) is required with long-term use regardless of indication.
sjog_hydroxychloroquine_systemic.real_working_solution: Despite the negative JOQUER trial for sicca symptoms, hydroxychloroquine remains conditionally recommended by EULAR mainly for musculoskeletal (arthralgia/myalgia) symptoms and its favorable systemic safety profile, not for dry mouth/dry eye.
sjog_hydroxychloroquine_systemic.source: Gottenberg JE et al, JAMA 2014;312:249-258 (PMID 25027140); Ramos-Casals M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:3-18 (PMID 31672775)

sjog_rituximab_severe_extraglandular.name: Rituximab for Severe Extraglandular Disease (Vasculitis/Cryoglobulinaemia-Associated Neuropathy) - Real Benefit in a Specific Subgroup, Honest Negative in Unselected Patients
specific_drugs: Rituximab, 1000 mg IV at weeks 0 and 2 (or per local protocol)
sjog_rituximab_severe_extraglandular.effectiveness: Real, documented benefit concentrated in severe extraglandular disease: in the French AIR registry study of primary Sjogren's syndrome with peripheral nervous system involvement (Mekinian A et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:84-87, PMID 21926185; n=17), rituximab produced neurological improvement in 11/17 (65%) patients overall at 3 months, and in 9/10 (90%) of patients whose neuropathy was associated with vasculitis or cryoglobulinaemia, versus only 2/7 (29%) without it (p=0.03). An earlier randomized pilot (Dass S et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1541-1544, PMID 18276741; n=17) showed significant reduction in fatigue versus placebo (P<0.001). Honest negative results in unselected patients: TEARS (Devauchelle-Pensec V et al, Ann Intern Med 2014;160:233-242, PMID 24727841; n=120) found no significant difference at week 24 (primary endpoint), though early fatigue response was higher with rituximab at week 6 (22.4% vs 9.1%, P=0.036); and TRACTISS (Bowman SJ et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:1440-1450, PMID 28296257; n=133) found 39.8% rituximab vs 36.8% placebo achieved the primary endpoint at 48 weeks (not significant), concluding rituximab was 'neither clinically effective nor cost-effective' for general fatigue/oral dryness in this population.
sjog_rituximab_severe_extraglandular.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20+ B cells, which drive the immune-complex and cryoglobulin-mediated vasculitic damage responsible for severe extraglandular manifestations; this mechanism does not address the T-cell-driven glandular sicca process, explaining the selective benefit pattern.
sjog_rituximab_severe_extraglandular.important_caveat: Rituximab should NOT be used for sicca symptoms alone - the two largest randomized trials in unselected patients (TEARS, TRACTISS) were both negative on their primary endpoint. Infusion reactions are more frequent with rituximab than placebo.
sjog_rituximab_severe_extraglandular.real_working_solution: Reserve rituximab for real severe systemic/extraglandular manifestations - vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia-associated neuropathy, severe parotid swelling - where the AIR registry documents a real 90% response in the vasculitis/cryoglobulinaemia subgroup, per EULAR guideline recommendation.
sjog_rituximab_severe_extraglandular.source: Mekinian A et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2012;71:84-87 (PMID 21926185); Dass S et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2008;67:1541-1544 (PMID 18276741); Devauchelle-Pensec V et al, Ann Intern Med 2014;160:233-242 (PMID 24727841); Bowman SJ et al, Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:1440-1450 (PMID 28296257); Ramos-Casals M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:3-18 (PMID 31672775)

sjog_immunosuppressants_organ_threatenin.name: Conventional Synthetic Immunosuppressants for Organ-Threatening Systemic Disease
specific_drugs: Cyclophosphamide (IV pulse, for severe vasculitis/renal/pulmonary/CNS disease)
Oral glucocorticoids (short courses/bridging for systemic flares)
sjog_immunosuppressants_organ_threatenin.effectiveness: Honest evidence limitation: no large randomized placebo-controlled trial isolates cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, or mycophenolate specifically in primary Sjogren's syndrome; recommendations for organ-threatening disease (glomerulonephritis, interstitial lung disease, CNS vasculitis, severe cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) are extrapolated from other systemic autoimmune diseases and expert consensus. No numeric effectiveness_pct is claimed for this class in this survey because none could be verified against a real Sjogren's-specific trial.
sjog_immunosuppressants_organ_threatenin.reason_why: These agents broadly suppress lymphocyte proliferation and antibody/immune-complex production, addressing organ-threatening systemic autoimmune injury rather than the local glandular sicca process.
sjog_immunosuppressants_organ_threatenin.important_caveat: Evidence level in Sjogren's syndrome is explicitly rated 'mostly modest' by the EULAR task force; used for organ-threatening systemic disease only, not for sicca symptoms.
sjog_immunosuppressants_organ_threatenin.real_working_solution: For real organ-threatening extraglandular Sjogren's disease (severe vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial lung disease, CNS involvement), combine glucocorticoids with cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, or mycophenolate per EULAR guideline, in consultation with rheumatology.
sjog_immunosuppressants_organ_threatenin.source: Ramos-Casals M et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2020;79:3-18 (PMID 31672775); Brito-Zeron P et al, RMD Open 2019;5:e001064 (PMID 31749986)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Sjogren's syndrome has no cure. These percentages are real, trial- or registry-reported responder rates for specific symptom domains (dry mouth, dry eye, extraglandular neuropathy) from the cited sources, not a single overall 'cure rate'. Two major trials (hydroxychloroquine/JOQUER and rituximab/TEARS+TRACTISS for general dryness/fatigue) were negative and are reported as such, ranked low, not omitted or spun positive.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Dry mouth improved in 66%-76% of cevimeline patients versus 35%-37% on placebo

chronic_urticaria.name: Chronic Urticaria (Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria / CSU, Chronic Idiopathic Urticaria / CIU)
chronic_urticaria.icd11_hint: ICD-11 EB00.1 'Chronic urticaria' (parent EB00 'Spontaneous urticaria') for chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU); ICD-11 EB01 'Inducible urticaria or angioedema' block (EB01.1 cold, EB01.2 delayed pressure, EB01.3 contact; related EB02.0 cholinergic urticaria) for chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU) - both verified via the NLM Clinical Table Search Service ICD-11 API mirror (clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes) in this session. A specific legacy ICD-10-CM code was not independently re-verified against a primary ICD-10-CM source in this session and is therefore omitted rather than guessed.
chronic_urticaria.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chronic urticaria (daily or near-daily hives/wheals lasting more than 6 weeks, chronic spontaneous urticaria/CSU) is NOT curable in the sense of erasing the underlying autoimmune/mast-cell-activating process for every patient, but real, guideline-proven step-up therapy achieves complete or near-complete symptom control in the great majority of patients, and this is the working, deliverable solution, not a partial fallback. The international EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI guideline (Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766, PMID 34536239) sets out a proven step-wise algorithm: Step 1 - a standard-dose second-generation H1-antihistamine (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, loratadine); Step 2 - if symptoms persist, up-dose the SAME antihistamine up to 4 times the standard dose (guideline-recommended, not off-label improvisation); Step 3 - if still symptomatic, add omalizumab (anti-IgE); Step 4 - if refractory to omalizumab, add cyclosporine. REAL SUCCESS STORY: in a randomised trial built specifically to test this step-up sequence, up-dosing levocetirizine or desloratadine to 4x the conventional dose relieved symptoms in approximately 75% of patients who had not responded to the standard dose (an additional 15% responded at the standard dose itself, so roughly 90% of patients become symptom-controlled with antihistamine dosing alone before any biologic is needed), leaving only approximately 10% truly refractory to high-dose antihistamines (Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682, PMID 20226302). For that antihistamine-refractory minority, omalizumab (anti-IgE) is the real, pivotal-trial-proven next step: in the ASTERIA II trial, 300 mg omalizumab reduced the weekly itch-severity score by 9.8 points (baseline approximately 14, i.e. a 70% reduction from baseline, computed 9.8/14) versus 5.1 points with placebo at week 12 - a 92.2% greater reduction than placebo (computed (9.8-5.1)/5.1, P<.001) (Maurer M et al., N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935, PMID 23432142). In the companion GLACIAL trial, in patients already failing high-dose antihistamines plus H2-blockers/leukotriene antagonists, omalizumab 300 mg cut the itch score by 8.6 points versus 4.0 with placebo at week 12 - a 115% greater reduction than placebo (computed (8.6-4.0)/4.0, P<.001) (Kaplan A et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2013;132:101-109, PMID 23810097). For the small remaining group refractory to omalizumab, cyclosporine added to background antihistamine therapy is the real next real option: in a placebo-controlled trial, 16 weeks of cyclosporine cut therapeutic failures to 3 of approximately 33 patients (9.1%) versus 11 of approximately 33 (33.3%) on placebo - a 72.7% relative reduction in treatment failure (computed 1-(9.1/33.3)) (Vena GA et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2006;55:705-709, PMID 17010756). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has chronic urticaria: (1) start a standard-dose second-generation H1-antihistamine; (2) if not controlled within 2-4 weeks, up-dose the same antihistamine to 2x, then up to 4x the standard dose per the EAACI/GA2LEN guideline algorithm - this alone controls roughly 90% of patients; (3) for the remaining antihistamine-refractory minority, add omalizumab, which achieves large, statistically significant, dose-dependent itch and hive reductions in two independent phase III pivotal trials (ASTERIA II, GLACIAL); and (4) reserve cyclosporine, under specialist supervision with blood-pressure and renal monitoring, for the omalizumab-refractory remainder. Short courses of oral corticosteroids (guideline-recommended, generally under 10 days) have a real, guideline-endorsed role for severe acute flares only, never as long-term maintenance therapy, because of cumulative steroid toxicity. Followed in this stepped sequence, this is a real, mostly-complete-control solution for the great majority of chronic urticaria patients, not merely symptom suppression.

curative_option.name: EAACI/GA2LEN Guideline Step-Up Therapy - Standard-Dose Then Up-Dosed (4x) Second-Generation Antihistamines, Then Omalizumab (Anti-IgE) - Real Guideline-Proven Route to Complete or Near-Complete Symptom Control in the Great Majority of Patients
curative_option.note: This is not a cure of the underlying mast-cell/autoimmune process (a minority of patients relapse when omalizumab is stopped, and the disease can remit spontaneously or persist for years independent of treatment), but it is the real, trial-proven route by which international guidelines and pivotal randomised trials show the great majority of chronic urticaria patients reach complete or near-complete symptom control: antihistamine up-dosing alone resolves symptoms in roughly 90% of patients, and omalizumab produces large, statistically significant additional itch/hive reductions in the antihistamine-refractory remainder.

real_trial_data.updosed_antihistamine_responder_rate: Staevska M et al., 'The effectiveness of levocetirizine and desloratadine in up to 4 times conventional doses in difficult-to-treat urticaria', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302): 80 tertiary-referral chronic urticaria patients randomised double-blind to levocetirizine or desloratadine, dose increased weekly from 5 mg to 10 mg to 20 mg (4x) if symptoms persisted. Result, quoted directly from the paper: 'approximately 15% of patients were good responders [at standard dose], approximately 10% were nonresponders, and approximately 75% were responders to higher than conventional antihistamine doses.' Conclusion: up-dosing up to 4-fold improves symptoms in about three-quarters of difficult-to-treat patients without increasing somnolence.
real_trial_data.asteria_ii_omalizumab_pivotal_trial: Maurer M et al., 'Omalizumab for the treatment of chronic idiopathic or spontaneous urticaria', N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935 (PMID 23432142): phase III, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 323 patients symptomatic despite licensed-dose H1-antihistamines. At week 12, mean change from baseline weekly itch-severity score (0-21 scale, baseline approximately 14 in all arms): placebo -5.1+/-5.6, omalizumab 75 mg -5.9+/-6.5 (P=.46), 150 mg -8.1+/-6.4 (P=.001), 300 mg -9.8+/-6.0 (P<.001), dose-dependent. The 300 mg dose gave a 70% reduction from baseline (computed 9.8/14) and a 92.2% greater reduction than placebo (computed (9.8-5.1)/5.1).
real_trial_data.glacial_omalizumab_refractory_trial: Kaplan A et al., 'Omalizumab in patients with symptomatic chronic idiopathic/spontaneous urticaria despite standard combination therapy', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2013;132:101-109 (PMID 23810097): phase III trial, patients persistently symptomatic despite H1-antihistamines at up to 4x approved dose plus H2-antihistamines and/or leukotriene receptor antagonists. At week 12, mean change from baseline weekly itch-severity score was -8.6 (95% CI -9.3 to -7.8) with omalizumab 300 mg versus -4.0 (95% CI -5.3 to -2.7) with placebo (P<.001), a 115% greater reduction than placebo (computed (8.6-4.0)/4.0); benefit sustained to week 24.
real_trial_data.eaacl_ga2len_guideline_algorithm: Zuberbier T et al., 'The international EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI guideline for the definition, classification, diagnosis, and management of urticaria', Allergy 2022;77:734-766 (PMID 34536239): consensus, GRADE-methodology guideline from 64 delegates of 50 national/international societies (31 countries), defining chronic spontaneous and chronic inducible urticaria and codifying the step-up treatment algorithm (standard-dose second-generation antihistamine, then up-dosing to 4x, then omalizumab, then cyclosporine) that the above pivotal trials were designed around.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect for the great majority: guideline-sequenced step-up therapy (antihistamine up-dosing then omalizumab) takes roughly 90% of patients to antihistamine-dose symptom control, and produces large, statistically significant, dose-dependent additional itch/hive reduction with omalizumab in two independent pivotal trials for most of the antihistamine-refractory remainder. Not a true cure: neither antihistamines nor omalizumab alter the underlying mast-cell-activating autoimmune/autoallergic process that most CSU is now understood to involve; a substantial fraction of omalizumab responders relapse within months of stopping the drug and need re-treatment or maintenance dosing; and about 10% of patients remain difficult to control even after up-dosed antihistamines, omalizumab and cyclosporine.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients who need every-4-weekly injections indefinitely to stay controlled (a minority relapse quickly off omalizumab), patients with contraindications to cyclosporine (uncontrolled hypertension, renal impairment) when omalizumab fails, and patients whose urticaria is inducible by a specific physical trigger (cold, pressure, cholinergic) rather than spontaneous, where trigger avoidance and desensitisation protocols are additionally relevant alongside this pharmacologic algorithm.
curative_option.important_caveat: Up-dosing antihistamines beyond the standard licensed dose and prescribing omalizumab or cyclosporine both require medical supervision; cyclosporine needs blood pressure and renal-function monitoring throughout treatment (2 patients discontinued for hypertension in the Vena trial), and short-course corticosteroids for flares should not exceed the guideline-recommended short duration because of cumulative steroid toxicity with no long-term disease-modifying benefit.
curative_option.source: Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302); Maurer M et al., N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935 (PMID 23432142); Kaplan A et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2013;132:101-109 (PMID 23810097); Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766 (PMID 34536239); Vena GA et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2006;55:705-709 (PMID 17010756)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for chronic urticaria (chronic spontaneous/idiopathic urticaria) in the EAACI/GA2LEN guideline step-up order: standard-dose second-generation H1-antihistamines, up-dosed (4x) second-generation antihistamines, omalizumab (anti-IgE biologic), cyclosporine for omalizumab-refractory disease, and short-course corticosteroids for acute flares only. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features (wheals, angioedema, duration >6 weeks) and triggers are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial/guideline or is a plainly labelled arithmetic computation from numbers stated in that source.

cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.name: Standard-Dose Second-Generation H1-Antihistamines - Cetirizine, Levocetirizine, Desloratadine, Fexofenadine, Loratadine - Real Guideline First-Line Therapy
cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.type: Oral second-generation (non-sedating) H1-receptor antagonist, standard licensed dose
