cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.effectiveness: Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302): in 80 tertiary-referral chronic urticaria patients started on levocetirizine or desloratadine 5 mg (standard dose), approximately 15% became good responders/symptom-free at this conventional dose (13 of 80 patients symptom-free at 5 mg in the reported breakdown).
cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.reason_why: Second-generation H1-antihistamines block the histamine H1 receptor on cutaneous mast cells/sensory nerves and vascular endothelium, reducing the wheal-and-flare response and pruritus that drive chronic urticaria's core symptoms, without the sedation of first-generation agents.
cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.important_caveat: The EAACI/GA2LEN guideline explicitly recommends against first-generation sedating antihistamines for chronic urticaria; standard-dose second-generation antihistamines control only a minority of patients (approximately 15% per Staevska et al.), so guideline-directed up-dosing is the expected next step, not a treatment failure requiring an entirely different drug class.
cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.real_working_solution: A standard-dose second-generation oral antihistamine is real, guideline-mandated first-line therapy for every chronic urticaria patient and should be tried before any escalation, but most patients will need up-dosing to reach control.
cu_standard_dose_second_gen_antihistamin.source: Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302); Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766 (PMID 34536239)

cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.name: Up-Dosed (Up to 4x Standard Dose) Second-Generation Antihistamines - Real Guideline-Endorsed Step 2, Highest-Responder-Rate Option in the Whole Algorithm
cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.type: Oral second-generation H1-antihistamine at 2x to 4x the standard licensed dose, same drug
specific_drugs: Levocetirizine up to 20 mg once daily (4x standard 5 mg dose)
Desloratadine up to 20 mg once daily (4x standard 5 mg dose)
Cetirizine, fexofenadine and other second-generation agents up-dosed by the same guideline-endorsed principle
cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.effectiveness: Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302): double-blind RCT, 80 difficult-to-treat chronic urticaria patients, dose escalated weekly from 5 mg to 10 mg to 20 mg. 'Approximately 75% were responders to higher than conventional antihistamine doses,' with only approximately 10% remaining true nonresponders even at 4x dose; of 28 patients unresponsive to 20 mg desloratadine, 7 became symptom-free switched to 20 mg levocetirizine. Quality of life improved with up-dosing without an increase in somnolence.
cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.reason_why: Chronic urticaria mast-cell histamine release in difficult-to-treat patients is often incompletely blocked at the standard H1-receptor occupancy achieved by the licensed dose; higher doses increase receptor occupancy and block-effect without crossing into first-generation-level CNS penetration, which is why efficacy rises with dose while sedation does not.
cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.important_caveat: Up-dosing is specifically the guideline-recommended step (not off-label improvisation) per EAACI/GA2LEN, and non-response to one up-dosed antihistamine does not predict non-response to a different up-dosed antihistamine (18 levocetirizine nonresponders in the trial did not benefit from 20 mg desloratadine, but a subset of desloratadine nonresponders did respond to levocetirizine), so a trial of an alternate agent before moving to omalizumab is reasonable.
cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.real_working_solution: Up-dosing the same second-generation antihistamine to 2x, then up to 4x the standard dose, per the EAACI/GA2LEN guideline, is the real, single highest-yield step in the whole treatment algorithm, controlling roughly three-quarters of patients who failed the standard dose.
cu_updosed_antihistamines_4x.source: Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302); Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766 (PMID 34536239)

cu_omalizumab_anti_ige.name: Omalizumab (Anti-IgE Monoclonal Antibody) - Real Pivotal-Trial-Proven Step 3 for Antihistamine-Refractory Chronic Urticaria (ASTERIA II and GLACIAL)
specific_drugs: Omalizumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (the dose proven effective in both pivotal trials; 150 mg and 75 mg doses showed smaller, dose-dependent effect)
cu_omalizumab_anti_ige.effectiveness: Maurer M et al. (ASTERIA II), N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935 (PMID 23432142): phase III RCT, 323 patients symptomatic despite licensed-dose antihistamines. At week 12, weekly itch-severity score fell 9.8 points with omalizumab 300 mg versus 5.1 with placebo (P<.001) - a 70% reduction from baseline (computed 9.8/14) and 92.2% greater reduction than placebo (computed (9.8-5.1)/5.1). Kaplan A et al. (GLACIAL), J Allergy Clin Immunol 2013;132:101-109 (PMID 23810097): phase III RCT in patients already failing high-dose antihistamines plus H2-blockers/leukotriene antagonists; itch score fell 8.6 points with omalizumab 300 mg versus 4.0 with placebo at week 12 (P<.001) - a 115% greater reduction than placebo (computed (8.6-4.0)/4.0), sustained to week 24.
cu_omalizumab_anti_ige.reason_why: Omalizumab binds free circulating IgE, lowering free IgE and down-regulating high-affinity IgE receptors (FceRI) on mast cells and basophils, which reduces mast-cell releasability and histamine release regardless of whether the triggering autoantibody or autoallergen has been identified - the mechanistic basis for its efficacy even in 'idiopathic' (autoimmune-mechanism) chronic urticaria.
cu_omalizumab_anti_ige.important_caveat: Omalizumab requires 4-weekly injections; benefit is dose-dependent (75 mg showed no significant effect over placebo in ASTERIA II) and a meaningful fraction of responders relapse within weeks to months of stopping, requiring maintenance dosing; serious adverse event rate was numerically higher in the 300 mg group (6%) than placebo (3%) in ASTERIA II, though overall safety was comparable across groups.
cu_omalizumab_anti_ige.real_working_solution: 300 mg omalizumab every 4 weeks is the real, twice-independently-pivotal-trial-proven next step for chronic urticaria that remains symptomatic despite up-dosed antihistamines, producing large and statistically significant itch and hive reductions.
cu_omalizumab_anti_ige.source: Maurer M et al., N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935 (PMID 23432142); Kaplan A et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2013;132:101-109 (PMID 23810097); Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766 (PMID 34536239)

cu_cyclosporine_refractory.name: Cyclosporine (Ciclosporin) - Real Step 4 Option for Omalizumab-Refractory Chronic Urticaria
cu_cyclosporine_refractory.type: Oral calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant, added to background antihistamine therapy
specific_drugs: Cyclosporine A, weight-based oral dosing (trial used up to 5 mg/kg/day initially, reduced to approximately 3 mg/kg/day from day 28), continued with background cetirizine
cu_cyclosporine_refractory.effectiveness: Vena GA et al., 'Cyclosporine in chronic idiopathic urticaria: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial', J Am Acad Dermatol 2006;55:705-709 (PMID 17010756): 99 patients with severe recalcitrant chronic idiopathic urticaria, randomised three-armed trial (16-week cyclosporine, 8-week cyclosporine+8-week placebo, 16-week placebo), all on background cetirizine. Fewer therapeutic failures with 16-week cyclosporine (3 patients) than with 16-week placebo (11 patients) or 8-week cyclosporine (8 patients); across the approximately 33-patient arms this is a therapeutic-failure rate of approximately 9.1% (3/33) with 16-week cyclosporine versus approximately 33.3% (11/33) with placebo - a 72.7% relative reduction in treatment failure (computed 1-(9.1/33.3); exact per-arm denominators not stated in the abstract, so this is an approximate computation from the 99-patient/3-arm total). Symptom scores significantly improved with cyclosporine over placebo at both 8 and 16 weeks.
cu_cyclosporine_refractory.reason_why: Cyclosporine inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation and directly suppresses mast cell and basophil mediator release, addressing the autoimmune/autoallergic mechanism (functional autoantibodies against the high-affinity IgE receptor or IgE itself) implicated in a large subset of chronic spontaneous urticaria that is refractory to antihistamines and anti-IgE therapy.
cu_cyclosporine_refractory.important_caveat: Cyclosporine carries real toxicity risk - hypertension (2 discontinuations for hypertension in this 99-patient trial) and nephrotoxicity - and requires regular blood pressure and renal function monitoring; the trial's dosing was not constant throughout (reduced after day 28), which the authors note may have been less effective than sustaining the higher dose, so this is a lower-bound efficacy estimate.
cu_cyclosporine_refractory.real_working_solution: Cyclosporine added to background antihistamine therapy, under specialist monitoring, is the real, trial-proven step for the omalizumab-refractory minority of chronic urticaria patients.
cu_cyclosporine_refractory.source: Vena GA, Cassano N, Colombo D, Peruzzi E, Pigatto P; Neo-I-30 Study Group, J Am Acad Dermatol 2006;55:705-709 (PMID 17010756); Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766 (PMID 34536239)

cu_short_course_corticosteroids_flares.name: Short-Course Oral Corticosteroids - Real Guideline-Endorsed Option for Severe Acute Flares Only, Not for Long-Term Maintenance
cu_short_course_corticosteroids_flares.type: Short course of oral corticosteroid (e.g., prednisolone), guideline-recommended duration generally under 10 days
specific_drugs: Prednisolone or equivalent oral corticosteroid, short course only, added on top of background antihistamine therapy for a severe flare
cu_short_course_corticosteroids_flares.effectiveness: No dedicated placebo-controlled randomised trial quantifying a numeric response rate for short-course corticosteroids specifically in chronic urticaria flares was found in this search; the EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI guideline (Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766, PMID 34536239) endorses a short corticosteroid course as an option for severe exacerbations based on expert consensus and long clinical experience with corticosteroids' anti-inflammatory, mast-cell-mediator-suppressing effect, not a specific trial percentage.
cu_short_course_corticosteroids_flares.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids broadly suppress the inflammatory cascade and reduce vascular permeability and mediator release, giving rapid relief during a severe flare, but chronic use produces cumulative toxicity (osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, adrenal suppression) with no evidence of disease-modifying benefit in chronic urticaria.
cu_short_course_corticosteroids_flares.important_caveat: This entry is deliberately NOT given a numeric effectiveness_pct or a ranked-table row, in line with a no-fabrication rule, because no verifiable randomised trial number for this specific use was located in this session; it is included only as a real, named-guideline-endorsed short-term rescue option, explicitly not for maintenance.
cu_short_course_corticosteroids_flares.real_working_solution: Reserve a short course of oral corticosteroids strictly for severe acute flares, on top of (not instead of) the antihistamine/omalizumab/cyclosporine step-up algorithm, and avoid repeated or prolonged courses.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Percentages below come from different outcome measures (responder rates, itch-score reductions relative to placebo, itch-score reduction from baseline, therapeutic-failure-rate reduction) across different trials and are not directly comparable to each other as a single 'cure rate' - see each row's metric field for exactly what was measured. Short-course corticosteroids for flares are deliberately excluded from this table because no verifiable numeric trial effectiveness for that specific use was found (see exhaustive_medicine_survey note).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Omalizumab 300 mg vs placebo, antihistamine+H2/LTRA-refractory patients (GLACIAL trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 115% greater reduction in weekly itch-severity score than placebo at week 12 (-8.6 vs -4.0 points, computed (8.6-4.0)/4.0, P<.001); phase III RCT in patients already failing up to 4x-dose antihistamines plus H2-antihistamines/leukotriene antagonists.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kaplan A et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2013;132:101-109 (PMID 23810097)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Omalizumab 300 mg vs placebo, standard-antihistamine-refractory patients (ASTERIA II trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92.2% greater reduction in weekly itch-severity score than placebo at week 12 (-9.8 vs -5.1 points, computed (9.8-5.1)/5.1, P<.001); phase III RCT, 323 patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Maurer M et al., N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935 (PMID 23432142)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Up-dosed (up to 4x) levocetirizine/desloratadine, difficult-to-treat chronic urticaria
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Approximately 75% of standard-dose non-responders became responders when the same antihistamine was up-dosed up to 4x the conventional dose (quoted directly from the paper); double-blind RCT, 80 tertiary-referral patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Staevska M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125:676-682 (PMID 20226302)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cyclosporine + background antihistamine vs placebo + background antihistamine (16-week therapeutic-failure rate)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 72.7% relative reduction in treatment-failure rate with 16-week cyclosporine versus placebo (approximately 9.1% [3/33] vs approximately 33.3% [11/33] therapeutic failures, computed 1-(9.1/33.3); per-arm denominator approximated from 99 total patients across 3 arms, not stated exactly in the abstract). Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 99 patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Vena GA et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2006;55:705-709 (PMID 17010756)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Omalizumab 300 mg, weekly itch-score reduction from baseline (ASTERIA II)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 70% reduction in weekly itch-severity score from baseline at week 12 (-9.8 of a baseline approximately 14 on the 0-21 scale, computed 9.8/14, P<.001 vs placebo).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Maurer M et al., N Engl J Med 2013;368:924-935 (PMID 23432142)

chronic_urticaria.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Chronic urticaria (chronic spontaneous urticaria, CSU, and chronic inducible urticaria, CIndU) is USUALLY not an emergency: recurring wheals, and even the angioedema seen in a substantial subset of patients (baseline angioedema prevalence 40.7-53.1% across the three omalizumab pivotal trials in antihistamine-refractory CSU - Zazzali JL et al., 'Angioedema in the omalizumab chronic idiopathic/spontaneous urticaria pivotal studies', Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2016;117:370-377, PMID 27424128), are mast-cell/histamine-mediated, typically affect the lips, periorbital area, hands, feet or genitals, and are usually NOT immediately life-threatening. However, when angioedema in a chronic urticaria patient involves the tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate, pharynx or larynx, it can mechanically obstruct the upper airway - this is a real emergency REGARDLESS of whether the patient also meets the multi-system NIAID/FAAN clinical criteria used elsewhere in this knowledge base for anaphylaxis (Sampson HA et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2006;117:391-397, PMID 16461139). Per Kaplan AP, Greaves MW's review 'Angioedema' (J Am Acad Dermatol 2005;53:373-388, PMID 16112343), angioedema causing throat/neck tightness, voice change or hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, drooling, stridor, or dyspnea reflects a mechanical airway threat that can occur WITHOUT the hypotension, widespread urticaria/flushing, or GI symptoms that define anaphylaxis, and - unlike classic IgE/mast-cell anaphylaxis - airway-threatening angioedema does not reliably or rapidly resolve with epinephrine alone. THEREFORE: any chronic urticaria patient reporting new tongue, mouth, throat or neck swelling, voice change, drooling, difficulty swallowing, or breathing difficulty MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue/routine-consultation flow entirely and be routed to emergency services / the nearest emergency department immediately for airway assessment and management, whether or not the full anaphylaxis symptom complex is also present. If systemic features (hypotension, widespread urticaria, respiratory wheeze, GI symptoms) ARE also present together with the airway signs, treat as anaphylaxis per this knowledge base's anaphylaxis entry (immediate intramuscular epinephrine) rather than as isolated angioedema. The AI's role here is only to recognise either pattern and route to immediate emergency care; distinguishing the precise mechanism (mast-cell/histaminergic vs any bradykinin contribution) and all subsequent emergency management belong to the treating emergency physician.

chronic_spontaneous_vs_chronic_inducible.finding: The international EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI urticaria guideline (successor of the earlier EAACI/GA2LEN/EDF/WAO guideline series) divides chronic urticaria (wheals and/or angioedema recurring for more than 6 weeks) into chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) - wheals/angioedema occurring without a specific, identifiable external trigger, known or unknown cause - and chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU) - wheals reproducibly triggered by a definable physical or environmental stimulus (cold, heat, pressure/delayed-pressure, exercise/sweating [cholinergic], solar exposure, vibration, water [aquagenic], or contact with a specific substance). Verified via the NLM Clinical Table Search Service ICD-11 API mirror in this session: CSU maps to ICD-11 EB00.1 'Chronic urticaria' under parent EB00 'Spontaneous urticaria'; CIndU maps to the ICD-11 EB01 'Inducible urticaria or angioedema' block (subtypes include EB01.1 cold urticaria, EB01.2 delayed pressure urticaria, EB01.3 contact urticaria, EB02.0 cholinergic urticaria).
chronic_spontaneous_vs_chronic_inducible.source: Zuberbier T et al., 'The international EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI guideline for the definition, classification, diagnosis, and management of urticaria', Allergy 2022;77:734-766, PMID 34536239; ICD-11 codes verified via NLM Clinical Table Search Service (clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd11_codes) in this session

autoimmune_subtype_anti_ige_receptor_aut.finding: A biologically distinct autoimmune subtype of CSU (often called Type IIb autoimmune CSU, aiCSU) is driven by circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against the alpha subunit of the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcepsilonRI) or, less commonly, against IgE itself; these autoantibodies cross-link IgE receptors on mast cells/basophils and trigger degranulation independent of any external allergen. This mechanism was first demonstrated by Hide M et al., who showed that IgG fractions from the serum of chronic idiopathic urticaria patients induced histamine release from basophils that was neutralised by a soluble FcepsilonRI-alpha construct. A later classification by Sabroe RA et al. of 78 chronic idiopathic urticaria patients' sera found: 26% had immunoreactive, histamine-releasing anti-FcepsilonRI autoantibodies; 15% had immunoreactive anti-FcepsilonRI autoantibodies without histamine-releasing activity; 9% had anti-IgE-like autoantibodies; 9% had a mast-cell-specific histamine-releasing factor; and 41% had no identifiable serum factor - and patients with histamine-releasing serum activity had significantly more severe urticaria. The multinational PURIST study (182 CSU patients) found 59% were ASST-positive, 58% IgG anti-FcepsilonRI/anti-IgE positive, and 25% basophil-activation-test positive, but only 15/182 (8%) met all three criteria for confirmed aiCSU; confirmed aiCSU patients had significantly higher disease activity (UAS7 21 vs 9, P<0.016), lower total IgE, and higher anti-thyroid-peroxidase antibody levels than non-aiCSU patients - i.e. autoimmune CSU is a real, mechanistically distinct, more-severe minority subtype, not simply a lab curiosity.
autoimmune_subtype_anti_ige_receptor_aut.source: Hide M et al., 'Autoantibodies against the high-affinity IgE receptor as a cause of histamine release in chronic urticaria', N Engl J Med 1993;328:1599-1604, PMID 7683772; Sabroe RA et al., 'Classification of anti-FcepsilonRI and anti-IgE autoantibodies in chronic idiopathic urticaria and correlation with disease severity', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;110:492-499, PMID 12209101; Schoepke N et al., 'Biomarkers and clinical characteristics of autoimmune chronic spontaneous urticaria: Results of the PURIST Study', Allergy 2019;74:2427-2436, PMID 31228881

recurring_wheals_over_6_weeks.finding: The defining clinical feature is recurrent wheals (wide, itchy, erythematous/pale-centred swellings of the superficial skin) and/or angioedema (deeper swelling of the dermis/subcutis or mucosa) persisting for more than 6 weeks, distinguishing chronic urticaria from acute urticaria (under 6 weeks). Individual wheals are typically evanescent, each lesion resolving within 24 hours without residual bruising or scarring, but new wheals continue to appear, so the overall eruption is continuously or intermittently present for weeks to years.
recurring_wheals_over_6_weeks.source: Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766, PMID 34536239

angioedema_in_a_subset.finding: Angioedema (deep swelling, most often of the lips, eyelids/periorbital area, tongue, or extremities, typically lasting longer than individual wheals - up to 72 hours) occurs in a real, substantial minority-to-near-half subset of chronic urticaria patients, not in all of them. In the three omalizumab pivotal trials of antihistamine-refractory CSU, baseline angioedema prevalence was 47.5% (ASTERIA I), 40.7% (ASTERIA II) and 53.1% (GLACIAL, the more severe/refractory population). In an independent 5-year prospective cohort of 139 chronic urticaria patients, angioedema co-existed with or appeared during the disease course in 40% of patients and was itself associated with a longer overall disease duration.
angioedema_in_a_subset.source: Zazzali JL et al., Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2016;117:370-377, PMID 27424128; Toubi E et al., 'Clinical and laboratory parameters in predicting chronic urticaria duration: a prospective study of 139 patients', Allergy 2004;59:869-873, PMID 15230821

clinical_diagnosis_with_limited_targeted.finding: Chronic urticaria is primarily a clinical diagnosis made from history (duration >6 weeks, wheal appearance/evanescence, presence/absence of an identifiable inducing trigger) and physical examination; the international guideline explicitly recommends AGAINST broad, unfocused laboratory panels for straightforward CSU. Recommended baseline workup is limited (differential blood count and CRP/ESR mainly to screen for an underlying systemic disease or to exclude urticarial vasculitis), with further tests only pursued when history suggests a specific cause. For suspected chronic inducible urticaria, the diagnostic step is standardized physical provocation testing matched to the suspected trigger (e.g. ice-cube application for cold urticaria, exercise/hot-bath challenge for cholinergic urticaria, calibrated pressure application for delayed pressure urticaria) rather than serology.
clinical_diagnosis_with_limited_targeted.source: Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766, PMID 34536239

autologous_serum_skin_test_for_the_autoi.finding: The autologous serum skin test (ASST) - intradermal injection of the patient's own serum, with a positive test defined as a red serum-induced wheal at least 1.5 mm larger in diameter than the saline-control response at 30 minutes - is the bedside screening test historically used to flag patients likely to have functional anti-FcepsilonRI/anti-IgE autoantibodies. In the original validation series (155 CIU patients), ASST sensitivity was 65-71% and specificity 78-81% for identifying patients with basophil-histamine-releasing serum activity. The 2009 EAACI/GA2LEN task force consensus, however, is explicit that the ASST is a test for autoreactivity, NOT a specific or confirmatory test for autoimmune urticaria: it has only moderate specificity for true functional autoantibodies (detected definitively only by a basophil histamine release assay or basophil activation test) but a high negative predictive value, and can also be positive in some non-CSU patients. In the PURIST study, ASST-positivity (59% of 182 CSU patients) alone did not equal confirmed autoimmune CSU (only 8% met all three confirmatory criteria); the basophil histamine release assay (88% predictive) and basophil activation test (69% predictive) are the stronger confirmatory tools when the autoimmune subtype specifically needs to be established, with ASST used as the accessible first-line screen.
autologous_serum_skin_test_for_the_autoi.source: Sabroe RA et al., 'The autologous serum skin test: a screening test for autoantibodies in chronic idiopathic urticaria', Br J Dermatol 1999;140:446-452, PMID 10233264; Konstantinou GN et al., 'EAACI/GA2LEN task force consensus report: the autologous serum skin test in urticaria', Allergy 2009;64:1256-1268, PMID 19650847; Schoepke N et al., Allergy 2019;74:2427-2436, PMID 31228881

ruling_out_underlying_and_associated_cau.finding: Because chronic urticaria (particularly the autoimmune subtype) clusters with autoimmune thyroid disease, targeted screening for anti-thyroid antibodies is part of the diagnostic framework: in the 139-patient prospective cohort, anti-thyroid antibodies were positive in 12% of chronic urticaria patients versus none of the normal-individual comparison group (P=0.001), and their presence tracked with longer disease duration (though, unlike ASST-positivity, not independently with severity). The broader diagnostic framework per the international guideline is to look for and address identifiable exacerbating or causal contributors on a history-driven, not shotgun, basis - chronic infection, NSAID/aspirin hypersensitivity, and (rarely) an underlying systemic or neoplastic disease in atypical/refractory presentations - while recognising that in the majority of CSU cases no external cause is ever identified (idiopathic CSU).
ruling_out_underlying_and_associated_cau.source: Toubi E et al., Allergy 2004;59:869-873, PMID 15230821; Zuberbier T et al., Allergy 2022;77:734-766, PMID 34536239

spontaneous_remission_rates_over_time.finding: In a prospective 1-3 year follow-up of 220 adults with chronic urticaria/angioedema, 35% of all patients were completely symptom-free at 1 year and a further 28.9% had decreased symptoms, but the course differed sharply by subtype: spontaneous remission occurred in 47.4% of patients with idiopathic (no identifiable cause) urticaria versus only 16.4% of patients with physical/inducible urticaria - i.e. chronic inducible urticaria has a distinctly worse spontaneous-remission prognosis than idiopathic CSU. In an independent prospective cohort of 139 chronic urticaria patients followed for 5 years, disease persisted beyond 1 year in more than 70% of cases, and 14% of patients still had active disease at the 5-year mark; longer disease duration was significantly associated with the presence of angioedema, a positive autologous serum skin test, and anti-thyroid antibodies - i.e. the autoimmune-leaning phenotype tends to run a more protracted natural course.
spontaneous_remission_rates_over_time.source: Kozel MM et al., 'Natural course of physical and chronic urticaria and angioedema in 220 patients', J Am Acad Dermatol 2001;45:387-391, PMID 11511835; Toubi E et al., Allergy 2004;59:869-873, PMID 15230821

real_symptom_control_achievable_even_whe.finding: Although the spontaneous natural course above shows chronic urticaria can persist for years in a meaningful minority of patients, this does not mean those patients are left with uncontrolled disease while waiting for remission: in the ASTERIA I randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of patients who remained symptomatic on licensed-dose H1-antihistamines, add-on omalizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks produced a complete response (weekly Urticaria Activity Score, UAS7 = 0, i.e. entirely wheal- and itch-free) in 35.8% of patients by week 12, versus 8.8% on placebo, and well-controlled disease (UAS7 <= 6) in 51.9% versus 11.3% on placebo (both P<0.0001) - real, randomised-trial evidence that structured step-up therapy (second-generation H1-antihistamines first, then omalizumab for antihistamine-refractory disease) can independently achieve durable, complete or near-complete symptom control for a substantial share of patients whose disease has not yet spontaneously remitted, rather than leaving them to wait out the natural history above untreated.
real_symptom_control_achievable_even_whe.source: Saini SS et al., 'Efficacy and safety of omalizumab in patients with chronic idiopathic/spontaneous urticaria who remain symptomatic on H1 antihistamines: a randomized, placebo-controlled study', J Invest Dermatol 2015;135:67-75, PMID 25046337

common_variable_immunodeficiency.name: Primary Immunodeficiency (Common Variable Immunodeficiency, CVID)
common_variable_immunodeficiency.icd11_hint: ICD-11 4A02 Predominantly antibody deficiencies (WHO ICD-11 foundation category covering CVID; the live ICD-11 foundation/linearization browser is a JavaScript single-page application that could not be machine-rendered in this session, so the exact fourth-character subcode for CVID (expected 4A02.0 'Common variable immunodeficiency' based on the published ICD-11 antibody-deficiency structure) is NOT independently machine-verified here and should be confirmed against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool before clinical/billing use). Older, well-established ICD-10 crosswalk: D83 'Common variable immunodeficiency' (subtypes D83.0-D83.9).
common_variable_immunodeficiency.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: CVID patients require override of the routine doctor-approval queue for immediate real-world urgent guidance in two real, evidence-based scenarios. (1) SEVERE/ACUTE INFECTION: because CVID is fundamentally an antibody deficiency, any CVID patient presenting with signs of severe or overwhelming infection (e.g. pneumonia with hypoxia, sepsis, meningitic symptoms) must be triaged as a real infectious emergency requiring same-day empiric antibiotics and hospital-level care, not routine outpatient queueing -- in the largest 4-decade natural-history cohort, 94% of CVID patients had a history of infections, and noninfectious complications carried an 11-fold higher hazard of death (HR 10.95, p<0.0001) than infection alone (Resnick ES, Moshier EL, Godbold JH, Cunningham-Rundles C, 'Morbidity and mortality in common variable immune deficiency over 4 decades', Blood 2012;119(7):1650-1657, PMID 22180439). (2) LYMPHOMA / AUTOIMMUNE / GRANULOMATOUS SURVEILLANCE: CVID carries a real, quantified, elevated risk of lymphoid malignancy and autoimmune/granulomatous complications that requires active hematology/immunology monitoring, not passive follow-up -- in the same 473-patient cohort, 8.2% developed lymphoma, 28.6% developed hematologic or organ-specific autoimmunity, and 9.7% developed granulomatous disease (Resnick ES et al, Blood 2012, PMID 22180439); in the European CVID registry, the clinical phenotype of polyclonal lymphocytic infiltration was independently associated with a 5-fold increased risk of progression to lymphoid malignancy (Chapel H, Lucas M, Lee M, Bjorkander J, Webster D, Grimbacher B, Fieschi C, Thon V, Abedi MR, Hammarstrom L, 'Common variable immunodeficiency disorders: division into distinct clinical phenotypes', Blood 2008;112(2):277-286, PMID 18319398). Any CVID patient with new unexplained lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cytopenia, chronic diarrhea/malabsorption, or unexplained weight loss needs urgent (not routine-queue) hematology-oncology/immunology referral for malignancy and autoimmune-complication work-up, since noninfectious complications -- not acute infections -- are the dominant driver of excess mortality in this disease.

clinical_phenotype_classification.finding: The largest European CVID registry cohort (334 patients, 7 centers, mean follow-up 25.6 years / 9461 patient-years) defined 5 distinct, largely non-overlapping clinical phenotypes: no complications, autoimmunity, polyclonal lymphocytic infiltration, enteropathy, and lymphoid malignancy. 83% of patients fit only one of these phenotypes. Polyclonal lymphocytic infiltration was the only identified clinical predictor, carrying a 5-fold increased risk of progression to lymphoid malignancy.
clinical_phenotype_classification.source: Chapel H, Lucas M, Lee M, Bjorkander J, Webster D, Grimbacher B, Fieschi C, Thon V, Abedi MR, Hammarstrom L, 'Common variable immunodeficiency disorders: division into distinct clinical phenotypes', Blood 2008;112(2):277-286 (PMID 18319398)
clinical_phenotype_classification.confidence: high - direct findings from this landmark multicenter registry study

exclusion_based_nosology.finding: CVID is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion within the broader inborn-errors-of-immunity classification: applying refined ESID registry clinical criteria to existing CVID datasets reclassified 8% of adults and 27% of children (176 of 1704 patients originally labeled CVID) into 22 other, more specific immunodeficiency diagnoses, showing both the progress of genetic diagnostics and the historical lack of a single standardized CVID case definition.
exclusion_based_nosology.source: Seidel MG, Kindle G, Gathmann B, Quinti I, Buckland M, van Montfrans J, et al; ESID Registry Working Party, 'The European Society for Immunodeficiencies (ESID) Registry Working Definitions for the Clinical Diagnosis of Inborn Errors of Immunity', J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2019;7(6):1763-1770 (PMID 30776527)

original_pagid_esid_diagnostic_criteria.finding: The original PAGID (Pan-American Group for Immunodeficiency)/ESID (European Society for Immunodeficiencies) consensus paper established the foundational tiered diagnostic-criteria framework (definite/probable/possible categories) used to classify primary antibody deficiencies including CVID, which subsequent international consensus documents have built on and refined.
original_pagid_esid_diagnostic_criteria.source: Conley ME, Notarangelo LD, Etzioni A, 'Diagnostic criteria for primary immunodeficiencies. Representing PAGID and ESID', Clin Immunol 1999;93(3):190-197 (PMID 10600329)
original_pagid_esid_diagnostic_criteria.confidence: moderate - this paper's title, authorship, and journal record are session-verified via PubMed, but PubMed carries no indexed abstract for it (title-only record), so its specific numeric diagnostic thresholds could not be independently re-extracted in this session and should be confirmed against the full-text criteria before clinical use

international_consensus_document.finding: In 2016, four major international allergy/immunology societies (AAAAI, EAACI, WAO, ACAAI) jointly produced the International Consensus Document (ICON) on Common Variable Immunodeficiency Disorders -- the current cross-society consensus reference for CVID diagnosis, classification, and management, compiled by an international multi-committee author group with independent external expert review.
international_consensus_document.source: Bonilla FA, Barlan I, Chapel H, Costa-Carvalho BT, Cunningham-Rundles C, de la Morena MT, Espinosa-Rosales FJ, Hammarstrom L, Nonoyama S, Quinti I, Routes JM, Tang ML, Warnatz K, 'International Consensus Document (ICON): Common Variable Immunodeficiency Disorders', J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2016;4(1):38-59 (PMID 26563668)
international_consensus_document.confidence: high for the document's existence, purpose, and authorship (verified from its PubMed methods abstract); the abstract itself describes only the consensus-development methodology rather than listing specific numeric diagnostic criteria, so exact lab thresholds are not quoted here as session-verified numbers -- see the diagnostic_framework section for what could be verified

infection_burden.finding: In the largest published single-center natural-history cohort (473 CVID patients followed over 4 decades in New York), 94% of patients had a documented history of infections, and 22.6% had a markedly low IgG below 100 mg/dL at some point.
infection_burden.source: Resnick ES, Moshier EL, Godbold JH, Cunningham-Rundles C, Blood 2012;119(7):1650-1657 (PMID 22180439)

noninfectious_complication_spectrum.finding: 68% of the same 473-patient cohort also had at least one noninfectious complication: hematologic or organ-specific autoimmunity 28.6%, chronic lung disease 28.5%, bronchiectasis 11.2%, gastrointestinal inflammatory disease 15.4%, malabsorption 5.9%, granulomatous disease 9.7%, liver disease/hepatitis 9.1%, lymphoma 8.2%, and other cancers 7.0%.
noninfectious_complication_spectrum.confidence: high - these are the primary reported percentages from this specific cohort; the independent ESID registry cohort below corroborates the same clinical clustering pattern in a much larger, separate population

recurrent_sinopulmonary_infection_patter.finding: Respiratory tract infections and their complications (recurrent sinusitis, otitis, pneumonia) are the most prominent clinical problem at both initial diagnosis and during long-term follow-up. In a 224-patient multicenter Italian cohort followed a mean of 11 years, IVIG reduced acute pneumonia and acute otitis episodes, but chronic sinusitis and chronic lung disease still progressed over time in all age groups, including children, despite ongoing immunoglobulin replacement.
recurrent_sinopulmonary_infection_patter.source: Quinti I, Soresina A, Spadaro G, Martino S, Donnanno S, Agostini C, Claudio P, Franco D, Maria Pesce A, Borghese F, Guerra A, Rondelli R, Plebani A; Italian Primary Immunodeficiency Network, 'Long-term follow-up and outcome of a large cohort of patients with common variable immunodeficiency', J Clin Immunol 2007;27(3):308-316 (PMID 17510807)

enteropathy_autoimmunity_granuloma_clust.finding: In the European Society for Immunodeficiencies registry cohort of 2212 CVID patients across 28 centers, enteropathy, autoimmunity, granulomas, and splenomegaly formed a statistically interrelated cluster of features that tended to co-occur in the same patients, whereas bronchiectasis behaved as an independent complication not associated with the other features. Early disease onset (before age 10) occurred in 33.7% of patients overall (39.8% of male patients), and diagnostic delay averaged 4-5 years.
enteropathy_autoimmunity_granuloma_clust.source: Gathmann B, Mahlaoui N, CEREDIH, Gerard L, Oksenhendler E, Warnatz K, Schulze I, Kindle G, Kuijpers TW, et al; European Society for Immunodeficiencies Registry Working Party, 'Clinical picture and treatment of 2212 patients with common variable immunodeficiency', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2014;134(1):116-126 (PMID 24582312)

cellular_immune_and_onset_features.finding: In a 248-patient cohort followed 1-25 years, 40% of patients had impaired T-cell proliferation to one or more mitogens (directly related to serum IgG level), and median age of symptom onset was 23 years in males and 28 years in females, with diagnosis typically following several years later (mean age at diagnosis 29 years in males, 33 years in females).
cellular_immune_and_onset_features.source: Cunningham-Rundles C, Bodian C, 'Common variable immunodeficiency: clinical and immunological features of 248 patients', Clin Immunol 1999;92(1):34-48 (PMID 10413651)

pneumonia_risk_phenotype.finding: A 5-year multicenter prospective study of 201 CVID patients (1365 patient-years of follow-up) identified a specific high-pneumonia-risk clinical phenotype: patients with low IgG and IgA levels at diagnosis, an IgA level under 7 mg/dL, and/or pre-existing bronchiectasis were significantly more likely to have pneumonia episodes despite immunoglobulin replacement.
pneumonia_risk_phenotype.source: Quinti I, Soresina A, Guerra A, Rondelli R, Spadaro G, Agostini C, Milito C, Trombetta AC, Visentini M, Martini H, Plebani A, Fiorilli M; IPINet Investigators, 'Effectiveness of immunoglobulin replacement therapy on clinical outcome in patients with primary antibody deficiencies', J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322 (PMID 21365217)

core_diagnostic_triad.finding: CVID's core diagnostic framework, as codified in the original PAGID/ESID consensus criteria and carried forward by the 2016 international ICON consensus document, rests on three pillars: (1) a marked reduction in serum IgG together with a marked reduction in at least one of IgA or IgM, (2) poor or absent specific antibody response to vaccination (e.g. impaired polysaccharide/protein vaccine response or absent isohemagglutinins), and (3) exclusion of other defined causes of hypogammaglobulinemia (e.g. other genetically defined primary immunodeficiencies, secondary causes such as protein-losing states, malignancy, or drug effects) before the CVID label is applied.
core_diagnostic_triad.source: Conley ME, Notarangelo LD, Etzioni A, Clin Immunol 1999;93(3):190-197 (PMID 10600329); Bonilla FA et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2016;4(1):38-59 (PMID 26563668)
core_diagnostic_triad.confidence: moderate-high - this triad is the standard, widely-taught CVID diagnostic framework and both cited source papers are session-verified as real, on-topic consensus documents; however, the exact numeric laboratory thresholds (precise IgG/IgA/IgM cutoffs by age, exact vaccine-response criteria) are set out in these documents' full text, which was not independently re-extracted in this session, so clinicians should confirm exact cutoffs against the primary ICON/ESID/PAGID documents rather than this summary alone

real_measured_immunoglobulin_levels_in_d.finding: In the 473-patient 4-decade natural-history cohort, median immunoglobulin levels at the time of study were IgG 246 mg/dL, IgA 8 mg/dL, and IgM 21 mg/dL, illustrating how far below normal reference ranges these three isotypes fall in diagnosed CVID.

exclusion_of_other_inborn_errors_of_immu.finding: Because CVID overlaps clinically with numerous other, more specific inborn errors of immunity, the ESID registry's refined clinical working-definition criteria reclassified 8% of adults and 27% of children who had originally carried a CVID label into 22 distinct, genetically or clinically better-defined immunodeficiencies -- concrete evidence that rigorous exclusion of alternative/secondary causes is a real, load-bearing step in the CVID diagnostic pathway, not a formality.
exclusion_of_other_inborn_errors_of_immu.source: Seidel MG et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2019;7(6):1763-1770 (PMID 30776527)

immunoglobulin_trough_level_and_monitori.finding: Once diagnosed and started on immunoglobulin replacement, trough IgG level is used as an ongoing monitoring parameter: in the 2212-patient ESID registry cohort, patients with very low IgG trough levels under 4 g/L had poor clinical outcomes, while higher trough levels were associated with a reduced frequency of serious bacterial infections, though no single universal 'protective' trough level could be defined because of the added role of structural lung disease.
immunoglobulin_trough_level_and_monitori.source: Gathmann B et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2014;134(1):116-126 (PMID 24582312); Quinti I et al, J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322 (PMID 21365217)

overall_mortality_and_survival_deficit.finding: In the 473-patient 4-decade cohort, 19.6% of patients died during follow-up, a significantly shorter survival than age- and sex-matched general-population controls (p<0.0001). In an earlier 248-patient cohort from the same center, 20-year survival after CVID diagnosis was only 64% in males and 67% in females, compared with an expected 92% (males) and 94% (females) survival in the general population over the same period.
overall_mortality_and_survival_deficit.source: Resnick ES et al, Blood 2012;119(7):1650-1657 (PMID 22180439); Cunningham-Rundles C, Bodian C, Clin Immunol 1999;92(1):34-48 (PMID 10413651)

noninfectious_complications_drive_excess.finding: The risk of death was 11-fold higher for CVID patients who had developed noninfectious complications compared with those who had not (hazard ratio 10.95, p<0.0001). Mortality was specifically associated with lymphoma, any form of hepatitis, functional or structural lung impairment, and gastrointestinal disease with or without malabsorption -- but, notably, was NOT significantly associated with bronchiectasis, autoimmunity, other (non-lymphoma) cancers, granulomatous disease, or prior splenectomy in this cohort.

lymphoma_and_malignancy_risk.finding: Lymphoma developed in 8.2% of the 473-patient cohort, and other cancers in a further 7.0%; female patients were more likely to develop lymphoma than males (p=0.04). In the separate European CVID registry cohort, the clinical phenotype of polyclonal lymphocytic infiltration carried a 5-fold increased risk of progression to lymphoid malignancy, identifying it as the single strongest clinical predictor of malignancy risk found in that study.
lymphoma_and_malignancy_risk.source: Resnick ES et al, Blood 2012;119(7):1650-1657 (PMID 22180439); Chapel H et al, Blood 2008;112(2):277-286 (PMID 18319398)

mortality_trend_improving_with_modern_ca.finding: Despite the real excess mortality documented above, the European CVID registry analysis found a considerable reduction in mortality in the most recent 15 years of the registry compared with earlier decades, consistent with the effect of more systematic immunoglobulin replacement, complication surveillance, and modern supportive/antimicrobial care over time.

infection_control_under_immunoglobulin_r.finding: Under long-term immunoglobulin replacement, a meaningful fraction of CVID patients become effectively infection-free: in a 5-year multicenter prospective study, 21% of CVID patients (and 24% of a comparison X-linked agammaglobulinemia cohort) remained infection-free throughout the study period, and IVIG produced a clear, sustained reduction in pneumonia incidence after initiation. This is real-world evidence that regular immunoglobulin replacement substantially normalizes day-to-day infection risk for most patients, even though chronic non-infectious complications (autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, enteropathy, chronic lung/sinus disease) are not fully prevented by IgG replacement alone and require their own ongoing monitoring.
infection_control_under_immunoglobulin_r.source: Quinti I et al, J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322 (PMID 21365217); Quinti I et al, J Clin Immunol 2007;27(3):308-316 (PMID 17510807)

common_variable_immunodeficiency.CURABILITY_NOTE: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) is the most common clinically significant primary antibody deficiency in adults, and while the underlying B-cell/antibody defect itself has no cure comparable to the HSCT/gene-therapy cures now available for SCID, regular immunoglobulin (Ig) replacement therapy is a real, guideline-standard, genuinely near-normalizing treatment that converts CVID from a historically infection-lethal disease into a condition compatible with a near-normal infection burden for most patients. The clearest real-world demonstration: Busse PJ et al. reviewed 50 laboratory-confirmed CVID patients before and after starting IVIG and found that the proportion who had ever had pneumonia fell from 84% (42/50) pre-treatment to 22% (11/50) after a mean 6.6 years of IVIG therapy -- a real ~74% relative reduction in pneumonia burden, with most of the residual cases occurring only in the first year of treatment before adequate dosing was established (J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;109(6):1001-1004, PMID 12063531). Consistent with this, Quinti I et al.'s 5-year multicenter IPINet prospective cohort of 201 CVID patients on long-term Ig replacement (1,365 patient-years of follow-up) found that 21% of CVID patients remained completely infection-free throughout the study, with a documented reduction in pneumonia episodes after Ig initiation (J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322, PMID 21365217). Lucas M et al.'s 22-year, 90-patient single-center cohort further showed that when Ig dose is individually titrated (0.2-1.2 g/kg/month) against each patient's own breakthrough-infection history rather than a fixed trough target, most CVID patients can be kept free of breakthrough bacterial infections at trough IgG levels of 5-17 g/L -- i.e. the real lever is individualized dose, not a single universal trough number (J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125(6):1354-1360.e4, PMID 20471071). Honest limit: Ig replacement treats the antibody-deficiency/infection axis of CVID, not the disease's other real face -- immune dysregulation. Resnick ES et al.'s 473-patient, four-decade New York cohort found that even with treatment, 68% of CVID patients develop at least one noninfectious complication (autoimmune cytopenia/organ-specific autoimmunity 28.6%, chronic lung disease 28.5%, granulomatous disease 9.7%, lymphoma 8.2%), that 19.6% died over follow-up (significantly reduced survival vs age/sex-matched population controls, p<0.0001), and that the risk of death was about 11-fold higher in patients with noninfectious complications than in those with infections alone (hazard ratio 10.95, p<0.0001) (Blood 2012;119(7):1650-1657, PMID 22180439). So Ig replacement is real and near-normalizing for the infection side of CVID -- the correct, guideline-standard, cure-first-framed first-line treatment below -- but it is not by itself a cure for the whole disease; the immune-dysregulation complications (managed separately, below) remain the major open problem in CVID care.

curative_option.name: Regular Immunoglobulin Replacement Therapy (IVIG or SCIG) -- the Real, Guideline-Standard, Near-Normalizing Best-Evidence Treatment for CVID
curative_option.type: Disease-modifying antibody replacement therapy (lifelong)
specific_drugs: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) -- e.g. Privigen, Gamunex-C, Octagam, Gammagard Liquid -- typically infused every 3-4 weeks
Subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG) -- e.g. Hizentra, Cuvitru, Gammanorm -- typically self-infused weekly or biweekly at home
Facilitated subcutaneous immunoglobulin (fSCIG) with recombinant human hyaluronidase (Hyqvia) permitting less-frequent, monthly-interval dosing

real_outcome_data.pneumonia_incidence_pre_vs_post_ivig: Proportion of CVID patients with a history of pneumonia fell from 84% (42/50) pre-IVIG to 22% (11/50) post-IVIG over a mean 6.6 years of therapy (n=50) - Busse PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;109(6):1001-1004 (PMID 12063531)
real_outcome_data.multicenter_complete_infection_free_rate: 21% of CVID patients remained completely infection-free during a 5-year, 1,365-patient-year multicenter prospective cohort on Ig replacement (n=201 CVID patients) - Quinti I et al., J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322 (PMID 21365217)
real_outcome_data.individualized_dosing_infection_preventi: Individually titrated Ig doses of 0.2-1.2 g/kg/month, adjusted to each patient's own breakthrough-infection history, kept most of a 90-patient CVID cohort free of breakthrough bacterial infections at trough IgG levels of 5-17 g/L over 22 years of follow-up - Lucas M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125(6):1354-1360.e4 (PMID 20471071)
real_outcome_data.autoimmune_hemolytic_disease_recurrence_: In a 326-patient CVID cohort, recurrent autoimmune hemolytic disease (ITP/AIHA/Evans syndrome) occurred significantly more often in patients not yet receiving maintenance IVIG than in those already on it (p<0.0001) - Wang J, Cunningham-Rundles C, J Autoimmun 2005;25(1):57-62 (PMID 15994061)

curative_option.note: This is a real, guideline-standard (AAAAI/ACAAI Joint Task Force Practice Parameter for the Diagnosis and Management of Primary Immunodeficiency, Bonilla FA et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2015;136(5):1186-1205, PMID 26371839) disease-modifying pathway, not a genetic/cellular cure: it does not correct the underlying B-cell defect, but it is the real, first-line, near-normalizing treatment for the infection burden of CVID. SCIG (Gardulf A et al., Lancet 1995;345(8946):365-369, PMID 7845120) achieves serum IgG levels comparable to IVIG with a low systemic-reaction rate and is a real guideline-recognized alternative route, particularly for patients with IVIG intolerance or venous-access difficulty; route efficiency (IV vs SC) also varies with disease phenotype and FCGRT genotype (Gouilleux-Gruart V et al., Clin Exp Immunol 2013;171(2):186-194, PMID 23286945).

cvid_ivig_replacement.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) Replacement, Real First-Line Near-Normalizing Treatment
specific_drugs: IVIG products (e.g. Privigen, Gamunex-C, Octagam, Gammagard Liquid), infused every 3-4 weeks, dose individually titrated (typically 0.2-1.2 g/kg/month) against breakthrough-infection history
cvid_ivig_replacement.effectiveness: Proportion of CVID patients with a history of pneumonia fell from 84% (42/50) pre-treatment to 22% (11/50) after a mean 6.6 years of IVIG (n=50); trough IgG levels of 5-17 g/L kept most of a separate 90-patient cohort breakthrough-infection-free over 22 years
cvid_ivig_replacement.reason_why: Regular exogenous IgG replaces the antibody repertoire CVID patients cannot make themselves, restoring opsonization and neutralization of encapsulated bacteria (the dominant cause of pneumonia/sinopulmonary infection in CVID) that drive most of the disease's infectious morbidity.
cvid_ivig_replacement.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-standard, near-normalizing first-line treatment for the infection burden of CVID.
cvid_ivig_replacement.source: Busse PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;109(6):1001-1004 (PMID 12063531); Lucas M et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010;125(6):1354-1360.e4 (PMID 20471071)

cvid_scig_replacement.name: Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin (SCIG) Replacement, Real Equally-Effective Alternative Route
specific_drugs: SCIG products (e.g. Hizentra, Cuvitru, Gammanorm), self-infused weekly or biweekly at home; facilitated SCIG with recombinant hyaluronidase (Hyqvia) permits monthly dosing
cvid_scig_replacement.effectiveness: In a 165-patient, 33,168-infusion, 434-patient-year safety cohort, serum IgG concentrations reached with SCIG were comparable to IVIG, and 83% of patients (137/165) had zero systemic adverse reactions, with no severe or anaphylactoid reactions recorded in any infusion
cvid_scig_replacement.reason_why: Subcutaneous absorption delivers the same replacement IgG as the intravenous route (avoiding the high peak-trough swings of IVIG) while allowing home self-administration; efficiency of the SC vs IV route also depends on CVID clinical phenotype and neonatal Fc receptor (FCGRT) genotype.
cvid_scig_replacement.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-recognized, equally effective alternative to IVIG, especially for patients with IVIG intolerance or poor venous access.
cvid_scig_replacement.source: Gardulf A et al., Lancet 1995;345(8946):365-369 (PMID 7845120); Gouilleux-Gruart V et al., Clin Exp Immunol 2013;171(2):186-194 (PMID 23286945)

cvid_prophylactic_antibiotics.name: Prophylactic Antibiotics for Breakthrough Infections Despite Adequate Ig Replacement, Real Guideline-Recommended Adjunct
cvid_prophylactic_antibiotics.type: Antimicrobial prophylaxis (adjunct, not a substitute for Ig replacement)
specific_drugs: Prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. azithromycin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or co-trimoxazole) considered per guideline for patients with recurrent breakthrough sinopulmonary infections or established bronchiectasis despite adequate trough IgG
cvid_prophylactic_antibiotics.effectiveness: No dedicated CVID-specific randomized-trial effectiveness percentage was found and none is invented here; use is guideline-recommended (AAAAI/ACAAI Practice Parameter, Bonilla FA et al., PMID 26371839) and targeted at the specific high-pneumonia-risk phenotype (low IgG/IgA at diagnosis, IgA <7 mg/dL, and/or bronchiectasis) identified by Quinti I et al., J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322 (PMID 21365217)
cvid_prophylactic_antibiotics.reason_why: In patients who keep having bacterial sinopulmonary infections despite an individually adequate Ig trough, chronic low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis reduces the bacterial burden/exacerbation frequency in the damaged airway (as in non-CVID bronchiectasis), complementing rather than replacing Ig replacement.
cvid_prophylactic_antibiotics.real_working_solution: Partial/adjunctive - real, guideline-recommended supportive measure for a defined breakthrough-infection subgroup; not a substitute for Ig replacement and not independently quantified in CVID-specific trials.
cvid_prophylactic_antibiotics.source: Bonilla FA et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2015;136(5):1186-1205 (PMID 26371839); Quinti I et al., J Clin Immunol 2011;31(3):315-322 (PMID 21365217)

cvid_immunosuppressants_autoimmune.name: Immunosuppressants for CVID-Associated Autoimmune Complications (ITP/AIHA/Evans Syndrome, Enteropathy), Real Adjunct Treatment
cvid_immunosuppressants_autoimmune.type: Immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory therapy (adjunct, for the autoimmune-dysregulation face of CVID, not the antibody deficiency itself)
specific_drugs: Corticosteroids (e.g. prednisone/prednisolone) for acute autoimmune cytopenia
Anti-Rh(D) immunoglobulin for ITP in Rh-positive, non-splenectomized patients
Rituximab (anti-CD20), with or without splenectomy, for refractory or recurrent ITP/AIHA/Evans syndrome
Maintenance IVIG itself, shown to reduce autoimmune hemolytic disease recurrence
cvid_immunosuppressants_autoimmune.effectiveness: In a 326-patient CVID cohort, 11% (35/326) had autoimmune hematologic disease (ITP, AIHA, or Evans syndrome); recurrences were significantly more frequent in patients not yet on maintenance IVIG than in those already receiving it (p<0.0001); corticosteroids, anti-Rh immunoglobulin, and splenectomy (11 patients) were the other treatments used
cvid_immunosuppressants_autoimmune.reason_why: CVID's immune dysregulation drives autoantibody-mediated destruction of blood cells independent of (and sometimes preceding) the antibody-deficiency diagnosis; standard autoimmune-cytopenia therapies (steroids, anti-Rh Ig, rituximab, splenectomy) treat this dysregulation directly, while adequate maintenance Ig replacement appears to additionally reduce recurrence risk.
cvid_immunosuppressants_autoimmune.real_working_solution: Partial - real, effective control of autoimmune flares and reduced recurrence on maintenance IVIG, but this treats a distinct complication of CVID, not the antibody deficiency itself.
cvid_immunosuppressants_autoimmune.source: Wang J, Cunningham-Rundles C, J Autoimmun 2005;25(1):57-62 (PMID 15994061)

cvid_glild_monitoring_management.name: Monitoring and Management of Granulomatous-Lymphocytic Interstitial Lung Disease (GLILD) in CVID, Real but Still Unproven-Optimal Treatment Area
cvid_glild_monitoring_management.type: Immunosuppressive therapy plus structured pulmonary monitoring (for a CVID immune-dysregulation complication, not the antibody deficiency itself)
specific_drugs: Glucocorticosteroids (monotherapy, for remission induction and/or maintenance)
Rituximab, alone or combined with azathioprine, as a steroid-sparing regimen
Mycophenolate mofetil as an alternative steroid-sparing agent
Structured monitoring: pulmonary function tests with carbon-monoxide diffusion capacity, high-resolution chest CT, per the ESID/ERS-endorsed e-GLILDnet framework
cvid_glild_monitoring_management.effectiveness: A systematic review of 42 studies/233 GLILD patients found treatment response rates 'varied widely' across regimens and that quantitative, well-controlled effectiveness data are lacking, so no single reliable effectiveness percentage can be honestly stated here; a qualitative trend toward fewer GLILD relapses with rituximab-containing regimens versus corticosteroid monotherapy was reported. An international e-GLILDnet survey of 161 clinicians (47 countries) found only 19% had access to a standardized diagnostic/management protocol, confirming this remains a real unmet-evidence area rather than an established cure
cvid_glild_monitoring_management.reason_why: GLILD reflects CVID's lymphoproliferative/granulomatous immune-dysregulation face rather than its antibody deficiency, so it does not respond to Ig replacement and instead requires direct immunosuppression of the aberrant lymphocytic infiltration, guided by regular pulmonary-function and imaging monitoring because relapse is common.
cvid_glild_monitoring_management.real_working_solution: No definitive answer yet - real, actively used treatments exist (rituximab +/- azathioprine appears to have a qualitative edge over steroid monotherapy) but current evidence cannot support a specific verified effectiveness percentage; this is an honest area of ongoing research (e-GLILDnet/ESID/ERS), not a claimed cure.
cvid_glild_monitoring_management.source: Lamers OAC et al., Front Immunol 2021;12:606099 (PMID 33936030); van de Ven AAJM et al., Front Immunol 2020;11:606333 (PMID 33324422)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (pre/post relative and absolute infection-reduction rates from one cohort, a multicenter complete-infection-free rate, and an infusion-safety rate) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes, not a claim that a single number captures 'how good' each option is in isolation, or a head-to-head trial comparison. Adjunct therapies for autoimmune complications and GLILD are deliberately omitted from this ranked table because no honestly computable, real numeric effectiveness percentage was found in the verified literature for them (see exhaustive_medicine_survey for their real, non-fabricated qualitative evidence).

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG replacement, relative reduction in proportion of patients with pneumonia
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in proportion of CVID patients with a history of pneumonia, pre- vs post-IVIG, n=50, mean 6.6 years therapy
ranked_high_to_low.source: Busse PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;109(6):1001-1004 (PMID 12063531)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG replacement, absolute pneumonia-free rate after treatment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of CVID patients with no pneumonia after starting IVIG (39/50), mean 6.6 years therapy
ranked_high_to_low.source: Busse PJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2002;109(6):1001-1004 (PMID 12063531)

ranked_high_to_low.name: SCIG replacement, freedom from systemic adverse reactions
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion of SCIG patients with zero systemic adverse reactions across 434 patient-years/33,168 infusions, n=165
ranked_high_to_low.source: Gardulf A et al., Lancet 1995;345(8946):365-369 (PMID 7845120)

reactive_arthritis.name: Reactive Arthritis
reactive_arthritis.icd11_hint: ICD-10 M02 Reactive arthropathies (M02.3- Reiter's disease, coded by joint site, e.g. M02.30 unspecified site; M02.9 Reactive arthropathy, unspecified) - confirmed via NLM Clinical Tables ICD-10-CM API (clinicaltables.nlm.nih.gov/api/icd10cm) this session. The WHO ICD-11 browser was not accessible for confirmation this session, so no ICD-11 code is stated here rather than guess one.
reactive_arthritis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real emergencies in reactive arthritis (ReA) must bypass routine doctor-approval-queue scheduling and trigger immediate real-world urgent care, not routine review: (1) ACUTE/RECURRENT UVEITIS - a real, sight-threatening complication. Any new eye redness, pain, photophobia, or blurred vision in a patient with (or suspected of having) ReA needs same-day ophthalmology assessment, not routine follow-up. In a tertiary ocular-immunology cohort of 25 patients with the ocular (Reiter's) subtype followed a mean of 48.5 months, 84% had uveitis, and despite systemic treatment, sight-threatening complications still accumulated over time - cataract in 56%, glaucoma in 16%, cystoid macular edema in 28% - showing that recurrent/chronic uveitis in this disease is a real cumulative threat to vision, kept from causing permanent loss (mean final visual acuity 20/25 in this treated cohort) only by prompt, sustained ophthalmologic care, never delayed review (Kiss S, Letko E, Qamruddin S, Baltatzis S, Foster CS, 'Long-term progression, prognosis, and treatment of patients with recurrent ocular manifestations of Reiter's syndrome', Ophthalmology 2003;110(9):1764-1769, PMID 13129875). (2) POSSIBLE SEPTIC ARTHRITIS - the acute presentation of ReA (a hot, swollen joint after a recent GI/GU infection) is clinically difficult to distinguish from septic arthritis, a joint-destroying and life-threatening emergency if missed or if immunosuppressive treatment is mistakenly started on top of it. Any acutely hot, swollen, or systemically unwell joint in this context must be treated as a possible septic-arthritis emergency requiring urgent synovial fluid aspiration, Gram stain, and culture before a diagnosis of ReA is accepted or treatment for it is started (Selmi C, Gershwin ME, 'Diagnosis and classification of reactive arthritis', Autoimmun Rev 2014;13(4-5):546-549, PMID 24418301).

symptoms.classification: Reactive arthritis (ReA, historically called Reiter's syndrome) is a sterile, post-infectious inflammatory arthritis that develops roughly 1-6 weeks after a triggering infection at a distant mucosal site, in a genetically susceptible (usually HLA-B27-positive) host. Two real, PMID-verified trigger categories: (1) GASTROINTESTINAL - Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and Yersinia. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 24 studies estimated the proportion of these enteric infections that go on to cause ReA: Campylobacter 1.71% (95% CI 0.49-5.84%), Salmonella 3.9% (95% CI 1.6-9.1%), Shigella 1.0% (95% CI 0.2-4.9%), Yersinia 3.4% (95% CI 0.8-13.7%), and combined across all four pathogens about 2.6% (95% CI 1.5-4.7%) (Pogreba-Brown K, Austhof E, Tang X, et al., 'Enteric Pathogens and Reactive Arthritis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses of Pathogen-Associated Reactive Arthritis', Foodborne Pathog Dis 2021;18(9):627-639, PMID 34255548). This is consistent with the broader estimate that genetic susceptibility makes only about 1-15% of infected individuals go on to develop ReA (Selmi C, Gershwin ME, 'Diagnosis and classification of reactive arthritis', Autoimmun Rev 2014;13(4-5):546-549, PMID 24418301). (2) GENITOURINARY - Chlamydia trachomatis is the classic genitourinary trigger, with metabolically active organism identifiable in the synovium of some patients even years after the triggering infection (Carter JD, Inman RD, 'Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis: hidden in plain sight?', Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol 2011;25(3):359-374, PMID 22100286). HLA-B27 association is real and strong but not universal: in a Finnish cohort of 63 hospitalised patients with reactive salmonella arthritis, 88% were HLA-B27 positive, and HLA-B27-positive patients had significantly higher acute-phase inflammatory markers and were the only ones who went on to develop chronic/recurrent disease or radiological sacroiliitis (Leirisalo-Repo M, Helenius P, Hannu T, et al., 'Long-term prognosis of reactive salmonella arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 1997;56(9):516-520, PMID 9370874). In a separate US referral cohort of 25 patients with the classic triad and ocular involvement, 85% were HLA-B27 positive (Kiss S et al., Ophthalmology 2003;110(9):1764-1769, PMID 13129875).
symptoms.clinical_presentation: The classic triad - remembered as 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree' - is arthritis + urethritis/cervicitis + conjunctivitis/uveitis, though the complete triad occurs in only a minority of real patients; incomplete presentations (arthritis alone, or arthritis plus a single extra-articular feature) are more common in practice (Jubber A, Moorthy A, 'Reactive arthritis: a clinical review', J R Coll Physicians Edinb 2021;51(3):288-297, PMID 34528623). Typical joint pattern: asymmetric oligoarthritis, predominantly of the lower limbs (knees, ankles), often with enthesitis (Achilles tendon, plantar fascia) and dactylitis ('sausage digit'); axial involvement (inflammatory low back pain, sacroiliitis) can occur, placing ReA within the spondyloarthritis disease spectrum (PMID 34528623). Extra-articular features: anterior uveitis/conjunctivitis, urethritis/cervicitis (which may itself be sterile, post-Chlamydia), and mucocutaneous lesions such as circinate balanitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, and oral ulcers (PMID 34528623). In a tertiary referral cohort of 25 patients with the ocular subtype, the antecedent infection was urethritis in 68% and 44% had mucocutaneous lesions (Kiss S et al., Ophthalmology 2003;110(9):1764-1769, PMID 13129875).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: There is no single, universally validated formal diagnostic/classification criterion set for ReA analogous to the ASAS axial-spondyloarthritis criteria; diagnosis remains predominantly clinical, built on the temporal link between a preceding GI/GU infection and a subsequent sterile inflammatory arthritis (Jubber A, Moorthy A, J R Coll Physicians Edinb 2021;51(3):288-297, PMID 34528623; Inman RD, 'Classification criteria for reactive arthritis', J Rheumatol 1999;26(6):1219-1221, PMID 10381032, an editorial specifically highlighting the absence of one validated criterion set for this disease). HLA-B27 testing supports rather than confirms the diagnosis, and carries real prognostic weight - HLA-B27-positive status tracks with higher risk of chronicity, sacroiliitis, and uveitis (Leirisalo-Repo M et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1997;56(9):516-520, PMID 9370874). Because the acute presentation (a hot, swollen joint after a recent infection) is clinically difficult to distinguish from septic arthritis, and starting immunosuppressive treatment on an undiagnosed septic joint is dangerous, synovial fluid aspiration with Gram stain and culture to rule out septic arthritis is a mandatory step before a diagnosis of ReA is accepted - true ReA synovial fluid is inflammatory but culture-negative for the causative organism, unlike septic arthritis (Selmi C, Gershwin ME, Autoimmun Rev 2014;13(4-5):546-549, PMID 24418301).
symptoms.natural_history: The genuinely good real story, and the one that should be led with: the great majority of reactive arthritis cases resolve completely within 6-12 months, especially when the triggering infection is identified and treated. In the largest available long-term cohort - 50 patients with reactive salmonella arthritis followed a mean of 11.0 years (range 5-22) after the acute episode - 20 of 50 (40%) had recovered completely, 10 (20%) had only mild residual joint symptoms, and 8 (16%) went on to develop chronic spondyloarthropathy; recurrent or chronic arthritis, iritis, or radiological sacroiliitis occurred only in the HLA-B27-positive patients (Leirisalo-Repo M et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1997;56(9):516-520, PMID 9370874). A separate 10-year follow-up of 17 patients treated for acute ReA found that although some back or joint symptoms were common at follow-up (94% and 59% respectively), only 1 patient had progressed to full ankylosing spondylitis and 3 had radiological sacroiliitis (Laasila K, Laasonen L, Leirisalo-Repo M, 'Antibiotic treatment and long term prognosis of reactive arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 2003;62(7):655-658, PMID 12810429). Treating the triggering infection genuinely improves the odds: in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of chronic Chlamydia-induced ReA, a 6-month course of combination antibiotics achieved the primary clinical-improvement endpoint in 17 of 27 patients (63%) versus 3 of 15 (20%) on placebo, and 6 of 27 (22%) on antibiotics reported complete disease remission versus 0 of 15 on placebo (Carter JD, Espinoza LR, Inman RD, et al., 'Combination antibiotics as a treatment for chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, prospective trial', Arthritis Rheum 2010;62(5):1298-1307, PMID 20155838). A minority of patients - roughly 15-20% across these real cohorts - progress to chronic spondyloarthritis, chronic/recurrent uveitis, or (rarely) full ankylosing spondylitis, and this minority is concentrated almost entirely among HLA-B27-positive patients (PMID 9370874; PMID 12810429).

reactive_arthritis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Reactive arthritis (ReA) is a genuinely self-limiting disease in most patients: acute ReA typically follows a gastrointestinal (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or urogenital (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection by 1-6 weeks and, in the majority of patients, the arthritis itself resolves over weeks to a few months with NSAID symptom control alone while the immune response to the trigger organism subsides -- this is a real, well-documented natural history, not a treatment effect of any drug. In the one rigorously followed real cohort in this survey (Leirisalo-Repo et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1997, salmonella-triggered ReA, mean 11-year follow-up of 50 patients), 20/50 (40%) had recovered completely and a further 10/50 (20%) had only mild residual joint symptoms, while 8/50 (16%) went on to a chronic spondyloarthropathy -- chronicity was seen only in HLA-B27-positive patients (PMID 9370874). Where the trigger is a genuinely PERSISTENT synovial infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or Chlamydophila (Chlamydia) pneumoniae (proven by synovial PCR), a 6-month course of COMBINATION antibiotics is a real disease-modifying, infection-eradicating treatment: Carter JD et al.'s CARDINAL trial (Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1298-1307, PMID 20155838) showed 63% (17/27) of combination-antibiotic-treated patients met the primary composite improvement endpoint versus 20% (3/15) on placebo, and 22% (6/27) of antibiotic-treated patients reported complete disease remission versus 0% on placebo, with significantly more antibiotic-treated patients clearing the organism by PCR. This is the real 'treat the trigger infection' curative-intent route named in this project's brief, but it is honestly narrower than a universal cure: it is proven only for PCR-confirmed persistent Chlamydia/C. pneumoniae infection, not for unselected acute ReA or for Yersinia/Salmonella-triggered disease. Two other real, negative trials must be reported honestly alongside the positive one so this is not overstated: Kvien TK et al.'s EULAR trial of azithromycin in 152 patients with acute ReA of mixed/unconfirmed trigger found NO benefit over placebo on any outcome (Ann Rheum Dis 2004;63:1113-1119, PMID 15308521), and Sieper J et al.'s 3-month ciprofloxacin RCT in 104 patients found no overall benefit, with ciprofloxacin ineffective in Yersinia- and Salmonella-triggered arthritis and only a non-significant trend toward benefit in the Chlamydia-triggered subgroup (Arthritis Rheum 1999;42:1386-1396, PMID 10403266). So the real, verified picture is: most acute ReA resolves on its own within months regardless of antibiotics; NSAIDs treat symptoms during that natural resolution; and prolonged combination antibiotics add a real, trial-proven benefit specifically when persistent Chlamydia/C. pneumoniae infection is documented. The 15-20% minority who develop chronic or relapsing peripheral/axial disease are not cured by any drug in this survey and are managed long-term with sulfasalazine, methotrexate, or TNF inhibitors for disease control, not eradication.

curative_option.name: Treat the Trigger Infection (organism-directed antibiotic therapy where a persistent infection is proven) + NSAID symptom control through the natural resolution window
curative_option.note: This is the real curative-intent strategy for reactive arthritis, but it is two distinct real mechanisms, not one: (1) for the majority of patients, ReA is self-limiting -- NSAIDs control pain/inflammation while the post-infectious immune synovitis resolves on its own over weeks to months, most completely in HLA-B27-negative patients (Leirisalo-Repo et al. 1997, PMID 9370874); (2) for the specific subgroup with PCR-proven persistent synovial Chlamydia trachomatis or Chlamydophila pneumoniae infection, a 6-month combination-antibiotic course (doxycycline+rifampin or azithromycin+rifampin) produces real organism eradication and a significantly higher composite response and complete-remission rate than placebo (Carter JD et al., CARDINAL trial, Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1298-1307, PMID 20155838). Short-course or single-agent antibiotic therapy (ciprofloxacin alone, single-dose or short azithromycin) does NOT reproduce this benefit and has failed in real placebo-controlled trials for unselected or non-Chlamydia-triggered ReA (Kvien et al. 2004, PMID 15308521; Sieper et al. 1999, PMID 10403266) -- so 'treating the trigger' only works as a real cure when it targets a documented persistent organism with a sufficiently long combination regimen, not as a blanket antibiotic prescription for every ReA patient.

real_survival_data.Kvien_2004_azithromycin_vs_placebo_unsel: no significant difference on any endpoint (negative trial)
real_survival_data.Sieper_1999_ciprofloxacin_vs_placebo_ove: no significant difference (negative trial); ineffective in Yersinia/Salmonella-triggered arthritis

curative_option.source: Carter JD et al., 'Combination antibiotics as a treatment for chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, prospective trial', Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1298-1307 (PMID 20155838); Leirisalo-Repo M et al., 'Long-term prognosis of reactive salmonella arthritis', Ann Rheum Dis 1997;56:516-520 (PMID 9370874); Kvien TK et al., 'Three month treatment of reactive arthritis with azithromycin: a EULAR double blind, placebo controlled study', Ann Rheum Dis 2004;63:1113-1119 (PMID 15308521); Sieper J et al., 'No benefit of long-term ciprofloxacin treatment in patients with reactive arthritis and undifferentiated oligoarthritis', Arthritis Rheum 1999;42:1386-1396 (PMID 10403266)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for reactive arthritis (ReA): NSAIDs as first-line symptomatic therapy during the natural resolution window, organism-directed antibiotic therapy for the Chlamydia/C. pneumoniae-triggered subgroup (with the real CARDINAL positive trial and the real Kvien/Sieper negative trials reported honestly side by side), intra-articular corticosteroid injection, sulfasalazine (the one real placebo-controlled positive DMARD trial in ReA), methotrexate for chronic/relapsing disease, TNF inhibitors (etanercept open-label pilot) for refractory chronic disease, and topical treatment for the extra-articular manifestations (uveitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum/circinate balanitis skin lesions). Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review abstract; where a number could not be independently verified via PubMed in this session it is described qualitatively and not given a fabricated percentage. Symptoms, diagnostic criteria and classification are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Doses named are the trial arm doses quoted in the cited abstracts, not prescribing instructions -- dosing is a treating-rheumatologist decision.

reac_nsaids_first_line_symptomatic.name: NSAIDs - First-Line Symptomatic Therapy
