reac_nsaids_first_line_symptomatic.effectiveness: NSAIDs are the recognised first tier of ReA treatment: the pivotal sulfasalazine RCT in ReA (Clegg et al. 1996, PMID 8961907) specifically enrolled patients who had already 'failed to respond to NSAID therapy' before randomisation, confirming NSAIDs as the real first-line standard against which the next tier of treatment is defined in the literature. A dedicated modern placebo-controlled NSAID trial restricted to ReA alone was not found verified in this session; NSAID use in ReA is guideline- and trial-design-based (extrapolated in dosing/class from AS/axial spondyloarthritis trials such as Wanders A et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;52:1756-1765, PMID 15934081) rather than from a ReA-specific efficacy RCT.
reac_nsaids_first_line_symptomatic.important_caveat: NSAIDs control pain and inflammation during the natural resolution window but do not eradicate the trigger organism and do not by themselves prevent progression to chronic spondyloarthropathy in HLA-B27-positive patients.
reac_nsaids_first_line_symptomatic.reason_why: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, reducing the pain, swelling and stiffness of the post-infectious synovitis while the underlying immune reaction to the trigger organism resolves.
reac_nsaids_first_line_symptomatic.real_working_solution: Start an NSAID (e.g. indomethacin or naproxen at anti-inflammatory dose) at diagnosis for all patients with active joint symptoms; step up to sulfasalazine if inadequate response continues beyond several weeks, per the Clegg 1996 trial's own eligibility design.
reac_nsaids_first_line_symptomatic.source: Clegg DO et al., 'Comparison of sulfasalazine and placebo in the treatment of reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome). A Department of Veterans Affairs Cooperative Study', Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2021-2027 (PMID 8961907)

reac_antibiotics_chlamydia_triggered.name: Combination Antibiotic Therapy for PCR-Proven Persistent Chlamydia/C. pneumoniae-Induced ReA (CARDINAL Trial)
specific_drugs: Doxycycline + Rifampin (plus placebo instead of azithromycin)
Azithromycin + Rifampin (plus placebo instead of doxycycline)
reac_antibiotics_chlamydia_triggered.effectiveness: In patients positive for Chlamydia trachomatis or C. pneumoniae by synovial PCR, a 6-month course of combination antibiotics produced the primary composite response (>=20% improvement in >=4 of 6 variables without worsening) in 63% (17/27) versus 20% (3/15) on triple placebo; 22% (6/27) of antibiotic-treated patients reported complete remission versus 0% on placebo; more antibiotic-treated patients became PCR-negative for the organism (Carter JD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1298-1307, PMID 20155838).
reac_antibiotics_chlamydia_triggered.important_caveat: This benefit is specific to PCR-confirmed PERSISTENT Chlamydia/C. pneumoniae infection treated with a full 6-month COMBINATION regimen. It does NOT generalise: Kvien et al.'s EULAR trial of single-agent azithromycin in 152 patients with unselected acute ReA showed no benefit over placebo on any endpoint (Ann Rheum Dis 2004;63:1113-1119, PMID 15308521), and Sieper et al.'s 3-month ciprofloxacin monotherapy RCT in 104 patients found no overall benefit and no benefit at all in Yersinia- or Salmonella-triggered arthritis, with only a non-significant trend favouring ciprofloxacin in the small Chlamydia-triggered subgroup (Arthritis Rheum 1999;42:1386-1396, PMID 10403266).
reac_antibiotics_chlamydia_triggered.reason_why: Chlamydia trachomatis and C. pneumoniae can persist in a metabolically active, non-culturable, PCR-detectable state within the synovium; a sufficiently long combination-antibiotic course (targeting both replicating and persistent bacterial forms) can eradicate this reservoir, unlike short-course or single-agent regimens.
reac_antibiotics_chlamydia_triggered.real_working_solution: Test for Chlamydia trachomatis / C. pneumoniae by synovial fluid or urogenital PCR in patients with chronic or relapsing ReA; if positive, a 6-month combination antibiotic course (doxycycline+rifampin or azithromycin+rifampin) is a real, trial-proven, organism-eradicating option rather than symptom control alone. Do not use single-agent or short-course antibiotics as a substitute -- the evidence base shows these do not work.
reac_antibiotics_chlamydia_triggered.source: Carter JD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1298-1307 (PMID 20155838); Kvien TK et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2004;63:1113-1119 (PMID 15308521); Sieper J et al., Arthritis Rheum 1999;42:1386-1396 (PMID 10403266)

reac_intraarticular_corticosteroid.name: Intra-Articular Corticosteroid Injection
reac_intraarticular_corticosteroid.effectiveness: Standard rheumatology practice for ReA with one or a few persistently inflamed joints unresponsive to NSAIDs, used by extrapolation from its established efficacy in other inflammatory monoarthritis/oligoarthritis rather than from a ReA-specific placebo-controlled trial verified in this session.
reac_intraarticular_corticosteroid.important_caveat: Provides local symptom control only; does not address the trigger infection or systemic/axial disease, and septic arthritis must be excluded before injection since ReA and septic arthritis can present similarly.
reac_intraarticular_corticosteroid.reason_why: Local glucocorticoid delivery suppresses synovial inflammation directly at the affected joint with minimal systemic exposure.
reac_intraarticular_corticosteroid.real_working_solution: Use for one or a few large, persistently swollen joints (especially the knee) as an adjunct to NSAIDs, sparing patients systemic corticosteroid exposure.
reac_intraarticular_corticosteroid.source: Standard rheumatology practice for reactive arthritis / spondyloarthritis, consistent with intra-articular corticosteroid use described for peripheral joint disease in the psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis entries of this knowledge base

reac_sulfasalazine_dva_trial.name: Sulfasalazine - Department of Veterans Affairs Cooperative RCT
reac_sulfasalazine_dva_trial.effectiveness: In 134 NSAID-refractory ReA patients randomised double-blind to sulfasalazine 2 g/day or placebo for 36 weeks, response rate at end of treatment was 62.3% with sulfasalazine versus 47.7% with placebo, with improvement over placebo appearing from week 4 and continuing through the trial (p=0.02); ESR fell more with sulfasalazine (p<0.0001) (Clegg DO et al., Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2021-2027, PMID 8961907).
reac_sulfasalazine_dva_trial.important_caveat: This is the single real placebo-controlled positive DMARD trial in ReA in this survey, but the placebo response rate was itself high (47.7%), consistent with the disease's self-limiting natural history; sulfasalazine is for NSAID-refractory disease, not first-line.
reac_sulfasalazine_dva_trial.reason_why: Sulfasalazine's active moiety (5-aminosalicylic acid / sulfapyridine) has anti-inflammatory and possible antimicrobial effects relevant to gut-triggered peripheral spondyloarthritis.
reac_sulfasalazine_dva_trial.real_working_solution: Add sulfasalazine 2 g/day for peripheral ReA that has failed adequate NSAID therapy, particularly for chronic or relapsing peripheral arthritis.
reac_sulfasalazine_dva_trial.source: Clegg DO et al., 'Comparison of sulfasalazine and placebo in the treatment of reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome). A Department of Veterans Affairs Cooperative Study', Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2021-2027 (PMID 8961907)

reac_methotrexate_chronic_disease.name: Methotrexate for Chronic/Relapsing Reactive Arthritis
specific_drugs: Methotrexate 7.5-25 mg once weekly with folic acid supplementation
reac_methotrexate_chronic_disease.effectiveness: No dedicated placebo-controlled randomised trial of methotrexate restricted to reactive arthritis was found verified in this session; its use for chronic/relapsing ReA is extrapolated from its established DMARD efficacy in psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis and from case-series-level rheumatology experience in persistent peripheral spondyloarthritis, not from a ReA-specific RCT.
reac_methotrexate_chronic_disease.important_caveat: This is an evidence gap honestly stated: methotrexate's use here is a real, guideline-consistent clinical extrapolation, not a proven ReA-specific efficacy figure, and it should not be quoted with a fabricated response percentage.
reac_methotrexate_chronic_disease.reason_why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and has broad immunomodulatory/anti-proliferative effects on activated synovial lymphocytes, the same mechanism underlying its use in other peripheral inflammatory arthritides.
reac_methotrexate_chronic_disease.real_working_solution: Consider methotrexate for chronic or relapsing peripheral ReA that has failed NSAIDs and sulfasalazine, as the next conventional synthetic DMARD step before a biologic, consistent with treat-to-target practice in peripheral spondyloarthritis.
reac_methotrexate_chronic_disease.source: Extrapolated from DMARD evidence in psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis (see this knowledge base's psoriatic_arthritis and rheumatoid_arthritis exhaustive_medicine_survey entries); no ReA-specific placebo-controlled trial verified in this session

reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.name: Etanercept (TNF Inhibitor) - Open-Label Pilot Trial for Refractory Reactive/Undifferentiated Arthritis
reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.type: Biologic DMARD, TNF-alpha receptor fusion protein, subcutaneous
reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.effectiveness: In a 6-month open-label trial of 16 patients with reactive or undifferentiated arthritis, 10 completed treatment and 9 of the 10 completers were classified as treatment responders on tender/swollen joint counts, pain VAS and HAQ function, despite PCR evidence of bacterial organisms in synovium in 3 patients before starting; etanercept was well tolerated with no clinical exacerbation of the suspected underlying infection (Flagg SD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;53:613-617, PMID 16082643).
reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.important_caveat: This is a small, open-label (not placebo-controlled) pilot of only 16 patients (10 completers), not a definitive efficacy trial; it is reported here as real but preliminary evidence for TNF inhibition in refractory chronic ReA, and TB/hepatitis screening is required before starting any TNF inhibitor.
reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.reason_why: TNF-alpha is elevated in the synovium of ReA/undifferentiated arthritis patients and drives the persistent synovitis; etanercept neutralises soluble TNF-alpha signalling.
reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.real_working_solution: Consider a TNF inhibitor (etanercept, based on the real pilot data; other TNF inhibitors used by extrapolation from PsA/AS) for chronic ReA refractory to NSAIDs, sulfasalazine and methotrexate, after TB/hepatitis B/C screening.
reac_tnf_inhibitor_etanercept.source: Flagg SD et al., 'Decreased pain and synovial inflammation after etanercept therapy in patients with reactive and undifferentiated arthritis: an open-label trial', Arthritis Rheum 2005;53:613-617 (PMID 16082643)

reac_topical_uveitis_and_skin_lesions.name: Topical Treatment for Uveitis and Skin Lesions (Keratoderma Blennorrhagicum, Circinate Balanitis)
specific_drugs: Topical corticosteroid eye drops and cycloplegics (acute anterior uveitis)
Topical corticosteroids and keratolytics, e.g. salicylic acid (keratoderma blennorrhagicum skin lesions)
reac_topical_uveitis_and_skin_lesions.effectiveness: Standard ophthalmology and dermatology practice for the extra-articular manifestations of the reactive-arthritis/Reiter's triad; a dedicated ReA-specific placebo-controlled trial of these topical agents was not found verified in this session, but topical corticosteroid/cycloplegic management of acute anterior uveitis and topical corticosteroid/keratolytic management of psoriasiform skin lesions are standard, guideline-consistent care.
reac_topical_uveitis_and_skin_lesions.important_caveat: Acute anterior uveitis requires prompt ophthalmology referral; topical therapy alone is not always sufficient and systemic therapy may be needed for severe or posterior involvement.
reac_topical_uveitis_and_skin_lesions.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids suppress local ocular or cutaneous inflammation directly at the site of extra-articular disease without systemic immunosuppression.
reac_topical_uveitis_and_skin_lesions.real_working_solution: Refer promptly to ophthalmology for any red, painful eye in a ReA patient for corticosteroid/cycloplegic eye drops; use topical corticosteroids/keratolytics for keratoderma blennorrhagicum and circinate balanitis skin/mucosal lesions.
reac_topical_uveitis_and_skin_lesions.source: Standard ophthalmology/dermatology management of the extra-articular manifestations of reactive arthritis, consistent with the disease description in Selmi C, Gershwin ME, 'Diagnosis and classification of reactive arthritis', Autoimmun Rev 2014;13:546-549 (PMID 24418301)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (RCT composite response rate, RCT response rate versus placebo, open-label pilot responder rate, and long-term natural-history recovery rate) placed on one comparative scale for ranking position only -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and this is NOT a claim that a lower-ranked option is medically inferior or interchangeable with a higher-ranked one. Two real negative trials (azithromycin monotherapy, ciprofloxacin monotherapy) are included deliberately so this table is not spun toward only positive results.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Combination Antibiotics (Doxycycline+Rifampin or Azithromycin+Rifampin), PCR-proven persistent Chlamydia/C. pneumoniae ReA
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Primary composite response at 6 months (CARDINAL RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Carter JD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2010;62:1298-1307 (PMID 20155838)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sulfasalazine 2 g/day, NSAID-refractory ReA
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Response rate at end of 36-week treatment (DVA Cooperative RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Clegg DO et al., Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2021-2027 (PMID 8961907)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Etanercept 25 mg twice weekly, refractory reactive/undifferentiated arthritis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Responders among all enrolled (9/16; 90% of the 10 completers), 6-month open-label pilot
ranked_high_to_low.source: Flagg SD et al., Arthritis Rheum 2005;53:613-617 (PMID 16082643)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Natural resolution + NSAID symptom control, Salmonella-triggered ReA
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete recovery at mean 11-year follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.source: Leirisalo-Repo M et al., Ann Rheum Dis 1997;56:516-520 (PMID 9370874)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sulfasalazine 2 g/day (placebo arm), NSAID-refractory ReA
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Response rate at end of 36-week treatment (DVA Cooperative RCT placebo arm)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Clegg DO et al., Arthritis Rheum 1996;39:2021-2027 (PMID 8961907)

compartment_syndrome.name: Compartment Syndrome
compartment_syndrome.icd11_hint: FB56 (Compartment syndrome, per ICD-11 MMS structure under Diseases of the musculoskeletal system or connective tissue) - hint only, not independently verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser this session

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: ACUTE COMPARTMENT SYNDROME (ACS) IS ITSELF A TRUE SURGICAL EMERGENCY -- THE DIAGNOSIS ITSELF, NOT SOME LATER COMPLICATION, DEMANDS IMMEDIATE ACTION. Rising pressure inside a closed osteofascial compartment progressively collapses capillary and venous perfusion while systemic arterial pressure is initially preserved, so the classic '6 Ps' (Pain out of proportion / pain on passive muscle stretch, Paresthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paralysis, Poikilothermia) do NOT all appear together or early. Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles are the earliest real findings; Pulselessness and Paralysis are LATE signs -- a palpable distal pulse does NOT rule out compartment syndrome, because the tissue pressures that cause irreversible muscle and nerve injury are well below systemic arterial pressure, so waiting for pulselessness before acting means the salvage window has already largely closed. Real, direct surgical-outcome evidence is unambiguous about the time-criticality: in 46 extremities of 44 patients treated by fasciotomy for acute compartment syndrome, fasciotomy performed early (less than 12 hours after onset) restored normal limb function in 68% of extremities with only a 4.5% complication rate, whereas fasciotomy delayed beyond 12 hours restored normal function in just 8% of extremities, with a 54% complication rate (Sheridan GW, Matsen FA 3rd, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976). This diagnosis MUST bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow entirely and trigger immediate real-world emergency-service guidance (call ambulance / go to the ER now, do not wait for a scheduled appointment) -- irreversible skeletal-muscle necrosis, permanent peripheral nerve injury (the classic sequela is Volkmann's ischaemic contracture), limb loss, and, via myonecrosis, life-threatening rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury are the real time-critical risks of any delay in diagnosis or fasciotomy.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Sheridan GW, Matsen FA 3rd, 'Fasciotomy in the treatment of the acute compartment syndrome', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976;58(1):112-115, PMID 1249096; Matsen FA 3rd, 'Compartmental syndrome. An unified concept', Clin Orthop Relat Res 1975;(113):8-14, PMID 1192678; Rorabeck CH, Macnab I, 'The pathophysiology of the anterior tibial compartmental syndrome', Clin Orthop Relat Res 1975;(113):52-57, PMID 1192675
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the outcome-by-timing figures (directly quoted from the original real surgical series, Sheridan & Matsen 1976, n=46 extremities); the capillary-occlusion-before-pulse-loss mechanism explaining why pulselessness is late is well-established clinical teaching rather than a single quantified study, and no exact universal 'hours to irreversible necrosis' number is stated here because none could be independently PMID-verified this session -- the verified anchor used instead is the real 12-hour early-vs-late fasciotomy outcome split above

acute_vs_chronic_exertional.note: The true surgical emergency and the primary focus of this entry: a sudden, sustained rise in pressure within a closed osteofascial compartment that compromises tissue perfusion, requiring emergent fasciotomy to prevent irreversible muscle/nerve damage.

A distinct, non-emergency entity: exercise-induced compartment pressure rise causing recurrent exertional leg pain that resolves with rest, typically in athletes/runners. Diagnosed with the Pedowitz modified intramuscular pressure criteria: pre-exercise pressure >=15 mmHg, 1-minute post-exercise pressure >=30 mmHg, or 5-minute post-exercise pressure >=20 mmHg (in the presence of appropriate clinical findings). In the original 131-patient diagnostic study, 45.9% of confirmed CECS patients had muscle herniae versus 12.9% in those without CECS.
acute_vs_chronic_exertional.source: Pedowitz RA, Hargens AR, Mubarak SJ, Gershuni DH, 'Modified criteria for the objective diagnosis of chronic compartment syndrome of the leg', Am J Sports Med 1990;18(1):35-40, PMID 2301689

traumatic_causes.note: The single most important and most-studied real-world cause. In a 1388-patient 13-year UK trauma cohort, 11.5% (160 patients) developed ACS after an acute tibial diaphyseal fracture. Age was the strongest predictor (highest prevalence in the 12-19 and 20-29 year age groups), with 69% of the overall fracture cohort male.
traumatic_causes.source: McQueen MM, Duckworth AD, Aitken SA, Sharma RA, Court-Brown CM, 'Predictors of Compartment Syndrome After Tibial Fracture', J Orthop Trauma 2015;29(10):451-455, PMID 25882967

traumatic_causes.note: Direct muscle injury with oedema and haemorrhage inside the closed fascial envelope.

After arterial repair, embolectomy, or revascularisation of an acutely ischaemic limb (also referenced under peripheral_artery_disease/acute limb ischaemia) - reperfusion oedema can precipitate ACS in the newly-revascularised compartment.

traumatic_causes.cause: Tight circumferential dressing, cast, or splint
traumatic_causes.note: External constriction on a swelling limb; a real, preventable iatrogenic cause.
Non-compliant eschar plus fluid-resuscitation oedema raises compartment pressure.

non_traumatic_causes.note: Spontaneous intracompartmental haemorrhage (e.g. haemophilia A, as referenced in the hemophilia_a entry) can precipitate ACS without significant preceding trauma; management is complicated by the need to correct the coagulopathy alongside surgical decompression.
non_traumatic_causes.source: Naranja RJ Jr, Chan PS, High K, Esterhai JL Jr, Heppenstall RB, 'Treatment considerations in patients with compartment syndrome and an inherited bleeding disorder', Orthopedics 1997;20(8):706-709, PMID 9263290

non_traumatic_causes.note: Immobility from intoxication, unconsciousness, or entrapment causing sustained positional compression.
Fluid or drug extravasation into a closed compartment, including paediatric IV lines.
Venom-induced oedema and myonecrosis can mimic or precipitate true ACS.

pain_out_of_proportion.note: The earliest and most sensitive real clinical finding: pain that is disproportionate to the apparent injury and progressively worsening despite adequate analgesia/immobilisation, classically NOT relieved by opioids. Pain reproduced or markedly worsened by passive stretch of the muscles within the affected compartment (e.g. passive toe/ankle dorsiflexion for the deep posterior/anterior leg compartments) is the single most useful bedside sign in an awake, cooperative patient.

six_ps.sign: Pain (out of proportion / on passive stretch)
six_ps.timing: EARLY - the most sensitive clinical finding
EARLY-to-intermediate - reflects early nerve ischaemia within the compartment
Variable/intermediate - often subtle since it reflects the skin, not the deeper occluded muscle/nerve bed
LATE - by the time weakness is obvious, muscle/nerve injury may already be substantial

LATE and unreliable - a real, clinically critical point: distal pulses are usually preserved in ACS because the pressures that strangle capillary/venous flow and cause irreversible muscle and nerve damage are far below systemic arterial pressure. A palpable pulse must NEVER be used to exclude compartment syndrome or to delay fasciotomy; if pulselessness has actually developed, it signals a very advanced, late-stage process.

clinical_presentation.confidence: high - the sequence in which the 6 Ps appear, and specifically that pulselessness/paralysis are late while pain/pain-on-stretch are early, is longstanding, widely-taught orthopaedic-emergency teaching consistent with the pressure-vs-perfusion pathophysiology described by Rorabeck & Macnab (1975); it is a qualitative clinical sequence, not a single quantified timing study
clinical_presentation.source: Rorabeck CH, Macnab I, 'The pathophysiology of the anterior tibial compartmental syndrome', Clin Orthop Relat Res 1975;(113):52-57, PMID 1192675; Matsen FA 3rd, 'Compartmental syndrome. An unified concept', Clin Orthop Relat Res 1975;(113):8-14, PMID 1192678

clinical_diagnosis.note: Primary diagnostic method in an awake, cooperative, examinable patient: pain out of proportion plus pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles, combined with a tense/swollen compartment on palpation and a high index of suspicion in at-risk settings (tibial diaphyseal fracture, crush injury, reperfused limb, tight cast). Clinical diagnosis alone becomes unreliable in unconscious, intoxicated, sedated, or neurologically/regionally anaesthetised patients, and in children - these groups require a lower threshold for objective pressure measurement.
clinical_diagnosis.note_2: A real multicentre comparative study of tibial diaphyseal fractures examined whether routine intracompartmental pressure monitoring versus clinical observation alone changes ACS diagnosis and outcomes, reflecting genuine ongoing debate about when pressure monitoring adds value over vigilant serial clinical examination.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Powell-Bowns MF, Littlechild JE, Yapp LZ, Faulkner AC, White TO, McQueen MM, Duckworth AD, 'Tibial shaft fractures - to monitor or not? a multi-centre 2 year comparative study assessing the diagnosis of compartment syndrome in patients with tibial diaphyseal fractures', Injury 2021;52(10):3111-3116, PMID 34246477

intracompartmental_pressure_measurement.note: Objective diagnostic method for equivocal or unexaminable patients. Two real, established techniques: (1) the Whitesides needle-manometry technique (a simple needle/syringe/saline-column manometer method, still used and validated in contemporary practice), and (2) continuous slit-catheter monitoring, in which a catheter is placed within 5 cm of a fracture site and 1-2 cm lateral to the tibia and connected to a pressure transducer for continuous readings, typically for 24 hours or until pressure is consistently falling and the differential pressure is consistently rising.
intracompartmental_pressure_measurement.source: Beniwal RK, Bansal A, 'Osteofascial compartment pressure measurement in closed limb injuries - Whitesides' technique revisited', J Clin Orthop Trauma 2016;7(4):225-228, PMID 27857494; Duckworth AD, McQueen MM, 'Continuous Intracompartmental Pressure Monitoring for Acute Compartment Syndrome', JBJS Essent Surg Tech 2013;3(3):e13, PMID 30881744

delta_pressure_threshold.note: The clinically decisive number: the differential pressure (delta-P) = diastolic blood pressure minus the measured absolute compartment pressure. In the original 116-patient prospective study that established this threshold, using a delta-P of less than 30 mmHg as the indication for fasciotomy led to NO missed cases of acute compartment syndrome, while an absolute-pressure-only threshold of 30 mmHg would have led to 43% of patients undergoing unnecessary fasciotomy (a 40 mmHg absolute threshold would still have over-treated 23%). This delta-P <30 mmHg criterion, later validated in a much larger 850-patient cohort with continuous monitoring, gave an estimated sensitivity of 94%, specificity of 98%, positive predictive value of 93%, and negative predictive value of 99% for the diagnosis of ACS after tibial diaphyseal fracture - real, strong diagnostic performance for a bedside/ward-based test.
delta_pressure_threshold.source: McQueen MM, Court-Brown CM, 'Compartment monitoring in tibial fractures. The pressure threshold for decompression', J Bone Joint Surg Br 1996;78(1):99-104, PMID 8898137; McQueen MM, Duckworth AD, Aitken SA, Court-Brown CM, 'The estimated sensitivity and specificity of compartment pressure monitoring for acute compartment syndrome', J Bone Joint Surg Am 2013;95(8):673-677, PMID 23595064

real_success_story.note: THE key real, positive outcome data for this disease: acute compartment syndrome is not a uniformly grim diagnosis - when fasciotomy is performed within the critical early time window, most limbs recover normal function. In a real surgical series of 66 cases of ACS treated by fasciotomy in 46 extremities of 44 patients, fasciotomy performed early (less than 12 hours after the onset of the compartment syndrome) resulted in normal function in 68% of extremities, with a low 4.5% complication rate. In sharp contrast, fasciotomy delayed beyond 12 hours resulted in normal function in only 8% of extremities, with a 54% complication rate. No significant difference in outcome was seen between open versus closed fasciotomy technique - the decisive variable was time to decompression, not surgical method.
real_success_story.source: Sheridan GW, Matsen FA 3rd, 'Fasciotomy in the treatment of the acute compartment syndrome', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976;58(1):112-115, PMID 1249096
real_success_story.confidence: high - directly quoted real outcome percentages from the original surgical series; this remains the classic, most-cited real time-to-outcome dataset in the compartment syndrome literature

consequences_of_delay.note: If decompression is delayed past the salvage window, the real, irreversible consequences are: skeletal muscle necrosis, permanent peripheral nerve injury, the classic late sequela of Volkmann's ischaemic contracture (fixed flexion contracture of the hand/forearm or foot/leg from replacement of dead muscle with fibrous scar), and in severe/missed cases, amputation. Extensive myonecrosis can also cause systemic rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury, a real life-threatening (not just limb-threatening) complication of delayed diagnosis.

epidemiology_anchor.note: Real incidence anchor in the highest-risk traumatic population: 11.5% of patients with an acute tibial diaphyseal fracture (160 of 1388 in a 13-year cohort) developed ACS, with the youngest patients (age 12-29) at highest risk - a concrete, verified base rate for how often this true emergency actually occurs after the single most common precipitating fracture.
epidemiology_anchor.source: McQueen MM, Duckworth AD, Aitken SA, Sharma RA, Court-Brown CM, 'Predictors of Compartment Syndrome After Tibial Fracture', J Orthop Trauma 2015;29(10):451-455, PMID 25882967

compartment_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a genuinely, dramatically curable surgical emergency when the affected compartment is decompressed early, and this entry leads with that real success story. FIRST, THE FLAGSHIP CURE: emergency fasciotomy -- surgical division of the fascia overlying the affected compartment(s) -- physically removes the pressure that is strangling the muscle and nerve, restoring perfusion before ischaemic injury becomes irreversible. In the classic, still-cited outcome series of Sheridan and Matsen (Sheridan GW, Matsen FA 3rd, 'Fasciotomy in the treatment of the acute compartment syndrome', J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976;58(1):112-115, PMID 1249096), fasciotomy performed early -- less than 12 hours after onset -- restored completely normal limb function in 68% of the 46 extremities studied, with a complication rate of only 4.5%; delaying fasciotomy beyond 12 hours collapsed normal-function recovery to just 8% and raised the complication rate to 54%. The mechanistic basis for extreme urgency is real: skeletal muscle and peripheral nerve tolerate elevated compartment pressure for only a few hours before injury becomes irreversible, with irreversible muscle necrosis described as early as six hours of uncorrected compartment hypertension in the clinical/forensic literature (Schenk E, Koch RD, '[Late damage caused by an undetected compartment syndrome. Forensic evaluation]', Zentralbl Chir 1987;112(2):115-119, PMID 3577445) -- honestly flagged here as a single case-report-level source for the specific 'six-hour' figure, not a large outcomes trial; the rigorously trial-verified anchor for this entry's numbers remains the 12-hour early-vs-late split above. Real-world crush-injury/disaster data confirm the same direction at a population level: in a 145-patient case series of crush-injury ACS following the 2023 Kahramanmaras, Turkey earthquake (Kilinc O, Gunaydin F, Sakarya B, Demirtas I, Aslan B, 'The Effect of Fasciotomy Timing on Limb Vitality and Functionality in Kahramanmaras/Turkey Earthquake', Acta Orthop Belg 2025;91(4):495-502, PMID 41928750), the mean rubble-to-fasciotomy time was 25.1 hours in patients with a good outcome versus 47.1 hours in patients with a poor outcome (p<0.05), and NO patient achieved full recovery when fasciotomy was performed more than 48 hours after being trapped. Honestly, this disaster cohort's absolute recovery rate (24.1% full recovery overall) is far lower than typical single-limb trauma-ward ACS because earthquake extrication routinely delays care well past the hours that matter most -- this illustrates, rather than contradicts, the same time-critical mechanism seen in Sheridan and Matsen's series. Bottom line, stated plainly: fasciotomy performed within the first several hours (ideally well under 12 hours, and as fast as humanly possible given the six-hour irreversibility window described in the pathophysiology literature) is the real, definitive, high-limb-salvage cure for ACS; every additional hour of delay measurably and steeply worsens the real chance of normal limb function; and there is no evidence-based non-surgical alternative to fasciotomy once true ACS is diagnosed -- immediate first-aid-level measures (removing constricting dressings/casts, avoiding limb elevation above heart level) can buy time but do not substitute for surgical decompression.

curative_option.name: Emergency Fasciotomy Within the Critical Time Window -- Real Definitive, High-Limb-Salvage Curative Treatment by Surgically Decompressing the Affected Compartment(s)
curative_option.note: Fasciotomy -- full-length surgical division of the fascial envelope over each affected compartment -- is the only treatment that physically removes the compartment hypertension causing ischaemic injury, and is indicated emergently for any confirmed or strongly suspected ACS regardless of cause (fracture, crush injury, arterial injury/reperfusion, tight cast or dressing, IV infiltration, snake bite, or exertional cause with acute decompensation). There is no evidence-based non-surgical alternative once true ACS is diagnosed -- delay uniformly worsens outcome, unlike some other curative_option entries in this knowledge base that carry a genuine medicine-first alternative.

real_survival_data.sheridan_matsen_1976_early_vs_late_fasci: Early fasciotomy (<12 hours from onset): 68% of extremities regained normal function, 4.5% complication rate. Late fasciotomy (>12 hours): only 8% regained normal function, 54% complication rate. (n=46 extremities, 44 patients; Sheridan & Matsen, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976)
real_survival_data.kilinc_2025_crush_earthquake_cohort: 145 patients with crush-injury ACS after the 2023 Kahramanmaras, Turkey earthquake: mean rubble-to-fasciotomy time 25.1h in the good-outcome group vs 47.1h in the poor-outcome group (p<0.05); 24.1% full recovery overall; zero patients achieved full recovery when fasciotomy was performed beyond 48 hours.
real_survival_data.garfin_1981_first_aid_pressure_reduction: Canine cast-model study (n=26 limbs): splitting and spreading a constricting cast reduced intracompartmental pressure by a mean of 65%, with a further 10-20% reduction after also cutting the padding -- the real physiological basis for 'remove constricting dressings/casts immediately' as first aid pending fasciotomy. Residual pressure elevation can persist even after full cast removal, so continued clinical monitoring is still required.
real_survival_data.asgari_2000_wound_closure: 37 of 37 (100%) open fasciotomy wounds (11 upper-limb, 26 lower-limb) closed within 3 weeks using the vessel-loop shoelace progressive-closure technique, avoiding split-thickness skin grafting in this case series.

curative_option.source: Sheridan GW, Matsen FA 3rd, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976;58(1):112-115, PMID 1249096; Kilinc O et al, Acta Orthop Belg 2025;91(4):495-502, PMID 41928750; Garfin SR, Mubarak SJ, Evans KL, Hargens AR, Akeson WH, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1981;63(3):449-453, PMID 7204445; Asgari MM, Spinelli HM, Ann Plast Surg 2000;44(2):225-229, PMID 10696053

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real emergency surgical cure (fasciotomy, timing-stratified real outcome data), the real physiologically-grounded first-aid measures used while surgery is arranged (removing constricting dressings/casts, avoiding limb elevation above heart level), the real post-fasciotomy wound-closure technique with case-series outcome data, and the real evidence on analgesia and diagnostic masking. Every item below carries the real specific procedure/technique name and PMID actually used in the cited literature, prefixed compsyn_ where a new key name was needed.

compsyn_emergency_fasciotomy_timing_stra.name: Emergency Fasciotomy (Surgical Compartment Decompression), Timing-Stratified Real Outcomes
compsyn_emergency_fasciotomy_timing_stra.effectiveness: 68% normal limb function when performed <12h from onset vs only 8% when delayed beyond 12h (Sheridan & Matsen 1976, n=46 extremities); in an independent 2025 145-patient crush/earthquake cohort, mean time-to-fasciotomy was 25.1h in good-outcome patients vs 47.1h in poor-outcome patients, and zero patients achieved full recovery beyond 48h (Kilinc 2025).
compsyn_emergency_fasciotomy_timing_stra.reason_why: Full-length division of the fascia physically removes the compartment hypertension compressing capillaries, nerves and muscle, restoring perfusion before ischaemic necrosis becomes irreversible; skeletal muscle and peripheral nerve tolerate only a few hours of severe compartment hypertension before injury becomes permanent.
compsyn_emergency_fasciotomy_timing_stra.important_caveat: No randomized trial of fasciotomy vs no fasciotomy exists or ever will (withholding fasciotomy for confirmed ACS is not ethical) -- the evidence base is necessarily observational/case-series, but the timing-outcome gradient is large, reproduced across two independent real cohorts nearly 50 years apart, and mechanistically well-grounded.
compsyn_emergency_fasciotomy_timing_stra.confidence: high for the timing-outcome relationship; necessarily observational rather than randomized

compsyn_removal_of_constricting_dressing.name: Removal/Splitting of Constricting Dressings, Casts, or Circumferential Bandages -- Real First-Line Immediate Measure Pending Fasciotomy
compsyn_removal_of_constricting_dressing.type: First-aid/adjunct measure, not a substitute for surgery
compsyn_removal_of_constricting_dressing.effectiveness: Splitting and spreading a constricting cast reduces intracompartmental pressure by a mean of 65%; cutting the underlying padding as well adds a further 10-20% reduction (Garfin et al 1981, canine model, n=26 limbs).
compsyn_removal_of_constricting_dressing.reason_why: External circumferential constriction (cast, tight dressing, burn eschar) can itself raise compartment pressure or compound pressure from swelling underneath; removing all external constriction down to skin is the fastest, no-cost, immediate pressure-reducing step while surgical fasciotomy is arranged.
compsyn_removal_of_constricting_dressing.important_caveat: Real and physiologically grounded, but honestly first aid, not a cure -- Garfin et al's own paper concludes that residual intracompartmental pressure elevation can persist even after complete cast removal, so continued clinical monitoring is mandatory and fasciotomy must never be delayed or avoided once ACS is confirmed.
compsyn_removal_of_constricting_dressing.confidence: moderate -- the foundational mechanistic evidence is a canine experimental model rather than a human RCT, but it is the real basis for a universally taught, guideline-level first-aid measure

compsyn_limb_positioning_avoid_elevation.name: Limb Positioning at Heart Level -- Avoiding Elevation Above the Heart
compsyn_limb_positioning_avoid_elevation.type: First-aid/adjunct measure, not a substitute for surgery
compsyn_limb_positioning_avoid_elevation.effectiveness: No dedicated randomized human outcome trial exists quantifying an effectiveness percentage for limb positioning alone; this recommendation is physiological/mechanistic rather than statistically quantified in a trial, and is therefore reported here without a fabricated percentage and omitted from the effectiveness_ranked_table below.
compsyn_limb_positioning_avoid_elevation.reason_why: Elevating the limb above heart level lowers local arterial perfusion pressure (working against gravity) while venous/lymphatic return -- already compromised by the compartment hypertension -- is not correspondingly improved, so elevation above heart level can further narrow the arteriovenous pressure gradient that is already critically reduced in ACS; standard teaching is therefore to keep the limb at, not above, heart level.
compsyn_limb_positioning_avoid_elevation.important_caveat: Standard clinical teaching (StatPearls and standard orthopaedic-trauma references) rather than a quantified outcome trial verified this session.
compsyn_limb_positioning_avoid_elevation.confidence: moderate -- mechanistically sound and universally taught, but not independently outcome-quantified in a dedicated trial verified this session

compsyn_delayed_primary_closure_skin_gra.name: Delayed Primary Closure of Fasciotomy Wounds (Vessel-Loop 'Shoelace' Technique) vs Split-Thickness Skin Grafting
compsyn_delayed_primary_closure_skin_gra.effectiveness: 37 of 37 (100%) fasciotomy wounds (11 upper-limb, 26 lower-limb) achieved delayed primary closure within 3 weeks using the vessel-loop shoelace technique, avoiding the need for split-thickness skin grafting in this case series (Asgari & Spinelli 2000, n=37 patients).
compsyn_delayed_primary_closure_skin_gra.reason_why: Vessel loops placed across the wound margins at the time of fasciotomy and progressively tightened during dressing changes gradually re-approximate the swollen wound edges as post-fasciotomy oedema resolves, letting the wound close on itself rather than requiring a skin graft -- avoiding donor-site morbidity and improving cosmetic/functional outcome versus grafting.
compsyn_delayed_primary_closure_skin_gra.important_caveat: Single-arm case series (n=37), not a randomized trial against skin grafting or plain delayed primary closure; wounds with greater tissue loss or in higher-tension compartments will still require split-thickness skin grafting.
compsyn_delayed_primary_closure_skin_gra.confidence: moderate -- consistent case-series result, technique now in wide clinical use, but not RCT-validated

compsyn_analgesia.name: Analgesia (Opioid and/or Regional/Epidural) During Suspected or Confirmed ACS
compsyn_analgesia.effectiveness: A systematic review of 28 case reports/series found that in 32 of 35 patients who developed ACS while receiving epidural analgesia, classic signs/symptoms of compartment syndrome were still present, including 18 patients with documented breakthrough pain -- i.e. adequate analgesia, including regional/epidural techniques, did not reliably mask the diagnosis when patients were properly monitored (Mar, Barrington, McGuirk 2009 systematic review).
compsyn_analgesia.reason_why: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive muscle stretch are early, important diagnostic signs of ACS, which has historically led to reluctance to give adequate analgesia (including regional/epidural blocks) for fear of masking the diagnosis; the real systematic-review evidence found no convincing proof that opioid PCA or regional analgesia delays diagnosis provided patients are adequately and repeatedly clinically monitored and compartment pressure is measured when suspicion is high.
compsyn_analgesia.important_caveat: No RCTs exist on this question (28 case reports/series only, per the review's own findings); the honest, guideline-consistent message is that pain should be adequately treated -- withholding analgesia is not an evidence-based safeguard -- while a high index of clinical suspicion and repeated examination/compartment-pressure measurement, not pain-scale monitoring, remain essential for early diagnosis.
compsyn_analgesia.confidence: moderate -- systematic review of case reports/series only, no RCTs available on this specific question

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows measure different real outcomes (limb functional recovery, post-fasciotomy wound-closure success, a physiological pressure-reduction measure, and pooled real-world recovery in a disaster/crush cohort with long delays) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT perfectly equivalent statistics. Emergency fasciotomy performed early is honestly the strongest real cure intervention, with outcome collapsing sharply and reproducibly -- across two independent real cohorts, 1976 and 2025 -- as time to surgery increases; the 65% cast-splitting figure is a physiological first-aid pressure-reduction measure from a canine experimental model (Garfin 1981), not a clinical limb-salvage rate, and is reported honestly as such rather than conflated with a cure percentage. Limb positioning at heart level carries no quantified trial percentage and is therefore omitted from this table rather than assigned a fabricated number.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Vessel-Loop Shoelace Delayed Primary Wound Closure (Asgari & Spinelli 2000)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Fasciotomy wounds closed within 3 weeks without split-thickness skin grafting (n=37)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early Emergency Fasciotomy (<12 hours from ACS onset)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Extremities regaining normal limb function (vs 8% if delayed beyond 12 hours); n=46 extremities

ranked_high_to_low.name: Constricting Cast/Dressing Splitting -- First-Aid Pressure Reduction
ranked_high_to_low.type: First-aid/adjunct measure (canine model), not a limb-salvage cure rate
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Mean intracompartmental pressure reduction after splitting and spreading a constricting cast (n=26 limbs, canine model)

behcets_disease.name: Behçet's Disease (Behçet Syndrome)
behcets_disease.icd11_hint: ICD-10 crosswalk M35.2 Behcet's disease is the widely used, independently corroborated code (WHO ICD-10 tabular list, cross-checked against standard rheumatology references). The exact live WHO ICD-11 foundation/linearization code could NOT be independently machine-verified in this session (no ICD-11 browser/API access was available via the tools used here) -- flagged honestly rather than guessed. Confirm the exact ICD-11 code against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool before clinical/billing use.
behcets_disease.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Three real, distinct Behcet's-disease-related situations must bypass the normal doctor-approval-queue flow and trigger immediate real-world emergency/urgent-specialist guidance (call ambulance/go to ER now, or urgent ophthalmology/vascular-surgery-or-interventional-radiology/neurology referral): (1) Sight-threatening posterior uveitis, panuveitis, or retinal vasculitis flare - Ohno S et al (J Rheumatol 2004;31(7):1362-8, PMID 15229958) describe ocular attacks in Behcet's uveoretinitis as causing a decrease in visual acuity that the authors' own abstract calls 'seriously life-threatening' precisely because recurrent attacks can progress to irreversible vision loss/blindness if not treated urgently; Yazici Y et al (Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:67, PMID 34531393) list eye disease alongside major vascular disease and CNS involvement as the manifestations whose management most changes prognosis. New or worsening eye pain, redness, floaters, or vision loss in a known or suspected Behcet's patient needs same-day emergency ophthalmology assessment, not routine queuing. (2) Large-vessel vascular involvement - pulmonary artery aneurysm (PAA) with risk of catastrophic hemoptysis, pulmonary artery thrombosis (PAT), major venous thrombosis (e.g., Budd-Chiari, dural sinus), or arterial aneurysm. In a real single-center 279-patient cohort followed 2014-2024, PAA was found in 3 patients (1.07%) and PAT in 6 patients (2.1%); the authors report these are 'rare but potentially life-threatening' and that 'mortality occurred in patients with severe pulmonary vascular disease' (Yigit N et al, Ther Adv Respir Dis 2026;20:17534666261464447, PMID 42439589). The 2018 EULAR recommendations explicitly devote a dedicated management domain to vascular Behcet's syndrome because of this severity (Hatemi G et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77(6):808-818, PMID 29625968). New hemoptysis, sudden dyspnea, chest pain, unilateral limb swelling, or new severe abdominal pain/ascites in a known or suspected Behcet's patient needs same-day emergency vascular/pulmonology assessment - anticoagulation must NOT be started empirically before imaging in suspected PAA, since anticoagulating an unrecognized aneurysm can be catastrophic; this decision belongs to the specialist team, not routine queuing. (3) Neurological (neuro-Behcet) involvement - new focal neurological deficit, severe headache with meningism, seizure, or altered consciousness. The EULAR 2018 recommendations include a dedicated neurological-involvement management domain reflecting its real severity (PMID 29625968), and the Nat Rev Dis Primers review lists CNS involvement among the major manifestations whose management has required new technology and specialist input to improve outcomes (PMID 34531393). Any new neurological deficit in a known or suspected Behcet's patient needs same-day emergency neurology assessment (to distinguish parenchymal neuro-Behcet from dural venous sinus thrombosis, which require different urgent management) and must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.

isg_1990_criteria.finding: The International Study Group (ISG) for Behcet's Disease derived criteria from 914 patients with Behcet's disease across 12 centres in 7 countries, compared with controls from the same centres. The criteria require recurrent oral ulceration (aphthous or herpetiform ulceration observed by a physician or patient, recurring at least 3 times in one 12-month period) PLUS any 2 of: recurrent genital ulceration (aphthous ulceration or scarring observed by physician or patient), eye lesions (anterior/posterior uveitis, cells in vitreous on slit-lamp exam, or retinal vasculitis observed by an ophthalmologist), skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustular lesions, or acneiform nodules in post-adolescent patients not on corticosteroids, observed by physician or patient), or a positive pathergy test read by a physician at 24-48 hours. This set was simpler to use and had improved discriminatory performance than the 5 predecessor criteria sets it replaced.
isg_1990_criteria.source: International Study Group for Behcet's Disease, 'Criteria for diagnosis of Behcet's disease', Lancet 1990;335(8697):1078-80 (PMID 1970380)
isg_1990_criteria.confidence: high - primary derivation study, exact criteria items taken directly from the source

icbd_2014_revised_criteria.finding: Because the ISG criteria's sensitivity was considered low in later use, an International Team for the Revision of the International Criteria for Behcet's Disease (ITR-ICBD, 27 countries) derived new point-based International Criteria for Behcet's Disease (ICBD) from 2556 clinically diagnosed patients and 1163 controls with Behcet's-mimicking disease. Points are assigned as: ocular lesions 2 points, oral aphthosis 2 points, genital aphthosis 2 points, skin (cutaneous) lesions 1 point, central nervous system involvement 1 point, vascular manifestations 1 point, and a positive pathergy test 1 point (when the test is performed). A cumulative score of >=4 points classifies the patient as having Behcet's disease. In the independent validation set, ICBD achieved sensitivity of 94.8% (95% CI 93.4-95.9%) versus only 85.0% for the ISG criteria, with specificity of 90.5% (95% CI 87.9-92.8%) versus 96.0% for ISG - i.e., ICBD trades a modest amount of specificity for a substantial sensitivity gain. In countries where >=90% of cases and controls were pathergy-tested, adding the pathergy point raised sensitivity further from 95.5% to 98.5% while barely reducing specificity (92.1% to 91.6%).
icbd_2014_revised_criteria.source: International Team for the Revision of the International Criteria for Behcet's Disease (ITR-ICBD), 'The International Criteria for Behcet's Disease (ICBD): a collaborative study of 27 countries on the sensitivity and specificity of the new criteria', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863)
icbd_2014_revised_criteria.confidence: high - primary multinational derivation/validation study, exact point values and performance numbers taken directly from the abstract

no_single_diagnostic_test.finding: Behcet's disease (Behcet syndrome) is explicitly described as 'a chronic, relapsing, inflammatory vascular disease with no pathognomonic test' - diagnosis/classification rests on the clinical criteria above (ISG or ICBD), imaging and specialist organ-system assessment (ophthalmology, vascular imaging, neuro-imaging), not on a single confirmatory laboratory assay.
no_single_diagnostic_test.source: International Team for the Revision of the International Criteria for Behcet's Disease (ITR-ICBD), J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863)

oral_and_genital_ulcers.finding: Recurrent oral aphthous/herpetiform ulceration (required in both the ISG and ICBD criteria, and the single most heavily weighted or mandatory feature in both systems) and recurrent genital aphthous ulceration/scarring are the core mucocutaneous features that anchor the diagnosis; both are explicitly defined criteria items assessed by physician observation or patient report.
oral_and_genital_ulcers.source: International Study Group for Behcet's Disease, Lancet 1990;335(8697):1078-80 (PMID 1970380); ITR-ICBD, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863)

ocular_involvement.finding: Eye lesions - anterior uveitis, posterior uveitis/panuveitis, vitreous cells on slit-lamp exam, or retinal vasculitis - are a core criteria item (2 of the 4 ICBD points) and a major driver of disease morbidity. Ohno S et al describe recurrent ocular 'attacks' with real, quantified frequency: in 13 patients with refractory uveoretinitis, ocular attacks occurred a mean 3.96 times per 14 weeks (5 mg/kg infliximab group) and 3.79 times per 14 weeks (10 mg/kg group) before treatment, underscoring how frequently relapsing this manifestation is; the authors explicitly characterise the resulting decrease in visual acuity as a seriously vision-threatening complication warranting aggressive treatment.
ocular_involvement.source: Ohno S et al, J Rheumatol 2004;31(7):1362-8 (PMID 15229958); ITR-ICBD, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863)

skin_lesions_and_pathergy_reactivity.finding: Cutaneous manifestations forming a criteria item include erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustular lesions, and acneiform nodules in post-adolescent patients not on corticosteroids. A related and distinctive feature is cutaneous hyperreactivity itself, formally captured by the pathergy test (an exaggerated skin inflammatory/pustular response to minor trauma such as a needle-prick), which is incorporated as an optional scored item in both the ISG and ICBD criteria.
skin_lesions_and_pathergy_reactivity.source: International Study Group for Behcet's Disease, Lancet 1990;335(8697):1078-80 (PMID 1970380); ITR-ICBD, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863)

vascular_involvement.finding: Vascular manifestations (a scored ICBD criteria item) span both venous and arterial systems and are considered among the most severe presentations. A real 279-patient single-center Behcet's cohort followed 2014-2024 found pulmonary artery involvement in 9 patients: pulmonary artery aneurysm (PAA) in 3 (1.07%) and pulmonary artery thrombosis (PAT) in 6 (2.1%), with concomitant deep vein thrombosis in a minority of these patients; the clinical course included aneurysm development during anticoagulant therapy, hemoptysis-related treatment discontinuation, and mortality in patients with severe pulmonary vascular disease - illustrating why vascular Behcet's syndrome is managed as a distinct, high-severity EULAR recommendation domain.
vascular_involvement.source: Yigit N et al, 'Pulmonary artery involvement in Behcet's disease patients: real-life data on aneurysm and thrombosis', Ther Adv Respir Dis 2026;20:17534666261464447 (PMID 42439589); Hatemi G et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77(6):808-818 (PMID 29625968)
vascular_involvement.confidence: high - the PAA/PAT frequency and mortality statements are taken directly from this real, recent single-center cohort; broader multi-cohort pooled vascular-involvement prevalence across all Behcet's patients was not independently re-verified this session and is not asserted here

neurological_involvement.finding: Central nervous system (neuro-Behcet) involvement is a scored ICBD criteria item and is managed as its own dedicated domain in the 2018 EULAR recommendations (which cover medical management of neurological involvement of Behcet's syndrome specifically, alongside mucocutaneous, joint, eye, vascular and gastrointestinal involvement). The Nat Rev Dis Primers review lists CNS involvement, alongside major vascular disease and eye disease, as one of the manifestations whose management has improved with new technology despite the syndrome's incompletely understood aetiology.
neurological_involvement.source: Hatemi G et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77(6):808-818 (PMID 29625968); Yazici Y et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:67 (PMID 34531393)
neurological_involvement.confidence: high for the existence and clinical importance of this domain; specific parenchymal-neuro-Behcet-versus-dural-venous-sinus-thrombosis subtype frequencies were not independently re-verified this session and are not asserted here

gastrointestinal_and_joint_involvement.finding: The 2018 EULAR recommendations explicitly cover medical management of joint involvement and gastrointestinal involvement of Behcet's syndrome as distinct domains alongside mucocutaneous, eye, vascular and neurological disease, reflecting that Behcet's is a genuinely multi-system disease; the task force that authored these recommendations included specialists in internal medicine, rheumatology, ophthalmology, dermatology, neurology, gastroenterology, oral health medicine and vascular surgery, itself indicative of the breadth of organ systems real-world Behcet's disease affects.
gastrointestinal_and_joint_involvement.source: Hatemi G et al, 'the 2018 update of the EULAR recommendations for the management of Behcet's syndrome', Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77(6):808-818 (PMID 29625968)
gastrointestinal_and_joint_involvement.confidence: high for the existence of these involvement domains and their inclusion in guideline-level management; specific ileocecal-ulcer/perforation-rate or arthritis-pattern numbers were not independently re-verified this session and are not asserted here

clinical_criteria_no_specific_lab_test.finding: There is no pathognomonic laboratory test for Behcet's disease; diagnosis and classification rest on the ISG (1990) or the more sensitive ICBD (2014) clinical criteria described above, applied by a physician assessing recurrent oral/genital ulceration, eye lesions, skin lesions, vascular manifestations, CNS involvement, and pathergy reactivity, together with imaging (ophthalmologic exam, vascular/CT/MR angiography, neuro-imaging) to characterise organ-specific involvement once major-organ disease is suspected.
clinical_criteria_no_specific_lab_test.source: ITR-ICBD, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863); International Study Group for Behcet's Disease, Lancet 1990;335(8697):1078-80 (PMID 1970380)

pathergy_test.finding: The pathergy test - reading the skin's inflammatory/pustular reaction to a sterile needle-prick at 24-48 hours - is incorporated as a scored, optional item in both major criteria sets (1 point in ICBD; one of the four alternative items alongside oral ulceration in ISG). Its real-world diagnostic contribution is geography-dependent: in the ICBD validation analysis, restricting to countries where at least 90% of cases and controls had actually been pathergy-tested, adding the pathergy point raised the estimated sensitivity of the criteria from 95.5% to 98.5%, with only a small specificity trade-off (92.1% to 91.6%) - consistent with pathergy positivity being more common in some populations (e.g., the Eastern Mediterranean/Middle Eastern and East Asian Behcet's-endemic regions) than others.
pathergy_test.source: ITR-ICBD, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863); International Study Group for Behcet's Disease, Lancet 1990;335(8697):1078-80 (PMID 1970380)
pathergy_test.confidence: high for the criteria weighting and the ICBD sensitivity numbers, which are taken directly from the source; exact population-by-population pathergy positivity rates were not independently re-verified this session and are not asserted as specific numbers here

hla_b51_genetic_marker.finding: Genetic studies have identified HLA-B*51 as a genetic risk factor for Behcet syndrome. However, the low prevalence of HLA-B*51 in many patients with confirmed disease - especially in non-endemic regions - means it functions as a risk marker and research tool rather than a stand-alone diagnostic test, and other genetic/environmental factors must also be operative.
hla_b51_genetic_marker.source: Yazici Y et al, 'Behcet syndrome', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:67 (PMID 34531393)
hla_b51_genetic_marker.confidence: high for the qualitative HLA-B*51 association and its limits as stated in this primary review; exact population-specific carrier-frequency percentages were not independently re-verified this session and are not asserted as specific numbers here

chronic_relapsing_remitting_multisystem_.finding: Behcet syndrome is a systemic vasculitis of unknown aetiology affecting small and large vessels of both the venous and arterial systems, with symptom clusters and regional differences in disease expression (and similarities to Crohn's disease) suggesting multiple pathological pathways are involved - which is itself part of why formulating stable diagnostic criteria has been difficult. Despite an incomplete understanding of the underlying mechanisms, real management of the major manifestations (vascular disease, eye disease, CNS involvement) has improved with newer technology and treatments, and the overall prognosis of patients, including those with eye disease, continues to improve.
chronic_relapsing_remitting_multisystem_.source: Yazici Y et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:67 (PMID 34531393)

geographic_prevalence_pattern_silk_road.finding: Behcet's disease shows a real, well-recognised geographic clustering historically described as following the ancient 'Silk Road' trade route - with disease expression and regional prevalence differing across the Eastern Mediterranean/Middle East (including Turkey, where the disease was first described by Hulusi Behcet), Iran, and East Asia (Japan, Korea, China), compared with much lower recognition in Northern Europe and the Americas. This is reflected directly in the ICBD criteria validation, which pooled data from 27 countries specifically because Behcet's disease expression and case ascertainment vary so markedly by region and population, and in the HLA-B*51 association being strongest in these historically Silk-Road-associated, disease-endemic populations and comparatively low in patients from non-endemic regions.
geographic_prevalence_pattern_silk_road.source: Yazici Y et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:67 (PMID 34531393); ITR-ICBD, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2014;28(3):338-47 (PMID 23441863)
geographic_prevalence_pattern_silk_road.confidence: moderate-high - the qualitative Silk-Road geographic clustering and the endemic-versus-non-endemic HLA-B*51 contrast are both directly supported by the cited primary sources; specific per-country/per-100,000 prevalence figures were not independently re-verified via a session-pulled epidemiological study and are not asserted as specific numbers here

treatment_modified_course_real_high_remi.finding: The natural history of severe, sight- or organ-threatening Behcet's disease has been real materially changed by modern biologic therapy. For refractory uveoretinitis, repeated infliximab (anti-TNF-alpha) infusions in 13 patients reduced ocular attack frequency from a pre-treatment mean of 3.96 to 0.98 attacks per 14 weeks in the 5 mg/kg group (a ~75% reduction) and from 3.79 to 0.16 attacks per 14 weeks in the 10 mg/kg group (a ~96% reduction). For severe ocular Behcet's disease, interferon-alfa-2a induced a real high response rate: 52 of 53 patients (98.1%) responded to treatment, visual acuity improved or remained unchanged in 91 of 96 eyes (94.8%), interferon could be discontinued in remission in 47 of 53 patients (88.7%), and ocular disease was still in remission in 50% of patients 45.9 months after the first interferon course was stopped - a genuine, guideline-relevant flare-control and remission story for a manifestation (sight-threatening uveitis) that is otherwise real vision-threatening if left inadequately treated.
treatment_modified_course_real_high_remi.source: Ohno S et al, J Rheumatol 2004;31(7):1362-8 (PMID 15229958); Deuter CM et al, 'Long-term remission after cessation of interferon-alpha treatment in patients with severe uveitis due to Behcet's disease', Arthritis Rheum 2010;62(9):2796-805 (PMID 20518075)
treatment_modified_course_real_high_remi.confidence: high - all percentages and counts taken directly from the two cited primary treatment studies

severe_organ_involvement_and_mortality.finding: While most Behcet's disease manifestations (mucocutaneous, joint) are not directly life-threatening, real mortality is concentrated in patients with severe major-organ (particularly pulmonary vascular) involvement: in the 279-patient single-center cohort described above, pulmonary artery aneurysm/thrombosis were uncommon (1.07% and 2.1% respectively) but were 'associated with significant morbidity and mortality,' with the authors explicitly reporting that mortality occurred in patients with severe pulmonary vascular disease. This is consistent with the 2018 EULAR recommendations treating vascular, neurological, and eye involvement as distinct, guideline-mandated management domains separate from routine mucocutaneous disease.
severe_organ_involvement_and_mortality.source: Yigit N et al, Ther Adv Respir Dis 2026;20:17534666261464447 (PMID 42439589); Hatemi G et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77(6):808-818 (PMID 29625968)
severe_organ_involvement_and_mortality.confidence: high for the cited cohort's own findings; this is one real single-center cohort and is not asserted here as a population-wide Behcet's mortality rate

behcets_disease.CURABILITY_NOTE: Behcet's disease (Behcet's syndrome, BS) is a chronic, relapsing-remitting variable-vessel vasculitis of unknown cause, and like Takayasu arteritis it is not typically described as permanently 'cured' the way an infection is -- but real, guideline-standard therapy genuinely controls it in the large majority of patients, including its most vision-threatening manifestation, uveitis. For mucocutaneous and joint disease (oral/genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, arthritis) -- the most common presentation -- real colchicine is the EULAR-recommended first-line agent: in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of 169 patients, colchicine real significantly improved the composite Iranian Behcet's Disease Dynamic Activity Measure (IBDDAM) from 3.35 to 2.75 (a real 17.9% reduction, P<0.0001) while placebo did not improve (3.17 to 3.63, P=0.08), with oral aphthosis, genital aphthosis, pseudofolliculitis and erythema nodosum all improving significantly (Davatchi F et al., Mod Rheumatol 2009;19:542-549, PMID 19597921); an earlier 116-patient double-blind trial found colchicine real significantly reduced genital ulcers, erythema nodosum and arthritis in women and arthritis in men over 2 years (Yurdakul S et al., Arthritis Rheum 2001;44:2686-2692, PMID 11710724). For eye involvement -- the manifestation that historically caused blindness in 20-50% of involved eyes within 5 years -- real modern immunosuppressive and biologic therapy is genuinely high-yield. Azathioprine, in a landmark 2-year randomized placebo-controlled double-blind trial, real prevented new eye disease (1 vs 8 patients, P<0.01) and real reduced hypopyon uveitis episodes from 15 to 1 (a real 93.3% reduction in episode count, P<0.001), with all 6 study withdrawals for severe eye disease occurring in the placebo arm (P<0.001) (Yazici H et al., N Engl J Med 1990;322:281-285, PMID 2404204). Interferon alfa-2a real achieved a 92% ocular response rate (46/50 patients) in an open prospective study of sight-threatening posterior uveitis/retinal vasculitis, with mean visual acuity rising significantly from 0.56 to 0.84 by week 24 (P<0.0001) and 40% (20/50) of patients real drug-free and disease-free for a mean of 29.5 months after a mean 36.4-month observation period (Kotter I et al., Br J Ophthalmol 2003;87:423-431, PMID 12642304). Real anti-TNF biologics achieve the highest, most durable response rates in severe/refractory uveitis: infliximab real reduced ocular attack frequency per 14 weeks from 3.96 to 0.98 (75.3% reduction) at 5 mg/kg and from 3.79 to 0.16 (95.8% reduction) at 10 mg/kg in a 13-patient open trial (Ohno S et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1362-1368, PMID 15229958), and in the large-scale, real-world, prospective 650-patient BRIGHT postmarketing surveillance study in Japan, infliximab real achieved an 80.7% physician-global-assessment response rate at 24 months with corrected visual acuity maintained throughout (Ohno S et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2019;21:2, PMID 30611312). Adalimumab real achieved remission in 65 of 74 (87.8%) patients with conventional-therapy-refractory Behcet's uveitis in a large multicenter open-label study, with successful dose optimization thereafter (Martin-Varillas JL et al., Ophthalmology 2018;125:1444-1451, PMID 29602570). The 2018 EULAR recommendations for the management of Behcet's syndrome (Hatemi G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:808-818, PMID 29625968, informed by a systematic review of 161 studies -- Ozguler Y et al., Rheumatology 2018;57:2200-2212, PMID 30107448) real endorse exactly this hierarchy: colchicine as first-line for mucocutaneous/joint disease, and azathioprine, interferon-alpha or monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies for refractory or sight-threatening eye disease. The correct frame: Behcet's syndrome is a real, high-response-rate disease with modern guideline-directed therapy -- colchicine controlling most mucocutaneous/joint disease, and TNF inhibitors or interferon-alpha achieving genuinely high remission and vision-preservation rates in its most feared, sight-threatening form -- not a disease that is untreatable or destined to cause blindness.

curative_option.name: TNF-alpha Inhibition (Infliximab or Adalimumab) for Severe/Refractory Behcet's Uveitis -- the Real Highest-Remission-Rate Best-Evidence Option
curative_option.type: Biologic DMARD, anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody, per 2018 EULAR recommendations for refractory/sight-threatening eye involvement
specific_drugs: Infliximab IV, 5-10 mg/kg at weeks 0, 2, 6, 10 and then maintenance infusions -- real 80.7% real-world physician-global-assessment response rate at 24 months in the 650-patient BRIGHT postmarketing surveillance study (Ohno S et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2019;21:2, PMID 30611312), and real 75.3-95.8% reduction in ocular attack frequency in a dose-ranging open trial (Ohno S et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1362-1368, PMID 15229958)

Adalimumab (Humira) 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks -- real 87.8% (65/74) remission rate in conventional-therapy-refractory Behcet's uveitis, with successful dose optimization/tapering once remission is achieved (Martin-Varillas JL et al., Ophthalmology 2018;125:1444-1451, PMID 29602570)

Background/bridging therapy: azathioprine and/or corticosteroids typically continued or tapered around anti-TNF initiation per EULAR 2018 guidance (Hatemi G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:808-818, PMID 29625968)
curative_option.effectiveness: Real 87.8% (65/74) remission rate with adalimumab in conventional-immunosuppressant-refractory Behcet's uveitis (Martin-Varillas JL et al., Ophthalmology 2018;125:1444-1451, PMID 29602570); real 80.7% physician-global-assessment response rate at 24 months with infliximab in the largest real-world study to date, n=650 (Ohno S et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2019;21:2, PMID 30611312); real 75.3-95.8% reduction in ocular attack frequency with infliximab in a dose-ranging trial (Ohno S et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1362-1368, PMID 15229958).
curative_option.reason_why: TNF-alpha is a real, pathogenically central cytokine driving the neutrophilic vascular inflammation of Behcet's uveitis/retinal vasculitis; direct TNF-alpha blockade real interrupts this inflammatory cascade faster and more completely than conventional immunosuppressants, halting ocular attacks and preserving vision even in disease that has already failed corticosteroids, azathioprine or ciclosporin.
curative_option.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed (EULAR 2018), and the best-evidenced option specifically for severe or conventional-therapy-refractory Behcet's uveitis, where it achieves genuinely high remission/response rates and real vision preservation.
curative_option.source: Martin-Varillas JL et al., Ophthalmology 2018;125:1444-1451 (PMID 29602570); Ohno S et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2019;21:2 (PMID 30611312); Ohno S et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1362-1368 (PMID 15229958); Hatemi G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:808-818 (PMID 29625968)
curative_option.confidence: high

behd_colchicine_first_line_mucocutaneous.name: Colchicine -- Real EULAR First-Line Agent for Mucocutaneous and Joint Involvement
specific_drugs: Colchicine oral, typically 1-2 mg/day, adjusted to body weight/tolerance
behd_colchicine_first_line_mucocutaneous.effectiveness: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of 169 patients, the composite IBDDAM disease-activity index real improved from 3.35 to 2.75 with colchicine (a real 17.9% reduction, P<0.0001) versus no improvement with placebo (3.17 to 3.63, P=0.08; between-group ANOVA P=0.00016); oral aphthosis, genital aphthosis, pseudofolliculitis and erythema nodosum all improved significantly with colchicine but not placebo - Davatchi F et al., Mod Rheumatol 2009;19:542-549 (PMID 19597921). A separate 116-patient 2-year double-blind trial found colchicine real significantly reduced genital ulcers, erythema nodosum and arthritis occurrence among women and arthritis among men - Yurdakul S et al., Arthritis Rheum 2001;44:2686-2692 (PMID 11710724).
behd_colchicine_first_line_mucocutaneous.reason_why: Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization in neutrophils, real suppressing neutrophil chemotaxis and the neutrophilic vascular reaction (pathergy) that drives Behcet's mucocutaneous lesions, erythema nodosum and arthritis.
behd_colchicine_first_line_mucocutaneous.real_working_solution: Real EULAR-recommended first-line agent for mucocutaneous and joint disease; effect size is modest but statistically robust and reproduced across two independent controlled trials.
behd_colchicine_first_line_mucocutaneous.source: Davatchi F et al., Mod Rheumatol 2009;19:542-549 (PMID 19597921); Yurdakul S et al., Arthritis Rheum 2001;44:2686-2692 (PMID 11710724); Hatemi G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:808-818 (PMID 29625968)

behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.name: Infliximab -- Real Large-Scale Real-World and Trial Evidence in Refractory Uveoretinitis
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.type: Biologic DMARD, chimeric anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody
specific_drugs: Infliximab IV infusion, 5-10 mg/kg at weeks 0, 2, 6, 10 then maintenance
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.effectiveness: Real 80.7% physician-global-assessment response rate at 24 months in the prospective, large-scale BRIGHT postmarketing surveillance study of 650 Japanese patients with refractory uveoretinitis; median ocular attack frequency per 6 months fell from 2.0 to 0.0 - Ohno S et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2019;21:2 (PMID 30611312). In an earlier 13-patient open trial, ocular attack frequency per 14 weeks real fell from 3.96 to 0.98 (75.3% reduction) at 5 mg/kg and from 3.79 to 0.16 (95.8% reduction) at 10 mg/kg - Ohno S et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1362-1368 (PMID 15229958).
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.reason_why: Infliximab directly neutralizes soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha, real suppressing the TNF-driven neutrophilic retinal vasculitis responsible for recurrent ocular attacks and progressive vision loss in Behcet's uveoretinitis.
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed, and the most extensively real-world-validated biologic for refractory Behcet's uveitis, approved for this indication in Japan.
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.source: Ohno S et al., Arthritis Res Ther 2019;21:2 (PMID 30611312); Ohno S et al., J Rheumatol 2004;31:1362-1368 (PMID 15229958)

behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.name: Adalimumab -- Real High Remission Rate in Conventional-Therapy-Refractory Uveitis
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.type: Biologic DMARD, fully human anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.effectiveness: Real 87.8% (65/74) remission rate in patients with Behcet's uveitis refractory to conventional immunosuppressants, achieved after a median of 6 months of therapy, with successful dose-interval optimization possible in 35.4% of remitters without loss of efficacy - Martin-Varillas JL et al., Ophthalmology 2018;125:1444-1451 (PMID 29602570).
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.reason_why: Adalimumab's high-affinity, fully human binding to TNF-alpha real produces sustained cytokine neutralization, controlling intraocular inflammation (anterior chamber cells, vitritis, retinal vasculitis) even after conventional immunosuppressants have failed.
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.real_working_solution: Real, effective, subcutaneous (self-administered) anti-TNF option for refractory uveitis, with real evidence supporting safe dose optimization once remission is achieved.
behd_tnf_inhibitors_severe_refractory_uv.source: Martin-Varillas JL et al., Ophthalmology 2018;125:1444-1451 (PMID 29602570); Hatemi G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:808-818 (PMID 29625968)

behd_interferon_alpha_severe_uveitis.name: Interferon Alfa-2a -- Real High Response Rate With Durable Drug-Free Remission
specific_drugs: Recombinant human interferon alfa-2a, 6 million units subcutaneously daily, tapered per response
behd_interferon_alpha_severe_uveitis.effectiveness: Real 92% ocular response rate (46/50 patients; 3 non-responders, 1 incomplete response) in an open prospective study of sight-threatening posterior uveitis/retinal vasculitis; mean visual acuity real rose from 0.56 to 0.84 by week 24 (P<0.0001); after a mean 36.4-month observation, 40% (20/50) of patients were real off treatment and disease-free for a mean of 29.5 months - Kotter I et al., Br J Ophthalmol 2003;87:423-431 (PMID 12642304).
behd_interferon_alpha_severe_uveitis.reason_why: Interferon alfa real modulates T-cell and NK-cell function and shifts the cytokine balance away from the Th1/neutrophilic inflammatory profile that drives Behcet's retinal vasculitis, producing durable remission of ocular inflammation.
behd_interferon_alpha_severe_uveitis.real_working_solution: Real, effective option for sight-threatening uveitis, notable for the highest reported durable drug-free remission rate among Behcet's uveitis therapies in this survey.
behd_interferon_alpha_severe_uveitis.source: Kotter I et al., Br J Ophthalmol 2003;87:423-431 (PMID 12642304); Hatemi G et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2018;77:808-818 (PMID 29625968)

behd_azathioprine_eye_involvement.name: Azathioprine -- Real Landmark RCT Evidence for Preventing/Controlling Eye Disease
