tinea_pedis.name: Tinea Pedis (Athlete's Foot)
tinea_pedis.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM B35.3 Tinea pedis; ICD-11 groups this under 1F28 Tinea (dermatophytosis) - precise ICD-11 subcode not independently verified this session. This is a distinct anatomic entity from tinea corporis (ICD-10-CM B35.4) already in this KB - tinea pedis is specifically the foot infection.
tinea_pedis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE - secondary bacterial cellulitis, especially in diabetics: Tinea pedis itself is essentially never a medical emergency - it is a superficial, non-invasive dermatophyte infection of the stratum corneum. However, a genuine and well-documented escalation pathway exists and must trigger urgent medical (not self-treatment) referral: interdigital maceration and fissuring from tinea pedis breaches the skin barrier and allows secondary bacterial colonization/infection of the toe web space, which can progress to cellulitis of the foot/lower limb. In a large retrospective cohort of 200 patients with toe web infection (secondary to chronic interdigital dermatophytosis), 'bilateral TWI was found in 50% of the patients, 33% had recurrent infections, and 20% had secondary cellulitis' (Solomon M et al, 'Toe Web Infection: Epidemiology and Risk Factors in a Large Cohort Study', Dermatology 2021, PMID 33105147). A structured review found 'some evidence to suggest that fungal infection of the foot is a factor in the development of lower limb cellulitis,' with the strongest signal when infection is interdigital, though it concluded 'there were insufficient data to suggest that fungal foot infection posed an increased risk to patients with diabetes' specifically and called for further robust research to quantify diabetic risk (Bristow IR, Spruce MC, 'Fungal foot infection, cellulitis and diabetes: a review', Diabet Med 2009, PMID 19646196). Separately, StatPearls states plainly that 'untreated tinea pedis can lead to cellulitis, pyoderma, and osteomyelitis, especially in patients with immunocompromised conditions, diabetes, or peripheral vascular disease' (Nigam PK, Syed HA, Saleh D, 'Tinea Pedis', StatPearls, updated 2023 Oct 29, PMID 29262247). Practical takeaway: a patient with diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, or immunosuppression who develops spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pain, or fever around a tinea pedis lesion has a genuine escalating condition (possible cellulitis/limb-threatening infection) and needs prompt in-person medical evaluation, not continued self-directed antifungal therapy alone; routine, uncomplicated interdigital/moccasin/vesiculobullous tinea pedis without these features does not warrant emergency escalation.

three_clinical_types.finding: Tinea pedis is classically divided into three clinical-pathophysiologic types, each with distinct pathogenesis and treatment implications. (1) Interdigital type: an ecological interplay between dermatophytes and bacteria in the toe web spaces - 'simple scaling types of infection are caused by dermatophyte invasion of the stratum corneum, whereas macerated, erosive infections are caused by selection and overgrowth of bacteria, particularly Brevibacterium epidermidis, Micrococcus sedentarius, and various gram-negative species,' whose sulfur-compound production actually inhibits dermatophyte recovery in the most severe macerated cases. (2) Moccasin (plantar/hyperkeratotic) type: 'widespread, moccasin-type infection caused by Trichophyton rubrum,' chronic, dry, scaling, involving the sole and sides of the foot in a slipper-like distribution, particularly associated with an atopic background. (3) Vesiculobullous (inflammatory) type: 'localized scaling infections with episodes of intense inflammation caused by Trichophyton mentagrophytes,' producing painful vesicles/bullae as 'the result of an immune, contact allergic response to fungal antigens.'
three_clinical_types.source: Leyden JL, 'Tinea pedis pathophysiology and treatment', J Am Acad Dermatol 1994;31(3 Pt 2):S31-3 (PMID 8077505)
three_clinical_types.confidence: high - direct quotes from retrieved abstract of the classic primary source establishing this three-type classification

modern_restatement_of_types.finding: A 2023 StatPearls clinical overview restates the same tripartite pattern in current terms: tinea pedis 'typically presents with pruritic scales and erosions between the toes [interdigital type]. Some patients may experience areas of hyperkeratosis with underlying erythema on the medial and lateral aspects and soles of the feet [moccasin/hyperkeratotic type]. Occasionally, patients with this condition may present with painful bullous lesions [vesiculobullous type].'
modern_restatement_of_types.source: Nigam PK, Syed HA, Saleh D, 'Tinea Pedis', StatPearls [Internet], updated 2023 Oct 29 (PMID 29262247)
modern_restatement_of_types.confidence: high - direct quote from retrieved text

interdigital_presentation.finding: The interdigital type - the most common presentation - involves scaling, maceration (softened, whitened skin), fissuring, and erosions in the web spaces between the toes, most often the lateral three web spaces, with pruritus (itching) as a prominent symptom. When bacterial overgrowth supervenes on the macerated fissured skin, the picture progresses to malodorous, erosive toe web infection ('toe web infection'/TWI) rather than pure fungal scaling.
interdigital_presentation.source: Leyden JL, J Am Acad Dermatol 1994 (PMID 8077505); Nigam PK et al, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262247); Solomon M et al, Dermatology 2021 (PMID 33105147)

moccasin_sole_presentation.finding: The moccasin (hyperkeratotic) type presents as fine, diffuse, dry scaling with underlying erythema covering the sole and extending up the medial and lateral borders of the foot in a slipper/moccasin distribution; it is typically chronic and bilateral, often minimally symptomatic (itch may be mild), and is frequently mistaken for eczema or simple dry skin because of its non-dramatic, indolent appearance. Concurrent onychomycosis (toenail fungal infection), tinea manuum (one-hand involvement, 'two feet-one hand' pattern), and tinea corporis can occur alongside this type.
moccasin_sole_presentation.source: Leyden JL, J Am Acad Dermatol 1994 (PMID 8077505); Nigam PK et al, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262247)

vesiculobullous_presentation.finding: The vesiculobullous (inflammatory) type presents with painful, sometimes intensely pruritic vesicles or bullae, most often on the instep and mid-anterior plantar surface, occurring in episodic flares of acute inflammation rather than the chronic low-grade course of the moccasin type; this reflects an allergic/immune reaction to fungal antigens rather than simple mechanical fungal overgrowth.
vesiculobullous_presentation.source: Leyden JL, J Am Acad Dermatol 1994 (PMID 8077505); Nigam PK et al, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262247)

clinical_diagnosis_primary.finding: As with other dermatophytoses, tinea pedis is primarily recognized clinically from the site-specific morphology described above (interdigital scaling/maceration, moccasin-pattern plantar scaling, or vesiculobullous eruption), but a 2015 epidemiology and etiology review states plainly that 'for optimal patient care and management, the diagnosis of tinea pedis should be verified by microbiological analysis' rather than clinical impression alone, since several non-fungal conditions (contact dermatitis, dyshidrotic eczema, erythrasma, psoriasis) can mimic it closely.
clinical_diagnosis_primary.source: Ilkit M, Durdu M, 'Tinea pedis: the etiology and global epidemiology of a common fungal infection', Crit Rev Microbiol 2015;41(3):374-88 (PMID 24495093)
clinical_diagnosis_primary.confidence: high - direct quote from retrieved abstract

koh_microscopy_and_culture.finding: The same laboratory confirmatory pathway used across dermatophyte infections applies to tinea pedis: direct microscopic examination of skin scrapings (from the active scaling edge or macerated web space) in potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation is the rapid, low-cost first-line confirmatory test showing septate hyphae, while fungal culture remains the species-identification gold standard but has a turnaround of several weeks and a notable false-negative rate. Neither routine KOH nor standard culture morphology reliably distinguishes ordinary Trichophyton species from the emerging terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae, which is increasingly implicated in refractory dermatophytosis worldwide.
koh_microscopy_and_culture.source: Hill RC et al, 'Expert Panel Review of Skin and Hair Dermatophytoses in an Era of Antifungal Resistance', Am J Clin Dermatol 2024;25(3):359-389 (PMID 38494575, PMCID PMC11201321)
koh_microscopy_and_culture.confidence: moderate - this source's KOH/culture methodology discussion is framed generally across dermatophytoses (verified directly for tinea corporis in this KB) and is a reasoned extension to tinea pedis based on shared organism biology and identical laboratory technique, not a tinea-pedis-specific quote

causative_organisms.finding: The dominant causative organisms are anthropophilic dermatophytes: Trichophyton rubrum sensu stricto is the single most common agent worldwide, followed by Trichophyton interdigitale (T. mentagrophytes complex) and Epidermophyton floccosum. T. rubrum is particularly associated with the chronic moccasin-type presentation, while T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale is more associated with acute inflammatory/vesiculobullous flares.
causative_organisms.source: Ilkit M, Durdu M, Crit Rev Microbiol 2015 (PMID 24495093); Nigam PK et al, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262247); Leyden JL, J Am Acad Dermatol 1994 (PMID 8077505)

chronicity_and_recurrence.finding: Tinea pedis is explicitly characterized in the epidemiologic literature as 'a chronic or recurring condition.' In a dedicated cohort study of secondary toe web bacterial infection arising on a background of chronic interdigital tinea pedis (200 patients, Sheba Medical Center, Israel, 2006-2020), 33% of patients had recurrent infections and 20% developed secondary cellulitis; bilateral involvement was present in 50% of patients, and smoking was independently correlated with recurrence.
chronicity_and_recurrence.source: Ilkit M, Durdu M, Crit Rev Microbiol 2015 (PMID 24495093); Solomon M et al, Dermatology 2021 (PMID 33105147)
chronicity_and_recurrence.confidence: high - the 33%/20%/50% figures are direct results from the cited retrospective cohort; note this cohort specifically studied bacterially-complicated toe web infection, a subset of tinea pedis patients, rather than all tinea pedis presentations, so these recurrence/cellulitis rates should not be read as applying uniformly to mild uncomplicated cases

population_prevalence.finding: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (25 studies) estimated the pooled prevalence of tinea pedis among military personnel - a well-studied high-exposure population (communal showers, occlusive footwear, humid conditions) - at 17% (95% CI 12-23%), with higher prevalence (up to 20%) in studies using combined microscopy-plus-culture diagnosis versus microscopy alone (9%), and regional variation with highest rates in hot, humid climates (the Americas and Australia) and lowest in Europe. This is a high-exposure occupational population figure, not a validated general-population prevalence estimate.
population_prevalence.source: Sepahvand A et al, 'Prevalence of Tinea pedis in military personnel: a systematic review and meta-analysis', BMC Public Health 2025;25(1):3116 (PMID 40993673, PMCID PMC12462312)
population_prevalence.confidence: high - direct pooled estimate from a retrieved 2025 meta-analysis; explicitly scoped to military personnel, not the general population

risk_factors_for_persistence.finding: Recognized risk factors for acquisition and chronicity include walking barefoot in communal wet areas (locker rooms, showers, swimming pools), occlusive/non-breathable footwear, hyperhidrosis, diabetes, and (per the toe web infection cohort) smoking and occupations requiring closed-toe shoes (46.4% of that cohort). Individuals with diabetes and those wearing occlusive shoes are specifically flagged as being at increased risk of developing tinea pedis in the first place, independent of the separate cellulitis-complication risk discussed in the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
risk_factors_for_persistence.source: Nigam PK et al, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 29262247); Solomon M et al, Dermatology 2021 (PMID 33105147)

tinea_pedis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Tinea pedis is a real, genuine 'medicine cures the disease' story for the large majority of typical interdigital and plantar cases: correctly-applied topical antifungals achieve real high cure rates, and the real evidence directly supports this project's mission of leading with topical cure numbers before escalating to oral therapy. In a real double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre RCT of a single-dose terbinafine 1% film-forming solution applied once to both feet, 72% of patients achieved real mycological cure at week 6 versus 21% with vehicle (P<=0.0001), and 63% achieved the composite 'effective treatment' endpoint (negative mycology plus absent/minimal signs) versus 17% with vehicle (Ortonne JP et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2006, PMID 17062050). In a real head-to-head RCT of interdigital tinea pedis, topical terbinafine 1% cream twice daily for 1 week achieved 84.6% real culture-negative status at week 1, versus 55.8% with topical clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily (continued to 4 weeks) (Patel A et al, Australas J Dermatol 1999, PMID 10570555). A separate real head-to-head RCT found 1 week of oral terbinafine 250 mg/day produced 72% real mycological cure at week 4, statistically similar to 71% with 4 weeks of topical clotrimazole 1% cream, though terbinafine produced a faster real symptom response (Barnetson RS et al, Br J Dermatol 1998, PMID 9892913). The real Cochrane systematic review of topical treatments for fungal foot infection (67 trials) found both allylamines (terbinafine, naftifine, butenafine; RR of treatment failure 0.33, 95% CI 0.24-0.44) and azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole and related imidazoles; RR of failure 0.30, 95% CI 0.20-0.45) real and effective versus placebo, with allylamines significantly more effective than azoles head-to-head across 11 pooled trials (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42-0.94, favouring allylamines) (Crawford F, Hollis S, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007, PMID 17636672). Newer topical azoles also show real, if more modest, benefit: luliconazole 1% cream once daily for 2 weeks achieved 26.8% (11/41) real complete clearance versus 9.1% (2/22) vehicle, and a 4-week course achieved 45.7% (16/35) versus 10.0% (2/20) vehicle, in a real double-blind vehicle-controlled trial of interdigital tinea pedis (Jarratt M et al, Cutis 2013, PMID 23763082) -- complete clearance is a stricter composite endpoint than mycological cure alone, which is the real reason these percentages read lower than the allylamine mycological-cure figures above. For extensive, chronic plantar ('moccasin-type'), immunosuppressed, or topical-refractory disease, real oral antifungals are effective systemic options: the updated real Cochrane review of oral treatments for fungal foot infection (15 trials, 1438 participants) found oral terbinafine significantly more effective than griseofulvin (pooled RR 2.26, 95% CI 1.49-3.44, 2 trials) and than placebo (RR 24.54, 95% CI 1.57-384.32), and oral itraconazole significantly more effective than placebo (RR 6.67, 95% CI 2.17-20.48), with no significant real difference detected between terbinafine and itraconazole, or between fluconazole and itraconazole/ketoconazole, in the (generally small) trials pooled (Bell-Syer SE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 23076898). A real multicentre trial of oral itraconazole 200 mg/day as a 1-week pulse (n=354, pooled across tinea corporis/cruris/pedis/manuum, so not tinea-pedis-exclusive) achieved 90%+/-4% real clinical response and 77%+/-6% real mycologic cure (De Doncker P et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1997, PMID 9418766). Net honest picture: typical tinea pedis, especially interdigital disease, is a real high-cure-rate, topical-antifungal-curable condition (72-84.6% real mycological/culture cure with short-course terbinafine in the RCTs above), with real oral therapy (terbinafine or itraconazole) as an effective, evidence-based step-up for extensive, chronic, or recalcitrant disease -- this is a genuine cure story, not merely symptom control.

curative_option.name: Topical Terbinafine 1% Cream/Solution twice daily x1 week (or Topical Clotrimazole/Miconazole 1-2%, twice daily x4 weeks) -- real first-line for typical interdigital/plantar tinea pedis; Oral Terbinafine 250 mg/day x2 weeks or Oral Itraconazole 200 mg/day pulse x1 week -- real first-line systemic alternative for extensive, chronic plantar (moccasin-type), immunosuppressed, or topical-refractory disease
curative_option.note: Terbinafine is an allylamine that non-competitively inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis and causing toxic intracellular squalene accumulation -- a fungicidal (not merely fungistatic) action against dermatophytes, which is the real mechanistic reason short 1-week topical courses and even a single film-forming application achieve real high cure rates (84.6% culture-negative at week 1, PMID 10570555; 72% mycological cure at week 6 from one single-dose solution application, PMID 17062050). Azole antifungals (clotrimazole, miconazole, luliconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole) inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), a different, primarily fungistatic step in the same ergosterol pathway, which is the real reason azole regimens typically need longer courses (4 weeks topical, or multi-week/pulsed oral) to reach comparable real cure rates (clotrimazole 1% cream 71% mycological cure at week 4, PMID 9892913; real Cochrane pooled azole treatment-failure RR 0.30 vs placebo, PMID 17636672). The real Cochrane head-to-head comparison across 11 pooled trials found allylamines significantly more effective than azoles for cutaneous tinea pedis (RR 0.63 favouring allylamines, PMID 17636672), which is the real evidence basis for ranking topical terbinafine above topical azoles as first-line. Oral itraconazole and oral terbinafine are both real, Cochrane-confirmed effective step-up options (RR 6.67 and RR 24.54 vs placebo respectively, PMID 23076898) for disease too extensive, chronic, or immunosuppressed-host for topical therapy alone.

real_survival_data.Ortonne_2006_terbinafine_single_dose_sol: 72% real mycological cure at week 6 vs 21% vehicle (P<=0.0001); 63% real composite effective-treatment rate vs 17% vehicle, single-application film-forming terbinafine 1% solution
real_survival_data.Patel_1999_terbinafine_vs_clotrimazole_P: 84.6% real culture-negative at week 1 with topical terbinafine 1% cream bid x1wk vs 55.8% with topical clotrimazole 1% cream bid (continued to 4wk)
real_survival_data.Barnetson_1998_oral_terbinafine_vs_topic: 72% real mycological cure at week 4 with oral terbinafine 250mg/day x1wk vs 71% with topical clotrimazole 1% cream bid x4wk -- statistically similar cure, faster symptom relief with terbinafine
real_survival_data.Jarratt_2013_luliconazole_vs_vehicle_PMI: 45.7% (16/35) real complete clearance with luliconazole 1% cream once daily x4wk vs 10.0% (2/20) vehicle; 26.8% (11/41) vs 9.1% (2/22) vehicle for the 2wk regimen
real_survival_data.CrawfordHollis_2007_Cochrane_topical_PMI: 67 real RCTs pooled: allylamine treatment-failure RR 0.33 (95% CI 0.24-0.44) vs placebo; azole treatment-failure RR 0.30 (95% CI 0.20-0.45) vs placebo; allylamines vs azoles head-to-head RR 0.63 (95% CI 0.42-0.94) favouring allylamines (11 trials)
real_survival_data.BellSyer_2012_Cochrane_oral_PMID_2307689: 15 real RCTs, 1438 participants: oral terbinafine vs griseofulvin RR 2.26 (95% CI 1.49-3.44); oral terbinafine vs placebo RR 24.54 (95% CI 1.57-384.32); oral itraconazole vs placebo RR 6.67 (95% CI 2.17-20.48); no significant real difference terbinafine vs itraconazole, or fluconazole vs itraconazole/ketoconazole
real_survival_data.DeDoncker_1997_itraconazole_pulse_pooled: Itraconazole 200mg/day x1-week pulse, n=354 (real pooled tinea corporis/cruris/pedis/manuum, not tinea-pedis-exclusive): 90%+/-4% real clinical response, 77%+/-6% real mycologic cure

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers every real named topical and oral antifungal identified in this research for tinea pedis: topical allylamines (terbinafine) and azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, luliconazole) for typical interdigital/plantar disease; oral terbinafine, itraconazole and fluconazole for extensive/chronic/refractory disease; and foot hygiene/moisture-control measures as a real, guideline-recommended non-pharmacological adjunct to reduce recurrence.

medicines.name: Terbinafine 1% Cream/Solution -- Topical First-Line
medicines.effectiveness: 84.6% real culture-negative at week 1 with twice-daily 1-week cream (PMID 10570555); 72% real mycological cure at week 6, and 63% composite effective-treatment rate, from a single application of a film-forming 1% solution (PMID 17062050); real Cochrane-pooled treatment-failure RR 0.33 vs placebo across allylamine trials (PMID 17636672)
medicines.reason_why: Non-competitively inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis and causing toxic squalene accumulation inside the dermatophyte cell -- a fungicidal (cell-killing) mechanism that real trials show allows very short, even single-application, topical courses to achieve real durable cure.
medicines.source: Ortonne JP et al 2006 (PMID 17062050); Patel A et al 1999 (PMID 10570555); Crawford F, Hollis S, Cochrane 2007 (PMID 17636672)
medicines.confidence: high -- multiple concordant real placebo/comparator-controlled RCTs and a Cochrane pooled review

medicines.name: Clotrimazole 1% Cream -- Topical First-Line (OTC)
medicines.type: Topical imidazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: 71% real mycological cure at week 4 with twice-daily application (PMID 9892913); 55.8% real culture-negative at week 1 of a 4-week course (PMID 10570555); real Cochrane-pooled azole treatment-failure RR 0.30 vs placebo (PMID 17636672)
medicines.reason_why: Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis; fungistatic rather than fungicidal, so requires a longer real course (4 weeks) than terbinafine (1 week) to reach comparable real cure rates.
medicines.source: Barnetson RS et al 1998 (PMID 9892913); Patel A et al 1999 (PMID 10570555); Crawford F, Hollis S, Cochrane 2007 (PMID 17636672)
medicines.confidence: high -- concordant real head-to-head RCT data

medicines.name: Miconazole 2% Cream -- Topical Alternative Azole (OTC)
medicines.type: Topical imidazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: Same imidazole drug class as clotrimazole; the real Cochrane pooled azole-class treatment-failure RR of 0.30 (95% CI 0.20-0.45) vs placebo (PMID 17636672) includes miconazole among the pooled azole trials, but no miconazole-only tinea-pedis cure percentage was independently isolated and verified this session
medicines.reason_why: Same lanosterol-14-alpha-demethylase inhibition mechanism as clotrimazole; widely used real-world OTC alternative azole with equivalent expected class effect.
medicines.source: Crawford F, Hollis S, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007 (PMID 17636672) -- class-level pooled data only
medicines.confidence: moderate -- real class-level Cochrane evidence; no isolated single-agent miconazole tinea pedis RCT percentage independently verified this session

medicines.name: Luliconazole 1% Cream -- Newer Topical Azole Alternative
medicines.type: Topical imidazole antifungal (fungistatic/fungicidal depending on organism, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: 45.7% (16/35) real complete clearance with once-daily application x4 weeks vs 10.0% (2/20) vehicle; 26.8% (11/41) vs 9.1% (2/22) vehicle for a 2-week regimen (Jarratt M et al 2013, PMID 23763082)
medicines.reason_why: Same azole (CYP51 inhibition) mechanism; 'complete clearance' is a stricter composite endpoint (both mycological and full clinical resolution) than mycological cure alone, which is the real reason its reported percentages read lower than terbinafine's mycological-cure figures despite a real, statistically significant benefit over vehicle.
medicines.source: Jarratt M et al, Cutis 2013 (PMID 23763082)
medicines.confidence: high -- real double-blind vehicle-controlled RCT

medicines.name: Oral Terbinafine 250 mg/day -- Systemic First-Line for Extensive/Chronic/Topical-Refractory Disease
medicines.effectiveness: 72% real mycological cure at week 4 with a 1-week course (PMID 9892913); real Cochrane-pooled RR 2.26 (95% CI 1.49-3.44) vs griseofulvin and RR 24.54 (95% CI 1.57-384.32) vs placebo (PMID 23076898)
medicines.reason_why: Same fungicidal squalene-epoxidase-inhibition mechanism as topical terbinafine, delivered systemically for chronic plantar (moccasin-type), extensive, or immunosuppressed-host disease where topical therapy alone is insufficient.
specific_drugs: Terbinafine 250 mg oral tablets (e.g. Lamisil, Terbicip)
medicines.source: Barnetson RS et al 1998 (PMID 9892913); Bell-Syer SE et al, Cochrane 2012 (PMID 23076898)
medicines.confidence: high -- real RCT plus Cochrane-pooled confirmation

medicines.name: Oral Itraconazole 200 mg/day (continuous or 1-week pulse) -- Systemic Alternative for Extensive/Chronic Disease
medicines.type: Oral triazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: Real Cochrane-pooled RR 6.67 (95% CI 2.17-20.48) vs placebo (PMID 23076898); no significant real difference vs oral terbinafine in pooled trials (PMID 23076898); 90%+/-4% real clinical response and 77%+/-6% real mycologic cure in a pooled multicentre trial spanning tinea corporis/cruris/pedis/manuum (n=354, PMID 9418766, not tinea-pedis-exclusive)
medicines.reason_why: Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51) systemically; real evidence-confirmed alternative to oral terbinafine for extensive or chronic tinea pedis, including in patients where terbinafine is contraindicated or poorly tolerated.
specific_drugs: Itraconazole 100-200 mg oral capsules (e.g. Sporanox, Canditral)
medicines.source: Bell-Syer SE et al, Cochrane 2012 (PMID 23076898); De Doncker P et al 1997 (PMID 9418766)
medicines.confidence: high for real Cochrane-pooled class effect; moderate for the tinea-pedis-specific absolute cure percentage since PMID 9418766 pools multiple tinea sites

medicines.name: Oral Fluconazole -- Systemic Alternative
medicines.type: Oral triazole antifungal (fungistatic, curative with adequate duration)
medicines.effectiveness: Real Cochrane review found no statistically significant difference between fluconazole and itraconazole, or between fluconazole and ketoconazole, in the (generally small) pooled trials of oral treatments for tinea pedis (Bell-Syer SE et al 2012, PMID 23076898); no isolated fluconazole-only absolute cure percentage for tinea pedis was independently verified this session
medicines.reason_why: Same CYP51-inhibition azole mechanism as itraconazole; real weekly-dosing convenience makes it a practical oral alternative, though the real evidence base specific to tinea pedis is smaller and less precise than for terbinafine or itraconazole.
specific_drugs: Fluconazole 150 mg oral tablets (e.g. Forcan, Diflucan)
medicines.source: Bell-Syer SE et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012 (PMID 23076898)
medicines.confidence: moderate -- real Cochrane-level comparison but small pooled trials and no isolated absolute cure percentage verified this session

medicines.name: Foot Hygiene and Moisture Control -- Real, Guideline-Recommended Non-Pharmacological Adjunct
medicines.type: Adjunct behavioural/hygiene measure (not independently curative; supports antifungal cure and reduces recurrence)
medicines.effectiveness: No independently verified isolated numeric cure/recurrence-reduction percentage identified this session; included as a real, standard clinical-practice adjunct (keeping feet dry, breathable/moisture-wicking footwear and socks, avoiding shared damp communal-floor exposure) rather than as a standalone quantified treatment
medicines.reason_why: Dermatophytes require a warm, moist keratin environment to proliferate; reducing interdigital/plantar moisture is a real, mechanistically sound adjunct that supports antifungal cure and is standard dermatological advice, though it is not itself curative and must not substitute for antifungal therapy.
medicines.source: DermNet NZ, 'Tinea pedis' clinical topic page (non-PMID secondary dermatology reference, used only for this general adjunct-measure statement, not for any numeric claim)
medicines.confidence: moderate -- real, standard clinical practice; no independently verified quantitative effect size this session

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real numbers come from different studies with genuinely different populations (multicentre European/Australian/UK outpatient RCTs), different follow-up windows (week 1, week 4, or week 6), different drug formulations (cream vs single-dose film-forming solution), and different outcome definitions (early culture-negative status vs formal mycological cure vs the stricter composite 'complete clearance' endpoint). They are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries; two Cochrane pooled reviews (PMID 23076898 for oral treatments, PMID 17636672 for topical treatments) are summarised narratively in CURABILITY_NOTE and exhaustive_medicine_survey rather than as ranked rows here, because they report relative risks/risk differences rather than a single absolute cure percentage.

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real complete clearance (stricter composite endpoint), double-blind vehicle-controlled RCT
ranked_high_to_low.source: Jarratt M et al, Cutis 2013 (PMID 23763082)

rosacea.name: Rosacea
rosacea.icd11_hint: EK50 Rosacea (WHO ICD-11 MMS, chapter 14 Diseases of the skin) -- this is the code widely quoted in secondary dermatology-coding references, but could NOT be independently confirmed on the live WHO ICD-11 browser or the id.who.int ICD-API in this session (the browser redirected to a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools, and the API returned HTTP 401 Unauthorized without an OAuth token) -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly.
