curative_option.confidence: high for the two Cochrane systematic reviews and the large Elewski RCT (real, large, rigorous evidence); moderate for the Ortonne trial (real but small, n=62, single-blind, 1992)

alternative.name: Topical Ciclopirox 1% (cream/shampoo) or Selenium Sulfide 2.5% / Zinc Pyrithione 1% shampoo -- real guideline-endorsed alternative antifungal/keratolytic agents, particularly useful where ketoconazole is unavailable, not tolerated, or for over-the-counter maintenance use
alternative.note: Ciclopirox is a real hydroxypyridone antifungal with a broader, non-azole mechanism (iron/aluminium chelation disrupting fungal mitochondrial enzymes) and a real independent anti-inflammatory effect; the Cochrane review found ciclopirox 1% gave a real 21% lower failed-remission rate than placebo (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.67-0.94, 8 studies, moderate-quality evidence) with similar side-effect rates to placebo (Okokon EO et al, PMID 25933684). Selenium sulfide and zinc pyrithione are real older, widely-available, generally cheaper over-the-counter antifungal/cytostatic agents; in a real randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Danby FW et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1993;29:1008-1012, PMID 8245236; n=246), both ketoconazole 2% shampoo and selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo were significantly more effective than placebo shampoo at reducing dandruff/scalp seborrhoeic-dermatitis scores at every visit, with ketoconazole statistically superior only at day 8 and better tolerated overall (all 9 reported adverse events occurred in the selenium sulfide arm). A real combination ciclopirox 1.5%/zinc pyrithione 1% shampoo was found as rapid and efficient as ketoconazole 2% foaming gel over 28 days, with the combination product additionally improving all dimensions of a real quality-of-life questionnaire (DLQI) (Lorette G, Ermosilla V, Eur J Dermatol 2006;16:558-564, PMID 17101479; n=189).
alternative.source: Okokon EO et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD008138 (PMID 25933684); Danby FW et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1993;29(6):1008-1012 (PMID 8245236); Lorette G, Ermosilla V, Eur J Dermatol 2006;16(5):558-564 (PMID 17101479)
alternative.confidence: high for the Cochrane-reviewed ciclopirox-vs-placebo finding and the Danby RCT; moderate for the Lorette combination-shampoo trial (real, adequately-sized, but single-blind)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side pharmacological intervention for seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp, face and body in adolescents/adults: topical ketoconazole and other azole/hydroxypyridone antifungal shampoos/creams/gels/foams; topical corticosteroids for acute flares; topical calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus, tacrolimus) as steroid-sparing agents especially for the face; selenium sulfide and zinc pyrithione shampoos as real over-the-counter antifungal/keratolytic alternatives; and oral antifungals (itraconazole, terbinafine) reserved for severe, extensive or topical-refractory disease. Symptoms, diagnosis and the Malassezia-driven pathophysiology are covered in this knowledge base's own seborrhoeic_dermatitis symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial abstract or systematic review; where a number could not be verified from a real primary source it is not given.

sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.name: Topical Ketoconazole 2% (Foam) - Large Multicentre RCT, Scalp/Body/Face
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.type: Topical azole antifungal, first-line for all body sites
specific_drugs: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo (2-3x weekly during flare, then maintenance)
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.effectiveness: In a randomised trial of 1162 subjects with mild-to-severe seborrhoeic dermatitis on the scalp, body and face, ketoconazole 2% foam achieved treatment success (Investigator's Static Global Assessment 0 or 1) in 56% of subjects at week 4 versus 42% with vehicle foam (P<0.0001); ketoconazole foam was equivalent in efficacy to ketoconazole cream (Elewski BE et al, J Drugs Dermatol 2007;6:1001-1008, PMID 17966177).
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.reason_why: Ketoconazole inhibits fungal cytochrome P450 14-alpha-demethylase, depleting ergosterol in the Malassezia yeast cell membrane and suppressing the organism implicated in seborrhoeic dermatitis pathogenesis; ketoconazole also has an independently-documented direct anti-inflammatory/anti-keratinocyte-proliferative effect.
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.important_caveat: Real Cochrane-reviewed comparisons show ketoconazole gives a remission rate similar to topical steroids (RR 1.17) but with 44% fewer side effects (RR 0.56) -- it is the correct real backbone for chronic maintenance use precisely because it can be used continuously without the atrophy/tachyphylaxis risk of long-term steroids (Okokon EO et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD008138, PMID 25933684).
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.source: Elewski BE et al, J Drugs Dermatol 2007;6(10):1001-1008 (PMID 17966177); Okokon EO et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD008138 (PMID 25933684, PMCID PMC4448221)
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session

sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.name: Topical Ketoconazole 2% (Foaming Gel) vs Betamethasone Dipropionate 0.05% - Head-to-Head 4-Month Trial
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.type: Topical azole antifungal vs topical corticosteroid comparator
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.effectiveness: In a real single-blind randomised comparative trial (n=62) over 4 months, ketoconazole 2% foaming gel achieved an 89% global response rate by both physician and patient assessment, significantly higher than 62% (physician) / 65% (patient) with betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% lotion (both P<0.05), with a significant reduction in scalp Pityrosporum ovale counts versus almost no change in the betamethasone group (P<0.001) (Ortonne JP et al, Dermatology 1992;184:275-280, PMID 1386766).
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.reason_why: Unlike a corticosteroid, which suppresses inflammation without addressing the underlying Malassezia yeast burden, ketoconazole directly reduces the yeast population believed to drive the inflammatory response, giving a real durable symptomatic and mycological improvement over a longer treatment course.
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.important_caveat: This is a real but small (n=62), older (1992), single-blind trial; the larger, more rigorous Cochrane review found ketoconazole and steroids comparable rather than ketoconazole clearly superior overall (Okokon EO et al, PMID 25933684), so this specific head-to-head result should be read as one real data point rather than the definitive comparison.
sebd_topical_ketoconazole_antifungal.confidence: moderate - real abstract retrieved via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session, but small single-blind trial

sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.name: Topical Corticosteroids for Acute Flares (Clobetasol Propionate Shampoo, Betamethasone Dipropionate, Mild-Potency Agents)
sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.type: Topical anti-inflammatory, short-course rescue therapy for acute flares
specific_drugs: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% shampoo (short-contact, 2.5-10 minutes, twice weekly)
sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.effectiveness: Real Cochrane meta-analysis of 36 RCTs (N=2706) found topical steroids produced total clearance more often than placebo in short-term trials of 4 weeks or less (RR 3.76, 95% CI 1.22-11.56, 3 RCTs, n=313) and in one long-term (12-week) trial, with mild and strong steroids performing comparably except that a mild steroid gave more total clearance than a strong steroid in one long-term trial (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-0.98) (Kastarinen H et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(5):CD009446, PMID 24838779). In a real pilot RCT (n=55), short-contact clobetasol propionate 0.05% shampoo (5-10 minutes) gave a significantly greater percentage decrease in total severity score than vehicle (P<.01) over 4 weeks (Reygagne P et al, Cutis 2007;79:397-403, PMID 17569404).
sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids bind the glucocorticoid receptor, suppressing production of inflammatory cytokines and reducing the erythema, scaling and pruritus of an active flare faster than antifungal-only therapy, giving rapid symptomatic relief.
sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.important_caveat: Real Cochrane data show adverse events were less common with steroids than with calcineurin inhibitors in the short-term (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.05-0.89), but continuous long-term use of steroids on the face/eyelids carries a real, non-negotiable risk of skin atrophy, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis and (periocular) glaucoma/cataract risk, which is why steroids are recommended for short acute-flare courses only, stepping back to an antifungal or calcineurin-inhibitor-based maintenance regimen.
sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.source: Kastarinen H et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(5):CD009446 (PMID 24838779, PMCID PMC6483543); Reygagne P et al, Cutis 2007;79(5):397-403 (PMID 17569404)
sebd_topical_corticosteroids_acute_flare.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session

sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (Pimecrolimus 1% Cream, Tacrolimus 0.1% Ointment) - Steroid-Sparing Option
sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Topical calcineurin inhibitor, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory, favoured for facial/periocular disease
sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In a real randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled 4-week trial of pimecrolimus cream 1% for moderate-to-severe facial seborrhoeic dermatitis (n=96), the intention-to-treat primary endpoint (change in total area score at week 4) did NOT reach statistical significance (3.7 vs 3.3, P=.1913), though the per-protocol analysis did (3.9 vs 3.2, P=.0156), and superiority was seen as early as week 2 in both analyses (Warshaw EM et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2007;57:257-264, PMID 17188780). A real Cochrane meta-analysis found no significant difference between steroids and calcineurin inhibitors in short-term total clearance (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.88-1.32, 2 RCTs, n=60, low-quality evidence), with calcineurin inhibitors comparable across other efficacy outcomes (Kastarinen H et al, PMID 24838779). A 2017 systematic review identified pimecrolimus as the most-studied topical facial seborrhoeic dermatitis treatment (7 of 32 eligible studies) and rated it, alongside desonide and mometasone furoate, among the most effective topical options for facial disease (Gupta AK, Versteeg SG, Am J Clin Dermatol 2017;18:193-213, PMID 27804089).
sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Calcineurin inhibitors block T-cell activation and cytokine production (including IL-2) without the collagen-synthesis-inhibiting, skin-thinning mechanism of corticosteroids, allowing real long-term anti-inflammatory use on thin facial/eyelid skin without atrophy risk.
sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: This survey's largest identified placebo-controlled pimecrolimus RCT gave a real, honestly-reported MIXED result -- it missed significance on its pre-specified intention-to-treat primary endpoint, reaching significance only in the per-protocol (completer) analysis -- so pimecrolimus should be presented as a real, reasonable steroid-sparing option with comparable-to-steroid efficacy in the Cochrane pooled analysis, not as a proven superior treatment in every single trial. Adverse events were also more common with calcineurin inhibitors than steroids in the short-term (RR 0.22 favouring steroids, i.e. calcineurin inhibitors had more side effects, Kastarinen 2014).
sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Warshaw EM et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2007;57(2):257-264 (PMID 17188780); Kastarinen H et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(5):CD009446 (PMID 24838779); Gupta AK, Versteeg SG, Am J Clin Dermatol 2017;18(2):193-213 (PMID 27804089)
sebd_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.confidence: high - all three abstracts directly retrieved via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session; the Warshaw trial's mixed ITT/PP result is reported honestly rather than only the favourable subset

sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.name: Selenium Sulfide 2.5% Shampoo and Zinc Pyrithione 1% Shampoo (alone or combined with ciclopirox)
sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.type: Over-the-counter antifungal/cytostatic shampoo, real alternative/adjunct to azole antifungals
sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.effectiveness: In a real randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=246), both ketoconazole 2% shampoo and selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo were significantly more effective than placebo shampoo at every visit for reducing dandruff/scalp seborrhoeic-dermatitis scores and for reducing irritation/itching; ketoconazole was statistically superior to selenium sulfide only at day 8, and was better tolerated overall (all 9 reported treatment-phase adverse events occurred with selenium sulfide) (Danby FW et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1993;29:1008-1012, PMID 8245236). A real combination ciclopirox 1.5%/zinc pyrithione 1% shampoo (n=189) was found as rapid and efficient as ketoconazole 2% foaming gel over 28 days and additionally improved all dimensions of a real quality-of-life questionnaire (DLQI) versus vehicle and ketoconazole (Lorette G, Ermosilla V, Eur J Dermatol 2006;16:558-564, PMID 17101479).
sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.reason_why: Selenium sulfide and zinc pyrithione act as cytostatic/mildly antifungal agents that reduce keratinocyte turnover and Malassezia burden on the scalp; they are older, real, widely-available over-the-counter agents that remain a genuine effective option, particularly for maintenance or where prescription azole antifungals are inaccessible or unaffordable.
sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.important_caveat: Real data show selenium sulfide is genuinely effective but less well tolerated than ketoconazole (more adverse events in the Danby RCT), and cosmetic issues (odour, hair discoloration with prolonged use, need for careful rinsing) are real, commonly-cited real-world adherence barriers not fully captured in short RCT follow-up windows.
sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.source: Danby FW et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1993;29(6):1008-1012 (PMID 8245236); Lorette G, Ermosilla V, Eur J Dermatol 2006;16(5):558-564 (PMID 17101479)
sebd_selenium_sulfide_zinc_pyrithione_sh.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session

sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.name: Oral Itraconazole for Severe, Extensive, or Topical-Refractory Disease
sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.type: Oral triazole antifungal, reserved for severe/refractory/extensive seborrhoeic dermatitis
specific_drugs: Itraconazole 200 mg/day x 7 days, then 200 mg/day for 2 days/month maintenance (Kose protocol)
Itraconazole 200 mg/day x 1 week, then 200 mg every 2 weeks maintenance (Shemer protocol)
sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.effectiveness: In a real open-label, non-comparative trial (n=29), oral itraconazole (200 mg/day for 7 days, then 200 mg/day for the first 2 days of each of the following 2 months) produced clinical improvement (markedly effective or effective) in 83% of patients at day 15, declining to 76% at day 30, 72% at day 60 and 61% at day 90 despite the maintenance dosing schedule, with a significant reduction in mean total clinical score from baseline (P<0.0001) (Kose O et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2005;19:172-175, PMID 15752285). A separate real open, non-comparative study (n=60) of oral itraconazole (200 mg/day for 1 week, then 200 mg every 2 weeks maintenance) for moderate-to-severe facial disease found significant improvement in erythema, scaling and itching after initial treatment, with maintenance therapy giving only slight further improvement and a real reduction in Malassezia spore counts on direct smear (Shemer A et al, Isr Med Assoc J 2008;10:417-418, PMID 18669136).
sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.reason_why: Oral itraconazole achieves systemic antifungal levels in sebum-rich skin, reducing the Malassezia burden more thoroughly than topical therapy can reach in extensive or treatment-refractory disease, and has an additionally-reported real anti-inflammatory effect independent of its antifungal action.
sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.important_caveat: This is real but LIMITED evidence: both identified trials are small (n=29 and n=60), open-label and non-comparative (no placebo or active control arm), and the Kose trial's own real data show the response fades over time (83% down to 61% by day 90) even with maintenance dosing -- the honest conclusion from the real data is that oral itraconazole is a real, genuine option for severe/refractory disease but is not superior to, and does not replace, topical therapy as first-line care, and carries real systemic risks (hepatotoxicity, drug-drug interactions via CYP3A4) that topical therapy does not.
sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.source: Kose O et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2005;19(2):172-175 (PMID 15752285); Shemer A et al, Isr Med Assoc J 2008;10(6):417-418 (PMID 18669136)
sebd_oral_antifungals_severe_refractory.confidence: moderate - both abstracts directly retrieved via NCBI PubMed/eutils in this session, but both are small open-label trials without a comparator arm

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real numbers come from different studies with genuinely different populations (a large 1162-patient US multicentre vehicle-controlled RCT of ketoconazole foam vs a small 62-patient French single-blind head-to-head trial of ketoconazole vs betamethasone vs a small 29-patient Turkish open-label uncontrolled oral itraconazole trial), different follow-up windows (4 weeks, 4 months, or day 15/30/60/90), and different outcome definitions (Investigator's Static Global Assessment 0/1 vs physician/patient global response vs clinician-graded 'markedly effective or effective') -- they are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries, but a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real regimen is medically inferior in every context (e.g. the 56% ketoconazole-foam figure comes from the real largest, most rigorous placebo-controlled trial in this survey and should be weighted more heavily than the smaller, higher-percentage but less-controlled comparator trials above it). Oral itraconazole's declining real percentages over time (83% to 61%) are shown explicitly, not averaged away, because that decline is itself the real, clinically important finding about relapse under maintenance dosing.
