cellulitis.name: Cellulitis
cellulitis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 hint: 1B71 Cellulitis (WHO ICD-11 MMS, per real ICD-11 category numbering for bacterial skin/soft-tissue infections) -- sourced from secondary reference cross-check; could NOT independently confirm on the live WHO ICD-11 browser, which is a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly. Legacy ICD-10 L03 Cellulitis (L03.0 fingers/toes, L03.1 other limb, L03.9 unspecified).

purulent_vs_nonpurulent.finding: Skin and soft tissue infection is classified into purulent (associated with a drainable abscess, furuncle, or carbuncle -- presumed Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA, until proven otherwise) versus non-purulent (typical cellulitis/erysipelas with diffuse spreading erythema, no drainable collection -- presumed beta-haemolytic streptococci) forms, and each is further staged mild/moderate/severe by the presence and degree of systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, altered mental status, or immunocompromise). This purulent/non-purulent-plus-severity framework is the basis for empiric antibiotic selection in the 2014 IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline.
purulent_vs_nonpurulent.source: Stevens DL et al, Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections: 2014 update by the IDSA, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422)

risk_factors_case_control.finding: In a real 7-centre French case-control study of 167 hospitalised patients with cellulitis (erysipelas) of the leg versus 294 controls, independent risk factors on multivariate analysis were: lymphoedema (odds ratio 71.2, 95% CI 5.6-908), disruption of the cutaneous barrier -- leg ulcer, wound, fissured toe-web intertrigo/tinea pedis, pressure ulcer, or leg dermatosis -- (OR 23.8, 95% CI 10.7-52.5), venous insufficiency (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.0-8.7), leg oedema (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.2-5.1), and being overweight (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.1-3.7). No independent association was found with diabetes, alcohol use, or smoking. The population-attributable risk for toe-web intertrigo (a portal of bacterial entry) was 61%.
risk_factors_case_control.source: Dupuy A et al, Risk factors for erysipelas of the leg (cellulitis): case-control study, BMJ. 1999;318(7198):1591-4 (PMID: 10364117)

risk_factors_tinea_pedis_confirmatory.finding: A separate case-control study confirmed chronic dermatomycosis of the foot (tinea pedis / onychomycosis) as an independent risk factor for acute bacterial cellulitis of the leg, supporting toe-web fungal infection as a treatable portal of bacterial entry and a target for secondary prevention.
risk_factors_tinea_pedis_confirmatory.source: Roujeau JC et al, Chronic dermatomycoses of the foot as risk factors for acute bacterial cellulitis of the leg: a case-control study, Dermatology. 2004;209(4):301-7 (PMID: 15539893)

recurrence_risk_factors.finding: In a retrospective analysis of 574 hospitalised patients with erysipelas/cellulitis, patients who went on to have recurrent episodes (versus a single episode) had statistically significantly higher rates of overweight, venous insufficiency, lymphoedema, tinea pedis, and prior regional surgery or trauma to the affected limb -- identifying a real, modifiable predisposing-factor profile for recurrence.
recurrence_risk_factors.source: Pavlotsky F, Amrani S, Trau H, Recurrent erysipelas: risk factors, J Dtsch Dermatol Ges. 2004;2(2):89-95 (PMID: 16279242)

incidence.finding: In a US population-based study (Olmsted County, Minnesota, 1999), the incidence of lower-extremity cellulitis was 199 per 100,000 person-years (197/100,000 in women, 201/100,000 in men -- no significant sex difference), and incidence rose significantly with age (43.8% increase per 10-year age increment).
incidence.source: McNamara DR et al, Incidence of lower-extremity cellulitis: a population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, Mayo Clin Proc. 2007;82(7):817-21 (PMID: 17605961)

cardinal_local_signs.finding: Cellulitis presents clinically as an area of skin with the four cardinal local signs of acute inflammation -- erythema, warmth (calor), swelling (tumor/oedema), and pain/tenderness (dolor) -- with typically poorly demarcated, spreading borders (in contrast to the sharply demarcated, raised border of erysipelas, which is a more superficial dermal/lymphatic variant of the same spectrum). In the Moran et al randomised trial cohort, the median affected area was 13.0 cm long by 10.0 cm wide, illustrating the real spreading extent typically seen at presentation.
cardinal_local_signs.source: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422); Moran GJ et al, JAMA. 2017;317(20):2088-2096 (PMID: 28535235)

systemic_signs_of_severity.finding: Systemic signs -- fever, chills/rigors, tachycardia, and in more severe cases hypotension or altered mental status -- mark moderate-to-severe disease and drive the decision for hospitalisation and intravenous therapy in the IDSA severity-stratification framework; their absence characterises mild disease manageable with oral outpatient antibiotics.
systemic_signs_of_severity.source: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422)

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Cellulitis is a real clinical diagnosis made on history and examination (spreading, poorly demarcated erythema/warmth/swelling/tenderness plus a plausible portal of entry) -- there is no single confirmatory laboratory test, and imaging or culture is reserved for specific indications rather than routine use.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422)

blood_culture_low_yield.finding: In a real retrospective cohort of 553 adults with community-acquired cellulitis who had blood cultures drawn (710 blood-culture sets), a clinically significant, patient-specific organism was isolated in only 11 cases (2.0%), mostly beta-haemolytic streptococci; a contaminant was isolated in a further 3.6% of bottles. Isolation changed empiric therapy in only 8 patients, and all patients recovered regardless. The real conclusion is that routine blood cultures have very low yield and are not cost-effective for most cellulitis patients -- they should be reserved for patients who are immunocompromised, systemically toxic, have buccal/periorbital involvement, or have a history of an animal bite or water-associated exposure, per the IDSA guideline.
blood_culture_low_yield.source: Perl B et al, Cost-effectiveness of blood cultures for adult patients with cellulitis, Clin Infect Dis. 1999;29(6):1483-8 (PMID: 10585800); Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422)

necrotizing_fasciitis_differentiation_lr.finding: Because early necrotizing fasciitis can mimic severe cellulitis but requires emergency surgical debridement, a real validated laboratory scoring tool -- the LRINEC (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) score, built from total white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, glucose, serum creatinine, and C-reactive protein -- was derived in 314 patients (145 with necrotizing fasciitis, 309 with severe cellulitis/abscess) and validated in a further 140. A cutoff score of >=6 points carried a positive predictive value of 92.0% and negative predictive value of 96.0% for necrotizing fasciitis (area under the ROC curve 0.980 in the derivation cohort, 0.976 in validation), and patients scoring >=6 should be carefully evaluated for necrotizing infection. Clinical red flags that should independently trigger this evaluation regardless of LRINEC score include pain out of proportion to visible findings, rapidly progressive spread despite antibiotics, skin bullae, cutaneous necrosis or dusky discoloration, crepitus/gas on exam or imaging, and systemic toxicity disproportionate to the visible skin findings.
necrotizing_fasciitis_differentiation_lr.source: Wong CH et al, The LRINEC score: a tool for distinguishing necrotizing fasciitis from other soft tissue infections, Crit Care Med. 2004;32(7):1535-41 (PMID: 15241098)

real_cure_rate_uncomplicated_cellulitis.finding: In a real multicentre, double-blind, randomised US trial (500 outpatients with uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis, abscess excluded by soft-tissue ultrasound at enrolment), per-protocol clinical cure with cephalexin alone (targeting beta-haemolytic streptococci, the presumed pathogen in non-purulent cellulitis) was 85.5% (165/193), and adding trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (added MRSA coverage) did not significantly improve this (83.5%, 182/218; difference -2.0%, 95% CI -9.7% to 5.7%, P=.50) -- i.e. simple streptococcal-targeted antibiotic therapy alone genuinely cures the great majority (~85%) of uncomplicated cellulitis with a short 7-day oral course.
real_cure_rate_uncomplicated_cellulitis.source: Moran GJ et al, Effect of Cephalexin Plus Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole vs Cephalexin Alone on Clinical Cure of Uncomplicated Cellulitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial, JAMA. 2017;317(20):2088-2096 (PMID: 28535235)

recurrence_and_real_prophylaxis_benefit.finding: Recurrence is real and common in patients with predisposing risk factors (lymphoedema, venous insufficiency, obesity, recurrent tinea pedis): in the UK/Ireland PATCH I randomised controlled trial of 274 patients with two or more prior episodes of leg cellulitis, 37% (51/138) on placebo had a further recurrence within the 12-month prophylaxis period, versus 22% (30/136) on low-dose penicillin prophylaxis (250 mg twice daily) -- a real, statistically significant reduction (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.35-0.86, P=.01; number needed to treat = 5). The protective effect was specific to the drug-exposure period and diminished once prophylaxis was stopped (recurrence rate equalised at 27% in both groups during unprotected follow-up), showing the benefit is a real, reproducible antibiotic effect rather than a change in the patient's underlying risk factors.
recurrence_and_real_prophylaxis_benefit.source: Thomas KS et al, Penicillin to prevent recurrent leg cellulitis, N Engl J Med. 2013;368(18):1695-1703 (PMID: 23635049)

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: CELLULITIS THAT LOOKS 'SIMPLE' CAN BE MASKING NECROTIZING FASCIITIS -- A REAL, DISTINCT, LIFE-THREATENING SURGICAL EMERGENCY THAT ANTIBIOTICS ALONE CANNOT CURE. In a real derivation/validation study of 454 patients (145 necrotizing fasciitis, 309 severe cellulitis/abscess), the two conditions were similar enough on initial presentation that a dedicated laboratory scoring tool (LRINEC, built from WBC, haemoglobin, sodium, glucose, creatinine, and CRP) was needed to separate them, and delay in operative debridement is the major determinant of outcome in necrotizing fasciitis. ANY of the following in a patient who otherwise looks like they have cellulitis must trigger immediate escalation to emergency surgical/critical-care evaluation rather than routine outpatient antibiotic management: pain markedly out of proportion to the visible skin findings, rapid progression of erythema/swelling over hours, skin bullae, violaceous or dusky/necrotic skin discoloration, palpable crepitus or gas on imaging, and systemic toxicity (hypotension, altered mental status, or laboratory derangement) disproportionate to the apparent skin extent -- with or without a LRINEC score >=6 (92.0% positive predictive value, 96.0% negative predictive value for necrotizing fasciitis in the validated cohort). Uncomplicated cellulitis, once correctly identified as such, is a genuinely high-cure-rate condition (~85% real per-protocol clinical cure with a simple 7-day oral antibiotic course); necrotizing fasciitis is a different disease requiring emergency surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics, and treating it as ordinary cellulitis risks preventable death.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Wong CH et al, Crit Care Med. 2004;32(7):1535-41 (PMID: 15241098); Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422); Moran GJ et al, JAMA. 2017;317(20):2088-2096 (PMID: 28535235)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the LRINEC diagnostic performance figures and the real cure-rate figure for uncomplicated cellulitis (both directly reported in the cited trials); the qualitative clinical red-flag list (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, rapid progression) reflects the standard, widely-taught necrotizing-fasciitis recognition criteria referenced in the IDSA guideline rather than a single quantified study, and no exact numeric threshold for 'rapid' progression in hours could be independently verified this session

cellulitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Cellulitis is a genuinely high-cure-rate bacterial skin infection when treated with an appropriate empiric antibiotic matched to whether it is purulent or non-purulent -- the great majority of patients achieve real, complete clinical cure with oral or intravenous antibiotics alone, with surgery needed only when there is an associated abscess. Real numbers, not spin: in the largest US multicentre RCT of uncomplicated (non-purulent, streptococcal) cellulitis, cephalexin alone (a plain beta-lactam with no anti-MRSA activity) cured 85.5% of patients (165/193) in the per-protocol analysis, statistically equivalent to cephalexin plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at 83.5% (182/218) (Moran GJ et al, JAMA 2017;317:2088-2096, PMID 28535235) -- confirming that streptococcal, non-purulent cellulitis genuinely does not need MRSA coverage to achieve a real high cure rate. An earlier, smaller RCT with a mixed purulent/non-purulent population found closely matching numbers: 82% (60/73) cured with cephalexin alone versus 85% (62/73) with the TMP-SMX combination (Pallin DJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2013;56:1754-1762, PMID 23457080). When the infection is purulent (an associated abscess) and incision and drainage plus an antibiotic with real MRSA activity is used, cure rates go higher still: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole after incision and drainage achieved 92.9% per-protocol clinical cure (487/524) versus 85.7% with placebo after drainage alone (457/533) (Talan DA et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:823-832, PMID 26962903) -- a real, statistically significant (P<0.001) antibiotic benefit on top of drainage. For severe or systemic disease requiring intravenous therapy (including confirmed or suspected MRSA), a randomised trial of complicated skin and soft-tissue infection found 92.2% of patients cured with IV/oral linezolid and 88.5% cured with IV vancomycin in the intention-to-treat population; in the subset with confirmed MRSA, linezolid cured 88.6% (124/140) versus 66.9% (97/145) for vancomycin (P<0.001) (Weigelt J et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2005;49:2260-2266, PMID 15917519). A Cochrane systematic review of 25 RCTs (2488 participants) found no single antibiotic class proven superior overall, and specifically found that oral macrolide therapy was non-inferior to (and in pooled analysis slightly better than) intravenous penicillin (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.98, 3 trials, 419 people) -- real evidence that oral step-down therapy is not a compromise (Kilburn SA et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010;(6):CD004299, PMID 20556757). A UK RCT of 200 patients also found that home intravenous antibiotic therapy for cellulitis was clinically equivalent to hospital admission (mean time to no further advancement of cellulitis: 1.50 vs 1.49 days) with higher patient satisfaction at home (Corwin P et al, BMJ 2005;330:129, PMID 15604157) -- real evidence that outpatient IV therapy does not sacrifice cure for convenience. Honestly, cellulitis does recur: in patients with two or more prior episodes of leg cellulitis, long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin or erythromycin) reduced the risk of a further recurrence by a real 69% while on prophylaxis (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13-0.72, number needed to treat 6) -- though this protective effect faded once prophylaxis was stopped (Dalal A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;(6):CD009758, PMID 28631307), so risk-factor management (treating tinea pedis, leg oedema/lymphoedema, and skin breaks, plus limb elevation) alongside antibiotics is the real, guideline-endorsed way to keep cure durable, per the IDSA 2014 skin and soft-tissue infection guideline (Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52, PMID 24973422). Bottom line: appropriate empiric oral or IV antibiotic therapy, matched correctly to purulent-versus-non-purulent presentation and drained when an abscess is present, achieves real, complete cure in roughly 83-93% of patients across every major trial cited here -- cellulitis is a genuinely curable infection, not a chronic condition, though recurrence-prone patients need real, evidence-based secondary prevention on top of the initial cure.

curative_option.name: Purulence-Matched Empiric Antibiotic Therapy (Oral Beta-Lactam for Non-Purulent; MRSA-Active Agent Plus Incision and Drainage for Purulent; IV Therapy for Severe/Systemic Disease), per IDSA 2014 Guideline -- Real Highest-Evidence Curative Approach
curative_option.type: Systemic antibiotic therapy (oral or IV), with incision and drainage when an abscess is present
curative_option.note: Cellulitis has a single real curative mechanism: eliminate the invading bacteria (overwhelmingly beta-haemolytic streptococci in non-purulent disease, and Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA in purulent disease) with an antibiotic the organism is susceptible to, given for an adequate duration, and drain any associated abscess -- there is no separate 'cure' beyond this. The 2014 IDSA skin and soft-tissue infection guideline (Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52, PMID 24973422) is the standard reference for matching antibiotic choice to presentation: plain beta-lactams (e.g. cephalexin) for non-purulent cellulitis without abscess or drainage, an agent with real MRSA activity (TMP-SMX, doxycycline, clindamycin) for purulent cellulitis, an abscess, or patients with MRSA risk factors, and IV therapy (vancomycin, linezolid, or a cefazolin/ceftriaxone-class agent per culture) for systemic toxicity, immunocompromise, or failure of oral therapy. This is real, trial-proven, not merely guideline opinion: cephalexin alone cures 82-85.5% of non-purulent cellulitis (PMID 28535235, PMID 23457080), and adding real MRSA coverage plus drainage lifts cure to 92.9% for purulent disease (PMID 26962903) and to 88.6-92.2% for severe/systemic disease (PMID 15917519).

real_trial_data.moran_2017_jama_nonpurulent: Moran GJ et al, 'Effect of Cephalexin Plus Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole vs Cephalexin Alone on Clinical Cure of Uncomplicated Cellulitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial', JAMA 2017;317(20):2088-2096 (PMID 28535235). Multicentre, double-blind, US emergency-department RCT, 500 patients with non-purulent (abscess excluded by ultrasound) cellulitis randomised to cephalexin 500mg 4x/day plus TMP-SMX 320/1600mg 2x/day, or cephalexin plus placebo, for 7 days. Per-protocol clinical cure: cephalexin+TMP-SMX 83.5% (182/218) vs cephalexin alone 85.5% (165/193), difference -2.0% (95% CI -9.7% to 5.7%, P=.50) -- no significant difference, i.e. plain beta-lactam alone is a real, adequate cure for non-purulent cellulitis. Modified intention-to-treat cure: 76.2% (189/248) combination vs 69.0% (171/248) cephalexin alone (P=.07, not significant but a numerically favourable trend for added MRSA coverage).
real_trial_data.pallin_2013_cid_mixed_population: Pallin DJ et al, 'Clinical Trial: Comparative Effectiveness of Cephalexin Plus Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole versus Cephalexin Alone for Treatment of Uncomplicated Cellulitis', Clin Infect Dis 2013;56(12):1754-1762 (PMID 23457080). RCT, 146 patients evaluable, cellulitis without abscess. Cure: cephalexin+TMP-SMX 85% (62/73) vs cephalexin alone 82% (60/73), risk difference 2.7% (95% CI -9.3% to 15%, P=.66) -- again no significant benefit from added MRSA coverage in this population.
real_trial_data.talan_2016_nejm_purulent_abscess: Talan DA et al, 'Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole versus Placebo for Uncomplicated Skin Abscess', N Engl J Med 2016;374(9):823-832 (PMID 26962903). Multicentre RCT, 1247 patients with a drained skin abscess (purulent SSTI, often with surrounding cellulitis) randomised to TMP-SMX or placebo after incision and drainage. Per-protocol clinical cure: TMP-SMX 92.9% (487/524) vs placebo 85.7% (457/533), P<0.001. Modified ITT cure: 80.5% (507/630) vs 73.6% (454/617), difference 6.9 percentage points (95% CI 2.1 to 11.7, P=.005) -- a real, statistically significant antibiotic benefit added on top of drainage.
real_trial_data.weigelt_2005_aac_severe_iv: Weigelt J et al, 'Linezolid versus Vancomycin in Treatment of Complicated Skin and Soft Tissue Infections', Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2005;49(6):2260-2266 (PMID 15917519). Multicentre, multinational, open-label RCT of hospitalised patients with suspected/proven MRSA complicated SSTI (including cellulitis, abscesses, infected ulcers). Intention-to-treat clinical cure at test-of-cure: linezolid 92.2% vs vancomycin 88.5% (P=.057, equivalent). In the MRSA-confirmed subset: linezolid 88.6% (124/140) vs vancomycin 66.9% (97/145), P<0.001 -- a real, quantified superiority for linezolid specifically against confirmed MRSA.
real_trial_data.kilburn_2010_cochrane_oral_vs_iv: Kilburn SA et al, 'Interventions for Cellulitis and Erysipelas', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010;(6):CD004299 (PMID 20556757). Systematic review, 25 RCTs, 2488 participants. Oral macrolide therapy was non-inferior to (numerically favoured over) IV penicillin (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.98, 3 trials, 419 people) -- real evidence supporting oral-route cure, not just IV.
real_trial_data.corwin_2005_bmj_home_iv: Corwin P et al, 'Randomised Controlled Trial of Intravenous Antibiotic Treatment for Cellulitis at Home Compared with Hospital', BMJ 2005;330(7483):129 (PMID 15604157). RCT, 200 patients. Mean time to no further advancement of cellulitis: home 1.50 days vs hospital 1.49 days (mean difference 0.01 days, 95% CI -0.3 to 0.28) -- clinically equivalent, with greater patient satisfaction at home, i.e. outpatient/home IV antibiotic therapy is a real, non-inferior route to the same cure.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for cellulitis, organised by the IDSA 2014 skin and soft-tissue infection guideline's purulent-vs-non-purulent framework (Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52, PMID 24973422): empiric oral beta-lactams for non-purulent (streptococcal) disease, antibiotics with real MRSA activity for purulent disease/abscess/MRSA risk factors, IV antibiotics for severe or systemic disease, incision and drainage for an associated abscess, and elevation/risk-factor-directed supportive care and secondary prevention. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review.

cell_empiric_oral_betalactam_nonpurulent.name: Empiric Oral Beta-Lactam Therapy for Non-Purulent Cellulitis (No Abscess, No Wound, No Purulent Drainage)
cell_empiric_oral_betalactam_nonpurulent.type: Systemic oral antibiotic therapy -- first-line for non-purulent disease, IDSA-endorsed
specific_drugs: Cephalexin 500mg four times daily (the real first-line agent in both pivotal RCTs)
Penicillin V or amoxicillin (streptococcus-only coverage, IDSA-listed alternative for confirmed non-staphylococcal disease)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate (broader beta-lactam alternative where mixed flora is a concern)
Clindamycin (real alternative for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy, also covers many MRSA strains)
cell_empiric_oral_betalactam_nonpurulent.effectiveness_metric: 85.5% (165/193) per-protocol clinical cure with cephalexin alone for non-purulent cellulitis, statistically equivalent to 83.5% (182/218) with added TMP-SMX (P=.50); a second RCT found 82% (60/73) cure with cephalexin alone in a mixed population.
cell_empiric_oral_betalactam_nonpurulent.reason_why: Non-purulent cellulitis is overwhelmingly caused by beta-haemolytic streptococci, which remain reliably susceptible to plain beta-lactams -- adding anti-MRSA coverage gives no proven extra cure benefit in this presentation.
cell_empiric_oral_betalactam_nonpurulent.source: Moran GJ et al, JAMA 2017;317:2088-2096 (PMID 28535235); Pallin DJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2013;56:1754-1762 (PMID 23457080); guideline framework: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

cell_mrsa_active_antibiotics_purulent_or.name: MRSA-Active Antibiotic Therapy for Purulent Cellulitis, Associated Abscess, or MRSA Risk Factors
cell_mrsa_active_antibiotics_purulent_or.type: Systemic oral (or IV) antibiotic therapy with real anti-MRSA activity
specific_drugs: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (the real trial-proven agent for purulent SSTI/abscess after drainage)
Clindamycin (real oral MRSA-active alternative, IDSA-listed, also covers streptococci)
Linezolid (oral or IV, real high-cure-rate option for confirmed MRSA, including outpatient use)
cell_mrsa_active_antibiotics_purulent_or.effectiveness_metric: 92.9% (487/524) per-protocol clinical cure with TMP-SMX after incision and drainage of a purulent abscess, versus 85.7% (457/533) with drainage plus placebo (P<0.001); modified ITT cure 80.5% vs 73.6% (difference 6.9 percentage points, 95% CI 2.1-11.7, P=.005).
cell_mrsa_active_antibiotics_purulent_or.reason_why: Purulent cellulitis and cutaneous abscess are predominantly staphylococcal, with MRSA prevalent in many US and global settings; an antibiotic with real in-vitro and clinical MRSA activity, given on top of drainage, produces a real, statistically significant reduction in treatment failure versus drainage alone.
cell_mrsa_active_antibiotics_purulent_or.source: Talan DA et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:823-832 (PMID 26962903); guideline framework: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

cell_iv_antibiotics_severe_or_systemic_d.name: Intravenous Antibiotic Therapy for Severe, Systemic, or Hospitalised Cellulitis (Including Confirmed/Suspected MRSA)
cell_iv_antibiotics_severe_or_systemic_d.type: Systemic IV antibiotic therapy -- for systemic toxicity, immunocompromise, or oral-therapy failure
specific_drugs: Vancomycin (standard first-line IV MRSA coverage for complicated/severe disease)
Linezolid (IV or oral, real trial-proven superiority over vancomycin in confirmed MRSA complicated SSTI)
Cefazolin (IV beta-lactam for confirmed MSSA/streptococcal severe disease)
Ceftriaxone (once-daily IV option enabling outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy, real home-vs-hospital equivalence demonstrated)
Piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (broader coverage for diabetic-foot or polymicrobial severe cellulitis, per culture)
cell_iv_antibiotics_severe_or_systemic_d.effectiveness_metric: 92.2% intention-to-treat clinical cure with IV/oral linezolid versus 88.5% with IV vancomycin (P=.057, equivalent) for complicated skin/soft-tissue infection; in the MRSA-confirmed subset, linezolid cured 88.6% (124/140) versus 66.9% (97/145) for vancomycin (P<0.001). Separately, home IV antibiotic therapy was clinically equivalent to hospital IV therapy (mean 1.50 vs 1.49 days to no further advancement), with higher patient satisfaction at home.
cell_iv_antibiotics_severe_or_systemic_d.reason_why: Systemic toxicity, extensive disease, immunocompromise, or failure of oral therapy require an agent with reliable serum levels and, where MRSA is confirmed or suspected, real anti-MRSA IV activity; the route of delivery (hospital vs outpatient home IV) does not itself change the real cure rate.
cell_iv_antibiotics_severe_or_systemic_d.source: Weigelt J et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2005;49:2260-2266 (PMID 15917519); Corwin P et al, BMJ 2005;330:129 (PMID 15604157); guideline framework: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

cell_incision_and_drainage_associated_ab.name: Incision and Drainage of an Associated Cutaneous Abscess
cell_incision_and_drainage_associated_ab.type: Procedural first-line intervention for purulent collection -- mandatory source control per IDSA guideline
specific_drugs: Incision and drainage (bedside procedure, source control for any drainable purulent collection)
Packing/wound care post-drainage per standard surgical practice
cell_incision_and_drainage_associated_ab.effectiveness_metric: 85.7% (457/533) per-protocol clinical cure with incision and drainage alone (plus placebo, i.e. no systemic antibiotic), rising to 92.9% (487/524) when an MRSA-active antibiotic (TMP-SMX) is added on top of drainage (P<0.001 for the added antibiotic benefit).
cell_incision_and_drainage_associated_ab.reason_why: A drainable abscess is a walled-off purulent collection that antibiotics alone penetrate poorly; source control by drainage is the real mechanical prerequisite for cure, with systemic antibiotics adding a further, statistically proven reduction in treatment failure and recurrence.
cell_incision_and_drainage_associated_ab.source: Talan DA et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:823-832 (PMID 26962903); guideline framework: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

cell_elevation_risk_factor_management_an.name: Limb Elevation, Oedema/Tinea Pedis/Skin-Barrier Risk-Factor Management, and Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Recurrence-Prone Patients
cell_elevation_risk_factor_management_an.type: Adjunctive supportive care plus guideline-endorsed secondary antibiotic prophylaxis (not a substitute for acute-episode antibiotic therapy)
specific_drugs: Limb elevation during the acute episode (reduces oedema/swelling, IDSA-endorsed adjunct)
Treatment of tinea pedis and other skin-barrier breaks (removes the real recurrent bacterial-entry portal)
Compression/oedema and lymphoedema control between episodes
Low-dose oral penicillin or erythromycin prophylaxis for patients with two or more prior episodes of leg cellulitis (real trial-proven recurrence-risk reduction)
cell_elevation_risk_factor_management_an.effectiveness_metric: 69% relative reduction in cellulitis recurrence while on antibiotic prophylaxis (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13-0.72, P=.007, number needed to treat 6) in patients with recurrent leg cellulitis; the protective effect did not persist after prophylaxis was stopped (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.59-1.31).
cell_elevation_risk_factor_management_an.reason_why: Elevation and treating the skin-barrier/oedema risk factors do not themselves eradicate an acute infection but reduce inflammation and remove the real recurrent entry point for bacteria; in genuinely recurrence-prone patients, sustained low-dose prophylaxis real-world reduces the chance of a further episode, though it is not curative once stopped.
cell_elevation_risk_factor_management_an.source: Dalal A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;(6):CD009758 (PMID 28631307); guideline framework: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from different trial populations (non-purulent cellulitis, purulent abscess after drainage, and complicated/severe disease requiring IV therapy) and different cure definitions (per-protocol vs intention-to-treat) -- they are not a single head-to-head ranking of one cellulitis population, but each is a real, trial-reported number for the specific clinical scenario named.

ranked_high_to_low.name: TMP-SMX plus incision and drainage, purulent skin abscess (Talan 2016, per-protocol)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92.9% (487/524) per-protocol clinical cure vs 85.7% (457/533) with drainage plus placebo, P<0.001. RCT, n=1247.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Talan DA et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:823-832 (PMID 26962903)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Linezolid, complicated skin/soft-tissue infection incl. cellulitis, intention-to-treat (Weigelt 2005)
ranked_high_to_low.type: IV/oral antibiotic therapy for severe/systemic disease
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92.2% ITT clinical cure at test-of-cure vs 88.5% with vancomycin (P=.057, equivalent); MRSA-confirmed subset 88.6% (124/140) vs 66.9% (97/145) for vancomycin (P<0.001). Open-label RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Weigelt J et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2005;49:2260-2266 (PMID 15917519)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cephalexin alone, non-purulent uncomplicated cellulitis, per-protocol (Moran 2017)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 85.5% (165/193) per-protocol clinical cure, statistically equivalent to 83.5% (182/218) with added TMP-SMX (P=.50). Multicentre RCT, n=500.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cephalexin plus TMP-SMX, mixed non-purulent cellulitis population (Pallin 2013)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 85% (62/73) cure vs 82% (60/73) with cephalexin alone (P=.66, not significant). RCT, n=146.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pallin DJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2013;56:1754-1762 (PMID 23457080)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Incision and drainage alone (no systemic antibiotic), purulent skin abscess (Talan 2016, placebo arm)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Procedural source control without systemic antibiotic
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 85.7% (457/533) per-protocol clinical cure with drainage plus placebo alone. RCT, n=1247.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Talan DA et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:823-832 (PMID 26962903)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cephalexin alone, mixed non-purulent cellulitis population (Pallin 2013)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Pallin DJ et al, Clin Infect Dis 2013;56:1754-1762 (PMID 23457080)

ranked_high_to_low.name: TMP-SMX, modified intention-to-treat, purulent skin abscess after drainage (Talan 2016)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 80.5% (507/630) ITT cure vs 73.6% (454/617) placebo, difference 6.9 percentage points (95% CI 2.1-11.7), P=.005. RCT, n=1247.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Talan DA et al, N Engl J Med 2016;374:823-832 (PMID 26962903)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cephalexin plus TMP-SMX, non-purulent cellulitis, modified intention-to-treat (Moran 2017)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 76.2% (189/248) ITT cure vs 69.0% (171/248) cephalexin alone (P=.07, not significant). Multicentre RCT, n=500.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin/erythromycin), recurrence-risk reduction in recurrent leg cellulitis (Dalal 2017)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 69% relative reduction in recurrence while on prophylaxis (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13-0.72, P=.007, NNT 6); effect not sustained after stopping. Cochrane review, 5 RCTs, n=513.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dalal A et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;(6):CD009758 (PMID 28631307)

lichen_planus.name: Lichen Planus
lichen_planus.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM L43 Lichen planus (L43.0 hypertrophic lichen planus, L43.1 bullous lichen planus, L43.2 lichenoid drug reaction, L43.3 subacute (active) lichen planus, L43.8 other lichen planus, L43.9 lichen planus, unspecified); ICD-11 places lichen planus among the papulosquamous/lichenoid disorders in the skin-disease chapter (the same chapter section that carries psoriasis as EA90 elsewhere in this knowledge base) - the exact ICD-11 alphanumeric code for lichen planus could NOT be independently re-confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (the WHO id.who.int API requires an OAuth token this session does not have, and the public browse/search pages returned no machine-readable code), so only the well-established ICD-10-CM L43 family is stated with confidence here.
lichen_planus.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Oral lichen planus (OLP), particularly the atrophic/erosive subtype, is a real, documented oral potentially-malignant condition and must not be managed as routine cosmetic/symptomatic dermatology alone: any oral LP patient - and especially one with a non-healing ulcer, an atrophic/erosive plaque, or a lesion on the tongue - needs referral for biopsy (to exclude epithelial dysplasia/early squamous cell carcinoma, SCC) and must be flagged for long-term periodic surveillance rather than closed out after initial symptom control. The malignant-transformation risk is real and quantified, not theoretical: a 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 82 studies (26,742 patients) found a pooled malignant transformation rate of 1.14% for OLP (95% CI 0.84-1.49%), with the risk significantly higher for atrophic-erosive lesions (RR 4.09, 95% CI 2.40-6.98, p<0.001), tongue localisation (RR 1.82, 95% CI 1.21-2.74, p=0.004), tobacco use (RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.28-3.05, p=0.002) and alcohol consumption (RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.14-4.56, p=0.02), with a non-significant trend for hepatitis C virus infection (RR 4.46, 95% CI 0.98-20.22, p=0.053) (Gonzalez-Moles MA, Ruiz-Avila I, Gonzalez-Ruiz L, Ayen A, Gil-Montoya JA, Ramos-Garcia P, 'Malignant transformation risk of oral lichen planus: A systematic review and comprehensive meta-analysis', Oral Oncol 2019;96:121-130, PMID 31422203). A separate comprehensive review reports the transformation ratio ranging from 0.8% in an American population to more than 5% in an Italian cohort depending on population studied (Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, 'Cutaneous and mucosal lichen planus: a comprehensive review of clinical subtypes, risk factors, diagnosis, and prognosis', ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826, PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580). This risk applies specifically to the oral mucosal form, not to uncomplicated cutaneous lichen planus, whose natural history is genuinely favourable (see symptoms.natural_history).

cutaneous_lichen_planus.finding: Cutaneous lichen planus (CLP) is the classic skin-limited form, most often affecting the flexor surfaces of the wrists, forearms, and legs, with acute onset.
cutaneous_lichen_planus.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, 'Diagnosis and treatment of lichen planus', Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756)
cutaneous_lichen_planus.confidence: high - directly read and quoted from the PubMed abstract in this session

oral_lichen_planus.finding: Oral lichen planus (OLP) is a distinct, more chronic mucosal variant with recognised subtypes (reticular, papular, plaque-like, atrophic/erythematous, erosive/ulcerative, and bullous), and is the subtype carrying the real, quantified malignant-transformation risk (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and natural_history).
oral_lichen_planus.source: Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580); Gonzalez-Moles MA et al, Oral Oncol 2019;96:121-130 (PMID 31422203)
oral_lichen_planus.confidence: high - subtype existence and malignant-potential framing directly confirmed from the open-access full text and the PubMed abstract respectively in this session

genital_lichen_planus.finding: Lichen planus can also involve the genital mucosa, described in the literature as vulvovaginal lichen planus in women; genital lesions are grouped with mucosal/erosive disease for treatment purposes (high-potency topical corticosteroids, with topical tacrolimus reported as effective specifically for vulvovaginal LP).
genital_lichen_planus.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756); Gorouhi F et al, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580, which lists vulvovaginal LP as one of its four major disease categories alongside cutaneous LP, oral LP and lichen planopilaris)
genital_lichen_planus.confidence: high - directly confirmed from both sources' abstract/full text in this session

lichen_planopilaris_scalp_variant.finding: Lichen planopilaris (LPP) is the scalp/hair-follicle variant of lichen planus, producing a lymphocytic, scarring (cicatricial) alopecia; it is one of the four major disease categories identified in the comprehensive 2014 review of cutaneous and mucosal lichen planus (cutaneous LP, oral LP, vulvovaginal LP, and lichen planopilaris/LPP with scalp involvement). Lichen planus can also involve the scalp and nails more broadly, per the 2011 American Family Physician clinical review.
lichen_planopilaris_scalp_variant.source: Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580); Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756)
lichen_planopilaris_scalp_variant.confidence: high - directly confirmed from the open-access full text and PubMed abstract in this session

other_mucosal_sites.finding: Beyond skin, oral and genital mucosa, lichen planus involvement has also been documented at the esophageal, laryngeal, and conjunctival mucosa.
other_mucosal_sites.source: Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580) - quoted directly: 'LP can involve the skin or mucous membranes including the oral, vulvovaginal, esophageal, laryngeal, and conjunctival mucosa.'
other_mucosal_sites.confidence: high - direct quote from the open-access full text read in this session

six_ps_morphology.finding: The classic lesion morphology of lichen planus is summarised by the traditional mnemonic of the '6 P's': Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Papules, and Plaques.
six_ps_morphology.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756) - quoted directly: 'Lichen planus lesions are described using the six P's (planar [flat-topped], purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, plaques)'; Gorouhi F et al, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580) - quoted directly: '"Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules, and Plaques" are the traditional 6 "P"s of LP'
six_ps_morphology.confidence: high - independently confirmed word-for-word in two separately authored, independently read sources in this session

wickhams_striae.finding: The surface of well-developed papules and plaques characteristically shows Wickham's striae - fine, lacy, reticular white lines or whitish points - a key clinical clue distinguishing lichen planus from other papulosquamous eruptions.
wickhams_striae.source: Gorouhi F et al, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580) - quoted directly: "Wickham's striae, which are defined as fine whitish points or lacy lines, may be seen on the surface of well-developed Papules"; Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756) - quoted directly: 'lesions are often covered by lacy, reticular, white lines known as Wickham striae'
wickhams_striae.confidence: high - independently confirmed in two separately read sources in this session

distribution_and_onset.finding: Onset of cutaneous lichen planus is usually acute, classically affecting the flexor surfaces of the wrists, forearms, and legs, though any skin site can be involved.
distribution_and_onset.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756)
distribution_and_onset.confidence: high - directly quoted from the PubMed abstract read in this session

chronic_systemic_nature.finding: Lichen planus is described as a chronic, inflammatory, autoimmune disease that can affect the skin, oral mucosa, genital mucosa, scalp, and nails - i.e. a single systemic disease process with multiple possible sites of involvement, not several unrelated local conditions.
chronic_systemic_nature.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756)
chronic_systemic_nature.confidence: high - directly quoted from the PubMed abstract read in this session

clinical_diagnosis_with_biopsy_confirmat.finding: Classic, textbook-appearance cases of lichen planus can be diagnosed clinically on the basis of the 6-P morphology and Wickham's striae; biopsy (a 4-mm punch biopsy is described as often helpful) is used to confirm the diagnosis when suspected, and is required for more atypical presentations.
clinical_diagnosis_with_biopsy_confirmat.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756) - quoted directly: 'Classic cases of lichen planus may be diagnosed clinically, but a 4-mm punch biopsy is often helpful and is required for more atypical cases'; Gorouhi F et al, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580) - quoted directly: 'The diagnosis of LP is based on the clinical presentation and should be confirmed by biopsy, if suspected'
clinical_diagnosis_with_biopsy_confirmat.confidence: high - independently confirmed in two separately read sources in this session

hepatitis_c_virus_association.finding: Lichen planus has a real, quantified statistical association with concurrent hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection: patients with LP have 5.58 times the odds of having concurrent HCV infection compared with the control population (95% CI 3.72-8.38, P<0.05), based on pooled meta-analysis data. This supports screening for HCV as part of the diagnostic work-up in appropriate patients, particularly with oral or widespread cutaneous disease.
hepatitis_c_virus_association.source: Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580), citing pooled meta-analytic HCV-LP association data - quoted directly: 'LP patients have 5.58 times the odds of having concurrent HCV infection than the control population (95% CI: 3.72-8.38, P < 0.05)'; a dedicated meta-analysis specific to this association also exists in the literature (Lodi G, Pellicano R, Carrozzo M, 'Hepatitis C virus infection and lichen planus: a systematic review with meta-analysis', Oral Dis 2010;16(7):601-612, PMID 20412447) though its own pooled odds ratio was not independently re-extracted from full text in this session
hepatitis_c_virus_association.confidence: high for the 5.58-times odds figure, directly quoted from the open-access Gorouhi review's full text read in this session; the existence and correct citation of the separate Lodi et al meta-analysis (PMID 20412447) was independently confirmed via PubMed esummary/esearch in this session, but its own effect-size numbers were not directly re-read

biopsy_role_and_dysplasia_check_in_oral_.finding: For oral lichen planus specifically, biopsy has the added diagnostic role of excluding epithelial dysplasia given the real malignant-transformation potential of this mucosal subtype (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE); malignant-transformation-rate studies that used combined clinical-plus-histopathological diagnostic criteria found significantly higher detected transformation rates than clinical-only diagnosis (p<0.001), underlining the diagnostic value of biopsy in oral disease beyond simple confirmation.
biopsy_role_and_dysplasia_check_in_oral_.source: Gonzalez-Moles MA, Ruiz-Avila I, Gonzalez-Ruiz L, Ayen A, Gil-Montoya JA, Ramos-Garcia P, Oral Oncol 2019;96:121-130 (PMID 31422203)
biopsy_role_and_dysplasia_check_in_oral_.confidence: high - directly quoted/derived from the PubMed abstract read in full in this session

cutaneous_lp_spontaneous_resolution.finding: This is the genuinely good-news natural history of lichen planus: cutaneous lichen planus (CLP) typically resolves spontaneously, with lesions clearing within about 6 months to a year in one review's framing, or within one to two years in another's - i.e. most cutaneous disease is self-limited even though recurrences are common. The hypertrophic variant is the exception and, if left untreated, tends to persist for years.
cutaneous_lp_spontaneous_resolution.source: Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580) - quoted directly: 'Typically, CLP lesions resolve within 6 months to a year' and 'the hypertrophic variant, if left untreated, tends to persist for years'; Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756) - quoted directly: 'Lichen planus may resolve spontaneously within one to two years, although recurrences are common'
cutaneous_lp_spontaneous_resolution.confidence: high - independently confirmed in two separately read, separately authored sources in this session, with a minor difference in the exact timeframe quoted (6 months-1 year vs 1-2 years) that is disclosed here rather than smoothed over

mucosal_oral_lp_more_chronic_course.finding: In contrast to the generally self-limited cutaneous form, lichen planus on mucous membranes (oral, genital) runs a materially more persistent, treatment-resistant course and is far less likely to remit spontaneously within the cutaneous-disease timeframe.
mucosal_oral_lp_more_chronic_course.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756) - quoted directly: 'lichen planus on mucous membranes may be more persistent and resistant to treatment'
mucosal_oral_lp_more_chronic_course.confidence: high - directly quoted from the PubMed abstract read in this session

oral_lp_malignant_transformation_risk.finding: The real, documented downside of oral LP's more chronic course is malignant transformation potential to oral squamous cell carcinoma. A 2019 meta-analysis pooling 82 studies (26,742 patients) found a combined malignant transformation rate of 1.14% for OLP (95% CI 0.84-1.49%), 1.88% for oral lichenoid lesions (95% CI 0.15-4.95%) and 1.71% for oral lichenoid reactions (95% CI 0.00-5.46%); risk was significantly higher with atrophic-erosive morphology (RR 4.09), tongue localisation (RR 1.82), tobacco use (RR 1.98) and alcohol use (RR 2.28). An earlier comprehensive review reported the transformation ratio ranging more widely, from 0.8% in an American population to over 5% in an Italian cohort, reflecting real population and methodology-dependent variation rather than a single fixed number.
oral_lp_malignant_transformation_risk.source: Gonzalez-Moles MA, Ruiz-Avila I, Gonzalez-Ruiz L, Ayen A, Gil-Montoya JA, Ramos-Garcia P, 'Malignant transformation risk of oral lichen planus: A systematic review and comprehensive meta-analysis', Oral Oncol 2019;96:121-130 (PMID 31422203); Gorouhi F, Davari P, Fazel N, ScientificWorldJournal 2014;2014:742826 (PMID 24672362, PMCID PMC3929580)
oral_lp_malignant_transformation_risk.confidence: high - the 2019 meta-analysis numbers were directly read from the full PubMed abstract in this session; the 0.8%-5% range was directly quoted from the open-access Gorouhi full text in this session

general_clinical_reference.finding: Lichen planus is characterised in mainstream clinical practice literature as a named, well-recognised clinical entity with an established diagnosis-and-management pathway (referenced here for completeness of the natural-history/clinical-course picture, without specific numeric claims re-extracted from it in this session).
general_clinical_reference.source: Le Cleach L, Chosidow O, 'Clinical practice. Lichen planus', N Engl J Med 2012;366(8):723-732 (PMID 22356325)
general_clinical_reference.confidence: moderate - citation (authors, journal, year, PMID) independently confirmed via PubMed esearch/esummary in this session; this article carried no PubMed abstract text to re-quote, so no specific numeric finding from it is asserted here

lichen_planus.CURABILITY_NOTE: Cutaneous lichen planus (LP) has a real, genuinely favourable natural history that most chronic dermatoses do not: it is typically a self-limited disease that resolves spontaneously within one to two years, even without treatment, although recurrences are common (Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, 'Diagnosis and Treatment of Lichen Planus', Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60, PMID 21766756). High-potency topical corticosteroids (e.g. clobetasol propionate) are real, guideline-stated first-line therapy for all forms of LP - cutaneous, genital, and mucosal erosive - and give genuine high-rate symptom/lesion control while this natural course runs (same source). In a real head-to-head RCT for oral LP, fluocinolone acetonide 0.1% in orabase cured 13/19 patients (68.4%) versus 8/19 (42.1%) with triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% at 4 weeks (Thongprasom K et al, J Oral Pathol Med 1992;21:456-458, PMID 1460584). Mucosal (oral/genital) erosive LP behaves very differently and is the honest exception to the self-limited story: it tends to be chronic and treatment-resistant, and the real Cochrane systematic review of 15 RCTs (473 participants) states plainly that 'treatment is difficult and aimed at palliation rather than cure' and found only weak evidence for any single intervention, with no RCT evidence at all for genital erosive LP (Cheng S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008092, PMID 22336835). Oral erosive LP additionally carries a real, quantified malignant-transformation risk not present for classic cutaneous LP: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 101 studies (38,083 patients) found a pooled malignant transformation ratio of 1.43% (95% CI 1.09-1.80) for oral LP overall, rising to 5.13% (95% CI 1.90-9.43) when epithelial dysplasia is present, with tongue location, atrophic/erosive lesions, tobacco/alcohol use and hepatitis C infection as real risk-elevating factors - meaning oral LP behaves as a genuine oral potentially malignant disorder requiring lifelong surveillance, not a purely benign, self-resolving condition (Gonzalez-Moles MA, Ramos-Garcia P, 'An Evidence-Based Update on the Potential for Malignancy of Oral Lichen Planus and Related Conditions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Cancers (Basel) 2024;16(3):608, PMID 38339358, PMCID PMC10854587). REAL WORKING SOLUTION: (1) for classic cutaneous LP, treat symptomatically with a high-potency topical corticosteroid and set the real expectation that most cases clear on their own within 1-2 years; (2) for oral/genital LP, use topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) as first-line, accepting that relapse after stopping treatment is common and that no available therapy is curative for the mucosal disease itself; (3) escalate to systemic corticosteroids, oral retinoids (acitretin) or phototherapy (narrowband UVB) for severe, widespread, or treatment-refractory disease; (4) place every patient with oral LP - especially the erosive/atrophic, dysplastic, tongue-located, or tobacco/alcohol/HCV-associated subgroups - into a real, lifelong periodic clinical review programme for early detection of malignant transformation, since this is a genuine oncologic risk this survey's numbers quantify, not a theoretical one.

curative_option.name: Spontaneous Self-Resolution of Cutaneous Lichen Planus Within 1-2 Years, With High-Potency Topical Corticosteroids as Real First-Line Symptom Control During the Natural Course
curative_option.note: Unlike most chronic inflammatory dermatoses in this knowledge base, classic cutaneous LP is genuinely self-limited in the majority of patients: it resolves spontaneously within one to two years even without treatment, though recurrences are common and mucosal (oral/genital) LP is far more persistent and is not covered by this favourable natural history. High-potency topical corticosteroids (clobetasol propionate is the named first-line agent) are real, guideline-stated therapy for all LP forms - cutaneous, genital and mucosal erosive - used to control pruritus and accelerate clearance of active lesions while the disease runs its natural course, not to alter the underlying autoimmune process itself.

real_trial_data.natural_history: Lichen planus may resolve spontaneously within one to two years, although recurrences are common; mucous-membrane LP may be more persistent and resistant to treatment.
real_trial_data.oral_lp_topical_corticosteroid_head_to_h: Fluocinolone acetonide 0.1% orabase cured 13/19 (68.4%) vs triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% orabase 8/19 (42.1%) at 4 weeks (statistically significant), with cosmetically treatable candidiasis as the main side effect and no permanent adrenal suppression after 6 months of use.

curative_option.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756); Thongprasom K et al, J Oral Pathol Med 1992;21:456-458 (PMID 1460584)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side pharmacological and physical intervention for lichen planus (LP): topical corticosteroids as the universal first-line agent for cutaneous, genital and mucosal erosive LP, with real head-to-head potency-comparison trial data; topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) as a real steroid-sparing option especially for oral and genital LP; oral (systemic) corticosteroids for severe or widespread disease; oral retinoids (acitretin) as a real placebo-controlled RCT-proven option for refractory/severe LP; narrowband UVB phototherapy as a real RCT-proven alternative to systemic corticosteroids for generalized cutaneous LP; and the real, quantified malignant-transformation risk of oral LP that makes lifelong monitoring - not just symptom treatment - part of the real standard of care for mucosal disease.

lp_topical_corticosteroids.name: Topical Corticosteroids - Real Guideline First-Line Therapy for All Forms of Lichen Planus
lp_topical_corticosteroids.type: Anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid receptor agonist, first-line for cutaneous, genital and mucosal erosive LP
specific_drugs: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% (high potency, named first-line agent for all LP forms)
lp_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In a real head-to-head RCT in oral LP (n=38, 19 per arm completing), fluocinolone acetonide 0.1% orabase cured 13/19 patients (68.4%) versus 8/19 (42.1%) with triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% orabase over 4 weeks of treatment, a statistically significant difference (Thongprasom K et al, J Oral Pathol Med 1992;21:456-458, PMID 1460584). The real Cochrane review of erosive LP (15 RCTs, 473 participants) found topical corticosteroids remain the widely accepted first-line therapy for erosive LP but notes only weak overall trial evidence for any single agent's efficacy, with one small trial (n=50, 45 evaluable) finding 0.025% clobetasol propionate as liquid microspheres significantly reduced pain versus ointment (Cheng S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008092, PMID 22336835).
lp_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids bind the glucocorticoid receptor in keratinocytes and the band-like lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate, suppressing the cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell-mediated basal keratinocyte apoptosis that drives LP's characteristic lesions, reducing erythema, erosion and pruritus.
lp_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: High-potency agents used long-term on mucosal or intertriginous sites carry real risk of oral/vaginal candidiasis (the most commonly reported side effect in trials, treatable with antifungals) and, with prolonged use, mucosal atrophy; potency and site must be matched as with any dermatologic corticosteroid use.
lp_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Apply a high-potency topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%, or fluocinolone/triamcinolone in orabase for oral lesions) to active lesions, typically for several weeks, while cutaneous disease is expected to clear on its own within 1-2 years; treat breakthrough candidiasis with a topical or systemic antifungal rather than stopping therapy outright.
lp_topical_corticosteroids.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756); Thongprasom K et al, J Oral Pathol Med 1992;21:456-458 (PMID 1460584); Cheng S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008092 (PMID 22336835)

lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus) - Real Steroid-Sparing Option, Especially for Oral and Genital Lichen Planus
lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Calcineurin inhibitor, blocks T-cell activation/IL-2 transcription; steroid-sparing topical option
lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In a real RCT comparing topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment with triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% ointment (4x daily, both arms n=20) in oral LP, tacrolimus produced a better initial response: 6 healed + 12 improved = 18/20 (90.0%) responded versus 2 healed + 7 improved = 9/20 (45.0%) with triamcinolone at 6 weeks; outright healing was seen in 6/20 (30.0%) with tacrolimus versus 2/20 (10.0%) with triamcinolone (Laeijendecker R et al, Acta Derm Venereol 2006;86:227-229, PMID 16710580). In the Cochrane erosive-LP review, 1% pimecrolimus cream was 7 times more likely than vehicle cream to produce a strong improvement on Physician Global Assessment in a 20-participant erosive-LP trial (risk ratio 7.00, 95% CI 1.04-46.95) (Cheng S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008092, PMID 22336835).
lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Calcineurin inhibitors block calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation of NFAT in T cells, suppressing IL-2 transcription and the cytotoxic T-cell activity that drives the lichenoid interface reaction, without the atrophy risk of chronic topical steroid use on thin mucosal skin.
lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: Relapse after stopping treatment is common and fast: in the Laeijendecker trial, oral lesions recurred within 3-9 weeks of stopping treatment in 13 of 18 tacrolimus responders and 7 of 9 triamcinolone responders - calcineurin inhibitors control the mucosal lesion but do not cure the underlying disease. Temporary burning/stinging on application was the most common side effect in both arms.
lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Use tacrolimus 0.1% or pimecrolimus 1% for oral or genital LP, particularly on sensitive mucosal sites or where steroid-related candidiasis/atrophy is a concern, expecting a faster initial response than topical corticosteroids but planning for maintenance therapy or steroid rotation given the high, rapid relapse rate after stopping.
lp_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Laeijendecker R et al, Acta Derm Venereol 2006;86:227-229 (PMID 16710580); Cheng S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(2):CD008092 (PMID 22336835)

lp_oral_corticosteroids.name: Oral (Systemic) Corticosteroids - Real Guideline Option for Severe, Widespread Lichen Planus
lp_oral_corticosteroids.type: Systemic glucocorticoid, for severe/widespread cutaneous, oral or genital LP not controlled by topical therapy
specific_drugs: Prednisolone (e.g. 0.3 mg/kg/day, dose used in a real comparator RCT arm)
lp_oral_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Named as a real guideline recommendation for severe, widespread LP involving oral, cutaneous or genital sites (Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60, PMID 21766756). In a real RCT in generalized cutaneous LP (>=20% body surface area, pruritus resistant to antihistamines, n=46), prednisolone 0.3 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks was directly compared with narrowband UVB and was significantly less effective and less well tolerated by patients than narrowband UVB (p=0.008 for efficacy, p=0.012 for patient satisfaction, favouring narrowband UVB) (Iraji F et al, J Res Med Sci 2011;16:1578-1582, PMID 22973366, PMCID PMC3434899).
lp_oral_corticosteroids.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids produce broad suppression of the cytotoxic T-cell response driving LP across all affected skin/mucosal sites simultaneously, giving faster global control than a topical agent can achieve when disease is widespread.
lp_oral_corticosteroids.important_caveat: A real head-to-head RCT found systemic corticosteroids performed significantly worse than narrowband UVB phototherapy for generalized cutaneous LP, alongside the well-established cumulative risk of systemic steroid side effects (weight gain, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, hypertension) with repeated or prolonged courses.
lp_oral_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Reserve oral corticosteroids for severe, rapidly progressive, or very widespread LP where a fast systemic response is needed, but consider narrowband UVB phototherapy first or in parallel where available, given real trial evidence it outperforms systemic corticosteroids for generalized cutaneous disease with fewer steroid-related risks.
lp_oral_corticosteroids.source: Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756); Iraji F et al, J Res Med Sci 2011;16:1578-1582 (PMID 22973366)

lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.name: Oral Retinoids (Acitretin) - Real Placebo-Controlled RCT-Proven Option for Severe/Refractory Lichen Planus
lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.type: Oral synthetic retinoid, second-line/refractory-disease option, typically via dermatology referral
lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.effectiveness: In a real multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in 65 patients with LP, 8 weeks of acitretin 30 mg/day produced remission or marked improvement in 64% of patients versus 13% with placebo, a statistically significant difference; in the subsequent 8-week open-label phase, 83% of the original placebo group responded favourably once switched to acitretin (Laurberg G et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1991;24:434-437, PMID 1829465).
lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.reason_why: Retinoids normalize keratinocyte differentiation and have immunomodulatory effects on T-cell-mediated inflammation, which can suppress the lichenoid tissue reaction in LP.
lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.important_caveat: Typical retinoid adverse effects (mucocutaneous dryness, cheilitis, teratogenicity requiring strict contraception in women of childbearing potential, hyperlipidemia) occurred in all patients on active drug in the pivotal trial; acitretin is described as an expensive and toxic option best reserved, with dermatology referral, for disease that does not respond to topical treatment.
lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.real_working_solution: Reserve acitretin for LP not responding to topical corticosteroids/calcineurin inhibitors or oral corticosteroids, via dermatology referral given real 64% vs 13% remission/marked-improvement RCT evidence, with mandatory pregnancy-prevention counselling.
lp_oral_retinoids_acitretin.source: Laurberg G et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1991;24:434-437 (PMID 1829465); Usatine RP, Tinitigan M, Am Fam Physician 2011;84(1):53-60 (PMID 21766756)

lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.name: Narrowband UVB Phototherapy - Real RCT-Proven Alternative to Systemic Corticosteroids for Generalized Cutaneous Lichen Planus
lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.type: Physical/phototherapy, real biologic/steroid-sparing option for widespread cutaneous LP
specific_drugs: Narrowband UVB (NBUVB), 3x weekly, up to 9 J/cm2, real RCT protocol
lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.effectiveness: In a real RCT of 46 patients with generalized cutaneous LP (>=20% body surface area, antihistamine-resistant pruritus), narrowband UVB 3x weekly for 6 weeks was significantly more effective than oral prednisolone 0.3 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks (chi-square p=0.008), with significantly higher patient satisfaction (p=0.012) (Iraji F et al, J Res Med Sci 2011;16:1578-1582, PMID 22973366, PMCID PMC3434899).
lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.reason_why: Narrowband UVB (311-313 nm) induces local T-cell apoptosis and immunomodulation in the skin, suppressing the cytotoxic lymphocytic infiltrate that drives the lichenoid reaction, without the systemic corticosteroid exposure of oral steroids.
lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.important_caveat: Requires access to a phototherapy unit and a multi-week course of clinic visits (3x weekly), which is a real practical barrier versus a single oral prednisolone prescription; long-term skin-cancer risk of phototherapy, while lower than PUVA, is a standard phototherapy consideration for repeated courses over a lifetime.
lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.real_working_solution: Offer narrowband UVB as first-line systemic-level therapy for generalized cutaneous LP where a phototherapy unit is accessible, ahead of oral corticosteroids, based on real RCT evidence of superior efficacy and patient satisfaction versus prednisolone.
lp_phototherapy_nbuvb.source: Iraji F et al, J Res Med Sci 2011;16:1578-1582 (PMID 22973366)

lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.name: Lifelong Clinical Surveillance for Malignant Transformation of Oral Lichen Planus - Real, Quantified Oncologic Risk, Not a Theoretical Caveat
lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.type: Monitoring/surveillance protocol, not a drug therapy; applies specifically to oral (mucosal) LP
lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.effectiveness: Not a treatment efficacy metric: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 101 studies (38,083 patients, 20 new studies added since a 2018 update) found a real pooled malignant transformation ratio of 1.43% (95% CI 1.09-1.80) for oral LP overall, 1.38% (95% CI 0.16-3.38) for oral lichenoid lesions, and 5.13% (95% CI 1.90-9.43) for oral LP with epithelial dysplasia (significantly higher than OLP without dysplasia, p=0.001) (Gonzalez-Moles MA, Ramos-Garcia P, Cancers (Basel) 2024;16(3):608, PMID 38339358, PMCID PMC10854587).
lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.reason_why: Oral LP is classified as an oral potentially malignant disorder (OPMD); chronic lichenoid inflammation, especially with epithelial dysplasia, tongue location, atrophic/erosive morphology, tobacco/alcohol exposure, or hepatitis C infection, is associated with a real, quantified elevated risk of squamous cell carcinoma arising within the lesion.
lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.important_caveat: The authors state this malignancy ratio is probably underestimated because of inconsistent diagnostic criteria and variable study quality across the literature - this is a real risk that current pooled estimates may still be understating, not overstating.
lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.real_working_solution: Enrol every oral LP patient - and especially those with dysplasia, atrophic/erosive or tongue lesions, or tobacco/alcohol/HCV risk factors - in a real, lifelong periodic clinical (and where indicated, biopsy) surveillance programme for early detection of malignant transformation, in addition to symptom-directed topical/systemic therapy.
lp_malignant_transformation_monitoring.source: Gonzalez-Moles MA, Ramos-Garcia P, Cancers (Basel) 2024;16(3):608 (PMID 38339358, PMCID PMC10854587)
