familial_mediterranean_fever.name: Familial Mediterranean Fever
familial_mediterranean_fever.icd11_hint: ICD-10 E85.0 Non-neuropathic heredofamilial amyloidosis (WHO ICD-10; this category includes Familial Mediterranean fever) - confirmed via NLM Clinical Tables ICD-10-CM API. The exact WHO ICD-11 code could not be independently verified this session (WHO ICD-11 browser was not accessible for confirmation) and is therefore not stated as a specific code here.
familial_mediterranean_fever.CURABILITY_NOTE: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is NOT curable in the sense of removing its cause: it is an autosomal-recessive (occasionally dominant-acting) disease of gain-of-function mutations in MEFV, the gene encoding pyrin, and no drug below corrects the mutation or the resulting hyperactive pyrin inflammasome. What IS real, decades-proven and worth stating plainly as this disease's genuine success story: lifelong daily colchicine, started at diagnosis and never stopped, is a near-cure of FMF's morbidity and mortality. In the pivotal double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Zemer 1974, PMID 4606109), colchicine was shown superior to placebo for preventing attacks, and it has been the worldwide first-line standard of care ever since (EULAR 2016 and 2024 recommendations, PMID 26802180 and PMID 40234174). In the landmark long-term cohort of 1070 patients followed 4-11 years (Zemer 1986, PMID 3515182), colchicine-compliant, previously unaffected patients remained free of new amyloid nephropathy in 98.3% of cases versus a 48.9% cumulative rate of nephropathy in non-compliant patients (p<0.0001) - a 28-fold difference that shows colchicine's real, near-complete prevention of FMF's fatal complication (renal AA amyloidosis) when taken as prescribed. On the best available published estimate, roughly 80-90% of all FMF patients also achieve adequate attack control on colchicine alone (complement of the 10-20% colchicine-resistance rate reported by Ben-Zvi 2017, PMID 27860460, and the 5-10% resistant plus 5-10% intolerant split reported by Kacar 2020, PMID 32210604). THE REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the roughly 10-20% who are colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant: IL-1 blockade. Anakinra, in the only randomised placebo-controlled trial in colchicine-resistant FMF (Ben-Zvi 2017, PMID 27860460), roughly halved attack frequency (51.4% reduction) and brought 50% of patients to under one attack per month versus 0% on placebo. Canakinumab, in the CLUSTER phase 3 trial (De Benedetti 2018, PMID 29768139), achieved complete response (flare resolution, no further flare to week 16) in 61% of colchicine-resistant FMF patients at the approved 150 mg/4-week dose versus 6% on placebo (p<0.001), rising to 71% when dose-escalated to 300 mg/4 weeks; a real-world cohort of 30 colchicine/anakinra-resistant patients (Karabulut 2022, PMID 34550430) independently confirmed an 81.2% reduction in attack frequency on canakinumab. What is NOT cured: the MEFV mutation and the underlying pyrin-inflammasome hyperactivation persist for life; every therapy here is a continued, lifelong treatment, and stopping colchicine (non-compliance) restores the pre-colchicine-era risk of both attacks and fatal amyloidosis, as the 1986 cohort's non-compliant arm shows directly.

curative_option.name: Lifelong Colchicine Prophylaxis - Real Complete/Near-Complete Attack Control in the Great Majority of Patients and Near-Complete Prevention of AA Amyloidosis/Nephropathy (Zemer Cohort, 1070 Patients, 4-11 Years)
curative_option.note: FMF itself (the underlying MEFV gain-of-function pyrin-inflammasome mutation) is not curable - it is genetic and lifelong. But daily oral colchicine, taken for life, is a real, decades-proven, near-cure-grade intervention for the disease's two serious consequences: it controls attacks completely or near-completely in the great majority of patients, and it prevents the fatal complication (AA amyloidosis/nephropathy) in patients who take it as prescribed. This is described here as a near-cure of the disease's morbidity and mortality, not a cure of the mutation itself.

real_trial_data.pivotal_rct_1974: Zemer D et al., double-blind placebo-controlled trial of colchicine versus placebo in FMF (N Engl J Med 1974;291:932-934, PMID 4606109) - the first controlled trial establishing that colchicine, not placebo, prevents FMF attacks; this trial is the basis on which colchicine became, and remains, the worldwide first-line standard of care (confirmed as the founding RCT by both the 2016 and 2024 EULAR/PReS recommendations, PMID 26802180 and PMID 40234174).
real_trial_data.amyloidosis_prevention_cohort_1986: Zemer D et al., 'Colchicine in the prevention and treatment of the amyloidosis of familial Mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1986;314:1001-1005 (PMID 3515182) - 1070 FMF patients followed 4-11 years on colchicine. In 960 patients with no amyloidosis at baseline, proteinuria (the first sign of AA amyloid nephropathy) appeared in only 4 of the patients who adhered to colchicine, versus 16 of 54 who admitted non-compliance. Life-table cumulative rate of proteinuria: 1.7% (90% CI 0.0-11.3%) at 11 years in compliant patients versus 48.9% (90% CI 18.8-79.0%) at 9 years in non-compliant patients (p<0.0001) - i.e. compliant patients remained free of new nephropathy in 98.3% of cases (computed 100-1.7), a 28-fold difference in absolute risk. Among 86 patients who already had proteinuria (without nephrotic syndrome) when colchicine was started, proteinuria resolved in 5 and stabilised (no worsening for over 8 years in 40 of them) in 68 of 86 (79.1%, computed 68/86) - i.e. colchicine also halted progression in most patients who already had early kidney amyloid involvement.
real_trial_data.colchicine_resistance_and_intolerance_re: Ben-Zvi I et al. (Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:854-862, PMID 27860460): FMF is refractory to colchicine prophylaxis in 10-20% of patients (background statement used to define the RCT's colchicine-resistant enrolment population). Kacar M et al., systematic review (J Inflamm Res 2020;13:141-149, PMID 32210604): 'In most patients, treatment with colchicine can prevent attacks of fever and inflammation. However, 5%-10% of patients are resistant to colchicine treatment, while a similar percentage cannot tolerate colchicine' - i.e. on the most conservative published split, roughly 80-90% of patients (computed 100 minus 10-20%) achieve adequate attack control on colchicine alone, and the remaining 10-20% (resistant or intolerant) are the population for whom IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) is the real, trial-proven next step.
real_trial_data.guideline_position: EULAR recommendations for the management of FMF (Ozen S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651, PMID 26802180) and the 2024 update (Ozen S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909, PMID 40234174): colchicine is the recommended first-line, lifelong treatment for all FMF patients from the time of diagnosis, both to control attacks and to prevent amyloidosis; both versions of the guideline recommend an IL-1 inhibitor (anakinra or canakinumab) for patients who are colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect: on lifelong, adhered-to colchicine, the great majority of patients have complete or near-complete cessation of febrile/serosal attacks, and amyloid nephropathy is prevented in 98.3% of previously unaffected, compliant patients over 11 years (versus 48.9% cumulative nephropathy in non-compliant patients) - a real, decades-proven near-cure of the disease's morbidity and mortality. Not curative: the causative MEFV mutation and the underlying pyrin-inflammasome hyperactivation are not removed; colchicine must be continued for life, and stopping it (non-compliance) restores the high risk of both attacks and fatal amyloidosis seen in the pre-colchicine era.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: The 10-20% of patients who remain colchicine-resistant despite maximum tolerated dosing, and the overlapping 5-10% who cannot tolerate colchicine (usually gastrointestinal side effects) at an effective dose (Ben-Zvi 2017, PMID 27860460; Kacar 2020, PMID 32210604) - for this group, colchicine alone does not deliver the near-cure state, and IL-1 blockade is the real, trial-proven alternative (see exhaustive_medicine_survey and effectiveness_ranked_table).
curative_option.important_caveat: The 98.3%/48.9% amyloidosis figures come from one large, long-running but non-randomised cohort (Zemer 1986) comparing self-selected compliant versus non-compliant patients, not a randomised amyloidosis-prevention trial (a placebo-controlled trial specifically for amyloidosis was never done, for ethical reasons, once the 1974 RCT had shown colchicine prevents attacks). The original 1974 RCT abstract/results text could not be retrieved in machine-readable form this session (pre-1975 MEDLINE record with no structured abstract); its existence, title, journal and PMID are independently confirmed via NCBI PubMed, and its finding (colchicine superior to placebo for attack prevention) is independently corroborated by both EULAR guideline documents citing it as the foundational trial.
curative_option.source: Zemer D et al., 'A controlled trial of colchicine in preventing attacks of familial mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1974;291:932-934 (PMID 4606109); Zemer D et al., 'Colchicine in the prevention and treatment of the amyloidosis of familial Mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1986;314:1001-1005 (PMID 3515182); Ben-Zvi I et al., 'Anakinra for Colchicine-Resistant Familial Mediterranean Fever: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial', Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:854-862 (PMID 27860460); Kacar M et al., 'The Efficacy, Safety and Tolerability of Canakinumab in the Treatment of Familial Mediterranean Fever: A Systematic Review of the Literature', J Inflamm Res 2020;13:141-149 (PMID 32210604); Ozen S et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651 (PMID 26802180); Ozen S et al., 'EULAR/PReS endorsed recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF): 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909 (PMID 40234174)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for familial Mediterranean fever (FMF): lifelong colchicine as first-line prophylaxis, IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) for colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant disease, and NSAIDs for symptomatic relief of acute-attack pain. Diagnosis (MEFV genotyping, Tel Hashomer criteria) and clinical features are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial, systematic review or real-world cohort; derived percentages show their arithmetic.

fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.name: Lifelong Oral Colchicine - Real First-Line Standard of Care Since the 1974 RCT; Prevents Attacks in the Great Majority and Amyloidosis in 98.3% of Compliant Patients
fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.type: Microtubule-inhibiting alkaloid, oral, taken daily for life from diagnosis onward
specific_drugs: Colchicine tablets, typically 0.5-2 mg/day in adults, titrated to response and tolerability (dose ranges reported across EULAR-cited cohorts)
Colchicine 0.5 mg tablets (the strength marketed in India, e.g. Zycolchin 0.5 mg, Colchicort)
fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.effectiveness: Zemer 1974 (double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT, PMID 4606109): established colchicine's superiority over placebo for preventing FMF attacks - the founding trial cited by both the 2016 and 2024 EULAR/PReS recommendations as the basis for lifelong colchicine as first-line therapy. Zemer 1986 amyloidosis cohort (1070 patients, 4-11 years, PMID 3515182): among 960 patients with no baseline amyloidosis, cumulative proteinuria (new nephropathy) was 1.7% at 11 years in colchicine-compliant patients versus 48.9% at 9 years in non-compliant patients (p<0.0001) - 98.3% of compliant patients remained free of new nephropathy (computed 100-1.7). Among 86 patients who already had proteinuria without nephrotic syndrome, colchicine stabilised (no deterioration, for over 8 years in 40) 68 of 86 (79.1%, computed 68/86). Real-world resistance/intolerance rate: 10-20% (Ben-Zvi 2017, PMID 27860460) to 5-10% resistant plus 5-10% intolerant (Kacar 2020, PMID 32210604), meaning roughly 80-90% of patients achieve adequate attack control on colchicine alone.
fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.reason_why: Colchicine binds tubulin and disrupts microtubule polymerisation in neutrophils, blocking the neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion and NLRP3/pyrin-inflammasome-driven IL-1 release that the gain-of-function MEFV/pyrin mutation otherwise triggers, so the downstream sterile-serositis attacks and the chronic subclinical inflammation that deposits serum amyloid A protein as AA amyloid are both suppressed.
fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.important_caveat: Effect depends entirely on adherence - the 1986 cohort's own data show non-compliant patients had amyloidosis rates approaching the pre-colchicine era. Common dose-limiting side effect is diarrhoea/GI upset; dose reduction, temporary interruption or an evening-only schedule is used to keep patients on therapy per EULAR guidance. Colchicine has significant drug interactions (P-glycoprotein/strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, statins) requiring dose caution, as in gout.
fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.real_working_solution: Start colchicine at diagnosis and continue for life, titrating the dose upward for breakthrough attacks and downward only for intolerable side effects (never stopped outright) - this single measure is what converts FMF from a disease with a high lifetime amyloidosis/renal-failure risk into one where the great majority of adherent patients live attack-free or near-attack-free with normal kidney function.
fmf_colchicine_lifelong_therapy.source: Zemer D et al., 'A controlled trial of colchicine in preventing attacks of familial mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1974;291:932-934 (PMID 4606109); Zemer D et al., 'Colchicine in the prevention and treatment of the amyloidosis of familial Mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1986;314:1001-1005 (PMID 3515182); Ben-Zvi I et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:854-862 (PMID 27860460); Kacar M et al., J Inflamm Res 2020;13:141-149 (PMID 32210604); Ozen S et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651 (PMID 26802180); Ozen S et al., 'EULAR/PReS endorsed recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF): 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909 (PMID 40234174); Retail listings for Zycolchin/Colchicort (colchicine 0.5 mg, Indian brands) (medibuddy.in, medplusmart.com, accessed 2026-09-24)

fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.name: Anakinra - Real Randomised Placebo-Controlled Proof for Colchicine-Resistant FMF (Ben-Zvi 2017): Halved Attack Frequency, 50% Reached Under 1 Attack/Month Versus 0%
fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.type: Recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist, daily subcutaneous injection, added on top of continued colchicine
specific_drugs: Anakinra (Kineret) 100 mg subcutaneous daily, added to existing colchicine ≥1.5 to ≤3 mg/day (Ben-Zvi 2017 RCT regimen)
fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.effectiveness: Ben-Zvi I et al., randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:854-862, PMID 27860460): 25 colchicine-resistant FMF patients (12 anakinra, 13 placebo, 4-month treatment). Mean attacks per patient per month: 1.7 +/- 1.7 (anakinra) versus 3.5 +/- 1.9 (placebo), p=0.037 - a 51.4% reduction (computed (3.5-1.7)/3.5). Patients with a mean of <1 attack/month: 6 of 12 (50.0%) with anakinra versus 0 of 13 (0%) with placebo, p=0.005. Joint attacks per month: 0.8 +/- 1.6 versus 2.1 +/- 1.1, p=0.019. Quality-of-life VAS (0-10): 7.7 +/- 2.3 versus 4.2 +/- 2.9, p=0.045. Adverse events per patient per month were comparable (2.03 +/- 1.75 versus 3.34 +/- 2.5, p=0.22) with no severe adverse events.
fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.reason_why: Anakinra competitively blocks the IL-1 receptor, neutralising both IL-1alpha and IL-1beta downstream of the hyperactive pyrin inflammasome that drives FMF attacks in patients whose colchicine dose no longer suppresses that inflammasome activity adequately.
fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.important_caveat: Small RCT (25 patients); anakinra requires daily injections, which some patients find burdensome long-term compared with the less frequent canakinumab schedule. Not FDA-labelled specifically for FMF (labelled indications are rheumatoid arthritis, CAPS/NOMID, DIRA); use in FMF is guideline-recommended (EULAR 2016/2024) and trial-supported but off-label in most jurisdictions.
fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.real_working_solution: For a patient who remains symptomatic on maximum tolerated colchicine (colchicine-resistant FMF), adding daily anakinra is a randomised-trial-proven option that roughly halves attack frequency and brings half of patients to under one attack per month, while colchicine is continued unchanged (for its amyloidosis-preventing effect).
fmf_il1_anakinra_colchicine_resistant.source: Ben-Zvi I et al., 'Anakinra for Colchicine-Resistant Familial Mediterranean Fever: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial', Arthritis Rheumatol 2017;69:854-862 (PMID 27860460); Ozen S et al., EULAR recommendations, Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651 (PMID 26802180); Ozen S et al., 2024 update, Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909 (PMID 40234174)

fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.name: Canakinumab (Ilaris) - CLUSTER Phase 3 RCT: 61% Complete Response at Approved Dose Versus 6% Placebo, Rising to 71% With Dose Escalation; Real-World Cohort Confirms 81% Fewer Attacks
fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.type: Human monoclonal anti-interleukin-1 beta antibody, subcutaneous injection every 4-8 weeks, added on top of continued colchicine
specific_drugs: Canakinumab (Ilaris) 150 mg subcutaneous every 4 weeks (approved regimen)
Canakinumab 300 mg subcutaneous every 4 weeks (dose-escalation step for incomplete responders)
Canakinumab 150 mg subcutaneous every 8 weeks (extended/maintenance dosing after complete response)
fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.effectiveness: CLUSTER trial (De Benedetti F et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:1908-1919, PMID 29768139), the colchicine-resistant FMF cohort: at week 16, complete response (flare resolution and no further flare to week 16) in 61% with canakinumab 150 mg/4 weeks versus 6% with placebo (p<0.001). With inclusion of patients dose-escalated to 300 mg/4 weeks, complete response reached 71% of colchicine-resistant FMF patients. After week 16, extended dosing (every 8 weeks) maintained disease control in 46% of colchicine-resistant FMF patients. Most frequent adverse events were infections (173.3 per 100 patient-years), with serious infections in 6.6 per 100 patient-years. Real-world confirmation: Karabulut Y et al. (Rheumatol Int 2022;42:81-86, PMID 34550430), 30 colchicine- and/or anakinra-resistant adult FMF patients: mean attacks per 24 weeks fell from 8.3 at baseline to 1.56 at last visit on canakinumab - an 81.2% reduction (computed (8.3-1.56)/8.3, p<0.001); mean attack duration fell from 67.2 hours to 18.27 hours after 6 months (p<0.001). A separate real-world cohort (Kacar M et al., systematic review, J Inflamm Res 2020;13:141-149, PMID 32210604) similarly reports canakinumab as effective, safe and tolerable specifically in colchicine-resistant/intolerant FMF, which is its approved/reviewed niche.
fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.reason_why: Canakinumab is a full human monoclonal antibody that neutralises IL-1beta directly, the master cytokine released by the hyperactive pyrin inflammasome in FMF; unlike anakinra it has a long half-life allowing dosing every 4-8 weeks instead of daily.
fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.important_caveat: CLUSTER's 71% figure includes patients who needed dose escalation to 300 mg/4 weeks, a higher and more expensive dose than the approved 150 mg/4 weeks label dose; the 46% figure at extended (8-week) dosing shows that not all initial responders stay controlled on a less frequent schedule. Real-world cohort (Karabulut 2022) is small (30 patients), uncontrolled/observational, and drawn from two centres. Canakinumab does not replace colchicine, which is continued for its amyloidosis-preventing effect.
fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.real_working_solution: For colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant FMF (including patients who have already failed anakinra), canakinumab 150 mg every 4 weeks, escalated to 300 mg every 4 weeks if the flare does not fully resolve, is the trial-proven and real-world-confirmed next step, achieving complete response in roughly 6 or 7 of 10 patients where colchicine alone had failed.
fmf_il1_canakinumab_colchicine_resistant.source: De Benedetti F et al. (CLUSTER), 'Canakinumab for the Treatment of Autoinflammatory Recurrent Fever Syndromes', N Engl J Med 2018;378:1908-1919 (PMID 29768139); Karabulut Y et al., 'Canakinumab is effective in patients with familial Mediterranean fever resistant and intolerant to the colchicine and/or anakinra treatment', Rheumatol Int 2022;42:81-86 (PMID 34550430); Kacar M et al., 'The Efficacy, Safety and Tolerability of Canakinumab in the Treatment of Familial Mediterranean Fever: A Systematic Review of the Literature', J Inflamm Res 2020;13:141-149 (PMID 32210604); Ozen S et al., EULAR recommendations, Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651 (PMID 26802180); Ozen S et al., 2024 update, Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909 (PMID 40234174)

fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.name: NSAIDs for Acute-Attack Pain Relief - Real, Guideline-Supported Symptomatic Adjunct; No FMF-Specific Placebo-Controlled Responder-Rate Trial Was Retrieved This Session
fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.type: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, short course during an attack, used alongside (never instead of) continued daily colchicine prophylaxis
specific_drugs: NSAIDs are used as symptomatic analgesia for the pain of an acute FMF attack (abdominal, chest or joint serositis); no single agent is named as superior over another for FMF specifically in the sources reviewed this session
fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.effectiveness: The EULAR recommendations for the management of FMF (Ozen S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651, PMID 26802180) and the 2024 update (Ozen S et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909, PMID 40234174) address acute-attack symptomatic management as part of the overall FMF care pathway, alongside the disease-controlling therapies (colchicine, IL-1 inhibitors) covered above. A dedicated FMF-specific, placebo-controlled trial of NSAID pain relief during attacks, with a numeric responder rate, was searched for via NCBI PubMed this session and was not found; NSAID use in FMF attacks is real, widespread guideline-consistent clinical practice for symptom relief, but is reported here without an invented efficacy percentage.
fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.reason_why: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase, reducing the prostaglandin-mediated pain and inflammation of the serosal/synovial surfaces affected during an acute FMF attack - the same general anti-inflammatory analgesic mechanism used for other serositis and arthritis pain - but they do not act on the pyrin-inflammasome/IL-1 pathway that drives the attack itself the way colchicine or IL-1 blockade does.
fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.important_caveat: NSAIDs are symptomatic only: they do not reduce attack frequency, do not prevent amyloidosis, and are not a substitute for continued colchicine. Deliberately not included in the effectiveness_ranked_table below because no real numeric responder percentage specific to FMF attacks could be verified this session, consistent with this knowledge base's rule of never inventing a number.
fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.real_working_solution: Use an NSAID as short-course symptomatic pain relief during an acute attack on top of unchanged, continued daily colchicine (or IL-1 inhibitor if already on one) - it treats the pain of the attack, not the disease process, and does not replace disease-controlling therapy.
fmf_nsaids_acute_attack_symptom_relief.source: Ozen S et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651 (PMID 26802180); Ozen S et al., 'EULAR/PReS endorsed recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF): 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909 (PMID 40234174)
