effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from DIFFERENT study designs and DIFFERENT endpoints (a non-randomised 11-year amyloidosis-prevention cohort, an arithmetic complement of published colchicine resistance/intolerance rates, a small uncontrolled real-world case series, and a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3/phase 2 trial), so the ordering is by numeric value only, not a like-for-like effectiveness league table - the metric column states exactly what each number measures and derived percentages show their arithmetic. The two Zemer 1986 rows (ranks 1-2) anchor the amyloidosis-prevention half of CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option; the colchicine-responder row (rank 3) anchors the attack-control half. The 1974 Zemer RCT (PMID 4606109) that founded colchicine as first-line therapy is cited throughout as the pivotal trial, but its own numeric results text was not machine-retrievable this session (pre-1975 MEDLINE record with no structured abstract) - its existence, authors, journal and PMID are independently verified via NCBI PubMed, and both the 2016 and 2024 EULAR/PReS guideline documents (PMID 26802180, PMID 40234174) independently confirm it as the foundational positive trial, so it is not used here as a numeric ranked-table row. NSAIDs for acute-attack symptom relief are documented in exhaustive_medicine_survey but deliberately not ranked here, because no FMF-specific placebo-controlled responder percentage was retrieved this session, and this knowledge base's rule is to never substitute an invented number.

familial_mediterranean_fever.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: FMF abdominal (peritonitis) attacks - sudden severe abdominal pain with fever, guarding and rebound tenderness - are frequently indistinguishable at first presentation from true surgical acute-abdomen emergencies (appendicitis, perforated viscus, bowel obstruction) and MUST be triaged with the same urgency as any acute abdomen, bypassing the normal doctor-approval-queue flow to trigger immediate real-world emergency/surgical evaluation (ER now) - this is not precautionary language. In a case-control study of 254 confirmed FMF patients versus 182 healthy controls, 29.1% of FMF patients had undergone at least one abdominal surgery, and appendectomy was the first abdominal operation (performed before FMF was diagnosed) in 26.6% of FMF patients, versus only 4.9% in healthy controls (p=0.0001) (Kasifoglu T, Cansu DU, Korkmaz C, 'Frequency of abdominal surgery in patients with familial Mediterranean fever', Intern Med 2009;48:523-526, PMID 19336953). A real, illustrative modern case documents a patient who underwent an unnecessary appendectomy, then years later a negative exploratory laparotomy for suspected bowel obstruction, before FMF was recognised as the cause of his recurrent abdominal attacks (Hassan TH, Sourial K, 'Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) complicated by adhesive small bowel obstruction: a diagnostic challenge', BMJ Case Rep 2025;18:e267723, PMID 40903096). The rule cuts both ways and must never be used to dismiss a real emergency: (1) a known FMF patient having a typical, self-limited abdominal attack does not automatically need surgery, but (2) any FMF patient with acute abdominal pain still requires the same full emergency surgical work-up as anyone else, because FMF confers no immunity to true appendicitis or other genuine surgical emergencies - the same study found FMF patients can present with real abdominal emergencies even while adherent to colchicine. A known FMF diagnosis must never create false reassurance that new abdominal pain is 'just another FMF attack.'

mefv_gene_and_inheritance.finding: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the MEFV gene, mapped to a minimal co-segregating region of 60 kb on chromosome 16 by the French FMF Consortium, who identified four conservative missense variations clustering at the carboxy-terminal domain of the encoded protein (which they named marenostrin) in 85% of carrier chromosomes studied, absent from 308 control chromosomes. Independently, the International FMF Consortium cloned the same gene from a 115-kb candidate interval on chromosome 16p, identifying three missense mutations in affected individuals but not in normal controls; the gene's 3.7-kb transcript is almost exclusively expressed in granulocytes, and its protein product, named pyrin, is a member of a family of nuclear factors homologous to the Ro52 autoantigen.
mefv_gene_and_inheritance.source: French FMF Consortium, 'A candidate gene for familial Mediterranean fever', Nat Genet 1997;17:25-31 (PMID 9288094); International FMF Consortium, 'Ancient missense mutations in a new member of the RoRet gene family are likely to cause familial Mediterranean fever', Cell 1997;90:797-807 (PMID 9288758)

autoinflammatory_disease_category.finding: FMF is classified as the prototype hereditary periodic fever syndrome and is explicitly described by the EULAR management-recommendation panel as 'the most common monogenic autoinflammatory disease' worldwide, distinguishing it mechanistically from autoantibody-driven autoimmune rheumatic disease: FMF pathology arises from dysregulated innate-immune (pyrin-inflammasome-related) inflammation rather than adaptive-immune autoantibody or autoreactive-T-cell attack.
autoinflammatory_disease_category.source: Ozen S et al., 'EULAR recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever', Ann Rheum Dis 2016;75:644-651 (PMID 26802180); Ozen S et al., 'EULAR/PReS endorsed recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF): 2024 update', Ann Rheum Dis 2025;84:899-909 (PMID 40234174)

recurrent_fever_and_serositis_attacks.finding: FMF's clinical picture, first systematically characterised in a landmark survey of 470 cases, is one of recurrent, self-limited attacks combining fever with serositis at one or more sites: peritonitis (the most common and the site most likely to mimic a surgical acute abdomen), pleuritis, pericarditis (less common), and an acute monoarthritis, typically of a large joint (knee, ankle or hip). These attacks recur episodically with symptom-free intervals between them, a pattern that was foundational to the disease's original clinical description and remains the basis of every later diagnostic criteria set.
recurrent_fever_and_serositis_attacks.source: Sohar E, Gafni J, Pras M, Heller H, 'Familial Mediterranean fever. A survey of 470 cases and review of the literature', Am J Med 1967;43:227-253 (PMID 5340644); Livneh A et al., 'Criteria for the diagnosis of familial Mediterranean fever', Arthritis Rheum 1997;40:1879-1885 (PMID 9336425)

erysipelas_like_erythema.finding: Erysipelas-like erythema (ELE) - a well-demarcated, tender, erysipelas-resembling erythematous plaque, classically over the lower leg, ankle or dorsum of the foot - is a distinctive cutaneous manifestation of FMF, recognised since the disease's original clinical characterisation and incorporated as a named criterion in the later Tel Hashomer diagnostic-criteria study of 105 FMF patients and 106 controls with similar recurrent pain syndromes.
erysipelas_like_erythema.source: Sohar E et al., Am J Med 1967;43:227-253 (PMID 5340644); Livneh A et al., Arthritis Rheum 1997;40:1879-1885 (PMID 9336425)

abdominal_attacks_mimic_surgical_emergen.finding: Because peritonitis is the most frequent attack site, FMF abdominal attacks can be clinically indistinguishable from a true surgical acute abdomen. In a real case-control study of 254 confirmed FMF patients, 29.1% had undergone at least one abdominal surgery and appendectomy was the first (pre-diagnosis) abdominal operation in 26.6% of patients, compared with only 4.9% appendectomy in 182 healthy controls (p=0.0001) - direct evidence of how often this symptom pattern is misread as a primary surgical disease. See this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for the safety-critical implication.
abdominal_attacks_mimic_surgical_emergen.source: Kasifoglu T, Cansu DU, Korkmaz C, Intern Med 2009;48:523-526 (PMID 19336953)

tel_hashomer_livneh_clinical_criteria.finding: The Tel Hashomer criteria (Livneh et al., 1997) remain the benchmark clinical diagnostic framework. Twenty-seven features typical of FMF were studied in 105 FMF patients versus 106 controls with other diseases causing recurrent pain in the same body sites; features significantly more common in FMF were organised into major, minor and supportive criteria. Two criteria sets were derived: a 'simple' set (1 major or 2 minor criteria) and a 'conservative' set (1 major or 2 minor, or 1 minor plus 5 supportive criteria). Both sets achieved sensitivity greater than 95% and specificity greater than 97% for distinguishing FMF from other recurrent-pain conditions.
tel_hashomer_livneh_clinical_criteria.source: Livneh A et al., 'Criteria for the diagnosis of familial Mediterranean fever', Arthritis Rheum 1997;40:1879-1885 (PMID 9336425)

genetic_testing_mefv.finding: MEFV mutation genetic testing supports the clinical diagnosis, particularly in atypical or clinically ambiguous presentations. The gene was independently cloned and characterised by two consortia in 1997, each identifying missense mutations that co-segregate with disease and are absent from unaffected control chromosomes, establishing MEFV genotyping as a real, mechanistically grounded diagnostic adjunct to the clinical (Tel Hashomer) criteria rather than a replacement for them, since a minority of clinically diagnosed FMF patients do not have both MEFV alleles identified on routine testing.
genetic_testing_mefv.source: French FMF Consortium, Nat Genet 1997;17:25-31 (PMID 9288094); International FMF Consortium, Cell 1997;90:797-807 (PMID 9288758)

colchicine_response_as_diagnostic_suppor.finding: A favourable, sustained clinical response to colchicine prophylaxis is itself one of the criteria in the Tel Hashomer diagnostic framework, reflecting how specific and reproducible colchicine's effect is in genuine FMF - a diagnostic-support role that depends directly on the same real drug effect documented in this entry's natural-history section below.
colchicine_response_as_diagnostic_suppor.source: Livneh A et al., Arthritis Rheum 1997;40:1879-1885 (PMID 9336425)

amyloidosis_risk_and_the_real_colchicine.finding: Untreated, FMF's most serious long-term complication is renal AA amyloidosis leading to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure. This is also the disease's most dramatic, decades-proven treatment success story: in a prospective follow-up of 1070 FMF patients over 4 to 11 years after colchicine was advised, overall nephropathy prevalence fell to one-third of the pre-colchicine-era rate, and life-table analysis showed the cumulative rate of new proteinuria (the earliest marker of amyloid nephropathy) was only 1.7% at 11 years in patients compliant with colchicine prophylaxis, versus 48.9% at 9 years in noncompliant patients (p<0.0001) - a roughly 25-fold difference directly attributable to a single, inexpensive daily oral drug. The study's own conclusion states plainly that 'colchicine prevented amyloidosis in our high-risk population.' Even after amyloid nephropathy was already established, colchicine (at doses above 1.5 mg/day) stabilised or improved proteinuria in the majority of patients with preserved renal function, though not in those who had already progressed to nephrotic syndrome or uraemia. Colchicine's disease-modifying, amyloidosis-preventing effect was first proposed in 1972 and confirmed in the first double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 1974.
amyloidosis_risk_and_the_real_colchicine.source: Zemer D, Pras M, Sohar E, Modan M, Cabili S, Gafni J, 'Colchicine in the prevention and treatment of the amyloidosis of familial Mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1986;314:1001-1005 (PMID 3515182); Livneh A, Zemer D, Langevitz P, Laor A, Sohar E, Pras M, 'Colchicine treatment of AA amyloidosis of familial Mediterranean fever. An analysis of factors affecting outcome', Arthritis Rheum 1994;37:1804-1811 (PMID 7986228); Goldfinger SE, 'Colchicine for familial Mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1972;287:1302 (PMID 4636899); Zemer D et al., 'A controlled trial of colchicine in preventing attacks of familial mediterranean fever', N Engl J Med 1974;291:932-934 (PMID 4606109)

geographic_and_ethnic_prevalence_pattern.finding: FMF occurs with markedly increased frequency among populations of the Eastern Mediterranean basin - historically best documented among Sephardic Jewish, Armenian, Turkish and Arab populations - a pattern already evident in the disease's original 1967 survey of 470 cases and confirmed as a worldwide epidemiological pattern in a dedicated 2009 review devoted specifically to FMF's global distribution. This entry does not restate specific numeric prevalence/carrier-frequency percentages by ethnicity, because a primary source giving independently re-verifiable current figures was not extracted from full text in this research session; the qualitative geographic/ethnic pattern itself is well and repeatedly documented.
geographic_and_ethnic_prevalence_pattern.source: Sohar E et al., Am J Med 1967;43:227-253 (PMID 5340644); Ben-Chetrit E, Touitou I, 'Familial Mediterranean fever in the world', Arthritis Rheum 2009;61:1447-1453 (PMID 19790133)
geographic_and_ethnic_prevalence_pattern.confidence: moderate - the geographic/ethnic pattern itself is high-confidence and repeatedly documented; specific numeric prevalence percentages are deliberately omitted as not independently re-verified from full text this session

complement_deficiency_disorders.name: Complement Deficiency Disorders (Terminal Complement C5-C9 Deficiency and C1-Inhibitor Deficiency / Hereditary Angioedema)
complement_deficiency_disorders.icd11_hint: ICD-10 crosswalk: D84.1 'Defects in the complement system' covers both terminal complement component deficiencies (C5-C9, properdin, factor D) and hereditary angioedema due to C1-inhibitor deficiency/dysfunction (types I and II). The live WHO ICD-11 foundation/linearization browser is a JavaScript single-page application that could not be machine-rendered in this research session, so the exact ICD-11 code (expected under the 4A0- 'complement system disorders' block) is NOT independently machine-verified here and should be confirmed against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool before clinical/billing use.
complement_deficiency_disorders.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Complement deficiency disorders contain two real, distinct medical emergencies that must bypass the normal doctor-approval queue the moment they are suspected: (1) FULMINANT MENINGOCOCCEMIA / INVASIVE MENINGOCOCCAL DISEASE IN TERMINAL (C5-C9) OR PROPERDIN-DEFICIENT PATIENTS - any fever, rash, or systemic illness in a person with known or suspected terminal complement component deficiency, properdin deficiency, or pharmacologic terminal-complement blockade (e.g. eculizumab/ravulizumab therapy) needs same-day emergency evaluation and a very low threshold for empiric antibiotics, because these patients cannot mount a complement-mediated bactericidal/membrane-attack-complex response against Neisseria meningitidis and can deteriorate rapidly. Vaccination is NOT sufficient protection by itself: patients receiving eculizumab (a drug that pharmacologically recreates terminal complement C5 deficiency) have a 1,000- to 2,000-fold increased incidence of invasive meningococcal disease even after receiving meningococcal vaccination (McNamara LA, Topaz N, Wang X, et al, 'High Risk for Invasive Meningococcal Disease Among Patients Receiving Eculizumab (Soliris) Despite Receipt of Meningococcal Vaccine', MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2017;66(27):734-737, PMID 28704351), which is exactly why real-world management of these patients adds prophylactic antibiotics on top of vaccination rather than relying on vaccination alone. A Dutch national pedigree study found that 27% of complement-deficient relatives of meningococcal-disease patients had themselves already had meningococcal disease by the time of screening, rising to 38% for relatives with late (terminal) complement component deficiency specifically (Fijen CA, Kuijper EJ, te Bulte MT, Daha MR, Dankert J, 'Assessment of complement deficiency in patients with meningococcal disease in the Netherlands', Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105, PMID 10028078) - this is a population that has already proven, individually, that it faces a real and recurring risk of a rapidly fatal infection, not merely a theoretical one. Practical rule: any known complement-deficient or eculizumab/ravulizumab-treated patient presenting with fever, headache, neck stiffness, rash (especially non-blanching/petechial), or any other sign compatible with sepsis or meningitis must go to emergency care immediately for empiric antibiotics and blood cultures/lumbar puncture as indicated - this must never be queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow. (2) LARYNGEAL EDEMA / UPPER AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION IN C1-INHIBITOR DEFICIENCY (HEREDITARY ANGIOEDEMA) - HAE laryngeal attacks are a proven, real cause of death by asphyxiation, and dental/oropharyngeal procedures are a documented real trigger: Bork K and Barnstedt SE described four HAE patients who died of asphyxiation after tooth extraction, with laryngeal edema developing after a symptom-free latency of only 4 to 30 hours post-procedure, three of whom had never had a laryngeal attack before ('Laryngeal edema and death from asphyxiation after tooth extraction in four patients with hereditary angioedema', J Am Dent Assoc 2003;134(8):1088-1094, PMID 12956349). Laryngeal edema is not a rare complication in this disease: in a 123-patient cohort, 49.7% (61/123) experienced at least one laryngeal edema episode in their lifetime, mean age at first laryngeal edema was 26.2 years, nearly 80% occurred between ages 11 and 45, and the mean interval between symptom onset and maximum swelling development was 8.3 hours - a real but narrow window in which emergency treatment must be given before the airway closes (Bork K, Ressel N, 'Sudden upper airway obstruction in patients with hereditary angioedema', Transfus Apher Sci 2003;29(3):235-238, PMID 14572815). The US HAE Association Scientific Registry found that 36.9% of HAE-C1INH participants reported having a family member who died from an HAE attack (15.4% for HAE with normal C1-inhibitor), a real, patient-reported signal of how lethal untreated/undertreated laryngeal attacks are within affected families (Christiansen SC, Wilmot J, Castaldo AJ, Zuraw BL, 'The US Hereditary Angioedema Association Scientific Registry', Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2023;131(6):766-774.e8, PMID 37619776). Practical rule: any patient with known or suspected C1-inhibitor deficiency who reports throat tightness, voice change/hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, or tongue/facial/oropharyngeal swelling - especially after dental work, intubation, or minor trauma - must be treated as a laryngeal-edema emergency requiring immediate emergency-department attendance and disease-specific emergency therapy, never watchful waiting and never queued through the routine doctor-approval workflow.

complement_system_overview.finding: The complement system consists of plasma and membrane proteins that mediate the inflammatory response, immune modulation, and host defense. Activation occurs via the classical or alternative pathway, which converge at C3 and share a sequence of terminal components; four steps are critical to its function - classical pathway activation, alternative pathway activation, C3 convertase formation/C3 deposition, and membrane attack complex assembly/insertion. Because complement proteins are activated sequentially and subserve unique functions, complement deficiency states produce predictable, mechanism-specific defects, and complement is most important in host defense against encapsulated bacteria, especially Neisseria meningitidis but also Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
complement_system_overview.source: Figueroa JE, Densen P, 'Infectious diseases associated with complement deficiencies', Clin Microbiol Rev 1991;4(3):359-395 (PMID 1889047)
complement_system_overview.confidence: high - direct finding from this foundational review's abstract

terminal_pathway_mechanism.finding: Terminal complement components (C5, C6, C7, C8, C9) assemble the membrane attack complex (MAC), which forms a pore in the bacterial outer membrane and is the principal complement-mediated bactericidal mechanism against Neisseria species; deficiency of any terminal component prevents MAC formation and abolishes complement-mediated killing of Neisseria, which is why terminal complement deficiencies present specifically and repeatedly with neisserial infections rather than the broader pyogenic infection pattern seen with early classical-pathway or opsonic defects.
terminal_pathway_mechanism.source: Figueroa JE, Densen P, Clin Microbiol Rev 1991;4(3):359-395 (PMID 1889047); Rauscher CK, Fajt ML, Bryk J, Petrov AA, 'Clinical implications of C6 complement component deficiency', Allergy Asthma Proc 2020;41(5):386-388 (PMID 32867893)

pharmacologic_terminal_complement_blocka.finding: Eculizumab (and related C5-blocking agents such as ravulizumab), used therapeutically for conditions such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, pharmacologically recreates a terminal (C5) complement deficiency state and confers a real, very large increase in meningococcal disease risk even in vaccinated patients - a directly analogous acquired counterpart of the genetic terminal complement deficiencies covered here.
pharmacologic_terminal_complement_blocka.source: McNamara LA, Topaz N, Wang X, et al, 'High Risk for Invasive Meningococcal Disease Among Patients Receiving Eculizumab (Soliris) Despite Receipt of Meningococcal Vaccine', MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2017;66(27):734-737 (PMID 28704351)

c1_inhibitor_deficiency_mechanism.finding: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) due to C1-inhibitor deficiency is clinically characterized by relapsing skin swellings, abdominal pain attacks, and life-threatening upper airway obstruction; C1-inhibitor is the principal regulator of the contact (kallikrein-kinin) and classical complement pathways, and its deficiency or dysfunction leads to unregulated bradykinin generation, producing episodic, non-pitting, non-pruritic angioedema without accompanying urticaria (the classic feature distinguishing it from mast-cell/histaminergic angioedema).
c1_inhibitor_deficiency_mechanism.source: Bork K, Meng G, Staubach P, Hardt J, 'Hereditary angioedema: new findings concerning symptoms, affected organs, and course', Am J Med 2006;119(3):267-274 (PMID 16490473)

other_component_deficiencies_mechanism.finding: Deficiency of complement regulatory/alternative-pathway proteins such as complement factor I (CFI) impairs regulation of the alternative pathway, causing secondary consumption of C3 and predisposing to both recurrent infection with encapsulated organisms (particularly Neisseria meningitidis) and immune-dysregulatory disease (rheumatologic, neurologic, and renal manifestations including atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome/glomerulopathy); properdin deficiency, an X-linked positive regulator of the alternative pathway, similarly predisposes specifically to meningococcal disease.
other_component_deficiencies_mechanism.source: Rajabi E, Kheirabadi MC, Olyaei NA, et al, 'Complete Complement Factor I (CFI) deficiency: a systematic review of forty-nine patients including three novel cases', BMC Immunol 2025;26(1):54 (PMID 40713518); Fijen CA et al, Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105 (PMID 10028078)

terminal_complement_C5_C9_deficiency.finding: Genetic deficiency of any terminal complement component (C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9) prevents membrane attack complex formation. C6 deficiency is described as the most common terminal complement component deficiency and can present even later in life with Neisseria meningitidis infection. Acquired, pharmacologic terminal (C5) blockade with eculizumab/ravulizumab produces a clinically analogous state.
terminal_complement_C5_C9_deficiency.source: Rauscher CK et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2020;41(5):386-388 (PMID 32867893); McNamara LA et al, MMWR 2017;66(27):734-737 (PMID 28704351)

c1_inhibitor_deficiency_hae.finding: The International/Canadian Hereditary Angioedema Guideline classifies C1-inhibitor-related HAE into Type I (reduced antigenic C1-inhibitor level and reduced function) and Type II (normal or elevated but dysfunctional C1-inhibitor protein, with reduced function), both with low C4; a separate, newer category - HAE with normal C1-inhibitor (HAE-nl-C1INH, including genetically defined subtypes such as those linked to F12, ANGPT1, PLG, and KNG1 mutations) - has normal C1-inhibitor level, function, and C4, and is diagnosed on clinical grounds plus, where available, genetic testing.
c1_inhibitor_deficiency_hae.source: Betschel S, Badiou J, Binkley K, et al, 'The International/Canadian Hereditary Angioedema Guideline', Allergy Asthma Clin Immunol 2019;15:72 (PMID 31788005)

other_complement_component_deficiencies.finding: Deficiencies of early classical-pathway components (C1q, C2, C4) are real, described entities most classically associated with lupus-like autoimmune disease and recurrent pyogenic (not specifically neisserial) infection; deficiencies of alternative-pathway regulators (complement factor I, factor H) and the alternative-pathway positive regulator properdin are real entities that predispose specifically to recurrent meningococcal disease and, for factor I, additionally to immune-dysregulatory disease including atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.
other_complement_component_deficiencies.source: Rajabi E et al, BMC Immunol 2025;26(1):54 (PMID 40713518); Fijen CA et al, Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105 (PMID 10028078)
other_complement_component_deficiencies.confidence: high for properdin/factor I associations; the C1q/C2/C4-lupus association is well-established teaching but was not re-derived from a freshly fetched primary source in this session and is therefore stated only in general terms

recurrent_neisseria_infections_terminal_.finding: In a Dutch national cohort, complement deficiency was found in 3% of 176 screened meningococcal disease patients overall, rising to 33% among patients whose meningococcal infection was due to uncommon or nongroupable serogroups - a real clinical clue that recurrent or serogroup-atypical meningococcal disease should prompt complement testing. Only 27% of identified complement-deficient relatives had themselves already had meningococcal disease at the time of screening (38% for late/terminal component deficiency, 18% for properdin deficiency), showing that many affected relatives are still at risk and had not yet had a recognized episode.
recurrent_neisseria_infections_terminal_.source: Fijen CA, Kuijper EJ, te Bulte MT, Daha MR, Dankert J, Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105 (PMID 10028078)

cfi_deficiency_infectious_and_dysregulat.finding: In a systematic review of 49 patients with complete complement factor I deficiency, 75.5% presented with infectious manifestations (36.7% specifically with sepsis), with encapsulated organisms - particularly Neisseria meningitidis - as the predominant pathogens; immune-dysregulatory manifestations were also common, involving rheumatologic (28.6%), neurologic (22.4%), and renal (16.3%) disease, and low or absent C3 and CFI levels were seen in most patients.
cfi_deficiency_infectious_and_dysregulat.source: Rajabi E et al, BMC Immunol 2025;26(1):54 (PMID 40713518)

recurrent_angioedema_without_urticaria_h.finding: HAE due to C1-inhibitor deficiency is characterized by recurrent, self-limited, non-pruritic swelling episodes without accompanying urticaria (skin swellings of the extremities, face, genitals, and trunk, plus abdominal pain attacks) that together made up 97.4% of all recorded edema episodes in a 221-patient cohort; less common episode locations included laryngeal edema (0.9% of episodes), soft palate (0.6%), tongue (0.3%), and headache (0.7%). Clinical symptoms started at a mean age of 11.2 (SD 7.7) years, and over a cumulative 5,736 patient-years of follow-up only 6.5% were symptom-free years.
recurrent_angioedema_without_urticaria_h.source: Bork K, Meng G, Staubach P, Hardt J, Am J Med 2006;119(3):267-274 (PMID 16490473)
recurrent_angioedema_without_urticaria_h.confidence: high; note the source abstract's total episode count is rendered ambiguously in the fetched text (appears as '131110', most plausibly a thousands-separator artifact for a number in the low-to-mid five-figure range) - the percentage-based and per-patient findings quoted above are unambiguous and are what is used here

ch50_ah50_functional_screening.finding: Total hemolytic complement (CH50, screens the classical pathway through C9) is the standard first-line functional screening test for a suspected complement deficiency; patients with a terminal complement component deficiency can be screened by checking CH50, which will be markedly reduced or absent. AH50 (alternative pathway hemolytic complement) is the analogous functional screen for alternative-pathway defects such as properdin or factor D deficiency. A markedly low or absent CH50/AH50 on a fresh, properly handled sample should be repeated before proceeding to individual component assays, since improper specimen handling can produce a spuriously low result.
ch50_ah50_functional_screening.source: Rauscher CK et al, Allergy Asthma Proc 2020;41(5):386-388 (PMID 32867893); Devonshire AL, Makhija M, 'Approach to primary immunodeficiency', Allergy Asthma Proc 2019;40(6):465-469 (PMID 31690396)

specific_complement_component_levels.finding: Once a functional screening assay (CH50/AH50) localizes the defect to the classical, alternative, or terminal pathway, specific antigenic and/or functional levels of individual components (C3, C4, C5, C6, C7, C8, C9, factor B, factor D, factor H, factor I, properdin) are measured to pinpoint the exact deficient protein; in the CFI-deficiency systematic review, immunological work-up in most patients showed low or absent levels of both C3 and CFI, illustrating this component-by-component localization approach in practice.
specific_complement_component_levels.source: Rajabi E et al, BMC Immunol 2025;26(1):54 (PMID 40713518)

c1_inh_level_function_and_c4_for_hae.finding: Diagnosis of C1-inhibitor-related HAE relies on C4 level (typically low, a useful and inexpensive first screen) plus C1-inhibitor antigenic level and C1-inhibitor functional (chromogenic) assay: Type I HAE shows low C1-inhibitor antigen and low function; Type II HAE shows normal or elevated C1-inhibitor antigen but low function (i.e., function must always be checked even if the antigenic level looks normal); HAE with normal C1-inhibitor shows normal C1-inhibitor level, function, and C4, and is instead identified through clinical criteria and, where available, genetic testing for the associated mutations.
c1_inh_level_function_and_c4_for_hae.source: Betschel S et al, Allergy Asthma Clin Immunol 2019;15:72 (PMID 31788005)

acquired_c1_inhibitor_deficiency_and_oth.finding: Angioedema without urticaria also occurs in acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency (typically associated with lymphoproliferative disease or autoantibodies to C1-inhibitor, presenting later in life without the family history seen in hereditary forms) and in ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema (a separate, drug-triggered bradykinin-mediated mechanism); both must be distinguished from hereditary C1-inhibitor deficiency, alongside mast-cell/histaminergic angioedema (which characteristically does present with urticaria and responds to antihistamines, unlike C1-inhibitor-deficiency-related angioedema).
acquired_c1_inhibitor_deficiency_and_oth.source: Betschel S et al, Allergy Asthma Clin Immunol 2019;15:72 (PMID 31788005)
acquired_c1_inhibitor_deficiency_and_oth.confidence: moderate-high - the general differential categories are stated in the cited international guideline; individual epidemiologic figures for each differential diagnosis were not independently re-extracted in this session

other_primary_immunodeficiencies_present.finding: Recurrent neisserial or other encapsulated-organism infection should also prompt evaluation for asplenia/hyposplenism, antibody (humoral) immunodeficiency, and other primary immunodeficiencies, since these share an overlapping clinical presentation of recurrent bacterial infection with encapsulated organisms; a stepwise initial screen (complete blood count with differential, serum immunoglobulins, complement levels) helps localize which arm of host defense - phagocytic, humoral, complement, or T-cell - is defective.
other_primary_immunodeficiencies_present.source: Reust CE, 'Evaluation of primary immunodeficiency disease in children', Am Fam Physician 2013;87(11):773-778 (PMID 23939499); Devonshire AL, Makhija M, Allergy Asthma Proc 2019;40(6):465-469 (PMID 31690396)
other_primary_immunodeficiencies_present.confidence: high for the general diagnostic-localization framework

family_history_and_inheritance.finding: Most terminal complement component deficiencies and factor I deficiency are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, while properdin deficiency is X-linked; family/pedigree screening is explicitly recommended once an index case is identified, since a Dutch cohort found that screening relatives of patients with meningococcal disease due to uncommon serogroups who were 5 years of age or older identified 30 of 33 complement-deficient families in the study. C1-inhibitor-related HAE is autosomal dominant, so first-degree relatives of an affected patient have a real, quantifiable risk and are a specific recommended screening population.
family_history_and_inheritance.source: Fijen CA et al, Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105 (PMID 10028078); Betschel S et al, Allergy Asthma Clin Immunol 2019;15:72 (PMID 31788005)

atypical_or_recurrent_meningococcal_sero.finding: Infection with an uncommon or nongroupable meningococcal serogroup, or recurrent meningococcal disease of any serogroup, is a real, specific clinical trigger for complement work-up: complement deficiency was found in 33% of patients with meningococcal disease due to uncommon serogroups versus 3% of all screened meningococcal disease patients.
atypical_or_recurrent_meningococcal_sero.source: Fijen CA et al, Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105 (PMID 10028078)

hae_diagnostic_delay_and_registry_demogr.finding: In the US Hereditary Angioedema Association Scientific Registry (485 HAE-C1INH, 26 HAE-nl-C1INH, and 70 idiopathic non-histaminergic angioedema participants collected 2009-2021), the delay to diagnosis was shorter for HAE-C1INH than for the combined HAE-nl-C1INH/INHA group (5 years versus 11 years), though both improved over time; morbidity surrogates (emergency department visits, hospitalizations, unnecessary abdominal surgeries, intubations) were described as strikingly high.
hae_diagnostic_delay_and_registry_demogr.source: Christiansen SC, Wilmot J, Castaldo AJ, Zuraw BL, Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2023;131(6):766-774.e8 (PMID 37619776)

infection_risk_without_prophylaxis_termi.finding: Complement-deficient relatives of meningococcal-disease patients identified through family screening had already had meningococcal disease themselves in 27% of cases overall by the time of screening, with a clearly higher cumulative risk for late (terminal) complement component deficiency (38%) than for properdin deficiency (18%) - real, quantified evidence that terminal complement deficiency in particular carries a substantial lifetime risk of invasive meningococcal disease if unrecognized and unprotected.
infection_risk_without_prophylaxis_termi.source: Fijen CA, Kuijper EJ, te Bulte MT, Daha MR, Dankert J, Clin Infect Dis 1999;28(1):98-105 (PMID 10028078)

vaccination_reduces_recurrence_real_comp.finding: In a Russian cohort of 45 patients with late complement component deficiency who had already had one to five prior meningococcal infections, 31 were vaccinated with a tetravalent (A/C/W135/Y) meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine and followed for 3-8 years: six new meningococcal infection episodes occurred in four of the 31 vaccinated patients, versus six episodes in six of 14 unvaccinated patients over the same period, and survival analysis showed a statistically significant reduction in the risk of contracting meningococcal disease among vaccinees compared with non-vaccinees (P<0.05).
vaccination_reduces_recurrence_real_comp.source: Platonov AE, Vershinina IV, Kuijper EJ, Borrow R, Käyhty H, 'Long term effects of vaccination of patients deficient in a late complement component with a tetravalent meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine', Vaccine 2003;21(27-30):4437-4447 (PMID 14505927)

cfi_deficiency_natural_course.finding: Across 49 published patients with complete complement factor I deficiency (cases from 1996 to November 2024), mean age at initial presentation was 7.19 (SD 9.75) years; the disease course spans a spectrum from asymptomatic to recurrent severe infection (75.5% with infectious presentation, 36.7% specifically with sepsis) and immune dysregulation (rheumatologic 28.6%, neurologic 22.4%, renal 16.3%), indicating a real and clinically significant, though heterogeneous, natural history if the deficiency is not identified and managed.
cfi_deficiency_natural_course.source: Rajabi E et al, BMC Immunol 2025;26(1):54 (PMID 40713518)

hae_untreated_attack_burden.finding: Over a cumulative 5,736 patient-years of follow-up in 221 HAE patients, only 6.5% were symptom-free years, meaning the great majority of a C1-inhibitor-deficient patient's life is punctuated by edema episodes if the disease is not adequately controlled; onset began at a mean age of 11.2 years, and women had a more severe disease course than men on average.
hae_untreated_attack_burden.source: Bork K, Meng G, Staubach P, Hardt J, Am J Med 2006;119(3):267-274 (PMID 16490473)

hae_laryngeal_attack_risk_and_real_morta.finding: In a 123-patient HAE cohort, 49.7% (61/123) experienced at least one laryngeal edema episode (596 episodes total), at a mean age of first occurrence of 26.2 years, with nearly 80% of laryngeal episodes occurring between ages 11 and 45; the mean interval from symptom onset to maximal swelling was 8.3 hours. Separately, four real, individually documented patient deaths from asphyxiation after tooth extraction were reported, with a symptom-free latency of only 4-30 hours after the procedure before fatal laryngeal edema developed, and in three of the four patients laryngeal edema had never occurred before. In the US HAE Association registry, 36.9% of HAE-C1INH participants (versus 15.4% of HAE-nl-C1INH participants) reported that a family member had died from an HAE attack - a real, patient-reported natural-history signal of mortality risk when laryngeal attacks are not promptly treated.
hae_laryngeal_attack_risk_and_real_morta.source: Bork K, Ressel N, Transfus Apher Sci 2003;29(3):235-238 (PMID 14572815); Bork K, Barnstedt SE, J Am Dent Assoc 2003;134(8):1088-1094 (PMID 12956349); Christiansen SC et al, Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2023;131(6):766-774.e8 (PMID 37619776)

clinical_takeaway.finding: Complement deficiency disorders split into two clinically distinct real emergencies sharing one root cause (a missing or malfunctioning complement protein): terminal (C5-C9) and alternative-pathway (properdin, factor I) deficiencies leave patients unable to kill Neisseria via the membrane attack complex, producing a real, quantified, substantial lifetime risk of invasive meningococcal disease (27-38% by the time of family screening) that is significantly reduced by meningococcal vaccination (P<0.05 in a real comparative cohort) - though vaccination alone is not fully protective, as shown starkly in eculizumab-treated patients (1,000- to 2,000-fold increased risk despite vaccination). C1-inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema) instead removes the brake on bradykinin generation, producing recurrent non-urticarial swelling that occupies the majority of a patient's life if untreated (93.5% of years affected) and, in its laryngeal form, is a real, individually documented cause of death by asphyxiation - most vividly seen in tooth-extraction-triggered fatalities occurring within 4-30 hours of a routine dental procedure. Both entities therefore demand the same clinical posture: recognize the pattern early (recurrent/atypical-serogroup meningococcal disease, or recurrent non-urticarial swelling with a family history), confirm with the correct functional/level-based complement assay, and treat the underlying risk aggressively rather than only the individual infection or swelling episode.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesized from all sources cited above in this entry
clinical_takeaway.confidence: high - each individual quantitative claim is independently sourced above; this is a narrative synthesis of already-cited findings, not a new independent data point

complement_deficiency_disorders.CURABILITY_NOTE: Complement deficiency disorders are genetic and are not curable at the root cause today - there is no gene therapy or transplant that restores normal complement protein function for either terminal complement deficiency or C1-inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency (hereditary angioedema, HAE). But this is a real example of prevention functioning as a near-total practical substitute for cure, with dramatic, trial-documented reductions in disease burden. (1) Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9/properdin/factor D): these patients are at markedly increased lifetime risk of recurrent invasive Neisseria meningitidis disease because the membrane attack complex cannot form. Real vaccine-response data in complement-deficient patients show that immunization with tetravalent (A/C/Y/W) meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine produces protective serum bactericidal antibody (SBA >= 8) in 85.7-92.5% of C2-deficient patients across all four serogroups (p<0.001 vs pre-vaccination titres) - Brodszki N et al., Vaccine 2015;33(15):1839-1845 (PMID 25707694). An earlier controlled study in late complement component-deficient (LCCD) individuals found capsular polysaccharide antibody after vaccination was comparable to normal individuals and that this antibody, not sub-capsular antibody, was what mediated meningococcal killing in both complement- and phagocyte-dependent bactericidal assays, supporting vaccination as a real preventive measure in this population - Andreoni J, Kayhty H, Densen P, J Infect Dis 1993;168(1):227-231 (PMID 8515116). The foundational review of complement deficiency states concluded that 'the availability of effective polysaccharide vaccines and antibiotics provides an immunologic and chemotherapeutic rationale for preventing and treating infection in patients with these deficiencies' - Figueroa JE, Densen P, Clin Microbiol Rev 1991;4(3):359-395 (PMID 1889047). (2) C1-inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema): modern targeted prophylactic therapy has converted a disease of unpredictable, sometimes airway-threatening swelling attacks into a largely controlled chronic condition, with real placebo-controlled trial reductions of roughly 50-87% in attack frequency depending on agent and dose: lanadelumab (HELP trial) cut the mean monthly attack rate from a placebo-period 1.97 to 0.26 with the 300 mg every-2-week dose, an 86.8% relative reduction (mean difference -1.71 attacks/month, 95% CI -2.09 to -1.33, p<0.001) - Banerji A et al., JAMA 2018;320(20):2108-2121 (PMID 30480729); nanofiltered C1-INH concentrate prophylaxis (the CHANGE study) cut attacks per 12-week period from 12.73 (placebo) to 6.26, a 50.8% reduction (p<0.001) - Zuraw BL et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363(6):513-522 (PMID 20818886); berotralstat 150 mg once daily (APeX-2) cut the monthly attack rate from 2.35 (placebo) to 1.31, a 44.3% reduction (p<0.001) - Zuraw B et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2021;148(1):164-172 (PMID 33098856); and for acute attacks, icatibant (FAST-3) cut the median time to 50%-or-greater symptom relief from 19.8 hours (placebo) to 2.0 hours, an 89.9% relative reduction in time-to-relief (p<0.001) - Lumry WR et al., Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2011;107(6):529-537 (PMID 22123383). These 2- to 10-fold real effect sizes are why the international WAO/EAACI HAE guideline now recommends long-term prophylaxis be offered to essentially all symptomatic HAE patients rather than reserved for the most severe cases - Maurer M et al., Allergy 2022;77(7):1961-1990 (PMID 35006617); Maurer M et al., World Allergy Organ J 2022;15(3):100627 (PMID 35497649).

curative_option.note: Neither condition has a cure for the underlying genetic complement defect. The two real best-evidence 'as-close-to-cure-as-exists' strategies are: (a) meningococcal vaccination plus antibiotic prophylaxis for terminal complement deficiency, which drives invasive meningococcal risk down toward that of the general population, and (b) modern targeted long-term prophylaxis for C1-INH deficiency/HAE, which drives attack frequency down 44-87% and, in individual responders, to near-zero attacks.

terminal_complement_deficiency.name: Meningococcal Vaccination Plus Antibiotic Prophylaxis - Real Best-Evidence Preventive Strategy for Terminal Complement Deficiency
terminal_complement_deficiency.type: Preventive immunization and chemoprophylaxis (not a cure of the underlying complement defect)
specific_drugs: Quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY, e.g. Menveo/MenQuadfi) plus serogroup B meningococcal vaccine (MenB, e.g. Bexsero/Trumenba), per WHO/national immunization guidance for complement-deficient patients
Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. daily penicillin or an equivalent agent per treating physician's regimen) in patients with recurrent invasive meningococcal disease despite vaccination

real_outcome_data.c2_deficient_vaccine_response: 85.7-92.5% of C2-deficient patients (n=22) achieved a protective serum bactericidal antibody titre (SBA >= 8) against all four vaccine serogroups (A, C, Y, W) after tetravalent meningococcal polysaccharide vaccination, with post-vaccination titres for serogroups C, Y and W statistically equal to healthy controls (p<0.001 vs pre-vaccination) - Brodszki N et al., Vaccine 2015;33(15):1839-1845 (PMID 25707694)
real_outcome_data.lccd_vaccine_antibody_function: Late complement component-deficient (LCCD) individuals (n=8) mounted capsular polysaccharide antibody responses comparable to unrelated normal individuals (n=7) and heterozygous family members (n=11); this capsular antibody, not sub-capsular antibody, mediated meningococcal killing in complement- and phagocyte-dependent bactericidal assays, supporting vaccination as protective in this group - Andreoni J, Kayhty H, Densen P, J Infect Dis 1993;168(1):227-231 (PMID 8515116)

terminal_complement_deficiency.source: Brodszki N et al., Vaccine 2015;33(15):1839-1845 (PMID 25707694); Andreoni J et al., J Infect Dis 1993;168(1):227-231 (PMID 8515116); Figueroa JE, Densen P, Clin Microbiol Rev 1991;4(3):359-395 (PMID 1889047)

c1_inhibitor_deficiency_hae.name: Modern Targeted Long-Term Prophylaxis - Real Best-Evidence Preventive Strategy for Hereditary Angioedema
c1_inhibitor_deficiency_hae.type: Prophylactic biologic/small-molecule and plasma-derived protein therapy (not a cure of the underlying SERPING1/C1-INH defect)
specific_drugs: Lanadelumab (Takhzyro), subcutaneous monoclonal antibody against plasma kallikrein
Berotralstat (Orladeyo), oral once-daily plasma kallikrein inhibitor
Plasma-derived or recombinant C1-inhibitor concentrate (e.g. Cinryze, Haegarda), given as scheduled prophylactic IV or subcutaneous injections

real_outcome_data.help_trial_lanadelumab: Mean monthly hereditary angioedema attack rate fell from a placebo-period 1.97 to 0.26 with lanadelumab 300 mg every 2 weeks during the 26-week treatment period (mean difference -1.71 attacks/month, 95% CI -2.09 to -1.33, p<0.001), an 86.8% relative reduction - Banerji A et al., JAMA 2018;320(20):2108-2121 (PMID 30480729)
real_outcome_data.change_study_c1inh_prophylaxis: Attacks per 12-week period fell from 12.73 with placebo to 6.26 with twice-weekly nanofiltered C1-inhibitor concentrate prophylaxis (p<0.001), a 50.8% reduction, in a 22-subject crossover trial - Zuraw BL et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363(6):513-522 (PMID 20818886)
real_outcome_data.apex2_berotralstat: Monthly attack rate fell from 2.35 with placebo to 1.31 with berotralstat 150 mg once daily (p<0.001, 44.3% reduction) and to 1.65 with the 110 mg dose (p=0.024, 29.8% reduction), n=120 - Zuraw B et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2021;148(1):164-172 (PMID 33098856)

c1_inhibitor_deficiency_hae.source: Banerji A et al., JAMA 2018;320(20):2108-2121 (PMID 30480729); Zuraw BL et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363(6):513-522 (PMID 20818886); Zuraw B et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2021;148(1):164-172 (PMID 33098856)

cdd_meningococcal_vaccination.name: Tetravalent (A/C/Y/W) Meningococcal Polysaccharide/Conjugate Vaccination in Complement-Deficient Patients
specific_drugs: Tetravalent meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine (historical trials) / modern MenACWY conjugate vaccine plus MenB vaccine per current guidance
cdd_meningococcal_vaccination.effectiveness: 85.7-92.5% of C2-deficient patients achieved protective serum bactericidal antibody titres (SBA >= 8) against all four serogroups (p<0.001 vs pre-vaccination); post-vaccination titres for serogroups C, Y, W were statistically equal to healthy controls
cdd_meningococcal_vaccination.reason_why: Complement-deficient patients cannot form the membrane attack complex needed to lyse Neisseria meningitidis directly, so they depend critically on opsonizing/bactericidal antibody to capsular polysaccharide for protection; vaccination supplies that antibody and capsular (not sub-capsular) antibody was shown to mediate meningococcal killing in both complement- and phagocyte-dependent bactericidal assays.
cdd_meningococcal_vaccination.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-recommended preventive measure for all patients with terminal complement pathway deficiency.
cdd_meningococcal_vaccination.source: Brodszki N et al., Vaccine 2015;33(15):1839-1845 (PMID 25707694); Andreoni J et al., J Infect Dis 1993;168(1):227-231 (PMID 8515116)

cdd_prophylactic_antibiotics.name: Long-Term Antibiotic Chemoprophylaxis in Terminal Complement Deficiency
specific_drugs: Daily oral penicillin or an equivalent antibiotic per treating physician's regimen, used alongside vaccination especially in patients with recurrent invasive meningococcal disease despite immunization
cdd_prophylactic_antibiotics.effectiveness: No dedicated randomized efficacy trial was identified in this session; the rationale is described qualitatively in the foundational complement-deficiency literature as a real chemotherapeutic complement to vaccination, not independently quantified as a percentage here
cdd_prophylactic_antibiotics.reason_why: Vaccination alone does not eliminate all invasive meningococcal risk in terminal complement deficiency (documented vaccine breakthrough/recurrent cases exist), so antibiotic prophylaxis is used as an additional real-world risk-reduction layer, particularly after a first invasive episode.
cdd_prophylactic_antibiotics.real_working_solution: Yes, as an adjunct to vaccination - real standard-of-care recommendation, though this session could not source a dedicated randomized-trial effectiveness percentage for antibiotic prophylaxis alone.
cdd_prophylactic_antibiotics.source: Figueroa JE, Densen P, Clin Microbiol Rev 1991;4(3):359-395 (PMID 1889047)
cdd_prophylactic_antibiotics.confidence: moderate - qualitative recommendation, no dedicated RCT-derived percentage found

cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.name: Nanofiltered C1-Inhibitor Concentrate - Acute Attack Treatment
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.type: Plasma-derived protein replacement, acute IV therapy
specific_drugs: Nanofiltered C1 inhibitor concentrate (Cinryze), 1000 units IV, one or two doses for an acute attack
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.effectiveness: Median time to onset of unequivocal relief from an acute attack was 2 hours with C1-inhibitor concentrate versus longer than 4 hours with placebo (p=0.02), n=68
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.reason_why: Directly replaces the deficient/dysfunctional C1-inhibitor protein, restoring control of the contact (kallikrein-kinin) and complement cascades that generate bradykinin-driven vascular permeability during an attack.
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-recognized acute treatment for HAE attacks.
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.source: Zuraw BL et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363(6):513-522 (PMID 20818886)

cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.name: Nanofiltered C1-Inhibitor Concentrate - Twice-Weekly Prophylaxis
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.type: Plasma-derived protein replacement, scheduled prophylactic IV/SC therapy
specific_drugs: Nanofiltered C1 inhibitor concentrate (Cinryze) 1000 units IV twice weekly, or subcutaneous C1-INH (Haegarda) per current dosing
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.effectiveness: 6.26 attacks per 12-week period with prophylactic C1-inhibitor concentrate versus 12.73 with placebo (p<0.001), a 50.8% reduction, in a 22-subject crossover trial (the CHANGE study), with significant reductions also in attack severity, duration, rescue-medication use and total days with swelling
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.reason_why: Maintaining a higher circulating trough level of functional C1-inhibitor continuously suppresses excess bradykinin generation before an attack can be triggered, rather than only treating attacks after they start.
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-recommended long-term prophylactic option for HAE.
cdd_c1_inhibitor_concentrate.source: Zuraw BL et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363(6):513-522 (PMID 20818886)

cdd_icatibant.name: Icatibant - Bradykinin B2-Receptor Antagonist for Acute HAE Attacks
cdd_icatibant.type: Small-molecule receptor antagonist, acute subcutaneous therapy
cdd_icatibant.effectiveness: Median time to 50% or more reduction in symptom severity was 2.0 hours with icatibant versus 19.8 hours with placebo (p<0.001, primary endpoint); median time to onset of primary symptom relief was 1.5 vs 18.5 hours (p<0.001); no icatibant-treated subject required rescue medication before symptom relief, n=88 (FAST-3 trial)
cdd_icatibant.reason_why: Bradykinin, not histamine, drives HAE swelling; icatibant directly blocks the bradykinin B2 receptor that mediates the vascular permeability and pain of an attack, so it interrupts the attack mechanism itself rather than treating a downstream allergic pathway.
cdd_icatibant.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-standard acute on-demand treatment for HAE attacks, including laryngeal attacks.
cdd_icatibant.source: Lumry WR et al., Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2011;107(6):529-537 (PMID 22123383)

cdd_lanadelumab.name: Lanadelumab - Monoclonal Antibody Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor (HELP Trial)
cdd_lanadelumab.type: Fully human monoclonal antibody, subcutaneous prophylactic therapy
specific_drugs: Lanadelumab (Takhzyro) 300 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks (most effective dose) or every 4 weeks
cdd_lanadelumab.effectiveness: Mean monthly attack rate fell from a placebo-period 1.97 to 0.26 with the 300 mg every-2-week dose (mean difference -1.71, 95% CI -2.09 to -1.33, p<0.001), an 86.8% relative reduction; the 300 mg every-4-week (-1.44, p<0.001) and 150 mg every-4-week (-1.49, p<0.001) doses were also significantly effective, n=125 randomized
cdd_lanadelumab.reason_why: Lanadelumab selectively and durably inhibits active plasma kallikrein, the enzyme that generates bradykinin from high-molecular-weight kininogen; because C1-INH deficiency leaves this pathway unchecked, direct kallikrein inhibition prevents the excess bradykinin generation that causes attacks before they start.
cdd_lanadelumab.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-recommended first-line long-term prophylactic therapy for HAE types I/II.

cdd_berotralstat.name: Berotralstat - Oral Once-Daily Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor (APeX-2 Trial)
specific_drugs: Berotralstat (Orladeyo) 150 mg once daily (most favorable benefit-risk dose) or 110 mg once daily
cdd_berotralstat.effectiveness: Monthly attack rate fell from 2.35 (placebo) to 1.31 with the 150 mg dose (p<0.001, 44.3% reduction) and to 1.65 with the 110 mg dose (p=0.024, 29.8% reduction) over 24 weeks, n=120 randomized; efficacy and safety were sustained through 48 weeks in the Part 2 extension
cdd_berotralstat.reason_why: Like lanadelumab, berotralstat blocks plasma kallikrein activity to suppress bradykinin generation, but as a small molecule it is taken orally once daily rather than by injection, giving HAE patients a real needle-free long-term prophylactic option.
cdd_berotralstat.real_working_solution: Yes - real, guideline-recognized oral long-term prophylactic option for HAE, an alternative for patients who prefer or need to avoid injections.
cdd_berotralstat.source: Zuraw B et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2021;148(1):164-172 (PMID 33098856); Wedner HJ et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2021;9(6):2305-2314 (PMID 33866032)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (acute time-to-relief reduction, vaccine seroprotection response rate, and long-term attack-rate reduction versus placebo) from different trials/populations placed on one comparative percentage scale for ranking purposes, not a claim that a single number captures 'how good' each option is in isolation, or a head-to-head comparison across the two distinct diseases (terminal complement deficiency vs C1-INH deficiency/HAE) covered by this entry.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lanadelumab 300 mg every 2 weeks for HAE prophylaxis (HELP trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in mean monthly attack rate vs placebo (0.26 vs 1.97 attacks/month), n=125

ranked_high_to_low.name: Meningococcal polysaccharide vaccination in C2-deficient patients

ranked_high_to_low.name: Berotralstat 150 mg/day for HAE prophylaxis (APeX-2 trial)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Relative reduction in monthly attack rate vs placebo (1.31 vs 2.35), n=120
