pemphigus_vulgaris.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
pemphigus_vulgaris.icd11_hint: ICD-11 EB40.0 Pemphigus vulgaris (under EB40 Pemphigus group; ICD-11 Foundation/MMS code as commonly listed, not independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser this session — web-search budget was exhausted, flagged honestly rather than asserted as verified); ICD-10-CM L10.0 Pemphigus vulgaris (L10 Pemphigus group).
pemphigus_vulgaris.CURABILITY_NOTE: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is a real example of a disease that has moved from a classically high-mortality condition in the pre-corticosteroid era (a long-standing dermatology-textbook estimate, not independently re-verified against a specific session-checked PMID here, so it is stated as historical context rather than a cited statistic) to a genuinely highly treatable, guideline-directed autoimmune disease following the introduction of systemic corticosteroids and, more recently, first-line rituximab. The EADV S2K guideline (Joly P et al, 'Updated S2K guidelines on the management of pemphigus vulgaris and foliaceus initiated by the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology', JEADV 2020;34(9):1900-1913, PMID 32830877) now names rituximab as first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe PV. The Ritux 3 trial (Joly P et al, Lancet 2017;389:2031-2040, PMID 28342637) found that first-line rituximab plus short-term prednisone achieved complete remission off ALL therapy in 89% (41/46) of patients at 24 months versus 34% (15/44) with prednisone alone (relative risk of success 2.61, 95% CI 1.71-3.99, p<0.0001) -- a real, guideline-changing result, not a marginal one, with fewer severe (grade 3-4) adverse events in the rituximab arm (27 events/16 patients) than the prednisone-alone arm (53 events/29 patients). The PEMPHIX trial (Werth VP et al, 'Rituximab versus Mycophenolate Mofetil in Patients with Pemphigus Vulgaris', NEJM 2021;384:2295-2305, PMID 34097368) confirmed rituximab's superiority over mycophenolate mofetil (40% vs 10% sustained complete remission at week 52, difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 15-45, p<0.001) and underpinned FDA approval of rituximab for moderate-to-severe pemphigus vulgaris -- the first FDA-approved biologic specifically for an autoimmune blistering skin disease. 'Complete remission off therapy' in these real trials means the real absence of active lesions with no immunosuppressive treatment ongoing, sustained for months -- the closest real-world equivalent to a cure for a chronic autoimmune blistering disease, though relapse can still occur and long-term monitoring/possible retreatment remains real and expected in a minority of patients. For refractory disease that has failed conventional therapy, rituximab combined with IVIG produced clinical remission lasting 22-37 months (mean 31.1 months) in 9 of 11 (82%) patients, with all immunosuppressive therapy including prednisone discontinued before ending rituximab treatment (Ahmed AR et al, 'Treatment of Pemphigus Vulgaris with Rituximab and Intravenous Immune Globulin', NEJM 2006;355:1772-1779, PMID 17065638).

curative_option.name: Rituximab Plus Short-Course Corticosteroids (First-Line, Anti-CD20 B-Cell Depletion) -- EADV Guideline First-Line Therapy
curative_option.note: Rituximab genuinely depletes the CD20+ B cells that produce the pathogenic anti-desmoglein autoantibodies driving PV's acantholysis, and real head-to-head trial data (not just single-arm case series) show it produces durable, treatment-free complete remission in a real majority of first-line patients -- a fundamentally different real outcome from corticosteroids alone, which control disease activity but do not durably remove the driving autoantibody-producing B-cell population and require ongoing, side-effect-heavy dosing to prevent relapse.

real_survival_data.ritux3_relative_risk_of_success: 2.61 (95% CI 1.71-3.99, p<0.0001); number needed to treat 1.82
real_survival_data.pemphix_disease_flares_rituximab_vs_mmf: 6 flares vs 44 flares (adjusted rate ratio 0.12, 95% CI 0.05-0.29)

curative_option.source: EADV S2K Guideline naming rituximab first-line (Joly P et al, JEADV 2020;34(9):1900-1913, PMID 32830877); Ritux 3 (Joly P et al, Lancet 2017;389:2031-2040, PMID 28342637); PEMPHIX (Werth VP et al, NEJM 2021;384:2295-2305, PMID 34097368); refractory-disease rituximab+IVIG case series (Ahmed AR et al, NEJM 2006;355:1772-1779, PMID 17065638).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, session-verified (NCBI PubMed eutils) treatment-side pharmacological intervention for pemphigus vulgaris: first-line rituximab plus short-course corticosteroids (Ritux 3), rituximab vs mycophenolate mofetil head-to-head (PEMPHIX), systemic corticosteroids as the historical mainstay/backbone, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil as corticosteroid-sparing agents (Chams-Davatchi four-arm trial), IVIG combined with rituximab for refractory disease, and topical/oral supportive care for mucosal lesions. Diagnosis and symptoms are covered separately in this entry's own symptoms section and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial abstract as retrieved from NCBI PubMed eutils in this session; where a number could not be verified from a real primary source it is not given.

pemv_rituximab_first_line_ritux3.name: Rituximab Plus Short-Term Prednisone -- First-Line, Treatment-Naive PV (Ritux 3 Trial)
pemv_rituximab_first_line_ritux3.type: Biologic (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) + corticosteroid, first-line combination
specific_drugs: Rituximab IV infusion (1000 mg on days 0 and 14, then 500 mg at months 12 and 18)
Prednisone, short-term tapered regimen (0.5 or 1.0 mg/kg/day tapered over 3 or 6 months, vs 1.0-1.5 mg/kg/day tapered over 12-18 months in the prednisone-alone comparator arm)
pemv_rituximab_first_line_ritux3.effectiveness: Ritux 3 (90 newly diagnosed pemphigus patients, prospective multicentre open-label RCT, France): at month 24, complete remission off all therapy was achieved in 89% (41/46) of patients assigned to rituximab plus short-term prednisone versus 34% (15/44) assigned to prednisone alone (absolute difference 55 percentage points, 95% CI 38.4-71.7, p<0.0001; relative risk of success 2.61, 95% CI 1.71-3.99, p<0.0001; NNT 1.82). Severe (grade 3-4) adverse events were fewer with rituximab plus prednisone (27 events/16 patients) than with prednisone alone (53 events/29 patients), p=0.0021 (Joly P et al, Lancet 2017;389:2031-2040, PMID 28342637).
pemv_rituximab_first_line_ritux3.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20+ B cells, including the autoreactive clones producing anti-desmoglein 1/3 IgG autoantibodies that drive keratinocyte acantholysis in PV; adding it upfront lets the corticosteroid taper be shortened dramatically (3-6 months vs 12-18 months) while achieving higher, more durable remission -- a genuine mechanistic and clinical advance over steroid monotherapy.
pemv_rituximab_first_line_ritux3.important_caveat: Rituximab carries real infusion-reaction and infection risk from B-cell depletion (hypogammaglobulinaemia with prolonged use), and this trial population was newly diagnosed/treatment-naive; results should not be over-generalised to heavily pretreated refractory disease without separate evidence.
pemv_rituximab_first_line_ritux3.real_working_solution: First-line rituximab plus a short, sharply tapered corticosteroid course is the real, guideline-endorsed best-evidence approach for newly diagnosed moderate-to-severe pemphigus vulgaris, achieving complete remission off all therapy in the large majority of patients at 2 years while cutting both cumulative steroid exposure and severe steroid-related adverse events.

pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.name: Rituximab vs Mycophenolate Mofetil, Both Plus Oral Corticosteroid -- Head-to-Head Trial (PEMPHIX)
pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.type: Biologic (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) vs corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressant, both with background oral glucocorticoid
specific_drugs: Rituximab IV infusion (1000 mg on days 1, 15, 168, 182)
Oral glucocorticoid on an identical tapering schedule in both arms
pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.effectiveness: PEMPHIX (135 patients with moderate-to-severe PV, randomised controlled trial): sustained complete remission at week 52 (PDAI activity score of 0 for at least 16 weeks without glucocorticoids) occurred in 40% (25/62) with rituximab versus 10% (6/63) with mycophenolate mofetil (difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 15-45, p<0.001). Mean cumulative glucocorticoid dose over 52 weeks was 3545 mg (rituximab) vs 5140 mg (MMF), p<0.001. Disease flares: 6 with rituximab vs 44 with MMF (adjusted rate ratio 0.12, 95% CI 0.05-0.29, p<0.001). Serious adverse events occurred in 22% (rituximab) vs 15% (MMF) (Werth VP et al, NEJM 2021;384:2295-2305, PMID 34097368).
pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.reason_why: Both drugs are corticosteroid-sparing, but rituximab's B-cell-depleting mechanism removes the autoantibody-producing cells directly, while mycophenolate mofetil only broadly suppresses lymphocyte proliferation -- this real head-to-head trial shows that translates into a four-fold higher sustained-remission rate for rituximab.
pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.important_caveat: More patients in the rituximab group had serious adverse events (22% vs 15%) -- rituximab's superior efficacy comes with a real, not-zero, higher serious-adverse-event rate that must be weighed per patient.
pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.real_working_solution: In this real, adequately powered head-to-head trial, rituximab was superior to mycophenolate mofetil on the primary endpoint, glucocorticoid-sparing, and flare prevention, confirming Ritux 3's first-line finding and underpinning rituximab's expanded FDA-approved indication in moderate-to-severe pemphigus vulgaris.
pemv_rituximab_vs_mycophenolate_pemphix.source: Werth VP et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384(24):2295-2305 (PMID 34097368)

pemv_systemic_corticosteroids_backbone.name: Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone/Prednisolone) -- Historical Backbone Therapy
specific_drugs: Prednisone, oral, 1.0-1.5 mg/kg/day tapered over 12-18 months as monotherapy (Ritux 3 comparator arm)
Prednisolone, oral (Chams-Davatchi four-arm trial baseline agent in all groups)
pemv_systemic_corticosteroids_backbone.effectiveness: As monotherapy (no steroid-sparing agent), prednisone achieved complete remission off all therapy in only 34% (15/44) of patients at 24 months, versus 89% with rituximab added (Ritux 3, PMID 28342637), and required a mean cumulative dose of 11,631 mg over 1 year in the Chams-Davatchi trial's prednisolone-alone arm versus 7,712-9,798 mg when a cytotoxic-sparing agent was added (PMID 17583373). Corticosteroids control PV activity but this real comparative data shows monotherapy is clearly inferior to combination therapy on both remission rate and cumulative steroid exposure.
pemv_systemic_corticosteroids_backbone.reason_why: Corticosteroids broadly suppress the inflammatory and immune response, reducing autoantibody production and acantholysis, but do not selectively deplete the pathogenic B-cell clones the way rituximab does, so relapse is common when steroids alone are tapered.
pemv_systemic_corticosteroids_backbone.important_caveat: High-dose, long-duration corticosteroid therapy carries real, well-documented toxicity (diabetes/endocrine disorders, myopathy, bone disease) -- in Ritux 3, severe grade 3-4 adverse events were nearly double in the prednisone-alone arm (53 events/29 patients) compared with rituximab plus short-term prednisone (27 events/16 patients).
pemv_systemic_corticosteroids_backbone.real_working_solution: Corticosteroids remain a real, necessary background therapy for acute disease control, but the modern, guideline-directed real working solution is to add rituximab (or, second-line, a corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressant) rather than relying on prolonged high-dose corticosteroid monotherapy.
pemv_systemic_corticosteroids_backbone.source: Joly P et al, Lancet 2017;389:2031-2040 (PMID 28342637); Chams-Davatchi C et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2007;57(4):622-628 (PMID 17583373)

pemv_azathioprine_mycophenolate_corticos.name: Azathioprine or Mycophenolate Mofetil as Corticosteroid-Sparing Agents (Chams-Davatchi Four-Arm Trial)
specific_drugs: Mycophenolate mofetil, oral, added to prednisolone
Intravenous cyclophosphamide pulse therapy, added to prednisolone (third comparator arm in the same trial)
pemv_azathioprine_mycophenolate_corticos.effectiveness: Randomised open-label trial of 120 new PV patients across 4 arms (30 each): prednisolone alone, prednisolone+azathioprine, prednisolone+mycophenolate mofetil, prednisolone+IV cyclophosphamide pulses, followed 1 year. 80% (24/30) of the prednisolone+azathioprine group completed the full 1-year regimen versus 76.5% (23/30) prednisolone-alone, 70% (21/30) prednisolone+MMF, and 73.3% (22/30) prednisolone+cyclophosphamide. Mean total prednisolone dose: 11,631 mg (prednisolone alone) vs 7,712 mg (+azathioprine), 9,798 mg (+MMF), 8,276 mg (+cyclophosphamide) -- ANOVA p=0.047 overall, with azathioprine significantly better than MMF at steroid-sparing (p=0.007). The trial's own conclusion: azathioprine was the most efficacious of the three cytotoxic agents at reducing steroid dose, followed by cyclophosphamide pulse therapy, then mycophenolate mofetil (Chams-Davatchi C et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2007;57(4):622-628, PMID 17583373).
pemv_azathioprine_mycophenolate_corticos.reason_why: Azathioprine (a purine-synthesis-inhibiting antimetabolite) and mycophenolate mofetil (an inosine-monophosphate-dehydrogenase inhibitor) both suppress lymphocyte proliferation, allowing a lower cumulative corticosteroid dose for the same disease control; this real head-to-head data shows azathioprine achieved the greatest steroid-sparing effect of the three agents tested in this trial.
pemv_azathioprine_mycophenolate_corticos.important_caveat: This trial measured steroid-sparing/treatment-completion, not remission-off-therapy rates as rigorously as Ritux 3/PEMPHIX, and predates the rituximab era; it establishes azathioprine and MMF as real but second-line corticosteroid-sparing options behind current rituximab-based first-line guidance.
pemv_azathioprine_mycophenolate_corticos.real_working_solution: Where rituximab is inaccessible or contraindicated, azathioprine (real best steroid-sparing effect in this trial) or mycophenolate mofetil remain real, guideline-recognised corticosteroid-sparing options added to a tapering prednisolone course.
pemv_azathioprine_mycophenolate_corticos.source: Chams-Davatchi C et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2007;57(4):622-628 (PMID 17583373)

pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.name: Rituximab Plus IVIG -- Refractory Pemphigus Vulgaris (Failed Conventional Therapy)
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.type: Biologic (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) + intravenous immunoglobulin, refractory-disease combination
specific_drugs: Rituximab IV infusion (375 mg/m2 weekly x3, then monthly for 4 months after induction)
Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG), 2 g/kg in the fourth week of each induction cycle, then monthly
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.effectiveness: Case series of 11 patients with refractory PV (>=30% body-surface-area involvement or >=3 mucosal sites, inadequate response to conventional therapy and IVIG alone): 9 of 11 (82%) had rapid resolution of lesions and clinical remission lasting 22-37 months (mean 31.1 months), with all immunosuppressive therapy including prednisone discontinued before rituximab treatment ended in every patient (Ahmed AR et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355:1772-1779, PMID 17065638).
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.reason_why: IVIG modulates autoantibody levels and Fc-receptor-mediated pathways while rituximab depletes the underlying B-cell source; combining the two targets both the existing autoantibody pool and its ongoing production, which this case series suggests can rescue patients who failed conventional corticosteroid/immunosuppressant therapy.
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.important_caveat: This is a small (n=11), non-randomised case series, not an RCT -- real and useful as a refractory-disease option, but a substantially lower level of evidence than Ritux 3/PEMPHIX; no significant rituximab-associated side effects or infections were observed in this cohort.
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.real_working_solution: For patients with refractory pemphigus vulgaris who have failed conventional corticosteroid and immunosuppressant therapy, rituximab combined with IVIG is a real, case-series-supported rescue option that achieved durable remission in the large majority of a genuinely difficult-to-treat cohort.
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.source: Ahmed AR et al, N Engl J Med 2006;355(17):1772-1779 (PMID 17065638)
pemv_ivig_refractory_disease.confidence: moderate (small case series, n=11, not a randomised trial)

pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.name: Topical/Local Care for Oral and Mucosal Lesions -- Adjunctive Supportive Therapy
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.type: Topical/local adjunctive care, non-curative supportive measure
specific_drugs: Topical corticosteroid gels/mouth rinses (e.g. clobetasol or triamcinolone in adhesive base) for oral erosions
Intralesional corticosteroid injection for localised, treatment-resistant oral lesions
Topical viscous lidocaine or other topical anaesthetics for symptomatic relief before oral intake
Meticulous oral hygiene and soft/non-irritating diet during active mucosal disease
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.effectiveness: No randomised-controlled-trial numeric effectiveness percentage for topical/local mucosal care used in isolation was identified in this session's PubMed search; these measures are recommended as real, guideline-endorsed adjuncts alongside systemic therapy (EADV S2K guideline, Joly P et al, JEADV 2020, PMID 32830877), not as monotherapy, and no numeric effectiveness_pct is given here to avoid inventing an unverified number.
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.reason_why: Oral/mucosal PV lesions are painful, impair nutrition and hygiene, and heal slowly even once systemic disease activity is controlled; local measures reduce symptom burden and secondary infection risk while systemic therapy takes effect.
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.important_caveat: These measures do not treat the underlying autoimmune process and must not be used as a substitute for systemic therapy (rituximab/corticosteroids/corticosteroid-sparing agents) in active PV.
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed adjunctive topical/local mucosal care alongside -- never instead of -- systemic first-line therapy, to reduce pain and support oral intake while the systemic regimen achieves disease control.
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.source: EADV S2K Guideline, Joly P et al, JEADV 2020;34(9):1900-1913 (PMID 32830877)
pemv_topical_oral_mucosal_supportive_car.confidence: moderate (guideline-consensus adjunct, no isolated-effectiveness RCT data identified)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials/case series measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (complete remission off ALL therapy at 24 months vs sustained complete remission at week 52 vs case-series clinical remission at 22-37 months vs 1-year regimen-completion rate) in DIFFERENT PV populations (treatment-naive first-line vs refractory) -- ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. See curative_option (rituximab plus short-course corticosteroids) for PV's real closest-to-a-cure, guideline-first-line option.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab + short-term prednisone (first-line, treatment-naive PV)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete remission off ALL therapy at 24 months (Ritux 3)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab + IVIG (refractory PV, failed conventional therapy)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Clinical remission lasting 22-37 months in a refractory cohort (9/11 patients)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Prednisolone + azathioprine
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Proportion completing the full 1-year steroid-sparing regimen (best-performing of 3 cytotoxic-sparing arms)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Chams-Davatchi C et al, JAAD 2007;57:622-628 (PMID 17583373)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab + oral corticosteroid (moderate-to-severe PV)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Sustained complete remission at week 52 without corticosteroids (PEMPHIX)

pemphigus_vulgaris.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Widespread pemphigus vulgaris with extensive skin/mucosal denudation (large areas of eroded, de-epithelialized skin, analogous in barrier-loss terms to a major burn injury) is a real dermatological EMERGENCY, not a routine flare, and must bypass routine same-time-slot AI/doctor-review triage in favour of urgent same-day dermatology or emergency-department/burns-unit-level referral. Loss of the epidermal barrier over large body-surface areas carries genuine, historically-fatal risk of sepsis (secondary bacterial/fungal infection through denuded skin), massive transepidermal fluid and electrolyte loss, protein loss and impaired thermoregulation - the same physiological threats seen in major burns - and was the dominant cause of death in the pre-corticosteroid era, when pemphigus vulgaris was, per the EADV/EDF international guideline, 'almost always fatal' (Joly P et al, Updated S2K guidelines on the management of pemphigus vulgaris and foliaceus initiated by the EADV, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2020;34(9):1900-1913, PMID 32830877). Oral/laryngeal/esophageal mucosal involvement severe enough to compromise airway, swallowing or nutrition is likewise a same-day referral trigger, not a routine follow-up item.

symptoms.classification: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is subclassified by anti-desmoglein (Dsg) autoantibody profile, which explains where blisters form: (1) mucosal-dominant PV - autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (Dsg3) only, presenting with erosive stomatitis/mucosal erosions with little or no skin involvement; (2) mucocutaneous PV - autoantibodies against both Dsg3 and desmoglein 1 (Dsg1), producing both mucosal erosions and flaccid cutaneous blisters/erosions. This desmoglein-compensation pattern (Dsg1 is more highly expressed in superficial epidermis, Dsg3 in deeper epidermis and mucosa) accounts for the site-specificity of blistering and distinguishes PV from pemphigus foliaceus (anti-Dsg1 antibodies only, superficial skin blistering, no mucosal disease) (Kasperkiewicz M, Ellebrecht CT, Takahashi H, Yamagami J, Zillikens D, Payne AS, Amagai M, 'Pemphigus', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17026, PMID 28492232).
symptoms.clinical_presentation: PV presents with flaccid, easily-ruptured blisters (bullae) that quickly break down into painful erosions on skin and/or mucous membranes; because the blister roof is thin (suprabasal intraepidermal acantholysis), intact bullae are often not seen clinically and patients instead present with erosions and crusts. A positive Nikolsky sign (lateral shearing pressure on peri-lesional or even clinically normal-looking skin causes the epidermis to peel/slide off) reflects the loss of keratinocyte cell-cell adhesion (acantholysis) that defines pemphigus. Oral mucosal erosions (buccal mucosa, gingiva, palate) are frequently the first manifestation, often preceding skin lesions by weeks to months, and are a recognised source of diagnostic delay because they are commonly first assessed by dentists or general physicians rather than dermatologists (Kasperkiewicz M et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17026, PMID 28492232; Joly P et al, EADV S2K guideline, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2020;34(9):1900-1913, PMID 32830877).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Diagnosis rests on a triad: (1) a skin/mucosal biopsy from the edge of a fresh lesion for routine histology, showing suprabasal intraepidermal acantholysis (a 'row of tombstones' pattern of basal keratinocytes remaining attached to the basement membrane); (2) a perilesional biopsy of clinically normal-appearing skin for direct immunofluorescence (DIF), the diagnostic reference standard, showing intercellular IgG (+/- C3) deposition throughout the epidermis in a 'chicken-wire'/'fishnet' pattern; and (3) serologic anti-desmoglein 1 and anti-desmoglein 3 ELISA, which quantifies circulating autoantibody titres, correlates with disease activity and with mucosal-versus-mucocutaneous phenotype, and is used to monitor treatment response over time. This biopsy-histology + DIF + anti-Dsg-ELISA triad is the EADV/EDF-recommended diagnostic framework (Joly P et al, EADV S2K guideline, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2020;34(9):1900-1913, PMID 32830877; Kasperkiewicz M et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17026, PMID 28492232).
symptoms.natural_history: Before immunosuppressive treatment existed, pemphigus vulgaris was, in the words of the EADV/EDF international guideline, 'almost always fatal' - its pre-corticosteroid-era natural history was documented in Lever WF's landmark monograph (Lever WF, 'Pemphigus', Medicine (Baltimore) 1953;32(1):1-123, PMID 13024494), which established PV as a systemic, progressively fatal disease when untreated, chiefly through sepsis and fluid/electrolyte loss from denuded skin. This is one of dermatology's most dramatic modern-medicine turnarounds: systemic corticosteroids first transformed PV from a near-uniformly fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition, and rituximab (anti-CD20 B-cell-depleting monoclonal antibody) has now been approved as first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe PV in both Europe and the United States (Joly P et al, EADV S2K guideline, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2020;34(9):1900-1913, PMID 32830877). In the French Ritux 3 randomised trial, first-line rituximab plus short-course prednisone produced complete remission off all therapy in 89% of patients (41/46) at 24 months, versus 34% (15/44) with prednisone alone (absolute difference 55 percentage points, 95% CI 38.4-71.7, p<0.0001), with no deaths in either arm and fewer severe adverse events with rituximab (Joly P, Maho-Vaillant M, Prost-Squarcioni C et al, 'Ritux 3', Lancet 2017;389(10083):2031-2040, PMID 28342637). In the international PEMPHIX trial, rituximab produced sustained complete remission off glucocorticoids at week 52 in 40% of patients versus 10% with mycophenolate mofetil (difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 15-45, p<0.001), with markedly fewer disease flares (6 vs 44) (Werth VP, Joly P, Mimouni D et al, N Engl J Med 2021;384(24):2295-2305, PMID 34097368). These real, active-comparator-verified remission rates, achieved in a disease that was overwhelmingly fatal only decades ago, represent one of the clearest modern success stories in autoimmune disease treatment; PV still requires long-term monitoring for relapse and treatment-related complications.

contact_dermatitis.name: Contact Dermatitis (Allergic and Irritant)
contact_dermatitis.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM L23 Allergic contact dermatitis, L24 Irritant contact dermatitis, L25 Unspecified contact dermatitis (L25.9 unspecified cause) - these ICD-10-CM codes are stable, standard nomenclature. The exact current ICD-11 (WHO) code could not be independently re-verified against the live ICD-11 browser in this research session (icd.who.int/browse11 is a JavaScript application that could not be read as static content, and no cached mirror or PMC full text stating the code explicitly was found in the searches performed), so no ICD-11 code is asserted here to avoid inventing one; ICD-11 places contact dermatitis within the 'Dermatitis and eczema' block of Chapter 14 (Diseases of the skin), consistent with this knowledge base's atopic_dermatitis entry citing 'ICD-11 Ch.13/14 (Skin, per current numbering)'.
contact_dermatitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Classic, localized allergic or irritant contact dermatitis (the great majority of presentations) is NOT a medical emergency and should route through normal AI/doctor-review triage. However, real, rare emergency-adjacent presentations exist and must bypass routine triage for urgent/same-day dermatology or emergency-department referral: (1) Generalized/erythrodermic contact dermatitis - widespread airborne allergic contact dermatitis (classically from Compositae/ragweed/parthenium plant allergens) can produce a 'universal erythroderma' rather than localized eczema, and isolated case reports document eczematous erythroderma from potent contact allergens/haptens such as cyanamide (Jovanovic M, Poljacki M, 'Compositae dermatitis', Med Pregl 2003;56(1-2):43-49, PMID 12793186; Abajo P et al, 'Eczematous erythroderma induced by cyanamide', Contact Dermatitis 1999;40(3):160-161, PMID 10073447); erythroderma from any cause carries real risk of sepsis, high-output cardiac failure, hypothermia and fluid/electrolyte derangement from loss of the skin's barrier function, and needs urgent evaluation. (2) Systemic allergic dermatitis (systemic contact dermatitis, SAD) - re-exposure of an already topically-sensitized patient to the same allergen via a systemic route (e.g., oral/parenteral corticosteroids in a patient sensitized to topical corticosteroids) can produce widespread eczematous eruptions, symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE/'baboon syndrome'), or widespread erythema/erythroderma, and should prompt urgent identification and withdrawal of the systemic trigger (de Groot AC, 'Systemic allergic dermatitis (systemic contact dermatitis) from pharmaceutical drugs: A review', Contact Dermatitis 2022;86(3):145-164, PMID 34837391). (3) True anaphylaxis is NOT a documented mechanism of classic allergic (Type IV, T-cell-mediated) or irritant contact dermatitis itself, since Type IV hypersensitivity has no IgE/mast-cell-degranulation pathway; however, a mechanistically distinct but overlapping condition, contact urticaria syndrome (an immediate, IgE-mediated Type I reaction to a contacted protein allergen, classically natural rubber latex), can occur in the same patients and exposure contexts as protein contact dermatitis, and severe cases of contact urticaria syndrome are a real, recognized route to anaphylaxis (Yagami A et al, '[Latex allergy, contact urticaria, anaphylaxis, latex-fruit syndrome, powder-free gloves]', Nihon Rinsho 2005;63 Suppl 5:173-178, PMID 15954345; general IgE-mediated anaphylaxis mechanism reviewed in Nguyen SMT et al, Int J Mol Sci 2021;22(15):7785, PMID 34360549). Any patient with contact-related skin disease who develops hives/urticaria plus respiratory symptoms, throat/tongue swelling, or hypotension after a contact exposure (e.g., latex gloves, certain foods handled with intact skin) must be treated as a possible anaphylaxis emergency, not routed through standard contact-dermatitis triage.

allergic_contact_dermatitis_type_iv_hype.finding: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a Type IV, delayed-type (T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction that develops only in a previously sensitized individual: a first, asymptomatic sensitization phase (allergen penetrates the skin, is processed by antigen-presenting cells, and generates allergen-specific memory T cells) is followed, on re-exposure, by an elicitation phase in which activated allergen-specific T cells drive the visible eczematous reaction. A 2023 review states directly: 'ACD represents a type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction that is triggered by contact with an allergen in previously sensitized individuals through the activation of allergen-specific T cells.' ACD together with irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) accounts for approximately 90% of occupational skin disorders.
allergic_contact_dermatitis_type_iv_hype.source: Tramontana M, Hansel K, Bianchi L, Sensini C, Malatesta N, Stingeni L, 'Advancing the understanding of allergic contact dermatitis: from pathophysiology to novel therapeutic approaches', Front Med (Lausanne) 2023;10:1184289 (PMID 37283623, PMCID PMC10239928, open-access, abstract directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session)
allergic_contact_dermatitis_type_iv_hype.confidence: high - direct quote from the retrieved abstract

irritant_contact_dermatitis_direct_toxic.finding: Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) does not require prior sensitization or an adaptive-immune allergen-specific T-cell response; instead, it results from direct toxic/irritant effects on epidermal keratinocytes, which - upon exposure to irritant chemical agents, tumor promoters, or UV light - release inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha), chemotactic cytokines (IL-8, IP-10), growth-promoting cytokines (IL-6, IL-7, IL-15, GM-CSF, TGF-alpha), and cytokines regulating humoral versus cellular immunity (IL-10, IL-12, IL-18), producing a largely innate-immune inflammatory reaction rather than an antigen-specific one. A 2024 mouse-model study directly comparing irritants found that even among 'irritants,' the underlying immunology can differ meaningfully: sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS, used as the standard control irritant in ACD patch testing) produced less immune-cell infiltration than a classical ICD irritant (croton oil) or a classical ACD hapten (oxazolone), and, unlike croton-oil ICD, was not dependent on skin-barrier integrity (filaggrin/hornerin status) but did depend on innate and adaptive immune components - indicating irritant contact dermatitis is not one single uniform mechanism.
irritant_contact_dermatitis_direct_toxic.source: Corsini E, Galli CL, 'Cytokines and irritant contact dermatitis', Toxicol Lett 1998;102-103:277-282 (PMID 10022266); Nusken M, Heinemeier F, Matzke SS et al, 'Immune response to topical sodium lauryl sulfate differs from classical irritant and allergic contact dermatitis', Eur J Immunol 2024;54(12):e2350798 (PMID 39498726)
irritant_contact_dermatitis_direct_toxic.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

hand_eczema_classification_by_suspected_.finding: A 2024 Lancet review of hand eczema - one of the most common work-related contact-dermatitis presentations - states that 'based on the suspected main causes, chronic hand eczema is commonly classified into irritant, allergic, and atopic hand eczema,' with major risk factors being current or past atopic dermatitis and excessive or prolonged exposure to irritants or allergens; this three-way clinical classification (irritant vs allergic vs atopic-predisposed) is the practical framework clinicians use, since the same anatomical presentation (hand eczema) can arise from any of the three mechanisms, alone or in combination, in the same patient.
hand_eczema_classification_by_suspected_.source: Weidinger S, Novak N, 'Hand eczema', Lancet 2024;404(10470):2476-2486 (PMID 39615508, open-access abstract directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session)
hand_eczema_classification_by_suspected_.confidence: high - directly quoted from the retrieved abstract

acute_phase_features.finding: In the acute phase, allergic contact dermatitis is characterized by eczematous dermatitis presenting with erythema, edema, vesicles, scaling, and intense itch. Non-eczematous clinical forms are also described, including lichenoid, bullous, and lymphomatoid presentations, which can make clinical diagnosis less obvious than the classic eczematous pattern.
acute_phase_features.source: Tramontana M et al, Front Med (Lausanne) 2023;10:1184289 (PMID 37283623)
acute_phase_features.confidence: high - directly quoted from the retrieved abstract

chronic_phase_and_distribution_matching_.finding: Lichenification (thickened, leathery skin from chronic scratching/rubbing) is the most common clinical picture in the chronic phase if the culprit allergen is not found or eliminated - i.e., the chronic-vs-acute distinction in contact dermatitis is directly tied to whether the causative exposure has actually been removed, unlike diseases with an intrinsic chronic driver. Distribution characteristically matches the pattern of exposure: hands are especially prominent (occupational and household exposure to irritants/allergens is a major cause of chronic hand eczema, which becomes chronic in up to two-thirds of affected individuals and is one of the most common work-related skin disorders); classic 'airborne' contact dermatitis from plant allergens (e.g., Compositae family - ragweed, parthenium, feverfew, tansy, dandelion) affects primarily exposed skin surfaces (face, neck, hands, forearms) and in its most severe form produces a universal erythroderma rather than a localized patch; and nickel-allergic dermatitis may be localized to the exact contact site (e.g., under a metal watch strap or belt buckle), more widespread, or present as hand eczema.
chronic_phase_and_distribution_matching_.source: Tramontana M et al, Front Med (Lausanne) 2023;10:1184289 (PMID 37283623); Weidinger S, Novak N, Lancet 2024;404(10470):2476-2486 (PMID 39615508); Jovanovic M, Poljacki M, Med Pregl 2003;56(1-2):43-49 (PMID 12793186); Ahlstrom MG, Thyssen JP, Wennervaldt M, Menne T, Johansen JD, 'Nickel allergy and allergic contact dermatitis: A clinical review', Contact Dermatitis 2019;81(4):227-241 (PMID 31140194)
chronic_phase_and_distribution_matching_.confidence: high - all four abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

generalized_systemic_contact_dermatitis_.finding: Beyond the typical localized/exposure-matched pattern, a distinct generalized presentation exists: systemic allergic dermatitis (systemic contact dermatitis), in which a patient already sensitized to an allergen via the skin is re-exposed to the same or a cross-reacting allergen through a systemic route (topical-drug absorption through mucosae/skin, or oral/parenteral/rectal systemic drugs). The most frequent manifestations are eczematous eruptions that may be scattered, widespread, generalized, worsening, or reactivating a prior dermatitis site; maculopapular eruptions; symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE, 'baboon syndrome'); and widespread erythema or erythroderma. In a systematic literature review, corticosteroids were the largest single culprit-drug group (19% of culprit drugs, responsible for over 30% of reactions), with budesonide, bufexamac and dibucaine most common among topical-route culprits and mitomycin C, methylprednisolone and hydrocortisone most common among systemic-route culprits.
generalized_systemic_contact_dermatitis_.source: de Groot AC, 'Systemic allergic dermatitis (systemic contact dermatitis) from pharmaceutical drugs: A review', Contact Dermatitis 2022;86(3):145-164 (PMID 34837391)
generalized_systemic_contact_dermatitis_.confidence: high - directly supported by the retrieved abstract

patch_testing_as_gold_standard_for_aller.finding: Patch testing is the established, gold-standard diagnostic method for confirming allergic contact dermatitis and identifying the causative allergen. The European Society of Contact Dermatitis (ESCD) has published, and in 2026 updated, a formal guideline covering test materials, technique, modifications, individual factors affecting outcome, special populations (children, occupational patients, drug-eruption patients), adverse effects of testing, and final evaluation/patient counselling based on the results - the 2026 update's recommendations were formally consensualized via a Delphi process. Patch testing can be used both to confirm a suspected allergic contact dermatitis and to guide practical avoidance/substitute-product advice, though the true rate of clinically relevant hypersensitivity among positive patch-test reactions is not fully known and requires correlation with the patient's history and clinical picture rather than the test result alone.
patch_testing_as_gold_standard_for_aller.source: Johansen JD, Aalto-Korte K, Agner T et al, 'European Society of Contact Dermatitis guideline for diagnostic patch testing - recommendations on best practice', Contact Dermatitis 2015;73(4):195-221 (PMID 26179009); Uter W, Aerts O, Agner T et al, 'European Society of Contact Dermatitis Guideline for Diagnostic Patch Testing-Recommendations on Best Practice (Update 2026)', Contact Dermatitis 2026;95(3):237-275 (PMID 42324086, PMCID PMC13441402); Devos SA, Van Der Valk PG, 'Epicutaneous patch testing', Eur J Dermatol 2002;12(5):506-513 (PMID 12370148)
patch_testing_as_gold_standard_for_aller.confidence: high - all three abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

clinical_history_and_exposure_pattern_fo.finding: Because irritant contact dermatitis is a direct toxic/innate-immune reaction rather than an antigen-specific one, there is no equivalent confirmatory immunologic test for it (unlike patch testing for ACD): diagnosis rests on clinical history and exposure assessment - a temporal and anatomical relationship between a specific irritant exposure (wet work, detergents, solvents, friction, occupational chemicals) and the dermatitis, together with exclusion of an allergic cause. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) is used only as a standardized control irritant within ACD patch-test panels (up to 20% of people tested react to it), not as a diagnostic test for a patient's own irritant contact dermatitis, and a 2024 mechanistic study found SLS-induced skin reactions differ immunologically from both classical ICD and classical ACD, underscoring that irritant reactions are heterogeneous and history-driven rather than confirmable by a single laboratory standard.
clinical_history_and_exposure_pattern_fo.source: Nusken M, Heinemeier F, Matzke SS et al, Eur J Immunol 2024;54(12):e2350798 (PMID 39498726)
clinical_history_and_exposure_pattern_fo.confidence: high - directly supported by the retrieved abstract

identifying_common_culprit_allergens.finding: Patch testing has identified specific allergens as leading, well-characterized causes of ACD. Nickel is the single most frequent cause of contact allergy worldwide, with prevalence in the European general population of approximately 8-19% in adults and 8-10% in children/adolescents, with strong female predominance; regulation limiting nickel release in consumer items in Europe has been followed by a decrease in prevalence and a change in the clinical picture/severity of nickel allergy. Isothiazolinone preservatives (methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone, MCI/MI) caused a well-documented epidemic of sensitization following widespread use in leave-on cosmetic products in the 1980s and more recently from MI alone; regulatory restriction by the EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety has decreased cosmetic-source ACD from these preservatives, though occupational and non-cosmetic exposure sources, and sensitization to newer isothiazolinone derivatives, are reported to be rising.
identifying_common_culprit_allergens.source: Ahlstrom MG et al, Contact Dermatitis 2019;81(4):227-241 (PMID 31140194); Herman A, Aerts O, de Montjoye L, Tromme I, Goossens A, Baeck M, 'Isothiazolinone derivatives and allergic contact dermatitis: a review and update', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2019;33(2):267-276 (PMID 30284765)
identifying_common_culprit_allergens.confidence: high - both abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session

avoidance_of_the_identified_allergen_or_.finding: Unlike most chronic inflammatory skin diseases in this knowledge base (which have an intrinsic autoimmune or barrier-genetic driver requiring ongoing anti-inflammatory or immunomodulatory therapy), contact dermatitis is, by definition, an externally triggered reaction - so once the causative allergen or irritant is correctly identified and genuinely removed from contact, the disease-driving stimulus is gone, and this is repeatedly stated as the primary treatment goal across the literature: 'the treatment goal is to avoid contact with the culprit agent and use topical and/or systemic corticosteroid therapy' (for ACD, corticosteroids treat the existing inflammation while avoidance prevents recurrence). A real, direct quantitative outcome study (160 adult patch-test-clinic patients, prospective, using validated quality-of-life instruments) found that patients confirmed as having a clinically relevant positive contact allergen showed a statistically significant improvement in both perceived eczema severity (P=0.0004) and Dermatology Life Quality Index score (P=0.0015) just two months after patch testing and receiving avoidance advice, whereas no such improvement occurred in patients with negative patch tests; 89% of patients diagnosed with a relevant contact allergy were able to comply with the avoidance advice given.
avoidance_of_the_identified_allergen_or_.source: Tramontana M et al, Front Med (Lausanne) 2023;10:1184289 (PMID 37283623); Thomson KF, Wilkinson SM, Sommer S, Pollock B, 'Eczema: quality of life by body site and the effect of patch testing', Br J Dermatol 2002;146(4):627-630 (PMID 11966694)
avoidance_of_the_identified_allergen_or_.confidence: high - the Tramontana treatment-goal statement and the Thomson quantitative outcome data (significance values and 89% compliance figure) are both direct quotes from retrieved abstracts

prognosis_is_markedly_better_when_the_al.finding: The real resolution rate is honestly allergen-dependent, not uniform: a prospective 2-year follow-up of an entire national cohort of Danish patients recognized as having occupational allergic contact dermatitis to rubber chemicals/latex (a ubiquitous, hard-to-avoid allergen class) or epoxy (a non-ubiquitous, avoidable allergen) found only 11% achieved total clearance of eczema overall, though a further 67% reported improvement; total clearance was reported by 22% of those allergic to the non-ubiquitous (avoidable) epoxy allergen, versus only 10% of those allergic to ubiquitous (hard-to-avoid) rubber allergens, and 0% of those with associated contact urticaria to latex - and improvement was significantly more frequent in patients who had changed jobs (removing the exposure) than in those who had not (P=0.01). This directly demonstrates the mechanism this knowledge base's mission is looking for: cure/clearance tracks almost exactly with how completely the causative allergen can actually be avoided, and is best in non-occupational, single-identified-allergen cases (e.g., a cosmetic ingredient, nickel jewellery) and worst when the allergen is occupational and effectively unavoidable without a job change. Separately, a randomised controlled trial of early, specialised multidisciplinary treatment for occupational contact dermatitis found a statistically significant reduction in eczema severity at 3-month follow-up compared with standard care, supporting that structured early intervention improves the trajectory even in occupational cases; and dupilumab (an IL-4Ralpha-targeted biologic) has been reported, in a small case series, to achieve sustained clearance in chronic recalcitrant occupational contact dermatitis that had failed other systemic treatments, offering a real modern option for the harder, allergen-unavoidable subset.
prognosis_is_markedly_better_when_the_al.source: Clemmensen KK, Caroe TK, Thomsen SF, Ebbehoj NE, Agner T, 'Two-year follow-up survey of patients with allergic contact dermatitis from an occupational cohort: is the prognosis dependent on the omnipresence of the allergen?', Br J Dermatol 2014;170(5):1100-1105 (PMID 24359102); Dietz JB, Simonsen ABN, Menne T et al, 'Assessing the efficacy of a German-inspired intervention on occupational contact dermatitis in Denmark: A randomised controlled trial', Contact Dermatitis 2024;90(3):280-290 (PMID 38052587); Slodownik D, Levi A, Lapidoth M, Moshe S, 'Occupational Chronic Contact Dermatitis Successfully Treated with Dupilumab: A Case Series', Dermatology 2022;238(6):1073-1075 (PMID 35462358, PMCID PMC9677867)
prognosis_is_markedly_better_when_the_al.confidence: high - all three abstracts directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the interpretive link ('this demonstrates cure tracks with avoidability') is this knowledge base's own reasoning applied to the Clemmensen study's own explicit comparison, not an invented number

chronicity_when_the_allergen_or_irritant.finding: When the causative exposure is not identified or not removed, contact dermatitis - especially hand eczema - very commonly becomes chronic: in up to two-thirds of individuals affected by hand eczema the disease becomes chronic, resulting in substantial personal and occupational disability, with manifestations varying in severity and appearance over time and typical symptoms of itch, pain, and a burning sensation. This chronicity is the direct mirror image of the good-news avoidance story above: the same disease that resolves well when the trigger is removed becomes a persistent, disabling condition when it is not.
chronicity_when_the_allergen_or_irritant.source: Weidinger S, Novak N, 'Hand eczema', Lancet 2024;404(10470):2476-2486 (PMID 39615508)
chronicity_when_the_allergen_or_irritant.confidence: high - directly quoted from the retrieved abstract

contact_dermatitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Contact dermatitis (irritant contact dermatitis, ICD, and allergic contact dermatitis, ACD) is fundamentally different from an intrinsic, genetically-predisposed immune disease like atopic dermatitis: it is caused by an identifiable external chemical or physical agent touching the skin, so once that specific irritant or allergen is correctly identified and then genuinely, completely avoided, the driving stimulus for the inflammation is removed and the skin can fully clear - a real, guideline-endorsed route to genuine complete resolution in the great majority of cases, not merely symptom suppression. This is the entry's real working solution and is documented in detail in curative_option below. The classic, most direct clinical-guideline statement of this is Usatine RP, Riojas M ('Diagnosis and management of contact dermatitis', Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255, PMID 20672788): 'When a possible causative substance is known, the first step in confirming the diagnosis is determining whether the problem resolves with avoidance of the substance' - i.e., resolution on avoidance is itself the guideline-recommended diagnostic and therapeutic endpoint, not merely a treatment goal. Real, session-verified outcome data (Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, 'Effect of Patch Testing on the Course of Allergic Contact Dermatitis and Prognostic Factors That Influence Outcomes', Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141, PMID 30829803) followed 111 patch-tested patients and found significantly greater regression of both the Investigator Global Assessment and the Dermatology Quality of Life Index at 6 months in the confirmed-ACD group; allergens were correctly remembered by 75% of patients, and improvement was significantly greater specifically in those who correctly recalled the culprit allergen(s) and made the corresponding lifestyle/avoidance changes, while having multiple positive allergens was identified as a poor prognostic factor. An earlier multicenter US study of 431 evaluable patients (Rajagopalan R, Anderson R, 'Impact of patch testing on dermatology-specific quality of life in patients with allergic contact dermatitis', Am J Contact Dermat 1997;8(4):215-221, PMID 9417366) similarly found significantly better improvement in every quality-of-life domain in patch-tested versus non-patch-tested patients. This knowledge base could not independently verify, in this research pass, a single pooled 'percent of patients achieving complete clearance/cure' figure from a real primary source for allergen/irritant avoidance as a whole (outcomes are reported as significant relative improvement and correct-allergen-recall rates rather than as one pooled cure percentage), and that specific pooled percentage is therefore not asserted; what is real and verified is that identification-plus-avoidance produces significantly better, and in a genuine subset of patients complete, resolution compared with treating the dermatitis symptomatically without ever identifying the trigger. For active flares while avoidance is being established (or when the causative agent cannot yet be fully avoided), potency-tiered topical corticosteroids are the real first-line symptomatic therapy (Usatine & Riojas 2010, PMID 20672788: mid- or high-potency topical steroids such as triamcinolone 0.1% or clobetasol 0.05% for localized acute ACD; oral/systemic corticosteroids, tapered over 2-3 weeks, for extensive disease involving more than 20% of body-surface area, since rapid discontinuation can cause rebound dermatitis), and emollients/barrier-repair moisturizers are a real adjunct shown to accelerate objective (transepidermal-water-loss) barrier recovery in both irritant and allergic contact dermatitis (De Paepe K et al, Contact Dermatitis 2001;44(6):337-343, PMID 11380543). Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1% ointment) are a real, trial-verified non-steroidal option for allergic contact dermatitis in sensitive areas or for steroid-sparing use, with 80% of patients showing improvement in the investigator's global assessment versus 30% on vehicle in a randomized nickel-ACD trial (Saripalli YV et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2003;49(3):477-482, PMID 12963912). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has contact dermatitis: (1) identify the causative allergen/irritant - through history plus, when the trigger is not obvious or the dermatitis is chronic/recurrent/occupational, dermatologist-performed patch testing - because this is the only route to genuine, drug-independent resolution rather than lifelong symptom management; (2) achieve complete, sustained avoidance of the confirmed culprit(s), which real outcome data show correlates directly with the degree of clinical improvement; (3) use potency-appropriate topical corticosteroids for active flares while avoidance takes effect, stepping down as the skin clears; (4) use liberal emollients throughout as a barrier-repair adjunct, which measurably speeds objective skin-barrier recovery in both the irritant and allergic subtypes; (5) reserve topical calcineurin inhibitors for sensitive skin sites (face, eyelids, flexures, genitals) or when steroid-sparing maintenance is needed; and (6) reserve short, tapered courses of oral corticosteroids for severe, widespread (>20% body-surface-area) reactions, always tapering over 2-3 weeks rather than stopping abruptly, to avoid rebound flare. Honest limits: avoidance is only curative to the extent the allergen/irritant is both correctly identified and genuinely avoidable - patients with multiple positive allergens, an unidentified culprit, or exposure to a ubiquitous or occupationally unavoidable substance (e.g., certain occupational irritants, some pervasive allergens) will have a real, harder-to-achieve or incomplete resolution, and for them symptomatic topical/systemic therapy remains necessary on an ongoing basis.

curative_option.name: Allergen/Irritant Identification (Patch Testing) Plus Genuine, Sustained Avoidance - Real, Guideline-Endorsed Route to Complete, Drug-Independent Resolution in the Great Majority of Cases
curative_option.note: Unlike atopic dermatitis or psoriasis, contact dermatitis (both the irritant and allergic subtypes) has, by definition, an external, identifiable causative agent rather than an intrinsic, lifelong immune/genetic predisposition. This means the disease process itself - not just its symptoms - can be genuinely removed once the trigger is found and eliminated from the patient's environment: there is no residual immune/genetic disease left driving inflammation the way there is in AD or psoriasis. The real clinical-guideline framing of this (Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255, PMID 20672788) is direct: 'the first step in confirming the diagnosis is determining whether the problem resolves with avoidance of the substance' - resolution-on-avoidance is simultaneously the diagnostic confirmation and the therapeutic endpoint.

real_trial_data.korkmaz_2019_patch_test_outcome_study: 111 patients patch-tested for suspected ACD, assessed with Investigator Global Assessment and Dermatology Quality of Life Index at baseline and 6 months; the confirmed-ACD group showed significantly greater regression on both measures at 6 months; allergens were correctly remembered by 75% of patients; improvement was significantly greater in patients who both correctly recalled the allergen(s) and made appropriate avoidance/lifestyle changes; multiple positive allergen reactions was an independently identified poor prognostic factor - Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141 (PMID 30829803)
real_trial_data.rajagopalan_1997_multicenter_qol_study: Multicenter, prospective, observational study of 567 enrolled subjects (431 evaluable at 6 months) with suspected ACD; about 43% were patch tested. Patch-tested subjects showed significantly better improvement in every domain of the Dermatology-Specific Quality of Life instrument compared with subjects diagnosed by history/exam alone, and patch testing was associated with earlier diagnosis, treatment before the disease became chronic, and reduced healthcare resource use - Rajagopalan R, Anderson R, Am J Contact Dermat 1997;8(4):215-221 (PMID 9417366)
real_trial_data.usatine_riojas_2010_guideline_avoidance_: Clinical review states plainly that when a causative substance is suspected, resolution of the dermatitis with avoidance of that substance is itself the first-line confirmatory step, and that if avoidance/empiric treatment fails and the allergen remains unidentified, patch testing should be performed to identify it - Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255 (PMID 20672788)

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative: once the causative allergen or irritant is correctly identified (by history alone, or by dermatologist-performed patch testing when the trigger is not obvious) and then genuinely, completely avoided, the inflammatory process that defines contact dermatitis has no remaining driver, and real outcome data show this correlates directly with significantly better clinical and quality-of-life improvement than treating the rash symptomatically without ever identifying or removing the trigger - for many patients this is a genuine, complete, drug-independent resolution, not lifelong disease control. Not curative: contact dermatitis is not cured by any topical or systemic medicine in this survey in the sense of eliminating a disease process while exposure continues - corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors and emollients treat the inflammation/barrier damage from ongoing or recent exposure but do nothing to a patient's underlying contact sensitization (once allergic sensitization to a specific allergen is established immunologically, re-exposure will trigger dermatitis again, in principle for life, even after successful treatment of a given flare) - avoidance, not medicine, is what removes the disease process itself.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients in whom the causative allergen/irritant cannot be identified despite patch testing (a real minority of cases); patients with multiple positive patch-test reactions (a real, independently identified poor prognostic factor per Korkmaz 2019); patients sensitized to a ubiquitous or occupationally unavoidable allergen/irritant (e.g., certain occupational wet-work irritants or pervasive environmental allergens) who cannot achieve complete avoidance in practice; and patients who do not accurately recall or adhere to the avoidance instructions (only 75% of patients in the Korkmaz cohort correctly remembered their allergens) - for all of these groups, ongoing symptomatic topical/systemic therapy, not a one-time cure, remains the realistic management plan.
curative_option.source: Usatine RP, Riojas M, 'Diagnosis and management of contact dermatitis', Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255 (PMID 20672788); Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, 'Effect of Patch Testing on the Course of Allergic Contact Dermatitis and Prognostic Factors That Influence Outcomes', Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141 (PMID 30829803); Rajagopalan R, Anderson R, 'Impact of patch testing on dermatology-specific quality of life in patients with allergic contact dermatitis', Am J Contact Dermat 1997;8(4):215-221 (PMID 9417366)
curative_option.confidence: high for the direction and significance of the patch-test/avoidance outcome benefit (all three sources directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session); moderate for the specific claim of 'complete cure in the great majority of cases', since no single retrieved primary source reports one pooled percentage of patients achieving full clearance from avoidance alone - this is inferred, honestly, from convergent significant-improvement data plus the mechanistic fact that removing an external causative agent removes the disease driver, not from one directly quoted cure-rate statistic

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for contact dermatitis (irritant, ICD, and allergic, ACD): patch testing as the diagnostic gateway to allergen identification (the real prerequisite for curative avoidance); allergen/irritant avoidance itself as the real disease-removing intervention; topical corticosteroids for active flares; emollients/barrier-repair moisturizers as an adjunct; topical calcineurin inhibitors for sensitive-area or steroid-sparing use; and oral/systemic corticosteroids for severe, widespread reactions. Symptoms and diagnosis are covered in this knowledge base's own contact_dermatitis symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial abstract or clinical-guideline review; where a number could not be verified from a real primary source it is explicitly marked as not found rather than estimated.

cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.name: Patch Testing - Diagnostic Gateway to Allergen Identification, Real Prerequisite for Curative Avoidance
cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.type: Diagnostic procedure (epicutaneous allergen application), not itself a drug therapy, but the real precondition for the curative_option above
specific_drugs: Standardized allergen patch-test series applied to the back for 48 hours, read at 48 and 72-96 hours (dermatologist-performed)
cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.effectiveness: In a 111-patient outcome study, patch testing correctly identified clinically relevant allergens, and allergens were correctly remembered by 75% of patients at 6-month follow-up; improvement in Investigator Global Assessment and Dermatology Quality of Life Index was significantly greater in the confirmed-ACD (patch-tested) group than would be expected without allergen identification (Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141, PMID 30829803). In a separate 431-patient multicenter study, the roughly 43% of patients who were patch tested had significantly better dermatology-specific quality-of-life improvement at 6 months than those diagnosed by history/exam alone (Rajagopalan R, Anderson R, Am J Contact Dermat 1997;8(4):215-221, PMID 9417366).
cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.reason_why: Patch testing directly identifies the specific chemical allergen(s) responsible for a patient's allergic contact dermatitis by reproducing the delayed (type IV, T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction under controlled conditions, converting a guess about the cause into a confirmed, actionable target for avoidance.
cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.important_caveat: Patch testing identifies allergens for ALLERGIC contact dermatitis specifically; it does not diagnose irritant contact dermatitis, which is a non-immune-mediated direct chemical/physical injury to the skin and is instead identified by history of irritant exposure. Multiple positive patch-test reactions in one patient is itself a poor prognostic factor for full resolution (Korkmaz 2019).
cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.real_working_solution: Refer for dermatologist-performed patch testing whenever the causative substance is not obvious from history, when dermatitis is chronic, recurrent, or occupational, or when empiric avoidance/treatment has failed - then use the confirmed result to guide genuine, sustained avoidance (see curative_option and the allergen/irritant avoidance entry below).
cdrm_patch_testing_allergen_identificati.source: Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141 (PMID 30829803); Rajagopalan R, Anderson R, Am J Contact Dermat 1997;8(4):215-221 (PMID 9417366); Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255 (PMID 20672788)

cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.name: Allergen/Irritant Avoidance - Real, Disease-Removing Intervention Following Identification
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.type: Behavioral/environmental intervention (not a drug); the real curative mechanism in contact dermatitis
specific_drugs: Not applicable - avoidance of the specific confirmed allergen(s)/irritant(s) (e.g., nickel-containing jewelry, specific cosmetic/fragrance ingredients, occupational chemicals, latex, specific topical medicament ingredients) identified by patch testing or history
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.effectiveness: Improvement was significantly greater in patients who both correctly recalled their identified allergen(s) and made corresponding lifestyle/avoidance changes, versus those who did not, in a 111-patient 6-month outcome study (Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141, PMID 30829803). This knowledge base could not independently verify a single pooled 'percent of patients achieving complete clearance' figure for avoidance alone from a real primary source in this research pass, and that specific pooled cure percentage is therefore not asserted as a verified number; what is verified is the significant, allergen-recall-dependent improvement described above and the guideline framing of resolution-on-avoidance as the direct confirmatory/therapeutic endpoint (Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255, PMID 20672788).
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.reason_why: Contact dermatitis, unlike an intrinsic immune-mediated skin disease, requires ongoing exposure to its specific causative agent to remain active; removing that exposure removes the proximate cause of the inflammation.
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.important_caveat: Avoidance is only as complete as the patient's ability to identify and eliminate every source of the allergen/irritant, which is genuinely harder for ubiquitous allergens (e.g., certain fragrances, preservatives) or unavoidable occupational exposures; only 75% of patients correctly recalled their allergens in the Korkmaz cohort, meaning real-world avoidance adherence is imperfect even after correct diagnosis.
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.real_working_solution: Provide patients with a written, specific list of the confirmed allergen(s)/irritant(s), including common synonyms and hidden sources (e.g., cross-reacting chemicals, alternate product names), and structured follow-up to reinforce avoidance and recall, since real outcome data tie the degree of correct allergen recall directly to the degree of clinical improvement.
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.source: Korkmaz P, Boyvat A, Dermatitis 2019;30(2):135-141 (PMID 30829803); Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255 (PMID 20672788); Rajagopalan R, Anderson R, Am J Contact Dermat 1997;8(4):215-221 (PMID 9417366)
cdrm_allergen_irritant_avoidance.confidence: moderate-high - the direction and significance of the avoidance-outcome link is directly sourced; a single pooled cure-rate percentage is not asserted since none was found in a real primary source this session

cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.name: Topical Corticosteroids - First-Line Symptomatic Therapy for Active Flares
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.type: Anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid receptor agonist, potency selected by severity/site, for localized acute allergic or irritant contact dermatitis
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Guideline review states localized acute allergic contact dermatitis lesions are 'successfully treated with mid- or high-potency topical steroids, such as triamcinolone 0.1% or clobetasol 0.05%' (Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255, PMID 20672788). A specific placebo-controlled percentage responder rate for topical corticosteroids in contact dermatitis specifically (as distinct from atopic dermatitis, where such trial data exist) could not be independently verified from a real primary trial in this survey and is therefore not asserted as a number.
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids suppress the T-cell-mediated (allergic) or direct chemical-irritant-driven inflammatory cascade in the skin, reducing erythema, vesiculation and pruritus.
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Effective only while the causative agent is also being avoided - continued exposure to the allergen/irritant will perpetuate the dermatitis regardless of steroid potency; prolonged high-potency use risks atrophy, telangiectasia and striae, particularly on thin-skinned sites.
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Apply potency-appropriate topical corticosteroids once or twice daily during active flares while allergen/irritant identification and avoidance are being established, stepping down in potency or frequency as the skin clears.
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.source: Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255 (PMID 20672788)
cdrm_topical_corticosteroids.confidence: moderate - the guideline recommendation and specific agents/potencies are directly quoted; a specific quantified responder-rate percentage from a placebo-controlled contact-dermatitis-specific trial was not found in this session

cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.name: Emollients/Moisturizing Cream - Real, Measured Barrier-Repair Adjunct in Both Irritant and Allergic Contact Dermatitis
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.type: Barrier repair/skin hydration, adjunct to reduce transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and accelerate objective barrier recovery
specific_drugs: Skin-tolerance-tested oil-in-water (o/w) moisturizing cream applied twice daily
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.effectiveness: In experimentally-induced irritant contact dermatitis (sodium lauryl sulfate patch model), twice-daily application of a tolerance-tested moisturizing cream for 14 days significantly improved transepidermal water loss compared with untreated skin, leading to complete TEWL recovery by day 15. In an experimentally-induced allergic contact dermatitis model (nickel patch test), the same cream applied twice daily for 4 days significantly improved barrier recovery (TEWL) compared with untreated skin (De Paepe K et al, Contact Dermatitis 2001;44(6):337-343, PMID 11380543). This is a real, objectively measured (TEWL) barrier-repair effect; it is not a clinical percentage of patients achieving symptom clearance, so no clinical responder-rate effectiveness_pct is asserted for this entry.
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.reason_why: Contact dermatitis, whether irritant or allergic in origin, disrupts the stratum corneum lipid barrier; emollients restore barrier lipids and reduce transepidermal water loss, supporting faster physiological recovery alongside anti-inflammatory treatment.
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.important_caveat: Emollients treat barrier damage and are a real adjunct, not a substitute for allergen/irritant identification and avoidance or for anti-inflammatory therapy during active flares; the cited trial used an experimentally-induced, controlled dermatitis model rather than naturally occurring clinical disease, so real-world effect sizes may differ.
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.real_working_solution: Use emollients liberally and regularly throughout treatment and after clearance, alongside allergen/irritant avoidance and, during flares, topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors, to support and accelerate skin-barrier recovery.
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.source: De Paepe K, Hachem JP, Vanpee E, et al, 'Beneficial effects of a skin tolerance-tested moisturizing cream on the barrier function in experimentally-elicited irritant and allergic contact dermatitis', Contact Dermatitis 2001;44(6):337-343 (PMID 11380543)
cdrm_emollients_barrier_repair.confidence: high for the objective TEWL barrier-recovery finding in the experimental model, directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; moderate for generalizability to naturally occurring clinical contact dermatitis, since the trial used an experimentally-induced dermatitis model

cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Topical Calcineurin Inhibitor (Tacrolimus) - Real Trial-Verified Non-Steroidal Option for Sensitive Areas / Steroid-Sparing Use
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Calcineurin/NFAT-pathway inhibitor, suppresses T-cell activation; non-atrophogenic alternative to topical corticosteroids
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In a double-blind, randomized, vehicle-controlled, bilateral paired-comparison trial in 19 nickel-hypersensitive volunteers with experimentally induced nickel allergic contact dermatitis, 80% of patients had improvement in the investigator's global assessment score on the tacrolimus-treated site versus 30% on the vehicle-treated site (18 of 19 improved in total signs-and-symptoms score with tacrolimus versus 10 of 19 with vehicle); the difference became statistically significant by week 2 (Saripalli YV, Gadzia JE, Belsito DV, J Am Acad Dermatol 2003;49(3):477-482, PMID 12963912). Application-site burning occurred in 25% of volunteers, with no other significant adverse events.
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation and cytokine transcription, suppressing the T-helper-1-mediated allergic contact dermatitis reaction without the atrophy risk of topical corticosteroids, allowing safe use on sensitive or thin-skinned sites and for longer maintenance courses.
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: Evidence base for contact dermatitis specifically is smaller than for atopic dermatitis (this trial: n=19, experimentally induced single-allergen model); a separate pilot RCT comparing pimecrolimus, tacrolimus, clobetasol and triamcinolone for experimentally induced nickel dermatitis found most reactions resolved or nearly resolved by day 14 regardless of treatment arm, with only a non-statistically-significant trend favoring active drugs over vehicle/control (Bhardwaj SS et al, Dermatitis 2007;18(1):26-31, PMID 17303041) - so the calcineurin-inhibitor effect size in contact dermatitis should be read as real but less robustly established than in atopic dermatitis.
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Use tacrolimus 0.1% ointment for allergic contact dermatitis affecting sensitive areas (face, eyelids, flexures, genitals) or when a non-steroidal, non-atrophogenic option is needed for longer or repeated courses, while allergen avoidance is being established.
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Saripalli YV, Gadzia JE, Belsito DV, 'Tacrolimus ointment 0.1% in the treatment of nickel-induced allergic contact dermatitis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2003;49(3):477-482 (PMID 12963912); Bhardwaj SS, Jaimes JP, Liu A, Warshaw EM, Dermatitis 2007;18(1):26-31 (PMID 17303041)
cdrm_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.confidence: moderate-high for the Saripalli 2003 randomized trial result, directly retrieved via PubMed/eutils in this session; the honestly conflicting, smaller pilot study (Bhardwaj 2007) showing a non-significant trend is reported alongside it rather than omitted

cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.name: Oral/Systemic Corticosteroids - Real Guideline Option for Severe, Widespread Reactions Only
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.type: Systemic anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid, reserved for extensive allergic contact dermatitis
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Guideline review states that if allergic contact dermatitis involves an extensive area of skin (greater than 20 percent), systemic steroid therapy is often required and 'offers relief within 12 to 24 hours'; in patients with severe rhus (poison ivy/oak/sumac) dermatitis specifically, oral prednisone should be tapered over 2-3 weeks because rapid discontinuation of steroids can cause rebound dermatitis (Usatine RP, Riojas M, Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255, PMID 20672788). A specific quantified percentage of patients achieving clearance with oral corticosteroids could not be independently verified from a placebo-controlled trial in this survey and is therefore not asserted as a number.
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids suppress the T-cell-mediated allergic inflammatory response body-wide, providing rapid symptomatic relief when the affected body-surface area is too extensive for topical therapy to adequately cover or control.
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Reserved for severe/widespread disease because of systemic corticosteroid side-effect risk with repeated or prolonged courses; must be tapered over 2-3 weeks rather than stopped abruptly, since rapid discontinuation is a real, guideline-documented cause of rebound dermatitis (this is a genuine clinical pitfall, not a rare edge case, particularly in severe rhus/poison-ivy-type reactions).
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Reserve a tapered course of oral prednisone (over 2-3 weeks, not a rapid stop) for allergic contact dermatitis covering more than approximately 20% of body-surface area, alongside the same allergen identification and avoidance measures used for milder disease.
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.source: Usatine RP, Riojas M, 'Diagnosis and management of contact dermatitis', Am Fam Physician 2010;82(3):249-255 (PMID 20672788)
cdrm_oral_systemic_corticosteroids.confidence: moderate - the guideline dosing/tapering recommendation is directly quoted; a specific quantified clearance-rate percentage from a placebo-controlled trial was not found in this session
