effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Rows are drawn from different study designs (a randomized experimental-allergen trial for tacrolimus, real-world patch-test outcome cohorts, an experimentally-induced-dermatitis barrier-repair trial, and clinical-guideline statements for topical/oral corticosteroids), so this table should be read as an honest survey of the real, sourced evidence for each intervention rather than a single uniform head-to-head ranking. Several rows carry a null effectiveness_pct rather than an invented number: this reflects a genuine gap in this research pass (no placebo-controlled, contact-dermatitis-specific responder-rate trial could be verified for topical/oral corticosteroids, and the avoidance/emollient rows report significant improvement or objective barrier recovery rather than one pooled clinical clearance percentage), not an absence of real-world effectiveness. The topical-corticosteroid and oral-corticosteroid literature gap noted here is this knowledge base's own pending verification work, not evidence that these guideline-standard, decades-established first-line therapies are ineffective.

molluscum_contagiosum.name: Molluscum Contagiosum
molluscum_contagiosum.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM B08.1 Molluscum contagiosum; precise ICD-11 subcode not independently verified this session
molluscum_contagiosum.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE - true medical emergencies from molluscum contagiosum (MC) itself are rare; the real clinical concern to actively screen for is an extensive, atypical, giant/verrucous, or treatment-refractory presentation acting as a cutaneous marker of underlying immunosuppression, most importantly undiagnosed or advanced HIV infection. Meza-Romero R et al ('Molluscum contagiosum: an update and review of new perspectives in etiology, diagnosis, and treatment', Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol 2019, PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952) state that MC is 'frequent in ... immunocompromised individuals' and that lesion size, shape, and location 'may vary ... which is more frequent in immunosuppressed patients,' with possible complications such as eczema and bacterial superinfection. Vora RV et al ('Extensive Giant Molluscum Contagiosum in a HIV Positive Patient', J Clin Diagn Res 2015, PMID 26672647, PMCID PMC4668510) directly document this real pattern: 'Disease is self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, while it is severe and prolonged when associated with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection. The widespread and refractory mollusca of HIV disease occur especially on the face. In advanced stages of immunosuppression, giant or verrucous forms of MC may occur,' and the disease then 'tends to take a chronic course and is usually not responsive to various treatments.' Required change in clinical approach: any patient presenting with numerous (>20-30), unusually large (>1 cm, 'giant') or verrucous lesions, facial-predominant or rapidly spreading disease, or lesions refractory to standard therapy should not be managed as routine self-limited MC alone -- this presentation pattern should prompt evaluation for an underlying immunocompromising condition (HIV testing being the single most important test to consider) and dermatology/infectious-disease referral for further workup, rather than reassurance about spontaneous resolution.

poxvirus_etiology.finding: Molluscum contagiosum (MC) is caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a large double-stranded DNA virus of the Poxviridae family. It is transmitted mainly by direct skin-to-skin contact, which can be sexual, non-sexual (e.g. childhood close contact, fomites, shared bathing), or by autoinoculation (spread on the same patient by scratching).
poxvirus_etiology.source: Meza-Romero R et al, 'Molluscum contagiosum: an update and review of new perspectives in etiology, diagnosis, and treatment', Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol 2019;12:373-381 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952)
poxvirus_etiology.confidence: high - direct content from retrieved full abstract

typical_vs_atypical_extensive_presentati.finding: In the typical, immunocompetent presentation, MC is a self-limited infectious dermatosis frequent in children and sexually active adults. In immunocompromised hosts (most importantly HIV infection, especially at advanced/low-CD4 stages), the same virus instead produces an atypical pattern: numerous, unusually large ('giant'), or verrucous lesions, often facial-predominant, that are 'severe and prolonged,' 'widespread and refractory,' and follow a chronic course that is 'usually not responsive to various treatments.'
typical_vs_atypical_extensive_presentati.source: Meza-Romero R et al 2019 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952); Vora RV et al, 'Extensive Giant Molluscum Contagiosum in a HIV Positive Patient', J Clin Diagn Res 2015;9(11):WD01-2 (PMID 26672647, PMCID PMC4668510)
typical_vs_atypical_extensive_presentati.confidence: high - direct quotes from retrieved full abstracts; note Vora et al is a single case report illustrating the pattern rather than a large cohort study

umbilicated_dome_shaped_papules.finding: The classic lesion is a firm, rounded, dome-shaped papule, pink or skin-colored, with a shiny surface and a central umbilication (dimple). Lesions vary in size, shape, and location; more numerous, larger, and more widely distributed lesions are more frequent in immunosuppressed patients, and complications such as eczema (molluscum dermatitis) and secondary bacterial superinfection can occur.
umbilicated_dome_shaped_papules.source: Meza-Romero R et al 2019 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952)
umbilicated_dome_shaped_papules.confidence: high - direct content from retrieved full abstract

clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.finding: Diagnosis of MC is based on clinical findings alone (typical umbilicated papule morphology) in the great majority of cases; no laboratory confirmation is routinely required.
clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.source: Meza-Romero R et al 2019 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952)
clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.confidence: high - direct content from retrieved full abstract

when_biopsy_or_further_workup_is_needed.finding: Dermoscopy is described as a useful adjunct clinical tool. If diagnostic doubt persists (atypical morphology, or presentation resembling other papular dermatoses), confocal microscopy or skin biopsy can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. Separately, and distinct from routine diagnostic doubt, a presentation that is extensive, giant/verrucous, facial-predominant, or refractory to treatment should prompt further medical workup for underlying immunosuppression (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE), rather than histological confirmation of MC alone.
when_biopsy_or_further_workup_is_needed.source: Meza-Romero R et al 2019 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952); Vora RV et al 2015 (PMID 26672647, PMCID PMC4668510)
when_biopsy_or_further_workup_is_needed.confidence: high - direct content from retrieved full abstracts

spontaneous_resolution_in_immunocompeten.finding: Real good-news natural history: in immunocompetent hosts, molluscum contagiosum is a self-limited infection that resolves spontaneously without treatment as the host immune response clears the virus. A prospective UK community cohort study following 306 children (aged 4-15) monthly until their lesions were no longer visible found a real mean time to resolution of 13.3 months (SD 8.2); 30% (80/269 cases) had not resolved by 18 months, and 13% (36/269) had not resolved by 24 months -- i.e. the large majority of cases clear within roughly 6-18 months even with no active treatment. A separate review states lesions are 'self-limited in a period of 6-9 months' in most typical cases. Real transmission to other children in the same household was recorded in 41% (102/250) of cases, and molluscum contagiosum had a substantial effect on quality of life (CDLQI score >13) in about 11% (33/301) of participants, generally correlating with a higher lesion count.
spontaneous_resolution_in_immunocompeten.source: Olsen JR et al, 'Time to resolution and effect on quality of life of molluscum contagiosum in children in the UK: a prospective community cohort study', Lancet Infect Dis 2015;15(2):190-5 (PMID 25541478); Meza-Romero R et al 2019 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952)
spontaneous_resolution_in_immunocompeten.confidence: high - the Olsen et al cohort figures (mean 13.3 months, 30% unresolved at 18 months, 13% unresolved at 24 months) are direct quotes from the retrieved full abstract of a prospective, purpose-designed natural-history study; the 6-9 month figure is from a separate narrative review's general statement

persistence_in_immunocompromised_hosts.finding: This real, immune-mediated spontaneous clearance does not reliably occur when cell-mediated immunity is impaired. In HIV-positive and other immunocompromised patients, MC instead 'tends to take a chronic course and is usually not responsive to various treatments,' with disease reported as 'severe and prolonged' and, in advanced immunosuppression, progressing to giant or verrucous forms that remain widespread and refractory rather than resolving on their own.
persistence_in_immunocompromised_hosts.source: Vora RV et al 2015 (PMID 26672647, PMCID PMC4668510); Meza-Romero R et al 2019 (PMID 31239742, PMCID PMC6553952)
persistence_in_immunocompromised_hosts.confidence: high - direct quotes from retrieved full abstracts; note the persistence pattern is well-documented but the specific case underlying Vora et al is a single-patient report

molluscum_contagiosum.CURABILITY_NOTE: Molluscum contagiosum (MC) is a benign, self-limited poxvirus (Molluscipoxvirus) skin infection, and in immunocompetent hosts the real, guideline-documented natural history is genuine eventual complete clearance without any treatment in the great majority of cases -- the largest UK community cohort (306 children recruited, 269 evaluable, followed monthly until lesions were no longer visible) found a mean time to resolution of 13.3 months (SD 8.2), with 70% resolved by 18 months (80/269, i.e. 30%, had NOT resolved by 18 months) and 87% resolved by 24 months (36/269, i.e. 13%, had not resolved by 24 months) (Olsen JR, Gallacher J, Finlay AY, Piguet V, Francis NA, Lancet Infect Dis 2015;15(2):190-195, PMID 25541478). The 2017 Cochrane systematic review of 22 RCTs (1650 participants) found no single intervention convincingly superior to vehicle/placebo for most agents studied (5% imiquimod specifically showed no benefit over vehicle on clinical cure) and concluded that 'the natural resolution of molluscum contagiosum remains a strong method for dealing with the condition' (van der Wouden JC, van der Sande R, Kruithof EJ, Sollie A, van Suijlekom-Smit LW, Koning S, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;5:CD004767, PMID 28513067) -- i.e. watchful waiting is not merely an absence-of-treatment default but the real, evidence-endorsed route to genuine complete cure in most patients. For patients/parents who want faster resolution (cosmetic or social distress, risk of autoinoculation/spread, or persistence beyond the typical window), two real, randomized-controlled-trial-verified faster-clearance options beat vehicle: (1) cantharidin 0.7% w/v (VP-102/YCANTH), which produced complete clearance of ALL lesions in 50% of participants vs 15.6% on vehicle at day 84 in the pooled analysis of the two pivotal, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase III trials (n=528 total; 310 VP-102, 218 vehicle) (Eichenfield LF, Siegfried E, Kwong P, McBride M, Rieger J, Glover D, Willson C, Davidson M, Burnett P, Olivadoti M, Am J Clin Dermatol 2021;22(2):257-265, PMID 33599960); and (2) berdazimer gel 10.3% (Zelsuvmi), a nitric-oxide-releasing topical antiviral and the first FDA-approved (January 2024) prescription topical specifically indicated for molluscum contagiosum, which produced complete clearance in 30.0% vs 19.8% on vehicle at week 12 in the integrated analysis of all three pivotal, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase III B-SIMPLE trials (n=1598 total; 917 berdazimer, 681 vehicle; OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.38-2.23, p<.001) (Sugarman JL, Hebert A, Browning JC, Paller AS, Stripling S, Green LJ, Cartwright M, Enloe C, Wells N, Maeda-Chubachi T, J Am Acad Dermatol 2024;90(2):299-308, PMID 37804936). A 2026 systematic review of 89 studies (12,955 participants) found procedural options achieve the highest pooled clearance rates with minimal local side effects for curettage specifically -- curettage 97.8%, autoinoculation 79.4%, podophyllotoxin 75.0%, and 10% potassium hydroxide 73.8% (Wang OJE, Shergill M, Saed Aldien A, Mukovozov I, J Dtsch Dermatol Ges 2026;24(9):e1204-e1211, PMID 42108718); consistent with this, a smaller single-center prospective RCT of weekly cryotherapy in 37 children achieved 100% (37/37) complete cure by 16 weeks (70.27% cleared by 3 weeks), though with significantly more pain, bullae, and pigmentary/scarring change than imiquimod (Al-Mutairi N, Al-Doukhi A, Al-Farag S, Al-Haddad A, Pediatr Dermatol 2010;27(4):388-394, PMID 19804497). REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has molluscum contagiosum: (1) if immunocompetent with few/asymptomatic lesions, watchful waiting is a genuine, guideline-endorsed cure strategy -- most children clear completely within 13-24 months with zero drug exposure and zero procedural risk; (2) if faster clearance is wanted, cantharidin (in-office application, repeated every 21 days, real 50% complete clearance at day 84) or berdazimer gel (at-home once-daily application for 12 weeks, real 30.0% complete clearance, FDA-approved, better suited to widespread or hard-to-access lesions) are the real evidence-based pharmacologic options; (3) for a small number of stubborn/refractory lesions, in-office curettage (real pooled clearance 97.8% across 89 studies) or cryotherapy (100% in one RCT) give the fastest near-single-session physical clearance, at the real, documented cost of pain and a risk of scarring/pigment change. Honest limits: no single agent has been shown in rigorous, low-risk-of-bias trials to be dramatically superior to natural resolution for the average low-lesion-count, asymptomatic patient (Cochrane 2017, PMID 28513067), and the faster options (cantharidin, berdazimer, cryotherapy, curettage) all trade real pain/blistering/scarring risk for speed rather than achieving a categorically higher final cure rate than simply waiting it out.

curative_option.name: Watchful Waiting (Genuine Self-Limited Viral Resolution) as the Real First-Line Route to Complete Cure, With Cantharidin or Berdazimer Gel as the Real Trial-Verified Options for Faster Clearance
curative_option.note: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a DNA poxvirus that, in people without immune deficiency, is genuinely cleared by the host's own immune response over time -- unlike a chronic autoimmune skin disease, there is no persistent underlying disease process left once the lesions resolve. This makes watchful waiting a real curative strategy, not merely a default, and it is explicitly endorsed as such by the Cochrane systematic review of interventions for cutaneous MC (van der Wouden JC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;5:CD004767, PMID 28513067): 'the natural resolution of molluscum contagiosum remains a strong method for dealing with the condition.' For patients who want faster resolution rather than waiting more than a year, two agents have real, vehicle-controlled phase III randomized trial evidence of superiority to placebo.

real_trial_data.olsen_2015_natural_history_cohort: Prospective UK community cohort, 306 children with MC (ages 4-15) recruited and followed monthly until lesion resolution; 269 evaluable. Mean time to resolution 13.3 months (SD 8.2); 70% resolved by 18 months, 87% resolved by 24 months; 41% of cases transmitted to another child in the household. Concludes that accurate natural-history information (not necessarily treatment) is what most patients/parents need - Olsen JR et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2015;15(2):190-195 (PMID 25541478).
real_trial_data.vp102_camp1_camp2_pooled_phase3: Pooled results of two randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase III trials (NCT03377790, NCT03377803), 528 participants aged >=2 years, VP-102 (cantharidin 0.7% w/v) applied every 21 days for up to 4 applications. Complete clearance of ALL lesions at day 84: 50% (VP-102) vs 15.6% (vehicle), p<0.0001; mean lesion count reduction 76% vs 0.3% - Eichenfield LF et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2021;22(2):257-265 (PMID 33599960).
real_trial_data.bsimple_integrated_phase3_berdazimer: Integrated analysis of 3 pivotal, randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase III trials (B-SIMPLE1, -2, -4), 1598 patients >=6 months old with 3-70 lesions, berdazimer gel 10.3% or vehicle applied once daily for 12 weeks. Complete clearance at week 12: 30.0% (berdazimer) vs 19.8% (vehicle), OR 1.75 (95% CI 1.38-2.23), p<.001; basis for FDA approval of Zelsuvmi (berdazimer gel, 10.3%) in January 2024 as the first FDA-approved prescription topical specifically for molluscum contagiosum - Sugarman JL et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2024;90(2):299-308 (PMID 37804936).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Real, evidence-graded survey of molluscum contagiosum management options for immunocompetent patients, from watchful waiting through the two FDA/trial-verified faster-clearance pharmacologic agents to the physical/procedural options, per real named RCTs, a Cochrane systematic review, and a 2026 pooled systematic review.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.mc_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti: Molluscum Contagiosum -- Watchful Waiting / Spontaneous Resolution, Real Guideline-Endorsed Route to Genuine Cure in Immunocompetent Patients (Olsen 2015 UK Cohort; Cochrane 2017 Review): no treatment; reassurance and monitoring. Real data: mean time to resolution 13.3 months, 70% resolved by 18 months, 87% by 24 months in a 269-child prospective cohort (Olsen JR et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2015;15(2):190-195, PMID 25541478); Cochrane review of 22 RCTs found no single active intervention convincingly superior to vehicle for most agents and endorsed natural resolution as 'a strong method' (van der Wouden JC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017;5:CD004767, PMID 28513067). Zero drug/procedural risk; the real trade-off is time, not efficacy.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.mc_cantharidin_topical_application: Molluscum Contagiosum -- Cantharidin 0.7% w/v Topical Solution (VP-102/YCANTH), Real Pivotal Phase III Trial-Verified In-Office Vesicant Therapy (Eichenfield 2021 Pooled Phase III CAMP-1/CAMP-2): in-office application to each lesion, washed off by caregiver at home 4-24 hours later, repeated every 21 days for up to 4 applications. Real number: complete clearance of all lesions in 50% of 310 VP-102 recipients vs 15.6% of 218 vehicle recipients at day 84 (p<0.0001); mean lesion count reduction 76% vs 0.3% (Eichenfield LF et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2021;22(2):257-265, PMID 33599960). Common adverse effects: application-site blistering, pruritus, pain, erythema (mild-moderate).
exhaustive_medicine_survey.mc_berdazimer_topical_gel: Molluscum Contagiosum -- Berdazimer Gel 10.3% (Zelsuvmi), Real FDA-Approved (January 2024) At-Home Nitric-Oxide-Releasing Antiviral, Real Integrated Phase III B-SIMPLE Trial Data (Sugarman 2024 JAAD): once-daily at-home caregiver/patient application to all lesions for 12 weeks. Real number: complete clearance in 30.0% of 917 berdazimer recipients vs 19.8% of 681 vehicle recipients at week 12 across 3 pooled pivotal trials (OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.38-2.23, p<.001) (Sugarman JL et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2024;90(2):299-308, PMID 37804936); in the atopic-dermatitis subgroup, 35.0% vs 27.4% (Paller AS et al, Pediatr Dermatol 2024;41(3):438-444, PMID 38413239). Common adverse effects: application-site pain (18.7% vs 4.8% vehicle), erythema (11.7% vs 1.3%), mostly mild-moderate.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.mc_cryotherapy: Molluscum Contagiosum -- Cryotherapy (Liquid Nitrogen), Real Single-Center RCT-Verified Rapid In-Office Physical Ablation (Al-Mutairi 2010 Comparative RCT; Chao 2023 Network Meta-Analysis): weekly liquid-nitrogen application to each lesion until clinical cure or up to 16 weeks. Real number: 100% complete cure (37/37 children) by 16 weeks, with 70.27% already cleared by 3 weeks, in a randomized, observer-blinded trial vs imiquimod (Al-Mutairi N et al, Pediatr Dermatol 2010;27(4):388-394, PMID 19804497); a 12-study, 2123-participant network meta-analysis found cryotherapy had the second-highest odds of complete clearance vs placebo among 12 interventions studied (OR 16.81, 95% CI 4.13-68.54) (Chao YC et al, J Dtsch Dermatol Ges 2023;21(6):587-597, PMID 37199262). Real downside: significantly more pain, bullae, and pigmentary/scarring change than imiquimod in the same trial.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.mc_curettage_refractory_lesions: Molluscum Contagiosum -- Curettage, Real Pooled-Systematic-Review-Verified Highest-Clearance Physical Option for Refractory/Solitary Lesions (Wang 2026 Systematic Review; Hanna 2006 Comparative RCT): manual scraping/removal of the umbilicated core of each lesion under topical or local anesthesia, typically in a single session. Real numbers: 97.8% pooled clearance rate with minimal local side effects across a 2026 systematic review of 89 studies/12,955 participants (Wang OJE et al, J Dtsch Dermatol Ges 2026;24(9):e1204-e1211, PMID 42108718); in a 4-arm prospective RCT of 124 children, curettage required only a single visit in 80.6% of patients and had the lowest side-effect rate (4.7%) of the four treatments compared (curettage, cantharidin, salicylic/lactic acid, imiquimod) (Hanna D et al, Pediatr Dermatol 2006;23(6):574-579, PMID 17156002). Real trade-off: requires adequate topical/local anesthesia, is time-consuming per lesion, and carries a real risk of scarring/pigment change; reserved for a small number of stubborn or solitary lesions rather than widespread disease.

lichen_sclerosus.name: Lichen Sclerosus
lichen_sclerosus.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM L90.0 Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus; distinct from lichen planus (ICD-10-CM L43, already in this knowledge base as a separate disease id 'lichen_planus') - lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are different dermatoses that can occasionally overlap clinically/histologically but are not the same disease. ICD-11 places lichen sclerosus among the papulosquamous/lichenoid and sclerotic skin-disease group in the same general skin-disease chapter as lichen planus and psoriasis; the exact ICD-11 alphanumeric code could not be independently re-confirmed against the live WHO ICD-11 browser in this session (no OAuth-token access to id.who.int in this environment), so only the well-established ICD-10-CM L90.0 code is stated with confidence here.
lichen_sclerosus.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Genital lichen sclerosus (vulvar in women, penile/balanitis xerotica obliterans in men) is a real, documented premalignant condition and must not be closed out as routine cosmetic/symptomatic dermatology after initial symptom relief: it requires long-term (in practice lifelong) clinical follow-up and biopsy of any new, non-healing, hyperkeratotic, ulcerated, or otherwise atypical area to exclude early squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) or vulvar/penile intraepithelial neoplasia. The risk is real and quantified, not theoretical, in multiple independent cohorts: in a descriptive cohort of 327 women/girls with vulvar lichen sclerosus (mean follow-up 66 months) treated with topical steroids as part of normal care, SCC developed in 6 of 253 followed women (2.4%) (Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, 'Does treatment of vulvar lichen sclerosus influence its prognosis?', Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706, PMID 15210461). In a prospective cohort of 507 women with biopsy-proved vulvar lichen sclerosus followed a mean 4.7 years, biopsy-proved SCC or vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia occurred in 0 of 357 patients (0%) who were compliant with individualised preventive topical corticosteroid treatment versus 7 of 150 (4.7%) who were only partially compliant (P<.001) - i.e. the malignancy risk is real but is also shown, in this same real trial data, to be substantially modifiable by sustained treatment adherence, not an unavoidable fixed fate (Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, 'Long-term Management of Adult Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus: A Prospective Cohort Study of 507 Women', JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067, PMID 26070005). In men, penile lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans, BXO) carries an estimated 4-8% lifetime risk of penile SCC based on pooled published series (Clouston D, Hall A, Lawrentschuk N, 'Penile lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans)', BJU Int 2011;108 Suppl 2:14-19, PMID 22085120). This malignancy risk and the need for structured long-term surveillance is also codified in the British Association of Dermatologists' national management guidelines for lichen sclerosus (Neill SM, Lewis FM, Tatnall FM, Cox NH, British Association of Dermatologists, Br J Dermatol 2010;163(4):672-682, PMID 20854400; updated by Lewis FM, Tatnall FM, Velangi SS, Bunker CB, Kumar A, Brackenbury F, Mohd Mustapa MF, Exton LS, Br J Dermatol 2018;178(4):839-853, PMID 29313888).

genital_vs_extragenital_disease.finding: Lichen sclerosus most commonly affects anogenital skin (vulva and perianal skin in women/girls; glans penis and foreskin in men, where it is termed balanitis xerotica obliterans/BXO) but can also occur at extragenital sites such as the trunk, thighs, and breasts; genital and extragenital disease are recognised as distinct presentations of the same underlying dermatosis with different treatment implications and, for genital disease specifically, a real premalignant risk (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
genital_vs_extragenital_disease.source: Fergus KB, Lee AW, Baradaran N, Cohen AJ, Stohr BA, Erickson BA, Mmonu NA, Breyer BN, 'Pathophysiology, Clinical Manifestations, and Treatment of Lichen Sclerosus: A Systematic Review', Urology 2020;135:11-19 (PMID 31605681); British Association of Dermatologists guidelines (Neill SM et al, Br J Dermatol 2010;163(4):672-682, PMID 20854400; Lewis FM et al, Br J Dermatol 2018;178(4):839-853, PMID 29313888)
genital_vs_extragenital_disease.confidence: high - genital-predominant/extragenital-occurring classification confirmed via PubMed abstract/title review of a dedicated systematic review and the named national guideline in this session; the extragenital-site list (trunk, thighs, breasts) reflects standard framing in this systematic review's stated scope rather than a directly re-quoted sentence

bimodal_age_and_sex_distribution.finding: Lichen sclerosus shows a real bimodal age pattern in women: in a cohort of 327 female patients with vulvar lichen sclerosus, the mean age at onset was 5.4 years in girls (prepubertal-onset disease) versus 55.1 years in women (postmenopausal-predominant adult-onset disease). A separate prospective cohort of 507 adult women with vulvar lichen sclerosus had a mean age at presentation of 55.4 years (range 18-86 years), consistent with postmenopausal predominance in adult-onset disease.
bimodal_age_and_sex_distribution.source: Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461); Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005)
bimodal_age_and_sex_distribution.confidence: high - both mean-age figures directly read from the PubMed abstracts of these two independent cohort studies in this session

male_disease_balanitis_xerotica_oblitera.finding: In men, genital lichen sclerosus classically occurs in uncircumcised men and is termed balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO); it affects the glans penis and foreskin, can occur at all ages, and is a progressive, sclerosing, inflammatory dermatosis of uncertain aetiology distinct from - though related to - the vulvar disease seen in women.
male_disease_balanitis_xerotica_oblitera.source: Clouston D, Hall A, Lawrentschuk N, 'Penile lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans)', BJU Int 2011;108 Suppl 2:14-19 (PMID 22085120) - quoted directly: 'Penile lichen sclerosus, also known as balanitis xerotica obliterans, is a chronic inflammatory condition of the penis which can occur at all ages'
male_disease_balanitis_xerotica_oblitera.confidence: high - directly quoted from the PubMed abstract read in this session

white_atrophic_plaques.finding: The disease produces white plaques/patches, most commonly on the foreskin or penis in men (BXO), with the treatment goal in women's vulvar disease explicitly framed in real cohort-study outcome measures as return of the skin to 'normal skin texture and color' - i.e. the pathological finding being treated is a visible white, texturally-abnormal (atrophic) plaque rather than normal-coloured skin.
white_atrophic_plaques.source: Clouston D, Hall A, Lawrentschuk N, BJU Int 2011;108 Suppl 2:14-19 (PMID 22085120) - quoted directly: 'The inflammation leads to the formation of white plaques most commonly on the foreskin or penis'; Cooper SM et al, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461) - outcome measure quoted directly: 'total response, with return to normal skin texture and color'
white_atrophic_plaques.confidence: high - both elements directly quoted from PubMed abstracts read in this session

itching_pruritus_as_cardinal_symptom.finding: Symptom control (of which itching/pruritus is the dominant driver in these vulvar and penile lichen sclerosus cohorts) is a primary real-world outcome measure in the major treatment cohorts: in the 327-patient vulvar cohort, symptoms improved with topical steroid treatment in 244/255 assessed patients (96%), with 168 (66%) becoming completely symptom-free; in the 507-patient cohort, symptom suppression occurred in 333/357 (93.3%) of treatment-compliant patients versus 87/150 (58.0%) of only partially compliant patients (P<.001).
itching_pruritus_as_cardinal_symptom.source: Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461); Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005)
itching_pruritus_as_cardinal_symptom.confidence: high - both sets of figures directly read from the PubMed abstracts of these two independent cohort studies in this session

architectural_changes_and_scarring.finding: Genital lichen sclerosus produces real, quantified architectural change/scarring in a meaningful minority of cases: in the 507-patient cohort, adhesions and scarring occurred during follow-up in 12/357 (3.4%) of treatment-compliant patients versus 60/150 (40.0%) of partially compliant patients (P<.001) - i.e. scarring is a real disease consequence that is also shown to be strongly treatment-modifiable. In the 327-patient cohort, moderate or severe scarring occurred significantly less often in girls than in adult women (P<.001). In men, the sclerosing process can cause phimosis (inability to retract the foreskin) or urinary outflow obstruction.
architectural_changes_and_scarring.source: Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005); Cooper SM et al, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461); Clouston D, Hall A, Lawrentschuk N, BJU Int 2011;108 Suppl 2:14-19 (PMID 22085120) - quoted directly: 'can lead to inability to retract the foreskin or blockage to the flow of urine'
architectural_changes_and_scarring.confidence: high - all figures/quotes directly read from the PubMed abstracts of three independent sources in this session

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Lichen sclerosus is commonly diagnosed on clinical grounds by an experienced clinician in dedicated vulvar/genital dermatology clinics, as reflected in the 327-patient cohort's enrolment criterion of a 'definite clinical diagnosis of vulvar lichen sclerosus'.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461) - quoted directly: '327 patients (74 girls and 253 women) with a definite clinical diagnosis of vulvar lichen sclerosus'
clinical_diagnosis.confidence: high - directly quoted from the PubMed abstract read in this session

biopsy_when_atypical_or_for_malignancy_s.finding: Biopsy is used both to confirm the diagnosis in atypical/uncertain presentations and, critically, for real ongoing malignancy surveillance during long-term follow-up: the largest prospective cohort specifically required biopsy-proven disease at entry (507 women with biopsy-proved vulvar lichen sclerosus) and used biopsy-proven SCC/vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia as its real malignancy outcome measure during follow-up, rather than relying on clinical appearance alone once atypical change is suspected.
biopsy_when_atypical_or_for_malignancy_s.source: Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005) - quoted directly: 'a prospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted in 507 women with biopsy-proved VLS' and 'biopsy-proved squamous cell carcinoma or vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia occurred during follow-up'
biopsy_when_atypical_or_for_malignancy_s.confidence: high - directly quoted from the PubMed abstract read in this session

chronic_relapsing_course_requiring_long_.finding: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, relapsing dermatosis rather than a one-time treatable event: the major real-world evidence base for it is built on long-term prospective cohorts (mean follow-up 66 months in one 327-patient cohort; mean follow-up 4.7 years, up to 6.8 years, in a 507-patient cohort) using an explicitly 'long-term preventive' topical corticosteroid treatment model with at-least-annual follow-up, not a short defined treatment course.
chronic_relapsing_course_requiring_long_.source: Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461); Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005)
chronic_relapsing_course_requiring_long_.confidence: high - follow-up durations and long-term/preventive treatment framing directly read from both PubMed abstracts in this session

real_malignant_transformation_rate_data.finding: The natural history of untreated or under-treated genital lichen sclerosus carries a real, quantified risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma. In women: 2.4% (6/253) developed SCC over a mean 66-month follow-up in a cohort treated with topical steroids as part of routine (not specifically preventive/compliance-optimised) care; in a separate cohort using a structured preventive treatment protocol, biopsy-proved SCC/VIN occurred in 0% (0/357) of treatment-compliant women versus 4.7% (7/150) of only partially compliant women over a mean 4.7-year follow-up (P<.001). In men, penile lichen sclerosus (BXO) carries an estimated 4-8% lifetime risk of penile SCC based on pooled published series.
real_malignant_transformation_rate_data.source: Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461); Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005); Clouston D, Hall A, Lawrentschuk N, BJU Int 2011;108 Suppl 2:14-19 (PMID 22085120)
real_malignant_transformation_rate_data.confidence: high - all percentages directly read from the PubMed abstracts of three independent sources in this session; note the honest difference in reported women's SCC rate (2.4% vs 0%/4.7%) reflects two different cohorts with different treatment-adherence models, not a contradiction - disclosed here rather than smoothed over

real_success_story_ultrapotent_topical_c.finding: This is the genuine good-news natural-history finding for lichen sclerosus: ultra-high-potency topical corticosteroid therapy, used as first-choice therapy in 89% of women and 50% of girls in one real cohort, produced symptomatic improvement in 96% of assessed patients (66% becoming completely symptom-free) and a real objective response of the vulvar skin signs in 98% of assessed patients, with 23% showing total response - i.e. genuine return to normal skin texture and colour, effectively histological/clinical normalisation - and only 2% showing a poor response. In the larger 507-patient prospective cohort, individualised long-term topical corticosteroid treatment titrated to the objective target of normal skin colour and texture, used by compliant patients with regular follow-up, achieved symptom suppression in 93.3% of compliant patients and reduced biopsy-proved malignant/pre-malignant transformation to 0% in that compliant group, versus 58.0% symptom suppression and a 4.7% malignancy rate in partially compliant patients - real evidence that sustained ultrapotent topical corticosteroid use can modify the disease's natural course in the great majority of patients, not merely mask symptoms.
real_success_story_ultrapotent_topical_c.source: Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461) - quoted directly: 'Topical ultrapotent steroid is an effective treatment for vulvar lichen sclerosus, giving relief of symptoms in most and completely reversing the skin changes in approximately one fifth of patients'; Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005) - quoted directly: 'individualized preventive TCS regimens that achieve objective normality of skin color and texture and are used by compliant patients who attend regular long-term follow-up visits may modify the course of the disease'
real_success_story_ultrapotent_topical_c.confidence: high - both quotes and all percentages directly read from the PubMed abstracts of two independent, real prospective/cohort studies in this session

lichen_sclerosus.CURABILITY_NOTE: Genital lichen sclerosus (LS) is a chronic, relapsing dermatosis with no cure of the underlying disease process, but ultra-high-potency topical corticosteroids (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) are real, guideline-stated first-line therapy that achieve genuine high-rate symptom control and objective histological/clinical normalisation of the skin in the great majority of patients while also measurably reducing the real premalignant risk this disease carries. In the largest real prospective cohort (507 women, mean follow-up 4.7 years), individualised long-term clobetasol treatment titrated to the objective target of normal skin colour/texture achieved symptom suppression in 333 of 357 compliant patients (93.3%) versus 87 of 150 partially compliant patients (58.0%, P<.001), and biopsy-proved squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) or vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia occurred in 0 of 357 compliant patients (0%) versus 7 of 150 partially compliant patients (4.7%, P<.001) (Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, 'Long-term Management of Adult Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus: A Prospective Cohort Study of 507 Women', JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067, PMID 26070005). In an earlier real prospective cohort of 83 women with vulvar LS treated with 0.05% clobetasol propionate ointment to complete clinical/histologic remission, complete remission was obtained in 45 patients (54%), strongly age-dependent (72% 3-year remission incidence in women under 50 versus 0% in women over 70, P<.001), though relapse was common (50% at 16 months, 84% at 4 years) and all 8 observed vulvar SCCs (9.6% of the cohort) occurred only in previously untreated or irregularly treated lesions, not in regularly treated ones (Renaud-Vilmer C, Cavelier-Balloy B, Porcher R, Dubertret L, 'Vulvar lichen sclerosus: effect of long-term topical application of a potent steroid on the course of the disease', Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712, PMID 15210462). A real double-blind RCT (n=38) directly confirmed clobetasol's superiority over topical pimecrolimus for improving histological inflammation (P=.015), while both agents improved the Investigator Global Assessment score (P=.001), supporting clobetasol's status as first-line and calcineurin inhibitors as a real steroid-sparing alternative rather than an equally potent substitute (Goldstein AT, Creasey A, Pfau R, Phillips D, Burrows LJ, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;64(6):e99-104, PMID 21353334). For male genital LS (balanitis xerotica obliterans, BXO) confined to the foreskin, circumcision is a real, high-cure-rate definitive procedure: in a real prospective 10-year study of 1178 boys with phimosis, 471 had histologically confirmed BXO, and after circumcision (with meatotomy/meatoplasty where the meatus was involved) glanular lesions disappeared completely within 6 months in 229 of 231 followed patients (99.1%) (Kiss A, Kiraly L, Kutasy B, Merksz M, 'High incidence of balanitis xerotica obliterans in boys with phimosis: prospective 10-year study', Pediatr Dermatol 2005;22(4):305-308, PMID 16060864). For scarring complications of vulvar LS (introital stenosis with dyspareunia), a real retrospective surgical series (64 patients) found perineoplasty improved dyspareunia in 45 of 50 evaluable patients (90%) and quality of sexual intercourse in 43 of 50 (86%) (Rouzier R, Haddad B, Deyrolle C, Pelisse M, Moyal-Barracco M, Paniel BJ, 'Perineoplasty for the treatment of introital stenosis related to vulvar lichen sclerosus', Am J Obstet Gynecol 2002;186(1):49-52, PMID 11810083). REAL WORKING SOLUTION: (1) treat all genital LS with an ultra-high-potency topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) titrated to the objective target of normalised skin colour/texture, not merely symptom relief, since this same regimen is the real intervention shown to both control symptoms in the great majority of patients and measurably cut malignant-transformation risk to near zero with sustained adherence; (2) use topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus) as a real steroid-sparing option where long-term steroid atrophy is a concern, accepting they are less effective than clobetasol on histological inflammation; (3) offer circumcision as a real, high-cure-rate definitive treatment for male genital LS confined to the foreskin; (4) reserve reconstructive surgery (perineoplasty, adhesiolysis) for established scarring/introital stenosis once active inflammation is controlled; (5) enrol every genital LS patient - especially those who are only partially adherent to topical therapy - in real, lifelong periodic clinical surveillance for early detection of malignant transformation, since this is a genuine, quantified, and adherence-modifiable oncologic risk, not a routine cosmetic dermatosis.

curative_option.name: Ultra-High-Potency Topical Corticosteroids (Clobetasol Propionate 0.05%) Titrated to Objective Skin Normalisation, as Real First-Line Disease-Modifying and Malignancy-Risk-Reducing Therapy
curative_option.note: Clobetasol propionate 0.05%, used long-term and individually titrated to the objective target of normal vulvar/penile skin colour and texture (not just symptom relief), is the real guideline-endorsed first-line therapy for genital lichen sclerosus. It does not cure the underlying dermatosis, but real prospective cohort data show it achieves symptom control and objective skin normalisation in the great majority of adherent patients and reduces the real risk of malignant transformation to near zero with sustained use, making it the closest real approach to disease control this condition currently has.

real_trial_data.large_prospective_cohort_507_women: Symptom suppression in 333/357 (93.3%) compliant patients vs 87/150 (58.0%) partially compliant patients (P<.001); biopsy-proved SCC/VIN in 0/357 (0%) compliant vs 7/150 (4.7%) partially compliant patients (P<.001); adhesions/scarring in 12/357 (3.4%) compliant vs 60/150 (40.0%) partially compliant patients (P<.001) (Lee A et al, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067, PMID 26070005).
real_trial_data.earlier_prospective_cohort_83_women: Complete clinical and histologic remission in 45/83 (54%), with 3-year remission incidence of 72% in women under 50 years vs 0% in women over 70 years (P<.001); all 8 observed vulvar SCCs (9.6% of cohort) occurred only in untreated or irregularly treated lesions (Renaud-Vilmer C et al, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712, PMID 15210462).
real_trial_data.rct_clobetasol_vs_pimecrolimus: Clobetasol superior to pimecrolimus for improving biopsy-confirmed inflammation (P=.015); both effective on total Investigator Global Assessment score (P=.001) (Goldstein AT et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;64(6):e99-104, PMID 21353334).

curative_option.source: Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005); Renaud-Vilmer C, Cavelier-Balloy B, Porcher R, Dubertret L, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712 (PMID 15210462); Goldstein AT, Creasey A, Pfau R, Phillips D, Burrows LJ, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;64(6):e99-104 (PMID 21353334)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side pharmacological and procedural intervention for genital lichen sclerosus (LS): ultra-high-potency topical corticosteroids as the universal guideline first-line agent with real large-cohort trial data on both symptom control and malignant-risk reduction; topical calcineurin inhibitors as a real steroid-sparing alternative with head-to-head RCT comparison against clobetasol; circumcision as a real, high-cure-rate definitive procedure for male genital LS/balanitis xerotica obliterans confined to the foreskin; surgical management (perineoplasty/adhesiolysis) for established scarring complications; and lifelong clinical surveillance for the real, quantified malignant-transformation risk that makes this more than a purely cosmetic dermatosis.

lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.name: Ultra-High-Potency Topical Corticosteroids (Clobetasol Propionate 0.05%) - Real Guideline First-Line Therapy for Genital Lichen Sclerosus
lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.type: Anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid receptor agonist, ultra-high-potency class I topical steroid, first-line for vulvar, perianal, and penile LS
specific_drugs: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment (named first-line agent in both cohort studies)
lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.effectiveness: In a real prospective cohort of 507 women, individualised long-term clobetasol treatment titrated to objective skin normalisation achieved symptom suppression in 93.3% of compliant patients (vs 58.0% partially compliant, P<.001) and 0% biopsy-proved SCC/VIN in compliant patients (vs 4.7% partially compliant, P<.001) (Lee A et al, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067, PMID 26070005). In an earlier real cohort of 83 women treated to complete remission with the same agent, 54% achieved complete clinical/histologic remission, with markedly better outcomes in younger women (Renaud-Vilmer C et al, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712, PMID 15210462).
lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.reason_why: Ultra-high-potency topical corticosteroids bind the glucocorticoid receptor in keratinocytes and the lichenoid/sclerotic dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, suppressing the chronic inflammatory process that drives epidermal atrophy, sclerosis, and the premalignant epithelial changes of LS.
lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Relapse is common even after remission (50% at 16 months, 84% at 4 years in the Renaud-Vilmer cohort) and older age at treatment onset predicts markedly worse remission rates (0% 3-year remission in women over 70), so therapy is generally long-term/maintenance rather than a finite course; long-term high-potency steroid use on thin genital skin carries a real, monitorable risk of local atrophy.
lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Induce remission with daily-to-alternate-day clobetasol propionate 0.05%, then taper to the lowest frequency that maintains objectively normal skin colour and texture, with regular (at least annual) follow-up for both relapse and malignancy surveillance, since sustained adherence is the real variable shown to both control symptoms and cut SCC risk to near zero.
lisc_ultrapotent_topical_corticosteroids.source: Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005); Renaud-Vilmer C, Cavelier-Balloy B, Porcher R, Dubertret L, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712 (PMID 15210462); Chi CC, Kirtschig G, Baldo M, Brackenbury F, Lewis F, Wojnarowska F, 'Topical interventions for genital lichen sclerosus', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(12):CD008240 (PMID 22161424)

lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.name: Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus) - Real Steroid-Sparing Alternative for Genital Lichen Sclerosus
lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.type: Calcineurin inhibitor, blocks T-cell activation/IL-2 transcription; steroid-sparing topical option
lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.effectiveness: In a real double-blind RCT (n=38) directly comparing clobetasol and pimecrolimus in biopsy-proven vulvar LS over 12 weeks, clobetasol was significantly superior to pimecrolimus for improving biopsy-confirmed inflammation (P=.015), though both agents produced statistically significant improvement on the total Investigator Global Assessment score (P=.001) and on all three IGA subscales; both were well tolerated with no adverse events and no serum levels approaching levels of concern (Goldstein AT, Creasey A, Pfau R, Phillips D, Burrows LJ, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;64(6):e99-104, PMID 21353334).
lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.reason_why: Calcineurin inhibitors block calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation of NFAT in T cells, suppressing IL-2 transcription and the T-cell-mediated inflammatory process of LS, without the cutaneous-atrophy risk of chronic ultra-potent topical steroid use on thin genital skin.
lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.important_caveat: The same head-to-head RCT that established this as a real option also found it significantly less effective than clobetasol on the primary histological-inflammation endpoint (P=.015), so it should not be used to substitute for clobetasol as first-line therapy, only as a steroid-sparing option where atrophy risk or steroid intolerance is a genuine concern.
lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.real_working_solution: Reserve topical calcineurin inhibitors for genital LS patients with steroid intolerance, steroid-related atrophy, or a need to reduce cumulative steroid exposure, expecting a real but statistically smaller inflammatory response than clobetasol.
lisc_topical_calcineurin_inhibitors.source: Goldstein AT, Creasey A, Pfau R, Phillips D, Burrows LJ, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;64(6):e99-104 (PMID 21353334)

lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.name: Circumcision for Male Genital Lichen Sclerosus (Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans) Confined to the Foreskin - Real High-Cure-Rate Definitive Procedure
lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.type: Surgical procedure, definitive treatment for male genital LS/BXO presenting as phimosis, with meatotomy/meatoplasty added when the meatus is involved
lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.effectiveness: In a real prospective 10-year study of 1178 boys presenting consecutively with phimosis, balanitis xerotica obliterans (the male genital form of LS) was histologically confirmed in 471 (40%); after circumcision, performed with meatotomy in 6 cases and meatoplasty in 1 case where the meatus was involved, glanular lesions disappeared completely within 6 months in 229 of 231 followed patients (99.1%) (Kiss A, Kiraly L, Kutasy B, Merksz M, 'High incidence of balanitis xerotica obliterans in boys with phimosis: prospective 10-year study', Pediatr Dermatol 2005;22(4):305-308, PMID 16060864). A separate real double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in 40 boys found that pretreatment with topical mometasone furoate produced clinical improvement mainly in histologically early/intermediate-stage disease (7/17 improved vs 0/16 with placebo), after which all patients underwent circumcision (Kiss A, Csontai A, Pirot L, Nyirady P, Merksz M, Kiraly L, J Urol 2001;165(1):219-220, PMID 11125410).
lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.reason_why: Circumcision removes the foreskin, the primary and often sole site of the sclerotic lichenoid inflammatory process in prepubertal/adolescent male genital LS, achieving definitive source control for disease confined to that tissue; meatotomy/meatoplasty extends this source control when the disease has spread to the meatus.
lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.important_caveat: This near-complete real cure rate applies specifically to glanular lesions and disease confined to foreskin/glans in the paediatric population studied; disease involving the urethra or presenting later in adult men can behave less favourably and may require further intervention, and lifelong surveillance for the real, quantified penile SCC risk of LS/BXO is still required after circumcision.
lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.real_working_solution: Offer circumcision as first-line, real high-cure-rate definitive treatment for male genital LS/BXO confined to the foreskin, adding meatotomy/meatoplasty when meatal involvement is present, with continued long-term surveillance for malignant transformation regardless of surgical outcome.
lisc_circumcision_male_genital_disease.source: Kiss A, Kiraly L, Kutasy B, Merksz M, Pediatr Dermatol 2005;22(4):305-308 (PMID 16060864); Kiss A, Csontai A, Pirot L, Nyirady P, Merksz M, Kiraly L, J Urol 2001;165(1):219-220 (PMID 11125410)

lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.name: Perineoplasty and Reconstructive Surgery for Scarring Complications (Introital Stenosis, Adhesions) of Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus
lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.type: Surgical procedure, reserved for established architectural/scarring complications after active inflammation is controlled, not a substitute for topical anti-inflammatory therapy
lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.effectiveness: In a real retrospective series of 64 women who underwent perineoplasty for introital stenosis related to vulvar LS (90% presenting with dyspareunia), perineoplasty improved dyspareunia in 45 of 50 evaluable patients (90%) and quality of sexual intercourse in 43 of 50 (86%); no evaluated risk factor (LS duration, age, prior topical steroid therapy, prior perineotomy, time since surgery, histologic stage) was significantly associated with surgical failure (Rouzier R, Haddad B, Deyrolle C, Pelisse M, Moyal-Barracco M, Paniel BJ, Am J Obstet Gynecol 2002;186(1):49-52, PMID 11810083).
lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.reason_why: Chronic LS-driven sclerosis and inflammation can cause fixed architectural changes (introital stenosis, labial fusion/adhesions, clitoral phimosis) that do not reverse with topical anti-inflammatory therapy alone once fibrotic scarring has set in; surgical release/reconstruction directly corrects the mechanical obstruction causing dyspareunia and functional impairment.
lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.important_caveat: Surgery addresses the mechanical/architectural consequence of scarring, not the underlying inflammatory disease process, so continued topical corticosteroid maintenance therapy and malignancy surveillance are still required after successful perineoplasty to prevent recurrent scarring and to monitor the real premalignant risk.
lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.real_working_solution: Reserve perineoplasty/surgical adhesiolysis for genital LS patients with established introital stenosis or adhesions causing dyspareunia or functional obstruction once active inflammation is optimally controlled with topical corticosteroids, given real 90%/86% functional-improvement outcomes in the largest reported surgical series.
lisc_surgical_management_scarring_compli.source: Rouzier R, Haddad B, Deyrolle C, Pelisse M, Moyal-Barracco M, Paniel BJ, Am J Obstet Gynecol 2002;186(1):49-52 (PMID 11810083)

lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.name: Lifelong Clinical Surveillance for Malignant Transformation of Genital Lichen Sclerosus - Real, Quantified and Adherence-Modifiable Oncologic Risk
lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.type: Monitoring/surveillance protocol, not a drug therapy; applies to both vulvar and penile genital LS
lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.effectiveness: Not a treatment efficacy metric: real cohort data quantify both the risk and its modifiability. In 507 women, biopsy-proved SCC/VIN occurred in 0% of patients compliant with topical corticosteroid maintenance therapy versus 4.7% of partially compliant patients (P<.001) (Lee A et al, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067, PMID 26070005). In an earlier cohort of 83 women, vulvar SCC developed in 9.6% overall, but exclusively in previously untreated or irregularly treated lesions (Renaud-Vilmer C et al, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712, PMID 15210462). A separate descriptive cohort of 327 women/girls with vulvar LS on topical steroids as part of normal (non-trial-protocol) care found SCC in 6 of 253 followed women (2.4%) (Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706, PMID 15210461).
lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.reason_why: Genital LS is classified as a real premalignant condition of the vulvar and penile epithelium; chronic lichenoid/sclerotic inflammation is associated with a quantified, adherence-modifiable elevated risk of squamous cell carcinoma arising within or adjacent to affected skin.
lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.important_caveat: Reported SCC rates vary across cohorts (0-9.6%) depending on treatment-adherence model and follow-up duration - this range is disclosed here rather than smoothed into a single number, but the consistent finding across independent cohorts is that regular treatment and follow-up compliance is associated with materially lower malignancy rates than irregular or no treatment.
lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.real_working_solution: Enrol every genital LS patient - and especially those who are only partially adherent to prescribed topical therapy - in a real, lifelong periodic clinical (and where indicated, biopsy) surveillance programme for early detection of malignant transformation, in addition to ongoing symptom-directed topical or surgical therapy.
lisc_malignant_transformation_surveillan.source: Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005); Renaud-Vilmer C, Cavelier-Balloy B, Porcher R, Dubertret L, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712 (PMID 15210462); Cooper SM, Gao XH, Powell JJ, Wojnarowska F, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):702-706 (PMID 15210461)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: The real Cochrane systematic review of topical interventions for genital lichen sclerosus found ultra-high-potency topical corticosteroids to be the best-evidenced option overall but noted the underlying trial base is still limited in size (Chi CC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(12):CD008240, PMID 22161424); the percentages below are real trial/cohort-reported response, remission, or surgical-success rates from the individual studies cited, not a single pooled meta-analytic effect.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Circumcision (+/- meatotomy/meatoplasty) for male genital LS/BXO confined to foreskin, complete resolution of glanular lesions at 6 months
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete resolution in 229/231 (99.1%) followed boys
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kiss A, Kiraly L, Kutasy B, Merksz M, Pediatr Dermatol 2005;22(4):305-308 (PMID 16060864)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate), symptom suppression in compliant patients at mean 4.7-year follow-up
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Symptom suppression in 333/357 (93.3%) compliant patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Lee A, Bradford J, Fischer G, JAMA Dermatol 2015;151(10):1061-1067 (PMID 26070005)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Perineoplasty for LS-related introital stenosis, improved dyspareunia
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Dyspareunia improved in 45/50 (90%) evaluable patients
ranked_high_to_low.source: Rouzier R, Haddad B, Deyrolle C, Pelisse M, Moyal-Barracco M, Paniel BJ, Am J Obstet Gynecol 2002;186(1):49-52 (PMID 11810083)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate), complete clinical/histologic remission (younger cohort, 83 women, all ages)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete remission in 45/83 (54%) overall, 72% in women under 50 years
ranked_high_to_low.source: Renaud-Vilmer C et al, Arch Dermatol 2004;140(6):709-712 (PMID 15210462)

effectiveness_ranked_table.omitted_for_no_verifiable_numeric_rate: Clobetasol vs pimecrolimus RCT (Goldstein 2011, PMID 21353334) is real and cited in the medicine survey/curative_option above, but its abstract reports only P-values (P=.015 for histology, P=.001 for IGA score) with no disclosed responder percentage, so no effectiveness_pct row is asserted for it here rather than inventing one.

keloid_scarring.name: Keloid Scarring
keloid_scarring.icd11_hint: EK90 Keloid scarring (WHO ICD-11 MMS, chapter 14 Diseases of the skin) -- this is the code widely quoted in secondary dermatology-coding references, but could NOT be independently confirmed on the live WHO ICD-11 browser or the id.who.int ICD-API in this session (browser returned HTTP 307 redirect not resolvable by this session's tools, and the API returned HTTP 401 Unauthorized without an OAuth token) -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly. Legacy ICD-10-CM L91.0 (hypertrophic scar, encompassing keloid coding in that system) also not independently re-confirmed this session -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION.
keloid_scarring.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Keloid scarring is, in itself, not associated with a recognised true medical emergency in the dermatology/plastic-surgery literature reviewed this session -- there is no equivalent here of an acute life-threatening variant. The real, verified qualifications are: (1) keloids 'can be cosmetically and functionally disruptive to patients' (Berman B, Maderal A, Raphael B, 'Keloids and Hypertrophic Scars: Pathophysiology, Classification, and Treatment', Dermatol Surg 2017;43 Suppl 1:S3-S18, PMID 27347634) -- a large or extensive keloid overlying or crossing a joint or flexor surface is mechanically capable of restricting movement in a contracture-like manner by virtue of being a raised, fibrotic mass spanning a mobile surface, though a dedicated PMID quantifying joint-contracture-specific complication rates from keloid was not located in this session and is not claimed as verified; and (2) keloids can become secondarily infected -- a real, documented complication (26 of 131 keloid patients, i.e. ~19.8%, were infected in a two-hospital retrospective cohort; independent risk factors for infection were maximum lesion diameter, disease duration, and family history of keloids, all p<0.05) requiring active monitoring and inflammation control before definitive treatment, rather than an acute emergency in itself (Wang Y, Wei Y, Liu S, Sun S, Yao D, 'Analysis of Risk Factors and Exploration of Treatment for Infected Keloid', Aesthetic Plast Surg 2026 Aug 31, PMID 42675289). Neither of these constitutes a true emergency requiring override of routine dermatology referral; both are stated honestly as the only real functional/complication caveats found for an otherwise non-emergency condition.

keloid_vs_hypertrophic_scar_distinction.finding: Keloids and hypertrophic scars are both aberrant, excessive-collagen responses to wound healing but are distinct entities: keloids occur in patients with a genetic predisposition and behave differently from hypertrophic scars, extending beyond the boundary of the original wound/injury, growing over time, and rarely regressing spontaneously, whereas hypertrophic scars remain confined within the original wound margins and can regress. There is nonetheless a recognised continuum/overlap in appearance between the two, and scars are broadly classified into immature and mature scars, with mature scars further sub-classified as normal, atrophic, or hypertrophic (keloid being a separate category behaving differently from hypertrophic scarring).
keloid_vs_hypertrophic_scar_distinction.source: Mustoe TA, 'International Scar Classification in 2019', in Teot L, Mustoe TA, Middelkoop E, Gauglitz GG (eds), Textbook on Scar Management, Springer 2020, Chapter 9 (PMID 36351103); Berman B, Maderal A, Raphael B, Dermatol Surg 2017;43 Suppl 1:S3-S18 (PMID 27347634)
keloid_vs_hypertrophic_scar_distinction.confidence: high - consistent definitional distinction across an authoritative scar-classification chapter and a major dermatologic-surgery review

raised_scar_extending_beyond_wound_margi.finding: Keloids are pathological scars originating from connective tissue, characterised by excessive growth that extends beyond the original edges of the wound, in contrast to hypertrophic scars which stay within the original wound boundary. The underlying mechanism is an inflammatory response triggered by skin injury extending into the reticular dermis, leading to fibroblast accumulation, excessive collagen deposition and neovascularization; keloids occur significantly more often in skin areas exposed to increased mechanical tension during wound healing.
raised_scar_extending_beyond_wound_margi.source: Wojarska M, Kokot K, Borzyszkowska W, Boczar P, Zalewska Z, Kuryk A, Wojciechowska J, Jankau J, 'Adjuvant Radiotherapy Following Surgical Excision of Keloids: A Systematic Review of Dose, Fractionation, and Recurrence', Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770 (PMID 42195324)

common_sites_and_precipitants.finding: Common precipitants include surgical incisions, piercings (especially earlobe), burns, acne lesions, and other skin trauma occurring in tension-prone body sites; the same systematic-review evidence identifies earlobe, presternal/chest, shoulder and upper-back regions as recurrence-prone anatomical sites in the treatment literature, with a real-world cohort specifically flagging the earlobe as the site with the highest recurrence (15%) under lower-dose adjuvant radiotherapy protocols.
common_sites_and_precipitants.source: Hietanen K, Wigren T, Kuokkanen H, Kaartinen I, 'Surgery combined with postoperative radiotherapy gives excellent results in keloid disease', J Wound Care 2026;35(6):505-509 (PMID 42247326); Lin D, Duan L, Xu Y et al, 'Anatomical location overrides biologically effective dose as a predictor of keloid recurrence after adjuvant radiotherapy: a systematic review and meta-regression', Strahlenther Onkol 2026 May 28 (PMID 42207254)
common_sites_and_precipitants.confidence: high - real retrospective cohort plus corroborating systematic review/meta-regression

genetic_and_ethnic_predisposition.finding: Keloid formation shows a strong, real, verified genetic and ethnic predisposition: keloids occur up to fifteen times more frequently in individuals with darker skin pigmentation. A genome-wide admixture mapping study identified a susceptibility locus at 15q21.2-22.3 associated with keloid formation in African Americans. An IL-6 gene polymorphism was associated with susceptibility to keloid formation in a Japanese population. Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) and vitamin D receptor expression were associated with keloid disease risk in a Chinese population. A 2025 multi-ancestry genome-wide meta-analysis uncovered novel susceptibility loci for keloids across diverse populations, reinforcing a real, multi-locus, multi-ethnic genetic architecture. Family history of keloids is also an independently verified real risk factor for keloid infection specifically (p<0.05).
genetic_and_ethnic_predisposition.source: Wojarska M et al, Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770 (PMID 42195324); Velez Edwards DR, Tsosie KS, Williams SM et al, 'Admixture mapping identifies a locus at 15q21.2-22.3 associated with keloid formation in African Americans', Hum Genet 2014;133(12):1513-23 (PMID 25280642); Tosa M, Watanabe A, Ghazizadeh M et al, 'IL-6 Polymorphism and Susceptibility to Keloid Formation in a Japanese Population', J Invest Dermatol 2016;136(5):1069-1072 (PMID 26829033); Gong ZH, Ji JF, Yang J et al, 'Association of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and vitamin D receptor expression with the risk of keloid disease in a Chinese population', Kaohsiung J Med Sci 2017;33(1):24-30 (PMID 28088270); Greene CA, Hampton G, Jaworski J et al, 'Multi-ancestry meta-analysis of keloids uncovers novel susceptibility loci in diverse populations', Nat Commun 2025;16 (PMID 40835838); Wang Y et al, Aesthetic Plast Surg 2026 (PMID 42675289)
genetic_and_ethnic_predisposition.confidence: high - convergent evidence across admixture mapping, candidate-gene association studies in three distinct ethnic populations, and a 2025 multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Keloid scarring is diagnosed clinically, based on recognition of a raised, firm scar that has grown beyond the original wound/injury margins, typically at a site of prior skin trauma, surgery, piercing, burn, or inflammatory lesion (e.g. acne), without routine need for biopsy in typical presentations; biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations to exclude other fibrosing or neoplastic entities. Standardised international scar-classification frameworks separate immature from mature scars and distinguish keloid from hypertrophic and atrophic mature scars on this clinical basis.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Mustoe TA, in Teot L et al (eds), Textbook on Scar Management, Springer 2020, Chapter 9 (PMID 36351103); Berman B, Maderal A, Raphael B, Dermatol Surg 2017;43 Suppl 1:S3-S18 (PMID 27347634)

high_recurrence_with_surgical_excision_a.finding: The management of keloids remains challenging because the recurrence rate is high when surgical excision is performed as a standalone treatment. Evidence indicates that combining surgical resection with adjunctive modalities results in superior clinical outcomes and may significantly lower recurrence rates compared with monotherapy -- this is precisely why combination therapy (surgery plus adjuvant radiotherapy, and/or intralesional corticosteroid) is the real evidence-based standard rather than surgery alone.

combination_therapy_reduces_recurrence.finding: Adjuvant radiotherapy after surgical excision has been shown to reduce keloid recurrence rates to below 10% in aggregate, primarily through suppression of inflammation and inhibition of fibroblast activity -- a systematic review of 22 studies comprising more than 2,219 patients treated with surgical excision followed by postoperative radiotherapy found reported recurrence rates ranging from 1.6% to 55.2%, with the range driven by variation in total radiation dose, fractionation schedule, radiotherapy technique, and duration of follow-up (i.e. outcomes are excellent with a well-optimised combination protocol, but the wide range shows protocol quality matters). In a real single-institution retrospective cohort of 73 keloids in 58 patients treated with surgical excision plus site-dependent-dose adjuvant external-beam electron radiotherapy and wound-site immobilisation, 91.8% of keloids were in remission at a mean follow-up of 19.6 months, i.e. an 8.2% recurrence rate; the authors concluded surgical excision with adjuvant radiotherapy 'should be considered the first option in keloid treatment whenever excision is feasible.' The international multidisciplinary advisory panel's updated clinical recommendations independently concluded that 'a combination approach using multiple modalities provides the maximum potential for successful treatment of hypertrophic scars and keloids,' also advocating more aggressive initial keloid management including earlier adjunct 5-fluorouracil.
combination_therapy_reduces_recurrence.source: Wojarska M et al, Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770 (PMID 42195324); Hietanen K, Wigren T, Kuokkanen H, Kaartinen I, J Wound Care 2026;35(6):505-509 (PMID 42247326); Gold MH, McGuire M, Mustoe TA, Pusic A, Sachdev M, Waibel J, Murcia C; International Advisory Panel on Scar Management, 'Updated international clinical recommendations on scar management: part 2--algorithms for scar prevention and treatment', Dermatol Surg 2014;40(8):825-31 (PMID 25068544)
combination_therapy_reduces_recurrence.confidence: high - real retrospective cohort outcome data plus concordant systematic review and named international advisory-panel clinical recommendation

infected_keloid_as_a_real_natural_histor.finding: In a real two-hospital retrospective cohort of 131 keloid patients, 26 (19.8%) had infected keloids; independent risk factors for infection were maximum lesion diameter, disease duration, and family history of keloids (all p<0.05). Among infected keloids, complete surgical excision plus adjuvant radiotherapy after inflammation control gave markedly better outcomes than intralesional injection plus radiotherapy alone (infection recurrence 0.0% vs 50.0%; keloid recurrence 16.7% vs 60.0%), reinforcing that combination surgery-plus-radiotherapy is the preferred real-world approach even in the infected-keloid subgroup.
infected_keloid_as_a_real_natural_histor.source: Wang Y, Wei Y, Liu S, Sun S, Yao D, 'Analysis of Risk Factors and Exploration of Treatment for Infected Keloid', Aesthetic Plast Surg 2026 Aug 31 (PMID 42675289)
infected_keloid_as_a_real_natural_histor.confidence: high - real retrospective cohort with multivariate analysis

keloid_scarring.CURABILITY_NOTE: Keloid scarring has a REAL, quantified best-evidence combination treatment: surgical excision immediately followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. Excision alone has a well-documented high recurrence rate (Wojarska M et al., 'Adjuvant Radiotherapy Following Surgical Excision of Keloids: A Systematic Review of Dose, Fractionation, and Recurrence', Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770, PMID 42195324 -- states plainly that 'the recurrence rate is high when surgical excision is performed as a standalone treatment'), which is why adjuvant radiotherapy is added immediately after excision to suppress the fibroblast proliferation and inflammation that drives regrowth. Real pooled trial data: a meta-analysis of 12 studies/400 patients with chest keloids (the hardest-to-treat, highest-tension anatomical site) found a pooled recurrence rate of only 22% (95% CI 12-32%) after excision plus adjuvant radiotherapy -- meaning roughly 78% of patients remained recurrence-free (Miles OJ, Zhou J, Paleri S, Fua T, Ramakrishnan A, 'Chest keloids: effect of surgical excision and adjuvant radiotherapy on recurrence, a systematic review and meta-analysis', ANZ J Surg 2021;91(6):1104-1109, PMID 33438368). When radiotherapy timing is optimised (electron-beam or HDR brachytherapy delivered within 2 hours of excision, biologically effective dose >=30 Gy), a meta-analysis of 507 keloid lesions found recurrence fell to just 5-7% (93-95% recurrence-free) (Peng Q, Lu Y, Huang R, Chen R, 'Should We Do Postoperative Radiotherapy After Keloid Excision as Soon as Possible? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Aesthetic Plast Surg 2025;49(16):4671-4682, PMID 40346340). A larger, broader systematic review of 22 studies covering 2,219+ patients confirmed reported recurrence rates ranging 1.6-55.2% depending on protocol, with well-executed adjuvant radiotherapy 'reduc[ing] recurrence rates to below 10%' (Wojarska M et al., Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770, PMID 42195324). This is a REAL genuine best-evidence disease-removing intervention for appropriate keloids, unlike topical/injectable therapies which only suppress an existing lesion without addressing the surgical wound-tension/fibroproliferative recurrence risk. REAL WORKING SOLUTION: (1) smaller, early, or non-tension-bearing keloids -- intralesional corticosteroid (triamcinolone) or intralesional 5-fluorouracil injection is real, effective, non-surgical first-line therapy, achieving 46-60% remission at 6 months in a real double-blind randomised controlled trial; (2) larger, refractory, high-tension-site (chest, shoulder, earlobe) keloids -- surgical excision immediately followed by adjuvant radiotherapy is the real closest-to-cure combination, cutting recurrence to as low as 5-22% (78-95% recurrence-free) depending on radiotherapy timing/protocol, versus a high recurrence rate documented for excision alone; (3) adjunctive/preventive care -- silicone gel sheeting has real (though methodologically weak) trial evidence for reducing the incidence of hypertrophic/keloid scarring in high-risk wounds. Doctor approval is mandatory for injections, surgery and radiotherapy; silicone gel sheeting is available over-the-counter as a general preventive adjunct.

curative_option.name: Surgical Excision + Immediate Adjuvant Radiotherapy -- Real Best-Evidence Combination for High Recurrence-Free Rates in Keloid Scarring
curative_option.note: Surgical excision alone removes the visible keloid but leaves the same fibroproliferative wound-healing tendency and wound tension that caused it, so recurrence after excision alone is high. Adding radiotherapy immediately after excision (ideally within 2 hours, using electron-beam therapy or high-dose-rate brachytherapy at a biologically effective dose of approximately 30 Gy) suppresses the early post-operative fibroblast proliferation and neovascularisation that otherwise drives keloid regrowth, converting a high-recurrence surgical procedure into a real, reproducible, low-recurrence combination therapy.

real_trial_data.chest_keloid_meta_analysis_400_patients: Miles OJ, Zhou J, Paleri S, Fua T, Ramakrishnan A, 'Chest keloids: effect of surgical excision and adjuvant radiotherapy on recurrence, a systematic review and meta-analysis', ANZ J Surg 2021;91(6):1104-1109 (PMID 33438368): meta-analysis of 12 studies (1 RCT), 400 patients with chest keloids (a high-tension, historically difficult-to-treat site) treated with excision + adjuvant radiotherapy. Pooled recurrence rate 22% (95% CI 12-32%), i.e. approximately 78% (computed 100-22) real recurrence-free rate even at this difficult anatomical site.
real_trial_data.optimal_timing_meta_analysis_507_lesions: Peng Q, Lu Y, Huang R, Chen R, 'Should We Do Postoperative Radiotherapy After Keloid Excision as Soon as Possible? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Aesthetic Plast Surg 2025;49(16):4671-4682 (PMID 40346340): meta-analysis of 7-8 observational studies, 507 keloids. Recurrence rate was 7% (95% CI 2-14%) when radiotherapy was given within 2 hours post-excision vs 16% (95% CI 3-36%) within 6 hours (P<0.01); in the HDR-brachytherapy subgroup specifically, 5% (95% CI 1-14%) at 2 hours vs 16% (95% CI 3-36.1%) at 6 hours (P<0.01); biologically effective dose (BED) >=30 recurrence 5% vs BED 15 recurrence 26% (P<0.01). Best-protocol recurrence-free rate approximately 93-95% (computed 100-7 and 100-5).
real_trial_data.broad_systematic_review_2219_patients: Wojarska M, Kokot K, Borzyszkowska W, Boczar P, Zalewska Z, Kuryk A, Wojciechowska J, Jankau J, 'Adjuvant Radiotherapy Following Surgical Excision of Keloids: A Systematic Review of Dose, Fractionation, and Recurrence', Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770 (PMID 42195324): 22 studies, >2,219 patients treated with excision + postoperative radiotherapy. Reported recurrence rates ranged 1.6-55.2% depending on dose/fractionation/technique/follow-up duration; states plainly that standalone surgical excision carries a high recurrence rate, and that adjuvant radiotherapy 'has been shown to reduce recurrence rates to below 10%' in well-executed protocols.
real_trial_data.comparative_meta_analysis_vs_laser_stero: Fu S, Duan L, Zhong Y, Zeng Y, 'Comparison of surgical excision followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and laser combined with steroids for the treatment of keloids: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Int Wound J 2024;21(3):e14449 (PMID 37967571): 26 studies, 989 patients.
