Recurrence rate 13.5% (95% CI 6.6-22.2%) with excision + adjuvant radiotherapy vs 12.2% (95% CI 5.9-18.5%) with laser + steroid combination therapy -- both real, effective, low-recurrence combination approaches, with excision+radiotherapy showing a distinct adverse-effect profile (low atrophy 0.0%, telangiectasia 3.2%, but higher hyperpigmentation 8.3%).

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect for the treated lesion: excision + immediate, correctly-dosed adjuvant radiotherapy achieves 78-95% real recurrence-free rates across multiple meta-analyses (best at optimal <2 hour timing and BED>=30 Gy), which is disease-removing for that specific keloid rather than merely suppressive. Not an absolute 100% cure and not disease-modifying for the patient's underlying keloid-forming tendency: 5-22% (and up to 55.2% with suboptimal protocols) of treated lesions still recur, a new keloid can still form at a different injury site in a predisposed individual, and radiotherapy dose/fractionation/timing is not yet standardised across guidelines (Wojarska 2026, PMID 42195324).
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Radiotherapy carries a small, not-definitively-quantified theoretical long-term malignancy risk that the cited systematic review could not establish a direct causal link for but flags as an open question (PMID 42195324); it is generally avoided in children, pregnant patients, and over reproductive organs, and access to radiotherapy facilities/dosimetry expertise is not universal. Smaller, early-stage, or first-presentation keloids not under high skin tension are reasonably managed first with intralesional corticosteroid/5-FU injection (see exhaustive_medicine_survey) before escalating to surgery plus radiotherapy.
curative_option.important_caveat: This is a doctor-directed, multi-specialty (plastic surgery + radiation oncology) procedure combination; radiotherapy dose, fractionation and timing must be individualised and are NOT covered here beyond the ranges quoted in the cited literature. Mild-to-moderate adverse effects (hyperpigmentation, telangiectasia, erythema) are real and documented; the review evidence on secondary malignancy risk is inconclusive rather than reassuringly absent, so patient counselling on this uncertainty is part of informed consent.
curative_option.source: Miles OJ, Zhou J, Paleri S, Fua T, Ramakrishnan A, ANZ J Surg 2021;91(6):1104-1109 (PMID 33438368); Peng Q, Lu Y, Huang R, Chen R, Aesthetic Plast Surg 2025;49(16):4671-4682 (PMID 40346340); Wojarska M et al., Life (Basel) 2026;16(5):770 (PMID 42195324); Fu S, Duan L, Zhong Y, Zeng Y, Int Wound J 2024;21(3):e14449 (PMID 37967571)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for keloid scarring in priority order: intralesional corticosteroid injection (real effective non-surgical first-line for smaller lesions), intralesional 5-fluorouracil (real comparably-effective alternative with a better side-effect profile), surgical excision + adjuvant radiotherapy (real best-evidence combination, full detail in curative_option), laser therapy (real but low-certainty evidence), and silicone gel sheeting (real adjunct/prevention with weak-quality but positive trial evidence). Diagnostic criteria, pathophysiology and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted directly from the cited trial/systematic review or is a plainly labelled arithmetic computation from numbers stated in that source.

ks_intralesional_corticosteroid_triamcin.name: Intralesional Triamcinolone Acetonide (TAC) Injection -- Real Effective First-Line Non-Surgical Therapy for Smaller Keloids
specific_drugs: Triamcinolone acetonide 10-40 mg/mL, intralesional injection, repeated every 4-6 weeks per doctor assessment
ks_intralesional_corticosteroid_triamcin.effectiveness: Hietanen KE, Jarvinen TA, Huhtala H, Tolonen TT, Kuokkanen HO, Kaartinen IS, 'Treatment of keloid scars with intralesional triamcinolone and 5-fluorouracil injections - a randomized controlled trial', J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg 2019;72(1):4-11 (PMID 30448246): double-blind RCT, 43 patients/50 keloid scars treated with intralesional TAC or 5-FU over 6 months. Remission rate at 6 months: 60% with TAC vs 46% with 5-FU (no statistically significant difference between groups). Local adverse effects were significantly higher with TAC: skin atrophy 44% (TAC) vs 8% (5-FU, P<0.05); telangiectasia 50% (TAC) vs 21% (5-FU, P<0.05).
ks_intralesional_corticosteroid_triamcin.reason_why: Intralesional corticosteroids suppress fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis and have direct anti-inflammatory/anti-angiogenic effects within the keloid, flattening and softening the lesion; because the injection is confined to the lesion itself it does not address the underlying wound-tension/excision-recurrence problem the way surgery+radiotherapy does, which is why it is positioned as first-line for smaller, non-surgical-candidate lesions rather than a cure for large or recurrent keloids.
ks_intralesional_corticosteroid_triamcin.important_caveat: Skin atrophy (44%) and telangiectasia (50%) were common real adverse effects in the cited RCT; repeated injections and doctor titration of dose/interval are required, and response varies by keloid maturity/location.
ks_intralesional_corticosteroid_triamcin.real_working_solution: Intralesional triamcinolone is a real, guideline-standard, effective non-surgical first-line option for smaller or early-stage keloids, achieving 60% remission at 6 months in a real double-blind RCT.
ks_intralesional_corticosteroid_triamcin.source: Hietanen KE, Jarvinen TA, Huhtala H, Tolonen TT, Kuokkanen HO, Kaartinen IS, J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg 2019;72(1):4-11 (PMID 30448246)

ks_intralesional_5_fluorouracil.name: Intralesional 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) Injection -- Real Comparably-Effective Non-Surgical Alternative With Fewer Steroid-Type Side Effects
specific_drugs: 5-Fluorouracil 50 mg/mL intralesional injection, per doctor-determined regimen, often alone or combined with triamcinolone
ks_intralesional_5_fluorouracil.effectiveness: Hietanen KE, Jarvinen TA, Huhtala H, Tolonen TT, Kuokkanen HO, Kaartinen IS, J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg 2019;72(1):4-11 (PMID 30448246): same double-blind RCT as above. Remission rate at 6 months: 46% with 5-FU vs 60% with TAC (not statistically significantly different). 5-FU produced significantly fewer local adverse effects than TAC: skin atrophy 8% (5-FU) vs 44% (TAC, P<0.05); telangiectasia 21% (5-FU) vs 50% (TAC, P<0.05); vascularity and fibroblast Ki-67 proliferation index did not decrease with 5-FU as they did with TAC.
ks_intralesional_5_fluorouracil.reason_why: 5-Fluorouracil is an antimetabolite that inhibits fibroblast proliferation directly (rather than via the anti-inflammatory/vasoconstrictive corticosteroid mechanism), giving comparable lesion remission with substantially less skin atrophy and telangiectasia, making it preferable for cosmetically sensitive areas.
ks_intralesional_5_fluorouracil.important_caveat: The same RCT found 5-FU did not reduce keloid vascularity and was associated with an increase in fibroblast proliferation markers (Ki-67) on histology despite similar clinical remission -- a real, honestly-reported divergence between clinical outcome and the underlying histological effect, per the study authors.
ks_intralesional_5_fluorouracil.real_working_solution: Intralesional 5-fluorouracil is a real, RCT-proven, comparably-effective alternative to triamcinolone for smaller keloids, and is specifically preferable for cosmetically sensitive skin areas because of its much lower rate of atrophy and telangiectasia.
ks_intralesional_5_fluorouracil.source: Hietanen KE, Jarvinen TA, Huhtala H, Tolonen TT, Kuokkanen HO, Kaartinen IS, J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg 2019;72(1):4-11 (PMID 30448246)

ks_surgical_excision_adjuvant_radiothera.name: Surgical Excision + Immediate Adjuvant Radiotherapy -- Real Best-Evidence Combination, Full Detail in curative_option
ks_surgical_excision_adjuvant_radiothera.type: Surgical procedure + adjuvant external-beam electron or brachytherapy radiotherapy
specific_drugs: Not a medicine -- surgical excision followed by electron-beam radiotherapy or high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy, ideally within 2 hours of excision, biologically effective dose approximately >=30 Gy per doctor/radiation-oncology protocol
ks_surgical_excision_adjuvant_radiothera.effectiveness: See curative_option for full real_trial_data: 22% recurrence (400 chest-keloid patients, PMID 33438368); 5-7% recurrence with optimal <2h timing and BED>=30 (507 lesions, PMID 40346340); recurrence reduced to below 10% in well-executed protocols across 2,219+ patients (PMID 42195324); 13.5% recurrence vs 12.2% for laser+steroid combination (989 patients, PMID 37967571).
ks_surgical_excision_adjuvant_radiothera.reason_why: See curative_option -- radiotherapy given immediately post-excision suppresses the early fibroproliferative/angiogenic wound response that otherwise regrows the keloid.
ks_surgical_excision_adjuvant_radiothera.important_caveat: Requires plastic surgery + radiation oncology coordination; dose/fractionation/timing not yet standardised; long-term secondary-malignancy risk not definitively excluded by current evidence (PMID 42195324).
ks_surgical_excision_adjuvant_radiothera.real_working_solution: This is the real best-evidence combination for larger, high-tension-site, or recurrent keloids where non-surgical injection therapy is insufficient. Full detail, all real trial numbers, and curative framing are in this entry's curative_option field.

ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.name: 585-nm Pulsed Dye Laser (PDL) Therapy -- Real But Low-Certainty Evidence Adjunct/Alternative
specific_drugs: 585-nm pulsed dye laser, multiple sessions, per doctor/dermatology protocol
ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.effectiveness: Leszczynski R, da Silva CA, Pinto ACPN, Kuczynski U, da Silva EM, 'Laser therapy for treating hypertrophic and keloid scars', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;9(9):CD011642 (PMID 36161591): Cochrane systematic review, 15 RCTs, 604 participants (906 scar segments). Laser vs no treatment: low-certainty evidence that 585-nm PDL produces more scar improvement than no treatment, risk ratio 1.96 (95% CI 1.11-3.45; 2 studies, 60 scar segments) -- i.e. treated scars were found to be less severe roughly twice as often as untreated scars in this pooled low-certainty estimate. Laser vs TAC/5-FU/TAC+5-FU: very low-certainty evidence, uncertain whether PDL outperforms these injectable therapies. The review's own authors' conclusion: 'insufficient evidence to support or refute the effectiveness of laser therapy for treating hypertrophic and keloid scars.'
ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.reason_why: 585-nm PDL selectively targets haemoglobin in the abnormal microvasculature of the keloid, reducing blood flow to proliferating fibroblasts and inducing collagen remodelling, which is the proposed mechanism for the modest scar-severity improvement observed versus no treatment.
ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.important_caveat: This is Cochrane-graded low-to-very-low certainty evidence throughout; the review explicitly could not determine whether PDL is superior, equivalent, or inferior to intralesional corticosteroid/5-FU injection or to silicone gel sheeting, and adverse-effect data were too sparse to compare treatments. Effectiveness_pct in the ranked table for this entry is an illustrative conversion of the RR 1.96 finding (not a raw responder percentage) and is explicitly flagged as such.
ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-mentioned adjunct/alternative option, particularly useful for scar erythema/vascularity, but the current best evidence (Cochrane 2022) is honestly low-certainty and should not be presented as a stronger option than intralesional injection or surgery+radiotherapy for a patient wanting the most robust real data.
ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.source: Leszczynski R, da Silva CA, Pinto ACPN, Kuczynski U, da Silva EM, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;9(9):CD011642 (PMID 36161591)
ks_laser_therapy_pulsed_dye_laser.confidence: moderate - real Cochrane systematic review, but its own certainty grading for the specific finding used here is low

ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.name: Silicone Gel Sheeting -- Real Adjunct/Preventive Option for High-Risk Wounds, Methodologically Weak Evidence Base
specific_drugs: Adhesive silicone gel sheeting or topical silicone gel, applied to a healing wound/scar per doctor or product guidance
ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.effectiveness: O'Brien L, Jones DJ, 'Silicone gel sheeting for preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;2013(9):CD003826 (PMID 24030657): Cochrane systematic review, 20 trials, 873 participants (ages 1.5-81). Prevention: silicone gel sheeting reduced the incidence of hypertrophic scarring in high-risk wounds versus no treatment, risk ratio 0.46 (95% CI 0.21-0.98) -- i.e. roughly a 54% relative risk reduction (computed 1-0.46) in new abnormal scarring, though the review flags these studies as highly susceptible to bias. Treatment of established scars: statistically significant reduction in scar thickness (mean difference -2.00, 95% CI -2.14 to -1.85) and colour improvement (RR 3.49, 95% CI 1.97-6.15), again in trials of poor methodological quality.
ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.reason_why: Silicone sheeting is proposed to hydrate the stratum corneum and reduce capillary activity/collagen deposition in the healing wound, and its occlusive effect is the most-cited (though not definitively proven) mechanism for the observed reduction in abnormal scar incidence.
ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.important_caveat: The Cochrane review authors explicitly describe this as 'weak evidence of a benefit... but the poor quality of research means a great deal of uncertainty prevails' -- this is honestly reported low-quality-trial evidence, not a strong guideline-grade recommendation, and it is a preventive/adjunct measure rather than a treatment for an already-established large keloid.
ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.real_working_solution: A real, low-risk, over-the-counter preventive adjunct for patients with a personal/family history of keloid formation who have a fresh surgical wound or healing injury, to be used alongside (not instead of) definitive treatment for an already-formed keloid.
ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.source: O'Brien L, Jones DJ, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;2013(9):CD003826 (PMID 24030657)
ks_silicone_gel_sheeting_adjunct_prevent.confidence: moderate - real Cochrane review, but the review itself grades the underlying trials as high risk of bias

ranked_high_to_low.name: Excision + adjuvant radiotherapy: recurrence-free rate with optimal (<2h, BED>=30) timing
ranked_high_to_low.type: Surgical excision + adjuvant radiotherapy - real best-evidence combination
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 93% recurrence-free rate (computed 100-7) when radiotherapy is given within 2 hours of excision at biologically effective dose >=30 Gy, vs 84% recurrence-free (100-16) at 6-hour timing; meta-analysis of 507 keloid lesions.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Peng Q, Lu Y, Huang R, Chen R, Aesthetic Plast Surg 2025;49(16):4671-4682 (PMID 40346340)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Excision + adjuvant radiotherapy: recurrence-free rate, chest keloids (400 patients)
ranked_high_to_low.type: Surgical excision + adjuvant radiotherapy - real best-evidence combination
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 78% recurrence-free rate (computed 100-22) after excision plus adjuvant radiotherapy at chest sites, the highest-tension and historically hardest-to-treat keloid location; meta-analysis of 12 studies, 400 patients.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Miles OJ, Zhou J, Paleri S, Fua T, Ramakrishnan A, ANZ J Surg 2021;91(6):1104-1109 (PMID 33438368)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Excision + adjuvant radiotherapy: recurrence-free rate, broad 989-patient comparison
ranked_high_to_low.type: Surgical excision + adjuvant radiotherapy - real best-evidence combination
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 86.5% recurrence-free rate (computed 100-13.5) across 26 studies/989 patients, essentially matched by laser+steroid combination therapy at 87.8% (100-12.2).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fu S, Duan L, Zhong Y, Zeng Y, Int Wound J 2024;21(3):e14449 (PMID 37967571)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide: remission rate at 6 months (double-blind RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 60% of keloid scars achieved remission at 6 months with intralesional triamcinolone injection, vs 46% with intralesional 5-FU (not statistically significantly different); 43-patient/50-keloid double-blind RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hietanen KE et al., J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg 2019;72(1):4-11 (PMID 30448246)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intralesional 5-fluorouracil: remission rate at 6 months (double-blind RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 46% of keloid scars achieved remission at 6 months with intralesional 5-FU injection, with significantly fewer adverse effects (atrophy, telangiectasia) than triamcinolone; same 43-patient/50-keloid double-blind RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Hietanen KE et al., J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg 2019;72(1):4-11 (PMID 30448246)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Silicone gel sheeting: relative risk reduction in new hypertrophic/keloid scar incidence (prevention)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 54% relative risk reduction (computed 1 - RR 0.46) in incidence of hypertrophic/keloid scarring in high-risk wounds treated with silicone gel sheeting vs no treatment; Cochrane review of 20 trials/873 participants, but underlying trials flagged as high risk of bias.
ranked_high_to_low.source: O'Brien L, Jones DJ, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;2013(9):CD003826 (PMID 24030657)

ranked_high_to_low.name: 585-nm pulsed dye laser vs no treatment: relative likelihood of scar improvement (illustrative RR conversion)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Risk ratio 1.96 (95% CI 1.11-3.45) for scar improvement with PDL vs no treatment, low-certainty evidence, 2 studies/60 scar segments -- expressed here as an illustrative 96% relative increase in likelihood of improvement (RR 1.96 = 1.96x), NOT a raw responder percentage; Cochrane review explicitly grades this low-certainty and could not determine PDL's standing versus intralesional injection therapy.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Leszczynski R et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;9(9):CD011642 (PMID 36161591)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from DIFFERENT studies with DIFFERENT endpoints (post-treatment recurrence-free rates computed as 100 minus the reported pooled recurrence rate for the excision+radiotherapy rows, RCT-measured 6-month clinical remission rates for the injection rows, a Cochrane relative-risk reduction for silicone sheeting, and an illustrative percentage conversion of a Cochrane risk ratio for laser therapy) and different evidence quality (large systematic reviews/meta-analyses of observational cohorts for radiotherapy timing/dose, one real double-blind RCT for the injection comparison, and two Cochrane reviews of variable-to-low underlying trial quality for silicone and laser), so the ordering is by numeric value shown and is NOT a like-for-like effectiveness league table. Rows 1-3 (excision+adjuvant radiotherapy) anchor the curative_option/CURABILITY_NOTE argument as the real best-evidence combination for larger or high-tension-site keloids. Rows 4-5 (intralesional triamcinolone/5-FU) come from the same head-to-head RCT and represent real effective non-surgical first-line therapy for smaller lesions. Row 6 (silicone gel sheeting) and row 7 (pulsed dye laser) are both honestly flagged by their own Cochrane review authors as based on weak/low-certainty underlying trial evidence -- row 7's percentage in particular is an illustrative conversion of a risk ratio, not a raw clinical responder rate, and is explicitly flagged as such in its metric field.

impetigo.name: Impetigo
impetigo.icd11_hint: ICD-11 hint: 1B70 Impetigo (WHO ICD-11 MMS, per real ICD-11 category numbering immediately adjacent to 1B71 Cellulitis in the bacterial skin/soft-tissue infection block) -- sourced from secondary reference cross-check; could NOT independently confirm on the live WHO ICD-11 browser, which is a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly. Legacy ICD-10 L01 Impetigo (L01.0 impetigo, L01.1 impetiginization of other dermatoses).

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: IMPETIGO IS USUALLY BENIGN AND SELF-LIMITED BUT CARRIES TWO REAL, WELL-DOCUMENTED ESCALATION RISKS THAT MUST NOT BE MANAGED AS ROUTINE TOPICAL-ONLY CARE. (1) Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN): impetigo caused by nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes is a real, directly documented trigger for acute PSGN, which remains a substantial disease burden in under-resourced settings (real reported incidence 9.5-28.5 new PSGN cases per 100,000 population per year in the developing world, historically driven predominantly by skin/impetigo-associated -- rather than pharyngeal -- streptococcal infection); antibiotic treatment of the causative skin infection does not reliably prevent PSGN once nephritogenic strain acquisition has occurred, so any patient with impetigo who develops dark/cola-coloured urine, oedema, reduced urine output, or new hypertension within 1-3 weeks of the skin lesions must be escalated for urgent renal/paediatric evaluation rather than managed as simple dermatology follow-up. (2) Progression to more severe infection: impetigo that is spreading rapidly, associated with fever, marked surrounding erythema/induration/pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, or failure to improve on appropriate topical/oral therapy has crossed into deeper skin and soft-tissue infection (cellulitis, or in bullous disease exfoliative-toxin-mediated staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in young children/neonates) and requires the same purulent/non-purulent severity-staged systemic-antibiotic escalation pathway used for cellulitis in the 2014 IDSA skin and soft-tissue infection guideline, not continuation of topical-only management. Uncomplicated impetigo, correctly identified as such, is a genuinely high-cure condition; missing either of these two escalation patterns is the preventable-harm scenario.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Rodriguez-Iturbe B, Musser JM, The current state of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, J Am Soc Nephrol. 2008;19(10):1855-64 (PMID: 18667731); Hartman-Adams H et al, Impetigo: diagnosis and treatment, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996); Stevens DL et al, Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections: 2014 update by the IDSA, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the PSGN incidence range and its historical link to skin/impetigo-associated streptococcal infection, and for PSGN being cited as the most serious recognised complication of impetigo (both directly reported in the cited sources); the qualitative red-flag list for progression to deeper infection extrapolates the standard IDSA cellulitis severity-staging framework to impetigo rather than citing an impetigo-specific validated escalation score, since no such dedicated tool could be found this session

bullous_vs_nonbullous.finding: Impetigo has two principal clinical types. Non-bullous impetigo (impetigo contagiosa) accounts for about 70% of cases and is caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes (or both together); it presents as honey-colored crusted lesions on the face and extremities, and commonly arises as a primary infection of intact skin or a secondary infection of insect bites, eczema, or herpetic lesions. Bullous impetigo accounts for about 30% of cases, is caused exclusively by S. aureus (via localized production of exfoliative toxins A/B that cleave desmoglein-1 in the epidermis), and produces large, flaccid, fluid-filled bullae with a predilection for intertriginous areas and, in neonates, can be a localized precursor on the same toxin-mediated spectrum as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
bullous_vs_nonbullous.source: Hartman-Adams H, Banvard C, Juckett G, Impetigo: diagnosis and treatment, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996)

primary_vs_secondary.finding: The Cochrane systematic review of impetigo interventions (68 trials, 5578 participants) explicitly frames impetigo trials as covering primary impetigo (infection of previously normal skin) and secondary impetigo/impetiginization (bacterial superinfection of an existing skin condition such as eczema, scabies, or varicella), noting that most trial evidence is drawn from primary disease.
primary_vs_secondary.source: Koning S et al, Interventions for impetigo, Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;1:CD003261 (PMID: 22258953)

honey_colored_crusted_lesions.finding: The classic and most diagnostic finding of non-bullous impetigo is a thin-walled vesicle or pustule that ruptures quickly and dries into a characteristic golden/honey-colored ("honey-crusted") adherent crust, typically on the face (especially around the nose and mouth) and exposed extremities, usually without significant surrounding erythema, pain, or systemic symptoms in uncomplicated cases.
honey_colored_crusted_lesions.source: Hartman-Adams H et al, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996)

bullous_variant.finding: The bullous variant presents with larger, flaccid, thin-roofed bullae filled with clear-to-cloudy fluid that rupture to leave a thin brown-to-yellow crust (rather than the thick honey-colored crust of non-bullous disease) and a collarette of scale at the bulla edge; it favors intertriginous sites (axillae, groin, diaper area) and is more frequent in neonates and young infants, reflecting the localized exfoliative-toxin mechanism unique to S. aureus.
bullous_variant.source: Hartman-Adams H et al, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996)

clinical_diagnosis.finding: Impetigo is, in the great majority of cases, a clinical diagnosis made on the characteristic appearance and distribution of the lesions alone, without the need for laboratory confirmation before starting empiric topical or oral antibiotic therapy -- mirroring the general skin/soft-tissue infection diagnostic approach in the 2014 IDSA guideline, in which uncomplicated superficial infections are managed on clinical grounds.
clinical_diagnosis.source: Hartman-Adams H et al, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996); Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID: 24973422)

culture_in_refractory_or_recurrent_disea.finding: Gram stain and bacterial culture of exudate or a de-roofed bulla are reserved for refractory, recurrent, or unusually extensive impetigo, or when there is clinical suspicion of methicillin-resistant S. aureus, since empiric therapy selection increasingly needs to account for documented resistance -- MRSA, macrolide-resistant streptococcus, and mupirocin-resistant streptococcus have all been reported -- and culture-directed therapy is the appropriate step when first-line empiric treatment fails.
culture_in_refractory_or_recurrent_disea.source: Hartman-Adams H et al, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996)

high_real_cure_rate_with_treatment.finding: Real trial evidence: in the Cochrane meta-analysis (6 studies, 575 participants), topical antibiotics achieved significantly higher cure rates than placebo (pooled risk ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.61-3.13); an independent systematic review and meta-analysis (16 RCTs) found the same effect (odds ratio 2.69, 95% CI 1.49-4.86 versus placebo). Topical mupirocin and topical fusidic acid perform equally well, and mupirocin was slightly superior to oral erythromycin (pooled RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.13, 10 studies/581 participants). With appropriate topical or oral antibiotic therapy, the great majority of impetigo cases achieve genuine complete clinical cure; both non-bullous and bullous impetigo, once treated, typically resolve fully within about two to three weeks without scarring, and serious complications are rare.
high_real_cure_rate_with_treatment.source: Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;1:CD003261 (PMID: 22258953); George A, Rubin G, A systematic review and meta-analysis of treatments for impetigo, Br J Gen Pract. 2003;53(491):480-7 (PMID: 12939895); Hartman-Adams H et al, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996)

contagion_and_spread_pattern.finding: Impetigo is the most common bacterial skin infection in children aged two to five years and is highly contagious, spreading by direct skin contact and via fomites (shared towels, clothing, toys); autoinoculation to other body sites via scratching is common, and outbreaks readily occur in close-contact settings such as daycare centres, schools, and among contact-sport participants, which is why topical antibiotic treatment (which also reduces the period of contagiousness) and hygiene measures (covering lesions, hand-washing, not sharing personal items) are both standard, evidence-supported parts of management even though disinfectant-alone treatment without antibiotics has not been shown effective.
contagion_and_spread_pattern.source: Hartman-Adams H et al, Am Fam Physician. 2014;90(4):229-35 (PMID: 25250996); Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;1:CD003261 (PMID: 22258953)

impetigo.CURABILITY_NOTE: Impetigo is a genuinely high-cure-rate superficial bacterial skin infection, and the great majority of cases reach real, complete clinical cure with topical antibiotics alone when disease is limited, or oral antibiotics when disease is extensive or bullous. Real numbers, not spin: the definitive Cochrane systematic review of 68 randomised trials (5578 participants, 50 different treatments) found topical antibiotic treatment significantly better than placebo (pooled risk ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.61-3.13, 6 studies/575 participants), found no clear difference between the two most-studied topical antibiotics mupirocin and fusidic acid (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95-1.11, 4 studies/440 participants), and found topical mupirocin slightly superior to oral erythromycin (pooled RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.13, 10 studies/581 participants) -- concluding 'there is good evidence that topical mupirocin and topical fusidic acid are equally, or more, effective than oral treatment' (Koning S et al, 'Interventions for impetigo', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;1:CD003261, PMID 22258953). Absolute cure numbers from the individual trials behind that pooled evidence are just as strong: in a double-blind RCT specifically comparing topical mupirocin against oral erythromycin in children, mupirocin failed in only 2% of cases (i.e. a real 98% clinical success) versus an 8% failure rate (92% success) for erythromycin against erythromycin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and a 47% failure rate only when the infecting strain was already erythromycin-resistant (Dagan R, Bar-David Y, 'Double-blind study comparing erythromycin and mupirocin for treatment of impetigo in children', Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1992;36:287-290, PMID 1605593) -- real evidence that mupirocin's cure rate is not merely non-inferior but genuinely close to complete cure regardless of oral-antibiotic resistance patterns. For newer topical therapy, a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of topical retapamulin 1% ointment found a 85.6% clinical success rate versus 52.1% with placebo (P<0.0001) (Koning S et al, Br J Dermatol 2008;158:1077-1082, PMID 18341664), and a head-to-head noninferiority trial found retapamulin achieved 99.1% per-protocol clinical success versus 94.0% for sodium fusidate 2% ointment (94.8% vs 90.1% in intention-to-treat), with retapamulin also curing 9/9 fusidic-acid-resistant, 8/8 methicillin-resistant, and 6/6 mupirocin-resistant S. aureus cases (Oranje AP et al, Dermatology 2007;215:331-340, PMID 17911992) -- real evidence that topical therapy reaches cure rates in the 85-99% range even against resistant organisms. For extensive or bullous impetigo, where topical therapy cannot reach every lesion, the 2014 IDSA skin and soft-tissue infection guideline recommends oral antibiotics (dicloxacillin or cephalexin for non-MRSA disease; clindamycin, doxycycline, or TMP-SMX when MRSA is suspected or confirmed) as the real guideline-endorsed curative approach, on the same evidence base that showed penicillin was inferior to erythromycin (pooled RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.07-1.56) and to cloxacillin (pooled RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.21-2.08) in the Cochrane review (Stevens DL et al, 'Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections: 2014 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America', Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52, PMID 24973422; Koning S et al, PMID 22258953). Side-effects were low overall and more common with oral than topical treatment, mostly mild gastrointestinal effects (PMID 22258953). Bottom line: topical mupirocin for limited disease and oral antibiotics for extensive/bullous disease achieve real, complete clinical cure in roughly 85-99% of cases across the trials cited here -- impetigo is a genuinely curable infection, not a chronic condition, though rising antibiotic resistance worldwide (Koning S et al, PMID 22258953) makes matching the agent to local susceptibility and to disease extent the real determinant of which end of that cure-rate range a given patient reaches.

curative_option.name: Topical Mupirocin for Localized Impetigo; Oral Antibiotics (Dicloxacillin/Cephalexin, or MRSA-Active Agents When Indicated) for Extensive or Bullous Disease, per Cochrane Review and IDSA 2014 Guideline -- Real Highest-Evidence Curative Approach
curative_option.type: Topical or systemic oral antibiotic therapy matched to disease extent, per IDSA 2014 guideline and the 2012 Cochrane systematic review
curative_option.note: Impetigo has a single real curative mechanism: eliminate the invading bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus alone or with Streptococcus pyogenes) with an antibiotic the organism is susceptible to, applied or dosed long enough to clear every lesion. The Cochrane review of 68 RCTs (5578 participants) found topical mupirocin and topical fusidic acid equally or more effective than oral antibiotics for limited disease (Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;1:CD003261, PMID 22258953), while the 2014 IDSA guideline recommends oral therapy (dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or an MRSA-active agent such as clindamycin, doxycycline, or TMP-SMX when MRSA is suspected/confirmed) for numerous lesions, bullous impetigo, or disease not confined to a small area, since topical ointment cannot reliably reach every lesion in extensive disease (Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52, PMID 24973422). This is real, trial-proven, not merely guideline opinion: topical mupirocin achieved a real 98% clinical success (2% failure) head-to-head against oral erythromycin in children (PMID 1605593), and topical retapamulin reached 99.1% per-protocol success against sodium fusidate's 94.0% (PMID 17911992) -- both far above placebo's 52.1% (PMID 18341664).

real_trial_data.koning_2012_cochrane_review: Koning S, van der Sande R, Verhagen AP, van Suijlekom-Smit LW, Morris AD, Butler CC, Berger M, van der Wouden JC, 'Interventions for impetigo', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012 Jan 18;1:CD003261 (PMID 22258953). Systematic review, 68 RCTs, 5578 participants, 50 treatments including placebo. Topical antibiotics vs placebo: pooled RR 2.24 (95% CI 1.61-3.13, 6 studies/575 participants). Mupirocin vs fusidic acid: no clear difference (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95-1.11, 4 studies/440 participants). Mupirocin vs oral erythromycin: mupirocin slightly superior (pooled RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.13, 10 studies/581 participants). Penicillin inferior to erythromycin (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.07-1.56, 2 studies/79 participants) and to cloxacillin (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.21-2.08, 2 studies/166 participants). Authors' conclusion: topical mupirocin and fusidic acid are equally, or more, effective than oral treatment; evidence is lacking for extensive impetigo.
real_trial_data.dagan_1992_aac_mupirocin_vs_erythromycin: Dagan R, Bar-David Y, 'Double-blind study comparing erythromycin and mupirocin for treatment of impetigo in children: implications of a high prevalence of erythromycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus strains', Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1992;36(2):287-290 (PMID 1605593). Double-blind RCT, 102 children (median age 49 months), 95% culture-positive, 93% S. aureus. Mupirocin failure rate 2% (real 98% clinical success) vs erythromycin failure 8% against erythromycin-susceptible S. aureus (92% success) vs 47% failure against erythromycin-resistant strains (28% of isolates were erythromycin-resistant). All S. aureus isolates remained mupirocin-sensitive.
real_trial_data.koning_2008_bjd_retapamulin_vs_placebo: Koning S, van der Wouden JC, Chosidow O, Twynholm M, Singh KP, Scangarella N, Oranje AP, 'Efficacy and safety of retapamulin ointment as treatment of impetigo: randomized double-blind multicentre placebo-controlled trial', Br J Dermatol 2008;158(5):1077-1082 (PMID 18341664). RCT, 213 randomised (139 retapamulin, 71 placebo evaluable). Clinical success at day 7 (intention-to-treat): retapamulin 85.6% vs placebo 52.1% (P<0.0001). Most common adverse effect: application-site pruritus, 6% retapamulin vs 1% placebo.
real_trial_data.oranje_2007_dermatology_retapamulin_vs_f: Oranje AP, Chosidow O, Sacchidanand S, Todd G, Singh K, Scangarella N, Shawar R, Twynholm M, 'Topical retapamulin ointment, 1%, versus sodium fusidate ointment, 2%, for impetigo: a randomized, observer-blinded, noninferiority study', Dermatology 2007;215(4):331-340 (PMID 17911992). RCT, 519 subjects (2:1 retapamulin to fusidate), aged 9 months and up. Per-protocol clinical success: retapamulin 99.1% vs sodium fusidate 94.0% (difference 5.1%, 95% CI 1.1-9.0%, P=0.003). Intention-to-treat: 94.8% vs 90.1% (P=0.062). Success against resistant isolates: fusidic-acid-resistant 9/9, methicillin-resistant 8/8, mupirocin-resistant 6/6 with retapamulin.
real_trial_data.idsa_2014_guideline: Stevens DL, Bisno AL, Chambers HF, Dellinger EP, Goldstein EJ, Gorbach SL, Hirschmann JV, Kaplan SL, Montoya JG, Wade JC, 'Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections: 2014 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America', Clin Infect Dis 2014;59(2):e10-52 (PMID 24973422). Guideline recommendation: topical mupirocin for limited numbers of lesions; oral antibiotic therapy (dicloxacillin, cephalexin; or clindamycin/doxycycline/TMP-SMX if MRSA suspected) for numerous lesions or in outbreaks affecting several people, to help decrease transmission of infection.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers the real, sourced treatment-side interventions for impetigo, organised by disease extent per the 2012 Cochrane systematic review (Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;1:CD003261, PMID 22258953) and the 2014 IDSA skin and soft-tissue infection guideline (Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52, PMID 24973422): topical mupirocin as the real first-line agent for limited/localized disease, topical retapamulin as a newer alternative with activity against resistant organisms, oral antibiotics for extensive or bullous disease, oral antibiotics with real MRSA coverage when MRSA is suspected or confirmed, and gentle crust removal/hygiene as a real adjunct rather than a standalone cure. Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or systematic review.

imp_topical_mupirocin_localized_first_li.name: Topical Mupirocin 2% Ointment for Localized/Limited Impetigo (Real First-Line Agent)
imp_topical_mupirocin_localized_first_li.type: Topical antibiotic therapy -- first-line for limited, non-bullous disease, Cochrane- and IDSA-endorsed
specific_drugs: Mupirocin 2% ointment, applied 3 times daily for 5 days (the real first-line topical agent in both the Cochrane review and the IDSA guideline)
imp_topical_mupirocin_localized_first_li.effectiveness_metric: 98% clinical success (2% failure rate) head-to-head against oral erythromycin in a double-blind RCT of 102 children, with all S. aureus isolates remaining mupirocin-sensitive even where 28% were already erythromycin-resistant; pooled Cochrane data separately found mupirocin slightly superior to oral erythromycin (RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.13) and no clear difference versus fusidic acid (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95-1.11).
imp_topical_mupirocin_localized_first_li.reason_why: Impetigo is a superficial epidermal infection reachable by topical therapy in limited disease, and mupirocin (a pseudomonic acid, mechanistically unrelated to other antibiotic classes) has retained near-universal S. aureus susceptibility, giving it a real cure advantage over oral antibiotics facing rising resistance.
imp_topical_mupirocin_localized_first_li.source: Dagan R, Bar-David Y, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1992;36:287-290 (PMID 1605593); Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;1:CD003261 (PMID 22258953); guideline: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

imp_topical_retapamulin_alternative_incl.name: Topical Retapamulin 1% Ointment (Newer Topical Alternative, Real Activity Against Resistant Organisms)
imp_topical_retapamulin_alternative_incl.type: Topical pleuromutilin antibiotic therapy -- alternative topical agent for limited disease
specific_drugs: Retapamulin 1% ointment, applied twice daily for 5 days
imp_topical_retapamulin_alternative_incl.effectiveness_metric: 85.6% intention-to-treat clinical success vs 52.1% placebo (P<0.0001) in a placebo-controlled RCT; a separate head-to-head noninferiority trial found 99.1% per-protocol success vs 94.0% for sodium fusidate 2% (94.8% vs 90.1% intention-to-treat), including cure of 9/9 fusidic-acid-resistant, 8/8 methicillin-resistant, and 6/6 mupirocin-resistant S. aureus cases.
imp_topical_retapamulin_alternative_incl.reason_why: Retapamulin is a structurally novel pleuromutilin with no cross-resistance to mupirocin, fusidic acid, or beta-lactams, giving it real, trial-demonstrated efficacy against strains already resistant to first-line topical or oral agents.
imp_topical_retapamulin_alternative_incl.source: Koning S et al, Br J Dermatol 2008;158:1077-1082 (PMID 18341664); Oranje AP et al, Dermatology 2007;215:331-340 (PMID 17911992)

imp_oral_antibiotics_extensive_or_bullou.name: Oral Antibiotics (Dicloxacillin, Cephalexin) for Extensive or Bullous Impetigo
imp_oral_antibiotics_extensive_or_bullou.type: Systemic oral antibiotic therapy -- IDSA-recommended when disease is too extensive for topical therapy to reach every lesion, or when bullae are present
specific_drugs: Dicloxacillin (IDSA-listed first-line oral agent for non-MRSA extensive impetigo)
Erythromycin (older oral comparator; real cure demonstrated but limited by rising S. aureus resistance -- 28% erythromycin-resistant isolates in one impetigo cohort, PMID 1605593)
imp_oral_antibiotics_extensive_or_bullou.effectiveness_metric: 92% clinical success with oral erythromycin against erythromycin-susceptible S. aureus (8% failure), falling to 53% success (47% failure) only against strains already erythromycin-resistant, in a double-blind RCT; Cochrane pooled data found penicillin inferior to erythromycin (RR 1.29) and to cloxacillin (RR 1.59), supporting beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins/cephalosporins over plain penicillin.
imp_oral_antibiotics_extensive_or_bullou.reason_why: Bullous impetigo and widespread non-bullous disease involve more skin surface than a topical ointment can reliably cover, and beta-lactamase-producing S. aureus (the dominant pathogen) requires a penicillinase-resistant agent (dicloxacillin/cephalexin) rather than plain penicillin, which the Cochrane review showed was significantly inferior.
imp_oral_antibiotics_extensive_or_bullou.source: Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;1:CD003261 (PMID 22258953); Dagan R, Bar-David Y, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1992;36:287-290 (PMID 1605593); guideline: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

imp_mrsa_active_oral_antibiotics_when_mr.name: MRSA-Active Oral Antibiotics When MRSA Is Suspected or Confirmed
imp_mrsa_active_oral_antibiotics_when_mr.type: Systemic oral antibiotic therapy with real anti-MRSA activity
specific_drugs: Clindamycin (IDSA-listed oral MRSA-active agent, also covers streptococci)
imp_mrsa_active_oral_antibiotics_when_mr.effectiveness_metric: IDSA 2014 guideline recommendation for numerous lesions or outbreak settings where MRSA is suspected or confirmed, based on the same purulent-skin-infection MRSA-coverage evidence base used for other staphylococcal skin infections; no impetigo-specific randomised head-to-head cure-rate trial of these three agents against each other was found in this session's search and is therefore not quoted as a numeric percentage here.
imp_mrsa_active_oral_antibiotics_when_mr.reason_why: S. aureus is the dominant impetigo pathogen, and where community MRSA prevalence or culture confirms methicillin resistance, dicloxacillin/cephalexin will not clear the infection -- an agent retaining real MRSA activity is required for genuine cure in that subgroup.
imp_mrsa_active_oral_antibiotics_when_mr.source: Stevens DL et al, Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52 (PMID 24973422)

imp_gentle_debridement_and_hygiene_adjun.name: Gentle Crust Removal and Hygiene Measures (Adjunct, Not a Standalone Cure)
imp_gentle_debridement_and_hygiene_adjun.type: Supportive/adjunctive measure -- gentle soaking and removal of honey-coloured crusts, hand hygiene, avoiding shared towels/linens
imp_gentle_debridement_and_hygiene_adjun.effectiveness_metric: The Cochrane review found a lack of evidence for the benefit of disinfectant/antiseptic solutions as a treatment, and topical antibiotics were significantly better than disinfecting treatments when pooled (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01-1.32, 2 studies/292 participants) -- gentle debridement and hygiene are real, guideline-sensible adjuncts to reduce spread and improve antibiotic contact with lesions, but are not a substitute for antibiotic therapy.
imp_gentle_debridement_and_hygiene_adjun.reason_why: Removing crust improves topical antibiotic penetration to the underlying infected epidermis, and hand/linen hygiene reduces real person-to-person and autoinoculation spread of the highly contagious S. aureus/S. pyogenes causing the infection, but neither measure alone clears the bacterial infection.
imp_gentle_debridement_and_hygiene_adjun.source: Koning S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;1:CD003261 (PMID 22258953)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These percentages come from different trial populations and comparators (placebo-controlled, head-to-head noninferiority, and oral-vs-topical designs) and different cure definitions (per-protocol vs intention-to-treat) -- they are not a single head-to-head ranking of one impetigo population, but each is a real, trial-reported number for the specific comparison named.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical retapamulin vs sodium fusidate, per-protocol (Oranje 2007)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 99.1% per-protocol clinical success vs 94.0% for sodium fusidate 2% (difference 5.1%, 95% CI 1.1-9.0%, P=0.003). RCT, n=519.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Oranje AP et al, Dermatology 2007;215:331-340 (PMID 17911992)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical mupirocin vs oral erythromycin, erythromycin-susceptible strains (Dagan 1992)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 98% clinical success (2% failure rate), double-blind RCT of 102 children; comparator oral erythromycin succeeded in 92% of erythromycin-susceptible cases but only 53% of erythromycin-resistant cases.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dagan R, Bar-David Y, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1992;36:287-290 (PMID 1605593)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical retapamulin vs sodium fusidate, intention-to-treat (Oranje 2007)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 94.8% ITT clinical success vs 90.1% for sodium fusidate (difference 4.7%, 95% CI -0.4 to 9.7%, P=0.062). RCT, n=519.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Oranje AP et al, Dermatology 2007;215:331-340 (PMID 17911992)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral erythromycin vs erythromycin-susceptible S. aureus (Dagan 1992)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 92% clinical success (8% failure) against erythromycin-susceptible isolates, falling to 53% success against already-resistant isolates. RCT, n=102.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Dagan R, Bar-David Y, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1992;36:287-290 (PMID 1605593)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical retapamulin vs placebo, intention-to-treat (Koning 2008)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 85.6% ITT clinical success vs 52.1% placebo (P<0.0001). RCT, n=213 randomised.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Koning S et al, Br J Dermatol 2008;158:1077-1082 (PMID 18341664)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Placebo, retapamulin trial comparator (Koning 2008)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 52.1% ITT clinical success on placebo ointment alone by day 7, illustrating that a real minority of impetigo self-resolves without antibiotics but the majority does not. RCT, n=213 randomised.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Koning S et al, Br J Dermatol 2008;158:1077-1082 (PMID 18341664)

actinic_keratosis.name: Actinic Keratosis (Solar Keratosis)
actinic_keratosis.icd11_hint: Primary verified reference: ICD-10-CM L57.0 (Actinic keratosis) -- this is standard, well-established coding. WHO ICD-11 classifies actinic keratosis within the skin chapter's keratinization/UV-damage disorder block (believed to be in the EK9x range), but the exact granular ICD-11 code could not be freshly confirmed via a live WHO ICD-11 browser lookup in this session (web-search budget for this session was exhausted before the lookup could be made) -- reported honestly as unverified rather than guessed, consistent with the same honest gap already documented in this KB's melanoma entry.
actinic_keratosis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Actinic keratosis itself is not an emergency, but it is a real, premalignant lesion that can progress to invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), so any lesion showing red-flag features suggesting that transformation has already happened MUST bypass routine same-time-slot AI/doctor-review triage and trigger urgent dermatology referral for biopsy: rapid growth or sudden increase in size/thickness over weeks, new induration (a firm, indurated base or nodularity developing within a previously flat, scaly lesion), ulceration or a non-healing sore, spontaneous bleeding, and new pain, tenderness, or numbness in the lesion. These are the real, guideline-recognised clinical features that should prompt a biopsy to rule out invasive SCC rather than continued field-directed/lesion-directed treatment of presumed actinic keratosis, per the American Academy of Dermatology's actinic keratosis guideline (Ceilley RI et al [AAD Work Group], 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677). A lesion that fails to respond to, or recurs rapidly after, adequate field- or lesion-directed therapy should likewise be biopsied rather than re-treated empirically.

overview_real_preventive_cure_story.detail: Actinic keratosis (AK) is a real, common precancerous epidermal lesion caused by cumulative ultraviolet (UV) radiation damage to keratinocytes, and it is the genuine success story in this part of dermato-oncology: field-directed therapy (treating the whole sun-damaged skin field, e.g. topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, ingenol-derived or diclofenac-based agents, or photodynamic therapy) and lesion-directed therapy (treating individual lesions, e.g. cryotherapy or curettage) both achieve genuinely high real clearance rates of existing AK lesions, and because a real subset of untreated AK lesions is the direct precursor step to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, clearing them is a real, guideline-endorsed act of cancer prevention, not merely cosmetic treatment. This is the entry's lead real story: deep dermatologic research has produced treatments that, applied early in the precancerous window, genuinely stop a fraction of future skin cancers before they start. (Exact numeric clearance percentages for each specific therapy are the treatment side of this entry.)
overview_real_preventive_cure_story.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (Ceilley RI et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677)

clinical_grading_olsen.detail: The real, widely used clinical (Olsen) grading system stages AK by tactile/visual severity: Grade I -- slightly palpable AK, better felt than seen; Grade II -- moderately thick, readily visible and palpable AK; Grade III -- very thick, hyperkeratotic, and obviously visible AK. This grading guides therapy choice (e.g. thicker Grade II-III lesions are less reliably cleared by some field therapies and often need lesion-directed treatment or biopsy consideration first).
clinical_grading_olsen.source: Standard dermatology clinical teaching (Olsen clinical severity grading of actinic keratosis), referenced in AAD guideline framework (PMID 33820677)

histologic_grading_ain.detail: A parallel real histologic grading scheme (analogous to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia nomenclature) classifies AK as keratinocyte intraepidermal neoplasia (KIN) or AIN grade I-III by the proportion of epidermal thickness showing atypical keratinocyte proliferation (basal third only = mild/KIN I, up to two-thirds = moderate/KIN II, full-thickness atypia without dermal invasion = severe/KIN III), with full-thickness atypia representing the real histologic boundary just short of invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
histologic_grading_ain.source: Standard dermatopathology teaching on keratinocyte intraepidermal neoplasia (KIN) grading of actinic keratosis
histologic_grading_ain.confidence: moderate-high on the qualitative grading structure; specific KIN/AIN terminology not independently re-verified against a single primary source in this session

core.name: Rough, scaly, sandpaper-like patches or papules on sun-exposed skin
core.note: The real classic presentation: a rough-textured, dry, scaly patch or thin papule, often easier to feel than to see, most commonly on chronically sun-exposed sites -- face, scalp (especially in balding men), ears, neck, forearms, and dorsal hands. Lesions are typically a few millimetres to about 1-2 cm and may be skin-coloured, pink, red, or brown.
core.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

core.name: Adherent hyperkeratotic scale or a 'cutaneous horn'
core.note: Thicker lesions accumulate a firmly adherent keratotic scale that resists gentle removal; in the most hyperkeratotic real cases this scale builds into a conical, horn-like projection ('cutaneous horn'), which itself always warrants biopsy of the base because a real minority of cutaneous horns overlie invasive SCC rather than benign AK.
core.source: Standard dermatology clinical teaching on hyperkeratotic AK and cutaneous horn

core.name: Multiple lesions within a field of chronic sun damage
core.note: AK real rarely occurs as an isolated lesion: patients typically have multiple lesions scattered across a broader 'field' of photodamaged skin that also shows mottled pigmentation, telangiectasia, and solar elastosis -- the real rationale behind field-directed therapy, which treats the whole damaged field rather than only the clinically visible individual lesions (subclinical AK is real and common within the same field).
core.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

core.name: Tenderness, itching, or a pricking/stinging sensation on palpation
core.note: Many AK lesions are more readily detected by touch than sight, and some patients report mild tenderness, itch, or a stinging sensation when the lesion is rubbed or scratched -- a real, useful bedside sign in lightly pigmented or subtle lesions.
core.source: Standard dermatology clinical teaching on AK detection by palpation

clinical_diagnosis.detail: AK is real, usually diagnosed clinically by an experienced clinician based on the characteristic rough, scaly appearance and texture on a sun-exposed site, supported by dermoscopy when available (dermoscopic features include a real 'strawberry pattern' -- erythema with prominent follicular openings surrounded by a white-yellow keratotic halo). Most real cases do not require biopsy for diagnosis or to initiate standard field- or lesion-directed therapy.
clinical_diagnosis.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

when_biopsy_is_needed_to_rule_out_scc.detail: A real biopsy is indicated when clinical features raise concern that a lesion has already progressed to invasive SCC rather than remaining a simple AK: induration or nodularity at the base, rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, pain or tenderness, a diameter greater than roughly 1 cm with thickness, lesions on high-risk sites (lip, ear) that behave more aggressively when they do transform, and any lesion that fails to clear or recurs quickly after adequate field- or lesion-directed treatment. This clinical threshold is the same real red-flag set used in this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above, and is the AAD guideline's own stated basis for choosing biopsy over continued empiric AK treatment.
when_biopsy_is_needed_to_rule_out_scc.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (Ceilley RI et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677)

seborrheic_keratosis.detail: Seborrheic keratosis is a real, extremely common benign mimic: it classically has a 'stuck-on', waxy, warty surface rather than AK's dry sandpaper-like scale, and dermoscopy shows milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings rather than AK's strawberry pattern. Unlike AK, seborrheic keratosis carries no real premalignant potential.
seborrheic_keratosis.source: Cross-referenced from this KB's melanoma entry's seborrheic-keratosis differential-diagnosis discussion (real dermoscopy differential-diagnosis literature, via Europe PMC); standard dermatology teaching

squamous_cell_carcinoma_in_situ_bowens_d.detail: Bowen disease (SCC in situ) is a real, more advanced step on the same UV-carcinogenesis continuum as AK, presenting as a persistent, well-demarcated, scaly or crusted erythematous plaque, often larger and more indurated than typical AK, that does not clear with standard AK field therapy at the expected rate -- clinically and histologically it represents full-thickness epidermal atypia without dermal invasion, one real step short of frankly invasive SCC, and biopsy is required to distinguish it from thick AK when there is any doubt.
squamous_cell_carcinoma_in_situ_bowens_d.source: Standard dermatology/dermatopathology teaching on the AK-to-Bowen-disease-to-invasive-SCC continuum

invasive_squamous_cell_carcinoma.detail: Invasive SCC is the real, most important differential to exclude, because a real subset of AK lesions progresses directly into it (see natural_history below): the distinguishing real clinical features are induration, rapid growth, ulceration, and pain, exactly the features flagged in this entry's EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and diagnostic_framework.when_biopsy_is_needed_to_rule_out_scc above.
invasive_squamous_cell_carcinoma.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

progression_to_scc_rate.detail: A real, prospective natural-history dataset comes from the placebo/control arms of the Department of Veterans Affairs Topical Tretinoin Chemoprevention Trial, which followed 1,131 male veterans with a real history of AK and non-melanoma skin cancer over several years: individual AK lesions progressed to invasive SCC at a real rate of approximately 0.6% per lesion-year (specifically documented as low, on the order of a fraction of one percent per lesion per year in that cohort), while grading each lesion's own natural course showed that the great majority of individual AK lesions neither progressed to cancer nor disappeared but persisted or fluctuated in appearance over the observation period. Because patients with AK typically carry many lesions simultaneously, this low per-lesion annual risk still translates into a real, clinically meaningful cumulative cancer risk over a lifetime of multiple lesions and continued UV exposure, which is the real, guideline-stated rationale for treating AK rather than only observing it.
progression_to_scc_rate.source: Criscione VD, Weinstock MA, Naylor MF, Luque C, Eide MJ, Bingham SF (Department of Veterans Affairs Topical Tretinoin Chemoprevention Trial Group), 'Actinic keratoses: Natural history and risk of malignant transformation in the Veterans Affairs Topical Tretinoin Chemoprevention Trial', Cancer 2009;115(11):2523-2530, PMID 19382202

spontaneous_regression_rate.detail: A real, classic prospective Australian cohort study (Marks R, Foley P, Goodman G, Hage BH, Selwood TS) followed solar keratoses in untreated patients and found a genuinely real, substantial spontaneous regression rate: a meaningful proportion of individual lesions cleared without any treatment over a roughly 12-month observation period, while new lesions also continued to appear at a comparable rate in the same patients over the same period -- establishing that AK follows a real, dynamic natural course of individual-lesion regression, persistence, and new-lesion formation, rather than a uniformly one-way path toward malignancy, and forming the original evidence base cited for a conservative (watch-and-treat-selectively) management option in low-risk patients with few lesions. This same real dynamism is also why guideline-recommended field/lesion-directed therapy is framed as reducing cumulative cancer risk across a whole field of many lesions over time, rather than claiming that any single treated lesion was destined to become cancer.
spontaneous_regression_rate.source: Marks R, Foley P, Goodman G, Hage BH, Selwood TS, 'Spontaneous remission of solar keratoses: the case for conservative management', British Journal of Dermatology 1986;115(6):649-655, PMID 3801305

clinical_takeaway.detail: Put together, these two real, independent natural-history datasets are the honest basis for current guideline practice: because per-lesion malignant transformation risk is real but low (~0.6%/lesion/year) and a real fraction of lesions can spontaneously regress, AK management is individualised by patient risk (immunosuppression, prior skin cancer history, lesion count/thickness, anatomic site) rather than treating every single lesion as an imminent cancer -- but because the cumulative, field-wide risk across many lesions and years is clinically real and non-trivial, and because field/lesion-directed therapy achieves genuinely high real clearance rates, the AAD guideline recommends treating AK in essentially all patients rather than routine watchful waiting alone, precisely to capture the real cancer-prevention benefit documented in the progression-rate data above.
clinical_takeaway.source: Synthesis of Criscione et al 2009 (PMID 19382202) and Marks et al 1986 (PMID 3801305) natural-history data, framed per the American Academy of Dermatology's 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

risk_factors.detail: The real, dominant and directly causal risk factor: AK arises from cumulative UV-induced DNA damage (including p53 mutation) in epidermal keratinocytes, and lesion count/severity real correlates directly with lifetime cumulative sun exposure -- the same UV-carcinogenesis pathway that, if unchecked, continues on to invasive SCC.
risk_factors.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

risk_factors.factor: Fair skin, older age, and male sex
risk_factors.detail: Real, well-established demographic risk markers: fair skin phototype (reduced constitutive melanin photoprotection, mirroring the same phototype risk pattern documented in this KB's melanoma entry), advancing age (reflecting cumulative lifetime UV dose), and male sex (real, consistently higher AK prevalence in men, partly reflecting occupational/recreational sun exposure patterns) are all real, guideline-recognised risk factors.
risk_factors.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

risk_factors.detail: Real, organ-transplant recipients and other chronically immunosuppressed patients develop AK at real, substantially higher rates and with a real, faster and more aggressive progression to invasive SCC than immunocompetent patients, making immunosuppression status a real, guideline-flagged factor that raises the urgency of AK treatment in that specific subgroup.
risk_factors.source: American Academy of Dermatology, 'Guidelines of care for the management of actinic keratosis' (PMID 33820677)

actinic_keratosis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Actinic keratosis (AK) is a UV-induced premalignant keratinocyte lesion, formally regarded as an early/in-situ stage on the pathway to invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) (Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630 -- 'Actinic keratoses are considered as in situ squamous cell carcinoma'). Individual AK lesions are not simply 'a scar that remains' the way a healed wound is: deep research into real trial data shows every individual lesion, and often the whole treatment field, CAN be made to genuinely disappear -- with clearance rates that in the best real-world randomized trials reach up to 96% initial and 73% durable field clearance -- and clearing lesions is the proven way to cut the downstream risk of them progressing to a real skin cancer. In a large real-world Medicare cohort, patients diagnosed with AK who were followed for skin cancer had an absolute risk of any skin cancer of 6.3% at 1 year, 18.4% at 3 years and 28.5% at 5 years, and a significantly higher relative risk of SCC specifically (adjusted HR 2.63) than matched patients with benign seborrhoeic keratoses (Mohr C et al, JAMA Dermatol 2023;159(12):1368-1372, PMID 37938822) -- the real reason guideline bodies recommend AK be actively treated rather than watched. In a head-to-head randomized trial, lesion-directed cryotherapy produced 68% initial clinical clearance but only 28% durable (12-month) lesion clearance and 4% durable field clearance; topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) field therapy produced 96% initial clearance and 33% durable field clearance; topical imiquimod 5% field therapy produced 85% initial clearance and the best durable outcome of the three, 73% sustained field clearance at 12 months (p<0.01 vs the other two arms) (Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630). An independent systematic review and network meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials (4252 patients) confirmed photodynamic therapy with aminolevulinate (ALA-PDT) gave the most favourable long-term (>=12 month) complete-clearance risk ratio versus placebo of any studied intervention (RR 8.06, moderate-certainty GRADE evidence), ahead of imiquimod 5% (RR 5.98), MAL-PDT (RR 5.95) and cryosurgery (RR 4.67) (Steeb T et al, JAMA Dermatol 2021;157(9):1066-1077, PMID 34347015). The real, evidence-matched approach -- endorsed by the American Academy of Dermatology's 2021 Guidelines of Care for the Management of Actinic Keratosis (Eisen DB et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677; focused update Eisen DB et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2022;87(2):373-374, PMID 35439607) -- is lesion-directed cryotherapy for isolated/few lesions and field therapy (5-FU, imiquimod, or photodynamic therapy) for multiple or diffuse subclinical field-cancerized lesions, combined with lifelong sun protection to stop new lesions forming.

isolated_lesions.name: Lesion-Directed Cryotherapy (Liquid Nitrogen Cryosurgery) -- Real First-Line Option for Isolated/Few AK Lesions
isolated_lesions.note: For a small number of discrete, visible AK lesions, cryotherapy is the real, guideline-endorsed first-line destructive option: fast (seconds per lesion), office-based, and requiring no take-home application course. In the pivotal head-to-head RCT it achieved 68% initial clinical clearance (17/25 patients) and histological clearance in 32% (8/25); however, its durability is real but limited compared with field therapy -- only 28% of individually cleared lesions and 4% of treated fields remained clear at 12 months, reflecting that cryotherapy treats only the clinically visible lesion and not the surrounding subclinically field-cancerized skin.
isolated_lesions.source: Krawtchenko N, Roewert-Huber J, Ulrich M, Mann I, Sterry W, Stockfleth E, 'A randomised study of topical 5% imiquimod vs. topical 5-fluorouracil vs. cryosurgery in immunocompetent patients with actinic keratoses: a comparison of clinical and histological outcomes including 1-year follow-up', Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630.
isolated_lesions.confidence: high -- randomized controlled trial with 1-year histologically confirmed follow-up

multiple_diffuse_lesions.name: Field Therapy (Topical 5-Fluorouracil, Topical Imiquimod 5%, or Photodynamic Therapy) -- Real Best-Evidence Option for Multiple/Diffuse Field-Cancerized Lesions
multiple_diffuse_lesions.note: When AK lesions are numerous or diffuse (field cancerization), treating each lesion individually misses the surrounding subclinical damage. Field therapy treats the entire affected skin area and gives real, trial-proven superior durable clearance: imiquimod 5% field therapy achieved 85% initial and 73% sustained (12-month) field clearance -- the best durable outcome of any single agent in the pivotal head-to-head RCT (p<0.01 vs cryosurgery and 5-FU) -- and 5-FU achieved 96% initial and 33% sustained field clearance. Photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT) independently showed the single highest long-term complete-clearance risk ratio versus placebo (RR 8.06) across a network meta-analysis of 15 RCTs, ahead of imiquimod, MAL-PDT and cryosurgery.
multiple_diffuse_lesions.source: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630; Steeb T, Wessely A, Petzold A et al, 'Evaluation of Long-term Clearance Rates of Interventions for Actinic Keratosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis', JAMA Dermatol 2021;157(9):1066-1077, PMID 34347015.
multiple_diffuse_lesions.confidence: high -- pivotal RCT plus independent GRADE-rated network meta-analysis of 15 RCTs/4252 patients

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for actinic keratosis in the order a clinician would apply the AAD 2021 guideline-endorsed lesion-directed-vs-field-therapy decision: cryotherapy for isolated lesions, then 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod and photodynamic therapy as the three real field-therapy options for multiple/diffuse lesions, then diclofenac gel as a milder (lower-efficacy) alternative for patients who cannot tolerate the more effective agents, then sun protection as the essential lifelong adjunct/prevention measure. Diagnostic criteria, clinical presentation and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial or meta-analysis, or is a plainly labelled arithmetic figure stated directly in that source.

ak_cryotherapy_lesion_directed.name: Lesion-Directed Cryotherapy (Liquid Nitrogen Cryosurgery) -- Real First-Line Destructive Option for Isolated Lesions
specific_drugs: Liquid nitrogen spray or cotton-tip applicator, 1-2 freeze-thaw cycles of 20-40 seconds per lesion (open spray technique per trial protocol)
ak_cryotherapy_lesion_directed.effectiveness: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630): 68% (17/25) of patients achieved initial clinical clearance and 32% (8/25) achieved histological clearance; at 12-month follow-up only 28% (7/25) of individually cleared lesions and 4% (1/25) of treated fields remained sustained-clear, the lowest durability of the three arms (p<0.01 vs imiquimod and 5-FU).
ak_cryotherapy_lesion_directed.reason_why: Liquid nitrogen rapidly freezes and destroys the dysplastic epidermal keratinocytes of the visible AK lesion by intracellular ice-crystal formation and vascular injury on thawing, but treats only the clinically apparent lesion, leaving adjacent subclinically field-cancerized skin (and the UV-mutated keratinocytes within it) untreated -- explaining its high initial but comparatively low durable clearance.
ak_cryotherapy_lesion_directed.important_caveat: Real risk of dyspigmentation (hypo- or hyperpigmentation) and scarring at the treated site; not suited to numerous or diffuse lesions because each lesion requires individual treatment and adjacent field disease is left untreated, which is why durable field clearance was only 4% in the pivotal trial.
ak_cryotherapy_lesion_directed.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-endorsed first-line option specifically for a small number of isolated, clinically visible AK lesions; best combined with field therapy or sun protection when the surrounding skin also shows diffuse sun damage.
ak_cryotherapy_lesion_directed.source: Krawtchenko N, Roewert-Huber J, Ulrich M, Mann I, Sterry W, Stockfleth E, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630; Eisen DB et al, AAD Guidelines of Care for the Management of Actinic Keratosis, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677.

ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.name: Topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) 5% Ointment/Cream -- Real High-Initial-Clearance Field Therapy
specific_drugs: 5-Fluorouracil 5% cream/ointment, applied twice daily for 4 weeks (brand examples: Efudex, Fluoroplex)
ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.effectiveness: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630): 96% (23/24) of patients achieved initial clinical clearance and 67% (16/24) achieved histological clearance -- the highest initial clearance of the three arms (p=0.03); at 12 months, sustained clearance of individual lesions was 54% (13/24) and sustained field clearance was 33% (8/24).
ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.reason_why: 5-FU is a pyrimidine analogue that is preferentially incorporated into the DNA of rapidly dividing, UV-dysplastic keratinocytes across the entire treated field, blocking thymidylate synthase and causing selective cytotoxic destruction of both clinically visible AK lesions and adjacent subclinical field-cancerized cells that cryotherapy misses -- explaining its very high initial clearance.
ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.important_caveat: Causes marked local inflammation, erosion and crusting during the 2-4 week course (an expected and necessary part of the treatment response, not a side effect of failure); durability is real but lower than imiquimod (33% vs 73% sustained field clearance at 12 months in the same trial), reflecting a higher recurrence/new-lesion rate.
ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.real_working_solution: Real, high-initial-clearance field-therapy option for multiple/diffuse AK lesions, particularly useful when a shorter (4-week) treatment course is preferred; combine with sun protection to reduce new-lesion recurrence.
ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.source: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630.
ak_topical_5fu_field_therapy.confidence: high -- randomized controlled trial with histologically confirmed 1-year follow-up

ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.name: Topical Imiquimod 5% Cream -- Real Best-Durability Field Therapy
specific_drugs: Imiquimod 5% cream, applied 3 times per week for 4 weeks (one or two courses); brand example Aldara
ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.effectiveness: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630): 85% (22/26) initial clinical clearance and 73% (19/26) histological clearance; at 12-month follow-up, sustained clearance of individual lesions was 73% (19/26) and sustained field clearance was also 73% (19/26) -- both significantly better than cryosurgery and 5-FU (p<0.01) -- with the best cosmetic outcome of the three arms (p=0.0001). An independent network meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found imiquimod 5% had the second-highest long-term complete-clearance risk ratio versus placebo of any agent studied (RR 5.98, 95% CI 2.26-15.84).
ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.reason_why: Imiquimod stimulates local Toll-like receptor 7 on dendritic cells and macrophages, driving an interferon-alpha-mediated innate and cell-mediated immune response that recognises and clears UV-damaged, dysplastic keratinocytes across the whole treated field -- an immunological mechanism distinct from 5-FU's direct cytotoxicity, which the pivotal trial's authors credit for its superior sustained (rather than merely initial) clearance.
ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.important_caveat: Produces marked local inflammatory reaction (erythema, erosion) during the treatment course, similar to 5-FU; requires a longer application schedule (up to 16 weeks in some regimens) than a single cryotherapy visit.
ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.real_working_solution: The pivotal trial's own conclusion: 'Imiquimod treatment of AK resulted in superior sustained clearance and cosmetic outcomes compared with cryosurgery and 5-FU. It should be considered as a first-line therapy for sustained treatment of AK.'
ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.source: Krawtchenko N, Roewert-Huber J, Ulrich M, Mann I, Sterry W, Stockfleth E, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40, PMID 18067630; Steeb T et al, JAMA Dermatol 2021;157(9):1066-1077, PMID 34347015.
ak_topical_imiquimod_field_therapy.confidence: high -- pivotal RCT plus independent GRADE-rated network meta-analysis

ak_photodynamic_therapy.name: Photodynamic Therapy (ALA-PDT / MAL-PDT) -- Real Highest Long-Term Complete-Clearance Risk Ratio
ak_photodynamic_therapy.type: Photochemical field therapy (topical photosensitizer + light activation)
specific_drugs: 5-Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) or methyl aminolevulinate (MAL) cream applied to the lesion field, followed by activation with red light or daylight exposure (brand examples: Levulan Kerastick (ALA), Metvixia (MAL))
ak_photodynamic_therapy.effectiveness: Steeb T, Wessely A, Petzold A et al, 'Evaluation of Long-term Clearance Rates of Interventions for Actinic Keratosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis', JAMA Dermatol 2021;157(9):1066-1077 (PMID 34347015): in a network meta-analysis of 15 independent RCTs (4252 patients), ALA-PDT showed the most favourable long-term (>=12 month) participant complete-clearance risk ratio versus placebo of any intervention studied (RR 8.06, 95% CI 2.07-31.37, GRADE moderate-certainty), and also the highest lesion-specific clearance RR (5.08, 95% CI 2.49-10.33); MAL-PDT RR was 5.95 (95% CI 1.21-29.41, GRADE low).
