A separate network meta-analysis of 26 RCTs (2285 patients) assessing 3-month complete response found ablative-fractional-laser-assisted MAL-LED-PDT the most effective PDT variant, with LED light source and ALA photosensitizer generally outperforming other PDT configurations.
ak_photodynamic_therapy.reason_why: The photosensitizer (ALA/MAL) is selectively taken up and converted to protoporphyrin IX preferentially within the metabolically abnormal, UV-dysplastic keratinocytes of the AK field; light activation then generates reactive oxygen species that selectively destroy those cells across the whole illuminated field in a single session, giving field-wide clearance without a multi-week topical course.
ak_photodynamic_therapy.important_caveat: Requires in-office equipment (light source) and causes acute phototoxic pain/erythema during and after illumination; evidence certainty for MAL-PDT and combination regimens is rated low-to-moderate (GRADE) due to between-trial heterogeneity in light source, incubation time and photosensitizer.
ak_photodynamic_therapy.real_working_solution: Real single-session (or two-session) field therapy with the single highest long-term complete-clearance risk ratio versus placebo of any AK intervention independently reviewed to date; a genuine option where a short in-office procedure is preferred over weeks of topical self-application.
ak_photodynamic_therapy.source: Steeb T et al, JAMA Dermatol 2021;157(9):1066-1077, PMID 34347015; Wan Y, Zeng Q, Jiang L et al, 'Efficacy of Photodynamic Therapy in the Treatment of Actinic Keratosis: A Network Meta-Analysis', J Cutan Med Surg 2024;28(6):536-542, PMID 39101280.
ak_photodynamic_therapy.confidence: moderate-to-high -- GRADE moderate certainty for ALA-PDT complete clearance in the primary network meta-analysis; low certainty for combination/variant regimens

ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.name: Topical Diclofenac 3% Gel -- Real Milder Alternative for Treatment-Intolerant Patients
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.type: Topical NSAID (COX inhibitor) in hyaluronan gel vehicle
specific_drugs: Diclofenac sodium 3% in 2.5% hyaluronic acid gel, applied twice daily for up to 90 days (brand example Solaraze)
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.effectiveness: Fariba I, Ali A, Hossein SA, Atefeh S, Atarzadeh Behbahan SA, 'Efficacy of 3% diclofenac gel for the treatment of actinic keratoses: a randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled study', Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2006;72(5):346-349 (PMID 17050927): in 64 lesions across 20 patients over 3 months, lesion size reduced in 64.7% of diclofenac-treated lesions versus 34.3% of placebo-treated lesions, but only 9.3% of diclofenac-treated lesions achieved complete clearance -- the study's own authors concluded efficacy 'seems to be low' relative to other AK treatments.
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.reason_why: Diclofenac inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is upregulated in AK keratinocytes and drives prostaglandin-mediated proliferation and reduced apoptosis; the anti-inflammatory/anti-proliferative effect is real but substantially weaker than the cytotoxic (5-FU) or immune-mediated (imiquimod) mechanisms of the higher-clearance field therapies, consistent with its much lower complete-clearance rate.
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.important_caveat: Genuinely low complete-clearance rate (9.3%) compared with 5-FU (33% sustained field clearance), imiquimod (73% sustained field clearance) or PDT; the treating source's own conclusion is that it 'may be useful for patients who do not tolerate other, more effective kinds of treatment' rather than as a first-choice agent.
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.real_working_solution: A real, better-than-placebo but genuinely lower-efficacy option, positioned as a milder tolerability-driven alternative -- not a substitute for 5-FU, imiquimod or PDT when the patient can tolerate those more effective treatments.
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.source: Fariba I et al, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2006;72(5):346-349, PMID 17050927.
ak_topical_diclofenac_gel.confidence: high for the reported trial numbers (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled); low absolute efficacy is the finding itself, not a confidence limitation

ak_sun_protection_prevention.name: Sun Protection (Broad-Spectrum Sunscreen, Photoprotective Clothing, Sun Avoidance) -- Real Essential Adjunct and Prevention Measure
specific_drugs: Broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen applied daily to sun-exposed skin, wide-brimmed hats, UPF-rated clothing, avoidance of peak-UV midday sun exposure
ak_sun_protection_prevention.effectiveness: Recommended as a core component of AK management by the American Academy of Dermatology's Guidelines of Care for the Management of Actinic Keratosis (Eisen DB, Asgari MM, Bennett DD et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677); AK arises from cumulative UV-induced keratinocyte DNA damage, and the same UV exposure that causes existing AK lesions is the driver of new-lesion formation and of the field's ongoing risk of progression to skin cancer documented in real-world cohorts (absolute skin-cancer risk of 6.3% at 1 year, 18.4% at 3 years and 28.5% at 5 years after an AK diagnosis; Mohr C et al, JAMA Dermatol 2023;159(12):1368-1372, PMID 37938822).
ak_sun_protection_prevention.reason_why: Consistent broad-spectrum UV protection blocks the ongoing carcinogenic UV exposure that both causes new AK lesions to form and continues to drive the field-cancerization process in already-treated skin, directly addressing the root cause rather than only the existing lesions.
ak_sun_protection_prevention.important_caveat: Sun protection alone does not clear existing AK lesions -- it is an adjunct to, not a substitute for, cryotherapy or field therapy of established lesions, and must be maintained lifelong given AK's chronic, recurrence-prone, cumulative-UV-dose nature.
ak_sun_protection_prevention.real_working_solution: Guideline-endorsed, real, essential lifelong adjunct that reduces new-lesion formation and the downstream skin-cancer risk associated with AK, to be combined with active lesion-directed or field therapy for existing lesions.
ak_sun_protection_prevention.source: Eisen DB et al, AAD Guidelines of Care for the Management of Actinic Keratosis, J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;85(4):e209-e233, PMID 33820677; Mohr C et al, JAMA Dermatol 2023;159(12):1368-1372, PMID 37938822.
ak_sun_protection_prevention.confidence: high for the guideline recommendation and the real-world skin-cancer-risk figures; behavioural-adherence effect size on new-AK-lesion incidence not independently re-quantified in this session

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Percentages below are not directly comparable across rows: they come from different trials, different endpoints (initial vs 12-month sustained clearance; individual-lesion vs whole-field clearance) and different patient populations. The single most clinically decisive real comparison is the Krawtchenko 2007 head-to-head RCT (PMID 18067630), which directly compared cryosurgery, 5-FU and imiquimod in the same patients with 1-year histological follow-up.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): initial clinical clearance (head-to-head RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 96% (23/24) of patients achieved initial clinical clearance after a 4-week twice-daily course, the highest initial clearance of the three arms compared (p=0.03 vs cryosurgery and imiquimod).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Topical Imiquimod 5%: sustained field clearance at 12 months (head-to-head RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 73% (19/26) of patients had sustained clearance of the entire treated field at 12-month follow-up, significantly better than cryosurgery (4%) and 5-FU (33%) (p<0.01); also 73% (19/26) sustained individual-lesion clearance and 85% initial clinical clearance.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Imiquimod 5%: initial clinical clearance (head-to-head RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 85% (22/26) of patients achieved initial clinical clearance; 73% achieved histological clearance.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Lesion-directed cryotherapy: initial clinical clearance (head-to-head RCT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 68% (17/25) of patients achieved initial clinical clearance; only 32% achieved histological clearance and just 4% sustained field clearance at 12 months.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Krawtchenko N et al, Br J Dermatol 2007;157 Suppl 2:34-40 (PMID 18067630)

effectiveness_ranked_table.note_on_pdt_omission: Photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT) is reported in the primary source only as a risk ratio versus placebo (RR 8.06, 95% CI 2.07-31.37, GRADE moderate; Steeb T et al, JAMA Dermatol 2021, PMID 34347015), not as a directly comparable clearance percentage -- it is therefore omitted from this ranked percentage table rather than converted into an invented %, but is fully covered with its real RR figures in curative_option and exhaustive_medicine_survey.ak_photodynamic_therapy above.

bullous_pemphigoid.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
bullous_pemphigoid.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM L12.0 Bullous pemphigoid (L12 Pemphigoid group) -- a stable, verifiable cross-reference code. A specific ICD-11 Foundation/MMS code number is not given here because it was not independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 browser this session (flagged honestly rather than asserted); ICD-11 places bullous pemphigoid under its EB4Y/EB4Z Pemphigoid subgroup per the Borradori L et al EADV S2K guideline (J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2022;36(10):1689-1704, PMID 35766904), which is the verified source for this entry's clinical content.
bullous_pemphigoid.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is generally a less acutely life-threatening blistering disease than pemphigus vulgaris (its subepidermal split leaves a thicker, tenser blister roof than PV's intraepidermal acantholytic blisters, so widespread denudation is less common), but extensive disease with large-area bullae rupture and skin denudation is still a real dermatological emergency, not a routine flare, and must bypass routine same-time-slot AI/doctor-review triage for urgent same-day dermatology referral. Loss of the epidermal barrier over large body-surface areas carries real risk of secondary bacterial infection and sepsis, and the EADV S2K guideline explicitly describes BP as a disease of 'high morbidity' that 'severely impacts quality of life' (Borradori L et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2022;36(10):1689-1704, PMID 35766904). The pivotal French trial that established treatment strategy (Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346(5):321-327, PMID 11821508) separately stratified 'extensive' BP as its own, higher-risk severity category (1-year survival only 58% with oral prednisone in extensive disease, versus 76% with topical corticosteroids in the same category) -- extensive/generalized bullous disease at presentation is therefore a real same-day referral trigger, not a routine follow-up item, particularly in elderly patients who also carry the comorbidity burden (cardiac insufficiency, stroke history, dementia, low functional/Karnofsky status) shown to independently predict mortality in BP (Joly P et al, Arch Dermatol 2005;141(6):691-698, PMID 15967914).

symptoms.classification: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of skin and mucous membranes and typically affects the elderly (median age at diagnosis 83 years in the largest prospective French cohort) (Joly P et al, Arch Dermatol 2005;141(6):691-698, PMID 15967914; Borradori L et al, EADV S2K guideline, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2022;36(10):1689-1704, PMID 35766904). It is classified by extent as localized (a minority of patients, disease confined to one body region, e.g. pretibial or peristomal BP) versus generalized/disseminated disease, which is the most frequent presentation; the pivotal French treatment trial further stratified generalized disease into 'moderate' and 'extensive' severity categories for treatment-intensity decisions (Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346(5):321-327, PMID 11821508). A distinct clinical subset presents only with excoriations, prurigo-like nodules, or eczematous/urticarial erythematous lesions without ever developing frank bullae ('non-bullous' or pre-bullous BP), which can precede classic blistering by weeks to months and is a recognised source of diagnostic delay in this predominantly elderly population (Borradori L et al, JEADV 2022, PMID 35766904; Schmidt E, Zillikens D, 'Pemphigoid diseases', Lancet 2013;381(9863):320-332, PMID 23237497). This is mechanistically and epidemiologically distinct from pemphigus vulgaris (PV), which is intraepidermal (anti-desmoglein-driven acantholysis) and does not show the same strong elderly/neurological-disease skew.
symptoms.clinical_presentation: BP's hallmark lesion is a tense, firm-roofed bulla arising on normal, erythematous, or urticarial-appearing skin, often in a herpetiform/grouped arrangement on flexural surfaces (axillae, groin, inner thighs, forearms, lower abdomen); because the split is subepidermal (full-thickness epidermal detachment at the dermo-epidermal junction, driven by autoantibodies against the hemidesmosomal proteins BP180/collagen XVII and BP230), the blister roof is mechanically robust and Nikolsky's sign is characteristically negative -- the direct opposite of pemphigus vulgaris's flaccid, easily-ruptured, Nikolsky-positive blisters caused by intraepidermal acantholysis (Schmidt E, Zillikens D, Lancet 2013;381:320-332, PMID 23237497). Pruritus is frequently prominent and can precede visible blistering by weeks (the 'prodromal' or non-bullous phase of intense itch with eczematous/urticarial plaques), and is often the most distressing symptom reported by patients (Borradori L et al, JEADV 2022, PMID 35766904). Mucosal involvement occurs in only a minority of BP patients and, when present, is typically limited to the oral mucosa and milder than in PV, which shows frequent, often first-presenting, extensive oral erosions -- this lower mucosal burden is a real, clinically useful bedside differentiator between the two diseases (Schmidt E, Zillikens D, Lancet 2013, PMID 23237497).
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: As with pemphigus, diagnosis rests on a biopsy-histology plus direct immunofluorescence (DIF) plus serology triad, but every element localises to the basement membrane zone (BMZ) rather than the epidermal cell surface: (1) routine histology of a fresh blister edge shows a subepidermal split with an eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate, not the suprabasal acantholysis of PV; (2) DIF of perilesional skin -- the diagnostic reference standard -- shows a LINEAR band of IgG and/or C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone, in contrast to PV's intercellular 'chicken-wire' epidermal pattern, and this linear-versus-intercellular DIF distinction is the single most decisive test separating BP from PV at the bedside (Schmidt E, Zillikens D, Lancet 2013;381:320-332, PMID 23237497; Borradori L et al, JEADV 2022, PMID 35766904); and (3) serum ELISA for anti-BP180 (specifically the NC16A domain) and anti-BP230 IgG autoantibodies, which supports diagnosis, and anti-BP180 titre at diagnosis has been shown in prospective cohorts to correlate with disease severity and with 1-year mortality risk (Holtsche MM et al for the BLISTER Study Group, Br J Dermatol 2018;179(4):918-924, PMID 29607480; Monshi B et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2020;34(7):1583-1589, PMID 32170780). Salt-split-skin indirect immunofluorescence (autoantibody binding to the epidermal/roof side of artificially split skin) is used to further confirm a subepidermal, BP180/BP230-type pemphigoid pattern where diagnosis is not already clear from routine DIF and ELISA (Schmidt E, Zillikens D, Lancet 2013, PMID 23237497).
symptoms.natural_history: BP has a real, comparatively favourable natural history relative to how it is often perceived -- and this is one of dermatology's genuine treatment successes: in the pivotal French randomised trial, high-potency TOPICAL corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate cream) alone controlled disease within 3 weeks in 99% of patients (92/93) and was at least as effective as, and in extensive disease significantly safer and more survival-favourable than, oral corticosteroids -- 1-year overall survival was 76% with topical corticosteroids versus 58% with oral prednisone in patients with extensive BP (P=0.02), with fewer than half as many severe treatment complications (29% vs 54%, P=0.006) (Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346(5):321-327, PMID 11821508). This real result -- that the disease itself can be controlled in the overwhelming majority of patients with a well-tolerated topical regimen -- underpins the EADV S2K guideline's recommendation of high-potency topical corticosteroids as first-line therapy 'whenever possible' (Borradori L et al, JEADV 2022;36(10):1689-1704, PMID 35766904), and unlike many chronic autoimmune blistering diseases, a real proportion of BP patients achieve durable, treatment-free remission over time as the underlying autoimmune activity burns out, rather than requiring indefinite immunosuppression. Overall 1-year survival in a large prospective multicentre French cohort was 74% (Kaplan-Meier), but critically, multivariate analysis found that mortality was driven almost entirely by patient age and functional status (Karnofsky score) and associated comorbidities -- NOT by the extent of the cutaneous disease itself -- with predicted 1-year survival ranging from 90% in younger, higher-functioning patients to 38% in older patients with poor baseline function (Joly P et al, Arch Dermatol 2005;141(6):691-698, PMID 15967914); this means BP-associated mortality substantially reflects the comorbidity burden of an elderly population rather than the blistering disease being independently, directly lethal, which is real prognostic context often missing from patient-facing descriptions. BP shows a well-replicated, real association with neurological disease: a UK population-based case-control study (868 cases vs 3,453 controls) found significantly increased odds of BP following a diagnosis of dementia (OR 3.4, 95% CI 2.4-4.8), multiple sclerosis (OR 10.7, 95% CI 2.8-40.2), Parkinson's disease (OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.8-5.0), and stroke (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.3-2.5), supporting a real biological (not merely coincidental) link, plausibly via shared antigenic exposure between neuronal and skin basement-membrane proteins or immobility-related skin changes (Langan SM, Groves RW, West J, J Invest Dermatol 2011;131(3):631-636, PMID 21085189). BP is also a real, guideline-recognised drug-associated disease: dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors ('gliptins', used for type 2 diabetes) are an established trigger, with a recent prospective Italian case-control study finding a strong overall gliptin-BP association (notably weaker for sitagliptin than other gliptins) and identifying that linagliptin-associated BP often presents as a distinct, BP180-NC16A/BP230-seronegative, clinically milder phenotype that can otherwise be missed by standard serology (Pira A et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2026;95(3):680-689, PMID 42173195).

bullous_pemphigoid.CURABILITY_NOTE: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) has a real, session-verified landmark trial showing that a simple, low-cost intervention -- high-potency topical corticosteroid applied over the whole body -- beats oral corticosteroids on survival itself, not just symptom control. Joly P et al, 'A Comparison of Oral and Topical Corticosteroids in Patients with Bullous Pemphigoid', N Engl J Med 2002;346(5):321-327 (PMID 11821508) randomised 341 patients: in the 188 patients with extensive disease, one-year survival was 76% with topical clobetasol propionate cream (40 g/day, whole-body application) versus 58% with oral prednisone (p=0.02); disease was controlled at 3 weeks in 99% (92/93) on topical clobetasol versus 91% (86/95) on oral prednisone (p=0.02); and severe complications occurred in only 29% (27/93) on topical clobetasol versus 54% (51/95) on oral prednisone (p=0.006). In the 153 patients with moderate disease, topical and oral corticosteroids performed equivalently on survival, disease control and complications. This is a genuine, guideline-changing result -- a topical, dose-titratable therapy that controls disease in the large majority of patients while being safer, and for extensive disease actually more effective at preventing death, than the historical oral-corticosteroid standard. The updated EADV S2K guideline (Borradori L et al, 'Updated S2K guidelines for the management of bullous pemphigoid initiated by the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV)', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2022;36(10):1689-1704, PMID 35766904) and its 2015 EDF-EADV predecessor (Feliciani C et al, Br J Dermatol 2015;172(4):867-877, PMID 25827742) both name high-potency topical corticosteroids as real first-line therapy on the strength of this trial. For patients who cannot use whole-body topical therapy or have widespread disease, oral corticosteroids (same trial's comparator arm, 91% three-week disease control) remain a real, effective first-line option, and doxycycline (BLISTER trial, Williams HC et al, Lancet 2017;389:1630-1638, PMID 28279484) is a real corticosteroid-avoiding initial strategy with significantly fewer severe/life-threatening/fatal treatment-related adverse events (18% vs 36% at 52 weeks, p=0.001) at the cost of somewhat lower 6-week blister control (74% vs 91%). Both the 2015 and 2022 EADV guidelines describe corticosteroid-based BP therapy as typically tapered and withdrawn over months once disease is controlled, consistent with BP's characteristically self-limited course in a real proportion of patients; a specific numeric 'durable drug-free remission' percentage was not identified as independently verified via PubMed in this session, so none is asserted here to avoid inventing a figure. For refractory disease failing corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents, rituximab is a real option supported by case-series evidence (Kasperkiewicz M et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;65(3):552-558, PMID 21641080).

curative_option.name: High-Potency Topical Corticosteroids (Clobetasol Propionate, Whole-Body Application) -- Real Best-Evidence First-Line Therapy (Joly 2002 NEJM Landmark Trial)
curative_option.note: Whole-body application of a high-potency topical corticosteroid achieves at least equivalent, and for extensive disease genuinely superior, real survival and disease-control outcomes compared with oral corticosteroids, while causing significantly fewer severe treatment complications -- a rare case where the safer, cheaper, more titratable option is also the more effective one on a hard endpoint (survival), not merely 'as good with fewer side effects'.

real_survival_data.joly2002_moderate_bp: no significant difference between topical and oral corticosteroids on survival, disease control, or complications

curative_option.source: Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346(5):321-327 (PMID 11821508); named first-line by the updated EADV S2K guideline (Borradori L et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2022;36(10):1689-1704, PMID 35766904) and its 2015 EDF-EADV predecessor (Feliciani C et al, Br J Dermatol 2015;172(4):867-877, PMID 25827742).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, session-verified (NCBI PubMed eutils) treatment-side pharmacological intervention for bullous pemphigoid (BP): high-potency topical corticosteroids as the landmark-trial first-line therapy, oral corticosteroids for widespread/whole-body disease, doxycycline and nicotinamide+tetracycline as real corticosteroid-avoiding/steroid-sparing options, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil as steroid-sparing agents, and rituximab for refractory disease. Diagnosis and symptoms are covered separately in this entry's own symptoms section and are not duplicated here. Every effect size below is quoted from the cited trial/case-series abstract as retrieved from NCBI PubMed eutils in this session; where a number could not be verified from a real primary source it is not given.

bulp_high_potency_topical_corticosteroid.name: High-Potency Topical Corticosteroid -- Clobetasol Propionate, Whole-Body Application (First-Line)
specific_drugs: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream, whole-body application, 40 g/day (tapered based on response)
bulp_high_potency_topical_corticosteroid.effectiveness: Joly 2002 (341 patients, randomised multicentre trial): in 188 patients with extensive BP, one-year survival was 76% with topical clobetasol vs 58% with oral prednisone (p=0.02); disease control at 3 weeks was 99% (92/93) vs 91% (86/95) (p=0.02); severe complications occurred in 29% (27/93) vs 54% (51/95) (p=0.006). In 153 patients with moderate BP, topical and oral corticosteroids were equivalent on all three outcomes (Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346:321-327, PMID 11821508).
bulp_high_potency_topical_corticosteroid.reason_why: Whole-body topical application delivers a very high local corticosteroid concentration directly to the subepidermal blister-forming site while producing lower systemic absorption/toxicity than an equivalent disease-controlling oral dose, which real trial data shows translates into fewer severe complications and, in extensive disease, better survival.
bulp_high_potency_topical_corticosteroid.important_caveat: Whole-body application of 40 g/day of a very potent topical steroid still carries real systemic absorption risk (adrenal suppression) with prolonged use and requires caregiver assistance for elderly/frail patients who often cannot self-apply to their entire body; it is more labour-intensive to administer correctly than a single oral tablet.
bulp_high_potency_topical_corticosteroid.real_working_solution: High-potency topical corticosteroid, applied whole-body, is the real, guideline-named (EADV 2022, EDF-EADV 2015) first-line therapy for BP, achieving disease control in the large majority of patients and, in extensive disease, significantly better survival and fewer severe complications than oral corticosteroids.
bulp_high_potency_topical_corticosteroid.source: Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346(5):321-327 (PMID 11821508); Borradori L et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2022;36(10):1689-1704 (PMID 35766904)

bulp_oral_corticosteroids_widespread_dis.name: Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisone/Prednisolone) -- Real First-Line Option for Widespread/Whole-Body Disease
specific_drugs: Prednisone, oral, 0.5 mg/kg/day (moderate disease) or 1 mg/kg/day (extensive disease), tapered (Joly 2002 regimen)
bulp_oral_corticosteroids_widespread_dis.effectiveness: Joly 2002: oral prednisone controlled disease at 3 weeks in 91% (86/95) of extensive-BP patients, with 58% one-year survival and 54% severe complications (vs 76% survival and 29% complications on topical clobetasol) (PMID 11821508). Williams 2017 (BLISTER trial): oral prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day) achieved three-or-fewer blisters at 6 weeks in 91% (92/101) of patients, versus 74% (83/112) on doxycycline, but with more related severe/life-threatening/fatal adverse events at 52 weeks (36% vs 18%, p=0.001) (Williams HC et al, Lancet 2017;389:1630-1638, PMID 28279484).
bulp_oral_corticosteroids_widespread_dis.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids broadly suppress the autoimmune/inflammatory process driving subepidermal blister formation and reliably control disease at a fixed, predictable oral dose, making them practical where whole-body topical application is not feasible (severe frailty, no caregiver, very widespread disease).
bulp_oral_corticosteroids_widespread_dis.important_caveat: Real trial data (Joly 2002, BLISTER) both show oral corticosteroids carry a materially higher rate of severe/life-threatening complications than topical clobetasol or doxycycline respectively -- the real trade-off is faster/more reliable short-term blister control against significantly worse long-term safety in this elderly, comorbidity-prone population.
bulp_oral_corticosteroids_widespread_dis.real_working_solution: Oral corticosteroids remain a real, effective first-line option for widespread BP where whole-body topical therapy is impractical, achieving disease control in the large majority of patients, though with a real and quantified higher severe-complication rate than topical clobetasol or doxycycline.
bulp_oral_corticosteroids_widespread_dis.source: Joly P et al, N Engl J Med 2002;346:321-327 (PMID 11821508); Williams HC et al, Lancet 2017;389:1630-1638 (PMID 28279484)

bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.name: Doxycycline -- Real Corticosteroid-Avoiding Initial Treatment Strategy (BLISTER Trial)
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.type: Tetracycline-class antibiotic, anti-inflammatory/MMP-inhibitory mechanism, corticosteroid-sparing initial strategy
specific_drugs: Doxycycline, oral, 200 mg/day, with localised adjuvant potent topical corticosteroid (<30 g/week) permitted during weeks 1-3
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.effectiveness: BLISTER trial (253 patients, UK/Germany, pragmatic non-inferiority RCT): starting on doxycycline gave three-or-fewer blisters at 6 weeks in 74% (83/112) of patients versus 91% (92/101) starting on prednisolone (adjusted difference 18.6%, within the predefined 37% non-inferiority margin). Related severe/life-threatening/fatal adverse events at 52 weeks were 18% (22/121) with doxycycline versus 36% (41/113) with prednisolone (adjusted difference 19.0%, 95% CI 7.9-30.1, p=0.001) (Williams HC et al, Lancet 2017;389(10079):1630-1638, PMID 28279484).
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.reason_why: Doxycycline is thought to act in BP through anti-inflammatory and matrix-metalloproteinase-inhibitory effects independent of its antimicrobial activity, giving real disease control without the systemic immunosuppression and corticosteroid toxicity burden that drives BP's high complication rate in oral-corticosteroid-treated (typically elderly) patients.
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.important_caveat: Doxycycline gives somewhat less complete short-term blister control (74% vs 91%) than prednisolone; the real trade-off, per the trial's own non-inferiority design and conclusion, is acceptable short-term control in exchange for a significant long-term safety advantage, not equivalent short-term efficacy.
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.real_working_solution: Starting BP treatment with doxycycline is a real, RCT-validated corticosteroid-sparing initial strategy that trades a real but bounded reduction in 6-week blister control for a significantly safer 52-week adverse-event profile, and is named as a real option in the updated EADV S2K guideline.

bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.name: Nicotinamide (Niacinamide) Plus Tetracycline -- Real Corticosteroid-Avoiding Combination (Fivenson 1994)
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.type: Vitamin B3 derivative + tetracycline-class antibiotic combination, corticosteroid-avoiding
specific_drugs: Nicotinamide, oral, 500 mg three times daily
Tetracycline, oral, 500 mg four times daily
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.effectiveness: Randomised, open-label trial of 20 BP patients (18 treated, 12 on nicotinamide+tetracycline, 6 on prednisone): 5 complete responses, 5 partial responses, 1 nonresponder and 1 with disease progression in the nicotinamide+tetracycline group (5/12 = 41.7% complete response) versus 1 complete response and 5 partial responses in the prednisone group. No statistically significant difference in response between groups; all 5 nicotinamide+tetracycline patients followed long-term remained disease-free during medication tapering, versus repeated flare-ups in 3 of the prednisone patients during tapering. Adverse effects were materially worse in the prednisone group, including one death from sepsis (Fivenson DP et al, Arch Dermatol 1994;130(6):753-758, PMID 8002646).
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.reason_why: Nicotinamide has real anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects (inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis and leukocyte migration relevant to BP's inflammatory blister formation) and, combined with tetracycline's independent anti-inflammatory action, provides real disease control without systemic corticosteroid exposure in this small trial.
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.important_caveat: This is a small (n=18), open-label pilot trial, not a large blinded RCT like BLISTER; the complete-response rate (41.7%) is numerically lower than doxycycline's 6-week blister-control rate in BLISTER, though the two trials used different response definitions and are not directly comparable.
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.real_working_solution: Nicotinamide plus tetracycline is a real, small-trial-supported corticosteroid-avoiding combination option for BP, with a signal of durable steroid-free remission in responders, though evidence is far less robust than the modern BLISTER doxycycline trial.
bulp_doxycycline_niacinamide_steroid_spa.source: Fivenson DP et al, Arch Dermatol 1994;130(6):753-758 (PMID 8002646)

bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.name: Azathioprine or Mycophenolate Mofetil Added to Oral Corticosteroid -- Steroid-Sparing Comparison (Beissert 2007)
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.type: Corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressants, added to systemic corticosteroid
specific_drugs: Azathioprine, oral, added to oral methylprednisolone
Mycophenolate mofetil, oral, added to oral methylprednisolone
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.effectiveness: Prospective multicentre RCT of 73 BP patients across 13 German dermatology departments: complete remission was achieved in 38 of 38 (100%) azathioprine-group patients after a mean of 23.8 +/- 18.9 days, versus 35 of 35 (100%) mycophenolate-mofetil-group patients after a mean of 42.0 +/- 55.3 days (both arms continued treatment until remission was reached, so 100% reflects the protocol's open-ended treatment design rather than a fixed-timepoint cure rate). Median cumulative methylprednisolone dose was similar between arms (4967 mg azathioprine vs 5754 mg mycophenolate mofetil). Grade 3-4 adverse effects occurred in 24% (9/38) of the azathioprine group versus 17% (6/35) of the mycophenolate group, with azathioprine causing significantly more liver-function-test toxicity (p<0.001 for elevated transaminases) (Beissert S et al, Arch Dermatol 2007;143(12):1536-1542, PMID 18087004).
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.reason_why: Azathioprine (purine-synthesis-inhibiting antimetabolite) and mycophenolate mofetil (inosine-monophosphate-dehydrogenase inhibitor) both suppress the lymphocyte-driven autoantibody production against hemidesmosomal BP180/BP230 antigens, letting corticosteroid dosing be brought down once remission is reached.
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.important_caveat: An earlier, larger controlled trial (Guillaume JC et al, Arch Dermatol 1993;129(1):49-53, PMID 8420491, n=100) found azathioprine added to prednisolone gave no significant benefit over prednisolone alone: complete remission at 28 days was 71% (prednisolone alone), 80% (plus azathioprine) and 71% (plus plasma exchange), and at 6 months 42%, 39% and 29% respectively, with azathioprine associated with more severe complications and no mortality difference among the three arms (14/98 deaths overall) -- a real, honestly-reported negative/neutral finding that predates and contrasts with Beissert 2007's steroid-sparing framing; azathioprine/mycophenolate mofetil's real value in BP is best supported as steroid-sparing/dose-reducing agents rather than as agents that improve remission rate over corticosteroids alone.
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.real_working_solution: Azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil, added to a tapering oral corticosteroid, is a real steroid-sparing strategy that let both Beissert 2007 arms reach complete remission with materially lower toxicity risk with mycophenolate mofetil; whether either agent improves the remission rate itself over corticosteroid monotherapy is not supported by the earlier, larger Guillaume 1993 controlled trial and should be represented honestly as steroid-sparing rather than remission-improving.
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.source: Beissert S et al, Arch Dermatol 2007;143(12):1536-1542 (PMID 18087004); Guillaume JC et al, Arch Dermatol 1993;129(1):49-53 (PMID 8420491)
bulp_azathioprine_mycophenolate_steroid_.confidence: high (both real RCTs; findings on remission-rate benefit are mixed/negative in the earlier, larger trial)

bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.name: Rituximab -- Refractory Bullous Pemphigoid Failing Conventional Therapy
specific_drugs: Rituximab IV infusion, 375 mg/m2 weekly x4, or 1000 mg twice 2 weeks apart; retreatment with 1000 mg twice 2 weeks apart used for relapse
bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.effectiveness: Case series of 17 patients with refractory autoimmune blistering dermatoses (pemphigus vulgaris n=8, pemphigus foliaceus n=2, bullous pemphigoid n=2, mucous membrane pemphigoid n=5): all lesions cleared in 14 of 17 patients overall, including both of the 2 BP patients in the cohort; 3 others had partial healing. Relapses occurred in 8 patients overall (including 1 of the BP patients), and retreatment with rituximab again produced complete or partial remission in relapsed patients. No serious rituximab-associated side effects were observed (Kasperkiewicz M et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;65(3):552-558, PMID 21641080).
bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.reason_why: Rituximab depletes CD20+ B cells, including the autoreactive clones producing anti-BP180/BP230 autoantibodies that drive hemidesmosome disruption and subepidermal blistering in BP, offering a real mechanistic route to control in patients who have failed corticosteroids and conventional steroid-sparing agents.
bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.important_caveat: The BP-specific evidence here is very small (only 2 of the 17 patients in this case series had BP), so the 100% (2/2) BP response should be read as an anecdotal-level signal, not a population-level effectiveness estimate; no larger BP-specific rituximab RCT was identified as independently verified via PubMed in this session.
bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.real_working_solution: Rituximab is a real, mechanistically-grounded rescue option for refractory BP that has failed corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents, with a small but genuine case-series signal of durable lesion clearance and safe retreatment on relapse.
bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.source: Kasperkiewicz M et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2011;65(3):552-558 (PMID 21641080)
bulp_rituximab_refractory_disease.confidence: low (n=2 BP patients within a mixed 17-patient case series, no larger BP-specific trial identified)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real percentages come from DIFFERENT trials/case series measuring DIFFERENT endpoints (protocol-defined complete remission with open-ended treatment duration vs fixed-3-week or fixed-6-week disease/blister control vs 1-year survival vs small case-series lesion clearance) in DIFFERENT BP populations (extensive vs moderate disease, treatment-naive vs refractory) -- ranking together is directionally useful, not strict apples-to-apples. See curative_option (high-potency topical corticosteroids) for BP's real best-evidence, guideline-first-line, survival-improving option (Joly 2002 NEJM).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Azathioprine + oral methylprednisolone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Protocol-defined complete remission, open-ended treatment duration, mean 23.8 days (Beissert 2007)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Beissert S et al, Arch Dermatol 2007;143:1536-1542 (PMID 18087004)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Mycophenolate mofetil + oral methylprednisolone
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Protocol-defined complete remission, open-ended treatment duration, mean 42.0 days (Beissert 2007)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Beissert S et al, Arch Dermatol 2007;143:1536-1542 (PMID 18087004)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Rituximab (refractory BP, n=2 within a 17-patient mixed case series)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete lesion clearance, small case series (2 of 2 BP patients)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kasperkiewicz M et al, JAAD 2011;65:552-558 (PMID 21641080)

ranked_high_to_low.name: High-potency topical clobetasol propionate, whole-body (extensive BP)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Disease control at 3 weeks (Joly 2002); this arm also had 76% 1-year survival vs 58% oral prednisone

ranked_high_to_low.name: Oral prednisone (extensive BP)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Disease control at 3 weeks (Joly 2002 comparator arm)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Doxycycline (initial treatment strategy)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Three-or-fewer blisters at 6 weeks (BLISTER trial; vs 91% for prednisolone in the same trial, but with double the severe-adverse-event rate)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Williams HC et al, Lancet 2017;389:1630-1638 (PMID 28279484)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Nicotinamide + tetracycline
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Complete response, small open-label pilot trial (5 of 12 patients; 5 more had partial response)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fivenson DP et al, Arch Dermatol 1994;130:753-758 (PMID 8002646)

hidradenitis_suppurativa.name: Hidradenitis Suppurativa
hidradenitis_suppurativa.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Two real, distinct emergencies must not be managed as routine hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) flares. (1) ACUTE SEVERE ABSCESS/CELLULITIS/NECROTISING FLARE: HS lesions are deep-seated abscesses and inflamed sinus tracts that can secondarily become superinfected; in the perineal/gluteal/genital region this carries a real, documented risk of progressing to Fournier's gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of the perineum). A published case describes a 42-year-old woman with severe untreated HS involving the axilla, perineum, lumbosacral region and bilateral gluteal areas who presented with fever, lethargy and shortness of breath, was found to be in septic shock, was diagnosed with Fournier's gangrene arising at pre-existing HS lesions, and died of multi-organ failure despite aggressive surgical debridement, antibiotics and intensive care (Khattar G, Bou Sanayeh E, Makram M, Rabah H, Abu Baker S, Khan S, Hong C, 'The Concomitant Occurrence of Hidradenitis Suppurativa and Fournier's Gangrene', Eur J Case Rep Intern Med 2024;11(6):004493, PMID 38846649). Any HS patient presenting with fever, systemic illness/lethargy, rapidly spreading erythema/induration beyond the usual lesion border, or a perineal/genital-region flare should be escalated for urgent surgical/infectious-disease evaluation rather than routed through standard non-urgent dermatology/doctor-approval queue timing. (2) RARE BUT REAL SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA (SCC) TRANSFORMATION IN CHRONIC SEVERE DISEASE: long-standing, severe (typically Hurley stage III) HS, especially in the perianal/gluteal/perineal region, carries a rare but real risk of malignant transformation to cutaneous SCC. A man with a 20-year history of Hurley stage III HS of the buttocks/perineum developed a chronic ulcerative lesion that rapidly enlarged into a 15 cm exophytic tumour confirmed as high-grade invasive SCC (Yamamura Y, Fujii K, Nakashima C, Usui S, Nishimura K, Otsuka A, 'Rapid Enlargement of Squamous Cell Carcinoma Arising From Hidradenitis Suppurativa During Bimekizumab Therapy', Cureus 2025;17(9):e92172, PMID 41084663); two further cases of HPV-16-positive cutaneous SCC arising in long-standing Hurley stage III HS have been reported (Abu Rached N, Kapynen R, Doerler M, Ocker L, Frost C, Haven Y, Bechara FG, 'HPV-16-Induced Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Hidradenitis Suppurativa: HPV Vaccination May Be Useful', Cancers (Basel) 2025;17(4):702, PMID 40002295); and a case of chronic HS that progressed to unresectable, ultimately fatal SCC after late surgical intervention led its authors to conclude wide surgical excision 'should at least be considered for all chronic HS patients due to high morbidity and malignant transformation risk' (Juviler PG, Patel AP, Qi Y, 'Infiltrative squamous cell carcinoma in hidradenitis suppurativa: A case report for early surgical intervention', Int J Surg Case Rep 2019;55:50-53, PMID 30685629). Any chronic, long-standing HS lesion (particularly in the perianal/gluteal/perineal region) that becomes non-healing, rapidly enlarging, exophytic, ulcerated, or friable should prompt urgent biopsy to exclude SCC rather than being assumed to be a routine HS flare, and should not wait for standard non-urgent doctor-approval queue timing.

hurley_staging_system.finding: Hidradenitis suppurativa severity is most widely staged using the three-tier Hurley staging system, which the major dermatology literature confirms 'is still widely used in severity rating' despite the availability of newer dynamic scoring tools: Hurley stage I (abscess formation, single or multiple, without sinus tracts or cicatrisation/scarring), Hurley stage II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tract formation and scarring, single or multiple widely separated lesions), and Hurley stage III (diffuse or near-diffuse involvement with multiple interconnected sinus tracts and abscesses across an entire anatomic area). A European S1 guideline explicitly recommends 'a Hurley severity grade-relevant treatment of HS' following a treatment algorithm keyed to these three stages.
hurley_staging_system.source: Nguyen TV, Damiani G, Orenstein LAV, Hamzavi I, Jemec GB, 'Hidradenitis suppurativa: an update on epidemiology, phenotypes, diagnosis, pathogenesis, comorbidities and quality of life', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2021;35(1):50-61 (PMID 32460374); Zouboulis CC, Desai N, Emtestam L et al., 'European S1 guideline for the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2015;29(4):619-644 (PMID 25640693)
hurley_staging_system.confidence: high - Hurley staging's three-tier structure and continued primary clinical use are consistently confirmed across the major guideline and review literature

hurley_staging_reliability_and_real_dist.finding: A dedicated inter/intra-rater reliability study (15 raters - plastic surgeons, general surgeons, dermatologists - independently staging 30 patient photographs at two time points) found Hurley staging reliable for rapid severity assessment: inter-rater reliability was moderate overall (kappa=0.59, 95% CI 0.48-0.70), moderate for stage I (kappa=0.45) and stage II (kappa=0.51), but almost perfect for stage III (kappa=0.81); intrarater reliability was substantial overall (kappa=0.65) and almost perfect for stage III (kappa=0.82); mean time to stage a photo was only 14 seconds. Separately, a prospective validation cohort of 355 real HS patients found the real-world distribution across stages was 88/355 (24.8%) Hurley stage I, 221/355 (62.3%) Hurley stage II, and 46/355 (13.0%) Hurley stage III, with a newer Severity Assessment of Hidradenitis Suppurativa (SAHS) score significantly correlating with Hurley stage (median SAHS 5 in stage I, 6 in stage II, 9 in stage III, P<0.001).
hurley_staging_reliability_and_real_dist.source: Ovadja ZN, Schuit MM, van der Horst CMAM, Lapid O, 'Inter- and intrarater reliability of Hurley staging for hidradenitis suppurativa', Br J Dermatol 2019;181(2):344-349 (PMID 30585304); Hessam S, Scholl L, Sand M, Schmitz L, Reitenbach S, Bechara FG, 'A Novel Severity Assessment Scoring System for Hidradenitis Suppurativa', JAMA Dermatol 2018;154(3):330-335 (PMID 29417136)
hurley_staging_reliability_and_real_dist.confidence: high - both are real, quantified, peer-reviewed validation studies with directly quoted kappa statistics and patient-distribution numbers

core_lesion_description.finding: Hidradenitis suppurativa is characterised by recurrent, painful, deep-seated nodules, abscesses and draining sinus tracts, most commonly in intertriginous (apocrine gland-bearing) areas, with lesion formation centred on follicular hyperkeratosis and occlusion within the pilosebaceous-apocrine unit followed by perifollicular inflammation, rupture and chronic architectural tissue change (fistulae and scarring in more advanced disease).
core_lesion_description.source: Nguyen TV, Damiani G, Orenstein LAV, Hamzavi I, Jemec GB, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2021;35(1):50-61 (PMID 32460374); Goldburg SR, Strober BE, Payette MJ, 'Hidradenitis suppurativa: Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and pathogenesis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82(5):1045-1058 (PMID 31604104)

anatomic_distribution.finding: Lesions occur predominantly after puberty in the apocrine gland-bearing areas of the body, most commonly the axillae, inguinal/groin and anogenital (perianal, perineal) regions, and also the submammary/inframammary folds and buttocks; distribution can be widespread in more severe (Hurley III) disease.
anatomic_distribution.source: Zouboulis CC et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2015;29(4):619-644 (PMID 25640693); Goldburg SR, Strober BE, Payette MJ, J Am Acad Dermatol 2020;82(5):1045-1058 (PMID 31604104)

associated_signs_and_symptoms.finding: Beyond the visible nodules/abscesses/sinus tracts, patients experience a real, quantified burden of chronic signs and symptoms - pain (mean numerical rating scale, NRS, score 3.99 across pooled studies), pruritus (mean NRS 4.99), malodour and suppuration/drainage - which correlate with poorer general and disease-specific quality of life (sexual distress, anxiety, depression, sleep disruption) when more intense. Low self-esteem and sexual dysfunction are also reported as chronic consequences of uncontrolled disease.
associated_signs_and_symptoms.source: Montero-Vilchez T, Diaz-Calvillo P, Rodriguez-Pozo JA, Cuenca-Barrales C, Martinez-Lopez A, Arias-Santiago S, Molina-Leyva A, 'The Burden of Hidradenitis Suppurativa Signs and Symptoms in Quality of Life: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021;18(13):6709 (PMID 34206415); Nguyen TV et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2021 (PMID 32460374)

clinical_diagnosis_no_pathognomonic_test.finding: In the absence of a pathognomonic laboratory test, hidradenitis suppurativa is diagnosed clinically, from direct observation of the characteristic lesions (recurrent nodules, abscesses, draining sinus tracts) in typical intertriginous locations together with the disease narrative (recurrence/chronicity over time). Phenotypic variation between patients renders diagnosis and severity assessment genuinely difficult in practice, and ultrasound imaging is described as an emerging (not yet routine) assessment tool for deep-seated lesions.
clinical_diagnosis_no_pathognomonic_test.source: Nguyen TV, Damiani G, Orenstein LAV, Hamzavi I, Jemec GB, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2021;35(1):50-61 (PMID 32460374)

diagnostic_delay_real_numbers.finding: Diagnostic delay in HS is real, large and, per a 2024 study, unimproved over time. A retrospective study of 285 patients diagnosed between January 2006 and December 2022 at a tertiary hospital found a mean diagnostic delay of 10.1 years, with no improvement over the study period; a delay of more than 5 years was significantly associated with earlier symptom onset, lesion location on the breasts and thighs, a follicular phenotype, and cardiovascular/psychiatric comorbidities, while smoking and BMI >=25 kg/m2 were also linked to longer delay. Conversely, a personal history of acne and greater disease severity were associated with earlier diagnosis. A separate major review independently confirms patients still experience 'significant diagnostic delay, up to several years.'
diagnostic_delay_real_numbers.source: Aparicio Martins I, Figueira Vilela B, Cabete J, 'Diagnostic Delay in Hidradenitis Suppurativa: Still an Unsolved Problem', Skin Appendage Disord 2024;10(2):129-132 (PMID 38572195); Nguyen TV et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2021 (PMID 32460374)
diagnostic_delay_real_numbers.confidence: high - directly quoted figures from a dedicated, real, 285-patient retrospective study

chronic_progressive_course_real_data.finding: HS is a chronic, inflammatory, recurrent, debilitating disease with a real average incidence of 6.0 per 100,000 person-years and an average prevalence of about 1% reported in Europe (a broader review places global prevalence in the range 0.00033-4.1%, but most likely 0.7-1.2% in European-US populations). A real, quantified, highly significant association exists between HS prevalence and current smoking (odds ratio 12.55) and overweight (odds ratio 1.1 per body-mass-index unit), and the disease is associated with obesity, metabolic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease (e.g. Crohn's disease), spondyloarthropathy and other follicular-occlusion/hyperergic diseases, as well as polycystic ovarian syndrome, depression, suicide and substance-use disorders. In a pooled meta-analytic HS cohort (4929 patients), mean disease duration at the time of study was 13.69 years, illustrating the disease's genuinely long, chronic course.
chronic_progressive_course_real_data.source: Zouboulis CC, Desai N, Emtestam L et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2015;29(4):619-644 (PMID 25640693); Nguyen TV et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2021 (PMID 32460374); Montero-Vilchez T et al, Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021;18(13):6709 (PMID 34206415)

quality_of_life_impact_real_numbers.finding: HS carries a real, exceptionally severe quality-of-life burden: a European S1 guideline states HS 'has the highest impact on patients' quality of life among all assessed dermatological diseases.' A dedicated systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies (4929 HS patients, mostly mild-to-moderate disease) found a mean Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) score of 10.70 (SD 2.16) - a substantial impairment - and confirmed that higher intensity of HS signs/symptoms (pain, pruritus, malodour, suppuration) correlated with poorer general and specific quality-of-life domains including sexual distress, anxiety, depression and sleep.
quality_of_life_impact_real_numbers.source: Zouboulis CC et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2015;29(4):619-644 (PMID 25640693); Montero-Vilchez T, Diaz-Calvillo P, Rodriguez-Pozo JA, Cuenca-Barrales C, Martinez-Lopez A, Arias-Santiago S, Molina-Leyva A, Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021;18(13):6709 (PMID 34206415)

rare_severe_complications_natural_histor.finding: At the extreme end of HS's natural history, real (rare but documented) severe complications occur in chronic, longstanding, usually Hurley stage III disease: necrotising soft-tissue infection (Fournier's gangrene) in the perineal/genital region, which has been fatal in a documented case, and malignant transformation to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, also documented as fatal when surgical intervention is delayed. These rare outcomes underscore that HS, left chronically uncontrolled over years to decades, is not merely a cosmetic or quality-of-life disease but carries real long-term morbidity and mortality risk (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE for full detail and sourcing).
rare_severe_complications_natural_histor.source: Khattar G, Bou Sanayeh E, Makram M, Rabah H, Abu Baker S, Khan S, Hong C, Eur J Case Rep Intern Med 2024;11(6):004493 (PMID 38846649); Juviler PG, Patel AP, Qi Y, Int J Surg Case Rep 2019;55:50-53 (PMID 30685629); Yamamura Y et al, Cureus 2025;17(9):e92172 (PMID 41084663)
rare_severe_complications_natural_histor.confidence: moderate-high - these are real, individually documented case reports rather than a population-level incidence rate for either complication, so absolute risk is not stated as a rate; rarity is described qualitatively per the cited sources

The current WHO ICD-11 MMS code for hidradenitis suppurativa could NOT be independently confirmed on the live WHO ICD-11 browser or the id.who.int ICD-API in this session (the browser is a JS-rendered app not fetchable by this session's tools, and the API requires an OAuth token this session does not have) -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly.
hidradenitis_suppurativa.CURABILITY_NOTE: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) has a REAL close-to-curative option, but it is surgical, not medical, and applies to a defined anatomical subset rather than the whole disease at once. Wide surgical excision (removing the entire affected apocrine-gland-bearing skin and sinus-tract field down to healthy tissue, not just draining individual abscesses) is the real disease-removing intervention for chronic, localized, Hurley Stage II-III disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies found the average recurrence rate after wide excision was 13.0% (95% CI 5.0-22.0%) -- i.e. roughly 87% of operated sites (computed, 100-13.0) do NOT recur -- versus 22.0% recurrence after local incision and 27.0% recurrence after deroofing (Mehdizadeh A, Hazen PG, Bechara FG, Zwingerman N, Moazenzadeh M, Bashash M, Sibbald RG, Alavi A, 'Recurrence of hidradenitis suppurativa after surgical management: A systematic review and meta-analysis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2015;73(5 Suppl 1):S70-7, PMID 26470621). Recurrence was lowest when the excision defect was closed with a skin flap (8.0% recurrence, ~92% no-recurrence, computed) or a skin graft (6.0% recurrence, ~94% no-recurrence, computed) rather than primary closure (15% recurrence, ~85% no-recurrence, computed) -- this is a real, quantified, close-to-curative outcome for the operated field, though it does not guarantee against new disease arising in a different, previously-unaffected apocrine-bearing area, since HS is a field disease. For patients who are not surgical candidates, or who have widespread moderate-to-severe inflammatory disease not yet localized enough for excision, biologic therapy is the real evidence-based medical alternative, though it is disease-controlling rather than curative: adalimumab (the first and still the only globally approved biologic specifically for HS) achieved a >=50% reduction in abscess/inflammatory-nodule count (HiSCR) in 41.8% (PIONEER I) and 58.9% (PIONEER II) of patients at week 12 with weekly dosing, versus 26.0% and 27.6% with placebo respectively (Kimball AB, Okun MM, Williams DA et al, 'Two Phase 3 Trials of Adalimumab for Hidradenitis Suppurativa', N Engl J Med 2016;375(5):422-434, PMID 27518661). The IL-17 inhibitors secukinumab (45% HiSCR at week 16 in SUNSHINE and 42-46% in SUNRISE, both significantly better than placebo's 31-34%; Kimball AB, Jemec GBE, Alavi A et al, Lancet 2023;401(10378):747-761, PMID 36746171) and bimekizumab (48-54% HiSCR50 at week 16 across BE HEARD I/II versus 29-32% placebo; Kimball AB, Jemec GBE, Sayed CJ et al, Lancet 2024;403(10443):2504-2519, PMID 38795716) have since shown real, statistically significant, similarly-sized responder-rate advantages over placebo in separate phase 3 trials (no head-to-head trial exists between the three biologics). REAL WORKING SOLUTION: (1) chronic, localized, Hurley II-III disease with recurrent sinus tracts/scarring in a defined field -- wide surgical excision with flap or skin-graft closure is the real closest-to-cure option, with ~87-94% of operated sites recurrence-free; (2) widespread moderate-to-severe inflammatory disease, or as a medical bridge before/after surgery -- adalimumab first-line, with secukinumab or bimekizumab as real trial-proven alternatives for adalimumab-inadequate-response or intolerant patients; (3) mild, early, or localized disease not yet requiring biologics or surgery -- topical/oral antibiotics and intralesional corticosteroid injections for acute flares provide real, guideline-endorsed symptomatic control while definitive therapy is arranged. Biologics and surgery both require mandatory doctor evaluation and monitoring.

curative_option.name: Wide Surgical Excision With Flap or Skin-Graft Closure - Real Closest-to-Cure Option for Chronic Localized (Hurley Stage II-III) Hidradenitis Suppurativa, With Adalimumab/IL-17 Inhibitor Biologics as Real Significant-Response Medical Alternatives
curative_option.note: Wide surgical excision physically removes the entire diseased apocrine-gland-bearing skin field -- sinus tracts, scarring, and surrounding at-risk tissue -- rather than draining or medically suppressing individual lesions, which is why it achieves durable, close-to-curative clearance of the treated site unmatched by any medical therapy. For patients whose disease is too widespread or inflammatory for excision, TNF-alpha inhibition (adalimumab) or IL-17 pathway inhibition (secukinumab, bimekizumab) gives a real, statistically significant reduction in abscess/inflammatory-nodule burden, but requires ongoing treatment to sustain the response -- it controls rather than removes the disease.

real_trial_data.wide_excision_meta_analysis_recurrence: Mehdizadeh A, Hazen PG, Bechara FG, Zwingerman N, Moazenzadeh M, Bashash M, Sibbald RG, Alavi A, 'Recurrence of hidradenitis suppurativa after surgical management: A systematic review and meta-analysis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2015;73(5 Suppl 1):S70-7 (PMID 26470621): meta-analysis of proportions across 22 included studies (of 1147 screened). Average recurrence: wide excision 13.0% (95% CI 5.0-22.0%, i.e. ~87.0% no-recurrence, computed); local incision 22.0% (95% CI 10.0-37.0%, ~78.0% no-recurrence, computed); deroofing 27.0% (95% CI 23.0-31.0%, ~73.0% no-recurrence, computed). Within wide excision, recurrence by closure method: primary closure 15% (95% CI 0-72%, ~85% no-recurrence, computed), flap closure 8.0% (95% CI 2.0-16.0%, ~92.0% no-recurrence, computed), grafting 6.0% (95% CI 0.0-24.0%, ~94.0% no-recurrence, computed).
real_trial_data.adalimumab_pioneer_i_ii: Kimball AB, Okun MM, Williams DA, Gottlieb AB, Papp KA, Zouboulis CC et al, 'Two Phase 3 Trials of Adalimumab for Hidradenitis Suppurativa', N Engl J Med 2016;375(5):422-434 (PMID 27518661): PIONEER I (n=307) and PIONEER II (n=326), randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials, adalimumab 40 mg weekly for 12 weeks. Clinical response (HiSCR): 41.8% vs 26.0% placebo in PIONEER I (P=0.003); 58.9% vs 27.6% placebo in PIONEER II (P<0.001).
real_trial_data.secukinumab_sunshine_sunrise: Kimball AB, Jemec GBE, Alavi A, Reguiai Z, Gottlieb AB, Bechara FG et al, Lancet 2023;401(10378):747-761 (PMID 36746171): SUNSHINE (n=541) and SUNRISE (n=543), identical phase 3 RCTs. HS clinical response at week 16, secukinumab 300 mg every 2 weeks: 45% (81.5/181) vs 34% (60.7/180) placebo in SUNSHINE (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-2.7, P=0.0070); 42% (76.2/180) vs 31% (57.1/183) placebo in SUNRISE (P=0.015), with the every-4-weeks arm reaching 46% (83.1/180) vs the same 31% placebo (P=0.0022). Responses sustained to week 52 in both trials.
real_trial_data.bimekizumab_be_heard_i_ii: Kimball AB, Jemec GBE, Sayed CJ, Kirby JS, Prens E, Ingram JR et al, Lancet 2024;403(10443):2504-2519 (PMID 38795716): BE HEARD I (n=505) and BE HEARD II (n=509), 48-week phase 3 RCTs. HiSCR50 at week 16, bimekizumab 320 mg every 2 weeks: 48% (138/289) vs 29% (21/72) placebo in BE HEARD I (OR 2.23, P=0.0060); 52% (151/291) vs 32% (24/74) placebo in BE HEARD II (OR 2.29, P=0.0032); the every-4-weeks arm in BE HEARD II reached 54% (77/144) vs the same 32% placebo (OR 2.42, P=0.0038). Responses maintained/increased to week 48.

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Curative-in-effect for the operated field: wide excision with flap or graft closure leaves ~92-94% of treated sites free of recurrence (computed from Mehdizadeh 2015, PMID 26470621), which is a real, durable, disease-removing outcome for that anatomical area. Not a systemic cure: HS is a field disease of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae, groin, perianal, inframammary), so a new site can still develop disease later even after a successful excision elsewhere, and even wide excision still carries a residual ~6-15% site recurrence risk. Biologics (adalimumab, secukinumab, bimekizumab) are NOT curative at all -- each achieves a real, statistically significant ~42-59% clinical response rate versus ~27-34% placebo, but the benefit requires continued dosing and a substantial minority of patients (about 40-58%) do not reach even a 50% lesion-count reduction.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Wide excision is not appropriate for early, mild, or non-localized (widespread, multi-region, still-acute-inflammatory) disease, where there is no discrete chronic field to remove and surgery would be premature; it also requires adequate wound-healing capacity and is not a rescue for an acute abscess flare. Biologics are not first-line for mild, localized, antibiotic-responsive disease, and adalimumab every-other-week dosing (rather than weekly) has been shown ineffective (Ingram JR et al, 'Interventions for hidradenitis suppurativa: a Cochrane systematic review incorporating GRADE assessment of evidence quality', Br J Dermatol 2016;174(5):970-8, PMID 26801356).
curative_option.important_caveat: No head-to-head randomized trial compares wide excision against biologics, or compares the three biologics against each other, so cross-trial responder-rate comparisons above are indirect. Surgery requires doctor/surgeon evaluation of disease extent and wound-closure planning; biologics require prescription-only initiation with infection/TB/hepatitis screening and ongoing monitoring given TNF-alpha/IL-17-inhibitor class risks.
curative_option.source: Mehdizadeh A et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2015;73(5 Suppl 1):S70-7 (PMID 26470621); Kimball AB et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375(5):422-434 (PMID 27518661); Kimball AB et al, Lancet 2023;401(10378):747-761 (PMID 36746171); Kimball AB et al, Lancet 2024;403(10443):2504-2519 (PMID 38795716)
curative_option.confidence: high

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for hidradenitis suppurativa in priority order: the three regulatory-trial-proven biologics (adalimumab, secukinumab, bimekizumab; full excision/biologic comparison in curative_option), wide surgical excision, topical/oral antibiotics for mild disease, and intralesional corticosteroids for acute flares. Diagnostic criteria, Hurley staging, pathophysiology and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial/review or is a plainly labelled arithmetic computation from numbers stated in that source.

hs_adalimumab.name: Adalimumab (Anti-TNF-alpha) - Real First Regulatory-Approved Biologic for Moderate-to-Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa (PIONEER I/II Phase 3 Trials)
specific_drugs: Adalimumab (Humira and biosimilars): 160 mg at week 0, 80 mg at week 2, then 40 mg subcutaneously weekly from week 4 (HS-specific induction/maintenance regimen)
hs_adalimumab.effectiveness: Kimball AB, Okun MM, Williams DA et al, 'Two Phase 3 Trials of Adalimumab for Hidradenitis Suppurativa', N Engl J Med 2016;375(5):422-434 (PMID 27518661): PIONEER I (n=307) and PIONEER II (n=326), randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials. Clinical response (HiSCR: >=50% reduction in abscess/inflammatory-nodule count, no increase in abscess/draining-fistula count) at week 12 with adalimumab 40 mg weekly: 41.8% vs 26.0% placebo in PIONEER I (P=0.003); 58.9% vs 27.6% placebo in PIONEER II (P<0.001).
hs_adalimumab.reason_why: TNF-alpha is a key pro-inflammatory cytokine driving the follicular-occlusion/inflammatory cascade of HS; adalimumab binds and neutralizes TNF-alpha, reducing the abscess and inflammatory-nodule burden that defines active disease.
hs_adalimumab.important_caveat: Response was inconsistent between the two identically-designed PIONEER trials (larger effect in PIONEER II); every-other-week dosing was ineffective in a Cochrane-reviewed meta-analysis of two trials, n=124 (Ingram JR et al, Br J Dermatol 2016;174(5):970-8, PMID 26801356). Requires prescription-only initiation with TB/hepatitis screening and doctor-directed monitoring.
hs_adalimumab.real_working_solution: First-line biologic for moderate-to-severe HS inadequately controlled by antibiotics; weekly (not every-other-week) dosing is required for real efficacy.
hs_adalimumab.source: Kimball AB et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375(5):422-434 (PMID 27518661); Ingram JR et al, Br J Dermatol 2016;174(5):970-8 (PMID 26801356)

hs_secukinumab.name: Secukinumab (Anti-IL-17A) - Real Phase 3 Trial-Proven Alternative Biologic for Moderate-to-Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa (SUNSHINE and SUNRISE Trials)
specific_drugs: Secukinumab 300 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks (higher-response schedule) or every 4 weeks
hs_secukinumab.effectiveness: Kimball AB, Jemec GBE, Alavi A et al, Lancet 2023;401(10378):747-761 (PMID 36746171): SUNSHINE (n=541) and SUNRISE (n=543), two identical phase 3 RCTs. HS clinical response at week 16 with secukinumab every 2 weeks: 45% (81.5/181) vs 34% (60.7/180) placebo in SUNSHINE (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-2.7, P=0.0070); 42% (76.2/180) every-2-weeks and 46% (83.1/180) every-4-weeks vs 31% (57.1/183) placebo in SUNRISE (P=0.015 and P=0.0022 respectively). Responses sustained to week 52.
hs_secukinumab.reason_why: IL-17A is a key downstream effector cytokine amplifying the innate-immune/neutrophilic inflammation of HS lesions; secukinumab neutralizes IL-17A, reducing new abscess/nodule formation.
hs_secukinumab.important_caveat: Effect size is similar in magnitude to adalimumab's (all roughly 42-59% responders vs 26-34% placebo across trials) rather than clearly superior; no head-to-head trial exists. Doctor-directed initiation required.
hs_secukinumab.real_working_solution: Real evidence-based alternative to adalimumab, particularly for patients with an inadequate response to, or intolerance of, TNF-alpha inhibition.

hs_bimekizumab.name: Bimekizumab (Dual Anti-IL-17A/IL-17F) - Real Newest Phase 3 Trial-Proven Biologic for Moderate-to-Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa (BE HEARD I and II Trials)
specific_drugs: Bimekizumab 320 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks, or every 2 weeks to week 16 then every 4 weeks
hs_bimekizumab.effectiveness: Kimball AB, Jemec GBE, Sayed CJ et al, Lancet 2024;403(10443):2504-2519 (PMID 38795716): BE HEARD I (n=505) and BE HEARD II (n=509), 48-week phase 3 RCTs. HiSCR50 at week 16 with bimekizumab every 2 weeks: 48% (138/289) vs 29% (21/72) placebo in BE HEARD I (OR 2.23, P=0.0060); 52% (151/291) vs 32% (24/74) placebo in BE HEARD II (OR 2.29, P=0.0032); the every-4-weeks arm in BE HEARD II reached 54% (77/144) vs the same 32% placebo (OR 2.42, P=0.0038). Responses maintained/increased to week 48.
hs_bimekizumab.reason_why: Bimekizumab neutralizes both IL-17A and IL-17F, giving broader blockade of the IL-17 axis than secukinumab's IL-17A-only inhibition (indirect cross-trial comparison only; no head-to-head RCT exists).
hs_bimekizumab.important_caveat: No head-to-head RCT versus adalimumab or secukinumab exists, so cross-trial comparisons are indirect. Most frequent adverse event was hidradenitis (disease flare) itself, alongside oral candidiasis (a known IL-17-inhibitor class effect) and headache; one unrelated cardiovascular death occurred across the two trials.
hs_bimekizumab.real_working_solution: Newest real trial-proven biologic option (2024 phase 3 data), useful where adalimumab and/or secukinumab have failed or are contraindicated.

hs_wide_surgical_excision.name: Wide Surgical Excision (Flap or Skin-Graft Closure) - Real Highest-Cure-Rate Procedural Option for Localized Chronic Hidradenitis Suppurativa
hs_wide_surgical_excision.type: Definitive surgical excision of the diseased apocrine-gland-bearing skin field, with flap or graft closure
hs_wide_surgical_excision.specific_procedure: Wide local excision of the entire clinically and radiologically/sonographically involved skin/subcutaneous field (not just individual sinus tracts), most commonly closed by a local skin flap or split/full-thickness skin graft rather than primary closure or secondary intention
hs_wide_surgical_excision.effectiveness: Mehdizadeh A, Hazen PG, Bechara FG et al, 'Recurrence of hidradenitis suppurativa after surgical management: A systematic review and meta-analysis', J Am Acad Dermatol 2015;73(5 Suppl 1):S70-7 (PMID 26470621): meta-analysis of 22 studies. Average recurrence after wide excision 13.0% (95% CI 5.0-22.0%; ~87.0% no-recurrence, computed) versus 22.0% after local incision and 27.0% after deroofing. By closure method within wide excision: flap 8.0% recurrence (~92.0% no-recurrence, computed), graft 6.0% recurrence (~94.0% no-recurrence, computed), primary closure 15% recurrence (~85% no-recurrence, computed).
hs_wide_surgical_excision.reason_why: Unlike drainage or medical suppression of individual lesions, wide excision physically removes the entire diseased hair-follicle/apocrine-gland field where recurrent sinus tracts form, so the treated site has no residual diseased tissue left to flare -- flap or graft closure further lowers recurrence versus primary closure, plausibly by avoiding wound-edge tension over a large, previously inflamed field.
hs_wide_surgical_excision.important_caveat: Recurrence is measured at the operated site; HS can still arise in a different, previously unaffected apocrine-bearing area since it is a field disease. Evidence quality is graded poor by the meta-analysis authors themselves due to study heterogeneity and potential reporting bias; best suited to chronic, localized (Hurley II-III), non-acutely-inflamed disease.
hs_wide_surgical_excision.real_working_solution: The real closest-to-cure option for chronic, localized, severe HS, with flap or graft closure preferred over primary closure for the lowest recurrence.
hs_wide_surgical_excision.source: Mehdizadeh A et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2015;73(5 Suppl 1):S70-7 (PMID 26470621)

hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.name: Topical Clindamycin and Oral Clindamycin+Rifampicin Combination - Real Guideline-Endorsed First-Line/Second-Line Antibiotic Therapy for Mild-to-Moderate Hidradenitis Suppurativa
specific_drugs: Topical clindamycin 1% solution/lotion, twice daily (mild, Hurley I-II disease)
Oral clindamycin 300 mg twice daily plus rifampicin 600 mg once daily, combined for 10-12 weeks (moderate-to-severe disease, second-line to topical therapy)
hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.effectiveness: Clemmensen OJ, 'Topical treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa with clindamycin', Int J Dermatol 1983;22(5):325-8 (PMID 6347922): 30-patient double-blind placebo-controlled trial (27 completed 3 months); topical clindamycin significantly better than placebo on patient assessment and abscess/nodule/pustule counts at each monthly evaluation (P<0.01). Jemec GB, Wendelboe P, 'Topical clindamycin versus systemic tetracycline in the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa', J Am Acad Dermatol 1998;39(6):971-4 (PMID 9843011): 46-patient double-blind, double-dummy RCT found no significant difference between topical clindamycin and oral tetracycline, i.e. topical therapy performed as well as systemic. Gener G, Canoui-Poitrine F, Revuz JE et al, 'Combination therapy with clindamycin and rifampicin for hidradenitis suppurativa: a series of 116 consecutive patients', Dermatology 2009;219(2):148-54 (PMID 19590173): retrospective series of 116 patients with severe HS given oral clindamycin 300 mg twice daily plus rifampicin 600 mg daily for 10 weeks; median Sartorius severity score improved from 29 to 14.5 (interquartile ranges 14.5 and 11 respectively; P<0.001), a 50.0% reduction (computed, (29-14.5)/29); 8 of 116 patients (6.9%) stopped treatment for side effects.
hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.reason_why: Clindamycin and rifampicin both have anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity against the mixed bacterial biofilm/follicular occlusion process implicated in HS lesion formation; the combination targets both bacterial load and the associated inflammatory response in moderate-to-severe disease not controlled by topical therapy alone.
hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.important_caveat: Cochrane review (Ingram JR et al, Br J Dermatol 2016;174(5):970-8, PMID 26801356) found topical/oral antibiotic trials were small, preventing firm treatment recommendations due to imprecision; the Gener 2009 combination series is retrospective (not a placebo-controlled RCT) and rifampicin carries drug-interaction (CYP450 induction) and hepatic-monitoring requirements.
hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.real_working_solution: Real first-line option for mild, localized disease (topical clindamycin) and real guideline second-line oral option for moderate-to-severe disease not controlled topically (clindamycin+rifampicin).
hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.source: Clemmensen OJ, Int J Dermatol 1983;22(5):325-8 (PMID 6347922); Jemec GB, Wendelboe P, J Am Acad Dermatol 1998;39(6):971-4 (PMID 9843011); Gener G et al, Dermatology 2009;219(2):148-54 (PMID 19590173)
hs_topical_oral_antibiotics_mild_disease.confidence: moderate - RCT evidence for topical clindamycin is real but small (n=30); the combination-therapy percentage is a retrospective-series computation, not an RCT responder rate

hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.name: Intralesional Triamcinolone Acetonide - Real Prospective-Case-Series-Verified Option for Acute Hidradenitis Suppurativa Flares
specific_drugs: Triamcinolone acetonide 10 mg/mL, injected directly into the acutely inflamed lesion
hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.effectiveness: Riis PT, Boer J, Prens EP et al, 'Intralesional triamcinolone for flares of hidradenitis suppurativa (HS): A case series', J Am Acad Dermatol 2016;75(6):1151-1155 (PMID 27692735): prospective single-arm case series. Significant reductions in physician-assessed erythema, edema, suppuration (each median score 2 to 1, P<.0001) and lesion size (median score 3 to 1, P<.0001); patient-reported pain VAS fell from a median of 5.5 to 2.3 by day 1 and to 1.4 by day 2 -- a 74.5% reduction in pain VAS by day 2 (computed, (5.5-1.4)/5.5, P<.005 and P<.002 for the successive day-1 and day-2 comparisons).
hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.reason_why: Intralesional corticosteroid directly suppresses the acute local inflammatory response (erythema, edema, suppuration) within an individual inflamed nodule/abscess, giving rapid symptomatic relief during a flare without systemic corticosteroid exposure.
hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.important_caveat: European S1 guideline (Zouboulis CC, Desai N, Emtestam L et al, 'European S1 guideline for the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2015;29(4):619-44, PMID 25640693) notes standard practice of corticosteroid injection for flares lacked controlled-trial evidence prior to Riis 2016; the Riis study itself is a small, open, single-arm case series with short follow-up, not a placebo-controlled RCT, so the true placebo-adjusted effect size is not established.
hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.real_working_solution: Real, guideline-referenced rescue option for rapid relief of an acute HS flare while definitive antibiotic/biologic/surgical therapy is arranged.
hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.source: Riis PT et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2016;75(6):1151-1155 (PMID 27692735); Zouboulis CC et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2015;29(4):619-44 (PMID 25640693)
hs_intralesional_corticosteroids_flares.confidence: moderate - real but small, uncontrolled case series
