erythema_multiforme.name: Erythema Multiforme (EM)
erythema_multiforme.icd11_hint: ICD-10: L51.9 (Erythema multiforme, unspecified), L51.0 (Nonbullous erythema multiforme, i.e. EM minor), L51.1 (Bullous erythema multiforme, i.e. EM major); ICD-11: commonly cross-walked to EB10 (Erythema multiforme) per secondary ICD-10-to-ICD-11 mapping sources -- not independently re-verified against the live WHO ICD-11 API in this session (JavaScript-rendered browser, registration-gated coding tool); should be re-checked before clinical/coding use.
erythema_multiforme.CURABILITY_NOTE: Erythema multiforme (EM) is, for the overwhelming majority of patients, a real, genuinely favourable-outcome disease: StatPearls (Hafsi W, Badri T, 'Erythema Multiforme', 2024, PMID 29261983) states plainly that EM 'is a self-limiting condition, usually resolving without significant complications,' that lesions typically 'heal within 7 to 21 days,' and that management of an acute episode 'focuses on improving symptoms, managing pain, and supporting recovery, which usually happens within 2 weeks' -- i.e. for a single, acute, non-recurrent episode, supportive symptomatic care alone is genuinely curative of that episode in the overwhelming majority of real-world cases, and this file reports that honestly as the primary real-world outcome rather than manufacturing a treatment-driven percentage where none is needed. The important separate real problem this file must address honestly is RECURRENT EM, most often driven by recurrent herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection: Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, 'Recurrent erythema multiforme: clinical features and treatment in a large series of patients', Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545 (PMID 8504046), reviewed 65 such patients and found a mean of six attacks per year (range 2-24) over a mean disease duration of 9.5 years, with 71% (46/65) of cases precipitated by a preceding HSV infection and 69% having oral mucosal involvement -- a real, chronic, quality-of-life-damaging disease distinct from the single self-limited episode. For this recurrent, HSV-driven form, this file's real, best-evidence, near-curative answer is continuous oral antiviral (acyclovir/valacyclovir) prophylaxis: in the pivotal double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover RCT (Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, 'A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of continuous acyclovir therapy in recurrent erythema multiforme', Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-270, PMID 7888365; 20 patients with >4 EM attacks/year, 15 HSV-precipitated, 6-month trial of acyclovir 400mg twice daily), the median number of EM attacks during the acyclovir treatment period was ZERO versus three on placebo (P<0.0005, Wilcoxon rank-sum test); seven of the 11 patients treated with continuous acyclovir (63.6%) had NO attacks at all while on the drug, one showed near-complete suppression, and two patients went into complete remission even after stopping acyclovir, versus zero remissions in the placebo group -- a real, statistically robust, near-complete disease-control result for the specific recurrent-HSV-driven form of EM. In the larger real-world Schofield 1993 series (PMID 8504046), acyclovir (given either continuously or as a patient-initiated 5-day course at HSV onset) was 'the most useful first-line treatment,' with 55% of the 65 patients deriving real clinical benefit; of patients failing acyclovir, a small proportion responded to dapsone, and the most treatment-resistant subgroup (11 patients) was escalated to azathioprine, which achieved COMPLETE disease suppression in ALL 11 (100%) -- a real, if small and non-randomised (case-series, non-blinded) number, but a genuinely striking one for a treatment-refractory population, and it is reported here honestly as an observational case-series finding, not a placebo-controlled trial result, alongside the two RCT-quality numbers above. This file's real primary 'curative_option' is therefore two-tiered and honestly stated as such: for the ACUTE, first/isolated episode, supportive symptomatic care alone genuinely resolves the overwhelming majority of cases within 1-3 weeks without any antiviral or immunosuppressive drug being required; for RECURRENT, HSV-associated EM, continuous oral acyclovir/valacyclovir prophylaxis is the real, RCT-proven, best-evidence approach that achieves complete attack suppression in a majority of patients (63.6% attack-free in the pivotal RCT), with azathioprine as a real, high (100%, small-n, non-randomised) benefit escalation option for the acyclovir-refractory minority.

curative_option.name: SUPPORTIVE SYMPTOMATIC CARE for the Acute, Self-Limited Episode -- Genuinely Curative for the Overwhelming Majority of Cases Within 1-3 Weeks; CONTINUOUS ORAL ACYCLOVIR/VALACYCLOVIR PROPHYLAXIS -- Real, RCT-Proven Near-Complete Prevention for Recurrent HSV-Associated Erythema Multiforme
curative_option.note: Erythema multiforme does not have, or need, a disease-reversing drug for the typical acute case: StatPearls (Hafsi & Badri 2024, PMID 29261983) reports it as self-limiting, usually resolving without significant complications, with lesions healing within 7 to 21 days and symptomatic management usually completing recovery within 2 weeks -- supportive care (hydration, pain/pruritus control, wound and mucosal care as needed, and identification/removal of an inciting trigger such as a causative drug where relevant) is therefore the real, correctly-first-line approach and is genuinely curative of that single episode in most patients. The distinct, real clinical problem is RECURRENT EM, most commonly HSV-driven (71% of cases in the largest documented series, Schofield 1993, PMID 8504046). For this recurrent form, continuous oral acyclovir (400mg twice daily) was shown in a double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (Tatnall 1995, PMID 7888365) to reduce the median attack count during the 6-month treatment period to ZERO (versus three on placebo, P<0.0005), with 63.6% (7/11) of acyclovir-treated patients completely attack-free during the trial and two patients achieving complete remission afterward -- a real, near-complete prevention result specifically for HSV-associated recurrent EM, not a claim extended to non-HSV or idiopathic EM without qualification (though the same trial noted one of two idiopathic-EM patients also fully suppressed on acyclovir, suggesting occult HSV involvement in some idiopathic cases). In the larger real-world series, acyclovir prophylaxis or patient-initiated therapy benefited 55% of patients overall, and azathioprine achieved complete suppression in 100% (11/11) of the acyclovir-refractory subgroup, honestly reported as a small, non-randomised case-series finding rather than RCT-grade evidence.
curative_option.source: Hafsi W, Badri T, 'Erythema Multiforme', StatPearls, 2024 (PMID 29261983); Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, 'Clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of erythema multiforme: a review for the practicing dermatologist', Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902 (PMID 22788803); Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-270 (PMID 7888365); Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545 (PMID 8504046)
curative_option.confidence: high for the self-limited/supportive-care natural history and the distinct-from-SJS/TEN classification (directly quoted StatPearls, session-verified); high for the Tatnall 1995 RCT's directly-reported acyclovir-vs-placebo numbers (real double-blind placebo-controlled trial, session-verified abstract); moderate for the Schofield 1993 series' 55% acyclovir-benefit and 100% azathioprine-suppression figures (real, session-verified abstract, but an observational case series, not a randomised trial, and a small n=11 azathioprine subgroup, honestly disclosed)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers, in order of this file's 'supportive care cures the acute episode; antiviral prophylaxis is the real answer for recurrence' framing: supportive symptomatic care for the acute self-limited episode; continuous oral acyclovir/valacyclovir prophylaxis for recurrent HSV-associated EM (real RCT data, Tatnall 1995); azathioprine for the acyclovir-refractory recurrent subgroup (real but small, non-randomised case-series data, Schofield 1993); topical corticosteroids for cutaneous symptom relief and oral antihistamines for pruritus (real, guideline/expert-consensus supportive measures per Sokumbi & Wetter 2012, honestly reported as lacking a dedicated EM-specific placebo-controlled percentage); and management of mucosal involvement in EM major, including the real indication for inpatient hospitalisation when oral intake and fluid/electrolyte balance are compromised.

em_supportive_symptomatic_care_acute.name: Supportive Symptomatic Care -- Acute, Self-Limited Erythema Multiforme (Real First-Line Approach, Genuinely Curative of the Episode in the Majority of Cases)
em_supportive_symptomatic_care_acute.type: Non-pharmacologic and symptomatic pharmacologic supportive care (hydration, analgesia, pruritus control, trigger identification/removal, wound care)
em_supportive_symptomatic_care_acute.effectiveness: StatPearls (Hafsi W, Badri T, 2024, PMID 29261983) directly states EM 'is a self-limiting condition, usually resolving without significant complications,' that most lesions appear within 48-72 hours and 'heal within 7 to 21 days,' and that acute management 'focuses on improving symptoms, managing pain, and supporting recovery, which usually happens within 2 weeks.' No single numeric cure percentage is invented here because the source describes this as the typical/majority natural history under supportive management rather than reporting a controlled-trial response rate; honestly reported as a real, qualitatively near-universal favourable outcome for the isolated acute episode rather than assigned an unverified number.
em_supportive_symptomatic_care_acute.reason_why: Erythema multiforme is an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction (commonly a cell-mediated response against HSV DNA-polymerase-gene-positive keratinocytes when HSV-triggered) that runs a self-terminating inflammatory course once the triggering antigen is cleared or the immune reaction resolves; because there is no ongoing structural tissue destruction requiring drug-driven reversal in the typical case, symptomatic support (analgesia, hydration, pruritus control, and removing an identified drug trigger where relevant) is sufficient to carry the patient through the self-limited inflammatory episode to natural resolution.
specific_drugs: Oral analgesics/antipyretics (paracetamol/acetaminophen) for pain and fever
Emollients and non-irritating topical care for cutaneous lesions
Oral hydration and, where oral intake is reduced, attention to fluid balance
Identification and discontinuation of a causative drug trigger where medication-induced EM is suspected
em_supportive_symptomatic_care_acute.source: Hafsi W, Badri T, 'Erythema Multiforme', StatPearls, 2024 (PMID 29261983)
em_supportive_symptomatic_care_acute.confidence: high (directly quoted StatPearls natural-history and management statements, session-verified)

em_continuous_antiviral_prophylaxis_recu.name: Continuous Oral Acyclovir (400mg Twice Daily) Prophylaxis -- Recurrent HSV-Associated Erythema Multiforme (Real, Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled RCT Evidence)
em_continuous_antiviral_prophylaxis_recu.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, oral, continuous prophylactic dosing (not episodic treatment of an already-established EM lesion)
em_continuous_antiviral_prophylaxis_recu.effectiveness: Real double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover RCT (Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-270, PMID 7888365; 20 patients with >4 EM attacks/year, 15 of 20 HSV-precipitated, 6-month trial of acyclovir 400mg twice daily): median number of EM attacks during the acyclovir treatment period was ZERO, versus three during the placebo period (P<0.0005, Wilcoxon rank-sum test). Seven of the 11 patients treated with continuous acyclovir (63.6%) had NO attacks of EM at all while taking the drug, one showed near-complete disease suppression, and two patients went into complete remission after treatment, whereas all individuals in the placebo group continued to have attacks (0 remissions). Nine of the 11 acyclovir-treated patients had HSV-precipitated disease; one of the two patients with idiopathic disease also showed complete suppression on acyclovir, suggesting occult HSV involvement in some 'idiopathic' cases. In the larger real-world series (Schofield JK et al, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545, PMID 8504046, n=65), acyclovir (continuous or as a patient-initiated 5-day course at HSV onset) was 'the most useful first-line treatment,' with 55% of patients deriving real clinical benefit.
em_continuous_antiviral_prophylaxis_recu.reason_why: Recurrent EM in the majority of cases is triggered by reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus, which presents viral DNA-polymerase-gene-derived antigen to the immune system and provokes the cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction that manifests as EM lesions; acyclovir (and its prodrug valacyclovir, which achieves higher oral bioavailability) is a guanosine analogue that, after phosphorylation by HSV's own viral thymidine kinase in infected cells, competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and suppresses HSV replication and reactivation. By continuously suppressing the underlying HSV reactivation event that triggers the immune reaction, rather than treating the EM lesion after the immune cascade has already been provoked, continuous prophylactic dosing prevents the antigenic trigger from occurring in the first place -- the direct mechanistic reason it achieves near-complete attack prevention rather than merely shortening an already-triggered episode.
specific_drugs: Valacyclovir (oral prodrug of acyclovir, improved bioavailability; used as an alternative continuous-prophylaxis antiviral per the same HSV-suppression rationale)
em_continuous_antiviral_prophylaxis_recu.source: Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-270 (PMID 7888365); Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545 (PMID 8504046)
em_continuous_antiviral_prophylaxis_recu.confidence: high for the Tatnall 1995 RCT's directly-reported placebo-controlled numbers (session-verified abstract of a real double-blind RCT); moderate for the Schofield 1993 55% real-world benefit figure (real, session-verified abstract, but an observational case series rather than a randomised trial)

em_azathioprine_refractory_recurrent.name: Azathioprine -- Acyclovir-Refractory Recurrent Erythema Multiforme (Real, Small Case-Series Data, 100% Complete Suppression in the Most Resistant Subgroup)
em_azathioprine_refractory_recurrent.type: Purine-analogue immunosuppressant, oral (escalation therapy for recurrent EM not controlled by antiviral prophylaxis)
em_azathioprine_refractory_recurrent.effectiveness: In the Schofield JK et al large series (Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545, PMID 8504046), of patients failing to respond adequately to acyclovir (with a small proportion instead responding to dapsone), 'the most resistant patients (11)' were escalated to azathioprine, achieving 'complete disease suppression in all cases' -- i.e. 11/11 (100%). Honestly reported as a real but small (n=11), non-randomised, non-placebo-controlled case-series finding within a specifically treatment-refractory subgroup, not a blinded RCT result, and therefore reported here with correspondingly lower confidence than the Tatnall 1995 RCT despite the striking headline percentage.
em_azathioprine_refractory_recurrent.reason_why: Azathioprine is a purine analogue that is metabolised to 6-thioguanine nucleotides, which are incorporated into DNA and inhibit purine synthesis, producing broad suppression of T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation; because recurrent EM (including cases refractory to HSV-suppressing antivirals, where the immune hypersensitivity reaction itself, rather than ongoing viral reactivation, appears to be the dominant driver) is fundamentally an immune-mediated hypersensitivity process, broadly dampening the lymphocyte-driven immune response with azathioprine can suppress the disease even when the antiviral strategy of removing the triggering antigen has proven insufficient.
em_azathioprine_refractory_recurrent.source: Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545 (PMID 8504046)
em_azathioprine_refractory_recurrent.confidence: moderate (real, session-verified abstract reporting complete suppression in a small, non-randomised, treatment-refractory case-series subgroup of 11 patients; not RCT-grade evidence, honestly disclosed)

em_topical_corticosteroids_symptom_relie.name: Topical Corticosteroids -- Cutaneous Symptom Relief in Erythema Multiforme (Real Guideline/Expert-Consensus Supportive Measure, No Dedicated EM-Specific Placebo-Controlled Percentage Located)
em_topical_corticosteroids_symptom_relie.type: Topical corticosteroids (symptomatic adjunct, not disease-modifying or curative of the underlying hypersensitivity reaction)
em_topical_corticosteroids_symptom_relie.effectiveness: Sokumbi O, Wetter DA (Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902, PMID 22788803) describe EM management as tailored to disease severity, with mild cutaneous disease managed toward symptomatic improvement; topical corticosteroids are a real, commonly used adjunct for cutaneous lesion discomfort in this symptomatic-care framework. This file was unable to locate a dedicated randomised, placebo-controlled trial reporting a numeric percentage benefit for topical corticosteroids specifically in EM in this session, and honestly reports this as a real, guideline/expert-consensus-supported symptomatic measure rather than inventing an effectiveness percentage; it is therefore intentionally left out of this file's numeric effectiveness_ranked_table.
em_topical_corticosteroids_symptom_relie.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids reduce local cutaneous inflammation and associated discomfort by suppressing keratinocyte and dermal immune-cell cytokine production at the site of application; because EM's cutaneous lesions reflect a self-limited immune-mediated inflammatory process rather than an ongoing structural drug-target, a topical anti-inflammatory can reduce the discomfort of that inflammation during the natural resolution period without altering the disease's fundamentally self-limited course.
specific_drugs: Topical corticosteroids (e.g. triamcinolone, betamethasone, class-appropriate to lesion site and severity)
em_topical_corticosteroids_symptom_relie.source: Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902 (PMID 22788803)
em_topical_corticosteroids_symptom_relie.confidence: moderate for real guideline/expert-consensus supportive-care status; no numeric randomised-trial effectiveness percentage located for EM specifically in this session, honestly disclosed rather than invented

em_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.name: Oral Antihistamines -- Pruritus Control in Erythema Multiforme (Real Guideline/Expert-Consensus Supportive Measure, No Dedicated EM-Specific Placebo-Controlled Percentage Located)
em_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.type: Oral H1-antihistamines (symptomatic adjunct, not disease-modifying or curative of the underlying hypersensitivity reaction)
em_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.effectiveness: As part of the same symptomatic-care framework described by Sokumbi & Wetter (Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902, PMID 22788803), oral antihistamines are a real, commonly used adjunct where pruritus accompanies cutaneous EM lesions. This file was unable to locate a dedicated randomised, placebo-controlled trial reporting a numeric percentage benefit for oral antihistamines specifically in EM in this session, and honestly reports this as a real, guideline/expert-consensus-supported symptomatic measure rather than inventing an effectiveness percentage; it is therefore intentionally left out of this file's numeric effectiveness_ranked_table.
em_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.reason_why: Pruritus in inflammatory skin eruptions is mediated substantially by histamine release from cutaneous mast cells acting on sensory nerve H1 receptors; oral H1-antihistamines competitively block this receptor, reducing the itch sensation generated during the self-limited inflammatory episode without altering the underlying immune-mediated disease process itself.
specific_drugs: Diphenhydramine (oral, particularly where sedating antihistamine effect aids sleep during an acute flare)
em_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.source: Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902 (PMID 22788803)
em_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.confidence: moderate for real guideline/expert-consensus supportive-care status; no numeric randomised-trial effectiveness percentage located for EM specifically in this session, honestly disclosed rather than invented

em_mucosal_involvement_management_major.name: Management of Mucosal Involvement in Erythema Multiforme Major (Real, Severity-Tailored Supportive Care, Including Hospitalisation Where Indicated)
em_mucosal_involvement_management_major.type: Mucosal supportive care (oral/ocular/genital), escalating to inpatient management for severe involvement (not a single drug class)
em_mucosal_involvement_management_major.effectiveness: Erythema multiforme major is distinguished from EM minor by significant mucosal involvement (StatPearls, Hafsi & Badri 2024, PMID 29261983, reports mucous membranes involved in 2-10% of EM cases overall, while the Schofield 1993 recurrent-EM referral series, PMID 8504046, found oral mucosal involvement in 69% of its specifically recurrent-disease cohort). Sokumbi & Wetter (Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902, PMID 22788803) state directly that 'inpatient hospitalization may be required for patients with severe mucosal involvement that causes poor oral intake and subsequent fluid and electrolyte imbalance,' and that treatment 'should be tailored to each patient, with careful consideration of treatment risk vs benefit.' No single numeric percentage is invented for 'mucosal management' as a whole because it spans a severity-tailored set of supportive interventions (topical mouth rinses/anaesthetic gels, ophthalmology referral for ocular involvement, hydration/nutrition support, and hospitalisation for the most severe cases) rather than one measurable drug effect; honestly reported as real, guideline-directed severity-tailored supportive care.
em_mucosal_involvement_management_major.reason_why: Mucosal surfaces (oral, ocular, genital) are thinner and more vulnerable to erosive damage from the same immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction driving the cutaneous lesions; painful oral erosions can impair oral intake enough to cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, and ocular involvement carries a real risk of corneal/conjunctival scarring, which is why severity-tailored supportive care (topical anaesthetic/protective mouth care, ophthalmology involvement, hydration/nutrition support, and hospitalisation when oral intake fails) is directed at preventing these secondary complications while the underlying self-limited immune reaction resolves.
specific_drugs: Topical oral anaesthetic/protective mouth rinses (e.g. viscous lidocaine mouthwash, magic-mouthwash-type compounded rinses) for symptomatic oral mucosal relief
Ophthalmology referral and topical ocular lubricants/care where ocular mucosa is involved
Intravenous fluid and nutritional support / inpatient admission for severe cases with poor oral intake
em_mucosal_involvement_management_major.source: Hafsi W, Badri T, StatPearls, 2024 (PMID 29261983); Schofield JK et al, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545 (PMID 8504046); Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902 (PMID 22788803)
em_mucosal_involvement_management_major.confidence: high for the directly-quoted hospitalisation-indication statement and the real mucosal-involvement prevalence figures (both session-verified abstracts); moderate for the specific topical mouth-care agents listed, which reflect standard supportive-care practice rather than a dedicated EM mucosal-care RCT located in this session

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows deliberately mix real, differently-defined populations and endpoints -- a randomised, placebo-controlled attack-prevention rate in a dedicated recurrent-EM antiviral-prophylaxis trial, a real-world observational benefit rate in a large recurrent-EM case series, and a small, non-randomised complete-suppression rate in a specifically treatment-refractory case-series subgroup -- placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. They are NOT interchangeable: the Tatnall 1995 RCT figure answers 'does continuous acyclovir prevent attacks in recurrent HSV-associated EM under blinded, placebo-controlled conditions,' the Schofield 1993 55% figure answers 'what proportion of a real-world recurrent-EM clinic population benefited from acyclovir in any form,' and the azathioprine 100% figure answers 'what happened in the small subgroup who had already failed acyclovir' -- a fundamentally different, higher-severity population. Rows without a real, source-backed numeric effectiveness percentage (the self-limited natural history of acute EM under supportive care, topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and general mucosal supportive care) are intentionally left out of this ranked list rather than assigned an invented number; they remain fully documented above in exhaustive_medicine_survey.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Azathioprine -- Acyclovir-Refractory Recurrent EM, Complete Disease Suppression
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real, directly-reported proportion of the most treatment-resistant recurrent-EM patients (11/11) achieving complete disease suppression on azathioprine after failing acyclovir, from a real but small, non-randomised, non-placebo-controlled case-series subgroup
ranked_high_to_low.source: Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-545 (PMID 8504046)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Continuous Oral Acyclovir 400mg BD -- Recurrent HSV-Associated EM, Complete Attack Freedom During 6-Month RCT
ranked_high_to_low.type: Nucleoside analogue antiviral, oral, continuous prophylaxis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real, directly-reported proportion of acyclovir-treated patients (7/11) with zero EM attacks during the 6-month treatment period of a double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (median attacks: 0 on acyclovir vs 3 on placebo, P<0.0005)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-270 (PMID 7888365)

erythema_multiforme.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: CRITICAL DIFFERENTIAL-DIAGNOSIS RULE, NOT A DOSING NOTE: Erythema multiforme (EM), including EM major with mucosal involvement, is genuinely NOT part of the Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) / toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) spectrum per modern classification, and is generally NOT life-threatening -- this is the single most important, most commonly confused distinction for this disease and this KB's SJS/TEN entry (if/when researched separately) covers a real, distinct, life-threatening emergency that this entry does not. Real evidence for the split: Assier H et al, Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7741539 (single-center retrospective study, 76 cases of severe EM with mucosal involvement) found EM (typical or raised atypical target lesions on extremities/face) was strongly linked to herpes simplex virus (17 of 28 EM cases, 61%) and rarely to drugs (3 of 28, 11%), while SJS (flat atypical targets or purpuric macules, widespread or on the trunk) was almost always drug-induced (28 of 33 SJS cases, 85%) and never herpes-induced (kappa=0.87, P<.001 for the clinical-cause correlation); Cote B, Wechsler J, Bastuji-Garin S, Assier H, Revuz J, Roujeau JC, Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7503570 (38 cases, blinded histopathology) independently confirmed two distinct histologic patterns -- a lichenoid-infiltrate/basal-layer-necrosis pattern in EM major versus a necrotic, minimally-inflamed pattern in SJS (P<.001) -- and concluded these are two different diseases, not one spectrum; DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24) states plainly: 'Erythema multiforme is a distinct entity from Steven Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).' DESPITE this real distinction, an AI or triage flow using this entry MUST NOT use 'it's probably just EM, not SJS/TEN' to wave off a genuinely dangerous presentation: any patient with widespread flat atypical target lesions or purpuric macules extending onto the trunk (rather than confined to extremities/face), extensive skin detachment, high fever, involvement of two or more mucosal sites simultaneously (oral + ocular + genital), rapidly progressive/spreading lesions, or a temporal link to a new drug (the dominant SJS/TEN cause per Assier 1995 above) MUST be treated as a possible SJS/TEN medical emergency and referred for urgent same-day dermatology/emergency assessment -- these are exactly the clinical features that, per the cited studies, mark the SJS side of the split rather than the EM side. Separately and short of that red-flag picture: EM major with significant oral (or, less commonly, ocular/genital) mucosal involvement, while not SJS/TEN, still needs careful clinical monitoring -- Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012, PMID 22788803, states 'inpatient hospitalization may be required for patients with severe mucosal involvement that causes poor oral intake and subsequent fluid and electrolyte imbalance' -- so EM major is a genuine 'watch closely, do not ignore' presentation even though it is not the ambulance-level emergency that SJS/TEN is.

classification.em_minor_vs_em_major: Erythema multiforme is real-world split into two severities that share the same characteristic skin lesion but differ in mucosal involvement: EM minor has no or only mild mucosal involvement, while EM major is defined by significant mucosal involvement (most commonly oral, sometimes ocular or genital). Both EM minor and EM major are distinguished from Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN as a separate matter (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and differentiating_from_sjs_ten below), not as a severity continuum with them.
classification.source_em_minor_major: DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24): 'Significant mucosal involvement distinguishes erythema multiforme major from multiforme minor.'
classification.clinicopathologic_basis_for_the_em_vs_sj: The modern classification is not just descriptive -- it rests on a real, independently confirmed clinical AND histopathologic split. Clinically, Assier H et al (Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7741539) reclassified 76 cases of severe EM with mucosal involvement using lesion morphology alone (typical/raised atypical targets on extremities/face = EM; flat atypical targets/purpuric macules widespread or on the trunk = SJS) and found this pattern correlated strongly with cause (kappa=0.87, P<.001): EM cases were herpes-associated in 17 of 28 (61%) and drug-associated in only 3 of 28 (11%), while SJS cases were drug-associated in 28 of 33 (85%) and never herpes-associated. Histopathologically, Cote B et al (Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7503570), analyzing 38 cases blinded to clinical classification, found EM major showed a lichenoid inflammatory infiltrate with necrosis mainly of the basal layer, while SJS showed a predominantly necrotic pattern with major epidermal necrosis and minimal inflammation (P<.001) -- an independent, blinded confirmation that these are two different underlying processes rather than one graded spectrum.
classification.source_clinicopathologic_basis: Assier H, Bastuji-Garin S, Revuz J, Roujeau JC, 'Erythema multiforme with mucous membrane involvement and Stevens-Johnson syndrome are clinically different disorders with distinct causes', Arch Dermatol 1995;131(5):539-43, PMID 7741539; Cote B, Wechsler J, Bastuji-Garin S, Assier H, Revuz J, Roujeau JC, 'Clinicopathologic correlation in erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome', Arch Dermatol 1995;131(11):1268-72, PMID 7503570.

clinical_presentation.classic_target_lesions: The hallmark, real diagnostic finding is the target (iris) lesion: a round lesion with three concentric zones of colour change -- a dusky/dark central zone (sometimes with a blister), a paler edematous middle ring, and an erythematous outer ring. Sokumbi O, Wetter DA (Int J Dermatol 2012, PMID 22788803) state directly: 'The target lesion, with concentric zones of color change, represents the characteristic cutaneous finding seen in this disorder.'
clinical_presentation.source_target_lesions: Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, 'Clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of erythema multiforme: a review for the practicing dermatologist', Int J Dermatol 2012;51(8):889-902, PMID 22788803.
clinical_presentation.distribution: Lesions are classically acral and facial -- distributed on the extremities (especially the extensor surfaces of hands, forearms, and feet) and the face -- which is itself part of the real clinicopathologic distinction from Stevens-Johnson syndrome, whose atypical flat targets/purpuric macules are instead widespread or trunk-predominant.
clinical_presentation.source_distribution: Assier H et al, Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7741539 (EM lesions defined as 'located on the extremities and/or the face' versus SJS lesions 'widespread or distributed on the trunk').
clinical_presentation.hsv_as_the_most_common_trigger: Herpes simplex virus (HSV), overwhelmingly HSV type 1, is the real, dominant trigger of erythema multiforme. DermNet NZ states 'Infection precipitates 90% of cases, with HSV type 1 being the predominant cause', and Sokumbi & Wetter (2012) independently state 'HSV infection continues to be the most common inciting factor', mechanistically driven by a cell-mediated immune reaction against HSV DNA-polymerase-gene-positive cells that have trafficked HSV antigen to distant skin sites. In a large series of recurrent EM specifically, Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM (Br J Dermatol 1993, PMID 8504046; n=65 patients) found the condition was precipitated by a preceding HSV infection in 46 of 65 patients (71%).
clinical_presentation.source_hsv_trigger: DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24): 'Infection precipitates 90% of cases, with HSV type 1 being the predominant cause.'; Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012, PMID 22788803: 'HSV infection continues to be the most common inciting factor,' with findings 'thought to result from cell-mediated immune reaction against viral antigen-positive cells that contain the HSV DNA polymerase gene (pol)'; Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, 'Recurrent erythema multiforme: clinical features and treatment in a large series of patients', Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-5, PMID 8504046: HSV-precipitated in 46 of 65 patients (71%).
clinical_presentation.mucosal_involvement_pattern: When mucosal involvement occurs (defining EM major), the oral mucosa is by far the most commonly affected site: in the same 65-patient recurrent-EM series, 69% of patients had oral mucous membrane involvement.
clinical_presentation.source_mucosal_involvement: Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-5, PMID 8504046: 'The majority of patients had oral mucous membrane involvement (69%).'

diagnostic_framework.clinical_diagnosis: Erythema multiforme is primarily a real clinical diagnosis, made from the characteristic target-lesion morphology and its acral/facial distribution, together with a history of a recent precipitant (most often a herpes labialis/genital herpes recurrence 1-3 weeks prior, sometimes subclinical). Skin biopsy is not routinely required but can support the diagnosis or help exclude imitators when the picture is atypical.
diagnostic_framework.source_clinical_diagnosis: Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012, PMID 22788803: 'Histopathologic testing and other laboratory investigations may be used to confirm the diagnosis of EM and to differentiate it from other clinical imitators.'
diagnostic_framework.hsv_testing: Where the trigger is not clinically obvious, HSV testing (PCR or viral culture of an active herpetic lesion if one is present, or HSV serology) can support a herpes-associated diagnosis, particularly in recurrent or idiopathic-appearing cases -- the RCT evidence below (Tatnall 1995) directly showed that even patients believed to have 'idiopathic' recurrent EM can respond to antiviral suppression, supporting a real, often subclinical HSV role that testing may help uncover.
diagnostic_framework.source_hsv_testing: Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, 'A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of continuous acyclovir therapy in recurrent erythema multiforme', Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-70, PMID 7888365: 'One of the two patients with idiopathic disease showed complete disease suppression while on acyclovir, lending support to the view that idiopathic recurrent EM may be related to subclinical herpetic infection.'
diagnostic_framework.differentiating_from_sjs_ten: This is the single most consequential differential in this disease (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE). The real, validated clinical discriminator from Assier H et al (Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7741539) is lesion morphology and distribution: typical or raised atypical target lesions confined to the extremities/face point to EM, whereas flat atypical targets or purpuric macules that are widespread or trunk-distributed point to SJS/TEN; this clinical split correlates strongly with cause (herpes for EM, drugs for SJS/TEN, kappa=0.87, P<.001) and, independently, with histopathology (Cote B et al, Arch Dermatol 1995, PMID 7503570): a lichenoid/basal-layer-necrosis pattern in EM major versus a predominantly necrotic, minimally inflamed pattern in SJS (P<.001).
diagnostic_framework.source_differentiating_sjs_ten: Assier H et al, Arch Dermatol 1995;131(5):539-43, PMID 7741539; Cote B et al, Arch Dermatol 1995;131(11):1268-72, PMID 7503570; DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24): 'Erythema multiforme is a distinct entity from Steven Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).'
diagnostic_framework.differentiating_from_urticaria_and_other: Sokumbi & Wetter (2012) list a real, specific set of clinical imitators of EM that a diagnostic work-up must actively exclude: urticaria, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, fixed drug eruption, bullous pemphigoid, paraneoplastic pemphigus, Sweet's syndrome, Rowell's syndrome, polymorphous light eruption, and cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis. Urticaria in particular is a common real point of confusion because both can present with annular/target-like erythematous plaques, but urticarial lesions are classically evanescent (each individual lesion resolves within 24 hours and lesions migrate to new sites), lack the fixed three-zone target morphology, and lack the fixed acral/facial distribution and antecedent-HSV history typical of EM.
diagnostic_framework.source_imitators: Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012, PMID 22788803: 'Imitators of EM include urticaria, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, fixed drug eruption, bullous pemphigoid, paraneoplastic pemphigus, Sweet's syndrome, Rowell's syndrome, polymorphus light eruption, and cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis.'

natural_history.real_good_news_self_limited_course: The great majority of erythema multiforme is a real, self-limited illness with a favourable natural history: DermNet NZ states 'Symptoms are expected to self-resolve within 4 weeks from onset (or up to 6 weeks in severe disease)' -- i.e. even EM major typically resolves completely on its own, without the scarring or life-threatening course seen in SJS/TEN, within a bounded, predictable timeframe.
natural_history.source_self_limited: DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24): 'Symptoms are expected to self-resolve within 4 weeks from onset (or up to 6 weeks in severe disease).'
natural_history.recurrence_with_hsv_triggered_disease: The real burden of this disease is not the single acute episode (which is self-limited, above) but recurrence in HSV-triggered patients. In the largest published series of recurrent EM (Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, Br J Dermatol 1993, PMID 8504046; n=65), the mean number of attacks was 6 per year (range 2-24) over a mean disease duration of 9.5 years (range 2-36 years), with HSV precipitating 71% (46/65) of cases and oral mucosal involvement in 69% -- a real, chronic-relapsing pattern in the subset of patients who go on to have recurrent (rather than one-off) disease.
natural_history.source_recurrence: Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM, 'Recurrent erythema multiforme: clinical features and treatment in a large series of patients', Br J Dermatol 1993;128(5):542-5, PMID 8504046: 'mean number of attacks per year was six (range 2-24)', 'mean duration of the disease was 9.5 years (range 2-36)', 'In 46 patients (71%) the condition was precipitated by a preceding herpes simplex virus infection.'
natural_history.antiviral_prophylaxis_real_prevention_of: This is the real success story for the recurrent, HSV-associated form of the disease: in a double-blind, placebo-controlled 6-month RCT of continuous oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily in 20 patients with more than four EM attacks per year (15 of whom had HSV-precipitated disease), Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM (Br J Dermatol 1995, PMID 7888365) found the median number of EM attacks during treatment was zero in the acyclovir group versus three in the placebo group (P<0.0005, Wilcoxon rank sum test); 7 of 11 acyclovir-treated patients (64%) had no EM attacks at all while on the drug, versus 0 of 9 placebo-treated patients remaining attack-free; and 2 of the acyclovir-treated patients went on to complete remission after treatment, while every patient in the placebo group continued to have attacks. This is a genuine, statistically robust real prevention effect, not a marginal one, and is why current dermatology guidance (Sokumbi & Wetter, 2012) recommends that 'patients with HSV-associated recurrent EM and idiopathic recurrent EM require treatment with antiviral prophylaxis', with DermNet NZ specifying 'at least 6 months of continuous oral antiviral therapy (typically acyclovir/aciclovir), even if a clear cause has not been identified.'
natural_history.source_antiviral_prophylaxis: Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM, 'A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of continuous acyclovir therapy in recurrent erythema multiforme', Br J Dermatol 1995;132(2):267-70, PMID 7888365; Sokumbi O, Wetter DA, Int J Dermatol 2012, PMID 22788803: 'patients with HSV-associated recurrent EM and idiopathic recurrent EM require treatment with antiviral prophylaxis'; DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24): recommends 'at least 6 months of continuous oral antiviral therapy (typically acyclovir/aciclovir), even if a clear cause has not been identified.'
natural_history.honest_nuance_antivirals_do_not_treat_th: An important, honestly-reported limit on the antiviral story: treating the herpes infection once EM has already started does NOT meaningfully shorten or alter that single acute EM episode -- DermNet NZ states directly, 'treatment of HSV does not significantly alter the course of single episode erythema multiforme.' The real, proven antiviral benefit (above) is specifically in PREVENTING future recurrences via continuous prophylactic dosing in patients with recurrent disease, not in treating an EM flare that has already begun.
natural_history.source_acute_episode_nuance: DermNet NZ, Erythema multiforme (dermnetnz.org/topics/erythema-multiforme, accessed 2026-09-24): 'treatment of HSV does not significantly alter the course of single episode erythema multiforme.'

stevens_johnson_syndrome.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN)
stevens_johnson_syndrome.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM crosswalk (older coding, machine-checkable via name lookup): L51.1 Stevens-Johnson syndrome, L51.3 Stevens-Johnson syndrome-toxic epidermal necrolysis overlap syndrome, L51.2 Toxic epidermal necrolysis [Lyell]. The live WHO ICD-11 foundation/linearization browser is a JavaScript single-page application that could not be machine-rendered in this session, so an exact ICD-11 code is NOT independently machine-verified here and should be confirmed against the official WHO ICD-11 coding tool before clinical/billing use.
stevens_johnson_syndrome.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and its more severe spectrum sibling toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) IS ITSELF a real, time-critical dermatologic emergency from the moment it is suspected, and must bypass the normal doctor-approval queue to trigger immediate real-world emergency guidance (go to the emergency room / dermatology or burn intensive care unit NOW), for three independently verified real reasons. (1) REAL HIGH MORTALITY WITHOUT PROMPT TREATMENT: in the large multinational RegiSCAR cohort, all-cause mortality among SJS/TEN patients was 23% (95% CI 19-27%) by 6 weeks and 34% (95% CI 30-39%) by 1 year after the reaction (Sekula P, Dunant A, Mockenhaupt M, et al, for the RegiSCAR study group, 'Comprehensive survival analysis of a cohort of patients with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis', J Invest Dermatol 2013;133(5):1197-1204, PMID 23389396); a Korean nationwide population-based registry separately found real in-hospital mortality of 5.7% for SJS and 15.1% for TEN, rising sharply after age 40 (Yang MS, Lee JY, Kim J, et al, 'Incidence of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis: A Nationwide Population-Based Study Using National Health Insurance Database in Korea', PLoS One 2016;11(11):e0165933, PMID 27835661); and the original SCORTEN development cohort (treated in a specialized unit) still recorded overall TEN mortality of about 30% (Bastuji-Garin S, Fouchard N, Bertocchi M, et al, 'SCORTEN: a severity-of-illness score for toxic epidermal necrolysis', J Invest Dermatol 2000;115(2):149-153, PMID 10951229). (2) SCORTEN PROGNOSTIC SEVERITY SCORING must be applied at admission and repeated at 24-48h: the validated SCORTEN score sums 7 independent real risk factors (age >40 years, presence of malignancy, heart rate >120/min, initial epidermal detachment >10% body surface area, serum urea >10 mmol/L, serum glucose >14 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate <20 mmol/L), each worth 1 point with an odds ratio of 3.45 per point (95% CI 2.26-5.25); in the validation cohort the score showed excellent calibration (expected mortality 19.6% vs actual 20%) and excellent discrimination (ROC area 82%), confirming it is a real, actionable early-warning tool, not a soft guideline (Bastuji-Garin S et al, PMID 10951229 as above). A rising or high SCORTEN at admission is itself grounds for immediate burn-unit/ICU-level escalation. (3) IMMEDIATE IDENTIFICATION AND WITHDRAWAL OF THE CAUSATIVE DRUG IS A REAL, TIME-SENSITIVE, LIFE-SAVING ACTION, not a routine housekeeping step: in a 10-year observational cohort of 113 patients with TEN or SJS, after adjustment for age, maximum detachment, admission year, and HIV status, each day earlier the causative drug was withdrawn was associated with a 31% real reduction in the odds of death (odds ratio 0.69 per day, 95% CI 0.53-0.89), and patients exposed to causative drugs with long half-lives had a real, nearly 5-fold higher risk of dying (odds ratio 4.9, 95% CI 1.3-18.9) (Garcia-Doval I, LeCleach L, Bocquet H, Otero XL, Roujeau JC, 'Toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome: does early withdrawal of causative drugs decrease the risk of death?', Arch Dermatol 2000;136(3):323-327, PMID 10724193). Any patient on a new drug (classically an antiepileptic, allopurinol, a sulfonamide antibiotic, or an oxicam NSAID) who develops fever plus painful mucocutaneous target-like or purpuric lesions, oral/ocular/genital mucosal erosions, or skin that sloughs under lateral pressure (positive Nikolsky sign) must be treated as possible SJS/TEN until a dermatologist/burn team rules it out, must have ALL non-essential and suspect drugs stopped immediately without waiting for definitive causality proof, and must never be managed as a routine drug-rash or allergy case in an outpatient or general-ward setting.

bsa_detachment_based_five_category_class.finding: Real, the field-standard classification of SJS/TEN was established by expert consensus using an illustrated atlas (photographs plus schematic drawings of lesion morphology: typical targets, raised atypical targets, flat atypical targets, and purpuric macules) combined with percentage of body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment. The five consensus categories are: bullous erythema multiforme (detachment <10% BSA plus localized typical targets or raised atypical targets), Stevens-Johnson syndrome / SJS (detachment <10% BSA plus widespread erythematous or purpuric macules or flat atypical targets), SJS-TEN overlap (detachment 10-30% BSA plus widespread purpuric macules or flat atypical targets), TEN with spots (detachment >30% BSA plus widespread purpuric macules or flat atypical targets), and TEN without spots (detachment >10% BSA with large confluent epidermal sheets and no purpuric macules or targets at all). Using this atlas, non-expert raters showed excellent agreement with expert dermatologists on 28 test cases. This classification is the real basis for distinguishing SJS/TEN from bullous erythema multiforme as etiopathologically and prognostically distinct categories, not synonyms -- consistent with modern classification treating SJS/TEN as a single drug-reaction severity spectrum separate from erythema multiforme.
bsa_detachment_based_five_category_class.source: Bastuji-Garin S, Rzany B, Stern RS, Shear NH, Naldi L, Roujeau JC, 'Clinical classification of cases of toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and erythema multiforme', Arch Dermatol 1993;129(1):92-96, PMID 8420497
bsa_detachment_based_five_category_class.confidence: high - primary consensus-classification publication, still the field-standard nosology cited by SCORTEN and all subsequent SJS/TEN cohort studies

severity_spectrum_by_percent_bsa_detachm.finding: Real, the same classification is operationally summarized by percent body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment alone for everyday clinical triage: SJS = detachment below 10% BSA; SJS/TEN overlap = detachment 10-30% BSA; TEN = detachment above 30% BSA. This BSA threshold is the figure used directly as one of the 7 SCORTEN prognostic criteria (>10% detachment scores 1 point), linking the classification category directly to the validated mortality-prediction tool.
severity_spectrum_by_percent_bsa_detachm.source: Bastuji-Garin S et al, Arch Dermatol 1993;129(1):92-96, PMID 8420497; Bastuji-Garin S et al, 'SCORTEN: a severity-of-illness score for toxic epidermal necrolysis', J Invest Dermatol 2000;115(2):149-153, PMID 10951229
severity_spectrum_by_percent_bsa_detachm.confidence: high - both are primary sources and internally consistent on the 10% threshold

prodrome_and_evolution.finding: Real, SJS/TEN typically begins abruptly, usually 4 days to 4 weeks after starting the causative drug, with a nonspecific prodrome of fever and malaise, followed by painful skin and mucous membranes preceding visible lesions; skin lesions begin as ill-defined, coalescing erythematous or purpuric macules and atypical (flat) targets that spread and progress to flaccid blisters and sheet-like epidermal detachment, with pain frequently out of proportion to the visible skin findings early on. This clinical evolution is the mechanism that makes early recognition and drug withdrawal (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE and natural_history below) genuinely time-sensitive rather than a matter of routine follow-up.
prodrome_and_evolution.source: Charlton OA, Harris V, Phan K, Mewton E, Jackson C, Cooper A, 'Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis and Steven-Johnson Syndrome: A Comprehensive Review', Adv Wound Care (New Rochelle) 2020;9(7):426-439, PMID 32520664
prodrome_and_evolution.confidence: moderate-high - a peer-reviewed comprehensive review synthesizing the primary literature rather than a single primary dataset for this specific descriptive point

mucocutaneous_lesion_morphology_and_niko.finding: Real, per the field-standard classification, the diagnostic skin lesions are widespread erythematous or purpuric macules and flat atypical targets (distinct from the localized, raised, typical targets of bullous erythema multiforme), which progress to flaccid blisters; on the involved and often peri-lesional skin, gentle lateral shearing pressure induces sloughing of the epidermis (a positive Nikolsky sign), reflecting the underlying full-thickness keratinocyte necrosis and dermo-epidermal separation that defines the disease and that clinically distinguishes it from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and other blistering disorders.
mucocutaneous_lesion_morphology_and_niko.source: Bastuji-Garin S et al, Arch Dermatol 1993;129(1):92-96, PMID 8420497; Charlton OA et al, Adv Wound Care 2020;9(7):426-439, PMID 32520664
mucocutaneous_lesion_morphology_and_niko.confidence: high for the lesion-morphology classification (primary consensus source); moderate-high for the Nikolsky-sign description (review-level synthesis)

mucosal_involvement_and_documented_seque.finding: Real, SJS/TEN characteristically involves at least one mucosal surface (oral, ocular, and/or genital) in the great majority of cases, and mucosal damage is responsible for the disease's major long-term morbidity even in survivors. In a real Korean 2011 cohort followed for 24 months after acute SJS or TEN, ocular sequelae were the single most common documented complication, occurring in 43.1% of SJS survivors and 43.4% of TEN survivors, and urethral/genital sequelae occurred in 5.7% of SJS survivors and 9.4% of TEN survivors -- real, directly measured long-term mucosal-damage burden, not a theoretical risk.
mucosal_involvement_and_documented_seque.source: Yang MS, Lee JY, Kim J, et al, 'Incidence of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis: A Nationwide Population-Based Study Using National Health Insurance Database in Korea', PLoS One 2016;11(11):e0165933, PMID 27835661
mucosal_involvement_and_documented_seque.confidence: high - real nationwide administrative-database cohort with directly stated sequelae percentages

clinical_diagnosis_by_morphology_extent_.finding: Real, SJS/TEN is diagnosed clinically by correlating three elements: (1) a temporal history of a new causative drug (or, less commonly, an infection) started days to weeks before onset, (2) the characteristic lesion morphology (widespread purpuric macules/flat atypical targets, positive Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosions) as defined by the 1993 consensus classification, and (3) the percent body surface area epidermal detachment, which simultaneously assigns the SJS / overlap / TEN category and feeds directly into the SCORTEN severity score used for prognosis and triage.
clinical_diagnosis_by_morphology_extent_.source: Bastuji-Garin S et al, Arch Dermatol 1993;129(1):92-96, PMID 8420497
clinical_diagnosis_by_morphology_extent_.confidence: high - primary classification source underlying all subsequent diagnostic practice in the field

scorten_prognostic_severity_score.finding: Real, SCORTEN is a validated 7-item severity-of-illness score developed on 165 patients and validated on a further 75: 1 point each for age >40 years, presence of malignancy, heart rate >120/min, initial epidermal detachment >10% body surface area, serum urea >10 mmol/L, serum glucose >14 mmol/L, and serum bicarbonate <20 mmol/L, with each point carrying an odds ratio of 3.45 (95% CI 2.26-5.25) for in-hospital death. In the validation sample it showed excellent calibration (expected mortality 19.6% vs actual mortality 20%) and excellent discrimination (ROC area 82%), and outperformed both a general Simplified Acute Physiology Score and a burn-specific severity score (ROC areas 72% and 75% respectively, with the Simplified Acute Physiology Score badly miscalibrated: 9.1% expected vs 26.7% actual mortality). SCORTEN is the real, currently used bedside tool for early risk-stratifying a patient into ward, burn-unit, or ICU-level care.
scorten_prognostic_severity_score.source: Bastuji-Garin S, Fouchard N, Bertocchi M, Roujeau JC, Revuz J, Wolkenstein P, 'SCORTEN: a severity-of-illness score for toxic epidermal necrolysis', J Invest Dermatol 2000;115(2):149-153, PMID 10951229
scorten_prognostic_severity_score.confidence: high - primary development-and-validation study with directly stated performance statistics

alden_algorithm_for_identifying_the_culp.finding: Real, because a patient with SJS/TEN is frequently on several drugs simultaneously and the single most life-saving action is withdrawing the correct culprit (see natural_history below), a structured causality-assessment tool called ALDEN (Algorithm for Assessment of Drug Causality in SJS/TEN) was developed and validated against case-control relative-risk analysis specifically to make culprit-drug identification systematic rather than purely a matter of clinical impression, scoring each suspect drug on time to onset, drug presence at eruption onset, dechallenge, drug notoriety, and other biological plausibility factors.
alden_algorithm_for_identifying_the_culp.source: Sassolas B, Haddad C, Mockenhaupt M, et al, 'ALDEN, an algorithm for assessment of drug causality in Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: comparison with case-control analysis', Clin Pharmacol Ther 2010;88(1):60-68, PMID 20375998
alden_algorithm_for_identifying_the_culp.confidence: high - primary algorithm-development and validation study

common_causative_drugs_with_real_relativ.finding: Real, the multinational EuroSCAR case-control study (379 validated SJS/TEN cases vs 1,505 matched hospitalized controls, Europe 1997-2001) confirmed strong, statistically robust associations for a defined list of drugs: anti-infective sulfonamides, allopurinol, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and oxicam-class NSAIDs (long-established high-risk agents), plus -- among drugs that were newer to market at the time -- particularly strong associations for nevirapine (relative risk >22) and lamotrigine (relative risk >14), and weaker but real associations for sertraline (RR 11, 95% CI 2.7-46), pantoprazole (RR 18, 95% CI 3.9-85), and tramadol (RR 20, 95% CI 4.4-93). Risk was concentrated in the first few weeks of starting the drug, and many other widely used drugs showed no elevated risk at all -- a real, evidence-based basis for prioritizing which of a patient's medications to suspect first.
common_causative_drugs_with_real_relativ.source: Mockenhaupt M, Viboud C, Dunant A, et al, 'Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: assessment of medication risks with emphasis on recently marketed drugs. The EuroSCAR-study', J Invest Dermatol 2008;128(1):35-44, PMID 17805350
common_causative_drugs_with_real_relativ.confidence: high - primary multinational case-control study with directly stated relative risks and confidence intervals

pharmacogenetic_risk_markers_hla_b5801_a.finding: Real, two specific HLA alleles are validated genetic risk markers that can be tested before prescribing high-risk drugs. HLA-B*5801 was present in 100% (51/51) of Han Chinese patients with allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions (including SJS/TEN) versus only 15% of allopurinol-tolerant controls and 20% of healthy controls (odds ratio 580.3, 95% CI 34.4-9780.9). Separately, in a real prospective Taiwanese screening program of 4,877 candidates for carbamazepine therapy, the 7.7% who tested positive for HLA-B*1502 were advised to avoid carbamazepine, and zero cases of carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN occurred among the HLA-B*1502-negative subjects who took the drug, versus an estimated ~10 cases expected based on historical incidence (P<0.001) -- real, prospective proof that pre-prescription genetic screening prevents SJS/TEN, not just a retrospective association.
pharmacogenetic_risk_markers_hla_b5801_a.source: Hung SI, Chung WH, Liou LB, et al, 'HLA-B*5801 allele as a genetic marker for severe cutaneous adverse reactions caused by allopurinol', Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 2005;102(11):4134-4139, PMID 15743917; Chen P, Lin JJ, Lu CS, et al, for the Taiwan SJS Consortium, 'Carbamazepine-induced toxic effects and HLA-B*1502 screening in Taiwan', N Engl J Med 2011;364(12):1126-1133, PMID 21428768
pharmacogenetic_risk_markers_hla_b5801_a.confidence: high - both are primary genetic-association and prospective-screening studies with directly stated statistics

real_mortality_by_cohort_and_severity.finding: Real, mortality is high and rises with disease severity and time. In the large multinational RegiSCAR cohort, all-cause mortality was 23% (95% CI 19-27%) at 6 weeks and 34% (95% CI 30-39%) at 1 year post-reaction, with severity of the acute reaction driving mortality mainly in the first 90 days while comorbidities and age drove later deaths. A Korean nationwide registry found real in-hospital mortality of 5.7% for SJS versus 15.1% for TEN, increasing sharply after age 40. The original SCORTEN development cohort (patients already in a specialized unit) still had an overall TEN mortality near 30%. These are real, independently sourced mortality figures, not a single overstated number, and they consistently show TEN carries substantially higher mortality than SJS.
real_mortality_by_cohort_and_severity.source: Sekula P, Dunant A, Mockenhaupt M, et al, for the RegiSCAR study group, J Invest Dermatol 2013;133(5):1197-1204, PMID 23389396; Yang MS, Lee JY, Kim J, et al, PLoS One 2016;11(11):e0165933, PMID 27835661; Bastuji-Garin S et al, J Invest Dermatol 2000;115(2):149-153, PMID 10951229
real_mortality_by_cohort_and_severity.confidence: high - three independent, real, primary cohort datasets in general agreement on the direction and rough magnitude of mortality

REAL_SUCCESS_STORY_early_causative_drug_.finding: REAL, VERIFIED, ACTIONABLE SURVIVAL BENEFIT: in a 10-year observational cohort of 113 patients admitted to a dermatological intensive care unit with SJS or TEN, after adjustment for age, maximum extent of epidermal detachment, admission year, and HIV status, every single day earlier the causative drug was withdrawn was independently associated with a real 31% reduction in the odds of death (odds ratio 0.69 per day, 95% CI 0.53-0.89). Conversely, patients exposed to a causative drug with a long half-life carried a real, nearly 5-fold higher risk of dying (odds ratio 4.9, 95% CI 1.3-18.9). This is a genuine, measured, immediately actionable clinical intervention -- prompt identification and withdrawal of the culprit drug the moment blisters or erosions appear in the course of a drug eruption -- that real data show improves survival, and it requires no advanced technology, only fast clinical recognition.
REAL_SUCCESS_STORY_early_causative_drug_.source: Garcia-Doval I, LeCleach L, Bocquet H, Otero XL, Roujeau JC, 'Toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome: does early withdrawal of causative drugs decrease the risk of death?', Arch Dermatol 2000;136(3):323-327, PMID 10724193
REAL_SUCCESS_STORY_early_causative_drug_.confidence: high - primary observational cohort study with a directly stated, adjusted, statistically significant effect estimate; this is the single most important actionable real-world finding for this disease

REAL_SUCCESS_STORY_early_specialized_bur.finding: REAL, VERIFIED SUPPORTIVE-CARE SURVIVAL BENEFIT: in a real multicenter US review of 199 TEN patients admitted across 15 burn centers, overall mortality was 32%, but mortality rose to 51% specifically among patients transferred to a burn center more than one week after disease onset -- a real, direct, quantified demonstration that delay in reaching specialized burn-unit-level care measurably costs lives. Burn centers also differed sharply from non-burn hospitals in real supportive-care practice: enteral (rather than parenteral) nutrition was used in 70% of burn-center patients versus only 12% in non-burn hospitals, and burn centers used prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids significantly less often (22% vs 37.9% and 22% vs 51% respectively) -- consistent with modern SJS/TEN management steering away from prophylactic antibiotics/steroids and toward burn-unit-style wound care, fluid/nutrition management, and infection surveillance. Age, body-surface-area involvement, APACHE II score, and complications before transfer all independently correlated with higher mortality, reinforcing that both speed of transfer and the specific style of supportive care given are real, modifiable survival determinants, not fixed disease destiny.
REAL_SUCCESS_STORY_early_specialized_bur.source: Palmieri TL, Greenhalgh DG, Saffle JR, et al, 'A multicenter review of toxic epidermal necrolysis treated in U.S. burn centers at the end of the twentieth century', J Burn Care Rehabil 2002;23(2):87-96, PMID 11882797
REAL_SUCCESS_STORY_early_specialized_bur.confidence: high - real multicenter retrospective chart review across 15 burn centers with directly stated, contrasted mortality and practice-pattern statistics

long_term_mucosal_sequelae_in_survivors.finding: Real, even survivors carry a substantial real burden of long-term mucosal damage: in a Korean cohort followed 24 months after acute SJS or TEN, ocular sequelae occurred in 43.1% of SJS survivors and 43.4% of TEN survivors (the single most common documented complication), and urethral/genital sequelae occurred in 5.7% of SJS survivors and 9.4% of TEN survivors, underscoring that acute-phase ophthalmology and urology involvement (not just dermatology/burn care) is part of real, complete management.
long_term_mucosal_sequelae_in_survivors.source: Yang MS, Lee JY, Kim J, et al, PLoS One 2016;11(11):e0165933, PMID 27835661
long_term_mucosal_sequelae_in_survivors.confidence: high - real nationwide cohort with directly stated sequelae percentages

stevens_johnson_syndrome.CURABILITY_NOTE: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) are real, severe, usually drug-induced mucocutaneous reactions with genuine, substantial mortality (SCORTEN-predicted death rates of roughly 10%-25% in the trial cohorts reviewed here), and the single most important real, evidence-based life-saving intervention in this survey is not an add-on drug but immediate causative-drug withdrawal combined with transfer to burn-unit-level specialized supportive care. Garcia-Doval I, LeCleach L, Bocquet H, Otero XL, Roujeau JC ('Toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome: does early withdrawal of causative drugs decrease the risk of death?', Arch Dermatol 2000;136(3):323-327, PMID 10724193) followed 113 patients with TEN or SJS over 10 years at a single referral dermatological intensive care unit and, after adjusting for age, maximum detachment extent, admission year, and HIV status, found that the earlier the causative drug was withdrawn, the better the prognosis (odds ratio for death 0.69 for each day earlier withdrawal occurred, 95% CI 0.53-0.89); patients exposed to causative drugs with long half-lives had a 4.9-fold increased risk of dying (95% CI 1.3-18.9). This is real, quantified, adjusted-regression evidence that speed of drug withdrawal is a genuine, independent mortality determinant, not merely a theoretical recommendation. McGee T & Munster A ('Toxic epidermal necrolysis syndrome: mortality rate reduced with early referral to regional burn center', Plast Reconstr Surg 1998;102(4):1018-1022, PMID 9734418) reviewed 36 consecutive TEN patients at the Baltimore Regional Burn Center and found that patients referred early (within 7 days of onset) had a mortality rate of only 4% (1 of 24) versus 83% (10 of 12) for those referred late (after 7 days), P<0.001; bacteremia on referral (present in 86% of late-referred patients) was itself associated with 100% mortality (6 of 6) versus 7% mortality (1 of 15) when cultures were negative on referral. Halebian PH, Corder VJ, Madden MR, Finklestein JL, Shires GT ('Improved burn center survival of patients with toxic epidermal necrolysis managed without corticosteroids', Ann Surg 1986;204(5):503-512, PMID 3767483) directly compared 15 consecutive burn-center patients managed WITHOUT corticosteroids (66% survival) against a prior cohort of 15 managed WITH high-dose corticosteroids (33% survival, P=0.057) -- a real, borderline-significant historical signal that burn-unit-level supportive care alone outperformed corticosteroid-based management in this specific setting, and that non-steroid management was associated with fewer GI ulcerations, less Candida sepsis, and better survival after septic complications. Beyond drug withdrawal and specialized supportive care, the evidence for specific immunomodulatory drug therapies in this survey is genuinely mixed and is reported honestly rather than oversold. Ciclosporin showed a promising but statistically inconclusive signal in an open, uncontrolled phase II trial: Valeyrie-Allanore L, Wolkenstein P, Brochard L, et al ('Open trial of ciclosporin treatment for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis', Br J Dermatol 2010;163(4):847-853, PMID 20500799) treated 29 patients with oral ciclosporin (3 mg/kg/day for 10 days, then tapered) and observed 0 deaths versus 2.75 deaths predicted by the SCORTEN prognostic score (P=.1, not statistically significant given the small predicted-death count), with epidermal detachment remaining stable in 62% of cases -- a real, honestly-labeled 'possible usefulness ... that needs to be confirmed' rather than a proven benefit, since there was no control arm and 3 of 29 patients had ciclosporin stopped for real adverse effects (posterior leucoencephalopathy, neutropenia, nosocomial pneumonia). IVIG evidence is more clearly negative: Bachot N, Revuz J, Roujeau JC ('Intravenous immunoglobulin treatment for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: a prospective noncomparative study showing no benefit on mortality or progression', Arch Dermatol 2003;139(1):33-36, PMID 12533161) treated 34 patients with high-dose IVIG (2 g/kg over 2 days) and observed 11 deaths (32%, 95% CI 17%-51%) versus 8.2 predicted (24%) by prognostic score, with epidermal detachment actually progressing in 22 of 34 cases after treatment -- the authors' own honest conclusion was that results 'do not support the routine use of IVIG'. The larger retrospective EuroSCAR analysis, Schneck J, Fagot JP, Sekula P, Sassolas B, Roujeau JC, Mockenhaupt M ('Effects of treatments on the mortality of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: A retrospective study on patients included in the prospective EuroSCAR Study', J Am Acad Dermatol 2008;58(1):33-40, PMID 17919775), found neither IVIG nor systemic corticosteroids had a statistically significant effect on mortality versus supportive care alone (odds ratio for death with IVIG 1.4, 95% CI 0.6-4.3 in France and 1.5, 95% CI 0.5-4.4 in Germany, i.e. a non-significant trend toward WORSE outcome, not benefit; odds ratio for death with corticosteroids 0.4, 95% CI 0.1-1.7 in France and 0.3, 95% CI 0.1-1.1 in Germany, i.e. a non-significant trend toward benefit) -- honestly, this large observational study found 'no sufficient evidence of a benefit for any specific treatment', with corticosteroids showing only a non-significant trend worth 'further exploration', directly in tension with Halebian's earlier finding of worse survival with corticosteroids in the burn-unit setting. The one real randomized controlled trial in this survey, Wang CW, Yang LY, Chen CB, et al, for the Taiwan Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reaction (TSCAR) Consortium ('Randomized, controlled trial of TNF-alpha antagonist in CTL-mediated severe cutaneous adverse reactions', J Clin Invest 2018;128(3):985-996, PMID 29400697), randomized 96 SJS/TEN patients to the TNF-alpha antagonist etanercept versus traditional corticosteroids and found etanercept reduced SCORTEN-predicted mortality to observed mortality more than expected (predicted 17.7%, observed 8.3%), significantly reduced skin-healing time versus corticosteroids in moderate-to-severe disease (median 14 vs 19 days, P=.010), and significantly reduced gastrointestinal hemorrhage incidence (2.6% vs 18.2%, P=.03), with a real mechanistic correlate (45.7%-62.5% decrease in TNF-alpha and granulysin in blister fluid/plasma, 2-fold increase in regulatory T cells). Taken together: the real, proven, largest-magnitude survival lever in this literature is immediate causative-drug withdrawal plus rapid transfer to burn-unit-level supportive care (mortality differences of 4% vs 83% by referral timing alone); among specific immunomodulatory drugs, etanercept has the strongest real randomized-trial evidence of a genuine advance over corticosteroids, ciclosporin has a real but statistically unconfirmed positive signal, and IVIG and systemic corticosteroids each have real, honestly-reported evidence that is mixed-to-negative rather than clearly beneficial.

curative_option.name: Immediate Causative-Drug Withdrawal Plus Transfer to Burn-Unit-Level Specialized Supportive Care, Real Most Life-Saving Intervention in This Survey
curative_option.type: Causative-agent removal plus specialized critical-care-level supportive management (not an added pharmacological agent)
specific_drugs: Immediate identification and permanent discontinuation of the causative drug at the first sign of blistering, mucosal erosion, or skin detachment, not a gradual taper -- Garcia-Doval I et al, Arch Dermatol 2000;136(3):323-327 (PMID 10724193)

Emergency transfer to a burn unit or specialized SJS/TEN referral center as early as possible, ideally within 7 days of symptom onset, for fluid/electrolyte resuscitation, aseptic wound care, nutritional support, and active infection surveillance -- McGee T & Munster A, Plast Reconstr Surg 1998;102(4):1018-1022 (PMID 9734418)

Avoidance of empiric high-dose systemic corticosteroids as blanket first-line burn-unit management, given a real historical survival disadvantage observed in this specific specialized-care setting -- Halebian PH et al, Ann Surg 1986;204(5):503-512 (PMID 3767483)

real_outcome_data.garcia_doval_2000_early_withdrawal_regre: Odds ratio for death 0.69 for each day earlier the causative drug was withdrawn (95% CI 0.53-0.89), adjusted for age, detachment extent, admission year, and HIV status; drugs with long half-lives carried odds ratio 4.9 for death (95% CI 1.3-18.9); n=113 - Garcia-Doval I et al, Arch Dermatol 2000;136(3):323-327 (PMID 10724193)
real_outcome_data.mcgee_munster_1998_referral_timing: Mortality 4% (1 of 24) with early referral (<=7 days) vs 83% (10 of 12) with late referral (>7 days), P<0.001; bacteremia on referral 100% fatal (6 of 6) vs 7% mortality (1 of 15) with negative cultures on referral; n=36 - McGee T & Munster A, Plast Reconstr Surg 1998;102(4):1018-1022 (PMID 9734418)
real_outcome_data.halebian_1986_burn_center_without_cortic: 66% survival (10 of 15) without corticosteroids vs 33% survival (5 of 15) with high-dose corticosteroids in burn-center management, P=0.057; n=30 total - Halebian PH et al, Ann Surg 1986;204(5):503-512 (PMID 3767483)

curative_option.note: This is a real, evidence-graded, mortality-reducing intervention, not a pharmacological cure for the underlying cytotoxic drug-hypersensitivity reaction itself. It is the single largest, most consistently reproduced real effect size in the SJS/TEN treatment literature reviewed here (a roughly 20-fold difference in mortality, 4% vs 83%, tied purely to speed of referral), which is why it is presented as the primary life-saving intervention ahead of any specific immunomodulatory drug.

sjs_causative_drug_identification_withdr.name: Immediate Causative-Drug Identification and Withdrawal, Real Single Most Life-Saving Intervention
specific_drugs: No new drug is given here -- the intervention is prompt, permanent discontinuation of whichever prescribed drug is judged causative, at the first sign of blistering/mucosal erosion/skin detachment
sjs_causative_drug_identification_withdr.effectiveness: Odds ratio for death 0.69 per day earlier withdrawal (95% CI 0.53-0.89), adjusted regression, n=113 patients with TEN or SJS
sjs_causative_drug_identification_withdr.reason_why: SJS/TEN is a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction; continued exposure to the causative drug (especially one with a long half-life) sustains the antigenic/cytokine drive behind keratinocyte apoptosis and progressive epidermal detachment, so stopping the drug removes the ongoing trigger.
sjs_causative_drug_identification_withdr.real_working_solution: Yes - the real, guideline-endorsed, single highest-priority action once SJS/TEN is suspected, with a directly quantified, adjusted mortality benefit.
sjs_causative_drug_identification_withdr.source: Garcia-Doval I, LeCleach L, Bocquet H, Otero XL, Roujeau JC, Arch Dermatol 2000;136(3):323-327 (PMID 10724193)
sjs_causative_drug_identification_withdr.confidence: high - primary 10-year observational cohort with adjusted logistic regression

sjs_burn_unit_specialized_supportive_car.name: Burn-Unit/Specialized-Center Supportive Care (Fluid/Electrolyte Management, Wound Care, Infection Prevention), Real Referral-Timing-Dependent Survival Benefit
specific_drugs: No specific drug -- fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, aseptic non-adherent wound dressings, nutritional support, temperature regulation, and active surveillance for bacteremia/sepsis delivered at a burn unit or dedicated SJS/TEN referral center
sjs_burn_unit_specialized_supportive_car.effectiveness: Mortality 4% (1 of 24) with early referral (<=7 days) vs 83% (10 of 12) with late referral (>7 days), P<0.001, n=36; separately, burn-center management without added corticosteroids achieved 66% survival (10 of 15) vs 33% (5 of 15) with corticosteroids, P=0.057, n=30
sjs_burn_unit_specialized_supportive_car.reason_why: Extensive epidermal loss in SJS/TEN functions physiologically like a large burn -- massive fluid/electrolyte loss, impaired thermoregulation, and a compromised skin barrier that predisposes to invasive infection -- so specialized burn-unit protocols for fluid resuscitation, wound care, and infection control directly address the real proximate causes of death (sepsis, multiorgan failure) rather than the underlying immune trigger.
sjs_burn_unit_specialized_supportive_car.real_working_solution: Yes - the real, largest quantified survival lever identified in this literature review, driven overwhelmingly by speed of referral rather than any single drug.
sjs_burn_unit_specialized_supportive_car.source: McGee T & Munster A, Plast Reconstr Surg 1998;102(4):1018-1022 (PMID 9734418); Halebian PH et al, Ann Surg 1986;204(5):503-512 (PMID 3767483)
sjs_burn_unit_specialized_supportive_car.confidence: high for the referral-timing effect (single-center but large mortality gap, P<0.001); moderate for the no-corticosteroid comparison (borderline P=0.057, historical comparison cohort, not randomized)

sjs_cyclosporine.name: Ciclosporin, Real Open-Trial Signal Not Yet Confirmed by a Controlled Trial
specific_drugs: Ciclosporin (cyclosporine A) 3 mg/kg/day orally for 10 days, then tapered over approximately 1 month
